# Q Fever

Q fever is an illness caused by a germ called *Coxiella burnetii*.  
This germ is very strong and can survive for months in dust and animal waste.  
It can spread through the air, especially when people breathe in tiny particles from infected animals.

Q fever can be either acute or chronic.  
Acute means it comes on suddenly.  
Chronic means it lasts a long time and can cause serious problems.

---

## How People Get Q Fever

The main way people get Q fever is by breathing in tiny particles from infected animals.  
These particles come from the birth fluids, milk, urine, or feces of infected animals.  
Sheep, cattle, and goats are the most common sources.  
The animals often show no signs of illness.

The germ can stay in the environment for a long time.  
It can travel far on the wind.  
People living near farms with infected animals can get sick even if they do not work with the animals.

You can also get Q fever by drinking raw milk from an infected animal.

The germ is so strong that just one tiny particle can cause infection.  
This makes it a concern for biological safety.

Person-to-person spread is very rare.

---

## Symptoms of Q Fever

### Acute Q Fever

The time from exposure to symptoms is usually 18 to 21 days.  
Some people have no symptoms at all.  
Others get sick suddenly with:

- High fever
- Severe headache
- Chills
- Extreme tiredness
- Muscle aches
- Loss of appetite
- Sweating

Fever can reach 40 degrees Celsius and last from 1 to more than 3 weeks.

Some people may have:

- A dry cough
- Pain in the chest that gets worse when breathing
- Crackling sounds in the lungs when breathing

These lung symptoms can be worse in older people or those who are already unwell.

The illness can also affect the liver.  
Symptoms include:

- Fever
- Tiredness
- Pain in the upper right side of the belly
- Swelling of the liver
- Yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice)

Headache and lung symptoms may not be present in these cases.

After recovery, some people report long-term fatigue.  
This is called post-Q fever fatigue syndrome.  
It can last for months.  
Symptoms include:

- Extreme tiredness
- Muscle pain
- Headaches
- Sensitivity to light
- Changes in mood or sleep

### Chronic Q Fever

Chronic Q fever happens in fewer than 5 out of 100 people.  
It can start weeks or even years after the first illness.

People with heart valve problems, aneurysms, or artificial blood vessel grafts are at higher risk.  
Pregnancy and weak immune systems also increase the risk.

Chronic Q fever often causes:

- Endocarditis (infection of the heart lining or valves)
- Hepatitis (liver infection)

Endocarditis may cause:

- Fever that lasts a long time
- Swelling of the liver or spleen
- Clubbing of the fingers
- Small spots on the skin (purpura)
- Blood clots that travel to other parts of the body

In some cases, people with chronic Q fever have no memory of having had the acute illness.

---

## Diagnosis of Q Fever

Q fever is hard to diagnose because early symptoms are like many other illnesses.  
It can look like the flu, viral infections, or other bacterial diseases.

Doctors may suspect Q fever if you have:

- A recent history of contact with farm animals
- Symptoms that do not improve with standard treatment

Tests used to confirm Q fever include:

- **Immunofluorescence assay (IFA)** – This test checks for antibodies in the blood. It is the most reliable method.
- **PCR test** – This test looks for the germ’s DNA in blood or tissue. It works best early in the illness.
- **Blood and tissue cultures** – These are rarely used because the germ is hard to grow in the lab.
- **Liver biopsy** – If the liver is involved, a small sample may be taken to check for granulomas (small areas of inflammation).

Chest X-rays may show signs of pneumonia.  
The lungs may look like they have bacterial pneumonia, but the actual cause is different.

Blood tests may show:

- Normal white blood cell count in some people
- Mildly high liver enzymes in others

---

## Treatment of Q Fever

### For Acute Q Fever

The main treatment is doxycycline.  
This is an antibiotic that works well against the germ.

Treatment usually lasts 14 days.  
You should take it until you feel better, have no fever for about 5 days, and have finished the full course.

For severe cases, treatment may need to be longer.

Doxycycline is safe for children over 8 years old.  
For younger children, the risk of tooth staining is low with short courses.  
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says short courses (5 to 10 days) are safe and effective.

Pregnant women should not take doxycycline after 32 weeks of pregnancy.  
Instead, they may be given trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.

### For Chronic Q Fever (Endocarditis)

Treatment is much longer.  
It usually lasts at least 18 months, and sometimes for life.

The recommended treatment is doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine.  
Hydroxychloroquine can affect the heart.  
So, your heart rhythm will be checked regularly with ECGs.

Doctors will monitor:

- Your symptoms
- Blood tests
- Antibody levels

Stopping treatment too early can lead to relapse.

Surgery may be needed to replace damaged heart valves.  
Some people get better without surgery, but this is rare.

### For Chronic Hepatitis

There is no clear best treatment.  
Doctors may use a combination of antibiotics, but the right choice is still being studied.

---

## Prevention of Q Fever

A vaccine is available in Australia.  
It is recommended for people at high risk, such as:

- Farm workers
- Slaughterhouse employees
- Dairy workers
- Wool sorters
- Herders

Before getting the vaccine, you must be tested.  
This is to check if you already have immunity.  
Vaccinating someone who is already immune can cause a severe reaction.

---

## Key Facts

- Sheep, cattle, and goats are the main sources of Q fever.
- The disease spreads mainly through the air from infected animals.
- Acute symptoms are like the flu. Lung symptoms can be worse in older or weak people.
- Chronic Q fever is rare but serious. It often affects the heart or liver.
- Diagnosis is done with blood tests or PCR testing.
- Acute Q fever is treated with doxycycline for 2 weeks or longer.
- Chronic Q fever needs long-term treatment, sometimes for life.
- A vaccine exists but is only available in Australia.

# Difficulty Swallowing

Some people have trouble swallowing. This is called dysphagia.  
With dysphagia, food or drink does not move smoothly from the throat to the stomach.  
You may feel like food or liquid gets stuck on the way down.  

Do not confuse dysphagia with a lump in the throat.  
A lump in the throat (called globus sensation) feels like something is stuck.  
But you can still swallow normally.  

---

## Problems from Swallowing Trouble

If you have trouble swallowing, you may accidentally breathe in saliva, food, or drink.  
This is called aspiration.  
Aspiration can cause a sudden lung infection called pneumonia.  
If it happens often over time, it can lead to long-term lung problems.  

People who have swallowing trouble for a long time often do not get enough food or drink.  
This can cause weight loss.  

---

## Why Swallowing Becomes Hard

Swallowing is a complex process.  
Your brain must control many small muscles in your throat and esophagus.  
These muscles must work together in the right order.  
They must squeeze strongly to push food from your mouth to your throat.  
Then they must push food down the esophagus.  

The top part of the esophagus must relax to let food in.  
The bottom part must relax to let food enter the stomach.  

Swallowing problems can happen if:  
- The brain or nerves are not working right  
- The muscles are weak or not working properly  
- There is a blockage in the esophagus  
- The esophagus does not move food well  

### Brain and Nerve Problems  
These can cause swallowing trouble:  
- Stroke  
- Parkinson disease  
- Multiple sclerosis  
- Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)  

People with these conditions usually have other symptoms too.  
Many already know they have one of these conditions.  

### Muscle Problems  
These can cause swallowing trouble:  
- Myasthenia gravis  
- Dermatomyositis  
- Muscular dystrophy  

### Blockages in the Esophagus  
A blockage can happen because of:  
- Esophagus cancer  
- Thin bands of tissue (rings or webs) inside the esophagus  
- Scar tissue from acid reflux or swallowing a harmful liquid  
- Eosinophilic esophagitis (inflammation from too many certain white blood cells)  
- Pressure from nearby organs, such as:  
  - An enlarged thyroid gland  
  - A bulge in a major chest artery (aortic aneurysm)  
  - A tumor in the chest  

### Movement Problems in the Esophagus  
These can cause swallowing trouble:  
- Achalasia (the lower esophagus does not relax and the esophagus does not move well)  
- Esophageal spasm (uncontrolled muscle contractions)  
- Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) – this can affect how the esophagus moves  

---

## How Doctors Check for Swallowing Trouble

Not every case of swallowing trouble needs urgent care.  
But certain signs mean you should see a doctor right away.  

### See a Doctor Right Away If You Have:  
- Drooling or cannot swallow anything at all  
- Losing weight because of swallowing trouble  
- Pain when swallowing  
- New weakness or problems with nerves, spine, or brain  
- Repeated lung infections from inhaling food or drink  

If the only sign is weight loss, you can wait about a week.  
But if you cough or choke every time you eat or drink, see a doctor sooner.  

### What Doctors Do  
Doctors start by asking questions about your symptoms and health history.  
Then they do a physical exam.  
What they find helps them decide what tests to do.  

### Questions Doctors Ask:  
- Do you have trouble with solid food, liquids, or both?  
- Does food come out your nose?  
- Do you drool or spill food from your mouth?  
- Do you cough or choke while eating?  

If you have equal trouble with solids and liquids, it may be a movement problem in the esophagus.  
If you start having trouble with solids and then liquids, it may be a growing blockage, like a tumor.  
If food comes out your nose or mouth, it may be a nerve or muscle problem, not an esophagus issue.  

### What Doctors Look For in the Exam:  
- Tremors (shaking) when at rest  
- Weakness in arms, legs, eyes, mouth, or face  
- Trouble doing repeated actions (like blinking or counting)  
- Problems walking or balancing  
- Skin changes, like rashes or thickened skin on fingers  
- Muscle wasting or twitching under the skin  
- Enlarged thyroid gland or other lumps in the neck  

---

### Common Causes and Their Signs

| Cause | Common Signs | Tests Used |
|------|--------------|------------|
| **Stroke** | Weakness on one side, trouble speaking, trouble walking | Brain CT or MRI |
| **Parkinson disease** | Stiff muscles, slow movement, shaking, balance issues | Doctor’s exam; sometimes brain CT or MRI |
| **Multiple sclerosis** | Symptoms come and go; vision problems, weakness, numbness | MRI; spinal tap |
| **ALS or related nerve diseases** | Muscle twitching, weakness, trouble chewing, swallowing, or talking | Nerve tests; blood tests; brain MRI |
| **Myasthenia gravis** | Droopy eyelids, weak eyes, muscles get weaker with use | Blood tests; nerve test; IV medicine to test strength |
| **Dermatomyositis** | Muscle weakness, rash, fever, fatigue, joint pain | Blood tests; nerve test; muscle biopsy |
| **Muscular dystrophy** | Weakness starting in childhood | Muscle biopsy; genetic testing |
| **Achalasia** | Trouble swallowing solids and liquids, regurgitation, chest discomfort | Barium swallow; esophageal manometry |
| **Esophageal spasm** | Chest pain, swallowing trouble that comes and goes | Barium swallow; esophageal manometry |
| **Eosinophilic esophagitis** | Reflux that does not improve with acid medicine | Endoscopy; biopsy |
| **Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma)** | Cold fingers, skin thickening, joint pain, heartburn, shortness of breath | Doctor’s exam; blood tests |
| **Peptic stricture** | Long history of heartburn | Endoscopy |
| **Esophagus cancer** | Getting worse swallowing, weight loss, chest pain | Endoscopy; biopsy |
| **Lower esophageal rings** | Swallowing trouble that comes and goes | Endoscopy; barium swallow |
| **Aortic aneurysm or tumor** | Pressure on esophagus | Barium swallow; X-rays; CT scan |
| **Swallowed caustic substance** | Trouble swallowing weeks or months after exposure | Endoscopy |

*Note: Not all signs appear in every person. These are common patterns.*

---

## Tests for Swallowing Trouble

If you have a complete or near-complete blockage, doctors will use a flexible tube to look inside your esophagus right away.  
This is called upper endoscopy.  
They may take a small tissue sample (biopsy) to check for eosinophilic esophagitis.  

If there is no blockage, doctors usually start with a barium swallow.  
You drink a liquid that shows up on X-rays.  
You may first drink plain barium, then barium mixed with food like a cracker or marshmallow.  

If the barium test shows a blockage, doctors do endoscopy to find the cause.  
This helps rule out cancer.  

If the barium test is normal or shows a movement problem, doctors do motility tests.  
You swallow a thin tube with pressure sensors.  
The sensors record how well the esophagus squeezes and relaxes.  

Another test is impedance testing.  
A small balloon is placed in the esophagus.  
It measures how much pressure it takes to expand.  
This helps doctors understand how the esophagus is working.  

---

## Treating Swallowing Trouble

The best treatment is to fix the cause.  

To help with symptoms, doctors often suggest:  
- Take small bites  
- Chew food well  

If swallowing trouble is from a stroke, a rehab specialist can help.  
They may teach you to:  
- Change your head position while eating  
- Retrain your swallowing muscles  
- Practice exercises to handle food in your mouth  
- Do strength and coordination exercises for your tongue  

If you are at high risk of choking, you may need to stop eating by mouth.  
You may be fed through a tube placed through your belly into your stomach or small intestine.  

---

## Important for Older Adults

Chewing, swallowing, tasting, and talking need healthy nerves and muscles in the mouth, face, and neck.  
These functions naturally weaken with age, even in healthy people.  

As you age:  
- The muscles for chewing get weaker and less coordinated  
- This is worse if you wear dentures  
- You may swallow larger pieces of food  
- This increases the risk of choking or breathing in food  

It also takes longer to move food from mouth to throat.  
This raises the chance of breathing in food.  

The most common causes of swallowing problems in older adults are:  
- Nerve or muscle diseases (like stroke, diabetes, Parkinson disease, ALS, or multiple sclerosis)  

Some treatments can make swallowing worse:  
- Certain medicines (like anticholinergics or diuretics)  
- Radiation to the head and neck

# Bronchiolitis – Simple Guide for Parents

## What Is Bronchiolitis?

Bronchiolitis is a common chest infection in young children.  
It starts like a cold.  
You might notice sneezing, a runny nose, or a cough.  
Later, your child may breathe faster or have noisy breathing.  

The infection usually gets better on its own.  
You can help your child feel better at home.  

## When to Get Help Right Away

Call 999 or go to A&E if your child:

- Is struggling to breathe. You might hear grunting sounds or see their tummy pulling in under their ribs.  
- Has pauses in their breathing.  
- Has blue skin, tongue, or lips.  
- Is very weak and won’t wake up or stay awake.  

If you think your child is seriously unwell, trust your gut. You know your child best.  

> **Find your nearest A&E**

### Important Safety Tips for A&E

- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you.  
- Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
- Bring any medicines your child takes.  

## When to Call Your Doctor or Call 111

Call your doctor for an urgent appointment or call 111 if your child:

- Has had a cold that is getting worse.  
- Is eating or drinking much less than usual.  
- Has not had a wet nappy for 12 hours or more.  
- Shows signs of dehydration (like dry lips, no tears, or sunken eyes).  
- Is under 3 months old and has a temperature of 38 degrees Celsius.  
- Is over 3 months old and has a temperature of 39 degrees Celsius or higher.  
- Feels hotter than normal when you touch their back or chest.  
- Feels sweaty.  
- Is very tired or very irritable.  

## What Are the Symptoms?

Early signs are like a cold:  
- Sneezing  
- Runny or blocked nose  
- Cough  
- Slight fever (38 degrees Celsius)  

Later, your child may have:  
- Breathing faster than normal  
- Trouble feeding or eating  
- Wheezing (noisy breathing)  
- Becoming fussy or irritable  

Symptoms are usually worst between day 3 and day 5.  
The cough usually improves after about 3 weeks.  

## How to Care for Your Child at Home

There is no special medicine for bronchiolitis.  
Most children get better without treatment.  
You can help your child feel better at home.

### Do These Things

- Give children’s paracetamol to babies and children over 2 months old.  
- Give ibuprofen to babies and children over 3 months old.  
- Do not give aspirin to any child under 16.  
- Use salt water drops in the nose if it is blocked.  
- Keep your child sitting upright when awake. This helps them breathe easier.  
- Offer plenty of fluids.  
  - For babies: give smaller feeds more often.  
  - For older children: offer extra water or diluted fruit juice.  

### Do Not Do These Things

- Do not smoke near your child.  
- Do not try to cool your child down with cool water sponges.  
- Do not take off all their clothes to lower their temperature.  

## What Causes Bronchiolitis?

Bronchiolitis is caused by a virus.  
The most common virus is called respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV.  

RSV spreads easily through coughs and sneezes.  
Almost every child gets RSV at least once before they turn 2.  

Most cases are mild.  
But some babies and children are at higher risk of serious illness, including:

- Babies under 6 months old  
- Babies born early (premature)  
- Babies or children with weak immune systems  
- Babies or children with long-term lung or heart problems

# Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia

This is a type of lung infection caused by a fungus called *Pneumocystis jirovecii*. It mainly affects people with weak immune systems. It is most common in people with HIV, those on long-term steroid medicine, and people who have had organ transplants.

## Who Is at Risk?

You are more likely to get this infection if you:
- Have HIV and your immune system is weak (CD4 count below 200 cells per microliter)
- Have had an organ transplant
- Have blood cancer
- Are taking strong medicines that lower your immune system

With better HIV treatment, fewer people with HIV now get this infection. But those who do not know they have HIV or are not on treatment still face a high risk.

## Symptoms

Most people have:
- Fever
- Trouble breathing
- A dry cough that lasts for days or weeks

The breathing trouble often gets worse over time.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will check your lungs and oxygen levels. Tests include:

- **Chest x-ray**: Often shows blurry areas in both lungs. But sometimes the x-ray looks normal.
- **CT scan**: Can show lung changes even when the x-ray is normal.
- **Pulse oximetry**: Measures how much oxygen is in your blood. Low levels can point to this infection, even if the x-ray is normal.
- **Blood tests**: Can show high levels of certain substances like beta-D glucan and LDH. These are not specific but can help support the diagnosis.

To confirm the infection, your doctor needs to find the fungus in a sample from your lungs. This can come from:
- A sputum sample (usually collected after a special breathing test)
- A sample taken during a bronchoscopy (a tube passed into the lungs)
- A sample from a breathing tube (if you are on a ventilator)

The best test to find the fungus is a PCR test. It is very sensitive. Other tests like fluorescent staining or special stains can also be used, but they are less reliable.

If the sputum test is negative, your doctor may do a bronchoscopy to get a better sample.

## Treatment

The main treatment is an antibiotic called trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX). It is usually given for 21 days.

You should start treatment even before the diagnosis is confirmed. The fungus can stay in your lungs for weeks, so early treatment helps.

Other options include:
- Trimethoprim with dapsone
- Clindamycin with primaquine
- Pentamidine
- Atovaquone (for mild cases)

Pentamidine can cause serious side effects, such as kidney damage, low blood pressure, and low blood sugar. It is not used as often because of this.

If your blood oxygen level is low (PaO2 below 70 mm Hg) or your pulse oximetry is below 92% while breathing room air, you will also get steroid medicine. Steroids help reduce lung swelling and improve breathing. The dose is slowly lowered over 21 days.

## Prognosis

This infection can be serious. The death rate is higher in people who are older, have had this infection before, or have very weak immune systems (especially those with HIV and CD4 counts below 50).

## Prevention

People at risk should take medicine to prevent this infection. This includes:
- People with HIV who have a low CD4 count (below 200)
- People who have had this infection before

The best preventive medicine is trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. If you cannot take it, other options are dapsone or inhaled pentamidine.

These preventive medicines are also used for people without HIV who are at high risk, such as transplant patients or those on strong immune-suppressing drugs.

## Key Points

- Think about this infection in anyone with a weak immune system, even if symptoms are mild or the chest x-ray looks normal.
- Test lung samples using special methods like PCR or fluorescent staining.
- Treat with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.
- Add steroids if your blood oxygen level is low.

# What You Need to Know About Liver Disease

Your liver helps clean your blood, make important chemicals, and store energy. When it does not work well, you have liver disease.

Liver disease can cause many different problems. Some of the most common signs are:

- Yellow skin or eyes (called jaundice)
- Less or no bile flow (called cholestasis)
- A larger than normal liver (called hepatomegaly)
- High blood pressure in the veins that carry blood from your gut to your liver (called portal hypertension)
- Fluid building up in your belly (called ascites)
- Brain problems from toxins that build up in the blood (called hepatic encephalopathy)
- Liver failure

Some people with liver disease do not have clear symptoms. Others may feel tired, unwell, lose their appetite, or lose a small amount of weight. These symptoms are common in many other illnesses. So, liver disease can be missed, especially in the early stages.

Below is a list of symptoms and complications linked to liver disease.

## Common Symptoms and Complications

### Jaundice
Your skin or the whites of your eyes turn yellow.

### Cholestasis
Your liver stops making or sending out bile properly.

### Hepatomegaly
Your liver becomes bigger than normal.

### Ascites
Fluid builds up in your belly. This can make your belly look swollen.

### Hepatic Encephalopathy
You feel confused or have trouble thinking clearly. This happens because harmful substances build up in your blood. Your liver usually removes these.

### Gastrointestinal Bleeding
You may bleed from the esophagus or stomach. This often happens because veins in these areas become swollen and twisted (called varices).

### Portal Hypertension
Blood pressure in the veins that bring blood from your intestines to your liver is too high.

### Skin Changes
You may see:
- Small, spider-like blood vessels on your face or chest
- Red palms
- A red face
- Itching

### Blood Problems
You may have:
- Fewer red blood cells (anemia) – this can cause tiredness
- Fewer white blood cells – this can make you more likely to get infections
- Fewer platelets – this can make you bleed more easily
- A higher risk of bleeding (coagulopathy)

### Hormone Problems
Your body may not use hormones properly. This can cause:
- High blood sugar even if you are not diabetic
- Feeling dizzy when you stand up
- Tiredness
- Dark patches on your skin
- Women may stop having periods and have trouble getting pregnant
- Men may have trouble getting or keeping an erection
- Men may lose muscle, grow breast tissue, or have smaller testicles

### Heart and Blood Vessel Issues
You may have:
- A faster heartbeat
- More blood pumped by your heart
- Low blood pressure

### General Symptoms
You may feel:
- Tired
- Weak
- Unusually thin
- Not hungry
- Sick to your stomach
- Fever
- Pain in your belly

> **Note:** Not everyone with liver disease will have all these symptoms. Some only show up when the liver is very damaged. These problems are more likely in advanced liver disease or liver failure.

# Ingrown Toenail

An ingrown toenail happens when the edge of your toenail grows into the skin beside the toe. This can cause pain, swelling, and redness.

## What to Look For

- You usually get it on your big toe, but it can happen on any toe.
- Your toe may be red, sore, and swollen.
- The nail may curve into the side of the toe.
- The toe can become infected.

Signs your toe is infected:
- Pus (yellow or white fluid) coming from the toe.
- You feel hot, shivery, or have a high temperature.

## What You Can Do at Home

Try these steps first. They can help ease the pain and prevent infection.

### Do These Things
- Soak your foot in warm water with salt. Do this for 15 to 20 minutes, 2 to 3 times a day.
- After soaking, dry your foot well.
- Wear shoes that are wide and comfortable. Avoid tight or pointy shoes.
- Take paracetamol or ibuprofen to help with pain.

### Do Not Do These Things
- Do not cut your toenail. Let it grow out naturally.
- Do not pick at the nail or skin around it.
- Do not wear tight or poorly fitting shoes.

## When to See a Doctor

See a doctor if:
- The pain and swelling do not get better after a few days of home care.
- Your toe is very painful, swollen, and pus is coming out.
- You have a high temperature or feel hot and shivery.
- You have diabetes. Foot problems can be more serious if you have diabetes.

## What a Doctor Can Do

A doctor can:
- Check your toe to confirm it is an ingrown toenail.
- Give you antibiotics if the toe is infected.

If the problem is serious, the doctor may refer you to a foot specialist.

### Foot Specialist (Podiatrist)

A foot specialist can:
- Cut away part of the nail.
- Remove the whole nail if needed.

You may get a local anaesthetic to numb the toe during the treatment. This means you will not feel pain.

Note: Not everyone can get a foot specialist through the NHS. Waiting times can be long. You can pay to see a foot specialist privately.

## How to Prevent Ingrown Toenails

To stop them from happening:
- Cut your toenails straight across, not in a curve.
- Do not cut them too short.
- Wear shoes that fit well and are not too tight.
- Keep your feet clean and dry. Dry them well after washing.

# Dementia with Lewy Bodies and Parkinson Disease Dementia

This condition includes two related types:  
- Dementia with Lewy bodies  
- Parkinson disease dementia  

Both involve a slow worsening of thinking and memory.  

## What Is Dementia with Lewy Bodies?

Dementia with Lewy bodies is a type of dementia that starts after age 60.  
It is the third most common form of dementia.  

It happens when abnormal clumps called Lewy bodies build up in brain cells.  
These clumps are made of a protein called alpha-synuclein.  
They mainly appear in the outer layer of the brain, called the cortex.  

The brain’s chemical messengers and nerve pathways between the deep brain and outer brain do not work properly.  

## What Is Parkinson Disease Dementia?

Parkinson disease dementia happens in people who already have Parkinson disease.  
It develops later in the disease, often after many years.  

Lewy bodies also form in a part of the brain called the substantia nigra.  
This area controls movement.  

About 25 to 30 out of 100 people with Parkinson disease will develop dementia.  
After 20 years of Parkinson disease, up to 83 out of 100 people may have dementia.  

## How Are These Two Conditions Related?

Lewy bodies appear in both conditions.  
Some experts believe they are part of the same larger brain disease.  
This disease affects both the central and peripheral nervous systems.  

Lewy bodies can also show up in people with Alzheimer disease.  
People with dementia with Lewy bodies may also have the same brain changes seen in Alzheimer disease.  

These three conditions—dementia with Lewy bodies, Parkinson disease, and Alzheimer disease—overlap a lot.  
More research is needed to understand how they are connected.  

## How Do These Conditions Progress?

Both dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson disease dementia get worse over time.  
There is no cure.  
The outlook is poor.  

## Dementia vs. Delirium

Dementia and delirium are not the same.  
Both affect thinking, but in different ways.  

| Feature | Dementia | Delirium |
|--------|----------|----------|
| Main problem | Memory loss | Trouble paying attention |
| Cause | Slow brain damage from disease | Sudden illness, infection, or medicine |
| Onset | Slow, over months or years | Fast, over hours or days |
| Reversible? | Usually not | Often yes |

Delirium can come and go.  
It may be caused by:  
- Certain medicines, especially those that affect the brain  
- Dehydration  
- Infections  

Always check for delirium in people with dementia.  

## Symptoms and Signs

Common symptoms include:  
- Unstable thinking (some days are better than others)  
- Seeing things that are not there (visual hallucinations)  
- Acting out dreams during sleep (REM sleep behavior disorder)  
- Movement problems like stiffness, slow movement, or tremors  

Other signs may include:  
- Falling often  
- Fainting  
- Dizziness when standing  
- Feeling very sleepy during the day  
- Strong reactions to certain mental health medicines  

## Diagnosis

There is no single test to confirm the diagnosis.  
Doctors make the diagnosis based on symptoms and exams.  

### Steps in Diagnosis

1. **Check for dementia**  
   - The person has trouble doing daily tasks.  
   - Their thinking has gotten worse over time.  
   - The problem is not due to delirium or a mental health issue.  

2. **Test thinking and memory**  
   - Talk to the patient and someone who knows them well.  
   - Do a quick mental check-up.  
   - If needed, do formal testing with a specialist.  

3. **Look for key signs of dementia with Lewy bodies**  
   A diagnosis is likely if **two or more** of these four core signs are present:  
   - Fluctuating thinking (good days and bad days)  
   - Seeing things that are not there  
   - REM sleep behavior disorder  
   - Movement problems like stiffness or slow movement  

   If only one sign is present, the diagnosis is possible but less certain.  

4. **Look for supporting signs**  
   These include:  
   - Falling often  
   - Fainting  
   - Dizziness when standing  
   - Excessive daytime sleepiness  
   - Bad reactions to certain mental health medicines  

5. **Rule out other causes**  
   Other brain diseases can cause similar symptoms.  
   Doctors must check for these.  

### How to Tell the Two Conditions Apart

- If movement problems come first and are worse than memory problems, it is likely Parkinson disease dementia.  
- If memory and thinking problems come first, especially trouble with planning or focus, it is likely dementia with Lewy bodies.  

### Important Notes

- People with dementia with Lewy bodies often seem drowsy or confused.  
  This is more like delirium than dementia.  
  Always check for delirium.  

- Movement problems in dementia with Lewy bodies can look like other brain diseases.  
  For example, progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) can cause similar stiffness and falls.  
  PSP also causes:  
  - Trouble moving eyes up and down  
  - Brain shrinkage in a specific area (seen on MRI)  

  These signs help doctors tell PSP apart from dementia with Lewy bodies.  

### Imaging Tests

- **CT and MRI scans**  
  These show no clear signs of Lewy body dementia.  
  But they help rule out other causes like stroke or tumors.  

- **SPECT scan with 123I-FP-CIT**  
  This test shows how well brain cells that use dopamine are working.  
  It can help confirm the diagnosis.  

- **PET scan with FDG**  
  This shows brain activity.  
  It may show patterns typical of Lewy body dementia.  

- **MIBG heart scan**  
  This checks the nerves in the heart.  
  In Lewy body dementia, these nerves are often damaged.  
  This test can help confirm the diagnosis.  

- **Polysomnography (sleep study)**  
  This can confirm REM sleep behavior disorder.  
  It helps support the diagnosis of dementia with Lewy bodies.  

### Final Diagnosis

Only an autopsy (exam of brain tissue after death) can confirm the diagnosis.  

## Treatment

There is no cure.  
Treatment focuses on helping the person live as well as possible.  

### Supportive Care

- Keep the home bright, calm, and familiar.  
- Use large clocks and calendars to help with time awareness.  
- Make the environment safe.  
  - Use alarms or monitoring systems if the person wanders.  
  - Remove tripping hazards.  

### Medicines

Medicines are used only when symptoms are severe and other steps do not help.  

- **Cholinesterase inhibitors** (like rivastigmine)  
  These may help improve thinking and memory.  
  They are often tried in both dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson disease dementia.  

- **Avoid certain medicines**  
  Some mental health drugs can make symptoms worse.  
  These include antipsychotics.  
  They can cause serious side effects in people with Lewy body dementia.  

## Key Points

- Lewy bodies appear in both dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson disease.  
  Experts think these may be part of the same brain disease.  

- Suspect dementia with Lewy bodies if:  
  - Dementia and movement problems start at about the same time  
  - There are memory problems, attention issues, vivid dreams, hallucinations, or strange thoughts  
  - There are problems with blood pressure, digestion, or bladder control  

- Suspect Parkinson disease dementia if:  
  - Movement problems come first  
  - Memory and thinking problems start years later  
  - Trouble with planning or focus appears early  

- Cholinesterase inhibitors (like rivastigmine) may help improve thinking.  
  They are used in both conditions.

# Sepsis and Septic Shock

## What Is Sepsis?

Sepsis is a serious reaction your body has to an infection. It happens when the infection spreads through your blood and causes your body to overreact. This reaction can damage your organs and make them stop working.

Septic shock is a life-threatening form of sepsis. It happens when sepsis causes very low blood pressure. This low pressure means your organs do not get enough blood. This can lead to organ failure.

## How Sepsis Starts

Normally, your body fights an infection in one place. For example, a bladder infection causes symptoms only in the bladder.

But in sepsis, the body’s response spreads everywhere. This is called a systemic reaction.

Sepsis often starts with a bacterial infection. It can also come from a fungal infection, though this is rare. The most common places for the infection to start are the lungs, the belly, or the urinary tract.

Sometimes, bacteria from the infection enter the blood. This is called bacteremia. When this happens, sepsis can develop.

In some cases, a skin abscess (a pocket of pus) can lead to sepsis. In rare cases, like toxic shock syndrome, toxins from bacteria can cause sepsis even if the bacteria do not enter the blood.

## Signs and Symptoms

At first, you may have a high fever or a low body temperature. You might feel cold and shiver. You may also feel weak.

As sepsis gets worse, you may:

- Have a fast heartbeat
- Breathe quickly
- Feel confused or less alert
- Have low blood pressure
- Urinate less than usual

Later, your body temperature may drop below normal. You may have trouble breathing. Your skin may feel cold and look pale or mottled (patchy). This means blood flow to your skin and organs is poor.

If blood flow stops to parts of your body, tissues can die. This can lead to gangrene.

When septic shock happens, your blood pressure stays low even after treatment. This is very dangerous and can be fatal.

## What Happens in the Body

Low blood pressure and tiny blood clots cause serious problems.

Your organs do not get enough blood. This makes them stop working properly.

Your heart tries to fix this by beating faster and pumping harder. But over time, the heart gets weak. It pumps less blood, so organs get even less.

When tissues do not get enough blood, they make more lactic acid. This makes your blood more acidic. This is called acidosis.

These problems create a cycle that gets worse over time.

- Your kidneys may stop working. You may make little or no urine. Waste builds up in your blood.
- Blood vessel walls may leak. Fluid escapes into your tissues. This causes swelling.
- Fluid builds up in your lungs. This makes breathing hard.
- Tiny blood clots use up your body’s clotting proteins. This can lead to dangerous bleeding.

## Who Is at Risk?

You are more likely to get sepsis if you:

- Are a newborn baby
- Are an older adult
- Are pregnant
- Have long-term health problems like diabetes or liver disease
- Have a weak immune system. This can happen if you take certain medicines (like chemotherapy or steroids) or have diseases like cancer or HIV
- Have recently taken antibiotics or steroids
- Have been in the hospital recently, especially in intensive care
- Have a medical device in your body, such as a catheter, tube, or breathing tube

Medical devices can bring bacteria into your body. Bacteria can also grow on the device. The longer the device stays in, the higher the risk.

Other risk factors include:

- Using illegal drugs. The needles and drugs are not clean. Each injection can bring bacteria into your blood. Drug users are also more likely to have HIV or other conditions that weaken the immune system.
- Having an artificial joint or heart valve. Bacteria can stick to these and enter the blood.
- Having an infection that does not get better with antibiotics. Some bacteria are resistant to antibiotics. If the infection does not improve, it may be caused by resistant bacteria that can lead to sepsis.

## How Doctors Diagnose Sepsis

Doctors suspect sepsis when someone with an infection suddenly has:

- A very high or very low body temperature
- A fast heart rate
- A fast breathing rate
- Low blood pressure

To confirm the diagnosis, doctors do tests.

They take a blood sample to look for bacteria. This is called a culture. It can take one to three days to grow the bacteria in the lab.

If you are already on antibiotics, the bacteria may not grow. In that case, doctors may remove a catheter and test its tip. If bacteria are found there, it means they are likely in your blood.

Doctors also test other fluids or tissues. These may include:

- Urine
- Fluid from the brain or spinal cord
- Wound samples
- Mucus from the lungs

They may also do imaging tests like:

- Chest x-ray
- Ultrasound
- CT scan
- MRI

These help find the source of the infection.

Other tests check for organ damage. These include:

- Blood tests to check for high lactic acid and waste products
- Blood tests to check platelet levels (cells that help blood clot)
- Pulse oximetry (a sensor on your finger) to check oxygen levels
- ECG (a test to check heart rhythm)

These tests help doctors see if shock is caused by sepsis or another problem.

## How Sepsis Is Treated

Sepsis is a medical emergency. Treatment starts right away in a hospital.

### Antibiotics

Doctors give antibiotics as soon as possible. They do not wait for test results. Delaying antibiotics lowers your chance of survival.

The first antibiotics are chosen based on:

- Where the infection started (lungs, bladder, skin, etc.)
- The most common bacteria in your area and hospital
- Whether the infection is likely to be caused by resistant bacteria

Often, two or three antibiotics are used together at first. Later, doctors switch to the one that works best against the specific bacteria.

### Fluids

People with septic shock get large amounts of fluid through a vein. This helps raise blood pressure.

Too little fluid does not help. Too much fluid can cause fluid to build up in the lungs, making breathing hard.

### Oxygen

You may get oxygen through a mask, nasal prongs, or a breathing tube. If needed, a machine called a ventilator helps you breathe.

### Remove the Source of Infection

If there is an abscess, doctors drain it. They remove or replace catheters, tubes, or other devices that may have caused the infection. Surgery may be needed to remove dead or infected tissue.

### Medicines to Raise Blood Pressure

If fluids do not raise blood pressure, doctors may give medicines that narrow blood vessels. These include norepinephrine.

These medicines raise blood pressure and improve blood flow to the brain, heart, and other organs.

But they can also reduce blood flow to some organs. Doctors use them carefully.

### High Blood Sugar

Some people with septic shock have high blood sugar. High sugar weakens the immune system. Doctors give insulin through a vein to lower blood sugar.

### Corticosteroids

If blood pressure stays low even after fluids, medicines, and treatment of the infection, doctors may give corticosteroids like hydrocortisone through a vein.

## Outlook

Without treatment, septic shock is almost always fatal.

Even with treatment, about 30 to 40 out of 100 people die.

Your chance of survival depends on many things:

- How quickly treatment starts
- What type of bacteria caused the infection
- Whether the bacteria are resistant to antibiotics
- Your overall health before the illness

Early treatment greatly improves your chances.

# Tension Headaches

## What Is a Tension Headache?

- A tension headache causes pain on both sides of your head, face, or neck.
- The pain lasts at least 30 minutes. It can go on for hours or even days.
- You may feel pressure or tightness across your head.
- The area may feel sore. Touching it can make the pain worse.
- You can still do your normal daily tasks. The headache does not stop you from doing things.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:

- You have headaches several times a week.
- Your headaches are very painful.
- Painkillers and relaxation activities do not help.
- You have a throbbing pain in the front of your head or on one side.
- You feel sick, throw up, or are bothered by light or noise.

These signs may mean you have a different kind of headache, such as a migraine or cluster headache.

## When to Get Urgent Help

Call 111 or get help online if:

- You or your child have a severe headache and:
  - Pain in the jaw when eating.
  - Blurred or double vision.
  - A sore scalp.
  - Numbness or weakness in the arms or legs.

Also call 111 or get help online if your child is under 12 and has:

- A headache that wakes them at night.
- A headache when they wake up in the morning.
- A headache that gets worse over time.
- A headache that starts or gets worse when coughing, sneezing, or bending down.
- A headache with vomiting.
- A headache with a squint (eyes pointing in different directions) or trouble looking up.

## When to Call 999 or Go to A&E

Call 999 or go to the emergency department if:

- You or your child has had a head injury, such as from a fall or accident.
- The headache came on suddenly and is extremely painful.

Also call 999 or go to A&E if:

- You or your child have a very painful headache and:
  - Sudden trouble speaking or remembering things.
  - Loss of vision.
  - Feeling drowsy or confused.
  - A very high temperature and symptoms of meningitis.
  - The white part of the eye is red.

If your child is under 12 and has:

- A headache with vision problems or trouble speaking, swallowing, balancing, or walking.
- A headache with drowsiness or constant tiredness.
- A headache that starts within 5 days of a head injury.

## How to Ease a Tension Headache

### Do These Things:

- Take painkillers like paracetamol, aspirin, or ibuprofen.
  - Paracetamol is the best choice if you are pregnant.
  - Children under 16 should not take aspirin.
- Try relaxing activities like walking, yoga, or massage.
- Change your sleep habits if poor sleep may be causing your headaches.
- Use a low, firm pillow.
- Try heat or cold packs if you have neck pain and headaches.

### Avoid These Things:

- Do not drink drinks with caffeine, such as tea, coffee, or cola.
- Try to cut down on caffeine if you drink it often.

## A Pharmacist Can Help

Talk to a pharmacist if you are unsure about:

- Which painkiller is best for you.
- What medicines are safe to take if you are pregnant.
- Treatments for sleep problems like insomnia, if poor sleep is causing your headaches.

## What Causes Tension Headaches?

Common causes include:

- Stress.
- Poor sleep, such as insomnia.
- Caffeine.

Taking painkillers too often or for too long can also cause headaches. These are called overuse or rebound headaches.

Tension headaches are not a sign of a serious health problem. They are not caused by a disease or injury.

# How Liver Disease Affects How Drugs Work in the Body

Liver disease can change how your body handles medicines. This includes how fast the body clears drugs, how the liver breaks them down, and how the drugs move through your body.

## How Liver Disease Changes Drug Handling

- The liver helps break down medicines. When it is not working well, this process can slow down.
- The liver also helps remove medicines from your blood. If blood flow to the liver is poor, this can slow removal.
- Some medicines are removed from the blood by the liver. If the liver is damaged, these medicines may build up in your body.
- The liver sends some medicines into the gut to be removed in the stool. If this process is not working, medicines may stay in your body longer.
- The gut and liver work together to recycle some medicines. Liver disease can disrupt this cycle.
- Some medicines are cleared by the kidneys. Liver disease can affect kidney function, which may change how medicines are cleared.

Sometimes, these changes mean that normal doses of medicine can build up in your body. This can lead to side effects or harm.

## Dose Adjustments Are Not Predictable

- There is no clear rule for changing medicine doses in people with liver disease.
- The amount of medicine that stays in your body does not match the type of liver damage.
- It also does not match how severe the damage is.
- Blood tests for liver function do not help predict how a medicine will behave in your body.

## Other Effects of Liver Disease on Medicines

- Even if the amount of medicine in your blood is normal, it can still have stronger effects.
- In long-term liver disease, your brain may become more sensitive to certain medicines.
- Opioids and sedatives (like sleeping pills) can cause confusion, drowsiness, or brain problems in people with liver disease.
- Even small doses of these medicines can trigger brain issues in people with cirrhosis.
- This happens because the brain’s response to medicines changes when the liver is damaged.

## Risks of Side Effects

- People with advanced liver disease do not have more side effects from medicines.
- But if a medicine harms the liver, these patients may not handle the damage as well.
- Their bodies may struggle to recover from liver injury caused by medicines.

# Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)

Polycystic ovary syndrome is a common health condition in women. It can cause irregular or missing periods. It often leads to weight gain. It can also cause symptoms from too much male hormone in the body. These include extra body hair and acne.

This condition affects 5 to 10 out of every 100 women. In the United States, it is the most common cause of infertility.

## What Causes PCOS?

The exact cause is not known. But it may be linked to a problem with how the body makes male hormones. This leads to higher levels of male hormones.

High male hormone levels can lead to:
- Weight gain
- Insulin resistance (when the body does not use insulin well)
- Increased risk of diabetes
- High blood pressure
- Heart and blood vessel problems
- Fatty liver (not caused by alcohol)

Too much estrogen and not enough progesterone can cause the lining of the uterus to grow too thick. This can lead to cancer of the uterus over time.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms often start during puberty and get worse over time. They vary from woman to woman.

Common signs include:
- Missed or irregular periods
- No periods at all
- Heavy or irregular vaginal bleeding
- Acne
- Extra body hair (especially on the face, chest, or back)
- Thinning hair or baldness
- Deep voice (rare)
- Larger muscles (rare)
- Breast size decrease (rare)

Many women with PCOS are overweight. But some are not. High insulin levels can make it hard to lose weight. Insulin resistance can also cause dark, thick skin in the armpits, neck, and skin folds (called acanthosis nigricans).

Other possible symptoms:
- Feeling tired
- Low energy
- Trouble sleeping (including sleep apnea)
- Mood swings
- Depression
- Anxiety
- Headaches

If a woman has metabolic syndrome, fat may build up around the belly.

## How Is PCOS Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tools to diagnose PCOS.

First, they check your symptoms. They may do:
- A pregnancy test
- Blood tests to check hormone levels
- An ultrasound of the pelvis

The ultrasound checks the ovaries for many small fluid-filled sacs (cysts). It also checks for tumors in the ovaries or adrenal glands. These tumors can cause similar symptoms.

A pelvic ultrasound uses a small device placed inside the vagina. It is not usually done in teenage girls because changes from puberty can make the results unclear.

If you have abnormal bleeding, your doctor may take a small sample of the uterine lining (endometrial biopsy). This checks for cancer.

Your doctor may also test:
- Blood pressure
- Blood sugar levels
- Cholesterol and other fats in the blood

These tests help check for metabolic syndrome and heart disease risk.

Imaging tests like CT scans or X-rays of the heart arteries may be done if needed.

Because PCOS is linked to depression and anxiety, your doctor will ask about your mood. If needed, you will be referred to a mental health professional.

## How Is PCOS Treated?

Treatment depends on your symptoms, age, and whether you want to get pregnant.

### Lifestyle Changes
- Exercise at least 30 minutes a day
- Eat fewer carbohydrates (like bread, pasta, potatoes, and sweets)
- Lose weight if you are overweight

Losing weight can:
- Help your body use insulin better
- Start regular ovulation
- Make your periods more regular
- Reduce body hair
- Lower the risk of uterine cancer

Weight loss surgery or GLP-1 medications may help women with both PCOS and obesity. These are not helpful for women with normal weight.

### Medications
**Birth control pills** (containing estrogen and progestin) or **progestin-only methods** (like an IUD or pills) are often used if you do not want to get pregnant. These help:
- Make periods more regular
- Lower male hormone levels
- Reduce acne and body hair
- Lower the risk of uterine cancer

**Metformin** is a diabetes medicine. It helps your body use insulin better. It can:
- Help with weight loss
- Restart ovulation and periods
- Lower insulin levels

If you take metformin and do not want to get pregnant, use birth control. Metformin does not help much with hair or acne. You will need regular blood tests to check sugar, kidney, and liver health.

**Liraglutide** and **orlistat** are medicines that can help with weight loss. Orlistat and inositols may also help reduce male hormone symptoms and improve insulin use.

### Fertility Treatments (If You Want to Get Pregnant)
If you are overweight and want to get pregnant, losing weight can help.

You may be referred to a fertility specialist. They may try:
- **Clomiphene** or **letrozole** – medicines that help the ovaries release an egg
- **Metformin** – if you have insulin resistance, it may help trigger ovulation
- **Follicle-stimulating hormone** – to help the ovaries work better
- **GnRH agonists** – to help control hormone release
- **Human chorionic gonadotropin** – to trigger ovulation

If medicines do not work, surgery may be an option. **Ovarian drilling** is done during laparoscopy. Small holes are made in the ovaries using heat or a laser. This lowers male hormone levels. It can help restart ovulation and improve chances of pregnancy. This surgery requires general anesthesia.

### Treating Excess Body Hair
No method removes all hair completely. But some help:
- **Eflornithine cream** – slows facial hair growth
- **Bleaching, plucking, waxing, or depilatory creams** – remove hair temporarily
- **Laser hair removal** – reduces hair over time

**Spironolactone** blocks male hormones. It can reduce body hair. Side effects include more frequent urination and low blood pressure (which may cause dizziness or fainting). It can harm a baby. So sexually active women must use birth control while taking it.

**Cyproterone** is a strong medicine that blocks male hormones. It helps many women with body hair. It is used in many countries but is not approved in the United States.

New treatments like GnRH agonists and antagonists are being studied. But they can weaken bones and lead to osteoporosis.

Losing weight can also slow down hair growth by lowering male hormone levels.

### Treating Acne
Acne is treated with:
- Benzoyl peroxide
- Tretinoin cream
- Topical or oral antibiotics

These treatments are used as they would be for any acne.

## Key Facts

- PCOS is the most common cause of infertility in the United States.
- It often starts in the teens or early 20s.
- It can lead to long-term health problems if not managed.
- Early treatment can prevent serious issues like diabetes, heart disease, and uterine cancer.
- Lifestyle changes are the first step in treatment.
- Many women with PCOS can live healthy lives with proper care.

# Crohn's Disease – Simple Guide

Crohn's disease is a long-term condition that affects your gut. It can cause a range of symptoms that come and go over time.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms can vary from person to person. They depend on which part of your gut is affected.

Common symptoms include:
- Diarrhoea
- Blood or mucus in your poo
- Stomach pain
- Pain around your bottom (anus)
- Feeling very tired or unwell
- Losing your appetite and losing weight
- In children: not growing as expected or delayed puberty

You may also have symptoms in other parts of your body, such as:
- Joint pain
- Sore eyes
- Skin rashes

Symptoms often come in waves. These are called flare-ups. They can last from a few days to several months. Then you may feel better for a while. This is called remission.

Most people first notice symptoms in their teens or twenties. But it can start at any age.

## When to See a Doctor

See your GP if:
- You think you might have Crohn's disease
- You already have Crohn's disease and your symptoms are getting worse
- Your current treatment is not helping

Go to your GP urgently or call NHS 111 if:
- Your poo is black or dark red
- You have bloody diarrhoea

You can call 111 or get help online.

## How Is Crohn's Disease Diagnosed?

There is no single test for Crohn's disease. It can take time to diagnose.

Your GP may:
- Do blood tests
- Test a sample of your poo

If your GP suspects Crohn's disease, you will be referred to a specialist in hospital.

Hospital tests may include:
- A thin tube with a camera is passed through your mouth or bottom to look inside your gut. This is called a colonoscopy, endoscopy, or gastroscopy.
- A small sample of tissue is taken from your gut. This is called a biopsy.
- Scans such as an MRI, CT scan, or ultrasound scan.

The specialist will use all the results to make a diagnosis.

## How Is Crohn's Disease Treated?

There is no cure for Crohn's disease. But treatments can help you stay well for long periods.

Your treatment will depend on your symptoms. You may need different treatments over time.

You will be cared for by a team of healthcare professionals. This includes a specialist doctor called a gastroenterologist. You will have regular check-ups and tests.

### Medicines

Medicines can help reduce inflammation, stop flare-ups, or ease symptoms.

Types of medicines include:
- Steroids to reduce swelling in your gut
- Mesalazine or sulfasalazine to reduce inflammation
- Immunosuppressants like azathioprine or mercaptopurine to calm your immune system
- Biological therapies like adalimumab or infliximab to target your immune system
- Painkillers, laxatives, or medicines to stop diarrhoea

Some people are given a special liquid diet instead of medicines. This is often used for children or people who cannot take steroids.

### Surgery

Surgery may be needed if:
- Your symptoms are only in one part of your gut
- Medicines are not working well
- You have serious complications

Surgery options include:
- Removing the damaged part of your gut and joining the healthy parts together (bowel resection)
- Creating a stoma – a small opening in your tummy to let waste leave your body (ileostomy or colostomy)

Surgery can help reduce symptoms. But symptoms may return in another part of your gut later.

Your surgeon will explain the risks and benefits of the operation.

## What You Can Do to Help Yourself

You can take steps to manage your condition and feel better.

### Do These Things

- Eat a healthy, balanced diet. Your healthcare team can help you plan meals to get all the nutrients you need.
- Keep a diary of your symptoms. Note what you eat, changes in your medicines, or stress levels. This can help you spot triggers.
- Get recommended vaccinations. If you take medicines that affect your immune system, you may need the flu vaccine or pneumococcal vaccine. Always check with your doctor first.
- Ask for a RADAR key if you need one. This unlocks accessible public toilets. You can usually get one from a charity.

### Avoid These Things

- Do not smoke. Smoking increases your risk of flare-ups.
- Do not change your diet drastically without talking to your healthcare team.
- Do not take non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen unless your doctor says it is safe.

## Possible Complications

Crohn's disease can lead to complications. These can be serious, but good treatment reduces the risk.

Over time, inflammation and damage in your gut can cause:
- A fistula – a tunnel that forms between your bowel and another part of your body, like your bladder, skin, or vagina
- An anal fissure – a small tear or sore near your anus
- A stricture – a narrow part of your gut that can block food from passing through
- A perforated bowel – a hole in the wall of your bowel
- Bowel cancer – if you are at high risk, you may be offered regular colonoscopies to check for this

Crohn's disease can also cause:
- Low levels of vitamins and minerals
- Joint problems
- Bone thinning
- Skin issues
- Eye problems
- Kidney or liver problems

## Support and Help

Living with Crohn's disease can be hard, both physically and emotionally.

You may be able to get social care and support if your illness affects your daily life.

Talk to your healthcare team. You may also find it helpful to connect with others who have Crohn's disease.
