# Toxocariasis

Toxocariasis is an infection in people caused by worm larvae from animals.  
The worms are called *Toxocara*.  
They usually infect dogs and cats.  
People get infected by accident.  

## How People Get Infected

The eggs of these worms live in soil.  
They come from the poop of infected dogs or cats.  
You can get the infection by touching dirty soil or sand.  
Then you touch your mouth.  
You can also get it from eating undercooked meat from infected animals like rabbits.  

Once inside your body, the eggs hatch in your intestines.  
The tiny worms then move through your body.  
They can travel to your liver, lungs, brain, or eyes.  
This movement causes damage.  
The damage comes from the worms and your body’s reaction to them.  

The worms do not grow into adult worms in people.  
But they can stay alive in your body for many months.  

## Symptoms

Toxocariasis can cause different symptoms.  
Some people have no symptoms at all.  
Others may have:  
- Fever  
- Loss of appetite  
- Swollen liver or spleen  
- Skin rash  
- Coughing or trouble breathing  
- Asthma-like symptoms  
- Eye problems, including blurry vision or loss of vision  

There are two main types of symptoms:  

### Visceral Larva Migrans (VLM)  
This happens when the worms move through your internal organs.  
It can cause fever, tiredness, and swelling in the liver or spleen.  
You may also have a rash or breathing problems.  

### Ocular Larva Migrans (OLM)  
This happens when the worms move into the eye.  
It often causes no symptoms at first.  
But it can lead to vision loss.  
Some people have a red, painful eye with swelling inside.  

## Diagnosis

Doctors diagnose toxocariasis using:  
- A blood test that checks for antibodies to *Toxocara*  
- Your medical history and symptoms  
- Eye exams if vision is affected  

The blood test is called enzyme immunoassay.  
It shows if you have ever been infected.  
But a positive result does not always mean you are sick now.  
Many people have had past infections.  

Imaging tests like CT or MRI can show small spots in the liver or lungs.  
Blood tests may show high levels of certain white blood cells called eosinophils.  
This is common in VLM.  

Biopsies (tissue samples) are not very helpful.  
The worms are hard to find in tissue.  
Stool tests are useless because the worms do not live in the intestines.  

For eye infections, an eye doctor must examine you.  
They look for white, oval spots in the back of the eye.  
These spots are caused by the body’s reaction to the worms.  

## Treatment

Most people with mild symptoms do not need medicine.  
The infection often goes away on its own.  

For mild symptoms like itching or rash:  
- Antihistamines can help.  

For moderate to severe symptoms:  
- Doctors may prescribe albendazole or mebendazole.  
- These medicines kill the worms.  
- The best length of treatment is not known.  

For severe symptoms:  
- Corticosteroids (like prednisone) may be used.  
- They reduce swelling and inflammation.  

For eye infections (OLM):  
- Steroids are very important.  
- They can be taken as pills or injected into the eye.  
- Albendazole may be used with steroids.  
- But it is not clear if this helps vision improve.  
- Most people still have some vision loss.  

Other treatments for eye infections include:  
- Laser therapy to kill worms in the eye  
- Freezing (cryotherapy)  
- Eye surgery in some cases  

## Prevention

You can prevent toxocariasis by:  
- Deworming dogs and cats regularly  
- Keeping pets away from areas where children play  
- Covering sandboxes when not in use  
- Washing hands after playing in dirt or sand  
- Washing fruits and vegetables before eating  
- Cooking meat thoroughly  

## Key Points

- *Toxocara canis* worms mainly infect dogs.  
- People get infected by accident, usually from soil with dog or cat poop.  
- You can also get infected from undercooked meat of infected animals.  
- In people, the infection causes two main problems:  
  - Visceral larva migrans: worms move through organs.  
  - Ocular larva migrans: worms move into the eye.  
- Eye infection can cause vision loss.  
- Diagnosis uses blood tests and symptoms.  
- Most cases of VLM do not need treatment.  
- For severe cases, use albendazole or mebendazole.  
- Steroids help reduce swelling.  
- For eye infections, use steroids, and sometimes medicine or surgery.  
- Deworming pets helps stop the spread of infection.

# Herniated Disc – Simple Explanation

A herniated disc happens when a disc in your spine gets damaged.  
The disc is like a cushion between the bones in your spine.  
It has a tough outer layer and a soft, jelly-like center.  

When the outer layer tears, the soft center can push out.  
This bulging part can press on nearby nerves.  
This pressure causes pain, numbness, or weakness.

---

## What Causes a Herniated Disc?

- Aging weakens the discs over time.  
- Injuries can damage a disc suddenly.  
- Being overweight puts extra stress on the spine.  
- Lifting heavy things the wrong way increases risk.  
- Repeated small injuries over time can also cause damage.

Most herniated discs happen in the lower back.  
They are most common in people aged 30 to 50.  
After age 50, the disc’s center starts to harden, so it’s less likely to bulge.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many people with a herniated disc have no symptoms.  
Even if a scan shows a bulging disc, it may not hurt.

But when symptoms do appear, they can range from mild to severe.  
Pain often gets worse with movement, coughing, sneezing, or bending forward.

Where the pain is felt depends on which disc is damaged and which nerve is affected.

- A herniated disc in the lower back often causes **sciatica**.  
  This is pain that runs down the back of the leg.  
- A herniated disc in the neck causes neck pain that may go down the arm or into the hand.  
- Pain that starts in one place and travels along a nerve path is called **radiating pain**.

Other possible symptoms:
- Numbness in the leg, arm, or hand  
- Weakness in a muscle  
- Trouble controlling the bladder or bowels (this is rare but serious)

If you lose control of your bladder or bowels, get medical help right away.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use imaging tests to see what’s happening in the spine.

- **MRI** (magnetic resonance imaging) gives a clear picture of soft tissues like discs and nerves.  
- **CT scan** (computed tomography) shows bone and soft tissue details.  
- **CT myelography** is used only if more detail is needed or if MRI can’t be done.

Sometimes doctors do nerve tests to check how well nerves are working.  
These tests include:
- Nerve conduction studies  
- Electromyography (EMG)

These help find which nerve is being pressed.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Most people get better without surgery.  
The disc often shrinks on its own over time.  
Most back pain improves within 6 weeks, no matter the cause.

### Pain Relief Options

- Use **cold packs** (like ice) or **heat pads** (like a heating pad).  
- Take over-the-counter pain medicine such as acetaminophen or NSAIDs (like ibuprofen).  
- If pain is severe, doctors may prescribe oral steroids or inject steroids near the spine.  
  But the benefit of these injections is still debated.

### Sleep Tips

- Sleep on a medium-firm mattress.  
- If you sleep on your back, place a pillow under your knees.  
- If you sleep on your side, use a pillow to keep your head in line with your spine.  
- Place a pillow between your knees to keep your hips and knees slightly bent.  
  This can ease back pain.

Avoid staying in bed for long periods.  
Traction (pulling the body) is not helpful and is not recommended.

### Physical Therapy and Exercise

As pain goes down, gentle exercise helps.  
It improves posture and strengthens back muscles.  
This reduces pressure on the nerves.

Start slowly. Stop any exercise that causes or increases pain.

---

### Surgery

Surgery is only needed if:
- Pain does not improve after weeks of treatment  
- You have muscle weakness  
- You lose feeling in a leg or arm  
- You lose control of your bladder or bowels (this is a medical emergency)

Surgery removes the part of the disc that is pressing on the nerve.  
This is called a **diskectomy**.  
Sometimes part of the bone over the nerve is also removed. This is called a **laminectomy**.

Most surgeries are done using small cuts and local or regional anesthesia.  
This means only part of the body is numbed.  
You may not need to stay in the hospital overnight.

Recovery time is usually 6 weeks to 3 months.  
Surgery often helps people feel better faster than non-surgical treatment.

But after about one to two years, most people—whether they had surgery or not—have similar results.

About 10 to 20 out of 100 people who have surgery for sciatica will have another disc herniate later.

---

## How to Prevent a Herniated Disc

You can’t always prevent a herniated disc, but you can lower your risk.

### Stay Active

- Exercise regularly.  
- Walking, swimming, and other aerobic activities improve fitness and strengthen muscles.

### Strengthen Core Muscles

Strong muscles in your belly, back, and buttocks help support your spine.  
This reduces strain on the discs.

Try these safe exercises:

#### Pelvic Tilts
- Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat.  
- Press your lower back into the floor.  
- Tighten your buttocks and stomach muscles.  
- Hold for 10 seconds.  
- Repeat 20 times.

#### Abdominal Curls
- Lie on your back with knees bent and feet on the floor.  
- Place hands on your chest.  
- Tighten your stomach muscles and slowly lift your shoulders off the floor.  
- Keep your head back—don’t touch your chin to your chest.  
- Lower slowly.  
- Do 3 sets of 10.

#### Knee-to-Chest Stretch
- Lie on your back.  
- Bring one knee toward your chest.  
- Hold for 10 seconds.  
- Lower and repeat with the other leg.  
- Do 10 times.

**Important:** Stop any exercise that causes pain.  
Breathe normally during each move.  
Talk to your doctor before starting an exercise plan if you have back pain.

### Maintain a Healthy Weight

Extra weight puts more pressure on your spine.  
Staying at a healthy weight helps protect your discs.

### Practice Good Posture

- Stand straight. Avoid slouching.  
- Sit with your feet flat on the floor.  
- Keep your knees slightly bent.  
- Keep your lower back against the chair.  
- Use a small pillow behind your lower back if needed.  
- Avoid crossing your legs.  
- Change positions often if you sit or stand for long periods.

### Learn to Lift Safely

- Keep your hips and shoulders lined up.  
- Do not twist your body while lifting.  
- Bend at your hips and knees, not your back.  
- Keep the object close to your body.  
- Use your legs to lift, not your back.  
- Avoid lifting heavy things over your head.

---

**Bottom Line:**  
Most herniated discs improve with time and simple care.  
Exercise, good posture, and safe lifting habits can help prevent them.  
If you have serious symptoms like weakness or loss of bladder control, seek medical help right away.

# Threadworms

Threadworms are small, white worms that can cause problems in the body.  
They are also called pinworms.

## Symptoms

You may see tiny white worms in your child’s stool.  
You may also notice intense itching around the bottom.  
The worms often come out at night while your child is sleeping.

## How to Get Help

If you think you or your child has threadworms, go to a pharmacy.  
You can buy medicine to treat threadworms at a pharmacy.

## Treatment

You can buy a medicine called mebendazole.  
It comes as a chewable tablet or liquid.  
You swallow it.

Treat everyone in your home who is over 2 years old.  
Even if they do not have symptoms, they should still take the medicine.  
This helps stop the worms from spreading.

Tell the pharmacist if:
- You need to treat a child under 2 years old.
- You are pregnant or breastfeeding.

The medicine may not be safe for these groups.  
You may need to see a doctor instead.

If you cannot take medicine, you can still get rid of threadworms.  
Use strict hygiene for 6 weeks.  
This includes washing hands, cleaning surfaces, and changing clothes and bedding.

## How Threadworms Spread

Threadworms spread when someone swallows their eggs.  
The worms lay eggs around the bottom.  
These eggs cause itching.  
When you scratch, the eggs get on your fingers.

The eggs can then get on:
- Clothes  
- Toys  
- Toothbrushes  
- Kitchen or bathroom surfaces  
- Bedding  
- Food  

Another person can catch the worms by touching these things.  
Then touching their mouth.  
The eggs can live for up to 2 weeks on surfaces.

Once swallowed, the eggs hatch in the gut.  
The worms grow into adult worms in 1 to 2 months.

## Preventing Re-infection

Children can get threadworms again after treatment.  
This happens if they swallow the eggs again.

To help stop this:
- Wash hands often, especially after using the toilet and before eating.  
- Keep fingernails short and clean.  
- Change underwear and bed sheets daily for 2 weeks.  
- Wash clothes and bedding in hot water.  
- Clean surfaces with a damp cloth.  
- Avoid sharing towels or toothbrushes.

# Sunburn

Sunburn happens when your skin gets too much ultraviolet light from the sun.  
It causes redness, pain, and sometimes blisters.  
The most harmful sun rays are in the UVB range, which is between 280 and 320 nanometers.

## What to Expect with Sunburn

Symptoms usually show up within 1 to 24 hours.  
They get worse over the next 72 hours.  
Most often, they peak between 12 and 24 hours after sun exposure.  

Your skin may turn red and feel hot.  
It might also swell, hurt when touched, or form blisters.  
In bad cases, you may feel sick.  
You could have a fever, chills, feel weak, or even feel dizzy.  
These symptoms happen when your body reacts to damaged skin.  
They are like the body’s response to a burn from heat.  

Days later, the burned skin may peel off.  
This is normal, but the new skin underneath is very sensitive to sunlight for weeks.

## Risks of Sunburn

Sunburn can lead to serious problems.  
You may get an infection in the damaged skin.  
Your skin may turn darker or lighter in patches.  
You are also much more likely to get skin cancer later in life.  
The peeling skin is especially sensitive to sun for several weeks.

## How to Treat Sunburn

Use cool, wet cloths on the burned area.  
You can also take over-the-counter pain medicine like ibuprofen or naproxen.  
These help reduce pain and swelling.  

Avoid using products with petroleum, like petroleum jelly, on severe burns.  
They can trap heat and make things worse.  

Aloe vera or other water-based lotions may help soothe the skin.  
But avoid creams with numbing medicine like benzocaine or diphenhydramine.  
These can cause an allergic reaction in some people.  

If you have blisters, treat them like a burn.  
Cover them with clean, sterile bandages.  
Use a healing ointment that fights germs.  

Some doctors may suggest a steroid medicine like prednisone for very bad sunburns.  
This is not always recommended and should only be done under a doctor’s care.

## How to Prevent Sunburn

Stay out of the sun during the middle of the day.  
Wear tight-weave clothing that covers your arms and legs.  
Wear a wide-brimmed hat and sunglasses.  
Use sunscreen every day, even on cloudy days.  

These simple steps can greatly lower your risk of sunburn.

# Polymyalgia Rheumatica

Polymyalgia rheumatica is a condition that causes pain and stiffness in the muscles. It mainly affects the neck, back, shoulders, and hips.

This condition usually starts in people over the age of 50. Women are more likely to get it than men.

The exact cause is not known.

It can happen at the same time as, before, or after another condition called giant cell arteritis. Some doctors believe these two conditions are part of the same problem.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms can start suddenly or slowly.

You may feel severe pain and stiffness in your neck, shoulders, back, and hips.

The stiffness is often worst in the morning or after sitting or lying down for a while.

Some people find it hard to get out of bed or do simple tasks like getting dressed.

You may feel weak, but your muscles are not damaged.

Other possible symptoms include:
- Fever
- Feeling unwell
- Low mood or depression
- Losing weight without trying

Some people also have symptoms of giant cell arteritis. This can include:
- Headaches
- Pain when chewing
- Muscle cramps or tiredness in arms or legs during activity
- Vision problems

If joint pain is very bad, the diagnosis may be rheumatoid arthritis instead.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tools to diagnose polymyalgia rheumatica.

### 1. Physical Exam
The doctor checks your symptoms and how your muscles feel.

### 2. Blood Tests
These help rule out other conditions and confirm inflammation.

- **Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)** and **C-reactive protein (CRP)**: These tests show if there is inflammation in the body. In polymyalgia rheumatica, both are usually very high.
  
- **Complete blood count (CBC)**: This checks for anemia and high platelet levels. These are common in this condition.

- **Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)**: This test checks for an underactive thyroid. This condition can cause muscle pain and weakness, so it must be ruled out.

- **Creatine kinase (CK)**: This test checks for muscle damage. In polymyalgia rheumatica, muscle damage does not happen. So, CK levels are normal.

- **Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies**: These are found in most people with rheumatoid arthritis. They are not found in polymyalgia rheumatica. This helps doctors tell the two apart.

### 3. Response to Treatment
Most people feel much better quickly when they start taking a corticosteroid medicine. This supports the diagnosis.

---

## How Is It Treated?

### Prednisone
This is a corticosteroid medicine. It is the main treatment.

- A low dose usually brings fast relief.
- If you also have giant cell arteritis, you may need a higher dose to prevent blindness.
- As your symptoms improve, your doctor will slowly lower the dose.
- Most people can stop the medicine in about 2 years.
- Some people need to stay on a low dose for several years.

### Sarilumab
This is a different medicine used in some cases.

- It may be used if prednisone does not work well.
- It may be used if you cannot lower the prednisone dose without symptoms returning.

### Side Effects
Corticosteroids can cause side effects, especially in older adults. These may include:
- Weight gain
- Trouble sleeping
- Mood changes
- Weak bones
- High blood pressure

Talk to your doctor about these risks.

---

## Watch for Warning Signs

Giant cell arteritis can start at any time—even after you feel better.

Tell your doctor right away if you have:
- Headaches
- Pain when chewing
- Cramps or tiredness in arms or legs when walking
- Vision changes or loss

These could be signs of a serious problem.

---

## More Information

The following resource may help:
- **Vasculitis Foundation: About Polymyalgia Rheumatica**  
  This site offers support and information for people with polymyalgia rheumatica.  
  It includes help finding a doctor, learning about research, and joining patient groups.

Note: The Manual is not responsible for the content of this website.

# Hiatus Hernia

A hiatus hernia happens when part of your stomach pushes up through a hole in your diaphragm. This can cause uncomfortable symptoms.

## Symptoms

You might not have any symptoms at all. Some people have no problems and do not know they have it.

If you do have symptoms, they can include:

- A burning feeling in your chest, especially after eating
- Bringing up food or bitter-tasting fluid from your stomach
- Feeling sick or being sick
- Bad breath
- A bloated feeling
- Trouble or pain when swallowing

These symptoms are also known as gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or GORD.

## When to See a Doctor

See your GP if:

- Your symptoms last longer than 3 weeks
- Your symptoms are very bad or getting worse
- Over-the-counter medicines from the pharmacy do not help

Get urgent help from your GP or NHS 111 if you have:

- Unexplained weight loss
- Trouble swallowing
- Frequent vomiting
- Blood in your vomit
- Pain in your upper tummy

You can call 111 or visit [111 online](https://www.111.nhs.uk) for help.

## How to Feel Better

You can take steps to reduce your symptoms.

### Do These Things

- Eat smaller meals more often
- Raise the head of your bed by 10 to 20 centimetres. This helps keep stomach acid down
- Lose weight if you are overweight
- Find ways to relax and reduce stress

### Avoid These Things

- Foods or drinks that make your symptoms worse
- Eating or drinking anything 3 to 4 hours before bedtime
- Tight clothes around your waist
- Smoking
- Drinking too much alcohol
- Stopping any medicine you were prescribed without talking to your doctor first

## Help from a Pharmacist

Talk to a pharmacist if you keep having symptoms.

They can suggest medicines like antacids or alginates. These can help ease your symptoms.

Take them with food or soon after eating. This works best because that’s when symptoms often happen.

These medicines help for a short time. They do not fix the problem. Do not take them every day for a long time.

If you are pregnant, a pharmacist can tell you which medicines are safe to use.

## Medical Treatment

If over-the-counter medicines and lifestyle changes do not help, your GP can prescribe stronger medicines.

If those do not work, your GP may do tests to check if your symptoms are caused by a hiatus hernia.

They may also prescribe long-term treatment for GORD.

Your GP might send you to a specialist. This is only if other treatments have not worked and your symptoms are very bad.

### Surgery

Surgery is usually done using keyhole techniques. This means small cuts in your tummy.

You will be asleep during the operation because it is done under general anaesthetic.

After surgery:

- It may take up to 6 weeks before you can eat normally
- It can take a few months to fully recover
- You may still have bloating, gas, or trouble swallowing for a while

There is a chance you may need more surgery in the future.

## What Causes a Hiatus Hernia?

Doctors do not know exactly what causes a hiatus hernia.

It is more common in people who are:

- Over 50 years old
- Pregnant
- Overweight

Anyone can get a hiatus hernia, but these factors increase the chance.

# Inborn Metabolic Disorders That Cause High Bilirubin Levels

Some people are born with conditions that affect how their body processes bilirubin. Bilirubin is a substance made when red blood cells break down. High levels of bilirubin can cause yellowing of the skin and eyes, known as jaundice.

There are two main types of high bilirubin:
- **Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia**: Bilirubin is not properly processed by the liver.
- **Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia**: Bilirubin is processed but not properly released into bile.

Below are the main conditions linked to these issues.

---

## Gilbert Syndrome

Gilbert syndrome is a common, harmless condition. It causes mild, ongoing high levels of bilirubin. But it does not cause any symptoms.

- It affects 3 to 10 out of every 100 people.
- It is caused by changes in a gene called *UGT1A1*. This gene helps make an enzyme that processes bilirubin.
- The gene change can be passed down in two ways: one parent can pass it on (autosomal dominant), or both parents must pass it on (autosomal recessive).

The liver does not take in bilirubin well. The enzyme that processes bilirubin works at a lower level than normal. But it is not as low as in other serious conditions.

Some people with this syndrome break down red blood cells slightly faster. But this does not cause anemia or make bilirubin levels worse.

The liver looks normal under a microscope.

This condition is often found by chance. A doctor may notice yellowing of the skin or eyes. Or a blood test may show high bilirubin levels. These levels usually stay between 2 and 5 mg/dL (34 to 86 micromol/L). They can go up during fasting or times of stress.

To tell Gilbert syndrome apart from liver disease:
- The bilirubin in the blood is mostly unconjugated.
- Other liver tests are normal.
- Bilirubin does not appear in the urine.

To tell it apart from hemolysis (too many red blood cells breaking down):
- There is no anemia.
- The number of young red blood cells is normal.

No treatment is needed. People with this condition do not have liver disease. They can be reassured that they are healthy.

---

## Crigler-Najjar Syndrome

This is a rare inherited condition. It affects the liver’s ability to process bilirubin.

- It is caused by a lack of the enzyme glucuronyl transferase.
- This enzyme helps make bilirubin water-soluble so the body can get rid of it.
- The problem comes from changes in the *UGT1A1* gene.

There are two types:

### Type 1 (Complete deficiency)
- This is the most severe form.
- It starts soon after birth.
- Bilirubin levels are very high.
- Without treatment, most children die from brain damage (kernicterus) by age one.
- Some may survive into adulthood with treatment.
- Treatment includes light therapy (phototherapy) and liver transplant.

### Type 2 (Partial deficiency)
- This form is less severe.
- Bilirubin levels are usually below 20 mg/dL (342 micromol/L).
- People with this type often live into adulthood without brain damage.
- The medicine phenobarbital can help. It boosts the weak enzyme.
- The usual dose is 1.5 to 2 milligrams per kilogram of body weight, taken three times a day.

---

## Dubin-Johnson Syndrome and Rotor Syndrome

These are rare, inherited conditions. They cause high levels of conjugated bilirubin. But they do not cause liver damage or other health problems.

- Both conditions cause jaundice.
- The liver works normally.
- There is no bile buildup (no cholestasis).
- Liver tests (aminotransferase and alkaline phosphatase) are normal.
- Bilirubin appears in the urine — unlike in Gilbert syndrome, where bilirubin does not appear in urine.

These conditions do not need treatment. They are harmless.

---

## Primary Shunt Hyperbilirubinemia

This is a rare, inherited condition. It runs in families and is harmless.

- The body makes more bilirubin than normal.
- This extra bilirubin comes from early red blood cell production and other sources, not from normal red blood cell breakdown.
- It is not linked to anemia or liver disease.
- The condition does not cause harm. No treatment is needed.

# Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC)

Primary biliary cholangitis is a long-term liver disease. It causes inflammation and scarring in the small tubes that carry bile from the liver. Over time, the tubes get blocked. This leads to more scarring. The liver becomes damaged. Eventually, this can lead to liver failure.

This condition is most common in women between the ages of 35 and 70. But it can also happen in men and women of any age. It sometimes runs in families.

## What the Liver and Bile Do

The liver makes bile. Bile is a thick, greenish-yellow fluid. It helps break down food during digestion. Bile also removes waste from the body. This includes bilirubin, extra cholesterol, and leftover drug products.

Bile moves through small tubes called bile ducts. These ducts carry bile from the liver to the gallbladder. Then it goes to the small intestine.

PBC only affects the small bile ducts inside the liver. It also affects the liver cells near these ducts.

Another condition, called primary sclerosing cholangitis, affects bile ducts both inside and outside the liver.

## How PBC Develops

PBC starts with swelling in the bile ducts. This swelling blocks the flow of bile. Bile then builds up in the liver cells. This causes more damage and swelling.

At first, the liver can repair itself. It makes new liver cells and connects them to the leftover structure of dead cells. But if the damage keeps growing, scar tissue forms. This scar tissue spreads through the liver. It does not help the liver work. It changes the liver’s shape and structure.

When scarring becomes widespread, the liver develops cirrhosis. Cirrhosis means the liver is severely damaged and cannot work well.

## What Causes PBC

Doctors do not know the exact cause. But it is likely due to an autoimmune reaction. This means the body’s immune system attacks its own tissues.

PBC often happens in people who have other autoimmune diseases. These include rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma, Sjögren syndrome, and autoimmune thyroiditis.

More than 95 percent of people with PBC have certain abnormal antibodies in their blood. These antibodies target mitochondria. Mitochondria are tiny parts of cells that make energy. But these antibodies do not cause the damage to bile ducts.

Other immune cells attack the bile ducts. Scientists do not know what starts this attack. It might be due to a virus or a toxic substance.

## Symptoms of PBC

PBC often starts slowly. About half of people have no symptoms at first.

Early symptoms may include:
- Itchiness
- Tiredness
- Dry mouth
- Dry eyes

Other problems may appear months or years later:
- Skin may turn darker
- Nerves may be damaged (called neuropathy)
- Pain or discomfort in the upper belly
- Small yellow bumps of fat in the skin (called xanthoma) or on the eyelids (called xanthelasma)
- Yellowing of the skin and eyes (called jaundice)
- Fluid buildup in the belly (called ascites)
- Swelling in the ankles and feet (called edema)

As the disease gets worse, any symptom of cirrhosis can appear. The body may not absorb fats well. This includes fat-soluble vitamins like A, D, E, and K.

Poor absorption of vitamin D can lead to weak bones (osteoporosis). Poor absorption of vitamin K can cause easy bruising and bleeding.

If fats are not absorbed, stools may be:
- Light-colored
- Soft
- Large
- Oily
- Very smelly (called steatorrhea)

The liver and spleen may get bigger. But as scarring grows, the liver shrinks.

## How Doctors Diagnose PBC

Doctors may suspect PBC in middle-aged women with tiredness or itchiness. But many people are diagnosed before symptoms appear. This happens when routine blood tests show liver problems.

During a physical exam, the doctor may feel:
- A firm, enlarged liver (in about 1 in 4 people)
- An enlarged spleen (in about 1 in 7 people)

If PBC is suspected, doctors do:
- Liver function blood tests
- Blood tests for specific antibodies
- Imaging tests
- Liver biopsy

**Imaging tests** check for blockages in bile ducts outside the liver. These include:
- MRI of the bile ducts (called MRCP)
- Ultrasound

If the results are unclear, a test called ERCP may be done. This uses an endoscope (a thin tube) passed through the mouth. A special dye is injected into the bile ducts. X-rays are then taken. If no blockages are found outside the liver, the problem is likely in the liver. This supports a diagnosis of PBC.

A **liver biopsy** is usually done. This means removing a small sample of liver tissue. The sample is looked at under a microscope. This confirms the diagnosis. It also helps doctors see how far the disease has progressed.

## How PBC Is Treated

There is no cure for PBC. But treatment can help:
- Ease symptoms
- Slow liver damage
- Treat complications

### Medications

- **Cholestyramine** can help with itchiness.
- **Rifampin**, **naltrexone** (an opioid medicine), **sertraline**, or **ursodeoxycholic acid with ultraviolet light** may also help with itchiness.

- **Ursodeoxycholic acid** is the main medicine used. It slows liver damage. It works best when started early. It can help people live longer. It also delays the need for a liver transplant.

- **Obeticholic acid** is used if ursodeoxycholic acid is not working well. It improves liver test results in many people. But it should not be used in people with advanced cirrhosis. It can make liver function worse.

- A medicine called **bezafibrate** (a fibrate) may also be used.

### Supplements

- **Calcium and vitamin D** are needed to prevent or slow weak bones (osteoporosis).
- Weight-bearing exercises, **bisphosphonates**, or **raloxifene** can also help protect bones.

- **Vitamin A, D, E, and K** supplements may be needed. These help correct vitamin deficiencies.
  - Vitamins A, D, and E are taken by mouth.
  - Vitamin K is taken by mouth or given as an injection.

### Lifestyle Changes

- Do not drink alcohol.
- Stop taking any medicines that can harm the liver.

### Liver Transplant

When PBC is advanced, a liver transplant is the best treatment. It can extend life.

After a transplant, PBC can come back in some people. But it rarely becomes serious.

## Outlook for PBC

PBC usually gets worse slowly. But the speed varies a lot.

Some people may not have symptoms for 2 years. Others may not have symptoms for 10 to 15 years.

Some people get very sick in just 3 to 5 years.

Once symptoms start, life expectancy is about 10 years.

Certain signs mean the disease may progress faster:
- Symptoms get worse quickly
- Older age
- Fluid buildup or other signs of cirrhosis
- Having another autoimmune disease, like rheumatoid arthritis
- Abnormal liver test results

Once jaundice appears, death may happen within months.

# Breast Abscess

A breast abscess is a painful lump in the breast. It contains pus, which is a thick fluid made of dead cells and bacteria.

The lump will feel swollen and warm to the touch.

## When to Seek Help

See your doctor right away if you have:
- A breast that hurts, feels warm, or looks red
- A lump or swelling in your breast

You can call NHS 111 or get help online.

## Symptoms of a Breast Abscess

You may notice:
- A lump or swelling in your breast
- Pain in your breast. It may feel warm or look red. (This can be harder to see on brown or black skin.)
- A high temperature
- Feeling unwell or tired

You are more likely to get a breast abscess if:
- You recently had a breast infection (mastitis)
- You have had a breast abscess before

## What Happens at Your GP Appointment

Your GP will check your breast. If they think you have an abscess, they will refer you to hospital.

At the hospital, you will have an ultrasound scan. This uses sound waves to create a picture of your breast. It helps doctors see if there is an abscess.

## Treatment for a Breast Abscess

You will need treatment in hospital.

The main treatment is draining the pus from the abscess. This can be done in two ways:
- A needle is used to draw out the pus. This may need to be done more than once. You may need to return to hospital each time.
- A small cut is made in the skin to drain the pus.

Before the procedure, you will get a local anaesthetic. This numbs the area so you do not feel pain.

Most people can go home the same day. You may be given antibiotics to take at home.

The abscess should heal completely in a few days or weeks.

## Breastfeeding During Treatment

You can and should keep breastfeeding if you can. It will not harm your baby.

Breastfeeding can help your breast heal faster.

If feeding is too painful, try expressing milk by hand or with a breast pump.

## What Causes a Breast Abscess

A breast abscess often starts with a breast infection called mastitis.

Mastitis happens when the breast becomes inflamed and infected. It is most common in women who are breastfeeding.

But it can also happen in women who are not breastfeeding, though this is less common.

If you treat mastitis quickly, you can lower your risk of getting an abscess.

# Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes – Simple Explanation

Ehlers-Danlos syndromes are genetic conditions. They affect the body’s connective tissues. These tissues hold your body together. They include skin, joints, and blood vessels.

The main problems are:
- Joints that move too much
- Skin that stretches easily
- Skin and tissues that break or tear easily

There is no cure. But treatment can help manage symptoms.

## How It Is Passed Down

Most people with this condition inherit it from a parent. It is usually passed down in an autosomal dominant way. This means one parent with the condition can pass it to their child.

But the condition is not the same in everyone. Different changes in genes cause different types. These gene changes affect the way collagen works. Collagen is a protein that gives strength and structure to tissues.

Some gene changes affect the type of collagen. Others affect enzymes that help build collagen.

## Types of Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes

There are 13 known types. The six most common are:

- Hypermobile type  
- Classic type  
- Vascular type  
- Kyphoscoliosis type  
- Arthrochalasia type  
- Dermatosparaxis type  

The hypermobile, classic, and vascular types are the most often seen.

There are also seven rare types.

## Symptoms and Signs

Symptoms vary a lot from person to person. But some signs are common in certain types.

Common symptoms include:
- Joints that move too much
- Skin that stretches far and returns to normal
- Scars that look thin and wide
- Wounds that heal slowly
- Blood vessels that are weak
- Skin that feels soft and velvety

You can stretch the skin on your forearm or hand by more than one and a half centimeters. The skin returns to normal when you let go.

Scars often form on bony areas like elbows, knees, and shins. These scars are usually thin and paper-like. They are less common in the hypermobile type.

Fleshy bumps called molluscoid pseudotumors can grow on scars or pressure points.

Joint movement can be extreme in the arthrochalasia, classic, and hypermobile types.

Bleeding is rare. But in the vascular type, blood vessels can tear or burst. This can cause bruising.

Small, hard lumps of calcium can sometimes be felt under the skin. X-rays can show them.

## How It Is Diagnosed

Doctors diagnose this condition based on symptoms and tests.

### Step 1: Look at the symptoms

Doctors check for:
- Joint hypermobility (joints that move too much)
- Skin that stretches too much

If you have frequent joint dislocations, slow healing wounds, or unusual scars, it may be a sign.

But many people have flexible joints without this condition. So, other conditions must be ruled out.

### Step 2: Ask simple questions

Doctors may ask:
- Can you touch the floor with your hands without bending your knees?
- Can you bend your thumb to touch your forearm?
- As a child, could you do the splits or twist your body in unusual ways?
- Did your kneecap or shoulder pop out more than once?
- Do you think you are “double-jointed”?

If you answer “yes” to two or more of these, you may have joint hypermobility.

### Step 3: Use the Beighton score

This is a test to measure joint flexibility. It checks:
- The little fingers
- The thumbs
- The elbows
- The knees
- The spine

Each joint that moves too much earns one point. A score of 5 or more means you have joint hypermobility.

### Step 4: Test the skin

Doctors measure how much the skin stretches. They check:
- Forearm and back of hands: more than 1.5 centimeters
- Neck, elbows, and knees: more than 3 centimeters
- Palm: more than 1 centimeter

If the skin stretches this far, it is considered hyperextensible.

### Step 5: Genetic testing

This is the best way to confirm the diagnosis. It can find changes in the genes linked to the condition. It is available for most types.

### Step 6: Skin biopsy (if needed)

A small skin sample may be taken. It is looked at under a microscope. This helps confirm the classic, hypermobile, and vascular types.

### Step 7: Heart and blood vessel tests

Echocardiography or other imaging tests check for heart or blood vessel problems. These can happen in some types.

## Outlook

Most people with Ehlers-Danlos syndromes live a normal life span.

But some types can be life-threatening. The vascular type can cause blood vessels to burst. This is serious and can be deadly.

## Treatment

There is no cure. But treatment can help prevent problems.

### General care:
- Avoid injuries. Wear protective clothing and padding.
- Be careful with physical activity. Avoid high-risk sports.

### Surgery:
- If surgery is needed, it must be done carefully.
- Doctors must stop bleeding well.
- Wounds are stitched with care.
- Tension on the skin and tissues must be avoided.

### Pregnancy:
- Pregnant women with this condition need special care.
- Close monitoring during pregnancy and delivery is essential.
- Genetic counseling is recommended for families.

## Key Facts

- Ehlers-Danlos syndromes are genetic conditions.
- There are 13 known types.
- Most people have very flexible joints and stretchy skin.
- The connective tissues are weak. This can lead to:
  - Heart valve problems
  - Eye damage (from weak eye tissue)
  - Blood vessel tears
  - Uterine rupture
- Diagnosis is based on symptoms and confirmed with genetic testing.

# Atrial Premature Beats

An atrial premature beat is an extra heartbeat. It happens when the upper chambers of the heart get an electrical signal too soon. This signal comes from a place in the heart that is not the normal starting point.

## What Causes Atrial Premature Beats?

- Many healthy people have these extra beats.
- They are more common in older adults.
- They often happen in people with lung problems, like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
- Drinking coffee, tea, or alcohol can trigger them.
- Some cold, allergy, or asthma medicines can make them worse.

## Do They Cause Symptoms?

Most of the time, these beats do not cause any symptoms.  
Sometimes, a person may feel their heart skip or flutter. This is called palpitations.

## How Is It Checked?

A doctor may notice an irregular pulse during a check-up.  
An electrocardiogram, or ECG, confirms the diagnosis.

### What Is an ECG?

An ECG is a test that records the electrical activity of the heart.  
It shows the heart’s electrical signals as waves on a screen or paper.  
Each wave stands for a different part of the heartbeat.

- The first wave, called the P wave, shows the upper chambers of the heart (atria) getting ready to contract.
- The next part, the QRS complex, shows the lower chambers (ventricles) contracting.
- The T wave shows the heart’s lower chambers preparing for the next beat.

An ECG can show many heart problems, including:
- A past heart attack.
- An abnormal heart rhythm.
- Poor blood flow to the heart.
- Thickened heart muscle.
- Weak spots in the heart wall, called aneurysms. These can form after a heart attack.

If the heart rhythm is not normal, the ECG can help doctors find where the problem starts.

## How Are Atrial Premature Beats Treated?

- Most of the time, no treatment is needed.
- If the beats happen often and cause strong discomfort, treatment may be needed.
- Medicines that help control heart rhythm are usually effective.
- If a cause is found, such as caffeine or a certain medicine, fixing that cause can help.

## More Information

The following resource may help you learn more:

**American Heart Association: Arrhythmia**  
This website gives clear information about heart rhythm problems.  
It covers risks, how to get diagnosed, and treatment options.

# Gilbert's Syndrome

## What Is Gilbert's Syndrome?

Gilbert's syndrome is a common condition. It affects how your liver works.  
It is passed from parents to children.  
It is caused by a change in a gene.  

The main sign is mild yellowing of the skin or eyes.  
This yellowing comes and goes.  
Many people with this condition do not have any symptoms at all.

## Symptoms

The most common symptom is mild jaundice.  
Jaundice means your skin or the white part of your eyes turns yellow.  
This yellowing may come and go.  
It can be harder to see on brown or black skin.  
But it is often easier to see in the white part of the eyes.  

Jaundice can also cause itchy skin.  
You may notice your pee is darker than usual.  
Your poo may be paler than normal.  

Many people with Gilbert's syndrome do not have any symptoms.

## How It Is Diagnosed

Doctors usually find out about Gilbert's syndrome through blood tests.  
These tests check how well your liver is working.  
A genetic test may be needed to confirm the diagnosis.  

Some people only learn they have it during tests for something else.  
This is because the condition often causes no symptoms.

## What You Can Do

You do not need treatment for Gilbert's syndrome.  
It does not harm your health or damage your liver.  
There is no cure, but you can take steps to help avoid symptoms.

### Things to Try

- Keep a record of when you get jaundice.  
- Try to avoid things that trigger it. These may include:  
  - Over-exercising  
  - Not getting enough sleep  
  - Drinking alcohol  
  - Not drinking enough fluids  

- Talk to your GP or pharmacist before taking any new medicine.  
- Some medicines, like statins for high cholesterol, may need closer monitoring.

## Causes

Gilbert's syndrome is inherited.  
This means you get it from your parents.  
A change in a gene affects your liver.  
This causes a substance called bilirubin to build up in your blood.  
Bilirubin is a natural waste product from red blood cells.  
Too much bilirubin can turn your skin and eyes yellow.

This condition is more common in men and people with type 1 diabetes.

## How It Affects Your Life

Gilbert's syndrome does not affect your health.  
It does not cause liver damage.  
It does not shorten your life.  

You may have a slightly higher chance of getting gallstones.  
But it does not increase your risk of other health problems.

## When to Seek Help

Call your GP right away or use NHS 111 if:

- You think you have jaundice and you have not been told you have Gilbert's syndrome.  
- You already know you have Gilbert's syndrome, but the yellowing is worse than usual.  
- The yellowing does not go away after a few days.

You can call 111 or get help online at [nhs.uk](https://www.nhs.uk).

# Appendicitis

Appendicitis is a sudden swelling and irritation of a small tube attached to the large intestine. It causes belly pain, loss of appetite, and tenderness in the belly.

Doctors usually diagnose it by checking your symptoms and doing a physical exam. Sometimes they use imaging tests like a CT scan or ultrasound. The main treatment is surgery to remove the appendix.

> **Note:** This information is about acute abdominal pain.  
> (See also: Acute Abdominal Pain)

---

## How Common Is Appendicitis?

In the United States, appendicitis is the most common reason for emergency belly surgery.  
More than 5 out of every 100 people will get it at some point in their lives.  
It most often happens in teens and young adults, but it can happen at any age.

Other problems can affect the appendix, such as small tumors, cancer, or growths.  
The appendix can also be affected by inflammatory bowel diseases like Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis.

---

## What Causes Appendicitis?

Appendicitis usually starts when the inside of the appendix gets blocked.  
The blockage can be caused by swollen tissue, a hard piece of stool (called a fecalith), a foreign object, a tumor, or even worms.  
When the appendix is blocked, it swells. Bacteria grow inside it. The blood supply weakens. This leads to swelling and pain.

If not treated, the appendix can die, break open, or become infected.  
If the broken appendix is caught by nearby tissue, it can form a pocket of infection called an abscess.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The most common signs of appendicitis are:

- Pain in the upper middle belly or around the belly button  
- A short time later, nausea and vomiting  
- Loss of appetite

After a few hours, the pain moves to the lower right side of the belly.  
The pain gets worse when you cough, move, or stretch.

Common signs doctors look for:

- Tenderness in the lower right belly, especially at a spot called the McBurney point  
  (This is the spot halfway between your belly button and the front of your hip bone.)

Other signs include:

- Pain in the lower right belly when the doctor presses on the left lower belly (Rovsing sign)  
- Pain when the doctor straightens your right leg while it is bent (psoas sign)  
- Pain when the doctor turns your bent leg inward (obturator sign)

A mild fever is common.  
Your rectal temperature may be between 37.7 and 38.3 degrees Celsius (100 to 101 degrees Fahrenheit).

Many people do not have the classic symptoms.  
More than half of patients have different or unclear signs.

In babies and young children, the pain may not stay in one place.  
Tenderness may be spread out or even missing.  
Bowel movements may be less frequent or stop.  
If you have diarrhea, the appendix may be behind the large intestine.

Sometimes, blood cells show up in the urine.

Older adults and pregnant women often have milder symptoms.  
Their pain may be less intense.  
Tenderness may be less obvious.

---

## How Is Appendicitis Diagnosed?

Doctors start by asking about your symptoms and doing a physical exam.

If the symptoms are clear, they may go straight to surgery.  
Waiting for imaging tests can increase the risk of the appendix breaking open.

If the symptoms are unclear or not typical, imaging tests are needed quickly.

- A CT scan is very accurate for diagnosing appendicitis.  
  It can also show other causes of belly pain.  
- Ultrasound is another option.  
  It is fast and does not use radiation.  
  This is especially good for children.  
  But it can be hard to use if there is gas in the intestines.  
  It is also less helpful for finding causes other than appendicitis.

Appendicitis is mainly diagnosed by symptoms and exam.  
Using imaging tests only when needed helps avoid unnecessary surgery.

Laparoscopy (a small camera through a tiny cut) can be used to both diagnose and treat appendicitis.  
It is especially useful in women with unclear lower belly pain.

Blood tests often show a higher white blood cell count.  
But this is not always true.  
A normal blood count does not rule out appendicitis.

---

## How Is Appendicitis Treated?

The main treatment is surgery to remove the appendix.

You will also get fluids through a vein and antibiotics.

There are two types of surgery:

- Open surgery: A single cut in the belly  
- Laparoscopic surgery: Several small cuts and a camera

Delaying surgery increases the risk of death.  
A 15% chance of removing a healthy appendix is considered acceptable.

The surgeon can usually remove the appendix even if it has broken open.  
Sometimes, the appendix is hard to find.  
It may be hidden behind the large intestine or nearby tissues.

There are some cases where surgery is not safe.  
If you have Crohn disease affecting the large intestine, surgery may be avoided.  
But if only the last part of the small intestine is affected and the large intestine is healthy, the appendix should still be removed.

Before surgery, you will get antibiotics through a vein.  
A type called a third-generation cephalosporin is preferred.

- If the appendix is not broken, no more antibiotics are needed after surgery.  
- If the appendix has broken open, antibiotics are given for 4 days after surgery.  
- If surgery is not possible, antibiotics alone can help you survive, even though they do not cure the problem.

Some studies have tried treating appendicitis with antibiotics only.  
Many patients get better during the hospital stay.  
But many later have a return of symptoms and need surgery within a year.

Because of this, surgery is still the best choice.  
This is especially true if a hard piece of stool (appendicolith) is seen on a CT scan.

If a large infected mass is found involving the appendix, the end of the small intestine, and the large intestine, removing the whole mass and reconnecting the intestines is best.

In later cases, if an abscess has already formed, the abscess is drained.  
This can be done using a needle guided by ultrasound or through open surgery.  
The appendix is removed later, after the infection is under control.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Without treatment, appendicitis can be deadly.

With early surgery, the death rate is less than 1% in areas with good medical care.  
Most people recover quickly and fully.

If the appendix breaks open or if there is an abscess or infection in the belly, the outcome is worse.  
Older age also makes recovery harder.

---

## Key Points

- If you have classic symptoms and signs, go straight to surgery. Do not wait for imaging tests.  
- If your symptoms are unclear, get a CT scan or, for children, an ultrasound.  
- Give a third-generation cephalosporin before surgery.  
- If the appendix has broken open, continue antibiotics after surgery.

# Varicella Vaccine (Chickenpox Vaccine)

This vaccine helps protect you from chickenpox.  
Chickenpox is a very contagious illness caused by a virus.  
It causes an itchy rash with small blisters on a red base.  
In some people, the virus can spread to the brain, lungs, or heart.  
This can lead to serious illness or even death.  
After you recover from chickenpox, the virus stays in your body.  
Years later, the virus can come back and cause shingles.

---

## Types of Varicella Vaccine

There are two types of varicella vaccine:

- Standard dose varicella vaccine  
- Combination vaccine that protects against measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella (MMRV)

Both vaccines contain a weakened form of the chickenpox virus.  
The virus is weak enough that it cannot cause chickenpox.  
But it is strong enough to help your body learn how to fight the real virus.  
This is called active immunization.

---

## When and How the Vaccine Is Given

The vaccine is given as a shot under the skin.  
It is a routine childhood vaccine.  
Children need two doses:

- First dose at 12 to 15 months of age  
- Second dose at 4 to 6 years of age

Children between 12 months and 12 years old may get the MMRV vaccine.  
This one shot protects against measles, mumps, rubella, and chickenpox.

People 13 years old and older who have never had chickenpox or the vaccine should get two doses.  
The two doses must be at least 4 weeks apart.

You should get two doses of the vaccine if you do not have proof of immunity and are likely to come into contact with chickenpox. This includes:

- Health care workers  
- People who live with someone who has a weak immune system  
- Teachers, child care workers, and people who work in group settings  
- People in schools, prisons, or military service  
- Women who could become pregnant  
- Teens and adults who live with children  
- International travelers

Do not get the vaccine if you had a serious allergic reaction to a past dose.  
This includes reactions like trouble breathing, swelling, or a rash.  
You should also not get it if you are allergic to neomycin, gelatin, or any other part of the vaccine.

The vaccine is not given to:

- Pregnant people  
- People with a weak immune system  
- People who have a parent, brother, or sister with immune system problems  
- People with cancer of the bone marrow or lymph system

You may not get the vaccine if you:

- Are taking certain antiviral medicines (acyclovir, famciclovir, or valacyclovir)  
- Recently received blood products  
- Have a moderate or severe illness right now

If you are sick, your doctor may wait until you feel better before giving the vaccine.

Children with HIV should not get the MMRV vaccine.  
But if their HIV is well-controlled with medicine, they can get the standard varicella vaccine.

Some health conditions may affect when or if you can get the vaccine.  
Check with your doctor if you are unsure.

---

## Side Effects of the Vaccine

The varicella vaccine is very safe.  
Most side effects are mild.

Common side effects include:

- Pain at the injection site  
- Swelling at the injection site  
- Redness at the injection site

A few people may get a mild rash that looks like chickenpox.  
If this happens, avoid close contact with people who have a weak immune system.  
Stay away until the rash is completely gone.

Do not give aspirin or similar medicines (salicylates) to children under 16 years old for 6 weeks after the vaccine.  
These medicines can cause a rare but serious illness called Reye syndrome.

For more details on side effects, read the package insert that comes with the vaccine.

---
