# Muscular Dystrophy – Simple Explanation

## What Is Muscular Dystrophy?

Muscular dystrophy is a condition that causes muscles to weaken over time.  
This weakness gets worse as you grow older.  
It can make it hard to walk, climb stairs, or lift things.  

There are many types of muscular dystrophy.  
Each type causes different symptoms.  
Symptoms can start at different ages.  
The speed at which symptoms get worse also varies.  

Muscular dystrophy is caused by a change in a gene.  
Genes are like instructions in your body.  
A changed gene can lead to muscle problems.  

Sometimes, the changed gene is passed from parent to child.  
But sometimes, a person is born with the changed gene even if their parents do not have it.  

Muscular dystrophy affects each person differently.  
It can make moving around harder.  
It can also affect how long you live.  
This depends on the type and how it affects your body.  

There is no cure for muscular dystrophy.  
But treatments can help you manage your symptoms.  
Different types need different treatments.  

---

## Symptoms of Muscular Dystrophy

The main symptom is muscle weakness.  
It gets worse over time.  

Symptoms can start at any age.  
Some types start in childhood.  
Others start in adulthood.  

Common signs include:  
- Trouble walking  
- Difficulty lifting objects  
- Falling more often than usual  
- Muscle pain  
- Stiff joints  

In young children, you might notice:  
- Floppy arms or legs  
- Taking longer to crawl or walk than other children  

---

## Types of Muscular Dystrophy

There are many types.  
The type you have affects:  
- What symptoms you have  
- How bad they are  
- When they start  
- How fast they get worse  

The most common type is Duchenne muscular dystrophy.  
It usually starts in early childhood.  
It mainly affects boys.  
It gets worse quickly.  

---

## What Causes Muscular Dystrophy?

Muscular dystrophy is a genetic condition.  
This means it is caused by a change in a gene.  
Different genes cause different types.  

The changed gene can come from a parent.  
Or it can happen by chance when you are born.  

If someone in your family has muscular dystrophy, you can get tested.  
This test checks if you have the changed gene.  

---

## How Muscular Dystrophy Affects Your Life

No two people are affected the same way.  
All types can make movement harder.  
How much it affects you depends on the type.  

Many people will need help moving.  
This might include using a wheelchair.  

Some types can also affect other parts of the body.  
This includes the heart, lungs, and spine.  

Muscular dystrophy can affect your life span.  
This depends on how severe your symptoms are.  
Your care team can talk to you about this.  

---

## Treatment for Muscular Dystrophy

There is no cure.  
But treatment can help you live better.  

You will work with a team of health experts.  
They will help you based on your type and symptoms.  

### Medical Treatments

You may have:  
- Physiotherapy to help with movement and ease pain  
- Medicines to slow the condition, such as steroids  
- Special medicines for heart problems, like ACE inhibitors or beta blockers  
- A pacemaker if your heart is affected  
- Surgery for spine problems like scoliosis or tight joints  
- A breathing machine if your lungs are weak  

### Support for Daily Life

You may also get help with everyday tasks.  
This support depends on your needs.  

You might need:  
- Occupational therapy to help with daily activities  
- Mobility aids like walking sticks, frames, or wheelchairs  
- Home changes like stair lifts or handrails  
- Help at home, school, or work  

---

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:  
- You or your child have signs of muscular dystrophy  
- You are worried about your child’s development  
- You are pregnant or planning a pregnancy  
- A family member has muscular dystrophy  

---

## Help and Support

You are not alone.  
Your care team will support you through treatment.  

You may also find comfort in talking to others with the same condition.  
Parents of children with muscular dystrophy can also share their experiences.  

There are charities that offer help and information.  

### Muscular Dystrophy UK

This charity supports people with muscular dystrophy and other muscle conditions.  
It also helps families and carers.  

- Website: [www.musculardystrophyuk.org](https://www.musculardystrophyuk.org)  
- Helpline: Call for advice and support  
- Support groups: Meet others with the condition  
- Peer support: Connect with people who understand your experience  

### Other Organisations

Other groups that offer help include:  
- Pathfinders Neuromuscular Alliance – for people with muscle weakness  
- Duchenne UK – for people with Duchenne muscular dystrophy and their families

# What Is Dementia?

Dementia is a long-term condition that slowly gets worse over time.  
It affects your thinking, memory, and ability to do everyday tasks.  
It is usually not reversible.  

Doctors diagnose dementia by talking to you and checking your mental and physical health.  
Tests like blood work and brain scans help rule out treatable causes.  
There is no cure, but treatment can help you live better.  
Some medicines may improve thinking and memory, depending on the type of dementia.

Dementia can happen at any age, but it mostly affects older adults.  
It is the main reason people move into nursing homes.

---

## Types of Dementia

Dementia can be grouped in different ways:

- Alzheimer disease or other types  
- Affects the outer brain layer (cortical) or deeper brain areas (subcortical)  
- Cannot be reversed or might be treatable

Do not confuse dementia with delirium.  
They are different, even though both affect thinking.

| Feature | Dementia | Delirium |
|--------|----------|----------|
| Main problem | Memory loss | Trouble paying attention |
| Cause | Brain damage from disease | Sudden illness, infection, or medicine side effects |
| Onset | Slow, over months or years | Fast, over hours or days |
| Reversible? | Usually not | Often yes, if treated quickly |

Other differences are listed in the table *Differences Between Delirium and Dementia*.

---

## What Causes Dementia?

Dementia can come from brain diseases or other health problems.

The most common types are:

- Alzheimer disease  
- Vascular dementia  
- Dementia with Lewy bodies  
- Frontotemporal dementia  

Dementia can also happen in people with:

- Parkinson disease  
- Huntington disease  
- Progressive supranuclear palsy  
- Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease  
- Gerstmann-Sträussler-Scheinker syndrome  
- Other prion diseases  
- Neurosyphilis (a brain infection from syphilis)  
- HIV infection  
- Brain injury (like repeated head hits in sports)  
- Certain brain tumors  

Some people have more than one type of dementia at the same time.  
The most common mixed type is Alzheimer disease with vascular dementia.

Some conditions can cause slow brain decline that may get better with treatment.  
These include:

- Normal-pressure hydrocephalus (fluid buildup in the brain)  
- Subdural hematoma (bleeding on the brain)  
- Low thyroid function (hypothyroidism)  
- Low vitamin B12 levels  
- Poisoning from lead or other toxins  

Some experts do not call these "dementia" because they can be fixed.  
But others use the term "reversible dementia" for these cases.

---

### Depression Can Look Like Dementia

Depression can cause memory and thinking problems.  
It used to be called "pseudodementia."  
Depression and dementia often happen together.  
Sometimes, depression is the first sign of dementia.

---

### Normal Aging and Memory Changes

As people get older, they may forget things more easily.  
They may take longer to remember names or details.  
This is normal and does not mean dementia.  
It does not stop people from doing daily tasks.

But early dementia can look very similar to normal aging.

---

### Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI)

MCI means memory and thinking are worse than expected for your age.  
But you can still do daily tasks.  
People with MCI are more likely to develop dementia.  
Up to half of them will get dementia within three years.

---

### Subjective Cognitive Decline (SCD)

SCD means you feel your memory or thinking is getting worse.  
But tests show your brain function is normal.  
People with SCD are more likely to develop MCI or dementia later.

---

### Things That Make Dementia Worse

Other health problems can make dementia symptoms worse.  
These include:

- Diabetes  
- Lung diseases like chronic bronchitis or emphysema  
- Infections  
- Kidney or liver disease  
- Heart failure  

Medicines can also make symptoms worse.  
This includes:

- Benzodiazepines (like some sleeping pills)  
- Anticholinergics (like some antidepressants, allergy medicines, or antipsychotics)  
- Alcohol, even in small amounts  
- Recreational drugs  

Kidney or liver problems can cause medicine to build up in the body.  
This can lead to side effects, even if you’ve taken the same dose for years.

---

### How Brain Diseases Spread

Some brain diseases spread slowly over time.  
A normal brain protein changes shape and becomes harmful.  
This harmful protein then causes other proteins to change shape too.  
This process can take years and affect many parts of the brain.  
The damaged proteins build up and are hard for the body to clear.

This spreading process may happen in:

- Alzheimer disease  
- Parkinson disease  
- Huntington disease  
- Frontotemporal dementia  
- ALS (a motor neuron disease)  

These harmful proteins are not as contagious as those in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.  
But they can still spread under certain conditions.

---

### Rapidly Progressive Dementia (RPD)

RPD means symptoms get much worse in 1 to 2 years.  
It is not the same as typical dementia.

Main symptoms include:

- Memory loss  
- Trouble with language or seeing things clearly  
- Poor planning or decision-making  

Other signs may include:

- Mood changes  
- Personality shifts  
- Hallucinations or delusions  
- Sleep problems  
- Confusion or drowsiness  
- Uncontrolled movements (like shaking or jerking)  
- Walking problems  
- Seizure-like events  
- Loss of balance  
- Parkinson-like symptoms  

The most common cause of RPD is prion disease.  
Other causes include:

- Autoimmune brain diseases  
- Paraneoplastic syndromes (linked to cancer)  
- Rare cases of Alzheimer disease, Lewy body dementia, frontotemporal dementia, or treatable causes (like infections or toxins)

---

## Classification of Some Dementias

| Cause | Examples |
|------|----------|
| Amyloid and tangles in brain | Alzheimer disease |
| Abnormal tau protein | Chronic traumatic encephalopathy, corticobasal degeneration, frontotemporal dementia, progressive supranuclear palsy |
| Abnormal alpha-synuclein protein | Dementia with Lewy bodies, Parkinson disease dementia |
| Autoimmune brain disease | Autoimmune dementia, post-encephalitis syndromes |
| Genetic mutation (Huntingtin gene) | Huntington disease |
| Blood vessel problems in brain | Binswanger disease, lacunar disease, multi-infarct dementia, strategic single-infarct dementia, CADASIL, CARASIL |
| Drug or toxin exposure | Alcohol-related dementia, heavy metal poisoning |
| Infections | Cryptococcosis (fungal), syphilis or Lyme disease (spirochetal), HIV |
| Paraneoplastic disorders | Cancer-related brain disease |
| Prion diseases | Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, some cases of Alzheimer, Parkinson, and frontotemporal dementia |
| Brain structure problems | Brain tumor, subdural hematoma, normal-pressure hydrocephalus, adult-onset leukodystrophies, multiple sclerosis |
| Treatable conditions | Depression, low thyroid, vitamin B12 deficiency |

---

## Symptoms of Dementia

Dementia affects thinking and memory in many ways.  
Symptoms start slowly.  
Family members may not notice at first.  
They may only notice when daily tasks become hard.

The first sign is often trouble remembering recent events.  
Early symptoms can look like normal aging or mild cognitive impairment.  
But over time, the problems get worse and clear.

Symptoms can be grouped into stages:

- Early  
- Middle  
- Late  

Personality changes and behavior problems can happen at any stage.  
Motor problems (like walking or movement issues) depend on the type of dementia.  
In vascular dementia, these problems often appear early.  
In Alzheimer disease, they usually come later.

Seizures are more common in people with dementia than in the general population.

Psychosis (seeing things that are not there, believing false things, or feeling paranoid) affects about 20% to 50% of people with dementia.  
The chance depends on the type and how far the disease has progressed.

Other health problems can make dementia worse.  
These include diabetes, lung disease, infections, kidney or liver disease, and heart failure.

Drinking alcohol, even in small amounts, can make dementia worse.  
It can shrink brain tissue over time.  
Most doctors recommend stopping alcohol if you have dementia.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Dementia

Doctors use several steps to diagnose dementia:

1. Talk to you and your family about symptoms  
2. Do a physical and brain exam  
3. Check mental function with simple tests  
4. Run blood tests and brain scans to rule out treatable causes  
5. Sometimes use detailed brain function tests (neuropsychological testing)

It is hard to know the exact type of dementia without looking at brain tissue after death.  
So, doctors focus on:

- Telling dementia apart from delirium and other conditions  
- Finding which parts of the brain are affected  
- Looking for causes that can be treated

---

### How Doctors Tell Dementia from Other Conditions

**Delirium:**  
This is a sudden change in thinking.  
It is often caused by illness, infection, or medicine.  
It can be fixed if treated fast.  
Doctors check attention first.  
Poor attention is a strong sign of delirium.  
But advanced dementia also causes poor attention.

# Cluster Headaches

Cluster headaches cause intense pain on one side of the head. The pain is usually around the eye or temple. It lasts from 30 minutes to 1 hour, but can be as short as 15 minutes or as long as 3 hours.

These headaches come with other symptoms. You may have a stuffy or runny nose. Your eye on the same side may water. Your eyelid may droop. Your face may look red. Some people also feel sick to their stomach.

The headaches happen in cycles. They often start suddenly and happen many times a day. They usually occur at the same time each day or night. A cycle can last 1 to 3 months. After that, you may have no headaches for months or even years.

Some people do not have a break between attacks. They have chronic cluster headaches.

Alcohol can trigger a headache during a cycle. But it does not cause headaches when you are not in a cycle.

## Who Gets Cluster Headaches?

Cluster headaches are rare. About 4 out of every 1,000 people in the United States get them. Men are more likely to have them than women. Most people first get them between the ages of 20 and 40.

## What Do Cluster Headaches Feel Like?

- The pain starts fast. It is very strong.
- It begins on one side of the head.
- It often starts with a stuffy or runny nose on one side.
- The pain spreads around the eye.
- It gets worse quickly and reaches its peak in just a few minutes.
- The pain often wakes you up from sleep.
- You cannot lie down. You may walk back and forth. Some people hit their head against a wall.

After the pain goes away:
- The eyelid on the same side may droop.
- The pupil in the eye may get smaller. This is called Horner syndrome.
- The area under the eye may swell.
- The eye may water.
- The face may look red.
- You may feel sick to your stomach.

## How Do Doctors Diagnose Cluster Headaches?

Your doctor will ask you about your symptoms. They will want to know:
- Where the pain is.
- How long it lasts.
- How often it happens.
- What other symptoms you have.

They will also check for other possible causes of your headaches. If your symptoms are not typical, they may do tests to rule out other problems.

## How Are Cluster Headaches Treated?

There are two main goals:
1. Stop a headache as soon as it starts.
2. Prevent future headaches.

### Treatments to Stop a Headache

These treatments work best when used at the first sign of pain.

- **Oxygen therapy**: You breathe in pure oxygen through a mask. This helps stop the headache.
- **Medicines**: A shot of a triptan or dihydroergotamine can help. These are medicines used for severe headaches.
- **Zolmitriptan**: This is a type of triptan. It can be taken as a pill or nasal spray.

Another option is **vagus nerve stimulation**. This is a noninvasive way to help control pain.

- You place a small handheld device on your neck.
- You feel a pulse in your neck. Place the device over that spot.
- The device sends a mild electric signal through your skin.
- The signal travels to the vagus nerve.
- The nerve sends a message to your brain to help reduce pain.

### Treatments to Prevent Future Headaches

Because cluster headaches are so painful and frequent, doctors often prescribe medicine to stop them from happening.

The following medicines may be used:
- **Prednisone**: A steroid taken by mouth. It works fast.
- **Nerve block**: A local anesthetic and steroid are injected into the back of your head. This is done in the doctor’s office.
- **Migraine prevention medicines**: These include divalproex, topiramate, valproate, and verapamil. They are taken every day.
- **Lithium**: A medicine that helps prevent attacks.
- **Monoclonal antibodies**: Such as galcanezumab. These are given as a shot.

**How these medicines are used:**
- Prednisone or a nerve block is often used first. They work quickly.
- Then, another medicine is used for long-term prevention.
- The nerve block must be done in the doctor’s office.
- All other treatments can be done at home.

## Important Notes

- Cluster headaches are not the same as migraines.
- You may need to try different treatments to find what works best.
- Always follow your doctor’s instructions.
- Do not stop taking medicine without talking to your doctor.

# Temporomandibular Disorder (TMD)

TMD is a condition that affects the jaw joint and the muscles around it. It can cause pain and other problems with your jaw.

## Symptoms of TMD

You may have TMD if you notice any of these:

- Pain around your jaw, ear, or temple
- Clicking, popping, or grinding sounds when you move your jaw
- Headaches, especially around your temples
- Trouble opening your mouth fully
- Your jaw locks in place when you try to open it

The pain may get worse when you chew. Stress can also make the pain worse.  
TMD can also make it hard to sleep well.

## When to Seek Urgent Help

Call 111 or get help online right away if you have:

- Trouble eating or drinking
- Loud clicking, popping, or grinding in your jaw
- Your jaw locks or you cannot open your mouth fully
- Pain in your jaw, ear, or side of your head
- Frequent or very bad headaches
- Pain or tenderness on the side of your head or scalp
- Vision problems, like double vision or losing sight in one or both eyes

These signs could mean you have a serious problem that needs fast treatment.

## How to Help Yourself

TMD often gets better on its own. But you can do things to feel better.

### Do These Things

- Eat soft foods like pasta, eggs, and soup
- Take paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain
- Use an ice pack or heat pack on your jaw. Wrap it in a tea towel first. Use whichever feels better
- Gently massage the sore muscles in your jaw
- Try to relax. Find ways to calm your mind and body

### Avoid These Things

- Do not chew gum or bite on pens or pencils
- Do not use your front teeth to bite hard food
- Do not yawn too wide
- Do not bite your nails
- Do not clench your teeth. Keep your teeth apart unless you are eating

## What a Doctor Might Suggest

Your doctor may recommend:

- Stronger painkillers if over-the-counter ones do not help
- Relaxation techniques to reduce stress
- Tips to help you sleep better

They might also suggest seeing other specialists:

- A dentist, if you grind your teeth at night
- A psychologist, if stress or anxiety is making your pain worse
- A physiotherapist, for jaw exercises and massage

If these treatments do not help, your doctor may refer you to a joint specialist. They can talk to you about other options, such as injections or surgery.

## What Causes TMD

TMD can happen for several reasons:

- Grinding your teeth, especially at night
- Worn-out joint tissue from long-term use
- A hit to the head or face
- High levels of stress
- A bite that is not even (your teeth do not line up properly)

# Pelvic Pain During Early Pregnancy

Pelvic pain is common in early pregnancy. It can be caused by serious or minor health problems. Some of these problems also cause vaginal bleeding. In some cases, the bleeding can be very heavy. This can lead to a dangerous drop in blood pressure and shock.

Pain in the upper belly or throughout the belly has similar causes in pregnant and non-pregnant people.

## What Can Cause Pelvic Pain?

Pelvic pain in early pregnancy can come from:

- Problems related to the pregnancy
- Gynecologic issues (problems with the female reproductive organs)
- Other medical conditions not related to the reproductive system
- Sometimes, no clear cause is found

### Most Common Pregnancy-Related Causes

- Normal changes in the body during pregnancy
- A miscarriage (also called spontaneous abortion). This can be:
  - Threatened (bleeding but the pregnancy may continue)
  - Inevitable (miscarriage will happen)
  - Incomplete (some tissue remains in the uterus)
  - Complete (all tissue has passed)
  - Missed (the baby has died but no tissue has passed)
  - Septic (infected tissue remains in the uterus)

The most serious pregnancy-related cause is a **ruptured ectopic pregnancy**. This happens when a pregnancy grows outside the uterus, usually in a fallopian tube. If the tube bursts, it can cause heavy bleeding.

### Gynecologic Causes

- **Ovarian torsion**: The ovary twists on itself. This is more likely during pregnancy because the ovary gets larger due to a hormone-producing structure called the corpus luteum.
- **Degenerating fibroid**: A non-cancerous growth in the uterus can break down and cause sudden, severe pain.
- **Ruptured corpus luteum cyst**: A fluid-filled sac on the ovary bursts, causing sharp pain.
- **Pelvic inflammatory disease**: An infection in the reproductive organs. This is rare during pregnancy.
- **Ovarian tumors**: These can be benign or cancerous. They may cause dull pain, bloating, or weight loss.
- **Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome**: This can happen after fertility treatments. It causes swelling, fluid buildup, and other serious symptoms.

### Other Common Causes

- **Appendicitis**: Inflammation of the appendix. The pain may be in an unusual spot because the growing uterus pushes the appendix up.
- **Urinary tract infection**: Infection in the bladder or kidneys. It causes burning, frequent urination, and sometimes fever.
- **Inflammatory bowel disease**: A long-term condition that causes belly pain, diarrhea, and sometimes blood in the stool.
- **Bowel obstruction**: Blockage in the intestines. It causes severe cramps, vomiting, and no bowel movements.
- **Gastroenteritis**: A stomach bug. It causes vomiting and diarrhea.

In late pregnancy, pelvic pain can also be caused by labor, other pregnancy complications, or the same non-pregnancy-related causes.

---

## How Is Pelvic Pain Evaluated?

If you have pelvic pain during early pregnancy, your doctor will check for serious conditions. These include:

- Ectopic pregnancy
- Septic abortion
- Appendicitis

Your doctor will:

- Check your vital signs (like blood pressure and heart rate)
- Do a physical exam
- Listen to the baby’s heartbeat
- Use ultrasound to look at the uterus and pelvis
- Run blood tests and urine tests

If needed, you may have more tests like MRI or CT scans.

---

## How Is Pelvic Pain Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause.

### Ectopic Pregnancy

- If the pregnancy is not ruptured, you may get a medicine called methotrexate.
- Or, you may have surgery to remove the pregnancy.
- If the tube has burst, you need emergency surgery right away.

### Miscarriage

- **Threatened miscarriage**: No treatment is needed. You may take pain medicine.
- **Inevitable, incomplete, or missed miscarriage**: You may take medicine to help the body pass the tissue. Or, you may have surgery to remove the tissue.
- **Septic miscarriage**: You need surgery to remove the tissue and antibiotics through a vein.

### Other Causes

- **Ruptured corpus luteum cyst** or **fibroid degeneration**: Pain medicine is usually enough.
- **Ovarian torsion**: Surgery is needed. If the ovary is still healthy, the doctor will untwist it. If it is damaged, the ovary or fallopian tube may need to be removed.

---

## Important Facts to Know

- Pelvic pain in early pregnancy should always make you think of ectopic pregnancy.
- Even if the pain seems minor, it could be a sign of a serious problem.
- If you have no clear cause for your pain, an ultrasound is usually needed.
- If you had a recent abortion or uterine procedure and now have fever, pain, or discharge, it could be a septic abortion.
- All pregnant women should have their blood type checked early in pregnancy.
- If you are Rh-negative and have vaginal bleeding or an ectopic pregnancy, you should get a shot called Rho(D) immune globulin. This prevents your body from making harmful antibodies.

---

## Summary

- Pelvic pain in early pregnancy is common but should never be ignored.
- Many causes are treatable, especially if found early.
- Always see a doctor if you have pelvic pain, especially with bleeding or fever.
- Early diagnosis and treatment can prevent serious harm to you and your baby.

# Erythema Multiforme

Erythema multiforme is a skin condition that causes red, raised patches. These patches often look like targets. They usually appear on both sides of the body at the same time.

## What Causes Erythema Multiforme?

Most cases are caused by a reaction to an infection. The most common infection is the herpes simplex virus. This virus also causes cold sores on the lips.

Some people get cold sores a few days before the rash appears.

Other causes include:
- Bacterial infections, such as *Mycoplasma*
- Certain medicines
- Vaccines
- Other viruses, especially hepatitis C
- Some autoimmune diseases, like systemic lupus erythematosus

Doctors do not fully understand how this condition starts. But they think the immune system plays a role. In some cases, no clear cause can be found.

## Symptoms

The rash appears suddenly. It starts as red bumps on the arms, legs, face, palms, and soles.

The red patches grow larger. They often have a pale ring inside and a purple or gray center. These are called target or iris lesions.

Small blisters may form in the rash. The patches may not hurt. But some people feel itching or a burning sensation.

Painful blisters often form on the lips and inside the mouth. Rarely, blisters can form in the eyes.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors look at the rash. They can usually tell it is erythema multiforme by its unique shape and pattern.

Sometimes it can look like a more serious condition called Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Doctors watch the person closely to make sure the diagnosis is correct.

## Treatment

Most people get better without treatment. The rash usually goes away in 2 to 4 weeks.

Some people have only one attack. Others have repeated attacks. Recurrences are more common if the cause is herpes simplex virus. Over time, attacks often become less frequent.

### Relief for Symptoms

If the rash itches, you can use:
- Creams or lotions with corticosteroids
- Antihistamine pills
- Numbing creams or sprays on the skin

If mouth blisters make eating hard:
- A numbing liquid like lidocaine can be used inside the mouth.
- If you cannot eat or drink enough, you may need fluids and nutrition through a vein (IV).

### Preventing Future Attacks

If you have frequent attacks and your doctor thinks herpes simplex virus is the cause, you may benefit from antiviral medicine.

Medicines like acyclovir, famciclovir, or valacyclovir can help. Take them at the first sign of a new outbreak.

Treating any underlying infection can also help prevent future episodes.

# Dysentery

## What is dysentery?

Dysentery causes diarrhoea that has blood and sometimes clear slime in it.  
You may also have a high temperature and tummy pain.  
These symptoms can last up to 7 days.

## When to get help

Call your GP or NHS 111 right away if:
- You or your child has diarrhoea with blood in it.

Tell the doctor if you have recently been abroad.

You can call 111 or get help online.

## What causes dysentery?

Dysentery spreads when you swallow poo from someone who is infected.  
This can happen through:
- Dirty water
- Food that has been handled by someone with dysentery
- Oral or anal sex with an infected person

## How is dysentery treated?

Your doctor may give you antibiotics, depending on what is causing the illness.  
You will need to give a poo sample so the doctor can find the cause.  
If your symptoms are very bad, you may need to go to hospital.

## How to feel better at home

Dysentery usually gets better on its own in about a week.  
The most important thing is to stay hydrated.

After seeing a doctor, you can help yourself by:
- Drinking plenty of water
- Making sure you pee regularly during the day
- Not feeling thirsty
- Using oral rehydration sachets mixed with water
- Eating when you feel ready – you do not need to avoid any foods

Do not take anti-diarrhoea medicine.  
It can make the illness worse.

## How to avoid catching or spreading dysentery

Wash your hands often with soap and water.  
Do this:
- After using the toilet
- Before preparing food or eating

Wash clothes, towels, or bedding that have poo on them in hot water.  
Clean toilet seats, taps, door handles, and flush handles every day.  
Use a condom on the penis or a dental dam during oral sex.  
Stay away from work, school, or nursery for at least 48 hours after your diarrhoea stops.

## How to stay safe when travelling

If you are going to a place with unsafe water, follow these steps:

### Do:
- Drink only bottled water or boiled tap water
- Brush your teeth with bottled or boiled water
- Wash your hands with soap and water after using the toilet and before eating or preparing food

### Do not:
- Eat ice cream or drink anything with ice
- Eat raw fruit or vegetables unless you washed them yourself with bottled or boiled water

# Induced Abortion – Simple Explanation

## About Abortion in the United States

- About half of all pregnancies in the United States are not planned.
- Of these unplanned pregnancies, about 4 out of 10 end in induced abortion.
- Most abortions happen in the first three months of pregnancy.

## Laws and Safety

- Each state has its own rules about abortion.
- These rules can include waiting periods or limits based on how far along the pregnancy is.
- In countries where abortion is legal, it is usually safe and complications are rare.
- Worldwide, unsafe abortions cause about 1 in 8 maternal deaths.
- Most of these deaths happen in places where abortion is illegal.

## Confirming Pregnancy

- You must be sure you are pregnant before having an abortion.
- Doctors often use an ultrasound to check how far along the pregnancy is.
- In early pregnancy, doctors may also use your medical history and a physical exam to estimate the pregnancy stage.
- If you are in the second trimester and have certain risk factors, such as a low-lying placenta or a scar from a past surgery on the uterus, more testing may be needed.

## Checking That the Abortion Is Complete

- The abortion is complete if the doctor sees the pregnancy tissue come out.
- Or, the doctor can use ultrasound during the procedure to check.
- If ultrasound is not used, blood tests can confirm the abortion is done.
- A blood test measures a hormone called beta-hCG.
- If the level drops by more than half within one week, the pregnancy is gone.

## Medicines and Care After the Procedure

- Antibiotics are given on the day of the abortion to prevent infection.
- These help fight infections like chlamydia.
- Doxycycline is a common antibiotic used.
- A dose of 200 milligrams is given before the procedure.
- Women with Rh-negative blood get a shot called Rho(D) immune globulin after the abortion.
- This shot helps protect future pregnancies.

## Pain Relief and Sedation

- First-trimester abortions usually only need local numbing medicine.
- Some doctors can also give sedation to help you relax.
- Later abortions usually need deeper sedation or general anesthesia.

## Starting Birth Control

- You can start any kind of birth control right after the abortion.
- This is true if the pregnancy was less than 28 weeks along.

## How Abortion Is Done

There are two main ways to end a pregnancy:

1. **Surgical method** – The doctor opens the cervix and removes the pregnancy tissue using suction or instruments.
2. **Medication method** – You take pills that cause the uterus to contract and empty.

The method used depends on how far along the pregnancy is.

### Surgical Method

- This method works for most pregnancies.
- For early pregnancies (under 14 weeks), doctors usually use suction curettage (suction D & C).
- For pregnancies between 14 and 24 weeks, doctors use dilation and evacuation (D & E).
- Before the procedure, the cervix is gently opened using medicine or small rods (like laminaria).

### Medication Method

- Pills can be used for pregnancies under 11 weeks.
- For these, you take mifepristone first, then misoprostol later.
- For pregnancies over 15 weeks, you take mifepristone first, then a prostaglandin medicine.
- Prostaglandins can be given in the vagina, under the tongue, or by injection.
- If you take the pills after 11 weeks, you should stay at the clinic for a while.
- This is because heavy bleeding can happen.

### Rare Surgery

- In very rare cases, a woman may need surgery to remove the pregnancy.
- This is called hysterotomy or hysterectomy.
- These surgeries are only used when other methods fail.
- They carry higher risks and can cause scarring in the uterus.
- This scar may break open in future pregnancies.

## Possible Complications

### Early Complications (Right After the Procedure)

- Very rare, but possible:
  - A small hole in the uterus (0.1%).
  - A rare injury to the intestines or other organs.
  - Heavy bleeding (0.06%).
  - This can happen from injury or if the uterus does not contract well.
  - A tear in the cervix (0.1% to 1%).
    - Most tears are small and heal on their own.
    - Some may need stitches.
- Anesthesia is safe for most people.
- Serious problems from anesthesia are very rare.

### Delayed Complications (Days or Weeks Later)

- Bleeding or infection (0.1% to 2%).
- These usually happen if some placenta stays behind.
- If you bleed heavily or feel sick, your doctor may do an ultrasound.
- The ultrasound can show if any tissue is still in the uterus.
- Mild swelling is normal.
- But if infection gets worse, it can spread to the belly lining or bloodstream.
- This can lead to serious illness.
- Scarring inside the uterus (Asherman syndrome) or blocked tubes from infection can cause infertility.
- Forcefully opening the cervix in later pregnancies may lead to a weak cervix.
- But with gentle methods and proper care, abortion does not raise the risk of problems in future pregnancies.

## Emotional Health

- Most women do not have serious emotional problems after an abortion.
- But some may feel upset if:
  - They had mental health issues before the pregnancy.
  - They felt strongly attached to the pregnancy.
  - They have little support from family or friends.
  - They feel judged by others.

## Key Points

- About 4 out of 10 unplanned pregnancies end in abortion.
- The two main methods are surgery (after opening the cervix) or medicine (to cause contractions).
- Always confirm pregnancy first.
- Use history, exam, or ultrasound to find out how far along the pregnancy is.
- For early surgery: use suction curettage (under 14 weeks).
- For later surgery: use dilation and evacuation (14 to 24 weeks).
- Open the cervix first with medicine or small rods.
- For medicine abortion under 11 weeks: take mifepristone, then misoprostol.
- For medicine abortion over 15 weeks: take mifepristone first, then a prostaglandin medicine.
- Serious complications (like uterine hole, heavy bleeding, or serious infection) happen in less than 1 out of 100 abortions.

# Finger Fractures

Finger fractures often happen when the fingertip is crushed. Two common types are avulsion fractures and crush fractures.

## What Happens in a Crush Injury?

- The fingertip becomes sore and swollen.
- The nail may turn blue-black and bulge upward.
- The skin under the nail (called the nail bed) can tear.
- The injury is very painful.
- After healing, the nail may stay bent or misshapen.

Sometimes, the area stays extra sensitive even after the bone has healed. This is called increased sensitivity.

## What Is an Avulsion Fracture?

- A tendon or ligament pulls off a small piece of bone.
- This often happens when something snaps or jerks the finger hard.

## How Do Doctors Know If a Finger Is Broken?

- If you think your finger is broken, see a doctor.
- The doctor will take x-rays from different angles to check for a break.
- X-rays help show the exact location and type of fracture.

## How Are Finger Fractures Treated?

### For Most Fractures

- Doctors wrap the fingertip in a protective covering.
- This can be a splint made of aluminum and foam.
- You wear it for about two weeks.

### For Blood Under the Nail

- If a lot of blood collects under the nail, it can cause pressure and pain.
- The doctor may make a tiny hole in the nail to drain the blood.
- This is called trephination.
- A needle or a heated tool is used.
- The hole is very small and the procedure takes just seconds.
- You may need to remove nail polish first.
- Pain medicine is usually not needed.

### For Severe Fractures

- If the bone is broken into many pieces, surgery may be needed.
- Surgery helps line up the bone pieces correctly.
- If the nail is badly damaged, the doctor may remove it.
- This allows the doctor to fix any tears in the nail bed.
- After repair, the finger is wrapped in a dressing to protect it.

### Do You Always Need to Remove the Nail?

- No. Most finger fractures do not require nail removal.
- The nail often stays in place unless it is severely damaged.

Always follow your doctor’s advice for care and healing.

# Atrial Fibrillation – Simple Guide

Atrial fibrillation is a condition where the heart beats in an irregular and often fast way.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may notice:
- Your heartbeat feels uneven or irregular.
- Your heart suddenly pounds, races, flutters, skips, or misses a beat. This is called palpitations.
- Your heart beats faster than 100 times per minute.
- You feel very tired.
- You find it harder to do physical activity.
- You have chest pain or tightness.
- You feel short of breath, dizzy, lightheaded, or like you might faint.

Some people have no symptoms at all. The condition may be found during a routine check-up or when testing for another issue.

Symptoms can come and go on their own. Or they may stop after treatment. Over time, some people always have symptoms.

## When to See a Doctor

Call your doctor if:
- You think you might have atrial fibrillation.
- You keep having heart palpitations, or they are getting worse.
- You already have atrial fibrillation, but your treatment is not helping.

## When to Call 999 (Emergency)

Call 999 right away if you have a fast or irregular heartbeat and any of these:
- Chest pain.
- Trouble breathing.
- Sweating.
- Feeling sick or being sick.
- Fainting, dizziness, or falling over.
- A severe headache.
- Weakness or numbness on one side of your face or body.
- Blurred vision or loss of sight.
- Confusion or trouble speaking.

### Important: A&E Safety Message
Do not drive yourself to the emergency department.  
The person you speak to on 999 will tell you what to do.

## How Is Atrial Fibrillation Treated?

You will have regular check-ups to make sure your symptoms are under control.

Your doctor may give you medicine to:
- Slow down your heart rate.
- Help your heart beat in a more normal rhythm.
- Reduce the risk of blood clots or stroke.

Other treatments may include:
- A procedure to burn or freeze a small part of the heart (ablation).
- A shock of electricity to reset your heart rhythm (electrical cardioversion).
- A device implanted under the skin to help control your heart rhythm (pacemaker or ICD).

If another health problem or medicine is causing your atrial fibrillation, treating that issue may help improve your symptoms.

## What Causes Atrial Fibrillation?

Atrial fibrillation happens when the heart’s electrical system does not work properly.

You can get it at any age, but you are more likely if:
- You are 55 or older.
- You are a man.
- You are overweight or have obesity.
- You smoke.
- You take certain medicines, such as levothyroxine, lithium, or some asthma medicines like salbutamol.
- You do long-distance running, cycling, or skiing.

It can also be caused by other health conditions, such as:
- High blood pressure.
- Heart failure.
- Problems with the mitral valve.
- Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.
- A heart attack.
- Chronic kidney disease.
- An overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism).
- Diabetes.
- Sleep apnoea.

## What Tests Are Done?

If your doctor thinks you have atrial fibrillation, they will refer you to a heart specialist.

At your appointment, the doctor will:
- Ask about your symptoms.
- Check your heart rate.

You may also have tests to:
- Rule out other causes.
- Check your heart rhythm.

These tests can include:
- An electrocardiogram (ECG) – a test that records the electrical activity of your heart.
- An echocardiogram (echo) – a scan that uses sound waves to show how your heart is working.
- A chest X-ray – to look at your heart and lungs.
- Blood tests – to check for other health problems.

## Support and Help

Living with a heart condition can be worrying. You are not alone.

You may find it helpful to:
- Join a local support group.
- Connect with others online who have atrial fibrillation.

### British Heart Foundation
Offers information and support for anyone affected by heart conditions.

- Website: [www.bhf.org.uk](https://www.bhf.org.uk)
- Heart Helpline: Call, email, or chat online with a cardiac nurse.
- Online community: Meet others with heart conditions.
- Support with everyday life: Practical advice and tools.

### MyHeart
Support for young people with heart conditions and their families.

- Website: [www.myheart.org.uk](https://www.myheart.org.uk)
- Helpline: 01737 363222

You can get help and feel more in control. Reach out to these groups when you need support.

# Hepatitis D – Simple Explanation

Hepatitis D is a liver infection caused by a virus. This virus cannot grow on its own. It needs another virus, called hepatitis B, to survive and spread.

Hepatitis D can happen in two ways:
- At the same time as a new hepatitis B infection (called coinfection).
- In someone who already has a long-term hepatitis B infection (called superinfection).

## How Hepatitis D Spreads

The virus spreads through contact with infected blood or body fluids. This can happen through:
- Sharing needles or syringes.
- Unprotected sex.
- Accidental needle sticks.
- From mother to baby during birth.

The virus lives in liver cells. These cells have a coating made of hepatitis B proteins.

Hepatitis D is not common everywhere. It is more common in some parts of the world, especially in certain countries. People who use drugs by injection are at higher risk. Unlike hepatitis B, hepatitis D is not common among men who have sex with men.

## What Symptoms to Watch For

Hepatitis D often causes more serious problems than hepatitis B alone. Symptoms depend on the type of infection:

- If you get hepatitis D at the same time as hepatitis B, your illness may be much worse than usual.
- If you already have a long-term hepatitis B infection, getting hepatitis D can suddenly make your symptoms much worse.
- If you have long-term hepatitis B, adding hepatitis D can make the disease progress faster and more severely.

## How Doctors Diagnose Hepatitis D

Doctors use blood tests to check for hepatitis D.

If you have signs of a sudden liver problem, your doctor will first rule out other causes of jaundice (yellow skin or eyes).

To check for viral hepatitis, your doctor will test your blood for:
- Antibodies to hepatitis A (IgM anti-HAV).
- Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).
- Antibodies to hepatitis B core (IgM anti-HBc).
- Antibodies to hepatitis C (anti-HCV) and hepatitis C RNA (HCV RNA).

If the test shows you have hepatitis B and your symptoms are severe, your doctor will test for hepatitis D antibodies (anti-HDV). A positive result means you are currently infected. These antibodies may not show up right away — sometimes it takes weeks after the illness starts.

## How Hepatitis D Is Treated

There is no cure for acute hepatitis D. Treatment focuses on helping your body recover.

- Do not drink alcohol. It can make liver damage worse.
- You do not need to stay in bed or follow a special diet. These are not proven to help.

For long-term hepatitis D, the main treatment is a medicine called interferon-alfa. A longer-acting version, pegylated interferon-alpha, may work just as well. Treatment usually lasts one year. It is not clear if longer treatment helps more.

Another medicine, bulevirtide, is available in Europe for treating hepatitis D. It is also being studied in clinical trials.

Hepatitis B and hepatitis D are treated separately. You must treat hepatitis B on its own.

## How to Prevent Hepatitis D

There is no vaccine to prevent hepatitis D.

But you can prevent hepatitis D by preventing hepatitis B. The hepatitis B vaccine protects against both viruses.

## Key Facts

- Hepatitis D only happens if you already have hepatitis B.
- Think about hepatitis D if your hepatitis B symptoms are very bad or getting worse.
- Treat and prevent hepatitis D the same way you treat and prevent hepatitis B.

# Bullous Pemphigoid

Bullous pemphigoid is a skin condition that causes large, itchy blisters.  
It happens when the body’s immune system attacks the skin by mistake.  
The immune system usually protects the body from germs.  
But in this condition, it wrongly targets the skin.  
This leads to blisters and red, swollen skin.

## Who Gets Bullous Pemphigoid?

- It mostly affects people over age sixty.  
- It can also happen in children, but this is rare.  
- It is not as serious as another blistering disease called pemphigus vulgaris.  
- It is not usually life-threatening.  
- It does not cause the skin to peel off in large areas.  
- Still, it can affect a large part of the body.  
- It can cause a lot of discomfort.

## What Causes Bullous Pemphigoid?

The exact cause is not known.  
But some things may trigger it, including:  
- Certain medicines: furosemide, spironolactone, sulfasalazine, antipsychotic drugs, penicillin, penicillamine, and etanercept.  
- Radiation therapy for breast cancer.  
- Exposure to strong sunlight (ultraviolet radiation).  
- Skin problems like psoriasis or lichen planus.  
- Some other health issues: diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, ulcerative colitis, and multiple sclerosis.

## Symptoms of Bullous Pemphigoid

- Itching is often the first sign.  
- Blisters may not appear for years.  
- Before blisters form, large, raised patches may show up.  
- These patches can look like hives.  
- The blisters are large, tight, and very itchy.  
- They are usually surrounded by normal skin or red, inflamed skin.  
- The blisters do not usually break open.  
- If they do break, they heal quickly.

### Where Do Blisters Appear?

- On skin that bends, such as the backs of the knees, underarms, insides of the elbows, and groin.  
- On skin that has been injured.  
- On the anus or genitals.  
- On the lower legs.  
- On skin near a stoma (an opening in the belly for waste to pass out).  
- A rare form affects the hands and feet. It can look like hand and foot dermatitis.  
- Blisters in the mouth are very rare.

### Photos of Bullous Pemphigoid

- Blisters, sores, and crusts on the arm.  
- Blisters and red, swollen skin on the foot.  
- Tight blisters, raw areas where blisters peeled off, and dark spots on the arm.  
- Blisters, sores, and crusts on the arm.

*(Photos show typical signs of the condition.)*

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- Doctors often recognize bullous pemphigoid by the look of the blisters.  
- But it can be hard to tell apart from other blistering skin diseases.  
- A skin biopsy is needed for a clear diagnosis.  
- A small sample of skin is taken from near a blister.  
- The sample is checked under a microscope.  
- Doctors look at which layer of skin is affected.  
- They also check for specific antibody deposits.  
- This helps confirm the diagnosis and rule out other conditions.

## How Is It Treated?

- Treatment aims to stop the immune system from attacking the skin.  
- It also helps reduce blisters and itching.

### First-Line Treatments

- Strong steroid creams like clobetasol are applied directly to the skin.  
- These creams can help reduce the need for pills.  
- For widespread blisters, a steroid pill called prednisone is used.  
- The dose is slowly lowered over time (called tapering).  
- Most people feel better in 2 to 10 months.  
- But treatment may need to continue for several years before stopping.

### Other Treatment Options

- A mix of nicotinamide and minocycline or tetracycline may help.  
- Dapsone, sulfapyridine, or erythromycin may be used alone.  
- Immune globulin given through a vein is used in some cases.  
- For severe cases that do not respond to other treatments, stronger drugs may be used.  
  - Methotrexate  
  - Azathioprine  
  - Mycophenolate mofetil  
  - Rituximab  
  - Omalizumab  
  - Cyclophosphamide

### Skin Care Tips

- Keep the affected skin clean to prevent infection.  
- Wear loose-fitting clothes to avoid irritation.  
- Most people do not need to stay in the hospital for treatment.

## Outlook

- Bullous pemphigoid is a long-term condition.  
- Medicines help control symptoms.  
- But medicines can cause side effects.  
- With treatment, most people feel better within months.  
- Some people need treatment for several years.

# Shin Splints

Shin splints cause pain and soreness in the front of your lower leg.  
This usually happens when you run or do other physical activity.  

The pain often goes away with rest and care.  
Most people feel better within a few weeks.

---

## What You Can Do to Feel Better

You can take steps to help your shin splints get better faster.

### Do These Things

- Take painkillers like paracetamol or ibuprofen.  
  You can use ibuprofen gel on your skin or take ibuprofen tablets if needed.  
- Put an ice pack on your shin for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours.  
  Use a bag of frozen vegetables wrapped in a towel if you don’t have an ice pack.  
- Switch to gentle activities like swimming or yoga while your leg heals.  
- When you start exercising again, do it on soft ground if possible.  
- Always warm up before you exercise.  
- Always stretch after you exercise.  
- Make sure your shoes support your feet well.  

### Do Not Do These Things

- Do not keep doing the exercise that caused the pain.  
- Do not go back to your old level of exercise too quickly.  
  Build up slowly over time.

---

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:

- You’ve tried rest and other steps to help.  
- But the pain is getting worse or not improving.

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and check your leg.  
If your shin splints are not getting better, your doctor may refer you to a physiotherapist.

---

## When to Get Help from NHS 111

Call NHS 111 or get help online if:

- Your pain is very bad.  
- You’ve hurt your shin in an accident.

You can call 111 or visit the NHS 111 website for help.

---

## Physiotherapy

Physiotherapy can help with shin splints.  
It is free on the NHS across the UK.  
But waiting times can be long.  
You can also get physiotherapy privately.

---

## Self-Referral for Help

You may be able to refer yourself directly to a physiotherapy or treatment service without seeing a doctor first.

To find out if this is possible in your area:

- Ask the staff at your GP surgery.  
- Check your GP surgery’s website.  
- Contact your local integrated care board.  
  Find your local board online.  
- Search online for “NHS treatment for shin splints near me.”

# Food Allergy

A food allergy happens when your body’s immune system overreacts to a food, usually a protein. This reaction can cause many different symptoms. Some people have skin rashes. Others have stomach or breathing problems. In rare cases, a food allergy can cause a life-threatening reaction called anaphylaxis.

## What Causes Food Allergies?

Almost any food can cause an allergy. But the most common triggers are:

- **In babies and young children:** Milk, soy, eggs, peanuts, and wheat.
- **In older children and adults:** Nuts and seafood.

Some people react to foods because they are also allergic to pollen. For example, eating apples or carrots can cause itching in the mouth if you are allergic to birch pollen. Some children with peanut allergy were first exposed to peanut oil in creams used for skin rashes. People who are allergic to latex may also react to bananas, kiwis, or avocados.

Food allergies are more common in children if a parent has a food allergy, hay fever, or asthma.

There are three main types of food allergies:

- **IgE-mediated allergies:** These cause fast reactions. Symptoms appear within minutes. They often start in infancy. They are linked to a family history of allergies.
- **T-cell-mediated allergies:** These cause slow, long-lasting symptoms. They often affect the stomach and intestines. They are most common in babies and young children.
- **Mixed allergies (IgE and T cells):** These reactions can be delayed or last a long time. They may cause skin rashes or stomach problems.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on the food, the type of allergy, and the age of the person.

- **Babies:** The most common sign is a skin rash (atopic dermatitis). This may come with stomach issues like nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
- **Children:** Many outgrow early symptoms. Over time, they may develop asthma or hay fever. This pattern is called the "atopic march."
- **Older children and adults:** Allergic reactions tend to be more serious. They may include hives, swelling, or anaphylaxis. Some people have a reaction only if they eat certain foods and then exercise soon after. The reason is not known. Some people also feel dizzy or faint after eating.

Certain symptoms may be linked to food allergies, such as:
- Cracked lips
- Mouth sores
- Stomach spasms
- Constipation
- Itching around the anus
- Skin irritation around the anus

T-cell-mediated allergies often cause stomach problems. These include:
- Ongoing or repeated belly pain
- Nausea
- Cramps
- Diarrhea

> **Tip:** If someone has ongoing stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, cramps, or diarrhea with no clear cause, think about food allergy.

## How Is Food Allergy Diagnosed?

Diagnosis starts with a detailed history of symptoms and what foods were eaten. Tests may include:

- **Allergen-specific blood test:** This checks for allergy antibodies in the blood.
- **Skin test:** A small amount of food is placed on the skin. The skin is then lightly pricked. A reaction shows a possible allergy.

A positive test does not always mean you are allergic. Both tests can give false results. Skin tests are faster and more sensitive, but they can give false positives more often.

If a test is positive, the food is removed from the diet. If symptoms go away, the food is slowly added back in a controlled way. This is called an oral challenge. It helps confirm the allergy.

If skin tests are not available or results are unclear, doctors may use:

- A food diary: Write down everything you eat and any symptoms. This helps find possible triggers.
- An elimination diet: You stop eating certain foods for a while. You only eat foods that are allowed. If symptoms improve, you slowly add back one food at a time.

> **Important:** Only test for foods that caused a reaction. Testing for many foods at once is not helpful and can lead to unnecessary food restrictions.

When using an elimination diet:
- Eat only the foods on the approved list.
- Use only pure, unprocessed foods. Many packaged foods contain hidden allergens.
- If no improvement happens in one week, try a different diet. T-cell allergies can take weeks to improve.

When adding back a food:
- Start with a small amount.
- Watch for symptoms for more than 24 hours.
- If symptoms return, the food is likely a trigger.

> **Note:** If symptoms come back after adding a food, this is the best sign of a true allergy.

### Sample Elimination Diets

| Food | Diet 1 (No beef, pork, fowl, milk, rye, corn) | Diet 2 (No beef, lamb, milk, rice) | Diet 3 (No lamb, fowl, rye, rice, corn, milk) |
|------|-----------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| Cereal | Rice products | Corn products | None |
| Vegetables | Artichokes, beets, carrots, lettuce, spinach | Asparagus, corn, peas, squash, string beans, tomatoes | Beets, lima beans, potatoes (white and sweet), string beans, tomatoes |
| Meats | Lamb | Bacon, chicken | Bacon, beef |
| Flour | Rice | Corn, 100% rye (regular rye bread has wheat) | Lima bean, potato, soybean |
| Fruits | Grapefruit, lemons, pears | Apricots, peaches, pineapple, prunes | Apricots, grapefruit, lemons, peaches |
| Fat | Cottonseed oil, olive oil | Corn oil, cottonseed oil | Cottonseed oil, olive oil |
| Beverages | Coffee (black), lemonade, tea | Coffee (black), lemonade, tea | Coffee (black), lemonade, juice from approved fruit, tea |
| Miscellaneous | Cane sugar, gelatin, maple sugar, olives, salt, tapioca pudding | Cane sugar, corn syrup, gelatin, salt | Cane sugar, gelatin, maple sugar, olives, salt, tapioca pudding |

> **If symptoms continue** after trying the above diets, a doctor may recommend an elemental diet. This uses special formulas made from broken-down proteins and nutrients. It is used only when other diets do not help.

## How Is Food Allergy Treated?

The main treatment is to avoid the food that causes the reaction.

- **For severe allergies:** Carry antihistamines to take at the first sign of a reaction. Always carry an epinephrine auto-injector. Use it if symptoms are serious, such as trouble breathing or swelling.
- **Antihistamines** help only with hives or swelling. They do not stop serious reactions.
- **Oral cromolyn** may help reduce allergic reactions to food.
- **Corticosteroids** are used for long-term treatment of certain stomach problems caused by food allergies.
- **Budesonide** (a type of steroid) is used to treat a condition called eosinophilic esophagitis in adults and children 11 years and older.
- **Immunotherapy** (oral or under-the-tongue) may help some people become less sensitive to certain foods.
- **Monoclonal antibodies** like omalizumab and dupilumab can help prevent severe allergic reactions.

> **Note:** Treatment plans are personalized. Work closely with your doctor.

## How Can Food Allergies Be Prevented?

For many years, doctors advised parents to avoid giving babies common allergens like peanuts. But new research shows that giving peanuts early can actually prevent peanut allergy in high-risk babies (those with eczema or egg allergy).

Current guidelines say:
- Do not delay introducing common allergens.
- Start adding foods like eggs and peanuts at about 4 to 6 months of age.
- This applies even to babies at higher risk.

## Key Points

- Food allergies are often caused by IgE (fast reactions) or T cells (slow, ongoing stomach issues).
- Do not confuse food allergies with other problems like lactose intolerance, irritable bowel syndrome, or food poisoning.
- If the allergy is not clear, use skin tests, blood tests, or an elimination diet.
- In an elimination diet, only eat foods on the list. Avoid processed foods unless they are safe.
- Other treatments include cromolyn, immunotherapy, and special antibodies.

# Paranasal Sinus Cancer

This is cancer that starts in the air-filled spaces around the nose. It most often begins in the maxillary or ethmoid sinuses.

## What Are the Sinuses?

The sinuses are air-filled spaces in the bones around your nose. They help lighten your skull and humidify the air you breathe.

- This type of cancer is rare in the United States.
- It is more common in Japan and among some groups in South Africa.
- Doctors do not know exactly what causes it.
- Smoking tobacco increases the risk.
- Breathing in certain types of wood dust or metal dust over time may also raise the risk.
- In some cases, the human papillomavirus (HPV) or Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) may be involved.
- Doctors do not believe long-term sinus infections cause this cancer.

> *For more information, see: Overview of Mouth, Nose, and Throat Cancers.*

## Where Are the Sinuses?

[Video showing the location of the sinuses]

[3D model showing the sinuses]

## Symptoms of Paranasal Sinus Cancer

Cancer in the sinuses can press on nearby parts of the face and nose. This causes symptoms such as:

- Pain in the face or head
- Feeling like one side of your nose is blocked
- Seeing double
- Frequent nosebleeds
- Ear pain or a feeling of fullness in the ear
- Numbness or tingling in the face
- Loose upper teeth near the affected sinus

Most people do not notice symptoms until the cancer is large. This is because the sinuses are hollow spaces. Early cancers can grow there without pressing on nearby tissues.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use two main methods to find and confirm the cancer:

1. **Imaging tests**  
   These include CT scans and MRI scans. They help doctors see the size and location of the tumor.

2. **Biopsy**  
   A doctor takes a small sample of tissue. They look at it under a microscope to check for cancer cells.

Doctors often use a thin, flexible tube with a camera (called an endoscope) to see inside the nose. They can use this tool to take a biopsy or remove small tumors.

## What Is the Outlook?

- The earlier the cancer is treated, the better the chance of recovery.
- Overall, about 60 out of 100 people with this cancer live at least 5 years after diagnosis.
- However, many people are diagnosed at a later stage, which makes treatment harder.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment usually includes a mix of surgery and radiation therapy.

- **Surgery**  
  Doctors can remove some tumors through the nose using an endoscope. This method helps protect the eye and other facial features. It leads to better appearance and function after surgery.

- **Radiation therapy**  
  This is often given after surgery if there is a high chance the cancer will come back.

- **Chemotherapy**  
  This may be used before or instead of surgery if the tumor is too large or in a hard-to-reach spot.

# Group B Strep

## What is Group B Strep?

Group B strep is a type of bacteria. It is common in pregnancy. Most women carry it without any problems. It does not usually harm you or your baby.

But there is a small chance it can pass to your baby during labour. This can make your baby sick.

## How Is It Treated?

If you have group B strep, you may get antibiotics during labour. This can greatly lower the chance your baby gets sick.

Your baby may need to be watched closely after birth. This helps catch any problems early.

## Signs of Infection in Babies

If your baby has group B strep, they may show signs like:

- Being very floppy or not moving much  
- Not reacting to sounds or touch  
- Having trouble breathing  
- Having a fever or being very cold  

Most babies get better completely with treatment. But some babies can get very sick. Serious problems can include blood infection (sepsis) or brain infection (meningitis).

These serious infections can cause long-term issues. These may include hearing loss or vision problems. In rare cases, they can be life-threatening.

## When to Get Help Right Away

Call 999 or go to A&E if your baby shows any of these signs:

- Being floppy or not responding  
- Breathing with grunts or working hard (you can see their chest or stomach moving a lot)  
- Breathing too fast or too slow  
- Temperature that is too high or too low  
- Skin that looks pale, blue, or blotchy  
- Not feeding well or bringing up milk  
- Heart beating too fast or too slow  

Your baby may need antibiotics in hospital right away.

> **Find your nearest A&E**

### Safety Tips for Going to A&E

- Do not drive yourself. Ask someone to take you.  
- Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
- Bring all your medicines with you.

---

## Group B Strep in Pregnancy

Group B strep is common. It usually does not cause any harm.

It is not tested for in most pregnancies. But it might be found by accident during other tests, like a urine test or a swab from the vagina.

### Risks During Pregnancy

If you have group B strep while pregnant:

- Your baby will likely be healthy  
- There is a small chance the bacteria can pass to your baby during labour  
  - This happens in about 1 in every 1,750 births  
- There is a very small chance of miscarriage or losing your baby  

### What Should You Do If You're Worried?

Talk to your midwife or doctor. They can explain the risks to your baby.

Ask if you should get tested. 

Routine testing is not recommended on the NHS. This is because group B strep is very common. Testing does not always predict if your baby will get sick. You can pay for a test privately if you want.

---

## What Happens If You Have Group B Strep?

If you test positive for group B strep, or if you’ve had a baby affected by it before, you may need extra care.

Your midwife may suggest:

- Talking about your birth plan  
- Giving birth in a hospital (this is not always needed)  
- Contacting your midwife as soon as labour starts or your waters break  
- Getting antibiotics through a drip during labour  
  - This can greatly reduce the risk of your baby getting sick  
- Staying in hospital for at least 12 hours after birth  
  - This helps your baby be watched closely  
  - This is not always needed  

---

## Watch for Symptoms After Going Home

Sometimes, signs of group B strep infection can appear up to 3 months after birth.

Look out for:

- Your baby being very floppy or not reacting  
- Grunting when breathing or breathing hard (watch their chest or stomach)  
- Breathing too fast or too slow  
- Temperature that is too high or too low  
- Skin that looks pale, blue, or patchy  
- Not feeding well or bringing up milk  
- Heart beating too fast or too slow  

If you see any of these signs, get help right away.

---

## Risks to Babies

Most babies with group B strep infection get better completely with treatment.

Some babies may get very sick. They can develop:

- Blood infection (sepsis)  
- Brain infection (meningitis)  

These can lead to lasting health problems. These may include:

- Hearing loss  
- Vision loss  

In rare cases, they can be fatal.

# Prostatitis Prostatitis is a condition that affects the prostate gland. It causes problems with urination and pain in the pelvic area. The pain is often in the area between the scrotum and anus. Some people also feel pain in the lower back, testicles, or tip of the penis. There are two main types: - One type is caused by a bacterial infection. - The other type is not caused by bacteria. This type is more common. The exact cause of the non-bacterial type is not fully known. It may be linked to muscle spasms in the pelvic area or problems with how the bladder and pelvic muscles work together. Doctors diagnose prostatitis based on symptoms and tests. They look at urine samples before and after a special prostate exam. They check for signs of infection and inflammation. Treatment depends on the type. --- ## What Causes Prostatitis? ### Bacterial Prostatitis This can be sudden (acute) or long-lasting (chronic). It is usually caused by bacteria that also cause bladder infections. Common bacteria include *E. coli*, *Klebsiella*, *Proteus*, and *Chlamydia*. We do not fully understand how these bacteria get into the prostate. In some cases, bacteria can hide in the prostate and survive antibiotics. This can happen if there are calcium deposits in the prostate. ### Nonbacterial Prostatitis This type is more common. It is not caused by infection. It may be due to muscle spasms in the pelvic floor or problems with how the bladder and pelvic muscles work together. The pressure from this can push urine backward into the prostate. This may cause inflammation or pain, even without infection. --- ## How Prostatitis Is Classified Doctors use a system with four types. The type is based on symptoms and test results from two urine samples. ### How the Tests Work 1. A urine sample is collected mid-stream (first sample). 2. A doctor gently presses on the prostate through the rectum (prostate massage). 3. The first 10 milliliters of urine after the massage is collected (second sample). Tests check for: - White blood cells (a sign of inflammation) - Bacteria (a sign of infection) | Type | Name | Key Features | Urine Test (Before Massage) | Urine Test (After Massage) | |------|------|--------------|-----------------------------|----------------------------| | I | Acute bacterial prostatitis | Sudden symptoms like fever, pain, trouble urinating | White blood cells: maybe present
Bacteria: maybe present | White blood cells: present
Bacteria: present | | II | Chronic bacterial prostatitis | Repeated infections with the same bacteria | White blood cells: maybe present
Bacteria: maybe present | White blood cells: present
Bacteria: present | | III | Chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome | Mainly pain and urinary problems | White blood cells: not present
Bacteria: not present | White blood cells: present (Type IIIa)
Bacteria: not present
White blood cells: not present (Type IIIb)
Bacteria: not present | | IV | Asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis | No symptoms. Found by chance during other tests | White blood cells: not present
Bacteria: not present | White blood cells: present
Bacteria: not present | **Note:** - Type IIIa is called "inflammatory" because white blood cells are found. - Type IIIb is called "noninflammatory" because no white blood cells are found. - The old name "prostatodynia" is no longer used. **+ / −** means the result may be present. **+** means the result is present. **−** means the result is not present. --- ## Symptoms of Prostatitis Symptoms vary by type, but most people have: - Trouble urinating - Frequent need to go - Urgent need to go - Feeling like the bladder is not empty - Needing to go at night - Pain in the pelvic area, lower back, testicles, or tip of the penis - Pain during or after ejaculation ### Type I: Acute Bacterial Prostatitis This comes on fast and is serious. Symptoms include: - High fever - Chills - Body aches - Feeling very unwell - Swollen, tender, or hard prostate This can lead to sepsis — a life-threatening reaction to infection. Signs of sepsis include: - Fast heartbeat - Fast breathing - Low blood pressure ### Type II: Chronic Bacterial Prostatitis This causes repeated infections. Symptoms come and go. They are usually milder than in acute cases. ### Type III: Chronic Prostatitis / Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome Pain is the main symptom. It can be severe and affect daily life. Other symptoms may include: - Pain when urinating - Pain during or after sex - Urinary problems The prostate may feel tender, but it is not swollen or soft. Types IIIa and IIIb look the same on exam. It is found by accident during other tests, like a prostate biopsy or semen analysis. --- ## How Doctors Diagnose Prostatitis ### Urine Tests Doctors check urine for white blood cells and bacteria. They take two samples: one before and one after prostate massage. ### When Prostate Massage Is Not Done It is not done in people with acute bacterial prostatitis. This is because it may spread bacteria into the blood. It may also cause harm, though this is not proven. ### Other Tests - If a person has fever and severe symptoms, blood cultures are done. - If antibiotics do not help, doctors may use imaging tests like ultrasound or CT scans. These check for abscesses or damage to the seminal vesicles. - For long-term cases, doctors may do: - Cystoscopy (a camera in the bladder) - Urine cell test (if blood is in the urine) - Urodynamic tests (to check bladder and muscle function) ### Other Conditions That Can Cause Similar Symptoms - Urethritis (infection in the urethra) - Perirectal abscess (a pus-filled lump near the rectum) - Urinary tract infection --- ## How Prostatitis Is Treated ### Type I: Acute Bacterial Prostatitis - Hospital care is needed if there are signs of sepsis. - Antibiotics are given through a vein.
