This site offers support and information for people with this condition and their caregivers. It includes help finding a doctor, learning about research studies, and joining patient groups.

# Polymyalgia Rheumatica

Most people with polymyalgia rheumatica feel very stiff muscles when they wake up.  
You might also feel very tired.  
You could feel down or sad.  
You may lose your appetite and lose weight.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main symptom is stiff muscles in the morning.  
This stiffness lasts longer than 45 minutes.  

Other possible symptoms include:  
- Feeling very tired  
- Not wanting to eat  
- Losing weight  
- Feeling sad or low  

See your doctor if you have pain and stiffness that lasts more than a week.  
Your doctor will check what is causing your symptoms.

It can be hard to diagnose polymyalgia rheumatica.  
The symptoms are similar to those of other conditions.  
One of these is rheumatoid arthritis.  
Your doctor will check for these other conditions first.  
They will rule them out before confirming a diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica.

## How Is It Treated?

The main treatment is a steroid medicine called prednisolone.  
This medicine helps reduce swelling and pain in your body.  
It eases your symptoms.

You will start with a moderate dose of prednisolone.  
Your doctor will slowly lower the dose over time.  
Most people need to take this medicine for 12 months to 2 years.  
This helps stop the symptoms from coming back.

## What Causes It?

The exact cause of polymyalgia rheumatica is not known.  
Experts think it may be due to a mix of genes and things in your environment.  

This condition is more common in older adults.  
Most people who get it are over 65 years old.  
It is very rare in people under 50.  
Women are more likely to get it than men.

# Infections Caused by Klebsiella, Enterobacter, and Serratia

These bacteria are normally found in the gut. They rarely cause illness in healthy people.

They can cause serious infections in people who are already unwell or have weak immune systems.

## What These Bacteria Can Cause

These bacteria are often found in hospitals. They mainly affect people who are already sick or have medical devices like catheters.

They can cause many types of infections, including:

- Bloodstream infections  
- Infections after surgery  
- Infections from IV lines or catheters  
- Lung infections (like pneumonia)  
- Urinary tract infections (like bladder or kidney infections)  

Some infections can get worse. They may lead to:

- Pockets of pus in the lungs  
- Pus in the space around the lungs  
- Spread of infection into the blood  
- A severe body-wide infection called sepsis  

### Specific Infections

- **Klebsiella pneumonia**: This is a rare but serious lung infection. It often causes thick, dark brown or red jelly-like spit. It is more common in people with diabetes or alcohol use disorder. It can also cause liver abscesses in people who are not in the hospital.

- **Serratia**: This type often causes urinary tract infections. It can also be found in the lungs and in wounds.

- **Enterobacter**: This type most often causes infections in hospitals. It can cause lung, urinary tract, or blood infections. It can also cause ear infections, skin infections, and sepsis in newborns.

## How Doctors Diagnose These Infections

Doctors take a sample of blood or infected fluid or tissue. They grow the bacteria in a lab to confirm the infection.

They also test which antibiotics will work best against the bacteria.

## How These Infections Are Treated

Doctors use antibiotics. The best choice depends on test results.

Common antibiotics include:

- Third-generation cephalosporins  
- Cefepime  
- Carbapenems  
- Fluoroquinolones  
- Piperacillin with tazobactam  
- Aminoglycosides  

But some bacteria are resistant to many antibiotics. So testing is very important.

### Special Cases

- Some *Klebsiella* bacteria make an enzyme called extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL). This enzyme can make certain antibiotics stop working during treatment.  
- Beta-lactamase inhibitors (like tazobactam, clavulanate, vaborbactam, avibactam) can help some of these bacteria respond to treatment.  
- Some *Klebsiella* bacteria make another enzyme called carbapenemase. These are very hard to treat.  
- A type called KPC (carbapenemase-producing *Klebsiella pneumoniae*) has been found around the world. This makes treatment very difficult.  
- Newer antibiotics that include special inhibitors can help. These include:  
  - Ceftazidime with avibactam  
  - Imipenem with relebactam  
  - Meropenem with vaborbactam  
- Other options that may work include:  
  - Eravacycline  
  - Cefiderocol  

### Enterobacter Challenges

- *Enterobacter* bacteria can become resistant to many common antibiotics, including third-generation cephalosporins.  
- They make an enzyme called AmpC beta-lactamase. This enzyme is not blocked by standard beta-lactamase inhibitors.  
- These bacteria may still respond to carbapenems like imipenem, meropenem, doripenem, or ertapenem.  
- Some *Enterobacter* bacteria are resistant to carbapenems too.  
- In these hard-to-treat cases, doctors may use:  
  - Ceftazidime with avibactam  
  - Meropenem with vaborbactam  
  - Imipenem with relebactam  
  - Tigecycline  
  - Eravacycline  
  - Cefiderocol  
  - Possibly colistin

# Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever (RMSF)

Rocky Mountain spotted fever is a serious illness caused by a type of bacteria. It can be deadly if not treated early. The illness spreads through bites from certain ticks.

## How You Get the Disease

- A tick that carries the bacteria bites you.
- The bacteria live inside your body’s cells, especially in blood vessels.
- The disease is not passed from person to person.

## Where It Happens

- It is most common in the southeastern and south central United States.
- These states include North Carolina, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Tennessee, and Missouri.
- It also happens in parts of Central and South America.
- The disease is most likely to occur from March to September.
- In southern states, it can happen all year.

## Who Is at Risk

- People who spend time outdoors in wooded or grassy areas.
- Children under 15 years old are more likely to get it.

## How Ticks Spread the Disease

- Ticks get the bacteria by feeding on infected animals, like mice.
- Female ticks can pass the bacteria to their babies.
- The main ticks that spread the disease are dog ticks and wood ticks.

## Symptoms

Symptoms start 3 to 12 days after a tick bite. They come on fast and can be severe.

### Early Symptoms (First Few Days)
- Severe headache
- Chills
- Extreme tiredness
- Muscle pain
- High fever that lasts 2 to 3 weeks in serious cases
- Dry, hacking cough
- Nausea and vomiting

### Rash (Usually Days 1 to 6)
- Starts on the wrists, palms, ankles, and soles.
- Spreads to the arms, neck, face, armpits, buttocks, and body.
- Begins as flat, pink spots.
- Later turns darker and slightly raised.
- Does not itch.
- Warm water, like a bath, makes the rash easier to see.
- After about 4 days, small purple spots (petechiae) appear due to bleeding under the skin.
- In severe cases, skin may die and turn black. This is called gangrene.

**Note:** Some people do not get a rash at all.

### Later Symptoms (If the Disease Gets Worse)
- Restlessness, trouble sleeping, confusion, or even coma
- Belly pain
- Lung problems, like pneumonia
- Heart damage
- Low blood count (anemia)
- Very low blood pressure
- In rare cases, death

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors look for signs and your history. They do not wait for test results to start treatment.

### What Doctors Check
- Do you live near woods or grassy areas?
- Do you have fever, headache, and muscle pain in spring, summer, or fall?
- Did you have a tick bite? (Many people do not remember.)

### Tests
- A skin sample from the rash is tested using a method called immunofluorescence assay. This helps find the bacteria.
- Blood tests check for antibodies to the bacteria. But these take 7 to 10 days to show results.
- Doctors often repeat the blood test weeks apart to see if antibody levels go up.
- A PCR test can find the bacteria faster than other tests.

**Important:** If doctors suspect RMSF, they start treatment right away—even before test results come back.

## Treatment

### Antibiotics Are Key
- Treatment starts as soon as the disease is suspected.
- Early treatment saves lives.

### The Main Medicine
- Doxycycline is the most common antibiotic used.
- It is taken by mouth if the illness is mild.
- It is given through a vein if the illness is severe.

### How Long to Take It
- Keep taking the medicine until you feel better and have no fever for 24 to 48 hours.
- You must take it for at least 7 days.

### Safety in Children
- Short courses (5 to 10 days) of doxycycline do not harm teeth or enamel in children of any age.
- The American Academy of Pediatrics and other experts support this.
- Long-term use (over 10 days) may stain teeth in children under 8, but short courses are safe.

### Pregnant Women
- Doxycycline is not usually used during pregnancy.
- Talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits.

### No Symptoms After a Tick Bite?
- Doctors do not give antibiotics if you have no symptoms.
- But you should call your doctor right away if symptoms start.

## Prevention

There is no vaccine. The best way to stay safe is to avoid tick bites and remove ticks quickly.

### How to Avoid Tick Bites
- Stay on trails and paths.
- Tuck your pants into your boots or socks.
- Wear long-sleeved shirts.
- Use repellent with DEET on your skin.
  - Use DEET carefully in very young children.
  - Some children have had bad reactions to it.

### Use Permethrin on Clothes
- Spray permethrin on clothing, shoes, and gear.
- It kills ticks on contact.

### Check for Ticks Often
- Look for ticks every day, especially in hairy areas and on children.
- Ticks must be attached for about 24 hours to pass the infection.
- Finding and removing ticks early stops the disease.

### How to Remove a Tick
- Use tweezers or a tick remover.
- Grasp the tick’s head close to the skin.
- Pull straight out slowly and steadily.
- Do not squeeze or crush the tick.
- Clean the bite area with alcohol.
- Do not use petroleum jelly, matches, or heat. These do not work and can cause harm.

### Make Your Yard Less Tick-Friendly
- Remove piles of wood, leaves, and brush.
- Cut tall grass and bushes around your home.
- This makes it harder for mice and other animals to hide.
- Mice carry ticks and spread the disease.

**Bottom Line:**  
- Watch for symptoms after being in tick areas.  
- Get treatment fast if you feel sick.  
- Prevent bites with clothing, repellents, and regular checks.

# Polio – Simple Guide

## What is polio?

Polio is a serious illness caused by a virus.  
The virus spreads through contact with the poo of an infected person.  
It is mainly found in Afghanistan and Pakistan.  

## How does polio spread?

The virus spreads easily from person to person.  
It often spreads when people do not wash their hands after using the toilet.  
Then they touch their mouth or food.  
It can also spread through contaminated food or water.  
It can spread through coughs or sneezes, but this is less common.  

You are very unlikely to get polio in the UK.  
This is because most people are fully vaccinated.  
Polio was stopped in Europe in 2003.  

There is a very small chance of catching it when travelling to countries where polio is still found.  
There is also a very small chance if someone who has been to one of these countries comes back to the UK and is not vaccinated.  

## How can you prevent polio?

The best way to prevent polio is to get vaccinated.  
Children in the UK are routinely vaccinated against polio.  
You can also get vaccinated before travelling abroad.  

## Polio vaccination

The polio vaccine is part of the NHS routine childhood vaccinations.  
Children get the vaccine at:  
- 8 weeks old  
- 12 weeks old  
- 16 weeks old  
- 3 years and 4 months old  
- 14 years old  

You need all five doses to be fully protected.  

You can check your child’s vaccination record in their red book.  
You can also call your GP surgery to check if you or your child are up to date.  

If you are not fully vaccinated, book an appointment with your GP.  
The vaccine is free on the NHS.  

You can get the polio vaccine at any time, even if you are not travelling.  
Even if you have had polio before, you should still get vaccinated.  
This protects you against other types of the virus.  

## Symptoms of polio

Most people who get polio do not have any symptoms.  
Some people have mild symptoms like:  
- A high temperature  
- Feeling very tired  
- Headaches  
- Being sick  
- A stiff neck  
- Muscle pain  

These symptoms usually last up to 10 days.  

In rare cases, polio can cause serious problems.  
This can include weakness or paralysis in the arms or legs.  
This can happen over just hours or days.  

If the muscles used for breathing are affected, it can be life threatening.  

Most people recover over time.  
Movement often returns slowly over weeks.  
But some people are left with permanent disability.  

## What to do if you or your child are unwell

Call 999 or go to A&E if:  
- You or your child cannot move part or all of your body  
- The body part feels stiff, floppy, or numb  
- You or your child are having trouble breathing or feel breathless  

**Find your nearest A&E**

### A&E safety tips

- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you.  
- Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
- Bring all your medicines with you.  

## When to get advice

Call 111 or check your symptoms online if you have flu-like symptoms and:  
- You are worried about a baby or child  
- You are 65 or older  
- You are pregnant  
- You have a long-term health condition (like diabetes, heart disease, lung disease, kidney disease, or a nervous system condition)  
- You have a weak immune system (for example, from chemotherapy or HIV)  
- Your symptoms do not get better after 7 days  

**Check your symptoms on 111 online** or call 111.  

## Treatment for polio

There is no cure for polio.  
But some care can help reduce the risk of long-term problems.  

This may include:  
- Rest in hospital  
- Painkillers  
- Help with breathing  
- Regular stretching and exercises to keep muscles and joints healthy  

If you have long-term problems, you may need:  
- Physiotherapy  
- Surgery  

## Long-term problems from polio

Polio can cause lasting health issues.  
Some people may be permanently paralysed.  
Others may need long-term care and support.  

Long-term problems can include:  
- Weak muscles  
- Stiff joints  
- Trouble swallowing  

If you had polio before, you may get symptoms again later in life.  
This can happen decades after the first illness.  
This is called post-polio syndrome.  
It can make your symptoms worse or cause new ones.

# Cancers That Are More Common in People With HIV

People with HIV are more likely to get certain types of cancer. Some of these cancers are so serious that they are used to diagnose AIDS. These include:

- **Kaposi sarcoma** – A type of skin cancer that causes dark spots on the skin or inside the body.
- **Burkitt lymphoma** – A fast-growing cancer of the lymph nodes.
- **Immunoblastic lymphoma** – A type of lymph node cancer that grows quickly.
- **Lymphoma in the brain or spinal cord** – A cancer that starts in the central nervous system.
- **Invasive cervical cancer** – A cancer of the cervix that has spread beyond the surface.

Other cancers that happen much more often in people with HIV include:

- **Hodgkin lymphoma**, especially the mixed cellularity and lymphocyte-depleted types.
- **Anal cancer** – A cancer of the anus.
- **Testicular cancer** – A cancer in the testicles.
- **Melanoma** – A serious type of skin cancer.
- Other cancers of the skin and the outer part of the eye.

Children with HIV can very rarely get a cancer called **leiomyosarcoma**.

People with HIV also have higher rates of many common cancers. These include:

- Lung cancer
- Cancers of the head and neck
- Cervical cancer
- Liver cancer (called hepatoma)

These higher rates may be due to greater exposure to viruses or harmful substances that cause cancer. For example:

- Hepatitis B and hepatitis C viruses can cause liver cancer.
- Human papillomavirus can cause cervical, anal, penile, and throat cancers.
- Smoking and drinking alcohol increase the risk of lung and head and neck cancers.

(For more information, see the topic on **Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Infection**.)

# Hyperthyroidism – Simple Explanation

Hyperthyroidism means your thyroid gland is overactive. It makes too much thyroid hormone. This speeds up many of your body’s normal functions.

## What Is the Thyroid Gland?

The thyroid gland is a small, butterfly-shaped organ in your neck. It makes hormones that control how fast your body uses energy. These hormones affect your heart, digestion, body temperature, mood, and how you grow.

There are two main thyroid hormones:
- **T4**: Thyroxine
- **T3**: Triiodothyronine

Your pituitary gland, in your brain, makes a hormone called TSH. TSH tells your thyroid how much hormone to make. If your body has too much thyroid hormone, the pituitary slows down TSH. If you have too little, it speeds up TSH.

## Who Gets Hyperthyroidism?

About 1 out of every 100 people in the United States has hyperthyroidism. It is more common in women between the ages of 20 and 50. It can happen at any age, including in babies and older adults.

## Common Causes

### Graves Disease
This is the most common cause. It is an autoimmune disease. Your immune system mistakenly attacks your thyroid. The attack causes the thyroid to make too much hormone. This condition often runs in families. It also causes the thyroid to grow larger.

### Toxic Multinodular Goiter
This happens when many small lumps (nodules) form in the thyroid. One or more of these lumps start making too much hormone. This is more common in older adults.

### Toxic Thyroid Nodule
A single lump in the thyroid makes too much hormone on its own. It does not need TSH to tell it to work. This lump is not cancer, but it can cause hyperthyroidism.

### Thyroiditis
This is inflammation of the thyroid. It can be caused by:
- A virus (subacute thyroiditis)
- Hormone changes after childbirth (silent lymphocytic thyroiditis)
- Long-term autoimmune disease (Hashimoto thyroiditis)

At first, the inflamed thyroid leaks stored hormones into the blood. This causes hyperthyroidism. Later, the hormone supply runs out, and the thyroid becomes underactive (hypothyroidism). In most cases, the thyroid returns to normal.

### Other Causes
- Taking too much thyroid hormone medicine
- Rarely, a tumor in the pituitary gland that makes too much TSH
- Certain medications:
  - Amiodarone (used for heart problems)
  - Interferon-alpha
  - PD-1 inhibitors (like nivolumab and pembrolizumab)
  - Alemtuzumab
  - Lithium (rarely)
- Too much iodine from some cough medicines or contrast dyes used in X-rays

Some rare causes include:
- A problem with the placenta during pregnancy
- A tumor in the ovary that contains thyroid tissue
- Thyroid cancer that has spread

## Symptoms

Most people with hyperthyroidism have a swollen thyroid gland (goiter). The whole gland may be larger, or there may be lumps inside.

Symptoms include:
- Fast heartbeat or irregular heartbeats
- Sweating more than usual
- Feeling nervous or anxious
- Trouble sleeping
- Losing weight even though you eat more
- Shaking hands (tremors)
- More frequent bowel movements, sometimes diarrhea
- Changes in menstrual periods in women

### Older Adults
Older adults may not have the usual symptoms. Instead, they may feel weak, confused, sad, or withdrawn. This is called “apathetic hyperthyroidism.”

Common symptoms in older adults:
- Weight loss
- Fatigue
- Heart problems like irregular heartbeats (atrial fibrillation), chest pain (angina), or heart failure
- Constipation (unusual, but possible)

Some older adults may still sweat a lot, feel nervous, have hand tremors, or have diarrhea.

### Eye and Skin Problems (in Graves Disease)
If Graves disease is the cause, you may notice:
- Puffiness around the eyes
- Eyes that feel dry or irritated
- Sensitivity to light
- Bulging eyes (eyes push forward)
- Double vision (seeing two images)
- Eyelids that do not close all the way

These eye changes happen because the muscles and tissues behind the eyes become inflamed. This can make it hard to move the eyes or keep them aligned.

The skin on the shins may become thick and lumpy, like an orange peel. It can be itchy and hard to touch.

Eye and skin symptoms can start before other signs of hyperthyroidism. They can also get worse even after the thyroid is treated.

## Thyroid Storm – A Medical Emergency

Thyroid storm is a sudden, severe overactivity of the thyroid. It is life-threatening.

Symptoms include:
- Extremely fast heartbeat
- High fever
- Severe weakness
- Restlessness or confusion
- Mood swings
- Altered awareness (even coma)
- Yellow skin or eyes (jaundice)
- Low blood pressure (shock)

Thyroid storm is usually caused by untreated or poorly treated hyperthyroidism. Triggers include:
- Infection
- Injury or surgery
- Poorly controlled diabetes
- Pregnancy or childbirth
- Stopping thyroid medication suddenly

It is rare in children.

Treatment happens in a hospital intensive care unit. Doctors use medicines to block thyroid hormone effects and treat complications like fever or confusion.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will check your symptoms and examine you. They may find a fast heart rate or a swollen thyroid.

Blood tests are used to confirm the diagnosis:
- A low level of TSH means the thyroid is overactive.
- High levels of T4 or T3 confirm hyperthyroidism.
- If Graves disease is suspected, blood tests look for special antibodies that attack the thyroid.

If a nodule is suspected, a thyroid scan may be done. This shows if a lump is making too much hormone.

- In Graves disease, the whole thyroid is overactive.
- In thyroiditis, the scan shows low activity due to inflammation.

## Treatment Options

Treatment depends on the cause and your health.

### Radioactive Iodine
This is the most common treatment. You swallow a pill with radioactive iodine. The thyroid takes it up and destroys part of the gland.

- It is not usually given to pregnant or breastfeeding women.
- You should avoid close contact with infants and young children for 2 to 4 days after treatment.
- Sleep in a separate bed, at least 6 feet away from your partner.
- Avoid pregnancy for 6 to 12 months.
- You may set off radiation alarms at airports. Carry a doctor’s note when traveling.

After treatment, most people need to take thyroid hormone replacement for life. This keeps your body functioning normally.

There is no proven link between radioactive iodine and cancer.

### Beta-Blockers
Medicines like propranolol or metoprolol help control symptoms:
- Slow a fast heart rate
- Reduce shaking
- Ease anxiety

They do not lower thyroid hormone levels. They are used while waiting for other treatments to work.

### Medications to Reduce Hormone Production
- **Methimazole** and **propylthiouracil** are the most common.
- They reduce how much hormone the thyroid makes.
- Methimazole is usually preferred because it is safer for the liver.
- Propylthiouracil may harm the liver in young people.
- Both can cross the placenta. Pregnant women are closely watched. These medicines can cause low thyroid levels or a goiter in the baby.

You take these pills by mouth. Doses start high and are adjusted based on blood tests. Most people see improvement in 2 to 3 months.

### Iodine
Iodine pills are used only in emergencies, like thyroid storm. They are not used long-term.

### Surgery (Thyroidectomy)
Surgery removes part or all of the thyroid gland.

It is used when:
- You are a child or teen with Graves disease
- You have a very large goiter
- You are allergic to or have bad side effects from medicines
- You do not want radiation treatment

More than 90% of people are cured. But most will need thyroid hormone replacement for life.

Risks include:
- Damage to the nerves that control your voice (hoarseness or voice loss)
- Damage to the parathyroid glands (which control calcium levels)

### Special Treatment for Graves Disease Eye and Skin Problems
- Raise the head of your bed to reduce eye swelling
- Use eye drops to keep eyes moist
- Tape eyelids shut at night to prevent dryness
- Selenium supplements may help
- Teprotumumab (a newer medicine) can help with eye bulging
- Diuretics (water pills) may reduce swelling
- Eyeglass prisms can help with double vision
- Steroid pills or eye radiation may be needed for severe eye issues
- Steroid creams can ease itchy, hard skin

Mild eye symptoms often go away on their own over time.

## Key Points

- Hyperthyroidism means your thyroid makes too much hormone.
- It speeds up your body’s functions.
- Graves disease is the most common cause.
- Symptoms include fast heartbeat, weight loss, sweating, anxiety, and tremors.
- Older adults may have different symptoms like fatigue and confusion.
- Eye and skin changes can happen with Graves disease.
- Thyroid storm is a life-threatening emergency.
- Blood tests confirm the diagnosis.
- Treatments include radioactive iodine, medicines, beta-blockers, and surgery.
- Most people need lifelong thyroid hormone replacement after treatment

# Rosacea

Rosacea causes redness and a stinging or burning feeling on your face.  
The redness may come and go.  
It can be harder to see on brown or black skin.

You can manage rosacea with treatments.  
These include creams, gels, or antibiotics.  
You might need to see a skin specialist.

You can also help by avoiding things that make symptoms worse.  
This includes alcohol, spicy food, and harsh skincare products.

---

## See a Doctor If:

- You have symptoms of rosacea

## Call 111 or see a doctor urgently if you have rosacea and:

- Your eye hurts  
- Your vision is blurry  
- Light hurts your eyes  
- Your eye is red  
- Your eye feels gritty  

These could be signs of a serious eye problem called keratitis.  
It needs treatment right away.

---

## Signs of Rosacea

The first signs of rosacea are:

- Redness across your nose, cheeks, forehead, chin, neck, or chest  
- The redness comes and goes, often lasting a few minutes  
- Your face may feel warm, hot, or painful  
- A burning or stinging feeling when you use water or skincare products  

The redness may be harder to see on brown or black skin.

Over time, the redness may stay on your face all the time.  
Tiny broken blood vessels may appear and stay on your skin.  
You may get small pink or red bumps on your face.  
Some bumps may have a yellowish fluid inside.

Other possible symptoms include:

- Dry skin  
- Swelling, especially around the eyes  
- Yellow or orange patches on the skin  
- Sore eyelids or crusts at the base of your eyelashes  
  - This is called blepharitis  
- Thickened skin, mainly on the nose  
  - This usually happens after many years

---

## Things That Can Make Rosacea Worse

We do not know what causes rosacea.  
But some things can make symptoms worse.  
These include:

- Drinking alcohol  
- Eating spicy food  
- Drinking hot drinks  
- Sunlight  
- Hot or cold weather  
- Exercise like running  
- Stress

---

## If You're Not Sure It’s Rosacea

Rosacea can look like other skin problems.  
These include:

- Acne  
- Contact dermatitis  
- Seborrhoeic dermatitis  
- Lupus  
- Keratosis pilaris

---

## Treating Rosacea

There is no cure for rosacea.  
But treatment can help control symptoms.  
Without treatment, rosacea can get worse.

Your doctor may suggest:

- Creams or gels to apply to your skin  
- Antibiotics taken by mouth for 6 to 16 weeks  

If the treatment does not help, your doctor may refer you to a skin specialist.

---

## What You Can Do to Help

Rosacea is not caused by poor hygiene.  
It is not contagious.  
But you can take steps to reduce symptoms.

If you know something like alcohol or spicy food makes your skin worse, avoid it.

### Do:

- Wear sunscreen every day with SPF 30 or higher  
- Try to avoid heat, sunlight, or humid weather  
- Cover your face in cold weather  
- Use gentle skincare products made for sensitive skin  
- Clean your eyelids at least once a day if you have sore eyelids or crusts  
- Manage stress through relaxation, exercise, or talking to someone

### Don’t:

- Drink alcohol  
- Drink hot drinks  
- Eat spicy food  
- Do too much aerobic exercise like running

# Lichen Sclerosus

Lichen sclerosus is a skin condition that causes inflammation.  
The exact cause is not known.  
It may be linked to the body’s immune system attacking its own skin.  
It most often affects the area around the genitals and anus.  

## What It Looks Like

Early signs include:  
- Skin that breaks easily  
- Easy bruising  
- Sometimes blisters  

The skin may feel itchy. The itch can be mild or very strong.  

In children, the skin changes can look like signs of abuse.  
This can cause worry and confusion.  

Over time, the skin becomes thin and weak.  
It may lose color in patches.  
Some areas may turn darker after healing.  
The skin can crack and feel rough.  
Some people develop thick, hard skin or scar tissue.  

In severe or long-term cases, the normal shape of the genitals can change.  
In women, the small lips and clitoris may shrink or disappear.  
In men, the foreskin may tighten or stick to the head of the penis.  

## Images of Lichen Sclerosus

These photos show the changes caused by lichen sclerosus:  
- Thin, pale skin on the labia  
- Pale patches on the head of the penis  
- Scarring and twisted shape around the anus  
- White patches and purple spots on the labia  
- Early fusion of the labia  

These images help show how the condition affects the skin.  
They are from public health resources and medical experts.  

## How It Is Diagnosed

Doctors often recognize lichen sclerosus by how the skin looks.  
This is especially true in later stages.  

A skin sample (biopsy) may be needed.  
This is important if:  
- The skin does not improve with basic treatments  
- The skin becomes thick or develops an open sore  

A biopsy helps rule out other problems.  
It also checks for cancer.  
People with lichen sclerosus have a higher risk of a type of skin cancer called squamous cell carcinoma.  

## How It Is Treated

Treatment uses strong steroid creams applied to the skin.  
These creams reduce inflammation and itching.  
They must be used carefully and as directed.  

The condition does not go away on its own.  
Long-term treatment is needed.  
Regular checkups are important.  

You should be checked for:  
- Skin cancer  
- Problems with sex or intimacy  

Emotional support is also important.  
The condition can affect self-esteem and mental health.  

## Key Facts

- Lichen sclerosus can cause bruising, itching, or blisters early on.  
- Later, the skin becomes thin, weak, and scarred.  
- Think about lichen sclerosus if skin problems in the genital or anal area do not go away.  
- Use long-term, strong steroid creams.  
- Get regular checkups.  
- Get help for emotional or sexual concerns.  
- There is a higher risk of skin cancer over time.

# Atrial Fibrillation and Atrial Flutter

Atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter are fast, irregular heart rhythms. They happen when the upper chambers of the heart (the atria) send out too many electrical signals. These signals make the atria twitch instead of pump normally. Some of these signals reach the lower chambers (the ventricles), making them beat too fast or too irregularly.

These conditions are more common in older adults and people with heart problems. Atrial fibrillation is much more common than atrial flutter. Many people with atrial flutter also have episodes of atrial fibrillation. The rhythms can come and go, or they can last for a long time.

---

## How the Heart Normally Works

The heart has a natural pacemaker. It sends out electrical signals to start each heartbeat. These signals travel through the heart in a clear path.

- The first signal makes the upper chambers (atria) contract.
- Then the signal moves to the lower chambers (ventricles), making them contract.
- After each beat, the heart resets itself for the next beat.

An electrocardiogram (ECG) records these electrical signals. It shows the heart’s activity as waves.

- The **P wave** shows the atria contracting.
- The **QRS complex** shows the ventricles contracting.
- The **T wave** shows the heart resetting.

An ECG can show many problems, including past heart attacks, poor blood flow to the heart, thickened heart walls, or abnormal heart rhythms.

---

## Atrial Fibrillation

In atrial fibrillation, the atria get too many electrical signals at once. These signals come from many places in the atria, not just one. The result is chaos.

- The atria do not pump blood well. They just quiver.
- Because the atria do not help push blood into the ventricles, the heart pumps about 10% less blood than normal.
- This drop in output is usually not a problem unless you already have heart disease.
- Only some of the chaotic signals get through to the ventricles.
- The ventricles beat in a fast and irregular pattern.
- Without treatment, the heart may beat 140 to 160 times per minute at rest. During exercise, it can be even faster.

On an ECG:
- The small waves from the atria are fast, irregular, and messy.
- The larger waves from the ventricles are also irregular.
- The ventricular rate can range from 60 to 150 beats per minute.

---

## Atrial Flutter

In atrial flutter, the electrical signals in the atria are more organized. They move in a loop.

- The atria contract very fast—250 to 350 times per minute.
- But the signals are too fast to all reach the ventricles.
- Usually, every second signal gets through.
- This leads to a ventricular rate of about 150 beats per minute.

On an ECG:
- The small waves from the atria are fast, regular, and look like a sawtooth pattern.
- The larger waves from the ventricles are regular and occur at about 75 beats per minute.

---

## Causes

Atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter can happen even if the heart is otherwise healthy. But they are more common when there are other heart problems, such as:

- High blood pressure
- Coronary artery disease
- Heart valve problems (especially the mitral or tricuspid valves)
- Heavy alcohol use
- Overactive thyroid gland
- A birth defect of the heart

High blood pressure and heart valve problems can cause the atria to grow larger. This makes it easier for abnormal rhythms to start.

---

## Risks and Complications

There are two main risks:

### 1. Blood Clots and Stroke
- The atria do not empty fully during each beat.
- Blood can pool and form clots inside the atria.
- If a clot breaks loose, it can travel to the brain and block a blood vessel.
- This can cause a stroke.
- A stroke can be the first sign of atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter.
- The risk is highest when the rhythm changes back to normal—either on its own or after treatment.

### 2. Poor Heart Pumping
- When the heart beats too fast, the ventricles do not have time to fill with blood.
- This means less blood is pumped out with each beat.
- Blood pressure can drop.
- This can lead to heart failure, especially in older adults or people with heart disease.
- In rare cases, very low blood pressure (shock) can happen.

> **Did You Know?**  
> Because blood can pool in the heart and form clots, atrial fibrillation is a major risk factor for stroke.

---

## Symptoms

Symptoms depend on how fast the heart beats.

- If the heart rate is normal or only slightly fast, you may feel no symptoms.
- If the heart beats too fast, you may feel:
  - Your heart racing or pounding (palpitations)
  - Tiredness or weakness
  - Dizziness or lightheadedness
  - Shortness of breath
  - Chest pain

In atrial fibrillation:
- The pulse is fast and always irregular.

In atrial flutter:
- The pulse is fast and can be regular or irregular.

If the heart does not pump well, you may feel weak, faint, or out of breath. Fast heart rates can cause chest pain or heart failure, especially in older adults or people with heart disease.

---

## Diagnosis

Doctors use several tests to diagnose these conditions.

### Electrocardiogram (ECG)
- This test records the heart’s electrical activity.
- It can show if the rhythm is atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter.

### Echocardiogram (Ultrasound of the Heart)
- This test uses sound waves to create a picture of the heart.
- It checks the heart valves and looks for blood clots in the atria.

### Blood Tests
- These tests check for an overactive thyroid gland, which can cause these rhythms.

---

## Treatment

Treatment has three main goals:
1. Slow down the heart rate.
2. Restore a normal rhythm if possible.
3. Prevent blood clots and stroke.

### 1. Slowing the Heart Rate
- Medications are used to slow the ventricles.
- Common medicines include:
  - Calcium channel blockers (like diltiazem or verapamil)
  - Beta-blockers (like propranolol or atenolol)
  - Digoxin (used if you have heart failure)

These medicines help the heart pump more efficiently.

### 2. Restoring Normal Rhythm
Sometimes the heart returns to normal on its own. But if it does not, doctors may use:

#### Electrical Shock (Cardioversion)
- A controlled electric shock is given to the heart.
- It is timed to avoid dangerous rhythms.
- This method works in 70 to 90% of people.

#### Medications
- Some drugs can help return the heart to a normal rhythm.
- Examples: vernakalant, amiodarone, flecainide, procainamide, propafenone, sotalol.
- These drugs work in about 25% to 65% of people.
- They can cause side effects.

> **Important:** Before cardioversion, doctors must prevent blood clots.  
> - If the rhythm has lasted more than 48 hours, you must take an anticoagulant (like warfarin or a NOAC such as apixaban, edoxaban, rivaroxaban, or dabigatran) for at least 3 weeks.  
> - Or, you may get a short-acting anticoagulant (like heparin) and have an echocardiogram. If no clot is seen, you can have cardioversion right away.  
> - If the rhythm has lasted less than 48 hours, you may not need anticoagulants before cardioversion.  
> - But you will need anticoagulants for at least 4 weeks after the procedure.

### 3. Ablation (A Procedure to Fix the Heart’s Wiring)
This is used when medicines and cardioversion do not work.

#### Ablation of the Atrioventricular Node
- The connection between the atria and ventricles is destroyed.
- This stops most signals from reaching the ventricles.
- The ventricles beat slower.
- But the heart now needs a permanent artificial pacemaker to keep it beating properly.

#### Pulmonary Vein Isolation
- This targets the area near the pulmonary veins in the atria.
- It can stop atrial fibrillation.
- Success rate: 60% to 80%.
- Risk of serious side effects: 1% to 5%.
- Usually only used in younger people with no major heart disease, or when other treatments fail.

#### Ablation for Atrial Flutter
- This procedure blocks the abnormal electrical circuit in the atria.
- It works in about 90% of people.
- It can cure the flutter permanently.

### 4. Preventing Blood Clots (Stroke Prevention)
Most people with atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter need long-term anticoagulants to prevent stroke.

Common anticoagulants:
- Warfarin
- Dabigatran
- Rivaroxaban
- Apixaban
- Edoxaban

> **The decision to use anticoagulants depends on your risk of stroke.**  
> You are at higher risk if you have:
> - Age 65 or older
> - High blood pressure
