# Reactive Arthritis

Reactive arthritis is a condition that causes joint pain and swelling. It happens after an infection, such as food poisoning or a sexually transmitted infection.

## Symptoms

Symptoms usually start 1 to 4 weeks after an infection.

Common signs include:
- Painful, stiff, hot, or swollen joints
- Feeling very tired

The knees and feet are most often affected. But hands, elbows, spine, and tendons around joints can also be involved.

Other possible symptoms:
- Sores in the mouth
- Pain when peeing
- Flaky skin on the palms of your hands or soles of your feet. The skin may have yellow pus underneath.
- A grey or white patchy rash on the penis
- Watery, sticky eyes (this is called conjunctivitis)
- Sore, red eyes that hurt in bright light or are blurry

## When to Seek Help

Call 111 or get help online right away if you have:
- Severe pain and swelling in one joint that started suddenly
- Pain that does not get better with simple painkillers like paracetamol
- Skin around a joint that feels hot or looks red (this may be harder to see on brown or black skin)
- Joint pain with a high temperature or chills
- Joint pain with sore eyes or vision problems
- Joint pain with pain when peeing, discharge from the penis or vagina, or a rash or sores on the genitals

See your GP if:
- You have joint pain and swelling that is new or unusual for you

## Treatment

Reactive arthritis is treated with medicines and other steps to reduce pain and swelling.

Medicines may include:
- Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) to reduce swelling and pain
- Steroids to reduce inflammation
- DMARDs or biological therapies to change how your immune system works
- Antibiotics if the infection that caused the arthritis is still present

Physical therapy, such as physiotherapy, can help keep your joints moving and strong.

Most people get better within 6 months. But for some, symptoms come back. In a few cases, reactive arthritis can lead to long-term joint problems like osteoarthritis or ankylosing spondylitis.

## What You Can Do to Feel Better

You can take steps to ease your symptoms:

### Do:
- Get enough rest, but try to move every day to keep your joints from getting stiff
- Do gentle stretching and strengthening exercises when your joints are not swollen
- Use a cold pack (wrapped in a towel) on sore, swollen joints
- Use a heat pack (wrapped in a towel) on stiff or sore muscles
- Take painkillers as your doctor recommends
- Follow your care team’s advice on what to do if your joint pain suddenly gets worse (this is called a flare-up)

## What Causes Reactive Arthritis

Reactive arthritis can follow an infection in your stomach, like food poisoning, or a sexually transmitted infection such as chlamydia.

Your immune system, which usually fights infections, mistakenly attacks your joints. This causes pain and swelling.

Sometimes the infection was so mild you don’t remember having it before your joint pain started.

# Paranasal Sinus Cancer – Simple Explanation

This type of cancer is rare. It usually starts in the lining of the sinuses near the nose. The most common type is called squamous cell carcinoma. Another type is adenocarcinoma. It most often begins in the maxillary or ethmoid sinuses.

We do not know what causes most cases. Symptoms often do not appear until the cancer is large. The outlook is usually not good.

> **Note:** This information is part of a larger guide on head and neck tumors.

---

## Who Gets This Cancer?

This cancer is rare in the United States. But it is more common in Japan and among some groups in South Africa, such as the Bantu people. Men over 40 years old are most likely to get it.

---

## What Might Cause It?

The exact cause is not known. Chronic sinus infections are not thought to cause this cancer. But some viruses may play a role in certain cases. These include:

- Human papillomavirus (HPV)
- Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)

Certain jobs or habits increase the risk. These include:

- Breathing in dust from certain woods, leather, or metals over time
- Smoking tobacco

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The sinuses are hollow spaces in the face. They can hold a growing tumor for a long time. So symptoms often do not show up early. When they do, they are caused by the tumor pressing on nearby parts of the face or head.

Symptoms include:

- Pain in the face or head
- Blocked nose or thick discharge from the nose
- Nosebleeds
- Double vision
- Ear pain or a feeling of fullness in the ear
- Numbness or tingling in the face
- Loose teeth in the upper jaw near the affected sinus
- A visible lump in the mouth or nose

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find and understand the cancer.

- **Endoscopy:** A thin tube with a camera is used to look inside the nose and sinuses.
- **Biopsy:** A small sample of tissue is taken during endoscopy. This is tested to confirm the type of cancer.
- **CT scan:** This creates detailed pictures of the sinuses and nearby areas.
- **MRI scan:** This gives even clearer images of soft tissues and helps see if the cancer has spread.

These tests help doctors find the tumor and check if it has spread to the brain, face, neck, lungs, or lymph nodes. This is called staging. Staging helps decide the best treatment.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the stage and location of the cancer.

### Surgery
For early-stage cancers, surgery is often the main treatment. The goal is to remove the entire tumor. Newer techniques, such as endoscopic surgery, can remove the tumor with less damage to healthy tissue. These methods can also help rebuild the area after surgery.

### Radiation Therapy
Radiation is often used after surgery if there is a high risk the cancer will come back. It may also be used instead of surgery if surgery is too risky or would cause serious side effects.

### Chemotherapy
Chemotherapy is sometimes used. It may be given before surgery to shrink the tumor. If the tumor gets smaller, surgery may be easier. If the tumor does not shrink, radiation therapy is used instead.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

The earlier the cancer is treated, the better the chance of recovery. The type of cancer also affects the outcome.

- Survival rates are slowly improving.
- About 40 out of 100 people will have the cancer come back.
- About 60 out of 100 people will still be alive five years after diagnosis.

This cancer is serious, but treatment can help many people live longer and better.

# Gastritis

Gastritis means the lining of the stomach is inflamed.

## What Is Gastritis?

- The stomach lining is usually strong and can handle strong acid.
- In gastritis, the lining becomes irritated and swollen.
- This can happen for many reasons, including infections, serious illness, injury, certain medicines, alcohol, or problems with the body’s defense system.

## Types of Gastritis

Gastritis is split into two main types:

### Erosive Gastritis
- This type causes both inflammation and damage to the stomach lining.
- It can start suddenly (acute) or slowly (chronic).
- It often affects people who are otherwise healthy.

### Nonerosive Gastritis
- This type causes changes in the stomach lining.
- The lining may thin out or change into a different kind of tissue.
- White blood cells build up in the stomach and cause swelling.
- The swelling can affect the whole stomach or just parts of it.

## Causes of Gastritis

### Erosive Gastritis
- Common causes: alcohol, serious illness, injury, and medicines like aspirin or other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
- Less common causes: Crohn disease, radiation, infections from viruses or bacteria, swallowing harmful chemicals, or injury from a tube put into the stomach.
- Even one baby aspirin a day can harm the stomach lining in some people.

### Nonerosive Gastritis
- Most often caused by a bacteria called *Helicobacter pylori*.

### Other Types
- Infections not caused by *H. pylori* are rare.
- Viral or fungal infections can happen in people who are very sick for a long time or have weak immune systems. This includes people with advanced HIV, cancer, or those on immune-suppressing medicines.
- Acute stress gastritis happens after a sudden illness or injury. It can follow burns, head injuries, or major bleeding. The exact reason is not clear, but it may be due to less blood flow to the stomach, more acid, or the stomach’s lining not healing well.
- Radiation therapy to the lower left chest or upper belly can irritate the stomach lining.
- Postgastrectomy gastritis happens after part of the stomach is removed. It often occurs where the stomach was sewn back together. It may happen because blood flow to the lining drops or because bile from the liver irritates the lining.
- Atrophic gastritis means the stomach lining becomes very thin and loses cells that make acid and digestive enzymes. It can happen when the body’s immune system attacks the stomach lining. It can also happen in people with long-term *H. pylori* infection or after stomach surgery.
- Eosinophilic gastritis: the cause is usually unknown. A type of white blood cell called eosinophils builds up in the stomach wall.
- Ménétrier disease: a rare condition. The stomach wall grows thick and forms large folds and fluid-filled sacs. The cause is not known, but it may be linked to an immune problem or *H. pylori* infection.

## Symptoms of Gastritis

- Most people with gastritis have no symptoms.
- When symptoms do appear, they can include:
  - Pain or discomfort in the upper belly.
  - Nausea.
  - Vomiting.
- These problems are often called indigestion.
- Severe forms like erosive gastritis or radiation gastritis can cause nausea and vomiting.
- Indigestion can happen with erosive gastritis, radiation gastritis, postgastrectomy gastritis, and atrophic gastritis.
- Mild indigestion can also happen with acute stress gastritis.

## How Gastritis Is Diagnosed

- Doctors often guess the diagnosis based on symptoms.
- If the diagnosis is unclear or symptoms do not improve, the doctor may do an upper endoscopy.
- During an upper endoscopy, a thin, flexible tube with a camera is used to look inside the stomach and part of the small intestine.
- The doctor can take a small tissue sample (biopsy) during the test to check for problems.

## Treatment of Gastritis

### General Treatments
- Medicines that reduce stomach acid help relieve symptoms.
- Antacids neutralize acid already in the stomach.
- Stop taking medicines that irritate the stomach, like aspirin or NSAIDs.

### Antacids
- Available without a prescription.
- Sold as tablets, chewable soft gels, or liquids.
- Common types:
  - Aluminum hydroxide – can cause constipation.
  - Magnesium hydroxide – can cause diarrhea.
  - Calcium carbonate – also common.
- Antacids can interfere with other medicines.
- Always talk to a pharmacist or doctor before using antacids if you take other medicines.

### Acid-Reducing Medicines
- **H2 blockers**: reduce acid production. More effective than antacids and easier to use.
- **Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs)**: very effective. Often used when there is bleeding. Usually taken for 8 to 12 weeks.

### Other Medicines
- **Sucralfate**: coats the stomach lining and helps it heal. Also protects it from irritation.

### If Caused by *H. pylori* Infection
- Antibiotics are needed to treat the infection.

### For Erosive Gastritis
- Avoid medicines that harm the stomach lining.
- Use PPIs or H2 blockers to protect the stomach.

### For Acute Stress Gastritis
- Most people get better when the main illness, injury, or bleeding is treated.
- Some people in intensive care may bleed heavily. This can be life-threatening.
- Doctors often give acid-reducing medicines after surgery or to people in intensive care to prevent this.
- These medicines also help treat ulcers that may form.

### For Heavy Bleeding
- Doctors may use heat to seal bleeding spots during endoscopy.
- If bleeding continues, surgery to remove part of the stomach may be needed. This is rare.

### For Other Types
- **Postgastrectomy gastritis** and **atrophic gastritis** have no cure.
- People with anemia from low vitamin B12 absorption due to atrophic gastritis must take vitamin B12 shots for life.
- **Eosinophilic gastritis**: may need corticosteroids or surgery if the stomach outlet is blocked.
- **Ménétrier disease**: removing part or all of the stomach may cure it. There are no good medicines for this condition.

# Pelvic Inflammatory Disease

Pelvic inflammatory disease, or PID, is an infection of the female reproductive organs. It can cause serious health problems if not treated.

## How to Lower Your Risk of PID

Always use a barrier method like a condom with a new sexual partner. This helps protect you from infections that can lead to PID.

## Signs and Symptoms of PID

PID often causes no symptoms at all. When symptoms do appear, they are usually mild.

You might notice one or more of these:

- Pain in the lower belly or pelvis  
- Deep pain during sex  
- Pain when peeing  
- Bleeding between periods or after sex  
- Heavier than normal periods  
- More painful periods  
- Unusual vaginal discharge, especially if it is yellow, green, or has a bad smell  

Some people become very unwell. Signs of this include:

- Severe belly pain  
- High temperature (fever)  
- Feeling sick or being sick  

## How PID Is Treated

If caught early, PID can be treated with antibiotics. The treatment usually lasts 14 days.

You will get a mix of antibiotics. This may include an injection and tablets. It is very important to take all the medicine as prescribed.

Do not have sex while you are on treatment. This helps make sure the infection goes away completely.

Your recent sexual partners should also be treated. This stops the infection from coming back and prevents it from spreading to others.

## What Causes PID

PID is usually caused by bacteria that move from the vagina or cervix up into the reproductive organs.

Many different bacteria can cause PID. In many cases, it is caused by a sexually transmitted infection (STI). Common ones include:

- Chlamydia  
- Gonorrhoea  
- Mycoplasma genitalium (a less well-known STI that is becoming more common)

In other cases, PID is caused by bacteria that normally live in the vagina but get into the wrong place.

## How to Prevent PID

Use a condom every time you have sex with a new partner. Keep doing this until both you and your partner have had a sexual health check.

Chlamydia is very common. Most people with it do not have any symptoms. That is why regular testing is important.

If you think you might have an STI, go to a sexual health clinic or genitourinary medicine clinic for help.

If you are having a gynaecological procedure, such as getting an intrauterine device (IUD) or having an abortion, get a check-up first. This helps reduce your risk of PID.

# Fatal Insomnia

Fatal insomnia is a very rare brain disease. It can be inherited or happen by chance. It causes serious sleep problems, movement issues, and eventually leads to death.

There are two types:
- **Fatal familial insomnia (FFI)**: This runs in families. It is caused by a change in a gene called *PRNP*.
- **Sporadic fatal insomnia (sFI)**: This does not run in families. It is not linked to a gene change.

## Symptoms

### Fatal Familial Insomnia (FFI)
- Most people start showing symptoms around age 40. Some start in their late 20s. Others may not show signs until their early 70s.
- The disease lasts from 7 to 73 months after symptoms begin.
- Early signs include:
  - Trouble falling asleep or staying asleep.
  - Problems with memory and thinking.
  - Trouble walking steadily (ataxia).
  - Mood changes or mental health issues.
- Later, some people may have:
  - High blood pressure.
  - Fast heartbeat.
  - High body temperature.
  - Excessive sweating.

### Sporadic Fatal Insomnia (sFI)
- People usually start showing symptoms a little later than those with FFI.
- The disease lasts a little longer than in FFI.
- Early signs include:
  - Problems with memory and thinking.
  - Trouble walking steadily (ataxia).
- Sleep problems are not common at first. But a sleep study can often find them.

## When to Suspect Fatal Insomnia

Think about fatal insomnia if someone has:
- Rapid worsening of memory and thinking.
- Mood or behavior changes.
- Trouble walking.
- Sleep problems.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

- A sleep study (polysomnography) can show that sleep is completely disrupted.
- Brain scans using FDG-PET or SPECT can show low activity in the thalamus (a part of the brain).
- Genetic testing can confirm FFI if a person has the *PRNP* gene change.
- MRI scans and tests on spinal fluid are not helpful for diagnosing fatal insomnia.
- A test called CSF RT-QuIC is usually negative in fatal insomnia.

## Treatment

There is no cure for fatal insomnia.  
Doctors can only help with symptoms.  
This is called supportive care.

# What Is Angina?

Angina is a feeling of pressure or pain in the chest. It happens when the heart muscle does not get enough oxygen-rich blood.

- Most people feel the discomfort under the breastbone.
- Angina usually starts during physical activity or stress.
- It often goes away when you rest.
- Doctors diagnose angina based on your symptoms, an electrocardiogram (ECG), and imaging tests.
- Treatment may include medicines like nitrates, beta-blockers, or calcium channel blockers. In some cases, doctors may open blocked blood vessels with a procedure or surgery.

In the United States, about 10 million people have angina. It is a sign of serious heart disease. Around 500,000 new cases are found each year. Women usually develop angina later in life than men.

---

## What Causes Angina?

Your heart needs a steady supply of oxygen-rich blood. The coronary arteries carry this blood from the main artery leaving your heart.

Angina happens when the heart needs more oxygen than the coronary arteries can deliver. This usually occurs when the arteries are narrowed.

- Narrowing is most often caused by fatty buildup in the arteries (called atherosclerosis).
- It can also happen if a coronary artery suddenly tightens (spasm).
- When blood flow to any tissue is too low, it is called ischemia.

When angina is caused by atherosclerosis, it usually starts during exercise or emotional stress. These situations make the heart work harder and need more oxygen.

If an artery is blocked by more than 70%, angina can happen even when you are at rest.

Other conditions can also cause angina:

- Severe anemia: This means you have too few red blood cells or not enough hemoglobin. Hemoglobin carries oxygen. Less oxygen means the heart may not get enough.
- High blood pressure: This forces the heart to work harder.
- Narrowed aortic valve: This blocks blood flow out of the heart.
- Leaky aortic valve: Blood flows backward, making the heart work harder.
- Thickened heart muscle (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy): This makes the heart pump less efficiently.

These conditions increase the heart’s need for oxygen. If the supply cannot keep up, angina occurs. Problems with the aortic valve can also reduce blood flow into the coronary arteries.

---

## Types of Angina

### Stable Angina
- Happens during physical activity or stress.
- Comes and goes in a predictable pattern.
- Usually goes away with rest.

### Vasospastic Angina (Variant Angina)
- Caused by a spasm in a large coronary artery.
- Often happens when you are resting, not during activity.
- Shows specific changes on an ECG during an attack.

### Unstable Angina
- The pattern of symptoms changes.
- Pain may be worse, happen more often, or occur with less effort or even at rest.
- This is a warning sign of a possible heart attack.
- It is considered an acute coronary syndrome.

### Nocturnal Angina
- A type of unstable angina.
- Happens at night while sleeping.

### Angina Decubitus
- A type of unstable angina.
- Happens when lying down, even without a clear cause.
- Gravity shifts fluid in the body, making the heart work harder.

---

## Symptoms of Angina

Most people feel pressure or aching under the breastbone. They may describe it as heaviness or discomfort, not sharp pain.

The discomfort can spread to:
- One or both shoulders
- Inside of one or both arms
- Back
- Throat, jaw, or teeth

### Older Adults
- May not feel pain under the breastbone.
- May feel pain in the back or shoulders.
- May think it is arthritis.
- May feel bloating, gas, or stomach discomfort after eating.
- May mistake this for indigestion or a stomach ulcer.
- Belching may seem to help.
- People with confusion or dementia may not be able to explain their pain.

### Women
- Often feel a burning or tender sensation.
- More likely to feel pain in the back, shoulders, arms, or jaw.

### Typical Angina Triggers
- Physical activity
- Emotional stress
- Cold weather
- Walking into the wind
- After a meal
- A strong emotion while resting
- A bad dream during sleep

Not everyone with poor blood flow to the heart feels angina. This is called silent ischemia. Doctors do not fully understand why some people have no symptoms. But most experts believe silent ischemia is just as serious as angina with symptoms.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Angina

Doctors start by listening to your symptoms. They ask about:
- The kind of pain
- Where it is
- When it happens
- What makes it better or worse

They also check for risk factors like high blood pressure, high cholesterol, or smoking.

### Electrocardiogram (ECG)
- May show normal results between attacks.
- May show changes during an attack.
- Can detect abnormal heart rhythms or electrical activity.

### Stress Testing
- Makes your heart work harder.
- Done by walking on a treadmill or riding a bike.
- If you cannot exercise, medicine is used to speed up your heart.
- Your heart is monitored with an ECG during the test.
- Abnormal results suggest poor blood flow to the heart.

After stress testing, doctors may do more tests:

### Echocardiography
- Uses sound waves to make pictures of the heart.
- Shows heart size, movement of the heart muscle, blood flow, and valve function.
- Done at rest and during exercise.
- If blood flow is poor, the heart muscle may not move normally.

### Radionuclide Imaging
- Uses a special dye and scanner to see blood flow to the heart.
- Helps find areas with poor blood supply.

### Coronary Angiography
- Uses X-rays and a special dye injected into the coronary arteries.
- Shows blockages or narrowing.
- The most accurate test for coronary artery disease.
- Helps decide if you need bypass surgery or a stent.

### Holter Monitor
- A small device worn for 24 to 48 hours.
- Records your heart’s electrical activity all day.
- Can catch silent ischemia or variant angina.

### Electron Beam CT
- Measures calcium in the coronary arteries.
- A higher calcium score means a greater chance of heart disease.
- Not used for everyone.
- Not reliable for predicting if you need a stent or surgery.
- Used in people at medium risk or with unclear symptoms.
- Involves radiation exposure.

### Multidetector Row CT (CT Angiography)
- Uses a fast CT scanner to see the coronary arteries.
- Noninvasive and very accurate at ruling out blockages.
- Useful if you cannot do a stress test or if the test was unclear.
- Can check if a stent or bypass graft is blocked.
- Can show heart anatomy and calcium in plaques.
- Not safe for pregnant women.
- You must hold your breath several times during the scan.
- Not good if your heart beats too fast. Medicine may be used to slow it.
- People who cannot take this medicine cannot have the test.
- Involves significant radiation.

### Cardiac MRI
- Uses magnets and radio waves to make detailed images.
- No radiation.
- Can show heart structure, blood flow, and how well the heart pumps.
- Can test if heart muscle damaged by a past heart attack can recover.
- Can check heart wall movement during stress.

---

## Treating Angina

### Lifestyle Changes
- Quit smoking — this is very important.
- Eat a healthy diet low in fat and sugar.
- Exercise regularly, if approved by your doctor.
- Lose weight if needed.

### Medicines
- Nitrates: Help widen blood vessels.
- Beta-blockers: Slow the heart rate and reduce workload.
- Calcium channel blockers: Help relax blood vessels and reduce heart strain.
- Other medicines may be used based on your needs.

### Revascularization Therapy
- Used if lifestyle changes and medicines do not help.
- Procedures to open blocked blood vessels:
  - Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI): A stent is placed to open the artery.
  - Coronary artery bypass graft (CABG): A surgeon uses a blood vessel to go around the blockage.

### When to Seek Help
- If symptoms get worse quickly, go to the hospital right away.
- This may mean you are having an acute coronary syndrome.

---

## Outlook for People with Angina

Your long-term outlook depends on several things:

- Age: Older people may have a worse outcome.
- How many arteries are blocked.
- How severe the blockages are.
- Whether you have diabetes.
- Other risk factors like smoking or high blood pressure.
- How well your heart pumps blood (heart failure).

If you have stable angina and your heart pumps normally, your outlook is usually good.

Microvascular angina (small artery problems) often causes ongoing pain, but the outlook is still better than for other types.

If your heart does not pump well, your outlook is much worse.

### Death Rate
- For people with angina and no other risk factors: about 1.4% per year.
- Higher for people with:
  - High blood pressure
  - Abnormal ECG results
  - History of heart attack
  - Diabetes

Even with risk factors, early treatment can improve your chances.

# Indigestion

Indigestion means your stomach is uncomfortable. It can happen after you eat or drink.

## What indigestion feels like

You might have one or more of these symptoms after eating or drinking:

- A burning pain in your chest. This is called heartburn.
- A full or swollen feeling in your belly.
- Feeling sick to your stomach.
- Burping or passing gas.
- Bringing up food or a bitter taste into your mouth.

## When it’s not indigestion

Stomach pain or back pain are not usually signs of indigestion. If you have these, you might be constipated.

## What causes indigestion

Indigestion often happens when stomach acid gets into your stomach lining or throat. This is called acid reflux.

Common causes include:

- Certain foods and drinks: coffee, tea, cola, alcohol, tomatoes, chocolate, fatty foods, or spicy foods.
- Being overweight.
- Smoking.
- Pregnancy.
- Stress or anxiety.
- Some medicines, like ibuprofen or aspirin.
- A hiatus hernia. This is when part of your stomach moves up into your chest.
- An open sore in your stomach lining. This is called a stomach ulcer.
- In rare cases, indigestion can be a sign of stomach cancer.

## When to see a doctor

See your doctor if you have any of these symptoms:

- You keep getting indigestion.
- You have severe pain.
- You lost a lot of weight without trying.
- You have trouble swallowing.
- You keep being sick.
- You have iron deficiency anaemia.
- You feel a lump in your stomach.
- You vomit blood or have blood in your poo.

These symptoms can mean something more serious is going on.

## How to treat indigestion at home

You do not always need to see a doctor for indigestion. You can try these steps at home.

### Do these things

- Cut down on tea, coffee, cola, or alcohol.
- Raise your head and shoulders when lying in bed. This helps stop acid from coming up at night.
- Lose weight if you are overweight.

### Avoid these things

- Do not eat 3 to 4 hours before going to bed.
- Do not eat rich, spicy, or fatty foods.
- Do not take ibuprofen or aspirin unless your doctor or pharmacist says it is safe. These medicines can make indigestion worse.
- Do not smoke.

## Help from a pharmacist

A pharmacist can suggest medicines to help with the burning or pain from indigestion.

Medicines that can help include:

- Antacids – they calm the acid in your stomach.
- Alginates – they form a barrier to stop acid from rising.
- Proton pump inhibitors – they reduce the amount of acid your stomach makes.

Some medicines work best when taken after eating. Always read the leaflet that comes with the medicine for instructions.

# Acute Interstitial Pneumonia (AIP)

Acute interstitial pneumonia is a rare and serious lung disease.  
It causes sudden and severe breathing problems.  
It looks like a condition called acute respiratory distress syndrome, or ARDS.  
It affects men and women equally.  
Most people who get it are over 40 years old.  
The cause is unknown.  

## Symptoms and Signs

You may suddenly feel feverish.  
You may have a cough.  
You may feel short of breath.  
Your breathing problems usually get worse over 7 to 14 days.  
Some people feel muscle aches, tired, or shivery before the main symptoms start.  
Your breathing may become very fast.  
A doctor may hear crackling sounds in both lungs when listening with a stethoscope.  

## Diagnosis

Doctors suspect AIP when you have these symptoms and signs.  
A chest X-ray may show signs of ARDS, such as fluid in both lungs.  
A high-resolution CT scan of the chest is often done.  
This scan shows patchy, cloudy areas in both lungs.  
It may also show solid areas in the lungs, especially near the outer edges.  
Small signs of scarring may be seen, but only in a small part of the lungs.  

Blood tests are not specific.  
They may show a high number of white blood cells.  
An arterial blood gas test often shows low oxygen levels in the blood.  
This is similar to what happens in ARDS.  

A bronchoscopy may be done.  
This test uses a thin tube to look into the lungs.  
It helps rule out other causes of breathing trouble.  
Fluid collected during this test usually shows many white blood cells, but this is not unique to AIP.  

A surgical lung biopsy is sometimes needed.  
This means taking a small sample of lung tissue.  
It is the best way to confirm AIP.  
The biopsy must show damage to the tiny air sacs in the lungs.  
This damage must not be caused by something else, like infection or injury.  
The biopsy helps rule out other serious lung diseases.  
These include bleeding in the lungs, a rare type of pneumonia, and a condition called organizing pneumonia.  

Biopsy is not always needed.  
But it carries risks.  
Doctors must weigh the benefits against the risks.  

## Treatment

There is no cure for AIP.  
Treatment focuses on supporting your body while it heals.  
Most people need a breathing machine.  
This machine helps you breathe.  
It uses the same methods used for ARDS.  
One method is low tidal volume ventilation.  
This means giving small breaths to protect the lungs.  

Steroid medicine is often used.  
It may help reduce lung inflammation.  
But there is no strong proof that it works.  

## Prognosis

The outlook is poor.  
More than half of people with AIP do not survive.  
Most who die do so within six months.  
Death is usually due to breathing failure.  

Some people survive the first serious episode.  
They may fully recover lung function.  
But the disease can come back.

# Felon

A felon is an infection in the soft part of the fingertip.  
It is usually caused by bacteria.  

The infection can create a pocket of pus inside the fingertip.  
This pus builds up pressure.  
The pressure can damage nearby tissue.  
The fingertip becomes very warm, swollen, and hard.  
It also causes severe throbbing pain.  

## How Doctors Diagnose a Felon

The doctor checks the affected finger.  
They look for signs of swelling, warmth, and pain.  
This helps them confirm the diagnosis.  

## Treatment for a Felon

The main treatment is draining the pus.  
The doctor makes a small cut in the fingertip.  
This allows the pus to come out.  
This relieves pressure and pain.  

You will also take antibiotics by mouth.  
These help kill the bacteria causing the infection.  

If treatment is delayed, the infection can spread.  
It may reach the bone, joint, or tendons.  
This can cause serious damage.  

Early treatment is key to a full recovery.

# Cellulitis – Simple Guide

## What is cellulitis?

Cellulitis is a skin infection.  
It causes pain, heat, and swelling in the skin.  
The skin often looks red, but this may be harder to see on brown or black skin.  
You might also see blisters on the skin.

You may feel unwell.  
You could have symptoms like fever, chills, or body aches.  
Your glands may swell and hurt.

Cellulitis can happen anywhere on the body.  
It is most common on the legs and feet.  
It can also happen on the hands, face, or near the eyes.

Cellulitis near the eye is very serious.  
The white part of the eye may turn red, but it does not always happen.

## When to get help right away

Call your doctor right away or use NHS 111 if:

- Your skin is painful, hot, and swollen.

Early treatment with antibiotics can stop the infection from getting worse.

You can call 111 or get help online at [nhs.uk](https://www.nhs.uk)

## When to go to A&E (Emergency Department)

Go to A&E or call 999 if you have cellulitis and any of these symptoms:

- A very high temperature  
- Shaking or feeling very cold  
- Fast heartbeat or fast breathing  
- Purple spots on your skin (this may be hard to see on brown or black skin)  
- Dizziness or feeling faint  
- Confusion or not knowing where you are  
- Cold, sweaty, or pale skin  
- Not responding or losing consciousness

These signs mean the infection may be spreading.  
This can be life threatening.

Find your nearest A&E: [NHS A&E finder](https://www.nhs.uk/service-search/urgent-care/)

### Important safety tips for A&E

- Do not drive yourself.  
- Ask someone to take you.  
- Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring all your medicines with you.

## How is cellulitis treated?

For mild cases, your doctor will give you antibiotic tablets.  
You will take them for about a week.

Your symptoms may get worse in the first two days of treatment.  
But they should start to improve after that.

If you do not feel better within 2 to 3 days, call your doctor.

Keep taking all your antibiotics, even if you feel better.  
Stopping early can make the infection come back.

Most people get well in 7 to 10 days.

If the infection is severe, you may need to go to hospital.  
You might get antibiotics through a drip in your vein.

## What you can do to help yourself

While taking antibiotics, do these things to help your recovery:

- Take paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain.  
- Raise the affected area on a pillow or chair when sitting or lying down. This helps reduce swelling.  
- Move the joint near the infected area, like your wrist or ankle. This keeps it from getting stiff.  
- Drink plenty of fluids to stay hydrated.  
- Do not wear compression stockings until you are fully well.

## How to lower your risk of getting cellulitis again

- Keep your skin clean and moisturised.  
- Clean any cuts or wounds right away. Use antiseptic cream.  
- Wear proper clothes and shoes to avoid cuts and scrapes.  
- Wear gloves if you work outside.  
- Treat athlete’s foot quickly if you have it.

## What causes cellulitis?

Cellulitis is caused by bacteria.  
The bacteria get into the deeper layers of your skin through a break.  
This break can be from a cut, insect bite, or dry, cracked skin.  
Sometimes the break is so small you can’t see it.

You cannot catch cellulitis from another person.  
It affects the deeper skin layers, not the surface.

You are more likely to get cellulitis if you:

- Have poor blood flow in your arms, legs, hands, or feet (for example, if you are overweight)  
- Have trouble moving around  
- Have a weak immune system (for example, from diabetes or chemotherapy)  
- Have lymphoedema (a condition where fluid builds up under the skin)  
- Use injected drugs  
- Have had recent surgery  
- Have had cellulitis before

If you are at higher risk, treat athlete’s foot as soon as you notice it.

# Cholera

Cholera is a serious infection of the small intestine.  
It is caused by a type of bacteria called *Vibrio cholerae*.  
This bacteria makes a poison that causes large amounts of watery diarrhea.  
The diarrhea can quickly lead to severe dehydration.  
Dehydration can cause low urine output and poor blood circulation.  
If not treated, this can lead to shock and death.

## How Cholera Spreads

Cholera spreads when people drink water or eat food that has been contaminated with the feces of infected people.  
This includes shellfish from polluted water.  
The bacteria can spread even if the infected person does not have symptoms.  
People in the same household as a sick person are at high risk.  
This is usually because they share the same water or food.  
Person-to-person spread is rare.  
It takes a large amount of the bacteria to cause infection.

## Where Cholera Is Found

Cholera is common in parts of Asia, the Middle East, Africa, South and Central America, and the Gulf Coast of the United States.  
In 2010, a major outbreak began in Haiti.  
It lasted until 2017 and spread to the Dominican Republic and Cuba.  
Over 820,000 people got sick.  
Nearly 10,000 died.  
Cases also spread to Europe, Japan, and Australia, causing small outbreaks.  
A large outbreak started in Yemen in 2016.  
It is still ongoing.  
Over 2.5 million people have been infected.  
Almost 4,000 have died.  
This is the largest and fastest-spreading cholera outbreak in modern history.  
At its peak in 2019, it made up more than 90% of all global cases.  
Haiti had a new outbreak in late 2022.  
This happened after the country had been free of cholera for three years.  
The outbreak is still happening.

Cholera outbreaks have increased worldwide since 2021.  
The number of reported cases doubled from 2021 to 2022.  
Seven countries in Africa and Asia reported more than 10,000 cases each in 2022.

In areas where cholera is common, outbreaks usually happen in warm months.  
Children, especially young or undernourished ones, are most at risk.  
In new areas, outbreaks can happen at any time.  
All age groups can get sick.

## What Causes Cholera

Only two types of *Vibrio cholerae* cause serious outbreaks: serogroups O1 and O139.  
Both the El Tor and classic types of O1 can cause severe disease.  
But most infections with the El Tor type are mild or cause no symptoms.  
The same is true for other *Vibrio cholerae* types that are not O1 or O139.

A milder form of stomach illness can be caused by other *Vibrio cholerae* types.  
These do not make the deadly toxin that causes severe diarrhea.

## Who Is at Risk

Some people are more likely to get sick.  
People with blood type O are more likely to be infected.  
The bacteria are killed by stomach acid.  
So people with low or no stomach acid are more at risk.  
This includes people taking medicines to reduce stomach acid.

People who live in areas where cholera is common often build up natural protection over time.

## Symptoms of Cholera

The time from infection to symptoms is usually 1 to 3 days.  
Cholera can cause no symptoms at all.  
It can cause mild diarrhea.  
Or it can cause a sudden, severe illness that can be deadly.

The first signs are sudden, painless, watery diarrhea and vomiting.  
Nausea is usually not a problem.  
In adults, diarrhea can be more than one liter per hour.  
But it is usually less.  
The stool often looks like white water with no solid parts.  
This is called "rice-water stool."

The loss of fluids and salts leads to extreme thirst.  
Urine output drops.  
Muscles cramp.  
People feel weak.  
Skin loses its firmness.  
Eyes sink in.  
Fingers become wrinkled.

Low blood volume causes thickened blood, low urine, and no urine.  
The body becomes very acidic.  
Potassium levels drop, but sodium stays normal.  
If not treated, blood pressure drops.  
Skin turns blue.  
A person may become confused or unconscious.  
Long-term low blood volume can damage the kidneys.

Without treatment, more than half of people with cholera will die.  
With proper treatment, fewer than 1 in 100 will die.

Most people stop carrying the bacteria within two weeks after diarrhea stops.  
Very few people become long-term carriers.

## How Cholera Is Diagnosed

Diagnosis is confirmed by testing a stool sample.  
A lab grows the bacteria on special plates.  
Then it checks the type of bacteria.  
This is called stool culture and serotyping.

Some labs can test for *Vibrio cholerae* using a method called PCR.  
A rapid test strip is available in remote areas.  
It can help find outbreaks quickly.  
But it is not always accurate.  
If the test is positive, it should be confirmed with a culture if possible.

Cholera must be told apart from other infections that cause similar symptoms.  
These include certain types of *Escherichia coli*, *Salmonella*, and *Shigella*.

Blood tests should be done to check salt levels, kidney function, and waste products in the blood.

## How Cholera Is Treated

The most important treatment is replacing lost fluids and salts.  
Oral rehydration solution (a mix of water, salts, and sugar) works for most people.  
For severe cases, fluids must be given through a vein (IV).

Antibiotics help shorten the illness and reduce the spread of bacteria.  
They are given to people 12 years and older, including pregnant women.  
The choice depends on which antibiotics the bacteria are sensitive to.  
Options include:
- Doxycycline
- Azithromycin
- Ciprofloxacin

Furazolidone is another option, but it is not available in the United States.  
Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) is also used.

## How to Prevent Cholera

To stop cholera from spreading:
- Human waste must be safely disposed of.
- Water must be cleaned before drinking.

In areas where cholera is common:
- Drink only boiled or chlorinated water.
- Cook vegetables and shellfish well.

Giving antibiotics to household contacts of sick people is not recommended.  
There is no strong proof it helps.  
Also, past outbreaks show that antibiotics can lead to resistant bacteria.

## Key Facts

- Only two types of *Vibrio cholerae* (O1 and O139) cause major outbreaks.
- These types make a toxin that causes severe, sometimes deadly diarrhea.
- Outbreaks happen when many people drink or eat contaminated water or food.
- Other *Vibrio cholerae* types cause milder illness that does not spread widely.
- Diagnosis is done with stool culture and testing.
- A rapid test can help in remote areas, but it must be confirmed.
- Rehydration is the most important treatment.
- Oral rehydration works for most cases.
- Severe cases need IV fluids.
- Antibiotics are used for people 12 years and older, including pregnant women.
- The choice depends on lab results.

# What Is Bronchiectasis?

Bronchiectasis is a long-term lung condition. It happens when the airways in the lungs become widened and thickened. This damage does not get better over time.

The airways are the tubes that carry air in and out of the lungs. When they are damaged, they do not work well. This leads to a buildup of mucus and repeated infections.

---

## How Bronchiectasis Develops

The airways have a natural defense system. This includes a layer of mucus and tiny hair-like structures called cilia. The cilia move back and forth. They push mucus up and out of the lungs. This helps clear out germs and dust.

When the airways are injured, this system breaks down. The cilia may be damaged or destroyed. Mucus builds up in the airways. This creates a place where bacteria can grow. The bacteria cause more damage. This leads to a cycle of infection and worsening lung damage.

---

## Causes of Bronchiectasis

Bronchiectasis can happen after:

- Severe or repeated lung infections
- Inhaling harmful substances like smoke, fumes, or dust
- A foreign object stuck in the airway
- Certain inherited conditions
- Weak immune systems
- Autoimmune diseases
- Lung surgery or tumors
- Acid from the stomach entering the lungs (as in severe reflux)

Some common causes include:

- **Cystic fibrosis** – a genetic disease that causes thick mucus
- **Primary ciliary dyskinesia** – a condition where cilia do not work properly
- **Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency** – a rare genetic disorder
- **Tuberculosis** – especially in areas with poor health care
- **Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis** – an allergic reaction to a fungus
- **Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)** or **asthma**
- **Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)** – when stomach acid flows back into the throat

In some people, no clear cause can be found.

---

## Symptoms of Bronchiectasis

Symptoms often start slowly. They may appear after a lung infection. Over time, they get worse.

Common symptoms include:

- A long-lasting cough that brings up thick mucus
- Coughing up blood (this is common and can be the first sign)
- Chest pain
- Recurrent pneumonia
- Wheezing or shortness of breath
- Feeling tired or weak
- Weight loss

Some people have flare-ups. These are times when symptoms suddenly get worse. Flare-ups are often caused by new infections.

---

## Complications

If not treated, bronchiectasis can lead to serious problems:

- **Pneumonia** – lung infection
- **Scarring of lung tissue** – this reduces lung function
- **Low oxygen levels in the blood** – this can cause fatigue and shortness of breath
- **High carbon dioxide levels in the blood** – this can lead to breathing problems
- **Cor pulmonale** – a type of heart failure caused by lung disease
- **Chronic respiratory failure** – when the lungs can no longer provide enough oxygen

These complications are more likely in people with severe or long-standing disease.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Bronchiectasis

Doctors use several tests to diagnose bronchiectasis:

- **Chest x-ray** – can show changes in the lungs, but may miss early cases
- **CT scan** – the most accurate test. It shows the exact shape and damage in the airways
- **Lung function tests** – measure how well the lungs work
- **Sputum culture** – a sample of mucus is tested to find the bacteria causing infection
- **Blood tests** – to check for immune problems, infections, or genetic conditions
- **Sweat test** – checks for cystic fibrosis
- **Bronchoscopy** – a thin tube is used to look inside the airways. This helps find blockages or tumors

Doctors may also test for:
- HIV
- Immunoglobulin levels
- Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis
- Tuberculosis
- Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

---

## Treatment of Bronchiectasis

Treatment aims to:

- Prevent infections
- Clear mucus from the lungs
- Reduce inflammation
- Treat the underlying cause

### Key Treatments

- **Vaccines** – to prevent flu, pneumonia, and other infections
- **Antibiotics** – to treat infections and prevent flare-ups
- **Chest physical therapy** – helps loosen and clear mucus
- **Inhaled medications** – to open airways and thin mucus
- **Bronchodilators** – help airways stay open
- **Inhaled corticosteroids** – used only in some cases
- **Mucolytics** – medicines that thin mucus (helpful for some people with cystic fibrosis)
- **Oxygen therapy** – if blood oxygen levels are low
- **Surgery** – rare, but may be needed if one part of the lung is severely damaged
- **Lung transplant** – for very severe cases, especially in people with advanced cystic fibrosis

### During Flare-Ups

When symptoms get worse, treatment includes:
- Antibiotics
- Bronchodilators
- Chest physiotherapy
- Sometimes oral steroids

People with cystic fibrosis may benefit from a special medicine called a CFTR modulator. This can reduce flare-ups.

### Bleeding from the Lungs

If you cough up a lot of blood, doctors may use a procedure called embolization. This blocks the bleeding blood vessel without surgery.

---

## Prevention of Bronchiectasis

You can lower your risk by:

- Getting childhood vaccines (measles, whooping cough)
- Getting yearly flu shots
- Getting pneumococcal and COVID-19 vaccines
- Getting RSV vaccine if recommended
- Avoiding smoking and secondhand smoke
- Avoiding harmful fumes, gases, and dust
- Not using mineral oil or petroleum jelly in the nose
- Watching young children to prevent them from inhaling small objects
- Treating acid reflux and swallowing problems early
- Getting treatment for immune system problems or genetic conditions

Early treatment of lung infections can also prevent long-term damage.

---

## Prognosis

The outlook depends on:
- The cause of the disease
- How well infections and complications are managed

People with other lung diseases like COPD or emphysema, or those with heart problems like pulmonary hypertension, tend to have a worse outcome.

With good care, many people can live well with bronchiectasis.

---

# Priapism (Long or Painful Erections)

A long or painful erection that lasts more than a few hours is a serious problem. It needs quick treatment to prevent lasting harm.

## When to Get Help Right Away

Call 999 or go to A&E if:
- You have an erection that lasts more than 3 to 4 hours.
- You have sickle cell disease and a painful erection that lasts more than 1 hour.

An erection this long must be treated in hospital as soon as possible. Delaying care can cause permanent damage to the penis.

> **Find your nearest A&E**

### Important Safety Tips for A&E

- Do not drive yourself to the hospital.
- Ask someone to drive you.
- Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.
- Bring all your medicines with you.

---

## What You Can Try at Home

These steps may help reduce a painful erection. But if the erection lasts more than 3 to 4 hours, get medical help right away.

### Do These Things:
- Try to urinate (pee).
- Take a warm bath or shower.
- Drink plenty of water.
- Go for a gentle walk.
- Try light exercises, like squats or running on the spot.
- Take painkillers such as paracetamol if you are in pain.

### Do Not Do These Things:
- Do not put ice or cold water on your penis. This can make the problem worse, especially if you have sickle cell disease.
- Do not have sex or masturbate. This will not make the erection go away.
- Do not drink alcohol.
- Do not smoke.

---

## Hospital Treatments for Priapism

If you go to hospital, doctors may use one or more of these treatments:

- A needle is used to drain blood from the penis. The area is numbed with a local anaesthetic.
- Tablets or injections are given directly into the penis.
- Surgery may be needed. A small cut is made to drain blood. You will be asleep under general anaesthetic.

---

## What Can Cause Priapism?

Priapism often happens in people with sickle cell disease.

Other causes include:
- Blood-thinning medicines, such as warfarin.
- Some antidepressants.
- Recreational drugs like cannabis and cocaine.
- Some medicines for high blood pressure.
- Other blood problems, such as thalassaemia and leukaemia.
- Some treatments for erectile dysfunction.

# Idiopathic Environmental Intolerance (IEI)

This condition causes repeated, unclear symptoms. People believe these symptoms come from exposure to common substances in the air, water, or food. Some also believe they are sensitive to electromagnetic fields like those from cell phones or Wi-Fi.

The symptoms can affect many parts of the body. But when doctors examine the person, there are no clear signs of illness.

There is no single agreed-upon definition. But IEI is generally described as having many symptoms after exposure to chemicals—whether you breathe them in, touch them, or eat them. These chemicals may be real or imagined. The key point is that no physical illness can be found.

---

## What Causes IEI?

The exact cause is not known. It is not due to a clear medical condition. Some people believe certain chemicals or electromagnetic fields trigger their symptoms. But no scientific proof links these exposures directly to the symptoms.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms vary widely. They can include:

- Fast or irregular heartbeat  
- Chest pain  
- Sweating  
- Trouble breathing  
- Feeling tired  
- Redness or warmth in the skin  
- Dizziness  
- Nausea  
- Feeling like you can’t breathe  
- Shaking  
- Tingling or numbness  
- Coughing  
- Hoarseness  
- Trouble focusing or thinking clearly  

Most people have more than one symptom. The symptoms often affect different parts of the body at the same time.

Many people list many possible triggers. These may be things they think caused their symptoms. Or they may be things found during past testing. Some people change jobs or move homes to avoid these triggers. Others avoid certain foods, wear masks in public, or stay away from public places.

When doctors examine them, they find nothing wrong. The physical exam is normal.

---

## How Is IEI Diagnosed?

Doctors must first rule out other conditions that can cause similar symptoms.

### Conditions to Rule Out:

- **Allergies** – such as hay fever or food allergies  
- **Asthma** – a lung condition that causes breathing problems  
- **Angioedema** – swelling under the skin  
- **Building-related illnesses** – when many people in the same building get sick at the same time  
- **Hormone problems** – such as carcinoid syndrome, pheochromocytoma, or mastocytosis  

To check for allergies, doctors may use skin tests or blood tests. An allergy specialist can help if needed.

If there are no clear signs of a rheumatic disease (like joint pain, skin rashes, or mouth sores), then blood tests for autoantibodies (like ANA or rheumatoid factor) are not needed. These tests often give false results when not needed.

---

## How Is IEI Treated?

### Avoiding Triggers (Sometimes)

Some people try to avoid things they think cause their symptoms. But many of these triggers are everywhere—like air, water, or food. Avoiding them can be very hard.

Going to extreme lengths to avoid triggers can hurt your life. It can lead to loneliness, stress, and high costs. Doctors advise against this.

Instead, a good relationship with your primary care doctor helps. They can listen, offer reassurance, and stop you from getting unnecessary tests or treatments.

### Psychological Support (Often Helpful)

Even if the cause is not clear, psychological support can help.

Some people resist this idea. But the goal is not to say their symptoms are “all in the mind.” The goal is to help them live better with their symptoms.

Useful approaches include:

- **Cognitive-behavioral therapy** – helps change how you think and react to triggers  
- **Desensitization** – slowly getting used to things you fear  
- **Graded exposure** – slowly facing fears in small steps  

These methods help reduce fear and avoidant behaviors.

If you also have a mental health condition like depression or panic attacks, medicine may help. But only if it is needed for that specific condition.

---

## Key Points

- IEI cannot be explained by a known physical illness.
- Doctors must first rule out other conditions with similar symptoms.
- Do not test for immune system problems unless there are clear signs of illness.
- Encourage psychological support, such as therapy and coping skills.
- Treat any coexisting mental health issues with medicine or behavior changes if needed.

# Mallet Finger

Mallet finger means the tip of your finger bends down and you cannot straighten it.  
It usually happens when a tendon in the fingertip gets injured.  

## What Causes Mallet Finger?

The tendon that straightens the fingertip is called the extensor tendon.  
This tendon connects muscle to bone.  
It can tear when the fingertip is forced to bend too far.  
A common cause is a ball hitting the fingertip, like a baseball.  
Because of this, mallet finger is sometimes called "baseball finger."  

One or more fingers can be affected.  
Sometimes the joint moves out of place (dislocated).  

When the tendon tears, it can pull a small piece of bone away.  
This is called an avulsion fracture.  
When this happens, the smooth surface of the bone at the joint also gets damaged.  

## Symptoms of Mallet Finger

- The finger hurts right after the injury.  
- It swells and may turn bruised.  
- The fingertip stays bent.  
- You cannot straighten it.  
- Sometimes blood collects under the nail.  
  This is called a subungual hematoma.  

## How Doctors Diagnose Mallet Finger

Doctors check the finger by looking and feeling it.  
They take X-rays to see if there is a broken bone.  
X-rays are taken from different angles to get a full view.  

## Treatment of Mallet Finger

Most people need a splint.  
The doctor will gently straighten the finger.  
Then they put a splint on it to keep the fingertip slightly bent upward.  
The splint must be worn for 6 to 8 weeks.  

Surgery is rarely needed.  
It may be required if:  
- A large piece of the joint bone is broken.  
- The joint is out of place.  

Following treatment carefully helps the finger heal properly.

# Lichen Sclerosus – Simple Explanation

Lichen sclerosus is a skin condition that causes itchy, white patches around the genitals or anus. These patches can bleed or hurt if you rub or scratch them.

There is no cure for lichen sclerosus. But you can manage the symptoms with treatment.

You can also take steps to protect your skin and reduce irritation.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Lichen sclerosus can happen at any age, including in children. It is more common in women over 50.

People with white, brown, or black skin can get it.

The skin may show patches that are:

- Itchy
- White in color
- Smooth or wrinkled
- Easy to damage – they may bleed or hurt if rubbed or scratched

These patches often appear on:

- The area around the opening of the vagina (called the vulva)
- The area around the anus
- The foreskin or tip of the penis

Sex can become painful. This is because the skin may shrink or tighten.

In men, the foreskin may tighten, making erections painful.

---

## What Can You Do to Help?

You can take steps to protect your skin and reduce irritation.

### Do These Things

- Wash with a gentle soap substitute instead of regular soap. Ask your doctor or pharmacist for a good product.
- Gently pat your genitals dry after peeing. Do not rub.
- Apply a barrier cream or ointment like petroleum jelly to the affected areas every day.
- Wear underwear made of cotton or silk. Avoid synthetic fabrics.
- Use a lubricant during sex if it feels uncomfortable.

### Avoid These Things

- Do not smoke.
- Do not scratch or rub the itchy areas.
- Do not use scented soaps, bubble bath, or shower gel.
- Do not wear tight underwear or tight clothes.
- Do not wash your underwear with detergent. Just rinse them with water.
- Do not use panty liners. If you must, use fragrance-free ones.
- Avoid activities like cycling or horse riding until your symptoms improve.
- If you use an emollient (a moisturizing cream), do not smoke or go near open flames. The cream can catch fire if it gets on clothes, bedding, or dressings.

---

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure for lichen sclerosus. But a strong prescription steroid ointment usually helps.

You may need to use the ointment every day for several months to get your symptoms under control.

Your doctor will tell you how often to use it.

After the first few months, you may switch to a weaker steroid ointment or a moisturizing cream to keep symptoms under control.

Always follow your doctor’s instructions about how and when to use your medicine.

---

## Possible Problems

Even with treatment, the skin can become scarred and tight over time.

This can cause:

- The vulva to shrink
- The clitoris and inner lips of the vagina to become smaller
- Pain when peeing or passing stool
- Pain during sex
- Pain when having an erection

If the condition is severe, you may need a small operation. For example:

- Surgery to widen the vagina
- Removal of the foreskin (called circumcision)

---

## Can It Lead to Cancer?

Lichen sclerosus slightly increases your risk of getting cancer on the vulva, penis, or anus.

The risk is low, but it’s important to check your skin regularly.

See your doctor if you notice:

- A lump
- Skin that feels thick or rough
- An open sore that does not heal

Early detection makes treatment easier.

---

## What Causes Lichen Sclerosus?

The exact cause is not known.

It may be linked to your immune system. Your immune system is your body’s way of fighting infections. In some cases, it may mistakenly attack your own skin.

Lichen sclerosus is:

- Not caused by an infection
- Not contagious – you cannot pass it to others through sex or close contact
- Not caused by poor hygiene

Rubbing or injuring the skin can trigger lichen sclerosus or make it worse.

# Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS)

Guillain-Barré syndrome is a rare condition that affects the nerves.  
It causes sudden muscle weakness and some loss of feeling in the hands and feet.  
The weakness usually gets worse over a few days to weeks.  
It often starts in the legs and moves up the body.  
Most people get better over time, but it can be serious.  
The body’s own immune system attacks the nerves.  
This is called an autoimmune reaction.

## What Causes Guillain-Barré Syndrome?

The exact cause is not fully known.  
But it often starts after an infection, surgery, or vaccination.  
In most cases, symptoms begin 5 days to 3 weeks after a mild illness.  
Common infections linked to GBS include:

- *Campylobacter jejuni* (a type of bacteria that causes food poisoning)  
- Certain viruses that affect the gut  
- Herpes viruses, such as Epstein-Barr and cytomegalovirus  
- *Mycoplasma* bacteria  

A few cases followed the swine flu vaccine in 1976.  
But later studies showed this link was not real.  
Some people have developed GBS after a Zika virus infection.  
Others have had it after having COVID-19.  
Some cancer treatments that boost the immune system can also cause a similar nerve problem.

If weakness lasts more than two months, doctors may diagnose a different condition called chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main symptom is muscle weakness.  
It is usually worse than any numbness or tingling.  
The weakness often starts in the legs and moves up the body.  
It can also start in the arms or face.  
The weakness is usually the same on both sides of the body.  
It often reaches its worst point within 3 to 4 weeks.  
Reflexes, like the knee-jerk, are lost.  
Bowel and bladder control are usually not affected.

In severe cases, the muscles in the face and throat become weak.  
This can make it hard to eat or drink.  
It may lead to dehydration or poor nutrition.  
About 1 in 5 people need a breathing machine because their lungs are too weak.  
This is a serious complication.

A few people have serious problems with their automatic body functions.  
These include sudden changes in blood pressure, heart rhythm, or digestion.  
They may also have trouble passing urine or have unusual pupil size.

One rare form, called Fisher variant or Miller-Fisher syndrome, causes only:

- Weak eye muscles  
- Poor balance  
- Loss of reflexes  

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose GBS based on symptoms and tests.  
The main test is a physical exam.  
Doctors look at muscle strength, reflexes, and sensation.  
They may also do:

- Nerve conduction studies (to check how well nerves send signals)  
- A spinal tap (to check the fluid around the spinal cord)  

These tests help confirm the diagnosis.  
But the diagnosis is mainly based on what the doctor sees.

## How Is It Treated?

GBS is a medical emergency.  
It needs close care in a hospital, often in an intensive care unit.  
Doctors must watch breathing and heart function closely.  
They check lung strength often.  
If lung strength drops too low, a breathing tube and machine are needed.  
Another warning sign is not being able to lift the head off the pillow.  
This often means the diaphragm is weak.

If a person cannot drink enough fluids, they get fluids through a vein.  
This helps keep the kidneys working.  
The arms and legs must be protected from injury.  
Pressure from lying in bed can cause sores.

Pain relief is important.  
Heat therapy can help ease pain.  
This makes it easier to start physical therapy early.  
Staying still for too long can cause stiff joints and muscle shortening.  
So, gentle movement of the joints should start right away.  
When the worst symptoms pass, active exercises can begin.  
Blood thinners may be given to prevent blood clots in people who are not moving.

### First Treatment: IV Immune Globulin (IVIG)

IVIG is the first treatment used.  
It works best when given early.  
It can be given in two ways:

- A single dose of 2 grams per kilogram of body weight over 1 to 2 days  
- Or 400 milligrams per kilogram once a day for 5 days  

Before IVIG, patients take acetaminophen and diphenhydramine to reduce side effects.  
IVIG helps even if given up to one month after symptoms start.

### Second Treatment: Plasma Exchange

Plasma exchange is used if IVIG does not work.  
It helps shorten the illness and reduces the chance of long-term weakness.  
It also lowers the risk of death.  
But it can cause low blood pressure.  
It may also be hard to start the IV line.  
Plasma exchange removes IVIG from the body.  
So, it should not be done while IVIG is being used.  
Wait at least 2 to 3 days after stopping IVIG.

### What NOT to Do

Do not use corticosteroids.  
They do not help and may make things worse.  
Eculizumab is being studied.  
It may help some people, but more research is needed.

## What Is the Outlook?

Most people survive GBS.  
Less than 4 out of 100 die from it.  
Most people get better over several months.  
But many adults still have some weakness after 3 years.  
More children have lasting weakness.  
Some people need retraining, braces, or surgery to help with movement.

About 5 out of 100 people get a new nerve problem called chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy after getting better.

## Key Points

- GBS usually starts with weakness in the legs that moves up the body.  
- It is often linked to a recent infection, surgery, or vaccine.  
- Doctors check for other conditions with similar symptoms, such as botulism or myasthenia gravis.  
- Tests like nerve studies and spinal tap help confirm the diagnosis.  
- Most people improve over time, but some have lasting weakness.  
- About 2 to 5 out of 100 develop a long-term nerve problem.  
- Care in a hospital is essential.  
- Start with IVIG. If it does not work, try plasma exchange.

# What Is Diverticular Disease?

Diverticular disease happens when small, balloon-like pouches form in the wall of part of the digestive system.

A single pouch is called a diverticulum.  
When there are two or more pouches, they are called diverticula.

The most common place for these pouches to form is in the large intestine, also known as the colon.

Pouches in the colon happen when the inner layer of the bowel pushes through the outer muscle layer.

Pouches can also form in the esophagus.  
They are rare in the stomach.  
A pouch in the small intestine is called a Meckel diverticulum.  
This condition is present at birth in about 2 out of every 100 people.

## Where Is the Large Intestine?

The large intestine is the last part of the digestive tract.  
It helps turn waste into stool.

When one or more pouches are found in the colon, the condition is called diverticulosis.  
Diverticulosis usually starts during middle age.

If the pouches become inflamed, the condition is called diverticulitis.  
Diverticulitis can happen with or without infection.

# Liver Disease

Your liver may not show any signs of trouble in the early stages.  
You might not feel sick at first.  

Later on, you could feel very tired.  
You might lose your appetite.  
Your skin and the whites of your eyes may turn yellow.  
This yellow color is called jaundice.

## What Are the Signs of Liver Disease?

Most liver problems do not cause symptoms early on.  
When symptoms do appear, your liver is already damaged.  
This damage is called cirrhosis.

Symptoms of cirrhosis include:

- Feeling very tired and weak all the time  
- Not wanting to eat, which can lead to losing weight  
- Losing interest in sex  
- Yellow skin and yellow eyes (jaundice)  
- Itchy skin  
- Feeling sick to your stomach or actually being sick

## How Is Liver Disease Treated?

The treatment depends on what type of liver disease you have.  
It also depends on how serious the damage is.

Some liver problems can improve with lifestyle changes.  
For example, if your liver disease is caused by drinking too much alcohol, stopping alcohol can help your liver heal.

Some types of liver disease, like certain kinds of hepatitis, need medicine to treat them.

If your liver is badly damaged and scarred, you may need a liver transplant.  
This means getting a new liver from a donor.

## How Can You Prevent Liver Disease?

The three main causes of liver disease are:

- Being overweight or obese  
- Having hepatitis that you do not know about  
- Drinking too much alcohol

You can lower your risk of liver disease by making simple changes:

- Try to keep a healthy weight  
- Do not drink too much alcohol

Vaccines are available for hepatitis A and hepatitis B.  
These are recommended if you are at higher risk of getting these infections.

### Important Note

You do not need to drink a lot of alcohol to harm your liver.  
Even drinking just a little more than the safe amount each day can cause damage over time.

# Herpetic Whitlow

Herpetic whitlow is a skin infection in the fingertip. It is caused by the herpes simplex virus.

This condition can cause severe pain, redness, and swelling in the finger. The soft part of the fingertip (the pulp) may be red and swollen, but it is not tight or hard. Some people also get a fever or swollen glands in the arm.

Small blisters appear on the front or back of the fingertip. They usually show up 2 to 3 days after the pain starts. The pain can feel like a deep infection called a felon. But herpetic whitlow is different because the fingertip is not tight and hard. Also, blisters are a clear sign.

The condition can look like other hand infections, such as paronychia or infections caused by the coxsackievirus. It will go away on its own, but it can come back.

## Important Points

- Do not cut into or drain the area if you think it is a felon or paronychia. This could be herpetic whitlow.
- Do not cut or drain the infected area. This can make it worse and spread the virus.
- Using a cream called acyclovir 5% on the skin may help shorten the first episode.
- Taking acyclovir pills (800 milligrams twice a day) right after symptoms start may help prevent future outbreaks.
- Keep open or leaking blisters covered. This helps stop the virus from spreading to others.

# What Is Coronary Artery Disease?

Coronary artery disease is when the blood flow to the heart muscle gets blocked or slowed down.

The heart needs a steady supply of oxygen-rich blood to work well. The coronary arteries carry this blood from the main artery (aorta) to the heart muscle.

When these arteries get narrow or blocked, the heart does not get enough blood. This can cause chest pain or a heart attack.

In rich countries, this disease causes more deaths than any other condition in both men and women. It causes about one in three deaths.

The most common cause is a buildup of fat and cholesterol in the artery walls. This is called atherosclerosis. It makes the arteries hard and narrow.

Men are more likely to die from this disease than women, especially between ages 35 and 55. After age 55, men’s risk goes down. Women’s risk keeps rising. After age 70 to 75, women’s risk is about the same as men’s.

---

## How the Heart Gets Blood

Like all body parts, the heart needs oxygen-rich blood and must get rid of waste.

Two main arteries carry blood to the heart:
- The right coronary artery
- The left coronary artery

These come off the aorta just after it leaves the heart.

The right artery splits into two smaller ones that go to the back of the heart.  
The left artery splits into two parts: the circumflex and the left anterior descending artery.

After the heart uses the blood, the waste-filled blood flows into small veins. These veins join a large vein called the coronary sinus. This vein returns the blood to the heart’s right side.

---

## What Causes Coronary Artery Disease?

Most cases happen because of a slow buildup of fat and cholesterol in the artery walls. This is called atherosclerosis.

This buildup can happen in any artery, not just the heart’s.

### The Main Cause:
- Atherosclerosis

### Other Causes:
- A sudden tightening (spasm) of a coronary artery. This can happen on its own or after using drugs like cocaine or nicotine.
- The artery does not widen when the heart needs more blood, such as during exercise. This is called endothelial dysfunction.
- Birth defects in the coronary arteries.
- A tear in the lining of a coronary artery (dissection).
- Autoimmune disease like lupus.
- Inflammation of the arteries (arteritis).
- A blood clot that moves from the heart into a coronary artery.
- Injury or radiation damage to the heart area.

As the fatty buildup grows, it bulges into the inside of the artery. This narrows the space for blood to flow.

Over time, calcium builds up in the fatty area. The more the artery narrows, the less blood reaches the heart muscle.

The heart needs more blood when you are active. If the blood supply is not enough during activity, the heart muscle does not get enough oxygen. This is called myocardial ischemia.

If the heart does not get enough blood, it cannot pump properly.

Even a small fatty area can break open suddenly. When it does, it often causes a blood clot to form.

This clot can block the artery completely. This leads to sudden, serious lack of blood flow. This is called an acute coronary syndrome.

Acute coronary syndromes include:
- Unstable angina (chest pain that comes and goes, even at rest)
- Two types of heart attack, depending on where and how blocked the artery is

In a heart attack, the part of the heart muscle that depends on the blocked artery dies. This is called myocardial infarction.

---

## Risk Factors for Coronary Artery Disease

Some risks cannot be changed:
- Getting older
- Being a man
- Having a close family member (like a father or brother) who had heart disease before age 55, or a mother or sister before age 65

Other risks can be changed or treated:
- High levels of LDL cholesterol (the bad kind)
- High levels of lipoprotein a
- Low levels of HDL cholesterol (the good kind)
- Diabetes
- Smoking
- High blood pressure
- Being overweight
- Not being physically active
- Poor diet
- High levels of C-reactive protein (a sign of inflammation)

Smoking more than doubles your risk of heart disease and heart attack. Secondhand smoke also raises your risk.

A poor diet can increase your risk. This includes:
- Not eating enough fiber
- Not eating enough vitamins C, D, and E
- Not eating enough plant-based foods (fruits and vegetables)
- Not eating enough fish oils (omega-3 fats)

Some health problems also raise your risk:
- Underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism)
- High levels of homocysteine (an amino acid)
- High levels of apolipoprotein B (a protein involved in fat movement in the blood)

It is not clear if infections play a role in causing this disease.

---

## How Is Coronary Artery Disease Treated?

Doctors aim to do three things:
1. Reduce the heart’s workload
2. Improve blood flow to the heart
3. Slow or reverse the buildup of fatty deposits

### Reducing the Heart’s Workload
- Control blood pressure
- Use medicines like beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers to help the heart beat more gently

### Improving Blood Flow
- Use medicines that relax the coronary arteries (like nitrates, calcium channel blockers, or ranolazine)
- Open narrowed arteries with a procedure called percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), which uses a balloon and stent
- Bypass blocked arteries with surgery (coronary artery bypass grafting or CABG)
- Use medicines to dissolve blood clots in the coronary arteries

### Slowing or Reversing Fatty Buildup
- Change your diet
- Exercise regularly
- Take certain medicines

These same steps are used to prevent the disease from starting.

### Minimally Invasive Bypass Surgery
This surgery uses small cuts instead of opening the chest wide.

Some versions use robots. The surgeon sits at a computer and controls small robotic arms. These arms hold special tools that move like human hands.

The surgeon sees a 3D image on a screen. The surgery needs only three small cuts:
- One for each robotic arm
- One for a camera

The breastbone is not cut open. This means shorter surgery time and shorter hospital stay than with traditional open-heart surgery.

### Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG)
This surgery connects a healthy blood vessel to the heart. The new path lets blood go around a blocked artery.

Doctors prefer using an artery instead of a vein because arteries are less likely to get blocked later.

One common method:
- Cut one of the internal mammary arteries (from the chest wall)
- Attach one end to the heart beyond the blockage
- Tie off the other end

If an artery cannot be used or if there are multiple blockages, a vein is used instead. The most common vein is the saphenous vein, which runs from the groin to the ankle.

One end of the vein is attached to the aorta. The other end is attached to the heart beyond the blockage.

Sometimes, both a mammary artery and a vein are used.

---

## How to Prevent Coronary Artery Disease

Changing your lifestyle can help prevent this disease. Many risk factors are linked, so changing one can help with others.

### Quit Smoking
- Quitting cuts your risk in half compared to people who keep smoking.
- It does not matter how long you smoked before quitting.
- Quitting also lowers your risk of dying after heart surgery or a heart attack.
- Avoid secondhand smoke.

### Eat a Healthy Diet
- Eat less saturated fat
- Avoid trans fats completely
- Eat more fruits and vegetables
- Eat more fiber
- Drink alcohol only in small amounts, if at all
- Eat fewer simple carbs like sugar, white bread, and white flour

Limit fat to 25 to 35% of your daily calories. Some experts say 10% is better for heart health.

A low-fat diet helps lower total cholesterol and LDL (bad) cholesterol.

The type of fat matters as much as the amount:
- Eat oily fish like salmon often (rich in omega-3 fats)
- Avoid trans fats

In the U.S. and many other countries, trans fats are banned in packaged foods, fast food, and restaurants.

### Types of Fat
There are three main types:

**Saturated fats**
- Have as many hydrogen atoms as possible
- Usually solid at room temperature
- Found in meat, dairy, and some processed oils
- A diet high in these fats increases heart disease risk

**Unsaturated fats**
- Have fewer hydrogen atoms than possible
- Usually liquid at room temperature
- Examples: olive oil, canola oil, corn oil
- Omega-3 fats (in fish) and omega-6 fats (in vegetable oils) are types of unsaturated fats

**Trans fats**
- Made by adding hydrogen to oils (a process called hydrogenation)
- Used in many fried and baked foods
- Now banned in many countries
- Increase bad cholesterol (LDL) and lower good cholesterol (HDL)
- Raise heart disease risk

Check food labels. If “hydrogenated” or “partially hydrogenated” fat is listed first, the product has trans fats.

Soft or liquid margarine has less trans fat than hard stick margarine.
