# Endometriosis

Endometriosis is a condition that can cause pain and other problems. It affects people who have periods.

## What are the symptoms?

You may have:
- Severe period pain that stops you from doing normal things.
- Heavy periods. You may need to change your pad or tampon every 1 to 2 hours. You might even bleed through your clothes.
- Pain when you pass urine (pee) or move your bowels (poo).
- Pain in your lower tummy or back (pelvic area).
- Pain during or after sex.
- Extreme tiredness (fatigue).
- Pain or bleeding in other areas, like your chest. This can cause shortness of breath or coughing up blood.
- Trouble getting pregnant.
- Low mood or anxiety.

These symptoms can happen during your period or at any time during your cycle.

Endometriosis often grows in the area around the womb. This includes the ovaries, fallopian tubes, and the lining of the pelvis. It can also affect the bladder, bowel, or, rarely, other parts of the body like the chest.

The pain happens because patches of endometriosis break down and bleed during your period. But the blood cannot leave your body. This causes irritation and pain.

## When to see a doctor

See your GP if:
- You think you might have endometriosis.
- Your symptoms are affecting your daily life, work, or relationships.
- You’ve had treatment from your GP but your symptoms are not getting better, or they are getting worse.

## How is endometriosis diagnosed?

It can take time to diagnose endometriosis. Your doctor may need to do several tests.

This is because the symptoms can be like those of other conditions, such as:
- Adenomyosis (when the womb lining grows into the muscle wall of the womb).
- Fibroids (non-cancerous growths in the womb).
- Pelvic inflammatory disease (an infection in the reproductive organs).
- Irritable bowel syndrome (a condition that affects the bowel).

### What happens at your GP appointment?

Your GP will:
- Ask about your symptoms.
- Ask if any close family members have had endometriosis.
- Do a physical exam, including a vaginal exam to check your tummy and pelvic area.
- Order blood tests.

Tell your GP everything you know about your symptoms. Be as clear and detailed as possible.

If your GP thinks you might have endometriosis, they may:
- Refer you to a gynaecologist (a doctor who specialises in women’s reproductive health).
- Give you medicines to help ease your pain.

### Further tests

You may need more tests, such as:
- An ultrasound scan – this can be done on your tummy or inside your vagina.
- An MRI scan – this gives a detailed picture of your internal organs.
- A laparoscopy – a small camera is put into your tummy through a tiny cut. This can confirm if you have endometriosis.

During a laparoscopy, the doctor may also remove some endometriosis tissue if it is safe to do so.

## How is endometriosis treated?

There is no cure for endometriosis. But treatment can help reduce your symptoms.

Your doctor will explain the benefits and risks of each treatment.

If your symptoms are very bad or other treatments are not working, you may be referred to a specialist endometriosis clinic.

### Medicines

Medicines are often the first step in treatment. They include:
- Painkillers like paracetamol or ibuprofen.
- Hormones, such as the combined contraceptive pill. These can help reduce pain.

You will not be given hormone medicines if you are trying to get pregnant.

### Surgery

Surgery may be an option if:
- Other treatments are not helping.
- You have a lot of endometriosis.
- Endometriosis is affecting your ability to have children.

Surgery can help by:
- Removing areas of endometriosis or fluid-filled sacs (cysts) on the ovaries.
- Removing the womb (hysterectomy) or ovaries (oophorectomy).
- Removing part of the bladder or bowel if endometriosis is affecting them.

You might need more surgery later if symptoms return or if scarring causes organs to stick together (adhesions).

## Support for living with endometriosis

Endometriosis can be hard to live with. It affects both your body and your emotions.

You can get help from:
- Your doctor.
- Other people with endometriosis.
- Support groups and organisations.

### Endometriosis UK

- Website: [https://www.endometriosis-uk.org/](https://www.endometriosis-uk.org/)
- Helpline: 0808 808 2227
- Web chat
- Online community
- Support groups

### The Endometriosis Foundation

- Website: [https://www.theendometriosisfoundation.org/](https://www.theendometriosisfoundation.org/)
- Online community
- Speak to a nurse

## How endometriosis affects your life

Endometriosis affects everyone differently.

Treatment usually helps reduce symptoms. But some people still have long-term pain and tiredness. This can affect work, relationships, and daily life for many years.

Most people find that their symptoms stop after menopause. But it is possible to still have symptoms after menopause.

# Nosebleeds

A nosebleed is when blood comes out of the nose.  
The amount of blood can be small or large.  
Some nosebleeds are just a nuisance.  
Others can be serious and even life-threatening.

## Where Nosebleeds Start

Most nosebleeds come from the front part of the nose.  
They start in a small area on the inside of the nose called the septum.  
This area has many tiny blood vessels.  
This is known as the Kiesselbach area.

Less common but more serious nosebleeds come from the back of the nose.  
These start near the vomer bone or from the lower or middle parts of the nasal structures.  
Back-of-the-nose bleeds are more likely in older people.  
They also happen more often in people with weak blood vessels or blood clotting problems.  
They can also happen after nose or sinus surgery.

## What Causes Nosebleeds

The most common causes are:

- Rubbing or blowing the nose too hard  
- Dry air making the inside of the nose dry and cracked  

Other causes are less common but can be serious.  
These include:

- Hardening of the blood vessels (arteriosclerosis)  
- Problems with blood clotting or low platelet count  
- A foreign object stuck in the nose (common in children)  
- Using illegal drugs like cocaine  
- Infections in the nose or skin around the nose  
- A rare inherited condition that causes weak blood vessels  
- A hole in the wall between the two sides of the nose (septal perforation)  
- Serious health problems like advanced HIV or liver disease  
- Tumors in the nose or sinuses

High blood pressure can make a nosebleed last longer.  
But it rarely causes a nosebleed on its own.

### Common Causes

| Cause | What to Look For | How It’s Checked |
|-------|------------------|------------------|
| Dry nose (like in cold weather) | The inside of the nose looks dry | Doctor checks with a light |
| Nose trauma (blowing, picking, injury) | Patient says they blew or picked their nose | Doctor asks questions and checks |
| Arteriosclerosis | More common in older adults | Doctor checks with a light |
| Blood clotting problems | History of bleeding from other areas, like gums | Blood test to check platelets and clotting |
| Foreign object in nose | Nosebleeds that keep coming back, bad smell from one side | Doctor checks with a special tool |
| Cocaine use | History of drug use, hole in the nose wall (in severe cases) | Doctor asks questions and checks |
| Infections (like rhinitis) | Crusty skin in the nose, pain, dryness | Doctor asks questions and checks |
| Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia | Tiny red spots on face, lips, mouth, fingers, toes | Family history, doctor exam, possible genetic test |
| Septal perforation | History of injury, surgery, or drug use | Doctor sees it during exam |
| Advanced HIV or liver disease | Known health problem, red or swollen nose lining | Doctor checks medical history and nose |
| Tumors in nose or sinuses | A lump seen in the nose or back of nose | CT scan to see inside the nose |

People with blood clotting problems or those on blood thinners are more likely to have nosebleeds.  
Their nosebleeds are often worse and harder to stop.

**CBC** = blood test to check blood cells and platelets  
**CT** = scan that shows detailed pictures of the inside of the nose  
**PT/PTT** = blood tests to check how well blood clots

## How Doctors Check Nosebleeds

Doctors start by asking about your health and how the nosebleed happened.  
They look inside your nose with a light or a special tool.  
They may do blood tests if they suspect a clotting problem.  
They may use a CT scan if they think there is a tumor or serious issue.

## How Nosebleeds Are Treated

If the nose is actively bleeding, the first step is the same for most cases.  
Press on the soft part of the nose for 10 to 15 minutes.  
This often stops the bleeding.

If the blood loss is large, the doctor may need to give blood.  
They decide this based on your symptoms, blood count, and vital signs.

If you have a blood clotting problem, the doctor will treat that too.

## Key Points

- Most nosebleeds come from the front of the nose.  
- They usually stop with direct pressure.  
- Always ask about bleeding problems, especially if you have a history of easy bruising or bleeding.  
- Always ask about medicines like aspirin, ibuprofen, or blood thinners.  
- These medicines can make nosebleeds worse.

# Osteochondrodysplasias

Osteochondrodysplasias are rare genetic conditions.  
They affect how bones, cartilage, or connective tissue grow.  
This leads to abnormal bone development.

The problem usually comes from changes in genes.  
These genes help build connective tissue.  
Connective tissue is the strong, fibrous material that holds the body together.  
It gives support and allows movement.

Each type of osteochondrodysplasia causes different symptoms.  
But all types lead to short stature.  
Short stature means an adult height of 4 feet 10 inches (147 centimeters) or less.  
This is true for both men and women.

Some types cause more shortening in the arms and legs.  
This is called short-limbed dwarfism.  
Other types cause more shortening in the trunk.  
This is called trunk-type dwarfism.

The most common form of short-limbed dwarfism is achondroplasia.  
People with achondroplasia often have:  
- Bowlegs  
- A large forehead  
- A nose that looks different (called a saddle nose)  
- An arched back  
- Joints that do not move as fully as they should

There is a serious form called thanatophoric dysplasia.  
It causes major chest and breathing problems in newborns.  
This form is often fatal shortly after birth.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Osteochondrodysplasias

Doctors use several tools to make a diagnosis.

**First, they look at symptoms and do a physical exam.**  
They check the shape of the bones and body.  
They also look at how the joints move.

**X-rays of the bones** are very helpful.  
They show how the bones are shaped and growing.

**Blood tests** can sometimes find the faulty genes.  
This is useful for predicting the condition before birth.

**Tests during pregnancy** can also help.  
A doctor may use a flexible camera to look at the baby inside the womb.  
This is called fetoscopy.  
Or they may use ultrasound to see the baby’s bones and body.

---

## How Osteochondrodysplasias Are Treated

Treatment depends on the specific condition and symptoms.

**Joint replacement surgery** may be needed.  
If joints do not move well, doctors can replace them with artificial ones.  
Hip replacement is common.

**Surgery to lengthen limbs** is possible.  
This can help increase a person’s final height.  
Surgery can also correct bowlegs.

**Growth hormone treatment** does not usually help people with achondroplasia.  
Their bodies do not respond to it.

But there is a medicine called vosoritide.  
It may help with bone growth.  
It is available for some people with achondroplasia.

Because the genetic causes are known, **genetic counseling** is helpful.  
It can guide families about risks and future pregnancies.

---

## Support and Resources

Organizations like **Little People of America** offer support.  
They provide medical information, community help, and advocacy.  
They help people with short stature live full lives.

Similar groups exist in other countries.  
They offer the same kind of support.

---

# Phlebitis (Superficial Thrombophlebitis)

Phlebitis is inflammation in a vein just under the skin. It often happens in the legs, but it can also happen in the arms or neck.

## Symptoms of Phlebitis

You may notice:
- Pain, soreness, or swelling in the area.
- Warm skin over the affected vein.
- Itchy skin.
- Skin that looks red, dark, or changes in texture. The skin may feel thick or hard.

Phlebitis is more common in people with varicose veins.  
It can be harder to see on brown or black skin.

## When to Seek Help

Call your doctor right away or use NHS 111 if you have:
- A throbbing or cramping pain in your leg, arm, or neck.
- Sudden swelling in your leg, arm, or neck.
- Warm skin around the painful area.
- Red or darkened skin near the pain.
- Swollen veins that feel hard or sore when touched.

These symptoms could be a sign of a deeper blood clot. This is called deep vein thrombosis. It needs quick treatment.

You can call 111 or get help online at 111.

## Treatments for Phlebitis

You may not need treatment if your symptoms are mild.

But treatment may be needed if:
- The pain is severe.
- The symptoms do not improve.

Treatment options include:
- Anti-inflammatory creams or gels for small areas.
- Compression stockings to help blood flow in the legs. These are not for everyone.
- Blood-thinning medicine to lower the risk of blood clots and prevent phlebitis from returning.

## What You Can Do to Feel Better

You can take steps to ease your symptoms:
- Keep using the affected leg or arm. Do not stop moving it.
- Raise your leg or arm when resting. This helps reduce swelling.
- Place a warm, damp cloth on the area. This can ease pain.
- Take paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain.  
  If you are on blood-thinning medicine, do not take ibuprofen unless your doctor says it is safe.

## Causes of Phlebitis

The exact cause is not always known. But it is often linked to:
- Varicose veins (swollen, twisted veins, usually in the legs).
- Conditions that make blood clot more easily, such as thrombophilia.
- Autoimmune diseases like Behçet’s disease (a rare condition that causes blood vessel inflammation).
- Injections or a small tube (cannula) placed in a vein.

Other things that raise your risk include:
- Getting older.
- Being overweight.
- Being pregnant.
- Having cancer.
- Having had phlebitis before.

# Laryngitis

Laryngitis means the voice box is inflamed.  
This usually happens because of a virus or overusing your voice.  
Your voice may sound weak or different.  
You might not be able to make any sound at all.  

Doctors usually diagnose laryngitis by talking to you and checking your throat.  
If your symptoms last more than two weeks, you may need a special test.  
This test uses a small camera to look at your voice box.  

Most cases of laryngitis go away on their own.  
Some causes need special treatment.  

## Types of Laryngitis

Laryngitis can be short-term or long-term.  
Short-term laryngitis usually gets better in one week.  
It can last up to three weeks.  
Long-term laryngitis lasts more than three weeks.  

The most common cause of short-term laryngitis is a virus.  
Bacteria or fungus can also cause it, but this is less common.  
These infections often happen after a virus.  

Coughing from other illnesses can also cause laryngitis.  
These include bronchitis, pneumonia, the flu, whooping cough, measles, and diphtheria.  

Using your voice too much — like shouting or singing — can cause laryngitis.  
Allergies, acid from the stomach coming up into the throat, or vomiting (as in bulimia) can also cause it.  
Breathing in smoke or strong fumes can irritate the voice box.  
Smoking or breathing in heated fumes can cause a condition called Reinke edema.  
This is a swelling in the vocal cords that makes the voice sound deeper or hoarse.  

Some medicines can cause serious swelling in the throat.  
This is rare but can be life-threatening.  
One example is a type of blood pressure medicine called an ACE inhibitor.  

## Symptoms of Laryngitis

The main symptom is a change in your voice.  
Your voice may be quieter than normal.  
Some people lose their voice completely.  

You may feel a tickle in your throat.  
Your throat may feel raw.  
You may keep clearing your throat.  

The symptoms depend on how bad the swelling is.  

In more serious cases, you may have trouble swallowing.  
You might feel pain in your throat.  
You could also have a fever or feel tired.  

Swelling in the voice box is rare.  
But if it happens, it can make breathing hard.  
You might make a high-pitched sound when breathing in.  

## How Doctors Diagnose Laryngitis

Doctors start by asking about your symptoms.  
They will look at your throat.  

Sometimes they use a small camera to see your voice box.  
This is called laryngoscopy.  
It is recommended if symptoms last more than two weeks.  

The camera may show redness or swelling in the voice box.  
If you have acid reflux, the inside of the voice box may be swollen and red.  
Long-term irritation, like from smoking, can cause white patches on the voice box.  
These patches are called leukoplakia.  

Doctors do not recommend giving steroid medicine for voice problems before looking at the voice box.  

A thick, grayish film in the throat or voice box can be a sign of diphtheria.  
This is a serious infection.  
If this is seen, doctors will act quickly.  

## Treating Laryngitis

There is no cure for viral laryngitis.  
It will get better on its own.  

You can help your voice recover by:  
- Resting your voice  
- Drinking plenty of fluids  
- Using a humidifier or breathing in steam  
- Taking cough medicine if needed  

Stopping smoking helps.  
Treating lung problems like bronchitis can also help.  

If laryngitis is caused by acid reflux, treating the reflux can help.  
If a medicine is causing the problem, your doctor may change it.  

Antibiotics do not help if the cause is a virus.  
They also do not help most cases of laryngitis.  
They are only used if a bacterial infection is likely.  
Antifungal medicine is only used if a fungus is the cause.

# Jock Itch (Tinea Cruris)

Jock itch is a skin infection caused by a type of fungus. It affects the groin area.

## What It Looks Like and Feels Like

- You may have a rash that itches a lot.
- The rash can also hurt or feel sore.
- The rash often starts in the skin folds near the genitals.
- It can spread to the inner thighs.
- It usually does not affect the scrotum much, or at all.
- The edges of the rash are red and scaly.

## Who Gets Jock Itch

- Men are more likely to get it than women.
- It is more common in warm weather.
- Wearing tight or wet clothes can make it worse.
- People with extra body weight are at higher risk.
- This is because skin folds can trap sweat and moisture.

## Why It Comes Back

- Jock itch often comes back.
- It can return if you have athlete’s foot or nail fungus.
- Fungi from those infections can spread to the groin.
- Flare-ups are more common in summer.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

- A doctor will look at your groin area.
- If the rash is not clear, the doctor may take a small skin sample.
- The sample is checked under a microscope to confirm it is a fungus.

## How It Is Treated

- Most people use a cream or lotion that fights fungus.
- Common creams include miconazole, naftifine, ketoconazole, and clotrimazole.
- Apply the cream to the rash as directed.
- Keep the area clean and dry.
- If the infection is large, very red, or not healing, you may need pills.
- Pills like itraconazole or terbinafine can help in these cases.

## Tips to Prevent It

- Wear loose, breathable clothes.
- Change out of wet clothes quickly.
- Dry your groin area well after showering.
- Avoid sharing towels or clothing.
- Treat athlete’s foot or nail fungus early to stop it from spreading.

# Dental Abscess

A dental abscess is a serious infection in your mouth. It can cause severe pain and swelling.

## Symptoms

You may have a dental abscess if you notice:

- A sharp, strong toothache that does not go away
- Pain in your gums
- Redness inside your mouth or on your face or jaw
- A bad taste in your mouth
- Swelling in your face or jaw
- Trouble opening your mouth wide
- Pain when chewing
- Sensitivity to hot or cold food and drinks
- A high temperature

## What to Do

A dental abscess will not get better on its own. You need to see a dentist right away.

### Call for urgent help if:

- You think you have a dental abscess
- You are having trouble breathing
- Your eye is swollen or painful, or you suddenly have trouble seeing
- You have a lot of swelling in your mouth

Do not go to a regular doctor’s office. They cannot treat dental problems.

### Call 999 or go to A&E if:

- You are having trouble breathing
- Your eye is swollen or painful, or you suddenly have vision problems
- Your mouth is very swollen

**Important:** Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you. Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring all your medicines with you when you go to A&E.

## Treatment

A dentist will treat a dental abscess by draining the pus. This helps reduce pain and swelling.

If the abscess is caused by a damaged tooth, you may need:

- Root canal treatment (the infected part of the tooth is removed)
- Or the tooth may need to be taken out

The dentist will use a local anaesthetic. This means you will not feel pain during the treatment.

After treatment, you may be given:

- Painkillers to take for a few days
- Antibiotics to fight the infection

## How to Feel Better While Waiting for Treatment

You can do a few things to help ease the pain:

- Take painkillers like ibuprofen or paracetamol
  - Children under 16 should not take aspirin
- Eat soft foods such as soup, scrambled eggs, mashed potatoes, and yoghurt
- Use a soft toothbrush to clean your teeth
- Avoid sugary foods and drinks
- Avoid very hot or very cold food and drinks

## Causes

A dental abscess happens when an infection in your mouth causes pus to build up under your teeth or gums.

You are more likely to get one if:

- A tooth has not grown through your gums properly (an impacted tooth)
- You have tooth decay or gum disease
- You have injured your teeth, gums, or mouth
- You are having radiotherapy or chemotherapy

Always get help quickly if you think you have a dental abscess. Early treatment can prevent serious problems.

# Measles – Simple Explanation

Measles is a serious virus that spreads easily. It mostly affects children who have not been vaccinated. It causes a high fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes, and a rash that spreads from the head down the body. Some people also get small white spots inside the mouth called Koplik spots. These spots are a clear sign of measles.

Measles can lead to serious problems like pneumonia or brain swelling. These complications can be deadly, especially in children who are poor, malnourished, or have weak immune systems.

Doctors usually diagnose measles by looking at symptoms. They may also test a sample from the nose, throat, or urine to confirm the virus. The test is called PCR.

There is no special medicine to cure measles. Treatment focuses on helping the person feel better. This includes rest, fluids, and fever reducers. Children with measles should get vitamin A. This helps reduce the risk of serious illness and death.

The best way to prevent measles is vaccination. The MMR vaccine protects against measles, mumps, and rubella. It is safe and very effective.

---

## How Common Is Measles?

- Around 10 million people get measles each year worldwide.
- About 100,000 people die from measles every year.
- Most deaths happen in children in poor areas with low vaccination rates.

Measles is rare in the United States because most children are vaccinated. The U.S. declared measles eliminated in 2000.

But cases have gone up in recent years:

- 2019: 1,274 cases (highest since 1992)
- 2020: 13 cases (due to the COVID-19 pandemic)
- 2023: 242 cases
- 2024: 285 cases
- 2025 (as of May 22): 1,046 cases and 3 deaths

Most cases in 2025 came from outbreaks. Outbreaks happen when many people get sick in a short time and are linked to each other.

---

## Why Are Cases Going Up?

Measles spreads fast when people are not vaccinated. Reasons include:

- Parents choosing not to vaccinate their children
- Disruptions in vaccine programs
- Travel to places where measles is common

In the U.S., the number of kindergartners getting vaccinated dropped from 95.2% in 2019–2020 to 92.7% in 2023–2024.

To stop measles from spreading, at least 92% to 95% of people in a community need to be immune. This is called herd immunity.

---

## How Does Measles Spread?

- The virus spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes.
- It can stay in the air for up to 2 hours in closed spaces.
- You can catch it even if you are not in the same room as the sick person.
- The virus does not live long on dry surfaces, so touching things is not a major risk.

You can spread measles 4 days before you show symptoms and for 4 days after the rash appears.

People with weak immune systems may spread the virus longer.

Travel to areas with measles outbreaks increases your risk.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Measles has stages:

1. **Exposure**: You come into contact with the virus.
2. **Incubation**: It takes 7 to 21 days (average 11–12 days) for symptoms to start.
3. **Prodrome (early symptoms)**: Fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes. This lasts 3 to 7 days.
4. **Koplik spots**: Small white spots with red edges inside the mouth. They appear 2 days before the rash and last 1–2 days.
5. **Rash**: Starts on the face, then spreads down the body. It may look darker on people with dark skin. The rash lasts 4 to 7 days.
6. **Recovery**: Symptoms go away about 7 days after the rash starts.

The rash fades quickly. It may leave a brown mark and then peel off. Fever drops at the same time.

Some people, especially those with weak immune systems, may not get a rash. They can get very sick, including severe lung disease.

---

## How Is Measles Diagnosed?

Doctors look for:

- Koplik spots (a sure sign of measles)
- A rash that spreads from head to toe
- Symptoms like fever, cough, and red eyes
- A history of exposure or travel

Lab tests are used to confirm:

- A swab from the nose or throat
- A urine sample
- A blood test

A blood test can show if your body is fighting the virus. But it takes time to get results.

All suspected cases must be reported to local health officials, even before test results come back.

A blood test may show low white blood cells or low platelets, but this is not needed to diagnose measles.

---

## What Else Could It Be?

Other illnesses can look like measles. These include:

- Rubella (German measles)
- Scarlet fever
- Drug rash
- Roseola
- Mononucleosis
- Kawasaki disease
- Some other viruses

Here’s how to tell them apart:

- **Rubella**: No early symptoms. Swollen glands behind the ears. Fever is mild. Rash lasts only a few days.
- **Drug rash**: No cough or early symptoms. Rash appears suddenly. You likely took a new medicine.
- **Roseola**: High fever first, then rash. Rash appears at the same time the fever goes down. Rare in children over 3 years old.

---

## How Is Measles Treated?

There is no cure for measles. Care focuses on making the person more comfortable.

- Rest and fluids
- Fever reducers (like acetaminophen or ibuprofen)
- Vitamin A for children (this reduces risk of death)

Children should get vitamin A:

- Ages 12 months and older: 200,000 IU once a day for 2 days
- Ages 6 to 11 months: 100,000 IU once a day for 2 days
- Under 6 months: 50,000 IU once a day for 2 days

If a child has signs of vitamin A deficiency (like night blindness, dry eyes, dry skin), they may need another dose 2 to 4 weeks later.

If a bacterial infection develops (like pneumonia), antibiotics are used.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

- In the U.S., about 1 to 3 out of every 1,000 children with measles die.
- In poor areas, the death rate is much higher — up to 3%.
- Worldwide, about 1 in 100 children with measles dies.

Risk of death is higher in:

- Babies under 1 year old
- Children with poor nutrition
- Children with low vitamin A
- Children who get pneumonia

---

## How Can Measles Be Prevented?

- People who have had measles are immune for life.
- Babies get protection from their mother’s antibodies for the first 6 to 12 months.
- The MMR vaccine is the best protection.

The MMR vaccine is given in two doses:

- First dose: between 12 and 15 months of age
- Second dose: between 4 and 6 years of age

Two doses are needed for full protection.

The vaccine is very safe and effective:

- One dose: 95% effective
- Two doses: 96% effective

Vaccination has reduced measles cases in the U.S. by 99%.

From 2000 to 2023, vaccines saved an estimated 60.3 million lives worldwide.

Some adults may need a booster:

- People born between 1957 and 1989 may have only had one dose.
- They should get a second dose if they are at high risk (e.g., students, health workers, travelers).
- People who got a dead measles vaccine between 1963 and 1967 should get the live vaccine now.

**Important:**
- The MMR vaccine is not safe during pregnancy.
- It is not safe for people with severe immune problems.
- It should not be given to people who had a serious allergic reaction to a previous dose or a vaccine ingredient.

---

## Key Points

- Vaccinate all children with MMR unless there is a medical reason not to.
- Measles spreads very easily — over 90% of unvaccinated people who are near a sick person will get it.
- Measles causes about 100,000 deaths each year, mostly in children in poor areas.
- Treat measles with rest, fluids, and fever control. Give vitamin A to children.
- If someone is exposed to measles, give the vaccine within 3 days. If not possible, give immune globulin within 6 days.

# Persistent Erection

A persistent erection means the penis stays hard for a long time without any sexual desire or excitement. It is painful and does not go away on its own. This condition happens most often in boys aged 5 to 10 and in men aged 20 to 50.

The penis has three sponge-like areas filled with blood. When blood flows into these areas, the penis becomes hard and stiff. Muscles around the base of the penis tighten and stop blood from leaving. This keeps the penis erect.

### Did You Know...

- Erections that last a long time can become very painful.
- If a boy or man has a painful erection that lasts more than a few hours, they should see a doctor right away.

---

## Types of Persistent Erection

### Ischemic Priapism (Low-Flow)

This is the most common type. Blood gets trapped in the penis and cannot flow out. New blood with oxygen cannot enter. The penis becomes starved of oxygen. This causes severe pain if the erection lasts more than 4 hours.

The shaft of the penis may be hard, but the tip (glans) may feel soft. If not treated quickly, this can cause lasting damage. It may lead to trouble getting an erection in the future. In some cases, tissue in the penis can die.

**Stuttering priapism** is a form of ischemic priapism. It comes and goes. The penis becomes erect for a while, then returns to normal. This pattern repeats over time.

### Nonischemic Priapism (High-Flow)

This type is less common. Blood flows too freely into the penis. It usually happens after an injury to the groin or penis. The blood flows in too fast and does not drain properly.

This type is less painful. The penis stays erect but is not fully hard. It does not cause tissue damage. The chance of lasting erection problems is much lower than with ischemic priapism.

---

## What Causes a Persistent Erection?

The exact cause is not always known. But it often involves problems with blood vessels, blood cells, or nerves in the penis.

### In Men

The most common cause is medicine used to treat erectile dysfunction.

- Pills like avanafil, sildenafil, tadalafil, and vardenafil.
- Injections into the penis, such as alprostadil.

These medicines can cause blood to stay in the penis too long.

### In Boys

The most common causes are blood disorders.

- Sickle cell disease.
- Less often, leukemia.

Other causes include:

- Prostate cancer (rare in boys).
- Injury to the penis or groin.
- Spinal cord injury.
- Certain medicines, such as:
  - Some antidepressants (like trazodone).
  - Blood pressure medicines.
  - Blood thinners.
  - Steroids.
  - Lithium.
  - Antipsychotic drugs.
  - Cocaine or amphetamines.

---

## When to See a Doctor

See a doctor right away if you or your child has:

- Severe pain.
- A painful erection lasting more than 4 hours.
- A child under 10 years old with an erection.
- A recent injury to the penis or groin.
- Fever or night sweats.

All cases of persistent erection need urgent medical care.

### What the Doctor Will Do

The doctor will ask about:

- How long the erection has lasted.
- Whether there is pain.
- Any recent injury.
- Past health problems like sickle cell disease.
- All medicines taken, including illegal drugs.

The doctor will do a physical exam. This includes checking the genitals, belly, and rectum. They may also test nerve function to check for spinal cord issues.

### Tests May Be Needed

Depending on the findings, the doctor may order tests such as:

- Blood tests to check for blood disorders.
- Urine tests to check for infection.
- Special blood tests for abnormal hemoglobin (like in sickle cell disease).
- Imaging scans (MRI or CT) if a spinal problem or cancer is suspected.
- Ultrasound of the penis to see blood flow.
- X-rays of blood vessels (angiography) if injury is suspected.

Sometimes, a doctor may test for drugs if they suspect illegal drug use.

---

## Treatment

This is an emergency. Do not wait. Treatment should start as soon as possible.

### Immediate Steps You Can Try

- Apply ice to the area.
- Climb stairs or walk around.

These may help, but they are not enough. Medical care is still needed.

### Medical Treatment

- The doctor will give a painkiller if needed.
- For ischemic priapism, the doctor may:
  - Inject medicine into the penis to narrow blood vessels.
  - Use a needle and syringe to draw out trapped blood.
  - Flush the veins with salt water to clear out old blood or clots.
- These steps may be repeated if needed.
- If they do not work, surgery may be needed. A small tube (shunt) is placed to redirect blood flow and restore normal circulation.

---

## Key Points

- A persistent erection is an emergency. It needs urgent medical care.
- The most common causes are medicines for erectile dysfunction and sickle cell disease.
- Treatment usually includes medicine injected into the penis and removal of trapped blood.

# Vascular Dementia

Vascular dementia affects how you think, feel, and behave.  
It happens when the brain does not get enough blood.  
This damage can happen suddenly or slowly over time.

## Symptoms of Vascular Dementia

You may notice these changes:

- Your thoughts slow down.  
- You have trouble planning or understanding things.  
- You find it hard to focus.  
- Your mood, personality, or behavior changes.  
- You feel confused or lost in familiar places.  
- You struggle to walk or keep your balance.  
- You may have memory problems or trouble with language.  
  - Many people with vascular dementia also have Alzheimer’s disease.

These problems can make everyday tasks harder.  
Over time, you may need help with basic self-care.

## Treatments for Vascular Dementia

There is no cure for vascular dementia.  
No treatment can bring back brain cells that are already damaged.  
But some treatments can help slow the condition down.

The goal is to treat the cause of poor blood flow to the brain.  
This may help protect your brain cells and slow their loss.

You can help by:

- Eating healthy meals every day.  
- Losing weight if you are overweight.  
- Quitting smoking.  
- Getting more physical activity.  
- Drinking less alcohol.  
- Taking medicines to control high blood pressure, lower cholesterol, or prevent blood clots.

Other helpful treatments include:

- Physical therapy to improve walking and balance.  
- Occupational therapy to help with daily tasks.  
- Activities like memory cafes to stay mentally active.  
- Talking therapies to support your mental health.

These treatments can improve your quality of life and help you stay independent longer.

## Causes of Vascular Dementia

Vascular dementia is caused by poor blood flow to the brain.  
This damage can happen in several ways:

- Small blood vessels in the brain become narrow or blocked.  
- A single stroke cuts off blood to part of the brain.  
- Many small strokes, called mini strokes or transient ischaemic attacks, cause widespread but small damage.

These issues are often linked to:

- High blood pressure  
- Diabetes  
- Smoking  
- Being overweight  

Taking steps to manage these conditions and live a healthier lifestyle may lower your risk of vascular dementia.  
But we do not yet know exactly how much risk can be reduced.

# What Are Tumor Antigens?

Cancer cells often make special molecules. These molecules are usually small protein pieces called peptides. They can get into the blood or show up on the outside of the cancer cell.

Any molecule that the body’s immune system can recognize is called an antigen. When the immune system sees an antigen, it starts a response to fight it.

Scientists have found these special cancer molecules in most types of human cancer. This includes:

- Burkitt lymphoma  
- Neuroblastoma  
- Melanoma  
- Osteosarcoma  
- Kidney cancer  
- Breast cancer  
- Prostate cancer  
- Lung cancer  
- Colon cancer  

The immune system’s job is to find these cancer molecules. Then it tries to destroy the cancer cells. But in many cases, the immune response is too weak to stop the cancer from growing.

## Types of Tumor Antigens

There are two main types of tumor antigens:

- **Tumor-associated antigens (TAAs)**: These are mostly found in cancer cells, but they can also appear in some normal cells.
- **Tumor-specific antigens (TSAs)**: These are found only in cancer cells. They are not in healthy cells.

TSAs and TAAs often come from inside the cell. They show up on the outside of the cancer cell. They are usually linked to a group of genes called the major histocompatibility complex or HLA genes.

But some cancer molecules on the cell surface do not come from these genes. These may still be good targets for new cancer treatments.

### Examples of Targetable Tumor Antigens

- **Mesothelin**: This molecule is found in high levels on many cancer cells. It is also found in some normal cells that line the chest and belly.
- **Claudin 18.2**: This is seen in many stomach cancers. It is also found in some pancreatic, esophageal, ovarian, and lung cancers.

## How Tumor Antigens Are Made

Scientists are still learning how these special molecules form. Here are some possible reasons:

- A virus can add new genes to a cell. For example, the human papillomavirus adds genes that make proteins in cervical cancer.
- Harmful chemicals can change genes that control cell growth. This can create new protein shapes (called neoantigens). These new shapes are not normal. They may come from genes like ras or p53.
- Other gene changes that are not directly linked to cancer genes can still create new protein shapes on the cell surface.
- Some proteins are made in much higher amounts than normal. For example, prostate-specific antigens or melanoma-related antigens.
- Some proteins are only made during early development. These are called carcinoembryonic antigens.
- In cancer cells, the cell membrane may not work right. This can expose hidden molecules that were once hidden inside the cell.
- When cancer cells die, they can release molecules that were once locked inside the cell or its parts.

## Link Between Immune Response and Tumor Mutations

Some research shows that the immune system’s reaction in cancer patients is tied to changes in the cancer cells’ genes. These changes can create new targets for the immune system to attack.

# Diabetic Retinopathy

Diabetic retinopathy is damage to the back of the eye caused by diabetes.

## What Happens in Diabetic Retinopathy

- High blood sugar weakens small blood vessels in the retina.
- These damaged blood vessels can leak blood and fluid into the retina.
- New blood vessels may grow in the retina. These new vessels are weak and can bleed or cause scarring.
- Scarring can pull the retina away from the back of the eye. This is called retinal detachment.
- If the center of the retina (the macula) swells from fluid, vision becomes blurry.

## Who Is at Risk

- Almost everyone with diabetes will have some eye changes after several years.
- People with high blood pressure are at much higher risk.
- Pregnancy can make retinopathy worse.
- Type 1 diabetes often leads to retinopathy about 5 years after diagnosis.
- Type 2 diabetes may go undetected for years. So retinopathy may already be present when the diagnosis is made.

## How Vision Is Affected

The amount of vision loss depends on:

- How well blood sugar is controlled.
- How well blood pressure is controlled.
- How long a person has had diabetes.

## Types of Diabetic Retinopathy

### Nonproliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (Early Stage)

- Small blood vessels in the retina leak fluid or blood.
- The retina may swell in some areas.
- Swelling can cause blurry vision or blind spots.
- If the swelling happens near the center of the retina, central vision becomes blurry.
- This condition is called macular edema.
- Vision loss may not happen even with serious damage.

### Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (Later Stage)

- Damage to the retina causes new blood vessels to grow.
- These new blood vessels are weak and can bleed into the eye.
- Scarring from these vessels can pull the retina away from the back of the eye.
- This can cause sudden, severe vision loss.
- Bleeding into the jelly-like center of the eye (vitreous) can block vision.
- Scarring can also cause a type of glaucoma called neovascular glaucoma.
- This type of glaucoma happens when new blood vessels block fluid drainage in the eye.
- This raises pressure inside the eye and can cause pain and vision loss.

### Symptoms of Proliferative Retinopathy

- Blurry vision.
- Floaters (dark spots or strings in your vision).
- Flashing lights.
- Sudden, severe, painless vision loss.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors use several tools to check for diabetic retinopathy:

- **Eye exam with dilated pupils**: The doctor uses a special light to look at the back of your eye.
- **Fluorescein angiography**: A dye is injected into your arm. It travels to the eye. A camera takes pictures of the blood vessels in the retina. This shows where blood is leaking and where blood flow is poor.
- **Optical coherence tomography (OCT)**: This is a scan that shows detailed images of the retina. It helps measure swelling in the macula and check how well treatment is working.

## How It Is Treated

### Control Blood Sugar and Blood Pressure

- Keeping blood sugar and blood pressure under control is the most important step.
- This helps slow or stop damage to the retina.

### Treat Macular Edema (Swelling in the Center of the Retina)

- Eye injections of special medicines are used.
- These medicines are called anti-VEGF drugs. Examples include ranibizumab, bevacizumab, aflibercept, and faricimab.
- These drugs reduce swelling and can improve vision.
- Some people get corticosteroid implants. These slowly release medicine into the eye.
- Dexamethasone implants help people with ongoing swelling.
- Fluocinolone implants are available in some countries for people with diabetes-related swelling.

### Laser Treatment

- A laser beam is aimed at the retina.
- This helps stop abnormal blood vessels from growing.
- It also reduces leakage from damaged blood vessels.
- Laser treatment may need to be done more than once.
- It rarely improves vision, but it often prevents further vision loss.

### Vitrectomy (Surgery)

- This is done if there is a lot of bleeding into the eye.
- The surgeon removes blood from the jelly-like center of the eye.
- This surgery can improve vision after bleeding or retinal detachment.
- It may also help treat macular edema.

## How to Prevent Diabetic Retinopathy

- Keep blood sugar levels under control.
- Keep blood pressure at normal levels.
- Have a yearly eye exam.
- During the exam, drops are used to widen the pupil so the doctor can see the back of the eye.
- Pregnant women with diabetes should have eye exams every 3 months.

For more information, visit the **National Eye Institute** website.  
This site offers helpful resources about eye health in both English and Spanish.  
It includes information for adults and children.  
You can search for topics using simple keywords.

# Sinusitis (Sinus Infection)

Sinusitis is when the spaces in your face around your nose become inflamed. It often happens after a cold or flu.

## Symptoms of Sinusitis

You may have:
- Pain or pressure in your face, especially around your cheeks, eyes, or forehead
- A stuffy or runny nose
- A reduced sense of smell
- Thick, green or yellow mucus from your nose
- A high temperature (fever)
- A headache
- Toothache
- Bad breath
- A cough
- A feeling of fullness or pressure in your ears
- Snoring at night
- A nasal-sounding voice when you speak

Young children may also:
- Be irritable
- Have trouble feeding
- Breathe through their mouth

## When to See a Pharmacist

Go to a pharmacist if:
- You think you have sinusitis
- Your child is 12 years old or older and you think they have sinusitis

A pharmacist can:
- Give you the same treatments a doctor would
- Offer advice
- Direct you to other medical help if needed

👉 [Find a pharmacy]

## When to See a Doctor

See a doctor if:
- You or your child has sinusitis symptoms and they do not improve after 7 days of treatment from a pharmacist or doctor
- You do not get better after 3 weeks of treating symptoms at home
- You keep getting sinusitis
- Your child is 11 years old or younger

## When to Get Urgent Help

Call 111 or get help online if:
- You feel very unwell
- Painkillers do not help or your symptoms get worse
- You have a weak immune system (for example, if you are having chemotherapy)

Call 111 if you need advice about a child under 5 years old.

👉 [Get help from 111 online]

## How to Treat Sinusitis at Home

You can often treat mild sinusitis at home by:
- Getting plenty of rest
- Drinking lots of fluids
- Taking painkillers like paracetamol or ibuprofen
  - Do not give aspirin to children under 16
- Avoiding things that trigger your allergies
- Not smoking
- Cleaning your nose with a salt water solution

### How to Make and Use a Salt Water Solution

1. Boil about 570 millilitres of water (1 pint). Let it cool.
2. Add 1 teaspoon of salt and 1 teaspoon of bicarbonate of soda to the water.
3. Wash your hands.
4. Stand over a sink. Cup your hand and pour a small amount of the solution into it.
5. Sniff the water into one nostril at a time. Breathe through your mouth. Let the water come out through the other nostril or into the sink.
   - Try not to let the water go down your throat.
6. Repeat steps 1 to 5 up to 3 times a day.
   - Make a fresh solution each time until your nose feels better.

If you have a high temperature or feel too unwell to do normal activities, stay at home. Avoid close contact with others until you feel better.

## Medical Treatments for Sinusitis

A pharmacist or doctor may prescribe:
- Steroid nasal sprays or drops to reduce swelling in your sinuses
  - You may need to use these for several months
- Antihistamines if allergies are causing your symptoms

Antibiotics are rarely needed. Most cases are caused by viruses, not bacteria.

## When You Might Need a Specialist

A doctor may refer you to an ear, nose, and throat specialist if:
- You still have symptoms after 3 months of treatment
- You keep getting sinusitis
- Your symptoms only affect one side of your face

The specialist may suggest surgery for some people.

### Surgery for Sinusitis

The surgery is called functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS).

You will be asleep during the surgery (under general anaesthetic).

The surgeon will:
- Remove some blocked tissue
- Or use a small balloon to open up the blocked sinuses, then remove the balloon

This helps improve airflow and drainage in your sinuses.

# Ulcerative Colitis

Ulcerative colitis is a long-term condition that causes inflammation and sores in the lining of the large intestine.  
It often causes bloody diarrhea.  
Some people also have joint pain or skin problems.  
People with this condition have a higher chance of getting colon cancer over time.  
Doctors diagnose it using a special camera test called colonoscopy.  
Treatment includes several types of medicine.  
In some cases, surgery may be needed.

---

## What Happens in Ulcerative Colitis?

The condition usually starts in the rectum.  
It can stay in the rectum only.  
Or it can spread up the large intestine.  
In rare cases, it affects most of the large bowel at once.  

The inflammation affects the inner layers of the colon wall.  
There is a clear line between healthy tissue and damaged tissue.  
In severe cases, the deeper muscle layer may also be involved.  

At first, the lining of the colon looks red, swollen, and fragile.  
The normal blood vessel pattern is lost.  
There may be small spots of bleeding.  
In severe cases, large sores form.  
These sores leak pus and blood.  
Small areas of healing tissue may stick up like islands.  
These are called pseudopolyps.  
Fistulas (tunnels between organs) and abscesses (pockets of infection) do not happen.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people have episodes of bloody diarrhea.  
These episodes come and go.  
There may be times when no symptoms are present.  

An episode often starts slowly.  
You may feel a strong need to pass stool.  
You may have mild cramps in the lower belly.  
You may see blood and mucus in your stool.  
Some cases begin after a stomach infection, such as from amoebas or bacteria.

If the problem is only in the rectum and lower colon:  
- Your stool may be normal or hard.  
- You may pass mucus with blood and white blood cells between bowel movements.  
- You usually do not have fever or other body-wide symptoms.

If the problem spreads higher in the colon:  
- You may have more than ten bowel movements a day.  
- The cramps can be very painful.  
- You may feel constant pressure in the rectum.  
- This does not go away at night.  
- The stool may be watery.  
- It often contains mucus, blood, and pus.

In rare cases, a serious form called toxic colitis can happen.  
It starts suddenly with violent diarrhea.  
You may have a high fever of 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit).  
You may have severe belly pain.  
You may have signs of infection in the belly, such as tenderness when touched.  
You may feel very ill overall.

Systemic symptoms are more common when the disease affects a large part of the colon.  
These include:  
- Feeling tired  
- Fever  
- Low red blood cell count (anemia)  
- Loss of appetite  
- Weight loss  

Joint pain and skin problems are more likely when you have these body-wide symptoms.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will check your stool.  
This helps rule out infections.  
A sigmoidoscopy is done.  
A small camera is used to look inside the lower colon.  
A small sample of tissue (biopsy) is taken for testing.

---

## How Is It Treated?

You can manage symptoms with diet changes and a medicine called loperamide.  
But do not use loperamide during a severe flare-up.  

Medicines used depend on how bad the disease is.  
Common treatments include:  
- 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA)  
- Steroid medicines  
- Other drugs based on your symptoms and disease severity  
- Medicines that affect the immune system (antimetabolites)  
- Biologic drugs  
- A Janus kinase inhibitor  
- A sphingosine 1-phosphate receptor modulator  

Surgery may be needed in some cases.

For details on specific medicines and dosing, see the section on Medications for Inflammatory Bowel Disease.  
For more guidance, refer to the American College of Gastroenterology’s 2019 guidelines for managing ulcerative colitis in adults.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Ulcerative colitis is a long-term condition.  
It comes and goes.  
Some people have only one attack and recover fully.  
But most have repeated flare-ups and periods of feeling better.

In a few people, the first attack becomes very severe.  
This can lead to heavy bleeding, a hole in the colon, or serious infection.  

People with disease only in the rectum (ulcerative proctitis) have the best outlook.  
They rarely need surgery.  
Their life expectancy is normal.  
But symptoms can be hard to control.  

Even if the disease starts in the rectum, it can spread up the colon over time.  
So doctors wait at least six months before calling it “localized.”  
If it spreads later, it is often harder to treat and more severe.

---

## Key Facts

- Ulcerative colitis starts in the rectum.  
- It can spread up the colon in a continuous way.  
- There are no normal patches of tissue between healthy and diseased areas.  

- Symptoms include cramps and bloody diarrhea.  
- These come and go over time.  

- Complications can include a severe form of colitis.  
- This can lead to a hole in the colon.  
- Long-term, the risk of colon cancer is higher.  

- For mild disease, use 5-ASA medicine as a suppository or by mouth.  

- For more widespread disease, use:  
  - High-dose steroid medicine  
  - Immune system drugs (like azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine)  
  - Biologic drugs (like adalimumab, infliximab, or vedolizumab)  
  - Tofacitinib, upadacitinib, or ozanimod  

- For severe, life-threatening disease:  
  - Use high-dose IV steroids or cyclosporine  
  - Add antibiotics (like metronidazole or ciprofloxacin)  
  - Use infliximab  
  - Surgery (removal of the colon) may be needed  

- About one in three people with widespread disease will eventually need surgery.

---

# Idiopathic Environmental Intolerance

This condition causes a range of symptoms that come and go. They seem to happen after exposure to low levels of common substances in the environment. These can include chemicals in the air, on surfaces, or in food. Some people also report symptoms after being near electromagnetic fields, like those from cell phones or Wi-Fi.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms can include:
- A fast heartbeat
- Chest pain
- Sweating
- Trouble breathing
- Feeling very tired
- Skin flushing (redness)
- Dizziness
- Nausea
- A feeling of choking
- Shaking
- Numbness
- Coughing
- Hoarseness
- Trouble focusing or thinking clearly

These symptoms do not always happen when a person is exposed to a substance. Sometimes they happen even when the exposure level is low. Other times, they happen even when the person has been around the substance before without problems.

## What Might Cause This?

Doctors do not know the exact cause. Some people think it may be linked to mental health. For example, it might be a type of somatic symptom disorder or an anxiety problem. Others think it could be a rare kind of allergic reaction. But there is no clear pattern in the body’s immune system that proves this.

Blood tests do not show consistent signs of immune system activity. This makes it hard to confirm a physical cause.

## Who Is Affected?

This condition is more common in women than in men.  
About 4 out of 10 people with chronic fatigue syndrome also have this condition.  
About 1 in 6 people with fibromyalgia also have this condition.

## What Triggers the Symptoms?

Common triggers include:
- Alcohol and drugs
- Caffeine and food additives
- Smells from carpets or furniture
- Fumes from fuel or car exhaust
- Paints and other building materials
- Perfumes and scented products
- Pesticides and weed killers
- Mobile phones and other wireless devices

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your symptoms and history. They may suspect this condition if:
- Your symptoms come back after being around a certain chemical.
- Your symptoms return at levels much lower than what you or others usually tolerate.
- Your symptoms go away when you leave the place where you feel unwell.
- Your symptoms happen after exposure to many different chemicals that are not related.

To rule out other causes, doctors may check for:
- Allergies (using skin or blood tests)
- Autoimmune diseases
- Mental health issues like depression or anxiety
- Building-related illnesses (sick building syndrome)

A doctor or mental health expert may do an evaluation if needed.

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure. But treatment can help you feel better and live a more normal life.

### Avoiding Triggers
You may try to avoid things you think cause your symptoms.  
But this can be hard. Many of these substances are everywhere.  
Also, the real cause may not be the thing you are avoiding. So avoiding it may not help.

### Psychotherapy
Talking with a mental health professional can help.  
The goal is not to say your symptoms are “all in your head.”  
The goal is to help you manage your symptoms and improve your daily life.

### Stay Connected
Avoiding people and places because of your symptoms can make things worse.  
Staying socially active is important for your well-being.

You are not alone. Support and treatment can make a real difference.

# Bronchiectasis – Simple Guide

## What is bronchiectasis?

Bronchiectasis is a long-term lung condition. It happens when the airways in your lungs are damaged. This damage makes it hard to clear mucus from your lungs.

You may have a cough that lasts a long time. You may also cough up a lot of mucus every day. You may get chest infections often.

## Symptoms of bronchiectasis

The main signs of bronchiectasis are:

- A cough that does not go away.
- Coughing up a lot of mucus every day. The mucus can be clear, white, yellow, or green.
- Getting chest infections often. These make you feel worse for days or weeks. You may feel tired, unwell, or have a fever.

Other possible symptoms include:

- Wheezing when you breathe.
- Feeling short of breath.
- Crackling, snoring, or squeaky sounds when you breathe.
- Feeling very tired.
- Coughing up blood, even just a few spots or streaks.
- Chest pain when you breathe or cough.

> **Note:** A cough or mucus can also be caused by other things like colds or chest infections. But if it lasts more than 3 weeks, it’s worth seeing a doctor.

---

## When to see a doctor

### See your GP if:

- You think you might have bronchiectasis.
- You’ve had a cough for more than 3 weeks.

### Call your GP right away or use NHS 111 if:

- Your cough is very bad or getting worse fast.
- You are coughing up a lot of mucus every day.
- You see blood in your mucus – even just a few spots or streaks.
- You feel short of breath, or more short of breath than usual.
- You already have bronchiectasis and now have signs of a chest infection, like a high temperature or chest pain when you breathe or cough.

You can call 111 or get help online at [nhs.uk/111](https://www.nhs.uk/111)

### Call 999 or go to A&E if:

- You are coughing up more than just a few spots of blood. This could mean serious bleeding in your lungs.
- You are struggling to breathe. You are gasping, choking, or can’t speak.

> **Find your nearest A&E** – search online or ask for help.

### A&E safety tips

- Do not drive yourself to A&E. Ask someone to take you. Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.
- Bring all your medicines with you.

---

## How bronchiectasis is diagnosed

Your GP will listen to your chest and ask about your symptoms.

They may do tests such as:

- Testing a sample of your mucus to check for infection.
- A chest X-ray.
- A breathing test to check how well your lungs work.
- Blood tests.

If these tests suggest bronchiectasis, you will be referred to a specialist. The specialist will do a CT scan to confirm the diagnosis.

You may also need more tests to find out what caused the condition.

---

## Treatment for bronchiectasis

Bronchiectasis cannot usually be cured. But treatment can help you feel better and stop your symptoms from getting worse.

You will work with a team of healthcare professionals. This may include your GP, a nurse, a physiotherapist, and sometimes a lung specialist.

You will have check-ups at least once a year. Your team will help you make a plan to manage your condition.

You may also need treatment for any other health problems that caused bronchiectasis.

### Clearing mucus from your lungs

A physiotherapist will teach you breathing exercises. These help you clear mucus from your lungs and airways.

They may also suggest a small handheld device. You breathe into it. It uses vibrations to loosen mucus.

You should do these exercises every day. This helps control your cough and lowers your risk of chest infections.

If your mucus is thick and hard to cough up, your team may suggest using a nebuliser. This machine turns a salt solution into a mist. You breathe it in to help loosen the mucus.

If you have trouble breathing, you may be offered pulmonary rehabilitation. This is a course led by a physiotherapist. It includes exercise classes and advice on managing your condition.

### Medicines

When you are unwell or your symptoms change, your doctor may ask you to give a sample of your mucus.

They will test it for infection. If there is an infection, you will need antibiotics.

You may be given a supply of antibiotics to keep at home. This is called a rescue pack. Your team will tell you when to take them.

If you get more than 3 chest infections a year, your specialist may suggest taking antibiotics every day to prevent infections.

You may also be given inhalers to help you breathe easier.

### Other treatments

If your symptoms are severe and medicines do not help, you may be offered:

- Oxygen therapy – breathing in oxygen through a mask or tube.
- Surgery – to fix damaged parts of your lungs.
- A lung transplant – in rare cases.

---

## What you can do to help yourself

You can take steps to feel better and avoid chest infections.

### Do:

- Exercise regularly. This keeps you fit and helps clear your lungs. Ask your care team for advice on safe exercises.
- Eat a healthy, balanced diet. Stay at a healthy weight. This helps with breathing and lowers your risk of infection.
- Wash your hands often. This helps stop germs spreading.
- Stay away from people who have colds, flu, or other infections.
- Get your yearly flu vaccine. Also get the pneumococcal vaccine and the COVID-19 vaccine when your GP recommends it.

### Don’t:

- Do not smoke. If you need help quitting, ask your GP or nurse. They can support you.

---

## How bronchiectasis affects your life

Bronchiectasis affects people in different ways. How it affects you depends on how bad your symptoms are and how often you get chest infections.

It is common to have bronchiectasis along with other lung conditions, such as asthma or COPD.

For some people, the condition gets worse over time. They may have serious breathing problems that affect daily life. In rare cases, it can be life-threatening.

But for others, symptoms are mild. With good treatment, they can live well and stay active.

---

## Support and help

You are not alone. There are many ways to get support.

### Asthma and Lung UK

This charity offers information and support for people with lung conditions, including bronchiectasis.

- Website: [www.asthmaandlung.org.uk](https://www.asthmaandlung.org.uk)
- Helpline: 0300 222 5800
- [Support in your area](https://www.asthmaandlung.org.uk/support)
- [Living with a lung condition](https://www.asthmaandlung.org.uk/living-with-lung-condition)

You can also join a local support group or connect with others online. Talking to people who understand your condition can help.

# Psoriasis

Psoriasis is a long-term skin condition that causes red, raised patches covered in silvery scales.  
It is not contagious.  
The skin cells grow too fast and build up on the surface.  
This causes thick, scaly patches that can be itchy or sore.

## What Causes Psoriasis?

The exact cause is not fully known.  
But it happens when the body’s immune system attacks healthy skin cells.  
This leads to fast skin cell growth and inflammation.

Genes play a big role.  
If someone in your family has psoriasis, you are more likely to get it.  
Certain genes are linked to a higher risk.

Triggers can start or worsen psoriasis.  
These include:
- Skin injuries (like cuts, burns, or scratches)
- Sunburn
- Infections (especially strep throat)
- HIV
- Stress
- Drinking alcohol
- Smoking
- Being overweight
- Some medicines (like beta-blockers, lithium, and certain arthritis or blood pressure drugs)

## What Does Psoriasis Look Like?

Psoriasis can appear in many ways.  
The most common type is called plaque psoriasis.  
It shows up as:
- Red, raised patches
- Covered in thick, silvery scales
- Usually on the elbows, knees, scalp, lower back, and buttocks
- Sometimes on the nails, genitals, or inside the mouth

The patches can be:
- Pink or red on light skin
- Darker, purplish, or gray on dark skin

The patches may:
- Be itchy or painful
- Crack and bleed
- Spread and join together

Other types of psoriasis include:
- **Guttate psoriasis**: Small, drop-like spots on the trunk, often after a throat infection
- **Inverse psoriasis**: Smooth, red patches in skin folds (like under the arms, behind the knees, or under the breasts)
- **Palmoplantar psoriasis**: Thick, scaly patches on the palms or soles
- **Pustular psoriasis**: White, pus-filled bumps on the hands or feet
- **Erythrodermic psoriasis**: A rare, severe form where most of the body turns red and peels
- **Nail psoriasis**: Pits, ridges, thickening, or nails that separate from the nail bed

## How Is Psoriasis Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose psoriasis by looking at the skin.  
They check the shape, color, and location of the patches.  
They may ask about your medical history and family history.

A skin biopsy is rarely needed.  
It may be done if the rash looks unusual or does not respond to treatment.

## How Is Psoriasis Treated?

Treatment depends on how bad the psoriasis is and where it is on the body.

### For Mild Psoriasis:
- Use creams or ointments on the skin
- Common options include:
  - Moisturizers (emollients)
  - Salicylic acid (to remove scales)
  - Coal tar (to reduce scaling and itching)
  - Corticosteroids (to reduce swelling and redness)
  - Vitamin D3 analogs (to slow skin cell growth)
  - Calcineurin inhibitors (for sensitive areas like the face or groin)
  - Tazarotene, roflumilast, or tapinarof (newer topical medicines)

### For Moderate to Severe Psoriasis:
- Use stronger treatments
- Options include:
  - Light therapy (ultraviolet light)
  - Oral medicines (like methotrexate, retinoids, or cyclosporine)
  - Biologic drugs (injected or infused medicines that target the immune system)
  - Small molecule drugs (oral medicines that block immune signals)

### For Specific Types:
- **Pustular psoriasis**: Treat with oral retinoids or light therapy
- **Inverse psoriasis**: Use mild steroid creams or ointments
- **Nail psoriasis**: Often needs systemic treatment (like biologics)
- **Erythrodermic psoriasis**: Needs urgent care, often in the hospital

### Light Therapy (Phototherapy):
- Uses ultraviolet light to slow skin cell growth
- Can be used when creams do not work
- Not for everyone — especially those with a history of skin cancer

## Psoriatic Arthritis

Some people with psoriasis also develop joint problems.  
This is called psoriatic arthritis.  
It can cause:
- Swollen, painful joints
- Stiffness, especially in the morning
- Tiredness
- Damage to joints over time

It can affect any joint, but often the fingers, toes, knees, or spine.  
Early treatment helps prevent long-term damage.

## How Common Is Psoriasis?

Psoriasis affects people of all ages and skin colors.  
But it may be under-diagnosed in people with dark skin.  
It can start at any age, but most often appears between ages 16 to 22 or 57 to 60.

Estimates vary:
- In children: 0 to 1.4% have psoriasis
- In adults: 0.5 to 11.4% have psoriasis

## How Does Psoriasis Affect Daily Life?

Psoriasis is not life-threatening.  
But it can affect your quality of life.  
You may feel self-conscious about your skin.  
It can take a lot of time to treat and care for the skin.  
You may need to wash clothes and bedding often.  
Some people feel stressed or sad because of how they look.

## Key Points

- Psoriasis is a long-term skin condition caused by the immune system.
- It runs in families and can be triggered by injury, infection, stress, or certain medicines.
- The most common type is plaque psoriasis: red, scaly patches on elbows, knees, scalp, and lower back.
- Other types include guttate, inverse, pustular, erythrodermic, and nail psoriasis.
- Psoriatic arthritis affects 5 to 30% of people with psoriasis and can cause joint damage.
- Diagnosis is based on how the skin looks and where it is.
- Mild psoriasis is treated with creams and ointments.
- Moderate to severe psoriasis may need oral medicines, injections, or light therapy.
- Light therapy is an option for people who do not want systemic medicines.
- Early treatment helps prevent joint damage and improves quality of life.

## Useful Resources

- **Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI)**: An online tool to measure how much of your body is affected
- **American Academy of Dermatology – Psoriasis Guidelines**: Trusted guidelines from top skin doctors
- **National Psoriasis Foundation**: Offers support, treatment info, and community groups
