# Allergic Conjunctivitis

Allergic conjunctivitis is when the eye becomes inflamed because of an allergy to something in the air.

## What Is the Conjunctiva?

The conjunctiva is the thin, clear layer that covers the white part of the eye and lines the inside of the eyelids.  
It has many immune system cells called mast cells.  
When you are exposed to an allergen, these mast cells release chemicals.  
These chemicals cause swelling and irritation in the eye.  
The reaction can last a short time or go on for a long time.

## Types of Allergic Conjunctivitis

There are several types of allergic eye problems:

### Seasonal Allergic Conjunctivitis  
This happens during certain times of the year.  
It is often caused by pollen from trees, grasses, or weeds.  
It usually starts in spring or early summer.  
Weed pollen can cause symptoms in summer and early fall.

### Perennial Allergic Conjunctivitis  
This happens all year long.  
It is most often caused by dust mites or animal dander.  
It is also called atopic conjunctivitis or atopic keratoconjunctivitis.

### Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis  
This is a more serious type.  
It often affects boys between the ages of 5 and 20.  
It is more common in people who also have eczema, asthma, or seasonal allergies.  
It comes back every spring and goes away in the fall and winter.  
Many children grow out of it by early adulthood.  
The cause is not always clear.

> **Note:** Inflammation from a virus or bacteria is not allergic. This is called infectious conjunctivitis.

## Symptoms

All types of allergic conjunctivitis cause strong itching and burning in both eyes.  
Symptoms usually affect both eyes the same.  
But sometimes one eye is worse than the other.

The eyes become red and may swell.  
The eye surface can look puffy.  
The eyelids may also itch badly.  
Rubbing or scratching can make the eyelid skin red, swollen, and wrinkled.

### Symptoms of Seasonal and Year-Round Allergic Conjunctivitis  
You may have a lot of thin, watery tears.  
Sometimes the tears are stringy.  
Your vision usually stays clear.  
You may also have an itchy, runny nose.

### Symptoms of Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis  
The eye discharge is thick, stringy, and sticky.  
This type can affect the cornea — the clear front part of the eye.  
In some people, small open sores (called corneal ulcers) form.  
These sores cause deep eye pain when light shines in.  
This is called photophobia.  
In rare cases, vision may be permanently affected.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor will look at your eyes and ask about your symptoms.  
They will check how your eyes look.  
Most of the time, no special tests are needed.  
The doctor can tell it is allergic conjunctivitis just by seeing the signs.

## How Is It Treated?

There are several ways to treat allergic conjunctivitis.

### Eye Drops
- Antihistamine eye drops like ketotifen can help mild cases.  
- These drops are available without a prescription.  
- If ketotifen does not work well, your doctor may prescribe stronger antihistamine drops like olopatadine or cetirizine.  
- Mast cell stabilizer drops like nedocromil may also help.  
- For long-term symptoms, cyclosporine eye drops may be used.

### Pain Relief
- Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory eye drops like ketorolac can ease pain.

### Stronger Anti-Inflammatory Drops
- Corticosteroid eye drops are very strong.  
- They reduce swelling fast.  
- But they should not be used for more than a few weeks.  
- They must be used only under close care from an eye doctor.  
- Long use can raise pressure inside the eye.  
- This can lead to glaucoma.  
- It can also cause cataracts.  
- It may increase the risk of eye infections.

### Oral Antihistamines
- Pills like fexofenadine, cetirizine, or hydroxyzine can help.  
- They are especially useful if your nose, ears, or throat are also itchy or runny.  
- These pills help with allergy symptoms all over the body.

### Other Helpful Steps
- Avoid things that cause your allergies.  
  This includes pollen, dust, and animal dander.  
- Use cold compresses on your eyes.  
- Use chilled artificial tears to soothe your eyes.

> **Important:** Always follow your doctor’s advice when using eye drops.  
> Do not use steroid eye drops for long without checking in with your eye doctor.

# Appendicitis – Simple Guide

## What is appendicitis?

Appendicitis is when the appendix, a small pouch attached to your large intestine, becomes inflamed and infected. It is not needed by your body, so it is safe to remove.

## Symptoms of appendicitis

- Pain usually starts in the middle of your tummy, near your belly button.
- After a few hours, the pain moves to the lower right side of your tummy.
- The pain gets worse over time.
- It hurts more when you move, cough, or press on your tummy.
- You may feel better when you pull your knees up to your chest.

Other possible symptoms include:

- Feeling sick or being sick
- Losing your appetite
- A high temperature (fever)
- Constipation or diarrhoea
- Needing to pee more than usual
- Sudden confusion (more common in older people)

Some people, especially young children, older adults, and pregnant women, may not have the usual pain. Their symptoms can be milder or in a different place.

If the appendix bursts, the pain may suddenly get better for a short time. Then the pain returns and spreads across your whole tummy. It becomes very painful to move.

## When to get help

### Call your doctor right away or use NHS 111 if:

- Your tummy pain is getting worse or does not go away
- The pain moves to the lower right side of your tummy

You can call 111 or get help online.

### Call 999 or go to A&E if:

- You have severe tummy pain
- You feel confused
- Your skin looks blotchy or paler than normal (on brown or black skin, check the palms of your hands or soles of your feet)
- You are having trouble breathing

These could be signs of a serious infection called sepsis.

> **Find your nearest A&E**

### A&E safety tips

- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 for an ambulance.
- Bring all your medicines with you.

## How doctors diagnose appendicitis

Doctors will check your tummy for pain and swelling.

You will need to go to hospital for tests. These may include:

- Blood tests
- A urine test
- An ultrasound scan or CT scan to look at your appendix
- A pregnancy test if you could be pregnant

There is no single test that always shows appendicitis. Symptoms can be like other conditions. Sometimes doctors wait a few hours to see how your symptoms change.

If doctors think you likely have appendicitis, or if your appendix may have burst, they may suggest surgery right away instead of waiting for more tests.

## Treatment for appendicitis

The usual treatment is surgery to remove the appendix. This is called an appendectomy.

### Surgery details

- You will be asleep during the operation (under general anaesthetic).
- Most surgeries are done using keyhole surgery. The surgeon makes small cuts and uses a camera and thin tools.
- In some cases, a larger cut is needed (open surgery).
- The surgeon removes the appendix and cleans the area if it has burst.
- The cuts are closed with stitches, clips, or glue.

### Antibiotics instead of surgery?

In some cases, doctors may treat appendicitis with antibiotics instead of surgery. This is only if:

- The infection has not spread
- Surgery is risky for you

If you have a lump in your tummy caused by the inflamed appendix (called an appendix mass), you will likely get antibiotics first. Surgery may be done a few weeks later if symptoms continue.

## Recovering from appendicitis

Most people feel better in 1 to 2 weeks. Recovery may take longer if the appendix burst.

### After surgery

- You will have small cuts on your tummy.
- Most stitches dissolve on their own and do not need to be removed.
- You may have pain in your tummy or around the cuts.
- You may have constipation or diarrhoea for a few days.

### In hospital

- You will rest in a recovery room, then move to a ward.
- You will get pain relief medicine.
- If you had keyhole surgery, you may go home the next day.
- If you had open surgery or complications, you may stay in hospital for a few days.

You can go home when doctors are sure you can eat, drink, and pass a stool.

You may be offered a follow-up appointment, but this is not always needed.

### At home

#### Do:

- Start your normal activities when you feel ready. You may need 1 to 2 weeks off work or school. Some jobs may need more time.
- Take painkillers if needed.
- Follow instructions for caring for your wounds.
- Be careful when showering. Change your dressings if they get wet.
- If you are constipated, eat high-fibre foods and drink plenty of fluids. You can use a mild laxative (ask a pharmacist for advice).
- If you are given antibiotics, take the full course as directed.
- Contact your hospital, GP, or nurse if you need help with recovery.

#### Don’t:

- Do not do sports or heavy lifting until you are fully recovered. Ask your doctor for advice.
- Do not drive until you can use a car safely and comfortably, including stopping quickly in an emergency.

## Risks if the appendix bursts

If the appendix bursts, it can cause serious problems:

- Infection in the lining of your tummy (peritonitis)
- A life-threatening reaction to infection (sepsis)
- A painful collection of pus (abscess)
- A blockage in your bowel
- Problems during pregnancy

These issues need urgent treatment with surgery and antibiotics. Do not delay getting help if you think your appendix may have burst.

# Salivary Gland Tumors – Simple Explanation

Most tumors in the salivary glands are not cancer. They usually happen in the parotid glands. The most common sign is a painless lump in the salivary gland area. Doctors often use a fine-needle aspiration biopsy to check the lump. Imaging tests like CT and MRI can help show where the tumor is and how big it is.

If the tumor is cancer, treatment usually includes surgery and radiation. The long-term outcome depends on how aggressive the cancer is.

---

## Where Salivary Glands Are

There are three main types of salivary glands:
- The large parotid glands (in front of the ears)
- The submandibular glands (under the jaw)
- The minor salivary glands (throughout the mouth and throat)
- The sublingual glands (under the tongue)

About 85% of salivary gland tumors happen in the parotid glands.  
About 10% happen in the submandibular glands.  
About 5% happen in the minor glands.  
Only about 1% happen in the sublingual glands.

Most tumors (75 to 80%) are not cancer. They grow slowly, are movable, painless, and usually appear as a single lump under the skin or inside the mouth. Some feel soft if they are filled with fluid. Most feel firm.

---

## What to Watch For: Symptoms

- A painless lump in the face, neck, or mouth is the most common sign.
- Most benign and cancerous tumors do not hurt at first.
- If the tumor is cancer, it may grow into nearby nerves. This can cause:
  - Pain
  - Numbness
  - Tingling
  - Weakness in the face
  - Loss of muscle control

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Salivary Gland Tumors

- **Fine-needle aspiration biopsy**: A thin needle is used to take a small sample from the lump. This helps doctors see what kind of cells are in the tumor.
- **CT scan or MRI**: These imaging tests show the size and location of the tumor. They also help check if the cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes or other parts of the body, such as the lungs, liver, bones, or brain.

Doctors often do these tests before deciding on treatment.

---

## How Salivary Gland Tumors Are Treated

### For Benign Tumors (Not Cancer)
- Surgery is the main treatment.
- If the surgery does not remove all the tumor, it may come back.

### For Malignant Tumors (Cancer)
- Surgery is the main treatment.
- Radiation therapy is often added after surgery, especially for aggressive cancers.
- Chemotherapy is not usually helpful unless there is a specific genetic change in the cancer. It may be used with radiation for high-grade cancers.

#### Specific Types of Cancer

**Mucoepidermoid Carcinoma**
- Treatment: Wide surgery to remove all cancer. Radiation after surgery for high-grade tumors.
- Low-grade type: 5-year survival rate is over 90%.
- High-grade type: 5-year survival rate is less than 50%.
- If cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes, those nodes are removed and radiation is given.

**Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma**
- Treatment: Wide surgery to remove the tumor.
- This cancer often grows along nerves, so it can come back in the same area.
- Spread to lymph nodes is rare, so lymph node treatment is not usually needed.
- Survival rates at 5 and 10 years are good.
- But the risk of dying from this cancer keeps rising over 30 years because it can spread late to the lungs.

**Acinic Cell Carcinoma**
- Prognosis is good after wide surgery.

**Carcinoma Ex Pleomorphic Adenoma**
- Treatment: Surgery to remove the entire tumor in the parotid gland.
- If cancer has spread to lymph nodes in the neck, a neck dissection is done.
- Some patients without lymph node spread may still get a neck dissection, depending on the case.

All surgeries aim to protect the facial nerve. This nerve controls facial movement. It is only removed if the tumor is directly attached to it.

---

## Key Points

- Only 20 to 25% of salivary gland tumors are cancer.
- The parotid gland is the most common site for these tumors.
- Cancerous tumors are usually firm, lumpy, and may stick to nearby tissues.
- Pain and nerve problems (like numbness or weakness) are common with cancer.
- If cancer is suspected, do a biopsy and imaging tests like CT or MRI.
- Treatment is usually surgery, and sometimes radiation therapy for certain cancers.

# Anal Fissure

An anal fissure is a small tear or sore in the lining of the anus. The anus is the opening at the end of the bowel where stool leaves the body.

## What Causes an Anal Fissure?

- A hard or large bowel movement can cause a tear.
- Frequent loose bowel movements may also lead to a fissure.
- Rarely, anal sex can cause a tear.
- The muscle around the anus (called the anal sphincter) may tighten too much. This spasm makes pain worse and slows healing.

Fissures can happen at any age. They are most common in babies.

## Symptoms

- Pain during or right after a bowel movement.
- Bleeding during or after a bowel movement. The blood is usually bright red.
- The pain can last from a few minutes to several hours. It returns with the next bowel movement.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor checks the anus by gently looking at it. This is usually all that is needed to make the diagnosis.

## Treatment

### 1. Make Bowel Movements Easier
- Take a stool softener.
- Eat more fiber. This can come from fruits, vegetables, and whole grains.
- Drink plenty of water.

These steps help prevent hard or large bowel movements. This reduces the chance of more tears.

### 2. Help the Fissure Heal
- Use a zinc oxide ointment. This protects the area and helps it heal.
- Use glycerin suppositories. These soften the stool and make bowel movements easier.

### 3. Ease Pain
- Apply a numbing cream like benzocaine or lidocaine to the anus.
- Soak in a warm (not hot) bath for 10 to 15 minutes after each bowel movement.

To do a sitz bath:
- Sit in a tub with a few inches of warm water.
- Or place a container of warm water on the toilet seat.
- Sit or squat in it for 10 to 15 minutes.

### 4. Treat Muscle Spasms
If the muscle around the anus keeps tightening, it can slow healing. To help:
- A doctor may inject botulinum toxin into the muscle. This relaxes it.
- Or you may apply nitroglycerin ointment or a cream like nifedipine or gel like diltiazem to the area.

These treatments help the muscle relax and let the fissure heal.

### 5. Surgery (if needed)
If other treatments do not work, surgery may be needed.
- The doctor cuts a small part of the internal anal sphincter muscle.
- This reduces muscle spasms and helps the fissure heal.

Surgery is usually safe and effective. Most people feel better quickly after the procedure.

# Temporal Arteritis – Simple Explanation

Temporal arteritis is a condition that causes inflammation in the blood vessels, especially those in the temples. It can lead to serious problems if not treated quickly.

## Symptoms

The most common symptoms include:

- Severe headaches that happen often
- Pain or soreness on the sides of your head (temples) or on your scalp
- Jaw pain when you chew or talk
- Vision problems, such as seeing double or losing vision in one or both eyes

You may also feel unwell in other ways, like:

- Having flu-like symptoms
- Losing weight without trying
- Feeling tired all the time
- Feeling low or sad

Some people with temporal arteritis also get another condition called polymyalgia rheumatica. This causes pain, stiffness, and swelling in the muscles around your shoulders, neck, and hips.

## When to Seek Help

If you think you might have temporal arteritis, you must act fast.

Call your doctor right away for an urgent appointment. Or use NHS 111 for help.

**Do not wait.** This condition can cause a stroke or blindness if it is not treated quickly.

If you have vision problems, you should see an eye doctor the same day.

## How It Is Diagnosed

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and check your temples.

You will likely have blood tests to check for signs of inflammation.

Then you will be referred to a specialist. They may do more tests, such as:

- An ultrasound scan of your temples to look at the blood vessels
- A biopsy: a small piece of the temporal artery is removed under local anaesthetic and checked in a lab

If you have vision problems, you will be seen by an eye specialist the same day.

## Treatment

Treatment starts as soon as possible, even before the diagnosis is confirmed. This is because of the risk of losing your sight.

The main treatment is a steroid medicine called prednisolone.

There are two stages:

1. **High dose at first** – for a few weeks to reduce swelling and control symptoms.
2. **Lower dose over time** – after symptoms improve. This may last for months or even years.

Some people need to take steroids for the rest of their life.

You will have regular check-ups to monitor your progress and check for side effects.

### Important: Steroids

- Do not stop taking steroids suddenly.
- Always follow your doctor’s instructions.
- Stopping too soon can make you very ill.

### Other Medicines You Might Need

You may also need other medicines to help with side effects or prevent complications:

- **Low-dose aspirin** – to lower the risk of a stroke or heart attack if the heart’s blood vessels are affected.
- **Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs)** – to protect your stomach from problems like indigestion or ulcers. These can happen when taking prednisolone.
- **Bisphosphonate therapy** – to help prevent weak bones (osteoporosis), which can happen with long-term steroid use.
- **Immunosuppressants** – to help reduce the amount of steroid you need and lower the chance of the condition coming back.

# Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis

This is a serious skin reaction. It can affect the skin, mouth, eyes, and other body parts. It is also called SJS or TEN.

## What Causes SJS and TEN?

Most cases are caused by medicines. The most common ones include:

- Sulfa drugs (like sulfasalazine)
- Antibiotics (like ampicillin, amoxicillin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins)
- Seizure medicines (like phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproic acid, lamotrigine)
- Pain relievers (like piroxicam, meloxicam)
- HIV medicines (like nevirapine)
- Other medicines (like allopurinol, chlormezanone)
- Immune checkpoint inhibitors (used in cancer treatment)

Some cases are not caused by medicine. Possible causes include:

- Infections (especially *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*)
- Vaccines
- Graft-versus-host disease (a problem after bone marrow transplants)

In children, an infection is the most likely cause. Most of these infections are from *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*.

Sometimes, no cause can be found.

## How Do SJS and TEN Work in the Body?

The exact reason is not fully known. But here is what scientists think:

- Some people’s bodies react badly to certain medicines.
- Their immune system attacks the skin cells.
- This attack causes the skin to die and peel off.
- A protein called granulysin may play a role in killing skin cells.
- Another protein, called Fas ligand, may also cause cell death.
- Some people may be born with a higher risk due to their genes.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms usually start 1 to 3 weeks after starting a medicine.

At first, you may feel sick. You may have:

- Fever
- Headache
- Cough
- Body aches
- Eye pain or redness

Then, red or purple spots appear. They often look like targets. They start on the face, neck, or upper body.

These spots grow fast. They join together and turn into large blisters. The skin may peel off in sheets.

This can happen in just 1 to 3 days.

Other symptoms include:

- Painful mouth sores
- Eye pain, redness, or vision problems
- Painful sores in the genitals
- Loss of nails or eyebrows
- Pain in the palms and soles
- In severe cases, the skin peels off easily when touched (called Nikolsky sign)

In very bad cases, the lining of the lungs may also peel off. This can cause:

- Cough
- Trouble breathing
- Pneumonia
- Low oxygen levels

Other problems can include:

- Kidney issues
- Liver problems

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors often recognize SJS and TEN by how the skin looks and how fast it gets worse.

A skin biopsy may be done. This means taking a small sample of skin to look at under a microscope. The test shows dead skin cells, which helps confirm the diagnosis.

Doctors must rule out other conditions. These include:

- Erythema multiforme (a milder rash)
- Viral rashes
- Other drug rashes
- Toxic shock syndrome (has different skin signs and more organ problems)
- Exfoliative erythroderma (a red, peeling rash that does not hurt as much and does not affect the mouth or eyes)
- Paraneoplastic pemphigus (a rare condition linked to cancer)
- Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (common in children, does not affect the mouth, and is caused by a staph infection)

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment must start early. It is best done in a hospital, often in a burn unit.

### General Care

- Stop all medicines that might be causing the reaction.
- Keep the patient in isolation to prevent infection.
- Give fluids, salts, blood, and nutrition as needed.
- Care for the skin like a burn. This includes daily cleaning and dressing changes.
- Treat infections if they happen.
- Do not use preventive antibiotics unless needed. They are not always helpful.

### Special Treatments

These are used in severe cases. But they are not always agreed on.

- **Cyclosporine**: This medicine helps calm the immune system. It may shorten the illness and lower the risk of death.
- **Plasmapheresis**: This is a blood filter. It removes harmful substances from the blood. It may help in some cases.
- **IV immune globulin (IVIG)**: This is a blood product. It may block harmful immune signals. But results are mixed. Some studies show no benefit, and one found higher death rates.
- **Corticosteroids**: These are strong anti-inflammatory medicines. Some doctors use them early. Others avoid them because they may increase infection risk. The evidence is not clear.
- **TNF-alpha inhibitors (infliximab, etanercept)**: These medicines reduce inflammation. They may help in severe cases.
- **Thalidomide**: This medicine was tested but is now not used. It increases the risk of death.

## What Is the Outlook?

SJS and TEN are very serious. They are like severe burns.

- The skin can peel off in large sheets.
- Fluids and salts are lost quickly.
- The body cannot eat or drink easily.
- The eyes may be damaged.
- Infection and organ failure are common.

Mortality (death rate) can be high:

- Up to 25% to 35% in adults
- Lower in children
- Lower if treatment starts early

With early care, survival for TEN can reach 90%.

### SCORTEN Score – Predicting Risk

Doctors use a tool called SCORTEN to predict how serious the illness is. It scores 7 factors in the first 24 hours after hospital admission.

| Risk Factor | Score |
|------------|-------|
| Age under 40 years | 0 |
| Age 40 or older | 1 |
| Cancer present | 1 |
| No cancer | 0 |
| Heart rate under 120 beats per minute | 0 |
| Heart rate 120 or higher | 1 |
| Blood urea nitrogen under 28 mg/dL | 0 |
| Blood urea nitrogen over 28 mg/dL | 1 |
| Skin loss less than 10% of body | 0 |
| Skin loss 10% or more | 1 |
| Bicarbonate level 20 mEq/L or higher | 0 |
| Bicarbonate level under 20 mEq/L | 1 |
| Blood sugar 250 mg/dL or lower | 0 |
| Blood sugar over 250 mg/dL | 1 |

**Total score and predicted death rate:**

- 0–1 risk factors: 3.2% chance of death
- 2 risk factors: 12.1% chance
- 3 risk factors: 35.3% chance
- 4 risk factors: 58.3% chance
- 5 or more risk factors: over 90% chance

## Key Points

- Most cases are caused by medicines. Infections, vaccines, and graft-versus-host disease can also cause it.
- Diagnosis is based on symptoms and skin appearance. A skin biopsy may be needed to confirm.
- Early treatment saves lives.
- Severe cases need care in a burn unit with intensive support.
- Eye problems need a specialist (ophthalmologist).
- Cyclosporine and plasmapheresis may help in serious cases.

# Sports-Related Concussion

## What Is a Concussion?

A concussion is a temporary problem with how the brain works. It happens after a hit to the head. There is no visible damage to the brain on imaging tests like CT scans or MRIs.

People who get concussions from sports are at risk for getting more than one. Getting multiple concussions can lead to serious long-term brain problems.

## Sports with Higher Risk

Sports that involve fast movement and body contact have the most concussions. These include football, rugby, ice hockey, and lacrosse. But even cheerleading and other sports carry some risk.

About one in five athletes in contact sports will have a concussion during a season.

Estimates of how many sports-related concussions happen in the United States range from 200,000 to 3.8 million per year. The numbers vary so much because many people do not get checked in a hospital after a head injury.

Concussions are not happening more often than before. But we are better at spotting them now. People now know that repeated head injuries can cause lasting harm.

## Risk of Getting Another Concussion

Unlike concussions from car crashes or falls, sports injuries can happen again and again. This makes repeat injuries more likely.

Athletes are especially at risk if they get another head hit before fully recovering from the first one.

Even after recovery, athletes who keep playing are two to four times more likely to get another concussion than those who never had one.

A second concussion can happen from a hit that is less severe than the first one.

Most people recover fully from one concussion. But some people who have had several concussions—even mild ones—develop long-term brain damage.

This condition is called chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE. It was first seen in boxers and was called dementia pugilistica. But CTE can happen in anyone who has had multiple concussions.

People with CTE may have brain damage that shows up on CT or MRI scans. They also have symptoms like those of dementia. These include:

- Trouble remembering things
- Problems with thinking clearly
- Changes in behavior
- Poor judgment and decision making
- Mood swings, anger, or violent behavior
- Depression
- Movement problems like those in Parkinson’s disease

Some well-known retired athletes who had many concussions have died by suicide. CTE may have played a role in some of these cases.

## Second-Impact Syndrome

Second-impact syndrome is a rare but very serious condition. It happens when a second concussion occurs before the first one has healed. The brain swells quickly and can be life-threatening.

Almost half of people with this syndrome do not survive.

## Symptoms of a Concussion

A person with a concussion may or may not lose consciousness. But they will have symptoms of brain problems. These include:

- Confusion: Looking dazed, not knowing who is playing or what the score is, or answering slowly
- Memory problems: Not remembering plays, assignments, or events just before or after the injury
- Vision issues: Seeing double
- Sensitivity to light
- Dizziness, unsteady walking, or poor balance
- Headache
- Nausea or vomiting
- Ringing in the ears (tinnitus)
- Loss of smell or taste

Some symptoms can last a few days to several weeks. These may include:

- Headaches
- Trouble remembering short-term events
- Difficulty focusing or paying attention
- Feeling tired all the time
- Trouble sleeping
- Mood changes like irritability or mood swings
- Sensitivity to light and noise

In teenagers, symptoms like irritability, tiredness, and trouble concentrating can be mistaken for normal teenage behavior.

## How Is a Concussion Diagnosed?

### See a Doctor

Anyone with concussion symptoms should see a doctor who knows how to treat head injuries. Some doctors are on site at big sports events. If not, team staff should be trained to spot concussions and know when to get help.

### Use Tools to Help

Free tools like the Sports Concussion Assessment Tool, 5th edition (SCAT5), are available online. You can download them to phones or tablets. They help coaches, trainers, and others check athletes on the field.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) also offers free tools and training for sideline staff. Look for their “Heads Up” programs.

### Watch for Hidden Symptoms

Athletes may hide or downplay their symptoms so they can keep playing. Doctors and staff must be aware of this.

### Imaging Tests

CT scans or MRIs are only done if doctors think there is a more serious injury. This could be bleeding inside the brain or a brain bruise.

### Brain Function Testing

Some sports programs test brain function before the season starts. If a concussion is suspected, the athlete is tested again. This helps doctors see if brain function has dropped.

## How Is a Concussion Treated?

### Rest Is Key

Rest your body and your brain. Avoid physical activity and mental tasks that are hard on the brain.

### Use Acetaminophen for Headaches

Take acetaminophen (like Tylenol) for headaches. It is the best choice after a minor head injury.

### Avoid Certain Activities

Do not go back to school, work, driving, drinking alcohol, or using computers, TV, or video games too much. These things can slow recovery.

### Watch for Worsening Symptoms

If symptoms get worse, take the person to the hospital right away.

### Did You Know?

Athletes often hide or minimize their symptoms so they can keep playing.

### Did You Know?

Acetaminophen is the safest medicine for pain after a minor head injury.

## Returning to Sports

You should not return to sports until all symptoms are gone. Follow these steps:

1. Start with light aerobic exercise (like walking or slow jogging).
2. Move to sport-specific training (like throwing or skating).
3. Do noncontact drills.
4. Try full-contact drills.
5. Return to full competition.

Do not go to the next step until all symptoms are gone at the current step.

Even if symptoms go away fast, wait at least one week after all symptoms are gone before returning to full play.

If the concussion was severe—such as losing consciousness for more than 5 minutes or losing memory of events from more than 24 hours before or after the injury—wait at least one month before returning to full competition.

If someone has had multiple concussions in one season, they must understand the risks. They (or their parents, if they are under 18) should talk to a doctor who has experience with brain injuries before deciding to keep playing.

# Blepharitis – Simple Guide

Blepharitis is an inflammation of the eyelids. It can cause discomfort and make your eyes feel irritated.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Blepharitis symptoms can come and go. They include:

- Sore or painful eyelids  
- Itchy eyes  
- A gritty or sandy feeling in your eyes  
- Flakes or crusts around the base of your eyelashes  
- Eyelids that stick together when you wake up in the morning  

These symptoms may get worse in the morning.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:

- Your symptoms do not get better  
- Your symptoms get worse  

Call your doctor right away or get help from NHS 111 if you have:

- Pain in your eyes  
- Changes in your vision, such as blurry vision or loss of vision  
- Very red eyes  

These could be signs of a more serious eye problem.

You can call 111 or get help online at [nhs.uk/111](https://www.nhs.uk/111)

## How to Treat and Prevent Blepharitis

### Do This:

- Clean your eyelids twice a day  
- Keep cleaning your eyelids even if your symptoms go away  

### Do Not Do This:

- Do not wear contact lenses while you have symptoms  
- Do not use eye makeup, especially eyeliner or mascara, while you have symptoms  

### How to Clean Your Eyelids

1. Wet a clean flannel or cotton wool with warm water.  
2. Place it on your closed eye for 5 to 10 minutes.  
3. Gently press and massage your eyelids for about 30 seconds.  
4. Use a clean cotton wool or cotton bud to wipe along the edge of your eyelids.  
5. You can mix a small drop of baby shampoo with water to help remove flakes or crusts.  

Be gentle. Do not rub hard.

## Help from a Pharmacist

A pharmacist can suggest products to help keep your eyelids clean. These may include:

- Pre-moistened eye pads or wipes  
- Special eyedrops  

They can help you choose the right product.

## Treatment from Your Doctor

If cleaning your eyelids does not help, your doctor may prescribe:

- An antibiotic cream or ointment to rub on your eyelid  
- Antibiotic eyedrops or tablets if you have a lump under the skin (cyst) or other eye problems  

If your blepharitis is very bad, or if you have other eye symptoms, your doctor may refer you to an eye specialist.

## What Causes Blepharitis?

Blepharitis can be caused by:

- A type of bacteria that lives on your skin  
- A skin condition like seborrhoeic dermatitis (a common skin problem that causes flaky, red skin)  
- Glands in your eyelids not making enough oil  

Blepharitis is not contagious. You cannot pass it to someone else.

# Diaphragmatic Hernia

A diaphragmatic hernia is a birth defect. It happens when part of the belly pushes up into the chest through a hole in the diaphragm. The diaphragm is the muscle that helps you breathe.

This condition can cause the lungs to not develop fully. It can also raise pressure in the blood vessels of the lungs. This makes it hard for the baby to get enough oxygen.

Doctors can find this problem before birth with ultrasound or MRI. After birth, they use chest X-rays and other imaging tests to confirm the diagnosis.

Treatment includes surgery to fix the hole. Babies often need special care in the hospital, including breathing support and long-term follow-up.

---

## Where the Hernia Happens

Most of the time, the hole is in the back and side of the diaphragm. This is called a Bochdalek hernia.  
About 85% of these holes are on the left side.  
In rare cases, there are holes on both sides.  
A small number of cases involve the front of the diaphragm (Morgagni hernia).

About 1 in every 4,000 babies is born with this condition.

Many babies with this defect also have other birth problems. Heart defects are the most common.

---

## What Moves Into the Chest

Belly organs like the intestines, stomach, liver, and spleen can push up into the chest.  
If the hole is large, the lung on that side may not grow properly.  
Even the other lung can be affected.

The blood vessels in the lungs may not develop well. This raises pressure in the lung blood vessels. This is called pulmonary hypertension.

Pulmonary hypertension can cause blood to flow backward in the heart. This means less oxygen reaches the body.  
Even with extra oxygen or a breathing machine, the baby may still struggle to get enough oxygen.

Heart function can also be weak. This makes treatment harder and increases the risk of serious problems.

---

## Signs and Symptoms

Most babies show signs of trouble right after birth.  
Some have severe breathing problems as soon as they are born.

When the baby cries or swallows air, the stomach and intestines fill with air.  
This makes them swell quickly.  
The belly organs push the heart and other chest structures to the other side.  
This squeezes the healthy lung and makes breathing worse.

The baby’s belly may look sunken or hollow. This is called a scaphoid abdomen.

Doctors may hear bowel sounds in the chest area.  
They may not hear breath sounds on the affected side.

In milder cases, breathing problems start a few hours or days after birth.  
The belly organs slowly move into the chest through a small hole.

In rare cases, the problem shows up later in childhood.  
It may happen after a stomach infection that causes sudden swelling of the intestines.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors can sometimes see the problem before birth using ultrasound or fetal MRI.

After birth, a chest X-ray is the main test.  
It shows if the stomach or intestines are in the chest.

If the hole is large, the X-ray shows many air-filled loops of intestine in the chest.  
The heart and other chest structures are pushed to the opposite side.

If the X-ray is taken right after birth, before the baby swallows air, the belly organs may appear as a solid, dark mass in the chest.

CT scans and MRI are used to get a clearer picture.  
They help doctors see the exact location of the hole.  
They also show which organs are in the chest.  
These scans help plan surgery and check for other birth defects.

An echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) is done to check for heart problems.  
This is especially important if the baby might need ECMO.

---

## How It Is Treated

If the baby is diagnosed before birth, delivery should happen at a hospital with a special newborn care unit.  
The hospital must have the ability to use ECMO.

In some cases, a fetal surgery called FETO may be done.  
This is done between 27 and 34 weeks of pregnancy.  
It helps the baby’s lungs grow.  
It can improve survival in severe cases, but it carries risks.

If a baby has breathing trouble after birth, doctors act fast.  
The baby must be placed on a breathing tube right away.  
This is called endotracheal intubation.

Do not use a bag and mask to give breaths.  
This can push more air into the belly organs.  
This makes breathing worse.

A special tube is placed through the nose into the stomach.  
It helps remove swallowed air.  
This prevents the belly organs from swelling and pressing on the lungs.

Before surgery, doctors work to treat high blood pressure in the lungs.  
They may use inhaled nitric oxide and other medicines.

They also make sure the baby’s blood chemistry, blood pressure, oxygen levels, and breathing are stable.

Low blood pressure that does not respond to medicine is common.  
This is due to low adrenal hormone levels.

Doctors may use special breathing machines.  
One type is high-frequency oscillating ventilation.

ECMO is often used.  
It is a machine that takes over the work of the heart and lungs.  
It is used for babies with very poor lung function.  
It can be planned ahead of time or used as a rescue when other treatments fail.

Surgery is needed to move the belly organs back into the belly.  
The hole in the diaphragm is then closed.

---

## Long-Term Care

After surgery, the baby needs ongoing care.  
This care is done by a team of specialists.

Some babies continue to have lung problems.  
They may have high blood pressure in the lungs.

They may also have acid reflux or other digestive issues.

Some babies have heart problems or delays in development.

Regular check-ups are needed to monitor health and support growth.

---

## Important Tips

- Never use a bag and mask to help a baby breathe if they have a diaphragmatic hernia.  
  This can make the problem worse.

---

## Key Points

- A diaphragmatic hernia lets belly organs move into the chest.  
  This can press on the lungs and cause breathing problems in newborns.

- The lungs may not grow fully.  
  Blood pressure in the lungs can rise.  
  Both make it hard to get enough oxygen.

- Doctors can find the problem before birth with imaging.  
  After birth, X-rays and other scans confirm the diagnosis.

- Treatment starts with a breathing tube.  
  Surgery is needed to fix the hole.  
  Many babies need ECMO to survive.

# Drug Allergies

Some people think they are allergic to a medicine when they just have a bad reaction. This is not always true.

For example, if you get an upset stomach after taking aspirin, you might say you are "allergic" to it. But this is not a true allergy. It is just a side effect.

True allergies happen when your body’s immune system reacts to a medicine. Your immune system is your body’s defense system. It fights off germs and other threats.

Aspirin can upset your stomach because it weakens the stomach’s natural protection against acid. This is not an allergy. It is a different kind of reaction.

Allergic reactions to medicines are not common. They are different from other side effects.

With allergic reactions, the amount of medicine you take does not matter. Even a small dose can cause a reaction. This is not true for most side effects.

Allergic reactions can be mild or very serious. They can even be life threatening.

Common signs of a drug allergy include:

- Skin rashes or itching
- Fever
- Trouble breathing, wheezing, or tightness in the chest
- Swelling in the throat or voice box, which can make it hard to breathe
- A sudden drop in blood pressure, which can be dangerous

Some allergic reactions are even rarer. They take days or weeks to appear. They can last for a long time.

These reactions happen when your body makes special proteins called antibodies. These antibodies attack your body’s own tissues after reacting with the medicine.

For example, they can damage red blood cells. This can lead to anemia. Or they can cause swelling in the skin, joints, or kidneys.

You cannot predict a drug allergy. It only happens after you have taken the medicine before without a reaction.

You may have taken the medicine by mouth, applied it to your skin, or had it injected. If you had no reaction before, you might still have a reaction later.

If you have a mild reaction, an antihistamine may help.

If you have a severe reaction, you may need an injection of epinephrine (also called adrenaline) or a steroid medicine like hydrocortisone.

Before giving you a new medicine, your doctor will ask if you have any known allergies.

If you have ever had a serious allergic reaction, wear a medical alert bracelet or necklace. It should list your allergies. For example, it could say “Penicillin Allergy.”

This helps doctors and nurses know what to avoid if you are in an emergency.
