# Tonsillitis

Tonsillitis means your tonsils are inflamed.  
The tonsils are the two lumps at the back of your throat.  

## What to look for

Your tonsils may be red and swollen.  
You may have a sore throat.  
You might find it hard to swallow.  

Other common signs include:  
- A high temperature  
- A cough  
- A headache  
- Feeling sick or being sick  
- Earache  
- Feeling very tired  

In more serious cases, you may notice:  
- Swollen, painful glands in your neck  
- White spots or patches on your tonsils  
- Bad breath  

## When to see a doctor

Call your doctor if:  
- Your symptoms last more than 7 days  
- You keep getting throat infections  

## When to get urgent help

Call NHS 111 now if:  
- You see pus on your tonsils  
- Your throat hurts so much you can’t eat or drink  

You can call 111 or get help online.

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:  
- A very bad sore throat that gets worse fast  
- Swelling inside your mouth or throat  
- Trouble speaking  
- Trouble swallowing  
- Trouble breathing  
- Can’t open your mouth  

These signs could mean you have a serious condition called quinsy.

Find your nearest A&E.

### A&E safety tips

Do not drive to A&E.  
Ask someone to drive you.  
Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
Bring your medicines with you.

## How to treat tonsillitis at home

Tonsillitis usually gets better on its own in a few days.  
But it can last longer.

To feel better:  
- Rest as much as you can  
- Drink cool drinks to soothe your throat  
- Take paracetamol or ibuprofen  
  - Do not give aspirin to children under 16  
- Gargle with warm salty water  
  - Children should not do this

### How to gargle with salty water

1. Put half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water.  
2. Stir until the salt dissolves.  
3. Swish the water around your throat.  
4. Spit it out. Do not swallow.  
5. Repeat as often as you like.

## Help from a pharmacist

Talk to a pharmacist if you have tonsillitis.  
They can help you choose the right treatment.  
They may suggest:  
- Lozenges with numbing, cleaning, or anti-inflammatory medicine  
- Throat sprays (though there is little proof they work)  
- Antiseptic mouthwashes

## Treatment from your doctor

Your doctor will check what is causing your tonsillitis.  

Most cases are caused by a virus.  
This type gets better on its own.  

Some cases are caused by bacteria.  
If this is the case, your doctor may give you antibiotics.

Your doctor will usually wait for test results before deciding.

## Surgery to remove tonsils

It is very rare to need surgery to remove the tonsils.  
This is only done if you keep getting severe tonsillitis.

## What causes tonsillitis?

Tonsillitis is most often caused by a virus.  
This can be the same kind of virus that causes a cold.  

It can also be caused by a bacterial infection.  
One common example is strep throat.

# Hip Surgery Recovery

Recovery starts as soon as possible after hip surgery. This helps you get stronger and keeps your other leg healthy.

At first, you can only do gentle muscle exercises. These are done while your leg is straight. Do not put a pillow under your knee. This can cause your hip and knee to stay bent too much.

Moving around slowly helps you walk again. How fast you recover depends on the type of surgery you had. If you had a hip replacement, you usually recover faster. You need less therapy and do better than if you had metal rods or plates put in.

How much weight you can put on your leg after surgery depends on your surgeon, your pain, your age, and your health. Many people need to stay in the hospital for therapy.

Your recovery can be different depending on how the surgery was done. Some people have the traditional back method. Others have a newer front method. Each has different rules and risks.

Here is what to expect after hip replacement surgery:

- **Day 1 to 2:** You may stay in bed or move around a little. You can put some weight on your leg if it feels okay.
- **Day 3 to 5:** You can put more weight on your leg, but not all of it.
- **Day 6 to 8:** You can put all your weight on your leg. Use a cane or walker to help.
- **After 4 to 8 days:** You can do walking exercises. Only if you can stand and balance well.
- **After about day 11:** You can start practicing going up and down stairs.

You will learn daily exercises. These help strengthen your stomach muscles and the front of your leg. Avoid lifting heavy things. Do not bend over, stoop, or jump for a long time.

Using one or two canes puts about the same stress on your hip. But using two canes can make daily tasks harder. Try to use just one.

Do not sit for long periods. Avoid low chairs. Use the arm of the chair to help you stand up. Keep your legs uncrossed while sitting.

Occupational therapists will teach you how to do everyday tasks safely. This helps you heal and move better. You may learn to:

- Keep your hip in the right position
- Wash dishes or iron while sitting on a high stool
- Use a pillow to raise your car seat when getting in and out
- Use long tools like reachers or shoe horns to avoid bending over

This teaching can happen in the hospital, in a rehab center, at home after leaving the hospital, or in an outpatient clinic.

(See also Overview of Rehabilitation.)

# Body Ringworm (Tinea Corporis)

Body ringworm is a skin infection caused by a type of fungus. It can appear on the face, chest, back, arms, and legs.

## What Does It Look Like?

- The rash often starts as a pink or red, round patch.
- The edges of the patch are raised and scaly.
- The center of the patch may look clearer than the edges.
- Sometimes the center becomes darker due to inflammation.
- The rash can be itchy, but not always.

## How Does It Spread?

- The fungus can spread quickly to other parts of your body.
- It can also spread to other people through close skin contact.
- You can get it from touching an infected person or animal.
- You can also get it from touching contaminated items like towels or clothing.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- A doctor will look at your skin.
- They may take a small sample of skin (a scraping) to check under a microscope.
- This helps confirm the infection is caused by a fungus.

## How Is It Treated?

- Most cases are treated with antifungal creams, lotions, or gels.
- Apply the medicine to the affected area twice a day.
- Keep using the medicine for 7 to 10 days after the rash is gone.
- Do not stop too soon. If you do, the infection may come back.
- It may take several days before you feel better.
- For more serious or widespread infections, a doctor may prescribe an oral antifungal medicine.
- These pills are taken for 2 to 3 weeks and are used when the infection is hard to treat.

## Common Medicines

- Topical (applied to skin): imidazole, ciclopirox, naftifine, terbinafine
- Oral (taken by mouth): itraconazole, terbinafine

## Important Notes

- Always follow your doctor’s instructions.
- Keep the skin clean and dry.
- Avoid sharing towels, clothing, or personal items.
- Wash your hands after touching the rash.

This condition is also known as tinea corporis. It is a type of fungal skin infection called dermatophytosis. The most common fungi that cause it are *Trichophyton* and *Microsporum*.

# Frostbite

Frostbite happens when skin and tissue freeze due to cold temperatures.

## What to Look For

Frostbite often starts with cold, painful, and numb skin.

As it gets worse, the skin may feel hard and frozen. It may also start to blister.

The most common places for frostbite are the fingers, toes, nose, and ears.

### Early Signs
- Skin feels cold and firm
- You may feel numbness, stinging, or burning
- The skin may hurt, throb, or ache
- Skin may look red or pale (redness can be hard to see on dark skin)

### Signs of Worse Frostbite
- Skin feels hard and frozen. It may look white, blue, or patchy
- Swelling and loss of feeling in the area
- Blisters filled with blood or clear or milky fluid
- Skin turns black and hard as it starts to die (this can be hard to see on dark skin)

## What to Do If You Think Someone Has Frostbite

Get indoors or into a sheltered place as soon as possible.

### Do These Things
- Remove gloves, rings, boots, and other tight clothing from the affected area
- Wrap yourself in a warm blanket, sleeping bag, or dry towel
- If your hands are affected, put them in your armpits to warm them
- If you're helping someone else, place their affected body part in your lap and gently warm it with your hands
- Place the affected area in warm (not hot) water. Dry it gently and cover it with a light dressing like gauze
- Raise the affected body part to help reduce swelling
- Take paracetamol for pain. Do not give aspirin to children under 16
- Drink a warm drink or water

### Do Not Do These Things
- Do not rub the affected area
- Do not use a fire, radiator, hot water bottle, or heat lamp to warm it
- Do not take a hot bath to warm up
- Do not drink alcohol

## When to Get Help Right Away

Call 999 or go to A&E if you’ve been in very cold weather and have:

- Hard, frozen skin
- Swelling and no feeling in the area
- Blisters with blood or clear or milky fluid
- Constant shivering, slurred speech, slow breathing, or feeling tired and confused

> Find your nearest A&E

## What Happens in the Hospital

Frostbite is treated in a hospital.

Doctors will:
- Warm the affected area slowly
- Remove dead skin if needed
- Give medicine to reduce swelling and prevent infection
- Perform surgery if the frostbite is very serious

You may need follow-up visits to check healing and deal with long-term issues like pain or stiffness.

## Possible Problems After Frostbite

Frostbite can cause serious damage.

- The skin and tissue may die. This is called gangrene.
- If the tissue dies, the affected part may need to be removed (amputation).
- Some people have lasting pain or stiffness in the area.
- You are more likely to get frostbite again if the same body part is exposed to cold.

## How to Prevent Frostbite

Wear warm, layered clothing in cold weather.

For example:
- Wear several loose layers, with a waterproof outer layer
- Wear a hat and scarf to protect your head, neck, and face
- Wear gloves or mittens for your hands and fingers
- Wear thick socks and boots for your feet and toes

Also:
- Eat and drink regularly when you’re in cold weather for long periods

Staying warm and dry is key to staying safe.

# Dyspepsia

Dyspepsia means pain or discomfort in the upper belly.  
It often comes back over time.  
People describe it in many ways.  
They may say they feel bloated, have gas, feel full too soon, or have a burning or gnawing pain.

---

## Common Causes of Dyspepsia

Here are some common reasons for dyspepsia.  
Each cause has its own signs and needs different tests.

### Cancer (in the esophagus or stomach)
- You may feel a dull, ongoing pain.
- Later, you might have trouble swallowing (esophagus) or feel full after eating a small amount (stomach).
- You may lose weight without trying.
- Tests: Upper endoscopy and abdominal CT scan.

### Celiac Disease
- Your bowel habits may change. You may have diarrhea, greasy stools, or bloating.
- You may have low iron levels without a clear reason.
- Tests: Blood tests and a small bowel biopsy.

### Heart Problems (coronary ischemia)
- Some people describe the pain as gas or indigestion, not chest pain.
- The pain may come when you are active.
- You may have risk factors like high blood pressure, high cholesterol, or diabetes.
- Tests: ECG, blood tests for heart damage, and sometimes stress testing.

### Slow Stomach Emptying (often from diabetes, a virus, or certain medicines)
- You may feel nauseous, bloated, or full after eating.
- Test: A scan that checks how fast your stomach empties.

### Certain Medicines
- Examples: Bisphosphonates, some antibiotics, estrogen, iron pills, NSAIDs, opioids, and potassium supplements.
- The symptoms start when you take the medicine.
- Your doctor will review your medicine list.

### Eosinophilic Esophagitis
- You have reflux symptoms that do not get better with acid-reducing medicines.
- Test: Upper endoscopy with a biopsy.

### Esophageal Spasm
- You feel chest pain, with or without trouble swallowing liquids or solids.
- Test: Barium swallow and esophageal manometry.

### Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
- You feel heartburn.
- You may taste acid or stomach contents in your mouth.
- Symptoms may get worse when lying down.
- Antacids often help.
- Tests: Clinical exam, and sometimes endoscopy or pH monitoring.

### Peptic Ulcer Disease
- You feel a burning or gnawing pain. It may get better after eating or taking antacids.
- Risk factors: Using NSAIDs, smoking, drinking alcohol, or having *Helicobacter pylori* infection.
- Test: Upper endoscopy with testing for *H. pylori*.
- Your doctor may suggest stopping NSAIDs.

---

### Important Note
Many people have test results that show problems like inflammation, slow movement in the gut, *H. pylori* infection, lactose intolerance, or gallstones.  
But these findings do not always match the symptoms.  
Fixing the problem does not always improve the pain.

---

## What Is Nonulcer Dyspepsia?

Nonulcer dyspepsia (also called functional dyspepsia) means you have ongoing upper belly pain or discomfort.  
Your physical exam and tests (like endoscopy, blood tests, or imaging) show no clear cause.  
This is a common reason for long-term dyspepsia.

---

## How Is Dyspepsia Evaluated?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and medical history.  
They may do tests to rule out serious causes.  
The need for testing depends on your age and other risk factors.

### When to Get an Endoscopy
- If you are over 60, you should have an endoscopy.
- If you are under 60, your doctor will decide based on your symptoms and risk factors.

---

## How Is Dyspepsia Treated?

### If a Specific Cause Is Found
- Your doctor will treat the cause directly.

### If No Clear Cause Is Found
- You will be watched over time.
- You will be reassured that your symptoms are not due to a serious illness.

### Medicines for Symptoms
- Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) help reduce stomach acid.
- H2 blockers also reduce acid.
- Sucralfate protects the lining of the stomach.
- These medicines are taken by mouth.

#### Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs)
- Examples: Dexlansoprazole, Esomeprazole, Lansoprazole, Omeprazole, Pantoprazole, Rabeprazole.
- Long-term use may raise a hormone called gastrin. But this does not cause cancer or serious changes.
- Side effects: Belly pain or diarrhea.

#### H2 Blockers
- Examples: Cimetidine, Famotidine, Nizatidine.
- Cimetidine may affect male hormones and cause sexual side effects.
- It can slow down how other medicines are broken down in the body.
- Side effects: Constipation or diarrhea.

#### Cytoprotective Agent
- Sucralfate helps protect the stomach lining.
- It may cause constipation.
- It can block other medicines from being absorbed.
- Do not take cimetidine, ciprofloxacin, digoxin, norfloxacin, ofloxacin, or ranitidine within 2 hours of sucralfate.

---

### Other Options If Symptoms Continue
- Tricyclic antidepressants may help some people.
- Prokinetic medicines (like metoclopramide or erythromycin) may help if you feel full too soon or have slow stomach movement.
- These are given as a liquid.

### Important Notes
- There is no strong proof that one medicine works better for certain symptoms (like reflux vs. fullness).
- Misoprostol and anticholinergics do not help with functional dyspepsia.

---

### Ranitidine Is No Longer Available
- Ranitidine (in pill, IV, or over-the-counter form) has been removed from the market.
- It had unsafe levels of a chemical called NDMA, which may cause cancer.
- Cimetidine and famotidine are safe alternatives.
- Proton pump inhibitors are also safe and do not contain NDMA.

---

## Key Points

- Chest pain that feels like gas could be a sign of a heart problem.
- Anyone over 60 with dyspepsia should have an endoscopy.
- For people under 60, the need for endoscopy depends on your symptoms and risk factors.
- If you do not have *H. pylori* or still have symptoms after treatment, your doctor may suggest trying acid-reducing medicine for 4 to 8 weeks.

# Carpal Tunnel Syndrome

Carpal tunnel syndrome causes pain and numbness in the hand. It happens when a nerve in the wrist gets squeezed.

## What Is the Carpal Tunnel?

The carpal tunnel is a narrow passageway in the wrist. It holds the tendons and the median nerve. The median nerve runs from the forearm into the hand. It gives feeling to the thumb, index finger, middle finger, and half of the ring finger.

The tunnel is made of bones, ligaments, and tendons. The median nerve lies on the palm side of the wrist.

## Who Gets Carpal Tunnel Syndrome?

This condition is very common. It affects many women between the ages of 40 and 59. It can affect one hand or both hands.

## What Causes Carpal Tunnel Syndrome?

Carpal tunnel syndrome happens when the median nerve gets squeezed. This can happen if the tissues around the nerve swell. It can also happen if thick bands of tissue form on the palm side of the wrist.

Some people are more likely to get it. These include:
- Pregnant women
- People with diabetes
- People with an underactive thyroid gland
- People with certain types of amyloidosis
- People with rheumatoid arthritis

Jobs that require repeated wrist movements, like using a screwdriver, can raise the risk. Using a computer keyboard that is too high or not in the right position may also play a role. Using vibrating tools for long periods is another possible cause. But in most cases, doctors do not know what causes the condition.

### How to Position Your Keyboard Properly

To help prevent carpal tunnel syndrome:
- Keep your wrist in a straight line with your forearm.
- Your hand should be slightly lower than your forearm.
- Never let your hand be higher than your forearm.
- Do not bend your wrist upward or downward.
- Place the keyboard low, so your hand is slightly below your elbow.
- Use a wrist pad to support your wrist.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may feel:
- Tingling in your thumb, index finger, middle finger, and half of the ring finger.
- Numbness in the same fingers.
- A burning or aching pain in the hand or forearm.
- Pain that wakes you up at night.

Shaking your hand may help bring back feeling. Over time, the muscles at the base of the thumb can get weaker and smaller. This is called atrophy.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will:
- Look at your hand and wrist.
- Ask about your symptoms.

They may also do:
- Nerve tests to check how well the nerve is working.
- Imaging tests like MRI or ultrasound, especially if surgery is being considered.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on how bad the symptoms are.

### Simple Steps That Help
- Wear a wrist splint at night. It keeps your wrist in a neutral position.
- Use mild pain relievers like acetaminophen or ibuprofen.
- Adjust your keyboard so your wrist stays straight.
- Avoid positions that stretch your wrist too much.

### Other Treatments
- Injections of a corticosteroid into the wrist can reduce swelling and relieve symptoms. This may help for weeks or months.
- If symptoms are severe, or if the muscles in your hand are shrinking, surgery may be needed.

### Surgery
A surgeon can cut the thick band of tissue that is pressing on the nerve. This relieves pressure and helps the nerve work better. Surgery is often very effective.

# Oral Thrush (Mouth Thrush)

Oral thrush is a common mouth infection. It is caused by a type of fungus called Candida.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Your mouth may feel sore and look red. You may see white patches on your tongue, inside your cheeks, on your gums, or in your throat.

The white patches do not come off easily. If you try to wipe them away, the area underneath may be red and can bleed.

### In Adults:
- You may have cracks at the corners of your mouth.
- You may not taste food the way you used to.
- You may have a bad taste in your mouth.
- You may feel pain in your mouth. This can include a sore tongue or sore gums.
- You may find it hard to eat or drink.

Oral thrush in adults is not contagious. You cannot pass it to someone else.

### In Babies:
- Your baby’s tongue may have a white coating. It can look like cottage cheese.
- The white coating does not come off when you wipe it.
- You may see white spots in your baby’s mouth.
- Your baby may not want to feed.
- Babies can pass the infection to their mother during breastfeeding. This can cause nipple thrush in the mother.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if you think you or your child has oral thrush.

## How Is It Treated?

Your doctor can prescribe a medicine called nystatin. It comes as a liquid.

To use it:
- Swish the liquid in your mouth for as long as you can.
- Then swallow it.

Follow your doctor’s instructions carefully.

## How to Prevent Oral Thrush

Oral thrush happens when a fungus called Candida grows too much in your mouth.

You are more likely to get it if you:
- Take antibiotics for a long time.
- Use asthma inhalers.
- Are having cancer treatment like chemotherapy.

### Do These Things to Help Prevent It:

- Brush your teeth twice a day.
- Clean your dentures every day.
- Go to your dentist for check-ups, even if you wear dentures.
- If you do not have teeth, brush your gums and tongue with a soft toothbrush.
- Rinse your mouth after eating or taking medicine.
- If you have diabetes, go to your doctor for regular check-ups.
- Sterilise your baby’s dummy regularly.
- Sterilise your baby’s bottle after every use.

### Do Not Do These Things:

- Do not wear dentures while you sleep.
- Do not keep wearing dentures if they do not fit well. See your dentist.
- Do not smoke.

# Vocal Fold Paralysis

Vocal fold paralysis affects how you speak, breathe, and swallow.  
It happens when the muscles in your voice box do not work properly.  
The left side is affected more often than the right.  
Women are more likely to have this condition than men, about 3 women for every 2 men.

Doctors diagnose this condition by looking directly at the voice box.  
They may need to do more tests to find the cause.  
If the cause cannot be fixed, surgery can help improve voice or breathing.

---

## What Causes Vocal Fold Paralysis?

The voice box gets signals from the brain through nerves.  
Paralysis can happen if there is a problem in any part of this pathway.  
The left nerve takes a longer path from the brain to the voice box.  
This makes it more likely to be damaged by pressure, pulling, or surgery.

Paralysis can be:

- One side affected (most common)  
- Both sides affected (less common but serious)

### Unilateral Paralysis (One Side Affected)

This is the most common type.  
About one-third of cases are due to cancer.  
Another third are caused by surgery or medical treatment.  
The rest have no clear cause, or are due to infection, nerve inflammation, or brain problems.

- Brain problems like tumors, strokes, or diseases that damage nerve coverings can cause paralysis.  
- Tumors at the base of the skull or neck injuries can damage the main nerve to the voice box.  
- Problems in the neck or chest can affect the nerve that controls the voice box.  
  These include aneurysms, heart disease, lung or thyroid cancer, or infections.  
- Injuries to the neck or spine, or surgeries in the neck or chest, can cause damage.  
- Exposure to poisons like lead, arsenic, or mercury can harm nerves.  
- Infections like diphtheria or Lyme disease can affect nerves.  
- Viral illnesses may also cause nerve problems.  
- Most cases with no known cause are likely due to nerve inflammation.

### Bilateral Paralysis (Both Sides Affected)

This is a serious condition.  
It can block the airway and make breathing very hard.  
It can happen after thyroid or neck surgery, long breathing tube use, neck trauma, or certain nerve and muscle diseases.

Paradoxical vocal fold motion (when the voice box closes when you try to breathe in) is a different condition.  
It is discussed elsewhere.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The voice box has two folds that move to open and close the airway.  
When paralyzed, these folds cannot move properly.  
This can affect speaking, breathing, and swallowing.  
Food or liquid may go into the windpipe.

The paralyzed fold usually sits 2 to 3 millimeters off center.

### In One-Sided Paralysis

- The voice sounds weak, breathy, or hoarse.  
- Breathing is usually not blocked because the healthy side still works.  
- During speaking, the paralyzed fold may move a little, but not during deep breaths.

### In Both-Sided Paralysis

- Both folds stay close to the center.  
- The voice may sound normal but weak and flat.  
- Breathing becomes hard, especially with activity.  
- You may make a high-pitched sound when breathing in (called stridor).  
- There is a risk of food or liquid going into the lungs (aspiration).

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use a special scope to look at the voice box.  
This is the best way to confirm paralysis.  
A more detailed version called strobovideolaryngoscopy shows how the folds vibrate.  
This helps doctors understand the problem better.

Finding the cause is very important.  
The doctor will ask about your medical history and do a physical exam.  
They will check for possible causes such as:

- Long-term exposure to heavy metals like lead, arsenic, or mercury  
- Side effects from certain medicines (like phenytoin or vincristine)  
- Autoimmune diseases like lupus or rheumatoid arthritis  
- Lyme disease  
- Sarcoidosis  
- Diabetes  
- Alcohol use disorder

Further tests may include:

- CT or MRI scans of the head, neck, and chest to look for tumors, blood vessel problems, or swelling  
- Thyroid scan to check the thyroid gland  
- Barium swallow to check swallowing  
- Endoscopy to look inside the esophagus or stomach

Sometimes, the voice box can be stiff and not move, even if the nerves are working.  
This is called joint fixation.  
It can happen after arthritis, neck injury, or long use of a breathing tube.  
Doctors can check for this during a scope under general anesthesia.

---

## How Is It Treated?

### For One-Sided Paralysis

Treatment focuses on improving the voice and preventing food from going into the lungs.

- **Augmentation**: A gel-like substance (like collagen, fat, or hyaluronic acid) is injected into the paralyzed fold.  
  This pushes the fold closer to the other side to help the voice sound better and reduce the risk of choking.

- **Medialization**: A small implant is placed next to the paralyzed fold.  
  It is placed during surgery under local anesthesia.  
  The doctor can adjust the size and position to match your voice.

- **Reinnervation**: A healthy nerve is connected to the paralyzed one.  
  This helps restore tone and position, but not full movement.  
  It is used in children and adults under 55 with long-term paralysis that will not get better.

Voice therapy can help if the folds can close enough.

### For Both-Sided Paralysis

The main goal is to keep the airway open.

- A breathing tube (tracheotomy) may be needed.  
  It can be temporary (for example, during a cold) or permanent.

- **Arytenoidectomy**: Part of the voice box is removed to open the airway.  
  This helps breathing but may make the voice worse.

- **Posterior laser cordectomy**: A laser is used to open the back part of the voice box.  
  This improves breathing and often keeps the voice working well.  
  It may prevent the need for a long-term breathing tube.

- **Selective reinnervation**: In rare cases, nerve surgery can help restore some function.  
  This is only used in carefully selected patients.

---

## Key Points

- Paralysis can happen anywhere along the nerve path to the voice box.  
- Most cases affect only one side. This mainly affects the voice.  
- Both sides affected is rare but dangerous. It can block the airway.  
- Diagnosis is done with a scope. Finding the cause often needs imaging (like MRI) and other tests.  
- People with both-sided paralysis often need a breathing tube at first.  
- Surgery can help improve voice or breathing, depending on the type of paralysis.

# Hives

Hives are red, itchy bumps on the skin. They look raised and often have a pale center. The bumps can appear anywhere on the body.

The skin swells because of chemicals released from cells in the skin. These chemicals make small blood vessels leak fluid. This causes the swelling. The itching can be strong.

Hives usually come and go. One bump may last a few hours, then fade. Another bump may appear later in a different spot. After a hive goes away, the skin looks normal.

## What Is Angioedema?

Hives can happen with angioedema. Angioedema is swelling under the skin, not on the surface. It can affect the face, lips, throat, tongue, or airways.

Swelling in the throat or airways can block breathing. This can be life threatening. If you have trouble breathing, get help right away.

## What Causes Hives?

Hives can be caused by an allergic reaction. But most of the time, they are not from an allergy.

### Allergic Reactions
Allergies happen when your body overreacts to a substance. This substance is called a trigger or allergen. It can be in food, medicine, insects, plants, or the air.

Common food triggers include eggs, fish, shellfish, nuts, and some fruits. Even a small amount of some foods can cause hives. For other foods, you need to eat more before a reaction happens.

Medicines can also cause hives. Antibiotics are a common cause. Some medicines cause hives without an allergy.

Some people have hives after touching certain things. For example, latex or a substance inhaled through the nose or lungs.

### Non-Allergic Causes
Hives can also happen without an allergy. Some causes include:

- Infections (like viral or bacterial infections)
- Certain medicines that do not cause an allergy
- Physical triggers like heat, cold, pressure, friction, or sunlight
- Autoimmune disorders (when the body attacks its own tissues)

In more than half of cases, doctors cannot find a cause for hives.

### Acute vs. Chronic Hives
Hives that last less than 6 weeks are called acute.  
Hives that last more than 6 weeks are called chronic.

Chronic hives can last for months or years. Sometimes they go away on their own.

## When to See a Doctor

You do not always need to see a doctor for hives. But you should seek help if:

- Your face, lips, tongue, or throat swells
- You have trouble breathing or wheeze
- Hives are very dark, turn into open sores, or last more than 48 hours
- You have a fever, swollen glands, yellow skin or eyes, weight loss, or other signs of a serious illness

### Call an ambulance if:
- You cannot breathe
- Your throat feels like it is closing

### Go to the emergency room or see a doctor soon if:
- Your symptoms are severe
- You feel weak, dizzy, or have a high fever or chills
- You are vomiting or have stomach pain or diarrhea

### See a doctor if:
- A bee sting causes hives or swelling (to get advice for future stings)
- You have other symptoms like fever, joint pain, weight loss, swollen glands, or night sweats
- Hives come back without a clear reason
- Hives last more than 2 days

If a child gets hives suddenly, they go away fast, and do not come back, a doctor visit is usually not needed. This is often due to a virus.

## How Doctors Evaluate Hives

Doctors start by asking questions. They want to know:

- How the hives look and how long they last
- If you have itching, trouble breathing, or swelling
- What you were doing before the hives started
- If you were near any possible triggers (like food, medicine, or insects)
- If you have had similar problems before
- If you have had recent infections, travel, or other health issues

Doctors also do a physical exam. They check for swelling in the face, lips, tongue, or throat. If there is swelling, they treat it right away.

They look at the hives. They check which parts of the body are affected. They may test for triggers by applying pressure, heat, cold, or sunlight to the skin.

Do not try to cause hives yourself. This could lead to a serious reaction.

### Possible Causes of Hives

| Cause | Common Features | Tests |
|------|------------------|-------|
| Medicines (like aspirin, antibiotics, or contrast dye) | Hives start within minutes to 48 hours after taking the medicine | Doctor’s exam |
| Foods (like nuts, fish, eggs, milk, or shellfish) | Hives start within minutes to hours after eating | Doctor’s exam, sometimes allergy testing |
| Infections (bacterial, viral, or parasitic) | Fever, chills, tiredness, or symptoms of the infection | Tests based on symptoms and travel history |
| Insect bites or stings | Hives start within seconds or minutes | Doctor’s exam |
| Physical triggers (cold, heat, pressure, sunlight) | Hives start within seconds or minutes of exposure | Doctor’s exam, testing with the trigger |
| Serum sickness (after a blood product or animal serum) | Hives start 7–10 days after exposure, with fever, joint pain, or swollen glands | Doctor’s exam |
| Contact allergens (like latex or meat) | Hives start within minutes to hours after touching | Doctor’s exam, sometimes allergy testing |
| Blood transfusions | Hives start within minutes after transfusion | Doctor’s exam |
| Autoimmune disorders (like lupus or Sjögren syndrome) | Hives last more than 24 hours, may be painful, do not fade when pressed | Blood tests, skin biopsy |
| Cancer (like lymphoma or digestive or lung cancer) | Weight loss, night sweats, cough, yellow skin, swollen glands | Tests based on symptoms |
| Chronic idiopathic hives (no known cause) | Hives happen daily or almost daily for 6 weeks or more | Doctor’s exam, blood tests, skin tests |
| Hormonal changes (like birth control pills or menstrual cycle) | Hives appear before periods and go away when they start | Doctor’s exam, blood tests |
| Mastocytosis (too many immune cells in the skin) | Small red spots that turn into hives when touched | Skin or bone marrow biopsy, blood tests |
| Other physical triggers (same as acute) | Hives appear quickly after exposure | Doctor’s exam, testing with the trigger |

Note: Not all features are always present. Some tests are only done if symptoms suggest a specific cause.

## Tests for Hives

Most people with one episode of hives do not need tests. But tests are often needed if:

- Hives look unusual
- They keep coming back
- They last a long time

Common tests include:

- Blood tests to check for infection, thyroid problems, or other issues
- A complete blood count
- Tests to check kidney and liver function
- Blood sugar and electrolyte levels

Allergy skin tests are done by an allergy specialist. They help find specific triggers.

Imaging tests or other blood tests are done only if the history and exam suggest a deeper problem.

A skin biopsy is done if the diagnosis is unclear. It is also done if a hive lasts more than 48 hours.

## Treating Hives

### Avoid Triggers
If you know what causes your hives, avoid it. If the cause is not clear, stop taking any non-essential medicines until the hives go away.

### Relieve Itching
- Bathe or shower with cool water
- Do not scratch
- Wear loose, soft clothing

### Medications
**Antihistamines** are the main treatment. They help reduce itching and swelling.

- Take them every day, not just when itches start.
- Common ones include cetirizine, loratadine, and diphenhydramine.
- Diphenhydramine can make you drowsy. It is not the best choice for many people.

Other antihistamines include fexofenadine, hydroxyzine, levocetirizine, and desloratadine.

Antihistamine creams and lotions are not helpful. They can make itching worse.

**Corticosteroids** (like prednisone) are used only for severe cases. They are taken by mouth for a short time. Long use can cause serious side effects.

Corticosteroid creams do not help.

**Epinephrine** is used for severe reactions or angioedema. It opens airways and reduces swelling. It is given in a hospital.

If you have had a severe reaction, carry an epinephrine autoinjector. Use it right away if symptoms return.

### Chronic Hives
About half of people with chronic hives get better without treatment within 2 years.

For those who do not improve, two medicines may help: omalizumab and dupilumab. These are given by injection.

## Special Advice for Older Adults

Older adults should avoid older antihistamines like diphenhydramine and hydroxyzine. These can cause:

- Drowsiness
- Confusion
- Trouble urinating
- Delirium

These side effects can be dangerous. Safer antihistamines are available.

## Key Points

- Hives are not always caused by allergies.
- In most cases, doctors cannot find a cause.

# Frozen Shoulder

Frozen shoulder means your shoulder hurts and feels stiff. The pain and stiffness do not go away on their own.

You can get better with pain relief and exercises. These help you move your shoulder again.

Your doctor or a physical therapist can give you exercises. Using a heat pack may also help with the pain.

It is not always clear why frozen shoulder happens. It can follow an injury, surgery, or it may be linked to diabetes.

## See a Doctor If:

- Your shoulder hurts and feels stiff for more than a few days.
- The pain is so bad that you cannot move your arm or shoulder.

## Symptoms of Frozen Shoulder

The two main signs are:

- Pain in your shoulder. It may get worse at night and wake you up.
- Stiffness. You cannot move your shoulder easily.

Frozen shoulder can take months or even years to get better. But most people do get better eventually.

## How to Treat Frozen Shoulder

Treatment has three main steps:

### Step 1: Ease the Pain
- Avoid movements that hurt.
- Move your shoulder gently.
- Start with paracetamol. Take it every 4 to 6 hours, up to the daily limit on the label.
- If paracetamol does not help, try ibuprofen. Stop taking it if it does not work.

### Step 2: Stronger Pain Relief
- Your doctor may give you stronger painkillers.
- Or they may give you a steroid injection into your shoulder.
- These are only used for a short time because they can cause side effects.

### Step 3: Get Movement Back
- Do gentle shoulder exercises at home.
- If the pain does not improve, your doctor may refer you to a physical therapist.

You may get a mix of these treatments. The right mix depends on how much pain and stiffness you have.

## Physical Therapy for Frozen Shoulder

Physical therapy helps you move your shoulder again.

A physical therapist will check how much movement you have. They will plan your treatment.

Most people need at least 6 weeks of therapy. The exact time depends on how fast your shoulder improves.

The therapist may use:

- Stretching exercises
- Strength exercises
- Advice on good posture
- Pain relief, including steroid injections

If you still have pain after your sessions, go back to your doctor or therapist. They may suggest more therapy or another treatment.

Many physical therapists work at doctor’s offices. In some places, you can see a physical therapist without first seeing a doctor.

You can also get physical therapy on your own, by paying for it privately.

## How to Help Yourself at Home

You can do things to ease the pain on your own.

### Do These Things:
- Follow the exercises your doctor or physical therapist gave you.
- Move your shoulder regularly. Keeping it still makes the pain worse.
- Take paracetamol every 4 to 6 hours, up to the daily limit.
- Use a heat pack or hot water bottle. Wrap it in a tea towel. Put it on your shoulder for up to 20 minutes at a time. You can buy heat packs at the pharmacy.

### Do Not Do These Things:
- Do not make up your own tough exercises. For example, using gym machines can make the pain worse.

## What Causes Frozen Shoulder?

Doctors do not always know why it happens.

Frozen shoulder occurs when the tissue around your shoulder joint becomes inflamed.

This tissue then tightens and shrinks. This causes pain and stiffness.

It can happen because:

- You had an injury or surgery that made it hard to move your arm.
- You have diabetes. It is not clear why, but it is important to keep up with your diabetes check-ups. This helps catch problems early.

# Pressure Injuries

A pressure injury is damage to the skin and deeper tissues. It often starts as a sore or open wound. It happens when pressure is applied to the skin for too long. This pressure squeezes soft tissues between bones and hard surfaces like beds or wheelchairs.

Pressure injuries are caused by:
- Long-lasting pressure on the skin
- Rubbing (friction) from clothes or bedding
- Shearing forces (when the body slides down a surface)
- Wet skin from sweat or incontinence

## Who Is at Risk?

You are more likely to get a pressure injury if you:
- Are over 65 years old
- Have poor blood flow or circulation
- Cannot move much (such as being in bed or in a wheelchair)
- Are underweight or not eating enough
- Cannot feel pain or pressure
- Have bladder or bowel incontinence

Children with serious nerve problems like spina bifida or cerebral palsy can also get pressure injuries.

In the United States, up to 3 million adults get pressure injuries each year. Among hospital patients, 5% to 15% have them. The rate is even higher in long-term care homes and intensive care units.

The term "pressure injury" is now preferred over "pressure ulcer." This is because early damage may not yet form an open wound. The National Pressure Injury Advisory Panel recommends this change.

## What Causes Pressure Injuries?

### Risk Factors

- **Age over 65**: Skin and blood vessels weaken with age. There is less fat under the skin, and blood flow slows down.
- **Limited movement**: This includes being in bed for long periods, being in a coma, having a spinal injury, or being very weak.
- **Skin irritants**: Urine or stool on the skin can damage it.
- **Poor healing**: Conditions like diabetes, poor blood flow from artery disease, or poor nutrition can slow healing.
- **Loss of feeling**: If you cannot feel pressure or pain, you may not notice early signs.
- **Incontinence**: Wet skin from urine or stool increases risk.

### Risk Assessment Tools

Doctors use tools to check your risk. Two common ones are:
- **Norton Scale**: Looks at physical health, mental state, ability to move, mobility, and incontinence.
- **Braden Scale**: Looks at how well you feel sensations, skin moisture, activity, movement, nutrition, and friction/shear.

Both tools give a score. A low score means higher risk. A score below 14 on the Norton Scale means you are at high risk.

Even though these tools are widely used, they do not always prevent pressure injuries. But using them with a doctor’s expert judgment is still recommended.

### How Pressure Injuries Develop

- **Pressure**: When skin is pressed for too long, blood flow stops. This starves the tissue of oxygen. If pressure is not relieved, damage can start in 3 to 4 hours. Common spots: tailbone, hips, ankles, and heels.
- **Friction**: Rubbing from sheets or clothes can wear away the skin’s surface.
- **Shearing forces**: When a person slides down in bed, deeper tissues move while the skin stays in place. This can damage blood vessels and cause injury.
- **Moisture**: Wet skin from sweat or incontinence becomes soft and weak. It breaks down more easily.

Muscle tissue is more sensitive to pressure than skin. So, damage can start deep in the muscle before the skin shows signs.

When blood flow stops and then returns, it causes more harm. This is called reperfusion injury. It leads to swelling and inflammation. The damage can be worse in older people or babies.

## What Do Pressure Injuries Look Like?

- They may be painful or itchy.
- But people with poor feeling may not notice them.
- They often start as red or purple areas on the skin.
- Over time, they can break open and form sores.

## What Can Go Wrong?

Pressure injuries can lead to serious problems:
- **Infections**: These are the most common issue. Bacteria grow in the wound and can spread.
  - Examples: skin infections, abscesses, joint infections, or deep tissue infections.
- **Osteomyelitis**: Infection in the bone. This happens in up to 32% of people with deep pressure injuries.
- **Marjolin ulcer**: A rare type of skin cancer that can form in long-standing wounds.
- **Sinus tracts**: Openings that connect the wound to deeper tissues, like the bowel.
- **Systemic infections**: Bacteria can enter the blood, leading to serious illness like blood infection, meningitis, or heart infection.

The more severe the injury, the higher the risk of these complications.

## How Are Pressure Injuries Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose pressure injuries by:
- Talking to you and checking your skin
- Looking at the wound’s size, depth, and appearance
- Checking for signs of infection

The wound is often on a bony area like the tailbone or heel.

Sometimes, other conditions can look like pressure injuries. These include:
- Poor blood flow in the legs
- Nerve damage from diabetes

These conditions can also be made worse by pressure, friction, and moisture.

### Wound Assessment

- It can be hard to see how deep the injury really is.
- Doctors take photos and recheck the wound over time.
- They use a system called the PUSH scale to track healing.

### Testing

- Routine wound swabs are not needed. All pressure injuries have many bacteria.
- A full nutrition check is important, especially for deep wounds.
- Blood tests like albumin or prealbumin are not reliable on their own.
- If infection is suspected, doctors may check blood counts and markers like CRP or procalcitonin.
- For suspected bone infection, a bone biopsy is the best test, but it is not always possible.
- MRI scans can show how far the injury has spread. They can also find hidden tunnels (sinus tracts) under the skin.

## How Are Pressure Injuries Treated?

Treatment includes many steps:

### 1. Reduce Pressure
- Turn the person every 2 hours.
- Use special mattresses or cushions that reduce pressure.
- Avoid letting the body stay in one position for more than 2 hours.
- Use pillows or padding to protect pressure points.

### 2. Care for the Wound
- Clean the wound gently with water or a mild solution.
- Use dressings that match the wound’s condition:
  - Clear films or hydrocolloids: for dry or lightly wet wounds
  - Alginates or gelling dressings: for wounds with a lot of fluid
  - Foam dressings: for wounds with any amount of fluid
- Remove dead tissue (debridement) if needed.

### 3. Treat Pain
- Use pain medicine as needed.

### 4. Fight Infection
- Use antibiotics if there is a confirmed infection.

### 5. Improve Nutrition
- Check if the person is getting enough protein and calories.
- Give supplements if needed.
- Good nutrition helps healing.

### 6. Surgery
- Surgery may be needed for large or deep wounds.
- It is often used when bones or tendons are exposed.
- Surgery works best when nutrition and other health issues are under control.

## What Is the Outlook?

- Early injuries heal well with proper care. Healing takes weeks.
- Deeper injuries take longer to heal.
- People with diabetes, poor nutrition, or poor blood flow may heal slowly.
- Even if the wound closes, long-term problems can happen if the person’s overall health is not managed.

## How Can Pressure Injuries Be Prevented?

Prevention is key. It includes:

### 1. Find High-Risk People
- Use risk tools like the Norton or Braden Scale.
- Let skilled staff do the assessment.

### 2. Reposition Often
- Turn the person every 2 hours.
- Use pillows or cushions to protect bony areas.
- Even on low-pressure beds, repositioning is needed.

### 3. Check Skin Daily
- Look at pressure points every day under good light.
- Check for redness, warmth, or sores.
- Teach patients and families to do daily checks.

### 4. Keep Skin Clean and Dry
- Wash skin gently with mild soap and water.
- Pat dry—do not rub.
- Use protective creams with zinc oxide or moisture barriers.
- Use antifungal powders or creams if needed.
- Avoid adhesive tape. It can pull off fragile skin.

### 5. Use Protective Padding
- Use sheepskin, foam pads, or special cushions.
- Change bedding and clothes often.

### 6. Protect Incontinent Patients
- Use synthetic dressings to keep urine and stool away from the skin.
- Clean and dry the area right after incontinence.

### 7. Avoid Immobilization
- Do not keep people in bed or in a chair longer than needed.
- Use the lowest dose of sedatives possible.
- Help people move as soon as it is safe.

## Key Points

- Pressure injuries can happen during hospital stays or long-term care, especially in older adults, babies, or people with incontinence or poor nutrition.
- Use both risk tools and expert judgment to find who is at risk.
- The injury may be deeper than it looks on the surface.
- Check for infection, bone infection, poor nutrition, or other problems in people with pressure injuries.
- Prevent and treat by:
  - Reducing pressure
  - Repositioning often
  - Using special cushions or beds
  - Keeping skin clean and dry
- Clean and dress wounds regularly.
- Use the right dressing for the wound’s fluid level.
- Treat pain with medicine.
- Treat infections with antibiotics.
- Consider surgery for large or deep wounds

# Lichen Sclerosus

Lichen sclerosus is a skin condition that often causes itching. It can also lead to scarring around the anus and genitals.

The exact cause is not known. But it may happen when the body’s immune system mistakenly attacks its own skin.

This condition mainly affects the skin around the anus and genitals. It can very rarely appear on other parts of the body.

## Symptoms of Lichen Sclerosus

At first, the skin may look bruised. It can also blister. Itching is common, and it can be very strong.

Over time, the skin may become thin. It may lose its normal color. Cracks and flaky patches can appear.

In some people, the skin becomes thicker instead of thinner.

If the condition goes on for a long time, scarring can change the shape of the area around the anus and genitals.

In children, the skin changes can look like signs of abuse. This can be upsetting. But it is not caused by abuse.

In rare cases, a type of skin cancer called squamous cell carcinoma can develop in skin that has had lichen sclerosus for many years.

## How Doctors Diagnose Lichen Sclerosus

Doctors look at the skin. They check how it looks and where it is affected.

Sometimes, doctors take a small sample of skin. They look at it under a microscope. This is called a biopsy.

A biopsy helps rule out skin cancer, especially if the skin is thickened.

## Treatment for Lichen Sclerosus

Doctors prescribe strong corticosteroid creams or ointments. These are applied directly to the skin.

Lichen sclerosus usually cannot be cured. It often causes scarring. So treatment is needed for a long time.

People with this condition need regular checkups. These checkups help find skin cancer early if it develops.

# Epididymitis – Simple Guide

## What is epididymitis?

Epididymitis is when the tube behind your testicle becomes inflamed.  
This causes pain and swelling in your testicles or the skin bag that holds them (the scrotum).

## Symptoms

You may notice:
- Pain in one or both testicles. The pain can come on suddenly or build up slowly.
- The scrotum feels tender, warm, and swollen.
- A lump or swelling around the testicle. This can be fluid buildup (called a hydrocele).

You might also have:
- Trouble peeing.
- A white, yellow, or green discharge from the tip of your penis.

## Causes

Most often, epididymitis is caused by an infection.

- In men under 35: Usually a sexually transmitted infection (STI), like chlamydia or gonorrhoea.
- In men over 35: Usually a urine infection.

Other causes can include:
- A urinary tract infection (UTI), especially if you have a large prostate, a catheter, or have had recent surgery on your groin, prostate, or bladder.
- Mumps.
- Tuberculosis.
- A certain heart medicine called amiodarone.
- A groin injury.
- Behçet’s disease (a rare condition that causes inflammation in the body).

If your infection is an STI, your doctor may suggest that your recent sexual partners (in the past 6 months) also get tested.

## When to See a Doctor

See your GP if you notice:
- A lump in your testicle.
- Swelling in your testicles.
- A change in the shape of your testicles.
- A change in how your testicles feel.
- One testicle getting bigger than the other.
- Ongoing aching or discomfort in your testicles.

A lump in the testicle can be a sign of testicular cancer.  
It is easier to treat if found early.

## When to Go to A&E (Emergency Room)

Go to A&E or call 999 if you have:
- Sudden, severe pain in your testicles or lower belly.

This could mean your testicle is twisted.  
This is an emergency. You need treatment in hospital right away.

> **Important:** Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you.  
> Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
> Bring your medicines with you.

## What Happens at the Doctor’s Appointment

Your doctor or nurse will:
- Examine your groin area.
- Take a swab from the tube that carries pee out (the urethra).
- Test your urine and blood.
- Do a rectal exam to check your prostate.

These tests help find the cause of the problem.

## Treatment

You will likely be given antibiotics.  
They may come as injections, tablets, or both.

- Take all the antibiotics as prescribed.
- Do not stop early, even if you feel better.
- You should start to feel better in a few days.
- Full recovery can take up to 3 months.

If symptoms continue after 3 months, you may need more tests.

## How to Help Yourself Recover

### Do these things:
- Take painkillers like paracetamol or ibuprofen.  
  If you have a history of seizures or fits, avoid ibuprofen if you are on certain antibiotics.  
  Ask a pharmacist for advice if unsure.
- Put a cold pack (or a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a towel) on your groin for 15–20 minutes at a time.
- Wear supportive underwear that holds your scrotum up.

### Do not:
- Have sex if you have chlamydia or gonorrhoea until you finish your full treatment.  
  Or wait at least 7 days after treatment starts.

## Key Points

- Epididymitis causes pain and swelling in the testicles.
- It is often caused by an STI in younger men or a urine infection in older men.
- Early treatment helps prevent long-term problems.
- A lump in the testicle can be a sign of cancer. See a doctor early.
- Sudden, severe pain needs emergency care.
- Always finish your full course of antibiotics.
- Supportive care like cold packs and painkillers can help with symptoms.

# Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) Vaccine

The RSV vaccine helps protect babies and older adults from a serious lung infection caused by the respiratory syncytial virus.

This virus can make babies very sick. It can also make older adults very sick, sometimes needing hospital care.

You can find more information about vaccines in the section called "Overview of Immunization."

---

## Types of RSV Vaccines

There are three RSV vaccines available:

- A nonadjuvanted RSV vaccine  
- An adjuvanted RSV vaccine  
- An mRNA-based RSV vaccine  

The first two vaccines are made from a part of the virus that cannot cause disease. They are inactivated and do not contain live virus.

The mRNA-based vaccine uses a small piece of genetic material. This tells your body how to make a protein from the virus. This helps your body learn to fight the real virus if you are exposed to it.

---

## Who Should Get the RSV Vaccine

### For Pregnant People

The nonadjuvanted RSV vaccine is recommended for pregnant people between 32 and 36 weeks of pregnancy.

It should be given from September through January in most of the continental United States.

You do not need another dose in the same pregnancy or in future pregnancies.

If you got the RSV vaccine in a past pregnancy, your baby should get a special antibody treatment instead of the vaccine.

In places where RSV season is different — like Alaska or tropical areas — follow local health advice. This may include guidance from the CDC or your local health department.

You should get the vaccine even if you have had RSV before.

### For Adults

All three RSV vaccines are recommended for adults aged 75 years and older.

For adults aged 60 to 74 years, the vaccine may be recommended based on a discussion with your doctor.

You may benefit most if you have any of the following health conditions:

- Lung problems such as asthma or COPD  
- Heart disease  
- Nervous system or muscle conditions  
- Kidney disease  
- Liver disease  
- Blood disorders  
- Diabetes  
- A weakened immune system (from illness or medicine)  
- Being frail  
- Living in a nursing home or long-term care facility  

Older adults and those with these conditions are at higher risk of serious illness from RSV.

---

## Who Should Not Get the RSV Vaccine

### Do not get the vaccine if you:

- Have had a severe allergic reaction (like anaphylaxis) to any part of the vaccine.

### Be careful before getting the vaccine if you:

- Are very sick with a fever or other serious illness.

Wait until you feel better before getting the vaccine.

---

## How the Vaccine Is Given

The RSV vaccine is given as one shot into the muscle.

The shot is 0.5 milliliters in size.

It is given once.

---

## Side Effects of the RSV Vaccine

Common side effects include:

- Pain at the injection site  
- Feeling tired  
- Muscle aches  
- Headache  
- Joint pain  

These side effects are usually mild and go away in a few days.

For more details about side effects, read the vaccine’s prescribing information.
