# Heart Failure Medicines: Simple Guide

Heart failure means your heart cannot pump blood well enough to meet your body’s needs. This can cause fluid to build up in your lungs and veins. It can also make your heart weaker or stiffer over time.

Medicines help in two main ways:
- They ease symptoms like shortness of breath and swelling.
- They help you live longer.

The right medicine depends on the type of heart failure you have.

---

## Types of Heart Failure and Which Medicines Help

### Systolic Heart Failure (HFrEF)
This is when the heart does not squeeze well.  
All of these medicines are helpful:
- ACE inhibitors
- Beta-blockers
- Aldosterone antagonists
- ARBs
- ARNIs
- SGLT2 inhibitors
- Digoxin
- Diuretics
- Vasodilators
- Ivabradine

### Diastolic Heart Failure (HFpEF)
This is when the heart does not relax properly.  
The following medicines are usually used:
- ACE inhibitors
- ARBs
- Aldosterone antagonists
- Beta-blockers
- SGLT2 inhibitors

### Mildly Reduced Heart Function (HFmrEF)
This is when the heart’s squeezing is only a little weaker.  
These medicines may help:
- ARNIs
- SGLT2 inhibitors

---

## Important Tips

- Take your medicine every day as your doctor tells you.
- Do not let your medicine run out.
- If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. But do not double up.

---

## How Each Medicine Works

### Aldosterone Antagonists
Aldosterone is a hormone that makes your body keep salt and water.  
These medicines block aldosterone.  
They help reduce fluid buildup.  
They also help you live longer and reduce hospital visits.

Examples: Spironolactone, Eplerenone

### ACE Inhibitors
ACE inhibitors stop your body from making a hormone called angiotensin II.  
This hormone causes your kidneys to keep salt and water.  
By blocking it, these medicines help your body get rid of extra fluid.  
They also widen blood vessels.  
This makes it easier for your heart to pump.  
They reduce symptoms, lower hospital visits, and help you live longer.

Examples: Captopril, Enalapril, Lisinopril, Ramipril

### Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers (ARBs)
ARBs work like ACE inhibitors.  
They block the same hormone (angiotensin II) but in a different way.  
They are used if you cannot take ACE inhibitors because of a dry cough.  
They help reduce fluid and improve heart function.

Examples: Losartan, Valsartan, Candesartan

### Angiotensin Receptor/Neprilysin Inhibitors (ARNIs)
This is a new type of medicine.  
It combines an ARB with a drug that blocks an enzyme called neprilysin.  
Neprilysin breaks down chemicals that help your body get rid of salt.  
By blocking it, the medicine helps your body remove more salt and water.  
This lowers blood pressure and eases the heart’s work.  
ARNIs help people live longer than ACE inhibitors alone.

Example: Valsartan plus sacubitril

**Important:** Stop taking ACE inhibitors at least 36 hours before starting this medicine.

### Beta-Blockers
These medicines slow your heart rate.  
They block a stress hormone that overworks your heart.  
They improve heart function over time.  
They help you live longer.  
They are used with ACE inhibitors.  
They may make symptoms worse at first, but get better over time.

Examples: Bisoprolol, Carvedilol, Metoprolol

### Digoxin
This is an old medicine.  
It makes each heartbeat stronger.  
It also slows a fast heart rate.  
It helps ease symptoms for some people with systolic heart failure.  
But it does not help you live longer.

Example: Digoxin

### Diuretics ("Water Pills")
These help your kidneys remove extra salt and water.  
They reduce swelling and fluid in the lungs.  
They are used when diet alone does not help.

#### Loop Diuretics
These are the most common for heart failure.  
They work well for moderate to severe cases.  
They can be taken by mouth or given through a vein in emergencies.

Examples: Furosemide, Torsemide, Bumetanide

#### Thiazide Diuretics
These are milder.  
They are often used if you also have high blood pressure.

Examples: Hydrochlorothiazide

#### Potassium-Sparing Diuretics
Loop and thiazide diuretics can cause low potassium.  
These medicines help keep potassium levels normal.  
They are often used with other diuretics.

Examples: Spironolactone, Eplerenone, Amiloride, Triamterene

Spironolactone is the most commonly used.  
It helps you live longer.  
It should not be used if your kidneys are very damaged.

**Note:** Diuretics can make it harder to control your bladder.  
You can time your dose so you are not at risk when a bathroom is not nearby.

### Ivabradine (Sinus Node Inhibitor)
This medicine slows the heart rate.  
It works on the heart’s natural pacemaker.  
It reduces the heart’s workload.  
It may help reduce hospital visits in some people with systolic heart failure.

Example: Ivabradine

### SGLT2 Inhibitors
These are diabetes medicines.  
They also help the heart and blood vessels.  
They lower blood sugar.  
But they help heart failure even if you do not have diabetes.

Examples: Dapagliflozin, Empagliflozin

- Dapagliflozin helps reduce symptoms and improve quality of life in systolic heart failure.
- Empagliflozin helps reduce hospital visits in diastolic heart failure.

**Do not use** if you have very low blood pressure or poor kidney function.

### Vasodilators
These medicines widen blood vessels.  
This makes it easier for the heart to pump.  
They are not used as often as ACE inhibitors or ARBs.  
But they can help if you cannot take those medicines.

Examples: Hydralazine, Isosorbide dinitrate, Nitroglycerin (patch or spray)

- Nitroglycerin is helpful if you have both heart failure and chest pain (angina).
- It is also used in sudden heart failure emergencies.
- The mix of hydralazine and nitrates works well, especially in people of African descent.

---

## Other Medicines That May Be Used

### Antiarrhythmic Drugs
If your heart beats irregularly, these medicines can help.  
They are used to fix abnormal heart rhythms.

### Other Heart-Pumping Drugs
Doctors have tried other medicines to make the heart pump harder.  
So far, none have helped.  
Some even made things worse and increased the risk of death.

---

## Summary Table of Common Heart Failure Medicines

| Medicine | What It Does | Key Points |
|--------|--------------|----------|
| **Aldosterone antagonists** | Block salt and water retention | Spironolactone and eplerenone help you live longer. Eplerenone causes fewer side effects in men. |
| **ACE inhibitors** | Widen blood vessels, reduce fluid | Main treatment for systolic heart failure. Help you live longer. |
| **ARBs** | Work like ACE inhibitors | Used if you cannot take ACE inhibitors due to cough. |
| **ARNIs** | Combine ARB and neprilysin blocker | Better than ACE inhibitors for some people with systolic heart failure. |
| **Beta-blockers** | Slow heart rate, reduce stress on heart | Used with ACE inhibitors. Improve heart function over time. |
| **Digoxin** | Makes heart beat stronger | Helps symptoms but does not extend life. |
| **Loop diuretics** | Remove salt and water | Furosemide, torsemide, bumetanide. Used for moderate to severe heart failure. |
| **Thiazide diuretics** | Mild fluid removal | Hydrochlorothiazide. Good for people with high blood pressure. |
| **Potassium-sparing diuretics** | Keep potassium in body | Spironolactone and eplerenone are best. Help you live longer. |
| **Ivabradine** | Slows heart rate | Helps some people with systolic heart failure. |
| **SGLT2 inhibitors** | Help heart and blood vessels | Dapagliflozin and empagliflozin. Help even without diabetes. |
| **Vasodilators** | Open blood vessels | Hydralazine, nitrates. Used if other medicines are not tolerated. |

---

## Side Effects

Side effects of ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics, and beta-blockers are listed in the table **Antihypertensive Drugs**.

Always talk to your doctor if you feel unwell or have new symptoms.

---

**Remember:**  
- Take your medicine every day.  
- Do not stop without talking to your doctor.  
- Keep your appointments.  
- Report any new or worsening symptoms.

# Atopic Eczema – Simple Guide

Atopic eczema causes itchy, dry skin.  
Your skin may also be red, white, purple, or grey.  
It can be lighter or darker than the skin around it.

You are more likely to have atopic eczema if your parent has it.  
Things like soap, laundry detergent, or certain fabrics can make it worse.

If you have atopic eczema, avoid triggers.  
Use moisturising creams often.  
Try not to scratch the skin.

The main treatments are:
- Moisturising creams, lotions, ointments, or gels (called emollients)
- Steroid creams, lotions, or gels applied to the skin (called topical corticosteroids)

---

## How to Know If It’s Atopic Eczema

Atopic eczema often shows up on the elbows, knees, and hands.  
In babies and young children, it often appears on the face.

Your skin may be:
- Itchy
- Dry, cracked, scaly, thickened, or crusty
- Red, white, purple, or grey
- Lighter or darker than the skin around it (this depends on your skin tone)
- Blistered or bleeding

Symptoms can start at any age.  
But they usually begin in babies and young children.  
Many people get better as they grow older.

You may have times when symptoms are worse (called flare-ups).  
You may also have times when symptoms are better.

---

## What Causes Atopic Eczema?

Doctors do not always know what causes it.

You are more likely to have it if:
- One or both of your parents have atopic eczema
- You or a close family member has asthma or hay fever

Things that can make it worse include:
- Contact with allergens or irritants like soap, laundry detergent, pets, certain fabrics, pollen, dust mites, or some foods
- Heat or sudden changes in temperature
- Skin infections, such as a staph infection
- Stress
- Hormonal changes, like during pregnancy

Atopic eczema is not contagious.  
You cannot catch it or pass it to someone else.

---

## What You Can Do to Help

### Do These Things

- Avoid things that make your eczema worse. This includes soap, laundry detergent, some fabrics, or pets.
- Use moisturising creams (emollients) on your skin at least twice a day.  
  Keep using them even when your skin feels better.
- Wash with an emollient instead of soap.
- Stay cool. Heat can make itching worse.
- Keep nails short.  
  Use anti-scratch mittens on babies to stop them from scratching and damaging the skin.

### Do Not Do These Things

- Do not scratch your eczema. Scratching can make it worse.  
  If it itches, gently rub the area with your finger instead.
- Do not share your emollients with anyone else.
- Do not put your fingers into the emollient pot.  
  Use a spoon or pump dispenser instead.
- Do not use aqueous cream. It can irritate the skin and make eczema worse.
- Do not change your diet unless a doctor tells you to.  
  This includes if you are breastfeeding a baby with eczema.
- Do not smoke or go near open flames if you use emollients.  
  Emollients are safe on the skin, but they can catch fire easily if they get on clothes, bedding, or dressings.

---

## Help from a Pharmacist

A pharmacist can help if you have small, dry, slightly itchy patches of eczema.

If your eczema is more severe, see a doctor.

---

## Treatment for Atopic Eczema

There is no cure for atopic eczema.  
But symptoms often improve as you get older.

Treatments can help control symptoms and make your skin feel better.

The main treatments are:
- Moisturising creams, lotions, ointments, or gels (emollients)  
  Use these on your skin and in the bath or shower.
- Steroid creams, lotions, or gels (topical corticosteroids)  
  Apply these to the affected skin as needed.

For more severe cases, your doctor may suggest:
- Special dressings
- Other medicines

Your doctor can prescribe treatment.  
Or you may be referred to a skin specialist (dermatologist).

Living with atopic eczema can be tough.  
If it affects your mood or mental health, you may be referred to a mental health specialist.

---

### See a Doctor If:

- You or your child have symptoms of atopic eczema
- Current treatments are not helping

---

### Get Urgent Help If:

You or your child have atopic eczema and:
- The skin is blistered, crusty, or leaking fluid
- The skin has pus-filled spots
- The area is painful, swollen, or warm to touch
- The eczema suddenly gets worse or spreads quickly
- You or your child has a high temperature or feel unwell

These signs may mean the eczema is infected.  
Or it could be a serious condition called eczema herpeticum.  
You may need antibiotics.

👉 Check your symptoms online at 111.nhs.uk (for people aged 5 and over).  
📞 Call 111 (for children under 5).

# Parkinson Disease – Simple Explanation

Parkinson disease is a long-term brain condition. It slowly gets worse over time. It affects how you move your body.

## What Are the Main Symptoms?

The main signs of Parkinson disease are:

- A shaking that happens when your body is at rest. This often starts in one hand.
- Stiffness in your muscles.
- Slow movements. You may find it hard to start moving.
- Trouble with balance and walking. You may shuffle or take small steps.

These symptoms usually start on one side of the body. They often get worse over time.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose Parkinson disease by looking at your symptoms and doing a physical exam.

They check for:
- Shaking when your body is still.
- Muscle stiffness.
- Slow or small movements.
- Problems with balance and walking.

They also ask about your medical history. This includes your family history, past jobs, and medicines you take.

If your symptoms do not improve with a medicine called levodopa, it may not be Parkinson disease.

A brain scan called dopamine ligand imaging can help. It shows if the brain is not making enough dopamine. This test can help rule out other causes.

## What Causes Parkinson Disease?

Most cases have no clear cause. This is called idiopathic Parkinson disease.

Some people get Parkinson disease at a young age. This is rare. It can be linked to genes.

Other causes of similar symptoms include:
- Certain medicines.
- Stroke or brain injury.
- Infections like encephalitis.

There are also other brain diseases that look like Parkinson disease but are different. These include:
- Multiple system atrophy.
- Progressive supranuclear palsy.
- Dementia with Lewy bodies.

These diseases do not respond as well to Parkinson medicines.

## What Happens in the Brain?

In Parkinson disease, brain cells that make dopamine die off. Dopamine helps control movement.

The loss of these cells happens in a part of the brain called the substantia nigra. This leads to less dopamine in the brain.

A protein called alpha-synuclein builds up in brain cells. It forms clumps called Lewy bodies. These clumps are a sign of Parkinson disease.

The problem may start in other parts of the nervous system before the brain. This includes the gut and the nerves that control the heart and digestion.

## Risk Factors

Some things may increase your risk of Parkinson disease:

- Being older.
- Having a family history of the disease.
- Living near farms or working with pesticides.
- Drinking well water over a long time.
- Exposure to carbon monoxide.

Some things may lower your risk:
- Drinking coffee or tea.
- Smoking (though this is not recommended due to other health risks).
- Being physically active.

## Other Symptoms You Might Have

Parkinson disease affects more than just movement. You may also have:

- Trouble sleeping. You may wake up often or have vivid dreams.
- REM sleep behavior disorder: You may talk, shout, or move your arms and legs during sleep.
- Loss of smell (anosmia).
- Constipation.
- Dizziness when standing up (orthostatic hypotension).
- Trouble swallowing.
- Urinary problems like needing to go often or not being able to start.
- Drooling.
- Depression or anxiety.
- Memory problems or confusion (dementia). This happens in about one in three people, usually later in the disease.

Some of these symptoms can appear before the movement problems.

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure, but treatments can help manage symptoms.

### Medicines

The most effective medicine is levodopa. It helps replace lost dopamine.

Levodopa is often combined with carbidopa. This helps it work better and reduces side effects.

Other medicines include:
- Amantadine – helps with movement and can reduce side effects.
- MAO-B inhibitors (like selegiline or rasagiline) – slow down dopamine breakdown.
- Dopamine agonists (like pramipexole or ropinirole) – mimic dopamine.
- COMT inhibitors – help levodopa last longer.

These medicines are often used early in the disease, especially in younger people with mild symptoms.

If the first medicines do not work well, doctors usually start levodopa. It can greatly improve quality of life.

Levodopa does not become less effective because of long-term use. It stops working because the disease gets worse.

### Surgery

For people whose symptoms do not improve with medicine, surgery may help.

Deep brain stimulation is a common option. It uses a device to send small electrical pulses to parts of the brain.

This surgery works best in people who:
- Do not have dementia.
- Do not have serious mental health problems.

### Lifestyle and Support

Exercise is very important. It helps with movement, balance, and mood.

Physical therapy, occupational therapy, and speech therapy can also help.

Adaptive tools (like special utensils or walkers) can make daily tasks easier.

## Key Points

- Parkinson disease is a brain condition that slowly gets worse.
- It causes shaking, stiffness, slow movement, and balance problems.
- Doctors diagnose it by checking your symptoms and doing a physical exam.
- A brain scan can help rule out other causes.
- The main treatment is levodopa with carbidopa.
- Other medicines can be used early or with levodopa.
- Surgery like deep brain stimulation may help if medicines do not work.
- Exercise and support from therapists are important.
- Some symptoms like sleep problems, constipation, and mood changes are common and should be treated.

If you or a loved one has these symptoms, talk to a doctor. Early treatment can make a big difference.

# Portal Hypertension

Portal hypertension means the blood pressure in the main vein that carries blood from your gut to your liver is too high.

This vein is called the portal vein.

## What Causes Portal Hypertension?

The most common cause is scarring in the liver. This scarring is called cirrhosis.

Cirrhosis makes it hard for blood to flow through the liver. This raises pressure in the portal vein.

Other causes include:
- Blood clots in the veins going to or from the liver
- A parasite infection called schistosomiasis
- Long-term alcohol use
- Metabolic dysfunction–associated liver disease (MASLD), formerly known as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)
- Chronic hepatitis C (a long-lasting liver infection)

## How the Blood Flows Through the Liver

The portal vein brings blood from your intestines, spleen, pancreas, and gallbladder to your liver.

Your liver uses this blood to process nutrients from food.

The portal vein splits into smaller branches inside the liver.

After the blood passes through the liver, it leaves through the hepatic vein and goes into the main bloodstream.

## Why Pressure Builds Up

Two things can raise pressure in the portal vein:
- More blood flowing through the veins
- Harder for blood to pass through the liver

When the liver is scarred, blood has a harder time flowing through it. This causes pressure to build up.

## What Happens When Pressure Is High?

The body creates new blood vessels to help blood flow around the blocked area. These are called collateral vessels.

These new vessels connect the portal vein to other veins that carry blood away from the liver.

Because these vessels bypass the liver, harmful substances (like toxins) can enter the main bloodstream.

The most dangerous collateral vessels form in the lower part of the esophagus and the upper part of the stomach.

These vessels become swollen and twisted. They are called varicose veins.

Esophageal varices and gastric varices are weak and can bleed easily.

Bleeding from these veins can be serious or even deadly.

Other collateral vessels can form on the belly wall or near the rectum.

## Effects on the Spleen

High pressure in the portal vein can make the spleen grow larger.

When the spleen is enlarged, it may trap too many blood cells.

This can lower your white blood cell count. That increases your risk of infection.

It can also lower your platelet count. That increases your risk of bleeding.

## Fluid Buildup in the Belly

High pressure can cause fluid to leak from the liver and intestines into the belly.

This fluid builds up and causes swelling. This condition is called ascites.

## Symptoms of Portal Hypertension

The high pressure itself does not cause symptoms.

But the problems it causes do.

### Swollen Belly (Ascites)
- The belly becomes big and tight.
- It can feel uncomfortable or painful.
- The swelling may be very noticeable.

### Enlarged Spleen
- You may feel a dull ache in the upper left side of your belly.

### Bleeding from Varicose Veins
- You may vomit blood or dark material that looks like coffee grounds.
- Your stool may be black and sticky.
- Less often, you may pass blood in your stool if the rectal veins bleed.

### Confusion or Drowsiness
- Toxins that should be cleaned by the liver reach the brain.
- This can cause confusion, trouble thinking, or drowsiness.
- This is called hepatic encephalopathy.

### Signs of Liver Failure
- You may bleed easily.
- You may feel very tired.
- You may have other signs of poor liver function.

## How Doctors Diagnose Portal Hypertension

Doctors look at your symptoms and do a physical exam.

They may feel your belly to check for a swollen spleen.

They may tap your belly to hear a dull sound. This can show fluid is present.

### Tests Doctors May Use

- **Blood tests** – to check liver function and blood cell counts.
- **Imaging tests** – such as ultrasound, MRI, or CT scan.
  - These can show blood flow, fluid in the belly, and abnormal blood vessels.
- **Endoscopy** – a thin tube with a camera is passed through the mouth to look at the esophagus and stomach.
  - This helps find varicose veins and check for bleeding.
- **Liver biopsy** – a small sample of liver tissue is taken to check for scarring.
- **Pressure test** – a thin tube is inserted through the neck and guided into the liver to measure pressure in the portal vein.

## Treatment of Portal Hypertension

### If You Are Bleeding

Bleeding from esophageal varices is an emergency.

Treatment includes:
- Blood transfusions to replace lost blood.
- Endoscopy to find the bleeding site.
- Rubber bands are used during endoscopy to tie off the bleeding veins.

### To Prevent Future Bleeding

Doctors may prescribe beta-blocker medicines. These include:
- Timolol
- Propranolol
- Nadolol
- Carvedilol

These medicines help lower pressure in the portal vein.

### If Bleeding Keeps Happening

A procedure called TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunting) may be done.

How TIPS works:
- A doctor inserts a tube through a vein in the neck.
- The tube is guided to the liver using X-rays.
- A small tunnel (shunt) is made between the portal vein and a hepatic vein.
- This lets blood flow around the liver and lowers pressure.

This helps stop bleeding and reduces pressure in the portal vein.

### Other Shunt Options

Sometimes, surgery is used to create a shunt. This is less common.

### Risks of Shunt Procedures

- The shunt may become blocked and need to be fixed.
- The shunt can cause hepatic encephalopathy (confusion or drowsiness).
- This happens because more toxins reach the brain.

### Liver Transplant

Some people need a liver transplant.

This is the only cure for severe liver damage and portal hypertension.

## Summary

- Portal hypertension means high pressure in the vein that carries blood from your gut to your liver.
- The most common cause is liver scarring (cirrhosis).
- It can lead to fluid in the belly, enlarged spleen, and dangerous bleeding from varicose veins.
- It can also cause confusion and other signs of liver failure.
- Doctors diagnose it using symptoms, exams, and tests like ultrasound, CT, MRI, or endoscopy.
- Treatment includes medicines, endoscopy, shunt procedures, or liver transplant.
- Early treatment can prevent serious complications.

# Cradle Cap

Cradle cap is a common skin condition in babies.  
It causes greasy, scaly patches on the skin.  
It usually appears on the scalp.  
It can also show up on the face, body, or in the nappy area.

The scales may look white or yellow.  
They can form a crust that flakes off.  
On the nappy area, you might see small, dry flakes.

The scales look similar on all skin tones.  
But the skin under them may look pink or red if your baby has white skin.  
If your baby has brown or black skin, the skin under the scales may look lighter or darker than the rest.

Cradle cap does not hurt.  
It does not itch.  
Your baby will not be bothered by it.

No one knows exactly what causes cradle cap.  
It is not contagious.  
You cannot catch it from another baby.

---

## What You Can Do to Help

You can gently treat cradle cap at home.  
The treatment is simple and safe.

### Do These Things

- Put a small amount of moisturiser or coconut oil on your baby’s scalp.  
  Gently rub it in.  
  This helps loosen the scales.

- Use a soft brush to gently brush your baby’s scalp.  
  Then wash the scalp with baby shampoo.

- If the scales are on other parts of the body, bathe your baby with water and moisturiser.  
  Do not use soap.

- Change wet or dirty nappies right away.  
  If the nappy area is affected, use a barrier cream to protect the skin.

- Your baby’s hair may come out with the scales.  
  This is normal.  
  The hair will grow back.

### Do Not Do These Things

- Do not use olive oil.  
  It may not be safe for baby skin.

- Do not use peanut oil.  
  It can cause an allergic reaction.

- Do not use soap, adult shampoos, or products with fragrance or perfume.  
  These can irritate your baby’s skin.

- Do not pick at the crusts.  
  Picking can cause infection.

---

## Ask a Pharmacist

A pharmacist can help you choose safe products.  
They can recommend:

- A moisturiser for your baby’s scalp  
- A fragrance-free baby shampoo  
- A barrier cream for the nappy area, if needed

---

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:

- The cradle cap does not improve after a few weeks of home care  
- The cradle cap covers your baby’s whole body  
- The crusts bleed or leak fluid  
- The skin around the patches looks swollen

Bleeding, fluid, or swelling could mean an infection.  
It could also be a different skin condition, such as eczema or scabies.  
A doctor can check and give the right treatment.

# Internal Tempomandibular Joint (TMJ) Problems

The most common problem inside the jaw joint is when the cushion between the jawbone and the skull moves forward. This is called internal TMJ derangement.

Often, this causes pain and a clicking or popping sound when you open your mouth. The cushion usually moves back into place when you open your mouth wide. But sometimes, it stays out of place. When this happens, your mouth may not open all the way.

Doctors diagnose this by asking about your symptoms and doing a physical exam. An MRI scan can confirm the diagnosis by showing the position of the cushion inside the joint.

Treatment includes pain medicine, resting your jaw, relaxing your jaw muscles, physical therapy, and using a special mouth device. If these do not help, surgery may be needed. Starting treatment early gives better results.

---

## What Causes TMJ Problems?

The cushion inside the joint can change shape. The ligaments that hold it can stretch out. The more these changes happen, the worse the problem can become.

If the cushion moves forward when your mouth is closed and does not move back when you open your mouth, this is called **disc derangement without reduction**.

This can cause:
- Your jaw to feel stuck or locked
- Pain in your ear or around the jaw
- A change in how your teeth fit together

If the cushion moves back into place at some point during mouth opening, this is called **disc derangement with reduction**.

This often causes a clicking or popping sound when you open your mouth. The sound may seem loud to you, but others nearby may not hear it. Pain can happen, especially when chewing tough foods.

About one in three people will have this type of problem at some point in their life.

All types of TMJ problems can cause inflammation in the tissues around the joint. This is called capsulitis. It can happen on its own or after an injury, arthritis, or infection.

---

## Symptoms of TMJ Problems

### Disc Derangement with Reduction
- A painless click or pop when opening your mouth
- The sound may seem loud to you, but others may not hear it
- Pain may happen when chewing hard foods

### Disc Derangement without Reduction
- No clicking or popping sound
- Your mouth cannot open very wide (less than 30 millimeters)
- Your jaw may move to one side when you open your mouth
- You may feel pain
- You may notice your bite feels different

These symptoms often start suddenly in someone who has had a clicking jaw for a long time. Sometimes, you wake up and cannot open your mouth fully.

In some cases, the symptoms go away on their own after 6 to 12 months.

### Capsulitis (Inflammation Around the Joint)
- Pain in the joint area
- Tenderness when you press on the joint
- Sometimes, your mouth cannot open fully

---

## How Doctors Diagnose TMJ Problems

### Step 1: Talk to You and Examine Your Jaw
Doctors ask about your symptoms and check your jaw movement.

### Step 2: Use MRI Scans
An MRI is done with your mouth in both open and closed positions. This shows the exact position of the cushion in relation to the jawbone.

### For Disc Derangement with Reduction:
- You open your mouth more than 10 millimeters (about the width of your thumb).
- You hear or feel a click or pop as the cushion moves back into place.
- The jawbone stays on top of the cushion as you open wider.
- A second, softer click may happen when you close your mouth.

### For Disc Derangement without Reduction:
- You try to open your mouth as wide as possible.
- The opening is measured. Normal is about 45 to 50 millimeters.
- If the cushion is out of place, your mouth opens less than 30 millimeters.
- Your jaw may move to the affected side.
- Pushing your jaw forward or closing it hard makes the pain worse.

### For Capsulitis:
- Doctors look at your history of injury, infection, or other joint problems.
- They check for extreme tenderness over the joint.
- They rule out other causes like muscle pain, arthritis, or jaw misalignment.
- Capsulitis can happen with any of these other conditions.

---

## How TMJ Problems Are Treated

### General Care
- Use pain medicine as needed
- Rest your jaw
- Relax your jaw muscles
- Do physical therapy
- Use a mouth device (oral appliance)

### For Disc Derangement with Reduction
- If you can open your mouth wide (about 40 millimeters, or the width of your index, middle, and ring fingers) without pain, no treatment is needed.
- If you have pain, take pain medicine like ibuprofen every 6 hours as needed.
- Some people benefit from using a device that gently moves the jaw to help the cushion return to its normal position.
- If the problem started less than 6 months ago, a special mouth device may be used. It is shaped like a horseshoe and fits over your teeth. It holds your jaw forward so the cushion can return to its normal spot.
- The device is slowly adjusted so your jaw can move back.
- If the cushion stays in place, it is “captured.”
- The longer the cushion stays out of place, the harder it is to fix.
- Surgery may be done to tighten the cushion, but results vary.

### For Disc Derangement without Reduction
- Pain medicine (like ibuprofen) is often enough.
- A mouth device may help if the cushion is not badly damaged. It can reduce pressure on the tissues behind the cushion. This may help them heal and form a new cushion-like structure.
- But long-term use can change your bite and jaw shape permanently.
- In some cases, you may be taught to gently stretch the cushion out of place. This can help your jaw open normally.
- If non-surgical treatments fail, surgery may be needed.

### For Capsulitis (Joint Inflammation)
- Start with pain medicine (NSAIDs or oral steroids)
- Rest your jaw
- Relax your jaw muscles
- A mouth device may be used for a short time while the inflammation goes down
- If this does not work, a steroid injection into the joint may help.
- Arthroscopic surgery (cleaning and flushing the joint) may be used if needed.

---

## Key Points

- The cushion inside the jaw joint can move forward due to jaw movement problems.
- It may stay out of place (without reduction) or move back (with reduction).
- With reduction, you often hear a click or pop. Your jaw may move to one side. You may have pain when chewing.
- Without reduction, you do not hear a click. Your mouth cannot open wide (less than 30 millimeters). Your jaw may move to one side.
- The tissues around the joint can become inflamed and painful (capsulitis).
- Pain medicine, mouth devices, and jaw exercises often help.
- Surgery is sometimes needed.

# Measles, Mumps, and Rubella Vaccine

This vaccine protects against three serious viral diseases: measles, mumps, and rubella.  
It is given as a shot under the skin.  
You need two doses to be fully protected.

## What the Diseases Do

**Measles**  
Causes a rash, high fever, and cough.  
It mostly affects children.  
It can lead to brain damage, pneumonia, or even death.

**Mumps**  
Makes the glands near the ears swell and hurt.  
It can also affect the testicles, brain, or pancreas.  
It is more dangerous in adults.

**Rubella (German measles)**  
Causes a runny nose, swollen glands, and a rash that starts on the face.  
In adults, it can cause joint pain.  
If a pregnant person gets rubella, they may lose the baby or the baby may be born with serious birth defects.

## How the Vaccine Works

The MMR vaccine contains live but weakened viruses.  
The viruses are too weak to cause disease.  
But they help your body learn how to fight the real viruses.  
This is called active immunity.

The vaccine protects against all three diseases at once.  
There are no separate vaccines for measles, mumps, or rubella anymore.  
The MMR vaccine can also be combined with the chickenpox vaccine (called MMRV).

## Who Should Get the Vaccine

### Children
- Get the first dose between 12 and 15 months of age.  
- Get the second dose between 4 and 6 years of age.

### Adults Born in 1957 or Later
- Should get one dose unless they have proof of vaccination.  
- Should not get the vaccine if they are allergic to any part of it.  
- Should not get it if lab tests show they are already immune.

### People Born Before 1957
- Are usually immune to all three diseases.  
- But health care workers born before 1957 should still get tested or vaccinated.

### Adults Who May Be Exposed to These Diseases
You should get a second dose if you:
- Work in health care and are not immune.  
- Go to college or another school after high school.  
- Travel to countries where measles, mumps, or rubella are common.  
- Are in an area with an outbreak.  
- Have HIV (unless your immune system is very weak).  
- Live with someone who has a very weak immune system.  
- Were vaccinated with an old killed measles vaccine (1963–1967).  
- Were vaccinated with an old killed mumps vaccine (before 1979) and are at high risk of mumps.

### People Who Could Become Pregnant
- Should be tested for rubella immunity.  
- If not immune, get the vaccine when not pregnant.  
- If pregnant, wait until after the pregnancy to get the vaccine.

### Travelers
- Babies 6 to 12 months old who travel abroad should get the vaccine if they are not already immune.  
- Get the vaccine at least 2 weeks before travel.

## Who Should Not Get the Vaccine

Do not get the MMR vaccine if you:
- Had a serious allergic reaction (like anaphylaxis) to any part of the vaccine or to a previous dose.  
- Have a very weak immune system due to leukemia, lymphoma, advanced HIV, chemotherapy, or long-term use of immune-suppressing medicines.  
- Are pregnant.  
- Are allergic to gelatin or the antibiotic neomycin.

If you get the vaccine, avoid getting pregnant for at least 28 days after.

If you are sick with a fever or a serious illness, wait until you feel better before getting the vaccine.

## Side Effects

Most people have no side effects.  
Some may have:
- A mild fever.  
- Feeling unwell.  
- A rash.  
- Temporary joint pain, especially in women.

Rare but serious side effects include:
- Brain inflammation.  
- Seizures caused by fever (febrile seizures).  
- A rare blood clotting problem.

The MMR vaccine does **not** cause autism.  
This has been proven by many studies.

For more details on side effects, read the package insert that comes with the vaccine.

The following resources are helpful.  
The Manual is not responsible for their content.

- European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC): Measles – Recommended Vaccinations  
- ECDC: Mumps – Recommended Vaccinations  
- ECDC: Rubella – Recommended Vaccinations

# Pelvic Organ Prolapse

Pelvic organ prolapse happens when the organs in your pelvis drop down. This can happen in women of any age, but it is more common after age 50.

## Symptoms

You may not have any symptoms. But if you do, they can include:

- A heavy or uncomfortable feeling in your lower belly or vagina.
- A bulge or lump inside your vagina. It might feel like something is coming out.
- Pain, discomfort, or numbness during sex.
- Trouble passing stool. You might feel constipated.
- Problems with your bladder. You might feel like your bladder is not emptying fully. You may need to go to the toilet more often. You might leak a small amount of urine when you cough, sneeze, or exercise.

Sometimes, a prolapse is found during a routine test, like a cervical screening.

## Treatment

Treatment depends on how bad the prolapse is and which organs are affected. Your doctor will also think about your age, your health, and whether you plan to have children.

If you have no symptoms, or the prolapse does not bother you, you may not need treatment.

If the prolapse is more serious or affects your daily life, your doctor may suggest:

- Hormone treatment: A cream, tablet, or ring with hormones that goes into the vagina.
- Vaginal pessary: A small device made of plastic or silicone. It goes into the vagina to support the pelvic organs.
- Pelvic floor exercises: A physiotherapist who specializes in women’s health can help you do these.
- Surgery: If the prolapse is severe, surgery may be an option. It can lift and support the organs.

You and your doctor will decide together which treatment is best for you.

### Important Note

Surgery using a mesh to support the vagina is no longer done on the NHS unless there is no other choice.

If you had mesh surgery before and think it is causing problems, talk to your GP or surgeon.

## Causes

Pelvic organ prolapse happens when the muscles and tissues that support the pelvic organs become weak.

It is more common as you get older, especially after menopause.

Things that can weaken these muscles include:

- Pregnancy and childbirth.
- Being overweight.
- Long-term constipation and straining when going to the toilet.
- A long-term cough.
- Pelvic surgery, such as a hysterectomy.

Some health conditions can also increase your risk, such as:

- Joint hypermobility syndrome.
- Marfan syndrome.
- Ehlers-Danlos syndromes.

## Support and Help

You will get support from your doctor or specialist.

You may also find it helpful to get support online.

Here are some national charities that can help:

### Bladder and Bowel UK

This group offers information and support for anyone with bladder or bowel problems.

- Website: [www.bbuk.org.uk](https://www.bbuk.org.uk)
- Helpline: 0161 214 4591
- Download the "Just Can't Wait" card: Helps you get access to toilets in public places.
- Join their private Facebook group: A safe space to connect with others.

# Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy (CRT)

## What is CRT?

Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) helps the heart beat more efficiently. It uses a special device to make the heart’s chambers contract at the right time. This can improve heart function and reduce symptoms.

## When is CRT Used?

Doctors consider CRT for people with heart failure who have certain heart rhythm problems. It works best in people with:

- Weak heart muscle (called dilated cardiomyopathy)
- A slow or abnormal electrical signal in the heart
- A wide QRS complex on an ECG (130 milliseconds or more)
- A very enlarged left ventricle (55 millimeters or more)
- A weak pumping ability (ejection fraction 35% or less)

## Signs of Heart Rhythm Problems

The heart has four chambers: two upper (atria) and two lower (ventricles). Normally, they contract in a smooth, timed way. But sometimes this timing breaks down. This is called dyssynchrony. It can happen in three ways:

- **Atrioventricular dyssynchrony**: The upper and lower chambers do not contract together.
- **Interventricular dyssynchrony**: The left and right lower chambers do not contract at the same time.
- **Intraventricular dyssynchrony**: Parts of the left lower chamber do not contract together.

## How is CRT Done?

CRT uses a device implanted under the skin, usually near the collarbone. Wires (leads) connect the device to the heart. The device sends small electrical pulses to help the heart beat in a better rhythm.

Most CRT devices have three leads:
- One in the right upper chamber (right atrium)
- One in the right lower chamber (right ventricle)
- One in the left lower chamber (left ventricle)

This is called biventricular pacing. It helps both lower chambers beat together.

The leads can be placed in two ways:
- Through a vein (transvenous)
- Through a small cut in the chest (surgical)

Another option is conduction system pacing. This targets the heart’s natural electrical system, such as the His bundle or left bundle branch. This method may be used in some patients.

## Who Benefits from CRT?

CRT helps people with heart failure who have moderate to severe symptoms. These include:

- Feeling very tired
- Having trouble breathing
- Being limited in daily activities

If you have heart failure and your symptoms are class II, III, or IV on the New York Heart Association scale, CRT can:
- Lower your chance of being hospitalized for heart failure
- Help you live longer

## Who Does Not Benefit?

CRT does not help everyone. It is not effective for:
- People with permanent atrial fibrillation (a common irregular heart rhythm)
- People with right bundle branch block
- People with a mild delay in the heart’s electrical signal (QRS less than 150 milliseconds)
- People with only a nonspecific conduction delay

## Summary

- CRT helps the heart beat more evenly.
- It is best for people with heart failure and specific heart rhythm issues.
- It can reduce hospital visits and improve survival.
- It does not help people with certain types of heart rhythm problems.

Always talk to your doctor to see if CRT is right for you.

# Murine (Endemic) Typhus

Murine typhus is a disease caused by bacteria. The bacteria are *Rickettsia typhi* and *Rickettsia felis*. These bacteria spread through rat fleas.

## What Causes Murine Typhus?

- The bacteria live inside the cells of other living things.
- They mainly live in rats and mice.
- People get infected when bitten by fleas that carry the bacteria.
- Fleas from rats, mice, and cats can spread the disease.

## Where Does It Happen?

- Murine typhus happens all over the world.
- It is rare, but more cases happen in some areas.
- In the United States, most cases are in suburban parts of Hawaii, Texas, and California.
- In these areas, the bacteria often live in opossums and cats.

## Symptoms of Murine Typhus

Symptoms start 6 to 18 days after infection.

- You may have shaking chills.
- You will get a fever.
- You will have a headache.
- The fever lasts about 12 days.
- A rash may appear a few days after the chills and fever.
- The rash starts on the chest or stomach.
- It then spreads to the arms and legs.

- Most people get better without serious problems.
- Older adults are at higher risk of serious illness or death.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several methods to find out if you have murine typhus.

- They look at your symptoms.
- They may take a small sample of the rash (a biopsy) and test it.
- They may use a test called PCR to find the bacteria quickly.
- They may do blood tests to check for antibodies to the bacteria.

- A single blood test is not enough.
- You need a second blood test 1 to 3 weeks later.
- The second test checks if your antibody level has gone up.
- This helps confirm the diagnosis, but it does not help right away.

## How Is It Treated?

- The main treatment is an antibiotic.
- Doxycycline is the most common antibiotic used.
- It is taken by mouth.
- You take it until you feel better and have had no fever for 48 hours.
- You must take it for at least 7 days.

- Some antibiotics can stain teeth in children under 8 if taken for more than 10 days.
- But a short course of doxycycline (5 to 10 days) is safe for children of all ages.
- It does not cause tooth staining or weaken tooth enamel.

## How Can You Prevent It?

- There is no vaccine for murine typhus.
- Prevention means avoiding contact with infected fleas.

To reduce the risk:

- Keep rats and other animals away from your home, workplace, and outdoor areas.
- Remove things that attract animals, such as piles of brush, rocks, junk, firewood, and food.
- Do not leave pet food out where animals can get to it.
- Wear gloves when handling sick or dead animals.

# Cystic Fibrosis

Cystic fibrosis is a long-term health condition. It affects the lungs and digestive system. It is caused by a change in a gene passed from both parents to their child.

## Symptoms of Cystic Fibrosis

Your body makes thick, sticky mucus if you have cystic fibrosis. This mucus can block airways and digestive organs. It can lead to many symptoms and make infections more likely.

### Lung Symptoms
- A cough that lasts a long time and brings up mucus.
- Wheezing and trouble breathing.
- Frequent chest infections.
- Frequent sinus infections.

### Digestive Symptoms
- Constipation.
- Stomach pain, bloating, and swelling.
- Large, greasy, and sticky stools that are hard to flush.

### Other Possible Symptoms
- Children may grow more slowly than expected.
- Adults may lose weight without trying.
- Fingers may swell and become rounder.
- Sweat is very salty. It can leave small white crystals on the skin.

Cystic fibrosis is often found soon after birth. It is part of the NHS newborn screening test. But some people are not diagnosed until they are teenagers.

## What Causes Cystic Fibrosis

Cystic fibrosis is inherited. It happens when a child gets a changed gene from both parents.

The changed gene makes mucus thick and sticky. This causes problems in the lungs and gut.

If a child gets the changed gene from only one parent, they will not have symptoms. But they can pass the gene to their own children.

If both parents carry the changed gene, their child has:
- A 1 in 4 chance of having cystic fibrosis.
- A 2 in 4 chance of not having the condition but being a carrier.
- A 1 in 4 chance of not having the condition and not being a carrier.

### Genetic Counselling

If you or your partner carry the changed gene or have cystic fibrosis, you can ask for genetic counselling. A specialist will talk with you about your options if you are thinking about having a baby.

Your GP or care team can help you get this support.

## How Cystic Fibrosis Is Diagnosed

All babies in the UK are tested for cystic fibrosis as part of the newborn blood spot test.

Tell the doctor if anyone in your family has cystic fibrosis.

If the blood test suggests cystic fibrosis, your baby will have a sweat test. This checks how salty the sweat is. People with cystic fibrosis usually have very salty sweat.

Older children and adults who might have cystic fibrosis will have a blood test and a sweat test.

### Carrier Testing

If a family member has cystic fibrosis or is a known carrier, you can ask to be tested. This is called carrier testing.

You can also ask for carrier testing if your partner has cystic fibrosis or is a carrier.

## Treatments for Cystic Fibrosis

There is no cure for cystic fibrosis. But treatments can help manage symptoms and improve quality of life.

You will work with a team of healthcare professionals. This may include:
- Specialist nurses and doctors.
- A physiotherapist.
- A dietitian.

### Medicines
- CFTR modulators: These medicines help the lungs work better by reducing the effect of the changed gene.
- Inhalers or medicines to open airways and make breathing easier.
- Medicines to help you cough up mucus.
- Antibiotics to treat infections.
- Steroid medicine to reduce swelling in the airways.

### Other Treatments
- Physiotherapy: A physiotherapist can teach you breathing and posture exercises to clear mucus from your lungs.
- Medical devices: Tools like inhalers and special masks can help with breathing and mucus removal.
- Diet and nutrition: A dietitian can help you eat a high-energy diet that is easy to digest. You may also need supplements to help your digestion.

Some people may need a lung transplant if other treatments are not working. But this is not an option for everyone.

## How Cystic Fibrosis Affects Your Life

Cystic fibrosis is a lifelong condition. It can shorten life. But new treatments mean many people with the condition now live well into middle age and beyond.

Living with cystic fibrosis can be hard. But it does not stop you from going to school, having a family, or working.

You will need ongoing care. If you or your child is diagnosed, you will be referred to a specialist cystic fibrosis care team.

These teams are based in larger NHS hospitals. They include doctors, nurses, physiotherapists, dietitians, and other experts. They provide treatment, support, and advice on living with the condition.

## When to See a Doctor

See your GP if:
- You or your child have symptoms of cystic fibrosis and have not been diagnosed.
- You are worried about your child’s growth or development.
- You are pregnant or planning a pregnancy, and someone in your or your partner’s family has cystic fibrosis.

## Support and Help

If you are a parent of a child with cystic fibrosis, or if you live with the condition, talking to others who have it can help.

Because of the risk of infection, people with cystic fibrosis should avoid close contact with each other.

But charities can help you connect with others who have the condition.

### Cystic Fibrosis Trust

The Cystic Fibrosis Trust offers useful information and support.

- [How we can support you](https://www.cysticfibrosis.org.uk)
- [Connect with others](https://www.cysticfibrosis.org.uk/connect)

This organization also links you to other helpful groups and resources.

# Ventricular Fibrillation (VF)

## What Is Ventricular Fibrillation?

Ventricular fibrillation is a serious heart rhythm problem.  
The lower chambers of the heart quiver instead of pumping blood.  
This means the heart cannot send blood to the brain or other organs.  
You will pass out right away.  
Without treatment, death happens within minutes.

## What Causes Ventricular Fibrillation?

VF happens when electrical signals in the heart go wild.  
These signals create many small, chaotic waves.  
An electrocardiogram (ECG) shows fast, irregular waves with no clear pattern.

In the past, VF was the first rhythm seen in about 75% of cardiac arrests.  
Now, it is seen in about 40% of cases.  
But this number is likely too low.  
Over time, VF often turns into a flat line on the ECG, which is called asystole.  
So, VF is still the final rhythm in many heart attacks and other heart problems.

Most people with VF have a known heart condition.  
Common causes include:  
- Heart damage from a past heart attack  
- Thickened heart muscle (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)  
- Enlarged heart (dilated cardiomyopathy)  
- Other heart conditions that cause dangerous rhythms

Some people have VF with no clear heart problem.  
These cases are called idiopathic ventricular fibrillation.

Certain conditions increase the risk of VF:  
- Low levels of key minerals in the blood  
- Too much acid in the blood  
- Low oxygen levels in the blood  
- Poor blood flow to the heart muscle

## VF in Children and Babies

Ventricular fibrillation is rare in infants and children.  
When cardiac arrest happens in young people, a flat line (asystole) is more common.

## How Is Ventricular Fibrillation Treated?

### Immediate Care

The first step is cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR).  
This includes chest compressions and rescue breaths.  
Defibrillation is also needed right away.  
Use a shock of 120 to 200 joules (biphasic) or 360 joules (monophasic).  
The shock must be delivered as soon as possible.

The chance of survival is very high if defibrillation happens within seconds.  
This is possible with an implantable defibrillator.  
If defibrillation is delayed, the success rate drops by about 10% every minute.

### Long-Term Treatment

People who have VF without a temporary or treatable cause are at high risk of future episodes.  
They are also at high risk of sudden death.

Most of these people need an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator.  
This device is placed under the skin.  
It checks the heart rhythm and delivers a shock if needed.

Many people also need medicine to help prevent fast or dangerous heart rhythms.  
These medicines can reduce the number of future episodes of ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation.

# Anemia in the Newborn

Anemia means there are too few red blood cells in the blood.

Red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to all parts of the body. They also carry waste carbon dioxide back to the lungs. When there are not enough red blood cells, the body does not get enough oxygen. This can cause tiredness and weakness.

The bone marrow makes new blood cells. After birth, the bone marrow makes very few new red blood cells for the first few weeks. This causes a normal drop in red blood cell count during the first few months of life. This is called physiologic anemia.

Very early babies (born before 37 weeks) have a bigger drop in red blood cells. This is called anemia of prematurity. It most often affects babies born before 32 weeks of pregnancy. It also affects babies who stay in the hospital for many days.

Anemia can happen if:
- Red blood cells break down too fast.
- A lot of blood is lost.
- The bone marrow does not make enough new red blood cells.

More than one of these can happen at the same time.

---

## Why Red Blood Cells Break Down Too Fast

When red blood cells break down too fast, it causes anemia. This process is called hemolysis.

High levels of bilirubin (a yellow substance made when red blood cells break down) build up in the blood. This can make the baby’s skin and the whites of the eyes look yellow. This is called jaundice.

### Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn
This happens when the mother’s blood has antibodies that attack the baby’s red blood cells. This can cause fast breakdown of red blood cells.

### Hereditary Problems
Some babies are born with abnormal red blood cells. For example:
- **Hereditary spherocytosis**: The red blood cells are round instead of round and flat. They break down easily.
- **G6PD deficiency**: Some babies lack a key enzyme in red blood cells. Certain medicines or chemicals during pregnancy can trigger fast breakdown of red blood cells in these babies.

### Hemoglobin Problems
Hemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. Some genetic conditions affect hemoglobin. One example is thalassemia. It can cause anemia in newborns, though this is rare.

### Infections
Infections that happen before, during, or after birth can also destroy red blood cells. These include:
- Toxoplasmosis
- Rubella
- Cytomegalovirus
- Herpes simplex virus
- Syphilis

---

## Blood Loss as a Cause

Blood loss can lead to anemia. It can happen in many ways.

### Blood Moving from Baby to Mother
If a large amount of the baby’s blood moves into the mother’s bloodstream through the placenta, the baby can lose a lot of blood. This is called fetal-maternal transfusion.

### Blood Trapped in the Placenta
If the baby is held above the mother’s belly too long before the umbilical cord is cut, some blood can stay in the placenta. This means the baby gets less blood.

### Twin-to-Twin Transfusion
In twins, blood can flow from one baby to the other. This causes anemia in one twin and too much blood in the other (called polycythemia).

### Placental Problems
- **Placental abruption**: The placenta separates from the uterus too early. This can cause bleeding in the mother and less oxygen for the baby.
- **Placenta previa**: The placenta covers the opening of the uterus. This can cause bleeding during pregnancy or delivery.

### Invasive Tests
Tests done during pregnancy that go into the mother’s body can cause blood loss in the baby. These include:
- Amniocentesis
- Chorionic villus sampling
- Umbilical blood sampling

### Injury During Delivery
- The baby’s liver or spleen can tear during delivery, causing internal bleeding.
- A vacuum or forceps used during delivery can cause bleeding under the baby’s scalp.

### Vitamin K Deficiency
Newborns are born with low levels of vitamin K. This vitamin helps blood clot. Without enough vitamin K, babies can bleed easily. This is called hemorrhagic disease of the newborn. To prevent this, all newborns get a vitamin K shot at birth.

### Inherited Bleeding Disorders
Babies born with hemophilia may bleed easily, especially during a hard delivery. This can lead to anemia.

### Frequent Blood Draws
Taking blood often, especially from premature babies, can add to anemia.

---

## Not Enough Red Blood Cells Made

Sometimes the bone marrow does not make enough red blood cells.

### Before Birth
Rare genetic problems can stop the bone marrow from making red blood cells. Examples include:
- Fanconi syndrome
- Diamond-Blackfan anemia

### After Birth
Some infections can stop the bone marrow from working right. These include:
- Cytomegalovirus
- Syphilis
- HIV

### Lack of Key Nutrients
The bone marrow needs certain nutrients to make red blood cells. A lack of:
- Iron
- Folate (folic acid)
- Vitamin E (rarely)

can cause anemia.

---

## Signs and Symptoms of Anemia

Most babies with mild or moderate anemia have no symptoms.

Some may be:
- Tired or sluggish
- Not feeding well

If a baby suddenly loses a lot of blood during labor or delivery, they may:
- Look pale
- Have a fast heartbeat
- Have low blood pressure
- Breathe fast and shallow
- Be in shock

If red blood cells break down too fast, the baby may also have:
- Yellow skin and eyes (jaundice)

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Anemia

### Before Birth
Doctors may use a prenatal ultrasound to look for signs of anemia in the baby.

### After Birth
Diagnosis is based on:
- The baby’s symptoms
- Blood tests

In some U.S. states, newborns are tested for certain causes of anemia, such as G6PD deficiency.

---

## Treatment of Anemia

### For Blood Loss
If a baby loses a lot of blood, they get fluids through a vein. Then they get a blood transfusion.

### For Hemolytic Disease
Treatment depends on how severe the anemia is. In very severe cases, an exchange transfusion is used. This means slowly removing some of the baby’s blood and replacing it with fresh donor blood. This lowers bilirubin and raises red blood cell count.

### Iron Supplements
Some babies are given liquid iron to help their bodies make more red blood cells.

### For Jaundice
If the baby has yellow skin and eyes, they may get phototherapy. This is also called “bili lights.” The baby lies under special lights that help break down bilirubin.

---

## Important Notes

- Most premature babies have mild anemia and do not need treatment.
- All newborns get a vitamin K shot at birth to prevent bleeding.
- Frequent blood draws can worsen anemia in premature babies.
- Early treatment can prevent serious problems.

# Meniscus Tear (Knee Cartilage Damage)

A meniscus tear is a tear in the soft cushion of tissue inside your knee. It often happens when you twist your knee during sports. But it can also happen from small injuries, like twisting when standing up.

## Symptoms of a Meniscus Tear

You may notice one or more of these signs:

- Pain in your knee or tenderness when you touch it  
- Swelling around your knee – this might not show up right away  
- Your knee feels stiff or hard to move  
- You cannot bend or straighten your knee fully  
- Your knee feels weak and gives way when you stand  
- A crunching or clicking noise when you move your knee  

These symptoms can feel like a sprain.

## What You Can Do to Feel Better

You can help your knee heal by doing these things:

### Do These Things

- Stop any activity that hurts your knee. Rest it for the first few days.  
- Put an ice pack (or a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a towel) on your knee for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours.  
- Wrap a bandage around your knee or wear a knee support. Take it off when you sleep.  
- Keep your leg raised on a pillow as much as possible. This helps reduce swelling.  
- Take paracetamol to help with pain. Follow the instructions on the packet.

### Do Not Do These Things

- Do not use heat packs or take hot baths.  
- Do not drink alcohol.  
- Do not massage your knee.  
- Do not carry heavy things.  
- Do not stop moving your knee completely. After a few days of rest, try gentle movements to keep it from stiffening.

## When to See a Doctor

Call your doctor if:

- Your knee pain stops you from doing normal things or keeps you awake at night  
- The pain is getting worse or keeps coming back  
- Your symptoms do not improve after a few days of home care  
- Your knee feels stiff for more than 30 minutes after you wake up

## When to Get Urgent Help

Call your doctor right away or use NHS 111 if:

- You have severe knee pain after a fall or injury  
- You cannot walk or put weight on your knee  
- The skin around your knee is swollen and feels hot  
- You have knee pain and feel unwell with a high temperature or chills  

You can call 111 or get help online at [nhs.uk](https://www.nhs.uk)

## When to Go to A&E (Emergency Department)

Go to A&E if:

- Your knee looks out of place, changed shape, or is pointing in a strange direction  
- You heard a crack when you injured your knee  
- You feel tingling or have no feeling in your knee, leg, or toes  

Find your nearest A&E at [nhs.uk](https://www.nhs.uk)

### A&E Safety Tips

- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 for an ambulance.  
- Bring your regular medicines with you.

## Help from a Pharmacist

A pharmacist can help you choose the right painkillers and recommend knee supports you can buy.

## Treatment Options

Most meniscus tears get better on their own over time. But it can take weeks or months.

Sometimes, your doctor may suggest physiotherapy. This is exercises to help reduce pain and improve strength and movement in your knee.

If the tear is serious, you may need surgery. The surgeon will use a small camera to repair or remove the damaged part of the knee cartilage. This is called arthroscopy.

# Uveitis Caused by Systemic Rheumatic Disease

Some autoimmune diseases that affect the whole body can cause eye inflammation.  
This type of eye inflammation is called uveitis.  
The uveal tract is the middle layer of the eye.  
When it becomes inflamed, it can cause eye pain, redness, and vision problems.  
These diseases include conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and ankylosing spondylitis.  
They are called systemic rheumatic diseases because they affect more than one part of the body.  
Inflammation in the eye is a common side effect of these conditions.  
Early treatment can help prevent vision loss.

# Kidney Infection

A kidney infection happens when bacteria get into one or both kidneys.

## What Causes a Kidney Infection?

Most kidney infections start in the bladder and move up the tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder. This is called ascending infection.

- The most common cause is a type of bacteria called *Escherichia coli*. It normally lives in the intestines.
- In healthy people, urine flow and the way the tubes close at the bladder stop bacteria from moving up to the kidneys.
- But if there is a blockage, bacteria can get trapped and cause infection.

Common causes of blockage include:
- A kidney stone
- A birth defect in the urinary system
- An enlarged prostate in men

Another cause is when urine flows backward from the bladder into the tubes leading to the kidneys. This is called reflux.

Pregnancy increases the risk of kidney infection. The growing baby presses on the tubes that carry urine. This slows down urine flow. Hormones also make the tubes wider and less active, which can let urine flow backward.

In rare cases, bacteria from another part of the body can travel through the blood to the kidneys. For example, a skin infection caused by staph bacteria can spread to the kidneys.

People with diabetes or a weak immune system are more likely to get a kidney infection. Their bodies have a harder time fighting off infections.

Very rarely, kidney infections are caused by tuberculosis, fungi, or viruses.

Some people get long-term (chronic) kidney infections. This usually happens when there is a serious problem in the urinary system, such as:
- A blockage in the urinary tract
- Large kidney stones that do not go away
- Urine flowing backward from the bladder into the tubes (common in young children)

Chronic infections can let bacteria enter the blood. This can lead to infections in the other kidney or in other parts of the body. Over time, chronic infection can seriously damage the kidneys.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms often start suddenly and include:
- Chills
- High fever
- Pain in the lower back, on one or both sides
- Nausea
- Vomiting

About one in three people also has symptoms of a bladder infection, such as:
- Needing to urinate often
- Pain or burning when urinating

The infected kidney may be swollen and tender. Doctors may feel pain when pressing on the lower back. The belly muscles may be tight.

If the tubes to the kidneys go into spasms, you may feel sharp, intense pain. This is called renal colic. It can happen if a kidney stone is moving.

In children, symptoms may be mild and hard to notice. They might just seem fussy, tired, or have a fever.

Older adults may not have typical symptoms. Instead, they may:
- Become confused or disoriented
- Have a fever
- Develop a serious blood infection (sepsis)

In chronic kidney infections, pain may be vague. Fever may come and go or not happen at all.

## How Is a Kidney Infection Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to check for a kidney infection.

### Urine Tests
- A sample of urine is checked under a microscope.
  - It looks for white blood cells, red blood cells, and bacteria.
- A urine culture is done.
  - This grows bacteria from the urine to find out what type is causing the infection.

### Blood Tests
- These check for:
  - High levels of white blood cells (a sign of infection)
  - Bacteria in the blood
  - Signs of kidney damage

### Imaging Tests
Imaging tests are used if:
- You have severe back pain (like in renal colic)
- You do not get better after 72 hours of antibiotics
- Symptoms come back after treatment
- You have long-term or repeated infections
- Blood tests show kidney damage
- You are a man (since men rarely get kidney infections)

Imaging tests like ultrasound or CT scans can show:
- Kidney stones
- Structural problems
- Other blockages in the urinary system

## How Is a Kidney Infection Treated?

### Antibiotics
- Antibiotics are started as soon as a kidney infection is suspected.
- Samples are taken for testing before treatment begins.
- The type and dose of antibiotic may be changed based on test results.
- The choice depends on:
  - How sick you are
  - Whether the bacteria are resistant to common antibiotics
  - Whether the infection started in a hospital (where bacteria are harder to treat)
  - Whether you have a weak immune system
  - Whether you have a urinary tract problem like a blockage

Most people can be treated at home with oral antibiotics if they:
- Do not have nausea or vomiting
- Are not dehydrated
- Do not have other serious health problems (like cancer, diabetes, or AIDS)
- Do not have signs of severe infection (like low blood pressure or confusion)
- Can control pain with oral pain medicine

If you need hospital care, antibiotics are given through a vein for 1 to 2 days. Then you can switch to pills.

Treatment usually lasts 5 to 14 days. For men with infection from the prostate (prostatitis), treatment may last up to 6 weeks.

After treatment, a final urine test is done to make sure the infection is gone.

### Surgery
Surgery is rarely needed. It may be done if:
- There is a long-term blockage in the urinary system
- A large kidney stone is causing the problem

In rare cases, if someone with chronic kidney infection is getting a new kidney, the infected kidney may need to be removed. This is because the new kidney is at high risk of infection. People who get a new kidney take medicines to prevent rejection. These medicines also weaken the body’s ability to fight infection.

## What Is the Outlook?

Most people recover fully from a kidney infection.

Recovery may be slower or complications may happen if:
- You needed hospital care
- The bacteria are resistant to common antibiotics
- You have a condition that weakens your immune system (like diabetes, cancer, or AIDS)
- You have a kidney stone

## How Can You Prevent a Kidney Infection?

If you have repeated kidney infections or the infection comes back after treatment, your doctor may suggest taking a low-dose antibiotic every day for a long time.

- The best length of time for this is not known.
- If the infection returns after stopping the medicine, you may need to keep taking it for life.

If you are a woman who can get pregnant and are taking an antibiotic, talk to your doctor. Some antibiotics are not safe during pregnancy. You may need to avoid pregnancy or switch to a safer medicine.

# Hand, Foot and Mouth Disease – Simple Guide

This illness is common, especially in children. It usually causes mild symptoms and gets better on its own.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The first signs often appear 3 to 5 days after catching the virus. They can include:

- A sore throat  
- A high temperature  
- Not wanting to eat  

A few days later, other symptoms may appear:

- Painful mouth ulcers (sores inside the mouth)  
- A rash of spots on the hands, feet, and sometimes the bottom or groin area  

The spots may be pink, red, or darker than the rest of the skin. They can turn into blisters. These blisters may look grey or lighter than the skin around them. They can be painful.

Symptoms are usually mild. Adults and children have similar symptoms.

## How to Treat It at Home

There is no cure for hand, foot and mouth disease. It will get better by itself in 7 to 10 days.

You can do these things to feel better:

- Drink cool fluids to soothe your mouth and stay hydrated  
- Avoid acidic drinks like fruit juice  
- Eat soft foods such as yogurt, mashed potatoes, or soup  
- Avoid hot, salty, or spicy foods  
- Take paracetamol or ibuprofen to ease pain or fever  

### Talk to a Pharmacist

A pharmacist can help you choose safe treatments for mouth ulcers. They can recommend:

- Gels, sprays, or mouthwashes to reduce pain  
- Products that are safe for children  

They can also tell you how much to use and for how long.

## When to See a Doctor

Call your GP if:

- Symptoms do not improve after 7 to 10 days  
- You are pregnant and get the illness  

Call your GP surgery before visiting. They may offer a phone call instead.

### Call 111 or Get Help Online If:

- You or your child has a very high temperature  
- You feel hot and shivery  
- You are worried about your child’s symptoms  
- Your child is not peeing as much as usual (this could mean they are dehydrated)  

You can call 111 or get help online.

## How to Stop It from Spreading

Hand, foot and mouth disease spreads easily. It is passed through:

- Coughs and sneezes  
- Poo  
- Fluid from blisters  

You can pass it on even before you feel sick. You are most likely to spread it in the first 5 days after symptoms start.

To reduce the risk of spreading it:

- Wash your hands often with soap and water  
- Wash children’s hands too  
- Use a tissue when you cough or sneeze  
- Throw used tissues in the bin right away  
- Do not share towels, cups, or cutlery  
- Wash dirty clothes and bedding in hot water  

## Should Your Child Stay Home from School or Nursery?

Keep your child home while they are too unwell to join in. But once they feel better, they can go back to school or nursery.

There is no need to wait until all the blisters have healed. Keeping them away longer will not stop the illness from spreading.

# Brucellosis – Simple Explanation

Brucellosis is an infection caused by bacteria called *Brucella*. These bacteria are found in animals and can spread to people.

## How People Get Brucellosis

You can get brucellosis in several ways:

- Touching fluids or waste from infected animals.
- Eating undercooked meat from infected animals.
- Drinking raw milk or eating dairy products made from raw milk.
- Breathing in tiny particles of the bacteria in the air.
- Very rarely, through contact with an infected person.

The most common sources are farm animals and raw dairy products. Deer, bison, horses, moose, caribou, hares, chickens, and desert rats can also carry the bacteria. People can get sick from these animals too.

Brucellosis is most common in rural areas. It often affects people who work with animals, such as meatpackers, veterinarians, hunters, farmers, livestock workers, and lab workers.

It is rare in the United States, Europe, and Canada. But it still happens in the Middle East, Mediterranean countries, Mexico, Central America, and among travelers to these places.

Because very few bacteria can cause infection—maybe only 10 to 100—*Brucella* bacteria are a concern for biological terrorism.

## Symptoms of Brucellosis

The time between exposure and getting sick can be as short as 5 days or as long as several months. On average, symptoms start about 2 weeks after exposure.

Symptoms can start suddenly or slowly.

**Sudden start:**
- Chills
- High fever
- Severe headache
- Joint pain and lower back pain
- Feeling very tired
- Sometimes diarrhea

**Slow start:**
- Mild tiredness
- Muscle pain
- Headache
- Neck pain
- Then fever rises in the evening

As the illness continues:
- Body temperature goes up to 40 to 41 degrees Celsius (104 to 106 degrees Fahrenheit).
- Then it slowly comes down during the morning.
- Sweating is heavy when the fever drops.

Fever often comes and goes for 1 to 5 weeks. Then there may be a break of 2 to 14 days with little or no symptoms. In some people, the fever returns again and again over months or years. This pattern is called “undulating fever.”

After the fever phase, other symptoms may appear:
- Loss of appetite
- Weight loss
- Belly pain
- Joint pain
- Headache
- Back pain
- Weakness
- Irritability
- Trouble sleeping
- Depression
- Mood swings

Constipation is common. The spleen may get bigger. Lymph nodes may be slightly or moderately swollen. Up to half of patients have a swollen liver.

## How Doctors Diagnose Brucellosis

Doctors use several tests to find brucellosis:

- **Blood culture**: This is the most common test. A sample of blood is sent to the lab to see if bacteria grow. It can take more than 7 days. Sometimes the lab needs to keep the sample for 3 to 4 weeks. Tell the lab if you might have brucellosis.
- **Bone marrow culture**: This test is more likely to find the bacteria than blood culture. It is often the best test.
- **Cerebrospinal fluid culture**: This test is used if the brain or spinal cord might be involved.
- **Blood tests (serology)**: Two blood tests are done, 3 weeks apart. A rise in the test result or a high level in the first test can confirm the disease. This test is not reliable for *B. canis*.
- **PCR test**: This test looks for the bacteria’s DNA in blood or tissue. It can give a positive result as early as 10 days after infection.

## How Doctors Treat Brucellosis

Most people need two antibiotics together. This lowers the chance of the illness coming back.

**For people over 8 years old:**
- Doxycycline plus rifampin
- Or doxycycline plus an aminoglycoside (like streptomycin or gentamicin)
- Or a fluoroquinolone (like ciprofloxacin) plus rifampin or doxycycline

**For children under 8 years old:**
- Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) plus rifampin

Treatment usually lasts 6 weeks. For severe cases, such as infection of the heart or brain, treatment may last longer and involve three antibiotics.

If you have severe pain in your back or joints, you may need pain medicine.

If the heart is infected, surgery is often needed in addition to antibiotics.

Even with treatment, about 5 to 15 out of 100 people get sick again. So all patients should be checked again for up to 1 year.

## Prevention of Brucellosis

You can prevent brucellosis by:

- Drinking only pasteurized milk.
- Avoiding cheese made from raw milk, especially if it has been aged less than 3 months.
- Wearing gloves and eye protection when handling animals or animal parts.
- Covering cuts or open skin before working with animals.
- Getting rid of infected animals and testing animals regularly.
- Vaccinating young cattle and pigs in some countries.

There is no vaccine for people. The animal vaccine is not safe for humans. It can cause infection.

After exposure to the bacteria, some high-risk people may take antibiotics to prevent illness. This is called postexposure prophylaxis.

**Recommended treatment after exposure:**
- Doxycycline plus rifampin for 3 weeks
- Or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (if you cannot take doxycycline)

But if you were exposed to the *B. abortus* (strain RB51) vaccine, do not use rifampin. This vaccine strain is resistant to rifampin.

## Key Facts

- Brucellosis spreads from animals to people through contact with fluids, raw meat, or raw milk.
- It usually causes fever and general symptoms like tiredness and body aches.
- It rarely affects specific organs like the brain, heart, liver, or bones.
- Most people get better in 2 to 3 weeks, even without treatment.
- But some people develop long-term or recurring illness.
- Diagnosis uses blood, bone marrow, or spinal fluid cultures and blood tests.
- Treatment uses two antibiotics for several weeks.
- All patients should be watched for up to 1 year for relapse.

## More Information

For more details, visit:
[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC): Brucellosis – Assessing Laboratory Risk Level and PEP](https://www.cdc.gov/brucellosis/)
