# Food Intolerance

Some people have trouble digesting certain foods. This is called a food intolerance.

## Common Types of Food Intolerance

- Lactose intolerance: Trouble digesting lactose, a sugar in milk and dairy products like cheese and yoghurt.
- Gluten intolerance: Trouble digesting gluten, a protein in wheat, rye, and barley. Found in bread, pasta, and many processed foods.
- Histamine intolerance: Trouble digesting histamine, a substance found in wine, cheese, and some fermented foods.
- Caffeine intolerance: Trouble with caffeine in coffee, tea, and some fizzy drinks.
- Alcohol intolerance: Trouble with alcohol in drinks.
- Sulphite intolerance: Trouble with sulphites, found in cider, beer, and wine.
- Salicylate intolerance: Trouble with salicylates, found in some fruits, vegetables, herbs, and spices.
- MSG intolerance: Trouble with monosodium glutamate, found in ripened fruits, cured meats, and savoury snacks.

## Symptoms of a Food Intolerance

Symptoms usually start a few hours after eating the food you are intolerant to.

Common symptoms include:
- Diarrhoea
- Bloating
- Passing gas (farting)
- Tummy pain

Other possible symptoms:
- Headache
- Feeling tired or weak
- Feeling sick (nausea)
- Constipation
- Joint pain
- Skin rashes

Symptoms can last a few hours or up to several days.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:
- You or your child keep getting symptoms after eating certain foods.
- The symptoms come back often.

## When to Call 999 (Emergency)

Call emergency services right away if you or someone else has:
- Swelling in the lips, mouth, throat, or tongue.
- Trouble breathing. You may wheeze, gasp, or feel like you can’t get enough air.
- A tight feeling in the throat or trouble swallowing.
- Skin, lips, or tongue turning blue, grey, or pale. On darker skin, check the palms of the hands or soles of the feet.
- Sudden confusion, drowsiness, or dizziness.
- Someone faints and does not wake up.
- A child becomes limp, floppy, or does not respond normally. Their head may fall to the side, back, or forward. They may struggle to lift their head or look at you.

You or the person may also have a rash that is swollen, raised, or itchy.

These signs can mean a serious allergic reaction. This needs urgent medical care in hospital.

## What Causes a Food Intolerance?

A food intolerance happens when your body cannot properly digest a certain food or ingredient.

It is not the same as a food allergy. A food allergy involves your immune system reacting strongly. A food intolerance does not involve the immune system.

This means you cannot have a life-threatening allergic reaction from a food intolerance.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor may refer you to a dietitian if they think you have a food intolerance.

Tests may include:
- A special diet: You stop eating the food you think causes problems. After a few weeks, you slowly add it back to see if symptoms return.
- Blood tests.
- A breath test if you might be lactose intolerant.
- Keeping a food and symptom diary: Write down what you eat and any symptoms you have. This helps find patterns.

### Home Tests

Some tests you can buy online or in stores claim to find food intolerances.

These are not recommended. There is not enough proof they work. They may tell you to avoid many foods. This can lead to poor nutrition and harm your health.

## How Is It Treated?

The main treatment is to avoid or reduce the food you are intolerant to.

This includes any food that contains the ingredient you cannot tolerate.

But do not stop eating any food without talking to your doctor or a dietitian first.

Why? Because cutting out foods without advice can mean missing important vitamins and minerals. This is especially important for children’s growth and development.

# Kaposi Sarcoma

Kaposi sarcoma is a type of cancer that starts in the blood vessels.  
It is caused by a virus called human herpesvirus type 8.  
This virus is found in many people, but it only causes cancer in some.  
The risk is much higher in people with weak immune systems.

There are five main types of Kaposi sarcoma:
- Classic (rare, mostly in older men in Europe)
- AIDS-related (common in people with HIV/AIDS)
- Non-epidemic (rare, not linked to HIV or Africa)
- Endemic (common in parts of Africa)
- Iatrogenic (caused by medicines after organ transplant)

## What It Looks Like

The most common sign is skin changes.  
These appear as purple, pink, brown, or red spots.  
The spots may grow together into larger patches or lumps.  
The lumps can be blue-violet or black.  
Some areas may swell.  
In rare cases, the lumps grow into soft tissue or even bone.

Less often, the cancer affects internal organs.  
The most common ones are the mouth, stomach and intestines, and lungs.  
Mouth sores look like bluish or purple spots.  
Stomach and intestine problems may cause bleeding.  
But they often do not cause symptoms.  
Lung problems can cause coughing or trouble breathing.

## How It Is Diagnosed

A doctor will take a small sample of the skin or tissue.  
This is called a biopsy.  
The sample is checked under a microscope to confirm the diagnosis.

If you have HIV or a weak immune system, your doctor will check for spread to internal organs.  
This may include a CT scan of the chest and belly.  
If the scan is normal but you still have symptoms, your doctor may do a scope test.  
For lungs, this is a bronchoscopy.  
For the stomach and intestines, it is an endoscopy.

## How It Is Treated

### For Small, Localized Skin Lesions
- You can remove one or a few spots with surgery.
- Freezing them with cold (cryotherapy) works well.
- Burning them with an electric current (electrocoagulation) is another option.
- A medicine called vinblastine can be injected directly into the spot.
- Interferon alfa can also be used this way.
- Topical treatments like imiquimod cream or alitretinoin cream may help.

### For Many Lesions or Widespread Disease
- Radiation therapy is used to treat larger areas.
- Chemotherapy is used if the cancer has spread to lymph nodes or other parts of the body.
- Radiation doses are usually between 10 and 20 gray (Gy).

### For AIDS-Related Kaposi Sarcoma
- The main treatment is antiretroviral therapy (ART).
- This medicine controls HIV and helps the immune system recover.
- Many people see their skin lesions improve with ART.
- Some medicines in ART may also slow the growth of blood vessels in the tumor.
- For mild cases, your doctor may add vinblastine injections into the spots.
- Pomalidomide is another option for slow-growing lesions.
- For more serious cases, you may get pegylated liposomal doxorubicin through a vein every 2 to 3 weeks.
- Paclitaxel is an alternative if doxorubicin does not work.

### For Transplant-Related Kaposi Sarcoma (Iatrogenic)
- The best treatment is to lower the dose of immunosuppressant medicines.
- This often causes the spots to shrink.
- If lowering the dose is not possible, other treatments are used.
- These include radiation, chemotherapy, or medicines like sirolimus.

### For Endemic Kaposi Sarcoma (in Africa)
- Treatment is hard and often focuses on relieving symptoms.
- It is not usually curable.

## Important Points to Remember

- Think about Kaposi sarcoma if you are an older man, from Africa, or have had an organ transplant or HIV.
- If you have a weak immune system, your doctor should check for spread to internal organs.
- Small skin spots can be treated with local methods like freezing, burning, or surgery.
- For many spots or spread to lymph nodes, use radiation and chemotherapy.

Treatment can help control the disease.  
But it does not usually extend life in people with advanced HIV.  
Infections are the main cause of illness and death in these patients.

# Rheumatic Fever – Simple Explanation

Rheumatic fever is a serious reaction that can happen after a throat infection caused by strep bacteria. It is not an infection itself. It is the body’s immune system reacting too strongly to the infection.

This reaction causes swelling and irritation in the joints, heart, skin, and nervous system.

## Who Gets Rheumatic Fever?

- It most often affects children between 5 and 15 years old.
- It is rare in children under 3 or over 21 in wealthier countries.
- It is more common in places with crowded homes, poor nutrition, and lower income.
- It can run in families, so some people may be more likely to get it.

## What Causes Rheumatic Fever?

- It starts with a strep throat infection that is not treated.
- It does not come from strep skin infections (like impetigo) or infections in other parts of the body.
- The exact reason why the body reacts this way is not fully known.

## Symptoms of Rheumatic Fever

Symptoms usually start 2 to 3 weeks after the throat infection goes away. They can vary from person to person.

### Common Symptoms:
- Joint pain and swelling
- Fever
- Chest pain or fast heartbeat
- Jerky, uncontrolled movements (especially in the face, hands, and feet)
- A flat, red rash with wavy edges
- Small, hard lumps under the skin

### Joint Pain:
- One or more joints become painful, warm, swollen, and red.
- Pain often moves from one joint to another (this is called migratory pain).
- Ankles, knees, elbows, and wrists are most often affected.
- The pain usually lasts 2 to 4 weeks.
- It does not cause long-term joint damage.

### Heart Problems:
- Some children have no symptoms at first.
- Others feel their heart beating fast or have chest pain.
- Inflammation around the heart can cause pain.
- Heart murmurs (odd sounds when blood flows through the heart) may appear.
- These murmurs can be a sign of valve damage.
- In some cases, heart failure can develop. This causes tiredness, shortness of breath, nausea, stomach pain, and a dry cough.

### Skin and Nervous System Symptoms:
- **Rash:** A flat, red rash with wavy edges. It may last less than a day.
- **Lumps:** Small, hard, painless bumps under the skin. They appear near affected joints and go away on their own.
- **Chorea:** Uncontrolled jerky movements. These often start after other symptoms go away. They may begin slowly and get worse over time. The movements stop during sleep. They can affect the face, hands, feet, and arms. Some children may make strange sounds with their mouth or tongue.

Chorea usually lasts 4 to 8 months. It can come back later.

## How Is Rheumatic Fever Diagnosed?

Doctors use a set of rules called the **modified Jones criteria** to diagnose rheumatic fever.

They look for:
- A recent strep throat infection
- Symptoms and signs of inflammation in the body

### Major Criteria (must be present):
- Inflammation of the heart (carditis)
- Jerky, uncontrolled movements (Sydenham chorea)
- A specific rash (erythema marginatum)
- Swelling and pain in several joints (arthritis)

### Minor Criteria:
- Joint pain without swelling or redness
- High levels of inflammation markers in blood tests
- Fever
- Abnormal heart rhythms

A child is diagnosed with rheumatic fever if they had a strep infection and:
- Two major criteria, or
- One major criterion and two minor criteria

### Tests Doctors Use:
- **Throat swab:** To check for strep bacteria.
- **Blood tests:** To look for signs of recent strep infection and inflammation.
- **ECG (electrocardiogram):** To check the heart’s rhythm.
- **Echocardiogram:** An ultrasound of the heart to check for valve damage or swelling.
- **Joint fluid test:** If needed, a doctor may take fluid from a swollen joint to rule out infection.

## Treatment of Rheumatic Fever

Treatment has three main goals:
1. Kill any leftover strep bacteria.
2. Reduce swelling and pain in the joints and heart.
3. Prevent future strep infections.

### Antibiotics:
- These are given to clear the strep infection.
- A long-acting penicillin shot is often used.
- Or, penicillin or amoxicillin by mouth for 10 days.

### Pain and Inflammation Relief:
- Aspirin is used in high doses for several weeks.
- It helps reduce pain and swelling, especially in the joints and heart.
- Other medicines like naproxen may work as well, but aspirin is usually preferred.

### For Severe Heart Inflammation:
- If the heart is badly inflamed, doctors may use a steroid medicine called prednisone.
- This is given by mouth or through a vein if needed.
- As the steroid dose goes down, aspirin is added.

### Activity:
- Children with joint pain, chorea, or heart problems should rest.
- Once the illness is over and there is no heart inflammation, normal activity can resume.
- Long bed rest is not helpful.

## Prevention of Rheumatic Fever

The best way to prevent rheumatic fever is to treat strep throat quickly and fully with antibiotics.

### For Children Who Have Had Rheumatic Fever:
- They need regular penicillin shots every 3 to 4 weeks.
- In some cases, penicillin is given by mouth instead.
- This is called **prophylaxis** – medicine to prevent infection.

### How Long to Continue Prophylaxis:
- Children without heart damage: 5 years or until age 21 (whichever is longer).
- Children with heart damage but no severe valve problems: 10 years or until age 21 (whichever is longer).
- Children with serious heart valve damage: often for more than 10 years. Some experts recommend lifelong treatment.
- People with severe heart damage who live around young children should take penicillin for life. Young children can carry strep bacteria and pass it on.

## Outlook (Prognosis)

- Rheumatic fever can come back, especially if strep infections are not treated.
- Sydenham chorea usually goes away in a few months. But it returns in about one-third of people.
- Joint pain and swelling do not last long.
- Heart inflammation can be serious and permanent, especially if strep infections keep coming.
- Some people keep heart murmurs and mild valve damage for life.
- Severe valve damage can lead to heart failure or irregular heartbeats later in life.

Early treatment and good follow-up care can help prevent long-term problems.

# Leptospirosis (Weil's disease)

Leptospirosis is an infection you can catch from dirty water or soil. It can also come from touching blood or meat from an infected animal.

## How You Can Get Leptospirosis

The infection spreads through the pee of infected animals. The most common animals are rats, mice, cows, pigs, and dogs.

You can get it if:
- Dirty water from rivers, lakes, or canals gets into your mouth, eyes, or a cut. This can happen when you swim, kayak, or fish.
- You touch the blood or flesh of an infected animal. This often happens when working with animals or animal parts.

It is very rare to get leptospirosis from pets, other people, or insect bites.

## Symptoms of Leptospirosis

Many people have no symptoms or only mild ones. Some people become very ill.

Common symptoms include:
- A high temperature
- Headache
- Body aches and pain
- Stomach pain
- Feeling sick or being sick
- Diarrhoea
- Redness in the white part of your eyes
- Yellowing of the skin or the white part of your eyes (this is called jaundice)

Yellow skin can be harder to see on black or brown skin. Always check the whites of your eyes.

## When to See a Doctor

See your GP if you think you were exposed to infected pee, water, or soil and you have:
- A high temperature or feel hot and shivery
- A headache
- Feeling sick or being sick
- Diarrhoea
- Body aches and pains
- Red eyes
- Loss of appetite

Call your GP right away or get help from NHS 111 if you have:
- Yellow skin or yellow eyes (jaundice)
- A rash
- Trouble passing urine
- Swelling in your ankles, feet, or hands
- Chest pain
- Trouble breathing

You can call 111 or get help online at NHS 111.

## Treatment

Your GP can treat leptospirosis with antibiotics. Most people feel better in a few days or weeks.

Take all your antibiotics as prescribed. Do not stop early, even if you feel better.

Use paracetamol or ibuprofen to help with pain, aches, or a high temperature.

If your symptoms are severe, you may need to go to hospital.

## How to Avoid Leptospirosis

Leptospirosis is rare in the UK. But your risk goes up if you:
- Do outdoor water sports, especially in tropical areas
- Work with animals or animal parts

### Do These Things to Stay Safe

- Wash your hands with soap and water after touching animals or animal products.
- Clean any cuts or scrapes right away.
- Cover cuts and grazes with waterproof plasters.
- Wear protective clothing if your job puts you at risk.
- Shower as soon as possible after being in water that might be dirty.
- Make sure your dog is vaccinated against leptospirosis. (There is no vaccine for people.)

### Avoid These Things

- Do not touch water or soil that might have animal pee in it.
- Do not touch dead animals with your bare hands.
- Do not drink water from rivers, canals, or lakes. Always boil or treat it first.

# Tendinitis and Tenosynovitis

## What Are Tendinitis and Tenosynovitis?

Tendinitis is when a tendon becomes inflamed.  
This often happens after the tendon has been damaged over time.  
Tenosynovitis is tendinitis with inflammation of the lining around the tendon.  

These conditions cause pain when you move the affected area.  
You may also feel tenderness when pressing on the tendon.  
Over time, ongoing swelling or damage can lead to scar tissue.  
Scar tissue can make movement harder or painful.  

Doctors usually diagnose these conditions by checking your symptoms and doing a physical exam.  
Sometimes imaging tests like ultrasound or MRI are used to confirm the diagnosis.  
Treatment includes rest, pain relievers, and sometimes injections.

---

## What Causes Tendinitis and Tenosynovitis?

The exact cause is often unclear.  
It is more common in middle-aged or older adults.  
As we age, tendons get less blood flow, which may make them more likely to get inflamed.  

Repeating the same motion over and over can harm tendons.  
Sudden or extreme strain, or doing more exercise than usual, can also cause problems.  
Some antibiotics called fluoroquinolones may raise the risk of tendon damage or rupture.  

Certain health conditions increase the risk:  
- Rheumatoid arthritis  
- Systemic sclerosis (a condition that causes thickening of the skin and tissues)  
- Gout  
- Reactive arthritis  
- Diabetes  
- Very high cholesterol levels (rarely)  
- Amyloidosis (very rare)  

In younger adults, especially women, a certain type of infection from gonorrhea can cause sudden, moving pain in tendons.  
This can happen even if there are no symptoms in the genitals.  

Some types of bacteria, like *Mycobacterium marinum*, can cause long-term infections in tendons.  
These infections lead to swelling and pain in the tendon area.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

You will feel pain when you move the affected tendon.  
You may also feel pain when someone resists your movement.  

For example:  
- If the back part of the lower leg tendon is inflamed, you may feel pain when you try to turn your foot inward.  

Sometimes the tendon sheath swells.  
Fluid may build up in the sheath.  
This can happen with infections, gout, or rheumatoid arthritis.  
Swelling may be visible or only felt when touched.  

When you press along the tendon, you will feel tenderness.  
The pain can be mild or severe.  

In systemic sclerosis, the tendon sheath stays dry.  
But moving the tendon inside the sheath can cause a rubbing feeling or sound.  
A doctor can hear this with a stethoscope.

---

## How Are They Diagnosed?

Doctors start by asking about your symptoms.  
They will examine the area and press on the tendon.  
They may do special movements to see if they cause pain.  

Imaging tests like ultrasound or MRI are not always needed.  
But they can help confirm the diagnosis.  
They can also rule out other problems.  
They can show if there is a tear in the tendon or signs of inflammation.

---

## How Are They Treated?

### Step 1: Reduce Pain and Inflammation
- Rest the affected area.  
- Use a splint or sling if needed.  
- Apply heat for long-term (chronic) pain.  
- Apply cold for sudden (acute) pain.  
- Take nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for 7 to 10 days.  

If gout is the cause, your doctor may prescribe indomethacin or colchicine.

### Step 2: Start Gentle Movement
After the pain and swelling go down, start gentle exercises.  
Do them several times a day.  
This helps restore movement.  
The shoulder is especially prone to stiffness, so exercise is very important here.

### Step 3: Corticosteroid Injections (If Needed)
A doctor may inject a long-acting steroid into the tendon sheath.  
This can help reduce pain and swelling.  
It is usually used when pain is severe or the problem has lasted a long time.  

The amount of medicine used depends on the location.  
It can range from 0.3 mL to 1 mL.  

To make sure the injection is in the right place, the doctor may add a numbing medicine (like lidocaine) through the same needle.  
If your pain goes away right away, it confirms the diagnosis.  

**Important:**  
- Do not inject the steroid directly into the tendon.  
- Pushing medicine into the tendon can weaken it.  
- This increases the risk of the tendon breaking.  
- The doctor can tell if they are in the tendon because there is strong resistance.  

After the injection, rest the nearby joint.  
This lowers the small risk of tendon rupture.  

Sometimes symptoms get worse for up to 24 hours after the injection.  
This is temporary and usually improves.

### Step 4: Surgery (Rarely Needed)
If symptoms do not improve, surgery may be needed.  
This is more common for long-term rotator cuff problems.  
Surgery can remove calcium deposits or repair the tendon.  
After surgery, physical therapy helps you regain strength and movement.  

Other reasons for surgery include:  
- Removing scar tissue that limits movement  
- Removing part of a bone that rubs against the tendon  
- Removing the inflamed lining of the tendon sheath (tenosynovectomy)

---

## Key Points

- Tendinitis and tenosynovitis are about inflammation.  
  Tendinopathy is about tendon damage over time, not inflammation.  

- Pain, tenderness, and swelling are usually worst along the path of the tendon.  

- Most cases are diagnosed by physical exam and specific tests.  
  Imaging like MRI or ultrasound may be used to confirm.  

- Treatment includes rest, heat or cold, NSAIDs, and sometimes steroid injections.  

- Never inject steroids directly into a tendon.  
  This can weaken it and increase the risk of rupture.

# Herpes Zoster Oticus

Herpes zoster oticus is a condition caused by a virus that affects nerves in the head. It involves the nerves that control hearing, balance, and facial movement.

The virus that causes herpes zoster oticus is the same one that causes chickenpox. After you have chickenpox, the virus stays in your body. It can come back later as shingles. This usually happens when your body’s defenses are weak. Things like cancer, AIDS, or certain medicines can weaken your body’s ability to fight infections.

When the virus comes back, it can travel along nerves. In herpes zoster oticus, it affects two nerves in the head:
- The seventh nerve, which controls facial muscles.
- The eighth nerve, which controls hearing and balance.

## Symptoms

You may have one or more of these symptoms:
- Severe pain in the ear.
- Blisters filled with fluid on the outer ear or inside the ear canal.
- Weakness or paralysis on one side of the face. This can look like Bell’s palsy.
- A spinning or moving feeling (vertigo). This can last for days or weeks.
- Hearing loss. This may get better, stay the same, or get worse over time.
- Rarely, you may have a headache, confusion, or a stiff neck.
- Sometimes other nerves in the head are affected too.

## Diagnosis

Doctors diagnose herpes zoster oticus by:
- Examining you in person.
- Taking a sample from the blisters to test in a lab.
- Doing an MRI scan if needed to rule out other causes.

The doctor will look at your symptoms and physical signs. They may take a small sample from the blisters to check for the virus. An MRI scan can help make sure the problem is not caused by something else, like a tumor or stroke.

## Treatment

Treatment focuses on relieving symptoms and helping your body fight the virus. Options include:
- Steroids like prednisone to reduce swelling and inflammation.
- Antiviral medicines such as acyclovir or valacyclovir. These may help shorten the illness, especially if your immune system is weak.
- Medicines to treat vertigo, such as diazepam.
- Pain relief with opioid medicines for severe pain.
- Surgery in rare cases to reduce pressure on the facial nerve if paralysis is complete.

It is not clear how much these treatments help. But doctors often use them to try to improve outcomes.

For people who have long-lasting pain after the blisters heal (called postherpetic neuralgia), other treatments may be used:
- Pain-relief patches applied to the skin.
- Medicines used to treat seizures.
- Certain types of antidepressants.

If you have full facial paralysis, surgery may be needed to relieve pressure on the facial nerve.

# Q Fever

## What is Q fever?

Q fever is an infection caused by bacteria. It can make you feel unwell, but many people do not have any symptoms at all.

## Symptoms of Q fever

You may not have any symptoms.  
If you do get symptoms, they usually start 2 to 3 weeks after you were infected.  
Symptoms can include:

- A high temperature  
- Aching muscles  
- Feeling very tired  
- Feeling sick  
- A sore throat  
- Swollen glands  

Most people feel better within 2 weeks.  
Some people have no symptoms at all.

## How Q fever spreads

Q fever is most often passed on through close contact with infected farm animals.  
The bacteria can spread when you breathe in tiny particles from infected animals.  
It can also spread through touch, especially if you touch:

- Afterbirth (placenta)  
- Blood  
- Urine  
- Feces  
- Animal skins, fur, or wool  

You can also get Q fever from drinking unpasteurised milk.  
This is less common.  

People who work with animals are more at risk.  
This includes farmers, vets, stablehands, and workers in slaughterhouses.

## When to see a doctor

See your doctor if you think you have Q fever and:

- You are pregnant – Q fever can cause miscarriage or harm to your baby, especially if you get it early in pregnancy  
- Your immune system is weak – for example, if you had an organ transplant or are having chemotherapy – the infection could affect your eyes or brain  
- You have heart valve disease – this means one or more of your heart valves are damaged or not working right  

Q fever is usually mild.  
But in rare cases, it can lead to serious health problems.

## Treatment

If your symptoms are bad or not improving, your doctor may give you antibiotics.  
You will likely take the antibiotics for 1 or 2 weeks.  
It is very important to take all the medicine, even if you start to feel better.  
Stopping early can make the infection worse.

## How to prevent Q fever

There is no vaccine for Q fever available in the UK.

If you work with animals, follow these steps to stay safe:

### Do

- Wash your hands often, especially after handling animals or animal products  
- Clean any cuts or scrapes right away and cover them with a plaster or dressing  
- Wear protective gear like waterproof gloves and goggles  
- Clean up animal afterbirth safely – do not leave it lying around  

### Don’t

- Do not help animals give birth if you are pregnant  
- Do not touch anything that has been near animal blood, urine, feces, or afterbirth – this includes clothes, boots, or gloves  
- Do not drink milk that has not been heated to kill bacteria (unpasteurised milk)  
- Do not eat in areas where animals are kept  

### Important

If you are pregnant, avoid contact with sheep and lambs during lambing season – from January to April.  
Do not touch anything that has been near sheep or lambs, such as gloves or boots.  
You may not have any symptoms if you get Q fever while pregnant.  
But it can still harm your baby.  
It is best to avoid any risk.

Also, be aware that sheep and lambs can carry another infection called toxoplasmosis.  
This can also harm a baby during pregnancy.

# Erythema Infectiosum (Parvovirus B19 Infection)

## What Is Erythema Infectiosum?

Erythema infectiosum is a viral illness caused by a virus called human parvovirus B19.  
It is also known as fifth disease or slapped-cheek disease.  
The name "fifth disease" comes from the fact that it is the fifth common viral illness that causes a rash in children.  
The other four are measles, rubella, chicken pox, and roseola.

This illness mostly affects children.  
It is most common in the spring.  
Outbreaks happen every few years, especially among children aged 5 to 7.

## How Does the Virus Spread?

The virus spreads through tiny droplets in the air when someone coughs or sneezes.  
It can also spread through contact with blood or blood products.  
People in the same household often get infected if one person has the virus.  
Some people can carry the virus and not show any symptoms.

Adults can also get infected.  
When adults get it, they may have different problems than children.

## What Happens in the Body?

The virus affects the body’s ability to make new red blood cells.  
This effect is usually mild and does not cause symptoms in most people.  
But in some children with certain blood disorders, it can cause serious problems.  
These include sickle cell disease or hereditary spherocytosis.  
In these children, the drop in red blood cells can lead to a sudden and severe anemia.  
This is called a transient aplastic crisis.

People with weak immune systems may also have long-lasting infections.  
This can lead to severe anemia because the body cannot make enough red blood cells.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The time from infection to symptoms is usually 4 to 14 days.  
At first, you may feel like you have a mild flu.  
This includes a low fever and feeling tired.

A few days later, your cheeks turn bright red.  
This is often called the “slapped-cheek” look.  
Then, a rash appears on your arms, legs, and trunk.  
The rash is usually not on the palms of your hands or soles of your feet.  
It may look like lacy, raised patches with clear centers.

The rash and illness usually last 5 to 10 days.  
But the rash can come back for several weeks.  
It may return when you are exposed to sunlight, exercise, heat, fever, or stress.

## What Are the Different Types of Problems Caused by the Virus?

| Problem | What Happens | Who It Affects |
|--------|--------------|----------------|
| Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) | Mild flu-like symptoms. Red rash on cheeks and body. | Mostly children, sometimes adults |
| Papular-purpuric gloves-and-socks syndrome | Red or purple spots on hands and feet. May include fever and sores in mouth or genitals. | Mostly children, sometimes adults |
| Transient aplastic crisis | Sudden drop in red blood cells. Causes severe anemia. | Children with blood disorders like sickle cell disease |
| Joint pain (arthralgia or arthritis) | Pain in small joints like fingers, wrists, knees, and feet. Often symmetric. May come with a rash. | Mostly adults, especially women |
| Pregnancy problems | Can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, or severe anemia in the baby. | Pregnant women |
| Long-term infection | No symptoms in many cases. Can cause severe anemia in people with weak immune systems. | People with weak immune systems |

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose this illness by looking at the rash.  
The rash has a very specific look and pattern.  
It is often enough to make the diagnosis.

In some cases, tests are needed.  
For example, if a child has a blood disorder, the doctor may check blood levels.  
They may also test for the virus or antibodies to it.

Pregnant women need special testing.  
They may have blood tests to check for antibodies.  
They may also have an ultrasound to check the baby’s health.

If the virus is still in the blood, a special test called PCR can find it.  
This test is used for people with long-term infections or for fetuses with serious problems.

## How Is It Treated?

There is no specific treatment for most people.  
You only need to treat the symptoms.

For example, you can take medicine to reduce fever or relieve discomfort.  
Rest and fluids are helpful.

If a person has a weak immune system and severe anemia, they may get a treatment called IV immune globulin.  
This helps the body fight the virus and start making red blood cells again.

## Key Facts to Remember

- Children often get a mild fever and feel tired at first.  
- A few days later, their cheeks turn bright red.  
- A rash then appears on the arms, legs, and trunk.  
- The rash usually does not affect the palms or soles.  
- The illness lasts about a week, but the rash can return for weeks.  

- The virus mildly affects red blood cell production.  
- This usually causes no problems.  
- But in children with sickle cell disease or other blood disorders, it can cause sudden severe anemia.  
- People with weak immune systems may have long-lasting infections.

- If a pregnant woman gets infected, there is a 2 to 6 percent chance the baby may die.  
- The risk is highest in the first half of pregnancy.

- Testing is usually only needed for children with blood disorders or adults with joint pain.  
- Most healthy children do not need testing.

- Treatment is focused on relieving symptoms.  
- People with weak immune systems may need IV immune globulin.

# Prostate Abscess

A prostate abscess is a pocket of pus that forms in the prostate gland. It happens when a bacterial infection becomes severe and does not get better with treatment.

## What Is the Prostate?

The prostate is a small gland in men. It sits just below the bladder and wraps around the tube that carries urine out of the body (the urethra). The prostate, along with nearby glands, makes most of the fluid in semen.

## Who Is at Risk?

Some men are more likely to get a prostate abscess. These include:

- Men who had radiation treatment for prostate cancer, including seed implants.
- Men who take certain diabetes medicines called SGLT2 inhibitors. These medicines can raise the risk of urinary and genital infections.

## Symptoms

Common signs of a prostate abscess include:

- Needing to urinate more often than usual.
- Pain or burning when you urinate.
- Trouble starting to urinate or feeling like your bladder is not empty.
- Pain in the area between the scrotum and the anus (the perineum).
- A fever.

Less common symptoms may include:

- Pain in the scrotum due to swelling of the tube that holds sperm (epididymitis).
- Blood in the urine.
- A thick, pus-like discharge from the urethra.

A doctor may find the prostate is swollen and tender during a rectal exam. This exam can be painful.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect a prostate abscess if a man has:

- Ongoing or repeated urinary tract infections.
- Pain in the perineum that does not go away.

To confirm the diagnosis, doctors may use:

- An ultrasound of the prostate. This uses sound waves to create a picture of the gland.
- A cystoscopy. This is a test where a thin tube with a camera is passed through the urethra to look inside the bladder and prostate.

Sometimes, a prostate abscess is found by accident during surgery or another test.

Not all men with a prostate abscess have pus or bacteria in their urine. Some may have no signs in a urine test.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment has two main parts:

1. **Antibiotics** – These kill the bacteria causing the infection. Common ones include ciprofloxacin or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.
2. **Drainage of pus** – The pus must be removed from the abscess.

There are two ways to drain the pus:

- A doctor may pass a thin tube through the urethra and then use a needle to puncture the abscess and drain the pus.
- Or, a doctor may insert a hollow needle through the skin between the scrotum and anus. The needle is used to suck out the pus.

Both methods help clear the infection and relieve symptoms. Treatment usually works well if started early.

# Inflammatory Bowel Disease

Inflammatory bowel disease, or IBD, is a long-term condition that affects your gut. It causes your bowel to become inflamed, which leads to uncomfortable symptoms.

## Symptoms of IBD

You may have IBD if you notice any of these signs:

- Diarrhoea that lasts more than four weeks.
- Pain in your tummy that does not go away.
- Blood or clear slime (mucus) in your poo.
- Bleeding from your bottom.
- Feeling very tired all the time.
- Losing weight without trying to.

These symptoms can come and go. They may be mild at first, but get worse over time.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if you have:

- Diarrhoea that lasts more than seven days.
- Tummy pain or bloating that keeps coming back.
- Blood or mucus in your poo.
- Unexplained weight loss.

## When to Go to A&E (Emergency Department)

Go to A&E or call 999 if you have:

- Severe tummy pain.
- Bleeding from your bottom that will not stop.
- A lot of blood — for example, the toilet water turns red or you see big clumps of blood.
- Vomiting blood, or throwing up something that looks like coffee grounds or soil.

> **Important:** Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to take you. Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
> Bring all your medicines with you when you go.

## Treatment for IBD

Your treatment will depend on how bad your symptoms are.

If you are very unwell, you may need to go to hospital.

Treatments can include:

- Medicines to reduce swelling and ease your symptoms. These may include steroids.
- Other medicines to help control your symptoms over time.
- Surgery to remove part of your bowel if your symptoms are very severe.

## What Causes IBD?

Doctors do not know exactly what causes IBD. But they believe it happens when your body’s immune system wrongly attacks your bowel.

This attack causes the bowel to become inflamed and damaged.

You are more likely to get IBD if a close family member has it. This includes parents, grandparents, or siblings.

## Help and Support

You are not alone. These organisations can help:

- **Crohn's and Colitis UK** – A charity that offers support, advice, and information for people with IBD.
- **IBD Registry** – A UK database that collects information on IBD. It includes Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, IBD unclassified, and other types of IBD.

# Swollen Gums

Swollen gums can happen as a side effect of some medicines. This swelling is not caused by infection.

The following medicines are most likely to cause swollen gums:

- Phenytoin  
- Valproate  
- Cyclosporine  
- Nifedipine and other medicines used to treat high blood pressure  
- High-dose birth control pills

When gums swell, they become larger all over. The tissue may look smooth or bumpy. It can grow so much that it covers part of the teeth. The extra tissue can be removed by a dentist or doctor. If possible, your doctor may switch you to a different medicine. Keeping your mouth very clean can help prevent the gums from swelling again.

Swollen gums can also be a sign of a serious problem. A type of mouth cancer called oral squamous cell carcinoma can start in the gums. This can make the gums look larger than normal. If you notice any unusual changes in your gums, see a doctor right away.

# What Is Vaginitis?

Vaginitis means inflammation or irritation of the vagina. It can be caused by an infection or by things that irritate the area.

It is very common for women to visit their doctor because of vaginitis. Millions of women each year have this problem.

## What Causes Vaginitis?

Vaginitis can be caused by:

- Bacteria
- Yeast (a type of fungus)
- Other germs
- Irritation from soaps, lotions, or other products
- Allergies to certain materials
- Hormonal changes, especially after menopause
- Damage to the vaginal tissue

Some causes are more common in certain groups of people.

### Infections

These are the most common causes of vaginitis:

- **Yeast infections**: Caused by an overgrowth of yeast in the vagina. They often cause thick, white, clumpy discharge and strong itching.
- **Trichomonal vaginitis**: Caused by a tiny parasite. It leads to a greenish-yellow, bubbly discharge and can cause itching and pain during sex or urination.
- **Bacterial vaginosis**: Not an infection, but a shift in the normal balance of bacteria in the vagina. It can cause a thin, gray or yellow-green discharge with a fishy smell.

### Other Causes

- **Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)**: This is an infection of the uterus, fallopian tubes, or other upper reproductive organs. It can start from an infection in the cervix, such as from chlamydia or gonorrhea.
- **Genital herpes**: This virus can cause blisters on the vulva, vagina, or cervix. It may also cause a vaginal discharge.
- **Irritation from products**: Soaps, detergents, bubble baths, sanitary pads, tampons, condoms, lubricants, and synthetic underwear can irritate the area.
- **Hormonal changes**: After menopause, lower estrogen levels make the vagina dry and thin. This can lead to irritation and infection.
- **Urinary or bowel incontinence**: If urine or stool stays on the skin for long, it can cause irritation and infection.
- **Damage to tissue**: Pregnancy, childbirth, surgery, injury, cancer, or radiation therapy can damage the vaginal tissue. This makes it easier for germs to enter.
- **Foreign objects**: In children, small items like tissue paper placed in the vagina can cause infection.
- **Sexual abuse**: This can lead to vaginal infections or sexually transmitted infections in children.

## Symptoms of Vaginitis

Common symptoms include:

- A change in vaginal discharge
- Itching in the genital area
- Redness or swelling
- Burning or soreness
- Pain during sex or when urinating
- A fishy smell (especially with bacterial vaginosis)

Some women have no symptoms at all. Others may have mild symptoms that come and go.

In rare cases, the skin folds around the vagina or urethra can stick together.

## How Is Vaginitis Diagnosed?

If you have a vaginal discharge with itching, odor, or other symptoms, see your doctor.

Your doctor will:

- Ask about your symptoms and health history
- Ask about your hygiene habits and products you use
- Ask if you are sexually active and about your sexual partners
- Do a pelvic exam

During the exam:

- The doctor uses a speculum to look inside the vagina and cervix.
- A small swab is used to collect a sample of discharge or fluid.
- The sample is checked under a microscope to find the cause.
- A sample from the cervix is tested for sexually transmitted infections.

The doctor may also press on your lower belly to check for pain. This helps rule out pelvic inflammatory disease.

If irritation or allergy is suspected, you may be asked to stop using certain products. Then, you try them one at a time to see which one causes the problem.

In children, the exam is done carefully by a trained doctor. A speculum exam may be done under anesthesia.

If a child has trichomonal vaginitis, the doctor will check for possible sexual abuse.

## Treatment of Vaginitis

Treatment depends on the cause.

### For Infections

- **Yeast infections**: Treated with antifungal medicines (creams, tablets, or pills).
- **Trichomonal vaginitis**: Treated with antibiotics (like metronidazole or tinidazole).
- **Bacterial vaginosis**: Treated with antibiotics (like metronidazole or clindamycin).

### For Other Causes

- If a foreign object is in the vagina, it is removed.
- If a product is causing irritation, stop using it.
- If tissue is damaged, treatment depends on the cause.

### For Symptom Relief

- Use cool compresses or sitz baths (sitting in warm water that covers only the genital area).
- Apply ice packs to reduce swelling and itching.
- Use a water bottle to gently rinse the area with lukewarm water.
- Take antihistamines to reduce itching. These can make you sleepy, which may help if itching keeps you awake.

## How to Prevent Vaginitis

You can lower your risk by:

- Washing the genital area with mild, unscented soap.
- Rinsing well and drying completely after washing.
- Wiping from front to back after using the toilet.
- Avoiding douching. It can remove good bacteria and make infections more likely.
- Using condoms during sex to reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections.
- Changing tampons, pads, or incontinence products often.
- Wearing cotton underwear and avoiding tight, synthetic clothing.
- Not using scented soaps, sprays, or lotions near the vagina.

## Important Notes

- **Douching is not safe**. It can harm the natural balance of the vagina and increase infection risk.
- **Leaving tampons in too long** can lead to infection. Change them every 4 to 8 hours.
- **Children can get vaginitis**. It often happens when they wipe from back to front after a bowel movement. This can move bacteria from the anus to the vagina.
- **Pinworms** can also cause vaginal symptoms in children.
- **Sexual abuse** is a possible cause of vaginitis in children. If a child has unexplained discharge or symptoms, this must be considered.

If you have any concerns about your vaginal health, talk to your doctor. Early diagnosis and treatment can prevent complications.

# Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)

Deep vein thrombosis is a blood clot in a deep vein, usually in the leg. It can be serious if not treated.

## Symptoms of DVT

You may have DVT if you notice any of these signs in one leg (rarily both legs):

- A throbbing pain in one leg, often in the calf or thigh
- Swelling in one leg
- The skin feels warm around the painful area
- The skin looks red or darker than normal
- Veins feel hard or sore when you touch them

These symptoms can also happen in your arm or tummy if the clot is there.

## When to Get Help

### Call your doctor right away or use NHS 111 if:
- You think you have DVT

You can call 111 or get help online.

### Call 999 or go to A&E if:
- You have DVT symptoms like pain and swelling
- You also have breathlessness or chest pain

A blood clot can travel to your lungs. This is called a pulmonary embolism. It can be life-threatening and needs emergency care.

### A&E Safety Tips
- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 for an ambulance.
- Bring all your medicines with you.

## Treatment for DVT

You may get a shot of a blood-thinning medicine called heparin while waiting for tests.

Main treatments include:
- Blood-thinning medicines like warfarin or rivaroxaban. You will likely take these for at least 3 months.
- Surgery to remove a clot or stop new clots from forming.

If you get DVT during pregnancy, you will get injections for the rest of your pregnancy and for 6 weeks after your baby is born.

## Who Is More Likely to Get DVT

You are more likely to get DVT if you:
- Are over 60 years old
- Are overweight
- Smoke
- Have had DVT before
- Take the contraceptive pill or hormone replacement therapy
- Have cancer or heart failure
- Have varicose veins

You are also more likely to get DVT if you:
- Are in hospital or have just left hospital, especially if you can’t move much
- Are staying in bed for long
- Are on a long journey (over 3 hours) by plane, car, or train
- Are pregnant or have had a baby in the last 6 weeks
- Are dehydrated (not drinking enough fluids)

Sometimes, DVT happens with no clear reason.

## How to Prevent DVT

You can lower your risk by making healthy choices.

### Do:
- Keep a healthy weight
- Stay active – take regular walks
- Drink plenty of fluids to stay hydrated

### Don’t:
- Sit still for long periods – get up and move every hour
- Cross your legs when sitting
- Smoke
- Drink too much alcohol

### If You’re on a Long Journey (3+ hours)
- Wear loose clothes
- Drink water often
- Avoid alcohol
- Walk around when you can

### If You’re Going into Hospital
Your healthcare team will check if you are at higher risk for DVT.

If you are at risk, you may get:
- Medicine to prevent clots
- Compression stockings (knee-high elastic socks that help blood flow)

You may need to keep taking treatment after you leave hospital. Clots can form weeks later.

You can also help protect yourself in hospital by:
- Walking around if you can
- Moving your toes and ankles (up and down, in circles) if you must stay in bed
- Doing any exercises your healthcare team gives you

# Inflammatory Vaginitis

This condition causes swelling and irritation in the vagina. It is not caused by common infections like yeast or bacteria.

It most often happens after menopause or when the body has low levels of estrogen.

## Symptoms

You may notice:
- Thick, white or yellow discharge from the vagina.
- Pain during sex.
- Pain or burning when urinating.
- Itching or irritation in the vagina.

Some people also feel:
- A burning sensation.
- Mild pain.
- Small amounts of bleeding.

The vaginal tissue may look thin and dry. The problem can come back.

Women who are past menopause or have early loss of ovarian function may also have other symptoms of menopause, such as:
- Dryness in the vagina and vulva.
- A strong need to urinate.
- Pain when urinating.

## How It Is Diagnosed

Your doctor will do a pelvic exam. They will also test your vaginal fluid.

Tests include:
- Measuring the pH level of the vaginal fluid.
- Looking at a sample under a microscope (wet mount).
- Checking for a fishy smell (whiff test).

The diagnosis is likely if:
- The vaginal pH is higher than 6.
- The whiff test does not show a fishy smell.
- The microscope shows mostly white blood cells and flat, immature cells (parabasal cells).

Your doctor will also check for signs of thin, dry vaginal tissue. These signs include:
- Small or fused inner lips of the vagina.
- Tissue that breaks easily.
- Pale color.
- Loss of normal folds in the vagina.

## Treatment

You will use clindamycin vaginal cream.  
- Apply 5 grams (about one full applicator) every night for 2 weeks.

If you have thin, dry vaginal tissue (genital atrophy), your doctor may suggest topical estrogen. This helps rebuild the tissue and ease symptoms.

Options for topical estrogen:
- Estradiol vaginal cream:  
  - Use 2 to 4 grams once a day for 1 to 2 weeks.  
  - Then use 1 to 2 grams once a day for 1 to 2 weeks.  
  - Then use 1 gram 1 to 3 times a week.
- Estradiol vaginal tablets: 4 or 10 micrograms, twice a week.
- Estradiol ring: One ring every 3 months. It slowly releases about 7.5 micrograms of estrogen each day.

Topical estrogen is usually the best choice for menopause-related vaginal dryness. It works well and has fewer side effects than hormone pills or other systemic treatments.

# Diphtheria-Tetanus-Pertussis Vaccine

This vaccine protects against three serious diseases: diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis.

## What the Diseases Do

- **Diphtheria** causes a sore throat and thick coating in the throat. The bacteria that cause it make a poison. This poison can harm the heart, kidneys, and nerves. Diphtheria used to kill many children.

- **Tetanus** (also called lockjaw) causes painful muscle spasms. It happens when bacteria get into a wound. The bacteria make a poison that affects the nervous system.

- **Pertussis** (also called whooping cough) is a very contagious lung infection. It is especially dangerous for babies under 2 years old and for people with weak immune systems.

## How the Vaccine Works

The vaccine contains parts of the bacteria that cause diphtheria and tetanus. These parts are weakened so they cannot cause disease. They are called toxoids.

It also contains small pieces of the bacteria that cause pertussis. These pieces are not alive and cannot cause illness.

Even though the vaccine does not contain live bacteria, it helps your body learn how to fight the real diseases. This is called building immunity.

There are two versions of this vaccine:

- **DTaP** – for children under 7 years old.
- **Tdap** – for people 7 years old and older, including teens and adults.

Tdap has smaller amounts of the diphtheria and pertussis parts. This is why the letters are lowercase. These smaller amounts are enough to protect older children and adults.

You can also get combination vaccines that include DTaP plus other vaccines. These are available in the United States and protect against hepatitis B, polio, and *Haemophilus influenzae* type b.

There is also a separate vaccine that only protects against tetanus and diphtheria. It is called the Td vaccine.

## When and How the Vaccine Is Given

- **DTaP** is given as 5 shots into a muscle.  
  The shots are usually given at:
  - 2 months old
  - 4 months old
  - 6 months old
  - 15 to 18 months old
  - 4 to 6 years old

- **Tdap** is given as 1 shot into a muscle.

Tdap is a routine vaccine for children. It is given once between 11 and 12 years old. This is called a booster shot.

People 13 years old and older who have never had Tdap should get it. They should also get it if they are not sure if they ever had it.

After the first Tdap shot, you need a booster every 10 years. You can use either Tdap or Td for these boosters.

Pregnant people should get a Tdap shot during every pregnancy. The best time is between 27 and 36 weeks of pregnancy.

After giving birth, people who have never had Tdap should get it.

If you get a wound and are over 7 years old, you may need a Tdap or Td shot to prevent tetanus. This is especially true if the wound is dirty or deep.

- If you have had Tdap before and get a wound, you may get Tdap or Td.
- If you have not had Tdap and get a wound, you should get Tdap.

## Who Should Not Get the Vaccine

Do not get the DTaP or Tdap vaccine if you:

- Had a serious allergic reaction (like anaphylaxis) to any part of the vaccine.

Do not get the vaccine if you have any of the following:

- A coma, very low alertness, or long-lasting seizures within 7 days after a previous dose.
- Seizures or another serious nervous system problem after a dose.
- Guillain-Barré syndrome within 6 weeks after a tetanus vaccine.
- Severe pain or swelling after a previous tetanus or diphtheria vaccine.

Some health conditions may affect when or if you should get the vaccine. Talk to your doctor.

If you are sick with a fever or a serious illness, your doctor may wait to give the vaccine until you feel better.

## Side Effects

Most side effects are mild and go away in 1 to 3 days. They may include:

- Soreness, pain, or redness where the shot was given
- Fever
- Crying or fussiness (especially in babies)
- Feeling tired
- Not wanting to eat
- Vomiting

Serious side effects are very rare. They include:

- A fever of 104.9 degrees Fahrenheit (40.5 degrees Celsius) or higher that starts within 2 days of the shot and has no other cause.
- Crying for more than 3 hours straight, and the crying cannot be calmed, within 2 days of the shot.
- A change in mental state, such as confusion or extreme sleepiness, within 7 days of the shot.
- A seizure within 3 days of the shot.
- Fainting or shock within 2 days of the shot.
- A fast, severe allergic reaction after the shot.

If a seizure happens within 3 days of the shot, or if there are signs of brain problems within 7 days, the vaccine is not given again.

Serious side effects are most often linked to the pertussis part of the vaccine. If they happen, the DTaP or Tdap vaccine will not be used again.

Instead, the Td vaccine will be used. This vaccine does not protect against pertussis, but it does protect against tetanus and diphtheria.

For more details on side effects, read the package insert that comes with the vaccine.

# Hamstring Injury

A hamstring injury happens when the muscles at the back of your thigh get damaged. It often occurs during sports or exercise.

## Symptoms

You may feel a sudden sharp pain in the back of your leg.  
The pain can be strong and sudden.  
You might feel a snap or hear a pop if the injury is serious.  
The back of your thigh may feel tender.  
Swelling and bruising can appear a few hours after the injury.  
You may find it hard to stand or walk on the injured leg.

## How to Treat It Yourself

You can treat a mild to moderate hamstring injury at home.  
Do this for the first 2 to 3 days using the PRICE method:

- **Protection**: Keep your leg safe from more harm.  
- **Rest**: Stop all activity. Do not put weight on the injured leg.  
- **Ice**: Put an ice pack (or a bag of frozen peas) on the injury. Wrap it in a tea towel. Use it for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours.  
- **Compression**: Wrap a bandage around your leg. It should feel snug but not tight. Take it off before you go to sleep.  
- **Elevate**: Keep your leg raised on a pillow as much as possible.

Avoid heat, hot baths, heat packs, massages, and alcohol for the first 3 days. These can make swelling worse.

When you can move your leg without pain, start moving it gently. This helps keep the muscle from getting stiff.

Most mild injuries get better in a few days.

### Talk to a Pharmacist

A pharmacist can help you choose pain relief or other treatments that may ease your symptoms.

## When to See a Doctor

Call NHS 111 or get help online if you think you have a hamstring injury and:

- The pain is very bad or getting worse  
- There is a lot of swelling or bruising, or it is getting worse  
- It hurts to walk or stand on the injured leg  
- Your leg feels very stiff or hard to move  
- It’s not getting better after treating it at home  
- You have a very high temperature  
- You feel hot but also cold and shivery – this could mean you have an infection

## Severe Injuries

Some hamstring injuries are serious.  
They can take weeks or months to heal.  
You may need help from a specialist doctor.

If your injury is not healing as expected, or you’ve had hamstring injuries before, see a physiotherapist.

A physiotherapist can teach you special exercises.  
These can help your leg heal faster.  
They can also help stop future injuries.

You can get free physiotherapy on the NHS.  
But there may be a long wait.  
Ask your GP surgery for advice on how to get help in your area.

In rare cases, surgery is needed.  
This is for the worst injuries, like a complete tear in the muscle.  
During surgery, the muscle is stitched back together.  
Recovery takes several months.

## How to Prevent Hamstring Injuries

You can lower your risk of injury by following these tips:

### Do

- Build up your fitness slowly if you haven’t exercised in a while.  
- Do not play tough sports like football until you are strong enough.  
- Always warm up before you exercise. This keeps your muscles flexible.  
- Stop exercising if you feel pain in your hamstrings.

### Don’t

- Do not exercise when you are tired. Tired muscles are more likely to get hurt.

# Stress Fractures

A stress fracture is a small crack in a bone. It often happens in the long bones of the foot, especially the metatarsals.

These fractures are not caused by a single injury like a fall or a blow. Instead, they happen from doing the same activity over and over. The bone gets stressed too much, and the muscles around it can no longer protect it.

Stress fractures can happen in the upper leg, pelvis, or lower leg. More than half happen in the lower leg. Many of these are in the foot bones called metatarsals. If the fracture is in the upper leg or pelvis, it may mean the bone is weak due to a condition like osteoporosis.

## Who Gets Metatarsal Stress Fractures?

Metatarsal stress fractures often happen in:

- Runners who suddenly increase how hard or how long they run
- People who are not used to physical activity and walk long distances while carrying a heavy load (like new soldiers)

The second metatarsal bone in the foot is the most common place for this injury. Other things that raise the risk include:

- A high-arched foot (called cavus foot)
- Shoes that do not absorb shock well
- Weak bones from osteoporosis

Stress fractures can also be a sign of the female athlete triad. This is a condition that includes missing menstrual periods, poor eating habits, and weak bones.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Pain in the front of the foot that starts after a long or hard workout is the most common early sign. The pain goes away when you stop exercising.

Over time, the pain starts sooner during activity. It can get so bad that you cannot keep going. The pain may even stay even when you are not walking or standing.

You might see swelling or redness. Or, the pain may only come when someone presses on the foot or squeezes it.

If you have deep pain in the groin or thigh when you stand or walk, you may have a stress fracture in the upper leg. This needs to be checked by a doctor who specializes in bones and injuries.

## How Are Stress Fractures Diagnosed?

Doctors usually start with an X-ray. But the X-ray may look normal at first. It can take two to three weeks for signs of healing to show up.

If the X-ray does not show the fracture, the doctor may use a bone scan or an MRI. These tests can find the injury earlier.

Women with stress fractures in the upper leg or pelvis may have weak bones. They may need more tests, like a dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan, to check bone strength.

## How Are Stress Fractures Treated?

The main treatment is to stop putting weight on the injured area.

For a foot fracture, this means not walking on the foot. You may need to use crutches. You should not walk on the injured foot until it heals.

Casting is sometimes used, but it is not the best choice. A wooden shoe or a special supportive shoe or boot is better. These help protect the bone without making the leg muscles shrink from not being used.

Healing takes between 6 and 12 weeks. It is important to rest and avoid activities that cause pain until the bone is fully healed.

# Eardrum Perforation

A perforation is a hole in the eardrum.

- The eardrum can develop a hole from an ear infection or from an injury.
- A hole in the eardrum can cause sudden ear pain.
- You might also bleed from the ear.
- You may lose some hearing.
- You might hear ringing or buzzing in the ear.

## What Causes a Hole in the Eardrum?

You can poke a hole in your eardrum with things like a cotton swab.  
You can also get a hole from something that hits your ear by accident. Examples include a low-hanging tree branch or a thrown pencil.  

If something goes through the eardrum, it can damage the tiny bones behind the eardrum. These bones help carry sound to the inner ear.  
Pieces of the broken bones or the object itself can go into the inner ear.  

A blocked tube that connects your middle ear to the back of your nose can also cause a hole. This tube helps balance pressure on both sides of the eardrum. If it is blocked, pressure builds up. This can burst the eardrum. This is called barotrauma.

A sudden change in outside pressure can also cause a hole.  
- A big increase in pressure, like from an explosion or a hard slap to the ear.  
- A big drop in pressure, like when you fly in an airplane or when strong suction is used on the ear.  

Doctors can cause a hole when they clean out the ear canal or remove a foreign object.  

A serious head injury can also cause a hole. This is more likely if the skull near the ear is broken.  

The most common cause of a hole that is not from an injury is a middle ear infection.

## What Are the Signs of a Hole in the Eardrum?

A middle ear infection that is strong enough to cause a hole is usually very painful. This is because fluid builds up behind the eardrum.  
But when the eardrum breaks, the fluid can drain out. This often reduces the pain.

An injury that causes a hole leads to sudden, sharp pain.  
- You may bleed from the ear.  
- You may lose hearing.  
- You may hear ringing or buzzing in the ear.  

There are two types of hearing loss:  
- Conductive hearing loss: Sound cannot reach the inner ear. This can happen if the tiny bones are damaged.  
- Sensorineural hearing loss: The inner ear or nerves are damaged. Sound reaches the inner ear, but the brain cannot understand it.  

The more serious the damage to the tiny bones or inner ear, the worse the hearing loss will be.

Damage to the inner ear can also cause vertigo. This is a feeling that you or your surroundings are spinning.  
Pus may start to come out of the ear within 24 to 48 hours. This is more likely if water or other material gets into the middle ear.

## How Is a Hole in the Eardrum Diagnosed?

A doctor will look inside your ear.  
They use a small light called an otoscope.  
This tool lets them see the eardrum clearly.

If you have hearing loss or vertigo, the doctor may do hearing tests before and after treatment.  
If the hole is large or if your symptoms are very bad, you will see a specialist. This is a doctor who treats ear, nose, and throat problems.

## How Is a Hole in the Eardrum Treated?

- Antibiotics may be needed.  
- Surgery may be needed in some cases.

Keep your ear dry.  
- Use a cotton ball with petroleum jelly in your ear when you shower or bathe.  
- Do not swim.

Most of the time, no special treatment is needed.  
But if the injury came from a dirty object, or if dirt or germs got into the ear, your doctor will give you antibiotic ear drops.  
Antibiotics may also be used if the ear becomes infected.

The eardrum usually heals on its own.  
If it does not heal within two months, surgery may be needed. This surgery is called tympanoplasty.

You may need surgery sooner if you have a serious injury. This is especially true if you have major hearing loss or severe vertigo.

If a hole is not repaired, you may get a long-term infection in the middle ear. This is called chronic suppurative otitis media.

If you still have hearing loss after the hole heals, it may mean the tiny bones are broken or stuck. These bones can be fixed with surgery.

If you still have hearing loss or vertigo more than a few hours after the injury, it may mean the inner ear was damaged.

# Pulmonary Embolism – Simple Guide

A pulmonary embolism is a serious blockage in a blood vessel in the lungs. It can be life-threatening if not treated quickly.

## Signs and Symptoms

You may have a pulmonary embolism if you suddenly:

- Feel short of breath.
- Have sharp chest pain that gets worse when you breathe in.
- Cough up blood.

You might also notice:

- Pain, redness, or swelling in one leg, especially in the calf.

This could be a sign of a blood clot in the leg. This is called deep vein thrombosis, or DVT.

## When to Get Help Right Away

Call your doctor for an urgent appointment or use NHS 111 if you:

- Suddenly have trouble breathing.
- Are coughing up blood.

You can call 111 or get help online.

Call 999 or go to A&E if you:

- Are struggling to breathe very badly.
- Have chest or upper back pain.
- Your heart is beating very fast.
- Someone has passed out.

These could be signs of a pulmonary embolism or another serious problem.

> Find your nearest A&E

### Important Safety Tips for A&E

- Do not drive yourself to A&E. Ask someone to take you or call 999 for an ambulance.
- Bring all your medicines with you.

## How It Is Treated

If your doctor thinks you have a pulmonary embolism, you will be sent to hospital.

At the hospital, you will likely get an injection of medicine to stop blood clots from getting bigger. This is called an anticoagulant.

You will get this injection before test results come back.

If tests confirm the diagnosis, you will continue with injections for at least five days.

You will also need to take anticoagulant tablets for at least three months.

If caught and treated early, most people make a full recovery.

## How to Lower Your Risk

A pulmonary embolism often starts when a blood clot in the leg breaks loose and travels to the lungs.

You can take steps to reduce your risk.

### If You Are in Hospital

Your medical team should take steps to prevent blood clots in your legs.

### If You Are Traveling

Long trips by bus, train, or plane can raise your risk of a blood clot, especially if the trip lasts more than four hours.

#### Do These Things

- Sit comfortably. Choose an aisle seat if you can.
- Wear loose clothing.
- Make sure you have enough space to move your legs.
- Drink water often.
- Get up and walk around regularly.
- Every 30 minutes, bend and straighten your legs, feet, and toes.
- Press the balls of your feet hard into the floor from time to time.
- Wear flight socks (compression socks).

#### Avoid These Things

- Sitting still for long periods without moving.
- Drinking alcohol.
- Drinking too much coffee or other drinks with caffeine.
- Taking sleeping pills.

Taking these steps can help keep your blood flowing and lower your risk of a dangerous clot.

# Osteoarthritis (OA)

Osteoarthritis is a common joint problem. It happens when the cartilage in a joint breaks down. Cartilage is the smooth tissue that covers the ends of bones where they meet to form a joint. When cartilage wears away, the bones rub against each other. This causes pain, stiffness, and swelling.

Over time, the bones around the joint may grow abnormally. This can cause bony bumps and thickening. The joint may also become less stable and move poorly.

## Who Gets Osteoarthritis?

Osteoarthritis is the most common joint disease. It often starts showing symptoms in your 40s or 50s. By age 80, almost everyone has some signs of it in their joints. But not everyone feels pain or has symptoms.

Only about half of people with joint damage from osteoarthritis actually feel symptoms.

Before age 40, men are more likely to get large joint osteoarthritis. This is often due to injury or a natural difference in joint shape, like a hip that is not formed normally.

After age 40, women are more likely to get it. By age 70, men and women are equally affected.

## Types of Osteoarthritis

There are two main types:

**Primary osteoarthritis**  
This happens without a clear cause. It often affects just one or a few joints.  
- It can be limited to certain joints like the hands, knees, or hips.  
- If it affects many joints, it is called generalized osteoarthritis.

**Secondary osteoarthritis**  
This is caused by another condition that harms the joint.  
- It can follow a serious injury.  
- It can come from birth defects in the joint.  
- It can be linked to diseases like hemochromatosis or Wilson disease.  
- It can follow an infection in the joint.  
- It can be caused by hormone problems, nerve issues, or other joint diseases.  
- It can also be caused by conditions that damage the cartilage, such as rheumatoid arthritis or psoriatic arthritis.

## How Osteoarthritis Develops

Joints normally work smoothly. They do not wear out from normal use. The cartilage in joints is mostly water and a special matrix. It has very few cells called chondrocytes. These cells take a long time to grow and repair.

The health of cartilage depends on movement. When you put weight on a joint, fluid is squeezed out. When you take the weight off, the cartilage fills back up with fluid and nutrients.

Osteoarthritis often starts with no clear cause. But it can begin after an injury, like a torn knee cartilage. It can also start when chemicals from the joint lining get into the cartilage. Or it can start when the body’s normal repair process goes wrong.

Being overweight can trigger problems in cartilage. Fat tissue releases chemicals that harm cartilage. Extra weight also puts more pressure on joints.

The body tries to fix the damage. Cells in the cartilage make more repair material. But this also causes the release of enzymes that break down cartilage. It also causes inflammation. This creates a cycle of damage that keeps going.

The cartilage cells eventually die. Once the cartilage is gone, the bone underneath becomes exposed. It gets hard and smooth, like ivory. This is called eburnation.

All parts of the joint can be affected. The bone under the cartilage becomes stiff and can die. It may form small fluid-filled pockets called cysts. The body tries to fix the bone, which causes it to thicken and grow bony spurs at the edge of the joint.

The bony spurs may form to help stabilize the joint. The cartilage may first thicken, but then it breaks down. The lining of the joint becomes inflamed and thick. The fluid inside the joint becomes thinner and more watery.

Tendons and ligaments around the joint become strained. This can cause pain and tightness. As the joint moves less, the muscles around it weaken. This makes the joint less stable.

In the knee, the meniscus (a piece of cartilage) can tear. It may break into pieces. This can cause pain and a feeling of the joint locking.

In the spine, osteoarthritis can cause thickening of ligaments. This can press on the spinal cord or nerves. It can cause back or leg pain that gets worse when walking. This is called neurogenic claudication.

The nerves in the spine are protected in small spaces. So nerve problems are less common. But some people may have trouble swallowing if bone spurs press on the esophagus. Rarely, blood flow to the spinal cord can be blocked.

Pain can come from many parts of the joint. This includes the bone, ligaments, joint lining, fluid sacs, joint capsule, muscles, tendons, disks, and the outer layer of bone. Pressure in the bone marrow can also cause pain.

## Symptoms and Signs

Osteoarthritis usually starts slowly. It often begins in one or a few joints.

**Pain** is the first sign. It may feel like a deep ache.  
- Pain gets worse when you stand or walk.  
- It gets better when you rest.  
- Over time, the pain may become constant.

**Stiffness** happens when you wake up or after sitting still.  
- It usually lasts less than 30 minutes.  
- It gets better with movement.

As the disease gets worse, the joint moves less. You may feel tenderness when you press on the joint. You may hear or feel a grating or crackling sound when you move the joint.

In larger joints like the knee, fluid may build up. This is called a joint effusion. The fluid is usually not inflamed. It has few white blood cells.

Bony growths can cause the joint to bend in a fixed way. This is called a contracture. Sudden or severe joint swelling is rare.

The disease often gets worse slowly. But sometimes it stops on its own, without warning.

## Which Joints Are Most Affected?

The most common joints affected are:

- The joints at the ends of the fingers (DIP joints) and middle finger joints (PIP joints). These can form bony bumps called Heberden and Bouchard nodes.
- The base of the thumb (carpometacarpal joint). This is often the most painful joint in the hand.
- The joints in the neck and lower back (vertebral joints).
- The big toe joint (first metatarsophalangeal joint).
- The hip joint.
- The knee joint.

### Spine Osteoarthritis

- In the neck and lower back, osteoarthritis can cause thickening of ligaments. This can press on the spinal cord or nerves.
- This can cause back or leg pain that gets worse when walking. This is called neurogenic claudication.
- Nerve problems (radiculopathy) can happen but are less common because nerves are well protected.
- Rarely, bone spurs in the neck can press on the esophagus and make swallowing hard.
- Rarely, blood flow to the spinal cord can be blocked.

### Hip Osteoarthritis

- You lose the ability to move the hip fully.
- Pain happens when you stand, walk, or turn the leg.
- Pain may be felt in the groin, hip, thigh, or knee.

### Knee Osteoarthritis

- The cartilage wears away, especially on the inside of the knee.
- The ligaments become loose. The joint feels unstable.
- Pain comes from the ligaments and tendons.

### Hand Osteoarthritis

- The space between the bones in the joint gets smaller.
- You feel pain, stiffness, and trouble using your hands.
- The joint lining may become inflamed.
- It mainly affects the finger joints and the base of the thumb.
- The second and third knuckles are less often affected. The wrists are usually not involved.
- **Nodal osteoarthritis** causes bony bumps on the finger joints.
- **Erosive osteoarthritis** causes severe damage seen on X-rays. It is not clear if this is a type of hand osteoarthritis or a different condition, such as calcium crystal disease.

## How Is Osteoarthritis Diagnosed?

### X-rays

Osteoarthritis should be suspected if you have slow-onset joint pain, especially if you are older.

If your doctor thinks you have osteoarthritis, they will take X-rays of the most painful joints.

X-rays can show:
- Bony spurs at the edge of the joint.
- Narrowing of the space between the bones.
- Hardening of the bone under the cartilage.
- Small fluid-filled pockets in the bone.
- Changes in bone shape.
- Sometimes, fluid buildup in the joint.

For knee X-rays, standing views with the knee bent are more accurate for seeing joint space loss.

It is common to have more pain than what the X-ray shows. The X-ray may look bad, but you feel little pain. Or the X-ray may look mild, but you have severe pain.

### Blood and Joint Fluid Tests

Blood tests are usually normal in osteoarthritis. But they may be done to rule out other diseases.

If there is fluid in the joint, your doctor may take a sample. This helps tell osteoarthritis apart from inflammatory arthritis.

In osteoarthritis:
- The fluid is clear and thick.
- It has fewer than 2,000 white blood cells per microliter.
