# Headaches

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:
- You keep getting headaches.
- Painkillers do not help and your headache gets worse.
- You have a strong, throbbing pain in the front or side of your head. This could be a migraine. It could also be a less common type called a cluster headache.
- You feel sick, throw up, and find light or noise painful.
- You often get headaches before or during your period.

## When to Get Urgent Help

Call 111 or get help online if:
- You or your child has a very bad headache and:
  - Your jaw hurts when you eat.
  - Your vision is blurry or double.
  - Your scalp is sore.
  - You have other symptoms like numbness or weakness in your arms or legs.

Also call 111 or get help online if your child is under 12 and has any one of these:
- A headache that wakes them up at night.
- A headache when they wake up in the morning.
- A headache that gets worse over time.
- A headache that starts or gets worse when coughing, sneezing, or bending down.
- A headache with vomiting.
- A headache with a squint (when the eyes point in different directions) or trouble looking up.

You can call 111 or get help from 111 online.

## When to Call 999 or Go to A&E

Call 999 or go to A&E if:
- You or your child has had a head injury, like from a fall or accident.
- You or your child has a headache that started suddenly and is extremely painful.

Also call 999 or go to A&E if:
- You or your child has a very bad headache and:
  - Suddenly has trouble speaking or remembering things.
  - Loses vision.
  - Feels very sleepy or confused.
  - Has a very high temperature and signs of meningitis.
  - The white part of the eye is red.

Also call 999 or go to A&E if your child is under 12 and has any one of these:
- A headache with vision problems or trouble speaking, swallowing, balancing, or walking.
- A headache with drowsiness or constant tiredness.
- A headache that starts within 5 days of a head injury.

## A&E Safety Tips

- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you. Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.
- Bring all your medicines with you.

## How to Feel Better at Home

Headaches can last from 30 minutes to several days.

### Do These Things:
- Drink plenty of water.
- Rest if you also have a cold or the flu.
- Try to relax. Stress can make headaches worse.
- Take paracetamol or ibuprofen.
- Stay at home and avoid others if you have a high temperature or do not feel well enough to do your normal activities.

### Avoid These Things:
- Do not drink alcohol.
- Do not skip meals, even if you are not hungry.
- Do not sleep longer than usual. This can make the headache worse.
- Do not stare at a screen for a long time. This can strain your eyes.

## What Can Cause Headaches

Common causes include:
- Having a cold or the flu.
- Stress.
- Drinking too much alcohol.
- Poor posture.
- Problems with your eyesight.
- Not eating regular meals.
- Not drinking enough fluids (this is called dehydration).
- Taking too many painkillers.
- Hormonal changes during your period or menopause.

Keeping a headache diary can help you find out what causes your headaches. Write down when the headache starts, how long it lasts, and what you were doing at the time.

# Submandibular Space Infection

This is a serious infection in the soft tissues under the jaw. It can spread quickly and may block the airway. It is not a true abscess, but it acts like one and is treated the same way.

## What Causes This Infection?

Most often, it starts from a tooth problem. It usually comes from an infected second or third lower molar tooth. Poor dental care, recent tooth removal, or injury to the jaw or mouth can also lead to this infection.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may feel pain in your teeth or jaw. The area under your chin and under your tongue becomes very hard and tender. The floor of your mouth may feel stiff and board-like. You may drool more than usual. You might have trouble opening your mouth or swallowing. You may also have a high-pitched sound when breathing, called stridor. This happens because the throat swells. Your tongue may push up against the roof of your mouth.

You may also have a fever, chills, and a fast heartbeat. This infection can block your airway in just a few hours. It is more likely to block the airway than other neck infections. The chance of dying from this condition is about 3 in 1,000.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose this by examining you. If the signs are not clear, they may order a CT scan to see the infection better.

## How Is It Treated?

The most important step is to keep your airway open. Swelling makes it hard to put a breathing tube in through the mouth. So doctors often use a thin tube passed through the nose while you are awake. This is done in a special room with a camera to guide the tube. Some people need a breathing tube placed directly into the windpipe through a cut in the neck. This is called a tracheotomy.

If you do not need a breathing tube right away, you will be watched closely. A small tube in the nose may help you breathe better for a short time.

Surgery is needed to drain the infection. The surgeon makes a cut and places drainage tubes deep under the jaw muscles. This reduces pressure and helps the infection heal.

You will also need antibiotics. These medicines must fight both types of bacteria found in the mouth: those that grow with oxygen and those that do not. Common choices include clindamycin, ampicillin with sulbactam, or high-dose penicillin.

# Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis

Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are serious skin conditions. They cause a rash, peeling skin, and sores inside the mouth, eyes, and other body openings.

These conditions can be life threatening. They often start with flu-like symptoms. Then the skin begins to peel off in large areas.

## What Causes These Conditions?

Most cases are caused by a reaction to a medicine. Common medicines that cause this include:
- Sulfa drugs and other antibiotics
- Seizure medicines like phenytoin and carbamazepine
- Some arthritis medicines like piroxicam
- A medicine used for gout called allopurinol

Some cases are caused by infections. Others are linked to:
- Certain vaccines
- A condition called graft-versus-host disease
- A weak immune system

In children, an infection is the most common cause.

Sometimes doctors cannot find the cause.

These conditions can happen at any age. They are more likely in people with:
- A bone marrow transplant
- Lupus
- Other long-term joint or connective tissue diseases
- HIV infection, especially if they also have a lung infection caused by *Pneumocystis jirovecii*

Some people have a family history of these conditions.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The condition usually starts with:
- Fever
- Headache
- Cough
- Eye pain and swelling
- Body aches

If it is caused by a medicine, symptoms usually appear 1 to 3 weeks after starting the medicine.

Next, a flat red or purple rash appears on the face, neck, and chest. It spreads to other parts of the body in an uneven pattern.

The rash grows larger. Blisters form in the center. The skin over the blisters is very loose. It can peel off with just a light touch.

The peeling skin is painful. The person feels very sick. They may have chills and a high fever.

Some people lose their eyebrows or fingernails. The palms of the hands and soles of the feet may also be affected.

Sores appear in the mouth, throat, eyes, genitals, anus, and sometimes the digestive or breathing tubes.

Mouth sores make eating hard. The mouth may hurt so much that the person drools. Closing the mouth is painful.

Eye sores cause severe pain. The eyes may swell and crust over. In some cases, the eyes can seal shut. Scarring can damage the eyes and affect vision.

Sores in the urethra (the tube that carries urine out) make urination painful and hard.

Sores in the digestive or breathing tubes can cause:
- Diarrhea
- Cough
- Pneumonia
- Trouble breathing

## How Much Skin Is Affected?

The amount of skin affected helps doctors decide which condition a person has.

- **Stevens-Johnson syndrome**: Less than 10% of the body is affected.
- **Toxic epidermal necrolysis**: More than 30% of the body is affected.
- **Overlap syndrome**: Between 10% and 30% of the body is affected.

Toxic epidermal necrolysis causes skin loss like a severe burn. It is just as dangerous.

## How Are These Conditions Diagnosed?

Doctors look at the skin and mouth sores. They check the symptoms and how fast the skin is peeling.

They may take a small sample of skin and look at it under a microscope. This is called a skin biopsy.

## How Are These Conditions Treated?

People with these conditions are hospitalized right away. They are often treated in a burn unit or intensive care unit.

All medicines that might be causing the problem are stopped immediately.

The skin loses fluids and salts through the open areas. Doctors give fluids and salts through a vein (IV) to replace what is lost.

The skin usually grows back on its own. Skin grafts are not needed, unlike with burns.

Doctors try to prevent infection. The person is kept in a clean, safe environment.

### Medicines Used in Treatment

There is no clear proof that any medicine helps people survive. But some doctors use certain medicines based on their experience.

**Cyclosporine**  
This medicine may help reduce the time with blistering and peeling. It may also improve survival chances.

**Corticosteroids**  
Some doctors give high doses early on. They believe this helps. Others avoid them because they may increase the risk of serious infection.

**Plasmapheresis**  
This is a blood treatment. The blood is removed from the body. The plasma (the liquid part) is separated and removed. The blood cells are returned. This removes harmful substances from the blood, such as medicines or immune system proteins that may be causing the damage.

**Immune globulin**  
This is a medicine made from human blood. It is given through a vein. It may help protect the skin, but it is not clear if it works.

**Immunosuppressants**  
These medicines calm down the immune system. They help stop it from attacking the body’s own tissues.

One type is called tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors. Examples include infliximab and etanercept. These are used to reduce the harmful immune response.

If an infection develops, doctors give antibiotics right away.

## What Is the Outlook?

The chance of survival depends on how much skin is lost.

- **Toxic epidermal necrolysis**:  
  - About 25 to 35 out of 100 adults die.  
  - The risk is higher in older adults with severe skin loss.  
  - Children have a better chance of survival.

- **Stevens-Johnson syndrome**:  
  - Fewer people die than in toxic epidermal necrolysis.

Recovery can take weeks to months. Some people have long-term problems, such as:
- Eye damage
- Skin scarring
- Nail loss
- Dry mouth or dry eyes

Early treatment improves the chances of recovery.

# Feeling Short of Breath

If you are having trouble breathing, it is important to act quickly. Some signs mean you need emergency help right away.

## When to Call 999 or Go to A&E

Call 999 or go to A&E immediately if you:

- Are gasping for air or choking.
- Cannot speak in full sentences.
- Feel tightness or heaviness in your chest.
- Have pain that moves to your arms, back, neck, or jaw.
- Your lips or skin look very pale, blue, or grey. On brown or black skin, check the palms of your hands.
- You feel suddenly confused or disoriented.

**Find your nearest A&E**

### Important Safety Tips for A&E

- Do not drive yourself to A&E.
- Ask a friend or family member to drive you.
- If you cannot get a ride, call 999 and ask for an ambulance.
- Bring all your regular medicines with you.

## If Your Child Is Short of Breath

Call 999 or go to A&E right away if your child:

- Is struggling to breathe. They may make grunting sounds or pull their stomach in under their ribs.
- Have lips or skin that are very pale, blue, or grey. On brown or black skin, check the palms of their hands.
- Are suddenly confused. They may be very agitated, acting strangely, or crying non-stop.
- Are limp, floppy, or not responding normally. Their head may fall to the side, back, or forward. They may not be able to lift their head or look at you.

**Find your nearest A&E**

## When to Call NHS 111

Call 111 or get help online if you:

- Are breathing more heavily than usual.
- Feel sick or are being sick.
- Are coughing up blood.
- Have pain or swelling in one leg.
- Feel your heart racing, beating too slowly, skipping a beat, or fluttering in your chest.

You can call 111 or visit the NHS 111 website for help.

## When to See Your GP

See your GP if:

- Your shortness of breath gets worse during normal daily activities.
- Your shortness of breath gets worse when you lie down.
- You are short of breath and have swollen ankles.
- You have been coughing for three weeks or longer.

It is always a good idea to get checked. You are not wasting time by asking for help. It is better to be safe.

## What Can Cause Shortness of Breath?

Shortness of breath can have many causes.

Common causes include:

- Asthma – a condition that makes it hard to breathe.
- A chest infection – like bronchitis or pneumonia.
- Being overweight.
- Smoking.
- A panic attack – a sudden feeling of fear that can make breathing hard.

But sometimes shortness of breath can be a sign of something more serious, such as:

- Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) – a long-term lung problem.
- Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis – scarring in the lungs.
- Heart failure – when the heart does not pump blood well.
- Lung cancer.

The treatment you need depends on what is causing your symptoms.

Do not try to guess what is wrong. Always see your GP for a proper check-up.

# Chronic Bilirubin Encephalopathy

This condition is brain damage caused by a substance called bilirubin building up in the brain. It mainly affects the deep parts of the brain that control movement and other basic functions.

Bilirubin is a waste product made when red blood cells break down. Normally, it stays in the blood and does not enter the brain. But sometimes it can get into the brain and cause damage. This happens when:

- The level of bilirubin in the blood is very high.
- The level of albumin in the blood is very low. Albumin helps carry bilirubin in the blood. This is common in premature babies.
- Other substances push bilirubin out of albumin. These include certain medicines like sulfisoxazole, ceftriaxone, and aspirin. It can also happen when babies are sick or have too much acid in their blood.

## Symptoms and Signs

In premature babies, the damage may not show any clear signs at first.

In full-term babies, early signs include:
- Being very sleepy or inactive.
- Not wanting to feed.
- Vomiting.

Later, more serious problems can appear, such as:
- Severe muscle stiffness.
- Eyes stuck in an upward position.
- Sudden, uncontrolled eye movements.
- Seizures.
- In the worst cases, death.

Long-term effects in childhood may include:
- Learning difficulties or low intelligence.
- A type of cerebral palsy that causes uncontrolled, writhing movements.
- Permanent hearing loss.
- Inability to look up with the eyes.

We do not know if mild cases cause smaller problems like trouble with coordination, attention, or learning.

## Diagnosis

There is no simple test to confirm this condition while a baby is alive.

Doctors make a guess based on symptoms and medical history. They look at the baby’s behavior, feeding, and movement.

The only way to be certain is to examine the brain after death, during an autopsy.

## Treatment

There is no treatment for brain damage once it has happened.

The only way to prevent this condition is to treat high bilirubin levels early. This means checking bilirubin levels in newborns and acting quickly if they are too high.

# Necrotizing Skin Infections

These are serious infections that cause skin and tissue to die. They are a severe form of a common skin infection called cellulitis.

## What Happens in These Infections?

- Bacteria enter the skin and spread quickly.
- The infection blocks small blood vessels. This cuts off blood flow to the tissue.
- Without blood, the tissue dies. Dead tissue is called necrotic.
- The body’s infection fighters, like white blood cells, can no longer reach the dead area.
- This lets the infection grow fast and become hard to control.
- Without treatment, the infection can lead to death.

## Types of Necrotizing Skin Infections

There are two main types:

- **Necrotizing fasciitis**: The infection spreads deep in the skin, along the layer that covers the muscles.
- **Necrotizing cellulitis**: The infection spreads in the outer layers of the skin.

Many different bacteria can cause these infections. Common ones include *Streptococcus* and *Clostridia*. Often, more than one type of bacteria is involved.

- A severe form caused by *Streptococcus* is sometimes called “flesh-eating disease” in the news. But it is not very different from other types.
- **Gas gangrene** is a type that affects muscle and nearby tissue. It is usually caused by *Clostridia*.

## How Do These Infections Start?

- They can start in small cuts, puncture wounds, or deep scrapes, especially if dirt or debris is in the wound.
- They may also start in surgical wounds or even in healthy skin with no visible injury.
- In some people, infections in the intestines — like from a hole in the bowel or a tumor — can lead to these skin infections.
- Bacteria from the gut can form a pocket of pus in the belly (an abscess) and spread to the skin.
- Or, the bacteria can travel through the blood to the skin and other organs.
- People with diabetes are more likely to get these infections.

## Signs and Symptoms

The infection often starts like a regular skin infection. But it gets worse fast.

- The skin may first look pale, then turn red or dark bronze.
- It feels warm and swells up.
- Pain is very strong.

Later, the skin turns purple. Large blisters form. The fluid inside is brown, watery, and may smell bad.

- Dead skin turns black. This is called gangrene.
- Some infections, especially those caused by *Clostridia* or mixed bacteria, make gas.
- The gas forms bubbles under the skin. You can feel a crackling sensation when you press the area.
- At first, the area hurts a lot. But as the tissue dies, the nerves stop working. The area may lose feeling.
- The muscles can also be affected as the infection spreads.

The person feels extremely sick. They may have:

- A high fever
- A fast heartbeat
- Confusion or trouble thinking
- Loss of consciousness
- Low blood pressure due to toxins and the body’s reaction (called septic shock)
- Toxic shock syndrome

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors look at the skin and ask about symptoms.

- They check for gas under the skin. This is a key sign.
- X-rays can show gas under the skin.
- Blood tests usually show a high number of white blood cells.
- Doctors take samples of blood or tissue to grow the bacteria in a lab. This helps identify the cause.
- But treatment starts right away — even before test results come back.

## How It Is Treated

Treatment must begin fast. It includes:

- Surgery to remove dead skin, tissue, and muscle. This is often a large operation.
- Antibiotics given through a vein (IV).
- In some cases, an arm or leg may need to be removed (amputation) to stop the infection.
- People need large amounts of IV fluids before and after surgery.
- If the person has toxic shock syndrome, they may get IV immune globulin.

## Outlook and Prognosis

- About 20 to 30 out of 100 people who get treatment die.
- Without treatment, almost everyone dies.

People who are older, have other health problems, or have advanced infection are more likely to die.

- Delay in diagnosis or treatment makes the outcome worse.
- Not removing enough dead tissue also makes it harder to survive.

# Transient Ischaemic Attack (TIA)

A transient ischaemic attack is a warning sign. It means a small stroke may happen soon. The symptoms go away quickly, but you still need medical care.

## Symptoms of a TIA

You can remember the main signs using the word FAST:

**Face**  
One side of the face may droop.  
You may not be able to smile.  
Your mouth or eye may look uneven.

**Arms**  
You may not be able to raise both arms.  
One arm may feel weak or numb.

**Speech**  
Your words may be hard to understand.  
You may slur your speech.  
You may not be able to speak at all.  
You may not understand what others are saying.

**Time**  
If you see any of these signs, call 999 right away.  
Even if the symptoms go away, get help fast.

## Treating a TIA

The symptoms of a TIA usually go away in minutes or hours.  
But you still need treatment to stop another TIA or a full stroke.

Your doctor will look at your health and decide the best treatment.

You will likely get advice on lifestyle changes.  
You may also get medicine to prevent blood clots.

In some cases, surgery may be needed.  
This surgery is called a carotid endarterectomy.  
It opens up the main blood vessels in your neck that carry blood to your brain.

## What Causes a TIA

A TIA happens when a blood vessel in your brain gets blocked.  
This stops blood from reaching part of your brain.

The blockage is usually a blood clot.  
The clot may have formed in another part of your body and moved to your brain.  
It can also be caused by pieces of fat or air bubbles.

These things raise your risk of a TIA:

- Smoking  
- High blood pressure  
- Being overweight  
- High cholesterol  
- Drinking too much alcohol  
- Having an irregular heartbeat called atrial fibrillation  
- Having diabetes  

People over 55 years old are more likely to have a TIA.  
People of Asian, African, or Caribbean background also have a higher risk.

## How to Prevent a TIA

A TIA is a warning that a full stroke could happen soon.  
It means you are at high risk of a serious stroke.

You can lower your risk, even if you’ve had a TIA or stroke before.

Do these things:

- Keep a healthy weight  
- Eat a balanced, healthy diet  
- Exercise regularly  
- Limit how much alcohol you drink  
- Do not smoke

# Hepatitis C – What You Need to Know

## What Is Hepatitis C?

Hepatitis C is a virus that causes liver inflammation.  
It spreads through contact with infected blood.  
It is not spread through casual contact like hugging or sharing food.

The virus is called HCV.  
It is a type of RNA virus.  
There are several types of HCV, called genotypes.  
These types vary by region and affect how well treatment works.

The virus can change over time in a person’s body.  
This makes it harder to treat and harder to create a vaccine.

## How Is Hepatitis C Spread?

Hepatitis C spreads mainly through blood.  
This can happen by sharing needles to inject drugs.  
It can also happen through tattoos or body piercings done with unsterile tools.

It can rarely spread through sexual contact or from mother to baby during birth.  
It does not spread through saliva, sweat, or casual touch.

Healthcare workers can get infected from needlestick injuries.  
But the risk is low.  
There is no need to stop infected workers from doing their jobs.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many people with hepatitis C have no symptoms at all.  
Some people may feel tired, lose their appetite, or feel unwell.  
Jaundice (yellowing of the skin or eyes) can happen but is not common.

In rare cases, the liver can become severely damaged very quickly.  
This is called fulminant hepatitis.  
It is very rare.

## What Happens Over Time?

About 75 out of 100 people with acute hepatitis C will develop a long-term infection.  
This is called chronic hepatitis C.

Chronic hepatitis C often causes no symptoms.  
But over time, it can damage the liver.  
About 20 to 30 out of 100 people with chronic hepatitis C will develop cirrhosis.  
Cirrhosis is scarring of the liver.  
It can take decades to develop.

In some cases, cirrhosis can lead to liver cancer.  
This is rare unless cirrhosis is already present.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use blood tests to check for hepatitis C.  
The first test looks for antibodies to the virus.  
This shows if you have ever been infected.

If the antibody test is positive, a second test checks for the virus itself.  
This test measures HCV RNA in the blood.  
It shows if the virus is still active.

You may need both tests to know if you have a current infection.

| Test | Acute Infection | Chronic Infection | Past Infection |
|------|------------------|-------------------|----------------|
| Antibody to HCV | Positive | Positive | Positive |
| HCV RNA | Positive | Positive | Negative |

Note: A past infection means you had the virus but your body cleared it or treatment worked.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment uses antiviral medicines.  
These are called direct-acting antivirals, or DAAs.  
They are very effective.  
They can cure the infection in most people.

Treatment should start soon after diagnosis.  
You do not need to wait to see if the body clears the virus on its own.

These medicines also reduce the chance of spreading the virus to others.

Avoid alcohol and medicines that harm the liver, like acetaminophen.  
They can make liver damage worse.

There is no need to rest in bed or follow special diets.  
These are not proven to help.

## How Can You Prevent Hepatitis C?

Do not share needles or other drug injection tools.  
Avoid getting tattoos or piercings with unsterile equipment.

Do not share personal items like razors or toothbrushes.  
They can carry blood.

Use protection during sex if you have multiple partners.  
This lowers the risk.

Healthcare workers should use gloves and other safety gear.  
But isolating patients is not needed.

There is no vaccine for hepatitis C.  
The virus changes too much for a vaccine to work.

There is no medicine to take before or after exposure to prevent infection.

## Key Facts

- Hepatitis C spreads through blood.  
- It often causes no symptoms.  
- About 75% of people with acute infection develop long-term infection.  
- Over time, 20 to 30% develop serious liver damage.  
- Some people with liver damage may get liver cancer.  
- Diagnosis uses two blood tests: one for antibodies and one for the virus.  
- Treatment with antiviral medicines should start right after diagnosis.  
- There is no vaccine.

## More Information

For more details, see the 2023 guidelines from the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases and the Infectious Diseases Society of America.  
Link: [Hepatitis C Guidance 2023 Update](https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciad319)

# Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms

This is a bulge in the large blood vessel (aorta) that runs through the chest.

## What Causes Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms?

- Most aneurysms are caused by hardening of the arteries (atherosclerosis).
- Some happen when the wall of the aorta weakens over time. This is called cystic medial necrosis.
- The part of the aorta near the heart may get bigger. This can cause the aortic valve to not close properly.
- When the valve does not close, blood leaks back into the heart. This is called aortic valve regurgitation.
- About half of people with this type of aneurysm also have Marfan syndrome, a condition that affects connective tissue.
- The other half have no clear cause. But many of them have high blood pressure.

Rare causes include:
- Syphilis infection.
- Bacteria from another infection (like pneumonia or a urinary tract infection) entering the blood and settling in the aorta. This can weaken the aorta and cause a bulge.

## Symptoms of Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms

Many people have no symptoms at all. The aneurysm may grow large without causing any pain or discomfort.

When symptoms do appear, they happen because the bulge presses on nearby parts of the body. The symptoms depend on where the aneurysm is.

Common symptoms include:
- Pain in the upper back.
- Coughing.
- Wheezing.
- Coughing up blood, if the bulge presses on or damages the windpipe.
- Trouble swallowing, if the bulge presses on the tube that carries food to the stomach (esophagus).
- A hoarse voice, if the bulge presses on the nerve to the voice box.

A group of symptoms called Horner syndrome can happen if nerves in the chest are pressed. These include:
- A small pupil in one eye.
- A drooping eyelid.
- No sweating on one side of the face.

You might also feel a strong pulse in your chest. A chest x-ray may show the windpipe shifted to one side.

If the aneurysm bursts, you will feel sudden, severe pain. The pain usually starts in the upper back. It can spread down the back and into the belly. It may also be felt in the chest and arms, like a heart attack.

You can quickly go into shock. This is a life-threatening condition caused by heavy internal bleeding. Without treatment, a burst aneurysm is always fatal.

## How Doctors Find a Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm

Doctors may find an aneurysm by accident. For example, a chest x-ray or CT scan done for another reason may show it.

If you have symptoms, your doctor may suspect an aneurysm. They may also notice signs during a physical exam, such as:
- A certain kind of heart murmur (a rumbling sound heard with a stethoscope).
- Physical features linked to Marfan syndrome.

To learn more, doctors use imaging tests:
- CT angiography: A special type of CT scan that shows blood vessels.
- Magnetic resonance angiography: A scan that uses magnets and radio waves to show blood vessels.
- Transesophageal echocardiography: A type of ultrasound where a probe is passed down the throat to get clear pictures of the heart and aorta.

These tests help doctors see the size and exact location of the aneurysm. They also help decide if surgery is needed.

## How Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms Are Treated

The goal is to fix the aneurysm before it bursts. This is much safer than treating a burst aneurysm.

### Monitoring Small Aneurysms

If the aneurysm is small, doctors will check it regularly with CT scans every 6 to 12 months. This helps track if it is growing.

### Medications

You will be given medicine to lower your blood pressure. This slows the growth of the aneurysm and lowers the risk of rupture.

- Beta-blockers.
- Calcium channel blockers.
- Other blood pressure medicines.

If you smoke, quitting is very important. Smoking makes the aneurysm grow faster and increases the risk of rupture.

### Surgery or Stent Graft

Doctors usually recommend repair when the aneurysm is 2.5 inches (about 5.5 to 6.0 centimeters) wide or larger.

For people with Marfan syndrome, surgery may be recommended even if the aneurysm is smaller. This is because their aneurysms are more likely to burst.

There are two main repair methods:

#### 1. Endovascular Stent Graft (Less Invasive)
- A stent graft is a tube made of fabric and metal mesh.
- Doctors insert it through a small cut in the groin.
- They guide it up the blood vessel to the aneurysm site.
- Once in place, the stent opens and forms a new path for blood flow.
- The stent stays in the body permanently.

This method:
- Does not require opening the chest.
- Causes less pain.
- Has a shorter hospital stay.
- Takes 2 to 4 hours.

#### 2. Open Surgery (More Invasive)
- This is done when a stent graft does not fit the shape of the aorta.
- It requires a large cut in the chest.
- Recovery takes longer and is more painful.

### Risk of Surgery

- The risk of death during stent graft repair is low.
- The risk is higher if the aneurysm has already burst.
- If a burst aneurysm is not treated, it will always be fatal.

### Treating Infection-Related Aneurysms

If the aneurysm is caused by syphilis or another infection:
- Doctors will give antibiotics to treat the infection.
- The aneurysm will still need to be repaired.

## Summary

- A thoracic aortic aneurysm is a bulge in the main blood vessel in the chest.
- It may not cause symptoms at first.
- It can burst, causing sudden, severe pain and death.
- Most are found by chance during imaging tests for other problems.
- Treatment includes medicine to lower blood pressure and surgery or stent grafts to fix the aneurysm.
- Early treatment is much safer than waiting for a rupture.
- Quitting smoking and controlling blood pressure are key steps in managing the condition.

# Nosebleed

A nosebleed means blood is coming out of your nose. It is usually not serious, but it can be worrying.

## How to stop a nosebleed at home

If you have a nosebleed:

- Sit down and lean forward.
- Keep your head tilted forward. Do not tilt it back.
- Pinch the soft part of your nose, just above your nostrils.
- Hold it for 10 to 15 minutes.
- Breathe through your mouth.

You can also hold a cold pack (or a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a tea towel) on the top of your nose. This may help, but there is not strong proof it works.

## When to see a doctor (GP)

See your doctor if:

- A child under 2 years old has a nosebleed.
- You have nosebleeds often.
- You feel weak, tired, or short of breath.
- Your skin looks paler than usual.
- You have a faster heartbeat or feel dizzy.
- You are taking medicine that stops blood from clotting, like warfarin.
- You have a condition that makes your blood not clot well, such as haemophilia.

Your doctor may test you for anaemia or other health problems.

## When to go to A&E (Emergency Department)

Go to A&E if you have a nosebleed and:

- It lasts longer than 15 minutes.
- The bleeding is heavy.
- You are swallowing a lot of blood and then vomiting.
- The bleeding started after a blow to your head.
- You feel weak, dizzy, or faint.
- You are having trouble breathing.

### Important safety message for A&E

- Do not drive yourself to A&E.
- Ask someone to drive you.
- Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.
- Bring all your medicines with you.

## Treatment in hospital

If a doctor sees you in hospital:

- They may use a small stick with a special chemical on it. They put it into your nose to stop the bleeding.
- If that does not work, they may pack your nose with soft gauze or sponge.
- You may need to stay in hospital for a day or two.

After the bleeding stops, your doctor may give you a cream to use inside your nose. This helps prevent scabs. Check the ingredients first. Do not use it if you are allergic to peanuts or soya.

## What causes nosebleeds?

Nosebleeds happen when the inside of your nose gets damaged. Common causes include:

- Picking your nose.
- Blowing your nose too hard.
- Dry air, especially in winter or in air-conditioned rooms.

Some nosebleeds need medical care. These often happen deeper inside the nose and are more common in adults. Causes include:

- A broken nose or injury to the face.
- Problems with blood vessels or blood clotting.
- Certain medicines, like warfarin.

Sometimes doctors do not know the cause.

## Who is more likely to have nosebleeds?

You are more likely to have a nosebleed if you are:

- A child.
- Over 45 years old.
- Pregnant.
- Have high blood pressure.

## After a nosebleed

To help prevent another nosebleed, do not:

- Blow your nose.
- Pick your nose.
- Drink hot drinks or alcohol.
- Do heavy lifting or hard exercise.
- Pick at scabs.
- Lie flat on your back.

Wait 24 hours before doing any of these things.

# Parapharyngeal Abscess

A parapharyngeal abscess is a serious infection in the deep part of the neck. It can be life-threatening if not treated quickly.

## What Is the Parapharyngeal Space?

The parapharyngeal space is a hidden area in the neck. It lies next to the throat muscles and inside the jawbone. It is split into two parts by a bony finger-like structure called the styloid process.

The back part of this space holds the main neck blood vessels and nerves. These include the carotid artery and the internal jugular vein.

Infections in this area usually start in the tonsils or throat. They can also come from a tooth infection or swollen lymph nodes nearby.

## Symptoms and Signs

Most people with this infection have:
- A high fever
- A severe sore throat
- Pain when swallowing
- Swelling in the neck that goes down to the hyoid bone

### If the Infection Is in the Front Part of the Space

- The jaw muscles become stiff, making it hard to open the mouth wide.
- The jaw angle feels hard and swollen.
- The tonsil and side of the throat bulge inward.

### If the Infection Is in the Back Part of the Space

- Swelling is more visible at the back of the throat.
- Jaw stiffness is mild or not present.
- The infection can spread to the carotid sheath (a bundle of blood vessels and nerves).
- This can cause:
  - Shaking chills
  - Very high fever
  - Germs in the blood
  - Nerve problems
  - Severe bleeding from a burst carotid artery

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect this infection when a patient has deep neck swelling and symptoms like fever and sore throat.

The best test is a contrast-enhanced CT scan. This scan shows the exact location and size of the abscess.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment must be fast and strong. It usually includes:

- Strong antibiotics given through a vein (IV)
- Surgery to drain the abscess

### Airway Care

This infection can block the airway. Doctors may need to help with breathing. This can mean using a breathing tube or a tracheostomy.

### Drainage Methods

- **Front abscesses**: Often drained through a cut inside the mouth.
- **Back abscesses**: Drained through a cut under the jaw (submaxillary fossa).

### Antibiotics After Surgery

- You will stay on IV antibiotics for several days after surgery.
- The type of antibiotic is based on lab tests of the infection.
- After IV treatment, you will take oral antibiotics for 10 to 14 days.

### Small Abscesses

In rare cases, small abscesses can be treated with IV antibiotics alone. No surgery is needed.

## Important Notes

- This is a serious condition. Do not delay care.
- Early treatment prevents life-threatening complications.
- Always follow your doctor’s instructions for antibiotics and follow-up.

# Mouth Growths

Growths can form in any part of the mouth or around it. This includes tissues like gums, muscles, nerves, and bones.

Common places for growths to appear:
- Lips
- Sides of the tongue
- Bottom of the mouth
- Back part of the roof of the mouth (soft palate)

Some growths cause pain or irritation. Others do not.

---

## What Causes Mouth Growths?

Mouth growths can be:
- Noncancerous (not cancer)
- Precancerous (may turn into cancer)
- Cancerous (cancer)

Most mouth growths are not cancer.

### Noncancerous Growth Causes

**Irritation** can cause noncancerous growths. These often happen from constant rubbing or biting. For example, braces or a sharp tooth edge can cause this. If the cause of irritation stays, the growth may come back after removal.

Long-term irritation can lead to changes that may become cancer.

**Ordinary warts** (called verrucae vulgaris) can spread to the mouth if you suck or chew on a wart on your finger. A different kind of wart, caused by a virus called human papillomavirus, can spread to the mouth through oral sex.

Warts in the mouth are best removed with surgery.

**Thrush** is a yeast infection. It often shows up as white, cheese-like patches in the mouth. These patches stick to the inside of the mouth. When you try to wipe them off, they leave a red, raw area.

Thrush is more common in people with diabetes, weak immune systems, or those taking antibiotics.

**Torus** is a hard, bony bump. It can form on the roof of the mouth (torus palatinus) or on the lower jaw near the tongue (torus mandibularis). It is common and harmless. You do not need to treat it unless it hurts when you eat or if you need a denture that covers it.

If you have many bony growths, especially along the jaw’s edge, it could be a sign of a rare inherited condition called Gardner syndrome. This condition causes many polyps in the colon, which can become cancer.

**Keratoacanthomas** are fast-growing lumps. They often appear on the lips or other sun-exposed skin like the face, hands, or forearms. They grow quickly—reaching about half an inch to one inch in size in a month or two. Then they slowly shrink and may go away on their own.

Doctors used to think all keratoacanthomas were harmless. Now, some believe they are slow-growing cancers. If a growth does not shrink, doctors recommend removing it.

**Cysts** are fluid-filled sacs. They can cause jaw pain and swelling. They often form near a wisdom tooth. As they grow, they can damage the jawbone.

Some cysts come back after surgery. Cysts can also form in the floor of the mouth. They are often removed if they make swallowing hard or if they look bad.

The most common mouth cyst is a **mucocele**. It forms in the lip when you accidentally bite it. This blocks a small salivary gland, and saliva builds up. Most mucoceles go away in a week or two. But if they bother you, they can be removed with surgery.

**Odontomas** are overgrowths of tooth tissue. They look like small, misshapen extra teeth or a mass of tooth material. In children, they can block normal teeth from coming in. In adults, they can push teeth out of place. If they grow large, they can make the jaw bigger. They are usually removed with surgery.

**Salivary gland tumors** are growths in the glands that make saliva. Most (75 to 80%) are not cancer. They grow slowly and usually do not hurt. They feel soft and move under the skin or inside the mouth.

The most common type is called a mixed tumor or pleomorphic adenoma. It mostly affects women over 40. This type can become cancer. It must be removed completely. If not fully removed, it may grow back.

Other noncancerous salivary gland tumors are also removed, but they rarely become cancer or grow back.

A **fibroma** is a small, firm growth. It is caused by long-term irritation. For example, it can form from constant rubbing by braces.

---

## Precancerous Changes

Some mouth areas may look like early signs of cancer. These include:
- White patches that do not wipe off
- Red patches that do not wipe off
- Mixed white and red patches

If any of these spots last more than two weeks and do not go away, they may be precancerous. They can turn into cancer if not treated.

**Leukoplakia** is a flat white patch. It forms when the inside of the mouth is irritated for a long time. The patch is white because the tissue thickens. This thickening is due to a substance called keratin, which also covers the skin.

**Erythroplakia** is a red, flat, or thin area. It happens when the mouth lining wears away. The red color comes from blood vessels showing through. Erythroplakia is a stronger warning sign of cancer than leukoplakia.

**Mixed white-red areas** contain both leukoplakia and erythroplakia. These areas can also become cancer over time.

---

## Risk Factors for Oral Cancer

People who use tobacco, alcohol, or both are at higher risk for oral cancer.

Chewing tobacco or snuff often causes cancer on the inside of the cheeks or lips.

Other common sites for oral cancer include:
- Sides of the tongue
- Bottom of the mouth
- Throat

Cancers caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), especially type 16, often appear at the back of the throat, base of the tongue, or tonsils. HPV is now a more common cause of these cancers than tobacco.

Rarely, cancer in the mouth comes from another part of the body. This can happen if cancer spreads from the lungs, breast, or prostate.

Oral cancer can look like many different things. But it often looks like a white, red, or mixed white-red spot that does not go away and does not wipe off.

---

## When to See a Doctor

You should see a doctor or dentist if you have:
- A lump or bump in the mouth that lasts more than two weeks
- A sore that does not heal
- A white, red, or mixed patch that does not go away
- Pain or trouble swallowing
- A growth that changes in size or shape

Even if a growth looks harmless, it should be checked. Cancer can look like a normal growth.

---

## How Doctors Evaluate Mouth Growths

Your doctor will:
- Look at the growth
- Ask about your health and habits (like smoking or drinking)
- Check your mouth and neck
- May take a small sample (biopsy) to test for cancer

A biopsy is the best way to know if a growth is cancer.

---

## Treatment of Mouth Growths

Treatment depends on:
- What is causing the growth
- Whether it is cancer or not
- How it affects your daily life
- How likely it is to become cancer

Most noncancerous growths can be removed with surgery. Some can go away on their own.

Cancerous or precancerous growths are usually removed. Some may need more treatment, like radiation or chemotherapy.

---

## Key Points

- Most mouth growths are not cancer.
- Warts, yeast infections, and repeated injury (like biting or rubbing) are common causes of noncancerous growths.
- Tobacco, alcohol, and HPV infection raise the risk of oral cancer.
- Because cancer can look like a normal growth, doctors often recommend a biopsy.
- Any mouth growth that lasts more than two weeks should be checked.

---

# Cluster Headaches

## What Are Cluster Headaches?

Cluster headaches are very painful headaches. They usually happen on one side of the head. The pain is often around the eye. The pain can start suddenly. It can make you feel very restless. You might want to move around or walk.

These headaches can come many times a day. They can last for weeks or months. Then they may stop for a while. Or they may come again without a break.

## Symptoms

The main symptoms include:

- Sharp, burning, or stabbing pain on one side of the head.
- Pain that is often around the eye.
- Headaches that happen at the same time each day or each year.
- Headaches that start and stop quickly, with no warning.
- Pain that makes you restless. You may feel the need to move or pace.
- Headaches that last from 15 minutes to 3 hours.

Other possible symptoms:

- One eye becomes red and watery.
- You feel sick to your stomach.
- One eyelid droops or swells.
- One pupil gets smaller than the other.
- Sweating on one side of the face.
- A blocked or runny nose on the same side as the pain.

## When to See a Doctor

See your GP if:

- You think you might have cluster headaches.
- Your headaches keep coming back.
- Painkillers like paracetamol or ibuprofen do not help.
- The pain is so bad it makes you restless or upset.
- You already have cluster headaches, but they are getting worse, lasting longer, or your usual treatments are not working.

## When to Get Urgent Help

Call 111 or get help online if you have a severe headache and:

- Pain in your jaw when you eat.
- Blurry or double vision.
- A sore scalp.
- Numbness or weakness in your arms or legs.

These could be signs of a serious condition called temporal arteritis.

## When to Call 999 or Go to A&E

Go to A&E or call 999 right away if you have either of these for the first time:

- One eyelid droops.
- One pupil is smaller than the other.

Even if you already know you have cluster headaches, these new symptoms need urgent care.

[Find your nearest A&E]

## What Happens at the Doctor’s Appointment

There is no single test to diagnose cluster headaches.

Your GP will ask you about:

- The kind of pain you feel.
- Where the pain is.
- How often the headaches happen.
- Other symptoms you have.

Other health problems can cause similar symptoms. Your GP may refer you to a specialist. You may need a brain scan to rule out other causes.

## Treatments

There is no cure for cluster headaches. But treatments can help ease the pain and stop future attacks.

Painkillers like paracetamol and ibuprofen do not work for cluster headaches.

### Treatments for When a Headache Starts

If a headache has already started, your doctor may suggest:

- A medicine called a triptan. It can be given as an injection or a spray into the nose.
- Breathing pure oxygen through a mask. This helps stop the pain.
- A device that sends small electrical pulses to the back of your neck.

In rare cases, if other treatments do not work, surgery may be an option. A small device may be placed in your body to help reduce pain.

### Treatments to Prevent Headaches

Your GP may prescribe medicine to help stop cluster headaches before they start. These can include:

- Corticosteroids.
- Verapamil.
- Lithium.

Talk to your GP about common triggers. Keeping a diary of your headaches can help you spot what causes them.

## What Causes Cluster Headaches?

The exact cause is not known.

They are more common in men in their 30s and 40s. They also run in families. If a close family member has them, you are more likely to get them.

Some things may trigger a cluster headache. These include:

- Smoking.
- Drinking alcohol.
- Strong smells like perfume, paint, nail polish, or petrol.
- Exercise.

Keeping a headache diary can help you find your personal triggers. This may help you avoid future attacks.

# Miliaria (Heat Rash)

Miliaria is also known as heat rash. It happens when sweat gets trapped under the skin. This can cause small bumps or blisters on the skin.

The rash usually appears in hot, humid weather. But it can also happen in cooler weather if a person is wearing too many clothes, is in the hospital, or is lying in bed for long periods.

## Types of Miliaria

There are different types of miliaria. They depend on how deep the sweat gets trapped in the skin.

### Miliaria Crystallina
- Sweat gets trapped just under the top layer of skin.
- It causes clear, tiny blisters that look like beads of water.
- These blisters break easily with light touch.
- The skin does not itch or feel sore.

### Miliaria Rubra (Prickly Heat)
- Sweat gets trapped in the middle layer of skin.
- It causes small, red, itchy bumps.
- The bumps feel prickly or stinging.
- This is the most common type of heat rash.

### Miliaria Pustulosa
- This is like miliaria rubra.
- But instead of red bumps, it causes small pus-filled bumps.
- It can look like tiny pimples.

### Miliaria Profunda
- Sweat gets trapped deep in the skin.
- It causes larger, firm bumps.
- These bumps are deeper in the skin than those in miliaria rubra.
- They can be painful.

## How Is Miliaria Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose miliaria by looking at the skin. They check the rash and ask about recent conditions.

For example:
- Was the person in a hot room?
- Were they wearing tight or heavy clothes?
- Were they lying in bed for a long time?

The rash often appears in areas where sweat builds up, like the neck, chest, or back.

## How Is Miliaria Treated?

The best way to treat miliaria is to keep the skin cool and dry.

### Steps to Help the Skin Heal
- Stay in a cool, air-conditioned room if possible.
- Wear loose, light clothing made of natural fabrics like cotton.
- Avoid thick creams or ointments that block the skin.
- Do not cover the skin with tight bandages or plastic wrap.

### For the Rash Itself
- Use a mild corticosteroid cream or lotion on the rash.
- Some people find relief when a small amount of menthol is added to the cream.
- Apply the cream only to the affected areas.
- Do not use corticosteroid creams for long periods without talking to a doctor.

### When to See a Doctor
- If the rash does not improve after a few days.
- If the skin becomes very sore, swollen, or starts to ooze.
- If you have a fever or feel unwell.

Miliaria usually goes away once the skin cools down and stays dry. Prevention is the best approach. Keep cool, wear loose clothes, and avoid sweating too much.

# Lymphedema

Lymphedema is swelling in a part of the body. It happens when fluid builds up in the tissues.

## What Is Lymph?

Lymph is a clear fluid that comes from the blood. It carries waste, proteins, and white blood cells. This fluid moves through a network of tubes called lymphatic vessels.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped parts of the body’s defense system. They are found in the neck, under the arms, and in the groin. They filter out harmful things like germs and cancer cells from the lymph fluid.

The lymphatic system helps the body fight infection and keep fluid levels balanced.

## What Causes Lymphedema?

Lymphedema happens when the lymphatic system cannot drain fluid properly. This causes fluid to build up and swell in the arms or legs.

There are two main types:

- **Primary lymphedema**: A problem from birth. The lymph vessels are not fully developed.
- **Secondary lymphedema**: Caused by damage to the lymph system later in life.

### Primary Lymphedema

This type is rare. It happens when a person is born with too few lymph vessels. These vessels can’t handle the amount of fluid they need to move.

It usually affects the legs. It rarely affects the arms.

The swelling may start at birth, but more often it shows up later in life. As the body grows and makes more fluid, the few lymph vessels can’t keep up.

The first sign is often puffiness in the foot. Shoes may feel tight at the end of the day. The foot may leave deep marks from the shoe.

In early stages, the swelling goes down when the leg is raised. Over time, the swelling gets worse. It does not go away completely, even after resting overnight.

### Types of Primary Lymphedema

| Type | When Swelling Starts | Notes |
|------|------------------------|-------|
| Congenital lymphedema | Before age 2 | A form called Milroy disease can also cause yellow skin and eyes, and diarrhea. |
| Lymphedema praecox | Between ages 2 and 35 | Often starts when a girl begins her period. A form called Meige disease can also cause extra eyelashes, a cleft palate, and swelling in the legs, arms, and face. |
| Lymphedema tarda | After age 35 | Some people with this type have family members who also have it. |

### Secondary Lymphedema

This is the most common type. It happens after injury or damage to the lymph system.

Common causes:
- Surgery that removes lymph nodes (especially for cancer)
- Radiation therapy
- Infections that scar the lymph vessels

For example, after breast cancer surgery, the arm on the same side may swell if lymph nodes under the arm are removed.

In rare cases, a tropical parasite called *Filaria* causes infection. This can scar the lymph vessels and lead to swelling.

In secondary lymphedema, the skin looks normal but is puffy. Pressing the skin does not leave a deep dent, unlike swelling from poor blood flow.

In severe cases, especially from *Filaria* infection, the limb can become very large. The skin becomes thick and wrinkled, like elephant skin. This is called **elephantiasis**.

## How Is Lymphedema Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose lymphedema based on symptoms.

Sometimes, imaging tests like CT scans or MRI scans are used. These help find where the blockage is.

In areas where *Filaria* infection is common, special tests may be needed to check for the parasite.

## How Is Lymphedema Treated?

There is no cure for lymphedema. But treatment can help reduce swelling and prevent it from getting worse.

### Common Treatments

- **Manual lymphatic drainage**: A therapist gently massages the limb to move fluid out.
- **Elevating the limb**: Lifting the arm or leg helps fluid drain.
- **Limb exercises**: Gentle movement helps the fluid move.
- **Compression bandages or stockings**: These apply pressure to help prevent fluid buildup.
- **Pneumatic compression devices**: These are sleeves or stockings that inflate and deflate to push fluid out.

For mild cases:
- Massage and elevation can help.
- Wearing compression stockings during the day can reduce swelling.

For more severe cases:
- People may use pneumatic compression devices every day for several hours.
- Once swelling goes down, they must wear special elastic stockings every day — from morning until bedtime.
- These stockings press hardest at the ankle and less at the top. This helps keep fluid from building up.

For arm swelling:
- Pneumatic sleeves work like stockings.
- Elastic sleeves are also available.

### Surgery

In some cases, surgery may help:
- Remove extra tissue under the skin.
- Create new pathways for lymph fluid to drain.

### How to Prevent Worsening

To keep symptoms from getting worse:
- Avoid heat (like hot baths or saunas).
- Avoid very intense exercise.
- Do not wear tight clothes or jewelry on the affected arm or leg.
- Keep the skin and nails clean and well cared for to prevent infection.
- Avoid medical procedures like blood draws, vaccines, blood pressure checks, or IVs in the affected arm.

These steps can help protect the limb and reduce the risk of serious problems.

# Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1)

Neurofibromatosis type 1 is a long-term health condition. It affects the nerves and skin.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Some people with NF1 have mild symptoms. Others have more serious problems.

Symptoms can appear at birth or in early childhood. Some show up later in life.

Common signs include:

- Light brown patches on the skin. These are called café-au-lait spots. They may be harder to see on brown or black skin.
- Extra freckles in the armpits or around the tops of the legs.
- Small lumps on or under the skin. These are called neurofibromas. They can be painful or itchy. They often appear during the teenage years or early twenties.
- Small yellow-brown spots on the colored part of the eye. These do not usually affect vision.
- Eye problems. These can include a squint, poor vision, or a bulging eye. A bulging eye can cause headaches or make you feel sick.
- A large head size and shorter than average height.
- Learning difficulties.

Your symptoms may change over time. Always tell your doctor about any new or changing symptoms.

## What Causes NF1?

NF1 is caused by a change in a gene. Genes are parts of your body that help control how it works.

Sometimes a parent with NF1 passes the changed gene to their child. This means the child will also have NF1.

But sometimes a child is born with NF1 even if neither parent has it.

If you have NF1, there is a 1 in 2 chance (50%) that you will pass the changed gene to each child you have.

## When to See a Doctor

See your GP if you think you or your child might have NF1.

Get urgent help if you or your child:

- Have ongoing or worsening headaches.
- Keep feeling sick or are actually sick.
- Have blurry vision or lose vision.

Use the 111 online service or call 111. Call 111 for children under 5 years old.

## How Is NF1 Treated?

There is no cure for NF1. But treatments can help manage symptoms and prevent problems.

You will work with a team of healthcare professionals. This may include:

- A brain doctor (neurologist).
- An eye doctor (ophthalmologist).
- A skin doctor (dermatologist).
- A doctor who treats children (paediatrician), if you are a child.

Treatment depends on your symptoms. It may include:

- Medicine to slow down or stop tumours from growing.
- Surgery to remove tumours that could cause harm.
- Radiation treatment (radiotherapy) for small tumours or leftover parts of a larger tumour after surgery.

If your symptoms are not causing any problems, your doctor may suggest waiting to see if any issues develop before starting treatment.

## How NF1 Affects Your Life

NF1 is a lifelong condition. It usually gets worse over time. But it affects each person differently.

You or your child should have a check-up at least once a year. This helps catch any changes early.

Children with NF1 should have their eyes checked every year. Adults should have eye checks every 2 years.

Blood pressure should be checked every year.

Many children with NF1 have learning difficulties. They may need extra help at school.

Because NF1 can lead to serious health problems, it may shorten life expectancy. Your care team can talk to you about this if you want more information.

## Support and Help

You are not alone. Healthcare professionals will support you and your family.

You may also find it helpful to connect with others who have NF1 or parents of children with NF1.

### Nerve Tumours UK

This charity offers support and information for people with NF1.

- Support for adults with NF1.
- Support for teenagers with NF1.
- Support for parents of children with NF1.

**Helpline:** 0300 102 17 22  
Open on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays from 9am to 5pm.

### Childhood Tumour Trust

This group supports children, young adults up to age 30, and their families.

- What you need to know about NF1.
- How to help your child.
- How to get support.

You can find more information and help through their website or by contacting them directly.

# Sialadenitis

Sialadenitis is an infection in a salivary gland. It is usually caused by a blockage in the gland’s tube or by not making enough saliva.  
Symptoms include swelling, pain, redness, and tenderness in the area.  
Doctors diagnose it by looking at the symptoms and doing a physical exam.  
Imaging tests like CT scans, ultrasounds, or MRIs can help find the cause if it is not clear.  
Treatment includes antibiotics.

---

## What Causes Sialadenitis?

Sialadenitis often happens when saliva flow slows down or when the tube that carries saliva gets blocked.  
It can also happen without a clear reason.  
The main salivary glands are in the cheeks (parotid), under the jaw (submandibular), and under the tongue (sublingual).

Sialadenitis is most common in the parotid gland.  
It often affects people in their 50s and 60s.  
It also affects people who are very sick and have dry mouth.  
It can happen in people with Sjögren syndrome, a condition that causes dry eyes and dry mouth.  
It may occur in teens and young adults who have anorexia.  
In children aged 1 to 18 years, a condition called juvenile recurrent parotitis can cause repeated swelling. The cause of this is not known.

The most common germ that causes this infection is *Staphylococcus aureus*.  
Other germs include streptococci, coliform bacteria, and some anaerobic bacteria.

Some people get swelling in the parotid gland after radiation treatment to the mouth or after radioactive iodine treatment for thyroid cancer.  
This swelling is not usually caused by bacteria, especially if there is no fever.

Juvenile recurrent parotitis affects children, most often between ages 4 and 6.  
It often goes away by the time they reach puberty.  
No clear cause has been found. Allergies, infections, genes, or autoimmune problems have not been proven to cause it.  
Except for mumps, this condition is the second most common cause of parotid swelling in children.

---

## Symptoms and Signs

People with sialadenitis often have fever and chills.  
They feel pain and swelling on one side of the face.  
The affected gland feels hard and tender all over.  
The skin over the gland may be red and swollen.  
If you press on the gland, pus may come out through the tube.  
This pus should be tested in a lab.  
If only one small area is swollen, it may be a pus-filled abscess.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

CT scans, ultrasounds, or MRIs can help confirm the diagnosis if the problem is not clear from the exam.  
MRI may not show a small stone blocking the tube.  
If pus comes out of the gland’s tube, it is sent to a lab for testing.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Antibiotics that work against *Staphylococcus aureus* are used first.  
Examples include dicloxacillin, a first-generation cephalosporin, or clindamycin.  
The treatment may be changed based on lab results.

More and more people are getting infections from a type of *Staphylococcus aureus* that is resistant to many antibiotics (called MRSA).  
This is especially true in older adults living in nursing homes.  
In these cases, a stronger antibiotic like vancomycin is often needed.

Rinsing the mouth with chlorhexidine 0.12% three times a day helps reduce germs in the mouth and keeps the mouth clean.

Other helpful steps include:
- Drinking plenty of fluids
- Chewing sugar-free gum or sucking on hard candy or lemon juice to make saliva flow
- Applying warm compresses to the area
- Gently massaging the gland
- Keeping good oral hygiene

If an abscess forms, it must be drained.

In rare cases, surgery may be needed for long-term or repeated infections.  
This can include removing part of the parotid gland, closing the tube that carries saliva, or removing the submandibular gland.

---

## Other Salivary Gland Infections

**Mumps** often causes swelling in the parotid gland.  
(See the table “Causes of Parotid and Other Salivary Gland Enlargement” for more details.)

People with HIV may have swelling in the parotid gland due to fluid-filled cysts in the gland or nearby lymph nodes.

**Cat-scratch disease**, caused by a bacterial infection, often affects the lymph nodes near the parotid gland.  
It can spread to the gland itself.  
The illness usually gets better on its own.  
But antibiotics may be given.  
If an abscess forms, it must be drained.

**Atypical mycobacterial infections** can spread from the tonsils or teeth to the salivary glands.  
The skin test for tuberculosis (PPD) may be negative.  
Diagnosis often requires a biopsy and lab testing of the tissue.  
Treatment is not always clear. Options include:
- Cleaning out the infected area
- Removing the infected tissue completely
- Using anti-tuberculosis medicines (rarely needed)

Salivary glands can also be affected by:
- **Sarcoidosis**, a condition that causes small lumps in organs
- **IgG4-related disease**, a rare immune condition that causes swelling in tissues

Sjögren syndrome can cause swelling in the parotid or submandibular glands.

# Gastritis

Gastritis means the lining of the stomach is inflamed.

## What Is Gastritis?

- The stomach lining usually handles strong acid well.
- In gastritis, the lining becomes irritated and swollen.
- This can happen for many reasons, including infections, serious illness, injury, certain medicines, alcohol, or problems with the body’s defense system.

## Types of Gastritis

Gastritis is split into two main types:

### Erosive Gastritis
- This type causes both inflammation and damage to the stomach lining.
- It can start suddenly (acute) or slowly (chronic).
- It often affects people who are otherwise healthy.

### Nonerosive Gastritis
- This type causes changes in the stomach lining.
- The lining may thin out or change into a different kind of tissue.
- White blood cells build up in the stomach and cause swelling.
- The swelling can affect the whole stomach or just parts of it.

## Causes of Gastritis

### Erosive Gastritis
- Common causes: alcohol, serious illness, injury, and medicines like aspirin or other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
- Less common causes: Crohn disease, radiation, infections from viruses or bacteria, swallowing harmful chemicals, or injury from a tube put into the stomach.
- Even one baby aspirin a day can harm the stomach lining in some people.

### Nonerosive Gastritis
- Most often caused by a bacteria called *Helicobacter pylori*.

### Other Types
- **Infectious gastritis** (not from *H. pylori*) is rare.
- **Viral or fungal gastritis** can happen in people who are very sick for a long time or have weak immune systems. This includes people with advanced HIV, cancer, or those on immune-suppressing medicines.
- **Acute stress gastritis** happens after a sudden serious illness or injury. It can follow burns, head injuries, or major bleeding. The exact reason is not clear, but it may be due to less blood flow to the stomach, more acid, or damage to the stomach’s protective layer.
- **Radiation gastritis** can happen if radiation therapy is used on the lower left chest or upper belly. This can irritate the stomach lining.
- **Postgastrectomy gastritis** happens after part of the stomach is removed. Inflammation often occurs where the stomach was sewn back together. This may happen because blood flow to the area is reduced or because bile from the liver irritates the stomach lining.
- **Atrophic gastritis** means the stomach lining becomes very thin and loses cells that make acid and digestive enzymes. It can happen when the body’s immune system attacks the stomach lining. It can also happen in people with long-term *H. pylori* infection or after stomach surgery.
- **Eosinophilic gastritis** is when a type of white blood cell called eosinophils builds up in the stomach wall. The cause is often unknown.
- **Ménétrier disease** is a rare condition. The stomach wall grows thick and forms large folds and fluid-filled sacs. The cause is not known, but it may be linked to an immune problem or *H. pylori* infection.

## Symptoms of Gastritis

- Most people with gastritis have no symptoms.
- When symptoms do appear, they can include:
  - Pain or discomfort in the upper belly.
  - Nausea.
  - Vomiting.
- These problems are often called indigestion.

### More Severe Forms
- Nausea and vomiting can happen with erosive gastritis, radiation gastritis, and other serious types.
- Indigestion is common with erosive gastritis, radiation gastritis, postgastrectomy gastritis, and atrophic gastritis.
- Mild indigestion can also happen with acute stress gastritis.

## How Doctors Diagnose Gastritis

- Doctors often guess the diagnosis based on symptoms.
- If the cause is unclear or symptoms do not improve, the doctor may do an upper endoscopy.
- During an upper endoscopy, a thin, flexible tube with a camera is passed through the mouth into the stomach.
- The doctor can look at the stomach lining and take a small tissue sample (biopsy) if needed.

## Treatment of Gastritis

### General Treatments
- Medicines that reduce stomach acid help relieve symptoms.
- Antacids neutralize acid already in the stomach.
- Stop taking medicines that irritate the stomach, like aspirin or NSAIDs.

### Antacids
- Available over the counter as tablets, chewables, or liquids.
- Common types:
  - Aluminum hydroxide (can cause constipation).
  - Magnesium hydroxide (can cause diarrhea).
  - Calcium carbonate.
- Antacids can interfere with other medicines.
- Always check with a pharmacist or doctor before using antacids if you take other medicines.

### Acid-Reducing Medicines
- **H2 blockers** reduce acid production. They work better than antacids and are easier to use.
- **Proton pump inhibitors** are stronger and are often used when there is bleeding.
- Most people take these medicines for 8 to 12 weeks.

### Other Medicines
- **Sucralfate** coats the stomach lining and helps it heal. It also protects it from irritation.

### If Caused by *H. pylori* Infection
- Antibiotics are needed to treat the infection.
- These are usually given with acid-reducing medicines.

### For Erosive Gastritis
- Avoid medicines that harm the stomach lining.
- Use proton pump inhibitors or H2 blockers to protect the stomach.

### For Acute Stress Gastritis
- Most people get better when the serious illness, injury, or bleeding is treated.
- Some people in intensive care units may bleed heavily. This can be life-threatening.
- To prevent this, doctors often give acid-reducing medicines after surgery or to people in intensive care.
- These medicines also help treat ulcers that may form.

### For Heavy Bleeding
- Doctors may use heat to seal bleeding spots during endoscopy.
- If bleeding continues, surgery to remove part of the stomach may be needed. This is rare.

### For Other Types
- **Postgastrectomy gastritis** and **atrophic gastritis** have no cure.
- People with anemia from low vitamin B12 absorption due to atrophic gastritis must take vitamin B12 shots for life.
- **Eosinophilic gastritis** may need corticosteroids or surgery if the stomach outlet is blocked.
- **Ménétrier disease** may be cured by removing part or all of the stomach.
- There are no good medicines to treat Ménétrier disease.

# Vision Loss

## What is vision loss?

Vision loss means you can’t see as well as you used to.  
You may notice changes in how you see things.  
It can happen slowly over time or suddenly.  
It can affect one eye or both eyes.

## Common symptoms

- You can’t see clearly.  
- You have trouble reading, watching TV, or seeing people’s faces.  
- Your eyes feel uncomfortable in bright light.  
- You struggle to see at night or in dim light.  
- You see blurry, double, or flashing images.  
- You notice a dark shadow moving across your vision.  
- You have pain in one or both eyes.  
- Your eyes feel sore or painful in bright light.

Vision loss can happen at any age.  
It is more common as you get older.

## When to get help

### See an optician if:
- You think your vision has changed.  
Early check-ups can help stop your vision from getting worse.

[Find an NHS sight test]

### Call your GP or NHS 111 if:
- Your vision suddenly changes (like blurriness, double vision, or flashing lights).  
- You see a dark shadow moving across your vision.  
- You have pain in one or both eyes.  
- Your eye is red and painful.  
- Your eyes hurt or feel uncomfortable in bright light.

You can call 111 or [get help from NHS 111 online].

### Go to A&E or call 999 if:
- You suddenly can’t see from one or both eyes.  
- You have sudden, severe eye pain.

[Find your nearest A&E]

### A&E safety tips
- Do not drive to A&E.  
- Ask someone to drive you.  
- Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
- Bring your medicines with you.

## Support if you have long-term vision loss

Everyone’s experience of vision loss is different.  
If your vision loss is permanent, support is available.

You may need help with:
- Making your home safer and easier to use (like for cooking or washing).  
- Using tools that help with low vision (like magnifiers or special phones).  
- Getting around and using public transport.  
- Applying for benefits and financial help.  
- Adjusting your workplace or finding a new job.  
- Studying at school, college, or university.  
- Talking therapies like counselling or cognitive behavioural therapy.

## Registering as sight impaired

If an eye doctor says you are severely sight impaired (blind) or partially sighted, you can register with your local council.

This can help you:
- Get support and services in your area.  
- Apply for benefits.

### More information:
- [RNIB: registering as sight impaired](https://www.rnib.org.uk)  
- [RNIB: criteria for certification](https://www.rnib.org.uk)  
- [GOV.UK: blind person's allowance eligibility](https://www.gov.uk)

## Royal National Institute of Blind People (RNIB)

RNIB is a national charity that helps people with vision loss.

- Website: [www.rnib.org.uk](https://www.rnib.org.uk)  
- Helpline: 0303 123 9999  
- [RNIB: practical and emotional support](https://www.rnib.org.uk)  
- [RNIB: coming to terms with sight loss](https://www.rnib.org.uk)

## Vision loss in children

Vision loss in children is rare.  
Most problems are found during routine eye checks.  
Talk to your health visitor or GP if you are worried about your child’s eyes.

## Causes of vision loss

Many things can cause vision loss.  
Some causes can be treated.  
Some conditions lead to permanent vision loss.

Your symptoms can help doctors guess what might be causing the problem.

## Treatments for vision loss

Treatment depends on what is causing your vision loss.

If your optician or GP thinks you have a medical condition, you will be sent to an eye specialist (ophthalmologist).

The eye specialist will explain what treatments are possible.  
These may include medicines or surgery.  
Some conditions cannot be treated.  
But treatments may still help stop your vision from getting worse.

If you have long-term vision loss, your doctor should refer you to local support services.  
These services can help you live well with your vision loss.

# Brain and Spinal Cord Tumors in Children

Brain and spinal cord tumors are the most common solid cancers in children under 15 years old.  
They are also the top cause of cancer-related deaths in children.  

Most children with these tumors do not have a clear cause.  
But two known risk factors are:  
- Exposure to high levels of radiation to the head  
- Certain inherited genetic conditions, such as neurofibromatosis  

## Most Common Types of Tumors

The most common brain and spinal cord tumors in children are:

- Astrocytomas  
- Medulloblastomas  
- Ependymomas  

These are listed in order of how often they occur.

## Signs and Symptoms

Many symptoms happen because pressure builds up inside the skull.  
This pressure can come from fluid buildup in the brain, called hydrocephalus.  

Common signs include:  
- Headaches  
- Feeling sick to your stomach  
- Vomiting  
- Being more irritable than usual  
- Feeling very tired or sleepy  
- Changes in mood or behavior  
- Trouble walking or keeping balance  

Other symptoms depend on where the tumor is.  
For example, some children may lose vision or have seizures.

## How Doctors Diagnose These Tumors

Doctors use two main tests to find and confirm a brain or spinal cord tumor:

1. **MRI scan**  
   - This is the best test for seeing brain and spinal cord tumors.  
   - It shows detailed pictures of the brain and spine.  
   - It can find tumors in hard-to-see areas like the back of the brain or around the spinal cord.  
   - CT scans may be used, but they are not as clear or helpful.

2. **Biopsy**  
   - A small sample of the tumor is taken during surgery.  
   - This helps doctors confirm the type of tumor.  
   - It also helps them learn how aggressive the tumor is.  
   - The World Health Organization has a system that uses both tissue and genetic details to classify tumors.

After the diagnosis is clear, doctors check if the tumor has spread.  
This is called staging.  
Staging includes:  
- An MRI of the whole spine  
- A spinal tap to check the fluid around the brain and spinal cord  
- Another MRI after surgery to see if any tumor remains  

Doctors also do a risk assessment.  
This looks at:  
- The child’s age  
- How much tumor is left after surgery  
- Genetic features of the tumor  
- Whether the cancer has spread  

## How These Tumors Are Treated

Treatment depends on the type, stage, and risk level of the tumor.  
Most children get a combination of treatments.

The main options are:

- Surgery to remove as much of the tumor as possible  
- Radiation therapy  
- Chemotherapy  
- Targeted therapy (drugs that attack specific parts of the cancer cells)  
- A mix of these treatments  

After surgery, most children need more treatment.  
This may include radiation, chemotherapy, or targeted therapy.

All children with a brain or spinal cord tumor should be considered for a clinical trial.  
These trials test new treatments and may offer better results.

Treating these tumors requires a team of specialists.  
This team includes:  
- Pediatric oncologists  
- Pediatric neuro-oncologists  
- Pediatric neurosurgeons  
- Neuropathologists  
- Neuroradiologists  
- Radiation oncologists  

All team members must have experience treating children with brain and spinal cord tumors.  
Radiation therapy for these tumors is complex.  
Children should go to a center with special experience in this type of treatment if possible.
