# Chest Tube Insertion

A chest tube insertion is a medical procedure. It is also called tube thoracostomy.

The doctor puts a tube into the space between the lung and the chest wall. This space is called the pleural space.

The tube helps drain air if the lung has collapsed. A collapsed lung is called pneumothorax.

The tube can also drain fluid from the pleural space. This fluid buildup is called pleural effusion. It is used when fluid builds up over time and cannot be removed all at once.

In some cases, this procedure is an emergency. It can save a person’s life.

The person stays awake during the procedure. But they may get a medicine to help them relax.

The doctor numbs the area between two ribs. Then they make a small cut. The tube is placed through the cut.

The tube is connected to a suction device. This helps pull out air or fluid.

After the tube is in place, a chest x-ray is usually done. This checks that the tube is in the right spot.

Serious problems are rare. But they can happen. Possible problems include:

- Pain in the chest  
- A hole in the lung or the diaphragm  
- Air trapped under the skin  
- Infection

If a large amount of fluid has been in the chest for weeks or months, removing it too fast can cause fluid to build up in the lung. This is called pulmonary edema.

Sometimes the tube needs to be replaced. This happens if the tube bends, comes out of place, or gets blocked by a blood clot.

# Hypothermia

Hypothermia means your body is too cold.  
Your body temperature drops below 35 degrees Celsius.  
This can happen in cold weather or after falling into cold water.

## Signs of Hypothermia

You or someone else may have hypothermia if you notice:

- Shivering  
- Skin that feels cold and looks pale, grey, or blue  
- Trouble speaking clearly  
- Slow breathing  
- Feeling very tired or confused  

A baby with hypothermia may:

- Feel cold to the touch  
- Be limp or floppy  
- Be unusually quiet and sleepy  
- Not want to feed  

## What to Do While Waiting for Help

If you think someone has hypothermia, act quickly.

### Do These Things:

- Move the person indoors or to a sheltered place as fast as you can.  
- Take off any wet clothes.  
- Wrap them in a blanket, sleeping bag, or dry towel.  
- Cover their head with a hat or scarf.  
- Give them a warm, non-alcoholic drink if they are awake and able to swallow.  
- Offer a small amount of sugary food, like chocolate.  
- Keep talking to them to help them stay awake.  
- Stay with them until help arrives.  

### Do Not Do These Things:

- Do not use a hot bath, hot water bottle, or heat lamp.  
- Do not rub their arms, legs, feet, or hands.  
- Do not give them alcohol to drink.  

These actions can make the situation worse.

## Hospital Treatment

If you go to hospital for hypothermia, you will get care right away.

- Doctors will check your heart rate.  
- You may get oxygen through a mask to help you breathe.  
- You may get warm fluids through a tube in your vein.  
- If your condition is serious, you may need care in intensive care.  

## What Causes Hypothermia?

Hypothermia happens when your body loses heat faster than it can make it.  
You can get it if:

- You are not wearing enough warm clothes in cold weather  
- You stay outside in the cold for too long  
- You fall into cold water  
- You wear wet clothes and get cold  
- You live in a cold home – older people living alone are at higher risk  

## When to Get Help

Go to A&E or call 999 if:

- You think you or your child has hypothermia  

### Important Safety Tips

- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you.  
- If you can’t get a ride, call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
- Bring your regular medicines with you when you go to hospital.

# Broken Wrist (Distal Radius Fracture)

A broken wrist often happens when someone falls onto an outstretched hand.

(See also: Overview of Broken Bones.)

Most broken wrists happen when the wrist bends backward. This type of break is called a Colles fracture. It is common, especially in older adults. Often, the small bone on the pinky side of the wrist (ulnar styloid) breaks too. Less often, the wrist bends forward during the fall. This is called a Smith fracture.

## What You Might Feel or See

A broken wrist can cause:
- Swelling
- A visible change in shape (deformity)
- Pain and tenderness

Swelling or the change in shape can press on a nerve in the wrist called the median nerve. If this nerve is hurt, you may feel numbness in the tip of your second finger. You may also have trouble moving your thumb to touch your little finger.

If the fall was very hard, the wrist bone (radius) can be pushed into itself. This makes the bone shorter.

Other problems can happen later, such as:
- Stiffness in the wrist
- A permanent change in the shape of the wrist
- Ongoing pain
- Arthritis in the wrist
- A rare condition called complex regional pain syndrome

These problems are more likely if the break goes into the wrist joint or if the bone is badly misaligned.

## How Doctors Diagnose a Broken Wrist

Doctors will take two X-rays:
- One from front to back
- One from side to side

These X-rays usually show the break. In some cases, a CT scan is needed to see if the joint is damaged.

Signs of a broken wrist on X-ray may include:
- The wrist bone bent backward
- A shape like a silver fork or dinner fork

## How a Broken Wrist Is Treated

The goal is to realign the bone and keep it still while it heals.

### Step 1: Try to Realign the Bone Without Surgery
Doctors often try to move the bone back into place without surgery. This is called closed reduction.

- Pain is managed in the emergency room with medicine or a numbing injection into the injured area.
- After the bone is realigned, the wrist is held still with a splint.

### Step 2: Use a Splint
- A volar splint is used. It goes on the palm side of the wrist.
- A sugar tong splint may also be used. It wraps around the wrist and forearm.

The wrist is kept in a position where the hand is slightly bent upward (15 to 30 degrees).

### Step 3: Surgery May Be Needed If:
- The joint is damaged or the break goes into the joint.
- The bone is too short after the injury.
- Closed reduction does not work.

Surgery is called open reduction with internal fixation (ORIF). It means the bone is fixed in place with metal plates, screws, or rods.

### How to Help Healing at Home
- Move your fingers every day.
- Move your elbow and shoulder every day, unless they are also in a splint.
- Keep your hand raised above heart level to reduce swelling.

## Key Facts

- Most broken wrists happen when the wrist bends backward. This is called a Colles fracture. It is common in older people.
- A broken wrist can cause swelling or a change in shape. This can hurt the median nerve, leading to numbness or weak thumb movement.
- X-rays from front to back and side to side usually show the break. Sometimes a CT scan is needed to see joint damage.
- Try to realign the bone without surgery and use a splint. If that does not work, or if the joint is damaged or the bone is too short, surgery may be needed.

# Sunburn

Sunburn happens when your skin gets too much ultraviolet light in a short time.

- Too much ultraviolet light causes sunburn.
- Sunburn makes your skin red, painful, and sometimes causes blisters.
- It can also cause fever, chills, and feeling weak.
- You can avoid sunburn by staying out of strong sunlight and using sunscreen.
- Cold water, moisturizers, and certain pain relievers can help ease the pain while your skin heals.

(See also: Overview of Sunlight and Skin Damage)

The amount of sun you need to get sunburned depends on your skin color and how well your skin makes pigment. It also depends on how strong the sun is on that day.

Sunburn makes your skin red and sore. Severe sunburn can cause swelling and blisters. Symptoms can start as soon as one hour after being in the sun. They usually get worse over the next one to three days. Most often, they peak between 12 and 24 hours after exposure. Some people with severe sunburn get a fever, chills, and feel very weak. In rare cases, they may go into shock. Shock means very low blood pressure, fainting, and extreme tiredness.

## Mild Sunburn

This photo shows red skin on the back and arms of a person with mild sunburn.

SINCLAIR STAMMERS/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY

## Severe Sunburn

Image

DR P. MARAZZI/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY

A few days after sunburn, people with fair skin may notice peeling skin. This peeling area often itches. The new skin underneath is very sensitive to sunlight for several weeks. Sunburned skin, especially peeling skin, can get infected. Dark spots called lentigines may appear. People who had bad sunburns as children are more likely to get skin cancer later in life—even if they do not get much sun after that.

### Did You Know...

- You can get sunburned on cloudy days. Light clouds do not block ultraviolet light.
- Even water-resistant sunscreen must be reapplied after swimming or sweating.

## How to Treat Sunburn

- Use cold compresses or cool water on the skin.
- Apply moisturizers that do not have perfume or numbing agents.
- Take nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen to reduce pain and swelling.
- Avoid petroleum jelly on severe sunburns.
- Do not use steroid creams on the skin. They do not work better than cool compresses.
- Avoid ointments with numbing agents like benzocaine or diphenhydramine. They can cause allergic reactions.
- Only use antibiotic creams if blisters are very bad.
- Most blisters break on their own. Do not pop them.
- Sunburn rarely gets infected. But if it does, healing takes longer.
- A doctor can check for infection and prescribe medicine if needed.

Your skin starts healing within a few days. Full healing can take weeks. After peeling, the new skin is thin and very sensitive to sunlight. Protect it for several weeks.

## How to Prevent Sunburn

- Stay out of strong sunlight.
- Wear protective clothing.
- Use sunscreen.

The best way to protect your skin is to avoid strong sunlight. Try not to be in bright sun around midday. This advice applies to everyone, even those with dark skin. The sun is less strong before 10 AM and after 4 PM.

If you must be in the sun:
- Find shade as soon as possible.
- Wear clothes that block UV rays.
- Use sunscreen.
- Wear a wide-brimmed hat.
- Wear sunglasses that protect against UV light.

Some materials block UV light. These include:
- Clothing
- Ordinary window glass
- Smoke
- Smog

But water does not block UV light well. UVA and UVB rays can go through a foot of clear water. Clouds and fog also do not block UV light. You can still get sunburned on a cloudy or foggy day.

Snow, water, and sand reflect sunlight. This means more UV light hits your skin. You burn faster at high altitudes. The air is thinner there, so more UV light reaches the ground. You also burn faster near the equator.

Sunlight helps your body make vitamin D. But most experts say it is safer to get vitamin D from food or supplements. Just 5 to 15 minutes of sun on your arms a few times a week is enough for most people.

Wear protective clothing to reduce sun damage. Tight-weave fabrics block more UV light than loose-weave ones. Special clothing with high sun protection is sold. It has a label with UPF and a number. The number shows how well it blocks UV light—just like sunscreen.

A wide-brimmed hat protects your face, ears, and neck. But you still need to use sunscreen on those areas.

Wear UV-protective, wrap-around sunglasses to protect your eyes and eyelids.

Apply sunscreen before going into strong sunlight. Sunscreen is a cream or lotion that blocks UV light. Older sunscreens only blocked UVB. Most new ones block both UVA and UVB.

Sunscreens come in many forms:
- Creams
- Lotions
- Gels
- Foams
- Sprays
- Powders
- Sticks

Self-tanning products do not protect your skin from UV light.

### Chemical Sunscreens

These contain ingredients that absorb UV light.  
- Cinnamates, salicylates, and PABA derivatives block UVB.  
- Benzophenones block both UVA and UVB.  
- Avobenzone and ecamsule block UVA.

### Barrier or Mineral Sunscreens

These contain zinc oxide or titanium dioxide. They reflect UV light and keep it from reaching your skin.  
- These used to be thick and white.  
- Now they are lighter and more transparent.  
- They still block almost all sunlight.  
- They can be mixed with chemical sunscreens for extra protection.  
- Some makeup also has zinc oxide or titanium dioxide.

All chemical sunscreen ingredients are absorbed into the body to some degree. Most are safe. But some may cause side effects. Experts are still studying them.

Mineral sunscreens use large particles. These do not get absorbed and are safe.  
Newer versions use tiny particles called nanoparticles. These may be absorbed. But they are thought to be safe. Still, they are being studied. If you are worried about nanoparticles, choose "non-nano" mineral sunscreens.

In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration rates sunscreens by SPF.  
- SPF 2 to 14: Low protection  
- SPF 15 to 29: Good protection  
- SPF 30 and above: Maximum protection

Sunscreens labeled "broad spectrum" protect against both sunburn and skin aging. They also lower your risk of skin cancer. These must have an SPF of 15 or higher.

Note: SPF only measures protection against UVB. There is no rating for UVA protection.

### For the best protection:
- Use a broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher.
- Use one ounce (about 30 milliliters) to cover your whole body.

Sunscreens can fail if:
- You do not use enough.
- You apply it too late. Apply it 30 minutes before going out in the sun.
- You do not reapply after swimming, sweating, or every 2 hours.
- Most people use less than half the amount needed.

### Did You Know...

One ounce of sunscreen (about the size of a shot glass) is needed to cover the whole body. Most people use less than half that amount.

Some people have allergic reactions to sunscreen.  
- You might react after applying it.  
- Or you might react after applying it and then going in the sun. This is called a photoallergic reaction.  
- A dermatologist can test for this if the cause is unclear.

## Are Tans Healthy?

No. A tan is not a sign of good health. Tanning has no health benefits. It is actually dangerous.

Any exposure to UVA or UVB light can harm your skin. Long-term sun exposure damages your skin and raises your risk of skin cancer. Tanning beds are just as harmful. The UVA light in them causes the same damage as UVB—wrinkles, uneven skin color, and skin cancer.

There is no safe tan.

### Self-Tanning Lotions

These do not tan your skin. They stain it. They give you a tanned look without UV exposure. So they are safe.

But they do not protect your skin from the sun. You still need to use sunscreen when in the sun.

Results vary. They depend on your skin type, the product used, and how you apply it.

### Supplements That Help

- *Polypodium leucotomos* (a tropical fern extract)
- Nicotinamide (a form of vitamin B3)

These are taken by mouth. They offer some protection from sun damage. But they are not a substitute for sunscreen, clothing, or shade.

# Bursitis

Bursitis is when a small fluid-filled sac near a joint becomes inflamed. This causes pain, swelling, and warmth in the joint area.

## Symptoms of Bursitis

You may have bursitis if one of your joints is:

- Painful – often a dull, aching pain  
- Tender to touch  
- Warmer than the skin around it  
- Swollen  
- More painful when you move it or press on it  
- Red – this can be harder to see on brown or black skin  

Bursitis can happen in any joint. It is most common in the shoulders, hips, elbows, or knees.

## How to Treat Bursitis at Home

You can help ease bursitis by doing these things:

- Rest the joint. Avoid moving it too much.  
- Do not do activities that press on the joint.  
- Use ice. Put an ice pack (or a bag of frozen peas) wrapped in a tea towel on the area for about 10 minutes.  
- Repeat every few hours during the day.  
- Take painkillers like paracetamol or ibuprofen to help with pain.  
- Use extra cushions when you sleep. This can protect and support the joint.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:

- Your symptoms do not get better after 1 to 2 weeks of home care  
- You have a high temperature or feel hot and shivery  
- You cannot move the joint at all  
- You have very sharp or shooting pain in the joint  

## Medical Treatments for Bursitis

Your doctor may suggest:

- Antibiotics – if the bursitis is caused by an infection. You will need to take them for at least 7 days.  
- A steroid injection into the joint – to reduce swelling. This is not used if the bursitis is caused by an infection.  
- A needle to drain fluid from the joint – to ease pain and swelling.  

In rare cases, surgery may be needed to drain or remove the inflamed bursa. This is only done if the bursitis is very bad or keeps coming back.

## How to Prevent Bursitis from Coming Back

Do these things to help stop bursitis from returning:

- Keep a healthy weight. Extra weight puts more pressure on your joints.  
- Clean any cuts on your joints right away. This helps prevent infection.  
- Warm up before you exercise or play sports.  
- Use padding when you put pressure on joints. For example, use knee pads when kneeling.  
- Take breaks if you do tasks that press on a joint, like kneeling for long periods.  

Avoid these things:

- Do not hit or bang your joints.  

## Self-Referral for Treatment

You may be able to get help for bursitis without seeing a doctor first. You can refer yourself directly to some services.

To find out what services are available near you:

- Ask the staff at your GP surgery  
- Check your GP surgery’s website  
- Contact your local integrated care board – find your local ICB online  
- Search online for “NHS treatment for bursitis near me”

# What Is Pelvic Organ Prolapse?

Pelvic organ prolapse happens when the muscles, tissues, and ligaments that hold your pelvic organs in place become weak or stretched. This can cause organs to drop down into the vagina. It is similar to a hernia.

This condition is common among women. It is hard to know exactly how many women have it. One study of 8,000 women found that 8.3% had symptoms of prolapse.

Treatment depends on your symptoms. If you do not have symptoms, you may not need treatment.

---

## What Parts Can Be Affected?

Pelvic organ prolapse can affect different parts of the female pelvis. These include:

- The front wall of the vagina (anterior wall)
- The back wall of the vagina (posterior wall)
- The top of the vagina (apical area)
- The uterus (uterine prolapse)

When the vaginal wall weakens, nearby organs can push into the vagina. Depending on which organ is involved, doctors may use different names:

- Cystocele: when the bladder pushes into the front of the vagina
- Urethrocele: when the urethra pushes into the front of the vagina
- Enterocele: when the small intestine pushes into the upper part of the vagina
- Rectocele: when the rectum pushes into the back of the vagina

When both the front and back walls of the vagina drop down and the top of the vagina also falls, this is called procidentia. Most women have more than one area affected.

---

## What Increases the Risk of Prolapse?

Certain things make it more likely that you will develop pelvic organ prolapse. These include:

- Having had children
- A long second stage of labor
- Giving birth through the vagina
- Using forceps or a vacuum during delivery
- Delivering a large baby
- Being overweight or obese
- Getting older
- Having had pelvic surgery
- Constant straining from constipation
- Lifting heavy objects often
- Long-term lung problems like chronic cough

Less common causes include nerve problems in the lower back and certain connective tissue disorders.

---

## How Is Prolapse Measured?

Doctors use a system called POP-Q to measure how severe the prolapse is. This system is widely used because it is clear and reliable.

The stages are:

- Stage 0: No prolapse. All organs are in their normal position.
- Stage I: The lowest part of the prolapse is more than 1 centimeter above the opening of the vagina.
- Stage II: The lowest part of the prolapse is between 1 centimeter above and 1 centimeter below the opening of the vagina.
- Stage III: The lowest part of the prolapse is more than 1 centimeter below the opening but not more than 2 centimeters shorter than the full length of the vagina.
- Stage IV: The organ has completely turned inside out and is outside the body.

This system uses clear, fixed points in the body. This makes it easy for doctors to agree on the stage.

The older Baden-Walker system is no longer used. It was not precise and gave different results when different doctors used it.

# Amebiasis

Amebiasis is an infection caused by a tiny parasite called *Entamoeba histolytica*. This parasite lives in the large intestine. In some cases, it can spread to the liver or other organs.

## How Amebiasis Spreads

- The parasite spreads when people swallow cysts (a dormant form of the parasite).
- Cysts can pass from one person to another through contact with feces.
- This can happen through oral-anal contact during sex.
- It can also happen by eating food or drinking water that has been contaminated with feces.
- In places with poor sanitation, food can become dirty if it is grown in soil fertilized with human waste.
- Fruits and vegetables can also be contaminated if they are washed in dirty water.
- People who are not clean, such as those who are incontinent or do not wash their hands well, can spread the parasite.
- This can happen in day care centers or mental health facilities, even in places with good sanitation.

## What the Parasite Looks Like

- The parasite has two forms:
  - A dormant form called a cyst.
  - An active form called a trophozoite.

Other types of amebas can infect the brain or the eye, but they do not cause intestinal infections.

## Symptoms of Amebiasis

Most people with amebiasis have no symptoms. But they can still spread the parasite.

If symptoms do appear, they usually start 1 to 3 weeks after infection. They may include:

- Diarrhea, sometimes with blood in the stool
- Belly cramps
- Weight loss
- Fever
- A tender belly when touched
- Severe diarrhea with mucus and blood (called dysentery)
- High fever and strong belly pain
- Dehydration from losing too much fluid
- Weakness and poor health over time
- Anemia (low red blood cells)

In rare cases, a lump (called an ameboma) can form in the large intestine.

If the parasite spreads to the liver, it can cause a liver abscess. Symptoms include:

- Fever
- Sweating
- Chills
- Weakness
- Nausea and vomiting
- Pain or discomfort in the upper right side of the belly

In very rare cases, the parasite can spread to the lungs, brain, or skin. Skin infections can happen around the buttocks, genitals, or wounds from surgery or injury.

## How Doctors Diagnose Amebiasis

Doctors use several tests to find out if someone has amebiasis.

- They test stool samples for signs of the parasite.
- The best tests look for a protein made by the parasite or for its genetic material.
- These tests are more accurate than looking at stool under a microscope.
- Microscopic tests often miss the parasite and cannot tell *Entamoeba histolytica* from other similar amebas that do not cause disease.
- If the parasite is in the liver, it may not show up in stool. In this case, doctors use imaging tests like ultrasound, CT scan, or MRI to look for a liver abscess.
- Blood tests can check for antibodies. These are proteins made by the body to fight the parasite.
- If a person gets better after taking medicine for amebiasis, doctors likely have the right diagnosis.

## How Amebiasis Is Treated

Treatment has two steps.

**Step 1: Kill the active parasites**
- Doctors give a medicine that kills the active form of the parasite.
- These medicines include tinidazole, metronidazole, secnidazole, or ornidazole.
- Nitazoxanide is another option being studied.
- Do not drink alcohol while taking these medicines or for several days after stopping them. Alcohol can cause nausea, vomiting, flushing, and headaches.

**Step 2: Kill the dormant cysts**
- The medicines above do not kill all the cysts in the intestine.
- A second medicine is needed to kill the remaining cysts and prevent the infection from coming back.
- This second medicine can be iodoquinol, paromomycin, or diloxanide furoate.
- Paromomycin is safe to use during pregnancy.
- Diloxanide furoate is not sold in stores in the United States. It can be made by some special pharmacies.

If someone is dehydrated, they are given fluids to replace lost water.

## How to Prevent Amebiasis

To lower your risk:

- Wash your hands well with soap and water, especially after using the toilet and before eating.
- Avoid sexual contact that can lead to fecal exposure.
- When traveling to areas with poor sanitation:
  - Do not eat raw foods like salads or uncooked vegetables.
  - Do not drink tap water or eat ice.
  - Boil water to kill the parasite.
  - Use a filter with a pore size of 0.1 or 0.4 microns to remove the parasite and other germs.
  - Add iodine or chlorine to water, but know that this may not work well if the water is cloudy or very cold.

Improving sanitation in areas where amebiasis is common is key to stopping the spread.

## More Information

The following resources may help:

- Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC): Yellow Book – Amebiasis
- CDC: Yellow Book – Food & Water Precautions
- CDC: Parasites – Amebiasis – General Information

# Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD)

## What is NAFLD?

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease means your liver has extra fat in it.  
This happens even if you do not drink much alcohol.  
Most people with NAFLD do not have any symptoms.  
Some people feel very tired or have pain under the right side of their ribs.

## Who is at risk?

You are more likely to get NAFLD if you:  
- Are overweight, especially if you have a large waist  
- Eat unhealthy foods  
- Do not get enough physical activity  
- Have type 2 diabetes  
- Have polycystic ovary syndrome  
- Have high blood pressure or high cholesterol  
- Are over 50 years old  

NAFLD is very common.  
Many people have it without knowing.

## How is NAFLD measured?

NAFLD has four stages.  
The stages show how much damage there is to your liver.  
Most people only have the first stage.  
This stage usually causes no problems.  
A few people go on to later stages with more serious liver damage.  
But healthy lifestyle changes can stop this from happening.

## Symptoms

Most people with NAFLD do not feel sick.  
It is often found during tests for something else.  
Some people have:  
- Feeling very tired  
- Feeling unwell overall  
- Pain or discomfort in the tummy under the right side of the ribs  

## When to see a doctor

See your GP if you:  
- Think you might have NAFLD  
- Think you are at higher risk of getting NAFLD  

## Treatment from your doctor or specialist

If you have NAFLD, you may not need medicine.  
Most people only need to make healthy lifestyle changes.  
You should have a check-up at least once a year.  
You may need tests every 2 to 3 years to check your liver.

If your liver is damaged (this is called fibrosis or cirrhosis), you will need to see a liver specialist.  
The specialist may prescribe medicine such as pioglitazone or vitamin E.  
In very severe cases, you may need a liver transplant.

If you have obesity, your doctor may suggest weight-loss treatments.  
These can include medicines or surgery.

## How you can help yourself

You can treat NAFLD or stop it from getting worse by making healthy changes.  
These changes can also lower your risk of other health problems like heart disease, kidney disease, high blood pressure, and type 2 diabetes.

### Do these things:

- Eat a healthy, balanced diet  
- Exercise regularly – aim for at least 150 minutes of activity each week  
- Lose weight if you are overweight  

### Avoid these things:

- Do not drink too much alcohol – limit yourself to no more than 14 units a week  
- Do not smoke  

## Support and information

Your GP or liver specialist will support you.  
There are also national charities that offer help and advice.

### British Liver Trust

This charity gives information and support to people with liver disease.  
- Website: [britishlivertrust.org.uk](https://www.britishlivertrust.org.uk)  
- Helpline: 0800 652 7330  
- Support groups for people with liver conditions  
- Advice on living with a liver condition  
- Tips on treating NAFLD with healthy eating and exercise

# Double Vision

Double vision means you see two images of one object.  
It can happen in one eye or both eyes.  

If double vision happens when only one eye is open, it is called **monocular double vision**.  
If it goes away when you close one eye, it is called **binocular double vision**.

---

## What Causes Double Vision?

### Monocular Double Vision (One Eye)

This happens when light does not pass straight through the eye to the back of the eye.  
It can cause more than two images.  
One image is clear. The others are blurry or dim.  

Common causes include:  
- A cataract (clouding of the eye’s lens)  
- Problems with the shape of the cornea, like keratoconus or surface damage  
- Uncorrected vision problems, especially astigmatism  
- Scarring on the cornea  
- A lens that has moved out of place  

Sometimes, people say they have double vision when they are not really experiencing it. This is called malingering.

### Binocular Double Vision (Both Eyes)

This happens when the eyes are not lined up properly.  
There are only two images, and both are clear.  

Common causes include:  
- Weakness in the nerves that control eye movement (third, fourth, or sixth cranial nerves)  
- Myasthenia gravis (a condition that causes muscle weakness)  
- Swelling or pressure in the eye area (like from thyroid disease or a tumor)

Most often, the eyes are misaligned because of a problem with the nerves that tell the eye muscles how to move.  
These nerve problems can be due to:  
- Stroke or blood vessel issues  
- Tumors or aneurysms pressing on the nerves  
- Infections or inflammation  
- Injury or trauma  
- Autoimmune diseases like myasthenia gravis or Guillain-Barré syndrome  
- Rare conditions like botulism or Wernicke encephalopathy

Pain may or may not be present, depending on the cause.

---

## Causes of Binocular Double Vision – Quick Guide

| Cause | Signs and Symptoms | How It’s Diagnosed |
|------|---------------------|--------------------|
| Stroke or blood vessel problem in the brain | Older adults, high blood pressure, diabetes, atherosclerosis | MRI scan |
| Aneurysm or tumor pressing on nerves | Sudden pain, other brain or nerve problems | Immediate CT or MRI scan |
| No clear cause (often small blood vessel issue) | Only double vision, no other symptoms | Watch and wait; eye doctor check |
| Infection or inflammation (like sinus infection) | Constant pain, fever, facial numbness, bulging eye | CT or MRI scan |
| Wernicke encephalopathy | History of heavy drinking, confusion, unsteady walking | Based on symptoms |
| Thyroid eye disease (Graves disease) | Eye pain, bulging eye, dry eyes, light sensitivity, weak eye muscles | Blood tests for thyroid function |
| Eye muscle inflammation (orbital myositis) | Pain in eye that gets worse when moving the eye, bulging eye | MRI scan |
| Eye injury (fracture or blood clot) | History of trauma, visible injury | CT or MRI scan |
| Tumor near the base of the skull or in the sinuses | Pain, bulging eye, other nerve problems | CT or MRI scan |
| Botulism | Weakness that starts in the face, trouble swallowing, dilated pupils | Blood and stool tests for toxin |
| Guillain-Barré syndrome (Miller Fisher variant) | Unsteady walking, no reflexes, eye movement issues | Spinal tap (lumbar puncture) |
| Multiple sclerosis | Fluctuating symptoms like numbness, weakness, vision problems | MRI of brain and spine |
| Myasthenia gravis | Double vision that comes and goes, droopy eyelid, muscle weakness that gets worse with use | Ice test, special nerve test, blood test |

---

## How Is Double Vision Evaluated?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms.  
They will check your eyes and nerves.  
They may order imaging tests like CT or MRI if there are warning signs.  
These signs include:  
- Sudden onset of double vision  
- Pain around the eye or head  
- Other neurological symptoms (like weakness, confusion, or trouble walking)  
- A history of stroke, diabetes, or cancer

If the double vision is mild and there are no warning signs, your doctor may wait to see if it gets better on its own.

---

## How Is Double Vision Treated?

There is no direct treatment for double vision.  
The treatment focuses on fixing the cause.  
For example:  
- Cataracts may need surgery  
- Thyroid disease needs medication  
- Nerve problems may need steroids or other treatments  
- Myasthenia gravis may need special medicine

---

## Key Points

- If you have double vision in just one eye and no other symptoms, it may go away on its own.  
- If you have warning signs like sudden pain, weakness, or confusion, you need imaging tests right away.

# Primary Cancerous Bone Tumors

Tumors that start in the bone are called primary bone tumors.  
These tumors can be noncancerous (benign) or cancerous (malignant).

When cancer is found, doctors stage it.  
Staging tells how far the cancer has spread.  
It includes how fast the cancer grows, how big it is, and whether it has spread to nearby tissues or other parts of the body.

(See also _Overview of Bone Tumors_ and _Overview of Cancer_.)

---

## Adamantinomas

Adamantinomas are rare bone cancers.  
They most often start in the shinbone (tibia).  
They usually affect young and middle-aged adults, but can happen at any age.  
They often cause pain.  
You may feel a lump under the skin.

These tumors grow slowly.  
They are low-grade cancers, so they are less likely to spread than other cancers.  
But spreading to the lungs can still happen, though it is rare.

To find out if someone has an adamantinoma, doctors take x-rays.  
They also take a small sample of tissue to look at under a microscope. This is called a biopsy.

To treat an adamantinoma, doctors remove it with surgery.  
They do not cut into the tumor.  
Cutting into it can spill cancer cells.  
If cells spill, the cancer may come back.

In rare cases, doctors may need to remove the entire leg.  
This happens only if the tumor is in a hard-to-reach spot or comes back after treatment.

---

## Chondrosarcomas

Chondrosarcomas are cancers made of abnormal cartilage cells.  
They usually affect middle-aged and older adults.  
They often start in flat bones like the pelvis or shoulder blade.  
But they can start in any bone or in tissues around bones.

Many chondrosarcomas grow slowly and are low-grade.  
This means they are less likely to spread.  
But some grow fast and are high-grade.  
These are more likely to spread.

To diagnose chondrosarcomas, doctors use x-rays.  
They also do a bone scan and an MRI.  
They take a tissue sample for a biopsy.

For low-grade chondrosarcomas, doctors scrape the tumor out of the bone.  
They use a special tool shaped like a scoop.  
They then kill any leftover cancer cells with cold (liquid nitrogen), a chemical (phenol), bone cement, or a special beam of energy (argon beam).  
Almost all low-grade tumors are cured with this treatment.

High-grade chondrosarcomas grow fast and are aggressive.  
They are more likely to spread.  
Doctors must remove them completely without cutting into the tumor.  
Cutting into it can cause the cancer to return.

Chondrosarcomas do not respond to chemotherapy or radiation.  
Amputation of the arm or leg is rarely needed.

---

## Chordomas

Chordomas are rare and cancerous.  
They usually start at the bottom of the spine (sacrum or tailbone) or near the base of the skull.  
A chordoma in the sacrum causes strong pain.  
One near the base of the skull can affect nerves, especially the optic nerve.

Symptoms can last for months or even years before diagnosis.  
Chordomas rarely spread to places like the lungs unless they are aggressive.  
But they often come back after treatment.

To diagnose a chordoma, doctors use MRI.  
They also do a biopsy.

Chordomas in the sacrum or tailbone can sometimes be cured with surgery.  
Chordomas near the base of the skull are hard to remove completely.  
Surgery usually cannot cure them.  
But radiation therapy can shrink the tumor and help reduce pain.

---

## Ewing Sarcoma of Bone

Ewing sarcoma is a cancer that affects more boys than girls.  
It most often appears in people aged 10 to 20 years.  
Most tumors start in the arms or legs, but they can start in any bone.  
Common symptoms are pain and swelling.  
The tumor can grow very large, sometimes filling the whole bone.  
It may also include a large mass of soft tissue.

To diagnose Ewing sarcoma, doctors take x-rays.  
X-rays show some details, but MRI gives a clearer picture of the tumor’s size.  
To confirm the diagnosis, doctors do a biopsy.

Treatment depends on whether surgery is possible and whether it works.  
Doctors use a mix of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy.  
This combination cures more than 60% of people with Ewing sarcoma.

---

## Lymphoma of Bone

Lymphoma of bone is a cancer that usually affects adults.  
It can start in any bone or in another part of the body.  
It can spread to the bone marrow.  
It often causes pain, swelling, and soft tissue buildup.  
The bone may break easily.

To diagnose lymphoma of bone, doctors take x-rays.  
They also do an MRI to see how much the soft tissue and bone are affected.

Treatment usually includes chemotherapy, with or without radiation.  
This works as well as removing the tumor with surgery.  
Amputation is rarely needed.  
If a bone is at risk of breaking, doctors may fix it with surgery to prevent a fracture.

---

## Osteosarcomas (Osteogenic Sarcoma)

Osteosarcoma is the most common type of primary cancerous bone tumor.  
(We count multiple myeloma as a blood cancer, not a bone cancer.)

It is most common in children and teens, but can happen at any age.  
Children with a family history of retinoblastoma or Li-Fraumeni syndrome have a higher risk.  
Adults over 60 are also at risk, especially if they have Paget disease of bone, have had radiation therapy for another cancer, or have areas of dead bone.

Osteosarcomas usually start near the knee.  
But they can start in any bone.  
They often spread to the lungs or other bones.  
They cause pain, swelling, soft tissue buildup, and trouble moving the joint.

Doctors take x-rays.  
But a biopsy is needed to confirm the diagnosis.  
People also get a chest x-ray and a chest CT scan to check for lung spread.  
A bone scan checks for spread to other bones.  
Doctors may also use MRI and PET-CT scans.

More than 65% of people live at least 5 years after diagnosis if the cancer has not spread.  
If chemotherapy kills almost all the cancer, the 5-year survival rate is over 90%.  
Surgery has improved.  
Doctors can usually save and rebuild the arm or leg.  
In the past, amputation was common.

Osteosarcomas are treated with a mix of chemotherapy and surgery.  
Chemotherapy is usually given first.  
Pain often gets better during this phase.  
Then doctors remove the tumor without cutting into it.  
Cutting into the tumor can spill cancer cells and cause a return.  
Chemotherapy continues after surgery.

# Erythema Multiforme – Simple Explanation

## What Is Erythema Multiforme?

The main sign of erythema multiforme is a rash.  
The rash starts as round, raised spots on the skin.  
Some spots may have rings around them.  
The spots can turn into blisters.  

The rash often appears on your hands and feet.  
It can spread to your tummy, chest, back, or face.  
It may feel itchy or burn.  

The rash can be red, pink, purple, or darker than the skin around it.  
It may also appear inside your mouth, on your lips, eyes, anus, or genitals.  
This can be painful.  

## When to See a Doctor

See your GP if:  
- You have symptoms of the rash.  
- The rash keeps coming back.  

Your doctor may be able to treat the cause of the rash.  

## When to Get Urgent Help

Call 111 or get help online if:  
- The rash is inside your mouth, on your lips, eyes, anus, or genitals.  
- The rash is painful.  
- You have trouble eating or passing urine.  
- You have a high temperature or body aches.  
- The rash started after you began a new medicine.  

## When to Go to A&E (Emergency Department)

Go to A&E or call 999 if:  
- The skin is red, swollen, blistered, or peeling.  
  - Redness may be harder to see on brown or black skin.  
- You are wheezing.  
- You feel tightness in your chest or throat.  
- You have trouble breathing or talking.  
- Your mouth, face, lips, tongue, or throat start swelling.  

These could be signs of a serious reaction. You may need urgent treatment in hospital.  

> **Find your nearest A&E**

### A&E Safety Tips

- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you.  
- Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
- Bring all your medicines with you.  

## Other Symptoms

You may also feel:  
- Unwell overall.  
- Tired or achy.  
- Have a headache.  
- Have a high temperature.  

## How It Is Treated

Most people get better on their own in 2 to 4 weeks.  
You may need:  
- Moisturisers or steroid creams to help with itching and healing.  
- Treatment for the infection causing the rash.  
  - For example, antiviral medicine if a virus is the cause.  

## What Causes It?

Erythema multiforme is often caused by an infection.  
Common causes include:  
- The herpes simplex virus (the same virus that causes cold sores).  
- Bacteria that cause lung infections like pneumonia.  

It can also be caused by some vaccines or medicines.  
These include:  
- Painkillers like ibuprofen (a type of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug).  
- Antibiotics.  
- Cholesterol-lowering medicines (statins).  
- Medicines for epilepsy.  

If a medicine is causing the rash, you may need to stop taking it.  
But **never stop any medicine without talking to your doctor first**.

# What Is Amyloidosis?

Amyloidosis is a group of rare diseases.  
In these diseases, certain proteins in the body fold incorrectly.  
These misfolded proteins clump together into long, thin fibers.  
The fibers build up in organs and tissues.  
This buildup can damage the organs and stop them from working properly.

The proteins that cause amyloidosis can come from different sources.  
Some come from genetic changes.  
Others come from long-term infections, inflammation, or blood cell disorders.  
In some cases, the cause is unknown.

The disease can affect just one organ.  
Or it can affect many organs at once.  
When many organs are involved, the disease can be very serious.

---

## What Are Amyloid Fibrils?

Amyloid fibrils are tiny, solid fibers.  
They form when normal proteins fold the wrong way.  
These misfolded proteins stick together.  
First, they form small clumps.  
Then, they grow into long, rigid fibers.

Many different types of proteins can misfold and form these fibers.  
Some are normal proteins.  
Some are changed by gene mutations.  
This is why there are many types of amyloidosis.

---

## What Are Amyloid Deposits?

Amyloid deposits are clumps of these fibers.  
They are very small—about 10 nanometers wide.  
They form a pattern called beta-pleated sheets.  
This pattern can be seen with special imaging.

The deposits also contain other substances:  
- A protein called serum amyloid P component  
- Sugar molecules called glycosaminoglycans

When doctors look at the deposits under a microscope:  
- They stain pink with a common dye (hematoxylin and eosin)  
- They react with special stains like periodic acid-Schiff or Alcian blue  
- They glow apple-green under polarized light after being treated with Congo red dye

Organs with amyloid deposits often look waxy or firm when examined after death.

---

## How Does Amyloidosis Develop?

For amyloidosis to happen, two things must occur:  
1. The body must make too many misfolded proteins.  
2. The body must fail to clear these proteins properly.

The amyloid deposits themselves do not break down or cause damage directly.  
But they take up space and block normal function.  
They can also cause physical harm to nearby cells.

Some early forms of the misfolded proteins—before they become fibers—can be toxic.  
These early forms can kill cells and cause disease symptoms.

---

## What Causes Amyloidosis?

### Systemic Amyloidosis (Affects Many Organs)

This type happens when misfolded proteins travel through the blood and build up in organs.

**AL Amyloidosis**  
- Caused by abnormal plasma cells making too much of a certain protein.  
- These proteins are parts of antibodies (immunoglobulin light chains).  
- The overproduction comes from a blood cell disorder.

**ATTR Variant (ATTRv) Amyloidosis**  
- Caused by a faulty gene passed down through families.  
- The gene makes a protein called transthyretin that misfolds easily.  
- This is a hereditary form.

**ATTR Wild-Type (ATTRwt) Amyloidosis**  
- Caused by normal transthyretin protein misfolding.  
- It happens in older adults, especially men.  
- Not inherited.

**AA Amyloidosis**  
- Caused by a protein called serum amyloid A.  
- This protein increases during long-term infections or inflammation.  
- It builds up in organs over time.

**Beta-2-Microglobulin Amyloidosis**  
- Can happen in people on long-term dialysis.  
- The protein builds up because dialysis does not remove it well.  
- Newer dialysis machines have reduced this risk.  
- A rare inherited form also exists.

### Localized Amyloidosis (Affects One Area)

This type happens when a protein is made in one organ and builds up there.  
It does not travel through the blood.

Common sites include:  
- Brain (as in Alzheimer disease)  
- Skin  
- Lungs  
- Bladder  
- Eyes  
- Breasts  
- Nerves

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on which organs are affected.  
They often come on slowly and are not specific.  
This can delay diagnosis.

### Kidneys
- Protein leaks into the urine (proteinuria)  
- In some cases, the tubes in the kidneys are damaged  
- This can cause waste to build up in the blood (azotemia)  
- Over time, this leads to nephrotic syndrome:  
  - Low blood protein levels  
  - Swelling in the body (edema)  
  - Fluid buildup in the tissues (anasarca)  
- Can progress to kidney failure

### Liver
- The liver gets bigger but usually does not hurt  
- Liver tests show problems with bile flow  
- Later, bilirubin levels rise (but jaundice is rare)  
- In some cases, pressure builds in the liver (portal hypertension)  
  - This can cause swollen veins in the esophagus (esophageal varices)  
  - Fluid builds up in the belly (ascites)

### Lungs and Airway
- Trouble breathing (dyspnea)  
- Hoarseness  
- Wheezing  
- Coughing up blood (hemoptysis)  
- Blockage in the airway

### Heart
- The heart muscle becomes stiff  
- This causes a type of heart failure called restrictive cardiomyopathy  
- The heart cannot fill properly between beats  
- This leads to heart failure  
- Irregular heartbeats or heart block can occur  
- Low blood pressure is common

### Nerves
- Tingling or numbness in the toes and fingers  
- This is common in AL and ATTRv amyloidosis  
- Autonomic nerves can be affected:  
  - Dizziness when standing (orthostatic hypotension)  
  - Problems with erections  
  - Sweating too much or too little  
  - Urine retention  
  - Digestive problems (constipation or diarrhea)

### Brain
- Bleeding in the brain (cerebral hemorrhage)  
- Some people have brief, sudden symptoms like weakness or confusion

### Digestive System
- Problems with movement in the esophagus  
- Slow movement in the intestines  
- Stomach does not empty well (gastric atony)  
- Poor absorption of nutrients (malabsorption)  
- Bleeding in the gut  
- Bowel blockage that is not caused by a physical block (pseudo-obstruction)  
- Enlarged tongue (macroglossia) is common in AL amyloidosis

### Soft Tissues
- Carpal tunnel syndrome  
- Trigger finger  
- Rupture of the biceps tendon  
- Narrowing of the spine (spinal stenosis)  
- These often appear before heart symptoms in ATTRwt amyloidosis

### Thyroid Gland
- A firm, symmetric, painless lump in the neck  
- Looks like the swelling in Hashimoto thyroiditis  
- Other hormone problems can also occur

### Lungs
- Small lumps in the lungs  
- Cysts  
- Lesions in the airways  
- Fluid around the lungs (pleural effusion)  
- Thickening in the lung tissue (interstitial deposits)  
- Most common in AL amyloidosis

### Eyes
- Cloudy areas in the eye (vitreous opacities)  
- Pupils look scalloped on the edges  
- Seen in some hereditary forms

### Skin and Blood Vessels
- Easy bruising, especially around the eyes (raccoon eyes)  
- Amyloid weakens blood vessels  
- Small injuries (like sneezing or coughing) can cause bleeding

---

## How Is Amyloidosis Diagnosed?

Diagnosis requires several steps.

### Biopsy
- A small sample of tissue is taken from the affected organ.  
- This is the only way to confirm amyloidosis.  
- Common biopsy sites: fat tissue under the skin, kidney, liver, or heart.

### Amyloid Typing
- Tests are done on the biopsy sample to identify the type of protein.  
- Methods include:  
  - Immunohistochemistry (uses antibodies to detect proteins)  
  - Genetic testing  
  - Mass spectrometry (most accurate method)

### Tests for Organ Damage
- Blood and urine tests  
- Imaging (ultrasound, CT, MRI)  
- Heart tests (echocardiogram, EKG)  
- Nerve function tests  
- Lung function tests

---

## How Is Amyloidosis Treated?

Treatment depends on the type of amyloidosis.

### Supportive Care
- Helps manage symptoms and improve quality of life.  
- Includes:  
  - Medicines for heart failure  
  - Diuretics for swelling  
  - Dialysis for kidney failure  
  - Nutritional support for digestive issues  
  - Pain relief  
  - Physical therapy for nerve or joint problems

### Type-Specific Treatments

**AL Amyloidosis**  
- Treat the underlying blood cell disorder.  
- Chemotherapy can stop the overproduction of abnormal proteins.  
- Stem cell transplant may be an option in some cases.

**AA Amyloidosis**  
- Treat the cause: infection, inflammation, or cancer.  
- Antibiotics, anti-inflammatory drugs, or cancer treatment can help.

**ATTRv Amyloidosis (Hereditary)**  
- Medicines that stabilize the transthyretin protein  
- Gene-silencing drugs that reduce protein production  
- These can slow or stop nerve damage

# Hand and Foot Dermatitis

This condition causes red, dry, scaly, and thick skin on the hands or feet. It can affect one or both areas.

It often starts with small blisters on the hands or feet. These blisters are sometimes called dyshidrotic dermatitis. But this name is misleading. The condition is not caused by sweating or problems with sweat glands.

Hand and foot dermatitis can be a sign of other skin conditions. These include atopic dermatitis (a type of eczema) or allergic contact dermatitis (a reaction to something that touches the skin).

Wet work is a common cause. This includes washing hands often or working with water or wet materials. Detergents make the problem worse. It is more common in people who have atopic dermatitis, hay fever, or asthma. These conditions together are called atopy.

The most severe form is called pompholyx. It causes small blisters that join together to form larger ones.

---

## Symptoms

The skin on the hands or feet may become red and dry. It may thicken and flake.

Small blisters can appear on the palms, sides of fingers, or soles of the feet. These blisters may itch.

The blisters can break open. This causes fluid to leak out. The area may then form a crust.

Blisters are often the first sign people notice.

Symptoms can come and go. The skin can get infected. Infections may be caused by bacteria or fungi.

Photos courtesy of Thomas Ruenger, MD, PhD.

---

## Diagnosis

Doctors look at the skin. They also ask about your medical history.

They use the look of the skin and your symptoms to make a diagnosis.

---

## Treatment

### Treat the Cause
If you know what triggers the condition, avoid it.

Avoid things that cause allergic reactions. These are called contact allergens.

Avoid frequent or long contact with water and detergents.

### Reduce Inflammation
Corticosteroid creams or ointments can reduce swelling and redness.

They are applied directly to the skin.

### Relieve Itching
Antihistamines can help with itching.

### Light Therapy
Phototherapy uses ultraviolet light. It can help improve the skin.

Sometimes, a special solution called psoralen is used before light treatment.

### Severe Cases
For very bad cases, doctors may prescribe corticosteroids by mouth or injection.

These are only used for a short time. Long-term use can cause side effects.

If long-term treatment is needed, doctors may use medicines like cyclosporine, mycophenolate, or methotrexate. These medicines lower the body’s immune response.

### Treat Infections
If the skin becomes infected, antibiotics are used. These treat bacterial infections.

Fungal infections are treated with antifungal medicines.

# Kidney Infection

A kidney infection is a serious condition. It needs treatment right away.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may have:
- Pain in your back or side
- A high temperature
- Feeling sick or being sick
- Diarrhoea
- Aching muscles and flu-like feelings
- Pain, burning, or stinging when you pee
- Needing to pee more often or urgently than usual
- Pee that looks dark or cloudy

In young children, symptoms may also include:
- Wetting the bed or their clothes
- Being very sleepy

A baby under 2 years old may only have a high temperature.

These symptoms can feel like other urinary tract infections, such as cystitis.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if you or your child have:
- Pain, burning, or stinging when peeing
- Needing to pee more often or urgently
- Dark or cloudy pee
- Symptoms that do not get better after taking antibiotics

## When to Get Urgent Help

Call your doctor right away or use NHS 111 if you or your child have:
- A very high temperature, or feel hot and shivery
- A low temperature below 36 degrees Celsius
- Pain in the lower tummy or in the back, just under the ribs
- Blood in the pee
- Feeling or being sick
- Not peeing all day
- You are pregnant

A kidney infection can become very serious if not treated. It can lead to sepsis, which is life-threatening.

Call 111 or get help online if you cannot see a doctor or if your symptoms are getting worse.

## When to Go to A&E (Emergency Department)

Go to A&E or call 999 now if you or your child:
- Are confused
- Are very drowsy
- Have trouble speaking

### A&E Safety Tips
- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you. Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.
- Bring all your medicines with you.

## How Is a Kidney Infection Treated?

### Treatment from Your Doctor

Your doctor will test your pee to check for infection.

The main treatment is antibiotics. You will take them as tablets for 7 to 14 days.

Most people feel better after about 2 weeks. Older adults or people with other health problems may take longer to get well.

### Treatment in Hospital

Some people need to go to hospital. This includes:
- People with long-term health conditions
- Pregnant women
- People with weakened immune systems

In hospital, you will get antibiotics through a drip. This works faster than tablets.

You will have blood and urine tests to check your health and make sure the treatment is working.

Most people go home after 3 to 7 days.

## What You Can Do to Feel Better

While you are being treated, try these things to help ease symptoms and prevent another infection:

### Do These Things
- Rest. It may take up to 2 weeks before you feel well enough to return to work.
- Drink plenty of fluids like water or squash. Sip small amounts if you feel sick.
- Take paracetamol to lower a high temperature and ease pain.
- Give your child liquid paracetamol if they are upset or uncomfortable. Check the label or leaflet. Ask a pharmacist or doctor if you are unsure.
- Ask your doctor how much fluid you can safely drink if you have kidney problems.
- Always try to empty your bladder completely when you pee.

### Do Not Do These Things
- Do not take ibuprofen unless your doctor says it is safe. It can harm your kidneys.
- Do not hold in your pee when you feel the need to go.

## What Causes a Kidney Infection?

A kidney infection is a type of urinary tract infection.

Urinary tract infections happen when bacteria get into the tube that carries pee out of your body (the urethra).

Most kidney infections start as a bladder infection (cystitis). But you can also get a kidney infection without having a bladder infection first.

You are more likely to get a kidney infection if you:
- Have kidney stones
- Have a weak immune system
- Have certain long-term health conditions

Urinary tract infections and kidney infections are more common in women, but anyone can get them.

# Arthritis in the Jaw Joint

Arthritis can affect the joint that connects your jaw to your skull. This joint is called the temporomandibular joint, or TMJ.

Several types of arthritis can affect this joint:

- **Infectious arthritis**: This happens when a germ, like a bacteria, gets into the joint and causes swelling and pain.
- **Traumatic arthritis**: This occurs after an injury to the jaw, such as a hard blow or a dislocation.
- **Osteoarthritis**: This is wear and tear on the joint over time. It often happens as people get older.
- **Rheumatoid arthritis**: This is a long-term condition where the body’s immune system attacks the joints, causing pain, swelling, and stiffness.
- **Secondary degenerative arthritis**: This is joint damage that happens after another problem, like an injury or another type of arthritis.

If you have pain, stiffness, or trouble moving your jaw, talk to your doctor. They can help find the cause and suggest treatment.

# Sepsis in Newborns – Simple Explanation

Sepsis is a serious reaction when an infection spreads through the blood. It can make a newborn very sick.

## Who Is at Risk?

Some newborns are more likely to get sepsis. These include babies who:

- Were born too early (premature)
- Weighed less at birth
- Had a low score on the APGAR test, needed help breathing at birth, or both
- Are male
- Had a mother with a low income
- Had a leak in the fluid around the baby before labor started
- Had a mother with an infection during pregnancy or a fever after delivery

## When Does Sepsis Happen?

Doctors divide sepsis into two types based on when it starts:

- **Early-onset sepsis**: Happens in the first 3 days of life.
- **Late-onset sepsis**: Happens after the baby is 3 days old.

Preterm babies are at higher risk for both types because their immune system is not fully developed. They also miss out on important infection-fighting antibodies from their mother because they were born too soon.

---

## Early-Onset Sepsis

This type happens during or just after birth. It can happen if the baby is exposed to certain germs during delivery.

### Risk Factors:
- The water breaks more than 18 hours before birth.
- The mother has an infection, such as a bladder infection or an infection in the lining of the uterus (called chorioamnionitis).
- The mother carries group B streptococcus (GBS) bacteria.
- The baby is born too early.

### Common Germs:
- *Escherichia coli* (E. coli)
- Group B streptococcus (GBS)

These germs are usually passed from the mother to the baby during a vaginal birth.

### Other Causes:
- Viruses like herpes simplex, enterovirus, adenovirus, or respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) can also cause early-onset sepsis.

---

## Late-Onset Sepsis

This type happens after the baby is 3 days old. It is often linked to hospital care.

### Main Risk Factor:
- Being born too early

### Other Risk Factors:
- Having a tube in a blood vessel, bladder, or breathing tube for a long time
- Taking antibiotics
- Using a breathing machine (ventilator)
- Staying in the hospital for a long time

### How It Happens:
The baby can get germs from the hospital environment. These include germs on tubes, IVs, or other medical equipment.

Antibiotics can also cause problems. They kill good bacteria in the body. This lets yeast (called *Candida*) grow and cause an infection.

### Other Causes:
- Viruses like herpes simplex, enterovirus, adenovirus, or RSV can cause late-onset sepsis.

---

## Signs and Symptoms

Newborns with sepsis often look very sick. They may:

- Be very sleepy or not wake up
- Not feed well
- Have a fever or feel cold to the touch
- Have a gray or pale color
- Breathe fast or have trouble breathing
- Stop breathing for short periods (apnea)
- Have cold hands and feet
- Have a swollen belly
- Vomit or have diarrhea
- Have seizures or tremble
- Show signs of jaundice (yellow skin or eyes)

### Specific Symptoms by Cause:
- Early-onset GBS infection can cause pneumonia (lung infection).

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Sepsis

Doctors look at the baby’s symptoms and do tests to find the cause.

### Tests Include:
- Blood tests
- Urine tests
- Spinal tap (a small amount of fluid is taken from the spine to check for infection)

### What the Tests Do:
- Doctors take samples of blood, urine, and spinal fluid.
- They grow the germs in a lab to see what is causing the infection.

### Other Tests:
- If the baby has breathing problems, a chest x-ray is done.

---

## How Sepsis Is Treated

### Antibiotics:
- Doctors give strong antibiotics through a vein (IV) right away if sepsis is suspected.
- Once the germ is identified, the antibiotic may be changed.

### Other Treatments:
- A breathing machine (ventilator) if the baby has trouble breathing
- Fluids through a vein to prevent dehydration
- Blood or plasma transfusions if needed
- Medicines to help keep blood pressure and circulation stable

---

## Outlook (Prognosis)

- Early-onset sepsis is deadly in about 18 out of 100 newborns.
- Late-onset sepsis is deadly in up to 12 out of 100 newborns.

Most babies who survive sepsis do not have long-term health problems.

**One exception:** Babies who survive meningitis (infection of the brain and its covering) may have lasting issues.

---

## How to Prevent Sepsis

### Group B Streptococcus (GBS):
- GBS used to be the top cause of early-onset sepsis.
- Now, most pregnant people are tested for GBS during pregnancy.

### Prevention Steps:
- If a pregnant person tests positive for GBS, or has had a baby with GBS before, they get antibiotics during labor.
- Antibiotics are not given if the baby is born by cesarean section before labor starts and before the water breaks.

### After Birth:
- Newborns are not given antibiotics unless they show signs of infection.
- Babies may be watched closely and tested for infection if they are at risk.
- Antibiotics are only used if the baby is actually sick.

# Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs)

## What is a UTI?

A urinary tract infection is an infection in the tubes or organs that carry urine out of your body. It often affects the bladder or the tube that carries urine out (urethra).

## Symptoms of a UTI

You may have a UTI if you notice any of these signs:

- A strong, sudden need to pee.
- Pain or a burning feeling when you pee.
- Needing to pee more often than usual.
- Needing to pee more often at night.
- Feeling like you must pee right away.
- Pee that looks cloudy or has a strong smell.
- Blood in your pee. It may look bright pink, red, or dark brown.
- Pain in your lower belly or in your back, just under your ribs.
- A high temperature, or feeling hot or cold.
- Shivering or chills.
- A very low temperature below 36 degrees Celsius.
- Feeling tired or weak.

If your only symptom is dark or smelly pee, you may just be dehydrated. Try drinking more water.

### Symptoms in Children

Children with a UTI may:

- Have a high temperature.
- Act irritable or unwell.
- Wet the bed or have accidents.
- Be sick.

### Symptoms in Older or Frail People

Older or frail people, or those with a urinary catheter, may show different signs:

- Confusion or sudden changes in behavior.
- Worsening incontinence (leaking pee).
- New shivering or shaking.

## What You Can Do Yourself

To feel better while you have a UTI:

- Take paracetamol up to four times a day to ease pain and reduce fever.
- Give children liquid paracetamol if needed.
- Rest and drink plenty of fluids.
- Aim to pass pale yellow urine regularly during the day.

Some people take cystitis sachets or drink cranberry juice to help prevent UTIs. These may help stop infections from starting. But they do not treat a UTI once it has started.

## When to See a Pharmacist

See a pharmacist if:

- You are a woman or girl aged 16 to 64.
- You are not pregnant or breastfeeding.
- You think you have a UTI.

A pharmacist can give you the same medicines a doctor would. They can also give advice or refer you to a doctor if needed.

👉 [Find a pharmacy near you]

## When to See a Doctor or Get Help

Call your doctor for an urgent appointment or use NHS 111 if you or someone you care for has a UTI and:

- You are 65 or older.
- Your child is 15 or younger.
- You have a very high or very low temperature.
- You feel hot or cold, or are shivering.
- You are a man, or were assigned male at birth and identify as trans or non-binary.
- You have diabetes.
- Your symptoms get worse quickly or do not improve in 48 hours.
- You keep getting UTIs (2 in 6 months or 3 in 12 months).
- You use a urinary catheter.
- You are pregnant.
- You have pain in your lower belly or in your back, just under your ribs.
- You see blood in your pee.
- You have a weakened immune system.

Some of these signs could mean you have a kidney infection. This can be serious and may lead to sepsis if not treated.

👉 Call 111 or get help online at [nhs.uk/111](https://www.nhs.uk/111)

## When to Go to A&E (Emergency Department)

Go to A&E or call 999 now if:

- You or your child is confused, very sleepy, or has trouble speaking.

### A&E Safety Tips

- Do not drive yourself to A&E. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 for an ambulance.
- Bring all your medicines with you.

## How UTIs Are Treated

If a pharmacist or doctor thinks you have a UTI, they may test your urine. But this is not always needed.

A doctor may:

- Give advice on self-care.
- Recommend a painkiller.
- Prescribe a short course of antibiotics.
- Suggest waiting 48 hours to see if symptoms go away on their own.

Take all your medicine as prescribed, even if you start to feel better.

### If UTIs Keep Coming Back

If you keep getting UTIs, see your doctor. They may:

- Prescribe a different antibiotic.
- Give you a low-dose antibiotic to take for up to 6 months.
- Prescribe a vaginal cream, gel, tablet, pessary, or ring with oestrogen if you are in perimenopause or have gone through menopause.
- Give you medicine to treat the infection and stop it from returning.
- Refer you to a specialist for more tests and treatment.

## What Causes UTIs?

Most UTIs happen when bacteria from poo get into the urethra (the tube that carries pee out of the body).

Women are more likely to get UTIs because their urethra is shorter than men’s. This makes it easier for bacteria to reach the bladder or kidneys.

Things that raise your risk include:

- Having sex.
- Being pregnant.
- Having kidney stones.
- Having an enlarged prostate (in men).
- Constipation (in children).
- Using a urinary catheter.
- Having a weak immune system (for example, from poorly controlled diabetes or chemotherapy).
- Not drinking enough fluids.

## How to Prevent UTIs

### Do These Things

- Always wipe from front to back after using the toilet.
- Keep the area around your genitals clean and dry.
- Drink plenty of fluids, especially water.
- Wash the skin around your vagina with water before and after sex.
- Pee as soon as possible after sex.
- Change nappies or incontinence pads right away if they are soiled.
- Wear cotton underwear.

### Avoid These Things

- Do not use scented soaps or lotions near your genitals.
- Do not hold in your pee when you feel the need to go.
- Do not rush when peeing. Try to empty your bladder fully.
- Do not wear tight underwear.
- Do not drink too much alcohol. It can irritate your bladder.
- Do not eat or drink too much sugar. It can help bacteria grow.
- Avoid condoms, diaphragms, or caps with spermicidal lube. Use non-spermicidal lube or try a different type of contraception.

### Other Ways to Prevent Recurrent UTIs

If you keep getting bladder infections (cystitis), you may find these helpful:

- D-mannose: a sugar you can take daily as a powder or tablet.
- Cranberry products: available as juice, tablets, or capsules to take daily.

Talk to your doctor before using these during pregnancy.

⚠️ Warning: D-mannose and cranberry products can have a lot of sugar.

⚠️ If you take warfarin, avoid cranberry products. They can affect how your medicine works.

# Hand and Foot Dermatitis

This condition causes skin problems on the hands and/or feet. It can be caused by an allergic reaction, irritation, or a skin condition called atopic dermatitis. The skin may become red, flaky, and thickened.

---

## What Causes Hand and Foot Dermatitis?

The skin’s outer layer swells between its cells. This swelling is called spongiosis. When the swelling gets too much, the connections between skin cells break. This creates tiny fluid-filled pockets called microvesicles.

On most parts of the body, these tiny pockets break open quickly and are not seen. But on the hands and feet, the skin is thicker. So the pockets stay longer and can be seen. When you see these visible blisters, it is called dyshidrotic dermatitis. The name is misleading because it has nothing to do with sweating or sweat glands.

The worst form of this condition is called pompholyx. It happens when many small blisters join together to form larger ones.  
- If it affects only the hands, it is called cheiropompholyx.  
- If it affects only the feet, it is called podopompholyx.  
- If it affects both hands and feet, it is called cheiropodopompholyx.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The skin may become red, flaky, and thick. It can then develop itchy blisters on the palms, sides of fingers, or soles of the feet. These blisters are called dyshidrotic dermatitis.

The blisters may break open. This leads to raw areas, oozing, and scabs. The blisters can be the first sign people notice.

Symptoms may come and go. They often get worse with certain triggers.

Common triggers include:
- Washing hands too often
- Working with water or wet materials
- Using soaps or detergents
- Having a history of allergies or sensitive skin

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose this condition by looking at the skin. They check the location and appearance of the rash.

### Other Conditions That Can Look Like Hand and Foot Dermatitis

These conditions can cause similar symptoms:

### Fungal Infection
- Causes redness, flaking, and itching.
- Can cause blisters, especially on hands and feet.
- A key clue: the rash often forms ring-shaped patterns. This happens because the fungus grows outward from the center.

### Palmoplantar Psoriasis
- Causes thick, red, scaly patches on the palms and soles.
- The edges of the patches are very clear and sharp.
- May include small, pus-filled bumps (sterile pustules).
- Often linked to other signs of psoriasis, such as nail changes or skin patches elsewhere.
- Unlike hand and foot dermatitis, true psoriasis does not cause blisters.

But sometimes, both conditions can happen at the same time. Or blisters from dermatitis can become infected. Or a person with psoriasis can develop an allergic reaction to a medicine. Or a skin injury can trigger psoriasis.

### Other Conditions That Affect Hands and Feet

These are not dermatitis but can cause similar skin changes:

- **Fungal infections** – such as tinea manuum (hand), tinea pedis (foot), or yeast infections
- **Viral infections** – such as herpetic whitlow or warts
- **Bacterial infections** – such as impetigo or rare mycobacterial infections
- **Parasitic infections** – such as scabies or cutaneous larva migrans
- **Hereditary palmoplantar keratoderma** – a rare inherited skin thickening
- **Hereditary epidermolysis bullosa** – a group of rare conditions where skin blisters easily
- **Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma** – a type of skin cancer
- **Lichen planus** – a rash with purple, itchy bumps
- **Pityriasis rubra pilaris** – a rare condition with red, scaly patches
- **Keratolysis exfoliativa** – a condition with ring-shaped redness and peeling on the palms and soles. It is not inflammation. It does not cause fluid-filled blisters. It may get worse with heat, sweating, rubbing, or water.
- **Hand-foot syndrome** – a side effect of some chemotherapy drugs. It causes tingling, swelling, and redness in the palms and soles. It can also cause pain, numbness, flaking, or blistering. It is not a skin allergy or infection.

---

## How Is It Treated?

### Treat the Cause When Possible
- Avoid things that irritate your skin.
- Stay away from known allergens.
- Limit contact with water and detergents.

### Supportive Care
- Use moisturizers to protect the skin.
- Wear gloves when doing wet work.

### Topical Treatments
- Topical corticosteroid creams can reduce swelling and itching.
- The strength of the cream depends on how bad the rash is.
- Antihistamines can help with itching.

### Light Therapy
- Narrow-band ultraviolet B (UVB) light can help.
- Soak PUVA: soak hands or feet in a special solution, then expose to UVA light.

### Infections
- If the skin gets infected, antibiotics (topical or oral) are needed.

### Severe Cases
- Short-term use of oral corticosteroids may help.
- For long-term treatment, doctors may use medicines like cyclosporine, mycophenolate, or methotrexate. These suppress the immune system.

Always follow your doctor’s advice. Do not use strong medicines without medical guidance.

# Problems with the Voice Box

This guide explains common noncancerous growths on the voice box. These growths can make your voice sound hoarse or weak.

---

## Types of Voice Box Growths

### Vocal Cord Polyps  
- These are often caused by a sudden injury, like shouting at a sports game.  
- They usually appear on just one side of the voice box.  
- Other causes include acid reflux, low thyroid levels, or long-term exposure to smoke or fumes.  
- When caused by these other issues, polyps often affect both sides.  
- Polyps are usually larger and stick out more than nodules.  
- They are most common in adults.

### Vocal Cord Nodules  
- These form on both sides of the voice box.  
- They are usually caused by long-term strain from yelling, singing, or speaking too loudly.  
- They can also happen when someone speaks in an unnatural low voice.  
- Nodules can occur in children as well as adults.

### Vocal Cord Granulomas  
- These are small areas of swelling caused by inflammation.  
- They often result from acid reflux that damages the voice box.  
- They can also happen after a breathing tube is placed during surgery.  
- Granulomas are most common in adults.

### Vocal Cord Papillomas  
- These are noncancerous, wart-like growths.  
- They are caused by certain types of human papillomavirus (HPV).  
- The virus can be passed from mother to baby during childbirth.  
- Most cases happen in children between 1 and 4 years old.  
- But they can appear at any age.  
- Early signs include a hoarse voice or a weak cry.  
- In some cases, the growths can block the airway and make breathing hard.

---

## How the Voice Box Works

- When you are not speaking, the voice cords form a V-shaped space.  
- This lets air pass freely into the windpipe.  
- The cords open when you breathe in.  
- They close when you swallow or speak.  
- A doctor can look at the voice cords using a mirror or a thin tube.  
- This check helps find problems like ulcers, granulomas, polyps, nodules, paralysis, or cancer.  
- All of these issues can change your voice.  
- Paralysis can affect one side or both sides of the voice cords.

---

## Symptoms of Voice Box Growths

- Hoarseness that lasts more than a few weeks.  
- A breathy or weak voice.  
- These symptoms usually get worse over days or weeks.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Voice Box Growths

- A doctor uses a mirror or a thin, flexible tube to look at the voice cords.  
- This is called laryngoscopy.  
- In some cases, the doctor takes a small sample of tissue.  
- This sample is checked under a microscope.  
- A biopsy helps confirm if the growth is a papilloma.  
- It also makes sure the growth is not cancer.

---

## Treatment for Voice Box Growths

### For Nodules and Granulomas  
- Rest your voice.  
- Avoid anything that irritates your voice box.  
- If voice strain is the cause, a speech therapist can teach you how to speak or sing without hurting your voice.  
- A speech therapist may use computer tools to help you avoid speaking too loudly or with too much tension.  
- People who use their voice a lot should stay well hydrated and eat a healthy diet.  
- Most nodules and granulomas go away with this care.  
- If granulomas do not go away, surgery may be needed.  
- But they often come back after surgery.

### For Polyps  
- Most polyps need surgery to remove them.  
- Surgery helps restore your normal voice.  
- After surgery, you may need speech therapy.  
- This helps you learn how to avoid harsh habits like yelling or screaming.

### For Papillomas  
- Surgery or laser treatment is used to remove the growths.  
- In severe cases, antiviral medicine may be given.  
- HPV vaccination in women can prevent the virus.  
- This lowers the chance of passing the virus to a baby during childbirth.  
- It also helps prevent papillomas in children.

# Orf

Orf is a virus that mainly affects sheep and goats.  
It can spread to people who have a cut, sore, or scratch on their skin.  
The virus enters your body through the open wound when you touch an infected animal or something the animal has touched.

## How Orf Affects You

Orf usually starts with a small spot on the skin.  
The spot may look red, blue, or darker on brown or black skin.  
It can feel itchy or tender.  
Over time, the spot turns into a blister.  
The blister is usually 2 to 3 centimetres wide. It can grow up to 5 centimetres.  
The blister may leak fluid before it forms a crust.  
The blister usually heals on its own in about 6 weeks.  
It does not need special treatment in most cases.

### Other Signs to Watch For

You may also feel unwell.  
This can include a high temperature.  
You might feel tired or weak.  
Your glands under your arm or inside your elbow may swell.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:

- A blister or mark on your finger, hand, arm, or face is not healing after 6 weeks.  
- The blister is painful, red, and swollen. You also have a high temperature.  
  (Redness can be hard to see on brown or black skin.)  
- You have a rash that looks like a target or bull’s-eye. It has a dark centre, a lighter ring around it, and a darker outer ring.  
- You have many blisters.  
- You have large, painful blisters.  
- Blisters keep coming back.

## How You Can Get Orf

You can get orf if you touch an infected animal.
