This includes touching the animal’s bedding, fencing, or other surfaces it has touched.  
You are more likely to get it if you work with sheep or goats often.  
This includes farmers or people who bottle feed lambs.

Orf causes scabs around the animal’s nose and mouth.  
These scabs can spread to the legs and teats.  
The virus spreads easily between animals.  
It is not usually serious for the animals.

Sheep and goats can be vaccinated against orf.  
But people can still get infected from both vaccinated and unvaccinated animals.  
It is very rare for one person to pass orf to another person.

## How to Treat Orf

There is no special medicine for orf.  
The blister will usually go away in about 6 weeks.  
Cover the blister with a waterproof dressing.  
This keeps it clean and dry.  
It also helps stop it from getting infected.

If the blister becomes infected, you may need antibiotics.  
If the blister does not heal on its own, your doctor may suggest:

- A special cream  
- Freezing the area to remove the blister (cryotherapy)  
- A small surgery to remove the affected skin

## How to Lower Your Risk of Getting Orf

You can take steps to protect yourself:

- Wear latex gloves when touching sheep or goats.  
- Cover any cuts, sores, or scratches with a waterproof dressing.  
  Do this especially when handling animals.  
- Wash your hands with warm water and soap after touching animals.  
- Vaccinate your sheep and goats against orf.  
- Clean and disinfect barns, sheds, and animal areas regularly.

# Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD)

This condition affects the nerves in the eyes and spinal cord. It can also affect other parts of the brain and spinal cord.

It is not the same as multiple sclerosis, even though it was once thought to be a type of it.

## What Causes NMOSD?

The body’s immune system attacks parts of the nervous system. It targets two main things:

- A protein called aquaporin 4, found in certain brain and spinal cord cells.
- Or a protein called MOG, found on the protective covering of nerves.

This attack causes damage to nerve cells and their protective layers. This damage leads to symptoms.

There are three types of NMOSD:

- **Type 1**: The blood test shows antibodies to aquaporin 4.
- **Type 2**: The blood test shows antibodies to MOG.
- **Type 3**: The blood test shows no antibodies. But the person still has NMOSD.

## Symptoms and Signs

Common symptoms include:

- Loss of vision
- Muscle spasms
- Weakness in the legs or arms
- Trouble controlling the bladder or bowels

Specific patterns of symptoms may include:

- Severe eye pain and vision loss in both eyes at the same time.
- Vision loss that affects only the top or bottom half of what you see.
- Complete loss of vision (20/200 or worse).
- A full spinal cord problem, often with sudden muscle spasms.
- Constant hiccups, nausea, or vomiting. This happens because a small part of the brain is affected.
- A spinal cord injury that covers three or more connected sections.

## How Is NMOSD Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to diagnose NMOSD:

- **MRI scans** of the brain and spinal cord.
- **Visual evoked potentials** – a test that checks how fast the eyes send signals to the brain.

These tests help tell NMOSD apart from multiple sclerosis.

Key differences:

- NMOSD often affects three or more connected sections of the spinal cord.
- MS usually affects only one section.
- NMOSD rarely causes brain white matter lesions. MS often does.
- The shape and location of the damage look different on MRI scans.

The visual evoked potential test can show nerve damage even before symptoms appear.

Blood tests check for two types of antibodies:

- Anti-aquaporin 4 antibodies – found in some people with NMOSD.
- Anti-MOG antibodies – found in others.

Some people have NMOSD but no antibodies. They are called double-antibody negative.

## Treatment

There is no cure for NMOSD. But treatment can help prevent attacks, slow the disease, and reduce disability.

### Main Treatments

- **Corticosteroids** – medicine to reduce swelling and inflammation.
- **Immunomodulatory or immunosuppressive drugs** – medicines that calm the immune system.

### Specific Medicines

- **Eculizumab** – for people with aquaporin 4 antibodies. It blocks part of the immune system.
  - Side effects: lung infections, headaches, pneumonia.
  - You must get a meningococcal vaccine before starting this medicine.
  - You will need close monitoring.

- **Satralizumab** – blocks a signal that causes inflammation.
  - Used for people with aquaporin 4 antibodies.
  - Watch for infections like urinary tract or lung infections.

- **Inebilizumab** – removes certain immune cells.
  - Used for people with aquaporin 4 antibodies.
  - Watch for infections.

- **Rituximab** – removes B-cells, a type of immune cell.
  - Shown to reduce relapses in studies.
  - Other similar medicines may also be used.

- **Methylprednisolone and azathioprine** – often used together.
  - These are strong anti-inflammatory and immune-suppressing medicines.

- **Plasma exchange** – a treatment that removes harmful antibodies from the blood.
  - Used if steroids do not help.

### Medicines to Avoid

- **Natalizumab** and **fingolimod** – these medicines do not help and may make NMOSD worse.

### Treating Symptoms

- **Baclofen** or **tizanidine** – help reduce muscle spasms.
- Other symptom treatments are similar to those used for multiple sclerosis.

## Key Points

- NMOSD damages the nerves in the eyes and spinal cord.
- It is often linked to antibodies against aquaporin 4 or MOG.
- Common symptoms: vision loss, muscle spasms, weakness, and bladder or bowel problems.
- Diagnosis uses MRI scans and visual evoked potential tests.
- Treatment includes steroids and medicines that calm the immune system.
- Eculizumab, satralizumab, inebilizumab, and rituximab are options for some people.
- Avoid natalizumab and fingolimod – they can be harmful.

# Postpolio Syndrome

Postpolio syndrome happens many years after a person has had polio.  
It causes muscles to feel tired, weak, and sometimes painful.  
It often shows up decades after the original illness.

Some people who had polio later develop this condition.  
It is more common in older adults.  
It is also more likely if the original polio was severe.

The muscles that were affected by polio may get weaker.  
They may also shrink in size.  
This is not always due to postpolio syndrome.  
Other health problems can cause similar symptoms.

Common causes of new weakness include:
- Diabetes
- A slipped disk in the spine
- Joint wear and tear (osteoarthritis)

The exact cause of postpolio syndrome is not known.  
It may be linked to aging.  
The nerves that were damaged by polio may not work as well over time.

## How Doctors Diagnose Postpolio Syndrome

Doctors consider postpolio syndrome if:
- A person had polio in the past
- They now have new muscle weakness that gets worse over time

## How Postpolio Syndrome Is Treated

There is no cure for postpolio syndrome.  
Treatment focuses on helping the person feel better and stay active.

Supportive care is key.  
This includes:
- Rest when needed
- Managing pain
- Using assistive devices if needed

Physical therapy can help.  
A physical therapist will design a safe exercise plan.  
The plan depends on which muscles are weak.  
Exercises are tailored to the person’s needs and abilities.

Exercise programs are designed to:
- Keep muscles strong
- Prevent further weakness
- Improve daily function

Always work with a trained professional.  
Do not start new exercises without guidance.

# Otosclerosis

Otosclerosis is a condition that can cause hearing loss. It often starts in younger adults, usually between the ages of 30 and 50.

## Symptoms

You may notice one or more of these signs:

- Your hearing gets worse slowly over time. This can happen in one ear or both ears.
- You hear ringing, buzzing, or other noises in your ears. This is called tinnitus.
- You feel dizzy.
- You have trouble keeping your balance.

These symptoms can develop over several years.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:

- You think your hearing is getting worse over time.
- You have tinnitus that happens often or all the time.
- Your tinnitus is getting worse.
- Your tinnitus is affecting your life. For example, it is making it hard to sleep, focus, or it is making you feel anxious or sad.

## What Happens at Your Doctor Visit

If you have symptoms, your doctor will:

- Look inside your ears with a special tool.
- Send you for a hearing test. This test checks how well you can hear different sounds.

You may be referred to a specialist. This could be:

- An audiologist. They do detailed hearing tests.
- An ear, nose, and throat doctor. They are also called ENT doctors. They will look inside your ears. They may order a CT scan. This is a type of scan that shows detailed pictures of your inner ear.

## Treatment Options

There are two main ways to treat hearing loss from otosclerosis:

### Hearing Aids

- These devices make sounds around you louder.
- They can help you hear better in daily life.
- They do not stop your hearing from getting worse over time.

### Surgery

- The surgeon removes a small bone in your ear called the stapes.
- The removed bone is replaced with a small plastic or metal implant.
- This surgery usually works very well to improve hearing.
- It is most often done on one ear at a time.

Your ear, nose, and throat doctor will help you decide which treatment is best for you. They will consider your hearing, your symptoms, and your lifestyle.

# Aortic Dissection

Aortic dissection is a serious condition where blood pushes through a tear in the inner layer of the aorta. This creates a false channel inside the aorta wall. The tear can happen on its own or after bleeding inside the aorta wall. The dissection can start anywhere along the aorta and spread forward or backward into other blood vessels.

High blood pressure is a major risk factor. The most common symptom is sudden, severe pain in the chest or back. The pain often feels like a tearing or ripping. It may move as the dissection spreads. Some people faint. Others may have signs of poor blood flow to organs, such as a stroke, a heart attack, or kidney problems.

Doctors use imaging tests to diagnose aortic dissection. These include transesophageal echocardiography, CT scans with contrast, MRI, or contrast aortography. These tests show the tear and the false channel.

Treatment focuses on lowering blood pressure quickly. Doctors also monitor the dissection with repeated imaging. Surgery is needed for dissections in the upper part of the aorta. It may also be needed for some lower aorta dissections. For certain lower aorta cases, doctors can use a stent graft placed through a blood vessel instead of open surgery.

People who are Black, male, older, or have high blood pressure are at higher risk. The condition is most common in people aged 50 to 65. For those with inherited connective tissue disorders, it often happens between ages 20 and 40.

---

## What Causes Aortic Dissection?

Aortic dissection often happens in people whose aorta has weakened over time. Common causes include:

- Inherited conditions like Marfan syndrome or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome  
- Atherosclerosis (hardening of the arteries)  
- High blood pressure  
- High cholesterol  
- Smoking  
- Cocaine use  
- Heart valve problems, such as a bicuspid aortic valve  
- Narrowing of the aorta (coarctation)  
- Inflammation of blood vessels (like in giant cell arteritis or Takayasu arteritis)  
- Injury from accidents or medical procedures  
- Certain rare genetic syndromes (like Loeys-Dietz or Turner syndrome)

High blood pressure is the most common factor. It plays a role in more than two out of three cases.

When the inner layer of the aorta tears, blood rushes into the middle layer. This creates a false channel. The channel can grow longer or shorter, depending on the direction of the tear.

---

## How Aortic Dissection Affects the Body

The process starts with inflammation in the aorta wall. The muscle cells in the wall die. The structure weakens. The elastic fibers break. Then the layers of the aorta separate.

The false channel can reconnect with the main blood channel later. This keeps blood flowing through the aorta.

Serious problems can happen:

- Blood flow to major organs can be blocked. This can cause a stroke, heart attack, kidney failure, or bowel damage.  
- The aortic valve can stretch and leak, leading to heart failure.  
- The aorta can burst through the outer layer. This can cause deadly bleeding into the chest or around the heart.  
- The false channel can block blood to the legs, arms, or spinal cord. This can cause weakness or paralysis.

These risks are highest in the first two weeks after the dissection starts. If the false channel seals off and stops connecting to the main channel, the risk goes down.

Some cases do not have a clear tear. These are called variants. They include:

- Bleeding inside the aorta wall without a visible tear  
- A bulge in the aorta wall without a blood clot or false channel  
- A tear caused by a broken plaque in atherosclerosis

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people feel sudden, intense pain in the chest or upper back. The pain often feels like a tear or rip. It may move as the dissection spreads.

About 1 in 5 people faint. This can happen from severe pain, low blood pressure, or blocked blood flow to the brain.

Low blood pressure and fast heartbeat may mean active bleeding.

Some people have signs of poor blood flow to organs. These include:

- Stroke  
- Heart attack  
- Belly pain from poor blood flow to the intestines  
- Kidney problems  
- Weakness or paralysis in the legs

These happen when the false channel blocks blood to a specific area.

About 1 in 4 to 1 in 3 people have weak or missing pulses in their arms or legs. The blood pressure in one arm or leg may be much higher than the other. This is a bad sign.

A doctor may hear a heart murmur if the aortic valve is leaking. This can lead to heart failure. Fluid buildup around the heart can cause trouble breathing and swelling in the neck veins.

Fluid in the space around the lungs can cause shortness of breath. Blockage in a leg artery can cause cold, pale, or numb limbs.

Kidney blockage can cause little or no urine.

> **Quick Tip:** About 20 to 30% of people with aortic dissection have weak or missing pulses.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Aortic dissection must be considered in anyone with:

- Sudden chest or back pain  
- Unexplained fainting  
- Sudden belly pain  
- Stroke  
- Sudden heart failure  
- Unequal blood pressure or pulses in the arms or legs

A chest X-ray is usually the first test. It often shows a widened area in the chest. A bulge may show where the tear started. Fluid in the left side of the chest is common.

If the X-ray suggests dissection, doctors do a more detailed scan right away. This is after the patient is stable.

The best tests are:

- **Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE):** A probe is passed down the throat. It gives clear images of the heart and aorta. It is very accurate and can be done quickly at the bedside. It does not need contrast dye.  
- **CT angiography (CTA):** A CT scan with contrast dye. It is fast and widely available. It is often the first test used. It is very accurate.  
- **Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA):** Gives very clear images. But it takes longer and is not good for emergencies. It is best for stable patients with ongoing or past symptoms.

**Contrast aortography** is used only when surgery is planned. It shows the exact location and extent of the tear. It also helps decide if other heart surgery is needed.

Doctors also do an echocardiogram to check the aortic valve. This helps decide if it needs repair or replacement.

An electrocardiogram (ECG) is done in most cases. But it does not confirm dissection. It may look normal or show signs of a heart attack or valve leak.

Blood tests can help rule out a heart attack. They may show:

- A mild rise in white blood cells  
- Low red blood cell count if blood has leaked  
- High levels of certain enzymes if the intestines or bowel are affected

A cardiothoracic surgeon should be involved early in the process.

---

## How Is It Treated?

All patients with aortic dissection need to be in an intensive care unit. They need:

- Continuous blood pressure monitoring through an artery  
- A catheter in the bladder to track urine output

Blood should be prepared in case surgery is needed. Usually, 4 to 6 units of packed red blood cells are ready.

If the patient is unstable, they may need a breathing tube.

The main treatment is medicine to lower blood pressure and slow the heart rate. Beta-blockers are often used first.

For dissections in the upper aorta, surgery is usually needed. This involves replacing the damaged part with a synthetic tube.

For some lower aorta dissections, doctors can use a stent graft. This is placed through a blood vessel in the groin. It seals the tear from the inside.

Medical treatment alone may be enough for stable patients with dissections only in the lower aorta.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

About 1 in 5 people die before reaching the hospital. Without treatment, the risk of death is about 1 to 2% every hour after symptoms start.

Without surgery, more than half of patients die within one month.

With treatment:

- About 1 in 5 patients with type A dissection (upper aorta) die in the hospital  
- About 1 in 10 patients with type B dissection (lower aorta) die in the hospital

Long-term survival is good for type A dissections treated with surgery. More than 90% survive 1 and 3 years after discharge.

For type B dissections treated only with medicine, about 78% survive 3 years.

---

## Key Points

- Aortic dissection often starts near the heart or just below the left arm artery.  
- It can happen in people with weak aorta walls from genetic conditions or injury. High blood pressure is a common factor.  
- The main symptom is sudden, severe chest or back pain. It often feels like a tear.  
- Other symptoms depend on which blood vessels are blocked. These can include stroke, heart attack, kidney failure, or leg weakness.  
- Diagnosis is done with imaging tests like TEE, CTA, or MRA.  
- Blood pressure and heart rate must be lowered quickly with medicine.  
- Surgery is needed for most upper aorta dissections.  
- Medical treatment alone may be enough for stable lower aorta dissections.

# Seasonal Allergies

Seasonal allergies happen when your body reacts to tiny particles in the air. These particles only appear at certain times of the year. The most common triggers are pollens from trees, grasses, and weeds. Mold spores can also cause these allergies.

## What Causes Seasonal Allergies?

- Seasonal allergies are also called hay fever. This name is confusing because they do not cause fever and they can happen in any season.
- They happen when your body overreacts to pollen or mold spores in the air.
- The timing of your symptoms tells you what you are allergic to.

### Pollen by Season

- **Spring:** Tree pollens (like oak, birch, elm, and alder).
- **Summer:** Grass pollens (like Bermuda, timothy, and Johnson grass) and some weeds (like Russian thistle and English plantain).
- **Fall:** Ragweed is the main cause.

### Where You Live Matters

- In the western United States, mountain cedar pollens are common from December to March.
- In dry areas, grasses pollinate for longer periods.
- In the fall, weeds like sagebrush and Russian thistle can cause symptoms.

You might be allergic to more than one type of pollen. This means your allergy season could last from early spring to late fall.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Your nose, eyes, throat, and sinuses can all be affected. Symptoms often come on suddenly or slowly.

### Nose and Throat

- Itchy nose, mouth, or throat.
- Runny nose with clear, watery mucus.
- Stuffy nose.
- Swollen, bluish-red nasal lining.
- Headaches from blocked sinuses.
- Sinus infections (sinusitis) can happen if sinuses stay blocked.

### Eyes

- Itchy, watery, or red eyes.
- Swollen eyelids.
- Contact lenses can make eye irritation worse.

### Other Symptoms

- Frequent sneezing.
- Coughing or wheezing (especially if you have asthma).
- Trouble sleeping.
- Feeling irritable.

### Asthma and Allergies

Many people with seasonal allergies also have asthma. The same allergens can trigger both conditions.

## How Are Seasonal Allergies Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and when they happen.

### Typical Signs

- Symptoms appear only during certain seasons.
- Itchy nose and eyes are common.
- Symptoms go away when the season ends.

### Tests (If Needed)

- A skin test may be done. A small amount of allergen is placed on your skin and then pricked. If you are allergic, the area swells and turns red.
- A blood test can check for allergy antibodies. This is used if skin testing is not possible.

### No Test Needed?

Most people do not need tests. Your symptoms and timing are usually enough to make the diagnosis.

## How Are Seasonal Allergies Treated?

There are many ways to feel better. The best treatment depends on your symptoms.

### First-Line Treatments

- **Corticosteroid nasal sprays** are often the most effective. They reduce swelling and itching in the nose.
  - Use them every day, even when you feel fine.
  - Side effects are rare but can include nosebleeds or a sore nose.

- **Antihistamines** help with itching, sneezing, and runny nose.
  - Available as pills, nasal sprays, or eye drops.
  - Can be used alone or with other medicines.

- **Decongestants** help clear a stuffy nose.
  - Available as pills or nasal sprays.
  - Do not use nasal sprays for more than 3 to 5 days. Long use can make congestion worse.

### Combination Medicines

- Many over-the-counter pills combine antihistamines and decongestants.
- Do not take decongestants if you have high blood pressure unless your doctor says it is safe.
- Do not use these combination pills if you take a certain type of antidepressant (monoamine oxidase inhibitors).
- These pills are not safe for young children.

### Side Effects of Antihistamines

- Drowsiness.
- Dry mouth.
- Blurry vision.
- Constipation.
- Trouble urinating.
- Confusion or feeling dizzy.

### Other Medications

- **Cromolyn nasal spray** helps prevent symptoms. It must be used every day to work.
- **Azelastine** and **ipratropium** are prescription nasal sprays. They help with runny nose and swelling. They can cause drowsiness.
- **Montelukast** is a pill that reduces inflammation. It helps with a runny nose. It is used only if other medicines do not work. Side effects can include mood changes, anxiety, depression, or unusual muscle movements.

### Sinus Irrigation

- Use a saline (salt and water) solution to rinse your sinuses.
- This helps clear mucus and soothe the nasal lining.
- Use a neti pot or a squeeze bottle. Follow instructions carefully.

### Stronger Treatments (Short-Term)

- If symptoms are very bad, your doctor may prescribe a short course of oral or injected corticosteroids.
- These are only used for a few days (less than 10).
- Long-term use of corticosteroids can cause serious side effects.

### Eye Care

- Use artificial tears or plain eyewashes to soothe itchy eyes.
- Avoid wearing contact lenses during allergy flare-ups.
- **Over-the-counter eye drops** with antihistamines and a blood vessel constrictor can help.
  - They may not work as well as prescription drops.
  - They can cause side effects like dryness or stinging.
- **Prescription eye drops** with cromolyn can prevent symptoms. Use them before you expect to be exposed to allergens.
- **Corticosteroid eye drops** are used for severe eye symptoms. An eye doctor must check your eyes regularly during treatment to watch for increased pressure or infection.

### Oral Antihistamines for Eye and Body Symptoms

- Pills like fexofenadine can help if your ears, nose, or throat are also affected.

## Allergen Immunotherapy (Desensitization)

This treatment helps some people with severe allergies.

### How It Works

- You are given small, increasing doses of the allergen.
- The goal is to teach your immune system not to overreact.
- The first dose is tiny and safe.
- Over time, the dose is slowly increased.
- Eventually, your body stops reacting to the allergen.

### When It’s Used

- When symptoms are very bad.
- When you cannot avoid the allergen.
- When regular medicines do not help.

### How It’s Given

- **Allergy shots** (injections under the skin).
- **Sublingual tablets** (placed under the tongue).

### Safety

- You must stay in the doctor’s office for at least 30 minutes after each dose.
- This is to watch for serious reactions.
- If you use sublingual tablets and have no reaction after the first dose, you can take later doses at home.

### Best Time to Start

- Begin treatment after the pollen season ends.
- Starting during pollen season can cause more side effects.
- Treatment works best when taken every year, all year long.

### What to Carry

- Always carry a self-injecting epinephrine pen.
- It can save your life if you have a severe allergic reaction.
- Use it if you feel symptoms like trouble breathing, swelling, or dizziness.

## Summary

- Seasonal allergies are common and happen at certain times of year.
- They are caused by pollen, mold, or other airborne particles.
- Symptoms include itchy eyes, runny nose, sneezing, and congestion.
- Diagnosis is based on symptoms and timing.
- Treatments include nasal sprays, pills, eye drops, and sometimes immunotherapy.
- Avoid allergens when possible.
- See your doctor if symptoms are severe or do not improve with treatment.

# Carpal Tunnel Syndrome

Carpal tunnel syndrome causes pain, numbness, tingling, or weakness in your fingers, hand, or arm.

Your symptoms may come and go. They often get worse at night.

## When to See a Doctor

See a doctor if:
- Your symptoms are getting worse.
- Your symptoms are not improving after trying home treatments.

## Symptoms of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome

You may notice:
- Aching or pain in your fingers, hand, or arm.
- Numbness in your hand.
- Tingling or a pins-and-needles feeling.
- A weak thumb or trouble holding things.

These symptoms usually start slowly and may not happen all the time.

## How to Treat Carpal Tunnel Syndrome at Home

Carpal tunnel syndrome can improve on its own, especially if it is caused by pregnancy.

### Wear a Wrist Splint

A wrist splint keeps your wrist straight. It helps reduce pressure on the nerve.

Wear it at night while you sleep. You may need to wear it for up to 6 weeks before you feel better.

You can buy wrist splints at pharmacies or online.

### Stop or Reduce Activities That Cause Problems

Avoid things that make you bend your wrist often or grip tightly. This includes:
- Using vibrating tools at work.
- Playing musical instruments that require tight gripping.

### Use Painkillers

Painkillers like paracetamol or ibuprofen can help with short-term pain.

But they do not fix the cause of carpal tunnel syndrome. Do not rely on them for long-term relief.

### Try Hand Exercises

Some people find that hand exercises help ease symptoms. There is not much strong evidence, but they may help a little.

## What Happens at Your Doctor’s Appointment

Your doctor can often tell if you have carpal tunnel syndrome by asking about your symptoms and checking your hand.

If they are unsure, they may refer you to a hospital for:
- A nerve test to check how well your nerves are working.
- An ultrasound scan or MRI scan to look at your wrist.

## Treatment from Your Doctor

If a wrist splint does not help, your doctor may suggest a steroid injection into your wrist.

The injection reduces swelling around the nerve. This can ease your symptoms.

But the injection is not always a cure. Symptoms can return after a few months. You might need another injection.

### Self-Referral for Treatment

You may be able to get help for carpal tunnel syndrome without seeing a doctor first.

To find out if this is possible in your area:
- Ask the staff at your GP surgery.
- Check your GP surgery’s website.
- Contact your local integrated care board.
- Search online for NHS treatment for carpal tunnel syndrome near you.

## Surgery for Carpal Tunnel Syndrome

If your symptoms are getting worse and other treatments have not worked, your doctor may refer you to a specialist.

Surgery usually cures carpal tunnel syndrome. You and the specialist will decide together if surgery is right for you.

During surgery:
- A local anaesthetic is used to numb your wrist.
- A small cut is made in your hand.
- The tight tissue around the nerve is cut to relieve pressure.

The operation takes about 20 minutes. You can go home the same day.

It may take about a month to return to normal activities.

## What Causes Carpal Tunnel Syndrome

Carpal tunnel syndrome happens when the space in your wrist (called the carpal tunnel) swells. This puts pressure on a nerve in your hand.

You are more likely to get carpal tunnel syndrome if you:
- Are overweight.
- Are pregnant.
- Do work or hobbies that involve repeated wrist bending or tight gripping, such as using vibrating tools.
- Have health conditions like arthritis or diabetes.
- Have a family member with carpal tunnel syndrome.
- Have had a wrist injury before.

# Listeriosis

Listeriosis is an infection caused by bacteria called *Listeria*. It can affect many parts of the body. These include the blood, brain, skin, eyes, and unborn babies. It can also cause serious infections in newborns. In rare cases, it can affect the heart.

The symptoms depend on which part of the body is infected. If a pregnant person gets infected, it can lead to the death of the baby. The only way to confirm the infection is through lab tests. Treatment usually involves antibiotics like penicillin or ampicillin. Sometimes, another antibiotic called an aminoglycoside is added. Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole is also used in some cases.

---

## What Is *Listeria*?

*Listeria* are tiny bacteria. They do not have a protective coating. They can live in both air and water. They are found in soil, animals, birds, and seafood. They can also live in the intestines of people and animals.

There are several types of *Listeria*, but only one, *L. monocytogenes*, causes serious illness in people.

This bacteria is not a common cause of food poisoning. But when it does cause illness, it can be very serious. In the United States, about 1,600 people get listeriosis each year. About one in six older adults who get it die. From 2020 to 2022, fewer cases were reported. This may be because fewer people were tested during the pandemic.

Infections are most common in the summer. The highest risk is for newborns, adults 65 and older, and people with weak immune systems. This includes people with advanced HIV. Pregnant people are also at higher risk, especially if they are Hispanic.

Listeriosis is a disease that must be reported to health officials in the United States. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention tracks outbreaks using a national system. This helps find and stop outbreaks quickly.

---

## Symptoms of Listeriosis

### Blood Infection (Bacteremia)
This is rare. It causes high fever but no clear signs of infection in one area. Symptoms usually start about 5 days after eating contaminated food. But they can start anytime from 0 to 29 days later.

The bacteria can spread to other parts of the body. This can cause infections in the heart, belly, bones, joints, gallbladder, liver, or lungs.

Some people get stomach symptoms like nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. These usually start within 24 hours of eating contaminated food. They last 1 to 3 days.

If a pregnant person gets a blood infection, it can spread to the baby. This can cause early labor, infection of the placenta, or the death of the baby.

### Brain Infection (Meningitis)
Meningitis from *Listeria* is less common now. This is due to better food safety. It still happens in about 20 to 30% of cases worldwide. In the United States, it causes 2 to 8% of cases. The death rate is 15 to 29%.

It is most common in newborns. It also affects people over 60, those with alcohol use disorder, and people on immune-suppressing medicines. It also affects people with cancer, diabetes, liver or kidney disease, or pregnancy.

Some cases progress to brain swelling. This can cause confusion, weakness, or problems with movement. Rarely, it causes a type of brain infection called rhombencephalitis. This can cause loss of balance, tremors, or trouble with eye movement.

### Eye and Lymph Node Infection (Oculoglandular Listeriosis)
This is rare. It causes swelling in the eye and nearby lymph nodes. It can start after the bacteria enter the eye. If not treated, it can spread to the blood or brain.

---

## How Is Listeriosis Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose listeriosis by testing blood or spinal fluid. The lab must know that *Listeria* is suspected. This is because the bacteria look like other harmless bacteria under the microscope.

Stool tests are not usually needed for stomach infections.

A newer test called PCR can give results faster. It works well and matches the results of culture tests.

Antibody tests are not helpful for making treatment decisions. They only show past exposure.

---

## How Is Listeriosis Treated?

### For Mild Illness
If you are healthy and have mild fever or stomach symptoms, you may not need antibiotics. The illness will go away on its own.

But if you are at high risk, treatment should start right away.

### For Pregnant People
If a pregnant person has listeriosis, they must get IV ampicillin or amoxicillin right away. Treatment should last at least 2 weeks. This helps protect the baby.

### For High-Risk Adults and Immune-Weakened People
If you are over 60 or have a weak immune system, and you have mild fever or stomach symptoms, take oral amoxicillin or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.

Delaying treatment can lead to serious harm or death.

### For Brain Infection (Meningitis)
Treat with IV ampicillin for at least 21 days. In severe cases, a second antibiotic called gentamicin is often added. This is based on lab results, even though real-world proof is limited.

Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, fluoroquinolones, linezolid, meropenem, and rifampin are also used in some cases.

Cephalosporin antibiotics do not work. They should not be used. Some cases have failed with vancomycin.

### For Heart Infection (Endocarditis) and Other Severe Infections
Use IV ampicillin every 4 hours plus gentamicin. Treat for 6 weeks.

For blood infection alone, treat for 2 weeks after the fever goes away. Combination therapy is usually not needed.

### For Eye or Localized Infections
Use oral ampicillin or amoxicillin. Treatment is usually short.

---

## How to Prevent Listeriosis

*Listeria* can grow even in the refrigerator. A small amount of contamination can become a large amount over time. This is especially dangerous for ready-to-eat foods that are not cooked again before eating.

People at high risk should avoid these foods:

- Soft cheeses made from unpasteurized milk (like feta, Brie, Camembert, queso fresco, queso blanco)
- Raw (unpasteurized) milk and milk products. Even pasteurized products can be contaminated.
- Refrigerated hot dogs, deli meats, pâtés, and meat spreads. These must be heated until steaming hot before eating.
- Refrigerated smoked seafood (like lox, nova-style, kippered, or jerky). These must be cooked before eating.

---

## Key Points

- *Listeria* is common in nature but causes illness in only about 1,600 people in the U.S. each year.
- Most cases come from contaminated food.
- The highest risk is for newborns, adults 65 and older, pregnant people, and people with weak immune systems.
- Infection during pregnancy can harm or kill the baby.
- Treatment usually includes ampicillin or amoxicillin, sometimes with gentamicin.
- High-risk people should avoid certain foods to prevent infection.

# Metabolic Syndrome

Metabolic syndrome is a group of health problems that happen together. It raises your risk for serious diseases.

## What Is Metabolic Syndrome?

Metabolic syndrome means you have several health issues at once. These include:

- A large waist size (extra fat around your belly)
- High blood pressure
- High blood sugar (or insulin resistance, which can lead to type 2 diabetes)
- Unhealthy levels of fats in your blood, like cholesterol and triglycerides

Having extra fat in your belly is a key sign. It is more dangerous than fat stored in other areas like your hips.

## Who Is at Risk?

You are more likely to get metabolic syndrome if you store fat in your belly. This is common in:

- Most men
- Women after menopause

Even people who are not overweight can have too much belly fat. This can still raise your risk.

## Health Problems Linked to Metabolic Syndrome

Extra belly fat increases your risk of:

- Heart disease (coronary artery disease)
- High blood pressure
- Type 2 diabetes
- Unhealthy cholesterol and fat levels in the blood (dyslipidemia)
- Fatty liver disease (liver with too much fat)
- Gout (a painful joint condition)
- Polycystic ovary syndrome (in women)
- Kidney disease
- Sleep apnea (a breathing problem during sleep)
- Erectile dysfunction (in men)

Chronic stress can also raise your risk. It may change your hormones. This can cause belly fat to build up and make your body less able to use insulin properly (insulin resistance). Stress can also lower your good cholesterol (HDL).

Smoking increases your risk too. It raises triglycerides and lowers good cholesterol.

Metabolic syndrome does not cause symptoms. You may not know you have it until a health problem shows up.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors check for metabolic syndrome using:

- Waist size
- Blood pressure
- Blood tests after fasting (no food for at least 8 hours)

### Waist Size
- Measure your waist at the level of your belly button.
- A larger waist means higher risk.
- The risk level depends on your sex and ethnic group.

### Blood Tests
- Fasting blood sugar
- Fasting triglycerides (a type of fat in the blood)
- HDL cholesterol (the "good" kind)

### Diagnosis Criteria
You may have metabolic syndrome if you have a large waist and two or more of the following:

- Waist size: 40 inches or more in men, 35 inches or more in women
- Fasting blood sugar: 100 mg/dL or higher
- Blood pressure: 130/85 mm Hg or higher
- Triglycerides: 150 mg/dL or higher
- HDL cholesterol: less than 40 mg/dL in men, less than 50 mg/dL in women

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment focuses on lowering your risk of heart disease, diabetes, and other serious problems.

### Lifestyle Changes (First Step)
- Be more physically active every day
- Eat a heart-healthy diet
  - Less salt
  - Less sugar
  - Less unhealthy fat
  - More fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins

### Medications (If Needed)
- **For high blood sugar or diabetes:** Medicines like metformin or thiazolidinediones help your body use insulin better.
  - Exercise also helps lower blood sugar and improves insulin use.
- **For high blood pressure:** Medicines called antihypertensives can help.
- **For high cholesterol or fats in the blood:** Statins are often used to lower these levels.
- **For obesity:** Medicines like orlistat, phentermine, or liraglutide may help.
  - In some cases, weight-loss surgery (metabolic or bariatric surgery) is recommended.

### Other Important Steps
- Quit smoking
- Manage stress
  - Try deep breathing, meditation, counseling, or therapy

### Control Other Risks
- If you have other risk factors for heart disease, treat them too.
- For example, if you smoke, stop.

## Key Points

- Metabolic syndrome is common. Over 40% of adults over 50 in the United States may have it.
- Children and teens can get it too, but we do not know how many.
- It often has no symptoms. You may not know you have it.
- Early treatment can prevent serious health problems.
- Lifestyle changes are the most important first step.
- Medicines and surgery may help if lifestyle changes are not enough.

(See also: Obesity)

# Tendonitis

Tendonitis is when a tendon becomes inflamed. Tendons connect your muscles to your bones. This can happen in your knees, elbows, shoulders, and other joints.

## Symptoms of Tendonitis

You may have tendonitis if you notice:

- Pain in a tendon that gets worse when you move it  
- Trouble moving the joint  
- A grating or crackling feeling when you move the tendon  
- Swelling, and sometimes warmth or redness in the area  

If the pain starts suddenly and is very bad, you may have torn (ruptured) a tendon. You might also hear a popping or snapping sound at the time.

## What to Do If You Think You Have Tendonitis

### See a Doctor If:
- You hurt a joint and your symptoms do not get better after a few weeks

### Call NHS 111 If:
- You are in a lot of pain  
- You think you may have torn a tendon  

You can call 111 or get help online.

---

## How to Treat Tendonitis at Home

For 2 to 3 days, try these steps to help reduce pain and support the tendon:

- **Rest**: Avoid moving the tendon as much as possible for 2 to 3 days  
- **Ice**: Put an ice pack (or a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a tea towel) on the area for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours  
- **Support**: Wrap the area with an elastic bandage, use a tube bandage, or wear a soft brace. These are available at pharmacies. Make sure it is snug but not too tight  

Take off the bandage or brace before you go to bed.

When you can move the area without pain, start moving it gently. This helps keep the joint from getting stiff.

To avoid making it worse, avoid:
- Lifting heavy things  
- Strong gripping or twisting motions  
- Playing sports until the tendon has healed  

---

## Can a Pharmacist Help?

Yes. A pharmacist can help you choose the best painkiller. They may suggest:
- Paracetamol  
- Ibuprofen  
- Ibuprofen gel to rub on your skin  

They can give you advice on how to use these safely.

---

## Medical Treatment for Tendonitis

If you need medical help, your doctor may:
- Prescribe a stronger painkiller  
- Suggest using ibuprofen gel on your skin  

If the pain is severe, lasts a long time, or you cannot move the joint well, you may be referred for physiotherapy. You can also see a physiotherapist on your own.

If physiotherapy does not help, you may be referred to:
- A doctor who specialises in bones and muscles (orthopaedic specialist)  
- A local musculoskeletal clinic  

Some people with serious tendonitis may be offered:
- Steroid injections to reduce pain for a short time  
- Surgery to remove damaged tissue or repair a torn tendon  

---

## Self-Referral for Treatment

You may be able to get help for tendonitis without seeing a doctor first. You can refer yourself directly to some services.

To find out what is available in your area:
- Ask the staff at your GP surgery  
- Check your GP surgery’s website  
- Contact your local integrated care board (ICB) – [find your local ICB](https://www.england.nhs.uk/your-nhs-local-system/find-your-icb/)  
- Search online for “NHS treatment for tendonitis near me”  

---

## How to Prevent Tendon Problems

Tendonitis often happens from:
- Sudden, sharp movements  
- Repeating the same motion over and over  
- Poor posture or technique during work or sports  

This kind of injury is also called repetitive strain injury.

You cannot always prevent tendonitis. But you can lower your risk by:

### Do:
- Warm up before you exercise  
- Stretch gently after exercising  
- Wear supportive shoes or insoles when you exercise  
- Take breaks during repetitive tasks  

### Don’t:
- Overuse muscles that are already tired  
- Start a new sport without training first  
- Do the same repetitive movements for long periods without stopping

# Septic Abortion – Simple Explanation

## What Is Septic Abortion?

Septic abortion is a serious infection in the uterus. It can happen during or just after a miscarriage or an abortion. This is a medical emergency and needs quick treatment.

It usually happens when the uterus is cleaned out using dirty tools or unclean methods. This is more likely to happen if the abortion is done by someone without medical training. It can also happen if the person doing the procedure does not use clean tools or clean hands. This often occurs because of laws, lack of health care access, or personal reasons.

Another cause is when a miscarriage is not complete. If some tissue stays in the uterus, it can get infected. This is more likely if the neck of the uterus (cervix) is open.

## What Causes the Infection?

The infection is caused by bacteria. Common ones include:
- *Escherichia coli*
- *Enterobacter aerogenes*
- *Proteus vulgaris*
- Hemolytic streptococci
- Staphylococci
- Some types of anaerobic bacteria, like *Clostridium perfringens*

One or more of these bacteria can cause the infection.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms usually start within 24 to 48 hours after the abortion. They include:
- Chills
- Fever
- Vaginal discharge
- Pain in the lower belly or pelvis
- Swelling or tenderness in the lower belly (peritonitis)
- Vaginal bleeding
- Cervix that is open
- Passing tissue from the vagina

If the uterus is torn during the procedure, you may have sudden, severe pain in the lower belly or pelvis.

In serious cases, the infection can lead to septic shock. This can cause:
- Low body temperature
- Very low blood pressure
- Little or no urine
- Trouble breathing

If the infection is caused by *Clostridium perfringens*, you may also see:
- Low platelet count
- Bruising under the skin
- Dark urine
- Pale skin (anemia)
- Yellow skin or eyes (jaundice)
- Red or brown urine (due to blood in the urine)

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors will check your vital signs and do a physical exam of your belly and pelvis.

They will take blood samples to test for bacteria. This helps choose the right antibiotics.

They will also run blood tests to check:
- Your white blood cell count
- Liver function
- Electrolyte levels
- Blood sugar
- Kidney function (BUN and creatinine)
- Blood clotting (if you are bleeding a lot or your liver is not working right)

An ultrasound is done to check if any tissue is still in the uterus. This can help explain the infection.

If you have severe pain and signs of infection, doctors may suspect a hole in the uterus. But ultrasound may not always show this.

If you have signs of blood infection (septicemia), doctors will test for:
- Group A strep
- *Clostridia* bacteria

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment must start right away. It includes:

### 1. Strong Antibiotics
You will get antibiotics through a vein (IV). These are broad-spectrum, meaning they fight many types of bacteria.

A common treatment is:
- Clindamycin 900 mg every 8 hours
- Gentamicin 5 mg per kg once a day
- Plus ampicillin 2 grams every 4 hours (if needed)

Another option is:
- Ampicillin
- Gentamicin
- Metronidazole 500 mg every 8 hours

The antibiotics may be changed later based on test results.

### 2. Remove Remaining Tissue
Once you are stable, the doctor will remove any leftover tissue from the uterus. This is done to stop the infection from spreading.

### 3. Imaging Tests
If you are bleeding or have signs of organ damage, you may need more imaging. This could include MRI or other scans.

## Key Points to Remember

- Septic abortion is most often caused by dirty tools or unclean methods during an abortion.
- It is more common when abortions are done by people without medical training.
- It can also happen if a miscarriage is not complete and tissue stays in the uterus.
- Symptoms like fever, chills, vaginal discharge, and belly pain usually start within two days.
- Severe pain in the belly or pelvis may mean the uterus was torn.
- If you think you have septic abortion, start antibiotics right away and remove the tissue from the uterus as soon as possible.
- Blood tests are needed to guide treatment and check your overall health.

# Pityriasis Rosea – Simple Explanation

Pityriasis rosea is a skin condition that causes many small, scaly patches on the skin.  
The patches are usually light pink, tan, or rose-colored.  
It is not a serious condition and usually gets better on its own.

---

## What Causes Pityriasis Rosea?

Doctors are not sure what causes it.  
But it may be linked to a virus, such as human herpesvirus type 6, 7, or 8.  
It is not contagious. You cannot catch it from someone else.

Some medicines can cause a rash that looks like pityriasis rosea.  
These include:  
- ACE inhibitors  
- Hydrochlorothiazide  
- Captopril  
- Barbiturates  
- Metronidazole  
- Allopurinol  

If you are taking any of these medicines and get a rash, talk to your doctor.

---

## Who Gets Pityriasis Rosea?

It most often affects people between the ages of 10 and 35.  
Women are more likely to get it than men.

If a woman gets pityriasis rosea during pregnancy, especially in the first 15 weeks, there is a higher chance of having a baby too early (premature birth) or a stillbirth.  
But this does not happen in all cases.

---

## Symptoms of Pityriasis Rosea

The first sign is usually one large, scaly patch on the body.  
Doctors call this the "herald patch."  
It is about 1 to 4 inches across (2 to 10 centimeters).  
It often appears on the chest, back, or stomach.

This first patch may appear alone for a few days.  
Then, within 1 to 2 weeks, smaller patches show up on the body.

The new patches often appear on the trunk, arms, and legs.  
They are most common along the spine and spread outward.

- In people with light skin, the patches are usually pink, tan, or rose-colored.  
- In people with dark skin, the patches may look purple, very dark, or both.

In children, the rash often starts in the groin or underarms and spreads outward.  
Children and pregnant women may have little or no scaling.

Most people feel some itching.  
Some have mild itching. Others have strong itching that is hard to live with.

Some people feel unwell before the rash appears.  
They may have:  
- A low fever  
- Headache  
- Joint pain  
- Loss of appetite  
- A general feeling of being sick  

But some people have no early symptoms. The rash may appear without warning.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor can usually tell if you have pityriasis rosea just by looking at your skin.  
They will pay close attention to the shape, size, and pattern of the rash.  
The herald patch is a key clue.

No special tests are usually needed.  
But if the doctor is unsure, they may do a skin test or blood test to rule out other conditions.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Most people do not need treatment.  
The rash usually goes away on its own in 5 weeks.  
Sometimes it can last up to 2 months.

For itching, you can try:

- **Sunlight**: Natural sunlight may help reduce itching and clear the rash faster.  
- **Artificial light**: Light therapy (like UV light from a special lamp) can also help.  
- **Topical corticosteroids**: Creams or ointments applied to the skin can reduce itching. Use them only for a short time.  
- **Oral corticosteroids**: These are pills. They are only used if the itching is very bad and other treatments do not work.

**Acyclovir** is an antiviral medicine.  
It may help if you are in the early stage of the illness and have many patches or flu-like symptoms.  
Pregnant women with pityriasis rosea may be offered acyclovir.  
But this medicine does not lower the risk of premature birth or stillbirth.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

The rash usually goes away without treatment.  
Most people feel better in 5 weeks.  
Some may take up to 2 months to fully recover.

The skin may stay slightly darker or lighter in the area where the rash was.  
This usually fades over time.

There are no long-term health problems from pityriasis rosea.  
It does not come back in most people.

---

If you have any concerns, talk to your doctor.  
They can help you manage symptoms and make sure there is no other cause for your rash.

# Bartholin’s Cyst – Simple Guide

## What Is a Bartholin’s Cyst?

- A Bartholin’s cyst is a soft lump on one side of the opening of the vagina.
- It can be small and not cause any pain.
- It may grow to the size of a pea or even a golf ball.
- Some people feel discomfort when walking, sitting, or having sex.
- One side of the vaginal lips may look larger or swollen.

## When the Cyst Gets Infected

- If the cyst becomes infected, it can turn into an abscess.
- An abscess is a painful, swollen area filled with pus.
- Signs of an infected cyst include:
  - Pus coming from the lump
  - A bad smell from the lump
  - Feeling unwell or having a high temperature
  - Severe pain around the lump
  - The area becoming red, hot, and swollen

> Note: Redness can be hard to see on dark skin. Look for warmth, swelling, or tenderness instead.

## When to See a Doctor

### See your GP if:
- You notice a lump near your vagina.

### Get urgent help (call 111 or go online) if:
- The lump gets bigger and more painful in just hours or days
- You see pus in the lump
- You feel unwell or have a high temperature
- The lump becomes very tender, swollen, hot, and red

These signs may mean the cyst is infected and needs treatment.

You can call 111 or get help online at 111.nhs.uk.

## What a Bartholin’s Cyst Looks Like

- It appears as a soft lump on one side of the vaginal opening.
- It may be hidden inside the opening.

> Image credit: Richard Usatine MD / Science Photo Library

## What Happens at the GP Appointment

- The doctor will look at the lump.
- They will check for signs of infection.
- You can ask for someone to be in the room with you during the exam.
  - This can be a friend, family member, nurse, or trained staff.
- If the doctor is unsure what the lump is, they may refer you for more tests.

## How to Care for a Bartholin’s Cyst at Home

Most cysts go away on their own. But you can do things to feel better.

### Do:
- Sit in a warm bath a few times a day for 3 to 4 days.
- Use a clean cloth or cotton wool soaked in warm water.
- Hold it gently on the lump for a few minutes at a time.
- Take ibuprofen or paracetamol to help with pain.

### Do Not:
- Do not try to squeeze or drain the cyst yourself.
- This can cause infection and make things worse.

## What If the Cyst Breaks Open?

- If the cyst bursts on its own, this is normal and can ease the pain.
- Keep the area clean and dry to prevent infection.
- Wash with water and mild soap.
- Avoid using harsh products or douches.

## Treatment for an Infected Cyst

- If the cyst is infected, you will be given antibiotics.
- If antibiotics do not help, or if the cyst keeps coming back, you may need a small procedure.

### The Procedure
- The doctor will make a small cut in the cyst to drain the fluid.
- They may leave a small opening so fluid can keep draining.
- Or they may place a thin tube (called a catheter) into the cyst.
  - The tube stays in place for about 4 weeks.
  - Then it is removed.
- The procedure can be done under local anaesthetic (you stay awake) or general anaesthetic (you are asleep).

### During the Procedure
- The doctor may take a sample of fluid from the lump.
- This is tested to check for infection.

## Key Points to Remember

- A Bartholin’s cyst is a lump near the vaginal opening.
- It often goes away on its own.
- Warm baths and pain relief can help with discomfort.
- Do not try to drain it yourself.
- See a doctor if the lump gets worse, has pus, or you feel unwell.
- Early treatment can prevent complications.

# Fevers During Pregnancy

A high fever during the first three months of pregnancy can be harmful to your baby.

A fever above 39.5 degrees Celsius (103 degrees Fahrenheit) in the first trimester may lead to:

- Losing the baby early (spontaneous abortion)
- Problems with the baby’s brain or spine

A fever later in pregnancy may increase the chance of going into labor too early (preterm labor).

Treating the fever is important. First, doctors will try to find and treat the cause of the fever.

To lower your body temperature, you may be given medicine called antipyretics. These help reduce fever.

If your body temperature is very high, doctors may use cooling blankets to help bring it down.

# Problems With Amniotic Fluid

Amniotic fluid is the liquid that surrounds your baby inside the uterus. This fluid and your baby are held inside a sac called the amniotic sac. Problems with amniotic fluid can happen in several ways:

- Too much fluid for how far along your pregnancy is  
- Too little fluid for how far along your pregnancy is  
- Infection in the fluid, the amniotic sac, or the placenta (called an intraamniotic infection)

---

## Too Much Amniotic Fluid

Too much amniotic fluid is called polyhydramnios or hydramnios. It can stretch your uterus and make it hard to breathe.

This can happen because of:

- Birth defects in the baby, especially a blockage in the baby’s esophagus or urinary tract  
- Carrying more than one baby (twins, triplets, etc.)  
- Diabetes in the mother  
- Anemia in the baby, such as when the mother’s blood attacks the baby’s blood (called hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn)  
- Other health problems in the baby, like infections or a genetic condition  
- In many cases, doctors do not know the cause

Too much fluid can lead to:

- Early labor  
- Water breaking early (prelabor rupture of membranes)  
- Placental abruption (placenta detaching too soon)  
- The baby being in a bad position, which may require a cesarean delivery  
- Severe breathing problems for the mother  
- The umbilical cord slipping out before the baby (umbilical cord prolapse)  
- The uterus not being able to contract well after delivery (uterine atony)  
- Heavy bleeding after delivery (postpartum hemorrhage)  
- Loss of the baby before birth (fetal death)

---

## Too Little Amniotic Fluid

Too little amniotic fluid is called oligohydramnios. It can happen because of:

- Poor blood flow between the uterus and placenta. This can happen if the mother has high blood pressure or if the placenta detaches too early (placental abruption)  
- Some medicines  
- The membranes around the baby breaking too early  
- A pregnancy that goes past 42 weeks  
- A chromosome problem in the baby  
- Birth defects in the baby’s urinary tract, especially the kidneys  
- A pregnancy that lasts too long  
- The baby not growing as expected (intrauterine growth restriction)  
- Loss of the baby before birth (fetal death)

In many cases, doctors do not know the cause.

Some medicines can cause too little fluid. These include:

- ACE inhibitors (like enalapril or captopril) – used for high blood pressure or heart failure  
- NSAIDs (like ibuprofen) – used for pain or inflammation

These medicines are usually avoided during pregnancy. But in rare cases, they may be needed to treat serious heart problems.

Too little fluid can cause:

- The baby not growing as expected (intrauterine growth restriction)  
- Limb or facial problems (if the fluid is very low and the problem starts early in pregnancy)  
- Lungs not developing fully  
- The baby not being able to handle labor, which may lead to a cesarean delivery  
- Loss of the baby before birth (fetal death)

---

## Symptoms of Amniotic Fluid Problems

Most women do not feel any symptoms when there is too much or too little amniotic fluid.

You might notice that your baby is moving less than before.

If there is too much fluid, you might:

- Have trouble breathing  
- Have painful contractions before your due date

Other conditions that cause fluid problems may cause symptoms of their own.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Amniotic Fluid Problems

Doctors use several tools to check for problems:

- A physical exam  
- Ultrasound  
- Tests to find the cause

Doctors may suspect a problem if:

- Your belly is much bigger or smaller than expected for your stage of pregnancy  
- Your baby is not moving as much as it should

Sometimes, the problem is found by chance during an ultrasound. If a problem is found, the ultrasound can show how much fluid is present.

If too much or too little fluid is found, doctors look for a cause. For example:

- They may check your vagina and cervix to see if the membranes broke too early  
- They may do blood tests to check for conditions like diabetes  
- They may use ultrasound and other tests (possibly amniocentesis) to check for birth defects or genetic problems in the baby

---

## Treatment of Amniotic Fluid Problems

Treatment includes:

- Regular ultrasounds to check the baby’s growth and fluid levels  
- Monitoring the baby’s heart rate  
- Treating any health problems in the mother  
- Removing extra fluid, if needed  
- Delivering the baby

Doctors do ultrasounds often to track the baby’s growth and fluid levels. They also check the baby’s heart rate when the baby is still and when it moves. This test is called nonstress testing. It helps check if the baby is doing well.

Any health problems in the mother, such as diabetes or high blood pressure, are treated.

When there is too much fluid:

- Doctors rarely remove the extra fluid  
- But they may remove it with a needle through the belly if:
  - Labor starts too early  
  - The mother has serious symptoms

In some cases, doctors plan to deliver the baby around 39 weeks if there is too much fluid.

When there is too little fluid:

- Most experts recommend delivery between 36 and 37 weeks, depending on how the baby is doing

# Hyperparathyroidism – Simple Explanation

Hyperparathyroidism means your body has too much calcium. This can cause health problems over time.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many people with hyperparathyroidism have no symptoms at all. Some may only find out they have it during tests for another issue.

If you do have symptoms, they can include:

- Feeling very tired
- Aches and pains in your joints, hands, arms, feet, or legs
- Weak muscles
- Feeling sick or being sick
- Not wanting to eat
- Constipation
- Stomach pain
- Always feeling thirsty
- Needing to pee more than usual
- Feeling low or sad (depression)

## What Causes It?

Your body needs calcium to keep your bones and teeth strong. A small group of glands in your neck called the parathyroid glands control how much calcium your body has.

Hyperparathyroidism happens when these glands make too much calcium. There are two main reasons:

- **Primary hyperparathyroidism**: One or more of your parathyroid glands grow a non-cancerous lump. This causes too much calcium.
- **Secondary hyperparathyroidism**: Another health problem, like long-term kidney disease, lowers your calcium. Your glands then work harder to fix it, which can lead to too much calcium.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors check for hyperparathyroidism using blood and urine tests.

Most people find out they have it by accident when getting tests for something else.

If you have hyperparathyroidism, your doctor may suggest more tests to check your health and plan treatment. These can include:

- Ultrasound scans
- X-rays
- Bone density scans

## What Are the Treatments?

You will be referred to a specialist if you are diagnosed.

Treatment depends on your calcium levels, your symptoms, and your overall health.

You may not need treatment if your calcium levels are only slightly high and you have no symptoms.

If you do need treatment, surgery is the most common option. The surgeon removes part or all of the parathyroid glands in your neck.

If surgery is not possible or you do not want it, your doctor may give you medicine to lower your calcium levels.

After surgery, you may still need medicine if your calcium levels stay high.

> **Important**: Do not change your diet to lower calcium unless your doctor tells you to. Changing your diet without advice can make your symptoms worse or cause new problems.

## What Can Happen If It’s Not Treated?

Untreated hyperparathyroidism can lead to serious health issues, including:

- **Osteoporosis**: Bones become weak and more likely to break
- **Kidney stones**: Hard lumps that form in your kidneys
- **High blood pressure**: This raises your risk of heart disease and stroke

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if you think you might have hyperparathyroidism.

# Metabolic Syndrome

Metabolic syndrome is a group of health problems that happen together.  
It increases your risk for heart disease, stroke, and type 2 diabetes.  

## What Is Metabolic Syndrome?

You have metabolic syndrome if you have at least three of the following five conditions:

- A large waist size (extra fat around your belly)  
- High blood pressure  
- High blood sugar (glucose) when you have not eaten for a while  
- High levels of triglycerides (a type of fat in the blood)  
- Low levels of good cholesterol (HDL)  

These problems are linked to having too much fat around your middle.  
This kind of fat is more dangerous than fat stored in your hips or thighs.  

## Who Gets Metabolic Syndrome?

More people get metabolic syndrome as they get older.  
In the United States, about 23 out of 100 adults have it.  
Among people aged 60 to 69, about 44 out of 100 have it.  
Among people aged 70 and older, about 42 out of 100 have it.  

Children and teens can also develop this condition.  
But doctors do not have a single clear rule to define it in young people.  

## Why Does It Happen?

Extra fat around your belly causes problems in your body.  
This fat sends too many fatty acids into your liver and muscles.  
This leads to fat building up in your liver and muscles.  

Your body starts to resist insulin.  
Insulin is a hormone that helps control blood sugar.  
When your body resists insulin, your blood sugar goes up.  
Your body makes more insulin to try to fix this, which can cause health issues.  

You may also develop:  
- High blood pressure  
- Bad cholesterol levels (high triglycerides, low HDL)  
- High levels of uric acid (which can lead to gout)  
- A blood that is more likely to clot  
- Chronic low-grade inflammation  

Some experts believe long-term stress may play a role.  
Stress can change your hormones.  
These changes may lead to belly fat, insulin resistance, and low good cholesterol.  

## Risks of Metabolic Syndrome

Having metabolic syndrome raises your risk for:  
- Sleep apnea (a condition where breathing stops during sleep)  
- Fatty liver disease (when fat builds up in the liver)  
- Kidney disease that lasts a long time  
- Polycystic ovary syndrome (in women)  
- Low testosterone or trouble getting an erection (in men)  
- Smoking (which makes triglycerides worse and lowers good cholesterol)  

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors check for metabolic syndrome using simple tests.  
They look at:  
- Your waist size  
- Your blood pressure  
- Your blood sugar after fasting  
- Your cholesterol and triglyceride levels  

If you have a family history of type 2 diabetes, especially if you are 40 or older,  
your doctor may test you even if you do not have symptoms.  
You should be tested if your waist size is too big for your sex and race.  

### Diagnosis Criteria

You are diagnosed with metabolic syndrome if you meet **three or more** of these five criteria:

| Condition | Men | Women |
|--------|-----|-------|
| Waist size | 102 cm or more (40 inches or more) | 88 cm or more (35 inches or more) |
| Fasting blood sugar | 100 mg/dL or more (5.6 mmol/L or more) | 100 mg/dL or more (5.6 mmol/L or more) |
| Blood pressure | 130/85 mm Hg or higher | 130/85 mm Hg or higher |
| Triglycerides | 150 mg/dL or more (1.7 mmol/L or more) | 150 mg/dL or more (1.7 mmol/L or more) |
| HDL cholesterol | Less than 40 mg/dL (1.04 mmol/L) | Less than 50 mg/dL (1.29 mmol/L) |

## How Is It Treated?

The best way to treat metabolic syndrome is to make healthy lifestyle changes.  
These changes can improve or even reverse the condition.

### Lifestyle Changes

- Eat a heart-healthy diet  
- Exercise regularly  
- Lose weight if needed  

A heart-healthy diet means:  
- More fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins  
- Less salt, sugar, and unhealthy fats  

Exercise should include:  
- Aerobic activity (like walking, swimming, or biking)  
- Strength training (like lifting weights or using resistance bands)  

Behavioral therapy can help you stick to your plan.  
It teaches you how to make lasting changes.  

### Medications

If lifestyle changes are not enough, your doctor may prescribe medicine.  

- **Metformin** helps your body use insulin better.  
- **Statins** lower bad cholesterol and reduce heart disease risk.  
- **Thiazolidinediones** (like rosiglitazone or pioglitazone) improve insulin sensitivity.  

Weight loss of about 7% can often reverse metabolic syndrome.  
If that does not work, treat each problem separately to reach healthy goals.  
Medicines are very effective when used correctly.  

### For Obesity

If you are very overweight, your doctor may suggest:  
- **Anti-obesity medicines** (like orlistat, phentermine, or liraglutide)  
- **Metabolic or bariatric surgery** (if needed)  

These options can help you lose weight and improve your health.  

### Other Important Steps

- Quit smoking  
- Manage stress with deep breathing, meditation, or counseling  
- Stay active — even if you do not lose weight, exercise helps your heart  

## Key Points

- Extra fat around your belly leads to high blood sugar, high blood pressure, bad cholesterol, and insulin resistance.  
- If you have three or more of these problems, you have metabolic syndrome.  
- It is very common, especially in people over 60.  
- Check your waist size, blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol levels.  
- Focus on healthy eating, regular exercise, and managing other risks.  
- If lifestyle changes are not enough, medicines or surgery may help.

# Lice Infestation – Simple Explanation

Lice are tiny insects that live on or in your body. They feed on your blood. They are not a sign of poor hygiene. Anyone can get lice.

## How Lice Spread

- Lice spread most often through close contact with another person.
- They can also spread through shared clothing, hats, combs, brushes, or bedding.
- Lice do not jump or fly. They crawl.
- Lice are not linked to being dirty or poor.

## Types of Lice

There are three types of lice. Each lives in a different part of the body.

### Head Lice
- Live in the hair on your head.
- Most common in children aged 5 to 11.
- Less common in people with Black hair.
- Spread by close contact or shared items like combs and hats.
- Can be hard to see, but their eggs (called nits) are easier to spot.

### Body Lice
- Live in clothing and bedding, not on the skin.
- Found in people with poor hygiene or in crowded living conditions.
- Spread by sharing dirty clothes or bedding.
- Can carry serious diseases like typhus, trench fever, and relapsing fever.

### Pubic Lice (Also Called “Crabs”)
- Live in pubic hair and around the anus.
- Usually spread through sexual contact.
- Can also spread to children through close contact with parents.
- Can live in other body hair, like chest, leg, beard, mustache, or eyelashes.
- Spread by sharing towels, bedding, or clothing.

## What Lice Look Like

- Lice are tiny, wingless bugs.
- They are about 1/8 inch (3 millimeters) long.
- They are hard to see with the naked eye.
- Their eggs (nits) are small, shiny, and stick tightly to hair near the scalp.

## Symptoms of Lice

- **Head lice**: Itching on the scalp. Some children feel nothing at all.
- **Body lice**: Itching and small red spots on the skin. These spots often appear on the shoulders, buttocks, and belly. Scratching can cause skin breaks and infections.
- **Pubic lice**: Itching in the genital area. Blue-gray marks may appear on the chest, buttocks, or thighs. Lymph nodes may swell. If lice get into the eyelashes, the eyes may itch, burn, or feel irritated.

## How Doctors Diagnose Lice

- Doctors look for live lice or their eggs (nits).
- For head lice: A fine-tooth comb is used on wet hair. Lice are often found at the back of the head or behind the ears.
- Nits are hard to remove. They stick tightly to hair and do not fall off easily.
- For pubic lice: A special light or microscope may be used to see them. Dark brown spots (louse waste) may be seen on skin or underwear.
- Body lice and their eggs are found in the seams of clothes and bedding.

## How to Treat Lice

### For Head and Pubic Lice

- Use special shampoos, creams, or lotions. These are available over the counter or by prescription.
- Follow the instructions carefully.
- Treat all family members at the same time.
- Repeat treatment in 7 to 10 days to kill new lice that hatch.

#### Common Treatments

- **Pyrethrins plus piperonyl butoxide**: Over-the-counter shampoo or cream. Apply for 10 minutes, then rinse.
- **Permethrin**: Prescription cream or liquid. Works well. Apply as directed.
- **Spinosad**: Prescription liquid. Apply to dry hair and scalp. Leave on for 10 minutes. Rinse with warm water. Avoid eyes. If live lice are still seen after 7 days, repeat treatment.
- **Malathion**: Prescription medicine. Kills both lice and eggs. It is strong, flammable, and smells bad. Must stay on the skin for 8 to 12 hours. Not used first because of risks.
- **Lindane**: Prescription lotion or shampoo. Not used anymore. It can be harmful and many lice are now resistant.

#### If Lice Are Hard to Kill

- Ivermectin is a pill. Doctors may prescribe it if lice do not respond to other treatments.

### Removing Nits (Eggs)

- Most treatments kill lice but not all nits.
- Dead nits do not need to be removed, but many people choose to.
- Use a fine-tooth comb to remove nits.
- Some products (shampoos, gels, sprays) help loosen nits.
- A hot hair dryer for 30 minutes may help kill nits.
- Nits grow out with the hair. If no nits are within 1/4 inch (0.64 cm) of the scalp, there are no live lice.

### For Lice in the Eyelashes

- Use petroleum jelly for 8 to 10 days.
- Use special eye drops (fluorescein).
- Take ivermectin by mouth.
- Use petrolatum salve or physostigmine ointment.
- A doctor may remove lice one by one with a tool.

### For Body Lice

- Do not use medicine on the skin.
- Lice live in clothes and bedding.
- Wash all clothing and bedding in hot water.
- Dry items in a machine at 130° F (54° C) for at least 30 minutes.
- If items cannot be washed, seal them in a plastic bag for 2 weeks.
- Heat is key. Dry items at 149° F (65° C) or higher.

## Cleaning Clothes and Bedding

- Wash all clothing, bedding, and towels in hot water.
- Dry them in a hot dryer for at least 30 minutes.
- Items that cannot be washed can be sealed in a plastic bag for 2 weeks.
- You do not need to throw away personal items unless they are very dirty.

## School or Work

- There is no need to keep a child out of school or an adult out of work just because of lice.
- Lice are not a health risk that spreads easily in schools or workplaces.
- Focus on treating the person and cleaning shared items.

## Important Notes

- Lice are not dangerous, but they can be itchy and annoying.
- Lice are becoming resistant to some medicines.
- Always follow treatment instructions.
- Treat everyone in the household at the same time.
- Check for lice again after 7 to 10 days.

If you are unsure what to do, talk to a doctor or nurse. They can help you choose the best treatment.

# Enlarged Prostate

An enlarged prostate is common in men over 50. It can cause problems with peeing.

## Symptoms

You may have trouble starting to pee.  
Your pee may come out slowly or weakly.  
You may need to pee more often.  
You might wake up at night to pee.  
You may feel like your bladder is not empty after you pee.  
You may dribble after you finish peeing.  

These symptoms usually get worse slowly over time.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:
- You have trouble peeing.
- You need to pee more often.

Don’t feel embarrassed. Doctors see these issues all the time.

Call NHS 111 or get help online if:
- Your pee looks pink, red, or brown.
- You have pain when you pee.
- You cannot pee at all.

## How It’s Diagnosed

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms.  
They may check your tummy and penis.  
They may put a finger in your bottom to feel your prostate. This is called a rectal exam.

You may be asked to keep a diary for 3 days.  
Write down how much you drink and how often and how much you pee.

Your doctor may do tests, such as:
- A urine test.
- A blood test called a PSA test.

You may be referred to a specialist. They may do more tests, such as:
- A urine flow test. You pee into a machine that measures how fast you pee.
- An ultrasound scan of your bladder.
- A cystoscopy. A small camera is used to look inside your bladder.

## Treatment Options

Not everyone needs treatment.  
Treatment depends on how bad your symptoms are.

If symptoms are mild, your doctor may suggest lifestyle changes first.

If symptoms get worse, you may need medicine or surgery.

### Medicines

You may be offered medicine if your symptoms are moderate or severe.  
Medicines can help with:
- Starting to pee.
- Peing more often or urgently.
- Slowing down prostate growth.

Common medicines include:
- Tamsulosin, doxazosin, or alfuzosin – help you pee more easily.
- Oxybutynin or tolterodine – help with needing to pee often or urgently.
- Finasteride or dutasteride – reduce hormone levels to slow prostate growth.

These medicines can cause side effects.  
Your doctor will explain the benefits and risks.  
You will have regular check-ups to see how well the medicine is working.

### Surgery

Surgery may be an option if medicine does not help or your symptoms are severe.

The most common surgery is called TURP.  
It removes part of the prostate through a thin tube passed up the penis.

Other options include:
- Using lasers, electricity, steam, or water to remove or destroy part of the prostate.
- Putting a small device in the prostate to keep the tube open.
- Making small cuts in the prostate to widen the tube.
- Removing part of the prostate with surgery.

Your surgeon will explain your choices.  
They will talk about the risks and benefits of each option.

### Support and Other Treatments

You can get help to manage symptoms.  
This includes:
- Pads, special pants, or sheaths to handle leaks or dribbling.
- A urinary catheter – a tube to drain pee if you cannot empty your bladder.
- Bladder training – slowly increasing how long you hold your pee.
- Pelvic floor exercises – to strengthen muscles that control your bladder.

## What You Can Do to Help

### Do These Things:
- Cut down on alcohol and caffeine. They make you pee more.
- Drink less fluid before bed or before going out. But drink enough during the day.
- Eat more fibre. This helps prevent constipation. Constipation can press on your bladder.
- Stay at a healthy weight. Being overweight can make symptoms worse.
- Wait a few seconds after you finish peeing. Then try again to empty your bladder.
- After peeing, press gently with your fingers. Place them 3 finger widths behind your scrotum. Move them forward and up toward the base of your penis. This can help push out the last drops.
- Ask your doctor or pharmacist if any other medicines you take could make your symptoms worse.

### Avoid These:
- Do not strain or push when you pee. Try to relax.
- Do not drink too little fluid. This can cause infections.

## What Causes an Enlarged Prostate?

It may be linked to changes in hormone levels as you age.  
It is more common in men over 50.  
It can run in families.

An enlarged prostate is not cancer.  
It does not raise your risk of getting prostate cancer.
