# Sleep Paralysis

Sleep paralysis means you are awake but cannot move or speak.  
You might feel like someone is in the room with you.  
You might also feel pressure on your chest, as if something is pushing you down.

These feelings can last for a few seconds to several minutes.  
They can be very frightening.

---

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if you often have sleep paralysis and you feel:

* very anxious or scared about going to bed  
* tired all the time because you are not sleeping well

---

## What Happens During Sleep Paralysis

While you are asleep, your body is relaxed.  
Your brain stays awake during sleep paralysis.  
You are aware of your surroundings but cannot move your body.  
You may not be able to speak or open your eyes.  
You might feel a presence in the room.  
You might feel pressure on your chest.  
You may feel scared or panicked.

---

## How to Help Prevent Sleep Paralysis

You can reduce your chances of sleep paralysis by improving your sleep habits.

### Do These Things

* Aim for 7 to 9 hours of sleep each night.  
* Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day.  
* Exercise regularly, but not within 4 hours of bedtime.

### Avoid These Things

* Do not eat a large meal before bed.  
* Do not smoke before bed.  
* Do not drink alcohol or caffeine before bed.  
* Try not to sleep on your back. This position can make sleep paralysis more likely.

---

## Treating Sleep Paralysis

Your doctor may check for other health problems that could be causing sleep paralysis.  
These include trouble sleeping or stress from past trauma.

If another condition is found, treating it may help.  
If not, your doctor may refer you to a sleep specialist.

### Treatment from a Sleep Specialist

You may be given a medicine that is usually used to treat depression.  
The doctor may prescribe a low dose of this medicine.  
This can help reduce sleep paralysis.

You may also be offered a type of talking therapy called cognitive behavioural therapy.  
This helps you change thoughts and habits that make sleep paralysis worse.

# Pinworm Infection

Pinworm infection is caused by a small worm that lives in the intestines.  
The worm is called *Enterobius vermicularis*.  
It is most common in school-aged children.  
Adults who live with infected children, caregivers, people in long-term care homes, and those who have oral-anal contact during sex are also at risk.

The main symptom is itching around the anus or in the vagina.  
Many people have no symptoms at all.  
Some people scratch the area, which can lead to skin sores.  
In rare cases, the worms can move into the vagina and cause irritation or infection.  
Very rarely, they can cause problems in the belly area.

Pinworm infection affects more than one billion people worldwide.  
It is most common in children.  
One study found about 1 in 5 young children in Europe had pinworms.

Because children often get pinworms, their family members and caregivers are also at risk.  
People in long-term care homes are also more likely to get infected.  
The infection can spread through sexual contact that involves the mouth and anus.

---

## How Pinworms Spread

Pinworm eggs become infectious within a few hours after they leave the body.  
The eggs can live on surfaces like clothes, bedding, furniture, rugs, and toys.  
People can pick up the eggs on their hands and then put their hands in their mouth.  
This is how they swallow the eggs and become infected.

Thumb sucking increases the risk.  
People can also get reinfected by touching the area around the anus and then touching their mouth.

The worms grow in the lower part of the intestines.  
It takes 2 to 6 weeks for them to become adults.  
The female worm comes out of the anus at night to lay eggs.  
The eggs are sticky and cause itching.  
The movement of the worm and the sticky coating on the eggs make the area itch.

Pinworm eggs can survive on surfaces for up to 3 weeks at room temperature.

---

## What to Look For

Most people with pinworms do not have any symptoms.  
Some people have itching around the anus.  
Scratching can cause skin sores.  
In some cases, a secondary skin infection can develop.

If the worms move into the vagina, it can cause itching and irritation.  
Very rarely, they can travel further into the female reproductive system and cause problems in the belly.

Some people believe pinworms cause stomach pain, trouble sleeping, or seizures.  
But there is no strong proof that pinworms cause these problems.  
Pinworms have been found in the appendix in some cases of appendicitis.  
But this may just be a coincidence.

---

## How to Diagnose Pinworm Infection

You can check for pinworms by looking for them around the anus.  
The best time to look is 1 or 2 hours after going to bed at night, or in the morning before getting out of bed.

You can also use a piece of clear tape to collect eggs.  
Press the tape gently against the skin around the anus.  
Then place the tape on a glass slide and look at it under a microscope.  
This is called the cellophane tape test.

The eggs are small and oval.  
They are about the size of a grain of sand.  
They have a thin shell and contain a tiny worm inside.

To make the eggs easier to see, a small drop of toluene can be added between the tape and the slide.  
This removes air bubbles and helps clear the view.

Do this test for 3 mornings in a row if needed.  
If a child has vaginal itching or discharge, the same test can be done at the opening of the vagina.

In some cases, eggs can be found under fingernails.  
Less often, eggs may show up in stool, urine, or vaginal samples.

---

## How to Treat Pinworm Infection

Treatment is only needed if the person has symptoms.  
The infection is usually not serious.  
But many parents want treatment when their child has pinworms.

Three medicines are used: mebendazole, pyrantel pamoate, or albendazole.  
Take one dose of any of these medicines.  
Take a second dose 2 weeks later.  
This treatment works in more than 90% of cases.

The medicine kills the worms but not the eggs.  
That is why a second dose is needed.

To help with itching, you can use a cream or ointment on the skin around the anus.  
Some creams contain carbolic acid or other ingredients that reduce itching.

---

## How to Prevent Pinworms

Reinfection is common.  
Eggs can still be passed in the stool for up to 1 week after treatment.  
Eggs that were already in the environment can live for 3 weeks.

It is common for more than one person in a household to get infected.  
Treating the whole family may be needed.

To stop the spread of pinworms:

- Wash hands with soap and warm water after using the toilet.  
- Wash hands after changing diapers.  
- Wash hands before handling food.  
- This is the most effective way to prevent infection.  
- Wash clothes, bedding, and toys often.  
- If someone is infected, take a shower every morning to wash off eggs from the skin.  
- Vacuum floors and furniture to remove eggs.  
- Avoid oral-anal contact during sex.

---

## Key Facts

- Pinworm infection is the most common worm infection in the United States.  
- It mostly affects school-aged children and younger kids.  
- Adults who care for children, family members of infected children, people in long-term care homes, and those who have oral-anal contact during sex are also at risk.  
- The infection is usually not harmful.  
- Reinfection is common.  
- Pinworm eggs can live in the environment for up to 3 weeks.  
- Eggs can be swallowed after touching the mouth following scratching or handling dirty items like clothes or bedding.  
- Most people have no symptoms.  
- The main symptom is itching around the anus.  
- Diagnosis is done by collecting eggs in the morning with clear tape and checking them under a microscope.  
- You can also find the female worm in the area around the anus at night.  
- If symptoms are present, treat with mebendazole, pyrantel pamoate, or albendazole.  
- Take the medicine once, then again 2 weeks later.

# Heel Bursitis

Bursitis means swelling and pain in a small, fluid-filled sac. These sacs help reduce rubbing between tissues and bones.

This type of bursitis happens at the bottom of the heel bone.

## Symptoms

- The heel may hurt and throb.
- The pain often gets worse when walking barefoot on hard floors.
- The heel may feel warm to the touch.
- The heel may look slightly swollen.
- The pain is usually worst when your heel first hits the ground while walking or running.

## Diagnosis

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and check your heel. They will not need an X-ray or scan to make the diagnosis.

## Treatment

- Your doctor may give you a shot into the heel. The shot contains medicine to reduce pain and swelling.
- You should wear shoes with soft soles.
- Add extra padding under the heel for protection.
- Avoid walking barefoot on hard surfaces.

# Herpetic Whitlow (Whitlow Finger)

Herpetic whitlow is a painful infection on your finger. It is caused by a virus called herpes simplex.

## Symptoms

You may notice:
- Swelling and pain in your finger
- Blisters or open sores on your finger
- Red or darker skin around the affected area
- Feeling unwell, with a high temperature

The infection usually starts on the top of your finger or thumb.

## When to See a Doctor

See a doctor if:
- You think you have herpetic whitlow
- Your symptoms get worse
- You have a very high temperature
- You feel hot and shivery

Getting help early makes treatment more effective. It can also stop the infection from spreading.

## Treatment from a Doctor

If you see a doctor within 48 hours of your symptoms starting, you may be given antiviral tablets.

These tablets can help your finger heal faster.

If you do not see a doctor within 48 hours, the infection will usually go away on its own in 2 to 3 weeks.

## What You Can Do at Home

You can help ease your symptoms by:
- Taking painkillers like paracetamol or ibuprofen
- Keeping your finger clean and covered with a dressing
- Avoiding touching the infected finger

### Do This:
- Keep the finger clean and covered with a bandage or dressing
- Take painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen to reduce pain
- If you have a child with whitlow, try to stop them from sucking their thumb

### Do Not Do This:
- Do not touch the infected finger with your other hand
- Do not touch other people with your infected finger
- Do not squeeze or try to drain the blisters
- Do not touch other parts of your body with the infected finger, especially your eyes
- If you wear contact lenses, use your other hand to put them in and take them out
- If you wear contact lenses, consider using glasses until the infection heals

## Causes

Herpetic whitlow is caused by the herpes simplex virus.

You can catch it by touching a cold sore or blister on another person who has the virus.

You are more likely to get it if:
- You have had cold sores before
- You have had genital herpes
- You have a weak immune system (for example, if you have diabetes or are having chemotherapy)

Your first time getting herpetic whitlow is usually the worst.

# What You Need to Know About Fungal Skin and Nail Infections

Fungal infections of the skin and nails are called dermatophytoses.  
They are caused by fungi that feed on keratin.  
Keratin is a protein found in the outer layer of skin, hair, and nails.  
When nails are infected, it is called onychomycosis.

These infections can appear in different places on the body.  
Symptoms depend on where the infection is.  
Doctors diagnose them by looking at the skin and testing skin scrapings.  
Treatment depends on the location but always includes antifungal medicine.

## Types of Fungi That Cause Infections

Some fungi can cause disease.  
Two main types are yeasts and molds.  
Yeasts are single-celled. An example is *Candida albicans*.  
Dermatophytes are molds. They grow in long threads.  
They need keratin to survive.  
They live only on the outer layer of skin, hair, or nails.  
The most common types that infect people are *Epidermophyton*, *Microsporum*, and *Trichophyton*.  
These infections do not spread deep into the body.  
This is different from yeast infections like candidiasis.

## How the Infection Spreads

You can get these infections from:
- Another person
- An animal
- Rarely, from soil

The fungus can stay in the body for a long time.  
Most people do not get sick from it.  
But some people do.  
This happens when their immune system is weak.  
This can be due to:
- Injury to the skin that affects blood flow
- A genetic condition
- Diseases like diabetes or HIV

## Common Types of Fungal Infections

- **Tinea barbae**: Infection of the beard area
- **Tinea capitis**: Infection of the scalp
- **Tinea corporis**: Infection of the body (like the arms or legs)
- **Tinea cruris**: Infection of the groin area (jock itch)
- **Tinea pedis**: Infection of the feet (athlete’s foot)
- **Dermatophytid reaction**: A skin rash that appears elsewhere in the body due to a fungal infection in another area

## What the Infections Look Like

The symptoms depend on where the infection is.  
The severity depends on the fungus and how strong your body’s defenses are.

Most of the time, the skin has mild symptoms.  
You may have a rash that itches a little.  
The edges of the rash are raised and flaky.  
The rash may go away and come back.

Sometimes the infection causes more serious problems.  
For example:
- Blisters or large fluid-filled sores on the feet
- A swollen, painful lump on the scalp called a kerion

## How Doctors Diagnose the Infection

Doctors look at the skin and where the rash is.  
They may take a small sample of skin or nail.  
They test it under a microscope using a special solution called potassium hydroxide, or KOH.  
This helps them see the fungus.

For nail infections, the best test is a special stain on nail clippings.  
This test is called periodic acid-Schiff stain.

In some cases, doctors grow the fungus in a lab.  
This is only needed for:
- Scalp infections (to find if an animal is the source)
- Nail infections (to check if a non-fungal mold is causing the problem)
- Severe infections with swelling, pus, or hair loss

## Other Conditions That Can Look Like Fungal Infections

Some other skin problems can look like fungal infections.  
These include:
- Folliculitis decalvans: A rare condition that causes bald patches with pus
- Bacterial skin infections
- Scarring hair loss conditions like discoid lupus erythematosus, lichen planopilaris, and pseudopelade
- Dissecting cellulitis: A deep skin infection

## How the Infection Is Treated

Treatment depends on where the infection is.  
Most cases need antifungal medicine.  
This can be a cream or a pill.

### For Skin Infections

Topical antifungal creams are usually enough.  
Over-the-counter options include:
- Terbinafine (kills the fungus quickly)
- Econazole or ciclopirox (best if a yeast infection is possible)
- Clotrimazole
- Miconazole

Terbinafine works faster than other OTC creams.  
It kills the fungus instead of just stopping its growth.

### For Nail and Scalp Infections

Oral antifungal pills are usually needed.  
These are stronger and work better for deep infections.  
Treatment can last several weeks to months.  
The dose and length depend on the location.

### For Itching and Swelling

Sometimes doctors add a mild steroid cream to help with itching and swelling.  
But steroids can make the fungus grow faster.  
So they should be used carefully.

Do not use over-the-counter creams that mix steroids and antifungals.  
These can hide the real problem.  
They can delay proper diagnosis and treatment.

Always get a proper test (like a KOH wet mount or culture) before starting treatment.  
This helps make sure you are getting the right medicine.

# Fungal Infection of the Nails

A fungal infection of the nails is called onychomycosis.

- About 1 in 10 people have this condition.
- It most often affects the toenails, not the fingernails.
- It is more common in older adults, especially men.
- It is also more common in people with poor blood flow in the feet, diabetes, a weak immune system, athlete’s foot, or nail problems.

This infection often comes back, even after long treatment.

## What Causes This Infection?

Most cases are caused by a type of mold called dermatophytes.

- These molds can spread through direct contact with an infected person.
- They can also spread by touching surfaces where the mold lives, like a bathroom floor.

## What Are the Signs?

The nails look different but do not itch or hurt.

- In mild cases, the nails have white or yellow spots.
- A white, powdery substance may slowly build up under the nail.
- In more serious cases, the nails become thick, twisted, and discolored.
- The nail may pull away from the nail bed.
- Dead nail material can collect under the free edge of the nail.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will:

- Look at your nails.
- Take a sample of nail debris or a small piece of nail.
- Examine the sample under a microscope.
- Sometimes grow the fungus in a lab to identify it.
- Use a test called PCR to make many copies of the fungus’s genes. This helps find the exact type of fungus.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment is usually only needed if the infection is very bothersome or if you are at risk for serious problems.

- People with diabetes or poor blood flow in the feet are at higher risk for a serious skin infection called cellulitis.
- Oral antifungal drugs are the most effective treatment.
- Common oral drugs include terbinafine, fluconazole, and itraconazole.
- These drugs must be taken for several months.
- The nail will not look normal until new, healthy nail grows in. This can take 12 to 18 months.
- The old, damaged nail will not improve. Only the new nail growing from the base will look healthy.

Topical treatments (applied directly to the nail) are less effective on their own.

- Ciclopirox is a nail polish with antifungal medicine. It works best when used with an oral drug.
- Efinaconazole and tavaborole are newer antifungal medicines you apply to the nail.
- They are not as strong as oral drugs but can help when used together.
- They are an option for people who cannot take oral drugs.

## How to Prevent It from Coming Back

To lower the chance of getting the infection again:

- Keep your nails short and trimmed.
- Dry your feet completely after bathing, especially between the toes.
- Wear socks that absorb sweat.
- Use antifungal foot powder or cream.
- Avoid wearing old shoes if possible. They may still have fungus spores.

# Roseola

Roseola is a common viral illness in young children. It usually gets better on its own within a week.

## What to Watch For

Your child may have:
- A sudden high temperature
- Cold-like symptoms such as a sore throat, runny nose, or cough
- Not wanting to eat
- Swollen eyelids or swollen glands in the neck

These symptoms last 3 to 5 days. Then a rash appears.

### The Rash
- Looks like pinkish-red spots, patches, or bumps
- May be harder to see on brown or black skin
- Starts on the chest, tummy, and back
- Spreads to the face, neck, and arms
- Is not usually itchy or painful
- Fades and disappears within 2 days

## When to Get Help Right Away

Call NHS 111 or see a GP urgently if your child:
- Is under 3 months old and has a temperature of 38 degrees Celsius or higher (or you think they have a high temperature)
- Is 3 to 6 months old and has a temperature of 39 degrees Celsius or higher (or you think they have a high temperature)
- Has a high temperature that lasts 5 days or more
- Refuses fluids or feeds
- Seems very unwell or different from normal
- Still has a high temperature even after taking paracetamol or ibuprofen
- Shows signs of dehydration – such as dry nappies, sunken eyes, or no tears when crying

### If You or Your Child Has a Weakened Immune System

Talk to a GP if you or your child has a weak immune system and has been around someone with roseola. The illness can be more serious in this case.

## When to Go to A&E (Emergency Department)

Call 999 or go to A&E if your baby or young child has:
- Blue, grey, pale, or blotchy skin, lips, or tongue  
  (On black or brown skin, check the palms of the hands and soles of the feet)
- A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it  
  (This is the same sign as in meningitis)
- Trouble breathing  
  (You might hear grunting, or see the stomach pulling in under the ribs)
- Breathing very fast or struggling to breathe
- A weak, high-pitched cry that is not like their usual cry
- Not responding normally or not interested in feeding or playing
- Sleeping more than usual or hard to wake

> **Find your nearest A&E**

### A&E Safety Tips
- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you. Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.
- Bring all your medicines with you.

## How to Care for Your Child at Home

You can usually care for your child at home. Most children feel better within a week.

### Do This
- Let your child rest if they feel unwell.
- Make sure they drink plenty of fluids.
- Give children’s paracetamol or children’s ibuprofen if the high temperature makes them uncomfortable.  
  Always check the correct dose on the bottle.
- Keep your child at home while they have a high temperature.  
  This is when roseola is most likely to spread.

### Do Not Do This
- Do not cover your child with too many clothes or blankets.
- Do not give aspirin to anyone under 16 years old.
- Do not give both ibuprofen and paracetamol at the same time unless a doctor tells you to.
- Do not give paracetamol to a child under 2 months old.
- Do not give ibuprofen to a child under 3 months old or who weighs less than 5 kilograms.
- Do not give ibuprofen to children with asthma.

## When Can Your Child Return to Nursery?

Once the high temperature is gone, your child can go back to nursery if they feel well enough.  
You do not need to wait until the rash disappears.

# High Blood Pressure

High blood pressure means your blood pushes too hard against the walls of your blood vessels.  
It is called hypertension when your blood pressure stays high over time.

## What Is High Blood Pressure?

Your blood pressure is high if:
- Your top number (systolic) is 130 or higher, or
- Your bottom number (diastolic) is 80 or higher, or
- You are taking medicine for high blood pressure.

This definition comes from large studies showing that higher blood pressure increases the risk of heart disease and stroke.

Nearly half of all adults in the United States have high blood pressure.  
Many do not know they have it.  
About 80% of people with high blood pressure are told they need treatment.  
But only about half actually get treatment.

Even with treatment, only 26% of people have their blood pressure under control.  
Among those who are treated but still have high blood pressure, almost 60% have a reading of 140 over 90 or higher.

High blood pressure is more common in non-Hispanic Black adults (58%) than in non-Hispanic White adults (49%), non-Hispanic Asian adults (45%), or Hispanic adults (39%).

Among people who are told to treat their blood pressure, control is better in non-Hispanic White adults (31%) than in non-Hispanic Black adults (20%), non-Hispanic Asian adults (24%), or Hispanic adults (23%).

Blood pressure goes up as you get older.  
About two out of three people over age 65 have high blood pressure.  
If you have normal blood pressure at age 55, you have a 90% chance of getting high blood pressure later in life.

Even though high blood pressure is common in older adults, treatment is still very important.  
It lowers your risk of serious health problems.

## High Blood Pressure During Pregnancy

High blood pressure that starts during pregnancy is different.  
It may go away after the baby is born.  
See separate sections on pregnancy-related high blood pressure and preeclampsia.

## Blood Pressure Categories for Adults

The American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association set these categories:

| Category | Blood Pressure Reading |
|--------|------------------------|
| Normal | Less than 120 over 80 |
| Elevated | 120 to 129 over less than 80 |
| Stage 1 Hypertension | 130 to 139 (top number) OR 80 to 89 (bottom number) |
| Stage 2 Hypertension | 140 or higher (top number) OR 90 or higher (bottom number) |

If your top and bottom numbers fall into different categories, your category is the higher one.

Note: Blood pressure in babies, children, and teens is much lower than in adults.

## What Causes High Blood Pressure?

There are two main types:

- **Primary hypertension** (no clear cause): This is the most common type. It affects about 85% of people.
- **Secondary hypertension** (has a clear cause): This is less common. It can be caused by:
  - Overactive adrenal glands (primary aldosteronism)
  - Sleep apnea
  - Kidney disease
  - Narrowed kidney arteries

## How Does High Blood Pressure Work?

Your blood pressure depends on:
- How much blood your heart pumps (cardiac output)
- How tight your blood vessels are (vascular resistance)

In most people with high blood pressure:
- The heart pumps about the same amount of blood as normal.
- The blood vessels are tighter than normal.

This pattern is common in primary hypertension and in cases caused by overactive adrenal glands, tumors, or kidney problems.

In some people:
- The heart pumps more blood than normal.
- The blood vessels do not tighten enough for the amount of blood being pumped.
- Later, the blood vessels tighten and the heart returns to normal pumping.

Some conditions that make the heart pump more blood (like overactive thyroid, abnormal blood vessel connections, or leaky heart valves) can cause high top numbers only.  
This is called isolated systolic hypertension.

Some older adults have high top numbers but normal or low heart output.  
This happens because the large blood vessels lose their flexibility.

Some people with very high bottom numbers have a weak heart that pumps less blood.

Blood volume often goes down when blood pressure goes up.  
But in some cases, blood volume stays normal or even increases.  
For example:
- Blood volume is high in primary aldosteronism and kidney disease.
- Blood volume is low in pheochromocytoma (a rare tumor).

## What Are the Symptoms?

High blood pressure usually has no symptoms.  
You may not feel anything even if your blood pressure is very high.

Symptoms only appear when high blood pressure causes damage to organs like the heart, brain, or kidneys.

If blood pressure is extremely high (top number 180 or higher, or bottom number 120 or higher), it may not cause symptoms.  
This is called a hypertensive urgency.

If high blood pressure causes serious problems like chest pain, heart failure, stroke, or kidney failure, it is called a hypertensive emergency.

## Eye Changes from High Blood Pressure

High blood pressure can damage the blood vessels in your eyes.  
This is called hypertensive retinopathy.

Signs in the eyes include:
- Narrowed blood vessels
- Bleeding
- Fluid leaks
- Swelling of the optic nerve (papilledema)

These changes are grouped into four grades, with higher grades meaning worse damage:

- **Grade 1**: Only the blood vessels are narrowed.
- **Grade 2**: Blood vessels are narrowed and stiff.
- **Grade 3**: Bleeding and fluid leaks appear, along with vessel changes.
- **Grade 4**: Swelling of the optic nerve (papilledema).

The higher the grade, the greater the risk of serious health problems.

## How Is High Blood Pressure Diagnosed?

You need more than one blood pressure reading to be sure you have high blood pressure.  
Blood pressure changes throughout the day.  
It is usually higher during the day and lower at night.

Your doctor will:
- Take your blood pressure several times
- Ask about your health history
- Do a physical exam
- Run tests to find the cause and check for organ damage

## Tests Your Doctor May Order

- Urine test (to check for protein)
- Spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (to check kidney health)
- Blood tests for:
  - Kidney function
  - Potassium, sodium, calcium levels
  - Blood sugar
  - Cholesterol
  - Thyroid function
- An electrocardiogram (ECG) to check your heart

## How Is High Blood Pressure Treated?

There is no cure for primary high blood pressure.  
But treatment can prevent serious problems.

Treatment includes:
- Lifestyle changes
- Medicine (if needed)

### Lifestyle Changes

- **Lose weight** if you are overweight.
- **Exercise regularly** (at least 30 minutes most days).
- **Stop smoking**.
- **Sleep at least 6 hours each night**.
- **Eat more fruits and vegetables**.
- **Cut down on salt**.
- **Limit alcohol**.

### Medicines

Your doctor may prescribe one or more of these:
- Diuretics (help your body get rid of extra fluid)
- ACE inhibitors (help relax blood vessels)
- Angiotensin II receptor blockers (help relax blood vessels)
- Calcium channel blockers (help relax blood vessels)

If your high blood pressure has a clear cause (like a tumor or kidney problem), fixing that cause may lower your blood pressure.

## What Is the Goal Blood Pressure?

For most people, including those with kidney disease or diabetes, the goal is:
- Less than 130 over 80

Lowering blood pressure below 130 over 80 keeps your risk of heart attack, stroke, and kidney disease even lower.

Older adults, including frail ones, can usually handle a bottom number as low as 60 to 65 without harm.  
But going lower than that may cause dizziness or other side effects.

Lowering the top number to around 120 may help some people.  
But it can also cause dizziness, light-headedness, or worsen kidney function.

This is especially important for people with diabetes.  
For them, a top number below 120 or a bottom number near 60 increases the risk of side effects.

## Measuring Blood Pressure at Home

It is best if you or a family member checks your blood pressure at home.  
But you must be trained to do it right.  
Your blood pressure monitor must be checked regularly to stay accurate.

## What Is the Outlook?

The higher your blood pressure, the worse your outlook.  
The more damage you have in your eyes, heart, brain, or kidneys, the greater your risk of serious problems.

The top number (systolic) is a better predictor of heart attacks and strokes than the bottom number.

Controlling your blood pressure can prevent most complications and help you live longer.

Without treatment:
- If you have eye damage (Grade 3), your chance of surviving one year is less than 10%.
- If you have eye damage plus swelling of the optic nerve (Grade 4), your chance of surviving one year is less than 5%.

# Knee Sprains and Related Injuries

A knee sprain happens when the strong bands of tissue (ligaments) that connect the thighbone to the shinbone are torn. The knee also has cushioning pads (menisci) made of cartilage. These pads can be injured too.

## What Can Go Wrong in the Knee

The knee has several important parts that keep it stable:

- **Collateral ligaments** are on the sides of the knee.  
  - The **medial collateral ligament** is on the inside of the leg.  
  - The **lateral collateral ligament** is on the outside of the leg.  
  These ligaments stop the knee from bending too far sideways.

- **Cruciate ligaments** are inside the knee joint.  
  - The **anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)** is in front.  
  - The **posterior cruciate ligament (PCL)** is in back.  
  These two ligaments cross each other like an X. They stop the knee from moving too far forward or backward.

- **Menisci** are two C-shaped pads of cartilage between the thighbone and shinbone. They help the knee absorb shock and stay steady.

The most often injured parts of the knee are:
- The medial collateral ligament
- The anterior cruciate ligament

Which part is hurt depends on how the knee was hit.

### How Injuries Happen

- **Medial collateral ligament and ACL**  
  These can be torn if the knee is hit from the side while the foot is planted. This often happens in sports like football. The injury is worse if the knee twists at the same time.

- **Lateral collateral ligament and ACL**  
  These can be damaged when force pushes the knee outward. This can happen if the inside of the leg is pushed.

- **ACL and PCL**  
  These can be injured when the knee is forced to straighten too much.

- **Menisci**  
  These can be torn when a person is standing on one foot and the knee twists suddenly.

## Symptoms of a Knee Sprain

Some people hear or feel a pop when the injury happens. This often means the ACL is torn.

Common symptoms include:
- Pain in the knee
- Swelling
- Stiffness
- Bruising
- A feeling that the knee might give way or buckle
- Muscle spasms (sudden, tight muscle contractions)

Where the pain is depends on which part is injured.

The severity of symptoms depends on how bad the injury is.

### Mild Injury
- Swelling appears within a few hours.
- It may take more than 24 hours for swelling to fully appear.
- Pain is usually mild or moderate.

### Moderate Injury
- Pain is moderate or severe.
- Pain gets worse when moving or bending the knee.

### Severe Injury
- Pain can be severe, moderate, or mild.
- Some people cannot walk without help.

Sometimes a torn meniscus causes the knee to lock. This means the knee cannot bend or straighten.

A strong force can also break a bone in the knee. It can also damage the tendons that help straighten the leg (knee extensor injuries).

## How Doctors Diagnose Knee Injuries

Doctors look at your symptoms and how the injury happened.

They may do:
- A physical exam
- X-rays to check for broken bones
- Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) if needed

### Physical Exam and Stress Testing

Doctors test the knee by gently moving the leg in certain ways. This is called stress testing. It helps them find torn ligaments.

But stress testing is often delayed. The knee is usually too painful at first. Swelling and muscle spasms can also make it hard to test right away.

Doctors usually wait a few days until the pain and swelling go down before doing stress testing.

### X-rays

Doctors take an x-ray if the knee is very painful or swollen. This checks for broken bones.

You are more likely to have a broken bone if:
- You feel sharp pain in a specific spot on the knee.
- You cannot bend your knee.
- You cannot put any weight on the injured leg.
- You are over 55 years old.

### MRI

An MRI is not usually done right away. It may be done if:
- A serious injury is suspected.
- Symptoms do not improve after several weeks of rest and care.

## Treatment for Knee Sprains

Most knee sprains can be treated without surgery.

### Immediate Care: PRICE

Most mild to moderate injuries are treated with:
- **Protection**: Avoid activities that hurt the knee.
- **Rest**: Do not use the knee much.
- **Ice**: Apply ice packs for 15 to 20 minutes every few hours.
- **Compression**: Wrap the knee with an elastic bandage to reduce swelling.
- **Elevation**: Keep the leg raised above heart level when possible.

A compression bandage may help. A splint or knee immobilizer may be used in some cases. These devices keep the knee from bending. They are mostly used for serious injuries like large ligament tears or fractures.

### Fluid Drainage

If a lot of fluid builds up in the knee, doctors may drain it. This helps reduce pain and muscle spasms.

### Exercises

- People with mild or moderate injuries are usually told to do exercises to strengthen the knee.
- If the injury is severe, exercises are delayed until after surgery.

### Surgery

Some serious injuries need surgery. This includes:
- Large tears in ligaments
- Major meniscus tears

Surgery is usually done using a small camera and tools through tiny cuts. This is called arthroscopic surgery.

After surgery, recovery takes time. Physical therapy and exercises are part of healing.

# Myeloma

## What are the main signs of myeloma?

You may notice these signs if you have myeloma:

- Pain in your back, hips, shoulders, or ribs.
- Feeling very tired for no clear reason.
- Finding it hard to breathe.
- Weakness in your muscles.
- Frequent headaches.
- Feeling very thirsty all the time.
- Needing to pass urine more often than usual.
- Losing weight without trying.

Sometimes myeloma does not cause any symptoms at first. You might only find out you have it after a blood test done for another reason.

## What tests are used to check for myeloma?

If your doctor thinks you might have myeloma, they will refer you to a specialist. The specialist will do tests to check for cancer.

The main tests usually include:

- A CT scan or an MRI scan. These take detailed pictures of your body.
- A bone marrow biopsy. A small sample of your bone marrow is taken and tested in a lab.

## What treatments are used for myeloma?

Myeloma can be hard to treat. The treatment you get depends on:

- How you are feeling and what symptoms you have.
- Whether the myeloma has returned after treatment.
- Your age and your general health.

You might not need treatment right away. Some people only start treatment when symptoms get worse.

You may be offered a mix of treatments. These can include:

- Chemotherapy to kill cancer cells.
- Radiotherapy to target cancer in one area.
- Targeted medicines that attack cancer cells in specific ways.
- Steroids to help reduce swelling and control symptoms.
- Bisphosphonates to help protect your bones from thinning.

Your specialist team will:

- Explain each treatment, what it can do, and what side effects to expect.
- Work with you to create a treatment plan that fits your needs.
- Help you manage any side effects you may have.

If you have questions or feel worried, talk to your specialist team. They are there to help.

## What causes myeloma?

We do not know exactly what causes myeloma. But some things may increase your risk:

- Being overweight.
- Having a close family member with myeloma.
- Being of Black African or African Caribbean background.
- Having a condition called MGUS or pernicious anaemia.

Myeloma is more common as you get older. It is slightly more common in men.

- Suddenly lose feeling in their arms or legs.
- Cannot walk or stand.
- Suddenly feel confused.
- Cannot control their bowels or bladder.

These could be signs of spinal cord compression. This is a serious condition that needs emergency treatment.

### A&E safety message (for 999 only)
Do not drive yourself to the emergency department. The person you speak to on 999 will tell you what to do.
