# Nasal Polyps

Nasal polyps are soft, fleshy growths inside the nose or sinuses.  
They form where the lining of the nose swells and becomes thick.  
These growths often appear near the openings of the sinuses in the cheekbones.

They look like small, clear, jelly-like bumps.  
They grow because the nose lining stays inflamed for a long time.  
About 1 in 100 to 25 in 1,000 people have nasal polyps.  
Men are slightly more likely to get them than women.

---

## What Causes Nasal Polyps?

Certain conditions make nasal polyps more likely.  
Allergic reactions in the nose can lead to polyps.  
Long-term infections in the nose and sinuses also increase the risk.  
Cystic fibrosis is a serious condition that often causes polyps.  
Some types of fungal infections in the nose can cause bleeding polyps.  
Polyps may also appear in people with a rare disease called eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.  
Another rare condition, primary ciliary dyskinesia, can also cause polyps.  

A single polyp on one side of the nose may be a sign of a tumor.  
It can also happen if something foreign gets stuck in the nose.  
Nasal polyps are strongly linked to:

- Allergy to aspirin  
- Chronic sinus infections  
- Asthma  
- Allergic rhinitis (hay fever)

---

## Symptoms of Nasal Polyps

You may have a blocked nose.  
You might feel mucus dripping down the back of your throat.  
Your nose may feel stuffy all the time.  
You may sneeze often.  
You may have a runny nose.  
You may feel pressure or pain in your face.  
Your eyes may itch.  
You may lose your sense of smell or notice it is weaker.  
This loss of smell is a strong sign of nasal polyps.

Because your nose is blocked, you may have trouble sleeping.  
This can make your daily life harder.  
You may snore more because air cannot flow easily through your nose.

---

## How Are Nasal Polyps Diagnosed?

Doctors start by asking about your symptoms.  
They will look inside your nose with a small tool called a nasal speculum.  
If the polyps are deep inside, they may use a thin, flexible tube with a light (endoscope) to see better.  
This is called rhinoscopy.  
Looking at the nose with a scope is the best way to find polyps.

A polyp looks like a clear, soft, teardrop-shaped bump.  
When it is fully grown, it looks like a peeled grape without seeds.

Sometimes, doctors need imaging tests.  
A CT scan shows the sinuses and bones in the nose and face.  
It helps check how bad the polyps are.  
It also helps plan surgery if needed.  
An MRI is used less often.  
It helps tell the difference between polyps and other growths.  
It also shows how much soft tissue is involved.

Some polyps are too deep to see with a scope.  
Only a scan can show them.

A biopsy may be done in rare cases.  
This means taking a small piece of tissue to test.  
It is usually done if there is only one polyp.  
This helps rule out cancer.  
If the tissue has many eosinophils (a type of white blood cell), it may mean the polyp is caused by allergies or fungus.  
It may also mean the polyp is more likely to come back.

---

## How Are Nasal Polyps Treated?

The first treatment is a steroid spray for the nose.  
Common sprays include fluticasone, mometasone, beclomethasone, and flunisolide.  
Use 1 or 2 sprays in each nostril twice a day.  
This can shrink or even remove small polyps.  
A short course of oral steroids (taken by mouth) for one week may also help.  
Some special sprayers have two openings—one for the nose and one for the mouth.  
These help deliver the medicine more effectively.

For people with large polyps on both sides or severe chronic sinus infections, biologic medicines may help.  
These include omalizumab, dupilumab, mepolizumab, and benralizumab.  
They can shrink polyps and improve symptoms.  
Dupilumab and mepolizumab may also improve your quality of life.  
These medicines are safe for most people.

If medicine does not work, surgery may be needed.  
Polyps that block the airway or cause repeated sinus infections are removed.  
A single polyp may be removed to check for tumors.

Polyps often come back.  
This happens unless the cause—like allergies, infection, or inflammation—is treated.  
After surgery, using a steroid spray every day helps prevent new polyps.  
In severe cases that keep coming back, surgery may be done to open the sinuses.  
This is usually done using a thin scope through the nose.  
The most common surgeries are maxillary sinusotomy and ethmoidectomy.

# Herpetic Whitlow

Herpetic whitlow is an infection in the fingertip caused by a virus.

The virus is the same type that causes cold sores or fever blisters.

The virus gets into the skin through a small cut or break.

The fingertip becomes painful and swollen.

The area is tender but not hard like a bacterial infection.

Small blisters filled with fluid appear on the finger.

These blisters may not show up right away. They can appear two or three days after the pain starts.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors look at the blisters and how the finger feels.

The finger is soft, not firm.

This helps them tell the difference from a bacterial infection called a felon.

Sometimes the condition looks like other hand infections.

## How It Is Treated

The infection will go away on its own over time.

But it can come back.

Using antiviral medicine on the skin can help the first episode get better faster.

Taking antiviral medicine by mouth, such as acyclovir, may help prevent future outbreaks.

This is especially useful for people who have had the infection more than once.

Cover any open or leaking blisters.

This stops the virus from spreading to others.

Surgery is not needed.

The infection will heal without surgery.

# Acromegaly

Acromegaly is a condition where your body makes too much growth hormone.  
This can cause your hands, feet, and other body parts to grow larger over time.  
It can also lead to tiredness, sleep problems, and other health issues.

## Early Signs of Acromegaly

The first signs often include:  
- Swollen hands and feet  
- Feeling very tired  
- Trouble sleeping  

Later, you may notice:  
- Your body growing larger  
- Frequent headaches  

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if you think you might have acromegaly.  
Early treatment can stop your symptoms from getting worse.

## What Causes Acromegaly?

Most of the time, acromegaly is caused by a small, non-cancerous growth (tumour) in the pituitary gland.  
This gland is located at the base of your brain.  
It controls many of your body’s hormones, including growth hormone.  
When the tumour grows, it makes your body produce too much growth hormone.

Acromegaly is not usually passed down from parents to children.

## Symptoms of Acromegaly

Symptoms can appear slowly and may include:  
- Swollen hands and feet  
- Feeling tired or having trouble sleeping  
- Sleep apnoea (a condition where you stop breathing for short times during sleep)  
- Excessive sweating  
- Numbness or weakness in your hands  
- In children and teenagers: very fast or unusual growth in height (called gigantism)  
- Larger feet, fingers, head, tongue, or neck  
- Headaches  
- Joint pain  
- Skin that is thicker and oilier than normal  
- A deeper voice  
- Irregular periods in women  
- Trouble getting or keeping an erection in men  

Most people develop acromegaly between the ages of 30 and 50.  
But symptoms can start at any age.

## Treatment for Acromegaly

Treatment aims to stop your body from making too much growth hormone.  
Options include:  
- Surgery to remove the tumour in the pituitary gland  
- Radiotherapy to shrink the tumour and lower hormone levels  
- Injections or tablets to reduce growth hormone levels  

Treatment usually stops the overproduction of growth hormone.  
It also helps improve your symptoms.

After treatment, you will need regular check-ups with a specialist.  
They will check how well your pituitary gland is working.  
They will also make sure your treatment is still right for you.

## Possible Health Problems from Acromegaly

If left untreated, acromegaly can raise your risk of:  
- Type 2 diabetes  
- High blood pressure (also called hypertension)  
- Heart disease  
- Bowel polyps (small growths in the large intestine that can become cancerous)  

You will have regular health checks to watch for these problems.  
This includes a colonoscopy to check your bowel for polyps.

# Atherosclerosis – Simple Explanation

Atherosclerosis is a condition where hard deposits build up inside the arteries. These deposits are called plaques. They can make the inside of the arteries narrower. This can slow or block blood flow.

The plaques are made of fat, immune cells, muscle cells, and connective tissue.

## What Causes Atherosclerosis?

Many things can raise your risk of developing atherosclerosis. Some you can change. Some you cannot.

### Things You Cannot Change
- Age: Risk goes up as you get older.
- Family history: If a close family member had heart or blood vessel problems early in life, your risk may be higher.
- Being male: Men are more likely to get it than women, especially at younger ages.

### Things You Can Change
- High cholesterol: Too much bad cholesterol (LDL) or not enough good cholesterol (HDL).
- Diabetes: High blood sugar harms blood vessels over time.
- High blood pressure: This stresses the artery walls.
- Smoking: Tobacco damages the lining of arteries.
- Being overweight or obese: Extra weight increases risk.
- Not being active: Sitting too much raises risk.
- Poor diet: Eating too much saturated fat, sugar, and processed foods is harmful.
- High levels of certain fats and proteins in the blood: For example, high levels of a protein called apolipoprotein B or a substance called lipoprotein (a).
- High levels of a marker called C-reactive protein (CRP): This shows inflammation in the body.
- High levels of small, dense LDL cholesterol: This type of cholesterol is more likely to cause harm.
- Drinking too much alcohol: This can raise blood pressure and harm the heart.
- Stress, depression, or anxiety: These can affect heart health.
- Having had a heart transplant or radiation therapy to the chest: These can damage arteries.
- Kidney disease: This can worsen other risk factors.

Some of these risk factors often happen together. This group is called the **metabolic syndrome**. It includes belly fat, high blood pressure, high blood sugar, and unhealthy cholesterol levels.

### How These Risk Factors Work
- **High cholesterol**: Bad cholesterol gets into the artery wall. It can become damaged (oxidized). This triggers inflammation and attracts immune cells.
- **High blood pressure**: It damages the inner lining of arteries. This makes it easier for plaque to form.
- **Diabetes**: High blood sugar harms the lining of blood vessels. It also increases inflammation and damage from free radicals.
- **Smoking**: Chemicals in tobacco poison the inside of arteries. Smoking also makes blood thicker and more likely to clot.
- **Lipoprotein (a)**: This is a type of bad cholesterol that runs in families. High levels increase heart attack and stroke risk.
- **Apolipoprotein B (apoB)**: This protein is found on bad cholesterol particles. It helps carry fat into artery walls. More of these particles mean higher risk.
- **Small, dense LDL**: This type of cholesterol is more likely to get trapped in artery walls and cause damage.
- **C-reactive protein (CRP)**: High levels mean there is inflammation in the body. This may signal a higher risk of a plaque breaking open.
- **Infections**: Some infections, like *Chlamydia pneumoniae*, may trigger inflammation in blood vessels.
- **Genes**: Certain genes can increase your risk. Even if each gene has a small effect, having many of them raises your risk.

## Where Does Atherosclerosis Happen?

Atherosclerosis can affect any large or medium-sized artery. Common places include:
- The arteries that supply blood to the heart (coronary arteries)
- The arteries in the neck (carotid arteries)
- The arteries in the brain (cerebral arteries)
- The main artery in the body (aorta)
- Arteries in the arms and legs

## What Are the Symptoms?

Atherosclerosis often has no symptoms at first. It can go undetected for years.

Symptoms appear when the plaque grows or breaks open. This can block blood flow.

### Common Symptoms by Area Affected
- **Heart**: Chest pain when walking or exercising (angina). Sudden, severe chest pain (heart attack).
- **Brain**: Weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking that comes and goes (transient ischemic attack or TIA). Sudden weakness or paralysis (stroke).
- **Legs**: Pain in the legs when walking, which goes away with rest (intermittent claudication). Pain at rest, especially at night.
- **Aorta or other large arteries**: A pulsing lump in the abdomen (aneurysm). Sudden, severe pain. Sudden loss of pulse in an arm or leg. Sudden death.

Plaques that are unstable can break open. This can cause a blood clot to form right away. This clot can block blood flow and cause a heart attack or stroke.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

If you have symptoms, your doctor will check your medical history and do a physical exam.

Tests may include:
- Ultrasound of the neck or leg arteries
- CT or MRI scans
- Angiography (a special X-ray that shows blood flow)

If you have no symptoms, routine testing is not usually needed. Your doctor will use your risk factors to estimate your risk.

## How Is It Treated?

The goal is to slow or stop plaque growth. In some cases, plaques can shrink.

### Lifestyle Changes
- **Eat a healthy diet**: Focus on vegetables, fruits, whole grains, lean proteins, and healthy fats. Limit saturated fats, sugar, and processed foods.
- **Stop smoking**: Quitting helps your arteries heal. HDL (good cholesterol) goes up within a month.
- **Be physically active**: Aim for at least 30 minutes of movement most days.
- **Lose weight** if you are overweight.
- **Limit alcohol**: If you drink, do so in moderation.

### Medicines
- **Statins**: These lower bad cholesterol and reduce inflammation. They help prevent heart attacks and strokes, even if your cholesterol is normal.
- **Antiplatelet drugs**: These prevent blood clots. Aspirin is common.
- **Blood pressure medicines**: Such as ACE inhibitors or beta-blockers. These help protect the heart and blood vessels.
- **Medicines for diabetes**: To keep blood sugar under control.

## Key Points

- Atherosclerosis is the most common and serious type of artery disease.
- It is the leading cause of death worldwide.
- It often starts early in life and grows slowly over decades.
- Many risk factors can be changed with lifestyle and medicine.
- Plaques that are unstable can break open and cause sudden heart attacks or strokes.
- Even if you have no symptoms, managing risk factors is key to prevention.
- Stopping smoking, eating well, staying active, and taking medicines as needed can greatly reduce your risk.

> **Note**: If you have a family history of early heart disease, talk to your doctor. You may need earlier or more frequent screening.

# Ovarian Cancer, Fallopian Tube Cancer, and Peritoneal Cancer

These three cancers are closely related. They start in different parts of the female reproductive system but often behave similarly.

- **Ovarian cancer** starts in the ovaries.
- **Fallopian tube cancer** starts in the tubes that carry eggs from the ovaries to the uterus.
- **Peritoneal cancer** starts in the lining of the abdomen.

These cancers are often found at a late stage. They may not cause symptoms until they have spread.

---

## Who Gets Ovarian Cancer?

- Most cases happen in women between the ages of 50 and 70.
- In the United States, about 1 in 70 women will develop ovarian cancer.
- It is the fifth leading cause of cancer death in women.
- In 2023, it is expected to cause about 19,710 new cases and 13,270 deaths.

---

## How These Cancers Are Related

Ovarian and fallopian tube cancers share many features:
- They cause similar symptoms.
- They are diagnosed the same way.
- They are treated the same way.

Because of this, doctors often talk about them together. Fallopian tube cancer is rare.

---

## The Female Reproductive System

The ovaries are two small organs that make eggs and hormones. They are located in the lower belly.

There are many types of ovarian cancer. They start in different kinds of cells.

- **Epithelial carcinomas** (over 90% of cases) start on the surface of the ovaries.
- **Germ cell tumors** start in the cells that make eggs. These are more common in women under 30.
- **Stromal cell tumors** start in the connective tissue of the ovaries.

Sometimes, cancer from other parts of the body can spread to the ovaries.

---

## How Ovarian Cancer Spreads

Ovarian cancer can spread in several ways:

- It grows directly into nearby tissues.
- It sheds cancer cells into the fluid inside the abdomen.
- It travels through the lymph system to other parts of the pelvis and abdomen.
- Less often, it spreads through the blood. If it does, it may show up in the liver or lungs.

---

## Risk Factors for Ovarian Cancer

You are more likely to get ovarian cancer if you:

- Are older (age is the biggest risk factor).
- Have a mother, sister, or daughter with ovarian cancer.
- Have never had a child.
- Had your first child after age 35.
- Started your periods before age 12.
- Went through menopause after age 50.
- Have had cancer of the uterus, breast, or colon.
- Have a family history of any of these cancers.

Taking **birth control pills** lowers your risk.

About 15% of ovarian cancers are linked to changes in the *BRCA1* and *BRCA2* genes. These same genes are also linked to some breast cancers.

When these gene changes run in families, it is called hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome.

- Women with a *BRCA1* gene change have a 20% to 40% chance of getting ovarian cancer in their lifetime.
- Women with a *BRCA2* gene change have a lower risk.
- These gene changes are more common in women of Ashkenazi Jewish descent.

---

## Symptoms of Ovarian Cancer

In early stages, ovarian cancer often causes no symptoms.

When symptoms do appear, they are often vague and easy to miss. They include:

- Bloating or swelling in the belly.
- Feeling full quickly when eating.
- Loss of appetite.
- Belly or pelvic pain.
- Needing to urinate more often.
- Changes in bowel habits.

As the cancer grows, the belly may swell. This can happen because:

- The ovary gets bigger.
- Fluid builds up in the abdomen (called ascites).

Later symptoms may include:

- Pain in the pelvic area.
- Feeling weak from anemia.
- Losing weight without trying.

Rarely, certain types of tumors can make hormones. This can cause:

- Too much growth of the lining of the uterus.
- Breast swelling.
- Excess body hair (if male hormones are made).
- Symptoms of an overactive thyroid (if thyroid-like hormones are made).

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Ovarian Cancer

Diagnosing ovarian cancer early is hard. Symptoms often do not appear until the cancer is large or has spread. Many other conditions can cause the same symptoms.

If a doctor finds a swollen ovary during a check-up, or suspects cancer based on symptoms, they will do:

- **Ultrasound** – to look at the ovary and see if it is a cyst or a solid mass.
- **CT scan or MRI** – to get a clearer picture of the inside of the belly and pelvis.
- **Blood tests** – to check for certain substances that may be higher in people with cancer (like CA 125).

High levels of CA 125 do not mean you have cancer. But they can help support a diagnosis when combined with other findings.

To confirm cancer, a **biopsy** is needed. This means taking a small sample of tissue to examine under a microscope.

There are two main ways to do this:

### 1. Laparoscopy
- A thin tube with a camera is inserted through a small cut near the belly button.
- Doctors use tools through the tube to take tissue samples.
- They can also remove the ovaries and fallopian tubes if needed.
- This is often used when cancer is thought to be early.

### 2. Open Surgery
- A larger cut is made in the belly.
- Doctors can see the organs directly.
- They check for cancer spread and remove as much cancer as possible.

After surgery, doctors stage the cancer. Staging tells how far the cancer has spread.

### Stages of Ovarian Cancer

- **Stage I**: Cancer is only in one or both ovaries or fallopian tubes.
- **Stage II**: Cancer has spread to the uterus or nearby tissues in the pelvis, or is on the peritoneum.
- **Stage III**: Cancer has spread outside the pelvis to lymph nodes or other parts of the abdomen.
- **Stage IV**: Cancer has spread to distant organs, like the lungs or liver.

---

## Treatment of Ovarian Cancer

Treatment depends on the type and stage of cancer.

Most women need surgery and often chemotherapy.

### Surgery
- The ovaries, fallopian tubes, and uterus are usually removed.
- If cancer has spread, nearby lymph nodes and other tissues are also removed.
- This is called **cytoreductive surgery** – the goal is to remove all visible cancer.

For women with early-stage cancer who still want to have children:
- Doctors may remove only the affected ovary and fallopian tube.

For advanced cancer:
- Doctors try to remove as much cancer as possible.
- Sometimes, chemotherapy is given before or after surgery.

### Chemotherapy
- Most women get chemotherapy after surgery.
- It helps kill any cancer cells left behind.
- For early-stage, less aggressive cancers, some women may not need more treatment after surgery.

### Special Cases
- **Germ cell tumors**: These can often be cured with surgery and a few types of chemotherapy. Radiation is rarely used.
- **Advanced cancer**: This often comes back. After treatment, doctors check blood levels of cancer markers (like CA 125) to see if any cancer remains.

If cancer returns after treatment:
- Doctors may give more chemotherapy.
- Different drugs or drug combinations may be used.

---

## Prognosis (Outlook)

Your chance of recovery depends on the stage of cancer.

- Early-stage cancer has a better outlook.
- If cancer is aggressive or cannot be fully removed during surgery, the outlook is worse.
- About 70% of women with stage III or IV cancer will have the cancer come back.

---

## Prevention

There is no routine screening test for ovarian or fallopian tube cancer.

But if you have a family history of ovarian or breast cancer, talk to your doctor about genetic testing.

### Genetic Testing
- If you have a first- or second-degree relative with ovarian or breast cancer, especially in Ashkenazi Jewish families, you may want to be tested for *BRCA1* and *BRCA2* gene changes.

### Preventive Surgery
- Women with *BRCA1* or *BRCA2* gene changes may choose to have both ovaries and fallopian tubes removed, even if they do not have cancer.
- This removes the risk of ovarian cancer and lowers the risk of breast cancer.

---

### Did You Know?

If you have a mother, sister, or daughter with ovarian or breast cancer, talk to your doctor about genetic testing.

---

## More Information

The following websites offer helpful resources in English:

- **Foundation for Women's Cancer**  
  Offers information on gynecologic cancers, clinical trials, research, educational courses, and personal stories.

- **National Cancer Institute: Ovarian, Fallopian Tube, and Primary Peritoneal Cancer**  
  Provides general info on causes, prevention, treatment, and coping with these cancers.

- **National Cancer Institute: BRCA1 and BRCA2: Cancer Risk and Genetic Testing**  
  Explains the *BRCA* genes, the benefits and risks of genetic testing, and what a positive result means.

# Ebola Virus Disease

Ebola is a serious illness caused by a virus.  
It spreads when you come into contact with body fluids from someone who is infected.  
These fluids include blood, vomit, saliva, sweat, urine, feces, and semen.  
It can also spread from wild animals, especially bats, monkeys, baboons, and chimpanzees.

Ebola is mainly found in parts of Central and West Africa.  
It has never spread from person to person in the UK.

---

## Who Is at Risk?

You are at risk if you:
- Travel to a country where Ebola is found.
- Have close contact with someone who has Ebola.
- Eat raw or undercooked meat from wild animals in areas where Ebola is found.

The most recent outbreaks have happened in:
- Uganda  
- Guinea  
- Democratic Republic of Congo  

---

## How to Avoid Ebola

If you are planning to travel to a place where Ebola is found, talk to a travel clinic before you go.  
It’s best to do this 4 to 6 weeks before your trip.  
But you can still get advice even if you are leaving at short notice.

### Do These Things

- Wash your hands often with soap and water.  
- Wash and peel fruits and vegetables before eating them.  
- Stay away from anyone who has symptoms of Ebola.  
- Use a condom for sex for at least 3 months after someone has recovered from Ebola.

### Do Not Do These Things

- Do not eat raw or undercooked meat from wild animals in countries where Ebola is found.  
- Do not touch a person who has Ebola or who has died from Ebola.  
- Do not touch their body fluids, clothes, bedding, or anything they have touched.  
- Do not touch wild animals, especially bats, monkeys, baboons, or chimpanzees.

---

## Symptoms of Ebola

Symptoms can start 2 to 21 days after infection.  
They often come on suddenly.  
The first signs are like the flu.  
They include:

- A high temperature  
- Feeling very tired  
- A headache  

Other symptoms may include:

- Feeling sick and vomiting  
- Diarrhoea and stomach pain  
- A rash on the skin  
- Yellowing of the skin or eyes  
- Blood in your stool  
- Many bruises on your body  
- Bleeding from the ears, eyes, nose, or mouth

---

## Treatment for Ebola

Ebola is a medical emergency.  
You must get help right away.  
You will be treated in a hospital in isolation.  
You will need care in an intensive care unit.

Treatment focuses on helping your body fight the illness.  
This includes:

- Getting fluids through a tube in your vein to prevent dehydration  
- Getting help with breathing if needed  

There is no cure for Ebola, but early care can improve your chances of recovery.

---

## When to Get Help

Call NHS 111 if:
- You have been to a country where Ebola is found and now have symptoms.  
- You have been near someone who has been to a country where Ebola is found and now have symptoms.

Stay at home and avoid close contact with others.  
Do not share towels, bedding, or other personal items.  
Wait for instructions from a health professional.

If you are travelling and start to feel unwell with Ebola symptoms, get medical help right away.

# Hepatitis E – Simple Explanation

Hepatitis E is a liver infection caused by a virus. The virus spreads through the mouth, usually by drinking water or eating food that has been contaminated with feces.

The infection causes symptoms like loss of appetite, tiredness, nausea, vomiting, fever, and yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice).

Most people get better on their own. But in rare cases, the illness can become very serious, especially in pregnant women. In pregnancy, the risk of severe liver failure and death is higher.

There are four types of the hepatitis E virus. All can cause the same kind of illness.

---

## Types of Hepatitis E Virus

### Types 1 and 2
- These types spread through water that has been polluted with feces.
- Outbreaks happen when clean water is not available.
- They spread from person to person through the fecal-oral route.
- Outbreaks have happened in parts of Asia, Africa, Latin America, and Russia.
- These outbreaks look like hepatitis A outbreaks.
- Sporadic cases (single cases not linked to an outbreak) also happen.
- No outbreaks have been reported in the United States or Western Europe.
- Most cases in the U.S. and Europe are in travelers who came back from areas with poor sanitation.
- Some cases happen in people who did not travel.

### Types 3 and 4
- These types do not cause outbreaks.
- They cause single, isolated cases.
- They spread through food, especially undercooked or raw meat.
- Cases have been linked to eating pork, deer meat, and shellfish.

---

## Can Hepatitis E Become Chronic?

For many years, doctors thought hepatitis E only caused short-term illness. But now we know that type 3 can cause long-term infection in people with weak immune systems.

This includes:
- People who had organ transplants
- People getting cancer treatment
- People with HIV

In these people, the virus can stay in the body for months or years. This can lead to ongoing liver damage.

---

## Symptoms of Hepatitis E

You may feel:
- Not hungry
- Tired
- Sick to your stomach
- Vomiting
- Fever

Later, your skin and eyes may turn yellow. This is called jaundice.

The illness can be worse in pregnant women. They are more likely to get severe liver problems and even die.

---

## How Is Hepatitis E Diagnosed?

Doctors test for hepatitis E using a blood test that looks for antibodies to the virus.

If you have symptoms of acute hepatitis (sudden liver illness), your doctor will first rule out other causes of jaundice.

They will test for hepatitis A, B, and C. These tests include:
- Blood test for hepatitis A antibodies
- Test for hepatitis B surface antigen
- Blood test for hepatitis B core antibodies
- Blood test for hepatitis C antibodies and a special test for hepatitis C virus RNA

If all these tests are negative, but you have symptoms and recently traveled to a high-risk area, your doctor may test for hepatitis E antibodies (IgM anti-HEV) if the test is available.

---

## How Is Hepatitis E Treated?

There is no specific medicine to treat acute hepatitis E. Most people get better with supportive care.

Supportive care means:
- Rest
- Staying hydrated
- Eating a healthy diet
- Avoiding alcohol (it can harm the liver)

For chronic hepatitis E (in people with weak immune systems), doctors may use a medicine called ribavirin. Studies show it can help clear the virus when taken for 12 weeks.

There is no scientific reason to avoid certain foods or to stay in bed. These are not proven to help.

If you have hepatitis E, you must report it to your local or state health department.

---

## How to Prevent Hepatitis E

Good hygiene helps stop the spread:
- Wash your hands often, especially after using the toilet and before eating
- Use safe water and food
- Boil water if you are unsure it is clean

The virus does not spread easily from person to person. So, isolating sick people is not needed.

A vaccine for hepatitis E is available in China. It is not available in the United States.

The vaccine:
- Works well in men, with about 95% protection
- Is safe
- But we do not yet know how well it works in women, children, or people with weak immune systems
- We also do not know how long the protection lasts
- We do not know if it prevents mild or silent infections

---

## Key Points

- Hepatitis E usually spreads through contaminated water or food.
- Most people recover without treatment.
- Pregnant women are at higher risk for serious illness and death.
- Type 3 hepatitis E can cause long-term infection in people with weak immune systems.
- Think about hepatitis E if you recently traveled to a high-risk area.
- Test for hepatitis E antibodies if the test is available.
- Treat acute cases with rest, fluids, and no alcohol.
- For chronic cases, ribavirin may help.
- A vaccine is available in China but not in the United States.

# Bird Flu – Simple Explanation

Bird flu is a sickness caused by a type of flu virus that usually lives in wild birds and farm chickens.

## What Causes Bird Flu?

- The virus comes from several types of flu A.  
- It mainly spreads among birds.  
- It rarely spreads to people.  
- It can only spread to people if the virus changes in a way that lets it infect human cells.  
- So far, almost all human cases happened after close contact with sick birds.  
- Bird flu does not spread easily from one person to another.

## Cases in the United States

- The first human case of H5N1 bird flu in the U.S. was in Colorado in 2022. The person likely touched infected chickens.  
- A second case happened in Texas in 2024. The person worked on a dairy farm.  
- In 2024, H5N1 was found in dairy cows in several states.  
- The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) are watching the situation closely.

## Cases in China

- H7N9 bird flu started in China in 2013.  
- A big wave of cases happened between 2016 and 2017. Nearly 800 people got sick.  
- Since then, only a few cases have been reported.  
- Worldwide, over 1,500 people have been infected since 2013. At least 615 people have died.  
- Most cases happened in places where people buy live chickens from markets.

Other bird flu strains have also caused rare cases in people.

## Symptoms of Bird Flu

People with bird flu may have:

- Fever  
- Cough  
- Sore throat  
- Body aches  
- Eye redness or swelling (called conjunctivitis)  
- Trouble breathing  
- Pneumonia

These symptoms are like the flu, but they can be much worse.

## How Is Bird Flu Diagnosed?

- A doctor takes a swab from your nose or throat.  
- The sample is tested in a lab.  
- You should see a doctor if you have flu-like symptoms and:  
  - You were near birds in an area where bird flu is known to be present.  
  - You were near someone who has bird flu.

## How Is Bird Flu Treated?

- Doctors give antiviral medicines.  
- The medicines used are baloxavir, oseltamivir, or zanamivir.  
- These drugs help people get better faster.  
- They can also help prevent serious illness or death.

## How to Prevent Bird Flu

- Do not touch sick or dead birds, chickens, or cows.  
- Do not eat raw or undercooked food. This includes unpasteurized milk and dairy.  
- In the United States, the milk you buy is safe.  
  - All milk is tested.  
  - No live, active virus has been found in pasteurized milk.  
  - Dairies must use milk only from healthy animals.  
  - Pasteurization is required for all milk sold in stores.  
- In China, chickens are being vaccinated to stop H5 and H7 bird flu.  
  - This helps stop the virus from spreading from wild birds to farm birds.  
  - Farm birds are more likely to spread the virus to people.  
- If a group of birds gets sick, the whole group is destroyed. This stops the virus from spreading.

## Vaccines

- A vaccine for H5N1 bird flu is available in the U.S.  
  - It will be given if public health leaders decide it is needed.  
- The regular flu shot does not protect against bird flu.

# Necrotising Fasciitis – Simple Explanation

Necrotising fasciitis is a serious skin infection. It can spread fast and is life-threatening if not treated right away.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms can start suddenly and get worse in just a few hours or days.

Early signs include:
- Severe pain near a cut, burn, or bite. The pain feels much worse than it should.
- Swelling around the injured area.
- Flu-like symptoms such as a high temperature, headache, and feeling very tired.

Later signs may include:
- Feeling sick and vomiting.
- Diarrhoea.
- Confusion or trouble thinking clearly.
- Dark spots or blisters on the skin. These can be black, purple, or grey. On darker skin, they may be harder to see.

## When to Get Help Right Away

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:
- A cut or wound that hurts much more than expected.
- A cut or wound plus flu-like symptoms like a high temperature, headache, or muscle aches.
- Sudden confusion.
- Black, purple, or grey spots or blisters near a cut or wound.

> **Find your nearest A&E**

### Important Safety Tips for A&E
- Do not drive yourself. Ask someone to take you or call 999 for an ambulance.
- Bring all your regular medicines with you.

## How Is It Treated?

This infection must be treated in hospital as soon as possible.

Treatment usually includes:
- Strong antibiotics to fight the infection.
- Surgery to remove the infected tissue.

Even if the treatment works, you may have lasting changes. These can include:
- Scarring.
- Trouble moving the affected area.
- In some cases, the loss of a limb (amputation).

You may need more surgery and physiotherapy to help you recover and get back to normal.

## What Causes It?

Necrotising fasciitis happens when bacteria get into the deep layers of your skin through a wound.

Common entry points include:
- Cuts and scratches.
- Burns or scalds.
- Insect bites.
- Surgery wounds.
- Injecting drugs.

You are more likely to get this infection if you have:
- Diabetes.
- A weak immune system.

## Important Notes

- Necrotising fasciitis is very rare.
- Its symptoms can look like those of a common skin infection, such as cellulitis.
- But it is much more serious and needs urgent care.

# Avian Influenza – Simple Explanation

## What Is Avian Influenza?

Avian influenza is a type of flu that mainly affects birds.  
It is caused by certain types of flu virus A.  
These viruses usually infect wild birds and farm chickens.  
Some of these viruses can also infect people.  
Most human cases come from contact with infected birds.  
Human-to-human spread is rare.

## Which Types of Avian Influenza Affect People?

The most common types that have infected people are H5, H7, and H9.  
The H5N1 and H7N9 types have caused the most serious human cases.  
Other types have also caused some infections.  
Wild birds often do not get sick from these viruses.  
But the viruses can kill farm chickens quickly.  
Some marine animals, like seals, can also get infected.  
There have been rare cases of people getting sick after contact with infected seals.

## How Do People Get Infected?

People can get infected by breathing in virus particles from sick birds.  
They can also get infected through direct contact with bird fluids.  
These fluids include saliva, mucus, or droppings.  
The virus can change over time.  
If it changes in a way that lets it attach to human cells, it can infect people.  
All flu viruses can change quickly.  
This means avian viruses could gain the ability to spread easily between people.  
This could happen through natural changes or by mixing with human flu viruses.  
If this happens, it could lead to a global flu outbreak.

## What Should You Do If You Are Infected?

Any case of human flu caused by an influenza A virus that is not H1 or H3 must be reported to health officials.

## Specific Cases of Avian Influenza

### H5N1
- The first human cases were found in Hong Kong in 1997.  
- Eighteen people were sick.  
- Many had serious breathing problems.  
- Three out of ten people died.  
- The outbreak stopped by killing all infected farm birds.  
- H5N1 returned in 2003 and 2004.  
- Cases still happen, mostly in Asia and the Middle East.  
- Two cases have been reported in the United States:  
  - One in Colorado in 2022. The person had contact with infected poultry.  
  - One in Texas in 2024. The person worked on a dairy farm.  
- H5N1 was found in dairy cows in several U.S. states in 2024.  
- The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the Food and Drug Administration, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture are watching the situation closely.

### H5N6
- Over 50 human cases have been reported since 2014.  
- All cases happened in the Western Pacific region.  
- Most were in mainland China.

### H5N8
- The first human cases were reported in February 2021.  
- Seven poultry workers in Russia got sick.  
- All had mild or no symptoms.  
- No one passed the virus to another person.  
- The risk to the general public is very low.

### H7N9
- A major outbreak happened in China in early 2013.  
- About one in three people who got sick died.  
- Most serious cases were in older adults.  
- There was no sustained spread from person to person.  
- Some limited spread between people has been seen.  
- People got sick from touching or being near infected birds.  
- This often happened in live bird markets.  
- These markets see more activity before Chinese New Year.  
- China’s sixth wave of H7N9 peaked in 2016–2017 with nearly 800 cases.  
- Since then, only a few cases have been reported.  
- Worldwide, over 1,500 human cases and at least 615 deaths have been reported since 2013.  
- Some cases outside China happened in people who had recently visited mainland China.

### Other Types
- H7N3: One case in Canada.  
- H7N7: Several cases in the Netherlands.  
- H7N4 and H9N2: Mostly in China, and one case in Vietnam in 2024.

## Symptoms of Avian Influenza

The symptoms are like those of regular flu.  
They include fever, cough, sore throat, and body aches.  
But avian flu can be much more serious.  
It can lead to severe pneumonia.  
The death rate is higher than with regular flu.  
This depends on the virus type.

## How Is Avian Influenza Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and recent exposure.  
You may have been near sick birds, dairy cows, or a person with flu.  
A test is done using a swab from your nose or throat.  
If you have a lung infection, a sample from your coughed-up mucus may be used.  
The test is called RT-PCR.  
It checks for the virus.  
Do not try to grow the virus in a lab.  
It is very dangerous and needs special safety steps.  
All suspected or confirmed cases must be reported to health authorities.

## How Is Avian Influenza Treated?

Two main medicines are used:  
- Oseltamivir (sold as Tamiflu)  
- Zanamivir (sold as Relenza)  

These are called neuraminidase inhibitors.  
They work best if started within 48 hours of symptoms.  
Another medicine, baloxavir marboxil (sold as Xofluza), is also used.  
It is for people 12 years and older.  
It works best if taken within 48 hours of symptoms.  
It is not used for severe cases or people in hospitals.  

Some viruses, like H7N9 and H5N1, do not respond to older flu medicines like amantadine and rimantadine.  
Some cases of H7N9 and H5N1 have also shown resistance to oseltamivir.

## How Can You Prevent Avian Influenza?

- Avoid touching sick or dead birds.  
- Avoid contact with farm chickens, wild birds, and dairy cows.  
- Do not eat raw or undercooked food.  
- Avoid unpasteurized milk and dairy products.  
- In the United States, tests show that commercial milk does not contain live virus.  
- Pasteurization kills the virus.  
- Dairies must use milk from healthy animals.  
- All milk sold in stores must be pasteurized.

### Controlling the Spread
- Infected bird flocks are found and destroyed.  
- China vaccinates farm birds against H5 and H7 flu.  
- This helps stop the virus from spreading from wild birds to farm birds.  
- Farm birds are more likely to spread the virus to people.

### Vaccines
- A human vaccine for H5N1 is available in the United States.  
- It is only used if health officials decide it is needed.  
- The regular flu shot does not protect against avian flu.

## Key Points

- Avian flu mainly affects birds.  
- Some types can cause serious illness and death in people.  
- Most human cases come from contact with infected birds.  
- Human-to-human spread is rare but possible.  
- Do not try to grow the virus in a lab. It is very dangerous.  
- Treat with oseltamivir or zanamivir.  
- Or use baloxavir marboxil if you are 12 or older and have mild flu symptoms within 48 hours.

# Tetanus-D Diphtheria Vaccine

This vaccine helps protect you from two serious infections: tetanus and diphtheria. Both are caused by bacteria. These bacteria make poisons that can harm your body.

## What the Vaccine Does

The Td vaccine contains weakened versions of the poisons made by the tetanus and diphtheria bacteria. These weakened poisons are not harmful. But they teach your body’s defense system how to fight the real bacteria if you are ever exposed.

Your body learns to recognize the bacteria and can stop them before they cause illness. This is called active immunization.

The Td vaccine is for people 7 years old and older. It is mostly used in teens and adults.

There are two other vaccines that also protect against whooping cough (pertussis).  
- One is for children under 7 years old. It is called DTaP.  
- The other is for teens and adults. It is called Tdap.

## When and How to Get the Vaccine

The Td vaccine is given as a shot into a muscle.

### For Children
The DTaP vaccine is a routine childhood vaccine. It is given in five shots:  
- At 2 months old  
- At 4 months old  
- At 6 months old  
- Between 12 and 18 months old  
- Between 4 and 6 years old

### For Teens and Adults
After finishing the DTaP series, teens get one booster shot of Tdap at age 11 to 12 years.

Because protection against whooping cough fades over time, people over age 16 should get a Tdap booster if they have not had one before.

After the Tdap booster, you should get a Td or Tdap booster every 10 years.

### After a Wound
If you get a cut, scrape, or other injury that breaks the skin, you may need a booster shot if:
- It has been 5 or more years since your last Td or Tdap shot.
- You have not had a Tdap shot before and are over age 7.

In these cases, your doctor may give you a Td or Tdap shot to prevent tetanus.

### Who Should Not Get the Vaccine
Do not get the Td vaccine if:
- You had a serious allergic reaction (like anaphylaxis) to a previous dose.
- You had a serious allergic reaction to any part of the vaccine.

Also, do not get the vaccine if:
- You developed Guillain-Barré syndrome within 6 weeks after a previous tetanus vaccine.
- You had severe pain or swelling after a previous tetanus or diphtheria vaccine.

If you are sick with a fever or a serious illness, your doctor may wait to give the vaccine until you feel better.

Some health conditions may affect when or if you should get the vaccine. Talk to your doctor if you are unsure.

## Side Effects

Serious side effects are very rare. They include:
- Severe allergic reaction
- Severe shoulder pain
- Muscle weakness

Mild side effects are common and usually go away in a few days. They include:
- Soreness, pain, or redness at the injection site
- Fever
- Feeling tired
- Headache
- Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or stomachache

If you had Guillain-Barré syndrome within 6 weeks after a tetanus vaccine, talk to your doctor before getting another dose.

For more details on side effects, read the package insert that comes with the vaccine.

# Molar Pregnancy – Simple Explanation

A molar pregnancy does not always cause symptoms.  
You might find out during your first ultrasound scan.  
Or you might learn about it after a miscarriage.

## When to Call a Midwife or Doctor

If you are pregnant and have any of these signs, call your midwife or doctor right away:

- Vaginal bleeding or a dark discharge  
- Feeling sick often (severe morning sickness)  
- Your bump seems bigger than it should be for how far along you are  
- Any other symptoms that worry you

## What Happens If You Have a Molar Pregnancy

If your midwife or doctor thinks you have a molar pregnancy, you will need:

- Blood tests to check your pregnancy hormone level  
- An ultrasound scan  
- A visit to a specialist doctor (a gynaecologist) or a pregnancy assessment clinic

The pregnancy hormone is often much higher than normal in a molar pregnancy.

## Finding Out You Have a Molar Pregnancy

You may not have any symptoms at all.  
Or you may have some signs of pregnancy, like nausea or a growing bump.

You might find out during your first ultrasound scan, usually between 8 and 14 weeks of pregnancy.  
Some people find out after a miscarriage.

Learning you have a molar pregnancy can be very hard.  
Your doctor or midwife can help you understand what comes next and where to get support.

## Treatment for a Molar Pregnancy

A molar pregnancy cannot grow into a healthy baby.  
It will not survive.

Sometimes the body ends the pregnancy on its own, like a miscarriage.  
If that does not happen, treatment is needed.

The most common treatment is a procedure to remove the pregnancy tissue from the womb.  
You will be asleep during the procedure.  
You will get a general anaesthetic.

In some cases, medicine can be used to end the pregnancy instead.

## After Treatment – Follow-Up Care

After treatment, you will need regular blood and urine tests.  
These tests check your pregnancy hormone level.  
It must go back to normal.

Very rarely, some molar pregnancy cells stay in the womb.  
They can grow or spread to other parts of the body.  
This is a rare type of cancer called an invasive mole or choriocarcinoma.

If this happens, it can usually be treated successfully with chemotherapy.

## Support and Help

Recovering from a molar pregnancy can take time.  
It can be hard on your body and your emotions.

Your specialist team can help you with advice and support.  
They may know of local services that can help.

You can also get support and information from:

- Molar Pregnancy Support & Information  
- Miscarriage Association  
- Tommy’s: molar pregnancy – information and support  
- Charing Cross Hospital Trophoblast Disease Service

# Fibromyalgia – Simple Explanation

Fibromyalgia is a long-term condition that causes widespread pain and other symptoms. It is not caused by joint problems or inflammation. Many people with fibromyalgia feel a deep ache in their muscles, tendons, and soft tissues. They also often feel stiff, tired, and have trouble thinking clearly. Sleep problems are common. Other symptoms may include headaches, stomach issues, or bladder problems.

There is no specific test for fibromyalgia. Doctors diagnose it based on your symptoms and by ruling out other conditions.

---

## What Causes Fibromyalgia?

The exact cause is not known. But research suggests it may be linked to how the brain and nervous system process pain. Some people develop fibromyalgia after a viral illness, a serious injury, or a stressful event. However, treating these past events with antibiotics or antiviral medicines does not help.

Sleep problems may play a role. Poor sleep, especially not getting deep sleep, can make symptoms worse. Emotional stress can also trigger or worsen symptoms.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

- Pain that spreads across both sides of the body, above and below the waist, and in the spine area.
- Aching, stiff muscles that often start slowly and get worse with fatigue or overuse.
- Feeling very tired, even after a full night’s sleep.
- Trouble focusing, remembering things, or thinking clearly – often called “brain fog.”
- Headaches, including migraines or tension headaches.
- Digestive issues like bloating, gas, or changes in bowel habits (irritable bowel syndrome).
- Bladder problems such as frequent urination or discomfort (interstitial cystitis).
- Tingling or numbness in the hands and feet, often moving from one area to another.

Other health problems can make fibromyalgia worse. For example:
- Joint pain from arthritis.
- Sleep issues from sleep apnea or depression.

Many people with fibromyalgia are high achievers. They may be stressed, anxious, or feel overwhelmed. Some may also feel sad or depressed.

---

## How Is Fibromyalgia Diagnosed?

Doctors look for:
- Widespread pain lasting at least three months.
- Pain on both sides of the body, above and below the waist, and in the spine area.
- No clear cause found after testing.

The diagnosis is based on symptoms, not on physical exam findings. In the past, doctors looked for specific tender spots. But this method is no longer used because it is hard to measure and the spots can change over time.

### Tests to Rule Out Other Conditions

Your doctor may order blood tests to check for:
- Thyroid problems (hypothyroidism).
- Hepatitis C.
- Inflammation (using ESR or C-reactive protein).
- Muscle damage (using creatine kinase).

Fibromyalgia does not cause abnormal results in these tests. So normal results do not rule out fibromyalgia.

Other tests are only done if your history or exam suggests another condition.

---

### Common Mistakes in Diagnosis

- Fibromyalgia is often missed in men, children, and teens.
- A condition called systemic exertional intolerance disease (SEID), also known as chronic fatigue syndrome, can cause similar symptoms. It also shows normal test results.
- Polymyalgia rheumatica causes pain mainly in the shoulders and hips, especially in the morning. It is more common in older adults and causes high levels of inflammation in blood tests.
- In people with other rheumatic diseases like rheumatoid arthritis or lupus, fibromyalgia can be hard to spot. It may be mistaken for a flare-up of the main disease.

> **Tip:** If you have more pain and stiffness than expected, think about fibromyalgia — or a flare-up of another condition like rheumatoid arthritis or lupus.

---

## How Is Fibromyalgia Treated?

There is no cure, but many treatments can help reduce symptoms.

### Lifestyle Changes

- **Exercise:** Gentle stretching and aerobic activity (like walking, swimming, or biking) help reduce pain and improve energy. Do stretching exercises every day. Hold each stretch for about 30 seconds. Repeat 5 times.
- **Heat:** Apply warm packs or take warm baths to ease muscle stiffness.
- **Massage:** Gentle massage can help relax tight muscles.
- **Sleep:** Good sleep is very important. Avoid caffeine and screens before bed. Get a regular sleep schedule. Ask your doctor to check for sleep disorders like sleep apnea.
- **Stress management:** Try deep breathing, meditation, or counseling. These can help reduce stress and improve mood.

### Medications

Medications are used to help with sleep, pain, and mood. They are not a cure, but they can help.

- **Sleep aids:** Low-dose tricyclic antidepressants (like amitriptyline) or cyclobenzaprine taken at bedtime can help you sleep better and reduce pain. Start with a low dose and increase only if needed.
- **Antidepressants:** Duloxetine is a good option if you feel very tired or sad.
- **Pain relievers:** Pregabalin and gabapentin may help if you have severe sleep problems or nerve pain.
- **Side effects:** These medicines can cause drowsiness, dry mouth, or other issues. Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects.

> **Important:** Do not use opioid painkillers. They are not helpful and can cause harm.

### Other Treatments

Some people find relief from:
- Capsaicin cream (a natural substance from chili peppers).
- Biofeedback (learning to control body functions like heart rate).
- Massage therapy.
- Hypnotherapy (a type of guided relaxation).
- Chiropractic care.

These are not strong treatments, but they may help some people. They are part of official guidelines for fibromyalgia care.

### Review Your Medicines

Some medicines can make sleep worse. Talk to your doctor about all your medicines. Stop or change any that interfere with sleep.

If you have anxiety, depression, or bipolar disorder, treat those too. They can make fibromyalgia worse.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Fibromyalgia usually lasts a long time. But it can improve on its own if stress goes down. It may come back from time to time.

With good treatment, most people can live well. They can keep working, stay active, and enjoy life.

But symptoms often do not go away completely. The outlook is worse if mood problems like depression are not treated.

---

## Key Points to Remember

- Think about fibromyalgia if you have long-term pain, stiffness, and tiredness with no clear cause.
- Check for thyroid problems, hepatitis C, and inflammation with blood tests.
- Rule out other conditions like chronic fatigue syndrome or polymyalgia rheumatica.
- In people with other rheumatic diseases, fibromyalgia can be hidden. It may look like a flare-up, but tests show no new activity.
- Treat fibromyalgia with exercise, better sleep, stress control, and nonopioid pain relievers.
- Avoid opioid painkillers. They do not help and can cause harm.

# Listeriosis

Listeriosis is an infection caused by a type of bacteria called *Listeria monocytogenes*.  
You usually get it by eating food that is contaminated with the bacteria.

## How You Get Listeriosis

- The bacteria can be in dairy products, raw milk, vegetables, meats, or ready-to-eat foods that do not need cooking.
- The bacteria can grow in the refrigerator and survive in the freezer.
- Pasteurization kills the bacteria in milk and dairy products.
- Cooking or reheating food to a high temperature kills the bacteria.
- But the bacteria can hide in cracks and hard-to-reach spots in food factories. They can then get back into food.
- If the food does not need more cooking after you buy it, the bacteria stay in it and you eat them.
- The bacteria do not change the taste, smell, or look of the food.

Foods linked to past outbreaks include:
- Soft cheeses like feta, Brie, Camembert, and queso fresco
- Deli salads like coleslaw
- Unpasteurized milk
- Cold cuts and hot dogs
- Smoked salmon
- Undercooked chicken

## Who Is at Risk

Listeriosis is rare. In the United States, about 1,600 people get the serious form each year.  
About 1 in 6 of these people die.

You are more likely to get a serious case if you are:
- Pregnant
- A newborn baby
- 65 years old or older
- Have a weak immune system (such as from HIV)

Pregnant women are more likely to get listeriosis than others.  
Hispanic pregnant women are at even higher risk.

## What Happens If You Get Listeriosis

Most people have flu-like symptoms:
- Chills
- Fever
- Muscle aches
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Diarrhea

These symptoms usually go away in 1 to 3 days.

In some cases, the bacteria spread into the blood and infect other parts of the body. This is called invasive listeriosis.  
It can affect:
- The brain and spinal cord (causing meningitis)
- The eyes
- Heart valves (causing endocarditis)
- Joints
- The uterus and baby in pregnant women

Rarely, pus-filled areas (abscesses) form in the brain or spinal cord.

## Effects on Pregnancy

Listeriosis can cause:
- Miscarriage
- Stillbirth
- Premature birth

Pregnant women usually do not get very sick.  
But the infection can pass to the baby.  
The baby may get a serious infection in the blood (sepsis) or in the brain (meningitis).  
Many newborns who get the infection near or during birth do not survive.

## Did You Know?

Pregnant women are especially at risk.  
Listeriosis can cause pregnancy loss or early labor.  
It can also harm the baby.

## Symptoms of Listeriosis

Most people have:
- Chills
- Fever
- Muscle aches
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Diarrhea

These symptoms usually last 1 to 3 days.

If the infection spreads, symptoms depend on where the bacteria are:
- Meningitis: headache, stiff neck, confusion, trouble balancing
- Infection in the uterus or placenta: miscarriage or stillbirth
- Newborns: blood infection (sepsis) or meningitis. Many die.

## How Doctors Diagnose Listeriosis

Doctors confirm the infection by testing:
- Blood
- Fluid around the brain and spinal cord (cerebrospinal fluid)

They take a sample and send it to a lab.  
The lab grows the bacteria.  
If they find the bacteria, the diagnosis is confirmed.

## How Listeriosis Is Treated

Antibiotics can cure the infection.

- People with mild symptoms and healthy immune systems often get better without antibiotics.
- Antibiotics are needed for:
  - People with weak immune systems
  - Pregnant women
  - Newborns
  - People with severe symptoms

For serious infections like meningitis or heart infections:
- Doctors give ampicillin and gentamicin through a vein (IV).
- If you are allergic to penicillin, doctors use sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim instead.

For eye infections:
- Doctors may give erythromycin by mouth.
- Or they may give trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole through a vein.

## How to Prevent Listeriosis

The bacteria can grow in the fridge.  
Even lightly contaminated food can become very dangerous over time.

Take extra care if you are:
- Over 65 years old
- Pregnant
- Have a weak immune system

Avoid these foods unless they are heated:
- Soft cheeses made from unpasteurized milk (like feta, Brie, queso fresco, queso blanco, Camembert)
- Raw (unpasteurized) milk and cheeses made from it
- Refrigerated ready-to-eat foods (like hot dogs, deli meats, pâtés, meat spreads) unless heated to 165 degrees Fahrenheit (73.9 degrees Celsius) or until steaming hot
- Refrigerated smoked seafood (like nova-style, lox, kippered, smoked, or jerky) unless cooked

Other steps to reduce risk:
- Put leftovers in shallow, covered containers.
- Refrigerate them within 2 hours.
- Use them within 3 to 4 days.
- Keep your refrigerator at 40 degrees Fahrenheit (4.4 degrees Celsius) or colder.
- Keep your freezer at 0 degrees Fahrenheit (-17.8 degrees Celsius) or colder.

## More Information

For more details, visit:
**Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: Listeriosis**  
This site has information on outbreaks, high-risk groups, and how to stay safe.
