# High Blood Pressure

Your chance of having high blood pressure goes up as you get older.  
Being Black or having a close family member with high blood pressure also increases your risk.

High blood pressure usually has no symptoms.  
You may not know you have it unless you get your blood pressure checked.

If you have high blood pressure, you are more likely to develop serious health problems.  
These include heart disease, kidney disease, and dementia.

You can lower your blood pressure by making healthy changes to your daily life.  
These include eating better, moving more, and drinking less alcohol.

Many people need medicine to keep their blood pressure under control.  
Your doctor will choose the best medicine for you.

---

## Find Out If You Are at Risk

High blood pressure is very common, especially in older adults.  
It often has no signs, so you might not know you have it.

You are more likely to have high blood pressure if you:

- Are older  
- Have a parent, brother, or sister with high blood pressure  
- Are Black African, Black Caribbean, or South Asian  
- Eat too much salt  
- Are overweight  
- Smoke  
- Drink too much alcohol  
- Feel stressed for a long time

---

## Signs of High Blood Pressure

High blood pressure usually does not cause any symptoms.  
Most people with it do not feel sick.

In rare cases, it can cause:

- Headaches  
- Blurry vision  
- Chest pain  

But the only way to know for sure if you have high blood pressure is to get it checked.

---

## Risks of High Blood Pressure

When your blood pressure is too high, it puts extra pressure on your blood vessels, heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes.  
If it is not treated, it can lead to serious health problems, such as:

- Heart disease  
- Heart attacks  
- Strokes  
- Heart failure  
- Kidney disease  
- Vascular dementia  

Even a small drop in blood pressure can lower your risk of these problems.

---

## How to Lower Your Blood Pressure

You can help lower your blood pressure by making healthy changes to your lifestyle.

### Do These Things

- Eat a healthy, balanced diet  
- Exercise regularly — aim for at least 150 minutes of activity each week  
- Lose weight if you are overweight

### Avoid These Things

- Do not eat too much salt — avoid salty foods or adding salt to your meals  
- Do not drink too much alcohol — limit yourself to no more than 14 units a week  
- Do not drink too much caffeine — this includes coffee, tea, and cola  
- Do not smoke

---

## Medicine for High Blood Pressure

Your doctor may prescribe medicine if:

- Your blood pressure is very high  
- You are at higher risk of heart attack or stroke  
- Your blood pressure stays high even after you make healthy lifestyle changes

There are many types of blood pressure medicine.  
The one you get depends on how high your blood pressure is, your age, and your ethnicity.

Most medicines come in tablet form and are taken once a day.  
You may need more than one medicine to keep your blood pressure in check.

---

## Get Your Blood Pressure Checked

Get your blood pressure checked at a pharmacy or doctor’s office if:

- You think you might have high blood pressure  
- You are at risk of high blood pressure  
- You are 40 or older and have not had a check in over 5 years

Some pharmacies charge a small fee for a blood pressure check.  
Some workplaces also offer free checks — ask your employer.

---

## When to Get Help from NHS 111

Call 111 or get help online if you:

- Often have headaches or blurry vision  
- Have chest pain that comes and goes  
- Are worried about other symptoms that might be linked to high blood pressure

---

## When to Call 999

Call 999 right away if you have:

- Sudden chest pain that does not go away  
- The pain feels like squeezing, pressure, burning, or indigestion  
- Pain that spreads to your arm, neck, jaw, stomach, or back  
- Chest pain with sweating, nausea, dizziness, or shortness of breath  

You could be having a heart attack. You need emergency treatment in hospital.

---

### Important Safety Message for 999 Calls

Do not drive yourself to the hospital.  
The person you speak to on the phone will tell you what to do.

# Psoriatic Arthritis – Simple Explanation

Psoriatic arthritis is a long-term condition that causes joint pain and swelling. It happens in people who have psoriasis, a skin disease. Some people get the joint problems first. Others get the skin issues first. The joint and skin symptoms do not always match in how bad they are.

This condition is not caused by a virus or bacteria. The exact cause is not known. But it runs in families. It is more common in people with certain genes. It is also more common in people with HIV.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

### Skin and Nail Changes
- You may have red, scaly patches on your skin.
- These patches can appear on the scalp, ears, belly, or around the belly button.
- The patches may be hidden and not noticed at first.
- Your nails may have small pits or become thick and discolored.

### Joint Problems
- The joint pain often affects fingers and toes, especially the joints closest to the fingertips and toes (distal interphalangeal joints).
- The joint pain is often uneven. One side of the body may be worse than the other.
- Some people get a "sausage finger" or "sausage toe" — the whole finger or toe swells up.
- This swelling is called dactylitis. It does not happen in rheumatoid arthritis.
- Some people get severe joint damage over time. This can make the fingers or toes look bent or shortened.

### Back and Spine Pain
- Some people have pain in the lower back or buttocks.
- This is more common in men and in people with a certain gene (HLA-B27).
- The pain often comes and goes on one side of the body.

### Tendon Pain
- Pain can happen where tendons attach to bones.
- Common spots: back of the heel (Achilles tendon), front of the knee (patellar tendon), or elbow.
- This is called enthesopathy.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will look at your symptoms and medical history. They will check for:
- Skin or nail changes
- Joint swelling or pain
- Family history of psoriasis

They may do blood tests to rule out other types of arthritis. For example:
- A test for rheumatoid factor (RF) is usually negative in psoriatic arthritis.
- A test for anti-CCP antibodies is also usually negative. This helps tell it apart from rheumatoid arthritis.

Imaging tests like X-rays or MRI can show:
- Damage to the joints at the ends of fingers and toes
- Bone changes like cupping or thinning
- Swelling in the fingers or toes
- Changes in the spine or sacroiliac joints

The diagnosis is based on what the doctor sees and finds during the exam.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment aims to:
- Reduce joint pain and swelling
- Control skin symptoms
- Prevent joint damage

Your treatment plan depends on which parts of your body are affected. For example:
- If your hands and feet are affected, you may need one type of medicine.
- If your back is affected, you may need a different medicine.

### Common Treatments

#### For Joint Pain in Hands, Feet, and Other Areas
- **Methotrexate** – A pill taken once a week. It helps with both skin and joint symptoms. You will also take folic acid daily to reduce side effects.
- **Sulfasalazine** – A pill taken once a day. It may help after 3 months. Your blood counts and liver tests will be checked regularly.
- **Leflunomide** – A pill taken once a day. It helps with joint pain.
- **Hydroxychloroquine** – Not usually used. It can make psoriasis worse in some people.
- **Apremilast** – A pill that helps with skin and joint symptoms. Side effects include diarrhea, nausea, and mood changes.
- **TNF inhibitors** – These are injections or infusions. They help with both joints and skin. Examples: adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab.
- **IL-17 inhibitors** – These are injections. They help with skin and joint symptoms. Examples: secukinumab, ixekizumab.
- **IL-12/23 and IL-23 inhibitors** – These are injections. They help with skin and joint symptoms. Examples: ustekinumab, guselkumab.
- **JAK inhibitors** – A pill taken daily. Example: tofacitinib. It helps with joint pain. But it can raise the risk of infections and blood clots.
- **Abatacept** – An injection or infusion. It helps with joint pain. It can be used with other medicines.

#### For Back and Spine Pain
- **TNF inhibitors** – These are very helpful for back pain.
- **IL-17 inhibitors** – These can also help with back pain.
- **JAK inhibitors** – These may help with back pain too.

### Important Notes About Medicines
- Some medicines can increase the risk of infections.
- Some can cause liver problems. Your doctor will check your liver with blood tests.
- Alcohol use should be limited. It can harm the liver, especially in people with psoriasis.
- You may need regular blood tests to check your blood counts and liver health.

---

## Key Points

- Psoriatic arthritis is a long-term joint problem that happens in people with psoriasis.
- The skin and joint symptoms do not always match in severity.
- Joint pain often affects fingers and toes, especially the joints closest to the fingertips.
- The joint pain is often uneven — one side of the body may be worse than the other.
- Diagnosis is based on symptoms, physical exam, and tests to rule out other conditions.
- Treatment uses medicines called DMARDs. The choice depends on which parts of the body are affected.
- Early treatment helps prevent joint damage and keeps you feeling better.

Always talk to your doctor about your treatment plan. They will help you choose the best medicine for your needs.

# Ebola Vaccine – Simple Explanation

This page explains the Ebola vaccine in clear, easy-to-understand language.

---

## Which Ebola Vaccine Is Available?

The **rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine** is the only Ebola vaccine available in the United States.  
It is also allowed in the European Union, Canada, and several countries in Central, East, and West Africa.

This vaccine only protects against one type of Ebola virus: the *Zaire ebolavirus* species.  
It does **not** protect against other types of Ebola virus or against Marburg virus.

Marburg virus causes a disease that is similar to Ebola but is a different virus.

Another vaccine option uses two shots: **Ad26.ZEBOV** and **MVA-BN-Filo**.  
These two vaccines are not available in the United States.  
They were used during an Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.  
They protect against the *Zaire ebolavirus* species.

---

## How the Vaccines Work

### rVSV-ZEBOV Vaccine

- This is a live-attenuated recombinant viral vaccine.
- It contains a weakened but still live version of the Ebola virus.
- The virus is made in a lab and changed so it cannot cause disease.
- Even though it is weakened, it still helps your body learn how to fight the real Ebola virus.
- This strong response from your immune system is called active immunization.

The vaccine is stored in Switzerland.  
It can be sent quickly to areas where an Ebola outbreak is happening.

### Ad26.ZEBOV and MVA-BN-Filo Vaccines

- These are vector vaccines.
- They contain harmless genetic material from the Ebola virus.
- This genetic material is carried into your body by a different, harmless virus (called a vector).
- The body sees this and builds protection against Ebola.
- These vaccines do not cause Ebola disease.

---

## Who Should Get the Ebola Vaccine?

### rVSV-ZEBOV Vaccine

This vaccine is given as **one shot into a muscle**.

It is recommended for people **18 years and older** who are at high risk of exposure to Ebola because of their job. This includes:

- People helping to respond to an Ebola outbreak.
- Health care workers at federally approved Ebola treatment centers in the U.S.
- Lab workers or staff at high-security labs (biosafety level 4) that handle live Ebola virus in the U.S.
- Lab workers or staff at labs in the Laboratory Response Network.

### Ad26.ZEBOV and MVA-BN-Filo Vaccines

These are given as **two separate shots into a muscle**, spaced apart.

They are recommended for people **1 year and older** who live in or travel to areas where Ebola is spreading or common.

---

## Who Should Not Get the Ebola Vaccine?

Do not get the vaccine if you:

- Had a serious allergic reaction (like anaphylaxis) to any part of the Ebola vaccine.
- Are allergic to rice protein. (Rice protein is used in making these vaccines.)

If you have a weak immune system, such as from HIV or from taking certain medicines like corticosteroids or chemotherapy, you may not be able to get the vaccine.  
Talk to your doctor before getting vaccinated if you have a weak immune system.

If you have a high fever or a serious infection, wait until you feel better before getting the Ad26.ZEBOV and MVA-BN-Filo vaccines.

---

## Vaccines and Pregnancy or Breastfeeding

### Pregnant People

- Do not get the Ad26.ZEBOV and MVA-BN-Filo vaccines before giving birth.
- If you are pregnant and cannot avoid Ebola exposure, talk to your doctor.
- Your doctor can help you decide if the benefits of the vaccine outweigh the risks.
- If you choose to get the vaccine while pregnant, it is best to get it during the second trimester or early third trimester.
- The vaccine is not given during the first trimester or late in the third trimester.

### Breastfeeding People

- Similar advice applies to people who are breastfeeding.
- If the risk of Ebola is high (like during an outbreak), the vaccine may be given.
- Talk to your doctor about the benefits of breastfeeding for your baby versus the risk of getting Ebola.

---

## Side Effects of the Ebola Vaccine

### Common Side Effects (for all three vaccines)

- Pain and swelling at the injection site.
- Muscle and joint pain.
- Headache.
- Feeling tired.

### rVSV-ZEBOV Vaccine – Additional Common Side Effects

- Redness at the injection site.
- Feeling feverish.
- Nausea (upset stomach).
- Joint pain, swelling, or stiffness.
- Rash.
- Sweating more than normal.

### Ad26.ZEBOV and MVA-BN-Filo Vaccines – Additional Common Side Effects

- Warmth at the injection site.
- Chills.

### Children 1 to 17 Years Old – Most Common Side Effects

- Pain at the injection site.
- Feeling tired.
- Less energy.
- Less appetite.
- Feeling irritable.

For more details about side effects, read the package inserts that come with the vaccine.

---

## More Information

The following resources are in English and may help you learn more:

- **Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC):** *Ebola Disease Basics*
- **CDC:** *Ebola Vaccine Information Statement*

Note: The Manual is not responsible for the content of these websites.

# Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS)

You can get MERS from touching infected camels.  
You can also get it from being close to someone who has it.

Good hygiene and staying away from camels can help you avoid MERS when you travel.

## What are the main symptoms of MERS?

You may have:
- A high temperature
- A cough
- Trouble breathing or shortness of breath

You might also have:
- Diarrhoea
- Feeling sick or being sick
- Muscle aches
- Shivering (chills)

Symptoms usually start 5 or 6 days after infection.  
But they can show up anytime between 2 and 14 days after exposure.

## When to get help

Call your doctor right away or call NHS 111 if:
- You recently travelled to an area where MERS is a risk
- You were close to someone with MERS
- You think you might have MERS

Tell the doctor or nurse about your travel and any contact with camels.

If you get sick while abroad, get medical help right away.  
Do not wait until you return home.

Call 999 if you:
- Have serious trouble breathing – like gasping, choking, or not being able to speak
- Have pale, blue, or blotchy skin, lips, or tongue  
  (On brown or black skin, check the palms of your hands or soles of your feet)
- Suddenly feel confused – for example, you do not know where you are

### Important: A&E safety message (for 999 only)
Do not drive yourself to the emergency department.  
The person on the phone will tell you what to do.

## What causes MERS?

MERS is caused by a virus.  
It usually spreads from camels through:
- Touching them
- Being bitten
- Eating camel meat or drinking camel milk
- Eating or drinking things that touched camel spit, urine, or faeces

You can also catch it from close contact with an infected person.

MERS is most common in the Middle East, especially Saudi Arabia.  
It has also been found in parts of Africa and south Asia.

The chance of catching MERS is very low for most people.

## How to stay safe while travelling

There is no vaccine for MERS.  
But you can take steps to lower your risk.

### Do these things:
- Stay away from camels – do not touch, pet, or ride them
- Avoid farms, barns, or markets where camels are kept
- Wash your hands often with soap and warm water  
  Especially before or after being near camels or camel areas
- If you buy food at a market, only eat it if:
  - It is well cooked
  - Or you washed and peeled it yourself

### Do not do these things:
- Do not eat raw or undercooked camel meat
- Do not drink unpasteurised camel milk
- Do not eat products made with unpasteurised camel milk, like yoghurt
- Do not touch or go near sick animals

## How is MERS treated?

MERS can be serious and may be life-threatening.  
If you have it, you will likely be treated in hospital in a special room to stop the virus from spreading.

Treatment focuses on easing your symptoms, such as:
- Medicine to lower your temperature
- Medicine to ease pain
- Help with breathing if needed

# Periodic Limb Movement Disorder and Restless Legs Syndrome

This information is about two sleep problems:  
- **Periodic limb movement disorder (PLMD)**  
- **Restless legs syndrome (RLS)**

Both can make it hard to sleep well. They cause unusual movements or feelings in the arms or legs.

---

## What Causes These Conditions?

- PLMD is more common in middle-aged and older adults.
- More than 3 out of 10 people with RLS also have PLMD.
- The exact cause is not fully known. It may be linked to how the brain uses a chemical called dopamine.
- These conditions can happen:
  - On their own
  - When stopping certain medicines
  - When using stimulants, some antidepressants, or medicines that block dopamine
  - During pregnancy
  - In people with long-term kidney or liver problems
  - In people with low iron levels or anemia
  - In people with diabetes
  - In people with nerve problems
  - In people with neurological diseases like multiple sclerosis or Parkinson disease
  - In people with spinal cord issues

For RLS, family history can play a role. More than one in three people with RLS have a close relative with the same problem.

Other risk factors include:
- Sitting too much
- Smoking
- Being overweight

PLMD is often seen in people with narcolepsy or REM sleep behavior disorder.

---

## Symptoms

### Periodic Limb Movement Disorder (PLMD)

- Your legs or arms twitch or kick during sleep.
- Movements happen every 20 to 40 seconds.
- You may wake up briefly many times during the night.
- You usually do not notice the movements.
- You do not feel odd sensations in your limbs.
- You may feel tired during the day.
- Your bed partner may complain about being kicked.

### Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS)

- You feel a strong need to move your legs, arms, or other parts of your body.
- This urge is often linked to odd feelings like crawling, tingling, or aching.
- The urge gets worse when you are still or lying down.
- It is worst in the evening or at night.
- You move your legs to feel better — by stretching, kicking, or walking.
- This makes it hard to fall asleep or stay asleep.
- Stress can make symptoms worse.
- Some people have symptoms only once in a while.
- Others have them every day.

---

## How Are They Diagnosed?

### For RLS:
- Doctors can often diagnose RLS just by talking to you.
- They will ask about your symptoms and sleep habits.
- Your bed partner may help describe what they see.

### For PLMD:
- A sleep study called **polysomnography** is needed.
- This test records brain activity, heart rate, breathing, and muscle movements during sleep.
- It shows repeated bursts of muscle activity in the legs or arms.
- The test can also check if you have RLS at the same time.

### Medical Tests:
- All patients should have blood tests to check for:
  - Anemia
  - Low iron levels
  - Kidney problems
  - Liver problems
- These tests help find possible causes.

---

## How Are They Treated?

### First Step: Iron Supplements
- If your iron level is low, take iron pills.
- Your doctor will check your ferritin level (a measure of stored iron).
- If ferritin is below 50 micrograms per liter, take iron supplements.
- Take ferrous sulfate with 100 to 200 milligrams of vitamin C at bedtime.
- This is the first treatment for both RLS and PLMD.

### Second Step: Medication
- If iron does not help, or if you are not low in iron, your doctor may prescribe:
  - **Gabapentin enacarbil** — this is the best first medicine.
  - It is taken once a day with food, a few hours before bedtime.
  - Common side effects: feeling sleepy or dizzy.
  - It is less likely to cause worsening symptoms over time than other medicines.

Other medicines may be used in some cases:

- **Gabapentin** — helps with RLS, especially if you have pain.
- **Pregabalin** — may help with RLS and pain. Side effects include dizziness and sleepiness.
- **Dopaminergic drugs** (like pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine, or levodopa/carbidopa):
  - These can help but have serious side effects.
  - They can cause:
    - Symptoms getting worse before the next dose
    - Symptoms spreading to arms or other areas
    - Worsening after stopping the medicine
    - Nausea
    - Dizziness when standing up
    - Uncontrollable urges (like gambling or overeating)
    - Trouble sleeping
  - These medicines are not safe for long-term use.

- **Benzodiazepines**:
  - Can help you sleep better.
  - Do not reduce leg movements.
  - Can cause dependence, worsen sleep apnea, or make you sleepy during the day.
  - Use with care.

- **Opioids**:
  - May help if symptoms are very severe and painful.
  - Use with caution because they can cause addiction, side effects, and tolerance.

### Lifestyle Tips
- Practice good sleep habits:
  - Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day.
  - Avoid caffeine and alcohol before bed.
  - Keep your bedroom quiet, dark, and cool.
  - Avoid screens before sleep.
  - Stay active during the day, but not right before bed.

---

## Key Points

- **PLMD** causes repeated twitching or kicking of the arms or legs during sleep.
  - It can break your sleep and make you tired during the day.
  - You usually do not notice the movements.
  - Your bed partner may notice them.

- **RLS** causes a strong urge to move your legs or arms.
  - It often comes with odd feelings like crawling or tingling.
  - It gets worse when you are still or lying down.
  - It makes it hard to fall asleep or stay asleep.

- **Diagnose RLS** based on your symptoms and history.
- **Use a sleep study (polysomnography)** if PLMD is suspected.

- **Start with iron supplements** if your iron level is low.
- **Then try gabapentin enacarbil** if symptoms continue.
- Avoid long-term use of dopamine medicines.
- Use other medicines only when needed and with care.

# Spinal Muscular Atrophies (SMAs)

Spinal muscular atrophies are genetic conditions. They cause nerve cells in the spinal cord and brain stem to break down. This breakdown leads to muscle weakness and muscle loss over time.

There are five main types of spinal muscular atrophy. Each type causes different levels of muscle weakness and loss.

- Some people may need to use a wheelchair.
- Some people may not live as long as usual.
- Doctors diagnose the condition based on symptoms, family history, muscle and nerve tests, and blood tests.
- There is no cure. But physical therapy and braces can help with movement and daily tasks.

(See also _Overview of the Peripheral Nervous System_.)

These conditions are passed down through families. A child must inherit one faulty gene from each parent to have the condition. The condition affects nerves in the brain and spinal cord, as well as nerves in the rest of the body.

---

## Symptoms of Spinal Muscular Atrophies

The first four types show up in babies and children.

### Type 0
This is the most serious type. It starts before birth. The baby moves less than normal in the womb. After birth, the baby is very weak and has no muscle tone. Reflexes are missing. Joints do not move well. Both sides of the face are paralyzed. Heart problems are present at birth. The muscles that help with breathing are very weak. Most babies die within the first few months because they cannot breathe well. This is called respiratory failure.

### Type 1
This type appears at birth or within a few days. It is almost always clear by 6 months of age. Babies have no muscle tone. They do not have normal reflexes. They struggle to suck, swallow, and later breathe. Most children die within the first year. All children with this type die by age 4. Death is usually due to breathing problems.

### Type 2
This type shows up between 3 and 15 months. Fewer than one in four children learn to sit. None can crawl or walk. Reflexes are missing. Muscles are weak. Swallowing may be hard. Most children use a wheelchair by age 2 or 3. The condition can be life-threatening in early childhood, often due to breathing issues. But some children live longer with stable weakness. Many have a curved spine (scoliosis).

### Type 3
This type starts between 15 months and 19 years. It gets worse slowly. People with this type often live longer than those with types 1 or 2. Some live a normal life span. Weakness and muscle loss begin in the hips and thighs. Later, it spreads to the arms, feet, and hands. How long a person lives depends on whether breathing problems develop.

### Type 4
This type starts in adulthood. It usually begins between ages 30 and 60. Muscles in the hips, thighs, and shoulders slowly become weak and waste away.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Spinal Muscular Atrophies

Doctors look for signs of weakness and muscle loss in young children. A family history of the condition can help with diagnosis.

Tests include:

- **Electromyography and nerve conduction studies**: These tests check how well nerves and muscles work.
- **Blood test**: This test finds the faulty gene in 95 out of 100 people with the condition.
- **Muscle biopsy**: In rare cases, a small piece of muscle is taken for testing.

If a family has a history of spinal muscular atrophy, a test called amniocentesis can be done during pregnancy. This test checks if the unborn baby has the faulty gene.

---

## Treatment for Spinal Muscular Atrophies

There is no cure. But treatments can help.

### Physical and occupational therapy
These help improve movement and daily skills. Therapists teach children how to feed themselves, write, or use a computer.

### Braces and assistive devices
These can help with walking, sitting, and other activities.

### Medications

- **Nusinersen**  
  This medicine may help with muscle movement. It may also delay disability and death.  
  It is given as a shot into the space around the spinal cord.  
  The doctor numbs the area first. Then a needle is placed between two bones in the lower back. This is like a spinal tap.  
  The medicine is given in four doses over 2 months. After that, it is given every 4 months.

- **Onasemnogene abeparvovec-xioi**  
  This is used for children under 2 years old. Only one dose is needed.  
  It is given through a vein in the arm over 1 hour.  
  It may help children reach key milestones. These include sitting without help, eating, rolling over, and walking on their own.

- **Risdiplam**  
  This is used for people 2 years old and older.  
  It is taken as a liquid or through a feeding tube once a day.  
  It may help people live longer. It may also reduce the need for breathing machines.

# Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP)

## What is HSP?

HSP is a condition that causes a rash. The rash looks like raised red or purple spots. These spots look like small bruises.

You may also have joint pain or swelling. You might also have tummy pain.

HSP is not contagious. It cannot spread to other people.

## Symptoms of HSP

- The rash usually appears on the legs, bottom, tummy, chest, or back.
- The spots may be many or just a few.
- The rash does not fade when you press a glass against it.
- You may have pain or swelling in your joints, like your knees or ankles.
- You may have tummy pain.

## When to Get Help

### Call your GP right away or use NHS 111 if:
- You or your child has a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it.
- You do not feel unwell otherwise.

This could be HSP.

You can call 111 or get help online at [nhs.uk](https://www.nhs.uk).

### Call 999 or go to A&E if:
- The rash does not fade when a glass is pressed against it.
- You feel very unwell.
- You have pain when looking at bright lights.
- You have a stiff neck.

This could be a serious illness like meningitis.

### A&E Safety Tips
- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you.
- Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.
- Bring all your medicines with you.

## How HSP is Treated

HSP usually gets better on its own in a few weeks. You can rest at home and take care of yourself.

There is no special treatment for HSP.

### Pain Relief
- You can take paracetamol to help with pain.
- Do not take ibuprofen unless your doctor says it is safe. It can harm your kidneys.

### Going Back to Normal Life
- Your child can go back to school or nursery when they feel well.
- You can return to work when you feel up to it.

### Kidney Check-Ups
- You will need regular check-ups for 6 to 12 months.
- These check-ups help make sure your kidneys are working well.
- At each visit, you may need to give a urine sample and have your blood pressure checked.
- These checks can happen at home, at your GP’s office, or in hospital.

### Hospital Treatment
- You may need to go to hospital if HSP affects your kidneys.
- In hospital, you may be given strong medicines like steroids to help with symptoms.

## Risks of HSP

- Most people with HSP get better completely.
- Kidney problems from HSP usually get better without treatment.
- In some cases, HSP can be serious and last for several months.
- There is a small chance that the kidneys could be permanently damaged. This is called chronic kidney disease.
- That is why regular check-ups are important.

### Can HSP Come Back?
- Yes, you can get HSP more than once.
- If symptoms return, see a doctor right away.

# Rare Types of Stomach Inflammation

Gastritis means the lining of the stomach is inflamed. It can happen for many reasons. These include infection with a bacteria called *Helicobacter pylori*, certain medicines like painkillers, drinking too much alcohol, stress, or the body attacking itself. Some rare conditions can also cause it.

---

## Ménétrier Disease

This is a rare condition. It mostly affects adults between 30 and 60 years old. Men are more likely to get it than women.

The stomach lining in the middle part of the stomach becomes very thick. The lower part of the stomach does not get thickened.

The glands in the stomach lining shrink. The small pits in the lining grow larger. The stomach makes more mucus. There is little inflammation, but the lining gets much thicker.

The body loses too much protein through the stomach. This causes low levels of albumin in the blood. This is the most common lab finding.

As the disease gets worse, the stomach makes less acid and less digestive juice. This leads to low acid levels in the stomach.

Symptoms are not specific. They include:
- Pain in the upper belly
- Nausea
- Losing weight
- Swelling in the body (edema)
- Diarrhea

To diagnose this disease, doctors use a scope to look inside the stomach. They take a small sample of tissue from deep in the lining. Or they may do a small surgery to get a full-thickness sample.

Other conditions that can look like Ménétrier disease include:
- Lymphoma: This can cause many ulcers in the stomach.
- MALT lymphoma: This is a type of cancer that affects the immune cells in the stomach lining.
- Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome): This causes the stomach to make too much acid and can also thicken the stomach folds.
- Cronkhite-Canada syndrome: This rare condition causes polyps in the stomach and intestines. It leads to diarrhea and protein loss.

Treatments used include:
- Medicines that reduce stomach acid
- Medicines that calm the nervous system
- Steroid medicines

None of these treatments work well for everyone. In severe cases, part or all of the stomach may need to be removed, especially if protein loss is very bad.

---

## Eosinophilic Gastritis

This condition happens when a type of white blood cell called eosinophils builds up in the stomach lining. It can affect the inner lining, the layer under it, and the muscle layer. It often starts in the lower part of the stomach.

Most cases have no known cause. But it can be linked to a worm infection.

Symptoms include:
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Feeling full quickly after eating small amounts

To diagnose it, doctors use a scope to take a tissue sample from the affected area.

Steroid medicines can help if the cause is unknown. If the opening from the stomach to the small intestine becomes blocked, surgery may be needed.

---

## MALT Lymphoma

This is a rare type of cancer. It starts in the immune cells in the stomach lining. The lining becomes full of these cells. It can look like Ménétrier disease when seen with a scope.

But a lab test of the tissue shows it is different.

If the cancer is only in the stomach, treating the *Helicobacter pylori* infection can cure it in many cases.

---

## Gastritis from Other Body-wide Diseases

Some diseases that affect the whole body can also cause stomach inflammation. These include:
- Sarcoidosis
- Tuberculosis
- Amyloidosis
- Other similar conditions

The stomach problem is usually not the main issue.

---

## Gastritis from Physical Causes

Radiation and swallowing strong poisons (especially strong acids) can damage the stomach lining.

If a person gets more than 6 gray of radiation to the whole body, the stomach lining can become severely damaged. The lower part of the stomach is usually more affected.

Possible complications include:
- Narrowing of the opening from the stomach to the small intestine (pyloric stenosis)
- A hole in the stomach wall (perforation)

---

## Infection-Related Gastritis

Infection of the stomach with bacteria is rare. The only common cause is *Helicobacter pylori*. Other bacteria usually only enter the stomach after:
- Poor blood flow to the stomach
- Swallowing strong poisons
- Radiation exposure

On X-rays, gas can be seen outlining the stomach lining.

This condition can cause sudden, severe belly pain. It is a medical emergency. It has a very high risk of death. Surgery is often needed.

People who are very weak or have a weak immune system can get stomach infections from viruses or fungi. These include:
- Cytomegalovirus
- Candida
- Histoplasmosis
- Mucormycosis

These infections should be considered if a person has a stomach lining that is covered in pus or has sores in the stomach, esophagus, or small intestine.

# Listeriosis – Simple Guide

## What is listeriosis?

Listeriosis is an infection caused by a type of bacteria called *listeria*.  
It does not always cause symptoms.  
If you do get symptoms, they are often mild and feel like the flu.

## What are the symptoms?

Most people have no symptoms.  
If you do get symptoms, they may include:  
- A high temperature  
- Chills  
- Aches and pains  
- Feeling sick or being sick  
- Diarrhoea  

If you are pregnant, you might also have:  
- A stomach ache  
- Your baby moving less than usual  

Babies with listeriosis may:  
- Be irritable  
- Feed less than normal  

## How do you get listeriosis?

You usually get it from eating food that has *listeria* bacteria in it.  
The bacteria can be in many types of food, especially chilled, ready-to-eat foods.  
These include:  
- Cold cooked meats (like sliced ham or salami)  
- Smoked or cured fish (including in sushi)  
- Cooked shellfish  
- Soft cheeses (like brie and camembert) and blue-veined cheeses  
- Pâté (including vegetable pâté)  
- Pre-made sandwiches and salads  
- Pre-cut fruit (like melon slices)  
- Unpasteurised milk and dairy products made from it  

These foods do not always have the bacteria.  
If you eat them and feel fine, you do not need to worry.  
But if you get symptoms, see a doctor.

You can also get listeriosis from:  
- Someone who is infected – for example, if they touch food without washing their hands  
- Close contact with farm animals – especially sheep or cows that are giving birth  

## Who is at higher risk?

Listeriosis is usually not serious for healthy people.  
But some people are more at risk of serious illness.  
This includes:  
- Anyone who is pregnant  
- Newborn babies  
- People with long-term health conditions like cancer, diabetes, liver disease, or kidney disease  
- People on treatments that weaken the immune system (like chemotherapy or steroid tablets)  
- Older adults – the older you are, the higher the risk  

If you are pregnant and get listeriosis, it can cause:  
- Miscarriage  
- Stillbirth  

In babies and people with weak immune systems, listeriosis can lead to serious problems like:  
- Sepsis (a life-threatening infection in the blood)  
- Meningitis (infection of the brain and spinal cord covering)  

## When to get help

Call your GP right away or use NHS 111 if you:  
- Are pregnant and think you have listeriosis  
- Have a health condition that weakens your immune system and think you have listeriosis  
- Are having treatment that weakens your immune system and think you have listeriosis  
- Think your baby might have listeriosis  

You can call NHS 111 or get help online.  
If you are pregnant, you can also call your midwife for advice.

## When to go to A&E (Emergency Department)

Go to A&E or call 999 if you or your child have:  
- A severe headache and a stiff neck  
- Pain when looking at bright lights  
- A fit (seizure)  
- Sudden confusion  
- Feeling very sleepy or hard to wake  
- A rash that does not fade when you press a glass over it  
  - The rash may look like bruises or tiny red spots  

These could be signs of meningitis caused by listeriosis.  
This needs urgent hospital treatment.

### A&E Safety Tips

- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you.  
- If you can’t get a ride, call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
- Bring all your medicines with you.

## How is listeriosis treated?

Most people get better on their own in a few days.  
You can treat it at home by:  
- Resting  
- Drinking plenty of fluids  

If you are at higher risk (like being pregnant or having a weak immune system), you may need antibiotics.  
Your doctor will decide if you need them.

## How to avoid listeriosis

You can lower your risk by following these steps:

### Do this:
- Keep chilled ready-to-eat foods cold.  
  - Make sure your fridge is at 5 degrees Celsius or below.  
- Eat chilled ready-to-eat foods within 4 hours of taking them out of the fridge.  
- Use foods by their use-by date.  
- Follow storage instructions on food labels.  
  - Opened food should be used within 2 days unless the label says otherwise.  
- Keep raw food separate from ready-to-eat food.  
- Follow cooking instructions on packaging.  
  - Cook or reheat food until it is steaming hot all the way through.  
  - This includes frozen vegetables.  
- Wash your hands often with soap and water, especially before handling food.

### Avoid these foods if you are at risk:
If you are pregnant or have a weak immune system, avoid:  
- Cold-smoked or cured fish (like smoked salmon or gravlax) unless cooked until steaming hot  
- Soft cheeses (like brie and camembert) unless cooked until steaming hot  
- All types of pâté (including vegetable pâté)  
- Unpasteurised milk and dairy products  
- Any undercooked food  

Also avoid:  
- Close contact with farm animals that are giving birth or have just given birth  
  - This includes sheep and cows  

## Important reminder

Eating these foods does not always cause listeriosis.  
You only need to worry if you get symptoms.  
If you do, seek help right away.

# Gallstones

Gallstones are hard pieces of material that form in the gallbladder.  
The gallbladder is a small organ under the liver. It stores bile, a fluid that helps digest fat.

Most people with gallstones do not have any symptoms.  
When symptoms do occur, the most common one is biliary colic.  
Biliary colic is a sudden, severe pain in the upper right side of the belly.  
Gallstones do not cause indigestion or trouble with eating fatty foods.

Serious problems can happen if gallstones block the bile ducts.  
These problems include:
- Inflammation of the gallbladder (cholecystitis)
- Blockage of the bile ducts (choledocholithiasis)
- Infection in the bile ducts (cholangitis)
- Inflammation of the pancreas (gallstone pancreatitis)

Doctors usually find gallstones using an ultrasound scan of the belly.  
If gallstones cause symptoms or complications, the gallbladder must be removed.

---

## Who Is at Risk for Gallstones?

You are more likely to get gallstones if you:
- Are a woman
- Are overweight or obese
- Are older
- Are of American Indian descent
- Eat a Western-style diet (high in fat and sugar)
- Lose weight very quickly
- Have a family history of gallstones

In the United States, over 15 out of 100 people aged 60 to 75 have gallstones.  
Most problems in the bile system are caused by gallstones.

---

## How Gallstones Form

### Biliary Sludge
Before gallstones form, a thick, sticky substance called biliary sludge may build up in the gallbladder.  
Sludge is made of:
- Calcium bilirubinate (a type of pigment)
- Tiny cholesterol crystals
- Mucus (mucin)

Sludge often forms when the gallbladder does not empty well.  
This can happen during pregnancy or when someone is on total parenteral nutrition (a special feeding method).

Most sludge goes away when the cause is fixed.  
But sometimes sludge turns into gallstones.  
It can also move into the bile ducts and block them.  
This can lead to:
- Biliary colic
- Infection in the bile ducts (cholangitis)
- Inflammation of the pancreas (pancreatitis)

---

### Types of Gallstones

#### Cholesterol Stones
These are the most common type in Western countries.  
They make up more than 85% of all gallstones.

For these stones to form, three things must happen:
1. Bile must have too much cholesterol.
   - Normally, cholesterol is mixed with bile salts and lecithin to stay dissolved.
   - Too much cholesterol can happen with obesity or diabetes.
   - It can also happen if the body makes too little bile salt (as in cystic fibrosis) or too little lecithin (a rare genetic condition).

2. The extra cholesterol must come out of the liquid and form tiny solid crystals.
   - This process is faster when there is too much mucin or other proteins in the bile.

3. The tiny crystals must stick together and grow into larger stones.
   - Mucin helps form a scaffold for the crystals to grow on.
   - Poor gallbladder movement (due to high cholesterol in bile) traps the crystals and helps them grow.

#### Black Pigment Stones
These are small, hard stones made of calcium bilirubinate and other calcium salts.
They are more common in people with:
- Liver disease from long-term alcohol use
- Chronic breakdown of red blood cells (hemolysis)
- Older age

#### Brown Pigment Stones
These are soft and greasy. They are made of bilirubinate and fatty acids.
They form when there is:
- Infection in the bile ducts
- Inflammation
- Parasites (like liver flukes, common in parts of Asia)

Gallstones grow slowly — about 1 to 2 millimeters per year.  
It can take 5 to 20 years for a stone to grow big enough to cause problems.

Most gallstones form in the gallbladder.  
But brown pigment stones usually form in the bile ducts.

After gallbladder removal, stones can still form in the bile ducts.  
This is especially true for brown pigment stones, which can form behind narrow areas (strictures) due to poor flow and infection.

---

## Symptoms and Signs

About 80% of people with gallstones never have symptoms.  
The other 20% may have:
- Biliary colic (the most common symptom)
- Inflammation of the gallbladder (cholecystitis)
- Serious infections (cholangitis)

### Biliary Colic
This is a sudden, sharp pain in the upper right side of the belly.  
It can also spread to the back or shoulder.

The pain:
- Starts suddenly
- Gets worse in 15 minutes to 1 hour
- Stays steady for up to 12 hours (usually less than 6 hours)
- Fades slowly over 30 to 90 minutes
- Leaves a dull ache

The pain is often so bad that people go to the emergency room.

Other common symptoms:
- Nausea
- Some vomiting

Fever and chills do not happen unless the gallbladder becomes infected.

There may be mild tenderness in the upper right belly.  
But there is no sign of peritoneal irritation (like rebound tenderness or guarding).

Between attacks, people feel fine.

### What Triggers the Pain?
- The pain can follow a heavy meal.
- But fatty foods are not a specific cause.
- Gas, bloating, and nausea are common in many conditions.
- These symptoms are not unique to gallbladder disease.

They happen just as often in:
- Peptic ulcer disease
- Functional gastrointestinal disorders

> **Important Note:**  
> Fatty foods do not cause biliary colic.  
> Gas, bloating, and nausea are not signs of gallbladder disease.

### When to Worry
- If the pain lasts more than 12 hours, especially with vomiting or fever, you may have:
  - Acute cholecystitis
  - Pancreatitis
- Biliary colic can happen even if the gallbladder is not inflamed.
- The number or severity of attacks does not always match how bad the gallbladder is.

---

## How Gallstones Are Diagnosed

### Ultrasound Scan
This is the best test to find gallstones.  
It is 95% accurate at finding stones and sludge.

Ultrasound can also show:
- Sludge
- Blockages
- Gallbladder wall thickening

### Other Imaging Tests
- CT scan and MRI can be used if ultrasound is unclear.
- Endoscopic ultrasound is very good at finding small stones (less than 3 millimeters).  
  It may be needed if other tests are not clear.

### Blood Tests
Blood tests are usually normal if there are no complications.  
They may show signs of infection or liver problems if complications are present.

### Incidental Findings
Many people find out they have gallstones by accident.  
This happens when an ultrasound or other scan is done for another reason.

About 10 to 15 out of 100 gallstones are calcified.  
These can be seen on a plain X-ray.

---

## Treatment

### For Symptomatic Gallstones
- The best treatment is laparoscopic cholecystectomy (removal of the gallbladder).
- In some cases, doctors may try to dissolve the stones using a medicine called ursodeoxycholic acid.
  - This only works for small cholesterol stones.
  - It takes months to years.
  - Stones often come back after stopping the medicine.

### For Asymptomatic Gallstones
- No treatment is needed.
- Doctors recommend watching and waiting (expectant management).
- Most people choose not to have surgery.
  - They do not want the cost, risk, or discomfort of surgery.
  - The gallbladder may never cause a problem.

But if symptoms start, surgery is needed.  
Pain will likely return.  
Serious complications can happen if the gallbladder is not removed.

---

## Prognosis

- About 2 out of 100 people with silent gallstones will develop symptoms each year.
- The most common symptom is biliary colic.
- Once symptoms start, pain returns in 20 to 40 out of 100 people each year.
- About 1 to 2 out of 100 people each year develop serious complications, such as:
  - Cholecystitis
  - Bile duct blockage
  - Infection in the bile ducts
  - Pancreatitis

---

## Key Points

- Gallstones are common, but 8 out of 10 people with them have no symptoms.
- Abdominal ultrasound is 95% accurate at finding gallstones.
- Once symptoms start (usually biliary colic), pain returns in 20 to 40 out of 100 people each year.
- Most people with symptomatic gallstones should have laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

# What Are Gallstones?

Gallstones are hard pieces of material that form in the gallbladder.  
The gallbladder is a small, pear-shaped organ under the liver.  
It stores bile, a fluid made by the liver to help digest food.  
When you eat, the gallbladder squeezes and sends bile into the small intestine.

Most gallstones are made of cholesterol.  
Cholesterol is a type of fat that normally dissolves in bile.  
But if the liver makes too much cholesterol, it can build up in the gallbladder.  
This causes tiny crystals to form.  
These crystals grow over time into gallstones.

Other types of gallstones are made of calcium or bilirubin.  
Bilirubin is a substance found in bile.  
Stones made of bilirubin are called pigment stones.  
Black pigment stones form in the gallbladder.  
Brown pigment stones form in the bile ducts.

Gallstones can stay in the gallbladder.  
Or they can move into the bile ducts.  
When they block the ducts, they can cause serious problems.

Some people have gallstones but never feel any symptoms.  
About 80 out of 100 people with gallstones do not have any problems.  
These are called silent gallstones.

## What Causes Gallstones?

Certain things increase your chance of getting gallstones.  
These include:

- Being a woman  
- Being older  
- Being American Indian  
- Being overweight  
- Losing weight very fast (such as on a very low calorie diet or after weight-loss surgery)  
- Eating a typical Western diet (high in fat and processed foods)  
- Having a family history of gallstones  

In the United States, more than 15 out of 100 people aged 60 to 75 have gallstones.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most gallstones do not cause pain or other issues.  
But if a stone moves and blocks a duct, it can cause pain.

The pain is called biliary colic.  
It usually starts in the upper right side of the belly, under the ribs.  
It can spread to the back or shoulder.  
The pain builds up over 15 to 60 minutes.  
It lasts for up to 12 hours.  
It is often very strong and may send people to the emergency room.

The pain usually gets better over 30 to 90 minutes.  
It leaves a dull ache.  
People often feel sick to their stomach and may vomit.

Eating a large meal can trigger this pain.  
But it does not matter if the meal is fatty or not.  
Gallstones do not cause belching or bloating.

Most of the time, the pain goes away on its own.  
But it can come back.  
About 20 to 40 out of 100 people have another attack each year.

If the blockage lasts, the gallbladder can become inflamed.  
This is called acute cholecystitis.  
Inflammation can lead to infection.  
You may get a fever.

If a stone blocks the main bile duct or the area where the bile and pancreatic ducts meet, it is more serious.  
This can cause:

- Swelling of the bile ducts  
- Fever and chills  
- Jaundice (yellow skin or eyes)  

This combination means you have a serious infection called acute cholangitis.  
Bacteria can spread into the blood.  
This can cause a life-threatening condition called sepsis.  
Pus pockets (abscesses) can also form in the liver.

A stone that blocks the area where the bile and pancreatic ducts meet can also block the pancreatic duct.  
This can cause pancreatitis — inflammation of the pancreas.  
This causes severe pain.

In rare cases, the gallbladder wall can break open.  
This is called perforation.  
It lets bile leak into the belly.  
This causes severe inflammation called peritonitis.

A large gallstone can also get stuck in the small intestine.  
This blocks the flow of food and causes a condition called gallstone ileus.  
This is rare but more likely in older adults.

> **Did You Know?**  
> Fatty foods do not cause more pain than other foods.  
> Most gallstones do not cause any symptoms.

## How Are Gallstones Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect gallstones if you have the typical upper belly pain.  
Sometimes gallstones are found by chance during another test.

The best test for gallstones is ultrasound.  
It uses sound waves to create images of the gallbladder.  
It finds gallstones in the gallbladder about 95 out of 100 times.  
It is less accurate for stones in the bile ducts.  
But it can show if the ducts are swollen.

If the ultrasound is unclear, other tests may be needed:

- **MRI** or **CT scan** – to look at the gallbladder and bile ducts  
- **MRCP** – a special MRI that shows the bile and pancreatic ducts  
- **Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)** – a thin tube with a camera and ultrasound is passed through the mouth into the stomach and small intestine. It gives a clearer picture of the gallbladder and ducts  
- **ERCP** – a procedure that uses a flexible tube to look inside the bile and pancreatic ducts. A dye is injected so doctors can see blockages on X-rays

During ERCP, doctors can also remove stones from the ducts.

Blood tests are also done.  
They check how well the liver is working.  
If a stone blocks a bile duct, the liver tests will be abnormal.  
This shows that bile is backing up in the liver.

## How Are Gallstones Treated?

If gallstones do not cause symptoms, no treatment is needed.  
Changing your diet, such as eating less fat, does not help.

If gallstones cause repeated pain, surgery to remove the gallbladder is the most common treatment.  
This surgery is called cholecystectomy.

About 90 out of 100 gallbladder removals are done using a laparoscope.  
This is a small camera and tools inserted through small cuts in the belly.  
It causes less pain, shorter hospital stays, better healing, and faster recovery.

The rest of the surgeries are done with a larger cut in the belly.  
This is called open surgery.

In some cases, doctors may use medicine to dissolve gallstones.  
The medicine is a type of bile acid taken by mouth.  
It can dissolve small stones in 6 months.  
Larger stones may take 1 to 2 years.  
But many stones never dissolve.

This treatment works best when:
- The stones are made of cholesterol  
- The gallbladder opening is not blocked  

Even if the stones go away, half of people get new ones within 5 years.  
This treatment is only used when surgery is too risky, such as in people with serious health problems.

A medicine called ursodeoxycholic acid can also help prevent stones in people who are losing weight fast after surgery or on a very low calorie diet.

Most stones in the bile ducts can be removed during ERCP.  
During this procedure, doctors cut the muscle at the end of the bile duct.  
This is called endoscopic sphincterotomy.  
It opens the duct so stones can pass into the intestine.

If stones do not come out on their own, doctors use a small basket to pull them out.

Cutting the duct helps prevent future blockages.  
But it can cause side effects.  
These include:
- Inflammation of the pancreas (pancreatitis)  
- Bleeding  
- Infection  
- A tear in the duct  
- Narrowing of the duct later on (stricture)

Most people who have ERCP and sphincterotomy later have their gallbladder removed.  
This is because stones in the gallbladder can still move into the ducts and cause more blockages.

> **Did You Know?**  
> Gallstones do not cause belching or bloating.

# Poisoning

Poisoning happens when someone swallows, touches, or breathes in a harmful substance.

## Common Causes of Poisoning

Some things that can cause poisoning include:
- Medicines like paracetamol, ibuprofen, or antidepressants
- Cleaning products such as bleach or laundry detergent
- Alcohol and drugs
- Certain plants and mushrooms
- Pesticides
- Chemicals found in some workplaces
- Carbon monoxide (a colourless, odourless gas from faulty heaters or stoves)

## Signs and Symptoms

Symptoms may not start right away. They can appear a few hours or even days later.

Symptoms can include:
- Feeling sick or being sick
- Diarrhoea
- Feeling very sleepy
- Blurred vision
- High temperature (fever)
- Confusion
- Trouble breathing
- Seizures (fits)
- Losing consciousness

The symptoms depend on what caused the poisoning.

## When to Get Help

Call 999 or go to A&E right away if:
- You think you, a child, or someone else swallowed, touched, or breathed in something harmful
- Someone has lost consciousness
- Someone has stopped breathing
- You or someone else is having severe trouble breathing – you can’t speak, are choking, or gasping
- You or someone else is having a seizure (fit)

## What to Do While Waiting for Help

If you think someone has been poisoned, do these things:
- Start CPR if the person is not breathing and is not responding.
- Put the person in the recovery position if they are unconscious but still breathing.
- Keep checking if they are breathing. If they are awake, keep talking to them to make sure they stay alert.
- Look around for the container, packaging, or medicine that might have caused the poisoning.
- Bring the substance or its container to the hospital if you can.
- If the person vomits, save some of the vomit in a clean container. This can help doctors find out what caused the poisoning.

Do not:
- Try to make the person sick. This can cause choking or stop them from breathing.
- Give the person anything to eat or drink.

## Getting to the Hospital

Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you. Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring all your medicines with you when you go to the hospital.

## When to Call NHS 111

Call NHS 111 if:
- You are not sure if something you or someone else swallowed, touched, or breathed in is harmful.

## Treatment in Hospital

Poisoning must be treated in hospital. It can make you very ill and can be life threatening.

Treatment depends on what caused the poisoning. It may include:
- Medicines that counteract the poison (antidotes)
- A special charcoal drink that can help block some poisons
- Fluids given through a needle in the vein to treat dehydration
- Treatments to remove the poison from your body, such as filtering it from the blood

If you have no symptoms, you may not need treatment. But you will still need to be watched closely for several hours in case you become unwell later.

# Immunoglobulin A–Associated Vasculitis (IgAV)

IgAV is a condition where small blood vessels become inflamed.  
It mostly affects children.  
The inflammation happens in small blood vessels in the skin, gut, and kidneys.  
It was once called Henoch-Schönlein purpura.

## What Happens in IgAV?

The body makes abnormal immune complexes.  
These contain a protein called IgA.  
They build up in small blood vessels.  
This causes inflammation and damage.

Possible triggers include:  
- Viruses that cause colds or sore throats  
- Strep infections  
- Certain medicines  
- Some foods  
- Insect bites  
- Vaccines  

The most common problem is a rash.  
It shows up as purple spots on the skin.  
It usually starts on the feet and legs.  
It can also appear on the arms or trunk.  
The spots feel raised and may look like bruises.  
They can start as itchy bumps that turn into purple marks.  
New spots may appear over several days or weeks.

Many people also have:  
- Fever  
- Joint pain, especially in the ankles, knees, hips, wrists, and elbows  
- Swelling around the joints  

Abdominal pain is common.  
It feels like cramps.  
It can be severe.  
Some people have blood in their stool.  
This may not be visible but can be found in a test.  
In children, a rare but serious problem is intussusception.  
This is when part of the intestine folds into itself.  
It can block the bowel.

Most people get better in about four weeks.  
But symptoms can come back after a break.  
In most cases, the disease goes away without lasting harm.  
However, a few people develop long-term kidney problems.

Adults are less likely to get intussusception.  
But they are more likely to have lasting kidney damage than children.

## How Is IgAV Diagnosed?

Doctors look at the symptoms and physical exam.  
In children, a clear rash and symptoms are often enough to make the diagnosis.  
No biopsy is needed in most children.

In adults, a biopsy is usually needed.  
A small sample of skin is taken.  
It is tested for IgA deposits in the blood vessel walls.  
This test is called direct immunofluorescence.

A urine test checks for blood or protein in the urine.  
This shows if the kidneys are involved.  
Blood tests check kidney function and blood counts.  
If kidney function is getting worse, a kidney biopsy may be done.  
This helps predict how the kidneys will do over time.  
If many kidney filters are damaged or if crescents form, kidney failure may get worse.

## How Is IgAV Treated?

Treatment focuses on relieving symptoms.  
It is not always needed.

If a medicine is causing the problem, stop taking it.  
Otherwise, treatment is mainly about comfort.

For children:  
- Pain relief is the main treatment.  
- Steroids or other immune drugs are usually not needed.  
- Most children get better on their own.

For adults:  
- Steroids like prednisone can help with belly pain.  
- They may also help with severe joint pain or kidney problems.  
- A short burst of strong steroids through a vein (IV) may be used.  
- This is followed by daily oral steroids.  
- Another medicine to calm the immune system may be added.  
  - These include mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, rituximab, or cyclophosphamide.  
- These treatments aim to reduce kidney damage.  
- But it is not clear if steroids help the kidneys in the long run.

## Key Facts

- IgAV is inflammation of small blood vessels.  
- It happens more often in children than adults.  
- Common signs include:  
  - Purple rash on the legs and feet  
  - Joint pain and swelling  
  - Belly pain  
  - Blood in the stool  
  - Kidney problems  
- Symptoms usually go away in about four weeks.  
- They can come back later.  
- A skin biopsy can confirm the diagnosis if needed.  
- The test looks for IgA in blood vessel walls.  
- Treatment is mainly about managing symptoms.  
- Adults may need steroids or other immune drugs if symptoms are severe.

# Cancer of the Uterus – Simple Explanation

This document explains uterine cancer in plain language. It covers what it is, what causes it, how it is found, how it is treated, and how to lower your risk.

---

## What Is Uterine Cancer?

The most common type of uterine cancer starts in the lining of the uterus. This lining is called the endometrium. The cancer is called endometrial cancer.

- Endometrial cancer mostly affects women after menopause.
- It often causes unusual bleeding from the vagina.
- Doctors diagnose it by taking a small sample of tissue from the lining of the uterus. This is called a biopsy.
- Treatment usually means removing the uterus, ovaries, and fallopian tubes. Sometimes nearby lymph nodes are also removed. After surgery, radiation therapy may be used. In some cases, chemotherapy or hormone therapy is also needed.

---

## Types of Uterine Cancer

Most uterine cancers start in the endometrium. These are called endometrial cancers.

- About 75 to 80 out of 100 endometrial cancers are adenocarcinomas. These start in gland cells.
- A smaller number of uterine cancers are sarcomas. These start in muscle or connective tissue.
- Sarcomas grow faster and are harder to treat than other types.

Less than 5 out of 100 uterine cancers are sarcomas.

---

## Who Gets Uterine Cancer?

Endometrial cancer is more common in high-income countries where more people are overweight.

- In the United States, it is the 4th most common cancer in women.
- In 2023, about 66,200 new cases were expected.
- About 13,030 women died from this cancer in 2023.
- About 80 out of 100 new cases are found early, when the outlook is good.
- The other 20 out of 100 cases are more advanced or aggressive.

In the United States:
- Black, American Indian, and Alaska Native women have higher rates of this cancer.
- Black women have the highest death rate from this cancer.

Most women with endometrial cancer are between 55 and 64 years old.

---

## Types of Endometrial Cancer

There are two main types:

### Type I
- More common.
- Grows slowly.
- Responds to the hormone estrogen.
- Often found in younger women, women with obesity, or women going through perimenopause (the years just before and after the last period).
- Prognosis is usually good.

### Type II
- Less common (about 10 out of 100 cases).
- Grows faster and is more aggressive.
- Usually found in older women.
- Prognosis is not as good.

---

## What Causes Uterine Cancer?

Certain conditions increase the risk of endometrial cancer.

### Risk Factors:
- High levels of estrogen and low levels of progesterone
- Being over 45 years old
- Being overweight or obese
- Using tamoxifen for 2 years or longer
- Having Lynch syndrome (a hereditary condition that raises the risk of colon and other cancers)
- Having radiation therapy to the pelvis (the area that holds the uterus, bladder, and rectum)

### Conditions That Raise Estrogen and Lower Progesterone:
- Being overweight
- Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) or other problems with ovulation
- Starting periods early or going through menopause late
- Never being pregnant
- Taking estrogen alone after menopause (without a progestin)
- Having a tumor that makes estrogen

Estrogen makes the lining of the uterus grow. Progesterone (or a synthetic version called progestin) helps thin that lining. When estrogen is high and progesterone is low, the lining can grow too much, which raises cancer risk.

Taking birth control pills that have both estrogen and progestin lowers the risk of endometrial cancer.

Medications or herbal products with estrogen can cause cancer if not taken with a progestin.

### Tamoxifen
- This drug treats breast cancer.
- It blocks estrogen in the breast but acts like estrogen in the uterus.
- It can raise the risk of endometrial cancer, especially in postmenopausal women.
- If you are taking tamoxifen and have unusual vaginal bleeding, tell your doctor right away.

### Heredity
- In about 5 out of 100 women with endometrial cancer, family history plays a role.
- About half of these cases are linked to Lynch syndrome.
- People with Lynch syndrome have a high risk of colon cancer and other cancers.

---

## Symptoms of Uterine Cancer

The most common early symptom is abnormal vaginal bleeding.

This includes:
- Bleeding after menopause
- Bleeding between periods
- Periods that are heavier, longer, or irregular

About 6 to 19 out of 100 women who bleed after menopause have endometrial cancer.

Even a small amount of blood, or pink, red, or brown spotting, should be checked by a doctor.

Women with sarcoma (a rare, aggressive type) may also have:
- Pain or pressure in the pelvis or lower belly

---

## How Is Uterine Cancer Diagnosed?

### Step 1: Suspect Cancer
Doctors may suspect cancer if:
- A woman has abnormal vaginal bleeding
- A Pap test shows cells from the uterus

### Step 2: Biopsy
- A small sample of tissue is taken from the lining of the uterus.
- This is called an endometrial biopsy.
- It is done in the doctor’s office and is accurate more than 90% of the time.

### Step 3: Ultrasound
- A small device is placed in the vagina to take pictures of the uterus.
- This helps see if the lining is thick or if there are other problems.
- But a biopsy is still needed to confirm cancer.

### Step 4: Dilation and Curettage (D and C)
- If the biopsy is unclear, doctors may scrape more tissue from the uterus.
- This is done under anesthesia.
- A thin tube with a camera (hysteroscope) is used to look inside the uterus at the same time.

### Step 5: Tests to Check for Spread
If cancer is found, doctors may do:
- Blood tests
- Tests to check kidney and liver function
- A chest x-ray (if needed)
- CT scan or MRI (if cancer may have spread)

### Staging
Staging tells how far the cancer has spread. There are four stages:

- **Stage I**: Cancer is only in the body of the uterus. It may have spread to an ovary in some cases.
- **Stage II**: Cancer has spread into the muscle wall of the uterus or into the cervix.
- **Stage III**: Cancer has spread to nearby tissues, the vagina, or lymph nodes.
- **Stage IV**: Cancer has spread to the bladder, intestines, or distant organs.

---

## How Is Uterine Cancer Treated?

### Surgery
Surgery is the main treatment. The most common surgery is a hysterectomy.

- The uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries are removed.
- This is called a total hysterectomy and salpingo-oophorectomy.

There are three ways to do this surgery:

1. **Open surgery**: A large cut is made in the abdomen.
2. **Laparoscopic surgery**: Small cuts are made near the navel. A camera and thin tools are used.
3. **Vaginal surgery**: The organs are removed through the vagina.

All methods take about 1 to 2 hours and require general anesthesia.

After surgery:
- You may have vaginal bleeding and pain.
- Recovery can take up to 6 weeks.

### Laparoscopic Surgery
- Small tools and a camera are inserted through tiny cuts.
- The camera sends images to a monitor.
- The surgeon watches the screen and uses the tools to cut and sew.

### Robotic-Assisted Laparoscopic Surgery
- Same as laparoscopic surgery.
- But robotic arms hold the tools.
- The surgeon sits at a console and uses hand controls to move the robot.
- The camera gives a 3D, high-definition view.

Benefits of laparoscopic or vaginal surgery:
- Shorter hospital stay
- Less pain
- Fewer complications
- Faster return to normal activities

### Lymph Node Removal
- Nearby lymph nodes are usually removed during surgery.
- A pathologist checks them to see if cancer has spread.
- This helps decide if more treatment is needed.

### Sentinel Lymph Node Dissection
- Instead of removing all lymph nodes, doctors remove only the first one(s) that cancer is likely to spread to.
- This is called the sentinel lymph node.
- To find it, doctors inject a blue or green dye or a radioactive substance into the cervix.
- During surgery, they look for nodes that are blue, green, or give off a signal.
- These nodes are tested for cancer.
- If no cancer is found, no other nodes are removed (unless they look abnormal).

### Treatment by Stage

- **Stage I**: Hysterectomy and removal of ovaries and tubes usually cure the cancer.
- **Stage II or III**: Surgery is done, followed by radiation therapy. Sometimes chemotherapy is added.
- **Stage IV**: Treatment includes surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, and sometimes hormone therapy with a progestin.
