# Whooping Cough

## What is whooping cough?

Whooping cough causes long spells of coughing. These coughing spells can make it hard to breathe. Some people, especially children, may make a loud "whoop" sound when they try to breathe in after coughing.

## Why is whooping cough dangerous?

Babies under 12 months old are at highest risk. Whooping cough can cause serious problems such as:
- Not drinking enough fluids (dehydration)
- Trouble breathing
- Pneumonia (a lung infection)
- Seizures (fits)

Older children and adults usually have milder symptoms. But the cough can still cause:
- Pain in the ribs
- A hernia (a bulge in the tummy or groin)
- Ear infections
- Leaking urine when you cough

## What are the symptoms?

At first, whooping cough feels like a cold. You may have:
- A runny nose
- A sore throat
- A mild fever (this is rare)

After about a week, you or your child will start to cough more. The coughing spells:
- Last several minutes
- Are worse at night
- May cause a loud "whoop" sound when breathing in
- Can make your face turn red
- May cause thick mucus to come up, which can lead to vomiting
- Can make it hard to breathe, especially in babies

The cough can last for weeks or even months.

## When to get help

### Call your GP or NHS 111 right away if:
- Your baby is under 6 months old and has coughing symptoms
- You or your child have a very bad cough that is getting worse
- You’ve been near someone with whooping cough and you’re pregnant

Use the NHS 111 online service for children aged 5 and over. Call 111 for children under 5.

### Call 999 or go to A&E if:
- Your lips, tongue, face, or skin suddenly turn blue or grey (on darker skin, check the palms of the hands or soles of the feet)
- You or your child are struggling to breathe (breathing is shallow)
- You or your child have chest pain that gets worse when coughing or breathing – this could mean pneumonia
- Your child has a seizure (fit)

Find your nearest A&E.

### A&E safety tips:
- Do not drive yourself to A&E. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 for an ambulance.
- Bring all your medicines with you.

## How is whooping cough treated?

Treatment depends on your age and how long you’ve had the cough.

### Antibiotics
- You may be given antibiotics if you’ve had the cough for less than 2 weeks.
- This helps stop the infection from spreading to others.
- Antibiotics do not make your symptoms go away faster.
- You must finish the full course of antibiotics, even if you feel better. Stopping early can let the infection come back.

### Hospital care
- You or your baby may need hospital treatment if:
  - The cough is very severe
  - Your baby is under 6 months old

## How to feel better at home

### Do:
- Rest as much as possible
- Drink plenty of fluids (water, juice, soup)
- Take paracetamol or ibuprofen if you or your child are in pain or uncomfortable
  - Always check the instructions on the packet or leaflet
  - Make sure the medicine is safe for your child’s age

### Don’t:
- Never give aspirin to anyone under 16 years old

## The whooping cough vaccine

The whooping cough vaccine protects children and babies from getting the disease.

### Routine vaccinations:
- Babies get the vaccine at 8, 12, and 16 weeks as part of the 6-in-1 vaccine.
- Children get a booster at age 3 years and 4 months as part of the 4-in-1 pre-school booster.

### If you are pregnant:
- You should have the whooping cough vaccine around 20 weeks of pregnancy.
- This helps protect your baby in the first few weeks of life.
- If you are past 20 weeks and haven’t been offered the vaccine, talk to your GP or midwife.

It is important to have all routine NHS vaccinations. This protects your child and others around them.

# Treating Stable COPD

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) has two main parts to treatment:  
- Managing stable COPD  
- Treating flare-ups  

This guide focuses on stable COPD.

## What Is the Goal of Treatment?

The main goals are to:
- Prevent flare-ups  
- Help your lungs work better  
- Improve your ability to move and do daily activities  

## How to Treat Stable COPD

### Stop Smoking
Smoking makes COPD worse. Quitting helps slow lung damage and can improve your life.  
Even if you’ve had COPD for years, quitting still helps.  

To quit smoking, try more than one method at once. These include:
- Pick a day to quit and stick to it  
- Join a support group  
- Work with a counselor or therapist  
- Use nicotine replacement (like gum, patches, inhalers, lozenges, or sprays)  
- Take medicine like varenicline or bupropion  
- Get support from your doctor  

Quitting is hard. Many people try more than once. But every attempt helps.  

**What happens when you quit?**  
- In the first year, your lung function may improve.  
- If you keep smoking, your lungs get worse faster.  
- If you start smoking again, your lung function drops.  
- If you stay quit, your lungs stay healthier longer.  

### Use Medicines
Medicines help open your airways and make breathing easier.  

**Main medicines:**
- Beta-agonists (help relax airway muscles)  
- Anticholinergics (also help relax airway muscles)  

These two types work about the same.  
- If you have mild COPD, use medicine only when you feel short of breath.  
- If you have moderate to severe COPD, use medicine every day to help your lungs and let you move more.  

**Other medicines can help reduce flare-ups:**
- Anticholinergics  
- Inhaled steroids  
- Long-acting beta-agonists  

But daily use of these medicines does not slow lung damage over time.  

**Choosing the right medicine:**
- Your doctor will help pick the best one for you.  
- Consider cost, how easy it is to use, and your symptoms.  

**How to use inhalers at home:**
- Use a metered-dose inhaler or dry powder inhaler.  
- Avoid nebulizers at home. They can get dirty and cause infections.  
- Nebulizers deliver medicine to the upper airways, which is less effective.  

**How to use a metered-dose inhaler correctly:**
- Breathe out fully.  
- Put the inhaler in your mouth.  
- Breathe in slowly and deeply.  
- Hold your breath for 3 to 4 seconds.  
- Breathe out slowly.  

Use a spacer with your inhaler. It helps medicine reach deep into your lungs. Some spacers tell you if you’re breathing in too fast.  

If your inhaler is new or hasn’t been used in a while, prime it with 2 to 3 sprays. Check the label for exact instructions.  

**How to use a dry powder inhaler:**
- You must breathe in very fast and deep.  
- This helps break up the powder so small particles reach the deepest parts of your lungs.  

### Use Oxygen Therapy
Oxygen therapy can help you live longer if your blood oxygen level is low.  

**Who needs oxygen?**
- If your blood oxygen level is below 55 mm Hg while at rest  
- Or if your oxygen level is below 88% while at rest  

**How to use oxygen:**
- Use it for 24 hours a day if possible.  
- Using it only at night is less helpful.  

**Benefits of oxygen:**
- Helps your blood carry oxygen better  
- May improve sleep and mental clarity  
- Helps your heart and lungs work better  
- Can help you walk farther without getting short of breath  

**Check your oxygen level:**
- Measure it at rest and during activity.  
- If you have advanced COPD but don’t meet the oxygen criteria at rest, your doctor may suggest a sleep study.  

**Oxygen during sleep:**
- If you drop below 88% oxygen during sleep, you may need oxygen at night.  
- This can help prevent worsening of lung pressure.  
- But it is not proven to help you live longer.  

**Oxygen during flights:**
- Airplane cabins have lower oxygen levels.  
- If you have COPD, you may need extra oxygen during flights.  

**When you need oxygen on a plane:**
- If your blood oxygen level is 68 mm Hg or lower at sea level  
- If you have high carbon dioxide levels  
- If you have severe anemia  
- If you have heart or brain problems  

**What to do:**
- Tell the airline when you book your flight.  
- Most airlines no longer provide oxygen.  
- Rent or buy a portable oxygen concentrator.  
- Bring extra batteries for the flight and possible delays.  

**Safety tip:**
- Never smoke or cook with open flames while using oxygen. It can cause fire.  

### Get Vaccines
Vaccines help prevent infections that can make COPD worse.  

**All people with COPD should get:**
- A flu shot every year  
- Pneumococcal vaccine (to prevent pneumonia)  
- RSV vaccine (for adults over 60, including those with COPD)  
- COVID-19 vaccine (including boosters)  

**If you are near someone with the flu:**
- Your doctor may give you medicine (like oseltamivir or zanamivir) to prevent infection.  
- Start treatment within 2 days of exposure.  
- If you get flu symptoms, start medicine right away.  

### Eat Well
COPD can make it hard to eat enough. You burn more energy just breathing.  

**Problems:**
- You may lose weight  
- You may not eat enough because you feel short of breath  
- Inflammation in your body can break down muscle  

**What to do:**
- Eat a balanced diet with enough calories  
- Eat small meals often instead of large ones  
- Exercise to keep your muscles strong  

**If you are underweight:**
- Talk to your doctor or dietitian.  
- You may benefit from extra nutrition supplements.  

**If you are overweight:**
- Try to lose weight slowly.  
- Focus on healthy eating and activity.  

**Medicines to boost appetite or build muscle:**
- These have not worked well in studies.  
- They are not recommended.  

### Join a Pulmonary Rehabilitation Program
Pulmonary rehab helps you move better and feel stronger.  

**What it includes:**
- Exercise training  
- Education about COPD and your medicines  
- Advice on managing daily tasks  
- Support for mental health and lifestyle  

**Benefits:**
- You can do more without getting out of breath  
- You feel better and more independent  
- You may feel less tired and anxious  

**Note:**
- Rehab does not improve lung function.  
- It helps you live better with your lungs.  

**How it works:**
- Start with light walking or cycling.  
- Gradually increase time and effort over 4 to 6 weeks.  
- Goal: Walk 20 to 30 minutes without stopping.  
- For very severe COPD, aim for 30 minutes at 1 to 2 miles per hour.  

**Exercise tips:**
- Do exercise 3 to 4 times a week to keep fit.  
- Use oxygen if needed.  
- Monitor your oxygen level.  

**Upper body strength:**
- Strength training helps with daily tasks like dressing and cleaning.  
- It improves your ability to do work and care for yourself.  

**Save energy:**
- Learn ways to do tasks with less effort.  
- Pace yourself.  
- Talk to your doctor about sexual activity. You can still enjoy it with energy-saving tips.  

**Virtual rehab:**
- You can join rehab online.  
- It helps improve exercise ability.  
- It may not help as much with quality of life or shortness of breath.  
- If in-person rehab is hard to reach, virtual rehab is a good choice.  

### Surgery (For Severe COPD)
Surgery is only for a few people with very severe COPD.  

**Options:**
- Lung volume reduction surgery  
- Lung transplant  

These are major surgeries. They are only done when other treatments fail.  

## Key Points

- Use short-acting medicines to relieve symptoms fast.  
- Use inhaled steroids, long-acting medicines, or a mix to reduce flare-ups.  
- Quit smoking. Use more than one method to increase your chances.  
- Eat well, stay active, and join a rehab program.  
- Use oxygen if your blood oxygen is low.  
- Get all recommended vaccines.  
- Talk to your doctor about your treatment plan.  

This information is based on the 2024 Global Strategy for COPD from the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD).  
Visit [www.goldcopd.org](http://www.goldcopd.org) for more details.

# Q Fever

Q fever is a disease caused by a type of bacteria called *Coxiella burnetii*.  
These bacteria mainly live in sheep, cattle, and goats.  
The bacteria can survive for months in dust and animal waste.  
Even one tiny bacterium can cause an infection.  

Q fever can spread through the air.  
People get sick when they breathe in tiny droplets from infected animals.  
It can also spread through raw (unpasteurized) milk from infected animals.  
It does not spread easily from person to person.  

Q fever happens all over the world.  
It is more common in people who work with animals or live near farms with infected animals.

---

## Who Is at Risk?

You are more likely to get Q fever if you:
- Work as a veterinarian
- Work in a meat processing plant
- Work in a slaughterhouse or dairy
- Are a livestock farmer
- Work in a lab with sheep
- Live within several miles downwind of a farm with infected animals

---

## Symptoms of Q Fever

Symptoms usually start 9 to 28 days after exposure.  
Some people have no symptoms or only mild ones.  
Others have flu-like symptoms, including:
- High fever
- Severe headache
- Chills
- Extreme tiredness
- Muscle aches
- Loss of appetite
- Sweating

You may also have a dry cough, chest pain, or trouble breathing.  
This happens because the lungs are affected.  
This lung problem is called pneumonia.

In some cases, the liver becomes involved.  
You may feel pain in the upper right side of your belly.  
You might also have yellowing of the skin or eyes.  
This is called jaundice.

If a woman is infected during pregnancy, she has a higher chance of:
- Losing the baby early (miscarriage)
- Giving birth before the due date

Some people develop a long-term tiredness after Q fever.  
This is called post-Q fever fatigue syndrome.  
It can last for months or years.  
Symptoms include:
- Severe tiredness
- Muscle pain
- Headaches
- Sensitivity to light
- Mood changes
- Trouble sleeping

---

## Chronic Q Fever

Chronic Q fever is a serious form of the disease.  
It affects fewer than 5 out of 100 people who get Q fever.  
It can start weeks or even years after the first infection.  

You are more likely to get chronic Q fever if you:
- Are pregnant
- Have a weak immune system (from illness or medicine)
- Have a heart valve problem

Chronic Q fever often affects the heart lining and heart valves.  
This is called Q fever endocarditis.  
It can also affect bones, artificial joints, and the liver.

Without treatment, most people with Q fever survive.  
But untreated Q fever endocarditis is almost always deadly.  
With treatment, fewer than 5 out of 100 people die.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Q Fever

Doctors use several tests to confirm Q fever:
- Blood tests to check for antibodies
- A test called PCR to find the bacteria in the blood
- A chest x-ray if you have a cough or breathing problems
- A biopsy (small tissue sample) from infected areas

Symptoms alone are not enough to diagnose Q fever.  
They are similar to other illnesses.  
Doctors will ask if you have been near farms or animals.

Antibody tests are not useful right away.  
You need to take the test twice — once when you first get sick and again 3 to 6 weeks later.  
A rising level of antibodies shows the infection is real.

PCR testing can find the bacteria faster than blood tests.

---

## Treatment of Q Fever

Most people with Q fever are treated with antibiotics.  
The main medicine is doxycycline.  
It is taken by mouth.

For mild cases:
- You take the medicine until you feel better and have no fever for about 5 days
- You must take it for at least 7 days
- Most people need about 2 weeks of treatment
- Severe cases may need longer treatment

Doxycycline is safe for children when used for 5 to 10 days.  
It does not cause tooth staining or weaken tooth enamel in children of any age.

If the heart is affected, treatment lasts much longer.  
You may need medicine for months or even years.  
Most people take doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine.  
Both are taken by mouth.

Doctors check your health regularly.  
They do blood tests and physical exams to decide when treatment can stop.

Even with treatment, the medicine may not fully fix the damage.  
Surgery may be needed to replace damaged heart valves.

---

## How to Prevent Q Fever

You can reduce your risk by:
- Only drinking milk that has been pasteurized
- Avoiding raw milk and dairy products
- Using good hygiene in animal farms
- Testing animals for the bacteria
- Keeping animal areas clean and safe

In Australia, a vaccine is available for people at high risk.  
It is used for:
- Slaughterhouse workers
- Dairy workers
- Livestock farmers
- Lab workers who handle sheep

The vaccine is not available in the United States.

Before giving the vaccine, doctors test your blood and skin.  
If you already have immunity, the vaccine can cause a strong reaction at the injection site.  
So it is not given to people who are already immune.

# Hay Fever

Hay fever is a common condition that happens when your body reacts badly to pollen.  
Pollen is a fine powder from plants.  
It is most common in the spring and summer months.  
It usually starts in late March and lasts until September.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may have one or more of these symptoms:

- You sneeze a lot.  
- You cough.  
- Your nose runs or feels blocked.  
- Your eyes are itchy, red, or watery.  
- Your throat, mouth, nose, or ears feel itchy.  
- You cannot smell things well.  
- You have pain in your forehead or sides of your head.  
- You get headaches.  
- You feel very tired.

These symptoms can last for weeks or even months.  
A cold usually goes away in 1 to 2 weeks.  
Hay fever does not go away that fast.

## How to Manage Hay Fever at Home

There is no cure for hay fever.  
You also cannot stop it from happening.  
But you can take steps to feel better when pollen levels are high.

### Do These Things

- Put a small amount of petroleum jelly (like Vaseline) around your nose.  
  This helps trap pollen before it gets in.  
- Wear wraparound sunglasses.  
  This keeps pollen out of your eyes.  
- Wear a mask or a wide-brimmed hat when you go outside.  
  This helps stop pollen from getting into your nose and mouth.  
- Shower and change your clothes after being outside.  
  This washes pollen off your skin and hair.  
- Keep windows and doors closed as much as possible.  
  This keeps pollen out of your home.  
- Vacuum your home regularly.  
  Use a damp cloth to dust.  
  This stops dust and pollen from floating in the air.  
- Use a pollen filter in your car’s air vents if you have one.  
- Use a vacuum cleaner with a HEPA filter.  
  This traps tiny particles like pollen.

### Avoid These Things

- Do not cut grass or walk on grass.  
  This can stir up pollen.  
- Do not spend too much time outside when it is warm, humid, or windy.  
  These conditions make pollen levels higher.  
- Do not keep fresh flowers in your house.  
  They can bring in pollen.  
- Do not smoke or be around smoke.  
  Smoke makes your symptoms worse.  
- Do not dry clothes outside.  
  Clothes can pick up pollen while drying.  
- If possible, do not let pets come inside.  
  Pets can carry pollen on their fur.

## Help from a Pharmacist

Talk to a pharmacist if you have hay fever.  
They can help you choose the right treatments.  
They may suggest:

- Antihistamine drops, tablets, or nasal sprays.  
- Steroid nasal sprays.

Some antihistamines can make you sleepy.  
Ask your pharmacist for a non-sleepy type if you need to stay alert.

## Treatment from Your Doctor

Your doctor may prescribe a steroid spray if your symptoms are bad.  
This helps reduce swelling and itching in your nose.

If steroids and other treatments do not help, your doctor may refer you for immunotherapy.

Immunotherapy means you get small, regular doses of pollen.  
This can be in the form of a shot or a tablet.  
Over time, your body learns to tolerate pollen better.  
This treatment usually starts a few months before hay fever season begins.

Immunotherapy is not available in all areas.  
It is a specialist treatment and may not be offered everywhere.

## What Causes Hay Fever?

Hay fever happens when your body overreacts to pollen.  
Pollen is a fine powder from trees, grasses, and weeds.  
When you breathe in pollen or it touches your eyes, nose, mouth, or throat, your body treats it as a threat.  
This causes the symptoms of hay fever.

# Agitation, Confusion, and Muscle Paralysis in Seriously Ill Patients

Patients in the intensive care unit often feel restless, confused, or uncomfortable. Some may become delirious. These feelings are hard on patients. They can also make care harder and put patients at risk. In serious cases, patients might pull out tubes or IV lines. This can be dangerous.

## What Causes Agitation and Confusion?

Agitation and confusion in a very sick patient can come from many sources. These include:

- The original illness
- New health problems
- Medical treatments
- The ICU setting itself

It is very important to know that muscle paralysis does not stop pain or distress. A patient who is paralyzed can still feel pain and fear.

### Common Causes

| Cause | Examples |
|------|----------|
| **Medical conditions** | Head injury, shock, poisoning, or overdose |
| **Pain and discomfort** | From injuries, surgery, breathing tubes, IVs, blood tests, or stomach tubes |
| **Health problems** | Low oxygen, low blood pressure, infection, organ failure, or blood clots in the lungs |
| **Medicines** | Painkillers, sleep aids, some heart or allergy medicines, or withdrawal from alcohol or drugs |
| **ICU environment** | Loud noises, bright lights, constant medical checks, lack of sleep, fear of dying, or worry about medical procedures |

Older adults are especially affected by the ICU environment.

## How to Check for Agitation and Confusion

Before giving sedatives for restlessness, doctors should:

- Look at the patient’s medical chart
- Do a full physical exam

This helps find the real cause of the problem.

## How to Treat Agitation and Confusion

### Treat the Root Cause

Fix the underlying problem. For example:

- Give oxygen if the patient is low on oxygen
- Treat infections
- Control blood pressure
- Manage pain
- Adjust or stop medicines that cause confusion

### Improve the Environment

Make the ICU more calming and easier to understand:

- Keep the room dark and quiet at night
- Limit interruptions during sleep
- Put clocks, calendars, and windows in the room
- Allow TV or radio to help patients stay aware of time and the world
- Let family members visit
- Use the same nurses as much as possible

### Use Medicines When Needed

Medicines are used only when needed and based on the main symptoms:

- **Pain** → Use pain relievers
- **Anxiety or trouble sleeping** → Use sedatives
- **Hallucinations or severe confusion** → Use small doses of antipsychotic medicine

If a patient needs strong sedatives, they may need a breathing tube. This is to protect the airway and breathing.

Many medicines are available. Short-acting ones are usually better. They let doctors check the patient’s brain function often. They also help when the patient is being taken off the breathing tube.

## Key Points

- Agitation and confusion can come from the illness, complications, treatment, or the ICU setting.
- A full history and physical exam often point to the cause.
- Treat the cause first. This includes giving pain relief and making the ICU more comfortable.
- Use sedatives like lorazepam, propofol, dexmedetomidine, or ketamine for any remaining restlessness.
- Muscle paralysis only hides pain and distress. A paralyzed patient may still be suffering.

# Gas in the Digestive System

Gas is normal in the digestive system. It can come out through the mouth as a burp or through the bottom as a fart.

## Common Gas Symptoms

There are three main gas-related symptoms:

- Burping too much  
- Feeling bloated or swollen in the belly  
- Passing gas too often  

Burping often happens right after eating or when you are stressed. Some people feel tightness in the chest or stomach before burping. This tightness goes away when the gas comes out.

Many people think they pass more gas than normal. But most people pass gas 13 to 21 times a day. This can be half a quart to one and a half quarts (0.5 to 1.5 liters). Some people pass gas more or less often. The gas may or may not smell.

The gas in your belly can catch fire because it contains hydrogen and methane. But this is not a common problem. Working near open flames is safe. However, in rare cases, gas has exploded during certain medical procedures like colonoscopy or surgery. This only happens if the bowel was not cleaned out well and electric tools were used.

In the past, doctors thought babies crying a lot (called colic) were caused by gas. Now, most doctors do not believe this. Tests show these babies do not have extra gas in their bellies. The real cause of colic is still unknown.

## What Causes Gas?

The cause of gas depends on the symptom.

### Why People Burp

- Swallowing air  
- Drinking fizzy drinks  

Most people swallow a little air when they eat or drink. But some people swallow more air without knowing it. This can happen when they eat too fast, chew gum, smoke, or feel anxious. Extra saliva from heartburn, bad dentures, certain medicines, or nausea can also cause more air to be swallowed.

Most of the air you swallow comes back up as a burp. Very little goes into the intestines. The small amount that does get absorbed into the blood. Very little of it comes out as gas.

### Why People Pass Gas

Gas in the bottom comes from bacteria in the large intestine. These bacteria always make some gas. But more gas can be made when:

- You eat certain foods  
- Your body cannot absorb food properly (called malabsorption)

Foods that make more gas include:

- Beans, cabbage, and other vegetables  
- Fruits like apples, pears, and prunes  
- Milk and dairy products  
- Foods with sugar alcohols like sorbitol (used in sugar-free gum and candy)  
- Fruits with fructose (like honey, berries, and some plants)  
- Foods with complex carbs like pretzels, bagels, and wheat germ  

A group of foods called FODMAPs (fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols) are hard to digest. They are quickly broken down by gut bacteria, which causes more gas and discomfort.

Many people cannot digest lactose, the sugar in milk. This is called lactose intolerance. It causes gas, bloating, and diarrhea after eating dairy.

Malabsorption can also cause gas. This happens when the body lacks enzymes to break down certain sugars. For example, people with lactase deficiency make a lot of gas when they eat milk.

Other conditions that cause malabsorption include:

- Tropical sprue  
- Celiac disease  
- Pancreatic insufficiency  

Some people naturally have more or different types of bacteria in their gut. Others may have a problem with how the muscles in the gut move. These differences can explain why some people pass more gas than others. Keeping a diary of gas frequency can help your doctor understand your symptoms.

### Why People Feel Bloating

Bloating can happen with digestive problems like:

- Slow stomach emptying (gastroparesis)  
- Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)  
- Ovarian cancer  
- Colon cancer  

Some medicines that calm the nervous system (anticholinergics) can slow stomach emptying and cause bloating.

Sometimes bloating is not from the belly at all. For example, some people have a heart attack and only feel bloated or have a strong urge to burp. But many people who feel bloated do not have any serious illness.

Doctors do not fully understand how gas causes bloating. Most people who feel bloated do not have extra gas in their system. But some people, especially those with IBS, are more sensitive to normal amounts of gas. People with eating disorders like anorexia or bulimia may also feel bloated and worry a lot about it.

The main issue in many cases may be a gut that is too sensitive. A problem with how the gut muscles move can also make symptoms worse.

## When to See a Doctor

Most gas symptoms do not need urgent care. But see a doctor if you have:

- Unintentional weight loss  
- Blood in your stool  
- Chest pain or bloating in the chest  

If you feel bloated in the chest and have chest pain, see a doctor right away. This could be a sign of heart disease.

If you have gas symptoms and also have other warning signs, abdominal pain, or diarrhea, see a doctor within a week.

If you have no warning signs, you can see a doctor later, but not right away.

### What the Doctor Will Do

The doctor will ask about your symptoms and medical history. Then they will do a physical exam.

The exam and your answers can help the doctor guess what is causing your symptoms. They may suggest tests.

For too much burping, the doctor will look for reasons you swallow air. This includes diet, gum chewing, or smoking.

For too much gas, the doctor will check your diet and look for signs of malabsorption, like diarrhea or greasy, smelly stool.

The doctor will ask:

- How your symptoms relate to meals (timing, food type, amount)  
- How often you have bowel movements  
- The color and texture of your stool  
- If you have lost weight  

For bloating or gas, the doctor will check for signs of serious illness. They may do:

- An exam of your belly  
- A rectal exam  
- For women, a pelvic exam  

### Common Causes of Gas Symptoms

| Cause | Typical Signs | Tests Needed |
|------|----------------|--------------|
| Swallowing air | Burping, may happen when eating fast, chewing gum, or feeling anxious | Doctor’s exam |
| Carbonated drinks | Burping after drinking soda | Doctor’s exam |
| Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) | Belly pain linked to going to the bathroom, changes in stool, starts in teens or 20s | Doctor’s exam, stool test, blood tests |
| Slow stomach emptying (gastroparesis) | Nausea, belly pain, early fullness, vomiting | Upper endoscopy or special scan to check stomach emptying |
| Eating disorders (anorexia, bulimia) | Long-term bloating, especially in young women who are thin but still worried about weight | Doctor’s exam |
| Chronic constipation | Hard, infrequent bowel movements over a long time | Doctor’s exam, anorectal manometry (tests muscle pressure) |
| Ovarian or colon cancer (rare) | New, ongoing bloating in middle-aged or older adults; colon cancer may have blood in stool | Pelvic ultrasound, colonoscopy |
| Foods that cause gas | Symptoms start after eating beans, dairy, certain fruits, or vegetables | Doctor’s exam, food diary, elimination diet |
| Lactose intolerance | Bloating, cramps, diarrhea after milk or dairy | Breath test for hydrogen |
| Celiac disease | Pale, bulky, smelly, oily stools; weakness, poor appetite, diarrhea; often starts in childhood | Blood tests, small intestine biopsy |
| Tropical sprue | Smelly, oily, soft stools; nausea, weight loss, diarrhea | Blood tests, small intestine biopsy |

*Note: Some tests are done for all girls and women of childbearing age, like a pregnancy test.*

*Upper endoscopy uses a thin tube with a camera to look at the esophagus, stomach, and first part of the small intestine.*

### When Tests Are Needed

Doctors usually do not test for gas unless other symptoms suggest a serious problem.

For example, if you have diarrhea, the doctor may test for malabsorption.

But if you are middle-aged or older and suddenly have ongoing bloating, especially if you never had digestive issues before, the doctor may test for ovarian or colon cancer.

## How Gas Is Treated

Doctors often tell people with long-term bloating or gas that their symptoms are not dangerous. They are not caused by a serious illness.

### For Burping

Burping is hard to stop because it often comes from swallowing air without knowing it. You can try:

- Eating slowly and calmly  
- Not chewing gum  
- Avoiding fizzy drinks  
- Breathing through your mouth using your diaphragm  
- Treating any related stomach problems like ulcers  

### For Passing Gas

To reduce gas, avoid foods that cause it. Try cutting out one food at a time:

1. Start with beans, cabbage, and other gas-causing vegetables  
2. Then avoid milk and dairy  
3. Then cut back on fresh fruits  
4. Then try limiting certain vegetables and other foods  

Limit sorbitol and fructose. These are in sugar-free gum, some candies, and fruit juices.

Adding roughage like bran or psyllium seeds may help move things through the gut. But it can make symptoms worse for some people.

### For Gas Pain

Aromatherapy oils like peppermint (in slow-release form) may help ease cramps and gas pain.

# Encephalitis

Encephalitis is an inflammation of the brain. It can start with symptoms like the flu.

## Symptoms of Encephalitis

At first, you may have a high temperature and a headache. These are common flu-like signs.

Over hours, days, or weeks, more serious symptoms can appear. These include:

- Feeling confused or not knowing where you are
- Having seizures or fits
- Acting differently than usual
- Trouble speaking clearly
- Weakness or loss of movement in parts of your body
- Losing consciousness

If you or someone else has any of these serious symptoms, call 999 for an ambulance right away.

## Treatment for Encephalitis

You must go to hospital if you have encephalitis. Getting treatment early improves your chances of recovery.

Doctors will treat the cause. Treatment may include:

- Antiviral medicines if a virus is causing the illness
- Steroid injections to reduce swelling in the brain
- Medicines to calm an overactive immune system
- Antibiotics if a bacterial infection is the cause
- Antifungal medicines if a fungus is the cause
- Painkillers to ease pain or reduce a high temperature
- Medicine to stop seizures or fits
- Help with breathing, such as oxygen through a mask or a breathing machine (ventilator)

How long you stay in hospital depends on your condition. It can be a few days, several weeks, or even months.

## Preventing Encephalitis

Not all cases of encephalitis can be prevented. But some infections that cause it can be avoided with vaccines.

Vaccines that help prevent certain types of encephalitis include:

- The measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. This is given to all children in England as part of routine care.
- The Japanese encephalitis vaccine. This is recommended for people travelling to certain parts of Asia.
- The tick-borne encephalitis vaccine. This is recommended for travellers going to some parts of Europe and Asia. It is not needed in the UK.
- The rabies vaccine. This is recommended for people going to areas where rabies is common and medical care may be hard to reach.

Check the GOV.UK website to learn about rabies risks in animals in different countries.

Talk to your GP if you are unsure if your vaccines are up to date. Or if you are planning to travel abroad and need advice on which vaccines you should have.

# Dengue

Dengue is a serious illness caused by a virus.  
It spreads when a certain kind of mosquito bites a person who has the virus and then bites someone else.  
The mosquito that spreads dengue is called the *Aedes* mosquito.  

Dengue is common in many countries, especially in tropical areas.  
It is found in parts of Africa, the Americas, Southeast Asia, the Pacific Islands, and the Mediterranean.  
It is most common in Southeast Asia, but outbreaks also happen in the Caribbean, Central and South America, and Oceania.  

In 2024, about 3,500 cases of dengue were brought into the United States by travelers.  
But worldwide, it is estimated that 50 to 100 million people get dengue each year.  
Around 20,000 people die from dengue every year.  

The dengue virus is a small germ that lives in the blood.  
There are four different types of the dengue virus.  
The virus stays in a person’s blood for 2 to 7 days after infection.  
If a mosquito bites that person during this time, the mosquito can become infected.  

A mosquito can bite more than one person.  
This means one infected mosquito can spread the virus to several people.  
The virus can also pass from a pregnant woman to her baby, or through blood transfusions and organ transplants.  
But these cases are rare.  

---

## Symptoms of Dengue

After being bitten, it takes 3 to 15 days for symptoms to start.  
Then, a person suddenly gets a high fever, chills, and a severe headache.  
Pain behind the eyes gets worse when the eyes move.  
Back pain and extreme tiredness come on quickly.  
Severe aches in the muscles and joints happen in the first few hours.  
This is why dengue is sometimes called “breakbone fever.”  

The fever can rise to as high as 40 degrees Celsius.  
The heart rate may be slower than normal for the fever level.  
The eyes may look red.  
Some people get a red flush or a rash on the face.  
Lymph nodes in the neck, under the arms, and in the groin may swell.  

The fever and other symptoms last 2 to 4 days.  
Then, the fever drops fast.  
The person sweats a lot and may feel better for about one day.  
After that, the fever may come back.  
This second fever is usually lower than the first.  
This pattern is called the “saddleback” fever.  

At the same time, a rash appears.  
It starts on the chest and spreads to the arms, legs, and face.  
The rash is flat and red, and it fades when pressed.  

Other symptoms can include a sore throat, nausea, vomiting, and signs of bleeding.  
These may include nosebleeds, gum bleeding, or blood in the stool.  

The 4th to 7th day of illness is the most dangerous time.  
If a person has warning signs during this time, they are at higher risk for serious dengue.  
Warning signs include:  
- Pain or tenderness in the belly  
- Vomiting that does not stop  
- Bleeding from the gums or nose  
- A swollen liver  
- Feeling very tired or restless  
- Blood that is thicker than normal (seen in blood tests)  

If these signs appear, the person may develop **dengue hemorrhagic fever**.  
This is a serious form of dengue.  
It causes low platelet counts, fluid leaking from blood vessels, and bleeding.  

If the person goes into shock, the illness is called **dengue shock syndrome**.  
This is life-threatening.  

Neurological problems are rare.  
But some people may have confusion, seizures, or a condition called Guillain-Barré syndrome.  

Mild cases of dengue usually get better in less than 3 days.  
In more serious cases, weakness and tiredness can last for weeks.  
Death is very rare.  

After having dengue, a person is protected for life against the same virus type.  
But protection against the other three types lasts only 2 to 12 months.  

Sometimes, a second dengue infection can be worse.  
This happens when a person has antibodies from a past infection that do not fully protect them.  
These antibodies can actually help the new virus spread more easily.  
This is called antibody-dependent enhancement.  

---

## How Dengue Is Diagnosed

Dengue is suspected in people who live in or have recently visited areas where dengue is common.  
It is especially likely if they have sudden fever, severe headache behind the eyes, body aches, swollen lymph nodes, and a rash.  

Doctors must rule out other similar illnesses.  
These include malaria, Zika virus, chikungunya, and leptospirosis.  

Tests used to diagnose dengue include:  
- Blood tests to check for dengue antibodies (serologic testing)  
- Tests to find a dengue protein (NS1 antigen) in the blood  
- PCR testing to detect the virus’s genetic material in blood  

Antibody tests are done using blood samples taken early in the illness and again later.  
But these tests can sometimes give false results because of other similar viruses, like Zika.  
The most accurate test is the plaque-reduction neutralization test.  
This is the gold standard but is only available in special labs.  

NS1 antigen tests are used in some countries, but not in the United States.  
PCR testing is done only in labs with special training.  

In rare cases, doctors can grow the virus in lab-grown cells or in special mosquitoes.  
But this is hard and not done often.  

A blood test may show low white blood cell counts early in the illness.  
By day 4 or 5, white blood cells may drop to 2,000 to 4,000 per microliter.  
The number of certain white blood cells (granulocytes) may be low.  

In severe cases, the blood becomes thicker (higher hematocrit), and platelets drop.  
This usually happens around day 4 to 6.  
A urine test may show some protein and a few small clumps of cells.  

---

## How Dengue Is Treated

There is no medicine that kills the dengue virus.  
Treatment focuses on relieving symptoms and supporting the body.  

Acetaminophen (like Tylenol) can be used to reduce fever and pain.  
But nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), including aspirin, should be avoided.  
These medicines can increase the risk of bleeding.  

Aspirin is especially dangerous in children.  
It can cause a rare but serious condition called Reye syndrome.  

People with dengue should drink plenty of fluids.  
They should rest and stay cool.  

If a person has severe dengue, they may need hospital care.  
This includes careful fluid replacement to prevent shock.  
Doctors will monitor blood levels and vital signs closely.  

---

## How to Prevent Dengue

The best way to prevent dengue is to avoid mosquito bites.  
Use insect repellent, wear long sleeves and pants, and sleep under mosquito nets.  
Keep windows and doors screened.  
Remove standing water where mosquitoes can breed.  

People with dengue should stay under mosquito nets until their fever has gone away for two full days.  
This stops them from spreading the virus to other people.  

In the United States, a dengue vaccine called CYD-TDV is approved.  
It is only for children and teens aged 9 to 16.  
They must have had a confirmed past dengue infection.  
The vaccine is only available in Puerto Rico, where dengue is common.  

The vaccine helps prevent severe dengue and hospitalization in people who have had dengue before.  
But it may make the disease worse in people who have never had dengue.  
For this reason, doctors must test for past infection before giving the vaccine.  

The World Health Organization and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration both recommend testing first.  
Only people who test positive for past dengue should get the vaccine.  
Three doses are given, six months apart.  

Another dengue vaccine, TAK-003, is available in Argentina, Brazil, Indonesia, the European Union, and the United Kingdom.  
It is being studied in the United States.  
This vaccine may protect against all four dengue virus types.  

---

## Key Points

- Dengue is spread by the bite of *Aedes* mosquitoes.  
- Dengue fever causes sudden high fever, severe headache behind the eyes, body aches, swollen lymph nodes, a rash, and intense joint pain.  
- It can lead to a serious, life-threatening illness with bleeding and shock.  
- Think of dengue if someone has these symptoms and has been in a high-risk area.  
- Diagnosis is done with blood tests for antibodies, virus proteins, or virus genes.  
- Treatment is focused on symptom relief and supportive care.  
- Prevention means avoiding mosquito bites and using vaccines only in people with past dengue infection.

# Aortic Dissection

An aortic dissection is a serious and often deadly condition. It happens when the inner lining of the main artery in the body (the aorta) tears. Blood then pushes through the tear and splits the middle layer of the artery wall from the outer layer.

## What Is the Aorta?

The aorta is the largest artery in the body. It carries oxygen-rich blood from the heart to the rest of the body. The part of the aorta that runs through the chest is called the thoracic aorta. Most aortic dissections happen in this area.

The wall of the aorta has three layers:

- **Inner layer (intima):** A thin lining.
- **Middle layer (media):** A thick layer that gives the artery strength.
- **Outer layer (adventitia):** A thin layer that supplies nutrients to the middle layer.

When the inner layer tears, blood flows into the middle layer. This creates a false channel inside the artery wall. As the tear grows, it can block blood flow to important organs.

## Who Is at Risk?

Aortic dissection is more common in men than women. It is more common in people of African ancestry, especially African-American people. It is less common in people of Asian ancestry.

Most cases happen in people aged 40 to 70 years.

## Causes

The most common cause is long-term high blood pressure. This weakens the artery wall over time.

More than two out of three people who have an aortic dissection have high blood pressure.

Other causes include:

- Hardening of the arteries (arteriosclerosis)
- Severe chest injury, such as from a car crash or fall
- Aging, which weakens the artery wall
- Genetic conditions like Marfan syndrome or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
- Birth defects in the heart or blood vessels, such as a narrowed aorta, a hole between the aorta and the lung artery, or a faulty aortic valve

In rare cases, a dissection can happen during a medical procedure, such as when a doctor inserts a tube into an artery or does heart surgery.

## Symptoms

Most people feel sudden, severe pain. The pain is often described as tearing or ripping.

- The pain usually starts in the chest.
- It often spreads to the back, between the shoulder blades.
- The pain may move as the tear grows. For example, it may move to the abdomen or lower back if blood flow to the intestines is blocked.

Some people faint from the pain.

### Possible Complications

- **Stroke:** If blood flow to the brain is blocked.
- **Heart attack:** If blood flow to the heart is blocked.
- **Kidney failure:** If blood flow to the kidneys is blocked.
- **Nerve or spinal cord damage:** This can cause numbness, tingling, or trouble moving an arm or leg.
- **Bleeding into the chest:** Blood can leak into the space around the heart. This can stop the heart from pumping properly. This is called cardiac tamponade and is life-threatening.
- **Leaky heart valve:** If the tear is near the heart, it can damage the aortic valve. This can cause heart failure.

## Diagnosis

Doctors use imaging tests to confirm aortic dissection. These tests include:

- CT angiography
- Magnetic resonance angiography
- Transesophageal echocardiography

These tests show the tear and how far it has spread.

### Signs Doctors Look For

- Weak or missing pulses in the arms or legs
- A difference in blood pressure between the two arms
- A new heart murmur heard through a stethoscope
- A widened aorta seen on a chest X-ray

A chest X-ray is often the first test. It can show a wider-than-normal aorta. But this can also happen with other conditions.

CT angiography is fast and accurate. It uses a special dye and a scanner to show the tear clearly.

Magnetic resonance angiography and transesophageal echocardiography can also find even small tears.

## Treatment

Treatment depends on where the tear is and how serious it is.

### Immediate Care

- People with aortic dissection go to an intensive care unit.
- Doctors watch heart rate, blood pressure, and breathing closely.
- Death can happen within hours of the start of the dissection.

### Medications

- IV medicines are given right away to lower heart rate and blood pressure.
- The goal is to keep blood pressure low enough to stop the tear from getting worse.
- But not so low that the brain, heart, or kidneys do not get enough blood.

### Surgery or Stent Graft

- **For tears near the heart (ascending aorta):** Surgery is almost always needed.
  - Surgeons remove the damaged part of the aorta.
  - They close the tear and replace the damaged section with a synthetic tube.
  - If the aortic valve is leaking, it is repaired or replaced.

- **For tears farther from the heart (descending aorta):** Doctors often use medicine instead of surgery.
  - In some cases, a stent graft is used.
  - A thin tube (stent graft) is guided through a blood vessel in the groin up to the damaged area.
  - The stent graft is opened inside the aorta. It creates a new path for blood to flow.
  - This keeps blood from pushing into the tear.

Stent grafts are less invasive than open surgery. They help more people survive and have fewer complications.

### When Surgery or a Stent Graft Is Needed

- If blood is leaking from the artery
- If blood flow to the legs or organs in the belly is blocked
- If the person has symptoms that do not go away
- If the tear is getting bigger
- If the person has Marfan syndrome

### Long-Term Care

Everyone who has had an aortic dissection must take medicine to keep blood pressure low. This usually lasts for life.

- Common medicines include:
  - Beta-blockers
  - Calcium channel blockers
  - ACE inhibitors (to lower blood pressure)
- If the person has hardening of the arteries, they may also take cholesterol-lowering medicine and change their diet.

Doctors watch closely for future problems, such as:

- Another dissection
- Aneurysms (bulges) in the weakened aorta
- More blood leaking through the aortic valve

If any of these happen, surgery may be needed.

## Prognosis

- About 20% of people die before they reach the hospital.
- Without treatment, many people die within the first two weeks.
- With treatment, most people survive long enough to leave the hospital.

Early diagnosis and fast treatment are key to survival.

# Hepatitis C

Hepatitis C often has no symptoms at first.  
You might not know you have it for years.  

Some people feel unwell.  
They may have muscle pain.  
They might have a high temperature.  
They could feel very tired.  
They may have stomach pain.  
They might feel sick or be sick.

These symptoms can feel like other illnesses.  
The only way to know if they are from hepatitis C is to get tested.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Hepatitis C usually does not cause symptoms until the liver is badly damaged.  
This means many people do not know they are infected.  

When symptoms do appear, they can include:  
- Muscle pain  
- A high temperature (fever)  
- Feeling tired all the time  
- Not wanting to eat  
- Stomach pain  
- Feeling sick or being sick  

If you have these symptoms, you should get tested.  
Only a test can tell if hepatitis C is the cause.

---

## How Is Hepatitis C Treated?

Hepatitis C can be cured with medicines.  
These medicines stop the virus from spreading in your body.  
You usually take them for several weeks.

In the past, treatment involved two medicines:  
- A weekly injection  
- A daily tablet  

Now, there are new tablet-only treatments.  
These are easier to take.  
They work better.  
They have fewer side effects.  
They also take less time to complete.

Medicines like sofosbuvir and daclatasvir are now used.  
More than 90 out of 100 people can be cured with these new medicines.

But being cured does not mean you are immune.  
You can get infected again.  
You must still take steps to protect yourself.

---

## How Do You Get Hepatitis C?

The virus spreads through blood.  
It is not spread through casual contact.

You can get hepatitis C by:  
- Sharing needles or other drug-injecting equipment  
- Sharing razors or toothbrushes that have blood on them  
- A pregnant woman passing it to her baby  
- Unprotected sex – but this is very rare  

In the UK, most cases happen in people who have used drugs by injection.  
About half of people who inject drugs have had hepatitis C.

### Blood Transfusions Before 1996

Before 1996, blood used in transfusions was not tested for hepatitis C.  
If you had a blood transfusion before 1996, you may have been infected.

If you had a transfusion before 1996 and have never been tested, talk to your doctor.  
You can also get a free home test for hepatitis C.  
You can find more information about support for people affected by infected blood.

---

## How Can You Prevent Hepatitis C?

There is no vaccine for hepatitis C.  
But you can lower your risk.

Do not share:  
- Needles or any drug-injecting equipment  
- Razors  
- Toothbrushes  

The risk of catching hepatitis C through sex is very low.  
But it may be higher if blood is present.  
This includes menstrual blood or small cuts during anal sex.

For long-term heterosexual couples, condoms are usually not needed.  
But it is a good idea to use them during anal sex or when having sex with a new partner.

# Corneal Ulcer

A corneal ulcer is a sore on the clear front surface of the eye. It happens when the outer layer of the eye is damaged and becomes infected. The infection can come from bacteria, fungi, viruses, or a rare germ called *Acanthamoeba*. It can start after an injury to the eye or from not getting enough nutrients. If the swelling and infection are not controlled, the eye tissue can die.

## What Causes a Corneal Ulcer?

Many things can cause a corneal ulcer. Some common causes include:

- Wearing contact lenses, especially while sleeping or if the lenses are not cleaned well.
- Eye injuries from scratches, foreign objects, or burns.
- Eye infections like herpes.
- Dry eyes or problems with the eyelids, such as not closing fully.
- Not eating enough protein or vitamin A.

Some conditions that affect the eye or body can also lead to ulcers. These include:
- Swelling under the cornea.
- Autoimmune diseases that damage the eye.
- Long-term eye infections.
- Nerve damage in the eye.

## How Does a Corneal Ulcer Develop?

The eye’s outer layer breaks down. This creates a sore. The area under the sore becomes inflamed. The body sends white blood cells to fight the infection. This causes a cloudy spot under the sore. Over time, the sore can get deeper and wider. It may fill with pus. The eye may become very red and painful.

In some cases, the sore can grow so deep that it breaks through the eye. This is serious and can lead to blindness. Blood vessels may grow into the cornea if the ulcer lasts a long time.

## What Are the Symptoms?

At first, symptoms may be mild. You might feel:
- A gritty feeling in the eye.
- Eye pain or aching.
- Redness in the white part of the eye.
- Sensitivity to light.
- Tears or watery eyes.

As the ulcer gets worse, the pain can become severe. The eye may hurt more when you blink. You may not be able to open your eye. The vision may become blurry.

Some ulcers cause intense pain. These are often caused by *Acanthamoeba*. Fungal ulcers tend to grow slowly but can last a long time. Bacterial ulcers, especially from *Pseudomonas*, can get worse very fast.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor uses a special light called a slit lamp to look at the eye. They put a drop of dye in the eye. This dye sticks to the sore and makes it easier to see. The doctor checks for signs of infection and damage.

The doctor may take a small sample from the sore. This is done with a tiny tool. The sample is tested to find the cause. This helps choose the right medicine.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment must start right away. Delaying treatment can lead to serious eye damage.

### General Treatment

- You will get antibiotic eye drops. These are used often—every 15 minutes at first, then every hour.
- For serious ulcers, stronger drops are used. These are made in special doses.
- You should not cover the eye with a patch. This can trap germs and make the infection worse.
- You may need drops to relax the eye muscles. These help reduce pain and prevent the iris from sticking to the lens.

### Specific Treatments by Cause

**Bacterial ulcers:**  
- Use of strong antibiotic drops like moxifloxacin or gatifloxacin.
- For severe cases, drops like tobramycin and cefazolin are used.

**Herpes simplex virus:**  
- Use of antiviral eye drops like trifluridine or ganciclovir.
- If drops are hard to use, oral medicine like valacyclovir or acyclovir can be used.

**Fungal ulcers:**  
- Antifungal drops like natamycin (best for plant-related fungi) or amphotericin B (best for yeast).
- For deep infections, oral antifungal medicine may be needed.

**Acanthamoeba ulcers:**  
- Special drops like propamidine, neomycin, and polyhexamethylene biguanide or chlorhexidine.
- These drops are used many times a day until the eye improves.
- Treatment may last several months.
- Oral medicine like ketoconazole or itraconazole may be added.
- In rare cases, a medicine called miltefosine is used.

### When Steroid Drops Are Used

Steroid drops can help reduce pain and light sensitivity. They can also help vision improve faster. But they can make the ulcer worse if used too soon.

Steroid drops are only used in special cases. They are not used if herpes is suspected. They must be prescribed by an eye doctor. The patient must be watched closely.

## When to See a Doctor

You should see an eye doctor right away if you have:
- Eye pain that does not go away.
- Redness that gets worse.
- Blurry vision.
- Sensitivity to light.
- A feeling like something is in your eye.

Even small ulcers should be checked. Most ulcers need to be tested to find the cause.

## Key Points

- A corneal ulcer is a sore on the front of the eye.
- It can be caused by infection, injury, dry eyes, or poor nutrition.
- Symptoms include pain, redness, light sensitivity, and blurry vision.
- Diagnosis is done with a special eye exam and testing.
- Treatment must start quickly and includes eye drops and sometimes hospital care.
- Steroid drops may help but are risky and must be used carefully.
- Always see an eye doctor for a corneal ulcer.

# Amyloidosis

Amyloidosis is a rare disease. It happens when proteins in the body fold the wrong way. These misfolded proteins clump together and form tough, fibrous deposits called amyloid fibrils. These deposits build up in tissues and organs. Over time, they can stop organs from working properly. This can lead to serious health problems, organ failure, or even death.

- The symptoms and how serious the disease is depend on which organs are affected.
- Doctors diagnose amyloidosis by taking a small sample of tissue (a biopsy) and looking at it under a microscope.
- There are many types of amyloidosis. More tests are needed to find out which type it is and what caused it.
- Treatment depends on the type of amyloidosis.

---

## What Causes Amyloidosis?

Proteins are long chains of molecules. They must fold into a specific shape to work right. In amyloidosis, some proteins fold the wrong way. These misfolded proteins stick together and build up in the body as amyloid deposits.

These deposits are made of long, tangled fibers. The body cannot break them down easily. They get in the way of normal organ function.

All the proteins involved come from inside the body. They do not come from food.

Some of these proteins are changed (mutated) versions of normal proteins. Others are normal proteins that just tend to fold wrong. Some proteins are made in higher amounts during other diseases, like tuberculosis or rheumatoid arthritis.

---

## Types of Amyloidosis

Amyloid deposits can be:

- **Systemic**: spread throughout the body
- **Localized**: found only in one organ or area

The severity of the disease depends on which organs are affected.

### Systemic Amyloidosis

There are four main types:

#### AL Amyloidosis (Light Chain Amyloidosis)

This happens when a type of immune cell called a plasma cell makes too many abnormal antibody parts called light chains. These parts build up and form amyloid.

Some people with AL amyloidosis also have a type of blood cancer called multiple myeloma. About 10 to 20 out of every 100 people with multiple myeloma develop AL amyloidosis.

Common places where amyloid builds up in AL amyloidosis include:
- Skin
- Heart
- Kidneys
- Nerves
- Tongue
- Intestines
- Liver
- Spleen
- Blood vessels

#### AA Amyloidosis

This type can happen after long-term infections or inflammation. It can also happen with some cancers.

It often causes kidney problems. But other organs may be affected too.

Common causes include:
- Tuberculosis
- Rheumatoid arthritis
- Familial Mediterranean fever

#### Hereditary Amyloidosis

This is a group of rare inherited diseases. They cause symptoms in adulthood.

The problem comes from a faulty gene. This gene makes a protein that folds the wrong way. The faulty protein forms amyloid.

The most common cause is a change in a protein called transthyretin. This protein is made in the liver.

The amyloid usually affects the kidneys, nerves, or heart.

#### ATTRwt (Wild Type Transthyretin) Amyloidosis

This type mostly affects the heart. It is more common in men than in women.

It is caused by a normal transthyretin protein folding the wrong way. The protein is not mutated. But it still forms amyloid.

Doctors do not yet know why the protein starts to misfold.

### Localized Amyloidosis

This happens when amyloid builds up in just one organ or tissue.

For example:
- In people with Alzheimer disease, amyloid builds up in the brain. This may play a role in causing the disease.
- Amyloid can also form in the skin, digestive tract, airways, or bladder.

---

## Symptoms of Amyloidosis

Too much amyloid in the body can stop organs from working right. Some people have few symptoms. Others have serious, life-threatening problems.

Common symptoms include:
- Feeling very tired
- Losing weight without trying

Other symptoms depend on where the amyloid builds up.

### If the heart is affected:
- Irregular heartbeats
- Heart failure
- Shortness of breath
- Feeling weak
- Fainting

### If nerves are affected:
- Tingling or numbness in fingers or toes
- Dizziness when standing up

### If kidneys are affected:
- Swelling in the feet and legs
- Swelling in the belly

### If the skin is affected:
- Easy bruising, especially around the eyes
- The tongue may get bigger (called macroglossia)

### Other possible effects:

| Organ or System Affected | Possible Problems |
|--------------------------|-------------------|
| Blood vessels | Easy bruising |
| Brain | Alzheimer disease, brain blood vessel problems |
| Digestive system | Constipation or diarrhea |
| Enlarged tongue | Weight loss, poor nutrient absorption |
| Heart | Irregular heartbeats, enlarged heart, heart failure |
| Kidneys | Swelling (edema), kidney failure |
| Liver | Enlarged liver |
| Lungs and airways | Trouble breathing, wheezing |
| Lymph nodes | Swollen lymph nodes |
| Musculoskeletal system | Carpal tunnel syndrome, spine narrowing, tendon tears |
| Nerves | Numbness, tingling, dizziness |
| Skin | Bruises, lumps (nodules) |
| Thyroid gland | Enlarged thyroid |

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Amyloidosis

Amyloidosis is hard to spot. It causes many different symptoms. Many of these symptoms also happen with other diseases.

Doctors may suspect amyloidosis if:
- A person has symptoms in more than one organ
- There is unexplained heart, kidney, or liver failure
- The tongue is unusually large (macroglossia)
- Several family members have heart or nerve problems
- An older man has heart symptoms without a clear cause

### The main test is a biopsy.

Doctors take a small sample of fat from the belly using a needle. This is called a fat pad biopsy. They look at the sample under a microscope.

If needed, doctors may take a sample from an affected organ. This could be the heart, kidneys, liver, or another organ.

After confirming amyloidosis, doctors do more tests. These help them:
- Find out which type of amyloidosis it is
- Check for any underlying disease that may be causing it
- See which organs are damaged

---

## Treatment for Amyloidosis

Treatment depends on the type of amyloidosis.

### For AL Amyloidosis

This type is linked to abnormal plasma cells. Treatment focuses on stopping these cells from making bad proteins.

- Chemotherapy and immunotherapy drugs are used.
- High-dose melphalan and stem cell transplant can help some people. But only 15 to 20 out of 100 people with new cases are able to have this treatment. It is risky and not safe for everyone.
- A combination of drugs (daratumumab, cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone) is very effective. This is called dara-VCd.
- If the disease comes back, other drug combinations are used.

### For AA Amyloidosis

This type is caused by long-term infection or inflammation.

Treatment focuses on fixing the underlying disease. This can reduce amyloid buildup.

- For AA amyloidosis caused by familial Mediterranean fever, the drug colchicine works very well.

### For Amyloidosis Caused by Transthyretin Protein

This includes both hereditary and wild type forms.

Medicines can help:
- Diflunisal, tafamidis, and acoramidis stabilize the transthyretin protein. This stops it from forming amyloid.
- These drugs slow down the disease, especially if the heart is affected.

Gene therapies like patisiran and vutrisiran reduce how much transthyretin the body makes. These help with nerve problems in hereditary cases. They also help people with heart disease live longer and need fewer hospital visits.

### Organ Transplants

In some cases, a transplant can help.

- A kidney or heart transplant may help people with organ failure from amyloidosis.
- For hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis, a liver transplant may be used. The liver makes the faulty protein. Removing it can slow the disease.
- A liver from someone with hereditary amyloidosis can be used in a "domino transplant." The liver still works well. It can save someone with liver failure.
- The person who gets the liver may still develop amyloidosis later. But the transplant can save their life in the short term.

---

## Prognosis (Outlook)

The outlook depends on:
- The type of amyloidosis
- Which organs are affected

If the heart is involved, the disease is the most serious. It can be very hard to treat and may lead to a poor outcome.

# Angina

## What is angina?

Angina is a type of chest pain.  
It can feel like pressure, tightness, or a squeezing sensation.  
The pain may also spread to your neck, jaw, shoulders, arms, or back.  

This pain usually happens during physical activity or times of stress.  
It often goes away after you rest or take your medicine.  

Angina is a warning sign.  
It means your heart is not getting enough blood.  

## When to call 999

Call 999 right away if you have:

- Chest pain that does not go away after resting or after taking your angina medicine  
- Sudden chest pain that feels like pressure, squeezing, or burning  
- Pain that spreads to your arm, neck, jaw, shoulder, stomach, or back  
- Chest pain with sweating, nausea, dizziness, or trouble breathing  

These could be signs of a heart attack.  
You need emergency treatment in hospital.  

> **Important:** Do not drive yourself to the hospital.  
> The person you speak to on 999 will tell you what to do.

## When to call NHS 111

Call 111 or get help online if you have:

- Chest pain or other angina symptoms that come and go  
- Angina that feels worse than before  
- Angina that happens more often  
- Angina that lasts longer  
- Angina that happens when you are resting  

## What causes angina?

Angina happens when your heart does not get enough blood.  

This is usually because the blood vessels to your heart are narrowed.  
This narrowing is often due to fatty deposits building up in the blood vessels.  
This condition is called coronary heart disease.  

In some people, the blood vessels tighten when they should not.  
This can also cause angina.  

You are more likely to get angina if you:

- Are a man aged 45 or older, or a woman aged 55 or older  
- Smoke  
- Drink more than 14 units of alcohol a week  
- Are overweight or have obesity  
- Have high blood pressure or high cholesterol  
- Have had a heart attack or a heart rhythm problem before  
- Have a close family member with heart problems  
- Have another health condition, such as diabetes, arthritis, or kidney disease  

## How is angina treated?

Your doctor may give you medicine to:

- Stop an angina attack when it happens (glyceryl trinitrate)  
- Reduce the chance of future attacks (beta blockers)  
- Lower your risk of a heart attack or stroke (low-dose aspirin or statins)  

In some cases, surgery may be needed.  
This can help improve blood flow to the heart.  
The two main types are coronary angioplasty and coronary artery bypass.  

## How to prevent angina attacks

You can take steps to help avoid angina attacks:

- Avoid things that trigger your symptoms. These include stress, cold weather, or large meals  
- Always carry your angina medicine with you  
- Use your medicine exactly as your doctor told you  
- Try to quit smoking if you smoke  
- Aim for a healthy weight  
- Eat a balanced diet  
- Stay as active as your symptoms allow  
- Cut down on alcohol if you drink more than 14 units a week  

## How angina affects your life

Angina increases your risk of a heart attack or stroke.  
Treating it and making healthy changes can lower this risk.  

With treatment, your symptoms should get better over time.  
They may even go away completely.  

If your symptoms are under control, you can usually keep doing most of your normal activities.  
This includes exercise and sex.  

But angina may affect your job if you do heavy physical work.  
It may also affect jobs that require driving large vehicles, like buses, coaches, or lorries.  

Your doctor will talk to you about any changes you may need.  
They will also tell you if you need to inform the DVLA about your condition.  

Before starting a new activity, talk to your doctor.  
Let them know if you are worried about exercising.  

Also think about practical steps:

- Always carry your angina medicine  
- Keep spare medicine at home or in your bag  
- Make sure you have enough medicine when you travel

# Itching

Itching is a common problem that can be very uncomfortable.  
It often leads people to see a skin doctor.  
When you scratch, your skin can get worse.  
Scratching can cause redness, swelling, and damage to the skin.  
It can also lead to infection.  
The skin may become thick, dry, and cracked.

---

## What Causes Itching?

Itching can start from many different things.  
Light touch, vibrations, or rough materials like wool can trigger it.  
Special nerve cells in the skin send the message "itch" to your brain.  
These nerve cells are different from those that feel pain or light touch.  
One specific receptor called MrgA3 plays a key role in causing the itch sensation.

---

## Why Do People Itch?

Itching can be a sign of a skin problem.  
It can also be a sign of a problem inside the body.  
Some medicines can cause itching as a side effect.  
(See the list of common causes of itching.)

---

## How Is Itching Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and medical history.  
They will check your skin for signs of disease.  
If no skin problems are found, your doctor may test for other health issues.

---

## How Is Itching Treated?

The main goal is to treat the cause of the itching.  
Supportive care includes:

- **Taking care of your skin**  
  - Limit how often you bathe.  
  - Use mild soaps.  
  - Avoid harsh detergents and fragrances.  
  - Moisturize your skin every day.  
  - Use a humidifier in dry rooms.

- **Topical treatments**  
  - Use creams or ointments on the skin.  
  - These can include moisturizers, anti-itch creams, or steroid creams.

- **Medicines taken by mouth**  
  - These may be needed for severe or ongoing itching.  
  - Options include antihistamines, steroids, or other drugs.

(See the list of common treatment options.)

---

## Special Considerations for Older Adults

Older adults often have more itching.  
This can be due to changes in the skin, nerves, and immune system.  
Dry skin, called xerotic eczema, is very common in older people.  
It often affects the legs and lower body.  
If itching is widespread and severe, it could be a sign of cancer.  
This is especially true if no other cause is found.  
Antihistamines can make older adults drowsy.  
So, doctors may lower the dose.  
They may suggest:  
- A non-drowsy antihistamine during the day.  
- A drowsy antihistamine at night.  
- Frequent use of moisturizing ointments.  
- Steroid creams when needed.  
- Light therapy (ultraviolet phototherapy) in some cases.  
These steps help reduce itching without causing too much sleepiness.

---

## Key Facts

- Itching is usually caused by a skin problem or an allergic reaction.  
- It can also be a sign of a deeper health issue.  
- If your skin looks normal but you still itch, check for internal causes.  
- Daily skin care helps prevent and ease itching.  
- Moisturizing, avoiding irritants, and limiting baths are important.  
- Creams or pills can help relieve symptoms.

# Chickenpox

Chickenpox is a common illness that mostly affects children. It is caused by a virus called the varicella-zoster virus. This virus is a type of herpes virus.

The main sign of chickenpox is a rash. The rash starts as small, red, itchy spots. These spots turn into fluid-filled blisters. The blisters then dry up and form crusts.

Most children get better without serious problems. But some children can get very sick. In rare cases, chickenpox can be deadly.

A vaccine can prevent chickenpox. Thanks to the vaccine, fewer people now get chickenpox than before.

---

## Who Gets Chickenpox?

- Chickenpox most often affects children.
- The vaccine has greatly reduced the number of cases.
- Adults and people with weak immune systems are more likely to get very sick.

---

## How Chickenpox Spreads

Chickenpox spreads easily. It can spread through:

- Airborne droplets from coughing or sneezing.
- Touching the fluid from the blisters.
- A pregnant woman passing the virus to her baby during pregnancy or after birth.

A person with chickenpox can spread the virus **two days before** the rash appears. They stay contagious until **all the blisters have crusted over**.

---

## Early Symptoms

Before the rash appears, a child may feel sick. Symptoms include:

- A mild headache.
- A moderate fever.
- Not wanting to eat.
- Feeling generally unwell.

Younger children may not show these early signs. Adults often have worse symptoms.

---

## The Rash

The rash usually starts 7 to 21 days after infection.

It begins as small, flat, red spots. These spots often appear first on the chest and face. Later, they may spread to the arms, legs, scalp, and inside the mouth.

The spots change quickly:

- Within 6 to 8 hours, each spot becomes raised.
- It turns into a fluid-filled blister.
- The blister then dries and forms a crust.

New spots keep appearing for several days. This means that at any one time, you can see spots in different stages — some flat, some blistered, some crusted.

This pattern is a key sign of chickenpox.

Some people have only a few spots. Others have many, even on the scalp or inside the mouth.

The worst of the illness usually lasts 4 to 7 days.

---

## Sores in the Mouth

Sores in the mouth break open quickly. They become raw and painful. This can make eating and drinking hard.

Sores can also appear on the eyelids, in the throat, rectum, or vagina.

---

## Rare but Serious Problems

In rare cases, the virus can spread to other parts of the body. This can cause serious infections in the lungs, brain, heart, or liver.

These serious problems are more likely in:

- Newborn babies.
- Adults.
- People with weak immune systems.

Examples of weak immune systems include:

- People with HIV.
- People taking certain medicines that lower immunity.
- People on high doses of corticosteroids.

---

## Reye Syndrome

Reye syndrome is a rare but very serious condition. It can happen in children under 18 after they take aspirin while having chickenpox.

This condition can cause brain swelling and liver damage.

**Do not give aspirin to children with chickenpox.**

Reye syndrome can start 3 to 8 days after the rash begins.

---

## Chickenpox During Pregnancy

If a woman gets chickenpox while pregnant, she is at risk of serious illness. She may even die.

The virus can also pass to the baby. This can cause:

- Birth defects.
- Low birth weight.
- Skin scars.
- Illness in the newborn.

The risk is highest if the mother gets chickenpox in the first or early second trimester.

---

## Can You Get Chickenpox More Than Once?

No. Once you have had chickenpox, you are protected for life.

But the virus stays in your body in a quiet state. Later in life, it can become active again. When it does, it causes a different illness called **shingles**.

There is a vaccine to help prevent shingles. It is recommended for older adults.

---

## How Is Chickenpox Diagnosed?

A doctor can usually tell if someone has chickenpox just by looking at the rash and symptoms.

In most cases, no special tests are needed.

Sometimes a blood test or a sample from a blister may be taken. This is only done if the diagnosis is unclear.

Antibodies are proteins made by the body to fight infections. A blood test can check for these.

---

## How Is Chickenpox Treated?

Most children with mild chickenpox only need to feel better. There is no need for special medicine.

### For Mild Cases:

- Use cool, wet cloths on the skin to ease itching.
- Keep the skin clean with soap and water.
- Wash hands often.
- Keep nails short to avoid scratching.
- Wear clean, dry clothes.
- Take antihistamines if itching is very bad.
- Try oatmeal baths to soothe the skin.

Scratching can spread the virus and cause scars. It can also lead to a bacterial skin infection.

### If a Bacterial Infection Develops:

- Antibiotics may be needed.

### For People at Risk of Severe Illness:

Some people need antiviral medicine. These include:

- Healthy people 12 years or older who are not vaccinated (18 or older for one medicine).
- People with eczema.
- People with long-term lung problems.
- People who take aspirin or other salicylates for a long time.
- People on corticosteroids.
- People who got chickenpox from someone they live with (these cases are often worse).

Antiviral medicines like acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir can help reduce symptoms and shorten the illness.

They work best if started within 24 hours of the first signs.

For people over 1 year old with weak immune systems, doctors may give acyclovir through a vein (IV).

Pregnant women with chickenpox are at high risk. Some experts recommend antiviral medicine for them.

---

## Prognosis (Outlook)

- Healthy children almost always recover fully.
- Before the vaccine, about 4 million people got chickenpox each year in the United States.
- About 100 to 150 people died each year from complications.

Adults get sicker than children. The risk of death is higher in adults.

People with weak immune systems are at greater risk.

Vaccinated people who get chickenpox usually have milder cases. Fewer of them die.

---

## How to Prevent Chickenpox

### Vaccination

The best way to prevent chickenpox is through vaccination.

The vaccine contains a weakened form of the virus. It helps the body learn how to fight the real virus.

There are two types of vaccines in the United States:

1. A standard two-dose varicella vaccine.
2. A combination vaccine that protects against measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella (MMRV).

Children are vaccinated at:

- 12 to 15 months old.
- A second dose at 4 to 6 years old.

Older children and adults who have never had chickenpox or the vaccine can also be vaccinated. They need two doses, 4 to 8 weeks apart.

### Who Should Not Get the Vaccine?

Do not get the vaccine if you:

- Had a serious allergic reaction to a previous dose or a vaccine ingredient.
- Have a weak immune system (including those on high-dose corticosteroids).
- Take aspirin regularly.
- Are pregnant or plan to become pregnant in the next 1 to 3 months.
- Are very sick at the time of vaccination.

### Other Ways to Prevent Spread

- Keep infected people away from others until all blisters are crusted.
