### Ad26.ZEBOV and MVA-BN-Filo – additional common side effects:
- Warmth at the injection site
- Chills

### In children 1 to 17 years old:
- Pain at the injection site
- Tiredness
- Less energy
- Less appetite
- Being irritable

For more details on side effects, see the vaccine’s prescribing information.

---

# Histoplasmosis

Histoplasmosis is an infection caused by a fungus called *Histoplasma capsulatum*.  
It usually starts in the lungs.  
In some cases, it can spread to other parts of the body.

## How You Get Histoplasmosis

You get histoplasmosis by breathing in tiny spores from the fungus.  
The fungus grows in soil and dust that have bird or bat droppings in them.  
People who work with soil are at higher risk.  
This includes chicken farmers, construction workers, and cave explorers.  
The risk is highest when activities stir up dust, like cutting down trees or building.  
Exploring caves with bats also increases the risk.

## Where Histoplasmosis Is Common

Histoplasmosis is most common in the eastern and midwestern United States.  
It is often found along the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys.  
It can also happen in the southern United States.  
The infection occurs in parts of Central and South America, Africa, Asia, and Australia.  
Outbreaks linked to bat caves have been reported in many countries, including the United States.  
These outbreaks have happened in Florida, Texas, and Puerto Rico.

## Types of Histoplasmosis

There are three main types:

### 1. Acute Pulmonary Histoplasmosis  
This is the first stage of the infection.  
It affects only the lungs.  
It usually stays in the lungs and does not spread.

### 2. Progressive Disseminated Histoplasmosis  
This happens when the infection spreads through the blood to other organs.  
It can affect the brain, spinal cord, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, adrenal glands, digestive system, or bone marrow.  
This form is rare in healthy adults.  
It mostly happens in very young children, malnourished infants, or people with weak immune systems.  
This includes people with HIV/AIDS, organ transplant recipients, or those on immune-suppressing medicines like corticosteroids.

### 3. Chronic Cavitary Histoplasmosis  
This form slowly causes holes (cavities) to form in the lungs.  
The infection does not spread beyond the lungs.  
It develops over several weeks.

## Symptoms of Histoplasmosis

Most people do not have symptoms.  
Some people feel sick and have a fever and cough.  
They may also have trouble breathing.  
Symptoms usually start 3 to 17 days after breathing in the spores.  
They often feel like the flu.  
Most people get better in 2 weeks.  
Symptoms rarely last longer than 6 weeks.

If you breathe in many spores, you may get pneumonia.  
You may feel very short of breath.  
You could be sick for months.

Acute pulmonary histoplasmosis is rarely deadly.  
But it can become serious in people with weak immune systems, like those with AIDS.

Symptoms start slowly.  
You may feel tired, weak, or just not well.  
Symptoms can get worse slowly or very fast.

Pneumonia can develop, but it is usually mild.  
It is more serious in people with AIDS.  
Rarely, the infection causes meningitis.  
This is swelling of the tissues around the brain and spinal cord.  
It causes a severe headache and a stiff neck.  
The liver, spleen, and lymph nodes may get bigger.  
Less often, sores can form in the mouth or intestines.  
Rarely, the adrenal glands are damaged.  
This can lead to Addison disease.

Even with treatment, histoplasmosis can be deadly in people with AIDS.

In chronic cavitary histoplasmosis, symptoms come on slowly.  
You may have a cough and trouble breathing that gets worse over time.  
Other symptoms include weight loss, night sweats, a low fever, and feeling unwell.  
Most people get better without treatment.  
But breathing problems can keep getting worse.  
Some people cough up blood, sometimes in large amounts.  
Lung tissue is destroyed.  
Scar tissue forms.  
Lung damage or a secondary bacterial infection can eventually be fatal.

## How Doctors Diagnose Histoplasmosis

Doctors use several tests to diagnose histoplasmosis.

- They take samples of sputum, urine, or blood.  
- They may use a thin tube (bronchoscope) to collect samples from the lungs.  
- They may do a biopsy to take tissue from the liver, bone marrow, or lymph nodes.  
- These samples are sent to a lab to grow the fungus and check for signs of infection.

Doctors may also test your blood and urine for proteins made by the fungus.  
They may test for the fungus’s DNA in your blood or urine.

A chest x-ray is often done to look for signs of lung infection.

Some rare forms of histoplasmosis need help from an infection specialist for diagnosis and treatment.

## How Histoplasmosis Is Treated

Antifungal medicines are used to treat histoplasmosis.

### Acute Pulmonary Histoplasmosis  
Most healthy people do not need medicine.  
If symptoms do not improve after a month, doctors may prescribe itraconazole by mouth.  
If you develop severe pneumonia, you may get amphotericin B through a vein.  
After that, you may switch to itraconazole by mouth.

### Progressive Disseminated Histoplasmosis  
This form always needs treatment.  
If the infection is severe, you get amphotericin B through a vein.  
Then you switch to itraconazole by mouth.

If you have AIDS and get histoplasmosis, you may need to take itraconazole for life.  
But if your immune system improves, you may stop after one year.  
This is only if your CD4 count (a measure of immune strength) reaches 150 or more cells per microliter of blood.

### Chronic Cavitary Histoplasmosis  
Itraconazole or, for more serious cases, amphotericin B can kill the fungus.  
But treatment cannot fix lung damage that has already happened.  
Most people still have breathing problems, like those with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.  
Starting treatment early helps prevent more lung damage.

## Outlook for Histoplasmosis

- Acute pulmonary histoplasmosis almost always gets better on its own.  
- Chronic cavitary histoplasmosis can be deadly.  
- Without treatment, progressive disseminated histoplasmosis kills more than 90% of people.

# Diphtheria

## What is diphtheria?

Diphtheria is a serious infection caused by bacteria.  
It can cause a thick grey-white coating in your mouth, throat, or nose.  
It can also cause swollen glands in your neck.  
Some people get skin blisters or sores instead.

## Symptoms of diphtheria

You may have:
- A thick grey-white coating on the back of your throat, nose, or tongue.
- A high temperature (fever).
- A sore throat.
- Swollen glands in your neck.
- Trouble breathing or swallowing.

Skin diphtheria can cause:
- Pus-filled blisters on your legs, feet, or hands.
- Large open sores with red, sore skin around them.

Symptoms usually start 2 to 5 days after you catch the infection.

## How diphtheria spreads

Diphtheria spreads easily from person to person.  
It spreads when an infected person coughs or sneezes.  
It can also spread through close contact with an infected person.  
You can catch it by sharing cups, cutlery, clothes, or bedding with someone who is infected.

## When to get help

Call your GP or use NHS 111 right away if:
- You have been to a country where diphtheria is found and now have symptoms.
- You have been close to someone who has diphtheria.

You can call 111 or get help online.

If you are travelling and feel unwell, get medical help right away.  
Do not wait until you return to the UK.

Call your GP before going in. They may want to talk to you over the phone first.

## Treatment for diphtheria

You will need:
- Antibiotics to kill the bacteria.
- Medicines to stop the harmful effects of the toxins made by the bacteria.
- Cleaning of any skin sores if you have skin diphtheria.

Treatment usually lasts 2 weeks.  
Skin sores usually heal in 2 to 3 months but may leave a scar.

Anyone who has been close to someone with diphtheria will also need antibiotics.  
They may also need a diphtheria vaccine.  
A contact tracing team will reach out to people who need treatment.

## How to prevent diphtheria

The best way to avoid diphtheria is to be fully vaccinated.

### Vaccines for children

Children in the UK get the diphtheria vaccine as part of routine childhood vaccinations.  
The doses are given at:
- 8 weeks old
- 12 weeks old
- 16 weeks old  
(These are part of the 6-in-1 vaccine – three separate shots.)

Then again at:
- 3 years and 4 months old (4-in-1 pre-school booster)
- 14 years old (3-in-1 teenage booster)

### Vaccines for travel

If you are travelling to certain parts of the world, you may need a booster shot.  
You should get a booster if your last diphtheria vaccine was more than 10 years ago.

Risks are higher in:
- Africa
- South America
- India
- South east Asia
- Eastern Europe

### Free vaccines on the NHS

You may be able to get a free combined vaccine that protects against diphtheria, tetanus, and polio.  
Ask your GP surgery about this.

# Neurofibromatosis

Neurofibromatosis is a group of genetic conditions. These conditions run in families. They cause tumors on nerves. The tumors can be non-cancerous or cancerous. The condition also often causes dark spots on the skin. It can affect many parts of the body. Doctors diagnose it based on physical signs and symptoms. Non-cancerous tumors can be removed with surgery. Cancerous tumors are treated with radiation or chemotherapy.

Neurofibromatosis is a condition that affects both the nervous system and the skin.

## Types of Neurofibromatosis

There are three main types:

- Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)  
- NF2-related schwannomatosis (formerly called NF2)  
- Non-NF2 schwannomatosis (formerly called schwannomatosis)

These names come from a group of experts who updated the rules for diagnosing these conditions. The new names better reflect how doctors now use both symptoms and gene tests to make a diagnosis.

## Symptoms and Signs

The symptoms vary by type.

**Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1):**  
- Many light brown spots on the skin (called café-au-lait spots)  
- Skin folds in the armpits or groin that are darker than normal  
- Small lumps under the skin (neurofibromas)  
- A tumor on the nerve that connects the eye to the brain (optic pathway glioma)  
- Small growths in the eye (Lisch nodules)  
- Bone problems like a bent leg bone or a missing part of the skull  
- A change in a gene called NF1

**NF2-related schwannomatosis:**  
- Tumors on both hearing nerves (bilateral vestibular schwannomas)  
- A shared gene change in two different tumors (like schwannomas, meningiomas, or ependymomas)  
- Or: One hearing nerve tumor and a family history of NF2  
- Or: Two or more meningiomas  
- Or: A gene change in blood or other normal tissue

**Non-NF2 schwannomatosis:**  
- Tumors on nerves under the skin (not in the skin itself)  
- These tumors are not on the hearing nerves  
- A gene change in the SMARCB1 or LZTR1 genes  
- Or: A pattern of gene changes in two different tumors on chromosome 22  
- Or: No known gene change, but at least two confirmed nerve tumors

## How Doctors Diagnose Neurofibromatosis

Doctors use a checklist of signs and symptoms to make the diagnosis. They do not rely on one test alone.

### Step-by-step diagnosis:

1. **Physical exam**  
   Doctors check the skin, bones, and nervous system.  
   They look for café-au-lait spots, skin folds, tumors, and bone issues.

2. **Brain MRI or head CT scan**  
   These scans are used if a person has symptoms like headaches, vision problems, or balance issues.  
   They help find tumors in the brain or nerves.  
   For children with NF1 who cannot have a full eye exam, an MRI can check for tumors on the optic nerve.

3. **Genetic testing**  
   This is done if a person has signs of neurofibromatosis but does not meet all the clinical rules.  
   It can confirm the diagnosis when symptoms are unclear.

Most people with NF1 are found during a routine check-up, a visit for skin changes, or because a family member has the condition.

## Treatment

There is no single treatment that works for all types of neurofibromatosis. Treatment depends on the type and symptoms.

### For NF1:
- Small tumors on the skin can be removed with a laser or heat (electrocautery).  
- Larger tumors may need surgery.  
- Surgery can cause loss of feeling or movement in the area.  
- Tumors often grow back after surgery.  
- For large tumors that cannot be removed, a medicine called selumetinib may help. It is used in children 2 years and older.  
- Most tumors on the optic nerve do not cause symptoms. Doctors just watch them over time.  
- If a tumor grows and causes vision problems, chemotherapy is used.

### For NF2-related schwannomatosis:
- Tumors on the hearing nerves are usually treated with surgery.  
- Slow-growing tumors may not need surgery right away.  
- For fast-growing tumors, a medicine called bevacizumab may help.  
- This medicine slows blood vessel growth in tumors.  
- Hearing care is very important. All patients should see an audiologist (hearing specialist).

### For non-NF2 schwannomatosis:
- There is no cure.  
- Treatment focuses on managing pain.  
- Surgery may be done if a tumor causes severe pain or nerve problems.  
- A team of specialists should care for these patients.

## Genetic Counseling

If one parent has neurofibromatosis, each child has a 50% chance of inheriting it.  
If neither parent has it, the chance for future children is unclear.  
New gene changes happen often, especially in NF1.

## Key Points

- There are three types: NF1, NF2-related schwannomatosis, and non-NF2 schwannomatosis.  
- All are caused by changes in certain genes.  
- NF1 often causes skin spots, nerve tumors, and bone problems.  
- NF2 causes tumors on both hearing nerves.  
- Non-NF2 schwannomatosis causes many nerve tumors, but not on the hearing nerves.  
- Diagnosis is based on physical signs and symptoms.  
- Brain scans are used if there are nervous system symptoms.  
- Tumors that cause pain or problems can be removed.  
- Cancerous tumors are treated with chemotherapy.  
- Bevacizumab may help some hearing nerve tumors.  
- Non-NF2 schwannomatosis is managed with long-term pain care.  
- Genetic testing is helpful if the diagnosis is not clear.

# Coronaviruses and Severe Respiratory Illnesses (MERS and SARS)

Coronaviruses are a group of viruses that can cause breathing problems.  
They range from mild colds to serious lung infections that can be deadly.  

There are many types of coronaviruses.  
Most of them infect animals.  
Four types commonly infect people and cause mild cold-like symptoms.  

Three other types can cause very serious illness.  
These have caused major outbreaks of deadly pneumonia in recent years.  

## What Are the Three Serious Coronaviruses?

- **SARS-CoV-2** is a new coronavirus.  
  It was first found in late 2019.  
  It causes a disease called coronavirus disease 2019, or COVID-19.  
  This is covered in a separate section.  

- **MERS-CoV** was found in 2012.  
  It causes a serious lung disease called Middle East respiratory syndrome, or MERS.  

- **SARS-CoV-1** was found in 2003.  
  It caused a global outbreak of severe acute respiratory syndrome, or SARS.  
  The outbreak started in China near the end of 2002.  

These three viruses spread from animals to people.  
They are called zoonotic viruses because they jump from animals to humans.

---

## Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS)

MERS is a serious lung infection caused by a coronavirus.  
It causes symptoms like the flu, but much worse.  

The virus that causes MERS is a type of coronavirus.  
It was first found in Jordan and Saudi Arabia in 2012.  

As of 2021:  
- Over 2,500 people were confirmed to have MERS.  
- More than 900 people died from it.  
- Most cases happened in Saudi Arabia.  
- New cases still appear in Saudi Arabia.  

The largest outbreak outside the Arabian Peninsula happened in South Korea in 2015.  
It started when a traveler returned from the Middle East.  

Cases have also been reported in:  
- Europe  
- Asia  
- North Africa  
- The Middle East  
- The United States  

Most of these cases involved people who were brought to these countries for care or got sick after visiting the Middle East.  
Very few cases have been reported since 2019.  

In some Middle Eastern countries, dromedary camels are likely the main source of the virus.  
But we do not yet know exactly how the virus moves from camels to people.  

MERS is more common in men.  
It is also more dangerous in older adults and people with long-term health problems.  
These include diabetes, heart disease, or kidney disease.  
About one in three people who get MERS die from it.  

The virus spreads through close contact with an infected person.  
It can also spread through tiny droplets in the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes.  
People are not contagious before they start showing symptoms.  

Most person-to-person spread happens among healthcare workers.  
They care for sick patients without proper protection.  

Symptoms usually appear about 5 days after infection.  
But they can show up as early as 2 days or as late as 14 days after exposure.  

Most people have:  
- Fever  
- Chills  
- Body aches  

Many also have a cough.  
About one in three people also have:  
- Diarrhea  
- Vomiting  
- Stomach pain  

### How Is MERS Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect MERS in people who:  
- Have a serious lung infection  
- Recently traveled to or live in an area where MERS is known to spread  
- Had close contact with someone who may have MERS  

To test for MERS:  
- Doctors take samples from the nose, throat, and lungs at different times.  
- They test these samples for the virus.  
- Blood tests are also done to check for the virus or antibodies.  

Blood tests are done for anyone who had close contact with a possible MERS case.  

### How Is MERS Treated?

There is no specific medicine to cure MERS.  
Doctors treat the symptoms.  

For fever and body aches:  
- Acetaminophen or ibuprofen can help.  

To stop the virus from spreading:  
- The infected person is placed in a special room.  
- The room has a ventilation system that limits the spread of germs.  
- Anyone entering the room must wear:  
  - A special mask  
  - Eye protection  
  - A gown, cap, and gloves  

Doors to the room should stay closed.  
People should enter and leave only when needed.  

---

## Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS)

SARS is a serious lung infection caused by a coronavirus.  
It causes flu-like symptoms, but they are much worse.  

No new cases have been reported since 2004.  

SARS symptoms are similar to those of other common respiratory viruses.  
But they are more severe, especially in older adults.  

Doctors only suspect SARS if a person has been near someone who had SARS.  

If SARS is suspected:  
- The person is placed in a special room.  
- The room has a ventilation system to stop germs from spreading.  

### What Caused the SARS Outbreak?

SARS was first found in China in late 2002.  
It spread worldwide.  
By mid-2003:  
- Over 8,000 people were infected.  
- About 800 people died.  
- Cases were reported in Canada, the United States, and other countries.  

No new cases have been reported since 2004.  
But SARS is not completely gone.  
The virus still lives in animals and could return.  

The virus likely came from civets.  
Civets are cat-like animals sold in live animal markets.  
They were eaten as food.  
We do not know exactly how the civets got infected.  
But bats are believed to be the original source of the virus in nature.  

SARS is much more serious than most other coronaviruses.  
Most coronaviruses only cause colds.  
But MERS and COVID-19 are also serious diseases caused by coronaviruses.  

### How Does SARS Spread?

SARS spreads through:  
- Close contact with an infected person  
- Airborne droplets from coughs or sneezes  

### What Are the Symptoms of SARS?

Symptoms include:  
- Fever  
- Headache  
- Chills  
- Body aches  

These are followed by:  
- A dry cough  
- Trouble breathing (in some cases)  

Most people recover in 1 to 2 weeks.  
But some get very sick.  
About 10% of people with SARS die.  

### How Is SARS Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect SARS only if:  
- A person has a fever  
- And a cough or trouble breathing  
- And has been near someone with SARS  

Tests can be done to find the virus in the body.  

### How Is SARS Treated?

There is no specific cure for SARS.  
Treatment depends on the severity of symptoms.  

- People with mild symptoms do not need special treatment.  
- People with moderate breathing problems get extra oxygen.  
- People with severe breathing problems may need a machine to help them breathe.  

Isolation in a special room with good air control helped stop the 2003 outbreak.  
This method kept the virus from spreading and eventually ended the outbreak.

# Peritonitis

Peritonitis is a serious infection of the lining inside your tummy.  
It can cause severe pain and other serious symptoms.  
If not treated quickly, it can lead to life-threatening problems.

## Symptoms of Peritonitis

You may have:
- Pain in your tummy that gets worse over time
- A very high temperature, or feel hot and shivery
- A fast heartbeat (your heart beats much faster than normal)
- Not being able to pee, or peeing much less than usual
- Loss of appetite
- Feeling sick or being sick
- A swollen tummy

If you are on kidney dialysis, check your fluid bag.  
If the fluid looks cloudy or has white bits in it, this could be a sign of infection.

## When to Seek Help

Call your doctor right away or use NHS 111 if you have any of these symptoms.  
Do not wait. Peritonitis can get worse very quickly.

## What Causes Peritonitis

The lining of your tummy (called the peritoneum) covers your internal organs.  
If this lining gets infected, it can cause peritonitis.  
This often happens because of another health problem, such as:

- A burst stomach ulcer
- A burst appendix
- Inflammatory bowel diseases like Crohn’s disease or diverticulitis
- Inflammation of the pancreas (pancreatitis)
- Recent surgery
- Injury to the tummy
- Pelvic inflammatory disease
- Liver scarring (cirrhosis)

In rare cases, bacteria can get into the equipment used for peritoneal dialysis.  
This can cause infection in people with kidney failure.

## Treatment for Peritonitis

You will need to go to hospital for treatment.  
The main treatment is antibiotics given through a drip into your vein.

If you have kidney dialysis, your doctor may change your treatment plan until the infection clears.

### Eating During Treatment

Peritonitis can make it hard to eat or digest food.  
If you cannot eat normally, you may need:

- A feeding tube put through your nose into your stomach
- Or a tube placed directly into your stomach using keyhole surgery
- If a tube is not possible, you may get liquid nutrition through a drip into your vein

### Surgery for Peritonitis

If the infection has damaged part of the tummy lining, surgery may be needed to remove the damaged area.

Pus-filled swellings (abscesses) can form.  
These may need to be drained using a needle under local anaesthetic.

You may also need surgery to fix the original cause.  
For example, a burst appendix must be removed.

# Urticaria (Hives)

Urticaria is a skin condition that causes raised, red, itchy patches. These patches can move from one place to another on the body. They often appear suddenly and go away within hours or days.

Sometimes, urticaria is linked to a deeper swelling called angioedema. This swelling can happen in the face, lips, hands, feet, or genitals. It can also affect the intestines and cause belly pain that comes and goes. If the swelling blocks the airway, it can be life-threatening. This can happen if the throat or tongue swell too much.

---

## What Causes Hives?

Hives happen when certain cells in the skin release chemicals. These chemicals cause fluid to leak into the skin. This leads to swelling and itching.

The release of these chemicals can be due to:

- An allergic reaction
- A problem with the immune system
- Direct irritation from certain medicines or substances
- Physical or emotional stress

### Allergic Causes
- You may have an allergic reaction to a food, medicine, insect sting, or infection.
- Your body makes antibodies that react to a trigger. This causes the skin cells to release chemicals.

### Immune System Problems
- In some cases, your body’s immune system attacks its own cells by mistake.
- This can cause the skin cells to release chemicals even without a clear trigger.

### Non-Allergic Causes
- Some medicines can directly cause skin cells to release chemicals.
- Stress, heat, cold, sunlight, or pressure on the skin can also trigger hives.
- Hormonal changes, such as those during the menstrual cycle, may cause hives in some people.

---

## Types of Urticaria

There are two main types:

### Acute Urticaria
- Lasts less than six weeks.
- Most common type.
- Often caused by an allergic reaction to food, medicine, insect bites, or an infection.

### Chronic Urticaria
- Lasts more than six weeks.
- Often has no clear cause.
- May be linked to an autoimmune condition.
- Can last for months or even years.

---

## Common Causes of Hives

### Acute Hives
- **Allergens**: Pollen, dust, pet dander, latex.
  - Hives appear within minutes or hours after contact.
- **Medicines**:
  - Aspirin, NSAIDs (like ibuprofen), or other drugs that block certain body chemicals.
  - Some medicines directly cause skin cells to release chemicals (like opioids or contrast dye).
  - ACE inhibitors (used for blood pressure) can raise levels of a chemical that causes hives.
- **Physical Triggers**:
  - Cold, heat, sun, pressure, vibration, or sweating.
  - Hives appear within seconds or minutes of exposure.
- **Infections**:
  - Bacterial (like strep or *H. pylori*).
  - Viral (like hepatitis, HIV, or Epstein-Barr virus).
  - Parasitic (like worms or *Giardia*).
  - Hives may go away after the infection is treated.
- **Foods**:
  - Peanuts, tree nuts, fish, shellfish, eggs, milk, wheat, soy.
  - Hives appear within minutes to hours after eating.
- **Insect Bites or Stings**:
  - Hives appear within seconds or minutes.
- **Serum Sickness**:
  - Happens 7 to 10 days after a shot or medicine.
  - Symptoms include hives, fever, joint pain, swollen glands, and belly pain.
- **Blood Transfusions**:
  - Hives appear within minutes of starting the transfusion.

### Chronic Hives
- **Autoimmune Diseases**:
  - Lupus, Sjögren syndrome, thyroid disease, or other immune-related conditions.
  - Signs depend on the disease (e.g., dry eyes, joint pain, rash, fatigue).
- **Cancer**:
  - Rare, but possible. Often linked to stomach, lung, or lymph node cancers.
  - Symptoms include weight loss, night sweats, cough, or blood in stool.
- **Unknown Cause (Idiopathic)**:
  - Most common cause of chronic hives.
  - No clear reason found.
- **Medicines or Substances**:
  - Long-term use of any medicine (prescription, over-the-counter, or herbal) can cause hives.
  - Stopping the medicine may help.
- **Hormonal Changes**:
  - Hives that happen during the second half of the menstrual cycle and go away with your period.
  - May be linked to birth control pills or hormone therapy.
- **Physical Triggers**:
  - Same as for acute hives (cold, heat, pressure, etc.).
- **Systemic Mastocytosis**:
  - A rare condition where too many mast cells build up in the body.
  - Skin may have small brown spots that turn into hives when touched.
  - May also cause flushing, stomach pain, or headaches.

> **Note**: If you have recently traveled to a developing country, tell your doctor. This can help find the cause.

---

## How Is Urticaria Diagnosed?

There is no single test for hives. Doctors rely on:

- Your medical history
- A physical exam
- Tests only if a specific cause is suspected

### Tests May Include:
- Blood tests to check for infections or autoimmune diseases
- Thyroid tests (TSH, antibodies)
- Tests for immune system problems (like ANA, RF, anti-CCP)
- Tests for blood proteins (cryoglobulins, complement levels)
- Skin biopsy (if mastocytosis or vasculitis is suspected)

---

## How Is Urticaria Treated?

### Step 1: Remove the Cause
- Stop any medicine or food that may be causing the hives.
- Avoid known triggers (like cold, heat, pressure, or stress).

### Step 2: Treat Symptoms
- Use non-sedating antihistamines (like cetirizine or loratadine).
- These help reduce itching and swelling.
- Avoid hot baths, tight clothes, and scratching.
- Cool baths or cold compresses can help relieve itching.

### Step 3: Severe Cases
- If hives are severe or not controlled, your doctor may prescribe stronger medicines.
- In rare cases, steroids or other treatments may be needed.

> **Important**: Topical creams (like steroid or antihistamine creams) do not help with hives.

---

## Special Considerations for Older Adults

Older adults should be careful with certain antihistamines. These include:

- Hydroxyzine
- Diphenhydramine

These medicines can cause:
- Drowsiness
- Confusion
- Trouble urinating
- Delirium

They should only be used if needed and under close supervision.

---

## Key Points

- Hives can be caused by allergies or by other body reactions.
- Most short-term hives are due to an allergic reaction.
- Most long-term hives have no clear cause or are due to an autoimmune problem.
- If you have other symptoms (like fever, joint pain, or belly pain), see your doctor to find the cause.
- First-line treatment is non-sedating antihistamines and avoiding triggers.
- Creams and ointments on the skin do not help treat hives.

# Seborrheic Dermatitis

This is a long-term skin condition. It causes flaky, greasy patches on skin areas that make a lot of oil. These areas include the scalp, face, hairline, and around the ears. It can also appear on other parts of the body.

## What Causes It?

The exact cause is not known. But some people react to a type of yeast called *Malassezia*. This yeast lives naturally on the skin. It may play a role in causing the condition.

## Who Gets It?

This condition is most common in:
- Babies, usually in the first three months of life.
- Adults between the ages of 30 and 70.

It often runs in families. Some people are more likely to get it because of their genes. Cold weather can make it worse.

It is also more common and more severe in people with:
- Parkinson disease.
- HIV infection.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The condition usually starts slowly. It causes flaky skin on the scalp. This is often called dandruff. It may itch, but it does not cause hair loss.

In more serious cases, you may see:
- Yellow or red, scaly bumps.
- These can appear along the hairline, behind the ears, on the eyebrows, in the skin folds beside the nose, and on the chest.

### In Babies Under One Month Old

- Thick, yellow, crusty rash on the scalp (called cradle cap).
- Yellow flakes behind the ears.
- Red pimples on the face.
- A stubborn diaper rash often happens at the same time.

### In Older Children and Adults

- Thick, hard-to-remove flakes on the scalp.
- Large, dry patches of skin.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look at the skin. They check where the rash is and how it looks. This helps them make the diagnosis.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the age and the severity of the condition.

### For Adults and Older Children

- Use a shampoo with ketoconazole. This fights the yeast on the skin.
- Use the shampoo twice a week until the symptoms improve.
- Then use it once a week to keep it under control.
- Other shampoos can also help. These include:
  - Shampoos with pyrithione zinc.
  - Shampoos with selenium sulfide.
  - Shampoos with salicylic acid and sulfur.
  - Shampoos with tar.
- Use these shampoos daily or every other day until the dandruff is gone.
- Then use them twice a week to prevent it from coming back.

If itching does not go away:
- Apply a corticosteroid solution to the scalp.

For the beard and eyebrow areas:
- Treat them the same way as the scalp.

For the face and other sensitive areas:
- Use only mild corticosteroids, like 1% to 2.5% hydrocortisone cream.
- Do not use these creams for long periods. They can thin the skin and cause other problems.

For mild cases:
- Use an antifungal cream like ketoconazole or another type.

For long-term treatment or when antifungals do not work well:
- Doctors may prescribe calcineurin inhibitors. These are medicines called pimecrolimus and tacrolimus.

Treatment often takes many weeks. If the condition comes back after stopping treatment, you can start again.

### For Babies

- Wash the scalp daily with a mild baby shampoo.
- Gently rub in 1% to 2.5% hydrocortisone cream or fluocinolone oil.
- For severe cases, use antifungal creams like 2% ketoconazole or 1% econazole.

### For Young Children with Thick Scaly Rash on the Scalp

- Apply mineral oil, olive oil, or a corticosteroid gel or oil.
- Use a soft toothbrush to gently rub it in at bedtime.
- Wash the scalp daily until the thick scale is gone.

# Leg Cramps

## What Are Leg Cramps?

A leg cramp is a sudden, sharp pain in a leg muscle.  
It usually lasts only a short time.  
The pain can make it hard to move the leg.  
The cramp may last a few seconds or up to 10 minutes.  

After the cramp ends, the muscle may feel sore for up to a day.

## Where Do Cramps Happen?

Cramps most often happen in the calf muscle.  
This is the muscle at the back of your lower leg, below the knee.  
They can also happen in the feet or thighs, but this is less common.

## What You Can Do Yourself

### When a Cramp Happens

Try stretching the muscle.  
Gently massage the muscle.  
This may help ease the pain.  
Standing up and putting weight on the leg can also help.  

You can take paracetamol or ibuprofen after the cramp is over.  
These medicines help with soreness.  
But they do not work during the cramp.  
They take too long to start working.

### How to Prevent Cramps

Do regular calf-stretching exercises.  
These may help reduce how often cramps happen.  
They may not stop cramps completely.

### How to Stretch Your Calf Muscles

1. Stand facing a wall.  
2. Reach your arms forward until your hands touch the wall.  
3. Keep your feet flat on the floor.  
4. Lean forward. Press your hands against the wall.  
5. You should feel a stretch in your calf.  
6. Hold the stretch for 2 or 3 seconds.  
7. Stand up straight again.  
8. Repeat this 5 times.  
9. Do this exercise for 5 minutes, three times a day.  
10. Do the last session just before bed.

If your cramps get less often, you may only need to do this once or twice a day.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:

- Cramps keep you awake at night.  
- You have numbness or swelling in your legs.  
- A cramp lasts longer than 10 minutes.

## What a Doctor Can Do

Your doctor will check your legs and ask about your health.  
They will try to find the cause of your cramps.  
Then they will suggest a treatment.

Treatments may include:

- Stretching exercises.  
- Quinine tablets, if exercise does not help.

Quinine is not safe for everyone.  
Your doctor will explain the risks and side effects before giving it.

## What Causes Leg Cramps?

Some common causes of leg cramps are:

- Getting older.  
- Doing too much exercise, especially in hot or humid weather.  
- Being pregnant, especially in the later stages.  
- Some medicines, such as those for high cholesterol (statins) or high blood pressure (diuretics).  
- Not drinking enough fluids (dehydration).  
- Liver problems from drinking too much alcohol.

In some cases, the cause is not known.

# Kneecap Dislocation

A kneecap dislocation happens when the kneecap moves out of its normal position. It almost always moves to the outside of the knee. This is not the same as a full knee dislocation, which is a much more serious injury.

## Who Gets Kneecap Dislocations?

Most people who have this problem are teenage girls. Many have a long-term issue with how the kneecap fits in the knee joint.

Some people’s kneecaps pop back into place on their own before they get medical help.

## How Does It Happen?

Kneecap dislocations often happen when someone suddenly changes direction. They can also happen when the knee twists or gets hit. This can occur during sports like soccer, gymnastics, or when swinging a bat in baseball.

## What Injuries Can Happen?

Sometimes the kneecap dislocation causes a small piece of bone and cartilage to break off. This can happen in the kneecap or the thigh bone near the knee.

## What Problems Can Follow?

Over time, some people develop joint pain and stiffness. This is called osteoarthritis.

People with a long-term kneecap problem may have more dislocations or partial dislocations.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors check the knee by looking and feeling it.

X-rays are always taken to make sure there is no broken bone.

### Signs of a Dislocation

If the kneecap is still out of place, you can see and feel it on the outside of the knee. The person will hold the knee slightly bent and will not want to straighten it.

If the kneecap popped back into place on its own, the knee may be swollen. The area around the kneecap will likely be tender.

### X-rays

X-rays are taken even if the kneecap has popped back in. This helps rule out a broken bone.

---

## How Is It Treated?

The main steps are to put the kneecap back in place and keep the knee still.

### Putting the Kneecap Back

Doctors move the kneecap back into place. Most people do not need medicine to help with pain or to relax.

The patient lies down with the hip bent. The doctor gently pushes the kneecap toward the inside of the knee while slowly straightening the leg. You may feel or hear a small click when the kneecap moves back.

After the kneecap is back, the doctor checks if the knee feels stable. They move the knee through its full range of motion.

### After the Kneecap Is Back

- If the knee feels stable, the person uses crutches and wraps the knee with an elastic bandage.
- If the knee feels loose or unstable, a knee brace is needed to keep it still.

### When Surgery Is Needed

Some people need surgery if:
- There is a broken piece of bone and cartilage.
- The kneecap keeps coming out again.

These people are referred to an orthopedic surgeon for care.

---

## Key Points

- Kneecap dislocations are common and not the same as a full knee dislocation, which is much more serious.
- They happen most often in teenage girls with a long-term kneecap problem.
- If the kneecap is still out, it is easy to see and feel. Always take X-rays to check for a broken bone.
- The kneecap must be put back in place.
- The knee must be kept still after the kneecap is back.
- If there is a broken piece of bone or cartilage, or if the kneecap keeps coming out, see an orthopedic surgeon.

# Infections Caused by Klebsiella, Enterobacter, and Serratia

Klebsiella, Enterobacter, and Serratia are types of bacteria. They are similar and belong to a group called gram-negative bacteria. These bacteria can cause infections in hospitals or long-term care facilities.

## Where These Infections Happen

These bacteria can infect:
- The bladder or lungs (causing pneumonia, bladder infections, or kidney infections)
- Vein catheters used to give medicine or fluids
- Burns
- Wounds from surgery
- The bloodstream (which can lead to serious illness)

These infections are rare in healthy people. Most often, they happen in people who are already sick or whose body’s defenses are weak. They also often affect people who have medical devices like catheters, drains, or breathing tubes.

## When These Infections Occur

These bacteria live in the intestines of many healthy people. But they usually do not cause harm unless the person is very sick or in a hospital.

Infections from these bacteria are often caught in hospitals or long-term care homes. They are more common in people with:
- Weak immune systems
- Chronic health problems like diabetes
- Alcohol use disorder
- Old age

## Rare Cases Outside Hospitals

Sometimes Klebsiella causes pneumonia in people who are not in a hospital. This usually happens in:
- Older adults
- People with diabetes
- People with alcohol use disorder
- People with weak immune systems

This type of pneumonia causes:
- A bad cough
- Coughing up thick, dark brown or dark red mucus
- Pus-filled areas in the lungs or in the space between the lungs and chest wall (called empyema)

One type of Klebsiella can make a poison that harms the colon. This can cause bleeding and inflammation in the colon. This condition is called antibiotic-associated colitis.

This happens after taking antibiotics. The antibiotics kill good bacteria in the gut. Then Klebsiella can grow out of control and make the poison. But most cases of antibiotic-associated colitis are actually caused by a different bacteria called Clostridioides difficile.

## How Doctors Diagnose These Infections

Doctors suspect an infection if you are in a hospital or long-term care facility and have symptoms.

To confirm the infection, doctors take a sample from:
- Sputum (mucus from the lungs)
- Lung secretions (collected using a small tube)
- Blood
- Urine
- Infected tissue

The sample is tested in a lab. It is stained and grown in a culture. Doctors can see the bacteria under a microscope. This helps identify the type of bacteria.

Other tests may be needed depending on the infection. These can include:
- X-rays
- Ultrasound
- CT scans

The bacteria are also tested to see which antibiotics will work best. This is called susceptibility testing.

## How These Infections Are Treated

All infections caused by these bacteria are treated with antibiotics given through a vein (intravenously).

Common antibiotics used include:
- Cephalosporins
- Cefepime
- Carbapenems
- Fluoroquinolones
- Piperacillin/tazobactam
- Aminoglycosides

But sometimes these bacteria are resistant to many antibiotics. So doctors always do a test to find the best antibiotic.

If the infection was caught in a hospital or care facility, it may be harder to treat. That is because bacteria in these places often resist many antibiotics.

# Hives

Hives cause a rash that is very itchy.  
The rash may look red, but this can be hard to see on brown or black skin.

You can often treat hives at home with antihistamines from a pharmacy.  
If the rash does not improve, your doctor may give you stronger antihistamines or steroid tablets.

## When to seek urgent help

Call your doctor right away or use NHS 111 if:

- The rash does not get better after 2 days  
- You are worried about your child’s rash  
- The rash is spreading fast  
- The rash keeps coming back (you may be allergic to something)  
- You have a high temperature and feel unwell  
- You have swelling under the skin (this is called angioedema)

You can call 111 or get help online at [nhs.uk/111](https://www.nhs.uk/111)

## When to call 999

Call emergency services right away if:

- Your lips, mouth, throat, or tongue swell suddenly  
- You are breathing very fast or struggling to breathe  
- You feel like you are choking or gasping for air  
- Your throat feels tight or you cannot swallow  
- Your skin, tongue, or lips turn blue, grey, or pale  
  - On black or brown skin, check the palms of your hands or soles of your feet  
- You feel very confused, very sleepy, or dizzy  
- Someone passes out and will not wake up  
- A child is limp, floppy, or not responding normally  
  - Their head may fall to the side, back, or forward  
  - They may not be able to lift their head or look at you

You or the person who is unwell may also have a rash that is swollen, raised, or itchy.

These signs can mean a serious allergic reaction.  
This needs emergency treatment in a hospital.

[Find your nearest A&E department](https://www.nhs.uk/service-search/urgent-care/)

## What hives look like

The main sign of hives is an itchy rash.  
The rash can:

- Appear as raised bumps or patches  
- Be any size or shape  
- Show up anywhere on the body  
- Stay in one place or spread to other areas  
- Feel itchy, stinging, or burning  
- Look pink or red on white skin  
- Be harder to see on brown or black skin

## Treatment from a doctor

Your doctor may give you:

- A menthol cream to soothe the skin  
- Antihistamines to reduce itching  
- Steroid tablets if the rash is severe

If the hives do not go away with treatment, your doctor may refer you to a skin specialist.  
This is a doctor who focuses on skin problems.

# Rhabdomyosarcoma – Simple Explanation

Rhabdomyosarcoma is a type of cancer that starts in cells that can become muscle. It can grow in any muscle in the body. This cancer can cause different symptoms depending on where it is.

## Who Gets This Cancer?

- Rhabdomyosarcoma is the third most common solid cancer in children, not including brain tumors.
- About 400 to 500 children in the United States get this cancer each year.
- It makes up about 3 out of every 100 childhood cancers.
- It is the most common cancer in a group called soft-tissue sarcomas.
- Two out of every three cases happen in children under 7 years old.
- It is more common in white children than in Black children. This is mostly because it is less common in Black girls.
- It is slightly more common in boys than in girls.

Even though adults can get this cancer, it is very different in adults than in children. The type of cancer, where it starts, and how it behaves are not the same.

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

Most children do not have fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Instead, they usually have:

- A hard lump that can be felt.
- Problems caused by the tumor pressing on nearby organs.

### If the cancer is in the eye or nose area:
- Watery eyes
- Eye pain
- Eye bulging
- Blocked nose
- Voice changes
- Thick, yellow or green discharge from the nose

### If the cancer is in the genital or urinary area:
- Belly pain
- A lump in the belly
- Trouble peeing
- Blood in the urine
- Vaginal tumors may cause a mass sticking out of the vagina and discharge with blood

### If the cancer is in an arm or leg:
- A hard, firm lump that does not move easily
- It can appear anywhere on the arms or legs

The cancer often spreads to nearby lymph nodes. It can also spread to the lungs, bone marrow, or other lymph nodes. But these spread areas usually do not cause symptoms.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- Doctors use CT scans or MRI scans to look at the tumor.
- MRI is better for tumors in the head and neck.
- A biopsy (taking a small sample of the tumor) or removing the whole tumor is needed to confirm the diagnosis.

To check if the cancer has spread, doctors do:
- A CT scan of the chest
- A PET-CT scan
- A bone scan
- A bone marrow test (taking a sample from both hips)

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment uses more than one method. The main treatments are:

- Surgery
- Chemotherapy (medicine to kill cancer cells)
- Radiation therapy (using high-energy beams to kill cancer cells)

### Surgery
- Doctors try to remove the entire tumor if it can be done safely.
- If removing the tumor would damage an organ, they may not do it. The cancer responds well to chemotherapy and radiation, so it is better to avoid major surgery if it could cause long-term harm.

### Chemotherapy
- All children get chemotherapy, no matter their risk level.
- Common medicines used are:
  - Vincristine
  - Actinomycin D (also called dactinomycin)
  - Cyclophosphamide
  - Doxorubicin
  - Ifosfamide
  - Etoposide
- Other medicines like topotecan and irinotecan also work against this cancer.

### Radiation Therapy
- This is used when:
  - Some cancer remains after surgery.
  - The cancer is in a high-risk group.
  - The cancer is in a hard-to-treat area.

## What Is the Outlook?

The chance of recovery depends on several things:

- Where the cancer is located
  - Better outcomes if it is in the head or neck (not near the brain) or in the genitourinary area (not the bladder or prostate)
- Whether the tumor was completely removed
- If the cancer has spread to other parts of the body
- The child’s age
  - Worse outlook for babies under 1 year or teens over 10 years old
- The type of cancer cells (embryonal type has a better outcome than alveolar type)

Doctors use all these factors to place each child into a risk group:
- Low-risk
- Intermediate-risk
- High-risk

Treatment is stronger for higher-risk children. Survival rates vary:
- Over 90% for low-risk children
- Less than 50% for high-risk children

# Abnormal Heart Rhythms – Simple Explanation

## What Are Abnormal Heart Rhythms?

An abnormal heart rhythm means your heart beats in a way that is not normal. It might beat too fast, too slow, irregularly, or use a wrong path for its electrical signals.

- Your heart has four chambers. They work together to pump blood.
- The heart muscle contracts in a set order. This keeps blood moving through your body.
- The heart’s rhythm is controlled by electrical signals.
- These signals start in a small area called the sinus node, in the top right chamber of the heart.
- The speed of the heart’s beats depends on how often the sinus node sends out signals.
- Your nervous system and certain hormones control how fast the heart beats.

## How the Heart’s Electrical System Works

- The sinus node starts each heartbeat with an electrical signal.
- The signal spreads through the upper chambers (atria), making them squeeze and push blood into the lower chambers (ventricles).
- The signal then reaches the atrioventricular node, which acts like a gate.
- This node delays the signal so the upper chambers can finish squeezing before the lower chambers get the signal.
- After the delay, the signal travels down a pathway called the bundle of His.
- It splits into two branches—one for each lower chamber.
- The signal spreads through the lower chambers, making them squeeze and push blood out of the heart.

## What Causes Abnormal Heart Rhythms?

The most common cause is a problem with the heart itself. This includes:

- Coronary artery disease
- Heart valve problems
- Heart failure

Other causes include:

- Some medicines (both prescription and over-the-counter)
- Birth defects in the heart’s electrical system
- Changes in the heart’s electrical system that come with aging

Some people have no clear cause for their abnormal rhythm.

### Fast Heart Rhythms (Tachycardia)

These can start on their own or be triggered by:

- Exercise
- Stress
- Drinking too much alcohol
- Smoking
- Stimulant drugs (like those in cold or allergy medicines)
- An overactive thyroid gland

### Slow Heart Rhythms (Bradycardia)

These can be caused by:

- Pain
- Hunger
- Tiredness
- Digestive problems like diarrhea or vomiting
- Swallowing, which can overstimulate the vagus nerve

In rare cases, the vagus nerve can slow the heart so much that it stops for a moment. But this usually fixes itself.

An underactive thyroid gland can also cause slow heart rhythms.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Some people feel their heart racing, fluttering, or skipping. This is called palpitations.

- Not everyone feels their heart rhythm changes.
- Some people feel normal heartbeats, especially when lying on their left side.
- The symptoms can range from mild to life-threatening.

Important facts:

- A serious heart rhythm may cause no symptoms at all.
- A mild rhythm may cause very strong symptoms.
- The real danger comes from how well the heart pumps blood, not just the rhythm.

When the heart does not pump well, you may feel:

- Weakness
- Tiredness
- Shortness of breath
- Dizziness
- Light-headedness
- Fainting (called syncope)

Fainting happens when the heart cannot keep blood pressure high enough. If the problem continues, it can lead to death.

Abnormal rhythms can also make other heart problems worse, like chest pain or trouble breathing.

If you have symptoms, you should see a doctor right away.

> **Did You Know?**  
> Some harmless rhythms can feel very bad. Some dangerous rhythms cause no symptoms at all.

## How Are Abnormal Heart Rhythms Diagnosed?

### Your Doctor Will Ask:

- Is your heartbeat fast or slow?
- Is it regular or irregular?
- Does it last a short time or a long time?
- Does it cause symptoms?

They will also ask:

- Does it happen when you are resting or only during activity?
- Does it start and stop suddenly or slowly?

### The Main Test: Electrocardiogram (ECG)

- An ECG records the electrical activity of your heart.
- It shows a picture of your heart’s rhythm during a short time.
- It can show if your heart is beating too fast, too slow, or irregularly.
- It can also show if there is a past heart attack, poor blood flow to the heart, or thickened heart muscle.

### If the Problem Is Not Always Present

- A portable ECG monitor (called a Holter monitor or event monitor) may be used.
- You wear it for 24 to 48 hours, or up to two weeks.
- It records your heart rhythm all the time or when you press a button during symptoms.
- You keep a diary of your symptoms and what you were doing.
- This helps the doctor match your symptoms to your heart rhythm.

### For Rare or Dangerous Rhythms

- A small device can be implanted under the skin near the collarbone.
- It records heart rhythms over a long time.
- It sends data to your doctor without pain.

### Hospital Testing

- People with serious symptoms are often admitted to the hospital.
- Their heart rhythm is watched all the time on a monitor.
- This helps catch problems quickly.

### Other Tests

- **Exercise stress test**: Your heart is checked while you walk on a treadmill.
- **Blood pressure during exercise**: Measures how your blood pressure changes with activity.
- **Echocardiogram**: Uses sound waves to check the heart’s structure and function.
- **Electrophysiologic testing**: A thin tube (catheter) is guided into the heart. Tiny electrodes at the tip send signals to test how the heart responds. This helps find the cause and best treatment.

### Reading an ECG

An ECG shows waves that represent different parts of the heartbeat:

- **P wave**: The upper chambers (atria) are getting ready to squeeze.
- **QRS complex**: The lower chambers (ventricles) are squeezing.
- **T wave**: The lower chambers are recovering after squeezing.

An ECG can show:

- Past heart attacks
- Abnormal heart rhythms
- Poor blood flow to the heart
- Thickened heart muscle
- Bulges in the heart wall (aneurysms), which can happen after a heart attack

It can also show where an abnormal rhythm starts in the heart. This helps doctors find the cause.

## How Are Abnormal Heart Rhythms Treated?

Treatment depends on the type and cause of the rhythm.

### Common Treatments

- **Medicines** to slow a fast heartbeat
- **Pacemaker** to help a slow heartbeat
- **Electric shock** to stop a fast rhythm
- **Ablation** to destroy a small area of heart tissue that causes the problem

### For Mild but Troubling Rhythms

- Just knowing the rhythm is harmless may be enough.
- Changing or adjusting medicines can help.
- Avoiding alcohol, caffeine, and smoking may reduce symptoms.
- Avoiding intense exercise may help if symptoms only happen during activity.
- You may need to stop driving until your doctor says it’s safe.

### Antiarrhythmic Medicines

- These help stop fast heartbeats that cause serious symptoms.
- No one medicine works for everyone.
- You may need to try several before finding one that works.
- Some medicines can make the rhythm worse or cause new problems.
- They can also cause side effects.

### Artificial Pacemakers

- These are small devices placed under the skin, usually near the collarbone.
- Wires connect the device to the heart.
- The device sends electrical signals to make the heart beat when it’s too slow.
- It acts like a backup for the heart’s natural pacemaker.

### Electric Shock (Cardioversion or Defibrillation)

- A shock stops the heart for a moment.
- After a second or two, the heart often restarts with a normal rhythm.
- This works for fast, dangerous rhythms.
- It does not work if the heart has no electrical activity at all.
- Shocks are usually given through a device on the chest.
- Some people with serious risks get a permanent device called an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD).

### Ablation

- This destroys a small area of heart tissue that causes the abnormal rhythm.
- It can cure some types of arrhythmias.
- It is done using a catheter with tiny electrodes.

## What Is the Outlook?

- Most abnormal heart rhythms do not cause symptoms.
- They do not harm the heart’s ability to pump blood.
- They are usually not dangerous, though they can cause worry.
- Some harmless rhythms can lead to more serious ones.

### When Is It Serious?

- If the heart cannot pump blood well, the rhythm is serious.
- Where the rhythm starts matters:
  - Rhythms starting in the lower chambers (ventricles) are more serious.
  - Rhythms in the upper chambers (atria) are less serious.
  - Rhythms starting in the natural pacemaker (sinus node) or the atrioventricular node are usually the least serious.

But there are exceptions. Each case is different.

## More Information

For more details, visit:

**American Heart Association: Arrhythmia**
