# Flu

Flu feels like a very bad cold.  
It can come on fast and make you feel unwell.

## What flu symptoms are like

You may have:
- A sudden high fever
- Body aches and pains
- Feeling very tired or weak
- A dry cough
- A sore throat
- A headache
- Trouble sleeping
- No appetite
- Diarrhoea or stomach pain
- Feeling sick or being sick

Children can have the same symptoms.  
They may also have ear pain or seem less active than usual.

## How to feel better at home

If you have flu, you can help yourself get better by:
- Taking it easy and resting
- Wearing warm clothes and staying in a warm room
- Taking paracetamol or ibuprofen to lower your fever and ease pain
- Drinking plenty of water to stay hydrated  
  (Your pee should be light yellow or clear)
- Giving paracetamol or ibuprofen to your child if they are upset or in pain  
  (Check the label or ask a pharmacist or doctor if you are unsure)

## When to get help

Call your doctor right away or use NHS 111 if:
- You are worried about your baby or child
- You are 65 years old or older
- You are pregnant
- You have a long-term health problem, such as diabetes, heart disease, lung disease, kidney disease, or a condition affecting your brain or nerves
- You have a weak immune system (for example, from chemotherapy or HIV)
- Your symptoms do not get better after 7 days

You can call 111 or get help online at [nhs.uk/111](https://www.nhs.uk/111)

## When to go to A&E (Emergency Department)

Go to A&E or call 999 if you:
- Have sudden chest pain
- Have trouble breathing
- Cough up a lot of blood

Find your nearest A&E at [nhs.uk/a-and-e](https://www.nhs.uk/a-and-e)

### Important safety tips for A&E

- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to take you or call 999 for an ambulance.
- Bring all your medicines with you.

## How to stop flu from spreading

Flu spreads easily.  
You can pass it on for the first 5 days of being sick.

Germs from coughs and sneezes can live on your hands and on surfaces for up to 24 hours.

To stop spreading flu:
- Wash your hands often with warm water and soap
- Cover your mouth and nose with a tissue when you cough or sneeze  
  (If you don’t have a tissue, cough or sneeze into the bend of your elbow, not your hand)
- Throw used tissues in the bin right away
- Stay at home and avoid others if you feel too unwell to do normal things

## Flu vaccine

The flu vaccine helps protect you from getting flu.  
It is safe and works well.

The NHS offers the flu vaccine every year in autumn or early winter to people at higher risk of serious illness.  
This includes some adults and children.  
Talk to your doctor or pharmacist to see if you are eligible.

# Lice

Lice are tiny insects that live on people. They can be found on the scalp, body, pubic area, or eyelashes.

There are three main types of lice:
- Head lice
- Body lice
- Pubic lice

Each type spreads in different ways:
- Head lice spread through close contact, like touching heads.
- Body lice spread in places that are crowded and dirty.
- Pubic lice spread through sexual contact.

The symptoms, signs, and treatment depend on where the lice are.

## What You Need to Know

- Head lice and pubic lice live directly on the skin.
- Body lice live in clothing and bedding, not on the skin.
- To confirm lice, you must see live lice or live eggs (nits).
- Head lice and pubic lice are treated with a special cream or lotion applied to the skin.
- A common treatment is a pyrethroid medicine.
- If the cream or lotion does not work, a doctor may prescribe a pill called ivermectin.
- Body lice are treated by cleaning clothes and bedding and by treating any skin irritation.

Lice are found all over the world. They do not spread disease, but they can cause itching and discomfort.

# Lichen Simplex Chronicus

Lichen simplex chronicus is a long-term skin problem. It causes intense itching. The itching gets worse when you scratch or rub the skin.

## What Causes It

You get this condition from scratching or rubbing your skin over and over. Scratching makes the skin itch more. That makes you want to scratch again. This creates a cycle that is hard to break.

Sometimes the scratching starts for no clear reason. Other times it begins because of another skin problem. But even after the original cause is gone, the itching may continue.

The nerves in your body may start to react more strongly to itching. This can make the problem worse.

This condition is more common in people who feel anxious or stressed. It also affects people who have eczema, hay fever, or asthma. These conditions make you more likely to feel itchy.

## Where It Happens

Lichen simplex chronicus can appear anywhere on the body. It often affects areas you can reach easily, such as:

- The upper chest  
- Arms  
- Neck  
- Legs  
- Genital area  

It rarely affects areas that are hard to reach, like the middle to upper back.

It can also affect the area around the anus (called pruritus ani) or the genitals (called genital itching).

## What It Looks Like

In the early stage, the skin looks normal. But it itches.

Over time, the skin becomes dry, flaky, thick, and darker. This change is called lichenification. The skin starts to feel tough and leathery.

Photo courtesy of Karen McKoy, MD.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors diagnose lichen simplex chronicus by:

- Looking at your skin  
- Asking about your symptoms and habits  
- Sometimes taking a small skin sample for testing (called a biopsy)  

If you have itching around the anus or genitals, the doctor may test for other possible causes, such as:

- Lichen planus  
- Pinworms  
- Trichomoniasis  
- Hemorrhoids  
- Vaginal discharge  
- Fungal infections  
- Warts  
- Contact dermatitis  
- Psoriasis  
- Lichen sclerosus  

## How It Is Treated

The goal is to stop the itching and break the cycle of scratching and rubbing.

### Treatments include:

- **Corticosteroid creams or ointments**  
  These reduce swelling and itching.  
  You can put a thick layer on the skin. Then cover it with plastic wrap and leave it on overnight. This helps the medicine work better.  
  Some special tapes are soaked in corticosteroids. They help reduce itching and protect the skin from scratching.  
  For small spots, a doctor may inject a long-lasting corticosteroid under the skin.

- **Antihistamines**  
  These are pills that help reduce itching. They are often taken at night to help you sleep.

- **Moisturizers (emollients)**  
  These keep the skin soft and less itchy.

- **Capsaicin cream**  
  This cream is made from chili peppers. It can help reduce itching over time.

### If a cause is found

If the doctor finds a reason for the itching, they will treat that cause. For example, if you have a fungal infection, they will give you medicine for that.

### Special care for the genital or anal area

When the problem is around the anus or genitals, the best treatment is a corticosteroid cream. It helps reduce swelling and itching quickly.

## Key Points

- Scratching makes the itching worse.  
- The skin becomes thick and leathery over time.  
- Treatment focuses on stopping the itch and breaking the cycle.  
- Avoid scratching or rubbing the skin.  
- Use medicine as directed by your doctor.  
- Keep the skin moisturized.  
- Seek help if the itching does not go away.

# Early or Premature Menopause

Menopause usually happens between the ages of 45 and 55.  
But if it happens before age 45, it is called early or premature menopause.  

It can happen on its own.  
It can also be caused by medical treatments like radiation therapy or surgery to remove the ovaries.  

## What Causes Early or Premature Menopause?

You are more likely to have early menopause if it runs in your family.  

Other things that increase your risk include:  
- Starting your periods at a young age  
- Smoking  
- Being underweight  

Certain medical treatments can also cause early menopause.  
These include:  
- Radiation therapy  
- Chemotherapy  
- Some hormone medicines  
- Surgery to remove the ovaries  

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main sign is not having regular periods.  
Or your periods may stop completely before you turn 45.  

Other common symptoms include:  
- Sudden hot flashes or night sweats  
- Dryness in the vagina  
- Trouble sleeping  
- Feeling low or anxious  
- Less interest in sex  
- Trouble remembering things or focusing  

## How Is It Treated?

The main treatments are medicines that replace the hormones your body is no longer making.  
These include the combined contraceptive pill or hormone replacement therapy.  

It is important to replace these hormones if you are under 45.  
This helps protect your bones and heart.  

But if you have had certain cancers, such as some types of breast cancer, you may not be able to take hormone treatments.  

You can also make lifestyle changes to feel better and stay healthy.  
These include:  
- Exercising regularly  
- Eating foods rich in calcium, like yoghurt and milk  

## What Problems Can It Cause?

Early menopause can lead to health problems later in life.  
You are more likely to get:  
- Weak bones (osteoporosis)  
- Heart disease  

It can also affect your mood and mental health.  
If you are struggling emotionally, help is available.  
You can get talking therapies through the NHS without needing to see a doctor first.  

## Fertility and Early Menopause

Early menopause means it may be harder to get pregnant.  
But you may still be able to have children.  

Options include:  
- Using your own frozen eggs in IVF  
- Using donor eggs in IVF  
- Surrogacy  
- Adoption  

## When to See a Doctor

See a doctor if you think you are having menopause symptoms.  

If you are under 45 and have these symptoms, your doctor may do blood tests to check your hormone levels.

# Ischemic Stroke

An ischemic stroke happens when blood flow to part of the brain stops suddenly. This causes brain cells to die. The damage is permanent and shows up on brain scans like MRI.

## What Causes an Ischemic Stroke?

The most common causes are:

- A blood clot blocking a large brain artery.
- A clot that travels from the heart to the brain (called an embolism).
- A small artery deep in the brain getting blocked (called a lacunar stroke).
- A narrowed artery combined with low blood pressure, which reduces blood flow to certain brain areas.

One-third of strokes have no clear cause. These are called cryptogenic strokes.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your symptoms and do a physical exam. They also do a brain scan to rule out bleeding and confirm a stroke. The scan shows where the damage is and how big it is.

## Risk Factors

Some things increase your risk of stroke. These can be changed:

- High blood pressure
- Smoking
- High cholesterol
- Diabetes
- Insulin resistance
- Belly fat
- Sleep apnea
- Drinking too much alcohol
- Not being active
- Eating a poor diet (high in bad fats and calories)
- Stress or depression
- Heart problems like irregular heartbeat, heart valve disease, or recent heart attack
- Narrowed carotid arteries in the neck
- Using drugs like cocaine or amphetamines
- Blood that clots too easily
- Inflammation of blood vessels
- Using birth control pills or hormone replacement therapy

Some risk factors cannot be changed:

- Having had a stroke before
- Being male or female
- Race or ethnicity
- Getting older
- Family history of stroke

## How Does a Stroke Damage the Brain?

The brain has backup blood vessels. These can help keep blood flowing if one artery is blocked. But if the backup system is weak or damaged, the brain can still be starved of blood.

Brain cells start to die if blood flow drops below 5% of normal for more than 5 minutes. If the blood flow is only slightly low, damage may take hours to happen. But if blood flow is very low for more than 15 to 30 minutes, all the brain tissue in that area dies.

Damage happens faster when you have a fever. It slows down if you are cold. If blood flow is restored quickly, some damaged brain tissue may survive.

The damage comes from:

- Swelling in the brain
- Tiny blood clots forming
- Cells dying on purpose (apoptosis)
- Cells dying from lack of oxygen (necrosis)
- Inflammation that causes more swelling and clots

Cells die because:

- They run out of energy
- Their internal balance is broken (especially calcium builds up)
- Free radicals damage cell membranes
- Harmful brain chemicals build up
- The brain becomes too acidic

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on which part of the brain is affected. They can appear suddenly or slowly.

### Common Stroke Patterns

| Stroke Type | Symptoms |
|-------------|----------|
| **Middle cerebral artery** | Weakness on one side of the body (worse in arm and face), trouble speaking, numbness, vision loss on one side, confusion |
| **Anterior cerebral artery** | Weakness in the leg, bladder control problems, confusion, poor judgment, not talking, trouble walking |
| **Posterior cerebral artery** | Vision loss in one or both eyes, memory problems, eye movement issues, jerky movements |
| **Ophthalmic artery** | Loss of vision in one eye |
| **Vertebrobasilar system** | Dizziness, trouble swallowing, slurred speech, double vision, balance problems, weakness on one side, confusion, coma |
| **Lacunar infarcts** | Pure weakness in one side of the body, numbness, unsteady walking, trouble with hand movements |

Some strokes get worse over time. This is called an evolving stroke. It can take 24 to 48 hours to reach full severity.

In most cases, symptoms get worse quickly—within minutes. This is common in embolic strokes.

In other cases, symptoms grow slowly. This is more common in atherothrombotic strokes.

A stroke is called submaximal if some function remains after it is done. This means some brain tissue is still at risk.

- Embolic strokes often happen during the day. Headache may come before symptoms.
- Thrombotic strokes often happen at night. People wake up with symptoms.

Lacunar strokes cause specific patterns like pure weakness or numbness. They do not cause confusion or speech problems.

Multiple small strokes can lead to memory loss and thinking problems (called multi-infarct dementia).

Seizures can happen at the start of a stroke, especially with embolic strokes. They can also happen months or years later due to scarring.

Fever can sometimes develop after a stroke.

## How Is It Treated?

### Immediate Treatment

- If the stroke is recent and safe, doctors may give medicine to dissolve the clot (like tPA or tenecteplase).
- In some cases, a doctor can remove the clot using a special device (mechanical thrombectomy).
- These treatments work best when done quickly—within hours of symptoms starting.

### Long-Term Treatment

- Surgery to open blocked neck arteries (carotid endarterectomy) or place a stent.
- Medicine to prevent new clots (antiplatelet drugs like aspirin).
- Medicine to prevent blood clots (anticoagulants) if needed.
- Control of risk factors: blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, weight, and lifestyle.

### Rehabilitation

After the stroke, physical therapy, speech therapy, and occupational therapy help you recover.

## Prognosis

How well you do after a stroke depends on how bad it was.

Doctors use the NIH Stroke Scale to measure how serious the stroke is. The score helps predict recovery.

- Mild stroke: Score 1–4
- Moderate stroke: Score 5–15
- Moderate to severe: Score 16–20
- Severe: Score 21–42

People with older age, low awareness, trouble speaking, or brain stem signs tend to do worse.

Those who are younger and improve early tend to do better.

- About half of people with moderate to severe weakness can care for themselves and walk.
- Most with mild symptoms recover well.
- Only about 10% have full recovery.
- Most lasting problems are permanent after 12 months.

After a stroke, the risk of another stroke is high. About 25% of people who recover from their first stroke have another one within 5 years.

About 20% of people die in the hospital after an ischemic stroke. The risk goes up with age.

## Key Points

- Stroke symptoms can look like other conditions. These include seizures, infections, migraines, and mental health issues.
- Some clues help tell the type of stroke:
  - Embolic strokes: Symptoms appear fast, often during the day.
  - Thrombotic strokes: Symptoms grow slowly, often noticed in the morning.
  - Lacunar strokes: Only cause weakness or numbness, no confusion or speech problems.
- Always check for heart problems (like irregular heartbeat) and narrowed neck arteries.
- Test blood for diabetes, high cholesterol, and clotting issues.
- Do not lower blood pressure too fast after a stroke unless needed.
- Use a checklist to decide if clot-busting medicine is safe.
- Act fast. The sooner treatment starts, the better the chance to save brain tissue.
- Prevent future strokes by managing risk factors and using medicine like aspirin, statins, or surgery if needed.

# Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms

## What Is an Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm?

An abdominal aortic aneurysm is a bulge in the wall of the aorta. The aorta is the main blood vessel that carries blood from the heart to the rest of the body. This bulge happens in the part of the aorta that runs through the belly.

The aneurysm can grow slowly over time. In some cases, it can burst open. When it bursts, it can cause life-threatening bleeding.

## Who Is at Risk?

Abdominal aortic aneurysms are most common in older men. Smoking greatly increases the risk. High blood pressure also raises the risk, especially if you smoke.

Some people inherit a tendency to develop aneurysms. If a close family member has had one, you may be more likely to get one.

The most common cause is atherosclerosis. This is when fatty deposits build up in the artery walls. This weakens the wall over time.

Other causes include infections in the aorta. These can come from heart infections or serious body-wide infections. Inflammation of blood vessels can also weaken the aorta.

## Symptoms

Many people with an abdominal aortic aneurysm have no symptoms at all. The aneurysm may be found by chance during a test done for another reason.

Some people feel a pulsing in their belly. This is like a strong heartbeat in the middle of the abdomen.

If the aneurysm is leaking or growing, it can cause deep, constant pain. The pain may be in the belly, back, or sides. It can be very severe.

If the aneurysm bursts, the pain is sudden and extreme. You may also feel dizzy, weak, or faint. Your blood pressure may drop quickly. This can lead to shock. A burst aneurysm is often deadly. It is always fatal if not treated right away.

> **Did You Know:** Small aneurysms rarely burst.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors often find aneurysms during routine tests. You may not have any symptoms.

A doctor may feel a pulsing lump in your belly. They may also hear a whooshing sound with a stethoscope. This sound comes from blood rushing through the aneurysm.

An ultrasound scan is the most common test. It uses sound waves to show the size and shape of the aneurysm. It is safe and does not use radiation.

A CT scan gives a more detailed picture. It can show the exact size and shape. It may use a special dye injected into a vein. But it does use radiation.

An MRI scan can also show the aneurysm clearly. But it may not be available as quickly as ultrasound or CT.

An abdominal X-ray may show calcium in the aneurysm wall. But it does not give much detail.

Doctors may repeat scans every few months. This helps track how fast the aneurysm is growing.

> **Screening is recommended** for some men over 65 who have smoked or have a family history of aneurysms. Even if you feel fine, a simple ultrasound can catch an aneurysm early.

## Treatment

Small aneurysms (less than 2 inches wide) rarely burst. You may not need surgery. But you will need regular checkups.

Your doctor may prescribe medicines to lower your blood pressure. You may also take medicine to lower cholesterol. Aspirin may help reduce the risk of blood clots.

Quitting smoking is the most important step. It slows the growth of the aneurysm and lowers the risk of rupture.

If the aneurysm is larger than 2 to 2.5 inches wide, your doctor will likely recommend repair. This is because larger aneurysms are more likely to burst.

For people with Marfan syndrome, aneurysms can burst at smaller sizes. So repair may be needed when the aneurysm is about 1.5 inches wide.

> **Did You Know:** You can live with a small aneurysm. But treatment is usually needed once it reaches a certain size.

### Repair Options

There are two main ways to repair an aneurysm:

1. **Traditional surgery**
2. **Endovascular stent graft repair**

#### Traditional Surgery

You will be asleep under general anesthesia. The surgeon makes a cut from below the breastbone to just below the belly button.

The damaged part of the aorta is removed. A synthetic tube (called a graft) is sewn in place. The graft takes over the job of carrying blood.

The cut is then closed. Recovery takes several weeks. You may need to stay in the hospital for a week or more.

This method is often used for younger, healthier people. The results can last a long time.

#### Endovascular Stent Graft Repair

This is a less invasive option. You stay awake but feel no pain. A regional anesthetic numbs your body from the waist down.

A thin tube (catheter) is guided through a blood vessel in the groin. It is moved up to the aneurysm.

Inside the catheter is a stent graft. It looks like a collapsible, mesh tube. Once in place, it is opened. It forms a new path for blood flow.

The aneurysm is now sealed off. Blood flows through the stent, not the weak spot.

This method has a faster recovery. It is often used for older adults or people in poor health.

### Choosing the Right Treatment

Your doctor will consider your age, health, and the shape of your aorta. They will also look at how fast the aneurysm is growing.

- Open surgery is often best for younger, healthier people.
- Endovascular repair is often better for older or sicker people.

### Emergency Repair

If the aneurysm bursts or is about to burst, you need emergency treatment.

You will need surgery right away. This is a life-threatening emergency.

The risk of death during emergency surgery is about 50%.

Endovascular stent graft repair has a lower risk. The death rate is about 20 to 30%.

If the aneurysm bursts, the kidneys may be damaged. This is because blood flow to the kidneys is cut off. Or because of low blood pressure from shock.

If kidney failure happens after repair, survival chances are very low.

> **Key Point:** Early detection and treatment can save your life. If you are at risk, talk to your doctor about screening.

# Cholera

Cholera is a serious illness caused by bacteria.  
It spreads through dirty water and food that has been in dirty water.  
You can also get it from food handled by someone who is infected.

## How to Reduce Your Risk

Wash your hands often with soap and water.  
Only drink bottled water or water that has been boiled.  
Do not drink tap water unless you know it is safe.

## Symptoms of Cholera

You may have very watery diarrhoea.  
You may feel sick or be sick.  
You may have tummy pain.  
You may also become dehydrated.  
Dehydration means your body has lost too much fluid.  
Signs of dehydration include feeling very thirsty or having dark yellow, strong-smelling urine.

## When to See a Doctor

See a doctor if you have been in an area where cholera is common and you have:  
- severe watery diarrhoea and vomiting  
- signs of dehydration, like being very thirsty or having dark yellow urine  

Tell the doctor if you have recently been in a place where cholera is found.  
You may need treatment to prevent dangerous dehydration.

## Where Cholera Is Found

Cholera is not found in the UK.  
It mainly occurs in parts of Africa and Asia.  
It is more common in places without clean water and proper sanitation.

You can get cholera from:  
- drinking dirty water  
- eating food, especially shellfish, that has been in dirty water  
- eating food that someone who is infected has touched

The chance of getting cholera while travelling is very low.

## How to Stay Safe When Travelling

### Do

- Wash your hands with soap and water often.  
  Do this after using the toilet and before preparing or eating food.  
- Drink only bottled water or boiled tap water.  
- Use bottled or boiled water to brush your teeth.

### Don’t

- Do not eat raw fruits or vegetables unless you have washed them yourself with clean water.  
- Do not eat shellfish or other seafood.  
- Do not have ice in your drinks.

## Cholera Vaccine

There is a vaccine for cholera, but most people do not need it.  
It is usually only recommended if:  
- you are going to a place where cholera is common and you will be in remote areas without medical care  
- you are working in aid or disaster relief in a place where a cholera outbreak is likely

The vaccine comes as a drink.  
Adults need two doses.  
The doses are given 1 to 6 weeks apart.  
Protection lasts up to 2 years.

You must have both doses at least one week before you travel.

## Getting the Vaccine

You may be able to get the cholera vaccine for free on the NHS.  
Ask your GP surgery if you need it.

## Treating Cholera

The main treatment is drinking plenty of fluids.  
This includes rehydration solution.  

Rehydration solution is a powder you mix with water.  
It helps replace the salts, sugars, and minerals lost through diarrhoea.  
You can buy it at most pharmacies.

If you are very ill, you may need hospital care.  
In hospital, you may get:  
- fluids through a tube in your vein  
- antibiotics to help fight the infection

# Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Vaccine

## What is HPV?

Human papillomavirus, or HPV, is the most common sexually transmitted infection.  
It can cause skin warts.  
It can also cause genital warts.  
Some types of HPV can lead to certain cancers.  
The type of HPV matters.  
Different types cause different health problems.

## How Does the HPV Vaccine Work?

The HPV vaccine helps prevent infection with certain types of HPV.  
It is very effective at stopping the most dangerous types.  
It protects against the types that cause most cases of genital warts and cervical cancer.  
The vaccine does not protect against all types of HPV.  
So, you still need regular Pap tests.  
Pap tests can find early signs of cervical cancer.  
The vaccine gives long-lasting protection.  
Most people who get the vaccine stay protected for many years.

## Types of HPV Vaccines

There are three types of HPV vaccines.  
Only one is available in the United States: the 9-valent vaccine.

### 9-Valent HPV Vaccine (9vHPV)
- Protects against HPV types 6 and 11.  
  These cause more than 90% of visible genital warts.  
- Protects against HPV types 16 and 18.  
  These cause about 70% of cervical cancers.  
  They also cause about 90% of anal cancers.  
- Protects against types 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58.  
  These together cause 10% to 20% of cervical cancers.

### Quadrivalent HPV Vaccine (4vHPV)
- Protects against types 6, 11, 16, and 18.

### Bivalent HPV Vaccine (2vHPV)
- Protects against types 16 and 18.

The 9-valent vaccine is the only one used in the United States.

The vaccine is made using a special method.  
It uses a protein from the outer shell of the HPV virus.  
This protein is not harmful.  
It cannot cause infection or cancer.  
The body uses this protein to learn how to fight HPV.  
The protein forms tiny particles that look like the real virus.  
But they are not real viruses.  
They are called virus-like particles.

## Who Should Get the HPV Vaccine?

The HPV vaccine is a routine shot for children.  
It is recommended for both boys and girls.

### For Children and Teens (Ages 9 to 26)
- Give the vaccine at age 11 or 12.  
- You can start as early as age 9 if a child has been sexually abused or assaulted.  
- The vaccine is also recommended for anyone up to age 26 who has not been fully vaccinated.

### For Adults (Ages 27 to 45)
- The vaccine is not routine for adults.  
- Doctors should talk with patients about whether it is right for them.  
- This is called shared decision-making.  
- The decision should be based on personal health, risk, and lifestyle.

Outside the United States, other vaccines may be used:
- For girls: 4vHPV or 2vHPV
- For boys: 4vHPV, including those who have sex with men

## Who Should Not Get the HPV Vaccine?

You should not get the HPV vaccine if you:
- Had a serious allergic reaction (like anaphylaxis) to a previous dose.  
- Are allergic to yeast.  
- Are pregnant.

If you are pregnant, do not get the vaccine.  
But you do not need a pregnancy test before getting the shot.  
If you find out you are pregnant after starting the series, stop the shots.  
Wait until after your pregnancy to finish the series.

## When to Wait Before Getting the Vaccine

Do not get the vaccine if you are very sick with a fever or other serious illness.  
Wait until you feel better.  
This is the main caution.

## How Is the Vaccine Given?

The vaccine is given as a shot into the muscle.  
Each dose is 0.5 milliliters.

### For Children and Teens (Ages 9 to 14)
- Two doses are needed.  
- First dose at age 9 to 14.  
- Second dose 6 to 12 months later.  
- The minimum time between doses is 5 months.  
- If the second dose is given too soon (less than 5 months after the first), a third dose is needed.

### For Teens and Adults (Age 15 and Older)
- Three doses are needed.  
- First dose at age 15 or older.  
- Second dose 1 to 2 months after the first.  
- Third dose 6 months after the first.  
- Minimum time between first and second dose: 4 weeks.  
- Minimum time between second and third dose: 12 weeks.  
- Minimum time between first and third dose: 5 months.  
- If a dose is given too soon, it must be repeated.

### For Adults Aged 27 to 45
- If you started the vaccine series as a child (age 9 to 14), you can finish with two doses.  
- If you started at age 15 or older, you need three doses.  
- This depends on your age when you started and your doctor’s advice.

### For People with Weakened Immune Systems
- This includes people with HIV.  
- They must get the 3-dose series.  
- This is true no matter their age when they start.

## Side Effects of the HPV Vaccine

Most people have no serious side effects.  
Common side effects include:
- Pain, swelling, redness, itching, or bruising at the injection site.  
- Fever.  
- Nausea.  
- Dizziness.

These side effects are usually mild.  
They go away in a few days.  
If you have concerns, talk to your doctor.

The following resources are in English and may help you learn more.  
The Manual is not responsible for the content of these websites.

- **Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP):**  
  ACIP Recommendations: Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Vaccine

- **Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC):**  
  HPV (Human Papillomavirus)

# Hiatus Hernia

A hiatus hernia happens when part of the stomach pushes up through a hole in the diaphragm.

The diaphragm is the muscle that separates your chest from your belly. The esophagus, the tube that carries food from your throat to your stomach, normally passes through a small opening in the diaphragm called the hiatus.

When part of the stomach bulges through this opening, it is called a hiatus hernia.

---

## What Causes a Hiatus Hernia?

Doctors do not always know why a hiatus hernia happens. But it is more common in people who:

- Are over 50 years old  
- Are overweight, especially women  
- Smoke  

It may also happen if the tissues that hold the esophagus in place stretch or weaken.

Some people are born with a diaphragm that has a larger opening. This can lead to a hernia. Injuries to the chest or belly can also cause a hernia.

---

## Types of Hiatus Hernia

There are two main types:

### 1. Sliding Hiatus Hernia (Most Common)

- The part where the esophagus meets the stomach, and some of the stomach, move up through the diaphragm.
- This is the most common type.
- More than 40 out of 100 people in the United States have this type.
- It becomes more common as people get older, especially after age 60.

### 2. Paraesophageal Hiatus Hernia

- The place where the esophagus meets the stomach stays in its normal spot below the diaphragm.
- But part of the stomach pushes up through the diaphragm and sits next to the esophagus.

---

## Symptoms of Hiatus Hernia

### Sliding Hiatus Hernia

- Most people have no symptoms.
- If symptoms do occur, they are usually mild.
- They often include heartburn or indigestion, especially when lying down after eating.
- Leaning forward, straining, lifting heavy things, or being pregnant can make symptoms worse.
- Less than half of people with a hiatus hernia have acid reflux.

### Paraesophageal Hiatus Hernia

- Often causes no symptoms.
- But it can get stuck or squeezed by the diaphragm.
- This can cut off blood flow to the stomach. This is a serious and painful problem called strangulation.
- It needs emergency surgery.
- Symptoms may include:
  - Chest pain
  - Bloating
  - Burping
  - Trouble swallowing

### Rare Symptoms

- Small or large bleeding from the lining of the hernia can happen in either type.
- This may cause black or bloody stools or vomiting blood.

---

## How Is a Hiatus Hernia Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find a hiatus hernia:

- **Chest x-ray** – Can show a large hernia.
- **Barium swallow x-ray** – You drink a liquid that contains barium. It coats the inside of your esophagus and stomach. This makes any problems easier to see on x-rays.
- **Upper endoscopy** – A doctor uses a thin, flexible tube with a camera (called an endoscope) to look inside your esophagus and stomach.

---

## How Is a Hiatus Hernia Treated?

### For Sliding Hiatus Hernia

- If you have no symptoms, no treatment is needed.
- If you have reflux symptoms, your doctor may prescribe a medicine called a proton pump inhibitor. This medicine lowers the amount of acid in your stomach.
- Other helpful steps include:
  - Raise the head of your bed when sleeping.
  - Eat smaller meals.
  - Lose extra weight.
  - Stop smoking.
  - Do not lie down or exercise right after eating.
  - Avoid tight clothes.
  - Limit or avoid:
    - Citrus juices (like orange juice)
    - Colas and other sodas
    - Alcohol
    - Coffee and other caffeinated drinks
    - Spicy foods
    - Acidic foods
    - Fatty foods

### For Paraesophageal Hiatus Hernia

- If it causes symptoms, surgery is usually needed.
- The goal is to prevent strangulation.
- Surgery can be done in two ways:
  - **Laparoscopic surgery** – Small cuts in the belly. A camera and thin tools are used.
  - **Thoracoscopic surgery** – Small cuts in the chest. A camera and thin tools are used.
  - In some cases, a full open surgery is needed.

Surgery helps return the stomach to its normal position and strengthens the area around the hiatus to prevent it from happening again.

# Lichen Planus

Lichen planus is a skin and mouth condition. It can cause rashes, sores, and other changes in your body. It is not contagious. Most people get better over time, and it usually does not come back.

## Symptoms of Lichen Planus

You may have one or more of these symptoms:

- Small, raised, shiny, purple-red spots on your arms, legs, or body.  
  - You might see thin white lines on the spots.  
  - The rash can be harder to see on dark skin.

- White patches inside your mouth.  
  - These can appear on your gums, tongue, or the inside of your cheeks.

- A burning or stinging feeling in your mouth.  
  - This often gets worse when you eat or drink.

- Bald patches on your scalp.  
  - The hair may fall out in small areas.

- Red, sore patches on your vulva.  
  - This can be painful or itchy.

- Nails that become rough, thin, or have grooves in them.

- Ring-shaped purple or white patches on your penis.

Your skin rash may be very itchy. But it does not always itch.

## Treatments for Lichen Planus

Most skin cases get better on their own in 9 to 18 months.

Your doctor may give you creams or ointments to help with the rash and itching.

If the creams do not help, or if your condition is severe, your doctor may suggest:

- Steroid tablets to reduce swelling and inflammation.  
- Light therapy. This uses a special kind of light to treat the skin.

Mouth lichen planus can last for years.  
Your doctor may give you mouthwashes or sprays to ease pain and burning.

You cannot pass lichen planus to someone else.  
It usually does not return after it clears up.

## How to Help Ease Lichen Planus at Home

You can take steps at home to feel better. The steps depend on where the lichen planus is.

### Lichen Planus on the Skin

- Wash with warm water only.  
  - Do not use soaps or body washes.  
  - These can make the rash worse.

- Wash your hair over a sink or in the bath.  
  - This keeps shampoo from touching your skin.

- Use a moisturizer (emollient) on the rash.  
  - Your doctor may prescribe this.

- Try not to scratch your skin.  
  - Scratching can make the rash worse and cause scars.

### Lichen Planus on the Genitals

- Take showers instead of baths.  
  - Baths can make the area more irritated.

- Use a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a clean towel.  
  - Hold it on the area to reduce itching and swelling.

- Wear loose clothes.  
  - Avoid tights or tight underwear.

- Dry yourself carefully after using the toilet.  
  - Do not rub the area.  
  - This helps prevent urine from irritating the skin.

- Use a lubricant during sex if it hurts.  
  - This can make sex more comfortable.

### Lichen Planus in the Mouth

- Avoid salty, spicy, or acidic foods.  
  - Also avoid alcohol if they make your mouth sore.

- Brush your teeth gently twice a day.  
  - This keeps your gums healthy.

- Use a mouthwash that does not have alcohol.  
  - Alcohol can make mouth sores worse.

# Erysipeloid

Erysipeloid is a skin infection caused by a type of bacteria called *Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae*.  
This bacteria lives in animals like fish, shellfish, birds, pigs, and insects.  
It can spread to people through cuts or scratches when handling animals or animal products.

## How the Infection Happens

The bacteria enter the body through a break in the skin.  
This often happens when someone handles raw meat, fish, or shellfish.  
It can also happen in slaughterhouses or when working with animal bones or shells.  
Bites from cats or dogs can also cause the infection.

The bacteria can hide inside the body’s immune cells.  
This helps it avoid being destroyed by the body’s defenses.  
It can then spread to other parts of the body, though this is rare.

## What the Infection Looks Like

### Local Skin Infection (Most Common)
- A red, raised, hard rash appears within one week of injury.  
- The rash is usually on the hand, but can be on other parts of the body.  
- It starts as a small bump and slowly grows larger.  
- The skin turns purple or dark red.  
- It may itch or burn.  
- The edges of the rash spread slowly over time.  
- Swelling is sharp and clear at the edges.  
- The hand may become stiff and hard to use.  
- The rash can last up to three weeks.  
- About one in three people also get swollen lymph nodes or red streaks in the skin (lymphangitis).

### Widespread Skin Infection (Rare)
- The rash spreads over large areas of the body.  
- The center of the rash may clear while the edges grow outward.  
- Blisters may form on the skin.  
- Red streaks may appear in the skin.  
- Most people do not have fever or other general symptoms.

### Serious Infection (Rare)
- The bacteria can enter the bloodstream.  
- This can lead to joint infections (septic arthritis) or heart infections (infective endocarditis).  
- The heart infection often affects the aortic valve.  
- It can be life-threatening.  
- People without known heart problems can still get this infection.  
- Infections in the brain, abdomen, or bones are very rare.

## How It Is Diagnosed

- A doctor takes a small sample of skin from the edge of the rash.  
- This sample is sent to a lab to grow the bacteria.  
- A full-thickness skin sample works better than a needle poke.  
- A swab from a raised bump may also help.  
- For joint or heart infections, samples from the joint fluid or blood are needed.  
- Blood tests often do not show the bacteria.  
- The bacteria can be mistaken for other bacteria in the lab.  
- A special test called PCR can quickly detect the bacteria.  
- This test is very helpful if heart infection is suspected.

## How It Is Treated

### For Mild Skin Infection
- Antibiotics are used for 7 to 10 days.  
- Options include:
  - Penicillin V or ampicillin (500 mg by mouth every 6 hours)  
  - Amoxicillin (500 mg by mouth every 8 hours)  
  - Ciprofloxacin (250 mg by mouth every 12 hours)  
  - Clindamycin (300 mg by mouth every 8 hours)  
- Cephalosporins are also effective.  
- If you are very allergic to penicillin, other options like daptomycin or linezolid may be used.  
- Tetracyclines and macrolides are not reliable anymore.

### For Severe Skin or Body-Wide Infection
- Stronger antibiotics are given through a vein.  
- Options include:
  - Penicillin G (2 to 3 million units IV every 4 hours)  
  - Ceftriaxone (2 grams IV once a day)  
  - A fluoroquinolone like ciprofloxacin (400 mg IV every 12 hours) or levofloxacin (500 mg IV once a day)

### For Heart Infection (Endocarditis)
- Penicillin G is the best choice.  
- Treatment lasts 4 to 6 weeks.  
- Cephalosporins or fluoroquinolones can be used if needed.  
- **Important:** The bacteria is resistant to vancomycin.  
- Vancomycin is often used for other similar infections, but it will not work here.  
- Fast testing is needed to avoid using the wrong medicine.

### For Joint Infection (Arthritis)
- Same antibiotics and doses as for heart infection.  
- Treatment lasts at least one week after fever goes away or fluid stops building up.  
- The infected joint may need to be drained with a needle.

## Key Facts

- Erysipeloid usually starts from a cut or scratch when handling animals or animal products.  
- It often happens in people who work with fish, shellfish, or raw meat.  
- A red, hard, purple rash appears on the skin within a week.  
- It may itch or burn.  
- About one-third of people also have swollen lymph nodes or red streaks.  
- Bloodstream infection is rare but can lead to joint or heart problems.  
- Diagnosis is best done by growing the bacteria from a skin sample.  
- If heart infection is suspected, fast testing is critical.  
- The bacteria is resistant to vancomycin.  
- Treatment depends on the location and severity of the infection.  
- Penicillin, ciprofloxacin, and other antibiotics are effective.

# Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)

BPPV is a common condition that causes brief spells of dizziness.  
It happens when you move your head in certain ways.  
The dizziness feels like you or your surroundings are spinning.  
This is not dangerous, but it can be very unsettling.

## What Happens in BPPV?

- Tiny calcium particles in your inner ear move out of place.
- These particles end up in a part of the ear that controls balance.
- When you move your head, the particles shift and send wrong signals to your brain.
- Your brain thinks you are moving when you are not.
- This causes a sudden feeling of spinning or dizziness.

The inner ear has three loops that help you stay balanced.  
The back loop is most likely to get affected.  
The particles collect and act like a sludge.  
They make the fluid in the loop move too much.  
This overstimulates the nerves in the ear.  
The result is a false sense of motion.

## Who Gets BPPV?

- BPPV is more common as people get older.
- It can make balance worse in older adults.
- Poor balance can lead to falls and injuries.
- Sometimes BPPV starts after a head injury.

## What Causes BPPV?

Most cases happen after a change in head position.  
For example:
- Turning your head while getting out of bed.
- Lying down or rolling over in bed.
- Looking up to reach something high.

The calcium particles may move out of place because of:
- Normal aging
- Ear infections
- Head or ear injury
- Being in bed for a long time
- Ear surgery

Some people with BPPV also have other health problems, such as:
- Other inner ear issues (like Meniere disease)
- Blocked blood flow to the inner ear
- A tumor in the brain or spinal cord

## What Are the Symptoms?

- Sudden dizziness that lasts only seconds to a few minutes.
- The dizziness happens when you move your head.
- You may feel sick to your stomach or throw up.
- Your eyes may jerk quickly in one direction, then slowly drift back.
- This eye movement is called nystagmus.
- You do not lose your hearing.
- You do not hear ringing in your ears.

The dizziness can come and go over days or weeks.  
It often gets better on its own.  
But it can be scary.  
It may cause falls if it happens while you are walking, driving, or doing other activities.

## How Is BPPV Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose BPPV based on:
- Your symptoms
- When the dizziness happens
- A physical exam

The most common test is the Dix-Hallpike maneuver.  
Here’s how it works:
- You sit on a table with your head turned 45 degrees to one side.
- You lie back quickly, keeping your head turned and hanging slightly over the edge.
- You wait 5 to 10 seconds (sometimes up to 30 seconds).
- If you have BPPV, dizziness and eye jerking will start.
- The dizziness lasts 10 to 30 seconds, then fades.
- If you repeat the test, the dizziness gets weaker each time.

This fading is called fatigue or habituation.  
It helps doctors tell BPPV from more serious brain problems.

If the doctor is unsure, they may order imaging tests.  
For example, a special MRI scan with contrast dye.  
This helps rule out serious causes like stroke or a brain tumor.

## How Is BPPV Treated?

Most people get better with simple head movements.  
Medicines are not usually helpful.  
They can even make symptoms worse.

### The Epley Maneuver

This is the most common treatment.  
It moves the loose particles out of the balance canal.  
It works in about 90 out of 100 people.

How it works:
- You sit on a table.
- Your head is turned to one side.
- You lie back quickly, keeping your head turned.
- You hold this position for about 30 seconds.
- You turn your head to the other side and hold it for 30 seconds.
- You roll onto your side and stay there for 30 seconds.
- You sit up slowly.

After the move, you should stay upright or half-upright for 1 to 2 days.  
This helps keep the particles in the right place.

To check if it worked:
- Try the head movement that caused dizziness before.
- If you feel no dizziness, the move worked.

If symptoms come back, repeat the maneuver.  
You can learn to do it at home.

### Brandt-Daroff Exercise

This is another safe way to treat BPPV at home.

How to do it:
- Sit up straight.
- Turn your head 45 degrees to one side.
- Lie down on your side, keeping your head turned.
- Stay in this position for 30 seconds or until dizziness stops.
- Sit up again.
- Repeat on the other side.
- Do 5 cycles on each side.
- Repeat 3 times a day for about 2 weeks.

Do this until the dizziness stops when you do the exercise.

### Other Cases

Sometimes the side canal, not the back canal, is affected.  
In these cases, rolling your body like a log can help relieve symptoms.

### When Treatment Doesn’t Work

If the head moves do not help, your doctor will look for other causes.  
These could be serious conditions that need different treatment.

Surgery is very rare.  
It is only considered if all other treatments fail.

# Measles

Measles starts with cold-like symptoms. A rash appears a few days later. The rash begins on the face and behind the ears. It then spreads to the rest of the body.

See your doctor if you or your child might have measles. Rest, drink plenty of water, and take painkillers to feel better.

Measles can cause serious health problems. These include pneumonia and meningitis. It can also harm your baby if you get measles while pregnant.

The MMR vaccine gives lifelong protection against measles, mumps, and rubella. Ask your doctor if you or your child have had the vaccine.

---

## When to Seek Help Right Away

Call your doctor or NHS 111 if you or your child:

- Think you have measles  
- Are under 1 year old and have been near someone with measles  
- Are pregnant or have a weak immune system and have been near someone with measles  
- Have not had measles or two doses of the MMR vaccine and have been near someone with measles  
- Have a high temperature that does not go down after taking paracetamol or ibuprofen  
- Are having trouble breathing – you feel more out of breath than usual  
- Your baby or young child is not feeding well or is drinking less than usual  
- You or your child are peeing less than normal (or your baby has fewer wet nappies)  
- You or your child feel very unwell or you are worried something is seriously wrong  

Measles spreads easily. Call your doctor before going in. They may want to talk to you on the phone. Or they may ask you to come to a special area of the clinic.

You can also call 111 or get help online.

---

## When to Go to A&E (Emergency Department)

Go to A&E or call 999 if you or your child has measles and:

- Has a seizure (fit)  
- Is having severe trouble breathing – gasping, choking, or unable to speak (babies may grunt or their stomach pulls in under the ribs)  
- Cannot stay awake – eyes stay closed for more than a few seconds  
- Suddenly becomes confused – your child is very upset, acts differently, or cries non-stop  
- Your child is limp, floppy, or not responding normally – head may fall to the side, back, or front, or they struggle to lift their head or look at your face  
- Has a rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it  
- Has a stiff neck or finds light painful or uncomfortable  

---

### A&E Safety Tips

Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you. Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring all your medicines with you.

---

## Symptoms of Measles

Measles starts with cold-like symptoms. A rash appears a few days later. Some people also get small spots in their mouth.

### Cold-Like Symptoms

Early signs of measles include:

- A high temperature  
- A runny or blocked nose  
- Sneezing  
- A cough  
- Red, sore, watery eyes  

### Spots in the Mouth

Small white spots may appear inside the cheeks and on the back of the lips a few days after the first symptoms. These spots last a few days.

### The Measles Rash

The rash usually appears a few days after the cold-like symptoms.

It starts on the face and behind the ears. Then it spreads to the rest of the body.

The rash spots may be raised. They can join together to form large, blotchy patches. The rash is not usually itchy.

On white skin, the rash looks red or brown. It may be harder to see on brown or black skin.

---

## How to Care for Yourself or Your Child

Measles usually starts to get better in about a week.

After seeing your doctor, you can do these things to feel better and stop spreading the virus:

- Rest and drink plenty of fluids like water to avoid dehydration  
- Give your child paracetamol for children or ibuprofen for children if they are in pain or upset – check the label or leaflet to make sure it is safe for your child. Ask a pharmacist or doctor if you are unsure  
- Adults can take paracetamol or ibuprofen for a high temperature  
- Use cotton wool soaked in cooled boiled water to gently clean crusts from your eyes or your child’s eyes  

### Important

Stay away from nursery, school, or work for at least 4 days after the rash first appears.

Avoid close contact with babies, pregnant people, or anyone with a weak immune system.

---

## Possible Complications

Measles can cause serious health problems if it spreads to the lungs or brain.

These problems include:

- Pneumonia (infection in the lungs)  
- Meningitis (infection in the lining of the brain and spinal cord)  
- Blindness  
- Seizures (fits)  

These problems are rare. But babies and people with weak immune systems are more at risk.

---

### Measles During Pregnancy

If you get measles while pregnant, it can harm your baby.

It may cause:

- Miscarriage or stillbirth  
- Premature birth (before 37 weeks of pregnancy)  
- Your baby being born with a low birthweight  

If you are pregnant and have been near someone with measles, get medical advice right away.

---

## Get the MMR Vaccine

The MMR vaccine prevents measles. It also protects against mumps and rubella.

The MMR vaccine is offered to all children in the UK. Two doses give lifelong protection.

Ask your GP surgery if you are not sure you or your child have had the vaccine. It is free on the NHS.

# Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA)

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a serious condition that causes inflammation in small and medium-sized blood vessels. This inflammation can damage organs. The most commonly affected organs are the kidneys, nose, and lungs. But any organ can be involved.

The disease often starts with problems in the nose or lungs. Later, kidney problems may appear. Some people have symptoms in many organs at the same time.

Symptoms depend on which organs are affected. They can come on slowly or suddenly. The full picture of the disease may take years to develop.

## What Causes GPA?

The exact cause is not known. But the body’s immune system seems to play a role. Most people with active disease have a certain kind of antibody in their blood called ANCA.

## How Does GPA Affect the Body?

In the nose, the lining becomes inflamed. It may look bumpy and break easily. Sores, thick crusts, and holes in the nose can form. The nose may become weak and collapse (called saddle nose).

In the lungs, inflammation can cause nodules, holes in the lung tissue, or bleeding. This can lead to coughing up blood, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

In the kidneys, the tiny filters become inflamed. This can cause blood and protein in the urine. Swelling and high blood pressure may develop. In severe cases, kidney failure can happen quickly.

Other organs can also be affected. These include the ears, eyes, skin, nerves, heart, and joints.

## What Are the Symptoms?

### Nose and Sinuses
- Frequent nosebleeds
- Thick, yellow or bloody discharge
- Pain in the sinuses
- Recurrent sinus infections that do not get better with antibiotics
- A hole in the septum (the wall between the nostrils)
- A weak or collapsed nose (saddle nose)

### Ears
- Ear infections
- Hearing loss
- Dizziness
- Pain in the ear

### Eyes
- Red, swollen eyes
- Pain or vision problems
- Inflammation of the tear ducts, eye lining, or deeper eye tissues
- Swelling behind the eye (can press on the optic nerve and cause blindness)
- Double vision

### Lungs
- Cough
- Chest pain
- Shortness of breath
- Coughing up blood
- Nodules or holes in the lung tissue

### Kidneys
- Swelling in the legs or face
- High blood pressure
- Blood or protein in the urine
- Rapid loss of kidney function (called rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis)

### Skin
- Purple spots (purpura)
- Tender lumps under the skin
- Sores or ulcers
- A mottled skin pattern (livedo reticularis)

### Nerves
- Numbness, tingling, or weakness in the arms or legs
- Pain in the limbs
- Weakness in muscles (especially if multiple nerves are involved)

### Other Organs
- Rarely, lumps can form in the breast, prostate, or other organs.

## How Is GPA Diagnosed?

Diagnosis is not always easy. Doctors look for signs in the nose, lungs, kidneys, and blood.

### Tests That Help
- **Blood tests**: Check for signs of inflammation and kidney function.
- **Urine test**: Looks for blood or protein in the urine.
- **Antibody test (ANCA)**: Most people with active GPA have a specific antibody in their blood.
- **Imaging**: CT scans of the chest and sinuses can show damage in the lungs and nose.
- **Biopsy**: A small sample of tissue is taken from an affected organ. This is the best way to confirm the diagnosis.

A biopsy of the nose rarely gives a clear answer. A lung or kidney biopsy is more likely to show the disease.

### Important Notes
- A positive ANCA test does not always mean you have GPA. Some people with other diseases also test positive.
- ANCA testing should only be done if the doctor suspects GPA based on symptoms.
- A positive ANCA test does not rule out infections like tuberculosis or fungal infections. These must still be checked for.

## How Is GPA Treated?

Treatment depends on how severe the disease is.

### For Severe Cases
These include life-threatening problems like lung bleeding, rapid kidney failure, or serious nerve damage.

- Hospital care is needed right away.
- High-dose corticosteroids are used to reduce inflammation.
- Another medicine is added: either **rituximab** or **cyclophosphamide**.
- Rituximab is usually preferred because it has fewer serious side effects than cyclophosphamide.
- After 3 to 6 months, cyclophosphamide is stopped and replaced with a safer medicine like methotrexate or azathioprine.
- Avacopan may be used to help reduce the dose of corticosteroids.
- Plasma exchange (removing blood and filtering it) is not proven to help and is not usually needed.

### For Less Severe Cases
- Corticosteroids and methotrexate are used to start treatment.
- Rituximab can be used instead of methotrexate.
- The corticosteroid dose is slowly lowered and may be stopped.

### To Keep the Disease in Check (Maintenance)
- Rituximab is very effective at preventing relapses.
- Other options include methotrexate, azathioprine, or mycophenolate mofetil.
- Some people need to stay on treatment for years or even for life.
- A low dose of corticosteroid may be used to help prevent flares.

### Special Treatments
- **Sinus irrigation** with salt water helps reduce crusts and infections.
- **Mupirocin nasal ointment** may be used to prevent staph infections.
- **Subglottic stenosis** (narrowing of the voice box) is hard to treat. Injections of corticosteroids and gentle stretching can help avoid surgery.

### Kidney Transplant
- Kidney transplants can work well for people with kidney failure.
- The risk of GPA coming back after transplant is lower than with dialysis.

## What Is the Outlook?

- With treatment, about 80% of people go into remission.
- But about half of them will have a relapse later.
- Relapses can happen during treatment or even years after stopping treatment.
- Restarting treatment usually brings the disease under control again.
- Most people will have some long-term health problems from the disease or from the medicines.

## Key Points

- GPA causes inflammation in small and medium-sized blood vessels.
- It often affects the kidneys, nose, and lungs.
- Symptoms can include nosebleeds, cough, blood in the urine, swelling, and high blood pressure.
- Diagnosis is confirmed with blood tests (ANCA) and tissue biopsy.
- Relapses are common.
- Treatment uses corticosteroids and another medicine to stop the disease.
- Long-term treatment may be needed to prevent flares.
- Early treatment improves the chance of recovery.

# Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy and Becker Muscular Dystrophy

These are two types of muscle diseases that run in families. They cause muscle weakness that gets worse over time. Both affect boys more than girls.

## What Causes These Conditions?

- A problem in a gene called the *dystrophin* gene causes these diseases.
- This gene helps make a protein that keeps muscles strong.
- The gene is on the X chromosome.
- Boys have only one X chromosome. If they get the faulty gene from their mother, they will have the disease.
- Girls have two X chromosomes. If one is faulty, the other one usually keeps them healthy. So girls rarely get the disease, but they can carry the faulty gene.

## Differences Between the Two Conditions

| Feature | Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy | Becker Muscular Dystrophy |
|--------|-------------------------------|----------------------------|
| Onset | Starts between ages 2 and 3 | Starts around age 12 or later |
| Severity | Severe | Milder |
| Walking ability | Most need a wheelchair by age 12 | Many can walk into adulthood |
| Life expectancy | Usually into late teens or early 20s without help | Often into 30s or 40s |
| Muscle protein | Almost no functional dystrophin | Some dystrophin, but not working well |

## Symptoms

### Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy

- Weakness starts in the legs and hips.
- A boy may walk later than other children.
- He may have trouble running, jumping, or climbing stairs.
- He falls often and may break bones.
- He walks with a waddle and walks on his toes.
- Shoulder muscles get weak over time.
- Muscles may look bigger but are not strong.
- Heart muscle weakens over time. This can cause heart rhythm problems.
- By age 14, about one in three boys has heart issues. By age 18, all do.
- Heart problems do not cause symptoms early because the boy does not exercise much.
- Some boys have mild learning difficulties, especially with speaking and understanding words.
- Arms and legs may tighten at the joints. Elbows and knees cannot straighten fully.
- Spine may curve abnormally (scoliosis).
- Calf muscles may grow larger and be filled with fat and other tissue.
- Breathing muscles get weaker. This increases the risk of pneumonia and other lung infections.
- Without breathing help, most boys live only into their 20s.
- With a breathing machine (mechanical ventilator), many live into their 30s or longer.

### Becker Muscular Dystrophy

- Weakness is less severe and starts later.
- Most boys can walk until at least age 15.
- Many stay able to walk into adulthood.
- The pattern of weakness is similar to Duchenne, but slower.
- Very few need a wheelchair.
- Most live into their 30s or 40s.

## How Doctors Diagnose These Conditions

Doctors look for signs like:
- A boy who is weak and getting weaker.
- A family history of muscle weakness in boys.

### Tests Used

- **Blood test**: Checks for high levels of an enzyme called creatine kinase. This enzyme leaks out of damaged muscles. High levels suggest muscle disease, but not always muscular dystrophy.
- **Genetic test**: Looks at DNA from a blood sample. It checks for problems in the *dystrophin* gene.
- **Muscle biopsy**: A small piece of muscle is taken and looked at under a microscope. This shows if there is little or no dystrophin protein.
  - In Duchenne: No dystrophin or almost none.
  - In Becker: Some dystrophin, but not enough or not working right.

### Heart Tests

- All boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy get heart tests at diagnosis or by age 6.
- These tests check how well the heart is working.

### Testing for Family Members

- Close family members can have a blood test to see if they carry the faulty gene.
- Pregnant women can have tests on the baby during pregnancy to see if the baby will be affected.

## Treatment

There is no cure for either condition. But treatments can help slow the disease and improve quality of life.

### General Treatments

- **Physical therapy**: Helps keep muscles strong and flexible.
- **Ankle or leg braces**: May help with walking or standing.
- **Surgery**: May be needed to fix tight muscles or correct a curved spine.
- **Diet**: Boys need fewer calories because they are less active. They should avoid overeating.

### Breathing Support

- Some boys use special masks that help them breathe.
- If the mask is not enough, doctors may place a tube in the windpipe (tracheostomy).
- The tube connects to a machine that helps air go in and out of the lungs (mechanical ventilator).
- This can help boys live into their 30s or longer.

### Heart Medications

- Boys with heart problems may take medicines like:
  - Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors
  - Beta-blockers

### Medications for Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy

- **Prednisone or deflazacort**: These are steroid medicines.
  - Given to boys over age 4 who have clear muscle weakness.
  - Taken by mouth every day.
  - Benefits:
    - Helps keep strength longer.
    - Lets boys walk a few more years.
    - Helps heart and lungs work better.
    - Can add 5 to 15 years to life.
  - Side effects:
    - Weight gain
    - Puffy face
    - More risk of bone and spine problems
- **Newer medicines** for some boys with certain gene changes:
  - Eteplirsen, golodirsen, viltolarsen, casimersen, ataluren, or delandistrogene moxeparvovec
  - These help the body make more dystrophin.
  - The protein is not perfect, but it works better than none.
  - They can help reduce symptoms.

> **Note**: These newer medicines are not tested well for Becker muscular dystrophy. They are not used for that condition.

### Genetic Counseling

- Families should talk to a genetic counselor.
- This helps them understand the risk of passing the gene to future children.

## More Information

The following English-language resource may be helpful. The Manual is not responsible for its content.

**Muscular Dystrophy Association**  
Provides information on research, treatment, technology, and support for people with Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy.

# Rubella (German Measles)

Rubella is a viral infection. It can cause a rash and other symptoms.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main sign of rubella is a spotty rash.  
The rash starts on the face or behind the ears.  
It then spreads to the neck and body.  

The rash appears 2 to 3 weeks after you catch the virus.  
On white skin, the rash looks red or pink.  
On brown or black skin, the rash may be harder to see. But it still feels rough or bumpy.  

You may also have:
- Swollen lumps in your neck or behind your ears
- Pain in your fingers, wrists, or knees
- A high temperature
- Coughing
- Sneezing and a runny nose
- Headaches
- A sore throat
- Eyes that are sore and red

## How Long Does It Last?

Rubella usually gets better in about a week.  
You can feel unwell for a few days.  
Stay at home until you feel better.  
Rest as much as you can.  
Drink plenty of fluids like water or squash.  
Take paracetamol or ibuprofen if you feel unwell.  
Do not give aspirin to children under 16.

## Rubella and Pregnancy

Rubella is rare during pregnancy.  
But if you get it while pregnant, it can harm your baby.  

It can cause:
- Losing the baby (miscarriage)
- Serious health problems after birth, such as:
  - Problems with sight
  - Hearing loss
  - Heart problems
  - Brain damage

The risk is highest if you get rubella in the first trimester (first 12 weeks).  
There is little risk to your baby if you get rubella after week 20 of pregnancy.

### Call Your Doctor Right Away If:
- You are pregnant and have a new rash
- You have been close to someone who has rubella

Call your midwife, maternity unit, or GP.  
Tell them you are pregnant and may have rubella.

## How to Prevent Rubella

The MMR vaccine protects you from rubella, measles, and mumps.  
It is safe and free on the NHS in the UK.  

All children in the UK should get two doses of the MMR vaccine.  
Two doses give long-term protection.  

Ask your GP surgery if you or your child have had the vaccine.  
They can give it to you for free if you haven’t.

# Acupuncture

Acupuncture is a treatment from traditional Chinese medicine. It is one of the most accepted forms of complementary therapy in Western countries.

A practitioner inserts very thin needles into specific points on your body. These points are in the skin and the tissues underneath.

The idea is that this helps balance the flow of energy in your body. This energy is called qi. It moves through pathways called meridians.

The treatment usually does not hurt. You might feel a tingling or warm sensation. Sometimes the needle is gently twisted, warmed, or moved to increase the effect.

Other ways to stimulate the same points include:

- Pressing on them (called acupressure)
- Using a low-power laser (called low-level laser therapy)
- Sending a small electric current through the needle (called electroacupuncture)

---

## What Is Acupuncture Used For?

Scientists have found it hard to study acupuncture well. It is difficult to hide the treatment from patients and researchers. Some fake treatments still use real pressure points. This means the fake treatment is not truly harmless.

In countries like China, where acupuncture is more common, there are more studies. But these studies often include other parts of traditional Chinese medicine, not just acupuncture.

The World Health Organization has reviewed the evidence. They list conditions where acupuncture may help. These include:

- Side effects from cancer treatment
- Feeling down or sad (depression)
- Painful periods
- Pain of any kind
- Headaches
- High blood pressure
- Symptoms after surgery
- Some problems during pregnancy
- Problems after a stroke

The World Health Organization also gives clear guidelines on how to do acupuncture safely and well. These are called the WHO benchmarks for the practice of acupuncture.

---

## Possible Side Effects and Risks

Acupuncture is generally safe when done by a trained person. But side effects can happen. A 2023 review of many studies found the following:

- Headaches
- Dizziness
- Feeling sleepy
- Nausea
- Fainting
- Injury to body tissues
- Infection

Most of these side effects were mild. A few could be serious, but they are rare.
