# Herpes Simplex Virus Infections

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is a common virus that can cause repeated infections.  
It affects the skin, mouth, lips, eyes, and genitals.  
Two types exist: HSV-1 and HSV-2.  

HSV-1 usually causes cold sores on the lips or mouth.  
It can also cause eye infections or genital sores.  
HSV-2 usually causes sores on the genitals.  

The virus spreads through close contact with someone who has an active infection.  
You can get it even if the person has no visible sores.  
The virus lives in nerve cells after the first infection.  
It can come back later and cause symptoms.  

Common triggers for a return of symptoms include:  
- Too much sun  
- Fever or illness  
- Stress  
- Weak immune system  
- Unknown reasons  

Recurrent outbreaks usually get milder over time.  
They also happen less often.  

## Types of Infections Caused by HSV

### Skin and Mouth Infections (Most Common)
- Clusters of small, painful blisters on red skin  
- These blisters can break open and form sores  
- They often appear on the lips, mouth, or genitals  

### Eye Infections
- Can cause pain, redness, and blurry vision  
- May lead to scarring or vision loss if not treated  

### Brain and Nervous System Infections
- Can cause serious brain inflammation (encephalitis)  
- Can cause swelling of the lining around the brain (meningitis)  
- Can be life-threatening in newborns (neonatal herpes)  

### Other Serious Cases
- In people with weak immune systems, the virus can spread through the body  
- Rarely, it can cause severe liver problems without skin sores  
- In people with HIV, the infection can be very severe  
  - It may cause long-lasting sores in the esophagus, intestines, or anus  
  - It can also cause pneumonia, brain infection, or meningitis  

### Other Skin Reactions
- Some people develop a rash called erythema multiforme after a herpes outbreak  
- This may be due to the body’s immune response to the virus  
- Eczema herpeticum is a serious skin infection that happens in people with eczema  
  - It causes many painful blisters in areas with eczema  

## How Doctors Diagnose HSV

Doctors often recognize HSV by looking at the sores.  
The rash has a typical look: small blisters on red skin.  

If needed, lab tests can confirm the diagnosis.  
Tests may include:  
- Swab from a blister or sore  
- PCR test (checks for virus DNA)  
- Virus culture (grows the virus in a lab)  
- Blood test (checks for antibodies to the virus)  

For brain infections:  
- A sample of spinal fluid is tested with PCR  
- An MRI scan of the brain may be done  

A Tzanck test can help find the virus in a blister.  
It uses a scraping from the sore and special stains.  

HSV must be told apart from herpes zoster (shingles).  
Shingles usually causes more pain and larger blisters.  
The blisters follow a specific path on one side of the body and do not cross the middle.  

If sores keep coming back, do not heal, or do not respond to treatment,  
a weak immune system may be the cause.  
HIV infection is one possible reason.  

## How Doctors Treat HSV

### For Mild Infections
- Oral medicine: acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir  
- For cold sores on the lips: topical penciclovir or docosanol cream  

### For Eye Infections
- A special eye drop called trifluridine is used  
- Treatment should be done with help from an eye doctor  

### For Severe Infections
- IV acyclovir is given through a vein  
- This is used for brain infections, newborns, or people with weak immune systems  

### Important Notes
- Starting medicine early helps reduce symptoms and healing time  
- Medicine does not stop future outbreaks  
- Even if treatment starts early, the virus stays in the body and can return  

## Key Points

- HSV most often causes skin or mouth sores.  
- It can also cause eye problems and serious brain infections.  
- Newborns and people with weak immune systems are at higher risk.  
- The virus stays in the body forever and can come back.  
- Diagnosis is often based on the look of the sores.  
- Lab tests help confirm the diagnosis in high-risk cases.  
- Treatment with antiviral medicine helps in severe cases.  
- Early treatment improves outcomes.  
- If sores keep coming back or do not heal, check for immune system problems.

# Fevers During Pregnancy

A fever during pregnancy can be risky. Here is what you need to know.

## First Trimester (First 3 Months)

If you have a fever above 103 degrees Fahrenheit (39.5 degrees Celsius) in the first trimester, it can increase the chance of:

- Losing the baby (miscarriage)
- The baby being born with brain or spine problems

## Later in Pregnancy

Later in pregnancy, a fever can raise the risk of:

- Going into labor too early (preterm labor)

## What You Can Do

Doctors will treat the cause of the fever. You can also take acetaminophen to bring down your temperature. If your fever is very high, doctors may use cooling blankets to help lower it.

Always talk to your doctor if you have a fever during pregnancy. Do not wait to get help.

# Psoriatic Arthritis

## What Is Psoriatic Arthritis?

Psoriatic arthritis causes pain, swelling, and stiffness in your joints.  
It often happens in people who also have psoriasis.  
Psoriasis is a skin condition that causes dry, scaly patches.  
It can also affect your nails.  

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if you have:
- Joint pain that comes and goes
- Swollen joints
- Stiff joints, especially in the morning

You should see a doctor even if you do not have psoriasis.  
These symptoms need to be checked.  

## Symptoms of Psoriatic Arthritis

You may notice:
- Pain, swelling, or stiffness in one or more joints
- Swollen fingers or toes (like sausages)
- Changes in your nails – they may turn yellow, become thick, or have small dents
- Feeling very tired or low on energy

Your symptoms may be worse when you first wake up.  
They may get better after you move around or exercise.  

Some people also have skin symptoms of psoriasis at the same time.  
These include dry, scaly patches on the skin.  

## What Happens at Your Doctor’s Appointment

If your doctor thinks you have psoriatic arthritis, they will refer you to a specialist.  
This specialist is called a rheumatologist.  

You may have some tests, including:
- Blood tests to check for signs of inflammation
- A joint fluid test – a small amount of fluid is taken from a swollen joint and tested
- X-rays, ultrasound scans, or MRI scans to look at your joints

## Treatments for Psoriatic Arthritis

Medicines are the main way to treat psoriatic arthritis.  
If one medicine does not help, talk to your doctor.  
Another medicine might work better for you.  

### Medicines

- **Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)**: These are tablets, creams, or gels. They help with mild pain and swelling.
- **Steroid injections**: A doctor injects a steroid medicine into a joint. This can reduce pain and swelling.
- **Disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs)**: These are used for more serious symptoms. They take several months to work. Keep taking them even if you do not feel better right away.
- **Biological treatments**: These are usually given as injections. They are used if DMARDs do not help.

### Other Treatments

Your doctor may refer you to:
- A **physiotherapist** – they teach you safe exercises to strengthen your joints and protect them from damage.
- An **occupational therapist** – they help you make changes at home or work. For example, they may suggest tools that make daily tasks easier.

## Things You Can Do to Feel Better

### Do These Things

- **Exercise regularly** – try low-impact activities like walking, swimming, or yoga. These help keep your joints strong and protected.
- **Lose weight if you are overweight** – extra weight puts more pressure on your joints. Losing weight can ease your symptoms.
- **Cut down on alcohol** – if you are taking medicine, alcohol can make it less effective or cause side effects.

### Avoid These Things

- **Do not smoke** – smoking can make your symptoms worse.
- **Do not use herbal remedies** – they can interfere with your medicine and cause problems.

## What Causes Psoriatic Arthritis?

Some people with psoriasis go on to develop psoriatic arthritis.  
It can happen years after the skin symptoms start.  

Like psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis happens when your immune system attacks healthy tissue in your joints.  
The immune system is your body’s defense system.  

It is not clear why some people with psoriasis get joint problems and others do not.

# Salivary Stones

Salivary stones are small hard lumps made of calcium salts. They can block the tubes that carry saliva from the glands to the mouth. This blockage can cause pain, swelling, and sometimes infection.

Most salivary stones form in adults. About 80 percent start in the submandibular glands. These stones block the Wharton duct. The rest mostly form in the parotid glands and block the Stensen duct. Only about 1 percent form in the sublingual glands. Around one in four people with a stone has more than one.

## The Main Salivary Glands and Their Tubes

There are three main salivary glands:
- Two parotid glands (one on each side of the face, near the ears)
- Two submandibular glands (under the jaw)
- Two sublingual glands (under the tongue)

Each gland has a tube that carries saliva into the mouth.

## What Causes Salivary Stones?

Most salivary stones are made of calcium phosphate. Small amounts of magnesium and carbonate are also present. People with gout may form stones made of uric acid.

Stones form when saliva slows down or stops moving. This is called salivary stasis. It can happen if you are very weak, dehydrated, not eating much, or taking certain medicines that reduce saliva.

If stones keep coming back, the gland may become infected. This is called sialadenitis.

## What Are the Symptoms?

A blocked stone causes swelling and pain. The pain often starts after eating. That is because eating makes the glands make more saliva. The swelling and pain may go away after a few hours. Sometimes you feel a sudden rush of saliva when the pain eases.

Some stones cause no symptoms. Others cause symptoms only sometimes.

If a stone is near the opening of the tube, you might see it or feel it with your finger.

## How Are Salivary Stones Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose salivary stones by examining you. They may ask about your symptoms and check the area.

If the stone is not clear on exam, your doctor may give you something to make your mouth water. This could be lemon juice, hard candy, or another sour food. If your symptoms come back when your mouth waters, it likely means you have a stone.

Imaging tests may be used if the diagnosis is unclear:
- CT scan: very good at finding stones
- Ultrasound: also very good, especially for small or hard-to-see stones
- Sialography: a special X-ray with dye. It is not used as often now.

Plain X-rays are not always helpful. Most stones in the submandibular glands show up on X-rays. But most stones in the parotid glands do not. So X-rays can miss many stones.

Ultrasound is used more often now. It can find 60 to 95 percent of all stones, whether they show up on X-rays or not. It is also very accurate at ruling out stones.

MRI is being studied more. It may be better than ultrasound or sialography at finding small stones or stones deep in the ducts.

## How Are Salivary Stones Treated?

You can try simple steps first:
- Drink plenty of fluids
- Use things that make your mouth water, like lemon wedges or sour candy, every 2 to 3 hours
- Gently massage the gland area

These steps can help the stone pass on its own. They can also help relieve pain.

If the stone is near the opening of the tube, your doctor or nurse may be able to push it out with their fingers.

A small tool may be used to gently open the tube. This can help the stone come out.

If these methods do not work, surgery may be needed.

- Stones near the opening can be removed through the mouth.
- Stones deep in the gland may need the whole gland removed.
- Stones up to 5 millimeters in size can often be removed using a small camera and tools through the mouth (endoscopy).

If there is a risk of infection, your doctor may give you antibiotics early to prevent it.

## Key Facts

- About 80 percent of salivary stones form in the submandibular glands.
- A doctor’s exam is usually enough to diagnose a stone. But sometimes imaging tests like CT or ultrasound are needed.
- Many stones pass on their own or with simple steps like sucking on sour candy. But some stones need endoscopy or surgery to remove.

# Transient Global Amnesia

Transient global amnesia is a sudden and short-term loss of memory.  
It affects memories from before, during, and after the event.  
The exact cause is not known.  

## Who Gets It?

This condition usually happens in people between the ages of 50 and 70.  
It is slightly more common in men than in women.  

## Possible Causes

Doctors do not know what causes transient global amnesia.  
Some possible causes include:  
- Seizures  
- Migraines  
- Problems with blood flow in the veins  
- Temporary blockage of blood vessels to the memory part of the brain (such as from a small blood clot)  
- Emotional or psychological stress  

But there is no strong proof that any of these actually cause the condition.  

## Things That Can Trigger It

Some events may start an episode. These include:  
- Jumping into very cold or very hot water  
- Heavy physical activity  
- Strong emotional stress  
- Pain  
- Medical procedures  
- Sexual intercourse  
- A Valsalva maneuver (trying hard to push out air without letting it escape, like when straining during a bowel movement)  

Most of the time, no clear trigger can be found.  

## Conditions That Look Like It

Some things can cause memory problems that seem like transient global amnesia. These include:  
- Drinking too much alcohol  
- Taking moderate amounts of certain sedatives (like barbiturates)  
- Using certain illegal drugs  
- Taking small doses of some sedatives, especially midazolam and triazolam  

## Symptoms

People with transient global amnesia suddenly lose the ability to remember recent events.  
They also cannot form new memories.  
They may not remember events from the past either.  

They stay alert and aware.  
They often repeat the same question or phrase because they forget what they just said.  
They may be confused about the time or place.  
But they usually still recognize people they know.  
They can answer questions that do not depend on memory.  

Memory loss usually lasts about 6 hours.  
Most episodes last between 2 and 12 hours.  
In rare cases, memory loss lasts from 30 minutes to 24 hours.  

Most people have only one episode in their life.  
But some people may have more than one, especially if seizures or migraines are the cause.  
About 5 to 25 out of 100 people have repeated episodes.  

After the episode ends, confusion goes away quickly.  
Full recovery is normal.  
But people usually do not remember what happened during the episode.  

## How It Differs from Alcohol or Drug-Related Amnesia

Amnesia from alcohol or drugs can also affect memory.  
It can make it hard to focus, think clearly, or remember new things.  
But it is different in these ways:  
- People only forget events that happened just before or during the time they were affected.  
- Confusion only lasts while they are under the influence.  
- Memory problems come back only if they drink the same amount of alcohol or take the same amount of the drug again.  

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors diagnose transient global amnesia based on symptoms.  
They also do tests to rule out other causes.  

Tests may include:  
- Blood tests to check for infections, electrolyte imbalances, or problems with the kidneys or liver  
- Blood tests to check for alcohol or clotting issues  
- Urine tests to check for illegal drugs  
- Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain  
- Electroencephalogram (EEG) to check for seizure activity in the brain  

An MRI may not show anything unusual right after the episode.  
But after a few days, it may show small spots in the hippocampus.  
The hippocampus is a part of the brain that helps with memory.  
These spots may mean blood flow was reduced in that area.  

If episodes happen more than once, doctors may do a more detailed evaluation.  

## Treatment

There is no specific treatment for transient global amnesia.  
It does not cause lasting harm.  
It rarely comes back.  

If doctors find a cause, they treat that cause.  
For example, if seizures are the cause, they may prescribe medicine to prevent seizures.

# Epiglottitis – Simple Explanation

## What is epiglottitis?

Epiglottitis is a serious condition that makes it hard to breathe.  
It can happen very quickly.  
The main sign is trouble breathing.  
You may feel better when you lean forward.

## When to call 999

Call 999 right away if you think you or your child has epiglottitis.  
Stay upright until help arrives.  
Lying down can make breathing worse.  
Do not drive yourself to hospital.  
The person on the phone will tell you what to do.

## Symptoms

The main symptom is very hard breathing.  
You or your child may also have:

- Very fast or very slow breathing  
- A high-pitched, rasping sound when breathing in  
- A sore throat that feels very bad  
- A high temperature  
- A hoarse or croaky voice  
- Pain when swallowing  
- Drooling (saliva runs out of the mouth)  
- Pale, grey, or blue skin – especially on the hands, feet, lips, gums, or inside the eyelids  
- Feeling very tired or very restless and irritable  

If a child has epiglottitis, they may not want to lie down.  
They will lean forward with their neck stretched out while sitting.

## Treatment

You will need to go to hospital if you have epiglottitis.  
You will likely need oxygen through a tube in your nose or a face mask.  
If breathing is very hard, you may need a tube in your throat or a hole in your neck to help you breathe.  
You will get antibiotics through a vein if an infection is the cause.  
Tests may be done to check the swelling in your windpipe and find the cause.  
These tests can include:

- A laryngoscopy: a small camera is used to look at your throat  
- A throat swab: a cotton-like stick is used to take a sample from your throat  
- Blood tests  
- An X-ray or CT scan  

Most people get better with treatment.  
You may need to stay in hospital for a few days.

## Causes

The most common cause is a bacteria called *Haemophilus influenzae type b* (Hib).  
Hib spreads through coughing, sneezing, or touching dirty surfaces.  
Other causes include:

- Injury to the throat, like being hit or drinking very hot liquids  
- Smoking, especially illegal drugs like cannabis or crack cocaine  
- A weak immune system

## How to prevent epiglottitis

The best way to prevent epiglottitis is to get the Hib vaccine.  
The NHS offers two vaccines:

- The 6-in-1 vaccine: given at 8, 12, and 16 weeks old  
- The Hib/Men C vaccine: a booster given at 1 year old  

If you or your child did not get these vaccines as a baby, talk to your GP about getting them now.  
Not smoking also lowers your risk of getting epiglottitis.

# Secondary and Atypical Parkinsonism

Parkinsonism means symptoms like slow movement, stiffness, and tremors. But not all parkinsonism is the same. Some types are caused by other problems. Here’s what you need to know.

---

## What Is Secondary Parkinsonism?

Secondary parkinsonism happens when something else causes parkinson-like symptoms. It is not Parkinson disease.

- The main cause is medicines that block dopamine.
- Dopamine is a brain chemical that helps control movement.
- When dopamine does not work well, movement becomes slow and stiff.

---

## What Is Atypical Parkinsonism?

Atypical parkinsonism is a group of serious brain diseases that look like Parkinson disease at first. But they are different.

- They are not Parkinson disease.
- They affect the brain in different ways.
- They do not respond well to Parkinson medicines.
- They often get worse faster than Parkinson disease.
- They may cause other problems like memory loss, balance issues, or speech problems.

Examples include:
- Progressive supranuclear palsy
- Dementia with Lewy bodies
- Corticobasal ganglionic degeneration
- Multiple system atrophy
- Frontotemporal lobar degeneration
- Wilson disease
- Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation
- Juvenile Huntington disease (Westphal variant)
- Some spinocerebellar ataxias

---

## What Causes These Conditions?

Parkinsonism can be caused by:

- Medicines
- Toxins (poisons)
- Other brain diseases
- Brain injuries
- Infections
- Rare genetic conditions

### Common Causes of Secondary Parkinsonism

The most common cause is medicine.

**Medicines that cause parkinsonism:**
- Antipsychotic drugs (used for mental health conditions)
- Some anti-nausea and stomach medicines (like metoclopramide)
- Medicines that lower dopamine levels (like tetrabenazine or reserpine)
- In some countries: cinnarizine and flunarizine

**Other medicines:**
- Lithium (used for mood disorders) can cause parkinsonism in some people.
- Long-term use may lead to symptoms that go away when the medicine is stopped.

**Illicit drugs:**
- A contaminant in some illegal drugs (called N-MPTP) can cause sudden, permanent parkinsonism.
- This happened in people who used IV drugs.

### Toxins That Cause Parkinsonism

- **Carbon monoxide poisoning:** Can damage brain areas that control movement.
- **Methanol:** Found in bad moonshine. Can cause brain damage and parkinsonism.
- **Manganese:** Found in mining or industrial work. Can cause slow movement, stiffness, and walking problems. Also linked to illegal drug use.

### Other Medical Conditions

- **Stroke (cerebrovascular disease):** Can cause stiffness and slow movement, especially in the legs. Symptoms are often the same on both sides.
- **Brain tumors near movement areas:** Can cause symptoms on one side of the body.
- **Chronic traumatic encephalopathy:** Seen in people with repeated head injuries (like boxers, athletes, soldiers).
- **Normal-pressure hydrocephalus:** Fluid builds up in the brain. Causes walking problems, memory loss, and bladder issues.
- **Hypoparathyroidism:** Low calcium levels can cause brain changes and movement problems.
- **Viral brain infections (like West Nile):** Can cause temporary or permanent parkinsonism.
- **Post-encephalitic parkinsonism:** A rare condition after a past brain infection (like the 1915–1926 epidemic).

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms of secondary and atypical parkinsonism are similar to Parkinson disease.

- Trembling at rest
- Stiff muscles
- Slow movement
- Trouble with balance

But there are differences:
- Symptoms may start on one side or both sides.
- Problems with thinking, memory, or speech may appear early.
- Falls happen early and often.
- Walking may be very unsteady.
- Some people have jerky movements or unusual body postures.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose this by:

- Talking to you about your symptoms.
- Reviewing your medicines and past health.
- Doing a physical exam.
- Checking how you respond to levodopa (a common Parkinson medicine).

**Key clue:** If levodopa does not help much, it is likely not Parkinson disease.

Doctors may also use brain scans (like MRI) to look for signs of other brain problems.

---

## Signs That Suggest a Different Condition

If your doctor sees any of these, they may suspect a different brain disease:

- Trouble moving your eyes up or down
- Overactive reflexes (like a knee jerk that is too strong)
- Sudden jerking movements (myoclonus)
- Problems with blood pressure, bladder, or digestion (autonomic issues)
- Poor coordination (cerebellar ataxia)
- Severe muscle stiffness (dystonia)
- Trouble copying hand movements
- Early memory loss or confusion
- Falls early in the illness
- Needing a wheelchair soon after symptoms start

---

## How Is It Treated?

### Treat the Cause

- If a medicine is causing the problem, stop it if safe to do so.
- If a toxin is the cause, avoid it.
- If a brain tumor or infection is found, treat it.

### Medicines

- Parkinson medicines (like levodopa) often do not help much.
- Amantadine or benztropine may help with symptoms from antipsychotic drugs.
- But these medicines can make memory problems worse.
- They may also increase brain damage over time.
- So they should be used only when needed and for a short time.

### Physical and Lifestyle Help

- Stay as active as possible.
- Exercise every day if you can.
- Physical or occupational therapy can help.
- Therapists can teach you how to move safely.
- They can help you make your home safer (like adding grab bars).
- Adaptive tools (like walkers or special utensils) may help.

### Nutrition

- Eat healthy, balanced meals.
- Good nutrition helps your body stay strong.

---

## Key Points

- Parkinsonism can be caused by medicines, toxins, brain diseases, stroke, tumors, infections, or injuries.
- If a medicine or toxin is the cause, stopping it may improve symptoms.
- If levodopa does not help, it is likely not Parkinson disease.
- Look for signs like early falls, memory loss, or eye movement problems.
- Treat the cause if possible.
- Stay active and safe with physical help and home changes.

# Shin Splints

Shin splints cause pain in the lower legs.  
The pain usually comes from running or walking hard.  
You can also get it from hiking or other activities that put stress on your legs.

## Where the Pain Happens

Pain can be in the front or side of your lower leg.  
It can also be on the back or inner side of your lower leg.  
The exact spot depends on which muscles are affected.

## What Causes Shin Splints

Running or walking hard puts repeated stress on your leg muscles and tendons.  
This stress can cause pain.  
If your foot turns outward too much when you walk or run, it can make shin splints worse.

## Symptoms

You may feel pain when you start moving.  
The pain often gets better as you keep going.  
At first, the pain only happens right when your foot hits the ground.  
If you keep running, the pain can happen with every step.  
Eventually, the pain may stay all the time.  
The pain usually goes away when you rest.

## How Doctors Diagnose Shin Splints

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms.  
They will check your legs and feet.  
They will look for signs of pain and swelling.  
They may also ask about your activity level and how long the pain has lasted.

## Treatment

Stop running or walking hard until the pain goes away.  
Use ice on the painful area for 15 to 20 minutes at a time.  
You can take pain medicine like ibuprofen or acetaminophen.  
These can help reduce pain and swelling.

You can still stay in shape by doing other exercises.  
Swimming or using a stationary bike are good choices.

When the pain starts to fade, do gentle stretching and strengthening exercises.  
One helpful exercise is the bucket-handle exercise.  
These exercises help prevent the pain from coming back.

Wear shoes that support your feet well.  
Look for shoes with strong heels and good arch support.  
Avoid running on sloped or very hard surfaces.  
These surfaces can make shin splints worse.

## Prevention

Wear good shoes that fit well.  
Use insoles if your feet need extra support.  
Avoid running on uneven or hard ground.  
Warm up before you exercise.  
Stretch your legs after activity.  
Slowly increase how much you run or walk.  
Do not push through pain.

# Aphasia

Aphasia makes it hard to talk, understand others, read, or write.  
It can be very frustrating and upsetting.  

## What Causes Aphasia?

Aphasia happens when the part of your brain that handles language gets damaged.  
The most common cause is a stroke.  
Other causes include:  
- A serious head injury  
- Bleeding in the brain  
- Infections in the brain  
- A brain tumour  
- Dementia  
- Long-term damage from alcohol or drug use  

Aphasia can happen to anyone.  
But it is more common in people over 65.  
This is because older people are more likely to have a stroke or dementia.  

There are different types of aphasia.  
The type depends on which part of the brain is damaged.  

## What Are the Symptoms?

Aphasia affects people in different ways.  
Common signs include:  
- Not being able to find the right words  
- Speaking very slowly or with long pauses  
- Using short or broken sentences  
- Repeating words or mixing them up  
- Making up words or sounds  
- Not understanding what others are saying, especially if you can’t see them  
- Trouble reading or writing  

## What Should You Do If You Think Someone Has Aphasia?

Call 999 right away if someone suddenly has:  
- One side of the face drooping or not moving  
- Weakness or numbness in one arm or one side of the body  
- Trouble speaking clearly  
- Slurred speech or confusion when talking  
- Blurred vision or sudden loss of sight in one or both eyes  

These are signs of a stroke.  
A stroke needs emergency treatment.  

> **Important:** Do not drive yourself to hospital.  
> The person on the phone at 999 will tell you what to do.  

## How Is Aphasia Treated?

There is no cure for aphasia.  
But most people get better with speech and language therapy.  

A speech and language therapist will:  
- Check your speaking, listening, reading, and writing  
- Help you improve your communication skills  
- Teach you new ways to talk and connect with others  

Therapy may include:  
- Matching words to pictures  
- Sorting words into groups  
- Repeating words or rhyming  
- Practising non-verbal ways to communicate, like drawing, gestures, or facial expressions  
- Using technology, such as voice-activated phones or photo apps  
- Using special apps or computer programs to practice  

Therapy can be done:  
- One-on-one  
- In a group  
- In person  
- Online  

Your family, friends, or caregivers will often be part of the therapy.  
They can learn how to help you communicate better.  

## Living with Aphasia

Aphasia can affect your daily life.  
It can make you feel frustrated, lonely, or sad.  
It may affect your relationships and your independence.  

But support can help.  
Talking therapies and help from your care team can improve your mood and confidence.  

If aphasia was caused by a stroke, head injury, or brain tumour:  
- Most people improve, especially in the first few months  
- Some people keep getting better for months or even years  
- A few people recover fully  

If aphasia is caused by a condition that gets worse over time, like dementia:  
- The symptoms will likely get worse  
- The focus of treatment is on learning new ways to communicate  
- This can include drawing, gestures, or using technology  

## Support and Help

You are not alone.  
Many people with aphasia and their families find support helpful.  

### Stroke Association  
- Offers information and support after a stroke  
- Website: [www.stroke.org.uk](https://www.stroke.org.uk)  
- Helpline: 0303 3033 100

### Aphasia Reconnect  
- Provides online and in-person support groups  
- Offers buddy programs to connect people with aphasia

- Phone: 07885 288943

## Tips for Managing Aphasia

You and the people around you can do things to help:  
- Speak slowly and clearly  
- Use simple words and short sentences  
- Use pictures, gestures, or writing to help explain  
- Let the person with aphasia take their time  
- Be patient and listen carefully  
- Avoid finishing their sentences unless asked  

With time, support, and therapy, many people with aphasia can still live full and meaningful lives.

# Unplanned Weight Loss

Weight loss that happens without trying can take weeks or months. It may be a sign of a serious health problem. It can also raise the risk of death. The cause might be clear, like ongoing diarrhea from a digestive issue. Or it might be hidden, like an undiagnosed cancer.

This guide is for people who come in because they are losing weight. It does not cover weight loss that is expected from a known long-term illness, such as advanced cancer or severe lung disease.

Doctors usually consider weight loss important if you lose more than 5% of your body weight or 5 kilograms in 6 months. But this rule does not tell the difference between losing fat and losing muscle. Losing muscle can be more serious. Also, swelling in the body (edema), which can happen in heart or kidney disease, can hide muscle loss.

You may have other symptoms along with weight loss. These can include not wanting to eat, fever, or sweating at night. You might also show signs of not getting enough nutrients. These signs depend on which vitamins or minerals you are missing.

About 5 out of every 100 people in the United States lose a lot of weight without trying each year. The chance goes up with age. In older adults, it can be as high as 20 out of 100. In nursing homes, it can be as high as 60 out of 100. Unplanned weight loss is linked to a higher risk of dying from any cause, including cancer or heart disease.

---

## What Causes Unplanned Weight Loss?

You lose weight when your body burns more calories than you take in. This can happen if your body uses more energy or if you are not absorbing food well. Some conditions that raise energy use can make you hungry. But more often, weight loss happens because you are not eating enough. In these cases, your appetite is low.

Sometimes more than one thing causes the weight loss. For example, cancer can make you lose your appetite. It also makes your body burn more calories.

---

## Common Causes of Unplanned Weight Loss

### If You Are Hungry But Still Losing Weight

- Overactive thyroid
- Uncontrolled diabetes
- Problems with digesting food (malabsorption)

### If You Are Not Hungry and Losing Weight

- Depression or other mental health issues
- Cancer
- Side effects from medicines
- Drug or alcohol use

---

### Causes and Clues to Look For

| Cause | Signs and Symptoms | How to Check |

| Alcohol use | History of heavy drinking | Look for skin changes, nerve problems, liver issues |
| Drug or medicine use | History of using drugs or certain medicines | Review all medicines, do a drug test if needed |
