# Altitude Sickness

You can get altitude sickness if you are at a high place. This usually means more than 2,500 metres above sea level. It often happens when you go up too fast.

## What Is Altitude Sickness?

Altitude sickness happens when your body does not have enough time to adjust to less oxygen in the air at high places.

You are more likely to get it if you climb or travel to a high place quickly.

You can get altitude sickness in places like:
- Mount Everest in Nepal
- Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania
- Some parts of the Alps
- La Paz in Bolivia

You cannot get altitude sickness in the UK because it is not high enough.

## Symptoms of Altitude Sickness

Symptoms usually start 6 to 10 hours after you reach a high place.

Common symptoms include:
- A headache
- Not wanting to eat
- Feeling sick or being sick
- Feeling very tired or weak
- Dizziness
- Trouble sleeping

Sometimes, symptoms get worse and become serious. These can be life-threatening.

## When to Get Help Right Away

Go to a lower altitude and get medical help right away if you or someone else:
- Feels very unwell
- Is confused or cannot think clearly
- Has trouble walking or balancing
- Sees or hears things that are not real
- Feels short of breath, even when resting
- Coughs or spits up foam or blood
- Has blue or grey skin, lips, tongue, or nails  
  (On brown or black skin, check the palms of the hands or soles of the feet)
- Is very sleepy or hard to wake up

If you can, go down 300 to 1,000 metres right away.

## What to Do If You Get Altitude Sickness

If you feel unwell at a high altitude:
- Tell someone you are with that you are not feeling well.
- Stay at the same height until you feel better.
- Do not climb or travel higher until you feel better.
- You can take painkillers like ibuprofen or paracetamol for a headache.
- You can also take medicine for nausea (feeling sick).

Most people feel better in 1 to 3 days.

If you feel better, you can slowly go higher again.

## If Symptoms Do Not Improve

If your symptoms do not get better after 1 day, go down in altitude if you can. Try to go down 300 to 1,000 metres.

## Treatment for Altitude Sickness

Most people get better by resting and staying at the same height.

You may be given medicine to help with symptoms.

If your symptoms are serious, you may need:
- Steroid medicine
- Medicine to lower blood pressure
- Oxygen through a mask

In rare cases, you may need to be treated in a special sealed room (called a hyperbaric chamber) that gives you more oxygen.

## How to Lower Your Risk

You can take steps to reduce your chance of getting altitude sickness.

### Do These Things:
- Climb or travel up slowly. This gives your body time to adjust.
- Spend a few days at a place below 2,500 metres before going higher.
- Take a rest day at the same height every 3 to 4 days if you are above 3,000 metres.
- Drink enough water. Do not get dehydrated.
- Talk to your doctor or a travel clinic if you have had altitude sickness before.  
  They may give you medicine to help prevent it.

### Do Not Do These Things:
- Do not go from a low place (below 1,200 metres) to a high place (above 3,500 metres) in one day.
- Do not fly directly to a high-altitude place. If you must, rest for one full day before going higher.
- Do not sleep more than 500 metres higher than you did the night before if you are above 3,000 metres.
- Do not drink alcohol while climbing or travelling at high altitudes.

# Zika Virus Infections – Simple Explanation

## What Is the Zika Virus?

The Zika virus is a virus spread by certain types of mosquitoes.  
It is similar to the viruses that cause dengue, yellow fever, and West Nile virus.  
Most people who get the virus do not feel sick.  
Some people may have a fever, a rash, joint pain, or red eyes.  
These symptoms are usually mild and last about 4 to 7 days.  
In rare cases, the virus can cause serious brain problems in adults.

## Zika Virus and Pregnancy

If a pregnant woman gets the virus, it can pass to her baby.  
This can cause serious birth defects.  
These include a small head size (called microcephaly), eye problems, and other developmental issues.  
This group of problems is called congenital Zika syndrome.

All babies born to mothers who had Zika during pregnancy should have their brain development checked for at least 2 years.  
This is true even if the baby looks normal at birth.

## How Is Zika Spread?

The main way Zika spreads is through bites from *Aedes* mosquitoes.  
These mosquitoes live near people and bite during the day.  
They also bite at night.  
They breed in standing water, like in old tires, flowerpots, or buckets.

The two main types of mosquitoes that carry Zika are:
- *A. aegypti* – found mostly in the southern United States, near the border with Mexico and in southern California.
- *A. albopictus* – found in many parts of the southeast, up through the Midwest, and in southern California.

*A. aegypti* bites mostly humans.  
*A. albopictus* bites humans and other animals that do not spread the virus.

Zika can also spread in other ways:
- Through unprotected sex (vaginal, anal, or oral).
- From a pregnant woman to her unborn baby.
- Through blood transfusions (rare).
- Through organ or tissue transplants (theoretical risk).
- Through sharing sex toys.

The virus can stay in semen longer than in blood or other fluids.  
Men can pass the virus to their partners even if they do not feel sick.  
Women can also pass the virus to men through sex, even if they have no symptoms.

Zika has been found in breast milk, but it is not clear if babies can get infected through breastfeeding.  
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention still recommends breastfeeding because the benefits outweigh the risks.

## Where Is Zika Found?

Zika was first found in monkeys in Uganda in 1947.  
It was not a big concern until large outbreaks happened in the South Pacific in 2007.  
In 2015, it spread to South America, Central America, the Caribbean, and parts of Africa and Asia.

As of May 2025, there are no active Zika outbreaks in any country.

Zika can spread to new areas if the right mosquitoes are present.  
Because the same mosquito that carries Zika also carries dengue and chikungunya, Zika can spread where those diseases are found.

## Who Is at Risk?

People who live in or travel to areas with Zika are at risk.  
Travelers returning from these areas can carry the virus in their blood.  
If they are bitten by a mosquito, that mosquito can spread the virus to others.

In the United States, local outbreaks have happened in Miami-Dade County, Florida, and Brownsville, Texas.  
But no local transmission has been reported since 2019.

## How Is Zika Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect Zika if a person has symptoms and has been in a high-risk area.  
But symptoms are similar to other diseases like dengue, malaria, and chikungunya.  
So lab tests are needed to confirm the diagnosis.

Tests include:
- RT-PCR: This finds the virus in blood or urine. It works best in the first week of illness.
- IgM antibody test: This checks for antibodies in the blood. But it can give false results because of other similar viruses.
- PRNT: This test confirms the results of the IgM test and helps rule out other viruses.

For pregnant women:
- If they have symptoms and have been in a high-risk area, they should be tested with RT-PCR and possibly IgM.
- If they have no symptoms, testing is not usually needed unless they recently traveled to a high-risk area or had sex with someone at risk.
- If a baby has signs of congenital Zika syndrome, the mother and baby should be tested.

For non-pregnant people:
- Testing is only needed if symptoms are severe.
- Testing men without symptoms is not recommended.

Doctors in the United States must report all confirmed cases to the CDC.

## How Is Zika Treated?

There is no medicine to cure Zika.  
Treatment focuses on helping the body recover.

You should:
- Rest.
- Drink plenty of fluids to stay hydrated.
- Use acetaminophen to reduce fever and pain.

Do not use aspirin or other NSAIDs (like ibuprofen) unless dengue has been ruled out.  
This is because these medicines can increase the risk of bleeding.  
Zika has been linked to serious bleeding problems in some people.

If a pregnant woman tests positive for Zika, she should have regular ultrasounds every 3 to 4 weeks to check the baby’s growth and development.  
She should also see a specialist in high-risk pregnancies.

## How Can You Prevent Zika?

There is no vaccine to prevent Zika.  
The best way to prevent it is to avoid mosquito bites.

To avoid mosquito bites:
- Use insect repellent.
- Wear long sleeves and long pants.
- Stay in places with screens or air conditioning.
- Remove standing water around your home.

Pregnant women should not travel to areas with active Zika outbreaks.  
If travel is necessary, talk to your doctor first and take strong steps to avoid mosquito bites.

Because Zika can spread through sex:
- Men and women who live in or have traveled to high-risk areas should avoid sex or use condoms every time they have sex.
- This includes vaginal, anal, and oral sex.
- This is especially important if a woman is pregnant or trying to become pregnant.

## Key Facts

- Zika is mainly spread by mosquitoes.
- Most people do not have symptoms.
- When symptoms do occur, they are usually mild.
- Zika during pregnancy can cause serious birth defects.
- All babies born to mothers with Zika should be checked for brain development for at least 2 years.
- Test pregnant women who have been in high-risk areas or had sex with someone at risk.
- Treat fever with acetaminophen. Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs until dengue is ruled out.
- Pregnant women should not travel to areas with active Zika outbreaks.
- Prevention means avoiding mosquito bites and using protection during sex.

# Hepatitis B Vaccine

This vaccine helps protect you from hepatitis B.  
Hepatitis B is a virus that causes liver inflammation.  
It can lead to long-term liver problems, including liver scarring and liver cancer.

---

## Types of Hepatitis B Vaccines

There are three main hepatitis B vaccines in the United States.  
There are also three combination vaccines that protect against hepatitis B and other diseases.

All hepatitis B vaccines used in the U.S. are made in a lab.  
They contain only a small, harmless part of the hepatitis B virus — a protein.  
The body learns to recognize this protein.  
If you are later exposed to the real virus, your body can fight it off.

The combination vaccines include protection against:
- Hepatitis A
- Polio (inactivated)
- *Haemophilus influenzae* type b (Hib)
- Diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis (DTaP)

These combination vaccines are sold as:
- HepB/HepA
- DTaP/HepB/IPV
- DTaP/HepB/Hib/IPV

---

## When and How the Vaccine Is Given

The hepatitis B vaccine is given as an injection into a muscle.  
Most people need 2 or 3 doses to be fully protected.

If you were vaccinated and later exposed to the hepatitis B virus, your doctor may test your blood.  
This test checks how well your body is protected.  
If your protection is low, you may need another dose.

### For Babies and Children

The hepatitis B vaccine is a routine childhood vaccine.  
Most babies get 3 doses of a combination vaccine:
- First dose: shortly after birth
- Second dose: at 1 to 2 months old
- Third dose: at 6 to 18 months old

If a baby did not get the first dose at birth, start the series as soon as possible.

### For Teens

Teens who have not been vaccinated should get the vaccine between 11 and 15 years old.  
They may need 2 or 3 doses, depending on the vaccine used.

### For Adults Ages 19 to 59

All adults in this age group who have never been vaccinated should get the hepatitis B vaccine.  
The number of doses depends on the vaccine used — 2, 3, or 4 doses.

### For Adults 60 and Older

The vaccine is recommended for adults 60 and older who have certain risk factors.  
These include:
- Working in jobs where you might touch blood or body fluids (like health care, cleaning, or police work)
- Traveling to countries where hepatitis B is common
- Having a long-term liver problem (such as hepatitis C, liver scarring, fatty liver, liver damage from alcohol, or autoimmune liver disease)
- Having kidney failure and needing dialysis
- Using illegal drugs by injection
- Having more than one sex partner in the past 6 months
- Needing treatment or testing for a sexually transmitted infection
- Being a man who has sex with men
- Living with or having sex with someone who has hepatitis B
- Having HIV
- Working in or living in places where hepatitis B is common (such as drug treatment centers, HIV clinics, prisons, or dialysis centers)

The vaccine may also be offered to adults 60 and older who do not have risk factors, if they want protection.

For adults 60 and older with diabetes, talk to your doctor about whether the vaccine is right for you.

The combination vaccine can be used in adults 18 and older who need protection from hepatitis A or B and have not been vaccinated before.

---

## Who Should Not Get the Vaccine

Do not get the hepatitis B vaccine if:
- You had a serious allergic reaction (like anaphylaxis) to any part of the vaccine
- You are allergic to baker’s yeast (used in making the vaccine)

If you are sick with a fever or a serious illness, wait until you feel better before getting the vaccine.

---

## Side Effects

Common side effects include:
- Soreness, redness, or swelling where the shot was given
- Mild fever
- Feeling tired
- Headache

A serious allergic reaction is very rare.

For more details on side effects, read the package insert that comes with the vaccine.

# Brain Aneurysm – Simple Guide

Most brain aneurysms do not need treatment.  
Treatment is only needed if there is a risk the aneurysm could burst.  
It may also be needed if the aneurysm has already burst.

We do not know exactly what causes most brain aneurysms.  
But some things can raise your risk.  
These include smoking and high blood pressure.

You can lower your risk by quitting smoking.  
You can also lower your blood pressure.  
These steps may help stop the aneurysm from growing or bursting.

---

## Call 999 if you or someone else suddenly has:

- A headache that is extremely painful and does not go away  
- One side of the face drooping or feeling weak  
- Trouble smiling  
- Weakness or numbness in one arm or one side of the body  
- Trouble lifting both arms at the same time  
- Slurred speech or trouble speaking  
- Confusion or trouble finding the right words  
- Blurred vision or loss of sight in one or both eyes

---

### A&E Safety Advice (for 999 calls only)

Do not drive yourself to hospital.  
The person you speak to on 999 will tell you what to do next.

---

## When to See a Doctor

Call your GP or get help from NHS 111 if you:

- Keep getting headaches that do not go away  
- Headaches are getting worse  
- Have pain above or around your eye  
- Have any other symptoms of a brain aneurysm that do not go away

You can call 111 or get help online.

---

## Support and Help

Finding out you have a brain aneurysm can be frightening.  
Talk to your doctor for medical advice.  
You may also find it helpful to talk to others who have been through the same thing.

### Headway

Support for anyone affected by brain injury.

- Website: [www.headway.org.uk](https://www.headway.org.uk)  
- Helpline: 0808 800 2244  
- Online communities available

### Brain and Spine Foundation

Help and information for people with brain conditions, including brain aneurysm.

- Website: [www.brainandspine.org.uk](https://www.brainandspine.org.uk)  
- Helpline: 0808 808 1000  
- Join a support group

---

## Symptoms of a Brain Aneurysm

Most brain aneurysms are small and cause no symptoms.  
They are often found by chance during a scan for another problem.

If the aneurysm is larger, you may notice:

- A headache  
- Pain above or around your eye  
- Double vision or other changes in your sight  
- Dizziness or balance problems  
- Numbness or weakness on one side of your face  
- Trouble concentrating or speaking  
- Problems with short-term memory

If the aneurysm bursts, it causes bleeding in the brain.  
This is called a subarachnoid haemorrhage.

The main sign is a sudden, very severe headache.  
People often describe it as a "thunderclap headache" – like a loud bang in the head.

---

## Treatment for a Brain Aneurysm

Small aneurysms that do not cause symptoms usually do not need treatment.  
They often stay small and rarely burst.

You may only need regular scans to check if the aneurysm is growing.

### Surgery for a Brain Aneurysm

Surgery is needed if the aneurysm might burst or if it already has burst.

There are two main types of surgery:

- **Surgical clipping**: A small metal clip is placed on the blood vessel in the brain. This stops blood from flowing into the aneurysm.  
- **Endovascular surgery**: A coil or small wire mesh is placed inside the aneurysm. This slows blood flow and helps a blood clot form to seal it.

Your surgeon will talk to you about which option is best for you.  
They will explain the risks and benefits.

Both types of surgery use general anaesthetic.  
This means you will be asleep and will not feel any pain during the operation.

---

## What Causes a Brain Aneurysm?

We do not always know what causes brain aneurysms.  
But some things increase your risk:

- Smoking  
- High blood pressure  
- A close family member who had a brain aneurysm  
- Injury to a blood vessel in the brain  
- Using drugs like cocaine  
- Certain inherited conditions, such as autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome

---

## What You Can Do to Help

If you have a brain aneurysm, you can take steps to lower the risk of it growing or bursting.

### Do:

- Stop smoking if you smoke  
- Keep your blood pressure at a healthy level  
- Get your blood pressure checked at a pharmacy or GP clinic  
- Eat a balanced diet  
- Exercise regularly  
- Lose weight if you are overweight

### Do Not:

- Drink too much alcohol  
- Use illegal drugs

---

### Driving

You may not be allowed to drive if you have a brain aneurysm.  
Your doctor will tell you if it is safe to drive.  
They will also advise if you need to inform the DVLA.

# Megaloblastic Macrocytic Anemias

This condition happens when your body does not make healthy blood cells. It is most often caused by low levels of vitamin B12 or folate.

Your bone marrow makes blood cells in a faulty way. This affects red blood cells the most, but it can also affect white blood cells and platelets.

## What Causes This Anemia?

The most common causes are:

- Low vitamin B12 levels  
- Low folate levels  

### Low Vitamin B12

The most common reason for low B12 is a condition called pernicious anemia. This happens when your stomach does not make a substance called intrinsic factor. This substance helps your body absorb vitamin B12.  
Autoimmune problems can cause this. It can happen at any age, not just in older people. It is more common in young women with certain stomach problems or a *Helicobacter pylori* infection.  
Other causes include:
- Surgery that removes part of the stomach or small intestine (like gastric bypass)
- Crohn disease
- Tapeworm infection in the intestines

A diet with no animal products (like vegan diets) can cause low B12, but this is rare in most countries.

### Low Folate

Folate deficiency is rare in countries where grain products are fortified with folic acid.  
But it can happen if you:
- Eat very little food (restrictive diet)
- Drink too much alcohol
- Have an eating disorder like anorexia

Other causes include:
- Celiac disease
- Tropical sprue
- Short bowel syndrome

Folate needs go up during pregnancy. It also goes up in people with certain blood disorders that destroy red blood cells. In these cases, low folate can develop.

### Other Causes

Some medicines can cause this problem. These include:
- Chemotherapy drugs (like hydroxyurea)
- Some medicines used to prevent organ rejection after transplant

Rare metabolic disorders can also cause it. One example is hereditary orotic aciduria.

Low copper levels can cause similar changes in blood cells. This can lead to anemia that is large, normal-sized, or even small red blood cells.

## How Does This Condition Work?

Your body needs DNA to make healthy blood cells. When DNA production is blocked, the cells grow too big. But they do not mature properly.

RNA continues to work. This makes the cells large with large nuclei. The cells in the bone marrow grow too fast in the cytoplasm but not in the nucleus. This mismatch causes abnormal cells called megaloblasts.

These abnormal cells die inside the bone marrow. This means your body cannot make enough healthy red blood cells. This is called ineffective blood cell production.

Because the problem affects all blood cells, you may have:
- Fewer new red blood cells (reticulocytopenia)
- Fewer white blood cells (leukopenia)
- Fewer platelets (thrombocytopenia)

Large, oval-shaped red blood cells (macro-ovalocytes) enter the bloodstream.  
Neutrophils (a type of white blood cell) have more than the usual number of lobes in their nucleus. This is called hypersegmentation.  
Small pieces of leftover cell nucleus (Howell-Jolly bodies) can be seen in red blood cells.

If you also have iron deficiency, kidney disease, or poor iron use, you may not get large red blood cells even with this condition.

## What Are the Symptoms?

This anemia develops slowly. You may not notice symptoms until the anemia is severe.

Common symptoms include:
- Diarrhea
- Sore or swollen tongue (glossitis)
- Loss of appetite

Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause nerve problems. These include:
- Tingling or numbness in hands and feet (paresthesias)
- Trouble walking or balance problems

These nerve problems can become permanent if not treated early.

Sometimes, tingling is the first sign of B12 deficiency — even before anemia develops.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will do several tests:

### Blood Tests
- Complete blood count (CBC)
- Red blood cell size and shape (RBC indices)
- Reticulocyte count (new red blood cells)
- Blood smear (examined under a microscope)

### What the Tests Show

- Red blood cells are larger than normal (macrocytic). The average size is over 100 femtoliters.
- The red blood cells vary in size (anisocytosis) and shape (poikilocytosis).
- Many red blood cells are oval and large (macro-ovalocytes).
- The red blood cell size variation is high (high RDW).
- Howell-Jolly bodies are often seen.
- Few new red blood cells are in the blood (reticulocytopenia).
- Neutrophils have more than five lobes (hypersegmentation).
- In severe cases, white blood cells and platelets are low.
- Platelets may look odd in size and shape.

### Vitamin Levels

Your doctor will check:
- Vitamin B12 level
- Folate level

A B12 level below 200 picograms per milliliter (pg/mL) means deficiency.  
A folate level below 2 nanograms per milliliter (ng/mL) means deficiency.  
Red blood cell folate below 150 ng/mL also means deficiency.

If B12 levels are between 200 and 300 pg/mL, the test is not clear. In this case, your doctor may check:
- Methylmalonic acid (MMA)
- Homocysteine (HCY)

In vitamin B12 deficiency:
- Both MMA and homocysteine are high.

In folate deficiency:
- Only homocysteine is high.

Kidney problems can raise methylmalonic acid levels. So your doctor must consider kidney function.

If B12 deficiency is confirmed, your doctor may test for antibodies against intrinsic factor.

Your doctor will also look for the cause of the deficiency.

## How Is It Treated?

You need to take the right vitamin supplement.

Always check for vitamin B12 deficiency before giving folate.  
Giving folate when B12 is low can fix the anemia but hide the nerve damage. This can let nerve problems get worse.

### Treatment Steps

- Give vitamin B12 if you are low in it.
- Give folate if you are low in it.
- Stop or reduce medicines that cause this problem, if possible.
- Treat the underlying cause of the deficiency.

For example:
- Treat celiac disease
- Treat *Helicobacter pylori* infection
- Change diet if needed

## Key Points

- Megaloblasts are large, immature red blood cells with loose DNA.
- The most common causes are low vitamin B12 or low folate.
- Use a complete blood count, red blood cell tests, reticulocyte count, and blood smear to check for this.
- Test vitamin B12 and folate levels. Consider methylmalonic acid and homocysteine if needed.
- Treat the cause of the vitamin deficiency.

# Prion Disease with Diarrhea and Nerve Problems

This is a rare type of prion disease. It starts by affecting nerves outside the brain. This causes ongoing diarrhea and numbness in the feet.

(See also: Overview of Prion Diseases.)

In 2013, doctors found this disease in a family in Britain. A similar case was later found in a family in Italy.

This disease is different from other prion diseases in several ways:

- It is caused by a unique change in a specific gene called the prion gene.
- The abnormal prion proteins build up in nerves all over the body. This includes nerves that control automatic body functions like blood pressure. In most other prion diseases, the prions only build up in the brain.
- It causes unusual symptoms like diarrhea.
- It gets worse very slowly over time.

Symptoms usually start when people are in their 30s. They have constant watery diarrhea and a bloated belly. They may also lose weight.

Because the nerves that control body functions are damaged, some people cannot empty their bladder (urinary retention). Others may leak urine (urinary incontinence). Their blood pressure may drop when they stand up. This can make them feel dizzy or lightheaded (orthostatic hypotension). They may also lose feeling in their feet.

Later, in their 40s or 50s, people may have trouble thinking clearly. Some may have seizures.

The disease can last for decades. People may live up to 30 years after symptoms first appear.

There is no cure right now. Treatment focuses on easing symptoms and improving quality of life.

# Food Poisoning

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may feel sick or be sick.  
You may have diarrhoea.  
You may have tummy pain.  
You may have a high temperature.  
You may feel generally unwell.

These symptoms usually start within a few hours or a few days after eating bad food.  
Sometimes they do not start for a few weeks.

## How to Treat Food Poisoning at Home

Most cases get better on their own within a week.  
You can treat it at home.  
The most important thing is to drink plenty of fluids.  
This helps prevent dehydration.

### What to Do

- Stay at home and rest.  
- Drink lots of fluids like water or squash.  
- If you feel sick, take small sips.  
- Keep feeding your baby with breast milk or formula.  
- If your baby is being sick, try giving small feeds more often.  
- For babies on formula or solid foods, give small sips of water between feeds.  
- Eat when you feel able.  
- Avoid fatty or spicy foods.  
- Take paracetamol if you are in pain.  
- Always check the leaflet before giving medicine to a child.

### What Not to Do

- Do not drink fruit juice or fizzy drinks. They can make diarrhoea worse.  
- Do not make baby formula weaker. Use it at the usual strength.  
- Do not give children under 12 years medicine to stop diarrhoea.  
- Do not give aspirin to children under 16.

## When to Call 111

Call 111 now if:

- You are worried about a baby under 12 months.  
- Your child stops breast or bottle feeding while ill.  
- A child under 5 years has fewer wet nappies.  
- You or your child (5 years or older) still feel dehydrated after using rehydration sachets.  
- You or your child keep being sick and cannot keep fluids down.  
- You or your child have bloody diarrhoea or blood from the bottom.  
- You or your child have diarrhoea for more than 7 days or vomiting for more than 2 days.

111 will tell you what to do.  
They can arrange a phone call with a nurse or doctor if needed.

## When to Call 999 or Go to A&E

Go to A&E or call 999 if you or your child:

- Vomit blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.  
- Have green vomit (adults).  
- Have yellow-green or green vomit (children).  
- May have swallowed something poisonous.  
- Have a stiff neck and pain when looking at bright lights.  
- Have a sudden, severe headache.  
- Have a sudden, severe tummy ache.  
- Have blue, grey, pale, or blotchy skin, lips, or tongue.  
  - On brown or black skin, check the palms of the hands or soles of the feet.  
- Have trouble breathing or are breathing very fast and shallow.  
- Are confused or not acting like themselves.

### What We Mean by Severe Pain

Severe pain:
- Is always there and so bad it’s hard to think or talk.  
- Stops you from sleeping.  
- Makes it hard to move, get out of bed, go to the bathroom, wash, or dress.

Moderate pain:
- Is always there.  
- Makes it hard to concentrate or sleep.  
- You can still get up, wash, or dress.

Mild pain:
- Comes and goes.  
- Is annoying but does not stop you from doing daily tasks.

## A&E Safety Tips

- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you.  
- Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
- Bring any medicines you take with you.

## Pharmacist Can Help

Talk to a pharmacist if:

- You or your child (over 5 years) have signs of dehydration, like dark or smelly pee or peeing less than usual.  
- You are older, have a weak immune system, or have other health problems that raise your risk of dehydration.  
- You need to stop diarrhoea for a few hours.

They may suggest:
- Oral rehydration powder to mix with water.  
- Medicine to stop diarrhoea for a few hours, like loperamide.  
  - This is not safe for children under 12.

# Nonatheromatous Arteriosclerosis

This condition is a normal part of aging. It affects the main arteries, especially the aorta and its large branches.

It causes the artery walls to thicken and lose their flexibility.

## What Is Arteriosclerosis?

Arteriosclerosis means the arteries become stiff and thick. This can happen in different ways.

The most common type is atherosclerosis. It is the most serious form. It leads to heart disease and stroke.

Atherosclerosis happens when fatty material builds up inside the artery wall. This buildup forms a plaque. The plaque contains fat, immune cells, muscle cells, and connective tissue. It may also contain blood clots and calcium.

## Types of Nonatheromatous Arteriosclerosis

There are two main types that do not involve fatty plaques:

- Arteriolosclerosis  
- Mönckeberg arteriosclerosis

These types cause the inner layer of the artery to thicken. They also damage the elastic layers inside the artery wall.

The middle layer of the artery (called the media) shrinks and weakens. This makes the artery open up wider than normal. This is called ectasia.

Wider arteries are more likely to bulge (aneurysm) or tear (dissection).

## Risk Factors and Causes

High blood pressure is a major cause of this condition in the aorta. It also increases the risk of aneurysms.

Damage to the inner lining of the artery can lead to blood clots. These clots can break loose and block blood flow elsewhere. Or they can cause the artery to close completely.

## Symptoms and Detection

Most people do not feel any symptoms. The condition is often found by chance during imaging tests done for other reasons.

Symptoms only appear when complications develop. The most common complication is an aneurysm.

## Treatment

There is no specific treatment for nonatheromatous arteriosclerosis.

Doctors focus on managing common risk factors for heart and blood vessel problems. These include:

- High blood pressure  
- High cholesterol  
- Diabetes

Controlling these conditions helps slow the disease and prevent serious problems.

## Key Points

- Nonatheromatous arteriosclerosis makes artery walls thick and stiff. It does not involve fatty plaques.
- The two types are arteriolosclerosis and Mönckeberg arteriosclerosis.
- Risk factors include diabetes, high blood pressure, and aging.

# Toxic Shock Syndrome

Toxic shock syndrome is a serious and fast-moving illness. It can cause high fever, a rash, very low blood pressure, and problems with many organs. It is caused by harmful substances made by two types of bacteria: *Staphylococcus aureus* and group A streptococci.

## What Causes Toxic Shock Syndrome?

Toxic shock syndrome happens when harmful substances from bacteria get into the body. These bacteria can be found in:

- Wounds that are infected
- Tampons, especially superabsorbent ones
- Contraceptive devices in the vagina, like diaphragms or menstrual caps
- After surgery, even if the wound seems small
- The uterus after childbirth
- The nose after nose surgery, if bandages are used

*Staphylococcus aureus* can grow on a tampon or other vaginal product. It can also infect a wound.  
Group A streptococci usually cause infection in the skin or deeper tissues under the skin.

About half of people with streptococcal toxic shock syndrome have bacteria in their blood.  
About half also have a severe skin infection called necrotizing fasciitis.

## Symptoms of Toxic Shock Syndrome

Symptoms come on quickly and get worse fast over a few days.  
You may have a very high fever.  
Your blood pressure drops to a dangerous level.  
Your organs—like the kidneys, liver, heart, and lungs—may stop working properly.

Other symptoms include:
- A red, sunburn-like rash over the whole body, including the palms and soles
- The skin may peel off later
- Swelling in the body from fluid buildup
- Trouble with blood clotting, which can cause more bleeding
- Diarrhea
- Muscle pain
- Red eyes
- Sore throat
- Confusion or delirium

### If the Cause Is Streptococci:
- The infected area is usually very painful
- Gangrene (dead tissue) can form around the wound
- You may feel very sick and weak
- Breathing problems are common
- Even with treatment, 20 to 60 out of 100 people die

### If the Cause Is Staphylococci:
- Skin peeling, especially on the palms and soles, is more common
- Peeling usually starts 3 to 7 days after symptoms begin
- About 8 out of 100 people die
- Most people who survive get better completely

If the cause is a tampon, the illness can come back.  
It often returns within 4 months if tampons are still used.  
Recurrences are usually milder.  
To avoid this, women who have had toxic shock syndrome should not use tampons or any other vaginal products like diaphragms, caps, or plugs.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your symptoms and do a physical exam.  
They also do blood tests to check how well your organs are working.

They take samples of blood and infected tissue to grow bacteria in a lab.  
This helps confirm the cause.

Imaging tests like MRI or CT scans may be used to find where the infection is.

After you leave the hospital, blood tests may be done to check if the infection is fully gone.  
These tests can also help find complications from streptococcal infection.

## How Is It Treated?

You will be admitted to the hospital, often in intensive care.  
You will get fluids through a vein to help your blood pressure and organs.

Medicines to raise blood pressure may be needed.  
Many people need help breathing with a machine called a ventilator.

All tampons, diaphragms, and other foreign objects in the vagina are removed right away.

Antibiotics are started as soon as possible, even before the bacteria are identified.  
Once the bacteria are known, the antibiotics are adjusted.

For severe cases, you may get intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG).  
This is a medicine made from blood of healthy people. It helps your body fight the infection.

Infected areas, like wounds or the vagina, are cleaned out with water (irrigated).

If the wound is badly infected, surgery may be needed.  
This can include removing dead or infected tissue.  
In rare cases, a limb may need to be removed if gangrene has spread.

## How to Prevent Toxic Shock Syndrome

Women who use tampons can lower their risk by:

- Not using superabsorbent tampons
- Using the least absorbent tampon that works for you
- Switching between tampons and pads
- Changing tampons every 4 to 8 hours

If you have had toxic shock syndrome from *Staphylococcus aureus*, you should not use tampons, diaphragms, menstrual caps, or any other product inserted into the vagina.  
This helps prevent the illness from coming back.

# Thrush in Men and Women

Thrush is a common condition caused by a fungus. It can affect men and women. It often causes itching, soreness, and a white discharge that looks like cottage cheese.

Most people get better within 1 to 2 weeks with treatment.

---

## When to See a Doctor

See a doctor if you:

- Have thrush symptoms for the first time  
- Are under 16 or over 60 years old  
- Get thrush more than 4 times in 12 months  
- Have tried treatment but it did not work  
- Are pregnant or breastfeeding  
- Have a weak immune system (for example, due to diabetes, HIV, or chemotherapy)

You can also visit a sexual health clinic if you think you have thrush.

[Find a sexual health clinic]

---

## Symptoms of Thrush

### In Women

- White discharge from the vagina  
- The discharge often looks like cottage cheese  
- It usually does not smell  
- Itching or irritation around the vagina and vulva  
- Pain or stinging when you pee or during sex

### In Men

- Redness, soreness, or burning around the head of the penis  
- Redness or soreness under the foreskin  
- White discharge (like cottage cheese)  
- A bad smell  
- Trouble pulling back the foreskin

### In Other Areas

Thrush can also affect skin in places like the armpits, groin, or between fingers.

This causes a red, itchy, or painful rash. The rash may have white or yellow flakes. It might be harder to see on darker skin.

Sometimes thrush causes no symptoms at all.

---

## Treating Thrush

You need antifungal medicine to treat thrush. This can be:

- A tablet you swallow  
- A tablet you put inside the vagina (called a pessary)  
- A cream to apply to the skin

Most people feel better within 7 to 14 days of starting treatment.

You do not need to treat your partner unless they also have symptoms.

### If Thrush Keeps Coming Back

If you get thrush more than 4 times in a year, you may need treatment for up to 6 months.

Your doctor can help find the cause. For example, your period, sex, or other health issues might be linked.

They will tell you how often to use treatment.

---

## What Causes Thrush

Thrush is not a sexually transmitted infection. But sex can sometimes trigger it. It can also be passed on during sex, though this is rare.

Thrush is caused by a fungus called candida. This fungus is usually harmless.

It grows when the balance of bacteria in your body changes. This can happen if:

- Your skin is irritated or damaged  
- You are taking antibiotics  
- You have uncontrolled diabetes  
- You have a weak immune system (for example, from HIV or chemotherapy)  
- You are on hormone replacement therapy  
- You are pregnant

---

## How to Feel Better and Prevent Thrush from Coming Back

You can take steps to ease symptoms and stop thrush from returning.

### Do These Things

- Wash the area with water and a gentle moisturizer (like E45 cream)  
- Dry the area well after washing  
- Wear cotton underwear  
- Avoid sex until the thrush is gone, if sex causes pain

### Do Not Do These Things

- Do not use soap, shower gel, or scented products  
- Do not use douches or deodorants in the vagina or on the penis  
- Do not wear tight underwear or tights

### Important Note

If you have sex during treatment, know that antifungal creams can damage condoms and diaphragms. This means your birth control may not work. Use a different method of contraception.

---

## Can a Pharmacist Help?

You can buy antifungal medicine from a pharmacy if you have had thrush before and know the symptoms.

A pharmacist can help you pick the right treatment. They can also offer a private space if you feel shy.

Do not use antifungal medicine more than twice in 6 months without talking to a pharmacist or doctor.

# Epidemic Typhus

Epidemic typhus is a serious illness caused by a germ called *Rickettsia prowazekii*.  
It spreads from person to person through body lice.  
The main symptoms are a very high fever, a severe headache, and a rash.

---

## What Causes Epidemic Typhus?

The germ *Rickettsia prowazekii* lives in humans.  
It spreads when body lice bite a person and then leave behind their feces.  
If the feces get into a bite wound, a cut, or the eyes or mouth, the germ can enter the body.  
This is how the disease spreads.  
In the United States, people can get it from flying squirrels.  
Fleas or lice on flying squirrels can carry the germ and pass it to people.

Children under 10 years old rarely die from this illness.  
But older people are at higher risk of dying.

---

## Symptoms and Signs

After 7 to 14 days, symptoms start suddenly.  
You will feel very sick with a high fever and a severe headache.  
Your temperature can reach 40 degrees Celsius within a few days.  
It stays high for about two weeks, with only a small drop in the morning.  
The headache is intense and affects your whole head.

A rash appears on the fourth to sixth day.  
It starts as small, pink spots.  
It spreads fast, mainly on the chest, underarms, and upper body.  
It usually does not appear on the palms, soles, or face.  
Later, the rash turns darker and becomes raised.  
In serious cases, the rash turns into small purple or black spots.  
These can be signs of bleeding under the skin.

Some people may have an enlarged spleen.  
Very sick people often have low blood pressure.  
If the illness gets worse, you may have:  
- Weak blood vessels  
- Kidney problems  
- Brain symptoms like confusion or seizures  
- Large bruises that turn black  
- Gangrene in fingers or toes  
- Pneumonia  

These are warning signs that the illness is serious.

---

## Brill-Zinsser Disease

Years after the first infection, the illness can come back.  
This is called Brill-Zinsser disease.  
It happens when your body’s defenses weaken.  
The germ stays in your body and wakes up again.  
This return is usually mild.  
It can happen at any time of year and in any place.  
It does not need lice to spread.  
But lice can pick up the germ from a person and pass it on.

Symptoms are mild.  
They are like those of the original illness.  
You may have a fever that comes and goes for about 7 to 10 days.  
The rash may be weak or not appear at all.  
There are no deaths from Brill-Zinsser disease.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and check your body.  
They may take a small sample of the rash and test it with a special stain.  
This test can find the germ.  
Blood tests can help confirm the diagnosis.  
But they are not useful right away.  
You need two blood tests — one early and one later.  
A lab test called PCR can also detect the germ in blood or tissue.

If you have lice, and you have been in a place where this disease is common, your doctor may suspect epidemic typhus.

---

## How Is It Treated?

The main treatment is a medicine called doxycycline.  
You take it until you feel better, your fever is gone for 24 to 48 hours, and you have taken it for at least 7 days.  
If you cannot take doxycycline, your doctor may try to help you tolerate it through a special process called desensitization.

Some older medicines can stain teeth in young children.  
But the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says that a short course of doxycycline is safe for children under 8.  
Studies show that a 5 to 10 day course does not harm tooth color or strength.

If doxycycline is not an option, a second medicine called chloramphenicol can be used.  
But this medicine is not available in the United States.  
It can also cause serious blood problems.  
If used, your blood must be checked often.

People who are very sick may have fluid leak from blood vessels.  
This can cause swelling in the lungs or brain.  
So, fluids given through a vein must be used carefully.  
The goal is to keep blood pressure up without making swelling worse.

---

## How Can It Be Prevented?

Stopping lice and keeping clean are the best ways to prevent this disease.  
Vaccines used to work well, but they are no longer available.  
To kill lice:  
- Dust the body with a medicine called malathion or lindane.  
- Wash bedding and clothes in hot water (over 54 degrees Celsius).  
- Dry them on high heat.  
- For items you cannot wash, dry-clean them or seal them in a plastic bag for 2 weeks.  
- Treat bedding and clothes with a spray called permethrin.

---

## Key Points

- Epidemic typhus happens all over the world.  
- Humans are the main carrier of the germ.  
- It spreads through body lice when their feces get into wounds or mucous membranes.  
- A rash starts as small pink spots. It spreads fast and later turns dark and raised.  
- Older people are more likely to die from this illness.  
- Signs like low blood pressure, kidney failure, brain problems, or black bruises mean the illness is serious.  
- Think about epidemic typhus if you have a fever, rash, and lice, and you have been in a high-risk area.  
- Confirm the diagnosis with a skin biopsy and special testing.  
- Treat with doxycycline.  
- Brill-Zinsser disease can return years later when your body is weak. It is mild and not deadly.

---

## More About Brill-Zinsser Disease

- It is a return of epidemic typhus after many years.  
- It happens when your body’s defenses drop.  
- The germ stays in your body and wakes up again.  
- You may have had the illness before or lived in a place where it is common.  
- The symptoms are mild.  
- Fever comes and goes for about 7 to 10 days.  
- The rash is often weak or missing.  
- There are no deaths from this condition.

# What Are Blistering Disorders?

A blister is a small bubble filled with fluid. It forms under a thin layer of dead skin. The fluid inside is mostly water and proteins. It comes from skin that has been damaged.

Most blisters happen after an injury. Examples include burns or skin that has been rubbed too much. These blisters only affect the top layer of skin. They usually heal fast. They do not leave scars.

Some blisters are not from injury. They can be a sign of a serious illness that affects the whole body. These blisters start deeper in the skin. They can spread over large areas. They take longer to heal. They may leave scars.

Many conditions can cause blisters. But three autoimmune diseases are especially serious:

- Bullous pemphigoid  
- Dermatitis herpetiformis  
- Pemphigus vulgaris  

In an autoimmune disease, the body’s immune system makes a mistake. The immune system usually fights germs and infections. But in these diseases, it attacks the body’s own skin.

Other autoimmune blistering diseases include:

- Mucous membrane pemphigoid  
- Pemphigoid gestationis  
- Epidermolysis bullosa  
- Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita  
- Linear immunoglobulin A disease  
- Pemphigus foliaceous  

Other causes of blisters include:

- Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome  
- Toxic epidermal necrolysis  
- Severe cellulitis  
- Certain drug rashes  

Blisters from burns or rubbing (like from tight shoes or shoveling) are common. But these are not considered blistering disorders.

# Non-Allergic Rhinitis

Non-allergic rhinitis means your nose is blocked or runny, but it is not caused by allergies.

## Symptoms

You may have:
- A blocked or runny nose
- Sneezing
- An itchy nose
- A weaker sense of smell

Sometimes, a crust forms inside your nose. This crust can smell bad. It may bleed if you try to remove it.

## What You Can Do at Home

Non-allergic rhinitis is not dangerous. But it can make daily life harder.

You can often treat it yourself.

Try to avoid things that make your symptoms worse.

A pharmacist can help you choose medicines that may work. These include:
- Antihistamines
- Nasal sprays to clear a blocked nose
- Salt water sprays or rinses to clean the inside of your nose

You can buy nasal sprays without a doctor’s prescription. But do not use them for more than one week. Using them longer can make your symptoms worse.

If you have a fever or feel too unwell to do your normal activities, stay home. Avoid close contact with others until you feel better.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:
- Your symptoms get worse
- You have asthma symptoms or your asthma gets worse
- Your symptoms keep you from sleeping or doing normal activities
- You do not know what is causing your symptoms
- Pharmacy medicines are not helping

## Treatment from a Doctor

Non-allergic rhinitis often gets better on its own.

If needed, your doctor may prescribe a stronger nasal spray.

They may also check if any medicine you are taking is causing your symptoms. If so, they may change it.

If your symptoms are very bad or the cause is unclear, your doctor may refer you to a specialist. The specialist can do more tests and offer more treatment.

## Causes

Common causes include:
- A cold
- Weather changes, like very hot or cold air, or high humidity
- Exercise
- Smoke, perfume, or paint fumes
- Alcohol and spicy food
- Hormone changes during pregnancy, puberty, or from hormone replacement therapy or the contraceptive pill
- An underactive thyroid
- Some medicines, such as ACE inhibitors, beta blockers, aspirin, and anti-inflammatory painkillers like ibuprofen
- Using decongestant nasal sprays too often

## Important Note

Non-allergic rhinitis is not the same as allergic rhinitis. Allergic rhinitis is caused by allergies, like hay fever. Non-allergic rhinitis is not caused by allergies.

# Myelophthisic Anemia – Simple Explanation

This condition happens when the bone marrow gets filled with abnormal cells or scar tissue. This stops the bone marrow from making enough healthy blood cells.

## What Causes Myelophthisic Anemia?

The most common cause is cancer that has spread to the bone marrow. Cancers like breast cancer or prostate cancer are often the source. Less often, kidney, lung, adrenal, or thyroid cancers cause this.

Other causes include:
- A type of blood cancer called primary myelofibrosis.
- Blood disorders like polycythemia vera or essential thrombocythemia that turn into myelofibrosis.
- Diseases that cause scar tissue in the bone marrow, such as autoimmune diseases or gray platelet syndrome.
- Infections or inflammatory diseases that form granulomas (clumps of immune cells).
- Rare inherited diseases that cause fat buildup in the body, like Gaucher disease.

In all these cases, the bone marrow space gets replaced. This means it can no longer make enough red blood cells, white blood cells, or platelets.

## What Happens in the Body?

When the bone marrow is damaged, the body tries to make blood in other places. This often happens in the spleen and liver. This is called extramedullary hematopoiesis.

The spleen may grow larger. This is called splenomegaly. In severe cases, a very large spleen can press on the stomach. This can cause:
- Feeling full quickly after eating.
- Weight loss.
- Pain in the upper left side of the belly.
- High pressure in the liver’s blood vessels (portal hypertension).

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may feel tired, weak, or short of breath. These are signs of anemia.

You may also have symptoms from the underlying disease. For example, if cancer is the cause, you may have unexplained weight loss or pain.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find out if you have this condition.

### Blood Tests
- A complete blood count checks your red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.
- A blood smear shows the shape and size of your blood cells under a microscope.

In this condition, blood tests often show:
- Red blood cells that are all different sizes and shapes (anisocytosis and poikilocytosis).
- Many abnormal red blood cells, including some that still have a nucleus (nucleated red blood cells).
- Teardrop-shaped red blood cells (called dacrocytes).
- White blood cells that are not fully mature.
- Low platelet counts. The platelets that are present may be large and oddly shaped.

### Bone Marrow Test
A bone marrow biopsy is usually needed to confirm the diagnosis. This test looks at the inside of the bone marrow.

The bone marrow may be hard to draw fluid from. So doctors often take a small piece of bone marrow tissue instead.

The test can show:
- Scar tissue in the marrow.
- Abnormal cells replacing normal marrow.
- Blood cell production in the spleen or liver, but it does not work well.

### Other Tests
X-rays or scans may show bone changes. These can include:
- Extra bone growth (myelosclerosis).
- Bone damage from cancer (like lytic or osteoblastic lesions).

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure for the anemia itself. Treatment focuses on the cause and symptoms.

### Treat the Underlying Cause
- If cancer is the cause, treat the cancer.
- If it is due to a blood disorder, treat that condition.

### Supportive Care
- Blood transfusions are given when anemia is severe.
- Folic acid supplements help the body make new blood cells.

### Specific Treatments for Primary Myelofibrosis
- Medicines that block a certain enzyme (JAK2 inhibitors) can help reduce symptoms.
- In some cases, a bone marrow transplant may be an option.

## Key Points

- Myelophthisic anemia means the bone marrow is filled with abnormal cells or scar tissue.
- This stops the marrow from making enough blood cells.
- The most common cause is cancer that has spread to the bone marrow.
- Other causes include blood disorders, infections, and rare inherited diseases.
- Signs include tiredness, a large spleen, and abnormal blood cells seen on a blood smear.
- A bone marrow biopsy is needed to confirm the diagnosis.
- Treatment focuses on the cause and includes blood transfusions and folic acid.
- For primary myelofibrosis, special medicines or bone marrow transplant may help.

# Gonorrhea – Simple Explanation

Gonorrhea is a common infection passed through sex. It is caused by a type of bacteria called *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. The bacteria can live in the lining of the urethra, cervix, rectum, throat, or the front part of the eye.

## How Gonorrhea Spreads

- Gonorrhea spreads during vaginal, anal, or oral sex.
- It can spread even if there is no ejaculation.
- The chance of getting it from an infected woman during unprotected sex is about 22%.
- The chance of getting it from an infected man is higher, especially when the man has sex with a woman or another man.
- A pregnant person with gonorrhea can pass the infection to their baby during childbirth.
- Children with gonorrhea may have been sexually abused. This is a serious sign and needs medical attention.

## Symptoms of Gonorrhea

Most people with gonorrhea do not have symptoms. But when symptoms do appear, they depend on where the infection is.

### In Men
- Some men have no symptoms.
- Others may feel mild pain in the tube that carries urine out of the body (urethra).
- They may have pain when urinating.
- A yellow or green discharge may come from the penis.
- The opening of the penis may be red and swollen.
- The infection can spread to the testicles, causing swelling and pain on one side.

### In Women
- Most women have no symptoms.
- If symptoms occur, they usually start about 10 days after infection.
- They may feel discomfort in the genital area.
- There may be a yellow or green vaginal discharge.
- Pain during sex is possible.
- If the urethra is infected, urination may be painful or frequent.

The infection can spread up into the uterus, fallopian tubes, or nearby areas. This can cause:
- Severe lower belly pain.
- Fever.
- A condition called pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), which can affect fertility.

In rare cases, the infection spreads to the area around the liver. This causes:
- Pain in the upper right side of the belly.
- Fever.
- Vomiting.

### In the Rectum
- This can happen after unprotected anal sex.
- Most people have no symptoms.
- Some may have:
  - Constipation.
  - Itching.
  - Bleeding.
  - A cloudy discharge from the rectum.
  - Red, raw skin around the anus.
  - Mucus or pus in the stool.

A doctor may use a small tube to look inside the rectum to check for signs of infection.

### In the Throat
- This can happen after unprotected oral sex.
- Most people have no symptoms.
- Some may have a sore throat.

### In the Eyes
- This happens if infected fluid touches the eye.
- It causes swelling of the eyelids.
- The eye may produce a thick, pus-like discharge.
- In adults, usually only one eye is affected.
- In newborns, both eyes are often affected.
- If not treated early, it can lead to blindness.

### In the Skin and Joints (Disseminated Gonococcal Infection)
- This is rare.
- The infection spreads through the blood to the skin and joints.
- Symptoms include:
  - Fever.
  - Feeling unwell.
  - Pain, swelling, and tenderness in the joints (arthritis).
  - Red, warm skin over the joints.
  - Small, red, painful spots on the arms and legs (sometimes filled with pus).
- In very rare cases, the infection can reach the heart or brain.

### In Children
- Gonorrhea in children is a sign of possible sexual abuse.
- In girls, the vulva may be red, swollen, and irritated.
- There may be a vaginal discharge.
- In boys, the urethra may be infected, causing pain when urinating.

## How Doctors Diagnose Gonorrhea

Doctors use tests to find the bacteria. The most common test is called NAAT (nucleic acid amplification testing). It finds the genetic material of the bacteria.

- A sample of discharge from the cervix, vagina, penis, throat, or rectum is tested.
- A urine sample can also be used.
- The test is very accurate and can also check for chlamydia at the same time.

Sometimes, doctors use a culture:
- This means they try to grow the bacteria in a lab.
- It helps check if the bacteria are resistant to certain antibiotics.

### How Samples Are Taken
- **For men:** A swab is taken from the penis. If there is no discharge, a swab is gently inserted into the urethra. Men should not urinate for at least 2 hours before the test.
- **For women:** A doctor checks the pelvis and takes a swab from the cervix. Women who cannot have a pelvic exam can use a urine sample or collect a vaginal swab themselves.
- **For throat or rectum:** A swab is taken from the throat or rectum.
- **For skin sores:** Blood and swabs from the urethra, cervix, and rectum are tested.
- **For joint pain:** A doctor uses a needle to draw fluid from the joint (called arthrocentesis) and tests it.

Doctors often test for other STIs at the same time, such as syphilis and HIV.

## Who Should Be Screened for Gonorrhea?

Screening means testing people who have no symptoms. It helps find infections early.

### Women
- All sexually active women under age 25 should be tested every year.
- Women 25 or older should be tested every year if they:
  - Have had an STI before.
  - Have many sex partners.
  - Have sex with someone who has many partners.
  - Use condoms inconsistently.
  - Work in sex work.

### Pregnant Women
- All pregnant women under age 25 should be tested.
- Women 25 or older with risk factors should be tested during the first prenatal visit.
- If still at risk, they should be tested again in the third trimester.
- After treatment, they should be retested within 3 months.

### Men Who Have Sex With Men
- All should be tested at least once a year.
- Those at higher risk (such as those with HIV, many partners, or partners with many partners) should be tested every 3 to 6 months.

### Transgender and Gender Diverse People
- People with a cervix under age 25 should be tested every year.
- Those 25 or older with a cervix should be tested every year if at risk.
- People without a cervix should be tested based on their sexual behaviors and anatomy.
- Rectal swabs are used for testing if they have had anal sex.

### Other Men
- Not routinely screened, but testing is available.
- It is often offered to men in high-risk settings like clinics, STI centers, or correctional facilities.

## How Gonorrhea Is Treated

- A single shot of an antibiotic called ceftriaxone is given into a muscle.
- Pregnant people get the same treatment.
- If someone is allergic to ceftriaxone, another antibiotic is used.

### If the Infection Has Spread
- If the infection has spread to the skin, joints, or other parts of the body, hospital treatment is needed.
- Antibiotics are given through a vein or by injection.
- Fluid in the joints is drained.

### After Treatment
- If symptoms return, doctors may test again to check if the infection is gone.
- They may test for antibiotic resistance.

### Treating Both Gonorrhea and Chlamydia
- Many people have both infections at the same time.
- Doctors often treat both at once with ceftriaxone.
- This is because the symptoms are similar and it is common to have both.

### What You Should Do After Treatment
- Do not have sex until treatment is complete.
- All sex partners from the past 60 days should be tested and treated.
- If partners were exposed in the past 2 weeks, they are treated right away without waiting for test results.

### Expedited Partner Therapy
- Doctors may give you medicine to give to your sex partners.
- This helps them get treated even if they do not see a doctor.
- It is helpful if partners are unlikely to seek care.
- But seeing a doctor is better because they can check for allergies and other infections.

## How to Prevent Gonorrhea

You can lower your risk by:
- Using a condom every time you have oral, anal, or vaginal sex.
- Reducing the number of sex partners.
- Avoiding high-risk partners (those with many partners or who do not use condoms).
- Being in a mutually monogamous relationship or choosing abstinence.
- Getting vaccinated if a vaccine is available for the STI.
- Getting tested and treated early to stop spreading the infection.
- Telling your sex partners if you have an STI so they can be tested and treated.

# Menopause

Menopause and the time before it, called perimenopause, can cause many changes in your body and mind. These changes can affect your daily life, including how you feel at home, with friends, and at work.

Everyone experiences menopause differently. Some people have many symptoms. Others have few or none.

Symptoms often start months or years before your periods stop. This is the perimenopause.

---

## Common Symptoms of Menopause and Perimenopause

### Changes in Your Periods
- Your periods may become irregular. They might come more often or less often.
- Eventually, your periods will stop completely.

### Mood and Brain Changes
- You may feel sad, anxious, or have mood swings.
- You might feel less confident in yourself.
- You may have trouble remembering things or focusing on tasks. This is sometimes called "brain fog."

### Physical Symptoms
- You may get hot flushes. These are sudden waves of heat in your face, neck, or chest. You might feel dizzy.
- You may have trouble sleeping. Night sweats can make this worse. This can leave you tired and grumpy during the day.
- Your heart may beat faster or feel more noticeable.
- You may get more headaches or migraines than before.
- You may feel pain in your muscles or joints.
- Your body shape may change. You may gain weight, especially around your waist.
- Your skin may become dry and itchy.
- You may feel less interested in sex.
- Your vagina may feel dry. Sex may be painful, itchy, or uncomfortable.
- You may get more urinary tract infections.
- Your teeth may feel sensitive. Your gums may hurt or have other problems.

---

## Lifestyle Changes That Can Help

Healthy habits can ease symptoms and help you feel better now and in the future.

### Do These Things
- Get enough rest. Try to go to bed and wake up at the same time every day.
- Eat a balanced diet with lots of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins.
- Eat foods high in calcium, like milk, yogurt, and kale. This helps keep your bones strong.
- Exercise regularly. Try walking, running, dancing, or other activities where your feet and legs carry your weight.
- Try relaxing activities like yoga, tai chi, or meditation.
- Talk to people who understand what you are going through. This could be family, friends, or coworkers.
- Talk to your doctor before trying herbal supplements or other natural remedies.

### Avoid These Things
- Do not smoke.
- Do not drink more than the recommended amount of alcohol.

---

## Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT)

HRT is a safe and effective treatment for most people going through menopause or perimenopause. Your doctor will explain any risks.

HRT replaces the hormone oestrogen, which your body makes less of during menopause.

There are different types and doses of HRT. Your doctor will help you find the right one. Most people find their symptoms improve with the right treatment.

### How Oestrogen Is Taken
- Skin patches
- Gel or spray applied to the skin
- Implants under the skin
- Tablets

### If You Have a Womb (Uterus)
- You will also need to take progesterone. This protects the lining of your womb from the effects of oestrogen.
- Taking both hormones together is called combined HRT.

### How Progesterone Is Taken
- Patches that also contain oestrogen
- IUS (a small device placed in the womb)
- Tablets

### Low Sex Drive?
- If you have low sex drive and HRT does not help, your doctor may suggest testosterone.

---

## When to See a Doctor or Nurse
- If you think you are going through perimenopause or menopause.
- If you are unsure about your symptoms or how to manage them.

You can also talk to a pharmacist for advice on treatments and lifestyle changes.

# Understanding Inherited Muscle Disorders

This section explains rare muscle conditions that are passed down through families. These conditions affect how muscles work and can cause weakness from birth or early infancy.

---

## What Are Muscular Dystrophies?

Muscular dystrophies are genetic conditions that cause muscles to weaken over time. They happen because of problems in one or more genes that help muscles stay strong and work properly.

- The muscles break down and try to repair themselves, but this process does not work well.
- A muscle biopsy (a small sample of muscle tissue) can show these changes.
- There is no cure for these conditions.
- Treatment focuses on helping people stay as strong and independent as possible.

### Most Common Types

- **Duchenne muscular dystrophy**: This is the most severe form. Symptoms start in early childhood. Muscle weakness gets worse quickly.
- **Becker muscular dystrophy**: This is similar to Duchenne but less severe. Symptoms start later and progress more slowly.
- **Myotonic dystrophy**: This is the second most common type. It causes muscles to stay tight after use and affects many body systems.
- **Facioscapulohumeral dystrophy**: This is the third most common. It mainly affects muscles in the face, shoulders, and upper arms.

### Other Types

Other forms include:
- Emery-Dreifuss dystrophy
- Limb-girdle dystrophy
- Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy
- Congenital muscular dystrophies

Each type affects different muscles and has its own genetic cause.

---

## Other Inherited Muscle Disorders

Some other inherited muscle conditions include:
- **Congenital myopathies**: These are muscle problems present at birth. They affect how muscles contract.
- **Myotonia congenita**: This causes muscles to stay tight after use. It is often present from birth.
- **Familial periodic paralysis**: This causes sudden episodes of muscle weakness or paralysis. It can come and go.

---

## Conditions That Affect Muscle Metabolism

Some inherited conditions affect how muscles make energy. These include:
- Mitochondrial disorders (problems with energy-making parts in cells)
- Glycogen storage diseases (problems storing energy in muscles)

These are not covered in detail here. Only conditions that mainly affect muscles are discussed.

---

## Congenital Muscular Dystrophy

Congenital muscular dystrophy means muscle problems that are present at birth or in the first few months of life.

- It is not one single disease. It is a group of rare conditions that all start early in life.
- These conditions are caused by changes in genes. The changes are passed down from parents.
- The genes involved help build the outer layer of muscle fibers. When these genes are faulty, muscles do not work well.

### Signs and Symptoms

- Babies are often described as “floppy” because their muscles are weak.
- They may have trouble feeding, moving, or holding up their heads.

### How It Is Diagnosed

- Doctors suspect the condition if a baby is very floppy at birth.
- A muscle biopsy helps tell the difference between congenital muscular dystrophy and congenital myopathy.
- Blood tests check for muscle proteins.
- Imaging tests like ultrasound or MRI can show muscle damage.
- Genetic testing may help confirm the diagnosis.

### Treatment and Care

- There is no cure.
- Care is focused on managing symptoms and keeping the person as strong and independent as possible.
- A team of specialists helps with:
  - Orthopedic care (for bones and joints)
  - Heart health
  - Breathing support
  - Nutrition
  - Physical therapy
- Supportive care helps maintain movement and function.

---

- **Muscular Dystrophy Association**: Offers information on research, treatments, new technology, and support for people with muscular dystrophy.
