  A simple summary for patients.

- **American Academy of Sleep Medicine**:  
  Detailed patient information about healthy sleep and treatment options for sleep disorders.

# Chalazion and Stye (Hordeolum)

## What Are Chalazia and Styes?

A **chalazion** is a lump inside the eyelid. It happens when an oil gland gets blocked. It is not an infection. It can feel like a small pimple deep in the eyelid.

A **stye** is usually caused by a bacterial infection. It forms at the base of an eyelash. The infection often comes from a type of bacteria called staphylococcus.

Some people get only one stye in their life. Others get them again and again. Rarely, a stye forms in a deeper gland inside the eyelid. This is called an internal stye.

## Symptoms

### Chalazion Symptoms

- At first, the eyelid may swell.
- You may feel mild pain or irritation.
- These early symptoms usually go away in a few days.
- After that, a round, painless lump grows slowly over the first week.
- The lump may keep growing. It can press on the eye and cause blurry vision.
- A red or gray spot may appear on the inside of the eyelid.

### Stye Symptoms

- The eyelid edge becomes red and tender.
- Pain starts at the edge of the eyelid.
- A small, round, sore bump forms.
- The eye may water more than usual.
- Bright light may hurt your eye.
- You may feel like something is in your eye.
- Usually, only a small part of the eyelid swells. But sometimes the whole eyelid swells.
- A tiny yellow spot often appears in the center of the bump. This is usually at the edge of the eyelid.
- The stye usually breaks open after 2 to 4 days. It releases a small amount of fluid, often pus. Then the pain and swelling go away.

### Internal Stye Symptoms

- Pain, redness, and swelling happen on the inside of the eyelid.
- Symptoms are usually worse than with an external stye.
- In rare cases, the swelling is very bad. You may also have a fever or chills.

## How Are They Diagnosed?

- A doctor will look at your eyelid.
- The doctor can tell if it is a chalazion or a stye just by examining it.

## How Are They Treated?

### Warm Compresses

- The best first step is to use warm compresses.
- Apply a warm, damp cloth to the eyelid for 5 to 10 minutes.
- Do this 2 to 3 times a day.
- Warmth helps the lump come to a head and drain on its own.

### Chalazion Treatment

- Most chalazia go away on their own in 2 to 8 weeks.
- Warm compresses can help them go away faster.
- If the lump does not go away after several weeks, or if it affects your vision, a doctor can drain it.
- A doctor may also inject medicine into the lump to reduce swelling.
- Antibiotics do not help because chalazia are not caused by infection.
- If a chalazion does not go away after treatment, a doctor may take a small sample of tissue. This is to check for eyelid cancer.

### Stye Treatment

- Warm compresses are the best treatment.
- They help the stye break open and drain.
- If a stye does not go away with compresses, a doctor can drain it.
- Internal styes rarely break open on their own. A doctor may need to drain them with a small cut.
- Internal styes are more likely to come back.

### Antibiotics

- Eye drops or ointments with antibiotics are sometimes used.
- But they usually do not help much. Most styes get better on their own in a few days.
- Oral antibiotics (pills) may be given if the infection spreads to the area around the eye.
- They may also be used after surgery for an internal stye.

# Angioedema – Simple Explanation

Angioedema is when part of your body swells up suddenly.  
The swelling can happen anywhere, but it often affects the face, hands, feet, or genitals.  

You may also have a rash that is raised and itchy.  
This rash is called hives.  

The swelling can be mild or very serious.  
Some cases need emergency care.

---

## When to Call 999 (Emergency)

Call 999 right away if you or someone else has any of these signs:

- Lips, mouth, throat, or tongue swell up quickly.  
- You are breathing very fast or having trouble breathing.  
- You feel like you are choking or gasping for air.  
- Your throat feels tight or you cannot swallow.  
- Your skin, tongue, or lips turn blue, grey, or pale.  
  - If you have dark skin, check the palms of your hands or soles of your feet.  
- You feel very confused, very sleepy, or dizzy.  
- Someone passes out and will not wake up.  
- A child is limp, floppy, or not responding normally.  
  - Their head may fall to the side, back, or forward.  
  - They may not be able to lift their head or look at you.

You or the person may also have a swollen, raised, or itchy rash.

These signs can mean a serious allergic reaction.  
You may need urgent treatment in hospital.

---

## When to See a Doctor Soon

Call your doctor or use NHS 111 if:

- A part of your body swells up suddenly.  
  - This could be your hands, feet, or genitals.

You can call 111 or get help online at [nhs.uk](https://www.nhs.uk)

---

## What Happens in Angioedema?

- The body swells quickly in one area.  
- The swelling may be itchy or painful.  
- It often comes with hives (raised, itchy spots on the skin).  
- The face is most often affected.  
  - This includes the lips, tongue, and eyelids.  
- Hands, feet, and genitals can also swell.  
- Sometimes the stomach swells, which causes pain.  
- In rare cases, the throat swells.  
  - This can make it hard to breathe.  
  - This is a medical emergency.

---

## How Is Angioedema Treated?

- If the swelling is mild and small, you may not need treatment.  
- If the swelling is severe or affects your lips, tongue, or throat, you will likely need emergency care in hospital.

Treatments include:

- Finding and avoiding the cause.  
  - If a medicine is causing the swelling, your doctor may switch you to a different one.  
- Antihistamine tablets.  
  - Examples: cetirizine, fexofenadine, loratadine.  
- Steroid tablets.  
  - Example: prednisolone.  

If you have a type of angioedema that keeps coming back (hereditary angioedema), you may need special medicine to prevent attacks.

You will have regular check-ups to see if your treatment is working.  
If your symptoms do not get better or get worse, you may need to go back to hospital for more tests and care.

---

## Types of Angioedema

There are different kinds of angioedema:

- **Allergic angioedema** – caused by an allergy to something like food, medicine, or insect stings.  
- **Non-allergic angioedema** – not caused by an allergy.  
- **Idiopathic angioedema** – the cause is unknown.  
- **Hereditary angioedema** – a rare type passed down in families. It can cause repeated swelling attacks.

# Oropharyngeal Squamous Cell Carcinoma – Simple Explanation

This document explains oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma in plain language. It covers what it is, who gets it, symptoms, how it is diagnosed, how it is treated, and what the outlook is.

---

## What Is Oropharyngeal Cancer?

Oropharyngeal cancer is cancer in the back part of the throat. It can start in:

- The tonsils  
- The base of the tongue (back third)  
- The soft part of the roof of the mouth (soft palate)  
- The sides and back walls of the throat  

Over 95 out of 100 cases of oropharyngeal cancer are a type called squamous cell carcinoma. This means the cancer starts in the flat, thin cells that line the inside of the throat.

---

## What Causes Oropharyngeal Cancer?

The main causes are:

- **Human papillomavirus (HPV)** – This is a common virus. HPV type 16 causes most HPV-related oropharyngeal cancers.  
- **Tobacco use** – Smoking or chewing tobacco increases risk.  
- **Alcohol use** – Drinking a lot of alcohol raises the risk.  

HPV is now the leading cause of this cancer in many countries. It is more common in younger people than in the past.

### Risk Factors for HPV-Related Cancer
- Having many sexual partners  
- Having frequent oral sex  

People with HPV-positive cancer have a 16 times higher risk of getting this cancer than those without HPV.

In Europe and North America, HPV causes about 7 out of 10 cases of oropharyngeal cancer.

### Risk Factors for Non-HPV-Related Cancer
- Older age – Most cases happen in people over 60  
- Men are more likely to get it than women (more than twice as many men)  
- Heavy smoking – More than 1.5 packs a day increases risk by about 3 times  
- Heavy drinking – 4 or more drinks a day increases risk by about 7 times  
- Smoking and drinking together – This combination increases risk by 30 times  

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms can vary depending on where the cancer starts. Common signs include:

- A sore throat that does not go away  
- Pain when swallowing  
- Trouble swallowing  
- A lump in the neck – often soft and not painful  
- Slurred speech  
- Ear pain  

These symptoms are similar to those of a cold or sore throat. Because of this, people often wait months before seeing a doctor.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

To diagnose oropharyngeal cancer, doctors use several steps:

### 1. **Laryngoscopy**
A doctor uses a small camera to look inside the throat. This helps see any abnormal areas.

### 2. **Biopsy**
If a suspicious area is found, a small sample of tissue is taken. This is tested in a lab to check for cancer.

### 3. **Imaging Tests**
These help find out how far the cancer has spread. Common tests include:

- CT scan of the neck and chest  
- PET scan of the neck and chest  

### 4. **HPV Testing**
Doctors test the tumor for HPV. This is important because HPV status affects treatment and outlook.

- **HPV DNA test** – This directly checks for the virus.  
- **p16 test** – This is a protein marker. It is often high in HPV-positive cancers. It is used as a sign of HPV infection.

---

## How Is It Staged?

Staging tells doctors how big the tumor is, whether it has spread to lymph nodes, and if it has spread to other parts of the body.

The stage is based on three things:

- **T** – How big the main tumor is and how far it has grown into nearby tissues  
- **N** – Whether cancer has spread to lymph nodes in the neck  
- **M** – Whether cancer has spread to distant organs (like the lungs or liver)

### Staging for HPV-Positive Cancer

| Stage | Tumor Size | Lymph Node Spread | Distant Spread |
|-------|------------|-------------------|----------------|
| I     | Small tumor (up to 4 cm) | No spread or limited spread | None |
| II    | Small tumor | Spread to more lymph nodes | None |
| III   | Any size tumor | Spread to more lymph nodes | None |
| IV    | Any size tumor | Any lymph node spread | Yes, cancer has spread |

### Staging for HPV-Negative Cancer

| Stage | Tumor Size | Lymph Node Spread | Distant Spread |
|-------|------------|-------------------|----------------|
| I     | Small tumor | No spread | None |
| II    | Medium tumor | No spread | None |
| III   | Large tumor | No spread | None |
| IVA   | Large or growing tumor | Limited spread | None |
| IVB   | Very advanced tumor | Any spread | None |
| IVC   | Any size tumor | Any spread | Yes, cancer has spread |

**Note:** HPV-positive cancers tend to grow slower and respond better to treatment. They are often found earlier and have a better outcome.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the stage, location, and HPV status of the cancer.

### Surgery
Surgery is now used more often than in the past.

- **Transoral laser microsurgery (TLM)** – A laser is used through the mouth to remove small tumors. This avoids open surgery and has fewer side effects.
- **Transoral robotic surgery (TORS)** – A robot with tiny arms and a camera is used. The surgeon controls it from a console. The robot helps see and reach hard-to-reach areas. It causes less damage than open surgery.

For larger tumors, surgery may be followed by radiation or chemotherapy.

### Radiation Therapy
Radiation uses high-energy beams to kill cancer cells.

- It can be used alone for early-stage cancer.
- It is often combined with chemotherapy for advanced cancer (called chemoradiation).
- **Intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT)** is used to protect healthy tissue and reduce long-term side effects.

### Neck Lymph Node Treatment
Because the throat has many lymph nodes, cancer often spreads there.

- If lymph nodes do not shrink after radiation or chemoradiation, surgery may be needed to remove them.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

The 5-year survival rate for oropharyngeal cancer is about 52%. But this number depends on HPV status.

- **HPV-positive patients** – More than 80% survive 5 years without cancer returning.  
- **HPV-negative patients** – Less than 50% survive 5 years without cancer returning.

HPV-positive cancers respond better to treatment. This is because:

- The cancer cells grow more slowly  
- Patients are often younger and healthier  
- The body’s immune system may help fight the cancer

High levels of the p16 protein are linked to better outcomes in both HPV-positive and HPV-negative cancers.

---

## Key Points

- Most oropharyngeal cancers are caused by HPV infection.  
- Common symptoms include a sore throat, trouble swallowing, and a lump in the neck.  
- Diagnosis involves a camera exam, biopsy, and imaging tests.  
- Surgery using lasers or robots is now a common option. It avoids open surgery and causes less harm.  
- Radiation therapy, sometimes with chemotherapy, is used for early or advanced cancer.  
- HPV-positive cancers have a much better chance of being cured than HPV-negative ones.  
- Doctors are studying ways to use less intense treatment for HPV-positive cancers to reduce side effects.

# Strongyloidiasis – Simple Explanation

Strongyloidiasis is an infection caused by a tiny worm called *Strongyloides stercoralis*. This worm is a type of roundworm.

## How People Get Infected

- Most people get infected by walking barefoot on soil that has the worm larvae in it.
- The larvae can go through the skin and enter the body.
- The worm lives in the small intestine and lays eggs there.
- The eggs hatch into larvae, which come out in the stool.
- In the soil, the larvae grow into a form that can infect people again.

## Who Is at Risk?

- The infection is most common in warm, wet areas like the tropics and subtropics.
- It is also found in rural parts of the southern United States.
- People with weak immune systems are at higher risk for serious problems.
- This includes people with cancer, those on certain medicines that lower immunity, or those who had an organ or bone marrow transplant.
- People with advanced HIV (AIDS) are less likely to get the severe form of the infection.

## Symptoms

Most people do not have any symptoms.

When symptoms do happen, they can include:
- A red, itchy rash where the larvae entered the skin.
- Coughing or wheezing when larvae pass through the lungs.
- Belly pain, diarrhea, or loss of appetite.
- Weight loss over time.

If the infection becomes severe, it can cause:
- Trouble breathing or coughing up blood.
- Blockage or bleeding in the intestines.
- Problems absorbing food and nutrients.
- Inflammation of the brain and spinal cord (meningitis).
- A brain abscess (a pocket of infection in the brain).
- Liver problems (hepatitis).
- Serious infections in the blood or inside the belly (peritonitis).

Severe infections can be deadly, especially in people with weak immune systems.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors look for the worm or signs of infection using:
- Stool samples: They check for worm larvae under a microscope.
- Blood tests: These look for antibodies (the body’s defense proteins) against the worm.
- Sputum (phlegm) samples: Used if the infection is severe.
- Chest x-rays: To check for lung problems.
- Endoscopy: A thin tube is passed through the mouth into the small intestine to take tissue samples.

A high number of a certain type of white blood cell (eosinophils) in the blood is common in this infection.

Blood tests can show if you have been infected, but they cannot tell if it is a new or old infection. They also cannot always tell the difference between this worm and other similar worms.

## Treatment

Everyone with strongyloidiasis must be treated.

For most cases:
- Doctors give a medicine called ivermectin. It is taken by mouth.
- Another option is albendazole, also taken by mouth.
- Ivermectin works better than albendazole.

Important note:
- If you have been in Africa and might have *Loa loa* worm infection, doctors will test you first.
- Ivermectin can cause serious brain swelling if you have both worms at once.

For severe cases (hyperinfection or disseminated infection):
- Doctors give ivermectin right away.
- Treatment continues until no worm larvae are found in stool or sputum for two weeks.
- These are life-threatening emergencies. Treatment must start fast.

If your immune system is weak, you may need more than one round of medicine.

If bacteria spread in the body (a common complication), antibiotics are used.

To check if the infection is gone:
- Doctors test stool samples again after treatment.
- If worms are still found, treatment is repeated.

## Prevention

You can reduce your risk by:
- Using clean toilets and proper sanitation.
- Avoiding direct skin contact with soil in areas where the worm is common.
- Always wearing shoes when walking outside.
- Using a tarp or mat when sitting on the ground.

This infection affects about 614 million people worldwide. It is one of the most common worm infections spread through dirty soil.

# Rheumatic Fever

Rheumatic fever usually starts 1 to 5 weeks after a throat infection.  
It can cause a high temperature, joint pain, and trouble breathing.

You will need medicine to treat rheumatic fever.  
You may also need long-term care for heart problems.  
This care helps prevent rheumatic fever from coming back.

Rheumatic fever happens after a bacterial infection in the throat or on the skin.  
It is not caused by the bacteria directly.  
Instead, your body’s immune system reacts too strongly.  
It attacks healthy tissue by mistake.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:
- You have had rheumatic fever before and now have a sore throat.
- You think rheumatic fever has come back.
- You recently had a bacterial throat infection and now have symptoms of rheumatic fever.

## Symptoms of Rheumatic Fever

Symptoms usually appear 1 to 5 weeks after a throat infection.  
They can include:
- A high temperature.
- Pain and swelling in your joints. This often affects the ankles, knees, wrists, or elbows.  
  Your joints may look red, but this may be hard to see on brown or black skin.
- Chest pain, trouble breathing, or a fast heartbeat.
- Jerky, uncontrolled movements in your hands, feet, or face.
- Small lumps under your skin.
- Pale-red spots on your arms or belly. These may be hard to see on brown or black skin.

## How Rheumatic Fever Is Treated

If you or your child is diagnosed with rheumatic fever, treatment will help ease symptoms and reduce swelling.

You may need:
- Antibiotics to treat the infection.
- Painkillers in tablet, capsule, or liquid form.
- Steroids if the pain is very bad.
- Medicines to control jerky, uncontrolled movements.

Resting in bed is also important.  
It helps your body heal.

### Recovery

Most people get better within about 3 months.  
Some may take longer to recover.

### Long-Term Care

If you’ve had rheumatic fever once, it can come back.  
Treat sore throats early to lower the risk.

You may need to take antibiotics for several years to prevent it from returning.

The chance of it coming back is lower after 5 years without an episode.  
Younger people are more likely to have it return.

Rheumatic fever can also damage your heart over time.  
This damage may not show up for years.  
You may need regular check-ups and treatment later in life.

Always ask your doctor what long-term care you need.

## What Causes Rheumatic Fever

Rheumatic fever happens after a bacterial infection in the throat or on the skin.  
Most people with such infections do not get rheumatic fever.

It is not caused by the bacteria itself.  
It is caused by your immune system.  
Your immune system fights the infection but then attacks your own healthy tissue.

Doctors do not know exactly why this happens.  
But your genes may increase your risk of getting rheumatic fever.

# Vestibular Neuronitis – Simple Explanation

## What Is Vestibular Neuronitis?

Vestibular neuronitis is a condition that causes a sudden, severe spinning sensation. This spinning feeling is called vertigo. It usually lasts for a few days to a couple of weeks. The problem comes from inflammation in a nerve that helps control balance. This nerve is part of the eighth cranial nerve.

Some people may still feel unsteady after the main episode is over. This is because the balance system may not fully recover.

Sometimes people use the term "viral labyrinthitis" to describe this condition. But there is a key difference. Vestibular neuronitis only causes vertigo. Viral labyrinthitis also causes ringing in the ears or hearing loss, or both.

Doctors think a virus may be the cause. But the exact reason is not known. The condition usually affects only one side of the body.

---

## Symptoms and Signs

- You will have one sudden, very bad episode of vertigo.
- The vertigo feels like the room is spinning.
- You may feel sick to your stomach and throw up.
- Your eyes will move in a jerky way. This is called nystagmus.
- The eye movements will be toward the side that is not affected.
- The eye movements are steady and horizontal. They happen without you trying.
- The fast part of the eye movement points toward the healthy ear.

The most important clue is that you do **not** have ringing in the ears or hearing loss. This helps doctors tell the difference between vestibular neuronitis and other conditions like Meniere disease or labyrinthitis.

The symptoms slowly get better over days or weeks. But some people still feel off-balance, especially when they move their head quickly. This may be due to lasting damage to the balance system.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

To make sure this is not another serious condition, your doctor may order tests:

- **Hearing test** – to check if your hearing is normal.
- **Eye movement test** – this checks how your eyes move when your balance system is tested. It includes a caloric test.
- **MRI scan of the head** – this looks at the brain and nerves. Special attention is given to the inner ear area. This helps rule out tumors, bleeding, or stroke.

The MRI may show swelling in the balance nerve. This supports the diagnosis of inflammation.

---

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure for the inflammation itself. But treatment helps you feel better while your body heals.

### Short-term relief:
- Medicines to stop nausea and vomiting (like prochlorperazine or promethazine).
- Antihistamines or benzodiazepines to calm the dizziness.
- A short course of steroid medicine (cortisone) that is stopped quickly.

If you are vomiting a lot, you may need fluids and salts through a vein (IV). This helps prevent dehydration.

### Important:
Do not take dizziness medicines for more than a few weeks. These drugs can slow down your body’s natural recovery. This is especially true for older adults.

### Long-term help:
- Vestibular rehabilitation therapy – this is a type of physical therapy.
- A trained therapist will guide you through exercises.
- These exercises help your brain learn to use other senses to keep your balance.

---

## Key Points

- You will have a sudden, severe spinning feeling. It lasts for days to weeks.
- You may feel sick and throw up.
- Your eyes will move in a jerky way toward the healthy side.
- You will **not** have hearing loss or ringing in the ears.
- Tests are needed to rule out other serious problems like tumors or stroke.
- Treatment focuses on relieving symptoms.
- Medicines like anti-nausea drugs, antihistamines, or benzodiazepines can help.
- Steroids may also be useful.
- Physical therapy can help with long-term balance problems.

# Fibromyalgia

Fibromyalgia causes pain, tiredness, trouble sleeping, and a feeling of mental fog. The pain affects soft parts of the body like muscles, tendons, and ligaments all over the body.

## What Is Fibromyalgia?

- Fibromyalgia is not a dangerous or life-threatening condition.
- It is common, especially in women. It is about seven times more common in women than in men.
- It usually starts in young or middle-aged women, but it can also happen in men, children, and teens.
- It used to be called fibrositis or fibromyositis syndrome.
- It is not an autoimmune disease. But some people with fibromyalgia also have other long-term health problems like rheumatoid arthritis or lupus.
- Fibromyalgia is not the same as myofascial pain syndrome. But both cause pain that comes from the nervous system. Myofascial pain is mostly in the muscles. Fibromyalgia causes pain all over the body and other symptoms too.

## What Causes Fibromyalgia?

- People with fibromyalgia feel pain more strongly than others.
- Their brain and nerves react more to pain signals.
- The exact cause is often unknown.
- Poor sleep, repeated strain, injuries, and stress may play a role.
- How a person handles stress may matter more than how much stress they have.
- Some people with fibromyalgia also have connective tissue diseases like rheumatoid arthritis or lupus.
- Infections like Lyme disease or possibly COVID-19 can trigger fibromyalgia in some people.
- Traumatic events, such as accidents or serious emotional stress, may also start it.

## What Are the Symptoms?

- Most people feel a deep ache, stiffness, and pain all over the body.
- The pain can be in any soft tissue — muscles, tendons, or ligaments.
- Common areas: neck, upper shoulders, chest, ribs, lower back, thighs, arms, and around joints.
- Less often, the lower legs, hands, and feet are painful or stiff.
- Symptoms may come and go (flare-ups) or stay all the time (chronic).
- Pain often gets worse with tiredness, overuse, or physical strain.
- Some spots on the body are very tender when pressed. These are called tender points.
- During flare-ups, muscles may tighten or spasm.
- Many people have trouble sleeping and feel anxious, tense, or sad.
- Fatigue is very common.
- Many have trouble focusing, remembering things, or thinking clearly. This is often called “brain fog.”
- Some people are perfectionists or have a high-pressure personality.
- Other common problems include:
  - Migraines or tension headaches
  - Irritable bowel syndrome (bloating, constipation, diarrhea, stomach pain)
  - A bladder problem called interstitial cystitis (pain when urinating)
  - Tingling or numbness in both sides of the body
- Other health issues can make fibromyalgia worse. These include:
  - Inflammatory arthritis (like rheumatoid arthritis)
  - Sleep problems from sleep apnea or depression

## How Is Fibromyalgia Diagnosed?

There is no single test for fibromyalgia. Doctors diagnose it based on symptoms and by ruling out other conditions.

### Key signs doctors look for:
- Pain in many parts of the body
- Pain on both sides of the body
- Pain above and below the waist
- Pain in the spine, chest, or lower back
- Fatigue that is a major symptom
- Symptoms lasting at least three months

### What doctors do:
- They do a full physical exam.
- They may do blood tests to check for other diseases.
- Blood tests can show if someone has antinuclear antibodies (ANA). This is common in lupus and other autoimmune diseases.
- But a positive ANA test alone does not mean you have fibromyalgia. Many healthy people, especially women, have it.

### Why diagnosis can be hard:
- Fibromyalgia shares symptoms with other long-term conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and ankylosing spondylitis.
- A doctor can often tell the difference by examining the body and reviewing symptoms.

## How Is Fibromyalgia Treated?

There is no cure, but treatment can help you feel better. The best results come from combining several approaches.

### Lifestyle Changes That Help:
- **Reduce stress** through deep breathing, meditation, or mindfulness.
- **Talk to a counselor** or mental health professional.
- **Stretch gently** every day. Hold each stretch for 30 seconds. Repeat 5 times.
- **Exercise regularly** on a set schedule. Start slow and build up.
  - Good choices: walking, using a treadmill, exercise bike, elliptical machine, or swimming.
- **Apply heat** to sore areas.
- **Get a massage** to help relax tight muscles.
- **Sleep well**. This is very important.

### Tips for Better Sleep:
- Avoid caffeine and other stimulants in the evening.
- Sleep in a quiet, dark room with comfortable bedding.
- Do not eat or watch TV in bed.
- Stick to a regular sleep schedule.

### Medications That May Help:
- **Tricyclic antidepressants** like amitriptyline. These are taken at bedtime to help with sleep, not depression.
- **Cyclobenzaprine**, a muscle relaxant. Taken at bedtime to help sleep.
  - These medicines are safer than sleeping pills, which can be addictive.
  - Side effects may include drowsiness and dry mouth, especially in older adults.
  - Taking them during the day can cause drowsiness.

- **Pain relievers** like acetaminophen or NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen) can help with pain.
- **Opioids** are not used. They can harm sleep, lead to addiction, and stop working over time.

- **Pregabalin**, **duloxetine**, and **milnacipran** are sometimes used.
  - These are not painkillers in the usual sense.
  - They may help a little when used with sleep improvement, exercise, and stress management.

- **Local anesthetics** like lidocaine can be injected into very tender spots.
  - This helps only for that one spot.
  - It should not be used often.
  - It does not help with pain all over the body.

### Other Helpful Treatments:
- **Capsaicin cream** (applied to skin)
- **Biofeedback** (learning to control body functions)
- **Massage therapy**
- **Hypnotherapy**
- **Chiropractic care**
- Other complementary or alternative therapies

## What Is the Outlook?

- Fibromyalgia is usually long-term.
- It may improve on its own if stress goes down.
- Even with treatment, many people still have some symptoms.
- With the right care, most people can live well and manage their symptoms.

# Mallet Finger

## What Is Mallet Finger?

The main sign of mallet finger is that you cannot straighten the tip of your finger.  
The finger may also hurt and look swollen.

## Symptoms

You may notice:
- The tip of your finger bends down and will not stay straight.
- Pain or tenderness in the finger.
- Swelling or bruising on the finger.

## What to Do Before Seeing a Doctor

If you think you have mallet finger, do these things while waiting for medical help:
- Keep your hand raised above your heart to reduce swelling.
- Take painkillers if you need them.
- Take off any rings from the finger.

## Getting Help

Call NHS 111 or visit the 111 online service if:
- You cannot straighten your finger.
- The finger is painful or tender.
- The finger is swollen or bruised.

## Treatment

Your finger must stay straight while it heals.  
A doctor or nurse will put a splint on the end of your finger.  
The splint will keep the tip of your finger straight.  
You can still bend the middle joint of your finger.

You will need to:
- Keep the splint dry. Wet skin under the splint can become sore.
- Wear the splint for 6 to 8 weeks.  
  Only take it off to clean your finger and the splint.

If the injury does not heal, you may need to wear the splint for another 8 weeks.

In rare cases, surgery may be needed.

## How to Clean Your Finger and Splint

Clean your finger and splint every day.  
It helps to have someone assist you.

Always keep the fingertip straight when the splint is off.

Steps:
1. Place your finger flat on a table.
2. Cut the tape and gently slide the splint off.
3. Wash the finger and splint with soap and water.
4. Dry both the finger and splint completely.
5. Slide the splint back on, making sure the fingertip stays straight.
6. Put new tape in place.  
   The middle joint can move, but the injured joint must not move.

## Recovery

It can take several months for your finger to feel normal again.  
You may still feel:
- Tenderness
- Swelling
- Redness

Redness may be harder to see on brown or black skin.

You may need to take time off work, depending on your job.

## What Not to Do

- Do not bend your finger. Bending it will stop the injury from healing.
- Do not do sports or any activity that uses your hands.

## Additional Information

About 6 to 8 weeks after your injury, your doctor or nurse may give you hand exercises to help with recovery.

# Chest Pain

Chest pain is a common reason people go to the doctor.  
Many people know it can be a sign of a serious health problem.  
They often come in even if the pain is mild.  
Some people with serious conditions ignore the pain or downplay it.  
How people feel pain can be very different.  
Men and women may describe the pain in different ways.  
No matter how the pain is described, it should never be ignored.  
Always find out what is causing it.

---

## What Causes Chest Pain?

The heart, lungs, food pipe, and large blood vessels send pain signals through the same nerves in the chest.  
A problem in any of these organs can cause pain in the chest.  
But the pain can also be felt in other areas.  
This is called referred pain.  
It may show up in the arms, back, jaw, or even the belly.  
Pain from the chest area can feel like pressure, tearing, gas, indigestion, burning, or aching.  
Sometimes it feels sharp or like a needle.  
Some people do not think they are in pain.  
They say it is just discomfort.

---

## What Can Cause Chest Pain?

Many different health problems can cause chest pain.  
These include issues with the heart, lungs, stomach, nerves, or muscles and bones in the chest.  

### Some causes are life-threatening and need urgent care:

- Heart attack or unstable chest pain (acute coronary syndrome)  
- A tear in the main blood vessel in the chest (aortic dissection)  
- Air trapped in the chest cavity that presses on the heart (tension pneumothorax)  
- A hole in the food pipe (esophageal rupture)  
- A blood clot in the lung (pulmonary embolism)

### Other causes are serious but not always life-threatening.

### The most common causes are:

- Problems with the chest wall (muscles, ribs, or cartilage)  
- Inflammation of the lining around the lungs (pleuritis)  
- Digestive issues like acid reflux, stomach spasms, ulcers, or gallstones  
- Heart-related chest pain (angina or heart attack)

In some cases, doctors cannot find a clear cause even after full testing.

---

### Common Causes of Chest Pain – What to Look For

| Cause | What It Feels Like | How It’s Diagnosed |
|------|---------------------|--------------------|
| **Heart attack or unstable chest pain** | Sudden, heavy pressure in the chest. Pain may spread to the jaw or arm. Pain comes with activity and goes away with rest. | ECG, blood tests for heart damage, sometimes an ultrasound of the heart or heart catheterization |
| **Aortic dissection** | Sudden, sharp, tearing pain that moves to the back. May cause fainting, stroke, or weak legs. One arm may have a weaker pulse than the other. | Blood tests, chest X-ray, CT scan, or ultrasound of the heart |
| **Inflammation of the heart muscle (myocarditis)** | Fever, shortness of breath, tiredness, chest pain. Often follows a recent virus or infection. | ECG, blood tests, heart ultrasound, or MRI |
| **Inflammation of the lining around the heart (pericarditis)** | Sharp pain that gets worse when breathing, swallowing, or lying down. Eases when sitting up. | ECG, blood tests, heart ultrasound |
| **Rupture of the food pipe** | Severe pain after vomiting or a medical test. Air under the skin may be felt. | Chest X-ray, special test using contrast dye |
| **Pancreatitis** | Pain in the upper belly or chest. Worse when lying flat. Eases when leaning forward. May include vomiting, fever, and shock. | Blood test for pancreas enzymes, CT scan of the belly |
| **Gallbladder problems** | Pain in the upper right belly or chest after eating. Not linked to exercise. | Ultrasound of the gallbladder, sometimes a special scan |
| **Esophageal motility disorders** | Long-term pain that may come with trouble swallowing. | Barium swallow, esophageal pressure test |
| **Acid reflux (GERD)** | Burning pain that moves from the belly to the throat. Worse when bending over or lying down. Eases with antacids. | Doctor’s exam, sometimes endoscopy or testing |
| **Stomach ulcer** | Recurring vague pain in the belly. Often eased by food or antacids. More common in people who smoke or drink a lot. | Doctor’s exam, sometimes endoscopy, test for bacteria |
| **Pulmonary embolism** | Sharp pain with breathing, shortness of breath, fast heartbeat. May have mild fever or cough up blood. More likely with risk factors. | ECG, chest X-ray, blood tests, sometimes CT scan of the lungs |
| **Tension pneumothorax** | Severe shortness of breath, low blood pressure, neck veins swollen, one side of the chest has weak breath sounds. | Clinical exam, chest X-ray, sometimes bedside ultrasound |
| **Pneumonia** | Fever, chills, cough, sometimes thick mucus. May have shortness of breath and signs of lung infection. | Chest X-ray |
| **Pneumothorax** | Pain with breathing, weak breath sounds on one side, sometimes air under the skin. | Chest X-ray, sometimes ultrasound or CT scan |
| **Pleuritis** | Pain when breathing or coughing. May follow a cold or lung infection. | Doctor’s exam, sometimes chest X-ray |
| **Cancer in the chest** | Pain that may come and go. May include chronic cough, weight loss, fever, or swollen neck glands. | Chest X-ray, CT scan, sometimes bone scan |
| **Muscle or bone pain in the chest** | Pain that lasts for days. Gets worse with movement or pressure. | Doctor’s exam, tenderness on touch |
| **Fibromyalgia** | Constant pain in many parts of the body, including the chest. Often includes fatigue and poor sleep. | Doctor’s exam, tender spots on the body |
| **Shingles (herpes zoster)** | Sharp, band-like pain on one side of the chest. A rash with blisters appears later. Pain may start before the rash. | Doctor’s exam |
| **No clear cause** | Pain with no obvious reason. No warning signs. | Diagnosis after ruling out other causes |

> **Note:**  
> - **1** = Immediate life threat  
> - **2** = Possible life threat  
> - **3** = Uncomfortable but usually not dangerous  

---

## What Tests Are Done?

Most people with chest pain should have:
- A pulse oximeter to check oxygen levels  
- An ECG (electrocardiogram) to check the heart  
- A chest X-ray to look at the lungs and heart  

If heart problems are suspected:
- Blood tests to check for heart damage  
- An ultrasound of the heart (echocardiogram)  
- A CT scan of the heart or a heart catheterization  

---

## What Are Red Flag Signs?

These signs mean the pain could be serious.  
You should get help right away if you have:
- Fast or slow heartbeat  
- Low blood pressure  
- Fast breathing  
- Confusion or pale skin  
- Sweating  
- Trouble breathing  
- One side of the chest with weaker breath sounds or pulses  
- New heart murmur  
- A drop in blood pressure when you breathe in (more than 10 mm Hg)

---

## How Is Chest Pain Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause.  
If the cause is not clearly harmless, you will likely be admitted to the hospital.  
You will be watched closely and tested further.  

Pain is treated with:
- Acetaminophen (Tylenol)  
- Opioids (like morphine) if needed  

Pain relief from medicine does not mean the problem is not serious.  
Always keep looking for a life-threatening cause.

If a blood clot in the lung is likely:
- Blood thinners (anticoagulants) should be started right away.  
- Waiting can be deadly.  
- Treatment can begin while tests are still being done.

---

## Special Considerations for Older Adults

Older people are more likely to have serious causes of chest pain.  
They may take longer to recover, but they can still get better with proper care.  
Doctors often use lower doses of medicine.  
They increase the dose slowly.  
Many older adults have other long-term health problems, like kidney disease.  
These can make diagnosis and treatment harder.

---

## Key Points

- Always rule out life-threatening causes first.  
- Heart attacks and blood clots in the lungs often do not cause classic symptoms.  
- Most people should get:  
  - Pulse oximetry  
  - ECG  
  - Blood tests for heart damage  
  - Chest X-ray  
- Testing must be fast.  
  - If you have a heart attack with certain changes on the ECG, you must get treatment within 90 minutes.  
- If a blood clot in the lung is likely, start blood thinners right away.  
  - Waiting can be fatal.

# Acute Necrotizing Ulcerative Gingivitis (ANUG)

ANUG is a painful gum infection. It can cause fever, bad breath, and a general feeling of being unwell.

## What Causes ANUG?

- The mouth has many types of bacteria. Normally, they do not cause harm.
- If these bacteria grow too much, they can cause an infection in the gums.
- Poor cleaning of the teeth and mouth makes this more likely.
- Stress, not eating well, not getting enough sleep, and smoking also increase the risk.
- ANUG is more common in people who already have mild gum disease.
- It is more likely to happen after a stressful event, like a big exam or military training.
- People with weak immune systems are more at risk. This includes people with HIV/AIDS or those on certain medicines that lower immunity.
- ANUG is not spread from person to person.

### Did You Know...

- ANUG used to be called "trench mouth."
- The name came from soldiers in World War I who got this infection while living in the trenches.

## Symptoms of ANUG

- The gums become painful and start bleeding easily.
- You may make more saliva than usual.
- Your breath may smell very bad.
- You may feel sick and have a fever.
- The gums between your teeth look like they are missing or have holes.
- Sores form on the gums. These sores are covered with a grayish layer of dead tissue.
- Talking, eating, or swallowing hurts.
- The glands under your jaw may swell.
- A mild fever may develop.

## How Is ANUG Diagnosed?

- A dentist will look at your mouth and gums.
- If your breath smells very bad, the dentist may suspect ANUG right away.
- The look of your gums often confirms the diagnosis.
- If the gums do not improve quickly with treatment, the dentist may do more tests to rule out other causes.

## How Is ANUG Treated?

### Step 1: Professional Cleaning
- A dentist will clean your teeth gently and thoroughly over several days.
- This helps remove the bacteria and dead tissue.

### Step 2: Rinses at Home
- Rinse your mouth with salt water.
- Or use a mix of half water and half regular hydrogen peroxide from the drugstore.
- Or use chlorhexidine, an antiseptic mouthwash.
- Rinsing is better than brushing at first. Your gums are too sore for brushing.
- After a few days, you can start brushing gently with a soft toothbrush.
- You can also use a washcloth to wipe your teeth.

### Step 3: Antibiotics (if needed)
- If you cannot get a cleaning right away, your doctor may give you antibiotics by mouth.
- Common antibiotics include metronidazole, amoxicillin, clindamycin, erythromycin, or tetracycline.

### Step 4: Good Daily Care
- Brush your teeth every day.
- Floss every day.
- Rest as much as you can.
- Drink plenty of fluids.
- Eat healthy, nutritious foods.
- Take pain medicine if needed.
- Avoid smoking.
- Avoid hot or spicy foods.

## Prevention and Long-Term Care

- Good oral hygiene is the best way to prevent ANUG.
- Brush your teeth twice a day.
- Floss every day.
- Avoid smoking.
- Manage stress.
- Eat a balanced diet.
- Get enough sleep.

## Useful Resources

- **Mouth Healthy**  
  This site gives general advice on oral health.  
  It includes tips on healthy eating, how to pick good toothbrushes and toothpaste, and how to find a dentist.

- **National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research**  
  This government website has information on oral health in both English and Spanish.  
  It explains common terms and shares the latest research on dental diseases.

# Glandular Fever

Glandular fever is a common illness. It mostly affects people between 15 and 24 years old.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may have:
- A high temperature
- Swollen glands in your neck, head, armpits, elbows, or groin
- A sore throat
- A rash that may be hard to see on black or brown skin
- Headaches
- Feeling very tired

## How to Feel Better at Home

Glandular fever will get better on its own. Most people start to feel better in 2 to 4 weeks.

You can help ease your symptoms by:
- Taking it easy and resting
- Drinking plenty of fluids
- Sipping fluids often if swallowing is painful
- Taking painkillers like paracetamol or ibuprofen
  - Do not give aspirin to children under 16

Avoid:
- Heavy lifting
- Playing sports or doing other hard physical activities

## How to Stop It from Spreading

Glandular fever spreads through spit. You can pass it on by:
- Kissing someone
- Sharing cups, glasses, or cutlery
- Giving blood

You can spread the virus even before you feel sick. You may still be able to pass it on for several months after you feel better.

You can return to work or school when you start to feel better.

To stop spreading the illness:
- Wash your hands often
- Wash any items that may have spit on them
- Do not kiss others
- Do not share cups or cutlery
- Do not give blood

## When to Get Help

### See a Doctor if you have:
- A very high temperature or feel hot and shivery
- A severe sore throat
- Swelling on both sides of your neck (swollen glands)
- Extreme tiredness or feeling completely worn out
- A sore throat that does not improve

### Call NHS 111 if you have:
- Trouble breathing
- More shortness of breath than usual
- Pain or difficulty swallowing

### Call 999 if you:
- Cannot swallow, even your own spit
- Are gasping for air or choking
- Cannot speak because of breathing trouble
- Have severe stomach pain

> **Important:** Do not drive yourself to the emergency department.  
> The person you speak to on 999 will tell you what to do next.

## Find Your Nearest A&E

Check your local hospital’s emergency department page to find the nearest one.

# Legionella Infections

Legionella pneumophila is a type of bacteria.  
It most often causes a serious lung infection called pneumonia.  
This infection can also affect other parts of the body.  

## How People Get Infected

The bacteria live in water.  
You can get infected by breathing in tiny droplets of water that are contaminated.  
This often happens from showers, air conditioners, or hot tubs.  
The bacteria do not spread from person to person.  

## What Happens When You Are Infected

There are two main types of illness:  
- **Legionnaires’ disease** – a serious lung infection.  
- **Pontiac fever** – a milder illness that feels like the flu.  

### Legionnaires’ Disease

The symptoms usually start 2 to 10 days after exposure.  
You may feel very sick with a high fever and chills.  
You may also have body aches, headache, or confusion.  
Other common symptoms include nausea, stomach pain, diarrhea, and a dry cough.  
Some people have trouble breathing, sharp chest pain, or cough up blood.  
In severe cases, your heart may beat slower than normal for your fever.  

The death rate for this illness is about 10 to 15% in most cases.  
It can be much higher in older adults, people in the hospital, or those with weak immune systems.  

### Pontiac Fever

This is a mild illness.  
It feels like a bad case of the flu.  
It does not affect the lungs.  
It goes away on its own without treatment.  
It does not cause long-term problems.  

## How Doctors Diagnose Legionella Infections

Doctors use several tests to find out if you have a Legionella infection.  

### Common Tests

- **Urine test** – This test checks for one specific type of Legionella bacteria.  
  It is accurate 3 days after symptoms start.  
  It only finds about 65% to 90% of all cases because it misses other types.  

- **Sputum or lung fluid culture** – A sample of mucus or fluid from the lungs is tested.  
  This test can confirm the infection.  
  But it takes 3 to 5 days to get results because the bacteria grow slowly.  
  Blood cultures are not useful.  

- **PCR test** – This test looks for the bacteria’s DNA.  
  It is fast and can help track how the infection spread.  

- **Antibody blood test** – This test checks for signs of infection in your blood.  
  It may take time to show results.  
  A fourfold rise in antibodies or a high level in the first test is considered positive.  

- **Fluorescent antibody test** – This is rarely used.  
  It requires special training and is not always reliable.  

### Imaging and Blood Tests

- A chest X-ray is done to check the lungs.  
  It often shows patchy areas of infection that grow quickly.  
  This can happen even if you are getting treatment.  
  Small amounts of fluid around the lungs may also be seen.  

- Blood tests often show low sodium or low phosphate levels.  
  Liver enzymes and a marker of inflammation (C-reactive protein) are often high.  

## How Doctors Treat Legionella Infections

### For Legionnaires’ Disease

- **Fluoroquinolones** – These are strong antibiotics.  
  Examples include levofloxacin and moxifloxacin.  
  They are given by mouth or through a vein.  
  Treatment lasts 7 to 14 days.  
  For people with very weak immune systems, treatment may last up to 3 weeks.  

- **Azithromycin** – This is another effective antibiotic.  
  It is taken for 5 to 10 days.  
  It works well and is often preferred.  

- **Clarithromycin and erythromycin** – These are less effective.  
  They are only used for mild cases in healthy people.  

- **Doxycycline** – This is an option for mild pneumonia in healthy people.  

- **Rifampin** – This medicine is not recommended.  
  It has not been proven to help.  
  It can cause harm.  

### For Pontiac Fever

No treatment is needed.  
The illness goes away on its own.  
It does not cause lasting health problems.  

## Key Facts

- Legionella bacteria most often cause lung infections.  
  They rarely affect other organs, like the heart.  

- The infection comes from breathing in contaminated water droplets.  
  It does not spread from person to person.  

- Diagnosis is best done with a urine test, PCR test, or culture of lung fluid.  
  Culture tests are accurate but take several days.  

- Treatment is with a fluoroquinolone or azithromycin.  
  Doxycycline can be used for mild cases in healthy people.

# Haemophilus influenzae Infections

Haemophilus influenzae are bacteria that can cause infections in the lungs and airways. These infections can spread to other parts of the body.

## How the Infection Spreads

- The bacteria spread through sneezing, coughing, or touching someone who is infected.
- Many types of Haemophilus live in the nose and throat of healthy people. They usually do not cause harm.
- One type causes a sexually transmitted disease called chancroid.
- Other types can cause infections in the heart, brain, lungs, or liver. These are rare.

The most common type that causes illness is Haemophilus influenzae.

This bacteria can infect children and sometimes adults.

## Who Is at Higher Risk?

You are more likely to get this infection if you:
- Are a child, especially a boy
- Are Black or Native American
- Work or go to a day care center
- Live in a crowded home
- Have a weak immune system
- Do not have a spleen
- Have sickle cell disease

## Types of Infections

One type, called Haemophilus influenzae type b, is more likely to cause serious illness.

In children, this type can enter the blood and spread to:
- Joints
- Bones
- Lungs
- Skin on the face and neck
- Eyes
- Urinary tract
- Other organs

It can cause two serious and sometimes deadly infections:
- **Meningitis**: Swelling of the brain and spinal cord coverings and the fluid around them.
- **Epiglottitis**: Swelling of the flap that covers the windpipe when you swallow.

Some strains cause:
- Ear infections in children
- Sinus infections in children and adults
- Lung infections in adults, especially those with long-term lung problems or HIV/AIDS

Symptoms depend on where the infection is in the body.

## How Doctors Diagnose the Infection

To find out if you have a Haemophilus influenzae infection, doctors:
- Take a sample of blood, pus, or another body fluid.
- Send it to a lab to grow the bacteria.
- Test for the bacteria’s genes.

If you have symptoms of meningitis, doctors do a spinal tap. This means they take a small sample of fluid from around the brain and spinal cord.

Finding the bacteria in a sample confirms the diagnosis.

After the bacteria are found, doctors test which antibiotics will work best. This is called susceptibility testing.

## How the Infection Is Treated

Antibiotics are used to treat Haemophilus influenzae infections.

The type of antibiotic depends on:
- How serious the infection is
- Where in the body it is
- The results of the antibiotic tests

### Meningitis

- Must be treated right away.
- You will get antibiotics through a vein (IV). Common ones are ceftriaxone or cefotaxime.
- Steroid medicine may help protect the brain from damage.

### Epiglottitis

- Must be treated right away.
- You may need help breathing.
- A breathing tube may be placed in the windpipe.
- In rare cases, a small hole is made in the windpipe (tracheostomy).
- Antibiotics like ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, or cefuroxime are given through a vein.

### Other Infections

- These are treated with antibiotics taken by mouth.
- Common ones include:
  - Amoxicillin with clavulanate
  - Azithromycin
  - Cephalosporins
  - Fluoroquinolones
  - Omadacycline
  - Lefamulin
  - Clarithromycin

If a child has a serious Haemophilus influenzae infection, they are hospitalized. They are kept in isolation for 24 hours after starting antibiotics. This stops the bacteria from spreading to others through the air.

## How to Prevent Infections

- Children are routinely vaccinated against Haemophilus influenzae type b.
- The Hib vaccine has greatly reduced serious cases of meningitis, epiglottitis, and blood infections.

If someone in your home has a serious Haemophilus influenzae type b infection:
- Any child under 4 who is not fully vaccinated should get the vaccine.
- All other household members (except pregnant women) should take the antibiotic rifampin to prevent infection.

If two or more children in a day care or nursery get this infection within 60 days:
- All adults and children who were in contact with them should take an antibiotic.

# Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS)

Myelodysplastic syndrome is a condition that affects the blood and bone marrow.  
It can cause tiredness, more bleeding than normal, and frequent infections.  
Some people have no symptoms at first.  

Anyone can get MDS.  
It is more common in people over 70.  
It is also more common in men.  
Some people with certain genetic conditions are more likely to get it.  

Doctors diagnose MDS by testing a sample of your bone marrow.  

Treatment depends on your situation.  
It may include chemotherapy or a stem cell transplant.  

---

## Common Symptoms of MDS

Symptoms of MDS are not always clear.  
They can be like symptoms of other health problems.  
You may not notice any symptoms at first.  
Sometimes MDS is found during a blood test done for another reason.  

If you do have symptoms, they can include:  
- Feeling tired or weak  
- Getting out of breath when doing light activity  
- Bleeding more than usual (like frequent nosebleeds, bleeding gums, or heavier periods)  
- Bruising easily  
- Getting sick often or taking longer to get better  
- Looking paler than usual (this may be harder to see on brown or black skin)  
- A rash that looks like small bruises under the skin  
- The rash does not fade when you press a glass against it  

Symptoms usually start slowly and get worse over time.  

---

## Who Is More Likely to Get MDS

MDS can happen to anyone.  
The cause is not known in most cases.  
Rarely, it can be linked to chemotherapy or radiotherapy for another cancer.  

You may be more likely to get MDS if:  
- You are over 70 years old  
- You are a man  
- A close family member has had MDS or a type of blood cancer called acute myeloid leukaemia  
- You have worked with benzene (a chemical found in petrol, cigarette smoke, and the rubber industry)  
- You have certain genetic conditions, such as Down’s syndrome  

---

## Tests for MDS

If your doctor thinks you might have MDS, they will refer you to a blood specialist.  
You may need tests to check for MDS.  

One common test is a bone marrow biopsy.  
This means taking a small sample from your bone marrow.  
The sample is taken using a needle, usually from the back of your hip.  
The sample is then checked for signs of MDS.  

Before the test, you will get a local anaesthetic to numb the area.  
You may also be given medicine to help you relax.  

---

## Treatments for MDS

MDS often grows slowly.  
You may not need treatment right away.  

Your treatment will depend on:  
- How bad your symptoms are  
- The type of MDS you have  
- How fast your symptoms are likely to get worse  
- Your risk of MDS turning into acute myeloid leukaemia  
- Your age  
- Your general health  

If you have low-risk MDS and few symptoms, you will likely just have regular check-ups.  
These include blood tests.  
You may need treatment later if your condition gets worse.  

If you have higher-risk MDS, treatment may include:  
- Chemotherapy  
- A stem cell transplant  
- Medicines called immunosuppressants  
- Targeted medicines  
- Immunotherapy  

You will also get treatments to help with symptoms.  
These are called supportive treatments.  

Your specialist team will:  
- Explain your treatment options, benefits, and possible side effects  
- Work with you to make a treatment plan  
- Help you manage any side effects  

You will have regular check-ups and tests during and after treatment.  

If you have any symptoms or side effects that worry you, talk to your doctor.  
You do not need to wait for your next appointment.  

---

### See a Doctor If:

- You think you might have MDS

# Trisomy 18

Trisomy 18 is a condition that happens when a baby has an extra chromosome 18.  
This extra chromosome causes many health problems.  
It is also called Edwards syndrome.

## What Causes Trisomy 18?

A baby gets one chromosome 18 from each parent.  
In trisomy 18, the baby has three copies of chromosome 18 instead of two.  
This extra chromosome changes how the baby’s body and brain develop.

Most of the time, the extra chromosome comes from the mother.  
The chance of this happening goes up when the mother is older.  
In rare cases, part of chromosome 18 can attach to another chromosome.  
This is called a translocation.

Girls are more likely to have trisomy 18 than boys.  
The ratio is about 3 girls to every 1 boy.

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

Babies with trisomy 18 often have many health problems.  
These problems are present at birth or show up during pregnancy.

### During Pregnancy

Ultrasound scans may show:
- Too much amniotic fluid (polyhydramnios)
- A small placenta
- Only one artery in the umbilical cord
- Slow growth in the womb

### At Birth

Babies with trisomy 18 are usually small.  
They often have:
- Low birth weight
- Weak muscle tone (hypotonia)
- Little muscle and fat under the skin

Their faces look different.  
They have:
- A small head (microcephaly)
- A large back of the head (prominent occiput)
- Ears that are low and shaped oddly
- A small mouth and jaw
- A pinched look to the face

Other common features include:
- Hands that stay clenched, with the index finger covering the other fingers
- Missing crease on the little finger
- Extra skin folds, especially on the neck
- Small or underdeveloped fingernails
- A short big toe that bends upward
- Feet that are turned inward or shaped like a rocker (clubfeet or rocker-bottom feet)

### Heart and Other Organ Problems

Many babies have serious heart problems.  
Common ones are:
- Patent ductus arteriosus (a hole in the heart)
- Ventricular septal defect (a hole in the wall between the heart chambers)

Other organs may also be affected.  
This includes the lungs, diaphragm, stomach, intestines, kidneys, and ureters.

Boys may have undescended testes.  
This means the testicles did not move down into the scrotum.

### Seizures

About 3 out of 10 children with trisomy 18 have seizures.  
These can be full-body, partial, or a mix.

### Muscle and Belly Problems

Many children have:
- Hernias (when part of the intestine pushes through the belly wall)
- A gap between the muscles in the belly (separation of the rectus muscles)

## How Is Trisomy 18 Diagnosed?

### Before Birth

Doctors can suspect trisomy 18 during pregnancy.  
This can happen if:
- Ultrasound shows unusual body parts or slow growth
- Blood tests show abnormal levels of certain markers
- Noninvasive prenatal screening (NIPS) finds a possible problem

NIPS uses a blood sample from the mother.  
It checks for pieces of the baby’s DNA in the mother’s blood.  
But NIPS is not always accurate for trisomy 18.  
It can miss some cases or give false alarms.

If NIPS shows a possible problem, more testing is needed.

To confirm the diagnosis, doctors take a sample of fluid or tissue from the pregnancy.  
This is done through:
- Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) – done early in pregnancy
- Amniocentesis – done later in pregnancy

The sample is tested using:
- Karyotype (a detailed picture of the chromosomes)
- FISH (a test that looks for extra chromosome 18)
- Chromosomal microarray (a test that checks for small changes in DNA)

Sometimes, the extra chromosome is only in the placenta.  
This is called mosaicism.  
If CVS shows trisomy 18, doctors may do amniocentesis or wait for a postnatal test to be sure.

### After Birth

If a baby is born with signs of trisomy 18, a blood test can confirm it.  
This test checks the baby’s chromosomes.

## How Is Trisomy 18 Treated?

There is no cure for trisomy 18.  
The extra chromosome cannot be removed.

Treatment focuses on helping the baby feel better and live as comfortably as possible.

### Supportive Care

Most children need help with:
- Feeding (using a tube in the nose or stomach)
- Breathing (if they have trouble breathing)
- Pain relief
- Seizure control

Some families choose to treat serious health problems.  
Others choose not to do surgery or invasive tests.  
This is a personal decision based on the baby’s condition and family values.

### Care Team

A team of specialists often helps.  
This may include:
- Doctors
- Nurses
- Physical therapists
- Speech therapists
- Feeding specialists

Early therapy is important.  
It can help the child grow and develop as much as possible.

### Family Support

Support for parents and caregivers is very important.  
Counseling and support groups can help families cope.

## What Is the Outlook?

Trisomy 18 is a serious condition.  
More than half of babies do not live past the first week.  
Fewer than 1 in 10 live past their first birthday.

But some children live much longer.  
There are now reports of adults with trisomy 18.  
Each child is different.  
Some live with support for many years.

# Recurrent Miscarriage

Recurrent miscarriage means you have had two or more miscarriages.

A miscarriage is when a pregnancy ends before 20 weeks. Each miscarriage should be checked by a health care provider. This helps decide if further testing is needed.

## What Can Cause Recurrent Miscarriage?

The cause may come from the woman, the man, the baby, or the placenta.

### In the Woman

Common causes in women include:

- Problems with the shape of the uterus or the neck of the uterus (cervix)
- Growths in the uterus called polyps
- Scar tissue inside the uterus, called adhesions
- Weak cervix, which can open too early (cervical insufficiency)
- Chromosome problems in the woman
- Long-term health issues that are not well managed, such as:
  - An underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism)
  - An overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism)
  - Diabetes
  - High blood pressure
  - Chronic kidney disease
- A condition called antiphospholipid syndrome. This makes blood clot too easily. It can cause miscarriages after 10 weeks of pregnancy. The clots can harm the placenta and stop nutrients from reaching the baby.

The more miscarriages a woman has had, the higher the chance of another one. But the risk depends on the cause. Overall, women who have had several miscarriages have about a 1 in 4 chance of having another one.

### In the Man

Chromosome problems in the man can also lead to recurrent miscarriages. Certain issues in the sperm may increase the risk. It is not clear if a man’s age over 35 increases the risk.

### In the Baby

Common causes in the baby include:

- Problems with the baby’s chromosomes or genes
- Birth defects (structural problems)

Chromosome issues in the baby cause about half of all miscarriages. These are more common in early pregnancy.

### In the Placenta

Problems with the placenta can also cause miscarriage. These include:

- Long-term health conditions that are not well controlled, such as:
  - Lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus)
  - Chronic high blood pressure

In up to half of all cases, no clear cause is found.

## How Is Recurrent Miscarriage Diagnosed?

If you have had two or more miscarriages, you may want to see a doctor before trying to get pregnant again.

The doctor will check for possible causes. This may include:

- Genetic tests to look for chromosome problems in both you and your partner
- Imaging tests to check the shape of the uterus. These can include:
  - Ultrasound
  - Sonohysterography
  - Hysterosalpingography
- Blood tests to check for:
  - Antiphospholipid syndrome
  - Diabetes
  - Hormone imbalances
  - Thyroid problems

A diagnosis of recurrent miscarriage is made if you have had two or more miscarriages.

## How Is Recurrent Miscarriage Treated?

If a cause is found, treatment may help.

Some causes can be treated. This can improve the chance of a healthy pregnancy. Treatment depends on the specific cause.

# Compartment Syndrome

## What Is Compartment Syndrome?

Compartment syndrome causes pain in a part of your body. The pain can start suddenly or build up over time.

You can get this condition in any muscle. It most often affects the lower legs and forearms.

## When to Get Help Right Away

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have sudden, severe pain in any part of your body.

If compartment syndrome is causing the pain, you need surgery as soon as possible.

### What We Mean by Severe Pain

Severe pain means:
- The pain is always there and so bad you can’t think clearly or talk.
- You cannot sleep because of the pain.
- It is very hard to move. You may struggle to get out of bed, go to the bathroom, wash, or dress.

### What We Mean by Moderate Pain

Moderate pain means:
- The pain is always there.
- It makes it hard to focus or sleep.
- You can still get up, wash, or dress, but it is difficult.

### What We Mean by Mild Pain

Mild pain means:
- The pain comes and goes.
- It is annoying but does not stop you from doing your normal daily tasks.

### A&E Safety Tips

- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you. Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.
- Bring all your medicines with you when you go to A&E.

## When to See Your Doctor

See your GP if:
- You keep getting pain, numbness, swelling, or trouble moving a body part when you exercise.

Your GP can check if the problem is compartment syndrome or something else.

## Symptoms of Compartment Syndrome

Common symptoms include:
- Pain in a muscle. It may feel like a burning or deep ache. Moving the body part can make the pain worse.
- Swelling or bulging in the muscle.
- Numbness, weakness, or a tingling feeling.
- The area feels tight. You may have trouble moving the part.

### Sudden Onset (Acute) Compartment Syndrome

This type starts quickly. It can happen after an injury. It can also happen if a bandage or cast is too tight.

### Gradual Onset (Chronic) Compartment Syndrome

This builds up over time. It often happens after exercise. The symptoms go away when you rest.

## How It Is Treated

Treatment depends on whether the condition comes on suddenly or gradually.

### Sudden (Acute) Compartment Syndrome

You will need surgery right away to reduce pressure in the muscle.

The surgery is called a fasciotomy. The surgeon makes cuts around the muscle to let the pressure out.

Sometimes, skin from another part of your body is used to cover the wound. This is called a skin graft.

After surgery:
- You will get medicine to help with pain.
- You may need physiotherapy to help you move the affected area again.

### Gradual (Chronic) Compartment Syndrome

You may not need treatment. Many people get better without surgery.

To help relieve symptoms, try:
- Avoiding the activity that caused the problem. For example, if running hurts, try cycling instead.
- Taking anti-inflammatory painkillers to reduce pain and swelling.
- Getting physiotherapy.
- Using shoe inserts (orthotics) if you start running again.

If these steps do not help, surgery may be an option. The surgery is similar to the one used for sudden compartment syndrome.

# Vaginal Wall Prolapse

This condition happens when organs in the pelvis push into the vagina. It can affect the front or back of the vagina.

## What Happens in Vaginal Wall Prolapse?

- **Front of the vagina (anterior)**: The bladder or urethra can push into the vagina. This is called a **cystocele** or **urethrocele**.
- **Back of the vagina (posterior)**: The small intestine or rectum can push into the vagina. This is called an **enterocele** or **rectocele**.

Many women have more than one type at the same time. A cystocele often happens with a urethrocele. An enterocele and rectocele can also happen together.

The main causes are weak tissues that support the organs. These tissues can weaken from childbirth, aging, or heavy lifting.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may feel:
- Fullness or pressure in the pelvis or vagina.
- A heavy or falling feeling in the pelvic area.
- A bulge that sticks out into the vagina or through the vaginal opening.
- This bulge may get worse when you cough, strain, or lift something heavy.

Some women have no symptoms at all, especially with mild prolapse.

Other possible symptoms include:
- Leaking urine when you cough, sneeze, or laugh (stress incontinence).
- Trouble starting to urinate or not being able to empty your bladder completely.
- Feeling like you haven’t finished passing stool.
- Constipation or needing to push with your fingers into the vagina to help pass stool (called splinting).
- Problems with sex, such as pain or feeling self-conscious about changes in your body.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will do a pelvic exam. You will be asked to lie down and then to strain, as if you are having a bowel movement.

- To check for a **cystocele**, your doctor will pull back the back wall of the vagina and look at the front wall.
- To check for an **enterocele** or **rectocele**, your doctor will pull back the front wall of the vagina and look at the back wall.
- A rectovaginal exam may be done. This means your doctor will check the back of the vagina and the rectum at the same time.

You may also be asked to stand on a stool with one knee up and strain. This can help find problems that are not seen when lying down.

Your doctor will also check for urinary incontinence if needed.

The **POP-Q system** is used to measure how severe the prolapse is. It gives a clear picture of the problem.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on your symptoms and how much the prolapse affects your life.

### First, try non-surgical options:
- **Pelvic floor exercises** (like Kegel exercises). These help strengthen the muscles that support the pelvic organs.
- **Pessary**: A small device placed in the vagina to hold the organs in place. It is removable and can be used long-term.

These treatments work well for many women, especially if symptoms are mild.

### Surgery may be an option if:
- The non-surgical treatments do not help.
- You want surgery and your symptoms are bothersome.
- The prolapse is severe.

Surgery aims to fix the weak tissues and support the organs in their normal position.

### Important Notes:
- If you have no symptoms, you do not need treatment.
- Treatment is about improving your quality of life, not just fixing the anatomy.
- You and your doctor will decide the best plan based on your needs and preferences.

## Key Facts

- Vaginal wall prolapse means organs push into the vagina.
- It can happen in the front (bladder or urethra) or back (intestine or rectum).
- Many women have more than one type at once.
- Symptoms include pressure, fullness, bulging, and trouble with urination or bowel movements.
- Diagnosis is done with a pelvic exam, including straining and special checks.
- Treatment starts with exercises or a pessary. Surgery is an option if needed.
- No treatment is needed if there are no symptoms.

# Salivary Gland Cancer

Cancer in the salivary glands is rare. Most growths in these glands are not cancer.  

The most common type of salivary gland cancer is called mucoepidermoid carcinoma. This cancer starts in the cells that make saliva. It can appear in small glands on the roof of the mouth. It can also form as a lump in one of the larger salivary glands. These larger glands are located under or behind the lower jaw.

## Where the Main Salivary Glands Are

(See also: Overview of Mouth, Nose, and Throat Cancers.)

## Signs of Salivary Gland Cancer

Most salivary gland cancers start as a painless lump.  
As the lump grows, it may start to hurt.  
The pain can get worse when you eat. This is because eating makes your salivary glands make more saliva.  
If the cancer spreads to nearby nerves, you may feel numbness or tingling in part of your face.  
You might also have trouble moving your face.

## How Doctors Diagnose Salivary Gland Cancer

Doctors take a small sample of tissue from the gland if they think it might be cancer.  
This is called a biopsy.  
They look at the tissue under a microscope to check for cancer.  
If cancer is found, doctors do imaging tests to see how far it has spread.  
These tests include CT scans and MRI scans.  
Some salivary gland cancers can spread to other parts of the body.  
So doctors may also check the lungs, liver, bones, and brain with imaging tests.

## How Salivary Gland Cancer Is Treated

Most people with this cancer have surgery first.  
The surgeon removes the cancer and nearby tissue.  
Doctors try hard to protect the facial nerve during surgery.  
After surgery, many people get radiation therapy.  
This treatment uses high-energy beams to kill any remaining cancer cells.  
Radiation therapy is used when needed, based on the type and stage of cancer.
