# Chickenpox

Chickenpox causes itchy spots. The spots turn into blisters. Then they form scabs. The rash can appear anywhere on the body. This includes inside the mouth.

Most people get better in 1 to 2 weeks. You can feel better by using cooling creams, antihistamines, and paracetamol.

You can catch chickenpox by being in the same room as someone who has it. You can also catch it by touching objects that have fluid from the blisters on them.

---

## What to expect with chickenpox

The main sign of chickenpox is an itchy rash with spots. The rash can appear anywhere on the body.

Before or after the rash shows up, you may feel:

- Hot or have a fever
- Have body aches
- Feel generally unwell
- Lose your appetite

Chickenpox happens in three stages. New spots can appear while older ones are turning into blisters or scabs.

### Stage 1: Small spots appear

The spots can:

- Show up anywhere on the body
- Appear inside the mouth or around the genitals — these can be painful
- Spread out or stay in one area
- Be red, pink, darker, or the same color as your skin
- Be harder to see on brown or black skin

### Stage 2: Spots turn into blisters

The spots fill with fluid. They become blisters. The blisters are very itchy. They may break open.

### Stage 3: Blisters turn into scabs

The blisters dry up and form scabs. Some scabs are flaky. Others may leak fluid.

---

## How to care for chickenpox at home

Stay away from school, nursery, or work until all the spots have formed scabs. This usually takes about 5 days after the first spots appear.

You do not need to see a doctor. You can treat chickenpox at home.

### Do these things

- Drink plenty of fluids. Try ice lollies if your child is not drinking.
- Take paracetamol to ease pain or discomfort.
- Cut your child’s fingernails short. Put socks on their hands at night to stop them scratching.
- Use cooling creams or gels from the pharmacy.
- Talk to a pharmacist about antihistamine medicine to help with itching.
- Take baths in cool water. Gently pat your skin dry. Do not rub.
- Wear loose, soft clothes.

### Do not do these things

- Do not use ibuprofen unless a doctor tells you to. It can cause serious skin infections.
- Do not give aspirin to anyone under 16 years old.
- Do not scratch the spots. Scratching can leave scars.

### Important

Do not be near newborn babies, pregnant women, or people with weak immune systems. Chickenpox can be dangerous for them.

---

## How chickenpox spreads

You can pass chickenpox to others from 2 days before your spots appear until all the spots have scabs. This usually lasts about 5 days after the spots first show up.

The rash usually appears 1 to 3 weeks after you catch the virus.

You can catch chickenpox from:

- Being in the same room as someone with it
- Touching objects that have fluid from the blisters on them
- Being near someone with shingles, if you have never had chickenpox before

You cannot catch shingles from someone with chickenpox. But someone with shingles can pass chickenpox to you if you have never had it.

# Peritonsillar Abscess and Cellitis

This condition affects the throat and surrounding tissues. It is most common in teenagers and young adults.  
It causes a very bad sore throat on one side of the throat.  
Other symptoms include trouble swallowing, a muffled or "hot potato" voice, and difficulty opening the mouth wide.  
The voice sounds like you are speaking with something hot in your mouth.  
The uvula (the small piece of tissue hanging at the back of the throat) may move to one side.  

A doctor must check for this condition.  
The best way to confirm it is by using a needle to draw fluid from the swollen area.  
Treatment includes antibiotics, draining any pus, staying well hydrated, pain relief, and sometimes surgery to remove the tonsil.  

---

## What Causes This Condition?

The infection starts in the tonsils.  
It spreads to the soft tissues around the tonsil.  
This can lead to either an abscess (a pocket of pus) or cellulitis (swelling and infection in the tissue).  
The infection usually affects only one side of the throat.  
It happens between the tonsil and a muscle in the throat wall.  
Multiple types of bacteria are usually involved.  
The most common bacteria are *Streptococcus* and *Staphylococcus*.  
*Bacteroides* is the most common type of bacteria that grows without oxygen.  

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may feel a worsening sore throat on one side.  
You may have trouble swallowing.  
You may have a fever.  
You may feel ear pain.  
Your neck glands may swell on one side.  

Common signs include:  
- Trouble opening your mouth wide (trismus).  
- A voice that sounds muffled or like you are speaking with something hot in your mouth.  
- A very ill appearance: you may look tired, upset, anxious, or hard to comfort.  
- Drooling.  
- Bad breath.  
- Redness and swelling of the tonsil.  
- Pus or white patches on the tonsil.  

An abscess causes a clear bulge above the tonsil.  
It pushes the soft palate and uvula to the opposite side.  
It also causes more severe jaw stiffness than cellulitis.  

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor will check your throat and ask about your symptoms.  
If you have a severe sore throat and the following signs, you likely have this condition:  
- Trouble opening your mouth wide.  
- A "hot potato" voice.  
- The uvula is pushed to one side.  

All such patients need a needle test.  
The doctor uses a needle to draw fluid from the swollen area.  
If pus comes out, it is an abscess.  
If no pus comes out, it is cellulitis.  

Ultrasound can help guide the needle.  
It shows the best place to drain the fluid.  
Ultrasound is very good at finding the problem.  
But it is not always perfect at telling the difference between an abscess and cellulitis.  

A CT scan of the neck may be needed if:  
- The physical exam is hard to interpret.  
- The diagnosis is unclear.  
- The doctor needs to rule out other serious infections in the neck.  

---

## How Is It Treated?

### For Cellulitis:
- You will get high-dose penicillin through a vein or by mouth.  
- You will drink plenty of fluids.  
- Most people feel better within two days.  
- If you cannot take penicillin, your doctor may use a first-generation cephalosporin or clindamycin.  
- After testing the fluid, your doctor will prescribe antibiotics based on the results.  
- You will take these antibiotics for ten days.  

### For Abscess:
- The doctor will drain the pus.  
- This is usually done in the emergency room.  
- You will get local anesthesia to numb the area.  
- Sometimes, sedation is used to help you relax.  
- Some doctors use a needle to drain the pus.  
- Others make a small cut to drain it.  
- Ultrasound may help guide the needle if the abscess is small or hard to see.  

Most people can go home after treatment.  
Some may need to stay in the hospital for:  
- IV antibiotics.  
- IV fluids.  
- Monitoring of the airway.  

### Tonsillectomy (Tonsil Removal):
- In rare cases, the tonsil is removed right away.  
- This may happen if the patient is young or not able to cooperate.  
- It may also happen if the patient already needs tonsil removal for other reasons, such as frequent tonsillitis or sleep apnea.  
- If you have had many episodes of tonsillitis, your doctor may schedule a tonsillectomy 4 to 6 weeks after the infection clears.  
- This helps prevent the abscess from coming back.

# Bursitis

Bursitis is when a small, fluid-filled cushion in your body becomes inflamed and painful.

These cushions are called bursae. They sit where skin, muscles, tendons, or ligaments rub over bones. They help reduce friction and protect your body from wear and tear.

## What Causes Bursitis?

Bursitis usually happens when a bursa is overused or irritated.  
It can also be caused by an injury.  
Some health conditions can lead to bursitis, including:
- Gout
- Pseudogout
- Rheumatoid arthritis  
- Infections, especially those caused by a type of bacteria called *Staphylococcus aureus*

In many cases, doctors do not know the exact cause.

## Where Does Bursitis Happen?

The shoulder is the most common place for bursitis.  
But it can also happen in the:
- Elbows
- Hips (called trochanteric bursitis)
- Pelvis
- Knees
- Toes
- Heels (called Achilles tendon bursitis)

People with shoulder bursitis often also have inflammation in the tendons around the shoulder. These tendons help move and hold the shoulder in place. This condition is called rotator cuff tendinitis.

## Symptoms of Bursitis

Bursitis usually causes pain and makes movement hard.  
The exact symptoms depend on where the bursa is inflamed.

For example:
- Shoulder bursitis makes it painful to raise your arm out to the side, like when putting on a jacket.
- Elbow bursitis may cause swelling but little pain or trouble moving.

### Acute Bursitis

This type comes on quickly, over hours or days.  
The area is painful when moved or touched.  
If the bursa is near the skin, like in the knee or elbow, the skin may look red and swollen.  
Bursitis caused by infection or gout can be very painful. The area may feel warm to the touch.

### Chronic Bursitis

This type happens when acute bursitis keeps coming back.  
It can also happen after repeated injuries.  
Over time, the walls of the bursa may thicken.  
If you use the area too much, the inflammation can get worse.  
Long-term pain and swelling can make it hard to move.  
This can weaken the muscles.  
Flare-ups can last for months and may return often.

## How Doctors Diagnose Bursitis

Doctors look at your symptoms and examine the painful area.

They may:
- Test fluid taken from the bursa with a needle
- Use imaging tests like X-rays, MRI, or ultrasound

If a bursa near the skin is swollen—like in the knee or elbow—the doctor may take a sample of fluid.  
This helps check for infection or gout.

X-rays are often done if:
- The bursitis does not improve with treatment
- It keeps coming back
- The doctor suspects another joint problem, like arthritis

MRI or ultrasound may be used to see bursitis in deeper areas, like under muscles.

## How Bursitis Is Treated

Treatment depends on the cause and how bad the bursitis is.

### For Acute Bursitis (Not Caused by Infection)

- Rest the joint. Use a splint if needed.
- Apply ice to the painful area.
- Take nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) to reduce pain and swelling.
- After rest, do physical therapy to help regain movement.

Sometimes a doctor gives a stronger pain reliever.  
A local anesthetic and corticosteroid may be injected into the bursa.  
This is often done for shoulder bursitis.  
It can help relieve pain within a few days.  
The injection may need to be repeated after a few months.

Draining fluid from the bursa with a needle can also help reduce pain.

If the pain is very bad, a doctor may give a corticosteroid pill, like prednisone, for a few days.  
As the pain goes down, you can start gentle exercises to improve movement.

### For Chronic Bursitis (Not Caused by Infection)

Treatment is similar, but rest and splints are less helpful.  
Physical therapy is often key.  
Exercises can help rebuild strength and restore full movement.

Surgery to remove the bursa is rare.

### For Infected Bursae

Infected bursae must be drained.  
Antibiotics are given, often to treat *Staphylococcus aureus*.

## Important Notes

Bursitis often comes back if the root cause is not treated.  
This includes conditions like:
- Gout
- Rheumatoid arthritis
- Repeated overuse

Treating the underlying cause helps prevent future flare-ups.

# Miscarriage

## What Are the Signs of a Miscarriage?

You may have a miscarriage if you notice:
- Bleeding from your vagina
- Cramps or pain in your lower belly

Sometimes, you may not have any symptoms. You might only learn about the miscarriage during a routine pregnancy scan.

If you have any of these signs, get help from a doctor or midwife right away.

> Learn more about bleeding during pregnancy and what might cause it.

## What Happens If You Think You’re Having a Miscarriage?

If you have symptoms, you will likely be sent to a hospital for tests.

A doctor will usually do an ultrasound scan. This uses sound waves to create a picture of your womb and shows whether the pregnancy is still going.

If the scan confirms a miscarriage, you will talk to your doctor or midwife about your next steps.

You may choose to:
- Wait 1 to 2 weeks for the pregnancy tissue to pass on its own
- Take medicine to help the tissue pass
- Have a small procedure to remove the tissue if you do not want to wait

## What Causes a Miscarriage?

There are many possible reasons for a miscarriage. But in most cases, doctors do not find a clear cause.

Most miscarriages are not caused by anything you did.

The most common reason is that the baby has an abnormal number of chromosomes.

Chromosomes are the parts of your cells that carry your baby’s genetic instructions. They tell the baby how to grow.

If the baby has too many or too few chromosomes, the baby cannot develop properly. This often leads to a miscarriage.

Most people who have a miscarriage go on to have a healthy pregnancy later.

## How Can You Reduce the Risk of a Miscarriage?

Most miscarriages cannot be prevented.

But you can take steps to lower your risk:
- Do not smoke
- Do not drink alcohol
- Do not use drugs
- Be at a healthy weight before getting pregnant
- Eat a balanced diet
- Take steps to avoid infections

These choices can help support a healthy pregnancy.

# Problems with Periods

Many women have issues with their periods. Common problems include:

- Not having periods at all  
- Having periods that are irregular  
- Bleeding too much during periods  
- Bleeding between periods  

There are many reasons why periods might be missing, irregular, heavy, or happen between normal times. For example, polycystic ovary syndrome can cause missed or irregular periods.  

Periods and period problems happen in women who are not pregnant and who are in their childbearing years. Bleeding that looks like a period in women who are pregnant or past menopause is not the same. The causes and how doctors check it are different in these cases.  

All women of childbearing age who have unusual bleeding from the vagina should have a pregnancy test. If a woman is pregnant, she needs to be checked for problems with the pregnancy.  

If a woman is close to menopause or has symptoms of menopause, her doctor should check her history. Blood tests may be needed to check hormone levels. This helps confirm if menopause has started.  

Women who have had menopause and then start bleeding from the vagina should be checked for cancer of the reproductive organs.  

Pelvic vein problems (once called pelvic congestion syndrome) are a common cause of long-term pelvic pain. These problems can also cause abnormal bleeding during periods.

# Cryptosporidiosis

Cryptosporidiosis is an infection in the gut caused by a tiny parasite called *Cryptosporidium*.  
It causes stomach cramps and diarrhea.

## How You Get the Infection

You can get this infection by:

- Drinking water that has been contaminated with the parasite.
- Eating food that has been contaminated with the parasite.
- Touching surfaces or objects that have the parasite on them.
- Being close to someone or an animal that is infected.

The parasite is found in the poop of infected people and animals.  
It can get into water, soil, or food.  
Even a small amount of the parasite can cause infection.

The eggs of the parasite are very tough.  
They do not die from freezing.  
They also survive in chlorine used in swimming pools and drinking water.

When you swallow the eggs, they travel to your intestines.  
The eggs release a young form of the parasite.  
This form enters the cells lining your intestines.  
The parasite grows, multiplies, and makes new eggs.  
You then pass these eggs in your stool.

One infected person or animal can pass millions of eggs in their stool.  
Just a few eggs can start an infection.  
This makes it easy for the infection to spread.  
It often spreads in places like day care centers or petting zoos.

## Where It Happens

Cryptosporidiosis is common in children in areas with poor sanitation.  
It can also happen to travelers visiting such areas.  
In the United States, outbreaks happen when people swallow contaminated water in pools, water parks, or lakes.  
It can also spread from contact with infected cattle or other people in child care centers.

People with a weak immune system, especially those with advanced HIV, are more likely to get this infection.  
They are also more likely to have serious and long-lasting symptoms.

## What You Should Know

- People with a healthy immune system often do not need treatment.  
  Their body can fight off the infection on its own.

## Symptoms

Symptoms usually start about 7 days after infection.  
They include:

- Stomach cramps
- Watery diarrhea
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Loss of appetite
- Fever
- Feeling weak

Symptoms usually last 1 to 2 weeks.  
But you can still pass the parasite in your stool for several weeks after feeling better.

In people with a weak immune system, symptoms may start slowly.  
Diarrhea can be very bad — more than 5 to 10 liters of watery stool per day in some people with HIV.  
The diarrhea can last for a long time.

Cryptosporidiosis is also linked to poor nutrition in children in areas with poor sanitation.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors test a sample of your stool to look for the parasite.  
They may test for:

- A protein made by the parasite (antigen test).
- The parasite’s DNA (genetic material).

Doctors may also look at the stool under a microscope to find the eggs.  
But this method is not always reliable.  
You may need to give more than one sample to find the parasite.

If you have long-lasting diarrhea and stool tests do not show the cause, your doctor may use a thin tube to look inside your upper digestive tract.  
This is called an endoscopy.  
They may take a small piece of tissue from your intestine to test.  
The parasite can be seen in this tissue.

## Treatment

### For People with a Healthy Immune System

- Most people get better on their own.
- If diarrhea is severe or lasts a long time, a medicine called nitazoxanide can help.
- This medicine is taken by mouth.

### For People with a Weak Immune System (like those with HIV)

- The most important treatment is to control the HIV infection with antiretroviral medicines.
- When the immune system gets stronger, diarrhea usually improves.
- Nitazoxanide may help reduce diarrhea and other symptoms, but it does not cure the infection.
- Doctors may also try another medicine called paromomycin.
- Sometimes, a mix of paromomycin and nitazoxanide is used to help ease symptoms.

If diarrhea is very bad, you may need fluids to prevent dehydration.  
This may be given through a vein in a hospital.

## Prevention

You can help stop the spread of cryptosporidiosis by:

- Washing your hands often, especially after using the toilet, changing diapers, touching animals, or working in soil.
- Keeping toilets and bathrooms clean.
- Avoiding drinking or swallowing water from:
  - Swimming pools
  - Hot tubs
  - Water parks
  - Lakes
  - Rivers
  - Oceans
  - Tap water in areas with poor sanitation
- Only drinking water that has been boiled or filtered properly.
- Eating only cooked food when traveling.
- Avoiding unpasteurized milk and juice.

### Water Filters

Use filters that:
- Use reverse osmosis.
- Are labeled “tested and certified by NSF/ANSI Standard No. 53 or No. 58 for cyst removal/reduction.”

Other filters may not remove the parasite.

### When There Is an Outbreak

Public health officials may tell people to:

- Boil all water used for drinking, brushing teeth, or washing food.
- Eat only cooked food.
- Avoid unpasteurized milk and juice.

### For Travelers

- Be careful about what you eat and drink.
- Wash your hands often with soap and water.
- Alcohol-based hand sanitizers do not work against this parasite.

# Trigger Finger

Trigger finger causes pain, stiffness, or a clicking sound when you move your finger or thumb. Sometimes, the finger gets stuck in a bent position.

## What Are the Symptoms?

- You may feel pain at the base of the finger or thumb when you move it or press on it.
- Your finger or thumb may feel stiff, especially in the morning.
- You might hear a click when you move the finger or thumb.
- As the condition gets worse, you may feel pain even when your hand is still.
- You might feel a small lump in your palm.
- The finger may get stuck in a bent position and then suddenly snap straight.
- Over time, the finger may not bend or straighten fully.

See your doctor if you think you have trigger finger. They will look at your hand and suggest the best treatment.

## How Is Trigger Finger Treated?

Some people get better without any treatment. But if it is not treated, the finger may stay bent permanently. This can make daily tasks hard.

If you need treatment, your doctor may suggest:

- **Rest** – Avoid activities that make the pain worse.
- **Medication** – Painkillers called non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can help reduce pain and swelling.
- **Splinting** – A plastic splint holds the finger still to reduce movement and help it heal.
- **Steroid injection** – A medicine injected into the hand to reduce swelling and help the tendon move freely.
- **Surgery** – A small operation to open the tight part of the tendon sheath. This lets the tendon move again.

Surgery is usually only done if other treatments do not work. It is very effective—up to 100% of the time. But if your job involves hard physical work, you may need 2 to 4 weeks off to recover fully.

## What Causes Trigger Finger?

Tendons are strong cords that connect muscles to bones. In your hand, tendons help move your fingers.

The tendons on the palm side of your hand run through a tunnel made of strong tissue. This tunnel holds the tendons in place. A protective covering around the tendon makes a small amount of fluid. This fluid helps the tendon slide smoothly when you bend or straighten your fingers.

Trigger finger happens when the tendon or its covering becomes inflamed and swollen. The tendon can no longer move easily through the tunnel. It may form a small lump. This makes it hard to bend or straighten the finger.

When the tendon gets stuck, it can click painfully as you straighten the finger.

We do not know exactly why this happens. But some things can make it more likely:

- Being a woman
- Being over 40 years old
- Having certain health conditions

Another hand condition called Dupuytren’s contracture can also raise your risk. In Dupuytren’s contracture, the tissue in the palm thickens. This causes one or more fingers to bend into the palm.

Long-term health problems like diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis are also linked to trigger finger.

# Autoimmune Metaplastic Atrophic Gastritis

This is a long-term condition you are born with. It causes your body’s immune system to attack cells in your stomach. These cells help make stomach acid and a protein called intrinsic factor. When these cells are damaged, your stomach makes less acid. It also makes less intrinsic factor.

Because of this, your body cannot absorb vitamin B12 well. This can lead to serious health problems over time.

## What Causes This Condition?

You are born with a tendency to get this disease. It runs in families and can be passed down from parent to child.

Your blood contains special proteins called antibodies. These attack your stomach cells and their parts. The main targets are:
- Parietal cells (the cells that make stomach acid)
- Intrinsic factor (the protein needed to absorb vitamin B12)
- A pump in the cells that makes acid (called H+,K+-ATPase)

Some people with this condition also have another autoimmune disease called Hashimoto thyroiditis. About one in three people with Hashimoto thyroiditis also have this stomach condition.

## What Problems Can This Cause?

This condition can lead to several serious health issues:

### Vitamin B12 Deficiency
Without enough intrinsic factor, your body cannot absorb vitamin B12 from food. This can cause:
- A type of anemia called pernicious anemia
- Nerve problems, such as numbness or tingling in hands and feet
- Weakness and balance issues

### Stomach Cancer
People with this condition have a three times higher risk of stomach cancer. This risk is even higher if:
- The stomach lining has changed in many areas
- The changes look like intestinal tissue (called intestinal metaplasia)

### Neuroendocrine Tumors
Low stomach acid causes other stomach cells to grow too much. This can sometimes turn into a tumor. These are rare but can be serious.

### Types of Stomach Changes
- **Atrophic gastritis**: The stomach lining becomes thin and weak.
- **Intestinal metaplasia**: Stomach cells change to look like intestinal cells. This is a warning sign for cancer.
- **Multifocal atrophic gastritis**: The damage is spread out in many areas of the stomach. This is more serious than damage in just one spot.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The condition itself often causes no clear symptoms. Some people feel mild discomfort in the upper belly.

The symptoms of vitamin B12 deficiency may not show up right away. Over time, you may feel:
- Tired all the time
- Weak
- Numb or tingly in your hands and feet
- Trouble walking or balancing

These nerve problems can happen even if your blood count is normal.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

There are no symptoms that clearly point to this condition. It is often found during tests for other problems, such as:
- Unexplained tiredness
- Belly pain
- Low blood counts

### Tests Used
- **Endoscopy**: A doctor uses a thin tube with a camera to look inside your stomach.
- **Biopsy**: Small pieces of stomach tissue are taken during the endoscopy and checked under a microscope.
- **Blood tests**: These check your vitamin B12 levels and look for antibodies in your blood.

You do not need to test for antibodies every time. But if your doctor suspects this condition, they may check for:
- Anti-parietal cell antibodies
- Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies

### Screening for Other Conditions
- All patients should be checked for thyroid problems, since this condition often happens with thyroid disease.

### Checking for Stomach Cancer Risk
Your doctor will look at your stomach tissue under a microscope. They will check for:
- How much the stomach lining is damaged
- Whether the cells look like intestinal cells
- How many areas are affected

### When to Have Follow-Up Endoscopies
- **Not needed every year** unless your first test was not clear or showed high-risk changes.
- **Repeat endoscopy every 3 to 5 years** may be reasonable if you are at higher risk for stomach cancer.
- Risk factors include:
  - Incomplete or widespread cell changes
  - Family history of stomach cancer
  - Coming from a country with high rates of stomach cancer (like Korea, Japan, or South America)

### Guidelines on Surveillance
- The American Gastroenterological Association says routine yearly checks are not needed.
- They also say that routine follow-up endoscopies are not helpful for most people with this condition.
- If you choose to have follow-up tests, you should know:
  - The benefits are small
  - Repeated tests can cause discomfort or harm
  - There is no strong proof that these tests save lives

- European guidelines recommend using high-quality cameras and special dyes during endoscopy for better detection of early cancer.
- They suggest endoscopy every 3 years for people with advanced stomach damage or intestinal metaplasia.
- One study found that 10 out of 100 people with this condition developed stomach tumors within 3 years.

### What Experts Recommend
- If your biopsy shows signs of autoimmune gastritis, your doctor may test for antibodies to confirm the diagnosis.
- All patients should be tested for thyroid disease.

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure. But you can stay healthy with one simple treatment:

- **Vitamin B12 shots**: You will need regular injections of vitamin B12. This replaces what your body cannot absorb.

You do not need any other treatment. The shots prevent anemia and nerve damage.

## Key Points

- This is a lifelong condition you are born with.
- It causes low stomach acid and poor vitamin B12 absorption.
- It increases your risk of stomach cancer and nerve problems.
- Diagnosis comes from endoscopy and biopsy.
- Treatment is vitamin B12 shots.
- Follow-up tests are not needed every year unless you are at high risk.
- Always talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits of repeat testing.

# What You Need to Know About Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)

Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are infections that spread through sexual contact. They can pass through blood, semen, vaginal fluids, or other body fluids. Skin-to-skin contact during oral, anal, or genital sex can also spread them.

## What Causes STIs?

STIs are caused by tiny germs. These include:
- Bacteria
- Viruses
- Parasites

Some of these germs can cause serious health problems if not treated.

## How Do STIs Spread?

STIs spread during sex. This includes:
- Oral sex
- Anal sex
- Genital sex

You do not need to have penetrative sex to get an STI. Some STIs can spread through skin-to-skin contact.

### Ways STIs Can Spread
- Having sex without protection (like a condom)
- Having many sex partners
- Not talking with your partner about safer sex
- Not getting tested or treated when needed
- Not treating both partners at the same time
- Not finishing your full course of medicine
- Traveling and having sex with new partners
- Sharing needles or medical tools that are not clean

### Other Ways STIs Can Spread
- A pregnant person can pass an STI to their baby during pregnancy or birth.
- A person with HIV can pass the virus to their baby through breastfeeding.
- Using unclean medical tools can spread HIV.
- Some infections can be passed through sex but are usually spread in other ways. For example:
  - Hepatitis A spreads through dirty food or water.
  - Hepatitis C spreads through blood.
  - Salmonella and Campylobacter spread through contaminated food or animals.
  - Shigella, Giardia, and Ameba spread through dirty water or food.

Some infections like pubic lice, scabies, molluscum contagiosum, and mpox can spread through skin contact. But they are only called STIs if they are passed during sex.

## What Are the Signs of an STI?

Symptoms can be different for each person. Some people have no symptoms at all.

Common signs include:
- Itching in the genital area
- A strange discharge from the penis or vagina
- Pain when peeing or during sex
- Sores, blisters, or rashes on the genitals or mouth

### Why Symptoms Matter
- Sores or broken skin make it easier to get other infections, like HIV.
- If an STI is not treated, it can spread through the blood and damage organs.

### Serious Problems from Untreated STIs
- **Syphilis** can cause heart, blood vessel, or brain problems.
- **HIV** can lead to severe infections and rare cancers.
- **HPV** can cause cancers of the cervix, vulva, vagina, anus, or throat.

### In Women
- Germs can move from the vagina up into the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries.
- This can cause scarring in the fallopian tubes.
- Scarring can lead to infertility or a dangerous pregnancy outside the uterus (ectopic pregnancy).
- Infection can also spread to the lining of the belly (peritoneum), causing a serious condition called peritonitis.
- This group of infections is called pelvic inflammatory disease.

### In Men
- Germs can enter the tube that carries urine (urethra).
- If not treated, this can cause:
  - Tight foreskin that cannot be pulled back
  - Narrowed urethra that blocks urine flow
  - A hole between the urethra and the skin of the penis
- In rare cases, germs can travel up to the testicles and cause infection in the tube that carries sperm.

### In Both Men and Women
- Some STIs cause long-term swelling in the genital area.
- Some cause infection in the urethra or rectum.

## How Are STIs Diagnosed?

Doctors use several methods to find STIs.

### What the Doctor Does
- Asks about your symptoms and sexual history.
- Examines the affected area.
- Takes a sample of blood, urine, or fluid from the penis, vagina, or cervix.

### Lab Tests
- Some tests look for the germ’s DNA or RNA.
- Others check for antibodies your body makes when fighting an infection.
- Tests are chosen based on what germ is most likely.

### Testing for Other STIs
- If you have one STI, your doctor will test for others.
- This is because people with one STI often have another.

## Should You Be Screened for STIs?

Screening means testing for an STI even if you have no symptoms.

You should be screened if:
- The infection is common.
- You are at higher risk (like having many partners).
- The infection can be dangerous (like during pregnancy).
- The test is simple and cheap.
- There is effective treatment.

Doctors recommend screening for:
- Chlamydia
- Gonorrhea
- Syphilis
- HIV

## How Are STIs Treated?

Most STIs can be treated successfully.

### Treatment by Type
- **Bacterial STIs** (like chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis) are treated with antibiotics.
- **Viral STIs** (like herpes, HIV, hepatitis B) are treated with antiviral medicines.

### Important Notes
- Some germs are becoming resistant to medicine. This makes treatment harder.
- Do not have sex until you and your partner are fully treated.
- Finish all your medicine, even if you feel better.
- Viral STIs like herpes and HIV last a lifetime. Medicine can control them but not cure them.

### Treating Complications
- If an STI causes a serious problem, like pelvic inflammatory disease, you will get stronger medicine.
- Treatment depends on the specific issue.

## How Can You Prevent STIs?

You can lower your risk by taking these steps:

### Practice Safer Sex
- Use a condom every time you have oral, anal, or genital sex.
- Use internal condoms, dental dams, or external condoms as barriers.

### Reduce Risk Factors
- Limit the number of sex partners.
- Avoid partners who have many partners or do not use protection.
- Be in a long-term, faithful relationship (mutual monogamy).
- Choose not to have sex (abstinence).

### Get Vaccinated
- Vaccines are available for:
  - HPV
  - Hepatitis A
  - Hepatitis B

### Take Preventive Medicine
- People at high risk of HIV can take medicine before exposure to prevent infection.
- Men who have sex with men and transgender women can take a daily antibiotic (doxycycline) within 3 days after sex without a condom to lower their risk of chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis.

### How to Use a Condom Correctly
- Use a new condom for each sexual act.
- Use the right size.
- Handle it carefully—avoid sharp nails, teeth, or jewelry.
- Put it on after the penis is hard and before any contact.
- Test the direction: roll it gently. If it resists, flip it over.
- Place it on the tip of the penis.
- Leave ½ inch at the tip to collect semen.
- Squeeze the air out of the tip.
- If uncircumcised, pull back the foreskin before rolling.
- Roll the condom down to the base.
- Smooth out air bubbles.
- Use only water-based lubricants with latex condoms.
  - Do not use oil-based products (like petroleum jelly, lotions, cooking oil).
- Hold the base of the condom during withdrawal.
- Pull out while the penis is still hard.

## More Information

For more details, visit:
[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC): Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)](https://www.cdc.gov/std)

# Asthma

Asthma is a condition that affects your breathing.  
It can cause wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath, or a tight feeling in your chest.  
An asthma attack happens when your symptoms become very bad and you struggle to breathe.  
This can be dangerous and needs quick action.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:
- You or your child have symptoms like wheezing, coughing, or trouble breathing.
- Your asthma is not getting better with your usual treatment.
- You are using your inhaler more often than usual.
- You need help learning how to use your inhaler correctly.
- Your symptoms stop you from doing normal activities or wake you up at night.

## When to Call 999 (Emergency)

Call 999 if:
- You or someone else is having an asthma attack and feels worse.
- You do not feel better after using the maximum dose of your reliever inhaler.
- You do not have your inhaler.

If symptoms do not improve after 10 minutes and an ambulance has not arrived, use your inhaler again if you have one. Use up to the same maximum dose.

### Important: A&E Safety Message
Do not drive yourself to the emergency department.  
The person on the phone will give you clear instructions.

## After an Asthma Attack

Even if you feel better after an asthma attack, see your doctor within 2 days.  
This helps you get advice to prevent another attack.

## Support and Help

You are not alone.  
Your healthcare team can help you manage asthma.  
You may also find it helpful to talk to others with asthma.

### Asthma and Lung UK
This charity gives information and support for people with asthma and other lung conditions.
- Website: [www.asthmaandlung.org.uk](https://www.asthmaandlung.org.uk)
- Helpline: 0300 222 5800
- Resources: Support in your area, living with a lung condition

### Allergy UK
This charity helps people with allergies, including those that can trigger asthma.
- Website: [www.allergyuk.org](https://www.allergyuk.org)
- Helpline: 01322 619898
- Resource: Asthma and allergies

### Beat Asthma
A website made for children and young people with asthma.
- Website: [www.beatasthma.co.uk](https://www.beatasthma.co.uk)
- Resource: Information for families and children

---

## What Are the Symptoms of Asthma?

The main signs of asthma are:
- Wheezing (a whistling sound when you breathe)
- Coughing
- Feeling short of breath
- A tight chest

Symptoms can be mild or very bad.  
They often come and go.  
They may be worse at night or early in the morning.

An asthma attack is when symptoms suddenly get much worse.  
You may find it hard to breathe.  
This can be life-threatening.

Triggers can include:
- Exercise
- Cold air
- Air pollution
- Allergies (like pollen, dust, mould, or pets)

Asthma often starts in childhood, but it can begin at any age.

---

## How Is Asthma Diagnosed?

If you or your child have asthma symptoms, your doctor or nurse will:
- Ask questions about your health and symptoms.
- Listen to your chest with a stethoscope.

You may need:
- A simple breathing test to check your lung function.
- A blood test in some cases.
- A peak flow meter to use at home for a few weeks. This measures how well your lungs work.

It can take time to diagnose asthma.  
Symptoms can change over time.  
Other conditions can cause similar breathing problems.

If asthma is likely, your doctor may give you asthma medicine to see if it helps.

---

## How Is Asthma Treated?

You will work with a care team.  
This includes your GP, nurse, or sometimes a hospital specialist.

Your care team will:
- Show you how and when to use your medicines.
- Teach you how to check your asthma.
- Help you avoid things that make your symptoms worse.
- Tell you what to do if your symptoms get worse.

All of this will be written in your asthma action plan.  
Bring this plan to every appointment.  
You will get a printed or digital copy.

You should have a check-up at least once a year.  
During this visit, your team will:
- Check that you are using your inhalers correctly.
- Make sure your asthma action plan is up to date.

---

### Asthma Inhalers

The main treatment for asthma is medicine you breathe in using an inhaler.  
Most people find inhalers work well to stop or prevent symptoms.

Your doctor may suggest one of these:
- An inhaler to use only when you have symptoms. This is called an anti-inflammatory reliever (AIR) inhaler.
- An inhaler to use every day to prevent symptoms, and also when you have symptoms. This is called a maintenance and reliever therapy (MART) inhaler.
- Two separate inhalers: one to use every day to prevent symptoms, and a blue reliever inhaler to use when symptoms start.  
  You should never use a blue reliever inhaler on its own.

---

### How to Use Your Inhaler

Using your inhaler correctly is very important.  
The medicine will not work if you do it wrong.

There are different types:
- Dry powder inhalers
- Pressurized metered-dose inhalers (pMDIs)
- Soft mist inhalers

A doctor, nurse, or pharmacist will show you how to use your specific inhaler.

---

### How to Dispose of Your Inhalers

Do not throw empty, unused, or expired inhalers in the bin.  
They can release gases that harm the environment.

Take them to your local pharmacy.  
They can dispose of them safely.

---

### Other Treatments

If inhalers are not enough, your care team may suggest:
- A stronger inhaler.
- Tablets that help you breathe easier, such as montelukast.

If your asthma is very severe and not controlled by inhalers or tablets, you may be offered:
- Injections of special medicines called biological therapies.

Your care team will explain the best treatment for you.  
They will also talk about any possible side effects.

---

### Hospital Treatment for an Asthma Attack

If your asthma attack does not improve, you may need hospital care.  
Treatments in hospital may include:
- Oxygen through a mask.
- A nebuliser to deliver high doses of medicine through a mask or mouthpiece.
- Steroid tablets or injections.

---

## What You Can Do to Help Manage Asthma

### Do These Things:
- Always carry your inhaler with you.
- Use your inhalers exactly as your care team tells you.
- Avoid things that trigger your symptoms. These can include:
  - Air pollution
  - Smoke (including secondhand smoke)
  - Pollen
  - Dust
  - Pets
- Exercise regularly.  
  Ask your doctor or nurse for advice if exercise makes your asthma worse.
- Keep a healthy weight.
- Get vaccinations like the flu vaccine.  
  Viruses like the flu can make asthma worse.

### Do Not Do These Things:
- Do not smoke.  
  If you need help quitting, ask your doctor or nurse.
- Do not take medicines for other health problems without checking with a pharmacist or doctor.  
  Some medicines, like aspirin, ibuprofen, and beta blockers, can make asthma worse in some people.

---

## What Causes Asthma?

Asthma happens when the airways in your lungs become swollen.  
This makes them narrower and harder to breathe through.

In people with asthma, certain things can trigger symptoms.  
These include:
- Allergies (like eczema, hay fever, or food allergies)
- Exercise
- Smoke
- Cold air
- Infections (like colds or chest infections)

We do not fully understand what causes asthma.  
But you are more likely to get it if:
- You have allergies.
- Other people in your family have asthma, hay fever, eczema, or allergies.
- You were born early (prematurely) or had a low birth weight.
- You were exposed to air pollution or cigarette smoke as a child.
- You had breathing problems as a child, such as bronchiolitis or croup.
- You are overweight.

Asthma can also be caused by breathing in certain chemicals at work.

# Angina Pectoris – Simple Explanation

Angina pectoris is chest discomfort or pressure caused by a temporary lack of oxygen to the heart muscle. It does not cause permanent heart damage. The discomfort usually happens during physical activity or strong emotions. It often goes away when you rest or take a special medicine called nitroglycerin.

## What Causes Angina?

Your heart needs oxygen-rich blood to work well. If your heart works harder than normal, it needs more oxygen. But if the blood vessels that carry blood to your heart are narrowed, your heart may not get enough oxygen.

Narrowed blood vessels are usually caused by a buildup of fatty material in the arteries. This is called atherosclerosis. It is the most common cause of angina.

Other causes include:
- Sudden tightening of a coronary artery (spasm).
- A blood clot in a coronary artery (rare).
- A partial or temporary blockage in a coronary artery. This can cause angina, but if the blockage is complete, it usually causes a heart attack.

Your heart’s oxygen needs go up when:
- Your heart beats faster.
- Your blood pressure is high.
- Your heart muscle contracts strongly.

So, angina often happens when you are active or stressed. It usually stops when you rest.

Other health problems can also cause angina, even if your arteries are not blocked. These include:
- High blood pressure.
- Narrowing of the aortic valve (aortic stenosis).
- Leaking of the aortic valve (aortic regurgitation).
- Thickened heart muscle (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy).

These conditions make the heart work harder. They also reduce blood flow to the heart muscle during rest.

Low oxygen levels in the blood can also cause or make angina worse. This can happen with:
- Severe anemia (low red blood cells).
- Low oxygen in the air (hypoxia).

## How Angina Feels

Angina can feel like a dull ache, pressure, or a heavy weight in the chest. It is rarely described as sharp pain.

The discomfort is usually felt behind the breastbone. But it can spread to:
- The left shoulder.
- Down the inside of the left arm.
- To the fingers.
- Through to the back.
- Into the throat, jaw, or teeth.
- Sometimes down the inside of the right arm.
- Or in the upper belly.

It is never felt above the ears or below the belly button.

Some people have symptoms that are not typical. They may feel bloating, gas, stomach pain, or burning in the back, shoulders, arms, or jaw. These symptoms are more common in women. They may think they have indigestion. Belching may even make the symptoms feel better.

Some people feel short of breath. This happens because the heart’s pressure rises during a lack of oxygen. The pressure can build up in the lungs and make breathing hard.

Symptoms often take more than a minute to go away. Very brief, fleeting sensations are not usually angina.

Between attacks, your body may look and feel normal. But during an attack, you may notice:
- A faster heartbeat.
- Higher blood pressure.
- Heart sounds that seem farther away.
- A wider or less focused pulse at the chest.
- A fourth heart sound (S4) is common.
- A third heart sound (S3) may appear.
- A soft, blowing sound (murmur) may be heard if the heart valve does not close properly due to muscle damage.

## When Does Angina Happen?

Angina usually starts during physical activity or strong emotions. It lasts only a few minutes. It goes away when you stop moving or calm down.

The pattern is usually predictable. But sometimes, the same activity that was fine one day causes angina the next. This can happen because blood vessel tone changes from day to day.

Certain things can make angina worse:
- Exercising right after eating.
- Walking in cold weather.
- Walking into a strong wind.
- Being in cold air after being in a warm room.

Doctors use a system to rate how much activity causes angina. This helps track how bad it is.

### Canadian Cardiovascular Society Classification System for Angina

| Class | Activity That Causes Chest Pain |
|-------|-------------------------------|
| 1 | Strenuous, fast, or long activity. Not usual daily activities like walking or climbing stairs. |
| 2 | Walking fast. Walking uphill. Climbing stairs fast. After eating. In cold weather. In the wind. During strong emotions. |
| 3 | Walking even 1 or 2 blocks at a normal pace. Climbing one flight of stairs. |
| 4 | Any physical activity. Sometimes happens even at rest. |

Angina attacks can happen several times a day. Or you may go weeks or months without any attacks.

Sometimes attacks get worse over time. This is called crescendo angina. It can lead to a heart attack or death.

In some people, attacks get better or go away. This can happen if:
- New blood vessels grow around the blocked ones (collateral circulation).
- The damaged heart area dies (infarcts).
- Heart failure or leg pain from poor blood flow limits activity.

### Nocturnal Angina

This is angina that happens at night. It can be caused by:
- A vivid dream that changes your breathing, heart rate, or blood pressure.
- A sign of heart failure. It is similar to waking up short of breath.

Lying down increases blood flow to the heart. This stretches the heart muscle and makes it work harder. This raises the need for oxygen.

### Angina Decubitus

This is angina that happens when you are lying down, not just at night. It is often linked to:
- A slightly faster heart rate.
- A large rise in blood pressure.

These changes increase the heart’s need for oxygen. They may cause angina at rest. Or they may be caused by a blood clot forming after a plaque breaks open.

If angina does not go away, the heart’s oxygen need keeps rising. This makes a heart attack more likely.

## How Is Angina Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your symptoms first. They ask:
- Where is the pain?
- When does it happen?
- How long does it last?
- What makes it better or worse?

They also check for risk factors for heart disease, such as:
- Smoking.
- High blood pressure.
- High cholesterol.
- Diabetes.
- Family history of heart disease.

If your chest pain lasts more than 20 minutes, happens at rest, or is linked to fainting or heart failure, you may have a heart attack or unstable angina. You will need urgent care.

Chest discomfort can also come from other causes, such as:
- Acid reflux.
- Esophagus spasms.
- Indigestion.
- Gallstones.
- Inflammation of the chest wall (costochondritis).
- Anxiety or panic attacks.
- Fast heart rhythms.
- Aortic dissection.
- Pericarditis.
- Mitral valve problems.

Even if your heart arteries are not blocked, these can cause chest pain.

### Tests Used to Diagnose Angina

- **Electrocardiogram (ECG):** This test checks the heart’s electrical activity. It is always done.
- **Stress test with ECG:** You walk on a treadmill or ride a bike while your heart is monitored. This shows how your heart responds to activity.
- **Stress test with imaging:** This uses ultrasound (echocardiography), nuclear scans, PET scans, or MRI to see how well the heart pumps during stress.
- **CT angiography:** A scan that shows the heart’s blood vessels in detail.
- **CT fractional flow reserve (CT FFR):** A special CT test that checks if a blockage is serious enough to cause angina.
- **Coronary angiography:** A detailed X-ray of the heart’s blood vessels. This is done if you have serious symptoms, a positive stress test, or a serious blockage found on CT.

Noninvasive tests (like stress tests and CT scans) are usually done first. If needed, coronary angiography is used to plan treatment.

## How Is Angina Treated?

The goal is to reduce symptoms, prevent heart attacks, and improve your quality of life.

### Lifestyle Changes

- **Stop smoking.** Quitting smoking lowers your risk of heart attack. After 2 years, your risk is similar to someone who never smoked.
- **Control blood pressure.** High blood pressure makes the heart work harder. Treat it even if it is only slightly high.
- **Lose weight.** Weight loss can reduce angina symptoms.
- **Treat mild heart failure.** This can help reduce angina.
- **Avoid digitalis.** This medicine can sometimes make angina worse.
- **Lower cholesterol.** Eat a healthy diet and take statin medicines. This slows heart disease, may shrink some blockages, and improves blood vessel function.
- **Exercise.** Walking regularly helps you feel better, lowers your risk of heart problems, and improves your ability to be active.

### Medicines

- **Antiplatelet drugs:** These prevent blood clots. Aspirin is used for most people. Others include clopidogrel, prasugrel, or ticagrelor.
- **Beta-blockers:** These slow the heart rate and lower blood pressure. They reduce the heart’s need for oxygen.
- **Nitroglycerin:** This medicine gives fast relief during an angina attack. It opens blood vessels and improves blood flow.
- **Calcium channel blockers:** These relax blood vessels and reduce heart workload. They help control symptoms.
- **ACE inhibitors:** These lower blood pressure and protect the heart. They are used if you have high blood pressure or heart failure.

# Superficial Vein Blood Clot

This condition is when a blood clot forms in a vein close to the skin. It usually happens in the arms or legs.

## What Causes It?

- Most often, it happens in the legs.
- It can also happen in the groin or arms.
- In the arms, it often follows having a needle in the vein (IV).
- In the legs, it often happens in veins that are swollen and twisted (varicose veins).
- Most people with varicose veins do not get a blood clot.

## How It Works

- A small injury can cause a varicose vein to become inflamed.
- This type of clot causes strong swelling and pain.
- The clot sticks tightly to the wall of the vein.
- The clot is less likely to break loose and travel through the body.
- Superficial veins are near the skin and do not have strong muscles around them to push the clot loose.

## Special Case: Migrating Clots

- Sometimes, blood clots keep forming in different veins.
- This is called migratory phlebitis.
- It can be a sign of a serious illness, like cancer.
- When this happens with cancer, it is known as Trousseau syndrome.

## Symptoms

- Pain and swelling come on quickly.
- The skin over the vein turns red on light skin.
- On dark skin, the area may look purple or hard to see.
- The area feels warm and very tender.
- The vein feels hard under the skin, like a tight cord.
- The hard feeling can go along the whole length of the vein.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

- Doctors look at the area and check the symptoms.
- Most of the time, no tests are needed.
- If the clot is above the knee and not in a varicose vein, doctors may use ultrasound to check for a clot in a deeper vein.

## Treatment

- Most cases get better on their own.
- Use warm compresses to help with pain and swelling.
- Take pain medicine like aspirin or another nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID).
- The swelling and pain usually go down in a few days.
- But lumps and tenderness may last several weeks.
- If the clot is very large, doctors may give a medicine to prevent more clots (anticoagulant), such as heparin.

> **Note:** Always talk to your doctor before starting any new treatment.

# Goitre

A goitre is when the thyroid gland in your neck becomes swollen.

## Symptoms

- You may notice a lump or swelling at the front of your neck.  
- The swelling is usually not painful.  
- It often shows up at the lower front of your neck.  
- The lump can feel smooth or lumpy.  
- It may only be on one side of your neck.  

You might also have other signs, such as:  
- A cough that lasts a long time  
- A hoarse voice or changes in your voice  
- A feeling that something is stuck in your throat  
- Wheezing when you breathe  
- Trouble swallowing or breathing  

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if you think you have a goitre.  
It is usually not serious, but it’s best to get it checked.

## When to Go to A&E

Go to A&E or call 999 if you are having trouble breathing.  
Do not drive yourself. Ask someone to take you or call 999 for an ambulance.  
Bring your medicines with you.

## What Causes a Goitre

Your thyroid gland is in your neck. It helps control your energy, weight, and mood.  
A goitre happens when this gland becomes swollen.  

Common causes include:  
- Your thyroid working too fast (overactive)  
- Your thyroid working too slow (underactive)  
- Small, harmless lumps on the thyroid  
- Hormone changes during puberty, pregnancy, or menopause  
- Inflammation of the thyroid (thyroiditis)  
- An immune system problem, like Grave’s disease  
- Not getting enough iodine in your food – this is rare in the UK  
- Thyroid cancer – this is very rare  

## Treatment

Most goitres are small and do not cause problems.  
You may not need any treatment at all.  

Your doctor will do tests to find the cause.  
These may include blood tests and an ultrasound scan.  

If the goitre is caused by an underactive or overactive thyroid, medicine can help.  
If the goitre is making it hard to breathe or swallow, surgery may be needed.  
Surgery can remove part or all of the thyroid gland.

# Boils and Carbuncles

## What Are Boils and Carbuncles?

A boil is a painful lump under the skin. It starts in a hair root and is caused by a bacterial infection. The most common bacteria is *Staphylococcus aureus*.

A carbuncle is a group of boils that are connected under the skin. It causes deeper infection and can leave scars.

Boils are smaller and closer to the surface than deep skin abscesses.

## Who Gets Boils and Carbuncles?

Boils and carbuncles can happen to anyone. But they are more common in:

- People who are overweight
- People with weak immune systems
- Older adults
- People with diabetes
- People living in crowded places with poor hygiene
- People who have been around someone with a serious skin infection

## What Makes Boils More Likely?

Certain things increase the chance of getting boils:

- Bacteria on the skin or inside the nose
- Hot and humid weather
- Clogged hair roots (like in acne)

Methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus* (MRSA) is a type of bacteria that often causes these infections. It is hard to treat with common antibiotics.

## Where Do Boils Usually Appear?

Boils often show up on:

- The neck
- The breasts
- The face
- The buttocks

They can be very painful, especially if they are near sensitive areas like the nose, ear, or fingers.

A boil looks like a red, swollen lump. It may have a white or yellow tip. It can leak thick fluid that is mixed with dead tissue and blood.

## What Is a Carbuncle?

A carbuncle is a cluster of boils that are joined together under the skin. It is larger and deeper than a single boil.

A carbuncle can cause fever and make you feel unwell.

## How Are Boils and Carbuncles Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose them by looking at the skin.

They may take a sample from the boil to test for the type of bacteria. This helps guide treatment.

## How Are Boils and Carbuncles Treated?

### Drainage
If the boil is large or painful, a doctor may cut it open to drain the pus. This helps it heal faster.

### Warm Compresses
Use warm, wet cloths on the area several times a day. This helps the boil open and drain.

### Antibiotics
Antibiotics are often needed, especially if the infection is serious.

The antibiotics must work against MRSA.

You may not need antibiotics for a small boil that is not getting worse and is not painful.

You should take antibiotics if:

- The boil is larger than 5 millimeters
- A small boil does not get better after drainage
- You have more than one boil
- The redness is spreading
- You have a weak immune system
- You are at risk for heart infection (endocarditis)
- You have a fever

### Which Antibiotics Are Used?

Common choices include:

- Sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim: Take 800/160 mg to 1600/320 mg twice a day
- Clindamycin: Take 300 to 600 mg every 6 to 8 hours
- Doxycycline or minocycline: Take 100 mg every 12 hours

### Hospital Care

If you are in the hospital and have many boils, and MRSA is common there, you may need to stay in a separate room.

You will be treated like someone with a serious skin infection, based on test results.

## How Can Boils Be Prevented?

Boils often come back. You can lower your risk by:

- Washing your skin daily with soap that contains chlorhexidine gluconate and alcohol
- Or using soap with 2 to 3% chloroxylenol

If you keep getting boils, treat the causes:

- Lose weight if you are overweight
- Control your blood sugar if you have diabetes
- Avoid work or jobs that expose you to skin irritants
- Treat bacteria in your nose if you carry *Staphylococcus aureus* or MRSA

If you still get boils despite these steps, your doctor may suggest:

- Rifampin plus another oral antibiotic

## Key Points

- Watch for a red, painful lump in a hair root. It may leak pus with dead tissue and blood. This is a sign of a boil.
- Get a sample tested if you have a boil or carbuncle.
- Have the boil drained if it is large or painful.
- Use antibiotics that work against MRSA if:
  - You are not feeling well
  - You have a weak immune system
  - You are at risk for heart infection
  - The boil is larger than 5 millimeters
  - You have more than one boil
  - The redness is spreading

# Mouth and Throat Cancer

This guide explains mouth and throat cancer in simple terms. It covers what it is, what causes it, how it shows up, how doctors diagnose it, how it is treated, and how to prevent it.

---

## What Is Mouth and Throat Cancer?

Mouth and throat cancer starts in the lips, the roof, sides, or floor of the mouth, the tongue, the tonsils, or the back of the throat.

- It can look like a sore that does not heal.
- It may appear as a lump or a patch that is red or white.
- It can also be a growth or a change in color in the mouth or throat.

---

## Types of Mouth and Throat Cancer

The most common type is **squamous cell carcinoma**. This means the cancer starts in the thin, flat cells that line the inside of the mouth and throat.

Other types are rare. These include:
- Verrucous carcinoma (a warty type of cancer)
- Malignant melanoma (a type of skin cancer that can appear in the mouth)
- Kaposi sarcoma (a rare cancer linked to a virus)

---

## What Increases the Risk of Mouth and Throat Cancer?

The main risk factors are:

- Using tobacco
- Drinking alcohol heavily
- Having a human papillomavirus (HPV) infection

### Tobacco Use

Tobacco use is a major cause of mouth and throat cancer. This includes:
- Smoking cigarettes, cigars, or pipes
- Chewing tobacco or betel quid (a mix that includes tobacco)
- Using snuff (a form of smokeless tobacco)

In the U.S., smoking more than two packs of cigarettes a day is the biggest tobacco risk. Cigar smoking also raises the risk. Pipe smoking increases the risk for cancer on the part of the lip that touches the pipe. Chewing tobacco or snuff raises the risk for cancer on the inside of the cheeks, gums, or lips.

### Alcohol Use

Drinking a lot of alcohol over time increases the risk. The more you drink, the higher the risk.

### Tobacco and Alcohol Together

Using both tobacco and alcohol greatly increases the risk. This combination is much worse than either one alone. People who keep using tobacco and alcohol after being treated for cancer are more than twice as likely to get another cancer in the mouth or throat.

### Human Papillomavirus (HPV)

HPV is a virus that can cause genital warts. It can also spread to the mouth during oral sex. Some types of HPV are linked to mouth and throat cancer.

- HPV-related cancers are becoming more common, especially in younger people in North America and northern Europe.
- The number of sexual partners and how often you have oral sex are important risk factors.
- Certain strains of HPV are more likely to cause throat cancer, and less likely to cause mouth cancer.

Vaccines against HPV can help prevent some of these cancers. But it takes many years for the benefits to show because cancer develops slowly.

### Other Risk Factors

- **Sex:** About 3 out of 4 cases happen in men.
- **Age:** The risk goes up as you get older.
- **Sun exposure:** Too much sun on the lips can cause lip cancer.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on where the cancer is.

### Mouth Cancer

- Often does not hurt at first.
- Later, it may cause pain when swallowing or speaking.
- It may look like a sore that does not heal.
- The sore may be flat or slightly raised.
- It can be red (called erythroplakia) or white (called leukoplakia).
- Cancers on the lip or inside the mouth often feel hard and stuck to the tissue underneath.
- Noncancerous lumps usually move easily.
- Dark or brown spots on the gums, tongue, or inside the mouth can be a sign of cancer.
- A dark, flat spot like a freckle (called a smoker’s patch) can appear where a cigarette or pipe is held.

### Throat Cancer

- Causes pain in the throat that gets worse when swallowing.
- Makes it hard to swallow or speak.
- Can cause ear pain.
- Sometimes, a lump in the neck is the first sign.

When cancer makes eating hard, people often lose weight.

---

## How Is Mouth and Throat Cancer Diagnosed?

Doctors use several steps to find and confirm cancer.

### Step 1: Look and Feel

Doctors check the mouth and throat during a physical exam. They look for any unusual spots, sores, lumps, or color changes.

If they see something strange, they take a small sample of tissue. This is called a **biopsy**.

Only a biopsy can tell for sure if a spot is cancer.

### Step 2: Use a Special Tool

If no clear growth is seen but symptoms are present, doctors use a mirror or a thin, flexible tube (called an endoscope) to look inside the throat.

They take a biopsy from any abnormal area seen.

### Step 3: Imaging Tests

If cancer is found, doctors do imaging tests to see how big it is and if it has spread.

These tests include:
- Computed tomography (CT scan)
- Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
- A combination of PET scan and CT scan

These tests help doctors see:
- The size and location of the cancer
- If it has spread to nearby tissues
- If it has reached lymph nodes in the neck

Doctors may also use:
- Laryngoscopy (to see inside the voice box)
- Bronchoscopy (to see inside the airways)
- Esophagoscopy (to see inside the food pipe)

### Early Detection Is Key

Finding cancer early makes it much easier to cure. Doctors and dentists should check the mouth and throat at every routine visit.

They should pay special attention to the area under the tongue. This is where lumps often go unnoticed until they are large.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

The chance of recovery depends on:
- Where the cancer started
- How far it has spread
- What caused it

### Survival Rates

- For tongue cancer that has not spread to lymph nodes: Over 80% of people live at least 5 years after diagnosis.
- For cancer in the floor of the mouth that has not spread: About 75% live at least 5 years.
- If the cancer has spread to lymph nodes, survival drops.
- For lower lip cancer: About 90% live at least 5 years. This cancer rarely spreads.
- For upper lip cancer: It tends to be more aggressive and spreads more easily.
- For throat cancer overall: About 52% live at least 5 years.

But if the cancer is caused by HPV, survival is much better — over 75%.  
If it is not caused by HPV, survival is less than 50%.

---

## How Can You Prevent Mouth and Throat Cancer?

You can lower your risk by:

- Not using tobacco
- Limiting alcohol
- Avoiding too much sun on your lips
- Using sunscreen on your lips
- Getting the HPV vaccine

The HPV vaccine helps prevent some types of HPV that cause mouth and throat cancer.

---

## How Is Mouth and Throat Cancer Treated?

Treatment depends on the size, location, and stage of the cancer.

The main treatments are:
- Surgery
- Radiation therapy
- Chemotherapy (often used with radiation)

### For Mouth Cancer

- Surgery is usually the first treatment.
- Doctors remove the cancer and sometimes nearby lymph nodes.
- This surgery can change how you look and may affect your ability to speak or eat.
- Reconstructive surgery can help restore appearance and function.
- Missing teeth or jaw parts can be replaced with artificial devices.
- Speech and swallowing therapy may be needed after surgery.
- Radiation or chemoradiation (radiation with chemotherapy) is used after surgery if the cancer is advanced.

If surgery is not possible, radiation therapy is used instead.

Chemotherapy is not used at first, but it may be added if the cancer has spread to many lymph nodes.

### For Throat Cancer

- Surgery is often the first treatment.
- Newer methods let doctors operate through the mouth, without cutting the neck.
- Some surgeries use a laser guided by an endoscope.
- Others use a robot. The surgeon controls the robot from a console while watching the surgery on a screen.

Radiation therapy, or chemoradiation, can be used:
- After surgery
- As the first treatment

Doctors often use radiation for early-stage cancers. They add chemotherapy for more advanced cases.

A special type of radiation called **intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT)** targets the cancer more precisely. This can reduce side effects.

### Side Effects of Radiation

Radiation to the mouth and throat can cause:
- Dry mouth (because the salivary glands are damaged)
- More tooth decay and dental problems
- Slow healing of jawbone after dental work
- Osteoradionecrosis (bone and tissue loss in the treated area)
- Skin changes if the neck is treated
- Voice changes or trouble swallowing if the throat or voice box is treated

### Preparing for Radiation

Before radiation:
- All dental problems must be fixed.
- Teeth that might cause problems should be removed.
- Wait for healing before starting radiation.

### After Radiation

Good dental care is very important. After radiation:
- The mouth heals poorly.
- If you need a tooth pulled, it can lead to serious problems.

To stay healthy:
- See your dentist regularly.
- Brush and floss every day.
- Use fluoride at home every day.
- If you ever need a tooth removed, ask about **hyperbaric oxygen therapy**. This treatment can help the jaw heal and prevent bone loss.
