# Bunion

A bunion is when the joint at the base of your big toe sticks out. This can make the toe look crooked.

## What Causes a Bunion?

- The big toe or the bone it connects to moves out of place.
- This shift causes a bump to form at the base of the big toe.
- The bump may become painful and swollen.
- A fluid-filled sac called a bursa can form over the joint. This sac can become inflamed and painful.

### Hallux Valgus and Bunions

- Hallux valgus is a condition where the base of the big toe points outward and the tip of the toe points inward toward the second toe.
- This misalignment causes the bunion.
- The bunion is the bump that forms at the base of the big toe.

## What Makes Bunions Worse?

- Rolling your foot inward too much (pronation) can contribute.
- Wearing tight shoes or shoes with pointed toes can make the problem worse.
- Injuries to the foot can also play a role.
- Over time, the joint may develop osteoarthritis. This means the cartilage in the joint wears down.
- Bone spurs may grow in the joint.
- Gout can cause sudden flare-ups. These make the bunion red, painful, and swollen.

## Symptoms of a Bunion

- Pain when wearing narrow or tight shoes.
- The bump gets bigger over time.
- The area around the joint becomes red, warm, and swollen.
- Pain and swelling spread around the whole joint.
- You may find it hard to move the joint.

## How Is a Bunion Diagnosed?

- Your doctor will ask about your symptoms.
- They will examine your foot.
- They may take a sample of fluid from the joint if it is very swollen and painful. This helps rule out infection or gout.
- X-rays are not always needed. But they may be used to see how much damage has happened to the joint.

## Treatment for a Bunion

### Non-Surgical Options

- Wear shoes with a wide toe box. This gives your toes more room.
- Use bunion pads. These protect the painful bump.
- Try toe spacers. These help keep your toes in a better position.
- Use orthotic devices. These are inserts placed inside your shoe. They help reduce pressure on the joint.

- If pain remains, your doctor may suggest:
  - Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) to reduce pain and swelling.
  - A corticosteroid injection with a numbing medicine. This can ease pain and swelling.
  - Removing fluid from the bursa using a needle. This is called aspiration.

### Surgery

Surgery may be needed if:
- The pain is severe.
- You have trouble walking.
- Non-surgical treatments do not help.
- Scar tissue is limiting movement.

Surgery can:
- Remove the bony bump.
- Realign the bones and joints.
- Release tight tissues.

Surgery is called a bunionectomy. It is usually considered only when other treatments fail.

# Blood in Your Urine

## When to Seek Help Right Away

Call your doctor for an urgent appointment or get help from NHS 111 if you see blood in your urine. This is true even if:

- You feel fine otherwise  
- This is the first time it has happened  
- There is only a small amount of blood  
- You are not sure it is blood  

Blood in your urine can look bright pink, red, or dark brown.

You can call 111 or get help online at 111.nhs.uk.

## Why It’s Important to Get Checked

Blood in your urine can be a sign of cancer. If caught early, cancer is easier to treat. That is why it is important to get it checked.

## What Happens at Your Doctor’s Appointment

If you have blood in your urine, your doctor will:

- Ask you about your symptoms  
- Check inside your bottom (rectal exam) if needed  
- Check your vagina if you are a woman  

They may also:

- Ask you to give a urine sample  
- Order a blood test  
- Give you antibiotics if they think you have an infection  
- Refer you to a specialist for more tests  

## Possible Causes of Blood in Urine

Blood in your urine can come from any part of your urinary system. This includes:

- Your bladder  
- Your kidneys  
- Your urethra (the tube that carries urine out of your body)  

Other symptoms can help point to the cause. But do not try to diagnose yourself. See your doctor if you think you have blood in your urine.

## When It Might Not Be Blood in Your Urine

It may not be blood in your urine if:

- You recently ate beetroot – this can make your urine look pink  
- You started a new medicine – some medicines can turn your urine red or brown  
- You are bleeding from your bottom instead  
- It is happening during your period  

Always get it checked if you are unsure.

# Pityriasis Rosea – Simple Explanation

Pityriasis rosea is a skin rash that comes and goes on its own. It is not dangerous and does not spread from person to person. Most people do not need treatment.

This rash is more common in people between the ages of 10 and 35. Women get it more often than men.

## What Causes Pityriasis Rosea?

Scientists think a virus may cause this rash. Some research points to certain types of herpes viruses.  
Some medicines can also cause a rash that looks like pityriasis rosea. These include:
- ACE inhibitors
- Hydrochlorothiazide
- Captopril
- Barbiturates
- Metronidazole
- Allopurinol

## What Does the Rash Look Like?

The rash usually starts with one large, scaly patch. This is called the **herald patch**. It appears on the chest, back, or arms.

Within 7 to 14 days, smaller patches appear. These are oval and pink, fawn, or reddish. They often show up on the trunk, arms, and legs.

The patches have a slightly raised, scaly edge. This looks like a collar around the patch. The rash can look like ringworm, but it is not caused by a fungus.

In people with dark skin, the patches may look more purple or darker than pink. In people with light skin, the patches are usually pink or red.

Most people feel itchy. Some have strong itching. In children and pregnant women, the rash may have more bumps and less scaling.

Some people get the rash in the armpits or groin area. This is called **inverse pityriasis rosea**. The patches spread outward from these areas.

The rash often follows the natural lines of the skin. When many patches appear on the back, they can form a pattern like a Christmas tree.

Some people feel unwell before the rash appears. They may have a headache, feel tired, or have joint pain. This happens in only a few people.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors can usually tell if you have pityriasis rosea just by looking at your skin. They check the shape, color, and pattern of the rash.

If the rash looks unusual, the doctor may test for other conditions. These include:
- Ringworm (a fungal infection)
- A different skin fungus called tinea versicolor
- A rash caused by medicine
- Psoriasis
- A rare skin condition called parapsoriasis
- A skin condition called pityriasis lichenoides chronica
- Lichen planus
- Syphilis

If the rash affects the palms of the hands or the soles of the feet, or if there is no herald patch, the doctor may test for syphilis.

## How Is It Treated?

Most people do not need treatment. The rash goes away on its own in about 5 weeks.

Sunlight can help the rash clear faster. You can use natural sunlight or artificial light (like a sunlamp) carefully.

If you are itchy, you can use:
- Creams that reduce itching
- Oral antihistamines (pills that help with itching)
- Topical corticosteroids (anti-inflammatory creams)

Some studies suggest that a short course of the medicine acyclovir may help if:
- The rash is widespread
- You have flu-like symptoms
- You get the rash early in the illness

Pregnant women should be offered acyclovir. This is because pityriasis rosea during the first 15 weeks of pregnancy is linked to early birth or loss of the baby.  
However, using acyclovir has not been proven to prevent these problems.

## Key Facts

- Pityriasis rosea is a skin rash that goes away on its own.
- It may be caused by a virus or certain medicines.
- It starts with one large scaly patch (herald patch).
- Then, smaller oval patches appear on the body, often in a pattern along skin lines.
- The rash is diagnosed by how it looks and where it appears.
- Treatment is only needed for itching. Options include creams, pills, or sunlight.
- Pityriasis rosea in early pregnancy can be linked to serious problems.
- Pregnant women should be offered antiviral medicine, even though it has not been proven to help prevent complications.

# Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes – Simple Explanation

Ehlers-Danlos syndromes are rare conditions you are born with. They affect the body’s connective tissue. This tissue holds your body together and gives it strength and flexibility.

## What Causes Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes?

- A problem in one of several genes causes the body to make weak connective tissue.
- Connective tissue is the tough, fibrous material that supports your skin, joints, blood vessels, and organs.

## Types of Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes

There are 13 known types.  
Six are common. Seven are rare.  
Each type affects different genes and causes different symptoms.  
All types lead to weak connective tissue. This can cause problems in joints, bones, and internal organs.

## Common Symptoms

People with this condition often have:

- Joints that move too much (very flexible)
- Skin that stretches easily and snaps back
- Wounds that heal slowly or scar badly
- Blood vessels that are weak and can break
- Small, hard lumps under the skin
- Bleeding that is hard to stop from small cuts
- Injuries that cause wide, open wounds
- Frequent sprains and joint dislocations
- A curved spine (like a humpback)
- Flat feet
- A chest that looks different
- A clubfoot (a foot that turns inward)
- Hernias (when part of the intestine pushes through the belly wall)
- Diverticula (small pouches in the intestine)
- Rarely, the intestine can bleed or tear
- Heart valve problems that cause leaks

## Pregnancy and Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes

- Pregnant women with this condition may give birth early.
- The uterus may tear during labor because the tissues are weak.
- Healing after an episiotomy or cesarean section can be hard.
- The baby may be born early if the sac around the baby breaks too soon.
- Both mother and baby may bleed too much during delivery.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tools to diagnose Ehlers-Danlos syndromes:

- They look at your symptoms and do a physical exam.
- They may do genetic testing to find the faulty gene.
- A skin sample may be taken and looked at under a microscope.
- Imaging tests like echocardiograms check the heart and blood vessels.

## Outlook (Prognosis)

- Most people with Ehlers-Danlos syndromes live a normal life span.
- Some types can lead to serious or life-threatening problems, especially bleeding.

## Treatment

There is no cure. The body’s connective tissue cannot be fixed.

But you can manage the condition:

- Prevent injuries. Wear protective clothing and padding if needed.
- Cuts are hard to stitch because the skin is weak. Doctors often use medical glue or tape instead.
- Surgery is risky. It needs special care and extra blood available.
- Pregnant women must be cared for by a doctor who specializes in childbirth.
- Family members may want genetic counseling to learn about the risk of passing the condition to children.

## Key Points

- This is a lifelong condition you are born with.
- It affects joints, skin, blood vessels, and organs.
- There is no cure, but symptoms can be managed.
- Early diagnosis and careful care help prevent serious problems.

# Tourette Syndrome

## What Is Tourette Syndrome?

Tourette syndrome causes repeated sounds or movements that you cannot control. These are called tics.

Tics can be simple or complex. They happen again and again, even when you do not want them to.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if you or your child has tics that have lasted for more than a year.  
The tics should include both sounds and movements.  
They should have started before the age of 18.

## Symptoms of Tourette Syndrome

The main sign of Tourette syndrome is tics.  
Tics are sudden, repeated actions or sounds you do not choose.

### Sounds (Vocal Tics)

You might make sounds like:
- Whistling
- Sniffing or clearing your throat often
- Making animal noises
- Repeating a word or phrase
- Swearing (this is rare)

### Movements (Motor Tics)

You might do movements like:
- Rolling your eyes or blinking fast
- Shrugging your shoulders
- Jerking or twitching your arms or legs
- Tightening your stomach muscles
- Jumping

Tics can get worse when you are stressed, excited, or tired.

Most people first notice tics around age 6.  
They often become more noticeable around age 10.

Tourette syndrome is more common in boys than in girls.

### Not All Tics Mean Tourette Syndrome

Many children have tics at some point.  
This does not always mean they have Tourette syndrome.

## Other Conditions Often Linked to Tourette Syndrome

People with Tourette syndrome often have other conditions too.  
These can include:
- OCD (obsessive compulsive disorder)
- ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder)

## How Is Tourette Syndrome Diagnosed?

Your doctor may suspect Tourette syndrome if:
- The tics started before age 18
- They have lasted for at least one year
- They include both sounds and movements

Your doctor will ask:
- When the tics started
- How often they happen
- If anyone in your family has Tourette syndrome
- If you or your child have other conditions like OCD or ADHD

If needed, your doctor will refer you to a specialist.  
This could be a brain and nerve doctor (neurologist) or a children’s doctor (paediatrician).

The specialist may do tests to check for other causes.  
These tests can include:
- An EEG (a test that checks brain activity)
- An MRI scan (a picture of the brain)
- A blood test

These tests help rule out other possible causes.

## Treatment for Tourette Syndrome

There is no cure for Tourette syndrome.  
But treatment can help if the tics are causing problems.

### Options for Treatment

- **Behavioural therapy** – This helps you learn new ways to manage tics.
- **Medicine** – This may be used if therapy does not help.

The type of medicine depends on whether you or your child also has ADHD or OCD.

Medicines can have side effects.  
Your doctor will talk to you about what to expect.

## What You Can Do to Help

Learning about Tourette syndrome can help you understand it better.  
It can also help you find ways to manage the tics.

### Things That Can Help

- Stick to a regular daily routine.
- Get plenty of physical activity.
- Have a calm bedtime routine.  
  Avoid phones, tablets, and screens before bed.
- Try to avoid stressful situations.  
  Stress can make tics worse.
- Tell your child’s school about the diagnosis.  
  This helps them understand and support your child.

## Support and Help

You are not alone.  
There are many people and groups that can help.

### Tourettes Action

This charity offers support for anyone affected by Tourette syndrome.

- Website: [www.tourettes-action.org.uk](https://www.tourettes-action.org.uk)
- Online support groups
- Face-to-face support groups
- Help with work or employment
- Support in school or education

## Complementary Treatments

Some people try herbs, supplements, or other natural treatments.  
But there is little proof that these help with tics.  
Talk to your doctor before trying any of these.

# Fever in Babies and Children

## What Is Fever?

Everyone’s normal body temperature is a little different.  
It can go up and down during the day.  
The highest normal temperatures are often seen in young children.  
Many healthy children between 18 and 24 months old can have a temperature as high as 38.3 degrees Celsius (101 degrees Fahrenheit).  
But doctors usually say a child has a fever when the rectal temperature is 38.0 degrees Celsius (100.4 degrees Fahrenheit) or higher.

Fever is not always a sign of a serious illness.  
Some mild sicknesses can cause a high fever.  
Some serious illnesses may only cause a small rise in temperature.  
Parents often worry about fever.  
But a temperature taken at home is just as useful as one taken at the doctor’s office.

---

## How Fever Works

Fever happens when the body releases certain chemicals called cytokines.  
These chemicals tell the brain to raise the body’s normal temperature.  
The brain then makes more prostaglandins, which reset the body’s temperature control.  
This causes the fever.

Fever helps the body fight infections.  
It is not harmful in a healthy child.  
In fact, lowering the fever may make some illnesses last longer.  
But fever does make the body work harder.  
This can be risky for children with heart, lung, or brain problems.  
Fever can also trigger febrile seizures.  
These seizures are usually not dangerous, but they scare parents.  
They must be checked to rule out more serious conditions like meningitis.

---

## What Causes Fever?

The cause of fever depends on how long it lasts.

- **Acute fever** lasts 14 days or less.  
- **Acute recurrent or periodic fever** comes and goes with normal temperatures in between.  
- **Chronic fever** lasts more than 14 days.  
  When no cause is found, this is called fever of unknown origin, or FUO.

The height of the fever or how well a child responds to fever medicine does not tell us what is causing the fever.

---

## How Doctors Check for Fever

### For Acute Fever

The tests a doctor does depend on the child’s age.

Children under 36 months old need a full check for serious infections, even if they seem only mildly sick.  
This includes infections like meningitis, blood infection, or urinary tract infection.  
Even if the child has a clear cause like ear infection, a full check is still needed.  
If the child is treated at home, a follow-up call or visit is important.

### For Chronic Fever (FUO)

The doctor will look at the child’s age, medical history, and physical exam.  
Then, tests are chosen based on what might be causing the fever.

Too many tests done without a reason can be harmful.  
They can lead to false alarms and more stress.

The pace of testing depends on how the child looks.

- If the child looks very sick, testing must be fast.  
- If the child looks well, testing can be slower.

All children with FUO should have:

- A complete blood count (CBC)  
- Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP)  
- Blood cultures  
- Urine test and culture  
- Chest X-ray  
- Blood tests for electrolytes, kidney function, liver function, and albumin  
- HIV test  
- Tuberculosis test (skin test or blood test)

These results help guide further testing.

---

### What the Tests Can Show

- **Anemia** may point to malaria, heart infection, bowel disease, lupus, or tuberculosis.  
- **High platelet count** is a general sign of inflammation.  
- **High white blood cell count** may mean a serious bacterial infection.  
  A count over 10,000 per microliter is a red flag.  
- **Atypical lymphocytes** suggest a viral infection.  
- **Immature white blood cells** may mean leukemia.  
- **High eosinophils** may suggest parasites, fungus, cancer, allergies, or immune problems.

- **ESR and CRP** are signs of inflammation.  
  High levels make it less likely the fever is fake.  
  Normal levels can slow down testing.  
  But these tests can be normal even in serious cases.

- **Blood cultures** are done at least once in all children with FUO.  
  If heart infection is suspected, three cultures over 24 hours are needed.  
  A positive culture, especially for *Staphylococcus aureus*, may mean hidden infection in bones or organs.  
  Then, a heart scan or bone scan may be needed.

- **Urine test and culture** are important.  
  Urinary tract infections are a common cause of long-term fever.

- **Chest X-ray** is done even if the lungs sound normal.  
  It checks for signs of infection or swollen glands.

- **Blood tests** check kidney and liver health.

- **HIV test and TB test** are done because both can cause long-term fever.

---

### Other Tests, Done When Needed

- **Stool tests** if the child has diarrhea or has traveled to a high-risk area.  
  Some infections like *Salmonella* can cause fever without diarrhea.

- **Bone marrow test** if the child has enlarged liver or spleen, swollen glands, or low blood counts.  
  This test helps find cancer or blood disorders.

- **Blood tests for specific infections** if needed.  
  These include Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, cat-scratch disease, syphilis, and some fungal or parasitic infections.

- **Antinuclear antibody (ANA) test** for children over 5 years old with a family history of autoimmune disease or symptoms of such disease.  
  A positive result may mean lupus or another autoimmune condition.

- **Immunoglobulin levels** (IgG, IgA, IgM) are checked if the first tests do not find a cause.  
  Low levels may mean a weak immune system.  
  High levels may mean long-term infection or an autoimmune problem.

- **Imaging tests** (ultrasound, CT, MRI) are used if the child has ongoing fever and symptoms in the belly, head, or bones.  
  These can find abscesses, tumors, or swollen glands.

- **Sinus, mastoid, or bowel imaging** is only done if the child has symptoms in those areas.  
  But it may be needed later if the fever continues with no clear cause.

- **Eye exam** with a special light may help find eye inflammation (uveitis) linked to arthritis or leukemia.

- **Biopsy** (taking a small tissue sample) is only done if a specific organ is involved.

---

### Important Notes About Testing and Treatment

- Do not give fever medicine just to see if it helps.  
  It does not help find the cause.  
  It can hide serious infections.

- Antibiotics should not be used just to test if they help.  
  They can cause false-negative results and delay diagnosis.

- Do not use anti-inflammatory medicine unless juvenile arthritis is suspected.  
  Then, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are the first choice.

- Some children may be victims of medical child abuse.  
  This means a caregiver is making up or causing fever.  
  Hospital care may be needed in these cases.

---

## How to Treat Fever

The main goal is to treat the cause of the fever.

Fever in a healthy child does not always need treatment.  
It is part of the body’s way of fighting infection.  
It can help the child get better.

But fever medicine can make the child feel more comfortable.  
It may also help children with heart, lung, or brain problems.  
It may also help children with a history of febrile seizures.

### Fever Medicine

Common medicines used are:

- Acetaminophen  
- Ibuprofen

Acetaminophen is usually preferred.  
Ibuprofen can harm the stomach lining if used often.  
Some studies suggest a possible link between fever medicine and asthma.  
But in normal doses, these medicines do not make asthma worse.

- Use only one medicine at a time.  
- Do not mix acetaminophen and ibuprofen unless advised by a doctor.  
  Mixing them can lead to mistakes in dosing.

- Aspirin should never be given to children.  
  It can cause a rare but serious condition called Reye syndrome, especially if the child has a virus like flu or chickenpox.

### Non-Medicine Ways to Help

- Give a warm or lukewarm bath.  
  This can help lower the temperature.  
  Do not use cold water.  
  Cold water can make the child shiver and raise the temperature.

- Use cool cloths on the forehead or neck.  
- Dress the child lightly.  
- Keep the room at a comfortable temperature.

---

## Key Points

- Most short-term fevers are caused by viruses.  
- The cause and check-up for fever depend on the child’s age.  
  In young babies, fever can mean a serious infection.  
  It needs careful attention.  
- A small number of babies under 3 years old with fever and no clear cause may have bacteria in the blood.  
  This can be a sign of a serious infection.  
- Teething does not cause a high fever.  
- Fever medicine does not cure the illness.  
  But it can make the child feel better.

# What You Need to Know About Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)

Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are infections that spread through sexual contact. They can pass through blood, semen, vaginal fluids, or other body fluids. Skin-to-skin contact during oral, anal, or genital sex can also spread them.

## What Causes STIs?

STIs are caused by tiny germs. These include:
- Bacteria
- Viruses
- Parasites

Some of these germs can cause serious health problems if not treated.

## How STIs Spread

STIs spread most often during sex. This includes:
- Oral sex
- Anal sex
- Genital sex

You do not need to have full penetration to pass on an STI. Skin-to-skin contact can also spread some infections.

### Things that make STI spread more likely:
- Having sex without a condom
- Not knowing how to protect yourself during sex
- Not talking with your partner about safe sex
- Not talking with a doctor about your sexual health
- Not being able to get medical care
- Having an STI but not knowing it because you have no symptoms
- Not treating both partners at the same time
- Not finishing your full medicine treatment
- Traveling and having sex with new partners without protection

### Other ways STIs can spread:
- A pregnant person can pass some STIs to their baby during pregnancy or birth. These include:
  - Syphilis
  - Herpes
  - Chlamydia
  - Gonorrhea
  - HIV
  - Hepatitis B
  - HPV
- Breastfeeding (chestfeeding) can pass HIV to a baby.
- Using dirty medical tools can spread HIV.
- Some infections can be passed through sex but are not usually called STIs. This is because they usually spread in other ways. Examples:
  - Hepatitis A: spreads through food or water that has been touched by an infected person’s stool.
  - Hepatitis C: spreads through contact with infected blood.
  - Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigellosis, Giardiasis, and Amebiasis: usually spread through contaminated food or water, or contact with animals.

Some infections like pubic lice, scabies, molluscum contagiosum, and mpox can spread through skin contact. But they are only called STIs if they are passed during sex.

## What Are the Signs of an STI?

Symptoms can be very different from person to person. Some people have no symptoms at all.

Common signs include:
- Itching in the genital area
- A discharge from the penis or vagina
- Pain when peeing or during sex
- Sores, blisters, or rashes on the genitals or mouth

### Why symptoms matter:
- Sores or irritated skin make it easier for other infections, like HIV, to enter the body.
- If an STI is not treated, the germ can travel through the blood and infect other parts of the body. This can lead to serious health problems.

### In women:
- Germs can move from the vagina up into the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries.
- This can cause scarring in the fallopian tubes.
- Scarring can lead to:
  - Trouble getting pregnant (infertility)
  - A pregnancy that happens outside the uterus (ectopic pregnancy)
- Infection can also spread to the lining of the belly (peritoneum), causing a serious condition called peritonitis.
- Infections of the uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, or peritoneum are called pelvic inflammatory disease.

### In men:
- Germs can enter through the penis and infect the tube that carries urine (urethra).
- If not treated quickly, this can cause:
  - Tight foreskin that cannot be pulled back
  - Narrowing of the urethra, blocking urine flow
  - A hole between the urethra and the skin of the penis (fistula)
- In rare cases, germs can travel up the sperm-carrying tubes and infect the epididymis (the tube on top of each testicle).

### In both men and women:
- Some STIs can cause long-term swelling in the genital area.
- They can also cause infection in the urethra (urethritis) or rectum (proctitis).

## How Are STIs Diagnosed?

Doctors use several methods to find out if you have an STI.

### What the doctor does:
- Asks about your symptoms and sexual history
- Does a physical exam
- Takes a sample of blood, urine, or fluid from the vagina, cervix, or penis

### Lab tests:
- Some tests look for the germ’s DNA or RNA.
- Others check for antibodies your body makes when fighting an infection.
- The test used depends on which germ is most likely.

### Testing for other STIs:
- If you have one STI, your doctor will likely test for others.
- This is because people with one STI often have another.

## Should You Be Screened for STIs?

Screening means testing for an STI even if you have no symptoms.

You should be screened if:
- The infection is common
- You are at higher risk (like having many partners)
- The infection can be dangerous (like during pregnancy)
- The test is easy and cheap
- There is effective treatment

Doctors recommend screening for:
- Chlamydia
- Gonorrhea
- Syphilis
- HIV

## How Are STIs Treated?

Most STIs can be treated successfully.

### Treatment depends on the type:
- Bacterial STIs (like chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis) are treated with antibiotics.
- Viral STIs (like herpes, HIV, hepatitis B) are treated with antiviral medicines.

### Important points:
- Some germs have become resistant to certain medicines.
- This happens when medicines are not used correctly or are overused.
- You must finish all your medicine, even if you feel better.

### What to do during treatment:
- Do not have sex until you and your partner are fully treated and the infection is gone.
- Your sex partners should be tested and treated as soon as possible.
- Viral STIs like herpes and HIV cannot be cured. But medicines can help control them and reduce the risk of spreading.

### Treating complications:
- If an STI causes a serious problem, like pelvic inflammatory disease, you will get antibiotics.
- Treatment depends on the specific issue.

## How to Prevent STIs

You can lower your risk of getting an STI by taking these steps:

### Practice safer sex:
- Use a condom every time you have oral, anal, or genital sex.
- Use internal condoms, dental dams, or external condoms as barriers.

### Reduce your risk:
- Limit the number of sex partners.
- Avoid sex with people who have many partners or who do not use protection.
- Be in a long-term, faithful relationship (mutual monogamy).
- Choose not to have sex (abstinence).

### Get vaccinated:
- Vaccines are available for:
  - HPV (human papillomavirus)
  - Hepatitis A
  - Hepatitis B

### Take preventive medicine:
- People at high risk of HIV can take medicine before exposure to lower their risk.
- Men who have sex with men and transgender women can take a daily antibiotic (doxycycline) within 3 days after sex without a condom to reduce their risk of chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis.

### How to use a condom correctly:
- Use a new condom for each sexual act.
- Use the right size.
- Handle it carefully—avoid sharp nails, teeth, or jewelry.
- Put it on after the penis is hard and before any contact with your partner.
- Test the direction by gently rolling it a little. If it resists, turn it over and try the other way.
- Place it on the tip of the penis.
- Leave about half an inch at the tip to collect semen.
- Squeeze the air out of the tip.
- If uncircumcised, pull the foreskin back before rolling.
- Roll the condom down to the base.
- Smooth out any air bubbles.
- Use enough lubricant during sex.
- Use only water-based lubricants with latex condoms. Oil-based products (like petroleum jelly, lotions, cooking oil) can break latex.
- Hold the base of the condom during withdrawal.
- Pull out while the penis is still hard to avoid slippage.

# Acne

Acne causes spots on your face, back, or chest. Your skin might feel oily, warm, or sore when you touch it.

You can often treat mild acne with creams or gels from a pharmacy. If your acne is more serious, your doctor may give you stronger medicine or antibiotics.

Acne often starts during puberty because of hormone changes. But it can begin at any age. It also tends to run in families.

## Where Acne Shows Up

Acne most often appears on:

- Your face – almost everyone with acne gets it here  
- Your back – more than half of people with acne have it here  
- Your chest – about 1 in 7 people with acne get spots here  

### Types of Spots

There are six main types of acne spots:

- **Blackheads** – small dark or yellowish bumps. They are not dirty. The dark color comes from the skin’s natural lining.  
- **Whiteheads** – look like blackheads but are firmer. They do not come out when you squeeze them.  
- **Papules** – small red bumps that may hurt or feel tender.  
- **Pustules** – red bumps with a white tip in the middle. The white part is pus.  
- **Nodules** – large, hard lumps under the skin. They can be painful.  
- **Cysts** – the most serious type of spot. They are big, filled with pus, and look like boils. They can cause lasting scars.

## Seeing a Doctor

See your doctor if:

- Your acne is moderate or severe  
- Pharmacy treatments did not help  
- You have many spots on your chest and back, not just your face  
- You have painful lumps under your skin  
- You have scars or are at risk of scarring  
- Your acne is making you feel sad or anxious  

Your doctor may prescribe one or more of the following:

- Creams or gels that go on the skin (topical retinoids or antibiotics)  
- A cream called azelaic acid  
- Antibiotic tablets  
- For women, the combined contraceptive pill (a type of birth control pill)  

If your acne is very bad or does not improve with treatment, your doctor can refer you to a skin specialist (dermatologist).

Most treatments take 2 to 3 months before you see results. Be patient and keep using the medicine, even if you don’t see changes right away.

## Why Do I Have Acne?

Acne is most often caused by hormone changes during puberty. But it can start at any age.

Hormones make the oil glands near your hair roots produce more oil than normal. This is called sebum.

This extra oil changes a common skin germ called P. acnes. It makes the germ more active and causes swelling and pus.

Hormones also make the inside of your hair follicles thicker. This blocks the pores. Cleaning your skin does not remove these blockages.

### Other Possible Causes

- Acne often runs in families. If both your mother and father had acne, you are more likely to get it too.  
- Hormone changes during your period or pregnancy can cause acne in women.  
- Poor hygiene does not cause acne.  
- Sexual activity does not cause acne.

# Polymyalgia Rheumatica – Simple Explanation

Polymyalgia rheumatica is a condition that causes pain and stiffness in the muscles. It mainly affects people over 50 years old. Women are more likely to get it than men.

This condition is closely linked to another disease called giant cell arteritis. Some experts think they are part of the same illness process. Polymyalgia rheumatica is more common. Some people with polymyalgia rheumatica later develop giant cell arteritis. But many people with giant cell arteritis also have polymyalgia rheumatica.

The exact cause of polymyalgia rheumatica is not known. Tests like ultrasound and MRI show there may be mild inflammation in the joints and fluid sacs around the joints.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main symptoms are:

- Pain and stiffness in the shoulders, hips, neck, and upper or lower back.
- The stiffness is usually worse in the morning and lasts more than one hour.
- Pain can wake you up at night.
- The pain can be so bad that it is hard to get out of bed or do simple tasks.
- You may feel weak, but your muscles are not actually weak.

The pain is not caused by muscle damage. It comes from inflammation in the joints and fluid sacs around the joints.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose polymyalgia rheumatica based on your symptoms and medical history. They will also do tests to rule out other conditions.

### Common tests include:
- Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
- C-reactive protein (CRP)
- Blood count
- Thyroid function test
- Creatine kinase (CK) test

In most people with polymyalgia rheumatica:
- ESR is very high, often over 100 mm per hour.
- CRP is also high.

Other tests like electromyography, muscle biopsy, and rheumatoid factor are usually normal. These tests help rule out other diseases.

### How It Is Different From Other Conditions:

- **Rheumatoid arthritis**: Polymyalgia rheumatica does not cause joint damage or swelling in small joints. Rheumatoid factor is usually negative.
- **Autoimmune myositis**: In this condition, muscle weakness is the main problem. In polymyalgia rheumatica, pain is the main issue. Muscle tests are normal.
- **Hypothyroidism**: Thyroid levels are normal in polymyalgia rheumatica.
- **Multiple myeloma**: This disease shows abnormal proteins in the blood. These are not found in polymyalgia rheumatica.
- **Fibromyalgia**: Pain in polymyalgia rheumatica is more focused. ESR is usually high. Pain is felt when moving or touching the shoulders.

---

## How Is It Treated?

### First-line treatment: Corticosteroids

- A low dose of prednisone (15 to 20 mg once daily) is usually started.
- Most people feel much better within hours or days.
- This quick improvement helps confirm the diagnosis.

If giant cell arteritis is suspected, a higher dose of steroids may be needed. A full check for giant cell arteritis should be done.

### Monitoring treatment:
- Doctors watch your symptoms, ESR, and CRP.
- As symptoms improve, the steroid dose is slowly lowered.
- The goal is to use the lowest dose that keeps symptoms away.
- CRP is more useful than ESR for tracking treatment response. ESR can stay high in older adults for other reasons.

### Some people can stop steroids after about 2 years. Others need a small dose for many years.

- Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen are not strong enough to treat this condition.

### Other treatment options:
- **Sarilumab**: This is a newer medicine that blocks a certain protein in the body. It may help people who do not respond well to steroids or cannot lower their steroid dose.
- **Methotrexate**: This medicine may help some people reduce their steroid dose without a relapse. But the evidence is limited.
- **TNF inhibitors (infliximab and adalimumab)**: These medicines have not been shown to help.

### Side effects of long-term steroid use:
- High blood sugar (can lead to diabetes)
- High blood pressure
- Weak bones (osteoporosis)

To prevent weak bones:
- All patients on long-term steroids should take a bisphosphonate medicine.

---

## Important Warnings

- Giant cell arteritis can start at the same time as polymyalgia rheumatica or years later.
- Even if you feel better, you could still develop giant cell arteritis.
- Tell your doctor right away if you have:
  - Headache
  - Pain when chewing
  - Vision changes (blurred vision, double vision, or sudden vision loss)

These could be signs of a serious problem that needs urgent care.

---

## Key Points

- Polymyalgia rheumatica affects adults over 50.
- It causes pain and stiffness in the shoulders, hips, neck, and back.
- It is linked to giant cell arteritis. About 40 to 60% of people with giant cell arteritis also have polymyalgia rheumatica.
- Diagnosis is based on symptoms and test results like high ESR or CRP.
- A fast response to low-dose steroids supports the diagnosis.
- Treatment is with steroids, slowly reduced over time if possible.
- Always report new symptoms like headache, jaw pain, or vision changes to your doctor.

# Uterine Adenomyosis – Simple Explanation

Adenomyosis happens when tissue from the inside lining of the uterus grows into the muscle wall of the uterus. This can make the uterus larger. It may become twice or even three times its normal size.

## What Are the Symptoms?

- Periods are very heavy and painful.
- You may feel pain in your lower belly or pelvis.
- You may feel pressure in your bladder or rectum.
- Some women have pain during sex.
- Heavy bleeding can lead to low iron levels (anemia).

These symptoms often go away after menopause.

## Who Gets Adenomyosis?

- It mostly affects women between the ages of 35 and 50.
- Not all women with adenomyosis have symptoms.
- Some women with adenomyosis also have endometriosis or fibroids.

We do not know exactly how many women have adenomyosis. It is hard to diagnose, so the true number is unclear.

The cause is not known. It may be more common in women who have had more than one baby.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor may suspect adenomyosis during a pelvic exam. They will check the size, shape, and feel of your uterus.

- If the uterus feels larger, round, and softer than normal, it may be adenomyosis.
- Your doctor may order an ultrasound or an MRI to look at the uterus in more detail.
- A special ultrasound done through the vagina (transvaginal ultrasound) is often used.

To be sure of the diagnosis, doctors need to look at tissue from the uterus. The only way to get this tissue is to remove the uterus. This is called a hysterectomy.

## How Is It Treated?

There are several treatment options:

- A small device called an intrauterine device (IUD) that releases a hormone called levonorgestrel can help reduce heavy bleeding and pain during periods.
- Birth control pills may help some women, but they do not work for everyone.
- Pain relief medicine (analgesics) can help with pain.

If symptoms are very bad and other treatments do not help, a hysterectomy may be recommended. This surgery removes the uterus. It completely stops the symptoms.

# Thrombophilia

Thrombophilia means your blood is more likely to form clots than normal.  
If a clot forms, you may feel pain or other symptoms.  
Most people do not know they have thrombophilia until a blood clot happens.

## Symptoms of Thrombophilia

You may not have any symptoms at all.  
The first sign might be a blood clot.  
A blood clot can cause:

- Throbbing pain and swelling in one leg or arm  
- Sudden trouble breathing  
- Chest pain  
- Coughing up blood  
- Repeated miscarriages

### When to Seek Help Right Away

Call your doctor or get help from NHS 111 if you have:

- Pain in one leg, especially in the calf or thigh  
- Swelling in one leg  
- Skin on your leg that looks red, dark, or feels warm  
- Sudden trouble breathing  
- Coughing up blood  

These could mean you have a blood clot in your leg or lung.  
You might also have pain or swelling in your arm or belly instead.

You can call 111 or get help online.

### When to Call 999 or Go to A&E

Go to A&E or call 999 if you have:

- Very bad trouble breathing  
- Severe chest or upper back pain  
- A very fast heartbeat  
- Someone has passed out  

These could be signs of a serious blood clot in the lungs or another emergency.

[Find your nearest A&E]

### A&E Safety Advice (for 999 calls only)

Do not drive yourself to A&E.  
The person you speak to on 999 will tell you what to do.

## How Thrombophilia Is Diagnosed

You may have a blood test if:

- You had a blood clot with no clear cause (like being overweight or smoking)  
- A close family member has inherited thrombophilia  
- You have had three or more miscarriages  

The blood test checks for changes in your genes or blood cells linked to clotting.  
You may also have an ultrasound scan or a CT scan.  
These tests look at your blood vessels to find any problems.

## Treatment for Thrombophilia

There is no cure for inherited thrombophilia.  
This means you were born with it and it comes from your parents’ genes.  

Thrombophilia that develops later in life may improve if the cause is treated.  

If your risk of a blood clot is low, you may not need treatment.  

If you do need treatment, you will likely be given anticoagulant medicine.  
This medicine makes your blood less likely to clot.  
It does not break up clots already in your body.  
It helps stop new clots from forming.

## What You Can Do If You Have Thrombophilia

Many people with thrombophilia live normal lives.  
But you can take steps to lower your risk of blood clots.

### Do These Things

- Stay active and move around often  
- Try to lose weight if you are overweight  
- Drink plenty of water every day  
- Dehydration increases your risk of clots  
- Wear flight stockings or socks on long flights  
- A pharmacist can help you choose the right kind

### Avoid These Things

- Do not smoke  
- Do not drink too much alcohol  
- Alcohol can make you dehydrated  
- Avoid sitting still for long periods  
- Get up and move if you can

### Important Reminder

Always tell your doctor or nurse that you have thrombophilia.  
This is true before any medical procedure or if you start a new medicine.  
This includes birth control pills or other prescription medicines.  

Some medicines can be unsafe for you.  
You may need extra care or monitoring during medical treatments.

# Omphalocele

An omphalocele is a birth defect where some of the baby’s intestines or other organs push through the belly button area. The organs are covered by a thin, clear membrane. This condition needs surgery to fix.

## How Common Is It?

About 2 to 3 out of every 10,000 babies born have an omphalocele. It is less common than another similar condition called gastroschisis.

## What Happens in an Omphalocele?

The baby’s belly organs stick out through a hole in the belly wall near the belly button. The organs may be just a small part of the intestines. Or they may include most of the intestines, the stomach, and even the liver.

The exposed organs are at risk of drying out. This can lead to serious problems like:
- The baby losing too much body heat (hypothermia)
- Dehydration from water loss
- Infection of the organs

## Other Health Problems

Most babies with an omphalocele also have other birth defects. About two out of every three babies have at least one other problem. These can include:
- A blockage in the intestines
- Chromosome problems such as trisomy 18, trisomy 13, or Down syndrome (trisomy 21)
- Heart problems
- Kidney problems
- Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome

## How Is It Found?

Doctors can often see the omphalocele during a routine ultrasound scan before birth. If the baby has this condition, delivery should happen at a hospital with special teams trained to care for babies with complex birth defects.

## Care Right After Birth

When the baby is born, the doctor will cover the exposed organs right away. They will use a clean, wet, soft dressing. This keeps the organs safe and stops them from drying out. The dressing may be covered with plastic wrap.

The baby will also get fluids through a needle in a vein (IV). This helps replace lost fluids. The baby will also get antibiotics to prevent infection. These medicines are strong and work against many types of bacteria.

A small tube will be placed through the nose into the stomach. This helps drain stomach fluid and keeps the stomach from getting too full.

The baby needs more fluids than a healthy newborn. The amount is usually 1.5 to 2 times more than normal.

## Before Surgery

The baby will be checked for other health problems before surgery. This helps the care team plan the best treatment.

## Surgery

The goal is to put the organs back inside the belly and close the hole.

- If the hole is small, the surgeon may close it right away.
- If the hole is large, the belly may not be big enough to fit all the organs. In this case, the surgeon uses a special soft cover (a silo) made of silicone. This cover slowly shrinks over several days. As the belly grows, the organs move back inside. This process takes time.

The baby’s chance of survival and long-term health depends on how big the hole is. Larger holes are harder to fix and carry more risk.

# Gastrointestinal Bleeding

Bleeding can happen anywhere in the digestive system. This includes the mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and rectum.

Blood may be easy to see. This is called overt bleeding.  
Or, blood may be too small to see. This is called occult bleeding.  
Occult bleeding is found only by testing a stool sample with special chemicals.

## Signs of Bleeding

**Vomiting blood (hematemesis)** means the bleeding is in the upper part of the digestive system. This includes the esophagus, stomach, or first part of the small intestine.

- If blood is bright red, the bleeding is likely fast and ongoing.
- If blood looks like coffee grounds, the bleeding has slowed or stopped. The stomach acid has partly digested the blood.

**Blood in the stool** can appear in different ways:

- Black, sticky, tar-like stools (melena)
- Bright red blood (hematochezia)
- Blood in normal-looking stool if the bleeding is very small (less than a few teaspoons per day)

**Melena** usually comes from the upper digestive tract.  
The black color happens because blood has been in the stomach and intestines for several hours. Stomach acid and bacteria change the blood’s color.

Melena can last for several days after the bleeding has stopped.

**Hematochezia** usually comes from the large intestine.  
But it can also happen if there is very fast bleeding from the upper digestive tract.

## Symptoms of Blood Loss

A person who loses only a small amount of blood may feel fine.  
But serious or sudden blood loss can cause:

- A fast heartbeat
- Low blood pressure
- Less urine than usual
- Cold, sweaty hands and feet

Severe blood loss can lead to shock.  
Shock means the body is not getting enough blood.  
This can cause confusion, being disoriented, or feeling very sleepy.

Slow, long-term blood loss can lead to anemia.  
Anemia means the body does not have enough healthy red blood cells.  
Symptoms of anemia include:

- Feeling weak
- Getting tired easily
- Pale skin
- Chest pain
- Dizziness

People with heart disease may have chest pain (angina) or a heart attack if blood flow to the heart drops.

(See also: Overview of Digestive Symptoms.)

## Causes of Bleeding

Bleeding can come from three areas:

- Upper digestive tract
- Lower digestive tract
- Small intestine

The most common causes depend on age and where the bleeding is.

### Most Common Causes of Upper GI Bleeding

- Ulcers or sores in the esophagus, stomach, or first part of the small intestine
- Enlarged veins in the esophagus (esophageal varices)
- A tear in the esophagus from severe vomiting (Mallory-Weiss syndrome)

### Most Common Causes of Lower GI Bleeding

- Polyps in the large intestine
- Diverticular disease (small pouches in the colon wall)
- Hemorrhoids (swollen veins in the rectum or anus)
- Abnormal blood vessels (angiodysplasia or arteriovenous malformations)
- Inflammatory bowel disease (like ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease)
- Colon cancer

Other causes of lower GI bleeding include:

- A split in the skin around the anus (anal fissure)
- Ischemic colitis (inflammation from poor blood flow)
- Radiation damage to the large intestine

### Bleeding from the Small Intestine

This is rare.  
It can be caused by:

- Blood vessel problems
- Tumors
- A Meckel diverticulum (a small pouch in the small intestine)

## Risk Factors for Bleeding

Bleeding is more likely and more serious in people who:

- Have long-term alcohol use or liver disease
- Have inherited blood clotting problems
- Take certain medicines

Liver disease makes bleeding worse.  
A damaged liver makes fewer proteins that help blood clot.

### Medicines That Can Cause or Worsen Bleeding

- Anticoagulants (like heparin, warfarin, dabigatran, apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban)
- Drugs that affect platelets (like aspirin, other NSAIDs, and clopidogrel)
- Some antidepressants (like SSRIs)
- Medicines that weaken the stomach’s protective lining (like NSAIDs)

## When to See a Doctor

You should see a doctor right away if you have:

- Fainting
- Heavy sweating
- A fast heartbeat (over 100 beats per minute with no exercise)
- Vomiting or passing more than 1 cup (250 milliliters) of blood

If the only sign is blood on toilet paper after a bowel movement, you can wait 1 or 2 days.  
This is safe if you feel well and have no other warning signs.

## How Doctors Evaluate Bleeding

Doctors will ask about your symptoms and medical history.  
They will do a physical exam.

### What Doctors Ask

- Where do you think the bleeding is coming from?
- How much blood are you passing? (For example, a few teaspoons or several clots)
- How often does it happen?
- Did you vomit blood the first time you threw up, or only after several times?
- Is the blood mixed with stool, pus, or mucus?
- Is the blood only on the toilet paper or on the surface of the stool?
- Do you have pain during bowel movements?
- Have you had recent travel or eaten food that might have made you sick?
- Do you have abdominal pain, weight loss, or feel weak?
- Do you get bruises or bleed easily?
- Have you ever had digestive bleeding before?
- Have you had a colonoscopy?
- Do you have inflammatory bowel disease, liver disease, or bleeding problems?
- Are you taking aspirin, NSAIDs, anticoagulants, or alcohol?

### What Doctors Check During Exam

- Pulse, breathing rate, blood pressure, and temperature
- Signs of anemia (pale skin, tiredness)
- Signs of shock (fast heartbeat, fast breathing, cold hands, little urine, confusion)
- Skin spots (petechiae or bruises) that may mean a bleeding disorder
- Signs of liver disease (spider-like blood vessels, swollen belly, red palms)
- Enlarged spleen or swollen veins in the belly (signs of portal hypertension)

Doctors will do a rectal exam.  
They will check the stool color and test it for blood.  
They will look for tumors or fissures.

They will also check the anus for hemorrhoids.

## Tests for Bleeding

The tests depend on what the doctor finds during the history and exam.

### Four Main Types of Tests

1. Blood tests and lab work
2. Upper endoscopy (for upper GI bleeding)
3. Colonoscopy (for lower GI bleeding, unless it’s clearly hemorrhoids)
4. Angiography or CT angiography (if bleeding is fast or severe)

### Blood Tests

- Check blood count to see how much blood was lost
- Low platelet count increases bleeding risk
- Tests for blood clotting problems (PT, PTT)
- Liver function tests

Doctors usually do not test people with minor bleeding from hemorrhoids.

### Nasogastric Tube

If you vomit blood or dark material, the doctor may pass a thin tube through your nose into your stomach.  
They will suction out the stomach contents.

- Bloody or pink fluid means active bleeding in the upper GI tract.
- Dark or coffee-ground material means bleeding is slow or stopped.
- No blood seen does not rule out recent bleeding.

This tube may be used even if you did not vomit, but passed a lot of blood from the rectum.  
This is because the blood might have come from the upper digestive tract.

### Endoscopy

If the tube shows active bleeding or symptoms suggest upper GI bleeding, the doctor will do an upper endoscopy.

**Upper endoscopy** uses a flexible tube with a camera to look at the esophagus, stomach, and first part of the small intestine.  
The doctor can see the bleeding source and often treat it during the test.

### Sigmoidoscopy or Anoscopy

If you have symptoms of hemorrhoids, you may only need:

- Sigmoidoscopy (exam of the lower colon, rectum, and anus)
- Anoscopy (exam of the rectum with a short scope)

### Colonoscopy

All other people with blood in the stool should have a colonoscopy.  
This exam uses a flexible tube with a camera to look at the entire large intestine, rectum, and anus.

### Other Tests if Bleeding Source Is Not Found

If endoscopy does not find the cause, doctors may use:

- **Enteroscopy** – to look at the small intestine
- **Angiography** – a test that uses a catheter and dye to find bleeding vessels. Doctors can also stop bleeding during this test by blocking the vessel.
- **CT angiography** – a scan that uses dye and imaging to show blood vessels and possible bleeding sites.
- **Radionuclide scanning** – a test that uses a radioactive tracer to find the bleeding site.
- **CT enterography** – a scan to look at the small intestine for tumors.
- **Video capsule endoscopy** – you swallow a tiny camera that takes pictures as it moves through the intestines. It is best for the small intestine but not useful for the colon or stomach.

## Treatment of Bleeding

There are two main goals:

1. Replace lost blood with fluids through a vein. Sometimes a blood transfusion is needed.
2. Stop the bleeding.

# Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)

## What Are STIs?

STIs are infections that spread through sexual contact. They can affect anyone who has sex.

Some STIs cause clear signs. Others do not cause any symptoms at all.

## Signs of an STI

You might have an STI if you notice any of these:

- A strange discharge from your vagina, penis, or anus  
- Pain when you pee  
- Lumps, bumps, or growths near your genitals or anus  
- A rash on your skin  
- Bleeding from your vagina that is not your period  
- Itching around your genitals or anus  
- Blisters, sores, or warts near your genitals or anus  
- Warts in your mouth or throat (this is very rare)

The time it takes for symptoms to appear depends on the type of STI.

Many people with STIs have no symptoms. This means you can carry an infection and pass it on to others without knowing.

The only way to know for sure is to get tested.

### When to Get Tested

Wait 7 weeks after unprotected sex before getting tested. Some STIs take up to 7 weeks to show up in tests.

You should go to a sexual health clinic if:

- You think you might have an STI  
- A partner has symptoms of an STI  
- You had sex without a condom and are worried  
- You are pregnant and have symptoms of an STI  
- You are having casual sex without a condom with new partners — you may be at risk for HIV and other STIs  

Do not have sex — including oral sex — without a condom until you’ve been checked or tested.

[Find a sexual health clinic]

## What Happens at a Sexual Health Clinic

If you go to a sexual health clinic:

- The doctor or nurse will ask about your sex life  
- They may look at your genitals or anus  
- They will explain which tests you need  

Tests may include:

- A urine sample (pee)  
- A blood test  
- A swab from the urethra (the tube that pee comes out of)  
- A swab from inside your vagina or anus  

Some clinics offer home testing kits for certain STIs.

If you test positive for an STI, you should tell your current and past sexual partners. This helps them get tested and treated too.

If you do not want to tell them yourself, the clinic can contact them for you without saying your name.

## Treating STIs

Most STIs can be treated. The treatment depends on the type of infection.

Many STIs are treated with antibiotics.

Always take all your medicine as prescribed. Do not stop early, even if you feel better.

Do not have sex — including oral sex — until you and your partner(s) have finished treatment.

### Important

If you are being treated for an STI, tell your current and past partners. A sexual health clinic can help you contact them anonymously.

## Common Types of STIs

These are some common STIs:

- Chlamydia  
- Gonorrhoea  
- Trichomoniasis  
- Genital warts  
- Genital herpes  
- Pubic lice  
- Scabies  
- Syphilis  
- Human papillomavirus (HPV)  
- HIV

Each of these can be treated, but some need special care. Getting tested early helps you get better faster and protects your partners.

# Hyperparathyroidism

Hyperparathyroidism happens when one or more of the small glands in your neck make too much parathyroid hormone. This hormone helps control calcium in your blood. Too much of it raises your blood calcium level. This condition is called hypercalcemia.

Some people have no symptoms. Others may feel tired all the time. They might have body aches, trouble sleeping, bone pain, memory problems, trouble focusing, sadness, or headaches.

Doctors find this condition by testing your blood for calcium and parathyroid hormone levels. If the test shows high calcium and high parathyroid hormone, it likely means you have hyperparathyroidism.

The most common treatment is surgery to remove the overactive gland or glands.

---

## What Causes Hyperparathyroidism?

The most common cause is a non-cancerous growth called a parathyroid adenoma. This is usually a single growth. But in some people, it can run in families, especially if they have other hormone-related tumors.

Another cause is when all four parathyroid glands become too active. This is called hyperplasia.

---

## How Does It Work?

Parathyroid hormone raises calcium in your blood in three main ways:

- It helps your kidneys keep more calcium instead of losing it in urine.
- It pulls calcium and phosphate out of your bones.
- It helps your gut absorb more calcium by turning vitamin D into its active form.

There are three types of hyperparathyroidism:

- **Primary**: The parathyroid glands make too much hormone on their own.
- **Secondary**: A problem outside the parathyroid glands causes low calcium. This makes the glands work harder over time.
- **Tertiary**: The glands keep making too much hormone even when calcium levels are normal. This can happen after long-term secondary hyperparathyroidism.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many people do not feel any symptoms. The condition is often found by chance when a blood test shows high calcium.

When symptoms do appear, they are due to high calcium in the blood. These include:

- Feeling very tired
- Constipation
- Loss of appetite
- Nausea or vomiting
- Trouble thinking clearly
- Confusion
- Feeling sad or down

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use blood and urine tests to check for hyperparathyroidism.

A high calcium level found on a routine blood test may raise suspicion. If the level stays high on a second test, your doctor will check your parathyroid hormone level.

In primary hyperparathyroidism, the parathyroid hormone level is high even though calcium is high. This is not normal. In most cases, high calcium should lower the hormone level. If it does not, that is a sign of the disease.

In rare cases, the hormone level is only slightly high. But if calcium is high, this is still a sign of the disease.

Serum calcium levels are usually not above 12 milligrams per deciliter. But the active form of calcium in your blood is almost always high.

Low phosphate in the blood can point to hyperparathyroidism. This is especially true if your kidneys are passing more phosphate than normal.

If your bones are breaking down faster than normal, your blood test may show high levels of a liver enzyme called alkaline phosphatase.

Your urine may show normal or high calcium. Low calcium in the urine suggests a different condition called familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia.

If you have long-term kidney disease, you may have secondary hyperparathyroidism. But primary hyperparathyroidism can also happen at the same time.

In kidney disease, high calcium and normal phosphate suggest primary hyperparathyroidism. High phosphate suggests secondary hyperparathyroidism.

---

## Imaging Tests

Imaging tests are not used to confirm the diagnosis. They are used to find the exact location of the overactive gland before surgery.

These tests are not needed to decide if surgery is needed. But they can help the surgeon find the right gland.

Many imaging methods work well. These include:

- High-resolution CT scan, sometimes with a biopsy or hormone test from a neck vein
- Contrast-enhanced four-dimensional CT scan
- MRI
- High-resolution ultrasound
- Digital subtraction angiography
- Thallium-201 and technetium-99 scanning

Technetium-99 sestamibi is the most accurate test for finding a single overactive gland.

If the condition comes back after surgery, imaging is very important. It can find extra glands in unusual places in the neck or chest. Technetium-99 sestamibi is the best test for this. Sometimes, doctors use more than one test (like MRI, CT, or ultrasound) along with sestamibi to find the problem.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on how serious the condition is.

Some people with no symptoms may not need treatment right away. Doctors may just watch them closely.

But most people with symptoms, very high calcium, or weak bones need surgery.

Surgery to remove the overactive gland or glands is the most effective treatment. It cures the problem in most cases.

For people who cannot have surgery, doctors may use medicines to lower calcium levels.

---

## Key Points

- **Primary hyperparathyroidism** causes high calcium in the blood. It often causes no symptoms.
- The diagnosis is made when blood tests show high calcium and high parathyroid hormone.
- The most common cause is a single non-cancerous growth in one gland. But sometimes more than one gland is affected.
- If you have no symptoms, your doctor may just watch you. But surgery is usually needed if you have symptoms, very high calcium, or weak bones.
- **Secondary hyperparathyroidism** is most often caused by long-term kidney disease. It happens when your body has low calcium and vitamin D, and high phosphate.
- Treatment for secondary hyperparathyroidism includes:
  - Eating less phosphate
  - Taking phosphate binders
  - Taking vitamin D
  - Using a medicine called a calcimimetic
- Surgery is only used if the condition is very bad and does not respond to medicine.

# Short-Lasting Unilateral Neuralgiform Headache with Eye Redness and Tearing (SUNCT)

SUNCT is a rare type of headache. It feels similar to cluster headaches. Most people with SUNCT have sharp pain around one eye. The pain happens in short bursts, but it can come many times a day.

## What SUNCT Feels Like

- The pain is on one side of the head, usually around the eye.
- Each pain attack lasts from 5 seconds to more than 4 minutes.
- Some people have up to 200 attacks in one day.
- The eye on the painful side often looks red.
- The same eye may also water a lot.

## How SUNCT Is Related to Other Headaches

SUNCT and cluster headaches are similar. Doctors group them together as a type called trigeminal autonomic cephalgias. Other rare headaches in this group include chronic paroxysmal hemicrania and hemicrania continua.

## A Similar Condition: SUNA

SUNA is like SUNCT. It also causes short, sharp pain on one side of the head. But in SUNA, only one of the following happens:
- The eye is red, or
- The eye waters

It does not have both redness and watering at the same time.

## How Doctors Diagnose SUNCT

Doctors look at your symptoms to make a diagnosis. They may do a brain scan called an MRI. This helps rule out other causes, like a tumor or injury.

## How SUNCT Is Treated

### To Stop Pain Right Away
- A medicine called lidocaine is given through a vein. This helps stop the pain quickly.

### To Prevent Future Attacks
- Doctors may prescribe antiseizure medicines. These include:
  - Lamotrigine
  - Topiramate
  - Gabapentin
- Doctors may also inject medicine near the nerve that supplies the eye. This can block or calm the nerve to reduce attacks.

These treatments can help reduce how often attacks happen and how bad they feel.

# Cirrhosis – Simple Guide

Cirrhosis is a serious condition where the liver becomes scarred and damaged. It can cause many health problems.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many people do not feel sick at first. But over time, symptoms may appear.

Early signs of cirrhosis can include:
- Feeling tired all the time
- Losing your appetite
- Losing weight without trying
- Feeling sick or being sick
- Pain in your tummy
- Blood vessels showing through your skin
- Redness on your palms – this may be harder to see on brown or black skin

As the condition gets worse, you may notice:
- Bleeding or bruising easily
- Itchy skin
- Fingers that are wider or curved (clubbed fingers)
- White nails
- Yellow skin or the white part of your eyes (this is called jaundice) – this may be harder to see on brown or black skin
- Swelling in your tummy, legs, ankles, or feet
- Shaking hands
- Slurred speech
- Confusion or trouble thinking clearly
- Vomiting blood
- Very dark or black poo

Men may also have:
- Larger breasts than usual
- Smaller testicles

## Who Is More Likely to Get Cirrhosis?

You are more likely to get cirrhosis if you:
- Drink a lot of alcohol over many years
- Have hepatitis B or hepatitis C
- Are overweight or have obesity
- Have type 2 diabetes
- Have non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
- Have an autoimmune liver disease (like autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis, or primary sclerosing cholangitis)
- Have a genetic condition (like haemochromatosis, Wilson’s disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, or cystic fibrosis)

## How Is Cirrhosis Treated?

There is no cure for cirrhosis. But treatment can slow it down and help prevent serious problems.

Treatment depends on the cause. For example:
- If you have hepatitis B or C, you may take antiviral medicines.
- If you drink alcohol, stopping is very important.

Other treatments may include:
- Laxative medicine to help clear toxins from your body
- Beta blockers to reduce the risk of bleeding
- Diuretics (water pills) to reduce swelling
- Antibiotics to treat or prevent infections and internal bleeding
- Treatment for weak bones
- A liver transplant if your liver is very damaged

You will work with a team of healthcare experts. This may include:
- A liver doctor (hepatologist)
- A digestive system doctor (gastroenterologist)
- A dietitian or nutritionist
- A specialist for alcohol support

## What Can You Do to Help?

You can take steps to stay healthy and slow down the damage.

### Do These Things:
- Eat a healthy, balanced diet
- Exercise regularly
- Try to keep a healthy weight
- Talk to a pharmacist or doctor before taking any medicine – including herbal remedies. Some can harm your liver.
- Get your flu vaccine and pneumococcal vaccine on time

### Do Not Do These Things:
- Do not drink alcohol
- Do not smoke

## When to See a Doctor

### See your GP if:
- You think you might have cirrhosis

### Call 111 or get help online if:
You have been diagnosed with cirrhosis and:
- Your skin or the white part of your eyes look yellow
- You are short of breath or find it harder to breathe than usual
- You have swelling in your tummy, legs, ankles, or feet

You can call 111 or visit [111 online](https://111.nhs.uk)

### Call 999 or go to A&E if:
You have been diagnosed with cirrhosis and:
- You are vomiting blood
- Your poo is very dark or black
- You suddenly feel confused or have slurred speech

Find your nearest A&E [here](https://www.nhs.uk/service-search/A-and-E/LocationSearch/1)

### A&E Safety Tips:
- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to take you or call 999 for an ambulance.
- Bring all your medicines with you.

## Support and Help

You are not alone. There are people and groups ready to help.

### British Liver Trust
This charity gives information and support to anyone affected by liver disease.

- Website: [www.britishlivertrust.org.uk](https://www.britishlivertrust.org.uk)
- Helpline: 0800 652 7330 (open Monday to Friday, 9am to 3pm)
- Support groups
- Online community

You can reach out for help, advice, and connection.

# Schistosomiasis

Schistosomiasis is an infection caused by tiny parasitic worms called *Schistosoma*. These worms enter the body through the skin when a person swims or walks in dirty freshwater. The worms travel through the blood and settle in the intestines or bladder. The infection can cause serious health problems over time.

## What Causes Schistosomiasis?

- The worms are called *Schistosoma*.
- They enter the body through the skin when you touch contaminated freshwater.
- The worms do not come from swallowing water. They go in through the skin.
- There are seven types of *Schistosoma* that can infect people.
- The most common types are *S. mansoni*, *S. haematobium*, and *S. japonicum*.
- Other types are less common: *S. mekongi*, *S. malayensis*, *S. intercalatum*, and *S. guineensis*.

### Where Does It Happen?

- *S. haematobium*: Found in Africa, parts of the Middle East, Turkey, and India.
- *S. mansoni*: Found in Africa, parts of the Middle East, South America, and some Caribbean islands.
- *S. japonicum*: Found in parts of Asia, especially China, the Philippines, Thailand, and Indonesia.
- *S. mekongi* and *S. malayensis*: Found in Southeast Asia.
- *S. intercalatum* and *S. guineensis*: Found in Central and West Africa.

### How Is It Spread?

- People are the main hosts for most types.
- For *S. japonicum*, animals like dogs, cats, pigs, and goats can carry the worms.
- For *S. mekongi*, dogs are the main animal hosts.
- The worms need freshwater snails to grow and multiply.
- Snails act as a middle step in the life cycle.
- The only way the disease spreads is through contact with infected freshwater.
- It does not spread in the United States, Canada, or Puerto Rico.

## How the Infection Works

- Adult worms live in blood vessels in the intestines or bladder.
- The worms lay eggs. Some eggs pass out in stool or urine. Others stay in the body and cause damage.
- Eggs that leave the body hatch in freshwater and release tiny larvae called miracidia.
- These larvae enter snails and multiply.
- The snails then release thousands of new larvae called cercariae.
- Cercariae swim in water and can enter human skin within minutes.
- Once in the skin, they lose their tail and become new worms called schistosomulae.
- These travel through the blood to the liver.
- In the liver, they grow into adult worms.
- The adults then move to their final home: the intestines or bladder.
- Eggs appear in stool or urine 1 to 3 months after infection.

### How Long Do the Worms Live?

- Adult worms can live 3 to 7 years in the body.
- Female worms are 7 to 20 millimeters long.
- Male worms are slightly smaller.

## What Are the Symptoms?

### Early Symptoms (Acute Phase)

- Skin rash where the worms entered.
- Fever, chills, nausea, stomach pain, diarrhea, tiredness, and muscle aches.
- These symptoms usually appear a few weeks after infection.

### Long-Term Symptoms (Chronic Phase)

- Bloody stool: This happens with *S. mansoni*, *S. mekongi*, *S. intercalatum*, and *S. japonicum*.
- Blood in the urine: This happens with *S. haematobium*.
- Over time, the body’s reaction to the eggs can cause scarring in the liver, bladder, or intestines.
- This can lead to serious problems like enlarged liver or spleen, blocked blood flow, or bleeding in the stomach.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Diagnosis means finding out if you have the infection. Tests include:

- **Stool or urine tests**: Doctors look for worm eggs under a microscope.
  - Use urine for *S. haematobium*.
  - Use stool for other types.
  - You may need to give more than one sample because eggs are not always in every sample.
- **Blood tests**: These check for antibodies (the body’s response to infection).
  - They can show if you were infected, but not how many worms you have.
  - They cannot tell if the infection is still active.
- **DNA or antigen tests**: These detect worm material in blood, urine, or stool.
  - They are very accurate and useful for checking if treatment worked.
- **Biopsy**: In rare cases, doctors take a small sample of tissue from the intestines or bladder.
  - This can show eggs and the body’s reaction to them.

### How to Read the Test Results

- *S. haematobium* eggs are large and have a sharp point at one end.
- *S. mansoni* eggs are large and have a small spine on the side near the back.
- *S. japonicum* eggs are rounder and have a small, hard-to-see spine.
- *S. intercalatum* eggs are long and often bulge in the middle. They are passed in stool.
- *S. mekongi* eggs are smaller than *S. japonicum* eggs and have a tiny spine.

### Special Cases

- If you have symptoms but no eggs in your stool or urine, a biopsy may help.
- For liver problems, ultrasound can show scarring and an enlarged spleen.
- For brain or spinal cord issues, doctors look for signs in scans and test spinal fluid.

## How Is It Treated?

### Acute Infection (Katayama Fever)

- This is a severe early reaction.
- Doctors may use a steroid medicine (like prednisone) for 5 days to reduce swelling and fever.
- After symptoms improve, treatment with praziquantel starts.
- A second dose of praziquantel is given 4 to 6 weeks later, after the worms have fully grown.

### Chronic Infection

- The main treatment is praziquantel.
- For *S. mansoni*, *S. haematobium*, and *S. intercalatum*: One day of medicine, taken in two doses.
- For *S. japonicum* and *S. mekongi*: One day of medicine, taken in three doses.
- Praziquantel kills adult worms but not young worms or eggs.
- So, if you were recently exposed, treatment is delayed for 6 to 8 weeks to let the worms grow.

### Side Effects

- Common side effects are mild: stomach pain, diarrhea, headache, dizziness.
- These usually go away quickly.

### Checking if Treatment Worked

- After treatment, you should be tested again 1 to 2 months later.
- Doctors check for live eggs in stool or urine.
- A live egg has a tiny worm inside it.
- If live eggs are found, you need another round of treatment.

## How to Prevent Schistosomiasis

- **Do not swim or wade in freshwater** in areas where the disease is common.
- **Do not swallow water**, even if it looks clean.
- **Do not let your skin touch freshwater** in risky areas.
- If you must use freshwater for bathing:
  - Boil it for at least 1 minute, then cool it.
  - Or add 1 milligram of chlorine per liter of water and wait 30 minutes.
- Water stored in a tank for 1 to 2 days is usually safe because the worms die without a host.
- If you fall into a river or lake, **dry off quickly with a towel** to remove any worms before they enter your skin.
- **Dispose of human waste properly** to stop worms from getting into water.
- In areas where many people are infected:
  - The World Health Organization recommends giving praziquantel once a year to everyone over 2 years old.
  - This includes adults, pregnant women after the first trimester, and nursing mothers.
  - Treatment should cover at least 75% of the population.
  - Schools often give medicine to children.
  - Programs to kill snails and teach people about the disease also help.

### For Travelers

- A single dose of praziquantel can help reduce the number of worms in people who were exposed.
- It is not needed for everyone, but may be used in high-risk areas.

### Immunity

- People who live in infected areas often get less sick over time.
- This may mean the body builds some protection.

### Vaccines

- Scientists are working on a vaccine, but none is available yet.

## Key Facts

- *Schistosoma* is the only worm that enters through the skin.
- Over 250 million people worldwide are infected.
- When worms enter the skin, they turn into new worms and travel to the liver.
- They then move to the intestines or bladder.
- Eggs in the liver cause scarring and can block blood flow.
- This can lead to an enlarged spleen, bleeding in the stomach, and other serious problems.
- Eggs in the intestines can cause bloody stool.
- Eggs in the bladder can cause blood in the urine and bladder infections.
- The main treatment is praziquantel.
- To avoid infection: avoid freshwater in risky areas, boil or treat water, or let it sit for a day.
