# Hyperaldosteronism

Hyperaldosteronism means your body makes too much of a hormone called aldosterone. This can cause fluid buildup, high blood pressure, muscle weakness, and sometimes short periods of paralysis.

## What Causes Hyperaldosteronism?

- A noncancerous tumor in one adrenal gland can cause this condition. This is called Conn syndrome or primary hyperaldosteronism.
- Sometimes both adrenal glands make too much aldosterone.
- It can also happen as a response to other health problems, such as a narrowed kidney artery. This is called secondary hyperaldosteronism.
- Eating large amounts of real licorice can cause the same symptoms. Real licorice contains a chemical called glycyrrhizin that acts like too much aldosterone. Most candies sold as "licorice" are not real licorice and do not cause this problem.

## How Aldosterone Works

- The adrenal glands make aldosterone.
- Aldosterone tells your kidneys to keep more salt (sodium) and get rid of more potassium.
- The body controls aldosterone in two main ways:
  - A hormone from the pituitary gland called ACTH helps control it.
  - A system involving the kidneys and blood pressure (called the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system) is the main control.

## Symptoms of Hyperaldosteronism

- High blood pressure is common.
- Low potassium levels may cause:
  - Weakness
  - Tingling in the hands or feet
  - Muscle cramps
  - Short periods of paralysis
- Some people feel very thirsty and need to urinate often.
- Low potassium often causes no symptoms at first.

## How Doctors Diagnose Hyperaldosteronism

Doctors check your blood for:
- Sodium levels
- Potassium levels
- Aldosterone levels
- Renin levels

- Low potassium in the blood can point to hyperaldosteronism.
- But some people with the condition have normal potassium levels.
- High aldosterone and low renin suggest a tumor in one adrenal gland (Conn syndrome).
- High aldosterone and high renin suggest another cause, like a kidney artery problem.

Doctors may give a medicine called spironolactone or eplerenone to see if your sodium and potassium levels improve. This helps confirm the diagnosis.

Imaging tests like CT or MRI can show if there is a tumor in the adrenal glands. In some cases, doctors take blood samples from each adrenal gland to find which one is making too much hormone.

## Treatment of Hyperaldosteronism

### If a Tumor Is Found
- The tumor can usually be removed with surgery.
- After surgery, potassium levels usually return to normal.
- Blood pressure returns to normal in about half to three out of every five people.

### If No Tumor Is Found
- If both adrenal glands are overactive, surgery is not usually helpful.
- Removing both glands is rare and can cause adrenal insufficiency. This means your body can no longer make enough important hormones. You would need to take hormone medicine for life.
- Instead, doctors often use medicines that block aldosterone:
  - Spironolactone helps control symptoms.
  - Eplerenone works like spironolactone but does not affect male hormones.
- Spironolactone can cause side effects in men, such as:
  - Breast swelling
  - Lower sex drive
  - Trouble getting or keeping an erection
- Because of these side effects, doctors often choose eplerenone for men.
- Other medicines for high blood pressure are also available and work well.

## Summary

- Hyperaldosteronism is caused by too much aldosterone.
- It can be due to a tumor or other health issues.
- Symptoms include high blood pressure, weakness, and low potassium.
- Diagnosis includes blood tests and imaging.
- Treatment may involve surgery or medicines.
- Eplerenone is often preferred over spironolactone in men.
- Most people can manage the condition well with treatment.

# Symptoms of Sepsis

Sepsis is a serious condition. It can be life threatening.  
It happens when your body overreacts to an infection.  
The reaction can damage your own organs and tissues.

Sepsis can be hard to spot.  
The symptoms can look like other illnesses, such as the flu or a chest infection.  
You should act fast if you think someone might have sepsis.

## Signs of Sepsis in Babies and Young Children

Call 999 or go to A&E if your baby or young child has any of these signs:

- Skin that is blue, grey, pale, or has blotchy patches  
  (On brown or black skin, check the palms of the hands or soles of the feet)  
- A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it  
  (This is the same as the rash seen in meningitis)  
- Trouble breathing  
  (You might hear grunting sounds or see the stomach pulling in under the ribs)  
- Breathing very fast or feeling breathless  
- A weak, high-pitched cry that is not like their usual cry  
- Not responding normally  
- Not interested in feeding or playing  
- Sleeping more than usual or hard to wake up

They may not have all these signs.  
But if you are worried, call for help right away.

## Signs of Sepsis in Adults and Older Children

Call 999 or go to A&E if an adult or older child has any of these signs:

- Acting confused or not making sense  
- Slurred speech  
- Skin that is blue, grey, pale, or blotchy  
  (On brown or black skin, check the palms of the hands or soles of the feet)  
- A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it  
  (This is the same as the rash seen in meningitis)  
- Trouble breathing  
- Feeling breathless  
- Breathing very fast

They may not have all these signs.  
But if you are worried, call for help right away.

## What to Do if You Go to A&E

Do not drive yourself to A&E.  
Ask someone to drive you.  
Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring all your medicines with you.  
This helps the doctors treat you better.

## When to Call 111

Call 111 now if you, your child, or someone you care for:

- Feels very unwell or something feels seriously wrong  
- Has not passed urine all day (for adults and older children)  
- Has not passed urine in the last 12 hours (for babies and young children)  
- Keeps vomiting and cannot keep food or milk down (for babies and young children)  
- Has swelling or pain around a cut or wound  
- Has a very high or very low temperature  
- Feels hot or cold to the touch  
- Is shivering

You do not need to be sure it is sepsis.  
It is better to call 111 if you are unsure.  
They can tell you what to do.  
They can arrange a phone call with a nurse or doctor.  
They can send an ambulance if needed.

## Who Is More Likely to Get Sepsis

Anyone with an infection can get sepsis.  
But some people are at higher risk. These include:

- Babies under 1 year old, especially if born early (premature)  
- Babies whose mothers had an infection during pregnancy  
- Adults over 75 years old  
- People with diabetes  
- People with a weak immune system  
  (This includes people on chemotherapy or who recently had an organ transplant)  
- People with certain genetic conditions that affect the immune system  
  (Such as Down’s syndrome or sickle cell disease)  
- People who have recently had surgery or a serious illness  
- Women who have just given birth, had a miscarriage, or had an abortion

If you are at higher risk and feel unwell, get medical help right away.  
Tell the doctor or nurse about your health conditions or risk factors.

You cannot catch sepsis from another person.  
Sepsis happens inside your own body when it overreacts to an infection.

## Treatment for Sepsis

Sepsis needs hospital treatment right away.  
It can get worse very quickly.

You should get antibiotics within 1 to 6 hours of arriving at the hospital.

If sepsis is not treated early, it can lead to septic shock.  
This can cause your organs to stop working.  
This is life threatening.

You may need more tests and treatments depending on your symptoms.  
These can include:

- Care in an intensive care unit  
- A machine to help you breathe (called a ventilator)  
- Surgery to remove infected tissue

You may need to stay in hospital for several weeks.  
Recovery can take time.

# Viral Conjunctivitis

Viral conjunctivitis is an eye infection caused by a virus.  
It spreads easily from person to person.  
Most cases are caused by a type of virus called adenovirus.  
Symptoms include redness, soreness, and watery eye discharge.  
Some people also feel pain from bright light.  

The condition usually gets better on its own.  
It does not need antibiotics.  
In rare cases, severe symptoms may need special eye drops.  

---

## What Causes Viral Conjunctivitis?

Viral conjunctivitis can happen with a cold or other viral illness.  
It may be linked to measles, chickenpox, rubella, or mumps.  
Most often, it is caused by adenovirus.  
In some cases, it is caused by enterovirus or herpes simplex virus.  

A severe form called epidemic keratoconjunctivitis is caused by certain adenovirus types.  
These include types Ad 5, 8, 11, 13, 19, and 37.  
Some adenovirus types are linked to eye problems.  
For example, HAdV-D is linked to conjunctivitis.  
HAdV-D53 and HAdV-D54 are linked to outbreaks of severe eye infection.  

Pharyngoconjunctival fever is caused by adenovirus types 3, 4, and 7.  
This causes sore throat, fever, and eye redness.  

A rare form called acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis is caused by enterovirus type 70.  
It has caused outbreaks in Africa and Asia.  

The Ebola virus and the virus that causes COVID-19 can also cause eye redness and watering.  
These viruses can also cause body-wide symptoms.  
If you have eye redness, body aches, and have traveled to a high-risk area, wear protective gear.  
Healthcare workers should use proper protection when seeing such patients.  

---

## Symptoms and Signs

Symptoms usually start 5 to 12 days after exposure.  
Redness and watery discharge begin in one eye.  
They often spread to the other eye quickly.  
The eyes may feel gritty or irritated.  

Small bumps called follicles may appear on the inside of the eyelid.  
The lymph node in front of the ear may swell and hurt.  

Many people have been near someone with eye infection.  
Or they recently had a cold or upper respiratory infection.  

In epidemic keratoconjunctivitis, the eyes may be very sensitive to light.  
You may feel like something is in your eye.  
The white part of the eye may swell and look puffy.  

Fibrin and white blood cells can form a film on the eyelid.  
This is called a pseudomembrane.  
It can cause blurry vision.  
Inflammation in the cornea can also blur vision.  

Even after the redness and discharge go away, small cloudy spots may remain in the cornea.  
These spots can last up to two years.  
They are seen with a special eye light called a slit lamp.  
These spots can cause halos or starburst patterns around lights.  
In rare cases, they can reduce vision.  

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose viral conjunctivitis by looking at the eyes.  
They check for redness, discharge, and swelling.  
They may also check for swollen lymph nodes.  

It can be hard to tell viral from bacterial conjunctivitis.  
The symptoms are often similar.  
Testing is not always needed.  

Special lab tests can grow the virus.  
But these are rarely used.  
Quick tests like NAAT or rapid antigen tests can help.  
They are useful if the eye problem is severe.  
They help rule out other serious conditions like orbital cellulitis.  

Certain signs can help tell viral from bacterial infection:  
- Clear eye discharge suggests viral infection.  
- Thick, yellow-green discharge suggests bacterial infection.  
- Swollen lymph node in front of the ear is more common in viral cases.  
- Swelling of the white part of the eye (chemosis) is seen in epidemic keratoconjunctivitis.  

If you have eye pain or light sensitivity, the doctor may use a special dye called fluorescein.  
This helps see damage on the cornea.  
It is done with a slit lamp.  

This test can show if herpes simplex virus is causing the problem.  
Corticosteroid eye drops can make herpes worse.  
So doctors must rule out herpes before using them.  

---

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure for viral conjunctivitis.  
It gets better on its own.  
Most people feel better in 1 to 3 weeks.  

The main treatment is cool compresses.  
They help reduce discomfort.  

To stop the virus from spreading:  
- Wash your hands often with soap and water.  
- Use hand sanitizer if soap is not available.  
- Do not touch your eyes with dirty hands.  
- Do not share towels, pillows, or eye makeup.  
- Avoid swimming in pools.  
- Do not cover your eye with a patch.  
- Keep the eye clean and free of discharge.  

Children with eye infection should stay home from school.  
This helps stop the spread.  

If you have severe light sensitivity or blurry vision, your doctor may prescribe steroid eye drops.  
These drops reduce swelling and pain.  
They are usually prescribed by an eye doctor.  

But steroid drops must not be used if herpes is present.  
They can make herpes worse.  
So doctors check for herpes first.  

Another type of eye drop called cyclosporin A may help.  
It is less effective than steroids.  
But it can be used if steroids are not safe.  

In severe cases, a doctor may remove a pseudomembrane during an exam.  
This helps prevent scarring and long-term eye problems.  

---

## Key Points

- Most viral conjunctivitis is caused by adenovirus or enterovirus.  
- It spreads easily and is very contagious.  
- Clear discharge, swollen lymph nodes, and eye swelling help tell it from bacterial infection.  
- Diagnosis is usually based on symptoms and eye exam.  
- Treatment is simple: cool compresses and steps to prevent spreading.  
- Most people get better without medicine.

# Scabies: What You Need to Know

Scabies is a skin problem caused by tiny mites. These mites live in the top layer of your skin and cause strong itching.

## How Scabies Spreads

- Scabies spreads easily through close physical contact.
- It often spreads through families or groups living in the same place.
- The mites can live on items like towels, bedding, and clothes for a short time.
- But the mites die quickly when they are away from a human body.
- Animal mites can cause itching, but they do not stay on people or need treatment.

## What Causes Scabies

- A tiny mite called *Sarcoptes scabiei* causes scabies.
- The female mite burrows into the skin and lays eggs.
- The eggs hatch into baby mites in a few days.
- The itching happens because your body reacts to the mites, their eggs, and their waste.

## Symptoms of Scabies

- The main symptom is strong itching, especially at night.
- You may see thin, raised lines on the skin. These are the mite tunnels.
- One end of the line may have a tiny bump. That is where the mite is.
- Scratching can break the skin and lead to infection.
- Bumps can appear on many parts of the body, including the hands, wrists, elbows, underarms, waist, and buttocks.
- In adults, the face is usually not affected.
- In babies and young children, the face, scalp, palms, and soles can be affected.
- In older adults, the itching may be strong but the skin may not look very different. This makes it hard to diagnose.
- In people with dark skin, scabies may cause thick, raised patches.
- In warm climates, people may have small red bumps with few visible tunnels.

### Pictures of Scabies

- One photo shows small red bumps and scratches between the fingers.
- Another shows thick, raised areas on the soles of a baby’s feet.
- These pictures show common signs of scabies.

## Severe Scabies (Crusted Scabies)

Some people get a very bad form of scabies. This is called crusted scabies or Norwegian scabies. It happens in people who:

- Have a weak immune system (from HIV, blood cancer, or long-term use of steroids).
- Have serious physical or mental disabilities.
- Are Aboriginal Australians.

In severe cases:
- The skin becomes thick and crusty, especially on the palms, soles, or scalp.
- The thick skin does not usually itch.

## Scabies Incognito

This is a rare form of scabies that happens in people who use steroid creams on their skin for a long time. It can be hard to spot because the skin looks different than usual. Finding the mites is also harder.

## How Doctors Diagnose Scabies

- Doctors look at your skin and ask about your symptoms.
- They may use a magnifying lens to see the tunnels.
- They may take a small skin scraping and look at it under a microscope to find mites, eggs, or waste.

## How Scabies Is Treated

### For Older Children and Adults

- Use a cream called permethrin or another medicine that kills mites.
- Apply the cream from your neck down to your toes.
- Leave it on for 8 to 14 hours, then wash it off.
- Repeat the treatment one week later.

### For Infants and Young Children

- Use permethrin cream on the head and neck, but avoid the eyes and mouth.
- Apply it all over the body, including skin folds, fingernails, toenails, and the belly button.
- Put mittens on babies to stop them from putting the cream in their mouth.
- You can also use a sulfur ointment at night. Wash it off in the morning.
- Do not use lindane. It can be harmful.

### For Children 4 Years and Older and Adults

- Use a liquid called spinosad.
- Apply it to all skin from the neck down, including the soles of the feet.
- If you are bald, apply it to your scalp, forehead, hairline, and temples.
- Let it dry for 10 minutes before dressing.
- Leave it on for 6 hours, then shower or bathe.
- Repeat the treatment one week later.
- Avoid getting it in your eyes.

### For People Who Can’t Use Skin Creams

- Ivermectin is a pill that can be taken by mouth.
- Take two doses, one week apart.
- It works well for people who can’t use skin creams or have severe cases, especially those with weak immune systems.

## After Treatment

- Itching and bumps may last up to 3 weeks after treatment.
- This is because your body still reacts to dead mites in the skin.
- You can use a mild steroid cream or an antihistamine pill to help with itching.
- If the skin is broken and infected, you may need antibiotics.

## Treating Everyone in the Household

- Anyone who has been close to someone with scabies should be treated, even if they do not have symptoms.
- Wash all clothes, towels, and bedding in hot water.
- Dry them in a hot dryer or iron them.
- If you can’t wash them, put them in a sealed plastic bag for at least 3 days.

Scabies is not caused by poor hygiene. It can affect anyone, no matter how clean they are.

# Swollen Ankles, Feet, and Legs (Oedema)

Swelling in your ankles, feet, or legs is called oedema. It happens when fluid builds up in these areas.

## What to Look For

- Your ankles, feet, or legs may look puffy or swollen.
- The skin may look shiny or stretched.
- The skin may change color.
- You may feel discomfort, stiffness, or pain.
- If you press on the skin, it may leave a dent that takes time to go away.

## How to Help Reduce Swelling at Home

Try these steps to help reduce swelling:

- **Raise your legs** on a chair or pillows when you sit.
- **Move around** with gentle exercise like walking. This helps blood flow.
- **Wear comfortable shoes** with a low heel and soft soles.
- **Keep your feet clean and dry**. Use moisturizer to prevent dry skin and infections.

Avoid:

- Standing or sitting in one place for too long.
- Wearing tight clothes, socks, or shoes.

## Common Causes

Swelling is often caused by:

- Sitting or standing in the same position for too long.
- Eating too much salty food.
- Being overweight.
- Being pregnant.
- Some medicines, such as blood pressure pills, birth control pills, hormone treatments, antidepressants, or steroids.

It can also be caused by:

- An injury like a sprain or strain.
- An insect bite or sting.
- Problems with your kidneys, liver, or heart.
- A blood clot.
- An infection.

## When to See a Doctor

Call your doctor if:

- One or both ankles, feet, or legs are swollen.
- The swelling does not get better after a few days of home care.
- The swelling gets worse.

## When to Get Urgent Help

Call 111 or get help online if:

- Swelling happens in just one leg, foot, or ankle with no clear reason, like an injury.
- The swelling is very bad, painful, or comes on suddenly.
- The swollen area is red or feels hot.
- You have a high temperature or feel hot and shivery.
- You have diabetes and your feet, ankles, or legs are swollen.

## When to Call 999 (Emergency)

Call 999 if you have:

- Trouble breathing or feel short of breath.
- A tight, heavy, or painful chest.
- Coughing up blood.

These could be signs of a blood clot in your lungs. This needs emergency treatment in hospital.

## Important Safety Note

Do not drive yourself to the emergency department.  
When you call 999, the person on the phone will tell you what to do.

## Treatment

If swelling does not go away on its own, your doctor will check what is causing it.

Your doctor may suggest:

- Losing weight.
- Eating less salt.
- Changing your medicines if needed.

Talk to your doctor about making changes to your lifestyle. They can help you find the best plan for your health.

# Multiple Myeloma – Simple Explanation

Multiple myeloma is a type of cancer that starts in plasma cells. Plasma cells are a kind of white blood cell that helps fight infections. In this disease, the plasma cells grow out of control and make abnormal proteins. These abnormal cells damage nearby bone and cause other health problems.

## Who Gets Multiple Myeloma?

- In the United States, about 1 in every 132 people will get this cancer in their lifetime.
- Most people are around 70 years old when they are diagnosed.
- Black people are twice as likely to get it as White people.
- Men are slightly more likely than women to develop it.
- The exact cause is not known. But some things may play a role, like genetics, radiation, or exposure to certain chemicals.

In 2024, doctors expect about 35,780 new cases and about 12,540 deaths from this cancer in the U.S.

Survival is getting better. Many people now live more than 10 years after diagnosis.

---

## What Happens in the Body?

The cancerous plasma cells make a special protein called M-protein. This protein can be found in the blood or urine.

- About half of patients make IgG protein.
- About one in five make IgA protein.
- Some patients make only light chains (called Bence Jones protein), which show up in the urine.
- A small number of patients make IgM or IgD proteins. IgD is more common in people of Asian descent.
- IgE myeloma is very rare.

Some patients do not have M-protein in their blood or urine. But a special test can still find abnormal light chains in these people.

### Bone Problems

The cancer cells destroy bone. This causes:
- Pain, especially in the back, ribs, pelvis, or skull.
- Weak bones that break easily, even with little injury.
- Vertebral collapse, which can press on the spinal cord and cause weakness or paralysis.

The bone damage is caused by:
- Tumors growing inside the bone.
- Chemicals released by the cancer cells that break down bone and stop new bone from forming.

Too much bone breakdown can lead to high levels of calcium in the blood. This is called hypercalcemia.

### Kidney Problems

Many patients have kidney issues. This can happen because:
- Light chains from the cancer build up in the kidneys.
- High calcium levels also harm the kidneys.

### Anemia

Most patients have anemia. This means they have too few healthy red blood cells. Causes include:
- Kidney disease.
- The cancer cells blocking normal blood cell production in the bone marrow.
- Other causes like iron or vitamin B12 deficiency.

### Infections

The immune system does not work well. This makes patients more likely to get bacterial infections.

Some treatments can also increase the risk of viral infections, like shingles (herpes zoster).

### Other Problems

- Amyloidosis: A rare condition where abnormal proteins build up in organs. It happens in about 1 in 10 patients, especially those with lambda light chains.
- Rarely, tumors can form outside the bone, such as in the nose, throat, or other tissues.

---

## Types of Multiple Myeloma

| Type | What It Means |
|------|---------------|
| **Extramedullary plasmacytoma** | Tumor outside the bone marrow, often in the upper airway. |
| **Solitary plasmacytoma of bone** | One tumor in a bone. May not make M-protein. |
| **Osteosclerotic myeloma (POEMS syndrome)** | Bone thickening, nerve damage, enlarged organs, hormone problems, skin changes, and M-protein. |
| **Nonsecretory myeloma** | No M-protein in blood or urine. But abnormal light chains may still be found. |

---

## Symptoms and Signs

Common symptoms include:
- Ongoing bone pain, especially in the back or chest.
- Weak bones that break easily.
- Feeling very tired (from anemia).
- Frequent infections.
- Swelling, numbness, or tingling in hands or feet (from nerve damage).
- Increased thirst and dry mouth (from high calcium).
- Trouble passing urine or kidney problems.

Some people have no symptoms at first. The disease is found during routine blood or urine tests.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to confirm the diagnosis.

### Blood and Urine Tests
- Complete blood count (CBC): Checks for anemia and other blood problems.
- Kidney and calcium levels: High calcium or low kidney function can signal myeloma.
- Protein tests: Look for M-protein in blood and urine.
- Free light chain test: Finds abnormal light chains even if M-protein is not seen.

### Imaging Tests
- X-rays: Show bone damage, like holes in the bone.
- MRI or PET-CT scan: More detailed than X-rays. Used if there is pain or nerve symptoms.
- Bone scans: Usually not helpful for this disease.

### Bone Marrow Test
- A small sample of bone marrow is taken from the hip bone.
- Doctors look for too many plasma cells.
- A diagnosis is made if 10% or more of the cells are plasma cells.
- But sometimes, the sample may show fewer than 10% even if the person has myeloma. The test is still important.

### Other Tests
- Cytogenetic tests (like FISH): Check for specific gene changes in the cancer cells. These help predict how the disease may behave and guide treatment.

### Diagnosis Criteria
To confirm myeloma, doctors look for:
- Clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow or a tumor.
- M-protein in blood or urine.
- Organ damage (anemia, kidney problems, high calcium, or bone damage).

If no M-protein is found, doctors may still diagnose myeloma if:
- Bence Jones protein is high in urine (over 200 mg in 24 hours).
- Free light chain levels are abnormal.
- Bone damage is present and not caused by cancer elsewhere.
- Plasma cells are seen in the bone marrow.

---

## Treatment

Treatment depends on symptoms and how advanced the disease is.

### For People With Symptoms or Organ Damage
- Chemotherapy: Kills cancer cells.
- Steroids: Help reduce inflammation and kill some cancer cells.
- Newer medicines:
  - Proteasome inhibitors (like bortezomib, carfilzomib, ixazomib).
  - Immunomodulatory drugs (like lenalidomide, thalidomide, pomalidomide).
  - Monoclonal antibodies (like daratumumab, isatuximab, elotuzumab).
- Drugs that target a protein called B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) using antibodies or special immune cells (T cells).

### For Some Patients
- High-dose chemotherapy followed by stem cell transplant using the patient’s own stem cells (autologous transplant).
- Radiation therapy: Used for painful or dangerous bone areas that do not respond to medicine.

### For Complications
- Treat anemia with blood transfusions or medicines.
- Treat high calcium with fluids and medicine.
- Treat kidney problems with fluids and special drugs.
- Prevent or treat infections with vaccines and antibiotics.

### For Relapsed or Refractory Disease
If the cancer comes back or does not respond to treatment, doctors may use:
- Different combinations of the same medicines.
- Newer treatments like CAR T-cell therapy or bispecific antibodies.

---

## When to Start Treatment

Not all patients need treatment right away.

Patients with no symptoms or organ damage may wait. But treatment is needed if:
- More than 60% of bone marrow cells are plasma cells.
- MRI shows one or more bone lesions.
- Free light chain levels are very high (over 100 mg/L).

These signs mean the disease is active and likely to cause problems soon. Even though early treatment does not yet improve survival, it may prevent complications.

Patients without these signs usually do not need treatment until symptoms appear.

---

## Prognosis (Outlook)

Multiple myeloma is not curable. But many people live more than 11 years after diagnosis.

Worse outcomes are linked to:
- Advanced stage of disease.
- Low blood albumin.
- High levels of beta-2 microglobulin.
- High lactate dehydrogenase (LDH).
- Certain gene changes in the cancer cells.
- High numbers of cancer cells in the blood.
- Poor kidney function at diagnosis.

If kidney function improves with treatment, the outlook is better.

Because the disease is serious and eventually fatal, it is important to talk about end-of-life care. This includes:
- Advance directives (like a living will).
- Decisions about feeding tubes.
- Plans for pain relief and comfort.

---

## Key Points

- Cancerous plasma cells make abnormal proteins and destroy bone.
- Bone damage causes pain, fractures, and high calcium.
- Anemia and kidney problems are common.
- About 1 in 10 patients develop amyloidosis, especially those with lambda light chains.
- Tests include blood and urine protein tests, free light chain testing, bone marrow biopsy, and imaging.
- Treatment includes chemotherapy, steroids, newer drugs, and sometimes stem cell transplant.
- Not all patients need treatment right away. It depends on symptoms and test results.
- Survival is improving, but the disease is not curable.

---

# Brain and Spinal Cord Birth Defects – Simple Explanation

Birth defects in the brain or spinal cord can cause a range of health problems. Some are very mild. Others can be life-threatening.

## What Are These Defects?

- These problems can happen early in pregnancy or later.
- They are called neural tube defects when they form in the first few weeks of pregnancy.
- Other types, like hydrocephalus and microcephaly, develop later in pregnancy.

## What Are the Signs?

Many babies with these defects have visible differences in their head or back.

If the brain or spinal cord is damaged, symptoms can include:
- Trouble learning or thinking clearly
- Seizures
- Paralysis
- Inability to control the bladder or bowels
- Loss of feeling in parts of the body

The level of disability depends on where the damage is and how serious it is.

## How Are They Diagnosed?

### Before Birth
Doctors can often find these defects during pregnancy using:
- Amniocentesis: A small sample of fluid around the baby is taken.
- Prenatal ultrasound: A scan that shows the baby’s body.
- Fetal MRI: A detailed picture of the baby’s brain and spine.
- Cell-free DNA screening: A blood test from the mother that checks for certain genetic problems in the baby.

### After Birth
After the baby is born, doctors use:
- CT scan: A series of X-rays that create pictures of the brain and spine.
- MRI: A scan that gives very clear pictures of soft tissues like the brain and spinal cord.

If a defect is found, parents may need emotional support and genetic counseling. This helps them understand the chances of having another child with a similar problem.

## How Are They Treated?

### Surgery
Some defects can be fixed with surgery. This is often done soon after birth.
- For example, if there is an opening in the spine or a swelling, surgery can close it.
- Surgery cannot fix brain or spinal cord damage that has already happened.
- But it can stop more damage and help the child do better.

With quick surgery, some children grow up with almost normal abilities.

## How Can They Be Prevented?

### Folate (Folic Acid)
All women who are able to get pregnant should take a daily vitamin with folate.
- Start 3 months before getting pregnant.
- Keep taking it for the first 3 months of pregnancy.

Women who have had a baby with a neural tube defect are at higher risk of having another affected baby.
- They should take a higher dose of folate.
- Start 3 months before getting pregnant again.
- Keep taking it for the first 3 months of pregnancy.

Folate does not prevent all cases. But it can greatly lower the risk.

The following resource may help:

# Catarrh

Catarrh is when your nose, sinuses, and throat become irritated. This causes extra mucus and swelling. It is your body’s way of fighting off infection or irritation.

## Symptoms of Catarrh

You may have catarrh if you have:
- A blocked nose that does not go away
- A feeling like something is stuck in your throat
- Needing to swallow or cough often to clear your throat
- Mucus slowly dripping down the back of your throat (called postnasal drip)
- A crackling or popping feeling in your ears

These symptoms usually last a few days. But sometimes they can last longer.

## What Causes Catarrh

Catarrh happens when your body reacts to:
- Infections like colds, flu, or sinus infections
- Air pollution or cigarette smoke
- Allergies to things like pollen, dust, or animal fur
- Growth in the nose called nasal polyps

## What You Can Do to Feel Better

Catarrh often gets better on its own. The mucus and phlegm are not harmful. They help your body clear out infection.

### Try These Things

- Drink plenty of water every day.
- Sip ice cold water when your throat feels sticky. This can help clear it without coughing or swallowing.
- Use a humidifier in your room. It adds moisture to the air and helps loosen mucus.
- Sleep with an extra pillow. This helps you lie more upright and makes breathing easier.
- Gargle with salt water. It can soothe a sore throat.
- Rinse your nose with salt water. This helps clear mucus and reduce swelling.

### How to Rinse Your Nose with Salt Water

1. Boil one pint of water. Let it cool down.
2. Add one teaspoon of salt and one teaspoon of baking soda to the water.
3. Wash your hands well.
4. Stand over a sink. Cup your hand and pour a small amount of the solution into it.
5. Sniff the water into one nostril at a time. Breathe through your mouth. Let the water come out through the other nostril or into the sink.
6. Do not let the water go down your throat.
7. Repeat steps 1 to 6 up to three times a day until your nose feels better.

Make a fresh solution each time. You do not need to use all of it.

## Help from a Pharmacist

A pharmacist can help you with:
- Decongestant medicines to reduce swelling in your nose
- Salt water nose rinses. You can buy them in bottles, sprays, or small packets.

## When to See a Doctor

See a doctor if:
- Your symptoms last more than a few weeks
- You are not getting better

Your doctor will check to make sure nothing else is causing your symptoms. For example, nasal polyps can cause long-term catarrh.

## Treatment from a Doctor

Your doctor may suggest:
- Decongestant medicines
- Salt water nose rinses

If your catarrh is caused by nasal polyps, your doctor may prescribe:
- Steroid spray or drops for your nose
- Surgery to remove the polyps if the medicine does not help

Always follow your doctor’s advice. Do not use medicine without talking to a healthcare professional first.

# Ovarian, Fallopian Tube, and Peritoneal Cancer

This guide explains ovarian, fallopian tube, and peritoneal cancers in simple terms. These cancers are closely related and often treated the same way.

---

## What You Need to Know

- Ovarian cancer is often deadly because it is usually found at a late stage.
- The most common type is called high-grade serous cancer. It behaves the same way in the fallopian tubes and the lining of the belly (peritoneum).
- Symptoms are often missing or vague. This makes early detection hard.
- Diagnosis starts with imaging tests and blood tests. A tissue sample is needed to confirm cancer.
- Treatment includes surgery and chemotherapy. Surgery removes as much cancer as possible.
- In the United States, about 1 in 70 women will get ovarian cancer. It causes more deaths than any other gynecologic cancer.

---

## Who Is at Risk?

Ovarian cancer mostly affects women who are near or past menopause. The average age at diagnosis is 63.

### Things that increase your risk:
- A close family member (like a mother or sister) had ovarian cancer.
- You never gave birth.
- You had your first period early.
- You had menopause late.
- You or a family member had breast, endometrial, or colon cancer.

### Things that lower your risk:
- Using birth control pills for several years.
- Having a mutation in the *BRCA1* or *BRCA2* genes (these are linked to breast cancer too).

About 1 in 5 women with high-grade serous ovarian cancer has a *BRCA* gene change. These genes help fix damaged DNA. When they are not working, cancer risk goes up.

Other genes like *TP53*, *PTEN*, and *MLH1* can also raise cancer risk when changed.

Women under 30 are more likely to get germ cell cancers. A rare condition called XY gonadal dysgenesis can also raise the risk.

---

## What the Cancer Looks Like

Ovarian cancers come in many types. Most start in the outer layer of the ovary (epithelial cells). The rest come from other types of cells.

### Main types of epithelial ovarian cancer:
- High-grade serous (most common)
- Low-grade serous
- Endometrioid
- Clear cell
- Mucinous

High-grade serous cancer is the most common. It often spreads before it is found. Studies show it usually starts in the fallopian tubes, not the ovaries.

Mucinous cancers are more likely to be found early. They make up nearly a third of early-stage cases.

### Other types of ovarian cancer:
- Germ cell tumors (from egg-making cells)
- Sex-cord stromal tumors (from hormone-making cells)
- Cancers that spread from other organs (like breast or colon)

---

## How Cancer Spreads

Ovarian cancer can spread in several ways:
- It grows into nearby tissues.
- It sheds cells into the belly cavity. These cells can grow on other organs.
- It moves through the lymph system to the pelvis and around the aorta.
- Less often, it spreads through the blood to the liver or lungs.

---

## Signs and Symptoms

Many women have no symptoms at all. When symptoms do appear, they are often mild and easy to ignore.

Common symptoms include:
- Bloating
- Feeling full quickly
- Upset stomach
- Changes in bowel habits
- Needing to urinate often
- Unexplained weight loss
- Belly pain or pressure

Later, you may notice:
- Pain in the pelvis
- Swelling in the belly from fluid buildup (ascites)
- Weakness and tiredness
- Anemia (low blood count)

A lump in the pelvis may be found during a routine exam. It may feel hard, irregular, and stuck in place.

Some tumors make hormones. This can cause:
- Too much thyroid activity (hyperthyroidism)
- Feminine traits (feminization)
- Male traits (virilization)

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

If your doctor suspects ovarian cancer, they will do:

- An ultrasound (to look at the ovaries)
- A CT or MRI scan (if cancer is likely to be advanced)
- Blood tests to check for CA 125, a marker that can be high in ovarian cancer

You may be referred for cancer if you have:
- An unexplained mass in the ovary
- Ongoing bloating
- Changes in bowel habits
- Unexplained weight loss
- Belly pain

A mass in a postmenopausal woman is more likely to be cancer. In younger women, harmless cysts can look like cancer.

If you have a pelvic mass and fluid in the belly, cancer is likely. But sometimes a rare condition called Meigs syndrome causes the same signs. It is not cancer.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the stage, grade, and type of cancer.

### Standard treatment steps:
1. Surgery to remove the uterus, both ovaries, and fallopian tubes (hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy).
2. Surgery to remove as much cancer as possible (cytoreductive surgery).
3. Chemotherapy after surgery (usually with carboplatin and paclitaxel).

For early-stage cancers (confined to one ovary), surgery alone may be enough. Survival is over 90% in these cases.

For more advanced cancers, chemotherapy is needed. It helps kill any remaining cancer cells.

### When surgery is not possible:
- Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (chemo before surgery) may be used.
- This is often better for people who are not healthy enough for major surgery.

### Fertility-sparing options:
- For young women with early, low-risk cancer, doctors may keep the uterus and one ovary if safe.

### When neoadjuvant chemo is used:
- It is helpful if cancer has spread to the liver, lymph nodes, or lungs.
- It can also help if cancer is widespread in the belly.

A large study found that neoadjuvant chemo followed by surgery caused fewer complications than surgery first, with the same long-term survival.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Survival depends on how far the cancer has spread.

- Stage I: 85% to 95% survive 5 years
- Stage II: 70% to 78% survive 5 years
- Stage III: 40% to 60% survive 5 years
- Stage IV: 15% to 20% survive 5 years

The outlook is worse if:
- The cancer is high-grade.
- Surgery cannot remove all visible cancer.

The best outcome happens when surgery leaves behind only tiny amounts of cancer (less than 1 cm or even microscopic).

About 7 out of 10 women with advanced cancer will have a return of the disease.

---

## How Can You Prevent It?

- Using birth control pills for 5 years cuts your risk by half.
- Using them for 10 years or more cuts your risk by 80%.

If you have a *BRCA1* or *BRCA2* gene change:
- Talk to a gynecologic oncologist about risk reduction.
- Removing both ovaries and fallopian tubes (risk-reducing surgery) lowers your risk of ovarian cancer and also helps lower breast cancer risk.
- Birth control pills may help reduce risk, but they are not a substitute for surgery if you are a good candidate.

Studies show that oral contraceptives reduce ovarian cancer risk by 50% in women with *BRCA* mutations. The benefit is greatest after 3 to 5 years of use.

Other forms of birth control (like rings, IUDs, or patches) have not been studied for this benefit.

---

## Key Takeaways

- Ovarian cancer mostly affects women near or past menopause.
- Risk goes up with family history, not having children, early periods, late menopause, and certain gene changes.
- Symptoms are vague and often ignored. Bloating, fullness, and belly pain are common.
- If cancer is suspected, start with an ultrasound. Blood tests like CA 125 may help.
- Treatment usually includes surgery and chemotherapy.
- There is no good screening test for average-risk women.
- High-risk women (like those with *BRCA* mutations) should be checked regularly with ultrasound and CA 125.

---

For more details, visit:
**National Cancer Institute: Ovarian, Fallopian Tube, and Primary Peritoneal Cancer**  
This website has information on causes, genetics, prevention, treatment, screening, and support.
