# What You Need to Know About *C. difficile* Colitis

*C. difficile* colitis is an inflammation of the large intestine that causes diarrhea. It happens when a certain type of bacteria, called *C. difficile*, grows too much in the gut and releases harmful substances.

This condition usually starts after someone takes antibiotics.

---

## What Causes *C. difficile* Colitis?

Antibiotics can kill off the good bacteria in your gut. This lets *C. difficile* bacteria grow out of control.

*C. difficile* bacteria make toxins. These toxins damage the lining of the large intestine. This causes inflammation and diarrhea.

Some people carry *C. difficile* in their intestines without getting sick. But if the bacteria grow too much, they can cause illness.

A stronger strain of *C. difficile* has been found in hospitals. This strain makes more toxins. It causes worse symptoms. It spreads more easily. And it is harder to treat with antibiotics.

Almost any antibiotic can cause this problem. But the most common ones are:

- Clindamycin  
- Penicillins (like ampicillin and amoxicillin)  
- Cephalosporins (like ceftriaxone)  
- Fluoroquinolones (like levofloxacin and ciprofloxacin)

The problem can happen even after just a few days of taking antibiotics.

It can also happen after some cancer treatments.

The risk is higher when antibiotics are taken by mouth. But it can also happen with injections into the muscle or through a vein.

---

## Who Is at Risk?

You are more likely to get *C. difficile* colitis if you:

- Are older  
- Have other serious health problems  
- Stay in the hospital for a long time  
- Live in a nursing home  
- Have had surgery on your stomach or intestines  
- Take medicine that reduces stomach acid

Medicines that reduce stomach acid include:

- Proton pump inhibitors  
- H2 blockers

These are used to treat heartburn and stomach ulcers.

Sometimes, the bacteria come from your own gut. *C. difficile* is common in newborns and healthy adults. It is also common in people in hospitals.

But it only causes illness when it grows too much.

People can spread the bacteria to others. The best way to stop this is by washing hands carefully.

You can also get the bacteria from pets or from surfaces in the environment.

Even without antibiotics, serious events like surgery can upset the balance of gut bacteria. This can allow *C. difficile* to grow and cause illness.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms usually start 5 to 10 days after starting antibiotics. But they can start as early as the first day or as late as 2 months later.

Symptoms can range from mild to very serious.

Mild symptoms:
- Loose or watery stools

More serious symptoms:
- Bloody diarrhea  
- Belly pain or cramps  
- Fever  
- Nausea (less common)

In the worst cases, the illness can be life-threatening. This is called fulminant colitis. It can cause:

- Severe dehydration  
- Fast heartbeat  
- Low blood pressure  
- A hole in the large intestine

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect *C. difficile* colitis if you have diarrhea after taking antibiotics.

They will test your stool. The test looks for:

- Toxins made by *C. difficile*  
- A special enzyme from the bacteria  
- The bacteria’s DNA using a test called PCR

Sometimes, a doctor uses a thin, flexible tube to look inside the lower part of the large intestine. This is called sigmoidoscopy.

If they see a specific kind of inflammation called pseudomembranous colitis, they know it is *C. difficile*.

If the problem is higher in the colon, they may use a longer tube called a colonoscope.

Imaging tests like X-rays or CT scans may be done if the doctor suspects a serious complication, such as a hole in the intestine or a very large intestine.

---

## How Is It Treated?

### Step 1: Stop the Problem Antibiotic
If you are still on the antibiotic that caused the problem, your doctor will stop it unless it is absolutely needed.

After stopping the antibiotic, symptoms usually improve in 10 to 12 days.

### Step 2: Use a New Antibiotic
If symptoms are bad or do not go away, you will be given a different antibiotic that works against *C. difficile*.

The most common treatments are:
- Vancomycin (taken by mouth)  
- Fidaxomicin (taken by mouth)

Fidaxomicin is better at preventing the illness from coming back.

### Do Not Use Diarrhea Medicines
Medicines like loperamide slow down the movement of the gut. They are not safe during *C. difficile* infection.

These medicines can make the illness worse. They keep the harmful toxins in the intestine longer.

### Severe Cases Need Hospital Care
If the illness is very serious, you may need to be in the hospital. You may get:

- Fluids through a vein  
- Electrolytes (like sodium, magnesium, calcium, and potassium)  
- Blood transfusions

### Surgery May Be Needed
In rare cases, surgery is required. This may include removing the large intestine. This is done only when the illness is life-threatening.

### Recurrent Cases
About 15 to 20% of people get symptoms again after treatment.

If it comes back once, you will get another course of the same antibiotic.

If it keeps coming back, you may get a different antibiotic for several weeks.

### Fecal Transplant
For people who keep getting sick, a fecal transplant may help.

This means putting healthy stool from a donor into your colon.

The donor’s stool is tested to make sure it is safe.

The transplant can be done in several ways:
- As an enema  
- Through a tube in the nose  
- Through a colonoscope

A pill made from healthy donor stool is also available and works well.

The goal is to restore the normal balance of good bacteria in your gut. This helps prevent the illness from returning.

### Bezlotoxumab
This is a special medicine given through a vein. It works by blocking one of the toxins made by *C. difficile*.

It is used with standard antibiotics. It lowers the chance that the diarrhea will come back.

---

## Key Points to Remember

- *C. difficile* colitis is caused by an overgrowth of harmful bacteria in the gut.
- It usually happens after taking antibiotics.
- Symptoms range from mild diarrhea to severe illness.
- Diagnosis is done with stool tests or by looking inside the colon.
- Treatment includes stopping the problem antibiotic and using a different one.
- Do not use diarrhea medicines unless your doctor says it is safe.
- Fecal transplants and bezlotoxumab can help prevent repeat infections.
- Good handwashing helps stop the spread of the bacteria.

# Heart Failure

Heart failure means your heart is not pumping blood as well as it should. This can cause several symptoms.

## Symptoms of Heart Failure

You may notice these signs:

- Trouble breathing when you walk or do normal activities.
- Feeling very tired all the time.
- Getting out of breath even when you are resting.
- Swelling in your ankles or legs.
- Feeling dizzy or fainting.
- A cough that does not go away.
- A fast heartbeat.

Some people get these symptoms suddenly. This is called acute heart failure.

Others get them slowly over weeks or months. This is called chronic heart failure.

## Treatments for Heart Failure

Your treatment will depend on what is causing your heart failure.

Most people need a mix of lifestyle changes and medicines.

### Lifestyle Changes
- Eat healthy foods.
- Stay active with regular exercise.
- Stop smoking.

### Medicines
- You may need more than one medicine.
- These help control your symptoms and slow the disease.

### Devices
- Some people need a small device placed in the chest.
- This helps keep your heart beating in a normal rhythm.

### Surgery
- You might need surgery to fix blood flow in the heart.
- In rare cases, a heart transplant may be needed.

You will likely need treatment for the rest of your life.

In some cases, heart failure can be cured. For example, if your heart valves are damaged, fixing or replacing them may solve the problem.

## Causes of Heart Failure

Heart failure often happens when more than one problem affects the heart.

Common causes include:

- **Coronary heart disease**: The blood vessels that feed the heart get blocked by fatty material. This can cause chest pain or a heart attack.
- **High blood pressure**: This forces the heart to work harder. Over time, this can weaken the heart.
- **Cardiomyopathy**: A problem with the heart muscle that makes it weak or stiff.
- **Heart rhythm problems**: Like atrial fibrillation, where the heart beats too fast or irregularly.
- **Heart valve problems**: Valves that do not open or close properly.
- **Congenital heart disease**: Heart problems you are born with.

Other conditions can also lead to heart failure, such as:

- Being very overweight.
- Low red blood cell count (anaemia).
- Drinking too much alcohol.
- An overactive thyroid gland.
- High blood pressure in the lungs (pulmonary hypertension).

# What You Need to Know About Sexually Transmitted Infections

## What Are Sexually Transmitted Infections?

A sexually transmitted infection (STI) is an infection passed from one person to another during sex. This includes oral sex, anal sex, or vaginal sex. The infection can spread through body fluids like semen, vaginal fluid, or blood. It can also spread through skin-to-skin contact.

When an STI causes clear signs of illness, it is called a sexually transmitted disease (STD).

Many different types of germs can cause STIs. These include bacteria, viruses, and parasites. Each type acts differently. Some are easy to treat. Others are harder to treat or can last a long time.

## Types of STIs

### Bacterial STIs
These are caused by bacteria. They can usually be cured with antibiotics.

- Syphilis  
- Chlamydia  
- Gonorrhea  
- Chancroid  
- Lymphogranuloma venereum  
- Granuloma inguinale  
- Infections caused by mycoplasma

### Viral STIs
These are caused by viruses. They cannot be cured, but medicines can help control them.

- Human papillomavirus (HPV)  
- Genital herpes  
- Hepatitis B  
- HIV (the virus that causes AIDS)

### Parasitic STIs
These are caused by tiny animals that live on or in the body.

- Trichomoniasis (caused by a single-celled parasite)  
- Scabies (caused by tiny mites)  
- Pubic lice (caused by lice that live in pubic hair)

### Other Infections That Can Be Spread Sexually
Some infections are not mainly spread through sex. But they can still be passed during sex. These include:

- Molluscum contagiosum  
- Salmonella infection  
- Shigella infection  
- Campylobacter infection  
- Amoeba infection  
- Giardia infection  
- Zika virus  
- Mpox (formerly called monkeypox)  
- Cytomegalovirus  
- Hepatitis A  
- Hepatitis C

## How STIs Spread

Sex involves close contact with the skin and mucous membranes of the genitals, mouth, or rectum. This makes it easy for germs to pass from one person to another.

Some STIs cause sores or swelling. These can make it easier for other infections, like HIV, to enter the body.

## How Common Are STIs?

STIs are still very common around the world.

In 2020, about 374 million new cases of curable STIs happened in people aged 15 to 49.

In the United States in 2018, about 26 million new STI cases were reported. Half of these cases were in people aged 15 to 24.

## Why Are STIs Hard to Control?

Several things make it hard to stop the spread of STIs:

- Having sex without protection and with many partners  
- People and doctors often feel uncomfortable talking about sex  
- Not enough money to pay for testing, treatment, or new tools  
- If only one partner is treated, the other can get the infection again  
- Not finishing the full course of medicine can lead to drug-resistant infections  
- Travel around the world helps spread STIs quickly

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on the type of infection.

Many STIs cause sores or ulcers on the genitals. They may also cause:

- Discharge from the penis or vagina  
- Itching or burning  
- Pain when peeing or during sex  
- Swollen glands in the groin  
- Fever or tiredness

### Common Types of Genital Sores

| Finding | Other Features | Likely Cause |
|--------|----------------|--------------|
| One painless sore | Hard, not very tender | Syphilis |
| Clusters of small, painful sores | May have blisters | Herpes |
| Shallow, painful sore | Ragged edges, red around it | Chancroid |
| Small bump or sore, often unnoticed | Very painful swollen glands, sometimes fever | Lymphogranuloma venereum |
| Raised bump that breaks open and grows | Smelly, bumpy tissue | Granuloma inguinale |
| Multiple shallow sores | Seen on skin, not just genitals | Scabies |
| Multiple shallow sores | Lice or their eggs seen in pubic hair | Pubic lice |

Other causes of sores include:
- Mouth sores from syphilis  
- Skin irritation from other conditions  
- Rare cancers  
- Injury or trauma

## How Are STIs Diagnosed?

Doctors use several methods to find STIs.

- They ask about your health and sexual history.  
- They do a physical exam to look for signs like sores, discharge, or swollen glands.  
- They may take a sample from a sore or from the vagina, penis, or rectum.  
- They test the sample using a lab test called a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT), or they may grow the germ in a culture.  
- They may do a blood test to check for certain infections.

Sometimes, tests are not available. Or the results take time. In these cases, doctors use symptoms and exam findings to decide on treatment.

## How Are STIs Treated?

Most STIs can be treated with medicine.

- Bacterial STIs are treated with antibiotics.  
- Viral STIs are treated with antiviral medicines. These do not cure the infection but help control it.  
- Some STIs need treatment for complications, like pain or swelling.

### Important Treatment Tips

- Both you and your sex partner should be treated at the same time.  
- Do not have sex until both of you have finished treatment and are fully better.  
- If you do not finish your medicine, the infection may come back or become resistant to drugs.  
- If you are unsure whether you will follow up, your doctor may start treatment based on symptoms alone.

### Viral STIs

Herpes and HIV are lifelong infections. There is no cure yet. But medicine can help keep the virus under control. You should use safer sex methods to avoid passing the infection to others.

## How Can STIs Be Prevented?

Preventing STIs takes effort from everyone.

### Key Steps to Reduce Risk

- Teach doctors and the public about STIs and how to prevent them.  
- Avoid high-risk sex behaviors.  
- Make sure testing and treatment are easy to get.  
- Help find and treat recent sex partners of infected people.  
- Check in with people after treatment to make sure they are cured.

### Protection During Sex

- Condoms and dental dams, if used correctly, lower the risk of many STIs.  
- They work best when used every time you have sex.

### Vaccines

Vaccines are available for:
- Hepatitis A  
- Hepatitis B  
- Human papillomavirus (HPV)

These vaccines can prevent infection and related health problems.

### Preventing HIV

If you are not infected with HIV but are at high risk, you can take a daily medicine called PrEP. This greatly lowers your chance of getting HIV. It is most effective when taken every day and used with other prevention methods.

# Von Willebrand Disease

Von Willebrand disease is a condition you are born with. It happens when a key protein in your blood does not work right. This protein is called von Willebrand factor.

This protein helps your blood to clot. Without it, your blood does not clot well. This can cause you to bleed too much.

## What Is von Willebrand Factor?

The von Willebrand factor is found in your blood plasma, in your platelets, and in the walls of your blood vessels.

Platelets are small parts of your blood. They are made in your bone marrow. They travel in your blood and help stop bleeding.

When you get a cut, platelets stick to the damaged blood vessel. This starts the clotting process. The von Willebrand factor helps platelets stick to the blood vessel wall.

If the von Willebrand factor is missing or does not work, platelets cannot stick properly. This means bleeding may not stop as it should.

## How Many Platelets Do You Need?

Your blood usually has between 140,000 and 440,000 platelets per microliter.

If your platelet count drops below 50,000 per microliter, you may bleed more than normal after a small injury.

If your count falls below 10,000 to 20,000 per microliter, you may bleed even without any injury.

## Types of Von Willebrand Disease

There are three main types. All are inherited. This means you get them from your parents.

The types differ in how much von Willebrand factor is missing or not working.

The more you are missing, the higher your risk of bleeding.

## Acquired von Willebrand Disease

Some people do not inherit the condition. They develop it later in life.

This is called acquired von Willebrand disease.

It can happen in people with certain cancers or autoimmune disorders. In these cases, the body makes antibodies that attack the von Willebrand factor.

High numbers of platelets can also reduce the function of some forms of von Willebrand factor.

In some heart and blood vessel diseases, the von Willebrand factor breaks down too fast. This leads to less of it in the blood.

In all these cases, the result is the same: you may bleed more than normal.

## Symptoms

You may notice signs of von Willebrand disease early in life.

Many people with this condition have a parent who also had bleeding problems.

Common signs include:

- Easy bruising
- Bleeding that lasts longer than normal after a cut
- Heavy bleeding after tooth removal or surgery
- Heavy menstrual bleeding in women

Bleeding can get worse at times. But it can also improve.

Hormonal changes, pregnancy, infections, or inflammation can cause your body to make more von Willebrand factor. This can help your blood clot better for a while.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will do blood tests to check your platelet count and how well your blood clots.

They will also check for other conditions that can cause low platelet counts and bleeding.

In most cases of von Willebrand disease, your platelet count is normal.

The prothrombin time test is usually normal.

The partial thromboplastin time test is often longer than normal.

Your doctor will test how much von Willebrand factor is in your blood.

They will also test how well it works.

The von Willebrand factor carries another important clotting protein called factor VIII.

If the von Willebrand factor is low, factor VIII levels may also be low. This can cause the partial thromboplastin time test to be longer.

## Treatment

Not everyone with von Willebrand disease needs treatment.

Some people with mild cases never need medicine.

### Desmopressin

For some mild cases, doctors may give a medicine called desmopressin.

This medicine helps your body release more von Willebrand factor.

It can help prevent bleeding during surgery or dental work.

It may be given as a nasal spray or an injection.

### Clotting Factor Transfusions

If you have heavy bleeding, you may need a transfusion.

This is a transfusion of blood products that contain von Willebrand factor.

These include:

- Intermediate-purity factor VIII concentrates
- Recombinant von Willebrand factor

These are used when desmopressin does not work or is not safe.

### Other Medicines

Some medicines help blood clots form.

These include:

- Aminocaproic acid
- Tranexamic acid

They can be used alone or with desmopressin.

They are often used before or after surgery or dental work.

### For Heavy Menstrual Bleeding

Women with heavy periods due to von Willebrand disease may use:

- A short course of desmopressin through the nose
- Or oral tranexamic acid

These can help reduce bleeding during their period.

Always talk to your doctor before starting any treatment.

# Diarrhoea and Vomiting

Diarrhoea and vomiting are common. Most of the time, you can treat them at home.

The most important thing is to drink plenty of fluids. This helps prevent dehydration.

Rest as much as you can. Let your body recover.

You can buy medicines at a pharmacy to help. For example, rehydration powder helps replace lost fluids.

Diarrhoea and vomiting are usually caused by a stomach bug or food poisoning. But other things can cause them too.

---

## Call 111 now if:

- You are worried about a baby under 12 months old.
- Your child stops breastfeeding or drinking from a bottle while sick.
- A child under 5 years old shows signs of dehydration. For example, fewer wet nappies.
- You or your child (5 years or older) still feel dehydrated after using rehydration sachets.
- You or your child keep being sick and cannot keep any fluids down.
- You or your child have blood in the stool or bleeding from the bottom.
- You or your child have diarrhoea for more than 7 days, or vomiting for more than 2 days.

111 will tell you what to do. They can arrange a phone call with a nurse or doctor if needed.

---

## Call 999 or go to A&E if you or your child:

- Vomit blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
- Adults: vomit that is green.
- Children: vomit that is yellow-green or green.
- You think you or your child may have swallowed something poisonous.
- You or your child has a stiff neck and pain when looking at bright lights.
- You or your child has a sudden, severe headache.
- You or your child has a sudden, severe tummy ache.
- Skin, lips, or tongue are blue, grey, pale, or blotchy. On brown or black skin, check the palms of the hands or soles of the feet.
- You or your child are having serious trouble breathing. Or breathing very fast and short.
- You or your child are confused or not acting like themselves.

---

### What we mean by severe pain

**Severe pain:**
- Always there and so bad it’s hard to think or talk.
- You cannot sleep.
- It’s very hard to move, get out of bed, go to the bathroom, wash, or dress.

**Moderate pain:**
- Always there.
- Makes it hard to focus or sleep.
- You can still get up, wash, or dress, but it’s difficult.

**Mild pain:**
- Comes and goes.
- Annoying, but does not stop you from doing normal daily tasks.

[Find your nearest A&E]

---

## A&E safety tips

Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you. Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring all your regular medicines with you.

---

## How to treat diarrhoea and vomiting at home

Most cases can be managed at home. The key is to stay hydrated.

### Do:

- Stay at home and rest.
- Drink plenty of fluids like water or squash. Take small sips if you feel sick.
- Keep breastfeeding or bottle feeding your baby. If they are sick, try giving small feeds more often.
- For babies on formula or solid foods, give small sips of water between feeds.
- Eat when you feel ready. Avoid fatty or spicy foods.
- Take paracetamol if you are in pain. Always check the leaflet before giving it to a child.

### Don’t:

- Do not drink fruit juice or fizzy drinks. They can make diarrhoea worse.
- Do not make baby formula weaker. Use it at the usual strength.
- Do not give children under 12 years medicine to stop diarrhoea.
- Do not give aspirin to children under 16.

---

## A pharmacist can help

Talk to a pharmacist if:

- You or your child (over 5 years) show signs of dehydration. For example, dark or strong-smelling pee, or peeing less than usual.
- You are older, have a weak immune system, or have other health problems that raise your risk of dehydration.
- You need to stop diarrhoea for a few hours.

They may suggest:

- Oral rehydration powder. Mix it with water to make a drink.
- Medicine to stop diarrhoea for a few hours, like loperamide. This is not for children under 12.

---

## Causes of diarrhoea and vomiting

The most common causes are:

- A stomach bug.
- Food poisoning.

---

### Other causes of diarrhoea

- Some medicines can cause diarrhoea. Check the leaflet to see if this is a side effect.
- Food intolerance or food allergy.
- Irritable bowel syndrome.
- Anxiety.
- Appendicitis.
- Inflammatory bowel disease.
- Coeliac disease.
- Diverticular disease.
- Radiation treatment in the pelvic area.

---

### Other causes of vomiting

- Pregnancy.
- Migraine.
- Motion sickness.
- Inner ear infections, like labyrinthitis.
- Some medicines. Check the leaflet to see if this is a side effect.
- Reflux – when a baby brings up milk after feeding ("spitting up").
- Other infections, such as a urinary tract infection.

# Osteochondrodysplasias (Short-Limbed Dwarfism)

Osteochondrodysplasias are conditions where bones or cartilage do not grow normally.  
This leads to problems with the shape and size of the skeleton.  
Most people with these conditions have short arms and legs.  
The condition is often called short-limbed dwarfism.

## What Causes Osteochondrodysplasias?

These conditions are caused by changes in genes.  
The genes help control how connective tissue, bone, and cartilage grow.  
When a gene is changed, it can stop the body from making the right proteins.  
This causes bones and cartilage to develop in a faulty way.

## What Are the Symptoms?

People with osteochondrodysplasias are much shorter than average.  
Adult height is usually less than four feet ten inches.  
The body parts may not grow at the same rate.  
For example, the trunk may be normal size, but the arms and legs are short.

## Common Types of Osteochondrodysplasias

There are many different types.  
Each type has its own symptoms, cause, and outlook.  
Some types are mild. Others are serious and can be life-threatening.

### Types of Osteochondrodysplasias

| Condition | Main Features | How It Is Inherited | Faulty Gene |
|---------|---------------|---------------------|------------|
| Achondroplasia | Big forehead, flat nose, curved lower back, bowlegs | One parent passes it on | Fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) |
| Chondrodysplasia punctata | Bone spots on X-rays in babies, other body issues | Varies | Varies |
| Chondrodysplasia punctata (rhizomelic form) | Arms and legs very short, death in infancy | Both parents pass it on | PTS2 protein |
| Chondrodysplasia punctata (Conradi-Hünermann) | Arms and legs slightly short, uneven growth, mild | One parent passes it on | EBP protein |
| Chondroectodermal dysplasia (Ellis-van Creveld) | Short arms and legs, extra fingers, heart problems | Both parents pass it on | EVC and EVC2 genes |
| Diastrophic dysplasia | Severe short stature, bent thumbs, clubfoot | Both parents pass it on | SLC26A2 protein |
| Hypochondroplasia | Similar to achondroplasia but milder | One parent passes it on | FGFR3 gene (not all cases) |
| Mesomelic dysplasia (Langer type) | Forearms and lower legs short, face and spine normal | Both parents pass it on | SHOX and SHOXY genes |
| Metaphyseal chondrodysplasia | Some types cause poor digestion, low white blood cells | One or both parents pass it on | PTHR or COL10A1 genes |
| Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia | Mild short stature, normal spine, short fingers, hip problems | One or both parents pass it on | SLC26A2 gene (in some cases) |
| Pseudoachondroplasia | Normal face, short stature, curved spine | One or both parents pass it on | COMP protein |
| Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia | Curved spine, nearsightedness, flat face | One or both parents pass it on | COL2A1 or TRAPPC2 genes |

> **Note:** Some types have other names.  
> For example, mesomelic dysplasia is also called Nievergelt or Langer type.  
> Metaphyseal chondrodysplasia has many other names, like Jansen, Schmid, and McKusick.

> **AD = autosomal dominant** (one parent passes it on)  
> **AR = autosomal recessive** (both parents pass it on)  
> **XL = X-linked** (gene is on the X chromosome)

## How Are These Conditions Diagnosed?

Doctors look at the person’s body shape and growth.  
X-rays show how bones are formed.  
Some bone changes are unique to certain types.  
A full-body X-ray is done for every baby born with this condition, even if the baby does not survive.  
This helps doctors know what to expect and plan care.

Doctors can sometimes find the condition before birth.  
This is done with ultrasound or a special test during pregnancy.  
It works best when the baby’s arms and legs are very short.

Blood tests do not help find the cause.  
But if the gene change is known, a genetic test can confirm the diagnosis.

Genetic testing is useful if the diagnosis is unclear.  
It also helps families understand the risk of passing the condition to future children.

## How Are These Conditions Treated?

There is no cure.  
But some treatments can help with symptoms and improve quality of life.

- Surgery can make legs longer.  
- Surgery can fix bowlegs.  
- Joint replacement surgery can help with pain and movement.  
- Some people need surgery to protect the spine.

Growth hormone does not help most people with these conditions.  
But a medicine called vosoritide can help some people with achondroplasia grow a little more.  
It works by helping bones grow better.

Some people have weak bones in the neck.  
This can cause nerve damage.  
Before surgery, doctors check the neck bones.  
If they are weak, the head must be supported carefully during anesthesia.

## Genetic Counseling

Since most types are inherited, families can get help understanding the risks.  
Genetic counselors can explain how the condition is passed down.  
They can also help families plan for future children.

## Support and Resources

Organizations like **Little People of America** offer support and information.  
They help people with short stature and their families.  
They also advocate for better care and rights.

Other countries have similar groups.

## Key Facts

- Osteochondrodysplasias are inherited conditions.  
- They affect how bones and cartilage grow.  
- Most cause very short height and uneven body growth.  
- Diagnosis is based on physical signs and X-ray results.  
- Growth hormone does not usually help.  
- Treatments focus on improving movement, reducing pain, and preventing complications.

## More Information

**Little People of America**  
This group offers community support, medical advice, and resources for people with short stature.  
It is not part of this guide, but it may be helpful.

# Hypothyroidism (Underactive Thyroid)

Hypothyroidism means your thyroid gland is not working well.  
It makes too little thyroid hormone.  
This slows down many important body functions.

## What the Thyroid Gland Does

The thyroid gland makes hormones that control how fast your body’s chemical processes work.  
These hormones affect your heart rate, how you burn calories, your skin, growth, body heat, fertility, and digestion.

There are two main thyroid hormones:
- T4: Also called thyroxine.
- T3: Also called triiodothyronine.

The pituitary gland in your brain makes a hormone called TSH.  
TSH tells your thyroid gland how much thyroid hormone to make.  
If your body has too much thyroid hormone, the pituitary slows down TSH.  
If your body has too little, the pituitary increases TSH.

## Who Gets Hypothyroidism?

Hypothyroidism is common, especially in older women.  
About 1 in 10 older women have it.  
It can happen at any age.

Very severe hypothyroidism is called myxedema.

## Causes of Hypothyroidism

### Primary Hypothyroidism (Thyroid Gland Problem)

This is the most common type. It happens when the thyroid gland itself is damaged or not working.

**Most common cause in the U.S.: Hashimoto thyroiditis**  
Your immune system slowly attacks and destroys your thyroid gland.  
This leads to low thyroid hormone levels.

Other causes include:
- Thyroid inflammation (thyroiditis)
- Treatment for overactive thyroid or thyroid cancer
- Not getting enough iodine in your diet
- Radiation to the head or neck
- Inherited problems that stop the thyroid from making hormones

**Thyroiditis** can cause short-term or long-term hypothyroidism.  
- Hashimoto thyroiditis causes permanent low thyroid hormone levels.  
- Subacute thyroiditis is often caused by a virus. It usually causes only temporary problems.  
- Silent lymphocytic thyroiditis happens after childbirth. It also usually goes away on its own.

**Treatment for overactive thyroid or thyroid cancer** can cause hypothyroidism.  
- Radioactive iodine or certain medicines stop the thyroid from making hormones.  
- Surgery to remove the thyroid gland means no more hormone production.

**Iodine deficiency** is the most common cause in countries where salt is not iodized.  
But in the United States, iodine is added to salt and found in dairy products.  
So iodine deficiency is rare here.

**Radiation to the head or neck** (used to treat cancer) can damage the thyroid gland.

Some rare inherited conditions stop the thyroid from making or releasing hormones.

### Secondary Hypothyroidism (Pituitary Gland Problem)

This is rare.  
It happens when the pituitary gland does not make enough TSH.  
Without TSH, the thyroid gland cannot make enough hormones.

## Symptoms of Hypothyroidism

Low thyroid hormone levels slow down your body.  
Symptoms come on slowly and may be mild at first.  
They can be mistaken for depression, especially in older adults.

Common signs include:
- Face looks dull or expressionless.
- Voice sounds hoarse.
- Speech is slow.
- Eyelids droop.
- Eyes and face look puffy.
- Hair becomes thin, dry, and coarse.
- Skin becomes dry, rough, scaly, and thick.

Other common symptoms:
- Feeling tired all the time.
- Gaining weight without trying.
- Constipation.
- Muscle cramps.
- Feeling cold even when others are warm.
- Tingling or pain in the hands (carpal tunnel syndrome).
- Slow pulse.
- Palms and soles may look slightly orange (carotenemia).
- Outer parts of the eyebrows slowly fall out.

Some people, especially older adults, may:
- Feel confused or forgetful.  
  These signs can look like Alzheimer’s disease or other types of dementia.
- Have changes in their menstrual periods.

People with hypothyroidism often have high cholesterol.

If not treated, hypothyroidism can lead to:
- Anemia (low red blood cells).
- Low body temperature.
- Heart failure.

In serious cases, it can lead to myxedema coma.  
This is a life-threatening emergency.  
It causes:
- Very slow breathing.
- Seizures.
- Poor blood flow to the brain.

Myxedema coma can be triggered by:
- Cold exposure.
- Infection.
- Injury.
- Surgery.
- Sedative medicines.

## Hypothyroidism in Older Adults

Many older adults have some level of hypothyroidism.  
About 1 in 10 older women and 1 in 16 older men are affected.

Older adults may not have the usual symptoms like weight gain or feeling cold.  
When they do, the symptoms may be mild or hard to notice.

They may have different symptoms, such as:
- Losing weight.
- Confusion.
- Poor appetite.
- Stiff or painful joints.
- Muscle pain or weakness.
- More likely to fall.

Because symptoms are vague and common in older adults without thyroid problems, doctors may miss the diagnosis.

Some experts suggest yearly thyroid tests for people over 70.  
But most medical groups say routine screening is not needed unless you have symptoms.

## How Doctors Diagnose Hypothyroidism

Doctors look at your symptoms and do a physical exam.  
A slow pulse is a common sign.

Most people need only one blood test:  
This measures TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone).

- If TSH is high, it means your thyroid is underactive.
- If TSH is low, it may mean the problem is in the pituitary gland.

In rare cases, the pituitary gland does not make enough TSH.  
Then a second blood test checks the level of T4 (thyroxine).  
If T4 is low, the diagnosis is confirmed.  
Further tests may be done to check the pituitary gland.

## How Hypothyroidism Is Treated

You will need to take thyroid hormone every day.

The best treatment is synthetic T4 (levothyroxine).  
It comes in a pill form.  
It is safe, effective, and easy to use.

Another form, desiccated (dried) thyroid, comes from animal glands.  
It is not used much anymore.  
The amount of hormone in each pill can vary.  
This makes it less reliable than synthetic T4.

Treatment starts with a small dose.  
Too much hormone can cause serious side effects.  
The dose is slowly increased until blood tests show normal TSH levels.

Older adults usually start with a very small dose.  
They are more sensitive to side effects.

During pregnancy, your dose may need to be increased.  
This is important for the baby’s brain development.

In emergencies, such as myxedema coma, doctors give thyroid hormone through a vein.  
They may use T4, T3, or both.

You will likely need to take thyroid hormone for the rest of your life.

# Post-Herpetic Neuralgia

Post-herpetic neuralgia is a type of nerve pain that can happen after shingles. It causes pain in the same area where you had the shingles rash.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The pain usually starts while you still have the shingles rash. Or it can start soon after the rash has healed. In rare cases, it may start weeks or months after the rash is gone.

Symptoms can include:
- Aching, burning, or sharp pain in the skin
- Pain that lasts all the time or comes and goes
- Skin that is very sensitive to touch, pressure, or temperature changes
- Itchy skin
- Loss of feeling in the skin

The pain can be mild. But for some people, it is very severe.

## How Is It Treated?

Post-herpetic neuralgia can be hard to treat. But it usually gets better over time. This can take a few months to more than a year.

Your doctor will likely suggest medicines to help with the pain. These may include:

- **Paracetamol** or **paracetamol with codeine** – for mild to moderate pain. This helps some people, but it may not stop the pain completely.
- **Medicines for nerve pain** – such as amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, or pregabalin. These are used if paracetamol and codeine do not help.
- **Pain relief patches** with lidocaine – for mild pain or if other medicines are not right for you.
- **Tramadol** – for severe pain. This is only for short-term use.

Nerve pain medicines may take time to work. You will start with a low dose. Your doctor will slowly increase the dose over a few weeks. You will have check-ups to see how well it works and if you have any side effects.

If the pain is very bad, or if it stops you from doing daily tasks, your doctor may refer you to:
- A **cognitive behavioural therapist** – a type of talk therapy that helps you manage pain.
- A **neurologist** or a **specialist pain clinic** – they may offer stronger patches, injections, or more talk therapy to help.

## What Can You Do to Feel Better?

You can take steps to help ease your symptoms:

- Wear loose clothes made of cotton or silk. This helps avoid rubbing your skin.
- Cover sensitive skin with a bandage, cling film, or plastic wound dressing under your clothes.
- Hold an ice pack (or a bag of frozen vegetables) wrapped in a tea towel on the painful area. Do this for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours.
- Take cool baths or showers.
- Keep a daily pain diary. This helps you track your symptoms and see if treatments are working.

## What Causes It?

Post-herpetic neuralgia happens when nerves are damaged by shingles. The exact reason why some people keep having pain after shingles is not fully known.

It is more likely to happen if:
- Your shingles was severe
- The rash covered a large area of your body
- You are older
- You have other health problems, such as diabetes or a weak immune system

## How to Lower Your Risk

You can reduce your chance of getting post-herpetic neuralgia by:
- Getting treatment for shingles as soon as possible
- Getting the shingles vaccine if you are eligible

The shingles vaccine is available on the NHS for:
- People who turned 65 on or after 1 September 2023
- People aged 70 to 79
- People aged 50 and over with a severely weakened immune system

Talk to your GP to find out if you can get the vaccine.

# Non-Hodgkin Lymphomas – Simple Explanation

Non-Hodgkin lymphomas are a group of cancers that start in the lymph system.  
They happen when abnormal lymph cells grow out of control.  
These cells can be found in lymph nodes, bone marrow, the spleen, liver, and gut.  

Most people notice swollen lymph nodes.  
But some people do not have swollen nodes.  
Instead, they have abnormal lymph cells in their blood.  

The disease often spreads to many parts of the body when it is first found.  
Doctors usually need to take a sample of a lymph node or bone marrow to make a diagnosis.  
This sample is tested to confirm the type of lymphoma.  

Treatment depends on the type and stage of the disease.  
Options include:  
- Watching and waiting for slow-growing types with no symptoms  
- Chemotherapy  
- Targeted drugs that attack cancer cells  
- Immunotherapy, like special antibodies or modified immune cells  
- Radiation therapy, especially for early-stage disease  
- Stem cell transplants, usually only for aggressive types that come back or do not respond well  

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is more common than Hodgkin lymphoma.  
It is the sixth most common cancer in the United States.  
Each year, over 80,000 people are diagnosed.  
About 20,000 people die from it each year.  

This is not one single disease.  
It includes many different types of lymphocyte cancers.  
These types are grouped as either slow-growing (indolent) or fast-growing (aggressive).  
The risk goes up with age.  

---

## What Causes Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma?

The exact cause is not known.  
But some viruses may play a role in certain cases.  
These include:  
- Human T-cell leukemia-lymphoma virus  
- Epstein-Barr virus  
- Hepatitis B and C viruses  
- HIV  
- Human herpesvirus 8  

Infection with *Helicobacter pylori* also raises the risk.  

People at higher risk include those with:  
- Weak immune systems from birth (primary immunodeficiency)  
- Immune problems caused by medicines (like after organ transplants or for rheumatoid arthritis)  
- Autoimmune diseases (like rheumatoid arthritis or Sjogren syndrome)  
- Long-term inflammation or swollen lymph nodes  
- Exposure to some chemicals (like certain herbicides or insecticides)  

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is one of the most common cancers in people with HIV.  
Some people with HIV first show signs of lymphoma.  
All patients with lymphoma should be tested for HIV and hepatitis.  

Genetics also matter.  
Some gene changes increase the risk.  
If a close family member has lymphoma, your risk is higher.  

---

## How Does It Work in the Body?

Most non-Hodgkin lymphomas start in B cells.  
Some start in T cells or natural killer cells.  
The stage of cell development when the cancer begins affects how the disease behaves.  

Most lymphomas start in lymph nodes.  
But some start in other areas like the skin, gut, lungs, or brain.  
In some cases, the cancer spreads to the blood and bone marrow.  
This can look like leukemia.  

About 15% of patients have low levels of infection-fighting proteins (immunoglobulins) at diagnosis.  
This makes them more likely to get serious bacterial infections.  
They may need special immune treatments to help protect them.  

> **Note:** There is a lot of overlap between lymphoma and leukemia.  
> Both can cause swollen lymph nodes, abnormal blood cells, and bone marrow involvement.  

---

## How Are They Classified?

Doctors use detailed tests to classify non-Hodgkin lymphoma.  
These tests look at cell shape, protein markers, genes, and how the disease behaves.  

Two main systems are used:  
- The 2022 World Health Organization (WHO) classification  
- The 2022 International Consensus Classification  

Both systems help doctors group lymphomas into types that have similar behavior and treatment needs.  

Lymphomas are often split into two main groups:  
- **Indolent (slow-growing):**  
  - Grows slowly  
  - Responds to treatment but is rarely cured with standard methods  
- **Aggressive (fast-growing):**  
  - Grows quickly  
  - Responds well to chemotherapy  
  - Often curable  

In children, most non-Hodgkin lymphomas are aggressive.  
Slow-growing types like follicular lymphoma are rare in kids.  

Common aggressive types in children include:  
- Burkitt lymphoma  
- Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma  
- Lymphoblastic lymphoma  

These cancers can spread to unusual places like the gut, brain, spinal fluid, or testes.  
Treatment must include steps to protect the brain and spinal fluid.  

Treating these cancers also means managing side effects.  
Long-term risks include:  
- Second cancers  
- Heart or lung problems  
- Fertility issues  
- Delayed growth or learning problems  

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people first notice:  
- Swollen lymph nodes that are not painful  
- Nodes feel firm and rubbery  
- They may grow together into larger lumps  
- Swelling is often in the neck, armpits, groin, or upper thighs  

Some people have no swollen nodes but still have symptoms.  
Swollen nodes in the chest or belly can press on nearby organs.  
This can cause:  
- Trouble breathing or a swollen face (if the large vein in the chest is blocked)  
- Yellow skin or eyes (jaundice) if the bile duct is blocked  
- Swelling in the kidneys (if the tubes from kidneys are blocked)  
- Vomiting and constipation (if the intestines are blocked)  
- Swelling in the legs or fluid in the chest or belly (if lymph flow is blocked)  

Skin can also be affected.  
- B-cell lymphomas may cause red, raised bumps on the scalp or legs  
- T-cell lymphomas may cause red, flat patches or raised lumps on the skin  
- In darker skin, redness may be hard to see  

Some people have systemic symptoms:  
- Unexplained fever  
- Night sweats  
- Fatigue  
- Weight loss  

These symptoms often appear in fast-growing lymphomas.  
They may happen even if no swollen nodes are felt.  
Imaging tests like CT or PET scans are needed to find the cancer.  

Anemia (low red blood cells) is common.  
It can be caused by:  
- Bleeding from gut lymphoma  
- Destruction of red blood cells (hemolysis)  
- Lymphoma spreading to the bone marrow  
- Side effects of chemotherapy or radiation  
- Long-term inflammation  

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

To diagnose non-Hodgkin lymphoma, doctors do:  
- A biopsy of a swollen lymph node  
- A bone marrow test (aspiration and biopsy)  
- A PET/CT scan of the chest, belly, and pelvis to see how far the cancer has spread  
- An MRI of the brain or spine if there are neurological symptoms  

Doctors suspect lymphoma when someone has:  
- Painless swollen lymph nodes  
- Lymph node swelling found on a chest X-ray or CT scan done for another reason  

Other conditions can cause similar swelling:  
- Infections like mono, toxoplasmosis, or CMV  
- Early HIV infection  
- Acute leukemia  

Swollen nodes in the chest can also be caused by:  
- Lung cancer  
- Sarcoidosis  
- Tuberculosis  

Less often, a blood test shows too many lymphocytes.  
This can happen in:  
- Leukemia  
- EBV infection  
- A rare genetic condition called Duncan syndrome  

After diagnosis, more tests are done to stage the disease and check for causes or risk factors.  

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the type, stage, and how fast the cancer grows.  

For slow-growing lymphomas with no symptoms, doctors may choose:  
- Watch and wait (monitor closely without starting treatment)  

For more advanced or aggressive disease, treatment may include:  
- Chemotherapy  
- Radiation therapy (especially for early-stage disease)  
- Immunotherapy (like monoclonal antibodies or CAR T cells)  
- Targeted drugs (such as BTK inhibitors, PI3K inhibitors, or EZH2 inhibitors)  
- Stem cell transplant (in some cases, especially after relapse)  

Treatment plans vary widely based on the specific type of lymphoma.  
General rules apply to early vs. advanced disease and slow vs. fast-growing types.  

Special types like Burkitt lymphoma and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma are treated differently and are discussed separately.  

---

## What Is the Outlook?

The outlook depends on the type, stage, and the person’s health.  
In general:  
- People with T-cell or NK/T-cell lymphomas tend to have a worse outcome than those with B-cell lymphomas  
- Even within the same type, differences in the cancer cells affect survival  

The most widely used tool for predicting outcome is the **International Prognostic Index (IPI)**.  
It is used only for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.  

The IPI looks at five factors:  
- Age over 60 years  
- Poor physical condition (measured by a standard tool)  
- High levels of a blood enzyme (LDH)  
- Cancer in more than one area outside the lymph nodes  
- Advanced stage (stage III or IV)

# Nosebleeds

Nosebleeds can be light or heavy. They can be a small annoyance or a serious problem.

Some people get nosebleeds often. Others get them rarely.

If you swallow blood, it can upset your stomach. You may vomit it. Swallowed blood can also pass through your gut and show up in your stool as dark, sticky poop.

## The Nose

Watch a video to learn more about the nose.

### Front Nosebleed (Anterior Nosebleed)

Most nosebleeds come from the front of the nose. They start in small blood vessels in the soft cartilage that divides the two nostrils. This area has many blood vessels. Bleeding here can make a lot of blood. But most front nosebleeds are not serious, even if they look scary.

### Back Nosebleed (Posterior Nosebleed)

Bleeding from the back of the nose is rare but more dangerous. It comes from larger blood vessels. These are hard for doctors to reach. This type of nosebleed is harder to treat.

Back nosebleeds are more likely in people who:

- Have hardening of the arteries (atherosclerosis)
- Have a bleeding disorder
- Take blood-thinning medicines
- Have had nose or sinus surgery

## What Causes Nosebleeds?

Nosebleeds happen when the inside of the nose is irritated or when blood vessels break.

Many things can cause nosebleeds. People who take aspirin or other blood-thinning medicines, or who have a clotting problem, or who have hardening of the arteries, are more likely to get nosebleeds.

### Common Causes

- Blowing or picking your nose
- Dry air, especially in winter

### Less Common Causes

- Infections in the nose or sinuses
- Using illegal drugs, especially cocaine
- A foreign object stuck in the nose (common in children)
- A rare inherited condition called hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
- Tumors in the nose or sinuses
- Bleeding disorders
- Serious health problems like severe liver disease or advanced HIV

High blood pressure does not usually cause nosebleeds. But if you have high blood pressure, a nosebleed may last longer than normal.

### Signs and Clues by Cause

| Cause | Common Signs and How Doctors Check |
|-------|-----------------------------------|
| Blowing or picking the nose | Often clear during a doctor visit |
| Injury to the nose | Seen during the exam |
| Dry nose lining (common in cold weather) | Dryness seen during exam |
| Hardening of the arteries | Usually in older adults |
| Bleeding disorders | Frequent nosebleeds or bleeding from gums; blood tests needed |
| Foreign object in nose | Repeated nosebleeds; bad smell from one nostril |
| Cocaine use | A hole in the nasal wall; seen during exam |
| Sinus infection or cold | Thick or colored mucus; crusts in the nose |
| Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia | Large, visible blood vessels on face, lips, mouth, fingers, toes; often runs in families |
| Serious health problems | Known condition; changes in nose lining |
| Tumors in nose or sinuses | A visible mass; bulging side of nose; CT scan may be needed |

> **Note:** People with a bleeding disorder or on blood-thinning medicine may have worse bleeding. It can be harder to stop.

> **Note:** Symptoms listed are common but not always present.

> **CT** = a type of imaging test.

## When to See a Doctor

You should see a doctor if you have any of these:

- Feeling weak, dizzy, or faint when standing up
- Taking blood-thinning medicine
- Signs of a bleeding disorder (like easy bruising or bleeding)
- Bleeding that does not stop with pressure
- Many nosebleeds in a short time with no clear cause

Common blood-thinning medicines include:

- Aspirin
- Clopidogrel
- Warfarin
- Newer oral anticoagulants like rivaroxaban and apixaban

### Signs of a Bleeding Disorder

- Tiny red or purple spots on the skin (petechiae)
- Large bruises
- Bleeding gums
- Black, tarry stools
- Coughing up blood
- Blood in urine
- Bleeding from small cuts or while brushing teeth
- Heavy periods in women

If you cannot stop a nosebleed by pinching your nose, go to the hospital right away.

Even if the bleeding stops, go to the hospital if you have warning signs.

If the nosebleed stopped and you feel fine, call your doctor. You may not need to come in.

### What the Doctor Will Do

The doctor will ask about your symptoms and health history. Then they will do a physical exam.

They will ask:

- Did you blow or pick your nose recently?
- Have you had nosebleeds before? How were they stopped?
- Do you or a family member have a bleeding problem?
- Are you taking any blood-thinning medicines?

They will check for:

- High blood pressure
- Signs of heavy blood loss (like fast heartbeat or low blood pressure)

Then they will look inside your nose. They will check for the bleeding site. They will also check your skin for signs of bleeding problems.

For a front nosebleed, the doctor can usually see the source with a light and a tool to hold the nostrils open. Sometimes they use a headlamp or mirror. If the bleeding is heavy or keeps coming back, they may use a thin, flexible scope to look inside.

If the bleeding is from the back of the nose, it may be too hard to see because of the blood.

### Tests

Blood tests are not usually needed. But they may be done if:

- You have signs of a bleeding disorder
- You lost a lot of blood
- You have frequent or severe nosebleeds

A CT scan may be done if a foreign object, tumor, or sinus infection is suspected.

## How Nosebleeds Are Treated

All nosebleeds are treated like front nosebleeds at first.

People who lost a lot of blood get fluids through a vein. Rarely, they need a blood transfusion. Any known bleeding problem is treated.

### At Home: The 10-Minute Pinch Method

To stop a front nosebleed at home:

- Sit up straight.
- Pinch the soft part of your nose (just above the nostrils) for 10 full minutes.
- Do not let go during the 10 minutes.
- Do not pinch the bony part of your nose.

Other home tricks like ice packs, tissue paper, or tilting your head do not work.

If the bleeding does not stop after 10 minutes, try again for another 10 minutes.

If it still does not stop, see a doctor.

### At the Doctor’s Office

The doctor may put cotton soaked in numbing medicine and a medicine that closes blood vessels into the bleeding nostril. Then they will pinch your nose for 10 minutes. The cotton is removed after.

For minor bleeds, that may be all that is needed.

For more serious or repeated bleeding, the doctor may:

- Use a chemical (silver nitrate) or electric heat (electrocautery) to seal the bleeding spot
- Place a special foam sponge (nasal tampon) in the nose. It swells to stop the bleeding. It is removed after 2 to 4 days
- Use a special balloon to press against the bleeding area
- Pack the nose with gauze (this can be painful)

If these methods do not work, the doctor may use a long strip of gauze to pack one side of the nose. This is usually removed after 3 days.

### Back Nosebleed Treatment

Back nosebleeds are hard to stop. Pinching the nose does not help. It just makes blood run down your throat.

The doctor may place a special balloon in the nose and inflate it to press on the bleeding area. This is very uncomfortable. It can make breathing hard.

Before this, the doctor may give you a sedative through a vein. You will likely stay in the hospital. You will get oxygen and antibiotics to prevent infection.

The balloon or packing stays in place for 4 to 5 days.

This can be painful, but pain relief is available.

If the balloon or packing does not work, the doctor may:

- Use a small camera (endoscope) to find the bleeding vessel inside the sinus
- Close the main blood vessel feeding the area with a clip
- Use X-ray to guide a thin tube to the bleeding spot and inject material to block it (embolization)

## Key Points

- Most nosebleeds come from the front of the nose.
- Try the 10-minute pinch method to stop a nosebleed.
- If pinching does not stop the bleeding, see a doctor.
- Tell your doctor if you or a family member has a bleeding disorder.
- Tell your doctor if you take blood-thinning medicines like warfarin, clopidogrel, aspirin, or other NSAIDs.

# What Is Vertigo?

Vertigo makes you feel like you or the world around you is spinning.  
It can also make you feel unsteady or off balance.

You may feel better by sitting or lying down during an attack.  
Avoid sudden head movements during your daily routine.

Most people get better without treatment.  
The treatment you need depends on what is causing the vertigo.

---

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:
- Your vertigo does not go away.
- It keeps coming back.

Call your doctor right away or use NHS 111 if you have vertigo and:
- A very bad headache.
- You are being sick or feel very sick.
- A high temperature or you feel hot and shivery.

You can call 111 or get help online.

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have vertigo and:
- Double or lost vision.
- Hearing loss.
- Trouble speaking.
- Weakness, numbness, or tingling in an arm or leg.

If someone cannot be woken up, take them to A&E or call 999.

[Find your nearest A&E]

---

## A&E Safety Tips

Do not drive to A&E.  
Ask someone to drive you.  
Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring all your medicines with you.

---

## What Vertigo Feels Like

Vertigo feels like spinning.  
It can make it hard to keep your balance.  
This is more than just feeling dizzy.

An attack can last from a few seconds to several hours.  
In some cases, it can last for days or even months.

---

## How to Feel Better During Vertigo

Here are things you can do to help:

### Do:
- Lie still in a quiet, dark room to reduce the spinning feeling.
- Move your head slowly and carefully during daily tasks.
- Sit down right away if you feel dizzy.
- Turn on the lights if you get up at night.
- Use a walking stick if you are at risk of falling.
- Sleep with your head slightly raised on two or more pillows.
- Get out of bed slowly. Sit on the edge for a few minutes before standing.
- Try to stay calm. Stress and anxiety can make vertigo worse.

### Don’t:
- Do not bend over to pick things up. Instead, squat down.
- Do not stretch your neck. For example, avoid reaching up to high shelves.

---

## Treatment for Vertigo

Most people get better without treatment.

Your doctor will treat the cause.  
For example, if an ear infection is the cause, you may be given antibiotics.

You might also be given special exercises to help your balance.

Medicines called antihistamines can help reduce symptoms in some cases.

---

## What Causes Vertigo?

The most common cause is a problem in the inner ear.  
This part of the ear helps you stay balanced.

Common causes include:
- **Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV):** Specific head movements cause spinning.
- **Labyrinthitis:** An infection in the inner ear caused by a cold or flu virus.
- **Vestibular neuritis:** Inflammation of the nerve that sends balance signals from the inner ear to the brain.
- **Ménière’s disease:** A rare condition that can cause ringing in the ear (tinnitus) or hearing loss.

Other possible causes:
- Migraines.
- Some medicines. Check the leaflet that comes with your medicine to see if vertigo is a side effect.

Sometimes, doctors do not know the cause.

# Streptococcal Infections

Streptococci are bacteria that can cause many different types of infections.  
They are found in the body and can grow in the throat, skin, lungs, blood, and other areas.  
Some infections are mild. Others can be serious.  

The most common infections include:  
- Sore throat  
- Skin infections  
- Pneumonia  
- Blood infections  
- Infections of the heart or kidneys  

Symptoms depend on where the infection is in the body.  
Some people may have no symptoms at first.  

Infections caused by group A streptococci can lead to long-term problems.  
These include:  
- Rheumatic fever (affects the heart and joints)  
- Glomerulonephritis (a kidney problem)  

Most streptococcal bacteria respond to penicillin.  
But some strains are now resistant to other antibiotics like macrolides.  

---

## Types of Streptococci

Doctors first look at how the bacteria grow on a special culture plate made from sheep blood.  
This helps them group the bacteria by how they break down red blood cells.

- **Beta-hemolytic streptococci** cause clear areas around each colony.  
- **Alpha-hemolytic streptococci** (also called viridans streptococci) cause a greenish color around the colony.  
- **Gamma-hemolytic streptococci** do not break down blood cells at all.  

Next, doctors use the bacteria’s cell wall to divide them into 20 groups.  
These are called Lancefield groups A through H and K through V.  

Some bacteria were once grouped as "group D" streptococci.  
Now they are known as a different type of bacteria called *enterococci*.  
They still have the same marker as group D, but they are not the same.  

Groups K through V are less likely to cause serious illness.  
They mainly affect people with weak immune systems.  

Viridans streptococci are a special group.  
They are hard to classify.  
Some, like *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, are alpha-hemolytic.  
But they do not fit into any Lancefield group.  

---

## Diseases Caused by Streptococci

The most dangerous streptococcus is *Streptococcus pyogenes*.  
It is beta-hemolytic and belongs to group A.  
This is called group A beta-hemolytic streptococci, or GABHS.  

The two most common illnesses from GABHS are:  
- Sore throat  
- Skin infections  

Sometimes, problems appear weeks after the infection.  
These are not caused by the bacteria still being in the body.  
They are the body’s reaction to the past infection.  
They include:  
- Rheumatic fever  
- Kidney disease  

GABHS can spread through the skin and into nearby lymph nodes.  
This can cause:  
- Swollen, red lines under the skin (lymphangitis)  
- Swollen glands in the neck (lymphadenitis)  

It can also cause:  
- Abscesses near the tonsils  
- Ear infections  
- Sinus infections  
- Bloodstream infections  

The infection can get worse if the body cannot fight it well.  
This can lead to:  
- Blood poisoning (septicemia)  
- Infection after childbirth (puerperal sepsis)  
- Heart infections (endocarditis)  
- Lung infections (pneumonia)  
- Fluid around the lungs (empyema)  

Other streptococci cause fewer infections.  
They usually cause skin infections or heart infections.  
Some types are more common in certain groups:  
- Group B streptococci often affect newborns and women after childbirth.  

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Streptococcal Infections

Doctors use several tests to find out if a person has a streptococcal infection.

### Culture
A sample is taken from the throat or skin.  
It is placed on a special plate to grow the bacteria.  
This is the most reliable way to confirm the infection.

### Rapid Tests
A quick test can be done at the doctor’s office.  
It checks for group A streptococci in a throat swab.  
These tests are very accurate if they are positive.  
But they can miss some infections.  
So, a negative result should be checked with a culture, especially in children.  

### NAATs (Nucleic Acid Amplification Tests)
These are fast tests that use a method called PCR.  
They can give results in 15 to 30 minutes.  
They are more accurate than rapid tests.  
They are useful for quick decisions.

### Antibody Tests
These tests check for antibodies in the blood.  
They are not used to diagnose a current infection.  
Antibodies take weeks to build up after an infection.  
So, a high level means the infection happened in the past.  

These tests are helpful for diagnosing long-term problems like:  
- Rheumatic fever  
- Kidney disease  

Common antibody tests include:  
- ASO (antistreptolysin O)  
- Anti-DNase B  

These levels rise about one week after infection.  
They peak in 1 to 2 months.  
They can stay high for months.  

ASO levels go up in 75 to 80% of cases.  
So, 20% of people may not have a rise in ASO.  
Other tests can be used if needed.  

To confirm a past infection, doctors compare two blood samples:  
- One taken early in the illness  
- One taken 2 to 4 weeks later  

A rise of at least two times is considered positive.  

If a person takes penicillin early in the illness, it may delay the rise in ASO.  

People with skin infections from strep may not have a strong ASO response.  
But they may have a response to other antibodies like anti-DNase B or antihyaluronidase.  

---

## How Streptococcal Infections Are Treated

Most infections are treated with penicillin.  
This is the best choice for most cases.  

For sore throat, penicillin or a cephalosporin is the first choice.  
If a macrolide antibiotic is used, testing for resistance is important.  
Resistance to macrolides is increasing.  

For skin infections:  
- Use dicloxacillin or cephalexin if MRSA is not likely.  
- If MRSA is suspected, use:  
  - TMP/SMX  
  - Linezolid  
  - Doxycycline  
  - Clindamycin (only if resistance is low in your area)  

For infections caused by group B, C, or G streptococci:  
- Use the same antibiotics as for group A infections.  

---

## Key Points

- The most important streptococcus is *Streptococcus pyogenes*, also known as group A beta-hemolytic streptococci (GABHS).  
- The two most common illnesses from GABHS are sore throat and skin infections.  
- Long-term problems like rheumatic fever and kidney disease can happen weeks after the infection.  
- Rapid tests are very accurate if positive, but can miss some cases.  
  - Always confirm a negative result with a culture in children.  
- NAATs are faster and more accurate than rapid tests.  
- Penicillin or a cephalosporin is the best choice for sore throat.  
- Test for resistance if using macrolides.  
- For skin infections, choose the right antibiotic based on whether MRSA is likely.  
- Group B, C, and G streptococcal infections are treated the same way as group A infections.

# Tetanus

Tetanus is a serious illness caused by a poison made by a type of bacteria called *Clostridium tetani*.  
This poison causes muscles to tighten and become stiff.  
The illness is also known as "lockjaw" because it often affects the jaw and neck muscles.

## How Tetanus Happens

Tetanus usually starts after a cut, wound, or injury that breaks the skin.  
The bacteria can get into the body through dirty wounds.  
They are often found in soil and animal waste.  
They can survive for years in these places.

The bacteria do not need oxygen to live.  
This means they grow best in deep wounds where there is little oxygen.

Tetanus can enter the body through:
- Wounds that are dirty or have soil or animal waste in them
- Puncture wounds from needles, such as those used for tattoos or body piercings
- Wounds with dead tissue, like burns, frostbite, or crushed areas
- Injuries that have foreign objects in them, such as splinters, dirt, or bullet fragments

Sometimes the injury is so small that people do not even notice it.  
In rare cases, tetanus can happen after childbirth or an abortion if the uterus is damaged.  
In some parts of the world, poor hygiene can lead to tetanus in newborns if the umbilical cord stump gets infected.

The bacteria can form spores.  
Spores are a dormant form that helps the bacteria survive tough conditions.  
When conditions are good, the spores turn into active bacteria.

The bacteria make a poison (toxin) that travels through the body.  
This poison blocks signals from nerves to muscles.  
As a result, muscles contract without control.  
This causes stiffness and painful spasms.

## Who Is at Risk

Tetanus is rare in the United States.  
But it is more common in places where people do not get vaccinated.  
It can affect people of any age, including babies.

You are more likely to get tetanus if:
- You have not been vaccinated
- You have not had a booster shot in the last 10 years
- You are over 60 years old (immunity weakens with age)
- You have diabetes
- You take medicines that weaken your immune system
- You inject drugs
- You have a burn, surgical wound, or serious injury

## Symptoms of Tetanus

Symptoms usually start 5 to 10 days after the injury.  
But they can start as late as 50 days after the injury.

The main symptom is muscle spasms.  
These are sudden, painful contractions that happen without control.  
The muscles become stiff and hard.

Common signs include:
- Jaw and neck muscles tighten, making it hard to open the mouth or swallow
- Face muscles freeze in a fixed smile with raised eyebrows
- Back muscles tighten, causing the body to arch backward
- Spasms in the arms, legs, and stomach
- Spasms in the muscles that control the bladder and bowels, leading to constipation or trouble urinating

Even small things can trigger spasms.  
These include loud noises, a breeze, or a bump on the bed.

In some cases, spasms only happen near the wound.  
This is called localized tetanus.  
It can last for weeks.

Other symptoms include:
- Fast heartbeat
- Slight fever
- Heavy sweating
- Fluctuating blood pressure
- Inhaling saliva or food into the lungs, which can cause pneumonia
- Restlessness and irritability

Even when the illness is severe, people stay awake and aware.

In newborns, tetanus affects the whole body.  
It often leads to death.  
Babies may have spasms and trouble feeding in the first two weeks of life.  
Children who survive may lose their hearing.

> **Did You Know:**  
> Cleaning a dirty wound right away can help prevent tetanus.

## How Doctors Diagnose Tetanus

Doctors suspect tetanus when a person has muscle stiffness or spasms after a wound.  
They often focus on the jaw and back muscles.

Doctors may take a sample from the wound to test for bacteria.  
But this test is not always reliable.  
It can give a false result.  
So doctors do not depend on it alone.

Instead, they make the diagnosis based on symptoms and medical history.

## How Tetanus Is Treated

Tetanus is treated in a hospital intensive care unit.  
The room is kept quiet to avoid triggering spasms.

Treatment includes:
- Cleaning the wound thoroughly
- Removing dead tissue and foreign objects
- Giving human tetanus immune globulin (antitoxin) to stop the poison from causing more harm
- Giving antibiotics through a vein to kill the bacteria
- Treating symptoms with medicines

If the muscles become too stiff to breathe, a tube is placed in the windpipe.  
A machine called a mechanical ventilator helps the person breathe.

Medicines are used to:
- Reduce muscle spasms and stiffness
- Control pain and anxiety
- Stabilize heart rate and blood pressure

If swallowing is hard, fluids and nutrition are given through a tube in the vein or nose.

Constipation is common.  
Stool softeners are used.  
A tube may be inserted into the rectum to help with gas.

After recovery, people are given a tetanus vaccine unless they are already up to date on their shots.

> **Important:**  
> Having tetanus once does not protect you from getting it again.  
> You must get vaccinated to stay protected.

## Outlook for People with Tetanus

With proper treatment, most people recover.  
But the illness can be deadly.

You are more likely to die if:
- You are very young or very old
- You inject drugs
- Symptoms start quickly and get worse fast
- Treatment is delayed

## How to Prevent Tetanus

Preventing tetanus is much better than treating it.

The tetanus vaccine helps your body make antibodies.  
Antibodies are proteins that fight infection.  
They block the poison from causing harm.

It takes several weeks after vaccination for your body to build up protection.

There is no single vaccine just for tetanus.  
Instead, you get a combination vaccine called DTaP.  
It protects against three diseases:
- Diphtheria
- Tetanus
- Whooping cough (pertussis)

### Vaccination Schedule

**For children:**
- Five doses of DTaP vaccine are given:
  - At 2 months old
  - At 4 months old
  - At 6 months old
  - At 15 to 18 months old
  - At 4 to 6 years old

**For older children and adults:**
- One booster dose of Tdap vaccine is given at age 11 to 12.
- Adults 13 and older who have never had Tdap should get it.
- After that, a booster with tetanus and diphtheria (Td) or Tdap is given every 10 years.

**For pregnant women:**
- A Tdap booster is given during each pregnancy.
- The best time is between 27 and 36 weeks of pregnancy.
- This protects both the mother and the baby.
- Antibodies pass from the mother to the baby before birth.
- The baby is born with some protection against tetanus.

### What to Do After an Injury

If you get a wound:
- Clean it right away with soap and water.
- Use clean water and a clean cloth.

If you are not up to date on your tetanus shots:
- If it has been more than 10 years since your last shot, get a booster.
- If the wound is deep or very dirty, get a booster if it has been more than 5 years.
- If you have never been vaccinated, get three doses:
  - One right away
  - One month later
  - One month after that

Because the vaccine takes time to work, you may also get human tetanus immune globulin.  
This gives immediate protection.  
It comes from people who have strong antibodies against tetanus.
