# Ear Infections

## What Are the Signs of an Ear Infection?

You may have an ear infection if you feel:
- Pain inside your ear (earache)
- A high temperature
- Trouble hearing
- Fluid coming out of your ear
- A feeling of pressure or fullness in your ear
- Itching or irritation around your ear
- Dry, scaly skin around your ear

Babies and young children may also:
- Rub or pull at their ear
- Not respond to sounds
- Be fussy or restless
- Not want to eat
- Lose their balance

Most ear infections get better in 3 days. Some may last up to a week.

If you or your child has a high temperature or feel too unwell to do normal things, stay home. Avoid close contact with others until you feel better.

---

## When to See a Pharmacist

See a pharmacist if:
- Your child is between 1 and 17 years old and you think they have an ear infection.

A pharmacist can:
- Give the same treatments as a doctor
- Offer advice
- Direct you to other medical help

[Find a pharmacy]

---

## When to See a Doctor

See a doctor if:
- Your child is under 12 months old and you think they have an ear infection
- You have ear pain that does not improve after 3 days
- You or your child keep getting ear infections

---

## When to Get Urgent Help (Call 111 or Go Online)

Call 111 or get help online right away if you or your child have ear infection symptoms and:
- Feel very unwell
- Have a very high temperature or feel hot and shivery
- Have swelling around the ear
- Have fluid coming out of the ear
- Notice a change in hearing or new hearing loss
- Feel sick or are being sick (vomiting), feel dizzy, or have a severe sore throat
- Your child under 12 months old has earache in both ears
- You have diabetes, or a heart, lung, kidney, or brain condition
- You have a weak immune system (for example, from chemotherapy)

Call 111 if you need advice for a child under 5 years old.

[Get help from 111 online]

---

## What You Can Do to Feel Better

### Do These Things:
- Take painkillers like paracetamol or ibuprofen. Do not give aspirin to children under 16.
- Gently wipe away any fluid from the outside of the ear with cotton wool.

### Do Not Do These Things:
- Do not put cotton buds, your finger, or anything else inside your ear to remove earwax.
- Do not let water or shampoo get into your ear.
- Do not swim while you have an ear infection.
- Do not use decongestants or antihistamines. They do not help with ear infections.

---

## Treatment for an Ear Infection

Your doctor or pharmacist may give you:
- Antibiotic tablets or eardrops
- Antifungal or steroid eardrops
- Pain-relieving eardrops

Eardrops will not work if you do not use them correctly.

If there is a small lump or boil in your ear, your doctor may use a needle to drain the pus.

---

## How to Help Prevent Ear Infections

You cannot always stop ear infections, especially those caused by colds or flu.

But you can reduce your risk by:
- Making sure your child has had all their childhood vaccinations
- Keeping your child away from smoke
- Avoiding dummies (pacifiers) after 6 months of age
- Not putting cotton buds or your fingers in your ears
- Wearing earplugs or a swimming hat when swimming
- Keeping water and shampoo out of your ears during showers or baths. You can use cotton wool with petroleum jelly in your ear if it’s hard to keep water out
- Treating skin problems like eczema or allergies that affect your ears (for example, from hearing aids)

# Recurrent Pregnancy Loss

Recurrent pregnancy loss means losing two or more pregnancies.  
Each loss should be looked at carefully.  
This is not the same as being unable to get pregnant (infertility).

## What Can Cause Recurrent Pregnancy Loss?

The cause can come from the mother, the father, the baby, or the placenta.

### Common Causes from the Mother

- Problems with the shape of the uterus or cervix.  
  This includes growths like polyps or fibroids.  
  It can also include scar tissue or a weak cervix.

- Chromosome problems in either parent.  
  For example, a balanced translocation means the chromosomes are rearranged but not harmful to the parent.  
  However, this can cause pregnancy loss.

- Long-term health problems that are not well controlled.  
  These include underactive or overactive thyroid, diabetes, high blood pressure, or kidney disease.

- Blood clotting problems.  
  These are called acquired thrombotic disorders.  
  One example is antiphospholipid syndrome.  
  This condition can cause blood clots in the placenta.  
  It is linked to three or more losses after 10 weeks of pregnancy.  
  If you lose one or more normal pregnancies after 10 weeks, this condition may be suspected.  
  The link to inherited blood clotting problems is weaker.  
  The only one that might matter is a mutation called factor V Leiden.

### Possible Causes from the Father

- Certain problems in the sperm.  
  These can increase the chance of miscarriage.  
  The father’s age over 35 has been studied.  
  But the results are not clear.  
  Some studies say it raises risk. Others say it does not.

### Causes from the Placenta

- Long-term health issues that are not well managed.  
  These include lupus and chronic high blood pressure.

### Causes from the Baby

- Chromosome or genetic problems.  
  These are the most common cause of early pregnancy loss.  
  About half of all miscarriages are due to these issues.  
  They are more common in early pregnancy.  
  A type of chromosome problem called aneuploidy causes up to 80% of losses before 10 weeks.  
  It causes less than 15% of losses after 20 weeks.  
- Physical birth defects in the baby.

### Does Recurrent Loss Affect Future Pregnancies?

The risk of slow baby growth or early birth in future pregnancies depends on the cause of the past losses.

## How Is Recurrent Pregnancy Loss Diagnosed?

Diagnosis is based on your history of two or more miscarriages.

### Tests to Find the Cause

- Genetic testing of both parents.  
  This includes testing the tissue from the lost pregnancy if possible.  
  This helps rule out genetic causes.

- Blood tests for blood clotting issues.  
  These include tests for anticardiolipin antibodies (IgG and IgM), anti-beta2 glycoprotein I (IgG and IgM), and lupus anticoagulant.

- Blood test for thyroid function.  
  This checks if the thyroid is working properly.

- Blood test for diabetes.

- Imaging tests to check the shape of the uterus.  
  These include hysterosalpingography or saline infusion sonohysterography.

### What If No Cause Is Found?

In up to half of all cases, no cause is found.  
Testing for inherited blood clotting problems is not usually needed.  
It should only be done if a specialist in high-risk pregnancies is involved.

## How Is Recurrent Pregnancy Loss Treated?

- If a cause is found, treatment may be possible.  
- If no cause is found, the chance of having a healthy baby in the next pregnancy is between 27% and 75%.

## Key Facts

- Recurrent pregnancy loss means two or more miscarriages.  
- Causes can come from the mother, father, baby, or placenta.  
- Chromosome problems (especially aneuploidy) are behind about half of all recurrent losses.

# Salivary Gland Problems

Your salivary glands make saliva. Saliva helps you chew and swallow food. It also has natural chemicals that help break down food.

## What Can Go Wrong with Salivary Glands?

- Glands may not work right.
- Glands can get infected.
- Glands can get blocked by small stones.
- Glands can swell.

When glands do not work well, you make less saliva. This causes a dry mouth. A dry mouth can lead to tooth decay.

Infected or blocked glands cause pain. You may feel swelling and discomfort.

Doctors can check how much saliva you make. They may also take a small sample of gland tissue to test.

Some blockages can be removed. Some people need to use artificial saliva.

(See also: Dry Mouth)

---

## The Main Salivary Glands

There are three main pairs of salivary glands in your mouth:

- **Parotid glands**: These are the largest. They sit just behind your jaw, below and in front of your ears.
- **Sublingual glands**: These lie under the side of your tongue.
- **Submandibular glands**: These sit under the side of your jaw.

In addition, many small glands are spread throughout your mouth. All of them make saliva. Saliva helps you digest food.

---

## Where Are the Main Glands?

[Image: 3D model showing the location of the parotid, sublingual, and submandibular glands]

---

## Types of Salivary Gland Problems

- Glands not working properly
- Salivary stones
- Infections
- Swelling

---

### Glands Not Working Properly

This problem is more common in adults. It means the glands make too little saliva.

When you have too little saliva, your mouth feels dry. This is called dry mouth.

Some things that can cause dry mouth:

- Autoimmune diseases like Sjögren syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, and lupus
- Infections like HIV
- Certain medicines, such as:
  - Some antidepressants
  - Some allergy medicines
  - Some medicines for mental health
  - Some Parkinson’s medicines
  - Some sleep aids
  - Some blood pressure medicines
  - Methyldopa
  - Methamphetamine
- Chemotherapy or radiation treatment for cancer
- Radioactive iodine treatment for thyroid cancer

Dry mouth from radiation is often permanent, especially with high doses. Dry mouth from chemotherapy usually goes away after treatment ends.

But not all dry mouth comes from gland problems. Other causes include:

- Not drinking enough water
- Breathing through your mouth
- Stress or anxiety
- Getting older

As you age, your mouth may feel drier. But this is usually because of medicine, not aging itself.

Saliva protects your teeth. Without enough saliva, you get more cavities—especially on the roots of your teeth.

Severe dry mouth can make it hard to speak, chew, or swallow.

In rare cases, glands make too much saliva. This usually happens only when you eat sour foods. Just thinking about sour food can cause extra saliva.

---

### Salivary Stones

Stones form from salts in your saliva. They are more likely when you are dehydrated or take medicines that reduce saliva.

People with gout are also more likely to get stones.

Stones are most common in adults. Some people get more than one.

Stones block the tube (duct) that carries saliva from the gland to your mouth. When the duct is blocked, saliva builds up. This causes pain and swelling.

A blocked duct and trapped saliva can become infected.

Common signs of a blocked duct:

- Swelling and pain over the affected gland
- Pain gets worse after eating, especially sour foods like lemons or pickles
- The swelling may go down after a few hours
- A sudden rush of saliva may come out
- Some stones cause no symptoms at all

---

### Infections in Salivary Glands

An infection in a salivary gland is called sialadenitis.

Most infections happen when saliva flow is blocked or very low.

The parotid gland is most often affected.

Infections are more common in:

- People in their 50s and 60s
- People with long-term health problems and dry mouth
- People with Sjögren syndrome
- Teenagers and young adults with anorexia
- Children aged 1 to 18 with repeated parotid gland infections with no clear cause
- People who had radiation to the mouth or radioactive iodine for thyroid cancer

Mumps is a viral infection. It causes painful swelling of the salivary glands, usually the parotid gland. It can also affect other parts of the body. Mumps mostly happens in people who have not had the mumps vaccine.

In teens and young adults with anorexia, the most common bacteria is *Staphylococcus aureus*.

Some infections are caused by HIV or cat-scratch disease.

Symptoms of a bacterial infection:

- Fever and chills
- Pain and swelling on one side of the face
- Red, swollen skin over the gland
- A pus-filled lump (abscess) may form
- A small amount of pus may come out of the gland’s duct

---

### Swelling in Salivary Glands

Swelling can be caused by:

- Mumps in children
- Bacterial infections (like in the tonsils or teeth)
- Diseases more common in adults, such as:
  - AIDS
  - Sjögren syndrome
  - Diabetes
  - Sarcoidosis
  - Bulimia

Swelling can also come from tumors in the glands. Tumors can be cancerous or noncancerous.

- Cancerous tumors feel hard and may stick to nearby tissues.
- Noncancerous tumors are usually soft and can move around.

An injury to the lower lip—like biting it by accident—can damage small glands there. This can block saliva flow. The gland may swell and form a small, soft, bluish lump called a mucocele. This lump usually goes away on its own in a few weeks to months.

---

### Spotlight on Aging: Dry Mouth

Many older people have dry mouth.

Aging itself has only a small effect on mouth moisture.

But older people are more likely to have health problems that cause dry mouth. They are also more likely to take medicines that dry the mouth.

For some, dry mouth is just a minor annoyance. For others, it causes serious problems.

Dry mouth can make it hard to taste food, chew, swallow, speak, or wear dentures.

It also increases the risk of tooth decay and gum disease.

Dry mouth is usually a sign of another health issue or a side effect of medicine.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Salivary Gland Problems

Doctors use several methods:

- **Biopsy**: A small sample of gland tissue is taken and checked under a microscope.
- **Endoscopy**: A tiny camera is used to look inside the ducts.
- **Imaging tests**: Like CT scans or ultrasounds.
- **Pus culture**: If infection is suspected, doctors may collect pus from the duct and test it in a lab.

There is no perfect test to measure how much saliva you make.

But doctors can gently press on the glands (milk them) and watch the ducts for saliva flow.

Swelling from a blocked duct is often diagnosed by how pain changes with eating. If eating something sour (like lemon juice or hard candy) makes the pain better, a stone is likely.

If the cause is unclear, a biopsy may be done.

Imaging tests like CT, ultrasound, or MRI can show swelling or infection.

If pus can be squeezed out of the duct, it is sent to a lab to check for bacteria.

---

## How Doctors Treat Salivary Gland Problems

### For Dry Mouth

- Avoid medicines that reduce saliva
- Drink water often
- Brush and floss every day
- Use fluoride mouthwash
- See your dentist every 3 to 4 months
- Use artificial saliva (like carboxymethylcellulose) as a mouthwash
- Chew sugarless gum or suck on xylitol lozenges
- Some dentists recommend wearing a plastic mouth guard with fluoride gel at night to protect teeth

Medicines like cevimeline or pilocarpine can help some people make more saliva. But they do not work if the glands were damaged by radiation.

### For Salivary Stones

- Take pain relievers
- Drink extra fluids
- Gently massage the gland
- Use warm compresses
- Stimulate saliva with lemon juice, sour candy, or hard candy

If the stone does not pass on its own:

- A dentist may push it out by pressing on both sides of the duct
- A thin wire tool can be used to pull it out
- As a last option, surgery or endoscopy may be needed

### For Infections

- Take antibiotics
- Massage the gland
- Use warm compresses
- Stay well hydrated
- Chew sour candy or suck on hard candy to stimulate saliva
- Keep your mouth clean

If an abscess forms, it must be cut open and drained.

### For Swelling

Treatment depends on the cause.

- A mucocele that does not go away can be removed with surgery.
- Both noncancerous and cancerous tumors can usually be removed with surgery.

# Pericarditis – Simple Explanation

## What is pericarditis?

Pericarditis is when the sac around your heart becomes inflamed.  
This sac is called the pericardium.  
It normally holds a small amount of fluid to protect your heart.  
When it gets inflamed, it can cause pain and sometimes extra fluid builds up.

## Symptoms of pericarditis

The main symptom is chest pain.  
The pain is often sharp or stabbing.  
It may spread to your shoulders, arms, or tummy.  
The pain gets worse when you breathe in deeply, swallow, cough, or lie down.  
It often feels worse when you lie on your left side.  
The pain may get better when you sit up or lean forward.  

You might also feel hot and shivery.  
You could have a high temperature.  
You might cough or have painful joints.  

Pericarditis often happens after a viral infection.  
This could be a cold or the flu.

## When to get help

### Call your GP right away or use NHS 111 if you have chest pain that:

- Feels sharp or stabbing  
- Gets worse when you breathe in deeply, swallow, cough, or lie down  

You can call 111 or get help online at 111.nhs.uk.

### Call 999 immediately if you have sudden chest pain that:

- Spreads to your arms, back, neck, or jaw  
- Makes your chest feel tight or heavy  
- Comes with shortness of breath, sweating, or feeling sick  
- Lasts more than 15 minutes  

This could be a heart attack.  
You need emergency treatment in hospital.

> **Important:** Do not drive yourself to the hospital.  
> The person on the phone will tell you what to do.

## How doctors check for pericarditis

Your GP will listen to your heart with a stethoscope.  
Inflamed pericardium can change the sound your heart makes.  

To confirm the diagnosis, your GP may:

- Do blood tests  
- Refer you for a chest X-ray  
- Refer you for an electrocardiogram (ECG)  
- Refer you for an echocardiogram  

An ECG is a safe and painless test.  
Some GP surgeries can do it there.

## Treatment for pericarditis

Treatment depends on what is causing the problem.  

Most people are given anti-inflammatory painkillers.  
These help reduce pain and swelling.  
Ibuprofen is a common example.  

Sitting up or leaning forward can also help ease the pain.  

If the pain does not get better, your GP may prescribe:

- Colchicine – if painkillers do not work or if pericarditis keeps coming back  
- Steroids – if colchicine does not help  
- Antibiotics – if a bacterial infection is the cause  

Most people start to feel better within a few weeks.

## What causes pericarditis?

The most common cause is a viral infection.  
This could be a cold or the flu.  
The virus causes the pericardium to become inflamed.  

In some cases, bacteria or other health problems can cause it.  
But it is hard to find the exact cause in many people.

# What You Need to Know About Histoplasmosis

Histoplasmosis is a fungal infection. It starts in the lungs and can spread to other parts of the body. It is caused by a fungus called *Histoplasma capsulatum*. Most people do not know they are infected at first. The infection often has no symptoms. But it can cause serious illness in some people.

This infection is found around the world. It is common in parts of Central and South America, Africa, Asia, and Australia. In the United States, it is most common in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys. It also occurs in parts of northern Maryland, southern Pennsylvania, central New York, and Texas.

Outbreaks linked to bat caves have happened in many countries. In the U.S., they have been reported in Florida, Texas, and Puerto Rico.

## How the Infection Spreads

The fungus grows as a mold in soil. It thrives in places with bird or bat droppings. Tiny spores from the mold can become airborne. You get infected by breathing in these spores.

You are more likely to get infected when:

- Trees or buildings are being removed in areas with birds or bats.
- You are exploring caves.

The fungus changes from a mold to a small yeast when it enters the body. This change happens at body temperature.

## Who Is at Risk for Severe Infection?

Some people are more likely to get very sick. These include:

- People who breathe in large amounts of spores over a long time.
- Adults aged 55 years or older.
- Babies and young children.
- People with weak immune systems. This includes those with HIV/AIDS, organ transplant recipients, or people taking medicines that lower immunity (like steroids or drugs for rheumatoid arthritis).

## Types of Histoplasmosis

There are three main types of this infection.

### 1. Acute Primary Histoplasmosis

This is the most common form. It often causes mild or no symptoms. But some people have:

- Fever
- Cough
- Muscle aches
- Chest pain
- Feeling tired

Some people develop pneumonia. This shows up on a chest x-ray.

### 2. Chronic Cavitary Histoplasmosis

This form affects the lungs over a long time. It causes holes in the lungs. These look like those seen in tuberculosis. Symptoms include:

- A worsening cough
- Trouble breathing
- Weakness

The infection does not spread beyond the lungs.

### 3. Progressive Disseminated Histoplasmosis

This is the most serious form. The fungus spreads through the blood to other organs. It can affect the liver, spleen, lymph nodes, bone marrow, and more.

Symptoms are often vague and mild at first. They may include:

- Fever
- Fatigue
- Weight loss
- Weakness
- General feeling of being unwell

In people with HIV/AIDS, the illness can suddenly get worse.

Other possible problems include:

- Brain infection (meningitis or brain lesions)
- Infection of the adrenal glands (rare, but can cause a serious hormone problem)
- Severe pneumonia with low oxygen levels
- Low blood pressure
- Changes in mental state
- Muscle damage
- Blood clotting problems

### Fibrosing Mediastinitis

This is a rare, long-term condition. It causes scar tissue to build up in the chest. This scar tissue can block blood vessels or airways. It is thought to be caused by an overactive immune response to leftover fungal material.

### Eye Problems

Some people lose vision. But the fungus is not found in the eye. Antifungal medicine does not help. The link between the eye problem and histoplasmosis is not clear.

## How Is Histoplasmosis Diagnosed?

Doctors may suspect histoplasmosis if you have symptoms and live in or have visited an area where it is common.

Tests include:

- Chest x-ray: May show normal results, small spots, or holes in the lungs.
- Sputum, blood, or urine tests: To look for the fungus.
- Tissue biopsy: A sample of lung or other tissue may be taken.
- Blood or urine antigen tests: These detect a substance made by the fungus.

A lab test called culture can confirm the diagnosis. But it is risky for lab workers. So labs must be warned if histoplasmosis is suspected.

Microscopic exam of tissue or blood can show the yeast form of the fungus. This is especially helpful in people with HIV/AIDS.

Antigen tests are very useful. They are accurate and fast. The fungus is found in the blood in about 80% of severe cases. It is found in the urine in over 90% of severe cases.

Note: These tests can sometimes give a false positive. Other fungi can cause similar results.

## How Is Histoplasmosis Treated?

Not everyone needs treatment. Most mild cases go away on their own.

### For Mild to Moderate Infection

- Use a medicine called itraconazole.

### For Severe Infection

- Start with a strong medicine called liposomal amphotericin B.
- After the infection improves, switch to itraconazole to finish treatment.

### Other Medicines

- Fluconazole and voriconazole may not work as well.
- Posaconazole and isavuconazonium are active against the fungus. They may help some patients. But more research is needed to know when to use them.

### Monitoring During Treatment

- Check blood levels of itraconazole.
- Test urine and blood for fungal antigen to see if the treatment is working.

## What Is the Outlook?

- Acute primary histoplasmosis usually gets better on its own. Death is very rare.
- Chronic cavitary histoplasmosis can lead to serious lung damage and death.
- Without treatment, progressive disseminated histoplasmosis kills more than 9 out of 10 people.

## Key Facts

- Histoplasmosis is a common fungal infection.
- It spreads by breathing in spores from soil with bird or bat droppings.
- It is common in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys in the U.S.
- It can cause mild lung infection, long-term lung disease, or spread to other organs.
- Diagnosis uses lab tests on sputum, blood, urine, or tissue.
- Most mild cases do not need treatment.
- Severe cases need strong medicine like liposomal amphotericin B, followed by itraconazole.
- Untreated severe histoplasmosis is often fatal.
