# Broken Nose

A broken nose can happen if you hit your face. It can be painful and look bad, but it often gets better on its own.

## Signs and Symptoms

- Your nose hurts.
- Your nose is swollen and bruised.
- You hear a crunching or crackling sound when you touch your nose.
- Your nose looks different. It might be crooked or bent.
- You have trouble breathing through your nose.
- You may get black eyes from bruising under your eyes.
- You might have a cut on the bridge of your nose.
- You may have a nosebleed.

## What to Do at Home

Most broken noses can be treated at home. You should start to feel better in 3 days. Full healing takes about 3 weeks.

### Do These Things

- Put an ice pack (or a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a towel) on your nose for up to 15 minutes. Do this several times a day.
- Take paracetamol to help with pain.
- If you have a nosebleed:
  - Sit or stand up straight.
  - Lean forward slightly.
  - Pinch the soft part of your nose (just above the nostrils) for up to 15 minutes.
- Keep your head raised when lying down. Use extra pillows to help.
- Clean any small cuts or scrapes. Stop the bleeding, wash the area gently, and cover it with a plaster or dressing.

### Do Not Do These Things

- Do not try to push your nose back into shape if it looks crooked. Call NHS 111 for help.
- Do not wear glasses until the swelling goes down, unless you really need them.
- Do not blow or pick your nose until it is fully healed.
- Do not do hard exercise for the first 2 weeks.
- Do not play sports for at least 6 weeks. Avoid any activity where your face could be hit.

## When to Get Help

### Call NHS 111 if you have:

- A nose that is crooked after the injury.
- Swelling that has not gone down after 3 days.
- Pain that does not get better with painkillers.
- Trouble breathing through your nose after the swelling goes down.
- Frequent nosebleeds.
- A very high temperature, or you feel hot and shivery.

You can call 111 or use the NHS 111 online service.

### Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

- A nosebleed that will not stop.
- A big cut or open wound on your nose or face. This includes something stuck in the wound, like glass.
- Clear, watery fluid coming from your nose. This could mean you have a serious head injury.
- A severe headache with blurry or double vision.
- Eye pain and double vision.
- Neck pain or a stiff neck, with numbness or tingling in your arms.
- A purple swelling inside your nose. It may hurt or block your breathing.
- Other signs of a serious head injury, such as vomiting, passing out, or trouble speaking.

### A&E Safety Tips

- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you. Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.
- Bring all your regular medicines with you.

## Medical Treatment

### If Your Nose Is Crooked

A doctor may be able to fix the shape of your nose. This is called manipulation.

- You may need to wait a few days for the swelling to go down.
- The treatment should happen within 3 weeks of the injury. This is before the bones start to heal in their new position.
- The procedure uses local anaesthetic to numb your nose.
- It does not always make your nose look exactly the same as before, but it often helps.

### If You Have a Large Wound

- The wound will be cleaned in hospital.
- It will be closed with stitches or special strips.

Always get medical help if you are unsure. It is better to be safe.

# Shigellosis

Shigellosis is a serious infection of the intestines. It is caused by a type of bacteria called *Shigella*. The infection leads to stomach pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. The diarrhea often contains blood, mucus, or pus.

## What Causes Shigellosis?

The bacteria *Shigella* spread from person to person. The main way this happens is through contact with the stool of an infected person. This can happen if someone does not wash their hands after using the bathroom.

The bacteria can also spread through food or water that has been touched by an infected person. Objects like toys or doorknobs can carry the bacteria. Flies can pick up the bacteria from stool and spread it to food.

Sexual contact between men can also spread the infection.

You can get sick from swallowing as few as 10 to 100 of these bacteria. This is because the bacteria can survive the acid in your stomach.

## Who Gets Sick?

Shigellosis is most common in young children. It is also common in places with poor sanitation or crowded living conditions.

Adults usually have milder symptoms than children. But older adults and people with weak immune systems are at higher risk for serious illness.

## Symptoms

The time between exposure and getting sick is usually 1 to 4 days.

### In Adults

- You may feel sharp stomach pain.
- You may feel a strong need to pass stool, even when your bowels are empty. This is called tenesmus.
- You may pass solid stool that gives temporary relief.
- These symptoms come back and get worse over time.
- Diarrhea becomes frequent and loose. It may contain blood, mucus, or pus.
- Severe cases can lead to rectal prolapse (part of the rectum comes out) and loss of bowel control.

Some adults may not have a fever. Their diarrhea may not be bloody or contain mucus.

Most adults get better on their own. Mild cases last 4 to 8 days. Severe cases can last 3 to 6 weeks.

Serious dehydration and low blood pressure can happen in older adults with weak immune systems or in very young children. This can be life-threatening.

In rare cases, the illness starts suddenly. You may pass watery or clear stools. You may vomit and become very dehydrated fast. You may have confusion, seizures, or lose consciousness. In these cases, death can happen within 12 to 24 hours.

### In Children

- The illness starts suddenly with fever, irritability, or drowsiness.
- Children may lose their appetite, feel sick to their stomach, or vomit.
- They may have diarrhea, stomach pain, and a swollen belly.
- Within 3 days, the stool may contain blood, pus, and mucus.
- The number of bowel movements can go up to 20 or more per day.
- Dehydration and weight loss become severe fast.
- Without treatment, children can die in the first 12 days.
- If they survive, symptoms usually improve by the second week.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect shigellosis when someone has bloody diarrhea, especially in outbreaks or in areas where it is common.

A stool sample is tested to confirm the diagnosis. This is done through a lab test called a stool culture.

A newer test called PCR can also detect the bacteria. It is very accurate and fast.

Doctors may also look at a stool sample under a microscope. If white blood cells are seen, it suggests an infection.

Other conditions that cause similar symptoms include:
- Infections from *E. coli* bacteria
- *Salmonella* infection
- *Yersinia* infection
- *Campylobacter* infection
- Amebiasis (a parasite)
- *Clostridioides difficile* infection

## How Is It Treated?

Most people with mild shigellosis get better with rest and fluids. The main goal is to prevent dehydration.

### Fluids

- Drink plenty of water or oral rehydration solutions.
- In severe cases, fluids may be given through a vein (IV).

### Do Not Use Anti-Diarrhea Medicines

Medicines like loperamide can make the illness worse. They should not be used.

### Antibiotics

Antibiotics are not needed for healthy adults with mild symptoms.

But antibiotics are usually recommended for:
- Children
- Older adults
- People with weak immune systems
- People with severe symptoms

The following antibiotics are used:
- Ciprofloxacin (taken by mouth)
- Azithromycin (taken by mouth)
- Ceftriaxone (given by injection)

Some *Shigella* bacteria are resistant to common antibiotics like ampicillin, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX), and tetracyclines. Resistance is growing.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reported a rise in cases of extensively drug-resistant (XDR) shigellosis. This is especially a concern for:
- Men who have sex with men
- People living with HIV
- International travelers
- People experiencing homelessness

In these cases, stronger antibiotics like carbapenems may be needed. Treatment should be guided by an infectious disease specialist.

## How to Prevent Shigellosis

- Wash your hands well with soap and water before eating or handling food.
- Wash your hands after using the bathroom or changing diapers.
- Clean and disinfect surfaces that may be contaminated.
- Soak soiled clothes, sheets, and blankets in soapy water with disinfectant until they can be washed in hot water.
- Keep infected people away from others, especially in homes, schools, and childcare centers.
- Use proper isolation methods, especially for stool.

### Vaccines

Vaccines are being tested and show promise. But they may need to protect against many types of *Shigella* because immunity is only effective against the specific type you were exposed to.

## Key Facts

- *Shigella* bacteria cause a very contagious form of dysentery.
- People are the only source of the bacteria.
- Diarrhea may be watery at first. Later, it often contains blood, mucus, or pus.
- *Shigella dysenteriae* type 1 makes a toxin that can cause a serious condition called hemolytic-uremic syndrome. This is rare in the United States but can happen in travelers returning from high-risk areas.
- Severe dehydration and shock are most dangerous in young children and older adults with weak immune systems.
- Most people get better with fluids and rest.
- Give antibiotics to children, older adults, and people who are very ill or have weak immune systems.
- Many *Shigella* bacteria are resistant to common antibiotics. This makes treatment harder.

# What Is Pneumonia?

Pneumonia is an infection in the small air sacs of the lungs and the tissue around them.

- Pneumonia is one of the most common causes of death around the world.
- The most common symptom is a cough that brings up thick or colored mucus.
- Doctors usually diagnose pneumonia with a chest x-ray.
- Antibiotics are often used to treat pneumonia.
- Pneumonia is often the final illness in people with serious, long-term health problems.
- Some types of pneumonia can be prevented with vaccines.

In the United States, millions of people get pneumonia each year (not counting cases caused by COVID-19). In 2020, more than 47,000 people died from pneumonia in the U.S. It is the most common cause of death from infection in hospitals. It is also the most common cause of death from infection in poorer countries. Pneumonia is a common serious illness in children and babies.

(See also: Overview of the Respiratory System.)

---

## What Causes Pneumonia?

Pneumonia is caused by tiny germs. These include bacteria, viruses, mycobacteria, fungi, and parasites.

- Bacterial and viral infections are the most common causes.
- Other types—like those caused by fungi or parasites—are less common.
- The type of germ can depend on your age, health, where you live, and other factors.
- Sometimes more than one germ is involved. For example, the flu virus can lead to a bacterial infection in the lungs.

Your lungs are always exposed to germs. Your nose and throat have many bacteria. You also breathe in small amounts of germs from the air. You can also swallow or inhale germs from your mouth or stomach.

Your lungs have natural defenses that usually stop these germs from causing harm. These defenses include:

- The cough reflex, which helps push mucus and germs out.
- Cells in the airways that block germs and move mucus upward so you can cough it out.
- Proteins made by lung cells that attack germs.
- White blood cells in the lungs that are part of your immune system and fight infection.

Pneumonia happens when:

- Your lung defenses are not working well.
- You breathe in a large number of germs that overwhelm your defenses.
- A very strong germ enters your lungs.

Most often, pneumonia starts when germs from the upper airways get into the lungs. But sometimes germs come from the air, travel through the blood, or spread from another infected area nearby.

Where you are when you get pneumonia matters. Germs in hospitals are often more dangerous and harder to treat with antibiotics than germs in other places. People in hospitals or nursing homes are also more likely to have health problems that make pneumonia more likely.

### Types of Pneumonia

**Community-acquired pneumonia**  
This happens in people who live in the community and are not in a hospital.

**Hospital-acquired pneumonia**  
This is an infection you get while in the hospital.

**Health care–associated pneumonia**  
This happens in places like nursing homes or dialysis centers. It is treated like community-acquired pneumonia because the germs are usually the same.

**Aspiration pneumonia**  
This happens when you swallow or inhale large amounts of saliva, food, or vomit. It can happen if you have trouble swallowing (like after a stroke) or if you are not fully awake due to medicine, alcohol, or drugs.

**Obstructive pneumonia**  
This happens when something blocks the airways in the lungs, like a tumor. Bacteria build up behind the blockage and cause infection.

**"Walking" pneumonia**  
This is a mild form of community-acquired pneumonia. You may feel well enough to go to work or do normal activities. You do not need to stay in bed or go to the hospital.

### Who Is at Higher Risk?

Pneumonia is more likely in people with a weak immune system. This includes people who:

- Take certain medicines, like steroids or chemotherapy.
- Have diseases like HIV or cancer.
- Are infants or young children (their immune systems are still developing).
- Are very sick and their immune system is not working well.

Pneumonia can also happen after surgery, especially belly surgery, or after an injury, especially to the chest. Pain from surgery or injury can make it hard to breathe deeply or cough. If you do not cough, germs can stay in your lungs and cause infection.

Other people at risk include those who are weak, bedridden, paralyzed, or unconscious.

Other health problems that raise the risk of pneumonia include:

- Drinking too much alcohol.
- Smoking or vaping.
- Having diabetes.
- Having heart failure.
- Being older than 65 years.
- Having chronic lung disease like COPD.

These conditions can weaken the lungs or the immune system.

---

## What Are the Symptoms of Pneumonia?

The most common symptom is:

- A cough that brings up thick or discolored mucus.

Other common symptoms include:

- Chest pain.
- Chills.
- Fever.
- Trouble breathing.

Symptoms can vary depending on how much of the lungs are affected and what germ is causing the infection.

Some people also have digestive symptoms, such as:

- Nausea.
- Diarrhea.
- Loss of appetite.

Symptoms can be different in babies and older adults.

- Babies and young children may not have a fever.
- They may not be able to say they have chest pain.
- The only sign might be fast breathing or suddenly refusing to eat.
- Their cough may not bring up mucus.

In older adults, confusion can be the only sign of pneumonia.

### Possible Complications

Pneumonia can lead to serious problems, including:

- Low oxygen in the blood.
- Very low blood pressure (a life-threatening condition called sepsis).
- A lung abscess (a pocket of pus in the lung).
- Empyema (pus in the space between the lung and chest wall).
- Severe lung damage (called acute respiratory distress syndrome or ARDS).

When pneumonia is severe, the lungs cannot get enough oxygen into the blood. This makes you feel short of breath. Low oxygen levels can be life-threatening.

The germ causing pneumonia can enter the bloodstream. Or your body’s reaction to the infection can be too strong. This can cause very low blood pressure, which is dangerous. This condition is called sepsis.

Some types of pneumonia can cause a lung abscess or empyema. A lung abscess is a hole in the lung filled with pus. Empyema is pus in the space between the lung and the chest wall.

An overwhelming infection or a strong immune response can damage the lungs badly. This can lead to ARDS. People with ARDS breathe fast and shallow. They usually need a breathing machine (mechanical ventilator) for a long time.

---

## How Is Pneumonia Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tools to diagnose pneumonia:

- A chest x-ray (most common).
- Sometimes a CT scan of the chest.
- Tests to find the germ causing the infection.

A doctor listens to your chest with a stethoscope. Pneumonia often makes the lungs sound different. These sounds happen when airways are blocked or when the air sacs fill with fluid and cells.

Most of the time, a chest x-ray confirms pneumonia. But sometimes a CT scan is needed.

In mild cases, doctors may start treatment based on symptoms and the exam.

For people who are very sick and need hospital care, doctors test:

- Sputum (mucus from the lungs).
- Blood.
- Urine.

These tests help find the germ causing the infection.

In very sick people, or those with weak immune systems, doctors may use special methods to get sputum:

- A vapor treatment to make you cough deeply.
- A bronchoscope (a thin tube with a camera) inserted into the airways.

These methods give cleaner samples than regular coughing. They are more likely to show the true cause of pneumonia.

It is very important to find the germ when someone is very sick, has a weak immune system, or is not getting better with treatment. But even with testing, doctors cannot identify the exact germ in most cases.

---

## How Is Pneumonia Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause and how sick you are.

- Antibiotics (for bacterial infections).
- Antiviral, antifungal, or antiparasitic medicines (if needed).
- Support for breathing.

People with pneumonia need to clear mucus from their lungs. Deep-breathing exercises can help.

If you are short of breath or have low oxygen levels, you will get extra oxygen. This is usually given through small tubes in your nose (nasal cannula).

Rest is important, but staying in bed all the time can be harmful. You should move around and get out of bed when you can.

Doctors often start antibiotics right away if they suspect bacterial pneumonia—even before they know the exact germ. Starting antibiotics early can reduce the severity of the illness and lower the risk of serious complications, including death.

Sometimes pneumonia follows a viral infection like the flu. In these cases, doctors give antibiotics to treat the bacterial infection that may have developed.

When choosing an antibiotic, doctors consider:

- What type of pneumonia you have (e.g., community-acquired, hospital-acquired).
- Your age.
- Whether your immune system is working well.
- If you have other lung diseases.
- How severe the pneumonia is.
- If you have taken antibiotics in the past 90 days.
- What germs are common in your area and which antibiotics work against them.
- Test results, if available.

Doctors often choose a broad-spectrum antibiotic when:

- The pneumonia is severe.
- Your immune system is weak.
- You have hospital-acquired pneumonia or other risk factors

# Corns and Calluses

## What Are Corns and Calluses?

Corns and calluses are areas of thick, hard skin.  
They usually form on your feet, toes, or hands.  

Corns are small, hard lumps.  
Calluses are larger, rough patches of thick skin.  

They can be tender or painful.  

## What Causes Corns and Calluses?

They happen when skin rubs or presses too hard.  
This can happen from:  
- Wearing high heels  
- Wearing shoes that are too tight or too small  
- Not wearing socks with shoes  
- Lifting heavy things  
- Playing a musical instrument  

## When to See a Doctor

See a doctor if you have a corn or calluses and:  
- You have diabetes  
- You have heart disease or poor blood flow  
- The area bleeds, oozes pus, or has discharge  
- It does not get better after 3 weeks of home care  
- The pain is so bad it stops you from doing normal things  

### What Does Severe Pain Mean?

Severe pain means:  
- It is always there and so bad you cannot think or talk  
- You cannot sleep  
- It is hard to move, get out of bed, go to the bathroom, wash, or dress  

Moderate pain means:  
- It is always there  
- It makes it hard to focus or sleep  
- You can still get up, wash, or dress, but it is difficult  

Mild pain means:  
- It comes and goes  
- It is annoying but does not stop you from doing daily tasks  

## What You Can Do at Home

### Do These Things:

- Wear thick, cushioned socks  
- Wear shoes that are wide, comfortable, have a low heel, and soft soles  
- Use soft insoles or heel pads in your shoes  
- Soak your feet in warm water to soften the skin  
- Use a pumice stone or foot file every few days to gently remove hard skin  
- Apply moisturiser daily to keep skin soft  

### Do Not Do These Things:

- Do not try to cut off corns or calluses yourself  
- Do not walk long distances or stand for long periods  
- Do not wear high heels or tight, pointy shoes  
- Do not go barefoot  

## Help from a Pharmacist

A pharmacist can help you with:  
- Heel pads and insoles  
- Products to treat corns and calluses  
- Pain relief options  

## Medical Treatment

### Doctor’s Care

Your doctor can check if you have a corn or callus.  
They may:  
- Give you antibiotics if the area is infected  
- Refer you to a foot specialist if needed  

### Foot Specialist Care

A foot specialist, like a podiatrist, can help.  
They may:  
- Cut away the corn or callus  
- Use patches to soften the hard skin so it can be removed  
- Give you custom pads or insoles to reduce pressure on painful spots  

Note: Not everyone can get a foot specialist through the NHS.  
Waiting times can be long.  
You can pay to see a foot specialist privately.  

## Common Causes

Corns and calluses happen from repeated pressure or rubbing.  
Examples include:  
- Wearing high heels  
- Wearing shoes that do not fit  
- Not wearing socks  
- Lifting heavy weights  
- Playing a musical instrument

# Pulmonary Embolism That Is Not Caused by Blood Clots

Pulmonary embolism means a blockage in an artery in the lung. Most often, this blockage is a blood clot. But sometimes, it is caused by something else.

Other things that can block a lung artery include:
- Air bubbles
- Fat from broken bones
- Fluid from the womb during childbirth
- Infected material
- Foreign objects
- Tumors
- Cement used in joint surgery

When the blockage is not a blood clot, the symptoms may be different from those of a clot-related blockage.

Doctors diagnose this condition based on the patient’s symptoms and risk factors. They may not always need special tests.

Treatment focuses on helping the patient feel better. This includes giving oxygen, managing pain, and supporting breathing. The goal is to keep the patient stable while the body clears the blockage.

# Portopulmonary Hypertension

Portopulmonary hypertension is a condition where blood pressure is high in two places at once.  
One place is the blood vessels in the lungs.  
The other place is the vein that carries blood away from the liver.  

Doctors find no other reason for the high blood pressure in the lungs.  

High blood pressure in the lungs can happen in people who already have high pressure in the liver’s blood vessels.  
This liver problem is often caused by scarring of the liver, called cirrhosis.  

When both lung and liver blood pressure are high, it is called portopulmonary hypertension.  

## Symptoms

People with this condition often feel short of breath.  
They also feel tired all the time.  
Some people have chest pain.  
Others may cough up blood.  
Veins in the neck may look swollen.  
Legs can swell up too.  

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors suspect this condition in people with liver disease and high pressure in the liver’s blood vessels.  
They look at symptoms and do a physical exam.  

An electrocardiogram (ECG) and other tests may show that the right side of the heart is enlarged and working too hard.  
This is called cor pulmonale.  

To confirm the diagnosis, doctors do two tests:  
- An echocardiogram. This uses sound waves to create a picture of the heart.  
- Right heart catheterization. A thin tube is gently guided through a vein in the arm or leg into the right side of the heart.  
This test measures the pressure in the heart and in the main lung artery.  

## Treatment

The main goal is to lower the blood pressure in the lung arteries.  
Medicines that open up blood vessels (vasodilators) often help reduce the pressure.  

But the severity of the liver disease plays a big role in how well a person does.  
Some people with this condition cannot have a liver transplant.  
This is because the high lung pressure increases the risk of serious problems or death during the surgery.

# Allergic Rhinitis

Allergic rhinitis causes sneezing, an itchy nose, and a stuffy or runny nose.

It happens when your body reacts to something you are allergic to.

## Symptoms

You may have:
- Sneezing
- An itchy nose
- A runny or blocked nose
- Itchy, red, or watery eyes
- A cough
- An itchy roof of your mouth

These symptoms usually start within minutes of touching or breathing in something you are allergic to.

## Causes

Allergic rhinitis is caused by an allergic reaction.

Common triggers include:
- Pollen from trees, grass, and weeds (this is also called hay fever)
- Dust mites in your home
- Pet dander from animals like cats and dogs
- Mould spores
- Dust from wood, flour, or latex

You are more likely to have allergies if other people in your family do too. Allergies often run in families.

You may also have other conditions like eczema or asthma.

### Note:
Allergic rhinitis is not the same as non-allergic rhinitis. The latter is caused by things like colds, extreme temperatures, or humidity.

## How to Prevent Symptoms

You cannot always avoid what you are allergic to. But you can take steps to reduce your symptoms.

### Do this:
- Wear wraparound sunglasses to keep pollen out of your eyes.
- Use bedding and covers that are made for people with allergies.
- Wash your bedding at 60 degrees Celsius or higher.
- Dust with a damp cloth.
- Use a vacuum cleaner with a HEPA filter.
- Wash your pets at least once every two weeks.
- Groom your pets outside.
- Wash your pet’s bedding often.
- Clean any furniture your pet has been on.
- Keep your home dry and well-ventilated.
- Fix any damp or condensation problems.

### Do not do this:
- Do not let pets in your bedroom.
- Avoid going outside or hanging clothes to dry when pollen levels are high.

## Treating Allergic Rhinitis at Home

You can often manage allergic rhinitis without seeing a doctor.

Try to avoid things that cause your symptoms.

A pharmacist can help you choose medicines that may work, such as:
- Antihistamines – these help with sneezing, itching, and runny nose.
- Decongestant nasal sprays or drops – these clear a blocked nose. Do not use these in children under 6.
- Salt water nasal sprays or rinses – these clean out your nose.

You can buy nasal sprays without a prescription. But do not use them for more than a week. Using them longer can make your symptoms worse.

If you have a fever or feel too unwell to do your normal activities, stay home. Avoid close contact with others until you feel better.

## Seeing a Doctor

If over-the-counter medicines do not help, see your doctor.

Your doctor may prescribe stronger treatments, such as:
- Steroid nasal sprays – these reduce swelling in the nose.
- Prescription antihistamines – these are stronger than the ones you can buy.

If your symptoms are very bad or it is hard to find the cause, your doctor may refer you to a specialist. They can do tests and offer more treatment options.

If someone passes out and you are there: - Check for a pulse right away. - If there is no pulse, start CPR. - If there is a pulse, but the heart is very slow, give atropine or use a pacemaker. - If needed, use isoproterenol to keep the heart rate up while a temporary pacemaker is placed. Recovery takes a few minutes or longer. - Heart-related syncope usually happens without warning and recovery is quick. - Treatment depends on the cause. - If the cause is not clear, do not drive or use machinery. The next episode could be deadly.

# What Is Sinusitis?

Sinusitis is when the sinuses become inflamed.  
The sinuses are air-filled spaces in the bones around your nose.  
This condition is very common.  
It can be caused by a virus, bacteria, or allergies.

## What Are the Sinuses?

- The two frontal sinuses are above your eyebrows.  
- The two maxillary sinuses are in your cheekbones.  
- The two groups of ethmoid sinuses are on each side of your nose.  
- The two sphenoid sinuses are behind the ethmoid sinuses.

## Types of Sinusitis

There are several types of sinusitis:

- **Acute sinusitis** lasts less than 4 weeks.  
- **Chronic sinusitis** lasts more than 12 weeks.  
- **Subacute sinusitis** lasts between 30 and 90 days.  
- **Recurrent sinusitis** means you have four or more episodes of acute sinusitis each year.

## Causes of Sinusitis

- A cold or viral infection often blocks the sinuses.  
- Allergies can also cause swelling and blockage.  
- A crooked nose (deviated septum) makes it harder to drain sinuses.  
- Some people have a family history of sinus problems.  
- A tooth infection can spread into the maxillary sinus.  
- Fungi in the air can cause infection in some people.

## Symptoms of Sinusitis

Both acute and chronic sinusitis cause similar symptoms:

- Thick yellow or green mucus from the nose  
- Headache  
- Pain or pressure in the face  
- Blocked or stuffy nose  
- Tenderness or swelling on the face  
- Trouble smelling things  
- Bad breath  
- Cough, especially at night

### Where Is the Pain?

- **Maxillary sinusitis**: Pain in the cheeks, below the eyes, or toothache  
- **Frontal sinusitis**: Pain across the forehead  
- **Ethmoid sinusitis**: Pain behind or between the eyes, watery eyes, and a splitting headache  
- **Sphenoid sinusitis**: Pain that is hard to locate—may be in the front or back of the head

You may also feel tired, weak, or unwell.  
Fever and chills can happen, but they may mean the infection has spread.

Pain often gets worse when you lie down or bend forward.

## Complications of Sinusitis

If not treated, the infection can spread:

- To the eye area, causing swelling or vision changes  
- Into the eye itself, causing eye pain and vision problems  
- To the brain, causing severe headache and confusion

If you have these symptoms, see a doctor right away.

## How Is Sinusitis Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms.  
They may do one or more of the following:

- A physical exam of your nose and face  
- A CT scan of the head (only if symptoms are severe or long-lasting)  
- A nasal endoscopy (a thin tube with a camera is used to look inside the nose)  
- Blood tests (to check for allergies or immune problems)  
- X-rays of the teeth (if a tooth infection is suspected)

Sometimes, a CT scan is found by accident when done for another reason, like a head injury.

### Sinusitis in Children

Doctors suspect sinusitis in children if:

- Thick mucus from the nose lasts more than 10 days  
- The child feels very tired  
- There is a cough that lasts a long time  
- There is pain or discomfort in the face  
- Fever is rare

A CT scan may be used to confirm the diagnosis, but only if needed.  
This is because children are more sensitive to radiation.

## Treatment of Sinusitis

### For Acute Sinusitis

The goal is to clear the sinuses and treat the infection.

**Home remedies that help:**

- Breathe in steam from hot water  
- Use a warm, wet towel on your face  
- Drink warm liquids  
- Rinse your nose with saltwater (nasal irrigation)  
- Use a saltwater spray

**Medicines:**

- Decongestant nasal sprays (like phenylephrine or oxymetazoline) can help for a few days.  
  Do not use them longer than 3 days. They can make congestion worse.  
- Oral decongestants (like pseudoephedrine) are not very helpful and should be avoided.  
- Steroid nasal sprays reduce swelling. They take at least 15 days to work.  
- Antihistamines (like fexofenadine, cetirizine, or loratadine) may help if allergies are involved.

**Antibiotics:**

- Only used if the infection is bacterial.  
- Given for severe or long-lasting symptoms (like high fever or severe pain lasting more than 3 days).  
- Common antibiotics: amoxicillin/clavulanate or doxycycline.  
- Azithromycin, cephalosporins, and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole are no longer recommended due to resistance.

### For Chronic Sinusitis

- Antibiotics are used for 4 to 6 weeks.  
- Adults: doxycycline is preferred.  
- Children: amoxicillin/clavulanate is preferred.

If antibiotics do not work, surgery may be needed.

**Surgery options:**

- To clean out the sinuses and collect samples for testing  
- To improve drainage and reduce blockage

## Fungal Sinus Infections

Fungi are common in the air.  
Most people have them in their nose and sinuses without problems.

But in some cases, fungi cause serious issues.

### Fungus Balls

- Caused by *Aspergillus* fungus.  
- Happens in people with healthy immune systems.  
- Symptoms: facial pain, pressure, stuffy nose, and mucus.  
- Treatment: surgery to remove the fungus.

### Invasive Fungal Sinusitis

- A serious and dangerous condition.  
- Happens in people with weak immune systems.  
  This includes people with:  
  - Uncontrolled diabetes  
  - Cancer (like leukemia or lymphoma)  
  - Late-stage HIV  
  - Those on steroids or chemotherapy

**Symptoms:**

- Severe pain  
- High fever  
- Pus from the nose  
- Bulging eye (proptosis)  
- Loss of vision

**Diagnosis:** A small tissue sample is taken and tested under a microscope.

**Treatment:**

- Surgery to remove infected tissue  
- Strong antifungal and antibiotic medicines given through a vein  
- Treatment of the underlying illness (like diabetes or cancer)  
- Support for the immune system

This condition can be life-threatening and needs urgent care.

### Allergic Fungal Sinusitis

- A type of chronic sinusitis caused by an allergic reaction to fungi.  
- Causes thick mucus, severe nasal blockage, and growths called polyps.  
- Polyps block the sinuses and cause ongoing inflammation.

**Treatment:**

- Surgery to open the sinuses and remove polyps and fungus  
- Long-term use of steroid medicines (taken by mouth or applied inside the nose)  
- Antibiotics and antifungal medicines (sometimes applied directly or taken by mouth)  
- Even with treatment, the condition often comes back.

## Key Points

- Sinusitis is common and usually caused by viruses, bacteria, or allergies.  
- Symptoms include facial pain, congestion, mucus, and headache.  
- Acute sinusitis lasts less than 4 weeks. Chronic lasts more than 12 weeks.  
- Treatment includes home care, medicines, and sometimes surgery.  
- Fungal infections are rare but serious, especially in people with weak immune systems.  
- Always see a doctor if symptoms last more than 10 days or get worse.  
- Seek emergency care if you have eye swelling, vision changes, or confusion.

# Balanitis – Simple Guide

Balanitis is when the head of the penis becomes swollen, itchy, sore, or red.  
You might also feel pain when peeing.  
You could have a thick discharge from under the foreskin.  
You might see bleeding around the foreskin.  
There may be a bad smell.  
Some people have trouble pulling back the foreskin.  
This is normal in young children.

## When to See a Doctor

See a doctor if:
- You or your child has swelling, itching, soreness, or redness on the head of the penis.
- The symptoms do not get better after treatment.

Adults can also go to a sexual health clinic for help.

## What Causes Balanitis

Balanitis can happen for several reasons:
- Not cleaning the penis well.
- Some young boys are born with a tight foreskin. This makes it hard to pull back the skin to clean underneath.
- A yeast infection called thrush.
- A sexually transmitted infection like gonorrhoea or chlamydia. If this is suspected, you may be sent to a sexual health clinic.
- Irritation from soap, shower gel, or condoms.
- Diabetes. High sugar levels in the urine can lead to thrush.

## How Balanitis Is Treated

The treatment depends on what is causing the problem.

Your doctor may give you:
- A mild steroid cream or ointment to reduce swelling and itching.
- An antifungal cream or ointment to treat a yeast infection.
- Antibiotics if there is a bacterial infection.

If balanitis keeps coming back and medicine does not help, your doctor may suggest circumcision.  
Circumcision is surgery to remove the foreskin.

## What You Can Do to Help

### Do These Things

- Wash your penis every day with just water or a moisturising cream (emollient).
- Gently pull back the foreskin and wash the area with warm water.
- Dry the area gently after washing.
- If you use condoms, choose ones made for sensitive skin.
- Wash your hands before peeing or touching your penis.

### Do Not Do These Things

- Do not use soap or shower gel on the penis.

### For Parents: Caring for Your Child

- Wash your child’s penis every day with warm water.
- Dry it gently after washing.
- Change nappies often if your child wears them.

### Do Not Do These Things for Your Child

- Do not use soap, bubble bath, or baby wipes on your child’s penis.
- Do not try to pull back the foreskin if it is stuck in place. This can cause pain and injury.

# Huntington Disease

Huntington disease is a genetic brain disorder.  
It runs in families and can affect anyone, no matter their sex.  
Most people start showing symptoms in middle age, usually between 35 and 40 years old.  
The disease gets worse over time and leads to serious disability.

## What Happens in the Brain

The brain’s caudate nucleus shrinks.  
The brain cells that help control movement die off.  
Levels of key brain chemicals like GABA and substance P go down.

The disease is caused by a change in a gene on chromosome 4.  
This gene is called *huntingtin*.  
The change means a certain DNA pattern (CAG) repeats too many times.  
This leads to a faulty protein that builds up in brain cells.  
This buildup harms the cells and causes the disease.  
The more CAG repeats, the earlier symptoms start and the worse they are.  
When a father passes the gene to his child, the number of repeats can grow over generations.  
This can make symptoms appear earlier and be more severe in later family members. This is called anticipation.

## What the Disease Feels Like

Symptoms start slowly.  
They often begin with memory problems or mood changes.  
People may feel sad, lose interest in things, become irritable, or act in ways that upset others.  
Some may have thoughts of suicide.  
These mental health issues are more common in people with Huntington disease than in the general population.

Movement problems come next.  
These include jerky, uncontrolled movements (chorea), twisting motions (athetosis), sudden jerks (myoclonic jerks), and fake tics (called tourettism).  
These fake tics cannot be stopped.  
They are not the same as true tics.

Other signs include:  
- A strange, stiff walk that looks like a puppet’s.  
- Grimacing faces.  
- Trouble moving eyes quickly without blinking or jerking the head.  
- Trouble holding a movement, like sticking out the tongue or gripping something.  
- Poor balance and coordination (ataxia), which is often missed.

The disease gets worse over time.  
Walking becomes impossible.  
Swallowing becomes hard.  
Memory and thinking skills decline severely.  
Chorea often turns into slow, stiff movements (akinetic-rigid features).  
Most people need to live in a care home.  
Death usually happens 13 to 15 years after symptoms begin.

Some people also develop anxiety or obsessive-compulsive behaviors.

If symptoms start before age 20, it is called juvenile Huntington disease or Westphal variant.  
This form often causes seizures and slow, stiff movements (parkinsonism).

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors look at symptoms, medical history, and family history.  
A genetic test confirms the diagnosis.  
The test counts how many CAG repeats are in the gene.

- **26 or fewer repeats**: Normal.  
- **27 to 35 repeats**: Normal, but unstable. Children may get the disease.  
- **36 to 39 repeats**: Abnormal. Some people get symptoms, some do not.  
- **40 or more repeats**: Abnormal. Almost everyone will get symptoms. The more repeats, the earlier symptoms start.

Brain scans (like MRI) can show shrinkage in the caudate area and some brain tissue loss in the front part of the brain.

## How the Disease Is Treated

There is no cure.  
Treatment focuses on helping with symptoms and improving quality of life.  
Doctors also work to slow the disease’s progress, but no treatment has yet proven fully effective.

### For Chorea (Uncontrolled Movements)

A medicine called a VMAT-2 inhibitor is often used first.  
Examples: tetrabenazine and deutetrabenazine.  
These medicines lower dopamine levels in the brain.  
This helps reduce jerky movements.  
Doses are slowly increased until symptoms improve or side effects become too strong.  
These medicines can cause extreme tiredness, restlessness, or stiffness.  
They should not be used in people with depression.  
They can make depression worse and increase suicide risk.  
They are also expensive.  
Deutetrabenazine is often better tolerated than tetrabenazine.

### For Agitation and Movement Problems

Antipsychotic medicines can help with chorea and agitation.  
They are an option for people who cannot take VMAT-2 inhibitors.  
Examples:  
- Chlorpromazine  
- Haloperidol  
- Risperidone  
- Olanzapine  
- Clozapine

Doses are raised slowly until symptoms improve or side effects become too bad.  
Clozapine needs regular blood tests.  
It can lower white blood cell counts, which can be dangerous.

### Other Treatments Being Studied

Scientists are testing new ways to help.  
Some aim to reduce overactive brain signals.  
Others aim to improve energy in brain cells.  
Treatments that boost brain chemicals like GABA have not worked well.

### For Mental Health

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) may help with depression, anxiety, or obsessive thoughts.  
They may also help with impulsive or risky behaviors.

## Important Advice for Families

People with a close relative who has Huntington disease should get genetic counseling.  
This is especially true for women who may have children and men thinking about fathering a child.  
Counseling should happen before any genetic test.  
It helps people understand what the results could mean.  
It also helps reduce the risk of suicide.

## Key Points

- Huntington disease is a genetic brain disorder.  
- It causes memory loss, mood changes, and uncontrolled movements.  
- Symptoms usually start in middle age.  
- Most people need long-term care.  
- If symptoms and family history suggest the disease, offer genetic counseling before testing.  
- Use brain scans to help confirm the diagnosis.  
- Treat symptoms early.  
- Talk about end-of-life care as soon as possible.  
- Offer counseling to family members before testing.  
- This helps them prepare for results and lowers suicide risk.

# Broken Upper Arm

A broken upper arm happens when the upper part of the arm bone (called the humerus) breaks. This bone is part of the shoulder joint.

## How It Happens

- Most often, a broken upper arm happens after a fall onto an outstretched hand.
- Sometimes it happens from a direct hit to the arm.
- The broken pieces of bone usually stay close together or do not move far out of place.
- Because the pieces stay near each other, the bone often heals on its own.

## Who Is Affected

- Broken upper arms are common in older adults.
- They can happen to people of any age, but are more likely in older people.

## Symptoms

- The shoulder and upper arm hurt and swell.
- It is hard or painful to lift the arm.
- Sometimes, a nerve near the injury gets damaged.
- If a nerve is damaged, the arm may feel numb.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

- Doctors ask about the injury and your symptoms.
- They check the elbow and collarbone for other injuries.
- They take x-rays of the shoulder from different angles.
- If the x-rays are not clear, doctors may use a CT scan.
  - A CT scan uses x-rays and a computer to make a 3D picture of the injury.
- If you think you have a broken upper arm, see a doctor right away.

## Treatment

Most broken upper arms are treated with:

- A sling to keep the arm still.
- A swathe (a piece of cloth or strap) to help hold the sling in place.
- Exercises to move the shoulder joint through its full range of motion.

### Exercises to Prevent Stiffness

Moving the shoulder soon after the break helps prevent it from becoming stiff. This is especially important for older adults.

**Codman Exercises (for shoulder movement):**

1. Bend your waist forward.
2. Let the injured arm hang straight down.
3. Relax your arm and shoulder.
4. Bend your knees slightly.
5. Slowly swing your arm:
   - Side to side.
   - Back and forth.
   - In small circles, both clockwise and counterclockwise.
6. Shift your weight from one foot to the other as you swing the arm.
7. Gradually increase the size of the swings as you can tolerate.
8. Do each movement twice in one set.
9. Do several sets each day.

These exercises should cause only mild discomfort. Do them even if your arm is in a sling or sling and swathe.

> **Did You Know?**  
> Start range-of-motion exercises as soon as possible after the break—even if your arm is in a sling.

### When Surgery Is Needed

- If the bone breaks into many pieces, surgery may be needed.
- An orthopedic surgeon will realign the bone pieces.
- They may use metal plates, screws, or wires to hold the bone in place. This is called open reduction with internal fixation, or ORIF.
- In some cases, the shoulder joint may need to be replaced.

> **Note:** Always follow your doctor’s advice. Healing takes time, and proper care helps you recover better.

# Back Pain

Back pain is common. It can happen for many reasons.

Some causes include a muscle injury, like a pulled muscle.  
Other causes can be a trapped nerve, a slipped disc, or a long-term condition like arthritis.

Most back pain gets better on its own in a few weeks.  
You can do things to help it improve faster.

---

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:

- Your pain does not get better after a few weeks of home care.  
- The pain stops you from doing normal daily tasks.  
- The pain is very bad or getting worse.  
- You are worried about the pain or feel you cannot cope.

### What Does Severe Pain Feel Like?

Severe pain means:
- The pain is always there and so strong it is hard to think or talk.  
- You cannot sleep.  
- It is very hard to move, get out of bed, go to the bathroom, wash, or dress.

### What Does Moderate Pain Feel Like?

Moderate pain means:
- The pain is always there.  
- It makes it hard to focus or sleep.  
- You can still get up, wash, or dress, but it is difficult.

### What Does Mild Pain Feel Like?

Mild pain means:
- The pain comes and goes.  
- It is annoying but does not stop you from doing your usual activities.

---

## When to Get Urgent Help

Call 111 or get help online if you have back pain and:

- A high temperature (fever).  
- You lost weight without trying.  
- You notice a lump or swelling in your back.  
- Your back looks different or has changed shape.  
- The pain does not get better when you rest.  
- The pain is worse at night.  
- The pain gets worse when you sneeze, cough, or pass a stool.  
- The pain is in the top of your back, between your shoulders, not your lower back.

---

## When to Call 999 or Go to A&E

Go to A&E or call 999 if you have back pain and:

- Pain, tingling, weakness, or numbness in both legs.  
- Numbness or tingling around your genitals or buttocks.  
- Trouble peeing.  
- You cannot control your bladder or bowels (you pee or poo yourself).  
- Chest pain.  
- The pain started after a serious accident, like a car crash.

### A&E Safety Tips

- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to take you.  
- If you cannot get a ride, call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
- Bring all your medicines with you.

---

## What Causes Back Pain?

Back pain can come from many things.

Sometimes, it is caused by a muscle injury, like a strain.

Other times, it is due to a medical condition, such as:
- A slipped disc (when a disc in your spine moves out of place).  
- Sciatica (a nerve in your leg is pressed on).  
- Ankylosing spondylitis (a long-term condition that causes stiffness in the spine).

Very rarely, back pain can be a sign of something serious, like:
- A broken bone.  
- Cancer.  
- An infection.

---

## How to Help Yourself

Most back pain gets better in a few weeks.  
You can do simple things to feel better faster.

### Do These Things:

- Stay active. Try to keep doing your normal daily tasks.  
- Take ibuprofen if you need pain relief.  
- Paracetamol alone is not the best choice for back pain. But you can take it with another painkiller if needed.  
- Use an ice pack (or a bag of frozen peas) wrapped in a towel to reduce pain and swelling.  
- Use a heat pack (or hot water bottle) wrapped in a towel to ease stiffness or muscle spasms.  
- Try gentle exercises and stretches for back pain.

### Do Not Do These Things:

- Do not stay in bed for long periods.  
- Avoid lying down too much. Movement helps.

---

## Treatments Your Doctor May Suggest

If your pain is bad or not improving, your doctor may give you medicine.

This can include:
- Stronger painkillers.  
- Medicine to relax tight muscles.

If your pain does not improve after a few weeks, your doctor may suggest:

- Group exercise classes.  
- Physiotherapy (a trained therapist helps you move better and strengthen your back).  
- Manual therapy (a therapist gently moves your back muscles, bones, and joints).  
- Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) to help you manage pain and stress.  
- A nerve block (a treatment that stops some nerves from sending pain signals – only for long-term lower back pain).

If your back pain is caused by a condition like a slipped disc and other treatments have not worked, surgery may be an option.

# Medicines for Heart Failure

Heart failure means your heart does not pump blood as well as it should. This can cause symptoms like shortness of breath, tiredness, and swelling in the legs.

## Medicines to Help with Symptoms

These medicines help ease symptoms such as fluid buildup and breathing problems:

- **Diuretics** – Help your body get rid of extra fluid. This can reduce swelling and make it easier to breathe.
- **Nitrates** – Help widen blood vessels. This lowers pressure in your heart and makes it easier to pump.
- **Digoxin** – Helps your heart beat stronger and more regularly.

## Medicines for Long-Term Care and Better Survival

These medicines are used every day to help you live longer and stay healthier. They slow down the damage to your heart.

- **ACE inhibitors** – Lower blood pressure and reduce strain on the heart.
- **Beta-blockers** – Slow your heart rate and lower blood pressure. This helps your heart work better over time.
- **Aldosterone antagonists** – Help your body get rid of extra fluid and reduce stress on the heart.
- **ARBs** – Work like ACE inhibitors. They help lower blood pressure and protect the heart.
- **ARNIs** – A newer type of medicine. They combine two actions to help the heart work better and reduce hospital visits.
- **SGLT2 inhibitors** – Originally made for diabetes. They also help the heart by reducing fluid and lowering risk of hospitalization.
- **Sinus node inhibitors** – Slow the heart rate. This helps the heart fill with blood better and work more efficiently.

## What You Need to Know About Your Medicines

Your doctor or nurse should explain your medicines clearly. Make sure you understand:

- Always refill your prescriptions on time. Do not run out of medicine.
- Take your medicine every day, as directed. Do not skip doses.
- Know what side effects to watch for. These can include dizziness, nausea, or unusual tiredness.
- Know when to call your doctor. Call if you feel worse, have new symptoms, or have side effects.

# Colorectal Cancer – Simple Explanation

Colorectal cancer is cancer that starts in the large intestine (colon) or the rectum. It is one of the most common cancers in Western countries and the second leading cause of cancer deaths. But it can often be prevented or caught early.

---

## What Causes Colorectal Cancer?

- A family history of colorectal cancer raises your risk.
- Eating a diet high in fat, animal protein, and refined carbs, and low in fiber, increases your risk.
- Certain inherited conditions can cause colorectal cancer:
  - Familial adenomatous polyposis
  - Lynch syndrome
  - Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
  - Juvenile polyposis syndrome
  - MUTYH polyposis syndrome
- People with long-term ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease of the colon also have a higher risk. The longer the disease lasts and the more colon is affected, the higher the risk.

---

## How Does Colorectal Cancer Start?

- Most colorectal cancers begin as a small growth called a polyp on the inner lining of the colon or rectum.
- Over time, some polyps turn into cancer.
- As the cancer grows, it can spread into the wall of the colon or rectum.
- It can also spread to nearby lymph nodes.
- Because blood from the colon and rectum flows to the liver, cancer can spread to the liver after spreading to lymph nodes.

---

## Symptoms of Colorectal Cancer

Colorectal cancer often does not cause symptoms in the early stages. When symptoms do appear, they depend on where the cancer is and how advanced it is.

Common symptoms include:
- Blood in the stool (sometimes not visible to the eye)
- Feeling tired or weak (this can happen from slow bleeding)
- Crampy or severe belly pain
- Constipation or a change in bowel habits
- A feeling that the bowel is not empty after a movement
- Pain when sitting (if the cancer is in the rectum)

**Rectal cancer** often starts with bleeding during a bowel movement. Even if you have hemorrhoids or other common bowel issues, bleeding should always be checked by a doctor to rule out cancer.

---

## How Is Colorectal Cancer Diagnosed?

If you have symptoms or a positive screening test, your doctor will do more tests.

### Common Diagnostic Tests:
- **Colonoscopy**: A thin, flexible tube with a camera is used to look inside the colon. Any growths found are removed during the test.
- **CT scan**: This checks if the cancer has spread to other parts of the body, like the liver or lungs.
- **Genetic testing**: If you have a family history of certain cancers, you may be tested for Lynch syndrome or MUTYH polyposis syndrome.

### Other Tests:
- **Barium enema x-ray**: This can show tumors in the lower colon, but colonoscopy is better because it allows tissue samples to be taken.
- **Blood tests**: These do not diagnose cancer, but they help track treatment progress. For example, a blood marker called CEA can show if cancer returns after surgery.

---

## Treatment for Colorectal Cancer

Treatment depends on the stage of the cancer and where it is.

### Surgery
- For colon cancer: The cancerous part of the colon and nearby lymph nodes are removed. The healthy ends of the colon are joined together.
- For rectal cancer: The surgery depends on how far the cancer is from the anus.
  - If the rectum and anus must be removed, a colostomy is needed.
  - A colostomy is a new opening in the belly that lets waste leave the body into a bag.
  - If part of the rectum can be saved, the colostomy may be temporary. Later, the colon can be reconnected, and the colostomy closed.

### What Is a Colostomy?
- The colon is cut and the healthy end is brought to the skin.
- Stool passes through the opening into a bag.
- This gives the colon time to heal after surgery.
- Later, the two ends can be reconnected so stool passes normally again.

### Chemotherapy and Radiation
- These are used after surgery if the cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes.
- For rectal cancer, chemotherapy and radiation may be given before or after surgery to help shrink the tumor and improve survival.
- If cancer has spread to distant organs, surgery may still be done to relieve blockages or symptoms.
- Chemotherapy can shrink tumors and help people live longer, but it is not a cure in advanced cases.

### Special Treatments for Liver Spread
- If cancer has spread only to the liver, doctors may:
  - Remove the tumors surgically.
  - Inject chemotherapy or radioactive beads directly into the liver’s blood supply.
  - Use a small pump (under the skin or worn on a belt) to deliver treatment while staying mobile.
  - Use radiofrequency ablation (heat to destroy cancer cells).
  - Use focused radiation to relieve pain and symptoms.

### For People Who Cannot Have Surgery
- If the cancer blocks the colon and surgery is too risky, doctors can:
  - Use a probe with electric current (electrocautery) to shrink the tumor.
  - Place a stent (a mesh tube) to keep the colon open.
- These treatments can ease symptoms, but they do not help you live longer.

---

## Staging Colorectal Cancer

Staging shows how far the cancer has spread.

- **Stage 0**: Cancer is only in the inner lining of the colon.
- **Stage 1**: Cancer has grown into the deeper layers of the colon wall.
- **Stage 2**: Cancer has reached the outer layer of the colon.
- **Stage 3**: Cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes.
- **Stage 4**: Cancer has spread to other organs like the liver, lungs, or ovaries.

---

## Prognosis (Outlook)

- The earlier the cancer is found, the better the chance of a cure.
- If cancer is only in the inner lining, the 5-year survival rate is about 90%.
- If cancer has spread through the colon wall, survival is about 73–74%.
- If cancer has spread to other organs, survival is less than 20%.

---

## How to Prevent Colorectal Cancer

You can lower your risk by:

### Getting Screened
- Start screening at age 45.
- Screening can find polyps before they turn into cancer.
- Common screening tests include colonoscopy, stool tests, and other imaging.

### Changing Your Lifestyle
- Be more physically active.
- Keep a healthy weight.
- Limit alcohol.
- Do not smoke.
- Eat less red meat (beef, pork, lamb) and processed meats (hot dogs, lunch meats).
- Eat more fiber (vegetables, fruits, whole grains).

### Low-Dose Aspirin (for Some)
- Doctors may suggest a daily low-dose aspirin for adults aged 50 to 59 who have a higher risk of heart disease.
- This can help prevent both heart disease and colorectal cancer.

---

## After Treatment

After surgery, you will need follow-up care:
- A colonoscopy within 1 year.
- Another colonoscopy 3 years later if no polyps are found.
- Then every 5 years.
- Regular blood tests (like a complete blood count and liver tests).
- Blood tests for CEA (a cancer marker).
- CT or MRI scans every 6 to 12 months for 5 years.

These checks help find any return of cancer early.

---

## Key Points

- Colorectal cancer often starts as a polyp.
- It grows slowly and may not cause symptoms early.
- Screening saves lives by finding cancer early.
- Surgery is the main treatment.
- Lifestyle changes and sometimes low-dose aspirin can reduce your risk.
- Early detection leads to the best outcomes.

# Sudden Confusion (Delirium)

## When to See a Doctor

- If you or a loved one has been getting more forgetful or confused over time, see your doctor.
- This might not be serious, but it’s best to get it checked.
- In older adults, memory problems and confusion can sometimes be signs of dementia.

## When to Go to A&E or Call 999

- If someone suddenly becomes confused, go to A&E or call 999 right away.
- Many causes of sudden confusion need urgent care.
- Some causes can be life-threatening.

### A&E Safety Tips

- Do not drive yourself to A&E.
- Ask someone to drive you, or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.
- Bring all your medicines with you.

## How to Tell If Someone Is Confused

A confused person may:

- Have trouble thinking or speaking clearly.
- Not know where they are.
- Struggle to focus or remember things.
- See or hear things that are not there. (This is called hallucinations.)

Try asking them:
- What is your name?
- How old are you?
- What is today’s date?

If they seem unsure or cannot answer, they need medical help.

## What to Do While Waiting for an Ambulance

If you are with someone who suddenly became confused, you can help while waiting for medical help.

### Do

- Stay with them.
- Tell them who you are and where they are.
- Keep reassuring them.
- Use simple words and short sentences.
- Write down any medicines they are taking, if you can.

### Don’t

- Do not ask many questions at once.
- Do not stop them from moving unless they are in danger.

## Common Causes of Sudden Confusion

Sudden confusion can come from many different causes. Do not try to guess what is wrong. Get medical help right away.

Some common causes include:

- Infections – especially urinary tract infections in older adults or people with dementia.
- A stroke or a TIA (a mini-stroke).
- Low blood sugar in people with diabetes.
- A head injury.
- Some prescription medicines.
- Alcohol poisoning or withdrawal from alcohol.
- Using illegal drugs.
- Carbon monoxide poisoning – especially if others in your home also feel unwell.
- A severe asthma attack or other serious lung or heart problems.
- Certain types of seizures linked to epilepsy.

# Tinea Corporis (Body Ringworm)

Tinea corporis is a skin infection caused by a type of fungus.  
It affects the face, chest, back, arms, and legs.  
The infection causes a rash that looks like a ring.  

## What Does It Look Like?

The rash often forms a circle or oval shape.  
The outer edge is raised and scaly.  
The center may look clearer than the edges.  
On darker skin, the center may look darker than normal.  
This is called postinflammatory hyperpigmentation.  

Some people get round, scaly patches instead of rings.  
These patches have small bumps or tiny pus-filled spots.  
This is a rare form of the infection.  

## What Causes It?

The most common causes are three types of fungus:  
- *Trichophyton mentagrophytes*  
- *Trichophyton rubrum*  
- *Microsporum canis*  

These fungi live on the skin and can spread from person to person.  
They can also come from animals or contaminated surfaces.  

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor checks the rash by looking at it.  
They may take a small sample of skin from the edge of the rash.  
The sample is examined under a microscope after being mixed with a special liquid.  
This test helps confirm the infection.  

Other skin conditions can look like tinea corporis.  
These include:  
- Pityriasis rosea  
- Drug rashes  
- Nummular dermatitis  
- Erythema multiforme  
- Tinea versicolor  
- Erythrasma  
- Psoriasis  
- Secondary syphilis  

## How Is It Treated?

Mild to moderate cases are treated with antifungal creams, lotions, or gels.  
You apply the medicine to the skin twice a day.  
Keep using it for at least 7 to 10 days after the rash is gone.  
Most people use medicine for about 2 to 3 weeks.  

The following medicines work well:  
- Imidazoles (like clotrimazole or miconazole)  
- Ciclopirox  
- Naftifine  
- Terbinafine  

For severe or hard-to-treat cases:  
- The fungus *Trichophyton rubrum* can be harder to treat.  
- People with serious health problems may also have trouble getting better.  

In these cases, a doctor may prescribe an oral antifungal medicine.  
The most effective options are:  
- Itraconazole, 200 milligrams once a day  
- Terbinafine, 250 milligrams once a day  

Treatment lasts 2 to 3 weeks.  

## Key Points

- Tinea corporis usually causes a pink or red ring-shaped rash.  
- The outer edge is raised and scaly.  
- The center often clears up over time.  
- On darker skin, the center may look darker.  
- Diagnosis is based on how the rash looks and a skin test.  
- Mild cases are treated with antifungal creams or lotions.  
- Apply the medicine twice a day.  
- Keep using it for at least 7 to 10 days after the rash is gone.  
- Severe or stubborn cases may need oral medicine.

# Otosclerosis

Otosclerosis is a condition where abnormal bone grows in the ear. This extra bone affects how sound moves through the ear.

The most common spot for this problem is near the stapes. The stapes is one of three small bones that carry sound from the eardrum to the inner ear. When the stapes is blocked by extra bone, it cannot move well. This leads to hearing loss that gets worse over time.

Otosclerosis often runs in families. About half of all cases are passed down through genes. If one parent has otosclerosis, a child has a 25% chance of getting it. If both parents have it, the chance rises to 50%.

## Symptoms of Otosclerosis

Only about 1 in 10 people with otosclerosis will have hearing loss. When it happens, it usually starts in late teens or early twenties. In rare cases, hearing loss can begin as early as age 7 or 8.

Most people first notice the problem in one ear. But over time, more than half of people develop symptoms in both ears. The main symptom is hearing loss. It often starts slowly. Many people first notice they have trouble hearing low sounds or soft words like whispers. Some people also hear ringing or buzzing in the ear. Dizziness is very rare.

## Diagnosis of Otosclerosis

A doctor who specializes in hearing problems usually makes the diagnosis. These doctors use special hearing tests to find the cause of hearing loss. One test is called tympanometry. These tests help decide if more testing is needed. In some cases, a CT scan may be done to look at the bones in the ear.

## Treatment of Otosclerosis

A hearing aid can help most people hear better. Some people choose surgery instead. One surgery, called stapedectomy, removes part or all of the stapes and replaces it with a small artificial piece. This can improve hearing. But the surgery carries risks. Some people may lose more hearing or have balance problems after the surgery.

# Erythromelalgia

Erythromelalgia mainly affects the feet.  
It can also affect the hands, arms, legs, ears, and face.  
The main symptoms are burning pain, redness, and warm or hot skin.  
The pain often starts as an itchy feeling.  
Redness may look different on brown or black skin.  
You may also have swelling and sweat more than usual.  

The pain can last for a few minutes or several days.  
It may come and go.  
When the pain gets worse, it is called a flare-up.  
A flare-up can start slowly or suddenly.  
After a flare-up, your skin may feel cold.  
It may also look blue or grey.

---

## What Causes Erythromelalgia?

It is not always clear what causes erythromelalgia.  
Sometimes it is linked to another health problem.  
In some cases, it is caused by a faulty gene passed down from a parent.  
Flare-ups are often triggered by a rise in body temperature.  

Things that can raise your body temperature include:  
- Exercise  
- Wearing warm or tight clothes and shoes  
- Hot weather  
- Stress  
- Drinking alcohol  
- Eating spicy food  
- Not drinking enough fluids (dehydration)

---

## What Happens at Your Doctor’s Appointment?

If your doctor thinks you have erythromelalgia, they will refer you to a specialist.  
The specialist will check your symptoms and examine you.  
They may do blood tests.  
They may also do genetic tests to look for changes in your genes.

---

## How Is Erythromelalgia Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause.  
If another health problem is causing your symptoms, treating that problem may help.  
Most treatments aim to stop flare-ups.  

You may be given:  
- Creams  
- Gels  
- Sprays  
- Tablets  
- Medicines given through a vein  

In rare cases, surgery may be needed.  
Erythromelalgia can be hard to treat.  
You may need to try different treatments to find what works best for you.

---

## Things That Can Help

### Do These Things:
- Avoid things that trigger your symptoms  
- Wear loose clothing and shoes  
- Drink plenty of fluids  
- Try to manage stress  
- Cool your hands or feet with a fan or a cool (not cold) gel pack for a short time  
- Raise your hands or feet on a chair or pillow during a flare-up  

### Do Not Do These Things:
- Do not use cold water or ice on your hands or feet. This can damage your skin.  
- Do not drink alcohol or eat spicy food.

# Blepharitis

Blepharitis is swelling and irritation along the edge of the eyelid.  
It can happen suddenly (acute) or last for a long time (chronic).  

## What Causes Blepharitis?

- **Acute blepharitis** can be ulcerative (with sores) or nonulcerative (without sores).  
- **Chronic blepharitis** is often caused by:  
  - Problems with the oil glands in the eyelid (meibomian gland dysfunction).  
  - A skin condition called seborrheic dermatitis.  
  - Tiny mites called *Demodex* living in the eyelash roots.  

## What Are the Symptoms?

All types of blepharitis can cause:  
- Itching or burning along the eyelid edge.  
- Redness and swelling of the eyelid.  
- A gritty or foreign body feeling in the eye.  
- Eyes that water more than usual.  
- Sensitivity to light.  
- Irritation of the white part of the eye (conjunctiva).  

Itching is more common if the cause is an allergy.  
Symptoms are often worse in the morning.  
This is different from dry eye, where symptoms usually get worse later in the day.  

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor will look at your eyes using a special microscope called a slit-lamp.  
This helps see the eyelid edges and eye surface clearly.  

If the condition does not improve with treatment, a small sample of tissue may be taken for testing.  
This is to rule out rare conditions like eyelid cancer or immune system problems.  

## How Is It Treated?

### For Acute Blepharitis:
- **Ulcerative type (with sores):**  
  - Topical antibiotics (eye drops or ointment).  
  - If a virus is the cause, oral antiviral medicine may be used.  

- **Nonulcerative type (no sores):**  
  - Warm compresses to soothe the eyelids.  
  - Sometimes, a short course of steroid eye drops to reduce swelling.  

### For Chronic Blepharitis:
- **If oil glands are blocked:**  
  - Warm compresses.  
  - Eyelid cleaning with a gentle cleanser.  
  - Oral antibiotics like tetracycline or azithromycin.  

- **If caused by seborrheic dermatitis:**  
  - Warm compresses.  
  - Daily eyelid cleaning.  
  - Artificial tears to relieve dryness.  

- **If mites (*Demodex*) are the cause:**  
  - A special medicine like lotilaner to kill the mites.  

## What Is the Outlook?

- Acute blepharitis usually gets better with treatment.  
  - But it can come back.  
  - It may turn into chronic blepharitis.  

- Chronic blepharitis:  
  - Comes and goes over time.  
  - Can be hard to treat completely.  
  - Causes discomfort and looks unpleasant.  
  - Does not usually damage the cornea or cause vision loss.  

Long-term care is important.  
You must keep doing warm compresses and clean your eyelids regularly to prevent flare-ups.  

## Key Points

- Common types of blepharitis:  
  - Acute ulcerative: Often caused by staph bacteria or herpes virus.  
  - Acute nonulcerative: Usually due to allergies.  
  - Chronic: Often linked to blocked oil glands, seborrheic dermatitis, or mites.  

- Dry eyes often happen with chronic blepharitis.  

- Common symptoms:  
  - Itching and burning on the eyelid edge.  
  - Watery eyes, light sensitivity, and a gritty feeling.  

- Diagnosis is done with a slit-lamp exam.  

- If one eyelid is affected and symptoms do not improve, check for eyelid cancer.  

- Supportive care includes:  
  - Warm compresses.  
  - Cleaning the eyelids daily.  
  - Using artificial tears if eyes are dry.  

- Specific treatments:  
  - Antibiotics or antiviral medicine for acute cases.  
  - Steroid drops for severe inflammation.  
  - Antibiotics (topical or oral) for chronic cases.

# Cholera

Cholera is a serious illness that affects the intestines.  
It is caused by a type of bacteria called *Vibrio cholerae*.  
This bacteria leads to severe diarrhea that can be deadly if not treated.

## How People Get Cholera

- People get infected by eating food or drinking water that is contaminated.  
- Shellfish are a common source of contamination.  
- Cholera is rare in places with good sanitation.  
- It spreads easily in areas where human waste is not properly treated.  
- The bacteria pass out of the body in stool.  
- If people touch contaminated surfaces or eat contaminated food, they can get sick.

## Where Cholera Happens

- Cholera is most common in parts of Asia, the Middle East, Africa, and South and Central America.  
- Small outbreaks have happened in Europe, Japan, and Australia.  
- In the United States, cases are rare but can occur along the Gulf Coast.  
- Outbreaks happen where people lack clean water and safe waste disposal.  
- Poor living conditions and war can make outbreaks worse.

### Major Outbreaks

- A major outbreak in Haiti started after a 2010 earthquake.  
- It lasted until 2017.  
- Over 820,000 people got sick.  
- Nearly 10,000 people died.  
- A large outbreak in Yemen began in 2016 and is still ongoing.  
- Over 2.5 million people have been sickened.  
- Almost 4,000 people have died.  
- This is the largest and fastest-spreading cholera outbreak in modern history.  
- In 2019, it caused more than 90% of all global cholera cases.  
- Haiti had a new outbreak in late 2022, after being declared cholera-free for three years.  
- This outbreak is still happening.

- Cholera cases have increased worldwide since 2021.  
- The number of reported cases doubled from 2021 to 2022.  
- In 2022, seven countries in Africa and Asia reported more than 10,000 cases each.

## When Outbreaks Happen

- In areas where cholera is common, outbreaks often happen during war or civil unrest.  
- These events break down sanitation systems.  
- Outbreaks are more common in warm months.  
- Young children and undernourished children are most at risk.  
- In new areas, outbreaks can happen at any time and affect all ages.

## How Cholera Works in the Body

- You need to swallow many bacteria to get sick.  
- Stomach acid usually kills bacteria.  
- If you have less stomach acid, the bacteria can survive and reach the small intestine.  
- The bacteria grow and release a toxin.  
- This toxin forces the small intestine to release large amounts of salt and water.  
- The body loses this fluid through watery diarrhea.  
- The loss of water and salt is what causes death.  
- The bacteria stay in the intestines. They do not spread to other parts of the body.

## Who Is More Likely to Get Cholera

- Young children are more at risk.  
- Older adults are more at risk.  
- People who take medicine to reduce stomach acid are more at risk.  
  - Examples: omeprazole and famotidine.  
- People with type O blood are more likely to get infected.  
- People in areas where cholera is common slowly build some protection over time.

### Did You Know?

- Without treatment, more than half of people with cholera will die.

## Symptoms of Cholera

- Most people who are infected do not have any symptoms.  
- When symptoms appear, they usually start 1 to 3 days after exposure.  
- The first signs are sudden, painless, watery diarrhea and vomiting.  
- Fever is usually not present.  
- Diarrhea and vomiting can be mild or very severe.  
- In severe cases, adults can lose more than one quart (1 liter) of fluid per hour.  
- The stool looks like rice water — clear and milky.  
- Dehydration can become serious quickly.  
- Signs of dehydration include extreme thirst, muscle cramps, and weakness.  
- Urine output drops.  
- Eyes may sink into the face.  
- Fingers may become very wrinkled.  
- If not treated, dehydration can lead to kidney failure, shock, coma, and death.  
- With treatment, symptoms usually go away in 3 to 6 days.  
- Most people stop carrying the bacteria within 2 weeks.  
- A few people carry the bacteria without getting sick. These people are called carriers.

## How Doctors Diagnose Cholera

- A sample of stool is taken.  
- A swab may be used to collect a sample from the rectum.  
- The sample is sent to a lab.  
- The lab grows the bacteria to see if *Vibrio cholerae* is present.  
- Finding the bacteria confirms the diagnosis.  
- A test called PCR can find the bacteria’s DNA faster.  
- Blood and urine tests check for dehydration and kidney problems.

## How Cholera Is Treated

- Replacing lost fluids and salts is the most important step.  
- Most people can drink a special fluid solution to replace lost fluids.  
- This solution contains salt and sugar to help the body absorb water.  
- For very dehydrated people who cannot drink, fluids are given through a vein.  
- In emergencies, if IV fluids are not available, fluids can be given by mouth or through a tube in the nose.  
- After symptoms improve, people should keep drinking fluids to replace what they lost.  
- Drinking water is encouraged.  
- Solid food can be eaten once vomiting stops and hunger returns.  
- An antibiotic is usually given.  
  - It helps reduce diarrhea and makes it stop faster.  
  - It also lowers the chance of spreading the disease.  
- The antibiotic doxycycline is used for everyone, including children and pregnant women.  
- Other options are azithromycin and ciprofloxacin.  
- All are taken by mouth.  
- Doctors pick the best antibiotic based on local resistance patterns.  
- For children in low-resource areas, zinc supplements can help reduce symptoms and shorten the illness.

## How to Prevent Cholera

- Clean water is essential.  
- Safe disposal of human waste is critical.  
- In areas where cholera is common, follow these steps:  
  - Use only boiled or chlorinated water.  
  - Avoid raw vegetables.  
  - Avoid undercooked shellfish.  
  - Shellfish can carry other harmful *Vibrio* bacteria too.

### Vaccines

- In the United States, a vaccine called Vaxchora is available.  
- It is for people aged 2 to 64 who are traveling to cholera-risk areas.  
- It is taken by mouth in one dose.  
- It is not known how long protection lasts.  
- It may not last more than 3 to 6 months.  

- Three other vaccines are available outside the U.S.: Dukoral, ShanChol, and Euvichol.  
- These provide 60 to 85% protection for 2 to 3 years.  
- They are taken by mouth in two doses.  
- A booster dose is recommended after 2 years for people still at risk.
