# Edwards’ Syndrome

Edwards’ syndrome is a condition that affects babies from birth. It happens because of a change in the baby’s genes.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Babies with Edwards’ syndrome may have some or all of these problems:

- They are born with a low birth weight.
- Their ears are set low on the sides of their head.
- They may have a cleft lip or cleft palate. This means the lip or roof of the mouth does not close properly.
- They may have club foot. This means one or both feet are turned inward or twisted.
- They may have heart problems.
- They may have kidney or spine problems.
- They may have trouble breathing or digesting food.

Every child with Edwards’ syndrome is different. Some have more symptoms than others.

## What Causes Edwards’ Syndrome?

Edwards’ syndrome is caused by an extra chromosome 18. Most people have two copies of chromosome 18. A baby with Edwards’ syndrome has three copies.

This extra chromosome happens by chance. It is not caused by anything you did before or during pregnancy.

Your chance of having a baby with Edwards’ syndrome goes up as you get older. There is also a small chance it could happen again if you have had a baby with Edwards’ syndrome before.

You cannot prevent Edwards’ syndrome. It is not something you can avoid.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors can check for Edwards’ syndrome during pregnancy. They can also test your baby after birth.

### Screening During Pregnancy

You will be offered a screening test during your pregnancy. This test shows your chance of having a baby with Edwards’ syndrome.

At 10 to 14 weeks of pregnancy, you can have a combined test. This includes a blood test and an ultrasound scan. This is often called the 12-week scan.

If you miss the combined test or it cannot be done, you can have a different blood test between 14 and 20 weeks. This is called the quadruple blood screening test.

If the screening test shows a possible problem, you will be referred to a specialist. You may be offered more tests, such as:

- Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT)
- Amniocentesis
- Chorionic villus sampling (CVS)

These tests can tell you for sure if your baby has Edwards’ syndrome. They can also help you understand what this might mean for your baby and your family.

You do not have to have these tests. It is your choice. Talk to your midwife or doctor about what you want to do.

### Support During Screening

If you are told your baby might have Edwards’ syndrome, you may feel worried or upset. You are not alone.

_Antenatal Results and Choices (ARC)_ offers support and information about screening tests. They can help you understand your options.

- Call the helpline: 020 7713 7486  
- Available Monday to Friday, 10am to 5.30pm

## Types of Edwards’ Syndrome

There are three types of Edwards’ syndrome:

- **Full trisomy 18** – This is the most common type. It is also the most serious.
- **Mosaic trisomy 18** – This is less common. Some cells have the extra chromosome, others do not. Symptoms may be less severe.
- **Partial trisomy 18** – This is very rare. Only part of chromosome 18 is extra. Symptoms may be less severe.

Tests during pregnancy may not always show what type your baby has. After your baby is born, you may be offered more tests to find out the type.

## Help and Support

If your child has Edwards’ syndrome, you are not alone. Many people can help you.

### Talk to Your Healthcare Team

Your doctor and healthcare team will support you. They can answer your questions and help you make decisions.

### Connect with Others

You may find comfort in talking to other parents who have children with Edwards’ syndrome. Sharing your experiences can help.

### Charities That Can Help

There are charities that offer support for families affected by Edwards’ syndrome and for parents of sick or premature babies.

#### SOFT UK

SOFT UK supports families affected by Edwards’ syndrome (trisomy 18) or Patau’s syndrome (trisomy 13).

- Call the helpline: 0300 102 7638  
- Email: support@soft.org.uk  
- Join the SOFT UK forum: Talk with others about trisomy 13 and trisomy 18  
- Get SOFT UK support: Help for children and families, and support during pregnancy or after a miscarriage or stillbirth

#### Bliss

Bliss supports sick or premature babies and their parents.

- Email: hello@bliss.org.uk  
- Book a video call with a volunteer: Get support online

## Final Thoughts

Edwards’ syndrome is a serious condition. But many families find strength and support through their healthcare team and charities.

You can get help and information at every step. You are not alone.

# Bowlegs and Knock-Knees

There are two main types of knee or leg shape problems:  
- Bowlegs (genu varum)  
- Knock-knees (genu valgum)  

If these problems are not treated, they can lead to knee joint wear and tear later in life. This condition is called osteoarthritis.

---

## Bowlegs

Bowlegs are common in young children.  
Most children grow out of bowlegs by the time they are 18 months old.  
If bowlegs do not improve or get worse, a condition called Blount disease may be the cause.  
Blount disease affects the growth plate in the shin bone.  
Other bone problems, such as rickets, should also be checked for.

---

## Knock-Knees

Knock-knees are less common than bowlegs.  
Even if knock-knees are very noticeable, they often get better on their own by age 9.  
A rare bone disorder called skeletal dysplasia should be ruled out.  
Another rare condition, hypophosphatasia, should also be checked for.  
If the leg shape is still very abnormal after age 10, surgery may be needed.  
The surgery involves placing small metal staples on the inside of the thigh bone to help guide normal growth.

# Glaucoma – Simple Explanation

Glaucoma is a group of eye problems that slowly damage the optic nerve. This nerve sends pictures from your eye to your brain. Damage to this nerve can cause permanent vision loss.

- The most common cause is high pressure inside the eye.
- But some people get glaucoma even when eye pressure is normal.
- Vision loss from glaucoma happens very slowly. You may not notice it at first.
- If not treated, glaucoma can lead to total blindness.

## How Common Is Glaucoma?

- About 4 million people in the United States have glaucoma.
- Around 70 million people worldwide have it.
- It is the second leading cause of blindness in the world.
- In the United States, it is the second most common cause of blindness.
- Among Black and Hispanic people in the U.S., it is the top cause of blindness.
- Only about half of people with glaucoma know they have it.
- Glaucoma can happen at any age, but it is much more common after age 60.

## Who Is at Risk?

You are more likely to get glaucoma if you:

- Are over 40 years old
- Are Black
- Have a family member with glaucoma
- Are very nearsighted (for open-angle glaucoma) or very farsighted (for closed-angle glaucoma)
- Have diabetes
- Have high blood pressure
- Use steroid medicines for a long time
- Have had an eye injury or eye surgery

## What Causes Glaucoma?

Your eye makes a clear fluid that nourishes it. This fluid flows out through small drainage channels. When these channels get blocked, fluid builds up and pressure rises.

- The fluid is made in the back of the eye.
- It moves to the front of the eye.
- It leaves through tiny drainage channels near the edge of the iris and cornea.
- When the system works right, fluid flows in and out like a faucet and a sink drain.
- If the drain gets blocked, fluid backs up. Pressure rises. This can hurt the optic nerve.

Sometimes, eye pressure is normal but still too high for the optic nerve. This is called low-tension glaucoma. It is more common in Asian people.

### Types of Glaucoma

There are two main types:

### Open-Angle Glaucoma

- This is the most common type.
- The drainage channels are not blocked, but they do not work well.
- Tiny deposits slowly clog them over months or years.
- Pressure builds up slowly.
- There are no early symptoms. Vision loss happens slowly.

### Closed-Angle Glaucoma

- This is less common.
- The space between the iris and cornea is too narrow.
- The drainage channels get blocked or covered.
- This can happen suddenly (acute) or slowly (chronic).
- In the sudden form, pressure rises fast and causes serious symptoms.

## Symptoms of Glaucoma

### Open-Angle Glaucoma

- No pain.
- No early warning signs.
- Vision loss starts in the side (peripheral) vision.
- You may miss steps or parts of words when reading.
- You may have trouble driving.
- Over time, side vision loss gets worse.
- You may end up with tunnel vision: you see straight ahead, but not to the sides.
- If untreated, even tunnel vision is lost. Total blindness can happen.

### Acute Closed-Angle Glaucoma

- This is a medical emergency.
- Symptoms come fast: severe eye pain, headache, red eye, blurred vision.
- You may see rainbow-colored rings around lights.
- You may lose vision suddenly.
- You may feel sick to your stomach or throw up.
- Without treatment, vision can be lost in just 2 to 3 hours.

### Chronic Closed-Angle Glaucoma

- Symptoms come slowly, like open-angle glaucoma.
- You may have eye redness, mild pain, blurred vision, or headaches.
- The pain may go away after sleep.
- Eye pressure may be normal or slightly high.

If you have glaucoma in one eye, you are likely to get it in the other eye.

## How Is Glaucoma Diagnosed?

Your doctor will do a full eye exam if they suspect glaucoma. The exam has five parts:

1. **Eye pressure test**  
   - Done with a device called a tonometer.  
   - It is painless.  
   - Normal pressure is between 11 and 21 millimeters of mercury.  
   - But some people with glaucoma have normal pressure. Some with high pressure do not have glaucoma.

2. **Optic nerve check**  
   - The doctor uses an ophthalmoscope or other tools to look at the nerve.  
   - They check for signs of damage.

3. **Peripheral vision test (visual field test)**  
   - You look straight ahead while lights flash in different areas.  
   - The machine records where you can and cannot see.  
   - This helps find blind spots.

4. **Gonioscopy**  
   - The doctor uses a special lens to look at the drainage channels.  
   - This helps tell if the glaucoma is open-angle or closed-angle.

5. **Cornea thickness test**  
   - Thinner corneas increase your risk of glaucoma.  
   - But thin corneas do not mean you have glaucoma.

### Important Note

Some medicines for allergies, colds, or sleep can widen your pupils. This can block the drainage channels and cause closed-angle glaucoma.  
Older adults should have their eyes checked before taking these medicines.

## Why Early Detection Matters

- Glaucoma often causes no symptoms at first.
- Vision loss happens slowly and silently.
- The best chance to prevent blindness is to catch it early.
- People at high risk should have a full eye exam every 1 to 2 years.

## How Is Glaucoma Treated?

Once vision is lost, it cannot come back. But treatment can stop more loss.

The goal is to lower eye pressure and protect the optic nerve.

Treatment is lifelong. It may include:

- Eye drops
- Surgery

### Eye Drops

Most people with open-angle glaucoma use eye drops.  
People with closed-angle glaucoma usually need surgery instead.

Common types of eye drops:

| Type | How It Works | Side Effects | Notes |
|------|--------------|--------------|-------|
| Prostaglandin-like drops (e.g., latanoprost) | Help fluid drain better | Darker eye or skin color, longer eyelashes, eye pain, rash, possible eye inflammation | Safe for most people |
| Beta-blocker drops (e.g., timolol) | Reduce fluid made in the eye | Shortness of breath (if you have lung problems), slow heartbeat, tiredness, mood changes | Not for people with heart or lung issues |
| Cholinergic drops (e.g., pilocarpine) | Make pupil smaller, help fluid drain | Sweating, headache, shaking, nausea, more saliva | Less used now |
| Rho kinase inhibitor (e.g., netarsudil) | Helps fluid drain | Red eyes, broken blood vessels, eye deposits | Used in some cases |
| Alpha-adrenergic agonist drops (e.g., brimonidine) | Reduces fluid and helps drainage | High blood pressure, fast heartbeat, dry mouth, drowsiness | Can be dangerous for babies under 2 |
| Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., dorzolamide) | Reduce fluid made in the eye | Bad taste, rash, tiredness, kidney stones | Some are pills, some are eye drops |
| Osmotic diuretics (e.g., glycerin, mannitol) | Pull fluid out of the eye | More urine, dehydration, salt imbalance | Used only in emergencies |

### Emergency Treatment for Acute Closed-Angle Glaucoma

- This is a medical emergency.
- Doctors use strong medicines fast to lower pressure.
- Eye drops (like timolol, brimonidine, pilocarpine) are used first.
- Pills (like acetazolamide) or IV medicine (like mannitol) may be given.
- Laser surgery is done on both eyes right away.
- The other eye is treated because it is at high risk.

### Surgery

Surgery may be needed if:

- Eye pressure is very high
- Eye drops do not work
- You cannot use eye drops
- You have bad side effects from drops
- You already have serious vision loss

#### Laser Surgery

- **Laser trabeculoplasty**: Opens drainage channels for open-angle glaucoma.
- **Laser peripheral iridotomy**: Makes a small hole in the iris for closed-angle glaucoma.
- Done in a doctor’s office or clinic.
- Uses numbing eye drops.
- Most people go home the same day.
- Side effect: temporary rise in eye pressure (treated with drops).
- Rarely, the laser can burn the cornea, but it heals fast.

#### Glaucoma Filtration Surgery

- Doctors create a new drainage path to let fluid leave the eye.
- Done in a hospital or surgery center.
- You can usually go home the same day.
- Possible risks:
  - Infection in the eye (rare)
  - Cataracts get worse
  - Eye pressure too low
  - Swelling in the back of the eye

# Glue Ear

Glue ear means fluid builds up behind the eardrum. This can cause hearing loss.

The main sign is trouble hearing. It can happen in one ear or both ears.

Glue ear often gets better without treatment. But sometimes, fluid needs to be drained from the ear.

One way to drain the fluid is with small tubes called grommets. These are put into the ear during a short operation.

---

## When to See a Doctor

Take your child to a doctor if you notice any of these signs:

- They speak very loudly.
- People have trouble understanding them.
- They keep asking others to repeat what they said.
- They want the TV or music turned up very loud.
- They can’t hear people who are far away.
- They get distracted when people are talking.
- They seem tired or grumpy because it’s hard to listen.

---

## What Happens with Glue Ear

The most common symptom is temporary hearing loss. It can affect one or both ears.

Other possible symptoms include:

- Pain in the ear.
- Ringing or buzzing sounds in the ear (called tinnitus).
- Feeling dizzy or off balance.

If glue ear lasts a long time, it can slow down how well a child learns to talk. It can also make school harder.

Glue ear is more common in children. But adults can get it too. Adults have the same symptoms.

---

## What the Doctor Can Do

The doctor will often wait and see if the problem gets better on its own.

There is no medicine that works well for glue ear. Most cases clear up within 3 months.

Your child may be checked again over the next year. This helps make sure the problem does not get worse.

The doctor might suggest a treatment called autoinflation. This helps the fluid drain from the ear.

To do autoinflation, your child can:

- Blow up a special balloon using one nostril at a time.
- Swallow while holding both nostrils closed.

This must be done several times a day. It is not usually used for children under 3 years old.

If glue ear causes an ear infection, the doctor may give antibiotics.

---

## Hospital Care

Your child may be sent to a hospital specialist if:

- Their hearing problems are affecting how they learn or grow.
- They already had serious hearing loss before this.
- They have Down’s syndrome or a cleft lip and palate. These conditions make glue ear less likely to get better on its own.

The two main treatments in hospital are:

- Temporary hearing aids.
- Grommets (small tubes placed in the ear).

Sometimes, surgery to remove the adenoids (glands at the back of the nose) is needed. This is called an adenoidectomy.

The hospital specialist will help you choose the best treatment for your child.

---

### Grommets

A grommet is a tiny tube placed in the ear during a short operation.

It helps drain fluid and keeps the eardrum open.

The grommet will fall out on its own in 6 to 12 months as the ear heals.

It does not need to be removed.

# Pulmonary Embolism (PE)

Pulmonary embolism is a blockage in one of the blood vessels in the lungs.  
The blockage is usually caused by a blood clot that starts in a large vein in the leg or pelvis.  
The clot breaks loose and travels through the bloodstream to the lungs.  

## What Causes Pulmonary Embolism?

Most blood clots that cause PE start in the deep veins of the legs or pelvis.  
These clots are called deep vein thrombosis.  
Clots that reach the popliteal vein (just below the knee) or higher are more likely to break off and cause PE.  
Clots can also come from veins in the arms or chest, especially if there is a tube in a large vein (like a central line).  

Other things that can block the lung arteries include:  
- Air bubbles  
- Amniotic fluid (during childbirth)  
- Fat from broken bones  
- Infected material  
- Pieces of bone cement (used in joint surgery)  
- Foreign objects  
- Tumor cells  

### Risk Factors

Certain conditions increase your chance of getting a blood clot and PE.  
These include:  

- Being older than 60 years  
- Having cancer or certain blood disorders  
- Taking certain cancer medicines (like bevacizumab or thalidomide)  
- Using hormone treatments (like birth control pills or hormone replacement therapy)  
- Using testosterone  
- Having heart failure  
- Being unable to move for long periods (like after surgery, during long trips, or while in bed)  
- Having a tube in a large vein  
- Having an infection (especially severe ones like COVID-19)  
- Having kidney disease that causes swelling  
- Being very overweight  
- Being pregnant or recently gave birth  
- Having had a blood clot before  
- Having sickle cell disease  
- Smoking  
- Having had a stroke  
- Having inherited blood clotting problems (like Factor V Leiden or protein C deficiency)  
- Having a condition that makes the blood too thick (like high levels of certain clotting factors)  
- Having trauma or surgery  
- Having other conditions that reduce movement, damage veins, or make blood more likely to clot  

## How PE Affects the Body

When a clot blocks a lung artery, it can cause serious problems.  
The size and number of clots, the health of the lungs, how well the right side of the heart is working, and the body’s ability to dissolve clots all matter.  

Small clots may not cause any symptoms.  
They can break down quickly and go away in hours or days.  

Larger clots can cause:  
- Faster breathing (tachypnea)  
- Low oxygen in the blood (hypoxemia)  
- Low blood flow to the body (low cardiac output)  
- Collapse of small air sacs in the lungs (atelectasis)  
- Increased pressure in the lung arteries (pulmonary hypertension)  
- Fast heart rate (tachycardia)  
- Low blood pressure (hypotension)  

Most clots are broken down by the body over time.  
But some do not dissolve.  
These can stay in place and cause long-term high pressure in the lungs (chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension).  

### Types of PE

PE is grouped into three levels based on how serious it is:  

**High risk (massive PE):**  
- The right side of the heart is not working well  
- Blood pressure is low (systolic blood pressure below 90 mm Hg)  
- Or blood pressure drops by 40 mm Hg or more from normal for at least 15 minutes  

**Intermediate risk (submassive PE):**  
- The right side of the heart is not working well, but blood pressure is normal  
- Imaging shows the heart is enlarged or not pumping well  
- Blood tests show heart damage (elevated troponin or BNP)  
- This group is split into:  
  - Intermediate high risk: heart problems on imaging AND abnormal blood tests  
  - Intermediate low risk: heart problems on imaging OR abnormal blood tests  

**Low risk:**  
- No heart problems  
- Normal blood pressure  
- No signs of serious illness  

### Saddle Embolism

A saddle embolism is a large clot that blocks the main split in the lung artery.  
It goes into both the right and left lung arteries.  
This type is usually high or intermediate risk.  
But not always.  
The treatment does not depend on the shape of the clot.  

### Long-Term Effects

In 1 to 3 out of 100 people, PE leads to chronic high pressure in the lungs over months or years.  
This is called chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.  
It can lead to long-term heart failure on the right side.  

A large clot or many small clots can suddenly block major lung arteries.  
This can cause the right side of the heart to fail quickly.  
This can lead to shock or sudden death.  
The risk depends on how fast the pressure rises and how healthy the heart and lungs were before.  
People with heart or lung disease are at higher risk.  
But even young, healthy people can survive a PE that blocks more than half the lung blood flow.  

### Pulmonary Infarction

Sometimes, a clot cuts off blood to part of the lung.  
This can cause tissue damage called pulmonary infarction.  
It may show up on a chest X-ray as a wedge-shaped area near the outer edge of the lung.  
This is rare because the lungs have two blood supplies.  
Most cases are mild and heal completely.  
It usually causes chest pain (especially when breathing) and sometimes coughing up blood.  

## Symptoms and Signs

Many small clots cause no symptoms at all.  
When symptoms do appear, they are often vague and vary from person to person.  

Common symptoms:  
- Sudden shortness of breath  
- Chest pain that gets worse when you breathe in (pleuritic pain)  

Shortness of breath may be mild at rest but get worse with activity.  

Less common symptoms:  
- Cough (often due to other lung problems or enlarged lung arteries)  
- Coughing up blood (hemoptysis), especially if there is lung tissue damage  
- In older adults, confusion or changes in mental state may be the first sign  

Large clots can cause:  
- Low blood pressure  
- Fast heart rate  
- Feeling dizzy or lightheaded  
- Fainting (syncope)  
- Heart stoppage (cardiac arrest)  

Common signs:  
- Fast heart rate  
- Fast breathing  

Less common signs:  
- Low blood pressure  
- A loud second heart sound (rare in acute PE)  
- Crackles or wheezing (usually due to other lung problems)  
- Swollen neck veins (if the right side of the heart is failing)  
- A third heart sound (S3) or a heart murmur (from valve leak)  

Fever is usually mild unless caused by another illness.  

Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension causes:  
- Shortness of breath with activity  
- Easy tiredness  
- Swelling in the legs (over months to years)  

Some people with PE also have symptoms of deep vein thrombosis:  
- Pain in a leg or arm  
- Swelling in a leg or arm  
- Redness in a leg or arm  

But these leg symptoms are not always present.  

## How PE Is Diagnosed

Diagnosing PE is hard because symptoms are not clear and tests are not perfect.  
Doctors must think about PE when patients have:  
- Shortness of breath  
- Chest pain  
- Coughing up blood  
- Dizziness or fainting  
- Rapid heart rate  

PE should be considered when diagnosing:  
- Heart attack  
- Heart failure  
- COPD flare-up  
- Pneumothorax (collapsed lung)  
- Pneumonia  
- Sepsis  
- Acute chest syndrome (in people with sickle cell disease)  
- Anxiety with fast breathing  

A fast heart rate with no clear cause may be a clue.  
PE should also be considered in older adults with fast breathing and confusion.  

### Initial Tests

- **Pulse oximetry:** Measures oxygen in the blood. Low levels suggest PE.  
- **Chest X-ray:** Usually shows nothing specific. But it can show:

  - It can help rule out pneumonia.

# Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension

This condition causes pressure inside the skull to rise. The exact cause is not known.

## Who Gets This Condition?

- It is rare. Only about 1 in 100,000 people get it.
- It mostly affects women during their childbearing years.
- Overweight young women are 20 times more likely to get it than women at a normal weight.
- As more people become overweight, this condition is becoming more common.

## What Causes the Pressure to Rise?

- Doctors do not know the exact reason.
- Some people have smaller veins in the brain that carry blood out. These veins drain blood more slowly. This can cause blood to back up and raise pressure in the brain and skull.
- Being overweight may play a role. Extra fat around the belly may increase pressure in the chest. This can make it harder for blood to flow from the head to the chest. This may raise pressure inside the skull.
- The high pressure is not caused by a tumor, infection, blood clot, or blockage that stops fluid around the brain from draining.

In most cases, no single event leads to this condition.  
In children, it sometimes starts after stopping steroid medicine or using growth hormone.  
It can also start after taking tetracycline antibiotics or large amounts of vitamin A.

## What Are the Symptoms?

- Most people have daily or almost daily headaches.
- The headaches often affect both sides of the head.
- At first, the pain may be mild. It can get worse over time.
- Headaches may come with nausea, double or blurry vision, or ringing or pulsing noises in the head (called pulsatile tinnitus).
- Some people have no symptoms at all.

High pressure inside the skull can cause swelling of the optic nerve near the eye. This is called papilledema.  
Doctors can see this swelling by looking at the back of the eye with a special tool called an ophthalmoscope.

- The first sign of vision problems is loss of side vision.
- People may not notice this loss at first.
- They may bump into things without knowing why.
- Vision may blur suddenly, especially when changing position.
- The blurring may come and go.
- In later stages, vision stays blurry. Some people lose their sight quickly.
- Up to one-third of people lose some or all of their vision in one or both eyes.
- Once vision is lost, it usually does not come back—even if pressure is lowered.

Because vision loss can happen without warning, doctors must check vision often.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to diagnose this condition.

### Step 1: Doctor’s Evaluation
- The doctor asks about symptoms and does a physical exam.
- They may suspect the condition if they see swelling of the optic nerve during a routine eye exam.

### Step 2: Vision Tests
- The doctor checks the full field of vision, including side vision.
- They use an ophthalmoscope to look at the back of the eye.

### Step 3: Imaging Tests
- A magnetic resonance venography (MRV) checks the large veins in the brain.
  - This test shows if the veins are narrow or blocked.
  - Narrow veins may be the only sign found in some people.
- A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the brain checks for other problems that could raise pressure.

### Step 4: Spinal Tap (Lumbar Puncture)
- A needle is placed in the lower back to measure the pressure of the fluid around the brain.
- The fluid is also tested.
- In this condition, the fluid pressure is high—often very high.
- The fluid itself is usually normal.
- When fluid is removed, pressure in the head drops.
- The veins in the brain may open up more, allowing better blood flow.
- Headaches often improve right away.

These tests help rule out other causes of high pressure, such as a brain tumor.

## How Is It Treated?

The main goals of treatment are:
- To relieve symptoms
- To lower pressure inside the skull
- To protect vision

### Medications
- **Acetazolamide** or **topiramate** are often prescribed.
  - These pills help reduce the amount of fluid made in the brain.
  - They can lower pressure inside the skull.
  - Topiramate may also help with weight loss and reduce headaches.
- **Pain relievers** like aspirin or acetaminophen can help with headaches.
- Medications used to prevent or treat migraines (like topiramate) may also help.

### Stop Triggering Medications
- If you are taking tetracycline antibiotics or high doses of vitamin A, your doctor may tell you to stop them.

### Weight Loss
- If you are overweight, losing weight can help lower pressure in the skull.
- Losing just 10% of your body weight may improve or even cure the condition.
- If diet and exercise are not enough, your doctor may suggest weight loss medicine or bariatric surgery.

### Spinal Taps (Repeated)
- Some people need spinal taps more than once.
- This is done to remove fluid and lower pressure.
- It may be used if vision is at risk while waiting for other treatments.
- Doctors watch closely to see if pressure is going down.

### Surgery
- Surgery may be needed if vision is getting worse.
- It may help save vision.

#### Types of Surgery:
- **Optic nerve sheath fenestration**  
  - Small cuts are made in the covering of the optic nerve behind the eye.  
  - This lets fluid escape into the tissue around the eye.  
  - The fluid is then absorbed by the body.

- **Shunt**  
  - A thin tube is placed under the skin.  
  - It drains extra fluid from the brain or spinal cord.  
  - The tube leads to the abdomen, where the fluid is absorbed.

- **Stenting**  
  - A small wire mesh tube (stent) is placed in a narrowed vein in the brain.  
  - The stent is opened to widen the vein.  
  - This helps blood flow better and lowers pressure.

### Bariatric Surgery
- If you are obese and other weight loss methods fail, bariatric surgery may be an option.
- Examples include gastric bypass.
- If weight loss is maintained, the condition may go away completely.

## Important Notes

- The condition sometimes goes away on its own.
- But it can come back in 10 to 20 out of 100 people.
- Vision loss is the biggest concern.
- Because side vision is lost early, people often do not notice it.
- An eye doctor checks vision regularly, especially side vision.
- If vision gets worse, surgery may be needed to prevent total blindness.

Early treatment is key to protecting your sight.

# HIV and AIDS – Simple Guide

## How HIV Spreads

HIV spreads most often during sex without a condom. This includes vaginal, anal, or oral sex.  
It can also spread if you share needles or other drug injection tools.  

HIV is in certain body fluids. These include blood, semen, vaginal fluids, and anal mucus.  
The virus enters your body through cuts, sores, or mucous membranes.  

You **cannot** get HIV from:  
- Kissing  
- Hugging  
- Shaking hands  
- Sharing toilet seats  
- Sharing food, drinks, or household items like cups and cutlery  

## How to Prevent HIV

Use a condom every time you have sex. This is the best way to protect yourself and your partner.  
If you are at high risk of HIV, you can take daily medicine to prevent infection.  

If you think you were exposed to HIV in the last 72 hours, take emergency medicine right away.  
This is called post-exposure prophylaxis or PEP.  
It can stop you from getting HIV if taken early.  

You can get PEP at a sexual health clinic or from the emergency department at a hospital.  

If you think you were exposed to HIV more than 72 hours ago, see a doctor or go to a sexual health clinic.  
They can test you for HIV and give you advice.  

## Getting Tested for HIV

You can get tested at a clinic using a small sample of blood from your finger or saliva from your mouth.  
You can also order a home test kit.  

Home test kits give results in minutes.  
Make sure the kit you buy:  
- Says it is for self-testing  
- Has a CE mark  
- Shows the manufacturer’s name  
- Is not damaged and the seal is unbroken  

Pregnant women are offered an HIV test as part of routine antenatal screening.  
This test checks for HIV, hepatitis B, and syphilis.  

### What Your Test Result Means

If your result is **negative**, it means no HIV was found.  
But if you had a possible exposure in the last few weeks, you may need to test again later.  

If your result is **positive**, it means you may have HIV.  
You will need a follow-up blood test at a clinic.  
If that test is also positive, you will be referred to an HIV clinic.  
There, you’ll get more tests and talk about treatment.  

## Treating HIV

There is no cure for HIV.  
But you can take daily medicine to control the virus.  

The goal of treatment is to lower the amount of HIV in your blood to a level that cannot be detected.  
This is called an undetectable viral load.  

When your viral load is undetectable, you cannot pass HIV to others.  
This is true even during sex.  

You will be seen at a specialist HIV clinic.  
Healthcare staff will help you choose the right treatment.  

### Anti-HIV Medicines

You will take antiretrovirals. These are daily tablets.  
It usually takes about 6 months of daily treatment to reach an undetectable viral load.  

## Support and Help

If you are diagnosed with HIV, you will get support from healthcare professionals.  
They will help you through treatment and care.  

There are national charities that offer information and support.  
You may find it helpful to talk with others who have HIV.  
You can join online or local support groups.  

If you need to stop working or work part-time because of HIV, you can find out about social care and support options.

### Do

- Take PEP medicine within 72 hours if you think you were exposed to HIV  
- Use condoms every time you have sex – they protect against HIV and other STIs  
- Use water-based lubricants like K-Y jelly with condoms  
- Avoid oil-based lubes like Vaseline, massage oil, or baby oil – they can damage condoms  

### Don’t

- Never share needles, syringes, spoons, swabs, or drug liquids  
- Talk to a GP or drug counsellor about needle exchange programmes if you use drugs  

## Key Facts

- If you are on effective HIV treatment and have an undetectable viral load, you cannot pass HIV to others.  
- Early testing and treatment help you stay healthy and protect others.  
- You can live a full, healthy life with HIV if you get treatment and follow your doctor’s advice.

# Irregular Heart Rhythms from the Upper Heart Chambers

Some heart rhythms start in the upper chambers of the heart. These are called ectopic supraventricular rhythms. They often come from the atria.

Your doctor can find these rhythms using an electrocardiogram. This test records the electrical activity of your heart.

Many of these rhythms do not cause symptoms. You may not feel anything at all. If you have no symptoms, you may not need treatment.

## Types of Ectopic Supraventricular Rhythms

- **Atrial premature beats**: Extra heartbeats that start in the upper chambers. They happen early and can feel like a skipped beat.
- **Atrial tachycardia**: The upper chambers beat too fast. This can make your heart race.
- **Multifocal atrial tachycardia**: The upper chambers beat too fast and start from more than one spot. This can cause an irregular and fast heartbeat.
- **Nonparoxysmal junctional tachycardia**: A fast heartbeat that starts near the center of the heart. It does not come on suddenly and may last longer.
- **Wandering atrial pacemaker**: The heart’s natural pace-maker moves between different spots in the upper chambers. This causes a slightly irregular rhythm.

# Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (Long-Term Ear Infection)

This is a long-term ear infection that causes a hole in the eardrum. The hole lets fluid drain from the ear. The fluid is often pus.

## What Causes This Condition?

- A past ear infection (acute otitis media) can lead to this.
- A blocked tube that connects the middle ear to the back of the nose can cause it.
- Injury to the ear, chemical burns, or loud explosions can also cause it.

Flare-ups can happen after:
- A cold
- A throat or nose infection
- Water getting into the ear through the hole in the eardrum

## What Are the Symptoms?

- Hearing loss is common.
- The ear drains fluid all the time.
- The fluid may smell bad.
- The ear may not hurt, even when it is infected.
- Some people get polyps. These are small, soft growths that grow from the middle ear into the ear canal.
- The infection can damage the small bones in the middle ear. These bones help carry sound from the eardrum to the inner ear. When they are damaged, sound cannot reach the inner ear well. This causes conductive hearing loss.

## What Is a Cholesteatoma?

Some people with this condition develop a cholesteatoma. This is a noncancerous growth made of skin-like material. It can grow in the middle ear.

Symptoms of a cholesteatoma include:
- Fever
- Dizziness
- Ear pain

A cholesteatoma can destroy bone. It can lead to serious problems, such as:
- Infection in the inner ear
- Weakness or paralysis of the face
- A brain abscess

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor will look inside the ear. They will check for:
- Pus or skin-like material in a hole or pocket in the eardrum
- Fluid draining from the ear

To find the cause of the infection, the doctor may take a sample of the fluid from the ear.

If the doctor thinks there is a cholesteatoma, they may order:
- A CT scan
- An MRI scan

If there is new tissue growing on the eardrum that keeps coming back, the doctor may take a small sample (biopsy) to check for cancer.

## How Is It Treated?

### For Mild Flare-Ups
- Doctors prescribe antibiotic ear drops.
- People may also take antibiotics by mouth if the infection is severe.

### Keeping the Ear Dry
- Do not let water get into the ear when there is a hole in the eardrum.
- When bathing or showering, put a cotton ball with petroleum jelly in the ear.
- Do not swim.

### Surgery
- A hole in the eardrum can be repaired with a surgery called tympanoplasty.
- If the small bones in the middle ear are damaged, they can be fixed during the same surgery.

### If a Cholesteatoma Is Present
- It must be removed with surgery.
- The middle ear structures may need to be rebuilt.
- Because cholesteatomas can come back, a second surgery is often needed to check for return before rebuilding the ear.

## Important Notes

- This condition can cause serious problems if not treated.
- Early treatment helps prevent hearing loss and other complications.
- Always follow your doctor’s instructions.

# Impetigo

Impetigo causes sores or blisters on the skin.  
These sores burst open and leave crusty, golden-brown patches.  
The patches can look like cornflakes stuck to the skin.

You may need antiseptic cream or antibiotics to treat impetigo.  
If it keeps coming back, you might need an antiseptic body wash or a nasal ointment.  
Sometimes you need both.

You are more likely to get impetigo if your skin is already damaged.  
Keep cuts, scratches, and insect bites clean.  
Get treatment for skin problems like eczema or scabies.

---

## When to see a pharmacist

See a pharmacist if:
- You have symptoms of impetigo.
- Your child is 12 months old or older and has symptoms.

A pharmacist can give you the same medicines a doctor would.  
They can also give advice or send you to another doctor if needed.

## When to see a doctor

See a doctor if you or your child have impetigo and:
- Your child is 11 months old or younger.
- You are breastfeeding and the sores are on your breasts.
- You have a weak immune system, such as from chemotherapy.
- The symptoms have changed or gotten worse after treatment.
- You had impetigo in the past year and it has come back.

Impetigo is very contagious.  
Call the doctor’s office before going in.  
They may suggest a phone call instead.

---

## Symptoms of impetigo

Impetigo starts with red sores or blisters.  
On brown or black skin, the redness may be hard to see.

The sores burst quickly.  
They leave crusty, golden-brown patches.

These patches can:
- Look like cornflakes stuck to the skin.
- Get bigger and spread to other areas.
- Itch or hurt sometimes.

The sores often appear on the face, especially around the nose and mouth.  
They also often appear on the hands.

After the blisters burst, you are left with golden-brown crusts.

In some cases, a yellow liquid comes out of the blisters.  
This liquid dries and forms a scaly edge around a scab.  
This is called bullous impetigo.

---

## Treatment for impetigo

A pharmacist or doctor will check if your symptoms are caused by a more serious skin infection, such as cellulitis.

If it is impetigo, they may give you:
- Hydrogen peroxide cream.
- Antibiotic cream or tablets.

Babies and people with a weak immune system may need antibiotic tablets.  
This helps stop the infection from getting worse.

---

### If impetigo keeps coming back

Your doctor may take a swab from your skin.  
They may also take a swab from inside your nose.

They might prescribe:
- An antiseptic body wash.
- A nasal ointment.
- Or both.

This helps remove the bacteria that cause impetigo.  
It can stop the infection from returning.

---

### Finish your treatment

Do not stop using the cream or taking the tablets early.  
Even if the sores start to look better, keep using the medicine as directed.

---

## How to prevent impetigo

Impetigo usually starts in skin that is already damaged.

You can get it from:
- A small cut.
- A scratch.
- An insect bite.
- A skin condition.

To help prevent impetigo:
- Wash cuts, scratches, and insect bites with warm water and soap.
- Treat skin conditions like eczema or scabies.

# Gonorrhea – Simple Explanation

Gonorrhea is a sexually transmitted infection caused by a type of bacteria called *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*.  
This bacteria can live in the urethra, cervix, rectum, throat, or eyes.  
It often causes irritation, pain, or a thick, pus-like discharge.

In rare cases, the infection spreads through the blood.  
This can cause skin sores, fever, and joint pain.  
The joint pain may move from one joint to another, or affect just one or a few joints.

Doctors diagnose gonorrhea using tests on samples from the urethra, cervix, rectum, throat, or joints.  
Tests include a special lab test called a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT), a Gram stain, or a culture.  
Many people with gonorrhea also have another infection called chlamydia.  
This happens in about 10% to 40% of cases, depending on the group.

Antibiotics are used to treat gonorrhea.  
But some bacteria are becoming resistant to common antibiotics.  
This makes treatment harder.

---

## How Gonorrhea Spreads

The bacteria only live in humans.  
It is almost always passed through sexual contact.  
This includes vaginal, anal, or oral sex.

- A woman can pass the infection to a man during vaginal sex.  
  The chance is about 22%.
- A man can pass it to a woman.  
  The chance is higher than 22%.
- For men who have sex with men, the risk is up to 42% during anal sex if condoms are not used.
- In the United States, over 1.5 million new cases happen each year.

Babies can get infected in the eyes during childbirth.  
Children can also get gonorrhea if they have been sexually abused.

---

## Symptoms and Signs

Most women with gonorrhea do not have symptoms.  
About 90% have no signs of infection.  
Men may also have no symptoms, but this varies.  
About 56% to 87% of men do not notice anything.

### In Men

- Symptoms usually start 2 to 14 days after exposure.
- You may feel mild pain in the urethra (the tube that carries urine out).
- This can get worse, with pain in the penis, pain when peeing, and a thick, yellow-green discharge.
- You may feel the need to pee often or urgently.
- A doctor may see a pus-like discharge from the urethra and redness at the opening.

**Epididymitis** (infection of the tube behind the testicle) can happen.  
It causes one side of the scrotum to become painful, swollen, and tender.

Rarely, men can get abscesses in glands near the urethra or in the prostate or seminal vesicles.

### In Women

- Symptoms usually start more than 10 days after exposure.
- You may have pain when peeing or a vaginal discharge.
- A doctor may see a thick, pus-like discharge from the cervix.
- The cervix may look red and bleed easily when touched.

You may also have urethritis (infection of the urethra).  
Pus may come out when pressure is applied to the lower front of the pelvis.

In rare cases, young girls who have been abused may have symptoms like pain when peeing, a pus-like vaginal discharge, and redness or swelling of the outer genitals.

### Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)

- This happens in 10% to 20% of women with untreated gonorrhea.
- It affects the uterus, fallopian tubes, and surrounding tissues.
- Symptoms include lower belly pain (often on both sides), pain during sex, and tenderness when the doctor touches the belly, ovaries, or cervix.

### Fitz-Hugh-Curtis Syndrome

- This is a rare condition where the infection spreads to the liver area.
- It causes pain in the upper right side of the belly, fever, nausea, and vomiting.
- It can feel like a liver or gallbladder problem.

### Rectal Gonorrhea

- Most people have no symptoms.
- It is more common in men who have receptive anal sex and in women who have anal sex.
- If symptoms occur, they may include:
  - Itching in the rectum
  - A cloudy or pus-like discharge from the rectum
  - Bleeding
  - Pain or discomfort when passing stool
  - Constipation

A doctor may see redness or pus on the inside of the rectum during a check-up.

### Throat Infection (Pharyngitis)

- Most people have no symptoms.
- Some may have a sore throat.
- The bacteria in the throat can look like other harmless bacteria.  
  So, testing is needed to tell the difference.

### Eye Infection (Conjunctivitis)

- The eye becomes red, swollen, and produces pus.
- This can happen if infected fluid touches the eye.

### Disseminated Gonococcal Infection (DGI)

- This is rare. It happens in less than 1% of people.
- It mostly affects women.
- The bacteria spread through the blood.
- Symptoms include:
  - Fever
  - Joint pain or swelling that moves from one joint to another
  - Pus-filled skin sores, usually on the arms or legs
  - Swelling or redness in tendons (like at the wrist or ankle)

In rare cases, DGI can cause serious problems like heart infection, brain infection, or liver infection.

The genital infection that started the DGI may have had no symptoms.

DGI can look like other serious illnesses, such as early hepatitis B or meningococcal infection.  
Some of these other conditions also cause genital symptoms.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Gonorrhea

Doctors use several tests:

### Nucleic Acid Amplification Tests (NAATs)

- These tests can detect gonorrhea and chlamydia.
- They can be done on a urine sample or a swab from the urethra, cervix, rectum, or throat.
- They are very accurate and are the most common test used.

### Gram Stain

- This test works well for men with a discharge from the urethra.
- It can show the bacteria under a microscope.
- It is not reliable for women, people with throat or rectal infections.

### Culture

- This test grows the bacteria in a lab.
- It is very accurate but hard to do because the bacteria are fragile.
- The sample must be sent to the lab quickly and kept in a special environment.
- Because NAATs are now used more often, not all labs can do cultures.
- If you need a culture, your doctor may need to contact a specialist.

Sometimes, another bacteria called *Neisseria meningitidis* can cause similar symptoms.  
It looks like gonorrhea under the microscope.  
If a Gram stain shows bacteria but the NAAT test is negative, a culture is needed to confirm the type.

In the United States, doctors must report confirmed cases of gonorrhea, chlamydia, and syphilis to public health officials.  
People should also be tested for syphilis and HIV.  
A test for chlamydia should be done at the same time.

---

## Who Should Be Screened?

Screening means testing people who do not have symptoms.  
It helps find infections early.

### Women

- All women under 25 who are sexually active should be tested every year.
- Women 25 or older should be tested every year if they:
  - Have had a past sexually transmitted infection
  - Have a new sex partner or more than one partner
  - Have sex with someone who has an STI
  - Use condoms inconsistently
  - Are in a relationship where their partner has other partners

Pregnant women under 25 should be tested at the first prenatal visit.  
Women 25 or older with risk factors should be tested again in the third trimester.  
If a pregnant woman has had gonorrhea, she should be retested 3 months after treatment.

### Men Who Have Sex With Men

- Test at least once a year if you have been sexually active in the past year.
- For insertive sex: use a urine test.
- For receptive anal sex: use a rectal swab.
- For oral sex: use a throat swab.
- Even if you use condoms, you should still be tested.

If you are at higher risk, such as:
- Having HIV
- Taking HIV prevention medicine
- Having many sex partners
- Having a partner with many partners

You should be tested every 3 to 6 months.

### Transgender and Gender Diverse People

- Test if you are sexually active.
- Testing depends on your body and your sexual activities.
- People with a cervix under 25 should be tested yearly.
- People with a cervix 25 or older should be tested yearly if at higher risk.
- Rectal swabs should be done based on your sexual history.

### Men Not in the Above Groups

- There is not enough evidence to say all men should be tested.
- But testing may be offered if you ask or if you are in a place with high rates of STIs, like a teen clinic or STI clinic.

# Gastritis

Gastritis means the lining of the stomach is inflamed.

## What Is Gastritis?

- The stomach lining is usually strong and can handle strong acid.
- In gastritis, the lining becomes irritated and swollen.
- This can happen for many reasons, including infections, serious illness, injury, certain medicines, alcohol, or problems with the body’s defense system.

## Types of Gastritis

Gastritis is split into two main types:

### Erosive Gastritis
- This type causes both inflammation and damage to the stomach lining.
- It can start suddenly (acute) or slowly (chronic).
- It often affects people who are otherwise healthy.

### Nonerosive Gastritis
- This type causes changes in the stomach lining.
- The lining may thin out or change into a different kind of tissue.
- White blood cells build up in the stomach and cause swelling.
- The swelling can affect the whole stomach or just parts of it.

---

## Causes of Gastritis

### Erosive Gastritis
- Common causes:
  - Drinking too much alcohol.
  - Stress from serious illness or injury.
  - Medicines like aspirin or other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
- Less common causes:
  - Crohn disease.
  - Radiation therapy.
  - Infections from bacteria or viruses (like cytomegalovirus).
  - Swallowing harmful chemicals.
  - Injury from a tube put through the nose into the stomach.
- Even one baby aspirin a day can harm the stomach lining in some people.

### Nonerosive Gastritis
- Most often caused by an infection with *Helicobacter pylori* bacteria.

### Other Types of Gastritis
- **Infectious gastritis** (not from *H. pylori*) is rare.
- **Viral or fungal gastritis** can happen in people who are very ill or have weak immune systems. This includes people with advanced HIV, cancer, or those on immune-suppressing medicines.
- **Acute stress gastritis** happens after a sudden serious illness or injury. It can be caused by burns, head injuries, or major bleeding—even if the injury is not in the stomach.
  - The exact reason is not clear, but it may be due to less blood flow to the stomach, more acid, or the stomach’s ability to protect itself being weakened.
- **Radiation gastritis** can happen if radiation therapy is given to the lower left chest or upper belly.
- **Postgastrectomy gastritis** happens after part of the stomach is removed.
  - Inflammation often happens where the stomach was sewn back together.
  - It may be caused by poor blood flow or too much bile (a greenish-yellow fluid made by the liver) reaching the stomach.
- **Atrophic gastritis** means the stomach lining becomes very thin and loses cells that make acid and digestive enzymes.
  - It can happen when the body’s immune system attacks the stomach lining.
  - It can also happen in people with long-term *H. pylori* infection.
  - It is also common after stomach surgery.
- **Eosinophilic gastritis** is when a type of white blood cell called eosinophils builds up in the stomach wall.
  - The cause is usually unknown.
- **Ménétrier disease** is a rare condition.
  - The stomach wall grows thick and forms large folds and fluid-filled sacs.
  - The cause is not known, but it may be linked to an immune problem.
  - It has also been linked to *H. pylori* infection.

---

## Symptoms of Gastritis

- Most people with gastritis have no symptoms.
- When symptoms do appear, they can include:
  - Pain or discomfort in the upper belly.
  - Nausea.
  - Vomiting.
- These problems are often called indigestion.

### More Severe Forms
- Nausea and vomiting can happen with:
  - Erosive gastritis.
  - Radiation gastritis.
- Indigestion is common with:
  - Erosive gastritis.
  - Radiation gastritis.
  - Postgastrectomy gastritis.
  - Atrophic gastritis.
- Mild indigestion can also happen with acute stress gastritis.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Gastritis

- Doctors often guess the diagnosis based on symptoms.
- If the diagnosis is unclear or symptoms do not improve, the doctor may do an upper endoscopy.
- During an upper endoscopy:
  - A thin, flexible tube with a camera is passed through the mouth into the stomach.
  - The doctor can see the inside of the stomach.
  - If needed, a small tissue sample (biopsy) is taken for testing.

---

## Treatment of Gastritis

### General Treatments
- Medicines that reduce or neutralize stomach acid help relieve symptoms.
- Stop taking medicines that irritate the stomach, like aspirin or NSAIDs.

### Antacids
- These neutralize acid already in the stomach.
- They are available over the counter as tablets, chewable gels, or liquids.
- Common types:
  - Aluminum hydroxide (can cause constipation).
  - Magnesium hydroxide (can cause diarrhea).
  - Calcium carbonate.
- Antacids can interfere with other medicines.
- If you take other medicines, talk to your pharmacist or doctor before using antacids.

### Acid-Reducing Medicines
- **H2 blockers** – reduce acid production.
- **Proton pump inhibitors** – reduce acid more strongly than H2 blockers.
- These medicines are often more effective than antacids.
- They are usually taken for 8 to 12 weeks.

### Other Medicines
- **Sucralfate** – coats the stomach lining and helps it heal.
- It also protects the stomach from irritation.

### Antibiotics
- If gastritis is caused by *H. pylori* infection, antibiotics are needed.
- These are taken with acid-reducing medicines.

### Special Cases

#### Erosive Gastritis
- Avoid medicines that harm the stomach lining (like NSAIDs).
- Use proton pump inhibitors or H2 blockers to protect the stomach.

#### Acute Stress Gastritis
- Most people get better when the serious illness, injury, or bleeding is treated.
- Some people in intensive care units may bleed heavily.
  - This can be life-threatening.
- Doctors often give acid-reducing medicines after surgery or to people in intensive care to prevent this.
- If bleeding happens:
  - Doctors may use heat to seal the bleeding spot during endoscopy.
  - If bleeding continues, surgery to remove part of the stomach may be needed.
  - This is rare.

#### Postgastrectomy Gastritis
- There is no cure.
- Treatment focuses on managing symptoms.

#### Atrophic Gastritis
- There is no cure.
- It can lead to low levels of vitamin B12.
- People with this problem need lifelong vitamin B12 shots.

#### Eosinophilic Gastritis
- May need corticosteroid medicines or surgery.
- This helps if the stomach outlet becomes blocked.

#### Ménétrier Disease
- Removing part or all of the stomach may cure it.
- There are no good medicines to treat this condition.

--- 

**Note:** Always talk to your doctor before starting or stopping any medicine.

# Genital Herpes

## What Is Genital Herpes?

Genital herpes is a common infection caused by a virus. It can cause blisters and sores in the genital area. You can pass it on even when you do not have visible sores.

## Symptoms of Genital Herpes

You may notice:

- Small blisters around your genitals, anus, thighs, or buttocks.
- The blisters break open and leave red, open sores.
- The sores may look less red on brown or black skin.
- Tingling, burning, or itching in the genital area.
- Pain when you pee.
- Unusual discharge from the vagina or penis.

### Where the Symptoms Appear

- Blisters can appear on the vagina.
- Blisters can appear on the penis in a group.
- Blisters and sores can also appear on the buttocks.

## When to See a Doctor

Go to a sexual health clinic as soon as you notice any symptoms.

Even if you have not had sex in a long time, you should still go. Blisters can take months or years to show up after infection.

## Treatment for Genital Herpes

There is no cure for genital herpes. But symptoms usually go away on their own. The blisters can come back later.

### First Time You Have Symptoms

If you go to a sexual health clinic within 5 days of symptoms starting, you may be given:

- Antiviral medicine to help stop the symptoms from getting worse.
- A cream to ease pain.

If you go after 5 days, you can still get tested to find out what is causing your symptoms.

### If Symptoms Come Back

If you have had genital herpes before and now have another outbreak:

- See your GP or a sexual health clinic.
- Antiviral medicine can help shorten the outbreak by 1 or 2 days if you start it right away.
- Most outbreaks go away on their own, so treatment is not always needed.
- Recurrent outbreaks are usually milder than the first one.
- Over time, outbreaks happen less often and are less severe.
- Some people never have another outbreak.

If you have more than 6 outbreaks in a year, your doctor may suggest taking antiviral medicine for 6 to 12 months.

If you still have outbreaks during this time, you may be referred to a specialist.

## How Genital Herpes Spreads

Genital herpes spreads very easily. You can pass it on:

- From the first sign of tingling or itching (before blisters appear).
- Until the sores are fully healed.
- Even if you have no symptoms at all.

You can get genital herpes through:

- Skin-to-skin contact with the infected area.
- Vaginal, anal, or oral sex.
- Touching a cold sore on someone else and then touching your genitals.
- Using fingers to move the virus from one person to your genitals.
- Sharing sex toys with someone who has herpes.

You **cannot** get genital herpes from:

- Towels
- Swimming pools
- Saunas
- Toilet seats

This is because these things do not involve direct skin-to-skin contact.

# Rabies

Rabies is a serious brain infection caused by a virus.  
The virus spreads through the saliva of infected animals.  
Bats are the most common source of rabies in the United States.  
Other animals that can carry the virus include raccoons, skunks, and foxes.  
Small rodents like squirrels, rats, mice, hamsters, and guinea pigs do not spread rabies.  
Rabbits and hares also do not spread the virus.

The virus enters the body through a bite.  
It can also enter through a scratch or open skin, or through the eyes, nose, or mouth.  
The virus travels along nerves to the brain.  
Once in the brain, it spreads to other parts of the body.  
The virus reaches the salivary glands, which is how it can spread to others.

---

## Symptoms of Rabies

You may feel pain or tingling at the site of the bite.  
The time it takes for symptoms to appear can vary.  
It usually takes 1 to 2 months, but it can take longer than a year.  
The speed of symptoms depends on how much virus entered and how close the bite was to the brain.

Early symptoms are not specific.  
They include fever, headache, and feeling unwell.  
Within days, two main types of symptoms appear.

**Furious rabies (about 80% of cases):**  
You may feel restless, confused, or very agitated.  
You may act strangely or have hallucinations.  
You may not be able to sleep.  
You may drool a lot.  
When you try to drink water, your throat muscles spasm and it hurts.  
This is called hydrophobia.

**Paralytic rabies (about 20% of cases):**  
You may feel weakness that spreads up your body.  
You may lose the ability to move your arms and legs.  
You do not have confusion or fear of water.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Rabies

Doctors suspect rabies if you have brain symptoms and a history of a bite or contact with a bat.  
Bat bites can be very small and easy to miss.

The best test is a skin sample from the back of the neck.  
A special test checks for the virus in the sample.  
Doctors may also test fluid from the spinal cord, saliva, or tissue.  
They can use a test called PCR to find the virus.  
Blood and spinal fluid may also be tested for signs of the virus.

Brain scans (CT or MRI) and brain wave tests (EEG) usually look normal or show only minor changes.

---

## Treatment of Rabies

There is no cure for rabies once symptoms start.  
Treatment focuses on keeping you comfortable and safe.  
You may need strong sedation to calm you down.  
Medicines like ketamine and midazolam are used.  
You will get care to manage pain and keep you breathing.

Most people die within 3 to 10 days after symptoms begin.  
Very few people survive.  
Most survivors had treatment *before* symptoms started.

Giving the rabies vaccine and immune globulin *after* symptoms start may make things worse.

---

## How to Prevent Rabies

Rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms begin.  
But it can be prevented with early action.

**If you are at risk of exposure, get the rabies vaccine before you are exposed.**  
This is recommended for:  
- Veterinarians  
- Animal handlers  
- People who explore caves (spelunkers)  
- Workers who handle the virus  
- Travelers to areas where rabies is common

**If you are bitten or scratched by an animal, or have contact with a bat, act fast.**  
Clean the wound well with soap and water.  
Get medical help right away.  
You will need two things:  
- The rabies vaccine  
- Rabies immune globulin (a medicine that gives you immediate protection)

**Do not touch or handle wild animals.**  
If an animal acts strangely, stay away.  
Look for signs of rabies:  
- Aggressive or wild behavior  
- Weakness or paralysis  
- No fear of people  
- Nocturnal animals seen during the day  
- Bats that make odd sounds or cannot fly well

If you see a suspicious animal, call local health authorities.  
They will remove the animal safely.

**Contact with a bat is always a reason to get treatment.**  
Bat bites can be tiny and hard to see.  
Even if you are not sure a bat bit you, get the vaccine and immune globulin.

---

## Key Facts

- Rabies kills tens of thousands of people each year worldwide.  
  Most cases happen in Africa and Asia.  
  Dog bites are the main cause there.

- In the United States, fewer than 3 human cases happen each year.  
  Most are from bats.  
  Raccoons, skunks, and foxes can also spread it.

- A bite site may hurt or tingle.  
  Then, either brain symptoms (restlessness, confusion) or paralysis can develop.

- If you have unexplained brain symptoms or weakness spreading up your body, doctors may test your skin, spinal fluid, or saliva.

- Once symptoms start, treatment only helps with comfort.  
  It does not cure the disease.

- Get the rabies vaccine before exposure if you are at risk.

- After a bite or contact with a bat, clean the wound and get the vaccine and immune globulin right away.

- If a raccoon, skunk, or fox bites you, treat it as rabies.  
- If you have any contact with a bat, get treatment even if you are not sure you were bitten.

# Dementia with Lewy Bodies and Parkinson Disease Dementia

This guide explains two types of dementia: dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson disease dementia. Both affect how the brain works and cause a slow decline in thinking, memory, and behavior.

---

## What Are These Dementias?

**Dementia with Lewy bodies** is a condition where brain cells slowly stop working. This happens because of small clumps of a protein called Lewy bodies that build up inside brain cells.

**Parkinson disease dementia** is a type of dementia that happens in people who already have Parkinson disease. It also involves Lewy bodies in the brain.

- Dementia with Lewy bodies is the third most common type of dementia.
- It usually starts in people over age 60.
- About 40 out of 100 people with Parkinson disease will develop Parkinson disease dementia.
- This usually happens after age 70, about 10 to 15 years after Parkinson disease is first diagnosed.

---

## How Dementia Is Different from Delirium

| Feature | Dementia | Delirium |
|--------|----------|----------|
| Onset | Slow and gradual | Sudden |
| Main problem | Memory and thinking | Attention and awareness |
| Can be reversed? | No | Yes, if treated quickly |

- Dementia slowly gets worse over time.
- Delirium comes on fast and often has a clear cause, like an infection or medicine.

---

## What Happens in the Brain?

In both dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson disease dementia, a protein called synuclein changes shape and builds up in brain cells.

- These clumps are called **Lewy bodies**.
- They damage brain cells and cause brain function to decline.
- The damaged protein can spread from one cell to another, like a chain reaction.
- This kind of protein is called a **prion**. Prions cause brain diseases like Creutzfeld-Jacob disease.

### Where the Lewy Bodies Form

- In **dementia with Lewy bodies**, Lewy bodies form in the outer layer of the brain (the cerebral cortex). This part controls thinking, memory, and language.
- In **Parkinson disease dementia**, Lewy bodies form in a deeper part of the brain called the **substantia nigra**. This area helps control smooth movement.

These two dementias may be different forms of the same disease. They share many features with Alzheimer disease, but the main damage comes from Lewy bodies, not the tangles and plaques seen in Alzheimer disease.

---

## Symptoms

### Dementia with Lewy Bodies

- Mental function can change quickly. One day a person may be alert and talk well. The next day, they may be sleepy, confused, or barely speak.
- Attention and alertness are often worse than memory at first.
- People have trouble planning, solving problems, or handling money.
- Drawing or copying shapes is harder than other tasks.
- Hallucinations are common. These are usually visual and detailed. They may include people or animals. The images can be scary.
- Delusions (false beliefs) are also common. These can be strange or bizarre.
- **Antipsychotic medicines** can make hallucinations and confusion worse. Some can cause serious side effects, like a life-threatening condition called neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
- Movement problems are similar to Parkinson disease: stiff muscles, slow movement, shuffling walk, stooping, and balance issues.
- Tremors may appear, but they are usually less severe than in Parkinson disease.
- Movement and thinking problems usually start within a year of each other.
- Sleep problems are common. Many people act out their dreams during sleep. This can hurt their partner.
- The autonomic nervous system may not work right. This can cause:
  - Fainting
  - Sweating too much or too little
  - Dry mouth
  - Constipation
  - Urinary problems

Most people live 6 to 12 years after symptoms start.

---

### Parkinson Disease Dementia

- Mental decline usually starts 10 to 15 years after movement problems begin.
- Memory and attention are affected.
- Thinking slows down.
- Problems with planning and complex tasks appear early and are common.
- Hallucinations and delusions are less common and less severe than in dementia with Lewy bodies.
- Movement problems like stiffness, slow motion, and balance issues are worse than in Parkinson disease without dementia.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tools to diagnose these dementias.

### Step 1: Check for Dementia

- Ask the person and their family about symptoms.
- Do a physical exam.
- Give a mental status test (simple questions and tasks).
- Use brain scans like CT or MRI to rule out other causes.

### Step 2: More Detailed Testing

- **Neuropsychologic testing** may be done. This takes 1 to 3 hours and checks memory, mood, attention, and thinking.
- This helps tell dementia apart from mild memory changes, depression, or early cognitive decline.

### Step 3: Rule Out Delirium

- Delirium can look like dementia, but it comes on fast and can be treated.
- It’s important to rule out delirium because treatment is different.

### Step 4: Identify the Type of Dementia

Doctors look for key signs:

- **Dementia with Lewy bodies** is more likely if:
  - Thinking problems and movement issues start at the same time or close together.
  - The person has visual hallucinations and fluctuating alertness.

- **Parkinson disease dementia** is more likely if:
  - Movement problems came first, and mental decline came years later.
  - Movement problems are worse than thinking problems.

### Final Diagnosis

- The only way to be sure is to examine brain tissue after death during an autopsy.
- This is not done while the person is alive.

---

## Treatment

There is no cure, but treatment can help manage symptoms and improve quality of life.

### General Support and Safety

- Keep the home bright, calm, and safe.
- Avoid loud noise or too many distractions.
- Use a daily routine for meals, bathing, and sleep.
- Explain any changes in routine or caregivers clearly.
- Encourage regular physical and mental activities.
- Break tasks into small steps as the disease progresses.

### Medications

- **Medications used for Alzheimer disease**, like **rivastigmine**, may help improve thinking and memory in both dementias.
- **Medications for Parkinson disease** can help with stiffness and tremors. But in dementia with Lewy bodies, they may make confusion and hallucinations worse.
- **Pimavanserin** is an antipsychotic medicine that can treat hallucinations and delusions in Parkinson disease. It is safer than older antipsychotics.
- **Older antipsychotic medicines** (first-generation) should be avoided. They can make movement problems worse.
- **Newer antipsychotics** (second-generation) may be used in low doses. But long-term use can cause:
  - Weight gain
  - High cholesterol
  - Increased risk of type 2 diabetes

### Caregiver Support

Caring for someone with dementia is hard. Caregivers can become tired or depressed.

To help caregivers:

- Learn about dementia and what to expect.
- Ask for help when needed. Options include:
  - Day care programs
  - Home visits by nurses
  - Housekeeping help
  - Live-in care
  - Counseling or support groups
- Take care of yourself. Keep your friends, hobbies, and personal time.

### Advance Planning

Before the person becomes too weak to make decisions:

- Talk with your doctor and loved ones about your wishes.
- Choose a health care proxy — someone legally allowed to make medical decisions for you.
- Write down your health care wishes.
- Make legal and financial plans (called advance directives).
- Discuss these plans early, not when a crisis happens.

As the disease gets worse, care focuses on comfort, not on trying to extend life.

---

For more details, visit:

**National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke's Dementia Information Page**  
- Information on treatments and outlook  
- Links to clinical trials  
- Available in English
