# Scarlet Fever

Scarlet fever is a bacterial infection. It causes a rash and other symptoms.

## What to Look For

The main sign is a rash. It feels rough, like sandpaper. The rash starts as small, raised spots.

You may feel sick first. This can include a high fever, a sore throat, and swollen glands in your neck.

The rash usually appears 12 to 48 hours after the first symptoms. It begins on the chest and tummy. Then it spreads to the rest of the body.

On light skin, the rash looks pink or red. On darker skin, the color change may be hard to see. But you can still feel the bumps.

Your tongue may start with a white coating. Later, the coating peels off. The tongue then turns red and swollen. It looks like a strawberry.

The rash does not cover the face. But your cheeks may look red. This redness can be harder to see on brown or black skin.

As the rash fades, the skin may peel. It can peel like sunburn.

These symptoms are the same in children and adults. But scarlet fever is more common in children.

## When to See a Doctor

See a doctor if you or your child has any of these:

- Symptoms of scarlet fever
- No improvement after a week of treatment
- Both scarlet fever and chickenpox at the same time
- Feeling unwell again weeks after the fever went away. This could mean a complication, like rheumatic fever
- Feeling unwell and you have been near someone with scarlet fever

Scarlet fever spreads easily. Call your doctor before going in. They may suggest a phone call instead.

## What Happens at the Doctor’s

The doctor can often tell if you have scarlet fever by looking at your tongue and rash.

Sometimes the doctor may:

- Swab the back of your throat with a cotton bud to test for bacteria
- Order a blood test

## Treating Scarlet Fever

If you have scarlet fever, your doctor will give you antibiotics.

Antibiotics help in three ways:

- You will feel better faster
- They lower the risk of serious problems, like pneumonia
- They make it less likely you will pass the infection to others

### Taking the Medicine

Take all the antibiotics as prescribed. Even if you feel better, finish the full course.

## How to Feel Better at Home

While taking antibiotics, you can do these things to feel more comfortable:

- Drink cool fluids, like water or juice
- Eat soft foods if your throat hurts
- Take painkillers like paracetamol to lower a high fever
  - Do not give aspirin to children under 16
- Use calamine lotion or antihistamine tablets to reduce itching

## How to Stop the Infection from Spreading

Scarlet fever spreads very easily. Do these things to protect others:

### Do

- Stay home from nursery, school, or work for at least 24 hours after starting antibiotics
- Wash your hands often with soap and water
- Use tissues when you cough or sneeze
- Throw used tissues in the bin right away

### Don’t

- Do not share cutlery, cups, towels, clothes, bedding, or baths with anyone else

# What Is Decreased Red Blood Cell Production?

Anemia means you have too few red blood cells. Red blood cells carry oxygen in your body. Anemia can happen if your body makes too few red blood cells, if they break down too fast, or if you lose blood.

When anemia is caused by low red blood cell production, it is called a hypoproliferative anemia. A test called a reticulocyte count can help find this type. If the count is too low for how severe the anemia is, it means your body is not making enough new red blood cells.

Your doctor will look at your red blood cell size to help figure out the cause. This is called the mean corpuscular volume, or MCV.

---

## Types of Anemia Based on Red Blood Cell Size

### Microcytic Anemia (Small Red Blood Cells)

This type happens when your body does not make enough healthy hemoglobin or when the hemoglobin is not made right. Causes include:

- Not having enough iron in your body (iron deficiency anemia)
- Problems moving iron in your body (iron-transport deficiency anemias)
- Issues using iron properly (some types of sideroblastic anemia and lead poisoning)

If you have microcytic anemia, your doctor will check your iron levels.

---

### Normocytic Anemia (Normal-Size Red Blood Cells)

This type means your red blood cells are the normal size. Common causes are:

- Low levels of a hormone called erythropoietin (EPO), which tells your body to make red blood cells
- Problems with EPO due to long-term inflammation or kidney disease
- Anemia caused by long-term illness (also called anemia of chronic disease)

Some serious bone marrow problems can also cause normocytic anemia. These include:

- Aplastic anemia (bone marrow stops working)
- Pure red cell aplasia (only red blood cells are affected)
- Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) – a group of disorders where bone marrow makes abnormal blood cells

---

### Macrocytic Anemia (Large Red Blood Cells)

This type happens when red blood cells are too big. It often comes from problems with DNA in the cells. Causes include:

- Not enough vitamin B12 or folate in your body
- Long-term alcohol use
- Certain medicines (like zidovudine, azathioprine, methotrexate, hydroxyurea, or imatinib)
- Toxins
- Liver disease
- Hemolysis (when red blood cells break down too fast)
- Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)

Some people with an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) also have large red blood cells, even if they do not have anemia.

---

## What the Blood Smear Can Show

A blood smear is a test that looks at your blood under a microscope. It can show different patterns:

- Anemia of chronic disease can show small, normal, or even large red blood cells.
- Myelodysplastic syndrome can cause small, normal, or large red blood cells.
- Anemia from hormone problems (like low thyroid) or lack of certain minerals (like copper) can also show different cell sizes.

---

## How Is Anemia Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause. Your doctor will find the reason for your low red blood cell count and treat that.

---

## Erythropoietin and Darbepoetin: Misuse in Sports

Erythropoietin and darbepoetin are medicines that help your body make more red blood cells. They are used to treat anemia in people with kidney disease or cancer.

Some athletes misuse these medicines to boost performance. They do this because more red blood cells mean more oxygen in the blood, which can help during long-distance sports.

But using these medicines without a medical need is dangerous. It can disrupt your body’s natural control of red blood cell production. If you stop using them, your body may suddenly make too few red blood cells. This can lead to serious health problems.

# Baker Cysts

## What Is a Baker Cyst?

A Baker cyst is a small, fluid-filled sac that forms behind the knee.  
It grows from a part of the knee joint.  
The sac holds joint fluid, which is a thick, slippery liquid that helps the knee move smoothly.

## What Causes a Baker Cyst?

The cyst forms when extra joint fluid builds up.  
This fluid gets trapped and pushes out from the joint.  
Common causes include:  
- Rheumatoid arthritis  
- Osteoarthritis  
- Other types of joint inflammation  
- Overusing the knees

Most Baker cysts do not cause any symptoms.  
Some become noticeable when they swell.  
They can grow as big as a baseball.  
They may stretch down into the calf muscle.

## What Happens If the Cyst Breaks?

The fluid inside the cyst can suddenly burst.  
This can cause sudden pain and swelling behind the knee or in the calf.  
The leaked fluid can irritate nearby tissues.  
This may cause symptoms like those of a blood clot in the leg.  
A blood clot in the leg is called deep vein thrombosis.

In rare cases, a bulging or broken cyst can press on a vein behind the knee.  
This can cause swelling and inflammation in the vein.  
This condition is called thrombophlebitis.

## How Is a Baker Cyst Diagnosed?

A doctor will ask about your symptoms.  
They will feel the area behind your knee and calf.  
They may notice a soft lump or swelling.

If needed, the doctor may order imaging tests.  
These include:  
- Ultrasound  
- MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)  
- Arthrography

These tests help confirm the diagnosis.  
They also help rule out a blood clot.  
They show how big the cyst is and how far it extends.

## How Is a Baker Cyst Treated?

### Pain Relief
- Take nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for pain.  
- If you cannot take NSAIDs, your doctor may suggest another pain reliever.

### Fluid Removal and Injections
- If arthritis causes ongoing knee swelling, your doctor may use a needle to drain fluid from the knee.  
- This is called joint aspiration.  
- After draining, the doctor may inject a steroid medicine.  
- This helps reduce swelling and may shrink the cyst.  
- The doctor may also drain the cyst directly and inject medicine into it.

### Surgery
- Surgery to remove the cyst is rare.  
- It is only considered if other treatments do not work.

### If the Cyst Breaks
- If the cyst breaks, the fluid is usually absorbed by the body.  
- Pain is treated with NSAIDs or another pain reliever.  
- If the broken cyst causes inflammation in the vein behind the knee, treatment includes:  
  - Rest in bed  
  - Keep your leg raised  
  - Use warm compresses  
  - Take blood-thinning medicine (like warfarin)

# Bacterial Vaginosis

## What Is Bacterial Vaginosis?

Bacterial vaginosis is a common condition in women. It happens when the natural balance of bacteria in the vagina changes.

It is not an infection passed from one person to another through sex. But sex can sometimes trigger it.

## Symptoms

You may notice:
- A thin, white or greyish discharge from the vagina.
- A strong fishy smell, especially after sex.
- The discharge may be watery.

Many women do not have any symptoms at all.  
About half of women with bacterial vaginosis feel no changes.

It does not usually cause itching or soreness.

## When to See a Doctor

Go to your doctor or a sexual health clinic if:
- You think you have bacterial vaginosis.
- You are pregnant.  
  Bacterial vaginosis can sometimes cause problems during pregnancy.  
  Getting treated can help protect your baby.

## Treatment

Bacterial vaginosis is treated with antibiotics.  
These can come as tablets, gels, or creams.

Your doctor or clinic will give you the right medicine.

If you have a same-sex partner, they may also need treatment.

### If It Comes Back

It is common for bacterial vaginosis to return, often within a few months.

If it comes back, you will likely get more antibiotics.

If you get it more than four times in a year, your doctor may suggest using a special antibiotic gel.  
You put this in your vagina.  
You may need to use it for several months to stop it from coming back.

Your doctor will tell you how long to use the treatment.

They can also help you find out what might be causing it.  
For example, sex, your period, or certain products.

## What Causes It?

The vagina has a mix of good and bad bacteria.  
Bacterial vaginosis happens when the balance shifts.

We do not fully understand why this happens.  
But certain things can increase your risk:

- Being sexually active (but women who are not sexually active can also get it).
- Having a new sexual partner.
- Using an IUD (a small device placed in the uterus to prevent pregnancy).
- Using scented soaps, sprays, or wipes near the vagina.

Bacterial vaginosis is not an STI.  
But having it can make you more likely to get an STI.

This is because bacterial vaginosis can make the vagina less acidic.  
A less acidic vagina is less able to fight off infections.

# What Are Temporomandibular Disorders?

Temporomandibular disorders, or TMD, are a group of conditions that affect the jaw joint, the muscles that move the jaw, and the nearby nerves and ligaments.

These problems often cause pain in the jaw, face, or neck. They can also cause trouble with jaw movement. For example, the jaw may make clicking or popping sounds. Or it may not open as wide as it should.

People usually seek medical help when the pain or jaw problems are bad enough to interfere with daily life.

TMD can have many causes. Most often, it comes from problems in the jaw muscles or the ligaments around the jaw joint. Sometimes, the joint itself is damaged or out of place.

A loose or overly flexible jaw joint can also play a role.

## What Happens in the Jaw Joint?

The jaw joint connects the lower jaw to the skull. It is made up of the rounded end of the lower jaw (called the condyle) and a socket in the skull (called the glenoid fossa).

Between these two bones is a small disc made of tough tissue. This disc acts like a cushion. It helps the joint move smoothly.

Unlike most joints, the jaw joint does not have cartilage like the rest of the body. Instead, it has a special type of tough tissue called fibrocartilage.

The disc can move out of place. This is called an internal derangement. When this happens, the joint may not work right. It can cause pain, clicking, or trouble moving.

Causes of disc problems include:

- A sudden injury, like a whiplash from a car crash
- Repeated small injuries from habits like clenching or grinding your teeth
- Chewing gum a lot
- Jaw thrusting or pushing the jaw forward
- Certain diseases like rheumatoid arthritis or juvenile arthritis
- Infections in the jaw area
- A sudden change in how the teeth fit together, such as after a blow to the face

## How Are TMDs Diagnosed?

Doctors start by asking about your symptoms and doing a physical exam.

Imaging tests like X-rays or MRI are not always needed. But they may be used if the diagnosis is unclear or if the doctor needs to see inside the joint.

### Key Signs of TMD

- Pain when pressing on the jaw joint while opening your mouth
- Jaw pain that spreads to the face, neck, or head
- Jaw that clicks, pops, or locks when you open or close it
- Difficulty opening your mouth wide

### Conditions That Can Feel Like TMD

Some other health problems can cause similar symptoms. These include:

- Sinus infections
- Headaches from tension or migraines
- Arthritis in the jaw or neck
- Tooth pain
- Nerve pain in the face or jaw
- Problems with the ear, such as ear infections or blocked ear tubes
- Neck injuries or muscle problems
- Heart issues
- Rare conditions like tumors or aneurysms

### What the Doctor Checks

The doctor will ask you to describe your pain. They will also check for tender spots in the jaw muscles and neck.

They will press on the muscles around your jaw. These include the temporalis, masseter, and medial pterygoid muscles.

They will also check for trigger points. These are tight spots that cause pain in other areas when pressed.

The lateral pterygoid muscles are hard to feel, so they are not checked directly.

The doctor will watch you open your mouth as wide as you can. If one side hurts, your jaw may move toward that side.

They may use a stethoscope or their fingers to listen or feel the joint. This helps them detect clicking, popping, or a catching sensation.

To check how the jaw moves, the doctor may place their fingers just in front of your ears. They gently press inward as you move your jaw. Or they may place their little fingers in your ear canals and press forward.

Most adults can open their mouth at least 40 millimeters. This is about the space between the front teeth of the top and bottom jaws.

A simple way to check this: try to fit three fingers (middle, ring, and pinky) into your mouth. They should fit up to the last joint of your fingers.

Imaging is not usually needed. But it may be used if the doctor needs to see inside the joint. For example, to check for a displaced disc or joint damage.

# Stress Fractures of the Foot

## What Is a Stress Fracture?

A stress fracture is a small crack in a bone.  
It happens from repeated stress, not from a single injury like a fall or a blow.  
These cracks often happen in the bones of the foot, especially the midfoot bones called metatarsals.  
They are sometimes called "march fractures" because soldiers who march long distances often get them.

## How Do Stress Fractures Happen?

Your bones take a lot of pressure when you walk, run, or jump.  
Muscles and tendons usually protect your bones by absorbing the shock.  
But if you do too much too soon, or if your muscles are weak, the bones can get damaged.  
This repeated stress can lead to a small crack in the bone.

## Who Is at Risk?

You are more likely to get a stress fracture if:
- You suddenly increase how much you run or walk.
- You are not used to physical activity.
- You have high arches in your feet.
- Your shoes do not cushion your feet well.
- You have weak bones (a condition called osteoporosis).

Women and girls who train hard and do not eat enough food are at higher risk.  
They may stop having their monthly periods.  
They may also develop weak bones.  
This combination is called the female athlete triad.  
It includes:
- Missing periods (amenorrhea)
- Poor eating habits (disordered eating)
- Weak bones (osteoporosis)

## Symptoms

Pain in the foot often starts after a long or hard workout.  
The pain may go away when you stop moving.  
But over time, the pain comes back sooner.  
It can get so bad that it hurts even when you are not walking.  
The pain may last even when you are not putting weight on the foot.  
The foot may look swollen or tender.  
Pressing on the foot can cause pain.

If you have deep pain in the groin or thigh when you walk, you may have a stress fracture in the upper leg bone near the hip.  
This needs medical attention.

## Diagnosis

Your doctor will start with an x-ray.  
But x-rays may not show the crack right away.  
It can take two to three weeks for the crack to appear on an x-ray.  
If the x-ray is normal but you still have pain, your doctor may order a bone scan or an MRI.  
These tests can find the crack earlier.

Women with stress fractures should talk to their doctor about testing for weak bones.  
Some women with fractures in the pelvis or upper leg may have weak bones that were not noticed before.

## Treatment

The main treatment is rest.  
You must stop putting weight on the injured foot or leg.  
You may need to use crutches.  
You may also wear a special shoe or boot to protect the foot.  
In some cases, a cast is needed.

Healing can take up to 12 weeks.  
During this time, you can stay active by doing exercises that do not put weight on your feet.  
Swimming is a good choice.  
It keeps your heart and lungs strong without stressing the injured bone.

If you have a stress fracture in the upper leg near the hip, see a specialist.  
This type of fracture needs careful care.

# Stomach Ulcer

A stomach ulcer is a sore in the lining of your stomach.  
The main sign is pain in your tummy.  
The pain is usually in the upper part of your tummy.  
It can feel like a burning sensation.  
The pain often gets worse at night.

## Symptoms of a Stomach Ulcer

The main symptom is tummy pain.  
You may also have:  
- Indigestion  
- Heartburn (a burning feeling in your chest)  
- Bloating  
- Feeling sick or being sick  

## What Causes a Stomach Ulcer

Most ulcers are caused by a type of bacteria called *H pylori*.  
This bacteria can live in your stomach and cause irritation.  
Another common cause is using painkillers like ibuprofen every day.  
Smoking increases your risk.  
The older you get, the more likely you are to get a stomach ulcer.

## How a Stomach Ulcer Is Treated

Treatment depends on what is causing the ulcer.

If you have *H pylori*, you will likely be given antibiotics.  
You may also be given medicine to lower the amount of acid in your stomach.  
These medicines help the ulcer heal.

Treatment can last from one week to two months.  
Your doctor may test you again after treatment to check it worked.

If your symptoms come back, talk to your doctor.  
You may need a different medicine or to take medicine for longer.

Your doctor may also suggest:  
- Quitting smoking  
- Stopping or changing medicines that make your symptoms worse  
- Getting help for stress, anxiety, or depression, as these can make your symptoms worse

## Things You Can Do to Help

After seeing your doctor, you can take steps to feel better and prevent the ulcer from coming back.

### Do

- Eat smaller meals  
- Finish your evening meal 3 to 4 hours before bedtime  
- Try to stay at a healthy weight  
- Manage your stress  

### Don’t

- Do not take painkillers like ibuprofen without talking to your doctor  
- Avoid foods or drinks that make your symptoms worse. These can include fatty or spicy foods, coffee, and chocolate  
- Do not smoke  
- Do not drink too much alcohol  

## Possible Problems from a Stomach Ulcer

If you do not treat a stomach ulcer, it can lead to serious health issues.  
These problems can be life-threatening.

Possible complications include:  
- Bleeding in your stomach or intestines  
- Low iron levels (iron deficiency anaemia) from blood loss  
- A hole in your stomach wall, which can cause a serious infection in your tummy  
- A higher risk of stomach cancer if *H pylori* is not treated

## When to See a Doctor

Call your doctor if:  
- Your indigestion does not get better with treatment  
- Your tummy pain keeps coming back  

## When to Get Urgent Help

Call your doctor right away or use NHS 111 if you have ulcer symptoms and:  
- Your tummy pain is getting worse or does not go away  
- You have lost your appetite  
- You feel full after eating just a small amount  
- You have lost weight without trying  
- You feel a lump in your tummy  
- It hurts or is hard to swallow  
- You keep being sick (vomiting)  
- You feel very tired all the time  

You can call 111 or get help online.

## When to Call 999 or Go to A&E

Go to A&E or call 999 if you have:  
- Vomiting blood that looks bright red  
- Vomiting that looks like coffee grounds  
- Blood in your poo  
- Poo that is black, sticky, and very smelly  
- Severe tummy pain  
- Pain when you touch your tummy  
- Sudden chest pain  

### Find your nearest A&E

### A&E Safety Tips

- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you.  
- If you cannot get a ride, call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
- Bring all your medicines with you when you go.

# Polyhydramnios

Polyhydramnios means there is too much fluid around the baby in the womb.  
This condition can cause problems for both the mother and the baby.  
It is diagnosed using an ultrasound scan to measure the amount of fluid.  
Treatment focuses on managing any health issues in the mother that may be causing the extra fluid.  
If symptoms are very bad or if early labor starts, doctors may remove some of the fluid.

## What Causes Polyhydramnios?

- The cause is unknown in many cases.  
- The baby may have a birth defect, such as a blockage in the gut or kidneys.  
- Carrying more than one baby (twins, triplets, etc.) can increase the risk.  
- The mother may have diabetes.  
- The baby may have low blood count (anemia), including a type caused by the mother’s blood reacting with the baby’s blood.  
- The baby may have an infection or a genetic condition.

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

Many women have no symptoms.  
Sometimes the belly grows faster than expected for how far along the pregnancy is.  
In severe cases, the belly may stretch so much that breathing becomes hard.  
Some women also get painful early contractions.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

An ultrasound scan is used to check the amount of fluid.  
A full ultrasound is done to look for any birth defects in the baby.  
Tests are done on the mother if a health problem is suspected.  

Doctors often suspect polyhydramnios when the belly is bigger than expected.  
But guessing the fluid level by eye is not reliable.  
So, doctors use a number to measure the fluid accurately.  

Two main methods are used:

- **Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI):** This adds up the fluid depth in four parts of the uterus.  
  - Normal AFI is between 5 and 24 centimeters.  
  - AFI of 24 centimeters or more means there is too much fluid.

- **Single Deepest Pocket (SDP):** This measures the largest single area of fluid.  
  - Normal SDP is between 2 and 8 centimeters.  
  - SDP of 8 centimeters or more means there is too much fluid.

Neither method is perfect.  
AFI can wrongly suggest too little fluid.  
SDP can wrongly suggest too much fluid.  

Doctors usually use the AFI to define polyhydramnios.  
A normal AFI is above 5 and below 24 centimeters.  
An AFI of 24 centimeters or more means there is too much fluid.

## How Is It Treated?

- Delivery is usually planned around 39 weeks of pregnancy.  
- In some cases, doctors may remove some fluid through a needle (called amnioreduction).  
- This is only done if the mother is very uncomfortable.  
- There is no clear rule on how much fluid to remove or how fast.  
  - Some doctors remove about one liter of fluid over 20 minutes.  
- Any health problem in the mother, like diabetes, must be well managed.

## Monitoring During Pregnancy

- If the AFI is 30 centimeters or more, monitoring should start as early as 32 weeks.  
  - This includes a weekly test to check the baby’s heart rate (nonstress test).  
  - But this testing has not been proven to lower the risk of baby death.  
- If the AFI is between 24 and 30 centimeters, weekly testing is not needed.  
- All women with polyhydramnios should have an ultrasound every 4 weeks.  
  - This checks for a large baby and looks at the baby’s body for any problems.

## Key Points

- Polyhydramnios means too much fluid around the baby.  
- It can be caused by birth defects, multiple babies, maternal diabetes, or other baby health issues.  
- It raises the risk of early labor, early water breaking, breathing problems for the mother, baby lying in a bad position, or baby death.  
- It can also cause problems during labor and delivery.  
- If polyhydramnios is suspected, get an ultrasound to measure fluid levels.  
  - Use either the AFI or the SDP.  
  - Also, check for possible causes, including a full ultrasound of the baby.  
- Only remove fluid if the mother has serious symptoms.  
- Start weekly heart rate checks as early as 32 weeks if the AFI is 30 centimeters or more.

# Dehydration in Children

Dehydration means the body has lost too much water. It usually happens when a child is vomiting, has diarrhea, or both.

- Dehydration happens when the body loses more water than it takes in.
- The body also loses important minerals called electrolytes.
- Electrolytes help the body work properly. They include sodium, potassium, chloride, and bicarbonate.
- Dehydration can be serious and even life-threatening if not treated.

## What Causes Dehydration in Children?

Children can become dehydrated when:

- They lose too much fluid from vomiting or diarrhea.
- They do not drink enough fluids.

Vomiting and diarrhea are the most common causes. But not every episode leads to dehydration.

Other causes include:

- Severe burns over large areas of the body.
- Sweating too much, such as during very hot weather or intense exercise.

Children may not drink enough fluids when they are sick. This can happen with:

- A sore throat.
- A serious illness of any kind.

Some children do not drink enough because they are being neglected.

Newborns may have trouble feeding. This can happen if they are not breastfeeding or bottle feeding well. This can sometimes lead to dehydration.

## Signs of Dehydration in Children

### Seek medical help right away if your infant shows any of these signs:

- The soft spot on the head is sunken.
- The eyes look sunken.
- No tears when crying.
- Dry mouth.
- Very little urine.
- Low energy or hard to wake up.

### Mild to moderate dehydration may cause:

- Dry mouth and dry lips.
- Thirst.
- Urinating less often.
- Less interest in playing or being active.

### Severe dehydration is an emergency. Signs include:

- Feeling very sleepy or weak.
- No tears when crying.
- Bluish skin color (this is called cyanosis).
- Fast breathing.

Severe dehydration can cause the salt level in the blood to become too high or too low. This can make the child feel worse and can lead to:

- Seizures.
- Coma.
- Brain damage.

In the worst cases, severe dehydration can be fatal.

## How Doctors Diagnose Dehydration

Doctors check the child’s symptoms and look for signs of dehydration.

They may:

- Weigh the child to see if they have lost weight.
- Do blood and urine tests if the child is moderately or severely dehydrated.

Weight loss over just a few days is a strong sign of dehydration. The amount of weight lost helps the doctor decide how serious the dehydration is.

Blood and urine tests help the doctor check the levels of electrolytes and how much fluid the child needs.

## How Dehydration Is Treated

The main treatment is replacing lost fluids and electrolytes.

### For mild dehydration:

- Give fluids by mouth.
- Use special drinks called oral rehydration solutions (ORS).
- ORS is not always needed for mild cases.

### If your child is vomiting:

- Start with small sips every 10 minutes.
- If the child keeps the fluid down, slowly increase the amount and space out the sips.
- If vomiting continues, stop giving fluids and call a doctor.

### If your child has diarrhea only:

- Give larger amounts of fluid less often.

### If your child has both vomiting and diarrhea:

- Give small sips of ORS every 10 minutes.
- If the diarrhea gets worse, the child may need to go to the hospital for fluids through a vein (IV).

### If your child cannot drink or is very weak:

- They may need fluids through a vein (IV).
- Or, a thin tube may be passed through the nose into the stomach to give fluids.

### For infants:

- Breast milk (human milk) is the best choice. It has all the fluids and minerals a baby needs.
- If the baby is not breastfeeding, give oral rehydration solution (ORS).
- ORS comes as powder to mix with water or as ready-to-use liquid.
- It is sold without a prescription at drugstores or grocery stores.

### How much ORS to give:

- Give about 1½ to 2½ ounces for every pound the child weighs in 24 hours.
- For example, a 20-pound child should get 30 to 50 ounces in 24 hours.
- A 10-kilogram child should get 1,000 to 1,650 milliliters in 24 hours.

This amount helps fix dehydration and meets daily fluid needs.

### After vomiting stops:

- Resume breastfeeding or formula feeding as soon as possible.
- For older children, start with small sips of clear broths, soups, clear sodas, gelatin, or diluted juice (half juice, half water).
- Popsicles made from diluted juice are also okay.

### Do not use:

- Plain water – it has no salt and is not enough.
- Undiluted juice – too much sugar and can make diarrhea worse.
- Sports drinks – high in sugar and may irritate the stomach.

### For children over 1 year old:

- ORS is a good option, especially for moderate dehydration.
- Once vomiting stops, the child can go back to their normal diet.

Always talk to a doctor if you are unsure about how to treat dehydration.

# Bedwetting in Children

Bedwetting is when a child wets the bed at night. It is common and usually not a sign of a serious problem.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:
- You have tried home steps to help, but your child still wets the bed.
- Your child started wetting the bed again after being dry for more than six months.

## Why Children Wet the Bed

Many things can cause bedwetting. These include:
- Not feeling the need to pee while asleep.
- Making more pee at night than the bladder can hold.
- Stress at home or at school.

Bedwetting can also be linked to health issues like diabetes or constipation.

## What You Can Do at Home

### Do These Things

- Let your child drink enough water during the day.
- Help your child go to the toilet about 4 to 7 times a day. This includes going just before bedtime.
- Work with your child to set up a reward system. For example, give a sticker each time they use the toilet before bed.
- Use waterproof covers on the mattress and duvet to protect them.
- Make sure your child can get to the toilet easily at night.

### Avoid These Things

- Do not punish your child. They cannot control this, and it can make the problem worse.
- Do not give drinks with caffeine, like cola, tea, or coffee. These can increase how much pee your child makes.
- Do not wake your child up at night to use the toilet. This does not help in the long run.

## Treatments from Your Doctor

If bedwetting continues, your doctor can suggest treatments such as:
- A bedwetting alarm. This wakes your child when they start to pee, helping them learn to wake up before wetting the bed.
- Medicine to reduce how much pee your child makes at night.

Your doctor will check if the treatment is working. They can also help you if you feel stressed or overwhelmed.

If these treatments do not help, your child may be referred to a specialist doctor.

# What You Need to Know About Salmonella Infections

Salmonella is a type of bacteria. There are two main types: *S. enterica* and *S. bongori*. Together, they include more than 2,500 different kinds.

Some of these kinds have common names. For example, *S. enterica* subspecies *enterica* serotype Typhi is often called *Salmonella* Typhi.

Scientists group Salmonella bacteria based on how well they infect people.

## Group 1: Bacteria That Only Infect Humans

These bacteria are very good at infecting people. They do not infect animals.

- *Salmonella* Typhi
- *Salmonella* Paratyphi A
- *Salmonella* Paratyphi B (also called *S.* Schottmülleri)
- *Salmonella* Paratyphi C (also called *S.* Hirschfeldii)

These types cause a serious illness called enteric fever, also known as typhoid fever.

## Group 2: Bacteria That Mostly Infect Animals

These bacteria mainly infect animals. They rarely cause illness in people.

But some of them can still make people sick. These include:
- *Salmonella* Dublin – found in cattle
- *Salmonella* Arizonae – found in reptiles
- *Salmonella* Choleraesuis – found in pigs

## Group 3: Bacteria That Can Infect Many Different Animals and People

This group has more than 2,000 kinds. Examples include *Salmonella* Enteritidis and *Salmonella* Typhimurium.

These bacteria cause a common illness called salmonella gastroenteritis. It leads to stomach pain, diarrhea, and fever.

This group causes about 85 out of every 100 salmonella infections in the United States.

# Infectious Arthritis – Simple Explanation

Infectious arthritis is an infection inside a joint. It happens when bacteria, viruses, or fungi get into the fluid and tissues of a joint. Most often, it is caused by bacteria. But sometimes, viruses or fungi can cause it.

## What Happens in Infectious Arthritis?

- Bacteria, viruses, or fungi can travel through the blood or come from a nearby infection.
- Pain, swelling, and fever usually start within hours or a few days.
- A doctor will take fluid from the joint using a needle and test it.
- Antibiotics are started right away, even before the test results come back.

There are two main types:

- Acute infectious arthritis
- Chronic infectious arthritis

---

## Acute Infectious Arthritis

This type starts suddenly and is usually caused by bacteria.

- Most cases of infectious arthritis are acute.
- It can happen in healthy people and in people with risk factors.
- The cartilage inside the joint can be damaged or destroyed within hours or days.

Sometimes, arthritis appears after an infection in another part of the body, like the genitals or the gut. This is not a true joint infection. The joint becomes inflamed because of the body’s reaction to the infection. This is called **reactive arthritis**.

---

## Chronic Infectious Arthritis

This type develops slowly over several weeks.

- Very few cases are chronic.
- It mostly affects people with risk factors.

The joints most often affected are:

- Knee
- Shoulder
- Wrist
- Hip
- Elbow
- Fingers

Most infections affect just one joint. But sometimes, more than one joint is involved.

Some bacteria have special habits:

- The bacteria that cause Lyme disease usually affect the knee.
- Gonococci (which cause gonorrhea) and some viruses (like hepatitis) can affect many joints at once.
- Mycobacteria are more likely to cause long-term joint infections.

---

## What Causes Infectious Arthritis?

Most infections come from bacteria. They can reach the joint in several ways:

- From a nearby infection, like a bone infection or a wound.
- Through the bloodstream.
- Directly, if the joint is touched during surgery, an injection, or a bite from a person or animal.

### Acute Infectious Arthritis

This is usually caused by bacteria or viruses.

Different bacteria cause infection in different age groups:

- **Newborns**: Group B streptococci, *E. coli*, other gram-negative bacteria, and *Staphylococcus aureus*.
- **Infants and young children**: *Staphylococcus aureus*, streptococci, gram-negative bacteria, and *Kingella kingae*.
- **Older children and adults**: *Staphylococcus aureus*, streptococci, and gonococci.

Other bacteria that can cause joint infections:

- Spirochetes (like those that cause Lyme disease and syphilis).

Viruses that can cause joint infections:

- HIV
- Parvovirus
- Rubella
- Mumps
- Hepatitis B
- Hepatitis C

### Risk Factors for Acute Infectious Arthritis

These things increase your chance of getting infectious arthritis:

- A past joint infection
- An artificial joint or recent joint surgery
- Using needles to inject drugs
- Long-term health problems like diabetes, lupus, lung or liver disease
- Being older
- Alcohol use disorder
- Having sex with many partners or without condoms
- Conditions that harm joints, like rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, or joint injury from an accident
- Bloodstream infection (bacteremia)
- Hemophilia
- Being on dialysis
- Skin infections
- Sickle cell disease

For example, if you have pneumonia or a serious blood infection, bacteria can travel to your joints and cause infection.

Even children without any risk factors can get this condition. About half of children with joint infections are under 3 years old. But vaccines for *Haemophilus influenzae* and *Streptococcus pneumoniae* are helping to reduce cases in young children.

### Risk Factors for Chronic Infectious Arthritis

These increase the chance of long-term joint infection:

- Rheumatoid arthritis
- HIV infection
- A weak immune system (from cancer or certain medicines)
- An artificial joint

> **Did You Know?**  
> If you have long-term arthritis like rheumatoid arthritis and suddenly get pain and swelling in one joint, see your doctor right away. You might have an infection—even if you do not have a fever.

---

## Symptoms of Infectious Arthritis

You may have:

- Severe joint pain
- Swelling in the joint
- Fever
- Redness and warmth around the joint

Depending on the cause, you might also have:

- Symptoms of Lyme disease (like a rash)
- Swollen glands (lymph nodes) if the infection came from a bite wound

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find out if you have infectious arthritis.

### Tests Include:

- **Joint fluid test**: A needle is used to remove fluid from the joint. This fluid is checked for white blood cells and tested for bacteria or other germs.
- **Blood tests**: These help find bacteria in the blood.
- **Sputum, spinal fluid, or urine tests**: These may be done to find the source of the infection.
- **X-rays, MRI, or ultrasound**: These help see the joint and check for fluid buildup or abscesses.

Doctors often suspect infectious arthritis if you have:

- Severe joint pain with no clear cause
- A mix of symptoms that are common in this condition

If the joint fluid test shows bacteria, the lab can grow them and test which antibiotics will work.

Sometimes, the bacteria are hard to grow. This is true for gonorrhea, Lyme disease, and syphilis.

Doctors may also test the joint fluid for DNA from gonococci or mycobacteria to help guide treatment.

X-rays help rule out other joint problems.

MRI or ultrasound may be used if the joint is hard to examine or if there is a lot of fluid or pus.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment includes:

- Antibiotics or antifungal medicines
- Removing pus from the joint
- Splinting the joint
- Physical therapy
- Pain and fever relief medicines

### Antibiotics

- Start antibiotics as soon as possible—even before the lab finds the germ.
- At first, doctors give antibiotics through a vein (IV) so the medicine reaches the joint fast.
- The first antibiotics are chosen based on the most likely bacteria.
- Most people start to feel better within 48 hours if the treatment works.
- Once the lab results come back, the antibiotic may be changed to match the germ’s sensitivity.
- IV antibiotics are given for 2 to 4 weeks.
- Then, oral antibiotics are taken by mouth for another 2 to 6 weeks.

### Infections That Are Hard to Treat

- If the infection does not go away with normal antibiotics, it may be caused by mycobacteria or fungi.
- Fungal infections are treated with antifungal medicines.
- Mycobacterial infections need a mix of antibiotics and long treatment.
- These infections take months to treat.

### Viral Infections

- Viruses usually get better on their own.
- Antibiotics do not help with viral infections.

### Removing Pus

- Pus is removed with a needle (aspiration) to prevent joint damage.
- If the needle does not work (like in the hip), a small scope (arthroscopy) or surgery may be needed.
- Sometimes, a tube is left in the joint to drain pus over time.
- Aspiration may be done more than once.

### Splinting and Therapy

- The joint is splinted (kept still) for a few days to reduce pain.
- Then, physical therapy starts to strengthen muscles and prevent stiffness or loss of movement.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

- Infections caused by most bacteria can destroy joint cartilage within hours or days.
- Infections from gonococci usually do not cause permanent joint damage.
- People with rheumatoid arthritis often do not fully recover use of the infected joint.
- The risk of death is higher in people with rheumatoid arthritis and joint infection.

---

This website offers clear, helpful information about all types of arthritis, including infectious arthritis. It also gives advice on living with arthritis.

# Pleurisy – Simple Guide

## What Is Pleurisy?

Pleurisy causes sharp pain in your chest when you breathe in.  
The pain can get worse when you cough, sneeze, or move.  
It may also spread to your shoulders or back.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor right away if you have:
- Sharp chest pain that only happens when you breathe in or cough
- Chest pain that does not get better after a few days
- A small amount of blood in your spit or phlegm
- Trouble breathing often

You can call 111 or get help online.

## When to Go to A&E (Emergency Department)

Go to A&E or call 999 if you have:
- Sudden chest pain that lasts 15 minutes or longer
- Chest pain that spreads to your arms, back, neck, or jaw
- Trouble breathing
- Coughing up more than a few spots of blood
- Coughing up blood and also having trouble breathing, a very fast heartbeat, or pain in your chest or upper back

These signs could mean a serious problem, like a heart attack or a blood clot in the lungs.

**Find your nearest A&E**

> ⚠️ Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to take you. Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
> Bring all your medicines with you.

## What Happens at the Doctor’s Office

Your doctor will check you and listen to your chest.  
They may send you to a specialist if they are not sure what is causing your symptoms.  
You might need tests, such as:
- Blood tests
- A chest X-ray
- An ultrasound scan
- A CT scan

## How Pleurisy Is Treated

Most people get better in a few days without needing treatment.  
If a bacterial infection is causing the problem, you may need antibiotics.  
To ease the pain, you can:
- Take painkillers like paracetamol or ibuprofen
- Rest in a position that feels best. Lying on the painful side may help.

You may need to stay in hospital if your symptoms are very bad or caused by a serious condition, such as a blood clot in the lungs or tuberculosis.

# Pediatric Growth Plate Fractures

Children’s bones have special areas called growth plates. These plates help bones grow longer. The growth plate is the weakest part of a child’s bone. It can break before other parts of the bone.

Growth plates close as a child gets older. This usually happens by age twenty. But the exact age varies by bone.

When a child’s bone breaks, the growth plate is often involved. A doctor will use an X-ray to check for a growth plate fracture.

## How Growth Plate Fractures Are Classified

Doctors use the Salter-Harris system to describe the type of growth plate break. The type helps predict how well the bone will heal.

Here is a simple way to remember the types:

- **Type I**: The break goes straight across the growth plate.
- **Type II**: The break starts in the growth plate and goes up into the bone above it.
- **Type III**: The break starts in the growth plate and goes down into the bone below it.
- **Type IV**: The break goes through the bone above, the growth plate, and the bone below.
- **Type V**: The growth plate is crushed, like being squashed under heavy pressure.

The more serious the break, the higher the risk of problems with bone growth. Types III, IV, and V are more serious than Types I and II.

## Signs of a Growth Plate Fracture

A child with a growth plate fracture may have:
- Pain in the area of the growth plate
- Swelling around the growth plate
- Trouble moving the injured limb
- Inability to put weight on the injured limb

## How Doctors Diagnose Growth Plate Fractures

Doctors use X-rays to look for a fracture. If the X-ray is unclear, the doctor may take an X-ray of the same area on the other side of the body for comparison.

Sometimes, the X-ray looks normal even if there is a fracture. This is common with Type I and Type V fractures.

If a fracture is suspected but not seen on the X-ray, the doctor will treat it as if it is broken. The child will wear a splint or cast. The child will return in a few days. If pain and tenderness continue, the doctor will confirm the fracture.

## How Growth Plate Fractures Are Treated

Treatment depends on the type of fracture.

- **Type I and Type II**: These are often treated with closed reduction and immobilization. This means the doctor gently moves the bone back into place and puts a cast or splint on it.
- **Type III and Type IV**: These often need surgery. The doctor will open the skin and use metal pins, screws, or plates to hold the bone in place. This is called open reduction with internal fixation, or ORIF.
- **Type V**: These are serious. They almost always cause problems with bone growth. Children with this type need to see a pediatric orthopedic specialist.

## Important Facts

- The growth plate is weaker than other parts of the bone. It breaks more easily than ligaments or other bones.
- Children with Type III, IV, or V fractures have a higher chance of long-term problems with growth.
- If a fracture is not clearly seen on the X-ray but is still suspected, compare the injured side with the healthy side.
- Type III and IV fractures often need surgery (ORIF) to heal properly.

# Gastritis

Gastritis means the lining of the stomach is inflamed.

## What Is Gastritis?

- The stomach lining is usually strong and can handle very strong acid.
- In gastritis, the lining becomes irritated and swollen.
- This can happen for many reasons, including infections, serious illness, injury, certain medicines, alcohol, or problems with the body’s defense system.

## Types of Gastritis

Gastritis is split into two main types based on how bad it is:

### Erosive Gastritis
- This type causes both inflammation and damage to the stomach lining.
- It can start suddenly (acute) or slowly (chronic).
- It often happens in people who are otherwise healthy.
- It is usually caused by alcohol, stress from serious illness, or medicines like aspirin and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
- Some people can get it from a single baby aspirin taken every day.
- Other causes include radiation, infections, swallowing harmful chemicals, or injuries like a tube going into the stomach.

### Nonerosive Gastritis
- This type does not cause visible damage to the lining.
- The lining may become thin or change into a different kind of tissue.
- White blood cells build up in the stomach and cause swelling.
- The swelling can affect the whole stomach or just parts of it.

## Causes of Gastritis

- **Erosive gastritis** is often caused by alcohol, stress from serious illness, or medicines like aspirin and NSAIDs.
- **Nonerosive gastritis** is most often caused by a bacteria called *Helicobacter pylori*.
- Infections from other germs (like viruses or fungi) are rare but can happen in people with weak immune systems, such as those with advanced HIV, cancer, or who take immune-suppressing medicines.
- **Acute stress gastritis** happens after a sudden illness or injury, even if the injury is not to the stomach. Examples include major burns, head injuries, or heavy bleeding.
- The exact reason stress causes gastritis is not fully known. It may be due to less blood flow to the stomach, more acid, or the stomach lining not healing well.
- **Radiation gastritis** can happen if radiation therapy is used on the lower left chest or upper belly.
- **Postgastrectomy gastritis** happens after part of the stomach is removed. It often occurs where the stomach was sewn back together. It may be due to poor blood flow or too much bile (a greenish-yellow fluid from the liver) touching the stomach lining.
- **Atrophic gastritis** means the stomach lining becomes very thin and loses cells that make acid and enzymes. It can happen when the body’s immune system attacks the stomach lining. It can also happen in people with long-term *H. pylori* infection or after stomach surgery.
- **Eosinophilic gastritis** is rare. The cause is often unknown. It happens when a type of white blood cell called eosinophils builds up in the stomach wall.
- **Ménétrier disease** is a rare condition. The stomach wall grows thick and forms large folds and fluid-filled sacs. The cause is not clear, but it may be linked to an immune problem or *H. pylori* infection.

## Symptoms of Gastritis

- Most people with gastritis have no symptoms.
- When symptoms do happen, they can include:
  - Pain or discomfort in the upper belly.
  - Nausea.
  - Vomiting.
- These symptoms are often called indigestion.
- Severe forms like erosive gastritis, radiation gastritis, postgastrectomy gastritis, and atrophic gastritis can cause indigestion.
- Mild indigestion can also happen with acute stress gastritis.

## How Gastritis Is Diagnosed

- Doctors often guess gastritis based on symptoms.
- If the diagnosis is unclear or symptoms do not improve, the doctor may do an upper endoscopy.
- During an upper endoscopy, a thin, flexible tube with a camera is used to look inside the stomach and part of the small intestine.
- The doctor can take a small sample of tissue (a biopsy) from the stomach lining to check under a microscope.

## How Gastritis Is Treated

### General Treatments
- Medicines that reduce stomach acid help relieve symptoms.
- Antacids neutralize acid that is already in the stomach.
- People should stop taking medicines that irritate the stomach, like aspirin and NSAIDs.

### Antacids
- These are available over the counter as tablets, chewable tablets, or liquids.
- Common types include:
  - Aluminum hydroxide (can cause constipation).
  - Magnesium hydroxide (can cause diarrhea).
  - Calcium carbonate.
- Antacids can interfere with other medicines. Always check with a pharmacist or doctor before using them if you take other drugs.

### Acid-Reducing Medicines
- **H2 blockers** reduce acid production. They are more effective than antacids and easier to use.
- **Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs)** are stronger and are often used when there is bleeding. Most people take them for 8 to 12 weeks.

### Other Medicines
- **Sucralfate** coats the stomach lining and helps it heal. It also protects it from irritation.

### Antibiotics
- If gastritis is caused by *H. pylori* infection, antibiotics are needed to treat the infection.

### Special Cases

- **Erosive gastritis**: Avoid stomach-irritating medicines. Use PPIs or H2 blockers to protect the stomach.
- **Acute stress gastritis**: Most people recover when the main illness, injury, or bleeding is treated.
- Some people in intensive care units can have serious bleeding from this type. To prevent it, doctors often give acid-reducing medicines after surgery or to critically ill patients.
- If bleeding continues, doctors may use heat to seal the bleeding spot during endoscopy. If bleeding does not stop, surgery to remove part of the stomach may be needed. This is rare.
- **Postgastrectomy gastritis** and **atrophic gastritis** have no cure.
  - People with anemia from low vitamin B12 absorption due to atrophic gastritis must take vitamin B12 shots for life.
- **Eosinophilic gastritis** may need corticosteroids or surgery if the stomach outlet is blocked.
- **Ménétrier disease** may be cured by removing part or all of the stomach. There are no good medicines to treat it.

# Osteomyelitis

Some people are more likely to get osteomyelitis. This includes people who have had it before, those with diabetes, or those with a weak immune system.

Osteomyelitis causes strong pain. It often affects the feet, legs, or back. Other signs can include swelling, a limp, and a high temperature.

Doctors treat osteomyelitis with antibiotics. If the symptoms are serious, you may need to stay in the hospital. Surgery may also be needed.

---

## Who is more likely to get osteomyelitis

Anyone can get osteomyelitis, but your risk is higher if you:

- Have had osteomyelitis before  
- Have diabetes, especially if you also have a foot ulcer  
- Have broken a bone  
- Have a wound from an injury  
- Have had an infection  
- Have had surgery  
- Have a weak immune system (for example, from chemotherapy or a condition like HIV)

Children may also be more likely to get it after a cold, flu, or chickenpox.

---

## Symptoms of osteomyelitis

Osteomyelitis usually causes strong pain. It most often affects the legs, but it can affect other areas.

Other symptoms include:

- Swelling in the area  
- The area feels warm to the touch  
- The skin looks red. This may be harder to see on black or brown skin  
- A limp (more common in children)  
- A high temperature

---

## Treatment for osteomyelitis

Osteomyelitis is treated with antibiotics. You may need to stay in the hospital, or you might be able to take the medicine at home.

You will usually take antibiotics for 4 to 6 weeks. If the infection is severe, you may need to take them for up to 12 weeks. It is important to finish the full course, even if you start to feel better.

If treatment starts within 3 to 5 days of the infection beginning, it often clears up completely.

You can take painkillers to help with the pain. If the infection is in a long bone, like an arm or leg, you may be given a splint to keep it still.

---

### Surgery for osteomyelitis

You may need surgery if:

- Pus builds up in the bone and needs to be drained  
- The infection presses on something important, like the spinal cord  
- The infection has lasted a long time and damaged the bone

If the bone is damaged, surgery is needed to remove the damaged part. This is called debridement.

After debridement, there may be a hole in the bone. This space may need to be repaired.

Sometimes more than one surgery is needed. Doctors may use muscle or skin from another part of your body to repair the area near the infected bone.

# Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE)

SSPE is a rare and serious brain disease. It usually starts months to years after a person has had measles. The disease slowly gets worse over time. It often leads to death.

## What Causes SSPE?

SSPE is caused by a long-lasting infection with the measles virus. The virus stays in the brain and slowly damages it.

## Who Gets SSPE?

SSPE is very rare in the United States and Western Europe. This is because most people get the measles vaccine. But it can still happen, especially in people who did not get vaccinated.

Before the vaccine, SSPE occurred in about 7 to 300 out of every million people who had natural measles. It happened in about 1 out of every million people who got the measles vaccine. The cases after vaccination are likely due to hidden measles before the shot.

Boys are more likely to get SSPE than girls.

The younger a child is when they get measles, the higher their risk of developing SSPE later. Most people with SSPE get symptoms before age 20.

Recent outbreaks of measles show that SSPE may be more common than we thought. It could affect 40 to 1,700 out of every million people who get measles. This is a big concern because more unvaccinated people are getting measles.

## Symptoms of SSPE

At first, the symptoms are mild. They may include:

- Trouble doing well in school  
- Forgetting things  
- Getting angry easily  
- Being unable to focus  
- Trouble sleeping  

Later, the person may have:

- Strange visions or thoughts (hallucinations)  
- Sudden jerking movements in the arms or legs (myoclonic jerks)  
- Seizures that affect the whole body  

The person’s thinking and memory get worse. They may lose the ability to speak clearly.

Other symptoms include:

- Stiff or twisted muscles  
- Bending the body backward (opisthotonos)  
- Trouble swallowing  
- Loss of vision  
- Damage to the optic nerve  

The eyes may also show signs of damage, such as inflammation in the back of the eye.

In the final stages, the brain’s control center for body functions may be affected. This can cause:

- Fluctuating body temperature  
- Sweating a lot  
- Changes in heart rate and blood pressure  

## How Is SSPE Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect SSPE in young people who have memory loss and muscle twitching.

To confirm the diagnosis, doctors do several tests:

- **Blood and spinal fluid tests** – These check for measles antibodies.  
- **Electroencephalogram (EEG)** – This records brain activity. In SSPE, the EEG shows regular, high-voltage waves that repeat every few seconds.  
- **Brain scans (CT or MRI)** – These can show brain shrinkage or damage in the white matter.  
- **Spinal fluid exam** – The fluid pressure and cell count are usually normal. But the protein level is often high, especially a type called globulin. This can make up 20% to 60% of the total protein in the fluid.

If the results are unclear, a brain biopsy may be needed. This means taking a small sample of brain tissue for testing.

## How Is SSPE Treated?

There is no cure for SSPE. Treatment focuses on helping the person feel better and managing symptoms.

Doctors may use:

- Medicines to stop seizures (anticonvulsants)  
- Supportive care to help with breathing, nutrition, and comfort  

Some medicines like isoprinosine, interferon alfa, and lamivudine have been tried. But they are not proven to help. Most antiviral drugs do not work well for SSPE.

## What Is the Outlook for SSPE?

SSPE almost always leads to death within 1 to 3 years. Pneumonia is a common cause of death.

A few people may have periods when symptoms get better, followed by worsening. But these remissions are rare and temporary.

# Salmonella Infections – Simple Explanation

Salmonella is a type of germ that can make you sick. It is a kind of bacteria that is found in the intestines of animals and people.

## How People Get Infected

You usually get infected by eating food that has been contaminated with Salmonella. Common sources include:

- Undercooked chicken, eggs, beef, or pork
- Raw milk or unpasteurized dairy products
- Contaminated seafood or fresh fruits and vegetables
- Foods that contain raw eggs, like homemade cookie dough or salad dressings

Salmonella can get into eggs before they are laid. It can also get into food during processing, such as in slaughterhouses. Poor hand hygiene by food workers who have not washed after using the toilet can also spread the germ.

Other rare sources of infection include:

- Carmine red dye (used in some foods and cosmetics)
- Contaminated marijuana

Some animals carry Salmonella in their intestines. These include:

- Reptiles like snakes, lizards, and turtles
- Amphibians like frogs
- Birds, especially baby chicks

Up to 90% of pet reptiles and possibly many amphibians carry Salmonella. This is why it is important to avoid letting young children touch these animals.

In the past, many infections in the United States came from small pet turtles. A law was passed to ban the sale of turtles with shells less than 4 inches long. This helped reduce infections. But some people still sell these turtles illegally, and infections still happen.

## Who Is at Risk?

Stomach acid usually kills Salmonella. But if you have low stomach acid, you are more likely to get sick. This can happen in:

- Babies under one year old
- Older adults
- People taking antacids or medicines that reduce stomach acid (like famotidine or omeprazole)
- People who have had part of their stomach removed

## What Happens When You Are Infected?

Salmonella causes inflammation in the intestines. This leads to a condition called gastroenteritis. Symptoms usually start 12 to 48 hours after eating contaminated food.

Common symptoms include:

- Nausea
- Crampy stomach pain
- Watery diarrhea
- Fever
- Vomiting

Most people feel better in 1 to 4 days. But some people may have severe symptoms that last longer.

Even after symptoms go away, some people still carry the germ in their stool. These people are called carriers. They can spread the germ to others.

Some adults develop joint pain weeks or months after the diarrhea ends. This is called reactive arthritis. It often affects the hips, knees, or the back of the heel.

## When the Infection Spreads

In some cases, Salmonella enters the bloodstream. This is called bacteremia. It can spread to other parts of the body and cause serious problems, such as:

- Infections in bones or joints
- Infections in the urinary tract or lungs
- Infections on artificial joints, heart valves, or blood vessel grafts
- Infection of the aorta (the main artery in the body)

These infections can lead to abscesses (pockets of pus) and long-term illness.

You are more likely to have the infection spread if you are:

- An infant
- An older adult, especially in a nursing home
- Someone with sickle cell anemia or malaria
- Someone with a weak immune system (like from HIV or cancer)
- Someone taking medicines that lower your immune system (such as cancer drugs or transplant medicines)

## Symptoms of Serious Infection

If the infection spreads, you may have new symptoms, such as:

- Pain or tenderness over a bone or joint
- Shortness of breath (if the heart is affected)
- Pain in the back or abdomen (if the aorta is infected)

Most people recover fully. But those with serious health problems or complications may not do as well.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

To find out if you have a Salmonella infection, your doctor will take a sample. This can be:

- Stool (poop)
- Pus from an abscess
- Blood
- A swab from the rectum

The sample is sent to a lab. There, the bacteria are grown and tested. This confirms the diagnosis.

The lab also tests which antibiotics will work best against the bacteria.

In some cases, the lab may test the germ’s genetic material to help track outbreaks.

People at risk for serious infection may need extra tests to check for complications.

## How Is It Treated?

### For Mild Infections (Gastroenteritis)

- Drink plenty of fluids to replace lost water.
- Fluids can be taken by mouth or through a vein if you are very sick.

Antibiotics are not usually needed. They do not help you feel better faster. In fact, they can make you carry the germ longer in your stool.

But antibiotics are given if you are at high risk for serious infection. This includes:

- Babies under one year old
- Older adults in nursing homes
- People with HIV or other immune system problems
- People with artificial joints, heart valves, or blood vessel grafts

Common antibiotics used include:

- Ciprofloxacin
- Azithromycin
- Ceftriaxone

Children are usually given trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.

### For Bloodstream Infections (Bacteremia)

- Antibiotics are given for several weeks.
- Common choices: azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone.

### For Abscesses

- The abscess must be drained by surgery.
- Antibiotics are given for several weeks.

### For Infections in Joints, Heart Valves, or the Aorta

- Surgery is usually needed.
- Antibiotics are given for weeks or months.

## How to Prevent Salmonella Infections

You can reduce your risk by following these steps:

- Cook poultry, eggs, and ground beef thoroughly.
- Do not eat or drink anything with raw eggs or raw (unpasteurized) milk.
- Wash fruits and vegetables well before eating.
- Wash your hands after using the toilet or changing a diaper.
- Wash your hands, cutting boards, and utensils with soap after touching raw meat or poultry.
- Wash your hands with soap after touching reptiles, amphibians, birds, or baby chicks.
- Wash your hands after touching pet feces.

### Special Advice for High-Risk People

- Young children should not touch reptiles, amphibians, baby chicks, or other young birds.
- Do not keep reptiles or amphibians in homes with infants.

### If You Are Infected

- Do not prepare food for others until you are fully well.

### For Travelers

- Take steps to avoid diarrhea while traveling. This includes drinking safe water and eating well-cooked food.

## Vaccines

There is no vaccine to prevent Salmonella infections. But there are vaccines available to prevent typhoid fever, which is a more serious type of Salmonella infection.

## More Information

For more details, visit the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) website.
