# Bulging Eyes (Exophthalmos)

Your eyes may look like they are sticking out more than normal. You might also see more of the white part of your eyes than usual.

## When to Seek Help

### Call your doctor right away or use NHS 111 if:
- One or both of your eyes are bulging.

You can call 111 or get help online at [111.nhs.uk](https://www.111.nhs.uk).

### Call 999 or go to A&E right away if:
- Your child’s eyes have just started bulging.
- Your eyes have just started bulging and you are having changes in your vision. This could mean you see wavy lines, flashing lights, or you are losing your sight.
- Your eyes have just started bulging and you have a very bad headache and feel sick.

> Find your nearest A&E: [NHS A&E Finder](https://www.nhs.uk/service-search/a-and-e)

### Important Safety Tips for A&E
- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you. Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.
- Bring all your medicines with you.

---

## What to Look For: Symptoms

You may have bulging eyes if:
- Your eyes look like they are sticking out more than normal.
- Your upper eyelids cover less of your eyes. Your eyes may look wide open.
- You can see more of the white part of your eyes.

Other symptoms depend on what is causing the bulging. You might also have:
- Pain in your eyes.
- Trouble closing your eyes or moving them.
- Dry eyes, or a feeling like there is dirt or sand in your eyes.
- Pain when looking at bright lights.

---

## What Can Cause Bulging Eyes?

A common cause is an overactive thyroid gland. This is when the small gland in your neck makes too much thyroid hormone.

Less common causes include:
- Infection or injury near or behind your eyes.
- Bleeding behind your eyes or problems with blood vessels behind your eyes.
- Tumours, including those from neuroblastoma or some soft tissue sarcomas.

---

## How Bulging Eyes Are Treated

Treatment depends on the cause.

You might need:
- Eye drops.
- Medicine to treat infections, swelling, or thyroid problems.
- Surgery if the bulging does not improve after other treatments.

If the cause is not clear, your doctor may refer you to a specialist. You may need more tests to find the cause.

---

## What You Can Do to Feel Better

### Do These Things:
- Use extra pillows to keep your head raised when lying down.
- Wear sunglasses if bright light hurts your eyes.
- If you wear contact lenses, take them out and wear glasses instead. This gives your eyes a rest.

### Avoid These Things:
- Do not smoke.
- Do not drink too much alcohol.
- Avoid smoky, dry, or dusty places for long periods.
- Do not stay too long in very dry, heated, or air-conditioned rooms.

# Aphasia

Aphasia is a problem with language. It can make it hard to understand words or to speak. It can also affect reading and writing.

Aphasia happens when parts of the brain that control language are damaged. This damage can happen in the outer layer of the brain or in the deep connections between brain areas.

Doctors diagnose aphasia by talking with the patient and doing tests. They may use brain scans like CT or MRI to find the cause.

How well a person recovers depends on the cause, how much the brain is damaged, and the person’s age.

There is no single medicine for aphasia. But speech therapy can help many people get better.

Most right-handed people have language in the left side of the brain. About two-thirds of left-handed people also have language in the left side. The other one-third have language in the right side.

The main parts of the brain involved in language are:

- The back and upper part of the temporal lobe (this includes the Wernicke area)
- The lower part of the parietal lobe next to it
- The back and lower part of the frontal lobe, just in front of the area that controls movement (this includes the Broca area)
- The deep white matter pathways that connect these areas

If any part of this area is damaged — by a stroke, tumor, injury, or disease — language problems can occur.

The rhythm, tone, and emphasis of speech (called prosody) usually involve both sides of the brain. But sometimes only the non-dominant side is affected.

Aphasia is not the same as learning problems in childhood. It is also not the same as problems with the muscles used to speak (dysarthria).

---

## What Causes Aphasia?

Aphasia often comes from sudden brain damage. Examples include:

- Stroke
- Head injury
- Brain infection (encephalitis)

When the cause is sudden, aphasia does not get worse over time.

Sometimes aphasia gets worse slowly. This can happen with:

- A growing brain tumor
- Dementia

---

## Types of Aphasia

Aphasia is split into two main types: receptive and expressive.

### Receptive Aphasia (also called sensory, fluent, or Wernicke aphasia)

- The person cannot understand spoken or written words.
- They may not recognize pictures, sounds, or touch signals.
- This happens when the Wernicke area in the left side of the brain is damaged.
- Many people with this type also lose the ability to read (called alexia).

### Expressive Aphasia (also called motor, nonfluent, or Broca aphasia)

- The person has trouble saying words.
- They understand what others say and can think clearly.
- This happens when the Broca area in the left side of the brain is damaged.
- It often causes problems with writing (called agraphia).
- Reading aloud is also hard.

There are other types of aphasia. They can overlap. No system of classification is perfect. The best way to describe aphasia is to list the specific problems a person has.

---

### Types of Aphasia (Summary)

| Type | Brain Area Damaged | Common Causes | Speech Pattern | Other Features |
|------|--------------------|---------------|----------------|----------------|
| **Anomic** | Small damage anywhere in the left language areas | Stroke, bleeding, injury, tumor | Fluent speech, but trouble naming things | Can’t name objects. Speaks in roundabout ways. Understands and repeats well. Can read and write. |
| **Broca (nonfluent)** | Large damage in left frontal or frontoparietal area | Stroke, bleeding, injury, tumor | Slow, effortful speech. Short sentences. Few words. | Can understand. Hard to repeat. Writing is slow and hard. |
| **Conduction** | Deep area under the left temporal or parietal lobe | Stroke, bleeding, tumor | Speaks fluently, but makes word errors | Understands well. Can’t repeat words correctly. Reading is fine. Writing is fine. |
| **Global** | Large damage in left frontotemporoparietal area | Stroke, bleeding, injury, tumor | Very poor speech. Few words. Hard to understand | Can’t understand, can’t repeat, can’t read, can’t write. |
| **Transcortical Motor** | Left frontal area (not Broca or Wernicke) | Stroke, encephalitis, bleeding, injury, tumor | Like Broca aphasia, but can repeat words well | Speech is slow. Can’t write well. But repetition is good. |
| **Transcortical Sensory** | Left temporoparietal area (not Broca or Wernicke) | Stroke, encephalitis, bleeding, injury, tumor | Like Wernicke aphasia, but can repeat words well | Can’t understand. Speaks fluently but nonsense. Can’t read. |
| **Wernicke (fluent)** | Large damage in left temporoparietal area | Stroke, tumor | Fluent speech, but full of wrong or made-up words | Can’t understand. Can’t repeat. Can’t read. Writing is fluent but wrong. |

> **Note:**  
> - The damaged area is usually in the left side of the brain.  
> - Paraphasic speech means using the wrong word, a mispronounced word, or a mix of words that make no sense.

---

## Symptoms of Aphasia

The most common symptom is trouble naming things. This happens in all types of aphasia.

---

## How Is Aphasia Diagnosed?

Doctors must tell aphasia apart from other communication problems. These include:

- Severe slurred speech (dysarthria)
- Hearing loss
- Vision problems (especially when reading)
- Problems using the hands to write

A doctor may check for aphasia by asking simple questions and doing tests.

### Bedside Tests

These tests look at:

- **Spontaneous speech:** Is speech fluent? How many words are said? Does the person start talking? Are there pauses or errors?
- **Naming:** Can the person name common objects? If not, do they describe them? (For example, “the thing you use to tell time” for “clock”.)
- **Repetition:** Can the person repeat a sentence like “no ifs, ands, or buts”?
- **Comprehension:** Can the person follow simple and complex commands? Can they point to objects when named?
- **Reading and writing:** Can the person read aloud? Can they write on their own? Can they write what is said to them?

### Formal Testing

A neuropsychologist or speech therapist may do more detailed tests. These help find small problems and plan treatment.

Examples of formal tests:
- Boston Diagnostic Aphasia Examination
- Western Aphasia Battery
- Boston Naming Test
- Token Test
- Action Naming Test

### Brain Imaging

Scans like CT or MRI are needed. They show the size and location of brain damage. They help find the cause — such as a stroke or tumor.

Further tests may be done to find the root cause.

---

## How Is Aphasia Treated?

### Treat the Cause
- If a tumor causes swelling, steroids may help.
- If a stroke is the cause, treatment can prevent more damage.

### Speech Therapy
- This is the most helpful treatment.
- It improves communication after stroke.
- It helps people use their remaining language skills.

### Augmentative Communication Devices
- For people who can’t recover basic language, these tools help.
- Examples:
  - A picture book with daily needs
  - A communication board with symbols
  - A computer with voice output

These tools help patients and caregivers communicate.

---

## What Is the Outlook for Aphasia?

Recovery depends on:

- The cause of the brain damage
- How big and where the damage is
- How severe the language problems are
- How well the person responds to therapy
- Age, education, and overall health (to a lesser degree)

Children under 8 years old often recover language even after major brain damage.

For older children and adults, most recovery happens in the first 3 months after brain injury. Some improvement can continue for up to a year.

---

## Key Points

- Language is in the left side of the brain for most right-handed people and about two-thirds of left-handed people.
- Describe aphasia by listing the specific problems (like naming, repeating, understanding) because types overlap and no system is perfect.
- At the bedside, test the person’s ability to name, repeat, understand, read, and write.
- Do brain imaging to find the cause.
- Consider formal testing by a specialist.
- Treat the cause if possible.
- Recommend speech therapy.

# Folliculitis and Skin Abscesses

## What Are Folliculitis and Skin Abscesses?

Folliculitis and skin abscesses are infections that cause pus-filled lumps in the skin.  
They happen when bacteria get into the skin.  
These lumps can be small and close to the surface.  
Or they can be deeper and affect more than just the hair follicles.

Folliculitis is a small infection in a hair follicle.  
It looks like a tiny red or white bump at the base of a hair.  
Other types of abscesses can form on the skin or deeper in the skin.  
They do not always start in a hair follicle.

Most skin abscesses are caused by a type of bacteria called *Staphylococcus aureus*.  
This bacteria causes pus to build up under the skin.  
A tough strain of this bacteria, called MRSA, is now common.  
MRSA does not respond to many common antibiotics.

Bacteria can enter the skin through a small cut, scrape, or puncture.  
Sometimes, there is no clear wound.  
People who live in crowded places, have poor hygiene, or have long-term skin problems are more likely to get these infections.  
People with a weak immune system, obesity, older age, or diabetes are also at higher risk.  
Some people get repeated infections for no clear reason.

Doctors may help prevent repeat infections by having people:  
- Wash their whole body with antibacterial soap.  
- Put antibiotic cream inside their nose.  
- Take antibiotics by mouth.

---

## Folliculitis

Folliculitis is an infection in a single hair follicle.  
It shows up as a small red or white bump at the base of a hair.  
You might have just one bump or many.  
Each bump may itch or hurt a little.  
But you will not feel sick overall.

Some people get folliculitis after using a hot tub or whirlpool that is not clean.  
This is called “hot tub folliculitis” or “hot tub dermatitis.”  
It is caused by a germ called *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*.  
Symptoms can start as soon as 6 hours or as late as 5 days after using the hot tub.  
The skin under a bathing suit—like the chest, back, and buttocks—is most often affected.

Some people get mild folliculitis in areas that stay wet and rub a lot.  
This can happen under sports gear or on the buttocks.

Infected hairs may fall out easily.  
They may also be pulled out.  
But new bumps often appear in the same area.

Sometimes, stiff hairs in the beard area (or any shaved area) curl back into the skin after shaving.  
This causes irritation and redness.  
But there is no infection.  
This is called pseudofolliculitis barbae.  
It is not true folliculitis.

For severe or recurring folliculitis, doctors may take a sample of pus.  
They send it to a lab to grow the bacteria.  
This helps them pick the right antibiotic.

Treatment for folliculitis includes:  
- Antiseptic soaps or creams applied to the skin.  
- Antibiotics applied directly to the skin.  
- Oral antibiotics for large areas of infection.

Hot tub folliculitis usually gets better on its own.  
But the hot tub must be properly cleaned with chlorine to stop it from coming back.  
This also protects others from getting sick.

Pseudofolliculitis barbae (ingrown hairs) can be treated in different ways.  
Results vary.  
You may need to stop shaving for a while.

---

## Skin Abscesses

Skin abscesses are painful, warm lumps filled with pus.  
They form under the skin and can appear anywhere on the body.  
They are usually red and raised.  
They can be from one inch to several inches wide.

There are two main types: furuncles and carbuncles.

### Furuncles (Boils)

Furuncles are small, painful abscesses.  
They start in a hair follicle and spread to nearby tissue.  
They are common on the neck, face, breasts, and buttocks.  
They can be very painful, especially in sensitive areas like the nose, ear, or fingers.

A furuncle looks like a red, swollen, pus-filled bump.  
It may hurt when touched.

### Carbuncles

Carbuncles are clusters of furuncles.  
They are connected under the skin.  
They are larger and more serious than single boils.

If not treated, abscesses may grow and burst.  
They release a thick, white or pink fluid.  
The infection can spread to nearby skin and lymph nodes.  
You may get a fever and feel unwell.

Doctors usually diagnose abscesses by looking at them.  
Sometimes, they take a sample of pus to test for the bacteria.

An abscess may go away on its own.  
Warm compresses can help it drain faster.  
But often, a doctor must cut it open and drain the pus.

After draining, the doctor checks that all the pus is out.  
They may rinse the area with salt water.  
Large abscesses—over 5 centimeters (about 2 inches)—may need gauze packing to keep them open while healing.

If the abscess is fully drained, antibiotics are usually not needed.  
But antibiotics by mouth may be given if:

- The abscess did not heal after drainage.  
- You have a weak immune system.  
- The infection spread to nearby skin (called cellulitis).  
- You have many abscesses.  
- You are at risk for a heart infection (endocarditis).  
- The abscess is on the middle of the face.  
- You have a fever.

People who keep getting boils can prevent them by:  
- Washing their skin with special antiseptic soap.  
- Taking antibiotics for 1 to 2 months.

# Metabolic Syndrome

Metabolic syndrome often has no symptoms.  
You usually find out you have it during a routine blood test or health check-up.

We do not know exactly what causes metabolic syndrome.  
It is linked to insulin resistance. This means your body does not use insulin well.  
It may also be linked to carrying too much fat around your belly.

## What to do if you think you are at risk

See your doctor if you think you might be at risk.

## Signs and symptoms

You may not feel any symptoms.  
Most people only learn they have metabolic syndrome after a blood test or check-up.

## How to check your risk

Metabolic syndrome is very common.  
We do not know what causes it.  
It is linked to insulin resistance.  
It may also be linked to having too much fat around your waist.

You are more likely to develop metabolic syndrome if you:

- Are overweight or have obesity  
- Eat a lot of foods high in saturated fat  
- Do not get enough physical activity  
- Are of Hispanic or South Asian descent  
- Smoke cigarettes  
- Drink a lot of alcohol  

Your risk goes up as you get older.

## Treatment options

Treatment usually starts with lifestyle changes.  
You may also be given medicines to help with:

- Losing weight  
- Improving how your body uses insulin and controls blood sugar  
- Lowering bad cholesterol  
- Reducing high blood pressure

## How to prevent metabolic syndrome

The best way to prevent metabolic syndrome is to live a healthy lifestyle.  
This also helps treat it and lowers your risk of serious health problems.

### Do these things:

- Try to lose weight if you are overweight  
- Eat less saturated fat  
- Eat fewer meats and dairy products  
- Eat more fruits, vegetables, and whole grains  
- Be active for at least 150 minutes each week  
- Spread your activity over at least 4 or 5 days  
- Try to cut down or stop smoking if you smoke

### Avoid these habits:

- Do not sit for long periods without moving

# Anal Fissure

An anal fissure is a small cut or sore in the skin around the anus. It can cause sharp pain and sometimes bleeding, especially when you pass a bowel movement. Most people find the pain starts during a bowel movement and lasts for hours. The pain often returns with the next bowel movement.

## What Causes an Anal Fissure?

Most fissures happen when you pass a hard or large stool. Frequent loose bowel movements can also cause them. Rarely, anal fissures are caused by trauma, such as anal sex.

The muscles around the anus can tighten up when you have a fissure. This tightness reduces blood flow to the area. Less blood flow makes it harder for the wound to heal.

## Symptoms and Signs

Most fissures are in the middle of the back of the anus. Some may be in the front. Fissures that are not in the middle may be linked to other health problems, such as Crohn disease.

You may notice a small lump of skin near the bottom of the fissure. This is called a sentinel pile. You might also see a small bump near the top of the fissure. This is called a hypertrophic papilla.

The main symptoms are:
- Sharp pain during or right after a bowel movement
- Small amounts of bright red blood on the toilet paper or in the toilet bowl

A doctor will gently spread your buttocks to look at the area. The exam must be careful but thorough.

Chronic fissures can look like other serious conditions. These include anal cancer, syphilis, tuberculosis, and ulcers from Crohn disease. It is important to rule these out.

Fissures are common in babies. But long-term fissures are rare in children.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor can usually diagnose an anal fissure by looking at the area. If the fissure looks normal and is in the usual spot, no further tests are needed.

## How Is It Treated?

Most fissures heal with simple steps that reduce pain and trauma during bowel movements.

### Lifestyle and Home Care
- Eat more fiber. This makes your stool softer and easier to pass.
- Drink plenty of fluids.
- Use stool softeners if needed.
- Try fiber supplements like psyllium.

### Skin Protection and Relief
- Use a protective ointment with zinc oxide. It helps protect the skin and keeps the area moist.
- Use simple suppositories like glycerin. They help soften the stool and ease passage.
- Take warm (not hot) sitz baths for 10 to 15 minutes after each bowel movement. This can ease pain and help healing.
- Use a numbing cream or ointment like benzocaine or lidocaine for short-term pain relief.

### Medicines That Help the Muscle Relax
- Apply nitroglycerin ointment (0.2%) to the area. It helps relax the muscle around the anus.
- Use a cream with nifedipine (0.2%) or a gel with diltiazem (2%). These also relax the muscle.
- In some cases, a doctor may inject a medicine called onabotulinumtoxinA into the muscle. This helps it relax.

These medicines work by reducing pressure in the anal muscle. This improves blood flow and helps the fissure heal.

### Surgery
If the fissure does not heal after trying all other treatments, surgery may be needed. The most common surgery is called an internal anal sphincterotomy. This cuts a small part of the muscle to stop it from tightening. This breaks the cycle of pain and muscle spasm, allowing the wound to heal.

Healing takes time. Most people see improvement within a few weeks. Be patient and follow your doctor’s advice.

# Angioedema – Simple Explanation

Angioedema is swelling under the skin. It can happen in the face, throat, or other parts of the body.

## What Is Angioedema?

- Swelling happens just under the skin, not on the surface.
- It can affect the face, lips, tongue, throat, hands, feet, or genitals.
- It may make it hard to swallow or breathe.
- It can also affect the stomach and intestines, causing nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, or diarrhea.

## Common Causes

Angioedema can happen for many reasons:

- A reaction to a medicine or other substance (like food or insect stings).
- A rare inherited condition.
- A problem with the immune system.
- A rare side effect of some cancers.
- Sometimes, doctors do not know the cause.

## Hives and Angioedema

- Angioedema often happens with hives.
- Hives are small, raised, itchy spots on the skin.
- Hives are on the surface of the skin.
- Angioedema is deeper under the skin.
- Swelling from angioedema may not itch.

## Types of Angioedema

### Acute Angioedema

This type comes on suddenly after exposure to a trigger.

**Common triggers include:**

- Medicines like aspirin, other pain relievers (NSAIDs), blood pressure drugs (ACE inhibitors), and certain pain medicines (like morphine or codeine).
- Insect stings or bites.
- Allergy shots (immunotherapy).
- Certain foods — especially eggs, fish, shellfish, nuts, and some fruits.
- A special dye used in X-rays (called contrast agent).

**Note:** ACE inhibitors can cause angioedema without hives. The face and throat are most often affected. The stomach may also be involved.

- Small amounts of some foods can cause a reaction.
- Other foods (like strawberries) may only cause a reaction after a large amount is eaten.

### Chronic Angioedema

This type comes back over weeks or months.

- The cause is often unknown.
- It may be due to repeated exposure to a substance, like penicillin in milk or dyes in food.
- Some medicines, like aspirin, other pain relievers, or certain pain medicines, can cause it.
- It can be hereditary or acquired (not inherited but caused by another health problem).
- When no cause is found, it is called idiopathic angioedema.

## Symptoms

- Swelling may be worse on one side of the body.
- It can be painful or uncomfortable.
- Swelling can happen in the eyelids, lips, tongue, face, hands, feet, or genitals.
- Swelling in the throat or airways can make it hard to breathe or swallow.
- Swelling in the stomach can cause nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, or diarrhea.
- Many people also get hives.
- Hives usually start with itching.
- Hives come and go. One spot may last a few hours, then fade. Another may appear later.
- After a hive goes away, the skin looks normal.

## Serious Reactions

- Some people have a severe allergic reaction called anaphylaxis.
- This can cause a sudden drop in blood pressure.
- This can be life-threatening.

## When to See a Doctor

- See a doctor right away if you have angioedema.
- The cause is often clear, so tests are not usually needed.
- If swelling comes back and the cause is not clear, your doctor will ask about:
  - All medicines you take.
  - All foods and drinks you consume.
- If you have no hives or if others in your family have angioedema, your doctor may test for rare forms.

## Treatment

### For Mild Angioedema with Hives

- Take antihistamine pills. They help with itching and reduce swelling.
- If symptoms are severe, your doctor may prescribe corticosteroid pills.
  - These are only used for a short time.
  - Long-term use (more than 3 to 4 weeks) can cause serious side effects.
- Creams, ointments, or lotions with steroids do not help.

### For Angioedema Without Hives

- Antihistamines, steroids, and epinephrine may not help.
- If caused by an ACE inhibitor:
  - Symptoms usually go away in 24 to 48 hours after stopping the medicine.
- If symptoms do not go away, are severe, or get worse:
  - Doctors may give fresh frozen plasma.
  - They may use special medicines like ecallantide.
  - They may use a purified form of a protein called C1 inhibitor (made from human blood).

### For Idiopathic Angioedema (no known cause)

- A high dose of antihistamine pills may help.

## Emergency Treatment

If angioedema causes trouble breathing or swallowing, or if you feel faint:

- Get emergency help right away.
- Doctors may:
  - Give epinephrine under the skin or into a muscle. This helps reduce swelling.
  - Insert a breathing tube through the mouth or nose into the windpipe (intubation).
  - If the airway closes too fast, they may make a small cut in the neck and insert a breathing tube.

## What You Should Do

- Always carry a self-injecting syringe of epinephrine if you have had a severe reaction.
- Use it immediately if symptoms start.
- Take antihistamine pills after using epinephrine.
- Go to the hospital emergency department after a severe reaction.
  - You need to be checked and treated if needed.

# Sciatica – Simple Guide

## What is sciatica?

Sciatica is a type of pain that starts in your lower back or bottom. It runs down the back of one leg. It can go all the way to your foot and toes.

You may feel:
- Sharp, burning pain
- Tingling, like pins and needles
- Numbness
- Weakness in the leg

The pain can start suddenly or slowly. It often gets worse when you move, sneeze, or cough.

You might also have back pain. But the leg pain is usually worse.

> **Note:** If you only have back pain and no leg pain, you probably do not have sciatica.

## When to see a doctor

See your doctor if:
- Your pain has not improved after a few weeks of home care
- Your pain is getting worse
- The pain stops you from doing your usual activities

## When to go to A&E or call 999

Go to A&E or call 999 right away if you have sciatica and:
- Pain is in both legs
- You have serious or worsening weakness or numbness in both legs
- You have numbness around your genitals or around your bottom (anus)
- You have trouble starting to pee, cannot pee, or cannot control when you pee – especially if this is new for you
- You do not notice when you need to go to the toilet, or cannot control your bowels – especially if this is new for you

These signs could mean a serious problem with your back. You need treatment in hospital right away.

> **Important:** Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you. Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
> Bring all your medicines with you.

---

## How to ease sciatica pain at home

Sciatica often gets better in a few weeks to a few months. But it can last longer. It can also come back.

### Do these things to help:

- Keep doing your normal daily activities as much as you can
- Try regular exercises for sciatica
- Start gentle movement as soon as you can – even light activity helps
- Use heat packs on the painful areas – you can buy these at a pharmacy
- Talk to a pharmacist about painkillers. Paracetamol may not help much. It’s not clear how well medicines like ibuprofen work for sciatica

### Do not do these things:

- Do not stay sitting or lying down for long periods. Even if moving hurts, it is not harmful. Moving can help you get better faster.

---

## Treatments from your doctor

If you see a doctor, they may:
- Give you exercises and stretches to do
- Prescribe painkillers

They may also refer you for:
- Physiotherapy – this includes exercise advice and hands-on treatment like massage
- Psychological support – to help you manage the pain and stay positive

Physiotherapy is free on the NHS across the UK. But wait times can be long. You can also get it privately.

---

## Other treatments if needed

If your pain is very bad and home care or doctor treatments do not help, your doctor may refer you to a hospital specialist. They may suggest:
- A procedure to stop nerves from sending pain signals (radiofrequency denervation)
- A painkilling injection, such as an epidural
- Surgery – a type called decompression surgery can help some people

---

## Can you refer yourself for help?

Yes, in some areas, you can refer yourself directly to sciatica treatment services without seeing a doctor first.

To find out if this is possible where you live:
- Ask the staff at your GP surgery
- Check your GP surgery’s website
- Contact your local integrated care board (ICB)
- Search online for “NHS treatment for sciatica near me”

---

## How to reduce your risk of sciatica

You may get sciatica again. But you can take steps to help prevent it or reduce the pain.

### Do these things:

- Stay active – do regular exercise
- Use safe lifting techniques when carrying heavy things
- Keep good posture when sitting and standing
- Sit properly when using a computer
- Lose weight if you are overweight

### Do not do these things:

- Do not smoke – smoking increases your risk of sciatica

---

## What causes sciatica?

Sciatica happens when something presses on or rubs the sciatic nerve.

Common causes include:
- A slipped disc – when a soft cushion between the bones in your spine pushes out. This is the most common cause. It becomes more likely as you get older.
- Spinal stenosis – when the space in your spine where nerves pass through gets narrower.
- Spondylolisthesis – when one bone in your spine slips out of place.
- A back injury.

# Penicillins

Penicillins are a type of antibiotic.  
They kill bacteria.  
The exact way they work is not fully known.  
They may work by turning on natural enzymes that break down the outer wall of some bacteria.

> *For more information, see: Overview of Antibacterial Medications.*

---

## Types of Penicillins

Here are the main types of penicillins and how they are taken:

| Penicillin Type | How It Is Taken |
|------------------|-----------------|
| Penicillin G (injected form) | Injected into a vein or muscle |
| Penicillin G benzathine | Injected into muscle only |
| Penicillin G procaine | Injected into muscle |
| Penicillin V potassium | Taken by mouth |
| Ampicillin | Taken by mouth or injected |
| Ampicillin and sulbactam | Injected into a vein |
| Amoxicillin | Taken by mouth |
| Amoxicillin and clavulanate | Taken by mouth |
| Dicloxacillin | Taken by mouth |
| Nafcillin | Taken by mouth or injected |
| Oxacillin | Taken by mouth or injected |
| Piperacillin and tazobactam | Injected into a vein |

---

## How Penicillins Work in the Body

Amoxicillin can be taken with food.  
Penicillin G should be taken one hour before or two hours after eating.  
Amoxicillin is now used more often than ampicillin.  
It is better absorbed, causes fewer stomach problems, and does not need to be taken as often.

Penicillins spread quickly through body fluids.  
They reach most tissues, especially when there is swelling or inflammation.

All penicillins leave the body through the kidneys.  
Most of them end up in the urine.  
Injected penicillin G leaves the body very fast.  
Its half-life is about 30 minutes.  
But two special forms — benzathine and procaine — are made to last longer.

- Benzathine penicillin is slowly released from the muscle.  
- It takes longer to reach peak levels.  
- It stays in the body for up to 30 days.  
- Procaine penicillin is absorbed faster.  
- It reaches peak levels quicker.  
- It stays in the body for about one week.

The body clears procaine penicillin faster than benzathine penicillin.

---

## When Penicillins Are Used

Penicillins are used to treat many bacterial infections.  
They are especially good for infections caused by certain types of bacteria.

---

## Who Should Not Take Penicillins

Do not take penicillins if you have had a serious allergic reaction to them.  
This includes rash, swelling, trouble breathing, or anaphylaxis.

---

## Penicillins During Pregnancy and Breastfeeding

Penicillins are safe to use during pregnancy.  
Animal studies have not shown harm to the baby.  
Human data is limited, but they are still considered safe when needed.  
Penicillin G is very effective at preventing syphilis from passing from mother to baby.  
It can also treat both the mother and the baby if infected.

Penicillins pass into breast milk in small amounts.  
They are usually safe to use while breastfeeding.

---

## Side Effects of Penicillins

Common side effects include:

- Skin rash (most common)
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Diarrhea

Other side effects are rare.

Taking oral penicillins can sometimes cause a condition called black hairy tongue.  
This happens because the surface of the tongue becomes irritated and thickened.  
It is harmless and goes away when you stop taking the medicine.

---

## Dosing Tips

Most penicillins are removed from the body through the kidneys.  
If your kidneys are not working well, you may need a lower dose.  
This is especially true for penicillins that are not used against staph infections (like nafcillin, oxacillin, cloxacillin, and dicloxacillin).

A medicine called probenecid can slow down how fast penicillins leave the body.  
This keeps more of the antibiotic in your blood.  
It is sometimes used with penicillins to help them work better.

# Polio Vaccine

Polio is a serious virus that can affect the spine and brain.  
It can lead to lasting muscle weakness, paralysis, and in rare cases, death.  

Thanks to widespread vaccination, polio is now very rare in most parts of the world.  
But wild polio still happens in some areas.

(See also: Overview of Immunization.)

---

## Types of Polio Vaccine

There are two types of polio vaccine used around the world:

### Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV)

- This vaccine contains a killed piece of the poliovirus.  
- The piece cannot cause polio.  
- It still helps the body’s immune system learn how to fight the real virus.  
- This is the only polio vaccine used in the United States since 2000.  
- It can be given with other vaccines, such as:
  - Diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis (DTaP) vaccine  
  - Hepatitis B vaccine  
  - *Haemophilus influenzae* type b vaccine  

### Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV)

- This vaccine contains a weakened but still live form of the poliovirus.  
- It is taken by mouth.  
- In very rare cases (about 1 in 2.9 million doses), the weakened virus can change and spread to unvaccinated people.  
- This changed virus can cause polio in people who are not vaccinated.  
- Because of this risk, the United States stopped using OPV.  
- However, in some poorer countries, OPV is still used because it helps stop the spread of polio more easily than IPV.  
- The benefits of OPV in these areas often outweigh the small risk.

---

## How and When to Get the Polio Vaccine

### Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV)

- It is given as an injection into a muscle or under the skin.  
- It is a routine vaccine for children in the United States.  
- Four doses are needed:
  - First dose at 2 months of age  
  - Second dose at 4 months of age  
  - Third dose at 6 to 18 months of age  
  - Final dose at 4 to 6 years of age  

Polio is now very rare in the United States.  
But you may be at higher risk if you:
- Travel to areas where polio is still common  
- Work in a lab with materials that might contain the virus  
- Care for someone who has polio  

### For Adults

- If you were never vaccinated or only partly vaccinated, you need three doses of IPV.  
- Most adults born after 1955 in the United States were vaccinated as children.  
  - You can assume you are protected unless you know otherwise.  
- If you finished your polio shots but are at higher risk of exposure, you may get one booster dose.  

### Recent Outbreak in the United States

- In July 2022, a case of vaccine-derived polio was found in an unvaccinated person in New York State.  
- No other cases have been found in the U.S. since then.  
- But the virus was found in wastewater in several New York counties.  
  - This means the virus was spreading in the community.  
- People in those areas may be at higher risk.  
- Follow the latest advice from the New York State Department of Health.

---

## Who Should Not Get the Polio Vaccine

Do not get the vaccine if you:
- Had a serious allergic reaction (like anaphylaxis) after a past dose  
- Had anaphylaxis to any ingredient in the vaccine, such as:
  - Streptomycin  
  - Neomycin  
  - Polymyxin B  

Pregnant people who are not at risk of polio should not get the vaccine.  
There is no evidence it harms the baby.  
But if a pregnant person is at high risk of exposure and needs protection, the inactivated vaccine can be given.

If you are sick with a fever or a serious illness, wait until you feel better before getting the vaccine.

---

## Side Effects of the Polio Vaccine

Common side effects:
- Soreness, redness, or swelling at the injection site  
- Skin thickening at the site  
- Mild fever  
- Feeling irritable  
- Feeling tired  

These side effects are usually mild and go away in a few days.

Serious side effects are very rare.

For more details on side effects, read the package insert that comes with the vaccine.

---

## More Information

The following resources are in English and may help you learn more:

- Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC): Polio vaccine information statement  
- European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC): Poliomyelitis: Recommended vaccinations

# Toxocariasis – Simple Guide

## What is toxocariasis?

Toxocariasis is an infection caused by tiny worms. These worms live in the intestines of dogs, cats, and foxes. Their eggs can be found in animal poo.

You can get infected if you swallow soil, sand, or anything that has animal poo on it. The eggs must have been in the soil or sand for a few weeks or more to become dangerous.

You cannot catch toxocariasis from fresh animal poo. You also cannot pass it to another person.

## Is it serious?

Most people who swallow the worm eggs do not get sick. The eggs can hatch into small worm-like larvae. These larvae usually travel through the body but die without causing harm.

But in rare cases, the larvae can cause serious problems. They may affect the liver, lungs, or eyes. This can lead to serious health issues.

## What are the symptoms?

You only get symptoms if the larvae spread in your body. Symptoms depend on where the larvae go.

Common symptoms include:
- A high temperature
- Coughing or wheezing
- Stomach pain
- Itchy skin rash
- Red or painful eyes
- Changes in vision, such as seeing small dots, lines, or flashes of light
- Loss of vision (usually in one eye)

## When to get help

Call your doctor right away or use NHS 111 if you or your child:
- Ate soil, sand, or animal poo
- And have any of the following:
  - A high temperature
  - Coughing or wheezing
  - Stomach pain
  - Itchy rash
  - Red or painful eye
  - Changes in vision (like seeing dots, lines, or flashes)
  - Loss of vision

You can call 111 or get help online at [nhs.uk/111](https://www.nhs.uk/111)

## How is it treated?

You only need treatment if you have symptoms.

The main treatment is medicine to kill the worm larvae.

If the larvae affect your eye, you may also get steroid medicine. This helps reduce swelling and damage. In some cases, surgery may be needed to remove the larvae or fix vision problems.

## How to lower your risk

Toxocariasis is rare, but you can take simple steps to stay safe.

### Do these things:
- Wash your hands often, especially before eating
- Wear gloves when gardening
- Teach young children not to eat dirt or sand
- Wash fruits and vegetables before eating them
- Pick up dog and cat poo right away and put it in the bin
- Make sure your pets are treated for worms regularly

### Avoid these things:
- Letting pets poop in areas where children play, like sandpits or playgrounds
- Letting children play in places where animal poo might be present

Taking these steps helps protect you and your family. It also helps keep pets healthy and stops worms from spreading.

# Nausea and Vomiting During Early Pregnancy

Up to 8 out of 10 pregnant women have nausea or vomiting.  
These symptoms are most common and worst in the first three months of pregnancy.  
People often call this "morning sickness."  
But nausea or vomiting can happen at any time of day.  
Symptoms can be mild or very bad.  
Very bad vomiting is called hyperemesis gravidarum.

## What Is Hyperemesis Gravidarum?

Hyperemesis gravidarum means severe vomiting during pregnancy.  
It happens again and again.  
It stops you from drinking or eating enough.  
This can lead to serious dehydration.  
It may also cause low levels of important body chemicals.  
It can cause weight loss of more than 5 percent of your pre-pregnancy weight.

## What Causes Nausea and Vomiting?

We do not fully understand why nausea and vomiting happen in early pregnancy.  
But several things may play a role: how your body uses energy, hormones, your gut, and your mood.  
Higher levels of estrogen may be linked to worse symptoms.

## Common Causes

The most common causes of nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy are:

- Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (this is the most common cause)
- Hyperemesis gravidarum
- Gastroenteritis (a stomach bug)
- Prenatal vitamins with iron (these can cause nausea in some women)
- A rare condition called a hydatidiform mole (a growth in the uterus that is not a baby)

Vomiting can also come from other health problems not related to pregnancy.  
For example, appendicitis or gallbladder problems can cause vomiting.  
But the main symptom is usually pain, not just vomiting.  
Some brain or nervous system problems can also cause vomiting.  
But headache or other brain symptoms are usually the main issue.

### Causes of Nausea and Vomiting in Early Pregnancy

| Cause | What to Look For | How It Is Checked |
|------|------------------|-------------------|
| **Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy** | Mild, occasional nausea or vomiting at any time of day. Mostly in the first trimester. | Check your health history and do a physical exam. No tests needed if symptoms are mild. |
| **Hyperemesis gravidarum** | Vomiting that happens often and does not stop. You cannot keep food or fluids down. | Signs of dehydration (fast heartbeat, dry mouth, thirst). Urine test shows ketones. Weight loss over 5% of your pre-pregnancy weight. Blood tests check electrolytes, kidney function, liver, and magnesium. |
| **Hydatidiform mole** | Uterus is bigger than expected. No baby heartbeat or movement. Sometimes high blood pressure or vaginal bleeding. In later stages, swelling all over the body or grape-like tissue from the cervix. | Blood pressure check. Blood test for hCG (a pregnancy hormone). Thyroid test. Kidney and liver tests. X-ray of the chest. Ultrasound of the pelvis. A procedure called D and C may be done. |
| **Gastroenteritis** | Sudden vomiting that does not last long. Usually comes with diarrhea. | Physical exam. The belly feels soft and not tender. Sometimes stool tests. |
| **Bowel obstruction** | Sudden vomiting. Often happens after abdominal surgery, or if you have cancer in the belly, or a trapped hernia. | Pain that comes and goes. No bowel movement. Belly is swollen and hard. Imaging tests like X-rays, ultrasound, or CT scan may be used. |
| **Urinary tract infection or kidney infection** | Need to pee often, or feel burning when peeing. May have back pain or fever. | Urine test and culture. |

D and C = widening the opening of the uterus and removing tissue.  
hCG = human chorionic gonadotropin (a hormone made during pregnancy).

## How Is It Checked?

The main goal is to rule out serious or life-threatening causes.  
Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum are only diagnosed after other causes are ruled out.

## How Is It Treated?

Some women feel better by eating small meals often—5 to 6 times a day.  
Stick to simple foods like crackers, bananas, rice, applesauce, and dry toast.  
Try eating something before you get out of bed in the morning.

If you are dehydrated (for example, from severe vomiting), you may need fluids through a needle in your arm.  
You may get 1 to 2 liters of normal saline or Ringer’s lactate.  
Your doctor will fix any chemical imbalances in your blood.

After fluids are given, your doctor may add sugar (dextrose) to your IV fluids.  
But before giving sugar, you must get a shot of vitamin B1 (thiamine) to prevent brain damage.

If you still cannot eat or drink, your doctor may use a tube through your nose to feed you.  
This tube goes into your stomach or small intestine.  
A central IV line (a long tube in a large vein) is not used.  
It can cause serious infections or blood clots during pregnancy.

### Medicines That Can Help

| Medicine | Dose | How It Is Taken |
|--------|------|----------------|
| Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) | 10 to 25 mg | 3 to 4 times a day by mouth |
| Doxylamine | 25 mg | At bedtime by mouth |
| Promethazine | 12.5 to 25 mg | By mouth, injection, or rectal suppository every 6 hours as needed |
| Metoclopramide | 5 to 10 mg | Every 8 hours by mouth or injection |
| Ondansetron | 4 to 8 mg | Every 12 hours by mouth or IV as needed |

- Start with vitamin B6 alone.  
- Add other medicines if symptoms do not improve.  
- If you do not respond to the first treatment, try a long-acting version of doxylamine with vitamin B6.

Other things that may help:

- Ginger (250 mg capsules 3 to 4 times a day, or ginger lollipops)  
- Acupuncture  
- Motion sickness bands  
- Hypnosis  
- Switch to a children’s chewable vitamin with folate instead of prenatal vitamins

## Key Points

- Nausea and vomiting during pregnancy usually gets better on its own.  
- Eating small meals and avoiding strong smells can help.  
- Hyperemesis gravidarum is rare but serious. It causes dehydration, low body chemicals, and weight loss.  
- Always think about other possible causes of vomiting, especially if symptoms are severe or do not improve.

# Too Much Clotting in the Blood

Too much clotting means your blood forms clots too easily or too much. This is also called thrombophilia.

- Some people are born with a higher risk of clotting.
- Others develop the problem later in life.
- The symptoms depend on where the clot forms.
- Doctors check blood levels of certain proteins to find the cause.
- Some people need medicine to prevent clots.

(See also _How Blood Clots_.)

Most clotting problems affect the veins. A few also affect the arteries.

---

## What Causes Too Much Clotting?

Some causes are inherited. These are passed down in families. They happen because of changes in certain proteins in the blood that help control clotting. Examples include:

- **Activated protein C resistance** – a common inherited issue.
- **Low levels of antithrombin** – a protein that helps stop clots.
- **Low levels of protein C** – a protein that helps control clotting.
- **Low levels of protein S** – another protein that helps stop clots.
- **Low levels of protein Z** – a protein that helps prevent clots.
- **Prothrombin 20210 mutation** – a gene change that causes the body to make too much prothrombin, a protein involved in clotting.
- **High levels of clotting factors VIII, IX, and XI** – these proteins help form clots.

Some causes are not inherited. They happen after birth. These include:

- **Disseminated intravascular coagulation** – often seen in people with cancer. It causes too many clots to form.
- **Antiphospholipid syndrome** – sometimes seen in people with systemic lupus erythematosus. It makes the blood more likely to clot.
- **High homocysteine levels** – this can happen if you lack enough vitamin B6, vitamin B12, or folate.

Other things that increase clotting risk include:

- Not moving for long periods (like being paralyzed, sitting for hours in a car or plane, or staying in bed after surgery).
- A recent heart attack.
- Heart failure – when the heart does not pump blood well.
- Extra pressure on leg veins – from being overweight or being pregnant.

The risk is much higher if you have one of these conditions **and** a clotting disorder.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most inherited clotting problems do not cause problems until young adulthood. But clots can form at any age.

Symptoms depend on where the clot is.

### Clot in a Deep Vein (Deep Vein Thrombosis)
- Pain in the calf or thigh.
- Warmth, redness, and swelling in the leg.

### Clot in the Lungs (Pulmonary Embolism)
- Shortness of breath.
- Chest pain that gets worse when you breathe.

### Other Possible Clots
- In the arm (deep vein).
- In the abdomen (portal, mesenteric, or hepatic vein).
- In the brain (cerebral venous sinus thrombosis).

### Clot in a Superficial Vein (Superficial Thrombophlebitis)
- Swelling, pain, redness, and warmth in a vein just under the skin.

### Long-Term Effects of Deep Vein Clots
- Swelling that lasts.
- Skin color changes.
- Sores or ulcers on the leg or arm.

### Clots in Arteries
- Less blood reaches the tissue.
- This can damage or destroy tissue.
- Can cause a heart attack or stroke.
- Clots in leg or arm arteries cause coldness, pain, and sometimes numbness.

### Clotting Problems in Pregnancy
- Some women with clotting issues have repeated miscarriages.
- These often happen in the second or third trimester.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use tests to find the cause and location of clots.

### Blood Tests
- These check the levels and activity of proteins that control clotting.
- They help find inherited clotting disorders.

### Imaging Tests
- If a clot is suspected in the leg, an ultrasound is used.
- If a clot is suspected in the lungs, a CT scan or a special lung scan is done.

### When to Test
- People under 50 who get a clot with no clear reason (like surgery or injury) are more likely to have an inherited clotting problem.
- A family history of blood clots also raises suspicion.

---

## How Is It Treated?

### Medicine to Prevent Clots
- Anticoagulants are used to stop clots from forming.
- These include:
  - Heparin (given by injection).
  - Warfarin (taken by mouth).
  - Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs): dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban.

### How Treatment Works
- People in the hospital with a clot usually get heparin through a vein for a few days.
- Then they switch to a DOAC or warfarin by mouth.
- People not in the hospital may start on some DOACs right away, without heparin.
- Pregnant women only get heparin. Warfarin and DOACs can harm the baby.

### Monitoring
- People on warfarin need regular blood tests to check the right dose.
- DOACs do not need regular blood tests. They are just as effective as warfarin.

### Long-Term Treatment
- People with deep vein clots and no clear cause, or those who have had more than one clot, may need to take anticoagulants for life.
- The risk of bleeding is considered when deciding on long-term treatment.

### Other Treatments
- Inherited clotting disorders cannot be cured.
- High homocysteine levels are treated with vitamin supplements (B6, B12, folate).
- But it is not clear if this lowers clotting risk.
- Treatment also depends on where the clot is.

--- 

**Note:** Always follow your doctor’s advice. Do not stop or change your medicine without talking to them.

# Hepatitis B

Hepatitis B is caused by a virus.  
It spreads through blood, semen, or vaginal fluids.  

You can get it from:  
- Having sex without a condom or dam  
- Sharing needles when injecting drugs  
- Getting stuck by a used needle  
- Getting a tattoo or piercing with unsterilized tools  
- Receiving a blood transfusion in a country that does not test blood for hepatitis B  

In the UK, blood is tested for hepatitis B.  
So the risk from a blood transfusion here is very low.  

If you are pregnant and have hepatitis B, you can pass it to your baby during pregnancy or birth.  

## Symptoms of Hepatitis B

You may have:  
- A high temperature  
- Feeling very tired  
- Pain in your upper belly  
- Feeling sick or being sick  
- Itchy, raised patches on your skin (hives)  
- Yellowing of the skin or the whites of your eyes (jaundice)  

Most people have no symptoms or only mild ones.  
The infection usually lasts 1 to 3 months.  
If it lasts longer than 6 months, it is called chronic hepatitis B.  

## When to See a Doctor

See your GP if you think you might have hepatitis B.  

## How to Prevent Hepatitis B

### Get Vaccinated

The best way to prevent hepatitis B is to get the vaccine.  

In the UK, babies get the hepatitis B vaccine as part of the 6-in-1 vaccine.  
Babies born to mothers with hepatitis B get extra doses to lower their risk.  

Adults should get the vaccine only if they are at high risk. This includes:  
- Traveling to a country with high rates of hepatitis B  
- Having liver or kidney disease  
- Having HIV  
- Working in a job where you might come into contact with blood or body fluids  
  - Examples: healthcare workers, prison staff  

Your employer should arrange the vaccine if your job puts you at risk.  

If you are traveling, talk to a travel clinic, GP, nurse, or pharmacist before you go.  

### Other Ways to Stay Safe

To reduce your risk:  
- Always use a condom or dam during sex  
- Never share razors, toothbrushes, or needles with others  

## Treatment for Hepatitis B

Most people do not need treatment.  
The infection often clears up on its own.  

You may be given medicine to help with symptoms.  
This can include painkillers or medicine to stop nausea.  

Your GP will refer you to a liver specialist.  
They will check how well your liver is working.  

If the infection lasts more than 6 months, it is called chronic hepatitis B.  
This is usually treated with antiviral medicine.  
You may also get medicine to help with itching, pain, or sickness.  

You will need regular check-ups with a liver specialist.

# What Is a Bunion?

A bunion is a bump on the inside of the big toe joint.  
It happens when the big toe leans toward the other toes.  
This causes the bone at the base of the big toe to stick out.

## What Causes a Bunion?

The main cause is a change in the position of the big toe or the bone under it.  
Some people are born with foot shapes that make bunions more likely.  
Wearing tight or narrow shoes can make the problem worse.  
Over time, the joint may become stiff and painful.  
This can lead to joint damage and bone growths called spurs.

## Symptoms of a Bunion

The first sign is often pain when wearing certain shoes.  
The bump may feel tender or sore.  
The skin over the bump can become red and warm.  
A fluid-filled sac (bursa) may form on the inside of the joint.  
This can become swollen, painful, and inflamed.  
The joint may swell all around.  
The big toe may not move well.  
You may feel pain when trying to bend the big toe up.

## How Is a Bunion Diagnosed?

Your doctor can usually see a bunion during a physical exam.  
They will check the shape of your foot and how the big toe moves.  
They will also feel the joint for tenderness or swelling.  

If the joint is very red, hot, and swollen, it could be gout or an infection.  
In these cases, the doctor may take fluid from the joint to test it.  
If other joints are also affected, the doctor may check for a long-term joint disease.

X-rays are not always needed.  
But they can show how bad the bunion is.  
They can show joint damage, bone spurs, and how much the bones are out of place.  
On an X-ray, the big toe bone may look bent inward.  
The big toe may point outward.  
The joint space may be narrow.  
Bone spurs may be seen on the big toe bone or the bone of the big toe’s top part.

## How Is a Bunion Treated?

### First Steps: Non-Surgery Treatments

Wear shoes with a wide toe area.  
Choose shoes made of stretchy material.  
This can reduce pressure on the bump.  
Use bunion pads to protect the bump.  
Try toe spacers to keep the big toe in a better position.  
Custom shoe inserts (orthotics) can help take pressure off the joint.

If these do not help, your doctor may suggest other options.

### For Pain or Swelling in the Joint

If the bursa is swollen and painful, your doctor may drain the fluid and inject a medicine to reduce swelling and pain.  
This is called a corticosteroid injection.  
It can help with pain and swelling.

For joint pain, your doctor may suggest a pain reliever that reduces inflammation.  
This is called an NSAID.  
Or they may give a shot into the joint with a painkiller and steroid.

### For a Stiff Big Toe (Hallux Limitus or Rigidus)

If the big toe does not move well, your doctor may recommend special shoes or inserts.  
These help limit movement in the joint.  
Some people get relief from a corticosteroid shot.  
If pain continues, surgery may be needed.

### When Is Surgery Needed?

Surgery is not the first choice.  
It is only considered if other treatments do not help.  
Surgery can fix the bone shape and improve joint movement.  
It may be a good option if you cannot wear wide shoes.  
But even after surgery, you should still wear special shoe inserts.  
This helps prevent the bunion from coming back.

## Key Facts

- Wearing tight or pointed shoes can cause or worsen bunions.  
- Some people are more likely to get bunions because of their foot shape.  
- Overuse or injury can also play a role.  
- Early signs include pain and tenderness at the bump.  
- Later signs include swelling, redness, and trouble moving the big toe.  
- A doctor can usually diagnose a bunion just by looking and feeling the foot.  
- X-rays help show how bad the bunion is.  
- Start with shoe changes, pads, spacers, and inserts.  
- Surgery is only for severe cases that do not improve with other treatments.

# Kneecap Dislocations

A kneecap dislocation happens when the kneecap moves out of its normal position. It slips to the side and outside of the knee. This can happen when the ligaments that hold the kneecap in place are stretched or weak.

## Who Is Most Likely to Get a Kneecap Dislocation?

- These injuries are common in teenage girls.
- They often happen in people who have a natural shape in their knee that makes it less stable.
- Loose ligaments or bones that are slightly out of line can make the kneecap more likely to slip.

## How Does It Happen?

- The kneecap can slide out when someone suddenly changes direction.
- This often happens during sports like soccer, gymnastics, baseball (when swinging a bat), or ice hockey.
- It can also happen when someone trips or slips.

Sometimes the force that causes the dislocation can damage the cartilage behind the kneecap. It can also break off a small piece of the thighbone.

## What Are the Symptoms?

- The kneecap looks crooked or out of place.
- You feel sharp pain under the kneecap.
- The knee is tender and often swollen.
- You cannot straighten your leg.
- You may be able to move the kneecap side to side.
- You may not be able to walk.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor will examine your knee. They will check how it looks and feels.

Even if the kneecap pops back into place on its own, you should still see a doctor. The doctor will take X-rays from different angles to check for broken bones.

If the kneecap has moved back in place, the doctor may still suspect a dislocation. They look for signs like swelling, tenderness, and blood inside the joint.

> **Did You Know?**  
> If your kneecap moves out of place, see a doctor right away—even if it goes back in on its own.

## How Is It Treated?

### Step 1: Put the Kneecap Back in Place

- The doctor gently moves the kneecap back into its normal spot.
- This is called reduction.
- Most people do not need medicine to help with pain during this step.

### Step 2: Check the Knee’s Stability

- The doctor moves your knee through its full range of motion.
- If the knee feels stable, you will get an elastic bandage and crutches.
- If the knee feels unstable, you will wear a knee immobilizer.

### What Is a Knee Immobilizer?

- It is a device that holds the knee still.
- It keeps the knee from bending.
- You wear it for several days.

### Step 3: Recovery and Rehabilitation

- After the immobilizer is removed, you will need physical therapy.
- Physical therapy helps rebuild strength in the leg muscles.
- It also helps you regain full movement in the knee.

### When Is Surgery Needed?

Surgery may be needed if:

- A bone is broken.
- The cartilage inside the knee is damaged.
- The knee stays unstable after initial treatment.

### Types of Surgery

- **Arthroscopic surgery**: A small camera is inserted through a tiny cut. This helps the surgeon see and fix the problem.
- **Open surgery**: A larger cut is made. This is used for more serious injuries.

> **Note:** Surgery is not needed for everyone. It depends on the injury and how the knee responds to treatment.

# Bowel Polyps – Simple Explanation

## What Are Bowel Polyps?

Bowel polyps are small growths inside the large bowel.  
They usually do not cause any symptoms.  
Most people with polyps do not know they have them.

Sometimes, larger polyps can cause:
- A small amount of mucus or blood in your poo
- Bleeding from your bottom
- Changes in your normal bowel habits, like diarrhea or constipation
- Unexplained weight loss

## Can Polyps Turn into Cancer?

Most polyps are harmless.  
But in a small number of cases, a polyp can become cancer over many years.  
Bowel cancer screening helps find these polyps early.  
If found early, they can be removed before they turn into cancer.

## What Might Cause Polyps?

We do not know the exact cause.  
But you may be more likely to get polyps if:
- A close family member has had polyps or bowel cancer
- You are over 50 years old (about 1 in 4 people over 50 have at least one polyp)
- You have a long-term bowel condition like ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s disease
- You are overweight or smoke

## How Are Polyps Found?

Polyps are often found during a test for another bowel problem.  
They may also be found during bowel cancer screening.  
Your doctor may suggest a colonoscopy or a CT colonography scan if they think you might have polyps.

### Colonoscopy

A doctor uses a long, thin tube with a camera on the end.  
The tube goes into your bottom and moves up through your bowel.  
This lets the doctor see inside your bowel and check for polyps.  
The test is not usually painful, but it can feel uncomfortable.

### CT Colonography

This is a special scan that uses X-rays and a computer.  
It creates a detailed picture of your bowel.  
You will drink a special liquid before the scan to help see your bowel clearly.

## How Are Polyps Treated?

Most polyps are removed during a colonoscopy.  
A small wire loop on the tube cuts or burns off the polyp.  
This is called a polypectomy.  
The process is painless.

In rare cases, if there are many polyps or one is very large, surgery may be needed.  
Surgery removes part of the bowel.

### After Treatment

The removed polyp is sent to a lab for testing.  
The lab checks:
- If the polyp was completely removed
- If it might grow back
- If there are any signs of cancer

If the lab finds cancer, you will need more treatment.  
Your specialist will talk to you about what to do next.

## When to See a Doctor

See your GP if you have:
- Mucus or blood in your poo for 3 weeks or longer
- A change in your normal bowel habits
- Constipation that does not get better with treatment, or happens often and lasts a long time
- Unexplained weight loss

Don’t feel embarrassed. Doctors and nurses hear about these symptoms all the time.

## When to Get Urgent Help

Call NHS 111 or go online for help if you have:
- Diarrhoea that lasts more than 7 days
- Black or dark red poo
- Poo with blood in it (bloody diarrhoea)

You can call 111 or get help online.

## When to Go to A&E or Call 999

Go to A&E or call 999 if you:
- Are bleeding heavily from your bottom
- See a lot of blood – for example, the toilet water turns red or you see large blood clots

# Neonatal Hyponatremia

Hyponatremia means the level of sodium in the blood is too low.  
A normal sodium level is above 135 milliequivalents per liter.  
If the sodium level is too low, it can cause serious problems.  
Severe low sodium can lead to seizures or coma.  
Treatment uses a special salt solution given through a vein.  
The most common solution is 0.9% saline.  
In rare cases, a stronger salt solution (3%) is needed, especially if the baby is having seizures.

> Note: This information is about babies. Hyponatremia in adults is covered elsewhere.

---

## What Causes Low Sodium in Newborns?

The most common cause is dehydration from vomiting or diarrhea.  
When babies lose fluids, they may be given drinks that do not have much salt.  
This can make the sodium level drop too low.

A less common cause is when the body holds on to too much water.  
This happens when a hormone called antidiuretic hormone is released at the wrong time.  
This can be due to brain bleeding, brain infection, or very rarely, a brain tumor.

Another cause is giving infant formula that is too weak.  
This can lead to too much water in the body, also called water intoxication.

A final cause is when the baby’s body holds on to both salt and water.  
This happens in serious conditions like heart failure or kidney failure.

---

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

Babies with low sodium may show these signs:
- Nausea and vomiting
- Lethargy or lack of energy
- Headache (hard to tell in babies, but they may cry more or seem fussy)
- Seizures
- Low body temperature
- Weakness
- Coma

Babies with low sodium and dehydration often look very sick.  
The low sodium causes a drop in fluid outside the cells.  
The symptoms depend on how low the sodium is and how long it has been low.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect low sodium based on the baby’s symptoms.  
They confirm it with a blood test to check the sodium level.  
If the baby is dehydrated, the blood test may also show high levels of blood urea nitrogen.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment uses a special fluid given through a vein.  
The main solution is 5% dextrose with 0.45% to 0.9% saline.  
In rare cases, a stronger salt solution (3%) is used.

The amount of fluid given is based on how much fluid the baby is missing.  
The sodium level should be raised slowly.  
It should not go up more than 10 to 12 milliequivalents per liter per day.  
This slow rise helps protect the baby’s brain from damage.

For babies with low blood volume (hypovolemic hyponatremia), they need extra fluid with salt.  
The amount of salt needed is 10 to 12 milliequivalents per kilogram of body weight.  
For very young babies with severe low sodium, up to 15 milliequivalents per kilogram may be needed.  
In addition, the baby needs a daily amount of salt (3 milliequivalents per kilogram) in a dextrose solution.

If the baby is showing serious symptoms like extreme sleepiness or confusion, they need emergency treatment.  
This includes a 3% saline solution given through a vein right away.  
This helps prevent seizures or coma.

# Laryngeal Cancer

Laryngeal cancer starts in the voice box. The voice box is also called the larynx.

## What Is the Larynx?

The larynx is the part of the throat that holds the vocal cords. It sits just above the windpipe. The vocal cords help you make sounds when you speak.

## Common Symptoms

Laryngeal cancer often starts on the vocal cords. It can cause:

- A hoarse voice that lasts more than 2 to 3 weeks  
- A lump in the neck  
- Trouble swallowing or breathing  
- Pain in the throat or ear  
- Unexplained weight loss  

If you have hoarseness for more than 3 weeks, see a doctor.

Cancers in other parts of the larynx grow more slowly. They may not cause hoarseness at first. Instead, they can cause:

- Throat pain  
- Ear pain  
- Trouble swallowing or breathing  
- Weight loss  

Sometimes, the first sign is a lump in the neck. This happens when the cancer spreads to a lymph node.

## Causes and Risk Factors

Most laryngeal cancers are squamous cell cancers. This means they start in the thin, flat cells that line the inside of the larynx.

The main risk factor is smoking. Over 95% of people with laryngeal cancer are smokers. Drinking too much alcohol also raises the risk.

Laryngeal cancer is more common in men than women. Most people diagnosed are over 60 years old.

The number of new cases is going down. This is likely because fewer people are smoking now.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

To check for laryngeal cancer, your doctor will:

- Use a thin, flexible tube with a camera to look inside your throat. This is called laryngoscopy.  
- Take a small sample of tissue from the throat. This is called a biopsy.  
- Do imaging tests to see how far the cancer has spread. These may include:  
  - A chest x-ray  
  - A CT scan of the neck and chest  
  - A PET scan  

The biopsy is usually done in the operating room while you are asleep under general anesthesia.

## Prognosis (Outlook)

The outlook depends on how big the cancer is and how far it has spread.

- If the cancer is small and has not spread, about 85% to 95% of people live at least 5 years.  
- If the cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes, fewer than 48% live 5 years or more.  
- If the cancer has spread beyond the neck, about 35% live longer than 5 years.  

The cancer is harder to cure if it has grown into muscle, bone, or cartilage.

## Treatment Options

Treatment depends on the stage and location of the cancer.

### Early-Stage Cancer

For small cancers, doctors may use:

- Surgery  
- Radiation therapy  

If the vocal cords are affected, doctors often choose radiation therapy. This helps keep your voice normal.  

For very early cancers, microsurgery may be better. It uses a special scope with tiny tools or a laser. It can be done in one visit. It causes fewer problems with speaking and swallowing than regular surgery.

### Larger Tumors

For larger cancers that have spread a little into nearby tissue, doctors may use:

- Radiation therapy combined with chemotherapy (called chemoradiation)  

This can work as well as surgery and may protect your voice. But surgery may still be needed after treatment to remove any leftover cancer.

### Advanced Cancer

If the cancer has spread to bone or cartilage, doctors usually recommend:

- Surgery to remove part or all of the voice box (called a partial or total laryngectomy)  
- Follow-up radiation therapy  
- Sometimes chemotherapy  

If the cancer is too advanced for surgery or radiation, chemotherapy can help shrink the tumor and reduce pain. But it is unlikely to cure the cancer.

## Side Effects of Treatment

All treatments can cause side effects.

### Radiation Therapy

- Skin changes: redness, itching, or hair loss  
- Scarring  
- Dry mouth  
- Loss of taste  
- Rarely, damage to healthy tissue  

If you have teeth that will be in the radiation area, fix dental problems before treatment. Radiation can make future dental work harder and may cause serious jaw infections.

### Chemotherapy

Side effects depend on the medicine used. They may include:

- Nausea and vomiting  
- Hearing loss  
- Increased risk of infection  

### Surgery

Surgery can affect your ability to speak and swallow. You may need rehabilitation to learn new ways to do these things.

## How to Speak Without Vocal Cords

After surgery, you can still speak. You just need a new way to make sound.

The voice box makes sound by vibrating. The tongue, lips, and mouth shape those vibrations into words. Even without vocal cords, you can still shape sounds into words.

There are three main ways to make sound after laryngectomy:

### 1. Esophageal Speech

- No surgery or devices needed  
- You learn to swallow air into your esophagus (the tube from throat to stomach)  
- You push the air out to make a sound, like a belch  
- Hard to learn  
- Others may have trouble understanding you  

### 2. Tracheoesophageal Puncture (TEP)

- A small hole is made between the windpipe and esophagus  
- A one-way valve is placed in the hole  
- Air from the windpipe goes through the valve into the esophagus when you exhale  
- This makes sound that you shape into words  
- Takes time and practice  
- Often leads to clear, fluent speech  
- The valve must be cleaned every day  
- It needs to be replaced every few months  
- You may need to cover the neck opening with your finger to speak  
- If the valve fails, food or liquid can go into the windpipe  

### 3. Electrolarynx

- A small battery-powered device that vibrates  
- You hold it against your neck to make sound  
- The sound is mechanical and artificial  
- Easier to learn than esophageal speech  
- Others usually understand it well  
- You must carry it and replace batteries  
- Some people feel self-conscious using it
