# Lupus

Lupus is a long-term health condition. It happens when your body’s natural defence system attacks healthy parts of your body by mistake.

There is no cure for lupus. But many people find that their symptoms improve with treatment.

## What Are the Symptoms of Lupus?

Lupus can cause many different symptoms. Not everyone has all of them.

Common symptoms include:

- Pain in your joints and muscles  
- Feeling very tired, even after resting  
- A rash on your face, especially after being in the sun  
  - This rash often appears over your nose and cheeks  
- Headaches  
- Sores in your mouth  
- A high temperature (fever)  
- Losing your hair  
- Losing weight without trying  
- Swollen glands in your neck, under your arms, or in your groin  
- Feeling sad, low, or anxious  
- Pain in your chest or tummy  
- Fingers or toes changing colour when you are cold, stressed, or anxious  
  - This is called Raynaud’s

### Flare-Ups

Lupus often comes and goes. Symptoms may get worse for a few weeks or longer. This is called a flare-up.

After a flare-up, symptoms may improve or go away. This is called remission.

We do not know why symptoms flare up or calm down.

Some people have symptoms all the time. Others have long periods without symptoms.

### When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if you often have symptoms like those above.

Finding lupus early helps you manage it better.

## How Is Lupus Treated?

Your doctor may give you medicines to help control your symptoms.

These include:

- Anti-inflammatory medicines like ibuprofen  
- Hydroxychloroquine to help with tiredness, skin problems, and joint pain  
- Steroid tablets, injections, or creams for kidney issues and rashes  
- In severe cases, stronger medicines that calm your immune system  
  - These are called immunosuppressants or biological medicines

## What Can You Do to Help Manage Lupus?

Medicines are important. But you can also take steps to feel better and stay well.

### Do These Things

- Use sunscreen with a factor of at least 50  
- Wear a hat when you are in the sun  
  - You can get sunscreen on prescription if you have lupus  
- Learn to pace yourself  
  - This means doing small amounts of activity and resting when needed  
- Stay active every day, even on bad days  
  - Gentle movement like walking helps  
- Try relaxation techniques  
  - Stress can make symptoms worse  
- Tell your employer about your condition  
  - You may be able to change your work hours or duties  
- Ask for help from family, friends, or your healthcare team  
- Eat a healthy, balanced diet  
  - Include foods with vitamin D and calcium

### Avoid These Things

- Do not smoke  
  - Smoking makes lupus worse  
- Do not sit in direct sunlight  
- Avoid spending long times in rooms with fluorescent lights  
  - These can trigger symptoms

## What Causes Lupus?

Lupus is an autoimmune condition. This means your immune system attacks your own body by mistake.

Lupus is not contagious. You cannot catch it from someone else.

We do not fully understand what causes lupus. But possible triggers include:

- A viral infection  
- Some medicines  
- Sunlight  
- Puberty  
- Giving birth  
- Going through menopause

More women than men get lupus. It is also more common in women of African, Caribbean, Asian, or Chinese background.

# Chorea, Athetosis, and Hemiballismus

This page explains three types of involuntary movements: chorea, athetosis, and hemiballismus. These movements happen without control and can affect daily life.

---

## What Are the Three Types of Involuntary Movements?

### Chorea
- Chorea causes random, flowing, and unpredictable movements.
- The movements mostly affect the hands, feet, and face.
- They can look like they are part of a purposeful action, but they are not.
- You cannot stop them on purpose.

### Athetosis
- Athetosis is a slower form of chorea.
- It causes twisting, writhing motions, mainly in the hands and feet.
- The movements are not steady or rhythmic.
- The arms and legs may change position slowly and keep shifting.

### Hemiballismus
- Hemiballismus causes fast, wild, and uncontrolled flinging movements.
- It affects one side of the body — either the arm or leg, or both.
- The movements are large and hard to control.
- It is a more severe form of chorea.
- In rare cases, both sides of the body are affected. This is called ballismus.

---

## What Causes These Movements?

Chorea and athetosis happen when the brain’s control system for movement is not working right.

- The basal ganglia, a part of the brain, normally helps stop unwanted movements.
- When this system fails, the brain sends too many signals to move.
- Too much dopamine — a brain chemical — may be the reason.

Doctors should always try to find the cause of chorea. Treating the cause can help reduce or stop the movements.

---

## Huntington Disease

Huntington disease is the most common inherited brain disorder that causes chorea.

- It is a long-term condition that gets worse over time.
- It affects movement, thinking, and behavior.
- Medicines that reduce dopamine activity can help control the movements.
  - Examples: risperidone, olanzapine
- Other medicines that lower dopamine levels can also help.
  - Examples: deutetrabenazine, tetrabenazine
  - Reserpine used to be used but is no longer available in the United States.

These medicines may also help with mental health symptoms like:
- Impulsiveness
- Anxiety
- Hallucinations or delusions

But the benefits may be small and do not last long.

These medicines can also be used for chorea with no clear cause — if needed and carefully managed.

---

## Other Causes of Chorea

Chorea can also be caused by:

- Overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism)
- Low calcium levels (hypoparathyroidism)
- High blood sugar (hyperglycemia)
- Autoimmune diseases like lupus that affect the brain
- Certain medicines and drugs:
  - Levodopa (used for Parkinson disease)
  - Phenytoin (a seizure medicine)
  - Cocaine
  - Tricyclic antidepressants
  - Birth control pills
- Tardive dyskinesia — a side effect from some antipsychotic medicines.
  - This can cause chorea or other movement problems.
  - It can happen even if the person is not having other symptoms like tics or restlessness.
- Brain tumors or stroke in certain areas
- Pregnancy
- Autoimmune conditions
- Rare conditions linked to cancer (paraneoplastic syndromes)

---

## Specific Types of Chorea

### Sydenham Chorea
- This type can happen during or after rheumatic fever.
- It may be the first sign of rheumatic fever.
- It often improves on its own over time, even without treatment.

### Chorea from Stroke
- A stroke in a part of the brain called the striatum (caudate or putamen) can cause sudden chorea on one side of the body.
- The movements happen on the side opposite the brain injury.
- This type often improves over time.

### Chorea from Metabolic Problems
- Chorea caused by thyroid issues or high blood sugar often gets better when the problem is fixed.
- If the movements do not go away after several weeks of treatment, doctors should look for another cause, like a stroke.

### Chorea in Older Adults
- Chorea in people over 60 is not normal aging.
- It must be checked carefully.
- Possible causes include:
  - Toxins
  - Metabolic problems
  - Autoimmune diseases
  - Cancer-related conditions
  - Medicines

---

## Chorea During Pregnancy

Chorea that happens during pregnancy is called chorea gravidarum.

- It can happen in women who had rheumatic fever in the past.
- It usually starts in the first trimester.
- It often goes away on its own after delivery.
- Doctors should still check for the cause if needed.
- A similar problem can happen in women using birth control pills.

---

## Hemiballismus

Hemiballismus is caused by a brain injury, usually a stroke, in a small area called the subthalamic nucleus.

- The injury is on one side of the brain.
- The movements happen on the opposite side of the body.
- The movements are very strong and hard to control.
- It usually lasts 6 to 8 weeks and goes away on its own.
- If the movements are very severe, treatment may be needed:
  - Antipsychotic medicine for 1 to 2 months
  - Deep brain stimulation (a surgery that uses electrical signals to calm brain activity)

This treatment helps if medicines do not work.

# Abnormal Heart Rhythms – Simple Explanation

## What Are Abnormal Heart Rhythms?

An abnormal heart rhythm means your heart beats in a way that is not normal. It might beat too fast, too slow, irregularly, or use a wrong path for its electrical signals.

- Your heart has four chambers. They work together to pump blood.
- The heart muscle contracts in a set order. This keeps blood moving through your body.
- The heart’s rhythm is controlled by electrical signals.
- These signals start in a small area called the sinus node, in the top right chamber of the heart.
- The speed of the heart’s beats depends on how often the sinus node sends out signals.
- Your nervous system and certain hormones control how fast the heart beats.

## How the Heart’s Electrical System Works

- The sinus node starts each heartbeat with an electrical signal.
- The signal spreads through the upper chambers (atria), making them squeeze and push blood into the lower chambers (ventricles).
- The signal then reaches the atrioventricular node, which acts like a gate.
- This node delays the signal so the upper chambers can finish squeezing before the lower chambers get the signal.
- After the delay, the signal travels down a pathway called the bundle of His.
- It splits into two branches—one for each lower chamber.
- The signal spreads through the lower chambers, making them squeeze and push blood out of the heart.

## What Causes Abnormal Heart Rhythms?

The most common cause is a problem with the heart itself. This includes:

- Coronary artery disease
- Heart valve problems
- Heart failure

Other causes include:

- Some medicines (both prescription and over-the-counter)
- Birth defects in the heart’s electrical system
- Changes in the heart’s electrical system that come with aging

Some people have no clear cause for their abnormal rhythm.

### Fast Heart Rhythms (Tachycardia)

These can start on their own or be triggered by:

- Exercise
- Stress
- Drinking too much alcohol
- Smoking
- Stimulant drugs (like those in cold or allergy medicines)
- An overactive thyroid gland

### Slow Heart Rhythms (Bradycardia)

These can be caused by:

- Pain
- Hunger
- Tiredness
- Digestive problems like diarrhea or vomiting
- Swallowing, which can overstimulate the vagus nerve

In rare cases, the vagus nerve can slow the heart so much that it stops for a moment. But this usually fixes itself.

An underactive thyroid gland can also cause slow heart rhythms.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Some people feel their heart racing, fluttering, or skipping. This is called palpitations.

- Not everyone feels their heart rhythm changes.
- Some people feel normal heartbeats, especially when lying on their left side.
- The symptoms can range from mild to life-threatening.

Important facts:

- A serious heart rhythm may cause no symptoms at all.
- A mild rhythm may cause very strong symptoms.
- The real danger comes from how well the heart pumps blood, not just the rhythm.

When the heart does not pump well, you may feel:

- Weakness
- Tiredness
- Shortness of breath
- Dizziness
- Light-headedness
- Fainting (called syncope)

Fainting happens when the heart cannot keep blood pressure high enough. If the problem continues, it can lead to death.

Abnormal rhythms can also make other heart problems worse, like chest pain or trouble breathing.

If you have symptoms, you should see a doctor right away.

> **Did You Know?**  
> Some harmless rhythms can feel very bad. Some dangerous rhythms cause no symptoms at all.

## How Are Abnormal Heart Rhythms Diagnosed?

### Your Doctor Will Ask:

- Is your heartbeat fast or slow?
- Is it regular or irregular?
- Does it last a short time or a long time?
- Does it cause symptoms?

They will also ask:

- Does it happen when you are resting or only during activity?
- Does it start and stop suddenly or slowly?

### The Main Test: Electrocardiogram (ECG)

- An ECG records the electrical activity of your heart.
- It shows a picture of your heart’s rhythm during a short time.
- It can show if your heart is beating too fast, too slow, or irregularly.
- It can also show if there is a past heart attack, poor blood flow to the heart, or thickened heart muscle.

### If the Problem Is Not Always Present

- A portable ECG monitor (called a Holter monitor or event monitor) may be used.
- You wear it for 24 to 48 hours, or up to two weeks.
- It records your heart rhythm all the time or when you press a button during symptoms.
- You keep a diary of your symptoms and what you were doing.
- This helps the doctor match your symptoms to your heart rhythm.

### For Rare or Dangerous Rhythms

- A small device can be implanted under the skin near the collarbone.
- It records heart rhythms over a long time.
- It sends data to your doctor without pain.

### Hospital Testing

- People with serious symptoms are often admitted to the hospital.
- Their heart rhythm is watched all the time on a monitor.
- This helps catch problems quickly.

### Other Tests

- **Exercise stress test**: Your heart is checked while you walk on a treadmill.
- **Blood pressure during exercise**: Measures how your blood pressure changes with activity.
- **Echocardiogram**: Uses sound waves to check the heart’s structure and function.
- **Electrophysiologic testing**: A thin tube (catheter) is guided into the heart. Tiny electrodes at the tip send signals to test how the heart responds. This helps find the cause and best treatment.

### Reading an ECG

An ECG shows waves that represent different parts of the heartbeat:

- **P wave**: The upper chambers (atria) are getting ready to squeeze.
- **QRS complex**: The lower chambers (ventricles) are squeezing.
- **T wave**: The lower chambers are recovering after squeezing.

An ECG can show:

- Past heart attacks
- Abnormal heart rhythms
- Poor blood flow to the heart
- Thickened heart muscle
- Bulges in the heart wall (aneurysms), which can happen after a heart attack

It can also show where an abnormal rhythm starts in the heart. This helps doctors find the cause.

## How Are Abnormal Heart Rhythms Treated?

Treatment depends on the type and cause of the rhythm.

### Common Treatments

- **Medicines** to slow a fast heartbeat
- **Pacemaker** to help a slow heartbeat
- **Electric shock** to stop a fast rhythm
- **Ablation** to destroy a small area of heart tissue that causes the problem

### For Mild but Troubling Rhythms

- Just knowing the rhythm is harmless may be enough.
- Changing or adjusting medicines can help.
- Avoiding alcohol, caffeine, and smoking may reduce symptoms.
- Avoiding intense exercise may help if symptoms only happen during activity.
- You may need to stop driving until your doctor says it’s safe.

### Antiarrhythmic Medicines

- These help stop fast heartbeats that cause serious symptoms.
- No one medicine works for everyone.
- You may need to try several before finding one that works.
- Some medicines can make the rhythm worse or cause new problems.
- They can also cause side effects.

### Artificial Pacemakers

- These are small devices placed under the skin, usually near the collarbone.
- Wires connect the device to the heart.
- The device sends electrical signals to make the heart beat when it’s too slow.
- It acts like a backup for the heart’s natural pacemaker.

### Electric Shock (Cardioversion or Defibrillation)

- A shock stops the heart for a moment.
- After a second or two, the heart often restarts with a normal rhythm.
- This works for fast, dangerous rhythms.
- It does not work if the heart has no electrical activity at all.
- Shocks are usually given through a device on the chest.
- Some people with serious risks get a permanent device called an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD).

### Ablation

- This destroys a small area of heart tissue that causes the abnormal rhythm.
- It can cure some types of arrhythmias.
- It is done using a catheter with tiny electrodes.

## What Is the Outlook?

- Most abnormal heart rhythms do not cause symptoms.
- They do not harm the heart’s ability to pump blood.
- They are usually not dangerous, though they can cause worry.
- Some harmless rhythms can lead to more serious ones.

### When Is It Serious?

- If the heart cannot pump blood well, the rhythm is serious.
- Where the rhythm starts matters:
  - Rhythms starting in the lower chambers (ventricles) are more serious.
  - Rhythms in the upper chambers (atria) are less serious.
  - Rhythms starting in the natural pacemaker (sinus node) or the atrioventricular node are usually the least serious.

But there are exceptions. Each case is different.

For more details, visit:

# Broken Arm or Wrist

A broken arm or wrist can cause pain, swelling, bruising, and trouble moving the arm or wrist. The area may also change color or feel numb.

## When to Get Help

### Call NHS 111 if:
- The pain is very bad, or you cannot use your arm because of the pain.
- The pain is getting worse.
- There is a lot of swelling or bruising, or it is getting worse.
- Your arm or wrist feels very stiff or hard to move.
- You have a high fever, or you feel hot and shivery. This could mean an infection.

You can call 111 or get help online.

### Go to A&E or call 999 if:
- Your arm or wrist is numb, tingling, or has pins and needles.
- You have a deep cut that is bleeding a lot.
- A bone is sticking out through the skin.
- Your arm or wrist looks bent in a strange way or is at an odd angle.

Find your nearest A&E.

### Important Safety Tips for A&E
- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you. Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.
- Bring your regular medicines with you.

---

## Signs You May Have a Broken Arm or Wrist

You may have a break if your arm or wrist:
- Hurts suddenly after an injury.
- Swells up.
- Bruises.
- Is hard to move.

The area may also change color, change shape, or feel numb.

It can be hard to tell if it is broken, dislocated, or just badly sprained. An X-ray will help find out.

---

## What to Do While Waiting for Help

If you think your arm or wrist is broken, do these things while waiting:

### Do:
- Use a towel as a sling to support your arm.
- Put an ice pack (or a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a tea towel) on the injury for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours.
- Press a clean pad or dressing on any cut to stop bleeding.
- Take off rings, watches, or bracelets. Your hand or wrist may swell.
- Take painkillers like paracetamol or ibuprofen gel. You can take ibuprofen tablets if needed.

### Don’t:
- Eat or drink anything. You might need surgery, and you should not have food or drink before that.
- Try to use the injured arm or wrist.

---

## Treatment at Hospital

When you get to the hospital:
- The doctor will put your arm in a splint to keep it still.
- You will get medicine to help with the pain.

An X-ray will be taken to check if the bone is broken and how bad the break is.

### Casts and Splints
- A plaster cast may be used to keep your arm in place while it heals.
- Sometimes the cast is put on a few days later, after the swelling goes down.
- You may also be given a sling to support your arm.

### Moving Bones Back into Place
- If the bones are out of place, the doctor may gently move them back into position.
- You will get medicine so you do not feel pain during this.

### Surgery
- If the break is very bad, surgery may be needed to fix the bones.

Before you leave the hospital:
- You will get painkillers to take home.
- You will get advice on how to care for your cast.
- You will be told to come back for follow-up visits to check healing.

If you are over 50 and have broken your arm or wrist, ask your doctor about a fracture liaison service. This service helps prevent future breaks and keeps your bones strong.

Ask your GP surgery if there is a service near you.

---

## Healing and Recovery

Most people take 6 to 8 weeks to heal from a broken arm or wrist. It may take longer if the injury was severe.

### What to Do During Recovery

### Do:
- Keep your hand raised above your elbow as much as possible. Use a pillow at night to help.
- Follow the exercise plan your doctor or nurse gave you.
- Use your painkillers as needed to ease pain.

### Don’t:
- Get your cast wet. Use a waterproof cover from a pharmacy.
- Use anything to scratch under the cast. This can cause infection.
- Drive or lift heavy things until your doctor says it is safe.

---

## When to Call NHS 111 During Recovery

Call 111 if:
- The pain gets worse.
- You have a very high temperature or feel hot and shivery.
- Your cast breaks, or it feels too tight or too loose.
- Your fingers, wrist, or arm go numb.
- Your fingers, wrist, or arm look swollen or turn blue or white.
- You notice a bad smell or liquid coming from under the cast.

You can call 111 or get help online.

# What Is Pancreatitis?

Pancreatitis means the pancreas is inflamed.

There are two main types: acute and chronic.

## Acute Pancreatitis

- This is a sudden inflammation of the pancreas.
- It usually gets better over time.
- The pancreas returns to normal in both appearance and function.

## Chronic Pancreatitis

- This is long-term inflammation of the pancreas.
- The damage does not heal.
- The condition gets worse over time.
- It leads to serious loss of the pancreas’s ability to work properly.
- People with chronic pancreatitis may have sudden flare-ups that feel like acute pancreatitis.

## How Pancreatitis Affects the Pancreas

The pancreas has two main jobs:

1. **Helping with digestion (exocrine function)**  
   - Special cells in the pancreas make digestive juices.  
   - These juices contain enzymes and bicarbonate.  
   - The juices travel through tubes (ducts) to the small intestine.  
   - They help break down food.

2. **Controlling blood sugar (endocrine function)**  
   - Other cells in the pancreas make insulin.  
   - Insulin goes directly into the blood.  
   - It helps the body use sugar for energy.  

When pancreatitis happens, both of these jobs can be affected.

# Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia

This is a lung condition that causes sudden inflammation and scarring. The scarring blocks the tiny airways and air sacs in the lungs. This makes it hard to breathe.

It usually starts between the ages of 50 and 60. It affects men and women about equally. Smoking does not seem to raise the risk.

## Symptoms

Most people get worse over time. They have a cough that does not go away. They also feel short of breath when they walk or do light activity.

About half of people first feel sick like they have the flu. This includes cough, fever, tiredness, and a general feeling of being unwell. They may also lose weight.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors use several tests to find out if you have this condition.

- A chest CT scan gives detailed pictures of the lungs. It can show signs that match this disease.
- A chest x-ray may help, but it often does not show enough detail to be certain.
- Blood tests usually come back normal. There is no clear sign in the blood.
- When doctors listen to your lungs with a stethoscope, they often hear crackling sounds. Sometimes they hear squeaky sounds when you breathe in.
- Lung function tests show that your lungs do not hold as much air as they should.
- Blood oxygen levels are often low when you are at rest. They drop even more during exercise.

If the CT scan is not clear, doctors may take a small sample of lung tissue. This is called a biopsy.

- A bronchoscope is a thin tube with a camera. Doctors use it to get a small sample from the lungs.
- In some cases, a larger sample is needed. Then, doctors do a surgical biopsy.

## Treatment

The main treatment is steroid medicine. These are also called glucocorticoids or corticosteroids.

- Most people feel much better quickly after starting steroids.
- Some people get better and stay well. But others have symptoms return later.
- If symptoms come back, doctors give steroids again. This usually works well.

Treatment often lasts for several months. It is important to follow your doctor’s advice and not stop the medicine too soon.

# Diverticular Disease and Diverticulitis

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may have tummy pain. The pain is often in the lower left side of your belly. A few people feel it on the right side.

The pain may get worse after you eat. It often gets better after you pass a stool or pass gas.

You might have constipation. Or you might have diarrhoea.

You may see blood in your stool. You might also notice mucus (a slimy substance) in your stool.

You may feel bloated or have a swollen belly.

If your bowel becomes infected or inflamed, it is called diverticulitis. This can cause:

- Severe, ongoing tummy pain
- A high temperature
- Bleeding from your bottom
- Passing mucus from your bottom

These symptoms are similar to those of other gut problems, like irritable bowel syndrome.

## When to Seek Help

Call your doctor right away or use NHS 111 if you have:

- Blood or mucus in your stool
- Tummy pain that is getting worse or does not go away
- A high temperature, or you feel hot or shivery
- You keep being sick and cannot keep fluids down
- Diarrhoea that lasts more than 7 days
- Being sick for more than 2 days

You can call 111 or get help online at [nhs.uk/111](https://www.nhs.uk/111)

Call 999 or go to A&E if you or someone you care for:

- Has severe tummy pain and is vomiting, has a swollen belly, or cannot pass stool or gas
- Is bleeding heavily from the bottom
- Is confused, has pale or blotchy skin, has a very high or very low temperature, or is breathing fast or short of breath

These could be signs of a serious infection called sepsis.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask you about your symptoms.

You may need a blood test or a stool sample.

You might need more tests to check for diverticular disease or diverticulitis. These tests can also rule out other conditions.

Possible tests include:

- A colonoscopy: A thin tube with a camera is gently put into your bottom. It checks the inside of your large bowel.
- A CT scan: This takes detailed pictures of your tummy and bowel.

## How Is It Treated?

### For Diverticular Disease

- Use painkillers like paracetamol for pain.
- Use bulk-forming laxatives if you are constipated or have diarrhoea.
- Take medicines to ease stomach cramps if needed.

### For Diverticulitis

- Antibiotics are used if there is an infection.
- Painkillers like paracetamol can help with pain.

## What You Can Do to Feel Better and Prevent Problems

### Do These Things

- Eat a healthy, balanced diet. Include whole grains, fruits, and vegetables.
- There are no foods you must avoid. But if you eat little fibre, slowly increase how much you eat.
- Drink plenty of water when you increase fibre.
- Stop smoking if you smoke.
- Keep a healthy weight.

### Avoid These Things

- Do not take NSAIDs like ibuprofen. They can cause stomach problems.
- Do not take opioid painkillers like codeine. They can cause constipation and increase the risk of a hole in your bowel.

These steps can help reduce your risk of future problems.

# Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy and Becker Muscular Dystrophy

These are two rare muscle diseases that affect mostly boys. They are passed down through families in a pattern linked to the X chromosome.

Both diseases cause muscles to weaken over time. This weakness starts in the hips, thighs, and shoulders. It gets worse slowly. The muscles break down and do not repair well.

Becker muscular dystrophy starts later in life. It causes milder symptoms than Duchenne. People with Becker may stay able to walk into their twenties or later.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy starts earlier. It causes more severe weakness. Most boys with this disease lose the ability to walk by their teens.

## What Causes These Diseases?

These diseases are caused by changes in a gene called *dystrophin*. This gene helps make a protein that protects muscle cells.

When the gene is damaged, the body makes little or no dystrophin. Without this protein, muscle cells break down easily.

- In Duchenne, the body makes less than 5% of the normal amount of dystrophin.
- In Becker, the body makes some dystrophin, but it is not working right or is in low amounts.

About 1 in 5,000 to 6,000 male babies is born with one of these diseases. Most have Duchenne.

Girls can carry the faulty gene. They usually do not have symptoms. But some may have slightly higher levels of a muscle enzyme in their blood or larger calf muscles.

## How Are These Diseases Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect the disease based on symptoms, age when symptoms start, and family history.

Tests used to confirm the diagnosis include:

- Blood test: Shows very high levels of a muscle enzyme called creatine kinase.
- Genetic test: Looks at the *dystrophin* gene in a blood sample. This is the main test.
- Muscle biopsy: A small piece of muscle is taken and tested. It shows if dystrophin is missing or abnormal.

The most common test is a blood test called MLPA. It finds large changes in the *dystrophin* gene. If that test is normal but the disease is still suspected, a full gene sequence test may be done.

If genetic tests do not show a problem, a muscle biopsy can check for dystrophin directly.

- In Duchenne, no dystrophin is found.
- In Becker, dystrophin is present but is not normal or is in low amounts.

All boys with Duchenne should have heart tests (ECG and echocardiogram) at diagnosis or by age six. This checks for heart problems.

Parents who carry the gene can be tested. Prenatal testing is possible during pregnancy.

## How Are These Diseases Treated?

There is no cure. But treatments help slow the disease and keep the body working as long as possible.

### General Care

- Gentle exercise is encouraged. It helps keep muscles strong and prevents stiffness.
- Passive exercises (done by someone else) can help delay loss of movement.
- Leg braces help with walking and standing.
- Ankle-foot braces worn at night can prevent tightness in the ankles.
- Avoid being overweight. Less activity means lower calorie needs.

### Heart Problems

If the heart is affected, doctors may prescribe:
- An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACE inhibitor)
- A beta-blocker

These medicines can slow heart damage.

### Breathing Problems

As the disease progresses, breathing muscles weaken.

- Noninvasive ventilation (using a mask at night) helps.
- Later, some children may need a breathing tube (tracheotomy). This can help them live into their 30s and beyond.

### Surgery

Sometimes surgery is needed, especially for scoliosis (curved spine).

### Special Treatments for Duchenne

- **Prednisone or deflazacort**: These medicines help keep muscle strength longer. They also help breathing and heart health. But they can cause side effects like weight gain, mood changes, and bone thinning.
- **Genetic therapies**: For some boys with specific gene changes, special drugs may help. These include:
  - Eteplirsen
  - Golodirsen
  - Viltolarsen
  - Casimersen
  - Ataluren

These drugs are not effective for all boys. Their benefits are limited, but they may help some.

### New and Experimental Treatments

Research is ongoing. Some new treatments being studied include:
- Gene therapy
- Creatine supplements
- Drugs that block myostatin (a protein that limits muscle growth)
- Stem cell treatments
- Idebenone (an antioxidant)

## Key Facts

- Duchenne and Becker are inherited diseases that reduce a key muscle protein called dystrophin.
- Both cause worsening muscle weakness. This leads to trouble walking, frequent falls, heart problems, and early death from breathing failure.
- Exercise, braces, and orthotics help maintain movement and function.
- Prednisone or deflazacort helps slow muscle loss and improves breathing and heart health. Side effects are common.
- For some boys with specific gene changes, special genetic drugs may be used.
- Heart medicines can slow heart damage.
- Breathing support can help people live longer.

## Genetic Counseling

Families should talk to a genetic counselor. This helps understand how the disease is passed on and what future pregnancies might be like.

## Useful Resources

The following websites offer helpful information in English:

- **Muscular Dystrophy Association**: Research updates, treatment options, support, and technology for people with Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy.
- **National Organization for Rare Disorders**: Detailed information on both diseases, including standard and new treatments, plus links to related topics.
- **Muscular Dystrophy News Today**: A news site with updates and personal stories about living with muscular dystrophy.

# Nasopharyngeal Cancer

This is a type of cancer that starts in the back of the nose, just above the soft part of the roof of the mouth and near the top of the throat.

## Who Gets This Cancer?

- This cancer is rare in North America and Western Europe.
- It is more common in people of Chinese, especially southern Chinese, and Southeast Asian backgrounds.
- It is more common in Chinese people who moved to North America than in other Americans.
- It is less common in American-born Chinese people than in their parents or grandparents.

## What Causes This Cancer?

- The Epstein-Barr virus, which causes mono, is linked to this cancer.
- Some people may inherit a higher risk.
- Eating a lot of salted fish and foods with nitrites, especially as a child or young adult, increases the risk.

## What Are the Symptoms?

- A lump in the neck is often the first sign.
- You may feel fullness, pain, or hearing loss in one ear.
- The ear tube (eustachian tube) may become blocked, leading to fluid buildup in the middle ear.
- You may have ear pain, a swollen face, blood or pus from the nose, nosebleeds, or trouble moving part of the face or an eye.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- A doctor will look at the back of your nose using a small mirror or a flexible tube with a camera (endoscope).
- If a tumor is seen, a small sample of tissue is taken (biopsy) and checked under a microscope.
- Imaging tests are done to see how far the cancer has spread:
  - CT scan of the base of the skull.
  - MRI of the head, nose, and base of the skull.
  - PET scan to check the cancer and lymph nodes in the neck.

## What Is the Outlook?

- Early treatment leads to much better results.
- About 80 out of 100 people with early-stage cancer live at least 5 years after diagnosis.
- Fewer than half of people with advanced cancer (stage IV) live at least 5 years after diagnosis.

## How Is It Treated?

- Radiation therapy is the main treatment.
- Chemotherapy is also used, often with radiation.
- Surgery is rarely used because the area is hard to reach.
- If the cancer comes back, radiation may be given again.
- In rare cases, surgery may be tried. It can be done through the nose using a camera (endoscope). This method is often just as effective as more invasive surgery and causes fewer side effects.
