# Toxoplasmosis – Simple Guide

Toxoplasmosis is an infection caused by a tiny parasite.  
Most people do not notice any symptoms.  
But some people may feel unwell.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You might have flu-like symptoms such as:  
- A high temperature  
- A headache  
- A sore throat  
- Aching muscles  
- Swollen glands  
- Feeling very tired  
- Feeling sick or being sick  

Some people have more serious symptoms, including:  
- Confusion  
- Blurred vision  
- Slurred speech  
- Trouble walking steadily  

## Who Is at Risk?

Toxoplasmosis is usually not serious.  
It often gets better on its own.  

But it can cause serious problems if you:  
- Are pregnant  
- Have a weak immune system (for example, if you have HIV or are having chemotherapy)  
- Have severe symptoms like confusion, blurred vision, or slurred speech  

If you get toxoplasmosis while pregnant, it can harm your baby.  
It may cause miscarriage or serious health problems for the baby.  

If you have a weak immune system, the infection can affect your eyes, brain, heart, or lungs.

## When to Get Help

Call your GP right away or use NHS 111 if you:  
- Are pregnant or have a weak immune system and have any symptoms  
- Have blurred vision  
- Have trouble walking  

You can call 111 or get help online.

If you are pregnant, you can also call your midwife for advice.

Go to A&E or call 999 if you or someone else suddenly:  
- Becomes confused  
- Starts speaking in a slurred way  

Find your nearest A&E.

### A&E Safety Tips

- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you.  
- If you cannot get a ride, call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
- Bring all your medicines with you.

## How Is It Treated?

Most people get better without treatment.  

But you may need medicine if you:  
- Are pregnant  
- Have a weak immune system (for example, if you are on certain medicines or have HIV)  
- Have eye problems from the infection  

Babies born with toxoplasmosis are treated with antibiotics and sometimes other medicines.  

If you are very ill, you may need to stay in hospital.

## How to Prevent Toxoplasmosis

The parasite that causes toxoplasmosis can be found in:  
- Cat poo  
- Undercooked meat  
- Soil that has been touched by cat poo  

You can avoid getting it by following these steps.

### Do This

- Wear gloves when gardening. Wash your hands well after.  
- Wash your hands before you prepare food or eat.  
- Wash your hands, knives, and cutting boards well after handling raw meat.  
- Wash fruit and vegetables well to remove any dirt.  
- Cook meat thoroughly, especially lamb, pork, and venison.  
- Avoid touching cat litter or soil if possible.  
- If you must clean a cat litter tray, wear gloves and wash your hands well after.

### Do Not Do This

- Do not eat raw or undercooked meat.  
- Do not eat cured meats like salami or Parma ham.  
- Do not touch pregnant sheep or newborn lambs.  
- Do not feed your cat raw or undercooked meat.

### Important Facts

- You cannot catch toxoplasmosis from petting a cat.  
- You cannot catch it from having a cat as a pet.  
- You cannot catch it from being near someone who has it.

# Ankle Fractures – Simple Explanation

An ankle fracture means one or more bones in the ankle are broken.  
The most common bones to break are the inner part of the shin bone (tibia) and the outer part of the calf bone (fibula).  

These breaks can be stable or unstable.  
Stable means the bones stay in place.  
Unstable means the bones are out of alignment and may move.

## How Ankle Fractures Happen

Ankle fractures often happen when you twist your ankle while running or jumping.  
This is called an inversion injury.  

Your ankle is made up of bones and ligaments that form a strong ring.  
This ring connects the lower leg bones to the foot bones.  
The ring stays strong because of:

- Two bones:  
  - The inner ankle bone (medial malleolus of the tibia)  
  - The outer ankle bone (lateral malleolus of the fibula)  

- Two groups of ligaments:  
  - On the inside: the deltoid ligament  
  - On the outside: the anterior talofibular ligament, posterior talofibular ligament, and calcaneofibular ligament  

If one part of the ring breaks, another part is often damaged too.  
For example, if a bone breaks, a ligament may tear at the same time.  

If two or more parts of the ring are damaged, the ankle becomes unstable.  
Damage to the inner ligament (deltoid) also causes instability.

## Special Type: Maisonneuve Fracture

Sometimes, the top part of the calf bone (proximal fibula) breaks.  
This is called a Maisonneuve fracture.  

This can happen when:  
- The inner ankle bone (medial malleolus) is broken  
- The joint between the shin and foot (ankle mortise) is open  
- The lower part of the calf bone (distal fibula) is not broken  

A Maisonneuve fracture can damage the peroneal nerve.  
This nerve runs near the calf bone and controls movement and feeling in the foot.  

Without a break in the lower fibula, the joint can still be damaged if the ligament between the tibia and fibula tears.  
This often happens when the top of the fibula breaks.

## Symptoms

Pain and swelling start right at the injury site.  
They often spread around the whole ankle.

## How Doctors Check for a Fracture

Doctors use X-rays to look for breaks.  
They take X-rays from different angles: front, side, and a special view called the mortise view.  

They may use the Ottawa ankle rules to decide if X-rays are needed.  
X-rays are usually needed if:

- You are over 55 years old  
- You cannot walk without help right after the injury (even just four steps)  
- You have tenderness in the ankle area, within 6 centimeters of the back or tip of either ankle bone  

If the X-ray shows a break, the doctor will check if the ankle is stable.  
They will look at the bones and ligaments.  
They may also do a stress X-ray to see if the joint is loose.

## What the X-rays Show

- A break in the lower fibula shows as a gap or step in the bone.  
- A break in the inner ankle bone (tibia) is visible on the X-ray.  
- A break in the outer ankle bone (fibula) is also visible.  
- A Maisonneuve fracture shows up as a break in the upper fibula and a widened space on the inside of the ankle joint.

## Checking for Stability

Doctors check stability by looking at and gently touching the ankle.  
They may also check the knee.  
This is because a break in the upper fibula can happen with a break in the inner ankle bone.  

If a Maisonneuve fracture is suspected, the doctor will test the peroneal nerve.  
They ask you to lift your foot upward to see if the nerve is working.

## Treatment

Most stable ankle fractures are treated with a walking boot or cast.  
This keeps the ankle still while it heals.

Unstable fractures usually need surgery.  
The surgery is called open reduction with internal fixation (ORIF).  
This means the surgeon puts the bones back in place and holds them with metal plates and screws.

## Important Points

- If one part of the ankle ring is broken, another part is often broken too.  
- If two or more parts of the ring are damaged, the ankle is unstable.  
- Use the Ottawa ankle rules to decide who needs X-rays.  
- Check the ankle’s stability with a physical exam and X-rays.  
- Treat stable fractures with a boot or cast.  
- Treat many unstable fractures with surgery (ORIF).  

## Prognosis

Most people heal well if the ankle is stable and the bones are properly aligned.  
If the bones do not stay in place, arthritis can develop.  
The ankle may also break again in the future.  

Maisonneuve fractures are serious.  
They always need surgery to fix the joint and prevent long-term problems.

# Infectious Conjunctivitis (Pink Eye)

This is inflammation of the clear membrane that lines the eyelid and covers the white part of the eye. It is usually caused by a virus or bacteria.

## What Causes It?

- Many different viruses and bacteria can cause this condition.
- The most common cause is a virus, especially a type called adenovirus.
- Bacteria can also cause it.
- Some viruses that cause body-wide symptoms can also cause red, sore eyes. These include:
  - Measles
  - Mumps
  - Rubella
  - Chickenpox
  - Zika virus
  - Some cold and flu viruses
  - The virus that causes COVID-19 (SARS-CoV2)

### In Babies

- Newborns can get conjunctivitis during birth.
- They are exposed to bacteria in the mother’s birth canal.
- The bacteria involved are *Chlamydia trachomatis* or *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*.

### Special Types

- **Inclusion conjunctivitis**: A long-lasting form caused by certain strains of *Chlamydia trachomatis*. It spreads through sexual contact with someone who has a genital chlamydia infection. It can also rarely come from swimming in a pool that is not fully cleaned.
- **Trachoma**: Another type caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis*, but it is not spread through sex.
- **Gonococcal conjunctivitis**: Caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* (the bacteria that cause gonorrhea). It can spread to the eye through contact with genital fluids from an infected person.
- Fungal infections are rare. They mostly happen in people who:
  - Use steroid eye drops for a long time
  - Have eye injuries from things like plants or dirt

## What Are the Symptoms?

- The eye turns red because blood vessels swell.
- There is often a discharge from the eye.
- The discharge can make the eyelids stick together, especially after sleeping.
- The discharge can blur vision. Blinking may clear the blur.
- If the clear front part of the eye (the cornea) is infected, vision stays blurry even after blinking.
- The eye may feel irritated.
- Bright light can hurt the eye.
- In rare cases, long-term scarring can lead to lasting vision problems.

### Viral vs. Bacterial Conjunctivitis

| Feature | Viral Conjunctivitis | Bacterial Conjunctivitis |
|--------|------------------------|---------------------------|
| Discharge | Watery | Thick, white, green, or yellow |
| Cold or flu symptoms | Common | Less common |
| Swollen lymph node in front of ear | Often present | Usually not present |

Note: These signs are not always clear. Doctors cannot always tell the difference just by looking.

### Other Signs

- People with inclusion conjunctivitis or gonorrhea-related conjunctivitis often have symptoms of a genital infection, such as:
  - Discharge from the penis or vagina
  - Burning when urinating

### Newborn Conjunctivitis

- Causes redness and swelling of the eyelids.
- Pus comes out of both eyes.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose it by:
- Looking at the symptoms
- Examining the eye closely with a special magnifying tool called a slit lamp

In some cases, a sample of the eye discharge is sent to a lab to test for the cause. This is done when:
- The symptoms are very bad or keep coming back
- The doctor is unsure if it is bacterial
- *Chlamydia trachomatis* or *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* is suspected
- The person has a weak immune system (like advanced HIV)
- The person has had eye surgery (like a corneal transplant) or eye bulging from Graves disease

## What Is Pink Eye?

- The term "pink eye" is often used for conjunctivitis caused by a virus or bacteria.
- It means the eye looks pink or red due to swollen blood vessels.

### Epidemic Keratoconjunctivitis

- A severe form caused by certain strains of adenovirus.
- It spreads easily from person to person.
- It can cause outbreaks in schools or communities.
- Spread happens through contact with infected eye secretions.
- This can happen by touching someone or touching contaminated objects (like poorly cleaned medical tools).

#### Symptoms

- Redness
- Watery discharge
- Eye feels like there is sand or grit in it
- Pain when looking at bright light
- Swelling of the conjunctiva around the cornea
- Swollen lymph node in front of the ear on the affected side

#### How Long Does It Last?

- Symptoms usually last 1 to 3 weeks.
- Blurry vision can last for weeks or even months.

#### Treatment

- No specific treatment is needed. The condition goes away on its own.
- In severe cases, doctors may give steroid eye drops to reduce swelling and light sensitivity.

#### How to Prevent Spread

- Wash hands often with soap and water or use hand sanitizer.
- Do not share towels, washcloths, or bedding.
- Stay home from work or school for several days, or even weeks in severe cases.
- Do not swim in pools.

## How Is It Treated?

- For bacterial conjunctivitis:
  - Use warm, wet compresses to clean the eye.
  - Use antibiotic eye drops or ointment to treat the infection.
- For severe viral conjunctivitis:
  - Steroid eye drops may be used if vision is very blurry or light hurts a lot.
- For comfort with viral conjunctivitis:
  - Use cold compresses to reduce swelling and pain.
- To stop the infection from spreading:
  - Use hand sanitizer or wash hands well before and after touching the eye.
  - Do not touch the infected eye and then touch the other eye.
  - Keep used towels and washcloths separate from others.

## How Long Does It Last?

- Most people get better without treatment.
- Some bacterial infections can last a long time if not treated.

### Special Cases

- **Inclusion conjunctivitis**: Can last for months if not treated.
- **Newborn conjunctivitis**: Can cause blindness if not treated.

## When to Stay Home

- People with infectious conjunctivitis should stay home from work or school for a few days, just like when they have a cold.
- In severe cases, people may need to stay home for weeks.
- Avoid swimming in pools until the infection is fully gone.

# Human Papillomavirus (HPV)

HPV usually does not cause any symptoms. You may not know you have it.

In some people, HPV can cause small, painless growths around the vagina, penis, or anus. These are called genital warts.

Most HPV infections go away on their own. Your body clears the virus without any treatment. This usually happens within two years.

If you notice genital warts or other problems, see a doctor. You can get help for these issues.

HPV does not cause health problems for most people. But some types of HPV can lead to cancer.

These types are called high-risk HPV. They can cause:

- Cervical cancer  
- Anal cancer  
- Penile cancer  
- Vulval cancer  
- Vaginal cancer  
- Some types of head and neck cancer  

You can carry HPV for many years without any signs. You can have it even if you have not had sex in a long time or only had one partner.

You can get HPV through any kind of sexual contact. This includes:

- Skin-to-skin contact in the genital area  
- Vaginal sex  
- Anal sex  
- Oral sex  
- Sharing sex toys  

You do not need to have penetrative sex to get HPV. You can get it the first time you have sex.

HPV is very common. Most people will get some type of HPV in their life.

### How to Reduce Your Risk

There is no way to be 100% protected from HPV. But you can lower your risk.

- Using condoms can help reduce your risk. But condoms do not cover all the skin around the genitals. So they do not fully protect you.
- The HPV vaccine protects against the most common types of HPV that cause genital warts and cervical cancer. It also helps prevent some other cancers. The vaccine does not protect against all types of HPV.

# Panniculitis

Panniculitis is a condition where the fat just under the skin becomes inflamed.  
It can happen for many different reasons.  
Doctors diagnose it by looking at the symptoms and doing a skin biopsy.  
Treatment depends on what is causing the inflammation.

> **Note:** This condition is similar to a condition called erythema nodosum.

## Types of Panniculitis

There are two main types, based on where in the fat layer the inflammation happens:

- **Lobular panniculitis**: Inflammation mainly affects the fat cells.
- **Septal panniculitis**: Inflammation mainly affects the tissue walls between fat cells.

## What Can Cause Panniculitis?

Panniculitis can be caused by:

- Infections
- Autoimmune diseases (like erythema nodosum, lipodermatosclerosis, or polyarteritis nodosa)
- Cold exposure or injury to the skin
- Blood cancers (such as T-cell lymphoma)
- Rheumatic diseases (like systemic lupus erythematosus or systemic sclerosis)
- Problems with the pancreas (such as pancreatitis or pancreatic cancer)
- A rare genetic condition called alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may notice lumps under the skin that are:

- Tender to touch
- Red or purple in color
- Found most often on the legs and arms
- Sometimes found on the back, belly, breasts, face, or buttocks

In rare cases, the lumps can appear in the intestines, lungs, scrotum, or skull.

You may also feel unwell, with symptoms like:

- Fever
- General tiredness

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors will:

- Look at your skin and ask about your symptoms
- Take a small sample of the skin (a biopsy) to check for inflammation

The diagnosis is usually based on how the skin looks.  
A biopsy helps confirm the diagnosis.

## How Is It Treated?

There is no single cure for panniculitis.  
Treatment focuses on managing symptoms and treating the underlying cause.

Options include:

- Supportive care (like rest and pain relief)
- Medicines to reduce inflammation
- Medicines that suppress the immune system
- Treatment for the root cause (such as antibiotics for infection or chemotherapy for cancer)

Some medicines that have been used with limited success include:

- Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
- Antimalarial drugs
- Dapsone
- Thalidomide

For severe cases or when the disease affects internal organs, doctors may use:

- Corticosteroids (taken by mouth or through a vein)
- Other immune-suppressing or chemotherapy drugs

## Key Points

- Panniculitis can have many different causes.
- Doctors diagnose it by examining the skin and confirming with a biopsy.
- Treatment is focused on relieving symptoms and treating the underlying cause.
- Anti-inflammatory or immune-suppressing medicines may be used if symptoms are severe.

# Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE)

SSPE is a rare and serious brain disease. It can happen months or years after a person has had measles. It slowly gets worse and is usually fatal.

## What Causes SSPE?

- SSPE is caused by the measles virus.
- The virus can stay in the brain for a long time after a measles infection.
- It may not cause problems at first, but later it can become active again.
- The disease is not caused by the measles vaccine. People who get SSPE after vaccination likely had a mild measles infection before they were vaccinated.

## Who Gets SSPE?

- SSPE is very rare in the United States and Western Europe because of widespread measles vaccination.
- It is more common in boys than in girls.
- The risk is highest in children who get measles before they are 2 years old.
- Most cases start in children or young adults, usually before age 20.

## Symptoms of SSPE

The first signs may include:
- Trouble doing well in school.
- Forgetting things easily.
- Getting angry quickly.
- Being easily distracted.
- Trouble sleeping.
- Seeing or hearing things that are not there (hallucinations).

Later, the person may have:
- Sudden jerking movements in the arms, head, or body.
- Seizures.
- Uncontrolled muscle movements.
- A slow loss of thinking ability and speech.

As the disease gets worse:
- Muscles become stiff and hard to move.
- Swallowing becomes difficult.
- Some people choke on their saliva, which can lead to pneumonia.
- Vision may be lost, and the person may become blind.
- In the final stages, body temperature may rise. Blood pressure and heart rate may become abnormal.

## How Is SSPE Diagnosed?

A doctor will suspect SSPE if a young person has mental decline and muscle jerks.

To confirm the diagnosis, doctors may do:
- A test on fluid from around the brain (cerebrospinal fluid).
- A blood test to check for high levels of antibodies to the measles virus.
- An electroencephalogram (EEG) to check brain activity. This test often shows abnormal patterns.
- Brain imaging tests like MRI or CT scans. These can show changes in the brain.

If the cause is still unclear, a brain biopsy may be needed.

## Treatment for SSPE

There is no cure for SSPE. Nothing can stop the disease from getting worse.

But doctors can help with symptoms:
- Medicines to control or reduce seizures may be used.

## Prognosis for SSPE

- SSPE is almost always fatal.
- Most people die within 1 to 3 years after symptoms start.
- The main cause of death is pneumonia.
- Pneumonia happens because the disease weakens the body and makes it hard to control muscles, including those used for breathing and swallowing.
- Some people have times when they feel better, followed by times when symptoms get worse.

# Cervical Spondylosis – Simple Guide

## What Is Cervical Spondylosis?

Cervical spondylosis is a common condition that happens as you get older.  
It affects the neck area of your spine.  
It is caused by normal wear and tear over time.  
Many people have it but do not feel any symptoms.  

## Common Symptoms

You may feel:
- Pain or stiffness in your neck or shoulders.  
- Headaches that start at the back of your neck.  
- Pain that comes and goes.  

These symptoms can get better or worse over time.  

## When to Seek Help

Call your doctor right away if you have:
- Pain that is getting much worse.  
- Weakness or heaviness in your arms or legs.  
- Tingling in an arm, along with neck or arm pain.  
- Neck pain that gets worse when you move.  
- Pain between your shoulder blades.  
- A stiff neck.  
- Trouble keeping your balance.  

If you have any of these, call 111 or get help online.  

Call 999 immediately if you have:
- Trouble walking.  
- Loss of control over your bladder or bowels.  
- Sudden trouble with coordination. For example, you cannot button a shirt.  
- One side of the face droops (mouth or eye may look uneven).  
- You cannot raise both arms and keep them up.  
- Trouble speaking. Your words may be slurred or hard to understand.  

These could be signs of a serious problem.  

## How to Ease the Pain

You can try these steps to feel better:
- Do gentle neck exercises.  
- Sit and stand with good posture.  
- Take painkillers like paracetamol or ibuprofen.  

These can help reduce pain and stiffness.  

## Help from a Pharmacist

A pharmacist can help you choose the right painkiller.  
They may suggest a stronger one if needed.  

## Treatment from Your Doctor

Your doctor will decide what treatment you need based on your symptoms.  
They may give you more exercises to do.  
They may also tell you to keep doing your normal daily activities.  

If the pain has lasted a long time, your doctor may prescribe:
- A muscle relaxant.  
- Other medicine to help with pain.  

It can take a few weeks to feel better.  
But the pain and stiffness may come back.  

## Surgery – When It’s Needed

Surgery is only considered if:
- A disc in your neck is pressing on a nerve.  
- There is a problem with your spinal cord.  

Surgery does not always cure the problem.  
But it can stop your symptoms from getting worse.  

## Physiotherapy

If your symptoms do not improve after a few weeks, your doctor may suggest physiotherapy.  
Physiotherapy helps you move better and reduces pain.  

Waiting times for NHS physiotherapy can be long.  
You can also get physiotherapy privately.  

## What Causes Cervical Spondylosis?

Most people over 40 get some signs of cervical spondylosis.  
It happens because of normal ageing.  
The bones in your neck and the soft cushions between them wear down over time.  

You may be more likely to get it at any age if:
- You had a neck injury in the past.  
- Someone in your family has had the condition.

# Diarrhea Caused by *Clostridioides difficile*

A germ called *Clostridioides difficile* can cause serious diarrhea. This germ makes poisons that damage the large intestine. The condition is called pseudomembranous colitis. It usually happens after taking antibiotics.

## What Causes This Diarrhea?

Antibiotics can kill good bacteria in your gut. This lets *C. difficile* grow out of control. The germ makes poisons that cause diarrhea and damage the colon.

Some antibiotics are more likely to cause this problem. These include:
- Third-generation cephalosporins
- Penicillins like ampicillin and amoxicillin
- Clindamycin
- Fluoroquinolones

Other medicines, like some cancer drugs, can also lead to this issue.

Some people carry *C. difficile* in their gut without getting sick. This is called being a carrier. The germ can live in soil, water, and pets. It can spread easily in hospitals and nursing homes.

A very strong strain of *C. difficile* called BI/NAP1/027 is now common. It makes more poison, causes worse illness, and is harder to treat. It also spreads more easily.

## Symptoms

Diarrhea usually starts 5 to 10 days after starting antibiotics. But it can start as early as the first day or up to 2 months later.

Symptoms may include:
- Frequent, watery diarrhea
- Diarrhea with blood
- Belly cramps or pain
- Mild tenderness in the belly

In severe cases, you may feel very sick. You may have:
- High heart rate
- Swollen belly
- Severe pain
- Signs of infection spreading through the body

Rarely, the colon can swell dangerously (toxic megacolon), tear open, or cause a life-threatening infection.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will test your stool for *C. difficile*.

Tests may include:
- Glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) antigen test – finds the germ, but not whether it is making poison
- Toxin test – checks for active poison
- PCR test – looks for the gene that makes the poison

The PCR test is very sensitive but can stay positive even after you are cured. This makes it hard to interpret.

Doctors usually do more than one test. A common approach is:
1. First, do the GDH and toxin tests.
2. If both are positive or both are negative, the result is clear.
3. If one is positive and one is negative, use the PCR test to decide.

A single stool sample is usually enough. If the first test is negative, do not repeat it for at least 7 days unless your symptoms get worse.

A sigmoidoscopy (a test using a small camera) may be done if you have no bowel movement (ileus) or if the stool tests are unclear.

Imaging tests like X-rays or CT scans are used if the doctor suspects a serious problem like a hole in the colon or a swollen colon.

## How Is It Treated?

The main treatments are:
- Oral vancomycin
- Oral fidaxomicin

These are the best choices for most people.

**Fidaxomicin** is taken as 200 milligrams by mouth every 12 hours for 10 days. It is recommended by major health groups. It lowers the chance of the illness coming back.

**Vancomycin** is taken as 125 milligrams by mouth four times a day for 10 days. It is also effective and is used when fidaxomicin is not available.

Metronidazole is no longer the first choice. It may be used only if vancomycin or fidaxomicin are not available.

For very severe cases without bowel blockage:
- Vancomycin 500 milligrams by mouth or through a tube, four times a day
- Metronidazole 500 milligrams through an IV, every 8 hours

If you have a bowel blockage (ileus), a vancomycin enema can be used. This is 500 milligrams in 10 milliliters of saline, given into the rectum four times a day.

If you are taking an antibiotic that may have caused the problem, stop it as soon as possible. Switch to a different antibiotic if needed.

Some supplements like cholestyramine, *Saccharomyces boulardii*, and probiotics are often used. But there is no strong proof they help.

Nitazoxanide works about as well as vancomycin. But it is not commonly used in the United States.

In rare cases, surgery to remove the colon may be needed.

## Key Points

- Antibiotics can let *C. difficile* grow and cause serious diarrhea.
- The most dangerous antibiotics are third-generation cephalosporins, penicillins, clindamycin, and fluoroquinolones.
- Test stool for the germ and its poison to confirm the diagnosis.
- Treat with oral fidaxomicin or vancomycin.
- The illness often comes back. If it does, treat again with antibiotics. For repeated cases, consider fecal transplant or a medicine called bezlotoxumab.

# Acupuncture

Acupuncture is a treatment from traditional Chinese medicine. It is one of the most widely accepted alternative therapies in Western countries.

Some people who do acupuncture are not medical doctors. But some doctors, especially those who treat pain, are trained and licensed to do it.

Millions of people get acupuncture every day. (See also: Overview of Integrative, Complementary, and Alternative Medicine.)

---

## How Acupuncture Works

Acupuncture uses very thin needles. The needles go into the skin at specific points on the body.

These points are believed to affect the flow of energy in the body. This energy is called qi (pronounced "chee").

In traditional Chinese medicine, illness happens when the flow of qi is not balanced. Qi moves through pathways in the body called meridians. There are more than 2,000 points along these pathways.

Stimulating these points helps balance two forces: yin (calm, quiet, soft) and yang (active, bright, strong).

Sometimes the needle is twisted or warmed to increase the effect.

---

## Other Ways to Stimulate Acupuncture Points

You can also stimulate these points without needles. These include:

- Pressing on the point (called acupressure)
- Using a laser
- Using sound waves (ultrasound)
- Sending a small electric current through the needle (called electroacupuncture)

Most people do not feel pain during acupuncture. Some feel a tingling or warm sensation.

---

## What Acupuncture May Help With

Doctors and researchers are studying whether acupuncture helps with:

- Pain relief after surgery or dental work
- Nausea and vomiting during pregnancy
- Nausea and vomiting after surgery or chemotherapy
- Addiction
- Carpal tunnel syndrome
- Fibromyalgia
- Headaches
- Lower back pain
- Tiredness
- Joint pain

Research on acupuncture is hard to do. It is difficult to hide which people get real acupuncture and which get fake treatment.

Some studies use "sham" acupuncture. This means needles are placed in spots that are not real acupuncture points. But even these fake needles can press on real points. This makes it hard to know if acupuncture really works.

In some places, especially China, studies often show better results. This could be due to bias. Or it could be because the providers are using the full system of traditional Chinese medicine, not just acupuncture.

Acupuncture has been shown to help with some health problems. But more research is still needed.

The fake treatment used in studies is not truly a placebo. It still involves a real treatment with a provider. This makes it hard to compare.

Some researchers use a blunt needle covered in a plastic tube. The needle touches the skin but does not go in. But even this can press on real points.

Many top medical centers and health groups, including the World Health Organization, are still studying acupuncture.

---

## Possible Side Effects

Side effects are usually mild if the treatment is done correctly.

- Some people feel worse for a short time after treatment.
- Very rarely, needles can hurt muscles, nerves, or skin.
- Infection is rare but possible.
- Headaches, dizziness, fainting, or sleepiness can happen, but they are rare.
- Some people feel faint during treatment. They may need to lie down.
- People with serious bleeding problems or those on blood thinners may bruise or bleed more.
- Very rarely, deep needle placement can cause a collapsed lung or internal injury.

---

# Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2)

Neurofibromatosis type 2 is a long-term health condition.  
It often causes growths in the inner ear.  
These growths can lead to hearing loss, ringing in the ears, and balance problems.

The condition is caused by a change in a gene.  
This changed gene can be passed from a parent to a child.  
But sometimes, a person is born with the changed gene even if their parents do not have it.

## When to See a Doctor

See your GP if you think you or your child might have NF2.

Get urgent help from your GP or NHS 111 if you have:
- Headaches that do not go away or are getting worse
- Feeling sick or being sick often
- Blurred vision or loss of vision

Use the 111 online service or call 111.

Call 999 if you:
- Have a seizure (fit) for the first time
- Feel weak or numb on one side of your face or body

## What to Expect

Everyone with NF2 is affected differently.  
Most people need help and support to manage daily life.

Healthcare teams will be there to guide you through treatment.  
You may also find it helpful to connect with others who have NF2 or parents of children with NF2.

### Nerve Tumours UK

This charity offers support and information for people with NF2.

They have support groups for:
- Adults with NF2
- Teenagers with NF2
- Parents of children with NF2

Helpline: 0300 102 17 22  
Open on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays from 9am to 5pm.

## Symptoms of NF2

Most people with NF2 develop growths in the inner ear.  
These growths grow slowly.  
They can cause:
- Hearing loss
- Ringing or buzzing in the ears (tinnitus)
- Trouble keeping your balance

You can also get growths on the spinal cord or on the layers around the brain (meninges).  
These may not always cause symptoms.  
But if they do, you might have:
- Headaches
- Feeling sick or being sick
- Seizures (fits)
- Hearing loss
- Blurred or lost vision
- Weakness or numbness in the face
- Weakness, numbness, or tingling in the hands and feet
- Skin lumps or marks that are smooth and shiny

Symptoms usually start in the late teens or early twenties.  
But children can also have symptoms.

### NF2 in Children

Children with NF2 often have eye problems.  
These can include:
- A squint (one eye turning in or out)
- Cloudy patches in the eyes (childhood cataracts)

Other common signs in children are:
- Skin lumps or marks
- Trouble lifting or moving the feet (foot drop)

## What Causes NF2

NF2 is caused by a change in a gene.  
This gene change can be inherited from a parent.  
But it can also happen for the first time in a child, even if neither parent has it.

If you have NF2, each child you have has a 50% chance of inheriting the changed gene.

## How NF2 Is Diagnosed

If you have symptoms, your doctor may refer you to a hospital.  
You may have several tests, including:
- Hearing tests
- Eye exams
- Scans such as a CT scan or MRI scan

Depending on the results, you may see specialists.  
These can include:
- A hearing expert (audiologist)
- An eye doctor (ophthalmologist)
- A gene expert (geneticist)

### Genetic Testing

A genetic test can help confirm NF2.  
It may be offered if a close family member has NF2.

If the test shows you have NF2, the gene expert will explain the condition.  
They will answer your questions.  
They will also tell you the chance of your children having NF2.

## Treatments for NF2

There is no cure for NF2.  
But treatments can help manage symptoms.

Your treatment will depend on your symptoms.  
Options include:
- Hearing aids or cochlear implants  
  (a cochlear implant is a small device that helps send sound signals to the brain)
- Medicine to slow down tumour growth  
  (sometimes this can improve hearing)
- Surgery to remove tumours that could cause harm
- Radiation treatment for small tumours  
  (or leftover parts of a larger tumour after surgery)

Most people with NF2 will need surgery at some point.  
This is usually to remove tumours from the inner ear, brain, or spinal cord.

## How NF2 Affects Daily Life

NF2 is a lifelong condition.  
It often gets worse over time.

The size, location, and speed of tumour growth vary from person to person.  
For many, the condition affects daily life.

Tumours in the inner ear can lead to total hearing loss.  
You may also have trouble walking.  
You might need a wheelchair or other support.

You will need regular care from a team of specialists.  
This can include physiotherapists and hearing experts.  
You will have regular check-ups and scans to monitor your condition.

NF2 can affect how long you live.  
But this depends on your symptoms and how they impact you.  
Your care team can talk to you about life expectancy if you want to know more.

# What Are Urinary Tract Infections?

Urinary tract infections (UTIs) can happen in different parts of the urinary system.

## Where Infections Can Occur

- Infections in the upper part of the urinary system affect the kidneys. This is called pyelonephritis.
- Infections in the lower part affect the bladder, the tube that carries urine out of the body (urethra), or the prostate gland in men. These are called cystitis, urethritis, and prostatitis.

In real life, especially in children, it can be hard to tell exactly where the infection is. Infections can also move from one area to another.

Even though urethritis and prostatitis are infections of the urinary system, doctors usually use the term UTI to mean infections of the bladder or kidneys.

## What Causes UTIs?

Most bladder and kidney infections are caused by bacteria.

Other causes include:
- Fungi, especially a type called candida.
- Less often, bacteria called mycobacteria.
- Viruses.
- Parasites.

Fungi, viruses, and parasites usually cause infections in people who have weak immune systems. They are also more common in people with diabetes, blockages in the urinary system, or birth defects in the urinary tract. These infections can also happen after medical procedures involving the urinary system.

## Viruses and UTIs

Viruses do not usually cause UTIs in healthy people.

One exception is adenovirus. It can cause a rare type of bladder infection called hemorrhagic cystitis.

## Parasites and UTIs

Some parasites can cause UTIs. These include:
- Filariasis
- Trichomoniasis
- Leishmaniasis
- Malaria
- Schistosomiasis

Of these, only trichomoniasis is common in the United States. It is usually spread through sexual contact.

## Causes of Urethritis and Prostatitis

- Urethritis is most often caused by a sexually transmitted infection (STI).
- Prostatitis is usually caused by bacteria. It can also be caused by an STI in some cases.

# What Is a Urinary Tract Infection?

Urine in the bladder is normally clean. No germs are in it. The tube that carries urine out of the body (urethra) also has no germs, or only a very small number. But any part of the urinary system can get infected. When this happens, it is called a urinary tract infection, or UTI.

## The Parts of the Urinary System

The urinary system includes:
- The kidneys (filter waste from the blood)
- The ureters (tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder)
- The bladder (holds urine)
- The urethra (the tube that carries urine out of the body)

These parts can be hurt by:
- A car crash or a fall
- A gunshot or stab wound
- An accident during surgery

## Types of UTIs

UTIs are split into two main types based on where they happen:

### Lower UTIs
- Infections in the bladder (called cystitis)
- Infections in the urethra (called urethritis)
- Infections in the prostate (called prostatitis)

### Upper UTIs
- Infections in the kidneys (called pyelonephritis)

Infections can happen in one or both kidneys. UTIs can affect children and adults.

## What Causes UTIs?

Most UTIs are caused by bacteria. Some can be caused by viruses, fungi, or parasites.

### How Germs Get Into the Urinary Tract

The most common way germs enter is through the opening of the urethra. This is at the tip of the penis in men and near the vagina in women. Germs can travel up the urethra into the bladder. Sometimes they go all the way to the kidneys.

The second way is through the blood. This is rare. Germs travel through the blood and reach the kidneys.

### Bacteria Are the Main Cause

Over 85% of UTIs are caused by bacteria from the intestines or vagina. These germs usually get washed out when the bladder empties. But sometimes they stay and cause an infection.

- *Escherichia coli* (E. coli) is the most common germ that causes UTIs.
- UTIs are much more common in women than in men, especially between ages 20 and 50.
- Men have a longer urethra, so germs have a harder time reaching the bladder.
- In men aged 20 to 50, most UTIs are in the urethra or prostate.
- After age 50, UTIs become more common in both men and women, and the difference between the sexes is smaller.

### Things That Make UTIs More Likely

#### Problems in the Urinary Tract
- Blockages in the urinary system (like kidney stones or a narrowed urethra)
- A prostate tumor in men
- A bladder that does not empty fully (can happen after spinal cord injury or other nerve problems)
- A birth defect in the urinary system (like a pouch in the urethra)
- A valve that does not work right between the ureter and bladder. This lets urine and germs flow backward into the kidneys (more common in children with UTIs)
- A catheter (tube) put into the bladder by a doctor
- Sexual activity
- Using a diaphragm with spermicide
- A hole between the vagina and bladder or between the intestine and bladder

#### Infections in Men
- An enlarged prostate
- Infection in the prostate

#### Infections That Spread from the Blood (Rare)
- Germs in the blood (called septicemia)
- Infection in the heart valves (called infective endocarditis)

## Other Causes of UTIs

### Viruses
- The herpes simplex virus can infect the urethra. This makes urination painful and makes it hard to empty the bladder.
- Other viral infections of the bladder or kidneys are rare. They usually only happen if the immune system is weak. This can happen with cancer, HIV/AIDS, or certain medicines.

### Fungi (Yeasts)
- Fungi can cause UTIs. This is often called a yeast infection.
- *Candida* is the most common fungus that causes this.
- Yeast infections are more likely in people with weak immune systems or those with a bladder catheter.
- Fungi and bacteria can infect the kidneys at the same time.

### Parasites
- Some worms and tiny parasites can infect the urinary tract.

#### Trichomoniasis
- Caused by a tiny parasite spread through sex.
- In women, it can cause a thick, greenish-yellow, bubbly discharge from the vagina.
- It can also infect the bladder or urethra.
- In men, it often causes no symptoms. But it can still be passed to a partner.

#### Schistosomiasis
- Caused by a type of worm called a fluke.
- It can affect the kidneys, ureters, and bladder.
- It is a common cause of serious kidney failure in people in Africa, South America, and Asia.
- Long-term bladder infection can cause blood in the urine, blockage of the ureters, and may lead to bladder cancer.

#### Filariasis
- Caused by a threadworm.
- It blocks the lymph vessels. This lets lymph fluid leak into the urine (called chyluria).
- It can cause extreme swelling in the body (called elephantiasis).
- In men, this swelling can affect the scrotum.

# Lactose Intolerance

Lactose intolerance means your body cannot digest lactose. Lactose is a sugar found in milk and dairy products.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms can start a few minutes to a few hours after eating or drinking something with lactose.

Common symptoms include:
- Pain or discomfort in your tummy
- A bloated tummy
- Passing gas (farting)
- Tummy rumbling
- Diarrhoea or constipation
- Feeling sick or being sick

Some people also have:
- Headaches
- Feeling tired
- Pain in joints or muscles

These symptoms are not always related to digestion.

## What Foods Contain Lactose?

Lactose is in all animal milk, including:
- Cow’s milk
- Goat’s milk
- Sheep’s milk

It is also in many dairy products such as:
- Milk
- Butter
- Cheese
- Cream
- Yoghurt
- Ice cream

Many processed foods also contain lactose, including:
- Cereals
- Breads, crackers, cakes, biscuits, and pastries
- Sauces and salad dressings
- Diet and protein shakes

## What Causes Lactose Intolerance?

The most common cause is not making enough lactase. Lactase is the enzyme your body uses to break down lactose.

Lactose intolerance can start at any age. It can also be caused by:
- Inflammatory bowel disease
- Coeliac disease
- Bowel infections
- Bowel surgery
- Injury to the bowel

Some babies born early cannot digest lactose because their intestines are not fully developed. This usually improves as they grow.

Very rarely, a person is born with no ability to make lactase at all.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

If your doctor thinks you have lactose intolerance, they may suggest:

- A lactose-free diet: You stop eating foods with lactose for a while to see if your symptoms get better.
- Blood tests: These check your blood sugar levels after eating lactose.
- A breath test: You breathe into a machine to measure hydrogen gas. High levels mean your body is not digesting lactose well.

If your symptoms are very bad and do not improve, you may need a gastroscopy. This is a test where a thin, flexible tube is gently passed through your mouth and into your stomach. A tiny sample of tissue from your small intestine may be taken for testing.

Before the test, you may be given medicine to help with pain and to help you relax.

## How Is It Treated?

Most people can manage symptoms by eating less lactose or avoiding it completely.

If you think your child has lactose intolerance, talk to your doctor before cutting dairy from their diet. Dairy is important for growth and development.

Taking a lactase supplement before eating or drinking something with lactose can help some people. These supplements help your body break down lactose.

In some cases, lactose intolerance is caused by another health problem, like coeliac disease. Treating the main condition can help improve lactose intolerance.

## When to See Your Doctor

See your doctor if you have symptoms of lactose intolerance and:

- Your symptoms come back often, especially after eating
- You notice changes in your poo that are not normal for you, such as looser stools, more frequent poos, or constipation lasting 3 weeks
- You have blood in your poo for 3 weeks
- You have tummy bloating and pain for 3 weeks
- You are losing weight

## When to Call 999 (Emergency)

Call emergency services if you or someone else has any of these signs:

- Sudden swelling in the lips, mouth, throat, or tongue
- Very fast breathing or trouble breathing (you may wheeze, choke, or gasp for air)
- A tight feeling in the throat or trouble swallowing
- Skin, tongue, or lips turning blue, grey, or pale (on dark skin, check the palms of hands or soles of feet)
- Sudden confusion, drowsiness, or dizziness
- Someone faints and cannot be woken up
- A child is limp, floppy, or not responding normally (their head may fall to the side, back, or front, or they may struggle to lift their head or look at you)

You or the person may also have a rash that is swollen, raised, or itchy.

These signs can mean a serious allergic reaction. This needs emergency treatment in hospital.

# Anal Itching

Itching around the anus is a common problem. It can happen for many reasons. This condition is also called anal itching.

Sometimes people feel pain instead of itching. So, doctors must check for other serious causes, like an abscess or cancer.

---

## What Causes Anal Itching?

Most of the time, doctors do not find a clear cause. This is called idiopathic.

Other common causes include:

- **Poor hygiene**: Not cleaning enough leaves stool and sweat on the skin. This can cause irritation.
- **Over-cleaning**: Using strong soaps, wipes, or scrubbing too hard can dry out or irritate the skin. Some people may have a reaction to certain products.
- **Hemorrhoids**: Large external hemorrhoids can make cleaning hard. Large internal hemorrhoids can leak mucus or cause stool to stick to the skin. This leads to irritation.

In young children and older adults, leaking stool or urine can cause skin irritation. This can also lead to a yeast infection.

Once itching starts, it can get worse. Scratching makes the skin more irritated. This causes more itching. The skin can become raw and infected. This leads to even more itching.

Some creams or ointments used to treat itching or infection can also cause irritation. This can make the problem worse.

---

## Common Causes of Anal Itching

| Cause | Signs to Watch For | How It’s Checked |
|------|---------------------|------------------|
| **Inflammatory bowel disease** (like Crohn disease) | Pus from the anus, pain in the rectum or belly, a fistula, or diarrhea | Anoscopy, sigmoidoscopy, or colonoscopy |
| **Hemorrhoids** | Bleeding (small amount of blood on toilet paper or in the toilet) or a painful lump on the anus | Physical exam, sometimes anoscopy or sigmoidoscopy |
| **Bacterial infection** (from scratching) | Red, raw, or broken skin | Physical exam |
| **Yeast infection** (Candida) | Rash around the anus | Physical exam, sometimes skin scraping |
| **Pinworms** | Common in children, may affect other family members | Tape test to check for eggs |
| **Scabies** | Very itchy, especially at night, may itch elsewhere, thin red lines or bumps on skin | Physical exam, skin scraping |
| **Atopic dermatitis** | Itchy, red, oozing, or crusty rash | Physical exam |
| **Skin cancer** (like Bowen disease or Paget disease) | Scaly or crusty spot | Biopsy |
| **Psoriasis** | Thick, scaly patches on skin | Physical exam, may see patches elsewhere |
| **Skin tags** | Small flap of skin near the anus | Physical exam |

---

## Medications and Diet

Some medicines and foods can cause anal itching.

- **Antibiotics**: If you recently took antibiotics, they might be the cause.
- **Foods and supplements**: Beer, coffee, chocolate, spicy food, milk, nuts, tomatoes, citrus fruits, spices, or vitamin C pills may trigger itching in some people.

If you think a food or medicine is causing the problem, try stopping it for a while to see if the itching improves.

---

## Hygiene Problems

- **Sweating too much**: Especially when wearing tight or synthetic clothes. Try wearing loose cotton underwear and changing it often.
- **Too little cleaning**: Not cleaning enough can leave stool and sweat on the skin.
- **Too much cleaning**: Using harsh soaps, wipes, or scrubbing hard can irritate the skin.

Try changing your cleaning habits. Use only water or mild soap. Do not scrub hard.

---

## Irritants

Some products can irritate the skin:

- Local anesthetics
- Ointments
- Soaps
- Sanitary wipes

If you use any of these and the itching gets worse, stop using them.

---

## How Doctors Check for Anal Itching

Doctors will ask about your symptoms and medical history. They will do a physical exam.

They may do tests if needed, such as:

- Looking at skin scrapings
- Checking for pinworm eggs with a tape test
- Taking a sample of tissue (biopsy) if cancer is suspected
- Using scopes to look inside the rectum or colon

---

## How to Treat Anal Itching

- Treat any infection or serious condition, like cancer or a yeast infection.
- Stop using any food or product that seems to cause the problem.
- Use only gentle, non-irritating cleaning methods.
- Keep the area dry. Moisture can make itching worse.

---

## Key Points

- Most cases have no clear cause, but doctors should check for serious problems.
- Pinworms are common in children. Poor hygiene is a common cause in adults.
- Certain foods and soaps can cause itching.
- Clean the area gently. Do not use strong soaps or scrub hard.
- Keep the area dry to help reduce itching.

# Panniculitis

Panniculitis is when the layer of fat under your skin becomes inflamed.

## What Causes Panniculitis?

The exact cause is not known.  
But it can happen after an infection, injury, or exposure to cold.  
It may also be linked to certain health conditions, such as:

- Lupus  
- Pancreas problems  
- Inflammatory bowel disease  
- Polyarteritis nodosa  
- Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency  

Erythema nodosum is a common type of panniculitis.

## Symptoms

You may feel tender, red, or purple lumps under your skin.  
These lumps are called nodules.  
They form deep in the fat layer beneath the skin.  
They can be large—several centimeters across.  

The lumps most often appear on the legs and arms.  
They can also show up on the buttocks, chest, or face.  

You may also have signs of bodywide inflammation, such as:  
- Fever  
- Joint pain  
- Muscle pain  
- Feeling unwell  

## How Doctors Diagnose Panniculitis

Your doctor will examine your skin and ask about your symptoms.  
They may take a small sample of the lump or skin.  
This sample is looked at under a microscope.  
This test is called a biopsy.  
It helps confirm the diagnosis.

## How Panniculitis Is Treated

There is no single treatment for panniculitis.  
Doctors focus on relieving symptoms and treating any underlying cause.

Medications that reduce pain and swelling may help.  
These include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or NSAIDs.  

Other medicines that may be used include:  
- Drugs used to treat malaria  
- Dapsone  
- Thalidomide  

If your symptoms are getting worse, your doctor may prescribe:  
- Corticosteroids  
- Medicines that calm the immune system (immunosuppressants)  
- Chemotherapy drugs  

Your doctor will also treat any condition that is causing the panniculitis.

# Chlamydia

Chlamydia is a common infection. It spreads through sex without a condom.

Many people do not have any symptoms. You can still pass it on even if you feel fine.

## Symptoms of Chlamydia

Most people with chlamydia do not feel sick. You might not know you have it.

If you do have symptoms, they can start as early as one week or as late as several months after infection.

### Symptoms in Women

You may notice:
- A change in your vaginal discharge. It might be more than usual or look different.
- Bleeding after sex or between your periods.
- A burning feeling when you pee.
- Pain in your lower belly.

### Symptoms in Men

You may notice:
- A white, cloudy, or watery discharge from the tip of your penis.
- Itching or burning around your penis or testicles.
- Swelling or pain in your testicles.
- A burning feeling when you pee.

### Other Possible Symptoms

Chlamydia can also affect other areas if they come into contact with semen or vaginal fluid. These include:
- Pain, bleeding, or discharge from your bottom.
- A sore throat.
- Red, painful eyes with discharge.

## Getting Tested and Treated

You can get tested at a sexual health clinic or with your doctor.

Chlamydia is treated with antibiotics. You may take one pill or a course of tablets for 7 to 14 days.

Sometimes, treatment starts before your test results come back.

You may need to be tested again after treatment. This checks that the infection is gone.

If you are pregnant, you will be tested again four weeks after finishing treatment.

### Important

Do not have vaginal, anal, or oral sex until:
- You have finished all your medicine.
- Your test results show you no longer have chlamydia.
- Your partner has also finished treatment and tested negative.

## How to Prevent Chlamydia

Chlamydia spreads through vaginal fluid and semen. It can pass during sex without a condom.

If you are pregnant and have chlamydia, it can pass to your baby during birth.

### What You Should Do

- Use a condom every time you have vaginal or anal sex.
- Use a condom on the penis, or a latex or plastic square (called a dam) over the vagina during oral sex.
- Get tested once a year, or whenever you start a new sexual relationship.
- Finish all your medicine if you or your partner has chlamydia.

### What You Should Not Do

- Do not share sex toys.
- If you do share them, wash them well and cover them with a new condom before the next person uses them.

## Possible Complications

If chlamydia is not treated, it can cause serious health problems.

These include:
- Infection in the womb, fallopian tubes, or ovaries. This can lead to trouble getting pregnant or a dangerous pregnancy outside the womb.
- Infection in the testicles.
- Joint pain called reactive arthritis. This usually gets better after a few months.

The earlier you get treatment, the better your chances of avoiding these problems.

## Chlamydia During Pregnancy

If you are pregnant and have chlamydia, it can pass to your baby during birth.

This can cause:
- Eye infection (conjunctivitis) in your baby.
- Lung infection (pneumonia) in your baby.

Both of these can be treated with antibiotics. Early treatment helps your baby stay healthy.

# Febrile Seizures

Febrile seizures happen in children between 6 months and 5 years old. They occur when a child has a fever over 38 degrees Celsius. The fever is not caused by an infection in the brain or spinal cord. The child has never had a seizure without fever before.

Doctors diagnose febrile seizures only after ruling out other possible causes.

## What Are Febrile Seizures?

Febrile seizures are fairly common. About 2 to 5 out of every 100 children in this age group will have one. Most happen between 12 and 18 months of age.

There are two types: simple and complex.

### Simple Febrile Seizures
- Last less than 15 minutes.
- Affect the whole body.
- Do not happen more than once in 24 hours.
- Most febrile seizures are simple.

### Complex Febrile Seizures
- Last 15 minutes or longer.
- Affect only part of the body.
- Start in one area of the body.
- Happen more than once in 24 hours.

## What Causes Febrile Seizures?

- They can happen during viral infections, like the flu or human herpesvirus 6.
- They can also happen after some vaccines, such as the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine.
- Some children have a family history of febrile seizures. Twins are more likely to both have them if they are identical.
- Children with developmental delays may be at higher risk for future seizures.

## What Do Febrile Seizures Look Like?

- They often start when a child’s fever is rising fast.
- Most happen within the first 24 hours of fever.
- Higher fever is more likely to cause a seizure than how fast the fever rises.
- The seizure usually affects the whole body.
- Movements may be jerky (clonic), stiff (tonic), or limp (atonic).

After the seizure:
- The child may be sleepy for a few minutes to a few hours.
- Confusion or restlessness can happen but is less common.
- If the child stays very sleepy for more than an hour, or if one side of the body is weak, see a doctor right away. This could mean a serious brain problem.
- Most children return to normal quickly.

### Febrile Status Epilepticus
This is when seizures go on for 30 minutes or more. It can be continuous or come in waves with no recovery between them. This type of seizure can cause brain damage. It may lead to long-term problems like epilepsy.

## How Are Febrile Seizures Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose febrile seizures only after checking for other causes.

### When Testing Is Needed
- For simple febrile seizures: Only check for the cause of the fever. No other tests are needed.
- For complex seizures, or if the child has weakness, or signs of a serious illness: More tests may be needed.

### Tests That May Be Done
- **Cerebrospinal fluid test**: Only if the child is very young and shows signs of brain infection (like stiff neck or drowsiness). Also if seizures happen after several days of fever, or if the child is not fully vaccinated or is on antibiotics.
- **Blood tests**: To check for low blood sugar, low sodium, or other chemical imbalances. This is important if the child has been vomiting, had diarrhea, or is dehydrated.
- **Blood and urine cultures**: To find the source of the fever.
- **Brain MRI**: Only if the child has signs of brain problems, or if the seizure affects only one side of the body. Not needed for simple seizures.
- **EEG (brain wave test)**: Only if the seizure has local features or happens more than once. It is not helpful for predicting future seizures in children with normal brain exams.

If a child already has a known brain or developmental condition, the diagnosis may not be a febrile seizure.

## How Are Febrile Seizures Treated?

### Fever Medicine
- Fever medicine (like acetaminophen or ibuprofen) can help make the child feel better.
- But it does not prevent another seizure.

### Seizures Lasting Less Than 5 Minutes
- No special treatment is needed.
- Keep the child safe and calm.
- Watch them closely.

### Seizures Lasting 5 Minutes or More
- Medication is needed to stop the seizure.
- The child must be watched closely for breathing and heart problems.
- If the seizure does not stop, or if breathing stops, the child may need a breathing tube.

### Medications Used
- **Lorazepam** (given through a vein) is often used first. It can be given every 5 to 10 minutes, up to 3 times.
- If the seizure continues, **fosphenytoin** may be given through a vein over 15 to 30 minutes.
- Other medicines like **phenobarbital**, **valproate**, or **levetiracetam** may also be used.

### If IV Access Is Not Available
- For children over 2 years old, **diazepam rectal gel** or **intranasal midazolam** can be used at home or in an emergency.

### Preventing Future Seizures
- Some doctors give diazepam rectal gel to parents to use at home if a seizure lasts too long.
- This is only for children with a history of repeated seizures.

## What Is the Outlook?

- Most children grow up with no long-term problems.
- The chance of developing epilepsy later is slightly higher than in other children.
- The risk is about 2 to 6 percent after one simple febrile seizure.

## How Can Febrile Seizures Be Prevented?

- Parents should check their child’s temperature during illness.
- Give fever medicine if the child feels uncomfortable, even if it does not prevent seizures.
- Routine use of seizure medicine to prevent future febrile seizures is not usually needed.

### When Medicine Might Be Used
- If the child has complex seizures and signs of brain problems.
- If there is a strong family history of epilepsy and repeated seizures.
- If the child has had febrile status epilepticus.
- If seizures happen at least once every three months.

## Key Points

- Febrile seizures happen in children 6 months to 5 years old with fever over 38 degrees Celsius.
- The fever is not from a brain or spinal cord infection.
- The child has never had a seizure without fever.
- Simple seizures last less than 15 minutes and do not repeat in 24 hours.
- Complex seizures last 15 minutes or more, affect one side of the body, or repeat in 24 hours.
- No tests are needed for simple seizures.
- Tests are needed if the seizure is complex, or if the child has weakness or signs of a serious illness.
- Seizures lasting 5 minutes or more need medicine like lorazepam.
- The risk of future epilepsy is slightly higher after a febrile seizure.
- Giving fever medicine at the start of illness does not prevent febrile seizures.

# Diaphragmatic Hernia

A diaphragmatic hernia is a birth defect. It means there is a hole or weak spot in the diaphragm. The diaphragm is the muscle that separates the chest from the belly.

Because of the hole, some of the organs from the belly can move up into the chest.

This can make it very hard for the baby to breathe.

## What Happens in a Diaphragmatic Hernia

- The diaphragm is a muscle that separates the chest and belly.
- Most of these hernias happen on the left side of the body.
- The stomach, intestines, liver, or spleen can push through the hole into the chest.
- If the hole is large, the lung on that side may not develop fully.
- The other lung can also be squished by the organs in the chest.
- When the lungs are squished, the blood vessels in them get narrow.
- This causes high blood pressure in the blood vessels of the lungs.
- High pressure in the lung blood vessels means less blood can flow through the lungs.
- Less blood flow means less oxygen gets into the blood.

After birth, the baby starts to cry and breathe. The stomach and intestines fill with air. This makes them grow bigger fast. The growing organs push on the heart and the other lung. This causes serious breathing problems. These problems often start right after birth.

Some babies with this condition also have other birth defects. These can include heart problems, kidney problems, or chromosome issues.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors can find a diaphragmatic hernia before birth.

- They use a prenatal ultrasound to look at the baby in the womb.
- If needed, they use a fetal MRI to get more detail about the hole and how the lungs are developing.

After birth, doctors use these tests:

- A chest x-ray to see the hole and where the organs are.
- A CT scan or MRI to get a clearer picture of the defect and to check for other birth defects.
- An echocardiogram (a special ultrasound of the heart) to check for heart problems.

Finding the problem before birth helps the hospital prepare. The baby can be born in a center with special care teams. This can improve the chances of survival.

## How Doctors Treat It

Treatment depends on how serious the problem is.

### Before Birth
- In some cases, doctors may do a surgery on the fetus before birth.
- This surgery is called fetoscopic endoluminal tracheal occlusion (FETO).
- It helps the baby’s lungs grow bigger.
- This surgery is only done in certain medical centers.
- It is only used for fetuses who are likely to benefit.
- It carries risks, so it is not done for all babies.

### After Birth
- The baby will need help breathing.
- Doctors give oxygen through a tube in the windpipe.
- A ventilator helps move air in and out of the lungs.
- For very sick babies, a machine called ECMO may be used.
  - ECMO takes over the work of the lungs or both the heart and lungs.
  - It gives the baby time to heal.

- Surgery is done soon after birth.
- The surgeon moves the organs back into the belly.
- The hole in the diaphragm is closed.

Surgery is key to fixing the problem and helping the baby breathe normally.

# Head Lice and Nits

Head lice are tiny bugs that live in your hair.  
They can cause an itchy scalp.  
You might also see small brown or white eggs stuck to your hair.  
These eggs are called nits.

## What to Look For

Head lice are very small.  
They are no bigger than 3 millimeters.  
They are hard to see in your hair.  
The nits are attached to the hair close to the scalp.  
They look like tiny specks.  
They are either brown or white.

The only way to know for sure if someone has head lice is to find live bugs.  
You can do this by using a special fine-toothed comb.  
This is called a detection comb.  
You can buy it online or at a pharmacy.

## How to Get Rid of Head Lice

Start treatment as soon as you find lice.  
You do not need to see a doctor.  
Check everyone in your home or who spends time close to you.  
Treat anyone who has lice on the same day.

You do not need to keep your child home from school.  
You do not need to wash clothes in hot water.

### Wet Combing

Wet combing can remove lice and nits.  
Use a detection comb.  
You can buy it at a pharmacy or online.

To do wet combing:

- Wash your hair with regular shampoo.  
- Put a lot of conditioner on your hair.  
- Use the detection comb to go from the roots to the ends of your hair.  
- Do this for the whole head.  
- Then go through the hair again from root to tip.

It takes about 10 minutes for short hair.  
It takes 20 to 30 minutes for long, curly, or frizzy hair.

Do wet combing on day 1, day 5, day 9, and day 13.  
Check again on day 17 to make sure no lice are left.

### Medicated Lotions and Sprays

If wet combing does not work, try a medicated lotion or spray.  
These are available at pharmacies, supermarkets, or online.  
They work on all hair types.

The lice should die within one day.  
Some products come with a comb to remove dead lice and nits.  
You may need to repeat the treatment after one week.  
This kills any new lice that hatch.

Always read the instructions.  
Check if the product is safe for you or your child.  
If the lotion or spray does not work, talk to a pharmacist.  
They can suggest other options.

### Treatments That Do Not Work

Some treatments are not recommended.  
They are unlikely to help.  
These include:

- Products with permethrin  
- Lice repellent sprays or lotions  
- Electric combs for lice  
- Plant oils like tea tree oil, eucalyptus oil, or lavender oil  
- Herbal remedies for lice

These treatments do not reliably kill lice.  
They are not worth using.

# Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS)

Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) is a group of blood disorders. It happens when the bone marrow does not make healthy blood cells. The bone marrow may make too few or abnormal blood cells. This can lead to anemia, infections, or bleeding.

MDS can turn into a type of fast-growing blood cancer called acute myeloid leukemia. This happens in many people with MDS.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on which blood cells are most affected.

- If red blood cells are low, you may feel tired, weak, or pale.
- If white blood cells are low, you may get more infections or fevers.
- If platelets are low, you may bleed more easily or bruise easily.

Some people also have an enlarged liver or spleen. This can cause fullness in the belly.

## How Is MDS Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to diagnose MDS:

- A blood test to check your blood cell counts.
- A blood smear to look at the shape of your blood cells under a microscope.
- A bone marrow test. This means taking a small sample from your bone marrow to check for problems.

Doctors will rule out other causes of low blood counts. These include vitamin deficiencies, autoimmune diseases, or side effects from medicines.

The diagnosis is confirmed by finding abnormal blood cells and changes in the bone marrow. Doctors also look for specific gene changes or chromosome problems.

## What Causes MDS?

The exact cause of MDS is not known. But it is more common in older adults. This may be because of gene changes that build up over time.

Some things may raise your risk:
- Exposure to radiation.
- Exposure to certain chemicals like benzene.
- Past cancer treatment with chemotherapy or radiation, especially long or strong treatments.

Changes in chromosomes are often found in MDS. These changes can affect how blood cells grow.

## How Does MDS Affect the Body?

The bone marrow may be too full or too empty. The body makes blood cells poorly. This leads to low levels of red blood cells, white blood cells, or platelets.

Over time, people who need blood transfusions often build up too much iron in their body. This is called iron overload.

The blood and bone marrow cells may look abnormal under a microscope. In some cases, the bone marrow can become scarred. This is called myelofibrosis.

MDS can also cause blood cells to form outside the bone marrow. This can make the liver and spleen larger.

MDS is grouped into types based on blood and bone marrow tests. The type helps doctors predict how the disease may progress.

## Types of MDS

There are several types of MDS. Each has different features:

- **Refractory anemia**: Low red blood cells, but normal or high bone marrow. The red blood cells look abnormal.
- **Refractory anemia with ringed sideroblasts**: Same as above, but more abnormal iron-filled cells are seen in the bone marrow.
- **Refractory cytopenia with multilineage dysplasia**: Low counts in more than one type of blood cell. The cells look abnormal.
- **Refractory cytopenia with multilineage dysplasia and ringed sideroblasts**: Same as above, but with more iron-filled cells.
- **Refractory anemia with excess blasts (RAEB)**: Low counts in two or more blood cell types. More abnormal cells are found in the bone marrow. This type has a higher risk of turning into leukemia.
- **MDS unclassified**: MDS that does not fit into any other group.
- **MDS with isolated del(5q)**: A specific type that mainly affects women. It causes severe anemia and high platelet counts. It often responds well to a medicine called lenalidomide.
- **Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML)** and **juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML)**: These are mixed disorders. They have features of both MDS and another blood disease. They cause high levels of a certain white blood cell.
- **Chronic neutrophilic leukemia**: A rare type with high levels of a certain white blood cell. It does not involve a specific gene change linked to other cancers.

## How Is MDS Treated?

Treatment depends on your symptoms, your age, and the type of MDS.

### Supportive Care
Many people need regular blood or platelet transfusions. These help relieve symptoms like fatigue or bleeding.

Over time, repeated transfusions can cause too much iron in the body. This can harm the heart and liver. A medicine called an iron chelator can help remove extra iron.

### Medicines to Help Blood Production
- **Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESA)**: These help make more red blood cells. They work best in people with low levels of a certain hormone and who do not need frequent transfusions.
- **Growth factors (like G-CSF)**: These can help increase white blood cells. Used with ESA, they may improve red blood cell production in some people.
- **Luspatercept**: This medicine helps increase red blood cell levels in people with certain types of MDS who do not respond to ESA.

### Drugs That Target the Disease
- **Azacitidine**: This medicine helps slow the disease. It can help people live longer than with no treatment. It is given as a shot under the skin. Most people get it for 4 to 6 cycles. Treatment continues as long as it helps.
- **Decitabine**: This medicine also helps slow the disease. It can lead to remission in some people. It is used for all types of MDS.
- **Lenalidomide**: This medicine works well for people with MDS and a specific chromosome change (deletion 5q). It can reduce the need for blood transfusions.

### Immune System Treatment
For people with low bone marrow activity, medicines that calm the immune system can help. These include cyclosporine and antithymocyte globulin. They can improve blood counts and reduce the need for transfusions.

### Stem Cell Transplant
This is the only treatment that can cure MDS. It is best for younger, healthier people with higher-risk MDS. It replaces the faulty bone marrow with healthy stem cells from a donor.

## What Is the Outlook?

The outlook depends on the type of MDS and how advanced it is.

Some types are less likely to turn into leukemia. These include refractory anemia and refractory anemia with ringed sideroblasts.

Doctors use a system called the **Revised International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS-R)** to predict how the disease may progress. It looks at:

- The type of chromosome changes.
- The number of abnormal cells in the bone marrow.
- How low your blood counts are.

The more risk factors you have, the worse the outlook.

- People in the lowest risk group may live about 8 years on average.
- People in the highest risk group may live only about 10 months on average.

## Key Points

- MDS is a disorder where the bone marrow makes too few or abnormal blood cells.
- Most people have low red blood cells, but some also have low white blood cells or platelets.
- MDS often turns into a fast-growing blood cancer called acute myeloid leukemia.
- Azacitidine and decitabine can help reduce symptoms and slow the disease.
- Stem cell transplant is the only cure. It is best for younger, healthier people.

The following resource may be helpful:

**MDS Foundation**: Offers information on diagnosis, treatment, clinical trials, and centers of excellence for healthcare professionals.
