# Herpes Simplex Eye Infections

## What Are the Symptoms?

Herpes simplex eye infections usually affect just one eye.  
You may have eye pain.  
Your eye might be red.  
Your eye may water a lot.  
You may feel pain when looking at light.  
Your vision might be blurry.  
You might notice other changes in your eyesight.  
Your eyelid may be swollen.  
You might have blisters or a rash on your eyelid or the skin around your eye.

If you have had a cold sore before, you are more likely to get a herpes simplex eye infection.  
If you have had this infection before, it may not hurt as much over time.

## What Causes It?

The same virus that causes cold sores can also cause eye infections.  
You usually get the virus from skin-to-skin contact with someone who has a cold sore.  
Once you have the virus, it stays in your body for life.  
It usually does not cause any symptoms.  
But sometimes it can cause an eye infection.

Certain things can trigger the virus to become active again.  
These include illness, stress, bright light, or an injury to the eye.  
People with a weaker immune system are more likely to get an eye infection.

You are unlikely to pass the virus to someone else through an eye infection.  
But avoid touching your eye.  
Wash your hands often to stay safe.

## When to See a Doctor

See a doctor or go to an optician if:

- Your eye is red and not painful, but stays red for more than a few days.

Some opticians can treat certain eye conditions on the NHS.  
Check with them before you go.

If the cause of your red eye is not clear, you may be sent to an eye specialist for tests.

## When to Get Urgent Help

Call your doctor right away or use NHS 111 if you have:

- Eye pain  
- A red eye that is getting worse  
- Blurry vision or other changes in your eyesight  
- A swollen or irritated eyelid that is not improving

It might not be serious, but it could need quick treatment.  
You can call 111 or get help online at 111.

## When to Go to A&E

Go to A&E or call 999 if you have a red eye and:

- It hurts to look at light  
- Your eye is very dark red  
- One pupil is bigger than the other

Find your nearest A&E.

### A&E Safety Tips

Do not drive to A&E.  
Ask someone to drive you.  
Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring all your medicines with you.

## How Are These Infections Treated?

If your doctor thinks you have a herpes simplex eye infection, they will refer you to an eye specialist.  
You will usually be seen the same day so treatment can start fast.

You will likely be given:

- An antiviral medicine as eye ointment, eye drops, or sometimes tablets  
- Or an antiviral medicine with steroid eye drops to reduce swelling

Most infections get better in a few weeks.  
Treatment usually does not cause lasting damage to your eyesight.

It is common for these infections to come back.  
If you keep getting them, your doctor may suggest taking antiviral tablets every day to help prevent new infections.

If treatment does not work or if you keep getting infections, the clear front part of your eye (called the cornea) may scar.  
This can lead to vision loss.  
If this happens, you may need a cornea transplant.

## Important Tips

If you wear contact lenses, do not wear them until 24 hours after all your symptoms are gone.

# Lumbosacral Radiculopathy

This condition causes pain or other nerve problems that travel along the lower back and down one or both legs. It happens when nerves in the lower spine are squeezed or damaged. The most common causes are a bulging disk, bone spurs, or narrowing of the spine. In rare cases, a tumor or infection can cause it.

Pain often starts in the lower back or buttock. It moves down the back of the leg. It may go past the knee. The pain can feel like a sharp stab, a burning sensation, or a sudden jolt.

Some people also feel numbness or weakness in the leg. The pain may get worse when you cough, sneeze, or strain. This is common with a bulging disk.

## What Causes This Problem?

Most often, the nerves in the lower back are squeezed by:

- A bulging or torn disk
- Bone spurs from arthritis
- Narrowing of the spine (spinal stenosis)
- A slipped vertebra (spondylolisthesis)
- Rarely, a tumor or infection inside the spine

The nerves can also be squeezed outside the spine, in the pelvis or buttocks.

The nerves at the L5-S1, L4-L5, and L3-L4 levels are most often affected.

Pain that runs down the back of the thigh and below the knee is called sciatica. It comes from the sciatic nerve, which is made up of nerves from L4, L5, and S1.

Pain that runs down the front of the thigh comes from the femoral nerve. This is not sciatica. It comes from nerves at L1, L2, and L3.

The word "sciatica" is often used wrong. People use it for any lower back pain that goes down the leg. But this can cause confusion. It is better to describe the pain clearly instead.

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

- Pain that starts in the lower back or buttock
- Pain that moves down the back of the leg
- Pain that goes below the knee
- Burning, stabbing, or sharp pain
- Numbness or tingling in the leg
- Weakness in the leg or foot
- Pain that gets worse when you cough, sneeze, or strain

A doctor will check your strength, reflexes, and sensation. They may do simple tests to see if nerves are affected.

### Straight Leg Raise Test

You lie on your back. The doctor slowly lifts your leg while keeping it straight. If pain shoots down your leg when the leg is raised to about 60 degrees, it may mean nerve root compression.

If lifting the other leg causes pain in the affected leg, this is even more likely to mean nerve root compression.

### Slump Test

You sit with your back rounded and your neck bent forward. The doctor slowly lifts your leg. This test can also show nerve problems. It is more likely to find a problem, but it may also give a false positive.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will first ask about your symptoms and do a physical exam.

If you have nerve problems or symptoms that last more than six weeks, you may need:

- An MRI scan
- A CT scan
- Nerve tests (electrodiagnostic studies)

MRI and CT scans show the spine clearly. They can find bulging disks, bone spurs, or narrowing of the spine.

Nerve tests check how well nerves are working. They can confirm nerve damage and rule out other conditions, such as nerve problems in the leg or foot.

These tests may not show problems right away. It can take two weeks or more after symptoms start for changes to appear.

## How Is It Treated?

Most people get better with simple treatments. Surgery is only needed in some cases.

### First Steps

- Rest in bed for 1 to 2 days, lying on your back with your head slightly raised (about 30 degrees).
- Use over-the-counter pain relievers like acetaminophen or NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen).
- Try these for up to six weeks.

### Medicines for Nerve Pain

If the pain feels like burning or shooting, your doctor may prescribe medicine for nerve pain. Examples include:

- Gabapentin
- Other anticonvulsant medicines
- Low-dose tricyclic antidepressants

Start with a low dose at bedtime. Increase slowly to avoid side effects like drowsiness or dizziness.

**Be careful if you are older, at risk of falling, have heart problems, or have kidney disease.** These medicines can make you sleepy.

### Heat and Cold

Use heat or cold packs to help with muscle spasms. This can ease discomfort.

### Physical Therapy

A physical therapist can help you strengthen your back and improve movement. This can reduce pain and prevent future problems.

### Steroid Medicine

Steroids can help reduce swelling and pain. But they are not always helpful.

- **Oral steroids** (taken by mouth) may help some people with nerve pain for a short time. But they do not help if the pain is not from a nerve.
- **Epidural steroids** (injected into the spine) may help speed up pain relief. But they are only used if the pain is severe or does not go away.

A common steroid plan is:

- Start with 24 milligrams per day
- Reduce by 4 milligrams each day
- Finish in six days

### Surgery

Surgery is needed if:

- You have cauda equina syndrome (a serious condition affecting the nerves at the bottom of the spine)
- You have a clear disk problem and one of the following:
  - Muscle weakness that is getting worse
  - Other nerve problems that are getting worse
  - Severe pain that does not improve after six weeks of other treatments
  - Pain that stops you from working or doing daily tasks

The most common surgery is a diskectomy. The surgeon removes the part of the disk pressing on the nerve.

A smaller version, called microdiskectomy, uses a smaller cut and less bone removal.

Chemonucleolysis (a treatment using a special enzyme) is no longer used.

### What Makes Surgery Less Likely to Work?

Surgery is less likely to help if:

- Mental health issues are a big part of the problem
- Symptoms have lasted more than six months
- You do heavy physical work
- Back pain (not leg pain) is the main problem
- There is a chance of getting money from a lawsuit or insurance claim

## Key Points

- The most common cause is a bulging disk, bone spurs, or narrowing of the spine.
- Pain usually runs down the back of the leg, below the knee. It feels sharp, burning, or stabbing.
- You may lose feeling, strength, or have weak reflexes in the leg.
- Get an MRI or nerve tests if you have nerve problems or symptoms that last more than six weeks.
- Most people improve with rest, pain medicine, physical therapy, and nerve pain medicine.
- Surgery is an option if nerve problems are getting worse or if pain does not improve after six weeks of other treatments.

# Melanoma

Melanoma is a type of skin cancer. It starts in the cells that give skin its color.

## What Is Melanoma?

- Melanoma can start on normal skin or in a mole you already have.
- It may look like a flat or raised patch of skin. The color can be brown, black, gray, or red.
- It can also look like a firm lump that is black, gray, or red.
- Melanoma can have spots of different colors in one area.

## How Is Melanoma Diagnosed?

- Doctors check suspicious skin changes with a biopsy.
- A biopsy means they take a small sample of the skin.
- They look at the sample under a microscope to see if it is cancer.
- If the sample shows melanoma, they remove the whole growth.
- If the cancer has spread, doctors may use chemotherapy or radiation therapy.
- But if melanoma has spread, it is hard to cure.

## What Causes Melanoma?

- Melanocytes are the cells in your skin that make pigment.
- This pigment gives your skin its color.
- Sunlight makes these cells make more pigment.
- Too much sun exposure increases your risk of melanoma.

## How Common Is Melanoma?

- In 2023, about 97,610 new cases of melanoma were expected in the United States.
- About 7,990 people died from melanoma that year.
- Melanoma makes up less than 2% of all skin cancers.
- But it causes most skin cancer deaths.

## Where Does Melanoma Start?

- Most often, melanoma starts as a new spot on sun-exposed skin.
- About 1 in 3 starts in a mole you already have.
- It can also start in the eyes, mouth, genitals, rectum, brain, or under the nails.

## How Fast Does Melanoma Spread?

- Melanoma can spread quickly to other parts of the body.
- Once it spreads, it keeps growing and damages healthy tissue.

## Types of Melanoma

There are two main types:

- **Superficial spreading melanoma**: This is the most common type. It makes up 70% of cases. It often appears on women’s legs and men’s torsos. It is linked to a gene change called *BRAF*.
- **Nodular melanoma**: This type makes up 15% to 30% of cases. It can appear anywhere on the body. It grows fast.

## Risk Factors for Melanoma

You are more likely to get melanoma if you:

- Have had bad sunburns, especially blistering ones.
- Use tanning beds or get UV light treatments.
- Have had skin cancer before.
- Have a family member with melanoma.
- Have light skin or freckles.
- Have many moles, especially unusual ones.
- Have a weak immune system.
- Have a large birthmark made of pigment cells (called a congenital nevus).
- Have certain gene changes, like in *BRCA2* or *BRAF*.
- Are older.

People who have had melanoma are more likely to get another one.

Melanoma is rare in people with dark skin. But when it does happen, it often starts under the nails or on the palms and soles.

Melanoma is very rare in children. But a large birthmark made of pigment cells (over 8 inches wide) can increase the risk.

Pregnancy does not make moles turn into melanoma. But moles often get bigger and darker during pregnancy.

## How to Check for Melanoma

Everyone should learn the **ABCDEs of melanoma**. This helps you check your moles for warning signs.

### The ABCDEs of Melanoma

- **A – Asymmetry**: One half of the mole does not match the other half.
- **B – Borders**: The edges are ragged, blurred, or not smooth.
- **C – Color**: The color is not the same all over. It may have shades of brown, black, red, white, or blue.
- **D – Diameter**: The spot is wider than a pencil eraser (about 6 millimeters).
- **E – Evolution**: A new mole appears after age 30. Or an old mole changes in size, shape, or color.

## Symptoms of Melanoma

- Some melanomas are flat and look like brown patches with small black spots.
- Others are raised and have red, white, black, or blue spots.
- Some look like a firm red, black, or gray lump.
- Less than 10% of melanomas have no color. These can look pink, red, or light brown.
- These colorless melanomas may look like harmless skin growths or other types of skin cancer.

## How Is Melanoma Treated?

### Early Melanoma

- Doctors remove the cancer by cutting it out.
- They take a border of skin around the tumor—about half an inch or more.
- For very early melanoma (that has not grown deep), surgery can cure almost all cases.

### If Surgery Is Not Possible

- For people who are too sick for surgery, or who do not want surgery (for example, if the mole is on the face), doctors may use:
  - Imiquimod cream (a medicine that helps the body fight cancer).
  - Cryotherapy (using extreme cold to destroy the cancer).

### If Melanoma Has Spread

- Doctors may use:
  - Immunotherapy (medicines that help the body’s immune system fight cancer).
  - Targeted therapy (medicines that attack cancer cells with specific gene changes).
  - Chemotherapy (drugs that kill fast-growing cells).
  - Radiation therapy (using high-energy beams to kill cancer cells).

### Immunotherapy

- **Pembrolizumab** and **nivolumab** are medicines that help the immune system find and kill cancer cells.
- They work by blocking a protein called PD-1. This protein hides cancer cells from the immune system.
- When the protein is blocked, the immune system can attack the cancer.
- These medicines are very effective for melanoma that has spread.
- **Ipilimumab** is another immunotherapy. It helps activate immune cells to fight cancer.
- The combination of **nivolumab and ipilimumab** is often the best treatment.
- **Nivolumab and relatlimab** can also be used together.

### Targeted Therapy

- These medicines target cancer cells with specific gene changes.
- They work only on cells with certain mutations.
- For melanomas with a *BRAF* gene change, doctors may use:
  - Dabrafenib
  - Encorafenib
  - Vemurafenib
- If immunotherapy is not an option, a combination of these medicines can be used.

### Chemotherapy

- Drugs like **dacarbazine** and **temozolomide** are sometimes used.
- They do not help people live longer.
- But they may be used when no other treatment works.

### Radiation Therapy

- This is used when:
  - The cancer is in a hard-to-reach place.
  - The cancer comes back after being removed.
  - The cancer has spread to the brain.

### New Treatments

- Doctors are testing new medicines and vaccines.
- These aim to train the body to attack melanoma cells.

## Prognosis (Outlook)

- Melanoma can grow fast and cause death in a few months.
- The deeper the cancer grows into the skin, the harder it is to cure.
- Almost all early, shallow melanomas are cured by surgery.
- If the cancer grows deeper than about 1 millimeter, it is more likely to spread.
- If melanoma has spread to other parts of the body, the 5-year survival rate is about 35%.
- Some people live less than 9 months.
- But some people live for years in good health, even with spread.

## How to Prevent Melanoma

You can lower your risk by protecting your skin from the sun, starting in childhood.

### Ways to Protect Yourself

- **Avoid the sun**:
  - Stay in the shade.
  - Avoid being outside between 10 AM and 4 PM.
  - Do not use tanning beds, especially if you are young.
- **Wear protective clothing**:
  - Long-sleeved shirts.
  - Pants.
  - Hats with wide brims.
- **Use sunscreen**:
  - Use sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher.
  - Choose one that protects against both UVA and UVB rays.
  - Apply it as directed.
  - Reapply every 2 hours or after swimming or sweating.
  - Do not use sunscreen to stay in the sun longer.

Doctors are not sure if these steps prevent melanoma or death from melanoma. But using tanning beds, especially by young people, clearly increases the risk.

### After a Melanoma Diagnosis

- If you have had melanoma, you are more likely to get another one.
- You should have regular skin checks.
- If you have many moles, get a full-body skin exam at least once a year.
- Learn how to check your own skin for changes.
- Know the signs of melanoma.

For people with no risk factors, it is not clear if yearly skin exams reduce deaths from melanoma.

The following websites offer helpful information in English:

- **Melanoma Research Foundation**: Learn about types, research, and clinical trials.
- **American Cancer Society: Melanoma Skin Cancer**: Get info on detection, prevention, and treatment.

# Stevens-JJohnson Syndrome

This is a serious skin reaction that can happen after taking certain medicines or after an infection.

## What Causes It?

Some medicines can trigger this condition. These include:
- Certain epilepsy medicines
- Some antibiotics
- Anti-inflammatory painkillers

Common medicines linked to this reaction:
- Allopurinol
- Carbamazepine
- Lamotrigine
- Nevirapine
- Oxicam anti-inflammatories like meloxicam and piroxicam
- Phenobarbital
- Phenytoin
- Sulfamethoxazole and other sulfa antibiotics
- Sulfasalazine

In children, it can also be caused by infections such as colds, flu, cold sores, or glandular fever.

## Who Is at Higher Risk?

You are more likely to get this if:
- You have had it before after taking a certain medicine. You may get it again if you take that medicine or similar ones.
- You have a weak immune system. This can happen if you have HIV or AIDS, or are having chemotherapy.
- A close family member has had this condition. Some people inherit a higher risk.

Note: This condition is rare. The chance of getting it is low, even if you take a medicine that can cause it.

## What Are the Symptoms?

It often starts with flu-like symptoms:
- High temperature
- Sore throat
- Cough
- Joint pain

A few days later, a rash appears. The rash has round patches. The center is darker. The edges are lighter.

The rash usually starts on the upper body. It spreads quickly to the face, arms, legs, and genitals. It is not usually itchy.

Blisters form on the skin. They burst and leave painful sores. The skin peels easily.

You may also get blisters and sores in:
- Lips, mouth, and throat – this can make swallowing hard
- The tube that carries urine out – this can cause pain when peeing
- The eyes – this can cause eye pain, light sensitivity, or vision problems

## When to Get Help Right Away

Call 999 or go to A&E if you or your child:
- Has a rash with dark centers and lighter edges after an infection or starting a new medicine
- Has a rash that is itchy, red, swollen, blistered, or peeling
- Is wheezing
- Feels tightness in the chest or throat
- Has trouble breathing or talking
- Has swelling in the mouth, face, lips, tongue, or throat

These signs can mean a serious reaction. You need urgent medical care.

> **Find your nearest A&E**

### A&E Safety Tips

- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you. Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.
- Bring all your medicines with you.

## How Is It Treated?

You will be treated in hospital, often in intensive care.

If a medicine is causing the reaction, it will be stopped right away.

Treatment includes:
- Fluids through a vein to prevent dehydration
- Creams and dressings to protect and soothe the skin
- Strong painkillers to reduce pain
- Medicines to reduce swelling and prevent infection

Without treatment, the condition can become life-threatening.

## Recovery

Full recovery can take several weeks or months.

Your skin usually takes 2 to 3 weeks to heal. It may take longer if you get a skin infection.

You will likely feel very tired for a few weeks after leaving hospital.

If the reaction was caused by a medicine, you must avoid that medicine for life. You may also need to avoid similar medicines. Your doctor will explain this in detail.

# Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD)

Peripheral artery disease is a condition where the blood vessels in the arms or legs become narrowed. This happens because of a buildup of fatty material inside the blood vessels. When blood flow is reduced, the legs or arms do not get enough oxygen-rich blood. This can cause pain, sores, or even tissue death.

This guide focuses on PAD in the legs. PAD in the arms is less common but can happen.

---

## What Causes PAD?

PAD is caused by a condition called atherosclerosis. This means fatty deposits build up in the walls of blood vessels. Over time, this narrows the vessels and slows blood flow.

The same things that cause heart disease also raise your risk for PAD. These include:

- Smoking (including secondhand smoke)
- Diabetes
- High cholesterol (especially high bad cholesterol and low good cholesterol)
- Family history of heart or blood vessel disease
- High levels of a substance called homocysteine
- High blood pressure
- Getting older
- Being a man
- Being overweight

Most people with PAD also have heart disease or problems with blood flow to the brain.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

PAD can cause different types of symptoms. Some people have no symptoms at all. Others may have mild or severe problems.

### 1. No Symptoms (Asymptomatic)
Some people with PAD feel fine. But tests may show they have poor blood flow. They might not notice it during daily life, but walking tests can show problems.

### 2. Intermittent Claudication (Chronic Symptomatic PAD)
This is the most common symptom. It causes pain, cramping, or tiredness in the legs when walking. The pain goes away when you stop walking and rest.

- The pain usually starts in the calf, but can also be in the feet, thighs, hips, or buttocks.
- It happens because the muscles do not get enough blood during activity.
- The more severe the PAD, the shorter the distance you can walk before pain starts.

### 3. Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischemia (CLTI)
This is a serious form of PAD. It means blood flow is so poor that the leg or foot is at risk of damage or loss.

Symptoms include:
- Pain in the foot or leg at rest, especially at night.
- The pain gets worse when the leg is raised. It feels better when the leg is lowered below the heart.
- The foot may look dark red or purple when hanging down (called dependent rubor).
- The foot may feel cold and look thin and pale.
- Skin may sweat a lot or turn blue (cyanotic).
- Sores (ulcers) may form on the toes or heels, especially after a small injury.
- These sores often have black, dead tissue around them (dry gangrene).
- If the sores get infected, they can spread quickly (wet gangrene).
- People with nerve damage (like from diabetes) may not feel the pain from these sores.

### 4. Acute Limb Ischemia
This is a sudden blockage of blood flow. It is a medical emergency. It causes sudden, severe pain, coldness, numbness, and pale skin. It needs immediate treatment.

---

## How Does PAD Affect Different Parts of the Leg?

Where the blockage is affects where the symptoms appear.

- **Aortoiliac PAD** (in the main blood vessel and upper leg): Causes pain in the hips, thighs, or calves. Men may also have trouble with erections (called Leriche syndrome).
- **Femoropopliteal PAD** (in the thigh and lower leg): Causes calf pain during walking. The pulse below the thigh may be weak or missing.
- **Distal PAD** (in the lower leg or foot): The pulse in the thigh may be normal, but the pulse in the foot is weak or missing.

Most people with serious PAD have blockages in more than one area of the leg.

---

## Can PAD Affect the Arms?

Yes, but it is rare. PAD in the arms usually affects the left arm. It can cause tiredness in the arm during activity. In some cases, small clots can travel to the hand and block blood flow.

---

## How Is PAD Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to check for PAD.

### 1. Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI)
This is the most common test.

- It compares blood pressure in your ankle to blood pressure in your arm.
- A normal result is between 1.00 and 1.40.
- A result of 0.90 or lower means you likely have PAD.
- A result between 0.91 and 0.99 is borderline.

If the ABI is normal but you still have symptoms, your doctor may do an **exercise ABI**. You walk on a treadmill or lift your ankles. If the ABI drops by 20% after exercise, it means you have PAD.

If the ABI is over 1.40, it may mean the blood vessels are too stiff to measure properly. This can happen with calcium buildup in the vessel walls.

### 2. Toe-Brachial Index and Toe Pressure
If the ABI is high but PAD is still suspected, doctors may test the blood pressure in your toes.

- A toe pressure below 30 mm Hg means healing is unlikely.
- A toe pressure above 60 mm Hg means healing is possible.

### 3. Transcutaneous Oximetry (TcO2)
This test measures oxygen levels in the skin of the foot.

- A reading below 40 mm Hg means healing is unlikely.
- A reading below 20 mm Hg means you have serious poor blood flow.

### 4. Imaging Tests
These show the exact location and size of blockages.

- **Ultrasound**: Uses sound waves to see blood flow.
- **Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA)**: Uses a magnet and radio waves to create images.
- **CT Angiography (CTA)**: Uses X-rays and dye to show blood vessels.
- **Invasive Angiography**: A thin tube is inserted into a blood vessel to take pictures. This is used before surgery or procedures.

Imaging is not used to diagnose PAD. It is used to plan treatment.

---

## How Is PAD Treated?

Treatment focuses on improving blood flow, reducing symptoms, and preventing serious problems.

### 1. Manage Risk Factors
- Control blood sugar if you have diabetes.
- Lower cholesterol with medicine (like statins).
- Control blood pressure with medicine.
- Quit smoking — this is one of the most important steps.

### 2. Lifestyle Changes
- Walk regularly. Exercise helps improve blood flow and reduces pain.
- Lose weight if you are overweight.
- Eat a healthy diet.

### 3. Medications
- **Antiplatelet drugs** (like aspirin or clopidogrel): Help prevent blood clots.
- **Cilostazol**: Helps reduce leg pain during walking. It is used for claudication.
- **ACE inhibitors or ARBs**: Help lower blood pressure and protect the heart and kidneys.
- **Rivaroxaban**: A blood thinner used in some cases to reduce risk of heart attack or stroke.

### 4. Revascularization (Restoring Blood Flow)
If symptoms are severe or do not improve, doctors may open blocked blood vessels.

- **Endovascular treatment**: A thin tube is guided through a blood vessel to open the blockage. This may include balloon inflation or stent placement.
- **Surgery**: A bypass graft may be used to reroute blood around the blocked area.

These treatments are used for claudication that does not improve with medicine and exercise, or for serious cases like chronic limb-threatening ischemia.

### 5. Amputation
In some cases, parts of the foot or leg may be lost due to poor blood flow and infection. This is a last resort when healing is not possible.

---

## Key Points

- PAD most often affects the legs.
- Most people with PAD also have heart or brain blood vessel disease.
- The main symptom is leg pain when walking that goes away with rest. This is called claudication.
- Severe PAD can cause pain at rest, sores, or tissue death (gangrene).
- A low ankle-brachial index (0.90 or less) confirms PAD.
- Treatments include lifestyle changes, medicines, and procedures to improve blood flow.
- Early treatment can prevent serious problems like amputation.

---

> **Note**: If you have leg pain when walking, or sores that do not heal, talk to your doctor. Early diagnosis and treatment can make a big difference.

# Sudden Hearing Loss

Sudden hearing loss means you lose your hearing quickly. It usually happens over about three days. Or you might wake up and notice you can’t hear well.

This type of hearing loss usually affects only one ear. But if it is caused by medicine, both ears can be affected.

Some people also have other symptoms. These can include:
- Ringing in the ears
- Dizziness
- A feeling that you are spinning or moving when you are not

About 1 in 5,000 to 1 in 10,000 people get sudden hearing loss each year.

If your hearing loss comes on slowly, see the section on general hearing loss.

---

## What Causes Sudden Hearing Loss?

Doctors group the causes into three main types:

1. No clear cause
2. A clear event, like an injury or infection
3. An underlying health problem

In most cases, doctors cannot find a clear reason for the hearing loss. But they have some ideas. Possible causes include:
- Viral infections, especially herpes simplex virus
- The body’s immune system attacking the inner ear or its nerves
- Small blood vessels in the inner ear or its nerves becoming blocked

Different people may have different causes.

In some people, the cause is clear. These include:
- Head injury
- A big change in pressure (like when diving or lifting heavy weights)
- Certain medicines that harm the ears
- Infections

### Head Injury
A broken bone in the skull or a serious brain injury can damage the inner ear. This can cause sudden hearing loss.

### Pressure Changes
Sudden pressure changes—like when diving deep or straining during weightlifting—can create a small hole between the middle and inner ear. This is called a fistula. Some people are born with this hole. It can cause sudden hearing loss on its own or make hearing worse after an injury or pressure change.

### Medicines That Harm the Ears
Some medicines can damage the inner ear. These are called ototoxic medicines. They can cause hearing loss fast—sometimes in just one day. This is more likely if the dose is too high.

A few people have a rare genetic condition. It makes them more likely to lose hearing from a group of antibiotics called aminoglycosides. Anyone taking these antibiotics should have blood tests to check for dangerous levels.

### Infections
Some infections can cause sudden hearing loss during or right after the illness. These include:
- Bacterial meningitis
- Lyme disease
- Viral infections

In developed countries, the most common viruses are mumps and herpes simplex virus in the brain. Measles is a rare cause because most people are vaccinated.

### Underlying Health Problems
Sudden hearing loss can be the first sign of a serious health issue. These problems usually have other symptoms first. But sometimes, hearing loss is the first thing noticed.

These conditions include:
- A tumor on the nerve that carries sound to the brain (vestibular schwannoma)
- Multiple sclerosis
- Meniere disease
- A small stroke in the part of the brain that controls balance (cerebellum)
- A reactivated syphilis infection in people with HIV
- Cogan syndrome (an immune system problem that attacks the inner ear and eye)
- Blood vessel inflammation (vasculitis)
- Blood disorders like macroglobulinemia, sickle cell disease, or some types of leukemia

---

## How Doctors Evaluate Sudden Hearing Loss

Sudden hearing loss is a warning sign. You should see a doctor right away. Some causes need fast treatment.

If you have other nervous system symptoms—like weakness, numbness, or trouble with balance—your hearing loss might be a sign of a brain or nerve problem.

### What the Doctor Will Do

The doctor will ask about your symptoms and medical history. Then they will do a physical exam.

They will check:
- Which ear is affected (one or both)
- If you had a recent head injury, diving, or illness
- If you have ringing in the ears, ear discharge, dizziness, or balance problems
- If you have headaches, weakness, or changes in taste
- If you are taking any medicines that can harm the ears

The exam will focus on your ears and hearing. It will also check your nervous system.

### Common Causes and Their Features

| Cause | Typical Signs | Tests Needed |
|------|----------------|--------------|
| Unknown cause | Hearing loss in one ear only. No other symptoms. | MRI with contrast (gadolinium) |
| Infection (like meningitis, Lyme, mumps, herpes) | Hearing loss in one or both ears. Often with fever, headache, confusion. Lyme: rash and flu-like symptoms first. Mumps: pain in cheeks when swallowing. | Blood tests, spinal tap (lumbar puncture) |
| Head injury | Hearing loss in one ear. Sometimes fluid from the ear (blood, blood-tinged, or clear). | CT scan or MRI |
| Pressure changes (diving, weightlifting) | Hearing loss in one or both ears. Comes on during or right after the event. May have pain, dizziness, or a loud pop. | Tympanometry (ear test), balance test (electronystagmography) |
| Ototoxic medicines (aspirin, gentamicin, vancomycin, cisplatin, furosemide, ethacrynic acid, quinine) | Hearing loss in both ears. Sometimes dizziness or balance loss. Happens after starting or stopping the medicine. | Doctor’s exam. Sometimes blood tests for medicine levels |
| Vestibular schwannoma (tumor on hearing nerve) | Hearing loss in one ear. Often dizziness, vertigo, balance loss. May have facial droop, numbness, or taste changes. | MRI with contrast |
| Autoimmune inner ear disease | Hearing loss in both ears. Can come and go. Gets worse over time. | Blood tests |
| Other autoimmune or blood disorders (vasculitis, Cogan syndrome, macroglobulinemia, sickle cell, leukemia) | Hearing loss in one or both ears. May have joint pain or rash. | Blood tests |
| Meniere disease | Hearing loss in one ear. Often dizziness and ringing in the ear. | MRI with contrast |
| Multiple sclerosis | Hearing loss in one ear. May have weakness or numbness that comes and goes in different body parts. | MRI with contrast. Sometimes spinal tap |
| Stroke (in brain area for balance) | Hearing loss in one ear. May have trouble with balance or coordination. | MRI with contrast |
| Reactivated syphilis (in people with HIV) | Hearing loss in one or both ears. May have risk factors like unprotected sex or many partners. | Blood tests. Sometimes spinal tap |

> **Note:** An audiogram (hearing test) is always done. It is only listed as a needed test if it can confirm the diagnosis without other tests.

> **CT** = computed tomography (a type of scan)  
> **MRI** = magnetic resonance imaging (a type of scan)

### What Tests Are Done?

Most people need a hearing test (audiogram).  
If the cause is not clear, doctors usually do an MRI with contrast or a CT scan—especially if one ear is more affected.

Other tests depend on the likely cause. For example:
- After a head injury, an MRI is done.
- If you are at risk for sexually transmitted infections, blood tests for HIV and syphilis are done.

---

## How Is Sudden Hearing Loss Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause.

If the cause is known, treatment targets that cause.

If no cause is found, most doctors try corticosteroid medicine. These reduce swelling and inflammation.

Some doctors also give antiviral medicine (like valacyclovir or famciclovir) for herpes simplex virus. But there is no strong proof this helps.

### Recovery Outlook

When the cause is unknown:
- About half of people get their hearing back completely.
- Others get some improvement.
- Most improvement happens within 10 to 14 days.

If the hearing loss is from medicine:
- With some medicines (like aspirin or diuretics), hearing returns within 24 hours.
- With antibiotics or chemotherapy drugs, hearing loss may be permanent if the dose was too high.

---

## Key Points

- Doctors often do not know why sudden hearing loss happens.
- A few people have a clear cause, like head injury, infection, or certain medicines.
- In very rare cases, sudden hearing loss is the first sign of a serious health problem.
- Doctors use hearing tests, CT scans, MRI scans, and other tests to find the cause.
- Treatment focuses on the known cause.

---

**National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders**  
Learn about hearing loss and other communication problems. Includes information on hearing, balance, taste, smell, voice, speech, and language.

# Tuberculosis (TB)

## What is TB?

Tuberculosis is an infection caused by bacteria.  
It mainly affects the lungs.  
You can catch it from someone who has active TB and is coughing.

## Symptoms of TB

TB symptoms usually start slowly.  
You may have a cough that lasts more than 3 weeks.  
You might cough up mucus.  
Sometimes the mucus has blood in it.

You may feel very tired or weak.  
You might have a high temperature.  
You may sweat a lot at night.  
You may not feel hungry.  
You may lose weight without trying.

You may feel generally unwell.  
Children with TB may not grow or gain weight as they should.

If TB spreads to other parts of your body, you may have other symptoms.  
These can include:

- Swollen glands in your neck or other areas  
- Pain in your bones or joints  
- Swelling in your ankles  
- Pain in your tummy or pelvis  
- Constipation  
- Dark or cloudy urine  
- Headaches  
- Feeling sick  
- Confusion  
- A stiff neck  
- A rash on your legs, face, or other parts of your body

Some people have TB in their body but do not have any symptoms.  
This is called latent TB.  
Latent TB cannot spread to others.  
But it can become active later.

If you have symptoms, it is called active TB.  
Active TB can spread to others.

## How TB Spreads

TB spreads through the air.  
It spreads when someone with active TB coughs, sneezes, or talks.  
You can catch TB if you breathe in the tiny droplets from their cough.

You are more likely to catch TB if you spend a lot of time near someone with active TB.  
This includes living in the same house.

## Who is More Likely to Get TB?

Anyone can get TB.  
But some people are at higher risk.  
These include people who:

- Live with someone who has active TB  
- Were born in or lived in a country where TB is common  
- Have a weak immune system (for example, people with HIV, those who had a kidney transplant, or those on chemotherapy)  
- Are under 5 years old  
- Live in crowded or poor living conditions (such as people who are homeless)  
- Smoke regularly, drink a lot of alcohol, or use drugs  
- Have had TB before but did not finish treatment

## When to See a Doctor

See your GP if you have:

- A cough that lasts more than 3 weeks  
- Feeling very tired or weak without a clear reason  
- A high temperature or night sweats that do not go away  
- No appetite for food  
- Losing weight without changing your diet or exercise  
- Been around someone with TB who has symptoms (like a long cough)

## When to Get Urgent Help

Call 111 or go online for help if you:

- Cough up blood or mucus with blood in it

You can call 111 or get help online.

## When to Go to A&E (Emergency Department)

Go to A&E or call 999 if you have:

- A stiff neck and a severe headache  
- Pain when looking at bright lights  
- A seizure or fit  
- Sudden confusion or changes in behaviour  
- Weakness or loss of movement in part of your body

These could be signs that TB has spread to your brain.  
This is called TB meningitis.

Find your nearest A&E.

### A&E Safety Tips

- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you.  
- If you cannot get a ride, call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
- Bring all your medicines with you.

## Treatment for TB

The main treatment for TB is antibiotics.  
You must take them for at least 6 months.  
Even if you start to feel better, keep taking the medicine.

If you stop early, the TB can come back.  
It can be harder to treat later.

If TB has spread to your brain, spinal cord, or the area around your heart, you may also need steroid medicine for a few weeks.

If you have latent TB (no symptoms), you may still need to take antibiotics for 3 to 6 months.

## TB Vaccine (BCG)

There is a vaccine called BCG.  
It helps protect some people from getting TB or getting very sick from it.

It is recommended for:

- Babies in areas of the UK where TB is more common  
- Babies and children who live with someone who has TB  
- Babies and children who were born or lived in a country where TB is common  
- Babies and children whose parents or grandparents were born in a country where TB is common  
- People under 35 who will be living in a country with high TB rates for more than 3 months  
- People at work risk, such as healthcare workers who care for people with TB

The vaccine is not given to everyone.  
It is only given to those at higher risk.

# Ankle Sprains – Simple Explanation

Ankle sprains are very common. They happen when you twist your ankle, usually by turning your foot inward.

## What Happens in an Ankle Sprain?

- The most common injury is to the outer side of the ankle.
- This happens when the foot rolls inward, stretching or tearing the ligaments.
- Ligaments are strong bands that connect bones to each other.
- The main ligaments involved are:
  - Deltoid ligament (on the inside of the ankle)
  - Anterior and posterior talofibular ligaments (on the outside)
  - Calcaneofibular ligament (on the outside)

### How Sprains Happen

**Inversion (foot turns inward):**
- This is the most common cause of ankle sprains.
- It often tears the front part of the outer ligament first.
- Severe sprains can lead to long-term instability.
- In rare cases, it can also break the bone on the top of the foot (talar dome).

**Eversion (foot turns outward):**
- This puts stress on the inside of the ankle.
- The deltoid ligament is strong, so it usually does not tear.
- Instead, the inside bone (medial malleolus) may break off (avulsion fracture).
- Eversion can also:
  - Crush the outside of the ankle joint.
  - Cause a break in the lower part of the fibula (distal fibula fracture).
  - Tear the ligaments between the tibia and fibula just above the ankle (called a high ankle sprain).
  - In rare cases, force can travel up the fibula and break the top of the fibula near the knee (Maisonneuve fracture).

Repeated sprains can hurt your body’s ability to sense where your ankle is. This makes future sprains more likely.

Most ankle sprains are mild (1st or 2nd degree).

---

## Symptoms and Signs

Ankle sprains cause:
- Pain
- Swelling
- Muscle tightness or spasms

Where the pain and swelling are depends on the type of injury:

- **Inversion sprain:** Pain and swelling are worst on the front and outside of the ankle.
- **Eversion injury:** Pain and swelling are worst on the inside of the ankle.
- **Maisonneuve fracture:** Pain is felt in the upper fibula, and also on the inside and sometimes the outside of the ankle.
- **Severe sprain (complete tear):** Swelling is widespread. The ankle may look swollen and egg-shaped.

Tenderness (pain when pressing) is usually worst over the injured ligament, not the bone. If pressing on the bone hurts more than pressing on the ligament, a bone break may be present.

### Types of Sprains

**Mild (1st-degree) sprains:**
- Little pain and swelling.
- The ankle feels weak.
- It can heal in hours to a few days.

**Moderate to severe (2nd-degree) sprains:**
- Swelling and bruising are common.
- Walking is painful and hard.
- Healing takes days to weeks.

**Very severe (3rd-degree) sprains:**
- The whole ankle is swollen and bruised.
- The ankle feels unstable and cannot hold weight.
- Nerves may be damaged.
- The cartilage inside the joint may be torn.
  - This can lead to long-term pain, swelling, joint instability, early arthritis, and trouble walking.
- Healing takes 6 to 8 weeks.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Ankle Sprains

Doctors check your ankle with a physical exam. They look for:
- Pain
- Swelling
- Tenderness
- Stability

They may order:
- X-rays to rule out a broken bone.
- MRI only in rare cases.

### When X-rays Are Needed

Use the **Ottawa ankle and foot rules** to decide if x-rays are needed. These rules help doctors know when a break is possible.

### Stress Testing

Doctors test how stable the ankle is. One common test is the **anterior drawer test**:
- You lie down or sit with your knee slightly bent.
- The doctor holds your lower leg and pulls your heel forward.
- If the foot moves too far forward, it means the ligament is completely torn (3rd-degree sprain).

### High Ankle Sprains

These happen when the foot turns outward and causes pain in the joint just above the ankle.
- The area just above the ankle (distal tibiofibular joint) may be tender.
- The doctor may check for a break in the upper fibula if this type of injury is suspected.

### Other Injuries to Rule Out

Ankle sprains can feel like other injuries. Doctors must check for:
- A break at the base of the little toe bone (5th metatarsal avulsion fracture)
- Injury to the Achilles tendon
- A break in the top of the foot bone (talar dome fracture)

---

## Treatment of Ankle Sprains

Most sprains get better with simple care and early movement.

### For Mild Sprains (1st-degree)

- Use **PRICE**:
  - **P**rotection: Keep the ankle safe.
  - **R**est: Avoid putting weight on it at first.
  - **I**ce: Apply ice for 15–20 minutes every few hours.
  - **C**ompression: Wrap with a bandage to reduce swelling.
  - **E**levation: Keep the foot raised above heart level.
- Start walking and moving the ankle as soon as it feels okay (usually within a few days).
- Early movement helps healing.

### For Moderate Sprains (2nd-degree)

- Use **PRICE**.
- Immobilize the ankle with a splint or boot.
- Keep the ankle in a neutral position (not bent up or down).
- After a few days, start gentle movement and physical therapy.

### For Severe Sprains (3rd-degree)

- Immobilize the ankle with a cast.
- Surgery may be needed if the ligaments are completely torn.
- Physical therapy is essential after healing starts.

### High Ankle Sprains

- Usually need a cast for several weeks.
- Healing takes longer than regular sprains.

### Crutches

Use crutches for all sprains until you can walk normally.

---

## Key Points

- Always think about other injuries before calling it a sprain:
  - Break at the base of the 5th metatarsal
  - Achilles tendon injury
  - Talar dome fracture

- Use the **Ottawa ankle and foot rules** to decide if you need x-rays.

- Test joint stability with stress tests (like the anterior drawer test), but wait until swelling and pain go down.

- For mild sprains, start moving the ankle as soon as possible. This helps it heal faster.

# Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA) Renal tubular acidosis is a condition where the kidneys do not work properly. This causes too much acid to build up in the blood. ## How the Kidneys Normally Work Your body makes acid when it breaks down food. The kidneys remove this acid from the blood. They send it out of the body through urine. The small tubes in the kidneys, called tubules, do most of this work. In renal tubular acidosis, these tubes do not work right. ## What Goes Wrong in RTA There are two main problems that can happen: - The kidneys do not get rid of enough acid. This causes acid to build up in the blood. - The kidneys lose too much bicarbonate. Bicarbonate helps balance acid in the body. Losing it makes the blood more acidic. When the body’s acid and base levels are off, it can cause other problems. ## Problems That Can Happen - Low or high levels of potassium in the blood - Calcium building up in the kidneys. This can lead to kidney stones - Dehydration - Soft, weak bones that can bend or break (called osteomalacia in adults and rickets in children) ## Who Gets RTA? - Some children are born with it. It can be passed down in families. - Others get it later in life. It can be linked to other health problems like diabetes, sickle cell disease, or autoimmune diseases such as lupus. - It can also be caused by blockages in the urinary tract or certain medicines. Some medicines that can cause RTA include: - Acetazolamide - Amphotericin B - ACE inhibitors - ARBs (angiotensin II receptor blockers) - Potassium-sparing diuretics If RTA is not treated, it can damage the kidneys over time. This may lead to chronic kidney disease. ## Types of RTA There are four types. Types 1 and 2 are rare. Type 4 is the most common. Type 3 is very rare and is not discussed here. ### Types of Renal Tubular Acidosis | Type | Cause | What Goes Wrong | Symptoms and Problems | |------|-------|------------------|------------------------| | 1 | May be inherited or caused by autoimmune disease or certain medicines | Kidneys cannot release acid into urine | Blood is too acidic
Dehydration

Others only notice problems after the condition has been present for years. The symptoms depend on the type: - **Types 1 and 2:** Low potassium can cause muscle weakness, slow reflexes, or even paralysis. - **Type 1:** Kidney stones may form. These can damage kidney cells and lead to chronic kidney disease. - **Types 1 and 2:** Bone pain and weak bones can happen in adults. Children may get rickets. - **Type 4:** Potassium levels are usually high. But this rarely causes symptoms. If potassium gets too high, it can cause irregular heartbeats or muscle paralysis. ## How Doctors Diagnose RTA Doctors use blood and urine tests to check for RTA. - For types 1 and 2: They look for high acid levels, low bicarbonate, and low potassium in the blood. - For type 4: They check for high acid and high potassium in the blood. Urine tests and other tests help the doctor figure out which type of RTA a person has. ## How RTA Is Treated Treatment depends on the type. ### Types 1 and 2 - Drink a daily solution of sodium bicarbonate (baking soda). This helps neutralize acid from food. - This treatment eases symptoms and helps prevent kidney failure and bone disease. - Other special solutions are available. - Some people also need potassium supplements. ### Type 4 - The acid buildup is mild. Baking soda is often not needed. - High potassium levels are managed by: - Eating less potassium-rich food - Staying well hydrated - Using diuretics that help remove extra potassium - Changing or adjusting certain medicines ## More Information The following resource may help: **National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK)** This group offers health information in English and Spanish. # Ganglion Cyst

A ganglion cyst is a lump under the skin on your hand or wrist.  
It feels smooth and is usually not painful.  
But it can hurt when you move your hand or wrist.

If the lump hurts, you can take pain medicine.  
You can also use a wrist support to help.  
Do not try to pop or burst the lump yourself.  
This can lead to infection or damage your skin.

Most ganglion cysts do not need treatment.  
But if the lump causes pain or makes it hard to use your hand, treatment is possible.

---

## What a Ganglion Cyst Looks Like

- It is a smooth, soft lump under the skin.  
- It usually appears on the hand or wrist near a joint.  
- It can also appear on the top of your foot.  
- It can be very small, like a pea.  
- It can also be several centimetres wide.  
- It is often painless.  
- But it may hurt when you move the joint.  

You might only notice the lump.  
Or you might feel numbness or aching after using your hand.

---

## How to Care for a Ganglion Cyst at Home

Most ganglion cysts go away on their own.  
This can take a few months to a year.

If the lump hurts when you use your hand, try these steps:

### Do

- Take ibuprofen or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to reduce pain and swelling.  
- Use a wrist support or a compression wrap.  
  These are stretchy bandages you can buy at a grocery store or pharmacy.

### Do Not

- Do not try to pop or burst the cyst.  
  This can cause infection or harm your skin.

### A Pharmacist Can Help

A pharmacist can suggest pain medicine.  
They can also tell you how to use a wrist support or compression wrap if needed.

---

## Medical Treatment for a Ganglion Cyst

Most ganglion cysts do not need treatment.  
They often go away on their own.

But if the cyst causes pain or problems, your doctor may suggest:

- Draining the fluid from the cyst using a needle.  
- Injecting a medicine into the cyst to reduce swelling.  
- Removing the cyst with a small surgery.

After surgery, the cyst usually does not come back.  
But sometimes it can return.

---

## What Causes Ganglion Cysts?

The exact cause is not always clear.  
But sometimes a cyst forms after an injury.  
The injury can cause fluid to leak from a joint.  
This fluid builds up under the skin and forms a lump.

Ganglion cysts are much more common in women than in men.

# Broken Nose

A broken nose happens when the bones or cartilage in the nose are damaged. This can cause swelling, pain when touched, a wobbly nose, a crackling sound when you move it, nosebleeds, and bruising around the eyes.

## What Causes a Broken Nose?

The bones in the nose are the most commonly broken bones in the face. This is because the nose sticks out from the face and is in the center. A hard hit to the face can break the nose. Sometimes, other bones in the face can be broken too. These include the bones around the eye, the upper jaw, or the thin bone at the top of the nose that separates the nose from the brain. The tear ducts near the nose can also be injured.

## Symptoms of a Broken Nose

You may notice:
- A nosebleed after a face injury.
- A crooked or oddly shaped nose.
- Swelling around the nose.
- Pain when you press on the nose.
- A crackling or crunching sound when you move the nose.
- The nose feels loose or unstable.
- Cuts or scrapes on the nose.
- Bruising around the nose or eyes.
- A bent or crooked septum (the wall inside the nose).
- Trouble breathing through the nose.
- A purple or dark bulge inside the nose (this is a septal hematoma).
- Clear fluid leaking from the nose (this may be mixed with blood and could be cerebrospinal fluid).

## How Is a Broken Nose Diagnosed?

Doctors will look at your nose and face. They will check for swelling, shape, pain, and movement. They may also check for a cerebrospinal fluid leak.

X-rays of the nose are not useful. They do not show the injury well. If the doctor thinks other bones in the face are broken, they may order a CT scan. This is a special type of X-ray that shows bones in more detail.

Do not use glucose test strips to check for fluid from the nose. These tests are not accurate and can give wrong results.

## How Is a Broken Nose Treated?

### Immediate Care
- Use ice to reduce swelling.
- Take pain medicine as needed.
- If there is a septal hematoma (a blood-filled bulge inside the nose), it must be drained right away. If not, it can cause infection or damage the cartilage.

### Fixing the Shape
- If the nose looks crooked or blocks your breathing, it may need to be fixed.
- Doctors usually wait 3 to 5 days after the injury. This gives time for swelling to go down.
- The nose should be fixed within 2 weeks. After that, the bones start to heal in the wrong position.
- Adults can have the nose fixed with local numbing medicine.
- Children need general anesthesia (they are asleep during the procedure).

To fix the nose:
- A tool is gently pushed into the nose.
- It lifts the broken bone back into place.
- Pressure is applied on the outside of the nose to line it up.
- The nose is held in place with packing inside the nose and a splint on the outside.

**Packing inside the nose:**
- Used to hold the bones in place.
- Made of gauze, sponges, or similar material.
- Left in for 4 to 7 days.

**Splint on the outside:**
- Holds the nose straight.
- Left on for 7 to 14 days.

Antibiotics are given while the packing is in place. This helps prevent a rare but serious infection called toxic shock syndrome.

### Cartilage Injuries
- Most cartilage injuries do not need to be fixed.
- If the nose still looks crooked after swelling goes down, a minor procedure can fix it. This is done with local numbing medicine.

### Septal Fractures
- These are hard to keep in place.
- Often, surgery is needed later.

### Fractures of the Skull Base (Cribriform Plate)
- If the thin bone at the top of the nose is broken and fluid leaks from the nose, this is serious.
- You will need to stay in the hospital.
- You must lie flat with your head raised.
- A tube may be placed in your lower back to drain fluid.
- Antibiotics may be used, depending on the hospital.
- If the leak does not stop, surgery may be needed to fix the skull.

## Key Points

- The most important things to watch for are:
  - A blood-filled bulge inside the nose (septal hematoma).
  - Nosebleeds.
  - Trouble breathing.
  - A crooked nose.
  - A rare leak of brain fluid from the nose.

- X-rays of the nose are not needed.
- If there is a septal hematoma, drain it right away.
- Wait 3 to 5 days before fixing the nose. This helps reduce swelling.
- Most treatments are delayed to let the swelling go down.

# Erysipelas

Erysipelas is a type of skin infection. It affects the top layers of the skin. It is a form of cellulitis.

It is most often caused by a type of bacteria called streptococci.  
Other bacteria can also cause it. These include staphylococcus bacteria.  
One type of staphylococcus is called MRSA. MRSA is hard to treat with common antibiotics.

## Symptoms

The skin shows a red, raised patch.  
The patch is shiny and feels warm and firm.  
The edges are sharp and clear. They do not blend into the normal skin around them.  
The patch is painful to touch.  
It usually appears on the legs or face.  

You may also have a high fever.  
You may feel chills.  
You may feel very unwell overall.

In some cases, blisters form on the skin.

## Diagnosis

A doctor will look at the skin.  
The look of the red patch helps the doctor make the diagnosis.  

If you are very sick, the doctor may take a blood sample.  
The sample goes to a lab. The lab checks for the bacteria causing the infection.

## Treatment

You will need antibiotics.  
Oral antibiotics, like penicillin, can treat the infection.  

If the doctor thinks you have MRSA, they may prescribe:  
- Sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim  
- Clindamycin  
- Doxycycline  

These are taken by mouth.  

If the infection is severe, you may need stronger antibiotics.  
These are given through a vein. Examples are vancomycin or linezolid.  

You can use cold packs to help with pain and swelling.  
Pain medicine can also help with discomfort.  

If you have a fungal infection on your feet, it may have let the bacteria in.  
Treating the fungal infection can help prevent the skin infection from coming back.  

Wearing compression stockings on your legs can help reduce swelling.

# Bladder Pain Syndrome (Interstitial Cystitis)

Bladder pain syndrome is a long-term condition that causes pain and discomfort in the lower belly. It can also make you need to pee more often than usual.

## Symptoms

The main symptoms include:

- Sharp pain in the lower belly
- A sudden, strong need to pee
- Needing to pee more often than normal
- Pain that gets worse as your bladder fills up
- Pain that goes away after you pee
- Waking up at night to pee

Other possible symptoms are:

- Trouble starting to pee
- Leaking urine
- Blood in your urine

These symptoms can also happen with other health problems. For example, bladder cancer can cause similar signs. That is why doctors need to do several tests to rule out other causes before diagnosing bladder pain syndrome.

**Seek urgent medical help if you see blood in your urine and have lower belly pain.**  
Call 111 or see your doctor right away.

Blood in your urine can look bright pink, red, or dark brown.

## What Causes Bladder Pain Syndrome?

The exact cause is not known. But doctors think several things may play a role.

Possible causes include:

- Damage to the lining of the bladder. This can let urine irritate the bladder and nearby nerves.
- Problems with the muscles in the pelvic floor. These muscles help control peeing.
- An overactive immune system that causes inflammation.

Some people with bladder pain syndrome may have a long-term urinary infection that standard tests did not find.

Bladder pain syndrome is also linked to other long-term health issues, such as:

- Fibromyalgia
- Myalgic encephalomyelitis or chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS)
- Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)

## How Is It Diagnosed?

There is no single test to confirm bladder pain syndrome. Doctors will do several tests to rule out other conditions.

Tests may include:

- **Cystoscopy**: A thin camera is used to look inside your bladder.
- **Urine tests**: To check for infection or blood.
- **Ultrasound, MRI, or CT scan**: To look at your bladder and kidneys.
- **Urodynamics**: Tests to check how well your bladder and urethra work.
- **Vaginal swabs**: To check for infections.

Ask your doctor to explain each test and why it is needed.

## Treatments

There is no one treatment that works for everyone. You may need to try several options to find what helps you.

Talk to your specialist about the benefits and risks of each treatment.

### Medicines

You may take tablets or capsules to help with symptoms.

These include:

- Over-the-counter painkillers like paracetamol or ibuprofen
- Medicines for nerve pain, such as amitriptyline, gabapentin, or pregabalin
- Medicines like tolterodine, solifenacin, or mirabegron to reduce the urge to pee
- A prescription medicine that blocks a substance called histamine in the bladder
- Pentosan polysulfate sodium (Elmiron) – this may help reduce pain. It can only be prescribed by a specialist and is not right for everyone

### Bladder Instillations

Some medicines can be put directly into the bladder through a thin tube called a catheter.

These are called bladder instillations.

Examples include:

- Lignocaine – a local anaesthetic that numbs the bladder
- A mix of steroids, sodium bicarbonate, and heparin
- Hyaluronic acid or chondroitin sulphate – may help repair the bladder lining
- Antibiotics, sometimes with a local anaesthetic and steroid – to reduce swelling and fight infection

Evidence on how well these work is not strong. Ask your specialist to explain your options.

### Supportive Therapies

Some people find these helpful:

- **Physiotherapy**: A pelvic floor specialist can teach you how to relax tight muscles and ease pain.
- **Acupuncture**: May help reduce pain.
- **Talking therapies and counselling**: Can help you cope with the emotional impact of living with long-term pain.
- **TENS**: A small device sends gentle electrical pulses to relieve pain.
- **Pain management**: Ask your GP to refer you to a pain specialist.

### Surgery and Procedures

Surgery may be considered if you have visible damage in your bladder or other treatments have not worked.

Options include:

- **Cauterisation**: Using heat or a laser to seal ulcers inside the bladder.
- **Bladder distension**: Filling the bladder with fluid to stretch it. This can help with diagnosis and may ease symptoms for a while.
- **Botulinum toxin injections (like Botox)**: Injected into the bladder wall to reduce frequent peeing and pain.
- **Neuromodulation**: A small device is implanted to send electrical signals to nerves and reduce pain and urges to pee.

In very rare cases, and only as a last option, the bladder may need to be removed. If this happens, your surgeon will create a new way for urine to leave your body.

## What You Can Do to Help Yourself

You can take steps to feel better:

- **Reduce stress**: Try gentle exercise, warm baths, or mindfulness meditation.
- **Stay hydrated**: Drink water regularly throughout the day.
- **Keep a food diary**: If you notice that certain foods or drinks (like citrus fruits, coffee, or alcohol) make your symptoms worse, avoid them. But talk to your doctor first.
- **Stop smoking**: The chemicals in cigarettes can irritate your bladder.

# Bartholin Gland Cyst and Abscess

## What Are Bartholin Gland Cysts?

- Bartholin glands are small glands near the opening of the vagina.
- They make mucus to help lubricate the vagina.
- A cyst forms when the tube that carries mucus gets blocked.
- The blocked tube fills with mucus and swells up.
- These cysts are the most common large cysts on the vulva.
- They usually appear on one side of the vaginal opening.

## How Common Are They?

- About 2 out of every 100 women get a Bartholin gland cyst.
- They are most common in women in their 20s.
- As women get older, they are less likely to develop these cysts.

## What Causes a Cyst?

- The exact cause is often unknown.
- Rarely, a sexually transmitted infection like gonorrhea can cause a blockage.

## What Happens If a Cyst Gets Infected?

- A cyst can become infected and turn into an abscess.
- An abscess is a painful, pus-filled lump.
- The most common germ causing these infections is a type of staph bacteria called MRSA.
- MRSA is hard to treat with some antibiotics.

## Can These Cysts Lead to Cancer?

- Very rarely, cancer can start in the Bartholin gland.
- This is more likely in women over 40.

---

## Symptoms

### Cysts

- Most cysts do not cause any symptoms.
- Large cysts may cause:
  - A feeling of pressure or fullness in the vulva.
  - Pain when walking or sitting.
  - Pain during sex.
  - One side of the vulva looks bigger than the other.

### Abscesses

- Abscesses cause severe pain.
- The area is red, swollen, and very tender.
- You may have a fever.
- You might have a discharge from the vagina.
- The skin around the area may be warm and red (this is called cellulitis).
- Other sexually transmitted infections may be present at the same time.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- Your doctor will examine your vulva.
- If there is a discharge, they may test it for sexually transmitted infections.
- If there is pus in the abscess, they may take a sample to test for bacteria.
- For women over 40, doctors may suggest a biopsy to rule out cancer.

---

## Treatment

### For Mild Symptoms

- Soak in warm water several times a day (called a sitz bath).
- This can help reduce swelling and pain.

### For Abscesses

- A small cut is made to drain the pus.
- A small tube (catheter) is often left in place for 4 to 6 weeks.
  - The tube helps keep the opening open.
  - It allows fluid to drain and prevents the cyst from closing again.
- Another option is marsupialization.
  - The edges of the cyst are stitched to the skin outside.
  - This creates a permanent opening.

### Antibiotics

- Antibiotics are used if:
  - You have signs of cellulitis (red, swollen, warm skin).
  - You have a weak immune system.
  - You have diabetes that is not well controlled.
- Common antibiotics include:
  - Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (taken once or twice a day).
  - Or this medicine plus amoxicillin-clavulanate.
  - Or this medicine plus metronidazole.
- The choice of antibiotic depends on local infection patterns.

### When Hospital Care Is Needed

- If you have diabetes and it is not well managed, you may need IV antibiotics in the hospital.
- If you have a weak immune system, hospital care is also recommended.

### For Recurrent Cysts or Abscesses

- If cysts keep coming back, the entire gland may need to be removed.
- This is a surgical procedure.

### For Women Over 40

- Any new cyst or abscess should be checked with a biopsy.
- This helps rule out cancer.
- If a cyst has been there for years and has not changed, it does not need to be removed unless it causes pain or other problems.

---

## Key Points

- Bartholin gland cysts are fluid-filled lumps near the vaginal opening.
- They form when the gland’s tube gets blocked.
- The cause is usually unknown.
- Cysts can become infected and turn into abscesses.
- Abscesses are painful and often need drainage.
- Treatment includes drainage, a catheter, or surgery.
- Women over 40 should have new cysts checked for cancer.
- Surgery may be needed for repeated problems or if cancer is suspected.

# Jaundice in Newborns

## What Is Jaundice?

Jaundice means the skin and the whites of the eyes turn yellow.  
The yellow color in the eyes is also called scleral icterus.

Jaundice happens when a yellow substance called bilirubin builds up in the blood.  
This buildup is called hyperbilirubinemia.

Bilirubin comes from the breakdown of hemoglobin.  
Hemoglobin is the part of red blood cells that carries oxygen.  
Old or damaged red blood cells break down naturally, and bilirubin is made during this process.

The body sends bilirubin through the blood to the liver.  
The liver processes bilirubin so it can be removed from the body in bile.  
Bile is a fluid made by the liver to help digest food.

In the liver, bilirubin is changed by a process called conjugation.  
This makes it easier to get rid of.  
The processed form is called conjugated bilirubin.  
The form that has not been processed is called unconjugated bilirubin.

Bile flows from the liver through tubes called bile ducts into the small intestine.  
If the liver and bile ducts cannot handle bilirubin fast enough, it builds up in the blood.  
This causes hyperbilirubinemia.

As bilirubin levels rise, the whites of the eyes turn yellow first.  
Then the skin turns yellow.

More than half of all newborns get jaundice that can be seen in the first week of life.  
But it can be hard to see in babies with dark skin.

---

## Why Does Jaundice Happen in Newborns?

Most newborns have some unconjugated bilirubin in their blood during the first week.  
This usually causes mild jaundice that goes away in a week or two.

But other things can also cause jaundice.  
It is more common in premature babies.  
Their livers are not fully developed.  
Their feeding and bowel habits are not mature.  
And their bodies break down red blood cells faster.

---

## Risks of Jaundice

Whether jaundice is dangerous depends on:

- What is causing it  
- How high the bilirubin level is  
- Whether the bilirubin is conjugated or unconjugated

Some causes, like infections or biliary atresia, are dangerous no matter the bilirubin level.

In most cases of newborn jaundice, the level of unconjugated bilirubin matters most.

Very high levels of unconjugated bilirubin can be dangerous.  
They can harm the brain.

This brain damage is called bilirubin encephalopathy.

Bilirubin encephalopathy can lead to:

- Delayed development  
- Cerebral palsy  
- Hearing loss  
- Seizures  
- Death

### Acute Bilirubin Encephalopathy

This is when bilirubin starts to harm the brain.  
It causes:

- Being very sleepy or sluggish  
- Being irritable  
- Unusual muscle tone or muscle spasms  
- Poor feeding  
- A high-pitched cry  
- Seizures

If treated quickly, this stage can be reversed.  
If not treated, it leads to chronic bilirubin encephalopathy.

Chronic bilirubin encephalopathy is permanent brain damage.  
It is also called kernicterus.

This risk is higher in:

- Premature babies  
- Babies who are very sick  
- Babies given certain medicines

This condition is now rare.  
But it can be prevented with early diagnosis and treatment of high bilirubin.

Once brain damage happens, there is no treatment to fix it.

---

## Common Causes of Jaundice in Newborns

### 1. Physiologic Hyperbilirubinemia

This is normal in newborns.  
It happens for two reasons:

- Newborns break down red blood cells faster than older babies.  
  This makes more bilirubin.

- The newborn’s liver is not yet fully able to process and remove bilirubin.

Almost all newborns have this.  
It usually starts 2 to 3 days after birth.  
Jaundice that appears in the first 24 hours may be a sign of a serious problem.

This type of jaundice does not cause other symptoms.  
It goes away in about a week.

If jaundice lasts past 2 weeks, a doctor should check for other causes.

### 2. Breastfeeding (Chestfeeding) Jaundice

This happens in some breastfed babies in the first few days.  
It usually goes away in the first week.

It happens when the baby does not get enough milk.  
This can happen if the mother’s milk has not come in yet.

When babies eat less, they have fewer bowel movements.  
Less bowel movement means less bilirubin is removed from the body.

As the baby breastfeeds more and eats more milk, the jaundice goes away.

### 3. Human Milk Jaundice

This is different from breastfeeding jaundice.  
It usually starts near the end of the first week.  
It may go away by 2 weeks or last for several months.

It is caused by substances in human milk that slow down the baby’s ability to process and remove bilirubin.

### 4. Excessive Breakdown of Red Blood Cells (Hemolysis)

When red blood cells break down too fast, the liver gets overwhelmed.  
It cannot process all the bilirubin.

This is called hemolytic anemia.

Causes include:

- **Immune causes**:  
  The baby’s blood has antibodies that attack its own red blood cells.  
  This can happen if the baby’s blood type does not match the mother’s.  
  This is called Rh incompatibility.

- **Nonimmune causes**:  
  - A genetic lack of an enzyme called G6PD.  
  - Inherited red blood cell problems like alpha-thalassemia or sickle cell disease.

Some babies get a bruise under the skin during birth.  
This is called a hematoma.  
When the blood in the bruise breaks down, it can cause jaundice.

Babies born to mothers with diabetes may get extra blood from the placenta.  
When this blood breaks down, it can cause jaundice.

Transfused blood cells can also break down and raise bilirubin.

### Other Causes

- Severe infections, including sepsis  
- Underactive pituitary gland (hypopituitarism)  
- Underactive thyroid gland (hypothyroidism)  
- Certain inherited disorders  
- Blockage in bile flow from the liver

Some of these cause cholestasis.  
This means bile flow is reduced.  
It leads to conjugated bilirubin buildup.

Hypothyroidism slows down how the liver processes bilirubin.  
Sepsis can cause both cholestasis and hemolysis.

A urinary tract infection (UTI) without sepsis can cause jaundice.  
Infections the baby gets in the womb can also cause jaundice.  
These include:

- Toxoplasmosis  
- Cytomegalovirus  
- Herpes simplex virus  
- Rubella virus

Some inherited conditions that cause jaundice include:

- Cystic fibrosis  
- Dubin-Johnson syndrome  
- Rotor syndrome  
- Crigler-Najjar syndrome  
- Gilbert syndrome

Bile flow can be blocked by birth defects in the bile ducts, like biliary atresia.  
Cystic fibrosis can also damage the liver and block bile flow.

---

## How Doctors Check for Jaundice

Hospitals check newborns for jaundice often.  
Doctors look at the color of the eyes and skin.  
But they also test the bilirubin level before the baby goes home.

If jaundice is present, doctors try to find the cause.  
They want to rule out serious problems.

Babies with jaundice that lasts more than 2 weeks need a doctor’s check.

### Warning Signs

Call a doctor right away if the baby has:

- Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life  
- Jaundice that starts after 2 weeks of age  
- Being very sleepy or hard to wake  
- Poor feeding  
- Irritability  
- Trouble breathing  
- Fever

Also call if:

- Bilirubin levels are very high  
- Bilirubin levels are rising fast  
- Blood tests show bile flow is blocked

If a baby leaves the hospital the first day after birth, a follow-up visit to check bilirubin should happen within 2 days.

### What Parents Should Do at Home

If you see yellow in your baby’s skin or eyes, call the doctor right away.

The doctor will decide how urgent the visit needs to be.  
They will consider symptoms and risk factors like prematurity.

### What Doctors Do

Doctors ask about:

- When the jaundice started  
- How long it has lasted  
- If the baby is sleepy, feeding poorly, or acting differently  
- How often and how much the baby is fed  
- How well the baby latches on to the breast or bottle  
- Whether the mother feels her milk has come in  
- If the baby swallows and seems full after feeding  
- The color of the baby’s stool

Pale or light-colored stool may mean bile flow is blocked.

Doctors also ask about:

- The mother’s health during pregnancy (like diabetes)  
- The mother’s blood type  
- Medicines the mother took  
- Family history of inherited conditions
