# Scabies

The main sign of scabies is a very itchy rash. It often gets worse at night.

## What to Look For

- You may feel strong itching, especially when you are lying down at night.
- You may see a raised rash or small spots on your skin.

The spots can look red. On brown or black skin, they may be harder to see. But you should still be able to feel them.

Tiny mites burrow into the skin and lay eggs. This leaves thin lines with a small dot at one end.

The rash can show up anywhere on the body. But it often starts between the fingers.

The rash can spread and turn into tiny bumps. On white skin, these may look red.

After the rash goes away, it may leave behind dark marks. On brown or black skin, these marks may be darker than your normal skin tone.

The rash usually spreads over most of the body. But it rarely affects the head and neck.

It often appears:
- Between the fingers
- Around the wrists
- Under the arms
- Around the waist, groin, and bottom

However, older adults and young children may get the rash on their head, neck, palms of the hands, or soles of the feet.

People with a weak immune system can get a rare and very contagious form of scabies called crusted scabies. The main sign is a thick, flaky rash. This often affects the elbows, knees, hands, and feet.

# Chickenpox

Chickenpox is a common childhood illness caused by a virus called the varicella-zoster virus.  
The virus can also cause shingles later in life.  

Chickenpox spreads easily from person to person.  
It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes.  
It can also spread through direct contact with fluid from the blisters.  

The illness usually starts with a mild fever, tiredness, and headache.  
These symptoms happen 7 to 21 days after being around someone with chickenpox.  
They usually appear about one day before the rash shows up.  
Older children and adults tend to have worse symptoms than young children.  

The rash appears in waves.  
It starts as small red spots.  
These spots turn into fluid-filled blisters.  
The blisters then break and form crusts.  
The rash often appears on the skin and inside the mouth.  
It can also appear on the scalp.  

Chickenpox is most contagious just before the rash appears.  
It stays contagious until all the blisters have crusted over.  
This usually takes about 5 to 7 days.  
People who have had chickenpox before cannot spread it.  

Before the chickenpox vaccine was available, outbreaks happened every 3 to 4 years.  
They were most common in winter and early spring.  

## Who Gets Severe Chickenpox?

Most children recover without serious problems.  
But some people are at higher risk for serious illness.  
These include:  
- Adults  
- Babies less than one month old  
- People with weak immune systems  
- People with certain health conditions like cancer or lung disease  
- People on strong medicines that weaken the immune system  

## How Is Chickenpox Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose chickenpox by looking at the rash.  
The rash has a very typical look.  
If the diagnosis is unclear, a doctor may do a test.  

Tests may include:  
- A swab from the base of a blister sent to a lab  
- A blood test to check for recent infection  
- A test to find the virus in the blister fluid  

The most accurate test is a PCR test.  
It finds the virus’s genetic material.  
It is fast and reliable.  

A Tzanck smear can also be done.  
It uses a small sample from a blister.  
It can show signs of a herpes virus.  
But it cannot tell if it is chickenpox or shingles.  

## How Is Chickenpox Treated?

Most children with chickenpox only need home care.  
The main goals are to feel better and avoid infection.  

To relieve itching:  
- Use cool, wet cloths on the skin  
- Take baths with colloidal oatmeal  
- Use antihistamines if itching is bad  

Keep the skin clean.  
Wash often.  
Keep fingernails short.  
This helps prevent scratching and infection.  

Do not use antiseptics on the skin unless the blisters get infected.  
If a skin infection happens, antibiotics are needed.  

Do not go back to school or work until all the blisters have crusted over.  

For people at high risk of serious illness, doctors may give antiviral medicine.  
This includes:  
- Valacyclovir  
- Famciclovir  
- Acyclovir  

These are taken by mouth.  
They work best if started within 24 to 48 hours of the rash starting.  

For people with weak immune systems, or those at high risk, doctors may give antiviral medicine through a vein.  
This is called IV acyclovir.  

## What Is the Outlook?

Most children get better without problems.  
But serious illness can happen in:  
- Adults  
- People with weak immune systems  
- People on chemotherapy or steroids  
- People on certain medicines for autoimmune diseases  

## How Can Chickenpox Be Prevented?

Once you have had chickenpox, you are protected for life.  
You cannot get it again.  

To avoid getting chickenpox:  
- Stay away from people who have the rash  
- Wash hands often  
- Avoid sharing towels or clothes  

The best way to prevent chickenpox is vaccination.  
All healthy children should get the vaccine.  
Unvaccinated adults who have never had chickenpox should also get it.  

If someone at high risk is exposed to chickenpox, they may get a shot called varicella immune globulin.  
This helps prevent or reduce the illness.  
It is given to:  
- People with weak immune systems  
- Pregnant women who have not had chickenpox  
- Newborn babies whose mother got chickenpox just before or after birth  

For healthy children over one year old, the chickenpox vaccine can be given after exposure.  
This can prevent the disease or make it milder.  

## Key Points

- Chickenpox causes itchy, blistering spots on the skin.  
- The spots can also appear inside the mouth.  
- It can lead to serious problems like skin infections, lung infections, or brain swelling.  
- Antiviral medicine is used for people at high risk.  
  - Valacyclovir or acyclovir for people 12 years and older  
  - Famciclovir for people 18 years and older  
  - People with eczema, lung disease, or on steroids should also get antiviral medicine  
- IV acyclovir is used for people with weak immune systems or other high-risk conditions  
- All healthy children and unvaccinated adults should get the chickenpox vaccine  
- High-risk people exposed to chickenpox should get a shot called varicella immune globulin  
- Healthy children over one year old can get the vaccine after exposure

# Hepatitis B, Acute – Simple Explanation

## What Is Acute Hepatitis B?

Acute hepatitis B is a short-term liver infection caused by the hepatitis B virus. It lasts from a few weeks to 6 months.

The liver is an organ that helps clean your blood and digest food. When it is inflamed, it does not work as well.

## How Is Hepatitis B Spread?

Hepatitis B spreads through contact with blood or other body fluids from an infected person.

- It can spread when people share needles to inject drugs.
- It can spread through sexual contact.
- It can spread in close living situations, like prisons or mental health facilities.
- A pregnant woman can pass the virus to her baby during childbirth.

It can also spread through contact with saliva, tears, breast milk, urine, vaginal fluid, or semen, but this is less common.

Blood transfusions can spread the virus, but this is now very rare in the United States because all donated blood is tested.

Insect bites do not clearly spread hepatitis B.

Some people get hepatitis B with no known cause.

## Who Is at Risk?

- Babies born to mothers with hepatitis B.
- People who share needles to inject drugs.
- People with multiple sex partners.
- People living in close quarters with others.
- People with chronic liver disease.

Even people with no symptoms can spread the virus.

## What Happens If You Get Hepatitis B?

Most people recover fully from acute hepatitis B. But a small number develop chronic hepatitis B, which lasts longer than 6 months.

The younger you are when you get infected, the more likely you are to develop chronic hepatitis B:

- Babies: 90% chance
- Children aged 1 to 5: 25% to 50% chance
- Adults: About 5% chance

If hepatitis B becomes chronic, it can lead to serious liver problems over time, such as:

- Scarring of the liver (called cirrhosis)
- Liver cancer

## Symptoms of Acute Hepatitis B

Many people have no symptoms. Others may feel sick for a few weeks to 6 months.

Common symptoms include:

- Loss of appetite
- Feeling tired or unwell
- Fever
- Nausea or vomiting
- Yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice)

Some people also get:

- Joint pain
- Itchy red bumps on the skin (wheals)

If the infection becomes severe, it can cause fulminant hepatitis. This is a life-threatening condition.

In fulminant hepatitis:

- The liver stops working fast.
- Toxins build up in the blood and affect the brain.
- This can cause confusion, drowsiness, or coma.
- Without a liver transplant, it can be fatal.

People with both hepatitis B and hepatitis D have worse symptoms.

## How Is Hepatitis B Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect hepatitis if you have symptoms like jaundice.

They will do blood tests to check:

- How well your liver is working
- If your liver is damaged
- If you have the hepatitis B virus

Blood tests can find:

- Parts of the virus (antigens)
- Antibodies your body made to fight the virus
- The virus’s genetic material (DNA)

If the infection is severe, doctors also test for hepatitis D virus.

## How Is Acute Hepatitis B Treated?

There is no specific medicine for acute hepatitis B.

You should:

- Avoid alcohol. It harms the liver.
- Eat a normal diet. No special foods are needed.
- Rest as needed. Most people can return to work after the yellowing of the skin goes away.

If you have itching, a medicine called cholestyramine can help. It is taken by mouth.

If fulminant hepatitis develops, doctors use antiviral medicine. These are taken by mouth and can improve survival. The most common medicines are:

- Entecavir
- Tenofovir

The best treatment for fulminant hepatitis is a liver transplant. This gives the best chance of survival, especially for adults.

## How Can You Prevent Hepatitis B?

The best way to prevent hepatitis B is vaccination.

Vaccination is recommended for:

- All children, starting at birth
- All adults who want protection
- Unvaccinated adults at higher risk, including pregnant women
- People with chronic liver disease
- Family members and close contacts of people with chronic hepatitis B

If a pregnant woman has high levels of the virus, she may be given antiviral medicine during the last three months of pregnancy. This lowers the chance of passing the virus to her baby.

If you are not vaccinated and have been exposed to hepatitis B, you should get:

- A shot of hepatitis B immune globulin (given into a muscle)
- The hepatitis B vaccine

This combination prevents chronic hepatitis B in about 75% of people. It can also make the disease less severe.

If you have been exposed to blood from someone with hepatitis B:

- You will get a shot of immune globulin.
- If you are not vaccinated, you will also get the vaccine.
- If you have been vaccinated, you will have a blood test to check if you are still protected. If not, you will be vaccinated.

## More Information

For more details, visit the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website.  
[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: Hepatitis B](https://www.cdc.gov/hepatitis)  
This site includes information on symptoms, testing, treatment, and the vaccine.

# Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)

ARDS usually happens to people who are already very sick. It can happen if you have an infection, serious injury, or other serious health problems.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may have trouble breathing.  
You may take quick, shallow breaths.  
You might feel very short of breath, even when resting.

## When to Get Help Right Away

Call 999 or go to A&E immediately if you or someone else has:

- Very hard breathing. You can’t speak in full sentences. You feel like you’re choking or gasping.
- Sudden shortness of breath with pain in your arms, back, neck, or jaw.
- Sudden shortness of breath with a tight or heavy feeling in your chest.
- Sudden shortness of breath with nausea or vomiting.
- Sudden shortness of breath and coughing up blood.
- Sudden shortness of breath with pain or swelling in one leg.

> **Find your nearest A&E**

## Important Safety Tips for A&E

Do not drive yourself to A&E.  
Ask a friend or family member to drive you.  
Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring all your regular medicines with you when you go.

## Who Is at Risk?

ARDS usually affects people who are already very ill.  
It can happen after:

- A serious infection in the blood (sepsis)
- Pneumonia or other lung infections
- Inflammation of the pancreas (acute pancreatitis)
- Accidentally breathing in vomit or food
- Drowning
- Breathing in smoke
- Severe injuries, like from a car crash
- Receiving a blood transfusion
- Having a lung transplant

## How Is ARDS Treated?

ARDS is treated in hospital, often in a special unit called intensive care.

Treatment may include:

- Oxygen through a mask to help you breathe.
- A machine that helps you breathe if you can’t do it on your own.
- Medicines, such as antibiotics to fight infections.
- Fluids given through a tube in your vein.

## Important Facts

ARDS is a very serious condition.  
It can be life-threatening.  
Not everyone survives.  
Some people get better, but others may not.

# Cushing Syndrome

Cushing syndrome happens when your body has too much cortisol for a long time.  
Cortisol is a hormone that helps your body respond to stress.  
Too much cortisol can cause many health problems.

Cushing disease is a type of Cushing syndrome.  
It happens when the pituitary gland makes too much ACTH.  
ACTH is a hormone that tells the adrenal glands to make cortisol.  
A small tumor in the pituitary gland often causes this.

## What Causes Cushing Syndrome?

There are two main types: ACTH-dependent and ACTH-independent.

### ACTH-Dependent Causes
- A tumor in the pituitary gland (Cushing disease).
- A tumor in another part of the body that makes ACTH.  
  Examples: small cell lung cancer or carcinoid tumors.
- Taking ACTH as medicine.

### ACTH-Independent Causes
- Taking corticosteroid medicines for a long time.  
  These are often used to treat inflammation or immune problems.
- A tumor in the adrenal gland (adenoma or carcinoma).
- Rare causes:
  - A condition called primary pigmented nodular adrenal dysplasia.  
    This usually affects teens and young adults.
  - Bilateral macronodular hyperplasia.  
    This usually affects older adults.

Cushing syndrome means you have too much cortisol from any cause.  
Cushing disease means the extra cortisol comes from a pituitary tumor.

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

You may notice these physical changes:

- Your face looks round and full. This is called "moon face."
- You gain weight in your middle body.  
  You may have a large hump of fat on your upper back.  
  This is called a "buffalo hump."
- You get stretch marks on your skin.  
  These are often on the stomach, hips, or thighs.
- Your arms and legs become thin and weak.
- Your skin becomes thin and easy to bruise.
- Wounds heal slowly.
- You may have high blood pressure.
- You may get kidney stones.
- Your bones become weak (osteoporosis).
- You may have trouble controlling blood sugar (glucose intolerance).
- You may get sick more often.
- You may feel confused, sad, or anxious.
- Children may stop growing.

Women may have irregular periods.  
If a woman has an adrenal tumor, she may grow extra body hair.  
She may also lose hair on her head or have other signs of male-like features.

## How Is Cushing Syndrome Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect Cushing syndrome based on your symptoms.  
They will do tests to confirm it and find the cause.

Common tests include:

- A 24-hour urine test to check cortisol levels.
- A blood test at night to check cortisol levels.  
  Cortisol is usually low at night. If it is high, this may mean Cushing syndrome.
- A saliva test at night to check cortisol levels.
- A dexamethasone suppression test.  
  You take a medicine called dexamethasone.  
  If your cortisol stays high, this suggests Cushing syndrome.
- A blood test to check ACTH levels.  
  This helps find out if the problem is in the pituitary or elsewhere.

## How Is Cushing Syndrome Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause.  
The goal is to lower cortisol levels and fix the underlying problem.

### Supportive Care
- Eat more protein-rich foods.
- Take extra potassium.  
  This can be in your food or as a medicine.  
  Potassium-sparing medicines like spironolactone may also help.

### Medicines to Lower Cortisol
- Metyrapone: taken by mouth, helps block cortisol production.
- Ketoconazole: taken by mouth, helps block cortisol.  
  It can take time to work. It may harm the liver in some people.
- Mitotane: used less often. It blocks cortisol and can shrink tumors.
- Levoketoconazole: helps block cortisol production.
- Osilodrostat: helps block cortisol.
- Mifepristone: blocks the effects of cortisol in the body.

### Emergency Treatment
- Parenteral etomidate: given through a vein.  
  It blocks cortisol production quickly.  
  It is used only in very serious cases.  
  It is given slowly and adjusted based on blood tests.

### Surgery or Radiation
- If there is a tumor, surgery is often the first choice.
- Radiation therapy may be used if surgery is not possible or if the tumor comes back.

### Other Options
- Somatostatin analogs (like pasireotide) or dopamine agonists (like cabergoline) may help if the tumor keeps coming back or spreads.

## Key Points

- Cushing syndrome is often diagnosed by:
  - High cortisol levels at night (in blood or saliva).
  - High cortisol in a 24-hour urine test.
  - A dexamethasone test that does not lower cortisol.
- ACTH levels help tell if the problem is in the pituitary or elsewhere.
- Imaging tests (like MRI or CT scans) are used to find tumors.
- Tumors are usually treated with surgery or radiation.
- Medicines like metyrapone, ketoconazole, levoketoconazole, or osilodrostat can lower cortisol before surgery.
- Mifepristone blocks cortisol from working in the body.
- Pasireotide or cabergoline may help if the tumor returns or spreads.

# Rabies

Rabies is a serious virus that attacks the brain and spinal cord. It is almost always deadly once it reaches the brain.

## How Rabies Spreads

The virus is in the saliva of infected animals. It spreads when an infected animal bites a person. It can also spread if infected saliva touches a cut or open wound, or gets into the eyes, nose, or mouth.

In the United States, bats are the most common source of rabies. In other parts of the world, unvaccinated dogs are the main source.

The virus travels from the bite site along nerves to the brain. This can take 10 days or more—usually 30 to 50 days. The closer the bite is to the brain (like on the face), the faster symptoms appear.

Rarely, symptoms can show up months or even years after a bite.

## Who Gets Rabies

Rabies kills more than 59,000 people worldwide every year. Most cases happen in rural areas of Asia and Africa.

In the United States, only a few people die from rabies each year.

Many animals can carry the virus. These include:
- Dogs
- Cats
- Bats
- Raccoons
- Skunks
- Foxes

In the United States, rabies in dogs is rare because of vaccines. Most cases come from wild animals, especially bats.

In countries where dogs are not routinely vaccinated, most rabies deaths come from dog bites.

A few cases come from bites by monkeys kept as pets.

Rabies is very rare in:
- Rodents (like hamsters, rats, mice, squirrels)
- Rabbits
- Hares

Birds and reptiles do not get rabies.

> **Did You Know?**  
> - If a raccoon, skunk, or fox bites someone, assume it has rabies.  
> - Bats cause most rabies deaths in the United States.

## Symptoms of Rabies

The bite wound may hurt or feel numb. Bat bites often cause no pain or symptoms.

Symptoms usually start 30 to 50 days after a bite. But they can appear as early as 10 days or as late as over a year.

Early symptoms include:
- Fever
- Headache
- Feeling unwell

Then people may become:
- Restless
- Confused
- Very excited or agitated
- Hallucinate (see or hear things that are not there)
- Have trouble sleeping

Saliva production increases. The muscles in the throat and voice box spasm. These spasms are very painful. Even a light breeze or trying to drink water can trigger them.

Because of this, people with rabies often cannot drink. This is why the disease is sometimes called “fear of water” (hydrophobia).

As the disease gets worse, people become more confused and agitated. They may fall into a coma and die.

Causes of death include:
- Blocked airways
- Seizures
- Extreme weakness
- Paralysis

In about 20% of people, the first sign is tingling or weakness in the arm or leg that was bitten. The weakness spreads through the body. Thinking stays clear. Other symptoms like confusion or fear of water may not happen.

## How Doctors Diagnose Rabies

Doctors suspect rabies if a person has:
- A headache
- Confusion
- A history of being bitten by an animal or exposed to bats

But many people do not remember being bitten.

To check for the virus, doctors take samples of:
- Skin (usually from the neck)
- Saliva
- Cerebrospinal fluid (taken with a spinal tap)

A test called PCR is used to find the virus’s unique DNA in these samples. Multiple tests over time increase the chance of finding the virus.

## How to Prevent Rabies

The best way to avoid rabies is to avoid being bitten by animals, especially wild ones.

Do not touch wild animals. Do not try to help a sick animal. Sick animals may bite.

Signs that a wild animal may have rabies:
- It does not run away when people come near
- It is active during the day (nocturnal animals like bats, raccoons, skunks, and foxes usually come out at night)
- A bat makes strange noises or cannot fly well
- An animal bites without being provoked
- An animal is weak, acting wild, or very aggressive

If you see a sick animal, call local health officials. Do not try to catch it.

### Who Should Get the Rabies Vaccine?

The vaccine is given to people at high risk of exposure. This includes:
- Veterinarians
- Lab workers who handle animals that might have rabies
- People who live or stay more than 30 days in countries where rabies in dogs is common
- People who explore caves where bats live

The vaccine is given in two doses:
- First dose on day 0 (right away)
- Second dose on day 7

The injection site may be sore or swollen, but this is usually mild. Serious allergic reactions are rare.

The vaccine gives long-term protection. But protection fades over time. If you are still at risk, your doctor may test your antibody levels and give a booster if needed.

### What to Do After a Bite

If you are bitten:
1. Wash the wound well with soap and water for at least 5 minutes.
2. Use running water to flush out deep bites.
3. See a doctor right away.

The doctor will:
- Clean the wound with an antiseptic called benzalkonium chloride
- Trim any torn skin if needed

No test can tell right away if the virus was passed on. So, doctors often give two treatments right away:
- **Rabies immune globulin**: This gives immediate protection. It is injected around the wound if possible.
- **Rabies vaccine**: This helps your body make its own protection. It works slowly but lasts longer.

### When Is the Vaccine Needed?

It depends on:
- What kind of animal bit you
- Whether the animal looked sick
- Whether the bite was provoked
- Whether the animal can be watched or tested

#### If You Are Bitten by a Dog, Cat, or Ferret

- If the animal looks healthy and can be watched for 10 days, no vaccine is needed unless the animal gets sick.
- If the animal shows signs of rabies, you get the vaccine and immune globulin right away.
- If the animal stays healthy for 10 days, it did not have rabies when it bit you. No vaccine is needed.
- If the animal cannot be watched (like if it ran away), talk to public health officials. If rabies is possible, you get the vaccine right away.

#### If You Are Bitten by a Skunk, Raccoon, Fox, Bat, or Other Wild Carnivore

- These animals are treated as if they have rabies unless testing proves otherwise.
- You get the vaccine and immune globulin right away.
- The animal is usually put to sleep and tested for rabies.
- If the test is negative, the vaccine is stopped.

Bats often bite without being noticed. If you wake up and a bat is in the room, get the vaccine.

#### If You Are Bitten by Livestock, Small Rodents, Rabbits, or Hares

- Each case is reviewed by public health officials.
- Most bites from small rodents, rabbits, or hares do not need the rabies vaccine.

### If You Need Preventive Treatment

If you have not been vaccinated before:
- Get immune globulin and the first vaccine dose on day 0.
- Get 3 more vaccine doses on days 3, 7, and 14.
- If you have a weak immune system (like from AIDS or certain medicines), you get one more dose on day 28.

If you have been vaccinated before:
- Clean the wound right away.
- Get one dose of vaccine on day 0 and another on day 3.

## Treatment After Symptoms Start

Once symptoms appear, there is no cure. The disease is almost always fatal.

Treatment focuses on making the person as comfortable as possible. This may include:
- Pain relief
- Care in an intensive care unit
- Support for breathing and other body functions

In rare cases, people have survived with long-term care in an intensive care unit.

# Salivary Gland Stones

Salivary gland stones are small, hard, white lumps.  
They often form under your tongue.  
They can cause pain or swelling in your mouth.

## What You Can Do at Home

You may be able to help the stone come out by doing these things:

- Drink plenty of water.  
- Chew sugar-free gum or suck on sugar-free lozenges.  
- Gently massage the area around the stone.  

If you have pain or swelling:

- Take paracetamol or ibuprofen.  
- Suck on ice cubes or ice lollies to reduce swelling.

The pain and swelling will not go away until the stone is out.

### Important Warning

Do not use anything sharp to try to remove the stone.  
This could hurt you or cause an infection.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:

- You cannot remove the stone yourself.  
- The area around the stone becomes infected.  
  Signs of infection include:  
  - Pain  
  - Redness  
  - Pus (thick, yellow or white fluid)  
  - High temperature (feeling hot and shivery)

## What the Stones Look Like

- They are white and hard.  
- They are usually about the size of a pea.  
- Most form in a salivary gland under your tongue.  
- You may not be able to see them.

## Symptoms

You may have:

- A dull ache in your mouth that comes and goes.  
- Swelling that gets worse at times.  
- An infection around the stone.  
  Signs of infection include pain, redness, and a high temperature.

If you feel strong pain during meals, the stone may be blocking the gland completely.  
The pain usually lasts 1 to 2 hours.

## How Doctors Treat Them

Some small stones come out on their own.  
But you will still have symptoms until the stone is gone.

Your doctor may try to remove the stone using a thin, blunt tool.  
If that does not work, you may need to go to the hospital for removal.

## What Causes Them?

Doctors do not know exactly what causes salivary gland stones.  
There is no way to prevent them.  
They are not usually linked to other health problems.

After a stone is removed, it usually does not come back.  
But if you keep getting them, your doctor may suggest removing one of your salivary glands.

# Hemorrhoids

Hemorrhoids are swollen blood vessels in the lower part of the rectum or around the anus.  
They can cause itching, pain, or bleeding.  
Some types are very painful, especially when a blood clot forms inside them.  

## What Causes Hemorrhoids?

High pressure in the blood vessels around the anus can lead to hemorrhoids.  
This pressure can come from:  
- Being pregnant  
- Lifting heavy things often  
- Straining when you go to the bathroom, especially if you are constipated  

Hemorrhoids can be either inside the rectum or outside the anus.  
In rare cases, a different condition called rectal varices can look like hemorrhoids.  
This happens when blood pressure in the liver is high.  

## Types of Hemorrhoids

### External Hemorrhoids  
These are outside the anus.  
They are covered with skin-like tissue.  
They can become painful if a blood clot forms inside them.  
This causes a hard, purple lump that hurts a lot.  
Sometimes they break open and bleed a little.  
They can make cleaning the area hard.  

### Internal Hemorrhoids  
These are inside the rectum.  
They are covered with lining that is like the inside of the bowel.  
They usually appear in three main spots:  
- On the right side, front  
- On the right side, back  
- On the left side  

They can happen in both adults and children.  
They often do not cause pain.  
But they may bleed during or after a bowel movement.  
You might see blood on toilet paper or in the toilet bowl.  
They can also cause mucus to leak out.  
Some people feel like they did not finish going to the bathroom.  

### Strangulated Hemorrhoids  
This happens when a hemorrhoid sticks out and gets squeezed.  
The blood supply is cut off.  
This causes severe pain.  
In rare cases, the tissue can die and form an open sore.  

## How Are Hemorrhoids Diagnosed?

A doctor will look at your anus and rectum.  
This is usually enough to see painful or bleeding hemorrhoids.  
For painless bleeding, a doctor may use a small scope called an anoscope.  
This lets the doctor see inside the rectum.  

If you have rectal bleeding, the doctor must rule out more serious problems first.  
This may include tests like sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy.  
These tests check the whole colon for signs of cancer or other issues.  

### Grading Internal Hemorrhoids

Doctors use a grading system to describe how bad internal hemorrhoids are.  
This helps decide the best treatment.  

| Grade | What It Means |
|-------|---------------|
| I     | The hemorrhoid is swollen but does not come out. |
| II    | The hemorrhoid comes out when you strain, but goes back in on its own. |
| III   | The hemorrhoid comes out and must be pushed back in by hand. |
| IV    | The hemorrhoid stays out all the time. It cannot be pushed back in. |

## Treatment Options

### For External Hemorrhoids  
- Use stool softeners to make bowel movements easier.  
- Soak in warm water (sitz bath) several times a day.  
- Take pain relievers if needed.  
- If the hemorrhoid is very painful and has a clot, a doctor can remove it quickly.  
- This works best if done within the first 3 days of pain starting.  

### For Internal Hemorrhoids  
- Injection sclerotherapy: A medicine is injected into the hemorrhoid to shrink it.  
- Rubber band ligation: A small rubber band is placed around the base of the hemorrhoid.  
  This cuts off blood flow and causes it to fall off in a few days.  
- Infrared photocoagulation: A special light is used to seal the blood vessels.  

These treatments are usually done in a doctor’s office.  
They are not painful.  

### Surgery  
Surgery is only used when other treatments do not work.  
It can be very effective but is not needed for most people.  

## Key Points

- External hemorrhoids can get a blood clot and become very painful.  
  But they rarely bleed.  
- Internal hemorrhoids often bleed but are not usually painful.  
- Most external hemorrhoids get better with stool softeners, warm baths, and pain relief.  
- If a blood clot causes severe pain, removing it early can help fast.  
- Bleeding internal hemorrhoids can be treated with injections, rubber bands, or light.  
- Surgery is a last option but can work well when needed.  

Always talk to your doctor before assuming rectal bleeding is from hemorrhoids.  
Other serious conditions must be ruled out first.

# Broken, Wobbly, or Missing Teeth

Broken, wobbly, or missing teeth are serious dental problems. They need quick care. These issues often happen after a hard hit to the mouth. Sometimes, teeth that are already weak break or become loose when chewing.

## Broken Teeth

The front upper teeth are most likely to get hurt. If you feel a sharp pain when chewing or when eating something cold, you may have a small crack in a tooth. If the tooth is only cracked and no piece has broken off, your dentist can fix it with a simple filling. If the crack is deeper, you may need a crown. Sometimes, you may also need root canal treatment.

If a tooth does not hurt when you breathe on it or drink cold water, only the outer layer (enamel) is damaged. Even if a small piece of enamel is chipped, you do not need to see a dentist right away. If the middle layer (dentin) is cracked, the tooth will likely hurt when you eat or breathe on it. Most people with this kind of injury go to the dentist fast.

If the inner part of the tooth (pulp) is damaged, you may see a red spot or some blood in the crack. In this case, your dentist may need to do root canal treatment. This removes the damaged inner tissue before it causes serious pain.

### Layers of a Tooth

- **Enamel**: The hard outer layer.
- **Dentin**: The middle layer, softer than enamel.
- **Pulp**: The innermost part with nerves and blood vessels.

## Wobbly Teeth

If a tooth becomes loose after an injury, or if the gums bleed a lot, see a dentist right away. This could mean the root or the socket is broken. If a wobbly tooth is put back in place quickly and held steady, it usually stays in place for good. If a baby tooth in the front is very loose, it is often removed. This helps protect the permanent tooth growing underneath.

## Missing Teeth

If a baby tooth or a permanent tooth comes out completely, go to a dentist right away.

- **Baby teeth**: Do not try to put them back in. Putting them back can cause infection. It can also harm the permanent tooth growing underneath.
- **Permanent teeth**: These must be reinserted as soon as possible.

If you can, place the permanent tooth back in its socket right away. Do not touch the root. Gently rinse the tooth under cold water for 10 seconds. Do not scrub it. Scrubbing can damage the tissue on the root that helps the tooth reattach.

If you cannot put the tooth back in, wrap it in a clean, damp paper towel. Or, place it in a glass of milk. Milk helps keep the tooth alive during transport. If you are awake and not at risk of choking, you can hold the tooth in your mouth (between your cheek and gum) while going to the dentist.

If you cannot find the tooth, it may have gone into your lungs (aspirated) or been swallowed. A chest X-ray can check for a tooth in the lungs. But if the tooth was swallowed, it is not dangerous. Doctors usually do not do X-rays to look for a swallowed tooth.

People who get a tooth reinserted often take antibiotics for several days. If the tooth touched dirt, your doctor will check your tetanus shot. You may need a booster if your tetanus shot is not up to date.

If a permanent tooth is reinserted within 30 minutes to one hour, it has a good chance of staying in place. The longer the tooth is out of the socket, the lower the chance of success. The dentist will usually hold the tooth in place with a splint for 7 to 10 days. If the bone around the tooth is also broken, the splint may stay on for 6 to 10 weeks. Reinserted teeth will likely need root canal treatment later.

### Did You Know?

A container of milk can help keep a knocked-out tooth alive while you take it to the dentist.

# Scurvy

Scurvy happens when you do not get enough vitamin C in your food.  
Vitamin C comes mainly from fruits and vegetables.

## What are the signs of scurvy?

You may feel very tired and weak all the time.  
You might feel irritable or sad all the time.  
You could have pain in your joints, muscles, or legs.  
Your gums may swell and bleed.  
In severe cases, your teeth may fall out.  
You may notice red or blue spots on your skin, especially on your legs and feet.  
Your skin may bruise easily.

## When to see a doctor

See your doctor if you or your child are at risk of scurvy and have:

- Constant tiredness and weakness  
- Feeling irritable or sad all the time  
- Pain in joints, muscles, or legs  
- Wounds that keep opening or do not heal well  

## When to get urgent help

Call your doctor right away or use NHS 111 if you or your child are at risk of scurvy and have:

- Skin that bruises very easily  
- Swollen or bleeding gums  
- Swelling in your joints or legs  
- A high temperature (fever), or feel hot and shivery  
- Yellow skin or the white part of your eyes turning yellow (this is called jaundice – it may be harder to see on brown or black skin)

You can call 111 or get help online at [nhs.uk](https://www.nhs.uk)

## When to go to A&E (Accident and Emergency)

Go to A&E or call 999 if you or your child have:

- A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it  
- A sudden, severe headache – even if it has improved a little  
- A stiff neck  
- Trouble with light – it hurts to look at bright lights  
- Blurred or double vision  
- Stroke-like symptoms – such as slurred speech or weakness on one side of the body  
- Losing consciousness or having uncontrollable shaking (convulsions)  
- Severe chest pain or trouble breathing  
- Confusion or extreme drowsiness  

If your child is affected, they may seem limp or floppy.  
They may not respond normally.  
Their head might fall to the side, back, or forward.  
They may struggle to lift their head or look at your face.

[Find your nearest A&E](https://www.nhs.uk)

## Important safety tips for A&E

Do not drive to A&E.  
Ask someone to drive you.  
Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
Bring all your medicines with you.

## What causes scurvy?

Scurvy happens when you do not eat enough vitamin C for a long time.  
Vitamin C is found in fruits and vegetables.

Most people who eat poorly from time to time are not at risk of scurvy.

But you may be at higher risk if you:

- Have not eaten fresh fruit or vegetables for a while  
- Eat very little food – this can happen if you are sick all the time (for example, during chemotherapy) or have an eating disorder like anorexia  
- Smoke – smoking lowers how much vitamin C your body can use  
- Have a long-term problem with drugs or alcohol that affects your eating habits  
- Have a poor diet while pregnant or breastfeeding – your body needs more vitamin C during these times  

Babies, children, and older adults who struggle to eat a healthy diet are also more at risk.

## How is scurvy treated?

It is important to treat scurvy quickly.  
Without treatment, it can lead to serious health problems and can be life-threatening.

Mild scurvy can often be fixed by eating more vitamin C-rich foods like fresh fruit and vegetables.

Your doctor may also suggest taking vitamin C tablets (also called ascorbic acid) until you feel better.

Most people start to feel better within a few days.  
With treatment, most people make a full recovery.

Your doctor may refer you to a specialist if needed.  
This depends on what is causing your scurvy.

# Fungal Nail Infection (Onychomycosis)

This condition is a fungal infection of the nail or the skin under the nail.  
It can affect the nail itself, the area under the nail, or both.  
The nails often become thick, change color, and look odd.  
The most common colors are white or yellow.  

## Who Gets It?

About 1 in 10 people have this condition.  
It is more common in older adults.  
Men are more likely to get it than women.  
It is much more common in toenails than fingernails.  
Toenails are about 10 times more likely to be infected.  

## What Causes It?

Most cases are caused by a type of fungus called dermatophytes.  
The most common fungus is *Trichophyton rubrum*.  
This type of infection is also called tinea unguium.  
Some cases are caused by other types of molds.  
These include *Aspergillus*, *Scopulariopsis*, and *Fusarium*.  
In people with weak immune systems, the infection may be caused by yeast.  
This is called candidal onychomycosis.  
It usually affects the fingernails.  

## Risk Factors

You are more likely to get this infection if you:  
- Have athlete’s foot (tinea pedis)  
- Have a history of nail problems (like from psoriasis)  
- Are older  
- Are a man  
- Live with someone who has athlete’s foot or fungal nail infection  
- Use public showers or pools often  
- Have poor blood flow in your legs or feet  
- Have diabetes  
- Have a weak immune system  

## How It Looks

There are three main patterns:  

**Distal subungual:**  
The nail gets thick and yellow.  
Debris builds up under the nail.  
The nail may start to pull away from the skin.  

**Proximal subungual:**  
The infection starts near the cuticle.  
This type is often a sign of a weak immune system.  

**White superficial:**  
White, chalky patches spread under the surface of the nail.  
The nail stays thin at first.  

## How It Is Diagnosed

Your doctor will look at your nails.  
They may take a sample from under the nail.  
They will check it under a microscope using a special solution.  
They may grow the fungus in a lab (culture).  
They may use a test called PCR to find the fungus.  
They may also examine a nail clipping under a microscope after special staining.  

If you have athlete’s foot, your doctor may suspect fungal nail infection.  
Certain signs make the diagnosis more likely:  
- The third or fifth toenail is affected  
- The first and fifth toenails on the same foot are affected  
- Only one nail is affected  

If you keep getting athlete’s foot, you may have a hidden fungal nail infection.  

It is important to tell the difference between fungal infection and other nail problems like psoriasis or lichen planus.  
The treatments are different.  
So, your doctor will usually confirm the diagnosis with a test.  

To get a good sample for testing:  
- Take scrapings from the front part of the nail that is still attached  
- Use a small tool to reach deeper under the nail  
- Avoid taking debris from the very tip of the nail, as it often does not contain live fungus  

## When to Treat

Not all cases need treatment.  
Many people have mild or no symptoms.  
Some people do not have any problems from the infection.  
The strongest medicines can cause liver damage or interact with other drugs.  

You may want treatment if:  
- You have had a skin infection in the leg (cellulitis) before  
- You have diabetes or poor blood flow in your legs  
- The infection causes pain or discomfort  
- You feel self-conscious about the look of your nails  
- You want your nails to look better (this is debated)  

## Treatment Options

### Oral Medicines (Taken by Mouth)

The most effective treatments are:  
- Terbinafine: 250 milligrams once a day for 12 weeks (6 weeks for fingernails)  
- Or, take terbinafine for one week each month until the nail is clear  
- Itraconazole: 200 milligrams twice a day for one week each month for 3 months  

Terbinafine works better than itraconazole.  
It clears the infection in 75 to 80 out of 100 people.  
Itraconazole clears it in 40 to 50 out of 100 people.  
But the infection can come back in up to half of people.  

You do not need to wait until the nail looks completely normal.  
The medicine stays in the nail even after you stop taking it.  
This helps prevent the fungus from coming back.  
But the old nail will not get better.  
Only the new nail that grows will look normal.  

Fluconazole is another option, but it is less effective.  

### Topical Treatments (Applied to the Nail)

Newer creams and nail polishes can get through the nail.  
They are better than older ones.  
Examples include:  
- Efinaconazole  
- Tavaborole  
- Ciclopirox 8%  
- Amorolfine  

These are used for mild cases.  
They can also help when used with oral medicine.  
They are especially useful if the infection is hard to treat.  

A nail polish with efinaconazole 10%, ciclopirox 8%, or amorolfine 5% can work in some cases.  
It is not available in the United States.  
It can cure about 3 out of 10 people when used alone.  
It helps improve results when used with oral medicine.  

### New and Experimental Treatments

Researchers are testing new ways to deliver terbinafine.  
These may improve how well the medicine works.  

## How to Prevent It from Coming Back

To reduce the chance of the infection returning:  
- Cut your nails short  
- Dry your feet well after bathing  
- Wear socks that absorb sweat  
- Use antifungal foot powder  
- Do not wear old shoes that may still have fungus  
- Throw away old shoes if possible  

## Key Points

- Fungal nail infection is common, especially in older men and people with poor blood flow, diabetes, or nail problems.  
- Look for thick, yellow, or white nails.  
- Confirm the diagnosis with a test.  
- Treatment is only needed if the infection causes problems or symptoms.  
- Terbinafine is the most effective medicine.  
- Prevent relapse by keeping feet dry, cutting nails short, and throwing away old shoes.

# What Is Gastritis and Peptic Ulcer Disease?

Gastritis and peptic ulcer disease affect the inner lining of the stomach or the first part of the small intestine, called the duodenum.

These conditions happen when the lining gets damaged.

## What Causes the Damage?

The stomach can be damaged by:

- Stomach acid (a strong liquid that helps break down food)
- Digestive enzymes (substances that help digest food)
- A bacterial infection called *Helicobacter pylori*
- Some medicines, like aspirin and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)

Smoking increases your risk of getting ulcers. It also makes ulcers harder to heal. The more cigarettes you smoke each day, the higher your risk.

In rare cases, a tumor in the duodenum or pancreas can cause too much stomach acid. This tumor releases a hormone called gastrin. This leads to more acid in the stomach and can cause ulcers.

## How Does the Stomach Protect Itself?

The inside of the stomach has natural defenses:

- Special cells make mucus. This mucus forms a thick layer over the stomach lining.
- The mucus protects the stomach from acid and digestive enzymes.
- These cells also make bicarbonate. This helps reduce the acid’s strength.

When these defenses fail, the stomach lining can get damaged. This can happen if you have a *Helicobacter pylori* infection or take aspirin or NSAIDs.

## How Are These Conditions Treated?

There are many treatments available. They help reduce stomach acid and heal the lining.  
For more details, see: *Medications for the Treatment of Stomach Acid*

# Cough

Most coughs come from a cold or the flu.  
Other causes include smoking, heartburn, allergies, and infections like bronchitis or COVID-19.  
Sometimes, mucus from the back of your nose drips down your throat and causes a cough.  
A cough is very rarely a sign of something serious, like lung cancer.

## When to see a doctor

See your doctor if:
- Your cough lasts more than three weeks.
- You are losing weight without trying.
- You have a weak immune system. This can happen if you are having chemotherapy or have diabetes.

Call your doctor right away or get help from NHS 111 if:
- Your cough is very bad or gets worse fast. For example, you are coughing hard and cannot stop.
- You feel very unwell.
- You have chest pain.
- The side of your neck is swollen and hurts (swollen glands).
- You have trouble breathing.
- You are coughing up blood.

You can call 111 or get help online at [111.nhs.uk](https://www.111.nhs.uk).

## How to treat a cough at home

You usually do not need to see a doctor for a cough.  
You can help yourself by:
- Getting plenty of rest.
- Drinking lots of fluids.
- Staying at home and avoiding others if you have a fever or feel too unwell to do your normal activities.

You can also try:
- Paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain.
- A drink made with hot lemon and honey. (Do not give this to babies under 1 year old.)
- A herbal remedy called pelargonium. (Only for people aged 12 or older.)

There is not much proof that these help. Hot lemon and honey work about the same as cough medicines.

### How to make a hot lemon and honey drink

1. Squeeze half a lemon into a mug of hot water.
2. Add 1 to 2 teaspoons of honey.
3. Drink it while it is still warm. (Do not give hot drinks to young children.)

## Important notes

Some medicines and herbal products are not safe for everyone.  
For example, some are not safe during pregnancy.  
Always read the leaflet or ask a pharmacist before taking any medicine.  

## What a pharmacist can help with

If you have a cough, you can ask a pharmacist about:
- Cough syrup.
- Cough medicine. (Some of these should not be given to children under 12.)
- Cough sweets.

These will not stop your cough completely.  
But they may help you cough less.  

Decongestants and cough medicines that contain codeine will not stop your cough.

# Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE)

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, is a brain disease that gets worse over time. It can happen after repeated head injuries or exposure to blast waves.

This condition was first seen in boxers in the 1920s. Today, we know it can affect retired professional or college athletes, especially those who played American football or ice hockey. It can also affect soldiers who had brain injuries from explosions.

We do not yet know why only some people with repeated head injuries develop CTE. We also do not know how many head injuries or how severe they must be to cause CTE. One study found that about 3.7 out of every 100 professional football players in the United States may have CTE.

In the brain, CTE causes a certain protein to build up in abnormal ways. This protein forms clumps in areas near blood vessels, in the folds of the brain, and under the surface of the brain.

## Symptoms of CTE

The first signs of CTE often include at least one of the following:

- Feeling sad, hopeless, or easily upset  
- Acting without thinking, getting angry quickly, or being aggressive  
- Trouble remembering things, making decisions, or thinking clearly  
- Problems with movement, such as slow or shaky movements, unsteady walking, or slurred speech

There are two main patterns of how symptoms appear:

1. Mood and behavior problems start in young adulthood, such as in a person’s 30s. Memory and thinking problems come later.
2. Memory and thinking problems start later in life, such as in a person’s 60s. Mood and behavior changes may happen after the thinking problems begin.

## How CTE Is Diagnosed

Doctors look at a person’s history and symptoms to consider a diagnosis of CTE. The main clues are:

- A history of head injuries  
- Symptoms that match what is seen in CTE  
- No other clear cause for the symptoms

These same rules are used in research studies.

Standard brain scans like CT or MRI usually look normal in people with CTE. There is currently no reliable test to confirm CTE while a person is alive.

The only way to be sure someone has CTE is to examine the brain after death, during an autopsy.

## Treatment for CTE

There is no cure for CTE. Treatment focuses on helping the person live as well as possible.

If dementia develops, support measures can help. These include:

- Keeping the living space bright, cheerful, and familiar  
- Placing large clocks and calendars in the room to help with time awareness  
- Using safety systems, such as alarms or monitoring devices, if the person wanders

## How to Prevent CTE

The best way to prevent CTE is to avoid repeated head injuries.

If someone has had a concussion, they should rest and slowly return to sports. People who have had multiple concussions should be told about the risks of continuing to play contact sports.

# Jaundice in Adults

Jaundice means your skin and the whites of your eyes look yellow.  
This happens when there is too much bilirubin in your blood.  
Bilirubin is a yellow substance made when your body breaks down old red blood cells.  

## What Causes Jaundice?

Your liver helps remove bilirubin from your blood.  
It sends bilirubin into a fluid called bile.  
Bile flows through tubes called bile ducts into your intestines.  
Most bilirubin leaves your body in your stool.  
A small amount leaves in your urine.  

If your liver or bile ducts are not working well, bilirubin builds up in your blood.  
This causes the yellow color in your skin and eyes.  

Many people with jaundice also have dark urine and pale or light-colored stool.  
This happens when bilirubin cannot leave the body through the stool.  
So more bilirubin goes into the urine.  

High bilirubin levels can cause itching all over the body.  
But jaundice itself usually does not cause other symptoms in adults.  
In newborns, very high bilirubin levels can cause brain damage.  

## Serious Problems from Liver Disease

If your liver is seriously damaged, you may have other symptoms.  
These include:  
- Nausea  
- Vomiting  
- Belly pain  
- Small red lines like spider webs on the skin (called spider angiomas)  

Men may notice:  
- Enlarged breasts  
- Smaller testicles  

Liver disease can also cause:  
- **Ascites**: Fluid builds up in the belly  
- **Coagulopathy**: You may bleed or bruise easily  
- **Hepatic encephalopathy**: Brain function gets worse because toxins build up in the blood  
- **Portal hypertension**: High pressure in the veins going to the liver  
  - This can cause bleeding in the esophagus or stomach  

## Not All Yellow Skin Is Jaundice

Eating a lot of foods high in beta-carotene can make your skin look yellow.  
These foods include carrots, squash, and some melons.  
But your eyes do not turn yellow.  
This is not jaundice.  
It is called carotenemia.  
It is not linked to liver problems.  

> **Did You Know?**  
> Eating too many carrots can make your skin look yellow, but this is not jaundice.

## Common Causes of Jaundice

Jaundice in adults can be caused by many things.  
Most causes involve:  
- Liver damage  
- Blockage in the bile ducts  
- Too many red blood cells breaking down  

### Most Common Causes

- **Hepatitis**: Inflammation of the liver  
  - Often caused by a virus  
  - Can also be caused by autoimmune problems or certain drugs  
  - Can be short-term or long-term  
  - Short-term viral hepatitis is a common cause of jaundice in healthy young adults  

- **Alcohol-related liver disease**:  
  - Caused by drinking too much alcohol over many years  
  - Damage usually takes 8 to 10 years of heavy drinking  

- **Blocked bile duct**:  
  - Most often caused by a gallstone  
  - Can also be caused by cancer (like in the pancreas or bile ducts)  
  - Rare liver diseases like primary biliary cholangitis or primary sclerosing cholangitis  

- **Toxic reactions to drugs, medicines, or herbs**  
  - Some medicines can harm the liver  
  - Examples: amoxicillin/clavulanate, chlorpromazine, azathioprine, oral contraceptives  
  - Some herbal products like kava, green tea extract, or germander  
  - High doses of acetaminophen (Tylenol)  
  - Poison from certain mushrooms  

- **Hereditary conditions**  
  - Gilbert syndrome: Mild increase in bilirubin, but usually no symptoms  
  - Other rare conditions like Dubin-Johnson syndrome  

- **Too many red blood cells breaking down (hemolysis)**  
  - Can be caused by drugs, toxins, infections (like malaria), or inherited blood disorders  
  - Can also be due to enzyme problems like G6PD deficiency  

- **Wilson disease**:  
  - Copper builds up in the liver  
  - Causes tremors, trouble speaking, poor coordination, mood changes  
  - A ring around the eye (Kayser-Fleischer ring) may be visible  
  - Tests check copper levels in blood and urine  

- **Surgery complications**  
  - Scarring of bile ducts after surgery  
  - Poor blood flow to the liver after major surgery  

## How Doctors Diagnose Jaundice

Jaundice is easy to see.  
But finding the cause takes a doctor’s exam and tests.  

### Warning Signs – See a Doctor Right Away

- Severe belly pain  
- Drowsiness, confusion, or agitation  
- Blood in stool or black, tarry stool  
- Vomiting blood  
- Fever  
- Easy bruising or bleeding under the skin (tiny dots or larger spots)  

If you have any of these, see a doctor right away.  
If you have no warning signs, see a doctor within a few days.  

### What the Doctor Will Do

1. Ask about your symptoms and medical history  
2. Do a physical exam  

The doctor will ask:  
- When the yellow color started  
- When your urine became dark (this often happens before jaundice)  
- If you have itching, tiredness, changes in stool, or belly pain  
- If you have had liver problems before  
- If you have had surgery on the bile ducts  
- What medicines, alcohol, or herbal products you use  
- If anyone in your family has had liver problems  

The doctor will also ask about risk factors for hepatitis:  
- Working in day care  
- Living in a long-term care facility or prison  
- Traveling to areas where hepatitis is common  
- Having anal sex  
- Eating raw shellfish  
- Using injected drugs  
- Getting hemodialysis  
- Sharing razors or toothbrushes  
- Getting a tattoo or piercing  
- Working in health care without hepatitis vaccine  
- Having had a blood transfusion before 1992  
- Having sex with someone who has hepatitis  
- Being born between 1945 and 1965  

During the exam, the doctor will check for:  
- Fever  
- Low blood pressure  
- Fast heartbeat  
- Easy bruising  
- Skin rash  
- Changes in mental state  
- Swelling or lumps in the belly  

### Tests Doctors May Order

- **Blood tests**  
  - Check bilirubin levels  
  - Test how well your liver is working  
  - Check if your blood can clot  
  - Test for hepatitis viruses or autoimmune antibodies  
  - Check for anemia or infection  

- **Imaging tests**  
  - **Ultrasound**: First test to check for blockages in the bile ducts  
  - **CT scan**: Shows detailed images of the liver and bile ducts  
  - **MRI**: Gives clear pictures of the bile ducts  
  - **MRCP**: Special MRI that shows bile and pancreatic ducts clearly  
  - **ERCP**: A tube is passed through the mouth into the intestine. A dye is injected into the ducts, and x-rays are taken  

- **Liver biopsy**  
  - A small sample of liver tissue is taken  
  - Done if the cause is unclear or if certain diseases are suspected  

## Treatment of Jaundice

There is no treatment for jaundice itself in adults.  
The goal is to treat the cause.  

### If the Cause Is Known

- **Hepatitis**: Often gets better on its own.  
  - But it can become long-term.  
- **Blocked bile duct**: A procedure can open it.  
  - This is often done during ERCP.  
  - Tools are passed through a tube to remove a gallstone or open a blocked duct.  

### Itching

- Itching often goes away as the liver improves.  
- If it is bad, a medicine called cholestyramine can help.  
- But it does not work if the bile duct is completely blocked.  

## Special Considerations for Older Adults

In older adults, jaundice may not cause the same symptoms as in younger people.  
Symptoms may be mild or hard to notice.  

For example:  
- Older adults with hepatitis may have little belly pain.  
- Confusion may be mistaken for dementia.  
  - But it could be due to hepatic encephalopathy.  
  - This happens when the liver cannot remove toxins from the blood.  
  - These toxins reach the brain and affect thinking.  

In older adults, a blocked bile duct is more likely to be caused by cancer.  
Doctors suspect cancer if:  
- You have lost weight  
- You have only mild itching  
- You have no belly pain  
- You have a lump in your belly  

## Key Points

- Severe liver damage can lead to serious problems like brain issues and bleeding.  
- Acute viral hepatitis is a common cause of jaundice in young, healthy people.  
- See a doctor right away if you have jaundice.  
- Cholestyramine can help with itching.

# Restricted Growth (Dwarfism)

## What is restricted growth?

The main sign of restricted growth is being short.  
You might have other symptoms depending on the cause.

Restricted growth can happen for many reasons.  
Most often, it is due to genes passed down from your parents.  
It can also be caused by low levels of growth hormone.  
Poor nutrition can also play a role.

Doctors usually find out about restricted growth at birth or during childhood.  
They use tests to check for the cause.  
These tests may include blood tests, genetic tests, and X-rays.

Treatment can include growth hormone medicine.  
Surgery is sometimes needed, but it is rare.  
You may also need treatment for other health issues linked to your condition.

How restricted growth affects your life depends on the cause and your treatment.  
Some people grow taller with treatment.  
Others may need help with daily tasks.

### See a doctor if:

- Your child is not growing as fast as other children their age

---

## Support and help

If you or your child has restricted growth, doctors and nurses will help you.  
You may also find it helpful to talk to others who have the same condition.  
Parents of children with restricted growth can also offer support.

Here are some national charities that can help:

- **Little People UK** – Offers support, information, and social events for people with restricted growth.
- **Restricted Growth Association** – Provides information and resources for people with restricted growth.
- **Child Growth Foundation** – Runs a support line, gives information, and organizes events for families affected by growth conditions.

---

## Symptoms of restricted growth

The main symptom is being short.  
It is often defined as being less than 147 centimetres (4 feet 10 inches) tall as an adult.

There are two types:

- **Proportionate** – Your arms and legs are the right size compared to the rest of your body.
- **Disproportionate** – Some parts of your body grow differently. For example, your arms and legs may be shorter than normal.

Symptoms may be noticed at birth.  
Or they may show up later when a child is not growing as expected.

You or your child may also have other symptoms.  
These depend on what is causing the restricted growth.

---

## Causes of restricted growth

Most cases are due to genes from your parents.  
This can happen if your parents are short.  
It can also happen if you have a genetic condition.

Other causes include:

- Not having enough growth hormone
- Rare genetic conditions like Turner syndrome, Noonan syndrome, or Prader-Willi syndrome
- Problems with bone development, such as achondroplasia

---

## How is restricted growth diagnosed?

Doctors often spot restricted growth at birth.  
Sometimes it is not noticed until a child is not growing as expected.

If your doctor suspects restricted growth, they may suggest:

- Blood tests
- Genetic tests
- X-rays

### Screening during pregnancy

If you or a family member has a known genetic condition, you may be offered screening tests during pregnancy.  
These tests can check if the baby might have restricted growth.

---

## Treatment for restricted growth

The main treatment is growth hormone medicine.  
Surgery to make arms or legs longer is possible but rare.  
You may also need treatment for other symptoms.

### Growth hormone

Growth hormone helps children grow taller.  
It works for many types of restricted growth.  
But it does not help with bone development problems like achondroplasia.

Types of growth hormone medicine include:

- **Somatropin** – A daily injection used for many causes of restricted growth.
- **Somatrogon or somapacitan** – A weekly injection. Only used if you lack growth hormone.

How well treatment works depends on the cause.  
Treatment usually continues until growth stops or your child reaches their target height.

### Treatment for bone development problems

If you have a condition like achondroplasia, treatment focuses on managing symptoms, not on making you taller.

You may need:

- Physiotherapy to help with movement and pain
- Orthodontics to fix teeth problems
- Treatment for ear infections or sleep apnoea
- Surgery to straighten legs or reduce pressure on the spine

---

## How restricted growth affects your life

How it affects your life depends on the cause, other symptoms, and treatment.

Some people grow to average or near-average height with treatment.  
Others stay much shorter than average.

Most people with restricted growth live a normal lifespan.  
But some conditions can affect how long you live.

### Daily life with restricted growth

If you are much shorter than most people, you may need changes to help with:

- Doing tasks at home
- Moving around and driving
- Going to school or work
- Finding clothes that fit
- Joining in sports and other activities

Depending on your needs, you may qualify for disability benefits.  
These can help cover the cost of adaptations and support.

# Cryptosporidiosis

Cryptosporidiosis is an infection caused by a tiny parasite called *Cryptosporidium*.  
You can get it by putting something in your mouth that has been touched by infected feces.  
The main symptom is watery diarrhea.  
You may also have stomach cramps, nausea, or feel weak.  
Most healthy people get better on their own in a few weeks.  
But for people with HIV, especially those with advanced disease, the illness can last a long time and be very serious.  

## How the Infection Works

The *Cryptosporidium* parasite lives inside the cells of the small intestine.  
You get infected by swallowing the parasite in the form of oocysts.  
These oocysts are tiny, tough shells that protect the parasite.  
Once inside your body, the oocysts break open and release the parasite.  
The parasite then moves into the lining of your intestines and starts to grow and multiply.  
It makes new oocysts.  
Some oocysts are thick-walled and can survive in the environment.  
These are the ones that can spread the infection.  
Other oocysts are thin-walled and can cause a new infection inside your own body.  
The thick-walled oocysts are passed in your stool.  
They can infect others if they get into your mouth.  
You only need a very small number of oocysts—fewer than 100—to become sick.  
The oocysts are very hardy.  
They can survive in chlorinated water, like in swimming pools and public water supplies.  
This makes it easy for the infection to spread.  

## Who Gets It and How

*Cryptosporidium* can infect many animals.  
The most common types that cause illness in people are *C. parvum* and *C. hominis*.  
Other types can also infect people, but less often.  
You can get infected by:  
- Drinking or eating food or water that has been contaminated with feces  
- Swimming in pools, hot tubs, lakes, or rivers that are dirty  
- Touching something that has been touched by an infected person or animal  
- Being around animals like cattle, especially young ones  
- Traveling to places with poor sanitation  

The infection is common in parts of Africa and southern Asia.  
In the United States, about 823,000 people get cryptosporidiosis each year.  
About 10% of these cases are linked to travel.  
From 2009 to 2017, there were 444 outbreaks in 40 states and Puerto Rico.  
The number of outbreaks has been rising each year.  
This may be because doctors are using better tests to find the parasite.  
The most common causes of outbreaks are:  
- Swallowing water in pools or water playgrounds  
- Being around infected cattle  
- Close contact with infected people in child care centers  

In 1993, over 400,000 people in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, got sick from contaminated city water.  
The water system failed during heavy rain.  

People at higher risk include:  
- Children  
- Travelers to developing countries  
- People with weak immune systems  
- Health care workers who care for sick people  

Outbreaks often happen in day care centers.  
The parasite is hard to kill.  
It spreads easily in places where young children wear diapers.  

In people with HIV, especially those not on treatment, the diarrhea can last for months or years.  

## What the Illness Feels Like

The time from infection to symptoms is about one week.  
Up to 80% of infected people will get sick.  
Symptoms start suddenly.  
You will have watery diarrhea and stomach cramps.  
You may also feel nauseous, lose your appetite, have a fever, or feel tired.  
Most people get better in 2 to 3 weeks.  
But some may stay sick for a month or longer.  
Even after your symptoms go away, you may still pass the parasite in your stool for weeks.  
Some children in poor areas carry the parasite without showing any symptoms.  
This can lead to poor growth and malnutrition.  

In people with weak immune systems, the illness may start more slowly.  
But the diarrhea can be much worse.  
Without treatment, the infection can last a lifetime.  
Some people with HIV lose more than 5 to 10 liters of fluid a day through diarrhea.  
The intestines are the most common place the parasite lives.  
But it can also spread to the liver, pancreas, or lungs.  

## How It Is Diagnosed

Doctors test your stool to find the parasite.  
The best test is a special lab test that looks for a protein from the parasite in your stool.  
This test is more accurate than looking at the stool under a microscope.  
Looking at stool under a microscope can find the parasite, but it is not always reliable.  
The parasite is hard to see.  
Special staining or special microscopes are needed.  
You may need to give more than one stool sample because the parasite does not show up every time.  
Some labs use a test that looks for the parasite’s DNA.  
This test can also tell which type of parasite you have.  
A small sample of intestine tissue can show the parasite, but this is not common.  
Blood tests are not useful for diagnosing an active infection.  
They are mainly used for tracking outbreaks.  

## How It Is Treated

For healthy people, the infection usually gets better on its own.  
If symptoms last a long time, a medicine called nitazoxanide can help.  
This medicine is taken by mouth.  
It can shorten the illness.  

For people with HIV, the most important treatment is antiretroviral therapy (ART).  
This medicine helps your immune system get stronger.  
When your immune system improves, the diarrhea often gets better.  
Nitazoxanide may help reduce symptoms in people with HIV.  
But it does not always cure the infection, especially in people with very weak immune systems.  

For people with severe illness and weak immune systems, doctors may try other medicines.  
One is called paromomycin.  
It can be used alone or with nitazoxanide.  
These medicines may help reduce diarrhea and improve how well your body absorbs food and medicine.  
Severe cases may need fluids given through a vein.  
Nutrition support may also be needed.  

## How to Prevent It

You can prevent cryptosporidiosis by taking simple steps:  
- Make sure public water is treated properly  
- Wash your hands well after using the toilet or changing diapers  
- Wash your hands after touching animals or their waste  
- Wash your hands before eating or preparing food  
- Do not swallow water when swimming in lakes, rivers, pools, or hot tubs  
- Use safe sex practices  
- Be extra careful when traveling to places with poor sanitation  

If you are traveling, follow food and water safety rules.  
Boil water for 1 minute (3 minutes at high altitudes) to kill the parasite.  
Only water filters with a pore size of 1 micron or smaller can remove the parasite.  
Look for filters labeled “absolute 1 micron” or certified under NSF/ANSI standards 53 or 58.  
Alcohol-based hand sanitizers do not work against this parasite.  
Wash your hands with soap and water instead.  

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has detailed advice for the general public and for people with weak immune systems.  

Stool from infected people is very contagious.  
Use strict hygiene when caring for someone with the illness.  
Follow special safety rules when handling stool samples in labs.  

## Key Points

- The parasite spreads easily.  
  - It can be passed in stool for weeks after symptoms go away.  
  - You only need a few oocysts to get sick.  
  - The oocysts are hard to remove with normal water filters.  
  - They survive in chlorine.  

- Watery diarrhea is common.  
  - It usually gets better on its own in healthy people.  
  - But in people with advanced HIV, it can last a long time and be life-threatening.  

- Diagnosis is best done with a stool test for parasite protein.  
  - Microscopic tests are less reliable and need special tools.  

- For healthy people:  
  - Use nitazoxanide if symptoms last.  

- For people with HIV:  
  - Start antiretroviral therapy (ART).  
  - This helps the immune system and often improves symptoms.  

- Nitazoxanide can help with symptoms in people with HIV.  
  - But it does not always cure the infection, especially in those with very weak immune systems.  

## More Information

The following resources may help:  
- U.S. Department of Health and Human Services: Guidelines for treating HIV in children  
- Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC): Cryptosporidium Prevention & Control  
- CDC: Cryptosporidium Prevention & Control – For people with weak immune systems  
- CDC: Yellow Book – Cryptosporidiosis  
- CDC: Yellow Book – Food & Water Precautions  
- European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control: Cryptosporidiosis
