# Laryngitis

Laryngitis means your voice box is inflamed.  
The voice box is the part of your throat that helps you make sounds.

## What Causes Laryngitis?

Most often, a virus causes laryngitis.  
A bacterial infection is a rare cause.  
The most common virus is the one that causes the common cold.  
Laryngitis can also happen with bronchitis or other infections in the upper airways.

Other causes include:  
- Using your voice too much  
- Allergies  
- Breathing in certain medicines  
- Cigarette smoke or other irritants  

Long-term laryngitis (lasting more than 3 weeks) can be caused by:  
- Acid reflux from the stomach  
- Lingering bronchitis  
- Frequent vomiting, as in bulimia  

## What Are the Symptoms?

Your voice may become hoarse.  
You might lose your voice completely.  
These changes can happen within hours or a day.  

Your throat may feel raw or tickly.  
You may keep wanting to clear your throat.  

In more serious cases, you might also have:  
- A fever  
- Feeling unwell  
- Trouble swallowing  
- A sore throat  

Symptoms depend on how bad the inflammation is.

## How Is Laryngitis Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms.  
They will listen to your voice.  

For long-term laryngitis, your doctor may look down your throat.  
They may use a small mirror or a thin, flexible tube to see the voice box.  
This can show redness or swelling in the throat lining.  

If hoarseness lasts more than a few weeks, your doctor may check for throat cancer.  
If they see a thin layer of dead tissue, they may suspect diphtheria.

## How Is Laryngitis Treated?

Rest your voice. Do not speak.  
Avoid whispering. It can make things worse.  
Drink plenty of fluids.  
Use steam to soothe your throat.  
Take cough suppressants if needed.  

If you smoke, stop. Smoking makes laryngitis worse.  
If you have bronchitis, treat that too.  

Antibiotics are only used if a bacteria causes the infection.  
They do not help if a virus is the cause.  

If acid reflux is the problem, treatment can help.  
If a medicine is causing the issue, your doctor may change it.

# Tick-Borne Encephalitis (TBE)

Tick-borne encephalitis is a rare illness. It spreads through tick bites. It can also spread through raw (unpasteurised) milk or dairy products.

In the UK, this illness is very rare. But it is more common in parts of Europe, Russia, China, and Japan.

You can lower your risk by avoiding tick bites. You can also get a vaccine if you are going to a high-risk area.

## Symptoms of TBE

Most people do not feel sick after a tick bite. But some people get flu-like symptoms about a week later. These include:

- A high temperature  
- Feeling very tired  
- Headache  
- Body aches  
- Feeling sick  

These symptoms usually go away on their own. But in a few people, the virus spreads to the brain. This can cause more serious symptoms a few days or weeks later.

Serious symptoms include:

- A stiff neck and a severe headache  
- Pain when looking at bright lights  
- A fit (seizure)  
- Confusion, strange behaviour, or slurred speech  
- Weakness or loss of movement in part of the body  
- Face drooping on one side  

## When to Seek Help

### Call your GP or NHS 111 right away if:

You were bitten by a tick or visited a place with ticks in the past month. And you now have:

- Feeling hot and shivery  
- Headaches  
- Aching muscles  
- Feeling sick  

Or you have a circular rash. This could be a different tick-borne illness called Lyme disease.

You can call 111 or get help online at 111.

Tell the doctor or nurse if you think you were bitten by a tick.

### Call 999 or go to A&E if:

You or someone else has:

- A stiff neck and a severe headache  
- Pain when looking at bright lights  
- A fit (seizure)  
- Confusion, sudden changes in behaviour, or slurred speech  
- Weakness or loss of movement in part of the body  
- Face drooping on one side  

Find your nearest A&E.

### A&E Safety Tips

- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you. Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
- Bring all your medicines with you.

## Are You at Risk?

The risk of getting TBE is very low.

Ticks that carry the virus are found in:

- Most of Europe (including the UK)  
- Russia  
- Parts of China and Japan  

Ticks live in woodlands, grassy areas, parks, and gardens.

In the UK, only a very small number of ticks carry the virus. Even if you are bitten, the chance of getting seriously ill is very low.

TBE can also spread through raw (unpasteurised) milk or dairy products.

## How to Reduce Your Risk

### Avoid Tick Bites

To lower your risk when you are outside:

- Check your clothes and skin often for ticks. Brush them off before they bite. Wear light-coloured clothes so ticks are easier to see.  
- Stay on clear paths. Avoid brushing against plants.  
- Use insect repellent on your skin. You can also buy clothes treated with repellent.  
- Wear long trousers and long-sleeved tops. This makes it harder for ticks to bite you.  

Ticks can be very small. They grow bigger after they bite and feed on your blood.

### Remove a Tick That Bit You

If you find a tick on your skin, remove it as soon as possible.

To remove it safely:

1. Use fine-tipped tweezers or a tick removal tool. You can buy these at pharmacies, vets, or pet shops.  
2. Grasp the tick as close to your skin as you can. Pull it straight up slowly and firmly.  
3. Do not squeeze or crush the tick. This can make you sick.  
4. Throw the tick away. Clean the bite area with antiseptic or soap and water.  

The chance of getting sick after a tick bite is low. You do not need medical help unless you start to feel unwell.

### Important

Tick bites usually do not hurt. You may not notice one unless you see the tick on your skin.

Always check your skin and hair after being outside.

## TBE Vaccine

The TBE vaccine is recommended if you are visiting a country where the virus is common. This is especially important if you plan to spend time outdoors.

You need at least two injections. The second injection must be at least two weeks after the first. Get the first shot at least one month before your trip.

You must pay for the vaccine yourself. You can get it at travel health clinics or pharmacies that offer travel health services.

## Treatment for TBE

TBE can be life-threatening if it reaches the brain. If you are very ill, you will need hospital treatment.

Treatment may include:

- Medicine to fight the virus  
- Fluids given through a vein  
- A machine to help you breathe (ventilation)  
- Surgery to remove fluid from the brain (this is rare)  

There is no cure for TBE. Treatment focuses on helping your body recover.

# Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and Other Motor Neuron Diseases

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and other motor neuron diseases (MNDs) slowly damage the nerves that control movement.  
These diseases get worse over time.  
They affect the brain, spinal cord, or both.  
The damage leads to muscle weakness, shrinking, and twitching.  
Some people also have trouble speaking, swallowing, or breathing.  
Emotions may change suddenly and without reason.

Doctors diagnose these diseases by checking nerve function.  
They use tests like nerve conduction studies and electromyography.  
They also do MRI scans and blood tests.  
These help rule out other possible causes.  
There is no cure.  
Treatment focuses on helping people feel better and stay as independent as possible.

## What Is ALS?

ALS is the most common type of motor neuron disease.  
MNDs can affect nerves in the brain and spinal cord (central nervous system) and nerves in the rest of the body (peripheral nervous system).  
Most cases have no known cause.  
About 1 in 7 cases are due to a family history.  
These cases are linked to a change in a gene called SOD1.  
The name and symptoms depend on which part of the movement system is most affected.

**Myopathies** are different.  
They affect the muscles themselves, not the nerves.  
They cause similar symptoms but come from muscle problems.

## Types of Motor Neuron Diseases

There are two main types: upper motor neuron diseases and lower motor neuron diseases.  
Some diseases, like ALS, have features of both.

### Upper Motor Neuron Diseases

These affect nerves in the brain that send signals to the spinal cord.  
Symptoms include stiffness, awkward movements, and clumsiness.  
It often starts in the face, mouth, or throat.  
Then it spreads to the arms and legs.

### Lower Motor Neuron Diseases

These affect nerves in the spinal cord or brain stem that connect to muscles.  
They cause muscle weakness, shrinking, twitching, and cramps.  
The first signs often appear in one hand, foot, or tongue.

Some lower MNDs include:
- Spinal muscular atrophy
- Polio (a viral infection that attacks nerve cells in the spinal cord)
- Postpolio syndrome (a condition that appears years after polio)

## How Doctors Tell the Difference

Doctors look at physical signs to tell if the problem is in the upper or lower motor neurons.

| Feature | Upper Motor Neuron Problem | Lower Motor Neuron Problem |
|--------|----------------------------|----------------------------|
| Reflexes | Stronger than normal | Weak or missing |
| Muscle size | Normal at first | Shrinks over time |
| Twitching | Not present | Common |
| Muscle tone | Stiff | Loose or soft |

Doctors also check for myopathy (muscle disease).  
Here’s how they tell the difference:

| Feature | Lower Motor Neuron Problem | Myopathy (Muscle Disease) |
|--------|----------------------------|----------------------------|
| Weakness pattern | More in hands and feet than arms and legs | More in arms and legs than hands and feet |
| Twitching | May happen | Does not happen |
| Reflexes | Weak or missing | Usually normal |

## How Doctors Diagnose ALS and Other MNDs

Doctors look for:
- Slowly getting worse muscle weakness
- No numbness or tingling (no sensory problems)

Tests include:
- MRI scan of the brain and neck
- Nerve and muscle tests (electrodiagnostic tests)
- Blood tests to check for other treatable conditions

## How Doctors Treat ALS and Other MNDs

There is no cure.  
Treatment focuses on managing symptoms and improving quality of life.

### Medicines That May Help

- **Riluzole**: May help people live 2 to 3 months longer.
- **Edaravone**: May slow the loss of function.
- **Sodium phenylbutyrate/taurursodiol**: A combination medicine that may slow decline. It can be used with other medicines.
- **Tofersen**: For people with ALS caused by a specific gene change (SOD1 mutation).  
  It slows disease progress.  
  It must be given into the spinal fluid through a special injection.

### Medicines for Specific Symptoms

- **Spasticity (muscle stiffness)**: Baclofen
- **Muscle cramps**: Phenytoin
- **Excess saliva**: Strong anticholinergic medicines like glycopyrrolate, amitriptyline, benztropine, trihexyphenidyl, transdermal hyoscine, or atropine
- **Pseudobulbar affect (sudden emotional outbursts)**: Amitriptyline, fluvoxamine, or a mix of dextromethorphan and quinidine

### Surgery

For some people with swallowing problems, surgery may help a little.  
But results are limited.

## Key Points

- Think about motor neuron disease if someone has muscle weakness in many areas but no numbness or tingling.
- Suspect ALS if a person has both upper and lower motor neuron signs and weakness in the face.
- Do an MRI of the brain and nerve tests to rule out other causes.
- The main treatment is supportive care.  
  This includes a team of specialists to help with daily living and symptoms.
- Riluzole may help people live a little longer.  
  Edaravone may slow the worsening of symptoms.

# Diphtheria – Simple Explanation

Diphtheria is a serious infection that affects the throat and sometimes the skin. It is caused by a type of bacteria called *Corynebacterium diphtheriae*. This bacteria can spread easily from person to person.

Some types of this bacteria make a strong poison. This poison can harm the heart, kidneys, and nerves. The infection can be deadly if not treated quickly.

---

## How Diphtheria Spreads

- The bacteria spread through tiny droplets in the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes.
- It usually grows in the mouth or throat.
- It can also spread through direct contact with open sores on the skin of an infected person.

---

## Who Gets Diphtheria?

- Diphtheria is rare in countries where children are well vaccinated.
- In the United States, fewer than 5 cases happen each year.
- But the bacteria still exist in many parts of the world.
- Outbreaks can happen if people are not vaccinated or if booster shots are missed.

Diphtheria is more common in:
- Parts of Asia
- The South Pacific
- The Middle East
- Eastern Europe
- Venezuela, Haiti, and the Dominican Republic

Outbreaks have happened in Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar, South Africa, Sudan, Pakistan, and India since 2011.

---

## Types of Diphtheria

### 1. Respiratory Diphtheria (Affects the Throat)

This is the most serious form. It starts with:
- A sore throat
- Trouble swallowing
- Hoarseness
- Feeling unwell
- Low fever (100.4 to 102°F or 38 to 38.9°C)
- Fast heartbeat

Children may also have:
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Chills
- Headache

The neck may swell, making it look like a bull’s neck. This swelling can block the airway.

A thick, gray layer called a **pseudomembrane** forms in the throat. It is made of dead cells, bacteria, and other material. This layer can:
- Block the airway
- Make breathing very hard
- Cause a loud, gasping sound when breathing
- Break loose and block the airway completely

The poison from the bacteria can also:
- Paralyze nerves in the face, throat, arms, and legs
- Make it hard to swallow or move
- Paralyze the diaphragm (the main muscle for breathing)
- Cause breathing failure

The poison can also:
- Damage the heart muscle
- Cause fast or irregular heartbeats
- Lower blood pressure
- Lead to heart failure or death

Severe infection can also harm the kidneys.

### 2. Skin Diphtheria

This form affects only the skin. It is more common in adults with poor hygiene, such as people who are homeless.

It causes:
- Red, scraped areas on the skin
- Open sores that do not heal
- Sores that may be painful and ooze

These sores can look like eczema, psoriasis, or impetigo.

---

## Symptoms Summary

- Sore throat
- Fever
- Swollen neck glands
- Thick gray coating in the throat
- Trouble breathing
- Weakness or paralysis in arms, legs, or face
- Fast or irregular heartbeat
- Skin sores that do not heal

Symptoms usually start about 5 days after exposure.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Diphtheria

Doctors look for:
- A sore throat with a gray coating
- Swollen neck glands
- No vaccination history

They take a sample from the throat or skin and send it to a lab to grow the bacteria (called a culture).

If the heart is affected, doctors do an **electrocardiogram (ECG)** to check heart function.

To confirm the infection, they may test for the diphtheria poison.

---

## How Diphtheria Is Treated

### For Respiratory Diphtheria

- The person is admitted to the hospital, often in intensive care.
- They get an injection of **antitoxin** to stop the poison from causing more harm.
- They are given antibiotics like penicillin or erythromycin for 14 days.
- They must stay in isolation until two lab tests show no more bacteria.

### For Skin Diphtheria

- Doctors clean the sores with soap and water.
- People take antibiotics for 10 days.

---

## Recovery and Aftercare

- Recovery can take weeks or months.
- Even after feeling better, people must not return to normal activities too soon.
- If the heart was damaged, even light exercise can be dangerous.
- People who have had diphtheria must still get vaccinated. Infection does not protect you from getting it again.

---

## How to Prevent Diphtheria

- Vaccination is the best way to prevent diphtheria.
- Children should get the DTaP vaccine.
- Older children and adults should get the Tdap booster.
- Adults should get a Td booster every 10 years.

If you have been near someone with diphtheria:
- You will be tested.
- You will be given antibiotics for 7 days.
- If the test shows you have the bacteria, you will take antibiotics for 17 days total.
- This is true even if you are vaccinated. Vaccines do not always prevent infection.

---

## Key Facts

- About 5 to 10 out of 100 people with diphtheria die.
- The risk is higher if:
  - You wait too long to see a doctor
  - You are not vaccinated or only partly vaccinated
  - The infection affects the heart or kidneys

---

# Baker’s Cyst

A Baker’s cyst is a soft lump behind the knee.  
It can cause pain, tightness, stiffness, or trouble bending the knee.  
Symptoms often get worse after walking.

The lump may go away on its own.  
It may also improve when the cause is treated.  
Pain relief and physical therapy can help.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:
- You have a lump on your body and you do not know what it is.

Call 111 or get help online if you have:
- Sudden worsening pain or swelling in your leg
- Swelling, bruising, or warm skin on your leg
- Red or darkened skin on your leg (harder to see on brown or black skin)
- Swelling that changes in firmness — gets harder or softer

These could be signs of a burst cyst or a blood clot in the leg.  
This type of blood clot is called deep vein thrombosis, or DVT.

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have leg pain and swelling, **and**:
- Trouble breathing
- Chest pain

These could be signs of a blood clot in the lungs.  
This is called a pulmonary embolism.  
It can be life-threatening and needs emergency care.

> Find your nearest A&E

### A&E Safety Tips
- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you.  
- If you can’t get a ride, call 999 for an ambulance.  
- Bring your medicines with you.

---

## What a Baker’s Cyst Feels Like

The main sign is a soft lump behind the knee.  
The lump may be easier to see when you are standing.  
It may be the only symptom you notice.  
But you might also have:
- Pain in the knee or leg
- Tightness or stiffness in the knee
- Aching in the knee
- Trouble bending the knee
- A clicking sound in the knee

Your symptoms may get worse after walking.

---

## How a Baker’s Cyst Is Treated

Not all Baker’s cysts need treatment.  
In children, they often go away on their own.

If the cyst is caused by another condition, treating that condition usually helps.  
Other treatments may include:
- Painkillers
- A shot of medicine (hydrocortisone) into the knee
- Physical therapy
- Draining fluid from the cyst
- Surgery to fix knee damage — removing the cyst itself is rare

It can take a few months to a few years for the cyst to get better.

---

## What You Can Do at Home

You can do simple things to ease pain, swelling, and other symptoms.  
These steps also help if the cyst bursts.

If the cyst bursts, symptoms will be worse for a few weeks until the swelling goes down.

### Do These Things:
- Rest your knee as much as possible.
- Use an ice pack (or a bag of frozen vegetables) wrapped in a tea towel.  
  Apply it for about 10 minutes at a time.  
  Repeat every few hours if needed.
- Raise your leg on a pillow when sitting or lying down.
- Take ibuprofen or paracetamol to help with pain and swelling.

---

## What Causes a Baker’s Cyst

Sometimes there is no clear cause — especially in children.

In adults, it usually happens when another problem damages the knee joint.  
Common causes include:
- A knee injury
- Osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis
- Gout

Anyone can get a Baker’s cyst.  
But it is most common in people aged 35 to 70.

# Prostate Abscess

A prostate abscess is a pocket of pus that forms in the prostate gland.  
It usually happens as a complication of a bacterial infection in the prostate.  

The most common bacteria that cause this are gram-negative bacteria.  
Less often, the bacteria *Staphylococcus aureus* is responsible.  

Men who have had prostate cancer treated with radiation, including radiation seeds, may have a higher chance of developing an abscess.  
Newer diabetes medicines called SGLT2 inhibitors may also raise the risk of urinary and genital infections.  
This could increase the chance of a prostate abscess.  

## Symptoms of Prostate Abscess

You may have symptoms like those of a bladder infection.  
These include:  
- Needing to urinate often  
- Pain or burning when you urinate  
- Trouble passing urine  
- Pressure or pain in the area between the scrotum and anus  

Less common signs include:  
- Swelling or pain in the testicle  
- Blood in the urine  
- A thick, pus-like discharge from the urethra  
- Fever (this does not always happen)  

When a doctor checks your prostate with a finger inserted through the rectum, they may feel tenderness or a soft, fluid-filled area.  
But the prostate may also feel normal or just slightly larger.  

## Diagnosis of Prostate Abscess

Doctors suspect an abscess if you have ongoing pain in the perineal area and keep getting urinary infections even after antibiotic treatment.  
In this case, you will likely have a prostate ultrasound.  
Sometimes, a cystoscopy (a small camera inserted into the urethra) is also needed.  

Many abscesses are found by accident.  
They may show up on a CT scan done for another reason.  
They can also be seen during prostate surgery or other procedures.  
If the abscess bulges into the urethra or breaks open during a procedure, it becomes obvious.  

A urine test may show white blood cells or bacteria.  
But sometimes the test looks normal.  
Blood cultures may be positive in some cases.  

## Treatment of Prostate Abscess

Treatment has two main parts: antibiotics and drainage.  

Antibiotics are started right away, even before test results come back.  
A fluoroquinolone antibiotic like ciprofloxacin is often used.  
This medicine gets into the prostate tissue well.  

Drainage is also needed.  
The abscess can be drained in two ways:  
- Through the urethra (using a small tube)  
- Through the skin between the scrotum and anus (using a needle)  

Both methods help remove the pus.  
Treatment must include both antibiotics and drainage to be effective.

# Tonsillar Cellulitis and Tonsillar Abscess

This condition happens when bacteria infect the tissues around the tonsils.  
A tonsillar abscess is a pocket of pus that forms behind the tonsils.

## What Causes It?

Bacteria from a throat infection can spread deeper into nearby tissues.  
The most common bacteria are streptococci and staphylococci.  
When these bacteria grow too much, they can cause a pus-filled abscess.  
Abscesses can form near the tonsils (peritonsillar) or on the side of the throat (parapharyngeal).  
A peritonsillar abscess pushes into the throat.  
A parapharyngeal abscess can push into the neck.  
A parapharyngeal abscess is larger and more serious than a peritonsillar abscess.  
This condition is most common in teenagers and young adults.

## Symptoms

Swallowing causes sharp pain.  
The pain often spreads to the ear.  
You have a very sore throat.  
You feel sick and have a fever.  
You may tilt your head toward the side with the abscess to ease the pain.  
You may have trouble opening your mouth because the jaw muscles spasm.  
This is called trismus.  

Cellulitis causes redness and swelling above the tonsil and on the roof of the mouth.  

A peritonsillar abscess or some parapharyngeal abscesses push the tonsil forward.  
The uvula (the small soft piece at the back of the throat) swells and may move to the opposite side.  
You may speak as if you are holding a hot potato in your mouth.  
This is called a "hot potato" voice.  
You may drool more than usual.  
The tonsils look red.  
White patches may appear on the tonsils.  
Lymph nodes in the neck become swollen.  
You may have very bad breath.

## How It Is Diagnosed

A doctor checks your throat.  
They may use imaging tests like a CT scan or ultrasound.  
They may use a needle to check for pus.  

A peritonsillar abscess is often diagnosed if you have:  
- A very bad sore throat  
- Trouble opening your mouth  
- A "hot potato" voice  
- A uvula pushed to one side  

If a peritonsillar abscess is suspected, the doctor may use ultrasound to find it.  
They may use a needle to draw out pus.  
The pus is sent to a lab to grow bacteria and find the cause.  

If the doctor is unsure about a parapharyngeal abscess, they may use a CT scan or ultrasound to check.

## How It Is Treated

You will get fluids and antibiotics.  
Antibiotics like penicillin or clindamycin are given by mouth or through a vein.  
The antibiotic may be changed based on lab results.  
You will take antibiotics for 10 days.

If there is no abscess, the infection usually starts to improve within two days.  

If there is a peritonsillar abscess, the doctor must drain the pus.  
They numb the area with a spray or injection.  
Ultrasound may help guide the needle.  
Antibiotics are continued by mouth or through a vein.  
Most people can go home, but some need a short hospital stay to get IV antibiotics and to monitor breathing.

Peritonsillar abscesses often come back.  
To prevent this, the tonsils may be removed in a surgery called tonsillectomy.  
This is usually done 4 to 6 weeks after the infection clears.  
It may be done sooner if antibiotics do not work.  
Tonsillectomy may also be done right away in rare cases.  
This includes when a person is young and has had many throat infections.  
It may also be done if the person has obstructive sleep apnea.  

If a parapharyngeal abscess is present, surgery is usually needed to drain the pus.

# Typhus

Typhus is a disease spread by bites from infected lice, mites, or fleas.  
It is very rare in the UK.  

You can lower your risk by using insect repellent and keeping clean.  
Wash your body and your clothes often.  

## What to do if you think you have typhus

Symptoms can include:  
- A high temperature  
- A headache  
- A rash (this may be harder to see on black or brown skin)  
- Feeling sick or being sick  
- Feeling very unwell  

If you have these symptoms and:  
- You recently came back from a trip abroad  
- You are planning to travel abroad  

You should get medical advice right away.  

### If you are in England:  
- See your doctor (GP)  
- Call 111  
- Get help online at 111  

### If you are abroad:  
- Check your travel insurance for medical help  
- Look up health advice for your destination on GOV.UK  

Early diagnosis is important.  
If typhus is not treated quickly, it can be life-threatening.  

## How you get typhus

You can get typhus from a bite by lice, mites, or fleas that carry the disease.  
These bugs often live on small animals like mice, rats, cats, dogs, and squirrels.  
They can also be on your clothes, skin, or hair.  

Typhus is most common in parts of Africa, South America, and Asia.  
It is more likely in places where:  
- Cleanliness is poor  
- People live in crowded spaces  
- There are many bushes and grassy areas  

## How to reduce your risk when travelling

There is no vaccine for typhus.  
But you can protect yourself.  

### Do this:  
- Use insect repellent with DEET  
- Wear long-sleeved shirts and long trousers  
- Wash and shower regularly  
- Wash and change your clothes often  

### Do not do this:  
- Do not wear clothes or use bedding that might have body lice  

## Symptoms of typhus

You may have:  
- A high temperature  
- A headache  
- A rash (this may be hard to see on black or brown skin)  
- Feeling sick or being sick  
- Feeling very unwell  

## Treatment for typhus

If your doctor thinks you have typhus, they will likely do a blood test or take a small sample of skin.  

Antibiotics are used to treat typhus.  
You usually start taking them before your test results come back.  
This is because test results can take up to a week.  

Most people feel better within two days of starting treatment.  
Keep taking all your antibiotics, even if you feel better.  

Some people with severe symptoms may need to go to hospital.

# Flail Chest

A flail chest happens when three or more ribs in a row break in two or more places. This causes a section of the chest wall to become loose and move differently from the rest of the chest.

This loose section is called a flail segment. It moves the wrong way when you breathe. When you breathe in, it moves inward instead of outward. When you breathe out, it moves outward instead of inward. This is called paradoxical motion.

A flail chest is a sign that the lung underneath may also be injured.

## What Causes a Flail Chest?

- A strong force to the chest, like from a car crash or fall.
- One rib can break in more than one place.
- When three or more ribs in a row break in two or more places, the section between them becomes unstable.

## Why Is a Flail Chest Dangerous?

- The same strong force that breaks the ribs often bruises the lung. This is called a pulmonary contusion.
- The loose chest section makes breathing harder.
- Pain from the broken ribs makes it hard to take deep breaths.
- This can lead to poor oxygen levels and lung infections.

## How Is Flail Chest Diagnosed?

Doctors check your symptoms and do a physical exam.

- They look for the flail segment moving the wrong way when you breathe.
- If you are in pain or not fully awake, it may be hard to see the movement.
- If you are on a breathing machine, the flail segment will not move paradoxically. But doctors can still see it move more than normal when the lungs inflate.
- Doctors may feel the chest to check for a crackling sensation (crepitus) from broken bones.
- A chest X-ray can show broken ribs and lung bruising. It does not show damage to the cartilage.

## How Is Flail Chest Treated?

Treatment depends on how severe the injury is.

- **Oxygen**: You will get humidified oxygen to help your lungs work better.
- **Pain relief**: Medicines for pain can help you breathe more deeply and comfortably.
- **Breathing support**: If you cannot breathe well on your own, you may need a breathing machine (mechanical ventilation).
- **Fluid balance**: Doctors will carefully watch your fluid levels. Too little fluid can hurt the lungs. Too much fluid can cause swelling in the lungs.
- **Surgery**: In some cases, surgery to fix the broken ribs may help. This is considered if:
  - You cannot stop using the breathing machine.
  - The chest is badly deformed.
  - You are still struggling to breathe even with pain control.
  - You need surgery for another reason, like a chest injury.

Surgery may reduce the risk of pneumonia, shorten your hospital stay, reduce time on a breathing machine, and lower the chance of death.

# What You Need to Know About Ringworm (Tinea)

Ringworm is a common skin infection caused by a type of fungus. It is not caused by worms, even though the name suggests it. The infection gets its name from the ring-shaped rash it can cause.

## What Causes Ringworm?

- Ringworm is caused by fungi called dermatophytes.
- These fungi feed on keratin, a protein found in the outer layer of skin, hair, and nails.
- The fungi live on the skin, hair, or nails. When they grow too much, they cause an infection.
- The most common fungi that cause ringworm are *Epidermophyton*, *Microsporum*, and *Trichophyton*.
- These fungi can live on your body without causing problems. They only cause infection when your skin is weak or your immune system is not working well.
- Conditions like diabetes, cancer, or HIV can make you more likely to get ringworm.
- Ringworm does not spread to the inside of your body, like your blood or organs.

## Where Can Ringworm Happen?

Ringworm can appear on many parts of the body. The name changes depending on the location:

- **Feet**: Called athlete’s foot (tinea pedis)
- **Beard area**: Called beard ringworm (tinea barbae)
- **Body**: Called body ringworm (tinea corporis)
- **Groin**: Called jock itch (tinea cruris)
- **Scalp**: Called scalp ringworm (tinea capitis)

Sometimes, a ringworm infection in one place can cause a rash to appear in another place that is not infected. This is called a dermatophytid reaction.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on where the infection is.

- Most of the time, the rash looks like a red, scaly ring.
- The edges are raised and may be itchy.
- The center of the ring may look clear or slightly lighter.
- The rash can come and go over time.
- In some cases, the skin becomes very inflamed.
- You may see blisters or fluid-filled spots, especially on the feet.
- On the scalp, the area can swell, become painful, and sometimes leak pus. This is called a kerion.

## How Is Ringworm Diagnosed?

Your doctor will check your skin and ask about your symptoms.

- They may take a small sample of skin or nail.
- They will look at the sample under a microscope to see if fungus is present.
- For scalp or nail infections, they may send the sample to a lab to grow the fungus. This helps them find the exact type of fungus.
- Knowing the type of fungus helps the doctor pick the best treatment.

## How Is Ringworm Treated?

Treatment depends on where the infection is.

- Most cases are treated with antifungal medicine.
- The medicine can be applied directly to the skin (topical) or taken as a pill.
- You must use the medicine for the full time, even if the rash goes away.
- In some cases, your doctor may give you a medicine to reduce itching and swelling.
- These medicines are not the same as antibiotics. They are made to fight fungus, not bacteria.

## Important Notes

- Ringworm is not caused by worms.
- It spreads easily through direct contact with infected skin or objects like towels, shoes, or combs.
- Keep the skin clean and dry to help prevent infection.
- Avoid sharing personal items like towels, hats, or razors.

If you think you have ringworm, see a doctor. Early treatment helps stop it from spreading and makes it easier to cure.

# Parkinson's Disease

Parkinson's disease affects how you move. It causes shaking, slow movement, and stiff muscles.

There is no cure for Parkinson's disease. But treatments can help you manage your symptoms and stay active for longer.

---

## Symptoms of Parkinson's Disease

The main signs of Parkinson's disease are:

- Shaking in one or more parts of your body, especially when at rest  
- Moving more slowly than usual  
- Muscles that feel tight and hard to move  

You may also have other symptoms, such as:

- Feeling sad or low (depression)  
- Feeling worried or tense (anxiety)  
- Trouble keeping your balance (this can lead to falls)  
- Not being able to smell things as well as before  
- Trouble sleeping  
- Trouble remembering things  

These symptoms can vary from person to person.

---

## Treating Parkinson's Disease

Treatments can help you move better and feel more in control.

Options include:

- Physical therapy to improve movement and balance  
- Occupational therapy to help with daily tasks  
- Medicines to help control symptoms  
- In some cases, brain surgery to reduce shaking and stiffness  

In the early stages, you may not need treatment. Your symptoms might be mild and not interfere with daily life.

But you will still need regular checkups with your doctor. This helps track your condition and adjust treatment if needed.

---

## What Causes Parkinson's Disease?

Parkinson's disease happens when nerve cells in a part of the brain called the substantia nigra slowly die.

These nerve cells make a chemical called dopamine. Dopamine helps your brain control movement.

When dopamine levels drop, your body has trouble moving smoothly. This causes the main symptoms of Parkinson's disease.

Scientists do not yet know exactly why the nerve cells die. Most experts believe it is due to a mix of genes and environmental factors.

# What Is Cancer?

Cancer happens when cells in the body grow out of control.  

These cells do not act like normal cells.  

They do not mature into specialized types of cells.  

They can grow into nearby tissues and damage them.  

Cancer can also spread to other parts of the body. It travels through the blood or the lymph system. This spread is called metastasis.

## The Body’s Defense Against Cancer

Your immune system helps protect you from cancer.  

It can find and destroy early cancer cells or abnormal cells before they grow.  

This is called immune surveillance.  

People born with weak immune systems or those who lose immune function later in life have a higher risk of cancer.  

This is especially true for cancers linked to viruses. Examples include certain types of lymphoma and Kaposi sarcoma.

## Can Cancer Be Treated?

Many cancers can be cured, especially if found early.  

Even when cancer is found later, long-term remission is often possible.  

Some early cancers found through screening tests may not grow or cause harm during a person’s lifetime.  

But for most cancers, finding them early gives the best chance of a cure.

## When Cure Is Not Possible

If cancer cannot be cured, treatment can still help.  

Options include surgery, chemotherapy, immune therapy, and radiation therapy.  

These treatments can help you live longer and feel better.  

But some people do not tolerate these treatments well.  

This is more common in people who are already weak or have other serious health problems.  

For these people, palliative care may be the best choice.  

Palliative care focuses on comfort, quality of life, and support.

# What Is Cancer?

## What Happens in Cancer?

Cancer starts when one cell in your body changes in a bad way.  
That cell no longer follows the normal rules.  
It begins to grow and divide without stopping.  
It can invade nearby healthy tissues.  
It can travel to other parts of the body.  
It can also make new blood vessels to feed itself.  

Cancer can start in any part of the body.  
As the bad cells grow, they form a lump called a tumor.  
A tumor is just a mass of abnormal cells.  
Tumors can be cancerous or not cancerous.  

Cancer cells from the original site can spread to other areas.  
This spread is called metastasis.

---

## Types of Cancer

There are two main types of cancer:  
- Cancers of the blood and blood-making parts of the body  
- Solid tumors (a solid lump of cells)

### Blood Cancers: Leukemias and Lymphomas

**Leukemias** start in the bone marrow.  
The bone marrow makes blood cells.  
In leukemia, bad cells take over the bone marrow.  
They crowd out healthy blood cells.  
This can lead to anemia, infections, and bleeding.

**Lymphomas** start in the immune system.  
They cause large lumps in the lymph nodes.  
Lymph nodes are found in the armpits, groin, chest, and belly.  
The lumps can grow big and cause pain or pressure.

### Solid Tumors: Carcinomas and Sarcomas

**Carcinomas** start in cells that line the skin, lungs, gut, and organs inside the body.  
Examples include:  
- Skin cancer  
- Lung cancer  
- Colon cancer  
- Stomach cancer  
- Breast cancer  
- Prostate cancer  
- Thyroid cancer  

Carcinomas are more common in older adults.

**Sarcomas** start in cells that form muscles, bones, blood vessels, and connective tissue.  
Examples include:  
- Leiomyosarcoma – cancer of smooth muscle in the gut wall  
- Osteosarcoma – bone cancer  

Sarcomas are more common in younger people.

---

## Most Common Cancers in Men and Women

The most common cancers are listed from most frequent to least frequent.  
These numbers are based on estimates for 2024 from the American Cancer Society.

### For Men:
1. Prostate cancer  
2. Lung cancer  
3. Colorectal cancer  
4. Bladder cancer  
5. Melanoma (a type of skin cancer)  
6. Kidney cancer  

### For Women:
1. Breast cancer  
2. Lung cancer  
3. Colorectal cancer  
4. Uterine cancer  
5. Melanoma (a type of skin cancer)  
6. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma  

> **Note:** Skin cancer is likely the most common cancer in both men and women.  
> But only melanoma is tracked in official reports.  
> Other types of skin cancer are not always reported.  
> So, skin cancer numbers are incomplete.  
> For this reason, skin cancer is usually left out of the main lists.

---

## Key Cancer Terms Explained

Here are common words used when talking about cancer:

- **Aggressiveness:** How fast a tumor grows and spreads.  
- **Benign:** Not cancer. A benign tumor does not spread.  
  It may still cause problems if it presses on nearby organs.  
- **Carcinogen:** Something that can cause cancer.  
  Examples include tobacco, radiation, and some chemicals.  
- **Carcinoma-in-situ:** Cancer cells that are still in the place where they started.  
  They have not spread into nearby tissue or other parts of the body.  
- **Cure:** When all cancer is gone and will not come back.  
- **Differentiation:** How much the cancer cells look like normal cells.  
  Poorly differentiated cells look very strange and grow fast.  
- **Grade:** How abnormal cancer cells look under a microscope.  
  The more abnormal they look, the more aggressive the cancer.  
- **Invasion:** The ability of cancer to grow into and destroy nearby tissue.  
- **Malignant:** Cancerous. Malignant cells can invade nearby tissue and spread.  
- **Malignant transformation:** The process by which a normal cell becomes cancerous.  
- **Metastasis:** Cancer that has spread to a new part of the body.  
- **Neoplasm:** A general term for any tumor, whether cancerous or not.  
- **Recurrence (relapse):** Cancer returns after treatment.  
  It can come back in the same place or in a new spot.  
- **Remission:** No signs of cancer after treatment.  
  But some cancer cells may still be in the body.  
- **Stage:** How far the cancer has spread.  
  Stage 1 means it is small and local.  
  Stage 4 means it has spread to other organs.  
- **Survival rate:** The percent of people who are still alive after a certain time.  
  For example, the 5-year survival rate is how many people are alive 5 years after diagnosis.  
- **Tumor:** A lump or mass of abnormal cells.

---

## Did You Know?

In medical words, the ending **-oma** often means a tumor or growth.  
The first part of the word tells you what the growth is made of.  

For example:  
- **Meningioma** is a tumor in the covering of the brain or spinal cord.  
  (Meninges = the covering)  

Many cancer names end in **-oma**, but not all **-omas** are cancer.  
For example:  
- A **hematoma** is a swelling caused by blood trapped under the skin.  
  It is not cancer.  
  (Heme = blood)

# Heavy Periods

Heavy periods mean you lose a lot of blood during your period.  
They can also last longer than 7 days.

You may have heavy periods if:
- You need to change your pad or tampon every 1 to 2 hours.
- You need to use two types of period products at once, like a pad and a tampon.
- Your period lasts more than 7 days.
- You pass blood clots bigger than a 10p coin (about 2.5cm across).
- You bleed through your clothes or bedding.
- You avoid normal activities like exercise or miss work because of your period.
- You often feel tired or short of breath.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if:
- Heavy periods are making your life harder.
- You’ve had heavy periods for a long time.
- You have severe pain during your period.
- You bleed between periods or after sex.
- You have heavy periods and other symptoms, like pain when peeing, pooping, or having sex.

## Treatment for Heavy Periods

Heavy periods do not always need treatment.  
But treatment can help if they are affecting your daily life.

Your doctor may suggest:
- Some types of contraception, like an intrauterine system (a small device placed in the womb) or the combined contraceptive pill.
- Medicine to reduce bleeding, such as tranexamic acid.
- Prescription painkillers that reduce inflammation, like mefenamic acid or naproxen.

If these treatments do not help, or your doctor thinks another condition is causing your heavy periods, they may refer you for tests or to a specialist.

### Specialist Treatments

If needed, a specialist may suggest:
- Removing the lining of the womb (a procedure called endometrial ablation).
- Removing fibroids if they are causing heavy bleeding.
- Removing all or part of the womb (a surgery called hysterectomy).

You may also have blood tests to check for conditions like iron deficiency anaemia.

## Causes of Heavy Periods

It is normal for some people to have heavy periods.  
They can be heavier at certain times, such as:
- When you first start your periods.
- After giving birth.
- As you get close to menopause.

Heavy periods can also be caused by:
- Problems with the womb or ovaries, such as polycystic ovary syndrome, fibroids, endometriosis, adenomyosis, or pelvic inflammatory disease.
- Conditions that make you bleed more easily, like Von Willebrand disease.
- Some medicines, including anticoagulants (blood thinners) and chemotherapy drugs.

Rarely, heavy periods can be a sign of womb cancer.

# Broken Upper Arm Bone (Proximal Humeral Fracture)

This type of fracture happens near the top of the upper arm bone, just above the surgical neck.  
Most of these breaks are small and do not move far out of place.  
They are often caused by falling onto an outstretched hand.  
A direct hit to the shoulder can also cause this injury.

## Who Gets This Injury?

This fracture is very common in older adults.  
Some people may have nerve damage that causes numbness on the side of the shoulder.  
In rare cases, a blood vessel near the shoulder can be injured.  
If the arm is not moved for just a few days, it can become stiff and hard to move again.  
This is especially true for older people.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The shoulder and upper arm hurt and swell.  
You will have trouble lifting your arm.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use X-rays to see the break.  
Sometimes they use a CT scan if the X-rays are unclear or if the break is complex.

The X-rays should include:
- A front view with the arm turned inward
- An oblique view that shows the shoulder from the side
- A special view to check the shoulder joint

A CT scan is used if the break is complicated or not clearly seen on X-rays.

## How Is It Treated?

Most people are treated with a sling and early movement exercises.  
Some may need surgery to fix the bone or replace the shoulder joint.

### One-Piece Fractures (Only One Part of the Bone Is Broken)

These fractures rarely need realignment.  
About 65 to 80 percent are treated with a sling.  
Some people also use a swathe (a band that holds the arm close to the body).  
Early movement exercises are important to prevent stiffness.

#### Codman Exercises (for Early Movement)

- Bend forward at the waist.  
- Let the injured arm hang straight down.  
- Keep your knees slightly bent.  
- Relax your shoulder and arm.  

Do these movements slowly:
- Swing your arm side to side
- Swing it forward and backward
- Make small circles, both clockwise and counterclockwise

As you swing, shift your weight from one foot to the other in the same direction.  
Gradually increase how far you swing.  
These exercises should cause only mild discomfort.  
Do each movement twice per set.  
Do several sets each day.  
Slowly increase how long you do them.

These exercises help all ages, but are especially helpful for older adults.

### Two or More Broken Pieces

If more than one part of the bone is broken, the arm is immobilized.  
You will be referred to an orthopedic surgeon.  
Surgery may be needed to fix the bone with metal plates and screws.  
In some cases, a shoulder replacement may be needed.

## Key Points

- Doctors classify the fracture by how many parts of the upper arm bone are broken or bent.  
- Most fractures (almost 80 percent) only need a sling.  
- Start moving your shoulder as soon as possible, especially if you are older.  
- Early movement helps prevent stiffness and improves recovery.

# Submandibular Space Infection

This is a bacterial infection in the soft tissues under the jaw and tongue.

## What Causes It?

Bacteria from a bad tooth can spread to the area under the tongue and jaw.  
People with poor dental care are more likely to get this infection.  
Those who recently had a tooth pulled or a broken jaw are also at higher risk.

## Symptoms

You will feel pain and tenderness under your tongue or under your jaw.  
The pain gets worse when you open your mouth wide or swallow.  
You may have a fever and chills.  
Swelling gets worse over time.  
You may drool more than usual.  
You may make a high-pitched sound when breathing in, like a squeak or gasp. This is called stridor.  
The swelling can block your airway.  
If the airway closes, you may not be able to breathe.  
This can happen quickly — within hours — and can be deadly.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors start by looking inside your mouth.  
They check for swelling, pain, and redness.  
If the exam is not clear, they may order a CT scan.  
But if the airway is already at risk, they do not wait for a scan.  
They start treatment right away.

## How It Is Treated

This infection needs fast treatment to keep your airway open.  
Doctors will place a breathing tube to help you breathe.  
They do this by guiding a thin tube through your nose into your windpipe.  
This is done using a small camera to see the way.  
Then, doctors cut open the infected area to drain the pus.  
If the breathing tube cannot be placed through the nose, doctors do a tracheotomy.  
This means they make a small cut in the front of your neck to put in a breathing tube.  
You will get antibiotics through a vein.  
The most common antibiotics are ceftriaxone and clindamycin.  
These medicines fight the infection.

# Motor Neurone Disease

## What is Motor Neurone Disease?

Motor neurone disease is a condition that affects nerves in your brain and spine. These nerves are called motor neurones. They send signals to your muscles to make them move.

Over time, these nerves stop working properly. This means your muscles do not get the messages they need to work.

The exact cause is not known. But for most people, it is likely a mix of genes and other factors.

## Who Can Get It?

Anyone can get motor neurone disease at any age. But it most often starts in people over the age of 50.

## Early Signs and Symptoms

You may notice these early signs:

- Trouble holding or gripping things with your hands
- Weakness in your legs or feet
- Frequent muscle twitches, spasms, or cramps that do not go away

These symptoms can feel like other, less serious problems. But it is important to see a doctor if you have them.

## How It Progresses

Motor neurone disease gets worse over time. This can take a few months or several years. Everyone’s experience is different.

As it gets worse, you may have trouble with:

- Breathing
- Swallowing
- Speaking
- Walking or moving
- Drooling more than usual
- Changes in mood or personality

You may not have all of these symptoms. And how fast they get worse can vary from person to person.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if you have:

- Trouble holding or gripping objects
- Weakness in your legs or feet
- Muscle twitches or cramps that last a long time or do not go away

## How It Is Diagnosed

If your doctor thinks you might have motor neurone disease, they will refer you to a specialist in brain and nerve conditions.

You may have:

- Blood tests
- Tests to check how well your nerves are working
- An MRI scan to rule out other possible causes

Diagnosing motor neurone disease can be hard at first. But as symptoms get worse, it becomes clearer.

## How It Affects Your Life

Motor neurone disease can affect many parts of your life, including:

- Your ability to move and walk
- Your speech and how you talk to others
- Your breathing, eating, and drinking
- Your emotions, thoughts, and behaviour
- Your relationships with family and friends

You will need ongoing care from a team of specialists. This may include:

- Physiotherapists
- Occupational therapists
- Speech and language therapists

As the disease gets worse, you may need:

- A wheelchair
- A breathing machine (ventilator)
- Tools to help you speak, such as a computer or tablet

Life expectancy depends on your symptoms and the type of motor neurone disease you have. Your care team can talk to you about this if you want to know more.

## Treatment and Support

There is no cure for motor neurone disease. But treatments can help you feel better and live as well as possible.

Your treatment will depend on your symptoms and the type of disease you have. You may need different treatments over time.

A team of healthcare professionals will support you. This team may include:

- A specialist nurse
- A brain and nerve doctor (neurologist)
- A physiotherapist
- An occupational therapist

### Medicines

You may be given medicines to help with:

- Muscle stiffness or cramps
- Drooling
- Shortness of breath

If you have a type called amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), you may be offered a medicine called riluzole. This can slow the disease down a little.

### Support for Symptoms

You may also get help with:

- Physiotherapy and exercises to keep your muscles as strong as possible
- Advice on eating and drinking to help you keep your weight up
- Equipment like walking frames, wheelchairs, or home changes like handrails and stair lifts
- Help with washing, bathing, and dressing
- Communication support. A speech and language therapist can teach you ways to talk better and suggest tools like voice computers
- Talking therapy, such as cognitive behavioural therapy, to help with anxiety, depression, or other feelings

You should meet with your care team every 2 to 3 months. This helps you talk about changes in your symptoms and how treatment is working.

## Causes

Motor neurone disease affects nerves that control your muscles. These nerves stop working properly.

We do not know exactly why this happens. But for most people, it is likely a mix of genes and other factors.

About 1 in 10 people with motor neurone disease have a family history of the condition. But having a family member with it does not mean you will get it too.

## Help and Support

Living with motor neurone disease can be hard, both physically and emotionally.

You are not alone. Support is available.

### Motor Neurone Disease Association (MNDA)

This group offers information and support for people with motor neurone disease, and for their families, friends, and carers.

- Website: [www.mndassociation.org](https://www.mndassociation.org)
- Helpline: 0808 802 6262
- Online forum: [MNDA online forum](https://www.mndassociation.org)

### Brain and Spine Foundation

This group gives help and information for anyone affected by brain or nerve conditions, including motor neurone disease.

- Website: [www.brainandspine.org.uk](https://www.brainandspine.org.uk)
- Helpline: 0808 808 1000
- Support groups: [Join a support group](https://www.brainandspine.org.uk)

You can find comfort and advice from others who understand what you are going through. Support groups, both in person and online, can make a big difference.

# Infantile Glaucoma

Infantile glaucoma is a rare condition that affects babies and young children. It happens when the eye’s drainage system does not form correctly. This causes fluid to build up inside the eye. The extra fluid raises the pressure inside the eye. High pressure can damage the nerve that sends vision signals from the eye to the brain. If not treated, this damage can lead to total blindness.

This condition can affect one eye or both eyes. It is more common in both eyes.

## How the Eye Normally Works

The eye makes a clear fluid called aqueous humor. This fluid is made behind the colored part of the eye. It flows through the center of the eye and then leaves through small drainage channels. If these channels do not work right, fluid builds up and pressure rises.

## Signs and Symptoms

Babies with infantile glaucoma often show three main signs:
- They blink too much (excessive blinking).
- They are very sensitive to light.
- They cry and have watery eyes.

The eye or eyes may also grow larger than normal. This happens because the high pressure stretches the eye’s outer layers. The cornea (the clear front part of the eye) becomes larger than normal, thinner, and sometimes cloudy. This can make vision blurry.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors look for the three main signs: excessive blinking, light sensitivity, and tearing. If they suspect glaucoma, they check the pressure inside the eye.

To get a full picture, the child may need to have an exam under general anesthesia. This allows the doctor to measure:
- The size of the cornea.
- The thickness of the cornea.
- The length of the eye.
- The angle where fluid drains out.
- The eye’s focusing power.

These tests help confirm the diagnosis.

## How It Is Treated

Treatment is always surgery. The goal is to open the blocked drainage system so fluid can leave the eye.

Surgery is done as early as possible. Common types include:
- Goniotomy.
- Trabeculotomy.
- Trabeculectomy.

Delaying surgery can lead to worsening cloudiness of the cornea. It can also cause permanent damage to the optic nerve. This damage shows as changes in the nerve’s shape. Without treatment, the child will likely become blind.

## Other Types of Glaucoma in Babies

Glaucoma can also happen in babies who have other eye problems. These include:
- Aniridia (missing part of the colored eye).
- Lowe syndrome.
- Sturge-Weber syndrome.

Glaucoma can also develop after eye injury or eye surgery, such as cataract removal. These cases are called secondary glaucoma.

# Otitis Media (Serous)

## What Is Serous Otitis Media?

Serous otitis media means fluid builds up in the middle part of the ear.  
This fluid is not an infection.  
It does not cause pain or pus.  
It can cause a feeling of fullness and mild hearing loss.

This condition often happens after an ear infection does not fully go away.  
It can also happen if the eustachian tube is blocked.  
The eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the back of the nose.  
It helps balance pressure in the ear.

Allergies and large adenoids are common reasons the eustachian tube gets blocked.  
Tumors can block it, but this is rare.  
This condition can happen at any age.  
It is most common in children after an ear infection.

## How Does Fluid Build Up?

Normally, the eustachian tube opens a few times a minute when you swallow.  
This lets air in and keeps pressure balanced.  
If the tube is blocked, air is absorbed from the middle ear.  
This lowers the pressure inside the ear.  
Lower pressure pulls fluid into the middle ear.  
This fluid stops the eardrum from moving well.  
That causes hearing loss.

## Symptoms

Most people feel a full or plugged-up feeling in the ear.  
You may hear popping or crackling when you swallow.  
Hearing may be slightly worse.  
Ear pain is rare.  
You may not notice any symptoms at all.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor will look in your ear with a special light called an otoscope.  
They may use a small device that pushes air into the ear.  
If the eardrum does not move normally, fluid may be present.  
A test called tympanometry checks for fluid in the middle ear.  
In adults and teens, the doctor may also check the nose and throat for tumors.

## Treatment

Most people get better without treatment.  
Decongestants and antibiotics do not help.  
They are not needed.

If allergies are the cause, the doctor may give you antihistamines or a steroid nasal spray.  
These help reduce swelling and blockage.

To help open the eustachian tube, you can try these steps:

- Close your mouth and pinch your nose shut.  
  Then gently blow out through your nose.  
  This is called the Valsalva maneuver.  
  Do this only if it feels safe.

- Pinch your nose and swallow.  
  Repeat this several times a day.  
  This helps push air into the middle ear.

- A doctor can use a special syringe to blow air into your nose.  
  They block one nostril and ask you to swallow.  
  This is called politzerization.  
  It forces air into the eustachian tube.

If symptoms last more than 1 to 3 months, the doctor may suggest a small surgery called a myringotomy.

### Myringotomy

The doctor makes a tiny hole in the eardrum.  
This lets fluid drain out.  
A small tube is placed in the hole.  
This tube helps air get into the middle ear.  
It keeps pressure balanced.

The tube usually falls out on its own in 6 to 12 months.  
Some types stay longer.  
If it does not come out, the doctor removes it.  
Sometimes the hole does not close.  
Then surgery may be needed to close it.

### For Children

Children with long-term fluid in the ear may need treatment to help their speech and language develop.  
If the child has large adenoids, the doctor may suggest removing them.  
This is called an adenoidectomy.

### After Surgery

Children can wash their hair and swim.  
But some doctors say to avoid deep water unless using earplugs.  
If fluid drains from the ear, call the doctor.  
This may mean an infection.

### Avoiding Pressure Changes

Do not scuba dive or fly in airplanes if possible.  
Changes in air pressure can hurt your ears.  
If you must fly:

- For young children: Give them a bottle or pacifier to suck on.  
  This helps open the eustachian tube.

- For older children and adults:  
  If the plane is going up (pressure drops), try yawning, chewing gum, or swallowing.  
  If the plane is going down (pressure rises), pinch your nose, close your mouth, and gently blow out through your nose.  
  This is the Valsalva maneuver.

## Managing Allergies

If allergies are causing the problem, try to avoid things that trigger your allergies.  
This may include dust, pollen, or pet dander.  
Your doctor may suggest allergen immunotherapy.  
This is a treatment that helps your body stop reacting to allergens over time.

# Heartburn and Acid Reflux

Heartburn feels like a burning pain in the middle of your chest.  
You may also taste sour liquid in your mouth.  
This happens when stomach acid moves up into your throat.

### What causes heartburn and acid reflux?

No one knows the exact cause for everyone.  
But some things can make it worse.  
These include:  
- Eating spicy, fatty, or acidic foods  
- Drinking coffee, alcohol, or chocolate  
- Being overweight  
- Smoking  
- Stress or anxiety  
- Hormone changes during pregnancy  
- Some medicines, like ibuprofen  
- A hiatus hernia (when part of your stomach moves up into your chest)  
- A stomach ulcer  
- A bacterial infection in your stomach

### When to see a doctor

See your doctor if:  
- You have heartburn most days  
- Lifestyle changes and over-the-counter medicines do not help  
- You feel food getting stuck in your throat  
- You are sick often  
- You lose weight without trying

Your doctor can check for serious problems.  
They can also give you stronger treatments if needed.

If your symptoms get worse, call 111 or go to 111.nhs.uk.

---

## Symptoms of Acid Reflux

The main signs are:  
- A burning pain in the middle of your chest  
- A sour or bitter taste in your mouth

You might also have:  
- A cough that won’t go away  
- Frequent hiccups  
- A hoarse voice  
- Bad breath  
- A bloated belly or feeling sick

Symptoms often get worse:  
- After eating  
- When lying down  
- When bending over

---

## How to Feel Better at Home

Small changes can help reduce heartburn.

### Do these things:

- Eat smaller meals more often  
- Try to lose weight if you are overweight  
- Find ways to relax and reduce stress

### Avoid these things:

- Foods or drinks that trigger your symptoms  
- Eating or drinking 3 to 4 hours before bedtime  
- Wearing tight clothes around your waist  
- Smoking  
- Drinking too much alcohol  
- Stopping any medicine without talking to your doctor first

### Try this tip:

Lift the head of your bed by 10 to 20 centimetres.  
Use books, bricks, or a bed riser.  
This helps keep stomach acid from moving up.

Do not use extra pillows.  
This can push on your belly and make heartburn worse.

---

## Help from a Pharmacist

Talk to a pharmacist if you keep getting heartburn.

They can suggest medicines like:  
- Antacids – these calm stomach acid  
- Alginates – these form a barrier to stop acid from rising

Take these medicines with food or soon after eating.  
They work better when taken with food.

These medicines help for a short time.  
They do not fix the root cause.  
Do not take them every day for long periods.

If you are pregnant, a pharmacist can tell you which medicines are safe.

---

## Treatment from Your Doctor

If you have acid reflux, your doctor may prescribe a medicine called a proton pump inhibitor (PPI).  
This medicine lowers the amount of acid your stomach makes.

Common PPIs include:  
- Omeprazole  
- Lansoprazole

You will usually take this medicine for 4 to 8 weeks.  
The length depends on how bad your symptoms are.

If your symptoms come back after stopping the medicine, go back to your doctor.  
You may need to take it long-term.

### Important:

If the PPI does not help, your doctor may try a different medicine called an H2 receptor antagonist.  
An example is famotidine.

---

## Tests and More Serious Treatment

If medicines do not help or your symptoms are very bad, your doctor may refer you to a specialist.

They may do tests such as:  
- A gastroscopy – a thin tube with a camera goes down your throat into your stomach to check for problems  
- Tests to see if you have a bacteria in your stomach that causes heartburn  
  - If so, you will take antibiotics and a PPI together

In some cases, surgery may be needed.  
This can help stop acid from coming up into your throat.  
Surgery may involve your stomach or food pipe (oesophagus).

# High Levels of Clotting Proteins: Factor VIII, IX, and XI

High levels of certain clotting proteins—Factor VIII, Factor IX, and Factor XI—can increase your risk of blood clots in the veins. These clots can travel to the lungs and cause serious problems.

These proteins are made in the liver. They help your blood to clot when you are injured. Factor VIII travels in the blood in an inactive form. It stays attached to another protein called von Willebrand factor. When a blood vessel is damaged, Factor VIII becomes active and helps start the clotting process.

Factor VIII levels are often inherited. But they can also go up if you have long-term inflammation or other serious health issues.

High levels of Factor VIII are linked to a higher chance of developing a blood clot in a vein. This is called venous thromboembolism, or VTE. The link was first found in a large study called the Leiden Thrombophilia Study. People with Factor VIII levels above 150 IU/L had nearly five times the risk of VTE.

High levels of Factor IX and Factor XI are also linked to a higher risk of VTE. One large study found that Factor XI, but not Factor IX, still raised the risk of VTE even after adjusting for age, sex, race, body weight, and diabetes.

High levels of von Willebrand factor are also linked to a higher risk of VTE.

---

## How Doctors Check for High Clotting Protein Levels

Doctors can test your blood to measure the levels of Factor VIII, Factor IX, and Factor XI.

These tests measure both the amount of the protein (antigen level) and how well it works (activity level).

It is important to test these levels when you are not taking blood thinners. Some blood thinners can affect the results.

- **Warfarin** changes the levels of several clotting proteins, including Factor IX and Factor X. It can make test results less accurate.
- **Direct oral anticoagulants** (like apixaban, rivaroxaban, and dabigatran) can also make activity levels look lower than they really are.
- However, **antigen levels** (the amount of protein) are not affected by direct oral anticoagulants.

Always tell your doctor about any blood thinners you are taking before testing.

---

## How High Levels Are Treated

If you have high levels of Factor VIII, IX, or XI and you have had a blood clot, your doctor will treat you with blood thinners.

Blood thinners help prevent new clots from forming.

- **Direct oral anticoagulants** (like apixaban, rivaroxaban, and dabigatran) are effective.
- **Vitamin K antagonists** (like warfarin) are also effective.

These medicines are used to treat blood clots in people with high levels of these clotting proteins.

If high Factor VIII levels are due to another health problem—like long-term inflammation—your doctor will also treat that condition.

# Typhoid Fever – Simple Explanation

Typhoid fever is an illness caused by a type of bacteria called *Salmonella* Typhi.  
It causes a high fever and stomach pain.  

This bacteria only lives in people.  
It spreads when someone with the infection touches food or water after using the bathroom.  
The bacteria can also be in urine, but this is less common.

## How Typhoid Fever Spreads

- People with typhoid fever pass the bacteria in their stool.  
- If hands are not washed well after using the bathroom, the bacteria can get on food or water.  
- Water can become unsafe if sewage is not treated properly.  
- Flies can carry the bacteria from stool to food.  
- The infection can also spread through close contact, like during play or certain types of sex.  

Some people carry the bacteria without feeling sick.  
They can still spread the disease.  
These people are called carriers.  
One famous carrier was a cook named Mary Mallon, known as Typhoid Mary.

You are more likely to get typhoid fever if:
- You have low stomach acid (older adults or people on acid-reducing medicine).  
- You are taking antibiotics (they can weaken the body’s natural defenses).  

## What Happens in the Body

The bacteria travel from the gut into the blood.  
They can then infect other parts of the body, such as:
- Liver, spleen, and gallbladder  
- Lungs  
- Joints  
- Kidneys  
- Heart valves  
- Brain and spinal cord coverings  
- Bones  

These serious infections usually happen if treatment is delayed or not given.

## Symptoms of Typhoid Fever

Symptoms start about 8 to 14 days after infection.  
They come on slowly.  
You may feel:
- Fever  
- Headache  
- Sore throat  
- Muscle and joint pain  
- Stomach pain  
- Dry cough  
- Loss of appetite  

After a few days, the fever rises to 103 to 104 degrees Fahrenheit (39 to 40 degrees Celsius).  
It stays high for 10 to 14 days.  
Then it slowly goes down by the fourth week.  

You may feel very tired.  
Your heartbeat may be slow.  
In severe cases, you may become confused or lose consciousness.

A rash of flat, pink spots may appear on the chest and belly in 5 to 30 out of 100 people.  
At first, you may be constipated.  
After two weeks, diarrhea may start.  

In rare cases (1 to 2 out of 100), the intestine can tear or bleed.  
This can be life-threatening.  

If the infection spreads to other organs, you may have symptoms from those areas.

About 1 in 10 people who are not treated may get sick again about two weeks after the fever goes away.

## How Doctors Diagnose Typhoid Fever

To confirm the illness, doctors take samples of:
- Blood  
- Stool  
- Urine  
- Sometimes other body fluids or tissue  

These samples are sent to a lab to grow the bacteria.  
The lab also tests which antibiotics will work best.

## How Typhoid Fever Is Treated

Antibiotics are the main treatment.  
Doctors may use one of these:
- Ceftriaxone (given by injection)  
- Fluoroquinolones (like ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, or moxifloxacin) – taken by mouth or injection  
- Azithromycin (taken by mouth)  

Antibiotic resistance is common, especially in areas where typhoid is common.  
It is also rising in the United States due to travelers returning from infected areas.

If the illness is very severe, doctors may give corticosteroids by injection.  
This helps when someone is confused, unconscious, or in shock.

While you have a fever:
- Stay in bed.  
- Drink clear liquids to help with diarrhea.  
- Do not take aspirin, laxatives, or enemas.

Some people get sick again after treatment ends.  
This second illness is usually milder but is treated the same way.

Carriers must report to local health officials.  
Health workers will help stop the spread.  
Carriers cannot work with food until tests show no bacteria are present.  
Long-term antibiotics (4 to 6 weeks) can clear the bacteria in many carriers.  

If a carrier has gallbladder problems, surgery to remove the gallbladder may help.  
But it does not always remove all the bacteria.

## Prognosis (Outlook)

Without treatment, 10 to 15 out of 100 people die.  
With treatment, only about 1 out of 100 dies.  
Most deaths happen in people who are very young, very old, or malnourished.

Full recovery can take weeks or months.

Signs of a serious case include:
- Not responding to touch or voice (stupor)  
- Coma  
- Shock  

These signs mean the illness is dangerous.

## How to Prevent Typhoid Fever

If you are traveling to areas where typhoid is common:
- Avoid raw vegetables and foods left out at room temperature.  
- Do not drink tap water.  
- Do not use ice unless you know it is safe.  
- Use only sealed bottled water for drinking and brushing teeth.  

You can safely eat:
- Food that is served very hot right after cooking  
- Sealed bottled or canned drinks  
- Hot tea or coffee  
- Fruit that you peel yourself  

Two vaccines can help prevent typhoid fever:
- An oral vaccine (taken by mouth) – works for people 6 years and older  
- An injected vaccine – works for people 2 years and older  

The oral vaccine is 40 to 80% effective.  
The injected vaccine is 50 to 80% effective.  
Both have few side effects.

Get vaccinated if you:
- Are traveling to high-risk areas  
- Live with or have close contact with a carrier  
- Work in a lab with *Salmonella* bacteria  

You need a booster:
- Every 2 years after the injected vaccine  
- Every 5 years after the oral vaccine  

## More Information

For more details, visit:
**Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC): Typhoid Fever**  
This site has helpful information for travelers and others at risk.
