# Dengue

Dengue is a disease spread by mosquitoes.  
It is found in tropical areas around the world.  
These include parts of Africa, Asia, Central and South America, the Caribbean, Pacific islands, and some southern areas of North America.  
There is also a risk in parts of southern Europe during spring to November.  
Countries in Europe where dengue has been found include Croatia, France, Italy, Spain, Portugal, and Madeira.  
Dengue is not found in the UK.  
You cannot catch dengue from another person.

## Who is at risk?

You can get dengue if you are bitten by a mosquito that carries the virus.  
The mosquitoes that carry dengue bite during the day.  
Some people are more at risk of serious illness.  
This includes people who:  
- are very young  
- are older  
- are pregnant  
- have a weak immune system  
- have health problems like asthma, diabetes, high blood pressure, or a condition that makes you bleed more easily  
- have had dengue before  

If you are in one of these groups, think carefully before travelling to areas where dengue is common.

## Symptoms of dengue

Dengue does not always cause symptoms.  
If you do get symptoms, they usually start 4 to 10 days after being bitten by an infected mosquito.  
Symptoms can feel like flu.  
They include:  
- a high temperature  
- a severe headache  
- pain behind your eyes  
- muscle and joint pain  
- feeling sick or being sick  
- swollen glands  
- a rash with flat or slightly raised spots that may cover large parts of your body  

## Severe dengue

Some people get a more serious form of dengue a few days after they first feel ill.  
This is rare.  
You may feel better at first, with your temperature going down.  
But then, 24 to 48 hours later, you may get worse symptoms.  
These include:  
- severe stomach pain  
- repeated vomiting  
- fast breathing  
- bleeding gums or nose  
- extreme tiredness  
- feeling restless or unable to relax  
- blood in your vomit or stool  

Severe dengue is very serious.  
It needs quick treatment in hospital.

## What to do if you think you have dengue

### Call your doctor or get help from NHS 111 if:
- You feel unwell after travelling to a country where dengue is found  
- You have symptoms like high temperature, headache, eye pain, or rash  

Check your symptoms online at 111 or call 111.  
Tell the person you speak to about your recent travel.  
Get medical advice quickly if you have symptoms while travelling.

### Call 999 or go to A&E if:
- You have been to a country where dengue is found  
- You have symptoms of severe dengue  

Severe dengue can be life-threatening if not treated fast.  
Go to a hospital as soon as possible if you get these symptoms while travelling.

### A&E safety tips:
- Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you.  
- Or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.  
- Bring any medicines you take with you.

## How to treat dengue

Most people feel better in a few days.  
There is no medicine that cures dengue.  
But you can help ease your symptoms by:  
- resting as much as possible  
- drinking plenty of fluids to stay hydrated  
- taking paracetamol to lower your temperature and ease pain  

Do not take anti-inflammatory painkillers like ibuprofen or aspirin.  
These can make bleeding worse if you have dengue.

If you have severe dengue, you will need to stay in hospital until you recover.

## How to prevent dengue

The best way to avoid dengue is to stop mosquito bites.  
This is especially important if you are in a country where dengue is found.

### Do these things:
- Wear long-sleeved shirts and long trousers, especially in the early morning and early evening  
- Use insect repellent on your skin. Choose one with DEET for best protection  
- Keep windows and doors closed when possible  
- Use window or door screens, or blinds to block mosquitoes  
- Sleep under a mosquito net that has been treated with insecticide — even during the day  

### Dengue vaccine

There is a vaccine that can help protect against dengue.  
It is only for people who have had dengue before, or might have had it.  
It is recommended for those travelling to areas where dengue is common.  
You need to get advice from a travel clinic.  
The vaccine is not free. You will have to pay for it yourself.

# Ingrown Toenail

An ingrown toenail happens when the edge of the nail grows into the skin next to it. This causes pain and discomfort.

## What Causes an Ingrown Toenail?

- Wearing shoes that are too tight.
- Walking in a way that puts extra pressure on the toes.
- Having toes that are wide or rounded at the tip.
- Cutting the nails too short or too curved.
- Being born with a nail shape that naturally curves inward.
- In young people, a rare bone growth under the nail (called an osteochondroma) can cause the problem.
- In older adults, swelling in the feet can increase the risk.
- If the area becomes infected, it can lead to a condition called paronychia.

## Symptoms

- Pain at the side of the toenail, especially near the corner.
- The pain may start as a mild ache, especially when wearing certain shoes.
- Over time, the skin may become swollen and red.
- In long-term cases, a soft, pink lump (called granulation tissue) may appear, especially in younger people.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- A doctor will look at your toe and ask about your symptoms.
- Redness, swelling, and pain may mean there is an infection.
- If you are under 20 and keep getting ingrown toenails, your doctor may order an X-ray to check for a bone growth under the nail.
- If there is a pink lump around the toe but no ingrown nail, it could be a rare type of skin cancer called amelanotic melanoma. A small sample of tissue (biopsy) is needed to confirm this.

## How Is It Treated?

- For mild cases, you can gently push a small piece of cotton between the nail and the skin using a thin toothpick. This can ease the pain right away. If you keep doing this, it may help the nail grow straight.
- If your shoes are too tight, try wearing shoes with more room in the toe area.
- In most cases, especially if there is an infection, the best treatment is to remove part or all of the ingrown nail. This is done after numbing the toe with a local anesthetic.
- After the nail is removed, a small soft tube may be placed between the nail and the skin. This keeps the area open so it can heal.
- If the problem keeps coming back, a chemical (like sodium hydroxide or phenol) can be used to stop the nail from growing back in that area. This is a permanent solution.
- Do not use phenol if you have poor blood flow in your feet. This can cause serious problems.

# Sleep Apnea

Sleep apnea is a serious condition. It happens when your breathing stops many times during the night. These stops last long enough to wake you up. They also lower the amount of oxygen in your blood and raise the amount of carbon dioxide.

## What Happens in Sleep Apnea?

- You may feel very tired during the day.
- You may snore loudly.
- You may gasp or choke during sleep.
- You may stop breathing for a few seconds.
- You may wake up suddenly with a snort.

Sleep apnea can lead to serious health problems. It can raise your risk of heart disease, stroke, and early death.

Doctors often use sleep tests to confirm the diagnosis. These tests show how bad the problem is.

Treatment options include:
- A machine that sends air into your airway (CPAP).
- A mouth device made by a dentist.
- Surgery in some cases.

Sleep apnea is very common. Over one billion people worldwide have the most common type—obstructive sleep apnea.

---

## Types of Sleep Apnea

There are two main types:

1. **Obstructive sleep apnea**
2. **Central sleep apnea**

Some people have both types.

### Obstructive Sleep Apnea

This is the most common type. It happens when your throat or upper airway closes during sleep.

Your upper airway goes from your nose and mouth down to your voice box. These parts can shift when you breathe.

This type affects about 8 to 16 out of every 100 adults. It is more common in people who are overweight. But not everyone with this condition is overweight.

Doctors diagnose obstructive sleep apnea when:
- You stop breathing during sleep.
- You have 5 or more breathing stops per hour.
- Each stop lasts more than 10 seconds.

### Risk Factors for Obstructive Sleep Apnea

- Being overweight.
- Getting older.
- Drinking too much alcohol.
- Using sedatives or sleeping pills.
- Having a narrow throat or thick neck (this can run in families).
- Low thyroid hormone levels (hypothyroidism).
- Acid reflux at night (GERD).
- A rare condition called acromegaly (too much growth hormone).
- Having had a stroke.
- Family history of sleep apnea.

> **Did You Know?**  
> People with obstructive sleep apnea should avoid alcohol and sleep aids, especially before bedtime.

### In Children

In kids, the causes include:
- Enlarged tonsils or adenoids.
- Some dental problems (like a large overbite).
- Being overweight.
- Birth defects (like a small lower jaw).
- Severe seasonal allergies that block the nose.

Most children with this problem snore. Other signs may include:
- Restless sleep.
- Sweating at night.
- Bedwetting.
- Mouth breathing during the day.
- Morning headaches.
- Trouble focusing.
- Behavior issues like hyperactivity.
- Slow growth.

Excessive sleepiness is less common in children than in adults.

### Central Sleep Apnea

This type is rare. It happens when the brain does not send the right signals to control breathing.

The brain stem controls breathing. It senses carbon dioxide levels in the blood. When carbon dioxide builds up, the brain tells your breathing muscles to work harder.

In central sleep apnea, the brain stem does not respond properly. So breathing slows down or stops during sleep.

Causes include:
- Stroke.
- Brain infection (encephalitis).
- Birth defects in the brain.
- Opioid pain medicines.
- Other medications.
- Living at high altitude.
- Heart failure.
- A brain tumor (very rare).

Unlike obstructive sleep apnea, central sleep apnea is not linked to being overweight.

One rare form, called Ondine curse or CCHS, affects newborns. These babies breathe poorly or not at all unless they are fully awake.

---

## Symptoms of Sleep Apnea

Most people do not notice their own symptoms. A partner, roommate, or family member often sees them first.

In all types of sleep apnea:
- Breathing may slow down or stop.
- Breathing may stop for up to a minute.
- Then breathing starts again.

Common effects include:
- Feeling sleepy during the day.
- Feeling tired all the time.
- Feeling irritable.
- Waking up with a headache.
- Trouble thinking clearly.
- Trouble concentrating.

People who are very sleepy are at higher risk of accidents. This includes driving, using heavy machines, or doing other dangerous tasks.

Sleepiness can hurt your work, your sex life, and your relationships.

Low oxygen levels can cause:
- Irregular heartbeats (atrial fibrillation).
- High blood pressure.

### In Obstructive Sleep Apnea

- Loud snoring is the most common symptom.
- But most people who snore do not have sleep apnea.
- Snoring in sleep apnea is often loud and disruptive.
- It may be followed by gasping, choking, or sudden snorts.
- You may wake up choking and scared.

In the morning, you may not know your sleep was broken many times. Some people wake up with a sore throat or dry mouth.

If the condition is severe:
- You may snore loudly and gasp many times at night.
- You may feel sleepy during the day and fall asleep at unexpected times.

You may have trouble staying asleep.

If you live alone, daytime sleepiness may be the main sign. Over time, this can hurt your work and your life.

You might fall asleep while watching TV, in meetings, or even while driving at a red light.

Memory may suffer. Your sex drive may drop. Relationships may suffer because you are tired and irritable.

If you live with others, your loud, restless sleep can bother your partner or roommates.

Obstructive sleep apnea increases your risk of:
- Stroke.
- Heart attack.
- Irregular heartbeats.
- High blood pressure.

Men in middle age who have more than 30 breathing stops per hour are at higher risk of dying early.

> **Did You Know?**  
> Only a few people who snore have sleep apnea. But almost everyone with sleep apnea snores.

### In Central Sleep Apnea

- Snoring is not common.
- Breathing is irregular and stops for short periods.
- You may have trouble staying asleep.
- You may wake up early.

#### Cheyne-Stokes Respiration

This is a type of central sleep apnea. Breathing:
- Gets faster.
- Then slows down.
- Stops for a short time.
- Then starts again.
- The cycle repeats every 30 seconds to 2 minutes.

### Obesity-Hypoventilation Syndrome

Some people with extreme obesity have this condition. It is also called Pickwickian syndrome.

It happens when:
- Extra fat makes it hard to move the chest.
- Extra fat below the diaphragm presses on the lungs.
- This leads to shallow, weak breathing.
- Extra fat around the throat blocks the airway.
- The brain’s control of breathing may not work right.

This can cause central sleep apnea.

---

## How Is Sleep Apnea Diagnosed?

Doctors start by asking about your symptoms.

They may use questionnaires to check for:
- Excessive daytime sleepiness.

The best way to confirm sleep apnea is to monitor your breathing during sleep.

### Home Sleep Test

You can do a test at home. A small device records:
- Your breathing.
- Your heart rate.
- Airflow through your nose.
- Oxygen levels in your blood.

### Polysomnography (Sleep Lab Test)

This is a more detailed test. You sleep overnight in a lab.

The test measures:
- Brain waves (using electrodes on your head).
- Eye movements.
- Oxygen levels (using a sensor on your fingertip or ear).
- Airflow (using sensors near your nose and mouth).
- Chest movements (using a band around your chest).

The test gives a number called the **apnea-hypopnea index (AHI)**.

- AHI counts how many times you stop breathing or breathe too lightly per hour of sleep.
- A higher AHI means more severe sleep apnea.
- Doctors use the AHI, your symptoms, and other test results to make the diagnosis.

Sometimes, extra tests are needed to check for complications like:
- High blood pressure.
- Irregular heartbeats.

---

## How Is Sleep Apnea Treated?

Treatment focuses on:
- Reducing risk factors.
- Treating the sleep apnea itself.

Support groups can help you and your family cope.

### Lifestyle Changes

- Avoid alcohol and sedatives, especially before bed.
- Do not use sleep aids or antihistamines that make you drowsy.
- Sleep on your side or raise the head of your bed.
- Use a special device that keeps you from lying on your back.
- Lose weight if you are overweight.
- Quit smoking.
- Treat nasal infections and allergies.
- Treat thyroid problems or acromegaly if present.

Weight loss helps, but it can be hard if you are tired and sleepy. In such cases, weight-loss medicine or bariatric surgery may be recommended.

### Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP)

This is the main treatment for obstructive sleep apnea, especially if you are very sleepy.

- You wear a mask over your nose or face.
- A machine sends a steady stream of air into your airway.
- The air pressure keeps your throat open while you breathe.

You can use CPAP with or without humidified air. Humidified air may feel more comfortable.

You need close follow-up for the first two weeks. A health provider will help you:
- Get the right mask fit.
- Learn how to use the device.
- Stay motivated.

Many people find CPAP hard to use. They stop using it or use it only sometimes.

# Alcohol-Related Liver Disease

Alcohol-related liver disease does not cause symptoms at first.  
You may not notice any problems until the liver is seriously damaged.

Later, you might notice:
- Feeling sick  
- Losing weight  
- Not feeling hungry  
- Yellowing of the eyes or skin (this is called jaundice)  
- Swelling in the ankles or belly  
- Feeling confused or very sleepy  
- Vomiting blood or passing blood in your stool  

Because there are no early symptoms, many people find out they have liver damage only when they get tests for something else.  
Or they learn about it when the liver is already badly damaged.

If you drink too much alcohol often, tell your doctor.  
They can check if your liver is hurt.

---

## Treating Alcohol-Related Liver Disease

There is no medicine that treats alcohol-related liver disease directly.  
The most important step is to stop drinking alcohol.  
It is best to stop for good.

Stopping drinking helps protect your liver from more harm.  
It also gives your liver the best chance to heal.

If you are used to drinking a lot, stopping can be very hard.  
But help is available.  
Local alcohol support services can give you advice, support, and medical help.

In very serious cases, the liver may stop working.  
If it does not get better after you stop drinking, you may need a liver transplant.

You will only be considered for a liver transplant if:
- You have serious liver damage from cirrhosis  
- You have stopped drinking alcohol  

All liver transplant centers require you to stay away from alcohol for the rest of your life.  
You must also not drink while waiting for a transplant.

---

## Preventing Alcohol-Related Liver Disease

The best way to prevent this disease is to stop drinking alcohol or stay within the recommended limits.

The NHS says:
- Men and women should not drink more than 14 units of alcohol per week on a regular basis  
- If you drink 14 units a week, spread it over 3 days or more  
- If you want to cut down, try to have several days each week with no alcohol  

One unit of alcohol is about:
- Half a pint of regular beer  
- One small pub measure (25 milliliters) of spirits  

Even if you have drunk heavily for years, cutting down or stopping will help your liver and your health.  
The benefits start quickly and keep going over time.

# Mastoiditis

Mastoiditis is an infection in the small air spaces behind the ear. It often starts after a middle ear infection. This condition can be serious and needs quick treatment.

## What Causes Mastoiditis?

- A middle ear infection can spread to the mastoid bone.
- The mastoid bone has small air spaces. These can fill with fluid.
- Bacteria can grow in this fluid. The most common bacteria is the same one that caused the ear infection.
- The infection can damage the walls between the air spaces. This causes the spaces to merge together. This is called coalescent mastoiditis.

## How Does the Infection Spread?

- The infection may drain through a hole in the eardrum.
- It can also push through the bone behind the ear. This forms a painful lump under the skin.
- In rare cases, the infection can spread to the brain. This can cause a brain abscess or a blood clot in a large vein.
- Sometimes, the infection can break through the tip of the mastoid bone. It then drains into the neck. This is called a Bezold abscess.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms usually start a few days to weeks after a middle ear infection. They include:

- Fever
- A deep, throbbing pain in the ear
- Redness, swelling, and tenderness behind the ear
- The ear may look pushed forward and down
- Pus coming from the ear

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- Doctors look at the ear and the area behind it.
- A CT scan is often done. This helps see how far the infection has spread.
- A sample of any fluid from the ear is tested to find the bacteria.
- If no fluid is draining, a small cut may be made in the eardrum to collect a sample.
- Blood tests may show signs of infection, but they are not always helpful.

## How Is It Treated?

- Treatment starts right away with strong antibiotics given through a vein.
- The most common antibiotic is ceftriaxone. It works well in the brain and spinal fluid.
- The dose depends on age and weight. Adults get 1 to 2 grams once a day. Children get 50 to 75 milligrams per kilogram of body weight.
- Treatment lasts at least two weeks.
- Other antibiotics like vancomycin or linezolid may be used if needed.
- After the infection is under control, oral antibiotics may be used. A quinolone is one option.
- The final choice of antibiotic depends on test results from the fluid sample.

### If There Is a Pus Collection Behind the Ear

- A surgery called a mastoidectomy is often needed.
- The surgeon drains the pus.
- The infected air spaces in the bone are removed.
- A new path is made from the mastoid to the middle ear to help fluid drain.

### If the Eardrum Does Not Break Open

- A small tube is placed in the eardrum. This is called a tympanostomy tube.
- It helps fluid drain from the middle ear.

### After Surgery

- You will use ear drops for 2 to 3 weeks.
- The drops are fluoroquinolone type. They are safe for a hole in the eardrum or a tube.
- Keep the ear dry during bathing and showers.
  - Use a cotton ball with petroleum jelly to block the ear canal.
- Do not swim.
- Do not use ear drops that contain neomycin, tobramycin, or polymyxin if you have a hole in the eardrum or a tube.
  - These drops can harm hearing.

## Possible Complications

If not treated, mastoiditis can lead to:

- Hearing loss
- Spread of infection into the bloodstream (sepsis)
- Infection of the brain lining (meningitis)

## Key Points

- Mastoiditis is a serious infection behind the ear.
- It often follows a middle ear infection.
- Symptoms include pain, swelling, fever, and pus from the ear.
- Diagnosis is based on exam and imaging.
- Treatment includes strong antibiotics and sometimes surgery.
- Early treatment prevents serious problems.

# Candidiasis (Yeast Infection)

Candidiasis is an infection caused by a type of yeast called *Candida*.  
Yeast is a kind of fungus.  
*Candida* lives on your skin and in your mouth, gut, and vagina.  
It usually does not cause problems.  
But sometimes it grows too much and causes an infection.

## Where Candidiasis Happens

Candidiasis often shows up in warm, damp areas of the body.  
These include:  
- The skin folds under the arms  
- The groin area  
- Between fingers and toes  
- The space under the breasts  
- The area around the penis, especially if not circumcised  
- The navel  
- The nails and skin around the nails  
- The mouth  
- The vagina  
- The esophagus (the tube from the mouth to the stomach)

In rare cases, *Candida* can spread through the blood and affect deeper tissues.  
This is serious and can be life-threatening, especially in people with weak immune systems.

## What Causes Candidiasis

Certain things can make it more likely for *Candida* to grow out of control.  
These include:  
- Hot and humid weather  
- Wearing tight or synthetic underwear  
- Not cleaning the skin well  
- Not changing diapers or underwear often, especially in babies and older adults  
- Having diabetes  
- Having HIV or AIDS  
- Taking corticosteroids or other medicines that weaken the immune system  
- Taking antibiotics  
- Being pregnant  
- Being overweight  
- Having other skin problems like intertrigo or psoriasis

Antibiotics kill good bacteria that normally keep *Candida* in check.  
This lets *Candida* grow more easily.  
Corticosteroids and medicines after organ transplants can also lower your body’s ability to fight infection.  
Inhaled steroids for asthma can sometimes cause mouth infections.

## Symptoms of Candidiasis

Symptoms depend on where the infection is.

### Skin Infections
- A bright red rash in skin folds or the navel  
- Skin may break down or peel  
- Small pus-filled bumps may appear around the edges  
- Itching or burning pain  
- A rash around the anus may look raw, white, or red and itches

### Diaper Rash in Babies
- Red, irritated skin in the diaper area  
- May have white patches or small sores

### Vaginal Infection (Yeast Infection)
- Thick, white or yellow discharge that looks like cottage cheese  
- Itching, burning, and redness inside and around the vagina  
- Common in pregnant women, women with diabetes, or those on antibiotics

### Penile Infection
- Red, raw, itchy, or painful rash on the head of the penis  
- More common in men with diabetes, uncircumcised men, or men whose partners have a vaginal yeast infection

### Thrush (Mouth Infection)
- White, creamy patches on the tongue or inside the cheeks  
- Patches can be scraped off and may bleed  
- Can be painful  
- Common in babies  
- In adults, it may mean the immune system is weak (due to cancer, diabetes, or HIV)

### Angular Cheilitis (Corners of the Mouth)
- Cracks or small cuts at the corners of the mouth  
- Can be caused by licking lips, sucking thumbs, or poorly fitting dentures  
- Moisture in the area helps yeast grow

### Nail Infection (Candidal Paronychia)
- Painful redness and swelling around the nail  
- The nail may turn white or yellow  
- The nail may pull away from the nail bed  
- Common in people with diabetes or weak immune systems  
- Also common in people who wash their hands often or have wet hands a lot

### Chronic Mucocutaneous Candidiasis
- Thick, crusted, red, pus-filled areas on the skin  
- Often on the nose and forehead  
- Looks like psoriasis  
- People with this condition often get thrush too

## How Doctors Diagnose Candidiasis

Doctors look at the rash or the white patches.  
They can often tell it is candidiasis just by seeing it.  
To be sure, they may take a small sample from the skin or mouth.  
They scrape off a bit of the skin or residue with a tool.  
They then look at it under a microscope.  
They may also grow the fungus in a special dish to confirm the diagnosis.

## How Candidiasis Is Treated

Treatment depends on where the infection is.

### Skin Infections in Skin Folds
- Use antifungal creams, powders, or solutions on the skin  
- Common medicines include miconazole, clotrimazole, oxiconazole, ketoconazole, econazole, ciclopirox, and nystatin  
- Keep the area dry  
- Use drying solutions like Burow solution or antiperspirant creams  
- Dry skin helps the infection heal and prevents it from coming back  
- If many skin folds are infected, doctors may give antifungal pills like fluconazole

### Vaginal Infection
- Use antifungal creams or suppositories inserted into the vagina  
- Or take antifungal pills like fluconazole by mouth

### Diaper Rash in Babies
- Change diapers more often  
- Use super-absorbent or ultra-absorbent diapers  
- Apply an antifungal cream to the skin  
- Common creams contain butoconazole, clotrimazole, fluconazole, ketoconazole, or miconazole

### Nail Infection
- Keep the area dry and protected from water  
- Use antifungal creams or take antifungal pills  
- These infections can be hard to treat and may take time to heal

### Thrush
- In adults:  
  - Use antifungal tablets or lozenges that dissolve in the mouth  
  - Gargle with liquid nystatin and either spit it out or swallow it  
  - Take antifungal pills like fluconazole  
- In babies:  
  - Use liquid nystatin  
  - Apply it with a finger or cotton swab to the inside of the cheeks

### Chronic Mucocutaneous Candidiasis
- Take fluconazole pills every day for a long time

## Prevention Tips

- Keep skin dry, especially in skin folds  
- Change clothes and diapers often  
- Avoid tight or synthetic clothing  
- Wash hands well, especially after using the bathroom  
- Avoid licking lips or sucking thumbs  
- Use proper dentures and keep them clean  
- If you take antibiotics, talk to your doctor about ways to prevent yeast infections

Always follow your doctor’s advice when treating candidiasis.

# Nasal Polyps

Nasal polyps are soft, non-cancerous growths inside the nose. They can block your nasal passages and cause discomfort.

## Symptoms

You may have nasal polyps if you notice:
- A blocked nose
- A runny nose
- Mucus slowly dripping down the back of your throat (postnasal drip)
- A weaker sense of smell or taste
- Snoring

These symptoms can feel like a cold. But colds usually go away in a few days. Nasal polyps do not get better on their own. They need treatment.

If the polyps block your sinuses, you may also have signs of sinus infection. These include facial pain, pressure, and thick mucus.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if you:
- Think you might have nasal polyps
- Have trouble breathing
- Notice your symptoms are getting worse
- See changes in your sense of smell

## Treatment

Your doctor can check your nose with a special tool. They will look for polyps.

Most people with nasal polyps are given steroid nose drops or a steroid spray. These help shrink the polyps.

Sometimes, your doctor may give you steroid tablets. These are usually taken for up to two weeks to reduce swelling.

Always follow your doctor’s instructions. Use the medicine as directed and for the full time they say.

### Surgery

If your symptoms do not improve after about 12 weeks, your doctor may suggest surgery.

Surgery removes the polyps. Most people feel better after surgery.

But polyps often grow back. This usually happens within a few years.

### After Surgery

You may need to keep using a steroid nasal spray after surgery. This helps stop polyps from coming back quickly.

## What You Can Do at Home

After seeing your doctor, a pharmacist can help you choose:
- A steroid nasal spray that does not need a prescription
- A salt water wash (also called a saline rinse or nasal douche) to clear your nose

### How to Make a Salt Water Wash at Home

1. In a clean bowl, mix 1 level teaspoon of salt and 1 level teaspoon of bicarbonate of soda.
2. Add about 1 pint of cooled boiled water.
3. Wash your hands before starting.
4. Stand over a sink. Cup your hand and pour a small amount of the mixture into it.
5. Sniff the mixture up one nostril. Let it come out the other side.
6. Repeat at least 3 times in each nostril, or until your nose feels clear.
7. You can gargle any leftover mixture to help clear mucus from the back of your throat.

Check the mixture is not too hot before using. Do not swallow it. It may make you feel sick.

Do not use this salt water wash for children.

## Causes

We do not fully understand what causes nasal polyps.

But some people are more likely to get them. This includes people who:
- Have asthma
- Are sensitive or allergic to aspirin

Nasal polyps are rare in children.

# Anal Cancer

## What Is Anal Cancer?

Anal cancer is a type of cancer that starts in the anus.  
The most common sign is bleeding when you pass stool.  
Other symptoms can include pain, a feeling that you still need to go to the bathroom, or a lump that can be felt during a rectal exam.  
Some people have no symptoms at all.

## How Common Is Anal Cancer?

In the United States, about 10,540 people are diagnosed with anal cancer each year.  
Around 2,190 people die from it each year.

## What Types of Anal Cancer Are There?

The most common type is squamous cell cancer.  
Other types include:
- Basal cell cancer  
- Bowen disease (a type of early skin cancer)  
- Extramammary Paget disease  
- Cloacogenic cancer  
- Malignant melanoma  
- Lymphoma  
- Various types of sarcoma  

Cancer can spread through the lymph system. It often moves to the lymph nodes in the groin.

## What Increases the Risk of Anal Cancer?

You are more likely to get anal cancer if you:
- Have a human papillomavirus infection, especially types 16 and 18  
- Have had anal sex  
- Have long-term anal fistulas (tunnels from the anus to the skin)  
- Have had radiation to the anal area  
- Have leukoplakia (white patches in the anus)  
- Have had lymphogranuloma venereum (a sexually transmitted infection)  
- Have HIV  
- Have genital warts (condyloma acuminatum)  
- Smoke cigarettes  

HPV infection is the biggest risk factor. It causes more than 80% of anal cancers.

## What Happens When HPV Causes Anal Cancer?

HPV can cause changes in the cells of the anus.  
These changes may look normal or slightly abnormal.  
They are called anal intraepithelial neoplasia.  
They are graded as I, II, or III.  
Higher grades are more likely to turn into cancer.  
People with HIV are more likely to have these changes.

A study called ANCHOR showed that treating high-grade changes can reduce the chance of getting anal cancer by 57%.  
The U.S. Department of Health supports screening for high-risk people, especially those with HIV.  
But major medical groups have not yet made formal screening recommendations.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The most common symptom is bleeding when you pass stool.  
Some people feel pain or pressure in the anus.  
Some feel they did not fully empty their bowels.  
Some have no symptoms at all.  
A lump may be felt during a rectal exam.

## How Is Anal Cancer Diagnosed?

A doctor will use a rigid anoscope to look inside the anus.  
This is a short, rigid tube with a light.  
A biopsy is done to confirm cancer.  
A small sample of tissue is taken and tested in a lab.

If you have other symptoms like changes in bowel habits or belly swelling, your doctor may do a flexible sigmoidoscopy, proctoscopy, or colonoscopy.  
These tests check the lower bowel or the whole colon.

If the cancer is near the edge of the anus, a skin biopsy may be needed.  
This is done by a dermatologist or surgeon.

Even if you have hemorrhoids or known diverticulosis, any rectal bleeding should be checked for cancer.

After diagnosis, imaging tests are done to see if the cancer has spread.  
These include:
- CT scan of the chest, belly, and pelvis  
- MRI scan  
- PET scan  

These tests help find cancer in other parts of the body.

## How Is Anal Cancer Treated?

The main treatment is a combination of chemotherapy and radiation therapy.  
This is called chemoradiation.  
It is used in most cases.  
It works well for squamous cell cancers of the anus.

Tumor shrinkage can continue for up to six months after treatment.  
It is okay to wait and watch during this time.  
Surgery is not needed right away if the cancer is shrinking.

Surgery is used only if:
- The cancer does not shrink completely after chemoradiation  
- The cancer comes back after treatment  

The surgery used is called abdominoperineal resection.  
It removes the anus and part of the rectum.  
A permanent colostomy is needed after this surgery.

# Unplanned Weight Loss

Unplanned weight loss means you are losing weight without trying. You are not on a diet or doing anything to lose weight.

Your weight can go up and down a little. This is normal. But doctors worry when you lose more than about 10 pounds (4 to 5 kilograms). Or if you are a smaller person, they worry if you lose 5% of your body weight. This kind of weight loss can be a sign of a serious health problem.

You may also have other symptoms. These can include not feeling hungry, fever, pain, or sweating at night. These signs may come from the illness causing the weight loss.

---

## What Can Cause Unplanned Weight Loss?

Most of the time, weight loss happens because you are not eating enough calories. Your body needs a certain number of calories to stay strong. If you take in fewer than your body needs, you lose weight.

There are a few reasons why you might eat less:

- You have less appetite.
- You have a problem in your gut that stops your body from absorbing nutrients. This is called malabsorption.

Sometimes, your body burns more calories than normal. For example, an overactive thyroid gland can cause this. In some cases, both problems happen at once. For example, cancer can make you lose your appetite and also make your body burn more energy. This leads to fast weight loss.

Almost any long-term serious illness can cause weight loss. Examples include severe heart failure or lung disease. But these conditions are usually already known before weight loss starts.

This guide focuses on weight loss that is the first sign of a new illness.

We can group the causes into two types:

- People who are hungry but still lose weight.
- People who are not hungry and eat less.

### If You Are Hungry But Still Losing Weight

The most common causes are:

- An overactive thyroid gland (hyperthyroidism).
- Uncontrolled diabetes.
- Problems in the gut that stop your body from absorbing nutrients (malabsorption).

### If You Are Not Hungry and Eat Less

The most common causes are:

- Emotional problems like depression.
- Cancer.
- Side effects from medicines.
- Drug use or addiction.

---

## When to See a Doctor

Because many different health problems can cause unplanned weight loss, doctors usually need to do a full check-up.

Some signs are serious and mean you should see a doctor right away. These include:

- Fever and night sweats.
- Bone pain.
- Trouble breathing, coughing, or coughing up blood.
- Feeling very thirsty and needing to urinate more.
- Headaches, jaw pain when chewing, or new vision problems (like double vision or blurry spots) in people over 50.

If you have any of these warning signs, see a doctor as soon as possible.

If you do not have these warning signs, you should still see a doctor when you can. Waiting a week or so is usually safe.

---

### What Happens at the Doctor’s Visit?

The doctor will ask you questions and do a physical exam.

They will want to know:

- How much weight you lost and how long it took.
- If your clothes fit looser.
- If you have less appetite or eat less.
- If you have trouble swallowing.
- If your bowel habits have changed.
- If you feel tired, unwell, have fevers, or sweat at night.
- If you have a history of any illness that causes weight loss.
- What medicines you take, including prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicines, herbal products, or illegal drugs.
- If your life has changed recently. For example, did you lose a loved one? Did you lose your job or independence? Do you no longer eat with others?

During the physical exam, the doctor will check:

- Your temperature, heart rate, breathing, and blood pressure.
- Your heart, lungs, stomach, head, neck, breasts, nervous system, rectum, genitals, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, joints, and skin.
- Your mood.

Your weight will be measured. Your body mass index (BMI) will be calculated. This number uses your height and weight to help assess your health.

---

### Common Causes and What Doctors Look For

| Cause | Common Signs | How Doctors Check |
|------|--------------|-------------------|
| Adrenal gland problems | Belly pain, tiredness, dark skin, dizziness | Blood tests |
| Alcohol use disorder | History of heavy drinking | Physical exam, liver tests |
| Anorexia nervosa | Fear of gaining weight, no periods in young women | Doctor’s exam, sometimes blood tests or heart test |
| Cancer | Night sweats, tiredness, fever | Tests based on where cancer might be |
| Depression | Sadness, low energy, low sex drive, trouble sleeping | Doctor’s exam |
| Diabetes (new or uncontrolled) | Hunger, thirst, more urination | Blood sugar test |
| Medicines or drugs | Amphetamines, cocaine, opioids, herbal or OTC products like caffeine, St. John’s wort, or weight-loss supplements | Review of what you take |
| Fungal infections (in lungs or body) | Fever, night sweats, cough, shortness of breath | Tests of sputum, blood, or tissue |
| Giant cell arteritis (in people over 50) | Headache, jaw pain, vision problems | Blood tests, ultrasound, or biopsy |
| Parasite infections (in gut) | Fever, belly pain, bloating, gas, diarrhea | Stool test |
| HIV (late stage) | Fever, cough, shortness of breath, swollen glands, diarrhea, fungal infections | Blood test |
| Kidney disease | Swelling in legs, tiredness, itchy skin, foamy urine | Blood and urine tests |
| Loss of taste | Often linked to nerve issues, certain medicines, or aging | Doctor’s exam |
| Malabsorption | Diarrhea, gas, oily stools | Stool tests |
| Dental problems | Tooth or gum pain, bad breath, missing or decayed teeth | Doctor’s exam |
| Sarcoidosis | Cough, shortness of breath, fever, tiredness, swollen glands | Chest X-ray, CT scan, biopsy |
| Heart valve infection | Fever, night sweats, joint pain, shortness of breath, tiredness | Blood cultures, heart ultrasound |
| Overactive thyroid | Hunger, heat intolerance, sweating, shaking, fast heartbeat, diarrhea | Blood tests |
| Tuberculosis | Fever, night sweats, cough, coughing up blood | Sputum test |

*Note: These signs are common but not always present. Some tests may be needed to confirm a diagnosis.*

---

### How Doctors Find the Cause

In about half of people, the doctor can guess the cause from symptoms and the physical exam.

Common tests include:

- Colonoscopy (for colon cancer).
- Mammogram (for breast cancer).

Other tests depend on what the doctor suspects.

If the doctor does not find a clear cause, they may do:

- A chest X-ray.
- Blood tests.
- Urine tests.

If these are normal, the doctor may repeat them in a few months to see if anything new shows up.

---

## How Is Unplanned Weight Loss Treated?

The main goal is to treat the underlying health problem.

To help you eat more, doctors may suggest:

- Encouraging you to eat.
- Helping you with meals.
- Offering foods you like or that have strong flavors.
- Giving small meals instead of large ones.

If these do not help, high-calorie drinks or food supplements may be used.

Tube feeding (feeding through a tube into the stomach) is only used in rare cases. It may help if the illness can be cured. But it may not be worth it if you are losing your ability to eat due to severe dementia.

---

## Special Considerations for Older Adults

Unplanned weight loss is more common in older adults. It affects up to 60% of people in nursing homes.

Older adults are more likely to lose weight because:

- They are more likely to have serious health problems.
- Normal aging changes can also cause weight loss.

Common age-related changes include:

- Less sensitivity to hunger signals.
- More sensitivity to signals that stop hunger.
- Slower stomach emptying (you feel full longer).
- Weaker sense of taste and smell.
- Loss of muscle mass (called sarcopenia).

Social isolation is also common. This can lead to eating less.

Depression and dementia are very common causes, especially in nursing homes.

Dental problems like gum disease or missing teeth become more common with age. These can make eating hard and affect digestion.

It is often hard to know which factor is the main cause.

Older adults may benefit from vitamin supplements, especially vitamin D and vitamin B12. But take them between meals or at bedtime. Otherwise, they may reduce your appetite at mealtime.

Help with shopping or feeding can also make a difference.

---

## Key Points

- Losing more than 10 pounds or 5% of your body weight over a few months is a red flag.
- Doctors use your symptoms and exam results to decide what tests to do.
- You usually do not need many tests to find the cause.

# Bird Flu

## What Are the Symptoms?

Bird flu can cause a high temperature.  
You may have a cough.  
You might feel short of breath.  
Your eyes may become red and sore.  

Other possible symptoms include:  
- A sore throat  
- A runny or blocked nose  
- Wheezing or sneezing  

Symptoms usually start about 4 to 6 days after contact with an infected bird.

## How Do You Get Bird Flu?

You can catch bird flu from close contact with infected birds.  
This includes touching the droppings of a sick bird.  
You can also get it from touching a dead bird that is infected.

Bird flu is found in many parts of the world, including the UK.  
Most human cases have happened in Asia and North Africa.

## What Should You Do If You Think You Have Bird Flu?

Call NHS 111 if you have bird flu symptoms and:  
- You have been near a bird in a country where bird flu is known to be present.  
- You have been near someone who has bird flu.

You can call 111 or get help online at 111.nhs.uk.

Call 999 if you are having serious trouble breathing.  
This means you are gasping, choking, or cannot speak.

## How Is Bird Flu Treated?

Doctors can treat bird flu with antiviral medicines.  
These medicines help your body fight the virus.

If you are very ill, machines can help you breathe.  
These machines support your lungs until you get better.

People who have been close to you may also be tested and treated.  
This helps stop the virus from spreading.

# Deep Vein Blood Clots (DVT)

A deep vein blood clot, or DVT, is a clot that forms in a deep vein. It usually happens in the leg, especially in the calf or thigh. It can also happen in the pelvis. DVT is the main cause of a lung clot, called pulmonary embolism.

DVT can happen when blood flow slows down, when the lining of a vein is damaged, or when the blood is more likely to clot than normal.

Some people with DVT have no symptoms. Others may feel pain or swelling in the leg or arm. A lung clot can happen right away. This is a serious problem.

Doctors check for DVT by asking about your symptoms and doing a physical exam. They confirm the diagnosis with a test called duplex ultrasonography. This test uses sound waves to look at blood flow in the veins.

Sometimes, a blood test called D-Dimer is used. If the result is normal, DVT is very unlikely. If the result is high, it does not mean you have DVT. More tests are needed to be sure.

Treatment is with blood thinners. These medicines help stop the clot from getting bigger and prevent new clots. With early and proper treatment, most people do well.

Long-term problems can include poor blood flow in the leg. This may cause swelling, pain, or skin changes. This is called post-thrombotic syndrome.

---

## Where DVT Usually Happens

DVT most often occurs in the legs or pelvis. It is rare in the arms (less than 5% of cases).

### Deep Veins in the Legs

- Clots in the upper leg (femoral or popliteal veins) are more likely to break off and travel to the lungs.
- About 90% of large clots are in the upper leg.
- About 10% of large clots are in the pelvis and upper leg.
- Clots in the lower leg (calf veins) are smaller. They are less likely to cause a lung clot. But they can grow and move up into the upper leg and cause a lung clot.
- About half of people with DVT also have a hidden lung clot.
- At least 30% of people with a lung clot have a DVT.

> **Important:** About half of people with DVT have a hidden lung clot.

---

## What Causes DVT?

Many things can raise your risk of DVT. These include:

- Cancer, especially lung, ovarian, stomach, brain, or pancreatic cancer
- Recent surgery or injury
- Long periods of not moving (like after surgery or during long travel)
- Blood that clots too easily
- Certain medical conditions

Cancer can increase the risk of DVT. In some cases, a hidden cancer may be the cause of a DVT with no clear reason. But doctors do not test everyone for cancer unless there are other warning signs.

---

## How DVT Develops

DVT usually starts in the small valves inside the veins. The clot is made of blood cells, clotting proteins, and a substance called thrombin. It has few platelets. Without treatment, the clot can grow or break off and travel to the lungs.

### Lower Leg DVT
Most often caused by:
- Not moving for a long time (like after surgery)
- Injury to the leg (like a broken bone)
- Blood that clots too easily

### Upper Leg or Arm DVT
Most often caused by:
- Damage to the vein from a tube (like a central line or pacemaker)
- Drug use (injection drugs)
- A tumor pressing on a large vein in the chest (superior vena cava syndrome)
- A tight space in the chest (thoracic outlet syndrome)
- Strenuous arm activity (rare, called effort thrombosis or Paget-Schroetter syndrome)

---

## Symptoms of DVT

DVT can happen in people who are walking around or in those who are sick or recovering from surgery.

In hospitalized patients, most clots start in the small veins of the calf. These clots often cause no symptoms and may go unnoticed.

When symptoms do appear, they can include:
- Aching or soreness in the leg or arm
- Tenderness along the vein
- Swelling in the leg or arm
- Redness or warmth in the area
- Veins under the skin that look bigger or feel hard

A sign called Homans sign (pain when you pull your foot up) may happen. But it is not reliable. It can be present in other conditions.

The most useful signs are:
- Swelling in the whole leg
- A difference of more than 3 centimeters in calf size (measured 10 cm above the ankle)
- Swelling that leaves an indentation when pressed (pitting edema)
- Visible or hard-to-feel enlarged veins

If you have three or more of these signs and no other likely cause, DVT is likely.

A low-grade fever can also happen. DVT may be the reason for a fever with no clear cause, especially after surgery.

If a lung clot happens, symptoms may include:
- Shortness of breath
- Sharp chest pain that gets worse when you breathe

---

### How Likely Is DVT? (Based on Symptoms)

| Symptom | How it helps |
|--------|-------------|
| Tenderness along the vein | Increases chance |
| Swelling in the whole leg | Increases chance |
| Calf swelling (more than 3 cm difference) | Increases chance |
| Pitting edema (indentation from pressure) | Increases chance |
| Dilated surface veins | Increases chance |
| Active cancer (treatment now or in past 6 months) | Increases chance |
| Immobilized leg (paralysis, cast, long travel) | Increases chance |
| Surgery causing immobility in past 4 weeks | Increases chance |

**Score:**
- 3 or more points = High chance of DVT
- 1 or 2 points = Moderate chance
- 0 points = Low chance

If another condition is just as likely, subtract 2 points.

---

## Conditions That Feel Like DVT

### Swelling in One Leg (Not DVT)
- Injury to soft tissue (like a sprain)
- Skin infection (cellulitis)
- Pressure on a pelvic vein
- Blocked lymph vessel in the pelvis
- A Baker’s cyst (a fluid-filled lump behind the knee) that blocks blood flow

### Swelling in Both Legs
- Some medicines (like certain blood pressure drugs, estrogen, or strong painkillers)
- Heart problems (especially right side)
- Low protein in the blood

### Calf Pain That Is Not DVT
- Poor blood flow in the leg (venous insufficiency)
- Skin infection (cellulitis)
- A burst Baker’s cyst (causes swelling, pain, and bruising)
- Torn muscle or tendon in the calf

---

## How DVT Is Diagnosed

### Ultrasound Test
This is the main test. It uses sound waves to see blood flow and check for clots. It is safe and painless.

### D-Dimer Blood Test
This test checks for a substance released when a clot breaks down. A normal result means DVT is very unlikely. A high result does not mean you have DVT. It can be high for other reasons. So more testing is needed.

### How Doctors Decide What to Test
Doctors first look at your symptoms and risk factors. Then they decide if you need an ultrasound or a blood test.

There is no single best testing plan. One common approach is shown in the figure "One Approach to Testing for Suspected DVT."

---

## How DVT Is Treated

### Blood Thinners
This is the main treatment. It helps prevent the clot from growing and stops new clots from forming.

- Treatment starts with an injection (heparin) — either standard or low-molecular-weight.
- Then you take a daily pill (like warfarin, dabigatran, or a factor Xa inhibitor).
- Or you can take a pill like rivaroxaban or apixaban for the whole treatment.

### Other Treatments (Rarely Needed)
- A filter in the large vein in the abdomen (inferior vena cava filter) — used only if you cannot take blood thinners or if clots keep coming back.
- Clot-busting drugs (thrombolytics) — used only in serious cases.
- Surgery — very rare.

### Supportive Care
- Use pain medicine as needed. Short-term use of NSAIDs (like ibuprofen) may help. But do not use them long-term — they can increase bleeding risk.
- Keep your leg raised when sitting or lying down. Use a pillow to support it. This helps reduce swelling.
- Move around as much as you can. Early movement does not increase the risk of a lung clot. It may help prevent long-term leg problems.

---

## Outlook for DVT

Without treatment, about 3% of people with leg DVT will die from a lung clot. This is rare with arm DVT.

Risk of another DVT is lowest after surgery or injury. It is highest if you have cancer, a DVT with no clear cause, or if a clot did not fully go away.

A normal D-Dimer test done 3 to 4 weeks after stopping blood thinners may mean a lower risk of another clot. This is more true in women than men.

It is hard to predict who will have long-term leg problems. Risk factors include:
- Clot in the upper leg
- Another DVT in the same leg
- Body mass index of 22 or higher

---

## How to Prevent DVT

# Shock

Shock is a serious medical emergency. It happens when blood flow to the body’s organs drops too low. This means organs do not get enough oxygen. Without oxygen, organs can stop working. If not treated quickly, shock can lead to death.

Most people with shock have low blood pressure. But blood pressure may not be low in the very early stages.

> **Did you know?**  
> Shock has nothing to do with sudden emotional stress. This is not the same as feeling shocked by bad news.

---

## What Causes Shock?

Shock can happen for several reasons:

- Losing too much blood  
- The heart not pumping well  
- Blood vessels becoming too wide (dilated)

### Low Blood Volume (Hypovolemic Shock)

This happens when there is not enough blood in the body. Causes include:

- Severe bleeding from an injury  
- Bleeding inside the body, such as from a stomach ulcer or a ruptured blood vessel  
- A pregnancy outside the uterus (ectopic pregnancy)  
- Severe burns  
- Bad vomiting or diarrhea  
- Pancreatitis (inflammation of the pancreas)  
- Kidney problems  
- Overuse of water pills (diuretics)  
- Untreated diabetes  
- Not drinking enough fluids, especially if someone has a physical or mental disability

### Heart Not Pumping Well (Cardiogenic Shock)

This happens when the heart cannot push blood out properly. Causes include:

- A heart attack  
- A blood clot in the lungs  
- A sudden problem with a heart valve (especially an artificial one)  
- An irregular heartbeat  
- Infection in the heart muscle or valves  
- Fluid building up around the heart (cardiac tamponade)  
- A tear in the heart wall

### Blood Vessels Too Wide (Distributive Shock)

This happens when blood vessels open up too much. This lowers blood pressure and reduces blood flow. Causes include:

- A severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis)  
- A serious bacterial infection (septic shock)  
- Overdose of certain drugs or poisons  
- Injury to the spinal cord or brain (neurogenic shock)  
- Hormone problems, such as adrenal insufficiency

---

## What Are the Symptoms of Shock?

Symptoms depend on the cause.

### If Shock Is Caused by Low Blood Volume or Poor Heart Pumping

- You feel tired, sleepy, or confused  
- Your skin feels cold and sweaty  
- Your skin looks pale, bluish, or gray  
- When you press your skin, it takes longer than normal to return to its normal color  
- Your pulse is weak and fast  
- You feel dizzy or faint when you try to sit up  
- You breathe fast  
- In later stages, breathing and pulse slow down  
- Urine output drops and may stop  
- You may fall into a coma and die if not treated

### If Shock Is Caused by Blood Vessels That Are Too Wide

- Your skin feels warm and red  
- Your pulse feels strong and fast (bounding)  
- Later, the skin becomes cold and sweaty, and you feel weak

In the early stages of shock—especially septic shock—some people may have no obvious symptoms. The only sign might be confusion, especially in older adults. Urine output may drop. Waste products may build up in the blood. Blood pressure may be low.

---

## How Is Shock Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose shock by checking your symptoms and doing tests.

### What Doctors Look For

- You are not alert or confused  
- You are not making urine  
- Your fingers or toes are blue  
- You have a fast heartbeat  
- You are breathing fast  
- You are sweating a lot

### Blood Tests

These help doctors understand what is happening:

- **Lactate test:** High levels mean your organs are not getting enough oxygen  
- **White blood cell count:** High or low levels can suggest infection  
- **Blood cultures:** To check for bacteria or other germs  
- **Kidney function test:** High creatinine means kidneys are damaged  
- **Heart damage test:** High troponin means the heart is injured

### Other Tests

Depending on the likely cause, doctors may do:

- Chest X-ray to check for pneumonia  
- CT scan to look for infection in the belly  
- Heart tests like EKG or imaging to check for heart problems

---

## How Is Shock Treated?

Shock is a medical emergency. You must get help right away.

### Immediate Steps

- Call emergency services immediately  
- Stop any major bleeding  
- Lay the person down  
- Keep them warm  
- Raise their legs above heart level

### In the Emergency Room

- Oxygen is given through a mask or breathing tube  
- Fluids are given through a vein (IV) very fast and in large amounts  
- If there is severe bleeding, a blood transfusion may be needed  
- Type O negative blood can be given quickly if there is no time to match blood type

### Medications

Doctors may give medicines to raise blood pressure. These are used only for a short time because they can cause side effects.

Medicines can:

- Tighten blood vessels (e.g., epinephrine, norepinephrine)  
- Help the heart pump better (e.g., dobutamine, milrinone)

### Treating the Underlying Cause

- **Heart attack:** Procedures like angioplasty or bypass surgery may be needed  
- **Damaged heart valve or heart wall tear:** Surgery may be required  
- **Fluid around the heart (cardiac tamponade):** A needle or surgery removes the fluid  
- **Infection (sepsis):** Antibiotics and surgery to remove the source of infection  
- **Bleeding:** Surgery to stop the bleeding  
- **Allergic reaction (anaphylaxis):** Steroid medicine may be given  
- **Hormone problems (e.g., adrenal insufficiency):** Steroid medicine may be given

---

## What Is the Outlook for Shock?

Shock is life-threatening. If not treated, it usually leads to death.

If treatment is given, recovery depends on:

- What caused the shock  
- The person’s age  
- Other health problems they have  
- How many organs are failing  
- How long it took to get treatment  
- What kind of treatment was given

If two or more organs stop working, this is called **multiple organ dysfunction syndrome**. This condition has a high risk of death. The more organs that fail, the higher the risk.

Even with treatment, the chance of death is high after a major heart attack or severe infection (septic shock), especially in older adults.

---

> **Key Takeaway:**  
> Shock is not the same as emotional shock. It is a serious medical emergency. If you suspect someone is in shock, call for help immediately. Do not wait.

# Aspergillosis

Aspergillosis is a lung condition caused by breathing in tiny pieces of a type of mould. This mould is common in soil, compost, dust, damp buildings, and air conditioning systems.

## What Causes Aspergillosis

You get aspergillosis by breathing in mould spores. The mould is found in:

- Soil
- Compost
- Rotting leaves
- Plants, trees, and crops
- Dust
- Bedding
- Damp buildings
- Air conditioning systems

You cannot catch this condition from another person or from animals.

## Symptoms

You may have:

- Trouble breathing
- A cough that brings up blood or thick mucus
- Wheezing
- A high temperature
- Unexplained weight loss
- Feeling very tired

If you already have a lung problem, your symptoms may get worse.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if you have:

- A cough that lasts more than three weeks
- A lung condition that is getting worse or harder to manage
- A weak immune system and symptoms of aspergillosis

Call 111 or get help online if you:

- Cough up blood

## What Happens at the Doctor’s

It can take time to diagnose aspergillosis. Your doctor will check if your symptoms are caused by something else, like a chest infection.

If your doctor is unsure, they may refer you to a specialist. The specialist may do tests such as:

- X-rays or scans of your chest
- Blood tests or tests on mucus from your lungs
- Allergy tests
- A bronchoscopy (a thin tube with a camera is used to look inside your lungs)

## Treatment

Treatment depends on the type of aspergillosis you have. It often aims to control your symptoms.

You may need to take:

- Steroid tablets
- Antifungal medicines

Some people need surgery.

Treatment can last for years or even your whole life.

If it is not treated well, it can damage your lungs.

## How to Lower Your Risk

You cannot avoid all mould, but you can reduce your risk, especially if you have a lung condition or a weak immune system.

### Do These Things

- Avoid places with lots of mould, like compost heaps and piles of dead leaves
- Open your windows several times a day to let fresh air in, especially when cooking or showering
- Wear a face mask when gardening or in dusty places
- Use a dehumidifier and an air purifier with a HEPA filter at home
- Keep your home between 18 and 21 degrees Celsius during cold weather

### Avoid These Things

- Do not dry clothes in your bedroom or living room. Dry them outside or in a tumble dryer
- Do not open windows if there is construction or digging nearby

These steps can help protect your lungs and lower your risk of getting aspergillosis.

# Altitude Illness

Altitude illness happens when you go to high places too quickly. At high altitudes, the air has less oxygen. This can make you feel sick.

## What Causes Altitude Illness?

As you go higher, the air pressure drops. The amount of oxygen in the air stays the same, but there is less oxygen in each breath.  
At 5,800 meters (19,000 feet), the oxygen level is about half of what it is at sea level.  
On the top of Mount Everest, it is only about one-third of the sea level amount.

Most people can climb to 1,500 to 2,000 meters (5,000 to 6,500 feet) in one day without getting sick.  
But about 25 out of 100 people who go to 2,500 meters (8,000 feet) get some form of altitude illness.  
At 4,340 meters (14,000 feet), about 40 out of 100 people get sick.  
Some groups, like religious pilgrims in Nepal or climbers on Mount Kilimanjaro, have even higher rates.  
This is often because they climb too fast.  
The highest place you sleep and how fast you climb are the biggest risks.

## Types of Altitude Illness

### Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS)
This is the mildest form.  
It causes a headache plus at least one of these:  
- Feeling very tired  
- Stomach problems like nausea or vomiting  
- Dizziness that does not go away  

AMS can happen to hikers, skiers, climbers, and anyone going to high altitudes.

### High-Altitude Cerebral Edema (HACE)
This is a serious brain problem.  
It happens when the brain swells.  
Symptoms include:  
- Severe headache  
- Trouble walking straight (loss of balance)  
- Confusion or changes in behavior  
- In severe cases, coma or death  

### High-Altitude Pulmonary Edema (HAPE)
This is a serious lung problem.  
It happens when fluid builds up in the lungs.  
Symptoms include:  
- Hard time breathing, even when resting  
- Feeling very weak  
- Dry cough that may turn into coughing up pink or bloody mucus  
- Lips or fingernails turning blue (cyanosis)  

HACE and HAPE are life-threatening. They need fast treatment.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose altitude illness based on your symptoms and what you have been doing.  
They will ask about your climb and check your body.  
Tests are not always needed, especially in remote areas.

For HAPE, doctors may use:  
- A chest X-ray to see fluid in the lungs  
- A pulse oximeter to check how much oxygen is in your blood  

For HACE, doctors may use brain scans (CT or MRI) if they are not sure.  
These scans can show brain swelling.  
Some signs, like small bleeds in the brain, can stay for months after the illness.

The Lake Louise Score is a tool used in research. It is not usually used in real-life medical care.

## How Is It Treated?

### For Mild or Moderate AMS:
- Stop climbing higher  
- Drink plenty of fluids  
- Take pain medicine like acetaminophen or ibuprofen  
- Sometimes take acetazolamide or dexamethasone  

### For Severe AMS:
- Go down right away  
- Drink fluids  
- Take pain medicine  
- Take acetazolamide or dexamethasone  

### For HACE or HAPE:
- Go down immediately  
- Use extra oxygen if available  
- Take medicine: dexamethasone for HACE, nifedipine or other similar drugs for HAPE  
- Use a pressure bag (if available) to help simulate lower altitude  

## How Can It Be Prevented?

- Climb slowly. Do not go higher than 300 meters (1,000 feet) per day after 2,500 meters (8,000 feet).  
- Take a rest day every 3 to 4 days when climbing above 2,500 meters.  
- Sometimes take medicine before and during the climb:  
  - Acetazolamide  
  - Dexamethasone  

Being fit does not protect you from altitude illness.  
Drinking water helps avoid dehydration. But it does not prevent AMS.  
Dehydration feels like AMS, so staying hydrated helps you tell the difference.  
Avoid strong painkillers (like opioids), sleeping pills, and heavy drinking, especially before bed.

## Key Facts

- About 20 out of 100 people who go to 2,500 meters (8,000 feet) in one day get altitude illness.  
- About 40 out of 100 people who go to 3,000 meters (10,000 feet) in one day get it.  
- The most common type is acute mountain sickness (AMS).  
- AMS causes headache plus tiredness, stomach issues, or dizziness.  
- HACE causes headache, loss of balance, and confusion.  
- HAPE causes shortness of breath, weakness, and coughing up blood.  
- Always treat symptoms early.  
- If you have HACE, HAPE, or very bad AMS, go down right away.  
- Prevent illness by climbing slowly and using medicine if needed.

# Croup

Croup is a condition that causes swelling in the windpipe and voice box.  
It is usually caused by a virus that spreads easily.  
The main symptoms are a cough, a loud squeaky sound when breathing in, and trouble breathing.

## What Causes Croup?

Croup is caused by a virus.  
The most common virus is called parainfluenza virus.  
Other viruses, like RSV or the flu virus, can also cause croup.  
Croup from the flu virus can be more serious and may affect older children too.  
The virus spreads through the air when someone coughs or sneezes.  
It can also spread by touching objects that have the virus on them.

Croup is most common in children between 6 months and 3 years old.  
Most children have only one episode of croup.  
Some children have repeated episodes, especially at night.  
These are called spasmodic croup.  
This type may be linked to allergies or sensitive airways, like in asthma.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Croup often starts like a cold.  
You may see a runny nose, sneezing, and a mild fever.  
Then the child gets a hoarse voice and a cough that sounds like a bark.  
This cough is loud and unusual.

The illness can be mild or very serious.  
In bad cases, the child has trouble breathing in.  
You may hear a loud squeaking noise with each breath in.  
This is called stridor.

About half of children have a fever.  
Symptoms are usually worse at night.  
They may wake up from sleep.  
In the morning, symptoms often get better.  
But they come back worse the next night.

The worst symptoms last 3 to 4 days.  
The cough then changes to a looser sound.  
This can worry parents.  
But it is normal and means the illness is getting better.

## How Is Croup Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose croup by listening to the child’s cough and breathing.  
The sound of the cough is a key clue.  
Sometimes, a doctor may take an x-ray of the neck or chest.  
This helps confirm the diagnosis.

## How Is Croup Treated?

For mild croup at home:
- Give plenty of fluids.
- Keep the child calm and resting.
- Use a cool-mist humidifier or run a hot shower to add moisture to the air.
- Take the child outside for cold night air, or to the kitchen to breathe cold air from the freezer.  
  These steps are safe and may help ease breathing.

For more serious croup:
- The child may need to go to the hospital.
- They may get oxygen through a mask or tube.
- They may get medicine called epinephrine through a nebulizer.  
  This helps reduce swelling in the airways.
- They may get a corticosteroid medicine by mouth or injection.  
  This also helps reduce swelling.

If a child has trouble breathing, a fast heartbeat, looks very tired, is dehydrated, or has blue or gray skin, they need urgent care.  
They will get oxygen and fluids through a vein.

Most children improve with treatment and can go home.  
Some children stay in the hospital if they are very sick.

Antibiotics are not used for croup.  
They only help if a bacterial infection develops, which is rare.  
In very severe cases, a child may need a breathing machine called a ventilator.

## What Is the Outlook?

Most children with croup get better completely.  
They do not have long-term problems.  
Croup is usually not dangerous if treated early.

# Bowel Cancer

Bowel cancer is when abnormal cells grow in the large bowel. It can cause several noticeable changes in your body.

## Symptoms of Bowel Cancer

You may have bowel cancer if you notice any of these signs:

- Your poo changes. It may become softer, or you may have more diarrhea or constipation than usual.
- You need to go to the toilet more or less often than you normally do.
- You see blood in your poo. It can be bright red or dark, almost black.
- You bleed from your bottom.
- You feel like you need to go to the toilet, even right after you’ve just gone.
- You have pain in your tummy.
- You can feel a lump in your tummy.
- Your tummy feels bloated or full.
- You lose weight without trying to.
- You feel very tired or out of breath. This can be a sign of anaemia, which can happen if bowel cancer causes slow bleeding.

## Tests and Next Steps

If your doctor thinks you might have bowel cancer, they will refer you to a specialist.

The main test is called a colonoscopy. A doctor uses a thin, flexible tube with a camera to look inside your bowel.

The test may feel uncomfortable, but it should not hurt. You will be given medicine to help you relax and reduce pain.

During the test, the doctor may take a small sample of tissue from your bowel. This is called a biopsy. It will be tested in a lab to check for cancer.

## Treatment for Bowel Cancer

Your treatment will depend on several things:

- How big the cancer is.
- Where the cancer is — in the colon, the rectum, or both.
- Whether it has spread to other parts of your body.
- If the cancer has certain genetic changes.
- Your age and overall health.

You may have more than one type of treatment. These can include:

- Surgery to remove the cancer.
- Chemotherapy to kill cancer cells.
- Radiotherapy to shrink the cancer.
- Targeted medicines that attack specific parts of cancer cells.
- Immunotherapy to help your body’s immune system fight the cancer.

Your specialist team will:

- Explain each treatment, including the benefits and possible side effects.
- Work with you to create a treatment plan that fits your needs.
- Help you manage any side effects you may have.

You can always ask questions or share your concerns with your specialist team.

## Causes of Bowel Cancer

We do not always know what causes bowel cancer. But some things can increase your risk.

You are more likely to get bowel cancer if:

- You are over 50 years old.
- You smoke.
- You are overweight.
- A close family member, like a parent or sibling, has had bowel cancer.
- You have inflammatory bowel disease. This includes Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis.
- You have small growths in your bowel called polyps.
- You have a rare inherited condition like Lynch Syndrome or familial adenomatous polyposis.

# Metabolic Dysfunction–Associated Liver Disease (MASLD)

## What Is MASLD?

MASLD is a condition where fat builds up in the liver.  
It was once called fatty liver or nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).  
The new name better reflects that this condition is linked to overall poor metabolic health, not just being overweight.

MASLD happens when fat collects in liver cells.  
This can happen in people who have at least one metabolic risk factor.  
Metabolic risk factors include:  
- Being overweight or obese  
- High blood pressure  
- High blood sugar or type 2 diabetes  
- High levels of fat in the blood (dyslipidemia)  
- Metabolic syndrome (a group of conditions that raise the risk of heart disease and diabetes)

People with MASLD usually drink little or no alcohol.  
The condition is not caused by drinking too much alcohol.

## What Is MASH?

MASH is a more serious form of MASLD.  
It means the liver has fat and also has signs of inflammation and damage to liver cells.  
MASH was once called nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH).

MASH can lead to scarring in the liver (fibrosis).  
Over time, this scarring can become severe and lead to cirrhosis.  
Cirrhosis can cause liver failure or liver cancer.

## How Is MASLD Diagnosed?

Most people with MASLD do not have symptoms.  
So, the condition is often found by chance during tests for other health problems.

To diagnose MASLD, doctors look for:
- Fat in the liver (seen on imaging tests or confirmed by biopsy)
- At least one metabolic risk factor
- Low alcohol use (less than 2 drinks a day for women, less than 3 for men)
- No signs of hepatitis B or C (checked with blood tests)

Common tests include:
- Ultrasound, CT scan, or MRI to see fat in the liver
- Blood tests to check liver function and rule out other liver diseases
- Tests to check for diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol

A liver biopsy is the most accurate way to confirm the diagnosis.  
But it is not always needed.  
Noninvasive tests like elastography (a type of ultrasound that measures liver stiffness) can help check for scarring.

## What Causes MASLD?

The exact cause is not fully known.  
But it is strongly linked to insulin resistance.  
Insulin resistance means the body does not use insulin well.  
This leads to more fat being stored in the liver.

Other possible causes include:
- Too much fat being made in the liver
- Poor removal of fat from the liver
- Genetic differences in how the body handles fat
- Changes in how the liver makes uric acid

Inflammation in the liver can lead to scarring.  
If scarring gets worse, it can lead to cirrhosis.  
Cirrhosis can cause serious problems like liver failure or liver cancer.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people with MASLD have no symptoms.  
Some may feel tired or unwell.  
Some may have a dull ache in the upper right side of the belly.

If the liver becomes severely scarred, signs may include:
- A swollen liver (felt during a physical exam)
- A swollen spleen (can be a sign of high pressure in the liver’s blood vessels)
- Low blood counts (due to pressure in the liver’s blood vessels)

People with cirrhosis may not have any obvious symptoms at first.

## How Is MASLD Treated?

The main treatment is to fix the underlying causes and risk factors.  
This includes:
- Losing weight (even a small amount helps)
- Eating a healthy diet
- Getting regular physical activity
- Controlling blood sugar, blood pressure, and cholesterol levels
- Stopping harmful medications or toxins

If you have moderate to severe scarring (F2 to F3), your doctor may prescribe a medicine called resmetirom.  
This medicine helps reduce fat and inflammation in the liver.  
It can also improve scarring in some people.

Other medicines like vitamin E or thiazolidinediones may help in some cases.  
But they are not always safe or effective.  
High-dose vitamin E is not safe for people with diabetes.

Many other treatments (like metformin, metronidazole, or special supplements) have not been proven to work.

New treatments are being studied.  
These include medicines that target different parts of the body’s metabolism.  
They may help reverse liver damage and scarring.

## What Is the Outlook?

The most important factor in predicting the future is how much scarring is in the liver.  
Scarring is the only sign that links to serious liver problems or the need for a liver transplant.

Simple fat in the liver (without inflammation or scarring) can stay stable or improve.  
But in some people, it can turn into MASH.

About 12 to 40 out of 100 people with MASLD will develop MASH over time.  
About 10 out of 100 people with MASLD will develop cirrhosis over 20 years.

Even small amounts of alcohol can make the disease worse.  
So, it is best to avoid alcohol completely.

If complications happen—like bleeding from enlarged veins in the esophagus (variceal hemorrhage)—the outlook becomes more serious.

## Key Points

- MASLD means fat in the liver linked to poor metabolic health.  
- MASH means fat in the liver with inflammation and damage.  
- Most people have no symptoms.  
- Diagnosis is based on fat in the liver, metabolic risk factors, and low alcohol use.  
- Blood tests and imaging can help confirm the diagnosis.  
- A liver biopsy is the most accurate test but is not always needed.  
- Treatment focuses on lifestyle changes and managing risk factors.  
- A medicine called resmetirom may help in some cases with moderate to severe scarring.  
- Avoid alcohol, even in small amounts.  
- The long-term outlook is usually good unless serious complications develop.
