# Spondylolisthesis

Spondylolisthesis means one of the bones in your lower back moves out of place.  
This can happen because of an injury or a long-term condition.  
You may feel pain in your lower back.  
The pain can also go down one or both legs.  
Doctors use imaging tests to confirm the diagnosis.  
Treatment focuses on reducing pain and stabilizing the spine.

## What Is the Spine?

Your spine is made of bones stacked on top of each other.  
These bones are called vertebrae.  
In spondylolisthesis, a vertebra in the lower back slips forward.  
This usually happens during the teenage years or young adulthood.  
It is often seen in athletes.  
It can be caused by a birth defect or an injury that breaks part of the bone.  
If both sides of the bone are damaged, the bone can slide forward over the one below it.  
In older adults, spondylolisthesis often happens because the discs between the bones wear down or because of joint arthritis.  
People who get this condition as adults may also develop narrowing of the spinal canal, called lumbar spinal stenosis.

## Symptoms

Mild cases may not cause any pain, especially in young people.  
When pain happens in teens, it usually affects only one side of the back.  
It may go down one leg.  
This pain can be linked to a broken bone.  
When adults have pain, it is usually felt in a specific spot on the lower back.  
It can go down both legs.  
This type of pain comes from a long-term condition.  
Standing up or leaning backward makes the pain worse.  
You may also feel numbness or weakness in your legs.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use imaging tests to find out if you have spondylolisthesis.  
X-rays of the lower back are the most common test.  
Sometimes, doctors use MRI or CT scans to get more detail.

## How Is It Treated?

### Rest and Sleep

Resting in bed for one to two days may help ease the pain.  
Staying in bed longer weakens your core muscles and makes your back stiffer.  
This can make pain worse and slow recovery.  
Sleep on a mattress that feels comfortable.  
If you sleep on your back, place a pillow under your knees.  
If you sleep on your side, use a pillow to keep your head in a neutral position.  
Place another pillow between your knees. Bend your hips and knees slightly if this helps your back.  
You can sleep on your stomach if it feels comfortable.

### Pain Relief

You can use cold packs or heating pads to help with pain.  
Over-the-counter pain medicines like acetaminophen or NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen) may help.  
Some people benefit from medicines that ease nerve pain. These include gabapentin, certain antiseizure drugs, or some antidepressants.  
If the pain is severe or does not go away, your doctor may prescribe oral corticosteroids or inject them into the space around the spinal cord.

### Physical Therapy

Exercises that strengthen and stretch your core muscles (belly, buttocks, and back) can help.  
These exercises support your spine and reduce pain.  
(See also: Low Back Pain: Prevention.)

# Skin Abscess

A skin abscess is a lump under your skin that holds pus.  
Pus is a thick fluid made of dead cells and bacteria.  

The lump is often round.  
It usually hurts when you touch it.  
It feels warm to the touch.  
The center of the lump may feel soft.

You may need to see a doctor to have the abscess treated.  
The doctor might drain the pus.  
You may also be given antibiotics.

## When to see a doctor

See your doctor if you have:

- A lump that is growing bigger  
- A lump that stays for more than two weeks  
- A hard lump that does not move when you press it  
- A lump or swelling in your breast  
- A lump and you have a weak immune system or a long-term health problem like diabetes  

Your doctor will check what is causing the lump.  
They will decide if you need treatment.

## When to get urgent help

Call your doctor right away or use NHS 111 if you have:

- A painful, red, or hot lump  
- A fever or chills  
- Redness or swelling spreading from the lump  
- Redness that is hard to see on brown or black skin  

You can call 111 or get help online at NHS 111.

## What a skin abscess looks like

A skin abscess is a lump or swelling under the skin.  
It can appear anywhere on your body.  
There are different types of abscesses.

The lump is often round.  
It feels sore and warm.  
The middle may feel soft.  
Pus may come out of the lump.  
You might have a high temperature.

On white skin, the abscess often looks red.  
On brown or black skin, the redness may be harder to see.

## How skin abscesses are treated

Treatment depends on the type of abscess.

The doctor may need to drain the pus.  
This means making a small cut in the skin.  
This lets the pus come out.  
You may get a local anaesthetic to numb the area.  
This means you will not feel pain during the procedure.

You may also be given antibiotics.  
These help fight the infection.

## What causes skin abscesses

Most skin abscesses are caused by an infection.

Bacteria live on your skin all the time.  
They usually do not cause harm.  
But sometimes bacteria get into your skin through a cut or a hair follicle.  
This can lead to pus forming and an abscess developing.

You are more likely to get a skin abscess if you:

- Smoke  
- Are overweight  
- Have diabetes  
- Are between 15 and 40 years old  
- Have a skin condition like eczema or skin inflammation

# Mallet Finger

Mallet finger is a condition where the tip of the finger bends down and cannot straighten on its own.  
It happens when the tendon that straightens the fingertip is torn or pulled off the bone.  
Sometimes, a piece of bone is also pulled off with the tendon.

## How It Happens

Most often, the injury occurs when the fingertip is hit hard by a ball.  
This force pushes the fingertip down too far.  
The tendon that pulls the fingertip up can tear away from the bone.  
The tear may include a small piece of bone from the end of the finger.

## Symptoms

The finger hurts right after the injury.  
It may swell and turn bruised.  
Sometimes, blood collects under the fingernail.  
This is called a subungual hematoma.

The tip of the finger stays bent down.  
You cannot straighten it on your own.  
But someone else can gently push it straight.  
This usually does not hurt much.

## How It Is Diagnosed

A doctor will look at your finger and check how it moves.  
X-rays are taken to see if there is a broken bone.  
The most useful view is the side view of the finger.  
If only the tendon is torn, the X-ray may look normal.

## Treatment

The main treatment is wearing a splint.  
The splint holds the fingertip straight for 6 to 8 weeks.  
You must keep the fingertip straight during this time.  
Do not let it bend, even when cleaning the finger.

If a piece of bone is broken off and it covers more than a quarter of the joint surface,  
or if the joint is out of place, surgery may be needed.  
In such cases, the doctor may refer you to a specialist.

# Palpitations

Palpitations mean you can feel your heart beating.  
You might feel it pounding, fluttering, racing, or skipping a beat.  
Sometimes you may also feel chest pain or have trouble breathing.  
These extra symptoms depend on what is causing the palpitations.

Palpitations are very common.  
Some people find them upsetting or scary.  
But most of the time, they are not a sign of a serious heart problem.  
Many people who have no heart disease still get palpitations.

---

## What Causes Palpitations?

Most people do not notice their heart beating.  
But if your heart beats faster or stronger than normal, you may feel it.  
This is usually a normal reaction.  
It is called sinus tachycardia.  
Common causes include:

- Exercise  
- Strong emotions like fear, anxiety, or pain  
- Low blood count (anemia)  
- Low blood pressure  
- Fever  
- Dehydration  

In other cases, palpitations come from a problem with the heart’s rhythm.  
This is called an arrhythmia.  
Arrhythmias can be harmless or serious.

### The Most Common Arrhythmias

These are usually harmless and happen in people with healthy hearts:

- Atrial premature beats  
- Ventricular premature beats  

You do not feel the early beat.  
You feel the next beat after a short pause.  
That next beat feels stronger than normal.  
You may think your heart skipped a beat.  
But it did not.

### Other Arrhythmias That Can Be Serious

These can be signs of a serious heart problem:

- Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT)  
- Atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter  
- Ventricular tachycardia  

These cause the heart to beat much faster than normal.  
Very slow heartbeats rarely cause palpitations.  
But some people do feel the slow rate.

Some arrhythmias happen in people with no serious health problems.  
Others are linked to serious heart disease or other health issues.

### Serious Heart Problems That Can Cause Palpitations

- Angina (chest pain from poor blood flow to the heart)  
- Heart attack  
- Congenital heart defects (like Brugada syndrome or long QT syndrome)  
- Problems with heart valves  
- Issues with the heart’s electrical system (like Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome)

### Health Problems Elsewhere in the Body That Can Cause Palpitations

- Overactive thyroid gland (hyperthyroidism)  
- Low oxygen in the blood (hypoxia)  
- Low potassium in the blood (hypokalemia)  
- Low magnesium in the blood (hypomagnesemia)  
- Certain medicines, illegal drugs, or substances  
  - Alcohol  
  - Caffeine  
  - Nicotine  
  - Digoxin  
  - Stimulants like albuterol, amphetamines, cocaine, epinephrine, ephedrine, and theophylline  
- Tumors in the adrenal glands that release too many hormones (pheochromocytoma)

### Risks of Fast Heartbeats

When the heart beats too fast, it may not pump blood well.  
This can cause dizziness, fainting, or even heart failure.  
Heart failure is more likely in people who already have heart problems.  
But it can happen in others if the heart beats too fast for too long.

A fast heart also needs more oxygen.  
If you already have narrowed heart arteries (coronary artery disease), a fast heart can cause chest pain or even a heart attack.

Some arrhythmias, especially ventricular tachycardia, can lead to sudden cardiac arrest.

---

## When to See a Doctor

Not all palpitations are caused by heart problems.  
But some heart problems are very serious.  
So it is best to get checked by a doctor.

### Go to the Emergency Room Right Away If You Have:

- Dizziness or fainting  
- Chest pain or pressure  
- Trouble breathing  
- Pulse rate over 120 beats per minute or under 45 beats per minute  
- Known heart disease or a family history of sudden death, fainting, or unexplained seizures  
- Palpitations during exercise, especially if you pass out

If you faint, have chest pain, or have trouble breathing, call emergency services.

### Call Your Doctor If You:

- Have occasional palpitations  
- Had an episode that stopped on its own  
- Do not have any warning signs  

Your doctor will decide how soon you need to be seen.  
They will consider your age, health history, and other symptoms.

---

## What the Doctor Will Do

The doctor will ask questions and do a physical exam.  
This helps them figure out what might be causing your palpitations.

### The Doctor Will Ask:

- How often the palpitations happen  
- How long they last  
- What makes them worse (like stress, activity, or caffeine)  
- What medicines or substances you take (including caffeine)

Sometimes the doctor will ask you to tap out the rhythm of your heartbeat.  
This helps them understand the pattern.

### The Physical Exam Includes:

- Checking your pulse, temperature, and blood pressure  
- Listening to your heart for unusual sounds  
- Listening to your lungs for signs of heart failure  
- Looking at and feeling your neck for an enlarged or swollen thyroid gland

Palpitations that come with other symptoms like shortness of breath, chest pain, weakness, fatigue, or fainting are more likely to be due to a serious heart problem.

---

### What Might Be Causing Your Palpitations?

| Feeling | Possible Cause |
|--------|----------------|
| A single skipped beat | Atrial premature beats or ventricular premature beats |
| Sudden fast heartbeat that stops suddenly | PSVT or Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome |
| Constant fast, irregular heartbeat | Atrial fibrillation |
| Fainting during palpitations | Ventricular tachycardia, inherited heart muscle diseases, atrial fibrillation, or heart rhythm disorders |
| Palpitations during exercise or stress | Normal heart response (sinus tachycardia), or poor blood flow to the heart |
| Family history of fainting or sudden death | Heart rhythm disorders or inherited heart muscle diseases |
| Bleeding, fever, pain, or fluid loss | Sinus tachycardia |
| Feeling hot, losing weight, bulging eyes, or neck swelling | Sinus tachycardia or atrial fibrillation from an overactive thyroid |

> Note: A doctor’s exam is always needed. These symptoms are common but not always present.

---

## Tests for Palpitations

Even if most causes are not serious, tests are usually done.

### 1. Electrocardiogram (ECG)

This test records your heart’s electrical activity.  
If done while you are having palpitations, it often shows the cause.  
But some problems only show up when you are not having symptoms.  
In that case, you may need to wear a monitor for a day or two (Holter monitor).  
Or you may use a longer-term device (event recorder).  
Some people get a small device placed under the skin (loop recorder).  
It records your heart rhythm all the time.  
You can check it later with a special reader.

Some fitness trackers and smartwatches can also track heart rate and rhythm.  
But they give less detailed information than medical devices.

### 2. Blood Tests

These help check for:

- Anemia (low blood count)  
- Imbalances in potassium, magnesium, and calcium  
- Signs of a heart attack (cardiac biomarkers)  
- Overactive thyroid (high thyroid hormone levels)  
- Hormone problems (like pheochromocytoma)

### 3. Imaging Tests

These may be needed if the ECG suggests heart disease:

- Echocardiography (ultrasound of the heart)  
- MRI of the heart (in some cases)

If you have symptoms during activity, you may need a stress test.  
This can include stress echocardiography or nuclear scanning.

### 4. Electrophysiologic (EP) Testing

This test is used if symptoms are severe and other tests did not find the cause.  
Small wires are passed through a vein into the heart.  
They record the heart’s electrical activity in more detail than an ECG.

---

## Treatment for Palpitations

### Step 1: Stop Triggers

- Stop caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, and other stimulants  
- Stop any medicine that may be causing the problem  
- If a needed medicine causes palpitations, your doctor may switch you to a different one

### Step 2: Reassurance and Medication

- If the palpitations are harmless (like atrial or ventricular premature beats), your doctor may just reassure you  
- If the palpitations are very bothersome, your doctor may prescribe a beta-blocker (a type of medicine that slows the heart)

### Step 3: Treat the Underlying Cause

- If there is a rhythm problem or another health issue, it will be treated  
- Doctors often start with medicines to control the rhythm (like digoxin, flecainide, verapamil, diltiazem, or amiodarone)  
- But these medicines can cause side effects or even new rhythm problems

### Step 4: More Advanced Treatments

For some arrhythmias (like atrial flutter or PSVT), **radiofrequency ablation** is often the best choice.  
This is a procedure that fixes the heart’s electrical pathway.

If medicines do not work or if the rhythm is dangerous, other treatments may be used:

- Direct current cardioversion (a shock to reset the heart rhythm)  
- Implanting a device that acts as both a pac

# Dandruff

Dandruff means you have white or grey flakes on your scalp and in your hair.  
Your scalp may also feel dry and itchy.

You can treat dandruff at home with anti-dandruff shampoo.  
You can buy this kind of shampoo at a pharmacy or grocery store.  
Use it every time you wash your hair.  
Keep using it for one month to see if your dandruff improves.

The most common reason for dandruff is a skin problem called seborrheic dermatitis.  
This is a condition that makes the skin on your scalp become inflamed and flaky.  
Dandruff can also happen if you are allergic to something in your hair products.

## See a doctor if:

- You still have dandruff after using anti-dandruff shampoo for a full month  
- Your dandruff is very bad or your scalp itches a lot  
- Your scalp looks red or swollen  
- You have flaky, itchy skin on your face or other parts of your body  

Your doctor can check your scalp.  
They can look for skin problems that might be causing your dandruff.

## What dandruff feels like

You will see white or grey flakes on your scalp and in your hair.  
The flakes are easier to see in dark hair.  
They may fall onto your shoulders when you move your head.  
Your scalp may feel dry and itchy.

## How to treat dandruff at home

Use an anti-dandruff shampoo.  
You can find these in pharmacies or supermarkets.  
Look for a shampoo with one of these ingredients:  
- Zinc pyrithione  
- Selenium sulphide (or selenium sulfide)  
- Ketoconazole  
- Coal tar with salicylic acid  

A pharmacist can help you pick the right shampoo and show you how to use it.  
Use the shampoo every time you wash your hair.  
Keep using it for one month.  
You may need to try more than one kind before you find one that works for you.

## What causes dandruff

Dandruff is not caused by not washing your hair enough.  
But if you do not wash your hair often, the flakes may be more obvious.  
Stress can make dandruff worse.  
Cold weather can also make dandruff worse.

# Lyme Disease

Lyme disease is an infection you can get from a tick bite.  
The bug that causes it is called *Borrelia*.  
It is a type of spiral-shaped bacteria.  
This kind of bacteria is called a spirochete.

## What Causes Lyme Disease?

Lyme disease is caused by a bacteria called *Borrelia*.  
In the United States, the most common type is *Borrelia burgdorferi*.  
A less common type, *B. mayonii*, has been found in the upper Midwest.  
In Europe and Asia, other types like *B. afzelii* and *B. garinii* cause the disease.

Ticks spread the bacteria.  
The main ticks that carry Lyme disease are:

- *Ixodes scapularis* – found in the Northeast and Midwest U.S.  
- *Ixodes pacificus* – found on the West Coast  
- *Ixodes ricinus* – found in Europe  
- *Ixodes persulcatus* – found in Asia

In the U.S., the white-footed mouse is the main animal that carries the bacteria.  
It passes the bacteria to ticks when they feed on it.  
Deer are hosts for adult ticks, but they do not carry the bacteria.  
Other animals like dogs can get Lyme disease too.

## Where Is Lyme Disease Found?

Lyme disease is most common in the United States.  
It was first noticed in 1976 in a town called Lyme, Connecticut.  
It is now reported in 49 states.  
But over 90% of cases happen in:

- Maine to Virginia  
- Wisconsin  
- Minnesota  
- Michigan

On the West Coast, most cases happen in northern California and Oregon.  
Lyme disease also happens in Europe, parts of Russia, China, and Japan.

## When Does Lyme Disease Happen?

Most cases happen in summer and early fall.  
This is when ticks are most active.  
People who live in wooded areas or walk through tall grass are more likely to get it.  
Children and young adults are most often affected.

## How Does Lyme Disease Spread?

The bacteria enter your body through a tick bite.  
The tick must be attached for more than 36 hours to pass the infection.  
After the bite, the bacteria move through your skin and into your body.  
They can spread to your joints, nerves, or heart.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Lyme disease has three stages:

1. Early localized  
2. Early disseminated  
3. Late

The first stage often has no symptoms.  
Then, the second stage may appear weeks or months later.  
The third stage can happen months or years after the bite.

### Early Stage: The Rash

The most common sign is a rash called erythema migrans.  
It appears at the site of the tick bite.  
It starts as a red spot.  
It often grows larger over time.  
It may look like a bull’s eye: a red center, a pale ring, and a red outer ring.  
But not everyone gets this pattern.  
Some people have a red rash with no clear center.  
Some have a rash with a blister or sore in the middle.

This rash is the best sign of Lyme disease.  
It usually appears within 3 to 32 days after the bite.

### Early Disseminated Stage

If the infection spreads, you may get other symptoms.  
These can include:

- Nerve problems (like weakness in the face, numbness, or tingling)  
- Heart issues (like a slow heartbeat or chest pain)  
- Joint pain or swelling

### Late Stage

If not treated, Lyme disease can cause long-term problems.  
These include:

- Joint pain and swelling (especially in the knees)  
- Nerve pain or brain issues  
- Memory problems or trouble focusing

## How Is Lyme Disease Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose Lyme disease in two main ways:

1. **Look at your symptoms and rash**  
   If you have the classic rash, doctors can often diagnose Lyme disease without tests.

2. **Use blood tests**  
   These tests look for antibodies your body makes to fight the bacteria.  
   They are not useful right away.  
   It can take weeks for your body to make enough antibodies.

Blood tests are most helpful if you have symptoms like joint pain, nerve problems, or heart issues.  
They are not needed if you only have the rash.

- A positive test must be confirmed with a second test.  
- A positive IgM test alone, especially long after the bite, may be wrong.  
- A positive IgG test means you were exposed to the bacteria in the past.  
  It does not mean you have an active infection now.

If your brain or spinal fluid is affected, a test called PCR may be done.  
This test can find the bacteria in the fluid.

### Important Notes

- Many people with tiredness, joint pain, or trouble thinking do **not** have Lyme disease.  
- If you never had the rash or other early symptoms, a positive blood test likely means you had Lyme disease in the past.  
- There is no proof that Lyme disease causes long-term fatigue or fibromyalgia-like symptoms.

## How Is Lyme Disease Treated?

Lyme disease is treated with antibiotics.  
The type and length of treatment depend on your symptoms.

### Early Lyme Disease (with rash only)

- Amoxicillin: 500 mg three times a day for 14 days  
- Doxycycline: 100 mg twice a day for 10 to 14 days  
- Cefuroxime axetil: 500 mg twice a day for 14 days  
- Azithromycin: 500 mg once a day for 7 days (if you cannot take the others)

### Nerve Problems (like facial weakness)

- Doxycycline: 100 mg twice a day for 14 to 21 days  
- Ceftriaxone: 2 grams once a day for 14 to 21 days (given through a vein)  
- Cefotaxime: 2 grams every 8 hours for 14 to 21 days (given through a vein)  
- Penicillin G: 3 to 4 million units every 4 hours for 14 to 21 days (given through a vein)

### Heart Problems

- Ceftriaxone: 2 grams once a day for 14 to 21 days (given through a vein)  
- Penicillin G: 3 to 4 million units every 4 hours for 14 to 21 days (given through a vein)  
- Doxycycline: 100 mg twice a day for 14 to 21 days  
- Amoxicillin: 500 mg three times a day for 14 to 21 days  
- Cefuroxime: 500 mg twice a day for 14 to 21 days

### Joint Pain (Arthritis)

- Amoxicillin: 500 mg three times a day for 28 days  
- Doxycycline: 100 mg twice a day for 28 days  
- Cefuroxime axetil: 500 mg twice a day for 28 days  
- Ceftriaxone: 2 grams once a day for 14 to 28 days (given through a vein)

### Rare Skin Condition (Acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans)

- Amoxicillin: 500 mg three times a day for 21 to 28 days  
- Doxycycline: 100 mg twice a day for 21 to 28 days  
- Cefuroxime: 500 mg twice a day for 21 to 28 days

### Special Cases

- Pregnant women can take amoxicillin: 500 mg three times a day for 14 days.  
- If a pregnant woman tests positive but has no symptoms, no treatment is needed.

### Other Treatments

- Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can help with pain and swelling.  
- If the heart beats too slowly, a temporary pacemaker may be needed.  
- If the knee is swollen and painful, fluid may be drained.  
- In rare cases, surgery may help if joint pain continues after antibiotics.

## How Can You Prevent Lyme Disease?

You can reduce your risk by avoiding tick bites.

### Wear Protective Clothing

- Stay on trails and paths.  
- Tuck your pants into your socks or boots.  
- Wear long-sleeved shirts.

### Use Repellents

- Apply repellent with DEET to your skin.  
- Use permethrin on your clothes. It kills ticks.  
- Use DEET with care in young children. It can cause side effects.

### Check for Ticks

- Check your body often, especially in hairy areas.  
- Check children and pets after being outdoors.  
- Look for ticks after spending time in wooded or grassy areas.

### Remove Ticks Safely

- Use tweezers to gently pull the tick straight out.  
- Do not squeeze or crush the tick.  
- Clean the bite area with alcohol.  
- Do not use matches, oil, or nail polish to remove ticks. These do not work.

### Do Not Use Antibiotics After a Tick Bite (Unless Needed)

A single dose of doxycycline after a tick bite can lower your risk.  
But doctors do not recommend this for everyone.

# Toxocariasis

Toxocariasis is an infection caused by roundworms that usually live in dogs and cats.  
These worms can spread to people, especially young children.

## How People Get Infected

- People get infected by swallowing roundworm eggs.  
- The eggs come from animal poop, especially from dogs and cats.  
- Children often get infected by eating dirt, sand, or soil that has been contaminated.  
- Sandboxes are a common place where this happens. Dogs and cats may poop in them, and children play there.  
- Children may touch contaminated sand and then put their hands in their mouths.  
- Adults can also get infected by touching dirty soil or surfaces, or by touching someone else’s unwashed hands.  
- People who eat non-food items like dirt, clay, or soil (a condition called pica) are at higher risk.  
- Rarely, people get infected by eating raw or undercooked meat from animals like rabbits or ducks that carry the worms.

## How the Infection Spreads in the Body

- After a person swallows the eggs, tiny worms called larvae hatch in the intestines.  
- The larvae break through the intestinal wall and travel through the blood.  
- They can go to any part of the body, such as the liver, lungs, heart, brain, or eyes.  
- The larvae cause damage and swelling in the tissues they reach.  
- The larvae do not grow into adult worms in people.  
- In dogs and cats, the larvae grow into adult worms.  
- In other animals like rabbits or ducks, the eggs hatch and the larvae form cysts in the body.  
- People can get infected by eating meat from these animals.

## Symptoms

Symptoms can appear a few weeks after swallowing the eggs.  
They depend on which part of the body is affected.

### If the worms affect internal organs (visceral larva migrans):

- Fever  
- Coughing or wheezing  
- Swollen liver  
- Swollen spleen  
- Skin rash  
- Trouble breathing  
- Loss of appetite

### If the worms affect the eye (ocular larva migrans):

- Usually only one eye is affected  
- No symptoms or only mild symptoms at first  
- The eye may become inflamed  
- Vision may become blurry or lost

## How Doctors Diagnose It

- Doctors suspect toxocariasis if a person has a fever, swollen liver, lung problems, or high levels of a certain type of white blood cell called eosinophils.  
- A blood test checks for antibodies. These are proteins the body makes to fight infection.  
- If the blood test shows antibodies to the roundworm, the diagnosis is confirmed.  
- In rare cases, a small sample of infected tissue (like from the liver) may be taken and tested for larvae or signs of inflammation.

## How It Is Treated

- Most people do not need treatment. The infection often goes away on its own.  
- If symptoms are bad, doctors may give medicine to kill worms. These medicines are called anthelmintics.  
- Common medicines are albendazole and mebendazole. They are taken by mouth.  
- For severe symptoms, doctors may also give corticosteroids to reduce swelling and inflammation.  
- If the eye is infected, an eye doctor will treat the person.  
- Treatment includes a steroid taken by mouth and a steroid applied directly to the eye.  
- Even with treatment, most people keep some vision loss.  
- In some cases, doctors use a laser to destroy worms in the eye.  
- Other treatments may include freezing the eye with a cold probe (cryosurgery) or surgery to fix eye damage.

## How to Prevent It

- Deworm dogs and cats regularly.  
- Wash hands with soap and water after playing with pets, after cleaning up pet waste, after being outside, and before eating or handling food.  
- Cover sandboxes when not in use to keep animals from pooping in them.  
- Teach children not to eat dirt, soil, or clay.

# Addison's Disease – Simple Explanation

Addison’s disease can cause many different symptoms. Some of the most common are:

- Feeling very tired all the time  
- Skin that is darker than the rest of your skin  
- Craving salty foods  

This condition happens when your body’s immune system attacks the adrenal glands by mistake. These glands are small organs near your kidneys. They make important hormones your body needs.

You will need to take medicine every day for the rest of your life. The medicine replaces the hormones your body is missing. This treatment helps you feel better and live a normal life.

Even though Addison’s disease can be hard to manage, treatment makes it possible to live well and stay healthy.

---

## When to See a Doctor

Call your doctor if you think you might have Addison’s disease.

---

## When to Call 999 (Emergency)

If you already have Addison’s disease and your symptoms suddenly get worse, call 999 right away. This could be a sign of an adrenal crisis. Get help if you have:

- A fast heartbeat  
- Feeling very dizzy or light-headed, especially when standing up  
- Severe stomach pain or pain in your side  
- Weak muscles, muscle pain, or muscle cramps  
- A headache that does not go away  
- Feeling sick (nausea) or vomiting  
- Feeling very sleepy, irritable, or confused  
- A seizure (fit)  
- Losing consciousness  

Even if you have already given yourself an emergency steroid injection, call 999. You still need urgent medical help.

---

## Support and Help

Healthcare teams will help you and your family manage Addison’s disease. You can also get support from others who have the condition.

### Addison’s Disease Self-Help Group (ADSHG)

This charity offers help and information for people with Addison’s disease and their families.

- Website: [www.addisonsdisease.org.uk](https://www.addisonsdisease.org.uk)  
- Learn what Addison’s disease is  
- Find useful resources  
- Join the Addison’s sanctuary of support  

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many symptoms of Addison’s disease are similar to those of other illnesses. They include:

- Extreme tiredness (fatigue)  
- Darker patches of skin, especially in skin folds or scars  
- Losing your appetite, losing weight, stomach pain, feeling sick, or craving salt  
- Feeling dizzy when standing up  
- Joint pain, weak muscles, or muscle cramps  
- Headaches  
- A mild fever  
- Feeling very thirsty and needing to pee often  
- Trouble focusing or thinking clearly  
- Feeling anxious or sad  

Addison’s disease most often affects adults between 30 and 50 years old. But it can also happen in children.

---

## What Causes Addison’s Disease?

The most common cause is the immune system attacking the adrenal glands by mistake.

This damage stops the glands from making the hormones your body needs.

Other causes include:

- Being born with larger-than-normal adrenal glands (congenital adrenal hyperplasia)  
- Infections like tuberculosis, meningitis, flu, cytomegalovirus, or HIV  
- Surgery to remove the adrenal glands  

---

## How Is Addison’s Disease Treated?

There is no cure for Addison’s disease. But medicine can help you feel well and stay healthy.

Your adrenal glands are not making enough hormones. One type of hormone they should make is called a steroid.

The main treatment is daily steroid medicine to replace the missing hormones.

You may be given:

- Hydrocortisone  
- Prednisolone  
- Fludrocortisone  

You must take your medicine every day. Always keep extra medicine on hand. Never run out.

You may need more medicine during stressful times, such as:

- When you are sick  
- Before or after surgery  
- During exams or other high-pressure events  

Your specialist will tell you when and how much extra medicine to take.

If you take steroids, carry a steroid emergency card with you at all times. It tells doctors you have Addison’s disease and that your medicine must not be stopped suddenly.

You can also get jewellery or wristbands with your condition and medicine details on them.

---

## How Does Addison’s Disease Affect Daily Life?

Addison’s disease is serious. You must remember to take your medicine every day. Sometimes your symptoms may get worse, or you may need emergency care.

But with treatment, you can live a full life with a normal life span.

You will have regular check-ups with your specialist. At these visits, you can talk about:

- How you are feeling  
- Whether your medicine is working well  
- How confident you feel about managing your condition  

---

## Addison’s Disease and Pregnancy

It is very important to manage Addison’s disease well during pregnancy. Poor control can lead to serious problems, including miscarriage.

If you are planning to become pregnant, talk to your specialist. They will help you stay healthy and manage your condition throughout your pregnancy.

# Chronic Suppurative Ear Infection

This is a long-term ear infection that lasts more than six weeks. It causes a hole in the eardrum. The ear drains fluid all the time. The fluid is often thick and may smell bad.

## What Causes This Condition?

This condition can start after a past ear infection. It can also happen because of:

- Blocked tubes in the ear
- Injury to the ear from trauma, burns, or loud blasts
- Problems from medical procedures, like ear tubes
- Certain birth conditions, such as Down syndrome, cleft lip or palate, or other rare genetic conditions

Living in poor conditions with dirty air or poor hygiene can make the problem worse. Getting a cold or having water get into the ear while bathing or swimming can also make it worse.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The most common signs are:

- Fluid draining from the ear all the time
- Hearing loss that gets worse over time
- No pain unless the bone around the ear becomes infected

The eardrum has a hole. The inside of the ear canal is swollen and full of raw, red tissue. The ear may look dirty or wet.

If a cholesteatoma is present, you may also have:

- Fever
- Dizziness
- Ear pain
- White, waxy material in the ear
- A soft, fleshy growth sticking out of the hole in the eardrum
- A blocked ear canal filled with thick, sticky fluid

Even if the ear does not drain all the time, hearing loss and occasional drainage can still happen. Some people feel better after using certain ear drops, but the problem comes back.

## What Is a Cholesteatoma?

A cholesteatoma is a growth of skin cells in the middle ear. It is not cancer. But it can grow and damage nearby bones and tissues. It can also cause serious infections.

The growth makes enzymes that break down bone and soft tissue. This can harm the eardrum and the small bones in the ear. It can also lead to:

- Infection in the inner ear
- Weakness or paralysis of the face
- Infection in the brain

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose this condition by looking in the ear with a special tool. They may take a sample of the fluid to test for bacteria.

If you have fever, dizziness, or ear pain, the doctor may order imaging tests. These include:

- CT scan
- MRI

These tests can show if the infection has spread to the inner ear, skull bones, or brain.

If the red, raw tissue in the ear keeps coming back, a small sample may be taken to check for cancer.

## How Is It Treated?

### Ear Drops

Use antibiotic ear drops twice a day for 10 to 14 days. The most common drops are:

- Ciprofloxacin
- Ofloxacin

Do not use ear drops with neomycin, tobramycin, or polymyxin if you have a hole in your eardrum or ear tubes. These can harm your hearing.

### Cleaning the Ear

If there is raw, red tissue in the ear, the doctor may remove it. They use small tools or a special stick with silver nitrate. This helps the ear heal.

After cleaning, the doctor may put in ciprofloxacin and dexamethasone drops for 7 to 10 days. Sometimes, these drops are used for 10 to 14 days without cleaning.

If the tissue keeps coming back, a biopsy may be needed. This checks for cancer.

### Oral Antibiotics

If the infection is severe, you may need pills. The most common ones are:

- Amoxicillin, taken three times a day for 10 days
- A type of cephalosporin antibiotic

Your doctor may change the medicine based on test results and how you respond.

### Surgery

Surgery is needed in some cases. It is used to:

- Fix certain types of holes in the eardrum
- Repair damaged small bones in the ear
- Remove a cholesteatoma

When a cholesteatoma is removed, the middle ear is rebuilt. Because the growth often comes back, a second surgery is usually done 6 to 12 months later. This check-up helps make sure the area is clean and healing.

## Important Facts to Remember

- This is a long-term ear infection with a hole in the eardrum and constant drainage.
- The middle ear is often damaged. In rare cases, the infection spreads to the skull or brain.
- Start treatment with ear drops.
- Use oral antibiotics if the infection is severe.
- Surgery is needed for certain types of holes, damaged bones, or cholesteatomas.

# Altitude Illness

Altitude illness happens when you go to a high place and your body does not get enough oxygen. It can affect hikers, skiers, climbers, and anyone who goes to high altitudes.

## What Causes Altitude Illness?

Air has less oxygen at high altitudes. The air is thinner, so your body gets less oxygen with each breath. The amount of oxygen in the air stays the same, but the pressure drops. This makes it harder for your body to get the oxygen it needs.

For example:
- At sea level, the air has normal oxygen.
- At 19,000 feet (5,800 meters), the air has only half the oxygen.
- In Denver, which is 5,300 feet (1,615 meters) high, the air has 20% less oxygen.

Most people can go up to 5,000 to 6,500 feet (1,500 to 2,000 meters) in one day without problems. But:
- About 25% of people who go to 8,000 feet (2,500 meters) get symptoms.
- About 40% of people who go to 14,000 feet (4,340 meters) get symptoms.

This illness is common in:
- Pilgrims in the Himalayas in Nepal.
- Climbers going up Mount Kilimanjaro in Kenya and Tanzania.

These people often go up too fast. Going up too fast is the biggest risk factor. Other risks include:
- How high you go.
- How high you sleep each night.

## Which Parts of the Body Are Affected?

The brain and lungs are most affected.

### Brain Problems
- **Acute mountain sickness (AMS)**: Mild form. Causes headache, tiredness, nausea, loss of appetite, and irritability.
- **High-altitude cerebral edema (HACE)**: Rare but dangerous. The brain swells with fluid. Causes confusion, trouble walking, and can lead to coma.

### Lung Problems
- **High-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE)**: Fluid builds up in the lungs. Can be deadly. Happens 24 to 96 hours after a fast climb above 8,000 feet (2,400 meters). Can happen even if you do not have AMS symptoms.

## Who Is at Risk?

Some people are more likely to get altitude illness. Risk increases if you:
- Have had altitude illness before.
- Live at sea level or very low altitudes.
- Go up too fast.
- Push yourself too hard.
- Sleep at a high altitude.

People with asthma, diabetes, heart disease, or mild COPD are not more likely to get altitude illness. But their health problems may get worse because of low oxygen levels.

- Asthma usually does not get worse at high altitudes.
- Short trips (less than a few weeks) to altitudes below 10,000 feet (3,000 meters) are safe for pregnant women and their babies.
- Being fit does not protect you from altitude illness.

## How the Body Adapts

Your body slowly adjusts to high altitudes. This is called acclimatization. It takes a few days to adjust to 10,000 feet (3,000 meters). It can take weeks to adjust to much higher altitudes. Some people can do normal activities above 17,500 feet (5,300 meters). But no one can fully adjust to living at altitudes above that.

## Common Symptoms

### Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS)
- Most common form of altitude illness.
- Usually starts at 8,000 feet (2,400 meters), but can happen lower in sensitive people.
- Symptoms start 6 to 10 hours after going up.
- Headache is the main symptom. Others include:
  - Dizziness
  - Loss of appetite
  - Nausea or vomiting
  - Tiredness
  - Weakness
  - Irritability
- Some say it feels like a hangover.
- Symptoms last 1 to 2 days.
- In rare cases, AMS gets worse and turns into HACE.

### High-Altitude Cerebral Edema (HACE)
- Brain swells with fluid.
- Symptoms:
  - Headache
  - Confusion
  - Trouble walking (unsteady or clumsy)
- Can get worse fast. Can lead to coma in hours if not treated.

### High-Altitude Pulmonary Edema (HAPE)
- Fluid builds up in the lungs.
- Usually starts 24 to 96 hours after a fast climb above 8,000 feet (2,400 meters).
- Can happen even without AMS symptoms.
- Causes most deaths from altitude illness.
- Can happen in people who live at high altitudes (called high-altitude resident HAPE).
- Can also happen when people return to high altitudes after a trip to lower elevations (called reentry HAPE).
- Respiratory infections can make HAPE more likely.
- Symptoms get worse at night when lying down.
- Mild: Dry cough, shortness of breath with light activity.
- Moderate: Shortness of breath even at rest, blue lips or nails (cyanosis).
- Severe: Gasping for breath, coughing up pink or bloody mucus, gurgling sounds when breathing.
- Can get worse fast. Can lead to breathing failure, coma, or death in hours.

### Other Common Signs
- Swelling in hands, feet, and face (especially in the morning). This is normal and goes away in a few days or after going down.
- Headache without other symptoms is common.
- Small bleeding spots in the eyes (retinal hemorrhages) can happen above 9,000 feet (2,700 meters). They are common above 16,000 feet (4,800 meters).
  - Most people have no symptoms.
  - If the bleeding affects the center of vision, you may see a small blind spot.
  - The spots go away in weeks and do not cause lasting damage.
  - If you notice a blind spot, go down to a lower altitude and see a doctor. You can go back up only after the bleeding is gone.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors mostly use symptoms to diagnose altitude illness.

For HAPE:
- Doctor listens to your lungs with a stethoscope. They may hear fluid.
- A chest x-ray can help confirm.
- Blood oxygen levels may be checked.

For HACE:
- A brain scan (CT or MRI) can help confirm, but it is not always needed.

## What Is Chronic Mountain Sickness?

Some people get sick after living at high altitudes for months or years.

**Chronic mountain sickness (Monge’s disease)**:
- Happens to people who live above 10,000 feet (3,000 meters) for a long time.
- Body makes too many red blood cells to carry oxygen.
- Too many red blood cells make the blood thick.
- This makes it hard for the heart to pump blood.
- Symptoms:
  - Tiredness
  - Shortness of breath
  - Aches and pains
  - Blue lips and skin (cyanosis)

**Treatment**:
- Removing blood (phlebotomy) helps for a short time.
- The best treatment is going down to a lower altitude.
- Acetazolamide may help.
- Full recovery takes months.
- People must stay at low altitude.

This disease is common in the Andes Mountains. It also happens in some high-altitude areas in Colorado.

In other places like Tibet, some people who move to high altitudes get a different form of chronic illness. They have high blood pressure in the lungs and heart problems, but not too many red blood cells.

## How Is It Treated?

### General Rule
- Going down to a lower altitude is the best treatment for all types of acute altitude illness.

### Mild AMS
- Stop going higher.
- Rest.
- Drink fluids.
- Use pain relievers like acetaminophen or ibuprofen for headache.
- Fluids do not treat AMS, but they help if you are dehydrated. Dehydration can feel like AMS.
- Most people feel better in 1 to 2 days.
- Sometimes doctors give acetazolamide or dexamethasone to help.

### Moderate or Severe AMS
- Go down at least 1,650 to 3,200 feet (500 to 1,000 meters).
- This often brings fast relief.
- Drink fluids.
- Use pain relievers.
- Take acetazolamide or dexamethasone.

### HACE
- Go down as far and as fast as possible.
- Use oxygen if available.
- Take dexamethasone.
- Acetazolamide may be added.

### HAPE
- Go down immediately.
- Use oxygen if available.
- Take nifedipine to lower blood pressure in the lungs.
- Avoid heavy exercise during descent. It can make the condition worse.
- Most people recover in 24 to 48 hours.
- Many are admitted to the hospital.
- Some can go home with oxygen if they have someone to watch them (like at a ski resort).

### If You Cannot Descend
- Use a hyperbaric bag (a portable pressure chamber).
- It simulates lower altitude by increasing air pressure inside the bag.
- You stay in the bag until symptoms improve.

# Bullous Pemphigoid

## What Is Bullous Pemphigoid?

Bullous pemphigoid is a skin condition that starts with an itchy rash.  
The rash can spread over large areas of the body.  
Over time, blisters may form.  
The blisters can be large and may contain fluid, blood, or pus.  
Some people also get blisters inside their mouth.  
These mouth blisters can make it hard to swallow.

The condition usually starts on the backs of the knees, inside the armpits, elbows, hands, feet, or stomach.  
The rash may look red or pink on white skin.  
On brown or black skin, it may look dark reddish-brown.  
Not everyone gets blisters.  
If you do, they may come and go for months or even years.  
In time, the condition often goes away on its own.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if you have:

- An itchy rash that lasts more than a few weeks  
- Many blisters or large, painful blisters  
- Blisters that keep coming back  
- Blisters in your mouth that make it hard to eat or swallow  
- Skin that feels hot, painful, or swollen  
- Redness in the skin, especially if you have brown or black skin (this may be harder to see)  
- A blister filled with pus or blood  

## How Is It Treated?

If your doctor thinks you have bullous pemphigoid, they may send you to a skin specialist.  
The main treatments are:

- Steroid creams applied to the skin  
- Steroid tablets taken by mouth  
- Antibiotics to help your skin heal and prevent new blisters  

These treatments help your skin heal.  
They also stop new rashes or blisters from forming.  
They lower the risk of infection.  
Your skin should heal without scars.  
But it may stay darker than before for a while.

### Important: Do Not Pop Blisters

Do not break blisters yourself unless a nurse has shown you how.  
Popping them can lead to infection.

## Possible Problems

Bullous pemphigoid can cause serious issues in some people.  
These problems can be life threatening, especially in older adults or those with other health issues.

The main risks are:

- Skin infections that can spread into the body (this is called sepsis)  
- Side effects from steroid treatment, such as high blood pressure, weak bones, or a higher chance of getting other infections  

Doctors will use the lowest possible dose of steroids for the shortest time.  
This helps reduce side effects.  
It is important to go to all your check-ups.  
This helps catch any problems early.

## What Causes Bullous Pemphigoid?

Bullous pemphigoid happens when your body’s immune system attacks your own skin.  
The immune system usually fights germs.  
But in this case, it mistakenly harms healthy skin.

We do not always know why this happens.  
But some things may trigger it, including:

- Certain medicines  
- Sunburn  
- Surgery  
- Burns

# Hand-Foot-and-Mouth Disease (HFMD)

Hand-foot-and-mouth disease is a common illness in young children.  
It is caused by certain viruses, including coxsackievirus A6, coxsackievirus A16, and enterovirus A71.  

The illness causes small blisters or sores on the hands, feet, mouth, and sometimes the area around the anus or genitals.  
These blisters can be painful but usually go away on their own in a few days.  

Some cases are not typical.  
These may cause a high fever.  
The blisters can spread to other parts of the body.  
They may turn into larger fluid-filled blisters or sores.  

The disease is most common in children under 10 years old.  
It feels similar to another virus illness called herpangina.  

Children with this disease often have a sore throat or mouth pain.  
They may not want to eat or drink because of the pain.  
Fever is also common.  

The blisters appear on the inside of the cheeks, tongue, and gums.  
They also show up on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet.  
Sometimes they appear in the diaper area.  
The blisters are usually painful but not serious.  
They heal without scarring.  

## What the Sores Look Like

- **Mouth sores**: Small blisters on the tongue and inside the mouth.  
  After the blisters break, they leave open sores.  
  These sores are red and can hurt when eating or drinking.  

- **Hand sores**: Blisters on the palms.  
  The skin around them may be red.  

- **Foot sores**: Blisters and red bumps on the soles of the feet.  
  They can also appear on the toes.  

- **Other areas**: In some cases, blisters may appear on the arms, legs, or buttocks.  

## Atypical Cases

Some cases of hand-foot-and-mouth disease are different.  
They may include:  
- Blisters that cover a large part of the body  
- Sores that appear mostly in areas where a child already has dry, itchy skin (eczema)  
- A rash with small, flat, red bumps on the face, buttocks, and arms  
- Purple spots on the skin  

After the illness, some children may lose their fingernails or toenails.  
This happens without pain.  
It usually happens during recovery.  

In rare cases, the virus can affect the brain or spinal cord.  
This can cause:  
- Aseptic meningitis (inflammation of the brain and spinal cord lining)  
- Encephalitis (inflammation of the brain)  
- Acute flaccid myelitis (AFM), a condition that causes muscle weakness  

These serious problems are more likely if the virus is enterovirus A71.  
In 2018, a group of such cases was seen in the United States.  

## Diagnosis

Doctors usually diagnose hand-foot-and-mouth disease by looking at the symptoms and the rash.  
They do not need special tests in most cases.  

## Treatment

There is no medicine to cure the virus.  
Treatment focuses on making the child feel better.  
- Use pain relief medicine as needed.  
- Use special mouth rinses or gels to ease mouth pain.  
- Keep the child well hydrated.  
  Offer cool drinks and soft foods.  

## Prevention

You can help stop the spread of the virus by:  
- Washing hands often, especially after changing diapers or using the toilet  
- Avoiding contact with open sores or saliva (like drool)  
- Not sharing cups, utensils, or toys  

There are three vaccines made from inactivated enterovirus A71.  
They are used in China.  
They are not yet approved for use in the United States.

# Kaposi Sarcoma

Kaposi sarcoma is a type of skin cancer.  
It causes flat, pink, red, or purple patches or bumps on the skin.  
It is caused by a virus called human herpesvirus type 8.  

This virus can lead to cancer, especially in people with a weak immune system.

---

## Types of Kaposi Sarcoma

There are five main types. Each type affects different groups of people and behaves differently.

### 1. Classic Kaposi Sarcoma
- Affects older men, often from Mediterranean, Eastern European, or Ashkenazi Jewish backgrounds.  
- Usually starts with one or two spots on the legs or feet.  
- Grows slowly.  
- Rarely spreads to other parts of the body.  
- Very unlikely to be deadly.

### 2. Endemic Kaposi Sarcoma
- Found in certain parts of Africa.  
- Affects children and young adults.  
- In children: Often starts in the lymph nodes. Can be sudden and severe. May be fatal.  
- In adults: Causes slow-growing skin spots, like classic Kaposi sarcoma. Rarely spreads. Not usually deadly.

### 3. Iatrogenic Kaposi Sarcoma
- Happens in people who take medicines that weaken the immune system.  
- These medicines are used after organ transplants.  
- Usually appears years after the transplant.  
- Can be serious. Spots may grow fast.

### 4. AIDS-Associated Kaposi Sarcoma (Epidemic)
- Affects people with AIDS.  
- Spots often appear within months.  
- Spreads quickly to the face, chest, mouth, and other areas.  
- Can affect lymph nodes and internal organs.  
- May cause bleeding in the stomach or intestines.  
- Sometimes, Kaposi sarcoma is the first sign of AIDS.

### 5. Non-Epidemic Kaposi Sarcoma
- A newer type.  
- Affects men who are HIV-negative but have sex with men.  
- Spots look like those in classic Kaposi sarcoma.  
- How serious it is is still being studied.

---

## Symptoms of Kaposi Sarcoma

- Spots or bumps on the skin.  
- Colors: Purple, pink, brown, or red.  
- Spots can grow large — up to several inches.  
- They may be flat or slightly raised.  
- They can turn blue-violet or black.  
- Swelling may happen around the spots.  
- In some cases, the cancer grows deep into soft tissues or even into bones.

### In the Mouth
- Spots are blue to violet.  
- Can cause pain when eating.

### In the Digestive Tract
- Spots may bleed heavily.  
- Often causes no symptoms at first.

### In People with AIDS
- Spots spread fast.  
- May appear on the face, chest, and inside the mouth.  
- Can cause pain when eating.  
- May spread to lymph nodes and organs.  
- Can cause blood in the stool.

---

## Did You Know?

- In the United States, most cases of Kaposi sarcoma happen in people with AIDS.  
- The iatrogenic type often shows up years after an organ transplant.  
- The endemic type in children is often serious and can be deadly.  
- The non-epidemic type is a recent discovery. It affects men who are HIV-negative and have sex with men.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Kaposi Sarcoma

- Doctors look at the skin spots.  
- They often do a **punch biopsy**.  
  - This means they remove a small piece of skin.  
  - The sample is checked under a microscope.  
  - This confirms the diagnosis.

For people with AIDS or a weak immune system:
- Doctors check if the cancer has spread.  
- They may do a CT scan of the chest and belly.  
- Other tests are done based on symptoms.

---

## Treatment of Kaposi Sarcoma

Treatment depends on the type, how many spots there are, and how fast the cancer is growing.

### For One or Two Spots
- Surgery to remove the spots.  
- Freezing them with extreme cold (cryosurgery).  
- Using an electric current to destroy them (electrocoagulation).  
- Applying a cream called imiquimod.  
- Using a gel called alitretinoin.  
- Injections of medicine directly into the spots (vinblastine or interferon alfa).  
- Some people with very few spots and no other symptoms choose not to treat them unless the cancer spreads.

### For Many Spots or Spread to Lymph Nodes
- Radiation therapy.  
- Chemotherapy.  
- The cancer often comes back. It is hard to cure completely.

### For Aggressive Cancer in People with a Normal Immune System
- Interferon alfa.  
- Chemotherapy given through a vein.  
- These treatments often work well.

### For People on Immunosuppressant Medicines
- Stopping or lowering the dose of these medicines may make the spots go away.  
- But if the medicines are needed for another health problem, the dose is lowered.  
- If the dose cannot be lowered, treatment includes surgery, chemotherapy, or radiation.  
- A medicine called sirolimus may also be used.  
- These treatments are less effective than in people with healthy immune systems.

### For People with AIDS
- Chemotherapy and radiation have not worked well.  
- The best treatment is **antiretroviral therapy (ART)**.  
  - This medicine controls HIV.  
  - It helps the immune system get stronger.  
- Some people with AIDS only need ART and spot removal.  
- Others need extra medicines like doxorubicin, paclitaxel, vinblastine, or pomalidomide along with ART.  
- Treating Kaposi sarcoma does not usually extend life for most people with AIDS.

### For the Endemic Type
- Hard to treat.  
- Doctors focus on making the person comfortable.  
- Pain relief and symptom control are key.  
- Spots are treated the same way as in classic Kaposi sarcoma.

---

# Ménière’s Disease

Ménière’s disease causes dizziness, balance problems, and hearing loss.  
It can make you feel like you or the world around you is spinning.  
You may also hear ringing or buzzing in your ears.  
Some people feel pressure or pain deep inside the ear.  
You might feel sick or be sick.

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if you have any of these symptoms:  
- A spinning feeling  
- Balance problems  
- Hearing loss  
- Ringing in the ears  
- Pressure or pain in the ear  
- Feeling sick or being sick

## When to Call 999 (Emergency)

Call 999 right away if you feel like you or everything around you is spinning AND:  
- One side of your face droops (your mouth or eye may look uneven)  
- You cannot raise both arms and hold them up  
- You have trouble speaking (your words may be slurred or hard to understand)  
- You suddenly have vision problems in one eye

These signs could mean you are having a stroke.  
A stroke is a serious emergency.  
Symptoms of a stroke come on very quickly.

> **Important:** Do not drive yourself to the hospital.  
> The person on the phone will tell you what to do.

## What to Expect

Symptoms of Ménière’s disease come and go.  
They can start suddenly and last from a few minutes to 24 hours.  
Some people have symptoms often. Others have them only once in a while.

Over time, your hearing may get worse.  
You may also have constant ringing in your ears.

## How It’s Treated

There is no cure for Ménière’s disease.  
But treatments can help you feel better.

Your doctor may give you medicine to stop dizziness and sickness.  
You may also get help for tinnitus (ringing in the ears).  
This can include therapy or sound treatments.  
Hearing aids can help if your hearing is affected.  
Balance problems can be improved with special exercises (vestibular rehabilitation).

In rare cases, surgery on the inner ear may be an option if symptoms are very bad and do not improve with other treatments.

Ménière’s disease can affect your daily life.  
It can make you feel anxious or low.  
Talking to a counselor or trying relaxation techniques like deep breathing can help.

## What You Can Do to Help Yourself

Symptoms can come without warning.  
Making some changes to your daily habits may help reduce how often they happen.

### Do These Things

- Always keep your medicine with you.  
- Be careful if you swim, climb ladders, or use heavy machines. Dizziness can make these activities dangerous.  
- Drink plenty of fluids every day.  
- Talk to your doctor about trying a low-salt diet.  
- Avoid caffeine. This includes tea, coffee, and chocolate.

### Avoid These Things

- Do not drive if you feel dizzy or if you think vertigo is coming on.  
- Do not drink alcohol.  
- Do not smoke.

# Postpoliomyelitis Syndrome

This condition causes new health problems years or even decades after a person had polio that caused paralysis.

It usually affects the same muscles that were weak or damaged during the original polio illness.

People who had polio in the past may start to feel more tired than usual. Their muscles may not work as well as they used to. They might also notice muscle weakness, twitching, or shrinking of muscles.

These symptoms often appear in older adults. They are more common in people who had severe polio at first.

The problem usually shows up in muscles that were already affected by the original polio infection.

Scientists believe the reason for this is that the body loses more nerve cells over time. These nerve cells help muscles work. The body already lost many of these cells during the original polio infection. Aging makes the loss worse.

There is no cure for postpoliomyelitis syndrome.

Treatment focuses on helping people feel better and stay as active as possible. It includes rest, physical therapy, and other supportive care.

# Hodgkin Lymphoma – Simple Explanation

Hodgkin lymphoma is a type of cancer that starts in a kind of white blood cell called a lymphocyte. It is different from other lymphomas because it has a special kind of cancer cell called a Reed-Sternberg cell.

## What Causes Hodgkin Lymphoma?

- The exact cause is not known.
- Some people may have a higher risk if they were exposed to the Epstein-Barr virus.
- There may be a family link in rare cases, but it is not contagious.
- There are no tests to check for this cancer in healthy people.
- People with certain immune system problems are at higher risk. These include:
  - Ataxia-telangiectasia
  - Klinefelter syndrome
  - Chédiak-Higashi syndrome
  - Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
  - HIV infection
  - Certain medicines after organ transplants
  - Autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis, celiac disease, Sjögren syndrome, and lupus

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people notice one or more swollen lymph nodes. These are often in the neck, but can also be in the armpit or groin. The swelling is usually not painful.

Some people have other symptoms, such as:
- Fever for no clear reason
- Night sweats
- Losing weight without trying
- Itching all over the body
- Feeling very tired
- A fever pattern that goes up and down over days or weeks (called Pel-Ebstein fever)

The symptoms depend on where the cancer is growing. For example:
- Swelling in the chest can cause coughing, chest pain, or trouble breathing.
- Swelling in the belly can cause pain or discomfort.
- Swelling in the liver can cause yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice).
- Swelling in the legs can cause them to get puffy (called lymphedema).
- Swelling near the spine or voice box can cause hoarseness or weakness in the arms or legs.
- Bone pain can happen if the cancer spreads to the bones.

These symptoms happen because the cancer affects how the body works. For example:
- Too few red blood cells cause tiredness and weakness.
- Too few white blood cells make infections more likely.
- Too few platelets can cause easy bruising or bleeding.
- The immune system does not work well, so infections like fungus or viruses are more common.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect Hodgkin lymphoma when a person has swollen lymph nodes that do not go away and are not painful. This is more likely if the person also has fever, night sweats, or weight loss.

To confirm the diagnosis, a doctor must take a sample of the lymph node. This is called a biopsy.

- The best way is to remove the whole node (excisional biopsy).
- If the node is near the skin, a needle can be used to take a sample (core needle biopsy).
- If the node is deep inside the body, surgery may be needed.

The sample is looked at under a microscope. Doctors look for Reed-Sternberg cells. These are large cancer cells with more than one nucleus. Their shape helps confirm the diagnosis.

Blood tests can show if the blood counts are low. But they are not enough to make the diagnosis. A biopsy is always needed.

## How Is It Staged?

Staging tells doctors how far the cancer has spread. This helps decide the best treatment and how likely it is to be cured.

There are four stages:
- Stage I: Cancer is in one area only (like one lymph node or one organ outside the lymph system).
- Stage II: Cancer is in two or more areas on the same side of the diaphragm (the muscle under the lungs).
- Stage III: Cancer is in areas on both sides of the diaphragm.
- Stage IV: Cancer has spread to organs outside the lymph system, like the liver, lungs, or bone marrow.

Stages I and II are called limited stage. Stages III and IV are called advanced stage.

Each stage can be labeled A or B:
- A means no fever, night sweats, or weight loss.
- B means one or more of these symptoms are present.

For example, someone with stage II and night sweats has stage IIB.

To stage the disease, doctors use:
- Blood tests (to check liver, kidney, and immune health)
- Tests for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C
- A combined PET-CT scan of the neck, chest, belly, and pelvis

This scan is the most accurate way to see how far the cancer has spread. It can also show if the cancer is still active after treatment.

If a PET-CT scan is not available, doctors use a contrast CT scan and a bone marrow biopsy.

MRI of the brain or spine is done only if there are symptoms like headaches, numbness, or weakness.

Most people do not need surgery to check the belly because the PET scan is very accurate and everyone gets chemotherapy, which treats the cancer wherever it is.

## How Is It Treated?

Most people with Hodgkin lymphoma can be cured. Treatment depends on the stage and other factors.

Common treatments include:
- Chemotherapy (medicine to kill cancer cells)
- Radiation therapy (high-energy beams to target cancer)
- Immunotherapy (drugs that help the immune system fight cancer)
- Stem cell transplant (in some cases)

Chemotherapy is the main treatment. It may be used alone or with radiation therapy.

Some people may need a stem cell transplant if the cancer comes back after initial treatment.

After treatment, people have regular checkups for 5 years. These include:
- Blood tests
- CT scans of the chest and pelvis
- Mammograms or breast MRIs (if they had radiation to the chest)
- Thyroid tests (if they had radiation to the neck)

## Long-Term Risks After Treatment

- Radiation therapy can increase the risk of other cancers later in life, such as lung, breast, or stomach cancer.
- Some people may develop non-Hodgkin lymphoma or leukemia years after treatment.
- These risks are low but real. Doctors will monitor for them.

## What Happens If the Cancer Comes Back?

If the cancer returns after treatment, it can still be cured in many cases.

- People who relapse after 12 months have a better chance of being cured than those who relapse earlier.
- Treatment for relapse often includes stronger chemotherapy and a stem cell transplant using the person’s own stem cells.
- This transplant is usually safe, with less than 1 to 2 out of 100 people dying from it.
- Immunotherapy drugs are also used to treat relapsed cases.

## Key Points

- Hodgkin lymphoma is a cancer of the lymph system.
- It is often curable with treatment.
- Early signs include painless swollen lymph nodes and unexplained fever, night sweats, or weight loss.
- A biopsy is needed to confirm the diagnosis.
- Staging helps guide treatment and predict outcomes.
- Most people are cured, but long-term follow-up is important.
- Fertility may be affected by treatment. Talk to your doctor about options to preserve it.

# Bell's Palsy

Bell's palsy causes one side of your face to feel weak or not move at all.  
This can happen over a few days.  

Other common signs include:  
- Drooling from one side of your mouth  
- A dry or watery eye on the affected side  
- Trouble closing your eye on the weak side  
- A drooping eyelid or corner of your mouth  
- Dry mouth  
- Loss of taste  
- Pain around your jaw or behind your ear  

In rare cases, both sides of your face may be affected.

---

## When to Get Help Right Away

Call 999 if someone:  
- Has one side of their face drooping (mouth or eye)  
- Cannot raise both arms and hold them up  
- Has trouble speaking (words are slurred or hard to understand)  

These signs could mean a stroke. A stroke is a serious emergency.  

---

## When to See a Doctor Soon

See a doctor urgently if you have any symptoms of Bell's palsy.  
It is best to get help within 72 hours.  
Early treatment works better.  

You can call NHS 111 or get help online at 111.nhs.uk.

---

## Treatment for Bell's Palsy

Your doctor may give you:  
- A 10-day course of steroid medicine (this helps reduce swelling)  
- Antiviral medicine, if needed (this fights viruses)  
- Eye drops or ointment to keep your eye moist  
- Special tape to keep your eye closed at night  

If you cannot close your eye, treatment helps protect your vision.  

---

## Recovery from Bell's Palsy

Most people get better within 6 months.  
Some people take longer to recover.  

See your GP again if your symptoms do not improve after 3 weeks.  

Some people have lasting effects, such as:  
- Ongoing face pain  
- A constantly watery eye  
- Trouble eating or drinking  
- Changes in taste  
- Sensitivity to loud sounds  

Living with Bell's palsy can be hard on your mood.  
You may feel sad, stressed, or anxious.  
Talk to your GP if this is affecting your mental health.  

You usually only get Bell's palsy once.  
But in rare cases, it can come back, sometimes years later.

# Heart Failure

Heart failure means the heart does not pump blood well.  
It can affect the left side, the right side, or both sides of the heart.  
The left side pumps blood to the body.  
The right side pumps blood to the lungs.

## What Happens in Heart Failure?

When the left side of the heart does not work well:  
- You may feel short of breath.  
- You may feel tired easily.  

When the right side of the heart does not work well:  
- Fluid builds up in the legs, ankles, or belly.  
- You may notice swelling in your legs or belly.

Both sides can be affected at the same time.  
Heart failure is not a single disease. It is a group of problems that cause the heart to fail.

## How Is Heart Failure Diagnosed?

Doctors start by asking about your symptoms and doing a physical exam.  
They may order tests to check your heart.  
Common tests include:  
- A chest X-ray to see the size of the heart and check for fluid in the lungs.  
- An echocardiogram to see how well the heart pumps.  
- Blood tests to check for a substance called BNP or NT-pro-BNP. These levels go up when the heart is under stress.

Other tests may be done to find the cause.  
These can include an ECG (electrocardiogram) or a scan of the heart.

## Who Gets Heart Failure?

About 6.5 million people in the United States have heart failure.  
More than 960,000 new cases happen each year.  
Around 26 million people worldwide have heart failure.

## How the Heart Works

The heart’s job is to pump blood.  
How well it works depends on:  
- How much blood fills the heart before it pumps (preload).  
- How hard the heart must push to send blood out (afterload).  
- How much oxygen and fuel the heart muscle gets.  
- How fast the heart beats and how regular the rhythm is.  
- How much healthy heart muscle is left.

**Cardiac output** is how much blood the heart pumps each minute.  
It depends on how much blood fills the heart and how fast the heart beats.

**Preload** is how much blood is in the heart just before it squeezes.  
If the heart is stretched too much, it may not pump well.

**Afterload** is how hard the heart must work to push blood out.  
High blood pressure makes afterload higher.

**The Frank-Starling principle** says that the more blood fills the heart, the harder it pumps—up to a point.  
After that, the heart cannot pump better, even if more blood comes in.

**Ejection fraction** is a number that shows how well the heart pumps.  
It is the percentage of blood pumped out with each beat.  
A normal ejection fraction is 50% or higher.  
A low ejection fraction means the heart is not pumping well.

**Force-frequency relationship** means that a faster heartbeat usually makes the heart pump harder.  
But in some heart failure cases, a faster beat makes the heart pump worse.

**Cardiac reserve** is the heart’s ability to work harder when needed.  
For example, during exercise, the heart can beat faster and pump more blood.  
It can also pull more oxygen from the blood.

## Why Does Heart Failure Happen?

The heart may fail because:  
- The heart muscle is damaged.  
- The heart valves do not work right.  
- The heart rhythm is abnormal.  
- The heart does not get enough oxygen or fuel.  
- The body has a high demand for blood (like in anemia or thyroid problems).  
- The heart is under too much pressure (like in high blood pressure).

Some diseases can damage the heart over time.  
These include:  
- Heart attacks  
- Viral infections of the heart  
- Certain cancer medicines  
- High blood pressure  
- Heart valve problems  
- Inherited heart muscle diseases

## Types of Heart Failure

There are two main types:

### Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF)  
- The heart muscle does not squeeze well.  
- Ejection fraction is 40% or less.  
- This is also called systolic heart failure.

### Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF)  
- The heart fills with blood but does not relax well.  
- Ejection fraction is 50% or higher.  
- This is also called diastolic heart failure.

Some people have an ejection fraction between 41% and 49%.  
They are now called having heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF).

### Other Ways to Describe Heart Failure

- **Left-sided heart failure** – affects the left side of the heart.  
- **Right-sided heart failure** – affects the right side.  
- **Biventricular failure** – both sides are affected.  
- **Acute heart failure** – comes on suddenly.  
- **Chronic heart failure** – lasts a long time.  
- **High-output heart failure** – the heart pumps a lot of blood, but still fails.  
- **Low-output heart failure** – the heart pumps too little blood.

## Symptoms and Signs

Symptoms depend on which side of the heart is affected.

### Left-Sided Heart Failure  
- Shortness of breath when walking or lying down.  
- Needing to sleep propped up on pillows.  
- Coughing, especially at night.  
- Feeling very tired.

### Right-Sided Heart Failure  
- Swelling in the legs, ankles, or feet.  
- Swelling in the belly (fluid buildup).  
- Feeling full quickly when eating.  
- Weight gain from fluid.

### Severe Cases  
- Pulmonary edema – fluid in the lungs.  
- Cardiogenic shock – the heart stops pumping enough blood.

### NYHA Classification of Heart Failure

This system rates how much activity causes symptoms:

| Class | What It Means | Example Activities |
|-------|----------------|--------------------|
| I | No symptoms with normal activity | Walking 8 km/h, playing sports |
| II | Mild symptoms with normal activity | Climbing stairs, gardening |
| III | Symptoms with light activity | Dressing, showering, walking slowly |
| IV | Symptoms even at rest | Cannot do light tasks without discomfort |

## How Is Heart Failure Treated?

Treatment has several goals:  
- Relieve symptoms.  
- Improve heart function.  
- Prevent hospital visits.  
- Help you live longer and feel better.

### Lifestyle and Diet Changes
- Eat less salt.  
- Weigh yourself daily.  
- Limit how much fluid you drink.  
- Stop smoking.  
- Exercise as your doctor says.  
- Maintain a healthy weight.

### Treat the Cause
- Control high blood pressure.  
- Treat diabetes.  
- Fix heart valve problems.  
- Treat abnormal heart rhythms.

### Medicines
Many medicines help.  
They include:  
- Diuretics – help remove extra fluid.  
- ACE inhibitors – lower blood pressure and reduce strain on the heart.  
- ARBs – similar to ACE inhibitors.  
- Beta-blockers – slow the heart and reduce strain.  
- Aldosterone blockers – help reduce fluid and protect the heart.  
- SGLT2 inhibitors – help the kidneys remove extra fluid and improve heart function.  
- Neprilysin inhibitors – help the heart pump better.  
- Ivabradine – slows the heart rate in some cases.  
- Other drugs may be used based on your needs.

### Devices
Some people need devices:  
- Implantable defibrillators – prevent sudden death.  
- Pacemakers – help the heart beat in a normal rhythm.  
- Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) – helps both sides of the heart beat together.

### Surgery or Transplant
In some cases, surgery or heart transplant may be needed.

### Care Team
You may work with a team of doctors, nurses, dietitians, and others.

## When to Get Help

Go to the hospital if you have:  
- Sudden shortness of breath.  
- Severe swelling in your legs or belly.  
- Trouble breathing when lying flat.  
- Rapid or irregular heartbeat.  
- Chest pain.  
- Dizziness or fainting.

## Prognosis (Outlook)

Heart failure often gets worse over time.  
But treatment can slow this down.  
After a hospital stay for heart failure, about 35% of people live 5 years.  
Some people live much longer with good care.

Poor signs include:  
- Low blood pressure.  
- Very low ejection fraction.  
- High levels of certain blood markers (like troponin, BUN, or sodium).  
- Poor ability to walk or exercise.

Tests like BNP, NT-pro-BNP, and risk scores can help predict how well someone may do.

Death can happen slowly or suddenly.  
Sudden death can happen without warning.

## Key Points

- Heart failure means the heart does not pump blood well.  
- Left-sided failure causes shortness of breath and fatigue.  
- Right-sided failure causes swelling in the legs and belly.  
- Ejection fraction helps classify heart failure.  
- Low ejection fraction = HFrEF.  
- Normal ejection fraction = HFpEF.  
- Think of heart failure in people with shortness of breath, fatigue, swelling, or a history of heart attack, high blood pressure, or valve problems.  
- Tests like echocardiogram and BNP help confirm the diagnosis.  
- Without treatment, heart failure usually gets worse.  
- Treatment includes lifestyle changes, medicines, devices, and sometimes surgery or transplant.
