# Epidemic Typhus

Epidemic typhus is a serious illness caused by a type of bacteria called *Rickettsia prowazekii*.  
It spreads through body lice.  
In some places, it can also spread from flying squirrels to people.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The illness starts suddenly, usually 7 to 14 days after infection.  
You will have a high fever.  
You will feel a strong headache.  
You will feel very tired and weak.  
A rash appears 4 to 6 days after the fever starts.  
The rash usually begins on the chest and spreads to the arms and legs.  

In some cases, the spleen may get bigger.  
If the illness is severe, blood pressure may drop too low.  
The kidneys may stop working properly.  
Gangrene (tissue death) or pneumonia may also develop.  

If not treated, epidemic typhus can be deadly.  
The risk of death goes up with age.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your symptoms.  
They may take a small sample of the rash to test.  
They may also do blood tests.

The rash test is the most reliable way to confirm the illness.  
Doctors use a special test called immunofluorescence assay on the rash sample.  
They may also use a test called PCR to find the bacteria faster.

Blood tests can show if your body is fighting the bacteria.  
But one blood test is not enough.  
You need a second test 1 to 3 weeks later.  
This helps show if your body is making more antibodies.  
This means the infection is real and not just a false alarm.

## How Is It Treated?

You will be given an antibiotic.  
The most common one is doxycycline.  
It is taken by mouth.

You must take the medicine until you feel better and have no fever for 24 to 48 hours.  
But you must take it for at least 7 days.

Doxycycline is safe for children of all ages when used for a short time.  
A short course (5 to 10 days) does not harm teeth or weaken tooth enamel.  
This is true even for children under 8 years old.

## How Can It Be Prevented?

Washing and drying clothes and bedding at high heat kills lice.  
This helps stop the spread of the disease.

Avoid contact with flying squirrels and their nests.  
Do not touch their droppings or nests.

If you have lice, your doctor may give you a medicine to kill them.  
These medicines are applied to the skin.  
But body lice live in clothes and bedding, not on the skin.  
So treating clothes and bedding is more important than treating the skin.

Wash clothes and bedding at least once a week in hot water (over 130 degrees Fahrenheit or 54 degrees Celsius).  
Dry them on high heat.  
If something cannot be washed, dry clean it or seal it in a plastic bag for 2 weeks.  
You can also treat clothes and bedding with permethrin, a special insecticide.

## Brill-Zinsser Disease

Brill-Zinsser disease is a return of epidemic typhus.  
It can happen years after the first infection.

Some of the bacteria stay hidden in your body.  
They can come back if your immune system is weak.

Symptoms are usually mild.  
They are like those of epidemic typhus.  
You may have a fever for about 7 to 10 days.  
You may not have a rash.

Diagnosis and treatment are the same as for epidemic typhus.

# What You Need to Know About COVID-19

COVID-19 can feel like a bad cold or flu.  
It can cause a high temperature, a new cough, and changes in your sense of smell or taste.

If you have symptoms, stay away from others.  
Meet outside if you must be around people.  
Do this until you feel better.

---

## Signs of COVID-19

You may have one or more of these signs:

- A high temperature. This means you feel hot to the touch on your chest or back. You do not need to use a thermometer.
- A new, ongoing cough. This means coughing a lot for more than an hour, or having 3 or more coughing episodes in 24 hours.
- You cannot smell or taste things the way you used to.
- Trouble breathing or feeling short of breath.
- Feeling very tired or worn out.
- Body aches or pain.
- Headache.
- Sore throat.
- A blocked or runny nose.
- Not feeling hungry.
- Diarrhoea.
- Feeling sick or being sick.

These signs are similar to those of colds and flu.  
Most people get better within a few weeks.  
But some people take longer to recover.  
For some, the illness can be serious.

---

## How to Stop Spreading COVID-19

If you have symptoms or tested positive, do these things to protect others:

- Cover your mouth and nose when you cough or sneeze.  
  Ask children to do the same.
- Clean surfaces you touch often.  
  This includes door handles, remote controls, and kitchen or bathroom surfaces.
- Stay away from other people.  
  This includes people you live with.  
  Stay apart until you feel better.
- Tell anyone who needs to come into your home that you have symptoms or tested positive.
- Ask friends, family, or neighbours to get food and other supplies for you.
- Avoid indoor or crowded places.  
  This includes public transport, large gatherings, or places with little fresh air.
- Wear a face covering when you cannot keep your distance from others.
- Tell healthcare staff if you have a positive test or symptoms.  
  This is important if you are going to a clinic or hospital.

---

## How to Lower Your Risk of Getting COVID-19

Wash your hands often with soap and water.  
Or use hand sanitiser.  
Try not to touch your eyes, nose, or mouth with unwashed hands.

### If You Are at Higher Risk

You are at higher risk if you are older, pregnant, or have a weak immune system.  
Or if your child is very young or has a long-term health condition.

If you are at higher risk, try to avoid people who have symptoms until they feel better.

You may also want to:

- Open windows and doors when meeting people indoors.  
  Or meet outside instead.
- Stay at least 2 metres away from others.  
  This is especially important indoors or in busy places.
- Work from home if you can.  
  Talk to your employer about how to stay safe at work.
- Wear a face covering when you cannot keep your distance.
- Ask people to wear a face covering or take a rapid test before meeting indoors.

---

## Who Can Get Treatment for COVID-19

Some people at highest risk of serious illness can get special treatments.  
These include:

- Nirmatrelvir plus ritonavir (sold as Paxlovid)
- Sotrovimab (sold as Xevudy)
- Molnupiravir (sold as Lagevrio)

Nirmatrelvir plus ritonavir and molnupiravir are medicines that fight the virus.  
A doctor will decide which treatment is best for you.

Some treatments come as pills you swallow.  
Others are given through a drip in your arm.  
This is usually done in a hospital or local clinic.

These treatments can help you feel better.  
They can also lower your risk of becoming seriously ill.

### Extra Help in Hospital

If you need to go to hospital, you may get other treatments.  
These are based on your condition.

---

## When to Get Help Right Away

Call your doctor or get help from NHS 111 if:

- You are worried about your or your child’s symptoms.  
  Or you are not sure what to do.
- The symptoms are getting worse.  
  Or they are not getting better.
- You or your child has other signs of illness.  
  This includes a rash, not eating, or feeling weak.
- You or your child has a high temperature for 5 days or more.  
  Or the fever does not go down with paracetamol.
- Your child is under 3 months old and has a temperature of 38 degrees Celsius or higher.  
  Or you think they have a high temperature.
- Your child is 3 to 6 months old and has a temperature of 39 degrees Celsius or higher.  
  Or you think they have a high temperature.

If you are at higher risk, get help sooner.  
This includes if you are pregnant, over 60, or have a weak immune system.

You can call 111 or get help online at 111.

---

## When to Call 999 or Go to A&E

Go to A&E or call 999 if:

- You or your child seems very unwell.  
  Or they are getting worse.  
  Babies and children can get worse very fast.
- You or your child has sudden chest pain.
- You or your child are so breathless that you cannot say a short sentence while resting.  
  Or breathing has suddenly gotten worse.  
  In babies, the stomach may pull in under the ribs.
- You or your child coughs up blood.
- You or your child collapses, faints, or has a seizure or fit for the first time.
- You or your child has a rash that does not fade when you roll a glass over it.  
  This is a sign of meningitis.

# Spondylolisthesis – Simple Explanation

Spondylolisthesis means one bone in your spine slips forward over the bone below it.  
The most common type is when the bone slips forward.  
It can happen anywhere in the spine, but it is most common in the lower back and neck.

Some people with spondylolisthesis have no pain.  
Others feel pain when walking or standing for long periods.

Treatment focuses on relieving symptoms.  
Physical therapy that strengthens the lower back is often helpful.

---

## Types of Spondylolisthesis

There are five main types. They are named based on what causes them.

### Type I: Congenital
- This happens because a part of the spine did not form properly before birth.
- It affects the upper joint part of the bone.

### Type II: Isthmic
- This is caused by a small crack or weak spot in a part of the bone called the pars interarticularis.
- This weak spot is also called spondylolysis.
- It often happens in young athletes.
- The most common spot is the lowermost lower back bone (L5).

### Type III: Degenerative
- This happens due to wear and tear over time.
- It is linked to joint arthritis in the spine.
- It usually affects people over 60 years old.
- It is much more common in women than in men.

### Type IV: Traumatic
- This is caused by a broken bone, dislocation, or other injury to the spine.

### Type V: Pathologic
- This is caused by serious problems like infection, cancer, or other bone diseases.

---

## Most Common Spine Levels

Spondylolisthesis most often affects:
- The bone between L3 and L4
- The bone between L4 and L5
- The bone between L5 and the pelvis (S1)

Types II and III are the most common overall.

---

## How the Slippage Is Measured

Doctors use X-rays to see how much the bone has slipped.  
They measure the slip as a percentage of the bone’s width.

- **Grade I:** Up to 25% slip
- **Grade II:** 25% to 50% slip
- **Grade III:** 50% to 75% slip
- **Grade IV:** 75% to 100% slip

The side view of the X-ray is used most often.  
Sometimes doctors take extra X-rays while you bend forward and backward.  
This helps check if the slip gets worse with movement.

---

## Symptoms and Risks

- Mild to moderate slippage (up to 50%) often causes little or no pain, especially in young people.
- Over time, slippage can narrow the space where nerves pass through. This is called foraminal stenosis.
- The slippage usually stays the same over time. It does not get worse quickly.

---

## Treatment

- Most people do not need surgery.
- Treatment focuses on easing pain and improving movement.
- Physical therapy with lower back strengthening exercises is often recommended.

# Premature Menopause

Premature menopause means your periods stop before you turn 40.  
This happens because your ovaries no longer release eggs regularly.  
Your ovaries also stop making the usual levels of female hormones.

Some women have no symptoms except that their periods stop.  
Others have trouble getting pregnant.  
Some have the same symptoms as women going through normal menopause.  
These include hot flashes, night sweats, and mood changes.

A blood test can confirm the diagnosis.  
Other tests help find the cause.  
Treatment with estrogen is often used.  
It is usually taken until about age 51, when most women go through menopause.

If you want to get pregnant, you may be offered fertility treatments.  
One option is to use eggs from another woman.  
The eggs are fertilized in a lab and placed in your uterus.

## What Happens in Premature Menopause?

Your ovaries make very little or no estrogen.  
You no longer release eggs regularly.  
Sometimes, your ovaries start working again for a short time.  
This means pregnancy is still possible, even though it is rare.

You still have thousands of eggs in your ovaries.  
Premature menopause does not mean you are aging faster.  
It only means your ovaries are not working the way they should.

## What Causes Premature Menopause?

Your ovaries hold egg cells in small sacs called follicles.  
Each follicle holds one egg.  
Premature menopause happens when the follicles do not work well.  
This can happen for many reasons.

- The number of follicles in your ovaries is lower than normal.  
- The follicles break down too fast.  
- The follicles do not respond well to hormones from the brain that tell them to work.

These problems stop your ovaries from releasing eggs and making hormones.

Common causes include:

- **Genetic problems**: Some people have abnormal chromosomes.  
  Examples: Turner syndrome, having a Y chromosome (which is rare in women), or Fragile X syndrome.  
- A family history of early menopause.  
- **Autoimmune disease**: Your body makes antibodies that attack your own tissues.  
  This can include your ovaries.  
- Metabolic problems, like enzyme deficiencies.  
- Viral infections, such as mumps.  
- Cancer treatments like chemotherapy or radiation.  
- Surgery to remove both ovaries.  
  This stops periods and causes menopause.  
- Surgery to remove the uterus.  
  This stops periods but does not cause most menopause symptoms if the ovaries still work.  
- Exposure to toxins, such as smoking.

If a Y chromosome is present, the risk of ovarian cancer increases.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Some women have no symptoms.  
They only notice that their periods become lighter or stop.  
This is called amenorrhea.

Others have trouble getting pregnant.  
They may also have symptoms like:

- Hot flashes  
- Night sweats  
- Mood swings

If the cause is a specific condition, you may have other symptoms.  
For example, if Turner syndrome is the cause, you may have physical or learning differences.

If an autoimmune disease causes premature menopause, you may also have other autoimmune conditions.  
These include:

- Thyroiditis (inflammation of the thyroid)  
- Vitiligo (loss of skin color)  
- Myasthenia gravis (muscle weakness)  
- Rheumatoid arthritis  
- Addison disease (a serious condition affecting the adrenal glands)

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect premature menopause if you are under 40 and have:

- Menopause-like symptoms  
- Few or no periods  
- Trouble getting pregnant

First, a pregnancy test is done.  
This rules out pregnancy as the cause of missed periods.

Then, blood tests check your hormone levels.  
Doctors measure estrogen and follicle-stimulating hormone.  
These tests may be repeated weekly for several weeks to confirm the diagnosis.

Other tests may be done to find the cause or check for related health problems.  
For example, if thyroid disease is suspected, thyroid hormone levels are tested.

Genetic testing and counseling may be offered if:

- You have learning problems, tremors, or balance issues  
- A close family member had early menopause  
- You are under 35 years old

A blood test for antimüllerian hormone can show how well your ovaries are working.  
It helps estimate your chances of getting pregnant after fertility treatment.

Bone density tests may be done to check for weak bones (osteoporosis).

## How Is It Treated?

If you do not want to get pregnant, you will be given one of the following:

- Birth control pills that contain estrogen and a progestin  
- A patch that delivers estrogen and a progestin  
- Menopausal hormone therapy (also called hormone replacement therapy)  
  This includes estrogen and a progestin or progesterone

These treatments are usually taken until about age 51.  
After that, your doctor will decide if you should keep taking them.

If you do not take estrogen until about age 51, your risk of:

- Weak bones (osteoporosis)  
- Dementia  
- Parkinson disease  
- Depression  
- Heart disease (coronary artery disease)

is higher.

Estrogen therapy helps with:

- Hot flashes  
- Night sweats  
- Vaginal dryness  
- Mood swings  
- Bone loss

Taking estrogen alone increases the risk of cancer in the lining of the uterus.  
To protect against this, most women also take a progestin or progesterone with estrogen.

Women who have had their uterus removed (hysterectomy) do not need to take a progestin or progesterone.

About 5 to 10 out of 100 women with premature menopause get pregnant on their own without treatment.

If you want to get pregnant, your doctor may suggest in vitro fertilization.  
This means using eggs from another woman.  
The eggs are fertilized in a lab.  
Then, the fertilized egg is placed in your uterus.

# What Is Stomach Cancer?

Stomach cancer is a condition where abnormal cells grow in the stomach.  
It can be hard to notice at first.  
Many symptoms are similar to other common stomach problems.  
This means you might not realize something serious is happening.

## Common Symptoms of Stomach Cancer

You may have one or more of these signs:

- Heartburn or acid coming up from your stomach  
- Trouble swallowing food or liquids  
- Feeling sick or actually being sick  
- Burping a lot  
- Feeling full very quickly, even after eating a small amount  

Other possible signs include:

- Losing your appetite  
- Losing weight without trying  
- Feeling a lump near the top of your tummy  
- Pain in the upper part of your tummy  
- Feeling very tired or weak  

If you already have a condition like acid reflux, you may have some of these symptoms often.  
You might get used to them over time.  
But if your symptoms change, get worse, or feel different from normal for you, see a doctor.

## Who Is More Likely to Get Stomach Cancer?

Anyone can get stomach cancer.  
The exact cause is not always known.  
But some people have a higher chance.  

You may be more likely to get it if you:

- Are over 50 years old  
- Are a man  
- Have had a long-term infection with a bacteria called H. pylori  
- Have long-term, serious acid reflux  
- Have a condition called gastritis (inflammation of the stomach lining)  
- Have a rare condition called pernicious anaemia (affects how your body uses vitamin B12)  
- Have a close family member who had stomach cancer  

Lifestyle habits can also play a role.  
Smoking, poor diet, and being overweight may increase your risk.

## How Is Stomach Cancer Checked?

If your doctor thinks you might have stomach cancer, they will refer you for a test.  
This test lets the doctor look inside your stomach.

The test is called a gastroscopy.  
It is a type of endoscopy.  
It uses a thin, flexible tube with a small camera on the end.

During the test:

- The doctor puts the tube through your mouth, down your throat, and into your stomach  
- The camera lets the doctor see the inside of your stomach  
- If anything looks unusual, the doctor may take a small sample of tissue  
- This sample is called a biopsy  
- The lab will check the tissue for cancer  

The test takes about 10 to 15 minutes.  
It is not usually painful, but it can feel uncomfortable.  

You may be offered help to feel more relaxed and comfortable, such as:

- A numbing spray for the back of your throat  
- Sedation (a medicine given through a small tube in your arm to help you relax)  

A gastroscopy can also check for problems in nearby areas, like the food pipe (esophagus) or the first part of the small intestine.

## Treatment for Stomach Cancer

Treatment depends on several things:

- What type of cancer you have  
- How big it is  
- Where it is in your stomach  
- If it has spread to other parts of your body  
- Your overall health  

Most people have surgery and chemotherapy.  
Some may also need radiotherapy or special medicines that target cancer cells.

Your care team will:

- Explain all your treatment options  
- Talk about the benefits and possible side effects  
- Work with you to make a plan that fits your needs  
- Help you manage side effects, including changes to your eating habits  
- Support you during recovery  

You will have regular check-ups during and after treatment.  
You may also have scans and other tests.

If you feel worried about any symptoms or side effects, talk to your doctor right away.  
You do not need to wait for your next appointment.

## When to See a Doctor

See your GP if you have:

- Trouble swallowing  
- A lump in your tummy  
- Lost a noticeable amount of weight  
- Other stomach cancer symptoms that do not improve after 3 weeks  
- Digestive symptoms that do not get better after 3 weeks of using your usual treatments  

## When to Call 111

Call 111 now if:

- You are being sick for more than 2 days  
- You have symptoms you are worried about but are not sure where to get help  

111 will tell you what to do.  
They can arrange a phone call with a nurse or doctor if needed.  

Go to [111.nhs.uk](https://111.nhs.uk) or call 111.

# Secondary Adrenal Insufficiency

This condition happens when your body does not make enough adrenocorticotropic hormone. This hormone tells your adrenal glands to make cortisol. Without enough of it, your adrenal glands do not work well.

## What Causes Secondary Adrenal Insufficiency?

- A problem with the pituitary gland (the master gland in your brain).
- A tumor in the pituitary gland.
- Damage to the pituitary gland from injury, infection, or surgery.
- A rare problem in the hypothalamus (a part of the brain that controls the pituitary).
- Long-term use of corticosteroid medicines, even inhaled, injected into joints, or applied to the skin.
- Stopping corticosteroid medicine after using it for more than four weeks.

When the hypothalamus does not send the right signals to the pituitary, it is sometimes called tertiary adrenal insufficiency.

## Symptoms

You may feel very tired. You may also feel weak. You might lose weight. You may have nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.

Your skin does not get darker. This is different from Addison disease.

Your blood levels of sodium and potassium are usually normal. If sodium is low, it is usually due to too much water in the blood.

If you have a problem with many hormones from the pituitary gland (panhypopituitarism), you may also have low thyroid function, low sex hormone levels, or low blood sugar.

If not treated, you could become very ill and go into a coma.

## When Is a Crisis More Likely?

A serious health crisis is more likely if you are treated for one hormone problem, such as low thyroid hormone, without also getting cortisol replacement.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will check your symptoms and do blood tests.

- Blood tests will show low levels of ACTH and low levels of cortisol.
- A test called the ACTH stimulation test checks how well your adrenal glands respond.
- A CT or MRI scan of your brain may be done to look for a tumor or damage in the pituitary gland.

### Confirmatory Blood Test Results

| Test | Result |
|------|--------|
| ACTH | Low (less than 5 picograms per milliliter) |
| Cortisol | Low (less than 5 micrograms per deciliter) |
| ACTH stimulation test | Normal or low response |
| 24-hour ACTH stimulation test | Cortisol should keep rising after 24 hours |

### Testing After Stopping Steroids

If you stopped taking corticosteroid medicine, your doctor may test your adrenal function.

- A small dose of cosyntropin (1 microgram) is given into a vein or muscle.
- Blood is tested 30 minutes later.
- Your cortisol level should rise to more than 20 micrograms per deciliter.

Some doctors prefer this low-dose test because it can better show if your adrenal glands are not working well.

### Insulin Stress Test

This test checks how well your body makes cortisol during stress.

- You are given insulin to lower your blood sugar.
- This should cause your cortisol to rise.
- The test is not safe for people with heart disease or seizure disorders.
- It is not used if you are already very ill.

## How Is It Treated?

You need to take a medicine that replaces cortisol.

### Common Medicines

- Hydrocortisone
- Prednisone
- Prednisolone

### How to Take the Medicine

- Take your medicine in 2 or 3 doses each day.
- Most people take 15 to 20 milligrams total per day.
- One common schedule: 10 milligrams in the morning, 5 milligrams at lunch, and 5 milligrams in the early evening.
- Another option: two-thirds of the dose in the morning, one-third in the evening.
- Do not take a dose right before bed. It may keep you awake.

### Extra Doses During Illness

If you get sick, have a fever, or are hurt, you may need extra medicine. Your body needs more cortisol during stress.

### Do You Need Other Medicines?

No. You do not need fludrocortisone. Your adrenal glands still make aldosterone, which helps control salt and water balance.

### Other Hormone Problems

If you have other hormone problems from the pituitary gland, such as low thyroid or low sex hormones, those need to be treated too.

## Key Points

- Secondary adrenal insufficiency is caused by low ACTH from the pituitary or hypothalamus.
- It can happen after long-term use of steroid medicine.
- Symptoms are similar to Addison disease, but your skin does not darken.
- Blood tests show low ACTH and low cortisol.
- You need cortisol replacement medicine.
- You do not need salt-regulating medicine like fludrocortisone.
- Other hormone problems may also be present.
- A crisis is more likely if you are treated for one hormone problem without replacing cortisol.

# Portal Vein Thrombosis

Portal vein thrombosis happens when a blood clot blocks or narrows the portal vein.  
This vein carries blood from the intestines to the liver.  

Most people do not notice any symptoms.  
But some people may have fluid build-up in the belly.  
Their spleen may get bigger.  
They may also have serious bleeding in the esophagus.  

Doctors can usually confirm the diagnosis with a special ultrasound test called Doppler ultrasonography.  
This test shows if blood flow in the portal vein is slow or stopped.  

If possible, doctors treat the cause of the clot.  
They also treat any problems caused by the blockage.  
Medicines may be used to dissolve the clot or stop it from getting bigger or coming back.  

---

## What Happens When the Portal Vein Is Blocked?

When the portal vein is blocked, pressure builds up in the blood vessels going to the liver.  
This is called portal hypertension.  

High pressure causes the spleen to grow larger.  
It also causes veins in the esophagus and stomach to swell and twist.  
These swollen veins are called varicose veins.  
They can burst and bleed heavily.  

Fluid may collect in the belly.  
This is called ascites.  
It is not common.  
But it can happen if the liver is already damaged or congested.  
It can also happen if a person gets a lot of fluids through a vein to treat heavy bleeding.  

If portal vein thrombosis happens in someone with liver scarring (cirrhosis), their health gets worse quickly.  

---

## What Causes Portal Vein Thrombosis?

Cirrhosis is a common cause.  
It slows blood flow through the liver.  
Slow blood flow makes clots more likely.  

Any condition that makes blood more likely to clot can cause this problem.  

Causes vary by age:  

- **Newborns:** Infection in the umbilical cord stump (the part left after the cord is cut)  
- **Older children:** Appendicitis (infection in the appendix that can spread to the portal vein)  
- **Adults:** Too many red blood cells, certain cancers (liver, pancreas, kidney, or adrenal gland), cirrhosis, injury, blood clotting disorders, surgery, or pregnancy  

Often, more than one condition causes the blockage.  
In about one third of people, the cause is never found.  

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people have no symptoms.  

In some people, problems slowly develop due to high pressure in the portal vein.  

If varicose veins form in the esophagus or stomach, they can burst.  
This can cause heavy bleeding.  
A person may vomit blood.  
The blood may pass through the digestive system.  
This makes the stool black, sticky, and very smelly.  
This is called melena.  

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect portal vein thrombosis if a person has:  

- Bleeding from varicose veins in the esophagus or stomach  
- An enlarged spleen  
- A known risk factor, such as umbilical cord infection in newborns or appendicitis in children  

Blood tests check how well the liver is working.  
But these tests often come back normal.  

Doppler ultrasonography is the main test.  
It shows if blood flow in the portal vein is weak or stopped.  

In some cases, doctors use MRI or CT scans to get more detail.  

---

## How Is It Treated?

Medicines are used to dissolve clots or prevent new ones.  

The cause of the blockage is treated if possible.  
Problems from high pressure in the portal vein are also treated.  

If a clot suddenly blocks the vein, a medicine that breaks up clots may be used.  
One example is tissue plasminogen activator.  

If the blockage develops slowly, a long-term medicine called an anticoagulant may be used.  
Heparin is one example.  
This medicine helps stop clots from growing or coming back.  
It does not dissolve clots that are already there.  

In newborns and children, the main cause is treated.  
For example, an infected umbilical cord or appendicitis is treated.  

Bleeding from varicose veins in the esophagus is treated in several ways:  

- A doctor uses a flexible tube with a camera (endoscope) to reach the esophagus.  
- Rubber bands are placed around the swollen veins to stop the bleeding.  
- Medicines like beta-blockers and nitrates lower pressure in the portal vein.  
- This helps prevent future bleeding.  
- A medicine called octreotide may be given through a vein.  
- It reduces blood flow to the liver.  
- This lowers pressure in the belly and helps stop bleeding.

# Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)

PCOS is a common condition that affects how a woman’s ovaries work. It can cause a range of symptoms. These symptoms often start in the late teens or early twenties.

## Symptoms of PCOS

You may have PCOS if you notice any of the following:

- Your periods are irregular. You might miss periods or have them very far apart.
- You have trouble getting pregnant. This is because your body may not release an egg regularly, or at all.
- You grow extra hair on your face, chest, back, or buttocks. This is called excessive hair growth.
- You gain weight easily, especially around your waist.
- Your hair on your head becomes thinner. You may notice more hair falling out.
- Your skin gets oily. You may also get acne.

PCOS can also raise your risk of health problems later in life. These include type 2 diabetes and high cholesterol.

## Treating PCOS

There is no cure for PCOS. But many of the symptoms can be managed.

Talk to your doctor if you think you might have PCOS.

If you are overweight, losing weight can help improve your symptoms. A healthy, balanced diet and regular physical activity can support weight loss.

Medicines are available to help with:

- Excessive hair growth
- Irregular periods
- Fertility problems

If fertility medicines do not work, your doctor may suggest a minor surgery called laparoscopic ovarian drilling. This uses heat or a laser to treat the part of the ovary that makes male hormones like testosterone.

With the right treatment, most women with PCOS can get pregnant.

## What Causes PCOS?

The exact cause of PCOS is not known. But it often runs in families.

PCOS is linked to hormone imbalances. One key issue is insulin resistance.

Insulin is a hormone that helps control blood sugar. In many women with PCOS, the body does not respond well to insulin. So the body makes more insulin to make up for it.

Too much insulin can lead to higher levels of male hormones like testosterone. This causes many of the symptoms of PCOS.

Being overweight or obese makes insulin resistance worse. It also increases the amount of insulin your body makes.

# Short-Lasting Unilateral Neuralgiform Headache with Eye Redness and Tearing (SUNCT)

SUNCT is a rare type of headache. It causes very frequent, short bursts of pain on one side of the head. It also causes symptoms like red eyes and tearing.

Another similar condition is SUNA. It also causes short, frequent headaches on one side of the head. But in SUNA, only one of the eye symptoms happens — either redness or tearing — not both.

Both SUNCT and SUNA are called short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headaches. They are linked to the trigeminal nerve, which controls feeling in the face.

SUNCT is similar to cluster headache. Both cause pain on one side of the head and affect the nerves around the eyes. Because of these similarities, doctors sometimes group them together.

## What Happens During a SUNCT Attack?

- The pain usually starts around the eye.
- Attacks happen very often — up to 200 times a day.
- Each attack lasts between 5 and 250 seconds.
- The most common eye symptom is redness.
- Tearing may also happen.

## How Is SUNCT Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose SUNCT based on your symptoms and a physical exam.

Imaging tests like MRI or CT scans are done to rule out other causes, such as a tumor in the pituitary gland.

SUNCT can look like trigeminal neuralgia. But there are key differences:

- SUNCT has no quiet period between attacks.
- The pain is mostly in the eye area, not the jaw or cheek.
- Touching the face does not trigger the pain.
- The medicine indomethacin does not help.

## How Is SUNCT Treated?

### To Stop a Series of Attacks
- IV lidocaine is the most effective treatment.
- In one study, giving IV lidocaine for 7 to 10 days stopped the attacks in most patients.

### To Prevent Future Attacks
- Antiseizure medicines can help. Examples include:
  - Lamotrigine
  - Topiramate
  - Gabapentin
- Blocking or stimulating the occipital nerve (a nerve at the back of the head) may also help.
  - This can be done with a shot of lidocaine and methylprednisolone.

### Treatment Success
- IV lidocaine works best.
- Lamotrigine is the next most effective.
- Oxcarbazepine is less effective than the others.

# Tourette Syndrome and Other Tic Disorders in Children and Adolescents

## What Are Tics?

- Tics are quick, repeated movements or sounds that happen without meaning.
- They are not under the person’s control.
- You can hold them back for a short time, but only with effort.
- Tics can be simple (like blinking) or complex (like making a series of movements or saying a word).

## What Is Tourette Syndrome?

- Tourette syndrome is a type of tic disorder.
- It happens when a person has both motor tics (movements) and vocal tics (sounds) for more than one year.
- The urge to do a tic feels like needing to sneeze or scratch an itch.
- The tic gives short relief from the urge.

## How Common Are Tics?

- Tics are common in children.
- Most tics are mild and go unnoticed.
- Boys are three times more likely than girls to have tics.
- Tourette syndrome affects 3 to 9 out of every 1,000 children.
- Tics usually start between ages 4 and 6.
- They get worse around ages 10 to 12.
- Most tics go away during the teenage years.
- About 1 in 100 children still have tics as adults.

## Other Conditions That Often Happen with Tics

Children with tics may also have:

- Trouble paying attention or being overly active (ADHD)
- Repeated thoughts or actions (OCD)
- Feeling worried or anxious
- Trouble learning at school

These other problems often cause more difficulty than the tics themselves.

- Some children with ADHD start having tics after taking stimulant medicine like methylphenidate.
- This does not mean the medicine caused the tics. It may just show that the child already had a tendency to develop tics.

Adolescents and adults with tics may also have:

- Feelings of sadness or low mood (depression)
- Mood swings or extreme highs and lows (bipolar disorder)
- Problems with alcohol or drugs (substance use disorder)

## Types of Tic Disorders

There are three main types:

1. **Provisional tic disorder**  
   - A child has tics (motor or vocal) for less than one year.

2. **Persistent tic disorder (chronic tic disorder)**  
   - A child has either motor tics or vocal tics (but not both) for more than one year.

3. **Tourette syndrome**  
   - A child has both motor and vocal tics for more than one year.

Most children start with a short-term tic disorder. Some later develop a longer-lasting one or Tourette syndrome.

## What Causes Tic Disorders?

- Doctors do not know the exact cause.
- Tics often run in families, so genes may play a role.
- Some brain infections or diseases like Huntington disease can cause tics.
- Using drugs like cocaine or amphetamines can also cause tics.
- These tics are not the same as the main tic disorders.

Some children who had a strep infection may suddenly get worse tics or OCD symptoms. This is called PANDAS.

- Doctors think the body’s immune system may attack the brain by mistake after a strep infection.
- But not all experts agree that PANDAS is real or linked to tics.

## What Do Tics Feel Like?

- Before a tic, a person may feel a strong urge in a part of the body.
- This feeling builds up, like the need to sneeze.
- Doing the tic gives quick relief.
- You can delay the tic for seconds or minutes, but only with effort.
- Stress and tiredness make tics worse.
- Tics are often worse when the body is relaxed, like when watching TV.
- Paying too much attention to a tic can make it worse.
- Tics do not happen during sleep.
- Tics rarely affect balance or coordination.
- Tics may get better when a person is focused on a task, like schoolwork.

- Severe tics can make daily life hard.
- They can cause anxiety in social situations.
- They can be physically or socially limiting.

## How Do Tics Change Over Time?

- Tics stay similar for a while, but they can change in type, strength, or how often they happen.
- They may start suddenly and get worse fast.
- They can happen many times an hour, then disappear for months.

## Types of Tics

### Simple Tics
- Last only a second or two.
- Examples: blinking, grimacing, jerking the head, shrugging shoulders, sniffing, grunting, throat clearing.

### Complex Tics
- Last longer and involve more than one movement or sound.
- Examples:
  - Doing a series of movements together (like turning the head and shrugging at the same time)
  - Making rude or sexual gestures (coprolalia)
  - Copying someone else’s movements (echopraxia)
  - Repeating words or sounds (echolalia)
  - Saying rude or offensive words (coprolalia)

> **Did You Know?**  
> Most people with Tourette syndrome do not shout out bad words. Coprolalia is rare.

## How Are Tic Disorders Diagnosed?

- A doctor will talk to the child and parents.
- The doctor will ask about symptoms and how long they have lasted.
- The doctor may check for other conditions like ADHD or OCD.
- To confirm Tourette syndrome, the doctor may need to watch the child over time.

## How Are Tic Disorders Treated?

### 1. Reassurance and Support
- If tics are mild, the best thing may be to stay calm and not focus on them.
- Tics often go away on their own.
- Parents, teachers, and classmates should understand that tics are not intentional.
- Punishing a child for tics will not help and may make things worse.

### 2. Comprehensive Behavioral Intervention for Tics (CBIT)
- This is a type of therapy that helps older children manage tics.
- It includes:
  - Learning to recognize when tics are about to happen.
  - Practicing new behaviors to replace tics.
    - For example, if a child has a shoulder shrug tic, they might stretch their arms out instead.
  - Learning relaxation techniques.
  - Getting information about tics and how they work.

### 3. Medications
Medications are only used if tics are causing real problems.

#### For Mild Tics:
- **Clonidine** and **guanfacine** can help.
- They also help with anxiety and ADHD.
- Side effects: drowsiness (can affect school or daily life).
- These medicines are not used for high blood pressure in children.
- Stopping them suddenly can cause a short rise in blood pressure.

#### For Severe or Hard-to-Control Tics:
- **Antipsychotic medicines** like aripiprazole, haloperidol, and pimozide can help.
- These are not used because the child has psychosis.
- They work well at low doses.
- Side effects (rare at low doses):
  - Restlessness
  - Stiff muscles
  - Symptoms like Parkinson’s disease (trembling, slow movement)
  - Long-term movement problems (tardive dyskinesia)

### Other Treatments

- If a child has trouble learning at school, they should be tested for learning problems.
- Support and special help can make a big difference.

- If a child has obsessive thoughts or compulsive actions, an antidepressant medicine (SSRI) may help.

- ADHD is hard to treat because stimulant medicines (like methylphenidate) can make tics worse.
- Sometimes a very low dose of a stimulant works without making tics worse.
- Or a non-stimulant medicine can be used instead.

## Key Points

- Tics are not a choice. They are not caused by bad behavior.
- Most tics go away on their own.
- Support and understanding are more helpful than punishment.
- Treatment can help if tics are causing distress or problems.
- Other conditions like ADHD, OCD, or anxiety often need attention too.

# Memory Loss (Amnesia)

## When to See a Doctor

- See your doctor if memory problems are making daily tasks harder.
- Memory issues are often not serious.
- Getting checked early can help treatment work better if you need it.

## If You're Worried About a Family Member

- If an older relative is becoming more forgetful, talk to a doctor.
- This could be a sign of dementia.
- A doctor can help you understand what is happening.

## What Can Cause Memory Loss

- Some memory loss is just part of getting older.
- Common and treatable causes include:
  - Stress
  - Anxiety
  - Depression
  - Trouble sleeping (insomnia)

- Rarely, memory loss can be a sign of a more serious condition like dementia.

- Do not try to figure out the cause yourself.
- Always see a doctor for a proper check-up.

## What Happens at the Doctor’s Visit

- Your doctor will ask you questions about your memory and daily life.
- It helps to bring someone who knows you well. They can share what they’ve noticed.
- Your doctor may send you to a memory specialist for a full check-up.
- You might need tests like brain scans to help find the cause.

- Treatment will depend on what is causing your memory problems.
- The right treatment can help improve your situation.

# Primary Aldosteronism – Simple Explanation

This condition happens when the adrenal glands make too much of a hormone called aldosterone. The adrenal glands are small organs above the kidneys. Too much aldosterone can cause health problems.

## What Causes Primary Aldosteronism?

- A non-cancerous tumor in one adrenal gland.
- Overactive tissue in both adrenal glands (called hyperplasia).
- A rare cancer in the adrenal gland.

Tumors are very rare in children. But the condition can still happen in children with adrenal cancer or overactive adrenal glands.

## What Does Aldosterone Do?

Aldosterone helps the body keep the right balance of salt and water. It makes the kidneys keep more salt and lose more potassium. This can lead to:
- High blood pressure.
- Low levels of potassium in the blood.
- More urine and more thirst.

Aldosterone also affects sweat glands, salivary glands, and the lining of the intestines.

## How Is Aldosterone Controlled?

The body controls aldosterone through a system involving the kidneys and blood pressure:
- When blood pressure drops or salt levels are low, the kidneys release a substance called renin.
- Renin turns a protein from the liver into a substance called angiotensin I.
- An enzyme in the lungs turns angiotensin I into angiotensin II.
- Angiotensin II tells the adrenal glands to make more aldosterone.

When aldosterone increases, the body keeps more salt and water. This raises blood pressure and reduces the need for renin. So the system turns itself off.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Some people have no symptoms at all. Others may have:
- High blood pressure that is hard to control.
- Weakness in the arms or legs.
- Tingling or numbness in the hands or feet.
- Muscle cramps or sudden weakness that comes and goes.
- Frequent urination and feeling very thirsty.
- High levels of sodium in the blood.
- Swelling is rare.

Low potassium levels are common, but not always present.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect this condition in people with high blood pressure and low potassium. But it is now also found in people with normal potassium levels and hard-to-control high blood pressure.

### Tests Used:
1. **Blood tests** to check:
   - Aldosterone levels.
   - Renin levels (a hormone from the kidneys).
2. **Salt loading test**:
   - You get a salt solution through a vein for 4 hours, or eat extra salt for 3 days.
   - Then your aldosterone is tested again.
   - In primary aldosteronism, aldosterone stays high even after salt.
3. **Imaging tests**:
   - CT or MRI scans of the adrenal glands.
   - These can show a tumor or enlarged glands.
4. **Adrenal vein sampling**:
   - A thin tube is placed into each adrenal vein.
   - Doctors measure aldosterone and cortisol levels in each side.
   - This helps tell if one gland is overactive (tumor) or both are (hyperplasia).

### What the Test Results Mean:
| Finding | Primary Aldosteronism | Secondary Aldosteronism |
|--------|------------------------|--------------------------|
| Blood pressure | Very high | High |
| Edema (swelling) | Rare | Common |
| Sodium in blood | Normal or high | Normal or low |
| Potassium in blood | Normal or low | Low |
| Renin | Very low | High |
| Aldosterone | High | High |

- If both renin and aldosterone are low, it may be due to something else, like eating too much licorice, Cushing syndrome, or Liddle syndrome.
- If both are high, it is likely secondary aldosteronism (caused by kidney or heart problems).

In children, Bartter syndrome is different. It causes high renin and low blood pressure. Gitelman syndrome is a milder version in adults.

## How Is It Treated?

### If There Is a Tumor:
- The tumor is removed with surgery.
- Surgery is done using small cuts (laparoscopy).
- After surgery:
  - Potassium levels return to normal.
  - Blood pressure goes down in all patients.
  - About half of patients no longer need blood pressure medicine.

### If There Is Hyperplasia (Both Glands Overactive):
- Surgery is not helpful.
- Instead, medicine is used to block the effects of aldosterone.
- Common medicines:
  - Spironolactone: Start with 50 mg once a day. Dose may be raised over 1 to 3 months to 50 to 100 mg once a day.
  - Amiloride: 5 to 10 mg once a day.
  - Eplerenone: A newer medicine. Start with 50 mg once a day, up to 200 mg twice a day.
- Eplerenone is better for men because it does not cause side effects like breast swelling or sexual problems (which can happen with spironolactone).

About half of people with hyperplasia still need extra blood pressure medicine.

## Key Points

- Think about this condition in people with high blood pressure and low potassium.
- Test blood for aldosterone and renin before and after a salt test.
- Imaging helps, but often doctors need to sample blood from both adrenal veins to know if it’s a tumor or overactive glands.
- Tumors are removed with surgery.
- Hyperplasia is treated with medicines like spironolactone or eplerenone.

# Ear Ringing or Buzzing

## What Is Tinnitus?

Tinnitus is a noise that comes from inside your ear. It is not a disease. It is a symptom of another problem.

The noise can sound like ringing, buzzing, roaring, whistling, or hissing. Some people hear more complex sounds. These sounds change over time.

The noise is often louder in quiet places. It is also harder to ignore when you are not focused on something else.

Tinnitus can be most annoying when you are trying to sleep.

Everyone experiences tinnitus differently. Some people are very bothered by it. Others do not mind it much.

## Types of Tinnitus

### Subjective Tinnitus

This is the most common type. Only you can hear the noise.

It comes from unusual activity in the part of your brain that handles sound. This activity often happens because of a problem in your ear.

Doctors do not fully understand how this happens.

### Objective Tinnitus

This is rare. Other people can sometimes hear the noise too.

The sound comes from real movement in the body. It may come from blood moving through nearby blood vessels.

The noise may match your heartbeat. It can be heard with a stethoscope. In rare cases, it can be heard with the ear alone.

## What Causes Tinnitus?

Many ear problems can cause tinnitus. Hearing loss is often linked to tinnitus.

Common causes include:

- Loud noise or explosions (this can damage your hearing)
- Getting older (this causes gradual hearing loss)
- Some medicines that harm the ear (called ototoxic medicines)
- Meniere disease (a condition that causes dizziness and hearing loss)
- Migraines
- Middle ear infections
- Blockages in the ear canal (like too much earwax, an infection, or a foreign object)
- Problems with the eustachian tube (the tube that connects your middle ear to the back of your nose)
- Otosclerosis (a bone growth problem in the middle ear)
- Temporomandibular joint disorders (jaw problems)

A rare but serious cause is a benign tumor on the nerve that connects your inner ear to your brain.

### Causes of Objective Tinnitus

This type is linked to blood flow near the ear. The noise often matches your heartbeat.

Causes include:

- Blood flowing too fast or in a rough way through the carotid artery or jugular vein
- Tumors in the middle ear that have many blood vessels
- Abnormal blood vessel connections in the brain covering (dura)
- Narrowed or blocked veins in the brain
- High pressure inside the skull (called idiopathic intracranial hypertension)
- Missing bone over a part of the inner ear canal
- Missing bone over a vein behind the ear
- Fluid in the middle ear that makes blood flow sounds louder

The most common sound is the noise of fast or rough blood flow in neck vessels.

This can happen if you have low red blood cell count (anemia), blocked arteries (atherosclerosis), or uncontrolled high blood pressure.

Small middle ear tumors called glomus tumors can also cause tinnitus. These tumors are small but close to the hearing parts of the ear. Blood flow through them can be heard.

Sometimes, abnormal blood vessel connections (arteriovenous malformations) form in the brain covering. If they are near the ear, you may hear blood moving through them.

Less often, muscle spasms in the roof of the mouth or in the small ear muscles cause clicking sounds. These sounds do not match your heartbeat.

These spasms may have no clear cause. But they can be linked to tumors, head injury, or nerve diseases like multiple sclerosis.

## When to See a Doctor

Not everyone with tinnitus needs to see a doctor. But some signs mean you should get checked.

See a doctor right away if you have:

- Tinnitus in only one ear
- Any new nervous system symptoms, such as trouble walking, balance problems, dizziness, vision issues, trouble speaking, or trouble swallowing

If you have tinnitus that started recently and no warning signs, call your doctor.

If you have pulsatile tinnitus (a noise that matches your heartbeat), see your doctor.

Most people with long-term tinnitus should still see a doctor, even if they have no warning signs.

### What the Doctor Will Do

The doctor will ask about your symptoms and health history.

They will do a physical exam.

They will check your ears and hearing. They will also check your nervous system.

They may use a stethoscope to listen near your ear and neck for sounds of objective tinnitus.

They may do tuning fork tests to check your hearing.

### Common Causes and Their Signs

| Cause | Typical Signs | How It’s Checked |
|------|----------------|------------------|
| Subjective tinnitus (usually a steady tone, often with hearing loss) | Noise in one or both ears, hearing loss | Hearing test (audiogram) |
| Noise damage (acoustic trauma) | History of loud noise exposure | Hearing test (audiogram) |
| Aging (presbycusis) | Slow hearing loss, family history | Hearing test (audiogram) |
| Ear pressure injury (barotrauma) | History of sudden pressure change (like diving or flying) | Hearing test (audiogram) |
| Brain tumors (like vestibular schwannoma) or nerve diseases (like multiple sclerosis or stroke) | Tinnitus and hearing loss in one ear, possible other nervous system issues | Hearing test (audiogram), MRI with contrast |
| Eustachian tube problems | Long history of hearing issues, trouble clearing ears during flights | Hearing test (audiogram), tympanometry |
| Ear infections (like otitis media, labyrinthitis, meningitis, syphilis) | History of infection | Hearing test (audiogram), sometimes spinal tap |
| Certain medicines (aspirin, some antibiotics, diuretics, chemotherapy drugs) | Tinnitus starts in both ears after starting medicine | Hearing test (audiogram) |
| Meniere disease | Repeated episodes of hearing loss, tinnitus, fullness in one ear, severe dizziness | Hearing test (audiogram), balance tests, MRI to rule out tumor |
| Ear canal blockage (wax, foreign object, infection) | Only one ear affected, visible blockage during exam | Doctor’s exam only |
| Blood vessel problems (arteriovenous malformations) | Constant pulsing noise in one ear, no other symptoms | MRI, CT scan, or special blood vessel imaging |
| Muscle spasms (palate or middle ear) | Irregular clicking or mechanical sounds | Physical exam during episode, sometimes MRI |
| Fast or rough blood flow in neck vessels | Humming or pulsing noise near neck | Exam, sometimes CT or MRI of blood vessels |
| Vascular middle ear tumors (like glomus tumors) | Constant pulsing noise in one ear, possible visible tumor | CT scan, MRI, angiography, hearing test |

Note: The signs listed are common but not always present.

CT = computed tomography  
MRI = magnetic resonance imaging

### Tests You May Need

- Most people should have a formal hearing test (audiogram).
- If you have tinnitus in one ear and hearing loss, you may need an MRI with contrast.
- If you have pulsatile tinnitus, you may need special blood vessel imaging (MRA, CTA, or conventional angiography).
- Doctors may use questionnaires to learn how tinnitus affects your daily life.

## How Is Tinnitus Treated?

Finding and fixing the cause of tinnitus often does not work.

But treating hearing loss (for example, with a hearing aid) helps about half of people.

Treating stress, anxiety, or depression can also help. These issues can make tinnitus worse.

Many people feel better when they learn their tinnitus is not caused by a serious illness.

Caffeine and other stimulants can make tinnitus worse. Try to avoid them.

### Ways to Manage Tinnitus

- Background sounds can help mask the noise. Try music, white noise, or a fan.
- A tinnitus masker is a small device worn like a hearing aid. It makes soft, neutral sounds.
- Some hearing aids have a built-in tinnitus masker.
- For people who are very hard of hearing, cochlear implants (a device placed in the inner ear) can reduce tinnitus in most cases. This is only for severe to profound hearing loss.

If standard methods do not help, consider a tinnitus clinic. They offer special treatments like behavioral therapy and sound stimulation.

## Key Points

- Most tinnitus is caused by harmless problems like loud noise, aging, Meniere disease, migraines, or certain medicines.
- In many cases, the cause is not known.
- Be concerned if tinnitus is in only one ear or if you have other nervous system symptoms.
- Tinnitus is rarely cured. But many people learn to live with it well using simple tools and support.

# Warts and Verrucas

A wart or verruca shows up as a small, rough bump on the skin.

You can treat warts and verrucas with creams, plasters, or sprays you buy from a pharmacy.

A doctor can freeze a wart or verruca so it falls off later. A foot specialist can also treat verrucas.

If you have a wart or verruca, cover it when swimming. Wash your hands often. Do not scratch it.

## See a doctor if:

- You are worried about a skin growth.
- A wart or verruca keeps coming back.
- The wart or verruca is very big or very painful.
- A wart bleeds or changes in shape or color.
- The wart is on your face or genitals.

## What Warts and Verrucas Look Like

Warts feel hard and rough. They often appear on the hands, fingers, palms, or knees.

Warts are usually the same color as your skin. On darker skin, they may look darker.

Verrucas are warts on the feet. They have small black dots under the thick skin.

Some warts are flat and yellow. These are called plane warts. You can have many of them.

Clusters of warts on the feet or hands are called mosaic warts.

Warts are not dangerous. But some people find them itchy, painful, or embarrassing. Verrucas hurt more — like stepping on a needle.

You can treat warts if they bother you, keep coming back, or hurt.

## Pharmacy Treatments

You can buy wart and verruca treatments at a pharmacy. These include creams, plasters, and sprays.

These treatments can take up to three months to work. They may irritate your skin. They do not always work.

Do not use these treatments on your face.

Your pharmacist can help you pick the best treatment for you.

## Medical Treatments

A doctor can freeze a wart or verruca with a cold treatment. It falls off a few weeks later. You may need more than one session.

Ask your doctor if the National Health Service covers this treatment in your area.

If the treatment does not work, or if you have a wart on your face, your doctor may send you to a skin doctor (dermatologist).

If you have a large or very painful verruca, your doctor may send you to a foot doctor (podiatrist).

A foot doctor can offer treatments such as:

- Stronger medicines than those sold in pharmacies.
- Freezing the verruca with liquid nitrogen (cryotherapy).
- Surgery using a scalpel or laser to remove the verruca.

You can also pay to see a foot doctor privately.

## How to Stop Warts and Verrucas from Spreading

Warts and verrucas are caused by a virus. The virus spreads through contact with dirty surfaces or skin-to-skin contact.

You are more likely to spread the virus if your skin is wet or broken.

It can take months for a wart or verruca to appear after you come into contact with the virus.

Here are things you can do to stop spreading it:

### Do:

- Wash your hands after touching a wart or verruca.
- Change your socks every day if you have a verruca.
- Cover warts and verrucas with a plaster when swimming.
- Be careful not to cut a wart while shaving.

### Don’t:

- Do not share towels, washcloths, socks, or shoes if you have a wart or verruca.
- Do not bite your nails or suck fingers that have warts.
- Do not walk barefoot in public places if you have a verruca.
- Do not scratch or pick at a wart.

# Tinnitus

Tinnitus means you hear noise in your ears when there is no outside sound.

About 10 to 15 out of every 100 people have tinnitus.

---

## Types of Tinnitus

**Subjective tinnitus**  
You hear the noise, but no one else can.  
This is the most common type.  
It happens when the brain’s hearing system becomes overactive.  
This overactivity may start after hearing loss or damage to the hearing pathway.  
It may be like phantom limb pain after an arm or leg is lost.  
It can also happen if sound does not reach the brain properly.  
This can be due to earwax blockage, middle ear infections, or blocked ear tubes.  
But it is more common in people with inner ear hearing loss.  
Up to 85 out of 100 people with inner ear hearing loss also have tinnitus.

**Objective tinnitus**  
This is rare.  
The noise is real and can be heard by a doctor.  
It comes from blood vessels near the ear.  
It can be caused by blood vessel problems like a narrowed artery or a tumor.  
It can also come from muscle spasms in the ear or throat.  
Because it can be a sign of a serious problem, it always needs more testing.

---

## What Causes Tinnitus?

Tinnitus can come from many causes.  
Some causes lead to subjective tinnitus.  
Others cause objective tinnitus.  
See the table for a list of possible causes.

---

## When to See a Doctor

You should see a doctor if you have any of these:

- A whooshing or pulsing sound in your ear, especially near the head or skull  
- Other symptoms like weakness, numbness, or trouble with balance  
- Tinnitus in only one ear  
- A doctor can hear the noise when checking your ear

---

## How Tinnitus Is Treated

Treating the cause can help reduce tinnitus.

- If hearing loss is the cause, using a hearing aid can help.  
- About half of people with hearing aids report less tinnitus.  
- Some hearing aids have built-in sounds that mask the tinnitus.  
- These sounds can make the tinnitus less noticeable.

Stress and mental health issues like depression can make tinnitus worse.  
Treating these problems may help reduce symptoms.  
Many people feel better when they learn tinnitus is not a sign of a serious illness.

Caffeine and other stimulants can make tinnitus worse.  
Try cutting them out to see if it helps.

There is no medicine or surgery that cures tinnitus.  
But some people find relief with:

- White noise machines or fans that cover the tinnitus sound  
- Tinnitus retraining therapy, which helps the brain get used to the noise  
- Cochlear implants: These are devices for people who are very deaf.  
  Over 85 out of 100 people with cochlear implants report less tinnitus.  
- A special device that sends small electrical pulses to the tongue and plays a custom sound in the ears.  
  This helps about 80 out of 100 people with moderate to severe tinnitus.

---

## Tinnitus in Older Adults

About 4 out of 10 people aged 60 to 69 have some hearing loss.  
Since tinnitus often happens with hearing loss, it is common in older adults.

---

## Key Facts

- Subjective tinnitus is caused by a problem in the hearing system.  
- Objective tinnitus is caused by a real sound from blood vessels or muscles near the ear.  
- The most common causes are loud noise, aging, Meniere disease, migraines, and certain medicines.  
- If you have tinnitus in one ear with hearing loss or dizziness, you may need an MRI scan.  
- If tinnitus comes with other nervous system symptoms, see a doctor right away.

# Lactose Intolerance

Lactose intolerance means your body cannot digest lactose, a sugar found in milk and dairy products. This happens because your body does not make enough of the enzyme lactase.

Lactase is made in the small intestine. It breaks down lactose into two simpler sugars: glucose and galactose. These simple sugars are then absorbed into your blood. If you do not have enough lactase, lactose stays in your gut. It draws water into your intestines, which causes diarrhea. Bacteria in your large intestine then ferment the undigested lactose. This creates gas, which leads to bloating, cramps, and flatulence.

## What Causes Lactose Intolerance?

Babies are born with high levels of lactase. This helps them digest milk. After weaning, most people’s lactase levels drop. This is normal. As a result, many older children and adults cannot digest much lactose.

Some people, especially those from Northern Europe, East Africa, and the Middle East, keep making lactase into adulthood. This is called lactase persistence. It is rare and has a genetic cause.

Lactose intolerance can also be temporary. It may happen after an intestinal infection or other illness. Once the gut heals, lactase production often returns.

Other sugar intolerances exist but are rare. For example:
- A lack of sucrase stops the body from digesting sucrose (table sugar).
- A lack of maltase and isomaltase stops the body from digesting maltose (a sugar in some grains).

## Symptoms of Lactose Intolerance

Symptoms usually start 30 minutes to 2 hours after eating or drinking something with lactose.

**In children:**
- Diarrhea
- Poor weight gain

**In adults:**
- Bloating
- Abdominal cramps
- Watery diarrhea
- Gas (flatulence)
- Nausea
- Loud gurgling sounds in the belly (borborygmi)
- A sudden need to go to the bathroom

Some people feel mild symptoms. Others may have more severe ones. But the symptoms of lactose intolerance are usually not as serious as those from other digestive problems like celiac disease or intestinal infections.

## How Is Lactose Intolerance Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms. They will want to know if your symptoms happen after eating dairy.

If your symptoms go away when you stop eating dairy, and come back when you start again, that is strong evidence of lactose intolerance.

Sometimes, a doctor may do a test to confirm.

### Hydrogen Breath Test

This test takes about 4 hours. You drink a liquid with a known amount of lactose. Your breath is tested for hydrogen gas at one-hour intervals.

- If your breath has high levels of hydrogen, it means your body did not digest the lactose.
- Bacteria in your gut produce hydrogen when they break down undigested lactose.

This test is the most common way to confirm lactose intolerance.

### Lactose Tolerance Test

This test is rarely used now. You drink a lactose solution. Your blood sugar is checked several times after.

- If your blood sugar rises, your body digested the lactose.
- If your blood sugar does not rise, and you have symptoms like bloating or diarrhea, you may be lactose intolerant.

## Treatment for Lactose Intolerance

You can manage lactose intolerance by changing your diet and using supplements.

### Avoid Lactose

- Stop eating or drinking milk and other dairy products.
- Check food labels. Lactose can be in many processed foods.
- Some dairy products are easier to digest:
  - Yogurt (often safe because it has natural lactase)
  - Cheese (lower in lactose than milk)
  - Lactose-reduced milk and other products (available in stores)

### Take Lactase Supplements

- These are available without a prescription.
- Take them just before eating or drinking something with lactose.
- They help your body break down lactose.

### Take Calcium Supplements

- If you avoid dairy, you may not get enough calcium.
- Calcium is important for strong bones.
- Your doctor may recommend a calcium supplement to prevent deficiency.

## Important Note: Lactose Intolerance vs. Cow’s Milk Allergy

Lactose intolerance is not the same as cow’s milk allergy.

- In lactose intolerance, the body cannot digest lactose.
- In cow’s milk allergy, the body’s immune system reacts to milk proteins. This causes allergic symptoms.

**Cow’s milk allergy symptoms:**
- Itching or rash
- Wheezing
- Vomiting
- Belly pain
- Reflux (when stomach contents come back up)

Cow’s milk allergy is more common in children. It is rare in adults.

## Did You Know?

Most adults around the world cannot digest lactose well. This is normal. Only a minority of people, especially those from certain regions, keep making lactase into adulthood.

# Legionnaires' Disease

You can get Legionnaires' disease by breathing in tiny water droplets that have bacteria in them.  
This usually happens in places like hotels, offices, or hospitals.  

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may have a cough that lasts for weeks.  
You might cough up blood.  
You could feel chest pain, especially when you breathe or cough.  
You may feel short of breath.  
You might have a high temperature.  
You may also feel like you have the flu.

## When to Seek Help

Call your doctor right away or use NHS 111 if you have any of these symptoms:

- A cough that has lasted three weeks or longer  
- Coughing up blood  
- Chest pain that comes and goes, or happens when you breathe or cough  
- Trouble breathing  

Tell them where you have been in the last ten days.  
For example, if you stayed in a hotel, spa, or hospital.

You can call 111 or get help online at 111.nhs.uk.

## How Do You Get It?

You get Legionnaires' disease by breathing in tiny water droplets that contain bacteria.  
The bacteria can grow in water systems in buildings.  
It is rare to get it at home.  

You can get it from:

- Air conditioning systems  
- Humidifiers  
- Spa pools and hot tubs  
- Taps and showers that are not used often  

You cannot get it from:

- Drinking water that has the bacteria  
- Being near someone who has the disease  
- Natural water like ponds, lakes, or rivers

## How Is It Treated?

Most people with Legionnaires' disease need to go to hospital.  
Doctors will give you antibiotics through a drip in your vein.  
You may need extra oxygen through a mask or tubes in your nose.  
You might need a machine to help you breathe.

When you start to feel better, you can take antibiotic tablets at home.  
Treatment usually lasts one to three weeks.  

Most people recover fully.  
But it can take a few weeks to feel like yourself again.

# Candidiasis (Skin and Mouth Infections)

Candidiasis is an infection caused by a type of yeast called *Candida*. The most common type is *Candida albicans*. This infection can affect the skin and the moist areas inside the body, like the mouth and genitals.

It often shows up in warm, damp areas of the body. These include skin folds, between fingers, the genitals, under the nails, and inside the mouth.

Symptoms depend on where the infection is. Doctors usually diagnose it by looking at the skin and testing a small sample.

Treatment includes drying the area and using antifungal medicines.

Most cases are mild and affect the skin or mouth. But in people with weak immune systems, the infection can spread and become serious.

This document covers skin and mouth infections. Other types of candidiasis are covered in other sections.

---

## What Causes Candidiasis?

*Candida* is a type of yeast. It lives on the skin and inside the body without causing harm most of the time.

It can grow too much and cause infection when conditions are right. These include:

- Warm, damp skin
- Tight or non-breathable clothes
- Poor hygiene
- Not changing diapers or underwear often
- Using antibiotics (they can kill good bacteria)
- Skin conditions like psoriasis
- Health problems that weaken the immune system

These include:
- Taking steroids or other immune-suppressing medicines
- Pregnancy
- Diabetes
- Hormone problems (like low thyroid or adrenal issues)
- Blood disorders
- HIV or AIDS
- Problems with certain immune cells

Candidiasis often appears in:
- Underarms
- Groin area
- Skin folds between the buttocks
- Between fingers
- On the head of the penis
- Under the breasts
- In the mouth (especially in people with weak immunity)
- Under the belly in people with obesity

Vaginal yeast infections are common in women.

Nail infections and infections around the nails (paronychia) can happen after bad manicures or from hands being in water too long.

Candidiasis in the mouth is a sign of weak immunity.

Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis is a long-term condition. It affects the skin, nails, and mouth. People with this condition have weak immune responses to *Candida*, but their body still makes normal antibodies.

This condition can run in families and may be linked to other hormone problems like low parathyroid or adrenal function.

---

## What Does Candidiasis Look Like?

### Skin Folds (Intertriginous Infections)
- Red, itchy patches
- The redness may be hard to see on darker skin
- Small bumps or pus-filled spots around the main patch

### Around the Anus (Perianal Candidiasis)
- White, soft, wet-looking skin
- Itching around the anus

### Vaginal Infections (Vulvovaginal Candidiasis)
- Itching
- Thick, white discharge

### Nail Infections (Candidal Paronychia)
- Painful, red swelling around the nail
- The nail may separate from the nail bed
- The area under the nail turns white or yellow

### Mouth Infections (Oropharyngeal Candidiasis)
- White patches on the inside of the mouth
- These patches can bleed if scraped

### Corners of the Mouth (Perlèche)
- Cracks or small cuts at the corners of the mouth
- Can be caused by licking lips, sucking thumbs, or dentures that don’t fit well
- Moisture in the corners helps yeast grow

### Chronic Mucocutaneous Candidiasis
- Thick, scaly, red, pus-filled patches
- Looks like psoriasis, especially on the nose and forehead
- Always includes long-term mouth infections

---

## How Is Candidiasis Diagnosed?

Doctors look at the skin and the symptoms.

They may take a small skin scraping and look at it under a microscope after mixing it with a special solution (potassium hydroxide).

This helps find the yeast and its thread-like forms.

A lab test (culture) is not usually helpful. *Candida* is found on most people’s skin and mouth, so a positive result does not mean you have an infection.

---

## How Is Candidiasis Treated?

Most cases are treated with:
- Drying agents
- Antifungal medicines

### Skin Folds (Intertriginous Infections)
- Use drying solutions like Burow’s solution for 15 to 20 minutes if the area is oozing
- Apply antifungal cream or powder twice a day
- Use miconazole powder twice a day for 2 to 3 weeks
- For large or severe cases, fluconazole (a pill) once a week for 2 to 4 weeks may be used
- You can use antifungal cream at the same time

### Diaper Rash (Candidal Diaper Rash)
- Change diapers more often
- Use super-absorbent or ultra-absorbent disposable diapers
- Apply an imidazole cream twice a day
- For babies with mouth infections, oral nystatin may be used

### Nail Infections (Paronychia)
- Keep the area dry and protected from water
- Use antifungal cream or pills
- Thymol in alcohol (4%) applied twice a day can help
- These infections are hard to treat and may come back

### Mouth Infections (Oral Candidiasis)
- Dissolve one 10-mg clotrimazole lozenge in the mouth 4 to 5 times a day for 14 days
- Or use nystatin liquid to swish and swallow
- In some cases, a pill like fluconazole may be needed

### Chronic Mucocutaneous Candidiasis
- Requires long-term treatment with fluconazole pills
