# Staphylococcal Food Poisoning

Staphylococcal food poisoning happens when you eat food that has a toxin made by *Staphylococcus aureus* bacteria.  
These bacteria are often on people’s skin.  
They can get into food if someone handling the food does not wash their hands well.  
If the food is left out at room temperature, the bacteria can grow fast and make the toxin.  
The food may look and smell normal, even though it is dangerous.  

## Symptoms

The symptoms start quickly after eating the contaminated food.  
They usually begin between 30 minutes and 8 hours after eating.  
The most common symptoms are nausea, vomiting, and stomach cramps.  
Diarrhea also often happens.  
Most people feel better within one day.  

Foods that are often linked to this illness include meats, poultry, dairy products, and eggs.  
A similar illness can happen with *Bacillus cereus* bacteria.  
This usually happens after eating rice or other foods that were reheated after being cooled or stored the wrong way.  

## Diagnosis

Doctors usually diagnose this illness based on your symptoms and what you ate.  
They do not need to test the food or your blood.  
The key clue is that symptoms started soon after eating a meal, such as one from a restaurant.  

## Treatment

The main treatment is to drink fluids to stay hydrated.  
You can use oral glucose-electrolyte solutions, broth, or bouillon.  
These help prevent or treat mild dehydration.  

If you are very dehydrated, you may need fluids through a needle in your vein.  
Common fluids used are Ringer’s lactate or normal saline.  

Medicines to stop vomiting, like ondansetron, may help if you cannot keep liquids down.  
These medicines are only used when needed.  

Antibiotics are not used.  
They do not help with this type of food poisoning.  
The body clears the toxin on its own.  
Most adults only need supportive care and fluids.

# Iron Deficiency Anemia

Iron is a key mineral your body needs to make healthy red blood cells. When your body does not have enough iron, it can lead to a condition called iron deficiency anemia.

- The most common cause is losing too much blood.
- You may feel tired, weak, or short of breath.
- You may look paler than usual.
- A simple blood test can show if your iron levels are low.
- Iron supplements help bring your iron levels back to normal.

(See also _Overview of Anemia_.)

Iron deficiency anemia usually develops slowly. It can take months for your body’s iron stores to run low. As your iron drops, your bone marrow makes fewer red blood cells. When your iron is gone, the red blood cells you do make are smaller than normal.

Iron deficiency is one of the most common reasons people get anemia. In adults, losing blood is the most common cause. In men and in women who no longer have periods, low iron usually means there is bleeding inside the digestive system. In women who still have periods, monthly bleeding is the most common cause. Not eating enough iron-rich foods can also lead to low iron, especially during times when your body needs more iron. These times include infancy, childhood, teenage years, and pregnancy. Some health problems can stop your body from absorbing iron properly. The most common of these is celiac disease.

### Did You Know...

- In the United States, most people do not get anemia from not eating enough iron. This is because many foods are now enriched with iron.

## Symptoms of Iron Deficiency Anemia

Symptoms often come on slowly. They are similar to those of other types of anemia. You may feel tired, weak, or pale.

Some people with severe iron deficiency develop a condition called pica. This means they crave things that are not food. The most common craving is for ice. Others may want to eat dirt, clay, or chalk.

## Diagnosis of Iron Deficiency Anemia

### Blood Tests

If a blood test shows you have anemia, your doctor will check for iron deficiency. With low iron, your red blood cells are smaller and paler than normal.

Your doctor will measure the amount of iron in your blood. They will also check the level of a protein called transferrin. This protein carries iron through your blood when it is not inside red blood cells.

The best test for iron deficiency measures a protein called ferritin. Ferritin stores iron in your body. Low ferritin levels mean your body is low on iron. But sometimes, ferritin levels can be normal even when you are low on iron. This can happen if you have liver damage, an infection, inflammation, or cancer.

## Treatment of Iron Deficiency Anemia

### Stop the Bleeding

The first step is to find the source of bleeding and stop it. This is the most important part of treatment.

Normal food usually does not provide enough iron to replace what is lost from long-term bleeding. Your body only stores a small amount of iron. So, you need to take iron supplements to rebuild your iron supply.

It usually takes 3 to 6 weeks to fix iron deficiency with supplements, even after bleeding has stopped. Most people take iron pills by mouth. These pills can make your stool look dark or black. They can also cause constipation.

To get the most benefit, take iron on an empty stomach, about 30 minutes before breakfast. Drink orange juice or take a vitamin C supplement at the same time. Vitamin C helps your body absorb iron better.

You should keep taking iron supplements for at least 6 months after your blood tests return to normal. This helps refill your body’s iron stores completely.

In some cases, iron is given through a vein (intravenously). This is used when you need a large amount of iron or when you cannot take pills.

Your doctor will do blood tests regularly to check your iron levels and make sure treatment is working.

Treating iron deficiency also helps fix pica. Once your iron levels are normal, the cravings usually go away.

# Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma – Simple Explanation

This information is about a type of cancer that starts in the mouth. It is called oral squamous cell carcinoma.

---

## What Is Oral Cancer?

Oral cancer starts in the mouth. It can appear between the lip line and the back of the tongue. It can also start on the roof of the mouth or the floor of the mouth.

About 35,000 people in the United States get this cancer each year. Most cases happen in people over age 50. It is more common in men than in women.

The most common type of mouth cancer is squamous cell carcinoma.

---

## Main Risk Factors

The biggest risks for this cancer are:

- Smoking tobacco
- Drinking alcohol

The more you smoke and drink, the higher your risk.  
If you smoke more than two packs of cigarettes a day and drink heavily, your risk goes up a lot.

Heavy drinking means:
- More than 6 ounces of hard liquor a day
- More than 5 ounces of wine a day
- More than 36 ounces of beer a day

When smoking and drinking happen together, the risk goes up even more.  
For women, the risk can be 100 times higher.  
For men, the risk can be 38 times higher.

Other things that can cause this cancer include:
- Long-term irritation in the mouth
- Poor dental health
- Overuse of mouthwash
- Chewing tobacco
- Using betel quid (a mix of areca nut, lime, and leaf)

Some oral cancers are linked to a virus called human papillomavirus (HPV).  
HPV is usually passed through sexual contact.  
But HPV is much more common in throat cancer than in mouth cancer.  
Even if HPV is found in a tumor, it does not always mean the virus caused the cancer.

Cancer on the lower lip is often caused by too much sun exposure.

---

## Signs and Symptoms

Early mouth cancer often has no symptoms.  
This means you may not feel pain or notice anything wrong.

Later, you might see:
- A red patch in the mouth
- A white patch in the mouth
- A sore that does not heal
- A lump or thickening in the mouth
- A sore that bleeds easily
- Trouble speaking or swallowing
- Pain in the mouth or jaw

Red patches (called erythroplakia) are more likely to be cancer than white patches.

White patches (called leukoplakia) are usually not cancer. But some can turn into cancer.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Most cases are found during a routine dental checkup.

Your dentist or doctor will look inside your mouth.  
They may use a special brush to take a small sample from any unusual area.

If the area looks suspicious, a biopsy is done.  
This means a small piece of tissue is removed and tested in a lab.

All patients with mouth cancer should have:
- A look at the throat and voice box (direct laryngoscopy)
- A look at the food pipe (esophagoscopy)

These tests check for another cancer in the throat or food pipe.

Imaging tests are also used:
- A CT scan of the head and neck
- A chest CT scan or X-ray
- Sometimes a PET/CT scan

These help find out how far the cancer has spread.

---

## Staging the Cancer

Staging tells doctors how big the tumor is and if it has spread.

| Stage | Tumor Size and Spread | Lymph Nodes | Distant Spread |
|-------|------------------------|-------------|----------------|
| I     | Tumor ≤ 2 cm, not deep | No spread | No spread |
| II    | Tumor > 2 cm but ≤ 4 cm | No spread | No spread |
| III   | Tumor > 4 cm OR spread to one node ≤ 3 cm | Spread to one node ≤ 3 cm | No spread |
| IVA   | Tumor > 4 cm OR spread to nodes | Spread to nodes ≤ 6 cm | No spread |
| IVB   | Tumor has spread to deep areas | Any node spread | No spread |
| IVC   | Any tumor size | Any node spread | Spread to other organs |

**Tumor size and depth**:
- T1: Small tumor, not deep
- T2: Larger or deeper tumor
- T3: Bigger or deeper tumor
- T4a: Tumor has spread to nearby bones or tissues
- T4b: Tumor has spread to very deep areas like the skull or major blood vessels

**Lymph node spread**:
- N1: One side, small node
- N2: One or more nodes on one side, larger
- N3: Large node or spread beyond the node

**Distant spread**:
- M0: No spread to other organs
- M1: Cancer has spread to other parts of the body

---

## Treatment

The main treatment is surgery.  
Surgery removes the cancer and some healthy tissue around it.

After surgery, radiation therapy may be needed.  
Chemotherapy is not used alone. But it may be used with radiation for advanced cases.

If the cancer has spread to the lymph nodes, a neck surgery may be done.  
This is called a neck dissection.  
It is usually done if the risk of spread is over 15 to 20 percent.

Reconstruction surgery helps restore normal mouth function.  
This can include using skin or tissue from other parts of the body.

Speech and swallowing therapy may be needed after surgery.

Radiation therapy is an option if surgery is not possible.

---

## Treatment for Lip Cancer

Cancer on the lip is treated with surgery.  
The goal is to remove the cancer and keep the lip working well.

If there are many abnormal cells on the lip, the doctor may:
- Cut off the top layer of skin
- Use a laser to remove the affected area
- Use a special surgery called Mohs surgery

After treatment, use sunscreen on the lip to protect it from the sun.

---

## Prognosis (Outlook)

If the cancer is found early and has not spread to the lymph nodes, the chance of surviving five years is high.

- Tongue cancer: Over 80% survive five years
- Floor of mouth cancer: About 75% survive five years
- Lip cancer: Over 90% survive five years

If the cancer has spread to the lymph nodes, survival rates go down.

Cancer often spreads first to nearby lymph nodes.  
Later, it may spread to the lungs.

Lower lip cancer rarely spreads.  
Upper lip cancer is more likely to spread and grow faster.

---

## Key Points

- The biggest risks are smoking and heavy drinking.
- Mouth cancer often has no symptoms at first.
- Regular dental checkups can help find cancer early.
- All patients should have tests to check for other cancers in the throat and food pipe.
- Imaging tests help show how far the cancer has spread.
- Surgery is the main treatment for most cases.

# Fatty Liver Disease

Fatty liver disease happens when fat builds up inside liver cells.  
This used to be called "fatty liver."  
The fat involved is a type called triglycerides.  

Most people with fatty liver do not feel sick.  
Some may feel tired.  
The liver may become larger and can be felt by a doctor during a check-up.  

Fatty liver can get worse over time.  
It may lead to scarring in the liver.  
Scarring can become serious and damage the liver permanently.  

## What Causes Fatty Liver?

The most common causes in the United States and other Western countries are:

- Drinking too much alcohol  
- Being overweight or obese  
- Having high blood pressure  
- Having high levels of fat in the blood (like cholesterol and triglycerides)  
- Having insulin resistance or diabetes  
- Taking certain medicines  
- Having a genetic condition that affects how the body handles fat  
- Being in the later stages of pregnancy  

Some medicines that can cause fatty liver include:
- Steroids  
- Tamoxifen  
- Some chemotherapy drugs  

Certain rare inherited conditions can also cause fatty liver.  
Examples include Gaucher disease, Wilson disease, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.  

Fatty liver during late pregnancy is rare.  
It is called fatty liver of pregnancy or microvesicular steatosis.  
It is usually treated as a different condition.  

**Important:** Eating high-fat foods alone does not cause fatty liver.  
But it can lead to weight gain and other health problems that increase the risk.  

## Inflammation and Scarring

Fatty liver may or may not be inflamed.  
When the liver is inflamed because of fat buildup, it is called steatohepatitis.  

Inflammation can lead to scarring.  
Scarring is called fibrosis.  
Fibrosis can get worse and turn into cirrhosis.  
Cirrhosis means the liver is badly scarred.  
This changes the liver’s shape and stops it from working well.  

## Types of Fatty Liver

Fatty liver that is not caused by alcohol is now called **metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD)**.  
This used to be called nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).  

MASLD usually happens in people who have fatty liver and at least one of these conditions:

- Extra body weight  
- High fat levels in the blood  
- High blood pressure  
- Insulin resistance or diabetes  

When MASLD causes liver inflammation, it is called **metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH)**.  
This used to be called nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH).  

MASH can lead to fibrosis and cirrhosis.  

## How Is Fatty Liver Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tools to check for fatty liver:

- **Blood tests**  
  These check for signs of liver damage or inflammation.  
  They also help rule out other liver problems, like viral hepatitis.  

- **Imaging tests**  
  These include ultrasound, CT scan, MRI, or FibroScan.  
  They can show if there is extra fat in the liver.  
  Some tests, like magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) or ultrasound elastography, can also show if there is scarring.  

- **Liver biopsy**  
  This is the most accurate test.  
  A doctor takes a small sample of liver tissue using a thin needle.  
  The sample is looked at under a microscope.  
  This test can confirm fatty liver and show how bad the damage is.  
  It can also show if the cause is alcohol or another condition.  

Doctors always ask about alcohol use.  
This is very important.  
Drinking too much alcohol can cause serious liver damage.  

## How Is Fatty Liver Treated?

The main goal is to treat the cause.  
This can stop or even reverse the problem.  

You should:

- Stop any medicine that might be causing fatty liver  
- Lose weight  
- Control diabetes, high cholesterol, and high blood pressure  
- Stop drinking alcohol  
- Eat a healthy diet, like the Mediterranean diet  

Losing weight helps reduce fat in the liver.  
It can also reduce inflammation and reverse scarring.  

Some people may need medicine.  
Doctors sometimes try:

- Vitamin E  
- Thiazolidinediones (medicines used for diabetes, like rosiglitazone and pioglitazone)  

But these are used less often now.  
They can cause side effects.  
High doses of vitamin E can be harmful.  

For people with advanced scarring, a new medicine called **resmetirom** may help.  
It can reverse fatty liver in 30% of patients.  
It can improve scarring in 25% of patients.  

New treatments are being tested in clinical trials.  
A liver specialist (hepatologist) can help decide if you might benefit from them.  

## What Is the Outlook?

Having fat in the liver is not always serious.  
But the cause of the fat buildup can be serious.  
If left untreated, fatty liver can lead to inflammation and scarring.  
This can cause permanent liver damage.  

If alcohol is the cause, stopping drinking can clear the fat from the liver.  
But if the cause is not found and fixed, the liver can keep getting worse.  

For example, if you keep drinking too much alcohol or keep taking a medicine that harms the liver, repeated injury can lead to cirrhosis.  
Cirrhosis means the liver is badly scarred and cannot work properly.

# Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)

Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is an infection in the upper part of a woman’s reproductive system. It can affect the cervix, uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries. In some cases, pus can collect and form an abscess.

PID is often caused by infections passed through sex. It can also be caused by other bacteria that normally live in the vagina.

## What Causes PID?

Bacteria move up from the vagina and cervix into the uterus and fallopian tubes. The most common causes are:

- *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* (gonorrhea)
- *Chlamydia trachomatis* (chlamydia)
- *Mycoplasma genitalium* (another sexually transmitted infection)

Other bacteria linked to vaginal infections, such as those that cause bacterial vaginosis, can also play a role. These include:

- *Haemophilus influenzae*
- *Streptococcus agalactiae*
- Certain types of bowel bacteria
- *Ureaplasma* species

Inflammation in the vagina makes it easier for these bacteria to move upward and cause infection.

## What Are the Symptoms?

PID often causes:

- Pain in the lower belly
- Fever
- Unusual vaginal discharge
- Bleeding between periods or after sex
- Pain during sex
- Pain when urinating

Some women have no symptoms at all. Even mild cases can lead to serious problems later.

## How Is PID Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect PID in women of childbearing age who have:

- Lower belly pain
- Unexplained vaginal discharge
- Irregular bleeding
- Pain during sex or urination

A pelvic exam checks for tenderness in the cervix, uterus, or ovaries. A doctor may also feel for a lump in the pelvic area, which could mean an abscess.

### Tests to Help Confirm PID

- **Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs)**: These test for gonorrhea and chlamydia in a sample from the cervix. They are very accurate.
- If NAATs are not available, a culture test may be used.
- A pregnancy test is always done. PID can look like an ectopic pregnancy, which is dangerous.
- Blood tests may show a high white blood cell count, but this is not reliable on its own.
- An ultrasound is often the first imaging test. It can show swelling, fluid, or abscesses in the fallopian tubes or ovaries.
- If the ultrasound is unclear or the patient does not improve, a CT scan may be done.

### When Is Surgery Needed?

If the diagnosis is still unclear after testing, or if the patient does not get better with antibiotics, a doctor may do a laparoscopy. This is a small surgery that lets the doctor see inside the belly. If pus is found in the abdominal cavity, it confirms PID.

### Important Notes

- If a woman is pregnant and has PID symptoms, the doctor must rule out ectopic pregnancy.
- Other causes of pelvic pain include endometriosis, ovarian cysts, ovarian torsion, and appendicitis.
- Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome can cause pain in the right side of the belly, like gallbladder disease. But it is linked to PID and can be confirmed with a pelvic exam or ultrasound.

## How Is PID Treated?

Antibiotics are the main treatment. They must cover:

- Gonorrhea
- Chlamydia
- Other bacteria from the vagina, including anaerobes

### Why Start Treatment Early?

- Test results can take days.
- Clinical signs are not always clear.
- Even mild cases can cause long-term damage.

So, doctors often start antibiotics right away if PID is suspected.

### Treatment Options

Treatment depends on how sick the woman is.

#### For Mild to Moderate PID (Outpatient)

- **Option 1**: A single shot of ceftriaxone, plus doxycycline and metronidazole by mouth for 14 days.
- **Option 2**: A single shot of cefoxitin with probenecid, plus doxycycline and metronidazole by mouth for 14 days.
- **Option 3**: A different IV antibiotic (like ceftizoxime or cefotaxime), plus doxycycline and metronidazole by mouth for 14 days.
- **Option 4**: Levofloxacin or moxifloxacin by mouth for 14 days, plus metronidazole twice a day for 14 days.

#### For Severe PID (Hospitalized)

- IV antibiotics are used.
- Common IV regimens include:
  - Ceftriaxone + doxycycline + metronidazole
  - Cefotetan or cefoxitin + doxycycline
  - Ampicillin/sulbactam + doxycycline
  - Clindamycin + gentamicin

Treatment continues until the fever is gone for at least 24 hours.

### Special Cases

- If a woman has a known allergy to cephalosporin antibiotics, levofloxacin or moxifloxacin may be used instead.
- If the patient does not improve after 72 hours of oral treatment, she should be rechecked and may need IV antibiotics.
- If treatment does not work, the infection may be caused by *Mycoplasma genitalium*. In this case, moxifloxacin is used for 7 to 14 days.

### When Is Hospitalization Needed?

A woman should be hospitalized if she has:

- Uncertain diagnosis (especially if surgery is needed)
- Is pregnant
- Has a high fever or severe pain
- Has a tubo-ovarian abscess
- Cannot keep oral medicine down (e.g., due to vomiting)
- Does not improve with outpatient treatment

### Abscess Treatment

If a pus-filled abscess forms in the fallopian tubes and ovaries:

- IV antibiotics are used for a longer time.
- Drainage may be needed. This can be done using a needle guided by ultrasound or CT scan.
- In some cases, surgery is required to drain the abscess.
- If the abscess bursts, emergency surgery is needed.
- Surgery should aim to save the reproductive organs when possible, especially in women who want to have children.

## Key Points

- PID is often caused by gonorrhea or chlamydia, but other bacteria can also cause it.
- Even mild cases can lead to long-term problems like infertility, chronic pain, and ectopic pregnancy.
- Doctors should suspect PID in any woman with pelvic pain, especially if she is sexually active.
- Testing is accurate, but treatment often starts right away if PID is suspected.
- Hospital care is needed for severe cases or if the patient does not respond to oral medicine.

# Cushing Syndrome – Simple Explanation

Cushing syndrome happens when your body has too much of a hormone called corticosteroid. This can happen in two main ways:  
- You take medicine that contains corticosteroids.  
- Your body makes too much corticosteroid on its own.

---

## What Causes Cushing Syndrome?

### 1. Taking Corticosteroid Medicine
Some people need strong corticosteroid medicine to treat serious health problems.  
These medicines are used for conditions like:
- Asthma
- Rheumatoid arthritis
- Lupus
- Severe skin problems

If you take high doses of this medicine for a long time, you can get Cushing syndrome.  
Even inhaled medicine (like for asthma) or cream on the skin can cause it in rare cases.

### 2. Tumors in the Body
Tumors can cause your body to make too much corticosteroid.  
- A tumor in the pituitary gland (a small gland at the base of the brain) can cause the adrenal glands to overwork. This is called Cushing disease.  
- A tumor in the adrenal glands (small glands on top of the kidneys) can make too much corticosteroid.  
- Some tumors in other places, like the lungs, can also make a hormone that tells the adrenal glands to make more corticosteroid.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

People with Cushing syndrome often have:
- A large, round face (called moon face)
- Extra fat around the middle of the body
- A hump of fat at the top of the back (called a buffalo hump)
- Thin arms and legs compared to the thick trunk
- Thin skin that bruises easily and heals slowly
- Purple or red stretch marks on the belly, chest, or thighs
- Muscle weakness and tiredness
- Weight gain without trying

Over time, high levels of corticosteroid can cause:
- High blood pressure
- Weak bones (osteoporosis)
- More frequent infections
- Higher risk of kidney stones
- Higher risk of diabetes
- Blood clots in veins
- Mood changes, such as depression or confusion

Women may have:
- Irregular periods
- More facial or body hair
- Hair loss on the scalp

Children with Cushing syndrome grow more slowly and are shorter than other children their age.

---

## How Is Cushing Syndrome Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to check for Cushing syndrome.

### Step 1: Test Cortisol Levels
Cortisol is the main corticosteroid hormone.  
It is normally high in the morning and lower at night.  
In Cushing syndrome, cortisol stays high all day.

Doctors may test:
- Urine (over 24 hours)
- Saliva (at night)
- Blood (in the morning)

### Step 2: Dexamethasone Suppression Test
You take a dose of dexamethasone (a medicine) at night.  
Then, doctors check your cortisol level the next morning.

- If cortisol drops, it may mean the problem is in the pituitary gland.
- If cortisol stays high, it may mean the problem is in the adrenal glands or another tumor.

### Step 3: Other Blood Tests
Doctors may check your ACTH level.  
ACTH is a hormone that tells the adrenal glands to make corticosteroid.

### Step 4: Imaging Tests
Imaging helps find tumors.  
Tests may include:
- MRI or CT scan of the brain (to look at the pituitary gland)
- CT scan of the chest or abdomen (to look for tumors in the lungs or other areas)
- X-ray of the chest

Sometimes, doctors take blood from veins near the pituitary to see if it is the source of the problem.

---

## How Is Cushing Syndrome Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause.

### If You Are Taking Corticosteroid Medicine
- Doctors will weigh the benefits of the medicine against the risks of Cushing syndrome.
- If possible, they will slowly lower your dose over weeks or months. This is called tapering.
- You must never stop the medicine suddenly. Your adrenal glands need time to recover.
- If you get sick or are under stress, you may need to take more medicine temporarily.
- Even after stopping, your adrenal glands may not work well for weeks or months. You may need to restart medicine if you get very ill.

### General Support
You can help your body by:
- Eating a diet high in protein and potassium
- Taking extra potassium if needed
- Treating high blood pressure
- Using blood thinners if you are at risk for blood clots
- Getting treatment for infections quickly

### Surgery or Radiation Therapy
- If a tumor is in the pituitary gland, surgery or radiation may be used to remove or destroy it.
- If a tumor is in the adrenal glands, surgery is often used to remove it.
- If both adrenal glands are removed, you will need to take corticosteroid medicine for life.
- If a tumor is in another part of the body, surgery is usually the first choice.

### Medications
These can help lower cortisol levels or block its effects:
- Metyrapone
- Ketoconazole
- Osilodrostat
- Levoketoconazole
- Mifepristone (blocks cortisol effects)
- Pasireotide (lowers ACTH, but may worsen diabetes)
- Cabergoline (may help in some cases)

These medicines are used while waiting for surgery or if surgery is not possible.

---

## What Is Nelson Syndrome?

Some people develop Nelson syndrome after both adrenal glands are removed to treat Cushing disease.

In Nelson syndrome:
- The pituitary tumor keeps growing
- It makes too much ACTH
- The skin becomes darker
- The tumor can press on nearby brain areas, causing headaches and vision problems

### Treatment for Nelson Syndrome
- Radiation therapy to the pituitary may help stop the tumor from growing
- Surgery to remove the pituitary tumor may be needed

---

## Key Points to Remember

- Cushing syndrome means too much corticosteroid in the body.
- It can be caused by medicine or by tumors.
- Symptoms include weight gain, a round face, thin skin, and muscle weakness.
- Diagnosis involves testing cortisol and ACTH levels and imaging scans.
- Treatment depends on the cause: stopping medicine, surgery, radiation, or medicine.
- Never stop corticosteroid medicine suddenly.
- After surgery, you may need to take medicine for life if both adrenal glands are removed.
- Nelson syndrome can happen after adrenal removal and needs careful follow-up.

# Typhoid Fever – Simple Explanation

Typhoid fever is a serious infection caused by a type of bacteria called *Salmonella enterica* serotype Typhi.  
This bacteria spreads through food or water that has been contaminated.  
It is not common in the United States, but it happens more often in travelers returning from areas where the disease is common.

In 2019, around 9.2 million people got typhoid fever worldwide.  
About 110,000 people died from it.  
The highest number of cases happened in parts of Southeast Asia, the Eastern Mediterranean, and Africa.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The first signs of typhoid fever usually appear 8 to 14 days after exposure.  
The more bacteria you swallow, the faster symptoms start.

Symptoms often begin slowly.  
You may feel very tired and weak.  
You will likely have a high fever.  
You may also have a headache, body aches, a sore throat, loss of appetite, and stomach pain.

Some people also have:  
- Trouble urinating  
- A dry cough  
- Nosebleeds  

Without treatment, your fever will rise over 2 to 3 days.  
It will stay high for 10 to 14 days.  
Then it will slowly go down by the end of the third week.  
By the fourth week, your temperature should return to normal.

A slow heartbeat (called relative bradycardia) often happens with the high fever.  
You may feel very weak and tired.

In severe cases, you may become confused, drowsy, or even lose consciousness.

About 5% to 30% of people develop small pink spots on the chest or belly.  
These are called rose spots.  
They appear during the second week and go away in 2 to 5 days.

Other common signs include:  
- An enlarged spleen  
- Low white blood cell count  
- Anemia  
- Liver problems  
- Protein in the urine  
- Mild blood clotting issues  

Some people may also get gallbladder inflammation or liver inflammation.

Later in the illness, you may have severe diarrhea.  
Some of this diarrhea may contain blood.  
In 20% of cases, the blood is only seen under a microscope.  
In 10% of cases, the blood is visible to the eye.

About 2% of people have serious bleeding in the intestines during the third week.  
This can be life-threatening.

If you have sudden belly pain, a fast heartbeat, and a high white blood cell count during the third week, you may have a hole in your intestine.  
This is called intestinal perforation.  
It happens in 1 to 2% of people and usually affects the lower part of the small intestine.

You may also get pneumonia during the second or third week.  
This can be caused by another infection, like pneumococcus.  
But the typhoid bacteria can also cause pneumonia directly.

The bacteria can spread to other parts of the body.  
This can lead to infections such as:  
- Bone infection (osteomyelitis)  
- Heart infection (endocarditis)  
- Brain infection (meningitis)  
- Abscesses in soft tissues  
- Kidney inflammation (glomerulitis)  
- Infections in the urinary or reproductive system

Sometimes, typhoid fever does not cause typical symptoms.  
It may only cause a fever, lung problems, or symptoms like a urinary tract infection.  
This can make it hard to diagnose.

Recovery can take several months.

In up to 10% of people who do not get treatment, symptoms come back about 2 weeks after the fever goes down.  
This is called a relapse.  
Surprisingly, taking antibiotics early in the illness can actually increase the chance of a relapse.  
If symptoms return, restarting antibiotics works quickly.  
Sometimes a second relapse happens.

---

## How Is Typhoid Fever Diagnosed?

If you have a fever and have been in a high-risk area, your doctor should think about typhoid fever.  
This is especially true if your fever lasts more than 3 days.  
Other warning signs include diarrhea, stomach pain, or constipation.

Your doctor will take samples of your blood, stool, and urine to test for the bacteria.  
Drug resistance is common.  
So, testing is needed to find the right antibiotic.

Blood cultures are most likely to find the bacteria in the first 2 weeks.  
But they are not always positive.  
Stool cultures are more likely to find the bacteria in weeks 3 to 5.

If all tests are negative but your doctor still suspects typhoid, a bone marrow sample may be taken.  
This test is very accurate.

The bacteria have two parts that trigger your immune system.  
Doctors can test your blood for antibodies to these parts.  
A fourfold increase in antibody levels over two weeks suggests typhoid fever.  
This is called the Widal test.

But this test is not reliable.  
It only works about 70% of the time.  
It can also give false results.  
Other types of Salmonella, and even liver disease, can cause false positives.

Other illnesses can look like typhoid fever.  
These include:  
- Other Salmonella infections  
- Rickettsia infections  
- Leptospirosis  
- Tuberculosis  
- Malaria  
- Brucellosis  
- Tularemia  
- Viral hepatitis  
- Psittacosis  
- Yersinia infection  
- Lymphoma

---

## How Is Typhoid Fever Treated?

Antibiotics are needed to treat typhoid fever.  
Drug resistance is common, especially in areas where typhoid is common.  
So, testing is essential to pick the right medicine.

The best choices are:  
- Ceftriaxone for 14 days  
- A fluoroquinolone for 7 to 10 days  
- Azithromycin for 7 days

Fluoroquinolones can be used in children, but with care.  
If the bacteria are resistant to fluoroquinolones, try azithromycin:  
- 1 gram on the first day  
- Then 500 milligrams once a day for 6 more days

Other antibiotics like amoxicillin, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, or chloramphenicol are not usually used.  
Resistance to these is high.  
They should only be used if lab tests show they work.

If you are very sick with confusion, drowsiness, or shock, your doctor may add steroids.  
Steroids help reduce severe symptoms.

For mild cases:  
- Take prednisone 20 to 40 milligrams once a day for 3 days

For severe cases:  
- Use dexamethasone: 3 milligrams per kilogram of body weight at first  
- Then 1 milligram per kilogram every 6 hours for 48 hours total

You should eat small meals often.  
Stay in bed while you have a fever.  
Avoid aspirin and other salicylates.  
They can cause low body temperature and low blood pressure.  
Also avoid laxatives and enemas.

If you have diarrhea, try a clear liquid diet.  
You may need IV fluids or nutrition if you cannot eat.

If you have a hole in your intestine, surgery is needed.  
You will also need strong antibiotics that cover common gut bacteria.

If symptoms come back, treat it the same way as the first illness.  
But you usually do not need to take antibiotics for more than 5 days.

---

## What About Carriers?

Some people keep the bacteria in their body even after they feel better.  
This is called being a carrier.  
About 3% of untreated people become long-term carriers.  
The bacteria live in the gallbladder and pass into the stool.  
They can spread the disease for more than a year.

Carriers must not handle food or care for children or sick people until they are proven free of the bacteria.

To check if someone is a carrier:  
- Do three stool tests, one each month  
- All three must be negative to rule out carrier status

If a person is a carrier, they may need long-term antibiotics.  
In some cases, surgery to remove the gallbladder (cholecystectomy) is needed.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Without antibiotics, about 10% to 15% of people die from typhoid fever.  
With early treatment, the death rate drops to about 1%.  
Most deaths happen in undernourished people, babies, and older adults.

If you are very sick — with confusion, coma, or shock — your outlook is worse.

Complications are more likely if treatment is delayed or not given at all.

---

## How Can You Prevent Typhoid Fever?

Clean water is key.  
Drink only water that has been boiled, filtered, or treated with chlorine.  
Do not drink water from taps or use ice unless you know it is safe.

Avoid raw leafy vegetables.  
Do not eat food that has been left out at room temperature.  
This includes salads, cooked foods, and street food.

Wash your hands often.  
Use soap and water, especially after using the toilet and before eating.

If you are a carrier, do not handle food or care for others until you are cleared.

Travelers to high-risk areas should:  
- Drink only safe water  
- Avoid raw or undercooked food  
- Wash hands often

## Key Points

- Typhoid fever is caused by a bacteria spread through contaminated food or water.  
- It causes fever, headache, body aches, stomach pain, and sometimes a rash or bloody

# What Is Colic?

Colic is when a healthy baby cries a lot for no clear reason.  
It usually starts in the first few weeks after birth.  
It is worst around 6 weeks old.  
It often stops suddenly by 3 to 4 months old.

Doctors often say a baby has colic if the baby cries more than 3 hours a day, more than 3 days a week, for more than 3 weeks.  
But some doctors also consider sudden, loud crying that lasts less than 3 hours a day to be colic.

The crying of colic usually:

- Is loud and high-pitched  
- Happens without any clear cause  
- Happens at the same time each day or night  
- Goes on for hours with no reason  
- Stops for short times when the baby seems calm and normal

## What Causes Colic?

Even though the word "colic" sounds like it means belly pain, there is no proof that babies with colic have a belly problem.  
Babies with colic may pass gas or have a bloated belly.  
But this happens because they cry a lot, not because of a belly illness.  
When babies cry, they swallow air. That causes gas and a swollen belly.

Most babies with colic eat well and grow normally.  
Some babies suck hard on pacifiers or toys.

## When to See a Doctor

Parents should worry and call a doctor right away if the baby’s crying is linked to any of these signs:

- Vomiting that is green, bloody, or shoots out forcefully  
- Changes in poop, like constipation, diarrhea, or poop with blood or mucus  
- A fever (rectal temperature over 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit) or very low temperature (under 97.0 degrees Fahrenheit)  
- Crying all day with very few calm moments  
- Lethargy — sleeping too much, not smiling, not looking at people, or sucking weakly  
- Not gaining weight  
- Trouble breathing  
- Bruises or other signs of injury

If the baby has any of these warning signs, see a doctor right away.

If the baby seems healthy and has no warning signs, parents can try simple things first:

- Feeding the baby  
- Burping the baby  
- Changing the diaper  
- Holding and cuddling the baby  

If the crying does not stop after these steps, call a doctor.  
The doctor can help decide how soon the baby needs to be seen.

Doctors start by asking questions about the crying.  
They ask about other symptoms and the baby’s health history.  
Then they do a physical exam.  
Most babies with colic look healthy during the exam.  
No tests are needed unless the doctor finds something unusual.

## How to Help a Baby with Colic

After the doctor checks the baby and says the baby is healthy, parents can try these things:

- Hold the baby close  
- Gently rock the baby  
- Pat the baby’s back  
- Use an infant swing  
- Play white noise — like rain, a fan, washing machine, vacuum, or hair dryer  
- Play soft music  
- Take the baby for a ride in the car  
- Let the baby suck on a pacifier  
- Burp the baby after feeding  
- Feed the baby — but do not overfeed  
- Wrap the baby snugly in a sleep sack (swaddling)

If the baby is tired, some of these tricks may only help for a short time.  
The crying may come back as soon as the baby stops being held or moved.  
This can make the baby even more tired.  
Sometimes it works better to put the baby in the crib while still awake.  
This helps the baby learn to calm down and fall asleep on their own.

Parents can try changing the baby’s formula for a short time.  
But this is only helpful if the baby has other signs like vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, or not gaining weight.  
Switching formulas often is not needed and should only be done if a doctor says so.

If the mother is breastfeeding, she may notice that her baby cries more after she eats certain foods.  
These include dairy, broccoli, cabbage, or drinks with caffeine like coffee, tea, or soda.  
She can try cutting out these foods to see if the baby cries less.  
She should also check if any medicines she takes — like decongestants — might be affecting the baby.  
Some ingredients in these medicines can pass into breast milk.

Coping with constant crying is hard on parents.  
It can cause stress and worry.  
Talking with a doctor can help.  
The doctor can give advice, offer reassurance, and support parents through this tough time.

# Stroke Rehabilitation

Rehabilitation after a stroke helps you keep or improve your movement, muscle strength, and control of your bowels and bladder. It also helps you regain your ability to think clearly and do daily tasks.

Your rehabilitation plan will depend on your life situation. This includes whether you plan to return home or to work. It also depends on your ability to take part in therapy, how well you learn, your motivation, and how you handle stress.

If the stroke affects your ability to understand what people say, it can make rehabilitation harder.

## When to Start Rehab

Start rehabilitation as soon as you are stable enough medically. This helps prevent new problems like stiff joints (contractures) and lowers the risk of depression.

You should start taking steps to prevent pressure sores (bed sores) even before you are fully stable.

You can begin sitting up once you are fully awake and your symptoms are no longer getting worse. This usually happens within 48 hours after the stroke.

## Early Movement

In the first weeks, your affected arms or legs may feel limp. A therapist will gently move each joint through its normal range of motion. Do this 3 to 4 times a day.

## Getting Around

Learning to get out of bed and move safely to a chair or wheelchair is very important. It helps your body and your mood.

Some problems need special therapy. These include:
- Trouble walking
- Muscle stiffness (spasticity)
- Loss of vision in part of your field of view (hemianopia)
- Trouble with coordination
- Trouble speaking or understanding language (aphasia)

# Hepatitis A

Hepatitis A is an infection that causes swelling and irritation of the liver. It is caused by a virus called the hepatitis A virus.

## How Hepatitis A Spreads

- The virus spreads when someone eats or drinks something that has been touched by an infected person’s stool.
- This often happens because of poor handwashing, especially after using the bathroom or changing diapers.
- People can spread the virus even before they feel sick.
- The virus can get into food, especially shellfish, if they come from water polluted with sewage.
- It can also spread in places like day care centers, where children and caregivers may touch contaminated diapers.
- Outbreaks often happen in areas with poor water treatment or sanitation.
- Hepatitis A does not stay in the body long. Once the illness is over, a person can no longer spread the virus.

## Who Gets Hepatitis A

- Hepatitis A is most common in children and young adults.
- In the United States in 2018, over 12,400 cases were reported. Experts think about 24,900 cases actually happened, because many go undetected or unreported.
- Worldwide, about 1.4 million people get hepatitis A each year.

## Symptoms of Hepatitis A

Most older children and adults with hepatitis A will have symptoms. These include:

- Not feeling hungry
- Feeling tired and unwell
- Vomiting
- Pain in the upper right side of the belly (where the liver is)
- Dark yellow urine
- Yellowing of the skin and eyes (called jaundice) — this happens in about 7 out of 10 people
- Itching all over the body

Young children under 6 years old often have no symptoms. If they do, they rarely get jaundice.

Some people may also have:

- Light-colored stools
- Itching all over the body

Symptoms usually go away in about 2 months. But they can last or come back for up to 6 months.

Hepatitis A does not cause long-term liver damage. It does not lead to cirrhosis (scarring of the liver). It rarely becomes very serious (called fulminant hepatitis), and this is less common than with hepatitis B.

Most people recover fully.

## How Doctors Diagnose Hepatitis A

- Doctors suspect hepatitis A if a person has symptoms like jaundice and has been around someone with the virus.
- Blood tests are used to check how well the liver is working.
- These tests measure liver enzymes and other substances made by the liver.
- If the liver tests are abnormal, more blood tests are done to check for the hepatitis A virus.
- These tests look for parts of the virus and for antibodies the body makes to fight it.

## How Hepatitis A Is Treated

- There is no special medicine for hepatitis A.
- People should not drink alcohol. Alcohol can harm the liver.
- There is no need to avoid any specific foods or to rest more than usual.
- If itching is a problem, a medicine called cholestyramine can help. It is taken by mouth.
- Most people can go back to work once the yellowing of the skin and eyes goes away.

## How to Prevent Hepatitis A

- Wash hands with soap and water after using the bathroom, after changing a diaper, and before handling food.
- Avoid drinking water that may be unsafe, especially when traveling to places with poor sanitation.
- Vaccination is the best way to prevent hepatitis A.

### Who Should Get the Hepatitis A Vaccine?

- All children should get the vaccine.
- Adults at higher risk should also get it, including:

  - People traveling to countries where hepatitis A is common
  - People who work with the hepatitis A virus in labs
  - People with long-term liver problems (like chronic hepatitis C)
  - Men who have sex with men
  - People who use illegal drugs
  - People who do not have a stable home or are homeless
  - People who are adopting a child from a country where hepatitis A is common — they should get the vaccine before the child arrives and for 60 days after
  - Pregnant women at risk of getting hepatitis A during pregnancy

People with long-term liver disease should get the vaccine because they are more likely to have serious problems if they get hepatitis A.

### What to Do After Exposure

- If someone who has not been vaccinated comes into contact with hepatitis A, they should get protection right away.
- Healthy people aged 1 to 40: One dose of the hepatitis A vaccine.
- People over 40, or those with weak immune systems or liver disease: A shot of immune globulin.

Immune globulin is a medicine made from blood of healthy people. It contains antibodies that help prevent or reduce the illness.

# Laryngeal Contact Ulcers

Laryngeal contact ulcers are small sores on the voice box. They can happen on one side or both sides. These sores form where the vocal cords meet.

## What Causes Laryngeal Contact Ulcers?

- Repeated loud or forceful voice use can hurt the voice box. This often happens when someone starts speaking or singing suddenly and loudly.
- Singers are more likely to get these sores because of how they use their voices.
- A breathing tube placed in the throat during surgery can cause sores if it is too big.
- Long-term coughing can irritate the voice box and lead to sores.
- Acid from the stomach flowing back into the throat (gastroesophageal reflux disease) can also cause or make sores worse.
- If the sores stay for a long time, they can turn into small growths called granulomas.

## What Are the Symptoms?

- Your voice may sound hoarse or weak.
- You may feel like there is a lump in your throat.
- Talking or swallowing may cause mild pain.

## How Are They Diagnosed?

- A doctor will look at your voice box using a special scope. This is called laryngoscopy.
- In some cases, a small sample of tissue may be taken to check for cancer or infection.

## How Are They Treated?

- The main goal is to treat the cause of the sores.
- If you have a cough, your doctor may help you stop it. This can be done with medicine or by changing habits.
- If acid reflux is a problem, you will need treatment to reduce stomach acid.
- If an infection is present, you may need antibiotics or antifungal medicine.
- Speech therapy can help you learn how to use your voice in a healthier way. This includes better coughing habits and reducing strain.
- In some cases, injections of a medicine called botulinum toxin can help.
- You will need regular checkups to see if the sores are healing.

## What Should You Know About Recurrence?

- These sores often come back.
- To lower the chance of them returning, you must keep up good voice habits.
- This includes staying hydrated, avoiding shouting, and not clearing your throat often.

---

# The Professional Voice

People who use their voice a lot for work—like singers, teachers, or actors—may have voice problems. These problems can include:

- A hoarse or breathy voice
- A lower pitch than normal
- Feeling tired when speaking
- A dry cough that does not help
- Needing to clear your throat often
- A sore throat

Most of these issues are not serious. They are often caused by overusing or straining the voice. Other health problems, like acid reflux, can make them worse.

## How Are These Voice Problems Treated?

- See a speech therapist or a doctor who knows about voice problems.
- Use computer tools to check your voice pitch, loudness, and sound quality.
- Work on reducing tension in your throat when speaking. Use visual and sound feedback from a computer to help.
- Follow a voice care plan. This means:
  - Avoid speaking too loudly.
  - Do not talk for more than one hour without a break.
  - Do not strain your voice.
  - Stop clearing your throat.
- If you have acid reflux, follow a treatment plan to reduce it.
- Drink enough water to keep your voice box moist.
- Before a performance, avoid:
  - Alcohol
  - Caffeine
  - Smoking
  - Secondhand smoke
  - Other breathing irritants like dust or fumes

# Airway Tumors

The windpipe, throat, and voice box can develop growths. These growths can press on or grow into the airway. This can make it hard to breathe. Sometimes, cancer from other parts of the body spreads to these areas.

Tumors in the windpipe are rare. Most are cancer and are found at a later stage. This means they have already spread to nearby tissue or lymph nodes.

The most common types of cancer in the windpipe are:
- Squamous cell carcinoma
- Adenoid cystic carcinoma
- Carcinoid tumors
- Mucoepidermoid carcinomas

The most common noncancerous (benign) airway tumor is a squamous papilloma. Other noncancerous conditions can also happen.

## Symptoms of Airway Tumors

You may notice:
- Trouble breathing
- A persistent cough
- Coughing up blood
- Wheezing or strange breathing sounds
- Trouble swallowing
- A hoarse voice

## How Doctors Diagnose Airway Tumors

Doctors may suspect a tumor if symptoms get worse slowly. They may also suspect it if common treatments do not help. For example, if asthma medicine does not stop wheezing.

If a tumor is suspected, doctors will do a test called bronchoscopy. This test uses a thin tube with a camera to look inside the airway. It can help clear blockages and take tissue samples for testing.

If cancer is found, more tests will be done to see how far it has spread. This is called staging.

## Treatment for Airway Tumors

Treatment depends on the type of tumor and how far it has spread.

**Surgery**  
Some tumors can be removed with surgery if possible.

**Radiation therapy**  
This uses high-energy beams to kill cancer cells. It may be used alone or with chemotherapy or targeted therapy.

**Other treatments to open blocked airways**  
If surgery is not an option, doctors can use less invasive methods to remove part of the tumor. These include:
- Laser treatment to burn away the tumor
- Photodynamic therapy using light and medicine
- Cryotherapy to freeze and destroy the tumor
- Endobronchial brachytherapy, which places a small radiation source inside the airway

If a tumor is pressing on the windpipe, doctors may:
- Place a stent (a small tube) to keep the windpipe open
- Use radiation therapy to shrink the tumor

## Outlook for Airway Tumors

The outlook depends on the type of cancer. Cancers that have spread to lymph nodes in the neck or chest, or that have grown into nearby tissues, tend to have a worse outcome.

# Acetaminophen Poisoning – Simple Explanation

Acetaminophen poisoning can harm your stomach and intestines within hours. It can also damage your liver. This liver damage may get worse over 1 to 3 days. If not treated fast, it can lead to liver failure and even death.

A large single dose of acetaminophen can cause serious harm. This happens if you take more than 150 milligrams per kilogram of body weight in 24 hours. For most adults, this is about 7.5 to 10 grams. The more acetaminophen you take, the greater the risk.

The level of acetaminophen in your blood helps doctors predict how bad the liver damage might be. The main treatment is a medicine called *N* - acetylcysteine. This medicine helps protect your liver and can stop serious damage.

> **Note:** This information is for people who may have taken too much acetaminophen. Always talk to a doctor or poison control center if you are worried.

---

## What Is Acetaminophen?

Acetaminophen is a common pain and fever medicine. It is in over 100 different products you can buy without a prescription. These include:

- Children’s liquid medicines
- Tablets and capsules for kids
- Cough and cold medicines
- Many prescription pills

Because it is in so many products, it is easy to take too much by accident. This makes acetaminophen overdose very common.

---

## How Does Acetaminophen Poisoning Work?

When you take acetaminophen, your liver breaks it down. One of the breakdown products is called NAPQI. This substance is dangerous. Normally, your liver has a natural defense called glutathione that neutralizes NAPQI.

But if you take too much acetaminophen, your liver runs out of glutathione. Then NAPQI builds up and harms liver cells. It can also damage other organs like the kidneys and pancreas.

Some people may be at higher risk. These include people with long-term alcohol use or poor nutrition. Their livers may not handle acetaminophen well. But even people with alcohol problems do not usually get liver damage from normal doses.

---

## Acute Acetaminophen Poisoning

To cause harm, a large amount of acetaminophen must be taken in 24 hours. The amount must be at least 150 milligrams per kilogram of body weight.

Some people may not feel sick at first. When symptoms do appear, they usually start after 48 hours. The symptoms happen in four stages:

### Stage 1: 0 to 24 hours after taking the medicine  
- Loss of appetite  
- Nausea  
- Vomiting  

### Stage 2: 24 to 72 hours after taking the medicine  
- Pain in the upper right side of the belly  
- Blood tests may show higher levels of liver enzymes (AST and ALT)  
- In severe cases, bilirubin and prothrombin time (INR) may also rise  

### Stage 3: 72 to 96 hours after taking the medicine  
- Continued vomiting  
- Signs of liver failure  
- Liver enzyme levels peak  
- Kidney problems or pancreatitis may occur  

### Stage 4: More than 5 days after taking the medicine  
- Liver damage may get better  
- Or it may get worse and lead to failure of multiple organs  
- This can be deadly  

> **Note:** Liver failure can happen even if you do not have severe symptoms early on.

---

## How Doctors Check for Poisoning

Doctors use blood tests to check for acetaminophen poisoning.

### Blood Test: Acetaminophen Level  
- A blood test measures how much acetaminophen is in your blood.  
- This test is most useful if done at least 4 hours after you took the medicine.  
- The test is not helpful if you took the medicine more than 24 hours ago.

### The Rumack-Matthew Nomogram  
- This is a chart doctors use to predict liver damage.  
- It uses your blood level and the time since you took the medicine.  
- It only works for one single large dose.  
- It does not work if you took the medicine slowly over time.

#### How the nomogram works:
- If your blood level is 150 micrograms per milliliter or less, and you have no symptoms, liver damage is very unlikely.  
- If your level is higher, liver damage is possible.  
- For extended-release pills, two blood tests are needed — one 4 hours after the dose and another 4 hours later.  
- If either test is above the danger line, treatment is needed.

> **Important:** If you are not sure when you took the medicine, doctors use the earliest possible time. This is called the "worst-case" estimate.

---

## What Tests Do Doctors Do?

If acetaminophen poisoning is suspected, doctors will do:

- Liver function tests (AST and ALT)  
- Prothrombin time (PT) and INR (to check blood clotting)  
- Kidney function tests (creatinine)  
- Blood pH and lactate levels (to check for acid buildup)

> **Note:** Mild increases in liver enzymes can happen in healthy adults who take normal doses of acetaminophen for a few days. These changes are usually temporary and not serious.

---

## Other Tests and Tools

- **Acetaminophen/cysteine adducts:** These are blood tests that show if you have been exposed to acetaminophen. But they do not prove liver damage.  
- **Other research tests:** Scientists are studying new blood markers like microRNA and HMGB-1. But these are not used in regular care yet.

---

## Treatment for Acetaminophen Poisoning

### 1. *N* - Acetylcysteine (The Main Treatment)
- This is an antidote that helps protect the liver.  
- It works by replacing the liver’s natural defense (glutathione).  
- It stops the toxic part of acetaminophen from harming liver cells.  
- It does not fix liver damage that has already happened.

#### When to give it:
- If liver damage is likely based on dose or blood level.  
- Best if given within 8 hours of taking the medicine.  
- Still helpful after 24 hours, even if the benefit is less clear.  
- If you are unsure, start treatment and keep going until the risk is ruled out.

#### How it is given:
- **Oral (by mouth):**  
  - First dose: 140 milligrams per kilogram of body weight.  
  - Then 17 more doses of 70 milligrams per kilogram every 4 hours.  
  - The medicine tastes bad. It is mixed with soda or fruit juice.  
  - Vomiting is common. If you vomit within 1 hour, repeat the dose.  
  - Anti-nausea medicine can help.

- **IV (through a vein):**  
  - First dose: 150 mg/kg in 200 mL of fluid, given over 15 minutes.  
  - Second dose: 50 mg/kg in 500 mL of fluid, given over 4 hours.  
  - Third dose: 100 mg/kg in 1000 mL of fluid, given over 16 hours.  
  - For children, the dose may need to be adjusted. Talk to a poison control center.

> **Note:** Both oral and IV forms work equally well.

#### When to stop treatment:
- Blood level of acetaminophen is below 10 micrograms per milliliter  
- INR is less than 2.0  
- AST and ALT levels are normal or have dropped by half from their peak  
- You feel well and have no symptoms

---

### 2. Activated Charcoal
- This is a powder that can trap poison in the stomach.  
- It may help if the acetaminophen is still in your stomach.  
- It is only useful if given within a few hours of taking the medicine.

---

### 3. Fomepizole (4-methylpyrazole)
- This medicine may help reduce the harmful breakdown of acetaminophen.  
- But the evidence is not strong. It is not a standard treatment.

---

### 4. Severe Cases (Massive Overdose)
- If someone takes more than 50 grams of acetaminophen, they may get very sick fast.  
- Symptoms include:  
  - Severe acid in the blood  
  - Extreme tiredness or confusion  
  - Coma  
  - High blood sugar  

- Treatment may include:
  - Continuous IV *N* - acetylcysteine until no acetaminophen is left in the blood  
  - Dialysis (a machine that cleans the blood)  
  - This is used if the blood level is over 900 micrograms per milliliter or if you are confused or have acid in your blood

> **Always consult a poison control center or toxicologist in these cases.**

---

## Liver Failure and Transplant

If the liver fails completely, the only treatment may be a liver transplant. This is rare but possible.

---

## Prognosis (Outlook)

With proper treatment, most people recover fully. The chance of dying is low.
