# Corneal Ulcer

A corneal ulcer is a sore on the clear front part of the eye. It is usually caused by an infection.

## What Causes a Corneal Ulcer?

- Infections from bacteria, fungi, viruses, or parasites like *Acanthamoeba* can cause ulcers.
- *Acanthamoeba* lives in dirty water and can get into the eye.
- A scratch or injury to the eye can start an ulcer.
- Severe dry eyes can also lead to ulcers.
- Wearing contact lenses, especially while sleeping or not cleaning them well, increases the risk.
- Viral ulcers, often from the herpes virus, can come back. Stress or no clear reason can trigger a return.
- Not getting enough vitamin A or protein can cause ulcers. But this is rare in the United States.
- If the eyelids do not close all the way, the eye can dry out and get irritated. This can lead to an ulcer.
- In-growing eyelashes, an eyelid that turns inward, or eyelid inflammation can also cause ulcers.

## What Are the Symptoms?

- The eye becomes red.
- You feel pain or aching.
- It feels like something is in your eye.
- You may cry more than usual.
- Bright light hurts your eye.
- The ulcer may look like a white or gray spot on the eye.
- In some cases, the ulcer spreads across the whole cornea and goes deep.
- Pus can build up behind the cornea. This may form a white layer at the bottom of the eye. This is called a hypopyon.
- The white part of the eye looks red and full of blood vessels.
- The deeper the ulcer, the worse the pain and the higher the risk of serious problems.

Even after healing, the eye may have a cloudy scar. This can affect your vision.

Other serious problems can happen, such as:
- Infection spreading deep into the eye.
- The cornea tearing open.
- The iris moving out of place.
- Damage to most or all of the eye’s tissue.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- A doctor will look at your eye with a special microscope called a slit lamp.
- The doctor may put in eye drops with a yellow-green dye called fluorescein.
- This dye sticks to damaged areas of the cornea. It makes the sore easier to see.
- In some cases, the doctor may gently scrape the surface of a large ulcer.
- The sample is sent to a lab to grow and find the cause of the infection.
- Once the cause is known, the doctor picks the right medicine to treat it.

## How Is It Treated?

- You will need eye drops right away. These may be antibiotics, antivirals, or antifungals.
- You must use the drops often. Sometimes every hour, day and night, for several days.
- Eye drops that widen the pupil, like atropine or scopolamine, can help with pain.
- These drops also lower the risk of other problems.
- In some cases, a corneal transplant may be needed.

> **A corneal ulcer is an emergency. It must be treated right away.**

# Calluses and Corns

Calluses and corns are thick, hard areas of skin.  
They form where the skin rubs against something or gets pressed.  
This usually happens over a bony part of the foot or hand.

## What Are Calluses?

Calluses are flat and spread out.  
They are usually not painful.  
They often form on the hands or feet.  
They can also form in other places if a person’s job causes repeated rubbing or pressure.  
For example, a violinist might get a callus on the jaw or collarbone.

## What Are Corns?

Corns are smaller and more focused.  
They are often painful.  
They can feel like a small, hard lump under the skin.  
Corns often form on the toes or the bottom of the foot.  
They can also form between the toes.

There are two main types of corns:

- **Hard corns** form on the tops or sides of toes.  
  They are common where bones stick out.
- **Soft corns** form between the toes.  
  The skin there stays moist, so the corn stays soft.

Corns can form when shoes do not fit well.  
Sometimes, a small corn on the foot or hand may be inherited.  
This type is very small and does not come from pressure.

## How Do They Look?

A corn looks like a small, round, hard disk.  
It may be yellow or tan.  
It is often surrounded by red, irritated skin.  
A corn can go deep into the skin.

A callus looks like a thick, tough patch of skin.  
It has no hard center.  
It is smooth and even in shape.

## What Causes Calluses and Corns?

They form when skin is pressed or rubbed over and over.  
This often happens on bony parts of the foot.  
Poorly fitting shoes are the most common cause.  
But they can also form from walking habits or foot shape.

## Symptoms

Calluses usually do not hurt.  
But if the rubbing is strong, they can become sore or burn a little.  
Sometimes, a callus near the toes can feel like nerve pain.

Corns are often painful when you press on them.  
A fluid-filled pocket (called a bursa) can form under a corn.  
This can make it more tender.

## How Are They Diagnosed?

A doctor checks the skin.  
They look at the shape, color, and location of the thickened skin.

To tell a corn from a wart, the doctor may gently scrape off the top layer of skin.

- A **corn** shows a clear, yellowish or tan core.  
  The skin underneath looks broken or damaged.
- A **wart** bleeds when scraped.  
  It has a rough, uneven edge.  
  It may have small black dots inside.  
  These dots are tiny blood vessels that have closed off.

Warts also break the natural lines on the skin.  
Calluses do not change these lines.

## How Are They Treated?

There are several ways to treat calluses and corns:

- **Manual removal**: A doctor or foot care specialist can gently scrape off the thick skin.
- **Keratolytics**: These are creams or liquids that help soften and remove thick skin.
- **Cushioning**: Pads or special insoles can protect the area and reduce pressure.
- **Change footwear**: Wearing better-fitting shoes helps prevent new ones from forming.
- **Fix foot problems**: If your foot shape causes pressure, a doctor may suggest changes in how you walk or stand.

In rare cases, surgery may be needed.  
This is only if other treatments do not work.

## How to Prevent Calluses and Corns

- Wear shoes that fit well.
- Use padding or insoles to protect pressure points.
- Avoid shoes that are too tight or too loose.
- Keep your feet healthy and dry.
- See a foot care specialist if you have diabetes or poor circulation.

## Key Facts

- Calluses and corns are caused by repeated pressure or rubbing.
- A corn has a hard center. A wart does not.
- When you scrape a corn, it does not bleed.  
  When you scrape a wart, it does bleed.
- You can use gentle scraping and special creams to remove thick skin.
- Cushioning and better foot support help stop new ones from forming.

# Neutropenia

Neutropenia means you have too few neutrophils in your blood.  
Neutrophils are a type of white blood cell that helps your body fight off infections.  
When you have too few neutrophils, you are more likely to get serious infections.

## What Happens When You Have Neutropenia?

- A low number of neutrophils makes it hard for your body to fight bacteria and some fungi.
- Without enough neutrophils, even mild infections can become life-threatening.
- Neutropenia often happens as a side effect of cancer treatments like chemotherapy or radiation.
- Doctors may suspect neutropenia if you get infections often or in unusual ways.

## How Is Neutropenia Diagnosed?

- A simple blood test checks your neutrophil count.
- If the cause is unclear, your doctor may take a sample of your bone marrow.
- The bone marrow sample is looked at under a microscope to see how well it is making blood cells.

## How Severe Is the Neutropenia?

The normal range for neutrophils is about 1500 per microliter of blood.  
When the count drops below this, the risk of infection goes up.  
The severity is split into three levels:

- **Mild**: 1000 to 1500 neutrophils per microliter  
- **Moderate**: 500 to 1000 neutrophils per microliter  
- **Severe**: Less than 500 neutrophils per microliter

When the count is below 500, the risk of infection is very high.  
Even bacteria that normally live in your mouth or gut can cause serious infections.

## What Causes Neutropenia?

There are two main reasons:

1. **Neutrophils are used up or destroyed too fast**  
   - Some infections (like certain bacterial infections) can use up neutrophils quickly.  
   - Some allergic reactions can cause the body to destroy neutrophils.  
   - Certain medicines, such as those for overactive thyroid, can cause this.  
   - In autoimmune diseases, the body makes antibodies that attack its own neutrophils.  
   - An enlarged spleen can trap and destroy neutrophils.

2. **The bone marrow does not make enough neutrophils**  
   - Cancer can affect the bone marrow’s ability to make blood cells.  
   - Viral infections like the flu can slow down production.  
   - Bacterial infections like tuberculosis can also affect the bone marrow.  
   - A condition called myelofibrosis damages the bone marrow.  
   - Low levels of vitamin B12 or folic acid can reduce neutrophil production.  
   - Radiation therapy that affects the bone marrow can cause neutropenia.  
   - Some medicines used in cancer treatment (chemotherapy) can harm the bone marrow.  
   - Toxins like benzene or insecticides can damage the bone marrow.  
   - A rare condition called aplastic anemia stops the bone marrow from making all types of blood cells.

Some rare inherited conditions also cause low neutrophil counts:

- **Cyclic neutropenia**: Neutrophil levels go up and down every few weeks.  
- **Chronic benign neutropenia**: Neutrophil levels stay low, but infections are rare.  
- **Severe congenital neutropenia**: Neutrophils do not mature properly. People with this condition get serious infections early in life.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Neutropenia itself does not cause specific symptoms.  
It is often found when you get an infection.

Common signs include:
- Fever
- Painful sores in the mouth or around the anus
- Pneumonia or other serious infections

In chronic neutropenia, you may feel fine if your neutrophil count is not extremely low.

If neutropenia is caused by medicine, you may have:
- Fever
- Rash
- Swollen glands

In cyclic neutropenia, symptoms come and go with your neutrophil levels.

> **Did You Know?**  
> Neutropenia often has no clear symptoms. Doctors usually only suspect it if you get infections often or in unusual ways.

## How Is Neutropenia Diagnosed?

Doctors use two main tests:

1. **Complete blood count (CBC)**  
   - This blood test measures your neutrophil count.  
   - A low count means you have neutropenia.

2. **Bone marrow exam**  
   - A small sample of bone marrow is taken with a needle.  
   - The sample is checked under a microscope.  
   - This helps doctors see if the bone marrow is making enough neutrophils.  
   - It also helps find if there is a hidden infection or disease like leukemia.

Doctors also:
- Ask about medicines or exposure to toxins.  
- Look for signs of infection or other health problems.  
- If you have stomach pain, they may do a CT scan of your belly.  
- If you have a fever, they will test your urine and blood.  
- They may do a blood culture to grow any bacteria that might be in your blood.  
- They may also do a chest x-ray to check for lung infections.

## How Is Neutropenia Treated?

The main goal is to treat any infection right away.

- If you have severe neutropenia and a fever, doctors treat you as if you have an infection, even if they do not yet know the cause.  
- You will be given strong antibiotics to fight common bacteria.  
- You may need to be hospitalized for close care.

Treatment depends on the cause and how severe the neutropenia is:

- **Stop or change medicines** that are causing the problem.  
- **Avoid toxins** like benzene or insecticides.  
- **Bone marrow may recover on its own** after a viral infection like the flu.  
- **Mild neutropenia** may not need treatment if you feel well.  
- **Severe neutropenia** can be deadly if not treated fast.  
  - You will likely be admitted to the hospital.  
  - You will get strong antibiotics right away.  
  - Fever is a key warning sign that you need urgent care.

### Medications to Help Neutrophil Production

- **Granulocyte colony stimulating factor (G-CSF)**  
  - This medicine helps your bone marrow make more neutrophils.  
  - It is given as a shot under the skin or into a vein.  
  - It helps prevent fevers, mouth sores, and infections.

### Other Treatments

- **Antithymocyte globulin** or other immune-suppressing medicines may be used if you have aplastic anemia.  
- Treating the main illness (like tuberculosis, leukemia, or other cancers) may fix the neutropenia.  
- In serious cases, a **bone marrow transplant** or **stem cell transplant** may be needed.  
  - This is used for conditions like severe aplastic anemia or leukemia.

> **Important**: If you have neutropenia and a fever, seek medical help right away.  
> Infections can spread quickly and become life-threatening.

# Relapsing Fever – Simple Explanation

Relapsing fever is a serious illness that causes repeated episodes of high fever. It is caused by bacteria called *Borrelia*. These bacteria are spread by lice or ticks.

## How Is It Spread?

- **Lice**: The human body louse spreads the disease. The louse gets infected when it bites a sick person. It does not pass the bacteria through its saliva or poop. But if the louse is crushed on your skin, the bacteria can enter through small cuts or bites.
- **Ticks**: Soft ticks (like *Ornithodoros*) and hard ticks (like *Ixodes scapularis*) can also spread the disease. These ticks bite at night and often go unnoticed. They get the bacteria from rodents. When they bite a person, the bacteria enter the skin through their saliva or waste.

## Where Does It Happen?

- **Louse-borne relapsing fever** is rare in the United States. It mainly happens in parts of northeast Africa (like Ethiopia, Sudan, Eritrea, and Somalia). It has also been seen in refugees from these areas in Europe.
- **Tick-borne relapsing fever** happens in many parts of the world. In the U.S., it is most common in the western states, especially in mountain cabins or caves. It is more likely in the spring and summer months.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The illness starts suddenly with:
- Chills
- High fever
- Severe headache
- Nausea and vomiting
- Muscle and joint pain
- Confusion or delirium

A rash may appear on the chest, arms, or legs. Some people may have:
- Bleeding under the skin or in the eyes
- An open sore (eschar) at the tick bite site
- Jaundice (yellow skin or eyes)
- Swollen liver or spleen
- Heart problems, especially in louse-borne cases

The fever lasts 3 to 5 days, then goes away suddenly. After about a week of feeling better, the fever comes back. This cycle can repeat 2 to 10 times. Each time, the symptoms are usually milder than before.

Later in the illness, some people may have:
- Eye problems
- Worsened asthma
- Skin rashes
- Nerve problems like meningitis or brain inflammation
- Miscarriage

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect relapsing fever if you have repeated fevers. The diagnosis is confirmed by looking at your blood under a microscope.

- The bacteria can be seen in blood samples during a fever.
- Special staining or darkfield microscopy helps find the bacteria.
- A test called PCR can detect *Borrelia miyamotoi* in the blood.

Blood tests for syphilis or Lyme disease may give false results. So they are not reliable for diagnosing relapsing fever.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the type of relapsing fever.

### For Tick-Borne Relapsing Fever:
- Take tetracycline, doxycycline, or erythromycin by mouth for 10 days.
- Dose: 500 mg every 6 hours (tetracycline or erythromycin), or 100 mg every 12 hours (doxycycline).

### For Louse-Borne Relapsing Fever:
- A single dose of tetracycline, erythromycin, azithromycin, or doxycycline works.
- Or a single shot of penicillin G in the muscle.

For children under 8 years old:
- Use erythromycin estolate, 10 mg per kilogram of body weight, three times a day.

If you are very sick, cannot keep food down, or have brain or nerve problems:
- You may need antibiotics through a vein (IV).
- Options include ceftriaxone, doxycycline, or penicillin G.

### Important Note:
- Start treatment as soon as possible during fever.
- You may have a reaction within 2 hours of starting antibiotics. This is called the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction.
- It can cause worse fever, chills, and a fast heartbeat.
- To reduce this reaction, take acetaminophen 2 hours before and after the first dose of antibiotics.
- This reaction is more common in louse-borne cases treated with penicillin.

### Other Care:
- Drink fluids or get IV fluids if you are dehydrated.
- Use acetaminophen with oxycodone or hydrocodone for severe headaches.
- Use prochlorperazine to treat nausea and vomiting.
- If heart failure happens, treat it specifically.

## What Is the Outlook?

- With treatment, most people recover fully.
- Without treatment, the disease can be deadly, especially in:
  - Very young children
  - Pregnant women
  - Older adults
  - People who are weak or malnourished
  - During louse-borne outbreaks

### Survival Rates:
- **Louse-borne relapsing fever**:
  - Untreated: 10% to 40% die.
  - Treated: 2% to 5% die.
- **Tick-borne relapsing fever**:
  - Untreated: less than 10% die.
  - Treated: less than 2% die.

## Key Facts to Remember

- Relapsing fever is caused by *Borrelia* bacteria.
- It spreads through lice or ticks.
- Symptoms include sudden chills, high fever, severe headache, nausea, vomiting, and body aches.
- Fever comes back in cycles, usually every 1 to 2 weeks.
- Each episode is usually milder than the last.
- Diagnosis is done by checking blood under a microscope.
- Treatment is with antibiotics like tetracycline, doxycycline, or erythromycin.
- Early treatment saves lives.
- A reaction after starting antibiotics is possible but can be managed.

# What Is Dermatitis?

Dermatitis means inflammation of the top layer of the skin.  
It causes redness, itching, swelling, and sometimes blisters, oozing, scabs, or flaky skin.

## What Causes Dermatitis?

- Dry skin can lead to dermatitis.  
- Touching certain substances can cause a reaction.  
- Some medicines can cause dermatitis.  
- Poor blood flow in the legs (varicose veins) can also be a cause.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Dermatitis causes:
- Red, itchy skin
- Flaky or scaly patches
- Open sores
- Fluid leaking from the skin
- Crusts on the skin
- Blisters (in some cases)
- Thickened skin (in long-term cases)

Long-term dermatitis can make the skin hard and cracked.  
Any type of dermatitis can become infected.

## How Is Dermatitis Diagnosed?

A doctor will:
- Look at your skin and ask about your symptoms.
- Check where the rash is and how long it has lasted.
- Ask if you have touched anything new or taken new medicines.

To confirm the diagnosis, the doctor may:
- Do a patch test to check for allergies.
- Run blood tests.
- Take a small sample of skin (biopsy) to test in a lab.

## How Is Dermatitis Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause and your symptoms.  
Common treatments include:

- Moisturizers to keep skin soft and prevent dryness.  
- Dressings to protect the skin.  
- Antihistamines to reduce itching.  
- Creams or ointments that reduce swelling and itching (like corticosteroids).  
- Other medicines that calm the immune system (if needed).  
- Antibiotics if there is an infection.  
- Injections or pills for severe cases.  
- Light therapy using ultraviolet light (phototherapy).

## How Can Dermatitis Be Prevented?

You can lower your risk by:
- Avoiding things that irritate your skin.  
- Staying away from known allergens.  
- Not touching substances that cause a reaction.

## Important Notes

- Dermatitis is a general term for many skin conditions that cause red, itchy rashes.  
- Eczema is another name for dermatitis, but it often refers to a specific type called atopic dermatitis.  
- Skin infections like fungal infections are not considered dermatitis.  

### Types of Dermatitis

Some types affect only certain areas:
- Contact dermatitis (like from poison ivy)
- Nummular dermatitis (coin-shaped rashes)
- Stasis dermatitis (from poor leg circulation)
- Lichen simplex chronicus (from long-term scratching)
- Seborrheic dermatitis (on oily areas like scalp or face)
- Hand and foot dermatitis

Other types can appear anywhere on the body:
- Atopic dermatitis (common in people with allergies or asthma)

Some types have a clear cause (like allergic contact dermatitis).  
Others have no known cause (like nummular dermatitis).

Chronic dermatitis lasts a long time.  
The hands are especially prone because they touch many things.  
Constant scratching or rubbing can make the skin thick and hard (called lichenification).

# Melanoma – Simple Explanation

Melanoma is a type of skin cancer. It starts in cells that give color to the skin, eyes, mouth, nose, throat, or other areas. It can also start in the brain or spinal cord.

If melanoma spreads to other parts of the body, it becomes much harder to treat. Early diagnosis and treatment are key to survival.

## How Common Is Melanoma?

In 2023, about 97,610 new cases of melanoma were expected in the United States. It caused about 7,990 deaths.

- About 2.6 out of every 100 white people will get melanoma in their lifetime.
- About 0.1 out of every 100 Black people will get it.
- About 0.6 out of every 100 Hispanic people will get it.

Melanoma makes up less than 2% of all skin cancers. But it causes most skin cancer deaths.

## Where Can Melanoma Develop?

Melanoma most often starts on the skin. But it can also start in:

- The mouth, genitals, or rectum (mucous membranes)
- The eye (especially the colored part of the eye)
- The thin layers covering the brain and spinal cord (leptomeninges)
- The skin under the fingernails or toenails

## What Does Melanoma Look Like?

Melanoma can be any size, shape, or color. It is often dark (brown, black, or blue), but it can also be red, pink, or skin-colored.

It can grow quickly and spread to other parts of the body. It spreads through the lymph system and blood vessels.

When it spreads, it may form small bumps near the original spot. These bumps may or may not be dark.

Sometimes, doctors find the spread before they find the original tumor.

## Risk Factors for Melanoma

You are more likely to get melanoma if you:

- Have had bad sunburns, especially blistering ones
- Use tanning beds or get repeated UV light treatments
- Have had other skin cancers before
- Have a family member with melanoma
- Have light skin, freckles, or red or blonde hair
- Have many moles, especially unusual ones
- Have a mole that is larger than 8 millimeters across
- Have more than 50 moles on your body
- Have a condition called atypical mole syndrome (many unusual moles)
- Have a family history of many unusual moles and melanoma
- Have a rare gene change (like in the BRCA2 gene)
- Are older
- Have a weakened immune system

If you have had melanoma once, you are more likely to get it again.

If you have a close family member with melanoma, your risk is much higher — up to 6 to 8 times greater.

People with dark skin get melanoma less often. But when they do, it often starts in the nails, palms, or soles of the feet.

About 30% of melanomas start in a mole. Half come from normal moles. Half come from unusual moles. Unusual moles can turn into melanoma.

Pregnancy does not make moles turn into melanoma. But moles can get bigger or darker during pregnancy. This is normal.

Very rare melanomas in children usually start in the brain or spinal cord or in large birthmarks.

## Watch for These Warning Signs

Check your skin often. See a doctor if you notice any of these changes:

- A mole that is not round or even
- A mole that has uneven edges
- A mole with more than one color (like black, brown, red, gray, or blue)
- A mole larger than 6 millimeters across (about the size of a pencil eraser)
- A new mole after age 30
- A mole that is changing in size, shape, or color
- A mole that bleeds, itches, or becomes sore
- A mole that has a rough or scaly surface
- A mole that looks inflamed or swollen around it

Even small changes can be a sign of trouble. Do not wait.

## How Is Melanoma Diagnosed?

The only way to know for sure if a spot is melanoma is to take a small sample of skin (a biopsy).

Doctors may use special tools to look at moles closely. But if a mole looks suspicious, a biopsy is needed.

The ABCDE rule helps spot possible melanoma:

- **A** – Asymmetry: One half does not match the other.
- **B** – Borders: Edges are ragged, blurred, or not smooth.
- **C** – Color: Colors are mixed or uneven.
- **D** – Diameter: Bigger than 6 millimeters.
- **E** – Evolution: The mole is changing over time.

You can learn to check your own skin. Look for new moles or changes in old ones.

If a doctor is unsure, they may take a deeper sample. This helps them see how deep the cancer has grown.

Even a mole that seems only slightly suspicious should be tested. Early diagnosis saves lives.

Biopsy is best done by removing the whole spot (excisional biopsy). But if the spot is in a sensitive or visible area, a smaller sample (shave biopsy) may be used.

For large or complex spots, doctors may take samples from several areas. This gives a better picture.

The pathologist will check the sample under a microscope. They will measure how thick the cancer is.

Do not have major surgery until the diagnosis is confirmed.

Some melanomas are tested for gene changes. This helps doctors pick the best treatment.

For example, if a gene called BRAF has a certain change, a drug called vemurafenib may help.

## Other Conditions That Can Look Like Melanoma

Some skin problems can look like melanoma. These include:

- Basal cell skin cancer
- Squamous cell skin cancer
- Seborrheic keratosis (a harmless skin growth)
- Atypical moles
- Blue nevi (dark moles)
- Dermatofibroma (a firm bump under the skin)
- Common moles
- Bruises (especially on hands or feet)
- Venous lakes (small blue bumps on lips or skin)
- Pyogenic granulomas (fast-growing red bumps)
- Warts with blood clots

## How Is Melanoma Treated?

The main treatment is surgery to remove the cancer.

For early-stage melanoma, doctors usually remove the cancer and a small border of healthy skin around it.

- For thin melanomas (less than 0.8 millimeters thick), a 1-centimeter border is usually enough.
- If the cancer is thicker, a wider border may be needed.
- If the cancer is thick or has broken through the skin, doctors may check the nearby lymph nodes.

For melanoma in the skin that has not spread, surgery is the best option.

For melanoma in the eye, the skin under the nail, or in the brain or spinal cord, treatment depends on the location.

For melanoma in the skin that is very early (melanoma in situ), surgery is the best choice.

Sometimes, doctors use special surgery called Mohs surgery. This removes the cancer layer by layer. They check each layer under a microscope until no cancer is left.

If surgery is not possible (because of health problems or the spot’s location), other treatments may help:

- Imiquimod cream (a medicine that boosts the immune system)
- Freezing with liquid nitrogen (cryotherapy)

But these treatments do not work well for deep cancers.

For melanoma that has spread or cannot be removed, doctors use:

- Immunotherapy (drugs that help the body fight cancer)
- Targeted therapy (drugs that attack specific gene changes in cancer cells)
- Radiation therapy (high-energy beams to kill cancer cells)

Examples of these drugs include:

- Pembrolizumab
- Nivolumab
- Ipilimumab
- Vemurafenib
- Dabrafenib
- Encorafenib

## What Is the Outlook?

Melanoma can grow fast and spread quickly. But if caught early, it is often curable.

- If melanoma is found early and has not spread, the 5-year survival rate is 99.6%.
- If it has spread to nearby lymph nodes, the survival rate is 73.9%.
- If it has spread to distant organs, the survival rate is 35.1%.

The thickness of the tumor at diagnosis matters a lot.

Melanoma in the mouth, genitals, or rectum (mucosal melanoma) often looks small when found. But it tends to be harder to treat.

The body’s immune system can help fight melanoma. If immune cells are found near the cancer, the outlook is better.

If the cancer is deep, has broken through the skin, or has spread into blood or lymph vessels, the outlook is worse.

There is a test that checks gene activity. It can help predict if a person with early melanoma is likely to have the cancer spread.

But this test is not yet part of standard guidelines. It should not be used alone to decide on treatment.

## How Can Melanoma Be Prevented?

Since UV light from the sun or tanning beds increases risk, take these steps:

- Stay in the shade, especially between 10 AM and 4 PM
- Avoid sunbathing and tanning beds
- Wear long-sleeved shirts, pants, and wide-brimmed hats
- Use sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher
- Use sunscreen that protects against both UVA and UVB rays
- Reapply every 2

# Shigellosis

Shigellosis is an infection caused by a type of bacteria called *Shigella*.  
These bacteria live in the stool of infected people.  
They can cause diarrhea that is watery or bloody.  
Bloody diarrhea is also called dysentery.  
Dysentery means passing small amounts of stool many times.  
The stool may contain blood, pus, and mucus.

## How Shigellosis Spreads

*Shigella* bacteria spread easily when hygiene is poor.  
The bacteria are passed in stool.  
They can get on hands, surfaces, food, or water.  
You can get infected if you touch something that has the bacteria and then touch your mouth.

You can get shigellosis by:
- Touching a diaper or toy that has infected stool on it.
- Eating food that was handled by someone who did not wash their hands after using the toilet.
- Drinking or swimming in water that has human waste in it.
- Sharing a bathroom or living space with an infected person.

The infection spreads easily in:
- Day care centers
- Nursing homes
- Refugee camps
- Group homes for people with intellectual disabilities
- Cruise ships
- Military camps
- Places with poor sanitation

Men who have sex with men can also pass the infection to each other.

Even a small number of *Shigella* bacteria can cause infection.  
This is because stomach acid does not kill them well.  
Once in the large intestine, the bacteria cause swelling and irritation.  
They are then passed out in stool, which can spread the infection.

## Symptoms of Shigellosis

### In Adults
- Mild cases: Low fever (100.4 to 102 degrees Fahrenheit) and watery diarrhea.
- Diarrhea starts 1 to 4 days after infection.
- Some adults do not have a fever.
- Mild symptoms usually go away in 4 to 8 days.
- Early symptoms: Belly cramps and a strong need to pass stool.
- Passing stool may ease the pain at first.
- Symptoms can get worse over time.

### In Children
- Symptoms start suddenly.
- Signs include fever, irritability, drowsiness, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and belly pain.
- Children often feel a strong need to go to the bathroom.
- Blood, pus, and mucus appear in the stool within 3 days.
- With treatment, symptoms usually go away by the second week.

### Severe Cases
Children are more likely than adults to have serious problems.  
Severe symptoms include:
- High fever (up to 106 degrees Fahrenheit)
- Confusion, seizures, or coma (this can happen if bacteria enter the blood)
- Severe dehydration (losing too much fluid)
- 20 or more bowel movements a day
- Part of the rectum sticking out of the body (rectal prolapse)
- Rarely, the intestine can swell or tear open
- Hemolytic-uremic syndrome (only if caused by *Shigella dysenteriae* type 1)

Hemolytic-uremic syndrome:
- Destroys red blood cells, causing anemia.
- Anemia leads to tiredness, weakness, and dizziness.
- Blood clots abnormally, which can stop the kidneys from working.
- Can cause seizures or strokes.

Severe dehydration can lead to shock and death.  
This is most dangerous for:
- Babies under 2 years old
- Older adults with long-term health problems
- People who are underweight

Some adults may develop:
- Joint pain (reactive arthritis)
- Eye inflammation (uveitis)
- Pain when urinating (urethritis)

These problems can appear weeks or months after the diarrhea ends.

## How Doctors Diagnose Shigellosis

Doctors suspect shigellosis if you have:
- Belly pain
- Fever
- Watery or bloody diarrhea
- Recent contact with someone who has the infection

To confirm the diagnosis:
- A stool sample is collected.
- The lab grows the bacteria from the sample.
- The lab also tests which antibiotics will work best.

Doctors may use a test called PCR to find the bacteria’s DNA faster.

## How Shigellosis Is Treated

### Fluids
- The main treatment is replacing lost fluids and salts.
- You can drink fluids with salt and sugar.
- For severe cases, fluids are given through a vein (IV).

### Antibiotics
- Antibiotics are not needed for mild cases in healthy adults.
- They are used for:
  - Very young or very old people
  - People with weak immune systems
  - People with moderate to severe infections

Common antibiotics include:
- Azithromycin
- Ciprofloxacin (for adults only)
- Ceftriaxone

Severe cases may need hospital care.  
This allows doctors to give IV fluids and treat serious problems like hemolytic-uremic syndrome.

### Do Not Use Diarrhea Medicines
- Medicines like diphenoxylate or loperamide can make the infection worse.
- They should not be used.

## How to Prevent Shigellosis

Good hygiene is key to stopping the spread.

### Everyone Should:
- Wash hands after using the toilet.
- Wash hands before preparing food.
- Wash hands before sex.
- Stay home from work or school until at least 2 days after diarrhea stops.
- Not prepare food for others if sick.

### If You Are Caring for Someone with Shigellosis:
- Wash hands with soap and water often.
- Especially before touching others or handling food.

### For Infected Children:
- Keep them away from other children.
- Dispose of diapers in a sealed trash can.
- Clean the diaper-changing area with disinfectant after each use.

### For Soiled Items:
- Flush stool from clothes, sheets, and blankets down the toilet.
- Wash these items in hot water.
- Clean the sink, toilet, and washing machine with disinfectant (like diluted bleach) after use.

### Do Not Swim
- Infected people should not go swimming.
- The bacteria can spread in pools and lakes.

### Isolation
- Talk to your doctor about how long to stay away from others.
- Precautions may be needed for several weeks.

### Vaccines
- No vaccine is available yet.
- Research is ongoing.

## More Information

For more details, visit:
**Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC): Shigellosis**  
This site explains how the infection spreads and how to prevent it.

# Celiac Disease – Simple Explanation

Celiac disease is a long-term condition where the body reacts badly to a protein called gluten. This reaction damages the small intestine and stops it from absorbing nutrients properly.

Gluten is found in wheat, rye, and barley. People with celiac disease must avoid all foods with these grains.

This condition runs in families. If one family member has it, others may be at higher risk.

---

## What Causes Celiac Disease?

Celiac disease is caused by a mix of genetics and the immune system reacting to gluten.

When a person with celiac disease eats gluten, their immune system attacks the lining of the small intestine. This causes damage to tiny finger-like parts called villi. These villi help absorb nutrients from food.

Without healthy villi, the body cannot take in enough vitamins and minerals.

---

## How Common Is Celiac Disease?

About 1 in 70 people worldwide may have celiac disease. But only about half of them are diagnosed.

It is more common in women than men.

The disease often starts in childhood, but it can appear at any age.

People with other health problems are more likely to have celiac disease. These include:
- Down syndrome
- Type 1 diabetes
- Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (an autoimmune thyroid disease)
- Lymphocytic colitis (a type of bowel inflammation)

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms vary widely. Some people have no symptoms at all. Others have clear signs.

### In Children:
- Poor growth or not gaining weight
- Tiredness and low energy
- Loss of appetite
- Pale skin
- Weak muscles
- Swollen belly
- Stools that are soft, large, pale, and smell bad

These symptoms often appear after starting to eat cereal or grain-based foods.

### In Adults:
- Tiredness and weakness
- Loss of appetite
- Mild or occasional diarrhea
- Stools that are pale, bulky, greasy, and smell bad (this is called steatorrhea)
- Weight loss (sometimes becoming underweight)
- Anemia (low iron or low folate)
- Sore mouth or tongue (glossitis)
- Cracks at the corners of the mouth (angular stomatitis)
- Mouth sores (aphthous ulcers)
- Bone pain or weak bones (due to low vitamin D and calcium)
- Women may stop having periods
- Both men and women may have trouble getting pregnant

### Skin Rash (Dermatitis Herpetiformis):
About 1 in 6 people with celiac disease get a very itchy rash.  
It shows up on the elbows, knees, buttocks, shoulders, and scalp.  
The rash gets worse when eating gluten.

---

## How Is Celiac Disease Diagnosed?

Diagnosis starts with symptoms and blood tests.

### Step 1: Blood Tests
These tests look for certain antibodies in the blood:
- Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody (tTG-IgA)
- Endomysial antibody (EMA)

These tests are very accurate. If both are positive, celiac disease is likely.

But if a person has low levels of a certain antibody (IgA), the test may not work. So doctors also check IgA levels at the same time.

If IgA is low, doctors test for IgG antibodies instead.

### Step 2: Small Intestine Biopsy
A small sample of tissue is taken from the small intestine during a procedure called an endoscopy.

This biopsy shows damage to the villi. The damage includes:
- Short or missing villi
- More immune cells in the lining
- Thicker glands in the lining

This test confirms the diagnosis.

But other conditions can cause similar damage. These include:
- Tropical sprue
- Bacterial overgrowth in the small intestine
- Eosinophilic enteritis
- Infections like giardiasis
- Lymphoma

So the biopsy must be read carefully.

### Step 3: Genetic Testing (HLA Testing)
A blood test can check for certain genes linked to celiac disease.

Over 95% of people with celiac disease have one of two genes: HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8.

If a person does **not** have these genes, they almost certainly do **not** have celiac disease.

This test is useful when blood tests and biopsies are unclear.

### Other Blood Tests
Doctors may also check for:
- Low iron (anemia)
- Low vitamin B12 or folate
- Low albumin (a protein in blood)
- Low calcium or potassium
- High alkaline phosphatase (a liver enzyme)
- Long blood clotting time

### Stool and Absorption Tests
These are not needed for diagnosis. But if done, they may show:
- High fat in the stool (steatorrhea)
- Poor absorption of sugar (D-xylose test)
- Poor absorption of vitamin B12 (Schilling test)

---

## How Is Celiac Disease Different from Gluten Sensitivity?

Some people have symptoms after eating gluten but do not have celiac disease.

This is called non-celiac gluten sensitivity (NCGS).

Key differences:
- No damage to the small intestine
- No abnormal blood tests for celiac disease
- No allergy to wheat

Symptoms are similar: bloating, gas, diarrhea, fatigue.

But NCGS does not cause long-term harm like celiac disease can.

Treatment is the same: avoid gluten.

---

## How Is Celiac Disease Treated?

The only treatment is a strict gluten-free diet.

This means avoiding:
- Wheat
- Rye
- Barley
- Any food that contains these grains

Gluten is hidden in many processed foods. Always read labels.

### What to Do:
- Work with a dietitian to learn what foods to avoid and what to eat.
- Join a support group. Helpful groups include:
  - Beyond Celiac
  - Celiac Disease Foundation

### Results:
- Most people feel better within 1 to 2 weeks.
- Symptoms go away quickly.
- The small intestine starts to heal.

But even a tiny amount of gluten can cause damage. So it’s important to avoid all gluten.

### Follow-Up:
- A repeat biopsy is done 3 to 6 months after starting the diet.
- If the intestine is still damaged, other causes (like lymphoma) must be checked.

Blood antibody levels go down when the diet is working. This helps track progress.

### Supplements:
If the body is missing key nutrients, supplements may be needed. These can include:
- Iron (for anemia)
- Folate (for low folate)
- Calcium
- Vitamin D
- A daily multivitamin

Some children who are very sick may need to stop eating for a while and get nutrition through a tube or IV.

### Refractory Celiac Disease:
If symptoms do not improve after going gluten-free, the diagnosis may be wrong. Or the disease may be refractory (hard to treat).

In these cases, doctors may use steroids to reduce inflammation.

---

## What Is the Long-Term Outlook?

With a strict gluten-free diet, most people live healthy lives.

But celiac disease can lead to serious problems if not treated.

### Possible Complications:
- Refractory celiac disease (does not respond to diet)
- Collagenous sprue (a rare, severe form)
- Intestinal lymphoma (a type of cancer)

Intestinal lymphoma is rare but more common in people with celiac disease. It usually appears 20 to 40 years after diagnosis.

Other cancers (like esophagus or throat cancer) are also more common.

But following a gluten-free diet greatly lowers the risk.

### When to Worry:
If someone who has been doing well on a gluten-free diet suddenly gets symptoms again, they should see a doctor.

Tests like endoscopy or capsule endoscopy may be done to check for lymphoma.

---

## Key Points

- Celiac disease is caused by an immune reaction to gluten.
- It damages the small intestine and stops the body from absorbing nutrients.
- It runs in families and can start at any age.
- Symptoms vary. Some people have no symptoms.
- Diagnosis uses blood tests and a small intestine biopsy.
- The only treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet.
- Supplements may be needed for missing vitamins and minerals.
- Sticking to the diet prevents serious health problems.
- Regular follow-up is important to stay healthy.

# Gastritis

Gastritis means the lining of the stomach is inflamed.

## What Is Gastritis?

- The stomach lining is usually strong and can handle very strong acid.
- In gastritis, the lining becomes irritated and swollen.
- This can happen for many reasons, including infections, serious illness, injury, certain medicines, alcohol, or problems with the body’s defense system.

## Types of Gastritis

Gastritis is split into two main types:

### Erosive Gastritis
- This type causes both inflammation and damage to the stomach lining.
- It can start suddenly (acute) or slowly (chronic).
- It often affects people who are otherwise healthy.

### Nonerosive Gastritis
- This type causes changes in the stomach lining.
- The lining may thin out or change into a different kind of tissue.
- White blood cells build up in the stomach and cause swelling.
- The swelling can affect the whole stomach or just parts of it.

---

## Causes of Gastritis

### Erosive Gastritis
- Common causes:
  - Drinking too much alcohol.
  - Stress from serious illness or injury.
  - Medicines like aspirin or other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
- Less common causes:
  - Crohn disease.
  - Radiation therapy.
  - Infections from bacteria or viruses (like cytomegalovirus).
  - Swallowing harmful chemicals.
  - Injury from a tube placed through the nose into the stomach.
- Even one baby aspirin a day can harm the stomach lining in some people.

### Nonerosive Gastritis
- Most often caused by an infection with *Helicobacter pylori* bacteria.

### Other Types of Gastritis
- **Infectious gastritis** (not from *H. pylori*) is rare.
- **Viral or fungal gastritis** can happen in people who are very ill or have weak immune systems. This includes people with advanced HIV, cancer, or those on immune-suppressing medicines.
- **Acute stress gastritis** happens after a sudden serious illness or injury. It can be caused by burns, head injuries, or major bleeding—even if the injury is not in the stomach.
  - The exact reason is not clear, but it may be due to less blood flow to the stomach, more acid, or the stomach’s ability to protect itself being weakened.
- **Radiation gastritis** can happen if radiation therapy is used on the lower left chest or upper belly.
- **Postgastrectomy gastritis** happens after part of the stomach is removed.
  - Inflammation often happens where the stomach was sewn back together.
  - It may be caused by poor blood flow or too much bile (a greenish-yellow fluid made by the liver) reaching the stomach.
- **Atrophic gastritis** means the stomach lining becomes very thin and loses cells that make acid and digestive enzymes.
  - It can happen when the body’s immune system attacks the stomach lining.
  - It can also happen in people with long-term *H. pylori* infection.
  - It is also common after stomach surgery.
- **Eosinophilic gastritis** is when a type of white blood cell called eosinophils builds up in the stomach wall.
  - The cause is often unknown.
- **Ménétrier disease** is a rare condition.
  - The stomach wall grows thick and forms large folds and fluid-filled sacs.
  - The cause is not known, but it may be linked to an immune problem.
  - It has also been linked to *H. pylori* infection.

---

## Symptoms of Gastritis

- Most people with gastritis have no symptoms.
- When symptoms do appear, they can include:
  - Pain or discomfort in the upper belly.
  - Nausea.
  - Vomiting.
- These problems are often called indigestion.

### More Severe Forms
- Nausea and vomiting can happen with:
  - Erosive gastritis.
  - Radiation gastritis.
- Indigestion is common with:
  - Erosive gastritis.
  - Radiation gastritis.
  - Postgastrectomy gastritis.
  - Atrophic gastritis.
- Mild indigestion can also happen with acute stress gastritis.

---

## How Gastritis Is Diagnosed

- Doctors often guess the diagnosis based on symptoms.
- If the diagnosis is unclear or symptoms do not improve, the doctor may do an upper endoscopy.
- During an upper endoscopy:
  - A thin, flexible tube with a camera is passed through the mouth into the stomach.
  - The doctor can see the inside of the stomach and small intestine.
  - If needed, a small tissue sample (biopsy) is taken for testing.

---

## Treatment of Gastritis

### General Treatments
- Medicines that reduce or neutralize stomach acid help relieve symptoms.
- Stop taking medicines that irritate the stomach, like aspirin or NSAIDs.

### Antacids
- These neutralize acid already in the stomach.
- Available over the counter as tablets, chewable gels, or liquids.
- Common types:
  - Aluminum hydroxide (can cause constipation).
  - Magnesium hydroxide (can cause diarrhea).
  - Calcium carbonate.
- Antacids can interfere with other medicines.
- Always check with a pharmacist or doctor before using antacids if you take other medicines.

### Acid-Reducing Medicines
- **H2 blockers** – reduce acid production.
- **Proton pump inhibitors** – reduce acid more strongly than H2 blockers.
- These are often more effective than antacids.
- Doctors usually prescribe proton pump inhibitors for gastritis with bleeding.
- Most people take these medicines for 8 to 12 weeks.

### Other Medicines
- **Sucralfate** – coats the stomach lining and helps it heal.
- It also protects the stomach from irritation.

### Antibiotics
- Used if gastritis is caused by *H. pylori* infection.
- A combination of antibiotics is usually needed.

### Special Cases

#### Erosive Gastritis
- Avoid medicines that harm the stomach lining (like NSAIDs).
- Use proton pump inhibitors or H2 blockers to protect the stomach.

#### Acute Stress Gastritis
- Most people recover fully when the serious illness, injury, or bleeding is treated.
- A small number of people in intensive care units may have heavy bleeding.
  - This can be life-threatening.
- Doctors often give acid-reducing medicines after surgery or to people in intensive care to prevent this.
- These medicines also help treat ulcers that may form.

#### Bleeding from Acute Stress Gastritis
- Doctors may use heat to seal bleeding spots during endoscopy.
- But bleeding can return if the serious illness continues.
- If bleeding does not stop, surgery to remove part of the stomach may be needed.
  - This is rare.

#### Postgastrectomy Gastritis
- There is no cure.
- Treatment focuses on managing symptoms.

#### Atrophic Gastritis
- There is no cure.
- It can lead to low levels of vitamin B12.
- People with this problem need lifelong vitamin B12 injections.

#### Eosinophilic Gastritis
- May need corticosteroid medicines or surgery.
- This helps if the stomach outlet becomes blocked.

#### Ménétrier Disease
- Removing part or all of the stomach may cure it.
- There are no good medicines to treat this condition.

--- 

**Note:** This information is for general understanding. Always talk to your doctor about your specific condition and treatment.

# Otosclerosis

Otosclerosis is a condition that affects the small bones in the inner ear. It causes too much new bone to grow in the wrong places. This most often happens near the oval window, a small opening in the inner ear.

This disease is one of many that can change the shape or strength of bones. Other conditions include:
- Tympanosclerosis
- Paget disease
- Branchio-oto-renal dysplasia
- Osteogenesis imperfecta
- Goldenhar syndrome

In otosclerosis, the body breaks down old bone and builds new bone in a harmful way. The stapes bone, which helps send sound to the inner ear, often becomes stuck. When this happens, sound cannot travel well through the ear. This causes conductive hearing loss.

Otosclerosis can also damage the inner ear’s sensory parts. This leads to sensorineural hearing loss. This type of hearing loss is more likely if the abnormal bone grows close to the fluid-filled part of the inner ear.

Otosclerosis often runs in families. About half of all cases are passed down through genes. If one parent has it, there is a 25% chance the child will get it. If both parents have it, the chance rises to 50%. Most cases are not caused by a single gene. Instead, many genes may be involved. One gene linked to otosclerosis is on chromosome 15. Recent research shows other genes may also play a role.

Some experts believe the measles virus may trigger otosclerosis in people who are already at risk due to their genes.

Otosclerosis is more common in White adults than in Black adults. About 10% of White adults have some signs of the disease. But only about 10% of these people actually develop hearing problems. In rare cases, hearing loss can start as early as age 7 or 8. Most people notice hearing loss during their late teens or early adult years. The hearing loss usually starts slowly and gets worse over time.

The condition often begins in one ear. But more than half of people with otosclerosis eventually develop symptoms in both ears.

Hearing aids can help improve hearing. Another option is surgery called stapedectomy. This surgery removes part or all of the stapes bone and replaces it with a small artificial device. This can restore hearing in many cases. But the surgery carries risks. These include further hearing loss or problems with balance. These risks must be carefully weighed before deciding on surgery.

# Infectious Arthritis

Infectious arthritis is an infection in the fluid and tissues inside a joint. It is usually caused by bacteria. Sometimes, viruses or fungi can also cause it.

- Bacteria, viruses, or fungi can travel through the blood or come from a nearby infection to reach a joint.
- Pain, swelling, and fever usually start within hours or a few days.
- A doctor will take fluid from the joint using a needle and test it.
- Antibiotics are started right away, even before test results are back.

There are two main types of infectious arthritis:

- Acute
- Chronic

---

## Acute Infectious Arthritis

Acute infectious arthritis caused by bacteria starts suddenly. Most cases are acute. It can happen in healthy people and in people with risk factors.

The cartilage inside the joint can be damaged or destroyed within hours or days.

Sometimes, arthritis develops after an infection in another part of the body, like the genitals or digestive system. This is not a true joint infection. It is called reactive arthritis. The joint becomes inflamed, but it is not infected.

---

## Chronic Infectious Arthritis

Chronic infectious arthritis develops slowly over several weeks. Few cases are chronic. It mostly affects people with risk factors.

The joints most often affected are the knee, shoulder, wrist, hip, elbow, and finger joints.

Most infections affect just one joint. But sometimes, more than one joint is affected.

Some bacteria have special patterns:

- The bacteria that cause Lyme disease usually affect the knee.
- The bacteria that cause gonorrhea can affect one or many joints at once.
- Viruses like hepatitis B or C, and some other bacteria, can also affect multiple joints.
- Mycobacteria are more likely to cause long-term joint infections.

---

## What Causes Infectious Arthritis?

Most infections are caused by bacteria. They usually reach the joint from a nearby infection, such as a bone infection or a wound. They can also travel through the blood.

A joint can also become infected during surgery, an injection, or from a bite wound.

### Acute Infectious Arthritis

This type is usually caused by bacteria or viruses.

Different bacteria cause infection in different age groups:

- **Newborns**: Group B streptococci, *Escherichia coli*, other gram-negative bacteria, and *Staphylococcus aureus*.
- **Infants and young children**: *Staphylococcus aureus*, streptococci, gram-negative bacteria, and *Kingella kingae*.
- **Older children and adults**: *Staphylococcus aureus*, streptococci, and gonococci.

Spirochetes (a type of bacteria) can also infect joints. These include the bacteria that cause Lyme disease and syphilis.

Viruses like HIV, parvovirus, rubella, mumps, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C can infect joints at any age.

### Risk Factors for Acute Infectious Arthritis

These increase the chance of getting the condition:

- A past joint infection
- An artificial joint or recent joint surgery
- Using needles to inject drugs
- Long-term health problems like diabetes, lupus, lung or liver disease
- Being older
- Alcohol use disorder
- Having sex with many partners or without condoms
- Ongoing joint damage from rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, or injury
- A bloodstream infection (bacteremia)
- Hemophilia
- Being on dialysis
- Skin infections
- Sickle cell disease

For example, bacteria from a lung infection (pneumonia) or a bloodstream infection (sepsis) can spread to a joint and cause infection.

Many children with joint infections have no known risk factors. About half of these children are under 3 years old. But routine childhood vaccines for *Haemophilus influenzae* and *Streptococcus pneumoniae* are helping to reduce cases in this age group.

### Risk Factors for Chronic Infectious Arthritis

These include:

- Rheumatoid arthritis
- HIV infection
- A weak immune system (from cancer or certain medicines)
- An artificial joint

> **Did You Know?**  
> If you have long-term arthritis like rheumatoid arthritis and suddenly get pain and swelling in one joint, see your doctor right away. You might have an infection—even if you do not have a fever.

---

## Symptoms of Infectious Arthritis

Symptoms depend on the cause. You might also have symptoms of Lyme disease. Or you might have swollen glands if the infection came from a bite wound.

---

## How Is Infectious Arthritis Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find the cause:

- **Joint fluid test**: A needle is used to remove fluid from the joint. The fluid is checked for white blood cells and tested for bacteria or other germs.
- **Blood tests**: These help find bacteria in the blood.
- **Sputum, spinal fluid, and urine tests**: These may be done to find the source of infection.
- **X-rays, MRI, or ultrasound**: These help see the joint and check for fluid or pus.

Doctors suspect infectious arthritis when someone has sudden, severe joint pain with no clear cause. They also look for other signs like fever, swelling, and redness.

The joint fluid is tested as soon as possible. The lab can grow and identify the bacteria in most cases. But some bacteria, like those that cause gonorrhea, Lyme disease, or syphilis, are hard to grow.

If bacteria grow, the lab tests which antibiotics will work best.

If the infection is caused by gonococci, the doctor may also test the urethra, cervix, rectum, and throat. They may also test for chlamydia, since many people with gonorrhea also have chlamydia.

To find the cause, doctors may test the joint fluid for DNA from gonococci or mycobacteria.

X-rays help rule out other joint problems. MRI is used if the joint is hard to examine or if fluid is hard to remove. Ultrasound or MRI can also show fluid buildup or abscesses (pockets of pus).

---

## How Is Infectious Arthritis Treated?

Treatment includes:

- Antibiotics or antifungal medicines
- Removing pus from the joint
- Splinting the joint, followed by physical therapy
- Pain and inflammation relief with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or other pain medicines

It is very important to start antibiotics as soon as infection is suspected—even before test results come back.

Doctors give antibiotics through a vein (IV) at first. This ensures the medicine reaches the joint quickly.

The antibiotics used are those that work against the most likely bacteria. They are given until the lab identifies the exact germ, usually within 48 hours.

If the treatment works, you should start to feel better within two days.

Once the lab results are back, the doctor may switch to a different antibiotic based on which one works best.

IV antibiotics are given for 2 to 4 weeks. Then, you take antibiotics by mouth for another 2 to 6 weeks.

If the infection does not go away with regular antibiotics, it may be caused by mycobacteria or fungi.

- Fungal infections are treated with antifungal medicines.
- Mycobacterial infections need a combination of antibiotics.
- Both types need long-term treatment.

Viral infections usually get better on their own. Antibiotics do not help with viruses.

Doctors often remove pus with a needle. This prevents it from building up and damaging the joint. If the needle does not work well (like in the hip), a small scope (arthroscopy) or surgery may be needed to drain the joint.

Pus may be drained more than once. Sometimes, a tube is left in place to drain the fluid over time.

The joint is splinted (kept still) for a few days to reduce pain. Then, physical therapy starts to strengthen muscles and prevent stiffness or permanent joint damage.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

- Infections caused by most bacteria can destroy joint cartilage within hours or days.
- Infections caused by gonococci usually do not cause permanent joint damage.
- People with rheumatoid arthritis often do not fully recover use of the infected joint.
- The risk of death is higher in people with rheumatoid arthritis and joint infection.
