# Recurrent Meningitis

Meningitis happens when the lining around the brain and spinal cord becomes inflamed.  
Recurrent meningitis means this inflammation happens more than once.  

Most often, recurrent meningitis is caused by germs.  
These germs can be bacteria or viruses.  

Sometimes, it is not caused by an infection.  
Other health problems can lead to repeated cases.  

(See also Overview of Meningitis.)

# Vocal Cord Contact Ulcers

## What Are Vocal Cord Contact Ulcers?

Vocal cord contact ulcers are raw sores on the lining of the voice box.  
They form where the vocal cords meet the cartilage at the back of the throat.  
These sores are not cancer.  
They are usually caused by overusing the voice in a forceful way.  
This often happens when a person starts speaking loudly or suddenly.

People who talk a lot for work are more likely to get these ulcers.  
This includes singers, teachers, preachers, salespeople, and lawyers.  
In some cases, the sores can turn into small lumps made of healing tissue.  
These lumps are called granulomas.

## What Causes Vocal Cord Contact Ulcers?

Stomach acid flowing back into the throat (called gastroesophageal reflux) can cause or make ulcers worse.  
This is also known as acid reflux.  
A breathing tube placed in the throat during surgery (called endotracheal intubation) can cause ulcers if the tube is too big.  
This is more likely if the tube rubs against the vocal cords.

> **Did You Know?**  
> Stomach acid that comes up into the throat can cause sores on the vocal cords.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may feel a mild pain when you speak or swallow.  
Your voice may sound hoarse.  
The hoarseness can be mild or severe.  
Some people notice the hoarseness gets worse over time.

## How Are They Diagnosed?

A doctor will look at your vocal cords using a thin, flexible tube with a camera.  
This is called a laryngoscope.  
The test is called laryngoscopy.  
It is done in the doctor’s office and takes just a few minutes.

Sometimes, the doctor takes a small sample of tissue from the sore.  
This is called a biopsy.  
The sample is checked under a microscope.  
This helps rule out cancer or tuberculosis.

## How Are They Treated?

### Rest the Voice
- Stop talking as much as possible.  
- Do not whisper. Whispering can hurt the vocal cords more.  
- Rest your voice for at least six weeks.  
- This gives the sores time to heal.

### Treat Acid Reflux
If acid reflux is the cause, treating it helps the ulcers heal.  
This includes:
- Taking antacids as directed.  
- Not eating for at least two hours before bedtime.  
- Sleeping with your head raised.  
  - Use extra pillows or raise the head of your bed.

### Other Treatments
- Antibiotics may be used to prevent infection while the sores heal.  
- Injections of botulinum toxin (Botox) may help in some cases.

### Prevent Future Problems
- See a speech therapist for voice therapy.  
- Learn how to use your voice in a healthy way.  
- This helps prevent the ulcers from coming back.

## Key Points

- Vocal cord contact ulcers are sores on the voice box.  
- They are often caused by overusing the voice or acid reflux.  
- Resting your voice is the most important step in healing.  
- Treating acid reflux helps the sores get better.  
- Voice therapy can prevent future problems.  
- Always see a doctor to rule out serious causes like cancer.

# Anorectal Abscess

An anorectal abscess is a pocket of pus near the anus or rectum.  
It usually starts in a small gland near the anus.  
The main symptoms are pain and swelling.  
Doctors usually diagnose it by examining the area.  
For deeper abscesses, they may use a CT scan or MRI of the pelvis.  
The only effective treatment is surgery to drain the pus.

## Types of Anorectal Abscesses

There are different kinds of abscesses, depending on where they are.

- A **perianal abscess** is close to the skin. It forms a bump that can be seen and felt.  
- An **ischiorectal abscess** is deeper. It goes past the muscle that controls bowel movements. It can spread to the other side of the anus, forming a shape like a horseshoe.  
- A **supralevator abscess** is very deep. It is above the pelvic floor muscle. It can reach the lining of the belly or nearby organs. This type often comes from diverticulitis or pelvic infections.  
- People with Crohn disease, especially when it affects the colon, can also get these abscesses.

Most abscesses are caused by more than one type of bacteria.  
Common bacteria include *Escherichia coli*, *Proteus vulgaris*, *Bacteroides*, streptococci, and staphylococci.

## Symptoms and Signs

- Superficial abscesses cause sharp pain.  
- The skin around the anus may be red, swollen, and tender.  
- Fever is uncommon with these.

- Deeper abscesses may hurt less.  
- But they can cause general illness symptoms like fever, chills, and tiredness.  
- There may be no visible signs on the skin.  
- A doctor may feel a soft, painful lump during a rectal exam.  
- High abscesses can cause lower belly pain and fever without any rectal symptoms.  
- In some cases, fever is the only sign.

## Diagnosis

Doctors begin with a physical exam.  
They may do an exam under anesthesia if the abscess is deep or hard to see.  
A CT scan is helpful if the abscess is deep or if Crohn disease is suspected.  
It can also show if the infection has spread into the belly.  
MRI of the pelvis and endoscopic ultrasound are other options.

- If you have a visible abscess on the skin, a normal rectal exam, and no signs of illness, you do not need imaging.  
- If the abscess is deep or if Crohn disease is likely, the doctor will do an exam under anesthesia at the time of drainage.

## Treatment

The key step is to cut open the abscess and drain the pus.  
This must be done quickly.  
It does not need to wait until the abscess forms a visible bump.

- Many abscesses can be drained in a doctor’s office or emergency room.  
- Deeper abscesses usually need surgery in an operating room.

Antibiotics are needed for some patients.  
You should get antibiotics if you have:

- A fever  
- A weak immune system  
- Diabetes  
- Severe skin swelling around the abscess

Common antibiotic choices include:
- Ciprofloxacin 500 milligrams every 12 hours through a vein  
- Metronidazole 500 milligrams every 8 hours through a vein  
- Ampicillin/sulbactam 1.5 grams every 8 hours through a vein

If you have very low white blood cell counts (less than 1,000 per microliter), you should get antibiotics alone.  
Antibiotics are not needed for healthy people with a simple, small abscess.

After drainage, some people develop an anorectal fistula.  
This is a small tunnel that forms between the rectum and the skin.  
It may need more treatment later.

## Key Points

- Anorectal abscesses can be close to the skin or deep inside.  
- Superficial abscesses can be diagnosed and drained in a doctor’s office or emergency room.  
- Deep abscesses often need a CT scan and surgery in the operating room.  
- All patients need prompt drainage.  
- Those with fever, a weak immune system, diabetes, or severe skin swelling should also get antibiotics.

# Vitamin Deficiency Anemia

This type of anemia happens when your body does not have enough vitamin B12 or folate. These vitamins are important for making healthy red blood cells.

## What Happens in Vitamin Deficiency Anemia?

- Your bone marrow makes red blood cells that are too big and not normal.
- These abnormal cells do not carry oxygen well.
- This leads to symptoms like feeling weak, tired, or short of breath.
- You may also look paler than usual.
- Nerves can stop working properly. This can cause tingling, numbness, or muscle weakness.
- In severe cases, confusion can happen. In older adults, this may look like memory problems or dementia.

## Causes of Vitamin Deficiency Anemia

- Not eating enough foods with vitamin B12 or folate.
- Problems in the gut that stop your body from absorbing these vitamins.
- A condition called pernicious anemia. This is an autoimmune disease. It stops your body from absorbing vitamin B12.
- Some cancer medicines can lower folate levels.
- Drinking too much alcohol can also lower folate levels.

## Symptoms

- Symptoms come on slowly.
- They are similar to other types of anemia: tiredness, weakness, and paleness.
- Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause nerve problems. These include tingling, numbness, or weakness in the hands and feet.
- Severe vitamin B12 deficiency can cause confusion.
- In older people, this confusion may be mistaken for dementia.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- A blood test checks for anemia.
- The doctor looks at your blood under a microscope.
- They check for large red blood cells and white blood cells with extra parts (called hypersegmented neutrophils).
- Blood tests also measure how much vitamin B12 and folate you have.
- Additional tests may be done to find the cause of low vitamin B12.

## Treatment

- The missing vitamin is replaced.
- For vitamin B12 deficiency:
  - You may get injections at first. These are given daily or weekly for several weeks.
  - Once your levels are normal, you may need an injection once a month.
  - You can also take vitamin B12 as a nose spray, a tablet under the tongue, or a swallowed tablet.
  - Some people need vitamin B12 supplements for life.
- For folate deficiency:
  - You take one tablet of folic acid every day.
  - This is usually enough to fix the problem.

## Important Notes

- Do not stop taking your supplements without talking to your doctor.
- Follow your doctor’s advice on how long to take the vitamins.
- If you have a long-term problem with absorption, you may need ongoing treatment.

# Spinal Muscular Atrophies (SMAs)

Spinal muscular atrophies are a group of inherited conditions. They cause muscles to weaken and shrink over time. This happens because nerve cells in the spinal cord and brain stem slowly stop working.

These conditions can start in infancy or childhood. Symptoms vary depending on the type. Common signs include weak muscles, low muscle tone, trouble sucking, swallowing, or breathing, and delays in reaching milestones like sitting or walking. In severe cases, children may not survive past early childhood.

Doctors diagnose SMA with genetic testing. There is no cure. Treatment focuses on helping people live as well as possible.

---

## What Causes SMA?

Most cases of SMA are caused by changes in a gene called *SMN1* on chromosome 5. These changes are usually inherited from both parents. The most common change is the loss of a part of the gene called exon 7.

Another gene, *SMN2*, can affect how serious the disease is. The more copies of *SMN2* a person has, the milder the symptoms may be. This helps explain why some children with SMA have different levels of severity.

In rare cases, SMA is caused by changes in other genes, not the *SMN1* gene.

---

## Types of SMA

There are five main types of SMA. They differ in how early symptoms start and how quickly they get worse.

### Type 0
- Symptoms begin before birth.
- The baby moves less in the womb.
- At birth, the baby is very weak and has low muscle tone.
- The baby may have facial weakness, no reflexes, heart problems, and joint stiffness.
- Most babies do not survive past 6 months due to breathing problems.

### Type 1
- Symptoms start before birth and become clear by 6 months of age.
- Babies are floppy at birth and have weak muscles.
- They have trouble sucking, swallowing, and breathing.
- Tongue twitching is common.
- Most children do not live past their first year. All die by age 4 without treatment.

### Type 2
- Symptoms appear between 3 and 15 months of age.
- Fewer than 25% of children learn to sit. None crawl or walk.
- Muscles are weak and may twitch. These twitches can be hard to see in young children.
- Reflexes are absent.
- Some children have trouble swallowing.
- Most use a wheelchair by age 2 to 3.
- The disease often leads to early death from breathing problems.
- In some cases, the disease stops getting worse. These children have lasting weakness and a high risk of spine curvature (scoliosis).

### Type 3
- Symptoms start between 15 months and 19 years of age.
- Muscle weakness is similar to type 1, but it gets worse slowly.
- Many people live a normal lifespan.
- Some cases are linked to enzyme problems, like low hexosaminidase.
- Weakness starts in the hips and thighs. It spreads to the arms over time.
- Life span depends on whether breathing problems develop.

### Type 4
- Starts in adulthood, between ages 30 and 60.
- Progresses slowly.
- Weakness mainly affects the hips and shoulders.
- Can be inherited in different ways: recessive, dominant, or X-linked.
- Hard to tell apart from a similar condition called amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), especially when only lower motor neurons are affected.

---

## How Is SMA Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect SMA in babies and children with unexplained muscle weakness and low muscle tone.

### Tests Used:
- **Electromyography (EMG)** and nerve conduction studies: These tests check how well nerves and muscles work. Nerve signals are normal, but muscles show signs of not getting signals from nerves.
- **Genetic testing**: This is the best way to confirm SMA. It finds the gene change in about 95% of people with the condition.
- **Muscle biopsy**: Done only in rare cases. It helps rule out other treatable causes and check if the condition is life-threatening.
- **Blood tests**: May show slightly high levels of certain enzymes like creatine kinase and aldolase.
- **Amniocentesis**: Done during pregnancy if there is a family history. It can detect SMA in the unborn baby.

---

## How Is SMA Treated?

There is no cure for SMA. Treatment focuses on supporting the body and improving quality of life.

### Supportive Care
- Physical therapy helps keep muscles and joints working well.
- Braces and special equipment can help with movement and posture.
- Devices from physical and occupational therapists help children do daily tasks like eating, writing, or using a computer.
- These tools can help children become more independent.

### Gene-Based Treatments

These medicines help the body make more of a protein that keeps motor neurons healthy.

#### Nusinersen
- Works by changing how the *SMN2* gene makes protein.
- Helps improve muscle function and may delay disability and death.
- Given as a shot into the spine (intrathecal injection).
- Must be given regularly.

#### Onasemnogene abeparvovec-xioi
- Used for children under 2 years old with two faulty *SMN1* genes.
- Uses a harmless virus to deliver a working *SMN* gene to nerve cells.
- Given as a one-time IV infusion over 1 hour.
- In studies, some children learned to sit, eat, roll over, and walk.
- Can cause serious liver problems.

#### Risdiplam
- Works by changing how the *SMN2* gene makes protein.
- Can be used in people 2 months old and older.
- Taken as a liquid, either by mouth or through a feeding tube, once a day.
- Common side effects include fever, diarrhea, and rash.

---

## Key Points

- If a baby or child has weak muscles and low muscle tone, check for SMA.
- EMG shows that muscles are not getting signals from nerves.
- Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis and identifies the type of SMA.
- Refer patients to physical and occupational therapists. They can help children do more on their own.
- Nusinersen, onasemnogene abeparvovec-xioi, or risdiplam may help improve movement and slow disease progress. They do not cure SMA.

# Neurofibromatosis

Neurofibromatosis is a group of inherited conditions. It causes soft, fleshy lumps under the skin and on nerves. It also causes light brown spots on the skin that look like coffee with milk.

## What Causes Neurofibromatosis?

A change in certain genes causes neurofibromatosis.  
Some people inherit the changed gene from a parent.  
Others get the change in the gene for the first time. This is not passed down from parents.  
The changed gene can be passed from parent to child.  
Each child of a parent with the condition has a 50% chance of getting it.  
The type of gene change affects how serious the condition is.

## Types of Neurofibromatosis

There are three main types: NF1, NF2, and schwannomatosis.

### NF1 (von Recklinghausen disease)

- Affects about 1 in 4,650 people.
- Causes lumps under the skin and on nerves.
- Lumps can grow on nerves in the skin, under the skin, or near the spine.
- Sometimes tumors grow on the nerves that connect the brain to the eyes.
- Bones and muscles can also be affected.

### NF2

- Affects about 1 in 25,000 people.
- Causes tumors on the nerves that carry sound from the inner ear to the brain.
- These tumors are called vestibular schwannomas or acoustic neuromas.
- Tumors can also grow in the brain or on the covering of the brain and spinal cord.
- These brain and spinal cord coverings are called meninges.
- Tumors on the meninges are not cancer.

### Schwannomatosis

- A rare condition.
- Causes tumors made mostly of Schwann cells.
- These tumors grow on nerves in the spine, head, and body.
- They do not grow on the nerves that carry sound from the ear to the brain.
- So people with this type do not get vestibular schwannomas.

## What Are the Symptoms?

### NF1

- Most people with NF1 have light brown spots on the skin. These are called café-au-lait spots.
- These spots are usually present at birth or appear in early childhood.
- Children without NF1 may have 2 or 3 of these spots.
- Children with NF1 usually have 6 or more.
- Lumps under the skin (neurofibromas) often appear between ages 10 and 15.
- These lumps can be small or large. There may be just a few or thousands.
- The lumps are usually the same color as the skin. Some may be pink or tan.
- Most do not cause pain or other problems.
- If a lump presses on a nerve, it can cause tingling, weakness, or pain.
- Some people have bone problems. These include a curved spine, crooked ribs, or bones in the arms or legs that are too big.
- If the bone around the eye is affected, the eye may bulge.
- Tumors can grow on nerves in the head. This can cause vision loss, dizziness, or weakness.
- Other possible problems:
  - A tumor on the nerve to the eye (optic glioma)
  - Small growths on the colored part of the eye (Lisch nodules)
  - Weak spots or blockages in blood vessels
  - A slightly larger head size
  - Learning problems
  - A rare type of blood cancer (leukemia)
  - Cancerous tumors in the brain or on nerves

Optic gliomas often do not cause symptoms.  
But if they grow large, they can press on the eye nerve and cause vision loss or blindness.  
These tumors are usually found by age 5.  
They rarely appear after age 10.

Neurofibromatosis usually gets worse slowly over time.  
As more lumps grow, more nerve problems may appear.

### NF2

- Tumors grow on the nerves that carry sound from the ear to the brain.
- These tumors press on the nerves and cause:
  - Hearing loss
  - Ringing in the ears (tinnitus)
  - Dizziness
  - Unsteadiness
  - Headaches
  - Weakness in parts of the face
- Symptoms can start in childhood or early adulthood.
- Other tumors may grow in the brain or on the brain’s covering (meninges).
- Some people get cataracts early in life.

### Schwannomatosis

- Tumors (called schwannomas) grow on nerves in the body.
- They do not grow on the nerves that carry sound from the ear to the brain.
- So people with this type do not get hearing problems from these tumors.
- Some people have many tumors. Others have only a few.
- The first sign is often pain. This pain can be anywhere in the body.
- The pain may become long-lasting and severe.
- Some people have numbness, tingling, or weakness in the fingers and toes.
- Symptoms appear when tumors press on nerves in the head, spine, or body.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tools to diagnose neurofibromatosis.

### What the Doctor Checks

- A full physical exam.
- Look for light brown skin spots (café-au-lait spots).
- Feel for lumps under the skin along nerves.
- Check for bone or eye problems.

### Imaging Tests

- Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT) scans.
- These tests look for tumors in the head and near the spine.
- Used if a person has nerve symptoms.

### Genetic Testing

- Done if a person has signs of neurofibromatosis but does not meet all the usual criteria.
- Helps confirm the diagnosis.

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure for neurofibromatosis.  
There is also no treatment that stops it from getting worse.

### For Lumps That Cause Problems

- Small lumps can be removed with a laser or electric heat (electrocautery).
- Larger lumps may need surgery.
- Sometimes, the nerve must be removed with the lump.

### For Cancerous Tumors

- Chemotherapy is used.

### For Vestibular Schwannomas (in NF2)

- Surgery is the main treatment.
- Slow-growing tumors may not need surgery right away.
- Fast-growing tumors may be treated with a medicine called bevacizumab.
  - This medicine blocks a substance that helps tumors grow.
- All people with NF2 should see an audiologist.
  - An audiologist checks hearing and balance.

### For Schwannomas (in non-NF2 schwannomatosis)

- Treatment focuses on managing pain.
- Surgery is only done if pain is not controlled or if the tumor causes weakness, numbness, or tingling.

## Genetic Counseling

- Neurofibromatosis can be passed from parent to child.
- If you have the condition and are thinking about having children, talk to a genetic counselor.
- Your child has a 50% chance of getting the condition.
- If you do not have the condition but your child does, your next child has a very small chance of getting it.

# Bullous Pemphigoid

Bullous pemphigoid is a long-term skin condition that causes large, itchy blisters.  
It mostly affects people over the age of sixty.  
It is not caused by an infection.  
It happens when the body’s immune system attacks the skin.  
The blisters form under the top layer of skin.  
The inside of the blisters is filled with fluid.  
The blisters are usually at least 10 millimeters wide.  
Mouth or other mucous membranes are rarely affected.  

## What Causes Bullous Pemphigoid?

No single cause has been proven.  
But some things may trigger it.  

### Possible Triggers
- Certain medicines:  
  - Furosemide (a water pill)  
  - Spironolactone (a blood pressure medicine)  
  - Omeprazole (a stomach acid medicine)  
  - Some cancer drugs like durvalumab, nivolumab, and pembrolizumab  
  - Sulfasalazine (for arthritis or bowel disease)  
  - Penicillin and other antibiotics  
  - Penicillamine (a medicine for rheumatoid arthritis)  
  - Etanercept (a medicine for autoimmune diseases)  
  - Some antipsychotic medicines  
  - Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (for diabetes)  

- Physical damage to the skin:  
  - Cuts, scrapes, or pressure  
  - Radiation treatment for breast cancer  
  - Sunlight (UV light)  
  - Anthralin (a medicine used for psoriasis)  

- Other skin problems:  
  - Psoriasis  
  - Lichen planus  
  - Some infections  

- Other health conditions:  
  - Diabetes  
  - Rheumatoid arthritis  
  - Ulcerative colitis  
  - Multiple sclerosis  

- Genetics and environment may also play a role.  

These triggers may cause the immune system to react in a way that harms the skin.  
One idea is that the triggers look like parts of the skin’s basement membrane.  
This causes the immune system to attack the skin by mistake.  
Another idea is that the triggers expose parts of the skin that the body usually ignores.  
Over time, the immune system may start attacking more parts of the skin.  
This is called epitope spreading.  
It can make the disease last longer.  

Some brain or mental health conditions may come before bullous pemphigoid.  
These include:  
- Multiple sclerosis  
- Schizophrenia  
- Dementia  
- Brain bleeds  
- Stroke  
- Delusional disorders  
- Personality disorders  
- Parkinson’s disease  

In rare cases, bullous pemphigoid may come before these conditions.  
One theory is that the immune system reacts to both brain and skin proteins.  
The protein BPAg1 is found in both the brain and the skin.  
Another theory is that some medicines used for brain or mental health problems may trigger the disease.  
But we do not fully understand how this happens.  

## Symptoms and Signs

The first sign is usually itching.  
The itching can start years before any rash appears.  
Blisters usually form on the trunk, inner elbows, behind the knees, and in skin folds.  
They can also form on normal-looking skin.  
Sometimes, the skin turns red or looks like hives before blisters appear.  
Blisters may also form at sites of injury, around stomas, or on the genitals and lower legs.  

A rare form called dyshidrotic pemphigoid affects the hands and feet.  
It can look like a type of hand and foot rash called dyshidrotic dermatitis.  

The blisters are usually tight and do not break easily.  
If they do break, they heal quickly.  

Other skin changes can include:  
- Red, swollen patches  
- Ring-shaped or irregular red spots  
- Small blisters around the edges of larger patches  

Very rarely, small blisters form in the mouth.  

Blood tests often show higher levels of white blood cells and eosinophils.  
Fever is uncommon.  

If you press or rub the skin near a blister, the top layer does not move.  
This is called a negative Nikolsky sign.  

Photos show:  
- Tight blisters, open sores, and scabs on the arm  
- Red patches with intact blisters and sores on the foot  
- Broken blisters and sores on the thigh  
- Both broken and unbroken blisters on a red base  
- Tight blisters, sores, and darkened skin on the arm  

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Diagnosis is based on skin tests and blood tests.  

### Key Tests
- A skin biopsy: A small piece of skin is taken from near a blister.  
  - This is checked under a microscope.  
  - It shows the type of blister and the cells inside.  
- Direct immunofluorescence: A test on the skin sample.  
  - It shows if antibodies and immune system proteins are stuck along the skin’s base layer.  
- Blood tests: Check for antibodies in the blood.  
  - These are called IgG antibodies to BPAg1 and BPAg2.  
  - They are found in about 75% of people with the disease.  

### How It Differs from Other Blistering Diseases

| Condition | Blisters | Mouth Sores | Itching | Skin Moves When Pressed? | Outlook |
|--------|--------|------------|--------|--------------------------|--------|
| Bullous pemphigoid | Tight blisters on red or normal skin | Rare | Common | No (negative) | Usually good; can be serious in older adults |
| Pemphigus vulgaris | Loose, soft blisters | Common, often in mouth | Rare | Yes (positive) | Can be life-threatening without treatment |

Other conditions that can look similar include:  
- Linear IgA disease  
- Erythema multiforme  
- Drug rashes  
- Mucous membrane pemphigoid  
- Paraneoplastic pemphigoid  
- Dermatitis herpetiformis  
- Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita  

## Treatment

Treatment aims to stop new blisters and reduce itching.  
It also helps prevent long-term side effects.  

### First-Line Treatments
- **Topical corticosteroids**: Strong creams like clobetasol 0.05% are used for small areas.  
  - They can reduce the need for oral medicines.  
- **Oral corticosteroids**: Prednisone is used for widespread disease.  
  - Start with 0.5 mg per kilogram of body weight each day.  
  - After a few weeks, lower the dose to 0.1 mg per kilogram per day.  
  - Most people get better in 2 to 10 months.  
  - Treatment may need to continue for years.  
  - If new blisters appear every few weeks, do not raise the dose.  

### Other Options
- **Anti-inflammatory medicines**:  
  - Tetracycline or minocycline with nicotinamide may help.  
  - Dapsone, sulfapyridine, or erythromycin may be used alone.  
- **IV immune globulin**: Used in rare cases.  

### For Severe or Hard-to-Treat Cases
- **Immunosuppressants**:  
  - Methotrexate  
  - Azathioprine  
  - Mycophenolate mofetil  
  - Cyclosporine  
- **Biologic drugs**:  
  - Rituximab  
  - Dupilumab  
  - Omalizumab  
  - IV immune globulin  

These drugs help reduce the need for long-term steroids.  

## Prognosis

Bullous pemphigoid is a long-term condition.  
It can be controlled with treatment.  
But treatment may cause side effects.  
Most people improve within months.  
However, some need treatment for several years.  

## Key Points

- Bullous pemphigoid mostly affects people over 60.  
- It is an autoimmune disease with no known cause.  
- Itching often starts years before a rash appears.  
- Mouth sores are rare.  
- A skin biopsy and blood tests are needed for diagnosis.  
- Use strong topical steroids when possible to avoid oral steroids.  
- Anti-inflammatory and immune-suppressing medicines can help lower steroid use.  
- Symptoms usually improve within months.  
- Treatment may be needed for years.

# Hidradenitis Suppurativa

Hidradenitis suppurativa is a skin condition that causes painful lumps under the skin. It often happens in areas like the armpits, groin, around the nipples, and near the anus.

The exact cause is not known. But it is not due to poor hygiene, using deodorants, powders, or shaving under the arms.

The condition usually starts after puberty. It happens when hair follicles (the tiny holes in the skin where hair grows) get blocked. This blockage leads to swelling and inflammation.

Blocked hair follicles can swell and form bumps. These bumps look like acne. But they are not the same as regular acne.

The blocked follicles can burst. This lets bacteria get in and cause infection. The infection leads to abscesses. Abscesses are pockets of pus under the skin.

Abscesses are painful. They can smell bad. They can grow deep into the skin. They often come back after healing.

Over time, the skin in the area becomes thick and scarred. Permanent tunnels (called sinus tracts) can form. These tunnels connect abscesses to the skin surface. They drain pus.

## How Severe Is It?

Hidradenitis suppurativa can be mild or severe.

- **Mild**: A few abscesses. Not much scarring.
- **Moderate**: More abscesses and scarring. Sinus tracts may form.
- **Severe**: Many abscesses. Deep sinus tracts. Skin damage is serious.

The condition can hurt a person’s quality of life. Pain and bad smell can cause embarrassment and stress.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look at the skin to make a diagnosis.

They check where the bumps and abscesses are. They also see if they keep coming back.

Sometimes, doctors take a sample of pus from deep abscesses. They send it to a lab to test for bacteria. This is called a culture.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on how bad the condition is.

### For Mild Cases

- A doctor may inject medicine into the area to reduce swelling.
- You may take antibiotics by mouth for 7 to 10 days. Examples: tetracycline, minocycline, erythromycin, or clindamycin.
- You may use clindamycin or resorcinol cream on the skin.
- You should wash the area with benzoyl peroxide.
- These treatments can be used alone or together.

### For Moderate Cases

- You may take the same oral antibiotics as for mild cases.
- You may also take rifampin, another antibiotic, for 2 to 3 months.
- Women may be given hormone-blocking medicines. These include birth control pills, spironolactone, or finasteride.
- A doctor may cut open abscesses to drain the pus.
- A doctor may open and drain sinus tracts.

### For Severe Cases

- You may get medicine through a vein or under the skin. These medicines reduce inflammation. Examples: infliximab, adalimumab, or secukinumab.
- You may take isotretinoin or acitretin by mouth for several months. These help reduce inflammation.
- If the condition does not improve, a doctor may remove the damaged skin and tissue.
- The doctor may repair the skin or use a skin graft.
- Laser treatment may be used to remove damaged skin or hair follicles.

---

## Other Helpful Steps

- Good hygiene will not cure the condition. But it helps keep the skin clean and healthy.
- Treat your skin gently. Avoid harsh soaps or scrubbing.
- Losing weight may help reduce symptoms.
- Avoid foods high in sugar and processed carbs. These are called high-glycemic foods.
- Psychological support can help with stress and emotional health.

You are not alone. Many people live with this condition. With the right care, symptoms can improve.

# AIDS Cholangiopathy

AIDS cholangiopathy is a blockage in the bile ducts. It happens when the bile ducts become narrowed. This narrowing is caused by infections that take advantage of a weak immune system.

(See also: How the Bile System Works.)

Before modern HIV treatment, this condition affected 1 in 4 people with AIDS. It was more common in people with very low immune cell counts (fewer than 100 of these cells per microliter of blood). The most common cause is a parasite called *Cryptosporidium parvum*. Other causes include cytomegalovirus, microsporidia, and *Cyclospora*.

Most people develop either a narrowing at the opening of the bile duct into the small intestine (papillary stenosis) or a condition where the bile ducts become scarred and stiff (sclerosing cholangitis). More than half of people have both problems.

## Symptoms

Common symptoms include:
- Pain in the upper right side of the belly
- Pain in the upper middle belly
- Diarrhea

Some people also have a fever or yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice).  
Severe pain usually means there is a blockage at the opening of the bile duct.  
Mild pain usually means the bile ducts are scarred and stiff.

The diarrhea comes from an infection in the small intestine. The most common cause is *Cryptosporidium*.

## Diagnosis

Doctors usually use ultrasound and a special procedure called ERCP.

Ultrasound is the first test. It is safe and very accurate (over 95% correct).  
But most people also need ERCP. This test can confirm the diagnosis. It also lets doctors take samples from the bile ducts and small intestine to find the cause of the infection. ERCP can also treat the problem by opening up blocked areas.

CT scans and MRI scans of the bile ducts may help support the diagnosis.

Abnormal liver blood tests often show high levels of alkaline phosphatase. This suggests bile is not flowing properly.

## Treatment

Treatment focuses on opening blocked bile ducts and treating the infection.

Endoscopic procedures are the main treatment.

- Doctors can cut the muscle at the opening of the bile duct (sphincterotomy) during ERCP. This helps relieve pain, jaundice, and infection.
- Narrowed areas (strictures) in the bile ducts can be opened with a stent placed during ERCP.
- Antibiotics or other medicines are used to treat the infection. But these medicines alone do not fix the damage in the bile ducts or relieve symptoms.

Ursodeoxycholic acid may help reduce scarring in the small bile ducts inside the liver. It may also help improve bile flow and reduce liver damage.

# Pemphigus Vulgaris

Pemphigus vulgaris is a rare and serious skin disease.  
It causes blisters on the skin and inside the mouth.  
It can also affect other moist areas in the body, like the nose and genitals.

## What Causes Pemphigus Vulgaris?

Your body’s immune system usually fights off germs like bacteria and viruses.  
It makes special cells and proteins called antibodies to do this.  
In pemphigus vulgaris, the immune system makes mistakes.  
It attacks healthy skin cells instead of germs.  
The antibodies target proteins that hold skin cells together.  
When these proteins are damaged, the skin cells fall apart.  
This causes blisters and open sores.

This disease is not contagious.  
It is not caused by poor hygiene or infection.  
It is an autoimmune disease, meaning the body attacks itself.

A similar skin problem called bullous pemphigoid can look like pemphigus vulgaris.  
But it is less serious and affects older adults more often.

## Who Gets Pemphigus Vulgaris?

This disease mostly affects middle-aged or older adults.  
Men and women are equally likely to get it.  
It is very rare in children.

## Symptoms

The main symptom is painful blisters.  
They are clear, soft, and can be any size.  
They often start in the mouth.  
They break easily and leave open, sore areas.

Blisters in the mouth can make it hard to eat, drink, or swallow.  
They may spread to the throat and cause more pain.  
Blisters can also appear on the skin.  
They break and leave raw, oozing wounds.  
These wounds can become infected.

The skin may peel off in sheets when touched lightly.  
This is very painful.  
The person may feel sick all over.  
The condition can be as serious as a severe burn.  
The skin leaks fluid and is at high risk for infection.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look at the blisters and the pattern of skin damage.  
They may take a small sample of skin for testing.  
This is called a skin biopsy.  
The sample is examined under a microscope.  
Special stains can show where the antibodies are in the skin.

This helps doctors tell pemphigus vulgaris apart from bullous pemphigoid.  
The two diseases affect different layers of the skin.  
The pattern of antibodies is also different.

## Treatment

Treatment is needed right away.  
Without treatment, the disease can be deadly.

Most people with moderate to severe disease are admitted to the hospital.  
Their skin is treated like a serious burn.  
They need careful cleaning and protection.

Doctors use strong medicines to calm the immune system.  
Corticosteroids are a key part of treatment.  
They are taken by mouth or given through a vein in the hospital.  
The dose is slowly lowered once the disease is under control.

For mild cases, treatment may start with a drug called rituximab.  
This drug helps reduce immune system activity.  
It may be used alone or with corticosteroids.  
Other immune-suppressing drugs like azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil are often added.

For moderate or severe cases, treatment usually starts with rituximab or high-dose corticosteroids.  
These are often combined with other immune-suppressing drugs.

Using immune-suppressing drugs helps lower the need for high doses of corticosteroids.  
This reduces side effects.

In some cases, doctors use immune globulin.  
This is a medicine made from donated blood.  
It is given through a vein and helps calm the immune system.

Some people may need plasma exchange.  
This is a process that filters harmful antibodies from the blood.  
It is used in very severe cases.

Some people can stop treatment after their symptoms go away.  
Others need to take low doses of medicine for years.

## Outlook

Without treatment, pemphigus vulgaris is often fatal.  
Most people die within five years.  
With treatment, most people survive.  
But the risk of death is still higher than for the general population.

The risk is higher if:
- The disease is widespread.
- High doses of corticosteroids or other immune-suppressing drugs are needed.
- The person has other serious health problems.

## Did You Know?

Pemphigus vulgaris is often deadly without treatment.  
But most people live long lives if they get proper care.

# Motion Sickness

Motion sickness causes nausea, stomach discomfort, vomiting, dizziness, pale skin, and sweating. It happens when your body feels motion, even if you are not moving.

It is caused by certain types of motion. These include back-and-forth or turning movements. It can also happen when your eyes, inner ear, and body feel different things at the same time.

You can reduce or prevent symptoms with changes in behavior or medicine.

Motion sickness is a normal reaction to motion. It affects only a few people in calm situations, like a smooth airplane ride. But almost everyone gets it in rough seas or during space travel.

You can get motion sickness from real movement, like riding in a car or boat. You can also get it when you think you are moving, even if you are still. This is called vection.

Some people are more likely to get motion sickness than others. Women are more likely than men. Children between 2 and 12 years old get it more often than adults. It is rare in babies under 2 years old.

Symptoms often get better with age. New cases in people over 50 are uncommon. But older adults may be more likely to get motion sickness from things like video games or virtual reality.

## What Causes Motion Sickness?

The main cause is too much activity in the inner ear balance system. This system can be overstimulated by real movement or by the feeling of movement.

A common example is playing video games or using virtual reality. These can cause motion sickness even if you are sitting still. This is called visually induced motion sickness or VIMS.

The inner ear has two parts. One senses turning movements. The other senses straight-line motion and gravity.

The brain and nervous system are involved too. Key parts include the inner ear, brainstem, parts of the brain that control balance, and the vomiting center.

We do not fully understand how it works. But motion sickness only happens if the inner ear and its nerve connections are working. People without a working inner ear system cannot get motion sickness.

Any kind of transport can cause motion sickness. This includes boats, cars, trains, planes, spacecraft, and amusement park rides.

One common cause is a mismatch between what your eyes see and what your body feels. For example:

- You see a still wall inside a moving boat. Your eyes say you are still. Your body says you are moving.
- You watch a fast-moving video while sitting still. Your eyes see motion. Your body feels no motion.

Another cause is a mismatch between turning and straight-line motion. This can happen in space, where there is no gravity.

In space, astronauts often get motion sickness at first. This is called space adaptation syndrome. It makes it hard to work during the first few days. But most people adjust after a few days.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Common symptoms include:

- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Pale skin
- Sweating
- A vague feeling of stomach upset

Other early signs may include:

- Yawning
- Breathing too fast
- Extra saliva
- Feeling sleepy

Other possible symptoms:

- Swallowing air (aerophagia)
- Dizziness
- Headache
- Tiredness
- Weakness
- Trouble focusing

You will not have pain, trouble breathing, weakness in one part of the body, or problems with vision or speech.

If you stay in motion for a long time, your body may adjust after a few days. But symptoms can come back if the motion gets worse or if you start again after a break.

If vomiting lasts a long time, it can lead to dehydration. This can cause low blood pressure, weakness, and low energy.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose motion sickness based on your symptoms and what you were doing.

You likely have motion sickness if you feel sick after being in a moving vehicle or in a situation that causes motion.

The diagnosis is usually clear. But in some people, especially older adults or those with no history of motion sickness, other serious problems must be ruled out.

These include brain bleeding or a stroke. This is especially important if you have sudden dizziness, vomiting, or other unusual symptoms.

If you have signs of a stroke — like weakness on one side, trouble speaking, or vision problems — you need urgent medical care.

## How Is It Treated?

There are several ways to treat motion sickness.

### Medicine to Prevent It
Take medicine before symptoms start. It works best when taken early. Options include:

- Anticholinergic drugs
- Antihistamines
- Drugs that block dopamine

Scopolamine and antihistamines are often used.

### Non-Medicine Ways to Prevent It
- Sit in the part of the vehicle that moves the least (like the middle of a boat or the front of a car).
- Sleep if you can.
- Get fresh air.
- Avoid alcohol, heavy meals, and too much drinking.

### Medicine to Stop Vomiting
If you start vomiting, take an anti-nausea medicine. It can be given by rectum or injection.

### Fluids and Electrolytes
If vomiting lasts a long time, you may need fluids and salts through a vein (IV). This helps prevent dehydration.

### Special Note for Pregnant Women
If you are pregnant, treat motion sickness the same way you would treat morning sickness. Use safe medicines and follow your doctor’s advice.

## Key Points

- Motion sickness is caused by too much inner ear activity or by conflicting signals from your eyes, body, and inner ear.
- Diagnosis is based on symptoms and history. It is usually easy to recognize.
- Medicine works best when taken before symptoms start. Scopolamine or antihistamines are common choices.
- If vomiting has started, serotonin blocker medicines are best.
- To reduce risk:
  - Sit where motion is least.
  - Rest or sleep if possible.
  - Keep the air fresh.
  - Avoid alcohol, heavy food, and too much drink.

# Lichen Planus

Lichen planus is a skin condition that causes an itchy rash.  
It starts as small, separate bumps that are red or purple.  
These bumps join together and become rough, scaly patches.  
The rash can appear on many parts of the body.  
It can also show up in the mouth or on the genitals.

## What Causes Lichen Planus?

The exact cause is not known.  
It may be a reaction by the body’s immune system.  
This reaction can be triggered by certain medicines.  
Common medicines linked to lichen planus include:  
- Blood pressure drugs (beta-blockers)  
- Pain relievers (NSAIDs)  
- Heart medicines (ACE inhibitors)  
- Diabetes pills (sulfonylureas)  
- Malaria medicines (antimalarials)  
- A drug used for rheumatoid arthritis (penicillamine)  
- Water pills (thiazides)  

It may also be linked to hepatitis B or C infections.  
Or to a liver condition called primary biliary cholangitis.  
Lichen planus is not contagious.  
It cannot be passed from one person to another.

## Symptoms of Lichen Planus

The rash almost always itches.  
Sometimes the itching is very strong.  
The bumps have sharp, angular edges.  
On light skin, the bumps look red or purple.  
On dark skin, they look brown or gray.  
When light hits the bumps from the side, they shine.  
New bumps can form where the skin is scratched or injured.  

After the rash goes away, some people are left with dark spots.  
This is called hyperpigmentation.  

The rash usually appears on both sides of the body.  
Common places include:  
- The chest and back  
- Inside of the wrists  
- The legs  
- The genital area  

The face is less often affected.  
On the legs, the rash can become very thick and scaly.  
It can also cause patchy hair loss on the scalp.  

Lichen planus is rare in children.  

About half of people with lichen planus also get it in the mouth.  
In the mouth, it often shows as white, lacy lines or patterns.  
These lines are called Wickham striae.  
They usually do not hurt.  
Some people do not even know they are there.  

But sometimes painful sores form in the mouth.  
These sores can make eating and drinking hard.  

In women, lichen planus often affects the vulva and vagina.  
Up to half of women with mouth lichen planus also have it on the vulva.  
This is often not diagnosed.  

In men, lichen planus commonly affects the head of the penis.  

Lichen planus can also affect the nails.  
This happens in up to 1 in 10 people.  
Some people only have mild changes.  
These include:  
- Discolored nail beds  
- Thin or brittle nails  
- Lines or ridges on the nails  

Others may lose their nails completely.  
Scarring can happen from the base of the nail to the skin under it.

## How Is Lichen Planus Diagnosed?

Doctors look at the rash and where it appears.  
They may also take a small sample of skin.  
This is called a biopsy.  
The sample is checked under a microscope.  

Other tests may be done.  
These include liver tests.  
Tests for hepatitis B and C are also done.  

## How Is Lichen Planus Treated?

If you have no symptoms, you do not need treatment.  
Stop taking any medicine that might be causing the rash.  
Do not take it again unless your doctor says it is safe.  

To relieve itching:  
- Use corticosteroid creams or lotions  
- Take corticosteroid pills  
- Get corticosteroid injections into the bumps  

Other medicines that may help include:  
- Acitretin  
- Griseofulvin  
- Dapsone  
- Hydroxychloroquine  
- Azathioprine  
- Apremilast  
- Cyclosporine  

Phototherapy uses ultraviolet light to treat the rash.  
It can be used alone or with a drug called psoralen.  
This combination is called PUVA.  
Another type uses a narrow band of ultraviolet B light.  
This is called narrowband ultraviolet B.  

For painful mouth sores:  
- Use a mouthwash with lidocaine before meals  
- Lidocaine is a numbing medicine  
- It forms a pain-killing coating in the mouth  
- Do not use more often than your doctor tells you  

Tacrolimus ointment can also help mouth sores.  
Other options include:  
- Corticosteroid creams, injections, or pills  
- Dapsone, hydroxychloroquine, or cyclosporine taken by mouth  
- Cyclosporine mouth rinses  

## What Is the Outlook for Lichen Planus?

Most people get better within 1 to 2 years.  
But it can last longer, especially if the mouth is involved.  
Treatment may be needed during flare-ups.  
Between flare-ups, no treatment is needed.  

People with painful mouth sores rarely get mouth cancer.  
The skin rash does not turn into cancer.  
Mouth sores often last for life.  

Lichen planus in the vagina or vulva can be long-lasting and hard to treat.  
It can cause scarring and lower quality of life.

# Urinary Incontinence in Adults

Urinary incontinence means you leak urine without meaning to. Some doctors only count it as a problem if you feel bothered by it. Many people do not talk to their doctor about it. Many doctors do not ask about it either. It can happen at any age. But it is more common in older adults and women. About 3 out of 10 older women and 1 out of 7 older men have it.

Incontinence can hurt your life. It can make you feel embarrassed, ashamed, or lonely. It can lead to sadness. Some older people end up in care homes because incontinence is hard for caregivers to manage. If you are in bed a lot, urine can irritate your skin. This can lead to pressure sores on your lower back. Older adults who feel a sudden need to pee are more likely to fall and break a bone.

(See also: Urinary Incontinence in Children and Overview of Voiding.)

---

## What Causes Urinary Incontinence in Adults

The causes can be different depending on your age.

As you get older, your bladder holds less urine. You may find it harder to hold your pee. Your bladder may squeeze on its own. This makes you need to go to the bathroom more often. Your bladder may not empty fully. After you pee, some urine stays in your bladder. This is called postvoid residual volume. It is normal for this to be less than 50 milliliters. In older adults, it may go up to 100 milliliters or more. The tissues that support the bladder and urethra also weaken.

**For women after menopause:**  
Estrogen levels drop. This can cause thin, dry, and irritated tissue in the urethra and vagina. The urethra becomes weaker. It does not close as tightly. This makes it easier to leak urine.

**For men:**  
The prostate gland grows larger. This can block the flow of urine. It makes the bladder work harder. The bladder may not empty fully. This can lead to incontinence. But a larger prostate alone does not always cause leaking. Many older men with a large prostate do not have incontinence.

**For younger people:**  
A short-term problem like a bladder infection or vaginal infection can cause temporary incontinence. This usually starts suddenly. You may leak only a little. It often gets better on its own or with simple treatment. Younger people usually have just one cause. Older adults often have more than one cause.

It helps to think of causes as either temporary or long-term. But these causes often mix together.

---

## How Doctors Check for Urinary Incontinence

Most people feel too shy to talk about leaking urine. They may not bring it up. But they might mention other symptoms like needing to pee often, waking up at night to pee, or having trouble starting to pee. All adults should be asked directly: “Do you ever leak urine?”

Do not assume that long-term incontinence cannot be fixed. Always check for urinary retention before treating overactive bladder.

> **Tip:** Most people are too embarrassed to bring up incontinence. Always ask about it.

---

## How Doctors Treat Urinary Incontinence

Treatment depends on the type and cause. But some steps help most people.

**Bladder training:**  
You learn to go to the bathroom on a schedule. This helps your bladder hold more urine and reduces leaks.

**Kegel exercises:**  
You tighten and relax the muscles that control your bladder. These exercises strengthen the muscles and help stop leaks.

**Medications:**  
Your doctor may prescribe medicine to help your bladder work better. But some medicines can make incontinence worse. If you are taking such medicines, your doctor may change the dose or timing. For example, a water pill (diuretic) might be taken earlier in the day so you are near a bathroom when it works.

**Treat the cause:**  
If an infection is causing the problem, it is treated. If a medicine is making it worse, it may be stopped or changed.

**General tips:**  
Even if you do not know the exact cause, some general steps help most people.

---

## Key Points

- Many people do not say they leak urine. Always ask about it.
- Incontinence is not a normal part of aging. It should always be checked.
- There are four main types: urge, stress, overflow, and functional.
- Even long-standing incontinence can often be improved or fixed.
- All incontinent patients should have:
  - A urine test (urinalysis)
  - A urine culture
  - Blood tests for kidney function (BUN and creatinine)
  - A check to see how much urine stays in the bladder after peeing (postvoid residual volume)
- Try bladder training and Kegel exercises.
- Treat the real reason your bladder is not working right.

# Febrile Seizures – Simple Explanation

A febrile seizure happens when a child has a seizure because of a fever. The fever must be at least 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit (about 38 degrees Celsius).

## What Is a Seizure?

A seizure is when the brain sends out too many electrical signals at once. This can cause:

- The body to shake or jerk uncontrollably
- Unusual movements that the child cannot control
- A change in awareness or alertness
- Strange feelings or sensations

A **convulsion** is when the body shakes violently and muscles become stiff.

## Who Gets Febrile Seizures?

- Febrile seizures happen in about 2 to 5 out of every 100 children between 6 months and 5 years old.
- They are most common in children between 12 and 18 months old.
- A seizure in a child 6 years or older with a fever is not called a febrile seizure.

## What Causes Febrile Seizures?

- Most febrile seizures are caused by a fever from a mild infection.
- Common infections include colds, ear infections, or other viral illnesses.
- The fever itself is the main cause. The infection is usually not serious.
- Febrile seizures are **not** caused by brain infections like meningitis or encephalitis.

## Family History

- Febrile seizures can run in families.
- Scientists have found several genes linked to febrile seizures.

## Types of Febrile Seizures

There are two types: simple and complex.

### Simple Febrile Seizure
- The whole body shakes.
- It lasts less than 15 minutes.
- The child loses consciousness.
- It happens only once in 24 hours.
- Over 90% of febrile seizures are simple.

### Complex Febrile Seizure
- The shaking lasts 15 minutes or longer.
- Only one side or one part of the body shakes.
- The child has more than one seizure in 24 hours.
- Children with complex seizures are more likely to have seizures later in life that are not linked to fever.

## After the Seizure

- After a seizure, the child may feel very tired or sleepy.
- This tired feeling can last a few minutes or up to a few hours.

## How Common Are Recurrent Seizures?

- About 20 to 35 out of every 100 children who have one febrile seizure will never have another.
- Children are more likely to have another seizure if:
  - They were under 1 year old when they had the first seizure.
  - A close family member has had febrile seizures.

## Long-Term Outlook

- Most children with simple febrile seizures grow up healthy.
- They do not develop epilepsy or other brain problems because of the seizure.
- But a febrile seizure can sometimes be the first sign of a hidden brain or nerve problem.
- Doctors may look back at the child’s history and see early signs of such a problem.
- In some cases, the signs do not appear until later.
- The seizure itself does not cause the brain problem.

### Risk of Future Seizures

- Children with a simple febrile seizure have a small chance (2 to 6%) of having seizures later that are not linked to fever.
- This risk is higher if the child had a complex seizure or has other risk factors, such as:
  - Developmental delays
  - A family history of seizures
  - Brain imaging that shows problems

## Febrile Status Epilepticus

- This is a very long seizure or several seizures that happen one after another without the child waking up between them.
- A febrile seizure lasting 30 minutes or more is called febrile status epilepticus.
- This is serious. Without quick treatment, it can cause brain damage.

## How Doctors Diagnose Febrile Seizures

If a child has a fever and a seizure for the first time, or seems very sick, they should go to the emergency room right away.

Doctors will:

- Ask questions about the child’s health and symptoms.
- Do a physical exam.
- Check for signs of serious illness.

They may do tests to rule out serious causes, such as:

- **Spinal tap (lumbar puncture):** A small amount of fluid is taken from around the spine to check for brain infections.
- **Blood tests:** To check blood sugar, calcium, magnesium, sodium, and other levels.
- **Urine and blood cultures:** To check for infections.
- **Brain imaging (MRI or CT scan):** To look at the brain. MRI is preferred, but CT may be used if MRI is not available.
- **EEG (electroencephalogram):** A test that checks brain activity. It may be done if the child has repeated seizures or other warning signs.

## How Febrile Seizures Are Treated

- Most febrile seizures last less than 5 minutes and stop on their own.
- No special treatment is needed beyond lowering the fever.

### If the Seizure Lasts 5 Minutes or More

- Doctors may give medicine to stop the seizure.
- The medicine is usually given through a vein (IV).
- If IV medicine is not possible and the child is over 2 years old, medicine can be given:
  - As a gel into the rectum.
  - As a liquid into the nose (intranasal).
- After treatment, the child is watched closely for breathing and blood pressure problems.

## Preventing Future Seizures

- Parents should watch for high fevers and treat them early.
- But febrile seizures often happen early in the fever, sometimes before parents even know the child is sick.

### When Medication Is Used to Prevent Seizures

Antiseizure medicine is usually not needed for children who have only a few simple febrile seizures.

But doctors may prescribe medicine if the child has:

- A complex febrile seizure and other brain or nerve problems (like cerebral palsy or abnormal brain scans).
- A strong family history of epilepsy and repeated febrile seizures.
- Febrile status epilepticus.
- More than 4 febrile seizures in one year.

### Emergency Medication at Home

- If a child has had a very long febrile seizure, the doctor may give a prescription for diazepam gel.
- This gel is put into the rectum during a future seizure.
- The child can be treated at home with this medicine.
- The same medicine may be given if a future seizure lasts more than 5 minutes.

## Key Points to Remember

- Febrile seizures are common in young children and usually harmless.
- They are caused by fever, not by brain disease.
- Most children do not need long-term medicine.
- The child’s brain is not damaged by a simple febrile seizure.
- Always seek medical help if a child has a seizure with a fever, especially the first time.

# Herpes Zoster Oticus

Herpes zoster oticus is a rare condition. It happens when a virus that caused chickenpox long ago becomes active again. This reactivation affects nerves in the head and ear.

The virus stays hidden in nerve cells for years. It can come back when the body’s defenses are weak. This can happen with cancer, chemotherapy, radiation, or HIV.

Usually, the virus causes a painful rash in one area of the skin. But in this rare case, it affects nerves near the ear and face.

## Symptoms

You may have:

- Severe pain in the ear
- Blisters in the ear or on the outer ear
- Weakness or paralysis on one side of the face (this can look like Bell palsy)
- Dizziness that lasts days or weeks
- Hearing loss (this may get better, stay the same, or get worse)

Blisters appear where the facial nerve sends feeling to the ear and outer ear. Headaches, confusion, or stiff neck are rare. Sometimes other nerves in the head are affected.

## Diagnosis

Doctors will look at your symptoms and exam results. They may take a sample from a blister to test for the virus. An MRI scan may be done to rule out other causes.

## Treatment

There is no proven cure, but these treatments may help:

- **Antiviral medicine** – Taken by mouth for 10 days. Examples: acyclovir or valacyclovir. These are often used in people with weak immune systems.
- **Steroid medicine** – Like prednisone. Start with 60 milligrams once a day for 4 to 7 days. Then slowly lower the dose over 2 weeks.
- **Surgery** – Only if the face is completely paralyzed and surgery is done within 2 weeks of the start. Before surgery, a test checks how much nerve function is lost. If the nerve signal drops by more than 90%, surgery may be an option.

For dizziness, medicine like diazepam can help. It is taken by mouth every 4 to 6 hours.

For pain, stronger pain medicine may be needed.

For long-term nerve pain after the rash heals (called postherpetic neuralgia), medicines like amitriptyline, nortriptyline, gabapentin, or pregabalin may help.

There is no strong proof that these treatments work. But they are the only options that might help. Doctors use them based on experience and possible benefit.

# Psoriatic Arthritis

Psoriatic arthritis is a type of joint problem that happens in some people who have psoriasis.  
Psoriasis is a skin condition that causes red, scaly rashes and thick, pitted nails.  

- Some people with psoriasis get joint pain and swelling.  
- The joints most often affected are in the fingers, toes, knees, hips, and spine.  
- Doctors diagnose psoriatic arthritis based on symptoms.  
- There is no single test to confirm the condition.  

## What Causes Psoriatic Arthritis?

The exact cause is not known.  
But some people are more likely to get it if they have a certain gene called HLA-B27.  
Having a family member with psoriasis also increases the risk.  

## Symptoms of Psoriatic Arthritis

- Inflammation often starts in the joints closest to the tips of the fingers and toes.  
- Other joints like the knees, hips, and spine can also be affected.  
- The upper body joints are often more involved than the lower ones.  
- Back pain can happen.  

- Swelling and joint changes can happen if inflammation lasts a long time.  
- The joint problems usually affect one side of the body more than the other.  
- Fewer joints are usually involved than in rheumatoid arthritis.  
- Tendons or ligaments where they attach to bones can become inflamed. This is called enthesitis.  
- Some people also have fibromyalgia. This causes muscle pain, joint stiffness, and tiredness.  

- The skin rash of psoriasis can appear before joint pain or after.  
- Sometimes the rash is hidden, like in the scalp, belly button, or skin folds.  
- The skin and joint symptoms may come and go together.  
- Sometimes the skin is worse. Sometimes the joints are worse.

## How Is Psoriatic Arthritis Diagnosed?

Doctors look for joint swelling and skin changes.  
They ask about your family history of psoriasis.  

- There is no test that can confirm psoriatic arthritis.  
- Blood tests check for a marker called rheumatoid factor. This helps rule out rheumatoid arthritis.  
- X-rays show how much joint damage has happened.  

## How Is Psoriatic Arthritis Treated?

The goal is to reduce skin rash and ease joint pain and swelling.  

### Medicines That Help

- **Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)**: These reduce pain and swelling.  
- **Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs)**: These slow down joint damage. Methotrexate is a common one.  
- **Cyclosporine**: This is a medicine that lowers the body’s immune response.  
- **Apremilast**: This is a pill that helps with both skin and joint symptoms.  
- **Biologic agents**: These are made from living materials. They target parts of the immune system that cause inflammation.  

#### Types of Biologic Agents

- **Tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors**: These include adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, certolizumab pegol, golimumab, and guselkumab. They are given by injection or infusion.  
- **Ustekinumab, secukinumab, and ixekizumab**: These are given by injection.  
- **Abatacept**: This is given by injection or infusion.  

TNF inhibitors are especially helpful for psoriatic arthritis.  

## What Is the Outlook?

- Psoriatic arthritis usually affects fewer joints than rheumatoid arthritis.  
- This means the outlook is often better than for rheumatoid arthritis.  
- But joint damage can still be serious if not treated.

# Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)

Polycystic ovary syndrome is a common condition in women. It affects how the ovaries work and causes hormone imbalances. It can lead to problems with periods, fertility, and other health issues.

PCOS affects 5 to 10 out of every 100 women. In the United States, it is the most common cause of infertility in women.

## What Is PCOS?

PCOS is diagnosed when a woman has at least two of these three signs:

- Irregular or missing periods (not ovulating regularly)
- High levels of male hormones (androgens), which can cause extra body hair or acne
- Ovaries that look full of small fluid-filled sacs (called cysts) on an ultrasound

Not all women with PCOS have cysts. And having cysts alone does not mean you have PCOS.

Many women with PCOS also have insulin resistance or are overweight. But some women with PCOS are not overweight.

## What Causes PCOS?

The exact cause of PCOS is not fully known. But research shows that:

- The body may make too much male hormone.
- Genes may play a role in how the body makes male hormones.
- Diet, lifestyle, and environmental factors may also affect the condition.
- Some women from certain racial or ethnic groups may have more metabolic or mental health issues linked to PCOS.

Hormones that control metabolism and reproduction are often out of balance. This can lead to:

- Insulin resistance
- Weight gain
- Type 2 diabetes
- High blood pressure
- High cholesterol
- Heart disease
- Infertility
- Irregular periods

The ovaries in PCOS often have many small cysts. These cysts are fluid-filled sacs that form around immature eggs. The ovaries may be larger than normal or have a thick outer layer.

## Health Risks of PCOS

PCOS can lead to serious health problems over time. These include:

- **Infertility** – because the ovaries do not release eggs regularly.
- **Endometrial cancer** – because the lining of the uterus builds up without being shed. This happens when a woman does not ovulate often.
- **Hirsutism** – extra hair growth in a male pattern (face, chest, back, stomach).
- **Insulin resistance** – the body does not use insulin well. This raises the risk of type 2 diabetes.
- **Obesity** – more common in women with PCOS, but it can also happen in women with normal weight.
- **Heart disease** – including high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and hardening of the arteries.
- **Metabolic syndrome** – a group of conditions that raise the risk of heart disease and diabetes.
- **Sleep apnea** – a condition where breathing stops during sleep.
- **Fatty liver disease** – fat builds up in the liver, even without alcohol use.
- **Mental health issues** – such as depression, anxiety, low self-esteem, and poor body image.

Women with PCOS are more likely to have early signs of heart disease. This includes calcium buildup in heart arteries and thickening of neck blood vessels.

## Symptoms of PCOS

Symptoms usually start during the teenage years. They often get worse over time.

Common symptoms include:

- Irregular or missing periods
- Trouble getting pregnant
- Mild weight gain or normal weight (some women are even underweight)
- Extra body hair in a male pattern (face, chin, chest, back, stomach, around the nipples)
- Acne
- Dark, thick skin in body folds (underarms, neck, elbows, knuckles) – this is a sign of insulin resistance

Some women may have more severe symptoms, such as:

- A deeper voice
- A larger clitoris
- Hair loss on the scalp (male pattern baldness)
- Less breast tissue

These signs suggest a more serious hormone problem and need further testing.

## How Is PCOS Diagnosed?

There is no single test for PCOS. Doctors use a combination of:

- A medical history and physical exam
- Blood tests
- An ultrasound

### Blood Tests

These tests check hormone levels and rule out other conditions:

- Testosterone – may be slightly high in PCOS
- Free testosterone – more sensitive, but harder to measure
- Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
- Prolactin
- Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
- Cortisol – to rule out Cushing syndrome
- 17-hydroxyprogesterone – to check for adrenal problems
- DHEAS – to check for adrenal tumors

A pregnancy test is also done to rule out pregnancy.

### Ultrasound

A transvaginal ultrasound checks the ovaries. It looks for:

- 12 or more small cysts in each ovary (2 to 9 mm in size)
- Ovarian volume over 10 milliliters

This test is not used in teenage girls unless needed.

### Diagnosis Criteria

Doctors use the Rotterdam criteria. You need at least two of these three:

1. Irregular or no periods (oligo-ovulation or anovulation)
2. Signs of high male hormones (hirsutism or high blood levels)
3. Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound

## Treatment for PCOS

Treatment depends on your symptoms, health goals, and whether you want to get pregnant.

### Goals of Treatment

- Reduce long-term health risks
- Improve symptoms
- Help with fertility if needed

### Hormonal Treatments

If you do not want to get pregnant, hormonal birth control is often the first choice. This includes:

- Combined pills (estrogen and progestin)
- Progestin-only pills
- A progestin-only IUD (like levonorgestrel)
- Other progestin medicines (like medroxyprogesterone)

These help:

- Make periods regular
- Lower male hormone levels
- Reduce acne and extra hair
- Protect the lining of the uterus from overgrowth

They also prevent pregnancy.

Some progestins (like drosperinone and dienogest) also help reduce male hormone effects.

### Managing Insulin Resistance

If you are overweight or have insulin resistance, lifestyle changes are key:

- Eat healthy foods
- Exercise regularly
- Lose weight if needed

Even a 5% to 10% weight loss can improve symptoms and help with ovulation.

If lifestyle changes are not enough, your doctor may prescribe:

- **Metformin** – a medicine that helps the body use insulin better. It is taken twice a day, starting at 500 mg.

Metformin helps:

- Lower blood sugar
- Improve insulin sensitivity
- Make periods more regular

But it does not help much with acne or extra hair. It may help with fertility in some women.

If you take metformin, your doctor will check your kidney and liver function and blood sugar levels regularly.

Metformin can cause ovulation. So you need to use birth control if you do not want to get pregnant.

### Newer Treatments Being Studied

- **Semaglutide** – a medicine used for weight loss and diabetes. In small studies, it helped women with PCOS lose weight and get regular periods.
- **Other insulin-sensitizing drugs** – like GLP-1 receptor agonists and thiazolidinediones – are being tested.
- **Gut bacteria treatments** – researchers are studying if changes in gut health can help PCOS.

### Fertility Treatment

If you want to get pregnant and are having trouble, see a fertility specialist. Treatments may include:

- Medicines to help the ovaries release eggs
- In vitro fertilization (IVF)

## When to See a Doctor

See your doctor if you have:

- Irregular or missing periods
- Excess body hair
- Acne that does not go away
- Trouble getting pregnant
- Weight gain that is hard to control
- Mood changes, fatigue, or sleep problems

## Key Points

- PCOS is common and often starts in the teens.
- It causes irregular periods, hormone imbalances, and fertility problems.
- Not all women with PCOS are overweight. Some are underweight.
- PCOS raises the risk of diabetes, heart disease, and endometrial cancer.
- Hormonal birth control helps many women manage symptoms and protect the uterus.
- Lifestyle changes (diet, exercise, weight loss) are important for all women with PCOS.
- Metformin can help with insulin resistance and regular periods.
- If you want to get pregnant, talk to a fertility specialist.
- Screen for mental health issues, sleep apnea, diabetes, and heart disease.

# Salivary Gland Problems

Your salivary glands make saliva. Saliva helps you chew and swallow food. It also has natural chemicals that help break down food.

- The glands can stop working properly.
- They can get infected.
- They can become blocked by small stones.
- When blocked, saliva builds up and causes pain.

If the glands do not make enough saliva, your mouth feels dry. This can lead to tooth decay.  
If the glands are blocked or infected, you may feel pain.  
Doctors can check how much saliva you make. They may also take a small sample of gland tissue to test.

Sometimes doctors can remove blockages. Some people need to use artificial saliva.

(See also: Dry Mouth)

---

## The Main Salivary Glands

There are three main pairs of salivary glands in your mouth:

- **Parotid glands**: These are the largest. They sit just behind your jaw, below and in front of your ears.
- **Sublingual glands**: These lie under the side of your tongue.
- **Submandibular glands**: These are under the side of your jaw.

In addition, many small glands are spread throughout your mouth. All of them make saliva. Saliva helps you digest food.

---
