| --- |

---

## Types of Salivary Gland Problems

- Glands not working right
- Salivary stones
- Infections
- Swelling

---

### Glands Not Working Right

This problem is more common in adults. It means the glands make too little saliva.  
When there is not enough saliva, your mouth feels dry. This is called dry mouth.

Some things that can cause dry mouth:

- Diseases like Sjögren syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, and lupus
- Infections like HIV
- Certain medicines: some antidepressants, antihistamines, antipsychotic drugs, Parkinson’s medicines, sleeping pills, methyldopa, diuretics, and methamphetamine
- Cancer treatments like chemotherapy or radiation to the head and neck
- Radioactive iodine treatment for thyroid cancer

Dry mouth from radiation is often permanent, especially if the dose is high.  
Dry mouth from chemotherapy usually goes away after treatment ends.

But not all dry mouth comes from gland problems. Other causes include:

- Not drinking enough water
- Breathing through your mouth
- Feeling anxious or stressed
- Getting older

As you age, your mouth may feel drier. But this is usually because of medicine, not age itself.

Saliva protects your teeth. Without enough saliva, you get more cavities—especially on the roots of your teeth.  
Severe dry mouth can make it hard to speak, chew, or swallow.  
It can also make dentures uncomfortable.

In rare cases, the glands make too much saliva. This usually happens only for a short time. It often happens when you eat sour foods. Just thinking about sour food can cause extra saliva.

---

### Salivary Stones

Stones can form from minerals in your saliva.  
They are more likely if you are dehydrated or take medicines that reduce saliva.  
People with gout are also more likely to get stones.  
Stones are most common in adults. Some people get more than one.

Stones block the tube (duct) that carries saliva from the gland to your mouth.  
When the duct is blocked, saliva backs up. This causes pain and swelling in the gland.

A blocked duct and trapped saliva can become infected with bacteria.

Common signs of a blocked duct:

- Swelling and pain over the affected gland
- Pain gets worse after eating, especially sour foods like lemons or pickles
- The swelling may go down after a few hours
- A sudden rush of saliva may come out
- Some stones cause no symptoms at all

---

### Infections in the Salivary Glands

An infection in a salivary gland is called sialadenitis.

Most infections happen when saliva flow is blocked or very low.  
The parotid gland is most often affected.

Infections are more common in:

- People in their 50s and 60s
- People with long-term health problems and dry mouth
- People with Sjögren syndrome
- Teenagers and young adults with anorexia
- Children aged 1 to 18 with repeated parotid gland infections with no clear cause
- People who had radiation to the mouth or radioactive iodine for thyroid cancer

Mumps is a viral infection that causes painful swelling of the salivary glands, usually the parotid gland.  
It can also affect other parts of the body.  
Mumps mostly happens in people who have not had the mumps vaccine.

In teens and young adults with anorexia, the most common bacteria is *Staphylococcus aureus*.

Some infections are caused by HIV or cat-scratch disease.

Symptoms of a bacterial infection:

- Fever and chills
- Pain and swelling on one side of the face
- Red, swollen skin over the gland
- A pus-filled lump (abscess) may form
- A small amount of pus may come out of the gland’s duct

---

### Swelling in the Salivary Glands

Swelling can be caused by:

- Mumps in children
- Bacterial infections in the tonsils or teeth
- Diseases more common in adults, such as AIDS, Sjögren syndrome, diabetes, sarcoidosis, and bulimia

Swelling can also come from tumors—either cancerous or noncancerous.

- Tumors that are cancerous feel hard and may stick to nearby tissues.
- Noncancerous tumors are usually soft and can move around.

An injury to the lower lip—like biting it by accident—can damage small glands in that area.  
This can block saliva flow.  
The gland may swell and form a small, soft, bluish lump called a mucocele.  
This lump usually goes away on its own in a few weeks to months.

---

### Spotlight on Aging: Dry Mouth

Many older people have dry mouth.  
Aging itself has only a small effect on mouth moisture.  
But older people are more likely to have health problems that cause dry mouth.  
They are also more likely to take medicines that dry the mouth.

For some, dry mouth is just a small annoyance.  
For others, it causes ongoing problems.  
It can make it hard to taste food, chew, swallow, speak, or wear dentures.

Dry mouth increases your risk of tooth decay and gum disease.  
Persistent dry mouth is usually a sign of another health issue or a side effect of medicine.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Salivary Gland Problems

Doctors use several methods:

- Biopsy: A small sample of gland tissue is taken and checked under a microscope.
- Endoscopy: A tiny camera is used to look inside the ducts.
- Imaging tests: Like CT scans or ultrasounds.
- Pus culture: If infection is suspected, doctors may collect pus from the duct and test it in a lab.

There is no perfect test to measure how much saliva you make.  
But doctors can gently press on the glands to see if saliva comes out.  
They may also ask you to eat something sour, like lemon juice, to see if saliva flows.

If swelling happens after eating, it may mean a stone is blocking the duct.  
If the sour food helps reduce the pain, a stone is likely.

If the cause is not clear, a biopsy or imaging test may be needed.

---

## How Doctors Treat Salivary Gland Problems

### For Dry Mouth

- Avoid medicines that reduce saliva
- Drink water often throughout the day
- Brush and floss your teeth every day
- Use fluoride mouthwash
- Visit your dentist every 3 to 4 months
- Use artificial saliva (like a mouthwash with carboxymethylcellulose)
- Chew sugarless gum or suck on xylitol lozenges
- Some dentists recommend wearing a plastic mouth guard with fluoride gel at night to protect teeth
- Medicines like cevimeline or pilocarpine can help some people make more saliva
- These medicines do not work well if the glands were damaged by radiation

### For Salivary Stones

- Take pain relievers
- Drink extra fluids
- Gently massage the gland
- Use warm compresses
- Stimulate saliva with lemon juice, sour candy, or hard candy
- A dentist may push the stone out by pressing on both sides of the duct
- If that does not work, a thin tool can be used to pull the stone out
- As a last option, surgery or endoscopy may be needed

### For Infections

- Take antibiotics
- Massage the gland
- Use warm compresses
- Stay well hydrated
- Chew sour candy or suck on hard candy to stimulate saliva
- Keep your mouth clean
- If an abscess forms, it must be cut open and drained

### For Swelling

Treatment depends on the cause.

- A mucocele that does not go away can be removed with surgery if it bothers you
- Both noncancerous and cancerous tumors can usually be removed with surgery

# Sports-Related Concussion

Concussions happen when the head gets hit during sports.  
They are a type of mild brain injury.  
You can get a concussion even if you do not lose consciousness.  

## What Are the Symptoms?

The most serious sign is losing consciousness.  
But many people do not pass out.  
Instead, they may show other signs, such as:  

- Feeling dazed or confused  
- Not knowing who is playing or what the score is  
- Answering questions slowly  
- Forgetting plays or assignments  
- Not remembering events before the injury (retrograde amnesia)  
- Not remembering events after the injury (anterograde amnesia)  
- Seeing double or being bothered by light  
- Feeling dizzy or unsteady  
- Having trouble walking or moving smoothly  
- Getting a headache  
- Feeling sick to your stomach or throwing up  
- Hearing ringing in the ears (tinnitus)  
- Losing your sense of smell or taste  

Some people have symptoms that last for days or weeks after the injury.  
These are called postconcussive symptoms.  
They can include:  

- Ongoing headaches  
- Trouble remembering things  
- Hard time focusing  
- Feeling tired all the time  
- Trouble sleeping  
- Mood changes like being irritable or moody  
- Being bothered by bright lights or loud noises  

Most people feel better within a few weeks to a few months.  

> **Important:** You can have a concussion even if you did not lose consciousness.

## How Is a Concussion Diagnosed?

A doctor checks you for signs of a concussion.  
This is done through a physical exam and questions about your symptoms.  

Brain scans like CT scans or MRIs are not needed for most concussions.  
This is because concussions do not usually cause visible damage to the brain.  
But a scan may be done if the doctor suspects a more serious brain injury.  

A scan is usually done if you have:  

- Lost consciousness  
- A low score on the Glasgow Coma Scale (a test of alertness)  
- Weakness or numbness on one side of the body  
- Confusion that does not improve  
- Any worsening signs  

Tools like the SCAT5 (Sports Concussion Assessment Tool, 5th edition) help coaches and trainers check athletes on the spot.  
These tools are part of the CDC "Heads Up" program, which teaches how to spot, respond to, and prevent concussions.  

Some sports teams do brain function tests before the season starts.  
They repeat the test after a concussion.  
This helps track recovery and decide when it is safe to return to play.

## How Is a Concussion Treated?

If you have any concussion symptoms, stop playing right away.  
Do not return to sports the same day.  

Rest is the most important treatment.  
Avoid:  

- Schoolwork or job tasks that require focus  
- Driving  
- Alcohol  
- Using computers, phones, or watching TV  
- Video games  
- Physical activity  

These things can make symptoms worse or last longer.  

For headaches, you can take acetaminophen.  
You can also use nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) if needed.  
But no medicine has been proven to speed up recovery.  

Family members should watch for warning signs.  
Take the person to the hospital if they show any of these:  

- Getting drowsy or hard to wake up  
- Weakness or numbness on one side of the body  
- Headache that gets worse  
- Vomiting more than once  
- Confusion or not recognizing people  
- Strange or unusual behavior  
- Seizures  

## What Is the Outlook?

Most people recover fully from a concussion.  
Some may have symptoms for several months.  

In rare cases, repeated head injuries can lead to a serious brain disease called chronic traumatic encephalopathy.  
This condition slowly gets worse over time.  
It can lead to death 10 to 15 years after symptoms start.

## Key Points

- A concussion is a temporary brain injury from a head blow.  
- You may lose consciousness, but many people only feel confused, forgetful, or unsteady.  
- Symptoms can go away quickly or last for weeks.  
- Anyone with concussion symptoms should stop playing and be checked by a trained doctor.  
- Tools like SCAT5 can help spot symptoms on the field.  
- Brain scans are only used if there are signs of a more serious injury.  
- After a concussion, you are more likely to get another one.  
- Do not return to sports until you have had no symptoms for at least one week.  
- Start physical activity slowly and build up over time.

# Shoulder Injury: Rotator Cuff and Bursa Problems

The muscles that hold your upper arm in the shoulder joint are called the rotator cuff. These muscles can get squeezed, become inflamed, or even tear.

This can happen from doing the same arm movements over and over. It can also happen from a sudden injury.

## What Causes This Problem?

- Repeating arm movements above your head can cause the rotator cuff to get pinched.
- This pinching can lead to swelling and pain.
- If you keep doing the same movements, the tendon can weaken and tear.
- A hard pull, stretch, or fall can also cause a sudden tear.

Sports that involve lifting arms over the head often lead to this problem. Examples include:
- Throwing a baseball
- Lifting heavy things over your shoulder
- Serving a tennis ball
- Swimming freestyle, butterfly, or backstroke

## What Are the Symptoms?

- Your shoulder hurts when you raise your arm above your head.
- The pain gets worse when your arm is at a 60 to 120 degree angle from your side.
- Later, the pain may happen even when you are not moving your arm.
- You may feel pain at night, especially when lying on the injured side.
- You may not be able to turn your arm outward normally if the tendon is torn.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and examine your shoulder.  
They may order an MRI scan to check for a tear in the rotator cuff.

## How Is It Treated?

### Rest
- Wear a sling for a few days if the pain is bad.
- Avoid lifting your arm above shoulder level.
- Avoid pushing or pulling with your arm.

### Exercise
- Start gentle exercises once the pain is gone when moving your arm.
- These exercises help strengthen the rotator cuff muscles.
- Stronger muscles help keep the shoulder balanced and reduce pinching.

### Medicine
- Your doctor may give you medicine to reduce swelling and pain.
- In some cases, a shot of medicine into the space above the rotator cuff (called the bursa) can help.

### Surgery
- Surgery may be needed if the rotator cuff is torn.
- Surgery can remove extra bone to make more room for the rotator cuff.
- This helps prevent pinching when you raise your arm.
- If the tendon is torn, surgery is usually the best option to fix it.

## Key Points

- Pain when raising your arm is a sign of a rotator cuff problem.
- Rest and exercise are often enough to heal mild cases.
- Severe pain or a tear may need surgery.
- Early treatment helps prevent long-term problems.

# Scrub Typhus

Scrub typhus is a disease caused by a type of bacteria called *Orientia tsutsugamushi*.  
It is spread by tiny mites known as chiggers.  
The disease is most common in parts of Asia and the Pacific region.

## What Causes Scrub Typhus?

The bacteria that cause scrub typhus live in small mites.  
These mites are called chiggers.  
They feed on wild animals like rats, voles, and field mice.  
When a chigger bites a person, it can pass the bacteria to them.  
The mites are both the carrier and the natural home of the bacteria.

Scrub typhus is found in a large area of Asia and the Pacific.  
This includes Japan, Korea, China, India, and northern Australia.

## Symptoms of Scrub Typhus

Symptoms usually start 6 to 21 days after being bitten.  
Most people feel sick suddenly.  
The first signs are fever, chills, and a severe headache.  
Swollen lymph nodes all over the body may also appear.

A dark, scabbed sore called an eschar often forms at the site of the bite.  
This sore starts as a red, hard bump about the size of a dime.  
It may blister, break open, and then form a black scab.  
Not all people get this sore.  
It is easier to see on light skin.

The fever usually rises to 40 to 40.5 degrees Celsius in the first week.  
The eyes may become red and watery.  
A rash appears on the chest and belly between the 5th and 8th day of fever.  
It can spread to the arms and legs.  
The rash may fade quickly or turn into raised, dark spots.

A cough is common in the first week.  
Some people develop lung problems in the second week.

In serious cases, the heart rate increases.  
Blood pressure drops.  
Confusion, drowsiness, or muscle twitching may occur.  
The spleen may become enlarged.  
Heart problems are more common with scrub typhus than with other similar diseases.

Without treatment, high fever can last two weeks or more.  
Then it slowly goes down.  
With treatment, fever usually drops within 36 hours.  
Most people recover quickly and fully.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your symptoms and medical history.  
They check your skin and lymph nodes.  
A small sample of the rash may be taken for testing.  
This test uses a special dye to find the bacteria.

Blood tests can help confirm the disease.  
But they are not useful right away.  
They are best done during recovery.  
A PCR test can detect the bacteria in the blood early in the illness.

Symptoms of scrub typhus are similar to those of other tick-borne diseases.  
But scrub typhus happens only in certain parts of Asia and the Pacific.  
An eschar with swollen nearby lymph nodes is a strong clue.

## How Is It Treated?

Antibiotics work best when started early.  
The main treatment is doxycycline.  
Take it until you feel better, have no fever for 48 hours, and have taken the medicine for at least 7 days.

Doxycycline is safe for children over 8 years old.  
For children under 8, the risk of tooth staining is low with short courses.  
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says it is safe to use for 5 days in mild cases and 10 days in high-risk cases.  
Research shows short courses do not harm tooth development.

Pregnant women can take trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.  
But only before 32 weeks of pregnancy.  
After 32 weeks, this medicine is not recommended.

For pregnant women or people allergic to doxycycline, azithromycin is a safe and effective option.

Chloramphenicol is another treatment.  
But it is not available in the United States.  
It can cause serious blood problems.  
If used, blood tests must be done regularly.

## How to Prevent Scrub Typhus

Clearing brush and trees helps reduce mite numbers.  
Spraying infested areas with long-lasting insecticides can also help.  
Use insect repellent like DEET when you are in areas where mites are common.

## Key Facts

- Scrub typhus is common in parts of Asia and the Pacific.  
- It is spread by chiggers, which are tiny mite larvae.  
- Symptoms start suddenly with fever, chills, severe headache, and swollen lymph nodes.  
- A dark scab may form at the bite site.  
- A rash appears and spreads over the body.  
- Doxycycline is the best treatment.  
- It works fast, even in severe cases.

# What Are Peripheral Artery Disorders?

Peripheral artery disorders mean that blood flow to the arms, legs, or trunk is not as good as it should be.

Most of the time, doctors use the term "peripheral artery disease" to talk about poor blood flow in the legs. This is usually caused by a condition called atherosclerosis. But these disorders can also affect the arms. They can have other causes too.

Problems with blood flow to the brain are called cerebrovascular disease.  
Problems with blood flow in the belly area are called abdominal aortic branch occlusion.

## How Blood Vessels Work

Blood vessels carry blood from the heart to the rest of the body.  
They can widen or narrow to control blood flow.  
This helps the body respond to changes like cold or exercise.

---

## What Causes Peripheral Artery Disease?

There are two main types: occlusive and functional.

### Occlusive Peripheral Artery Disease

This happens when something physically blocks or narrows the arteries.

The most common cause is atherosclerosis.  
Atherosclerosis means plaque builds up inside the artery walls.  
Plaque is made of cholesterol, fat, and a protein that helps blood clot.  
Over time, plaque makes the arteries narrower. This slows blood flow.

Another cause is fibromuscular dysplasia.  
This is a condition where the cells in the artery wall grow abnormally.  
It is not caused by plaque buildup.

### Functional Peripheral Artery Disease

This happens when the arteries do not work properly.  
They may narrow too much or not open enough.

Normally, arteries in the arms and legs open wider or get smaller.  
This helps control blood flow based on the body’s needs.  
For example, they open wider when you are warm or active.

In functional disease, the normal process goes wrong.  
The arteries may tighten too much or too often.  
Sometimes, the muscles in the artery walls suddenly contract.  
This is called a spasm.  
The spasm makes the artery narrow quickly.  
This cuts off blood flow for a short time.

In rare cases, the muscles in the artery walls do not tighten enough.  
This causes the arteries to open too wide.  
This can also affect blood flow.

Causes of this type include:

- A genetic problem in the blood vessels  
- Nerve problems that control artery size (especially the sympathetic nervous system)  
- Injuries  
- Certain medicines

Examples of functional peripheral artery disease are:

- Acrocyanosis  
- Erythromelalgia  
- Raynaud syndrome

# Trisomy 13

Trisomy 13 is a serious condition. It happens when a baby has an extra chromosome 13. This extra chromosome causes major problems in the baby’s body and brain.

The condition leads to:
- Severe learning and thinking problems.
- Heart problems.
- Problems with the shape of the face and eyes.
- A small size at birth.

Most babies with this condition do not live past the first few weeks of life. But some babies do survive longer, especially if they get certain medical treatments.

Trisomy 13 is also called Patau syndrome.

## How Common Is Trisomy 13?

Trisomy 13 happens in about 1 out of every 6,000 babies. This number comes from data on pregnancies that ended in miscarriage, stillbirth, or live birth.

About 80% of cases are due to a full extra chromosome 13. The extra chromosome usually comes from the mother. Older mothers have a higher chance of having a baby with this condition.

In most cases, the extra chromosome comes from a mistake during egg formation. But in rare cases, part of chromosome 13 can attach to another chromosome.

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

Babies with trisomy 13 are often smaller than expected for their stage of pregnancy.

They often have problems in the middle of the face and head. These include:
- A brain that did not split into two sides properly.
- A cleft lip or cleft palate.
- Small eyes or missing parts of the eye.
- A gap in the iris or retina.

The eyebrows are flat. The eyes often slant upward.

The ears are shaped differently and sit lower than normal. Many babies have hearing problems.

Some babies are born with holes in the scalp or small skin tunnels on the back of the head. Loose skin often hangs at the back of the neck.

The hands and fingers may look unusual. These include:
- A single crease across the palm.
- Extra fingers or toes.
- Fingernails that are curved and narrow.

About 6 out of 10 babies have serious heart problems. Some hearts are on the wrong side of the chest.

The genitals may not form normally. In boys, one or both testicles may not have dropped into the scrotum. In girls, the uterus may be shaped like a heart.

Babies often have breathing problems in the first weeks of life. They may stop breathing for short periods.

All babies with trisomy 13 have severe learning and thinking problems.

## How Is Trisomy 13 Diagnosed?

Doctors can suspect trisomy 13 before birth. This can happen if:
- An ultrasound shows growth problems or unusual body parts.
- A blood test on the mother shows a higher risk.

A test called noninvasive prenatal screening can also suggest a problem. It uses a blood sample from the mother to check for signs of chromosome issues.

But this test is not a final answer. It only shows a risk. A follow-up test is needed to confirm.

To confirm the diagnosis, doctors take a sample of tissue from the placenta (chorionic villus sampling) or amniotic fluid (amniocentesis). They then test the chromosomes in the lab.

After birth, a blood sample from the baby is tested to confirm the condition.

## How Is Trisomy 13 Treated?

There is no cure for trisomy 13. The extra chromosome cannot be removed.

But doctors can help with care and comfort. This is called supportive care.

In some cases, families and doctors may choose to offer:
- Breathing support with a machine.
- Feeding support through a tube.
- Surgery for heart problems, cleft palate, or feeding tubes.

These choices depend on the baby’s condition and what the family wants.

Most care focuses on making the baby as comfortable as possible. The goal is to improve the quality of life for the baby and the family.

Support for parents and caregivers is very important.

## What Is the Outlook?

Most babies with trisomy 13 do not live past the first few weeks of life.

About 1 in 10 babies live past their first birthday. Survival has improved over time, especially for babies who have surgery for heart or other problems.

# Chronic Pancreatitis

Chronic pancreatitis is a long-term condition where the pancreas becomes inflamed and damaged over time. This damage does not heal. The pancreas loses its ability to work properly.

## What Is the Pancreas?

The pancreas is a small organ in the upper part of your belly. It helps your body digest food and control blood sugar.

- It makes insulin, a hormone that helps control blood sugar.
- It makes digestive juices that flow into the first part of the small intestine (called the duodenum).
- These digestive juices contain enzymes that break down food.

## Acute vs. Chronic Pancreatitis

- **Acute pancreatitis** comes on quickly and usually gets better in a few days or weeks.
- **Chronic pancreatitis** lasts a long time. The inflammation slowly damages the pancreas. Over time, the pancreas becomes scarred and stops working well.

The scarring in the pancreas is a key sign of chronic pancreatitis. As the disease gets worse, the cells that make digestive enzymes are destroyed.

## Causes of Chronic Pancreatitis

In the United States, the most common causes are:

- Drinking too much alcohol over many years.
- Smoking cigarettes.

Other causes include:

- Certain inherited conditions, such as cystic fibrosis or hereditary pancreatitis.
- Autoimmune pancreatitis (when the body’s immune system attacks the pancreas).
- A very bad case of acute pancreatitis that leaves lasting damage.
- Blockage of the pancreatic duct by stones or a tumor.

In some people, doctors cannot find a clear cause. This is called idiopathic pancreatitis.

In some tropical countries (like India, Indonesia, and Nigeria), children and young adults can get chronic pancreatitis with no known cause. This is called tropical pancreatitis.

## Symptoms of Chronic Pancreatitis

### Abdominal Pain

- Pain in the upper belly is the main symptom.
- The pain can be mild or severe.
- It may come and go, or it may be constant.
- It often gets worse after eating.
- Sitting up or leaning forward may help ease the pain.
- Over time, the pain may become steady and less intense.

Later in the disease, the pain may go away. This happens because the pancreas can no longer make digestive enzymes.

### Poor Digestion (Pancreatic Insufficiency)

- The pancreas makes fewer digestive enzymes.
- Food is not broken down well.
- This leads to poor absorption of nutrients (malabsorption).
- Stools become large, greasy, and smell very bad (called steatorrhea).
- Stools may be light in color and may have oil droplets.
- The body does not get enough nutrients.
- This can lead to weight loss, poor health, and vitamin deficiencies.

### Other Problems

- A fluid-filled sac called a pseudocyst can form in the pancreas.
  - It can bleed or burst.
  - If it grows, it can cause pain or block the small intestine or bile duct.
- Over time, the cells that make insulin may be destroyed.
  - This can lead to diabetes.
- People with chronic pancreatitis have a higher risk of getting pancreatic cancer.

## How Is Chronic Pancreatitis Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tools to diagnose chronic pancreatitis:

### Imaging Tests

- **X-rays of the belly**: Can show calcium deposits in the pancreas.
- **CT scan**: Shows changes in the pancreas and checks for complications like pseudocysts.
- **MRI scan**: A special type called MRCP gives a clearer picture of the bile and pancreatic ducts.
- **Endoscopic ultrasound**: A thin tube with a camera and ultrasound probe is passed through the mouth into the stomach and small intestine. It helps find problems in the pancreas and ducts.
- **ERCP**: A thin tube is passed through the mouth into the small intestine. A dye is injected to see the ducts. Doctors can also use tools through the tube to remove stones or place a tube (stent) to open a blocked duct.

### Pancreatic Function Tests

- Stool tests check for fat or a digestive enzyme called elastase.
  - Low levels of elastase mean the pancreas is not working well.
- Blood tests may show:
  - High levels of certain enzymes (amylase and lipase), though this is less helpful than in acute pancreatitis.
  - High blood sugar, which may mean diabetes is developing.

### When Cancer Is Suspected

If symptoms get worse or the duct narrows, doctors may suspect pancreatic cancer. They may order:
- Blood tests
- MRI scan
- CT scan
- Endoscopic ultrasound

## Treatment of Chronic Pancreatitis

Treatment focuses on relieving pain, improving digestion, and managing complications.

### Stop Alcohol and Smoking

- Everyone with chronic pancreatitis should stop drinking alcohol and stop smoking.
- This is true even if alcohol was not the original cause.

### Pain Relief

- Pain is the hardest part to treat.
- Eating small meals (4 to 5 per day) that are low in fat may help reduce pain.
- Opioid painkillers may be needed, but they can lead to addiction if used too long.
- Doctors may also prescribe:
  - Tricyclic antidepressants
  - Gabapentin
  - Pregabalin
  - SSRIs (a type of antidepressant)
- These medicines may be used alone or with opioids.
- Results vary. Many people still have pain despite treatment.

### Autoimmune Pancreatitis

- If the cause is autoimmune, doctors may give corticosteroids.

### Endoscopic Treatments

- Doctors can use a scope to treat blockages in the ducts.
- They can drain a blocked duct or remove stones.
- Lithotripsy (shock waves) can break up large stones in the duct.

### Surgery

- Surgery may be an option if the duct is swollen or if there is a large mass in the pancreas.
- If the duct is swollen, a bypass can be made from the pancreas to the small intestine. This helps relieve pain in 70 to 80 out of 100 people.
- If the duct is not swollen, part of the pancreas may need to be removed.
  - Removing part of the pancreas also removes insulin-making cells.
  - This can lead to diabetes.
- Surgery is only done after the person has stopped drinking alcohol and can manage diabetes.

### Pseudocysts

- If a pseudocyst causes pain or grows too large, it may need to be drained.
- This can be done through the skin or using a scope.

### Pancreatic Enzyme Supplements

- These pills or capsules help break down food.
- They should be taken with every meal.
- They can make stools less greasy and help the body absorb food better.
- They may help with weight gain and fewer bowel movements.
- Some people also need to take acid-reducing medicines (like H2 blockers or proton pump inhibitors) with the enzymes.
- Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K) may also be needed as supplements.
- If symptoms do not improve, try eating even less fat.

### Managing Diabetes

- Pills that lower blood sugar usually do not work well for diabetes caused by chronic pancreatitis.
- Insulin is usually needed.
- But insulin can cause low blood sugar (hypoglycemia).
- This is because the pancreas also makes a hormone called glucagon, which helps balance insulin.
- Too much insulin can cause blood sugar to drop too low.
- Low blood sugar can lead to confusion, dizziness, or even a coma.

## Outlook

The long-term outcome varies. Some people live with mild symptoms. Others have severe pain and complications. Stopping alcohol and smoking can slow the disease. Early treatment helps prevent serious problems.

# Acute Necrotizing Ulcerative Gingivitis (ANUG)

This is a painful infection in the gums. It causes sharp pain, bleeding, and bad breath. Doctors diagnose it by looking at the mouth. Treatment includes cleaning the gums gently, better brushing and flossing, mouth rinses, and care to ease symptoms. If cleaning cannot happen right away, antibiotics may help.

## Who Gets ANUG?

ANUG is more common in people who smoke. It also affects those who are very tired, sick, or under a lot of stress. Other risk factors include:
- Not brushing or flossing well
- Not eating enough healthy food
- Having a weak immune system (like in HIV/AIDS or from certain medicines)
- Not getting enough sleep

Some people also have a yeast infection in the mouth called oral candidiasis. The main bacteria linked to ANUG are *Treponema*, *Selenomas*, *Bacteroides melaningenicus*, and *Fusobacterium*.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The problem often starts suddenly. You may feel tired or have a fever. The main signs are:
- Very sore gums that bleed easily
- More saliva than normal
- Very bad breath (sometimes so strong it is hard to stand)
- Open sores on the gums between the teeth and along the gum line
- The sores look like they were punched out with a hole in the middle
- A grayish film covers the sores
- Sores on the inside of the cheeks or tonsils are rare
- Swallowing or talking hurts
- Swollen glands in the neck

Sometimes there is no bad smell. The problem can also affect just one small area of the gums.

## How Is ANUG Diagnosed?

A doctor or dentist checks the mouth. If the gums do not improve with normal treatment, they may test the throat or do a blood test. This helps rule out other serious infections like diphtheria or a blood disorder.

## How Is ANUG Treated?

### Cleaning the Gums
A dentist gently removes dead tissue and plaque. This is done over several days. You can use a soft toothbrush or a clean washcloth to clean your teeth at home.

### Rinses
Rinse your mouth every hour with warm salt water. Or, rinse twice a day with:
- 1.5% hydrogen peroxide
- 0.12% chlorhexidine

Do this for the first few days after cleaning.

### Supportive Care
You must:
- Brush and floss gently at first
- Eat healthy foods
- Drink plenty of fluids
- Rest
- Take pain medicine if needed
- Avoid smoking, hot food, and spicy food

Most people feel much better within one to two days. Then, the cleaning can be finished.

### Antibiotics
If you cannot get cleaning right away, antibiotics can help. Use:
- Metronidazole 500 milligrams every 8 hours
- Amoxicillin 500 milligrams every 8 hours

Take the medicine for 72 hours after symptoms go away.

If you are very allergic to penicillin, use:
- Clindamycin 300 milligrams every 6 hours
- Erythromycin 250 milligrams every 6 hours
- Tetracycline 250 milligrams every 6 hours

### Yeast Infection in the Mouth
If you have a yeast infection in the mouth, it needs separate treatment. This is described in another guide.

### Surgery
If the gum shape changes and the tips of the gum between teeth are lost, surgery may be needed later. This helps prevent future gum disease.

# Opioids: Simple Explanation

Opioids are strong pain medicines. They come from the opium poppy plant. Some are made in labs. They are used to treat serious pain.

But opioids can be dangerous. They can make you feel very good. This can lead to misuse. Some people become dependent or addicted.

## What Are Opioids?

Opioids include:
- Codeine
- Oxycodone (sometimes with acetaminophen)
- Meperidine
- Morphine
- Pentazocine
- Hydromorphone
- Methadone (taken by mouth)
- Fentanyl (applied as a skin patch)

Heroin is also an opioid. It is illegal in the United States. But in some countries, it is used in medical treatment.

## Why Are Opioids Misused?

Opioids are widely available. They make people feel happy and relaxed. This makes them easy to misuse.

Most people who use opioids for short-term pain (like after an injury) do not become addicted.

But people who use opioids for long-term pain are more likely to develop a substance use disorder.

## Tolerance

After a few days of using opioids, your body may need more to feel the same effect. This is called tolerance.

Tolerance does not mean you are addicted. But it can make it harder to stop using the drug.

## Side Effects of Opioids

Opioids can cause:
- Drowsiness
- Feeling calm or happy (euphoria)
- Constipation
- Nausea or vomiting
- Flushed face
- Itching
- Confusion (especially in older adults)

Meperidine can cause seizures when it breaks down in the body.

Some opioids, when mixed with other drugs, can cause a serious condition called serotonin syndrome. Symptoms include:
- Confusion
- Shaking
- Muscle spasms
- Sweating
- High body temperature

Heroin users who inhale the drug may develop a rare brain condition. This can cause:
- Restlessness
- Lack of interest
- Poor balance
- Paralysis

This condition can get worse and may be deadly.

## Overdose: A Life-Threatening Emergency

Taking too much opioid can stop your breathing. This can lead to death.

In 2020, about 91,800 people died from opioid overdoses in the United States.

Signs of overdose:
- Breathing becomes very slow or stops
- Lungs fill with fluid
- Blood pressure drops
- Heart rate slows
- Pupils become very small (like pinpoints)
- Person becomes unconscious or dies

Mixing opioids with alcohol or other sedatives makes overdose more likely.

## Long-Term Problems

Opioids themselves do not cause many long-term health problems. But some people have:
- Chronic constipation
- Excessive sweating
- Sleepiness
- Lower sex drive

The biggest risks come from:
- Sharing needles
- Injecting unknown substances with opioids

## Withdrawal Symptoms

Stopping opioids after regular use can cause uncomfortable symptoms. But it is rarely life-threatening.

Symptoms can start as early as 4 hours after stopping. They peak in 2 to 3 days and usually go away in about a week.

Symptoms include:
- Anxiety
- Strong cravings
- Fast breathing
- Yawning
- Sweating
- Watery eyes
- Runny nose
- Dilated pupils
- Stomach cramps
- Restlessness
- Agitation
- High heart rate
- High blood pressure
- Goosebumps
- Shaking
- Muscle twitching
- Fever and chills
- Body aches
- Loss of appetite
- Nausea and vomiting
- Diarrhea

The more you used and the longer you used, the worse the symptoms.

## Opioids and Pregnancy

Using opioids during pregnancy is very serious.

Heroin and methadone pass through the placenta to the baby.

Babies born to mothers who used opioids may have withdrawal symptoms, including:
- Shaking
- High-pitched crying
- Jitters
- Seizures
- Fast breathing

If the mother uses opioids just before labor, the baby may have weak breathing.

## How Is Opioid Use Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose opioid use based on:
- What the person or others say
- Physical exam

If the cause of symptoms is unclear, doctors may test for:
- Low blood sugar
- Head injury

Urine tests can check for opioids.

Other tests may be done to check for complications.

## Treatment for Opioid Overdose

An opioid overdose is a medical emergency.

Doctors may use a machine called a ventilator to help breathing.

A medicine called naloxone is used to reverse the overdose. It works fast.

Naloxone is given by injection or nasal spray.

Some people become agitated or confused before waking up. They may need to be held safely for a short time.

Naloxone can cause withdrawal symptoms in people who are dependent on opioids. So it is only used when needed.

After treatment, people must be watched for several hours. If the opioid lasts a long time (like methadone), they may need to stay longer.

If symptoms come back, another dose of naloxone may be given. Or the person may be admitted to the hospital.

## Detoxification (Stopping Opioids)

There are two main ways to stop opioids:

1. **Cold turkey**: Stop all at once and let withdrawal happen.
2. **Substitution**: Switch to a safer drug, then slowly reduce the dose.

Both methods can be hard. Medicines like clonidine can help with withdrawal symptoms.

But clonidine can cause:
- Low blood pressure
- Drowsiness

Stopping clonidine can cause withdrawal symptoms like:
- Restlessness
- Trouble sleeping
- Irritability
- Fast heartbeat
- Headaches

## Substitution Therapy

This means replacing the opioid with a safer medicine. The dose is slowly lowered and then stopped.

Common medicines used:
- Methadone
- Buprenorphine

### Methadone

- Taken by mouth
- Blocks withdrawal and cravings
- Works longer than other opioids
- Usually taken once a day
- Dose is lowered slowly
- Must be taken at a licensed clinic every day
- Can cause abnormal heart rhythms
- Needs close monitoring

### Buprenorphine

- Works like an opioid but also blocks other opioids
- Can be prescribed by doctors in their office
- No need to go to a special clinic
- Used more often now than methadone

### Naltrexone

- Blocks the effects of opioids
- Has no opioid effects
- Must be fully detoxed before starting
- If not fully detoxed, it can cause severe withdrawal
- Works for 24 to 72 hours
- Can be taken once a day or 3 times a week
- Best for people who are very motivated to stay off opioids

## Maintenance Treatment

For people who keep using opioids, maintenance is often better.

This means taking a safe medicine every day for months or years.

Medicines used:
- Methadone
- Buprenorphine
- Naltrexone

This helps people live normal lives. They do not need to spend time getting illegal drugs.

The medicine does not make them drowsy or high. It helps them work, study, and care for family.

Some people do well with this treatment. For many, it is needed for life.

## Counseling and Support

No matter which treatment is used, ongoing counseling and support are essential.

Support can come from:
- Doctors and nurses
- Counselors
- Support groups
- Family and friends
- Other people with similar experiences

## Therapeutic Communities

Some programs help people rebuild their lives in a group setting.

Examples:
- Samaritan Daytop Village
- Phoenix House

People live together in a residential center for months or years.

They get training, education, and help to change their lives.

These programs help many people. But many drop out early.

They are expensive. Not everyone can afford them.

## Helpful Resources

These organizations offer support and information:

- **National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA)**  
  Government research and information on drug use.

- **Phoenix House**  
  Residential treatment centers in many states and Washington, DC.

- **Samaritan Daytop Village**  
  Helps people with addictions, including veterans, mothers and babies, and homeless people.

- **Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA)**  
  U.S. government agency that supports mental health and substance use treatment. Offers help finding treatment, hotlines, training, and data.

# Tinea Pedis (Athlete’s Foot)

Tinea pedis is a fungal infection of the feet.  
It is also called athlete’s foot.  
The fungus grows best in warm, damp places.  
Sweaty feet create the perfect environment for the fungus to grow.

## Types of Tinea Pedis

There are four main types.  
Some people have more than one type at the same time.

### Chronic Hyperkeratotic Tinea Pedis
- This type causes thick, scaly skin on the soles of the feet.  
- The skin may also be thick on the sides of the feet.  
- The pattern often looks like a moccasin boot.  
- It is usually caused by a fungus called *Trichophyton rubrum*.

### Chronic Intertriginous Tinea Pedis
- This type affects the skin between the toes.  
- The skin becomes red, itchy, and may crack or peel.  
- It most often affects the toes on the outside of the foot.

### Acute Ulcerative Tinea Pedis
- This type starts between the toes.  
- It spreads to the top or bottom of the foot.  
- The skin between the toes looks wet and soft.  
- It may have a scaly edge.  
- It is often caused by *T. mentagrophytes* var. *interdigitale*.  
- Bacteria can get into the skin and cause a secondary infection.  
- This can lead to redness, swelling, and pain.

### Vesiculobullous Tinea Pedis
- Small blisters form on the soles of the feet.  
- The blisters may join together to form larger ones.  
- This type is less common.  
- It often happens when feet are trapped in tight, warm shoes.  
- Heat and humidity can make it worse.

## How Doctors Diagnose Tinea Pedis

Doctors usually diagnose tinea pedis by looking at the skin.  
They check for signs like scaling, redness, and cracks.  
They also ask about your habits.  
For example, do you wear tight shoes? Do your feet sweat a lot?

If the skin does not look clearly like a fungal infection, the doctor may take a small skin sample.  
They will examine it under a microscope after mixing it with a special solution.  
This test is called a potassium hydroxide wet mount.

## Other Conditions That Can Look Like Tinea Pedis

Sometimes the skin on the feet looks like tinea pedis but is not.  
Other causes include:

- **Sterile maceration**: Skin that gets soft and breaks down from sweat and tight shoes.  
- **Contact dermatitis**: Skin irritation from materials in shoes.  
  - This can be from glue, rubber, or chemicals used in leather.  
- **Irritant contact dermatitis**: Skin damage from constant rubbing or moisture.  
- **Psoriasis**: A skin condition that causes thick, scaly patches.

## Pictures of Tinea Pedis

The following images show different types of tinea pedis:

- **Between toes**: Wet, scaly skin between the third and fourth toes.  
- **Moccasin pattern**: Thick, scaly skin on the soles and sides of the feet.  
- **Irregular scaling**: Scaly patches on the bottom of the foot.  
- **Top of foot**: Scales on the top of the foot.  
- **Lateral foot**: Red, scaly skin on the side of the foot.  
- **Subtle case**: Slight scaling between the toes that is hard to see at first.  
- **With nail infection**: Fungal infection in the toenails is also present.

## How Tinea Pedis Is Treated

### Antifungal Medicines
- Topical antifungals (creams, sprays, powders) are the first choice.  
- They are safe and work well for most people.  
- Treatment may need to continue for several weeks.  
- Recurrence is common.  
- Oral antifungals (pills) may be used if the infection is severe or does not respond.  
- Itraconazole and terbinafine are two common oral medicines.  
- Using a topical antifungal along with a pill may help prevent the infection from coming back.

### Keep Feet Dry
- Moisture makes the fungus grow.  
- Dry your feet well after bathing.  
- Pay special attention to the spaces between your toes.  
- Change your socks often.  
- Wear shoes that let air in.  
- Avoid tight, closed shoes, especially in warm weather.  
- Use drying agents such as:
  - Antifungal powders (like miconazole)  
  - Gentian violet (a liquid that dries the skin)  
  - Soaks with Burow solution (a 5% aluminum acetate solution)  
  - 20 to 25% aluminum chloride solution (a strong drying agent)

## Key Points

- Tinea pedis is the most common fungal infection of the skin.  
- It thrives in sweaty, warm feet.  
- Look for redness, scaling, cracking, or blisters between the toes or on the soles.  
- If you have these signs, think about tinea pedis.  
- Other conditions can look like it. These include:
  - Hand and foot eczema (dyshidrotic dermatitis)  
  - Psoriasis on the palms and soles  
  - Allergic reactions to shoe materials  
- Treat with antifungal creams or pills.  
- Keep your feet dry to prevent the infection from returning.

# Breast Pain

Many women have breast pain at some point. The pain can happen in one breast or both.

(See also: Overview of Breast Disorders.)

## What the Breasts Are

[Video available]

## What Causes Breast Pain

The cause of breast pain depends on where the pain is.

If the pain is in just one spot, it may be due to:

- A fluid-filled sac in the breast (called a cyst)
- A breast infection (rare, but possible)

If the pain is in the whole breast, it may be due to:

- Hormone changes
- Fibrocystic changes (common changes in breast tissue)
- Large breasts that stretch the tissues that support them
- A rare, widespread breast infection

If breast pain is the only symptom, it is usually not a sign of breast cancer.

Hormones like estrogen and progesterone can cause breast pain. These hormones rise before your period or during pregnancy. When they rise, they make the milk glands and tubes in the breast grow. The breasts also hold more fluid. This can make the breasts swell and hurt. The pain is often felt all over the breast. The breasts may feel tender when touched. This kind of pain often comes and goes with your period. It can last for months or years. Birth control pills or hormone therapy after menopause can also cause this kind of pain.

## When to See a Doctor

See a doctor if you have:

- Severe pain, redness, or swelling
- A lump in the breast
- A nipple that points inward
- Changes in the skin, like dimpling or redness

If you have severe pain, redness, or swelling, see a doctor within a day or two. These could be signs of an infection.

If the pain lasts more than one month, see a doctor.

Your doctor will ask you about your pain. They will want to know:

- When the pain happens (for example, around your period)
- If you have other symptoms
- What medicines you take (like birth control pills)

Your doctor will check your breasts and the area around them. They will look for lumps, skin changes, or tenderness. If nothing unusual is found, the pain is likely due to hormones or large breasts.

If you are pregnant, your doctor may do a pregnancy test. This is if you missed a period or feel sick in the morning. Other tests may be done based on your symptoms.

## How Breast Pain Is Treated

Mild breast pain often goes away on its own, even without treatment.

Pain that happens during your period can often be helped by:

- Acetaminophen
- A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), like ibuprofen

For severe period-related pain, your doctor may suggest:

- Danazol (a man-made hormone like testosterone)
- Tamoxifen (a medicine used to treat breast cancer)

These medicines reduce the effect of female hormones. This can help reduce swelling and pain. But they can cause side effects if used for a long time. So they are usually only used for a short time.

For breast pain during pregnancy, try:

- Wearing a firm, supportive bra
- Taking acetaminophen
- Or both

Stopping birth control pills or hormone therapy may help ease the pain.

Evening primrose oil, a natural supplement, may help some women with breast pain linked to periods or pregnancy.

If a specific problem is found, the doctor will treat that problem. For example, if a cyst is causing the pain, draining the fluid from it usually helps.

## Key Points

- Pain in one spot is often caused by a cyst.
- Pain in the whole breast is often due to hormones, fibrocystic changes, or large breasts.
- Breast pain alone is usually not a sign of breast cancer.
- See a doctor if the pain is severe or lasts more than one month.
- Tests are only needed if you have other symptoms.
- Treatment depends on the cause. Pain medicines like acetaminophen or NSAIDs can help in many cases.

# Hepatitis B – Acute

## What Is Hepatitis B?

Hepatitis B is a virus that causes liver infection.  
It spreads through contact with infected blood or body fluids.  
The virus can enter the body through broken skin or mucous membranes.  
It is not spread through casual contact like hugging or sharing food.

The virus has a complex structure.  
It has a core that holds its genetic material and an outer coat.  
The core contains DNA and an enzyme that helps the virus copy itself.  
The outer coat forms in the body’s cells.  
The body makes far more of this outer coat than needed.

Hepatitis B is the second most common cause of acute viral hepatitis.  
Hepatitis A is more common.  
Many people with hepatitis B do not know they are infected.  
This is more common than with hepatitis A.

In the United States, 2,045 cases of acute hepatitis B were reported in 2021.  
But experts believe the real number was about 13,300.  
This is because many cases go undetected or are not reported.

Hepatitis B can sometimes cause problems outside the liver.  
These include certain types of blood vessel disease, joint problems, kidney disease, and a rare blood disorder.  
The exact role of the virus in these conditions is not fully clear.  
But it may trigger the body’s immune system to attack its own tissues.

Sometimes, a person can be infected with both hepatitis B and hepatitis D at the same time.

---

## Symptoms of Acute Hepatitis B

Hepatitis B can cause many different types of liver illness.  
Some people have no symptoms at all.  
Others may have mild illness or severe liver failure.

Most people with acute hepatitis B have symptoms like:  
- Loss of appetite  
- Feeling tired and unwell  
- Fever  
- Nausea  
- Vomiting  
- Yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice)

These symptoms can last from a few weeks to six months.

About 5 to 10 out of every 100 people with acute hepatitis B develop a long-term infection.  
The younger the person is when infected, the higher the chance of long-term infection.

- Infants: 90% chance of long-term infection  
- Children aged 1 to 5 years: 25% to 50% chance  
- Adults: About 5% chance

If the infection becomes long-term, it can lead to serious liver damage.  
This includes scarring of the liver (cirrhosis).  
It can also lead to liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma).  
Liver cancer can develop even without cirrhosis.

---

## How Is Hepatitis B Diagnosed?

Doctors use blood tests to diagnose hepatitis B.  
These tests look for signs of the virus and the body’s response to it.

If a doctor suspects acute viral hepatitis, they will test for hepatitis A, B, and C.

The following tests are used:
- IgM antibody to hepatitis A virus (IgM anti-HAV)  
- Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg)  
- IgM antibody to hepatitis B core (IgM anti-HBc)  
- Antibody to hepatitis C virus (anti-HCV)  
- Hepatitis C RNA (HCV-RNA) using PCR testing

If any hepatitis B test is positive, more tests may be needed.  
These help tell if the infection is new, old, or long-term.

Additional tests may include:
- Hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg)  
- Antibody to hepatitis B e antigen (anti-HBe)  
- Hepatitis B DNA (HBV-DNA)  
- Antibody to hepatitis D virus (anti-HDV) if the infection is severe

There are three main blood markers for hepatitis B:

### HBsAg (Hepatitis B Surface Antigen)
- Shows up during the early stage of infection, before symptoms appear.  
- It means the person can spread the virus.  
- It usually goes away during recovery.  
- In some people, it stays in the blood.  
- If HBsAg stays and no protective antibody forms, the infection becomes long-term.

### HBcAb (Hepatitis B Core Antibody)
- This is an antibody to the virus’s core.  
- It appears when symptoms start.  
- It stays in the blood for years or life.  
- It is present in people who have had hepatitis B in the past.  
- In acute infection, it is mostly IgM type.  
- In long-term infection, it is mostly IgG type.  
- IgM anti-HBc is a strong sign of recent infection.  
- It can be the only sign during a short window between when HBsAg disappears and anti-HBs appears.

### HBeAg (Hepatitis B e Antigen)
- This protein is found only in people who are HBsAg positive.  
- It suggests the virus is very active and the person is highly contagious.  
- If anti-HBe is present instead, the virus is less active and less contagious.  
- HBeAg and anti-HBe help predict how the disease will progress.

### HBV-DNA
- This test finds the virus’s genetic material in the blood.  
- It shows if the virus is actively multiplying.

| Marker | Acute Infection | Chronic Infection | Past Infection | After Vaccination |
|--------|------------------|-------------------|----------------|-------------------|
| HBsAg | Positive | Positive | Negative | Negative |
| Anti-HBs | Negative | Negative | Positive | Positive |
| IgM anti-HBc | Positive | Negative | Negative | Negative |
| IgG anti-HBc | Negative | Positive | Variable | Negative |
| HBeAg | Variable | Variable | Negative | Negative |
| Anti-HBe | Negative | Variable | Variable | Negative |
| HBV-DNA | Positive | Positive | Negative | Negative |

Note: Anti-HDV should be tested if hepatitis B is confirmed and the illness is severe.

---

## How Is Acute Hepatitis B Treated?

There is no specific treatment to cure acute hepatitis B.  
Care focuses on helping the body recover.

You should avoid alcohol.  
Alcohol can make liver damage worse.

There is no need to limit food or activity.  
Bed rest is not helpful.

If the liver fails suddenly (fulminant hepatitis), treatment is urgent.

- Antiviral medicines like entecavir or tenofovir can help.  
- These medicines increase the chance of survival.  
- Liver transplantation is the best option for survival in adults.  
- Children have a better chance of recovery without a transplant.

All cases of viral hepatitis must be reported to public health authorities.

---

## How Can Hepatitis B Be Prevented?

Avoid high-risk behaviors:
- Do not share needles or syringes.  
- Use protection during sex.  
- Avoid sharing personal items like razors or toothbrushes.

Infected blood and body fluids can spread the virus.  
This includes blood, saliva, semen, and vaginal fluids.

Clean up spills with diluted bleach.  
Use gloves and other barriers when handling body fluids.

Do not isolate infected people.  
They do not need to be separated from others.

To prevent blood transfusion-related infection:
- Only give blood when needed.  
- Screen all blood donors for hepatitis B and C.  
- This has made post-transfusion hepatitis B and C very rare in the United States.

---

## Key Facts

- Hepatitis B spreads through blood or body fluids.  
- It can also spread through mucous membranes.  
- Diagnosis is done with blood tests for HBsAg and other markers.  
- Treatment is supportive.  
- About 5 to 10% of people with acute hepatitis B develop long-term infection.  
- Long-term infection can lead to cirrhosis or liver cancer.  
- All babies should get the hepatitis B vaccine at birth.  
- After exposure, a shot of hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) and the vaccine can help.  
- HBIG may not prevent infection, but it can reduce symptoms.  
- Babies born to mothers with hepatitis B have a 70% to 90% chance of getting infected during birth.  
- This risk drops sharply if the baby gets HBIG and the vaccine right after birth.  
- Pregnant women with high levels of the virus can take tenofovir in the third trimester to lower the risk.
