# Epiglottitis

Epiglottitis is a serious infection of the epiglottis and the tissues around it.  
The epiglottis is a small flap of tissue at the back of the throat.  
It closes off the windpipe when you swallow.  

This infection can block the airway.  
A blocked airway can stop you from breathing.  
This can be deadly.

## What Causes Epiglottitis?

Bacteria can infect the epiglottis.  
The most common cause used to be a bacteria called *Haemophilus influenzae* type B.  
But routine vaccination has made this infection very rare in children.  

Now, more cases happen in adults.  
Children can still get it from other types of bacteria.  
Adults and children who have not been vaccinated can still get infected with *Haemophilus influenzae* type B.

The infection causes swelling.  
This swelling can block the airway.  
This can lead to trouble breathing and death.

Children are more at risk than adults.  
This is because children have smaller airways.  
But adults can also die from this condition if not treated quickly.

Children with this infection often have bacteria in their blood.  
This can spread the infection to other parts of the body.  
These include the lungs, joints, brain coverings, heart sac, or skin.

## Symptoms of Epiglottitis

### In Children

Symptoms come on very fast.  
They can become life-threatening in just a few hours.  

Symptoms include:  
- Severe sore throat  
- Trouble swallowing  
- Pain when swallowing  
- Fever  
- Drooling  
- Voice sounds muffled or strange  

The back of the throat may look normal.  
Even though the throat is very sore.  

As the epiglottis swells, breathing becomes harder.  
At first, you may hear a high-pitched squeaking sound when breathing in.  
This is called stridor.  
Breathing gets worse quickly.  
The condition can get worse fast.

### In Adults

Symptoms are similar to those in children.  
They include:  
- Sore throat  
- Fever  
- Trouble swallowing  
- Drooling  

But in adults, symptoms usually take more than a day to develop.  
Adults have larger airways.  
So blockage is less likely and less sudden.  
Still, the airway can become blocked.  
If not treated, adults can die.

In both children and adults, the throat may look normal.  
So if someone has a very bad sore throat but no redness or swelling in the throat, doctors may suspect epiglottitis.

## How Is Epiglottitis Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect epiglottitis if someone has:  
- A very bad sore throat  
- Stridor or other signs of breathing trouble  
- A throat that looks normal  

If epiglottitis is suspected, the person is taken to the hospital right away.

Doctors look at the epiglottis using a thin, flexible tube with a camera.  
This is done in the operating room.  
This is the best way to see the swelling.

X-rays may be done if symptoms are mild.  
They help rule out other problems.

Doctors may take blood or tissue samples.  
These are sent to a lab to grow bacteria.  
This helps find the exact cause of the infection.

## How Is Epiglottitis Treated?

### Airway Care

The most important step is keeping the airway open.  

Children are taken to the operating room.  
A breathing tube is placed through the mouth into the windpipe.  
This tube keeps the airway open.  
It prevents swelling from blocking the airway.  

Adults who are having trouble breathing get a breathing tube.  
This is especially true if the airway is badly blocked.  
Adults who are breathing well may not need a tube.  
They can be watched closely in an intensive care unit.  

The breathing tube is usually needed for 60 hours or less.  

If a breathing tube cannot be placed, doctors may do a tracheotomy.  
This means making a small hole in the windpipe.  
A tube is placed in the hole to help the person breathe.

### Antibiotics

All people with epiglottitis get antibiotics.  
The most common one is ceftriaxone.  
The antibiotic may be changed later based on lab results.  

Antibiotics help kill the bacteria causing the infection.

## How Can Epiglottitis Be Prevented?

The *Haemophilus influenzae* type B (Hib) vaccine can prevent this infection.  
It is given to children as part of routine childhood vaccinations.  
This vaccine has greatly reduced cases of epiglottitis in children.  

Adults and children who have not been vaccinated are still at risk.  
Vaccination is the best way to stay safe.

# Trigger Finger (Stenosing Flexor Tenosynovitis)

Trigger finger happens when the tendons in your fingers become inflamed. Over time, this can cause thickening or a small lump to form. This makes it hard for the finger to move smoothly.

This condition often happens for no clear reason. But it is more common in people with rheumatoid arthritis or diabetes. Using your hands a lot, such as when using heavy gardening tools, may also play a role.

People with diabetes may have trigger finger at the same time as carpal tunnel syndrome. They may also have thickening of the tissue on the palm of the hand.

The problem starts when a small lump forms in the tendon. If the lump is near a tight band of tissue at the base of the finger, it can block the finger from straightening or bending. This can cause the finger to lock in a bent position. When it finally straightens, it may snap suddenly.

---

## How Is Trigger Finger Diagnosed?

### Patient Description
You may describe a painful snapping or locking feeling when you bend or straighten your finger.

### Physical Exam
Your doctor will ask you to open and close your hand. They may feel a tender lump at the base of the finger. They may also see the finger lock or snap during movement.

### Imaging
You do not need X-rays or other scans to diagnose trigger finger. The diagnosis is based on your symptoms and the physical exam.

---

## How Is Trigger Finger Treated?

### First Steps
- Wear a splint to keep the finger still.
- Use warm, moist compresses to ease pain.
- Take nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) to reduce swelling and pain.

These steps help many people feel better.

### If Symptoms Continue
If the first steps do not help, your doctor may suggest:
- A shot of corticosteroid medicine into the tendon area. This can reduce swelling and relieve pain quickly.
- Surgery, if the shot does not work. The surgery gently opens the tight band of tissue so the tendon can move freely again.

Surgery is safe and effective for most people.

# Aplastic Anemia

Aplastic anemia happens when the bone marrow stops making enough blood cells.  
The bone marrow is the soft part inside your bones. It makes red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.

When the stem cells in the bone marrow are damaged or destroyed, the marrow can stop working.  
This is called bone marrow failure.  
When this happens, your body makes too few red blood cells, white blood cells, or platelets.

Low red blood cells cause anemia.  
Low white blood cells make infections more likely.  
Low platelets cause easy bruising and bleeding.

The term "aplastic anemia" means that the bone marrow is not making most or all types of blood cells.  
If only red blood cells are affected, it is called pure red blood cell aplasia.

In many cases, doctors do not know the cause. This is called idiopathic aplastic anemia.  
When the cause is unknown, it may be due to an autoimmune problem.  
In an autoimmune problem, the body’s immune system attacks its own bone marrow stem cells.

Other causes include:

- Infections with certain viruses, such as parvovirus, Epstein Barr virus, or cytomegalovirus  
- Exposure to radiation  
- Contact with harmful chemicals like benzene  
- Some cancer treatments (chemotherapy) and certain medicines, such as chloramphenicol  
- Pregnancy  
- Liver infections (hepatitis)

## Symptoms of Aplastic Anemia

Symptoms usually appear slowly over weeks or months.

Low red blood cells cause tiredness, weakness, and pale skin.  
Low white blood cells make you more likely to get infections.  
Low platelets cause bruises that appear easily and bleeding that does not stop quickly.

## How Aplastic Anemia Is Diagnosed

Doctors use two main tests:

1. Blood tests  
2. Bone marrow exam

If you have symptoms of anemia, your doctor will do blood tests.  
If the blood tests show low levels of all blood cells, you will need a bone marrow exam.

A bone marrow exam means taking a small sample of bone marrow from your hip bone.  
A doctor looks at the sample under a microscope.  
If the sample shows very few bone marrow cells, you have aplastic anemia.

## Treatment for Aplastic Anemia

Treatment depends on how severe the condition is.

### Blood Transfusions
You may need transfusions of red blood cells and platelets.  
These help relieve symptoms like fatigue and bleeding.  
You may also get growth factors, which are medicines that help your body make more blood cells.

### Stem Cell Transplant
A stem cell transplant is the best treatment for many people with severe aplastic anemia.  
It can cure the disease.  
The transplant replaces damaged bone marrow with healthy stem cells from a donor.

If a transplant is not possible, doctors may give you medicines to calm down your immune system.  
These medicines are called antithymocyte globulin and cyclosporine.  
They help your bone marrow recover and start making blood cells again.

# Roseola Infantum (Commonly Called "Sixth Disease")

Roseola infantum is a common illness in babies and young children.  
It is caused by a virus called human herpesvirus 6B.  
Less often, it is caused by a similar virus called human herpesvirus 7.  

The illness causes a high fever and a rash.  
The rash usually shows up when the fever goes down.  
There are no signs of infection in one specific part of the body, like the ears or throat.  

Doctors usually diagnose it by looking at the child’s symptoms.  
There is no specific medicine to cure it.  
Treatment focuses on making the child feel better.

---

## What Causes Roseola Infantum?

The most common cause is human herpesvirus 6B.  
There are two types of this virus: type A and type B.  
Most cases of illness are due to type B.  
In rare cases, the virus can cause serious brain or liver problems in children with weak immune systems.  
This usually happens in children who have had a bone marrow transplant.

---

## When Does It Happen?

Roseola is most common in the spring and fall.  
Small outbreaks have been seen in childcare centers and schools.

---

## Symptoms and Signs

- The time from infection to symptoms is about 5 to 15 days.  
- The fever starts suddenly.  
- It reaches 103 to 105 degrees Fahrenheit.  
- The fever lasts 3 to 5 days.  
- The child may have no other symptoms like cough, sore throat, or ear pain.  
- Even with a high fever, the child usually stays awake and active.  
- Some children may have a seizure caused by the fever. This is called a febrile seizure.  
- Swollen glands in the neck and behind the ears are common.  
- Brain or liver problems are very rare.  

When the fever drops, usually on the fourth day, a rash appears.  
- The rash shows up first on the chest and belly.  
- It may spread to the face and arms and legs.  
- It looks like flat red spots or small raised bumps.  
- The rash lasts from a few hours to two days.  
- In some cases, the rash is so mild it goes unnoticed.  

In 7 out of 10 children, the classic rash does not appear at all.

> **Important Note:** The rash usually appears when the fever goes down.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors make the diagnosis based on the child’s symptoms and a physical exam.  
They may suspect roseola if a child between 6 months and 3 years old has:  
- A sudden high fever for 3 to 5 days  
- No other clear signs of illness  
- A rash that appears after the fever drops  

Testing is not usually needed.  
If testing is done, it can confirm the virus with blood tests or lab cultures.  
A special test called PCR can find the virus.  
This test is more often used to check for a virus that has come back after being inactive.

---

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure for roseola.  
Treatment focuses on helping the child feel better.  
This includes:  
- Giving plenty of fluids  
- Using fever reducers like acetaminophen or ibuprofen  
- Keeping the child comfortable  

For children with weak immune systems who have severe illness, such as brain infection, doctors may use antiviral medicines like foscarnet or ganciclovir.  
These medicines are not used for most children.  
There are no strong studies proving they work well in these cases.

# Anorectal Abscess

An anorectal abscess is a painful pocket of pus that forms inside the anus or rectum. It happens when bacteria get into a small gland in that area and cause an infection.

## What Is the Rectum and Anus?

- The **rectum** is the part of the digestive system just above the anus. It holds stool before it leaves the body.
- The **anus** is the opening at the end of the digestive system. Stool passes out of the body through this opening.

## How Does an Abscess Form?

- A small gland in the anus or rectum gets blocked.
- Bacteria grow inside the blocked gland and cause an infection.
- The infection fills the area with pus, which causes swelling and pain.
- Even though the anus has many bacteria, infections are rare because blood flows well to the area.
- When infection does happen, it is usually due to more than one type of bacteria.

## Who Is at Risk?

- People with Crohn disease are more likely to get abscesses.
- Abscesses can also happen after other conditions like diverticulitis or pelvic inflammatory disease.
- The abscess can be deep inside the rectum or close to the outside opening of the anus.

## Symptoms

- If the abscess is just under the skin:
  - The area is swollen and red.
  - It feels tender and very painful.
  - Some people may have a fever.

- If the abscess is deep inside the rectum:
  - It may not hurt as much on the outside.
  - But you may have a fever and pain in the lower belly.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- A doctor will examine the area.
- If there is no visible swelling, the doctor may insert a gloved finger into the rectum to feel for a tender lump.
- If the doctor thinks the abscess is deep or if Crohn disease is suspected, a CT scan of the belly may be done.
  - This scan shows the exact location and size of the abscess.

## How Is It Treated?

- The best treatment is to cut open the abscess and drain the pus.
- For a small abscess under the skin:
  - A local anesthetic numbs the area.
  - The doctor cuts into the abscess and drains the pus.

- For a deeper abscess:
  - The person is usually admitted to the hospital.
  - The abscess is drained in the operating room under general anesthesia.
  - This means the person is asleep during the procedure.

- Antibiotics are not always needed.
  - They are given only if:
    - You have a fever.
    - You have a weak immune system.
    - You have diabetes.
    - You have skin infection (cellulitis).
    - You have an infection in another part of the body.
  - People with low levels of a certain type of white blood cell (neutropenia) get antibiotics but usually do not need drainage.

## Possible Complications

- Even after proper treatment, a drained abscess can lead to a tunnel that forms between the anus or rectum and the skin.
- This tunnel is called an anorectal fistula.
- It may need more treatment later.

# Erythema Multiforme – Simple Explanation

Erythema multiforme is a skin reaction that causes specific types of rashes.  
It often appears as a sudden rash with a target or iris pattern.  
The inside of the mouth can also be affected.  
The rash usually goes away on its own.  
But it can come back again and again.  

This condition is most often caused by an infection.  
The most common infection is herpes simplex virus.  
It can also be caused by certain medicines.  
Other causes include other infections like hepatitis C.  
It can also happen in people with a condition called systemic lupus erythematosus.  

Doctors now believe erythema multiforme is a separate condition.  
It is not just a mild form of more serious skin diseases like Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis.

---

## What Causes Erythema Multiforme?

**Most cases** are caused by herpes simplex virus.  
Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) is more likely to cause it than type 2 (HSV-2).  
We do not know if the rash is a specific reaction to the virus or just a general response.  
Experts think the body’s immune system attacks skin cells that contain parts of the virus.  
This attack is done by certain immune cells called T cells.  

Some people may be more likely to get this rash because of their genes.  
The rash is rare, even though herpes simplex virus is common.  
Certain types of human leukocyte antigens are linked to a higher risk.

**Less often**, the rash is caused by:  
- Certain medicines  
- Vaccines  
- Other infections (like hepatitis C)  
- Systemic lupus erythematosus  

When the rash happens in someone with lupus, it is sometimes called Rowell syndrome.

---

## What Does Erythema Multiforme Look Like?

The rash appears suddenly.  
It shows up as red spots, bumps, blisters, or fluid-filled sacs.  
It often starts on the hands, feet, arms, legs, face, or palms.  
It can spread to the trunk (chest and back).  

The classic rash is called a target or iris lesion.  
It has a red center.  
This center is surrounded by a pale ring.  
Then there is a pink outer ring.  
The pattern looks like a target or a bullseye.  

The rash is usually not itchy.  
But some people do feel itchy.  

The rash can also affect the mouth.  
In the mouth, it may look like:  
- Target-like spots on the lips  
- Small blisters on the roof of the mouth or gums  
- Open sores (erosions) on the inside of the mouth  

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose erythema multiforme by looking at the rash.  
They check the shape, color, and location of the spots.  
A skin biopsy is rarely needed.  

Other conditions can look similar.  
These include:  
- Hives (urticaria)  
- Blood vessel inflammation (vasculitis)  
- A rare skin disease with blisters (bullous pemphigoid)  
- A rare immune disease (pemphigus)  
- A skin condition with blisters in a line (linear IgA dermatosis)  
- A rare skin disease with fever and white blood cells (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis)  
- A skin disease linked to gluten (dermatitis herpetiformis)  

If the mouth is affected, doctors must rule out:  
- Mouth sores that are not caused by infection (aphthous stomatitis)  
- Pemphigus  
- Herpes infection in the mouth (herpetic stomatitis)  
- Hand-foot-and-mouth disease  

If the rash covers a large area and includes the trunk and face,  
and if there are purple spots or blisters,  
it is more likely to be Stevens-Johnson syndrome.  
This is a more serious condition than erythema multiforme.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Most people do not need treatment.  
The rash goes away on its own.  

To help with symptoms, you can use:  
- Creams that reduce swelling and irritation (topical corticosteroids)  
- Creams that numb the skin (anesthetics)  
- Pills that reduce itching (oral antihistamines)  

If the rash keeps coming back, your doctor may suggest antiviral medicine.  
This is especially true if herpes simplex virus is likely the cause.  

Antiviral medicine may be used if:  
- You have more than five episodes in a year  
- The rash always comes back after a herpes outbreak  
- You have a history of herpes simplex virus  

Common antiviral medicines include:  
- Acyclovir 400 milligrams every 12 hours  
- Famciclovir 250 milligrams every 12 hours  
- Valacyclovir 1000 milligrams every 24 hours  

These medicines are taken daily to prevent future outbreaks.

---

## Key Points

- Erythema multiforme is often caused by herpes simplex virus.  
- It can also be caused by certain medicines.  
- The rash often has a target or iris pattern.  
- Lesions on the palms and soles are common and can help point to the diagnosis.  
- A skin biopsy is usually not needed.  
- Most people do not need treatment.  
- If the rash keeps coming back and herpes is likely the cause, antiviral medicine may help.

# Pneumonia in People With a Weak Immune System

Pneumonia is an infection in the lungs.  
It can be more serious in people whose immune system does not work well.  
A weak immune system means the body has a harder time fighting off infections.

People with a weak immune system are called immunocompromised.  
The immune system protects the body from germs that cause illness.

## What Causes Pneumonia in People With a Weak Immune System?

Pneumonia in these people can be caused by germs that do not usually make healthy people sick.  
It can also be caused by the same germs that cause pneumonia in healthy people.

Some common causes of a weak immune system include:

- Cancer and the medicines used to treat it  
- Problems with white blood cells (the cells that fight infection)  
- HIV infection  
- Certain medicines, such as steroids, chemotherapy drugs, or drugs for autoimmune diseases

### Common Germs That Cause Pneumonia

- *Pneumocystis jirovecii* – a fungus that usually does not cause harm in healthy people.  
  It can cause pneumonia when the immune system is weak.  
  This type of pneumonia is often the first sign of AIDS in people with HIV.

- Other fungi like *Aspergillus* and *Candida*  
- Bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, and *Haemophilus influenzae*  
- Viruses like cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex virus

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms can appear quickly or slowly.  
They may include:

- Feeling weak or tired  
- Coughing up thick or colored mucus  
- Trouble breathing  
- Fever  
- Shaking chills  
- Pain in the chest

People with *Pneumocystis jirovecii* pneumonia often have:

- A fever  
- Shortness of breath  
- A dry cough that does not produce mucus  
- Low oxygen levels in the blood, which can make breathing very hard

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to diagnose pneumonia in people with a weak immune system.

### Tests Used

- **Chest x-ray** – shows if there is infection in the lungs  
- **Sputum test** – a sample of mucus from the lungs is checked under a microscope  
- **Blood tests** – help find the germ causing the infection  
- **Pulse oximetry** – a small device on the finger or ear measures oxygen in the blood

Doctors may collect sputum in two ways:

- By giving a mist to help the person cough up deep mucus  
- By using a thin, flexible tube with a camera (bronchoscope) to get a sample directly from the lungs

Samples taken with a bronchoscope are more accurate than those coughed up on your own.

Blood samples are tested to see if bacteria grow in the lab.  
This helps identify the germ causing the infection.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on:

- The type of immune system problem  
- How sick the person is  
- The germ causing the infection

### Medicines Used

- **Antibiotics** – for bacterial infections  
- **Antivirals** – for viral infections  
- **Antifungals** – for fungal infections

Doctors often start with a broad-spectrum antibiotic.  
This type works against many different germs.  
If the person does not get better, they may add a medicine for viruses or fungi.

### Treating the Immune System

Doctors may stop or reduce medicines that weaken the immune system, such as chemotherapy or steroids, until the infection clears.

### Specific Treatment for *Pneumocystis jirovecii* Pneumonia

- The main treatment is a combination medicine called trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole  
- Other options include dapsone, atovaquone, clindamycin, or pentamidine  
- People with severe cases may also get prednisone, a medicine that reduces lung swelling and inflammation

## What Is the Outlook?

Pneumonia is harder to treat in people with a weak immune system.  
Even with treatment, the chance of death is higher than in healthy people.

The death rate for *Pneumocystis jirovecii* pneumonia is especially high.

## How Can It Be Prevented?

Doctors often give treatments to help protect people with weak immune systems.

### Ways to Prevent Pneumonia

- **Medicines to boost white blood cells** – for people whose immune system is weakened by cancer treatment  
- **Vaccines** – to prevent pneumonia caused by *pneumococcus* and *Haemophilus influenzae*  
- **Preventive medicine for *Pneumocystis jirovecii*** – trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole is used to prevent this type of pneumonia

### Side Effects of Preventive Medicine

- Skin rashes  
- Lower number of infection-fighting white blood cells  
- Fever

These side effects are more common in people with AIDS.

### Alternative Preventive Options

- Dapsone  
- Pentamidine

These are used if the main medicine is not tolerated.

# Treating a Sudden Worsening of COPD

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or COPD, has two main parts to treatment:  
- Managing the long-term, stable condition.  
- Treating sudden flare-ups when symptoms get worse.

When COPD suddenly gets worse, treatment includes:  
- Giving extra oxygen.  
- Using medicines to open the airways.  
- Giving steroids to reduce swelling.  
- Using antibiotics if an infection is likely.  
- Sometimes using a breathing machine without a tube (noninvasive ventilation) or with a tube (intubation and mechanical ventilation).

The main goals right away are to:  
- Make sure the body gets enough oxygen.  
- Bring blood pH back to near normal.  
- Open up blocked airways.  
- Treat the cause if it can be found.

The cause of a sudden flare-up is often not clear. But most flare-ups are caused by a virus or bacteria. Smoking, breathing in fumes or dust, and high levels of air pollution can also make flare-ups worse.

Some people with mild flare-ups can be treated at home if they have good support.  
But people who are older, frail, have other health problems, a history of breathing failure, or changes in blood gas levels should go to the hospital for care.

People with life-threatening flare-ups—such as very low oxygen levels that do not improve, severe acid buildup in the blood, new heart rhythm problems, or worsening breathing despite treatment—should go to the intensive care unit. Their breathing must be checked often.

---

## Oxygen During a COPD Flare-Up

Many people with COPD need extra oxygen during a flare-up—even if they do not need it all the time.  
Giving oxygen can sometimes make carbon dioxide levels go up. This is called hypercapnia.

This rise in carbon dioxide was once thought to happen because oxygen reduces the body’s natural drive to breathe. But even if carbon dioxide goes up, oxygen is still recommended.

Most people with COPD already have high carbon dioxide levels. So serious brain problems are rare unless carbon dioxide levels go above 85 mm Hg.

The goal for oxygen is to reach a level of about 60 mm Hg in the blood. Going higher gives little benefit and increases the risk of high carbon dioxide.

In most cases, low levels of oxygen help fix low oxygen levels in the blood.  
If a person needs high levels of oxygen, it may mean there is a serious problem like pneumonia or fluid in the lungs.

For people who are likely to have high carbon dioxide, oxygen is given through small tubes in the nose or a special mask. This allows better control. The person must be watched closely.

If a person gets worse during oxygen treatment—such as becoming very confused or very sleepy—they may need a breathing machine.

Many people who start using oxygen at home after a flare-up get better within 30 days and no longer need it.  
So, their need for home oxygen should be checked again 60 to 90 days after leaving the hospital.

---

## Breathing Support During a COPD Flare-Up

Noninvasive ventilation means using a mask to help with breathing. It does not require a tube in the throat.  
This method can help avoid the need for a breathing tube. It can also shorten hospital stays and lower the risk of death in people with severe flare-ups.

Noninvasive ventilation works best in people with a blood pH below 7.30 who are stable and not at immediate risk of stopping breathing.

It does not help much in people with mild flare-ups.  
But it may be used if blood gas levels get worse despite medicine or oxygen.  
It may also be used if a person is clearly heading toward needing a breathing tube but does not yet need one.

People with severe shortness of breath, overinflated lungs, and using extra muscles to breathe may feel better with this support.

If a person gets worse while using noninvasive ventilation, they will need a breathing tube and mechanical ventilation.

Signs that a breathing tube is needed include:  
- Worsening blood gas levels.  
- Confusion or drowsiness.  
- Extreme tiredness from breathing.

The settings on the breathing machine, how to manage care, and possible side effects are discussed elsewhere.

People at higher risk of needing a breathing machine long-term include those with:  
- Very low lung function (FEV1 less than 0.5 liters).  
- Poor blood gas levels (oxygen below 50 mm Hg or carbon dioxide above 60 mm Hg).  
- Severe limits on physical activity.  
- Poor nutrition.

If a person is at high risk, their wishes about breathing machines should be discussed and written down while they are well and not in the hospital. This is part of advance care planning.

But do not delay life-saving treatment just because of fear about needing a breathing machine. Many people recover fully and return to their normal life.

High-flow oxygen through the nose can also be used for people with breathing failure from COPD. It may be tried if a person cannot tolerate the mask used in noninvasive ventilation.

For people who need a breathing tube for more than two weeks, a tracheostomy (a small opening in the neck) is often helpful. It makes breathing easier, helps with speaking, and makes eating safer.

With a good pulmonary rehabilitation program—plus help with nutrition and mental health—many people who need long-term breathing support can eventually stop using the machine and return to their usual life.

Special programs exist for people who still need a breathing machine after recovery.  
Some can go off the machine during the day.  
With strong family support, some can go home with a breathing machine.

For people with long-term high carbon dioxide levels who were in the hospital for a flare-up, using a breathing machine at night can lower carbon dioxide and may help them live longer.  
But it does not improve quality of life. So, the decision should be made together with the patient.

---

## Key Tips

- Most people with a COPD flare-up need extra oxygen while in the hospital.  
- Inhaled medicines that open the airways (short-acting beta-agonists) are the main treatment.  
- Use antibiotics if the person has a flare-up and is coughing up thick, colored mucus.  
- For people with severe COPD, talk early about end-of-life care. This includes preferences about breathing machines and comfort care.

# Septic Abortion

Septic abortion is a serious infection in the uterus. It can happen just before, during, or after an abortion or a miscarriage. This is a medical emergency.

## What Causes Septic Abortion?

- The infection often happens when a procedure is done by someone who is not trained.
- It can also happen if the tools used are not clean or sterile.
- If the uterus is damaged during the procedure, germs can enter and cause infection.
- The infection can spread quickly and lead to serious harm or death.

This is most likely to happen when a woman cannot get safe, professional medical care. This may be due to lack of access to health services or personal reasons.

## Symptoms of Septic Abortion

Symptoms usually start within 24 to 48 hours after the abortion or miscarriage. They include:

- Chills
- Fever
- Vaginal discharge
- Vaginal bleeding
- Fast heartbeat

The opening of the uterus (cervix) may open wider. A miscarriage may happen if it has not already occurred. If the uterus is pierced during the procedure, the pain is usually very severe.

In some cases, the woman may become confused or disoriented. Her blood pressure may drop very low. This is called septic shock and is life-threatening.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several methods to confirm septic abortion:

- They ask about the recent procedure and symptoms.
- They do a physical exam to check for fever, low blood pressure, heavy bleeding, or pain in the belly or pelvis.
- They take blood tests to look for signs of infection.
- They send a blood sample to a lab to grow any germs. This helps find the right medicine to treat the infection.
- They use ultrasound to check if any pregnancy tissue is still in the uterus.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment must start right away. It includes:

- Strong antibiotics given through a vein (IV).
- Removal of any remaining pregnancy tissue from the uterus.

The tissue is removed using surgery through the vagina. This is called surgical evacuation. Two common methods are:

- Dilation and curettage (D & C)
- Dilation and evacuation (D & E)

These procedures are done by trained medical staff. They help clear the infection and prevent further harm.

## Important Notes

- Septic abortion can happen after any abortion or miscarriage procedure.
- It is most dangerous when done without proper training, clean tools, or safe equipment.
- Delaying treatment can lead to serious complications or death.
- Always seek medical help right away if you have symptoms after an abortion or miscarriage.

# Renal Tubular Acidosis

Renal tubular acidosis (RTA) is a group of kidney problems. The kidneys do not work right. They do not balance acid and certain minerals in the body. This can lead to long-term acid buildup in the blood and problems with potassium, calcium, and other minerals.

There are three main types of RTA:
- Type 1: The kidneys do not remove acid properly.
- Type 2: The kidneys do not reabsorb bicarbonate well.
- Type 4: The body does not make or use aldosterone properly.

Type 3 is very rare and is not discussed here.

Most people with RTA have no symptoms. Some may have signs of low potassium, low blood volume, or weak bones. In some cases, RTA can lead to chronic kidney disease.

## Types of Renal Tubular Acidosis

Here are the main features of each type:

| Feature | Type 1 | Type 2 | Type 4 |
|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| How common | Rare | Very rare | Common |
| What goes wrong | Kidneys cannot remove acid | Kidneys cannot keep bicarbonate | Body does not make or use aldosterone well |
| Blood bicarbonate level | Often below 15 | Usually 12 to 20 | Usually above 17 |
| Blood potassium level | Often low, but may rise with treatment | Usually low, gets lower with treatment | High |
| Urine pH | Above 5.5 | Above 7.5 if bicarbonate is normal; below 5.5 if bicarbonate is low | Below 5.5 |
| Note | Type 3 is very rare | | |

## Symptoms and Signs

Most people with RTA feel fine. Severe problems are rare but can be dangerous.

- Type 1 RTA can cause kidney stones or calcium deposits in the kidneys.
- Type 2 RTA can cause dehydration. This happens because the kidneys lose too much water and salt.
- Type 1 and type 2 RTA can cause muscle weakness, low reflexes, or even paralysis. This is due to low potassium.
- Bone pain, soft bones in adults (osteomalacia), or weak bones in children (rickets) can happen in type 2 and sometimes in type 1.
- Type 1 RTA often leads to chronic kidney disease.
- Type 4 RTA usually causes mild symptoms. But if potassium gets too high, it can cause heart rhythm problems or paralysis.

## How RTA Is Diagnosed

RTA is suspected when:
- Blood tests show acid buildup in the blood (metabolic acidosis) with a normal anion gap.
- Blood potassium is high with no clear reason.

Tests include:
- Arterial blood gas (ABG) to check blood acidity and rule out breathing problems.
- Blood tests for electrolytes, kidney function (BUN and creatinine), and urine pH.

More tests may be needed to find the type:
- **Type 1 RTA**: A test that makes the body more acidic. Normal kidneys lower urine pH to below 5.2 within 6 hours. In type 1, urine pH stays above 5.5.
- **Type 2 RTA**: A test using bicarbonate given through a vein. In type 2, urine pH goes above 7.5 and the body loses more bicarbonate than normal (over 15%).
- **Type 4 RTA**: A history of conditions linked to this type, high potassium, and normal or slightly low bicarbonate. Blood tests often show low renin and low aldosterone.

## Treatment

Treatment depends on the type of RTA.

- **Alkali therapy** is used to correct acid levels. This includes:
  - Sodium bicarbonate
  - Potassium bicarbonate
  - Sodium citrate
- These help bring blood bicarbonate to a normal level (22 to 24).
- Potassium citrate may be used instead if you have low potassium or kidney stones.

- **Vitamin D and calcium supplements** may be needed to help fix weak bones.
  - Vitamin D: 800 international units once a day by mouth.
  - Calcium: 500 mg three times a day (e.g., calcium carbonate 1250 mg three times a day).

- **Type 1 and type 2 RTA**: Treat low potassium with supplements.
- **Type 4 RTA**: Limit potassium in the diet. Sometimes a diuretic that removes potassium is used.

Untreated RTA in children can slow growth.

## Key Points

- RTA is a group of kidney problems that cause long-term acid buildup in the blood.
- It is most often due to low aldosterone (type 4), or problems removing acid (type 1), or not keeping bicarbonate (type 2).
- Think about RTA if blood tests show acid buildup with normal anion gap or high potassium with no clear cause.
- Check blood gas, electrolytes, kidney function, and urine pH.
- Use special tests to confirm the type (acid load test for type 1, bicarbonate infusion for type 2).
- Treat with alkali therapy. Correct low potassium in types 1 and 2. Limit potassium or use diuretics in type 4. Add other supplements as needed.

# Frostbite

Frostbite happens when part of your body freezes due to extreme cold.

- Freezing can kill skin and tissue.
- It can also harm nearby tissue that did not freeze.
- The affected area may feel numb. It may look white, swollen, blistered, or turn black and hard like leather.

## What Causes Frostbite?

Frostbite is caused by a mix of things:

- Freezing kills some cells. Others survive.
- Cold makes blood vessels get smaller. This cuts off blood flow to nearby tissue.
- Poor blood flow can cause blood clots in small blood vessels.
- These clots can stop blood from reaching tissue. This can cause the tissue to die.
- When blood flow returns, damaged tissue releases chemicals that cause swelling and more harm.
- As frozen tissue warms, harmful substances enter the blood.

Any part of the body can get frostbite if it is exposed to freezing temperatures.

The risk depends on:
- How cold it is.
- How long the body part was exposed.

People at higher risk include those with:
- Diabetes.
- Arteriosclerosis (hardened blood vessels).
- Blood vessel spasms (from smoking, some nerve problems, or certain medicines).
- Tight gloves or boots that cut off blood flow.

Hands, feet, face, and ears are most likely to be affected.

Wet skin or touching metal speeds up freezing. This is very dangerous.

## Signs and Symptoms of Frostbite

Symptoms depend on how deep the freezing goes.

**Shallow frostbite:**
- Skin turns white and numb.
- After warming, the skin peels.

**Slightly deeper frostbite:**
- Swelling and blisters appear.

**Deeper frostbite:**
- The area feels numb, cold, and hard.
- It looks pale and feels cold to the touch.
- Blisters form.
- Clear fluid in blisters means less damage.
- Blood-stained fluid in blisters means more serious damage.

**Dead tissue:**
- The area may turn gray and soft. This is called wet gangrene.
- Wet gangrene often needs amputation.
- More often, dead tissue turns black and hard. This is called dry gangrene.

## How Is Frostbite Diagnosed?

A doctor checks for:
- Signs of frostbite.
- A history of being in cold weather.

Frostbite looks different from other cold injuries. At first, it may look the same. After a few days, it becomes clear it is frostbite.

## How Is Frostbite Treated?

### First Aid

- Cover the person with a warm blanket. They may also have low body temperature (hypothermia).
- Warm the frostbitten area as soon as possible.
- Immerse the area in warm water.
  - Water should be no hotter than what feels comfortable to the caregiver.
  - Temperature: 98.6 to 102.2 degrees Fahrenheit (about 37 to 39 degrees Celsius).
- Do not rub the area with snow or anything else.
  - Rubbing causes more damage.
- Do not warm the area near a fire, with a heating pad, or an electric blanket.
  - You cannot feel pain in the frozen area. You might burn it without knowing.

**Important:**
- It is worse to thaw frostbitten tissue and then let it freeze again.
- If you must go back into freezing weather, do not thaw the area.
- Thawed feet are more likely to be hurt by walking.
- Protect the area from rubbing, pressure, or more injury.
- Clean and dry the feet. Cover them with clean bandages.
- Stay warm. Take pain medicine if possible.
- Get to a hospital as soon as you can.

### Hospital Care

- The frostbitten area is warmed in warm water baths (98.6 to 102.2 °F or 37 to 39 °C).
- Remove rings, watches, or jewelry before soaking.
- Full warming takes 15 to 30 minutes.
- Gently move the affected part during warming.
- Warming causes severe pain. You may need strong pain medicine.
- Do not break blisters.
- If blisters break, cover them with antibiotic ointment.

After warming:
- Gently wash the area.
- Dry it carefully.
- Wrap it in clean, sterile bandages.
- Keep it clean and dry to prevent infection.

**Medicines:**
- Ibuprofen (by mouth) or aloe vera gel (on skin) can reduce swelling.
- If infection occurs, antibiotics are needed.
- Some doctors give antibiotics to all people with deep frostbite to prevent infection.
- Some doctors use medicines given into a vein or artery to improve blood flow.
  - These help only in the first few days after injury.
- If you are not up to date on your tetanus shot, you may get a tetanus vaccine.

### Ongoing Care

- Eat healthy food. This helps your body make heat.
- Use warm whirlpool baths (about 98.6 °F or 37 °C) three times a day.
- Dry gently after each bath.
- Rest and allow time for healing.

Most people get better over several months.

- Amputation may be needed to remove dead tissue.
- Frostbite can look worse than it really is at first.
- Doctors often wait several months before deciding on amputation.
- Imaging tests can help:
  - Radionuclide scanning.
  - Microwave thermography.
  - Laser-Doppler flow study.
- These tests show which areas may heal and which will not.
- Areas that will not heal may need amputation.

### After Healing

Some people have long-term effects:
- Numbness in the area.
- Extra sensitivity to cold.

These changes may last a long time.

# Infectious Mononucleosis (Mono)

Infectious mononucleosis is caused by a virus called Epstein-Barr virus, or EBV.  
This virus belongs to the herpes family.  
Most people get infected with EBV at some point in their lives.  
The infection causes tiredness, fever, sore throat, and swollen glands.  
Tiredness can last for weeks or even months.  
In rare cases, serious problems can happen, such as blocked airways, a ruptured spleen, or nerve issues.  
Doctors diagnose mono based on symptoms or blood tests.  
There is no specific treatment. Care focuses on helping the body feel better.

---

## How EBV Spreads

EBV spreads through saliva.  
You can get it by sharing drinks, food, or kissing.  
It is not very contagious.  
The virus is not found in the environment.  
It only lives in humans.  
Most children get EBV before age five, but they often do not feel sick.  
Over 90% of adults have had EBV at some point.  
After the first infection, the virus stays in the body for life.  
It hides in certain white blood cells.  
The virus can come out from the mouth from time to time, even if you feel fine.  
This is called shedding.  
About 10 to 20 out of 100 healthy adults who have had EBV can spread the virus without showing symptoms.  
People with weak immune systems, such as those with HIV or who had an organ transplant, shed more virus and more often.

---

## What Symptoms You Might Have

Most young children do not feel sick when they get EBV.  
Symptoms usually appear in older children and adults.  
It takes about 30 to 50 days after exposure for symptoms to start.  
Tiredness is often worst in the first 2 to 3 weeks.  
It can last much longer.  

The most common symptoms are:

- Fever  
- Sore throat  
- Swollen glands  

Fever often peaks in the afternoon or early evening.  
It can reach 39.5 degrees Celsius, or even 40.5 degrees Celsius.  
Sore throat can be very painful.  
It may look like strep throat.  
Swollen glands are usually on both sides of the neck.  
They can be in any group of glands, but most often in the front and back of the neck.  
Sometimes swollen glands are the only sign.

Other possible symptoms include:

- Enlarged spleen  
- Mildly enlarged liver with tenderness when pressed  
- Swelling around the eyes  
- Small red spots on the roof of the mouth  
- Rash (less common)  
- Yellowing of the skin or eyes (rare)

An enlarged spleen happens in about half of all cases.  
It is usually biggest in the second and third week.  
It often feels only slightly enlarged and hard to feel.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Mono

Doctors suspect mono when you have the typical symptoms.  
They may do a test for heterophile antibodies.  
This test is quick and often used first.  
If the result is unclear, they may do a blood test to check for EBV-specific antibodies.  
Mono can look like strep throat.  
Both can cause sore throat, swollen glands, and fever.  
But mono often causes swollen glands in the back of the neck or all over the body.  
It also often causes an enlarged spleen or liver.  
Even if strep bacteria are found in your throat, you can still have mono.  
So, both infections can happen at the same time.

---

## How Mono Is Treated

There is no cure for mono.  
Treatment focuses on making you feel better.  
Rest is important during the worst part of the illness.  
You can slowly return to normal activities when your fever, sore throat, and tiredness go away.  
To prevent a ruptured spleen, avoid heavy lifting and contact sports for at least one month.  
Your doctor may use ultrasound to check if your spleen has returned to normal size.  

Corticosteroids (a type of medicine) can help if symptoms are very severe.  
They can reduce fever and ease a sore throat.  
But they are not needed for mild cases.  
They may help if you have a blocked airway, very low blood platelets, or a type of anemia.  

Antiviral medicines like acyclovir can reduce the amount of virus in your mouth.  
But they do not help most people feel better.  
There is no strong proof that these medicines should be used for mono.

---

## What to Expect in the Long Term

Mono usually gets better on its own.  
The worst part lasts about two weeks.  
About 20% of people feel well enough to return to school or work within one week.  
About half feel well enough in two weeks.  
Tiredness can last for several more weeks.  
In up to 10% of people, tiredness lasts for months.  

Death from mono is very rare.  
It happens in less than 1 out of 100 cases.  
Most deaths are due to serious complications like brain swelling, a ruptured spleen, or blocked airway.

---

## Key Facts

- EBV is very common.  
- The virus stays in your body for life.  
- It can come out from your mouth from time to time, even if you feel fine.  
- Only about 5% of people get EBV from someone who is sick with mono.  
- Common symptoms: tiredness, fever, sore throat, swollen glands, and enlarged spleen.  
- Rare but serious problems: brain issues, ruptured spleen, blocked airway, anemia, low blood platelets, and yellow skin.  
- A positive test for heterophile antibodies or EBV-specific antibodies helps confirm the diagnosis.  
- Early HIV infection can look like mono.  
  If you are at risk for HIV, your doctor should test for it.  
- Care is supportive.  
  Rest and avoid heavy lifting and contact sports.  
  Antiviral medicines are not needed.  
- Use corticosteroids only if you have serious complications like blocked airway, severe anemia, or very low blood platelets.

# Understanding Delirium and Dementia

Delirium and dementia are the most common reasons people have trouble thinking clearly. This means they cannot learn new things, remember what they know, or use their knowledge the way they used to.

Even though delirium and dementia can happen at the same time, they are very different.

## What Is Delirium?

- Delirium starts quickly. It can come on in hours or days.
- Your mental abilities can change from minute to minute.
- It is usually caused by another health problem.
- It can get better when the cause is treated.

## What Is Dementia?

- Dementia develops slowly over months or years.
- It gets worse over time.
- It does not go away. It is not reversible.

## How They Affect the Mind

- Delirium mainly affects your ability to focus and pay attention.
- Dementia mainly affects your memory, especially for recent events.

## Who Gets These Conditions?

- Both can happen at any age.
- But they are much more common in older adults.
- This is because the brain changes as we age.

## Key Differences Between Delirium and Dementia

| Feature | Delirium | Dementia |
|--------|----------|----------|
| **How it starts** | Suddenly, often with a clear start | Very slowly, hard to notice at first |
| **What causes it** | Usually another illness, like an infection, low fluid levels, or certain medicines | Usually a brain disease, such as Alzheimer disease, vascular dementia, or dementia with Lewy bodies |
| **First sign** | Trouble paying attention | Trouble remembering recent events |
| **Worse at night?** | Yes, usually worse at night | Often worse at night |
| **Awareness level** | Can be very alert one moment, then very slow the next | Usually normal until later stages |
| **Knows where they are?** | May not know their surroundings | Often loses track of time and place |
| **Talks clearly?** | Speech may be slow, confused, or not make sense | May struggle to find the right word |
| **Memory** | Can be poor, but it changes a lot | Memory loss is steady and gets worse |
| **How it gets worse** | Mental function goes up and down | Gets worse slowly, but steadily |
| **How long it lasts** | Days to weeks, sometimes longer | Usually lasts for life |
| **Need for treatment** | Needs urgent care | Needs care, but not always right away |
| **Can treatment help?** | Symptoms often go away when the cause is fixed | Treatment may slow it down, but it cannot stop or cure it |

# Nonerosive Gastritis

Nonerosive gastritis is a condition where the lining of the stomach is inflamed.  
It is often caused by a bacterial infection called *Helicobacter pylori*.  
Most people with this condition do not have any symptoms.  
The condition is found during a test called endoscopy.  
Treatment usually involves getting rid of the *H. pylori* bacteria.  
Sometimes, medicines that reduce stomach acid are also used.

(See also: How the stomach makes acid and an overview of gastritis.)

---

## What Happens in Nonerosive Gastritis

The stomach lining becomes inflamed.  
This inflammation is usually due to *H. pylori* bacteria.  
The damage does not break through the lining, so there are no open sores.  
This is why it is called "nonerosive."

---

## Symptoms and Signs

Most people with *H. pylori*-related gastritis feel fine.  
Some may have mild stomach discomfort.  
Others may feel full quickly or have a vague sense of unease in the stomach.  
These symptoms are not specific and can be caused by many other issues.

---

## How It Is Diagnosed

A doctor may find this condition during an endoscopy.  
An endoscopy is a test where a thin tube with a camera is passed through the mouth into the stomach.  
This test is usually done for other reasons, like checking for ulcers or bleeding.  
Testing for *H. pylori* is not needed in people with no symptoms.  
If the stomach lining looks inflamed, testing for *H. pylori* is recommended.

---

## How It Is Treated

### If *H. pylori* Is Present

The main treatment is to kill the bacteria.  
This is done with a combination of antibiotics.  
This treatment removes the risk of stomach cancer.  
*H. pylori* is known to cause cancer.  
Even if you have no symptoms, getting rid of the bacteria is important.  
It lowers your long-term risk of serious problems.

### If *H. pylori* Is Not Present

Treatment focuses on relieving symptoms.  
Medicines that reduce stomach acid can help.  
These include:  
- Histamine-2 receptor antagonists  
- Proton pump inhibitors  
- Antacids  

These medicines do not treat the cause, but they can make you feel better.  
They are used only if you have symptoms.

# Lyme Disease – Simple Explanation

Lyme disease is an infection caused by tiny bacteria. These bacteria are called *Borrelia*. The most common type is *Borrelia burgdorferi*. Another type, *Borrelia mayonii*, is less common and found in the United States.

The bacteria are spread by ticks. Ticks are small insects that feed on blood. They can carry the bacteria and pass them to people when they bite.

---

## How Do People Get Lyme Disease?

- Most people get Lyme disease when they go into wooded areas or walk through tall grass.
- They are bitten by ticks that carry the bacteria.
- The tick must stay attached for at least a day and a half to pass on the infection.
- The most common time for infection is summer and early fall.
- Children and young adults who live near woods are most at risk.

---

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

Lyme disease has three stages: early, early spread, and late.

### Early Stage (First Few Weeks)

- A red or dark spot appears at the bite site.
- The spot grows slowly and can get as big as 20 inches (50 centimeters).
- It often clears in the center, making it look like a bull’s eye.
- The spot may be warm but does not usually itch or hurt.
- It can appear on the thigh, buttock, trunk, or armpit.
- In people with dark skin, the spot may be hard to see.
- The rash shows up in about 75% of people.
- It usually goes away after 3 to 4 weeks.

> **Note:** About 25% of people never get this rash or do not notice it.

### Early Spread Stage (Days to Weeks After Rash)

- The bacteria spread through the body.
- Symptoms include:
  - Fatigue
  - Chills
  - Fever
  - Headache
  - Stiff neck
  - Muscle aches
  - Swollen or painful joints
- Some people get more red spots on other parts of the body.
- Others may have back pain, nausea, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes, or an enlarged spleen.
- These symptoms can last for weeks.
- They often feel like the flu, especially if the rash is not present.

> **Nervous system problems** can happen in about 15% of people:
> - Meningitis: causes headache and stiff neck.
> - Bell palsy: causes weakness on one or both sides of the face.

> **Heart problems** can happen in up to 8% of people:
> - Slow heart rhythm (called heart block).
> - Inflammation of the heart or the sac around it (causing chest pain).
> - These can cause dizziness or fainting.

### Late Stage (Months to Years After Infection)

- If not treated, problems can return months or years later.
- Arthritis is common. It affects more than half of people.
  - Swelling and pain in large joints, especially the knee.
  - The knee may be hot and swollen, but not always painful.
  - Pain can come and go for years.
  - Cysts can form behind the knee and burst, causing sudden pain.
  - In about 10% of people, knee problems last longer than 6 months.
- Some people have brain and nerve problems:
  - Trouble with memory, mood, speech, or sleep.
  - Numbness or sharp pains in the back, legs, or arms.

---

## How Is Lyme Disease Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tools to diagnose Lyme disease:

- A typical rash (especially erythema migrans).
- A history of being in a place where Lyme disease is common.
- Blood tests that look for antibodies (proteins made by the body to fight infection).

> **Important notes:**
> - Blood tests may not show results in the first few weeks of infection.
> - Antibodies can stay in the body for years, even after the infection is gone.
> - This means a positive test does not always mean you have active Lyme disease.
> - Doctors do not treat people based only on blood tests. They look at symptoms and exposure history.

Sometimes doctors take a sample of joint fluid or spinal fluid to test for the bacteria. They use a method called PCR to find tiny pieces of the bacteria’s DNA.

---

## How Is Lyme Disease Treated?

Antibiotics are the main treatment. They work well at all stages.

### Early Stage (Rash or Early Symptoms)

- Oral antibiotics: doxycycline, amoxicillin, or cefuroxime.
- Treatment lasts 10 to 14 days.
- If the infection is only in one area, 10 days may be enough.
- If you cannot take these medicines, azithromycin or erythromycin is used.
- Doxycycline is not given to children under 8 or to pregnant or breastfeeding women.

### Complications

- **Bell palsy:** Doxycycline by mouth for 2 to 3 weeks.
- **Meningitis:** Ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, or penicillin given through a vein for 2 to 3 weeks.
- **Arthritis:** Amoxicillin, cefuroxime, or doxycycline by mouth, or ceftriaxone through a vein for 4 weeks.
- **Heart block (serious rhythm problem):** Ceftriaxone or penicillin through a vein. A temporary pacemaker may be needed.
- **Mild heart issues:** Doxycycline, amoxicillin, or cefuroxime by mouth for 2 to 3 weeks.

> **After treatment:**
> - Antibiotics kill the bacteria in most people.
> - Arthritis often improves, but sometimes it lasts even after the bacteria are gone.
> - Some people still have fatigue, headaches, joint pain, or brain and nerve symptoms after treatment.
> - This is called post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome (PTLDS).
> - The cause is unknown. More antibiotics do not help.

### Pain Relief

- Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like aspirin or ibuprofen can help with joint pain.
- Fluid in the joint can be drained.
- Crutches may help if walking is painful.

---

## How Can Lyme Disease Be Prevented?

You can lower your risk by avoiding tick bites.

### Tips to Avoid Ticks

- Stay on trails when walking in the woods.
- Walk in the center of the path to avoid brushing against bushes.
- Do not sit on the ground or on stone walls.
- Wear long-sleeved shirts and long pants.
- Tuck pants into boots or socks.
- Wear light-colored clothes so ticks are easier to see.
- Use insect repellent with DEET on your skin.
- Use permethrin on clothes or wear clothes already treated with permethrin.

> **Ticks are tiny.** The most dangerous ones are young deer ticks (nymphs). They are smaller than a sesame seed.

### Check Your Body Daily

- Check your whole body every day after being outdoors.
- Pay special attention to hairy areas like the scalp, armpits, and groin.
- Ticks must be attached for more than a day and a half to pass on the disease. So checking early helps.

### How to Remove a Tick

- Use fine tweezers.
- Grasp the tick by the head or mouthparts where it is attached to the skin.
- Pull straight out slowly and steadily.
- Do not squeeze the tick’s body.
- Do not use petroleum jelly, alcohol, or a lit match.

> **After a tick bite:**
> - Doctors may give a single dose of doxycycline to prevent Lyme disease.
> - Or they may suggest watching the bite area and starting antibiotics only if a rash or symptoms appear.

---

## Key Facts

- Lyme disease is the most common tick-borne illness in the United States.
- It is found in 49 states.
- Most cases happen in the Northeast (from Maine to Virginia) and in Wisconsin, Minnesota, and Michigan.
- On the West Coast, most cases are in northern California and Oregon.
- Lyme disease also occurs in Europe, China, Japan, and parts of the former Soviet Union.
- Deer do not carry or spread the bacteria. They only provide blood for adult ticks.
- Ticks can carry other infections too, like babesiosis and anaplasmosis. You can get more than one infection at once.
