# Croup

Croup is a sudden swelling in the voice box and windpipe.  
It is most often caused by a virus called parainfluenza virus type 1.  
The main symptoms are a loud, barking cough and a high-pitched sound when breathing in.  
This high-pitched sound is called stridor.

Most children get better on their own.  
The illness usually lasts 3 to 4 days.  
Croup mostly affects children between 6 months and 3 years old.

---

## What Causes Croup?

The most common cause is the parainfluenza virus, especially type 1.  
Other viruses can also cause croup, but less often.  
These include:

- Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)  
- Adenovirus  
- Influenza viruses (types A and B)  
- Enterovirus  
- Rhinovirus  
- Measles virus  
- *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* (a type of bacteria)

Croup caused by the flu virus can be more serious.  
It can also affect older children.

Croup often happens in outbreaks.  
- Parainfluenza virus cases are more common in the fall.  
- RSV and flu cases are more common in winter and spring.

The virus spreads through the air when someone coughs or sneezes.  
It can also spread by touching things that have the virus on them.

---

## How Croup Affects the Body

The virus causes swelling in the voice box, windpipe, and airways.  
The swelling is worst just below the voice box.  
This makes it harder to breathe.  
The child must work harder to breathe.  
In rare cases, the child gets too tired.  
This can lead to too much carbon dioxide in the blood.

If the small airways get blocked, part of the lung may collapse.  
This is called atelectasis.

---

## Symptoms of Croup

Croup usually starts with cold-like symptoms.  
Then the child gets a barking cough.  
The cough may come in sudden bursts.  
The voice may sound hoarse.

These symptoms often get worse at night.  
The child may wake up suddenly with trouble breathing.  
They may breathe fast.  
Their chest may pull in with each breath.

In severe cases, the child’s lips or face may turn blue.  
Breathing becomes shallow and weak as the child tires.

The most obvious signs are:

- Loud, barking cough  
- High-pitched sound when breathing in (stridor)  
- Fast breathing  
- Pulling in of the chest with each breath

When a doctor listens to the chest, they may hear:

- Long, high-pitched breathing in  
- Stridor  
- Crackling sounds (if lower airways are involved)  
- Weak breath sounds (if part of the lung is collapsed)

About half of children have a fever.  
The child may seem better in the morning.  
But symptoms often come back at night.

Some children have repeated episodes.  
This is called spasmodic croup.  
Allergies or sensitive airways may play a role.  
But the symptoms are the same as regular croup.  
Spasmodic croup often starts after a viral infection.  
Fever is usually not present.

---

## How Is Croup Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose croup by the child’s symptoms.  
The barking cough is a key sign.

If the diagnosis is not clear, the doctor may order X-rays.  
An X-ray of the neck and chest can show a narrow area below the voice box.  
This is called the "steeple sign."  
It supports the diagnosis of croup.

Other serious conditions can cause similar symptoms.  
These include:

- Epiglottitis (swelling of the voice box cover)  
- Bacterial tracheitis (bacterial infection of the windpipe)  
- A foreign object stuck in the airway  
- Diphtheria (a rare bacterial infection)

These conditions are more serious.  
They come on faster.  
The child looks sicker.  
They may have a sore throat and not have cold symptoms.

A foreign object may cause coughing and stridor.  
But there is usually no fever or cold before it.

Diphtheria is very rare today.  
It is usually ruled out by checking if the child has had all their vaccines.  
It can be confirmed by testing a sample from the throat.

If a child looks very sick, the doctor may examine them in an operating room.  
This is to keep the airway open if needed.

All children with breathing trouble should have their oxygen level checked.  
If the oxygen level is low, blood tests may be done to check carbon dioxide levels.

> **Important:**  
> Epiglottitis, retropharyngeal abscess, and bacterial tracheitis make a child look much sicker than croup.  
> They do not cause a barking cough.

---

## How Is Croup Treated?

Most children can be treated at home.  
Keep the child calm and comfortable.  
Crying and tiredness can make breathing worse.

Use cool, moist air.  
A humidifier or a cold steam vaporizer may help.  
But it does not change how long the illness lasts.

Give fluids to keep the child hydrated.  
Use medicine to reduce fever if needed.

For children with moderate to severe croup, doctors may give:

- A single dose of a steroid medicine (like dexamethasone)  
- A breathing treatment with epinephrine (given through a nebulizer)

Steroid medicine helps reduce swelling.  
It can prevent hospitalization.  
It can also help children who are already in the hospital.  
A single dose of dexamethasone (0.6 mg per kilogram of body weight) is usually enough.  
The maximum dose is 10 milligrams.

Epinephrine helps open the airway quickly.  
It gives fast relief.  
But the effect only lasts a few hours.  
It does not cure the virus or shorten the illness.

Side effects of epinephrine can include a fast heartbeat.  
It is used mainly for children with moderate to severe symptoms.

Antibiotics are not needed.  
The viruses that cause croup do not lead to bacterial infections.

---

## When Is Hospital Care Needed?

Hospital care is needed if the child has:

- Trouble breathing that gets worse  
- Fast heart rate  
- Signs of tiredness  
- Blue lips or face  
- Low oxygen levels  
- Dehydration

Oxygen is given if the child’s oxygen level drops below 92%.  
A humidifier helps deliver the oxygen.

Blood tests may be done to check carbon dioxide levels.  
High carbon dioxide levels mean the child is too tired to breathe well.  
This may mean the child needs a breathing tube.

A breathing tube is used if the child cannot breathe on their own.

---

## Key Points

- Croup is a viral infection that affects the voice box and windpipe.  
- It mainly affects children from 6 months to 3 years old.  
- It is most often caused by parainfluenza virus type 1.  
- The main symptoms are a barking cough and stridor.  
- Symptoms are often worse at night.  
- Diagnosis is based on symptoms.  
- A neck X-ray may show a "steeple sign" to confirm the diagnosis.  
- Treatment includes cool, moist air, fluids, and sometimes steroids and epinephrine.  
- Most children recover fully.  
- Antibiotics are not needed.  
- Hospital care is needed for severe cases.

# Apnea of Prematurity – Simple Explanation

This condition happens in babies born too early. It means the baby stops breathing for a short time. This can happen in babies born before 37 weeks of pregnancy.

## What Is Apnea of Prematurity?

- The baby stops breathing for more than 20 seconds.
- Or, the baby stops breathing for less than 20 seconds but also has a slow heart rate (less than 100 beats per minute).
- Or, the baby’s skin turns blue (cyanosis).
- Or, the baby’s oxygen level drops below 85%.

These breathing pauses happen in babies who are born too early and do not have another serious health problem.

### Why Does It Happen?

- The baby’s brain and breathing system are not fully developed.
- This is called central apnea. It means the brain does not send the right signals to breathe.
- If the pause lasts a long time, the baby’s airway may also become blocked. This is called obstructive apnea.
- Sometimes, both types happen together. This is called mixed apnea.

### How Is It Diagnosed?

- Doctors watch the baby closely.
- They use monitors to check breathing and heart rate.
- They check for other serious causes like infections, heart problems, or brain issues.
- If the baby is breathing normally but still has pauses, it may be due to immaturity.

### Important Notes

- Do not assume the baby has apnea of prematurity right away.
- First, rule out other serious problems like infection, low blood sugar, or brain bleeding.
- Gastroesophageal reflux (GERD) does not cause apnea in preterm babies. Do not treat GERD just because of apnea.

## Treatment

- If the baby stops breathing, gently touch or rub them to wake them up.
- If they do not start breathing, give breaths using a bag and mask.
- If the baby has frequent or serious episodes, doctors may give a medicine called caffeine.
  - Caffeine helps the brain control breathing better.
  - It is safe and easy to give.
  - It is the most common treatment.
- If caffeine does not help, the baby may need continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP).
  - CPAP keeps the airway open with gentle air pressure.
- In rare cases, the baby may need a ventilator to help with breathing.

### When Is Treatment Stopped?

- Treatment continues until the baby is 34 to 35 weeks old (measured from the first day of the mother’s last period).
- The baby must not have any apnea that needs physical help for at least 5 to 7 days.
- After stopping treatment, the baby is watched for another 5 to 10 days to make sure no more episodes happen.

### Discharge from Hospital

- Some doctors keep the baby in the hospital for 7 days after stopping treatment.
- Others may let the baby go home with caffeine if it is working well.
- But this is not common.

## Prognosis (Outlook)

- Most babies outgrow apnea of prematurity by 40 weeks after the first day of the mother’s last period.
- By this time, 98 out of 100 preterm babies no longer have apnea.
- Babies born very early (23 to 27 weeks) may have apnea for several weeks.
- Death from this condition is very rare.
- Apnea of prematurity is not linked to sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).

## What Is Not Apnea?

- **Periodic breathing** is normal in babies.
  - It means the baby breathes normally for 5 to 20 seconds, then pauses for less than 20 seconds.
  - It is common in both full-term and preterm babies.
  - It is not dangerous and does not lead to apnea of prematurity.

## Key Points

- Apnea of prematurity is caused by an immature brain and breathing system.
- It can happen in babies born before 37 weeks.
- Breathing pauses may last more than 20 seconds or be shorter but come with a slow heart rate or low oxygen.
- Always check for other serious causes before diagnosing apnea of prematurity.
- Use physical stimulation first when breathing stops.
- If needed, give bag-valve-mask breaths.
- Caffeine is the most common and safest medicine for frequent or serious episodes.
- Do not treat gastroesophageal reflux (GERD) to fix apnea.
- Home monitoring does not improve outcomes.
- Only babies who stop having episodes without help should be considered for going home with a monitor.

# Mammography

A mammogram is an X-ray of the breast.  
It usually takes two or more pictures of each breast from different angles.  
The breast is gently pressed between two plastic plates.  
This helps spread out the breast tissue.  
It makes it easier to see any problems.

## Types of Mammograms

### Screening Mammograms
These are for women who do not have any breast symptoms.  
They are used to check for breast cancer early.  
This is done even if you feel fine.

### Diagnostic Mammograms
These are for women who have breast problems.  
You may need one if you have:
- A lump in your breast
- Breast pain or changes in the skin
- A breast lump that you can feel
- Abnormal results from a screening mammogram

A diagnostic mammogram may include extra views.  
These help the doctor get a clearer picture.

## Who Needs Mammograms?

Women who have no symptoms but have had breast cancer before may have a mammogram every year.  
They may have either a screening or a diagnostic mammogram.  
The choice depends on the rules at the imaging center.

## Radiation and Safety

A mammogram gives a small amount of radiation to the breasts.  
The amount is about 0.21 mSv.  
This is a low level compared to other X-ray tests.  
Still, radiation can be a concern.  
Breast tissue is sensitive to radiation.

For this reason, doctors often suggest mammograms only for women over 40.  
Older women have breast tissue that is less sensitive to radiation.  
Newer machines and digital imaging help lower the radiation dose.  
These tools make the test safer.

# Airway Tumors – Simple Explanation

Tumors can affect the airway in several ways.  
They can start in the airway itself.  
They can grow from nearby tissues and press on or invade the airway.  
Or, cancer from another part of the body can spread to the airway.

## Types of Airway Tumors

Primary tracheal tumors are rare.  
Most of them are cancerous.  
They are often found at a late stage, when they are already large or have spread.  
Other cancers, like thyroid or lung cancer, can grow into the airway.

### Most Common Cancerous Tumors in the Trachea

- Adenoid cystic carcinoma  
- Squamous cell carcinoma  
- Carcinoid tumor  
- Mucoepidermoid carcinoma

### Most Common Benign (Non-Cancerous) Airway Tumor

- Squamous papilloma  
  - This is often caused by a virus called human papillomavirus.

Other non-cancerous tumors can also occur:  
- Pleomorphic adenoma  
- Granular cell tumor  
- Benign cartilage tumor

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

People with airway tumors often have:

- Trouble breathing  
- A persistent cough  
- Wheezing (a whistling sound when breathing)  
- Coughing up blood  
- A high-pitched sound when breathing in (stridor)

Coughing up blood is rare.  
But when it happens, it is more likely with squamous cell carcinoma.  
It can help catch the cancer earlier.  
Wheezing or stridor is more common with adenoid cystic carcinoma.

Other signs like trouble swallowing or a hoarse voice can happen early.  
These usually mean the cancer is already advanced.

---

## How Are Airway Tumors Diagnosed?

A doctor may suspect a tumor if you have:

- Breathing problems that get worse over time  
- A cough that does not go away  
- Wheezing that does not improve with asthma medicine  
- Coughing up blood  
- No clear reason for your symptoms

If a tumor is suspected, you will need a test called **bronchoscopy**.  
This test uses a thin tube with a camera to look inside the airway.  
It can help both diagnose the tumor and treat blockages.  
During the test, the doctor can take a small sample of tissue for testing.

If cancer is found, more tests will be done to see how far it has spread.  
This is called staging.

---

## How Are Airway Tumors Treated?

Treatment depends on the type and stage of the tumor.

### Surgery
- If possible, the tumor is removed with surgery.  
- Common surgeries include removing part of the trachea, the voice box, or the area where the airway splits.  
- Up to half of the trachea can be safely removed and reconnected.  
- If lung or thyroid cancer has spread to the airway, surgery may still be an option if the area can be rebuilt.  
- After surgery, radiation therapy may be used if the cancer was not fully removed.

### Radiation Therapy
- Used when surgery is not possible.  
- Also used after surgery if cancer cells remain.

### Other Treatments to Open the Airway
- **Bronchoscopy**: A doctor can use tools to remove the tumor from inside the airway.  
- **Laser treatment**: Burns away the tumor.  
- **Photodynamic therapy**: Uses light and medicine to destroy cancer cells.  
- **Cryotherapy**: Freezes the tumor to destroy it.  
- **Endobronchial brachytherapy**: A type of radiation placed inside the airway.  
- **Stents**: A small tube placed in the airway to keep it open.  
  - Used when a tumor outside the airway is pressing on it.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

The outcome depends on the type of tumor.

### Squamous Cell Carcinoma
- This cancer often spreads to nearby lymph nodes and nearby tissues.  
- It comes back often after treatment.  
- Even with surgery, less than 40% of people live at least 5 years.

### Adenoid cystic Carcinoma
- This cancer grows slowly.  
- It often spreads to the lungs and along nerves.  
- It comes back after surgery, but slowly.  
- About 60% to 75% of people live at least 5 years because the cancer grows slowly.

---

## Key Points

- Primary tracheal tumors are rare.  
- Most are cancerous.  
- They are often found at a late stage.

- Think about airway tumors if you have:  
  - Breathing problems that get worse over time  
  - A cough that does not go away  
  - Wheezing or stridor  
  - Coughing up blood  
  - No clear cause for your symptoms

- Coughing up blood is rare.  
- It is more likely with squamous cell carcinoma.

- Treat the tumor with surgery if possible.  
- If surgery is not an option, use other treatments to destroy or remove the tumor and open the airway.

# Transient Global Amnesia

Transient global amnesia is a sudden memory problem. It causes confusion about recent events and an inability to form new memories. The memory problem usually lasts less than 24 hours. It often gets better on its own. But it can come back in some people. There is no special treatment unless another health issue is causing it.

## Who Gets It?

- About 3 to 8 out of every 100,000 people get it each year.
- Most people who get it are between 50 and 70 years old.
- The average age is 62.
- Men are slightly more likely to get it than women.

## What Causes It?

The exact cause is not known. But researchers think it may be linked to:

- Migraine-like changes in the brain
- Low oxygen levels in the brain
- Poor blood flow in brain veins
- Seizures
- Strong emotional stress

One theory is that a part of the brain called the hippocampus (which helps with memory) is sensitive to stress. When this area is damaged, memory problems can happen.

A separate, mild form of memory loss can happen after:

- Drinking too much alcohol
- Taking large doses of barbiturates (a type of sedative)
- Using certain illegal drugs
- Taking small doses of some benzodiazepines (like midazolam or triazolam)

This type of memory loss is not serious. It only affects memories from the time of drug use.

## Things That Can Trigger It

Some events may lead to transient global amnesia. These include:

- Jumping into very cold or very hot water
- Heavy physical activity
- Strong emotional stress
- Pain
- Medical procedures
- Sexual activity
- Holding your breath and pushing hard (Valsalva maneuver)

But in most cases, no clear trigger can be found.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main symptom is a sudden loss of memory. This includes:

- Inability to remember new things (anterograde amnesia)
- Trouble remembering recent past events (retrograde amnesia)

Some people may only have trouble remembering the past at first.

- Episodes usually last about 6 hours.
- Most last between 2 and 12 hours.
- Rarely, they can last from 30 minutes to 24 hours.

People often do not know where they are or what day it is. But they still know who they are.

Many people feel anxious or upset. They may keep asking the same questions, like:

- “Where are we?”
- “What happened?”

Their ability to speak, pay attention, understand space, and act socially stays normal.

As the episode ends, memory slowly returns. But they may never remember what happened during the episode.

### The Benign Form After Substance Use

This type of memory loss is different because:

- It only affects memories from the time of drug or alcohol use.
- It is tied to the time of intoxication.
- Once the person is sober, they are not confused.
- It only comes back if they use the same drug again in the same amount.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose transient global amnesia based on:

- The patient’s story
- A physical exam

They also do tests to rule out other serious causes.

### Tests That May Be Done

- **Brain imaging (MRI or CT scan):** To check for stroke or brain tumors.
- **Blood tests:** To check for anemia, clotting problems, or drug use.
- **Electroencephalogram (EEG):** To check for seizures. This test is only needed if seizures are suspected.

### Important: Rule Out Other Conditions

Before diagnosing transient global amnesia, doctors must make sure it is not:

- A stroke in the memory area of the brain
- A seizure-related memory problem
- A memory problem caused by psychological stress
- A memory issue from drugs or toxins
- Memory loss after a head injury

If episodes happen more than once, more testing may be needed.

## How Is It Treated?

- There is no specific treatment for transient global amnesia.
- If another health problem is found (like poor blood flow to the brain), that condition is treated.

## What Is the Outlook?

- The outlook is very good.
- Most people get better within 24 hours.
- Memory returns slowly as the episode ends.
- But people often do not remember what happened during the episode.

- About 15% of people have more than one episode.
- The risk of stroke is not higher than in the general population.

## Key Points

- This condition mostly affects people aged 50 to 70.
- Use a high-quality MRI scan of the brain to rule out other causes, like a stroke.
- Even if memories from the episode are lost, brain function usually returns to normal within 24 hours.
- Most people do not have another episode.

# Rare Inherited Blood Clotting Problems

Most inherited blood clotting problems are rare. They are not hemophilia. These rare conditions are passed down through families in a pattern called autosomal recessive. This means a person must inherit the faulty gene from both parents to have the condition.

Only people who have two copies of the faulty gene will have serious bleeding problems. People with just one copy usually do not have symptoms.

These rare clotting problems can affect clotting factors II, V, VII, X, XI, and XIII. The most common of these is factor XI deficiency.

---

## Factor XI Deficiency

People with low levels of factor XI often do not bleed more when their factor XI level is very low. This means we do not fully understand how factor XI works in normal clotting.

Because of this, your personal history of bleeding is very important. It helps doctors decide how to treat you.

---

## Other Rare Clotting Problems

For most of these rare clotting problems, a person needs more than 20 percent of normal clotting factor levels to stop bleeding normally.

Here is a table that shows the test results and treatment for each condition.

---

### Key Terms

- **PTT**: A blood test that checks how long it takes for blood to clot. A long time means clotting is slow.
- **PT**: A blood test that checks how long it takes for blood to clot. A long time means clotting is slow.
- **Fresh frozen plasma**: Blood plasma frozen soon after collection. It contains many clotting factors.
- **Cryoprecipitate**: A part of plasma rich in fibrinogen and other clotting factors.
- **Recombinant**: Made in a lab using genetic engineering.
- **Plasma-derived**: Made from human blood plasma.
- **Half-life**: How long a substance stays in the body before it breaks down.

---

### Summary

- Most rare inherited clotting problems are rare and need two faulty genes to cause symptoms.
- Factor XI deficiency is the most common of these.
- Your history of bleeding is more important than test results for some conditions.
- Treatment depends on the specific clotting factor missing.
- Some treatments replace the missing factor. Others stop clots from breaking down too soon.
- Always follow your doctor’s advice for testing and treatment.

# DiGeorge Syndrome

DiGeorge syndrome is a condition that a child is born with. It affects the immune system and can cause other health problems.

## What Happens in DiGeorge Syndrome?

- The thymus gland is missing or does not work well.
- The thymus helps make T cells. T cells are a type of white blood cell that fight infections.
- Without enough working T cells, the body cannot fight many infections well.
- Other problems are often present at birth.

### Common Birth Problems

- **Heart issues:** Many babies have a heart defect that is present at birth.
- **Parathyroid glands:** These glands help control calcium in the blood. In DiGeorge syndrome, they are often underdeveloped or missing.
  - Low calcium levels can cause muscle spasms.
  - Spasms usually start within the first two days after birth.
- **Face shape:** Babies often have distinct facial features, such as:
  - Ears that sit low on the head.
  - A small or receding jaw.
  - Eyes that are far apart.
  - A cleft palate (a split in the roof of the mouth).
- **Thymus gland:** This gland is missing or not working. So, the body makes too few T cells.
  - Fewer T cells mean more frequent and serious infections.
  - Infections often start soon after birth and keep coming back.
  - In some children, T cells may improve over time.

The outlook depends mostly on how serious the heart problem is.

## How Is DiGeorge Syndrome Diagnosed?

Doctors look for signs of the condition based on symptoms.

### Tests That Are Done

- **Blood tests:** These check:
  - How many blood cells are in the body.
  - How many T cells and B cells are present.
  - How well T cells work.
  - How well the parathyroid glands work.
  - How well the body makes antibodies after vaccines.
- **Chest x-ray:** This shows the size of the thymus gland.
- **Echocardiography:** This uses sound waves to make pictures of the heart.
  - It helps find heart defects.
- **Genetic tests:** These may be done to look for changes in the genes.

## How Is DiGeorge Syndrome Treated?

### For Children With Some T Cells

- The immune system may work well enough without treatment.
- Infections are treated right away when they happen.
- Calcium and vitamin D supplements are given by mouth.
  - These help prevent muscle spasms from low calcium.

### For Children With No T Cells

- Without treatment, the condition is life-threatening.
- A transplant of thymus tissue is needed to save the child’s life.
  - The thymus tissue is grown in a lab before transplant.
  - It is treated to remove mature T cells.
    - This prevents a serious problem called graft-versus-host disease.
    - This happens when donor T cells attack the child’s body.
- Stem cell transplant is another option.
  - This can also help fix the immune system.

### Heart Problems

- Sometimes the heart issue is more serious than the immune problem.
- Surgery may be needed to fix the heart.
- This can prevent heart failure or death.

# Heart Disease During Pregnancy

Heart problems are a leading cause of death during pregnancy.  
About one in four pregnancy-related deaths are due to heart conditions.  
In the United States, most heart issues in pregnancy come from birth defects in the heart.  
In parts of Southeast Asia, Africa, India, the Middle East, and some areas of Australia and New Zealand, a different kind of heart disease—rheumatic heart disease—is still common.

Even though many people with serious heart problems now live longer and better lives, pregnancy can still be very risky for some women.  
Pregnancy is not safe for women with certain high-risk heart conditions. These include:

- High blood pressure in the lungs (pulmonary hypertension) from any cause, including Eisenmenger syndrome  
- Narrowing of the aorta (coarctation of the aorta) if not fixed or if there is a bulge in the artery  
- Marfan syndrome with a large aorta (more than 4.5 centimeters wide)  
- Severe narrowing of the aortic valve (aortic stenosis)  
- Severe narrowing of the mitral valve (mitral stenosis)  
- A bicuspid aortic valve with a large ascending aorta (more than 50 millimeters wide)  
- A heart with only one working pumping chamber and weak heart function, whether or not the person had the Fontan procedure  
- Heart muscle disease (cardiomyopathy) with weak heart pumping (ejection fraction below 30%) or severe heart failure (New York Heart Association class III or IV)

---

## How Pregnancy Affects the Heart

Pregnancy puts extra strain on the heart.  
This strain can make existing heart problems worse.  
Some women may first notice heart problems during pregnancy.

The body changes in pregnancy.  
Blood volume goes up.  
The heart pumps more blood with each beat.  
Heart rate increases.  
Cardiac output (how much blood the heart pumps per minute) goes up by 30% to 50%.  
These changes peak between 28 and 34 weeks of pregnancy.

During labor, each contraction of the uterus raises cardiac output by about 20%.  
Pushing during the second stage of labor adds more stress.  
The blood returning to the heart increases because the uterus squeezes blood vessels.  
These heart stresses do not return to normal until several weeks after delivery.

---

## Signs and Symptoms of Heart Problems in Pregnancy

Some signs of heart problems can also happen in normal pregnancy.  
These include:

- Shortness of breath  
- Fast heartbeat  
- Swelling in the legs or ankles  
- A heart murmur (a sound heard through a stethoscope)  
- Swollen neck veins  
- A slightly enlarged heart seen on a chest X-ray

Murmurs that happen during the relaxation phase of the heartbeat (diastolic or presystolic) are more likely to mean a real heart problem.

Heart failure can lead to early labor or irregular heartbeats.  
The risk to mother or baby depends on how much physical activity causes symptoms.  
This is measured using the New York Heart Association (NYHA) classification.

The risk is higher if:

- Symptoms happen with light activity (NYHA class III)  
- Symptoms happen with little or no activity (NYHA class IV)

---

## How Heart Disease Is Diagnosed in Pregnancy

Diagnosis starts with a detailed medical history and physical exam.  
An echocardiogram (a heart ultrasound) is usually done.  
This test shows how well the heart is working.

Heart disease can run in families.  
Women with congenital heart disease should be offered genetic counseling.  
Fetal echocardiography may also be offered to check the baby’s heart.

---

## Treating Heart Disease During Pregnancy

Certain medicines are not safe during pregnancy.  
These include:

- Warfarin  
- ACE inhibitors  
- ARBs (angiotensin II receptor blockers)  
- Aldosterone antagonists (like spironolactone and eplerenone)  
- Thiazide diuretics  
- Some antiarrhythmia drugs (like amiodarone)

These medicines can harm the baby.  
They should be avoided.

For women with NYHA class III or IV heart failure:  
- Limit physical activity  
- Rest in bed or limit movement after 20 weeks

Most other treatments for heart failure and irregular heartbeats are used as in non-pregnant patients.  
But the doctor will choose safe options.

All pregnant women with heart disease need:

- Regular prenatal visits  
- Plenty of rest  
- Avoidance of gaining too much weight  
- Treatment of anemia (low red blood cells)

An anesthesiologist with experience in heart disease during pregnancy should be involved.  
They should be consulted before delivery.  
During labor, pain and anxiety are treated quickly to prevent a fast heartbeat.

Women are closely watched right after delivery.  
They continue to be followed by a heart doctor for several weeks after giving birth.

Before pregnancy, women with NYHA class III or IV heart failure should have their heart condition treated as well as possible.  
If needed, surgery should be done before conception.  
For women with severe heart disease or other high-risk conditions, early pregnancy termination may be advised.

Some women with poor heart function need:

- Digoxin (0.25 mg by mouth once daily)  
- Bed rest or limited activity starting at 20 weeks

Digoxin passes into the baby’s bloodstream.  
But newborns and children are less likely to be harmed by it.

ACE inhibitors and ARBs are not safe.  
They can damage the baby’s kidneys.

Aldosterone antagonists (like spironolactone and eplerenone) should be avoided.  
They can cause male babies to develop female traits.

Other heart failure treatments (like nonthiazide diuretics, nitrates, inotropes) may be continued during pregnancy.  
The decision depends on how serious the heart problem is and the risk to the baby.  
This is decided by a heart doctor and a pregnancy specialist.

---

## Key Points

- Pregnancy is not safe for women with certain serious heart conditions.  
  These include:  
  - High blood pressure in the lungs  
  - Unfixed narrowing of the aorta  
  - Marfan syndrome with a large aorta  
  - Severe aortic or mitral valve narrowing  
  - A bicuspid aortic valve with a large aorta  
  - A heart with one pumping chamber and weak function  
  - Heart muscle disease with weak pumping or severe heart failure

- Treat heart failure and irregular heartbeats during pregnancy like in non-pregnant women.  
  But avoid certain medicines: warfarin, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, aldosterone antagonists, thiazide diuretics, and some antiarrhythmics like amiodarone.

- Most pregnant women with atrial fibrillation (an irregular heartbeat) are treated with heparin (standard or low molecular weight).

- Preventive antibiotics (endocarditis prophylaxis) are needed in the same situations as for non-pregnant people with heart defects.

---

## Valve Problems During Pregnancy

Valve problems most often affect the mitral and aortic valves.  
Mitral stenosis is the most common valve issue in pregnancy.

Pregnancy makes the sounds from mitral and aortic stenosis louder.  
But it makes the sounds from mitral and aortic regurgitation (leaking valves) quieter.

Mild regurgitation is usually well tolerated.  
Stenosis (narrowing) is harder to handle.  
It can lead to serious problems for both mother and baby.

Mitral stenosis is especially dangerous.  
The fast heartbeat, extra blood volume, and higher heart output during pregnancy can quickly raise pressure in the lungs.  
This can cause fluid to build up in the lungs (pulmonary edema).

Atrial fibrillation (an irregular heartbeat) is also common in these women.

Treatment for mitral stenosis includes:

- Preventing a fast heartbeat  
- Treating fluid in the lungs  
- Treating atrial fibrillation  
- Sometimes surgery to open the valve (valvotomy)

For aortic stenosis:  
- Surgery before pregnancy is best if possible.

Ideally, valve problems are found and treated before pregnancy.  
Surgery is often recommended for severe cases.  
Antibiotics may be needed to prevent infection of the heart valves (endocarditis prophylaxis).

---

## Other Heart Conditions in Pregnancy

Other heart problems can also happen during pregnancy.  
These include congenital heart defects, arrhythmias, and heart muscle disease.  
Each case needs careful planning and monitoring.  
A team of specialists should manage care.

# Physical Therapy (PT)

Physical therapy helps people recover movement and function after injury, illness, or surgery. It focuses on the back, arms, and legs. The goal is to help you stand, balance, walk, and climb stairs more easily.

Therapists use many types of exercises and hands-on techniques. These include:

- Moving joints through their full range
- Building muscle strength
- Improving balance and coordination
- Practicing walking
- Getting the body ready for daily activities
- Learning how to move safely from one place to another
- Using a special table to help with standing

---

## Range-of-Motion Exercises

After a stroke or long time in bed, joints can become stiff. This can cause pain and make daily tasks harder. It can also lead to skin sores.

Stiffness is common with age, but most older adults can still care for themselves.

### How Therapists Help with Stiff Joints

A therapist holds your shoulder steady with one hand. With the other hand, they slowly raise your elbow as high as it can go. Over time, they raise it a little higher each session.

Before treatment, the therapist measures how far your joint can move. They use a tool called a goniometer. This helps track progress.

The therapist checks if stiffness comes from tight muscles or tight connective tissues (like ligaments and tendons).  
- If muscles are tight, the therapist can stretch them more firmly.  
- If tendons or ligaments are tight, gentle stretching is used. Sometimes surgery is needed first.

Warmth helps tissues stretch better and causes less pain. Therapists often use heat before stretching.

There are three types of range-of-motion exercises:

### Active Exercise  
You move your own limbs. You do this without help.

### Active-Assistive Exercise  
You try to move your limbs, but need a little help. A therapist may guide your arm or leg. Or they may use bands or other tools to help.

### Passive Exercise  
You do not move at all. The therapist moves your limbs for you. This helps prevent muscles from becoming permanently stiff.

Active-assistive and passive exercises are done gently. Some discomfort may happen, but it should not be severe.

To improve movement, the therapist moves the joint past the point of pain. But the movement should not cause pain that lasts after it stops.  
Slow, steady stretching works better than quick, hard pulls.

---

## Muscle-Strengthening Exercises

These exercises build stronger muscles. They work by slowly increasing resistance.

- When muscles are very weak, just moving against gravity helps.  
- As strength improves, therapists add resistance using stretchy bands or light weights.  

Over time, muscles grow bigger and stronger. You also gain more energy and endurance.

---

## Coordination and Balance Exercises

These help people who have trouble moving smoothly or staying upright. This often happens after a stroke or brain injury.

### Coordination Exercises  
You repeat useful movements. These involve more than one joint and muscle.  
Examples:  
- Picking up a cup  
- Touching your nose with your finger  

### Balance Exercises  
You start by holding onto parallel bars. A therapist stands right behind you.

You shift your weight side to side. Then, you shift forward and backward.  
Once you can do this safely, you practice without the bars.

---

## Walking Exercises (Ambulation)

Walking—on your own or with help—is often the main goal of therapy.

Before walking, you must be able to stand and balance.

You start by holding onto parallel bars. You shift your weight from side to side and front to back. The therapist stands in front or behind you to keep you safe.

Some people need more work on joint movement or muscle strength before walking. Some may need a brace or other support.

### Did You Know?

For people who struggle to walk, learning to move safely from bed to chair or from a wheelchair to the toilet can make a big difference. It helps them live on their own.

When ready, you start walking with parallel bars. Then you move to a walker, crutches, or a cane. Some people wear a special belt that the therapist can hold to prevent falls.

Once you can walk safely on flat ground, you learn to step over curbs or climb stairs.

- To go **up** stairs: Step up with your stronger leg first.  
- To go **down** stairs: Step down with your weaker leg first.

Remember: “Good leg up, bad leg down.”

Family members and caregivers should learn how to support you properly.

### How to Help Someone Walk

If someone needs help walking:

- Place your arm under their arm.  
- Grip their forearm gently.  
- Lock your arm by pressing your upper arm firmly against theirs.  
- This gives support at the shoulder if they start to fall.

Some people wear a special belt. Caregivers can grab the back of the belt to steady them.

---

## General Conditioning Exercises

These combine range-of-motion, strength, and walking exercises. They help people recover after being in bed for a long time.

They improve heart and lung health. They also help keep muscles strong and flexible.

---

## Transfer Training

This teaches people how to move safely between places. It is very important for people who have had a hip fracture, lost a limb, or had a stroke.

Being able to move from bed to chair, chair to toilet, or sitting to standing helps you stay at home.

If you cannot move on your own, you may need full-time help.

Caregivers can use special tools like a gait belt or harness to help.

The method used depends on:

- Can you put weight on one or both legs?  
- Can you balance well?  
- Are you paralyzed on one side?

Some tools can help. For example:
- A seat-lifting chair helps people stand up more easily.  
- A chair with a higher seat makes it easier to get up.

---

## Tilt Table

Some people feel dizzy when they stand up. This can happen after long bed rest or after a spinal cord injury. It is called orthostatic hypotension.

A tilt table helps the body adjust to standing.

You lie on your back on a padded table. A footboard and safety belt keep you in place. The table tilts slowly upward. The speed depends on how you feel.

The slow change helps your blood vessels learn to tighten and loosen properly. This helps control blood pressure when you change position.

You stay in the upright position for a short time. This should not last more than 45 minutes.

The tilt table is used once or twice a day. Results vary depending on the type and level of disability.

---

It explains the benefits of physical therapy.  
It also shows how to choose a good physical therapist.

# What Are Anxiety Disorders?

Anxiety disorders are long-lasting and strong feelings of fear and worry. They can lead to changes in how a person acts to try to feel safer. Each type of anxiety disorder is different. The differences come from what triggers the fear, the worry, and the actions a person takes to cope.

Everyone feels afraid or worried sometimes. That is normal.

**Fear** happens when you face a clear danger right now. For example, if a stranger enters your home or a car skids on ice.

**Anxiety** is a feeling of unease or nervousness. It is not always tied to a clear danger. You might feel anxious before a big event, after a scary moment, or even when nothing obvious is wrong.

Anxiety can cause physical changes. You might sweat, feel sick to your stomach, or have a racing heart. It can also change your behavior. You might avoid certain places, become angry, or act tense. Many people notice these changes but do not realize they are feeling anxious or afraid.

Some anxiety is helpful. It can push you to prepare, practice, or stay careful in risky situations. But when anxiety gets too strong, it causes serious problems. It can make daily life hard. When this happens, it is no longer normal. It is a mental health condition.

Anxiety disorders are the most common type of mental health problem. About one in three people will have one at some point in their life. But many people with anxiety do not get diagnosed. Anxiety can lead to thoughts about suicide or even suicide attempts.

The *Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders*, 5th edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR), lists the main types of anxiety disorders. They are listed roughly by when they usually start:

- **Separation anxiety disorder** – starts in childhood
- **Selective mutism** – starts in childhood
- **Specific phobia** – fear of animals, nature, blood, injections, or certain situations
- **Social anxiety disorder** – fear of being judged in social settings
- **Panic disorder** – sudden, intense panic attacks
- **Agoraphobia** – fear of being in places where escape might be hard
- **Generalized anxiety disorder** – constant, ongoing worry about many things
- **Substance-induced/medication-induced anxiety disorder** – caused by drugs or medicine
- **Anxiety due to another medical condition** – caused by a physical illness
- **Other specified anxiety disorder** – when symptoms are serious but do not fit any other category

Separation anxiety and selective mutism usually start in childhood. The other types usually begin in adulthood.

Always think about substance-induced or medical causes when someone has strong anxiety. Some medicines and health problems can cause anxiety.

Other mental health conditions often include strong anxiety. These include:

- Acute stress disorder
- Adjustment disorders
- Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD)

These are grouped separately in the DSM-5-TR because they come from trauma or very stressful events.

Anxiety disorders often happen with other health problems. Common ones include:

- Depression
- Substance use problems
- Personality disorders
- Other anxiety disorders
- Heart disease
- Asthma
- Migraine headaches
- Arthritis

Anxiety often comes before these other problems. Treating anxiety early can help prevent or reduce the chance of other issues later.

## What Causes Anxiety Disorders?

There is no single cause for anxiety disorders. They develop from a mix of biology, psychology, and life experiences.

Anxiety can run in families. Two main reasons are:

- A child may be born with a natural tendency to be shy or cautious. This trait is linked to a higher risk of anxiety later.
- Children can learn fear from their parents. They may also develop anxiety after early trauma, such as abuse or serious illness like asthma. These experiences may make a child more aware of their body and emotions. This can lead to panic attacks or social anxiety.

Many people develop anxiety without any clear cause. For example, most people with a fear of snakes have never been bitten. They did not have a scary experience with a snake.

Adults can also develop anxiety after stressful life events. These might include the end of a close relationship or surviving a disaster. But most people who go through such events do not develop an anxiety disorder.

Chemicals in the brain play a big role. The main ones are:

- GABA – helps calm the brain
- Glutamate – can increase alertness and worry
- Serotonin – affects mood
- Norepinephrine – affects energy and alertness
- Dopamine – affects motivation and reward

These brain chemicals help doctors choose the right medicine.

Some health problems can cause anxiety. These include:

- Asthma
- Irregular heartbeats
- Chronic lung disease (COPD)
- Heart failure
- Overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism)
- Cushing syndrome
- Tumors in the adrenal glands (pheochromocytoma)

Some medicines used to treat other health problems can also cause anxiety. These include:

- Asthma medicines: albuterol, corticosteroids, theophylline
- ADHD medicines: amphetamines and other stimulants
- Thyroid medicines: levothyroxine, liothyronine
- Allergy medicines: antihistamines and decongestants
- Seizure medicines: phenytoin
- Parkinson’s disease medicines: levodopa

Some substances and illegal drugs can cause anxiety. These include:

- Caffeine
- Cocaine
- MDMA (ecstasy)

Even some drugs meant to relax you can cause anxiety. For example, cannabis (marijuana) can make some people anxious. This can happen because of the drug itself or because it is mixed with another substance like PCP.

Stopping alcohol, sedatives, or other drugs can also cause anxiety.

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

Anxiety disorders are different from normal worry. They last longer than six months. They are too strong. They make life hard and cause real discomfort.

Anxiety can cause many physical symptoms. These include:

- Stomach problems: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea
- Breathing issues: shortness of breath, feeling like you are choking
- Body reactions: dizziness, feeling faint, sweating, hot or cold flashes
- Heart problems: fast heartbeat, heart pounding
- Muscle problems: tight muscles, chest pain or tightness

Keeping a diary of your anxiety and panic attacks can help. It helps you remember what happened. It also helps your doctor plan your treatment.

## How Are Anxiety Disorders Diagnosed?

Diagnosis is based on the DSM-5-TR guidelines. A doctor may suspect an anxiety disorder if:

- The anxiety causes strong distress.
- The anxiety gets in the way of daily life.
- The anxiety does not go away on its own in a few days.
- No other clear cause is found.

It is very important to check for other causes. These include:

- Medical problems like asthma or an overactive thyroid
- Medicines or illegal drugs

The doctor must also decide if the medical problem or substance is actually causing the anxiety.

If the anxiety is clearly caused by a medicine or drug, the diagnosis is **substance-/medication-induced anxiety disorder**.

If the anxiety is clearly caused by another health problem, the diagnosis is **anxiety disorder due to another medical condition**.

There are no blood tests or scans to diagnose anxiety disorders. But tests can help find medical problems that cause anxiety.

Diagnosis depends on a careful history. The doctor will ask about your symptoms, how long they last, and how they affect your life.

To tell one anxiety disorder from another, doctors often ask three key questions:

1. What situations make you feel afraid or worried?
2. What thoughts go through your mind when you feel anxious?
3. What do you do to avoid the anxiety?

## How Are Anxiety Disorders Treated?

Treatment works for most people. The main options are:

- Learning about anxiety (psychoeducation)
- Relaxation techniques
- Talking therapy, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT)
- Medicines (like benzodiazepines and SSRIs)

Important points to remember:

- Many types of treatment help with anxiety.
- Most people can be treated in a regular doctor’s office.
- It is important to know exactly which anxiety disorder you have. It is also important to know if you have other health problems.
- Treat any medical conditions that might be making anxiety worse. For example, treat asthma well.
- If you use alcohol or drugs, treat that at the same time as anxiety. People often use these to feel better. But stopping them can make anxiety worse.
- Exercise, good sleep, and cutting back on caffeine can help reduce anxiety.
- Your treatment plan should match your preferences and what care is available to you.
- Talking therapy and medicine work best when used together. This is true for most anxiety disorders.

# The Ears

The ears help you hear and stay balanced.  
They have three main parts: the outer ear, the middle ear, and the inner ear.  
All three parts work together to turn sound into signals your brain can understand.

---

## How the Ears Work

The outer ear catches sound waves.  
It funnels them through the ear canal to the eardrum.  
The eardrum vibrates when sound hits it.  
These vibrations move through the middle ear.  
In the middle ear, three tiny bones carry the vibrations to the inner ear.  
The inner ear turns the vibrations into nerve signals.  
These signals travel to the brain.  
The brain then turns the signals into sound.

The inner ear also helps you keep your balance.

---

## The Outer Ear

The outer ear is the part you can see.  
It is also called the pinna or auricle.  
It is made of cartilage covered with skin.  
Its shape helps catch sound and send it into the ear canal.  
The ear canal leads to the eardrum.  
The eardrum is a thin membrane.  
It separates the outer ear from the middle ear.

---

## The Middle Ear

The middle ear has the eardrum and a small air-filled space.  
Inside this space are three tiny bones.  
They are called the hammer, the anvil, and the stirrup.  
The hammer is attached to the eardrum.  
The anvil sits between the hammer and the stirrup.  
The stirrup fits into a small opening called the oval window.  
The bones help make sound louder as they pass it along.

Two small muscles are in the middle ear.  
The tensor tympani muscle is attached to the hammer.  
It tightens the eardrum to protect it from loud body sounds.  
The stapedius muscle is attached to the stirrup.  
When a loud noise happens, this muscle tightens.  
It makes the bones stiffer.  
This reduces how much sound gets through.  
This is called the acoustic reflex.  
It helps protect the inner ear from damage.

A small tube called the eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the back of the nose.  
It opens when you swallow, chew, or yawn.  
It lets air in and out of the middle ear.  
This keeps the pressure on both sides of the eardrum equal.  
If pressure is not equal, the eardrum can bulge or pull in.  
This can hurt and make hearing hard.  
You can relieve pressure by swallowing or "popping" your ears.  
This often helps when flying in an airplane.

The eustachian tube can get blocked during a cold or other upper respiratory infection.  
When it is blocked, fluid can build up in the middle ear.  
This fluid can become infected and cause pain.

---

## The Inner Ear

The inner ear has two main parts:  
- The cochlea – the part that helps you hear  
- The vestibular system – the part that helps you stay balanced

### The Cochlea

The cochlea is a small, coiled tube shaped like a snail shell.  
It is filled with fluid.  
Inside the cochlea is a structure called the organ of Corti.  
This contains about 20,000 special cells called hair cells.  
These cells have tiny hairlike parts called cilia.  
The cilia stick into the fluid.  
When sound vibrations reach the cochlea, they move the fluid.  
This makes the cilia move.  
The movement creates nerve signals.  
These signals go to the brain and are heard as sound.

Different parts of the cochlea respond to different sound pitches.  
High sounds affect hair cells near the round window.  
Low sounds affect hair cells near the top of the cochlea.  
If you uncoiled the cochlea, it would look like a piano keyboard.

The nerve signals travel along the cochlear nerve to the brain.  
The round window is a small, flexible opening.  
It connects the fluid-filled cochlea to the middle ear.  
It helps reduce pressure from sound waves.

Even with the protection of the acoustic reflex, loud noise can harm the hair cells.  
Once a hair cell is damaged, it does not grow back.  
Repeated exposure to loud noise causes more damage over time.  
This can lead to hearing loss.  
It can also cause ringing in the ears, called tinnitus.

### The Vestibular System

The vestibular system helps you stay balanced.  
It has two parts:  
- Two small fluid-filled sacs called the saccule and the utricle  
- Three fluid-filled tubes called the semicircular canals

The saccule and utricle sense movement in a straight line.  
They detect up and down or back and forth motion.

The semicircular canals are three tubes at right angles to each other.  
They sense head rotation.  
When you turn your head, the fluid inside the canals moves.  
The movement is stronger in one canal than the others, depending on the direction.  
Hair cells in the canals detect this movement.  
They send signals to the brain.  
The brain uses this information to help you stay balanced.

If the semicircular canals do not work right, you may lose your balance.  
You might feel dizzy or like you are spinning.  
This is called vertigo.  
It can happen during a cold or other illness.  
It can also happen due to other temporary or long-term problems.

# Cervical Insufficiency

Cervical insufficiency means the neck of the womb opens too early during pregnancy.  
This can lead to losing the baby in the second trimester.  
The opening happens without pain or contractions.  
It used to be called cervical incompetence.

## What Causes Cervical Insufficiency?

We do not fully understand what causes it.  
It may be due to weak or abnormal structure in the cervix.  
It might also be linked to inflammation or infection.  
These problems can be inherited or happen during life.

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

Most women do not feel anything until it is too late.  
Some women may feel pressure in the vagina.  
Others may notice light bleeding or spotting.  
Some have vague pain in the lower belly or back.  
Some have more vaginal discharge.

The cervix may feel soft.  
It may be thinning out or opening.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors may use a special ultrasound test through the vagina.  
This test checks the cervix from week 15 to week 24 of pregnancy.  
It is used if a woman has symptoms or risk factors.

Most women are not diagnosed until they have had at least one second-trimester loss.  
Doctors suspect cervical insufficiency if a woman has risk factors or certain signs.

If the diagnosis is unclear, doctors may do repeated ultrasounds.  
They check the length of the cervix every few weeks.  
This helps track changes.

Signs on ultrasound that suggest cervical insufficiency include:

- The cervix is 2.5 centimeters or shorter.  
- The cervix is opening.  
- The sac around the baby is pushing into the cervix.

## How Is It Treated?

The main treatment is a surgery called cervical cerclage.  
This means sewing the cervix closed with strong thread.  
The thread does not dissolve and stays in place.

Cerclage helps prevent early delivery in women who have had two or more second-trimester losses.  
It may be done based on past history alone.  
It may also be done based on ultrasound results and history.  
Or it may be done if the cervix is already opening during a physical exam.

### When Is Cerclage Done?

If a woman has a history of two or more second-trimester losses,  
cerclage is usually done in the first trimester.  
It can also be done before pregnancy starts.

If a woman is being watched with ultrasounds,  
cerclage is often done if the cervix is less than 2.5 centimeters long before week 24.  
This helps avoid unnecessary surgery.  
It also lowers the risk of early delivery.

Cerclage may help women who have had a previous early delivery with no clear cause.  
If the cervix is less than 2.0 to 2.5 centimeters long, cerclage may help.

If the cervix is already open and confirmed by exam,  
cerclage may be done in some women before week 24.  
But only if the procedure is possible and there are no signs of infection, bleeding, or labor.

This decision is not always clear.  
It depends on the doctor’s judgment and the woman’s choices.

If early labor is suspected after week 22 or 23,  
the baby’s lungs may be helped with medicine.  
The woman may also be told to rest more.

## Key Points

- Cervical insufficiency means the cervix opens too early.  
- This can cause loss of the baby in the second trimester.  
- It happens without pain or contractions.

- We usually cannot predict it before a woman has had a second-trimester loss.

- If a woman has risk factors or symptoms, do a vaginal ultrasound after week 15.

- Signs of cervical insufficiency on ultrasound:  
  - Cervix is 2.5 centimeters or shorter.  
  - Cervix is opening.  
  - The baby’s sac is pushing into the cervix.

- Treat women at risk with cervical cerclage.

# Feverfew

Feverfew is a plant with small leaves. People use the dried leaves to make capsules, tablets, and liquid extracts.

The parts of feverfew that may work in the body are called parthenolides and glycosides.

## What People Use Feverfew For

Many people take feverfew to help stop migraine headaches from happening.  
It is also used to reduce swelling and inflammation.  
Some people use it to feel better emotionally.  
It has been tried for asthma, pain during periods, skin redness and swelling (rosacea), joint pain (arthritis), and to fight cancer. But there is not strong proof for most of these uses.

## What Science Says About Feverfew

Six different studies looked at whether feverfew helps prevent migraines.  
The results were mixed.  
But one larger recent study did find a small drop in the number of migraines each month.  
The differences in results may be because the studies used different forms or amounts of feverfew.  
Newer studies are testing feverfew with other supplements like magnesium and CoQ10.

Studies on people with arthritis found that feverfew did not help with pain or swelling.  
There is no strong scientific proof that feverfew helps with any other health claims.

## Side Effects of Feverfew

Some people get mouth sores when taking feverfew.  
Others may get skin irritation or rashes.  
It can also cause mild stomach upset.  
Feverfew may change how food tastes.  
It may also make your heart beat faster.

Feverfew is not safe for children.  
It should not be used by women who are pregnant or breastfeeding.  
In pregnant women, feverfew may cause the uterus to tighten. This could lead to a miscarriage.  
It may also cause allergic skin rashes.

If you stop taking feverfew suddenly, your migraines may get worse.  
You might also feel nervous or have trouble sleeping.

People who are allergic to ragweed or plants like daisies, marigolds, or chrysanthemums may also react badly to feverfew.

Because feverfew can increase the risk of bleeding, stop taking it at least two weeks before any surgery.

## Interactions with Medicines

Feverfew may interact with blood-thinning medicines.  
It may also interact with medicines used to treat migraines.  
It can also affect nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), like ibuprofen or naproxen.  
Feverfew may make blood less able to clot by affecting platelets, which are parts of the blood that help stop bleeding.

## Advice on Using Feverfew

Feverfew might slightly reduce how often migraines happen.  
But any benefit is likely small.

Talk to your doctor before using feverfew if you:  
- Have hay fever or allergies to ragweed or related plants  
- Take blood-thinning medicines  
- Use medicines for migraines  
- Take nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)

Pregnant women should not take feverfew.
