# Niacin Deficiency

Niacin deficiency is rare in countries where people have enough to eat.  
When it does happen, it causes a condition called pellagra.  
Pellagra has three main signs: a skin rash, stomach and bowel problems, and brain and nerve issues.  

The skin rash often appears on areas exposed to sunlight.  
It can look scaly and turn dark or red.  
You may also have diarrhea and trouble thinking clearly.  
These symptoms can happen alone or together.  

Doctors usually diagnose niacin deficiency by looking at your symptoms.  
Treatment with niacin works well in most cases.  

---

## What Is Niacin?

Niacin is a type of vitamin.  
It helps your body turn food into energy.  
It is part of two important chemicals in your cells: NAD and NADP.  
These chemicals help your body’s cells work properly.  

You can get niacin from food.  
Good sources include liver, red meat, fish, chicken, beans, and whole grains.  
Some breads and cereals are also enriched with niacin.  

You can also get niacin from tryptophan, another substance in food.  
Tryptophan is found in dairy products like milk and cheese.  
So, if you do not eat enough niacin, foods with tryptophan can help make up for it.  

---

## Why Does Niacin Deficiency Happen?

### Primary Niacin Deficiency

This happens when you do not eat enough niacin or tryptophan.  
It is most common in places where people eat a lot of corn (maize).  
Corn has a form of niacin that your body cannot use unless it is treated with an alkali.  
This treatment is used when making tortillas.  
Without this step, the niacin in corn stays locked and cannot be absorbed.  

Corn protein also has very little tryptophan.  
This makes it harder for your body to make niacin from food.  

In some areas, people eat millet that has a lot of leucine.  
This may cause an imbalance in amino acids.  
This imbalance may make niacin deficiency worse.  

People with primary niacin deficiency often lack other B vitamins and protein too.  

### Secondary Niacin Deficiency

This happens when your body cannot use niacin properly.  
It can be caused by:  
- Long-term diarrhea  
- Liver disease (cirrhosis)  
- Heavy drinking of alcohol  

Pellagra can also happen in:  
- Carcinoid syndrome — when the body uses tryptophan to make other chemicals instead of niacin  
- Hartnup disease — when your body cannot absorb tryptophan from food  

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

### Skin Problems

You may get a rash that is red, scaly, and dark.  
The rash often appears on skin that is exposed to sunlight.  
It can look like a glove on the hands or a boot on the feet.  
You may also get a rash around the neck that looks like a necklace.  
This is called Casal necklace.  
The rash can also form a butterfly shape on the face.  

The rash gets worse when you are in the sun.  
It may be itchy or painful.  

### Mouth and Throat Problems

Your mouth may hurt.  
Your tongue may become red and swollen.  
You may have sores in your mouth.  
These sores can appear under your tongue, on your lips, or near your back teeth.  
You may also make more saliva than normal.  

### Stomach and Bowel Problems

You may feel a burning in your throat or chest.  
You may have stomach pain or bloating.  
Constipation is common.  
Later, you may feel sick to your stomach, vomit, or have diarrhea.  
The diarrhea may be bloody because the lining of your intestines becomes inflamed and breaks down.  

### Brain and Nerve Problems

You may have trouble thinking clearly.  
You may forget things, feel confused, or lose your sense of time and place.  
You may act strangely or have mood changes.  
You might feel very excited, very sad, or very anxious.  
You may have hallucinations or delusions.  
You may become disoriented or lose awareness of your surroundings.  

There is no clear proof that niacin levels affect blood pressure.  

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your symptoms to make a diagnosis.  
If you have a rash, mouth sores, diarrhea, and confusion, it is likely niacin deficiency.  

But sometimes the symptoms are not clear.  
Then, your doctor may ask about your diet.  
A history of eating little niacin or tryptophan can help.  

A good response to niacin treatment can confirm the diagnosis.  

Lab tests can help if the diagnosis is still unclear.  
A urine test can check how much niacin your body is using.  
Low levels of a substance called NMN in the urine suggest a niacin deficiency.  

---

## How Is It Treated?

The main treatment is niacin.  
The form called nicotinamide is used most often.  
It works well and does not cause flushing, itching, or tingling.  

You take nicotinamide by mouth.  
The usual dose is 250 to 500 milligrams each day.  

Because many people with niacin deficiency also lack other nutrients,  
a healthy diet with other B vitamins is important.  
This includes vitamins like riboflavin and pyridoxine.  

---

## Key Points

- Niacin deficiency causes pellagra.  
- It is most common in places where people do not have enough food.  
- Pellagra causes a rash that gets worse in sunlight, mouth sores, stomach problems, and brain issues.  
- Doctors usually diagnose it by looking at your symptoms.  
- Nicotinamide is the best treatment.  
- A good response to treatment helps confirm the diagnosis.

# Injection Drug Use

Drugs can be taken in different ways. You can swallow them, smoke them, snort them through the nose, or inject them. When you inject drugs, the effects come faster and are stronger.

There are three main ways to inject drugs:
- Into a vein (this is called intravenous injection).
- Into a muscle (this is called intramuscular injection).
- Under the skin (this is called subcutaneous injection).

Most people use the veins in their arms for intravenous injections. But if those veins get damaged from repeated use, some people switch to other veins. These can be in the thigh, neck, armpit, or feet.

(See also: Drug Use and Abuse.)

---

## Risks of Injecting Drugs

Injecting drugs is riskier than other ways of using drugs. You face not only the dangers of the drug itself but also the dangers of the injection process.

### Adulterants

Adulterants are extra substances added to drugs. They are often added without the user knowing. This is done to save money or to make the drug easier to use.

You do not know what you are getting. In street drugs like heroin or cocaine, these added substances can make the drug stronger or change how it affects your mind.

Some common adulterants include:
- Amphetamine
- Dextromethorphan
- Fentanyl
- Ketamine
- LSD

Each of these has its own effects. This makes it hard to know exactly what drug someone has used. Some adulterants are very strong. They can cause serious harm or even overdose.

### Fillers

Some people crush prescription pills, dissolve them in water, and inject the liquid. The pills contain fillers like cellulose, talc, or cornstarch. These fillers are not meant to be injected.

When injected, these fillers can get stuck in the lungs. This causes inflammation and can damage lung tissue.

Fillers can also harm the heart. They may damage the heart valves. This increases the risk of infection in the heart, a serious condition called endocarditis.

### Bacteria and Viruses

Using dirty needles, especially needles that someone else has used, can bring harmful germs into your body.

These germs can cause abscesses near the injection site. They can also travel through your blood to other parts of your body. This can lead to infections in the lungs, heart, brain, liver, or bones.

Infection of the heart valves (endocarditis) is a common and serious problem for people who inject drugs.

You can also get serious infections like botulism or tetanus through the injection site.

Sharing needles spreads dangerous infections. These include hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV.

### Injuries from Needles

Repeated bad injections can cause long-term damage.

- **Drug abuser’s elbow** happens when repeated needle use injures the muscle near the elbow. Over time, the muscle turns into scar tissue.
- **Skin sores** can form from injections under the skin (called skin popping).
- **Track marks** appear from repeated intravenous injections. These are lines of small dark dots (from needle holes) surrounded by dark or discolored skin.
- Scarring from repeated injections makes veins harder to use. It also slows blood flow and can cause more damage.

---

## How Doctors Find Out If Someone Is Injecting Drugs

Doctors use several ways to find out if someone is injecting drugs.

### Talking to the Person

Sometimes people come in asking for help to stop using drugs. They may admit their drug use.

Other people try to hide it.

### Watching for Signs

Doctors look for physical signs of drug use. They may notice:
- Track marks on the arms.
- Scars or sores under the skin.
- Changes in mood or behavior.

People who inject drugs may give other reasons for their marks. They might say they donated blood often, got bug bites, or had other injuries.

### Tests

Doctors may use questionnaires to learn more about drug use. They may also do urine or blood tests to check for drugs.

If someone is using drugs and injecting them, doctors will test for common infections. These include:
- Hepatitis B
- Hepatitis C
- HIV

---

## Treating Injection Drug Use

### Counseling

Most treatment starts with counseling. This helps people understand their drug use and learn how to stop.

### Medication

The type of treatment depends on the drug being used. Sometimes, doctors use safer drugs to replace the harmful ones. For example:
- Methadone can be used to help people stop using heroin.

### Support

Family and support groups help people stay on track. They provide encouragement and help prevent relapse.

### Treating Complications

If a person has a problem from injecting drugs, treatment is similar to treatment for the same problem from other causes.

- Abscesses are drained.
- Infections are treated with antibiotics.

### Harm Reduction

Because sharing needles spreads HIV and hepatitis, a harm-reduction program was created.

This program helps people who are not ready to stop using drugs. It gives them clean needles and syringes. This means they do not have to reuse someone else’s needle.

This reduces the spread of HIV and hepatitis. It also saves money for society.

---

## More Information

The following English-language resources may help. Note: The Manual is not responsible for the content of these websites.

- **National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA):**  
  A U.S. government agency that funds research on drug use. It shares information about drugs, research progress, treatment tools, and funding opportunities.

- **Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA):**  
  A U.S. health agency that leads efforts to improve mental and substance use health. It offers tools like treatment finders, free helplines, training for health workers, and public data on drug use.

# Chancroid

Chancroid is a sexually transmitted infection caused by a type of bacteria called *Haemophilus ducreyi*.  
It causes sores on the genitals or inside the genital area.  
It also causes swollen and painful lymph nodes in the groin.  
These swollen lymph nodes can fill with pus and sometimes form an abscess.

## What Causes Chancroid?

The bacteria *Haemophilus ducreyi* causes chancroid.  
This bacteria is a small, thin rod that looks a certain way under a microscope.  
It spreads through sexual contact.

Chancroid is rare in the United States and other high-income countries.  
It mostly happens in small outbreaks in certain areas.  
In poorer parts of Asia, Africa, and the Caribbean, it is a common cause of genital sores.

Like other sexually transmitted infections that cause sores, chancroid makes it easier to get HIV.

The bacteria can also cause sores on other parts of the skin, not just the genitals.

## Symptoms of Chancroid

Symptoms usually appear 3 to 7 days after exposure.  
Small, painful bumps show up on the genitals or inside the genital area.  
These bumps quickly turn into open sores.  
The sores are soft, shallow, and very painful.  
They have ragged edges that look like they are hanging over.  
The area around the sore is red.

The sores can be different sizes.  
They may join together to form larger sores.  
In some cases, the sores go deep and destroy tissue.

Swollen lymph nodes in the groin are common.  
This is called a bubo.  
A bubo is a large, tender lump made of swollen lymph nodes.  
The nodes may stick together.  
They can become soft and filled with pus.  
In some cases, they form an abscess.

The skin over the abscess may turn red and shiny.  
It can break open and drain pus.  
The infection can spread to other skin areas and cause new sores.

In rare cases, chancroid can lead to problems like tight foreskin (phimosis), narrowing of the urethra (urethral stricture), or a hole between the urethra and skin (urethral fistula).

## How Is Chancroid Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose chancroid based on your symptoms and a physical exam.  
Testing the bacteria is hard to do.  
The bacteria are hard to grow in a lab.  
Also, the sores often have many types of bacteria, which makes it hard to see the chancroid bacteria under a microscope.

If testing is available, a sample of pus from a swollen lymph node or fluid from the sore can be sent to a lab.  
Some labs can use a test called NAAT to find the bacteria.  
This test is very accurate.  
A culture test is less accurate.

You should also be tested for syphilis and HIV.  
You may also be tested for herpes.  
This is because other infections can cause similar sores.  
It is possible to have more than one infection at the same time.

## How Is Chancroid Treated?

You should start treatment right away, even before test results come back.  
The following antibiotics are effective:

- One dose of azithromycin (1 gram by mouth)  
- One dose of ceftriaxone (250 milligrams by injection)  
- Erythromycin (500 milligrams by mouth, three times a day for 7 days)  
- Ciprofloxacin (500 milligrams by mouth, twice a day for 3 days)

If you are being treated for another type of genital sore, your doctor may give you an antibiotic that also treats chancroid.  
This is especially important if testing is not possible.

If you have HIV and chancroid, treatment may take longer.  
Sores may take up to two weeks to heal.  
Swollen lymph nodes may take longer to go down.

If a bubo is very painful, a doctor can drain it.  
This helps relieve pain.  
But you must also take antibiotics for the infection to get better.

## What About Your Sexual Partners?

Your sexual partners from the past 10 days should be checked.  
They should be treated even if they do not have symptoms.  
This helps stop the infection from spreading.

## Follow-Up Care

After treatment, you should get tested for syphilis and HIV again 3 months later.  
This is important because chancroid increases your risk of getting HIV.

Always follow your doctor’s instructions.  
Finish all your medicine, even if you feel better.  
This helps make sure the infection is fully gone.

# Swollen Lymph Nodes

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped parts of your body’s defense system.  
They help fight infections and diseases.  
You can feel them under the skin in your neck, under your arms, and in your groin.  

Lymph nodes are part of the lymphatic system.  
This system helps your body get rid of waste and fight infections.  

Lymph is a clear fluid that moves through your body.  
It comes from your blood and collects around your cells.  
Some of this fluid goes back into your blood.  
The rest flows into tubes called lymphatic vessels.  

The lymph flows through the lymph nodes.  
The nodes filter out bad things like germs, damaged cells, and cancer cells.  
They destroy these harmful items.  

When there are many germs or cancer cells, the lymph nodes can swell.  
Sometimes, the germs can even cause an infection inside the node.  

Doctors call swollen lymph nodes "lymphadenopathy."  
If the swollen nodes are painful or red, or feel warm, doctors call it "lymphadenitis."  
This usually means there is an infection, often from a virus or bacteria.  

It is normal to feel a few small lymph nodes in healthy people.  
But if the nodes are larger and easy to feel, it may mean something is wrong.  

Some people say "swollen glands" when they mean swollen lymph nodes.  
But lymph nodes are not glands.  

Swollen nodes can happen in one area or in many areas.  
Other symptoms may appear, like a sore throat, runny nose, or fever.  
Sometimes, doctors find swollen nodes during a check-up for another problem.  

## What Can Cause Swollen Lymph Nodes?

Lymph nodes react when your body fights infections, inflammation, or cancer.  
Here are the most common causes:

### Most Common Causes
- Infections in the upper airways (like colds or sore throats)
- Infections in nearby skin or tissues

Sometimes doctors cannot find the cause.  
This is called idiopathic lymphadenopathy.  
But the swelling usually goes away on its own and does not cause harm.

### Most Serious Causes
- Cancer
- HIV infection
- Tuberculosis

But most people with swollen nodes do not have these serious conditions.  
For example, only about 1 in 100 people with swollen nodes has cancer.

## When to See a Doctor

Not everyone with swollen nodes needs to see a doctor right away.  
But certain signs mean you should get checked.  

See a doctor right away if:
- A node is 2 centimeters (almost an inch) or bigger
- The node is draining pus or fluid
- The node feels hard
- You have risk factors for HIV (like sharing needles or high-risk sex) or tuberculosis (like living with someone who has TB or moving from a high-risk area)
- You have a fever or are losing weight without trying

If a node is very painful or draining fluid, go to the doctor right away.  
Otherwise, call your doctor to talk about it.  

Your doctor will decide how soon you need to be seen.  
If you have no warning signs and feel fine, waiting a week or so is safe.

Your doctor will ask questions and do a physical exam.  
They will check:
- Where the nodes are swollen
- How long they have been swollen
- If they hurt
- If you had a recent injury (like a cat scratch or rat bite)
- If you have any signs of infection (like a sore throat, cough, fever, runny nose, tooth pain, or unexplained weight loss)

They will also check your body for other signs of illness.  
Swollen nodes in many areas may mean a body-wide problem.  
Swollen nodes in just one area may mean a local infection or a more serious disease.

Sometimes, the history and exam point to a clear cause.  
For example, a sore throat may explain neck node swelling.  
Other times, the cause is not clear.  

Warning signs like hard, large, long-lasting nodes that do not move when pushed may suggest cancer.  
Tenderness, redness, or warmth around a swollen node may mean an infection in the node.

*Note: These signs are common but not always present.  
CT = computed tomography; HIV = human immunodeficiency virus; STI = sexually transmitted infection.*

If your doctor suspects a specific illness (like TB in someone with HIV), they may test for that first.  

If no cause is found from the history and exam, more tests depend on:
- Which nodes are swollen
- Other symptoms you have

People with warning signs or widespread swelling should have:
- A complete blood count
- A chest X-ray

Your doctor may also test for:
- Tuberculosis
- HIV
- Mononucleosis
- Toxoplasmosis
- Syphilis

If you have joint pain or a rash, blood tests may check for lupus.

If cancer or lymphoma is suspected, a lymph node biopsy is needed.  
A biopsy may also be needed if swelling lasts 3 to 4 weeks and does not go away.

## How Are Swollen Lymph Nodes Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause.  
For example, if a bacterial infection is likely, your doctor may give antibiotics to see if the swelling goes down.

## Key Points

- In most cases, swollen nodes are caused by a nearby infection or a mild virus. These go away on their own.
- Testing is usually needed if you have warning signs, other symptoms, or risk factors for serious illness.
- If swelling lasts 3 to 4 weeks and does not improve, a biopsy may be needed.

# Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency (Central Diabetes Insipidus)

This condition happens when your body does not make enough vasopressin.  
Vasopressin is a hormone that helps your kidneys keep water in your body.  
Without enough of this hormone, your body loses too much water through urine.

You will feel very thirsty and need to drink a lot of water.  
You will also pass large amounts of very dilute urine.  
This can happen day and night.  
If you do not replace lost fluids, you can become dehydrated quickly.

## What Causes This Condition?

The problem starts in the brain.  
It affects the part of the brain that makes and stores vasopressin.  
This part is called the hypothalamus.  
The hormone travels from the brain to the back of the pituitary gland.  
That is where it is released into the blood.

The condition can be:
- **Complete**: No vasopressin is made.
- **Partial**: Only a small amount of vasopressin is made.

It can also be:
- **Primary**: A genetic problem that stops the brain from making the hormone.
- **Secondary**: Caused by injury, tumor, infection, or other illness that damages the brain or the connection between the brain and pituitary.

## Symptoms

The main symptoms are:
- Extreme thirst
- Passing large amounts of urine (3 to 30 liters per day)
- Needing to wake up many times at night to urinate

In primary cases, these are the only symptoms.  
In secondary cases, you may also have symptoms from the brain or pituitary problem.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use a test called the **water deprivation test**.  
You stop drinking fluids for a while under close medical supervision.  
This test must be done carefully.  
Serious dehydration can happen if not watched closely.

During the test:
- You are weighed each morning.
- Blood and urine samples are taken to check fluid balance.
- Urine is collected every hour to measure how concentrated it is.
- The test continues until your body loses at least 5% of your weight, or your urine stops getting more concentrated.

After dehydration, you get a dose of vasopressin.  
This is usually given as a shot or nose spray.  
Another urine sample is collected one hour later.

The results help doctors tell the difference between:
- Vasopressin deficiency
- Kidney problems that make the body ignore vasopressin
- Drinking too much water on purpose

### Normal Results:
- Urine becomes very concentrated after dehydration.
- Urine gets even more concentrated after the vasopressin shot.

### In Vasopressin Deficiency:
- Urine stays very dilute after dehydration.
- Urine becomes much more concentrated after the vasopressin shot.

### In Kidney Resistance to Vasopressin:
- Urine stays very dilute after dehydration.
- Urine does not get more concentrated after the vasopressin shot.

Doctors may also test blood levels of vasopressin or copeptin.  
Copeptin is a part of the same hormone.  
Low levels of these hormones suggest vasopressin deficiency.  
But these tests are not always available.

## Treatment

The main treatment is **desmopressin**.  
This is a man-made version of vasopressin.  
It works like your natural hormone.  
It helps your kidneys keep water in your body.

Desmopressin can be taken as:
- A pill
- A nasal spray
- A shot

It is very effective and usually works well.

In some cases, doctors may use other medicines.  
These include certain diuretics, like thiazides.  
They are not used often because desmopressin works so well.

Reducing salt in your diet can also help.  
Less salt means less fluid loss in your urine.

## Important Facts

- Vasopressin deficiency causes extreme thirst and large amounts of dilute urine.
- It can be caused by genetic problems or by brain or pituitary damage.
- The water deprivation test is the best way to diagnose it.
- People with this condition cannot concentrate urine when dehydrated.
- But they can concentrate urine after getting desmopressin.
- Low levels of vasopressin or copeptin confirm the diagnosis, but these tests are not always available.
- Always treat any correctable cause.
- Desmopressin is the main treatment. It replaces the missing hormone.

# Understanding and Evaluating Pain

Doctors want to understand your pain so they can find the cause and help you feel better. They will ask you questions about your pain and how it affects your daily life.

## What Doctors Ask About Your Pain

- Where exactly do you feel the pain?
- How would you describe the pain? For example, is it sharp, dull, or crampy?
- When did the pain start? Did you have an injury before it began?
- Did the pain come on suddenly or build up slowly?
- Is the pain always there, or does it come and go?
- Does the pain happen after certain things? For example, after eating, moving, or being in a certain position?
- What makes the pain worse?
- What, if anything, helps ease the pain?
- Does the pain stop you from doing normal things like working, walking, or spending time with family?
- Does it affect your sleep, your appetite, or your ability to use the bathroom?
- Does the pain change your mood? Do you feel sad, anxious, or hopeless?

## How Doctors Measure Pain Severity

Doctors need to know how bad your pain feels. They may ask you to rate your pain on a scale from 0 to 10.

- 0 means no pain.
- 10 means the worst pain possible.

They might also ask you to describe the pain as mild, moderate, severe, or excruciating.

For children or people who have trouble talking about their pain—such as after a stroke—doctors may use drawings of faces. The faces go from smiling to frowning to crying. You point to the face that matches how you feel.

## Finding the Cause of the Pain

Doctors look for physical causes of pain. Many long-term health problems cause pain. These include:

- Cancer
- Arthritis
- Sickle cell anemia
- Inflammatory bowel disease

They also check for short-term causes, such as:

- Cuts and wounds
- Burns
- Torn muscles
- Broken bones
- Sprained ligaments
- Appendicitis
- Kidney stones
- Heart attack

## How Doctors Check for Physical Causes

Doctors use simple tests to find the source of pain.

- They move your arms and legs gently to see if movement causes pain.
- They press on different spots on your body to find tender areas. These are called trigger points.
- They use different tools, like a blunt key or a sharp pin, to test your skin. This helps them check if you feel sensations normally.

## Considering Mental and Emotional Health

Pain can be affected by your mental health. Conditions like depression and anxiety can make pain feel worse.

- Depression and anxiety can be caused by long-term pain.
- Long-term pain can also lead to depression and anxiety.

Sometimes, a person has pain and signs of mental health issues, but no clear physical cause can explain the pain. This kind of pain is called psychogenic or psychophysiologic pain.

Doctors may ask about:

- Difficult experiences in childhood (called ACEs)
- Past trauma
- What you expect from treatment
- Ongoing stress in your life
- Past or current problems with alcohol, drugs, or medicine

Doctors always consider your culture and personal beliefs when they ask these questions.

## What You’ve Tried to Treat the Pain

Doctors want to know what you’ve done to manage your pain.

- What medicines have you taken? This includes over-the-counter pain relievers.
- What other treatments have you tried? For example, physical therapy, heat, or acupuncture.
- Did any of these help? How much?

If doctors suspect you are misusing opioids or other substances, they will do more tests and ask more questions. This is to keep you safe and help you get the right care.

# Osteonecrosis (Bone Death)

Osteonecrosis is when part of a bone dies. This can happen for specific reasons or for no clear reason. It can cause pain, make movement hard, lead to joint collapse, and cause joint wear and tear (osteoarthritis). Doctors diagnose it with X-rays and MRI scans. In early stages, surgery may slow or stop the damage. In later stages, replacing the joint may be needed to ease pain and keep function.

In the United States, about 20,000 new cases are diagnosed each year. The hip (top of the thigh bone) is most often affected. Next are the knee and shoulder (top of the upper arm bone). The wrist and ankle are less often involved. It is rare for the shoulder or other joints to be affected without the hip also being involved. A rare type called medication-related bone death in the jaw is linked to certain osteoporosis medicines. This type is different from bone death in other parts of the body.

## What Causes Osteonecrosis?

Osteonecrosis can happen for no known reason. It can also be caused by injury or other non-injury factors. The most common cause is injury.

## How Does Osteonecrosis Develop?

Bone needs blood to stay healthy. When blood flow stops to part of the bone, the bone cells die. This can happen because of blood clots, fat particles in the blood, or pressure from swelling. After the blood flow stops, the body tries to clean up the dead bone and replace it with healthy tissue. If the damaged area is small and not under heavy weight, healing may happen. But in about 80% of cases, especially when the damage is large and in a weight-bearing area, the bone collapses before healing can occur. The top of the thigh bone then becomes flat and uneven.

Osteonecrosis usually affects the ends of long bones. When this happens, the smooth surface on top of the bone (cartilage) becomes flat and rough. This leads to joint wear and tear (osteoarthritis) and more pain.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Pain is the main symptom. It often starts slowly and gets worse over time. It may happen in the hip, knee, shoulder, wrist, or ankle. The pain may not go away with rest. It may get worse when you move or put weight on the joint.

## How Is Osteonecrosis Diagnosed?

### X-rays

X-rays are usually the first test. They may not show anything early on. In the beginning, the bone may look denser in some areas and lighter in others. Later, a curved line may appear under the joint surface. This shows a crack in the bone. Then, the joint surface may collapse and flatten. Over time, the joint shows signs of wear and tear. If the cause is a body-wide problem, more than one bone may be affected.

If the doctor suspects osteonecrosis but X-rays are normal, an MRI scan is the next step. MRI is much better at finding early bone death. It can show damage before X-rays can. It is best to do an MRI early to prevent more damage. Both hips should be scanned. CT scans are rarely needed. They may help see joint collapse that X-rays and sometimes MRI miss. Bone scans are not very good at finding osteonecrosis. They are only used if MRI and CT are not possible.

Doctors may use staging systems to describe how far the disease has progressed. One common system is the ARCO system. It looks at the size and location of the damage, whether the bone is still round, and if there is joint collapse or arthritis.

Blood tests are usually normal. They do not help find osteonecrosis. But they can help find other health problems that might cause it, such as blood clotting issues, blood disorders, or high fat levels in the blood.

## How Is Osteonecrosis Treated?

- Rest the joint as much as possible.
- Physical therapy to keep movement and strength.
- Pain relief medicines like ibuprofen or similar drugs.
- Surgery to save the joint, such as removing dead bone or adding support.
- Joint replacement surgery if the joint is too damaged.

## How Can Osteonecrosis Be Prevented?

- Use steroid medicines only when needed. Use the lowest dose for the shortest time possible. Tell patients about the risk of bone death when long-term or high-dose steroids are used.
- Divers and workers in pressurized environments should follow safe rules for coming up from deep water or high pressure. This helps prevent decompression sickness, which can cause bone death.
- Limit alcohol use and stop smoking. These habits raise the risk.
- There is not enough proof that medicines like blood thinners, blood vessel dilators, or cholesterol drugs can prevent osteonecrosis in high-risk people.

## Key Facts

- Osteonecrosis can happen for no known reason. It can also be caused by injury or non-injury factors. The most common non-injury causes are steroid medicines and heavy alcohol use.
- Think about osteonecrosis if you have unexplained pain in the hip, knee, shoulder, wrist, or ankle. Also consider it after a fracture or joint injury if pain does not go away.
- X-rays can show osteonecrosis, but MRI is better at finding it early.
- Small areas of damage may heal on their own. But most larger areas, especially in the hip, get worse without treatment.
- Non-surgical treatments are not widely used because their benefits are not clear.
- Surgery is often needed to stop the disease from getting worse and to relieve pain, especially in the hip.

# What Is Pain?

Pain is a strong feeling that tells your body something might be wrong. It can be a warning sign of injury or damage.

Pain is not just a physical sensation. It also includes emotions and thoughts. Everyone experiences pain differently.

## How People Experience Pain

- Pain is shaped by life experiences.
- Your body, mind, and surroundings all affect how you feel pain.
- Your personal feelings, beliefs, and past experiences influence your pain.

Pain is the most common reason people go to a doctor.  
Some pain lasts a long time. Pain that lasts more than three months is called chronic pain.

In 2023, more than a quarter of adults in the United States had chronic pain.  
Nearly seven out of every 100 had high-impact chronic pain. This means their pain made daily life very hard.

Chronic pain is more common in women and older adults.  
The most common places for pain are the legs and feet.  
Next are the back, arms and hands, and the head.

Pain can feel sharp or dull.  
It can come and go or stay all the time.  
It can throb or feel steady.  
Some people find it hard to describe their pain.  
Pain can be in one spot or spread over a large area.  
The pain can be mild, moderate, or so strong it feels unbearable.

People handle pain in different ways.  
One person may struggle with a small cut.  
Another may not notice a serious injury during a sports game.  
Your mood, personality, and situation affect how much pain you can stand.

During a game, an athlete might not feel a bad bruise.  
But after the game, especially if the team lost, the pain may feel much worse.

Doctors always take your word about pain seriously.  
But some people cannot explain their pain well.  
This does not mean they are not in pain.  
Doctors watch for signs like wincing, holding a body part, or avoiding movement.

---

## Pain and Aging

Older adults often have pain.  
But they often say less about it than younger people.

Why?  
They may feel less pain because their body’s sensitivity changes.  
Or they may be more quiet about pain, thinking it is normal with age.

Many older adults have long-term pain.  
The most common cause is a problem with muscles, bones, or joints.

Chronic pain can hurt older adults in many ways:

- It makes it harder to do daily tasks.
- It can make people more dependent on others.
- It can cause poor sleep and tiredness.
- It can reduce appetite, leading to poor nutrition.
- It can stop people from going out or seeing friends.
- This can lead to loneliness and depression.
- It can make people less active.
- Less activity weakens muscles and reduces flexibility.
- This increases the risk of falls.

### Pain Relievers and Older Adults

Older adults are more likely to have side effects from pain medicines.  
Some side effects can be serious.

Pain medicines stay in the body longer in older adults.  
They may also be more sensitive to these medicines.

Many older adults take several medicines.  
This increases the chance that one medicine will react badly with another.

Older adults are more likely to have health problems that make side effects worse.

#### Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs)

NSAIDs include medicines like ibuprofen and naproxen.

These medicines can cause side effects.  
The risk is higher in older adults, especially if they have other health issues or take high doses.

For example:
- Older adults are more likely to have heart or blood vessel problems.
- Taking NSAIDs can raise the risk of heart attack, stroke, or blood clots.
- NSAIDs can harm the kidneys.  
  Kidney function tends to slow with age.  
  This makes kidney damage more likely.
- People with kidney, heart, or liver problems are at even higher risk.
- NSAIDs can cause stomach ulcers or bleeding.  
  Doctors may prescribe a medicine to protect the stomach, such as omeprazole or misoprostol.

If an older adult takes NSAIDs, they should see their doctor regularly.  
Doctors recommend:
- Use the lowest possible dose.
- Use them for only a short time.
- Take breaks between uses.

#### Opioids

Opioids are strong pain medicines.  
They are more likely to cause problems in older adults.

Older adults may be more sensitive to opioids.  
Even a short use can help with pain and improve movement.  
But it can also cause confusion or mental fog.

Opioids also increase the risk of falls.  
Long-term use can weaken bones and raise the risk of fractures.

They cause constipation and trouble passing urine.  
These problems are worse in older adults.

Older adults are more likely to have conditions or take medicines that make opioid side effects worse:

- **Dementia**: Opioids can make thinking problems worse.
- **Breathing problems** (like COPD or sleep apnea): Opioids can slow breathing.  
  In serious cases, breathing can stop.  
  This is a leading cause of death in opioid overdoses.
- **Liver or kidney problems**: The body cannot clear opioids well.  
  This can cause the medicine to build up and lead to overdose.
- **Other sedatives** (like diazepam, lorazepam, or clonazepam):  
  These can make you extremely sleepy and dizzy.  
  Both opioids and sedatives slow breathing.  
  Taking them together can be very dangerous.

Opioids can also lead to dependence or addiction.

Doctors usually choose pain medicines that are safer for older adults.  
For example, acetaminophen is often the first choice for mild to moderate pain without swelling.

Some NSAIDs (like indomethacin and ketorolac) and some opioids (like pentazocine) are usually not given to older adults.  
They carry too high a risk of side effects.

If opioids are needed:
- Doctors start with a low dose.
- The dose is increased slowly.
- The effects are watched closely.

Buprenorphine may be a good option, especially for older adults with kidney problems.  
It may cause fewer side effects than other opioids.

Non-medical help can also help.  
Support from family, caregivers, and other treatments can reduce pain and the need for medicine.

## How Pain Works in the Body

Pain starts when special sensors in your body detect harm.  
These sensors are called pain receptors.

They send signals as electrical messages through nerves.  
The signals go to the spinal cord and then to the brain.

Sometimes, the signal causes a quick reflex.  
This happens without the brain being involved.

For example:
- If you touch something hot, you pull your hand away fast.
- This reflex helps protect you from serious injury.

The same signal also goes to the brain.  
Only when the brain recognizes the signal as pain do you become aware of it.

Pain receptors and nerves work differently in different parts of the body.

- Skin has many pain receptors.  
  They can tell you exactly where the pain is.  
  They can also tell if the pain is sharp (like a cut) or dull (like pressure, heat, cold, or itching).

- Internal organs (like the intestines) have fewer pain receptors.  
  They give less clear signals.  
  The intestines can be damaged without causing pain.  
  But stretching or pressure can cause strong pain.  
  Even a small gas bubble can hurt.

The brain cannot always tell where the pain in the intestines comes from.  
The pain may feel spread out and hard to locate.

### Reflex Arc: A Quick Reaction

A reflex arc is the path a nerve signal takes during a reflex.

1. A tap on the knee activates a sensor.
2. The signal travels to the spinal cord.
3. The spinal cord sends a signal to a motor nerve.
4. The motor nerve tells a muscle to contract.
5. The leg jerks up.

This whole process happens without the brain being involved.

### Referred Pain

Sometimes, pain is felt in one place but comes from another.

This is called referred pain.

Why?  
Because signals from different body areas often travel on the same nerves in the spinal cord and brain.

For example:
- A heart attack may cause pain in the neck, jaw, arms, or belly.
- A gallbladder problem may cause pain in the back of the shoulder.

---

## Types of Pain

Pain can be acute or chronic.

### Acute Pain

- Comes on suddenly.
- Lasts only a few days or weeks.
- Often caused by injury or surgery.

Severe acute pain can cause:
- Anxiety
- Fast heartbeat
- Fast breathing
- High blood pressure
- Sweating
- Dilated pupils

### Chronic Pain

- Lasts for months or years.
- Does not usually cause the same physical reactions as acute pain.
- But it can lead to:
  - Depression
  - Poor sleep
  - Low energy
  - Poor appetite
  - Weight loss
  - Less interest in sex
  - Loss of interest in life

# Tissue Transplantation

Many types of body tissues can be transplanted. These include skin, bone, cartilage, adrenal tissue, fetal thymus, corneas, and complex transplants to rebuild the face or limbs.

(See also: Overview of Transplantation and Corneal Transplantation.)

---

## Composite Transplants (Hand, Arm, Face)

Composite transplants involve more than one type of tissue. These often include skin, soft tissues, and sometimes bones and muscles.  
In the United States, only four of these transplants were done in 2021.  
New medicines that lower the body’s immune response have made these surgeries possible.  
But these transplants are still controversial.  
They do not usually save lives.  
They cost a lot of money and use many medical resources.  
They can also cause serious health problems, including infections.

The first successful hand transplant happened in 1998.  
Since then, doctors have done double hand and upper arm transplants.  
Recovery of hand function varies.  
Some people get enough movement and feeling to do everyday tasks.

The first face transplant was done in 2005.  
Ethical concerns are even stronger for face transplants.  
The surgery is very hard.  
The medicines needed to prevent rejection can lead to serious infections.

After a transplant, patients take medicines to stop their body from attacking the new tissue.  
This is called immunosuppression.  
It usually starts with strong medicines given right after surgery.  
These include antithymocyte globulin or drugs that block certain immune signals.  
Then, patients take three types of medicines long-term:  
- A steroid medicine  
- A drug that stops immune cells from multiplying  
- A medicine that blocks a key immune system signal

Sometimes, patients also use creams on the skin.  
These creams contain the same types of medicines used in pills.

---

## Skin Grafts

Skin grafts can come from three sources:  
- The patient’s own body (autograft)  
- A donor (allograft)  
- A donor’s skin (allograft)

---

## Cartilage Transplants

Cartilage transplants help children born with missing or deformed noses or ears.  
They also help adults with serious injuries or joint damage, such as severe arthritis.  
Cartilage cells are less likely to be rejected by the body.  
This may be because the cells are protected by the surrounding tissue.  
Because of this, patients do not need to take medicines to stop rejection.  
It is not yet clear if cartilage transplants help people with arthritis in the long run.

---

## Bone Transplants

Bone transplants are used to fix large bone defects.  
This often happens after removing bone cancer.  
The donated bone does not contain living cells.  
But the dead bone structure helps the patient’s own bone cells grow into it.  
This acts like a scaffold to hold the area together while new bone forms.

Donated bones come from cadavers.  
They are frozen to reduce the chance of rejection.  
They are also treated with glycerol to keep any cartilage cells alive.

No medicines to suppress the immune system are needed after the transplant.  
Some patients make antibodies against the donor bone.  
But early checkups show no damage to the cartilage.

---

## Adrenal Grafts

Doctors have placed adrenal tissue from a patient’s own body into the brain.  
This has helped ease symptoms in some people with Parkinson disease.  
Other doctors have tried using adrenal tissue from unborn babies.  
This tissue was placed into the brain of people with Parkinson disease.  
It helped reduce stiffness and slow movements.  
But using tissue from unborn babies is controversial.  
There are strong ethical and political debates about this.  
So, large studies to test this treatment are unlikely.

Scientists are also testing pig cells that make hormones.  
These are being tested as a possible treatment.

---

## Thymus Transplants

Doctors have used thymus tissue from stillborn babies.  
This helps children with a rare condition called DiGeorge syndrome.  
These children are born without a working thymus.  
This causes serious problems with their immune system.  
Transplanting thymus tissue can help the immune system develop.

Because the child’s immune system is weak, they do not need medicines to stop rejection.  
But there is a risk of a serious side effect called graft-versus-host disease.

---

## Uterus Transplants

A few women with infertility due to missing or damaged uteruses have had uterus transplants.  
The surgery carries serious risks.  
Some women need more than one operation.  
They also face risks from the medicines used after transplant.  
These medicines lower the body’s ability to fight infections.  
Once a woman has finished having children, the transplanted uterus is removed.

# Changes in the Lips

The lips can change in size, color, or texture. Some changes are harmless. Others may signal a health problem. As people age, their lips often become thinner.

## Lip Sores

Lip sores (ulcers) can have many causes. A sore with hard edges might be a type of skin cancer. See the section on types of oral cancer for more information. See also the section on lips and sun damage.

Sores can also appear because of other health issues. These include:

- Erythema multiforme  
- Recurrent cold sores caused by the herpes simplex virus  
- Syphilis  

## Spots on the Lips

You may notice spots on your lips. Multiple small, brownish-black spots can be a sign of a rare inherited condition called Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. This condition causes growths in the stomach and intestines.

People who smoke may get brown spots on their lips. These spots appear where the cigarette touches the lip. They are not cancer.  

Freckles and irregular brown patches are common around the lips. These marks can stay for years. They are not a health concern.

## Kawasaki Disease

Kawasaki disease is a rare illness that mostly affects babies and children under 8 years old. The cause is unknown. It can make the lips dry, cracked, and sore. The inside of the mouth may also turn red.

## Other Common Lip Changes

- Sun damage  
- Swelling of the lips  

### Cold Sores

Cold sores are small, painful blisters on or around the lips. They are caused by a virus. They often come back.

## Cheilitis

Cheilitis means inflammation of the lips. It can cause pain, redness, cracking, and flaky skin.

### Angular Cheilitis

This is the most common type. It affects the corners of the mouth. It often happens when:

- Dentures do not fit well and do not keep the jaws apart  
- Teeth are worn down, leaving too little space between the upper and lower teeth  
- There is an infection with *Candida* fungus or *Staphylococcus aureus* bacteria  
- The diet lacks enough vitamin B2 or iron  

**Treatment:**

- Fix or replace dentures to reduce skin folds at the corners of the mouth  
- Use partial dentures, crowns, or implants to restore proper tooth size  
- Treat infections with medicine applied to the skin  
- Take vitamin B2 or iron supplements if levels are low  

### Other Types of Cheilitis

These affect the outer surface of the lips and the line where the lips meet the skin. Causes include:

- Infections  
- Sun damage  
- Certain medicines or skin irritants  
- Allergies  
- Other underlying health conditions  

**Treatment:**

- Apply petroleum jelly to keep the lips moist  
- Treat the cause, such as stopping a medicine, avoiding irritants, or managing an allergy  
- Treat any underlying health condition  

Always see a doctor if you notice new or unusual changes in your lips. Early care can prevent problems from getting worse.

# Chondromalacia Patellae

Chondromalacia patellae means the cartilage under the kneecap is softening.

This condition often causes pain around the knee.  
The pain usually happens when you go up or down stairs.  
It can also happen when you play sports that put pressure on the knee.  
Some people feel pain after sitting for a long time, like in a movie theater.  
The knee usually does not swell.

This problem may happen because the leg is not straight or is twisted.  
This can cause the kneecap to move poorly when you move your leg.  
It can also affect the muscles in the front of the thigh.

## How to Treat Chondromalacia Patellae

**Physical therapy**  
You will do exercises to help your knee move better.  
These exercises strengthen the muscles around the knee.  
They also help the kneecap move in the right way.

**Pain relief**  
You can use over-the-counter pain medicine.  
This helps reduce pain and discomfort.

**Ice**  
Apply ice to the knee for 15 to 20 minutes at a time.  
Do this several times a day, especially after activity.

**Rest**  
Children with this condition should stop doing activities that hurt the knee.  
This includes sports or games that require bending the knee.  
They should rest for several days.

**Surgery (rare)**  
If pain continues or comes back, a doctor may suggest a small surgery.  
This surgery uses a camera to smooth the underside of the kneecap.  
It is only done in rare cases.

# What Is a Limb Prosthesis?

A limb prosthesis is an artificial limb. It replaces a body part that is missing. Most often, this happens after an amputation.

## Why Do People Need a Prosthesis?

The main reasons for amputation are:

- Blood vessel problems, especially from diabetes or poor blood flow in the legs
- Cancer
- Serious injuries, like from car crashes, workplace accidents, or war
- Being born without a limb

In the United States, about 1 in every 200 people lives without a limb. Around 500 amputations happen every day. This number is likely to grow as more people get older and develop diabetes or blood vessel disease.

Most people who lose a limb are offered a prosthesis. The goal is to help them do everyday tasks on their own. These tasks include walking, eating, and getting dressed. A good prosthesis can help people live nearly as well as they did before the amputation.

## Who Helps with a Prosthesis?

Success with a prosthesis is more likely when a team of experts works together. The team may include:

- A surgeon
- A prosthetist (a specialist who makes and fits artificial limbs)
- A physical therapist

The prosthetist checks your overall health and abilities. They create a plan for your prosthesis. This includes designing it, fitting it, making it, adjusting it, and giving you care for life. They also teach you how to use and care for your prosthesis.

For more complex cases, the team may also include:

- A physiatrist (a doctor who treats physical disabilities)
- An occupational therapist (helps with daily tasks)
- A social worker
- A psychologist
- Your family

## Traveling with a Prosthesis

You may worry about going through airport security. Most of the time, you do not need to remove your prosthesis. If security asks you to, they must do it in private. This is because it may require taking off some clothes.

It can help to have a letter from your prosthetist. The letter should say:

- Your prosthesis has metal and electronic parts
- If you take it off for more than 10 to 15 minutes, it may be hard to put back on
- This is because the limb swells with fluid when not worn

## What Are the Goals of a Prosthesis?

Your goals can be simple or very active. For example:

- Walking around the house
- Going up and down stairs
- Running, jumping, or playing sports
- Climbing mountains or skydiving

The parts of the prosthesis are chosen to match your goals. New materials and designs make prostheses more comfortable and easier to use. The prosthetist works to make sure you are:

- Comfortable
- Stable when standing and walking
- Able to reach your personal goals

People who are healthy and motivated can do amazing things with a prosthesis. They can return to work, join the military, run races, or take part in sports.

## What Makes a Prosthesis Work Well?

Success depends on several things:

- Your other health problems
- Your physical strength and mental ability
- The shape and condition of your remaining limb
- How well the prosthesis fits and connects to your body

Fitting a prosthesis is a skilled job. It takes time and effort. You may need to adjust physically and mentally. Not everyone can use every type of prosthesis.

## Where Is the Amputation Done?

The doctor decides how much of the limb to remove. They consider many things, including:

- Removing dead or infected tissue
- Making sure blood flows well in the remaining limb
- Keeping muscles and their attachments to bones
- Stabilizing the bones
- Covering the end of the limb with muscle

## Getting Ready for Amputation

Losing a limb is hard. It affects your body and your sense of self. Doctors and prosthetists help you and your family understand:

- Why the amputation is needed
- What will happen before, during, and after surgery
- What to expect during the fitting process

People who understand the process and have realistic expectations are more likely to succeed. Sometimes, doctors connect you with someone who already uses a prosthesis and has adjusted well.

Before surgery, doctors try to get you as healthy as possible. They treat problems like:

- Poor nutrition
- Diabetes
- Heart or lung disease

Smoking slows healing. Quitting smoking is very important. If you are weak, you may do therapy and exercises to get stronger and more flexible.

## After Surgery

Right after surgery, the medical team starts helping you:

- Keep your joints moving to prevent stiffness
- Build strength and stay in shape
- Reduce swelling in the remaining limb

When you are ready, you can start to get used to the end of your limb. This includes:

- Massaging it
- Tapping it
- Using vibration
- Putting weight on it

You can start getting a prosthesis about 7 to 10 weeks after surgery. This is when the wound has healed and swelling has gone down. You also need enough strength and movement in your joints.

Your limb will keep changing for 6 to 18 months. Fluid leaves the limb, and muscles reshape. During this time, you may get one or more temporary sockets. These help you get used to using a prosthesis.

When your limb stops changing, you get a final prosthesis. A temporary prosthesis helps you learn how to handle pressure and movement.

Early rehab helps you recover faster and use your prosthesis better. If your amputation is planned, rehab can start before surgery. If it happens suddenly, rehab begins as soon as possible—sometimes the first day after surgery.

## Possible Problems After Amputation

Some people have problems after amputation. These include:

- Pain in the remaining limb
- Slow healing, often from poor blood flow
- Skin sores or breaks
- Skin infections
- Swelling in the remaining limb

These problems can come from the limb itself or from the prosthesis or socket.

## More Help and Information

The following resources may help. The Manual is not responsible for their content.

- **Amputee Coalition**: Offers education, support, and advocacy for people affected by limb loss. Also works to prevent limb loss.

- **U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs: Rehabilitation and Prosthetic Services**: Provides national programs and services to help veterans with disabilities stay healthy, independent, and active.

# Microscopy

Microscopy helps doctors see tiny germs in body samples. It can show if a germ is deeply in the tissue or just on the surface. Culture tests alone cannot always tell the difference.

Most samples are stained to make germs easier to see. The stain colors the germs so they stand out from the rest of the sample. But sometimes, doctors use a wet mount—this means no stain is used. Wet mounts help find fungi and some other germs.

Doctors choose a stain based on the kind of germ they think is present. No stain works perfectly. Some germs look similar under the microscope, even if they are different.

The most common stain is the Gram stain. It shows whether bacteria are gram-positive (they stay blue) or gram-negative (they turn red). It also shows the shape and how the bacteria are grouped—like in chains or clumps. It can also show white blood cells, which means there is likely a real infection, not just germs on the surface.

The Gram stain can guide early treatment with antibiotics. If the sample shows many different types of germs with different shapes and colors, it may mean the sample is dirty or there is more than one infection. If a sputum sample has many squamous cells (skin cells), it likely came from saliva and is not useful for diagnosis.

To do a Gram stain, lab workers put the sample on a slide and heat it to stick it down. Then they add four dyes in order: crystal violet, iodine, a decolorizer, and a counterstain (usually safranin).

---

## Acid-Fast and Modified Acid-Fast Stains

These stains help find:

- Mycobacteria (like the bacteria that cause tuberculosis)
- Some less common bacteria, such as *Nocardia*
- *Rhodococcus* and similar germs
- Oocysts (eggs) of certain parasites, including *Cryptosporidium*, *microsporidia*, *Cystoisospora*, *Cyclospora*, and *Balantidium coli*

To find mycobacteria in sputum, you need at least 10,000 germs per milliliter. But often, there are fewer. So the test may miss the germs. To improve results, several milliliters of sputum are treated with a strong chemical (sodium hydroxide) to remove mucus and other material. Then the sample is spun in a machine to concentrate the germs.

The acid-fast stain is more accurate than the Gram stain for these germs. But some non-mycobacteria can look similar and are hard to tell apart.

---

## Fluorescent Stains

Fluorescent stains make germs glow under special lights. They can find germs at lower levels—less than 10,000 germs per milliliter.

Examples include:

- Acridine orange: finds bacteria and fungi
- Auramine-rhodamine and auramine O: finds mycobacteria
- Calcofluor white: finds fungi, especially those that cause skin infections

Scientists can also attach a dye to an antibody that targets a specific germ. This method is called direct or indirect immunofluorescence. It should be more accurate and sensitive. But the results are hard to read. Only a few tests—like for *Pneumocystis* and *Legionella*—are widely available and used.

---

## Wet Mounts

Wet mounts are used without stains. They are helpful for seeing:

- Fungi
- Parasites, including worm eggs and larvae
- Clue cells in vaginal samples (a sign of bacterial vaginosis)
- Moving germs, such as *Trichomonas*
- *Treponema* (the germ that causes syphilis)

To see fungi better, doctors can add 10% potassium hydroxide to the sample. This dissolves skin and other tissue, making the fungi easier to see.

---

## India Ink Stain

India ink is a black liquid made of carbon. It is used to find *Cryptococcus neoformans* and other fungi with a capsule. The ink stains the background, not the germ. So the capsule around the germ shows up as a clear halo.

This test is used on samples like cerebrospinal fluid. But it is not as sensitive as a special antigen test for *Cryptococcus*. Also, white blood cells can look like they have capsules, which can cause confusion.

---

## Warthin-Starry and Dieterle Stains

These are silver stains. They help see:

- Spirochetes (spiral-shaped bacteria)
- *Helicobacter pylori* (a germ that causes stomach ulcers)
- Microsporidia (a type of parasite)
- *Bartonella henselae* (the germ that causes cat-scratch disease)

These stains make the germs appear dark against a light background.

---

## Wright Stain and Giemsa Stain

These stains are used to find:

- Parasites in blood
- *Histoplasma capsulatum* inside white blood cells and tissue cells
- Inclusions inside cells caused by viruses or *chlamydia*
- The active form of *Pneumocystis jirovecii* (a fungus that causes lung infections)
- Some bacteria that live inside cells

---

## Trichrome Stain (Gomori-Wheatley) and Iron Hematoxylin Stain

These stains are used to find parasites in the intestines.

- **Gomori-Wheatley stain**: Best for finding microsporidia. It may miss worm eggs and larvae. It also stains fungi and human cells, which can make results harder to read.

- **Iron hematoxylin stain**: Stains different parts of cells differently. It helps see cell structures and nuclei. But worm eggs may stain too dark to identify clearly.

# Problems with the Connection Between Nerves and Muscles

Nerves connect to muscles at a special spot called the neuromuscular junction.  
At this spot, the end of a nerve touches a special area on the muscle’s surface.  
This area has tiny receptors that pick up a chemical called acetylcholine.  
Acetylcholine is a signal messenger sent by the nerve.  
It tells the muscle to contract.  

When the nerve sends a signal, the muscle gets an electric impulse.  
This makes the muscle tighten or contract.  
After the signal is sent, the body breaks down acetylcholine.  
This stops the muscle from staying contracted too long.

> **Did you know?**  
> Some nerve gases used in chemical warfare block the normal flow of signals between nerves and muscles.

## Common Problems at the Neuromuscular Junction

These conditions affect how nerves talk to muscles:

- **Myasthenia gravis**  
- **Botulism**  
- **Eaton-Lambert syndrome**

Many medicines and harmful substances can also cause these problems.  
These include:

- Very high doses of some antibiotics  
- Certain insecticides (like organophosphates)  
- Chemical weapons (such as sarin gas and Novichok)  
- Curare  

Novichok was created in Russia. It has been used in attacks.  
Curare is used in surgery to relax muscles.  
It can also be used on poison darts to paralyze and kill animals.

Some of these substances stop the body from breaking down acetylcholine after the signal is sent.  
This causes muscles to stay active too long.

## What Happens in These Disorders?

Most of these problems reduce nerve signals.  
This leads to muscle weakness.  
But they do not affect your sense of touch.  
You will not feel numbness, tingling, or pins-and-needles.

Some disorders do the opposite.  
They cause nerves to send too many signals.  
This leads to constant muscle activity.  
Examples include:

- **Stiff-person syndrome**  
  Your body makes antibodies that attack nerves in the brain and spinal cord.  
  These nerves control muscle movement.  
  When they are damaged, muscles stay tight and stiff.  
  This makes movement hard.

- **Isaacs syndrome**  
  Nerves keep sending electrical signals to muscles.  
  This causes muscles to twitch and stay tight.  
  Normal activities like walking or exercising become very difficult.

Even though stiff-person syndrome starts in the brain and spinal cord, it still affects the neuromuscular junction.  
This causes muscles to stay contracted all the time.

# Diabetes During Pregnancy

Diabetes can make it harder to keep blood sugar levels under control during pregnancy. This is true for both type 1 diabetes (which needs insulin) and type 2 diabetes (which does not always need insulin). But pregnancy does not make eye, kidney, or nerve problems from diabetes worse.

## What Is Gestational Diabetes?

Gestational diabetes happens in about 4 out of every 100 pregnancies. It is more common in people of certain ethnic backgrounds, such as non-Hispanic Asian or Pacific Islander, and Hispanic or Latina women.

Women who have gestational diabetes are more likely to develop type 2 diabetes later in life.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) has clear guidelines for managing diabetes during pregnancy.

## How Is Diabetes Diagnosed in Pregnancy?

All pregnant women should be tested for gestational diabetes. This test usually happens between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy.

The most common test is the oral glucose tolerance test. But a single blood sugar test can also be used.

### Two-Step Testing (Recommended by ACOG)

1. First, you drink a sweet liquid with 50 grams of sugar.
2. One hour later, a blood test checks your blood sugar level.
   - If the result is over 130 to 140 mg/dL, you need a second test.
3. The second test uses 100 grams of sugar and measures blood sugar at fasting, and then at 1, 2, and 3 hours after drinking the liquid.

### One-Step Testing (Used Outside the U.S.)

Some groups use a single test with 75 grams of sugar. Blood sugar is checked before and 2 hours after drinking the liquid.

### When Is Gestational Diabetes Diagnosed?

The table below shows the blood sugar levels that mean you have gestational diabetes.

| Organization | Fasting (mg/dL / mmol/L) | 1-Hour (mg/dL / mmol/L) | 2-Hour (mg/dL / mmol/L) | 3-Hour (mg/dL / mmol/L) |
|--------------|---------------------------|--------------------------|--------------------------|--------------------------|
| Carpenter and Coustan | 95 / 5.3 | 180 / 10.0 | 155 / 8.6 | 140 / 7.8 |
| National Diabetes Data Group | 105 / 5.8 | 190 / 10.6 | 165 / 9.2 | 145 / 8.0 |

Note: This test uses 100 grams of sugar.

## How Is Diabetes Managed During Pregnancy?

Good control of blood sugar is key to a healthy pregnancy.

### What You Should Do

- Work with a team of experts. This team may include doctors, nurses, dietitians, and social workers.
- See a pediatrician who can care for your baby after birth.
- Get help right away if any health problem shows up during pregnancy, even if it seems small.
- Plan your delivery carefully.
- Make sure a trained pediatrician is present at birth.
- Have access to a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) in case your baby needs special care.

In some areas, there are special centers with experts who focus on diabetes during pregnancy.

## Key Points

- Diabetes during pregnancy raises the risk of:
  - A large baby (macrosomia)
  - Shoulder injury during delivery (shoulder dystocia)
  - High blood pressure (preeclampsia)
  - Needing a cesarean section
  - Stillbirth
  - Birth defects, if diabetes is not well controlled during early pregnancy
  - Miscarriage, if diabetes is not well controlled

- All pregnant women should be tested for gestational diabetes using a glucose tolerance test.

- If you have diabetes, aim to keep:
  - Fasting blood sugar below 95 mg/dL (5.3 mmol/L)
  - Blood sugar 2 hours after eating below 120 mg/dL (6.6 mmol/L)

- Start checking your baby’s health with tests at 32 weeks of pregnancy.

- Deliver your baby by 39 weeks of pregnancy.

- Adjust your insulin dose right after the placenta is delivered.

# Infantile Spasms

Infantile spasms are a type of seizure that affects babies.  
They happen suddenly and can be very hard to notice at first.  

## What Happens During a Spasm?

- The baby suddenly raises and bends their arms.  
- The neck and upper body bend forward.  
- The legs straighten out.  
- The whole body may jerk or stiffen.  

These movements can look like a startle.  
Sometimes only the head nods slightly.  

Spasms last only a few seconds.  
But they often happen in groups.  
A group can last several minutes.  
A baby may have many groups of spasms each day.  

Spasms usually start before the baby is one year old.  
They often stop by age five.  
But many children go on to have other types of seizures later.  

## What Causes Infantile Spasms?

Most babies with infantile spasms have a serious brain problem.  
Some common causes include:  

- Problems with how the body uses energy (metabolic disorders)  
- Genetic conditions (problems passed down in families)  
- Brain malformations (the brain did not form correctly)  
- Lack of oxygen at birth (can happen during labor or delivery)  
- Serious head injury around the time of birth  

Some rare conditions are linked to infantile spasms:  

- **Tuberous sclerosis complex** – a rare inherited condition that affects the brain, nerves, and skin.  
- **Sturge-Weber syndrome** – a condition that affects the brain and skin.  
- **Neurofibromatosis** – a condition that affects nerves and skin.  

Other rare causes:  

- Chromosome problems (like Down syndrome)  
- Brain or spinal cord structure issues  
- Infections the baby gets before birth (such as syphilis, Zika virus, or cytomegalovirus)  

In some cases, doctors cannot find a cause.  

## What Are the Signs?

- Babies may seem to startle or jerk suddenly.  
- They may have many spasms in a row.  
- Spasms often happen right after waking up.  
- Sometimes they happen when falling asleep.  

Many babies with infantile spasms also have:  

- Slow development  
- Delayed language skills  
- Trouble learning new things  

Some babies who were developing normally may:  

- Stop smiling  
- Lose skills they already had, like sitting up or rolling over  

Parents often notice these delays before the first spasm happens.  

## How Are Infantile Spasms Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find the cause.  

### Electroencephalography (EEG)  
- This test checks the brain’s electrical activity.  
- It is done while the baby is awake and while sleeping.  
- It can show a special pattern that is common in infantile spasms.  

### Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)  
- This scan takes detailed pictures of the brain.  
- It helps find brain damage or birth defects.  

### Blood and Urine Tests  
- These check for metabolic problems.  
- They can show if the body is not using food and energy properly.  

### Spinal Tap (Lumbar Puncture)  
- A small amount of fluid is taken from around the spinal cord.  
- This fluid is tested for infections or other problems.  

### Genetic Testing  
- If no cause is found, doctors may test the baby’s genes.  
- This can help find a genetic reason for the spasms.  

## How Are Infantile Spasms Treated?

Early treatment is very important.  
The sooner spasms are controlled, the better the chance for normal development.  

Three main medicines are used:  

### Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH)  
- Given as a shot into a muscle once a day.  
- Treatment usually lasts two weeks.  
- Then the dose is slowly lowered over several weeks.  

### Corticosteroid (like prednisone)  
- Taken by mouth every day.  
- Works like a natural hormone in the body.  

### Vigabatrin  
- Taken by mouth.  
- This is the best choice if the cause is tuberous sclerosis complex.  
- Other seizure medicines or special diets (like a ketogenic diet) have not been proven to help.  

### Surgery (in some cases)  
- If one small area of the brain is causing all the spasms, surgery may help.  
- Doctors may remove that part of the brain.  
- This is only done if it will not harm the baby’s ability to function.  

## Important Notes

- Infantile spasms are rare.  
- They need fast diagnosis and treatment.  
- Early care can improve a child’s long-term development.  
- Parents should talk to their doctor right away if they notice any unusual jerking or developmental delays.

# Medical Check-Up for People with Mental Health Symptoms

When someone has mental health symptoms, doctors do a medical check-up. This check-up looks for three main things:

- Medical problems that cause symptoms like mental illness.
- Medical problems that are made worse by mental illness or its treatment.
- Medical problems that happen at the same time as mental illness.

## Medical Problems That Look Like Mental Illness

Some medical conditions cause symptoms that seem like mental illness. For example:

- Confusion, disorientation, or sudden changes in thinking.
- Mood changes like sadness or feeling overly happy.
- Trouble sleeping.
- Memory problems.
- Strange behavior or personality changes.
- Hallucinations or delusions.

These symptoms can come from many different medical issues. Some of the most common causes include:

- Brain infections like encephalitis or meningitis.
- Low blood sugar or low oxygen levels.
- Dehydration or fever.
- Hormone problems, such as an underactive or overactive thyroid.
- Kidney or liver failure.
- Brain tumors or bleeding in the brain.
- Stroke or head injury.
- Vitamin deficiencies (like B12 or thiamin).
- Autoimmune diseases like lupus.
- Severe infections like HIV or syphilis.
- Certain types of seizures.

## Medicines and Substances That Cause Mental Symptoms

Many medicines can cause mental health symptoms. These include:

- Medicines for seizures, depression, or psychosis.
- Sleep aids or sedatives.
- Stimulant drugs.
- Some allergy medicines (antihistamines).
- Steroid medicines (like prednisone).
- Some antibiotics or blood pressure medicines.

Drugs like alcohol, amphetamines, marijuana, cocaine, hallucinogens, and PCP can also cause mental symptoms. This is especially true when used often or in large amounts.

Stopping alcohol, barbiturates, or benzodiazepines suddenly can cause anxiety and other mental symptoms, along with physical withdrawal signs.

## Mental Illness Can Lead to Physical Problems

People with mental illness can also get physical health problems. These problems may cause new or worse mental symptoms. For example:

- A person with schizophrenia may not eat enough, leading to poor nutrition.
- A person on lithium medicine may develop an underactive thyroid.
- Some mental health medicines can raise cholesterol levels.

Even if the physical problem is not the cause of the mental symptoms, it still needs to be treated.

## Important Points to Remember

- Do not assume that all mental symptoms in someone with a known mental illness are due to that illness.
- Some people with mental health symptoms have a medical problem that has not yet been found.
- These medical problems may be unrelated, caused by the mental illness, or caused by the treatment.

## When a Medical Check-Up Is Needed

A doctor should do a medical check-up if:

- The person has new mental health symptoms with no past history.
- The symptoms are different from what the person usually experiences.
- The symptoms are unusual for the person’s age or background. For example, psychosis in an older adult.

The goal is not to diagnose a mental illness. The goal is to find any medical condition that might be causing or affecting the mental symptoms.
