# Varicose Veins

Varicose veins are enlarged, twisted veins that appear in the legs.  
They are usually not painful.  
But some people feel heavy, tired, or sore legs.  
Some may feel pain or extra sensitivity in the legs.

## What Causes Varicose Veins?

Doctors do not always know the cause.  
In some cases, the valves in the veins do not work well.  
This lets blood flow backward and build up in the veins.  
In other cases, the vein walls are weak and stretch out.  
Varicose veins can also happen if blood pressure in the veins stays high for a long time.

Varicose veins often run in families.  
This suggests genes may play a role.  
Women are more likely to get them than men.  
This may be because of hormones like estrogen.  
Pregnancy can also raise pressure in the legs and pelvis.  
This can make varicose veins more likely.

Rarely, varicose veins are part of a rare condition called Klippel-Trénaunay-Weber syndrome.  
This condition includes abnormal blood vessels between arteries and veins.  
It also causes red or purple marks on the skin.

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

At first, the veins may feel tight and hard to touch.  
They may not be easy to see.  
Over time, they can grow larger and bulge out.  
They are easiest to see when standing.

You may feel fullness, tiredness, pressure, or pain in the legs.  
The skin around the ankles may change.  
It can become thick, dark, or dry.  
It may also get itchy or inflamed.  
These skin changes usually happen on the inside of the ankle.

Sores can form after a small injury.  
These sores are usually small, shallow, and painful.  
They are called venous stasis ulcers.

Varicose veins can sometimes get a blood clot.  
This causes pain and swelling.  
The skin over the vein may become thin.  
It can break open and bleed, even from a small bump.  
If bleeding happens at night and is not noticed, it can be dangerous.

> **Important:**  
> Varicose veins rarely cause skin sores or ulcers.  
> But a small injury can lead to a sore in a weak area.

## How Are Varicose Veins Diagnosed?

Your doctor will look at your legs and ask about your symptoms.  
This is usually enough to make the diagnosis.

A test called Doppler ultrasound may be used.  
It checks blood flow in the veins.  
It can show if blood is flowing backward.

A test called duplex ultrasound gives a clear picture of the veins.  
It is very accurate.  
But it is not always needed for every person.

## How Are Varicose Veins Treated?

Treatment helps ease symptoms.  
It can also improve how the legs look.  
In some cases, it helps prevent problems.

### Compression Stockings
Wear compression stockings every day.  
They help push blood up the legs.  
This reduces swelling and discomfort.

### Wound Care
If you have a sore or broken skin, keep it clean.  
Use special dressings to help it heal.

### Minimally Invasive Treatments
These treatments do not need big surgery.  
They are often used for cosmetic reasons.  
They can also help prevent new clots or skin changes.

- **Sclerotherapy:** A medicine is injected into the vein.  
  It irritates the inside of the vein.  
  This causes it to close off.  
  The vein turns into scar tissue and fades.  
  But some veins may open again over time.

- **Thermal Ablation:** Heat from a laser or radio waves is used.  
  It closes the vein from the inside.  
  This is done through a small tube placed in the vein.

### Surgery
Surgery may be done to tie off or remove the main veins in the leg.  
This helps reduce symptoms.  
But the results do not last forever.  
Many people get new varicose veins later.

> **Important:**  
> No treatment stops varicose veins from coming back.  
> You may need treatment more than once over time.

## Key Points

- Varicose veins are more common in women than in men.  
- Symptoms can include heaviness, tiredness, pressure, pain, or skin sensitivity.  
- Skin sores and ulcers are rare.  
  But a small injury can cause a sore.  
- Treatment options include compression stockings, injections, heat treatments, or surgery.  
- Varicose veins often come back, even after treatment.  
  You may need repeated treatments over time.

# Echinococcosis (Dog Tapeworm Infection)

Echinococcosis is an infection caused by tiny worms called *Echinococcus granulosus* and *Echinococcus multilocularis*. These worms live in the intestines of dogs and other animals like foxes and coyotes.

People can get infected when they accidentally swallow worm eggs. The eggs come from dog poop. Once inside the body, the eggs can grow into fluid-filled cysts in the liver, lungs, or other organs.

---

## How People Get Infected

- Dogs get the worm by eating infected meat from animals like sheep, goats, cattle, or pigs.
- The worms grow in the dog’s gut and pass eggs in their poop.
- These eggs can survive in soil for up to a year.
- The eggs can also stick to the fur of infected animals.
- People become infected by touching contaminated soil, animal fur, or food and then putting their hands in their mouth.

When a person swallows the eggs:
- The eggs hatch in the intestines.
- Tiny worm parts (called oncospheres) travel through the blood.
- They settle in organs like the liver or lungs.
- There, they grow into cysts over time.
- These cysts can get bigger and cause health problems.

---

## Where the Worms Are Found

- *Echinococcus granulosus* is common in sheep-raising areas such as the Mediterranean, Middle East, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, and South America. It is rare in parts of North America.
- *Echinococcus multilocularis* is mainly found in Central Europe, Alaska, Canada, and Siberia. It is rare in parts of the United States, including Wyoming, the Dakotas, and the upper Midwest.

---

## Symptoms of Echinococcosis

Symptoms depend on where the cysts form.

**If cysts are in the liver:**
- Belly pain
- Yellow skin or eyes (called jaundice)

**If cysts are in the lungs:**
- Chest pain
- Coughing up blood or fluid from the cyst

**In rare cases:**
- Hives
- A serious allergic reaction called anaphylaxis

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Echinococcosis

Doctors use several tests to find the infection.

- **Imaging tests** like ultrasound, CT scans, or MRI can show cysts in the liver or other organs.
- **Chest X-rays** can show cysts in the lungs.
- **Blood tests** check for antibodies. These are proteins made by the body to fight infections, including parasites.

These tests help confirm the diagnosis.

---

## How Echinococcosis Is Treated

Treatment depends on the type of worm and where the cysts are.

### For *Echinococcus granulosus* cysts:
- Doctors may remove the cyst with surgery.
- Or they may drain the cyst using a needle guided by ultrasound.
- After draining, they inject a salt solution into the cyst to kill the worms.
- Then they drain the solution out.

### For *Echinococcus multilocularis* cysts:
- These are usually removed with surgery.

### Medication:
- **Albendazole** is a medicine taken by mouth.
- It helps kill the worms and stop cysts from growing.
- It is given before and after surgery or drainage to prevent the infection from spreading if the cyst breaks open.
- It is usually taken for 1 to 6 months after treatment.
- It can also shrink or kill some cysts that cannot be removed.

### In severe cases:
- A liver transplant may be needed.

---

## How to Prevent Echinococcosis

You can reduce your risk by:

- Washing your hands carefully, especially after being outdoors or handling animals.
- Not eating food or drinking water that might be dirty with dog poop.
- Avoiding contact with dog feces, especially in areas where the infection is common.
- Keeping dogs away from animal carcasses and cleaning up their poop properly.

---

> *Note: This information is based on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and is intended for general understanding. Always talk to a doctor for medical advice.*

# Capillary Malformations

Capillary malformations are present at birth.  
They look like flat patches on the skin.  
The patches can be pink, red, or purple in color.

## What Is a Port-Wine Stain?

A port-wine stain is a type of capillary malformation.  
It is flat and ranges in color from red to purple.  
It can appear anywhere on the body.  
It often shows up on the face, scalp, neck, or arms and legs.

The stain gets darker over time.  
It may also become thicker and bumpy as a person ages.  
By middle age, it can be quite thick.  
The stain grows only as much as the person grows.  
It does not spread to new areas on its own.

A port-wine stain on the face, especially near the eye or forehead, can be a sign of a larger condition called Sturge-Weber syndrome.  
This syndrome affects the brain and eyes.  
It can cause seizures and glaucoma.  
In this condition, a similar blood vessel abnormality is found under the brain’s surface.

## How Are Capillary Malformations Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose capillary malformations by looking at the skin.  
They check the size, shape, and color of the patch.

In some cases, a brain scan may be needed.  
This is especially true if the patch is on the face.  
The scan helps rule out other problems.  
It can also check for signs of Sturge-Weber syndrome.  
The scan may include a special dye to get a clearer picture.

## How Are Capillary Malformations Treated?

There are two main treatment options:

### Vascular Laser Treatment
- This treatment uses a special light beam to target the blood vessels in the skin.  
- It works best when started early in life.  
- Starting treatment in infancy often leads to better results.  
- It can reduce thickening and bumps in the skin.  
- Multiple sessions are usually needed.  
- The treatment is not painful, but it may cause temporary redness or swelling.

### Cosmetic Creams
- A special cream can cover the patch.  
- The cream matches the patient’s skin color.  
- It is not a cure.  
- But it can help hide the patch.  
- It is useful for people who do not want or cannot have laser treatment.

Both options can improve how the skin looks.  
The choice depends on the person’s age, health, and personal preference.

# What Are Lymphomas?

Lymphomas are a type of cancer that starts in a kind of white blood cell called a lymphocyte.

Lymphocytes help your body fight infections.

There are two main types of lymphocytes:
- B cells
- T cells

B cells make antibodies. Antibodies help your body attack germs like bacteria and viruses.

T cells help control your immune system. They also help fight off viruses.

Lymphomas are similar to other cancers of white blood cells, such as leukemia.

All lymphocytes start in the bone marrow. From there, they travel through your blood and through a network of small tubes called lymphatic vessels.

Along this network, you have small clusters of lymphocytes called lymph nodes.

When lymphocytes become cancerous, they turn into lymphoma cells.

These cancer cells can stay in one lymph node. Or they can spread to other parts of your body, such as:
- The bone marrow
- The blood
- The spleen
- Any other organ

Cancer cells do not work like normal white blood cells. They cannot help your body fight infections.

## The Two Main Types of Lymphoma

There are two major types of lymphoma:
- Hodgkin lymphoma
- Non-Hodgkin lymphoma

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is more common than Hodgkin lymphoma.

There are many different kinds of non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

## How the Lymphatic System Helps Fight Infections

Your lymphatic system is part of your body’s defense system.

It includes:
- Lymphatic vessels (tubes that carry fluid)
- Lymph nodes (small glands that hold lymphocytes)
- Bone marrow (where blood cells start)
- Spleen (a filter for blood)

This system helps your body find and destroy germs.

## More Information

The following resource may help you learn more:

**Leukemia & Lymphoma Society**  
This group offers clear, full information about blood cancers.  
You can learn about:
- How doctors diagnose lymphoma
- What treatments are available
- How to get support and care

# Home Health Care

Home health care helps people who need medical care at home. It is often used when someone needs:

- Regular checks on their health
- Help with changing medicines
- Wound care or dressing changes
- Light physical therapy

## When Home Health Care Is Used

Home health care is common after a hospital stay. But you do not need to be in the hospital first. It is especially helpful for older adults.

It may also be used for:

- People who need long-term medical care each year
- People who are stable but have serious trouble doing daily tasks
- People with sudden or long-term health problems
- People who are nearing the end of life (end-of-life care)

Home health care is becoming more popular for long-term care. It can help avoid nursing homes. When planned well, it costs less than staying in a care facility.

## Who Provides Home Health Care?

Home health care is given by agencies. These agencies can be different sizes and owned by different groups. Some are certified.

To be certified, an agency must meet state rules and federal standards for Medicare. Certified agencies offer skilled nursing care. A doctor must approve the care plan. Nurses follow the doctor’s instructions. The doctor checks in when care needs to change.

## Communication Is Key

To keep patients safe and healthy, all health care workers must talk to each other. This includes nurses, doctors, and caregivers.

If a patient’s condition changes, the patient or caregiver must tell the nurse or doctor right away. This helps catch problems early and keep care on track.

## What Services Are Offered?

Home health care can include both medical and nonmedical help.

### Medical Services

- Nursing care
- Physical therapy and occupational therapy
- Hospice care and short-term relief for caregivers (respite)
- Equipment like wheelchairs, walkers, and commodes
- IV medicine
- Dialysis
- Nutrition through tubes or IV
- Breathing support machines
- Tests like blood work, X-rays, and heart checks

### Nonmedical Services

- Help with bathing, washing hair, using the toilet, and getting dressed
- Cleaning the home
- Emergency alert systems (like personal alarms)
- Security cameras
- Delivery of meals

# Pneumothorax

A pneumothorax happens when air gets into the space between the lungs and the chest wall. This air pushes on the lung and causes it to collapse. The lung is covered by a thin, double-layered membrane called the pleura. Normally, this space has no air. When air enters, the lung can only partly or fully collapse.

## Symptoms of Pneumothorax

Symptoms depend on how much air is in the space and how fast it builds up.

- You may feel sudden sharp chest pain.
- You may have trouble breathing.
- The pain can spread to your shoulder, neck, or belly.
- Some people have a dry, hacking cough.
- In mild cases, you may have no symptoms at all.
- In severe cases, you may feel dizzy, weak, or even go into shock.
- In rare cases, a pneumothorax can be life-threatening.

If the air builds up slowly, symptoms are usually milder. If it builds up fast, symptoms are worse.

Most people feel better over time. The body slowly absorbs the air. The lung may slowly reinflate on its own.

## How It Is Diagnosed

Your doctor will check you with a physical exam and imaging tests.

- A doctor listens to your chest with a stethoscope. If the lung is collapsed, the breathing sounds are weaker on that side.
- Tapping on the chest may make a hollow, drum-like sound.
- Air under the skin can cause a crackling feeling when touched.
- A chest x-ray shows the air pocket and the collapsed lung.
- A CT scan or ultrasound can also confirm the diagnosis.

## Types of Pneumothorax

### Primary Spontaneous Pneumothorax

This happens without any known cause. It often affects tall young men under 40, especially those who smoke tobacco or marijuana.

- It usually happens when a small weak spot on the lung bursts.
- Most people recover fully.
- About 3 out of 10 people will have it again.

### Secondary Spontaneous Pneumothorax

This happens in people with a known lung problem.

- It is more common in older adults with chronic lung disease.
- It often happens in people with COPD, cystic fibrosis, asthma, or other lung conditions.
- It can also happen in people with lung infections like tuberculosis or pneumonia.
- Because the lungs are already weak, symptoms are usually worse.
- The chance of it coming back depends on the cause.

### Catamenial Pneumothorax

This is a rare type that happens in women around the time of their period.

- It occurs within 48 hours of starting a period.
- It can also happen in women who take estrogen after menopause.
- It is caused by endometriosis in the chest.
- Endometriosis means tissue from the lining of the uterus grows in other places.
- This tissue may move to the lungs through a hole in the diaphragm or through blood vessels.

### Traumatic Pneumothorax

This happens after an injury or a medical procedure.

- It can happen after a chest injury.
- It can also happen during procedures like:
  - Thoracentesis (removing fluid from the chest)
  - Bronchoscopy (looking inside the airways)
  - Thoracoscopy (looking inside the chest)
- Ventilators (breathing machines) can cause lung damage, especially in people with COPD or severe lung injury.
- Divers and pilots are at higher risk because of pressure changes in the air or water.

## Treatment of Pneumothorax

### Small Pneumothorax

- A small pneumothorax may not need treatment.
- The body can absorb the air in a few days.
- Larger ones may take weeks to heal.

### Removing the Air

- If you have trouble breathing, the air can be removed.
- A thin tube (catheter) is placed into the chest.
- A syringe pulls the air out.
- The tube can stay in place to catch any new air.
- You should stop smoking. Counseling can help.

### Chest Tube

- A chest tube is used if the catheter does not work.
- It is placed through a small cut in the chest wall.
- It connects to a drainage system that lets air out but keeps air from coming back in.
- A suction machine may be used if air keeps leaking in.

### Surgery

Surgery may be needed in some cases.

- It is often done using a small camera (thoracoscope) through the chest wall.
- The surgeon repairs the leak in the lung.
- The inner and outer layers of the pleura are glued together to prevent future air leaks.
- Surgery is recommended for:
  - People at high risk, like divers or pilots, after the first episode.
  - People with secondary pneumothorax who are healthy enough for surgery.
  - People who have had the same side affected twice.
  - People whose lung does not heal on its own.

### Sealing the Pleural Space

If surgery is not possible due to poor health:

- A medicine like talc or doxycycline can be put into the chest through a tube.
- This causes the layers of the pleura to stick together.
- This stops air from building up again.
- This method is less effective than surgery.

## Summary

- A pneumothorax is a lung collapse caused by air in the space between the lung and chest wall.
- Symptoms range from mild to life-threatening.
- Diagnosis is done with a physical exam and imaging tests.
- Treatment depends on the size and cause.
- Small cases may heal on their own.
- Larger cases need air removal with a tube.
- Surgery can prevent future episodes.
- People with ongoing lung problems or high-risk jobs may need surgery after the first episode.

Always talk to your doctor about your symptoms and treatment options.

# Drug Interactions

Drug interactions happen when one medicine changes how another medicine works. This can happen when you take two or more medicines at the same time. It can also happen when you take a medicine with food or a dietary supplement.

## How Drug Interactions Work

- One medicine can make another medicine stronger.
- One medicine can make another medicine weaker.
- Sometimes, the change is harmful. This can cause side effects or make the medicine stop working.
- In rare cases, doctors may use a drug interaction on purpose to help treat a disease.

### Example of a Helpful Interaction

- A doctor may give two medicines together to treat HIV.
- One medicine, called ritonavir, changes how the other medicine, lopinavir, works.
- This makes lopinavir stay in the body longer and work better.

## Risks of Drug Interactions

- Some medicines are dangerous even when taken alone.
- Taking another medicine with them can make the risk of harm much higher.
- Always check with your doctor or pharmacist before starting a new medicine.

## Medicines That Can Cause Serious Interactions

Some medicines are more likely to cause serious problems when taken with others. These include:

- Medicines that treat heart rhythm problems (like quinidine)
- Cancer medicines (like methotrexate)
- Heart medicines (like digoxin)
- Mood stabilizers (like lithium)
- Asthma medicines (like theophylline)
- Blood thinners (like warfarin)

Other medicines are broken down in the liver. If you take two of these together, one can change how the other is processed. This includes:

- Anxiety medicines (like alprazolam)
- Depression medicines (like amitriptyline)
- Cholesterol medicines (like atorvastatin)
- Seizure medicines (like carbamazepine)
- HIV medicines (like protease inhibitors)
- Some blood pressure and diabetes medicines

## Medicines That Can Block Liver Processing

Some medicines stop the liver from breaking down other medicines. This can make the other medicine too strong. These include:

- Some cancer medicines (like cimetidine)
- Some antibiotics (like clarithromycin)
- Some antifungal medicines (like fluconazole)
- Some antidepressants (like fluoxetine)
- Some HIV medicines (like ritonavir)
- Grapefruit juice (can have the same effect)

## Medicines That Speed Up Liver Processing

Some medicines make the liver break down other medicines faster. This can make the other medicine too weak. These include:

- Some seizure medicines (like phenobarbital)
- Some blood pressure medicines (like bosentan)
- Some HIV medicines (like efavirenz)
- Some herbal products (like St. John’s wort)

> **Important:** Always check with your doctor or pharmacist before taking a new medicine with any of these. Use a trusted source like Drugs.com to check for possible interactions.

## Therapeutic Duplication

- This happens when you take two medicines that do the same thing.
- For example, taking one medicine for anxiety and another for sleep.
- Both medicines can make you very sleepy or dizzy.
- This can lead to serious side effects.

## Types of Drug Interactions

There are two main types of drug interactions:

### 1. Pharmacodynamic Interactions

- One medicine changes how your body responds to another.
- This happens at the level of the body’s cells or receptors.
- For example, two medicines that both slow down your heart can make it too slow.

### 2. Pharmacokinetic Interactions

- One medicine changes how the other is absorbed, moved through the body, broken down, or removed.
- This can change how much of the medicine is in your body.
- It can make the medicine stronger or weaker.
- It can also change how long the medicine stays in your body.
- These changes are often predictable.
- Doctors can watch for them by checking blood levels or watching for symptoms.

> **Always talk to your doctor or pharmacist** before starting, stopping, or changing any medicine. This helps keep you safe.

# Needle Biopsy of the Pleura or Lung

This is a medical test that takes a small sample of tissue from the lung or the lining around the lung. The sample is sent to a lab to check for disease.

---

## What Is a Pleural Biopsy?

A pleural biopsy takes tissue from the lining around the lung. This is called the pleura.

- It may be done if a test called thoracentesis did not find the cause of fluid buildup between the layers of the pleura.
- The doctor first cleans the skin and numbs the area.
- A special cutting needle is used to take a small piece of tissue from the pleura.
- The tissue is sent to a lab to check for problems like cancer or tuberculosis.
- This test correctly finds tuberculosis in about 80 to 90 out of 100 cases.
- It is less reliable for finding cancer or other conditions.

---

## What Is a Lung Biopsy?

A lung biopsy takes tissue from a lung tumor.

- It may be needed when a doctor needs to look at lung tissue to make a diagnosis.
- The skin is numbed first.
- The doctor uses imaging tools to guide the needle to the tumor. These tools include:
  - Chest CT scan
  - Navigational bronchoscopy
  - Ultrasound
- The needle collects a small sample of tissue or cells.
- The sample is sent to a lab for testing.
- If an infection is suspected, the lab can grow bacteria from the sample to find the cause.

---

## Possible Risks

Both types of biopsies can cause side effects. These are similar to those from thoracentesis, but bleeding and air in the chest (pneumothorax) are more common with biopsies.

- Bleeding can happen at the site.
- Air can leak into the space around the lung, which may cause the lung to collapse.

---

# Pain in an Arm or Leg

Pain in an arm or leg can affect all or part of the limb.  
If your pain is in one joint or several joints, see separate information on joint pain.  
The pain may come and go or stay all the time.  
It may get worse when you move, or it may not be linked to movement at all.  
Other symptoms often point to the cause.

---

## What Causes Limb Pain?

The most common causes are easy to spot from your story and symptoms.

### Injuries and Overuse
This section does not cover pain from injuries or overuse.  
Pain in one joint or many joints is covered elsewhere.

There are many possible causes.  
The most common ones are:

- Deep vein blood clot (DVT)  
- Skin infection (cellulitis)  
- Nerve root problem in the spine (radiculopathy)

Some causes are rare but serious.  
They need quick diagnosis and treatment.  
These include:

- Sudden blockage of an artery in the limb  
- Deep infection in soft tissues  
- Heart problem causing pain in the arm (without chest pain)

---

### Common Causes of Limb Pain

| Cause | What You Might Notice | How Doctors Check |
|------|------------------------|-------------------|
| **Skin infection (cellulitis)** | Redness (or darker color on dark skin), warmth, soreness, swelling | Doctor’s exam |  
| | Sometimes fever | Blood and tissue tests (if immune system is weak) |
| **Deep soft-tissue infection** (like myonecrosis or necrotizing infection) | Deep, constant pain that feels worse than it looks | Redness, warmth, soreness, tight swelling, fever |  
| | Sometimes crackling under the skin, bad-smelling fluid, blisters, dead skin, signs of serious illness (like confusion, fast heartbeat, pale skin, shock) | Blood and tissue tests |  
| | Imaging tests (X-ray, MRI) may be needed |
| **Bone infection (osteomyelitis)** | Deep, constant pain, often at night | Tenderness in the bone, fever |  
| | Often risk factors: weak immune system, IV drug use, known infection nearby or far away | X-ray, MRI, or CT scan |  
| | Sometimes bone culture |
| **Bone tumor** (in the bone or spread from another cancer) | Deep, constant pain, often at night | Tenderness in the bone |  
| | Often a history of cancer | X-ray, MRI, or CT scan |
| **Deep vein blood clot (DVT)** | Swelling, warmth, redness, sometimes bulging veins | Risk factors: blood clotting issues, recent surgery, long sitting, cancer |  
| | Ultrasound scan |
| | Sometimes blood test (D-dimer) |
| **Chronic vein problems (venous stasis)** | Mild ache with swelling, redness, warmth in lower leg | Sometimes small sores on the skin |  
| | Doctor’s exam |
| **Sudden poor blood flow (acute ischemia)** | Sudden, severe pain | Cold, pale, weak pulse, slow return of color after pressing nail |  
| | Sometimes long-term changes: thin skin, hair loss, pale color, sores |  
| | After a few hours: numbness, muscle soreness |  
| | Known history of poor blood flow in limbs | Immediate angiography (special X-ray of blood vessels) |
| **Poor blood flow over time (peripheral arterial insufficiency)** | Pain in legs when walking, goes away with rest | Low blood pressure in ankle compared to arm |  
| | Long-term changes: thin skin, hair loss, pale color, sores | Ultrasound |  
| | Sometimes angiography |
| **Nerve problem (plexopathy)** | Weakness, often reduced reflexes | Numbness in a nerve pattern |  
| | Usually need nerve tests (EMG and nerve conduction) | Sometimes MRI |
| **Thoracic outlet syndrome** | Pain and tingling from neck or shoulder into arm and hand | Doctor’s exam |  
| | Sometimes nerve tests or MRI |
| **Spine nerve problem (radiculopathy)** | Pain and numbness in a pattern along a nerve | Pain gets worse with movement |  
| | Often back or neck pain | Weakness and reduced reflexes in a nerve pattern |  
| | Usually need MRI | Sometimes nerve tests |
| **Nerve pain (polyneuropathy)** | Long-term burning pain, usually in both hands or both feet | Numbness, tingling, or pain from light touch |  
| | Often from alcohol use | Doctor’s exam |  
| | Sometimes nerve tests |
| **Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS)** | Burning pain, extreme sensitivity to touch, changes in skin color or temperature | Often follows an injury (even a small one) |  
| | Doctor’s exam |
| **Heart problem (acute coronary ischemia)** | Arm pain with no injury or soreness | Sweating, shortness of breath at same time |  
| | History of heart disease | ECG and blood test (troponin) |  
| | Sometimes stress test or heart angiography |
| **Muscle pain (myofascial pain syndrome)** | Pain and soreness along a tight muscle band | Pain gets worse with movement or pressure on a trigger point |  
| | Doctor’s exam |

---

## How Doctors Evaluate Limb Pain

It is very important to rule out sudden blockage of an artery.  
This is a medical emergency.

---

## How Limb Pain Is Treated

Treatment depends on the cause.  
Pain relief medicines can help ease the pain.

---

## Key Points

- Sudden, severe pain in a limb may mean a blocked artery.  
- The timing of the pain and signs like poor blood flow, swelling, or nerve issues help doctors find the cause.

# Help with Eating for People Who Are Dying or Have Severe Dementia

As people get close to the end of life, they often lose their appetite. People with advanced dementia also lose the ability to eat on their own. Family members may worry about this and ask doctors about feeding tubes or liquids through a vein. These are forms of nutritional support.

Family members often want to use nutritional support because food is linked to love, care, and kindness. Sharing meals is also a special time for families. Many people do not want to stop this tradition.

But nutritional support does not help. It does not make people live longer. It does not make them feel better. In fact, many doctors and nurses say it can make the final days more uncomfortable. 

People who are dying or have advanced dementia do not feel hungry. They are more comfortable when they eat and drink only when they want to. The body naturally slows down near the end of life. This includes the need for food and drink. In the past, people who were dying were not forced to eat. They were allowed to stop eating when they wanted. Doctors usually follow this practice today.

### Did You Know...

- Do not push or urge a person who is dying or has advanced dementia to eat more than they want.

If death is not expected within hours or days, doctors may try nutritional support for a short time. This is to see if it helps with comfort, clear thinking, or energy. But it often does not help. The person and their family should talk with the care team about when to start and when to stop nutritional support. This is especially important if it is not helping.

Even if nutritional support is not used, family members and caregivers can still help in gentle ways:

- Offer food slowly.
- Give small amounts of food and small sips of water.
- Offer favorite foods that are strong in flavor or easy to swallow.
- Let the person choose when and what to eat or drink.

Some medicines can help increase appetite. These include certain antidepressants, megestrol, or dronabinol. These medicines may help a person want to eat more.

Other care can also bring comfort:

- Brush the person’s teeth.
- Use wet swabs to keep the mouth moist.
- Offer ice chips.
- Use lip salve to prevent dry lips.

These actions help the person feel better. They also help family members feel more at ease. Hospice care teams can support both the person and their family.

Counseling can help family members who are unsure about whether to use nutritional support. It can help them make decisions that feel right for their loved one.

# Postinfectious Glomerulonephritis (PIGN)

This condition happens after an infection. It most often follows a specific type of strep infection. The kidneys become inflamed. This can cause problems with how the kidneys work.

Most children aged 3 to 15 get this condition. It is more common in crowded or low-income areas.

## What Causes Postinfectious Glomerulonephritis?

The most common cause is a type of strep bacteria. These are called nephritogenic strains. The two main types are:
- Type 12, which causes sore throat.
- Type 49, which causes skin sores (impetigo).

The kidney problem usually starts 6 to 21 days after the infection. Sometimes it can take up to 6 weeks.

A growing number of cases are linked to staph infections. These affect older people more.

Other causes include other bacteria, viruses, parasites, and fungi. Infections from heart valve problems or brain shunts can also lead to this condition.

The exact cause is not fully known. But it seems that parts of the bacteria stick to the kidney filters. This triggers an immune reaction. The body’s defense system attacks the kidneys by mistake. This causes swelling and damage.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms can be mild or very serious. Some people have no symptoms at all.

Common signs include:
- Blood in the urine. The urine may look dark, like cola, brown, or smoky.
- Protein in the urine. This can be mild or very high.
- Swelling in the face, hands, or feet.
- Less urine than normal.
- High blood pressure.
- Feeling tired or unwell.

Fever is rare. If fever is present, it may mean the infection is still active.

In rare cases, kidney failure can happen. This can cause fluid buildup in the body. It may lead to heart problems or very high blood pressure. Dialysis may be needed in about 1 out of every 100 children.

Some people still have blood in the urine or high blood pressure after they feel better. In rare cases, protein in the urine stays high even after recovery.

Symptoms from non-strep infections can look like other kidney diseases. These include blood vessel inflammation, blood clots in the kidneys, or side effects from certain medicines.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look for signs of a recent infection. They also check the urine and blood.

### Urine Test
The urine test often shows:
- Red blood cells that look abnormal.
- Red blood cell casts (a sign of kidney damage).
- White blood cells.
- Kidney cells.
- Protein.

A simple urine test can show if protein is high. The normal level is below 0.2. Levels above 2 are high. Some people have levels in the nephrotic range (3 grams or more per day).

### Blood Tests
- **Complement levels** drop during active disease. C3 and CH50 are the most important. These usually return to normal in 6 to 8 weeks.
- **Creatinine** levels may rise. But they usually do not get high enough to need dialysis.
- **Antibody tests** check for past strep infection. These include:
  - Antistreptolysin O (ASO)
  - Antihyaluronidase
  - Anti-DNAase

These antibodies go up after a strep infection. They stay high for months. But they are not specific to this condition.

### Kidney Biopsy
A small sample of kidney tissue may be taken. This is done only if the diagnosis is unclear.

The biopsy shows:
- Swollen and busy kidney filters.
- White blood cells in the filters.
- Swelling and growth of kidney cells.
- Clots in small blood vessels.
- Crescent-shaped areas in the kidney capsule (in severe cases).

The immune system leaves behind deposits in the kidney. These deposits are made of antibodies and other immune material. They are found under the kidney filter cells.

Immunofluorescence shows IgG and complement in a patchy pattern. Electron microscopy shows hump-shaped deposits under the filter cells.

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure that directly treats the kidney damage. Treatment focuses on helping the body heal.

Supportive care includes:
- Limiting salt, protein, and fluids in the diet.
- Treating swelling and high blood pressure.
- Using dialysis if kidney failure occurs.

Antibiotics may help prevent the condition if given within 36 hours of the infection. But they do not help once kidney damage has started.

## What Is the Outlook?

Most people get better. Kidney function returns to normal in 1 to 3 months.

Some people still have blood in the urine or protein in the urine for up to 5 years. Minor colds can cause these signs to return temporarily.

Kidney cells return to normal within weeks. But some scarring may remain.

In rare cases, the condition gets worse. About 10% of adults and 1% of children develop a more serious form of kidney disease.

## Key Points

- Think about postinfectious glomerulonephritis in children who had a sore throat or skin infection and now have kidney symptoms.
- Blood tests showing low complement levels confirm the diagnosis.
- A kidney biopsy can confirm the diagnosis but is rarely needed.
- Supportive care helps most people recover full kidney function.

# How Children Grow and Develop

Children grow and change fast between the ages of 1 and 13. Their bodies, minds, and emotions all develop quickly. They go from wobbling on their feet to running, jumping, and playing team sports. They also learn to read, talk, and do harder tasks. But every child grows at their own pace. Some grow faster in one area, others in another.

## What Affects a Child’s Development

Several things help shape how a child grows:

- **Family history:** Some traits run in families. For example, some children start walking or talking later than others, and this can be common in their family.
- **Food and nutrition:** Good food is very important. Without it, a child may not grow or learn as well.
- **Home and surroundings:** A child needs mental stimulation. If they are not given chances to learn and play, their growth may slow. But if they are given fun, safe, and engaging experiences, they grow faster.
- **Health problems:** If a child has a physical issue, like not being able to hear well, it can slow their ability to learn to talk.

Sometimes a child’s growth slows down for a short time. This is normal. Doctors use common milestones—skills most children reach by certain ages—to check if a child is growing as expected. For example, most children learn to walk by their first birthday. But it is okay if a child walks late and talks early. Skills can develop at different times.

---

## How Children Learn and Think

A child’s ability to understand, think, and reason is called intellect. This grows best when children are loved, cared for, and given chances to learn.

### What Children Learn at Different Ages

**At age 2:**  
Most children understand time in simple ways. They think everything in the past happened “yesterday” and everything in the future will happen “tomorrow.” They have a strong imagination. They may not know the difference between pretend and real.  

**By age 4:**  
Children understand time better. They know the day has morning, afternoon, and night. They can see how seasons change.

**From 18 months to 5 years:**  
A child’s word list grows fast—from about 50 words to thousands. They start naming things and asking questions. By age 2, they use two words together, like “more juice.” By age 3, they make simple sentences. Their speech gets clearer. By age 2, others can understand half of what they say. By age 4, they are easy to understand. A 4-year-old can tell a short story and talk with adults or other kids.

Even before 18 months, children enjoy being read to. By age 5, they can say the alphabet and recognize simple words. These skills are the first steps to learning to read. Most children begin reading by age 6 or 7, depending on how much they are read to and their natural ability.

**By age 7:**  
Children think in more complex ways. They can pay attention to more than one thing at once. For example, they understand that a tall, thin cup can hold the same amount of water as a short, wide one. They know medicine can taste bad but still help them feel better. They understand that a parent can be angry but still love them. They can see things from another person’s point of view. This helps them take turns in games or conversations. They follow game rules. They use what they see and think about different views to solve problems.

---

## How Children Feel and Behave

A child’s emotions and behavior depend on their age and their natural mood, or temperament.

Some children are cheerful and easy to care for. They adapt well to routines like sleeping, eating, and waking. They enjoy new things.  
Some children are more sensitive and find it hard to adjust. They may have irregular routines. They may react negatively to new situations.  
Some children are in between these two types.

### Crying
Crying is how babies talk before they can speak. They cry when hungry, uncomfortable, or upset. Babies cry the most—about 3 hours a day—at 6 weeks old. By 3 months, they usually cry only about 1 hour a day. Parents can try feeding, changing diapers, or checking for pain. If that does not help, holding or walking with the baby often calms them. Sometimes nothing works. Parents should not force food on a crying baby. If the baby is hungry, they will eat.

### Separation Anxiety (Around 8 Months)
Babies often get upset when separated from their parents. This can happen at bedtime or at child care. They may have tantrums. This can last for months. A favorite blanket or stuffed animal can help. It acts like a symbol of the parent.

### Tantrums (2 to 3 Years)
Children at this age test limits. They do things they are told not to, just to see what happens. They hear “no” a lot. This is normal. Tantrums are part of growing up. They help children show frustration when they cannot say how they feel. Parents can help by:
- Not letting children get too tired or too frustrated.
- Knowing their child’s patterns.
- Avoiding situations

# Breath-Holding Spells

A breath-holding spell happens when a child stops breathing by accident. The child then loses consciousness for a short time. This usually happens right after something scary, upsetting, or painful.

(See also: Overview of Behavioral Problems in Children.)

- Breath-holding spells affect between 0.1% and 5% of healthy children.
- They usually start in the first year of life.
- Most common at age 2.
- Over half of children stop having spells by age 4.
- Almost all children stop by age 8.
- A few may still have spells into adulthood.

These spells are not linked to epilepsy. But they may raise the chance of fainting later in life.

Almost all breath-holding spells are caused by something outside the child. This can be a physical event, like a fall. Or it can be an emotional event, like being scared or angry.

There are two types of breath-holding spells:

## 1. Cyanotic Breath-Holding Spell

This is the most common type. The child turns blue during the spell.

- The child cries out, then breathes out.
- The child does not breathe in again.
- The skin turns blue.
- The child loses consciousness.
- A brief seizure may happen, but it is rare.
- After a few seconds, breathing starts again.
- Skin color returns to normal.
- The child wakes up fully.

You can sometimes stop the spell by placing a cold cloth on the child’s face at the start.

Parents should not give in to the child’s behavior during a spell. This can make the problem worse. If spells happen often, try to avoid situations that trigger them.

Some children with this type of spell may benefit from iron supplements—even if they are not anemic.  
If the child has sleep apnea, treating that condition may also help.

## 2. Pallid Breath-Holding Spell

This type is less common. It happens after pain or a sudden shock.

- The child stops breathing.
- The heart slows down a lot.
- The child becomes pale and limp.
- The child loses consciousness quickly.
- If the spell lasts more than a few seconds:
  - Muscles may stiffen.
  - A seizure may happen.
  - The child may lose control of the bladder or bowels.
- After the spell, the heart speeds up.
- Breathing returns on its own.
- The child wakes up without help.

Because this type is rare, doctors may need to do more tests if spells happen often.  
An electrocardiogram (ECG) and an EEG can help find the cause. These tests check the heart and brain activity at the same time. This helps doctors tell if the problem is from the heart or the brain.

# Retropharyngeal Abscess

A retropharyngeal abscess is a pocket of pus that forms in the back of the throat.

## What Causes a Retropharyngeal Abscess?

- A bacterial infection causes the abscess.
- The infection often starts in the tonsils, throat, sinuses, adenoids, or nose.
- Many infections involve more than one type of bacteria.
- In some cases, HIV or tuberculosis can cause the infection.
- A sharp object, like a fish bone, can injure the back of the throat and lead to an abscess.

Lymph nodes in the back of the throat can become infected. These nodes usually shrink by age 4 to 5. That is why this condition mostly affects children between 1 and 8 years old. It is rare in adults.

## Symptoms

The main signs of a retropharyngeal abscess include:

- Pain and trouble swallowing
- High fever
- Swollen lymph nodes in the neck
- A muffled or hoarse voice
- Drooling, especially in children
- A squeaky or gasping sound when breathing in (called stridor)
- Stiff neck
- Children may hold their head tilted forward or back to breathe easier

The abscess can block the airway. This makes breathing hard. Children may lean forward and push their jaw out to open their airway. Adults often have severe neck pain but may not have stridor.

## Possible Complications

If not treated, the abscess can lead to:

- Blocked airway
- Bleeding around the abscess
- The abscess bursting into the airway (which can block breathing)
- Pneumonia
- Spasms in the voice box that make breathing worse
- Blood clots in the neck veins
- Infection spreading into the chest
- Widespread infection in the blood, which can cause organs to fail (called septic shock)

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor will suspect the condition if a child has:

- A very bad sore throat with no clear cause
- A stiff neck
- Stridor

To confirm the diagnosis, the doctor will use imaging tests:

- X-rays of the neck
- CT scan of the neck

These tests show the size and location of the abscess.

## How Is It Treated?

Most people recover well if treatment starts quickly.

Treatment includes two main steps:

1. **Antibiotics**  
   - You will get strong antibiotics through a vein (IV).
   - Common antibiotics used are ceftriaxone or clindamycin.

2. **Surgery to drain the abscess**  
   - A breathing tube is placed through the mouth into the windpipe to keep the airway open.
   - The doctor then cuts open the abscess to drain the pus.

This treatment helps prevent serious breathing problems and clears the infection.

# Hip Dislocations

Most hip dislocations happen when the hip is pushed backward. This often occurs during a car crash when the knee hits the dashboard and the leg is bent.

## What Can Go Wrong

- The sciatic nerve can be damaged.
- The ball of the thigh bone (femoral head) may lose its blood supply. This is called osteonecrosis. It can happen later and cause serious problems.

## Other Injuries That May Happen

- The kneecap (patella) may break.
- The back ligament of the knee (posterior cruciate ligament) may be torn.
- The hip socket (acetabulum) or the ball of the thigh bone may break.

## How a Dislocated Hip Looks

In a posterior dislocation:
- The leg is shorter than the other leg.
- The leg is pulled inward toward the body.
- The foot points inward.

Anterior dislocations are rare. In these cases:
- The leg is pushed outward.
- The foot points outward.

(See Overview of Dislocations for more information.)

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Hip Dislocations

### X-rays

Routine hip x-rays are usually enough to confirm a dislocation. They show the bones in the hip joint and whether they are out of place.

---

## How Doctors Treat Hip Dislocations

### Closed Reduction

The main treatment is to put the hip back in place without surgery. This should be done as soon as possible, ideally within six hours. Waiting longer increases the risk of osteonecrosis.

The patient must be relaxed and sedated. They lie on their back during the procedure.

There are three common methods:

### Allis Technique

- The leg is bent to 90 degrees at the hip.
- Gentle pulling is done on the leg to guide the bone back into place.
- A rigid board on the floor can help keep the body stable.
- A strap or brace holds the hips down to create counterpressure.

### Captain Morgan Technique

- The hips are held down with a sheet or belt.
- The dislocated leg is bent.
- The doctor places their knee under the patient’s knee and lifts up while pulling on the leg.
- This method may work better the first time than the Allis technique.

### Rocket Launcher Technique

- The doctor stands on the side of the injured hip, facing the patient’s feet.
- The leg is bent at the hip and knee to 90 degrees.
- The hips are held down with a sheet or by another person.
- The doctor squats and places the patient’s knee on their shoulder.
- The doctor pushes the knee inward and turns the foot outward to help move the hip.
- Then the doctor stands up and pulls down on the foot, using their shoulder as a pivot point.

After the hip is back in place:

### CT Scan

A CT scan is needed for all hips that are not artificial (native hips). This scan checks for:
- Fractures in the hip socket or thigh bone.
- Loose pieces of bone or cartilage inside the joint.

About 70 out of 100 people with a posterior hip dislocation also have a hip socket fracture.

If the scan shows a fracture or loose pieces:
- An orthopedic surgeon should be consulted.
- Surgery may be needed.

If the scan shows no fractures or loose pieces:
- The patient can go home.
- Use crutches.
- The foot can touch the floor for balance.
- Do not put any weight on the injured leg.
- Wait for a follow-up with an orthopedic doctor before putting weight on the leg.

---

## Dislocated Artificial Hip

After a total hip replacement, the new hip can come out of place without a major injury. This happens in up to 2 out of 100 people.

Posterior dislocations are more common.

### Treatment

- Closed reduction (putting the hip back in place without surgery) often works, especially for first-time dislocations.
- Sometimes, surgery is needed to fix the hip.

---

## Key Points

- Most hip dislocations are posterior.
- The leg is shorter, pulled inward, and turned inward.
- Use routine x-rays to confirm the diagnosis.
- Put the hip back in place as soon as possible, ideally within six hours.
- Delay increases the risk of bone damage.
- After reduction, do a CT scan to check for fractures or loose bone or cartilage pieces.

# Plague and Other Yersinia Infections

## What Is Plague?

Plague is a serious infection caused by a type of bacteria called *Yersinia pestis*.  
It mainly affects the lymph nodes or the lungs.  
The bacteria are spread mostly by rat fleas.  
Plague can cause fever, chills, swollen lymph nodes, headache, fast heartbeat, cough, trouble breathing, vomiting, and diarrhea.  
Doctors confirm the diagnosis by testing blood, spit, or pus from swollen lymph nodes.  
Antibiotics can save lives.  
Keeping infected people apart helps stop the disease from spreading.

In the past, big outbreaks of plague killed millions.  
This happened because there were many rats, crowded cities, and dirty living conditions.  
Today, plague happens only in small outbreaks or rare cases.

In the United States, over 90% of cases happen in rural or semi-rural areas of the Southwest.  
These include Arizona, California, Colorado, and New Mexico.  
Most cases are in people who camp or spend time outdoors.

Globally, most cases since the 1990s have been in Africa.  
The main countries are the Democratic Republic of Congo and Madagascar.  
Some cases also happen in Peru.

---

## How Plague Spreads

The bacteria that cause plague live in wild rodents like rats, mice, chipmunks, squirrels, prairie dogs, and wild rabbits.  
The rat flea carries the bacteria from one animal to another.  
When a wild animal dies, the fleas may jump to animals near homes.  
They can then bite pets, especially cats.  
If the fleas bite a person, they can pass the infection.  
People can also get infected through a cut or scratch when touching an infected animal.

Very rarely, plague spreads from person to person.  
This happens when someone breathes in tiny droplets from a cough or sneeze of an infected person.  
The bacteria go into the lungs and cause a type of pneumonia called pneumonic plague.  
This kind of spread usually only happens when people live close together or care for someone with pneumonic plague.

The plague bacteria could be used as a biological weapon.  
They can be spread through the air and inhaled.  
Small particles go deep into the lungs and cause pneumonic plague.  
Larger particles stay in the throat and cause throat plague.

---

## Symptoms of Plague

Plague comes in several forms.  
Each form has different symptoms.

### Bubonic Plague

This is the most common form.  
Symptoms can start a few hours to 12 days after exposure.  
Most often, they start 2 to 5 days after exposure.  
You may suddenly feel very cold and have a high fever, up to 106 degrees Fahrenheit (41 degrees Celsius).  
Your heartbeat becomes fast and weak.  
Your blood pressure may drop.

Soon after the fever starts, or at the same time, lymph nodes near the flea bite or scratch become swollen and painful.  
These swollen nodes are called buboes.  
They are hard, red, warm, and very tender.  
In the second week, pus may come out of the nodes.  
The liver and spleen may also get bigger.

A bump, sore, or black scab may form where the flea bit you.

You may feel restless, confused, disoriented, or unsteady on your feet.

The bacteria can spread through the blood.  
This can lead to lung infection, which causes pneumonic plague.

Without treatment, about 60% of people with bubonic plague die.  
Most die within 3 to 5 days.

### Pneumonic Plague

This is a lung infection caused by the plague bacteria.  
Symptoms start suddenly, usually 2 or 3 days after exposure.  
You will have a high fever, chills, fast heartbeat, and a severe headache.  
Within 24 hours, you will start coughing.  
At first, the cough brings up clear spit.  
Soon, the spit turns pink or bright red and looks foamy.  
It may look like raspberry syrup.

Breathing becomes fast and hard.

If not treated, pneumonic plague is almost always fatal.  
The risk of death stays high if treatment starts more than 24 hours after symptoms begin.

### Septicemic Plague

This is when the infection spreads into the blood.  
You may have nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and stomach pain.

The blood starts to clot too much.  
This blocks blood vessels.  
Eventually, the body runs out of clotting material.  
This causes bleeding.  
This condition is called disseminated intravascular coagulation.

Because blood flow is blocked, the limbs may turn black and die.  
This is why the disease was once called the Black Death.

Without treatment, many organs stop working.  
This can lead to death.

### Pestis Minor

This is a mild form of bubonic plague.  
Symptoms include swollen lymph nodes, fever, headache, and tiredness.  
These symptoms go away within a week.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Plague

Doctors need to act fast to diagnose plague.  
The longer they wait, the higher the risk of death.

To diagnose plague, doctors take samples of:
- Blood
- Spit (sputum)
- Pus from swollen lymph nodes

They look at the samples under a microscope.  
They also send them to a lab to grow the bacteria.  
They test the blood for antibodies to the bacteria.  
They may use fast tests to find the bacteria or its DNA.  
One such test is called polymerase chain reaction, or PCR.

If doctors suspect pneumonic plague, they take a chest X-ray.

---

## How Plague Is Treated

Treatment must start right away.  
It greatly reduces the chance of dying.

For pneumonic or septicemic plague, antibiotics must be given within 24 hours of symptom onset.

The main treatments are:
- Streptomycin
- Gentamicin

These are given as injections for 10 days, or until the fever has been normal for 3 days.  
Other effective antibiotics include:
- Doxycycline
- Levofloxacin
- Moxifloxacin
- Ciprofloxacin

People with pneumonic plague must be isolated.  
This stops the bacteria from spreading through the air.  
This is called respiratory isolation.  
It includes:
- Limiting who can enter the room
- Requiring staff near the patient to wear a mask, eye protection, a gown, and gloves

---

## How to Prevent Plague

You can reduce the risk of plague by:
- Removing things that attract rodents near your home.  
  This includes brush, rocks, junk, cluttered wood piles, and food.
- Wearing gloves when handling animals that might be infected.  
  This includes when skinning an animal.
- Using insect repellent like DEET when you are outdoors in areas where fleas are common.  
  This includes camping, hiking, or working outside.
- Using flea control products on pets.
- Not letting pets sleep in your bed if they go outside in areas where plague is found.

There is no plague vaccine available in the United States.

If someone has been near a person with pneumonic plague, doctors will:
- Check their temperature every 4 hours for 6 days.
- Give them antibiotics to prevent infection.

For people over 8 years old:  
- Doxycycline or ciprofloxacin

For children under 8 years old:  
- Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole

## Other Yersinia Infections

Other types of *Yersinia* bacteria, such as *Yersinia enterocolitica* and *Yersinia pseudotuberculosis*, live in animals worldwide.  
These bacteria can infect people, but the illness is usually much milder than plague.

You can get these infections by:
- Handling infected animals (for example, hunters)
- Eating or touching raw or undercooked meat
- Drinking water that is contaminated
- Drinking unpasteurized milk or eating dairy products from infected animals

Common symptoms include:
- Diarrhea (which usually goes away on its own)
- Sore throat
- Swollen lymph nodes in the lower right part of the belly
- Belly pain that feels like appendicitis

The bacteria can enter the blood, but they rarely spread beyond the intestines.

### Diagnosis

Doctors test:
- Blood
- Stool
- Spit
- Pus from swollen lymph nodes

### Treatment

Most people do not need antibiotics.  
The illness usually gets better on its own.  
But antibiotics are needed if the infection spreads to the blood or other organs.

### Prevention

To avoid these infections:
- Wash your hands with soap and water before eating or preparing food.
- Wash your hands after touching animals, especially their poop.
- Wash your hands after handling raw meat.
- Cook meat to the recommended safe temperature.
- Only drink pasteurized milk and eat pasteurized dairy products.
- Dispose of pet waste in a clean and safe way.

# Amebic Keratitis

Amebic keratitis is a rare eye infection caused by a tiny parasite called *Acanthamoeba*.  
It mostly affects people who wear contact lenses.  
The infection can cause serious damage to the eye if not treated early.

## How Common Is It?

Amebic keratitis affects about 1 in every 1 million people each year.  
This means about 2 eyes out of every 1 million are affected.

## Where Does the Parasite Come From?

The *Acanthamoeba* parasite lives in water, soil, sewage, and dust.  
It can also be found in tap water, showers, hot tubs, and air conditioning units.  
You can get infected if the parasite gets into your eye.

## Who Is at Risk?

Over 90 percent of cases happen in people who wear contact lenses.  
The risk goes up if you wear lenses while swimming or bathing.  
Using dirty or unsterile lens cleaning solutions also increases the risk.  
Soft contact lenses (except daily disposable ones) are more likely to cause problems.  
Using multi-purpose lens solutions or recalled solutions is risky.  
Poor cleaning habits with lenses can lead to infection.  
Some infections start after a scratch on the cornea.

## How Does the Infection Work?

The *Acanthamoeba* parasite has two forms:  
- A growing form called a trophozoite.  
- A tough, protective form called a cyst.  

The cysts are hard to kill.  
They can survive in harsh conditions.  
The parasite can enter the body through the eyes, nose, or broken skin.  
When it gets into the eye, it can cause severe inflammation and damage.

Both the cysts and the growing form can be found in the cornea during infection.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The infection causes intense pain.  
You may feel like something is in your eye.  
Your eye may be red and sensitive to light.  
You may cry more than usual.  
Your vision may become blurry.  
You will not have body-wide symptoms like fever or chills.  
The problem usually affects only one eye.  
In rare cases, both eyes can be affected.

At first, the eye may look like it has a herpes infection.  
Later, the cornea may show patchy cloudy areas.  
A ring-shaped pattern may appear.  
Inflammation in the front part of the eye is common.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

An eye doctor must examine you to confirm the diagnosis.  
A small sample of the cornea is taken.  
This sample is checked under a microscope.  
It is also grown in a special lab dish to see if the parasite grows.  

A lab test called PCR can detect the parasite’s DNA.  
This test is very accurate.  
Another test called in vivo confocal microscopy can spot cysts in the cornea.  
This test needs a skilled doctor to do it.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment must start early and be very strict.  
The first step is to gently remove the damaged surface layer of the cornea.  
This is called debridement.  

You will use strong eye drops.  
The drops include chlorhexidine or polyhexamethylene biguanide.  
You may use one or both.  
These drops are used every 1 to 2 hours for the first 3 days.  

Other eye drops like propamidine or hexamidine may also be used.  

Treatment lasts 6 to 12 months.  
It is slowly reduced as your eye heals.  
Stopping treatment too soon can cause the infection to come back.  

Most people do not need a cornea transplant.  
But if medicine does not work, a transplant may be needed.

## How Can You Prevent It?

Always follow your eye doctor’s and manufacturer’s instructions.  
Wash your hands well before touching your lenses.  
Use fresh lens solution every time.  
Do not reuse old solution.  
Do not add new solution to old.  
Never use tap water to clean or store lenses.  
Do not use homemade lens solutions.  

Avoid wearing lenses while swimming or bathing.  
Do not sleep with lenses in unless your doctor says it is safe.  
Avoid overnight wear unless approved.

## Key Points

- *Acanthamoeba* can cause a serious, long-lasting eye infection.  
- It mostly affects contact lens wearers.  
- See an eye doctor right away if you have eye pain and wear contact lenses.  
- Diagnosis is done by testing a sample from the cornea.  
- Tests include microscopy, culture, PCR, and special imaging.  
- Treatment includes debridement and strong eye drops.  
- Treatment lasts 6 to 12 months.  
- Do not stop treatment early.  
- Prevention is key. Follow all lens care rules.

# Tropical Sprue

Tropical sprue is a rare condition that affects the small intestine. It mainly happens in tropical and subtropical areas. The exact cause is not known, but doctors think an infection may play a role.

This condition causes the lining of the small intestine to become damaged. This damage stops the body from absorbing nutrients properly. As a result, people can become very low in important vitamins and minerals.

## Where It Happens

Tropical sprue is most common in:
- The Caribbean
- Southern India
- Southeast Asia

Both local people and visitors can get it. Visitors must have stayed in one of these areas for at least one month. Children rarely get this condition.

It is very rare in the United States. The number of cases worldwide has been going down over the past few decades.

## Symptoms

The most common symptoms are:
- Light-colored, soft, bulky, greasy, and very smelly stools (this is called steatorrhea)
- Long-term diarrhea
- Fever
- Feeling unwell all the time (malaise)
- Losing weight

Other symptoms can happen if the body lacks certain nutrients:
- A sore tongue can happen if you do not get enough vitamin B2.
- Anemia can happen if you lack iron, vitamin B12, or folate. This causes tiredness and weakness.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors suspect tropical sprue in people who:
- Live in or have recently visited a tropical or subtropical area
- Have anemia
- Have symptoms of poor nutrient absorption

To confirm the diagnosis, the doctor will:
- Take a small sample of tissue from the small intestine using a thin, flexible tube with a camera (called an endoscope).
- Look at the tissue under a microscope. The damaged lining will show clear signs of the disease.

A stool sample is also tested to rule out infections like parasites or bacteria.

Blood tests are done to check for low levels of nutrients and signs of undernutrition.

## Treatment

Most people recover fully with treatment. But some may get sick again.

Treatment includes:
- The antibiotic tetracycline, taken for up to six months.
- Folate supplements, taken by mouth.
- Vitamin B12 injections, given for several weeks.
- Other vitamins or minerals are added if needed.

Following this treatment plan helps the small intestine heal and restores normal nutrient absorption.

# Arginine Vasopressin Resistance

This condition is also called nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. It means your kidneys do not respond properly to a hormone called vasopressin. This hormone helps your body hold onto water. When it does not work, your kidneys make a lot of very dilute urine.

You can be born with this condition. Or it can happen later in life due to other health problems.

## What Happens in This Condition?

Your kidneys cannot concentrate urine. This means you pass large amounts of urine that are very watery. You may pass between 3 and 20 liters of urine each day.

You usually feel very thirsty. This helps your body stay balanced. Your blood sodium level stays near normal if you can drink enough water.

But if you cannot drink enough water, you may become severely dehydrated. This can raise your blood sodium level too high. High blood sodium can cause confusion, muscle twitching, seizures, or even coma.

In rare cases, very high urine output can cause swelling in the tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect this condition if you pass a lot of urine. In babies, parents may notice this first. If not, the first sign may be dehydration.

Tests include:

- A 24-hour urine collection to measure how much urine you make and how concentrated it is.
- Blood tests to check your electrolyte levels, especially sodium.

If you make more than 50 milliliters of urine per kilogram of body weight each day, this is a sign of polyuria (excessive urine).  
If your urine is very dilute (less than 300 milliosmoles per kilogram), this suggests either a lack of vasopressin or resistance to it.

In this condition, your urine stays dilute even when your body is low on fluid. Normally, your urine would be more concentrated when you are dehydrated.

If your urine is more concentrated (over 300 milliosmoles per kilogram), another cause is likely. For example, too much sugar in the urine or other kidney problems.

Your blood sodium level is usually only slightly high (142 to 145 milliequivalents per liter) if you drink enough water. But it can rise very high if you do not have access to water.

## How Is It Treated?

The main goal is to prevent dehydration. This means drinking enough water every day.

You should also:

- Eat less salt.
- Eat less protein.

If a medicine is causing the problem, stop it. Treat any underlying health issue.

If you still pass too much urine, your doctor may prescribe medicine. These include:

- Thiazide diuretics (like hydrochlorothiazide). These seem to help reduce urine output even though they are diuretics.
- Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as indomethacin.
- Amiloride.

These medicines work by reducing how much water reaches the part of the kidney that should respond to vasopressin.

## What Is the Outlook?

Babies born with this condition can suffer brain damage and lifelong learning problems if treatment is delayed. Early treatment is very important.

Even with treatment, children may grow more slowly. This is likely due to repeated dehydration.

All complications except for rare swelling in the urine tubes can be prevented by drinking enough water.

## Key Points

- People with this condition cannot concentrate their urine because their kidneys do not respond to vasopressin.
- They pass large amounts of dilute urine.
- They feel thirsty and usually have normal blood sodium levels if they can drink water.
- Think about this condition in babies who pass a lot of urine or in families with a history of it.
- Test urine volume and concentration over 24 hours.
- Check blood electrolytes.
- Confirm the diagnosis with a water deprivation test.
- Drink plenty of water every day.
- Eat less salt and less protein.
- Use medicine like thiazide diuretics or amiloride if needed.

# Cupping

Cupping is a practice used in traditional Chinese medicine.  
It is thought to boost blood flow to the area where the cup is placed.  
Better blood flow may help the body heal faster in that area.

A cup is placed on the skin.  
The air inside the cup is heated.  
In modern times, a rubber pump is often used to heat the air.  
The cup is quickly turned upside down and placed on the skin.  
The change in air pressure creates a vacuum.  
This vacuum pulls the skin up into the cup.  
The cup stays in place for several minutes.

Cupping may help ease neck pain and lower back pain.  
It has been used with acupuncture and moxibustion to treat nerve pain after shingles.  
It has also been tried for metabolic syndrome, facial paralysis, acne, and breathing problems.  
But there is not enough strong evidence to show it works well for these conditions.

Cupping can make the skin red.  
It may also cause a mild burn.
