# Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML)

PML is a serious brain disease caused by a virus called the JC virus.  
The JC virus usually stays quiet in the body after a person is infected as a child.  
It can become active again when the body’s immune system is weak.  

PML mostly affects people with weak immune systems.  
The most common cause is advanced HIV infection.  
It can also happen in people with certain cancers, rare immune disorders, or those who have had organ transplants.  
More recently, PML has been seen in people taking certain medicines that affect the immune system.  

PML damages the brain over time.  
It causes worsening brain problems.  
Most people with PML get worse over weeks or months.  
Death usually happens within one to nine months after symptoms start.  

## What Causes PML?

The JC virus is the cause of PML.  
This virus is very common.  
Most people are infected as children.  
After infection, the virus stays in the body in a quiet state.  
It can wake up when the immune system is not working well.  

The virus attacks cells in the brain that help protect nerve fibers.  
These cells are called oligodendrocytes.  
When they are damaged, nerve signals slow down or stop.  

People at highest risk for PML have weak cell-mediated immunity.  
This includes people with advanced HIV.  
It also includes people with blood cancers like leukemia or lymphoma.  
Other risks include rare immune disorders like Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.  
It can also happen after organ transplants.  

The risk of PML in people with advanced HIV goes up when the virus level in the blood is high.  
But the number of cases has gone down because better HIV medicines are now widely used.  

PML is now also seen in people taking certain immune-modifying medicines.  
These include:  
- Natalizumab (a monoclonal antibody)  
- Brentuximab vedotin (an antibody-drug combination)  
- Rituximab  
- Fingolimod  
- Dimethyl fumarate  

Doctors can test blood for antibodies to the JC virus.  
This test is called the JC virus index.  
Higher levels mean a higher risk of PML, especially in people taking natalizumab.  
But even people with low levels can still get PML.  

## What Are the Symptoms of PML?

The first sign of PML is often clumsiness.  
Many people have weakness on one side of the body.  
This is called hemiparesis.  
Other common symptoms include:  
- Trouble speaking or understanding words (aphasia)  
- Slurred speech (dysarthria)  
- Loss of vision in one side of the visual field (hemianopia)  

About two out of three people with PML have trouble with thinking, memory, or focus.  
This is due to damage in the outer layer of the brain.  

Some people may also have problems with balance, coordination, or feeling.  
Brain stem problems can cause issues with swallowing or eye movement.  

Headaches and seizures are rare.  
They are more likely in people with advanced HIV.  

The disease gets worse slowly and steadily.  
Most people do not get better.  
Death usually happens within one to nine months after symptoms begin.  

## How Is PML Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect PML in people with unexplained brain problems.  
This is especially true if the person has a weak immune system.  

The main test is a brain scan called MRI.  
It shows areas of damage in the brain’s white matter.  
These areas appear as bright spots on certain MRI images.  
In some cases, a contrast dye may make the edges of the lesions slightly brighter.  
CT scans can also show brain damage, but they are not as good as MRI.  

Another key test is a spinal tap.  
This collects fluid from around the spine.  
Doctors test this fluid for the JC virus using a method called PCR.  
A positive result means the virus is in the brain.  
When this result matches the brain scan, it is almost certain that the person has PML.  

Routine spinal fluid tests usually look normal.  
Blood tests for the JC virus are not useful for diagnosis.  
A brain biopsy can confirm PML, but it is rarely needed.  

## How Is PML Treated?

There is no cure for PML.  
Treatment focuses on supporting the patient and managing the underlying cause.  

For people with advanced HIV, starting or improving antiretroviral therapy can help.  
This treatment can slow the disease and improve survival.  
One-year survival has improved from 10% to 50% with better HIV medicines.  

But some people get a serious side effect called immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS).  
This happens when the immune system starts to recover.  
It can overreact to the JC virus.  
This causes more swelling and damage in the brain.  
Symptoms may get worse suddenly.  
MRI scans may show more contrast enhancement and brain swelling.  

Corticosteroids (steroid medicines) may help reduce swelling.  
In severe cases, doctors may stop antiretroviral therapy temporarily.  
This decision depends on how sick the person is.  

If PML happens in someone taking an immune-suppressing medicine, the medicine should be stopped.  
For some drugs, like natalizumab, doctors may do plasma exchange.  
This removes the medicine from the blood.  
It helps the body clear the drug faster.  

There is some early evidence that certain cancer drugs may help.  
These are called immune checkpoint inhibitors.  
They include pembrolizumab and nivolumab.  
They work by boosting the immune system.  
They may reduce the amount of JC virus in the brain.  
They may also improve the body’s ability to fight the virus.  
Some patients have had better symptoms.  
But this treatment is still experimental.  

## Key Points

- PML is caused by the JC virus.  
- It happens when the immune system is weak.  
- Common causes include advanced HIV, certain cancers, and some immune-modifying medicines.  

- Early signs include clumsiness, weakness on one side, trouble speaking, slurred speech, vision loss, and memory problems.  

- If someone has a weak immune system and is getting worse in their brain function, do an MRI and test spinal fluid for the JC virus.  

- Treat PML with supportive care.  
- Stop immune-suppressing medicines if possible.  
- For people with advanced HIV, start or improve antiretroviral therapy.  
- Watch closely for IRIS.  

- Early studies suggest pembrolizumab or nivolumab may help some people.  
- These drugs are not yet standard treatment.  
- More research is needed.

# Skin Care for the Residual Limb

Your skin where the prosthesis touches must be kept clean and checked often. This helps prevent skin damage and infection. Skin damage means the skin gets hurt and may form blisters or sores. Pain is often the first sign of a problem. If you feel any discomfort, take off the prosthesis right away and look at your skin.

Skin problems can be serious. You should see a health care provider if needed. Talk to your prosthetist too. They are the expert who makes, fits, and adjusts your prosthesis. Over time, you may learn to tell the difference between small issues and serious ones. But if something feels unusual, lasts a long time, hurts, or worries you, get it checked by a health care provider.

(See also: Overview of Limb Prosthetics.)

---

## Things That Increase Skin Problem Risk

Certain health conditions make skin problems more likely. These include poor blood flow in the legs (like peripheral arterial disease) and diabetes. These same conditions can lead to amputation. After amputation, they also raise the risk of skin damage and infection.

Some conditions, like diabetes or nerve problems, reduce your ability to feel pain. You may not notice skin damage or infection until it is serious. If you have these conditions, take off your prosthesis several times a day to check your skin. Look for redness or other signs of trouble. Others should check their skin at least once a day.

Skin problems are more likely if your residual limb has certain features. These include:
- Too much soft tissue at the end of the bone
- Loose skin
- Skin that was burned
- Skin that was grafted
- Thick or deep scars
- Bumps or sharp points on the bone

A well-fitting prosthesis helps prevent skin problems. But even a good fit can change over time. Your body changes every day. Muscles can shrink. Fluid levels can go up or down. These changes can affect how the limb fits in the socket.

If the top part of the socket is too tight, blood flow can slow down. This can cause swelling. Swelling increases pressure on the end of the limb. This can hurt the skin and deeper tissues. If the socket is too loose, pressure builds up on the end of the limb and on bony areas. This can cause skin damage.

---

## Skin Breakdown

Skin breakdown happens where pressure or rubbing happens. It is worse when pressure pushes up and down or side to side on the skin. Wet or sweaty skin is more likely to break down.

The first sign is redness and a burning feeling. This may be followed by pain, swelling, blisters, or open sores. Wearing the prosthesis when this happens makes the damage worse. It can also lead to infection.

You cannot stop all skin breakdown. But you can reduce the risk with these steps:

- Wash your residual limb twice a day with mild soap. Rinse well. Wash more often if you sweat a lot.
- Your prosthetist can give you special antiperspirant products for people with prostheses.
- Keep the prosthesis socket fitting well.
- Stay at a stable weight. Even small weight changes can affect fit.
- Eat healthy foods and drink water all day. This helps your skin stay healthy.
- If you have diabetes, keep your blood sugar under control.
- Make sure your prosthesis is aligned properly (especially if it is for a lower limb).

If you see signs of skin breakdown, see your prosthetist right away. They may need to adjust the prosthesis. Try not to wear the prosthesis until it is fixed. If the prosthesis is not the cause, or if adjusting it does not help, see a doctor.

---

## Skin Infection

Healthy, dry skin keeps bacteria and fungi in check. But the material between your skin and the prosthesis (like a gel or plastic layer) creates a warm, moist space. This helps bacteria and fungi grow. Damp skin is more likely to break down. This gives bacteria a way into your body. Infection can spread fast.

Signs of infection include:
- Tenderness
- Redness
- Open sores (ulcers)
- Pus (thick, yellow or white fluid)
- A bad smell (this may mean infection or poor cleaning)

If a mild infection gets worse, it can become cellulitis. This causes fever and feeling unwell. An abscess is a pocket of pus. It can also cause fever.

Any sign of infection needs medical attention. Get help right away if you have:
- The limb feels cold (this may mean poor blood flow)
- The area is red and tender
- The area smells bad
- Lymph nodes in the groin or armpit are swollen
- Pus or thick fluid is coming from the skin
- The skin turns gray and soft or turns black (this may mean gangrene)

Treatment for bacterial infection usually includes:
- Cleaning the area well
- Using a topical antibiotic (applied to the skin)
- Sometimes, removing dead skin or taking oral antibiotics

Do not wear the prosthesis until the infection is fully healed.

For fungal infections, use an over-the-counter antifungal cream.

Preventing skin breakdown also helps prevent infection.

---

## Other Skin Problems

Ingrown hairs and infected hair follicles (folliculitis) are not dangerous. But they can hurt or feel uncomfortable. Not shaving the hair on your residual limb can help prevent these issues.

Rough, warty bumps at the end of the limb are often caused by a poor-fitting socket. If not treated, this condition (called verrucous hyperplasia) can lead to serious infection.

If you see warty bumps:
- See your prosthetist right away for a socket adjustment.
- If the bumps do not go away in 2 to 4 weeks, see your doctor.
- Try not wearing the prosthesis for a week. Adjust the socket fit. This usually fixes the problem in 2 to 4 weeks.

# Idiopathic Telangiectasias (Spider Veins)

## What Are Telangiectasias?

- Telangiectasias are small, visible blood vessels under the skin.
- They look like thin red or purple lines or web-like patterns.
- They are also called spider veins.
- These veins are usually not harmful or dangerous.
- They are often caused for no known reason. This is called idiopathic.

## Where Do They Appear?

- Telangiectasias most often appear on the face.
- They can also appear on the legs or other parts of the body.
- They are usually not painful or itchy.
- But some people feel a mild burning or aching in the area.

## Why Do People Care?

- Most people do not have symptoms.
- Still, many people find even the smallest ones unattractive.
- They may feel self-conscious about their appearance.
- This can affect confidence or how they feel about themselves.

## How Are They Diagnosed?

- A doctor can diagnose them by looking at the skin.
- No special tests are needed.
- The doctor checks the skin and asks about your health history.

## Treatment Options

### Sclerotherapy

- This is a common treatment for spider veins.
- A doctor injects a special solution into the vein.
- The solution is a 0.3% liquid called sodium tetradecyl sulfate.
- The needle used is very thin.
- The treatment closes off the vein so it fades over time.
- The solution is injected directly into the blood vessel.

**What to Expect:**

- The treatment may cause some pain or discomfort.
- Some people use a numbing cream before the injection.
- A stronger solution called hypertonic saline (23.4%) is used sometimes.
- This causes more pain, but only for a short time.
- Large areas may need more than one treatment.
- Some people get darker spots on the skin after treatment.
- These spots usually fade over time, often completely.
- If the medicine leaks outside the vein or too much is used, the skin may break open or form a sore.

### Laser Treatment

- This uses light to close off the blood vessels.
- It works well for small spider veins.
- Larger areas may need more than one session.
- Some veins may stay or come back after treatment.

## Summary

- Telangiectasias are harmless but can be unsightly.
- They do not cause health problems.
- Many people choose treatment for cosmetic reasons.
- Sclerotherapy and laser treatment are both effective.
- Both may need more than one session.
- Side effects are usually mild and temporary.
- Talk to your doctor to decide which treatment is best for you.

# Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)

DIC is a serious condition where small blood clots form throughout the body. These clots block tiny blood vessels. The body uses up too many clotting materials to make these clots. This leaves too few clotting materials to stop bleeding. As a result, people with DIC may bleed too much.

## What Causes DIC?

DIC can start from many serious health problems. These include:

- Severe infections
- Complications from childbirth
- Surgery
- Serious injuries, such as head trauma
- Burns
- Frostbite
- Snake bites
- Certain cancers
- Aneurysms
- Large collections of abnormal blood vessels (cavernous hemangiomas)

A substance from the illness or injury triggers the body to make too many clots.

## How Fast Does DIC Develop?

DIC can happen suddenly or slowly.

- **Sudden DIC** often follows surgery, childbirth, or a severe infection.
- **Slow DIC** is more common in people with cancer or long-term health issues.

## Symptoms of DIC

### If DIC Comes On Suddenly

- Bleeding is the main symptom.
- Bleeding can be severe and hard to stop.
- It may happen at IV sites, in the brain, stomach, skin, muscles, or inside the body.
- Bleeding after surgery or childbirth can be life-threatening.

### If DIC Develops Slowly

- Clots in veins are more common than bleeding.
- Clots often form in the legs. This can cause swelling, redness, or pain.
- Some people have no symptoms at all.
- A clot can break loose and travel to the lungs. This can cause shortness of breath.
- In people with cancer, clots can also form in arteries. This can lead to:
  - Stroke
  - Heart attack
  - Blood clots in the arms or legs

## How Is DIC Diagnosed?

Doctors use blood tests to check for DIC.

- The blood test may show low platelet levels. Platelets are tiny pieces in the blood that help clots form.
- The blood may take longer than normal to clot.
- High levels of D-dimer mean the body is making more clots than usual.
- Low or falling levels of fibrinogen (a protein needed for clotting) also suggest DIC.

These test results help confirm the diagnosis.

## How Is DIC Treated?

### Treat the Underlying Cause

The most important step is to treat the main illness. This may be:

- An infection
- A problem during childbirth
- Cancer
- A serious injury

Once the main problem is treated, the clotting issues usually improve.

### Treat the Clotting Problems

- If DIC comes on suddenly, it is a medical emergency.
- Doctors may give platelets and clotting factors through a blood transfusion.
- This helps stop the bleeding.

- If DIC is mild and long-term, and clotting is the bigger problem, doctors may use a medicine called heparin.
- Heparin slows down the clotting process.
- It is used only when clots are more dangerous than bleeding.

Treating the root cause is key. Without it, the clotting problems will not get better.

# Selenium Toxicity

Selenium is a mineral your body needs to stay healthy.  
It helps make a special enzyme that breaks down harmful substances in the body.  
This enzyme works with vitamin E to protect your cells.  
Selenium also helps your body change thyroid hormones so they work properly.

Your blood levels of selenium depend on how much you eat.  
Normal levels range from 8 to 25 micrograms per deciliter of blood.  
This is the same as 0.1 to 0.3 micromoles per liter.

Taking too much selenium can cause harm.  
This can happen if you take more than 900 micrograms per day.  
High doses of selenium can lead to serious health problems.

Symptoms of too much selenium include:  
- Upset stomach  
- Nausea  
- Diarrhea  
- Hair falling out  
- Nails that become weak or change shape  
- Skin rashes  
- Tingling or numbness in hands and feet  
- Feeling very tired  
- Feeling irritable  
- A strong garlic smell in your breath

There is no clear number that shows when selenium levels become dangerous.  
Doctors do not have a standard level to define toxicity.

To diagnose selenium toxicity, your doctor will ask about your diet and supplements.  
They will check your symptoms and do a physical exam.  
They may also test your blood or urine to measure selenium levels.

The main treatment is to stop taking selenium supplements.  
You should also avoid foods that are very high in selenium.  
Your symptoms will slowly improve once you stop taking extra selenium.

# What Happens During a Mass-Casualty Weapon Incident

A mass-casualty weapon causes many injuries at once. These events overwhelm hospitals and emergency services because so many people need help. The weapons include:

- Germs that cause disease  
- Poisonous chemicals  
- Bombs and explosives  
- Radiation sources  
- Toxins (very strong poisons)

These weapons are sometimes called weapons of mass destruction. But that name is not always accurate. It suggests the weapon destroys buildings and roads. That is mostly true for bombs. But other weapons, like germs or poisons, do not destroy buildings. They make people sick instead.

The word "weapon" means someone used it on purpose. But some of these substances can also cause harm by accident. For example, a chemical leak from a truck or a power plant can make many people sick. Doctors and public health teams use the same methods to help people whether the event was intentional or accidental.

Sometimes, the danger is obvious. An explosion or a visible spill is easy to see. A person might even warn people ahead of time. But other dangers are harder to spot. Radiation, germs, or poisons can be spread without anyone noticing. The first sign might be that many people get sick at the same time and place. Doctors may not know right away if this is from a weapon or a natural illness. For example, vomiting and diarrhea from radiation exposure might first look like food poisoning.

Once released, these harmful substances can exist as solids, liquids, gases, or vapors. Tiny particles or droplets can float in the air. These are called aerosols. They can look like smoke, fog, mist, or fumes. Radiation can also spread as dust or debris. People can touch it or breathe it in. Or they can be harmed by radiation without touching anything.

The form of the substance affects how long it stays around and how people are exposed.

- Solids and thick liquids stay in the environment for more than a day. Some can last for weeks or even years.  
- Gases and thin liquids usually disappear in less than 24 hours.

How people are exposed matters a lot. Gases, vapors, and tiny particles can be breathed in. These affect the body quickly. Solids and liquids can get on the skin. They may be absorbed through the skin or transferred to the mouth if hands are not washed. Skin exposure usually takes longer to cause symptoms. Contaminated objects, like pieces of debris, can pierce the skin and put the substance directly into the body.

---

## How Doctors and Emergency Workers Respond

Doctors and emergency teams follow four main steps when responding to a mass-casualty incident:

1. **Preparedness**  
2. **Recognition**  
3. **Assessment and triage**  
4. **Treatment**

These steps often happen at the same time, especially when many people are hurt.

### 1. Preparedness

Being ready is key. Hospitals and communities need plans and supplies before an incident happens. These plans include:

- Bringing in extra staff  
- Reassigning beds, operating rooms, and blood supplies from regular care to emergency care  
- Setting up decontamination areas with sealed drains and protective gear  
- Stockpiling antidotes or having a way to get them fast  

Many hospitals run drills regularly. This helps staff know where to find emergency supplies and how to follow procedures, especially for decontamination.

### 2. Recognition

Some incidents are easy to spot. Explosions, gunshots, or car crashes are obvious. But biological or chemical attacks are harder to recognize.

Doctors and first responders may learn about an incident through:

- Intelligence reports  
- Warnings from the attacker  
- Dead animals or strange smells  
- Environmental sensors (if available)  

Sometimes, the only clue is that many people are suddenly sick with the same symptoms. Doctors look for patterns. For example, certain symptoms may point to a specific poison or germ. They may send samples to a lab for testing. But diagnosis and treatment often must start right away—especially for fast-acting chemicals.

### 3. Assessment and Triage

Triage means sorting people by how urgent their care needs are. Some people need help immediately. Others can wait.

In a mass-casualty event, medical teams must check many people quickly. They often have no time for long exams.

Triage is harder when there are no visible injuries. Some people may not be hurt at all but feel sick from stress. Stress can cause fast breathing, shaking, nausea, or weakness. These symptoms can look like poisoning, infection, or radiation sickness. Medical teams must learn to tell the difference.

To stay safe, trained teams set up three zones:

- **Hot zone**: The area right around the release. This is the most dangerous. Only emergency workers with full protective gear can enter.  
- **Warm zone**: The area just outside the hot zone. This is where people are cleaned. Full decontamination happens here. Workers may wear protective gear to check and treat people, especially if they were exposed to chemicals.  
- **Cold zone**: The safe area, like a hospital emergency room. People should be clean by the time they reach this zone. Staff here usually only need standard safety gear. But hospitals still need decontamination tools. Some people may arrive without being cleaned first.

---

## How People Are Treated

When dealing with mass-casualty weapons, doctors and responders focus on:

- Protecting themselves  
- Stabilizing the person’s condition  
- Stopping further exposure (moving people away from the danger, cleaning them)

The first step is often to open the airway. But for some chemicals, decontamination must happen right away. For certain nerve agents, an antidote may also be needed immediately.

The type of decontamination depends on the weapon.

- For germs or radiation in the air, people usually only get the substance on their skin or clothes. Most of these agents do not get through healthy skin fast. So removing clothes and showering is usually enough.  
- For some chemicals like sulfur mustard or liquid nerve agents, the substance gets into the skin right away. It can start causing damage fast. These people need to be cleaned right away. This stops more harm and stops the poison from spreading to others.

A special product called reactive skin decontamination lotion (RSDL) can stop nerve agents and sulfur mustard on the skin. It is not yet approved for use in eyes or open wounds. But soap and water also work well. Water alone is not as good for oily chemicals, but it can be used if soap is not available.

A weak bleach solution (made by mixing one part household bleach with nine parts water) is also effective. But it should not be used in eyes or open wounds.

In an emergency, any material that can soak up the chemical can help. This includes paper towels, tissues, clay-rich soil, or even bread. Apply it to the skin. Rub it in for up to two minutes. Then wash it off with lots of water.

Doctors check wounds and remove all dirt and debris. They then flush the wounds with plain water or salt water.

# Onchocerciasis (River Blindness)

Onchocerciasis is a disease caused by a type of worm called *Onchocerca volvulus*.  
It spreads when infected blackflies bite people.  
The blackflies live near fast-moving rivers and streams.  
This is why the disease is also called "river blindness."

## Who Gets It?

Many people live near fast-flowing rivers or streams.  
They are most at risk of getting this disease.  
Long-term travelers, like missionaries or aid workers, can also get it.  
The disease is most common in tropical areas of Africa.  
Small cases also happen in Yemen and near the border between Venezuela and the Brazilian Amazon.  
In the Americas, blindness from this disease is rare.  
Colombia, Ecuador, Mexico, and Guatemala have been declared free of the disease.

## What Happens in the Body?

A blackfly bites a person and injects tiny worm larvae into the skin.  
These larvae grow into adult worms over 12 to 18 months.  
The adult worms live in small lumps under the skin.  
Female worms can live up to 15 years.  
They are very long—33 to 50 centimeters.  
Male worms are shorter—19 to 42 millimeters.  
The female worms make tiny worms called microfilariae.  
These microfilariae move through the skin and can enter the eyes.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The disease mainly affects the skin and eyes.  
You may feel itchy skin.  
You may have rashes or skin that becomes thin and scarred.  
You may feel lumps under the skin.  
These lumps are called nodules.  
The microfilariae can damage the eyes.  
This can cause vision problems.  
In some cases, it leads to blindness.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors check for the tiny worms in the skin.  
They take a small sample of skin, called a skin snip.  
They look at it under a microscope.  
They may also check the front part of the eye with a special light.  
This is called a slit-lamp exam.  
They can see the microfilariae in the eye this way.  
A test called PCR can find the worm’s DNA in skin samples.  
This test is more sensitive but is only used in research labs.  
Blood tests for antibodies are not very helpful.  
They can give false results and cannot tell if the infection is current or past.  
If a lump is found under the skin, doctors can remove it and check for adult worms.  
But this is rarely needed.

## How Is It Treated?

The main medicine is ivermectin.  
It kills the tiny worms in the skin and eyes.  
It also reduces how many new tiny worms the female worms make.  
Ivermectin does not kill the adult worms.  
But over time, repeated doses make the adult worms less fertile.  
The medicine is taken as a single pill.  
It is given once every 6 to 12 months.  
The dose depends on body weight.  
Doctors do not know exactly how long treatment should last.  
Some people take it for several years.  
Treatment may stop if itching goes away and no tiny worms are found in skin or eye checks.  

Side effects of ivermectin are mild and rare.  
They are much less serious than side effects from another medicine called diethylcarbamazine.  
Diethylcarbamazine is not used because it can cause a dangerous reaction.  
This reaction can harm the skin and eyes.  
It can also cause heart problems.  
Mild reactions during ivermectin treatment are common.  
Severe reactions can be treated with a short course of steroid medicine.

Before giving ivermectin, doctors must check for another worm called *Loa loa*.  
This is important if the person has been in central Africa.  
Ivermectin can cause serious side effects in people with heavy *Loa loa* infections.

### New Treatments Being Studied

A medicine called moxidectin may work better than ivermectin.  
One dose of moxidectin reduces tiny worms more than one dose of ivermectin.  
Another medicine, doxycycline, kills bacteria that the worm needs to survive.  
This medicine kills more than 60% of female worms.  
It also stops the rest from making new worms.  
But it does not kill the tiny worms already in the body.  
Doxycycline is taken as a pill once or twice a day for 6 weeks.  
It is started one week after the first ivermectin dose.  
Studies show it helps clear tiny worms.  
But it does not clearly improve skin or eye health.  
Doxycycline may be an option for people in areas where *Loa loa* is common.  
But it has not been tested in people with very high *Loa loa* levels.

Surgery to remove skin lumps can help reduce tiny worms.  
But ivermectin is now the preferred treatment.

## How Can It Be Prevented?

No medicine prevents infection with this worm.  
But giving ivermectin once or twice a year to entire communities helps stop the disease.  
It controls hidden infections and lowers the chance of spreading.  
In West Africa, the disease was nearly wiped out.  
This happened through spraying insecticides on blackfly breeding sites.  
It also happened through giving ivermectin to infected people.  
This program ended in 2002.  
Today, large-scale treatment with ivermectin continues in areas where the disease still exists.

To avoid blackfly bites:  
- Stay away from fast-moving rivers and streams.  
- Wear long sleeves and pants.  
- Use insect repellent on skin and clothes.

## Key Facts

- Onchocerciasis is caused by a worm.  
- It spreads through blackfly bites.  
- It causes skin problems and eye damage.  
- It can lead to blindness.  
- Diagnosis is done by checking skin samples or the eye.  
- PCR testing can help in some cases.  
- Ivermectin is the main treatment.  
- It kills tiny worms and reduces new ones.  
- It does not kill adult worms.  
- Always check for *Loa loa* infection before giving ivermectin in central Africa.

# Liver Transplant

A liver transplant is a surgery to replace a damaged liver with a healthy one from a donor. It is the second most common type of solid organ transplant.

## Who Needs a Liver Transplant?

The main reasons people need a liver transplant include:

- **Cirrhosis** – This is scarring of the liver. It causes about 70% of transplants in the United States. In 10 to 20% of these cases, the cause is hepatitis C.
- **Fulminant hepatic necrosis** – This is sudden and severe liver failure. It causes about 8% of transplants.
- **Hepatocellular carcinoma** – This is a type of liver cancer. It causes about 7% of transplants.
- **Biliary atresia and metabolic disorders** – These are rare conditions that affect the liver and bile ducts. They mainly affect children and cause about 3% of transplants each.
- **Other liver diseases** – These include conditions that block bile flow (like primary sclerosing cholangitis) and those caused by the immune system attacking the liver (like autoimmune hepatitis). These cause about 8% of transplants.

For people with liver cancer, a transplant may be an option if:
- There is only one tumor and it is smaller than 5 centimeters.
- Or there are up to three tumors, and each is smaller than 3 centimeters.

If these conditions are met and the cancer has not spread outside the liver or into major blood vessels, the patient meets the **Milan criteria**. This helps doctors decide if a transplant is safe and likely to work.

For people with cancer that has spread to the liver, a transplant may only be an option if:
- The cancer started in the gut (neuroendocrine tumor).
- The cancer has not spread beyond the liver.
- The original tumor was removed.

## When a Liver Transplant Is Not Safe

These conditions make a transplant too risky and are called **absolute contraindications**:

- Very high pressure inside the skull (over 40 mm Hg) or low blood flow to the brain (under 60 mm Hg) in people with sudden liver failure.
- Severe high blood pressure in the lungs (mean pressure over 50 mm Hg).
- A serious infection in the blood (sepsis).
- Liver cancer that has spread to other parts of the body.

These conditions make it very likely the person will not survive the surgery or will not do well afterward.

## How the Surgery Is Done

### Donor Livers
- For people who get a liver from a deceased donor, doctors first check the liver during surgery. They make sure the cancer is not advanced or has not spread. If it has, the liver cannot be used.
- For living donors, a part of the liver is removed. This is called a lobar or segmental resection.

### Liver Storage
- The removed liver is cooled and kept in a special solution. It can be stored for up to 18 hours.
- The longer the liver is stored, the higher the chance it will not work well after transplant or that bile ducts will be damaged.

### The Transplant Surgery
- The patient’s damaged liver is removed. This is the hardest part of the surgery. It is hard because the patient often has high pressure in the liver’s blood vessels and trouble with blood clotting.
- Blood loss can be very high in rare cases — over 100 units. But machines that collect and reuse the patient’s own blood help reduce the need for blood from other people. On average, patients need 5 to 10 units of blood.
- The new liver is connected to the patient’s blood vessels and bile ducts.
- The new liver’s main vein (vena cava) is connected to the patient’s vena cava using a method called the "piggy-back" technique. This means no machine is needed to help blood flow during surgery.
- In some cases, the new liver is placed in a different spot in the body (called heterotopic placement). This is still experimental and has not worked well so far.

## Medicine After the Transplant

After the transplant, patients take medicines to stop their body from rejecting the new liver. These are called immunosuppressants.

Common medicines include:
- Anti-IL-2 receptor antibodies – given on the day of surgery.
- A calcineurin inhibitor – either cyclosporine or tacrolimus.
- Mycophenolate.
- Corticosteroids.

For most patients, corticosteroids can be reduced within weeks and often stopped after 3 to 4 months. The only exception is people with autoimmune hepatitis.

Compared to other organ transplants, liver transplants need the lowest doses of these medicines.

## Possible Problems After the Transplant

There can be complications after a liver transplant. These include infection, bleeding, blood clots, and problems with the new liver not working right.

## Survival After a Liver Transplant

### One Year After Transplant
- **Living donor liver**: 90% of patients survive. 82% of the transplanted livers still work.
- **Deceased donor liver**: 91% of patients survive. 85% of the transplanted livers still work.

### Three Years After Transplant
- 79% of patients survive.
- 72% of the transplanted livers still work.

### Five Years After Transplant
- 73% of patients survive.
- 65% of the transplanted livers still work.

People who had long-term liver disease (chronic) do better than those with sudden liver failure (acute).

After one year, most deaths are not from transplant problems. They are from the original disease coming back. For example:
- Cancer returning.
- Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NASH) returning.

### Recurrent Hepatitis C
- In the past, hepatitis C often came back and caused liver scarring in 15 to 30% of patients within 5 years.
- Today, new antiviral medicines make this very rare.
- Even if hepatitis C returns soon after transplant, it can be cured with medicine.

### Autoimmune Liver Diseases
- Conditions like primary biliary cirrhosis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, and autoimmune hepatitis can come back in 20 to 30% of patients within 5 years.

# Drowning

Drowning happens when someone is under water and cannot breathe.  
This can happen if water gets into the lungs.  
It can also happen if the voice box tightens and blocks the airway, even if no water gets into the lungs.

When a person drowns, the body does not get enough oxygen.  
Lack of oxygen can hurt the brain and other organs.  
Doctors check for low oxygen levels and other problems after a drowning.  
Treatment focuses on getting oxygen back to the body and fixing other issues.

Drowning can be serious but not deadly. This is called nonfatal drowning.  
It can also be deadly.  
More people are hospitalized for nonfatal drowning than die from it.  
Drowning is one of the top 10 causes of accidental death worldwide.

In the United States in 2023:
- Drowning was the top cause of injury-related death in children aged 1 to 4 years.
- It was the second leading cause of death in children aged 5 to 14 years, after car crashes.
- It was among the top 10 causes of unintentional death in people under 55 years old.

## Who is at higher risk of drowning?

Some people are more likely to drown. These include:
- People who have had alcohol or drugs that affect thinking and alertness.
- People with conditions that cause sudden loss of control, like seizures.
- People with heart rhythm problems, such as long QT syndrome.
- Children from African American or Native American families.
- Children who have not learned to swim and are not watched closely near water.
- Boys and men.
- People who do dangerous underwater breath-holding games.

More than half of adult drowning deaths involve alcohol.  
The more alcohol in the blood, the higher the risk of dying.

Seizures and heart rhythm problems raise the risk of drowning.

Boys and men are at much higher risk.  
About 80% of people over age 1 who drown are male.

## Where and how drowning happens

Drowning often happens in pools, hot tubs, lakes, rivers, and oceans.  
Even small amounts of water can be dangerous for young children.  
Toilets, bathtubs, buckets, and other containers with water can be deadly if a child falls in.

Diving into shallow water can cause serious injuries to the spine or head.  
These injuries can make drowning more likely.

### Dangerous underwater breath-holding behaviors (DUBBs)

These are risky activities done mostly by healthy young men.  
They try to stay underwater longer than normal.  
There are three types:

1. **Hyperventilation** – Breathing fast before going under water.  
   This lowers carbon dioxide in the blood.  
   It makes a person feel they can stay under longer.  
   But it increases the risk of passing out and drowning.

2. **Hypoxic training** – Holding breath while swimming.  
   This is done to improve underwater swimming.  
   It should only be done with trained rescuers nearby.

3. **Static apnea** – Holding breath while still underwater.  
   This is sometimes done as a game.

In all these cases, a person may pass out underwater.  
This is called a hypoxic blackout or breath-hold blackout.  
It can lead to drowning.

> **Did You Know?**  
> Breathing fast before going underwater can make drowning more likely.

## What happens in the body during drowning

When someone is under water, one of two things can happen:

- Water gets into the lungs.  
- The voice box tightens and blocks the airway.

In both cases, the lungs cannot send oxygen to the blood.  
Low oxygen levels can cause brain damage or death.

### Water in the lungs

Large amounts of water in the lungs cause drowning right away.  
Smaller amounts, especially if the water is dirty or has chemicals, can cause lung damage.  
This damage may not show up for hours after the person is out of the water.  
This is called secondary drowning.  
The lungs may keep losing oxygen.  
Freshwater can be absorbed into the blood.

### Voice box spasm

The voice box may tighten after a person is pulled from the water.  
This blocks air from getting in.  
No water enters the lungs.  
This is sometimes called dry drowning.

## Cold water and drowning

Cold water has both good and bad effects.

Cold makes muscles work poorly.  
It can also cause dangerously low body temperature, called hypothermia.  
This can make a person confused or unable to think clearly.

But cold water can help protect the body during lack of oxygen.  
It can trigger the mammalian diving reflex.  
This reflex slows the heart and sends blood to the heart and brain.  
This helps keep vital organs alive.

This reflex is stronger in children than in adults.  
So children have a better chance of surviving long submersion in cold water.

> **Did You Know?**  
> Children are more likely than adults to survive after being under water for a long time.

## Signs of drowning

People who are drowning usually cannot call for help.  
They may struggle to breathe.  
Children who cannot swim can go under in less than a minute.  
Adults may struggle longer.

After being rescued, people can have many different symptoms.  
Some are only a little anxious.  
Others may be unconscious or near death.

Symptoms can include:
- Being awake, drowsy, or unconscious.
- Not breathing.
- Gasping for air.
- Vomiting.
- Coughing or wheezing.
- Blue skin (a sign of low oxygen).

Some people do not show serious breathing problems for several hours after being pulled from the water.

Some people who survive long submersion may have brain damage.  
If they breathe in dirt, chemicals, or vomit, they can get lung infections or breathing problems.  
These problems may not show up for hours.

People who drown in cold water often have low body temperature.

## How doctors diagnose drowning

Doctors look at what happened and the symptoms.  
They check oxygen levels in the blood.  
They may take a chest x-ray to see lung damage.  
They check body temperature to see if the person has hypothermia.

Other tests may be needed if there is a chance of head or spine injury.  
These include x-rays or CT scans.  
An ECG and blood tests may be done to check for heart problems that could have caused the drowning.

## How drowning is treated

The most important step is to start resuscitation right away.  
This includes artificial breathing and CPR.

- Start rescue breathing before chest compressions.  
- Move the neck as little as possible if there is a spine injury.

People who were under water should go to the hospital, even if they seem okay.  
Use an ambulance if possible.

- People with mild symptoms may go home after a few hours of observation.  
- If symptoms last or oxygen levels are low, hospital care is needed.

Most people need extra oxygen.  
Some need high levels of oxygen or a breathing machine.

- If a person wheezes, medicine can help open the airways.  
- If an infection develops, antibiotics are given.

If the water was cold, the person may have hypothermia.  
They may need to be warmed slowly.

Spine injuries need special care.

## What to expect after drowning

The best chances of survival without brain or lung damage come from:
- Starting resuscitation right away (most important).
- Being under water for a short time.
- Being in cold water.
- Being young.

Some children have survived without brain damage after being under water for up to 60 minutes in cold water.  
Many people who need CPR can recover fully.  
Almost all people who are awake and alert when they reach the hospital recover fully.

People who had alcohol before drowning are more likely to die or have lasting damage.

## How to prevent drowning

- Do not drink alcohol or use drugs before or during swimming, boating, or watching children near water.
- Pools must follow local safety rules.  
  They should be surrounded by fences.  
  All doors and gates to the pool area must be locked.
- Children in or near water need constant supervision.  
  Supervision should be close enough to reach them in seconds.
- Even a few inches of water can be deadly.  
  Empty buckets, tubs, and containers right after use.
- Small children should wear approved life jackets or floatation devices near water.
- Air-filled toys like water wings or noodles are not safe.  
  They are not meant to keep people afloat.
- Swimming lessons reduce the risk of fatal drowning in children aged 1 to 4 years.  
  All children should learn to swim.  
  Even those who have lessons need to be watched near water.

- Swim with a buddy.  
  Only swim in areas with lifeguards.
- Learn how to escape rip currents: swim parallel to the shore, not toward it.
- People who do dangerous breath-holding games should be supervised and know the risks.
- You do not need to wait an hour after eating to swim.  
  There is no proof that eating causes cramps or drowning.

> **Did You Know?**  
> You do not need to wait an hour after eating to swim.

- Everyone should wear a life jacket approved by a trusted safety agency when in a boat.  
  This is required for nonswimmers and small children.
- Do not dive into shallow water.  
  This can cause serious spine injuries.

Community pools and swimming areas should:
- Have trained lifeguards.
- Keep life preservers, life jackets, and a shepherd’s crook (a long pole with a hook) nearby.
- Have access to automated defibrillators, airway tools, and phones to call emergency services.

# Bipolar Disorder in Children and Teens

Bipolar disorder means a person has strong mood swings. These swings include times of high energy and extreme mood (mania), times of deep sadness (depression), and times when mood is normal. Each of these mood changes can last for weeks or months.

This condition usually starts in the middle of teenage years or early twenties. It is very rare in young children.

Many children first show signs of depression. Some children used to be diagnosed with bipolar disorder if they had very strong and unstable moods. But now doctors know that most of these children do not have bipolar disorder. Instead, they are diagnosed with a different condition called disruptive mood dysregulation disorder.

## What Causes Bipolar Disorder?

There is a link to family history. Some genes may play a role. But there is no test that can tell for sure if someone has bipolar disorder.

Brain scans show that some parts of the brain are smaller in teens with bipolar disorder. These include the amygdala and the front part of the brain. Also, these brain areas do not grow normally during teenage years.

Some drugs can make symptoms worse or look like bipolar disorder. These include cocaine, amphetamines, PCP, and some antidepressants. Exposure to toxins like lead can also cause similar symptoms.

Certain health problems can cause mood changes that look like bipolar disorder. These include thyroid problems.

There have been a few reports of teens having mania after having a mild or no symptoms of COVID-19.

## What Are the Signs?

Bipolar disorder means repeated episodes of high energy and extreme mood (mania or hypomania). These are followed by episodes of deep sadness (depression). The sad times may happen more often than the high-energy times.

During a manic episode, a teen may feel very happy or very angry. Their mood can change quickly depending on the situation. They may talk very fast and feel like they do not need sleep. They may think too highly of themselves. They may act in dangerous ways, like having unsafe sex or driving recklessly.

In younger children, mood changes can be very strong. But they do not last long. They may last only a few minutes.

The condition often starts slowly. Children often have always been very hard to manage and have strong reactions to things.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use a mental health exam to make the diagnosis. They follow strict guidelines from the *Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders*, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR).

They also check for other possible causes. This includes testing for thyroid problems, brain infections, brain tumors, and drug use. A drug test may be done to check for illegal drugs or toxins.

The doctor will also ask about stressful events. These can include things like abuse or trauma.

## How Is It Treated?

### For Mania

The first treatment is a second-generation antipsychotic medicine. These work fast to calm down extreme mood swings. Examples include aripiprazole, lurasidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, and ziprasidone.

If these medicines do not help after trying two or three, a mood stabilizer may be used. These include lithium, divalproex, lamotrigine, and carbamazepine.

### For Depression

The first treatment is a second-generation antipsychotic plus a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI). These are types of antidepressants.

Lithium is another option. It can be used alone or with an SSRI.

Lithium has been shown to help reduce suicidal thoughts, lower depression, and improve daily life. These benefits are similar to what is seen in adults.

Antidepressants should never be used alone. They must be used with an antipsychotic or lithium.

It was once thought that antidepressants could cause mania. But now we know this is not true. However, they can still make symptoms worse in some teens with bipolar disorder.

Psychotherapy is also very important. It helps teens and families understand the illness and manage it better.

## Important Tips

- Second-generation antipsychotics like risperidone are the first choice for treating bipolar disorder in children and teens.
- Lithium can help reduce thoughts of suicide and improve mood and daily functioning.

## What Is the Outlook?

The long-term outlook varies. It gets worse with each episode. Risk factors for more episodes include:
- Starting the illness at a young age
- Severe symptoms
- Family history of mental illness
- Not taking medicine as prescribed

Teens who have mild to moderate symptoms and respond well to treatment often do very well. They stay on track with school, friends, and family.

But many teens do not take their medicine as they should. This makes long-term results worse.

We do not know much about how young children with very unstable moods will do over time.

## Key Points

- Bipolar disorder means mood swings between mania, depression, and normal mood. Each phase lasts weeks or months.
- It usually starts in the teenage years or early twenties. It is rare in young children.
- It often starts slowly. Children have always been very emotional and hard to manage.
- For mania, start with antipsychotic medicine. Then add mood stabilizers to prevent relapses.
- For depression, use a combination of antipsychotic medicine and an SSRI. Add lithium if needed.
- Psychotherapy is a key part of treatment.

# Acquired Kidney Cysts

Sometimes, fluid-filled sacs called cysts grow in the kidneys. These are called acquired cysts.

Most of the time, these cysts do not cause any problems. They do not harm kidney function. A person may have just one cyst or many cysts. The cysts can be in one kidney or both kidneys.

Doctors do not know what causes a single cyst. They also do not know the exact cause of multiple cysts. But having many cysts is more common in people with long-term kidney disease. It is especially common in people who have had dialysis for many years. More than half of people on dialysis for over 10 years will develop cysts.

## Symptoms

Most people with acquired cysts have no symptoms. But sometimes, people may notice:

- Blood in the urine  
- Pain in the side of the body (flank pain)  
- Signs of infection, such as fever and side pain

People with a transplanted kidney or those who have had dialysis for many years are at higher risk for kidney cancer. Because of this, some doctors check these people regularly using ultrasound or CT scans.

## How Cysts Are Found

Doctors often find acquired cysts by chance. This happens when a CT scan or ultrasound is done for another reason.

## Treatment

If a cyst keeps bleeding or gets infected, it may need to be drained. In rare cases, part of the kidney or the whole kidney may need to be removed. This is called a partial or complete nephrectomy.

If a cyst turns into kidney cancer, a nephrectomy may be needed. But this is very rare.

# Injection Drug Use

Some people who use drugs inject them into their body. This gives a faster or stronger effect than other methods.

Most people inject drugs into a vein in the arm. But some inject into the skin, muscle, or under the tongue.

People often use small veins in the arms. Over time, these veins can become damaged from repeated use. When this happens, some people learn to inject into larger veins in the neck, groin, or armpit.

## Risks of Injecting Drugs

People who inject drugs face dangers from the drugs themselves. They also face risks from dirty needles, fake drugs, and germs that may be in the drug.

## How Doctors Find Out If Someone Injects Drugs

Doctors ask about drug use. They also do a physical exam.

Some people will say they inject drugs. Others may not admit it. In those cases, doctors look for signs on the body.

Repeated injections can leave marks on the skin. These are called track marks. They look like thin lines of small dark spots. The skin around them may be darker or discolored. This happens because of long-term swelling and irritation.

Track marks are often on the arms or inside the elbows. But some people hide them by injecting in less obvious places, like the armpits.

Injecting under the skin (called skin popping) can cause round scars or open sores. There may also be signs of past infections or abscesses.

People with drug problems may try to explain away these marks. They might say they got them from donating blood, bug bites, or old injuries.

## Treating Injection Drug Use

Doctors treat both the drug use and any infections it causes.

People who inject drugs should be tested for serious infections. These include hepatitis, HIV, tuberculosis, syphilis, and other sexually transmitted diseases.

All people who inject drugs should get vaccines. These protect against hepatitis, flu, pneumonia, tetanus, and other infections.

The HIV crisis led to a movement called harm reduction. This means helping people stay safer while using drugs. It does not require stopping drug use.

For example, giving clean needles and syringes helps stop the spread of HIV and hepatitis. It is safer than sharing used ones.

If someone gets an infection from injecting drugs, treatment is the same as for other infections. This may include antibiotics for bacterial infections. Abscesses may need to be cut open and drained.

Treating infections can be hard. Some people have trouble getting a vein for medicine. Others do not follow their treatment plan. This makes recovery harder.

# Adnexal Torsion

Adnexal torsion happens when the ovary twists. Sometimes the fallopian tube twists too. This twisting cuts off the blood supply to these organs.

- The twist causes sudden, sharp pain.
- You may also feel sick to your stomach and throw up.
- This is a medical emergency. It needs quick treatment.

## What Causes Adnexal Torsion?

The ovary and fallopian tube hang from tissues that act like ligaments. If these tissues are long or loose, the ovary can twist.

Adnexal torsion is most common in women who are able to have children. It often happens when something is wrong with the ovary.

The following can make twisting more likely:

- Being pregnant and having a large cyst on the ovary called a corpus luteum cyst.
- Using fertility medicines that cause ovulation.
- The ovary is larger than normal. This is often due to a noncancerous (benign) tumor or cyst.
- You have had adnexal torsion before.

Noncancerous growths are more likely to cause twisting than cancerous ones.

Sometimes a normal ovary twists. This is more common in children and teens.

Usually, only one side is affected. Most of the time, only the ovary twists. But sometimes the fallopian tube twists too.

If blood flow is cut off for too long, the tissue can die. This can damage the ovary or fallopian tube. The organs may not work properly after that.

## Symptoms

When the ovary twists, you feel sudden, severe pain in your lower belly.

- The pain often comes with nausea and vomiting.
- Before the sudden pain, you may have had crampy pain that came and went for days or even weeks.
- This earlier pain may happen because the ovary twists and untwists several times.
- Your belly may feel tender when touched.
- The pain may be on one side or spread across your lower belly.
- Some women also have a fever or a fast heartbeat.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors look at your symptoms and do a physical exam.

They may use a special test called an ultrasound.

- The ultrasound uses a device placed inside the vagina. This is called transvaginal ultrasonography.
- It can show if the ovary is swollen or if there is a mass in it.
- A type of ultrasound called color Doppler can show if blood is still flowing to the ovary.

The only way to be sure of the diagnosis is to have surgery to look inside the belly.

## Treatment

If adnexal torsion is suspected, surgery is done right away.

The goal is to check for a twist and fix it if possible.

### Laparoscopy

- Doctors make one or more small cuts in the belly.
- They use a thin tube with a camera (laparoscope) to see inside.
- They use small tools through other cuts to untwist the ovary.
- If the fallopian tube is twisted, they untwist it too.
- This surgery is done in a hospital.
- You will be asleep during the procedure (general anesthetic).
- Most people go home the same day.

### Laparotomy

- This is used only if the ovary is very large.
- Doctors make a larger cut in the belly.
- They can see the organs directly without a camera.
- This surgery takes longer and requires a hospital stay.
- It may cause more pain than laparoscopy.

### What Happens During Surgery?

- If there is a cyst and the ovary can be saved, the doctor removes the cyst. This is called cystectomy.
- If the ovary has died from lack of blood, the doctor removes the ovary and fallopian tube. This is called salpingo-oophorectomy.
- If there is a tumor, the whole ovary is removed. This is called oophorectomy.

# Legg-Calvé-Perthes Disease

This condition affects the ball at the top of the thigh bone. It happens when the bone in this area loses its blood supply and starts to break down. The exact cause is not known. It mostly affects children between the ages of 5 and 10. Boys are more likely to get it than girls.

In most cases, only one hip is affected. But in about 1 out of every 10 cases, both hips are involved. The condition is more common in white children. It affects up to 29 out of every 100,000 children under 15 years old. About 1 in 10 cases runs in families, but no clear gene has been found yet.

## Symptoms

The main signs are:
- Pain in the hip
- Trouble walking (limping)
- Some children also feel pain in the knee

The pain comes on slowly. It gets worse over time. The child may not be able to move the hip fully. The muscles in the thigh may shrink and look smaller.

## How It Is Diagnosed

Doctors start by asking about symptoms and doing a physical exam.

X-rays are usually done next. Sometimes an MRI is needed to get a clearer picture.

At first, the x-rays may look normal or only show a small change. Later, the x-rays can show the bone breaking into pieces. The bone may also look lighter in some areas and denser in others.

If both hips are affected or if there is a family history, doctors will do a full-body x-ray to rule out other bone problems. This is important because other conditions need different treatments.

Doctors also check for other possible causes, such as:
- Low thyroid hormone levels
- Sickle cell anemia
- Long-term use of steroid medicine
- Past injury to the hip

## How It Is Treated

The main goal is to keep the top of the thigh bone round and the hip working well.

Treatment usually includes:
- Rest
- Keeping the leg still with casts or braces
- Bed rest for a long time

If the child is over 6 years old and the bone damage is serious, surgery may help. One type of surgery involves cutting the bone near the hip and repositioning it. This is done with metal screws. The child can start walking again sooner after this surgery.

Some early studies show that a medicine called bisphosphonate may help. But more research is needed to confirm this.

## Outlook

Without treatment, the condition usually lasts 2 to 3 years. It will eventually stop on its own. But the bone may not heal properly. This can lead to arthritis later in life.

With treatment, the long-term results are better. Children who are younger than 8 years old and who have less bone damage when first diagnosed tend to do the best. A key sign of better outcome is if the side part of the bone is still tall when the disease is first found.

# Bladder Cancer – Simple Explanation

Bladder cancer starts in the inner lining of the bladder. This lining is made of special cells that stretch when the bladder is full and shrink when it is empty. These same cells can also become cancerous in the tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder (the ureters) and in the kidney’s collecting area (the renal pelvis).

## How Common Is Bladder Cancer?

- About 83,190 new cases are found each year in the United States.
- More than 16,840 people die from bladder cancer each year.
- Men are about three times more likely than women to get this cancer.

## What Causes Bladder Cancer?

The biggest risk factor is smoking. It causes at least half of all new cases.  
Certain chemicals used in factories can also lead to bladder cancer. These include:
- Chemicals from oil and fuel (hydrocarbons)
- Dyes used in the dye industry (like naphthylamine)
- Chemicals used in rubber, electric, cable, paint, and textile factories

Exposure to these chemicals is going down over time.  
Long-term use of some medicines, especially cyclophosphamide, raises the risk.  
A parasite called schistosomiasis, bladder stones, long-term bladder infections, or using a catheter for a long time can also increase the risk. But these causes are rare.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The most common symptom is blood in the urine.  
Other signs may include:
- Pain or burning when you pee
- A strong, sudden need to urinate
- Feeling like you need to go often, even if your bladder is empty

These symptoms can feel like a bladder infection. In fact, bladder cancer and infection can happen at the same time.  
If you have low red blood cells (anemia), you may feel tired or look pale.

## How Is Bladder Cancer Diagnosed?

Doctors often first suspect bladder cancer when blood is found in the urine.  
This can be seen under a microscope or even with the naked eye if the urine looks red.

Tests used to confirm the diagnosis include:
- **Urine test (cytology):** A lab checks your urine for cancer cells.
- **Cystoscopy:** A thin, flexible tube with a camera is passed through the urethra into the bladder. This lets the doctor see inside the bladder.
- **Biopsy:** If anything looks abnormal, a small piece of tissue is taken and checked under a microscope.

Sometimes, bladder cancer is found by accident during imaging tests like a CT scan or ultrasound done for another reason.

If the cancer has grown into the bladder wall, more tests are needed:
- CT scan of the belly
- X-ray of the chest
- MRI scan to see how far the cancer has spread

Better tools to find and stage bladder cancer are helping doctors catch it earlier. This can lead to better results.

## How Is Bladder Cancer Treated?

### For Surface Cancers (only on the inside lining)

- The cancer can often be removed during cystoscopy.
- But new cancers often come back later in the bladder.
- To help prevent this, doctors may put medicine directly into the bladder after surgery. This includes:
  - BCG (a substance that boosts your immune system)
  - Chemotherapy drugs like gemcitabine, docetaxel, mitomycin C, or nadofaragene firadenoec-vncg

### For Invasive Cancers (grown into the bladder wall)

- These cancers cannot be removed with a cystoscope.
- The usual treatment is surgery to remove part or all of the bladder (cystectomy).
- Chemotherapy is often given before surgery. This has been shown to improve survival.
- Radiation therapy, alone or with chemotherapy, may be used in some cases to try to cure the cancer.

### If the Whole Bladder Is Removed

Doctors must create a new way for urine to leave the body.  
Common options include:

#### 1. **Ileal Conduit (Stoma)**
- A tube made from part of the intestine is used to carry urine from the kidneys to an opening in the belly.
- A bag is worn outside the body to collect urine.

#### 2. **Orthotopic Neobladder**
- A new bladder is built from part of the intestine.
- It is connected to the urethra.
- You learn to empty it by relaxing your pelvic muscles and pushing with your belly.
- Most people stay dry during the day, but some may leak at night.

#### 3. **Continent Urinary Diversion (e.g., Indiana Pouch)**
- A new reservoir is built from the intestine and connected to a stoma in the belly.
- You do not need a bag.
- You empty the reservoir by inserting a tube (catheter) through the stoma into the reservoir several times a day.

## If Cancer Has Spread Beyond the Bladder

- Treatment is usually chemotherapy.
- Several drug combinations work well, especially if the cancer has only spread to nearby lymph nodes.
- If the cancer responds well to chemo, surgery or radiation may be offered.
- But only a small number of people are cured.
- For those who are not cured, care focuses on relieving pain and supporting quality of life.

## What Is the Outlook?

- For slow-growing cancers that stay on the surface of the bladder, the chance of dying from cancer in 5 years is less than 5%.
- For cancers that grow into the bladder wall, the 5-year death rate is much higher—about 50%.
- If the cancer has spread beyond the bladder to lymph nodes or other organs, the outlook is much worse.

Early detection and treatment improve outcomes.

# Decompression Sickness

Decompression sickness happens when pressure drops too fast. This can happen when you come up too quickly from a dive, leave a pressurized chamber, or go to a high altitude. When pressure drops fast, gas that was dissolved in your blood and tissues forms bubbles. These bubbles can cause serious health problems.

Symptoms often include pain or nerve problems. In severe cases, it can be deadly. Doctors diagnose it based on your symptoms. The main treatment is recompression therapy. Good diving habits can prevent this condition.

## How It Happens

Gas dissolves in liquids when pressure is high. When you dive deep, the pressure increases. This makes more gas (like nitrogen or helium) dissolve in your blood and tissues.

When you come up, the pressure goes down. The extra gas can form bubbles in your body. These bubbles can appear in any tissue. They can also travel through your blood to other parts of your body. This is called arterial gas embolism.

Bubbles cause harm by:

- Blocking blood vessels
- Damaging or pressing on tissues
- Causing fluid to leak from blood vessels
- Triggering blood clots and inflammation

Nitrogen dissolves easily in fat. So areas with a lot of fat, like the brain and spinal cord, are more at risk.

## What the Symptoms Feel Like

Some people get symptoms within minutes after surfacing. Most people notice symptoms slowly. Early signs may include feeling unwell, tired, not hungry, or having a headache.

About half of people get symptoms within one hour after surfacing. Ninety percent get symptoms within six hours. Rarely, symptoms show up 24 to 48 hours later — especially if you fly after diving.

### Type I Decompression Sickness

This type mainly causes pain. The pain is often in joints, especially elbows and shoulders. It can also affect muscles. The pain feels deep and dull. It does not get worse when you move.

Other signs include:
- Swelling in the arms or legs
- Skin that looks patchy or discolored
- Itching
- Rash

### Type II Decompression Sickness

This type affects the nervous system and sometimes the lungs. Symptoms include:
- Weakness
- Numbness or tingling
- Trouble urinating
- Loss of bowel or bladder control

Headaches and tiredness may also happen, but these are not specific to this condition.

If the inner ear is affected, you may feel dizzy, hear ringing, or lose hearing.

Severe symptoms include:
- Seizures
- Slurred speech
- Vision loss
- Confusion
- Loss of consciousness

In the worst cases, this can lead to death.

### The Chokes

This is a rare but serious form. It affects the lungs. Symptoms include:
- Shortness of breath
- Chest pain
- Coughing

It is caused by fluid building up in the lungs. Large amounts of gas in the lung blood vessels can cause sudden collapse of the circulatory system. This can be fatal.

### Dysbaric Osteonecrosis

This is a late effect of repeated pressure exposure. It often happens without earlier symptoms. It is a type of bone death caused by long or frequent exposure to high pressure. It is common in people who work in pressurized environments or deep commercial divers.

It damages the joints in the shoulder and hip. Over time, this leads to chronic pain and disability. It can cause arthritis.

### Blood Clots

Legs that are immobile due to decompression sickness can lead to deep vein thrombosis. This is a blood clot in a deep leg vein. It can travel to the lungs and cause a pulmonary embolism.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors make the diagnosis based on your history and physical exam.

Imaging tests like CT or MRI can help rule out other conditions with similar symptoms. These include:
- Herniated spine
- Stroke
- Bleeding in the brain

These tests may show changes from decompression sickness. But they are not always accurate. So treatment should start based on symptoms, not waiting for test results.

Arterial gas embolism can look like decompression sickness. But both need the same emergency treatment.

### Comparison: Gas Embolism vs. Decompression Sickness

| Feature | Gas Embolism | Decompression Sickness |
|--------|--------------|------------------------|
| **Common Symptoms** | Loss of consciousness, often with seizures. Any diver who passes out soon after surfacing should be treated as having gas embolism. | Joint pain (most often in elbows or shoulders), nerve problems, or breathing issues. |
| **Less Common Symptoms** | Mild brain symptoms, signs of lung injury (like air under the skin or a collapsed lung) | Other nerve issues, breathing problems, or joint pain |
| **Onset** | Sudden, usually during or right after surfacing — even from just 1 meter deep | Usually gradual or sudden, but often starts at least one hour after surfacing. Can happen up to 24 hours after diving, especially after deep dives or long exposures |
| **Rare Onset** | Very rare after 24 hours | Can happen after flying soon after diving |
| **Cause** | Holding your breath or blocked airway while coming up. Air in the lungs expands and can damage lung tissue | Diving or being in a pressurized chamber, especially beyond safe limits |
| **Mechanism** | Air from the lungs enters blood vessels and blocks blood flow to the brain | Gas bubbles form when pressure drops too fast |
| **Emergency Care** | Keep airway open, control bleeding, give CPR or use a breathing machine if needed. Get to a recompression chamber fast. Keep the person flat to maintain blood pressure. If unconscious, place on side to prevent choking. Give 100% oxygen. Give fluids by mouth if awake, IV if not. | Same as above: keep airway open, give CPR or breathing support if needed. Get to a recompression chamber fast. Keep flat. Place unconscious people on side. Give 100% oxygen. Give fluids by mouth or IV. |
| **Note** | Repeated dives are often involved | Repeated dives are often involved |

*Recompression chamber* is a special room that increases pressure to treat decompression sickness.

For dysbaric osteonecrosis, X-rays may show joint damage. But this looks like other joint problems. MRI is usually needed to confirm the diagnosis.

### Important Tips

- If you think someone has decompression sickness, start treatment right away. Do not wait for tests.
- Time is critical. The faster treatment starts, the better the outcome.

## How It Is Treated

The main treatments are:

- High-flow 100% oxygen
- Recompression therapy
- Fluids to replace lost body fluids

Most people recover fully.

### Oxygen

Giving 100% oxygen helps remove nitrogen from the body. It works by creating a strong push for nitrogen to leave the blood and go into the lungs. This helps dissolve the bubbles faster.

### Fluids

For mild cases, alert people can drink water or oral rehydration fluids.

For serious cases, IV fluids (without sugar) are used. Dehydration can make the condition worse. So doctors may give large amounts of fluids to restore blood volume.

### Recompression Therapy

This is the most important treatment. It is needed for all patients except those with only mild symptoms like itching, skin changes, or tiredness. These may improve with oxygen alone.

But patients must be watched closely. Symptoms can get worse.

People with serious symptoms must be taken to a recompression chamber as fast as possible.

Do not delay transport for non-essential tests or procedures.

### Traveling After Treatment

If you need to fly, use a plane that keeps the cabin at normal pressure (1 atmosphere). If the plane is not pressurized, stay below 609 meters (2,000 feet) and keep giving oxygen.

Commercial planes are pressurized, but the air pressure is like being at 2,438 meters (8,000 feet). This can make symptoms worse.

Flying soon after diving can trigger symptoms.

Weigh the risks of flying against the risk of getting worse without treatment.

For mild cases (normal nerves and stable for 24 hours), flying later is unlikely to harm long-term recovery.

### Blood Clot Risk

Because of the risk of blood clots, doctors may check leg veins with ultrasound scans.

## How to Prevent It

You can avoid gas bubbles by:

- Staying within safe depth and time limits for diving
- Taking decompression stops when needed
- Following safe diving rules

Many divers use dive computers. These track depth and time. They calculate safe ascent times and stops.

Even with safe dives, cases can still happen.

Many divers also do a safety stop at 4.6 meters (15 feet) for a few minutes. But this does not stop all cases.

Dives close together (less than 24 hours apart) or dives at high altitudes need special planning.

## Key Points

- Half of all people with decompression sickness get symptoms within one hour of surfacing.
- Ninety percent get symptoms within six hours.
- If you suspect decompression sickness, give high-flow 100% oxygen right away.
- Get the person to a recompression chamber as fast as possible.
- Use ground transport or a plane that keeps cabin pressure at normal levels.
- Follow safe diving rules: limit depth and time, use decompression stops, and avoid repeated dives or flying soon after diving.
