# How the Adrenal Glands Work

The adrenal glands sit on top of each kidney.  
There are two adrenal glands, one on each kidney.

Each adrenal gland has two main parts:  
- The outer part, called the cortex  
- The inner part, called the medulla

Each part has a different job.

## The Adrenal Cortex

The adrenal cortex makes hormones.  
These hormones help your body manage stress.  
They also help control your blood pressure.  
They help balance salt and water in your body.  
They also help your body use sugar for energy.

## The Adrenal Medulla

The adrenal medulla makes hormones too.  
These hormones help your body react quickly to danger.  
They prepare your body for "fight or flight."  
They make your heart beat faster.  
They raise your blood pressure.  
They help your muscles get ready to act fast.

Both parts work together to keep your body balanced and ready for action.

# Vitiligo

Vitiligo is a condition where the skin loses its color in patches.  
This happens because the cells that make skin color (called melanocytes) are destroyed.

## What Vitiligo Looks Like

- The skin in some areas turns white.  
- The white patches can appear anywhere on the body.  
- The most common places are the face, hands, feet, elbows, knees, and around the mouth, eyes, and genitals.  
- The skin in these areas is very sensitive to sunlight.  
- Hair in the affected areas often turns white too.  
- The condition is most noticeable in people with darker skin.

## What Causes Vitiligo?

The exact cause is not known.  
But it may happen when the body’s immune system attacks the melanocytes.  
This is called an autoimmune reaction.

- Vitiligo sometimes runs in families.  
- It can also start for no clear reason.  
- It may be linked to other health problems, such as:  
  - Overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism)  
  - Underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism)  
  - Diabetes  
  - Addison disease  
  - Pernicious anemia  
- These links are not fully understood.  
- In rare cases, vitiligo starts after a skin injury, like a chemical burn or sunburn.  
- Emotional stress may also trigger it.  
- Some people develop vitiligo after receiving immunotherapy for skin cancer.

## How Doctors Diagnose Vitiligo

- Doctors usually diagnose vitiligo by looking at the skin.  
- A special light called a Wood light may be used to help confirm the diagnosis.  
- Skin biopsies are rarely needed.

## How Vitiligo Is Treated

There is no cure for vitiligo.  
But treatment can help some people regain skin color.  
Some people’s skin color returns on its own.

### Protect Your Skin from the Sun

- All areas with vitiligo are at high risk for sunburn.  
- Always cover these areas with clothing.  
- Use sunscreen every day.  
- Long-term sun exposure increases the risk of skin cancer.

### Creams and Ointments

- Strong corticosteroid creams can help small patches get color back.  
- A cream with calcipotriene (a form of vitamin D) and betamethasone (a corticosteroid) works better than either alone.  
- For sensitive areas like the face or groin, doctors may use other creams like tacrolimus or pimecrolimus.  
- Ruxolitinib cream is also available.  
  - It can help improve skin color.  
  - But the white patches may return after stopping the cream.

### Light Therapy (Phototherapy)

- A doctor uses special ultraviolet light in a clinic.  
- This treatment can help more than half of people get some color back.  
- It takes months to years to see results.  
- Treatment may need to continue for a long time.  
- It can increase the risk of skin cancer.

### Surgery and Tattoos

- For small patches that do not respond to other treatments, doctors may use skin grafts.  
- They may also transplant melanocytes (color-making cells) from healthy skin.  
- Tattooing is helpful for areas that are hard to treat, such as the lips, nipples, and fingertips.

### Bleaching Unaffected Skin

- Some people with large areas of vitiligo choose to bleach the rest of their skin.  
- This creates a more even skin tone.  
- It is done with a strong cream called hydroquinone.  
- The cream must be used many times over weeks or even a year.  
- It can cause strong skin irritation.  
- The results are permanent.  
- Once the skin is bleached, the color will not come back.

### Other Options

- Some people use makeup, skin stains, or bronzers to cover the white patches.  
- These are safe and easy to use.

## Important Notes

- Vitiligo is not contagious.  
- It does not cause pain or health problems beyond the skin.  
- But it can affect a person’s self-esteem and confidence.  
- Support and counseling can help.  
- Talk to your doctor about the best treatment for your situation.

# Trimethoprim and Sulfamethoxazole

Trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole are two antibiotics that work together to fight infections.  
They are often used together as a single medicine.  
Trimethoprim can also be used alone.

The two medicines work in different ways to stop bacteria from growing.  
Trimethoprim blocks a step that bacteria need to make a key part of their cells.  
Sulfamethoxazole blocks another step in the same process.  
When used together, they are more effective than either one alone.  
This combination often kills bacteria completely.

The fixed-dose combination comes in two forms:  
One tablet has 80 milligrams of trimethoprim and 400 milligrams of sulfamethoxazole.  
A stronger tablet has 160 milligrams of trimethoprim and 800 milligrams of sulfamethoxazole.  
The two medicines are always given in a 1 to 5 ratio.

---

## How the Body Handles These Medicines

Both medicines are taken by mouth.  
They are well absorbed into the bloodstream.  
They leave the body through the urine.  
They stay in the blood for about 11 hours.  
They reach many parts of the body, including the brain fluid and prostate gland.  
Trimethoprim builds up in the prostate.

---

## When This Medicine Is Used

This medicine works against many types of bacteria and some other germs.  
It is effective against:

- Many types of gram-positive bacteria, including some hard-to-treat staph infections  
- Many types of gram-negative bacteria  
- The protozoa that cause *Cystoisospora* and *Cyclospora* infections  
- The fungus that causes *Pneumocystis jirovecii* pneumonia

The medicine does **not** work against:

- Anaerobic bacteria (germs that grow without oxygen)  
- The bacteria that cause syphilis  
- The bacteria that cause tuberculosis  
- The bacteria that cause mycoplasma infections  
- The bacteria *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*  
- Many types of enterococci  
- Many strains of *Streptococcus pneumoniae*

It is not effective for strep throat.  
It will not prevent complications like rheumatic fever.

### Common Uses of the Combination (Trimethoprim/Sulfamethoxazole)

| Condition | Notes |
|--------|-------|
| Bacterial prostatitis | A good choice, especially if fluoroquinolones are not suitable |
| Uncomplicated bladder infection in women | Works as well as fluoroquinolones for short treatment (3 days), if resistance is low (<15%) |
| Preventing repeated bladder infections | Take half to one full tablet every night or every other night. For women with infections after sex, take after sex |
| Treatment and prevention of *Pneumocystis jirovecii* pneumonia | First-choice medicine for people with AIDS or cancer |
| Intestinal infections | Works for infections caused by *Shigella*, *Vibrio*, and *E. coli*, and for *Cystoisospora* and *Cyclospora* infections. But resistance is becoming more common |
| Infections caused by *Nocardia* and *Listeria monocytogenes* | Can be used in these cases |
| Skin infections from community-associated MRSA | First-choice oral treatment for mild cases |

Trimethoprim alone is used less often.  
It may be helpful for:

- Long-term bacterial prostatitis  
- Preventing or treating urinary tract infections in people allergic to sulfonamides

---

## When Not to Use This Medicine

Do not use this medicine if you have ever had a bad reaction to trimethoprim or sulfamethoxazole.  
It should be used with care if you have:

- Low levels of folic acid in your body  
- Liver problems  
- Kidney problems

---

## Use During Pregnancy and Breastfeeding

Animal studies show this medicine may cause birth defects.  
We do not have enough clear data from human studies.  
Avoid using it in the first trimester of pregnancy.  
It may increase the risk of neural tube defects.  
Avoid it near the time of delivery.

If you must use it during pregnancy, take 4 milligrams of folic acid every day.  
This helps protect the baby.

The medicine can raise bilirubin levels in the blood.  
This increases the risk of brain damage in the baby or newborn.  
This condition is called kernicterus.

Sulfamethoxazole passes into breast milk.  
Using this medicine while breastfeeding is usually not recommended.

---

## Side Effects

Common side effects include:

- Rash  
- Nausea  
- Vomiting  

These are the same side effects seen with other sulfonamide medicines.  
Trimethoprim causes similar side effects, but less often.

People with HIV/AIDS are more likely to have side effects.  
These include fever, rash, and low white blood cell counts.

Other possible side effects:

- Low folic acid levels (can lead to anemia and low blood cell counts)  
- High potassium levels in the blood (can be dangerous)  
- Kidney problems, including kidney failure in people with existing kidney issues  
- Liver damage (rare)  
- A condition that feels like meningitis but is not caused by infection

Folic acid can help prevent or treat low blood cell counts and anemia from long-term use.

Trimethoprim can reduce how much potassium your kidneys remove.  
This can lead to high potassium levels, which can be life-threatening.

---

## Dosing and Drug Interactions

Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole can affect other medicines.  
It may increase the effects of:

- Warfarin (a blood thinner)  
- Phenytoin (a seizure medicine)  
- Methotrexate (a cancer and autoimmune medicine)  
- Rifampin (a tuberculosis medicine)

Sulfamethoxazole can make blood sugar drop too low in people taking sulfonylurea diabetes medicines.

If you have kidney problems, your dose must be lowered.  
Use this medicine with caution if your kidneys are not working well.  
Other medicines may be better choices in these cases.

# Chronic Venous Insufficiency and Post-Thrombotic Syndrome

## What Is Chronic Venous Insufficiency?

Chronic venous insufficiency means the veins in your legs are damaged.  
This damage stops blood from flowing back to your heart the way it should.  
The problem can cause pain, swelling, and skin changes in your legs.

## What Is Post-Thrombotic Syndrome?

Post-thrombotic syndrome is a type of chronic venous insufficiency.  
It happens after a blood clot in a leg vein.  
The clot can damage the valves in the vein.  
This leads to long-term symptoms.

## Symptoms

You may notice:
- Swelling in your legs, especially at the end of the day.
- A heavy, tired, or achy feeling in your legs.
- Cramps or pain in your legs.
- Itching or scaly skin on your ankles.
- Skin that turns dark or brown.
- Open sores (ulcers) on your legs, often near the ankle.

The swelling often gets better when you lie down at night.  
But it comes back when you stand or sit for long periods.

## Causes

Your veins have small one-way valves.  
These valves keep blood moving up toward your heart.  
They stop blood from flowing backward.

Chronic venous insufficiency happens when:
- The veins get too wide.
- The valves get damaged.

This causes blood to pool in your legs.  
The pressure builds up.  
Fluid leaks into the tissues.  
This causes swelling and other symptoms.

### Most Common Cause

A past blood clot in the leg (deep vein thrombosis).  
The clot can leave scar tissue.  
This scar tissue can damage the valves in the vein.

### Other Risk Factors

- Injury to the legs.
- Getting older.
- Being overweight.
- Sitting or standing for long periods.
- Being pregnant.

Not everyone who has a blood clot in the leg will get post-thrombotic syndrome.  
But you are more likely to get it if:
- You had more than one blood clot in the same leg.
- The clot was in the upper leg or pelvis.
- You are overweight.

## Diagnosis

Your doctor will check your legs for swelling, skin changes, and varicose veins.  
They will ask about your symptoms and medical history.

Sometimes your doctor will use a special ultrasound test called duplex ultrasonography.  
This test checks blood flow in your legs.  
It helps rule out a new blood clot.

## Treatment

Treatment focuses on reducing swelling and healing any sores.

### 1. Elevate Your Legs

Lift your legs above your heart for at least 30 minutes.  
Do this at least three times a day.  
This helps reduce pressure in the veins.

### 2. Use Compression

Compression helps push fluid out of your legs.  
It reduces swelling and pain.

- Start with elastic bandages.  
- Once swelling goes down, switch to compression stockings.  
- These stockings are tighter at the ankle and looser higher up.  
- The higher the pressure, the better they work—but they may be harder to wear.

**How to use compression stockings:**
- Put them on when you wake up.
- Do this before your legs swell from standing or walking.
- Wear them all day.
- Take them off at night.

Some people find the stockings hard to wear.  
They may feel tight, uncomfortable, or unattractive.  
But they are very helpful if used correctly.

### 3. Intermittent Pneumatic Compression (IPC)

This uses a pump and inflatable leg sleeves.  
The sleeves squeeze your legs to push fluid out.  
It is used if stockings do not help or are not tolerated.

### 4. Wound Care

If you have a leg ulcer, proper care is key.

- Use special dressings that stay in place for several days.  
- Some dressings keep the wound moist to help healing.  
- The Unna boot uses bandages with zinc oxide.  
- These help protect the wound and support healing.

Healing takes time.  
Even small sores can take weeks or months to close.

### Medications and Surgery

Medicines do not help treat chronic venous insufficiency.  
Surgery is not usually needed.  
Skin grafts may be used for ulcers that do not heal.  
But even with a graft, the skin can break open again.  
This only happens if you do not keep using leg elevation and compression.

## Prevention

You can lower your risk by:
- Losing weight if you are overweight.
- Exercising regularly.
- Eating less salt.

If you have had a blood clot in your leg:
- Take blood-thinning medicine (anticoagulants) as directed.  
- This can help prevent post-thrombotic syndrome.

Compression stockings do not prevent the condition.  
But they are very useful for treating it.

## More Information

The following resource may help you learn more:

**Vascular Cures: Chronic venous insufficiency (CVI)**  
This site gives clear information about causes, diagnosis, and treatment.  
It is in English.  
Note: The Manual is not responsible for the content on this site.

# Cyclothymic Disorder

Cyclothymic disorder causes mood swings that are not as strong as those in bipolar disorder.  
These mood changes include mild highs and mild lows.  
The mood swings last for a few days at a time.  
They come and go in an unpredictable pattern.  
The mood changes must happen for more than half the days over a period of at least two years.  

Doctors diagnose this condition by talking to the person and learning about their history.  
There is no lab test or scan to confirm it.  

Treatment mostly focuses on education and support.  
Some people need medicine if their symptoms cause serious problems in daily life.

---

## What You Should Know

Cyclothymic disorder often leads to bipolar II disorder later in life.  
But it can also stay as a pattern of extreme moodiness without turning into a major mental health condition.

### Chronic Hypomania

A rare form of this disorder is called chronic hypomania.  
In this form, people feel overly happy and energetic most of the time.  
They often sleep less than six hours a night.  

People with chronic hypomania may:  
- Feel constantly cheerful and confident  
- Have too much energy  
- Make many plans without thinking them through  
- Spend money carelessly  
- Get too involved in other people’s lives  
- Act on sudden urges  
- Be too familiar with strangers  

---

## How It Affects People

Some people with this condition do well in careers.  
They may succeed in business, leadership, or creative work.  
But more often, the mood swings cause serious problems.  

These problems include:  
- Unstable jobs or school records  
- Frequent moves from one place to another  
- Repeated breakups in relationships or marriages  
- Trouble with alcohol or drug use  

---

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors use the *Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders*, 5th edition, Text Revision, to make the diagnosis.  
The following must be true for at least two years:  

- There are many times when the person feels mildly high or energetic, but not high enough to be called a full hypomanic episode.  
- There are many times when the person feels mildly down or sad, but not low enough to be called a major depression.  
- These mood changes happen on more than half the days during the two-year period.  
- The person does not go without symptoms for more than two months at a time.  
- The symptoms are not caused by another mental health condition, such as schizophrenia or delusional disorder.  
- The symptoms are not caused by a substance (like drugs or alcohol) or a medical condition (like an overactive thyroid).  

---

## How It Is Treated

- Doctors give support and education.  
- Some people need medicine if their symptoms cause serious problems.  

### Lifestyle Tips

- Try to find jobs with flexible hours.  
- People with creative talents may do well in the arts.  
- The ups and downs of this condition may be easier to manage in creative fields.  

### Medicines

- Mood stabilizers may help.  
- Common ones include lithium, valproate, carbamazepine, and lamotrigine.  
- Oral divalproex is often easier to take than lithium.  
- The choice of medicine depends on how much the condition affects daily life.  
- It also depends on whether the person gains benefits from being more energetic or creative.  

### Antidepressants

- These should be avoided unless the low mood is very bad and lasts a long time.  
- They can make mood swings worse or cause rapid cycling between highs and lows.  

### Support Groups

- Joining a support group can help.  
- Talking with others who have similar experiences can reduce feelings of isolation.  
- It can also help people feel understood and less alone.

# Isaacs Syndrome

Isaacs syndrome is a rare condition. It affects the nerves that control muscle movement.

## What Happens in Isaacs Syndrome?

- The nerves that tell muscles to move become overactive.
- This causes muscles to twitch and quiver all the time.
- The twitching can look like a bag of worms moving under the skin.
- Muscles in the arms and legs are most affected.
- Over time, muscles become stiffer and harder to relax.
- Some people also have more sweating than normal.
- Muscle cramps and sudden spasms can happen in the hands and feet.

## What Causes Isaacs Syndrome?

- The body makes an antibody that attacks part of the nerve cell membrane.
- This attack happens in the peripheral nerves. These are the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord.
- The condition may be linked to other health problems, such as:
  - Cancer
  - Myasthenia gravis
  - Thymus gland tumors
  - Hashimoto thyroiditis
  - Low vitamin B12 levels
  - Celiac disease
  - Other autoimmune or rheumatic diseases
- In some cases, the condition runs in families.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- Doctors look at your symptoms.
- They may do two tests:
  - Electromyography: This checks how well nerves and muscles work.
  - Nerve conduction studies: This measures how fast signals travel through nerves.
- These tests show clear signs of nerve overactivity.

## How Is It Treated?

- Medicines can help reduce symptoms.
- Antiseizure drugs like carbamazepine or phenytoin are often used.
- Other medicines that may help include gabapentin and valproate.
- Diazepam may also be used to calm muscle activity.
- Some people get better with immune globulin.
  - This is a liquid made from blood donations.
  - It contains many different antibodies.
  - It is given through a vein.
- Plasma exchange may also help.
  - This is a process that filters harmful substances from the blood.
  - It removes abnormal antibodies that are causing the problem.

## Important Notes

- Isaacs syndrome is rare.
- Early treatment can help improve symptoms.
- If you have other health issues, your doctor will check for them.
- Treatment plans are made based on your symptoms and test results.

# Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis

This is a rare condition. It causes non-cancerous growths in the airway. The cause is a virus called human papillomavirus.

The most common place for these growths is the voice box. This is called laryngeal papillomas.

The condition can happen at any age. But it is most common in children between 1 and 4 years old.

The growths can come back after treatment. In rare cases, they can turn into cancer. They may also spread to the windpipe or lungs.

## Symptoms

You may notice:
- A weak cry in babies
- A hoarse voice
- Trouble breathing in serious cases

## How It Is Diagnosed

Doctors use a special scope to look at the voice box. This is called laryngoscopy.

They may take a small sample of tissue. This is called a biopsy.

The growths can be one or many. They are seen during laryngoscopy.

The biopsy confirms the diagnosis.

## How It Is Treated

The main treatment is surgery to remove the growths.

The growths often come back within weeks or months. So more than one surgery may be needed.

You will need regular checkups. These include laryngoscopy and bronchoscopy to watch for new growths.

Surgery may use a pulsed-dye laser or photodynamic therapy.

In severe cases, doctors may try medicines. These include:
- Antiviral drugs like cidofovir
- Drugs that stop blood vessel growth, like bevacizumab

In some children, the growths shrink on their own when they reach puberty.

## How to Prevent It

A vaccine against human papillomavirus can help prevent this condition.

The vaccine works best against HPV types 6 and 11. These are the types most often linked to the growths.

The vaccine has been proven to work in adults. Its effect in children is still being studied. But it is expected to help reduce the number of cases.

# What Is Hepatitis?

Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver.  
The liver helps clean your blood and process food.  
Hepatitis is common all over the world.

Hepatitis can be:
- **Acute**: Lasts a short time.
- **Chronic**: Lasts for six months or longer.

Most people with acute hepatitis caused by a virus get better on their own.  
But some people go on to have long-term liver problems.

> **Did you know?**  
> - Vaccines can stop some types of viral hepatitis or make them less serious.  
> - Simple steps like washing hands and avoiding risky behaviors can also help prevent hepatitis.

---

## What Causes Hepatitis?

Hepatitis is most often caused by:
- A virus — especially one of five main types: A, B, C, D, or E.
- Drinking too much alcohol.
- Fatty liver disease due to how the body processes food and energy.
- Some medicines, such as isoniazid (used to treat tuberculosis).

### What Is Fatty Liver?

Your body turns food into energy through a process called metabolism.  
When this process goes wrong in the liver, fat builds up.  
This causes inflammation and can lead to liver damage.  
This condition is now called metabolic dysfunction-associated liver disease (MASLD).  
If it gets worse, it can become metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH).

> **Note:** MASLD used to be called nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).  
> MASH used to be called nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH).

Less common causes include:
- The body’s own immune system attacking the liver (autoimmune hepatitis).
- Inherited liver problems.
- Other infections like mononucleosis, herpes simplex, or cytomegalovirus.
- Infection with the virus that causes COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2).

Even if you have no symptoms of COVID-19, your liver may still become mildly inflamed.  
The more severe the illness, the more likely the liver is to be affected.

---

## Types of Hepatitis Viruses

Here’s what you need to know about each type.

### Hepatitis A

**How it spreads:**  
You get it by eating or drinking something that has been contaminated with the stool of an infected person.  
This usually happens due to poor hygiene or dirty water.

**Symptoms:**  
- Children often have no symptoms.  
- Older children and adults may feel sick, lose their appetite, vomit, or turn yellow (jaundice).

**What happens next:**  
- Most people recover fully.  
- It does not become a long-term problem.

**How to prevent it:**  
- Wash hands well, especially after using the bathroom and before handling food.  
- Avoid drinking untreated water.  
- Get the hepatitis A vaccine.  
  - All children should get it.  
  - Adults at risk should also get it.  
- If you are exposed, you can get the vaccine or a special shot called immune globulin.

---

### Hepatitis B

**How it spreads:**  
It spreads through contact with blood or body fluids like semen, vaginal fluids, or saliva.  
This can happen through:
- Sharing needles to inject drugs.
- Using unsterilized needles for tattoos.
- Having sex.
- A mother passing it to her baby during birth.

**Symptoms:**  
- More serious than hepatitis A.
- Can be deadly in some cases.
- Joint pain and itchy red bumps on the skin (hives) may also occur.
- If you have both hepatitis B and hepatitis D, the illness is worse.

**What happens next:**  
- It can become a long-term condition.
- Long-term infection raises the risk of liver cancer.

**How to prevent it:**  
- Avoid sharing needles or having unprotected sex with many partners.
- Get the hepatitis B vaccine.  
  - All babies should get it at birth.  
  - Adults at risk should also get it.
- If you are exposed (including babies born to infected mothers), get both the vaccine and a special shot called hepatitis B immune globulin.

---

### Hepatitis C

**How it spreads:**  
Through contact with blood or body fluids.  
This can happen through:
- Sharing needles to inject drugs.
- Using unsterilized needles for tattoos.
- Rarely, through sex.
- Rarely, from mother to baby during birth.

**Symptoms:**  
- Often no symptoms at first.
- Sometimes symptoms come and go — mild at first, then worse.

**What happens next:**  
- About 75 out of 100 people develop long-term infection.
- This can lead to serious scarring of the liver (cirrhosis).
- It can also lead to liver cancer — but only if cirrhosis has already developed.

**How to prevent it:**  
- Do not share needles.
- Avoid tattoos or piercings with unsterilized tools.
- There is no vaccine yet.

---

### Hepatitis D

**How it spreads:**  
Only happens if you already have hepatitis B.  
It spreads the same way: through blood or body fluids.

**Symptoms and risks:**  
- Makes hepatitis B much worse.
- Same prevention steps as for hepatitis B.

**How to prevent it:**  
- Get the hepatitis B vaccine.
- Avoid sharing needles or having unprotected sex.
- If you are exposed to hepatitis B, get both the vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin.

---

### Hepatitis E

**How it spreads:**  
Through eating or drinking something contaminated with the stool of an infected person.  
This usually happens due to poor hygiene or dirty water.  
Sometimes, eating meat from an infected animal can cause it.

**Symptoms:**  
- Can be severe, especially in pregnant women.

**What happens next:**  
- It usually does not become long-term.
- A vaccine is available — but only in China.

---

## What Are Immune Globulins?

- **Standard immune globulin** is a medicine made from blood plasma of healthy people.  
  It contains antibodies that help fight infections.  
  It is given by injection into a muscle or vein.

- **Hepatitis B immune globulin** is a special type made from blood of people with strong protection against hepatitis B.  
  It is used to prevent infection after exposure.  
  It is given by injection.

---

## Can a Mother Pass Hepatitis to Her Baby?

Yes.  
A mother with hepatitis B or hepatitis C can pass the virus to her baby during childbirth.  
But steps can be taken to prevent this.  
Babies born to infected mothers should get the hepatitis B vaccine and immune globulin right after birth.

# Hypereosinophilic Syndrome

This condition happens when your body makes too many eosinophils.  
Eosinophils are a type of white blood cell.  
They help fight infections and allergies.  
But too many can damage your organs.  

This syndrome is not caused by parasites, allergies, or other known reasons.  
It is defined by having more than 1,500 eosinophils in each microliter of blood.  
This high count must last for at least six months.  
It must also cause harm to one or more organs.  

Some people with this condition have a genetic change in their blood cells.  
This change leads to the overproduction of eosinophils.  
New tests have found that many cases are not truly "unknown" in cause.  

The old definition has limits.  
It misses some people who have the same harmful genetic changes.  
But their blood counts do not meet the old rules.  
Also, some people get serious organ damage before six months.  
They need treatment sooner.  

Any type of blood cell problem can cause the same organ damage.  

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on which organs are affected.  
They can be different in each person.  

### Common Symptoms by Body System

**General Symptoms (about half of people):**  
- Loss of appetite  
- Feeling tired  
- Fever  
- Muscle pain  
- Weakness  
- Losing weight  

**Heart and Lungs (more than 70% of people):**  
- Blood clots in the heart that can travel to other parts of the body  
- Heart muscle becomes stiff or thickened  
- Heart valves do not close properly  
- Coughing  
- Trouble breathing  
- Heart failure  
- Irregular heartbeat  
- Damage to the inner heart lining  
- Fluid in the lungs  
- Fluid around the lungs  

**Skin (more than half of people):**  
- Swelling under the skin (angioedema)  
- Skin that turns red when scratched (dermatographism)  
- Itching  
- Rashes (including eczema and hives)  

**Blood and Lymph System (more than half of people):**  
- Anemia (low red blood cells)  
- Swollen lymph nodes  
- Enlarged spleen  
- Blood clots in blood vessels  
- Low platelet count  

**Nervous System (more than half of people):**  
- Clots in the brain causing weakness or confusion  
- Changes in behavior or thinking  
- Stiffness in the limbs  
- Nerve problems in arms and legs  

**Digestive System (more than 40% of people):**  
- Belly pain  
- Diarrhea  
- Nausea  

**Immune System (about 40% of people):**  
- Immune complexes in the blood (like in serum sickness)  
- High levels of certain antibodies, especially IgE  

In rare cases, very high eosinophil counts (over 100,000 per microliter) can cause serious problems.  
These include brain or lung damage from lack of oxygen.  
This can lead to confusion, trouble breathing, or breathing failure.  
Blood clots in the heart can also happen.  

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors must rule out other causes first.  
These include parasites, allergies, and other diseases.  

They check for organ damage using tests.  
These tests include:  
- Blood tests for liver, muscle, kidney, and heart health  
- An electrocardiogram (ECG)  
- An echocardiogram (heart ultrasound)  
- Lung function tests  
- CT scans of the chest, belly, and pelvis  

A bone marrow test is also needed.  
This means taking a small sample of bone marrow from the hip bone.  
It helps check for abnormal blood cells.  

The test looks for specific gene changes.  
One common change is called *FIP1L1/PDGFRA*.  
Other similar gene changes may also be found.  

The test also checks if the problem is in a type of white blood cell called a T cell.  
This helps rule out a rare form of the disease.  

Doctors should consider this condition if:  
- You have high eosinophils in your blood more than once  
- The count is over 1,500 per microliter  
- No other cause is found  
- You have signs of organ damage  

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause and how serious the disease is.  

**Corticosteroids** are often used.  
They help reduce eosinophils and stop organ damage.  
They are usually given for severe cases.  

**Imatinib** is used if a specific gene change is found.  
This includes *FIP1L1/PDGFRA* or similar gene changes.  
Imatinib is a targeted drug.  
It blocks the abnormal signal that causes too many eosinophils.  
It works well in these cases.  

Other medicines may be used to control eosinophil levels.  
These include:  
- Hydroxyurea  
- Interferon alfa  
- Etoposide  
- Cladribine  

Supportive care is also important.  
This means treating symptoms and protecting organs.  

There is no fixed number of eosinophils that triggers treatment.  
But most doctors start treatment when the count is between 1,500 and 2,000 per microliter.  

---

## What Is the Outlook?

The most common cause of death is heart damage.  
Heart problems can happen even if the eosinophil count is not very high.  
The level or length of high counts does not predict heart damage.  

The outlook depends on how well the disease responds to treatment.  
People with the *FIP1L1/PDGFRA* gene change do much better when treated with imatinib.  
Other gene changes that respond to similar drugs also have better outcomes.  

---

## Key Points

- Hypereosinophilic syndrome means high eosinophils in the blood (over 1,500 per microliter).  
- It is not caused by parasites, allergies, or other known reasons.  
- The high count must last at least six months.  
- It must cause damage to organs.  

- This condition is linked to different blood cell disorders.  
- Some have a genetic cause.  

- The heart, lungs, spleen, skin, and nervous system are most often affected.  
- Heart damage can be life-threatening.  

- Test for organ damage using blood tests, ECG, heart ultrasound, lung tests, and CT scans.  

- Do a bone marrow test to find the cause.  
- Look for gene changes like *FIP1L1/PDGFRA*.  

- Use corticosteroids for high eosinophils or organ damage.  
- Use low-dose imatinib if a specific gene change is found.  
- Other medicines may help control blood cell counts.

# Kyphosis: A Humpback

Kyphosis is when the spine curves too much in the upper back. This can make the back look hunched or rounded.

## Types of Kyphosis

There are two main types:

### Flexible Kyphosis
- The spine can straighten when the child tightens their muscles.
- The bones in the spine are normal.
- Doctors do not know what causes it.
- Strengthening the back muscles may help.
- No special treatment is usually needed.

### Fixed Kyphosis
- The spine cannot straighten, even when muscles are tight.
- The bones in the upper back are shaped like wedges instead of rectangles.
- Usually, three or more bones are affected.
- Some babies are born with this condition, but it more often starts later in life.
- It most often begins during the teenage years.
- Rare causes include broken bones, infections, or cancer.
- The most common cause is a condition called Scheuermann disease.

## What to Watch For

Many children with kyphosis have no symptoms. But some may have:
- Mild, ongoing back pain.
- A rounded shoulder look.
- A visible hump in the upper back.
- A spine that curves more than normal.
- Long arms and legs compared to the body trunk. This can look similar to a rare condition called Marfan syndrome.

Kyphosis is often found during a routine check-up. A doctor may see it because of how the body looks. To confirm the diagnosis, the doctor will take x-rays of the spine.

## Scheuermann Disease

Scheuermann disease is the most common cause of fixed kyphosis. It usually starts during the teenage years. Boys are slightly more likely to get it than girls.

### What Causes It?
- The exact cause is unknown.
- It sometimes runs in families.
- It can happen with another spine problem called scoliosis, which is a sideways curve. When both happen, it is called kyphoscoliosis.

### What Is It?
- Scheuermann disease is a growth problem in the bones.
- It affects the growth plates in the spine during childhood.
- This happens when a child is growing fast.

### Symptoms
- A rounded upper back or hunched posture.
- Mild, ongoing back pain.
- Arms and legs that seem longer than the body.
- A more curved upper back than normal, either in one area or all along the upper spine.
- Severe cases may cause more pain and can make it hard to breathe deeply. This is because the chest cannot move well.

### How Is It Diagnosed?
- A school screening may find it.
- Doctors confirm it with x-rays of the spine.
- Sometimes, a magnetic resonance imaging scan (MRI) or a computed tomography scan (CT) is done.

## Treatment

Treatment depends on how severe the curve is.

### For Mild Kyphosis
- Reduce activities that put stress on the spine.
  - Avoid high-impact sports.
  - Do not lift heavy things.
- Avoid very strenuous activities.
- These steps can help reduce pain and stop the curve from getting worse.
- The spine may straighten a little with treatment.
- But pain and other symptoms may not go away completely.

### For More Severe Kyphosis
- A spinal brace may be needed.
- Sleeping on a firm bed may help.
- These treatments can reduce pain and stop the curve from getting worse.

### Surgery
- Surgery is rare.
- It may be needed if the curve gets worse even after treatment.
- Surgery can help straighten the spine.

## Key Points
- Kyphosis is a curve in the upper back that makes a hump.
- It can be flexible or fixed.
- Fixed kyphosis is often caused by Scheuermann disease.
- Most children have no symptoms, but some have back pain or a visible curve.
- X-rays are used to confirm the diagnosis.
- Treatment includes activity changes, braces, and sometimes surgery.

# Zinc Supplements

Zinc is a mineral your body needs in small amounts.  
The recommended daily amount for adults is 8 to 11 milligrams.  
You can get zinc from foods like oysters, beef, and fortified cereals.

## What People Say About Zinc Supplements

Some people believe zinc supplements can:
- Help reduce cold symptoms.
- Help babies recover faster from infections.
- Slow down a certain type of eye disease called age-related macular degeneration.
- Help wounds heal faster.

Zinc may also help your body use insulin better.

A mild lack of zinc can slow growth in children.  
This problem can be fixed with zinc supplements.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration gave special approval to a form of zinc called zinc acetate.  
This is to treat a rare disease called Wilson disease.  
This disease causes too much copper to build up in the body.

## What the Research Shows

### Cold Symptoms
Many studies have looked at zinc for colds.  
A major review of 34 studies found:
- Zinc does not help prevent colds.
- Zinc may shorten the length of a cold by a few days.
- Some people who take zinc report side effects like bad taste, upset stomach, or nausea.

Another review found:
- Zinc acetate and zinc gluconate work about the same for colds.
- Taking more than 100 milligrams per day does not help more.

A third study found:
- Zinc prevented 5 colds for every 100 people each month.
- The number needed to treat was 20 (meaning 20 people need to take zinc to prevent one cold).
- People on zinc got better 2 days faster than those not taking it.
- More people still had symptoms after 7 days if they did not take zinc.

### Infant Health
In developing countries, giving babies zinc and iron once a week for the first year of life:
- Lowers the risk of dying from diarrhea or lung infections.
- This is strong evidence from many studies.

Another review found:
- Zinc helps treat diarrhea in children over 6 months old who are not getting enough zinc or are malnourished.

### Eye Health
Taking zinc and antioxidants (like vitamin C, vitamin E, and lutein/zeaxanthin) every day:
- Slows the worsening of a serious eye disease called age-related macular degeneration.
- This is true for people with moderate to severe dry form of the disease.
- A 10-year study confirmed this benefit.

### Diabetes
New research shows zinc may help people with diabetes or prediabetes:
- A large review of 32 studies found zinc lowered blood sugar levels and improved long-term blood sugar control.
- The effect was stronger when zinc was taken with other supplements.
- The effect was weaker when only zinc was taken.

### Depression
Some studies suggest:
- Zinc, when taken with antidepressant medicine, may help reduce symptoms of depression.
- Experts in mental health recommend trying zinc supplements (in forms like chelated or picolinate) along with antidepressants for some people with depression.

## Side Effects of Zinc Supplements

Zinc is safe for most people when taken in normal amounts.  
But high doses can cause harm.

Common side effects of zinc lozenges include:
- Nausea.
- Vomiting.
- Diarrhea.
- Mouth irritation.
- Mouth sores.
- Bad taste.

Zinc is a trace metal.  
It can remove other important minerals from your body.  
Do not take more than 75 milligrams of zinc per day.  
Do not take this amount for more than 14 days.

Zinc sprays can irritate your nose and throat.  
Using zinc inside the nose may cause loss of smell.

## Drug Interactions

Zinc can interfere with some medicines.  
Take zinc at least 2 hours before or 4 to 6 hours after certain antibiotics.  
These include:
- Cephalexin.
- Tetracyclines.
- Quinolones.

Zinc may also affect other medicines:
- It may reduce the effect of cisplatin, a cancer drug.
- It may reduce the effect of dolutegravir, a medicine for HIV.
- It may lower levels of penicillamine, a medicine for rheumatoid arthritis.

# Meconium Aspiration Syndrome

This condition happens when a newborn baby breathes in a substance called meconium before birth. Meconium is a dark green, sticky material that builds up in a baby’s intestines before birth. Babies do not eat before birth, so this material is not waste from food. It is normal for babies to pass meconium after birth, but sometimes it is passed into the fluid around the baby in the womb.

## What Causes Meconium Aspiration Syndrome?

- Babies may pass meconium into the amniotic fluid before birth.
- This can happen normally, especially near or after the due date.
- It can also happen when a baby is under stress.
- Stress may be caused by low oxygen levels, infection, or other problems.
- When a baby is stressed, they may gasp. This can cause them to breathe in the fluid with meconium.
- If the baby breathes in this fluid, it can get into their lungs.

## What Happens in the Lungs?

- Meconium in the lungs causes irritation and swelling.
- This can lead to a lung infection.
- Meconium can block the airways.
- Blocked airways can cause parts of the lungs to collapse.
- If air gets in but cannot get out, the lung can become over-inflated.
- An over-inflated lung can burst.
- If the lung bursts, air can leak into the space around the lung.
- This is called a pneumothorax.

Babies with this condition also have a higher chance of having high blood pressure in the lungs. This is called persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn.

## Signs and Symptoms

Babies with meconium aspiration syndrome may show these signs:

- They breathe very fast and with effort.
- Their chest pulls in when they breathe in.
- They make a grunting sound when they breathe out.
- Their chest may look swollen or barrel-shaped if the lungs are over-inflated.
- Their skin or lips may look blue, gray, or whitish. This is called cyanosis.
- In babies with darker skin, the color change may be easier to see inside the mouth, nose, or eyelids.
- The umbilical cord, fingernails, or skin may have a greenish-yellow stain from meconium.
- Some babies may have low blood pressure.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look for:

- Meconium in the amniotic fluid at birth.
- Trouble breathing right after birth.
- Abnormal results on a chest x-ray.

If a baby has these signs, doctors will do a chest x-ray to confirm the diagnosis.

They may also take blood samples to check for infection.

## How Is It Treated?

- If the baby’s airway is blocked, doctors may gently suction the fluid and meconium out.
- Babies who struggle to breathe may need help breathing.
- A breathing tube may be placed in the windpipe.
- A machine called a ventilator may be used to help move air in and out of the lungs.
- Or, the baby may use CPAP. This gives a small amount of extra air pressure through prongs in the nose.
- Babies are treated in a special unit called the neonatal intensive care unit.
- The lowest possible settings are used on breathing machines to protect the lungs.
- Babies on a ventilator may get a special substance called surfactant. This helps keep the tiny air sacs in the lungs open.
- Doctors watch closely for serious problems like pneumothorax or high lung pressure.
- Babies are taken off breathing machines and oxygen as soon as it is safe to do so.
- If a bacterial infection is suspected, antibiotics are given through a vein.

## What Is the Outlook?

- Most babies with meconium aspiration syndrome survive.
- But the condition can be life-threatening if it is severe.
- Babies who survive may have a higher chance of later health problems, such as:
  - Asthma
  - Cerebral palsy
  - Delays in development

In rare cases, the condition can be fatal, especially if it leads to persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn.

# Avoidant Personality Disorder

This condition makes people avoid social situations. They fear being judged, rejected, or made fun of.

It is diagnosed by a doctor based on specific signs and symptoms.

Treatment includes talk therapy, and sometimes medicine for anxiety or depression.

---

## What Is Avoidant Personality Disorder?

People with this disorder feel deeply unsure of themselves. They try to protect themselves by staying away from people and social events.

They believe others will not like them. They expect to be criticized or rejected.

Even if they want to be with others, they stay away because they are afraid.

---

## How Common Is It?

About 2 out of every 100 people in the United States have this disorder.

More women than men are affected, but the difference is small.

---

## Other Conditions Often Seen With It

Many people with this disorder also have other mental health problems. These include:

- Depression
- Long-term low mood
- Obsessive thoughts and behaviors
- Anxiety, especially fear of social situations (social anxiety)

Some also have other personality disorders, like being overly dependent on others or having unstable relationships.

People with both social anxiety and avoidant personality disorder have worse symptoms and more trouble in daily life than those with just one condition.

---

## What Causes It?

Experts believe it starts in childhood. Some possible causes:

- Being rejected or left out by others as a child
- Being naturally shy or anxious in social settings
- Avoiding people early in life — even as young as age two

These early experiences may shape how a person sees themselves and others.

---

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

People with this disorder avoid social contact. They do this even at work or school. They fear being judged or rejected.

Examples:

- They turn down a promotion because they think coworkers will criticize them.
- They skip meetings or group events.
- They do not make new friends unless they are certain they will be liked.

They do not trust others until they are sure they are safe. They need repeated reassurance before they will join a group or form a close bond.

They want to be with people. But they are afraid to let others get close. They worry that if they open up, they will be hurt.

Because they avoid people, they often have no close friends or support system.

They notice even small signs of disapproval. They are always on guard for criticism.

They may seem tense or nervous. This can make others tease them. That makes their fear worse.

They feel bad about themselves. They think they are not good enough, not smart enough, or not worthy of being liked.

They believe they are awkward or unattractive. They think others are better than them.

They stay quiet and shy. They try to stay in the background. They fear speaking up because they think others will say they are wrong.

They do not talk about themselves. They fear being laughed at or humiliated.

They worry they will blush or cry if someone criticizes them.

They avoid new experiences or taking risks. They think the dangers are bigger than they really are.

They may use small problems as an excuse to stay home. They prefer a safe, predictable life.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor uses the DSM-5-TR to make the diagnosis.

To be diagnosed, a person must show a long-term pattern of:

- Avoiding social contact
- Feeling inadequate
- Being very sensitive to criticism or rejection

And they must have at least four of the following:

- Avoiding work tasks that involve talking to others because they fear criticism or rejection
- Not getting close to people unless they are sure they will be liked
- Being reserved in close relationships because they fear being laughed at or humiliated
- Always thinking about being criticized or rejected in social settings
- Feeling too unsure of themselves to join new social situations
- Seeing themselves as socially awkward, unattractive, or worse than others
- Avoiding new activities or risks because they fear embarrassment

These patterns must have started in early adulthood.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment helps people feel more confident and less afraid in social situations.

### Types of Therapy

- **Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT)**: Teaches practical social skills. Often done in groups.
- **Supportive therapy**: Helps people feel safe and understood. Therapists are kind and patient.
- **Psychodynamic therapy**: Looks at deep feelings and past experiences that affect current behavior.

### Group Therapy

Group therapy can help if the group has people with similar struggles.

### Medicines

- Medicine for anxiety (anxiolytics)
- Medicine for depression (antidepressants)

These may help reduce fear and improve mood.

But there are no strong studies proving that medicine alone works for this disorder.

### Important Notes About Treatment

- Many people with this disorder avoid getting help.
- Therapy works best when the therapist is patient and sensitive to the person’s fears.
- Group therapy can be very helpful for people with both social anxiety and avoidant personality disorder.

---

## Summary

Avoidant personality disorder is a pattern of avoiding people and social events due to fear of being judged or rejected.

It starts early in life and lasts into adulthood.

People with this disorder want to connect with others but are too afraid.

Treatment with therapy and sometimes medicine can help.

Supportive, patient-centered care is key.

# What Are Immunodeficiency Disorders? Your immune system protects your body from harmful invaders like bacteria, viruses, and fungi. When it does not work well, you get sick more often. You may also get sicker than usual and stay sick longer. ## Types of Immunodeficiency Disorders There are two main types: ### Primary Immunodeficiency - This type is present at birth. - It is caused by a problem in the genes you inherit. - It usually shows up in infancy or childhood. - Some types may not be found until adulthood. - These disorders are rare. ### Secondary Immunodeficiency - This type develops later in life. - It is caused by another illness or treatment. - It is more common than primary immunodeficiency. - It can be caused by long-term diseases like diabetes or cancer. - It can also be caused by certain medicines or radiation therapy. Some people with immunodeficiency live a normal life span. Others may have a shorter life span. Some disorders go away with treatment. Others last a lifetime. ## What Causes Immunodeficiency? ### Primary Causes - A change in a gene (called a mutation). - If the gene is on the X chromosome, the disorder is more common in boys. - About 60% of people with primary immunodeficiency are male. The immune system has several parts. Problems can happen in any of them: - **B cells** – These make antibodies that fight infections. - **T cells** – These help find and destroy harmful cells. - **Both B and T cells** – Problems in both types. - **Phagocytes** – These are cells that eat and destroy germs. - **Complement proteins** – These help immune cells kill bacteria. Most primary immunodeficiency disorders involve problems with B cells. ### Common Primary Immunodeficiency Disorders | Part of Immune System Affected | Disorder | |-------------------------------|--------| | B cells (antibody production) | Common variable immunodeficiency

C2, C3, C4, C5, C6, C7, C8, or C9 deficiency | ### Secondary Causes These can cause immunodeficiency later in life: - Long-term or serious illnesses like diabetes, cancer, or kidney disease. - Certain medicines, including chemotherapy and steroids. - Radiation therapy (rarely). - Poor nutrition (not getting enough food or key nutrients). - Old age. - Hospital stays. ### Illnesses That Can Cause Secondary Immunodeficiency | Type | Examples | |------|--------| | Blood disorders | Aplastic anemia, leukemia, multiple myeloma, sickle cell disease | | Cancers | Many types | | Chromosomal disorders | Down syndrome | | Infections | Chickenpox, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, HIV, measles, some bacterial infections | | Hormonal problems | Diabetes | | Kidney problems | Chronic kidney disease, nephrotic syndrome | | Liver problems | Chronic hepatitis, liver failure | | Autoimmune diseases | Systemic lupus erythematosus (lupus) | | Other | Spleen removal, alcohol use disorder, burns, undernutrition | ### Medicines That Can Cause Immunodeficiency - **Antiseizure drugs**: Lamotrigine, phenytoin, valproate - **Chemotherapy drugs**: Alemtuzumab, busulfan, cyclophosphamide, melphalan - **Corticosteroids**: Methylprednisolone, prednisone - **Immunosuppressants**: Azathioprine, cyclosporine, mycophenolate, sirolimus, tacrolimus - **Other targeted drugs**: Adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, rituximab, tocilizumab These medicines are used to treat other conditions. # Understanding Pituitary Disorders

The pituitary gland is a small organ at the base of the brain.  
It helps control other hormone glands in the body.  
These glands include the thyroid, adrenal glands, and reproductive organs.

The pituitary works closely with the hypothalamus.  
The hypothalamus is another part of the brain that helps manage the pituitary.

This overview covers the main types of problems that can affect the pituitary gland.

## Common Pituitary Problems

- **Pituitary tumors or growths**  
  These are abnormal cell collections in the pituitary.  
  They can press on nearby brain areas.  
  They may also change hormone levels.

- **Generalized hypopituitarism**  
  This means the pituitary gland is not making enough of most of its hormones.  
  This can affect growth, energy, and reproduction.

- **Selective hormone deficiencies**  
  The pituitary makes less of one or a few hormones.  
  One example is low levels of vasopressin.  
  Vasopressin helps the body keep the right amount of water.

- **Hormone overproduction**  
  The pituitary makes too much of one or more hormones.  
  This can cause serious health issues.  
  Examples include:
  - **Gigantism**: Extra growth in children before their bones stop growing.
  - **Acromegaly**: Extra growth in adults, especially in hands, feet, and face.
  - **Galactorrhea**: Milk leaking from the breasts in people who are not breastfeeding.
  - **SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion)**: Too much water retention in the body.
  - **Cushing disease**: Too much cortisol, a stress hormone, in the body.

# Eosinophilic Pneumonia

Eosinophilic pneumonia is a lung condition where a type of white blood cell called an eosinophil builds up in the lungs and often in the blood.

- Some health problems, medicines, chemicals, fungi, or parasites can cause this buildup.
- People may cough, wheeze, or feel short of breath. In some cases, breathing becomes so hard that it is life-threatening.
- Doctors use chest x-rays and blood tests to find the condition and figure out what is causing it, especially if a parasite might be the cause.
- Most people are given steroids to reduce swelling and ease symptoms.

---

## What Are Eosinophils?

Eosinophils are a type of white blood cell. They help the body fight infections and play a role in allergic reactions. Their numbers go up during allergies or inflammation. This includes asthma, which often happens with some types of eosinophilic pneumonia.

Unlike regular pneumonia, this condition is not caused by bacteria, viruses, or fungi in the tiny air sacs of the lungs. But the air sacs and airways can fill with eosinophils. In some cases, the walls of blood vessels in the lungs may also be affected. If asthma develops, the airways can get blocked with mucus.

---

## Löffler Syndrome

Löffler syndrome is a mild form of eosinophilic pneumonia.

- It may cause no symptoms at all.
- Or it may cause a dry cough, wheezing, or a low-grade fever.
- A chest x-ray and blood test are needed to confirm the diagnosis.
- It is often linked to a worm infection, especially from roundworms like *Ascaris lumbricoides*.
- In some people, no cause is found.
- The condition usually gets better on its own within one month.
- Doctors may give steroids to reduce symptoms and swelling.

---

## What Causes Eosinophilic Pneumonia?

The exact reason why eosinophils gather in the lungs is not fully known. But it may be due to an allergic reaction. Often, doctors cannot find the trigger. Still, some known causes include:

- Cigarette smoke (only in acute cases)
- Certain medicines, such as:
  - Penicillin
  - Aminosalicylic acid
  - Carbamazepine
  - Tryptophan
  - Naproxen
  - Isoniazid
  - Nitrofurantoin
  - Phenytoin
  - Sulfonamides (like sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim)
- Chemical fumes, such as from cocaine or nickel vapor
- Fungi, especially *Aspergillus fumigatus*
- Parasites, especially roundworms
- Other body-wide diseases, such as eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis

---

## Symptoms of Eosinophilic Pneumonia

Symptoms can be mild or very serious. They can come on quickly or develop slowly over time.

### Acute Eosinophilic Pneumonia

- Comes on fast, often within hours or days.
- Causes fever, chest pain that gets worse when breathing deeply, shortness of breath, and a cough.
- You may feel very unwell.
- Oxygen levels in the blood can drop quickly.
- Without treatment, it can lead to sudden breathing failure in a few hours or days.

### Löffler Syndrome

- May not cause any symptoms.
- Or it may cause mild breathing problems like coughing, wheezing, or shortness of breath.
- Most people get better quickly.

### Chronic Eosinophilic Pneumonia

- Develops slowly over days or weeks.
- Can become serious over time.
- May go away on its own, but often comes back.
- Can get worse over weeks or months.
- Without treatment, it can lead to severe shortness of breath.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to diagnose eosinophilic pneumonia.

### Chest X-ray
- Used first to look at the lungs.
- In acute cases, the x-ray usually shows changes.
- In chronic cases, the x-ray can help with the diagnosis.

### CT Scan of the Chest
- Often needed to get a clearer picture.
- Helps confirm the diagnosis in both acute and chronic cases.

### Blood Tests
- Check how many eosinophils are in the blood.
- In acute cases, the count may be normal.
- In chronic cases, the count is often very high—up to 10 to 15 times normal.

### Bronchoscopy
- A thin tube is passed into the lungs to collect fluid from the air sacs.
- A lab checks this fluid under a microscope.
- It usually shows clumps of eosinophils.

### Other Tests
- Stool tests may be done to check for worms or other parasites.
- Tests may also look for fungal infections.

### Pulmonary Function Tests
- Measure how well the lungs work.
- Check how much air the lungs can hold.
- Check how well air moves in and out.
- Check how well oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged.
- These tests help confirm the diagnosis.

---

## How Is It Treated?

### Steroids
- Most people are given steroids, such as prednisone.
- These reduce swelling and help the lungs heal.

### Acute Eosinophilic Pneumonia
- Steroids are usually needed.
- Most people get better quickly with treatment.

### Chronic Eosinophilic Pneumonia
- Steroids may be needed for many months or even years.
- Treatment may need to continue for a long time to prevent relapses.

### If You Have Wheezing
- You will be treated the same way as someone with asthma.
- This may include inhalers or other asthma medicines.

### If Parasites Are the Cause
- You will be given medicine to kill the worms or other parasites.

### If a Medicine Is the Cause
- The medicine will be stopped if possible.
- This can help the condition improve.

# External Otitis (Acute)

External otitis is an infection of the skin inside the ear canal. It usually happens quickly and is caused by bacteria. The most common bacteria is *Pseudomonas*. 

## What Causes External Otitis?

- Bacteria like *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, *Proteus vulgaris*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, or *Escherichia coli* often cause the infection.
- Fungi such as *Aspergillus niger* or *Candida albicans* can also cause it, but this is less common.
- Furuncles (boils) are usually caused by *Staphylococcus aureus* or a resistant form called MRSA.

### Things That Make It More Likely

- Using cotton swabs or other objects to clean the ear
- Allergies
- Skin conditions like psoriasis, eczema, or seborrheic dermatitis
- Water staying in the ear canal for long periods
- Hair sprays, hair dyes, or other irritants
- Wearing earplugs or hearing aids that do not fit well or are not cleaned

Cleaning the ear with cotton swabs can scratch the skin. These tiny scratches let bacteria get in. Swabs can also push wax and debris deeper into the ear. This buildup traps water and makes the skin soft and weak. This sets the stage for infection.

## Symptoms and Signs

### General Symptoms
- Pain in the ear
- Drainage from the ear
- Hearing loss if the ear canal swells shut
- Pain when you pull on the outer ear or press on the small bump in front of the ear (the tragus)

### Fungal Infection (Otomycosis)
- More itching than pain
- A feeling of fullness in the ear
- Grayish black or yellow spots (if caused by *Aspergillus niger*)
- A cotton-like material around the spots
- Thick, creamy white discharge (if caused by *Candida albicans*)
- A velvety look to the discharge

### Furuncles (Boils)
- Severe pain
- Drainage that is bloody or pus-like
- A red, swollen bump (like a pimple) in one spot

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- A doctor checks your ear and asks about your symptoms.
- The ear canal looks red, swollen, and full of wet, pus-filled debris.
- If the discharge is thick and looks like cotton, it may be a fungal infection.
- A sample may be taken to test for fungus or bacteria.

## How Is It Treated?

### Mild Cases
- Use 2% acetic acid (or white vinegar) and hydrocortisone drops.
- Put 5 drops in the ear 3 times a day for 7 days.
- This helps lower the acid level in the ear and reduces swelling.

### Moderate Cases
- First, gently remove the infected debris with suction or dry cotton swabs.
- Do not use water to rinse the ear.
- Add a topical antibiotic like ciprofloxacin or ofloxacin.
- Do not use neomycin/polymyxin because it can cause allergic reactions.
- If the ear canal is very swollen, a small wick is placed in the ear.
- The wick is soaked with Burow solution (5% aluminum acetate) or antibiotic drops, 4 times a day.
- The wick stays in for 24 to 72 hours. It may fall out on its own.
- After swelling goes down, drops can be put directly into the ear.

### Severe Cases
- You may need oral antibiotics like cephalexin or ciprofloxacin.
- Take cephalexin 500 mg 4 times a day for 10 days.
- Or take ciprofloxacin 500 mg 2 times a day for 10 days.
- The choice depends on test results.
- Quinolone antibiotics (like ciprofloxacin) are not safe for children. They can harm tendons and cartilage.
- Pain relief may be needed. This can include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or even stronger pain medicine for the first 1 to 2 days.

### Fungal Infection
- The ear must be cleaned well.
- Use an antifungal solution like gentian violet, cresylate acetate, nystatin, clotrimazole, or a mix of acetic acid and isopropyl alcohol.
- Do not use these if the eardrum is torn. They can cause severe pain or damage the inner ear.
- You may need several cleanings and treatments to fully clear the infection.

### Dry Ear Precautions
- Wear a shower cap when bathing.
- Avoid swimming.
- Use a blow dryer on low heat to dry the ear canal.

### Furuncles
- If the boil is ready to drain, a doctor may cut it open to let the pus out.
- If seen early, cutting it open does not help much.
- Topical antibiotics do not work.
- Take oral antibiotics that fight *Staphylococcus*.
- Pain medicine may be needed.
- Applying dry heat (like a warm cloth) can ease pain and help the boil heal faster.

## Prevention Tips

- After swimming, put a few drops of a 1:1 mix of rubbing alcohol and white vinegar into your ear.
- This helps dry the ear and changes the acid level to prevent infection.
- Do not use cotton swabs or any other object in your ear.
- Keep earplugs and hearing aids clean and fit well.

## Key Points

- Most cases are caused by bacteria, especially *Pseudomonas*.
- Fungal infections are less common and cause more itching and less pain.
- Pulling on the outer ear causes sharp pain in external otitis.
- Gently remove infected material with suction or dry swabs.
- Do not flush the ear with water.
- For mild cases: use acetic acid and hydrocortisone drops.
- For moderate or severe cases: clean the ear, use topical antibiotics (with a wick if swollen), and sometimes oral antibiotics.

# Bacterial Tracheitis

Bacterial tracheitis is a serious infection in the windpipe.  
It is caused by bacteria.  

This condition is rare.  
It can happen in children of any age.  
The most common bacteria are *Staphylococcus aureus* and streptococci.  

The infection starts quickly.  
It causes a loud squeaking sound when the child breathes in.  
This sound is called stridor.  
The child also has a high fever.  
They often cough up thick, pus-filled mucus.  

In rare cases, bacterial tracheitis happens after croup.  
Croup is swelling in the windpipe and voice box.  
It can also happen after a breathing tube is placed in the windpipe.  
This tube is put in through the mouth or nose.  

## How Doctors Diagnose Bacterial Tracheitis

Doctors look at the child’s symptoms.  
They use a thin tube with a light to look at the throat.  
This tool is called a laryngoscope.  
It helps the doctor see the inside of the throat.  

X-rays of the neck are often taken.  
These show changes in the windpipe.  
The pictures help doctors tell bacterial tracheitis apart from croup.  

## How Doctors Treat Bacterial Tracheitis

Very sick children need a breathing tube.  
This tube is placed into the windpipe.  
It keeps the airway open if swelling blocks it.  
This is called endotracheal intubation.  

The child gets antibiotics through a vein.  
This is called intravenous antibiotics.  
The medicine fights the infection.  

With proper treatment, most children get well.  
They recover fully.

# Feverfew

Feverfew is a plant with small leaves. People use the dried leaves to make capsules, tablets, and liquid extracts.

The plant contains chemicals called parthenolides and glycosides. These may help reduce swelling and relax certain muscles.

## What People Say About Feverfew

Some people believe feverfew can help prevent migraine headaches. It may also help ease menstrual pain, asthma, and arthritis.

In lab tests, feverfew stops blood cells from clumping together.

## What the Research Shows

A major review of studies looked at 6 trials with 561 people who had migraines.

The first 5 studies gave mixed results. But the largest and most recent study found that feverfew reduced migraines by about half a headache per month compared to a placebo.

Results varied between studies. This may be because different forms of feverfew were used, or different doses were given.

Some studies looked at combining feverfew with magnesium and CoQ10 for migraines. The results were unclear.

There are very few studies on feverfew for rheumatoid arthritis. One study found no clear benefit from taking feverfew by mouth.

## Side Effects of Feverfew

You may get mouth sores, skin irritation, a bad taste in your mouth, or mild stomach upset.

Stopping feverfew suddenly may make your migraines worse. It may also cause nervousness or trouble sleeping.

Do not take feverfew for two weeks before surgery. It may increase the risk of bleeding.

Feverfew is not safe during pregnancy. It may cause the uterus to contract and lead to early labor.

Feverfew is not recommended for children or for women who are breastfeeding.

## Drug Interactions

Do not take feverfew if you are using:

- Other medicines to prevent or treat migraines  
- Pain relievers like ibuprofen or naproxen (these are called NSAIDs)  
- Blood thinners like aspirin or clopidogrel  
- Warfarin (a blood thinner)

Always check with your doctor before combining feverfew with any medicine.

# Toxins as Weapons

A toxin is a poison made by a living thing. Some toxins can also be made in labs.  
Toxins are not infections. They do not spread from one person to another.  
This makes them more like chemical weapons than biological weapons.  
Toxins cause poisoning, not illness from germs.

Many toxins are known.  
But it is hard to make large amounts of most toxins.  
It is also hard to spread them widely.  
So most toxins are better for killing one person than for harming many.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention lists only four toxins as high threats:

- Botulinum toxin  
- Epsilon toxin from *Clostridium perfringens*  
- Ricin toxin  
- Staphylococcal enterotoxin B

Of these, only botulinum toxin is considered a top threat.

The epsilon toxin from *C. perfringens* is mostly of historical interest.  
Iraq reportedly worked on it in the 1980s.

---

## Botulinum Toxin as a Weapon

Botulinum toxin is a powerful poison made by a type of bacteria called *Clostridium botulinum*.  
There are 8 types of this toxin.  
Only 5 types can harm people.

You can get botulism from food, wounds, or infants.  
But mass harm could happen if many people eat or drink something poisoned.  
It could also happen if people breathe in a mist of the toxin.

The toxin blocks a chemical that nerves use to talk to muscles.  
This chemical is called acetylcholine.  
When it does not work, muscles become weak or stop working.

Paralysis usually starts at the top of the body.  
It shows up 12 to 36 hours after exposure.  
It can appear as early as 2 hours or as late as 8 days.  
The weakness moves down the body.  
The brain is not affected. So thinking stays clear.

Doctors diagnose the illness by looking at symptoms.

They give an antitoxin through a vein.  
The antitoxin only works on toxin still in the blood.  
It does not help with toxin already stuck to nerves.  
So it stops the illness from getting worse.  
But it does not fix symptoms that are already there.  
The earlier it is given, the better it works.

---

## Ricin and Abrin as Weapons

Ricin comes from castor beans.  
Abrin comes from jequirity beans, also called rosary peas.  
Both are plant poisons.

Ricin has been used in assassinations.  
But mass harm would likely come from breathing in a mist of ricin.

Symptoms depend on how the person was exposed.  
If inhaled, symptoms start 4 to 8 hours later.  
They include coughing, trouble breathing, and fever.  
Over the next 12 to 24 hours, many organs fail.  
This leads to breathing failure and often death.

Doctors diagnose the illness by symptoms.

There is no specific antidote or antitoxin.  
Treatment focuses on helping the person breathe.

---

## Staphylococcal Enterotoxin B as a Weapon

Staphylococcal enterotoxin B is one of seven toxins made by *Staphylococcus aureus* bacteria.  
It causes food poisoning when eaten.  
But it can also be used to harm many people.

Mass harm could happen if food is poisoned.  
It could also happen if people breathe in a mist of the toxin.

Symptoms appear 1 to 12 hours after eating.  
They appear 2 to 12 hours after breathing in the toxin.  
Some people may feel symptoms as early as 1.5 hours or as late as 24 hours.

At first, people feel like they have the flu.  
They may have fever, chills, headache, and body aches.

If the toxin is eaten, the person will have nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.  
These last 1 to 2 days.

If the toxin is inhaled, the person will cough, have chest pain, and often have a stuffy or runny nose.  
Eye irritation and redness can happen if the mist touches the eyes.  
In rare cases, inhalation can cause death.

In people who survive, fever can last up to 5 days.  
Coughing can last up to 4 weeks.

Special lab tests can help confirm the diagnosis.

There is no specific antidote or antitoxin.  
Doctors treat the person by easing symptoms.

# Squamous Cell Carcinoma

Squamous cell carcinoma is a type of skin cancer.  
It starts in the top layer of the skin.  
It grows into deeper layers of the skin.  
It usually appears on areas that get a lot of sun.

The cancer can grow quite large in one spot.  
It can spread to other parts of the body in later stages.  
A doctor must check any skin sore that does not heal.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor takes a small sample of the skin.  
This is called a biopsy.  
The sample is checked under a microscope.  
This test confirms if it is cancer.

## What Does It Look Like?

The look of squamous cell carcinoma can vary.  
Any sore on sun-exposed skin that does not heal should be checked.  
It may start as a red bump or flat patch.  
The surface may be scaly or crusty.  
It can grow into a hard lump or become thick and warty.  
Sometimes the lump is below the skin level.  
Over time, the center may break down and form an open sore.

Some examples:
- A thick, skin-colored bump on sun-exposed skin.
- A red, irregular patch on an arm or leg.
- Scaly, dark spots on the earlobe.
- A thick, hard lump on the lip.
- A large, open sore that grows and spreads.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the size, location, and how deep it goes.  
Most treatments aim to remove the cancer completely.

Common treatments include:
- Scraping and burning the tumor (curettage and electrodesiccation).
- Cutting out the cancer with surgery.
- Freezing the tumor with cold (cryosurgery).
- Using special creams (imiquimod or 5-fluorouracil).
- Using light therapy (photodynamic therapy).
- Radiation therapy, if needed.

Doctors watch patients closely after treatment.  
This is because squamous cell carcinoma can spread more than other skin cancers.

For cancers on the lip or other sensitive areas, surgery is often needed.  
It can be hard to cure these cancers completely.

For large cancers or those that come back, doctors may use a special surgery called Mohs surgery.  
This method removes the cancer layer by layer.  
Each layer is checked under a microscope right away.  
This keeps healthy tissue safe while removing all cancer.

If cancer has spread to nerves, radiation therapy is often used after surgery.

If the cancer has spread to distant parts of the body, radiation may help if the spread is limited.  
Chemotherapy does not work well for widespread spread.

For advanced or spreading cancer that cannot be removed by surgery, new drugs called PD-1 inhibitors can help.  
These include cemiplimab and pembrolizumab.

## What Is the Outlook?

Small cancers found early and treated well have a very good chance of cure.  
Most skin cancers on sun-exposed areas do not spread.  
But some do, especially if they are large or aggressive.

Cancers that are more likely to spread include those that:
- Are bigger than 2 centimeters across.
- Go deeper than 2 millimeters into the skin.
- Spread along nerves.
- Are near the ear or the edge of the lip.
- Are in scars.

About one in three cancers in the mouth or on mucous membranes have already spread by the time they are found.

Late-stage cancers are more likely to spread.  
They first spread to nearby skin and lymph nodes.  
Later, they can reach other organs.

The 5-year survival rate for cancer that has spread is about 34 percent, even with treatment.

## How Can It Be Prevented?

Squamous cell carcinoma is linked to sun exposure.  
You can lower your risk by protecting your skin.

Do these things:
- Stay in the shade when possible.
- Avoid being outside between 10 in the morning and 4 in the afternoon.  
  This is when the sun is strongest.
- Do not use tanning beds.
- Wear long-sleeved shirts, pants, and wide-brimmed hats.
- Use sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher.
- Choose sunscreen that protects against both UVA and UVB rays.
- Apply sunscreen as directed.  
  Reapply every 2 hours.  
  Reapply after swimming or sweating.
- Do not use sunscreen to stay in the sun longer.

## Key Points

- Think about squamous cell carcinoma if you have a sore on sun-exposed skin that does not heal.
- Spread is rare but more likely in cancers on the mouth, near the ear, on the lip, in scars, or that spread along nerves.
- Most treatments are local.  
  They include surgery, freezing, burning, creams, or light therapy.  
  Radiation may be used for large, recurring, or nerve-involved cancers.
- For advanced or spreading cancer, drugs like cemiplimab and pembrolizumab can help.

# Testicular Torsion

Testicular torsion happens when a testicle twists on its cord. This cuts off the blood supply to the testicle.

## What Is Testicular Torsion?

- This condition often happens in boys between 12 and 18 years old.
- It can also happen in babies or at any other age.
- Some boys are born with a shape that makes twisting more likely.
- If the blood flow is blocked, the testicle can die within 6 to 12 hours.
- This is a medical emergency. Quick treatment is needed.
