## Symptoms of Testicular Torsion

- Pain starts suddenly and is very bad.
- Swelling follows soon after.
- The pain may feel like it is in the belly.
- You may feel sick to your stomach or throw up.
- You might have a fever.
- You may need to urinate more often.
- Sometimes the pain goes away on its own but comes back later.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- A doctor will ask about your symptoms and do a physical exam.
- The doctor may use an ultrasound to check blood flow in the testicle.
- Ultrasound uses sound waves to make pictures of the inside of the body.

## How Is It Treated?

- The testicle must be untwisted quickly.
- Doctors may try to untwist it by hand during a physical exam.
- If this does not work, surgery is needed right away.
- During surgery, the doctor will untwist the cord.
- The doctor will also secure both testicles in place to prevent future twisting.
- This surgery helps stop the problem from happening again.

**Act fast.** If you or someone you know has sudden, severe testicle pain, go to the emergency room right away. Delay can lead to loss of the testicle.

# Pulmonary Contusion

A pulmonary contusion is a bruise of the lung. It happens when the chest is hit hard. The lung tissue bleeds and swells. There is no cut or tear in the lung.

This injury is common after a serious chest injury. It can be life-threatening. It often happens after a car crash, fall, or strong blow to the chest.

People with a lung bruise may also have other injuries. These can include broken ribs, a broken breastbone, or air in the space around the lung (pneumothorax).

Large bruises can make it hard for the lungs to deliver oxygen to the blood. This can lead to serious breathing problems. Later, the person may get pneumonia. In some cases, the lungs can fail completely, a condition called acute respiratory distress syndrome.

## Symptoms

The main symptom is pain. The pain comes from the chest wall being injured. Some people also have trouble breathing.

The chest is tender to touch. Other signs depend on any other injuries present.

## How It Is Diagnosed

Doctors suspect a lung bruise when breathing problems start after a chest injury. The symptoms often get worse slowly over time.

A chest x-ray is the usual test. It can show the bruised area as a dark spot. But the dark spot may not show up right away. It can take 24 to 48 hours for the bruise to appear on the x-ray.

A CT scan is more sensitive. It can find smaller bruises. But it is usually done only if doctors are checking for other injuries.

Patients are watched closely for breathing failure. Doctors check breathing and blood oxygen levels often. If oxygen levels drop or breathing gets hard, they may do more tests. These include measuring carbon dioxide levels or taking a blood sample from an artery.

## How It Is Treated

Treatment focuses on helping the body heal. It is not a cure for the bruise itself.

Pain relief is given as needed. This helps the person breathe deeply and avoid lung infections.

Oxygen is given if blood oxygen levels are low. For example, if the oxygen level is between 91% and 94%, extra oxygen may be needed.

Mechanical ventilation may be needed if breathing is very poor. This means the person is not getting enough oxygen or is holding too much carbon dioxide. This usually happens when oxygen levels fall below 90% while breathing room air, or when the blood oxygen level is below 65 mm Hg.

People with long-term lung disease (like COPD) or kidney disease are more likely to need a breathing machine.

# Loiasis

Loiasis is a disease caused by a type of roundworm called *Loa loa*.  
This worm is also known as a filarial worm.  
It is found only in rainforest areas of western and central Africa.

## How Loiasis Spreads

A fly called the African deer fly carries the worm.  
The fly bites a person and puts worm larvae into the skin through the bite.  
The larvae grow into adult worms inside the body.  
The adult worms live in the tissues under the skin and around the eyes.  
Female worms are about 1.5 to 3 inches long (4 to 7.5 centimeters).  

The adult worms make tiny worm babies called microfilariae.  
These tiny worms travel in the blood during the day.  
At night, they move into the lungs.  
When a fly bites a person during the day, it can pick up the microfilariae.  
The fly then passes the worms to another person when it bites again.

## What Happens in Loiasis

Most people with loiasis do not feel sick.  
Some people get itchy lumps on their arms or legs.  
These lumps are called Calabar swellings.  
They can appear anywhere on the body.  
They are caused by an allergic reaction to the worms moving through the body.  
In people who live in the area, the lumps usually last 1 to 3 days.  
In travelers, the lumps happen more often and are worse.

Sometimes the adult worms move across the eye.  
This can make the eye feel itchy or irritated.  
It can be scary to see a worm move across the eye.  
But it usually does not cause lasting eye damage.

In rare cases, the worms can affect the heart, kidneys, or brain.  
When this happens, symptoms are usually mild.  
Some people may have more protein or a little blood in their urine.

## How Doctors Diagnose Loiasis

Doctors look for signs of the disease in several ways.  
They may check a blood sample under a microscope.  
They take the blood between 10 in the morning and 2 in the afternoon.  
This is when the most tiny worms are in the blood.  
They can also see the worms moving under the eye’s clear covering.  
They may find worms that were removed from the eye or skin.

Doctors suspect loiasis in people who have eye worms or lumps and have been to western or central Africa.  
They confirm the diagnosis by finding the tiny worms in the blood or seeing the adult worms.

## How Loiasis Is Treated

The only medicine that kills both adult worms and tiny worms is diethylcarbamazine.  
You take it by mouth for 21 days.  
You may need to take it more than once to clear the infection.

Before giving diethylcarbamazine, doctors check for another worm infection called onchocerciasis.  
If you have both infections, diethylcarbamazine can cause serious side effects.  
In that case, doctors give you diethylcarbamazine and another medicine called ivermectin.

Diethylcarbamazine can cause serious or even deadly side effects, especially if the infection is severe.  
To lower this risk, doctors first check how many tiny worms are in your blood.  
If the number is high, they first reduce the number of tiny worms.  
They do this with another medicine called albendazole.  
Or they use a blood-filtering procedure called apheresis.  
This lowers the risk of bad reactions.

If the number of tiny worms is low, doctors give you diethylcarbamazine.  
They may also add albendazole if the first medicine does not work.

## How to Prevent Loiasis

If you plan to stay a long time in an area where *Loa loa* is found, you can take diethylcarbamazine to help prevent infection.

To avoid being bitten by the deer fly:

- Use insect repellent.  
- Wear clothing treated with permethrin.  
- Wear loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and long pants.  

The deer fly bites during the day.  
Mosquito netting on beds does not help.

# Spina Bifida – Simple Explanation

Spina bifida is a birth defect where the bones of the spine do not close properly around the spinal cord.  
It can range from mild to very serious.  
The exact cause is often unknown.  
But low levels of folate during pregnancy increase the risk.

Some children have no symptoms.  
Others have serious problems with movement and feeling below the affected area.

## What You Need to Know

- Spina bifida is one of the most serious birth defects that can allow a child to live a long life.  
- It happens in about 1 out of every 2,758 babies born in the United States each year.  
- It most often affects the lower back, especially the lower chest, lower back, or tailbone area.  
- The defect usually covers 3 to 6 spine bones.

## Types of Spina Bifida

### 1. Occult Spinal Dysraphism (OSD)
This type has no open wound.  
But there may be small signs on the skin over the lower back.  
These signs include:
- A small dimple or hole in the skin that goes deep.
- A patch of darker skin.
- One side of the buttocks is higher than the other.
- A tuft of hair in the lower back.

Even if the skin looks normal, the spinal cord may still be affected.  
Common issues include:
- A fatty lump (lipoma) near the spinal cord.
- The spinal cord is stuck in place (tethered cord).

### 2. Spina Bifida Cystica
This type has a sac sticking out from the back.  
The sac can contain:
- Only the protective covering of the spinal cord (meningocele).
- Part of the spinal cord itself (myelocele).
- Both the spinal cord and its covering (myelomeningocele).

In a myelomeningocele, the sac has a thin layer of tissue and a patch of nervous tissue inside.  
If the skin over the sac is broken, it can get infected easily.  
This can lead to meningitis, a serious brain and spinal cord infection.

## Common Problems with Spina Bifida

- **Hydrocephalus**: Fluid builds up in the brain.  
  This is common because many children have a brain abnormality called Chiari II malformation.

- **Syringomyelia**: A fluid-filled space forms inside the spinal cord.  
  This can cause more nerve damage.

- Other issues may include extra tissue or growths around the spinal cord.

## What Causes Spina Bifida?

There is no single cause.  
It likely comes from a mix of factors.

- Low folate levels during pregnancy are a major risk.  
- Some families have a history of the condition, so genes may play a role.  
- Certain medicines taken by the mother during pregnancy can raise the risk.  
  For example, valproate (a medicine for seizures or mood disorders).  
- Uncontrolled diabetes in the mother also increases the risk.

## Signs and Symptoms

Many children with mild forms have no symptoms.  
Others may have:
- Weakness or no movement in the legs.
- Trouble feeling touch, heat, or pain in the lower body.
- Problems with bladder or bowel control.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

### Before Birth
- A routine ultrasound scan can show the defect.  
- High levels of a protein called alpha-fetoprotein in the mother’s blood or amniotic fluid can suggest spina bifida.

### After Birth
- The defect is often visible on the baby’s back.  
- Doctors use imaging tests to see the spine and brain:
  - Ultrasound (for babies).
  - MRI (for more detail).
- X-rays of the spine, hips, and legs are done if needed.
- Brain scans (ultrasound, CT, or MRI) check for fluid buildup and spinal cord problems.

### Urinary System Check
After diagnosis, the bladder and kidneys must be tested.  
This includes:
- A urine test.
- Blood tests to check kidney function.
- An ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder.

Doctors may also test how much urine the bladder holds and how much pressure builds up when the bladder empties.  
This helps plan treatment.

Further tests like urodynamics or a voiding cystourethrogram may be needed based on earlier results.

## Treatment

Spina bifida needs care from many specialists.  
This includes neurosurgeons, urologists, orthopedic doctors, pediatricians, mental health experts, and social workers.

### Surgery
- The open spine or sac is closed as soon as possible after birth.  
- This is usually done within the first 72 hours.  
- The goal is to prevent infection and protect the spinal cord.

- If the sac is leaking fluid, antibiotics are started right away.  
- A sterile dressing covers the area.

- If the defect is large or hard to close, a plastic surgeon may help.

### Shunt for Brain Fluid
- If fluid builds up in the brain (hydrocephalus), a shunt is placed.  
- This drains extra fluid into the belly.  
- The shunt may be put in during the spine surgery.

### Bladder and Kidney Care
- Kidney function must be watched closely.  
- Any bladder or kidney infection must be treated fast.

- If the bladder does not empty well, a tube is used to drain urine.  
- This is called clean intermittent catheterization.  
- It is usually started between ages 2 and 3, or earlier if needed.

- This helps keep the bladder and kidneys healthy.  
- It also improves bladder control.

### Bowel Care
- Children are encouraged to sit on the toilet after meals to help with bowel control.  
- A healthy diet is important.  
- Stool softeners or laxatives may help prevent constipation.  
- This improves bowel control.

- Older children may use a special procedure: liquid is put into the bowel through a tube in the belly.  
- This helps clean out the bowel regularly.

### Bone and Muscle Care
- Early treatment is key.  
- If a foot is twisted (clubfoot), a cast is used.  
- Surgery may be needed after casting.

- Hip joints are checked often for dislocation.  
- Children are watched for:
  - Curved spine (scoliosis).
  - Weak muscles.
  - Muscle tightness or spasms.
  - Broken bones from weak bones.
  - Pressure sores from sitting or lying too long.

## Prognosis (Outlook)

The outcome depends on:
- How high the spinal defect is.
- How many other problems the child has.

Children with defects in the upper back (thoracic area) or those with:
- Curved spine (kyphosis),
- Fluid in the brain,
- Early kidney problems,
- Other birth defects,
have a harder time.

But with good care, most children do well.  
The main causes of death in older children are:
- Kidney failure.
- Problems with the brain shunt.

## How to Prevent Spina Bifida

- All women who could become pregnant should take folate.  
  Take 400 to 800 micrograms (mcg) of folate every day.  
  Start 3 months before getting pregnant.  
  Keep taking it through the first trimester.

- Women who have had a baby with spina bifida or another neural tube defect should take 4 milligrams (4,000 mcg) of folate daily.  
  This is a much higher dose.  
  They should start before pregnancy and continue through the first trimester.

## Key Points

- Spina bifida means the spine did not close properly.  
  It can include a sac that sticks out, with or without spinal cord tissue inside.

- A brain abnormality called Chiari II malformation is common.  
  It often causes fluid buildup in the brain (hydrocephalus).

- Low folate is a major risk.  
  Other risks include certain medicines, diabetes, and family history.

- Some children have no symptoms.  
  Others have weakness, numbness, or trouble with bladder and bowel control.

- No nerve signals to the legs can cause muscle loss and foot or spine problems.

- Test for spina bifida during pregnancy using ultrasound and blood tests.

- Treat the spine defect early.  
  Use a shunt if fluid builds up in the brain.  
  Treat bladder, bowel, and bone problems as needed.

- Prevent spina bifida by taking folate before and during early pregnancy.

# Numbness

Numbness means you cannot feel touch, pain, heat, cold, or the position of your body parts.  
It can happen in one area or spread to other parts of the body.  
Numbness is often a sign that the nervous system is not working properly.

When you lose feeling in your body, you may not know where your arms or legs are.  
This can make it hard to walk or keep your balance.  
You may also have trouble doing everyday tasks.

Some people use the word "numbness" when they feel tingling, pins and needles, or weakness.  
These feelings are not the same as numbness.  
But they often happen at the same time.  
The exact symptoms depend on what is causing the numbness.

If numbness lasts a long time, especially in the feet, it can lead to serious problems.  
You may have trouble walking or driving.  
You may fall more often.  
You might not feel pain from cuts, sores, or infections.  
This can delay treatment and make things worse.

---

## How the Body Feels Sensations

To feel things normally, your body follows a clear path:

1. Special nerve endings in your skin pick up signals like touch, heat, or pain.  
2. These signals travel through nerves in your skin to your spinal cord.  
3. The nerves join together in your spine to form nerve roots.  
4. The signals go up your spinal cord.  
5. They pass through the brain stem.  
6. Finally, they reach the part of your brain that understands and responds to the signals.

Some body areas use special networks called plexuses.  
Plexuses are groups of nerves that help send signals to specific areas.  
There are four main plexuses in the torso.

Another structure, called the cauda equina, is a bundle of nerves at the bottom of the spinal cord.  
It looks like a horse’s tail — that’s what “cauda equina” means in Latin.  
It sends feeling to the thighs, buttocks, genitals, and the area between them.  
This area is called the saddle area because it would touch a saddle when riding a horse.

---

## What Causes Numbness?

Numbness happens when any part of the sensation pathway stops working.  
This can be due to disease, injury, or certain medicines.

Many conditions can cause numbness. For example:

- Poor blood flow to nerves, such as in vasculitis or after a stroke  
- Injury to nerves, like from a fall or accident  
- Nerve damage from inherited conditions, such as Friedreich ataxia  
- Pressure on nerves, such as from swelling or sitting in one position too long  
- Infections that affect nerves, like leprosy, HIV, or Lyme disease  
- Inflammation that damages the outer layer of nerves, as in multiple sclerosis or Guillain-Barré syndrome  
- Problems with body chemistry, such as diabetes, vitamin B12 deficiency, heavy metal poisoning, or side effects from chemotherapy

Pressure on different parts of the pathway can come from many sources:

- **Pressure on nerves**: Repeating the same motion (like typing), or sitting with legs crossed for too long  
- **Pressure on spinal nerve roots**: A slipped disk, arthritis, or narrowing of the spine  
- **Pressure on the spinal cord**: A tumor, injury, or a collection of blood (hematoma) or pus (abscess)

---

## How Doctors Check for Numbness

Because many things can cause numbness, doctors ask questions carefully.  
They look for warning signs that need urgent care.

Go to the hospital right away if you have:

- Sudden numbness (within minutes or hours)  
- Sudden weakness with numbness  
- Numbness or weakness that spreads quickly up or down your body  
- Trouble breathing  
- Numbness in the thighs, buttocks, genitals, or saddle area  
- Loss of bladder or bowel control  
- Numbness on both sides of the body below a certain level (like below the chest)  
- Numbness in an entire arm or leg  
- Loss of feeling in the face or chest

If you do not have these warning signs, call your doctor.  
They will decide how soon you need to be seen.

Doctors start by asking:

- Which parts of your body are numb?  
- How fast did the numbness start?  
- Do you have other symptoms like tingling, weakness, trouble with bladder or bowel control, or vision problems?

The pattern of numbness helps doctors find the problem:

- Numbness in one arm or leg? Likely a nerve or spinal nerve root issue.  
- Numbness on one side of the body? Likely a brain problem.  
- Numbness on both sides below a certain level? Likely a spinal cord problem.  
- Numbness in both hands and feet? Likely a widespread nerve problem (polyneuropathy).

Doctors also ask about your medical history.  
They want to know if you have:

- Diabetes  
- Kidney disease  
- Infections like HIV or Lyme disease  
- A past stroke or arthritis  
- Family members with nerve problems  
- Use of medicines, alcohol, or drugs  
- Exposure to toxins

They do a full physical exam.  
This includes testing your sense of touch, temperature, reflexes, and muscle strength.

---

### Common Causes and Their Features

| Cause | Common Signs | How It’s Diagnosed |
|------|--------------|--------------------|
| Numbness in one arm and leg on the same side | Often due to stroke, brain tumor, or multiple sclerosis | MRI or CT scan of the brain |
| Numbness on the opposite side of the face and body | May happen with brain stem problems | MRI or CT scan of the brain |
| Numbness on the same side of the face and opposite side of the body | May happen with lower brain stem issues | MRI of the brain |
| Numbness in both arms and legs | Often due to spinal cord pressure or inflammation | MRI of the spinal cord |
| Numbness in the saddle area (thighs, buttocks, genitals) | Often with back pain and loss of bladder control | MRI of the spinal cord |
| Numbness and weakness in arms and shoulders | May follow spinal injury or a cyst in the spine | MRI |
| Numbness in both hands and feet | Often from diabetes, kidney disease, or vitamin deficiency | Nerve tests and blood tests |
| Numbness with tingling and weakness | May be from multiple sclerosis | MRI of brain and spine, spinal tap |
| Numbness in one arm or leg | May be from a pinched nerve in the spine | MRI or CT of spine |
| Numbness in a large area of one limb | May be from injury or cancer near a nerve network | Nerve tests, MRI |
| Numbness in one specific nerve area | Like carpal tunnel syndrome or knee nerve injury | Exam, sometimes nerve tests |

Note: Some conditions can be diagnosed just by the exam.  
Other tests are needed if the cause is unclear.

---

## Testing for Numbness

Tests are not always needed.  
For example, if the cause is clear — like carpal tunnel syndrome — rest or a splint may be enough.

But if the cause is not clear, doctors may do tests:

- **Nerve conduction studies and electromyography**: These tests check how well nerves and muscles work.  
  - Electrodes or small needles stimulate nerves.  
  - Doctors measure how fast signals travel.  
  - A needle in a muscle records its electrical activity when resting and when moving.

- **MRI or CT scans**: Used to look at the brain or spinal cord.  
  - MRI is preferred when possible.  
  - CT is used if MRI is not available.

If nerve tests suggest a widespread nerve problem, blood tests check for:

- Diabetes  
- Kidney disease  
- Vitamin B12 deficiency  
- Infections like HIV or Lyme disease

---

## Treating Numbness

The main goal is to treat the cause of numbness.  
If the cause can be fixed, numbness may improve.

Other treatments help relieve symptoms.  
For example, medicines can help with nerve pain.

Simple steps can also help:

- Wear well-fitting shoes and socks.  
- Check your shoes before wearing them — look for pebbles or sharp objects.  
- Check your feet every day for sores, redness, or signs of infection.  
- Be careful with hot or sharp objects if your hands are numb.

If you have trouble walking or feel unsteady, physical therapy can help.  
It teaches you how to move safely and avoid falls.

You may have trouble driving if you have numbness.  
Talk to your doctor about whether it is safe for you to drive.

---

## Key Points

- Numbness means you cannot feel touch, pain, heat, cold, or where your body parts are.  
- It often comes with tingling or other odd feelings.  
- Many things can cause numbness — from injury to disease.  
- It happens when the path from your skin to your brain is damaged.  
- If you have sudden numbness, weakness, or loss of bladder control, go to the hospital right away.  
- Tell your doctor which body parts are affected and how fast symptoms started.  
- This helps find the cause.  
- Tests usually start with nerve studies if nerves are involved, or MRI if the brain or spinal cord is involved.

# Sleep Problems from Body Clock Issues

Your body has a natural sleep-wake cycle. This is your body clock. It tells you when to feel awake and when to feel sleepy. 

Sometimes, this body clock does not match the outside world. For example, it may not match the light and dark times of day. When this happens, you may have trouble sleeping or feel very tired during the day.

These problems are called circadian rhythm sleep disorders.

## What Causes These Sleep Problems?

Your body clock can become out of sync in two main ways:

- **Internal causes**: Your body clock runs too early or too late. This can happen without any outside reason.
- **External causes**: Things like traveling across time zones or working night shifts can throw off your body clock.

These sleep problems can also happen in people with:
- Alzheimer disease
- Parkinson disease
- Brain injury from head trauma
- Brain infection (encephalitis)

## What Happens When the Body Clock Is Off?

When your body clock is out of sync, other body rhythms can also go off track. These include:
- Body temperature
- Hormone levels

This can cause:
- Trouble sleeping
- Feeling very sleepy during the day
- Nausea
- Feeling unwell
- Mood changes like irritability or sadness

Long-term problems may also increase your risk of:
- Heart disease
- Metabolic problems (like diabetes or weight gain)

## How Hard Is It to Adjust?

It is harder to adjust when your sleep schedule keeps changing. This is common with:
- Frequent long-distance travel (especially flying east)
- Rotating shift work (switching between night, evening, and day shifts)

Shifts that move your sleep time earlier (like flying east or switching from night to day shifts) are harder to adjust to. These are called counterclockwise shifts.

Most people feel better in a few days. But some people, especially older adults, may take weeks or even months to feel normal again.

## How Can You Feel Better?

Light is one of the strongest signals that helps reset your body clock.

To help your body adjust:
- Get bright light (sunlight or special light lamps) after you wake up.
- Wear sunglasses before bedtime to block light. This helps your body know it is time to sleep.

Taking melatonin before bed may also help. Melatonin is a natural hormone that helps you feel sleepy.

## Common Types of Circadian Rhythm Sleep Disorders

These are the main types:

- **Jet lag disorder**: Trouble sleeping and feeling tired after crossing multiple time zones.
- **Shift work disorder**: Sleep problems caused by working night shifts or rotating shifts.
- **Sleep phase disorders**: Your body clock is too early or too late. This means you fall asleep and wake up much earlier or later than normal.

## Important Notes

Some people try to fix their sleep problems with:
- Alcohol
- Sleep medicines
- Stimulants (like caffeine or energy pills)

These can make the problem worse over time. They are not a good long-term solution.

# Pemphigoid Gestationis

Pemphigoid gestationis is a rare skin condition that causes severe itching. It happens during pregnancy or shortly after giving birth.

## What to Expect

- The rash usually starts around the belly button.
- It often appears in the second or third trimester of pregnancy.
- The rash usually goes away within a few weeks or months after delivery.
- Most babies are not affected by the rash.
- Sometimes, a baby is born with a similar rash. This rash usually goes away on its own within a few weeks.
- The condition is caused by the body’s immune system attacking healthy skin. This is called an autoimmune reaction.
- The condition is rare.

## Symptoms

- The rash may start as red spots on the skin.
- These spots can be flat or raised.
- The rash often begins on the abdomen, near the belly button.
- Blisters then form. They are filled with fluid.
- The blisters can be small or large. They are irregular in shape.
- The rash is very itchy.
- The rash can spread to other parts of the body, including the arms, legs, chest, back, palms, and soles.
- The face and mouth are usually not affected.
- The rash can appear earlier in pregnancy or right after delivery.
- It often gets worse right after giving birth.
- It may come back in future pregnancies.
- It can also return when a woman uses birth control pills.
- It may also come back during a period or when an egg is released from the ovary (ovulation).

## Risks to the Baby

- Most babies are healthy.
- But if the baby is born too early or does not grow well in the womb, the risk of serious problems increases.
- In rare cases, the baby may not survive.

## How It Is Diagnosed

- A doctor will look at the rash and ask about your symptoms.
- Sometimes, a small sample of skin is taken from the rash area.
- This sample is tested for abnormal antibodies in the skin.

## How It Is Treated

- A corticosteroid cream is applied directly to the skin.
  - This helps reduce itching and swelling.
  - A common cream is triamcinolone.
- If the rash is widespread, a corticosteroid pill is taken.
  - A common pill is prednisone.
- Antihistamines that do not make you sleepy can also help with itching.
  - These are taken by mouth.
- Treatment helps relieve symptoms and makes you more comfortable.

# Byssinosis

Byssinosis is a lung condition that affects people who work with raw cotton, flax, or hemp.  
It causes the airways in the lungs to narrow.  
This makes it hard to breathe and causes chest tightness.  

The main cause is breathing in tiny particles from the raw materials.  
These particles contain a substance called bacterial endotoxin.  
This substance triggers the lung problem.  
Some people are more likely to get it because of their genes.  

## Who Gets Byssinosis?

People who work in textile mills are most at risk.  
Jobs that involve handling raw cotton, flax, or hemp carry the highest risk.  
The condition is more common in workers with long-term exposure.  

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may feel chest tightness and shortness of breath.  
Symptoms usually start on the first day of work after a break, like a weekend or vacation.  
They get better as you work through the week.  
This pattern is different from regular asthma.  

Over time, long-term exposure can lead to a serious lung condition.  
This condition has signs of both asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).  
COPD is a long-term lung disease that makes breathing harder.  

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your work history.  
They ask if you have worked with raw cotton, flax, or hemp.  
They also do lung function tests.  
These tests measure how well your lungs work.  
They can show if your airways are blocked.  

Workers in textile factories can be checked regularly.  
This includes reporting symptoms and doing lung tests.  
Early checks can catch the problem before it gets worse.  

## How Is It Treated?

The best way to treat byssinosis is to avoid the dust.  
Reduce your exposure to cotton, flax, or hemp dust.  
Medicines used for asthma and COPD can help.  
These include inhalers and other breathing medicines.  

Workplaces can reduce dust in several ways:  
- Wet the raw materials to keep dust down.  
- Improve air flow in the building.  
- Use exhaust hoods to pull dust away.  

For some jobs, wearing a face mask or respirator may be needed.  
This is in addition to other safety measures.  

If your symptoms do not go away, or if lung tests show serious blockage,  
you should be moved to a job with less dust exposure.

# Melatonin

Melatonin is a natural substance made in your brain. It helps control your sleep and wake times. The part of your brain that makes melatonin is called the pineal gland. It is in the center of your brain.

Melatonin in supplements can come from animals. But most is made in a lab. In some countries, melatonin is treated like a medicine and is regulated.

## What People Use Melatonin For

Many people take melatonin to help with sleep problems. It may help with insomnia. It can also help with jet lag. It may also help people who work night shifts.

If you are traveling across time zones, you can take melatonin on the day you leave. You can also take it for 2 to 4 nights after you arrive.

If you work rotating shifts, you can take melatonin before you go to bed.

Doctors are studying melatonin to see if it can help people with early Alzheimer disease. It may help reset their sleep schedule. It is also being studied for seasonal affective disorder. This is when a person feels sad or low during the winter months.

Melatonin is also used to help calm nerves before and after surgery. Most people feel anxious before surgery.

## What the Research Shows

Melatonin can affect your sleep schedule. It may help with jet lag or short-term sleep problems. But it does not seem to help with long-term sleep problems.

Scientists are testing melatonin in people with Alzheimer disease. It may help them sleep better. It may also reduce sundowning. Sundowning means confusion, restlessness, aggression, or anxiety that happens in the late afternoon or evening.

## Side Effects of Melatonin

Some people have side effects from melatonin. These can include:
- Headache
- Dizziness
- Nausea
- Feeling sleepy
- Feeling down or sad for a short time

Melatonin may make depression worse. We do not know if it is safe to use for a long time.

You should take melatonin only under a doctor’s care. This is especially true for children.

People with epilepsy should not take melatonin. It may make seizures more likely.

Melatonin may make autoimmune diseases worse. These are conditions where the body attacks itself, like lupus or rheumatoid arthritis.

Melatonin may lower fertility. We do not know if it is safe during pregnancy or while breastfeeding.

The amount of melatonin in different products can vary a lot. Labels do not always show the true amount. This can be dangerous.

More people are having serious side effects from melatonin. Some have needed hospital care. This includes children who accidentally took melatonin.

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine says older adults with dementia should avoid melatonin. It stays in their bodies longer than in younger people. This can cause drowsiness during the day.

## Drug Interactions

Melatonin can make warfarin stronger. Warfarin is a medicine that prevents blood clots. This can raise the risk of bleeding.

Melatonin can make some sleep medicines stronger. This includes benzodiazepines.

Melatonin can reduce the effect of seizure medicines. This may raise the risk of seizures.

Melatonin can make the side effects of methamphetamine worse.

Some medicines change how much melatonin your body has:
- Fluvoxamine, estrogen, and quinolone antibiotics can raise melatonin levels.
- Carbamazepine (a seizure medicine) and rifampin (an antibiotic) can lower melatonin levels.

## Recommendations

If you have trouble sleeping or want to prevent jet lag, you can try melatonin. But most people should talk to a doctor first. This is especially true if you plan to take it often.

Do not take melatonin if you:
- Have dementia
- Have epilepsy
- Have an autoimmune disease
- Are trying to get pregnant
- Are taking warfarin

# Cold Injury: What You Need to Know

Cold weather can make your body temperature drop too low. This is called hypothermia. Cold can also hurt your skin and tissues.

## Types of Cold Injury

- **Frostnip**: Cold damages skin but no freezing happens. Skin turns white or numb. It feels cold and tingly. It usually gets better fast when warmed.
- **Immersion foot**: This happens when feet stay wet and cold for a long time. It causes swelling, numbness, and pain. It can happen even in mild cold if feet stay wet.
- **Chilblains**: Small, itchy, red or purple spots on skin. They happen after cold exposure, especially if skin gets wet and then warms too fast.
- **Frostbite**: This is when skin and deeper tissues freeze. It can cause permanent damage. It often affects fingers, toes, nose, and ears.

## How to Treat Cold Injury

- Warm the injured area slowly. Use warm water or body heat. Do not use hot water or heating pads.
- Do not rub the area. This can cause more harm.
- Do not walk on frostbitten feet or toes. This can cause more damage.
- Seek medical help right away if you think you have frostbite or severe cold injury.
- Surgery may be needed later to remove dead tissue. This is done only when needed and often delayed.

## Who Is More at Risk?

You are more likely to get cold injury if you:
- Are very tired
- Have not eaten enough
- Are dehydrated
- Are in low oxygen conditions
- Have heart or blood vessel problems
- Are in contact with wet clothes or metal

## How to Prevent Cold Injury

Prevention is the most important step.

- Always be ready for cold, even if it does not feel very cold.
- Wear several layers of warm clothing. Wool or polypropylene works best. These materials stay warm even when wet.
- Wear a warm hat. You can lose a lot of body heat through your head.
- Keep your gloves and socks dry. Change them if they get wet.
- Wear insulated boots that fit well. They should not be too tight. Tight boots can cut off blood flow.

### Stay Warm from the Inside

- Drink plenty of fluids. Warm drinks help keep your body warm.
- Eat regular meals. Food gives your body energy to make heat.
- Avoid alcohol. It makes your skin warm on the outside but causes you to lose heat faster. It also makes you less aware of cold and less able to act to protect yourself.

### Watch for Warning Signs

- If your fingers, toes, nose, or ears feel cold or numb, warm them right away.
- Do not wait. Early action can stop serious injury.

Always take cold exposure seriously. Protect yourself before it’s too late.

# Fatty Acid Oxidation Disorders

These are rare health problems that affect how the body uses fat for energy.  
They happen when a child is born with missing or weak enzymes.  
Enzymes are special proteins that help break down fat.  
Without enough of these enzymes, the body cannot make enough energy from fat.  
This can slow down a child’s growth and learning.  

These disorders are passed from parents to children through genes.  
Both parents must carry one copy of the faulty gene.  
The child needs two copies of the faulty gene to have the disorder.  
So, the parents usually do not have the disorder themselves.  

Fats are a key source of energy for the body.  
The body constantly breaks down fat and rebuilds it to meet energy needs.  
Several enzymes help break down fat so the body can use it for energy.  

Children with this disorder are missing or have weak enzymes.  
This means their body cannot break down fat properly.  
They run out of energy.  
Harmful byproducts build up in the body.  
One of the most common missing enzymes is called medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase.  
Other missing enzymes include short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase, very long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, glutaric acidemia type II, and mitochondrial trifunctional protein.  
Most of these problems start in infancy.  

Treatment depends on which fats build up in the blood and body.  

---

## Medium-Chain Acyl-CoA Dehydrogenase Deficiency (MCADD)

MCADD is one of the most common inherited metabolic disorders.  
It is more common in people of Northern European background.  

Symptoms usually start after 2 to 3 months of age.  
They often appear when a child goes without food for a long time.  
They can also happen during illness or heavy exercise.  
The blood sugar level drops very low.  
This can cause confusion, drowsiness, or even coma.  
The child may feel weak, vomit, or have seizures.  
Over time, the child may grow and learn more slowly.  
The liver may become enlarged.  
The heart muscle may weaken.  
The heartbeat may become irregular.  
In rare cases, sudden death can happen.  

All babies in the United States are tested for MCADD at birth.  
A small blood sample is taken from the heel.  
Urine and other tissue tests may also be done.  
DNA testing can confirm the diagnosis.  

If a child has a serious episode, they need dextrose given through a vein.  
For long-term care, the child must eat often.  
They must never skip meals.  
They should eat a diet high in carbohydrates and low in fat.  
Carnitine supplements may help.  
Some children need cornstarch at night to keep blood sugar from dropping too low.  

The long-term outlook is usually good with proper care.  

---

## Long-Chain 3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA Dehydrogenase Deficiency (LCHADD)

LCHADD is the second most common fatty acid oxidation disorder.  
It causes symptoms similar to MCADD.  
It can also cause heart muscle problems.  
The heart walls may become weak and thick.  
Nerves in the hands and feet may be damaged.  
The liver may not work well.  

When a child exercises, muscle tissue can break down.  
This is called rhabdomyolysis.  
Damaged muscle releases a protein called myoglobin.  
This can turn the urine brown or red.  

A pregnant woman with a fetus who has LCHADD may have serious health problems.  
She may have breakdown of red blood cells.  
Her liver enzymes may be high.  
She may have low platelets.  
This condition is called HELLP syndrome.  

Doctors diagnose LCHADD by testing the blood for certain acids.  
They may also test skin cells to check enzyme levels.  
Genetic testing can show if a couple is at risk of having a child with this disorder.  
All babies in the United States are tested for LCHADD at birth.  

During a serious episode, the child needs fluids and glucose through a vein.  
They must rest in bed.  
Carnitine supplements are given.  

For long-term care, the child must eat often.  
They should avoid hard exercise.  
They need a diet high in carbohydrates.  
They also get supplements of triglycerides.  

---

## Very Long-Chain Acyl-CoA Dehydrogenase Deficiency (VLCADD)

This disorder is like LCHADD.  
But it often causes severe heart muscle problems.  

---

## Glutaric Acidemia Type II

Children with this disorder have low blood sugar when they have not eaten.  
This is called fasting hypoglycemia.  
They also have too much acid in the blood.  
This is called metabolic acidosis.  
They may have high levels of ammonia in the blood.  
This is called hyperammonemia.  

Doctors diagnose this by testing the blood for certain acids.  
Genetic testing is also available.  

Treatment is similar to MCADD.  
But some children may get riboflavin (vitamin B2) supplements.  

---

# Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (RPGN)

RPGN is a serious kidney condition that gets worse quickly. It causes sudden kidney damage. The damage happens in the tiny filters of the kidneys, called glomeruli. These filters become scarred and blocked. This leads to kidney failure in just weeks or months.

This condition is rare. It often starts after an infection or due to an autoimmune problem. Autoimmune means the body’s immune system attacks its own tissues.

---

## What Happens in RPGN?

- The kidneys stop working properly.
- Blood and protein leak into the urine.
- Swelling in the legs, face, or hands may occur.
- You may feel very tired, weak, or sick to your stomach.
- You might have a fever or joint pain.
- Some people cough up blood if the lungs are also affected.

Without treatment, most people will need dialysis or a kidney transplant.

---

## How Is RPGN Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find out if you have RPGN.

### Tests Include:
- **Blood tests** – to check kidney function and look for signs of infection or autoimmune disease.
- **Urine tests** – to check for blood and abnormal cells in the urine.
- **Kidney biopsy** – a small sample of kidney tissue is taken to see the damage.
- **Immunofluorescence test** – this helps identify the cause by showing where immune proteins are stored in the kidney.

### Key Signs of RPGN:
- Blood in the urine (hematuria).
- Abnormal red blood cells in the urine (dysmorphic RBCs).
- Red blood cell casts in the urine.
- High levels of creatinine in the blood (a sign of poor kidney function).

---

## Types of RPGN and Their Causes

There are different types of RPGN. Each type has a different cause. The type is found using special tests.

| Type | Cause | How Common |
|------|-------|------------|
| Anti-GBM antibody disease | The body attacks the kidney’s filter layer. If the lungs are also affected, it is called Goodpasture syndrome. | About 20% of cases |
| Immune complex RPGN | Caused by immune system problems after infections or autoimmune diseases like lupus. | About 50% of cases |
| Pauci-immune RPGN | The immune system attacks blood vessels in the kidneys. Linked to ANCA antibodies. | About 30% of cases |
| Double-antibody positive | Has features of both anti-GBM and pauci-immune types. | Very rare |

### Common Causes:
- After a strep infection (like strep throat).
- Lupus.
- Vasculitis (inflammation of blood vessels).
- Hepatitis B.
- Infections like endocarditis (heart infection).
- Certain cancers or abscesses.

---

## Symptoms of RPGN

You may notice:
- Feeling very tired or weak.
- Fever, nausea, or loss of appetite.
- Joint pain or belly pain.
- Swelling in your legs, feet, or face.
- Less urine than normal.
- Blood in your urine (urine may look pink, brown, or tea-colored).

Some people have sudden blood in the urine. Others have a slow start with vague symptoms.

If the lungs are involved, you may cough up blood or have trouble breathing.

---

## How Is RPGN Treated?

Treatment must start early. The sooner it starts, the better the chance of saving kidney function.

### Main Treatments:
- **Corticosteroids** – medicine to reduce swelling and immune system activity.
- **Cyclophosphamide** – medicine to stop the immune system from attacking the kidneys.
- **Rituximab** – another medicine that targets immune cells.
- **Plasma exchange** – a treatment that removes harmful antibodies from the blood.

### When Is Each Treatment Used?

- **Anti-GBM disease (including Goodpasture syndrome):**
  - Plasma exchange is used daily for 14 days.
  - Steroids and cyclophosphamide are given together.
  - This helps stop the body from making new harmful antibodies.

- **Pauci-immune RPGN (like granulomatosis with polyangiitis or microscopic polyangiitis):**
  - Steroids and cyclophosphamide or rituximab are used.
  - Plasma exchange may be used if kidney function is very poor or if lungs are bleeding.

- **Immune complex RPGN (like lupus or post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis):**
  - Steroids and cyclophosphamide or rituximab are used.
  - Plasma exchange is not always needed.

- **Idiopathic RPGN (no clear cause):**
  - Steroids and cyclophosphamide are usually given.
  - But there is not enough proof that this helps.

### Important Notes:
- Treatment works best when started before kidney damage is severe.
- If creatinine levels are high, treatment may still help if you do not need dialysis right away.
- Older people or those with infections may not tolerate strong treatments well.

---

## Can You Get a Kidney Transplant?

Yes, kidney transplants can work well for RPGN.

But you must wait until the disease is under control.

- For anti-GBM disease: Wait at least 12 months after anti-GBM antibodies are gone.
- For pauci-immune disease: Wait at least 6 months after the disease is quiet.
- ANCA levels do not need to be low before transplant.

The disease can come back in the new kidney. But the risk goes down over time.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Without treatment, most people will go on to kidney failure.

With early treatment, many people can keep their kidneys working.

### Good Signs (Better Outlook):
- Younger age.
- Low creatinine level at diagnosis.
- No severe swelling or low urine output.
- Early treatment before kidney damage is too bad.
- RPGN caused by post-infection or lupus.

### Poor Signs (Worse Outlook):
- Age over 60.
- Very high creatinine level.
- Little or no urine output.
- More than 75% of kidney filters are scarred.
- Pauci-immune type.

### Survival Rates:
- About half of people with pauci-immune RPGN get better with treatment.
- Less than 10% need dialysis.
- About 15% die within 5 years.
- Among those who do not respond to treatment:
  - Over 50% need dialysis.
  - About 40% die within 5 years.

---

## Key Points to Remember

- If you have sudden kidney problems with blood in your urine, see a doctor right away.
- Look for symptoms like fatigue, fever, nausea, or swelling.
- Blood and urine tests, plus a kidney biopsy, are needed to confirm RPGN.
- Start treatment early with steroids, cyclophosphamide, or rituximab.
- Plasma exchange may help in some cases.
- Kidney transplant is possible after the disease is under control.
- Early treatment saves kidneys and improves survival.

# Fourth Cranial Nerve Palsy

This condition affects how your eyes move up and down.  
It happens when the fourth cranial nerve does not work properly.  
The nerve controls one of the muscles that move the eye.

## What Causes This Problem?

Doctors often do not know the cause.  
When they do find a cause, it is usually a head injury.  
These injuries can happen in motorcycle crashes.  
They can also happen with smaller head injuries.  

Diabetes can cause this problem.  
It does so by damaging small blood vessels that feed the nerve.  
Rarely, a tumor, a bulge in a blood vessel (aneurysm), or multiple sclerosis is the cause.  
Sometimes the problem is present from birth.

## What Are the Symptoms?

One or both eyes may be affected.  
The affected eye cannot move inward and down.  
This causes double vision.  
One image appears above and slightly to the side of the other.  
Going down stairs becomes hard because you need to look down and inward.  

Tilting your head to the side opposite the affected eye can help.  
This position uses other eye muscles that are not affected.  
It helps both eyes focus on the same spot.  
This can make the double vision go away.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will look at how your eyes move.  
They will check for limited movement, especially when looking down and inward.  
If needed, your doctor may order a CT scan or an MRI of your brain.  
These tests help find the cause of the problem.

## How Is It Treated?

If a cause is found, it is treated.  
For example, if diabetes is the cause, blood sugar levels are managed.  
If a tumor or aneurysm is found, treatment depends on the situation.

Eye exercises may help improve eye movement.  
Prism glasses can also help.  
These glasses have special lenses.  
The lenses are thinner at the top and thicker at the bottom.  
They bend light so the images from both eyes line up.  
This reduces or removes double vision.

Most people get better over time.  
The nerve heals on its own.  
In some cases, surgery may be needed later.

# Thoracotomy

Thoracotomy is surgery to open the chest.  
It is done when other tests cannot give a clear answer or when they are not enough to treat a lung problem.

## Why Thoracotomy Is Done

The main reasons for this surgery are:

- Removing a lobe of the lung (lobectomy)  
- Removing an entire lung (pneumonectomy)  

Doctors most often do these surgeries to treat lung cancer.  
For lung and chest lining biopsies, doctors now usually use a less invasive method called video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery.  
This method is safer and causes less pain than open surgery.

## When Thoracotomy Is Not Safe

Thoracotomy is not recommended if you have:

- A recent heart attack or serious heart problem  
- A bleeding problem that cannot be fixed  
- Poor function in major organs like the heart, lungs, or kidneys  

These conditions make surgery too risky.

## How the Surgery Is Done

There are three main ways to open the chest:

- **Front or side cut**: A small cut, 6 to 8 centimeters long, is made between the ribs. This is used to reach the front part of the chest.  
- **Back and side cut**: This cut gives the surgeon access to the lining of the chest, the area where the lung connects to the chest, the center of the chest, and the whole lung.  
- **Middle chest cut**: The breastbone is split open. This is used when both lungs need to be reached, such as in lung volume reduction surgery.

## Risks of Thoracotomy

This surgery has more risks than other lung procedures.  
This is because it requires general anesthesia, causes major surgery trauma, and leads to a longer hospital stay and more pain after surgery.  

The most serious risks include:

- A hole between the airway and the chest cavity (bronchopleural fistula)  
- Heavy bleeding (hemorrhage)  
- Infection in the chest  
- Air leaking into the space around the lung (pneumothorax)  
- Bad reactions to the anesthesia used during surgery

# Undescended Testes and Retractile Testes

## What Are Undescended and Retractile Testes?

- **Undescended testes** means one or both testicles did not move down into the scrotum before birth. They stay in the belly or the groin area.
- **Retractile testes** means the testicles are in the scrotum but can pull back up into the groin easily. This happens as a reflex when the child is cold, scared, or touched.

## How Do Testes Normally Move?

- In a baby boy, the testicles form inside the belly.
- They usually move down through a small tube called the inguinal canal.
- This tube leads from the belly to the scrotum.
- The movement usually happens before birth, often in the last three months of pregnancy.

## What Happens After the Testes Move Down?

- After the testicles reach the scrotum, the tube usually closes.
- If the tube does not close completely, a small bulge called an **inguinal hernia** can form. This is when part of the intestine pushes through the open tube.
- An inguinal hernia may not cause pain. But doctors can often feel it during a check-up.

- Sometimes, fluid from the belly gets trapped around the testicles after the tube closes.
- This fluid forms a soft lump called a **hydrocele**.
- A hydrocele usually goes away on its own within the first year of life.

## Undescended Testes

- About 3 out of every 100 full-term baby boys are born with an undescended testicle.
- For babies born early (premature), the number is higher — about 30 out of every 100.
- If a close family member had undescended testes, the baby is more likely to have it too.
- Usually, only one testicle is affected. But in about 1 out of 10 cases, both testicles are undescended.

- Most undescended testicles are in the groin area. Some stay inside the belly.
- In full-term babies, about two-thirds of undescended testicles move down on their own by 4 months of age.
- For premature babies, this happens by 4 months after their due date.
- Testicles still in the belly at birth are much less likely to move down on their own.

- Undescended testicles usually do not cause pain or other symptoms.
- But they can cause problems later in life:
  - They may affect sperm production.
  - They increase the risk of testicular cancer.
  - Testicles in the belly can twist, causing sudden, severe pain.

- Most newborns with undescended testicles also have an inguinal hernia.

### How Are Undescended Testes Found?

- Doctors check the scrotum during the baby’s first exam and at every yearly well-child visit.
- If they cannot feel one or both testicles, they check to see if the testicles are just retracting into the groin.
- If the testicles are not found in a newborn, the doctor may do blood tests or other checks to rule out a condition that affects normal development of the genitals.
- Most cases are found in infancy. Some are found later, often after a growth spurt.
- If the testicles are not in the scrotum, the child should see a urologist — a doctor who treats the urinary system and male reproductive organs.
- In rare cases, doctors use ultrasound or MRI to locate the testicles.

### Treatment for Undescended Testes

- If the testicle has not moved down by 6 months of age in a full-term baby, or by 1 year of age in a premature baby, surgery is needed.
- The surgery moves the testicle into the scrotum.
- The doctor may use a small cut (open surgery) or a camera (laparoscopy) to do the surgery.
- If the baby has an inguinal hernia, the doctor fixes that at the same time.

### Long-Term Care

- Boys who had undescended testicles are at higher risk for testicular cancer later in life.
- After puberty, all males should check their testicles every month for lumps or changes.

## Retractile Testes

- Retractile testes are testicles that are in the scrotum but can move back into the groin.
- This movement happens as a reflex. It can be triggered by cold, fear, touch, or laughter.
- This is normal, especially in young boys and babies.
- Retractile testes do not cause cancer or other health problems.

### How Are They Checked?

- Doctors check the testicles during regular well-child visits.
- They make sure the testicles stay in the scrotum as the child grows.
- Most boys stop having this reflex by puberty. The testicles grow larger and stay in place.

### Treatment

- Retractile testes do not need surgery or any other treatment.
- No special care is needed.

# Binge-Eating Disorder

Binge-eating disorder is when a person eats a very large amount of food in a short time.  
They feel they have no control over their eating.  
This is not followed by actions like making themselves throw up or using laxatives.  

The condition is diagnosed based on clear signs and symptoms.  
Treatment often includes talk therapy or medicine.  

## Who Gets Binge-Eating Disorder?

About 1 to 2 out of every 100 women will have this disorder in their lifetime.  
Less than 1 out of every 100 men will have it.  
More than 3 out of every 100 teenage girls may have it.  
About 1 out of every 100 teenage boys may have it.  

This disorder is more common in people who are overweight or obese.  
It is not as common in people with anorexia or bulimia.  
People with binge-eating disorder are usually older when they are first diagnosed.  

Scientists are still studying whether genes or gut bacteria play a role.  
But no clear proof has been found yet.  

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

During a binge, a person eats much more than most people would in the same time and situation.  
They feel they cannot stop eating.  
After the binge, they may feel ashamed, sad, or guilty.  

Binge eating happens in episodes.  
It is not the same as eating a little bit all day long.  
There is no purging after the binge.  
This means no vomiting, no laxatives, no extra exercise, and no fasting.  

People with this disorder are often upset about their eating habits.  
They may feel depressed.  
They may worry a lot about their body shape or weight.  
These feelings are more common in people with obesity who binge eat than in others with similar weight who do not binge.  

This disorder is strongly linked to being overweight or obese.  
It can lead to serious health problems like high blood pressure and diabetes.  

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A mental health professional will ask questions and do an exam.  
The diagnosis is based on the *Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders*, 5th edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR).  

To be diagnosed, a person must meet all of these criteria:  

- They have binge eating episodes at least once a week for 3 months.  
- They feel they have no control over their eating.  
- They also have at least three of the following:  
  - They eat much faster than normal.  
  - They eat until they feel uncomfortably full.  
  - They eat large amounts even when not hungry.  
  - They eat alone because they feel embarrassed.  
  - They feel disgusted, sad, or guilty after eating.  

Binge-eating disorder is different from bulimia.  
People with bulimia also binge eat, but they then try to get rid of the food by vomiting, using laxatives, or exercising too much.  
People with binge-eating disorder do not do these things.  

## How Is It Treated?

The best treatment is cognitive behavioral therapy.  
This is a type of talk therapy that helps people change their thoughts and behaviors around food.  
Interpersonal psychotherapy is another option.  
It helps people improve their relationships and communication.  

Both types of therapy work well.  
About half of people improve with either treatment.  
The improvement usually lasts over time.  
These therapies do not cause major weight loss.  

Weight-loss programs that focus on behavior can help reduce binge eating at first.  
But many people start binge eating again later.  

Antidepressant medicines, such as SSRIs, can help reduce binge eating in the short term.  
But we do not know if they help in the long run.  

Lisdexamfetamine is a medicine used for moderate to severe binge-eating disorder.  
It can reduce the number of binge days.  
It may also lead to a small amount of weight loss.  
But we do not know how well it works over the long term.  

Other medicines that reduce appetite or help with weight loss may also help.  
But their long-term benefits are not clear.  

Bariatric surgery (weight-loss surgery) can help some people with binge-eating disorder.  
It may work by changing hormones and gut bacteria.  
In the short term, many people feel better.  
But after 10 years, about one-third of people who had surgery still have binge-eating episodes.  

## Key Points

- People with binge-eating disorder eat large amounts of food in a short time.  
- They do not try to get rid of the food by vomiting, using laxatives, or fasting.  
- They often have overweight or obesity.  
- Diagnosis is based on clear signs and symptoms.  
- Treatment includes talk therapy like cognitive behavioral therapy or interpersonal psychotherapy.  
- Medicine such as SSRIs or lisdexamfetamine may also be used.

# Green Tea

Green tea comes from the leaves of the same plant used to make regular tea.  
But the leaves are treated differently.  
Regular tea leaves are fermented.  
Green tea leaves are steamed instead and not fermented.  

You can drink green tea as a hot drink.  
You can also take it in pill or capsule form.  

Green tea has caffeine.  
But many green tea products have had the caffeine removed.  

Green tea is full of plant compounds called flavonoids, polyphenols, and catechins.  
These are antioxidants.  
Antioxidants help protect your body’s cells from damage.  

---

## Why People Use Green Tea

Some people take green tea to:  
- Help prevent cancer  
- Help prevent heart disease  
- Treat warts on the genitals  
- Lower fat levels in the blood  
- Ease joint pain from osteoarthritis  
- Reduce symptoms of menopause  
- Help with weight loss  
- Improve memory  
- Live longer  

---

## What Science Says About Green Tea

Most of the health claims for green tea are not strongly supported by science.  
But one use has some support:  
- Applying green tea directly to genital warts may help clear them.  

Some studies show that people who take green tea lose a small amount of weight.  

---

## Possible Side Effects

Side effects come from the caffeine in green tea.  
They include:  
- Trouble sleeping  
- Feeling anxious  
- Fast heartbeat  
- Shaking hands or body  

Pregnant women should not drink large amounts.  
Too much caffeine may raise the risk of miscarriage.  

Rare cases of liver damage have been reported.  
Drinking brewed green tea on an empty stomach may raise the risk of liver problems.  
But this has not been studied well.  

---

## Green Tea and Medicines

Green tea can affect how some medicines work.  

- Green tea may reduce how well warfarin works.  
  Warfarin is a medicine that prevents blood clots.  
  If green tea weakens it, you may be more likely to form clots.  

- Green tea may lower levels of:  
  - Nadolol (a medicine for high blood pressure)  
  - Atorvastatin and rosuvastatin (medicines that lower cholesterol)  

- If you stop taking green tea suddenly, lithium levels in your blood may rise.  
  Lithium is a medicine for mood disorders.  
  Higher levels can cause side effects.  

- Green tea may also reduce how much iron and folic acid your body absorbs.  
  Iron helps make healthy blood.  
  Folic acid is important for cell growth.  

---

## Advice on Using Green Tea

Green tea is generally safe for most people.  
But any health benefits are likely small.  

Avoid drinking large amounts, especially if you are pregnant.  
Do not drink green tea on an empty stomach.  

---

# Cardiac Catheterization – Simple Explanation

This is a medical test that uses a thin tube called a catheter. The tube goes through a blood vessel in your arm, leg, or neck. It moves into your heart or the blood vessels around your heart.

## What This Test Can Do

This test helps doctors see how your heart is working. It can:

- Take pictures of your heart and blood vessels.
- Find leaks in the heart or blood vessels.
- Take a small sample of heart muscle for testing.
- Use sound waves inside blood vessels to get detailed images.
- Measure how well your heart pumps blood.
- Check how your heart uses energy.

These results help doctors make a correct diagnosis. They also help decide the best treatment for you.

This test is also used to do certain treatments. For example, it can open blocked heart arteries.

## What to Expect Before the Test

Most people need to stop eating and drinking for 4 to 6 hours before the test.  
You usually do not need to stay in the hospital overnight unless you also have a treatment during the test.

## What Happens During the Test

The doctor puts the catheter into a blood vessel. They guide it to your heart using X-ray images.  
You will be awake but may get medicine to help you relax.  
The test takes about 30 to 60 minutes.

## When This Test Is Not Safe

Some health problems make this test riskier. These are called relative risks. They include:

- Poor kidney function (acute or long-term)
- Blood clotting problems
- Fever
- Allergy to the dye used in the test (if not treated ahead of time)
- Serious infection in the body
- Unstable heart rhythm
- Very high blood pressure
- Heart failure that is not under control

Doctors weigh the risks and benefits. If you are having a heart attack, the test may still be done even with these risks.  
Your doctor will decide if you need to stop or change your blood thinners before the test. This depends on your health, the type of test, and your risk of bleeding.

## Possible Problems After the Test

Most problems are minor and easy to fix.  
Serious problems are rare.  
The chance of dying during or right after the test is 0.1% to 0.2%.

Serious problems can include:

- Heart attack (0.1% chance)
- Stroke (0.1% chance)
- Severe allergic reaction
- Heart stopping
- Low blood pressure
- Seizures
- Kidney damage

The chance of stroke is higher in people over 80 years old.

Most problems come from:

- The dye used in the test
- The catheter touching or moving inside blood vessels
- The place where the catheter entered your body (the access site)

## Risk Factors for Problems

You are more likely to have problems if you have:

- Long-term kidney disease
- Chronic lung disease (like COPD)
- Diabetes
- Heart failure
- Are older
- Poor blood flow in your legs or arms
- Heart valve problems

The following resources may help you learn more. The Manual is not responsible for their content.

  A guide from the American College of Radiology on safe use of the dye used in tests.

  A report from major heart health groups. It sets standards for how cardiac catheterization labs should work.

# What Are Paraphilias and Paraphilic Disorders?

## What Is a Paraphilia?

A paraphilia is a strong and repeated sexual attraction to things that are not typical. This can include:

- Inanimate objects (like clothes or shoes)
- Children
- People who do not agree to sex (nonconsenting adults)
- Pain or humiliation of oneself or a partner

These thoughts or behaviors cause strong sexual arousal. They often start in late childhood or just before puberty. Once they begin, they usually last a lifetime.

## What Is a Paraphilic Disorder?

A paraphilic disorder happens when a paraphilia causes problems. This can mean:

- The person feels upset, ashamed, or guilty
- The person has trouble doing normal daily tasks
- The person harms someone else or might harm someone

If the behavior causes no harm and both people agree to it, it may be part of a healthy relationship. But if it causes distress or harm, it is a disorder.

## Common Types of Paraphilic Disorders

The most common types are:

- **Voyeuristic disorder**: Getting sexual pleasure from watching others without their knowledge.
- **Exhibitionistic disorder**: Getting sexual pleasure from showing one’s body to others without their consent.
- **Frotteuristic disorder**: Getting sexual pleasure from touching or rubbing against someone without their permission.
- **Sexual masochism disorder**: Getting sexual pleasure from being hurt or humiliated.
- **Sexual sadism disorder**: Getting sexual pleasure from hurting or humiliating another person.
- **Pedophilic disorder**: Having strong sexual urges toward children.
- **Fetishistic disorder**: Getting sexual pleasure from non-living things, like shoes or fabrics.
- **Transvestic disorder**: Getting sexual pleasure from wearing clothes of the opposite gender.

## Who Is Affected?

Most people with paraphilias are men. Many have more than one type of paraphilia. Some also have serious mental health issues, such as:

- Antisocial personality disorder (a pattern of ignoring rules and hurting others)
- Narcissistic personality disorder (a strong need to be admired and a lack of empathy)

## Important Facts

- Some paraphilias, like pedophilia, are against the law.
- People with these disorders may struggle to have loving, equal sexual relationships.
- Partners may feel used, unimportant, or like a tool in the relationship.
- The person with the disorder may feel trapped by their urges and may feel deep shame.

# Iodine Toxicity

Iodine is a mineral your body needs to make two important thyroid hormones: T4 and T3.

Iodine in food and the environment mostly comes in the form of iodide.

Most adults absorb about 80 percent of the iodide they take in. The thyroid gland takes up most of this iodide.

Most iodine in nature comes from seawater. A small amount gets into the air. Rain carries it to the ground near the sea.

Adding iodide to table salt helps people get enough iodine. A typical amount is 70 micrograms per gram of salt. Most adults need about 150 micrograms of iodine each day.

Pregnant women need more: 220 micrograms per day. Breastfeeding women need even more: 290 micrograms per day.

Toxicity can happen if you take in more than 1.1 milligrams of iodine per day over a long time.

Most people who take in too much iodine do not have thyroid problems. But some people, especially those who were low in iodine before, may develop overactive thyroid glands. This is called the Jod-Basedow phenomenon.

Oddly, too much iodine can also stop the thyroid from making hormones. This is called the Wolff-Chaikoff effect.

Because of this, too much iodine can lead to a goiter (swelling in the neck), underactive thyroid, or a serious condition called myxedema.

Very high doses of iodide can cause a metallic taste in the mouth. They can also cause more saliva, stomach upset, and skin problems like acne.

People who often get iodine from medical dyes used in X-rays or from the medicine amiodarone should have their thyroid checked regularly.

## How Is Iodine Toxicity Diagnosed?

Doctors usually check thyroid function with blood tests. They may also use imaging tests. These results are combined with your symptoms and medical history.

Measuring how much iodine your body gets rid of in urine is more accurate. But this test is not done often.

## How Is Iodine Toxicity Treated?

Treatment focuses on fixing any thyroid problems. If you are getting too much iodine, you should change your diet.

If you have an underactive thyroid caused by too much iodine, it often gets better within a few weeks after stopping excess iodine.

But some people do not get better. They may need to take thyroid hormone medicine for the rest of their lives.

# Transient Hypogammaglobulinemia of Infancy – Simple Explanation

This condition affects how babies make antibodies. Antibodies help the body fight infections.

## What Are Antibodies?

Antibodies are proteins made by the immune system.  
They protect the body from germs, cancer, and other harmful substances.  
If a baby does not have enough antibodies, they are more likely to get serious infections.

## How Babies Get Antibodies

At birth, a baby’s immune system is not fully ready.  
Most of the antibodies a baby has come from the mother.  
The mother passes these antibodies through the placenta before birth.  
These antibodies protect the baby from infections during the first few months.

Babies also get antibodies from breast milk if they are breastfed.  
These help protect the baby’s gut and lungs.

## When Antibody Levels Drop

By about 6 months of age, most babies start making their own antibodies.  
At the same time, the mother’s antibodies start to fade away.  
This is a normal process.

In some babies, making their own antibodies is delayed.  
This is called transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy.  
It means the baby’s antibody levels stay low between 3 and 6 months of age.  
The levels usually return to normal by 12 to 36 months.

## What Happens in This Condition?

Most babies with this condition do not get serious infections.  
It is not considered a true immune problem.  
But a few babies may get frequent infections.  
These can include:

- Infections in the sinuses  
- Lung infections  
- Digestive tract infections  
- Fungal infections (like candidiasis)  
- Meningitis (infection of the brain and spinal cord lining)

## Who Is More Likely to Have This?

This condition is more common in babies born early (premature babies).  
Premature babies get fewer antibodies from their mothers.  
This makes it harder for them to fight infections early in life.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors check blood levels of antibodies.  
They also test how well the baby’s immune system responds to vaccines.  
Most babies with this condition make normal antibodies after vaccines.  
They also make antibodies when exposed to germs.

## How Is It Treated?

Most babies do not need treatment.  
The condition often goes away on its own over time.  
But if a baby, especially a premature one, gets many infections, doctors may give antibiotics.  
This helps prevent more infections.

## How Long Does It Last?

The condition can last from a few months to a few years.  
It usually gets better without any special treatment.
