# Paragonimiasis

Paragonimiasis is a disease caused by a type of parasitic worm called a lung fluke.  
The most common type is *Paragonimus westermani*.  
Other similar worms can also cause the disease.

You get infected by eating raw, pickled, smoked, or undercooked freshwater crabs or crayfish.  
These animals can carry tiny worm larvae that are not killed by cooking or pickling.

Most people with the infection do not have any symptoms.  
But some people develop lung problems.  
These can include a long-lasting cough, chest pain, trouble breathing, or coughing up blood.

The worms can also travel to other parts of the body.  
If they reach the brain, they can cause seizures, trouble speaking, weakness in the arms or legs, or vision problems.  
If they reach the skin, they can cause itchy or painful lumps under the skin.

## How the Infection Works

The worm’s life cycle starts when eggs are passed in sputum (mucus from the lungs) or in stool.  
The eggs hatch in freshwater after 2 to 3 weeks.  
The tiny larvae (called miracidia) then enter a snail.  
Inside the snail, they grow and multiply.  
They leave the snail as free-swimming larvae (called cercariae).  
These cercariae then enter freshwater crabs or crayfish and form cysts (called metacercariae).  
When a person eats the infected crab or crayfish, the cysts come out in the gut.  
The worms then move through the body.  
They pass through the belly wall, go through the diaphragm, and reach the lungs.  
There, they grow into adult worms and form a capsule.  
The adult worms lay eggs, which leave the body in sputum or stool.

The worms can also reach other organs like the brain, liver, skin, or spinal cord.  
But in these places, the worms cannot complete their life cycle.  
The eggs cannot leave the body.  
Adult worms can live in the body for 20 to 25 years.

Other animals like pigs, dogs, and cats can also carry the worms.

## What Symptoms You Might Have

Many people have no symptoms at all.  
In the early stage, some people may have:  
- Diarrhea  
- Belly pain  
- Fever  
- Cough  
- Itchy skin rashes  
- Swollen liver or spleen  
- Lung problems  
- High levels of a certain type of white blood cell (eosinophilia)

In the long-term stage, the lungs are most affected.  
Symptoms include:  
- A cough that lasts a long time  
- Chest pain  
- Coughing up mucus or blood  
- Trouble breathing  

These symptoms can look like tuberculosis or another lung condition called Löffler syndrome.

Fluid may build up in the space around the lungs (pleural effusion).

If the worms reach the brain, they can cause brain lesions.  
This often happens within a year after lung symptoms start.  
Symptoms include:  
- Seizures  
- Trouble speaking  
- Weakness in arms or legs  
- Vision problems

Some people get skin lumps that move under the skin.  
These are painless or tender and contain immature worms.  
This is more common with one type of worm (*P. skrjabini*) but can happen with others.

## How Doctors Diagnose the Disease

Doctors look for the worm eggs in:  
- Sputum (mucus from the lungs)  
- Stool (bowel movement)  
- Fluid from the lungs or belly  

Eggs may also be found in fluid from the lungs or belly during special tests.

The eggs are hard to find because they are released only sometimes and in small numbers.  
Special lab methods can help find them.

Blood tests can also help.  
These tests look for antibodies (the body’s response to the worm).  
They are useful when the infection is mild or when worms are in the brain or other organs.

Imaging tests like chest X-rays or CT scans can show lung problems.  
They may show:  
- White patches in the lungs  
- Small lumps  
- Ring-shaped shadows  
- Cavities  
- Thickened lung lines  
- Lung abscesses  
- Fluid around the lungs  
- Air in the chest cavity  

But these images are not enough to confirm the disease on their own.

## How the Disease Is Treated

The best medicine is praziquantel.  
You take it by mouth, three times a day for two days.  
This is the first choice for all types of paragonimiasis.

Praziquantel also works for worms in the brain or other organs.  
But you may need more than one course of treatment.

If the worms are in the brain, doctors may give a short course of steroid medicine.  
This helps reduce swelling and inflammation caused by dying worms.

Triclabendazole is another option in areas where it is available.  
You take it once by mouth after a meal.  
For severe cases, you take it twice, 12 hours apart.

Surgery may be needed in rare cases.  
This includes removing skin lumps or brain cysts.

## How to Prevent the Disease

The best way to avoid infection is to never eat raw, pickled, smoked, or undercooked freshwater crabs or crayfish.  
This is especially important in areas where the disease is common.

## Where the Disease Is Found

The disease is most common in parts of Asia.  
This includes Korea, Japan, Taiwan, highland areas of China, and the Philippines.

Other areas with the disease include:  
- West and Central Africa (caused by *P. africanus*)  
- Parts of South and Central America (caused by *P. mexicanus*)  
- North America (caused by *P. kellicotti*)

These worms can also infect animals like pigs, dogs, and cats.

# Platelet Dysfunction

Platelets are small parts of blood that help stop bleeding by forming clots.  
They are made in the bone marrow and travel in the blood.  
A normal blood count has about 140,000 to 440,000 platelets in each microliter of blood.  
When the count drops below 50,000 platelets per microliter, bleeding can happen after even small injuries.  
The risk of serious bleeding usually only becomes high when the count falls below 10,000 to 20,000 platelets per microliter.  
At these very low levels, bleeding can happen without any injury.

When platelets do not work right, people may bleed too much.  
This can happen after injuries or even without any injury.  
Platelet problems can be caused by:

- A problem in the platelets themselves  
- Something outside the body that affects how platelets work

## Types of Platelet Problems

### Inherited Platelet Problems

Some people are born with platelet problems.  
The most common inherited platelet issue is von Willebrand disease.  
Other rare inherited conditions include Glanzmann disease, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, and Bernard-Soulier syndrome.  
Some of these conditions also cause skin problems, weak immune systems, or kidney problems.

### Acquired Platelet Problems

These problems are not inherited.  
They develop later in life.  
They are usually caused by:

- Certain medicines  
- Certain diseases

The most common medicines that affect platelets are:
- Aspirin  
- Other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)  
- Antiplatelet drugs like clopidogrel, used to prevent strokes and heart attacks

Diseases that can cause platelet problems include:
- Liver scarring (cirrhosis)  
- Multiple myeloma  
- Kidney disease  
- Lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus)

Some people also develop platelet problems after open-heart surgery that uses a heart-lung machine.

## Signs and Symptoms

Symptoms depend on how bad the problem is and what caused it.

People with inherited platelet problems often:
- Bruise easily  
- Bleed too much after small injuries  
- Bleed too much after minor surgery, like tooth removal  
- Boys may bleed a lot after circumcision  
- Women may first notice very heavy periods

Other signs include:
- Tiny red, purple, or brown spots on the skin (called petechiae)  
- Bruises after minor bumps or injuries

**Petechiae** are small spots on the skin or inside the mouth.  
They look like tiny dots.  
They can be red, purple, or brown.

**Ecchymoses** are large purple bruises.  
They often appear on the legs or arms.

## How Doctors Diagnose Platelet Problems

Doctors use blood tests to check for platelet problems.  
They look at:
- The number of platelets  
- How well the blood clots  
- How well the platelets work

If symptoms start after a person begins a new medicine, the doctor may think the medicine is the cause.  
If symptoms start early in life and the person is not on any medicines, the doctor may suspect an inherited problem.

The first test is a complete blood count (CBC).  
This test checks how many platelets are in the blood.  
If the count is low, the problem may be low platelets (called thrombocytopenia).  
If the count is normal but bleeding still happens, the doctor may suspect the platelets are not working right.

Other tests may include:
- Prothrombin time (PT)  
- Partial thromboplastin time (PTT)  

These tests measure how long it takes blood to clot.

Special tests called platelet function tests are also used.  
A blood sample is taken and tested to see how well platelets respond to triggers.  
Abnormal results can help find the cause of the problem.

## Treatment

Treatment depends on the cause.

If a medicine is causing the problem, stopping the medicine often fixes it.  
People with inherited platelet problems should avoid medicines that make bleeding worse.

For serious bleeding, treatment may include:
- Platelet transfusions  
- A medicine called desmopressin, which helps reduce bleeding

For bleeding during minor procedures or heavy periods, a medicine called tranexamic acid can help.  
This medicine makes blood clots stronger and helps stop bleeding.

# Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN)

Polyarteritis nodosa is a rare disease that causes inflammation in the walls of medium-sized arteries. This inflammation can block blood flow to organs and tissues. The kidneys, skin, joints, muscles, nerves, and gut are most often affected. The lungs are usually not involved.

The disease can affect any organ, but it most commonly harms the kidneys, skin, nerves, joints, muscles, and digestive system. It does not cause kidney inflammation in the tiny filters (glomeruli). The disease is rare. It affects about one person per million. It mostly affects adults in their 50s, and the risk goes up with age.

---

## What Causes Polyarteritis Nodosa?

Most cases have no known cause. About 20% of people with PAN have hepatitis B or C. The exact cause is not clear, but the body’s immune system seems to play a role. Some medicines may trigger the disease. In some people, the disease is linked to certain cancers like lymphoma or leukemia. It can also happen in people with rheumatoid arthritis or Sjögren syndrome.

A rare form of PAN is caused by a gene change in the *ADA2* gene. This form runs in families and is passed down through both parents. Another rare condition called VEXAS, caused by a gene change in the *UBA1* gene, can also lead to symptoms like PAN.

---

## How Does Polyarteritis Nodosa Work?

The disease causes swelling and damage in the walls of medium-sized arteries. This damage often happens where arteries split into two branches. The swelling can block blood flow. This leads to tissue damage or death (infarction). The artery walls can weaken and form small bulges (aneurysms). Over time, the damaged areas can scar and become thick.

The disease does not affect the small veins after capillaries. Early signs include white blood cells called neutrophils. Later, lymphocytes and plasma cells appear. The disease does not cause granulomas (clumps of immune cells). The inner layer of the artery can grow too thick, which can block blood flow. This can lead to blood clots and further damage.

The most commonly affected areas are the kidneys, skin, nerves, joints, muscles, and gut. The liver and heart are less often affected. Kidney damage happens, but it is not due to inflammation in the tiny kidney filters. Skin rashes from small vessel problems or lung inflammation are not typical of PAN.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

PAN can look like many other diseases. It can come on suddenly and last a long time. It can also start slowly and get worse over time. Symptoms depend on which organs are affected and how bad the damage is.

Common early symptoms include:
- Fever
- Feeling very tired
- Night sweats
- Loss of appetite
- Weight loss
- General weakness

Many people also have muscle pain and joint pain. Affected muscles may be tender and weak. Arthritis can occur.

### Symptoms by Organ System

**Nerves (Peripheral nervous system):**  
People often get nerve problems that are not the same on both sides. This is called multiple mononeuropathy. It can affect nerves in the legs, arms, or hands. Symptoms include weakness, numbness, or tingling. As more nerves are affected, it may feel like a symmetrical nerve problem.

**Brain and spinal cord (Central nervous system):**  
Headaches and seizures can happen. In rare cases, a stroke or brain bleed can occur. These may be linked to high blood pressure.

**Kidneys:**  
If the arteries in the kidneys are damaged, people may get high blood pressure. They may pass less urine, feel sick to their stomach, or have signs of kidney failure. Urine may show blood and protein, but not red blood cell casts. High blood pressure can get worse quickly. A burst aneurysm in a kidney artery can cause bleeding around the kidney. Severe cases can lead to kidney damage and kidney failure.

**Digestive system (Gut):**  
Inflammation in the liver or gallbladder causes pain in the upper right side of the belly. The gallbladder can burst, causing a medical emergency. Inflammation in the arteries of the intestines causes belly pain, nausea, vomiting, and sometimes bloody diarrhea. It can lead to poor digestion, bowel wall holes, or a sudden belly emergency. Aneurysms can form in the liver or main gut arteries.

**Heart:**  
Some people have blocked heart arteries. This may not cause symptoms, but it can cause chest pain. Heart failure can happen if the heart muscle is damaged by low blood flow or high blood pressure.

**Skin:**  
People may have a mottled skin pattern called livedo reticularis. They may also get skin sores, red lumps under the skin, blisters, or dead skin on fingers or toes. The lumps look like those in erythema nodosum, but they can break open and heal with scarring. A biopsy shows blood vessel damage in the deeper skin layers.

**Genitals:**  
Men may get swollen and painful testicles.

---

## How Is Polyarteritis Nodosa Diagnosed?

Diagnosis can be hard because symptoms are not always clear. Think about PAN if someone has:
- Unexplained fever
- Joint or muscle pain
- Skin lumps or sores
- Belly or limb pain
- New weakness in the foot or hand (footdrop or wristdrop)
- Rapidly rising blood pressure

The diagnosis is confirmed by:
- A biopsy showing damaged arteries
- An imaging test (arteriography) showing aneurysms in medium-sized arteries

MRI angiography can show small aneurysms, but it may miss very small ones. So, it is not the main test for diagnosis.

Biopsies should be taken from areas that are clearly affected. Good choices include skin, nerve, or muscle tissue. Biopsies of the kidney or liver are not usually helpful. They can give false negative results. They also carry a risk of bleeding if there are hidden aneurysms. Unlike in some other vasculitis diseases, the kidney tissue does not usually show heavy inflammation.

If no clear area is affected, nerve tests (EMG and nerve conduction studies) can help find the best place to biopsy.

If there are skin sores, a full skin biopsy is needed. It must include the deeper skin layers. A small punch biopsy that only takes the top skin layer will miss the disease.

Testicular biopsies are not recommended unless there are symptoms and no other good biopsy sites. The chance of finding the disease is low.

### Lab Tests

Lab results are not specific. Common findings include:
- High white blood cell count (up to 40,000 per microliter)
- Protein in the urine
- Blood in the urine (microscopic)
- High platelet count
- High levels of inflammation markers (ESR or CRP)
- Low blood protein (hypoalbuminemia)
- Low red blood cell count (anemia), often from blood loss or kidney failure
- High levels of certain antibodies in the blood

Liver enzymes are often slightly high. Testing for hepatitis B and C is important.

Other tests (like ANCA, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, ANA, complement levels, cryoglobulins) help rule out other diseases like lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, or Sjögren syndrome.

---

## How Is Polyarteritis Nodosa Treated?

Treatment depends on how severe the disease is.

For mild to moderate disease without serious nerve, kidney, gut, or heart problems:
- Use corticosteroids with methotrexate or azathioprine.

For severe disease with nerve, kidney, gut, or heart problems:
- Use corticosteroids with cyclophosphamide.

High blood pressure must be treated strongly and quickly.

If hepatitis B is present, it must be treated.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

With treatment, about 80% of people live at least 5 years. The outlook is worse for people with hepatitis B. The best chance for recovery is if the disease goes into remission within 18 months of diagnosis. Relapses are less common than in other vasculitis diseases.

Poor outcomes are more likely if:
- Kidney function is poor
- The gut is involved
- Nerves are affected

---

## Key Points

- Polyarteritis nodosa is a rare disease that inflames medium-sized arteries.
- It most often affects the kidneys (not the tiny filters), skin, joints, muscles, nerves, and gut.
- Think of PAN if someone has unexplained fever, joint pain, skin lumps, sores, belly or limb pain, new footdrop or wristdrop, or fast-rising blood pressure.
- Confirm the diagnosis with a biopsy or arteriography.
- Test for hepatitis B and C.
- Poor outcomes are more likely with kidney, gut, or nerve problems.
- Treat with corticosteroids and one of the following: cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, or azathioprine — based on how severe the disease is.

# Ventricular Premature Beats

A ventricular premature beat is an extra heartbeat. It starts in the lower chambers of the heart (the ventricles) before the next normal beat should happen.

## What Causes These Extra Beats?

- The heart’s normal beat starts in a small area called the sinus node, in the top right part of the heart.
- Sometimes, a beat starts in one of the lower chambers instead.
- These extra beats are common, especially in older adults.
- They can be triggered by:
  - Stress
  - Caffeine (in coffee, tea, soda, or chocolate)
  - Alcohol
  - Cold or allergy medicines that speed up the heart (like pseudoephedrine)
- They may also happen in people with:
  - Coronary artery disease (especially after a heart attack)
  - Heart failure
  - Heart valve problems

## What Are the Symptoms?

- Most people feel nothing at all.
- Some feel a fluttering or a skipped beat in the chest.
- This feeling is called palpitations.
- If the extra beats happen very often, they may cause dizziness or shortness of breath.
- In people with a healthy heart, these beats are not dangerous.
- But in people with heart disease, frequent extra beats can lead to serious heart rhythms. These can be life-threatening.

## How Are They Diagnosed?

- A doctor will use an electrocardiogram (ECG) to check the heart’s electrical activity.
- This test shows if the heart is beating normally or if there are extra beats.

## How Are They Treated?

### Lifestyle Changes
- If you are healthy, you may not need medicine.
- You can help prevent extra beats by:
  - Reducing stress
  - Avoiding caffeine
  - Avoiding alcohol
  - Not using cold or allergy medicines that speed up the heart

### Medicines
- Medicine is rarely needed because side effects can be worse than the problem.
- The main medicine used is a beta-blocker.
- Beta-blockers are used only if:
  - You recently had a heart attack
  - You have heart failure with symptoms
- In these cases, beta-blockers can help you live longer.

## More Information

The following resource may help you learn more:

- **American Heart Association: Arrhythmia**  
  This site explains your risk for heart rhythm problems. It also covers how they are diagnosed and treated.

# Chiropractic Care

Chiropractic is a type of treatment that focuses on the body’s structure, especially the spine. It is based on the idea that the spine and other joints affect how the nervous system works. When the spine is in good position, the body may work better and stay healthier.

Chiropractors use hands-on techniques to adjust the spine and other joints. They may also work on soft tissues like muscles and tendons. These adjustments aim to improve movement and reduce pain.

Chiropractors may also use other treatments, such as:
- Heat or cold packs
- Electrical stimulation
- Exercises to help with recovery
- Massage
- Pressure on certain points (acupressure)
- Advice on how to improve your daily habits, like your posture or work setup

Some chiropractors believe the body can heal itself. They think that spinal adjustments can fix small shifts in the bones of the spine. They say this helps a natural life force flow through the body. They believe this can help with many health problems.

Other chiropractors do not believe in this idea. They focus only on treatments that are supported by strong research. These treatments are mainly for muscle and joint problems.

## What Chiropractic Is Used For

There is good evidence that chiropractic care helps with:
- Low back pain

It may also help with some types of headaches, especially those caused by neck problems. But the relief does not last long. More research is needed to be sure.

Chiropractic care may also help with neck pain. Studies support this use.

Some chiropractors treat other conditions, such as:
- Asthma
- Bedwetting
- Tight neck muscles (torticollis)
- Ear infections in children

But there are very few high-quality studies on these uses. The current research does not show that chiropractic works well for these conditions.

## Possible Side Effects

Serious side effects from spinal adjustments are rare. But they can happen. These include:
- Worsening back pain
- Nerve damage in the neck
- Injury to blood vessels in the neck

Spinal adjustments are not safe for people with:
- Osteoporosis (very weak bones)
- Numbness, tingling, or weakness in an arm or leg

It is not clear if spinal adjustments are safe for people who:
- Have had spinal surgery
- Have had a stroke
- Have a blood vessel problem

Always talk to your doctor before starting chiropractic care, especially if you have any of these conditions.

# Schizophrenia in Children and Teens

Schizophrenia is a long-term brain condition. It affects how a person thinks, feels, and acts. It can make it hard to have normal relationships and do everyday tasks. The condition lasts for six months or longer.

## What Causes Schizophrenia?

- Scientists believe it is linked to chemical imbalances in the brain.
- It may also be tied to problems in brain development during pregnancy and early childhood.
- Doctors do not know the exact cause.
- Some people may inherit a higher chance of developing schizophrenia.
- It is not caused by bad parenting or tough experiences in childhood.

Recent studies show that using cannabis products increases the risk of psychotic disorders like schizophrenia and bipolar disorder in teens. This risk is not due to genetics. The legal use of marijuana may make some teens and parents think it is safe. But it is not.

## Symptoms

Children and teens with schizophrenia may have:

- Hearing or seeing things that are not there (hallucinations)
- Believing things that are not true (delusions)
- Feeling very suspicious of others (paranoia)
- Pulling away from family and friends
- Showing strange emotions or behaviors

In children, symptoms often start slowly and get worse over time. Thinking and learning may be more affected than in adults.

Teens may act withdrawn. They may have strange emotions. They may also have hallucinations, delusions, or paranoia.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

There is no single test for schizophrenia. Doctors make the diagnosis by:

- Watching how symptoms change over time
- Talking with the child and family
- Doing tests to rule out other possible causes

These tests check for:
- Brain infections
- Brain injuries
- Brain tumors
- Autoimmune diseases
- Use of certain medicines (like steroids) or illegal drugs

> **Did You Know?**  
> Schizophrenia is not caused by poor parenting or childhood struggles.

## Treatment

Schizophrenia cannot be cured. But treatment can help manage symptoms and improve daily life.

### Medicines
- Antipsychotic medicines can reduce hallucinations and delusions.
- Common medicines include haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine, and risperidone.
- Children are more likely to have side effects from these medicines.
- Side effects may include:
  - Shaking or tremors
  - Slow movements
  - Unusual body movements
  - Metabolic syndrome (a group of health problems that includes being overweight, type 2 diabetes, and high levels of fat in the blood)

### Support and Therapy
- Social skills training helps children learn how to interact with others.
- Vocational rehabilitation helps teens prepare for work or school.
- Counseling helps the child and family understand and cope with the condition.
- Educational support helps the child keep up in school.

Doctors almost always refer children to child psychiatrists. These are doctors who specialize in treating mental health issues in young people.

### Hospital Care
- A child may need to stay in the hospital if symptoms get worse.
- This helps doctors adjust medicine safely.
- It also keeps the child safe during tough times.

Treatment works best when the child, family, and doctors work together. Early help can make a big difference in long-term outcomes.

# Pelvic Venous Disorders

Pelvic venous disorders are a group of conditions that cause long-term pelvic pain. The pain often gets worse when you stand for long periods or during sex. These conditions are linked to swollen veins near the ovaries.

This condition used to have many different names. Now, doctors use the term pelvic venous disorders to cover all these problems. It includes issues like blocked veins or veins that do not close properly. The condition is grouped using a system based on symptoms, visible veins, and how the problem works in the body.

Many women have unusual vein shapes in the pelvis. Most of the time, this does not cause any symptoms. But in some women, it leads to pain or other problems.

We do not know exactly how many women have this condition. But it seems more common in women who have not gone through menopause.

## Symptoms and Signs

The most common symptom is long-term pelvic pain. The pain often feels like a dull ache. It can also feel sharp or throbbing. It usually affects one side, but sometimes both sides are involved.

The pain gets worse after standing for a long time, walking, or doing activities that push on the belly. Lying down often helps relieve the pain.

Some women feel pain that lasts for hours after sex. This is called postcoital ache. Deep pain during sex is also common.

Other symptoms include:
- A heavy or pressured feeling in the pelvis
- Painful periods
- More vaginal discharge than usual

If a vein is blocked, you may also have:
- Pain in the left side of the belly or back
- Blood in the urine (you might see it or it might only show up in a test)
- Swelling in the legs (less common)
- Pain in the legs when walking (called venous claudication)

You might see or feel swollen veins on the outside of the genitals, in the area between the genitals and the anus, or in the legs.

During a pelvic exam, your doctor might find that one area near the ovary is tender.

## How It Is Diagnosed

Diagnosis starts with your symptoms. You must have pelvic pain that lasts more than six months. The pain should get worse when standing or after sex. Your doctor should also find tenderness in the pelvis during an exam.

The first test is usually a pelvic ultrasound. This test uses sound waves to look at the veins. But it may not show the swollen veins if you are lying down. The test also helps rule out other causes of pelvic pain.

Some doctors may recommend more tests if needed. These include:
- Transabdominal ultrasound
- CT scan
- MRI scan
- Catheter venography (a special X-ray using a dye)
- Intravascular ultrasound

In catheter venography, a thin tube is placed into a vein. A dye is injected to see the blood flow. This can confirm if there are swollen veins.

If the pain is severe and no cause has been found, your doctor may do a laparoscopy. This is a small surgery where a camera is used to look inside the belly. But this test may miss swollen veins because of the position used and pressure from gas.

## Treatment

There is not strong scientific proof for the best treatment. But some options are commonly used.

### Conservative Treatments
- Take nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen to reduce pain and swelling.
- Wear compression shorts. These help improve blood flow. Do not use regular compression stockings.

### If Pain Persists and Is Severe

If the pain does not improve with these steps, treatment depends on the cause.

**If blood is flowing backward in the veins (reflux):**
- A minimally invasive procedure called embolization may help.
- A small tube is guided to the vein. Tiny coils or a special material are used to block the vein.
- This is done under local anesthesia and sedation.
- This treatment can reduce the need for pain medicine by up to 80%.
- Possible side effects include:
  - Bruising in the groin
  - Coils moving to another area
  - Allergic reaction to the dye used

**If a vein is blocked:**
- Doctors may use a stent (a small tube) to keep the vein open.
- Or they may use balloon angioplasty to widen the blocked vein.

**If other treatments fail:**
- Surgery may be an option. This can include tying off or removing the affected vein.

## Guidelines

The following professional groups have published advice on this condition:

- American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) – Chronic Pelvic Pain (2020, reaffirmed 2023)

## Key Points

- Pelvic venous disorders are caused by blocked veins or veins that do not close properly in the pelvis.
- The condition is most common in women who have not gone through menopause.
- Pain usually gets worse when standing or during sex.
- Other symptoms include:
  - A heavy or pressured feeling in the pelvis
  - Painful periods
  - More vaginal discharge
  - Pain in the left side of the belly or back
  - Blood in the urine (visible or not)
  - Swelling in the legs (less common)
  - Leg pain when walking (less common)
- Physical exam may show:
  - Swollen veins on the outside of the genitals, in the perineum, or in the legs
  - Tenderness near the ovaries
- Finding swollen veins on imaging alone does not mean you have the condition. Many women have these veins but no symptoms. Do not treat just because veins look swollen.
- Start with NSAIDs or compression shorts.
- If pain continues and is severe, consider:
  - Embolization
  - Stenting
  - Balloon angioplasty
- Surgery (tying off or removing the vein) may be needed if other treatments do not work.

# What You Need to Know About Lung Tumors

Lung tumors can be either:

- Not cancer  
- Cancer  

Even if a tumor is not cancer, it still needs medical check-up. This is because a noncancerous tumor can grow big enough to block your airway and make breathing hard.

How doctors treat a lung tumor depends on whether it is cancer or not.

## Noncancerous Lung Tumors

Noncancerous lung tumors can form in two main places:

### In the Trachea or Bronchial Tubes
These include:
- Hamartomas (the most common noncancerous lung tumor)
- Bronchial cystadenomas (grow in the main or smaller airways)
- Myoblastomas
- Papillomas

### In the Lung Tissue Itself
These include:
- Fibromas
- Hamartomas
- Leiomyomas
- Lipomas
- Neurofibromas
- Schwannomas
- Sclerosing hemangiomas

Doctors can tell what kind of noncancerous tumor it is by looking at the types of cells in it. For example, some are made of muscle cells, fat cells, or nerve cells.

Hamartomas are special. They are made of a mix of normal tissues that are not organized properly. These tissues can include cartilage, fat, and muscle.

Some noncancerous lumps in the lungs are not true tumors. They form because of swelling from an infection or an immune system problem. One example is sarcoidosis.

Most noncancerous tumors do not cause symptoms. But some may cause:
- Wheezing
- Coughing
- Trouble breathing

This usually happens if the tumor presses on or blocks an airway. It may also happen if the tumor grows large.

Doctors often find noncancerous lung tumors by accident. This happens when a chest x-ray or other scan is done for a different reason.

Most noncancerous tumors do not need treatment. But some may need surgery. Surgery is done to stop the airway from getting blocked.

### Did You Know?

In words like "carcinoma," the ending "-oma" means a lump, growth, or tumor. The first part of the word tells what the lump is made of.

For example:
- A meningioma is a tumor in the covering of the brain or spinal cord (called the meninges).
- Many cancer names end in "-oma," but not all lumps with "-oma" are tumors.

A hematoma is not a tumor. It is a swelling caused by blood collecting under the skin. The word "heme" means blood.

# Scrotal Pain

Scrotal pain means pain in the scrotum. This can happen in boys and men of any age.

## What Causes Scrotal Pain?

The most common causes are:

- **Testicular torsion**  
  The testicle twists inside the scrotum. This cuts off blood flow.

- **Torsion of a testicular appendage**  
  A small piece of tissue on the testicle twists. This causes pain.

- **Epididymitis or epididymo-orchitis**  
  Inflammation of the epididymis or both the epididymis and testicle. This is often due to infection.

There are other, less common causes. Your age, how fast the pain started, and other symptoms help doctors find the cause.

### Common Causes and Their Signs

#### Testicular Torsion
- Pain starts suddenly and is very bad.
- Only one side is affected.
- The pain does not go away.
- The reflex that pulls the testicle up is gone.
- The testicle sits higher than normal and is turned sideways.
- This happens most often in newborns and boys after puberty, but can happen in adults.
- Doctors use **color Doppler ultrasound** to check blood flow.

#### Torsion of a Testicular Appendage
- Pain builds up over a few days.
- Pain is in the top part of the testicle.
- The reflex that pulls the testicle up is still there.
- There may be a small fluid buildup (hydrocele) or a blue or black spot on the skin.
- This happens most often in boys aged 7 to 14.
- Doctors use **color Doppler ultrasound** to confirm.

#### Epididymitis or Epididymo-Orchitis
- Pain starts suddenly or over a few days.
- Pain is in the epididymis and sometimes the testicle.
- Urinary symptoms like frequent urination or pain when urinating.
- Recent heavy lifting or straining.
- The reflex that pulls the testicle up is still there.
- The scrotum may be swollen, red, and hard.
- Some men have discharge from the penis.
- This is common in boys and men after puberty.
- Doctors check urine and do tests for sexually transmitted infections.

#### Postvasectomy Pain
- You had a vasectomy.
- Pain during sex or ejaculation.
- Pain when you exercise.
- The epididymis may be tender or full.
- Doctors make a diagnosis based on your history and exam.

#### Trauma
- You had an injury to the genitals.
- Swelling may be present.
- There may be blood inside the testicle or a fluid collection (hematocele).
- Doctors use **color Doppler ultrasound** to check.

#### Strangulated Inguinal Hernia
- You have had a painless swelling in the groin for a long time.
- Now you have sudden or gradual pain.
- The scrotum has a large, soft lump.
- You may hear bowel sounds in the lump.
- The lump cannot be pushed back in.
- Doctors do a physical exam.

#### Immunoglobulin A–Associated Vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein Purpura)
- Purple spots on the skin, usually on the legs and buttocks.
- Joint pain or swelling.
- Belly pain.
- Kidney problems.
- This happens most often in boys aged 3 to 15.
- Doctors do a physical exam. Sometimes they take a skin sample.

#### Polyarteritis Nodosa
- Fever, weight loss, belly pain, high blood pressure, swelling.
- Skin has purple spots or lumps under the skin.
- This can cause poor blood flow to the testicles.
- This is most common in men aged 40 to 50.
- Doctors may do an angiography (a special X-ray of blood vessels).
- Sometimes they take a tissue sample.

#### Referred Pain
- Pain comes from another part of the body.
- The scrotum looks normal.
- Pain may come from:
  - Abdominal aortic aneurysm
  - Kidney stones
  - Nerve problems in the lower back
  - Appendicitis behind the belly
  - Tumors in the back of the belly
  - Pain after hernia surgery
- Doctors look at your symptoms and exam to find the real cause.

#### Orchitis (Usually Viral)
- Pain in the scrotum and belly.
- Nausea and fever.
- Swelling and redness in the scrotum.
- This can be caused by viruses like mumps, rubella, or others.
- Doctors test blood for signs of infection.

#### Fournier Gangrene
- Severe pain, fever, and a sick appearance.
- Redness, blisters, or dead skin.
- Sometimes you can feel gas under the skin.
- Some men had recent belly surgery.
- This is more common in older men with diabetes or poor blood flow.
- Doctors do a physical exam.

## How Is Scrotal Pain Evaluated?

You need fast care. If testicular torsion is not treated quickly, the testicle can be lost.

## How Is Scrotal Pain Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause.

- **Testicular torsion** needs emergency surgery. Surgery must happen within 12 hours of pain starting. Delayed surgery can cause permanent damage or loss of the testicle. Surgery untwists the testicle and fixes it in place to prevent future twisting.
- **Torsion of a testicular appendage** often gets better with rest and time.
- **Pain relief** may include strong pain medicine like morphine.
- **Infections** like epididymitis or orchitis need antibiotics.

## Special Considerations for Older Men

- Testicular torsion is rare in older men.
- When it does happen, symptoms are not typical. This makes diagnosis harder.
- Epididymitis, orchitis, and injury are more common in older men.
- Sometimes, an inguinal hernia, colon perforation, or kidney stones cause scrotal pain in older men.

## Key Points

- Always think about testicular torsion if a boy or teen has sudden scrotal pain. Quick diagnosis is critical.
- The most common causes are testicular torsion, torsion of a testicular appendage, and epididymitis.
- Color Doppler ultrasound is often used when the cause is unclear.
- If the scrotum and area around it look normal, the pain may be coming from somewhere else in the body.

# Chronic Widespread Pain

Chronic pain lasts for months or years.  
It is usually called chronic if it lasts more than three months.  
It can also continue for more than a month after an injury has healed.  
It may come and go over many months or years.  
It can be linked to long-term health problems like cancer, arthritis, diabetes, or fibromyalgia.  
It can also happen after an injury that does not fully heal.

Sometimes, nerves become more sensitive to pain.  
The original cause of pain may keep sending signals to nerves.  
This repeated activity can change the nerves and the cells that carry pain signals.  
This change is called neuroplasticity.  
It can make normal touches feel painful.  
It can also make real pain feel worse than it should.  
This is called sensitization.

Some areas of muscle or connective tissue become very tender.  
Touching these spots often causes pain that spreads to other parts of the body.  
These spots are called trigger points.

> **Did You Know:**  
> Chronic pain can get worse because the nervous system changes after repeated pain signals.  
> These changes can make pain last longer and feel stronger.

Long-term health problems like cancer, arthritis, diabetes, or fibromyalgia can cause chronic pain.  
Even a small injury can lead to long-term pain if nerves have become more sensitive.

Mental health matters.  
Anxiety and depression can make pain feel worse.  
They can also limit what people can do.  
People with chronic pain often worry about when the next pain will come.  
This fear can reduce natural pain-relieving chemicals in the body.  
This makes pain harder to control and can cause pain to continue even after the original cause is gone.

Sometimes the cause of pain is clear.  
For example, a past injury may have led to long-term back pain.  
Other times, the cause is not known.  
For example, someone may have ongoing headaches with no clear reason.

---

## Symptoms of Chronic Widespread Pain

Pain can happen in different places in different people.  
One person may have pain in the back.  
Another may have pain in the fingers.  
The pain can feel like throbbing, stabbing, burning, or stinging.  
It can be constant or come and go.  
The level of pain can change from day to day.

People with chronic pain often feel tired.  
They may have trouble sleeping.  
They may lose their appetite or their taste for food.  
They may lose weight.  
Their interest in sex may go down.

These problems build up slowly.  
Constant pain can stop people from doing things they enjoy.  
They may feel sad or anxious.  
They may stop doing normal activities.  
They may pull away from friends and family.  
They may focus too much on their health.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Chronic Widespread Pain

Doctors start by asking questions and doing a full exam.  
They want to find the cause of the pain and how it affects daily life.  
If no cause is found, the focus shifts to reducing pain and helping the person live better.

Doctors ask if the person feels sad, anxious, or sleeps well.  
These issues can make pain worse.  
If present, they must be treated to help with pain.  
A mental health evaluation may be needed.

If pain does not improve with medicine or other treatments, a team of health experts may help.  
This team works together to support the person’s overall well-being.  
Psychologists and psychiatrists help with emotional and mental health.  
Therapists help with physical and daily activities.  
Sleep experts, nutritionists, and others may join the team.  
The goal is to help the person manage pain and live as well as possible.

---

## Treating Chronic Widespread Pain

Treatment may include:

- Medicines to reduce pain  
- Physical methods like physical therapy  
- Psychological and behavior therapy  
- Special medical procedures

If a cause is found, doctors treat that cause.

Common treatments include:

- Pain medicines (analgesics)  
- Physical therapy or occupational therapy  
- Complementary methods like acupuncture, massage, or TENS (a device that sends small electrical pulses to nerves)  
- Counseling or therapy

If treatments do not work, doctors may refer the person to a pain clinic.

Most people on pain medicine find that pain levels change during the day.  
Pain can vary based on:

- How the nerves work  
- What activities are done  
- Stress levels  
- The dose and timing of medicine

Medicines used for chronic pain include:

- Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen or naproxen  
- Antiseizure medicines such as gabapentin and pregabalin  
- Antidepressants like SNRIs or TCAs

Sometimes, combining medicines works better than using just one.

Doctors usually start with acetaminophen or NSAIDs.  
NSAIDs help with pain and reduce swelling that often makes pain worse.  
But long-term or high-dose use can cause serious side effects.  
These include stomach irritation, bleeding, kidney problems, and higher risk of heart and blood vessel issues.

**Adjuvant analgesics** are medicines that help reduce pain by changing how nerves send signals.  
They do not block pain directly.  
Common ones include:

- Antidepressants like amitriptyline, bupropion, desipramine, duloxetine, nortriptyline, and venlafaxine  
- Antiseizure medicines like gabapentin and pregabalin  
- Local anesthetics (applied to the skin or taken by mouth)

**Opioids** are only used if other treatments fail.  
They are not first-choice medicines.  
They can cause serious side effects, including addiction, slowed breathing, and overdose death.  
They are most often used for moderate to severe pain from cancer or other life-limiting illnesses.  
They are also used in hospice care for people near the end of life.

Before prescribing opioids, doctors consider:

- What the usual treatment is  
- If other treatments could work  
- If the person is at risk for side effects  
- If the person might misuse the medicine

If there is a high risk of misuse, doctors may refer the person to a pain specialist or mental health expert.  
People with a history of addiction usually need this referral.

When opioids are prescribed, doctors explain:

- The nature of the condition (if known)  
- The risks and benefits of all treatment options  
- The risks of opioids, including addiction and side effects

Doctors ask about the person’s goals and expectations.  
They give written information about risks.  
The person must read and understand it before signing a consent form.

Doctors also tell people taking opioids to:

- Avoid alcohol and medicines for anxiety or sleep  
- Take the correct dose at the right time  
- Keep the medicine locked up and safe  
- Never share the medicine  
- Call the doctor if they feel drowsy or have side effects like confusion, constipation, or nausea  
- Dispose of unused pills properly  
- Keep naloxone (an overdose antidote) on hand  
- Learn how to use it and teach family members

Doctors follow safety rules when prescribing opioids.  
They usually ask the person to get prescriptions from only one doctor and fill them at the same pharmacy.  
They see the person often for checkups.  
They monitor how the medicine is used.  
They may test urine to check if the medicine is being taken correctly.  
They may ask the person to sign an agreement about safe use.

For people with pain from cancer or a terminal illness, side effects should not stop opioid use.  
Side effects can usually be managed.  
Addiction is less of a concern in these cases.

---

## Physical and Occupational Therapy

Physical and occupational therapists help people with chronic pain.  
They teach ways to move and do daily tasks with less pain.

If trigger points are present, therapists may use a cooling spray followed by gentle stretching.  
This method is called stretch and spray.  
It can reduce pain.

Wearing a support device (orthosis) can help some people.  
These devices support weak or damaged joints, muscles, ligaments, or bones.

Regular exercise can help.  
Walking every day may be better than staying in bed for back pain.

Therapists help people find ways to do daily tasks with less pain.

---

## Complementary and Integrative Treatments

Doctors may suggest these options:

- Acupuncture  
- Meditation, yoga, or tai chi  
- Chiropractic care, osteopathic manipulation, or massage  
- Therapeutic touch or Reiki

Other techniques can also help:

- Relaxation training  
- Distraction (like imagining a peaceful scene, such as lying on a beach)  
- Hypnosis  
- Biofeedback

These methods can help people manage pain better.

---

## Counseling and Therapy

Counseling can help people live better, even if pain does not go away.  
Doctors may suggest slowly increasing physical and social activities.  
People are encouraged not to let pain stop them from doing things.  
This approach often leads to less pain over time.  
Doctors praise progress and keep supporting the person.

Doctors may also talk with family or coworkers.  
They ask them not to focus too much on the person’s pain.  
For example, they should not keep asking about health or make the person avoid chores.

---

Some procedures can help when medicine and therapy do not work.

Doctors inject medicine near a nerve to reduce pain and swelling.

### Neurolysis
This destroys part of a nerve to reduce pain.  
It can be done by freezing the nerve (cryotherapy), burning it with radio waves (radiofrequency ablation), or using a chemical to damage it (chemoneurolysis).
