# Skin Infestation by Fly Larvae (Cutaneous Myiasis)

This condition happens when fly larvae get into the skin.  
The larvae are also called maggots.  
They come from certain types of flies with two wings.  

There are three main types of skin infestation:  
- Furuncular myiasis  
- Wound myiasis  
- Migratory myiasis  

Sometimes, the larvae can also get into other parts of the body.  
These include the nose and throat, the gut, or the urinary and reproductive organs.  

Most cases happen in tropical countries.  
In the United States, most cases are in people who recently came from these areas.

---

## Furuncular Myiasis

This type is often caused by bot flies.  
The most common cause in travelers returning to the United States is *Dermatobia hominis*.  
This fly lives in South and Central America.  

Other flies that cause this include:  
- *Cordylobia anthropophaga* in sub-Saharan Africa  
- *Cuterebra* species in North America  
- *Wohlfahrtia* species in North America, Europe, and Pakistan  

These flies do not usually lay eggs directly on people.  
They lay eggs on other insects, like mosquitoes.  
Or they lay eggs on things like clothes hanging out to dry.  

When the eggs touch the skin, they hatch.  
The tiny larvae then burrow into the skin.  
They grow in stages until they are full size.  
Full-grown larvae can be 1 to 2 centimeters long.  

If not treated, the larvae will eventually come out of the skin.  
They fall to the ground to finish their life cycle.  

Common symptoms include:  
- Itching  
- A feeling that something is moving under the skin  
- Sharp, shooting pain in some cases  

The first sign may look like a bug bite or a small abscess.  
But it can be told apart by a small hole in the center.  
There may be fluid draining from the hole.  
Sometimes, part of the larva can be seen at the opening.  

- *D. hominis* lesions often appear on the face, scalp, or arms and legs.  
- *C. anthropophaga* lesions usually show up on areas covered by clothes.  
  These include the head, neck, and back.  

There is no single best treatment.  
Options depend on what is available.  
Some people wait and see if the larva comes out on its own.  
Others use methods to force the larva out.  

Larvae need air to survive.  
Covering the hole with something can make them come closer to the surface.  
This makes it easier to remove them.  

Common coverings include:  
- Petroleum jelly  
- Nail polish  
- Bacon  
- A paste made from tobacco  

But if the larva dies during this process, it can be hard to remove.  
It may also cause a strong swelling or redness.  

Another way is to make a small cut and pull the larva out.  
A medicine called ivermectin can also help.  
It can kill the larva or make it move toward the surface.  
It can be taken by mouth or applied to the skin.  
The usual dose is 200 micrograms per kilogram of body weight.  
One dose is usually enough.  

---

## Wound Myiasis

This happens when fly larvae get into open wounds or moist areas like the mouth or nose.  
It is most common in people who live outdoors, have alcohol use disorder, or do not have good hygiene.  

The most common flies are green or black blowflies.  
Unlike housefly larvae, these can grow in healthy skin as well as dead or damaged skin.  

Treatment usually involves:  
- Washing the wound with water  
- Carefully removing the larvae by hand  

This helps clean the wound and stop the infestation.  

---

## Migratory Myiasis

This type is caused by flies that usually live in horses and cattle.  
The most common ones are *Gasterophilus intestinalis* and *Hypoderma* species.  

People get infected by touching animals that are infested.  
Less often, the flies lay eggs directly on a person’s skin.  

The larvae burrow under the skin.  
They move slowly through the tissue.  
This causes itchy, growing sores.  

These sores can look like another skin problem called cutaneous larva migrans.  
But there is a key difference:  
- Fly larvae are much bigger than the worms that cause cutaneous larva migrans.  
- The sores from fly larvae last longer.  

Treatment is similar to that for furuncular myiasis.  
It may include covering the hole to force the larva out,  
or removing it with a small cut.  
Medicine like ivermectin may also be used.

# Blastomycosis

Blastomycosis is a fungal infection. It mainly affects the lungs. The fungus that causes it is called *Blastomyces dermatitidis*.

## How You Get Blastomycosis

- The fungus lives in soil, especially near rivers.
- You can get infected by breathing in tiny spores from the soil.
- The spores enter your lungs when you breathe them in.
- The infection usually starts in the lungs.
- In some cases, the fungus spreads through the blood to other parts of the body.

## Where the Infection Can Spread

The fungus can spread to:
- The skin
- Bones
- The reproductive and urinary systems (including the prostate in men)
- The brain and the tissues covering it
- Other areas like the kidneys, spine, testes, ovaries, and lymph nodes

## Who Is at Risk

- Blastomycosis can happen in people with healthy immune systems.
- It may be more common and more serious in people with weakened immune systems.
- Unlike many other fungal infections, blastomycosis is not more common in people with AIDS.
- But when it does occur in people with AIDS, it tends to be more severe.

## Where Blastomycosis Is Found

Most cases happen in parts of North America, especially in:
- The Ohio and Mississippi River valleys (including parts of the middle Atlantic and southeastern U.S.)
- The northern Midwest
- Upstate New York
- Southern Canada near the Great Lakes and Saint Lawrence River

Rarely, cases are seen in the Middle East or Africa.

## Symptoms of Blastomycosis

Some people have no symptoms at all. Others may feel fine after a short time and not know they are sick.

When symptoms do appear, they can start suddenly or slowly. They include:
- Fever
- Chills
- Heavy sweating

Other possible symptoms:
- Chest pain
- Trouble breathing
- A dry or hacking cough
- Coughing up mucus (sputum)

The lung infection usually gets worse slowly. Some people get better without treatment.

In some people, the infection gets worse quickly.

When the fungus spreads beyond the lungs, it can cause problems in many areas. The most common sites are:
- Skin
- Bones
- Reproductive and urinary systems
- Brain and the tissues around it

### Skin Symptoms

- Small, raised bumps (papules) appear first.
- These bumps may have pus inside.
- Later, warty, raised patches form.
- These patches are surrounded by small, painless pus-filled spots (abscesses).

### Bone Symptoms

- The area over the infected bone may swell.
- It may feel warm and painful.

### Reproductive and Urinary Symptoms

**In men:**
- The tube on top of a testicle (epididymis) may swell and hurt.
- The prostate gland may become infected, causing pain or discomfort.

**In women:**
- Infection in the ovaries or fallopian tubes can cause abscesses.
- The lining of the uterus may become infected.
- The fallopian tubes may become infected.

### Brain and Nervous System Symptoms

- The fungus can spread to the tissues covering the brain and spinal cord.
- This causes a condition called fungal meningitis.
- Abscesses can form in the brain.
- Symptoms include headache and confusion.

## How Doctors Diagnose Blastomycosis

Doctors use several tests to find the infection:

- A sample of sputum (mucus from the lungs) or infected tissue is taken.
- The sample is sent to a lab to be checked under a microscope and grown in a culture.
- A chest x-ray is done to look for signs of lung infection.
- Blood and urine tests may be done to check for proteins (antigens) made by the fungus.
- A PCR test may be used. This test finds and copies tiny pieces of the fungus’s genetic material. This makes it easier to identify the fungus.

## How Blastomycosis Is Treated

- Antifungal medicines are used to treat the infection.
- For severe cases, a medicine called amphotericin B is given through a vein (IV).
- For mild to moderate cases, a medicine called itraconazole is taken by mouth.

### Treatment Time

- Most people start to feel better within a few days to weeks.
- But the medicine must be taken for 6 to 12 months or longer.
- Stopping early can cause the infection to come back.

### Without Treatment

- The infection slowly gets worse.
- In rare cases, it can be fatal.

Always follow your doctor’s instructions for treatment. Do not stop taking medicine early, even if you feel better.

# Growth Hormone Deficiency in Children

This guide explains growth hormone deficiency in children using simple, clear language.

---

## What Is Growth Hormone Deficiency?

Growth hormone deficiency means a child’s body does not make enough growth hormone. This hormone helps children grow taller.

This is the most common hormone problem in children involving the pituitary gland. It can happen alone or with other hormone problems.

When a child has this condition, they grow much more slowly than other children. They may be much shorter than their peers.

---

## What Causes Growth Hormone Deficiency?

There are two main types:

### 1. Isolated Growth Hormone Deficiency
- Only growth hormone is low.
- It can be present from birth (congenital) or develop later (acquired).
- About 25% of cases have a known cause.
- Causes include:
  - Problems with genes that control growth hormone.
  - Brain or pituitary problems present at birth.
  - Brain infections like meningitis.
  - Brain injury.
  - Radiation treatment to the brain (used for cancer).
  - Radiation to the spine (can also harm bone growth).

### 2. Generalized Hypopituitarism
- More than one hormone from the pituitary gland is low.
- This includes hormones that control:
  - Thyroid function.
  - Adrenal glands.
  - Reproductive organs.
  - Growth.
- It can also affect a hormone called vasopressin, which helps the body control water balance.
- Causes include:
  - Genetic problems passed down in families or new gene changes.
  - Birth defects, such as cleft palate or missing parts of the brain.
  - Tumors in the brain or pituitary.
  - Infections like tuberculosis or toxoplasmosis.
  - Inflammatory diseases that affect the brain or pituitary.
  - A rare condition called Langerhans cell histiocytosis, which can cause bone damage and diabetes insipidus.

---

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on the child’s age and the cause.

### Main Signs of Growth Hormone Deficiency:
- Very slow growth.
- Height below the 3rd percentile (shorter than 97% of children their age).
- Growth rate less than:
  - 6 cm per year before age 4.
  - 5 cm per year from age 4 to 8.
  - 4 cm per year before puberty.
- Teeth may come in later than normal.
- Bones mature more slowly than expected (bone age is more than 2 years behind actual age).
- The child’s body proportions stay normal — they are short but not oddly shaped.

### Other Possible Signs:
- Delayed or no puberty.
- Weight gain that is out of step with height — may appear overweight.
- Newborns with brain or pituitary problems may have:
  - Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia).
  - High bilirubin (jaundice).
  - Cleft palate.
  - Small penis (micropenis).
  - Other hormone problems.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Diagnosis uses several steps:

### 1. Growth Tracking
- Doctors measure height and weight.
- These numbers are plotted on a growth chart.
- For babies 0 to 2 years: use WHO growth charts.
- For children 2 years and older: use CDC growth charts.

### 2. Blood Tests
- **IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 levels** are checked.
  - IGF-1 is a protein made by the liver in response to growth hormone.
  - IGFBP-3 carries IGF-1 in the blood.
  - These levels help show if growth hormone is working.
  - IGF-1 levels change with age and are best compared to bone age, not just calendar age.
  - In young children, IGF-1 levels are naturally low — so low levels do not always mean deficiency.
  - In older children, low IGF-1 may suggest growth hormone deficiency.
  - But low IGF-1 can also happen with poor nutrition, emotional stress, celiac disease, or hypothyroidism. These must be ruled out.
  - IGFBP-3 is less affected by poor nutrition, so it helps in younger children.

- **Growth hormone levels** are not measured at random.
  - Growth hormone is released in bursts, not steadily.
  - Random blood tests are not useful.
  - Doctors use **provocative testing** to check if the body can make growth hormone when stimulated.
  - This test is not perfect — results can vary and are hard to repeat.
  - A normal result does not always mean the child is fine.
  - A single test should not be the only reason to start treatment.

### 3. Imaging Tests
- An MRI scan of the brain is done if growth is abnormal.
- It checks for tumors, birth defects, or other problems in the pituitary or brain.
- A hand X-ray is used to check bone age.

### 4. Other Blood Tests
- To rule out other causes of slow growth:
  - Thyroid function (TSH, thyroxine).
  - Kidney function (electrolytes, creatinine).
  - Signs of inflammation or infection (C-reactive protein, antibodies).
  - Blood count (to check for anemia or blood disorders).

### 5. Genetic Testing
- May be done if the child has physical signs of a genetic syndrome.
- Or if growth patterns do not match the family.

### 6. Additional Hormone Tests
- If growth hormone deficiency is suspected, doctors check:
  - Cortisol (adrenal hormone).
  - Thyroid hormone (TSH, free T4).
  - Sex hormones (LH, FSH).
  - Prolactin.

> **Important Note:** Random growth hormone levels are not helpful for diagnosis.

---

## How Is It Treated?

### 1. Growth Hormone Replacement
- Recombinant growth hormone is given as a daily injection under the skin.
- It is used for all children with confirmed growth hormone deficiency.
- Dose: 0.03 to 0.05 mg per kilogram of body weight, once daily.
- Results:
  - First year: growth may increase to 10 to 12 cm per year.
  - Later years: growth slows but stays faster than before treatment.
- Treatment continues until:
  - The child reaches a height that is acceptable.
  - Growth rate drops below 2.5 cm per year.

- **IGF-1 levels** are used to adjust the dose:
  - Goal: IGF-1 in the upper half of normal range (0 to +2 standard deviations).
  - If IGF-1 is too low, the dose can be increased by 10% to 20%.

### 2. Long-Acting Growth Hormone Options
- New weekly injections are available for children who only need growth hormone.
- These include:
  - **Lonapegsomatropin**: For children over 1 year old and weighing more than 11.5 kg.
  - **Somapacitan**: For children over 2.5 years old.
  - **Somatrogon**: For children over 3 years old.
- These are made to last longer in the body than daily shots.
- They have different starting doses and may need different monitoring.
- Studies show they work as well as daily injections for growth.
- Monitoring IGF-1 levels may be harder because of timing and how the drug works.

### 3. Other Hormone Replacements
- If other hormones are low, they must also be replaced:
  - **Cortisol**: Given daily for life if levels are low.
  - **Thyroid hormone**: Given daily for life if levels are low.
  - **Vasopressin (for diabetes insipidus)**: Given as a tablet or nasal spray for life.
  - **Sex hormones (testosterone or estrogen)**: Given if puberty does not start on time.

### 4. Special Cases
- **Children who had brain radiation for cancer**:
  - There was concern that growth hormone could cause cancer to return.
  - But studies show no increased risk.
  - Growth hormone can be started at least 1 year after cancer treatment ends.

---

## Should All Short Children Get Growth Hormone?

Some children are short but have no known medical cause. This is called **idiopathic short stature (ISS)**.

- ISS means:
  - Height is 2 standard deviations below average for age.
  - Growth rate is normal or near normal.
  - No signs of hormone or metabolic problems.
  - Growth hormone tests are normal (not deficient).
- Growth hormone may be used only if:
  - The child is very short (2.25 standard deviations below average).
  - Predicted adult height is below normal (under 150 cm for girls, under 160 cm for boys).

> **Important:** Doctors do not recommend giving growth hormone to every short child.

- Treatment results vary:
  - Some children grow 5 cm more as adults.
  - Others grow no more.
- Better results are seen when:
  - Treatment starts before age 9 in girls.
  - Treatment starts before age 10 in boys.
  - Growth speed increases in the first year.
  - IGF-1 levels rise after treatment.

- Some experts suggest trying treatment for 6 to 12 months.
  - Continue only if growth speed doubles or increases by 3 cm per year.
- But this approach is debated because:
  - It is expensive.

# Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis

This condition causes swelling in small and medium-sized blood vessels. This swelling can harm organs. It usually affects adults who have had asthma, nasal allergies, nasal polyps, or a mix of these.

- The exact cause is not known.
- At first, people may have a runny nose, asthma, or sinus pain for months or years.
- Later, symptoms can vary depending on which organs are affected.

## What Happens in the Body

The body’s immune system attacks blood vessels. This causes swelling (inflammation). The swelling can damage organs.

- The nerves, sinuses, skin, joints, lungs, gut, heart, and kidneys are most often affected.
- Clumps of immune cells form lumps called granulomas. These can grow under the skin or inside organs.
- Granulomas can damage healthy tissue and stop organs from working right.
- People with this condition have too many eosinophils. These are a type of white blood cell.
- High levels of eosinophils are called eosinophilia. This often means the body is reacting to an allergy or other problem.

## Symptoms

Symptoms can appear slowly over time. They may come and go in episodes.

### Early Symptoms
- Asthma that gets worse over time
- Runny nose that lasts a long time
- Sneezing and itchy eyes
- Pain in the face from sinus swelling

### Later Symptoms
- Feeling very tired and unwell
- Fever or night sweats
- Loss of appetite and weight loss
- Muscle and joint pain
- Trouble breathing or worse asthma
- Chest pain
- Skin rashes
- Belly pain or diarrhea
- Blood in the stool
- Numbness, tingling, or weakness in an arm or leg — sometimes sudden
- Confusion, seizures, or loss of consciousness

Kidney problems may not cause symptoms until the kidneys stop working. Other serious problems can include heart failure, heart attack, inflammation of the heart lining, or heart valve issues.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Diagnosis is not based on one test. Doctors look at all the signs and test results together.

### Tests Done
- **Blood tests**: Check for high levels of eosinophils. Test for certain antibodies linked to this disease. Check for signs of inflammation.
- **Urine tests**: Check if the kidneys are affected.
- **Chest x-ray**: Looks for lung problems.
- **Heart ultrasound (echocardiography)**: Checks for heart damage.
- **Biopsy**: A small sample of skin, muscle, or lung tissue is taken and looked at under a microscope. This can show if there are eosinophils or granulomas.

A biopsy may need to be done in a hospital. It helps confirm the diagnosis.

## Treatment

Treatment aims to reduce swelling and stop damage to organs.

- **Corticosteroids** (like prednisone) are used first. They reduce swelling.
- A second medicine that lowers the immune system (immunosuppressant) is also used.
- Common options include: rituximab, azathioprine, methotrexate, mepolizumab, or benralizumab.
- Cyclophosphamide is used only if the disease is very severe, especially if the heart is involved.

After symptoms improve, the dose of medicine is slowly lowered. Some people may stop taking medicine after a while. If symptoms return, treatment can start again.

Long-term use of these medicines can cause serious side effects. People should talk to their doctor about risks.

## What You Should Do

- Learn about your condition.
- Watch for new or worsening symptoms.
- Tell your doctor right away if you notice anything unusual.

## Outlook

The outlook is worse if the heart, brain, spinal cord, or nerves are affected.

## More Help

The following website may be useful:

**Vasculitis Foundation: About Eosinophilic Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis**  
This site offers support and information for people with this condition. It helps you find a doctor, learn about research, and join patient groups.

# Selective IgA Deficiency

## What Is Selective IgA Deficiency?

IgA is a type of protein in the blood that helps fight infections.  
Selective IgA deficiency means your body makes very little of this protein.  
Your levels of other important proteins, like IgG and IgM, are normal.  
This condition is the most common type of primary immunodeficiency.  
It means the problem is in your immune system from birth.

Many people with this condition have no symptoms.  
Some people get infections often, especially in the ears, sinuses, lungs, or gut.  
Some develop allergies like asthma or nasal polyps.  
Some develop autoimmune diseases such as celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, lupus, or chronic liver disease.  
Over time, a few people develop common variable immunodeficiency (CVID).  
In some cases, the condition goes away on its own.

## What Causes Selective IgA Deficiency?

The exact cause is not fully known.  
It may be linked to problems in B cells, which are immune system cells that make antibodies.  
The condition runs in families.  
If a close family member has it, your risk is about 50 times higher.  
Some people have changes in a gene called *TACI*.  
Others have certain patterns of genes in a region called the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class III.  
These gene patterns are linked to the condition.

Some medicines can cause IgA deficiency in rare cases.  
These include phenytoin, sulfasalazine, gold, and penicillamine.

## Symptoms and Signs

Most people with this condition feel fine and have no symptoms.  
Others may have frequent infections in the nose, lungs, or digestive system.  
Some have diarrhea, asthma, or nasal polyps.  
Some develop autoimmune diseases.

If you have had a blood transfusion or immune globulin treatment, you may develop antibodies against IgA.  
If you get exposed to IgA again, you could have a severe allergic reaction called anaphylaxis.  
This is rare but serious.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor may suspect this condition if you:  
- Have repeated infections  
- Had a severe reaction during a blood transfusion  
- Have a family history of IgA deficiency, CVID, or autoimmune disease  
- Are taking medicines that can cause IgA deficiency

To confirm the diagnosis:  
- Your blood is tested for levels of IgA, IgG, and IgM.  
- A low IgA level (less than 7 milligrams per deciliter) with normal IgG and IgM levels confirms the condition.  
- You are also tested for your ability to make antibodies after getting a vaccine.  
- Your antibody levels should rise at least two times after vaccination.

Testing family members is not usually needed.  
Most people with low IgA have no serious health problems.  
But if you have had a bad reaction to a blood transfusion, you should be tested.  
This is especially important if a family member has IgA deficiency.

## How Is It Treated?

You may need antibiotics when you get an infection.  
In severe cases, you may take antibiotics every day to prevent infections.  
Antibiotics are used for infections in the ears, sinuses, lungs, gut, or urinary tract.

Immune globulin therapy (IVIG) is not helpful for this condition.  
It contains mostly IgG and very little IgA.  
But it still carries a small risk of causing an allergic reaction in people who have anti-IgA antibodies.  
In rare cases, if you do not respond to vaccines and antibiotics do not work, a special type of immune globulin with almost no IgA may be tried. It may help a little.

You must avoid blood products that contain IgA.  
This includes most plasma and immune globulin.  
If you need a blood transfusion:  
- Only washed packed red blood cells should be used.  
- Other blood products must be IgA-deficient.  
- Any blood cells used must be washed to remove IgA.

You should wear a medical ID bracelet or necklace.  
This helps prevent accidental exposure to IgA-containing products.  
It can save your life if you have a severe allergic reaction.

## What Is the Outlook?

Most people with this condition live normal lives.  
Some get better on their own over time.  
A few develop CVID later in life.  
The outlook is worse if you develop an autoimmune disease.

## Key Points

- Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency.  
- You may have no symptoms or may have frequent infections or autoimmune diseases.  
- Some people develop CVID later; others get better without treatment.  
- Think about this condition if you have had a bad reaction to a blood transfusion, take certain medicines, or have repeated infections.  
- Confirm the diagnosis with blood tests for IgA, IgG, and IgM, and by checking your response to vaccines.  
- Use antibiotics when needed, and sometimes daily to prevent infections.  
- Avoid blood products and immune globulin that contain more than a tiny amount of IgA.

# Mesothelioma

Mesothelioma is a rare type of cancer. It starts in a thin layer of tissue that covers the lungs and lines the chest and belly.

## What Causes Mesothelioma?

- The main cause is exposure to asbestos.
- Asbestos is a group of natural minerals. It was used in building materials, car brakes, and some fabrics because it resists heat and holds its shape.
- You do not need to have worked with asbestos to get mesothelioma. Even small amounts of exposure can cause it.
- The cancer usually shows up 30 to 50 years after exposure.
- Smoking does not cause mesothelioma. But it can harm your lungs in other ways.

## How Can You Get Exposed?

- Workers in construction, shipbuilding, and manufacturing are at higher risk.
- You can also be exposed if you live with someone who works with asbestos. Fibers can come home on clothes or skin. This is called take-home exposure.
- Asbestos is found in tiny amounts in air, water, and soil. But this low-level exposure does not usually cause disease.

## Symptoms of Mesothelioma

- A constant pain in the chest is the most common symptom.
- Trouble breathing is also very common.
- If the cancer spreads, you may have:
  - Severe chest pain
  - A hoarse voice
  - Trouble swallowing
  - Swelling in the belly

## How Is Mesothelioma Diagnosed?

Diagnosing mesothelioma is not easy. Doctors use several steps:

- They ask about your past exposure to asbestos.
- They take pictures of your chest using X-rays or CT scans.
- They test fluid from around the lungs (pleural fluid).
- They take a small sample of tissue from the lining of the lungs (pleural biopsy).

These tests help doctors see if the cells are cancerous and if they are mesothelioma.

- There is no recommended screening test for people who were exposed to asbestos but have no symptoms.

## Treatment for Mesothelioma

There is no cure for mesothelioma. Treatment focuses on helping you feel better and live longer.

### Supportive Care
- Doctors help relieve pain and shortness of breath.
- They may remove extra fluid around the lungs to make breathing easier.

### Surgery
- Surgery may be an option if the cancer is found early.
- In later stages, surgery may be used to remove as much of the cancer as possible.

### Radiation Therapy
- Radiation can shrink tumors.
- It is often used to ease symptoms like pain.

### Chemotherapy
- Chemo can slow the cancer for a short time.
- It does not usually help people live much longer.

### Immunotherapy
- This treatment helps your body’s immune system fight cancer.
- Drugs like tremelimumab, pembrolizumab, nivolumab, and ipilimumab are used.
- Combining chemo and immunotherapy may help some people live longer in the short term.
- But long-term survival still remains low.

## Prognosis

- Mesothelioma is a serious illness.
- Even with new treatments, most people live between 6 and 18 months after diagnosis.

## How to Prevent Mesothelioma

- The best way to prevent mesothelioma is to avoid breathing in asbestos dust and fibers.
- Even though we use less asbestos today, people who were exposed decades ago are still getting sick.
- If you work with asbestos, follow safety rules to protect yourself and others.

# Gastroschisis

Gastroschisis is a birth defect where the intestines and other belly organs push out through a hole in the belly wall. The hole is usually to the right of the belly button. The baby’s organs are not covered by a protective sac.

This condition needs surgery to fix.

## How Common Is It?

Gastroschisis happens in about 1 out of every 2,500 babies born. It is more common than another similar condition called omphalocele.

## What’s Different About Gastroschisis?

In gastroschisis, the hole is not in the middle of the belly. It is usually to the right of the belly button. In omphalocele, the hole is in the middle, at the base of the belly button.

In gastroschisis, the intestines are not covered by a thin membrane. The intestines are swollen, red, and often stuck together with a sticky film. This happens because the intestines were exposed to the amniotic fluid during pregnancy. This exposure causes irritation and inflammation. Over time, this can lead to scarring, poor movement of the intestines, or blockages.

## Other Health Problems

Most babies with gastroschisis do not have other major birth defects. Only about 10 to 15% have other problems.

But about 1 in 4 babies with gastroschisis also have issues with their intestines. These include:
- The intestines are twisted (malrotation)
- Parts of the intestines are blocked or missing (intestinal atresia)

## Finding It Before Birth

Doctors can often spot gastroschisis before birth. They do this with:
- A blood test that shows high levels of a protein called alpha-fetoprotein
- An ultrasound scan

If the baby has gastroschisis, the mother should give birth at a hospital with a neonatal intensive care unit and pediatric surgery team.

## Care Right After Birth

When the baby is born, the doctor will cover the exposed organs right away. They use a clean, wet, soft dressing. This keeps the organs safe and prevents them from drying out. A plastic wrap may be placed over the dressing.

The baby will get fluids and antibiotics through a vein. The most common antibiotics are ampicillin and gentamicin. Sometimes, just covering the skin bacteria is enough.

A small tube will be placed through the nose into the stomach. This helps drain stomach contents and prevents bloating.

The baby needs more fluids than a normal newborn. The amount is usually 1.5 to 2 times more. This is because the exposed intestines lose a lot of fluid.

## Checking for Other Problems

Before surgery, doctors will check for other birth defects. They will do tests to make sure the heart, kidneys, and other organs are working well.

## Surgery to Fix the Problem

The goal is to put the organs back inside the belly and close the hole.

If the belly is small and cannot fit all the organs, the surgeon will use a special pouch made of silicone. This pouch is placed over the organs. Over several days, the pouch is slowly made smaller. This gives the belly more room. The organs slowly move back into the belly.

Once all the organs are inside, the hole is closed.

Some doctors now use a new method. They cover the hole with the baby’s own belly button or a special dressing. No stitches are used. But more research is needed to see if this method works as well.

## Recovery and Feeding

It can take several weeks before the baby’s intestines start working again.

The baby will not be able to eat by mouth at first. They will get nutrition through a tube into the vein (parenteral nutrition) or through a tube into the stomach (enteral nutrition). This may last for months.

Some babies have long-term problems with how their intestines move. This can cause ongoing feeding issues.

# Diabetes During Pregnancy

This guide explains what happens when a woman has diabetes during pregnancy. It covers the risks, how it is diagnosed, and how it is treated.

---

## What Is Diabetes During Pregnancy?

Diabetes is a condition where the body cannot control blood sugar levels properly. There are two main types:

- **Type 1 diabetes**: The body does not make insulin.
- **Type 2 diabetes**: The body does not use insulin well.

Some women have diabetes before they become pregnant. Others develop it only during pregnancy. This is called **gestational diabetes**.

---

## Gestational Diabetes

About 4 out of every 100 pregnant women develop gestational diabetes.

This type of diabetes is more common in women who:

- Are overweight or obese
- Have a family history of diabetes
- Are of non-Hispanic Asian/Pacific Islander or Hispanic/Latina heritage

If not treated, gestational diabetes can cause serious health problems for both mother and baby. It can even lead to the death of the baby.

### Why Does Gestational Diabetes Happen?

During pregnancy, the body needs more insulin. Insulin helps control blood sugar.

The placenta makes a hormone that blocks insulin. This is called **insulin resistance**. It gets worse as the pregnancy goes on.

If the body cannot make enough extra insulin, blood sugar levels rise. This leads to gestational diabetes.

Some women may have had diabetes before pregnancy but did not know it until they became pregnant.

---

## Risks of Diabetes During Pregnancy

If blood sugar is not well controlled, it can cause problems at different times in pregnancy.

### Early in Pregnancy

Poor blood sugar control increases the risk of:

- Major birth defects in the baby
- Miscarriage

### Late in Pregnancy

Poor blood sugar control increases the risk of:

- A baby weighing more than 9 pounds (4 kilograms) at birth
- High blood pressure during pregnancy (called preeclampsia)
- Shoulder dystocia (the baby’s shoulder gets stuck during delivery)
- Needing a cesarean delivery (C-section)
- Stillbirth (the baby dies before birth)

Babies born to mothers with diabetes are often larger than average. A large baby is harder to deliver through the vagina. This increases the chance of injury during birth. A C-section may be needed.

The baby’s lungs may also mature more slowly. This means the baby may not be ready to breathe on its own at birth.

### Risks for the Newborn

Newborns of mothers with diabetes are more likely to have:

- Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia)
- Low blood calcium (hypocalcemia)
- High levels of bilirubin (hyperbilirubinemia), which can cause jaundice (yellow skin and eyes)

---

## How Is Diabetes Diagnosed During Pregnancy?

Doctors check blood sugar levels to find out if a woman has diabetes.

### Routine Screening

Most doctors recommend testing all pregnant women for gestational diabetes between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy.

### Blood Tests

The first test is a fasting blood test. The woman does not eat or drink anything except water for at least 8 hours before the test. A blood sample is taken to check blood sugar.

But the best test is the **oral glucose tolerance test**. It has two parts:

1. The woman drinks a sweet liquid that contains glucose.
2. One hour later, a blood sample is taken to check blood sugar.
   - If the level is too high, the test continues.
3. The woman drinks a larger amount of glucose.
4. Three hours later, another blood sample is taken.
   - If the level is still too high, diabetes is diagnosed.

This test helps confirm if diabetes is present.

---

## Treatment of Diabetes During Pregnancy

The goal is to keep blood sugar as close to normal as possible. This lowers the risk of problems.

### What Doctors Do

- Involve a team of experts: nurses, dietitians, social workers, and a pediatrician.
- Check the mother and baby often.
- Treat any health issues right away, even small ones.
- Plan the delivery carefully.
- Make sure a pediatrician is present at birth.
- Have newborn intensive care ready if needed.

### How to Control Blood Sugar

- Follow a healthy diet. Avoid sugary foods.
- Exercise regularly.
- Take insulin if needed. Some women may also need oral medications.
- Check blood sugar several times a day at home using a blood sugar monitor.

If blood sugar drops too low, it can cause confusion or loss of consciousness. This is called **hypoglycemia**.

Women at risk for low blood sugar are given a **glucagon kit**. This is a medicine that raises blood sugar quickly.

- The woman is taught how to use it.
- A family member is also taught how to use it.
- If symptoms of severe low blood sugar happen, the woman or a family member can give the injection.

### Late in Pregnancy

Blood sugar tends to rise late in pregnancy. More insulin is usually needed.

### Monitoring the Baby

Doctors check the baby’s health with tests such as:

- Fetal heart rate monitoring
- Nonstress tests
- Biophysical profiles (using ultrasound)

These tests usually start at 32 weeks. They may start earlier if there are concerns, such as:

- The baby is not growing well
- The mother has high blood pressure

### Amniocentesis

In some cases, doctors take a sample of the fluid around the baby (amniotic fluid). This is called **amniocentesis**.

This test is done if:

- The woman had problems in past pregnancies
- The due date is unclear
- Blood sugar has not been well controlled
- Care during pregnancy has been poor
- The woman is not following her treatment plan

The test helps check if the baby’s lungs are mature enough to breathe air. This helps decide when the baby can be delivered safely.

### Starting Labor

If labor has not started by 39 weeks, doctors may use medicine to start labor. This is called **induction of labor**.

Most women with diabetes can have a vaginal delivery.

### During Labor and Delivery

Many women with diabetes need insulin through a tube in a vein during labor. This helps keep blood sugar under control.

### After Birth

- The baby’s blood sugar, calcium, and bilirubin levels are checked right after birth.
- The baby is watched closely for signs of low blood sugar, low calcium, or jaundice.

### After Delivery

- The need for insulin drops sharply right after birth.
- The body usually returns to its normal insulin needs within about one week.

### Gestational Diabetes After Pregnancy

- Gestational diabetes usually goes away after delivery.
- But many women who had gestational diabetes go on to develop type 2 diabetes later in life.

---

## Key Takeaways

- Diabetes during pregnancy can be managed well with care.
- Keeping blood sugar under control is the most important step.
- Regular checkups and tests help protect both mother and baby.
- After delivery, follow-up care is important to prevent future health problems.

# Scheuermann Disease

## What Is Scheuermann Disease?

Scheuermann disease is a condition that affects the spine in young people.  
It causes changes in the bones of the spine.  
These changes can lead to back pain and a rounded back.  
The rounded back is called kyphosis.  

The condition usually starts during the teenage years.  
It is slightly more common in boys than in girls.  
In one study, between 1 in 100 and 1 in 10 people had this condition.  

Doctors do not fully understand what causes Scheuermann disease.  
It may be due to injury to the growth plates in the spine.  
It may also be linked to inflammation in the spine.  
Some cases run in families.  

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people with this condition have a hunched back.  
Their shoulders may look rounded forward.  
They often have a dull, ongoing backache.  
Some people have long arms and legs compared to their trunk.  
This can make them look similar to people with another condition called Marfan syndrome.  

The normal curve in the upper back becomes more curved than normal.  
This curve can be spread out over many vertebrae or focused in one area.  

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use X-rays of the spine to confirm the diagnosis.  
In some cases, they may use a CT scan or an MRI.  
Some cases are found during school health checks for spine problems.  

The X-ray shows that at least three bones in the spine are wedge-shaped.  
The front of these bones is narrower than the back.  
The angle of the wedge is at least five degrees.  
This change usually happens in the lower part of the upper back and the top of the lower back.  

Over time, the edges of the bones may become rough or hard.  
The spine may curve forward more than normal.  
In some cases, the spine may also curve sideways.  

If the doctor suspects another bone disorder, they may take X-rays of the whole body.  
If they think the problem could be an infection in the spine, they may use a CT scan or MRI.  

## How Is It Treated?

Most people do not need surgery.  
Treatment focuses on reducing stress on the spine.  
This means avoiding heavy lifting and high-impact sports.  
It also means avoiding activities that strain the back.  

These changes can help reduce pain.  
They may also stop the curve from getting worse.  

In some cases, a back brace may help.  
The brace supports the spine and helps keep it in a better position.  
Resting on a firm bed may also be recommended.  

Surgery is very rare.  
It is only used if the curve is getting worse.  
Surgery can help correct the spine and stop further problems.  

## What Is the Outlook?

The condition usually lasts for several years.  
It can be mild and does not always get worse.  
Even after the pain stops, some spine curvature may remain.  
The condition often becomes quiet and does not change much after a while.

# Polycystic Kidney Disease (PKD)

Polycystic kidney disease is a condition you are born with. It causes many fluid-filled sacs to grow in both kidneys. These sacs slowly get bigger. As they grow, they damage the healthy parts of the kidneys.

## What Causes PKD?

- PKD is caused by a faulty gene passed down from a parent.
- There are two main types: one is inherited from just one parent. The other is inherited from both parents.
- The type you have affects when symptoms start and how serious they are.

## How the Kidneys Work

Your kidneys clean waste from your blood. They also help control blood pressure and make sure your body has the right balance of fluids and salts.

## What Happens in PKD?

- Cysts grow in the kidneys over time.
- The kidneys get larger but work less well.
- The blood flow to the kidneys drops.
- Scar tissue builds up in the kidneys.
- Cysts can get infected or bleed.
- Kidney stones can form.
- Over time, the kidneys may stop working well. This is called chronic kidney disease.
- Cysts can also form in other organs, like the liver and pancreas.

## Types of PKD

### Recessive PKD (Rare, starts in childhood)

- This type is rare and serious.
- Cysts grow fast and make the belly look swollen.
- Babies with this condition may not survive long after birth.
- The kidneys and liver are both affected.
- By age 5 to 10, children often develop high pressure in the blood vessels of the liver.
- Eventually, liver failure and kidney failure happen.

### Dominant PKD (Most common, starts in adulthood)

- This type is more common.
- Cysts grow slowly over time.
- Most people do not have symptoms until their 20s or 30s.
- Some people never know they have the disease.
- Symptoms can be mild or not noticeable at all.

## Symptoms of PKD

- Pain in the side or lower back
- Blood in the urine
- Needing to urinate often
- Severe cramp-like pain from kidney stones
- Feeling tired, sick to your stomach, or weak (from poor kidney function)
- Fever that lasts for weeks (if a cyst bursts)
- Frequent urinary tract infections
- High blood pressure (this happens in at least half of people with PKD)

## Complications of PKD

- About one in three people with the dominant type also get cysts in the liver. These do not harm the liver.
- Some people develop hernias in the belly.
- Some get pouches in the large intestine (diverticulosis).
- Heart valve problems can happen.
- Up to 1 in 10 people get weak spots in blood vessels in the brain. These can burst and cause a stroke.

## How Is PKD Diagnosed?

- Doctors may suspect PKD if you have a family history of the disease.
- An imaging test done for another reason may show large kidneys with cysts.
- Ultrasound, CT scan, or MRI can show the cysts in the kidneys and liver.
- These tests are usually only done when symptoms appear.
- There is no cure yet, and early diagnosis can cause problems (like trouble getting life insurance).
- Genetic testing can help you understand the chance that your children will inherit the disease.

## How Is PKD Treated?

### Treating Symptoms and Complications

- Urinary tract infections are treated with antibiotics.
- High blood pressure is treated with medicine. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are often used.
- These medicines help slow kidney damage.

### Other Treatments

- If a cyst causes severe pain, a doctor may drain fluid from it. This can help with pain but does not change the long-term outcome.
- In rare cases, a kidney may need to be removed if it causes serious problems.
- A new medicine called tolvaptan may help slow the disease in some adults with the dominant type.
- Tolvaptan can cause serious liver damage. Doctors will talk to a specialist before giving it.

### Long-Term Outlook

- More than half of people with PKD will eventually need dialysis or a kidney transplant.
- Dialysis helps clean the blood when the kidneys no longer work.
- A kidney transplant replaces a failing kidney with a healthy one.

## Where to Find More Information

The following organizations offer helpful information in English:

- American Kidney Fund (AKF)
- National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK)
- National Kidney Foundation (NKF)

# Schizotypal Personality Disorder (STPD)

This condition affects how a person thinks, feels, and behaves. It makes it hard to form close relationships. People with this disorder often see the world in unusual ways. They may act in odd or strange ways. They may also have trouble thinking clearly or speaking in a normal way.

Doctors diagnose this condition based on symptoms and behavior. There is no single test. Treatment includes medicine, talk therapy, and emotional support.

---

## What Causes Schizotypal Personality Disorder?

Scientists believe this disorder is mostly due to biology. It shares brain changes with schizophrenia. It is more common in people who have a close family member with schizophrenia or another serious mental illness.

---

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

People with this disorder often have no close friends. They may only feel close to their parents, siblings, or children. They feel very uncomfortable around others. They may talk to people only when they must. They feel different from others and do not fit in.

Even after being around people for a long time, they still feel anxious. They may say they are lonely and unhappy about their lack of relationships.

They often believe that ordinary things are about them. For example, they may think a news story or a song is meant just for them. They may believe in magic, mind reading, or special powers. They might think their actions can control other people or prevent bad things.

Their speech may be strange. It can be too vague, too detailed, or use odd words. They may dress in unusual or messy ways. They may act in odd ways, like not making eye contact or not following social rules.

They often feel suspicious. They may think others are trying to harm them or are against them.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor uses the DSM-5-TR to make a diagnosis. To be diagnosed, a person must show a long-term pattern of:

- Strong discomfort in close relationships  
- Strange thoughts, beliefs, or odd behavior  

And at least five of the following:

- Believing that everyday events are about them (but not full-blown delusions)  
- Holding unusual beliefs, like magic, telepathy, or clairvoyance  
- Having strange sensory experiences, like hearing a whisper of their name  
- Speaking in odd or confusing ways  
- Being suspicious or having paranoid thoughts  
- Showing emotions that do not match the situation  
- Acting in odd, strange, or unusual ways  
- Having no close friends except family  
- Feeling extreme social anxiety that does not go away, even with time  

These symptoms must start by early adulthood.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment helps people feel better and live more normally. It includes:

### Medicines
- Atypical antipsychotic medicines help reduce anxiety and strange thoughts.  
- Antidepressants can help with social anxiety and low mood.

### Talk Therapy
- Cognitive-behavioral therapy helps people learn how to act in social situations.  
- It teaches how to manage fear and anxiety.  
- It also helps people understand how others see them.

### Emotional Support
- Supportive therapy builds a safe, caring relationship.  
- It helps people develop healthier ways to handle stress and relationships.

---

## Important Notes

- This disorder often happens with other mental health problems.  
- Over half of people with this disorder have had major depression.  
- Many also have problems with alcohol or drug use.  
- Men may be slightly more likely to have this condition than women.

Treatment works best when it is consistent and tailored to the person. Early help can make a big difference.

# Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition Disease

This condition happens when small crystals build up in the joints. These crystals cause pain and swelling. It can feel like gout or rheumatoid arthritis.

- The crystals form in the joint fluid and cartilage.
- They cause inflammation and damage to the joint.
- Doctors confirm the diagnosis by looking at joint fluid under a microscope.
- There is no treatment that removes the crystals.
- Medicines can help reduce pain and swelling.

This disease mostly affects older adults. It affects men and women equally.

## What Causes This Disease?

We do not know exactly why some people get these crystals. But certain conditions increase the risk:

- A past injury to a joint, including surgery
- Gout
- A buildup of an abnormal protein in the body (amyloidosis)
- Too much calcium in the blood due to overactive parathyroid glands (hyperparathyroidism)
- Too much iron in the body (hemochromatosis)
- Too little magnesium in the blood (hypomagnesemia)
- Rare genetic conditions like hypophosphatasia, Gitelman syndrome, hypophosphatemic rickets, and familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia
- Getting older

Many people with this disease have none of these conditions. It rarely runs in families.

The crystals often appear in joints already damaged by osteoarthritis. But having crystals does not always mean you will have symptoms.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms can be very different from person to person.

Some people have sudden, painful joint flares. These often happen in the knees, wrists, or other large joints. The pain can feel like gout.

Others have long-term joint pain and stiffness in the arms and legs. This can feel like rheumatoid arthritis or osteoarthritis.

Compared to gout, CPPD flares:

- Can vary in how bad they are
- Often last longer
- Are harder to treat

Flares can cause fever. Some people feel no pain between flares. Some never feel pain, even with many crystals in the joint.

Unlike gout, people with this disease rarely get hard lumps of crystals under the skin (tophi).

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tools to diagnose this disease:

- **Joint fluid test**: A doctor takes a sample of fluid from an inflamed joint. They look at it under a special microscope. This can show calcium pyrophosphate crystals. These look different from the crystals that cause gout.
- **X-rays**: These can show crystal deposits in the cartilage. This can suggest the diagnosis.
- **Ultrasound**: This can also show crystals in the joint cartilage. It strongly suggests the disease.

Doctors often suspect this disease in older adults with joint pain and swelling that comes and goes.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment focuses on relieving pain and swelling during flares. It does not remove the crystals.

- **Drain fluid and inject steroids**: A doctor can remove extra fluid from the joint. They can then inject a steroid medicine directly into the joint. This helps reduce pain and swelling fast.
- **Pain and swelling medicines**: Pills can help control pain and swelling during flares.
- **Physical therapy**: Exercises to strengthen muscles and improve joint movement can help keep joints working well.

For acute flares, treatment is similar to gout.

- **Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)**: These pills are often the first choice. They help stop pain and swelling quickly.
- **Colchicine**: A low daily dose (usually one or two pills) can help reduce how often flares happen.
- **Oral steroids**: These pills work well for flares. They are especially helpful for people who cannot take NSAIDs or colchicine.
- **Other medicines**: If a person cannot take steroids, NSAIDs, or colchicine, other medicines that reduce inflammation and immune system activity (like anakinra injections) may help.

There is no long-term treatment that removes or reduces the crystals. Physical therapy can help maintain joint function.

## What Is the Outlook?

Most people recover from joint flares without lasting problems.

But in some people, the disease becomes long-term. This can lead to permanent joint damage. In severe cases, joints can become so damaged they look like those in a condition called neurogenic arthropathy (Charcot joints).

Unlike gout, there is no treatment that removes the crystals. This makes long-term control harder.

People who have frequent flares, especially younger people, should be checked for other health problems that might be causing the disease.

# Secondary Iron Overload

This condition happens when too much iron builds up in the body. It is not the same as the inherited type of iron overload. It usually affects people who have problems making healthy red blood cells.

## What Causes Secondary Iron Overload?

Secondary iron overload often happens in people with:

- Sickle cell disease  
- Thalassemia  
- Sideroblastic anemias  
- Other inherited anemias like hereditary spherocytosis  
- Myelodysplasia (a bone marrow disorder)

The extra iron comes from:

- The body absorbing too much iron from food  
- Taking iron supplements  
- Getting many blood transfusions

Each blood transfusion adds about 250 milligrams of iron. When a person gets more than 40 transfusions, iron starts to build up in the body.

In some people, the body makes a substance called erythroferrone. This substance lowers a natural blocker of iron absorption. This leads to more iron being taken in from food.

People with these blood disorders now live longer. So, iron overload is a major concern. It can damage the heart, liver, and hormone glands. It can even lead to death. But removing iron can help people live longer.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Iron overload can cause many problems. Some symptoms appear early. Others show up only after damage has happened.

Common early signs include:

- Feeling very tired  
- General weakness  
- Trouble with blood sugar control (this can lead to diabetes)  
- Low thyroid function (hypothyroidism)  
- In men: low sex drive and trouble getting or keeping an erection

The liver is the most commonly affected organ. It can become damaged and scarred. This is called cirrhosis. People with cirrhosis have a higher risk of liver cancer.

Liver problems may not cause clear symptoms at first. You might only feel tired or have pain in the upper right side of your belly. Your liver may be larger than normal.

Other signs include:

- Darkening of the skin (like a bronze color)  
- A skin condition called porphyria cutanea tarda  
- Joint pain and stiffness (arthropathy)  
- Heart problems, including heart failure

Liver disease is the most common cause of death. Heart failure is the second most common.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors check for iron overload using blood tests.

The first test is a serum ferritin test. This measures how much iron is stored in the body.

- In women, a level above 200 nanograms per milliliter is high.  
- In men, a level above 250 nanograms per milliliter is high.

High ferritin levels usually mean iron overload. But other conditions can raise ferritin too. These include:

- Inherited iron overload (hemochromatosis)  
- Liver disease from viruses, alcohol, or fatty liver  
- Cancer  
- Inflammatory diseases like rheumatoid arthritis  
- Obesity

If ferritin is high, doctors do more tests:

- Fasting serum iron: levels above 300 micrograms per deciliter are high  
- Transferrin saturation: this should be above 50% in iron overload

To rule out inherited iron overload, doctors may do a genetic test.

A transferrin saturation below 45% makes iron overload very unlikely.

## How Is It Treated?

The main treatment is iron chelation. This means using medicine to remove extra iron from the body.

### Chelation Medicine Options

**Deferoxamine**  
- Given as a slow injection under the skin at night  
- Used 5 to 7 nights a week  
- Dose: 40 to 50 milligrams per kilogram of body weight per day  
- For children over 3 years: 20 to 40 mg/kg/day, given over 8 to 12 hours, 5 to 7 days a week  
- Maximum dose: 40 mg/kg/day  

This treatment is hard to follow. It takes a lot of time and effort. Many people do not stick with it.

Side effects can include:

- Low blood pressure  
- Stomach upset  
- Allergic reactions (rare but serious)  
- Vision or hearing loss with long-term use

**Deferasirox**  
- Taken by mouth once a day  
- Starts at 20 mg/kg per day  
- Dose can be raised to 30 mg/kg per day if needed  
- Maximum dose: 40 mg/kg per day  
- If using granules: start at 14 mg/kg per day, max 28 mg/kg per day  

This medicine is easier to take than deferoxamine. It helps lower iron levels and can prevent serious problems.

Side effects happen in about 1 in 10 people. They include:

- Nausea  
- Belly pain  
- Diarrhea  
- Skin rash  

Liver and kidney function can be affected. Blood tests should be done every month. More often if you are at higher risk.

Treatment can be paused if ferritin drops below 500 nanograms per milliliter.

**Deferiprone**  
- Taken by mouth three times a day  
- Starts at 25 mg/kg per dose  
- Maximum: 33 mg/kg per dose, three times a day  

This medicine is used when deferasirox or deferoxamine do not work well.

It can also be used with deferasirox. The two work in different ways.

You must have blood tests every week to check white blood cells. This helps catch a rare but serious drop in white blood cells (neutropenia) early.

Ferritin is checked every 2 to 3 months. Treatment is paused if levels stay below 500 nanograms per milliliter.

### Other Treatments

- Diabetes is treated with medicine or insulin.  
- Heart problems are managed with heart medications.  
- Erectile dysfunction can be treated with medicine.  
- Joint pain may need pain relief or physical therapy.

If you have liver scarring (fibrosis) or cirrhosis from iron overload, you should be checked every 6 months for liver cancer. This includes a liver ultrasound and blood tests like alpha fetoprotein.

## Lifestyle Tips

- Eat a balanced diet. You do not need to avoid iron-rich foods like red meat or liver.  
- Drink alcohol only in small amounts. Alcohol can raise iron levels and damage the liver.  
- Do not take vitamin C supplements. They make your body absorb more iron.

## Key Points

- Secondary iron overload happens when the body gets too much iron.  
- It is caused by too much iron absorption, repeated blood transfusions, or too many iron supplements.  
- It can damage the liver, heart, skin, joints, and hormone glands.  
- It can lead to diabetes, heart failure, and liver cancer.  
- Diagnosis starts with a blood test for ferritin. High levels need more testing.  
- Treatment is usually iron chelation with medicine.  
- Early treatment can prevent serious damage and help you live longer.

It is based on the idea that energy flows through the body.  
Reiki practitioners use their hands to help move this energy.  
They may place their hands lightly on or just above the body.  
They do not press hard or make strong contact.

# Hypertensive Retinopathy

Hypertensive retinopathy is damage to the blood vessels in the retina caused by high blood pressure.  
The signs of this condition usually appear only after the disease has been present for a long time.  
A doctor checks the retina using a special eye instrument called an ophthalmoscope.  
This exam can show several changes in the blood vessels.

## What Happens in the Eyes

High blood pressure can cause the blood vessels in the retina to narrow.  
This narrowing is often the first sign.  
Over time, the blood vessels may become thick and stiff.  
This can cause the arteries to look like copper wires or silver wires.  
The place where an artery crosses a vein may become damaged. This is called arteriovenous nicking.  
This damage can increase the risk of a blockage in a retinal vein.

If blood pressure rises very quickly, the optic nerve at the back of the eye may swell.  
This is called optic disk edema.  
It can happen during a hypertensive crisis.  
A hypertensive crisis is a sudden and dangerous rise in blood pressure.

Leaking blood vessels can cause small, white spots on the retina.  
These are called cotton-wool spots.  
They are signs of poor blood flow to parts of the retina.  
Leaking vessels can also cause red, flame-shaped spots.  
These are called flame-shaped hemorrhages.  
Fatty deposits from leaking vessels can form yellow spots.  
These are called hard exudates.  
They may form a star shape in the center of the retina, especially if the blood pressure is very high.

## Why This Matters

High blood pressure is a major risk factor for other eye problems.  
These include blockages in the retinal arteries or veins.  
It also increases the risk of diabetic retinopathy.  
When high blood pressure and diabetes happen together, the risk of vision loss is much higher.  
People with hypertensive retinopathy are also at risk for damage to other organs.  
This includes the heart, kidneys, and brain.

## What You Might Feel

Most people do not notice any symptoms at first.  
Symptoms usually appear only when the damage is advanced.  
You may notice blurry vision.  
You might also see dark spots or missing areas in your vision.

## How It Is Diagnosed

Doctors diagnose this condition by asking about your blood pressure history.  
They will want to know how long you have had high blood pressure.  
They will also check your eyes with an ophthalmoscope.  
This exam shows changes in the blood vessels of the retina.

## How It Is Treated

The main treatment is to control your blood pressure.  
This is the most important step.  
Lowering blood pressure can slow or stop further damage.  
If you have vision loss, your doctor may treat the swelling in the retina.  
This can be done with laser treatment.  
Or, medicine may be injected into the eye.  
These medicines include corticosteroids or drugs that block a substance called VEGF.  
Examples of VEGF-blocking drugs are ranibizumab, pegaptanib, and bevacizumab.

## Key Points

- High blood pressure slowly damages the retina.  
- You may not notice any symptoms until the damage is serious.  
- Long-term high blood pressure causes permanent narrowing of the arteries.  
- It can cause arteriovenous nicking.  
- Arteries may look like copper wires or silver wires.  
- A sudden, severe rise in blood pressure can cause swelling of the optic nerve.  
- It can also cause flame-shaped bleeding, white spots, yellow deposits, and optic nerve swelling.  
- Diagnosis is based on your blood pressure history and an eye exam.  
- Treatment focuses on lowering blood pressure.  
- For vision problems, laser or eye injections may help.

# Achilles Tendon Tears

Achilles tendon tears happen when the strong cord that connects your calf muscle to your heel bone breaks.

- The tear often happens when you push your toes up toward your shin too hard.
- It can also happen during running, jumping, or sudden movements.
- The calf becomes very painful. Walking is hard, especially if the tear is complete.
- Doctors can usually tell if you have a tear by doing a physical exam.

## What Causes Achilles Tendon Tears?

- These injuries are common in athletes and middle-aged men who are not used to physical activity.
- They often happen when someone starts a new sport or activity without warming up or building up slowly.
- The injury usually occurs during running or jumping, especially in sports that require quick direction changes.
- The tendon tears when the foot is pushed up too far and too fast.

Rarely, the tendon can tear without any injury if you are taking certain medicines:
- Fluoroquinolone antibiotics (like ciprofloxacin)
- Corticosteroids

## What Are the Symptoms?

- You may feel like someone kicked you behind the ankle.
- You might hear a pop at the time of injury.
- The calf is very painful.
- Walking is difficult, especially with a full tear.
- The area may swell and turn bruised.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor will check your leg and foot. They may do the following:

- Squeeze your calf while you lie face down. If your foot does not move or barely moves, the tendon is likely torn.
- Ask you to lie face down with your knees bent. If your ankle does not hang down slightly, the tendon may be torn.
- Feel along the back of your heel while you stand on the injured leg. If you feel a gap, the tendon is torn.

Sometimes, doctors use imaging tests like MRI or ultrasound. But a physical exam is usually enough to make the diagnosis.

## How Is It Treated?

- You will be referred to an orthopedic surgeon.
- A splint or cast may be used for partial or complete tears.
- Some complete tears need surgery right away.
- Surgery may also be needed if a partial tear does not improve after 3 months.

### What You Should Do

- Do not put weight on the injured ankle.
- Use crutches to help you move.
- Wear the splint as directed.
- Follow your doctor’s advice.

The splint holds your foot in a downward position. This helps the tendon heal by keeping it from stretching. After a short time, your surgeon will decide if you need a cast or surgery.

# Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder

This is a mental health condition where a person feels disconnected from themselves or their surroundings. It is a type of dissociative disorder.

## What It Feels Like

You may feel like you are watching your own life from outside your body.  
You might feel unreal, like a robot, or like you have no control over your actions.  
You may feel emotionally numb or unable to feel anything.  
You might not be able to name or understand your own emotions.

You may also feel disconnected from your surroundings.  
The world may seem dreamlike, foggy, or unreal.  
People, objects, or everything around you may feel distant or artificial.  
Colors may seem dull. Sounds may seem too loud or too soft.  
Time may feel like it is moving too fast or too slow.  
Objects may look blurry, too big, too small, or flat.

These feelings are not just thoughts. They are real experiences for the person.  
But the person always knows these feelings are not true.  
They know they are not losing their mind or going crazy.

## How Common Is It?

Many people have had a brief moment of feeling detached at some point in their life.  
This happens in 25% to 75% of people at some time.  
But only about 1 to 2 out of every 100 people have this condition long-term.

## What Causes It?

This disorder often starts after a very stressful event.  
Common causes include:

- Emotional abuse or neglect as a child  
- Physical abuse  
- Seeing violence at home  
- Having a parent who is very ill or mentally unwell  
- Losing a loved one suddenly

Other triggers can include:

- Stress from relationships, work, or money  
- Depression  
- Anxiety  
- Using illegal drugs like marijuana, ketamine, or hallucinogens

## When Does It Start?

The condition usually begins around age 16.  
It can start in childhood.  
Only 5% of cases begin after age 25.  
It is very rare for it to start after age 40.

It affects men and women equally.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors will ask about your symptoms and how they affect your life.  
They will check for other possible causes, such as brain problems or other mental health issues.

To rule out other problems, doctors may do:

- A brain scan (MRI)  
- A test of brain waves (EEG)  
- A urine test to check for drugs

The diagnosis is based on the DSM-5-TR guidelines.  
You must have:

- Recurring or ongoing feelings of being detached from yourself or your surroundings  
- Awareness that these feelings are not real (you still know what is real)  
- Symptoms that cause serious distress or make daily life hard  
- No better explanation from another medical or mental health condition

Special questionnaires and interviews can help confirm the diagnosis.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment focuses on helping you manage stress and trauma.  
It also helps you deal with past experiences that may have made you more likely to feel this way.

### Psychotherapy (Talk Therapy)

Different types of therapy can help:

- **Cognitive therapy** helps you stop obsessing over feeling unreal.  
- **Behavioral therapy** teaches you to focus on tasks that take your mind off the feeling.  
- **Grounding techniques** use your five senses. For example:  
  - Listen to loud music  
  - Hold something cold, like ice  
  - Touch a textured object  
  - Name five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell, one you can taste  
  These help you feel more connected to the present moment.

- **Psychodynamic therapy** helps you understand and work through painful emotions or past experiences that you may have pushed away.

- **Tracking feelings in real time** means naming your emotions and dissociation as they happen during therapy. This helps you stay aware and in control.

### Medications

No medicine has been proven to directly treat this condition.  
But some people feel better when they take medicine for related problems, such as:

- Depression  
- Anxiety

Medicines that may help include:

- Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)  
- Lamotrigine  
- Opioid antagonists  
- Anti-anxiety medicines  
- Stimulants

These medicines work best when you also have depression or anxiety.

## What Is the Outlook?

Many people get better over time.  
Recovery is more likely if the cause was temporary or treatable.

Some people have symptoms for years or even decades.  
But even then, they can live full lives if they learn ways to manage the feelings.

If you can stay busy with work, hobbies, or conversations, you may feel less affected.  
You can distract yourself and stay focused on the outside world.

However, some people become very disabled.  
This can happen if the feeling of being disconnected is constant.  
It can also happen if you have ongoing anxiety or depression.

## Key Points

- You are not losing your mind. You know the feelings are not real.  
- The condition is not caused by brain damage or psychosis.  
- It is often linked to past trauma or stress.  
- Treatment can help you feel more connected and in control.  
- Recovery is possible, even if symptoms last a long time.

# How Life Changes Affect Older Adults

Older age often brings big changes. These can include retiring from work, moving to a new home, or losing someone close. Adjusting to these changes can be hard. Everyone handles them differently.

---

## Retirement

Retirement is one of the biggest changes many older adults face. How it affects health depends on how a person feels about it and why they retired.

- About one in three retirees struggle with changes like less money or a new role in life.
- Some people look forward to retirement and plan for it.
- Others must retire early because of health problems or losing their job.

Planning ahead can help. Counseling can also help retirees and their families if they are having a hard time. Many workplaces and local groups offer help with retirement planning.

> **Did You Know?**  
> Many employers and community groups offer free help with retirement planning.

---

## Moving to a New Home

Older adults may move more than once as they get older. Reasons for moving include:

- Moving to a retirement community with better services.
- Moving to a smaller home to make cleaning and maintenance easier.
- Moving to a warmer climate.
- Moving closer to family.
- Moving in with a relative.
- Moving into a care home.

People who do not adjust well to moving are more likely to be:

- Living alone.
- Feeling lonely.
- Low on money.
- Feeling sad or depressed.

Men often find moving harder than women.

Some older adults stay in a home they do not like because they cannot afford to move or do not know how. Social workers can help them explore options, like moving or making changes to their current home.

Many people feel stressed when moving because they feel they have no control. They also do not know what to expect in the new place.

For people with memory problems, moving away from familiar places can make confusion worse. It can also make them more dependent on others. This can lead to frustration.

Even if a move happens quickly, a little preparation can help reduce stress. If possible:

- Visit the new home ahead of time.
- Meet neighbors.
- Get to know the area.

These steps can make the move feel less scary.

---

## Grief, Depression, and Suicide Risk

Losing someone close is hard on older adults. It can affect:

- How often they see people.
- Their sense of belonging.
- Their money situation.
- Their health.

After losing a close person, some older adults get sicker. The death of a spouse affects men and women differently.

- Men are more likely to die in the two years after their wife dies, especially if her death was sudden.
- For women, the risk of dying after losing a husband is not clearly higher.

It is normal to feel sad, have trouble sleeping, or feel anxious after a loss. These feelings usually go away in a few weeks or months without medicine.

But if grief lasts too long, or if a person cannot do basic tasks like eating or bathing, or if they talk about ending their life, they need help from a doctor.

If a doctor finds signs of depression, they may refer the person to a mental health expert. Sometimes medicine can help with depression or anxiety.

### Screening for Depression

Checking for depression is an important part of a doctor visit. Caregivers and health workers should watch for signs of sadness or hopelessness. People who have lost someone are at high risk for suicide and worsening health.

- Suicide risk goes up with age.
- In the United States in 2022, older men were almost four times more likely to die by suicide than older women.

But suicide rates in older adults may be higher than reported. For example:

- Many deaths from opioid overdoses are not fully investigated.
- Some people choose not to eat or drink, and these deaths are not always recorded as intentional.

Older adults often do not talk about suicide. They also rarely ask for help. Doctors are less likely to offer mental health treatment to older adults than to younger people.

Even though older adults try suicide less often, they are more likely to die from it. This is because:

- They often use guns, which are more deadly.
- They are more likely to be sick or frail.
- They may avoid medical help.
- They often live alone, so no one notices a suicide attempt.

Because of this, the risk of dying by suicide is high for older adults who are thinking about it.

### What Can Help?

- Early screening for depression and suicidal thoughts is key.
- Doctors ask specific questions to check suicide risk, especially after a loss or if someone seems very sad.
- Counseling, support groups (like the National Widowers Organization), and medicine can help during tough times.
- Health workers should save the 988 Lifeline number in their phone and show older adults how to use it. They can call, text, or chat with a trained counselor.

---
