# Swelling During Late Pregnancy

Swelling in the feet, ankles, and lower legs is common during the last part of pregnancy.  
This happens because the body holds on to extra fluid.  
It is normal to have some swelling, especially in the third trimester.  
The medical term for this is edema.  
Sometimes the fingers also swell a little.  

If your hands swell more than a little, or if your face swells, you should see a doctor.  

## Why Swelling Happens

Your body makes more fluid during pregnancy.  
This is partly because your adrenal glands make more of certain hormones.  
These hormones cause your body to keep more fluid.  
Also, your growing baby pushes on blood vessels in your legs.  
This slows down blood flow back to your heart.  
As a result, fluid leaks out into the tissues around your legs.  

## Causes of Swelling

Most of the time, swelling is normal and not a problem.  
But sometimes it can be a sign of a serious health issue.  

### Preeclampsia  
This is a serious condition that only happens during pregnancy.  
It causes high blood pressure and extra protein in the urine.  
You may notice swelling in your face, hands, or feet.  
You may also gain weight quickly.  
Not all women with preeclampsia have swelling.  
If it gets worse, it can harm your brain, kidneys, lungs, or liver.  
It can also harm your baby.  

### Deep Vein Thrombosis  
This means a blood clot forms in a deep vein, usually in the leg.  
Pregnancy increases your risk.  
Your body makes more clotting factors to prevent heavy bleeding during childbirth.  
This makes clots more likely.  
If you are not moving much, blood can pool in your legs and form clots.  
If a clot breaks loose, it can travel to your lungs.  
This can block blood flow and cause a life-threatening condition called pulmonary embolism.  

### Peripartum Cardiomyopathy  
This is a rare but serious heart problem.  
It can happen late in pregnancy or after delivery.  
It causes shortness of breath, tiredness, and swelling in the legs.  

## Risk Factors

Some women are more likely to develop these serious conditions.  

### Risk Factors for Preeclampsia  
- You had preeclampsia in a past pregnancy  
- You are carrying more than one baby  
- You had high blood pressure before pregnancy  
- You have diabetes  
- You have kidney problems  
- You have an autoimmune disease  
- You had a molar pregnancy (a rare abnormal growth in the uterus)  

### Moderate Risk for Preeclampsia  
- This is your first pregnancy  
- You are overweight or obese  
- A close family member had preeclampsia  
- You are of African ancestry  
- You have a low income  
- You are 35 years old or older  
- You got pregnant through IVF  
- You have had a baby with low birth weight  
- You have had a bad pregnancy outcome before  
- It has been more than 10 years since your last pregnancy  

### Risk Factors for Deep Vein Thrombosis  
- You have had a blood clot before  
- You have a family history of blood clots  
- You have injured a leg vein  
- You have cancer, heart disease, or kidney disease  
- You smoke cigarettes  
- You are not moving much (after surgery or illness)  
- You are overweight or obese  

### Risk Factors for Peripartum Cardiomyopathy  
- You are 30 years old or older  
- You have had heart problems before  
- You are of African ancestry  
- You are carrying more than one baby  
- You had preeclampsia  
- You had high blood pressure before pregnancy  

## When to See a Doctor

You should go to the hospital right away if you have any of these warning signs:  
- Swelling in your hands that is more than mild (your hands look puffy or a ring won’t come off)  
- Swelling that gets worse quickly in any part of your body  
- Swelling in just one leg or calf, especially if it feels warm, red, or tender  
- Blood pressure of 140 over 90 or higher  
- Severe headache that won’t go away  
- Blurred or changed vision  
- Confusion  
- Pain in the upper belly  
- Trouble breathing  

If you do not have these warning signs, you can see your doctor.  
Waiting a few days is usually safe.  

## How Doctors Check for Swelling

Doctors want to rule out serious causes before saying the swelling is normal.  

They will ask:  
- When the swelling started  
- How long it has lasted  
- If lying on your left side helps or makes it worse  

They will also ask about your health history.  
They want to know if you have had:  
- Blood clots  
- Pulmonary embolism  
- Preeclampsia  
- High blood pressure  
- Heart problems  

During the exam, they will:  
- Check your blood pressure  
- Listen to your heart and lungs  
- Look at your eyes with a special light tool  
- Check for swelling in your legs, hands, and face  
- Feel for redness, warmth, or tenderness  

## Possible Causes and How They Are Diagnosed

| Cause | Common Signs | How It Is Checked |
|-------|--------------|-------------------|
| Normal swelling | Swelling in both legs, no pain | Doctor’s exam only |
| Preeclampsia | High blood pressure, swelling in face/hands/feet, headache, vision changes, belly pain | Blood pressure check, urine test for protein, blood tests for liver/kidney, blood count |
| Deep vein thrombosis | Swelling and pain in one leg, redness, warmth, tenderness | Ultrasound of the leg, sometimes a blood test (D-dimer) |
| Pulmonary embolism (if clot travels to lungs) | Chest pain, trouble breathing | CT scan of chest or lung scan |
| Peripartum cardiomyopathy | Swelling in both legs, shortness of breath, tiredness, trouble lying flat | Chest x-ray, EKG, echocardiogram, blood tests for heart stress |

If preeclampsia is suspected:  
- A urine sample is tested for protein  
- Blood tests check liver, kidneys, and blood count  
- High blood pressure plus high protein in urine means preeclampsia  
- If unsure, you may collect all your urine for 24 hours to test protein levels  

If deep vein thrombosis is suspected:  
- An ultrasound of the leg checks for blood clots  

If peripartum cardiomyopathy is suspected:  
- Tests include chest x-ray, EKG, echocardiogram, and blood tests for heart strain  

## How Swelling Is Treated

If swelling is caused by a serious condition, the condition is treated.  

If swelling is normal during pregnancy, you can reduce it by:  
- Lying on your left side to help blood flow  
- Resting with your legs raised above your heart  
- Wearing compression stockings  
- Wearing loose clothes that do not squeeze your legs  
- Avoiding tight socks or stockings with tight bands  

## Key Points

- Some swelling in the legs and ankles is normal during pregnancy.  
- It is most common in the third trimester.  
- Doctors can find serious causes using exams, blood pressure checks, blood and urine tests, and sometimes ultrasounds.  
- If swelling is due to pregnancy, it can be eased by lying on your left side, raising your legs, wearing support stockings, and wearing loose clothing.

# Heart Tests and Procedures Explained Simply

There are many tests that can show how your heart is built and how well it works. Some tests do not need surgery. Others need a small procedure inside your body.

Some tests can also be used to treat heart problems at the same time.

---

## Common Heart Tests

Here are the main tests used to check your heart.

### How Well Your Left Side of the Heart Works

These tests check how well the main pumping chamber of your heart is working.

- **Cardiac CT scan**: A special X-ray that takes detailed pictures of your heart.
- **Contrast ventriculography**: A test that uses dye and X-rays to see how your heart pumps.
- **Echocardiography**: Uses sound waves to make moving pictures of your heart.
- **Gated MRI**: A scan that uses magnets and radio waves to show heart movement.
- **MUGA scan**: A test that uses a small amount of radiation to track blood flow in your heart.
- **PET scan**: A scan that shows how well heart tissue is using energy.
- **SPECT scan**: A test that uses radiation to show blood flow in the heart muscle.

### Finding Out If You Have Blockages in Heart Arteries

These tests help find if your heart arteries are narrowed or blocked.

- **Coronary angiography**: A test that uses dye and X-rays to see the inside of your heart arteries.
- **Stress testing**: Checks your heart while you exercise or when medicine makes your heart work harder. It can use an ECG, an echo, or a scan.
- **Intravascular ultrasound**: A small camera on a thin tube that takes pictures inside your heart arteries.
- **Magnetic resonance angiography**: A scan that uses magnets to show blood vessels in the heart.
- **Multidetector CT coronary angiography**: A fast CT scan that shows heart arteries in detail.

### Checking If Heart Muscle Is Still Alive After a Heart Attack

These tests help find out if heart muscle is still healthy or if it is damaged.

- **Gated MRI**: Shows how well the heart muscle moves and if it is alive.
- **PET scan**: Shows how heart tissue uses energy. This helps find living tissue.
- **Resting SPECT scan**: A scan that checks blood flow in the heart when you are at rest.
- **Stress test with low-dose dobutamine and echo**: A test that uses a medicine to make your heart beat harder. An echo checks how the heart responds.

# Parts of a Limb Prosthesis

A limb prosthesis has four main parts:

- Interface  
- Suspension  
- Structural components  
- Appearance components  

---

## How the Prosthesis Connects to the Body

The prosthesis connects to your body through direct skin contact or through a special interface. This interface is a thin cushion worn over the part of your limb that is left after amputation.

### Gel Cushion Interface

- A gel cushion goes over your residual limb.  
- It protects your skin and helps spread pressure evenly.  
- If your limb has scars, sharp bones, or burns, you may need a custom-made interface.  
- It is best to have two identical interfaces.  
- Use one today and the other tomorrow.  
- This helps the interface keep its shape and last longer.  
- Replace the interface every 6 months.  
- If you are very active, replace it every 3 to 4 months.  

### Prosthetic Socks

- You can wear a prosthetic sock instead of or with a gel cushion.  
- Socks are made from wool, nylon, or synthetic materials.  
- Some socks have gel between the layers.  
- Socks come in different thicknesses.  
- Your residual limb changes size during the day.  
- This happens because of activity, weather, or other reasons.  
- You can add or remove socks to adjust the fit.  
- This helps keep the prosthesis comfortable all day.  
- If socks and pads do not help, your prosthetist can adjust the socket.  
- A prosthetist is a specialist who makes, fits, and adjusts prostheses.  

---

## How the Prosthesis Stays on the Limb

Suspension means how the prosthesis stays on your body. Some gel materials work better with certain types of suspension.

### Vacuum Suspension

- A pump removes air from the socket.  
- This creates a strong hold.  
- It also helps control fluid in the limb.  
- Urethane gel is best for this type of suspension.  

### Passive Suction

- When you put your limb in the socket, air is pushed out.  
- A seal stops air from coming back in.  
- This creates suction.  
- A one-way valve at the bottom of the socket lets air out.  

### Locking Pin System

- The interface has a small metal pin at the bottom.  
- The pin fits into a locking part in the socket.  
- To take off the prosthesis, press a release button.  
- The pin comes out and the prosthesis comes off.  

### Anatomical Suspension

- Natural bumps on bones (like at the knee, ankle, or elbow) help hold the socket in place.  

### Belts and Straps

- Belts or straps can hold the prosthesis on.  
- This is an option if you cannot use vacuum, suction, or pin systems.  

---

## The Main Parts of the Prosthesis

The prosthesis has these basic parts:

- Socket  
- Appendage (hand or foot)  
- Joint (wrist, elbow, shoulder, ankle, knee, or hip)  
- Connecting module that joins the appendage and joint to the socket  

### The Socket

- The socket is the part that holds your residual limb.  
- It is made of plastic.  
- It is the most important part.  
- It supports your body.  
- It sends movement forces to your limb.  

### Lower Limb Prostheses

- Microprocessor-controlled ankles and knees help you walk more safely.  
- They give better balance.  
- They use less energy.  
- They reduce stress on nearby joints and your spine.  

### Upper Limb Prostheses

- Body-powered prostheses need a working shoulder and arm.  
- You use a loop strap to control the hand or hook.  
- Myoelectric prostheses do not need a full working arm.  
- They use your body’s natural electrical signals.  
- Electrodes in the socket pick up muscle activity.  
- These signals control the hand, wrist, or elbow.  
- No other body movement is needed.  

---

## How the Prosthesis Looks

Some people want their prosthesis to look like a real limb.

### Natural Appearance

- Technicians cover the plastic and metal parts with soft foam.  
- The foam feels like real muscle and tissue.  
- This helps protect your clothes.  
- The shape can be made to match your other limb.  
- A synthetic skin is added.  
- It matches your skin color.  

### Performance-Style Design

- Some people, especially athletes, prefer a bare look.  
- They leave the plastic and metal parts exposed.  
- This makes the prosthesis lighter.  
- It allows more adjustments.  
- This can improve performance.

# Pelvic Fractures – Simple Explanation

A pelvic fracture means one or more bones in the pelvis are broken. The pelvis is the ring of bones at the base of your spine. It includes the pubic bone, the hip bones, the sacrum, and the sacroiliac joints.

These fractures can be mild or very serious. Some are stable and do not move much. Others are unstable and can shift, which can cause heavy bleeding.

Other injuries can happen at the same time. These may include damage to the bladder, urethra, intestines, or nerves.

---

## How Pelvic Fractures Happen

The pelvis is like a strong ring made of bones and tough ligaments. If the ring breaks in two or more places, it becomes unstable.

Most pelvic fractures happen from high-energy events. The most common causes are:
- Car crashes
- Falls from a height

Some fractures happen from small injuries, like a fall at home. These are more likely in older people with weak bones (osteoporosis).

In teens, small pieces of bone can pull off the pelvis during sports or sudden movements. This is called an avulsion fracture.

There are many ways to classify these injuries based on how they happened, where they are, and how stable they are.

---

## What You Might Feel

Most people with a pelvic fracture feel pain in the groin or lower back.

Pressing on the front of the pelvis or both hip bones can be very painful. This may mean the fracture is unstable.

You may or may not be able to walk. It depends on how bad the break is.

---

### Signs of Genitourinary or Gynecologic Injury

These signs mean the bladder, urethra, or female reproductive organs may be damaged:

- Blood in the urine
- No urine output
- Blood coming from the urethra (the tube that carries urine out)
- Swelling in the scrotum or perineum (the area between the genitals and anus)
- The prostate feels higher than normal during a rectal exam (called a high-riding prostate)
- Vaginal bleeding

---

### Signs of Intestinal or Rectal Injury

These signs mean the bowel may be damaged:

- Belly or pelvic pain
- Blood in the stool
- Later, signs of infection in the belly (peritonitis)

---

### Signs of Nerve Injury

These signs mean nerves may be damaged:

- Weakness in the legs
- Loss of feeling in the legs, rectum, or perineum
- Trouble controlling the bowels or bladder
- Trouble passing urine

If the fracture is unstable or causes severe bleeding, the risk of death is high.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Pelvic Fractures

Doctors look for pelvic fractures if you have:
- Pain in the pelvis or hip
- A history of major trauma (like a car crash or fall)

### X-rays
An X-ray of the pelvis is usually the first test. It can show most fractures.

If the bones are not lined up properly, the ring is broken. This means the injury is unstable.

Special X-ray views (like Judet views) may be needed to see the hip socket (acetabulum) clearly.

### CT Scan
A CT scan gives a more detailed picture than an X-ray. It is used when:
- The injury was from a high-energy event (like a car crash)
- The doctor needs to see all the broken pieces
- There is concern about other injuries

A CT scan is usually not needed for small, simple fractures from low-energy injuries (like a fall at home).

### Tests for Other Injuries
Doctors must check for other injuries first. These tests include:

- Urine test to check for blood in the urine
- Neurological exam to check nerve function
- Pelvic exam in women to check for vaginal injury
- Retrograde urethrogram (a special X-ray) if there is blood at the urethra

In men, doctors may do a rectal exam to check the position of the prostate. But this test is not always helpful.

If blood is seen at the urethra, a retrograde urethrogram is needed.

---

## How Pelvic Fractures Are Treated

### Stable Fractures
These are minor breaks that do not move much. They often only need:
- Pain relief
- Rest
- Walking if possible

Most people with stable fractures can go home after a short stay.

### Unstable Fractures
These breaks are serious and can move. They need immediate treatment to stop bleeding and stabilize the pelvis.

- A pelvic binder (a special bandage) is applied right away in the emergency room.
- This can stop or reduce bleeding.
- In some cases, a metal device (external fixator) is placed through the skin to hold the bones in place.

An orthopedic surgeon or trauma surgeon will decide if surgery is needed.

### Bleeding
If there is heavy bleeding:
- A pelvic binder is used first.
- If bleeding continues, doctors may:
  - Use a catheter to block the bleeding blood vessels (angiographic embolization)
  - Perform surgery to pack the pelvis and stop the bleeding
  - Use internal metal plates and screws (open reduction with internal fixation)

### Acetabular Fractures
These are breaks in the hip socket. They usually happen from high-energy injuries.

- If the bones are out of place, surgery is needed.
- If the break is in the back part of the socket, surgery may not be needed.
- An orthopedic surgeon should be consulted.

---

### When Surgery Is Needed

External screw fixation is used when:
- Bleeding continues or the person is unstable
- There are multiple injuries
- The patient needs to be stabilized before being moved for surgery

This treatment helps reduce complications and shortens hospital stay.

---

## Important Tips

- Wrap the pelvis with sheets or use a pelvic binder as soon as possible after injury.
- If bleeding does not stop, more treatment is needed: embolization, surgery, or internal fixation.
- For unstable fractures without major bleeding, use a pelvic binder in the emergency room. Surgery (ORIF) is the final treatment.
- Treat all other injuries at the same time.

---

## Key Points

- Serious pelvic fractures from high-energy events often come with bladder, urethra, or blood vessel damage.
- Some fractures, like those in the pubic bone, can happen from small falls, especially in older people with weak bones.
- Get a CT scan if the injury was from a high-energy event.
- Stabilize the pelvis, stop bleeding, treat other injuries, and manage pain.

# Problems After Dental Treatment

Some problems can happen after dental work. These include swelling, pain, bleeding, dry socket, bone infection, and jaw bone death. These are serious and need quick care.

---

## Swelling and Pain

Swelling is common after tooth removal or gum surgery.  
It often happens on the side of the face where the work was done.  
You can reduce swelling by using ice.  
Use a cold pack or a plastic bag with frozen peas or corn.  
This shape fits your face better than a regular ice pack.  
Put the cold pack on your cheek for 25 minutes.  
Take it off for 1 or 2 hours.  
Do this for the first 18 hours after the procedure.  

If swelling gets worse after 3 days, or if pain is very bad, you may have an infection.  
Call your dentist right away.

Pain after dental work can be mild, moderate, or strong.  
You can take over-the-counter pain medicine to help.  
Follow the label instructions.

---

## Bleeding

It is normal to have some bleeding after a tooth is pulled.  
Bleeding may look worse than it really is.  
A little blood mixes with saliva and can seem like a lot.  

To stop the bleeding:  
- Bite down gently on a clean gauze pad.  
- Hold it in place for at least one hour.  
- Do not keep checking it.  
- If bleeding does not stop after a few hours, call your dentist.  

You may need to repeat the gauze step 2 or 3 times.  
If bleeding continues, your dentist may clean the area and close it with stitches.

If you take blood-thinning medicine like warfarin or aspirin, tell your dentist at least one week before surgery.  
This includes even one aspirin every few days.  
Your doctor and dentist may decide to change your dose or stop the medicine for a few days.  
This helps reduce the risk of heavy bleeding.

---

## Dry Socket

A dry socket happens when the blood clot in the tooth hole is lost.  
This can happen after pulling a lower back tooth.  
The bone is then exposed, and healing slows down.

Symptoms:  
- Pain goes down for 2 or 3 days.  
- Then the pain suddenly gets much worse.  
- You may feel pain in your ear.  

The pain usually goes away on its own in 1 to 2 weeks.  
But your dentist can help relieve the pain faster.  
They can put a special dressing in the socket.  
The dressing has medicine to numb the pain.  

You may need to come back every 1 to 3 days to get the dressing changed.  
This continues until the pain stops when the dressing is left in place for a few hours.  

Some dentists use a special dressing that does not need to be removed.  
It has pain medicine, germ killer, and numbing medicine in it.  

If you still have pain, you can take nonsteroidal pain medicine (like ibuprofen) by mouth.

Smoking increases the chance of dry socket.  
If possible, do not smoke for several days before and after the tooth is pulled.  
Women who take birth control pills also have a higher risk.

---

## Bone Infection (Osteomyelitis)

Osteomyelitis is an infection in the jawbone.  
It is usually caused by bacteria.  
It most often affects the lower jaw.  

Signs of bone infection:  
- Fever  
- Swelling in the jaw  
- Pain when you touch the area  

Your dentist or doctor will take an x-ray to check for infection.  
You will need to take antibiotics for several weeks.

---

## Jaw Bone Death (Osteonecrosis of the Jaw)

Osteonecrosis of the jaw means part of the jawbone dies.  
This happens when the bone is exposed through the gum.  
It can cause:  
- Pain  
- Loose teeth  
- Pus coming from the gums  

This can happen after:  
- Tooth removal  
- Injury to the jaw  
- Radiation therapy to the head or neck (called osteoradionecrosis)  
- Long-term or high-dose use of bone-strengthening medicines  

Some people get this problem without any clear cause.  
It is linked to certain bone-strengthening medicines.  
The most common ones are:  
- Alendronate  
- Risedronate  
- Ibandronate  
- Zoledronate  

The risk is higher if you:  
- Are getting these medicines through a vein (IV)  
- Have had high doses of these medicines before (common in cancer treatment)  
- Have taken them for a long time  

The risk is low (about 1 in 1,000) for people taking these medicines in normal doses for osteoporosis (weak bones) for a short time.

Treatment includes:  
- Removing dead bone tissue (called debridement)  
- Taking antibiotics by mouth  
- Using special mouth rinses to kill germs

# Tornwaldt Cyst

A Tornwaldt cyst is a rare fluid-filled sac. It forms in the middle of the upper part of the throat behind the nose. This area is called the nasopharynx.

The cyst comes from a small piece of tissue left over from early development. It sits just under a muscle in the throat. The inside of the cyst is covered with the same kind of lining that covers the inside of the nose and throat.

Sometimes the cyst gets infected. When this happens, it can cause several problems:

- Thick, yellow or green fluid drains from the nose or throat.
- The fluid has a bad smell and a bad taste.
- The ear tube (eustachian tube) becomes blocked. This can cause ear pressure or hearing problems.
- The throat becomes sore.

You might see thick fluid coming out of a small opening in the back of the nose.

## How It Is Diagnosed

Doctors use a small camera to look at the back of the nose and throat. This is called nasopharyngoscopy.

If the camera does not show a clear picture, the doctor may order a CT scan or an MRI. These tests give a detailed view of the area.

## How It Is Treated

Treatment depends on the size and symptoms. Two common options are:

- **Marsupialization**: The doctor opens the cyst and stitches the edges to the throat wall. This keeps it open so fluid can drain.
- **Excision**: The doctor removes the entire cyst.

Both treatments help stop infection and relieve symptoms.

# Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD)

Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) damages the center of the retina. This part of the eye is called the macula. It is the most important area for clear, central vision.

- The center of your vision may become blurry or lose detail.
- Straight lines may look wavy or bent.
- A doctor can often see changes in the eye using special tools.
- Some people may benefit from vitamin supplements.
- Injections into the eye or laser treatments may be needed for some.

## What Is the Retina and Macula?

The retina is the layer at the back of your eye. It senses light and sends signals to your brain. The macula is the center part of the retina. It has many light-sensing cells. These cells give you sharp, clear vision. They help you see fine details and colors.

## Who Gets AMD?

AMD is the most common cause of serious vision loss in older adults. It affects men and women equally. It is more common in White people.

## What Causes AMD?

These things increase your risk of AMD:

- Getting older
- Family history of AMD
- Smoking
- Certain gene changes
- Heart disease (like hardening of the arteries)
- High blood pressure
- Being overweight
- Too much sun exposure
- Eating too few foods with omega-3 fatty acids (like some fish)
- Eating too few dark green leafy vegetables

There are two types of AMD:

1. **Dry AMD** – This is the most common type.
2. **Wet AMD** – This is less common but causes more serious vision loss.

All cases of AMD start as dry AMD. About 15% of people with dry AMD go on to develop wet AMD. About 85% of people with AMD have only the dry type.

### Dry AMD

- The macula gets thinner over time.
- Cells in the macula slowly die.
- Waste from light-sensing cells builds up and forms small yellow spots called drusen.
- Both eyes can be affected at the same time.
- There is no bleeding, scarring, or fluid in the macula.

### Wet AMD

- New, weak blood vessels grow from the layer behind the retina under the macula.
- These blood vessels leak blood and fluid.
- This causes swelling and damage.
- Over time, scar tissue forms under the macula.
- Wet AMD usually starts in one eye. It can later affect both eyes.

## What Are the Symptoms?

### Dry AMD

- Vision loss happens slowly over many years.
- You may not notice any symptoms at first.
- When symptoms do appear, they often affect both eyes.
- Colors may look faded.
- Fine details become hard to see.
- Reading becomes harder.
- A blind spot may grow in the center of your vision.
- Most people still have enough vision to read and drive.

### Wet AMD

- Vision loss happens fast — over days or weeks.
- It can get worse suddenly if a blood vessel bleeds.
- The first sign is often blurry, wavy, or distorted vision in the center.
- Side vision (peripheral vision) stays clear.
- Wet AMD usually affects one eye at a time.
- Reading or watching TV becomes hard.

AMD can cause severe vision loss. It may lead to legal blindness in the affected eye.

## How Is AMD Diagnosed?

A doctor checks your eyes using a special light and magnifying lens. This is called ophthalmoscopy. The damage to the retina is often visible before you notice any symptoms.

To confirm wet AMD, the doctor may:

- Take color photos of the retina.
- Use a test called fluorescein angiography.
- Use a scan called optical coherence tomography.

These tests help confirm the diagnosis and check how well treatment is working.

## How Is AMD Treated?

### For Dry AMD

- There is no treatment to fix damage from dry AMD.
- No treatment is needed for mild cases.
- Quitting smoking may lower your risk of getting AMD.

For people with moderate or advanced dry AMD in one eye, doctors recommend certain supplements:

- Zinc
- Copper
- Vitamin C
- Vitamin E
- Lutein and zeaxanthin (for people who have smoked or still smoke)
- Beta-carotene or vitamin A (for people who have never smoked)

**Important notes:**

- People who have smoked in the past 7 years should not take beta-carotene or vitamin A. These can raise the risk of lung cancer.
- Lutein and zeaxanthin are safer for them.
- Men who take these supplements may have a higher risk of prostate or urinary problems.
- Women may have a higher risk of stress incontinence.
- Beta-carotene can turn your skin yellow.

Eating more foods with omega-3 fatty acids and more dark green leafy vegetables may help slow AMD. But taking omega-3 supplements does not help.

### For Wet AMD

Medicines injected into the eye can stop new blood vessels from leaking. These medicines are called anti-VEGF drugs. They include:

- Ranibizumab
- Bevacizumab
- Aflibercept
- Brolucizumab

These drugs work by:

- Stopping new blood vessels from growing.
- Reducing swelling.

Injections are usually needed every 1 to 3 months. They can:

- Lower the risk of vision loss.
- Help restore reading vision in about one-third of people.

**Important notes:**

- Brolucizumab may cause more side effects than other similar drugs. These include eye inflammation or problems with the artery that supplies blood to the retina.
- Higher doses of aflibercept or a newer drug called faricimab may need fewer injections.

A device that delivers ranibizumab continuously into the eye was recalled. It is being redesigned and is not available right now.

### Other Treatments

- **Photodynamic therapy**: A special medicine is injected into a vein. Then, a laser is used to destroy abnormal blood vessels. This works best if the vessels are not directly under the macula.
- **Thermal laser**: This can destroy abnormal blood vessels before they cause more harm.
- Surgery is rarely used for wet AMD.

### Low-Vision Aids

These tools can help you see better if your vision is poor:

- Handheld magnifiers
- High-power reading glasses
- Telescopic lenses
- Closed-circuit TV magnifiers
- Computer software that makes text larger or reads it aloud
- E-books that let you change font size and contrast
- An implantable miniature telescope (for people with severe, permanent vision loss)

A low-vision specialist (an eye doctor who helps people with poor vision) can guide you on what tools are best.

## More Information

The following websites offer helpful information in English:

- **American Macular Degeneration Foundation**: Latest news on AMD. Tips for healthy living. Ways to support research on preventing, treating, and curing AMD.

- **National Eye Institute**: Learn about eye health for adults and children. Available in English and Spanish. Search for topics you want to know more about.

- **Prevent Blindness, Eye Diseases & Conditions**: Detailed info on AMD and other eye diseases. Covers treatments, including helpful supplements. Tips for living with low vision.

# Bone and Joint Tumors – Simple Explanation

## What Are Bone and Joint Tumors?

Bone tumors can be non-cancerous (benign) or cancerous (malignant).  
Cancerous tumors can start in the bone. These are called primary tumors.  
Cancerous tumors can also spread to the bone from another part of the body. These are called metastatic tumors.

### In Children

Most bone tumors in children are not cancer.  
Some are cancerous, but they start in the bone. Examples include osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma.  
Very few bone tumors in children come from cancer elsewhere in the body. Examples include neuroblastoma and Wilms tumor.  
Childhood leukemia and lymphoma can affect the bone marrow. This can show up as strange results on X-rays.

### In Adults

In adults, especially those over age 40, most bone tumors are not from the bone itself.  
They are cancer that has spread to the bone from another place.  
Only about 3,900 new cases of cancer that starts in the bone happen each year in the United States.  
This includes both children and adults.  
Multiple myeloma is a cancer of the bone marrow. It is not considered a primary bone tumor because it starts in blood-forming cells.

### Joint Tumors

Tumors in the joint area are very rare in both children and adults.  
Tenosynovial giant cell tumor is not cancer. But it can damage the joint cartilage.  
Synovial sarcoma is a cancer of soft tissue. It does not come from the joint lining. It rarely grows inside a joint.

---

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

Bone tumors often cause pain that gets worse over time.  
The pain may happen when you walk or stand.  
It can also happen at rest, especially at night.  
This is because the bone is being damaged by the tumor.  
Some tumors, like leukemia, lymphoma, or Ewing sarcoma, can also cause fever or other general symptoms like fatigue or weight loss.

---

## How Are Bone and Joint Tumors Diagnosed?

### Step 1: X-rays

X-rays are the first test used.  
They help find and describe a possible tumor.  
If the X-ray shows a tumor, even if it was found by accident during another test, more tests are usually needed.  
These may include CT scans or MRI scans.  
A biopsy may also be needed.  
But if the X-ray shows a classic sign of a non-cancerous tumor (like osteochondroma or enchondroma), and the child has no pain, no further tests are needed.

### Step 2: MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging)

MRI gives a very detailed picture of soft tissues and bone marrow.  
It is the best test for the arms and legs.  
Gadolinium contrast (a special dye) can help show cancer more clearly.  
Use contrast when cancer is a possible diagnosis.  
Do not use contrast for known or likely non-cancerous tumors like lipomas.  
Check kidney function before using contrast. Poor kidney function can cause harm.  
The MRI doctor will decide if contrast is needed and what extra scans to do.

### Step 3: CT (Computed Tomography)

CT gives a very clear picture of bone structure.  
It is better than MRI for seeing bone damage.  
It helps check if a bone is weak and at risk of breaking.  
It can also show if a tumor has calcium in it. This can help identify certain types of tumors.  
CT is used when MRI is not safe. For example, if a person has a pacemaker or cochlear implant.

### Step 4: Whole-Body Scans

If doctors suspect cancer has spread to many bones, a full-body scan is needed.  
A whole-body bone scan checks all bones at once.  
It is better than a scan of just one area.  
It helps find other hidden tumors.  
The patient already gets the full dose of radioactive material. Adding the full-body view takes only a little extra time.  
Whole-body PET-CT is another option. It combines a PET scan with a CT scan.

### Step 5: Biopsy

A biopsy is needed to confirm cancer.  
This means taking a small sample of the tumor.  
It is done when the tumor looks cancerous.  
It is also done if the tumor is not clearly benign.  
But if a person has many bone lesions and already has a known cancer, a biopsy may not be needed.

### Why Diagnosis Is Often Delayed

The most common reason for delay is that doctors do not think of a bone tumor.  
They do not order the right tests.  
Always consider a bone tumor if someone has:  
- Unexplained bone pain  
- Pain that gets worse at night or when resting  
- Pain that does not go away after treatment for injury or arthritis  
- A growing lump in the bone area  
- Pelvic pain or pain that feels like sciatica  
- Pain in the back, hip, or leg that does not improve with treatment

---

## Key Points

- In children, most bone tumors are not cancer. Some are cancer, but they start in the bone. Very few are from cancer that spread from elsewhere.  
- In adults over age 40, most bone tumors are cancer that spread from another part of the body.  
- Diagnosis starts with a medical history, physical exam, and X-rays.  
- Blood tests and advanced imaging are usually needed.  
- Signs of cancer on X-rays include:  
  - Bone damage  
  - Blurry or unclear edges  
  - Breaks in the outer bone layer  
  - Spread into soft tissues  
  - A broken bone from a minor injury  
- A biopsy is needed to confirm cancer.  
- Always think about a bone tumor if someone has ongoing, unexplained bone pain.

# How Doctors Diagnose Infections

Infections are caused by tiny living things like bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites.

Doctors look at your symptoms, do a physical exam, and consider your risk factors to decide if you have an infection.

First, they must figure out if your symptoms are from an infection or from another kind of illness.

For example, a cough and trouble breathing could mean pneumonia (a lung infection). But it could also mean asthma or heart failure, which are not infections.

A chest x-ray can help doctors tell the difference between pneumonia and other conditions.

Once doctors confirm you have an infection, they need to find out which specific germ is causing it.

Many different germs can cause the same illness. For example, pneumonia can be caused by viruses, bacteria, or, rarely, fungi.

The treatment depends on which germ is causing the infection.

There are many types of lab tests to find germs. These tests use samples from your body, such as blood, urine, sputum, or tissue.

The lab may:

- Stain the sample and look at it under a microscope  
- Grow the germ in a lab (this is called culturing)  
- Test for antibodies your body made against the germ  
- Test for antigens (parts of the germ that trigger your immune system)  
- Test for the germ’s genetic material (like DNA or RNA)

No single test can find every germ. Some tests work well for one germ but not for another.

Doctors choose the best test based on which germs they think are most likely.

Sometimes, doctors do several tests in a specific order. Each test helps narrow down the possibilities.

If the right test is not done, doctors might miss the cause of the infection.

Once the germ is found, doctors can test which medicines will work best against it. This helps them start the right treatment faster.

---

## Where the Lab Gets the Sample

The lab takes a sample from the part of your body that likely has the germ.

Common samples include:

- Blood  
- Sputum (mucus from deep in the lungs)  
- Urine  
- Stool (bowel movement)  
- Tissue  
- Cerebrospinal fluid (fluid around the brain and spinal cord)  
- Mucus from the nose, throat, or genital area  

Some samples, like sputum, stool, and mucus, normally have many harmless bacteria. Doctors must tell the difference between harmless bacteria and the ones causing your illness.

Other samples, like blood, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid, should not have any germs at all. If germs are found in these samples, it usually means there is an infection.

To avoid false results, the skin is cleaned with an antiseptic before taking a blood sample.

---

## Looking at the Sample Under a Microscope

Doctors can sometimes see the germ under a microscope.

Most samples are treated with special dyes (called stains). The stains make the germs stand out.

Some germs have a unique size, shape, and color after staining. This helps doctors identify them.

But many germs look alike under a microscope. Some are too small to see.

Viruses are too small to be seen with a regular microscope.

For bacteria, doctors often use a stain called Gram stain.

- **Gram-positive bacteria** look blue after staining  
- **Gram-negative bacteria** look red after staining  

Doctors can sometimes pick the right antibiotic based on whether the bacteria are gram-positive or gram-negative.

Gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria usually respond to different types of antibiotics.

Other stains can be used depending on the germ doctors suspect. Fungi can also be stained.

---

## Growing the Germ in the Lab (Culture)

Many samples have too few germs to see or test. So doctors try to grow the germ in the lab.

This process is called culture.

The sample is placed on a sterile dish or in a tube with nutrients that help germs grow.

Different nutrients are used depending on which germ is suspected.

Doctors may add substances to stop unwanted germs from growing.

Many germs, like those that cause urinary tract infections or strep throat, grow easily in culture.

Some germs, like the one that causes syphilis, cannot be grown in the lab.

Others, like the bacteria that cause tuberculosis, can be grown but take weeks.

Some viruses can be grown, but many cannot.

After the germ grows, doctors test it to identify it and see which medicines will work.

---

## Testing How Well Medicines Work Against the Germ

Doctors know which medicines usually work against certain germs. But germs can become resistant to medicines over time.

So doctors test how well different medicines work against the specific germ in your body.

This is called susceptibility testing.

They use cultures to do this. Once the germ is grown, doctors add different medicines to see which ones kill it.

They also test how sensitive the germ is to a medicine.

This tells them if a small or large amount of medicine is needed to kill the germ.

If a large amount is needed, doctors usually do not use that medicine.

Sometimes, genetic tests can find genes that make the germ resistant to certain medicines.

For example, MRSA (a type of staph infection) can be found by testing for the *mecA* gene.

But lab results do not always match what happens in your body.

Your body’s response to medicine depends on:

- How strong your immune system is  
- Your age  
- Other health problems you may have  
- How your body absorbs and processes the medicine  

---

## Tests for Antibodies and Antigens

Some germs, like the one that causes syphilis, cannot be grown in the lab.

For these, doctors use special tests called immunologic tests.

These tests look for:

- Antibodies  
- Antigens  

### Antibody Tests

Antibodies are proteins your body makes to fight infections.

They are made by white blood cells when they meet a germ.

It takes several days to weeks for your body to make enough antibodies to be detected.

Antibodies are specific to one type of germ. If you have antibodies to a germ, you have been exposed to it.

But antibodies can stay in your blood long after the infection is gone.

So finding antibodies does not always mean you are still infected.

Doctors may test for several antibodies, depending on what they suspect.

They often check how much antibody is in your blood.

To do this, they dilute your blood sample in half many times until the test no longer shows antibodies.

The more times they can dilute it before the test turns negative, the more antibodies were in your blood.

Because it takes time to make antibodies, early tests may be negative.

So doctors may take a sample right after you get sick and then another one weeks later.

If the antibody level goes up between the two tests, it likely means you have a current or recent infection.

### Antigen Tests

Antigens are parts of a germ that trigger your immune system.

Every germ has unique antigens.

Finding an antigen means the germ is present.

Antigen tests find the germ directly. This means doctors can diagnose an infection quickly.

These tests do not wait for your body to make antibodies.

They are useful for people whose immune systems are weak, such as those who had a bone marrow transplant or have advanced HIV.

To do an antigen test, doctors mix your sample with a special antibody that targets the suspected germ.

If the germ is in your sample, its antigens will stick to the test antibody.

Different methods can detect this match.

If the test is positive, the germ is likely causing your illness.

---

## Testing for the Germ’s Genetic Material

Tests that find the germ’s genetic material are called nucleic acid–based tests.

These tests look for DNA or RNA from the germ.

Each germ has unique parts of DNA or RNA.

Finding these parts means the germ is present.

One common test is called PCR. It makes many copies of a gene from the germ. This makes it easier to find.

Each genetic test is for only one specific germ.

For example, a test for hepatitis C virus only finds that virus.

These tests are only used when doctors already suspect a certain infection.

Most of these tests only check if the germ is present (qualitative testing).

But for some infections, like HIV and hepatitis C, tests can also measure how much germ is in your body (quantitative testing).

This helps doctors know how serious the infection is.

It also helps track how well treatment is working.

Some genetic tests can check for genes that make the germ resistant to medicine.

But these tests are not perfect.

Not all resistance genes are known.

The tests are expensive and not available everywhere.

They are only used for a few types of germs.

---

## Other Tests to Identify Germs

Some tests look at other features of germs that are not related to their DNA or RNA.

These are called non-nucleic acid–based identification tests.

For example, doctors may test:

- What substances the germ can grow in  
- What enzymes the germ makes (enzymes help the germ infect cells or spread)  
- Other parts of the germ, like proteins or fatty acids  

These tests help doctors identify the germ when other methods do not work.

# Understanding Gender Identity and Gender Dysphoria

Some people feel they are a man, some feel they are a woman, and others feel they are neither or both. This is called gender identity.  
Not everyone fits into the traditional idea of being only male or female.  
Some people describe themselves as genderqueer, nonbinary, or gender nonconforming.  
These terms are becoming more common and accepted in many cultures.  

The way people see gender can be different in different parts of the world.  
Most people are cisgender. This means their gender identity matches the sex they were assigned at birth.  

---

## What Do These Terms Mean?

Here are simple explanations of key terms:

- **Cisgender**: A person whose gender identity matches the sex they were born with.  
- **Gender binary**: The idea that there are only two genders — male and female.  
- **Gender dysphoria**: A strong feeling of discomfort or distress because a person’s gender identity does not match the sex they were assigned at birth.  
- **Gender expression**: How a person shows their gender through clothes, hairstyle, voice, or behavior.  
- **Gender identity**: A person’s inner sense of being male, female, both, neither, or something else.  
- **Gender nonconforming**: When a person’s gender expression or identity does not match the usual expectations for their assigned sex.  
- **Genderqueer**: A person whose gender identity does not fit the idea of only two genders. They may feel like both, neither, or a mix of genders.  
- **Trans-affirmative**: Being respectful and supportive of transgender and gender-diverse people.  
- **Transgender**: A general term for people whose gender identity or role is different from what is usually expected based on their sex at birth.  
- **Transition**: The process of living as the gender a person truly feels they are. This can include changing names, using new pronouns, wearing different clothes, or getting medical treatments like hormones or surgery.  

---

## Gender in Children

Many cultures are more accepting of girls who act or dress in ways that are usually seen as “boyish.”  
They are less accepting of boys who act or dress in ways that are usually seen as “girlish.”  
It is normal for some boys to pretend to be girls or mothers.  
They might wear their sister’s clothes or play with toys that girls usually play with.  
This kind of behavior is not a problem.  
It does not mean a child will grow up to be transgender.  
Most children who act this way do not have gender dysphoria later in life.  
But some young teens who feel this way may later identify as gay, lesbian, or bisexual.  

---

## What Is Nonbinary?

Nonbinary means a person’s gender is not just male or female.  
They may feel they are both, neither, or a mix of genders.  
Some nonbinary people feel their gender changes over time or in different situations.  
This is called gender fluid.  
Not all nonbinary people are transgender.  
Some are, but others are not.  

Nonbinary people may use pronouns like they/them/theirs.  
Some use new pronouns like ze/zir/hir or e/er/ers.  
Studies show that nonbinary people make up a large part of the gender-diverse community.  
This is especially true among teens and young adults.  
Most nonbinary people were assigned female at birth.  

---

## Changes in Gender Dysphoria Care

Before the 2010s, most people who came to clinics for help with gender dysphoria were assigned male at birth.  
Now, more young people assigned female at birth are seeking care.  
This is true around the world.  

Most people feel comfortable with their gender identity, their sex at birth, and how they act.  
But some people feel deep distress because their gender identity does not match their sex at birth.  
This is called gender dysphoria.  
It is listed in the DSM-5-TR, a guide used by doctors to diagnose mental health conditions.  
There are different rules for diagnosing it in children and in teens and adults.  

Just feeling different from gender norms is not a disorder.  
It is a normal part of human diversity.  
But if the mismatch between a person’s gender identity and their body causes serious distress or problems in daily life, a doctor may diagnose gender dysphoria.  
The diagnosis is based on the person’s distress, not just on their identity.  

---

## What Does Gender Dysphoria Feel Like?

People with gender dysphoria often feel anxious, sad, angry, or upset.  
They may feel like they do not belong in their own body.  
Some feel this way for a long time and it is very painful.  
They often want to change their body through medical treatments like hormones or surgery.  

We do not know exactly how many people have gender dysphoria.  
But studies show that between 0.02% and 0.1% of people meet the official criteria.  
Other surveys show higher numbers when people say they are transgender or gender diverse:  

- In adults:  
  - 0.5% to 0.6% say they are transgender.  
  - 0.6% to 1.1% say they are gender-incongruent or gender diverse.  

- In children and teens:  
  - 1.2% to 2.7% say they are transgender.  
  - 2.5% to 8.4% say they are gender-incongruent or gender diverse.  

Some experts say gender dysphoria is not a mental illness.  
It is more like a medical condition, similar to other differences in how bodies develop.  
The World Health Organization moved it from the mental health section to a new section on sexual health.  
This change helps reduce stigma.  
Other experts believe gender differences are just rare but normal parts of human diversity.  

---

## Health Challenges for Transgender People

Transgender people often face more health problems than others.  
This includes physical health issues, mental health struggles, and sexual health concerns.  
Many of these problems come from not being able to get good care.  
Not all mental health issues in this group are due to gender dysphoria.  
For example, some people have depression, anxiety, or substance use problems.  
Not everyone with gender incongruence has gender dysphoria.  
A diagnosis is only made when the distress is serious and lasts for at least six months.  

Sex and gender are not the same thing.  
They are separate parts of a person’s identity.  

---

## What Causes Gender Incongruence?

We do not fully understand what causes gender identity.  
But research suggests biology plays a big role.  
This includes genes and hormones during early pregnancy.  
Some studies found that identical twins are more likely to both have gender dysphoria than non-identical twins.  
This suggests genetics may be involved.  
Other studies did not find this link.  
Brain scans show that some people with gender dysphoria have brain features that match their gender identity, not their sex at birth.  

Family relationships and emotional bonds also affect how a person develops their gender identity.  

Rarely, gender dysphoria is linked to medical conditions like ambiguous genitals or genetic disorders such as Turner syndrome or Klinefelter syndrome.  
When a child is raised in a clear way — with a clear gender label — their gender identity usually develops normally, even if their genitals look different.  
But if the gender label is unclear, a child may feel confused.  
Experts still debate how much environment affects this.  

---

## What Are the Signs of Gender Incongruence?

This section talks about how people feel and act.  
It includes people who are gender-diverse but do not have gender dysphoria.  

---

## How Is Gender Dysphoria Diagnosed?

Doctors use two main systems:  
- The DSM-5-TR (used in the U.S. and many countries)  
- The ICD-11 (used in many other countries)  

---

## How Is Gender Dysphoria Treated?

Most adults and teens get hormone therapy to change their body in ways that match their gender identity.  
Some also get surgery, such as breast, genital, or facial surgery.  
Other treatments may include voice training or hair removal.  

Psychotherapy can help with mental health issues, transition challenges, or other problems.  
But it is not required to get medical or surgical care.  

The goal of treatment, according to global guidelines, is to help people feel comfortable in their own skin.  
The aim is to improve their health, mental well-being, and life satisfaction.  

Cross-dressing or gender nonconforming behavior is not a disorder.  
It does not need treatment if it does not cause distress.  
If treatment is needed, it is to reduce suffering and help the person live as they are.  
Trying to change a person’s gender identity — called conversion therapy — does not work.  
It can cause serious harm.  
It is unethical and illegal in some places.  

Most people with gender dysphoria do not want mental health treatment.  
They want medical help to change their body.  
They want to look and feel like the gender they are.  
When gender dysphoria is properly diagnosed and treated, many people feel much better.  
Treatment can include therapy, hormone therapy, and surgery.  

Surgery can help some people feel more at peace with their body.  
Experts say surgery should only be done after a full evaluation by a trained doctor.  
Patients are usually advised to live as their true gender for at least one year before surgery.

# Dermatitis Herpetiformis

Dermatitis herpetiformis is a skin condition linked to celiac disease. It causes groups of very itchy, red blisters and swollen patches on the skin.

## What Causes Dermatitis Herpetiformis?

- The body’s immune system wrongly attacks the skin.
- This happens when a person eats foods with gluten.
- Gluten is a protein found in wheat, rye, and barley.
- The immune system mistakes the skin for a threat and damages it.
- This damage causes the rash and intense itching.

## Who Gets This Condition?

- It can happen at any age.
- It is most common in adults between 30 and 40 years old.
- It is rare in Black and Asian people.

## Important Facts

- The name “herpetiformis” does not mean it is caused by the herpes virus.
- The word “herpetiformis” means the blisters appear in clusters, like some herpes rashes.
- People with this condition often have celiac disease, even if they do not have stomach problems.
- Some people also have other autoimmune diseases, such as:
  - Thyroid problems
  - Lupus
  - Sarcoidosis
  - Anemia from lack of vitamin B12
  - Diabetes
- There is a small chance of developing a type of cancer in the intestines called lymphoma.

## Symptoms

- Blisters and hives appear slowly or suddenly.
- They most often show up on:
  - Elbows
  - Knees
  - Buttocks
  - Lower back
  - Back of the head
- They can also appear on the face and neck.
- The itching and burning are usually very strong.
- The skin is very sensitive. Blisters often break quickly.
- This means doctors may not see many intact blisters.
- Blisters in the mouth can happen, but they usually do not cause pain.

### Things That Can Make It Worse

- Iodides and iodine products, such as:
  - Kelp and seaweed
  - Some skin cleansers
- Some experts also suggest avoiding iodized salt.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- A doctor takes a small sample of skin.
- The sample is checked under a microscope.
- The test looks for specific antibodies in the skin.
- Everyone with this skin condition is tested for celiac disease.

---

## How Is It Treated?

### 1. Gluten-Free Diet

- This is the main treatment.
- You must avoid all foods with wheat, rye, and barley.
- This diet helps control the disease and lowers the risk of cancer in the intestines.
- You must follow this diet strictly for 5 to 10 years to reduce cancer risk.

### 2. Medicines

- **Dapsone**:
  - Taken by mouth.
  - Usually relieves itching in 1 to 3 days.
  - Can cause anemia.
  - You must have blood tests regularly to check your blood counts.

- **Sulfapyridine** or **Sulfasalazine**:
  - Taken by mouth.
  - Used if dapsone does not work or causes side effects.
  - Can cause anemia and lower white blood cell counts.
  - This increases the risk of infection.
  - Blood tests are needed regularly.

### Can You Stop Medicines?

- Some people can stop taking medicine after the condition is under control.
- But many people need to keep taking medicine long-term.
- Even a small amount of gluten can cause a new outbreak.
- Sticking to a strict gluten-free diet is key to staying well.

---

# Blockage in the First Part of the Small Intestine

The first part of the small intestine, called the duodenum, can become blocked. This blockage can happen in several ways:

- The intestine may be missing a section. This is called atresia.
- The intestine may be too narrow. This is called stenosis.
- Something outside the intestine may press on it and block it.

Many babies with a blocked duodenum also have Down syndrome. This is a condition that affects how a person develops.

Doctors use imaging tests to find the blockage. These tests take pictures of the inside of the body.

Surgery is needed to fix the blockage. The surgeon will open the intestine and remove or repair the problem.

# Spinal Epidural Abscess

A spinal epidural abscess is a collection of pus in the space between the spine and the tough outer layer that covers the spinal cord. This buildup can press on the spinal cord and cause serious problems.

## What Causes a Spinal Epidural Abscess?

Most often, the abscess comes from bacteria that spread from another infection in the body. Common sources include:

- Skin infections near the spine  
- Infections in the bones of the spine  
- Heart valve infections (endocarditis)  
- Pressure sores (bedsores)  
- Dental infections  

It can also happen after certain medical procedures, such as:

- Spinal surgery  
- Inserting a tube into the space around the spinal cord (epidural catheter)

The most common bacteria are:

- *Staphylococcus aureus* (about 60% of cases)  
- *Escherichia coli* and other similar bacteria  
- Streptococci  

In rare cases, the cause is tuberculosis affecting the spine or drug use. In about one-third of people, doctors cannot find the exact cause.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The first sign is usually back pain. The area over the abscess may hurt when touched. The pain often gets worse when lying down and can become very severe.

Other symptoms may include:

- Fever  
- Weakness in the legs  
- Partial or full paralysis of the legs  
- Trouble controlling the bladder or bowels  
- Loss of feeling in the buttocks, genitals, or rectum (the saddle area)  
- Trouble walking  

If the abscess presses on nerves at the lower end of the spinal cord, it can cause a condition called cauda equina syndrome. Symptoms can get worse over hours or days.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect an abscess if you have:

- Unexplained back pain  
- Tenderness in the spine  
- Fever  
- A recent infection or dental procedure  

The main test is magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This scan shows detailed images of the spine and can find the abscess.

If MRI is not available, doctors may use:

- Myelography (a special X-ray of the spinal cord)  
- Followed by a CT scan  

Blood tests are done to check for signs of infection. Samples of blood and, if possible, pus from the abscess are sent to a lab. The lab grows the bacteria to find out which one is causing the infection.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment must start quickly to prevent lasting damage.

**Antibiotics** are always used. They are given right away, even before test results come back. The type of antibiotic is chosen based on the most common bacteria.

If the abscess is pressing on the spinal cord and causing serious problems, such as:

- Weakness or paralysis in the legs  
- Loss of bladder or bowel control  

Then surgery is needed right away to drain the pus.

A sample of the pus is sent to the lab to identify the exact bacteria. This helps doctors adjust the antibiotics if needed.

In some cases, antibiotics alone may be enough if the abscess is small and there are no serious symptoms. But if there are any signs of nerve damage, surgery is done immediately.

# Glycogen Storage Diseases

Glycogen storage diseases are rare conditions that affect how the body uses sugar.  
They happen when the body lacks certain enzymes needed to make or break down glycogen.  
Glycogen is a form of sugar stored in the liver and muscles.  
When these enzymes are missing, sugar builds up in the wrong places.  
This can cause low blood sugar or damage to organs and muscles.

These diseases are passed down through families.  
Most types are inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.  
This means a child must get a faulty gene from both parents.  
One type, called GSD type VIII/IX, is passed through the X chromosome.  
This affects boys more often than girls.

The number of babies born with these diseases ranges from 1 in 20,000 to 1 in 43,000.  
The rate depends on the population studied.

Symptoms vary by type.  
But most people have low blood sugar or muscle problems.  
Some have liver issues.  
Symptoms can start at birth or later in life.

Doctors suspect the disease based on symptoms and medical history.  
They may use imaging tests like MRI or tissue samples (biopsy) to check for abnormal sugar buildup.  
DNA testing confirms the diagnosis.  
In some cases, doctors test enzyme levels in liver, muscle, skin, or blood cells.  
For some types, they check how the body handles lactate during exercise.

Pompe disease (GSD type II) is now tested for in newborns in many U.S. states.

Treatment depends on the type.  
For liver forms, patients take uncooked cornstarch.  
This gives a steady supply of sugar.  
It helps keep blood sugar normal.  
For muscle forms, people should avoid heavy exercise.  
Some types need enzyme replacement therapy.  
Others may need special diets or medicines.

Prognosis and treatment depend on the specific type.

## Other Conditions That Look Like Glycogen Storage Diseases

Rare problems in sugar breakdown can cause similar symptoms.  
Deficiencies in certain enzymes can mimic the muscle or liver problems seen in GSDs.

- Low levels of phosphoglycerate kinase, phosphoglycerate mutase, or lactate dehydrogenase cause muscle pain and weakness.  
  These look like GSD types V and VII.  
- A problem with glucose transporter 2 causes liver issues.  
  This is like GSD types I, III, IV, and VI.  
  This condition is called Fanconi-Bickel syndrome.

---

## Types of Glycogen Storage Diseases

Below is a list of the main types, their causes, symptoms, and treatments.

### GSD I (von Gierke disease)

- **Most common type** of GSD I.  
  About 80% of cases are type Ia.  
- **Onset:** Before age 1.  
- **Symptoms:**  
  - Very low blood sugar  
  - High levels of lactic acid  
  - Large liver  
  - Later: liver tumors, kidney problems, high blood pressure, short height, high fat in blood, high uric acid, bleeding issues, anemia  
  - Type Ib also causes low white blood cells, frequent infections, and bowel problems  
- **Treatment:**  
  - Uncooked cornstarch every 4 to 6 hours  
  - Special formula without lactose  
  - Nighttime feedings are very important  
  - Avoid fructose and galactose  
  - Bicarbonate for acid buildup  
  - Allopurinol to lower uric acid  
  - Liver or kidney transplant may help  
  - For type Ib with low white blood cells: a medicine called G-CSF

  - Juvenile/adult forms: weak muscles, delayed movement, trouble breathing  
  - Type IIb: learning problems  
- **Treatment:**  
  - Enzyme replacement therapy (alglucosidase alfa)  
  - Heart transplant if heart is severely damaged

# Prenatal Testing for Genetic Disorders and Birth Defects This guide explains tests that can be done during pregnancy to check for certain health problems in the baby. These tests look for genetic disorders and birth defects. They can help parents make informed choices about their pregnancy. --- ## What Are Prenatal Tests? Prenatal tests are done before the baby is born. They check if the baby has certain health problems. These problems can be inherited from the parents or happen by chance during pregnancy. There are two main types of tests: - **Noninvasive tests** – These do not harm the baby. They use the mother’s blood or ultrasound. - **Invasive tests** – These involve taking a sample from the baby or placenta. They are more accurate but carry a small risk. Most women start with noninvasive tests. If the results are not normal, they may choose to have an invasive test to be sure. --- ## Noninvasive Prenatal Tests These tests are safe and do not harm the baby. They are often part of routine care. ### Common Noninvasive Tests - **Blood tests** – A small amount of blood is taken from the mother. It checks for: - Fetal DNA in the mother’s blood - Certain proteins and hormones made by the baby or placenta - **Ultrasound** – A scan uses sound waves to create pictures of the baby. It can check the baby’s size, position, and development. ### What These Tests Can Detect These tests can help find: - Chromosomal problems like Down syndrome, trisomy 13, or trisomy 18 - Neural tube defects such as spina bifida or anencephaly ### How the Tests Work - **Cell-free DNA test (cfDNA)**: This blood test checks tiny pieces of the baby’s DNA in the mother’s blood. It can be done as early as 10 weeks. It is very accurate for detecting certain chromosomal issues. - **Serum marker tests**: These blood tests measure levels of certain proteins and hormones. They are often done in the first and second trimesters. - **Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)**: A protein made by the baby. - **Pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A)**: Made by the placenta. - **Estriol**: A hormone made from baby’s substances. - **Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)**: Made by the placenta. - **Inhibin A**: Made by the placenta. - **Nuchal translucency scan**: This ultrasound measures a fluid-filled space at the back of the baby’s neck. A larger amount may suggest a higher risk of certain problems. ### What If a Test Is Abnormal? An abnormal result does not mean the baby definitely has a problem. It only means there is a higher chance. If this happens, the doctor may suggest an invasive test to confirm. ### Important Notes - Noninvasive tests are not perfect. They can miss some problems or give false alarms. - A false alarm means the test says there is a problem, but there is none. This can lead to more testing, which carries some risk. - Some parents choose not to have any testing. That is their personal choice. --- ## Ultrasound During Pregnancy Ultrasound is a common test during pregnancy. It has no known risks. It can show: - If the baby is alive - How many babies there are - How far along the pregnancy is - Where the placenta is - If the baby has any major birth defects, such as heart, brain, spine, kidney, or stomach problems If a blood test shows a high alpha-fetoprotein level, or if there is a family history of birth defects, the doctor may do an ultrasound to check the baby. But a normal ultrasound does not guarantee the baby is healthy. Some problems cannot be seen. --- ## Invasive Prenatal Tests These tests are more accurate but carry a small risk of miscarriage or harm to the baby. ### Amniocentesis - A needle is inserted through the mother’s belly into the amniotic fluid. - A small amount of fluid is taken and tested. - It is usually done after 15 weeks of pregnancy. - The fluid contains baby cells that can be tested for genetic and chromosomal problems. - It can also check for alpha-fetoprotein in the fluid, which helps detect brain and spine defects. **Risks of amniocentesis:** - Soreness for a short time - Light spotting or leaking of fluid (usually stops on its own) - Miscarriage (about 1 in 500 to 1,000) - Rare injury to the baby from the needle **After the test:** - Women with Rh-negative blood get a shot to prevent blood problems in future pregnancies. - The shot is not needed if the father also has Rh-negative blood. ### Chorionic Villus Sampling (CVS) - A small sample of tissue is taken from the placenta. - It can be done between 10 and 12 weeks of pregnancy. - It is done either through the vagina and cervix or through the belly. **How it is done:** - **Through the cervix**: A thin tube is passed through the vagina and cervix into the placenta. - **Through the belly**: A needle is inserted through the skin and into the placenta. **Risks of CVS:** - Miscarriage (about 1 in 500) - Light spotting after the test - Rarely, the test result is unclear, and another test is needed **Important:** - CVS does not check for brain or spine defects because it does not test amniotic fluid. - If needed, a later blood test or amniocentesis can check for these. **Advantages of CVS:** - Results come faster than amniocentesis. - If a problem is found early, parents can make decisions sooner. - It gives more time to prepare for a baby with special needs. ### Percutaneous Umbilical Blood Sampling (PUBS) - A needle is inserted through the mother’s belly and uterus into the umbilical cord. - A small amount of baby’s blood is taken and tested. - It is rarely used now. **When it is used:** - If the baby is thought to have severe anemia. - Blood can be given to the baby through the needle during the test. **Risks:** - Miscarriage (about 1 in 100) - This test is now mostly replaced by safer, faster tests using amniotic fluid or placenta samples. --- ## Testing Before Pregnancy (In Vitro Fertilization) If a couple uses in vitro fertilization (IVF), they can test the embryo before it is placed in the uterus. This is called **preimplantation genetic testing**. - It checks for certain genetic disorders or chromosomal problems. - It is expensive and needs special labs. - It is usually used by couples who have a high risk of passing on a serious genetic condition. Newer methods may make this testing cheaper and more available in the future. --- ## Should You Have These Tests? There is no right or wrong answer. Each family must decide what is best for them. Ask yourself: - How would I feel if I did not know the results? - Would knowing help me make better choices? - If the baby has a problem, would I consider ending the pregnancy? - If I would not end the pregnancy, would I still want to know? - Could knowing cause more stress than help? Some parents choose not to be tested.
