# Problems with Blood Clotting Caused by Antibodies in the Blood

Sometimes the body makes antibodies that stop blood from clotting properly. These are called circulating anticoagulants.

These antibodies are usually autoantibodies. That means the body makes them by mistake and they attack its own parts.

Some autoantibodies target specific clotting proteins. For example:
- One type attacks factor VIII.
- Another attacks factor V.

Other autoantibodies affect proteins that work with fats in the blood. These are called antiphospholipid antibodies.

In rare cases, these antibodies can cause bleeding. This happens when they bind to a mix of prothrombin and fats in the body.

## When to Suspect These Antibodies

You should think about this problem if:
- A person is bleeding too much.
- Blood tests show a longer time for blood to clot.
- The test stays long even when mixed with normal blood.

The two main tests are:
- Partial thromboplastin time (PTT)
- Prothrombin time (PT)

If the test result does not improve when mixed with normal blood, this may point to circulating anticoagulants.

## Autoantibodies and Blood Clots

Autoantibodies that target proteins and fats in the blood often cause blood clots. This is called the antiphospholipid syndrome.

This syndrome can cause clots in arteries or veins. It can lead to serious problems like stroke or deep vein thrombosis.

The exact reason why these antibodies cause clots is not fully known.

These antibodies often bind to a protein called beta-2-glycoprotein 1. But we do not yet know how this leads to clotting.

In some people, the antibodies bind to a mix of prothrombin and fats. This can lower the amount of prothrombin in the blood. This can cause bleeding.

## Antibodies Against Factor VIII and Factor IX

### Factor VIII Inhibitors

Some people with severe hemophilia A develop antibodies against factor VIII.

This happens in about 30 out of 100 people with severe hemophilia A.

It usually happens after repeated treatments with factor VIII replacement therapy.

People without hemophilia can also get these antibodies. This can happen:
- After childbirth.
- As part of a larger autoimmune disease.
- In older adults with no clear cause.

These antibodies can cause life-threatening bleeding.

### Factor IX Inhibitors

People with severe hemophilia B can also develop antibodies against factor IX.

This is less common. It happens in about 2 to 3 out of 100 people with hemophilia B.

## How Doctors Test for These Antibodies

A blood sample is mixed with normal blood. The test is done right away and again after a few hours.

If the clotting time stays long, it suggests the presence of an inhibitor.

This test is done for both factor VIII and factor IX.

## How These Antibodies Are Treated

### For People Without Hemophilia

If a person without hemophilia develops antibodies against factor VIII or IX, treatment may include:
- Cyclophosphamide
- Glucocorticoids
- Rituximab

Rituximab is a medicine that targets certain immune cells.

These medicines help stop the body from making the harmful antibodies.

In some people, the antibodies go away on their own.

### For People With Hemophilia

For people with hemophilia A and factor VIII inhibitors:
- Long-term, high-dose factor VIII replacement is used.
- This is called immune tolerance induction.
- It helps the body learn to accept factor VIII again.

For people with hemophilia B and factor IX inhibitors:
- Exposure to factor IX can cause severe allergic reactions.
- It can also cause kidney problems (nephrotic syndrome).
- A plan to reduce the body’s reaction to factor IX may help.
- This includes desensitization and immunosuppression.

## Treating Bleeding Episodes

### Recombinant Human Factor VIIa

This medicine is used to stop serious bleeding in:
- People with hemophilia A or B who have inhibitors.
- People without hemophilia who have factor VIII or IX antibodies.

It helps the blood clot even when factor VIII or IX is not working.

### Activated Prothrombin Complex Concentrates

This medicine can also treat bleeding in people with factor VIII inhibitors.

It contains factor IX. So it cannot be used in people with factor IX inhibitors.

### Emicizumab

This is a special medicine made in a lab.

It works like factor VIII but is not the same.

It links factor IX and factor X together to help blood clot.

It can be used to prevent or reduce bleeding in people with hemophilia A.

It works even if the person has factor VIII inhibitors.

### Concizumab

This is a medicine that targets a protein called TFPI.

TFPI stops blood from clotting too much.

By lowering TFPI, this medicine helps the blood clot better.

It can be used in people with hemophilia A or B.

It works even if factor VIII or IX is low.

### Marstacimab

This is another medicine that targets TFPI.

It works the same way as concizumab.

It is used for people with hemophilia A or B who do not have inhibitors.

### Fitusiran

This is a small piece of genetic material.

It works in the liver to reduce a protein called antithrombin.

Antithrombin stops clotting.

By lowering antithrombin, the body can clot better.

This medicine can be used in people with hemophilia A or B.

It works even if factor VIII or IX is low.

### Recombinant Porcine Factor VIII

This is a version of factor VIII made from pigs.

It is different from human factor VIII.

Some people with factor VIII inhibitors have antibodies that do not attack the pig version.

So this medicine can help stop bleeding in those people.

It is used only when other treatments do not work.

# Problems with the Fallopian Tubes and Pelvis That Can Cause Infertility

This page explains how issues with the fallopian tubes or other parts of the pelvis can make it hard to get pregnant. It also covers how doctors find these problems and what treatments are available.

---

## How the Fallopian Tubes and Pelvis Affect Fertility

The fallopian tubes carry the egg from the ovary to the uterus.  
Sperm must travel through the tubes to meet the egg.  
If the tubes are blocked or damaged, sperm cannot reach the egg.  
If the tubes are blocked, the egg or fertilized egg (zygote) cannot move to the uterus.  
The fertilized egg must reach the uterus to grow.  
If it does not, pregnancy cannot happen.

Abnormalities in the pelvis can also cause fertility problems.  
These include growths in the uterus, such as fibroids.  
They can stop the egg from attaching to the lining of the uterus.  
They can also block the fallopian tubes.

---

## Causes of Fallopian Tube and Pelvic Problems

### Fallopian Tube Problems

These can happen because of:

- Endometriosis (when tissue like the lining of the uterus grows outside the uterus)
- Pelvic infections, such as pelvic inflammatory disease
- A past pregnancy in the fallopian tube (ectopic pregnancy)
- A ruptured appendix
- Surgery in the pelvis or lower belly
- Infections like tuberculosis or inflammatory bowel disease

Bacteria from sexually transmitted infections can enter the vagina during sex.  
These bacteria can move up into the cervix, uterus, and fallopian tubes.  
Some infections, like chlamydia, may not cause any symptoms.  
But they can still damage the fallopian tubes over time.  
Scar tissue can form and block the tubes.

### Pelvic Abnormalities

These include:

- Fibroids or polyps in the uterus
- Scar tissue (adhesions) that form between organs in the pelvis
- Birth defects of the uterus or fallopian tubes

Adhesions often happen after surgery or infection.  
They are common after a procedure called dilation and curettage (D and C).  
Scarring can also happen in the cervix after infection, injury, or surgery.

---

## How Doctors Find These Problems

Doctors use several tests to check for blockages or other issues.

### Common Tests

- **Sonohysterography** – A salt solution is gently put into the uterus during an ultrasound.  
  This helps the doctor see the inside of the uterus and fallopian tubes.  
  If the solution flows through the tubes, they are not blocked.  
  This test is quick and does not need anesthesia.  
  It does not use radiation or contrast dye.  
  It is safer than other tests.

- **Hysterosalpingography** – X-rays are taken while a special dye is injected through the cervix.  
  The dye shows the shape of the uterus and tubes.  
  This test is done a few days after a period ends and before ovulation.  
  It does not need anesthesia.  
  Some people may have an allergic reaction to the dye.  
  It can give a false result – it may say the tubes are blocked when they are not.

- **Hysteroscopy** – A thin camera is inserted through the vagina and cervix into the uterus.  
  The doctor can see inside the uterus and remove small growths like polyps or fibroids.  
  This can improve the chance of pregnancy.

- **Laparoscopy** – A small camera is inserted through a tiny cut below the belly button.  
  The doctor can see the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries.  
  This is done under general anesthesia.  
  It is rarely used just to check for blockages.  
  But it can be used to treat problems like endometriosis or scar tissue.

### When Infections Are Suspected

If a pelvic infection is possible, doctors test for gonorrhea or chlamydia.  
Screening for sexually transmitted infections is part of routine care when trying to get pregnant.

---

## What Happens After the Tests?

- If the sonohysterography results are normal, some young women may get pregnant more easily afterward.  
  Doctors may wait to see if pregnancy happens before doing more tests.

- If the hysterosalpingography results are normal, fertility may also improve slightly.

- If a problem is found, doctors may treat it during the same procedure.  
  For example, they can remove a polyp or fibroid during hysteroscopy.

---

## Treatment Options

### If There Is a Pelvic Infection

- Antibiotics are used to treat the infection.

### If There Is Abnormal Tissue

- Doctors may remove fibroids, polyps, or scar tissue during surgery.  
- This can improve the chance of pregnancy.

### If the Fallopian Tubes Are Damaged

- Surgery may be an option for younger women with mild damage.  
  It can fix tubes damaged by an ectopic pregnancy, infection, or past sterilization.  
  But after surgery, the chance of a normal pregnancy is still low.  
  The risk of another ectopic pregnancy is higher.

- In most cases, **in vitro fertilization** is a better choice.  
  This method bypasses the fallopian tubes entirely.

### In Vitro Fertilization (IVF)

- Eggs are taken from the ovaries.  
- Sperm is used to fertilize them in a lab.  
- The fertilized egg is placed into the uterus.  
- IVF is often needed or recommended, especially for women under 30.

---

## Summary

- Blocked or damaged fallopian tubes can stop sperm from meeting the egg.  
- Problems in the pelvis can stop the egg from attaching to the uterus.  
- Tests like sonohysterography and hysterosalpingography help find these issues.  
- Sonohysterography is now preferred because it is safer and easier.  
- Surgery can fix some problems, but IVF is often the best option.  
- Early treatment improves the chance of a healthy pregnancy.

# Problems with Calcium Levels in the Body

Calcium is a mineral your body needs to work properly. It helps your muscles move, your nerves send signals, your hormones work, and your blood to clot. It also plays a role in many other body processes.

Your body keeps calcium levels in balance through three main ways:

- What you eat
- How much calcium your gut absorbs
- How much calcium your kidneys remove

Most people eat about 1000 milligrams of calcium each day. About 200 milligrams of calcium also come into the gut from bile and other digestive fluids. The amount of calcium your gut absorbs each day depends on two key substances: parathyroid hormone and active vitamin D. This absorption usually ranges from 200 to 400 milligrams per day. The rest — about 800 to 1000 milligrams — leaves the body in your stool.

Your kidneys remove about 200 milligrams of calcium each day. This amount also depends on the levels of parathyroid hormone and calcitonin in your blood.

Calcium levels inside and outside your cells are tightly controlled. Calcium moves in and out of cells through the cell membrane. It also moves into and out of small parts inside cells, like the endoplasmic reticulum, the sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle cells, and the mitochondria.

The most important form of calcium in the blood is **ionized calcium**. This is the active form your body uses. The level of ionized calcium inside cells is very low — less than one-thousandth of the level in the blood. Ionized calcium acts like a signal inside cells. It helps muscles contract, helps heart and smooth muscles respond to signals, and turns on certain enzymes and proteins.

Ionized calcium also helps other signals in the body work, such as cAMP and inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate. These signals help your body respond to many hormones, including epinephrine, glucagon, vasopressin, secretin, and cholecystokinin.

Even though calcium is so important inside cells, almost all of the calcium in your body — about 99% — is stored in your bones. It is mainly in the form of a hard mineral called hydroxyapatite. About 1% of the calcium in your bones can move in and out of the blood. This small amount helps balance calcium levels when needed.

Normal total calcium in the blood is between 8.8 and 10.4 milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL). About 40% of this calcium is attached to proteins in the blood, especially albumin. The other 60% is either free (ionized) or linked to other substances like phosphate and citrate.

Most labs measure total calcium — this includes all forms: bound, complexed, and free. But the most useful number is **ionized calcium**, because it is the active form in the blood. It does not always match total calcium levels.

- Ionized calcium is usually about half of the total calcium level.
- You can estimate ionized calcium using total calcium and albumin levels.
- Direct testing of ionized calcium is harder and is usually only done if a person has a condition that might change how calcium binds to proteins.

Normal ionized calcium levels usually range from 4.7 to 5.2 mg/dL (1.17 to 1.30 mmol/L). This range can vary slightly between labs.

## How the Body Controls Calcium

Calcium and phosphate work closely together. The body controls both using three main substances:

- Parathyroid hormone
- Vitamin D
- Calcitonin (to a lesser degree)

Calcium and phosphate can combine to form calcium phosphate. When the levels of calcium and phosphate in the blood are too high, this can form crystals in soft tissues. A safe level for the product of calcium and phosphate is less than 60 mg²/dL². If this number goes above 70 mg²/dL², the risk of crystal formation increases.

Calcium phosphate crystals can build up in blood vessels. This speeds up hardening of the arteries. This can happen even when the calcium-phosphate product is above 55 mg²/dL², especially in people with chronic kidney disease.

# Cervical Stenosis

Cervical stenosis means the opening in the cervix is narrow or closed.  
The cervix is the lower part of the uterus.  
It connects the vagina to the main body of the uterus.

## What Causes Cervical Stenosis?

Cervical stenosis usually happens because of another health problem.  
Common causes include:

- **Menopause** – The tissues in the cervix become thin and weak.  
- **Cervical cancer** – Cancer in the cervix.  
- **Endometrial cancer** – Cancer in the lining of the uterus.  
- **Surgery on the cervix** – For example, to treat abnormal cells that could become cancer.  
- **Endometrial ablation** – A procedure that destroys the lining of the uterus. It is used for heavy bleeding.  
- **Radiation therapy** – Used to treat cervical or endometrial cancer.

## What Problems Can Cervical Stenosis Cause?

Most women with cervical stenosis have no symptoms.  
But in some cases, it can cause:

- No periods (amenorrhea)  
- Painful periods (dysmenorrhea)  
- Unusual bleeding  
- Trouble getting pregnant (infertility) – because sperm cannot pass through the cervix

In rare cases, blood can build up in the uterus. This is called **hematometra**.  
It can cause pain or a feeling of fullness in the lower belly.

In very rare cases, pus can build up in the uterus. This is called **pyometra**.  
This often happens if the stenosis is caused by cancer.

## Symptoms of Cervical Stenosis

- Many women feel no symptoms.  
- Some women stop having periods or have painful periods.  
- Some have unusual bleeding.  
- Some have trouble getting pregnant.  
- If blood or pus builds up in the uterus, you may feel pain or a lump in the pelvic area.

## How Is Cervical Stenosis Diagnosed?

Doctors often find cervical stenosis during a pelvic exam.  
They may suspect it if:

- Periods stop or become painful after cervical surgery.  
- They cannot put a tool into the cervix for testing.  
  For example, to take a sample for a Pap test or HPV test.  
  Or to take a sample from the lining of the uterus.

To confirm the diagnosis, the doctor tries to pass a small probe through the cervix.  
If they cannot, the diagnosis is likely cervical stenosis.

If you have abnormal bleeding and cervical stenosis, your doctor may test for cancer.  
Tests may include:

- A Pap test or HPV test  
- An endometrial biopsy – a sample from the lining of the uterus

You do not need more tests if all of these are true:

- You are past menopause (your periods have stopped).  
- You have no symptoms.  
- There is no blood or pus in the uterus.  
- Your Pap test results are normal.

## How Is Cervical Stenosis Treated?

Treatment is only needed if you have symptoms, or if blood or pus is trapped in the uterus.

The main treatment is to widen the cervix.  
This is done by gently inserting small metal rods (dilators) through the cervix.  
The rods are slowly made larger to stretch the opening.

To keep the cervix open, the doctor may place a small tube (called a stent) in the cervix.  
The tube stays in place for 4 to 6 weeks.

# High Potassium in the Blood

High potassium in the blood is called hyperkalemia.  
It means the level of potassium in your blood is above 5.5 milliequivalents per liter.  
This can happen when your kidneys do not remove enough potassium.  
It can also happen when potassium moves out of your cells into your blood.  

Many things can cause high potassium at the same time.  
These include eating too much potassium, taking certain medicines, or having kidney problems.  
High potassium can also happen during diabetic ketoacidosis.  

High potassium can affect your muscles and your heart.  
It may cause muscle weakness.  
It can also cause dangerous heart rhythms.  
In serious cases, it can lead to a heart that stops beating.  

Doctors check for high potassium by testing your blood.  
Treatment depends on how high the level is.  
It may include changing your diet, adjusting your medicines, using a special resin, or getting emergency care like calcium, insulin, or dialysis.

---

## What Causes High Potassium?

### Pseudohyperkalemia

This is a false high reading.  
It happens when the blood sample is damaged.  
The most common reason is that red blood cells break open during the test.  
This can happen if the tourniquet is left on too long.  
It can also happen if you clench your fist too hard during the blood draw.  
High platelet counts or very high white blood cell counts can also cause this.  

### Real High Potassium

If your kidneys work normally, they can get rid of extra potassium.  
So, long-term high potassium usually means your kidneys are not working well.  
But other things often play a role too.  
These include eating or drinking too much potassium, or potassium moving out of your cells.  

If you take a large amount of potassium in a short time, even healthy kidneys may not keep up.  
But the high level usually goes away quickly.  

---

### Common Causes of High Potassium

| Cause | Examples |
|------|----------|
| **Medicines that keep potassium in the body** | ACE inhibitors, ARBs, cyclosporine, aliskiren, heparin, lithium, potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, tacrolimus, trimethoprim |
| **Low hormone levels** | Adrenal insufficiency |
| **Kidney problems** | Acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease, type 4 renal tubular acidosis, blocked urine flow |
| **Low blood volume** | Dehydration, poor circulation |
| **Too much potassium intake** | Eating high-potassium foods, taking potassium supplements, blood transfusions, IV fluids with added potassium, parenteral nutrition, potassium citrate, some antibiotics like penicillin G |
| **Potassium moving out of cells** | Beta-blockers, digoxin toxicity, tissue damage from tumors, severe burns, bleeding into soft tissues or the gut, rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown), inherited muscle disorders |
| **Low insulin or fasting** | Diabetes, not eating for long periods |
| **Other conditions** | Metabolic acidosis, intense exercise |

High potassium is common when kidney function is poor.  
It is also common after severe burns, muscle breakdown, major bleeding, or adrenal insufficiency.  
In chronic kidney disease, high potassium is rare unless you eat or drink too much potassium.  

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people with high potassium have no symptoms.  
The first sign is often a dangerous heart rhythm.  

In a rare condition called hyperkalemic familial periodic paralysis, muscle weakness can happen during attacks.  
It may get worse and lead to full paralysis.  

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several steps to find high potassium:

- A blood test checks your potassium level.  
- An ECG (heart tracing) looks for changes in your heart rhythm.  
- Your doctor reviews your medicines.  
- Tests check how well your kidneys are working.  

High potassium is often found during routine blood tests.  
It should be suspected in people with kidney disease, heart failure, blocked urine flow, or those on certain medicines like ACE inhibitors or potassium-sparing diuretics.  

If you have no risk factors and no heart changes, pseudohyperkalemia may be the cause.  
The lab may report if the blood sample was damaged.  
If this is suspected, the test should be repeated.  
Use a larger needle, avoid tourniquets, and do not clench your fist.  
Get the blood tested quickly after drawing.  

---

## How Is It Treated?

### For Mild High Potassium

- Reduce potassium in your diet.  
- Stop or change medicines that raise potassium.  
- Use a special resin like sodium polystyrene sulfonate, patiromer, or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate.  
These help remove potassium from your body through your bowel.

### For Moderate or Severe High Potassium

- Give insulin and glucose through a vein.  
- Give calcium through a vein.  
- Use an inhaled medicine that opens airways (beta 2-agonist).  
- Use dialysis, especially if kidney function is poor.  

Dialysis is often needed for people with chronic kidney disease.  
It is also used if the ECG shows serious changes.

---

## Key Facts

- Common causes include medicines that keep potassium, poor kidney function, adrenal insufficiency, and conditions that break down body tissues (like burns, muscle damage, or bleeding).  
- High potassium often causes no symptoms until it harms the heart.  
- Some people feel weak.  
- Early ECG changes: longer PR interval, shorter QT interval, tall and peaked T waves.  
- When potassium is over 6.5, the QRS complex gets wider. The P wave may disappear.  
- Later, the ECG shows a sine wave pattern. This can lead to ventricular fibrillation or a stopped heart.  
- For mild cases: use sodium polystyrene sulfonate, patiromer, or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate.  
- For moderate to severe cases: give insulin, glucose, calcium, and possibly an inhaled beta 2-agonist.  
- Use dialysis for people with chronic kidney disease or serious ECG changes.

# Problems with the Optic Nerve

## How the Eye and Brain Work Together

The back of your eye has a layer called the retina.  
This layer has tiny cells that can see light.  
These cells send signals through the optic nerve.  
The optic nerve carries these signals to your brain.  
Your brain then turns the signals into the pictures you see.

If the optic nerve is damaged, or if the path to the brain is damaged, you may lose your vision.  
The damage causes specific patterns of vision loss.  
Doctors can use these patterns to find where the problem is.

## How Vision Signals Travel to the Brain

Each eye sends signals through its own optic nerve.  
The two optic nerves meet at a point in the brain called the optic chiasm.  
At this point, half of the nerve fibers from each eye cross over to the other side.  
This means the right side of your brain gets information from the left side of what both eyes see.  
The left side of your brain gets information from the right side of what both eyes see.

Damage at any point along this path causes different kinds of vision loss.  
Where the damage happens determines what part of your vision is affected.  
Doctors use the pattern of vision loss to figure out where the problem is.

# Squamous Cell Carcinoma in Situ

This is a type of skin growth that starts in the top layer of the skin. It is not cancer that has spread deep into the skin or body. It was once called Bowen disease.

It most often appears on skin that gets a lot of sun. But it can also show up on skin that does not get much sun.

## What It Looks Like

- The skin changes can be one spot or several spots.
- The spots are red-brown in color.
- They are scaly or crusty on the surface.
- The skin does not feel hard under the spot.
- The spots often look like a thin, red patch of psoriasis or eczema.
- They can also look like a fungal skin infection.

## How It Is Diagnosed

- A doctor will take a small sample of the skin.
- This is called a biopsy.
- The sample is checked under a microscope.
- The test shows that the top layer of skin is abnormal.
- The abnormal cells are only in the top layer.
- The deeper layers of skin are not affected.

A doctor may suspect this condition if a rash does not get better with normal treatments for psoriasis or eczema.

## How It Is Treated

Treatment depends on the size, location, and appearance of the spot.

Your doctor may recommend one or more of the following:

- **Topical chemotherapy**: A medicine cream or ointment applied directly to the skin.
- **Curettage and electrodesiccation**: The doctor scrapes off the spot and uses an electric current to destroy any remaining cells.
- **Surgical excision**: The doctor cuts out the spot and a small area around it.
- **Electrocautery**: The doctor uses a heated tool to burn off the spot.
- **Cryosurgery**: The doctor freezes the spot with liquid nitrogen.

## How to Help Prevent It

Many skin cancers are linked to too much sun exposure. To lower your risk:

- **Stay out of the sun** when it is strongest. This is between 10 in the morning and 4 in the afternoon.
- **Seek shade** when outside.
- **Avoid sunbathing** and **tanning beds**.
- **Wear protective clothing**: long-sleeved shirts, long pants, and wide-brimmed hats.
- **Use sunscreen** every day:
  - Choose a sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher.
  - Pick one that protects against both UVA and UVB rays.
  - Apply it as directed.
  - Reapply every two hours.
  - Reapply after swimming or sweating.
- Do not use sunscreen to stay in the sun longer. It is not a full shield.

# Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency

This is a genetic condition. It means you are born with it. It happens when your body does not make enough of a special protein called alpha-1 antitrypsin. This protein helps protect your lungs and liver.

## What Causes This Condition?

- A change in a gene you inherit from your parents causes this condition.
- The gene tells your body how to make the alpha-1 antitrypsin protein.
- When the gene is changed, the protein may not work right or may not be made in enough amounts.
- People of Northern European background are more likely to have this condition than people of African, Asian, or Hispanic backgrounds.

## What Problems Can This Cause?

The main problems are:

- Liver damage
- Emphysema (a type of lung disease that makes breathing hard)

### Liver Problems

- The abnormal protein can build up in the liver.
- This can cause the liver to stop working well.
- Over time, this can lead to scarring of the liver, called cirrhosis.
- Scarring increases the risk of liver cancer.

### Lung Problems

- Without enough alpha-1 antitrypsin, harmful enzymes in the lungs can cause damage.
- This damage leads to emphysema.
- Smoking makes emphysema worse and can cause it earlier.
- Even people who never smoked can get emphysema from this condition.

Other rare problems can also happen. These include:

- Painful lumps or skin changes on the lower belly, buttocks, or thighs (panniculitis)
- Serious bleeding
- Weak spots in blood vessels (aneurysms)
- Inflammation in the intestines (ulcerative colitis)
- Inflammation in blood vessels (vasculitis)
- Kidney disease

## Symptoms

Symptoms can start at any age — in infancy, childhood, or adulthood.

### In Babies

- Yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice) appears in the first week of life.
- The liver may be larger than normal.
- Jaundice usually goes away by 2 to 4 months of age.
- But about 1 in 5 babies with this condition later develop cirrhosis.
- Some do not live past young adulthood.

### In Adults

- The most common symptom is emphysema.
- You may feel short of breath, especially when walking or doing light activity.
- You may cough and wheeze.
- These symptoms usually start after age 25.
- Smoking makes the symptoms come earlier and worse.
- If you never smoked, symptoms are usually mild.
- Most people who never smoked live a normal life span.

- About 1 in 10 adults who had no liver problems as babies later develop cirrhosis.
- This can lead to liver cancer.

### Panniculitis

- You may feel pain or tenderness in the lower belly, buttocks, or thighs.
- You may see red, hard lumps or patches on the skin.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect this condition if:

- A baby has jaundice and liver problems.
- A smoker gets emphysema before age 45.
- A non-smoker gets emphysema at any age.
- A person has liver problems with no clear cause.
- A person has panniculitis.
- A family member has emphysema or cirrhosis with no known cause.
- A family member has been diagnosed with this condition.

To confirm the diagnosis:

- Doctors do a blood test to check how much alpha-1 antitrypsin is in your blood.
- They may do a genetic test to find the specific gene change.
- These tests help determine the type of deficiency.

## How Is It Treated?

### General Care

- If you smoke, you must stop. Smoking makes lung damage much worse.
- Use medicines called bronchodilators (like albuterol) to open your airways and make breathing easier.
- Treat lung infections right away. Do not wait.

### Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Replacement Therapy

- You can get alpha-1 antitrypsin through a vein (IV).
- The protein comes from healthy donors’ blood.
- The blood is tested to make sure it is safe.
- This treatment is expensive.
- It helps slow down lung damage.
- It does not fix damage that is already done.
- It works best for people with mild symptoms and who do not smoke.

### Lung Transplant

- If you are under 60 and have severe lung damage, a lung transplant may be an option.
- Some centers may consider people up to age 70 if they are otherwise healthy.
- In some cases, lung volume reduction surgery may help.

### Liver Damage

- Alpha-1 antitrypsin replacement does not help liver damage.
- The liver damage is caused by the abnormal protein building up, not by low levels.
- If the liver is badly damaged, a liver transplant may be needed.
- The new liver makes normal alpha-1 antitrypsin.
- The new liver will not get damaged because the protein it makes is normal.

### Panniculitis

- Doctors may try medicines like dapsone, corticosteroids, or certain antibiotics (tetracyclines).
- These may help reduce swelling and pain.
- But it is not clear if they work well for everyone.

# Lightning Injuries

Lightning can hurt people in many ways. It can stop the heart, cause loss of consciousness, or lead to short-term or long-term nerve problems. Serious burns or deep tissue damage are rare.

Doctors diagnose lightning injuries by checking the person’s symptoms. They always do an electrocardiogram (ECG) and monitor the heart. Treatment focuses on supporting the body while it heals.

Even though fewer people die from lightning strikes now than in the past 50 years, about 30 people still die each year in the United States. Several hundred others are injured. About 1 in 10 people who are struck by lightning die.

Lightning usually hits tall or isolated things. This includes trees, towers, shelters, flagpoles, bleachers, and fences. A person standing in an open field might be the tallest thing around. Metal objects and water do not draw lightning. But if lightning hits them, the electricity can travel through them.

Lightning can strike up to 10 miles away from a storm. It can even hit when the sky is clear. This means danger can come without warning. Lightning can also travel from outdoor power lines into indoor devices like computers or phones.

The force of a lightning strike can throw a person several meters.

The way lightning injures the body is very different from how electric shocks from power lines or batteries do. For example, the amount of voltage or current does not predict how bad the injury will be. Lightning carries a lot of energy, but it flows for only a tiny fraction of a second—less than one thousandth of a second.

Because of this, lightning rarely causes serious skin wounds. It also rarely causes rhabdomyolysis (a condition where muscle tissue breaks down) or deep tissue damage. This is different from injuries caused by man-made electricity.

Some people may have bleeding inside the brain. This is usually due to secondary injury, not the lightning itself.

Lightning mainly affects the nervous system. It can damage the brain, the autonomic nervous system, and the nerves in the arms and legs.

---

## Key Facts

- Unlike injuries from power lines or batteries, lightning rarely causes serious skin burns or deep tissue damage.
- Lightning does not cause the same kind of damage as high-voltage electricity.

---

## What Happens After a Lightning Strike?

The electric shock from lightning can cause the heart to stop beating or beat irregularly. It can also cause brain symptoms like confusion, memory loss, or losing consciousness.

### Keraunoparalysis (Lightning Paralysis)

This is a common reaction. It causes:
- Weakness or paralysis in the legs and sometimes the arms.
- Cold, pale, or mottled skin.
- No pulse in the affected limbs.
- Numbness or loss of feeling.

This is likely due to damage to the nerves that control blood flow and movement. It usually goes away within a few hours. But in rare cases, some weakness may last.

Other possible signs of lightning injury include:

- Small burns on the skin. These may look like tiny dots or branching lines.
- A ruptured eardrum.
- Cataracts (clouding of the eye lens) that can appear within days.

The most common cause of death is heart failure right at the moment of the strike. This happens when the heart goes into a dangerous rhythm called ventricular fibrillation.

Nerve problems can include:
- Confusion.
- Trouble thinking clearly.
- Numbness or tingling in the arms and legs.

Long-term issues may include:
- Trouble sleeping.
- Trouble focusing or paying attention.
- Memory problems.
- Chronic pain.
- Problems with the nervous system, such as erectile dysfunction.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Lightning Injuries

Doctors look for heart and brain problems.

Some injuries are seen right away. Others are not. If someone is found unconscious or cannot remember recent events after a storm, doctors should suspect lightning injury.

All people struck by lightning must be checked for injuries from the fall or shock.

An ECG is done if the injury is serious or if heart problems are suspected.

Blood tests for heart damage are done if the person has:
- Chest pain.
- Abnormal ECG results.
- Changes in mental state.

If a person has ongoing confusion, worsening mental state, or signs of brain injury (like weakness on one side), a brain scan (CT or MRI) is needed.

---

## How Doctors Treat Lightning Injuries

Treatment is supportive. This means helping the body heal on its own.

CPR is used only if the person’s heart or breathing stops.

If an automated external defibrillator (AED) is available, it should be used right away for heart arrest.

People who are in cardiac arrest after a lightning strike have a better chance of survival than those in cardiac arrest from other causes. This is because lightning often causes a reversible heart rhythm.

In most mass casualty events, people in cardiac arrest are given low priority. But in lightning strikes, they are given high priority. This is because they are more likely to survive with quick help.

AEDs can fix the heart rhythm quickly. This means less need for complex trauma care.

Supportive care includes:
- Giving fluids only as needed to avoid swelling in the brain.
- Monitoring the heart and brain.

Most people who survive a lightning strike can go home unless there are signs of heart or brain injury.

---

## How to Prevent Lightning Injuries

Most lightning injuries can be avoided by following safety rules.

Always check the weather forecast before going outside. Have a plan to get to a safe place.

Stay aware of the weather while outside. If a storm starts, act fast.

When you hear thunder, you are already in danger. Seek shelter immediately.

Safe shelters include:
- Large, enclosed buildings.
- Fully enclosed metal vehicles (like cars or vans).

Avoid small, open shelters like gazebos, picnic shelters, or tents. They are not safe.

Wait at least 30 minutes after the last thunder or lightning before going back outside.

### If You Are Inside During a Storm

- Avoid touching plumbing (like sinks, showers, or bathtubs).
- Stay away from windows and doors.
- Do not use hard-wired phones, computers, video game consoles, or headsets connected by cables.

Cell phones, tablets, and laptops are safe to use if they are running on battery power. They do not attract lightning.

---

## Summary

- Lightning injuries mainly affect the heart and brain. They do not usually cause serious skin burns or deep tissue damage like man-made electricity does.
- If someone is found unconscious or confused after a storm, think about lightning injury.
- Check for injuries, heart problems, and brain damage.
- Treat with supportive care.
- Most lightning injuries can be prevented by following safety rules.

# Preventing Health Problems in Older Adults

Your goals for staying healthy as you age depend on your current health, how well you can do daily tasks, and your personal risks. Here’s what prevention means for different situations:

- If you are healthy and can take care of yourself: Focus on avoiding new health problems.
- If you have mild long-term health issues but still live independently: Focus on staying strong and avoiding a decline in your ability to do daily tasks.
- If you are frail and depend on others for help: Focus on avoiding accidents and serious complications that could make you even more dependent or lead to death.

---

## Healthy Lifestyle Choices

### Exercise

Regular physical activity is important at any age. It helps you stay strong and mobile.

- Strength training, like lifting weights, helps prevent muscle loss and weak bones.
- Aerobic exercise, such as walking or swimming, builds stamina and may lower your risk of heart and blood vessel problems.
- Dancing and tai chi are fun ways to stay active. They also improve balance, which helps prevent falls.

### Quitting Smoking

It’s never too late to stop smoking. Doing so helps:

- Boost your energy and endurance.
- Reduce symptoms like chest pain or leg cramps.
- Lower your risk of heart attacks, lung disease, and some cancers.

### Alcohol

Older adults process alcohol differently. Drinking more than one drink a day can raise your risk of injuries and other health issues.

---

## Medications and Vaccines

### Medications

Older adults are more sensitive to side effects from medicines. This is because the body changes with age and handles drugs differently.

- Some medicines can interact with each other or with food.
- These interactions are more common in older adults than in younger people.

To stay safe:

- Know the name of every medicine you take — both the brand and the generic name.
- Know why you are taking each medicine.
- Know how long you should take it.
- Know what to avoid while on the medicine — such as certain foods, drinks, or other medicines.
- Always bring all your medicines — both prescription and over-the-counter — to your doctor visits so your doctor can check them.

### Vaccines

Vaccines are very important for older adults. They help protect against serious illnesses.

You should get the following vaccines:

- **Pneumococcal vaccine**: Two types are available. This vaccine helps prevent pneumonia.
- **Tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis vaccine**: One dose if you’ve never had a pertussis shot. Then, a tetanus and diphtheria booster every 10 years.
- **Flu vaccine**: One dose every year.
- **Shingles vaccine**: Two doses, given 2 to 6 months apart, starting at age 50.

These vaccines are especially important because older adults are more likely to get pneumonia, tetanus, and shingles. The flu can also lead to serious problems like pneumonia in older adults.

---

## Preventing Injuries

Simple safety steps can help prevent injuries at home. These are the same steps that help younger adults — but they are especially important for older adults.

### Preventing Falls

Falls are a major cause of serious injury in older adults. To reduce your risk:

- Keep your home free of clutter.
- Secure loose rugs or remove them.
- Tuck in carpet edges and cover cords with tape or clips.
- Make sure rooms are well lit, especially hallways and stairs.
- Add handrails on stairs and grab bars in the bathroom.
- Install handrails near the toilet and in the shower or tub.
- Avoid using slippery bath oils.
- Talk to your doctor about stopping any medicines you don’t need.
- Use the lowest effective dose of any medicine you must take.
- Work on balance through exercise, dancing, or tai chi.

---

## Driving Safely

You may need to limit or stop driving if:

- Your vision is poor.
- Your reflexes are slow.
- Your overall health affects your ability to drive safely.

Do not drive if:

- You are taking medicine that makes you drowsy.
- You have trouble seeing at night.

# How the Body Gets Rid of Medicines

Your kidneys are the main organs that remove water-soluble medicines and waste from your body.  

Some medicines pass into the bile and go into the intestines. If the medicine is not reabsorbed in the intestines, it leaves the body through the stool.  

Other routes of excretion include the intestines, saliva, sweat, breast milk, and lungs. These routes usually play a small role.  

The only exception is the lungs. They can remove certain medicines that are inhaled, such as anesthesia gases.  

Medicines that pass into breast milk can reach a nursing baby. This may affect the baby’s health. See the table titled *Some Medications Contraindicated for Breastfeeding Mothers* for more information.  

The liver often changes medicines so they become more water-soluble. This makes it easier for the kidneys to remove them from the body.

# Infective Endocarditis – Simple Explanation

This is a serious infection of the inner lining of the heart. It is usually caused by bacteria or fungi. It can affect the heart valves and the tissue inside the heart.

## What Causes Infective Endocarditis?

The heart is usually strong against infection. But two things are needed for this infection to happen:

- A problem with the heart’s inner lining or valves.
- Germs in the blood.

Germs can enter the blood from infections in the mouth, skin, or other parts of the body. In some cases, very strong germs can cause infection even in a healthy heart.

## Types of Infective Endocarditis

There are different types, based on how fast the illness develops.

### Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis
- Develops slowly over weeks or months.
- Often starts without clear symptoms.
- Usually caused by streptococci (a type of bacteria).
- Often happens after a mild infection in the gums, gut, or urinary tract.

### Acute Bacterial Endocarditis
- Comes on fast, within days.
- Often linked to a clear source of infection.
- Usually caused by *Staphylococcus aureus* or other strong bacteria.
- Can affect healthy heart valves.

### Prosthetic Valvular Endocarditis
- Happens in people with artificial heart valves.
- Can happen within the first two months after surgery (early) or later (late).
- Early cases are often due to germs from surgery.
- Late cases are often due to mild infections in the body, like from the mouth.

## Symptoms and Signs

Symptoms can be vague and may come on slowly. They include:

- Fever
- Fatigue
- Weight loss
- Night sweats
- New or changing heart murmur
- Small red or purple spots on the skin (petechiae)
- Pain in the joints or muscles
- Swelling in the legs or belly

Some people have no symptoms at first. Others may have signs of organ damage, like kidney problems or brain issues.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

There is no single test that confirms the disease. Doctors use a mix of findings:

- **Blood cultures**: To find germs in the blood.
- **Echocardiogram**: An ultrasound of the heart to see if there are clumps of germs (vegetations) on the valves.
- **Other imaging tests**: May be used if needed.
- **Clinical criteria**: Doctors use guidelines to decide if the illness is likely endocarditis.

You should suspect endocarditis if you have:
- Fever with no clear cause.
- A heart murmur.
- A history of heart valve problems.
- Recent dental or medical procedures.
- A history of drug use.

If blood tests show germs, doctors must check for new heart murmurs and signs of clots in the body.

## Lab Tests

There are no lab tests that confirm endocarditis alone. But common findings include:

- Low red blood cell count (anemia).
- High white blood cell count.
- High inflammation markers (like ESR).
- Signs of immune system activity.

Urine tests may show blood or infection.

## Treatment

Treatment is long and serious.

### Antibiotics
- Given through a vein (IV) for 2 to 8 weeks.
- The type depends on the germ found.
- Home IV treatment is common.

### Surgery
- Needed if:
  - The heart valve is damaged.
  - The infection does not respond to antibiotics.
  - There is a large abscess or leaky valve.
  - A clot breaks off and blocks a blood vessel.

### Other Steps
- Remove any infected devices (like IV lines or catheters).
- Treat dental infections to stop germs from entering the blood.
- Do not use blood thinners if there is a brain clot.

Germs can hide in devices and form a protective layer (biofilm). This makes them hard to kill with antibiotics.

## Prognosis (Outlook)

- About 15 to 20 out of 100 people die in the hospital.
- About 40 out of 100 die within one year.
- Without treatment, the infection is always fatal.

Worse outcomes are more likely if:
- The person is older.
- The infection is caused by drug-resistant germs.
- There is a serious heart condition.
- Treatment is delayed.
- The aortic valve or multiple valves are affected.
- The vegetations are large.
- There are multiple types of germs in the blood.
- The infection is on an artificial valve.
- There is a mycotic aneurysm (a weak spot in a blood vessel).
- There is an abscess around the valve.
- A large clot breaks off and blocks a major blood vessel.

People with *Aspergillus* infection after valve surgery have a very poor chance of survival.

Right-sided endocarditis (affecting the tricuspid valve) has a better outcome than left-sided. This is because:
- The right side of the heart can handle more damage.
- Clots do not travel to the brain or other vital organs.
- *Staphylococcus aureus* infections on the right side respond better to treatment.

## Prevention

You can lower your risk by:

- Getting dental care before heart surgery.
- Keeping your mouth and skin clean.
- Removing infected IV lines or devices.
- Using good hygiene if you have a heart condition.

### Who Should Get Preventive Antibiotics?
- People with artificial heart valves.
- People who have had endocarditis before.
- People with certain heart defects.
- Heart transplant patients with valve problems.

Preventive antibiotics are now more focused on preventing infections from *enterococci* (a type of bacteria). This means:
- Vancomycin or amoxicillin with clavulanic acid may be used instead of older antibiotics.

## Key Points

- The heart is usually safe from infection.
- Endocarditis usually happens when the heart lining is already damaged.
- Common heart problems that raise risk:
  - Congenital heart defects.
  - Rheumatic heart disease.
  - Bicuspid or calcified aortic valves.
  - Mitral valve prolapse.
  - Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
  - Previous endocarditis.
  - Artificial heart valves or other devices.

### Heart Damage from Infection
- Abscesses in the heart muscle.
- Problems with the heart’s electrical system.
- Sudden valve leaks.

### Body-Wide Effects
- Immune system problems (like kidney damage).
- Clots that break off and block blood vessels.
- These clots can affect:
  - Lungs (especially with right-sided infection).
  - Kidneys.
  - Spleen.
  - Brain.
  - Skin.
  - Eyes.

### Diagnosis
- Get blood cultures.
- Use echocardiogram.
- Follow clinical guidelines (like the Duke or European Society of Cardiology criteria).

### Treatment
- Long course of IV antibiotics.
- Surgery may be needed for serious damage or resistant germs.

### Prevention
- Use antibiotics before high-risk procedures if you are at high risk.
- Keep your mouth and skin clean.
- Remove infected devices.

# Shinbone Twisting at Birth

Some babies are born with a twist in the shinbone.  
The shinbone is the main bone in the lower leg.  

Twisting of the shinbone is common at birth.  
The twist can be inward or outward.  

Outward twisting is normal as a child grows.  
It usually does not cause any problems.  

Inward twisting is also common at birth.  
Most children grow out of it by age 5 or 6.  

If the inward twist is very strong, it may be a sign of a nerve or muscle problem.  
It could also be a sign of a condition called Blount disease.  

A strong inward twist can cause a child to walk with toes pointing inward.  
This is called toeing-in.  
It can also lead to bowlegs.  

Doctors check for this by looking at the legs.  
They take measurements to see how much the bone is twisted.  

Most children do not need treatment.  
The bone usually straightens on its own by age 5 or 6.  

Some children with a severe twist may need special shoes.  
They might also need a cast or leg braces.

# Rifamycins

Rifamycins are a group of antibiotics. They kill bacteria by stopping the bacteria from making RNA. RNA is needed for bacteria to grow and multiply.

The following are rifamycins:
- Rifabutin
- Rifampin (also called rifampicin)
- Rifapentine
- Rifaximin

---

## Rifabutin, Rifampin, and Rifapentine

Rifabutin, rifampin, and rifapentine work the same way in the body. They have similar effects on bacteria and cause similar side effects.

You take these medicines by mouth. They are well absorbed and spread through the body. They reach many tissues and fluids, including the fluid around the brain and spinal cord.

Rifampin builds up in certain white blood cells. This helps clear bacteria from abscesses. The liver breaks down rifampin. Most of it leaves the body through the bile. A small amount leaves through the urine.

### What these medicines are used for

Rifampin works against:
- Most types of bacteria that have a thick outer layer (gram-positive)
- Some types of bacteria that have a thin outer layer (gram-negative)
- Certain types of *Mycobacterium* bacteria

Resistance to rifampin can develop quickly. So it is almost never used alone. It is always used with other antibiotics.

#### Tuberculosis
Rifampin is used to treat tuberculosis. It is part of a combination treatment.

#### Atypical mycobacterial infections
Rifampin works against many types of atypical mycobacteria. But it does not work against fast-growing types like *Mycobacterium fortuitum*, *M. chelonae*, or *M. abscessus*.

#### Leprosy
Rifampin is used with dapsone, and sometimes with clofazimine.

#### Staphylococcal infections
Rifampin is used for serious staph infections. This includes:
- Bone infections (osteomyelitis)
- Infections of heart valves with artificial parts (prosthetic valve endocarditis)
- Infections around artificial joints or other medical devices

It is used with other antibiotics that fight staph.

#### *Legionella* infections
Older studies suggest better results when rifampin is used with erythromycin. Using rifampin with azithromycin or a fluoroquinolone does not help more.

#### Pneumococcal meningitis
Rifampin can be used if the bacteria are sensitive to it. It is used with vancomycin. It may also be used if the bacteria are resistant to ceftriaxone or cefotaxime. It is also used if the response to treatment is slow.

#### Preventing meningitis in close contacts
Rifampin can be used alone to prevent meningitis in people who have been around someone with meningococcal meningitis or *Haemophilus influenzae* type b meningitis.

### Choosing between rifampin and rifabutin

- For tuberculosis, both rifampin and rifabutin work equally well in people with or without HIV.
- If you are taking HIV medicines (antiretroviral therapy), rifabutin is preferred. It does not lower the levels of these HIV medicines as much as rifampin does.
- For lung infections caused by *Mycobacterium avium* complex (MAC), rifampin is preferred unless you are on HIV medicine. Then rifabutin may be used.
- For widespread MAC infections, rifabutin is better than rifampin. It works better in lab tests and causes fewer drug interactions.

### Rifapentine

Rifapentine is used to treat:
- Active tuberculosis in the lungs
- Latent tuberculosis (when the bacteria are present but not causing symptoms)

### Who should not take rifampin or rifabutin

Do not take rifampin or rifabutin if you have had an allergic reaction to them.

### Pregnancy and breastfeeding

- Animal studies with rifabutin showed harm at high doses. But no good studies have been done in pregnant or breastfeeding women. Safety during breastfeeding is not known.
- Animal studies with rifampin and rifapentine show a risk to the baby at normal human doses. No good studies have been done in pregnant women.
- Because of possible cancer risk in animals, the maker does not recommend rifampin while breastfeeding.
- However, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says rifampin is safe during breastfeeding. You and your doctor should decide if you should stop breastfeeding or stop the medicine, based on how important the medicine is to you.

---

## Side Effects of Rifamycins

Common side effects include:
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Diarrhea
- Heartburn

More serious side effects include:
- Liver problems (the most serious)
- Stomach upset
- Brain and nerve issues
- Low blood cell counts

### Liver problems

Liver problems happen more often when rifampin is used with isoniazid or pyrazinamide. During the first week of treatment, rifampin may cause a temporary rise in bilirubin. Bilirubin is a substance in the blood. This rise is not dangerous and does not mean you should stop treatment.

### Brain and nerve issues

These can include:
- Headache
- Drowsiness
- Trouble walking (ataxia)
- Confusion

### Other serious reactions

Rash, fever, low white blood cells, low red blood cells, low platelets, kidney problems, and kidney damage can happen. These are usually due to an allergic reaction. They are more likely if you stop the medicine and restart it later. These problems go away when you stop taking rifampin.

### Rifabutin and eye problems

Rifabutin can cause eye inflammation. This can affect one or both eyes. The risk goes up with higher doses.

### Other changes

Rifampin, rifabutin, and rifapentine can turn your urine, saliva, sweat, mucus, and tears a reddish-orange color. This is normal and not harmful. But it can permanently stain soft contact lenses.

### Monitoring liver health

If you have liver disease, your doctor should check your liver function before starting rifampin. They should check it every 2 to 4 weeks during treatment. No dose changes are needed for kidney problems.

---

## Drug Interactions

Rifampin strongly affects liver enzymes. This can make many other medicines less effective.

Rifampin can reduce the effect of:
- Blood pressure medicines (ACE inhibitors)
- Atovaquone
- Barbiturates
- Beta-blockers
- Calcium channel blockers
- Chloramphenicol
- Clarithromycin
- Hormone birth control pills (oral and systemic)
- Steroids
- Cyclosporine
- Dapsone
- Digoxin
- Doxycycline
- Fluconazole
- Haloperidol
- Itraconazole
- Ketoconazole
- Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (delavirdine, nevirapine)
- Pain medicines (opioids)
- Phenytoin
- Protease inhibitors
- Quinidine
- Diabetes medicines (sulfonylureas)
- Tacrolimus
- Theophylline
- Thyroid hormone (thyroxine)
- Tocainide
- Tricyclic antidepressants
- Voriconazole
- Warfarin
- Zidovudine

Your doctor may need to change the dose of these medicines when you start or stop rifampin.

### Other medicines that affect rifampin

Some medicines, like protease inhibitors, azoles, and clarithromycin, slow down liver enzymes. This can raise levels of rifampin in your body. This increases the risk of side effects.

For example, eye inflammation (uveitis) is more common when rifabutin is used with clarithromycin or azoles.

---

## Rifaximin

Rifaximin is a type of rifamycin. It is not well absorbed when taken by mouth. About 97% of it passes through the gut and comes out in the stool.

### Uses of rifaximin

#### Traveler’s diarrhea
Rifaximin can be used to treat traveler’s diarrhea caused by certain types of *Escherichia coli* bacteria.

It does not work for diarrhea caused by other bacteria like *Shigella*, *Salmonella*, or *Campylobacter*. Because it is not absorbed into the blood, it is not safe for infections that spread through the body.

**Dosage for traveler’s diarrhea:**
- 200 milligrams by mouth every 8 hours
- For 3 days
- For adults and children over 12 years old

#### Other uses
Rifaximin may also be used for:
- Liver-related brain problems (hepatic encephalopathy)
- Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)

# Jaw Dislocation

A dislocated jaw is very painful. It is a serious dental emergency. You need to see a doctor or dentist right away.

Your mouth may not close. Your jaw might be twisted to one side.

Most of the time, a dislocated jaw happens when you open your mouth too wide. This can happen when you yawn, bite into a big sandwich, vomit, or during a dental visit.

It is more likely to happen if you have had a jaw dislocation before. It can also happen if your jaw is loose. This looseness may be due to a condition called temporomandibular disorder.

## How Doctors Fix a Dislocated Jaw

Doctors or dentists put the jaw back in place by hand. This is called manual reduction.

Here is how they do it:

- They wrap gauze around their fingers for protection.
- They place their thumbs inside your mouth, on the back teeth.
- They place their other fingers under the bottom of your jaw.
- They press down on the back teeth.
- They push your chin upward.
- They keep doing this until the jaw moves back into its normal position.

## Using a Barton Bandage

After the jaw is back in place, doctors may use a Barton bandage. This is a special wrap.

The bandage helps keep your jaw still. It stops the jaw from moving too much. This helps prevent another dislocation while the joint heals.

## What You Should Do After Treatment

- Wear the Barton bandage as directed.
- Do not open your mouth wide for at least six weeks.
- When you feel a yawn coming, put your fist under your chin. This stops your mouth from opening too far.
- Cut your food into small pieces. This makes it easier to eat without opening your mouth wide.
- If you have had more than one jaw dislocation, surgery may be needed.
- Surgery can tighten the ligaments that connect your jaw to your skull. This makes the joint more stable.

# How Food and Drugs Affect Each Other

Food and drugs can change how each other work in your body.  
This can affect how well your medicine works.  
It can also affect your nutrition and health.

## How Food Affects Drugs

Food can change how your body absorbs a drug.  
It can make the drug work faster, slower, or not at all.  
Some foods block the absorption of many antibiotics.  
This means the medicine may not work as well.

Food can also change how your body breaks down drugs.  
A high-protein diet can speed up the breakdown of some drugs.  
This happens because it activates a liver enzyme called cytochrome P-450.

Eating grapefruit can slow down the breakdown of some drugs.  
This is because grapefruit blocks a specific liver enzyme called cytochrome P-450 34A.  
Drugs affected include amiodarone, carbamazepine, cyclosporine, some calcium channel blockers, and statins.

Your gut bacteria can also affect how drugs work.  
Diets that change the balance of gut bacteria can strongly affect how your body handles certain medicines.

## Dangerous Food-Drug Combinations

Some foods can cause serious side effects when taken with certain drugs.  
For example, cheese contains a substance called tyramine.  
If you take a medicine called a monoamine oxidase inhibitor and eat cheese, you could have a sudden and dangerous rise in blood pressure.

## How Nutrition Affects Drug Response

Poor nutrition can change how your body handles drugs.  
Low energy and protein intake can reduce the levels of important liver enzymes.  
This can make your body absorb less medicine or break it down more slowly.

Low levels of calcium, magnesium, or zinc can also slow down how your body processes drugs.  
A lack of vitamin C can reduce the activity of drug-processing enzymes, especially in older adults.

## How Drugs Affect Nutrition

Many drugs change your appetite, how you absorb food, or how your body uses nutrients.
