# Amniotic Fluid Embolism

Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare but serious condition. It happens when fluid from around the baby gets into the mother’s blood. This fluid can contain tiny pieces of the baby’s skin or tissue.

When this happens, the mother’s body can have a strong reaction. This reaction can hurt the lungs and heart. It can also cause very heavy bleeding.

This condition is very rare. It usually happens during the later stages of pregnancy. It can also happen during an abortion in the first or second trimester. Among women who die suddenly during labor, this is one of the most common causes.

## Things That May Increase the Risk

The risk may be higher if the mother:

- Is older
- Is carrying more than one baby, such as twins or triplets
- Has too much fluid around the baby
- Has the placenta covering the opening of the uterus (placenta previa)
- Has the placenta stuck too tightly to the uterus (placenta accreta)
- Has the placenta separate from the uterus too early (placental abruption)
- Has had a serious injury to the belly
- Has eclampsia (a dangerous condition with seizures during pregnancy)
- Had labor started with medicine (induced labor)
- Has a tear in the cervix
- Had forceps used during delivery
- Has a tear in the uterus (uterine rupture)
- Had a cesarean delivery

## Signs and Symptoms

The body’s reaction usually happens during or just after labor and delivery. The mother may:

- Have a very fast or irregular heartbeat
- Have low blood pressure
- Have trouble breathing
- Stop breathing (respiratory failure)
- Have her heart stop (cardiac arrest)

The chance of death is very high.

A common problem is a condition called disseminated intravascular coagulation. This means small blood clots form all through the bloodstream. These clots use up the body’s clotting material. This leads to severe, uncontrolled bleeding. This needs emergency treatment.

## How It Is Diagnosed

Doctors will check the mother’s symptoms right away. They may do blood tests to see how well the blood is clotting.

Doctors diagnose amniotic fluid embolism based on sudden symptoms, especially:

- Heart stops suddenly
- Sudden trouble breathing
- Low blood pressure
- Heavy, uncontrolled bleeding

## How It Is Treated

This is a life-threatening emergency. A team of specialists must act fast. The mother needs intensive care.

Treatment includes:

- Immediate help from a medical emergency team
- Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) if the heart stops
- Medicines to help the uterus contract (to stop bleeding)
- Blood transfusions, including blood and blood components
- Medicines to help the blood clot
- Breathing support, such as a breathing machine
- Medicines to help the heart pump

If CPR does not bring back the heart’s rhythm, the baby must be delivered right away. This can be done using forceps, a vacuum device, or a cesarean delivery. Delivering the baby quickly can save the mother’s life. It can also save the baby if the baby is old enough to survive outside the womb.

Medicines to help the uterus contract are given to prevent more bleeding.

# Thiamin Deficiency

Thiamin deficiency can cause a condition called beriberi. It is most common in people who eat mostly white rice or refined carbs, especially in places where food is hard to get. It also happens often in people who drink too much alcohol.

Symptoms can include nerve problems, heart failure, and brain issues. Thiamin is given to both diagnose and treat the deficiency.

Thiamin is found in many foods. Good sources include whole grains, pork, liver, enriched cereals, nuts, beans, and potatoes. Thiamin helps your body use energy from food. It is especially important for your nerves and heart.

Thiamin is very safe. It does not cause harm, even in large amounts.

---

## What Causes Thiamin Deficiency?

### Primary Deficiency (Not Getting Enough Thiamin)

- You do not eat enough thiamin.
- This often happens when your diet is mostly white rice, white flour, or sugar.
- It can also happen if you are not eating enough of any kind of food. This may occur in young people with severe eating disorders or older adults who do not eat well.
- Other B vitamins are often low at the same time.

### Secondary Deficiency (Body Cannot Use Thiamin Well)

- Your body needs more thiamin than usual. This can happen during pregnancy, breastfeeding, with fever, or with overactive thyroid.
- You cannot absorb thiamin well. This can happen with long-term diarrhea.
- Your liver does not process thiamin properly. This can happen with liver disease.
- In people who drink too much alcohol, several problems happen together:
  - They eat little thiamin.
  - Their gut does not absorb thiamin well.
  - Their body uses thiamin faster.
  - There may be a problem with a key enzyme that needs thiamin.

---

## How Thiamin Deficiency Affects the Body

Without enough thiamin, your nerves and brain can be damaged. The thalamus, mammillary bodies, and cerebellum in the brain may shrink. Blood flow to the brain drops, and blood vessels in the brain become tighter.

Your heart may get bigger. The heart muscle fibers swell and break down. Fluid builds up in the spaces between the fibers. Blood vessels widen, which can cause swelling in the feet and legs. Blood may bypass normal paths and flow directly from arteries to veins. This can lead to heart failure with high blood flow.

---

## Symptoms and Signs

### Early Symptoms (Not Specific)

- Feeling tired
- Feeling irritable
- Trouble remembering things
- Trouble sleeping
- Pain in the chest
- Loss of appetite
- Stomach discomfort

### Dry Beriberi (Nerve Problems)

- Numbness or tingling in the toes and feet
- Burning pain in the feet, worse at night
- Cramps in the calves
- Pain in the legs
- Pain on the bottom of the feet
- Tenderness in the calf muscles
- Trouble standing up from a squat
- Loss of feeling in the toes
- Muscle wasting
- Over time, the same problems can spread to the arms

### Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome

This condition affects some people who drink too much alcohol and do not eat fortified foods.

**Wernicke Encephalopathy** (acute brain problem):
- Slow thinking or lack of energy
- Eyes move uncontrollably (nystagmus)
- Trouble walking (ataxia)
- Eyes cannot move properly (ophthalmoplegia)
- Confusion or drowsiness
- If not treated, it can lead to coma or death

**Korsakoff Psychosis** (memory and thinking problems):
- Confusion
- Trouble speaking clearly
- Making up stories to fill memory gaps (confabulation)
- Cannot remember recent events

This often follows repeated episodes of Wernicke encephalopathy.

### Cardiovascular (Wet) Beriberi (Heart Problems)

- Blood vessels widen
- Fast heartbeat
- Sweating
- Warm skin
- Build-up of lactic acid in the blood
- Later, heart failure develops:
  - Trouble breathing when lying flat
  - Swelling in the lungs
  - Swelling in the legs and feet
- In severe cases, blood pressure drops and shock can occur

### Infantile Beriberi

This happens in babies under 4 weeks old who are breastfed by mothers low in thiamin.

- Sudden heart failure
- Cannot cry (aphonia)
- No reflexes in the knees or elbows

### Important Note

Giving sugar through a vein (IV glucose) can make symptoms worse in people who are low in thiamin. This is because the body uses more thiamin when processing sugar.

---

## How Is Thiamin Deficiency Diagnosed?

- A good response to thiamin treatment is the main clue.
- If symptoms improve after taking thiamin, the diagnosis is likely.
- Other nerve problems (like from diabetes, alcohol use, vitamin B12 deficiency, or heavy metal poisoning) do not improve with thiamin.
- Nerve problems that affect only one nerve (mononeuropathy) or a few nerves (mononeuritis multiplex) are not caused by thiamin deficiency.

Check blood levels of electrolytes, including magnesium, to rule out other causes.

In unclear cases, doctors may test:
- Thiamin levels in red blood cells (low in deficiency)
- Thiamin in urine over 24 hours (low in deficiency)

Diagnosing heart-related beriberi can be hard if other heart problems are present. A trial of thiamin treatment can help confirm the diagnosis.

---

## How Is Thiamin Deficiency Treated?

- Give thiamin supplements. Dose depends on the symptoms.
- Make sure your diet includes enough thiamin, even if you feel fine.

**Important:** If you are at risk for thiamin deficiency, get thiamin before getting IV sugar. This is especially true for people who drink too much alcohol.

> **Key Tip:** Give 100 milligrams of thiamin through a vein before giving IV sugar to people at risk.

### Doses of Thiamin

- **Mild nerve problems:** 10 to 20 milligrams by mouth once a day for 2 weeks
- **Moderate or severe nerve problems:** 20 to 30 milligrams per day (one or more doses), for several weeks after symptoms go away
- **Swelling and fluid from heart problems:** 100 milligrams through a vein once a day for several days
- **Heart failure** is also treated with other medicines

### For Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome

- Give thiamin for several days.
- A common plan:
  - 500 milligrams through a vein every 8 hours for 2 days
  - Then 250 milligrams through a vein or muscle once a day for 5 more days
  - Also give other B vitamins
- Allergic reactions to IV thiamin are very rare.
- Eye movement problems may improve in a day.
- Memory and thinking problems may take 1 to 3 months to improve.
- Full recovery is often not possible, especially in brain-related cases.

### Other Important Points

- Thiamin deficiency often happens with other B vitamin deficiencies.
- So, doctors usually give a mix of water-soluble vitamins for several weeks.
- Eat a healthy diet with 1 to 2 times the daily recommended amount of vitamins.
- Stop drinking alcohol completely.

---

## Key Points

- Thiamin deficiency is more likely in people who eat mostly white rice, white flour, or other refined carbs, especially in areas with food shortages.
- It is also common in people who drink too much alcohol.
- Early signs are vague: tiredness, mood changes, poor memory, sleep issues.
- Specific problems include nerve damage, heart failure, and brain issues (especially in people who drink too much alcohol).
- Diagnosis is based on symptoms and how well you respond to thiamin treatment.

# Aging and Medications

Medications are the most common treatment used in medicine. They play a key role in helping older adults stay healthy and active. Without medications, many older adults would not live as long or function as well.

### Did You Know...

- Up to half of older adults do not take their medications exactly as their doctor told them to.
- Older adults are more likely to have side effects from medications than younger people.

---

## Why Older Adults Take More Medications

Older adults often have more than one long-term health problem. These can include high blood pressure, diabetes, or arthritis. Because of this, they usually take more medications than younger people.

Most of the medicines older adults take are for long-term conditions. These are taken every day for years. Some medicines are only used for a short time. These include treatments for infections, certain types of pain, or constipation.

- About 90% of older adults take at least one prescription medicine regularly.
- About 43% take at least five different prescription medicines every day.
- When over-the-counter medicines and supplements are included, the number of people taking multiple medicines is even higher.

People who are frail, in the hospital, or living in a nursing home usually take the most medicines.

Many prescription and over-the-counter medicines and supplements can be dangerous for older adults. Always check with your doctor or pharmacist before using them.

---

## Benefits of Medications

Medicines have helped improve the health and quality of life for older adults over the past few decades.

- **Vaccines** help prevent serious infections like the flu, RSV, COVID-19, and pneumonia. These used to cause many deaths in older adults.
- **Antibiotics** can treat serious bacterial infections such as urinary tract infections and pneumonia.
- **Blood pressure medicines** help prevent strokes and heart attacks.
- **Diabetes medicines**, including insulin, help control blood sugar. This allows people with diabetes to live normal lives. These medicines also lower the risk of eye and kidney damage.
- **Pain medicines** help people with arthritis stay active and keep doing daily tasks.

---

## Risks of Medications

Medicines can cause side effects. These are not the intended results. Side effects can be mild or serious.

Starting in late middle age, the risk of side effects increases. Older adults are more than twice as likely to have side effects as younger people. These side effects can be worse and may lead to:

- Feeling tired or dizzy
- Confusion
- Falls
- More doctor visits
- Hospital stays

### Why Are Older Adults More Sensitive to Medicines?

As people age, their bodies change in ways that affect how medicines work:

- The body holds less water and muscle, and more fat.
  - Medicines that dissolve in water become more concentrated in the body.
  - Medicines that dissolve in fat build up in fat tissue.
- The kidneys become less able to remove medicines from the body.
- The liver becomes less able to break down medicines.

Because of these changes, medicines stay in the body longer. This increases the chance of side effects.

For example:
- Digoxin is a medicine used for some heart problems.
- It dissolves in water and leaves the body through the kidneys.
- As people age, they have less water in their body and their kidneys work less well.
- This causes digoxin to build up in the body.
- This can lead to nausea or irregular heartbeats.
- To prevent this, doctors may prescribe a lower dose or switch to a different medicine.

Older adults are also more sensitive to the effects of many medicines. For example:

- Some anxiety medicines or sleep aids can make older adults feel more sleepy, dizzy, or confused.
- Blood pressure medicines can lower blood pressure too much in older adults.
  - This can cause dizziness, lightheadedness, or falls.

If you have these side effects, talk to your doctor.

---

## Anticholinergic Medicines

Some medicines have a side effect called anticholinergic effects. These include:

- Certain antidepressants (like amitriptyline and imipramine)
- Many allergy and cold medicines (like diphenhydramine)
- Some bladder control medicines (like oxybutynin and tolterodine)
- Many antipsychotic medicines (like chlorpromazine and clozapine)

Anticholinergic effects can cause:
- Confusion
- Blurred vision
- Constipation
- Dry mouth
- Trouble starting to urinate
- Dizziness or loss of balance

These effects are more common in older adults, especially those with memory problems.

### What Does "Anticholinergic" Mean?

Acetylcholine is a natural chemical in the body. It helps nerves talk to each other. It helps with memory, focus, and the function of the heart, lungs, bladder, and digestive system.

Some medicines block acetylcholine. This can cause problems in the body.

Even though some anticholinergic effects are helpful (like reducing tremors or nausea), most are not. Because older adults have less acetylcholine, these medicines can cause more harm than good. Doctors usually try to avoid these medicines in older adults when possible.

---

## Drug Interactions

Medicines can interact with:

- Other medicines (drug–drug interaction)
- A health condition (drug–disease interaction)
- Food (drug–food interaction)
- Herbal products (drug–herbal interaction)

Older adults are more likely to have these interactions because they often have more health problems and take more medicines.

For example:
- A medicine might make a health problem worse.
- A medicine might not work well if taken with food or another medicine.

### How to Reduce the Risk of Interactions

- Always tell your doctor and pharmacist about all medicines you take, including over-the-counter medicines and supplements.
- Ask your doctor or pharmacist before starting any new medicine, even if it is sold without a prescription.
- Do not take someone else’s medicine, even if their symptoms seem similar to yours.

---

## Not Taking Medicines as Directed

Not following your doctor’s instructions for taking medicine is risky.

- Up to half of older adults do not take their medicines as directed.
- This can happen because of side effects, cost, or confusion about the schedule.

It is not safe to:
- Skip doses
- Take too little
- Take too much

If a medicine causes side effects, do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor. There may be a safer way to manage the problem.

---

## How to Get the Most Benefit and Stay Safe

You and your caregivers can take steps to use medicines safely and effectively.

### Know Your Medicines and Health Conditions

- Keep a list of all your health problems and allergies.
- Keep a full list of all medicines you take, including over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, minerals, and herbal supplements.
- Update this list whenever you start or stop a medicine.
- Learn:
  - Why each medicine is prescribed
  - What benefits it should provide
  - What side effects to watch for
  - How to take it (time of day, with or without food, with other medicines)
  - What to do if you miss a dose
- Ask your doctor, nurse, or pharmacist to write down instructions. Write them down yourself if needed.

### Use Medicines the Right Way

- Take your medicines exactly as told.
- Use tools to help you remember:
  - Pill organizers
  - Alarm clocks
  - Smartphone apps
- Do not stop a medicine without talking to your doctor.
- If a medicine is too expensive, talk to your doctor or pharmacist about cheaper options.
- Throw away unused medicines properly. Do not keep them for later use unless your doctor says to.

### How to Safely Dispose of Medicines

- Follow the instructions on the label.
- Visit the Food and Drug Administration’s website for safe disposal tips.
- Take unused medicines to a pharmacy or local law enforcement site that accepts them.
- If no other option is available:
  - Mix the medicine with coffee grounds or kitty litter.
  - Put it in a sealed plastic bag or container.
  - Throw it in the trash.

Do not flush medicines unless the label says to.

---

## Work with Your Doctor and Pharmacist

- Get all your prescriptions from the same pharmacy if possible.
- Choose a pharmacy that checks for drug interactions and keeps a full record of your medicines.
- Bring all your medicines and supplements to every doctor visit.
- Review your medicine list with your doctor or pharmacist regularly.
  - Ask if you are taking the right medicines.
  - Ask if any medicines can be stopped.
- If your doctor changes a medicine, ask your pharmacist to check for possible interactions.
- Tell your doctor and pharmacist about all over-the-counter medicines and supplements you use.
- Ask your doctor before starting any new medicine.
- Report any new or unusual symptoms to your doctor or pharmacist.
- If the medicine schedule is too hard to follow, ask for help simplifying it.
- If you see more than one doctor, make sure each one knows all the medicines you take.
- Ask your pharmacist to print labels in large, clear text.
- Ask for easy-to-open containers and easy-to-hold packaging.

---

## Remembering to Take Medicines

To get the full benefit of your medicines, you must take them at the right time and in the right way.

Some medicines must be taken on an empty stomach. Others must be taken with food. Some must be taken at specific times of day.

For example:

- If taken with food or other drinks, they will not work well.

# Neuropathic Arthropathy

Neuropathic arthropathy is a condition where joints break down quickly. This happens because the nerves in the body are damaged. When nerves are damaged, you may not feel pain or know where your joints are. This can lead to injuries that go unnoticed.

The most common causes are diabetes and stroke. Other conditions can also cause this problem.

## What Causes Neuropathic Arthropathy?

Many health problems can lead to nerve damage. This includes:

- Diabetes
- Stroke
- Nerve damage from injury or tumors
- Certain rare inherited nerve diseases
- Spinal cord problems
- Leprosy
- Some types of cancer
- Congenital conditions (present from birth)

When nerves are damaged, the body cannot feel pain or know the position of the joints. This means small injuries can happen again and again. The body does not protect the joint because it does not feel pain.

Blood flow to the bone increases. This causes the bone to break down faster. Over time, this leads to joint damage.

Each injury makes the joint worse. Bleeding into the joint and tiny fractures can happen. These make the joint unstable. Ligaments become loose. Muscles weaken. Cartilage wears away fast.

All of this can lead to joint dislocation. Dislocations make the joint worse. In later stages, the joint may grow extra bone. This can cause swelling and deformity.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The joint problem usually starts years after the nerve damage begins. But once it starts, it can get worse very fast. It may destroy the joint in just a few months.

Pain is common at first. But because nerve damage reduces pain, the pain may be much less than expected for the amount of damage.

Early signs include:

- Swelling in the joint
- Fluid buildup (often with blood)
- The joint feels loose or unstable
- Partial dislocation (subluxation)
- Sudden dislocation

Later, pain may return if the joint breaks down fast. This can happen with fractures or blood buildup in the joint.

In advanced stages, the joint becomes very swollen. This is due to extra bone growth and large amounts of fluid. The joint shape changes because of dislocations and broken bones.

Pieces of bone or cartilage can break off and float inside the joint. This can cause a grating sound when the joint moves. The sound is often louder than the pain.

Most often, the knee or ankle is affected. But other joints can be involved too. The joint most affected depends on the cause.

- Diabetes often affects the foot and ankle.
- Stroke and tabes dorsalis often affect the knee and hip.
- Syringomyelia often affects the spine, shoulder, and elbow.

Usually, only one joint is affected. Sometimes two or three joints are involved. The small joints in the feet can be affected more widely.

Infections can develop in the joint. This is more likely in people with diabetes. Infections may not cause fever or feeling unwell. So, doctors must be very careful to check for infection.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect this condition in people with nerve damage who have joint problems. The joint damage is severe, but the pain is mild.

The main test is an X-ray. X-rays show joint damage. The changes may look like osteoarthritis at first.

Signs on X-ray include:

- Broken pieces of bone
- Bone loss
- New bone growing in odd shapes
- Loss of space between bones in the joint
- Joint swelling
- Joint dislocation

The bones may become bent or twisted. New bone often forms near the joint and can grow up the bone shaft. This is common in long bones like the thigh or shin.

Calcium can build up in soft tissues. Large, strange-shaped bone spurs may form around the joint. In the spine, large curved bone spurs (like a parrot’s beak) can appear even if there is no spine disease.

Neuropathic arthropathy gets worse faster than osteoarthritis.

## How Is It Treated?

### Treat the Underlying Cause

If the nerve damage is due to diabetes, controlling blood sugar may slow joint damage. Treating the root cause can help stop or slow the joint damage.

### Protect the Joint

If a small fracture is found early, even if there is no pain, treatment can help. Stabilizing the joint with a splint, special boot, or brace can prevent more injury.

This protection may stop the joint from getting worse. It may even prevent the condition in people at risk.

### Surgery

If the joint is badly damaged and unstable, surgery may be needed.

For very damaged joints, fusion surgery (arthrodesis) can help. This joins the bones together using metal rods, screws, and bone grafts.

For damaged hips or knees, joint replacement surgery may work. But patients with nerve damage have a higher risk of problems after surgery. These include:

- The new joint coming loose
- The new joint dislocating

## Key Points

- Neuropathic arthropathy is a fast-acting joint destruction.
- It happens when you cannot feel pain or know where your joints are.
- Common causes include diabetes and stroke.
- Joint damage is much worse than the pain suggests.
- The condition can destroy a joint in a few months.
- X-rays show joint damage that does not match the pain level.
- Always check for infection, especially in people with diabetes.
- Treat the cause when possible.
- Protect the joint with braces, boots, or splints.
- Surgery may be needed for severe joint damage.

# Kawasaki Disease – Simple Explanation

Kawasaki disease is a serious illness that causes swelling in blood vessels. It mainly affects children under 5 years old.

## What Causes Kawasaki Disease?

- The exact cause is not known.
- It may start after a child gets an infection.
- Some children are more likely to get it because of their genes.
- It is not contagious.

## Who Gets Kawasaki Disease?

- Most children with Kawasaki disease are under 5 years old.
- Rarely, babies under 4 months, teens, or adults can get it.
- Boys are slightly more likely than girls to get it.
- It is more common in children of Japanese or Korean descent.
- It happens all over the world.
- In the United States, about 4,000 to 5,500 children get it each year.
- It can happen any time of year, but it is most common in spring and winter.

## What Happens in the Body?

- The disease causes swelling in the walls of blood vessels all over the body.
- The swelling in the heart’s blood vessels is the most dangerous.
- The swelling can also affect the pancreas, kidneys, and other organs.

## Symptoms of Kawasaki Disease

The illness starts with a high fever that lasts at least 5 days.

- The fever is usually above 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit (38 degrees Celsius).
- The fever does not go down with fever-reducing medicines like acetaminophen or ibuprofen.
- The eyes become red, but there is no discharge.
- A red, patchy rash appears on the chest, back, diaper area, and inside the mouth or vagina.
- The rash can look like hives or the rash from measles or scarlet fever.
- The throat is red.
- The lips are dry, cracked, and red.
- The tongue is red and looks like a strawberry.
- The palms of the hands and soles of the feet turn red or purple.
- The hands and feet may swell.
- About 10 days after the illness starts, the skin on the fingers and toes begins to peel.
- The lymph nodes in the neck are often swollen and tender.
- The illness can last from 2 to 12 weeks or longer.

## Heart Problems

- If not treated, heart problems can start 1 to 4 weeks after the illness begins.
- A few children develop a bulge in a heart artery (called a coronary artery aneurysm).
- These bulges can burst or cause a blood clot.
- A blood clot can block blood flow to the heart and cause a heart attack.
- A heart attack can lead to sudden death.
- Treatment greatly lowers the risk of these serious heart problems.

Other possible issues include:
- Vomiting
- Diarrhea
- Painful swelling in the brain lining (meningitis)
- Swelling in the ears, eyes, liver, joints, urethra, or gallbladder

These problems usually go away without lasting harm.

## How Doctors Diagnose Kawasaki Disease

Doctors look for a fever lasting at least 5 days and at least 4 of the following 5 signs:

- Red eyes with no discharge
- Red, dry, cracked lips and a red strawberry-like tongue
- Swelling, redness, and peeling of the hands and feet
- Red, patchy rash on the body
- Swollen, tender lymph nodes in the neck

To confirm the diagnosis, doctors may do:

- Blood and urine tests
- Chest X-ray
- Tests of blood and throat samples
- These tests help rule out other illnesses like measles, scarlet fever, juvenile arthritis, or MIS-C

Doctors may also do:

- An electrocardiogram (ECG) to check the heart’s electrical activity
- An echocardiogram (ultrasound of the heart) to look for heart problems

- These heart tests are done right away if Kawasaki disease is suspected.
- They are repeated 1 to 2 weeks later.
- If the second test is normal, no more testing is needed.
- If the first test is abnormal, doctors may repeat the test at 6 to 8 weeks and again at 6 to 12 months.
- If the heart test shows a problem, a stress test may be done.
- If a bulge in a heart artery is found, a heart catheterization may be needed.

## Treatment of Kawasaki Disease

Treatment must start as soon as possible. The best results come when treatment begins within 10 days of symptoms.

The main treatments are:

- Immune globulin given through a vein (IV)
- Aspirin taken by mouth

- Immune globulin helps reduce swelling in blood vessels.
- Aspirin helps reduce fever, rash, and pain.
- Aspirin is given for at least 2 weeks, or longer if needed.

- If heart tests show no problems, aspirin can be stopped.
- If heart problems are found, the child may need to take aspirin for months or years.

**Important safety note:**
- Aspirin can cause a rare but serious illness called Reye syndrome if a child has the flu or chickenpox.
- To stay safe, children on long-term aspirin must get:
  - A yearly flu shot
  - The chickenpox vaccine at the right age
- If a child gets the flu or chickenpox, doctors may switch to a different medicine called dipyridamole instead of aspirin for a short time.

Children with large bulges in heart arteries may also need blood-thinning medicines (anticoagulants) to prevent clots.

## Outlook (Prognosis)

- With treatment, most children recover fully if their heart arteries are not affected.
- If heart problems are present, the outcome depends on how serious they are.
- In the United States, almost no children die from Kawasaki disease when treated early.
- Without treatment, some children can die suddenly and without warning.

- About two-thirds of the bulges in heart arteries go away within 1 year.
- Larger bulges are more likely to stay and need more treatment.
- Even if the bulges go away, children may have a higher risk of heart problems later in life.

Early treatment makes a big difference in recovery and long-term health.

# Papilledema

Papilledema means swelling of the optic nerve where it enters the eye. This swelling happens because pressure inside the skull is too high. If the optic nerve swells for other reasons, like high blood pressure or a blocked blood vessel in the eye, it is not called papilledema.

Most people with papilledema do not notice vision problems at first. But some may see their vision go gray for a few seconds. This is called a transient visual obscurations.

Papilledema is a sign that something is wrong inside the skull. It is almost always present in both eyes. Finding the cause is very important.

## What Causes Papilledema?

The most common cause is a condition called idiopathic intracranial hypertension. This means pressure in the fluid around the brain is high, but there is no tumor or other mass. It is also called pseudotumor cerebri.

Other causes include:
- Brain tumors
- Brain infections like meningitis or encephalitis
- Brain injury or bleeding
- Blood clots in the large veins of the brain
- Scarring in the brain’s covering (arachnoidal adhesions)

## What Are the Symptoms?

At first, vision is usually normal. But some people may have:
- Vision that goes gray for a few seconds
- Flickering vision
- Blurry or double vision

Other symptoms of high pressure in the skull may include:
- Headaches
- Nausea
- Vomiting

An eye doctor can see signs of papilledema during an eye exam. These signs include:
- Swollen and red optic nerve head
- Bulging and twisted veins in the retina
- Small bleeding spots around the optic nerve, but not in the rest of the retina

If the optic nerve swells for other reasons, like inflammation or poor blood flow, it is not papilledema.

In the early stages, vision and pupil reactions to light are usually normal. They only become abnormal when the condition is advanced.

Eye tests can show:
- A larger blind spot in the vision
- Loss of side vision with curved blind spots that follow the nerve pattern

## How Is Papilledema Diagnosed?

A doctor will do a full eye exam. Then, they will do brain imaging right away. This is to rule out serious problems like a tumor.

The most common imaging tests are:
- MRI of the brain with contrast
- CT scan of the brain with contrast

If a blood clot in a brain vein is suspected, a special scan of the veins (MR venogram or CT venogram) may be done.

To measure pressure in the fluid around the brain, a lumbar puncture may be done. This test is only done after a mass is ruled out. Doing a lumbar puncture when a brain tumor is present can be dangerous.

If the brain scan shows no tumor, the fluid pressure is high, and other causes are ruled out, the diagnosis is idiopathic intracranial hypertension. This is the most common cause of high pressure in the skull.

To measure swelling, doctors may use:
- A special eye test with a lens to compare the height of the swollen nerve to normal areas
- Optical coherence tomography (OCT), which measures the thickness of the nerve fibers

OCT helps track changes over time.

It is important to tell papilledema apart from other causes of a swollen optic nerve. These include:
- Optic neuritis (inflammation of the optic nerve)
- Ischemic optic neuropathy (poor blood flow to the nerve)
- Very low eye pressure (less than or equal to 5 mm Hg)
- Blocked retinal vein
- Eye inflammation (uveitis)
- Pseudo swelling from optic nerve drusen (tiny deposits in the nerve)

For optic nerve drusen, the best tests are:
- B-scan ultrasound
- OCT
- Fundus autofluorescence

## How Is Papilledema Treated?

The main goal is to treat the cause of high pressure in the skull.

For idiopathic intracranial hypertension, the first treatments are:
- Losing weight
- Medicines like acetazolamide or topiramate

If vision is at risk and medicines do not work, surgery may be needed. Types of surgery include:
- Ventriculo-peritoneal shunt (a tube to drain fluid)
- Optic nerve sheath fenestration (a small cut in the nerve covering)
- Stenting of a blocked brain vein

If pressure is not lowered, the optic nerve can become damaged. This can lead to permanent vision loss.

## Key Points

- Papilledema is swelling of the optic nerve caused by high pressure inside the skull.
- Both eyes are usually affected.
- The optic nerve looks swollen and red. Veins in the retina are thick and twisted. There may be small bleeds around the nerve.
- Eye changes usually appear before vision problems.
- Get brain imaging right away.
- If no tumor is found, do a lumbar puncture to check fluid pressure.
- Treat the underlying cause.

# Too Much Vitamin K

Too much vitamin K is very rare. It happens most often in babies who drink formula.

Vitamin K comes in two types:

- **Phylloquinone**: This type is found in plants. You get it from the food you eat. It works better in your body when you eat it with fat. This type is safe, even if you take a lot.
- **Menaquinone**: This type is made by bacteria in your gut. Your body makes only a small amount. In some countries, people use this type as a supplement.

Vitamin K helps your blood to clot normally. It also helps keep your bones and other tissues healthy.

Too much vitamin K can cause problems. It may lead to anemia. This happens when red blood cells break open. It can also cause jaundice. Jaundice in newborns can lead to brain damage. This brain damage is called kernicterus.

(See also: Overview of Vitamins.)

# Infection with *Dipylidium caninum*

*Dipylidium caninum* is a type of tapeworm. It can infect people, especially children. Most people do not have any symptoms.

This tapeworm lives in dogs and cats. Fleas carry the tapeworm. A person gets infected by swallowing a flea that has the tapeworm inside it. This usually happens when a young child puts a flea in their mouth.

The infection does not cause illness in most people. It goes away on its own. But you might see small, white segments in your stool. These are parts of the tapeworm.

## Treatment

You can treat the infection with a medicine called praziquantel. Take one dose by mouth. The dose depends on your weight.

Another medicine, niclosamide, can also be used. It is not available in the United States. If it is used, you take four tablets. Each tablet is 500 milligrams. Chew one tablet at a time and swallow it.

For children, the dose is based on weight. The maximum dose is 2 grams.

## What to Expect

The infection usually goes away by itself. It often clears up in about six weeks. You do not need treatment if you have no symptoms. But treatment can help clear the worm faster.

# Lymphocytopenia – Simple Explanation

Lymphocytopenia means you have too few lymphocytes in your blood.  
Lymphocytes are a type of white blood cell that help your body fight infections.  

## What Are Lymphocytes?

There are three main types of lymphocytes:  
- B cells  
- T cells  
- Natural killer cells  

Each type helps protect your body in different ways.  
B cells make antibodies that fight bacteria and other germs.  
T cells and natural killer cells help fight viruses, fungi, and parasites.  

A normal blood count has at least 1,500 lymphocytes per microliter in adults.  
In children, the normal count is above 3,000 per microliter.  
Low lymphocyte levels do not always mean your total white blood cell count is low.

## Common Causes of Low Lymphocytes

The most common causes are:  
- Viral infections, including HIV, flu, and the virus that causes COVID-19  
- Poor nutrition (undernutrition)  

Other causes include:  
- Fasting or not eating for a long time  
- Severe stress on the body  
- Use of steroid medicines like prednisone  
- Chemotherapy or radiation for cancer  
- Long-term use of steroid medicines  
- Certain autoimmune diseases like lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, or myasthenia gravis  
- Chronic infections such as HIV or miliary tuberculosis  
- Some cancers like leukemia or lymphoma  
- Sarcoidosis  
- Certain inherited immune disorders, such as DiGeorge syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, SCID, ataxia-telangiectasia, and WHIM syndrome  

Some of these conditions can cause low lymphocytes that last a long time or even for life.

## Symptoms of Lymphocytopenia

Many people with mild lymphocytopenia have no symptoms at all.  
When symptoms do appear, they are often due to the underlying cause.  

You might have:  
- Swollen lymph nodes or a swollen spleen (this can suggest HIV or cancer)  
- Cough, runny nose, or fever (this can suggest a viral infection)  
- Small tonsils or lymph nodes (this can suggest a genetic immune problem)  
- Painful, swollen joints and a rash (this can suggest lupus or rheumatoid arthritis)  

If your lymphocyte count is very low, you may get repeated infections.  
These infections can be caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites.  
Symptoms depend on where the infection is and what kind of germ is causing it.

## How Is Lymphocytopenia Diagnosed?

A blood test called a complete blood count is usually the first step.  
This test is often done for other reasons and may find low lymphocytes by chance.  

If you have frequent or serious infections, your doctor may do this test to check for lymphocytopenia.  

If your lymphocyte count is very low, your doctor may:  
- Test your blood for HIV and other infections  
- Take a sample of bone marrow to examine under a microscope  
- Test for specific types of lymphocytes (B cells, T cells, natural killer cells)  

In babies and young children with long-term low lymphocytes and low antibody levels, doctors may do genetic testing to look for inherited immune problems.

## How Is Lymphocytopenia Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause.  

If a medicine is causing low lymphocytes, stopping the medicine often helps.  
The lymphocyte count usually returns to normal within days.  

If HIV is the cause, treatment with at least three different antiviral medicines can help raise T cell levels and improve health.  

For people with low B cells and low antibody production, doctors may give gamma globulin.  
This is a medicine rich in antibodies. It helps prevent infections.  

For some inherited immune disorders, stem cell transplantation may be an option.  
This treatment can help rebuild the immune system.  

If you get an infection, your doctor will give you the right medicine.  
This could be an antibiotic, antifungal, antiviral, or antiparasitic drug.  
The medicine is chosen based on the type of germ causing the infection.

# Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)

DIC is a serious condition where blood clots form too quickly in the bloodstream. This happens when a substance called tissue factor gets into the blood. This triggers the body’s clotting system to overreact.

The body makes too much of a clotting enzyme called thrombin. This leads to the formation of many small clots in blood vessels. These clots can block blood flow and damage organs.

As clots form, the body uses up platelets and clotting proteins. This can lead to bleeding because the body runs out of the tools it needs to stop bleeding.

DIC can develop slowly over weeks or months. In this case, the main problem is blood clots in veins or arteries.

DIC can also develop very fast, over hours or days. In this case, the main problem is severe bleeding.

## What Causes DIC?

DIC most often starts when tissue factor enters the bloodstream. This can happen in several ways:

- **Problems during pregnancy:**  
  - Placenta separates too early from the uterus (placental abruption).  
  - A miscarriage caused by saline solution.  
  - A dead baby stays in the uterus too long.  
  - Amniotic fluid leaks into the mother’s blood.

- **Infections, especially serious bacterial infections:**  
  - Bacteria with a certain type of outer layer (gram-negative bacteria) can trigger clotting.

- **Cancer:**  
  - Cancers of the pancreas, stomach, bile ducts, lungs, prostate, or breast.  
  - A rare type of leukemia called acute promyelocytic leukemia.

- **Shock from any cause:**  
  - When blood flow to tissues drops, damaged tissue releases tissue factor.

- **Severe injuries:**  
  - Head injuries, burns, frostbite, or gunshot wounds.

- **Prostate surgery:**  
  - Prostate tissue can get into the blood and cause clotting.

- **Snake bites:**  
  - Some snake venoms contain enzymes that directly start clotting.

- **Severe blood breakdown:**  
  - This can happen during a bad blood transfusion reaction, especially if blood types do not match.

- **Large blood vessel problems:**  
  - Aneurysms or rare blood vessel tumors (cavernous hemangiomas) can damage blood vessel walls and cause clots.

DIC that develops slowly is often linked to cancer, aneurysms, or blood vessel tumors.

## How DIC Affects the Body

When DIC develops slowly, the main issue is blood clots. These can cause:

- Deep vein clots (deep venous thrombosis).  
- Clots in the lungs (pulmonary embolism).  
- Rarely, clots in the heart or arteries.

Bleeding is not common in slow DIC.

When DIC develops quickly and severely, the body runs out of platelets and clotting proteins. This causes:

- Severe bleeding.  
- Bleeding under the skin (bruises).  
- Bleeding from IV sites or needle punctures.  
- Bleeding in the stomach or intestines.

Small clots can block tiny blood vessels. This stops blood from reaching organs. This can lead to organ damage or failure.

The body also breaks down clots too slowly. This can damage red blood cells. This causes small, fragmented red blood cells (called schistocytes) and mild blood breakdown.

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

In slow DIC, you may notice signs of blood clots:

- Swelling, pain, or warmth in a leg (deep vein clot).  
- Shortness of breath or chest pain (lung clot).

In severe, fast DIC, you may see:

- Bleeding that does not stop after a needle stick.  
- Bruises that appear without injury.  
- Blood in the stool or vomit.

## How Is DIC Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect DIC if a patient is bleeding for no clear reason or has a blood clot. This is especially true if the patient has a known risk factor.

To check for DIC, doctors do blood tests:

- Platelet count.  
- Prothrombin time (PT).  
- Partial thromboplastin time (PTT).  
- Fibrinogen level in the blood.  
- D-dimer level (a sign that clots are being broken down).  
- A blood smear to look for damaged red blood cells.

## How Is DIC Treated?

The most important step is to treat the underlying cause. For example:

- Use antibiotics for a serious infection.  
- Remove a dead baby from the uterus.  
- Treat shock with fluids and other support.

If the cause is treated quickly, DIC often improves fast.

If bleeding is severe, doctors may give:

- Platelets to help stop bleeding.  
- Cryoprecipitate to replace fibrinogen.  
- Fresh frozen plasma to replace other clotting factors.

Heparin is sometimes used. It is helpful in slow DIC, especially when clots are forming in veins or arteries. This includes cases linked to cancer, aneurysms, or blood vessel tumors.

Heparin is rarely used in fast, severe DIC. The one exception is when a dead baby stays in the uterus.

## Key Points

- DIC usually starts when tissue factor gets into the blood.  
- This triggers both clotting and clot breakdown.  
- DIC often starts fast and causes bleeding and small clots. This can lead to organ failure.  
- Sometimes DIC starts slowly and causes clots instead of bleeding.  
- Fast, severe DIC causes low platelets, long clotting times, low fibrinogen, and high D-dimer levels.  
- Treating the cause is the top priority.  
- Severe bleeding may need replacement of platelets, fibrinogen, and clotting factors.  
- Heparin helps in slow DIC but is not usually used in fast DIC (except in a retained dead fetus).

# Pulpitis

Pulpitis is a painful condition caused by inflammation in the inner part of the tooth. This inner part, called the pulp, contains nerves and blood vessels.

## What Causes Pulpitis?

The most common cause is tooth decay. The second most common cause is injury to the tooth.

Mild inflammation may go away if the cause is treated. But severe inflammation can kill the pulp.

Pulpitis can lead to an infection. This infection may form a pocket of pus at the root of the tooth. This is called a periapical abscess.

An untreated tooth infection can spread to the jaw. It can also spread to other parts of the body, such as the brain or sinuses.

## What Is Inside a Tooth?

The tooth has several layers. The outer layer is the hard enamel. Beneath that is dentin. At the center is the pulp, which holds nerves and blood vessels.

## Symptoms of Pulpitis

Pulpitis causes strong tooth pain.  
If there is an abscess, the tooth becomes very sensitive to pressure.  
Tapping the tooth may cause sharp pain.

## How Is Pulpitis Diagnosed?

A dentist will examine your tooth.  
They may take dental x-rays.  
They will test the tooth for sensitivity.  
They may use a special tool called an electric pulp tester.

The electric pulp tester sends a small electric charge to the tooth.  
If you feel the charge, the pulp is still alive.  
But feeling the charge does not mean the pulp is healthy.

Dentists may also test the tooth with hot, cold, or sweet substances.  
If the pain stops within 1 to 2 seconds after the test, the pulp may still be healthy. This is called reversible pulpitis.  
If the pain lasts after the test, or if pain happens without a trigger, the pulp is likely too damaged to save. This is called irreversible pulpitis.

X-rays help dentists check the bone around the tooth.  
They look for signs of infection, such as a cyst or bone damage.

## How Is Pulpitis Treated?

The treatment depends on how bad the inflammation is.

### For Reversible Pulpitis

- The dentist removes the decayed part of the tooth.  
- They then fill the tooth to protect it.  
- Sometimes, they place a temporary filling with medicine to ease pain.  
- This temporary filling stays for 6 to 8 weeks.  
- After that, it is replaced with a permanent filling.  
- In most cases, the dentist places a permanent filling right away.

### For Irreversible Pulpitis

- The pulp is too damaged to save.  
- The only way to stop the pain is to remove the pulp.  
- This is done through root canal treatment.  
- In some cases, the tooth must be removed.  
- If you have signs of infection, such as a fever, the dentist may prescribe antibiotics.  
- If symptoms return or get worse, root canal treatment may need to be repeated.

## More Information

The following English-language resource may help:

**Mouth Healthy**  
This website gives general advice on oral health.  
It includes tips on nutrition.  
It helps you choose toothbrushes, toothpaste, and other products with the American Dental Association’s seal of approval.  
It also tells you how to find a dentist and when to see one.

# Phenylketonuria (PKU)

Phenylketonuria, or PKU, is a condition that affects how the body handles a certain type of building block used in proteins. This condition leads to serious brain problems if not treated early. The main cause is a missing or faulty enzyme that helps break down a substance called phenylalanine. When this enzyme is not working, phenylalanine builds up in the blood and harms the brain.

PKU can happen in people of all races. It is more common in some areas than others. It is passed down through families in an autosomal recessive pattern. This means a child must inherit one faulty gene from each parent to have the condition. The chance of a baby having PKU is about 1 in 10,000 in White and East Asian populations.

For more information on similar conditions, see the table on Phenylalanine and Tyrosine Metabolism Disorders. Also, read the guide on how to approach a patient with a suspected inherited metabolic disorder.

---

## How PKU Works in the Body

The body normally turns excess phenylalanine into another substance called tyrosine. This process needs a helper molecule called tetrahydrobiopterin, or BH4. If a gene is faulty, the enzyme that breaks down phenylalanine does not work. This causes phenylalanine to build up in the blood. The brain is most affected, possibly because the brain’s protective covering does not form properly.

Some of the extra phenylalanine turns into waste products called phenylketones. These are passed out in the urine. This is why the condition is called phenylketonuria. The amount of enzyme missing varies from person to person. This affects how severe the condition is.

---

## Signs and Symptoms of PKU

Most babies with PKU look normal at birth. But over the first few months, symptoms slowly appear as phenylalanine builds up.

The main sign of untreated PKU is severe intellectual disability. Children may also be very hyperactive. They may have trouble walking or moving normally. Some may have hallucinations or other mental health issues.

A common sign is a strong, unpleasant smell like mice. This comes from a substance in the urine and sweat. The child may also have lighter skin, hair, and eye color than other family members. Some develop a rash like infantile eczema.

If treatment is delayed, children may become extremely hyperactive. They may also have seizures that are hard to control.

---

## How PKU Is Diagnosed

### Newborn Screening

In the United States and many other countries, all newborn babies are tested for PKU. The test is done 24 to 48 hours after birth. A small blood sample is taken from the baby’s heel. This test checks for high levels of phenylalanine.

If the test shows a problem, a second test is done to measure phenylalanine levels directly. In classic PKU, levels are usually over 20 mg/dL. In milder cases, levels are below 8 to 10 mg/dL while eating a normal diet. Levels above 6 mg/dL need treatment.

To tell the difference between mild and classic PKU, doctors may do a gene test. Or they may test how much enzyme is in the liver. In mild cases, the enzyme works at 5% to 15% of normal.

### BH4 Deficiency

Some cases of PKU are caused by a problem with BH4, not the enzyme. This is called BH4 deficiency. It can be found by testing urine, blood, or spinal fluid for high levels of certain substances. Genetic testing can also help. It is very important to find this type because standard PKU treatment does not help the brain in these cases.

All babies with PKU should have a urine test for BH4 levels at diagnosis. This helps doctors choose the right treatment.

### Prenatal Testing

If a family has a history of PKU, a baby can be tested before birth. This is done using a sample from the placenta (chorionic villus sampling) or amniotic fluid (amniocentesis). The test looks for the same gene changes found in the family.

---

## How PKU Is Treated

Treatment for PKU must be followed for life. The main treatment is to limit the amount of phenylalanine in the diet.

### What to Eat

All natural foods contain some phenylalanine. But people with PKU can eat:

- Fruits and vegetables
- Some grains that are low in protein
- Special protein products that have had phenylalanine removed
- Special amino acid mixtures that do not contain phenylalanine

Many products are made just for people with PKU. These are available in stores and online.

Even though phenylalanine must be limited, the body still needs a small amount for growth and health. This is provided by carefully measured amounts of low-protein milk or other low-protein foods.

### Monitoring Levels

Blood tests are needed often to check phenylalanine levels. For children, the goal is to keep levels between 2 mg/dL and 6 mg/dL (120 to 360 micromol/L). This range helps prevent brain damage.

### Planning for Pregnancy

Women with PKU must start planning before they get pregnant. High phenylalanine levels during pregnancy can harm the baby. The baby may be born with a small head and developmental delays. Starting treatment early helps protect the baby.

### Other Treatments

- **Tyrosine supplements** are often given. This is because the body cannot make enough tyrosine when phenylalanine builds up. Tyrosine is needed for normal body function.
- **Sapropterin** is a medicine that helps some people with PKU. It is a synthetic form of BH4. All people with PKU should try it to see if it helps lower phenylalanine levels.

### Special Treatment for BH4 Deficiency

If the problem is not with the enzyme but with BH4, treatment is different. It includes:

- Tetrahydrobiopterin (1 to 5 mg per kg of body weight, taken three times a day)
- Levodopa and carbidopa (to help with brain chemicals)
- 5-OH tryptophan (another brain chemical)
- Folinic acid (10 to 20 mg once a day) if the issue is with a specific enzyme

Even with these extra treatments, the main goal is still to keep phenylalanine levels in the safe range.

---

## Prognosis (Outlook)

If treatment starts in the first few days of life, most serious problems can be avoided. The child can grow up with normal intelligence and good health.

But even with good treatment, some children may still have mild learning problems or mental health issues.

If treatment starts after 2 or 3 years of age, it may only help with extreme hyperactivity and seizures. It will not reverse earlier brain damage.

Children born to mothers with uncontrolled PKU during pregnancy are at high risk. The baby may be born with a small head and delayed development. This is why it is so important for women with PKU to keep their phenylalanine levels low before and during pregnancy.

---

## Key Points

- PKU is caused by a faulty gene that stops the body from breaking down phenylalanine.
- When phenylalanine builds up, it harms the brain. This can cause severe intellectual disability.
- In the U.S. and many other countries, all newborns are tested for PKU within two days of birth.
- The test uses a blood sample from the baby’s heel.
- A second test confirms high phenylalanine levels.
- Treatment is a lifelong diet low in phenylalanine.
- Starting treatment early prevents most serious problems.
- Blood levels must be checked often. The target range for children is 2 to 6 mg/dL.
- Women with PKU must plan ahead before pregnancy to protect their baby.
