# Positron Emission Tomography (PET)

## What Is PET?

PET is a type of medical scan that uses a special kind of radiation to show how well parts of your body are working.  
It is also called a radionuclide scan.  

A small amount of a radioactive substance is used in the scan.  
This substance is linked to a natural material your body uses, like sugar or oxygen.  
The combination is called a radioactive tracer.  

The tracer moves through your body and collects in areas that are very active.  
The more active a tissue is, the more tracer it takes up.  
This means it gives off more radiation.  

The PET scanner has many detectors arranged in rings.  
These detectors pick up the radiation from the tracer.  
The scanner takes pictures from many angles.  

A computer uses this data to make detailed images.  
The images are shown in colors.  
Different colors show different levels of activity.  

The images look like slices of your body.  
They can show which parts are working normally or abnormally.  
But PET does not show the exact shape or structure of organs and tissues as clearly as other scans.  

## How Is a PET Scan Done?

Before the scan, you may be asked to avoid alcohol, coffee, tea, tobacco, or any medicine that affects your mind.  
This helps make the results more accurate.  

A nurse will inject the radioactive tracer into a vein in your arm.  
It takes about 30 to 60 minutes for the tracer to reach the area being checked.  

You will lie on a narrow, padded table.  
The table slides into the PET scanner, which is a large circle.  
The part of your body being scanned must be inside the circle.  

You must stay still during most of the test.  
The scan usually takes 45 to 60 minutes.  
If your brain is being scanned, you may be asked to do mental tasks, like solving math problems.  
This helps show which parts of your brain are active.  

## Why Is PET Used?

PET helps doctors see how well your heart and brain are working.  
It can also help find cancer and other problems.  

For the heart, PET can show blood flow and how well the heart muscle is working.  
This helps doctors decide if you need heart surgery or a heart transplant.  

For the brain, PET can show which areas are most active during certain tasks.  
For example, it can show which parts of the brain are used when doing math.  

PET can help diagnose Alzheimer disease and Parkinson disease.  
It can also help doctors understand seizure disorders.  

PET can show where cancer is in the body.  
It can show if cancer has spread to other areas.  
It can also show how well cancer treatment is working.  

Most PET scans are done to check for cancer.  
Common cancers checked with PET include:  
- Lung cancer  
- Colorectal cancer  
- Esophageal cancer  
- Head and neck cancer  
- Lymphoma  
- Melanoma  

PET can also help doctors tell if swollen lymph nodes are due to cancer spreading or another cause.  

## PET Combined with CT

PET is often done with a CT scan.  
This is called PET-CT.  

CT gives clear pictures of the body’s structure.  
PET shows how well tissues are working.  

The two types of images can be viewed separately.  
Or, one can be placed on top of the other.  
This helps doctors see both structure and function at the same time.  

This is especially helpful for cancers in areas with many different tissues close together, like the neck or pelvis.  
It helps find cancer more precisely.  
It can also find cancer early after treatment.  

The whole test usually takes less than one hour.  

*Image provided by Jon A. Jacobson, MD.*

## Downsides of PET

The amount of radiation from a PET scan is about the same as from a CT scan.  
When both are done together, the total radiation is higher.  

The radioactive tracers used in PET only last a short time.  
So, the scanner must be near a place that can make the tracer quickly.  

PET scans are not available in all hospitals.  
They are only done in special medical centers.

# Skin Problems Caused by Overactive Immune Responses

Your body’s immune system helps protect you from illness. Sometimes, it can react too strongly to something. This strong reaction can cause skin problems.

The following skin conditions are mainly caused by an overactive immune system. This can happen in response to a medicine, an infection, or even cancer.

- **Acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis**  
  A sudden skin rash with fever. It happens when white blood cells build up in the skin.

- **Drug eruptions and reactions**  
  Skin rashes or other skin issues caused by a medicine. The skin may become red, itchy, or blister.

- **Erythema multiforme**  
  A rash that looks like target shapes. It often appears after an infection or medicine.

- **Erythema nodosum**  
  Painful red lumps under the skin, usually on the shins. It can be linked to infections or other health issues.

- **Granuloma annulare**  
  A ring-shaped rash that appears on the skin. It is not harmful but can last for months.

- **Panniculitis**  
  Inflammation of the fat layer under the skin. It causes painful lumps or nodules.

- **Pyoderma gangrenosum**  
  A serious skin condition with open sores that can grow quickly. It is linked to other health problems like arthritis or bowel disease.

- **Stevens-Johnson syndrome**  
  A severe reaction that causes blistering and peeling of the skin. It often starts with flu-like symptoms.

- **Toxic epidermal necrolysis**  
  A life-threatening skin reaction. The top layer of skin dies and peels off. It is a medical emergency.

# Types of Complementary and Alternative Medicine

Complementary and alternative medicine includes many different types of treatments. These are grouped into five main categories:

- Whole medical systems  
- Mind-body techniques  
- Biologically based practices  
- Manipulative and body-based therapies  
- Energy therapies  

Each category includes different methods. Some of these methods are supported by science. Others are not. Some methods overlap with more than one category.

---

## Whole Medical Systems

These are complete health systems with their own beliefs, ways to diagnose illness, and treatments.

### Ayurveda
- Aims to balance the body’s systems.  
- Uses diet, massage, herbs, meditation, detox methods, and yoga.  

### Homeopathy
- Based on the idea that a substance causing symptoms in large amounts can cure the same symptoms in tiny amounts.  
- The substances are often so diluted that they contain no measurable molecules.  

### Naturopathy
- Focuses on preventing illness and helping the body heal itself.  
- Treats the whole person, not just the symptoms.  
- Uses many methods, including:  
  - Acupuncture  
  - Counseling  
  - Exercise  
  - Guided imagery  
  - Homeopathy  
  - Water therapy  
  - Herbs  
  - Natural childbirth  
  - Nutrition  
  - Physical therapy  
  - Stress management  

### Traditional Chinese Medicine
- Aims to balance the body’s life force (called qi).  
- Believes in balancing two forces: yin and yang.  
- Uses:  
  - Acupuncture  
  - Massage  
  - Herbs  
  - Qi gong (a gentle movement and breathing practice)  

---

## Mind-Body Techniques

These methods use the mind to help the body stay healthy or heal.

### Biofeedback
- Uses machines to show body functions like heart rate or muscle tension.  
- Teaches people how to control these functions on their own.  

### Guided Imagery
- Uses mental pictures to help people relax.  
- Can help with sleep problems or emotional stress.  

### Hypnotherapy (Hypnosis)
- Puts people into a relaxed, focused state.  
- Helps change habits or behaviors that affect health.  

### Meditation (including mindfulness)
- Focuses attention on the present moment.  
- Helps calm the mind and reduce stress.  

### Relaxation Techniques
- Slow down body functions like heart rate.  
- Help reduce tension and stress.  

These methods are now used in many hospitals and clinics. They help with:  
- Chronic pain  
- Heart disease  
- Headaches  
- Sleep problems  
- Menopause symptoms  
- Preparing for childbirth  

They also help people with cancer manage symptoms and side effects of treatment.

---

## Biologically Based Practices

These use natural substances to support health.

### Botanical Medicine and Natural Products
- Uses plant or animal-based substances to treat symptoms or illness.  
- Example: Using cartilage to ease joint pain.  

### Chelation Therapy
- Uses a drug to bind to metals or minerals in the body.  
- Believed to remove harmful or excess amounts.  

### Diet Therapies
- Uses special eating plans to treat or prevent disease.  
- Examples:  
  - Macrobiotic diet  
  - Paleo diet  
  - Low-carb diet  
  - Mediterranean diet  
- Some people use these to improve health or remove toxins.  

---

## Manipulative and Body-Based Therapies

These involve moving or touching parts of the body to treat health issues.

### Chiropractic
- Focuses on the spine.  
- Adjusts the spine to improve nerve function.  
- May also use:  
  - Heat or cold therapy  
  - Electrical stimulation  
  - Massage  
  - Exercises  
  - Lifestyle advice  

### Cupping
- Uses heated cups placed on the skin.  
- Creates suction that pulls the skin up.  
- Left on for several minutes.  
- Thought to increase blood flow and reduce inflammation.  

### Massage
- Presses, rubs, and moves muscles and soft tissues.  
- Helps reduce pain, muscle tension, and stress.  

### Moxibustion
- Burns a dried herb (mugwort) near or on the skin.  
- Done over acupuncture points.  

### Reflexology
- Presses specific spots on the feet, hands, or ears.  
- Believed to connect to organs or body systems.  

### Gua Sha
- Rubs a smooth tool (like a coin or spoon) across the skin.  
- Usually done on the back, neck, or arms.  
- Also called scraping, coining, or spooning.  
- Thought to improve energy flow and remove toxins.  

**Note:** Some of these methods can leave marks or bruises. These may look like injuries. They are not harmful but can be mistaken for abuse.

There is little strong scientific proof that these methods work well for most conditions.

---

## Energy Therapies

These therapies focus on energy fields around the body (called biofields). They are based on the idea that a life force flows through the body and universe.

### Acupuncture
- Inserts very thin needles into the skin at specific points.  
- Believed to balance the body’s energy (qi) along pathways called meridians.  

### Qi Gong
- A gentle movement practice.  
- Uses posture, breathing, and meditation.  
- Aims to improve energy balance and healing.  

### Magnets
- Places magnets on the body.  
- Believed to reduce pain or help healing.  

### Reiki
- Practitioners use their hands to send energy into the body.  
- Believed to promote healing and balance.  

### Therapeutic Touch
- Practitioners use their hands near the body.  
- Does not always touch the person.  
- Believed to fix imbalances in the body’s energy field.  

**Important Note:** There is little scientific proof that energy fields or life force exist. These ideas are hard to test. So far, no strong evidence shows that these therapies work beyond a placebo effect.

---

## Summary

- Complementary and alternative medicine includes many different types of treatments.  
- Some are based on science. Others are not.  
- Many of these methods are now used in mainstream health care.  
- Always talk to your doctor before trying any new treatment.  
- Some methods may interact with medicines or treatments.  
- Be cautious with highly diluted products (like in homeopathy). They may not contain any active ingredient.

# Campylobacter Infections

## What Is Campylobacter?

Campylobacter is a type of bacteria. It lives in the gut of many farm animals and birds.  
It can cause illness in people.  
The most common illness is diarrhea that lasts a few days.  
In rare cases, the bacteria can spread into the blood.  
When this happens, it can cause serious infections in the heart, bones, or joints.

## Types of Campylobacter

There are several types of Campylobacter.  
The most common ones that make people sick are *C. jejuni*, *C. coli*, and *C. fetus*.  
These bacteria are curved, move around, and need a small amount of oxygen to grow.  
They are not killed by stomach acid in most people.

## Who Gets Sick?

*C. jejuni* is a common cause of food poisoning.  
It affects healthy people and those with weak immune systems.  
It causes diarrhea in all age groups.  
The highest number of cases happen in children aged 1 to 5 years.  
In some years, *C. jejuni* causes more diarrhea cases in the United States than *Salmonella* and *Shigella* combined.  
It can also cause meningitis in babies.

*C. fetus* and a few other Campylobacter types usually cause serious infections in adults.  
These infections are more likely in people with long-term health problems.  
Examples include diabetes, liver disease, cancer, or HIV/AIDS.  
*C. fetus* is rare.  
It mostly affects older adults, pregnant women, and people with other health issues.  
In pregnant women, it can lead to miscarriage in up to 7 out of 10 cases.  
Healthy people can get infected if they work with sick animals.  
People with low levels of certain immune proteins may have long-lasting or recurring infections.  
Low stomach acid (from medicine or disease) increases the risk of infection.

## How Do People Get Infected?

You can get infected through:

- Touching sick animals, like puppies  
- Eating or drinking contaminated food or water  
- Eating undercooked chicken or other poultry  
- Drinking raw milk that has not been pasteurized  

You can also pass the infection to others through contact with feces or during sex.  
But this is rare.  
It takes a large number of bacteria to cause illness.  
Still, infections do happen among men who have sex with men.  
In most cases, the source of the infection is not clear.

## Symptoms and Signs

The most common symptom is sudden diarrhea.  
It can be watery or bloody.  
The illness usually goes away on its own in a few days.

Other symptoms may include:

- Fever that comes and goes (between 38 and 40 degrees Celsius)  
- Belly pain, often on the right side (this can feel like appendicitis)  
- Headache  
- Muscle aches  

In some cases, people do not have diarrhea.  
Instead, they may have:

- Infection of the heart (endocarditis), more often caused by *C. fetus*  
- Joint pain and swelling (reactive arthritis), usually in one knee  
- Meningitis (infection of the brain and spinal cord lining)  
- A long-lasting fever with no clear cause  

Joint symptoms usually go away on their own in 1 week to several months.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose Campylobacter by testing a sample of your stool.  
They may use a culture or a rapid test that looks for the bacteria’s DNA.  
Blood tests may also be done if the infection has spread beyond the gut.  
This is more likely if you have a high fever, severe pain, or signs of infection in another part of the body.  
Stool samples may show white blood cells, which means there is an infection.

## How Is It Treated?

Most people with Campylobacter infection do not need antibiotics.  
Their symptoms go away on their own in a few days.  
If treatment is needed, the most common medicine is azithromycin.  
This medicine is often given to people at higher risk of serious illness.  
This includes people with weak immune systems, older adults, and pregnant women.

Ciprofloxacin was once used, but many bacteria are now resistant.  
It should only be used if a test shows the bacteria are sensitive to it.  
Even then, resistance can develop during treatment.

For infections outside the gut (like in the heart, bones, or joints), antibiotics are needed for 2 to 4 weeks.  
Common medicines include imipenem, gentamicin, ampicillin, and erythromycin.  
This long treatment helps prevent the infection from coming back.

# How the Immune System Works

## What the Immune System Does

The immune system protects your body from harmful invaders.  
These invaders include:

- Germs like bacteria, viruses, and fungi  
- Parasites such as worms  
- Cancer cells  
- Transplanted organs or tissues  

To do its job, the immune system must tell the difference between:

- Things that belong in your body (self)  
- Things that do not belong (foreign)  

**Antigens** are parts of invaders that the immune system can recognize.  
If the immune system sees an antigen as dangerous, it will start a response.  
Antigens can be on germs, parasites, cancer cells, or even on their own—like food particles or pollen.

A normal immune response has four steps:

1. It finds a harmful foreign substance.  
2. It turns on the body’s defenses.  
3. It attacks the invader.  
4. It stops the attack when the threat is gone.

If the immune system makes a mistake and attacks the body’s own tissues, it can cause an **autoimmune disease**.  
Examples include rheumatoid arthritis, Hashimoto thyroiditis, and lupus.

## Types of Immune System Problems

Immune system problems happen when:

- The body attacks itself (autoimmune disease)  
- The body cannot fight off infections (immunodeficiency)  
- The body overreacts to harmless things like pollen (allergic reaction)

---

## Parts of the Immune System

### Antibodies (Immunoglobulins)
Antibodies are proteins made by B cells.  
They stick tightly to specific invaders.  
They mark the invader for destruction or stop it from causing harm.  
Your body makes thousands of different antibodies.  
Each one targets a specific antigen.

### Antigens
Antigens are any substances the immune system can recognize.  
They trigger an immune response.

### B Cells (B Lymphocytes)
B cells are white blood cells that make antibodies.  
Each B cell makes antibodies for one specific antigen.

### Basophils
Basophils are white blood cells.  
They release histamine, which causes swelling and redness in allergic reactions.  
They also send signals to bring other white blood cells to the area.

### Cells
Cells are the basic building blocks of life.  
Each cell has a center (nucleus), fluid (cytoplasm), and a covering (membrane).

### Chemotaxis
Chemotaxis is how chemicals guide immune cells to a problem site.

### Complement System
This is a group of proteins that work together to defend the body.  
They can kill bacteria, help other cells find invaders, and attract immune cells to the area.

### Cytokines
Cytokines are messengers made by immune and other cells.  
They help control how the immune system responds.

### Dendritic Cells
Dendritic cells come from white blood cells.  
They live in tissues and help T cells find foreign invaders.

### Eosinophils
Eosinophils are white blood cells.  
They kill large invaders that cannot be eaten.  
They also help fight parasites and may help destroy cancer cells.  
They are also involved in allergic reactions.

### Helper T Cells
Helper T cells help B cells make antibodies.  
They turn on killer T cells.  
They also help macrophages eat infected or abnormal cells.

### Histocompatibility
This means how well tissues match.  
It is based on human leukocyte antigens (HLA).  
HLA helps the body tell self from nonself.  
It is used to check if a transplanted organ will be accepted.

### Human Leukocyte Antigens (HLA)
HLA are identification markers on all body cells.  
Each person has a unique mix of HLA.  
This helps the body know what belongs and what does not.  
HLA is also called the major histocompatibility complex.

### Immune Complex
An immune complex is an antibody stuck to an antigen.

### Immune Response
An immune response is what happens when the immune system reacts to an antigen.

### Interleukin
Interleukin is a type of cytokine.  
It is made by white blood cells to talk to other white blood cells.

### Killer (Cytotoxic) T Cells
Killer T cells find infected cells and cancer cells.  
They attach to them and destroy them.

### Leukocyte
Leukocyte is another name for white blood cell.  
Examples include monocytes, neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, and lymphocytes (B cells and T cells).

### Lymphatic System
The lymphatic system is a network of tubes and nodes.  
It moves fluid, germs, dead cells, and cancer cells to lymph nodes.  
There, they are filtered and destroyed.  
Immune responses often start in lymph nodes.

### Lymphocytes
Lymphocytes are white blood cells that handle specific immunity.  
B cells make antibodies.  
T cells help identify self vs. nonself.  
Killer T cells destroy infected or cancer cells.

### Macrophages
Macrophages are large cells made from monocytes.  
They eat bacteria and other invaders.  
They also help T cells find threats.  
They live in the lungs, skin, liver, and other tissues.

### Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC)
MHC is another name for human leukocyte antigens.

### Mast Cells
Mast cells live in tissues.  
They release histamine and other chemicals during allergic and inflammatory reactions.

### Molecule
A molecule is a group of atoms joined together to form a unique substance.

### Natural Killer Cells
Natural killer cells are white blood cells.  
They can find and kill abnormal cells like infected or cancer cells.  
They do not need to learn what to attack first.

### Neutrophils
Neutrophils are white blood cells.  
They eat and kill bacteria and other invaders.

### Phagocytes
Phagocytes are cells that eat and destroy invaders, dead cells, or cell parts.  
Neutrophils and macrophages are types of phagocytes.

### Phagocytosis
Phagocytosis is when a cell eats and destroys an invader, another cell, or a cell fragment.

### Receptor
A receptor is a molecule on a cell that fits a specific substance like a key fits a lock.

### Regulatory (Suppressor) T Cells
These T cells help stop the immune response.  
They prevent the body from attacking itself too much.

### T Cells (T Lymphocytes)
T cells are white blood cells that help with specific immunity.  
There are three types: helper, killer, and regulatory.

### White Blood Cells (Leukocytes)
White blood cells come in many types:  
- Monocytes  
- Neutrophils  
- Eosinophils  
- Basophils  
- Lymphocytes (B cells and T cells)  

Each type has a different job in fighting disease.

---

## How the Body Defends Itself

The body has several layers of defense:

1. Physical barriers  
2. White blood cells  
3. Immune molecules (like antibodies and complement proteins)  
4. Lymphoid organs (like lymph nodes and spleen)

### First Line of Defense: Physical Barriers

Your body has natural barriers that keep invaders out:

- Skin  
- Cornea of the eyes  
- Mucous membranes in the nose, mouth, lungs, gut, bladder, and reproductive system  

As long as these barriers stay intact, most germs cannot get in.  
If the skin is broken—like in a cut or burn—the risk of infection goes up.

These barriers also have protective secretions:

- Sweat  
- Tears  
- Mucus in the nose and lungs  
- Vaginal secretions  

These fluids contain enzymes that can kill bacteria.

### Second Line of Defense: White Blood Cells

White blood cells travel through the blood and tissues.  
They search for and attack invaders.  
This defense has two parts:

#### Innate Immunity (Natural Defense)
This is something you are born with.  
It works right away.  
It does not need to learn what to fight.

- **Phagocytes** (like macrophages, neutrophils, monocytes, and dendritic cells) eat invaders.  
- **Natural killer cells** are ready to kill cancer cells and virus-infected cells.  
- **Basophils and eosinophils** release chemicals that cause inflammation and help in allergic reactions.  
- Some of these cells can kill invaders directly.

#### Acquired Immunity (Adaptive Defense)
This defense learns and remembers.  
It takes time to start but works faster the next time.

- **B cells and T cells** are the main players.  
- They meet an invader, learn how to fight it, and remember it.  
- Next time, they respond faster and stronger.  
- B cells make antibodies.  
- T cells help B cells and kill infected or cancer cells.  

To recognize invaders, T cells need help from **antigen-presenting cells**.  
These cells eat an invader, break it into pieces, and show the pieces on their surface with HLA markers.  
A T cell with a matching receptor can then attach and become active.

Innate and acquired immunity work together.  
They send signals to each other using:

- Cytokines (immune messengers)  
- Antibodies  
- Complement proteins  

These substances are not inside cells.  
They float in body fluids like blood plasma.

Some of these substances cause **inflammation**.

### What Is Inflammation?

Inflammation happens when immune chemicals attract immune cells to a problem area.  
The body sends more blood to the area.  
Blood vessels widen and become leaky

# Ventricular Premature Beats (VPB)

Ventricular premature beats (VPB) are extra heartbeats that start in the lower chambers of the heart.  
They happen when electrical signals in the heart go wrong.  
This can be due to a loop of electrical activity or a cell firing too early.  

VPBs are very common.  
They happen in people with healthy hearts and in people with heart problems.  
Some people feel nothing.  
Others feel their heart skip or flutter.  

## What Causes VPBs?

VPBs can happen at random.  
Or they can follow a pattern.  
For example, every third beat (called trigeminy) or every second beat (called bigeminy).  

Certain things can make VPBs more likely.  
These include:  
- Anxiety or stress  
- Drinking alcohol  
- Caffeine  
- Some medicines that act like adrenaline  
- Low oxygen levels  
- Imbalances in body salts like potassium or magnesium  

Most VPBs are harmless.  
But they can sometimes be a sign of a heart problem.  
If VPBs get worse during exercise, it may mean the heart muscle is not getting enough blood.  

In rare cases, very frequent VPBs can weaken the heart muscle.  
This is called VPB-induced cardiomyopathy.  
It is more likely if the heart is already weak.  

Some people with normal heart structure still have VPBs.  
These are called idiopathic VPBs.  
They are often linked to a chemical called cAMP.  
They usually start in the right or left side of the heart’s outflow area.  

These VPBs have a specific look on an ECG.  
They look like a left bundle branch block.  
The electrical signal goes down and to the right.  
This shows as a tall positive wave in lead V1.  
A negative wave in lead AVL.  
And a flat wave in lead I.  

## How Do People Feel VPBs?

People often feel a skipped beat.  
They do not feel the VPB itself.  
They feel the next normal beat after it.  
This next beat feels stronger.  

If VPBs happen very often, especially every other beat, blood flow can drop.  
This may cause mild symptoms like dizziness or tiredness.  
Existing heart murmurs may get louder.  
This happens because the heart fills more and squeezes harder after the pause.  

## How Are VPBs Diagnosed?

The main test is an electrocardiogram (ECG).  
It shows the heart’s electrical activity.  
A VPB shows up as a wide, abnormal heartbeat.  
It has no early signal (P wave) before it.  
It is followed by a full pause.  

If your doctor suspects a heart problem, you may need:  
- A 24-hour heart monitor  
- An echocardiogram (a heart ultrasound)  

If your doctor thinks you might have blocked heart arteries, you may need an exercise test.  
This helps check blood flow to the heart.  
It also helps decide if you need more tests or treatment.  

## How Are VPBs Treated?

Most people with VPBs do not need treatment.  
This is especially true if the heart is healthy and there are no symptoms.  
Reassurance is often enough.  

Treatment is only needed if symptoms are bothersome.  

First choice:  
- Beta-blockers  
- Non-dihydropyridine calcium blockers (verapamil or diltiazem)  

These medicines work well for VPBs that start in the outflow areas of the right or left ventricle.  

Other antiarrhythmic medicines (class I or class III) are rarely used.  
They can increase the risk of death.  
They are not safe for people with heart disease.  

If VPBs do not respond to medicine and the heart is getting weaker, a procedure called ablation may help.  
This is done through a thin tube in the blood vessels.  
It destroys the small area of heart tissue causing the extra beats.  
Ablation is very effective for outflow tract VPBs.  

It may also be offered if symptoms are too hard to live with.  

For people with heart disease:  
- Frequent VPBs (more than 10 per minute) are linked to higher risk of death.  
- But no study has shown that medicine to stop VPBs improves survival.  

After a heart attack, people who take class I antiarrhythmic medicines have a higher risk of death.  
This is likely because the medicines cause more harm than good.  

Beta-blockers (a type II antiarrhythmic) are safe and helpful.  
They are part of standard care for heart disease.  
They help if you have heart failure or symptoms from VPBs.  

Verapamil and diltiazem should not be used if the heart muscle is weak.  

If VPBs get worse during exercise and you have heart artery disease, your doctor may consider:  
- Angioplasty (opening a blocked artery)  
- Bypass surgery  

## What Is the Outlook?

VPBs are not dangerous if your heart is healthy.  
No treatment is needed beyond avoiding triggers.  
These include caffeine, alcohol, stress, and lack of sleep.  

Treatment is only offered if:  
- Symptoms are very bothersome  
- VPBs are so frequent they weaken the heart and cause heart failure  

Other medicines that stop VPBs can cause more serious heart rhythm problems.  
They are not worth the risk.

# Occupational Therapy (OT)

Occupational therapy helps people do everyday tasks more easily. It is part of rehabilitation.

This therapy focuses on daily activities like:
- Eating
- Dressing
- Bathing
- Grooming
- Using the toilet
- Moving from a chair to a bed or toilet
- Cooking meals
- Using a phone or computer
- Managing money
- Taking medicine
- Shopping
- Driving

OT helps people do these tasks by improving key abilities:

- The ability to feel and move your body
- The ability to plan and carry out actions
- The desire to start a task and keep going until it is done

These abilities can be affected by illness, injury, or aging.

---

## What Can Make Daily Tasks Harder?

Here are common problems that can interfere with doing simple tasks:

### 1. Problems with Feeling and Moving
- Numbness or poor sense of touch
- Stiff joints or limited movement
- Weak muscles
- Getting tired easily
- Poor balance
- Trouble with small movements (like picking up a coin)

### 2. Problems with Thinking and Planning
- Trouble paying attention
- Getting distracted easily
- Hard to focus
- Poor judgment
- Can’t make decisions
- Memory problems
- Trouble solving problems

### 3. Problems with Motivation and Emotions
- Feeling no interest in doing things
- Depression
- Anxiety
- Feeling like you can’t do it
- Frustration
- Giving up too soon
- Trouble handling stress

---

## How Occupational Therapists Help

Therapists watch how you do daily tasks. They may do simple tests, like checking your balance. They also talk to your family, caregivers, or other doctors.

They visit your home to see what might make tasks harder. They look for dangers like:
- Poor lighting
- Cords on the floor
- Slippery floors

They suggest changes to make your home safer. For example:
- Use brighter lights
- Remove or secure cords
- Add grab bars in the bathroom
- Use a shower chair

They also check how much help your family can give.

Some therapists can test if you can still drive safely. If needed, they can help you relearn driving skills.

---

### Did You Know?

- Occupational therapists help people do daily tasks that have become hard because of illness or injury.
- Many tools are available to help. Examples include:
  - Grabbers to pick up things from the floor
  - Utensils with bigger handles
  - Tools with easier-to-use grips

---

## Working Together on Goals

You and your therapist work together to set goals. You decide what tasks are most important to improve.

For example:
- If you have trouble eating, you may practice using your fingers and hands with pegs on a board.
- If you forget things, you may play memory games.
- If you have a weak arm, you can learn new ways to dress, tie shoes, or fasten buttons.

As you get better, tasks become harder to keep improving.

---

## Tools That Help (Assistive Devices)

Therapists suggest tools to help you live more independently. They teach you how to use them. Some tools are made just for you.

| Problem | Tool |
|--------|------|
| Poor balance, weak legs, or dizziness | Canes, walkers, wheelchairs, shower chairs, grab bars, bathtub benches |
| Weak grip | Utensils with bigger handles, shoehorns with larger grips |
| Hard to reach things | Grabbers that pick up items from the floor or shelf |
| Shaking hands (tremors) | Weighted spoons, cups with lids, spoons that swivel |
| Trouble keeping things steady | Plates with raised edges and rubber bottoms to stop sliding |
| Hand problems | Tools with larger handles, spring-loaded or electronic tools |
| Hard to stand up from a chair | Raised toilet seats, seat-lifting chairs, chair leg extenders |
| Paralysis or serious movement limits | Computer or smartphone tools to help with daily tasks |
| Poor vision | Phones with big buttons or voice control, large-print or audio books |
| Poor hearing | Phones with flashing lights instead of rings, smartphones that turn speech into text |
| Memory problems | Phones that dial automatically, medicine organizers with alarms, pocket devices or apps that play reminders at the right time, wearable devices that track your location |

---

## Orthoses (Orthotic Devices)

Orthoses are special supports for joints, muscles, or bones. They are made to fit your body.

They are often used in shoes. They help:
- Shift your weight to different parts of your foot
- Prevent foot problems
- Help carry your weight
- Reduce pain
- Give support

Therapists can make and fit these devices. They are often expensive and may not be covered by insurance.

---

## Splints

Splints keep a joint straight. They help prevent a joint from freezing in a bent position.

This can happen if you do not move a limb for a long time. For example:
- After a stroke
- With arthritis

A splint holds the limb straight. This helps keep movement possible.

---

## Walking Aids

These tools help you walk or stay balanced.

- **Walkers** – Help with balance and support. Some have wheels.
- **Crutches** – Help carry weight and keep balance.
- **Canes** – Help with balance and support.

Each type has pros and cons. Therapists help you pick the best one for your needs.

---

## Wheelchairs

Wheelchairs help people who cannot walk.

- **Self-propelled models** – You push them yourself. They are stable and can go over rough ground or up curbs.
- **Pushed models** – Someone else pushes you. They are less stable and slower.

---

## Mobility Scooters

Scooters are battery-powered, wheeled carts.

- They have a steering wheel or tiller.
- You can go forward and backward.
- They have speed controls.

They work well on flat, solid surfaces inside and outside buildings.

They **cannot** be used on stairs or curbs.

They are good for people who can walk only short distances — for example, to and from the scooter.

---

## Prostheses

Prostheses are artificial limbs. They replace missing arms or legs.

If you have lost an arm, you may get a fake arm with a pincer. This helps you hold a spoon or fork.

Therapists help you learn how to use your artificial limb. They also teach you how to use other tools to do daily tasks.

---

# How to Prevent Frailty

Frailty means your body has less strength and energy to handle everyday stress. This can lead to disability even from small problems.

Signs of frailty include:
- Weak muscles
- Slow movement
- Losing weight without trying
- Losing muscle mass
- Getting tired easily when moving
- Falling often
- Trouble walking or moving around
- Inability to control bladder or bowel
- Getting sicker more often from long-term health issues

## Stay Active

Regular physical activity helps prevent or slow down frailty.

- Walking, swimming, or running are good types of aerobic exercise.
- People who stay active live longer and keep their ability to do daily tasks better than those who do not move much.
- Exercise can also improve your mood and mental sharpness.
- Lifting weights helps build stronger muscles and bones.
- Stronger muscles and bones lower your risk of falls and broken bones.

## Eat Well

A healthy diet can help prevent or reduce frailty.

- Good nutrition helps prevent many health problems linked to frailty.
- These include certain cancers, weak bones, being overweight, and not getting enough nutrients.
- Eating well may also lower your risk of serious illness and death.

## Get Help with Food and Nutrition

Talking to a dietitian can help if you are frail.

- Supplements like protein may help if you are not getting enough from food.
- Protein is important when you are also exercising.
- Experts suggest that healthy older adults should aim for 1.0 to 1.2 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight each day.
- This advice does not apply to people with kidney disease.

# Chondromalacia Patellae

Chondromalacia patellae means the cartilage under your kneecap has become soft.  
This softening can cause pain in your knee.  

This condition often starts in teens.  
People who run are more likely to get it.  
It may happen because the kneecap does not line up properly.  
When the kneecap is misaligned, the cartilage rubs against other bones when you bend your knee.  
This rubbing can damage the cartilage over time.  

## What You Might Feel

You may feel a dull, aching pain around or behind your kneecap.  
You will not see any swelling.  
Pain often gets worse when you:  
- Climb stairs  
- Play certain sports  
- Sit for long periods  
- Run  

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms.  
They will do a physical exam of your knee.  
They will not need an X-ray or scan to make the diagnosis.  

## How It Is Treated

### Exercises
Your doctor may suggest exercises to strengthen the muscles in front of your thigh.  
These muscles help straighten your leg.  
Stretching exercises can also help make your knee more flexible.  
Avoid activities that make the pain worse.  
This may mean resting your knee for a few days.  

### Pain Relief
You can use ice on your knee to reduce pain and swelling.  
Your doctor may recommend nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.  
These are medicines like ibuprofen or naproxen.  
They help reduce pain and swelling.  

### Surgery (Rare)
In some cases, the doctor may use a small camera called an arthroscope.  
The camera is about as wide as a pencil.  
It goes into the knee joint through a tiny cut.  
The doctor uses it to smooth the damaged cartilage.  
This is only done if other treatments do not help.

# Skin Color Changes: What You Need to Know

Skin, hair, and the colored part of the eyes get their color from a substance called melanin.  
Melanin is made by special cells in the skin called melanocytes.  
Most people have about the same number of these cells.  
The difference in skin color comes from how much melanin the cells make, not how many cells there are.

There are two main types of melanin in the skin:  
- Eumelanin, which gives skin a brown or black color.  
- Pheomelanin, which gives a reddish color.

Sunlight and other forms of ultraviolet light can make the skin make more melanin.  
Some diseases and health problems can also cause more melanin to be made.  
Other things can stop the skin from making melanin normally.

Problems with skin color are called pigmentation disorders.  
These can mean the skin has less color, no color at all, or too much color.  
The changes can happen in one small area or over a large part of the body.

### Less Color in the Skin (Hypopigmentation)
This means the skin has less melanin than normal.  
The skin may look lighter than usual.

### No Color in the Skin (Depigmentation)
This means the skin has lost all its melanin.  
The skin becomes white in the affected areas.

---

## Localized (Focal) Skin Lightening

This means only one or a few spots have less color.  
It often happens after:

- Skin injury  
- Skin inflammation, such as eczema or psoriasis  
- Burns  
- Exposure to certain chemicals, especially hydroquinone and phenols

Other conditions that can cause one or more spots to lose color include:

- Vitiligo (a condition that causes white patches on the skin, sometimes covering large areas)  
- Leprosy  
- Poor nutrition, such as in kwashiorkor  
- Some inherited conditions, like tuberous sclerosis complex, piebaldism, and Waardenburg syndrome  
- Morphea (a type of scleroderma that causes thick, hard patches on the skin)  
- Lichen sclerosus  
- Pityriasis versicolor (a fungal skin infection that causes light or dark patches)  
- Idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis (small white spots, often on sun-exposed skin)  
- Progressive macular hypomelanosis (a condition that causes slowly spreading white patches)  
- Skin that loses color after healing from a rash or injury (postinflammatory hypopigmentation)  
- Pityriasis alba (a mild skin condition that causes pale patches, often on the face)

### Morphea
This condition causes hard, thick patches on the skin.  
The patches often look white or lighter than the rest of the skin.  
They usually appear on the trunk or limbs.

*Photo: Multiple hard, white patches on the trunk. This is typical of morphea.  
Photo courtesy of Karen McKoy, MD.*

---

## Widespread Skin Lightening (Diffuse Hypopigmentation)

This means large areas of skin have less color.  
It is most often caused by:

- Albinism (a condition where the body makes little or no melanin from birth)  
- Vitiligo (a condition that causes white patches over large areas of the body)

---

## Extra Skin Color (Hyperpigmentation)

This means the skin has more melanin than normal.  
It often happens after skin inflammation from any cause.  
This is called postinflammatory hyperpigmentation.  
It usually affects only one or a few spots.

But hyperpigmentation can also be caused by:

- A disease in the body (systemic disorder)  
- Certain medicines or substances  
- Some types of cancer

When caused by these other issues, the darkening usually affects large areas of the skin.

# Carbohydrates, Proteins, and Fats

Carbohydrates, proteins, and fats are the three main types of nutrients in food.  
They are needed every day in large amounts.  
These nutrients make up 90% of the dry weight of your diet.  
They also provide all the energy your body uses.

All three give you energy in the form of calories.  
But they differ in how many calories they provide per gram:

- 4 calories per gram of carbohydrate or protein  
- 9 calories per gram of fat

Carbohydrates give energy the fastest.  
Fats give energy the slowest.

Your body breaks down these nutrients in the intestine.  
It turns them into their basic building blocks:

- Carbohydrates into sugars  
- Proteins into amino acids  
- Fats into fatty acids and glycerol

Your body uses these building blocks to make new substances.  
This includes making more carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.  
It uses them for growth, repair, and daily activities.

---

## Carbohydrates

Carbohydrates come in two forms: simple and complex.

### Simple Carbohydrates

Simple carbohydrates are small molecules.  
They include sugars like fructose (found in fruit) and sucrose (table sugar).  
Because they are small, your body breaks them down and absorbs them quickly.  
They give you energy fast.

They raise your blood sugar level quickly.  
Blood sugar is also a type of sugar.

Foods high in simple carbohydrates include:
- Fruits  
- Milk and dairy products  
- Honey  
- Maple syrup  
- Candy and cakes

These foods taste sweet because of the simple sugars.

### Complex Carbohydrates

Complex carbohydrates are made of long chains of simple sugars.  
Because they are larger, your body must break them down first.  
This takes longer, so they give energy more slowly.

They are less likely to turn into fat than simple carbohydrates.  
They raise blood sugar more slowly and keep it steady for longer.

Foods with complex carbohydrates include:
- Starches in bread, pasta, and other wheat products  
- Other grains like rye and corn  
- Beans and legumes  
- Root vegetables like potatoes and sweet potatoes

---

### Refined vs. Unrefined Carbohydrates

**Refined** means the food has been highly processed.  
During processing, fiber, bran, and many vitamins and minerals are removed.  
This makes the food easier to digest.  
But it also means it gives little nutrition.

Even though refined foods have the same number of calories as whole foods, they are not as healthy.  
Some refined foods are "enriched."  
This means vitamins and minerals were added back after processing.

A diet high in simple or refined carbohydrates increases your risk of:
- Obesity  
- Diabetes

If you eat more carbohydrates than your body needs, it stores the extra.  
Some is stored as glycogen in your liver and muscles.  
Glycogen is a form of stored energy.  
It can be used quickly when you need energy.

Your muscles use glycogen during intense exercise.  
The amount stored can give you energy for almost a full day.

Other body tissues store carbohydrates too.  
But they cannot use these stored forms for energy.

Most health experts recommend:
- 50 to 55% of your daily calories come from carbohydrates  
- Most of these should come from fruits, vegetables, beans, legumes, and unrefined grains

No more than 10% of your daily calories should come from added sugars.

**Added sugars** are syrups and sweeteners used in processed foods.  
They are listed on food labels.  
Examples include:
- Brown sugar  
- Corn syrup  
- Dextrose  
- Fructose  
- Glucose  
- High-fructose corn syrup  
- Honey  
- Lactose  
- Malt syrup  
- Molasses  
- Raw sugar  
- Sucrose  
- Turbinado sugar  
- Trehalose  
- Invert sugar

Sugars naturally found in fruit or milk are not added sugars.

---

### The Glycemic Index

The glycemic index (GI) measures how fast a food raises blood sugar.  
It ranges from 1 (very slow) to 100 (very fast, like pure glucose).

Foods with a low GI raise blood sugar slowly.  
Foods with a high GI raise blood sugar quickly.

Complex carbohydrates usually have a lower GI than simple ones.  
But there are exceptions.  
For example, fructose (fruit sugar) has a low GI.

Several things affect a food’s GI:

- **Processing**: Processed, refined, or finely ground foods tend to have a higher GI.  
- **Type of starch**: Some starches are digested faster than others.  
  - Potato starch is digested quickly.  
  - Barley starch is digested slowly.  
- **Fiber content**: More fiber means slower digestion and slower sugar absorption.  
- **Ripeness of fruit**: Riper fruit has more sugar and a higher GI.  
- **Fat or acid content**: Foods with more fat or acid are digested more slowly.  
- **Preparation**: Cooking or grinding food makes it easier to digest.  
  This increases the GI.  
- **Individual differences**: How your body processes food varies.  
  How well you chew and how fast you eat also matter.

---

### Why the Glycemic Index Matters

Foods with a high GI raise blood sugar fast.  
This causes a quick rise in insulin.  
Insulin helps lower blood sugar.  
But it can cause blood sugar to drop too low.  
This leads to hunger and cravings.

This cycle may lead to eating too many calories and gaining weight.

However, experts now believe that choosing low-GI foods does not help most people lose weight.

Low-GI foods do not cause big spikes in insulin.  
This helps you feel full longer.  
They also help maintain healthier cholesterol levels.  
They lower the risk of:
- Obesity  
- Diabetes  
- Complications from diabetes (in people who already have it)

But the glycemic index is not perfect.  
It does not tell the whole story.

For example:
- Potato chips have a lower GI than brown rice.  
  But potato chips are not a healthy food.  
- Some high-GI foods are rich in vitamins and minerals.

So, the glycemic index should only be used as a general guide.

It does not consider how much carbohydrate a food contains.  
That matters too.

The **glycemic load** takes both the GI and the amount of carbohydrate into account.

A food can have a high GI but a low glycemic load if it has little carbohydrate.  
Examples:
- Carrots  
- Bananas  
- Watermelon  
- Whole-wheat bread

These foods have little effect on blood sugar.

Glycemic load also considers how foods work together.  
The GI does not.

---

## Proteins

Proteins are made of smaller units called amino acids.  
They are strung together in long chains.  
Because they are complex, your body takes longer to break them down.  
This means they give energy slowly and last longer than carbohydrates.

There are 20 different amino acids.  
Your body can make some of them.  
But it cannot make 9 of them.  
These are called **essential amino acids**.

Everyone needs 8 of these essential amino acids:
- Isoleucine  
- Leucine  
- Lysine  
- Methionine  
- Phenylalanine  
- Threonine  
- Tryptophan  
- Valine

Infants also need a 9th one: histidine.

The body can use protein from different foods at different rates:

- Egg protein: 100% usable  
- Milk

# Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder

This condition causes physical symptoms that affect movement or the senses. It used to be called conversion disorder.

The symptoms happen without the person trying to make them. They are not due to a brain or nerve problem. The symptoms do not match what we know about how nerves and the brain work.

Stress or past trauma often play a role in starting or making the symptoms worse.

Doctors diagnose this condition after checking for other physical causes. They look at your medical history and do tests to rule out other illnesses.

Treatment starts with a strong, trusting relationship with your doctor. Therapy, hypnosis, and physical therapy can help some people.

(See also: Overview of Somatization.)

This disorder is a type of somatization. That means emotional or mental health issues show up as physical symptoms.

It usually starts in late childhood or early adulthood. But it can happen at any age. It is more common in women.

---

## What the Symptoms Feel Like

Symptoms often start suddenly. They may follow a stressful event.

The symptoms usually affect how you move or feel. For example:

- Trouble moving an arm or leg
- Weakness or paralysis in a limb
- Loss of feeling in part of the body
- Problems with balance or coordination
- Seizure-like shaking or loss of awareness
- Strange body positions that do not match known brain or nerve problems
- Blurred or double vision
- Blindness or deafness
- Trouble speaking or swallowing
- A feeling of a lump in the throat
- Trouble urinating

Some people have one episode. Others have symptoms come and go. Sometimes symptoms last for a long time. Most episodes are short.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose This Condition

Doctors use the *Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders*, 5th edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR) to help make the diagnosis.

First, they do a full medical check-up. This includes tests to rule out other illnesses.

The diagnosis is only made after all other possible causes are ruled out.

The symptoms must not match what we know about brain or nerve diseases. For example:

- A person may have weak foot movement when lying down but can walk on tiptoes normally.
- A doctor may feel the foot of a “paralyzed” leg push down when the other leg is lifted.
- A tremor may stop or change when the person is distracted, like when copying a movement with the other hand.
- A person may resist eye opening during a seizure-like event.
- A person may see only in a narrow tunnel, not the full field of vision.

To be considered a disorder, the symptoms must cause serious distress or make daily life hard. This includes problems at work, school, or in relationships.

---

## How This Condition Is Treated

A strong, trusting relationship with your doctor is key.

A team approach works best. This may include a psychiatrist and a doctor from another field, like a neurologist or internal medicine doctor.

Once other causes are ruled out, it helps to tell the patient: “Your symptoms are real. But they are not caused by a serious brain or body disease.”

This reassurance can help people feel better. Symptoms may improve over time.

The following treatments may help:

- **Hypnosis** can help people manage stress and how it affects their body.
- **Psychotherapy**, including cognitive-behavioral therapy, helps some people understand and manage their symptoms.
- **Physical therapy** can help people regain movement and strength.
- Any other mental health issues, like depression, should also be treated.

# Rat-Bite Fever

Rat-bite fever is an infection caused by two types of bacteria.  
One is called *Streptobacillus moniliformis*.  
The other is called *Spirillum minus*.  

## How People Get Rat-Bite Fever

Most people get the infection from a bite or scratch from an infected rat.  
Pet rats, wild rats, mice, and gerbils can carry the bacteria.  
Weasels can also spread the infection.  
In some cases, people get sick from drinking milk that has not been heated to kill germs.  
This kind of infection is called Haverhill fever.  

Streptobacillary rat-bite fever is common in the United States.  
Spirillary rat-bite fever is mostly found in Asia.  

## Types of Rat-Bite Fever

### Streptobacillary Rat-Bite Fever

This type is caused by *Streptobacillus moniliformis*.  
This bacteria lives in the mouth and throat of healthy rats, mice, and gerbils.  
It has a long, rod-like shape.  

You can get this infection from a rat bite or scratch.  
You can also get it from drinking unpasteurized milk that has the bacteria.  
This type causes joint pain.  

### Spirillary Rat-Bite Fever

This type is caused by *Spirillum minus*.  
This bacteria has a spiral shape.  

You usually get this infection from a rat bite.  
It is very rare to get it from eating food with the bacteria.  
This type causes swollen lymph nodes.  

## Symptoms

Both types cause fever that comes and goes.  
Both types also cause a rash.  

### Symptoms of Streptobacillary Rat-Bite Fever

The bite site usually heals fast.  
Symptoms start within a day to three weeks after the bite heals.  
You may feel chills.  
You may have a high fever.  
You may have a headache.  
You may feel sick to your stomach and throw up.  
You may have back pain and joint pain.  

A few days after the fever starts, a rash appears.  
The rash looks like small, flat, red spots.  
It usually shows up on the hands and feet.  

Without treatment, joint pain and joint infection can last for days or even months.  
The fever may come and go for weeks or months.  

Haverhill fever causes similar symptoms.  
But vomiting is worse.  
Your throat may also hurt.  

In rare cases, the bacteria can infect the heart.  
This can cause a serious condition called endocarditis.  
Abscesses can form in the brain or other parts of the body.  
These problems are rare but serious.  

### Symptoms of Spirillary Rat-Bite Fever

The bite site usually heals fast.  
But a few days to four weeks later, the area becomes red and swollen.  
You may get a fever that comes and goes.  
Your lymph nodes may swell.  
A rash can appear, but it is usually mild.  
Joint pain is rare.  

Without treatment, the fever may come and go for up to eight weeks.  

## How Doctors Diagnose Rat-Bite Fever

Doctors look at your symptoms to guess which type you have.  
They check if you have joint pain.  
That is more common in streptobacillary rat-bite fever.  
They check if you have swollen lymph nodes.  
That is more common in spirillary rat-bite fever.  

To confirm the diagnosis, doctors take a sample.  
For streptobacillary rat-bite fever, they take blood or fluid from a joint.  
They send the sample to a lab.  
There, they grow the bacteria to see if it is present.  
Sometimes they use special stains and look at the sample under a microscope.  
Blood tests can also help.  

For spirillary rat-bite fever, doctors take a sample of blood, joint fluid, or tissue near the bite.  
They look at the sample under a microscope.  
The bacteria can be seen this way.  
But they cannot grow the bacteria in a lab.  

Sometimes doctors use blood tests to check for antibodies.  
They may also use a test called PCR.  
This test finds tiny pieces of the bacteria’s genetic material.  
It can detect the bacteria quickly.  

## Treatment

Rat-bite fever is treated with antibiotics.  

For both types, doctors start with strong antibiotics given through a vein.  
Common ones are penicillin and ceftriaxone.  
After a few days, you switch to an oral antibiotic.  
These include ampicillin, amoxicillin, or penicillin.  

If you are allergic to penicillin, doctors give you doxycycline instead.  

If the bacteria have infected the heart, doctors use high doses of penicillin.  
They also add another antibiotic.  

## Outlook

Without treatment, about 1 in 10 people with rat-bite fever will die.  
With proper treatment, most people get better quickly.
