# Bullous Keratopathy

Bullous keratopathy means fluid-filled blisters form on the surface of the cornea.  
This happens when the inner layer of the cornea does not work properly.  
The cornea becomes swollen and cloudy.  

## What Causes Bullous Keratopathy?

The cornea needs to stay dry and clear to let light pass through.  
When the inner layer of the cornea fails, fluid builds up.  
This causes swelling and blisters on the cornea.  

The most common causes are:  
- Fuchs corneal endothelial dystrophy  
- Injury to the inner layer of the cornea during eye surgery  

**Fuchs dystrophy** is a genetic condition.  
It slowly damages the inner layer of the cornea.  
It often starts to cause symptoms between ages 50 and 60.  
It can run in families, but not everyone with the gene will get the condition.  

**Injury to the inner cornea** can happen during eye surgery.  
This includes cataract surgery.  
It can also happen if a lens placed inside the eye is not made right or is in the wrong place.  

If the problem happens after cataract surgery:  
- It is called *pseudophakic* if a lens is in place.  
- It is called *aphakic* if no lens is in place.  

## What Are the Symptoms?

Small blisters form under the surface of the cornea.  
These blisters are filled with fluid.  
The cornea swells and becomes cloudy.  

This leads to:  
- Blurry or poor vision  
- Trouble seeing contrast  
- Glare from lights  
- Pain when looking at bright light  

Sometimes the blisters break open.  
When they do, you may feel:  
- Sharp pain  
- A feeling like something is in your eye  

If a blister breaks, bacteria can get in.  
This can cause a corneal ulcer.  
A corneal ulcer is an open sore on the cornea.  
It can be serious and may lead to vision loss.  

## How Is It Diagnosed?

An eye doctor uses a special microscope called a slit lamp.  
This shows the blisters and swelling on the cornea.  

The doctor also measures the thickness of the cornea.  
They use a test called ultrasonic pachymetry.  
This test uses sound waves to measure how thick the cornea is.  

In Fuchs dystrophy, the doctor may see:  
- Tiny, raised spots on the inner surface of the cornea  
- A thickened layer at the back of the cornea  
- A wrinkled or “beaten metal” look on the back of the cornea  

Symptoms are usually worse when you first wake up.  
They improve during the day.  
This is because your eyes close at night.  
Moisture builds up and the cornea swells.  
When you open your eyes during the day, the cornea dries out a little.  

## How Is It Treated?

You must see an eye doctor for treatment.  

Treatment includes:  
- Eye drops or ointments that draw out fluid (like 5% sodium chloride)  
- Eye drops to lower pressure inside the eye  
- Soft contact lenses for short periods, if symptoms are mild to moderate  
- Antibiotics if there is an infection  

If these treatments do not help restore clear vision, a corneal transplant is usually needed.  
This surgery replaces the damaged cornea with healthy tissue.  
It often fixes the problem and restores good vision.  

## Key Facts

- Bullous keratopathy is caused by swelling of the cornea.  
- The most common causes are Fuchs dystrophy or injury during eye surgery.  
- Fluid-filled blisters form under the cornea’s surface.  
- This causes blurry vision, glare, and light sensitivity.  
- A slit-lamp exam shows the blisters and swelling.  
- A test measures how thick the cornea is.  
- You must see an eye doctor for treatment.

# Atelectasis

Atelectasis happens when part of a lung loses air and collapses.  
This can make it hard to breathe.  
It can also lead to low oxygen levels in the blood.  
In some cases, it can cause pneumonia.

## What Happens in the Lungs

Your lungs bring oxygen into your body and remove carbon dioxide.  
This happens in tiny air sacs called alveoli.  
These air sacs must stay open and full of air to work.  
The lungs have a natural elastic structure that helps keep them open.  
A special liquid called surfactant also helps keep the air sacs open.  
Taking deep breaths and coughing help keep the air sacs clear.  
Coughing pushes out mucus or other fluids that could block the airways.

If the air sacs close, they can no longer bring in oxygen.  
The more air sacs that close, the less oxygen gets into the blood.  
The body tries to fix this by narrowing blood vessels in the collapsed area.  
This sends blood to parts of the lung that are still working.

## Causes of Atelectasis

Atelectasis is often caused by one of two things:

- A blockage in the airways (bronchi or bronchioles)  
- Not taking deep breaths or being unable to cough

Blockages can come from inside or outside the airways.

**Inside the airways:**
- Mucus plugs  
- Tumors  
- A foreign object like a piece of food, a pill, or a toy

**Outside the airways:**
- A tumor pressing on the airway  
- An enlarged lymph node  
- Fluid in the space around the lung (pleural effusion)  
- Air in the space around the lung (pneumothorax)

When an airway is blocked, the air in the tiny air sacs beyond the blockage gets absorbed into the blood.  
This causes the air sacs to shrink and collapse.  
Bacteria and white blood cells can build up behind the blockage.  
This can lead to infection, especially if the blockage lasts for days or longer.  
If the collapse lasts for months, the lung may not fully open again.

Other things that reduce deep breathing or coughing can also cause atelectasis.  
These include:

- Strong painkillers (like opioids)  
- Sedatives  
- General anesthesia  
- Pain after chest or abdominal surgery  
- Chest or lung injuries  
- Pneumonia  
- Nerve or muscle problems  
- Being unable to move (immobility)  
- Chest deformities  
- Swelling in the belly (abdominal swelling)  
- Obesity

**Did You Know?**  
Taking deep breaths after surgery can help prevent atelectasis.  
People who smoke can lower their risk by stopping smoking at least 6 to 8 weeks before surgery.

## Symptoms of Atelectasis

Atelectasis often causes no symptoms at all.  
When symptoms do appear, the most common is shortness of breath.  
The severity depends on how fast it develops and how much of the lung is affected.

- If only a small part of the lung is affected, or if it develops slowly, you may feel little or no symptoms.  
- If a large part of the lung collapses quickly, you may feel very short of breath.

Other signs may include:

- Faster heart rate  
- Faster breathing  
- Bluish tint to the skin or lips (cyanosis)  
  - In people with darker skin, this may appear as a dark brown or black color  
  - It is easiest to see in the eyes, lips, and nail beds

Symptoms may also come from the cause of atelectasis.  
For example:
- Chest pain from an injury  
- Chest pain when breathing deeply from pneumonia

## How Doctors Diagnose Atelectasis

Doctors suspect atelectasis based on:

- Your symptoms  
- What they find during a physical exam  
- Your recent medical history (like surgery, injury, or use of certain drugs)

To confirm the diagnosis, they use:

- A chest x-ray  
- A CT scan of the chest

These tests show the area of the lung that has lost air.

Sometimes doctors do more tests to find the cause or remove the blockage.  
For example:
- Bronchoscopy: A thin tube with a camera is inserted into the airway to look inside and remove blockages.

## How Atelectasis Is Treated

Treatment focuses on two main goals:

1. Getting deep breathing to happen again  
2. Removing any blockage in the airways

**To help with deep breathing:**
- You may be asked to breathe deeply and cough often  
- You may use a device called an incentive spirometer to help you take deep breaths  
- Changing your position can help move mucus out of the lungs

**To clear blockages:**
- A health care provider may use suction to remove mucus  
- If suction does not work, a bronchoscopy may be needed  
- If a tumor is blocking the airway, treatment may include surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, or laser therapy  
- If mucus is thick, medicines may be given to thin it or open the airways

**If complications develop, you may need:**
- Extra oxygen  
- Antibiotics, if an infection is present  
- A breathing tube and machine to help you breathe (mechanical ventilation), in rare cases

## How to Prevent Atelectasis

You can lower your risk by:

- Taking deep breaths often  
- Coughing regularly  
- Moving around as soon as possible after surgery  
- Stopping smoking at least 6 to 8 weeks before surgery  
- Using an incentive spirometer after surgery  
- Changing positions to help clear mucus from the lungs

# Small-for-Gestational-Age Infant

An infant is called small for gestational age if their weight is below the 10th percentile for how far along the pregnancy is.  
This means the baby is smaller than most babies at the same stage of pregnancy.

Small babies may face health problems.  
These include low oxygen levels at birth, breathing in meconium (the baby’s first stool), too many red blood cells, low blood sugar, and trouble staying warm.

---

## What Is Gestational Age?

Gestational age is how far along a pregnancy is.  
It is measured in weeks.  
Doctors usually count from the first day of the mother’s last normal period.  
This is the standard way to track pregnancy progress.

But this method is not always exact.  
Ovulation and conception happen about two weeks after the start of the last period.  
So the count includes two weeks before the baby even begins to form.

If a woman has irregular periods, this method becomes even less accurate.

---

## Better Tools to Track Growth

The Fenton growth charts give a more accurate picture of how a baby is growing.  
They are used especially for premature babies.  
There are separate charts for boys and girls.

### Fenton Growth Chart for Preterm Boys  
*Source: Fenton T, Kim J. A systematic review and meta-analysis to revise the Fenton growth chart for preterm infants. BMC Pediatrics 13:59, 2013. Used with permission.*

### Fenton Growth Chart for Preterm Girls  
*Source: Fenton T, Kim J. A systematic review and meta-analysis to revise the Fenton growth chart for preterm infants. BMC Pediatrics 13:59, 2013. Used with permission.*

---

## Why Are Some Babies Small?

Some babies are small because of problems during pregnancy.  
These problems can be split into two types.

### Symmetric Growth Restriction

In this case, the baby’s height, weight, and head size are all similarly small.  
This usually happens early in pregnancy, often in the first three months.  
It is often due to a problem with the baby’s development.

Common causes include:
- Genetic conditions affecting the brain, heart, or kidneys.
- Infections in the first trimester, such as cytomegalovirus, rubella, or toxoplasmosis.

### Asymmetric Growth Restriction

Here, the baby’s weight is most affected.  
The head and brain grow more normally.  
This usually happens later in pregnancy, in the second or third trimester.  
It is often due to problems with the placenta or the mother’s health.

Common causes include:
- Poor blood flow in the placenta due to high blood pressure, preeclampsia, kidney disease, or long-term diabetes.
- Problems with the placenta in multiple pregnancies (like twins or triplets).
- The placenta aging too soon after the due date.
- The mother having low oxygen levels due to lung or heart disease.
- The mother not eating enough healthy food.
- Using fertility treatments to get pregnant.
- The mother being very young or over age 35.
- Having had a small baby in a past pregnancy.

Babies can also be small if the mother used opioids, cocaine, alcohol, or tobacco heavily during pregnancy.  
These substances can harm the baby’s growth.

Not all small babies are unhealthy.  
Some are just naturally small and healthy.  
Also, not every baby who grows slowly in the womb ends up being small for gestational age.

---

## What Do Small Babies Look Like?

Small babies look like other babies of the same age.  
Their skin, ears, and foot creases look normal.  
They act alert and are active.  
They want to feed and are usually not weak.

But they may look thin.  
They have less muscle and less fat under the skin.  
Their face may look sunken, like an older person’s face.  
The umbilical cord may look thin and small.

---

## How Are Small Babies Treated?

There is no special treatment to fix being small for gestational age.  
But doctors will treat any health problems the baby has.

Supportive care is key.  
This includes keeping the baby warm, checking blood sugar, and watching for breathing issues.

Prevention is important.  
Pregnant women should avoid alcohol, tobacco, and illegal drugs.  
These can harm the baby’s growth.

In some cases, doctors may give growth hormone to babies who are still very small at ages 2 to 4.  
This treatment lasts several years.  
It is only used when needed and after careful review of each case.

---

## What Is the Outlook for Small Babies?

If the baby does not have low oxygen at birth, the brain and nervous system usually develop well.  
Most full-term small babies do well in the long run.

But later in life, they may be more likely to develop heart disease, high blood pressure, or stroke.  
This may be due to changes in blood vessel development during pregnancy.

If the baby was small because of poor placenta function, good nutrition after birth can help them grow quickly.  
Some babies catch up fully in size and health.

If the baby was small due to genetic issues, infections, or the mother’s substance use, the outlook depends on the specific cause.  
These babies may face more long-term health challenges.

---

## Key Points

- A baby is small for gestational age if their weight is below the 10th percentile for how far along the pregnancy is.
- Problems early in pregnancy often cause symmetric growth restriction.  
  This means height, weight, and head size are all small.
- Problems later in pregnancy often cause asymmetric growth restriction.  
  This means weight is most affected, but the brain and head grow more normally.
- Small babies do not have the same health risks as premature babies of the same size.  
  They are not underdeveloped in their organs.
- Complications are usually due to the cause of the small size.  
  Common issues include low oxygen at birth, breathing in meconium, low blood sugar, too many red blood cells, and low body temperature.

# Subacute Combined Degeneration

This condition slowly damages the spinal cord. It happens because the body does not have enough vitamin B12.

## What Happens in the Body

- Nerve fibers that control movement and feeling are damaged.
- The body needs vitamin B12 to make a protective covering around some nerves. This covering helps nerves send signals fast.
- Without enough vitamin B12, this covering breaks down. This causes nerve damage.
- The damage can affect the spinal cord, the brain, the eyes, and nerves in the arms and legs.

## Who Is Affected

- This condition usually starts in people over the age of 40.
- It is often linked to a lack of vitamin B12.
- A lack of vitamin B12 can also cause anemia. One type of anemia, called pernicious anemia, is not caused by diet. It happens when the body cannot absorb vitamin B12 properly.

## Symptoms

- You may feel weak all over.
- Tingling, numbness, or a pins-and-needles feeling in both hands and feet.
- These feelings get worse over time.
- You may not feel vibrations or know where your arms and legs are in space.
- Your limbs may feel stiff.
- Movements become clumsy.
- Walking becomes hard.
- Reflexes may be too slow, too fast, or missing.
- Vision may become blurry in rare cases.
- You may feel irritable, tired, confused, or suspicious.
- Your mood may change quickly and without reason.
- In rare cases, memory problems or dementia can develop.

## How It Is Diagnosed

- A blood test checks your vitamin B12 levels.
- A CT scan or MRI may be done to rule out other causes of your symptoms.

## How It Is Treated

- Most people get vitamin B12 through injections right away.
- Injections are usually needed for life to prevent symptoms from coming back.
- If the vitamin B12 deficiency is mild and nerve damage has not started, large doses of vitamin B12 by mouth may work.
- The sooner treatment starts, the better the chance of full recovery.
- If treatment is delayed, symptoms may stop getting worse. But full recovery of lost function is less likely.

## Important Notes

- Early treatment leads to the best results.
- Do not wait to get help if you have symptoms like numbness, weakness, or confusion.

# Fluoroquinolones – Simple Explanation

Fluoroquinolones are a type of antibiotic. They kill bacteria by stopping the bacteria from copying their DNA. This is how they work.

## How Fluoroquinolones Work

These antibiotics block two important enzymes that bacteria need to copy their DNA. Without these enzymes, the bacteria cannot grow or multiply.

## Types of Fluoroquinolones

There are two main groups:

### Older Fluoroquinolones
- Ciprofloxacin
- Norfloxacin
- Ofloxacin

### Newer Fluoroquinolones
- Delafloxacin
- Gemifloxacin
- Levofloxacin
- Moxifloxacin

Some newer fluoroquinolones were taken off the market in the United States. They were removed because they caused serious side effects when taken by mouth. These include:
- Trovafloxacin – caused severe liver damage
- Gatifloxacin – caused low or high blood sugar; still used in eye drops
- Grepafloxacin – caused heart problems
- Temafloxacin – caused kidney failure, liver damage, anemia, blood clotting issues, and low blood sugar
- Lomefloxacin, sparfloxacin, and enoxacin – also removed due to serious side effects

## How Fluoroquinolones Are Taken

| Medicine | How It Is Taken |
|--------|----------------|
| Ciprofloxacin | By mouth or through a vein |
| Delafloxacin | By mouth or through a vein |
| Gemifloxacin | By mouth |
| Levofloxacin | By mouth or through a vein |
| Moxifloxacin | By mouth or through a vein |
| Norfloxacin | By mouth |
| Ofloxacin | By mouth or through a vein |

Some fluoroquinolones are also available as ear drops or eye drops.

## How the Body Handles Fluoroquinolones

- You should not take fluoroquinolones with antacids, calcium, iron, or other supplements. These can reduce how well the medicine works.
- The medicine spreads through most body fluids, including the lungs, prostate, and bile.
- Most fluoroquinolones are broken down in the liver and removed through the urine.
- Moxifloxacin is mostly removed through the bile (a fluid made by the liver).

## What Fluoroquinolones Can Treat

These antibiotics work against many types of bacteria, including:
- *Haemophilus influenzae*
- *Moraxella catarrhalis*
- *Mycoplasma* species
- *Chlamydia* species
- *Chlamydophila* species
- *Legionella* species
- Enterobacterales (a group of common bacteria)
- *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* (especially ciprofloxacin)
- *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* (the bacteria that cause tuberculosis)
- Some other types of mycobacteria
- Some types of staph bacteria that are not resistant to methicillin

Most types of MRSA (a tough kind of staph infection) are not affected by fluoroquinolones.

Older fluoroquinolones do not work well against strep bacteria or anaerobic bacteria (bacteria that grow without oxygen).

Newer fluoroquinolones work better against:
- Streptococci (including *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, even if it is not sensitive to penicillin)
- Some anaerobic bacteria

Delafloxacin is the newest and most powerful fluoroquinolone. It works against:
- Gram-negative bacteria (like *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*)
- Gram-positive bacteria (including MRSA)
- Anaerobic bacteria
- Atypical bacteria in the lungs

## Resistance to Fluoroquinolones

As more people use these antibiotics, some bacteria are becoming resistant. This is especially true for:
- *Escherichia coli*
- *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*
- *Streptococcus pneumoniae*
- *Neisseria* species

Because of this, fluoroquinolones are no longer the first choice for treating gonorrhea. But a single dose of ciprofloxacin can still cure gonorrhea if the bacteria are still sensitive to it.

## Common Uses of Fluoroquinolones

| Medicine | Use | Notes |
|--------|-----|-------|
| Fluoroquinolones (except moxifloxacin) | Urinary tract infections | Use when *E. coli* is resistant to trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole |
| Fluoroquinolones | Bacterial prostatitis | Effective treatment |
| Fluoroquinolones | Salmonella blood infection | Effective |
| Fluoroquinolones | Typhoid fever | Usually works well |
| Fluoroquinolones | Infectious diarrhea | Works against many causes (like *Campylobacter*, *Salmonella*, *Shigella*, *Vibrio*, *Yersinia*) |
| | | Not effective against *E. coli* O157:H7 or other dangerous *E. coli* types |
| | | Not effective against *Clostridioides difficile* (a cause of severe diarrhea) |
| Ofloxacin | *Chlamydia trachomatis* infections | Take for 7 days |
| Newer fluoroquinolones (delafloxacin, gemifloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) | Community-acquired pneumonia | Not first choice; other medicines are preferred |
| Ciprofloxacin | Legionella pneumonia | A top choice (or azithromycin) |
| Ciprofloxacin | Hospital-acquired pneumonia | Can be used early while waiting for test results |
| | | Works well against *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* |
| | | May be used with another antibiotic if the bacteria are resistant to many drugs |
| Ciprofloxacin | Long-term treatment of bone infections (osteomyelitis) | Good for long-term use because it works well in bones |
| Ciprofloxacin | Meningococcal prevention | Used to prevent spread of meningococcal disease |
| Ciprofloxacin | Anthrax prevention | Used during outbreaks, like after the 2001 bioterror attack |

## Who Should Not Take Fluoroquinolones

You should not take fluoroquinolones if:
- You had an allergic reaction to one before
- You have heart rhythm problems (like long QT interval)
- You have low levels of potassium or magnesium in your blood
- You have a slow heart rate (bradycardia)
- You are taking other medicines that can cause heart rhythm problems or slow the heart

Delafloxacin does not seem to cause heart rhythm problems.

Fluoroquinolones were once avoided in children because they might harm growing bones. But experts now say they can be used in special cases when no other medicine works. These include:
- *Pseudomonas* infections in people with cystic fibrosis
- Infections in people with weak immune systems
- Life-threatening infections in newborns and infants
- Severe *Salmonella* or *Shigella* infections in the gut

## Fluoroquinolones and Pregnancy or Breastfeeding

- Animal studies show some risk to the baby.
- Human data is limited.
- Use only if the benefit outweighs the risk and no safer option is available.

Fluoroquinolones pass into breast milk. They are not recommended during breastfeeding.

## Side Effects of Fluoroquinolones

These medicines have strong warnings because they can cause serious, long-lasting side effects. These include:

### Tendons
- Tendon pain or rupture (especially the Achilles tendon) can happen even after a short course.
- Stop the medicine at the first sign of pain.

### Nerves
- Numbness, tingling, burning, or weakness in hands or feet can happen soon after starting the medicine.
- These symptoms can be permanent.
- Stop the medicine if you notice any nerve symptoms.

### Brain and Nervous System
- Seizures (rare)
- Increased pressure in the brain (can cause headaches, vision problems)
- Mental changes like confusion, anxiety, depression, hallucinations, or mood swings
- Dizziness, trouble sleeping, nightmares, tremors
- Do not use if you have a brain or nervous system disorder.

### Muscle Problems
- Can make muscle weakness worse in people with myasthenia gravis.
- Avoid in these patients.

### Other Side Effects
- Upset stomach (about 5% of people) – due to irritation in the stomach
- Low blood sugar – especially if you are also taking diabetes medicine
- Heart rhythm problems – can lead to sudden death in rare cases
- Aortic aneurysm or tear – risk is higher in people with Marfan syndrome or known aneurysms
- *Clostridioides difficile* infection – causes severe diarrhea and colitis. This is strongly linked to fluoroquinolone use, especially the dangerous *C. difficile* type 027
- Allergic reactions – including rash, swelling, or anaphylaxis. Stop the medicine at the first sign of a rash, yellow skin, or other allergy signs
- Liver damage – stop the medicine if you develop jaundice or liver problems
- Sun sensitivity – you may burn easily in the sun. Avoid strong sunlight and wear protective clothing

- Diarrhea
- Low white blood cell count
- Anemia

# What Is Leukemia?

Leukemia is a type of cancer that starts in the white blood cells or in the cells that turn into white blood cells.

White blood cells are made in the bone marrow. Sometimes, the process goes wrong. Pieces of chromosomes can get mixed up. This causes the cells to grow too fast or not die when they should. This leads to leukemia.

## Types of Leukemia

There are four main types of leukemia. They are grouped by how fast they grow and what kind of white blood cells are affected.

- **Acute lymphoblastic leukemia**  
  This grows fast. It starts in early-stage lymphocytes.

- **Acute myeloid leukemia**  
  This also grows fast. It starts in early-stage myeloid cells.

- **Chronic lymphocytic leukemia**  
  This grows slowly. It starts in more mature lymphocytes.

- **Chronic myeloid leukemia**  
  This grows slowly. It starts in more mature myeloid cells.

**Acute leukemias** grow quickly. The cells are not fully developed.

**Chronic leukemias** grow slowly. The cells are more developed.

**Lymphocytic leukemias** come from lymphocytes or their parent cells. They can be acute or chronic.

**Myeloid leukemias** come from cells that make neutrophils, basophils, eosinophils, and monocytes. They can be acute or chronic.

## Problems Caused by Leukemia

Leukemia cells take over the bone marrow. They stop normal blood cells from forming. This can lead to:

- Low red blood cells → feeling tired and weak (anemia)
- Low normal white blood cells → higher risk of infections
- Low platelets → more bleeding or bruising (thrombocytopenia)

The cancer cells do not work like normal white blood cells. So they cannot help fight infections.

Leukemia cells can also spread to other parts of the body. This includes the liver, spleen, lymph nodes, testes, and brain.

## What Causes Leukemia?

For most people, the cause is unknown.

Some things can raise the risk:

- Exposure to high levels of radiation
- Some types of chemotherapy
- Certain chemicals like benzene, some pesticides, and chemicals in tobacco smoke

But even with these risks, very few people develop leukemia.

Some inherited conditions increase the risk:

- Down syndrome
- Fanconi anemia

In some people, changes in chromosomes cause leukemia.

A virus called HTLV-1 may cause a rare type of lymphocytic leukemia called adult T-cell leukemia. This virus is similar to HIV, which causes AIDS.

Infection with the Epstein-Barr virus (which causes mono) has been linked to a rare type of lymphocytic leukemia in parts of Asia and Africa.

## How Is Leukemia Treated?

Treatment depends on the type of leukemia. Common treatments include:

- Drugs, such as chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or targeted therapy
- Stem cell transplant in some cases
- Radiation therapy or surgery, if needed

Many types of leukemia can be treated well. Some can even be cured.

**Chemotherapy** uses drugs to kill fast-growing cells. It works on cancer cells because they grow fast. But it can also harm healthy cells.

**Immunotherapy** helps the body’s own immune system fight cancer.

**Targeted therapy** uses drugs that attack specific problems in cancer cells, like abnormal genes or proteins.

Immunotherapy and targeted therapy usually cause fewer side effects than chemotherapy. They are easier on the body.

Doctors pick the best treatment based on the type of leukemia.

Other problems from leukemia also need treatment:

- Blood transfusions if you are very anemic
- Antibiotics if you get an infection
- Platelet transfusions if you are bleeding

When treatment works, the number of leukemia cells drops. This is called remission.

If the leukemia comes back, it is called a relapse.

For some people, the disease returns and treatment no longer helps much. Quality of life becomes more important than trying to live a little longer. Comfort and dignity matter most.

You and your family should be part of these choices. There are many ways to give compassionate care, ease symptoms, and support you during this time.

This group gives clear information about leukemia for patients and caregivers. It also offers support and resources.
