All 50 states in the United States recognize advance directives. They are a simple legal way to share your wishes and have them respected.

But you do not need a formal document to express your wishes. If your wishes are clear and honest, and they follow standard medical care, they should still be honored.

## When Can You Make One?

You must be able to understand what you are doing and be able to say what you want. If you are too sick to understand or speak, you cannot make a new advance directive.

In most states, the directive only starts to be used after a doctor says you can no longer make your own health care decisions.

## What If You Don’t Have One?

If you do not have an advance directive, someone must step in to make decisions for you.

This person is called an **authorized surrogate**. They are chosen by state law or by a court.

## What Doctors Should Do

Doctors should:

- Get a copy of your living will and power of attorney for health care.
- Review the document with you regularly while you are still able to understand it.
- Keep the document in your medical record.

Federal law says hospitals and long-term care centers must clearly mark in your file if you have an advance directive.

## What You Should Do

- Give a copy of your power of attorney for health care to the person you chose to make decisions for you.
- Share copies with close family members or friends who may be involved in your care.
- This helps avoid confusion or arguments later.
- Keep a copy with your lawyer.
- Some states now offer online systems to store and find your advance directive. Check if your state has one.

# Keratomalacia

Keratomalacia is a serious eye problem. It happens when the eye’s clear front layer, called the cornea, becomes dry and cloudy. This is caused by a lack of vitamin A. It usually affects people who are not getting enough to eat.

## What Happens in the Eye

- The cornea and the membrane covering the eye (called the conjunctiva) dry out.
- Dry eyes can lead to sores on the cornea. These sores are called corneal ulcers.
- Bacteria can enter through these sores and cause infections.
- The tear glands do not make enough tears. This makes the eyes even drier.
- Some people develop white, foamy spots on the white part of the eye. These are called Bitot spots.
- A lack of vitamin A also affects the retina. This can cause night blindness. That means it is hard to see in low light.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors look at the eye. They check for dryness, ulcers, or cloudiness in the cornea. They also check if the person is undernourished. The diagnosis is based on these signs.

## How It Is Treated

- Antibiotic eye drops or ointments are used to treat any infection.
- Vitamin A must be replaced. This can be done with vitamin A supplements.
- A better diet is also needed. Eating foods rich in vitamin A helps the body heal.
- Treating the vitamin A deficiency and improving nutrition are just as important as treating the eye infection.

Treating the root cause—lack of vitamin A and poor nutrition—is key to full recovery.

# Hiccups

Hiccups happen when the diaphragm (the muscle under your lungs) suddenly contracts. This causes a quick closing of the voice box. The result is the familiar "hic" sound.

Short bouts of hiccups are very common.  
Hiccups that last more than two days are rare.  
Hiccups that last more than a month are even rarer but can be very upsetting.

## What Causes Hiccups?

Hiccups happen when nerves that control the diaphragm get irritated.  
They can also happen if the part of the brain that controls breathing is irritated.  
Men are more likely to get hiccups than women.

In most cases, doctors do not know the exact cause.  
But short-term hiccups are often caused by:

- Eating too much food
- Drinking alcohol
- Swallowing very hot or spicy food or drink

Long-lasting hiccups (more than two days) can have many causes. Some of these include:

### Problems in the Esophagus
- Acid reflux (when stomach acid flows back into the esophagus)
- Other issues with the esophagus

### Problems in the Abdomen
- Recent abdominal surgery
- Bowel problems
- Gallbladder disease
- Cancer that has spread to the liver
- Liver inflammation
- Pancreas inflammation

### Other Causes
- Pregnancy
- Inflammation of the lining around the diaphragm
- Inflammation of the lining around the heart
- Lung infection (pneumonia)
- Recent chest surgery
- Alcohol misuse
- Tumors or stroke in the back part of the brain
- Kidney failure

## How Are Hiccups Checked?

Doctors will ask about your symptoms and medical history.  
They may do a physical exam.  
Tests are usually not needed for short hiccups.  
But if hiccups last more than a few days, tests may be needed to find the cause.

## How Are Hiccups Treated?

If a clear cause is found, treatment focuses on that problem.  
For example:
- Medicines to reduce stomach acid for acid reflux
- Surgery or dilation to fix a narrowed esophagus

For symptom relief, some simple tricks may help. But they do not work for everyone.  
And there is not strong proof that they work.

Some people try:
- Holding their breath several times in a row
- Breathing deeply into and out of a paper bag

**Warning:** Do not use plastic bags. They can stick to your nose and block your airway.

Other tricks include:
- Swallowing dry bread
- Eating granulated sugar
- Chewing crushed ice
- Pulling on your tongue gently
- Triggering a gag reflex

Many home remedies exist, but most are not proven to work.

Long-lasting hiccups are hard to treat.  
Many medicines have been used, but results vary.

Effective options include:
- Baclofen – a medicine that calms nerve activity
- Chlorpromazine – a medicine that helps calm the brain
- Metoclopramide – a medicine that helps move food through the stomach
- Anticonvulsants like gabapentin – medicines used for nerve pain

Doctors may also try a trial of proton pump inhibitors (medicines that reduce stomach acid), even if acid reflux is not suspected.

For severe cases, chlorpromazine can be given as an injection into a muscle or through a vein.

In very rare cases, doctors may block the nerve to the diaphragm using a numbing medicine.  
This is done carefully to avoid serious side effects like trouble breathing or a collapsed lung.  
Even cutting the nerve on both sides does not always stop hiccups.

## Key Points

- The cause is usually not known.
- Rarely, hiccups are a sign of a serious health problem.
- Testing is often not helpful for short hiccups.
- But testing is important if hiccups last more than a few days.
- Many home remedies exist, but few are proven to work.
- No single treatment is clearly better than the others.

# Photosensitivity Reactions

Photosensitivity is a skin reaction caused by sunlight. It is sometimes called a sun allergy.

- Sunlight can cause the body’s immune system to react in a way that harms the skin.
- The skin may become itchy, red, swollen, or develop a rash.
- The rash only appears on skin that has been in the sun.
- Most reactions go away on their own without treatment.
- A doctor can usually diagnose it by looking at the skin and asking about your health and medicines.

Some people are more likely to have this reaction. It can run in families. Certain health conditions, like lupus or porphyria, can also make the skin more sensitive to sunlight.

---

## Types of Photosensitivity Reactions

### Solar Urticaria

- This is a type of hives that appears within minutes of sun exposure.
- The hives are red, itchy, and often go away in minutes or hours.
- Some people have this reaction for years or even for life.
- If a large area of skin is affected, a person may feel dizzy, weak, sick to their stomach, or have trouble breathing.

### Chemical Photosensitivity

Over 100 medicines and substances can make the skin react to sunlight. Some of these are more common than others.

There are two main types: phototoxicity and photoallergy.

#### Phototoxicity

- This reaction causes pain, redness, swelling, and sometimes dark or grayish skin color.
- It looks like a sunburn but only happens after using certain medicines or chemicals.
- It can be caused by:
  - Some antibiotics (like tetracyclines and diuretics)
  - Certain skin care products (like perfumes and coal tar)
  - Some plants (like limes, celery, and parsley)
- The chemicals in these plants are called furocoumarins. They make the skin more sensitive to sunlight.
- This reaction only happens on skin that has been in the sun.
- It usually shows up within hours after sun exposure.

#### Photoallergy

- This is an allergic reaction to sunlight.
- It causes redness, flaking, itching, blisters, or hives.
- It can be caused by:
  - Aftershave lotions
  - Sunscreens
  - Some antibiotics (like sulfonamides)
- The substance must be on the skin and the skin must be in sunlight for the reaction to happen.
- The rash can appear on skin that was not in the sun.
- It usually shows up 24 to 72 hours after sun exposure.

---

### Common Medicines and Substances That Cause Photosensitivity

| Type of Medicine or Substance | Examples |
|-------------------------------|----------|
| Antianxiety medicines | Alprazolam, Chlordiazepoxide |
| Antibiotics | Quinolones, Sulfonamides, Tetracyclines (especially doxycycline), Trimethoprim |
| Antidepressants | Tricyclic antidepressants |
| Antifungal medicines | Griseofulvin |
| Diabetes medicines | Sulfonylureas |
| Malaria medicines | Chloroquine, Quinine |
| Antipsychotic medicines | Phenothiazines |
| Cancer medicines | Dacarbazine, Fluorouracil, Methotrexate, Vinblastine |
| Diuretics | Furosemide, Thiazides |
| Acne medicines | Isotretinoin |
| Heart medicines | Amiodarone, Quinidine |
| Pain relievers | NSAIDs (especially piroxicam and ketoprofen) |
| Skin products | Chlorhexidine, Hexachlorophene, Coal tar, Fragrances |
| Plant chemicals | Furocoumarins (found in limes, celery, parsley) |
| Sunscreens | Some types can cause reactions |

---

### Polymorphous Light Eruption

- This is a common skin reaction to sunlight, especially UVA rays.
- It is more common in women and people from northern climates who do not get much sun.
- The rash appears as red bumps, raised red patches (plaques), or sometimes blisters.
- It only shows up on skin that has been in the sun.
- It usually appears 30 minutes to several hours after sun exposure.
- New patches can appear many hours or even days later.
- The rash usually goes away in a few days to a few weeks.
- Over time, many people become less sensitive to sunlight if they keep going out in the sun. This is called hardening.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Photosensitivity

- A doctor will look at your skin and ask about your health, medicines, and skin care products.
- They may ask about any medical conditions you have, like lupus.
- There are no special blood or lab tests for photosensitivity.
- If the rash only appears on sun-exposed skin, the doctor may suspect photosensitivity.
- If the cause is not clear, the doctor may do a test called phototesting.
  - This involves exposing small areas of skin to UV light.
  - The test is done when you are not using any medicine or product that could cause a reaction.
  - This helps the doctor figure out what type of reaction you have.

---

## How Photosensitivity Reactions Are Treated

### General Treatment

- Stop any medicine or chemical that may be causing the reaction. Always talk to your doctor first.
- For chemical photosensitivity, use a steroid cream on the skin and avoid the substance that causes the reaction.

### Solar Urticaria

- Doctors may prescribe antihistamines (to reduce itching and hives).
- Steroid creams or pills may help.
- Sunscreen can protect the skin.
- If these do not work, UV light therapy may be tried.
- Some people benefit from omalizumab, a medicine that helps reduce allergic reactions.

### Polymorphous Light Eruption

- Steroid creams or pills may help.
- Hydroxychloroquine (a medicine used for lupus) may be helpful.
- In some cases, doctors may slowly increase sun exposure to help the skin get used to sunlight. This is called phototherapy.

### Prevention

- Taking *Polypodium leucotomos* (a plant-based supplement) or nicotinamide (a form of vitamin B3) by mouth may help prevent symptoms in people who are sensitive to sunlight.

---

## How to Prevent Photosensitivity Reactions

- Everyone should avoid too much sun.
- If you are sensitive to sunlight, take extra care:
  - Wear long sleeves, pants, and hats.
  - Stay in the shade when possible.
  - Use sunscreen every day, even on cloudy days.
  - Reapply sunscreen often, especially after swimming or sweating.

For more information, see: *Prevention of Sunburn*

# Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE)

PACE is a health care program for older adults. Most people in the program are 55 or older. They qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid. They need care like that given in a nursing home. But they want to stay at home as long as possible.

## What PACE Offers

PACE gives you many kinds of care. The care team includes doctors, nurses, physical therapists, occupational therapists, social workers, dietitians, and drivers. The team works together to meet your needs.

You get care at a special center for adults. This center is open every day. PACE also provides transportation to and from the center. Some care can happen at your home.

The services include:

- Doctor and dentist visits  
- Adult day care  
- Help with daily tasks at home  
- Prescribed medicines  
- Social services  
- Therapy to help you stay strong and independent  
- Meals and advice on healthy eating  
- Hospital care when needed  
- Long-term care when needed  

The PACE team decides what care you need. The program must cover all services that Medicare and Medicaid pay for. It also includes any other care the team says is important.

You may have to pay a monthly fee. The amount depends on your income and the state you live in.

## Who Can Join PACE?

To join PACE, you must:

- Be 55 years old or older  
- Live in an area where a PACE program is available  
- Need the same level of care as someone in a nursing home (this is confirmed by your state)  
- Be able to live safely in your community with help from PACE  

## Where Is PACE Available?

PACE is only available in certain parts of the United States. You can check the PACE plan search tool to find out if there is a PACE program in your state.

PACE uses money from both Medicare and Medicaid. This helps cover the cost of your care.

# Paraneoplastic Syndromes

Paraneoplastic syndromes happen when cancer causes unusual symptoms. These symptoms come from substances in the blood. The substances can be hormones made by the tumor. Or they can be antibodies made by the immune system. These substances travel through the blood and affect organs far from the cancer. They can cause problems in many parts of the body. This includes the nervous system and hormone system. Symptoms may include changes in the brain, low blood sugar, diarrhea, or high blood pressure.

About one in five people with cancer will have a paraneoplastic syndrome. The cancers most often linked to these syndromes are:

- Lung cancer (most common)
- Kidney cancer
- Liver cancer
- Leukemia
- Lymphoma
- Breast cancer
- Ovary cancer
- Neuroendocrine cancer
- Stomach cancer
- Pancreatic cancer

To find a paraneoplastic syndrome, doctors often test the blood for the substance causing the symptoms. At first, treatment focuses on easing the symptoms. The best long-term solution is to treat the cancer itself.

---

## General Symptoms

People with cancer often have fever, night sweats, poor appetite, and weight loss. The conditions below are less common.

---

## Digestive System Problems

Some cancers cause watery diarrhea. This happens when the tumor releases substances into the blood. Some tumors in the intestine release too much protein into the stool. This can lower the amount of protein in the blood.

---

## Hormone-Related Problems

Small cell lung cancer can make a substance that tells the adrenal gland to make more cortisol. This can cause weakness, weight gain, and high blood pressure. This condition is called Cushing syndrome.

Small cell lung cancer can also make a substance called vasopressin. This causes the body to hold on to water. It can lower sodium levels in the blood. This may lead to weakness, confusion, and seizures.

High levels of calcium in the blood (hypercalcemia) can happen in people with solid tumors or leukemia. The cancer may release a substance like parathyroid hormone. This causes calcium to come out of the bones. The cancer can also invade bone directly, releasing calcium into the blood. High calcium levels can cause kidney failure and confusion. If not treated, this can lead to coma or death.

Some tumors in the pancreas make too many hormones. This can cause carcinoid syndrome. Symptoms include flushing, wheezing, diarrhea, and heart valve damage.

---

## Nervous System Problems

Polyneuropathy means the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord are not working right. It can cause weakness, numbness, and weak reflexes. Subacute sensory neuropathy is a rare form. It causes loss of feeling and poor coordination. It often shows up before the cancer is found. It causes little weakness.

Guillain-Barré syndrome is another nerve problem. It causes muscle weakness all over the body. It is more common in people with Hodgkin lymphoma.

Subacute cerebellar degeneration is rare. It can happen in people with breast cancer, ovary cancer, small cell lung cancer, or other solid tumors. It may be caused by an antibody that attacks the brain’s cerebellum. Symptoms include unsteady walking, poor arm and leg control, trouble speaking, dizziness, and double vision. These symptoms can appear before the cancer is found.

Uncontrollable eye movements (opsoclonus) and sudden jerks in the arms and legs (myoclonus) can happen in children with neuroblastoma.

Subacute motor neuronopathy affects the nerves in the spinal cord. It weakens the arms and legs. It can happen in people with Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

Some people get brain changes because their immune system makes antibodies against the tumor. These antibodies also attack brain tissue. This can cause confusion, memory problems, vision changes, and muscle weakness.

Eaton-Lambert syndrome happens in some people with small cell lung cancer. It causes extreme muscle weakness. The nerves fail to properly signal the muscles to move.

Subacute necrotizing myelopathy is very rare. It causes fast loss of nerve cells in the spinal cord. This can lead to paralysis.

---

## Skin Problems

Itching is the most common skin symptom in people with cancer. Flushing (redness and warmth) is also common. People may get brown, black, or bluish marks on the skin.

---

## Other Problems

Polymyositis means muscle weakness and soreness from muscle inflammation. If the skin is also inflamed, the condition is called dermatomyositis.

Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy can happen in people with lung cancer. It changes the shape of the fingers and toes. It can also cause painful swelling in some joints.

Cancer can cause changes in blood cells. Some people have too few red blood cells (anemia). Others have too many platelets (thrombocythemia). Some have too many white blood cells.

Cancers of the kidneys or liver can cause the body to make too many red blood cells. Other cancers can spread to the bone marrow. This can stop the body from making enough blood cells. This includes red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.

# Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)

A ventricular septal defect is a hole in the wall between the two lower chambers of the heart.  
This hole lets blood flow from the left side of the heart to the right side.  
The amount of blood that leaks depends on how big the hole is.

## What Happens in a VSD?

- Small holes often close on their own in early childhood.  
- Large holes let too much blood flow to the lungs.  
- This extra blood flow makes the heart work harder.  
- Over time, the blood vessels in the lungs can become damaged.  
- The heart may eventually fail.  
- In rare cases, the blood flow can reverse.  
- Then blood flows from the right side to the left side of the heart.  
- This can lead to serious health problems.

## Who Gets VSD?

- VSD is the second most common heart problem present at birth.  
- It happens in about 1 out of every 5 babies born with a heart defect.  
- It can happen alone or with other heart problems.  
- Examples include tetralogy of Fallot, complete atrioventricular septal defects, and transposition of the great arteries.

## How Does a VSD Affect the Body?

- The left side of the heart pumps blood to the body.  
- The right side pumps blood to the lungs.  
- A hole lets blood from the left side leak into the right side.  
- This extra blood goes to the lungs.  
- The lungs get too much blood.  
- The heart must pump harder to keep up.  
- Over time, this can damage the lungs and the heart.

## Symptoms of VSD

### Small VSDs
- Most babies with small holes have no symptoms.  
- They grow and develop normally.  
- They do not have trouble breathing or feeding.  
- They do not get sick often.

### Larger VSDs
- Symptoms usually start between 4 and 6 weeks of age.  
- The baby may breathe fast or have trouble feeding.  
- The baby may not gain weight well.  
- The baby may seem tired after feeding.  
- The baby may get lung infections often.  
- Over time, untreated large VSDs can lead to serious lung problems.  
- This can cause a condition called Eisenmenger syndrome.

## What Do Doctors Hear When Listening to the Heart?

- A small hole may cause a soft, short sound (murmur).  
- A larger hole causes a loud, harsh sound that lasts all through the heartbeat.  
- This sound is usually heard at the lower left side of the chest.  
- It can be heard in the first few days of life.  
- The heart’s second sound (S2) is normal in small holes.  
- In larger holes, the second sound may be louder or split.  
- A doctor may also hear a soft rumbling sound at the heart’s tip.  
- This happens because more blood flows through the mitral valve.

## How Is VSD Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find a VSD.

### Chest X-ray
- Shows the size of the heart.  
- Shows if the lungs have too much blood flow.  
- Small holes may not show anything abnormal.

### ECG (Electrocardiogram)
- Measures the heart’s electrical activity.  
- Can show if the heart muscle is thickened.  
- May show signs of strain in the right or both lower chambers.  
- Small holes usually have normal results.

### Echocardiogram (Echo)
- This is the main test to confirm a VSD.  
- It uses sound waves to make a moving picture of the heart.  
- It shows the size and location of the hole.  
- It shows how much blood is leaking.  
- It measures pressure in the right side of the heart.  
- It checks how well the heart is working.  
- This test is safe and painless.

### Cardiac Catheterization
- Not needed for most cases.  
- Used only if more detail is needed.  
- Helps measure pressure in the lungs.  
- Checks how much blood is going to the lungs.  
- Helps decide if surgery is needed.

## How Is VSD Treated?

### Small VSDs
- Often close on their own in the first few years.  
- No treatment is needed if the hole stays small.  
- Regular checkups are still important.

### Larger VSDs
- May need treatment to help the heart.  
- Medicines can help with symptoms of heart failure.  
- These include diuretics, digoxin, and ACE inhibitors.  
- These medicines help reduce swelling and make the heart work better.  
- They are used before surgery or to help babies grow while waiting.

### Surgery
- Recommended for babies who do not get better with medicine.  
- Recommended for babies who are not gaining weight.  
- Surgery is often done in the first few months of life.  
- Even babies with no symptoms may need surgery if the hole is large.  
- Surgery is usually done within the first year of life.  
- This helps prevent long-term lung damage.  
- The risk of death from surgery is less than 2%.  
- Possible side effects include a small leak left after surgery or a problem with the heart’s electrical system.

### Other Treatments
- Some holes can be closed using a thin tube (catheter).  
- This is not common and is only used in special cases.  
- It is not usually the first choice.

### Infection Prevention
- Antibiotics are not needed before surgery.  
- After surgery, antibiotics are needed for the first 6 months.  
- They are also needed if a small leak remains after surgery.

## Key Facts

- A VSD is a hole in the wall between the two lower heart chambers.  
- It causes blood to flow from the left side to the right side of the heart.  
- Large holes can cause serious lung problems over time.  
- This can lead to a condition called Eisenmenger syndrome.  
- Symptoms usually appear by 6 weeks of age.  
- A loud, harsh sound (murmur) is often heard at the lower left side of the chest.  
- Babies who do not improve with medicine or who are not growing well need surgery early.  
- Even babies with no symptoms should have large holes repaired by age 1.  
- Most children do very well after treatment.

## More Information

The following resources may help parents and caregivers understand heart defects and care for children.

- **American Heart Association: Common Heart Defects**  
  A guide to common heart problems in babies and children.

- **American Heart Association: Infective Endocarditis**  
  Information about heart infections and when antibiotics are needed.

# Bone Density Problems in Children

Bone density problems affect how strong and dense a child’s bones are. Weak bones break easily. Bones may also grow in an unusual way.

- These problems happen when the body does not recycle old bone cells properly.
- Common signs include bones that do not grow normally and bones that break easily.
- Doctors check for these problems using symptoms, x-rays, and sometimes blood tests.
- Treatments like medicine and surgery can help with some of the issues.

Bone density measures how much mineral is in the bone. Bones that are too dense or not dense enough are more likely to break.

Some bone density problems come from gene changes passed down from parents. Others come from poor eating habits, hormone issues, or other health problems.

Bone density problems are split into two types: low bone density and high bone density.

(See also: Overview of Bone Disorders in Children.)

---

## Low Bone Density in Children

Children’s bones are always growing and changing. Old bone is removed and new bone is made. This keeps bones strong.

In children with low bone density, this process is broken. This can happen because of a specific cause or because the child is not moving much. The result is less bone mass and weaker bones.

Weaker bones become thinner and more likely to break. Breaks can happen in the spine or in long bones like the arm and leg bones. This can slow down normal growth and make movement hard.

The main low bone density problems in children are:
- Osteogenesis imperfecta
- Osteoporosis
- Rickets

Causes of low bone density include:
- Not eating enough healthy food
- Low levels of vitamin D
- Gene changes
- Low levels of hormones like growth hormone, estrogen, or testosterone
- Health problems like celiac disease or chronic kidney disease
- Some medicines, such as steroids

To check for low bone density, doctors use a test called a DXA scan. This scan uses two types of x-rays on the spine and hip. These are the areas most likely to break.

The scan compares the child’s bone density to that of a healthy child of the same age, sex, and size. The result is called a Z-score. A lower Z-score means weaker bones. A Z-score of –2.0 or lower means the bones are too weak.

Doctors treat the cause of the problem when possible. Changes in lifestyle and medicine can also help.

---

## High Bone Density in Children (Osteopetroses)

High bone density problems are called osteopetroses. These are rare and inherited. They happen because of gene changes passed from parents to children.

Bones are made of cells that grow, live, and then get removed. This is a natural recycling process. In osteopetrosis, the body does not remove old bone cells. This causes bones to become too thick and dense.

Even though the bones are dense, they are actually weak and brittle. The shape of the bones can also change. The dense bone takes up space inside the bone. This leaves less room for bone marrow, where blood cells are made.

When bone marrow is crowded, the body may not make enough blood cells. This can lead to anemia (low red blood cells) and low platelets (which help stop bleeding). The spleen may also become overactive and destroy too many red blood cells.

Osteopetroses can be mild or very serious. Some children have symptoms at birth (early onset). Others develop symptoms later in life (delayed onset).

Most types of osteopetroses cause similar problems:
- Bones grow poorly
- Bones become thick but break easily
- Blood cell production drops, leading to infection or bleeding
- Bleeding can happen after small injuries, like nosebleeds from picking the nose or bleeding gums from brushing teeth

Extra bone in the skull can cause pressure inside the head. This can press on nerves and cause:
- Facial weakness or paralysis
- Loss of vision or hearing
- Changes in face shape and teeth

Bones in the fingers, feet, arms, legs, spine, and pelvis can also be affected.

### How Doctors Diagnose Osteopetroses

Doctors use:
- X-rays
- Blood tests
- Genetic tests

X-rays show bones that are very dense or oddly shaped. Sometimes, doctors find dense bones by accident when doing x-rays for another reason.

Blood tests can show:
- Low red blood cells (anemia)
- Low platelets (thrombocytopenia)

Genetic tests help confirm the diagnosis by finding the gene changes that cause the problem.

### How Doctors Treat Osteopetroses

Treatments include:
- Steroids (like prednisone)
- Stem cell transplantation
- Surgery
- Blood transfusions
- Antibiotics
- Orthodontic care

Steroids help reduce the formation of new bone cells. They may also help remove old bone cells. This can make bones stronger. Steroids can also ease bone pain and improve muscle strength.

Stem cell transplantation can cure some babies with early-onset osteopetrosis. But it may not fix kidney problems that are already present.

If nerves in the skull are pressed by bone, surgery may be needed to relieve the pressure. Surgery may also be used to reduce pressure inside the skull. Plastic surgery can fix serious face or jaw changes.

Teeth that are misaligned may need orthodontic treatment.

Minor bone breaks are treated with a cast or a traction device. Major breaks (where bones are separated or not moving) may need surgery.

Anemia and low platelets are treated with blood transfusions.

In rare cases, if the spleen is overactive, removing it can help with both anemia and bleeding.

Infections are treated with antibiotics.

Without treatment, early-onset osteopetrosis is often fatal in infancy or early childhood. Death usually comes from anemia, infection, or severe bleeding.

Late-onset osteopetrosis is usually mild and does not cause serious problems.

# Rhabdomyolysis – Simple Explanation

Rhabdomyolysis is a serious condition where muscle tissue breaks down. This can harm your kidneys and other organs.

## What Happens in Rhabdomyolysis?

Your muscles need certain chemicals and energy to work properly. When muscles are damaged, they break down. This releases muscle contents into the blood. These include a protein called creatine kinase and another protein called myoglobin.

Myoglobin can damage the kidneys. If too much gets into the urine, it can turn the urine red or brown.

## What Causes Rhabdomyolysis?

Many things can cause muscle damage. Common causes include:

- Crush injuries or pressure on muscles (like in car accidents)
- Electric shocks
- Seizures
- Tight muscles in a small space (compartment syndrome)
- Certain medicines, like statins
- Illegal drugs, such as cocaine or amphetamines
- Alcohol use
- Infections like the flu, coxsackievirus, or staph infections

Less common causes include:

- Low levels of potassium or phosphate in the blood
- Uncontrolled diabetes
- Genetic muscle diseases like Duchenne or Becker muscular dystrophy
- Extreme exercise or staying still for a long time
- Very low or very high body temperature (like in heatstroke or severe cold)

## What Are the Symptoms?

The classic signs are:

- Muscle pain
- Muscle weakness
- Urine that looks red or brown

But only less than 1 in 10 people with rhabdomyolysis have all three of these symptoms.

Many people have no muscle pain at all. When pain does occur, it usually affects the shoulders, thighs, lower back, or calves.

Red or brown urine means myoglobin is in the urine. A simple urine test can show this. But even if the urine looks normal, rhabdomyolysis can still be present. Myoglobin leaves the body quickly, so it may not show up in the urine.

Other symptoms depend on the cause. For example:

- Fever may happen if you have an infection.
- Confusion or changes in alertness may happen with drug use.

About 15% to 50% of people with rhabdomyolysis develop kidney problems. This risk is higher if you are dehydrated, have an infection, or have very high levels of creatine kinase in the blood.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect rhabdomyolysis based on your symptoms and history. They confirm it with blood and urine tests.

The main test is for creatine kinase (CK). A level more than 5 times the normal high limit usually means rhabdomyolysis.

Other tests may include:

- Urine test for myoglobin (especially if no red blood cells are seen)
- Blood tests for kidney function, potassium, calcium, phosphate, and other chemicals
- Tests for acid levels in the blood (lactic acidosis)
- Platelet count (low platelets can be a sign of serious problems)

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment has three parts:

1. Supportive care
2. Treat the cause
3. Treat any complications

### Supportive Care

- You will get fluids through a vein (IV) to help protect your kidneys.
- If you have trouble breathing, you may need a breathing machine.
- There is no strong proof that adding baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) to the fluids helps. In fact, it can be dangerous if you already have low calcium or high blood pH.

### Treat the Cause

- If pressure is building in a muscle area (compartment syndrome), surgery may be needed to relieve it.
- Infections are treated with antibiotics or other medicines.
- Any medicine that may have caused the problem (like statins) is stopped.
- Imbalances in blood chemicals (like potassium or calcium) are corrected.

### Treat Complications

- Kidney damage may need more IV fluids. In severe cases, dialysis is used.
- A serious blood clotting problem (disseminated intravascular coagulation) is treated with fresh frozen plasma.

## Key Points

- The classic symptoms (muscle pain, weakness, red or brown urine) happen in fewer than 10% of cases.
- A blood test showing creatine kinase more than 5 times the normal high level is usually needed to confirm the diagnosis.
- Treatment focuses on IV fluids, fixing the cause, and managing any complications.

# What You Need to Know About Cholesterol and Fats in the Blood

Your body needs fats to grow and to have energy. Fats also help make hormones and other important substances. If you have too much fat, it can build up in your blood vessels and inside your organs. This can block blood flow and harm your organs. It can lead to serious health problems.

## Types of Fats in the Blood

Two main types of fats are found in the blood:

- Cholesterol  
- Triglycerides

### Cholesterol

Cholesterol is a key part of your body’s cells. It is especially important for your brain and nerves. It helps make bile, which your body uses to digest fats and fat-soluble vitamins. Your body uses cholesterol to make vitamin D and hormones like estrogen, testosterone, and cortisol.

Your body can make all the cholesterol it needs. But you also get cholesterol from the food you eat.

### Triglycerides

Triglycerides are stored in fat cells. When your body needs energy, it breaks down triglycerides to use. Your intestine and liver make triglycerides from smaller fats called fatty acids. Some fatty acids your body makes. Others you must get from food.

## How Fats Move in the Blood

Fats like cholesterol and triglycerides do not mix with blood. Blood is mostly water. So fats must be wrapped in proteins and other substances to travel through the blood. These packages are called lipoproteins.

There are four main types of lipoproteins:

- Chylomicrons  
- High-density lipoproteins (HDL)  
- Low-density lipoproteins (LDL)  
- Very low density lipoproteins (VLDL)

Each type has a different job.

### What Each Lipoprotein Does

| Type | Where It Comes From | What It Does |
|------|---------------------|--------------|
| Chylomicrons | Made in the intestine from fats in food | Carry digested fats (triglycerides) to muscle and fat cells |
| High-density lipoprotein (HDL) | Made in the liver and small intestine | Takes cholesterol out of body tissues. Brings it to the liver to be removed or to cells that need it |
| Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) | Made from VLDL after it gives triglycerides to fat cells | Carries cholesterol to cells that need it |
| Very low density lipoprotein (VLDL) | Made in the liver | Carries triglycerides from the liver to fat cells |

Cholesterol carried by LDL is called LDL cholesterol.  
Cholesterol carried by HDL is called HDL cholesterol.

Your body controls how much of each lipoprotein it makes. It also controls how fast lipoproteins enter and leave the blood.

## How Lipid Levels Change

Cholesterol and triglyceride levels can change from day to day. This happens because of stress, what you eat, how active you are, your lifestyle, and changes in your body’s metabolism.

- Cholesterol levels can change by about 10% between tests.  
- Triglyceride levels can change by up to 25%.

Lipid levels can be:

- Too high (called dyslipidemia or hyperlipidemia)  
- Too low (called hypolipidemia)

These changes can happen because of aging, certain health problems (including inherited ones), some medicines, or lifestyle choices. For example, eating too much saturated fat, not being active, or being overweight can raise your lipid levels.

## Health Risks of High Lipid Levels

High levels of certain fats, especially cholesterol, can cause long-term damage.

### Atherosclerosis

High cholesterol, especially high LDL ("bad") cholesterol, can lead to a condition called atherosclerosis. This is when fatty material builds up in the walls of your blood vessels. This makes the vessels narrow and stiff. It increases your risk of heart attack or stroke.

But not all cholesterol is bad. High HDL ("good") cholesterol can help protect your heart. Low HDL cholesterol increases your risk.

### Triglycerides and Health Risks

The link between triglycerides and heart attack risk is not as clear. But very high triglyceride levels (over 500 milligrams per deciliter of blood) can cause pancreatitis. This is a painful and serious inflammation of the pancreas.

## How Doctors Check Your Lipid Levels

Doctors use a test called a lipid profile (or lipid panel). It measures:

- Total cholesterol  
- Triglycerides  
- LDL cholesterol  
- HDL cholesterol

You used to need to fast (not eat or drink anything except water) for 12 hours before this test. Now, in most cases, you do not need to fast.

### When to Get Tested

- Adults: Doctors usually check lipid levels every 5 years starting at age 20. This helps check your risk for coronary artery disease.
- Children and teens:  
  - If a child has risk factors (like a close family member with high cholesterol or heart disease at a young age), they should be tested between ages 2 and 8.  
  - If a child has no risk factors, they should be tested once before puberty (usually between ages 9 and 11) and again between ages 17 and 21.  
  - Testing is done using a nonfasting blood sample.

# Takayasu Arteritis – Simple Explanation

Takayasu arteritis is a rare condition that causes inflammation in the large blood vessels. It mainly affects the aorta and its branches, and sometimes the arteries in the lungs. It is most common in young women, usually between the ages of 15 and 30. The exact cause is not known. But it may involve the body’s immune system attacking the blood vessels.

This inflammation can lead to narrowed, blocked, widened, or bulging blood vessels. These changes can reduce blood flow to organs and limbs.

## Who Gets It?

- It is rare worldwide.
- It is more common in Asia, but it happens in all parts of the world.
- Women are much more likely to get it than men — about 8 women for every 1 man.
- The average age when it starts is between 15 and 30 years.

## What Happens in the Body?

The disease mainly affects large, elastic arteries. The most commonly affected are:

- The main artery from the heart (aorta)
- The arteries going to the arms (subclavian and innominate arteries)
- The carotid arteries (in the neck)
- The arteries going to the kidneys
- The pulmonary arteries (in the lungs)

Most people have narrowed or blocked arteries. About one in three people develop an aneurysm (a bulge in a blood vessel wall). The walls of the affected arteries become thick and uneven. This can block blood flow.

When the aorta is involved, the openings where major arteries branch off can become very narrow or even close completely. In about half of patients, the pulmonary arteries are also affected. Sometimes the medium-sized branches of the lung arteries are involved.

In the early stages, the outer layer of the artery wall fills with immune cells. Later, the middle layer becomes inflamed. This can cause damage, including dead tissue and giant cells. These changes look similar to those seen in another condition called giant cell arteritis.

The inflammation causes the artery walls to thicken. This leads to a smaller space inside the vessel. This can block blood flow completely.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many people first notice symptoms in one part of the body due to poor blood flow.

About half of patients have general symptoms like:

- Fever
- Feeling tired
- Night sweats
- Weight loss
- Joint pain

Using the arms a lot or holding them up for long periods can cause pain and tiredness.

Pulses in the arms or legs may be weak or missing. One arm or leg may feel cooler than the other. People may feel pain in the legs when walking — this is called claudication.

A whooshing sound (called a bruit) can often be heard with a stethoscope over:

- The arteries in the neck
- The upper arms
- The chest or belly
- The legs

Blood pressure may be lower in one or both arms. This is common.

If the arteries in the neck are affected, blood flow to the brain drops. This can cause:

- Dizziness
- Fainting
- Headaches
- Blurred or lost vision for a short time
- Mini-strokes
- Full strokes

A condition called subclavian steal syndrome can happen when a narrowed artery in the arm causes blood to flow backward in the neck artery. This can cause dizziness or fainting when lifting the arm.

Narrowing of the coronary arteries (those that supply the heart) can cause chest pain or a heart attack. If the aorta becomes very wide, it can cause blood to leak backward through the aortic valve. This is called aortic regurgitation. Over time, this can lead to heart failure.

Blockage in the lower part of the aorta can cause symptoms like high blood pressure, headaches, and leg pain when walking. This is similar to a condition called aortic coarctation.

If the arteries to the kidneys are narrowed, blood pressure can rise. This is called renovascular hypertension.

Pulmonary arteries can become narrowed or blocked. This can lead to high blood pressure in the lungs. It can also cause lung clots or tissue death (infarcts).

Because the disease is long-term, the body can create new blood vessels to bypass blocked ones. This means serious problems like sores or gangrene in the limbs are rare.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect Takayasu arteritis when:

- A young woman has symptoms of poor blood flow to an organ or limb.
- The pulses in the arms or legs are weak or missing.
- There are no signs of atherosclerosis (hardening of the arteries), which is common in older people.

Tests used to confirm the diagnosis include:

- Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA)
- CT angiography (CTA)
- Conventional angiography (aortic arteriography)

These tests show the blood vessels clearly. They can find:

- Narrowed or blocked arteries
- Irregular shapes in the blood vessel walls
- Bulging areas (aneurysms)
- Widened areas after a blockage
- New blood vessels forming around blocked areas

Blood pressure is checked in all arms and legs. But measuring it accurately can be hard. If both arteries to the arms are badly affected, blood pressure may only be measured correctly in the legs.

If both arm arteries and the lower aorta are blocked, blood pressure cannot be measured in any limb. In this case, doctors must measure pressure inside the main artery using a special catheter.

Other signs of hidden high blood pressure include:

- Changes in the back of the eye (hypertensive retinopathy)
- Thickened heart muscle (seen on an echocardiogram)

If high blood pressure is not found, it can be mistaken for symptoms of the disease itself.

Blood tests are not specific. They may show:

- Low red blood cell count (anemia of chronic disease)
- High platelet count
- Sometimes high white blood cell count
- High levels of inflammation markers (like ESR and CRP)

These tests do not confirm the disease, but they can help track how active it is.

### Signs of Active Disease

Doctors look for:

- New symptoms like fever, fatigue, weight loss, or loss of appetite
- New pain in the arms or legs when walking
- New whooshing sounds (bruits)
- New changes in blood pressure

### Imaging to Track the Disease

Even if symptoms go away and blood tests look normal, the disease can still be active. New damage can happen silently.

So, regular imaging of the aorta and large arteries is needed. MRA is usually the best test for young women because it does not use radiation or contrast dye.

### Tests Used to Diagnose and Monitor

| Test | When It’s Used | Notes |
|------|----------------|-------|
| Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) | First choice for most patients | No radiation. Good for young women. Shows vessel wall changes. Cannot see small branches well. |
| CT angiography (CTA) | When MRA is not possible | Can show calcium in arteries. May show wall thickness. Not clear if it helps track disease activity. |
| Conventional angiography | When surgery is planned | Gives detailed view of blood vessel shape. Involves a catheter and contrast dye. |
| PET scan with FDG | To find active inflammation | Shows areas with high cell activity. Does not show changes in blood vessel size. |

### Other Conditions That Can Look Like Takayasu Arteritis

Doctors must rule out other diseases that affect large blood vessels, such as:

- Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
- Marfan syndrome
- Infections in blood vessels (tuberculosis, fungus, syphilis)
- Fibromuscular dysplasia
- Blood clotting disorders
- Other inflammatory diseases (like ankylosing spondylitis, rheumatoid arthritis, Behçet syndrome, Kawasaki disease, sarcoidosis)

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment aims to reduce inflammation and prevent damage.

- **Corticosteroids** (like prednisone) are used first to calm the immune system.
- **Other immunosuppressants** (like azathioprine, methotrexate, or mycophenolate) may be added to help control the disease.
- **Aspirin** is often given to prevent blood clots.
- **Antihypertensive medicines** are used if blood pressure is high.
- **Surgery or procedures** may be needed if blood flow is severely blocked. These include bypass surgery or stent placement.

## What Is the Outlook?

- About 20% of people have one episode and then get better.
- The rest have recurring flare-ups or a slowly worsening disease.
- Even if symptoms and blood tests look normal, new damage can still happen in the blood vessels.
- A poor outcome is more likely if the disease keeps getting worse or if complications develop, such as:
  - High blood pressure
  - Aortic valve leak
  - Heart failure
  - Aneurysms

## Key Points

- Takayasu arteritis is rare and mostly affects young women.
- It causes inflammation in large blood vessels, especially the aorta and its branches.
- It can cause weak or missing pulses, unequal blood pressure, leg or arm pain when walking, dizziness, vision problems, strokes, and high blood pressure.
- Diagnosis is made with imaging tests like MRA or CTA.
- Treatment includes corticosteroids, other immune drugs, aspirin, and blood pressure medicines.
- Surgery may be needed if blood flow is blocked.
- Regular imaging and blood pressure checks are essential, even when symptoms improve.

# Anorexia Nervosa – Simple Explanation

Anorexia nervosa is a serious eating disorder. It causes people to eat very little food. They often feel they are too fat, even when they are very thin. They fear gaining weight and may keep losing weight even when it is dangerous.

## Who Gets Anorexia Nervosa?

- It usually starts during the teenage years or young adulthood.
- It is much more common in girls and women.
- It is rare in boys and men.
- It is very rare before puberty or after age forty.
- Up to 1.5 out of every 100 women will develop it in their lifetime.
- In places where food is hard to get, anorexia is rare.

## Two Types of Anorexia Nervosa

There are two main types:

**Restricting type:**  
- People eat very little food.  
- They do not eat large amounts of food at once (binge eat).  
- They do not make themselves vomit or use laxatives.  
- Some people exercise too much.

**Binge eating/purging type:**  
- People eat very little food.  
- They also eat large amounts of food at once (binge eat).  
- They may make themselves vomit or use laxatives.  
- Some use water pills (diuretics) to lose weight.

> **Did you know?**  
> Almost half of people with anorexia nervosa binge eat or purge.

## What Causes Anorexia Nervosa?

We do not fully know what causes it. But some things may increase the risk:

- Being a girl or woman.
- Growing up in a middle or upper class family.
- Being very careful, organized, or perfectionistic.
- Having high goals for success.
- Living in a culture that values being thin.
- Taking part in sports or activities that focus on body shape or weight (like gymnastics or ballet).
- Having a family history of eating disorders.

## Signs and Symptoms

Anorexia can be mild or very serious. It often starts with a strong focus on diet and weight, even if a person is not overweight.

People with anorexia nervosa may:

- Think about food all the time.
- Count calories or study diets.
- Hide, throw away, or hoard food.
- Collect recipes or cook meals for others.
- Skip meals or pretend to eat.
- Exercise too much.
- Wear many layers of clothes to hide their body.
- Weigh themselves many times a day.
- Feel bad about themselves if they gain even a small amount of weight.
- Say they are fat even when they are very thin.
- Deny that they have a problem.

They may also have physical signs:

- Low heart rate.
- Low blood pressure.
- Low body temperature.
- Hair growing on the body (fine and soft).
- Extra hair on the face or body.
- Muscle loss.
- Swelling in the hands, feet, or belly (called edema).
- Bloating, stomach pain, or constipation.
- Missed or irregular periods (in women).
- Weak bones (due to low bone density).

Vomiting or using laxatives can cause:

- Tooth damage.
- Swollen glands in the cheeks.
- Inflammation in the throat.

Many people with anorexia also feel sad or anxious.

## When to Be Concerned

Rapid or extreme weight loss can be life-threatening. The most dangerous problems are:

- Heart problems (like slow or irregular heartbeat).
- Dehydration.
- Low blood pressure.
- Low levels of potassium and sodium in the blood.
- Weak heart that does not pump well.
- Sudden death, often from heart rhythm problems.

Using laxatives, diuretics, or vomiting makes these risks worse.

## How Doctors Diagnose Anorexia Nervosa

Doctors look for signs and symptoms. They may:

- Ask about eating habits and feelings about weight.
- Measure height and weight.
- Calculate body mass index (BMI).
- Use special questionnaires to check for eating disorders.
- Do a physical exam.
- Run blood and urine tests.
- Check bone strength with a bone density test.
- Monitor heart rhythm with an ECG or longer heart test.

Doctors also rule out other causes of weight loss, such as:

- Depression.
- Schizophrenia.
- Problems with digestion (malabsorption).
- Drug use (like amphetamines).
- Cancer.

A diagnosis is more likely if:

- A person eats very little and has a low body weight (BMI under 17, or below the fifth percentile for age in children).
- They fear gaining weight.
- They have a distorted view of their body.
- They deny they are sick.

Even if a child has not lost weight, doctors may still diagnose anorexia if they are not growing as expected.

> **Did you know?**  
> Without treatment, nearly 5 out of every 100 people with severe anorexia die each year.

## How Anorexia Nervosa Is Treated

Treatment focuses on:

- Getting enough food and nutrients.
- Returning to a healthy weight.
- Changing unhealthy eating habits.
- Improving mental health.

### Getting Enough Food

- People may need to be hospitalized if they are very underweight or losing weight fast.
- Eating solid food is best.
- Sometimes, liquid nutrition supplements are used.
- In rare cases, a tube is placed through the nose and into the stomach to give food (nasogastric tube).

### Therapy

- Psychotherapy helps people learn healthy eating habits and return to a normal weight.
- Individual therapy helps people understand their thoughts and feelings.
- Family therapy is especially helpful for teens. It helps parents support their child and improve family relationships.
- Therapy usually lasts at least one year after weight is restored.
- It works best when started early (within 6 months of symptoms).

### Other Treatments

- Doctors treat health problems caused by anorexia. For example:
  - Calcium and vitamin D supplements for weak bones.
  - Medicines for depression or anxiety if needed.
- There are no medicines that directly treat anorexia.
- Some medicines used for other mental health conditions (like olanzapine) may help with weight gain.

### Regular Check-Ups

- People need to see a doctor often.
- A team of health experts may help, including:
  - A doctor.
  - A nutritionist (who helps plan meals and track calories).
  - A therapist.

## Outlook (Prognosis)

With treatment, many people improve. But outcomes vary:

- About half of people regain most or all of their lost weight. Their body and hormone problems often get better.
- About one in four improve some, gain some weight, but may go back to old habits later (relapse).
- About one in four have repeated relapses and continue to struggle with health and mental health issues.

Children and teens treated for anorexia do not have a better or worse chance of relapse than adults.

## Where to Get Help

The following organizations offer support and information in English:

- **National Eating Disorders Association (NEDA)**
- **National Association of Anorexia Nervosa and Associated Disorders (ANAD)**
- **National Institutes of Mental Health (NIMH), Eating Disorders**

# Nutrition in Everyday Health

Poor nutrition can make illness worse. Some health problems can also cause poor nutrition. Many people, especially older adults in the hospital, have hidden nutrition problems that need treatment. Hospitals often have teams of doctors, nurses, dietitians, and pharmacists to help find and fix these issues.

Eating too much can lead to long-term health problems. These include cancer, high blood pressure, being overweight, diabetes, and heart disease. Some rare inherited conditions need special diets. For example, people with galactosemia or phenylketonuria must avoid certain foods.

## How Doctors Check Nutrition

You should get a nutrition check if you have any of these:

- Unexplained weight loss or gain
- Signs of missing key nutrients
- Babies or children who are not growing or developing well

Doctors should check nutrition as part of a regular exam for:

- Babies and children
- Older adults
- People taking many medicines
- People with mental health conditions
- People with long-term health problems

To check your nutrition, your doctor will:

- Ask about your diet and recent weight changes
- Do a physical exam
- Sometimes order blood or other tests

If your doctor suspects you are not getting enough nutrition, they may check your blood levels. They may also do a skin test to see how well your immune system is working. Tests like skinfold measurements or bioelectrical impedance can help estimate how much body fat you have. These tests help find obesity.

### Talking About Your Diet

Your doctor will ask about:

- What you eat each day
- Whether you have lost or gained weight
- Risk factors for poor nutrition

A dietitian can help with a more detailed food history. This may include:

- A list of everything you ate in the past 24 hours
- A food questionnaire
- A food diary where you write down every meal and snack

The most accurate way to track your food is the weighed ad libitum diet. You weigh and write down every food you eat.

# Sickle Cell Disease – Simple Explanation

Sickle cell disease is a condition you are born with. It affects the red blood cells in your body. These cells carry oxygen to all parts of your body.

## What Happens in Sickle Cell Disease?

- Red blood cells are normally round and flexible.
- In sickle cell disease, some red blood cells become stiff and shaped like a sickle (a curved blade).
- These sickle-shaped cells do not carry oxygen well.
- They break apart easily and do not last as long as normal cells.
- This leads to a low number of healthy red blood cells, which causes anemia.

### Why This Matters

- The sickle-shaped cells can get stuck in small blood vessels.
- This blocks blood flow and stops oxygen from reaching parts of the body.
- Blocked blood flow can cause pain and damage to organs over time.
- Organs that can be affected include the spleen, kidneys, brain, bones, and heart.

## Common Symptoms

- **Anemia** – You may feel tired, weak, or pale.
- **Jaundice** – Your skin or the whites of your eyes may look yellow.
- **Pain** – This can happen in your bones, chest, or belly. It is called a sickle cell crisis.
- **Shortness of breath** – This can happen if your body does not get enough oxygen.
- **Fever** – This may mean you have an infection.
- **Swelling in the spleen or liver** – This can cause pain in the upper belly.

### Other Possible Problems

- **Acute chest syndrome** – A serious condition with chest pain and trouble breathing. It can be life-threatening.
- **Spleen problems** – The spleen may get too big or stop working properly.
- **Kidney problems** – You may have trouble passing urine or develop kidney stones.
- **Heart problems** – The heart may get bigger and not pump well.
- **Bone pain** – Especially in the hands, feet, and joints.
- **Leg sores** – These often appear near the ankles.
- **Priapism** – A painful, long-lasting erection in males. It can cause permanent damage.
- **Strokes** – Blocked blood flow to the brain can cause brain damage.

## Who Gets Sickle Cell Disease?

- It mostly affects people with African or Black American ancestry.
- About 8 out of 100 people with this background have one copy of the sickle cell gene. This is called **sickle cell trait**.
- People with sickle cell trait do not have the disease.
- They do not get pain crises.
- But they may have a higher risk of kidney problems or blood in their urine.
- About 3 out of 1,000 people with this background have two copies of the gene. These people have sickle cell disease.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- A blood test can show if you have sickle cell disease.
- A test called **hemoglobin electrophoresis** checks the type of hemoglobin in your blood.
- Newborns in the United States are tested at birth.
- Pregnant women can be tested to see if they carry the gene.
- If a baby is at risk, tests can be done during pregnancy using fluid from the amniotic sac or tissue from the placenta.

## How Is It Treated?

### Preventing Crises

- Avoid things that lower oxygen in your blood, like high altitudes or smoking.
- Stay warm. Cold can trigger a crisis.
- Get medical help fast for any illness, even a small cold.
- Get all recommended vaccines:
  - Pneumococcal
  - Meningococcal
  - Influenza
  - Haemophilus influenzae type b
  - COVID-19

### Medications

- **Hydroxyurea** – Helps make more healthy hemoglobin. This reduces pain crises and lung problems.
- **L-glutamine** – Helps protect red blood cells.
- **Crizanlizumab** – Reduces pain crises by keeping blood cells from sticking together.
- **Voxelotor** – Helps hemoglobin carry oxygen better and reduces anemia.

### Other Treatments

- **Folic acid** – A vitamin that helps your body make new red blood cells.
- **Blood transfusions** – Can help treat severe anemia or prevent strokes.
- **Stem cell transplant** – Can cure the disease in some people. It uses healthy stem cells from a donor.
- **Gene therapy** – A new treatment that fixes the faulty gene. It is now available in some cases.

### During a Crisis

- You may need to go to the hospital.
- You will get oxygen and fluids through a vein.
- Pain medicine will be given.
- Any cause of the crisis, like an infection, will be treated.

## What You Can Do

- Stay healthy and avoid infections.
- Drink plenty of water.
- Avoid extreme heat or cold.
- Exercise carefully and stop if you feel pain.
- See your doctor regularly.

## Sickle Cell Trait – Important Facts

- You do not have sickle cell disease.
- You do not get pain crises.
- You can pass the gene to your children.
- You may have a higher risk of:
  - Kidney problems
  - Blood clots in the lungs (pulmonary embolism)
  - Rare kidney cancer
- In very rare cases, sudden death can happen during extreme exercise or severe dehydration.

## Support and Resources

- **Sickle Cell Disease Association of America**  
  Offers education, support, and peer mentoring for people with sickle cell disease and their families.

# Botulism – Simple Explanation

Botulism is a serious illness caused by a poison made by a type of bacteria called *Clostridium botulinum*. This poison affects the nerves that control muscles. It can happen without a full infection if you swallow, inject, or breathe in the poison.

## What Causes Botulism?

The bacteria *Clostridium botulinum* makes a powerful poison called botulinum toxin. This toxin blocks signals from nerves to muscles. This causes muscle weakness and paralysis.

The bacteria can be found in soil, dust, and some foods. The poison is very strong. Even a tiny amount can make you very sick.

There are several types of the toxin. The most dangerous ones for people are types A, B, E, and rarely F and a mix of F and A.

- Type A is most common in the western United States.
- Type B is more common in the eastern United States.
- Type E is often linked to eating fish, especially in Alaska and around the Great Lakes.

The bacteria can make the toxin in two ways:
1. Inside your body (if you swallow the bacteria’s spores).
2. In food before you eat it (if the food already has the poison).

## Types of Botulism

### When the Poison Forms Inside Your Body

- **Wound botulism**: Happens when the bacteria grow in a wound and make the poison there.
- **Infant botulism**: The most common type. Babies get it by swallowing the bacteria’s spores. The spores grow in the baby’s gut and make the poison. This usually affects babies under one year old.
- **Adult enteric botulism**: Rare. Happens in adults who have had bowel surgery, have gut problems, or take certain medicines.

### When You Get the Poison from Outside

- **Food-borne botulism**: Happens when you eat food that already has the poison. This often comes from home-canned foods.
- **Iatrogenic botulism**: Happens when doctors give the toxin on purpose (like for muscle problems or cosmetic use). Very rarely, this can cause illness.
- **Inhalation botulism**: Happens when you breathe in the poison. This can happen by accident or on purpose, like in a bioweapon attack. The poison does not happen naturally in the air.

## How to Prevent Botulism

- **Do not eat food from swollen, leaking, or damaged cans.**
- **Do not eat home-canned food unless you know it was canned safely.**
- **Refrigeration does not stop the toxin.** The bacteria can make the poison even in the fridge (as low as 3 degrees Celsius).
- **Boiling food for 10 minutes kills the toxin.** But boiling does not kill the bacteria’s spores.
- **To kill the spores, food must be heated to 120 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes under pressure.**

## Symptoms of Botulism

Symptoms start slowly and get worse over time. They are the same in both eyes and both sides of the body.

Common early signs:
- Dry mouth
- Blurred or double vision
- Drooping eyelids
- Slurred speech
- Trouble swallowing

Later signs:
- Weakness that starts in the face and moves down the body
- Weakness in arms, legs, and chest muscles
- Trouble breathing
- No feeling changes (you still feel touch, pain, and temperature)
- No fever
- Slow or normal pulse
- Constipation

The most serious risk is **not being able to breathe**. This can happen if the muscles that help you breathe get weak.

## Complications

- **Breathing failure** – the main danger.
- **Pneumonia** – can happen if food or liquid gets into the lungs.
- Other infections from being in the hospital.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your symptoms and ask what you ate or where you were exposed.

Tests may include:
- Blood or stool tests to find the toxin.
- A special test called electromyography to check nerve and muscle function.

The test for the toxin is only done at special labs. Your local health department or the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) can help find one.

Botulism can look like other serious conditions, such as:
- Guillain-Barré syndrome
- Polio
- Stroke
- Myasthenia gravis
- Tick paralysis
- Poisoning from heavy metals, curare, or belladonna

## Treatment

Botulism is a medical emergency. You must go to the hospital right away.

### Key Treatments

- **Supportive care**: This means helping your body stay strong while it fights the poison.
- **Antitoxin**: A medicine that stops the poison from doing more harm. It is given through a vein.

#### Who Gets Which Antitoxin?

- **Adults and children over 1 year old**: Get a special antitoxin called heptavalent equine antitoxin (HBAT). It comes from the CDC.
- **Babies under 1 year old**: Do not get the equine antitoxin. They get a different medicine called human botulinum immune globulin.

#### Other Care

- **Breathing help**: If your breathing muscles get weak, you may need a breathing machine (mechanical ventilation).
- **Airway protection**: If you have trouble swallowing, you may need a tube in your stomach to feed you. This is safer than giving food through the mouth.
- **Wound care**: If you have wound botulism, the wound must be cleaned and treated with antibiotics like penicillin or metronidazole.

## Prevention

- Always check canned food for swelling, leaks, or bad smell. Throw it out if it looks bad.
- Use safe methods when canning food at home.
- Do not give honey to babies under one year old. It can carry the bacteria’s spores.

There is no vaccine for botulism. A vaccine used in the past is no longer made because it caused side effects and did not last long. New vaccines are being studied.

## Important Facts

- Botulism can come from food, wounds, or babies swallowing spores.
- It can also come from medicine or intentional use of the poison.
- The poison blocks nerve signals to muscles. This causes weakness that starts in the face and moves down the body.
- You still feel normal. Your mind stays clear. You do not lose feeling.
- Cooking kills the poison, but not the spores.
- Diagnosis is based on symptoms and lab tests for the toxin.
- Antitoxin must be given quickly. It comes from the CDC.
- With good care, most people survive.
