# Mallory-Weiss Syndrome

This condition happens when there is a small tear in the tissue where the tube from your throat meets your stomach.

## What Causes a Mallory-Weiss Tear?

- Forceful vomiting can cause the tear.
- Retching (dry heaving) or strong hiccups can also cause it.
- The tear can damage small blood vessels, leading to bleeding.

## What Are the Symptoms?

- You may see bright red blood when you vomit.
- Vomiting blood is called hematemesis.
- Some people feel sharp pain in the lower chest during the tear.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- Doctors suspect this condition if you vomit blood after vomiting hard.
- If the bleeding is light, doctors may wait to see if it stops on its own.
- If the bleeding is heavy or does not stop, doctors use a test called upper endoscopy.

### What Is Upper Endoscopy?

- A doctor uses a thin, flexible tube with a camera to look inside your esophagus and stomach.
- This test helps find the source of the bleeding.
- The doctor can often treat the bleeding during the same test.

## How Is It Treated?

- Most tears stop bleeding on their own.
- If bleeding continues, the doctor may use the endoscope to stop it.
- Methods include:
  - Using heat to seal the blood vessel.
  - Placing a small clip on the blood vessel to close it.
  - Injecting medicine into the blood vessel to stop the flow.

- In some cases, doctors may use a different test called angiography.
  - They inject medicine like vasopressin or epinephrine into the bleeding vessel to stop the bleeding.

- If you lose a lot of blood, you may need a blood transfusion.

- Surgery to fix the tear is very rare.

## Important Facts

- This condition was first seen in people with alcohol use problems.
- But anyone who vomits forcefully can get it.

> **Did You Know?**  
> Forceful vomiting can tear the esophagus.

# Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is a rare condition that affects the immune system.  
It causes problems with two types of immune cells: B cells and T cells.  
This weakens the body’s ability to fight infections.  

The main signs of the condition are:  
- Frequent infections  
- Skin rash (eczema)  
- Low blood platelet count (thrombocytopenia)  

This condition is passed down through families in an X-linked recessive pattern.  
This means it mostly affects boys.  
It is caused by a change in a specific gene.  
That gene makes a protein called WASP.  
This protein helps immune cells work properly.  
Without it, immune cells do not function well.  

Low platelet count happens because:  
- The body destroys platelets too quickly  
- The body does not make enough platelets  
- Platelets do not live as long as they should  

Because immune cells do not work well, people get infections from bacteria and viruses.  
Common infections include:  
- Pneumonia  
- Skin infections  
- Infections from the varicella zoster virus (chickenpox)  
- Infections from the herpes simplex virus (cold sores)  

Some people also develop cancer later in life.  
The most common types are:  
- Lymphoma (a cancer of the immune system)  
- Leukemia (a blood cancer)  

These cancers happen in about 1 out of 10 people over 10 years old with this condition.

---

## Symptoms and Signs

The first signs often involve bleeding.  
This can include:  
- Blood in the stool  
- Black, tarry stools (melena)  
- Purple spots on the skin (purpura)  
- Nosebleeds (epistaxis)  
- Blood in the urine (hematuria)  

Later, people often get repeated lung and breathing infections.  
They also develop a skin rash (eczema).  
They have a low number of platelets in the blood.

---

## How It Is Diagnosed

Doctors use several tests to diagnose Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.  

**Blood tests check for:**  
- Levels of infection-fighting proteins (immunoglobulins)  
- Number and size of platelets  
- How well white blood cells work  

**Key findings in the blood include:**  
- Low number of T cells  
- High levels of IgE and IgA  
- Low levels of IgM  
- Normal or low levels of IgG  
- Poor natural killer cell activity  
- Weak movement of white blood cells (neutrophil chemotaxis)  
- Low platelet count  

Some people do not make good antibodies to certain vaccines.  
Doctors test this by giving a pneumococcal vaccine and checking the response.  

Platelets in this condition are small and do not work well.  
The spleen destroys them faster than normal.  
This causes the low platelet count.  

Genetic testing can confirm the diagnosis if symptoms and blood tests suggest the condition.  
Family members should be tested if a child has this disease.

People with this condition need regular blood tests every 6 months.  
This helps catch cancer early.  
If symptoms suddenly get worse, more tests are needed.

---

## Treatment

There is no cure yet, but treatments can help manage symptoms.  

**Medicines to prevent infections:**  
- Antibiotics to prevent bacterial infections  
- Immune globulin (a medicine made from donated blood) to help fight infections  
- Acyclovir to prevent serious herpes virus infections  

**For bleeding due to low platelets:**  
- Platelet transfusions to stop or prevent bleeding  
- In rare cases, surgery to remove the spleen (splenectomy)  
  - This is not done often because it raises the risk of serious infections  

**Other medicines:**  
- Eltrombopag may be used in some cases  
  - It helps the body make more platelets  
  - It is used only when other treatments do not work  

**Best treatment option:**  
- Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (bone marrow transplant)  
  - This is the only treatment that can cure the condition  
  - It replaces the faulty immune system with a healthy one  

**New treatment under study:**  
- Gene therapy  
  - A small study showed good results in 8 patients  
  - After treatment, infections and skin rashes improved  
  - Bleeding and autoimmune problems also got better  
  - Patients were followed for up to 7.6 years  

Without treatment, most people with this condition do not live past age 15.  
Some do survive into adulthood, especially with early treatment.

# What Are Interstitial Lung Diseases?

Interstitial lung diseases are a group of conditions that affect the lungs. They cause problems in the tissue around the air sacs, the blood vessels, and the small airways in the lungs.

These diseases lead to swelling and scarring in the lungs. This makes it hard to breathe and causes a dry cough.

The lungs become stiff and shrink. This makes it harder to get oxygen into the blood. But the lungs usually still work well to remove carbon dioxide.

The changes in the lungs often look similar on imaging tests. But the diseases are not the same. They have different causes and treatments.

---

## How These Diseases Develop

In the early stages, white blood cells and fluid build up in the lung tissue. This causes inflammation.

If the inflammation lasts, it can lead to scarring. This scarring is called fibrosis.

Over time, the air sacs (alveoli) are destroyed. The lungs are left with thick-walled holes. These holes look like a beehive. This pattern is called honeycombing.

The result is a condition called pulmonary fibrosis.

---

## Unusual Interstitial Lung Diseases

These are rare forms of lung disease. They have unique causes and symptoms.

### Drug-Induced Interstitial Lung Disease

- Symptoms may come on slowly over weeks or months.
- Or they may start suddenly and be very severe.
- Common symptoms: shortness of breath and cough.

**Treatment:**
- Stop the medicine causing the problem.
- Steroids may help in some cases.

**Notes:**
- Many types of medicines can cause this.
- Older adults are more likely to have serious problems.
- Some medicines cause lung damage similar to lupus.
- The risk depends on the dose and how long the medicine was taken.

---

### Alveolar Hemorrhage Syndromes (Bleeding in the Lungs)

- Most common symptom: coughing up blood.
- Other signs: low red blood cell count (anemia) and kidney problems.

**Treatment:**
- Steroids and other immune-suppressing medicines (like cyclophosphamide).
- Blood transfusions if needed.
- Oxygen therapy if blood oxygen is low.

**Notes:**
- Blood leaks from tiny blood vessels in the lungs.
- This can happen due to an autoimmune reaction.
- Conditions linked to this include:
  - Goodpasture syndrome
  - Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
  - Lupus
  - Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis (iron buildup in lungs)
  - Drug reactions
- Severe bleeding can be life-threatening.

---

### Lymphangioleiomyomatosis

- Symptoms: trouble breathing, cough, chest pain, and sometimes coughing up blood.

**Treatment:**
- Lung transplant (in severe cases).
- Sirolimus medicine.

**Notes:**
- This rare disease affects young women.
- It can get worse during pregnancy.

---

### Important Note About Steroids

Steroids are also called corticosteroids or glucocorticoids.

---

## Causes of Interstitial Lung Diseases

These diseases can be caused by many different things.

| Cause | Examples |
|-------|----------|
| Autoimmune diseases | Myositis, Goodpasture syndrome, mixed connective tissue disease, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis, Sjögren syndrome, lupus |
| Breathing in dust | Bird droppings, molds |
| Medicines | Amiodarone, bleomycin, busulfan, carbamazepine, checkpoint inhibitors, chlorambucil, cocaine, cyclophosphamide, gold, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, sulfasalazine, sulfonamides |
| Chemicals | Aluminum powder, asbestos, beryllium, metals, sulfur dioxide, talc |
| Genetic conditions | Fabry disease, familial pulmonary fibrosis, Gaucher disease, Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome, neurofibromatosis, Niemann-Pick disease, pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, tuberous sclerosis |
| Unknown cause (idiopathic) | Acute interstitial pneumonia, cryptogenic organizing pneumonia, desquamative interstitial pneumonia, idiopathic pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, lymphoid interstitial pneumonia, nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, respiratory bronchiolitis-associated interstitial lung disease |
| Radiation therapy | For cancer treatment |
| Other conditions | Amyloidosis, chronic aspiration, eosinophilic pneumonia, lymphangioleiomyomatosis, pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis, sarcoidosis, vasculitis (inflammation of blood vessels) such as eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis and granulomatosis with polyangiitis |

> **Idiopathic** means the cause is unknown.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose These Diseases

Doctors use several tests to find out if someone has an interstitial lung disease.

### Common Tests

- **Chest x-ray** – Shows basic lung structure.
- **Chest CT scan** – More detailed than x-ray. Helps doctors see small changes in the lungs.
- **Pulmonary function tests** – Measure how well the lungs work. Often show that the lungs hold less air than normal.
- **Arterial blood gas test** – Checks oxygen and carbon dioxide levels in the blood. Also checks blood acidity.

### Confirming the Diagnosis

Sometimes, doctors need to look at lung tissue under a microscope.

- **Transbronchial lung biopsy** – A small sample is taken through a thin tube passed through the windpipe.
- **Video-assisted thoracoscopic lung biopsy** – A larger sample is taken during surgery using a camera and small tools.

### Blood Tests

- Blood tests are not used to confirm the disease.
- But they help rule out other similar conditions.

---

## How These Diseases Are Treated

Treatment depends on the type of disease.

### For Inflammation

- Doctors may prescribe steroids or other immune-suppressing medicines.
- These help reduce swelling in the lungs.

### For Scarring (Fibrosis)

- Special medicines may be used to slow down scar tissue growth.
- These help protect lung function.

### For Severe Cases

- Some people need a **lung transplant**.
- Others may need **mechanical ventilation** (a machine to help with breathing).
- This machine is connected to a monitor and helps deliver air to the lungs.

---

## Key Points

- Interstitial lung diseases affect the tissue around the air sacs in the lungs.
- They cause shortness of breath, cough, and stiff lungs.
- Scarring (fibrosis) can lead to permanent lung damage.
- Many causes exist, including medicines, dust, chemicals, and autoimmune diseases.
- Diagnosis uses imaging, lung function tests, and sometimes lung biopsies.
- Treatment depends on the cause and includes medicines, oxygen, and sometimes lung transplant.

# Cat-Scratch Disease

Cat-scratch disease is an infection caused by a type of bacteria called *Bartonella henselae*.  
It usually starts after a cat bites, scratches, or licks a person.  
Cats, especially kittens, carry this bacteria.  
The bacteria can stay in a cat’s blood for a while without making the cat sick.  
The most common way people get the disease is from contact with cats.  
But the cat flea can also spread the bacteria between cats.  
It may even spread the disease to people who have not touched a cat.

## Who Gets Cat-Scratch Disease?

Children are most likely to get this disease.  
Most people who get it say they were scratched, bitten, or licked by a cat.  
The cats are usually healthy.  
The disease is more common in warm, humid areas.  
It is also more common in wild or stray cats than in pets.

## What Are the Symptoms?

About 3 to 10 days after a scratch or bite, a small bump appears at the site.  
The bump is red, crusty, and usually not painful.  
Sometimes it turns into a small pus-filled sore.  

Within 2 weeks, the nearby lymph nodes swell.  
The nodes feel hard and tender at first.  
Later, they may feel soft and filled with fluid.  
They can drain through the skin.  

Other symptoms may include:  
- Fever  
- Feeling tired  
- Headache  
- Loss of appetite  

Most people get better on their own.  
But some people have unusual symptoms.  
These happen in about 1 in 10 cases.  
They are more common in adults.

### Unusual Symptoms

- **Eye problem with swollen neck glands**: One eye becomes red and sore. The gland in front of the ear swells. This happens in about half of the unusual cases.  
- **Nervous system problems**: These include confusion, seizures, vision loss in one eye, back pain, weakness in the legs, or problems with blood vessels in the brain.  
- **Liver and spleen problems**: The liver and spleen become inflamed and develop small lumps. This is rare.  
- **Fever with no clear cause**: Some people have a fever that lasts for weeks with no obvious reason.  
- **Heart infection**: In people with heart valve problems, the bacteria can cause a serious infection of the heart.  
- **Skin and organ problems in people with weak immune systems**: In people with weak immune systems, the bacteria can cause skin growths and fluid-filled pockets in the liver.  
- **Severe illness in people with AIDS**: People with AIDS can get very sick from this infection.

Most people recover fully.  
But serious nervous system or liver problems can be life-threatening or cause lasting damage.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose cat-scratch disease based on symptoms and tests.  
They may do blood tests to check for antibodies to the bacteria.  
They take two blood samples, 6 weeks apart, to see if the body is fighting the infection.  
They may also use a test called PCR on fluid from a swollen lymph node.  

If the diagnosis is unclear, doctors may test for other infections that cause similar symptoms.  
These include:  
- Tularemia  
- Tuberculosis  
- Brucellosis  
- Fungal infections  
- A sexually transmitted disease called lymphogranuloma venereum  

A lymph node biopsy may be done if cancer is suspected.  
It may also be done to confirm the diagnosis.  
The biopsy can show signs of infection or the bacteria itself.  
Special stains and lab tests can help find the bacteria in the tissue.  

People with weak immune systems or serious symptoms may need blood cultures.  
These tests take longer to give results.  
Lymph node fluid is rarely positive in culture.  
But the bacteria can sometimes be grown from a biopsy sample.  
Special lab dishes are needed to grow the bacteria.

## How Is It Treated?

Most people with cat-scratch disease do not need antibiotics.  
The illness usually gets better on its own.  

### For Mild Cases

- Apply warm compresses to the swollen area.  
- Take pain medicine like acetaminophen or ibuprofen.  
- If a lymph node is full of fluid, a doctor can drain it with a needle.  
- This helps relieve pain.

### For Severe Cases or People with Weak Immune Systems

Antibiotics are needed.  
They are also used if the disease spreads through the body.  
Common antibiotics include:  
- Azithromycin  
- Doxycycline  

Other options include:  
- Fluoroquinolones  
- Rifampin  
- Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole  

For serious nervous system problems, doctors may use more than one antibiotic.  
For heart infection, a strong antibiotic called gentamicin is given through a vein for 2 weeks.  

Treatment often lasts for weeks or even months.  
Lab tests showing how well the bacteria respond to antibiotics do not always match how well the person gets better.  

### Important Notes

- Antibiotics are not usually needed for healthy people with mild symptoms.  
- Azithromycin may help shorten the illness and reduce swelling in lymph nodes.  
- It may also lower the risk of the infection spreading.  
- People with weak immune systems or serious symptoms should get antibiotics.

# Mucous Membrane Pemphigoid

Mucous membrane pemphigoid is a long-term condition where the body’s immune system attacks the moist linings inside the body. This causes blisters and open sores. The most common areas affected are the mouth and eyes.

## What Are Mucous Membranes?

Mucous membranes are the wet, soft surfaces inside the body. They line the mouth, nose, throat, genitals, and the inside of the eyelids. These membranes help keep the body moist and protected.

## Who Gets This Condition?

This condition mostly affects older adults. Women are more likely to get it than men.

## What Causes Mucous Membrane Pemphigoid?

Your immune system normally fights off germs like bacteria and viruses. It makes special proteins called antibodies to do this. In autoimmune diseases, the immune system makes a mistake. It attacks the body’s own tissues instead of foreign invaders.

In mucous membrane pemphigoid, the immune system attacks the mucous membranes. The antibodies bind to these tissues and cause damage. This leads to blisters and open sores.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main symptom is painful blisters and sores in the mucous membranes. These sores can be red, swollen, and raw. They may heal with scars.

### In the Mouth

- Sores often appear on the gums and inside the cheeks.
- The roof of the mouth and the inside of the lips may also be sore.
- The sores burn or sting.
- You may not see blisters. Instead, you see raw, worn-down areas.

### In Other Areas

- Sores can form in the nose, throat, genitals, or around the anus.
- These sores heal with scars.
- Scarring in the throat can narrow the tube that carries food to the stomach. This makes swallowing hard.

### On the Skin

- Some people get blisters on the scalp, face, chest, or arms.
- The skin often scars after the blisters heal.

### In the Eyes

- Blisters do not form in the eyes.
- Both eyes become red, sore, and dry.
- The thin membrane covering the eye and lining the eyelid can shrink and scar.
- In serious cases, this can lead to vision loss or blindness.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors often suspect mucous membrane pemphigoid based on how the sores look. To confirm the diagnosis, they take a small sample of tissue from the affected area. They then examine it under a microscope.

Sometimes, special dyes are used to highlight the antibodies in the tissue. This helps confirm the diagnosis.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment aims to reduce pain, stop new sores from forming, and prevent scarring.

### First-Line Treatment

- **Corticosteroids** are used to reduce swelling and pain. They can be applied directly to the sores or injected into them.
- A combination of **doxycycline** and **nicotinamide** is taken by mouth. These medicines help control the immune system and reduce damage.

### For Severe Cases

- Doctors may prescribe stronger medicines that lower the activity of the immune system.
- These include drugs like dapsone, prednisone, rituximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, or cyclophosphamide.
- In some cases, immune globulin is given through a vein (IV) to help calm the immune system.

Treatment may need to continue for months or years. It is not always possible to cure the condition completely.

## What Is the Outlook?

- The condition usually gets worse slowly over time.
- It rarely goes away on its own.
- Even with treatment, it often does not go away completely.
- Some people with this condition have a higher chance of developing internal cancers.

## More Information

The following English language resource may be helpful. Please note that The Manual is not responsible for the content of this site.

# Pemphigoid Gestationis

Pemphigoid gestationis is a rare skin condition that happens during pregnancy or after childbirth.  
It causes intense itching and leads to small bumps, blisters, and fluid-filled sacs on the skin.  
The condition is not caused by a virus.  
It is not related to herpes, even though the rash can look similar to a herpes infection.

## What Causes Pemphigoid Gestationis?

The body’s immune system attacks the skin.  
This happens because of a specific antibody that targets a protein in the skin’s lower layer.  
This immune reaction is likely the main cause.

## How Common Is It?

It affects about 1 in every 50,000 to 60,000 pregnancies.  
It usually starts in the second or third trimester.  
But it can also begin in the first trimester or right after delivery.  
It often comes back in later pregnancies.  
Some women get it after using birth control pills.  
Flare-ups often happen within 24 to 48 hours after giving birth.  
They can also happen during periods or around ovulation.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The rash is very itchy.  
It often starts around the belly button.  
Then it spreads to other parts of the body.  
Blisters and large fluid-filled sacs are the most telling signs.  
Red, raised patches may also appear.  
The rash can affect the arms, legs, back, buttocks, palms, and soles.  
It usually does not affect the face or mouth.

The rash often gets worse during labor or right after delivery.  
Most women see improvement within a few weeks or months.

## What Happens to the Baby?

Most babies are not affected.  
Less than 5 percent of babies are born with mild skin changes.  
These skin issues go away on their own in a few weeks.  
In rare cases, the baby may have health problems.  
These risks are higher if the baby is born too early or is smaller than expected.  
The baby’s health may be affected if the placenta does not work well.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look at the rash and how it appears.  
A skin sample may be taken for testing.  
The test checks for a specific immune protein along the skin’s edge.  
This test confirms the diagnosis.

It can be confused with other itchy rashes of pregnancy.  
One common one is called polymorphic eruption of pregnancy.  
Pemphigoid gestationis usually starts near the belly button.  
Polymorphic eruption usually starts in stretch marks.

## How Is It Treated?

For mild symptoms:  
Use a steroid cream on the skin up to six times a day.  
A common cream is 0.1% triamcinolone acetonide.

For more severe symptoms:  
Take a steroid pill once a day.  
A common pill is prednisone, starting at 40 milligrams.  
This helps reduce itching and stops new rashes from forming.  
The dose is slowly lowered when symptoms improve.  
It may need to be increased again if symptoms get worse, such as during labor.

Steroid pills taken late in pregnancy and for short periods do not harm the baby.

To help with itching:  
Take a non-drowsy antihistamine by mouth.

## Monitoring the Baby

If the baby is growing normally:  
Have an ultrasound every four weeks.  
If the baby is not growing well:  
Have an ultrasound every two weeks.  
Also, do a nonstress test to check the baby’s heart rate and movements.

## Key Points

- Pemphigoid gestationis is an immune system problem.  
- It is not caused by herpes virus.  
- Most babies are healthy.  
- Look at where the rash starts.  
  - Pemphigoid gestationis often starts near the belly button.  
  - Polymorphic eruption usually starts in stretch marks.  
- Treat with steroid cream or, for severe cases, steroid pills.

# Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia

This condition happens when your body’s immune system makes mistakes. It creates antibodies that attack your own red blood cells. These antibodies treat your red blood cells like foreign invaders.

## What Causes It?

- The cause is often unknown. This is called idiopathic autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
- It can also happen with other health problems like lupus or lymphoma.
- Some medicines, such as penicillin, can trigger it.
- It can start suddenly or slowly.
- If it is caused by a virus or medicine, it may stop on its own after a while.
- In some people, the problem lasts for months or years.

There are two main types:

- **Warm antibody hemolytic anemia**: The antibodies attack red blood cells at normal body temperature.
- **Cold antibody hemolytic anemia (cold agglutinin disease)**: The antibodies become active when the body is cold.

### Paroxysmal Cold Hemoglobinuria

This is a rare form of cold antibody anemia. It happens when you are exposed to cold. Even small cold exposures—like drinking cold water or washing hands—can cause red blood cells to break down. An antibody sticks to the red blood cells in the cold. When the blood warms up, the cells break apart inside blood vessels. This often follows a viral illness. It can also happen in people with syphilis. The anemia can develop quickly or slowly, and its severity varies.

---

## Symptoms

Some people have no symptoms, especially if the red blood cell damage is mild and slow.

Others may feel tired, weak, or pale. They may also have:

- Shortness of breath
- Yellow skin or eyes (jaundice)
- Fever
- Chest pain
- Fainting
- Trouble breathing (a sign of heart problems)
- In severe cases, death

If the problem lasts for months, the spleen may grow larger. This can make you feel full in the belly or cause discomfort.

People with cold antibody anemia may have:

- Blue or gray hands and feet
- Pain in the hands and feet
- Sores (ulcers) on the skin

If the anemia is caused by another illness, the symptoms of that illness may be more noticeable. For example:

- Swollen, sore lymph nodes
- Fever

People with paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria may have:

- Severe back and leg pain
- Headache
- Vomiting
- Diarrhea
- Dark brown urine

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use blood tests to check for anemia and find the cause.

If your red blood cells are being destroyed too fast, your blood test may show:

- More young red blood cells (called reticulocytes)
- A higher level of bilirubin (a substance made when red blood cells break down)
- Lower levels of haptoglobin (a protein that binds to broken-down red blood cell material)

To confirm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, doctors test for antibodies on red blood cells or in the blood. This is called the Coombs test.

- **Direct Coombs test**: Looks for antibodies attached to red blood cells.
- **Indirect Coombs test**: Looks for antibodies in the blood plasma.

Other tests may help find the root cause of the immune system problem.

---

## How Is It Treated?

### Blood Transfusions

If your anemia is very severe, you may need a blood transfusion. This gives you new red blood cells quickly. Do not avoid a transfusion just because the blood is not a perfect match. A life-threatening anemia needs treatment right away. But transfusions do not fix the cause. They only help for a short time.

### Corticosteroids

For warm antibody anemia, doctors usually start with a steroid medicine like prednisone. You take a high dose at first. Then, over weeks or months, the dose is slowly lowered.

### Splenectomy

If steroids do not work or cause bad side effects, your doctor may suggest surgery to remove the spleen. The spleen is where antibody-covered red blood cells are destroyed. Removing it can help stop the damage.

### Other Medicines

- **Rituximab** and other immune-suppressing medicines may be used if steroids fail.
- These medicines are sometimes used with steroids from the start.

### Cold Antibody Anemia

For cold antibody anemia, the main treatment is to avoid cold. This includes:

- Wearing warm clothes
- Avoiding cold drinks and cold water
- Keeping your body warm

If the anemia is caused by another illness, like lymphoma, treating that illness may help.

In severe cases, doctors may use **plasma exchange**. This removes the harmful antibodies from your blood.

---

## Key Points

- Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is rare and can happen at any age.
- The immune system attacks your own red blood cells.
- Some people have no symptoms. Others feel tired, weak, or pale.
- Jaundice, fever, chest pain, and dark urine can happen.
- Blood tests are used to confirm the diagnosis.
- Treatment depends on the type and severity.
- Steroids are usually the first medicine.
- Surgery to remove the spleen may help in some cases.
- Avoiding cold is key for cold antibody anemia.
- In serious cases, blood transfusions or plasma exchange may be needed.

# What Is Culture?

Culture means growing germs in a lab using a special food-like substance.  
Growing more germs makes it easier to find out which germ is causing the illness.  
Culture also helps test which medicines can kill the germ.

You must talk to the lab about your patient.  
Most samples go on general growth media, like blood or chocolate agar.  
But some germs need special food or special growing conditions.  
These include special nutrients, special inhibitors, or specific temperature, oxygen, or carbon dioxide levels.  
Some germs also need longer growing times.

If you suspect a hard-to-grow germ, or if the patient is on antibiotics, tell the lab.  
Tell the lab where the sample came from.  
This helps the lab tell real germs from normal germs that live in that area.

---

## Special Growth Media for Common Germs

Some germs need special growth plates to grow.  
Here are the best choices for common germs:

| Germ | Best Growth Medium |
|------|--------------------|
| *Bacteroides* species | Kanamycin-vancomycin laked blood agar |
| *Bacteroides fragilis* | *Bacteroides* bile-esculin (with gentamicin and bile) |
| *Bordetella pertussis* | Bordet-Gengou agar with methicillin or cephalexin, or Regan-Lowe cephalexin agar, or horse blood-charcoal agar |
| *Burkholderia cepacia* | *Burkholderia cepacia* agar |
| *Campylobacter jejuni* or *C. coli* | *Campylobacter*-selective agars (like cefoperazone-vancomycin agar) |
| *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* | Tinsdale agar, cystine-tellurite blood agar, or Löffler coagulated serum medium |
| *Escherichia coli* or dangerous strains (like O157-H7) | MacConkey-sorbitol agar |
| *Francisella tularensis* | Blood-cystine agar or chocolate-cystine agar |
| *Legionella* species | Buffered charcoal yeast extract agar |
| *Leptospira* species | Fletcher or Stuart medium with rabbit serum, or *Leptospira* medium with bovine serum albumin-Tween 80 |
| *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* | Lowenstein-Jensen agar |
| *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* or *N. meningitidis* | Modified Thayer-Martin agar or New York City agar |
| *Salmonella* and *Shigella* species | Standard MacConkey or eosin-methylene blue agar.  
Alternative: Hektoen or xylose-lysine-desoxycholate agar, *Salmonella-Shigella* agar, or gram-negative or selenite enrichment broth |
| *Vibrio* species | Thiosulfate-citrate-bile salts-sucrose agar |
| *Yersinia* species | Cefsulodin-Irgasan-novobiocin agar |

---

## How to Collect a Sample

Collecting the sample correctly is very important.  
To find the cause of an infection, take the sample from the infected area.  
For skin sores, take the sample from the edge, not the center.

Swabs are not the best choice.  
If you must use a swab, use a flocked swab.  
It collects more sample than other types.  
If you are doing a molecular test, use a swab that works with that test.  
Using the wrong swab can give a false-negative result.

Wooden-shafted swabs can harm some viruses.  
Cotton-tipped swabs can harm some bacteria, like chlamydia.

---

### Blood Cultures

Blood cultures need clean skin.  
Clean the skin with a 70% isopropyl alcohol solution that has chlorhexidine gluconate or tincture of iodine.  
Take more than one blood sample.  
Get them from different sites if possible.  
Try to take them at the same time as a fever spike.

If only one blood sample grows germs, it is likely from skin germs that got into the sample by accident.  
This is called contamination.  
Blood cultures are often contaminated.  
This can lead to wrong treatment, harm to the patient, and extra costs.

If you take blood from a central line, also take blood from a regular vein.  
This helps tell if the germ is in the blood or just in the line.  
Catheter cultures usually grow germs faster and have more germs than blood from a vein.  
Some fungi, like molds (for example, *Aspergillus*), usually do not grow in blood cultures.

---

## How to Send the Sample to the Lab

Send all samples to the lab as fast as possible.  
Use the right container and medium.  
Keep conditions that stop normal germs from growing.  
To count the germs accurately, stop extra growth.  
Send the sample right away.  
If you must wait, keep it cold (refrigerated) in most cases.  

---

## Special Notes for Culture

Some cultures need special care.  
Follow the lab’s instructions carefully.

# Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL)

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is a serious type of cancer. It starts in the bone marrow. The bone marrow is the soft part inside bones where blood cells are made.

In ALL, the cells that should become a type of white blood cell called lymphocytes turn into cancer cells. These cancer cells grow very fast. They take over the bone marrow. This stops the bone marrow from making healthy blood cells.

## Who Gets ALL?

ALL can happen at any age. But it is the most common cancer in children. It makes up about three out of four leukemia cases in children under 15.

Most children with ALL are between 2 and 5 years old.

In adults, ALL is more common in people over 45.

## What Happens in the Body?

The cancer cells build up in the bone marrow. They destroy the healthy cells that make normal blood.

These healthy blood cells include:

- **Red blood cells** – carry oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body.
- **White blood cells** – help fight infections.
- **Platelets** – help stop bleeding by forming clots.

The cancer cells do not work like normal white blood cells. So they cannot help the body fight infections.

The cancer cells also travel through the blood. They can grow in other parts of the body, such as:

- The liver
- The spleen
- The lymph nodes
- The brain
- The testes

They can also spread to the thin layers of tissue around the brain and spinal cord. This is called leukemic meningitis.

When leukemia cells grow in other organs, they can cause damage. This can lead to:

- Anemia (low red blood cells)
- Liver problems
- Kidney problems
- Other organ issues

## Symptoms of ALL

Early symptoms happen because the bone marrow cannot make enough healthy blood cells.

### Signs of Low Red Blood Cells (Anemia)
- Feeling weak
- Feeling tired
- Looking pale
- Trouble breathing
- Fast heartbeat
- Chest pain

### Signs of Low White Blood Cells
- Fever
- Night sweats
- Frequent infections

### Signs of Low Platelets
- Easy bruising
- Nosebleeds
- Bleeding gums
- Bleeding inside the body, such as in the brain or belly

### Other Symptoms from Leukemia in Other Organs

- **In the brain:** Headaches, vomiting, vision problems, balance issues, hearing problems, or facial muscle weakness.
- **In the bones and joints:** Pain.
- **In the liver and spleen:** A full or heavy feeling in the belly. Sometimes pain.

## Did You Know?

About 8 out of 10 children with ALL are cured.

## How Is ALL Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find out if someone has ALL.

### Blood Tests
A complete blood count checks the levels of different blood cells. In ALL:
- White blood cell count may be low, normal, or high.
- Red blood cell count is usually low.
- Platelet count is usually low.
- Very immature white blood cells (called blasts) are found in the blood.

### Bone Marrow Test
A small sample of bone marrow is taken from the hip bone. This test confirms the diagnosis. It also helps doctors find the exact type of leukemia. This helps them pick the best treatment.

The sample is tested for changes in chromosomes. These changes help guide treatment.

### Other Tests
- Urine tests to check for problems in the kidneys.
- Imaging tests like CT scans or MRI scans if the brain or other organs are affected.
- An echocardiogram (a heart ultrasound) may be done before treatment. Some chemotherapy drugs can harm the heart.

## How Is ALL Treated?

Treatment usually includes:

- Chemotherapy (drugs to kill cancer cells)
- Other drugs like immunotherapy or targeted therapy
- Rarely, stem cell transplant or radiation therapy

### Chemotherapy Is the Main Treatment

Chemotherapy is given in stages. Each stage has a different goal.

#### 1. Induction
This is the first phase. The goal is to kill most of the cancer cells. This gives the bone marrow a chance to make healthy blood cells again.

You may need to stay in the hospital for days or weeks. This depends on how fast your body recovers.

A mix of drugs is used. The exact mix depends on your test results. One common mix includes:

- Prednisone (a steroid taken by mouth)
- Vincristine (a chemotherapy drug given through a vein)
- Daunorubicin (a chemotherapy drug given through a vein)
- Asparaginase (a drug given through a vein)
- Sometimes cyclophosphamide (a chemotherapy drug given through a vein)

The drugs are given over several days or weeks. The same mix may be repeated.

#### 2. Treatment of the Brain
Leukemia often spreads to the brain. So treatment starts early and may continue through all phases.

To treat or prevent brain involvement, doctors may:

- Inject chemotherapy drugs (like methotrexate, cytarabine, or steroids) directly into the fluid around the brain and spinal cord.
- Give high doses of these drugs through a vein.
- Use radiation therapy to the brain in some cases.

#### 3. Consolidation and Intensification
This phase keeps killing cancer cells in the bone marrow.

More chemotherapy is given. It may use the same drugs as in induction, or different ones.

For people at high risk of relapse (due to certain gene changes), a stem cell transplant may be done after remission.

#### 4. Maintenance
This phase lasts 2 to 3 years. It uses fewer drugs, sometimes at lower doses.

The goal is to keep the cancer from coming back.

### Special Cases

Older adults may not be able to handle the strong treatment used for children. For them, gentler treatment may be used. This may include:

- A milder form of induction chemotherapy
- Immunotherapy
- A gentler stem cell transplant

### Supportive Care During Treatment

During treatment, you may need:

- Blood transfusions to treat anemia
- Platelet transfusions to prevent bleeding
- Antibiotics or other medicines to treat infections
- IV fluids to help the body stay hydrated
- Medicines like allopurinol or rasburicase to remove harmful waste (like uric acid) from the body

These wastes are released when cancer cells die.

## What If the Cancer Comes Back?

Sometimes the cancer returns. This is called relapse.

It often comes back in the blood, bone marrow, brain, or testes.

- If it comes back in the bone marrow, it is a serious sign.
- If it comes back in the brain, doctors give chemotherapy directly into the spinal fluid, once or twice a week.
- If it comes back in the testes, radiation therapy to the testes is used along with chemotherapy.

### Treatment for Relapsed ALL

For people who relapse, the best chance of cure is high-dose chemotherapy followed by a stem cell transplant.

The stem cells must come from someone with a matching tissue type. This is called HLA matching.

- A sibling is the most common donor.
- Sometimes a matched unrelated donor is used.
- In rare cases, partially matched family members or umbilical cord blood can be used.

Stem cell transplants are rarely used in people over 65. The risks are too high, and the treatment is less likely to work.

### New Treatments for Relapsed ALL

Some people with relapsed ALL may get:

- **Monoclonal antibodies** – these are special proteins that attach to leukemia cells. They help the body’s immune system destroy the cancer.
- **CAR-T therapy** – a type of treatment that changes a patient’s own immune cells (T cells). These new cells are trained to find and kill leukemia cells.

### End-of-Life Care

For people who do not respond to treatment, further therapy may make them feel worse. It may not help.

In these cases, end-of-life care should be considered. This care focuses on comfort and quality of life.

## Prognosis (Outlook)

Before treatment was available, most people with ALL died within months.

Now, most children are cured. About 8 out of 10 children survive.

In adults, about 3 out of 10 to 4 out of 10 survive.

Most people go into remission after the first round of chemotherapy.

Children between 3 and 9 years old have the best chance of recovery.

Infants and older adults have a harder time.

Other factors that affect outcome include:

- The number of white blood cells at diagnosis
- Whether the cancer has spread to the brain
- The type of chromosome changes in the cancer cells

# Cannabidiol (CBD)

Cannabidiol, or CBD, is a substance found in the *Cannabis sativa* plant. This plant is also known as marijuana or hemp. It contains more than 80 different chemicals called cannabinoids. Two of the most well-known are CBD and tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC.

THC causes the “high” feeling people get from using cannabis. It may also help with some health issues. CBD does not cause a high. It does not make you feel “stoned” or “high.”

CBD comes in many forms. You can find it in softgels, tablets, capsules, oils, gum, liquid extracts, and vape juice. Some products have only CBD. Others have CBD plus other ingredients.

There are problems with how much CBD is listed on product labels. A study looked at 84 online CBD products. Only 30% of them had the correct amount of CBD on the label. Also, 21% of the products had THC in them, even though they did not say so.

---

## What People Use CBD For

A prescription form of CBD is approved to treat certain types of seizures.

Some people use CBD for other health concerns, including:

- Mood swings or mood disorders like bipolar disorder  
- Pain  
- Anxiety  
- Crohn disease  
- Diabetes  
- Trouble sleeping  
- Multiple sclerosis  
- Symptoms when stopping use of heroin, morphine, or other opioids  

---

## What the Research Shows

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved CBD for treating seizures in two rare and serious seizure disorders:

- Lennox-Gastaut syndrome  
- Dravet syndrome  

These conditions start in childhood. They cause frequent seizures and serious problems with learning and thinking.

Studies show that CBD helps reduce seizures in these children and adults. It also helps some people with other types of epilepsy that do not respond to other treatments. But more research is needed to see if CBD works for common forms of epilepsy.

There is some evidence that CBD may help with nerve pain. A large review of 16 studies found that people using cannabis-based medicines were slightly more likely to get at least half their pain relief than those using a placebo. But the benefit was small. The review also found that the risks of side effects may outweigh the benefits.

An oral spray made from cannabis has helped reduce muscle stiffness in people with multiple sclerosis.

Many studies are ongoing. You can find summaries of these studies on the National Institutes of Health website.

---

## Side Effects of CBD

CBD can cause side effects. These include:

- Dry mouth  
- Low blood pressure  
- Diarrhea  
- Less appetite  
- Mood changes  
- Feeling dizzy or light-headed  
- Tiredness  
- Skin rash  
- Trouble sleeping or poor sleep quality  
- Feeling sleepy  

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration warns strongly against using CBD during pregnancy.

CBD can also harm the liver. It can raise liver enzyme levels and cause liver damage.

---

## Drug Interactions with CBD

CBD is broken down in the body by two liver enzymes: CYP3A4 and CYP2C19. If you take other medicines that use these same enzymes, CBD can change how those medicines work.

This can raise the levels of those medicines in your blood. It can also raise CBD levels. This increases the risk of side effects.

CBD may increase the effects of these medicines:

- Seizure medicines (like brivaracetam, carbamazepine, clobazam, topiramate)  
- Medicines to prevent organ rejection after a transplant (like cyclosporine, tacrolimus)  
- Blood thinners (like warfarin)  
- Tricyclic antidepressants  
- Stomach acid reducers (like omeprazole) – this may cause diarrhea  
- Nicotine – it may make nicotine stay in your body longer  
- Lithium – it may increase the risk of lithium side effects  
- Ketamine – it may make ketamine work better as an antidepressant  
- Methadone  
- Thyroid medicine (like levothyroxine)

CBD can make you sleepy. If you take it with other sleep-inducing medicines, such as:

- Benzodiazepines  
- Phenobarbital  
- Morphine  
- Alcohol  

You may become too drowsy. This can be dangerous.

Some medicines have a very narrow safety range. This means even small changes in dose can cause harm. Examples include amiodarone. Use CBD with extra caution if you take these medicines. You may need close monitoring.

CBD can harm the liver. If you take other medicines that also harm the liver, such as:

- Acetaminophen (Tylenol)  
- Valproic acid  

The risk of liver damage goes up when you take them together.

Some medicines can lower the amount of CBD in your blood. These include:

- Certain seizure medicines  
- Rifampin (an antibiotic)

Tricyclic antidepressants may raise CBD levels in your blood. This could make CBD side effects worse.

# Growth and Weight Faltering in Children

Growth and weight faltering means a child is not gaining weight or growing as they should. This used to be called failure to thrive.

This problem can slow down a child’s development and growth.

## What Causes Growth and Weight Faltering?

Many things can cause this problem.

### Environmental and Social Factors

These are the most common causes. They happen when a child does not get enough good food.

- A caregiver may not give the child enough food.
- The caregiver may not know how to feed the child properly.
- The family may not have enough money for food.
- The home may be stressful or chaotic.
- A caregiver may be depressed or not able to care for the child well.
- Some caregivers give food that is not healthy or does not have enough calories.

Stress can also make a child lose their appetite. This means they eat less and do not grow well.

Some mothers do not make enough breast milk. In rare cases, the milk they do make has fewer calories than needed.

Children who feel stressed at home may grow more slowly. Stress can change the body’s hormones. This can stop growth hormones from working properly.

### Medical Problems

Some health problems can also cause poor growth and weight gain.

- Trouble chewing or swallowing (like with a cleft lip or cleft palate).
- Gastroesophageal reflux (when stomach contents come back up).
- Narrowing of the tube from the mouth to the stomach.
- Problems absorbing food in the intestines.
- Eating disorders.
- Infections.
- Tumors.
- Hormone or metabolism problems (like diabetes or cystic fibrosis).
- Heart, kidney, or liver disease.
- Genetic conditions (like Down syndrome or inherited metabolic disorders).
- Digestive diseases (like celiac disease or inflammatory bowel disease).
- Trauma (injury).
- HIV infection.

Sometimes, a child has both a medical problem and a hard home life. These two things together can make growth and weight faltering worse.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors check for growth and weight faltering by:

- Looking at the child’s growth chart over time.
- Measuring the child’s weight, height, and head size.
- Asking questions about feeding, health, and family life.
- Doing a physical exam.
- Running blood, urine, or stool tests if needed.
- Taking x-rays if necessary.

A child may be diagnosed if:
- Their weight or body mass index is much lower than expected.
- Their height or length drops below what is normal for their age and sex.
- Their weight percentile drops sharply over a short time, even if their actual weight is not low.

For example, if a baby goes from the 90th percentile to the 50th percentile in a few weeks, the doctor will be concerned.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause.

### For Poor Nutrition

All children with this problem need more nutritious food with enough calories.

- Mild to moderate cases: The child gets healthy, high-calorie meals or feedings on a regular schedule.
- Caregivers get help with feeding and may be taught better ways to feed the child.
- Families may get support with money, food, or mental health care.

### For Medical Problems

If a health issue is found, the child gets treatment for that problem.

- For example, a child with a cleft lip may need surgery.
- A child with celiac disease must avoid gluten.
- A child with reflux may need medicine.

### Severe Cases

If the child is very underweight or not growing at all, they may need to go to the hospital.

- A team of experts works together: nutritionists, social workers, feeding specialists, psychiatrists, and doctors.
- The team finds the cause and plans the best way to feed the child.

### If Abuse or Neglect Is Involved

If a child is not being cared for properly, they may need to be placed in foster care.

- The child’s progress is watched closely.
- If the child returns home, doctors keep checking their growth and health.

## What Is the Outlook?

The first year of life is very important for brain development.

- Children who are undernourished in the first year may not catch up fully, even if they grow taller later.
- In about half of these children, learning and thinking skills stay below normal.
- This includes problems with speaking and math.

Early help can make a big difference. The sooner treatment starts, the better the chance for recovery.

# Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI)

Osteogenesis imperfecta is a genetic condition that makes bones weak and easy to break.  
It is caused by problems with a protein called collagen, which helps build strong bones, ligaments, and tendons.  
Some people with OI also have hearing loss, blue-colored whites of the eyes, weak teeth, or loose joints.

Doctors usually diagnose OI based on symptoms and physical exams.  
There is no single test that works for everyone.  
Treatment may include growth hormone, special medicines for bones, and other therapies.

---

## Types of Osteogenesis Imperfecta

There are four main types of OI. Each type has different symptoms and severity.

- **Type I**: The mildest form.  
  Some people only have blue eyes.  
  Others have joint pain from loose joints.  
  Bones may break more often in childhood.

- **Type II**: The most serious form.  
  This type is often fatal at birth or shortly after.  
  Babies are born with many broken bones.  
  Limbs are short.  
  The skull is soft and feels like a bag of bones.  
  The eyes are blue.  
  Birth injuries can cause brain bleeding.  
  Some babies die soon after birth.

- **Type III**: A severe, ongoing form that is not fatal.  
  People with this type are short in height.  
  They have curved spines and many broken bones.  
  The face is often triangular-shaped.  
  The chest may be deformed.  
  The color of the eyes can vary.

- **Type IV**: A moderate form.  
  People with this type live into adulthood.  
  Bones break easily in childhood.  
  The eyes are usually normal in color.  
  Height is below average.  
  Early diagnosis is important so treatment can help.

Most people with these main types inherit the condition in an autosomal dominant way.  
This means one parent with the condition can pass it to their child.  
About 90 percent of people with these types have changes in two genes: *COL1A1* or *COL1A2*.  
These genes help make a key part of collagen.

There are also rarer types of OI (types V to XXI).  
These are caused by changes in other genes.

---

## Symptoms and Signs

- Hearing loss affects 50 to 65 percent of people with OI.  
  It can happen in any of the four main types.  
  It may start in childhood or later in life.

### Type I
- Blue eyes are common.  
  This happens because the eye’s outer layer is thin.  
  You can see the blood vessels underneath.  
- Joint pain from loose joints.  
- Bones may break more than usual in childhood.

### Type II
- This form is life-threatening at birth.  
- Babies are born with many broken bones.  
- Limbs are short.  
- The skull is soft and fragile.  
- The eyes are blue.  
- Birth trauma can cause brain bleeding.  
- Some babies die in the first days or weeks of life.

### Type III
- The condition gets worse over time.  
- People are short.  
- The spine curves.  
- Bones break many times.  
- The head is large.  
- The face looks triangular.  
- The chest may be shaped oddly.  
- Eye color can be any shade.

### Type IV
- This form is in the middle in severity.  
- Most people live into adulthood.  
- Bones break easily before adolescence.  
- Eye color is usually normal.  
- Height is below average.  
- Early diagnosis helps so treatment can begin.

---

## How OI Is Diagnosed

Doctors usually diagnose OI by looking at symptoms and doing a physical exam.  
There are no strict rules for diagnosis.

If the diagnosis is unclear, doctors may do:
- A test on a skin sample to check the type I collagen protein.  
- A genetic test to look for changes in the *COL1A1* and *COL1A2* genes.

In some cases, doctors can find severe OI before birth using a detailed ultrasound scan during pregnancy.

---

## How OI Is Treated

Treatment depends on the type and how severe the condition is.

### Medicines
- **Growth hormone**: Helps children grow better. It works best for types I and IV.
- **Bisphosphonates**: These medicines help strengthen bones.  
  They reduce pain and lower the chance of fractures.  
  Options include:
  - IV pamidronate: Given through a vein over 3 days.  
    Dose is based on weight.  
    Given every 4 to 6 months as needed.
  - Oral alendronate: A pill taken once a day.  
    Dose is based on weight.  
    Maximum dose is 20 milligrams per day.
- **Denosumab**: A medicine given as a shot.  
  It helps stop bone breakdown.  
  It may help some people with OI.  
  It is used when other treatments do not work well.

### Vitamin D
- Some people with OI are low in vitamin D.  
- Doctors may give vitamin D supplements if needed.

### Other Treatments
- **Surgery**: Helps fix broken bones or correct bone shape.  
- **Physical therapy**: Helps build strength and improve movement.  
- **Occupational therapy**: Helps with daily tasks and using tools.  
- **Cochlear implants**: May help with hearing loss in some cases.

# Cesarean Delivery

A cesarean delivery is a surgery to deliver a baby. The doctor makes a cut in the mother’s belly and uterus.

In the United States, more than one in three babies are born by cesarean delivery.

Doctors choose a cesarean delivery when they believe it is safer than a vaginal birth for the mother, the baby, or both. This may happen if:

- Labor is moving too slowly.
- The baby is in a position that makes vaginal birth hard, such as feet or buttocks first.
- The baby’s heart rate is not normal. This can mean the baby is in trouble.
- There is heavy bleeding during labor. This may mean the placenta is pulling away too soon.
- The placenta covers the opening of the uterus. This is called placenta previa.
- The mother has had one or more previous cesarean deliveries.

In the past, doctors said all future babies must be delivered by cesarean if a woman had one cesarean before. They were worried the scar on the uterus might open during labor. This is called uterine rupture.

Now doctors know that the risk of rupture is very low if the scar is in the lower part of the uterus and is a horizontal cut.

So, if a woman had only one previous cesarean delivery and the scar was a horizontal cut in the lower part of the uterus, she may choose to try a vaginal birth. This is called a trial of labor after cesarean, or TOLAC.

But if a woman has had more than one cesarean delivery, most doctors still recommend another cesarean delivery.

Women should talk with their doctor about the risks and benefits before deciding on TOLAC. Many hospitals use checklists to make sure the mother and baby are good candidates for a safe TOLAC.

If a woman chooses to try a vaginal birth after one cesarean delivery, she should give birth in a hospital that can do a cesarean delivery quickly. This is because:

- Only about 60 to 80 out of 100 women who try a vaginal birth after one cesarean delivery succeed.
- There is a very small chance the uterus might open during labor.

### Did You Know...

- If a woman had only one previous cesarean delivery with a horizontal cut in the lower part of the uterus, she can talk with her doctor about trying a vaginal birth for her next baby.

A cesarean delivery involves several medical professionals. These include an obstetrician, an anesthesiologist, nurses, and sometimes a pediatrician.

Medicines given through a vein, antibiotics, and blood transfusions help keep the mother and baby safe during the surgery.

The doctor can make the cut in the uterus in two places:

#### Lower Incision
- This is the most common type.
- The lower part of the uterus is thin and has fewer blood vessels.
- Less blood is usually lost during surgery.
- The scar heals stronger, so it is less likely to open in future pregnancies.
- This cut is usually horizontal.
- A vertical cut is only used if there are special risks, such as a problem with the placenta or if the baby is too big or in the wrong position.

#### Upper (Classical) Incision
- This is used less often.
- It is usually done when the placenta covers the cervix (placenta previa).
- It is also used when the baby lies across the birth canal.
- It may be used if the baby is born too early.
- It may be used if the baby has a birth defect.

After a cesarean delivery, women are encouraged to walk around soon. This helps prevent blood clots in the legs or pelvis. These clots can travel to the lungs and block blood vessels. This is called a pulmonary embolism.

A cesarean delivery causes more pain after surgery. It also means a longer stay in the hospital and a longer time to recover than a vaginal birth.

# Testicular Torsion

Testicular torsion is a serious medical emergency. It happens when the testicle twists on its cord. This twist cuts off the blood supply to the testicle.

## What Causes Testicular Torsion?

Some boys are born with a condition that makes the testicle move too freely in the scrotum. This is called a bell-clapper deformity. It happens when the testicle is not held tightly in place by the sac around it.

This loose attachment lets the testicle twist easily. It can twist on its own or after an injury. About 1 in 8 boys has this condition. But not all of them will have torsion.

Torsion most often happens between the ages of 12 and 18. It can also happen in babies. It is rare in men over 30. It is more common in the left testicle.

### How the Testicle Moves in the Scrotum

- Normally, the front two-thirds of each testicle is covered by a thin sac called the tunica vaginalis.
- This sac holds fluid and helps protect the testicle.
- The sac is attached to the back and side of the testicle. This limits how much the testicle can move.
- If the sac is attached too high, the testicle can move more freely. This increases the chance of twisting.

**A:** Normal attachment – the testicle moves only a little.  
**B:** Too high attachment – the testicle can rotate easily, which can lead to torsion.

---

## Symptoms and Signs

The pain starts suddenly and is very bad.  
You may feel sick to your stomach and throw up.  
The scrotum swells quickly and feels hard.  
You may have a fever.  
You may also feel the need to urinate more often.

The affected testicle is very tender.  
It may be higher than normal and lie sideways.  
The other testicle may also be sideways. This is because the same problem often affects both sides.  
The reflex that makes the testicle pull up when the inner thigh is touched (cremasteric reflex) is usually gone on the affected side.

Sometimes the twist fixes itself. But it can come back. When this happens, the pain may seem to start slowly.  
But most of the time, the pain comes on fast and goes away fast.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your symptoms and do a physical exam.  
They may use a test called color Doppler ultrasonography. This test shows blood flow in the scrotum. It helps confirm if the blood supply is cut off.

Torsion can look like another condition called epididymitis.  
With epididymitis, the pain and swelling come on more slowly.  
The pain usually starts in the back of the testicle.  
But both conditions can cause swelling and tenderness all over the scrotum.  
This makes it hard to tell them apart.

In most cases, a doctor can make a good guess just from the exam.  
If the diagnosis is unclear, imaging can help.  
Color Doppler ultrasound is the best choice.  
It is fast and shows blood flow clearly.

A different test using a special dye (radioisotope scan) can also help. But it takes longer and is not as useful.

---

## How Is It Treated?

### Step 1: Try to Untwist the Testicle by Hand

A doctor may try to untwist the testicle during the first exam.  
This is called manual detorsion.  
It is done quickly and without waiting for imaging.

The testicle usually twists inward.  
To fix it, the doctor turns it outward.  
For the left testicle, this means turning it clockwise when looking from the front.  
A simple way to remember: “Stand at the foot and open the book.”

You may need more than one turn.  
The pain should go away when the twist is fixed.  
Pain relief tells the doctor if the move worked.

### Step 2: Surgery

If manual detorsion does not work, surgery is needed right away.  
Surgery must happen within a few hours.  
The longer you wait, the less chance the testicle will survive.

- If treatment starts within 6 to 8 hours, the testicle can be saved in 80% to 100% of cases.
- After 12 hours, the chance of saving the testicle is almost zero.

During surgery, the doctor will fix the affected testicle in place.  
They will also fix the other testicle. This prevents torsion from happening on that side.

If manual detorsion works, surgery is still needed.  
But it can be done later, not right away.  
The goal is to fix both testicles to prevent future problems.

---

## Key Points

- Testicular torsion causes sudden, severe pain in the scrotum.  
- You may feel sick and throw up.  
- The scrotum swells and feels hard.  
- Fever and needing to urinate more often can also happen.  
- The cremasteric reflex is usually gone on the affected side.  
- The other testicle may also be sideways.  
- Even if you have a fever or urinate more often, it does not rule out torsion.  
- If symptoms suggest torsion, treatment should start right away.  
- Imaging is only needed if the diagnosis is not clear.  
- Try to untwist the testicle by turning it outward.  
- If that does not work, get surgery right away.
