# Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency

This condition is present from birth. It happens when the body does not make enough of a protein called alpha-1 antitrypsin. This protein helps protect the lungs. Without enough of it, the lungs can become damaged over time. This damage can lead to a lung disease called emphysema.

The body also stores a faulty form of this protein in the liver. This can cause liver problems in both children and adults.

A blood test can help find this condition. If the level of alpha-1 antitrypsin in the blood is below 80 milligrams per deciliter, it suggests the condition is present. A second test is needed to confirm the diagnosis. This second test checks the genes or the type of protein in the blood.

Treatment includes stopping smoking, using medicines to open the airways, treating lung infections early, and in some cases, getting replacement protein. Severe liver damage may need a liver transplant. The outlook depends mostly on how much lung damage has already happened.

---

## How the Condition Works

Alpha-1 antitrypsin stops certain enzymes from damaging lung tissue. These enzymes are made by white blood cells. The protein is made mostly in the liver and then moves into the blood. It travels to the lungs to do its job.

The amount and shape of the protein in the blood depend on the genes a person inherits. There are many different versions of these genes. The most common normal version is called PI*MM.

The most common cause of severe disease is having two copies of a faulty gene called Z. This is known as PI*ZZ. About 95% of people with serious lung or liver problems from this condition have this gene pattern.

This condition is more common in people of Northern European background. It is rare in people of Asian or African descent.

Even if someone has two Z genes, they may not get lung disease. Smoking greatly increases the risk. People with two Z genes who do not smoke still have a shorter life than people with normal genes. If they smoke, their life span is even shorter.

People with only one Z gene (PI*MZ) are at higher risk of lung damage if they smoke. Their lung function may decline faster than normal.

Other rare gene patterns include PI*SZ, PI*Z-null, and PI*null-null. The last two mean the body makes no alpha-1 antitrypsin at all. Some rare gene changes make a protein that does not work, even if the blood level is normal.

### Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Levels and Risk of Lung Damage

| Gene Pattern | Blood Level (mg/dL) | Risk of Emphysema |
|--------------|---------------------|-------------------|
| PI*ZZ        | 20–45               | High              |
| PI*MZ        | 90–210              | Slightly increased |
| PI*SZ        | 75–120              | Slightly increased |
| PI*SS        | 100–200             | Slightly increased |
| PI*MM        | 150–350             | Normal            |

*Note: Levels are measured in two ways. The values above are based on common lab tests.*

---

## What the Condition Feels Like

### In Babies
Babies with liver problems may have yellow skin and eyes (jaundice) in the first week of life. Their liver may also be larger than normal. The jaundice usually goes away by 2 to 4 months.

Some children or adults may develop scarring of the liver (cirrhosis). In rare cases, liver cancer can develop.

### In Adults
Adults with lung damage have symptoms like shortness of breath, coughing, wheezing, and long breaths out. These are signs of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

The severity of lung damage varies. Some people who smoke and have two Z genes have only mild lung problems. Others with two Z genes who do not smoke may have serious lung damage.

People found to have this condition during routine checks (and who have no symptoms) often have better lung function than those who are diagnosed because they are already sick.

Airflow problems are more common in men. They are also more likely in people with asthma, frequent lung infections, exposure to dust at work, or a family history of lung disease.

### Skin Problems
Some people develop a skin condition called panniculitis. This causes hard, painful lumps or patches under the skin. These usually appear on the lower belly, buttocks, or thighs.

---

## How the Condition Is Diagnosed

A doctor may suspect this condition if:

- A person who smokes gets emphysema before age 45.
- A person who does not smoke and has no job-related lung exposure gets emphysema at any age.
- A chest X-ray shows emphysema mainly in the lower lungs.
- There is a family history of emphysema or unexplained liver disease.
- A family member has this condition.
- A person has panniculitis.
- A newborn has jaundice or high liver enzymes.

The first test is usually a gene test. This checks for the faulty genes.

To confirm the diagnosis, a blood test is done. The level of alpha-1 antitrypsin must be below 80 mg/dL if tested with a common method. If tested with a different method, the level must be below 50 mg/dL.

---

## How the Condition Is Treated

### For Lung Problems
- Stop smoking. This is the most important step.
- Use medicines that open the airways (bronchodilators).
- Treat lung infections early.
- In some cases, get regular injections of purified human alpha-1 antitrypsin.

This protein replacement therapy helps keep the blood level above 80 mg/dL. This level is thought to protect the lungs.

The treatment does not fix damaged lungs. It only helps slow down further damage.

It is only used for people who:
- Do not smoke.
- Have two abnormal genes.
- Have mild to moderate lung problems.
- Have low blood levels of the protein.

It is not used for people with severe lung damage or those with one or more normal genes.

Lung volume reduction surgery is not recommended. It does not work as well in people with this condition as it does in others.

For people under 60 with very bad lung disease, a lung transplant may be an option.

### For Liver Problems
There is no treatment that replaces the missing enzyme. The problem is not a lack of enzyme. It is that the body makes a faulty version of the protein.

Treatment is supportive. This means helping the body stay as healthy as possible.

If the liver fails, a liver transplant may be needed.

### For Skin Problems
There is no clear treatment for panniculitis. Some doctors use:
- Dapsone
- Steroid medicines
- Tetracycline antibiotics

But the best treatment is not known.

---

## What the Future Holds

People with this condition who have never smoked often live a normal life span. Their lung function may be only mildly affected.

The most common cause of death is lung damage from emphysema. Liver disease, including liver cancer, is the second most common cause.

---

## Key Points

- Think about this condition if someone has:
  - Unexplained emphysema.
  - Liver problems, especially in babies.
  - Skin lumps or patches (panniculitis).
  - Unexplained lung or liver disease.

- Diagnose with a gene test. Confirm with a blood test showing levels below 80 mg/dL.

- Give protein replacement therapy only to people who:
  - Do not smoke.
  - Have two abnormal genes.
  - Have mild to moderate lung problems.
  - Have low blood levels of the protein.

- Consider a liver transplant if the liver fails.

# Esophageal Varices

Esophageal varices are swollen veins in the tube that carries food from your mouth to your stomach. These veins can break open and cause serious bleeding.

- The main cause is high blood pressure in the blood vessels around the liver.
- Most people with these varices do not feel any symptoms until they start bleeding.
- Bleeding can be very heavy. It can lead to shock or even death.
- Doctors use a special camera to see the inside of the esophagus and diagnose the problem.

Varices can also form in the upper part of the stomach, near where the esophagus connects. These are called gastric varices. They act the same way and can also bleed.

---

## What Causes Esophageal Varices?

The main cause is high pressure in the portal vein.

The portal vein carries blood from your intestines and other organs like the spleen, pancreas, and gallbladder to your liver. When this vein has too much pressure, it is called portal hypertension.

In high-income countries, the most common reason for portal hypertension is scarring of the liver, known as cirrhosis.

When the liver is scarred, blood cannot flow through it easily. So, the body creates new blood vessels to bypass the liver. These new vessels are called collateral vessels.

These new vessels form in certain places. The most dangerous ones are at the bottom of the esophagus and the top of the stomach. These vessels become twisted and enlarged. They are called varices.

Varices are weak and can burst without warning. When they burst, they cause heavy bleeding in the stomach or intestines.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people with varices feel fine until the veins start bleeding.

When bleeding happens, you may vomit bright red blood. Sometimes the amount is large.

The bleeding does not hurt.

If you lose a lot of blood, you may feel dizzy, weak, and sweaty. Your heart may beat fast. Your blood pressure may drop.

These signs mean you are in shock.

---

## How Are Varices Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect varices if you have long-term liver disease and start vomiting blood.

They use a thin, flexible tube with a camera on the end. This is called an endoscope.

They pass the endoscope through your mouth and into your esophagus. This lets them see the varices.

If they see them, they can treat the bleeding right away using the same tube.

---

## How Are Varices Treated?

You will likely get fluids through a needle in your vein to replace lost blood. If you lost a lot of blood, you may need a blood transfusion.

Doctors can stop the bleeding during the endoscopy.

The most common method is endoscopic banding. They place small rubber bands around the varices. This cuts off the blood flow and closes them.

A medicine called tranexamic acid may help the banding work better in some people.

Another method is injection sclerotherapy. Doctors inject a special substance into the varices. This seals them shut.

At the same time, they may give you medicine through a vein. This helps slow the bleeding. The medicines used are octreotide or vasopressin.

If the bleeding does not stop with these treatments, doctors may do a procedure called portosystemic shunting.

This surgery creates a new path for blood to flow. It moves blood around the liver instead of through it. This lowers the pressure in the portal vein and helps stop bleeding.

There are different types of shunting procedures.

One type is called transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunting, or TIPS. Doctors use X-rays to guide a thin tube into a vein in your neck. They thread it to the liver and create a new connection between the portal vein and a liver vein.

Less often, doctors do this surgery through the abdomen.

If you are in serious danger from heavy bleeding and must wait for the shunt, doctors may place a special tube in your esophagus. It has balloons that inflate to press on the varices. This stops the bleeding temporarily.

Another option is a metal stent that expands in the esophagus. It presses on the varices to stop bleeding.

People with liver disease and bleeding are at risk for infection. So, doctors give them antibiotics.

---

## Can Varices Bleed Again?

Yes. Even after treatment, varices can bleed again. This is more likely if your liver disease is still active.

Doctors may give you medicine like beta-blockers to help lower pressure in the portal vein.

If the problem keeps coming back, you may need a liver transplant. This is the only cure for advanced liver disease.

# Speech Therapy

Speech therapists help people who have trouble speaking or making sounds. They work with patients who have:

- Problems with speaking after a stroke or brain injury (aphasia)
- Weak or uncoordinated mouth and throat muscles (dysarthria)
- Trouble planning the movements needed to speak (verbal apraxia)
- Had their voice box removed (laryngectomy)

They find the best way for each person to communicate. Here’s how they help in different situations:

## For People with Expressive Aphasia
- Use a board with pictures or letters.
- Point to the picture or letter to say what they want.

## For Mild to Moderate Dysarthria or Apraxia
- Practice breathing exercises.
- Do exercises to strengthen mouth and throat muscles.
- Repeat words and sounds over and over.

## For Severe Dysarthria or Apraxia
- Use a special electronic device.
- Type messages on a keyboard.
- The device shows the message on a screen or prints it out.

## For People After Laryngectomy
- Learn to speak using a new voice.
- Use a small device called an electrolarynx.
- This device makes a sound that you can shape into words.

Speech therapists also help with swallowing problems. They can check how well you swallow and teach you ways to eat and drink safely.

# Health Issues in Teens

Teens are people who are growing from children into adults. Most teens are healthy, but this time of life can bring new challenges. To stay healthy and catch problems early, teens need support from parents or guardians. They also need regular checkups with a doctor.

## What Teens Need to Know About Their Health

Teens go through many changes. These include:

- Growing taller and stronger
- Learning to think more clearly
- Managing emotions
- Building friendships
- Becoming more independent
- Figuring out who they are, including their feelings about sex and gender

Some common health concerns during these years include:

- Problems with mental health, like sadness or worry
- Using drugs, alcohol, or tobacco
- Getting hurt by accidents or violence
- Weight issues, like being overweight
- Health problems that started in childhood and continue into teen years
- Injuries from sports or other activities

## Common Health Problems in Teens

The most common causes of death and serious injury in teens in the United States are:

- Accidents involving cars
- Accidents with guns
- Overdosing on drugs

Some teens also hurt themselves on purpose or are hurt by others. This includes suicide and homicide.

Head injuries are common, especially in sports. A head injury can affect the brain. This is called a concussion. If a teen has a concussion, they must see a doctor who knows how to treat it. They need time to rest before going back to school, sports, or using phones and computers. A trusted adult should help guide their return to normal activities.

Using drugs or alcohol is a serious health risk. It can lead to long-term problems. Doctors can help find these issues early. Early help can prevent bigger problems later.

Mental health issues can start during the teen years. These include:

- Depression
- Anxiety
- Other serious mental health conditions, like schizophrenia

The pandemic made mental health worse for many teens. They felt more lonely, stressed, or sad.

Sex and relationships become important topics. Teens may start to explore their feelings about sex and who they are attracted to. Important topics to talk about include:

- Who you are attracted to (your sexual orientation)
- How to build healthy relationships
- How to stay safe during sex
- How to prevent sexually transmitted infections (STIs)
- How to prevent pregnancy
- How to protect yourself from sexual abuse or other trauma
- How to understand your gender identity

Being overweight is common in teens. It often comes with other health problems, such as:

- Diabetes
- High blood pressure
- High levels of fat in the blood

Many teens live longer after surviving serious health problems that started when they were young.

Bad habits that start in the teen years can cause health problems now and later in life. These habits include:

- Eating unhealthy foods
- Not being active
- Smoking

About 4 out of 10 teens in the United States have a long-term health condition. These can include:

- Asthma
- Diabetes
- Inflammatory bowel disease

Cancer is rare in children, but some types are more common in teens. These include:

- Leukemia
- Lymphoma
- Bone cancers
- Rhabdomyosarcoma
- Thyroid cancer
- Brain and spinal cord tumors

# Getting Your Prosthesis

There are many types of artificial limbs. But once your doctor and team decide on your treatment plan, the fitting process usually follows the same steps no matter which type of prosthesis you get.

The fitting process works together with physical therapy and occupational therapy. These sessions help you learn how to use your new prosthesis.

## What a Prosthesis Is Made Of

A prosthesis has seven main parts:

- **Gel pad for the remaining limb**: A soft layer made of silicone or a similar material. It protects your skin and helps control pressure.
- **How the prosthesis stays on**: A system that connects the prosthesis to your body. This can be a strap, suction, or another method.
- **Socket**: A hard plastic part that holds your remaining limb. It fits over your limb and the gel pad. Some sockets have a soft inner layer to help reduce pressure.
- **Joints and end parts**: These include joints like the ankle, knee, wrist, or elbow. The end part could be a hand or foot.
- **Connection parts**: These link the joints and end parts to the main frame. They allow small adjustments.
- **Flesh-like shape**: A soft foam layer that looks like real muscle. It protects the inner parts and gives the prosthesis a natural look.
- **Artificial skin**: A thin layer that matches your skin tone. It goes over the foam to make the prosthesis look real.

## How the Prosthesis Is Made

First, your doctor or technician makes a mold of your remaining limb. This can be done by wrapping your limb with plaster bandages or using a digital scanner.

Next, a model of your limb is made from the mold. This model can be built by hand or created using a computer.

Then, a socket is shaped around this model. The socket is the part that holds your limb.

A test version of the prosthesis is built using this socket. This test version lets you try different parts and settings. The goal is to find the best setup for stability, comfort, and movement.

Once the best parts and design are chosen, the final socket is made. It is usually made from strong materials like carbon fiber.

The final prosthesis is then adjusted and fine-tuned. This ensures it fits well and works smoothly.

Finally, the outside appearance is added. You can choose a realistic look that matches your other limb. Or you can choose a design that shows the inner parts.

The whole fitting process takes between 7 and 18 visits. It also includes about 16 steps in the lab.

## Alternative: Bone-Integrated Prosthesis

Another option is called transcutaneous osseointegration. This method involves surgery to place a metal anchor directly into the bone of your remaining limb.

This anchor connects to the prosthesis. It changes how the prosthesis touches your body.

This option may help people who had problems with a regular socket. These problems can include pain, poor fit, or skin issues.

# Pulmonary Rehabilitation

Pulmonary rehabilitation helps people with long-term lung problems live better every day.  
It is a program that includes exercise, education, support, and advice to help you stay active and improve your health.

This program is for people with long-term lung diseases.  
Its main goal is to help you do as much as possible on your own.  
It can help you feel stronger and more in control of your life.

Most programs focus on chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or COPD.  
But they can also help people with other lung conditions, such as:

- Asthma  
- Bronchiectasis (when airways are permanently widened)  
- Long-term effects of COVID-19  
- Cystic fibrosis  
- Interstitial lung disease  
- Lung cancer  
- Neuromuscular disorders  
- Pulmonary hypertension  
- Sarcoidosis  

Pulmonary rehabilitation may help you:

- Breathe easier  
- Walk or move farther without getting out of breath  
- Feel better overall  
- Stay out of the hospital more often  

There is no strong proof that this program helps people live longer.  

It can help before and after surgery for people with lung cancer, severe COPD, or severe lung disease needing a lung transplant.

Most programs happen in a clinic or doctor’s office.  
Some happen in your home.  
More programs now use video calls or online tools.

You can start pulmonary rehabilitation even if your lung disease is not very bad.  
Even mild symptoms can improve with this program.  
It can help you breathe easier and move more.  
Sometimes, pulmonary rehabilitation is done together with cardiac rehabilitation.

The best programs use a team of experts.  
This team includes:

- A respiratory therapist  
- A physical therapist  
- A nurse  
- A doctor  
- A psychologist or social worker  
- A dietitian  

They work together to help you.  
Most people join for 8 to 12 weeks.  
But you must keep doing the exercises and skills at home.  
If you stop, you may lose the progress you made.

Supportive treatments can be used with pulmonary rehabilitation.  
These include:

- Oxygen therapy  
- Chest physical therapy  

These treatments can also help people who are not in a formal program.  
They can help those with long-term lung problems like cystic fibrosis or bronchiectasis.  
They can also help people with sudden lung issues like pneumonia.

---

## Joining the Program and Setting Goals

Before you start, your doctor will check your health and how well you can do daily tasks.  
This check happens in a hospital or clinic.  

The team will talk with you about your short-term and long-term goals.  
For example, an older person may want to walk their grandchild to the school bus.  
If they can only walk 300 feet because of shortness of breath, but need to walk 1,000 feet, the first goal might be to walk a little farther each week.  

The team will help you set goals that are realistic and encouraging.  
They will check your progress every week.  
This helps make sure you are moving forward.

The team will also look for things that might make it hard to succeed.  
These could include:

- Not having enough money  
- No way to get to the clinic  
- Trouble remembering how to use medicine devices  
- Problems at home with family or caregivers  

For example, if you have dementia, you may need simpler instructions.  
If your caregiver cannot help you at home, the team will find ways to support you.

Long-term goals are also set.  
The team will teach you how to notice changes in your breathing or health.  
If your symptoms get worse, you will know when to call your doctor.  
Your treatment plan may need to change based on how you are feeling.

---

## What the Program Includes

A pulmonary rehabilitation program has several parts:

### Exercise Training

This is the most important part of the program.  
It helps reduce weakness from not being active.  
It helps you breathe easier and move more.

Aerobic exercise and strength training are both important.

Walking is the main exercise.  
Most daily tasks require walking.  
Many programs use walking on a treadmill or outside.  
Some people prefer a stationary bike.  
Choose the exercise that feels best and is easiest to keep doing.

Arm exercises are also helpful.  
If you have shortness of breath when doing daily tasks like washing your hair or shaving, arm training can help.  
Lung disease can cause muscle loss.  
Some shoulder muscles help with both breathing and arm movement.  
Using these muscles too much can make you tired fast.

### Inspiratory Muscle Training

This helps strengthen the muscles you use to breathe.  
You use special breathing exercises and tools.  
It is usually done with regular exercise.

### Psychosocial Counseling

Many people with lung disease feel sad or anxious.  
Breathing problems can make these feelings worse.  
They can also affect your sex life and your ability to relax.  

Counseling, group sessions, and sometimes medicine can help.  
Family members may join counseling to help them cope.

### Nutrition Evaluation and Counseling

People with lung disease often have weight problems.  
Some lose weight and muscle.  
Others gain weight because they move less.  

The program helps you eat right.  
You will learn how to get enough calories without feeling too full.  
Feeling full can make breathing harder.  

For those who are overweight, losing weight can help.  
It reduces the strain on your breathing.

### Education

You will learn about your lung disease and your medicines.  
You will learn:

- When and how to take your medicines  
- What each medicine does  
- What side effects to watch for  
- How to use inhalers correctly  

The team will check how well you follow instructions.  
They will teach you and your family why it is important to take your medicines right.

You will also learn about:

- Quitting smoking  
- Breathing techniques, like pursed-lip breathing (breathing out slowly through closed lips to slow your breathing and reduce shortness of breath)  
- How to save your energy during daily tasks

# Echinacea

Echinacea is a wildflower that grows in North America.  
It contains many natural substances that can affect the body.  

## What People Say About Echinacea

Some people believe echinacea helps the body fight off infections.  
They say it can make colds shorter if taken right at the start.  
But well-designed studies have not found strong proof that this is true.  
Some people use echinacea on the skin to help wounds heal.  

## What the Research Shows

Studies on echinacea for colds give mixed results.  
One reason is that echinacea products are not all the same.  
Different parts of the plant are used.  
Different types of echinacea are used.  
This leads to different mixtures in the final product.  

A major review in 2014 looked at 24 studies with over 4,600 people.  
It tested many different echinacea products for cold prevention and treatment.  
The review found no clear benefit for preventing colds.  
But when researchers combined some of the prevention studies, they saw a small possible benefit.  
The benefit was between 10% and 20% less chance of getting a cold.  
The researchers said some products might have a weak effect.  

Another study reviewed many small trials.  
It looked at how echinacea affects cold prevention, symptom length, and safety.  
It found no clear benefit for preventing colds.  
It also found no effect on how long cold symptoms last.  
No serious safety problems were found.  
But the studies were very different from each other.  
This makes it hard to trust the results.  

One study followed 200 healthy children.  
It found that echinacea helped prevent respiratory infections.  
It also cut the need for antibiotics by 76.3%.  

Some lab studies looked at how echinacea affects immune cells.  
They studied bacteria found in the plant and the soil it grows in.  
These studies show possible immune effects.  
But we do not yet know if these effects happen in real people.  
More research is needed.  

## Side Effects of Echinacea

Most side effects are mild and go away quickly.  
They include dizziness, tiredness, headaches, and stomach upset.  
Echinacea should not be used by people with autoimmune diseases.  
This includes conditions like multiple sclerosis.  
It should also be avoided by people with advanced HIV, tuberculosis, or those who have had an organ transplant.  
This is because echinacea may boost certain immune cells.  
This could make these conditions worse.  
People with allergies to ragweed, chrysanthemums, marigolds, daisies, or similar plants may have an allergic reaction.  

## Drug Interactions

Echinacea can change how some medicines work.  
It can slow down or speed up certain liver enzymes.  
These enzymes help break down many medicines.  
Echinacea may affect medicines like:  
- Anabolic steroids  
- Some antifungal drugs  
- Methotrexate  
- Etoposide  
- Other cancer medicines  

Always talk to your doctor before using echinacea if you take any medicine.

# Understanding Gender Incongruence and Gender Dysphoria

## What Do These Terms Mean?

**Sex** is about your body. It includes things like your genitals, chromosomes, and hormones. Doctors use these to say if a person is male or female at birth.

**Gender identity** is how you feel inside. It is your sense of being a man, a woman, both, neither, or something else. This may match your sex at birth, or it may not.

**Gender incongruence** means you feel a strong and lasting mismatch between your gender identity and the gender you were assigned at birth.

**Gender dysphoria** is diagnosed when this mismatch causes serious emotional pain or makes daily life hard. It is not the mismatch itself that is the problem. It is the distress or difficulty it causes.

- Some people feel their gender does not match their sex at birth. These people are often called transgender or gender diverse.
- Not all transgender people have gender dysphoria. Some feel fine with their identity.
- When someone does have gender dysphoria, they may feel anxious, sad, or have trouble doing normal things.
- Doctors diagnose gender dysphoria based on the person’s emotional pain, not just on having a different gender identity.

## What Helps People Feel Better?

Treatment can help reduce distress. Options include:

- **Social transition**: Living as your true gender. This can mean using a new name, new pronouns, and dressing in a way that matches your gender identity. You do not need medical treatment to do this.
- **Psychotherapy**: Talking with a mental health professional. This can help with anxiety, depression, or other emotional challenges.
- **Hormone therapy**: Medicine that changes your body to match your gender identity. For example:
  - People assigned male at birth may take estrogen. This can lead to breast growth, less body hair, and softer skin.
  - People assigned female at birth may take testosterone. This can lead to facial hair, a deeper voice, and changes in body shape.
- **Surgery**: Some people choose surgery to change their body. This is called gender-affirming surgery. It is not for everyone.

## How Common Is This?

We do not know the exact number of people who are transgender or gender diverse.

- About 0.5% to 1% of adults say they are transgender.
- Among children and teens, the number is higher — from 1% to 8%.
- Only a smaller number of transgender people have gender dysphoria.

## Is Being Transgender a Mental Health Problem?

No. Feeling that your gender does not match your sex at birth is not a mental illness.

But some transgender people do feel emotional pain or struggle with daily life. If this happens, it is important to talk to a health care provider.

## What Is a Gender Transition?

A gender transition is the process of living as your true gender. It can include:

- Changing your name and how you dress.
- Using new pronouns (like “she,” “he,” or “they”).
- Taking hormones or having surgery.
- Telling family, friends, or coworkers about your identity.

You can choose to do any or all of these steps. You do not have to do them all.

Support from friends, family, or support groups can help. Health care providers can also guide you through the process.

## Key Terms Explained

Here are common words used when talking about gender:

- **Cisgender**: A person whose gender identity matches the sex they were assigned at birth.
- **Gender binary**: The idea that there are only two genders — male and female.
- **Gender dysphoria**: Distress caused by a mismatch between your gender identity and your sex at birth.
- **Gender expression**: How you show your gender through clothes, voice, behavior, and appearance.
- **Gender identity**: How you feel inside about your gender.
- **Gender nonconforming**: When your gender expression does not match what is expected for your sex at birth.
- **Genderqueer**: A person whose gender identity does not fit into the idea of just male or female. They may feel like both, neither, or something in between.
- **Trans-affirmative**: Being respectful and supportive of transgender and gender-diverse people.
- **Transgender**: A general term for people whose gender identity or role is different from what is usually expected based on their sex at birth.
- **Transition**: The process of living as your true gender. It can include social steps (like a new name) or medical steps (like hormones or surgery).

## Signs of Gender Incongruence or Dysphoria

Some children show signs as young as age 2 or 3.

But many people do not notice these feelings until later in life.

### What Might Children Show?

Children may:
- Want to wear clothes of the other gender.
- Say they are the other gender.
- Say they wish they were the other gender.
- Play only with toys or games that are usually for the other gender.
- Avoid activities that are seen as typical for their sex.
- Feel upset about their body, especially their genitals.

For example:
- A girl may say she wants to grow a penis and become a boy. She may stand to pee.
- A boy may dream of being a girl. He may not like rough play or sports. He may wish he did not have a penis or testicles.

Puberty can make distress worse. Some boys with gender dysphoria ask for treatment to stop their body from changing in a way that feels wrong.

### What About Adults?

Some people do not feel different until they are older. They may:
- Work jobs that match their birth sex.
- Get married to someone of the expected gender.
- Wear clothes that match their birth sex.

Some men may start by wearing women’s clothes. They may not admit their true feelings until later.

Once people accept their identity, many choose to live as their true gender. Some do this without hormones or surgery. Others use medical help.

Some people struggle with anxiety, depression, or thoughts of suicide. These problems can come from being rejected by family or society.

## How Is Gender Dysphoria Diagnosed?

A doctor or mental health professional makes the diagnosis.

Most children are seen when they are 6 to 9 years old.

The doctor will:
- Talk to you or your parents about your gender identity and how you express it.
- Ask about your past and current feelings.
- Review your medical and mental health history.
- Look for other problems like depression, anxiety, or substance use.
- Check for stress at home, school, or in the community.

### For Adults and Teens

To be diagnosed, you must:
- Feel that your body does not match your gender identity.
- Have felt this way for at least 6 months.
- Feel very upset or have trouble doing normal things because of this.

You must also have at least 2 of these:
- A strong wish to get rid of your sex characteristics.
- A strong wish to have the body of the gender you identify with.
- A strong desire to live as the other gender.
- A strong belief that you feel and act like the other gender.
- A strong desire to be treated as the other gender.

### For Children

To be diagnosed, you must have at least 6 of these:
- A strong wish to be the other gender.
- A strong preference for wearing clothes of the other gender.
- A strong wish to pretend to be the other gender.
- A strong preference for toys, games, or activities of the other gender.
- A strong preference for friends of the other gender.
- A strong dislike of toys, games, or activities of your own gender.
- A strong dislike of your body or genitals.
- A strong wish to have the body of the gender you identify with.

The child must also feel very upset or have trouble at school, with friends, or in other areas.

### Important Note

If a child says they want to be the other gender just to get special treatment, this is not likely gender dysphoria. For example, a boy who says he wants to be a girl because he thinks his sister gets more attention is probably not experiencing gender dysphoria.

## Treatment for Gender Dysphoria

The goal of treatment is to help you feel comfortable with who you are. It aims to improve your health, mental well-being, and happiness.

### What Treatments Are Available?

- **Hormone therapy**: Medicine that changes your body to match your gender identity.
- **Surgery**: Procedures to change your body. This includes breast, genital, or facial surgery.
- **Voice therapy**: Helps change your voice to match your gender identity.
- **Electrolysis**: A treatment to remove unwanted body hair.

### Do You Need Therapy?

Psychotherapy is not required before starting hormone therapy or surgery.

But it can help with:
- Treating depression or anxiety.
- Dealing with negative reactions from others.
- Finding a way to express your gender that feels right.
- Talking to family or friends about your identity.
- Planning your transition.

### Hormone Therapy and Fertility

- Hormone therapy can reduce fertility.
- It does not prevent pregnancy. You still need birth control if you want to avoid pregnancy.
- If you want to have children in the future, talk to your doctor about preserving your fertility before starting treatment.

### Surgery

Surgery is permanent. Doctors only recommend it after:
- You have worked with a trained health care provider.
- You have followed current medical standards.

Before surgery, doctors usually suggest:
- Using hormone therapy.
- Living full-time as your true gender for at least 1 year.

# Hypnotherapy

Hypnotherapy is a type of treatment that connects the mind and body. It comes from common mental health therapy practices in the West. The goal is to help people feel better physically and mentally.

A trained therapist guides you into a deep state of relaxation. You focus your mind on specific thoughts or feelings. You stay aware of what is happening around you. You are not asleep. You are just very focused and calm.

Some people learn how to do this on their own. They can use it to help themselves when needed.

---

## What Hypnotherapy Can Help With

Hypnotherapy can help with many health issues. It may help you:

- Reduce pain from long-term conditions
- Ease symptoms during menopause
- Sleep better at night
- Overcome strong fears or phobias
- Manage symptoms that come from stress or emotional issues (conversion disorders)
- Stop smoking
- Lose weight

It can also help during medical treatments. It may reduce pain and fear during procedures for both adults and children.

Some people find it helpful for:

- Irritable bowel syndrome
- Frequent headaches
- Asthma
- Skin problems like warts or psoriasis
- High blood pressure

It can also help with nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy. This is especially true when the nausea happens before treatment starts (anticipatory nausea).

In people with cancer or long-term pain, hypnotherapy may improve mood and overall well-being. This works best when people are open to trying it and believe it can help.

# Precautions and Side Effects During Blood Transfusions

Blood transfusions help the body carry oxygen better. They also replace lost blood and fix problems with blood clotting. Most people do well after a transfusion. But sometimes, side effects can happen.

Health care teams take steps to lower the risk of side effects. Before the transfusion, your blood is tested against the donor’s blood. This is called cross-matching. It checks for any bad reactions. This step is done for red blood cell transfusions, but not for plasma or platelet transfusions.

Before giving the blood, the team checks the labels on the blood bags. They make sure the blood is meant for you. Then, they give the blood slowly. Each unit usually takes 1 to 4 hours. Most side effects happen in the first 15 minutes. So, you are watched closely at the start. A nurse checks on you often. If you have a bad reaction, they stop the transfusion right away.

Most transfusions go well. But mild side effects can happen. Rarely, serious or even deadly side effects can occur.

## Common Side Effects

- Fever  
- Allergic reactions

## Serious Side Effects

- Too much fluid in the body  
- Lung damage  
- The body destroys the transfused red blood cells because of a blood type mismatch

## Rare Side Effects

- Graft-versus-host disease (the donated cells attack your body)  
- Infections  
- Problems from very large transfusions (poor clotting, low body temperature, low calcium or potassium levels)

---

### Fever

Fever can happen because of white blood cells in the donated blood. It can also be caused by chemicals released by those cells. Most hospitals in the United States remove white blood cells from donated blood to lower this risk.

You may feel hot, shiver, and have a headache or back pain. You might also get itchy skin or a rash.

Usually, taking acetaminophen (like Tylenol) is enough to lower the fever. If you had a fever before and need another transfusion, you may be given acetaminophen before the next one.

---

### Allergic Reactions

Symptoms include:
- Itching  
- Rash all over the body  
- Swelling  
- Dizziness  
- Headache  

Less common symptoms:
- Trouble breathing  
- Wheezing  
- Airway blockage  

Rarely, the reaction can be so bad it causes low blood pressure and shock.

If this happens, the transfusion stops. You will get an antihistamine. For more serious reactions, you may get hydrocortisone or epinephrine.

There are treatments that let people with past allergic reactions have transfusions safely. If you have repeated severe reactions, you may get washed red blood cells. Washing removes parts of the blood that can cause allergies. White blood cells and platelets are already removed from stored blood (this is called leukocyte reduction), so allergic reactions are rare.

---

### Fluid Overload

You can get more fluid than your body can handle. This can cause swelling in your arms, legs, or face. It can also make it hard to breathe.

This is the most common cause of death linked to transfusions. People with heart problems are at higher risk. Their transfusions are given more slowly and watched closely. If you get too much fluid, you will be given a medicine to help your body get rid of the extra fluid (a diuretic).

---

### Lung Injury

A rare but serious reaction called transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) can happen. It is caused by antibodies in the donor’s plasma. It can cause serious breathing problems.

TRALI is the second most common cause of death from transfusions. It happens in 1 out of every 5,000 to 10,000 transfusions. Many cases are mild and may not be noticed.

Most people with mild to moderate lung injury get oxygen and other care to help them breathe while their lungs heal.

---

### Destruction of Red Blood Cells

Even with careful blood typing and matching, a mismatch can still happen. This can be due to small differences in blood types or, very rarely, a mistake.

When this happens, your body attacks and destroys the new red blood cells soon after the transfusion. This is called a hemolytic reaction.

You may feel unwell or anxious during or right after the transfusion. You might have:
- Trouble breathing  
- Chest pressure  
- Flushing  
- Severe back pain  
- Cold, sweaty skin  
- Low blood pressure (shock)

In rare cases, this can be deadly.

If doctors suspect this, they stop the transfusion right away. They give treatment to help your breathing and blood pressure. They do blood and urine tests to confirm the red blood cells are being destroyed.

Sometimes the reaction happens later — within a month after the transfusion. These delayed reactions are usually mild. They may only show up during blood tests done to check your recovery.

These reactions happen when the donor blood has a rare blood type antigen that is not usually tested for.

---

### Graft-versus-Host Disease

This is a rare but serious problem. It mainly affects people with weak immune systems due to illness or medicine.

In this condition, the donated white blood cells attack your body’s tissues. Symptoms include:
- Fever  
- Rash  
- Low blood pressure  
- Low blood cell counts  
- Tissue damage  
- Shock

This can be deadly. But it can be prevented. People with weak immune systems get red blood cells and platelets that have been treated with radiation before transfusion.

---

### Infections

Even with strict testing and safe storage, infections can sometimes pass through blood transfusions. Blood donors are carefully checked. Blood is tested for many infections.

But sometimes, a donor is infected with a germ that is not yet detectable. This can happen if the infection is very new or if there is no test for that germ.

---

### Problems from Massive Transfusions

A massive transfusion means getting a full blood volume (about 10 units) in 24 hours or less. This can happen after a serious injury or during major surgery.

Main problems include:
- Poor blood clotting (coagulopathy)  
- Low body temperature (hypothermia)

Blood clotting fails because the transfused blood lacks clotting factors and platelets. To prevent this, doctors often give fresh frozen plasma and platelets along with the blood. Fresh frozen plasma contains clotting factors.

Massive transfusions can also cause:
- Low calcium levels (hypocalcemia)  
- Low potassium levels (hypokalemia)

Low calcium can cause muscle spasms and abnormal heart rhythms. Low potassium can cause muscle weakness and heart rhythm problems.

Blood is stored cold. Getting many units of cold blood can lower your body temperature. To prevent this, doctors use a special device that gently warms the blood as it goes into your body through the IV tube.

# Cervicitis – Simple Explanation

Cervicitis means inflammation of the cervix. The cervix is the lower part of the uterus that opens into the vagina.

This condition can be caused by an infection or by things that irritate the cervix but do not cause infection.

## What Causes Cervicitis?

Most cases of acute cervicitis are caused by a sexually transmitted infection (STI). The most common STIs are:

- *Chlamydia trachomatis*  
- *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* (gonorrhea)

Other possible causes include:

- Herpes simplex virus (HSV)  
- *Trichomonas vaginalis*  
- *Mycoplasma genitalium*

Sometimes, no cause is found.

The cervix can also become inflamed without infection. This can happen with:

- Bacterial vaginosis  
- Trichomoniasis  

Non-infectious causes include:

- Gynecologic procedures (like a Pap smear)  
- Foreign objects in the vagina (such as pessaries or birth control devices)  
- Chemicals in douches, creams, or gels  
- Allergies (such as to latex)

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many women with cervicitis have no symptoms at all.

When symptoms do occur, they may include:

- Vaginal discharge  
- Bleeding between periods  
- Bleeding after sex  
- Pain during sex

## How Is Cervicitis Diagnosed?

A healthcare provider will do a pelvic exam. They will look for:

- Discharge from the cervix (thick, white, or yellowish)  
- A cervix that bleeds easily when touched  
- Redness or swelling of the cervix

Tests are done to check for:

- Chlamydia  
- Gonorrhea  
- Bacterial vaginosis  
- Trichomoniasis  

If you have a fever, pain when the cervix is moved, or sores, it may mean you have pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) or herpes.

## How Is Cervicitis Treated?

Most women are treated for chlamydia and gonorrhea right away, even before test results come back.

This is especially true if:

- You are in an emergency room or urgent care clinic  
- You may not return for follow-up  
- Your symptoms strongly suggest an STI

### Treatment for Chlamydia:
- Azithromycin: One dose by mouth  
- Or doxycycline: Two pills twice a day for 7 days

### Treatment for Gonorrhea:
- Ceftriaxone: One injection (500 mg if under 150 kg, 1 gram if 150 kg or more)  
- Plus azithromycin: One dose by mouth

This is because some gonorrhea bacteria are becoming resistant to certain antibiotics.

After test results are known, treatment may be changed.

### If the Cause Is Herpes:
- Herpes does not go away. It stays in your body for life.  
- Antiviral medicine can help control outbreaks but will not cure the infection.

### If Cervicitis Persists After Treatment:
- Check again for chlamydia or gonorrhea.  
- If no cause is found, you may be treated for *Mycoplasma genitalium*.  
- Moxifloxacin: One pill once a day for 7 to 14 days (usually 10 days).

*Mycoplasma genitalium* can cause:

- Cervicitis  
- Pelvic inflammatory disease  
- Early childbirth  
- Trouble getting pregnant

Testing for this bacteria is only available in some labs.

### Important for Sexual Partners:
- If you have an STI, your partner must be tested and treated too.  
- Avoid sex until both you and your partner have finished treatment and are cured.

### Follow-Up Testing:
- All women with chlamydia, gonorrhea, or trichomoniasis should be tested again 3 months after treatment.  
- Reinfection is common.

## Key Points

- Acute cervicitis is usually caused by a sexually transmitted infection.  
- It can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease if not treated.  
- Many women have no symptoms.  
- Common symptoms are vaginal discharge and bleeding between periods or after sex.  
- Test for chlamydia, gonorrhea, bacterial vaginosis, and trichomoniasis.  
- Treat most women for chlamydia and gonorrhea at the first visit.

# Avoidant Personality Disorder

This is a mental health condition where a person avoids social situations because they fear being rejected, criticized, or made fun of.

## What It Feels Like

- People with this condition feel unsure of themselves.
- They believe they are not good enough or not worthy of being liked.
- They avoid people and social events to protect themselves from possible hurt.
- They worry that others will judge them or think badly of them.

## How Common Is It?

- About 2 out of every 100 people in the United States have this condition.
- It is slightly more common in women than in men.

## Other Conditions Often Seen With It

Many people with avoidant personality disorder also have other mental health issues, such as:

- Depression
- Obsessive-compulsive disorder
- Anxiety disorders, especially social anxiety
- Other personality disorders, like dependent or borderline personality disorder

When someone has both social anxiety and avoidant personality disorder, their symptoms are usually worse and harder to manage.

## What Causes It?

- Some people may be born with a tendency to feel anxious in social settings.
- Others may have been rejected, ignored, or teased during childhood.
- Avoidance of social situations can start as early as age 2.

## What Are the Signs?

People with this condition often do the following:

- Say no to job opportunities, like a promotion, because they fear coworkers will criticize them.
- Skip meetings or group events.
- Avoid making new friends unless they are certain the person will like them.
- Wait for repeated proof that others accept them before joining a group or forming a close bond.
- Stay quiet in conversations because they fear being mocked or embarrassed.
- Avoid trying new things because they fear looking foolish.
- Make excuses to stay out of activities, even if the real reason is fear of being judged.
- Choose a simple, predictable life to feel safe and in control.

They are very sensitive to any sign of disapproval. They watch others closely for clues that they are being judged. Their nervous or tense look may make others tease them, which can make their fears feel true.

They often feel too shy or unsure to speak up. They think they are not good at socializing. They believe they are unattractive or less capable than others. This makes it hard to start or keep relationships.

Even though they want to connect with others, they stay away because they fear being hurt. This leads to loneliness and a lack of support when they need it.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor or mental health professional will look at a person’s history and behavior.

They use a guide called the *Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision* (DSM-5-TR) to make a diagnosis.

To be diagnosed, a person must show at least four of the following:

- They avoid work or social activities that involve talking to others because they fear criticism or rejection.
- They do not get close to others unless they are sure they will be liked.
- They hold back in close relationships because they fear being laughed at or humiliated.
- They are always worried about being criticized or rejected in social settings.
- They feel too unsure of themselves to join new social situations.
- They see themselves as socially awkward, unattractive, or not as good as others.
- They avoid new activities because they fear embarrassment.

These patterns must have started in early adulthood and lasted for many years.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment can help people feel more confident and less afraid in social situations.

### Types of Therapy

- **Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT)**: This helps people learn better social skills. It works well in group settings.
- **Group therapy**: Groups with others who have similar struggles can be helpful.
- **Supportive individual therapy**: Therapy that is kind and understanding of the person’s fears.
- **Psychodynamic therapy**: This helps people understand deep-rooted feelings and past experiences that affect their behavior.

### Medications

- **Antidepressants**, like selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), can help reduce anxiety.
- **Antianxiety medicines** can also help lower fear and nervousness.

These medicines can make it easier for people to try new things and face social situations.

### Important Notes

- Some people with this condition may not want to seek help because they fear being judged by a doctor or therapist.
- Treatment works best when the person feels safe and respected.
- Combining therapy and medicine often gives the best results.

With the right support, people with avoidant personality disorder can improve their confidence and build better relationships.

# The Complement System

The complement system is a group of proteins in your blood.  
It helps your body fight infections.  
It works by starting a local reaction that causes inflammation.  
This inflammation helps your body attack harmful invaders.

Most complement proteins are inactive when they travel in the blood.  
They become active only when needed.  
Some complement proteins stay on the surface of your cells.

The complement system connects two parts of your immune system:

- It helps your body make more antibodies.  
- It helps your body remember past infections.  
- It kills foreign cells, like bacteria.  
- It removes waste from the body, such as dead cells and immune complexes.

These proteins also do other important jobs, such as:

- Attracting immune cells to the site of infection.  
- Triggering the release of chemicals from certain immune cells.  
- This happens even without the involvement of a specific type of antibody called IgE.

# Enterococcal Infections

Enterococci are a type of bacteria. They are round in shape and live in the intestines of healthy people. Most of the time, they do not cause harm. But sometimes they can cause infections.

There are many types of enterococci. Some types live in the gut without causing problems. These are called normal bacteria. They only cause illness if they get into parts of the body where they do not belong.

The two most common types that cause infections in people are *Enterococcus faecalis* and *Enterococcus faecium*.

Enterococci can cause the following infections:

- Infections of the bladder or kidneys (urinary tract infections)
- Bacteria in the blood (bacteremia)
- Infection of the heart valves (endocarditis)
- Skin infections or infections under the skin (cellulitis)
- Infection of the prostate gland (prostatitis)
- Infections in wounds
- Pockets of pus in the abdomen (abdominal abscesses)

The symptoms you have depend on where the infection is in your body.

## Treating Enterococcal Infections

Doctors usually treat these infections with antibiotics. They may also drain any abscesses.

Some types of enterococci are resistant to many antibiotics. This means the usual medicines do not work. Infections caused by these resistant types are harder to treat.

One type that is especially hard to treat is resistant to vancomycin. This kind of infection is very difficult to cure.

# Clindamycin

Clindamycin is an antibiotic. It stops bacteria from growing. It does this by blocking a part of the bacteria’s protein-making system.

## How Clindamycin Works in the Body

You can take clindamycin by mouth or through a vein. It spreads well through body fluids, but not into the fluid around the brain and spinal cord. It builds up in certain white blood cells. Most of the drug is broken down in the body. The broken-down parts leave the body through the bile and urine.

## When Clindamycin Is Used

Clindamycin works against many types of bacteria. It is similar to another antibiotic called erythromycin. But it does not work well against some bacteria.

It works well against:
- Many anaerobic bacteria (bacteria that grow without oxygen)
- Some strains of methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus* (MRSA) that are common in the community
- Some strains of *Streptococcus pneumoniae* that are resistant to erythromycin but still sensitive to clindamycin

It does **not** work well against:
- *Mycoplasma*, *Chlamydia*, *Chlamydophila*, and *Legionella* bacteria
- Most aerobic gram-negative bacteria
- Enterococci

Clindamycin is often used to treat infections caused by anaerobic bacteria. But some of these bacteria are now resistant to clindamycin, especially *Bacteroides fragilis*. Because these infections often involve other types of bacteria, clindamycin is usually used with another antibiotic.

Clindamycin is used in combination with other drugs for:
- Infections caused by toxin-producing streptococci (used with penicillin to reduce toxin production)
- Brain infection caused by *Toxoplasma* (used with pyrimethamine)
- Babesiosis or severe malaria (used with quinine)
- Pneumonia caused by *Pneumocystis jirovecii* (used with primaquine)

In areas where community-associated MRSA is common, clindamycin may be used for skin and soft-tissue infections. But its use depends on local resistance patterns.

Some MRSA strains are sensitive to clindamycin but resistant to erythromycin. This resistance can happen in two ways:
- The bacteria pump out erythromycin (efflux mechanism)
- The bacteria change their protein-making system (ribosomal target modification)

If the resistance is due to the efflux mechanism, clindamycin will likely work.  
If the resistance is due to ribosomal changes, clindamycin may not work. In some cases, the bacteria can become resistant to both clindamycin and erythromycin during treatment.

A test called the D test can help tell the difference. It uses two antibiotic disks on a culture plate. A “D” shaped zone of no growth near the erythromycin disk means the bacteria are resistant due to ribosomal changes. If the test is positive, clindamycin should not be used for serious infections.

Clindamycin does not reach the brain or spinal fluid well. So it is not used for most brain or spinal cord infections—except for *Toxoplasma* brain infection.

Topical clindamycin (applied to the skin) is used to treat acne.

## Who Should Not Use Clindamycin

Do not use clindamycin if you have had an allergic reaction to it.  
Use with care if you have a history of:
- Crohn’s disease (regional enteritis)
- Ulcerative colitis
- Antibiotic-related colitis

## Clindamycin During Pregnancy and Breastfeeding

Animal studies did not show harm to unborn babies. In human studies, clindamycin use in the second and third trimesters was not linked to more birth defects. It can be used during pregnancy if needed.

Clindamycin passes into breast milk. It is not recommended to use during breastfeeding.

## Side Effects of Clindamycin

The most serious side effect is diarrhea caused by *Clostridioides difficile* (formerly *Clostridium difficile*). This can lead to severe colitis (inflammation of the colon).  
Clindamycin causes this more than any other antibiotic. The risk is about 20 times higher than with no antibiotic. Other antibiotics like fluoroquinolones and cephalosporins increase the risk 5 to 10 times.

Other side effects include:
- Skin rash (usually mild to moderate)
- Severe skin reactions (rare, but possible, including toxic epidermal necrolysis)
- Longer heart rhythm (QT interval) in people with multiple risk factors
- Esophagitis (inflammation of the esophagus) if the pill is not taken with water

## Dosing

No dose change is needed for kidney problems.  
Clindamycin is taken every 6 to 8 hours.

# Mite Bites

Mites are small creatures related to spiders. Some mites can bite people and animals. These biting mites can carry diseases that spread to humans.

(See also: Introduction to Bites and Stings and Tick Bites.)

Mite bites are common. They cause very itchy skin rashes. The most common causes include:

- Chiggers (mite larvae) – these cause intense itching.
- Scabies – a skin condition caused by mites that burrow under the skin.
- Other itchy rashes and skin problems.

The skin around the bite can become red, swollen, or sore. In some parts of Asia and in Australia, chiggers can spread a serious illness called scrub typhus.

## Where Mites Come From

Mites that bite can come from many sources:

- Birds
- Rats and other small rodents
- Cats, dogs (especially young ones), and rabbits
- Pigs
- Straw, hay, seeds, and other plant materials

Some mites bite and then burrow under the skin. Scabies is caused by this kind of mite. Another type, called Demodex mites, causes a similar rash, sometimes called mange. Other mites, like chiggers or certain bird mites, do not burrow. They just bite the skin.

Some mites do not bite at all. But they can still cause allergic reactions. These include:

- Grocer’s itch – a skin rash from touching stored grains, cheese, or other foods.
- Wheezing – a breathing problem caused by dust mite waste in pillows, mattresses, and carpets.

## How to Treat Mite Bites

To relieve itching, you can use:

- Creams or lotions that stop itching.
- Pills that reduce itching (antihistamines).
- Steroid creams to reduce swelling and redness.

If mites have burrowed under the skin, your doctor may give you antibiotics by mouth.

For scabies, your doctor will apply a special cream with permethrin or a solution with lindane. This kills the mites.

A steroid cream may be used for a few days to help with itching. If you use permethrin or lindane, apply it first. Then use the steroid cream if needed.

# Vancomycin

Vancomycin is an antibiotic that kills bacteria.  
It works by stopping bacteria from building their outer shell, which they need to survive.

---

## How Vancomycin Works in the Body

Vancomycin does not get absorbed well if you take it by mouth.  
If you get it through an IV, it spreads into your bile and fluid around the lungs, heart, joints, and belly.  
It does not go well into the fluid around the brain and spinal cord, even if that fluid is inflamed.  
The body removes vancomycin unchanged through the kidneys.

---

## When Vancomycin Is Used

Vancomycin works against many types of bacteria, including:

- Most staphylococcus bacteria (like *Staphylococcus aureus*) that do not respond to penicillin or cephalosporin.
- Many types of enterococci (mostly *Enterococcus faecalis*).
- Some strains of *Corynebacterium*.
- Certain types of streptococci, including those that cause pneumonia.

Some bacteria are already resistant to vancomycin.  
This includes many enterococci and some staphylococci.

Vancomycin is used to treat serious infections such as:

- Infections caused by methicillin-resistant staphylococci (MRSA).
- Infections caused by staphylococci that are resistant to other antibiotics.
- Infections caused by streptococci when you cannot use penicillin or similar drugs.
- Infections caused by enterococci when you cannot use penicillin or similar drugs.
- Infections of the heart valves (endocarditis) caused by resistant staphylococci or enterococci.

Vancomycin is not the best choice for infections caused by staphylococci that are still sensitive to methicillin.  
For those, other antibiotics work better.

Vancomycin is often used with other antibiotics when treating heart valve infections caused by resistant staphylococci or enterococci.

Vancomycin can be used for meningitis caused by pneumococci that are not very sensitive to penicillin.  
But it does not go well into the fluid around the brain.  
This makes it less effective, especially if you are also taking dexamethasone.  
There have been cases where treatment failed when vancomycin was used alone.

Oral vancomycin is used to treat diarrhea caused by *Clostridioides difficile* (formerly *Clostridium difficile*).  
This is a serious type of bowel infection that can cause severe diarrhea.

For mild cases of *C. difficile* infection, vancomycin is preferred over metronidazole.  
For severe cases, vancomycin is also preferred.  
If metronidazole does not work, vancomycin is a good next choice.

However, the latest guidelines say that if available, fidaxomicin is better than vancomycin for *C. difficile* infection.  
This is because fidaxomicin has a lower chance of the infection coming back.

---

## Who Should Not Use Vancomycin

Do not use vancomycin if you have ever had an allergic reaction to it.

---

## Using Vancomycin During Pregnancy and Breastfeeding

Animal studies have not shown harm to unborn babies.  
But there is not enough clear evidence in humans.  
Use vancomycin during pregnancy only if your doctor says it is needed.

Oral vancomycin can be used safely during pregnancy to treat *C. difficile* diarrhea.

Vancomycin passes into breast milk.  
Because of this, it is best to avoid using it while breastfeeding.  
This is to protect the baby’s gut bacteria.  
But since the baby’s body does not absorb much of the medicine from the milk, serious side effects in the baby are unlikely.

---

## Side Effects of Vancomycin

The most common side effect is an allergic reaction.  
This can include itching, redness, or a rash.  
It can also happen if the medicine is given too fast.

To avoid this, vancomycin should be given slowly through an IV.  
It should be diluted and given over at least 60 minutes.  
The rate should not be more than 10 milligrams per minute.

Other possible side effects include:

- Low white blood cell count (this usually goes back to normal).
- Low platelet count (this usually goes back to normal).
- Kidney problems — this is rare unless you take high doses or other kidney-damaging medicines at the same time.
- Some studies suggest that using vancomycin with piperacillin/tazobactam may increase the risk of kidney damage.
- Swelling or pain in the vein during IV use (phlebitis) — this is uncommon.

Hearing loss is rare with current forms of vancomycin.  
But it becomes more likely if you are also taking other medicines that can harm hearing.

---

## How to Dose Vancomycin

For infections of the brain (meningitis), higher doses are needed than usual.

If your kidneys are not working well, you will need a lower dose.

For serious infections caused by methicillin-resistant staphylococci (MRSA), the goal is to keep the level of vancomycin in your blood at a certain level.  
This is measured by a test called the area under the curve (AUC).  
The target AUC is 400 to 600.

Doctors used to use trough levels (the lowest level just before the next dose) as a guide.  
But this is no longer recommended.

Now, doctors use better methods to find the right dose.  
These include:

- Taking blood samples at two times: 1 to 2 hours after the IV ends, and just before the next dose.
- Using computer software to calculate the AUC.
- Using a continuous IV drip to reach a steady level of 17 to 25 micrograms per milliliter.

These dosing rules apply only to MRSA infections.  
They should not be used for other types of bacterial infections.

Over the past 10 years, some bacteria have become harder to treat with vancomycin.  
For *Staphylococcus aureus*, the sensitivity is measured like this:

- Less than or equal to 2 micrograms per milliliter: sensitive (the medicine works).
- 4 to 8 micrograms per milliliter: intermediate (the medicine may not work well).
- More than 8 micrograms per milliliter: resistant (the medicine does not work).

Even if the bacteria are labeled as sensitive, infections with a vancomycin level of 2 or higher may not respond well to standard doses.  
If your condition is not improving, your doctor may switch to a different medicine.

---

# Making Health Care Decisions

## Who Can Make Health Care Decisions?

In most states, people who are 18 years old or older can make their own health care choices. This includes decisions about treatment, tests, and care.

Some younger people can also make their own health care decisions. These are called emancipated minors. They are under 18 but are treated as adults by law. This usually applies to those who are married, living on their own, earning their own income, in the military, or have a court order saying they are independent.

In some states, a person can give consent for medical care at a younger age than 18. For example, in Alabama, a person can give consent for medical care at age 14, even though they are not considered an adult until age 19.

## When Someone Cannot Make Health Care Decisions

A person keeps the right to make their own decisions until a court says they are legally unable to do so. This is called legal incapacity.

Only a court can decide if someone is legally incapacitated. Doctors cannot make this decision.

To declare legal incapacity, a court must find that:

- The person has a serious condition that affects their thinking. This could be a mental illness, dementia, a brain injury, or long-term drug use.
- The person cannot understand information or make decisions about their life.
- The person cannot take care of their basic needs like food, safety, or health without help.
- A guardian or conservator is the only way to protect the person.

If a court finds someone legally incapacitated, it may appoint a guardian or conservator. This person then makes decisions for the individual.

Today, most states use the word “incapacity” instead of “incompetency.” They also see incapacity as task-specific. This means a person might not be able to handle money but can still make their own medical choices or decide where to live.

## Supporting People Who Need Help

Many states now support alternatives to guardianship. These help people keep their rights while getting help.

**Supported decision-making** is one option. It lets a person with a disability make their own choices with help from trusted people. These helpers can be family, friends, or professionals. The person still makes the final decision.

The support agreement should clearly say who is helping and how. It must also say the person being supported is still in charge.

**Technology** can also help. Devices like emergency alert systems, health monitors, or medicine reminder apps can help people stay independent.

## When a Doctor Says Someone Cannot Make a Decision

Doctors can judge if a person can make a health care decision at a given time. This is called clinical incapacity.

A doctor may say someone lacks clinical capacity if they cannot:

- Understand their health condition.
- Understand the benefits and risks of treatment and other options.
- Make or share a decision about care.

Clinical incapacity is not permanent. It only applies to one decision at a time.

For example, a person may be able to decide to get IV fluids but not be able to decide whether to join a research study.

Even if someone has some trouble thinking clearly, they may still be able to choose a person to make decisions for them if they become unable to do so.

People who are drunk, confused, in a coma, very depressed, or very upset may not be able to make decisions right now. But they may get better and be able to decide again later.

Doctors also check if a person can carry out a decision. For example, someone with a broken leg may be able to decide to go home but not be able to do it safely. In that case, the care team helps by providing support.

People with dementia may need a mental health check. This includes testing memory, thinking, and judgment. Those with mild dementia may still understand their doctor’s advice and make some choices.

## What Happens If a Person Cannot Make a Decision?

Doctors must follow a person’s wishes if they are able to express them.

Doctors cannot ignore a person’s wishes unless:

- A court says the person is legally incapacitated.
- The person’s wishes are not safe or ethical.

If a doctor thinks a person lacks clinical capacity, they will ask someone with legal authority to make decisions. This could be a person named in a health care power of attorney or a legally appointed surrogate.

If the person or their family disagrees with the doctor’s decision, the court may get involved.

In an emergency, people are assumed to agree to any treatment needed to save their life. This rule is rarely challenged in court.
