# Tests to Look at the Liver and Gallbladder

Imaging tests help doctors see inside your body.  
They are very useful for finding problems in the bile ducts and gallbladder.  
These tests can show if there is a lump or growth in the liver.  
They can also find an infection in the liver, such as an abscess.  
They can detect a tumor in the liver.  

However, imaging tests are not always good at finding certain liver problems.  
They may not clearly show issues that affect the whole liver.  
For example, they may not clearly show liver inflammation or scarring.  
These conditions include hepatitis and cirrhosis.

# Problems Moving Both Eyes Together

When you have a conjugate gaze palsy, both eyes cannot move in the same direction at the same time.  
This can happen when looking left or right, up, or down.  

Palsy means weakness or loss of movement. It can be mild or complete.  

Most often, the problem affects side-to-side movement.  
Upward movement is affected less often.  
Downward movement is affected the least.  

You might notice that you cannot look in certain directions.  

There is no direct treatment for this condition.  
But doctors will try to treat the cause if they can find one.  

---

## Side-to-Side Eye Movement Problems

The most common cause is damage to the brain stem.  
The brain stem is the lower part of the brain.  
This damage is often due to a stroke.  

When this happens, moving your eyes past the center line is very hard.  
For example, if you are looking straight ahead, it is hard to move your eyes fully to the opposite side.  

Some people have milder problems.  
They may have trouble keeping their eyes fixed on one thing for long.  
They may also have nystagmus.  

Nystagmus means the eye moves quickly in one direction, then slowly drifts back.  
This happens over and over.  

Damage to the front part of the brain (the cerebrum) can also cause this problem.  
This is usually from a stroke.  
The weakness is often not as bad as when the brain stem is damaged.  
Symptoms may get better over time.  

---

## Up and Down Eye Movement Problems

It is normal for upward and downward eye movement to slow down as you get older.  
But a gaze palsy is much worse than normal aging.  

Upward movement is usually affected first.  

The most common cause is damage to the top part of the brain stem.  
This is called the midbrain.  
Damage can be from a stroke or a tumor.  

### Upward Gaze Palsy

When you have this problem, your pupils may be wide open.  
When you try to look up, your eye moves quickly up, then slowly drifts back down.  
This is nystagmus.  

### Parinaud Syndrome

This is a type of upward gaze palsy.  
It is often caused by a tumor near the pineal gland.  
This tumor presses on the part of the brain that controls eye movement.  
It can also be caused by a stroke.  

People with Parinaud syndrome tend to look down.  
Their eyelids are pulled back.  
Their pupils are wide open.  
They may also have nystagmus.  

### Downward Gaze Palsy

If only downward movement is affected, but upward movement is normal,  
the most likely cause is progressive supranuclear palsy.

# Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP)

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is a serious and sudden illness.  
It causes low platelet counts.  
It also causes damage to red blood cells.  
It can harm organs like the brain, kidneys, and gut.  

Some people with TTP feel confused or weak.  
Others may have kidney problems.  
The illness can be life-threatening if not treated quickly.  

Doctors diagnose TTP by checking blood tests.  
They look for signs of damaged red blood cells.  
They also check for very low levels of a protein called ADAMTS13.  

Treatment includes plasma exchange.  
This means replacing the patient’s plasma with healthy donor plasma.  
Steroid medicines are often used.  
Another medicine called rituximab is also used.  
A rare medicine called caplacizumab may be used in some cases.  

TTP is a type of blood vessel disease called thrombotic microangiopathy.  
It happens when a key enzyme called ADAMTS13 is missing or not working.  
This enzyme normally breaks down a large protein called von Willebrand factor.  
Without it, the large von Willebrand factor builds up and causes blood clots in small blood vessels.  

Another similar illness is hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS).  
HUS is often caused by a bacterial infection.  
It can also be linked to problems in the body’s immune system.  

---

## How TTP Works in the Body

TTP damages small blood vessels.  
It causes platelets and red blood cells to stick together and form clots.  
These clots block blood flow.  
This harms organs and causes low platelet counts and anemia.  

The clots form mainly in the tiny vessels between arteries and capillaries.  
The brain, stomach, and kidneys are most likely to be affected.  
Kidney damage is common, but severe kidney failure is rare in TTP.  

The clots in TTP are different from those in other diseases.  
They do not contain red blood cells or fibrin.  
They also do not cause the inflammation seen in vasculitis.  
Large blood vessel clots are uncommon.  

---

## What Causes TTP

TTP happens when the enzyme ADAMTS13 is missing or not working.  
This can be due to a gene problem (inherited) or an immune reaction (acquired).  

Most cases are acquired.  
The body makes an antibody that attacks ADAMTS13.  
This stops the enzyme from working.  

A rare inherited form is called Upshaw-Schulman syndrome.  
It is passed down through families and caused by a gene mutation.  

In many cases, doctors do not know why the body makes the harmful antibody.  
But certain factors increase the risk:  
- Being female  
- Using desmopressin (a medicine for some types of bleeding)  
- Being pregnant  
- Being Black (based on U.S. studies, this group has a much higher risk)  

---

## Symptoms of TTP

The inherited form often shows up in babies or young children.  
The acquired form usually affects adults.  

Symptoms can start slowly or come on suddenly.  
Without treatment, the illness gets worse and is often deadly.  

Anemia causes tiredness and weakness.  
Low platelets cause easy bruising or bleeding.  

Clots in small blood vessels can cause:  
- Weakness  
- Confusion  
- Seizures  
- Coma  
- Belly pain  
- Nausea or vomiting  
- Fast or irregular heartbeat  

Fever is not common in TTP.  

TTP and hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) have similar symptoms.  
But TTP more often causes brain problems.  
HUS more often causes kidney failure.  

---

## How Doctors Diagnose TTP

Doctors suspect TTP if a patient has:  
- Low platelet count  
- Anemia  
- Signs of damaged red blood cells  

They do a full blood test.  
This includes checking platelets, red blood cells, and other blood values.  

They also do a blood smear.  
This shows if red blood cells are broken into small pieces.  
These broken cells are called schistocytes.  

Other tests include:  
- Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) – high levels mean red blood cells are breaking down  
- Haptoglobin – low levels mean red blood cells are being destroyed  
- Bilirubin – high levels mean red blood cells are breaking down  
- Direct antiglobulin test – this must be negative in TTP  
- Coagulation tests – these should be normal in TTP  

Doctors also test for ADAMTS13 activity and antibodies.  
They do this to confirm the diagnosis.  

The PLASMIC score helps doctors estimate how likely TTP is.  
It helps guide treatment decisions.  

If TTP is suspected, treatment should start right away.  
Even before test results come back.  
This is because waiting can be dangerous.  

A diagnosis of TTP is likely if:  
- Platelet count is low  
- Blood smear shows broken red blood cells  
- Tests show red blood cells are being destroyed  
- Direct antiglobulin test is negative  
- Coagulation tests are normal  

If ADAMTS13 levels are below 10% and antibodies are found, it confirms most cases of TTP.  
These patients respond well to plasma exchange and immune-suppressing medicines.  

If ADAMTS13 levels are normal and no antibodies are found, TTP is unlikely.  
Other causes must be checked.  
These include:  
- Blood clots in many places (disseminated intravascular coagulation)  
- Infection (sepsis)  
- Hidden cancer with blood clots  
- Preeclampsia (a serious pregnancy condition)  
- Autoimmune diseases like lupus or scleroderma  
- Very high blood pressure  
- Kidney transplant rejection  
- Certain medicines (like quinine, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, or some cancer drugs)  

Some people have low ADAMTS13 but no antibodies.  
These patients may have the inherited form.  
They need genetic testing to confirm.  
They only need plasma infusions, not immune-suppressing drugs.  

Genetic testing is also needed if:  
- Symptoms start in childhood  
- Symptoms happen during pregnancy  
- The illness comes back  
- There is a family history of TTP  

If a person has low platelets and broken red blood cells with no other cause, doctors can suspect TTP.  

---

## How TTP Is Treated

Plasma exchange is the main treatment.  
It must start right away.  
It is done daily for days or weeks.  
It continues until blood counts and other tests return to normal.  

Most patients also get steroid medicines.  
Another medicine called rituximab is often used too.  

Caplacizumab is used in rare cases.  
It blocks the large von Willebrand factor from sticking to platelets.  
It may help speed up recovery.  
But it can increase the risk of bleeding.  
It does not cure TTP on its own.  
It may reduce the need for plasma exchange.  
But its role is still debated.  
The International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis recommends it only in certain cases.  

Without treatment, TTP is almost always fatal.  
With treatment, over 90% of patients recover fully.  

---

## Important Tips

- If a person has unexplained low platelets and broken red blood cells, think TTP.  
- Start plasma exchange right away.  

- Caplacizumab may help some patients.  
- But it can cause bleeding.  
- It is expensive and not always needed.  

Most people have only one episode of TTP.  
But about 40% of patients with a strong immune attack on ADAMTS13 will have a relapse.  
If symptoms return after stopping treatment, more immune-suppressing medicine may help.  
Patients must see a doctor quickly if symptoms come back.  

---

## Key Facts

- TTP destroys platelets and red blood cells in small blood vessels.  
- This causes low platelets, anemia, and organ damage.  
- The cause is usually a missing or faulty enzyme called ADAMTS13.  
- This is often due to an immune attack on the enzyme.  
- Rarely, it is due to a gene problem.  
- Without treatment, TTP is almost always fatal.  
- With fast treatment, over 85% of patients survive.

# Parathyroid Tumors

The parathyroid glands are small. They sit close to the thyroid gland in the neck.  
Their exact position can vary. Some people have four glands. Others may have more or fewer.  

These glands make a hormone called parathyroid hormone.  
This hormone helps control the amount of calcium in your blood and body tissues.  
It works by affecting your bones, kidneys, and gut.

Most parathyroid tumors are not cancer.  
They are harmless growths.  
But they still make too much parathyroid hormone.

Too much parathyroid hormone causes high levels of calcium in the blood.  
This condition is called hyperparathyroidism.  
High calcium in the blood is called hypercalcemia.

At first, high calcium may cause:  
- Feeling weak or tired  
- Constipation  
- Not wanting to eat  
- Trouble focusing  
- Memory problems  
- Needing to urinate more often  

If calcium levels get very high, it can cause confusion.  
In serious cases, it can lead to coma.  
If not treated, this condition can be life threatening.

---

## Parathyroid Adenoma

A parathyroid adenoma is a noncancerous tumor.  
It makes too much parathyroid hormone.  
This causes hyperparathyroidism.

High levels of parathyroid hormone cause:  
- Low levels of phosphate in the blood (hypophosphatemia)  
- Loss of calcium and phosphate from bones into the blood (bone breakdown)  
- Weakened bones (osteoporosis)

Most parathyroid adenomas are single and isolated.  
They are more common in older women.  
But some people get more than one adenoma.  
This can happen in rare inherited conditions called multiple endocrine neoplasia, or MEN.

MEN is a family condition.  
It causes several hormone-making glands to grow abnormal or cancerous tumors.  
Sometimes the glands just get bigger without forming tumors.

Most parathyroid adenomas do not cause symptoms.  
They are found when a blood test for another reason shows high calcium.  

If symptoms do appear, they are usually due to high calcium or kidney stones.

Doctors diagnose hyperparathyroidism when:  
- Blood tests show high calcium  
- Blood tests also show high parathyroid hormone  

If both are high, further tests are needed. These include:  
- Checking calcium levels in blood and urine  
- Checking phosphate levels in blood and urine  
- Imaging tests to check bone strength and look for kidney stones  

To find the tumor before surgery, doctors may use:  
- High-resolution CT scans  
- MRI scans  
- Ultrasound  
- Angiography  
- Biopsy (in some cases)

Treatment is usually surgery to remove the affected gland.  
For people with only slightly high calcium and no symptoms, doctors may choose to watch closely instead. This is called active surveillance.

Sometimes doctors prescribe medicine to lower parathyroid hormone.  
Medicines used include cinacalcet and etelcalcetide.  
These help reduce hormone release.

---

## Parathyroid Cancer

Parathyroid cancer is very rare.

Risk factors include:  
- Radiation treatment to the neck in the past  
- A family history of parathyroid tumors  
- Having multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndrome

Cancer in the parathyroid gland causes more severe hyperparathyroidism and higher calcium levels than a benign adenoma.

Symptoms come from high calcium.  
They include:  
- Weakness and fatigue  
- Constipation  
- Loss of appetite  
- Trouble concentrating  
- Memory problems  
- Confusion  
- Urinating more often

Doctors diagnose parathyroid cancer with:  
- Blood tests to check for high parathyroid hormone  
- Imaging tests to find the tumor  

Because some families have a history of this cancer, doctors may suggest genetic testing for other family members.

Treatment usually starts with surgery to remove the cancer.  
In some cases, radiation therapy or chemotherapy is also needed.

Parathyroid cancer grows slowly.  
If the surgeon removes the entire tumor, long-term survival is likely.  
If the cancer comes back, it usually grows slowly and stays in the neck area.  
In rare cases, it spreads to other parts of the body.

# What Is Homeopathy?

Homeopathy is a type of medicine that started in Germany in the late 1700s.  
It is based on the idea that "like cures like."  
This means a substance that causes certain symptoms in large amounts may help treat those same symptoms when used in very tiny amounts.  

The tiny amount is believed to help the body heal itself.  
Treatment is based on your personal health, lifestyle, and symptoms.  
It is not based on how chemicals or body systems work.  

Homeopathic remedies come from natural sources.  
These include plants, minerals, and other natural materials.  
They are made by diluting the substance many times.  
The more it is diluted, the stronger it is believed to be.  

Some remedies are so diluted that they contain no trace of the original substance.  
For example, a 30C dilution means the substance was diluted 100 times, 30 times in a row.  
This results in a final amount so small it is nearly impossible to measure.  

You can buy homeopathic products without a prescription.  
You can also get them from a homeopathic provider.  

---

## How Is Homeopathy Regulated?

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration regulates homeopathic remedies.  
Only remedies approved by the FDA can be made.  
The active ingredient is tested before it is diluted.  

But the FDA does not require the following for homeopathic products:  
- Proof that the active ingredient is what it says it is.  
- Proof that the remedy works.  
- Limits on how much alcohol (a common liquid used in dilution) the product can contain.  

However, the label must include:  
- The name of the manufacturer.  
- The word “homeopathic.”  
- At least one health condition the product is meant to treat.  
- Instructions for safe use.  
- The name of the active ingredient and how much it was diluted, unless exempt.  

---

## Is Homeopathy Effective?

The two main ideas in homeopathy are:  
- Like cures like.  
- The more diluted a remedy, the stronger it becomes.  

But science says this is not possible.  
A remedy with no active ingredient cannot have a real effect on the body.  
Any effect it has is likely due to the placebo effect.  

Some homeopathic products do contain active ingredients in measurable amounts.  
For example, Zicam contains zinc, which can have a real effect on the body.  

Many studies have looked at whether homeopathy works.  
A 2010 review of all major studies found no evidence that homeopathy works better than a placebo.  
The United Kingdom’s science committee reached the same conclusion after reviewing all the evidence.  

Australia’s government reviewed the evidence in 2013.  
It found no proof that homeopathy works for 61 health conditions.  
For 7 other conditions, there was no strong evidence at all.  

Later reviews confirmed these findings.  
They showed that homeopathy does not work better than a placebo.  
The quality of the studies on homeopathy is generally low.  

Still, some people use homeopathy for conditions where standard medicine has no clear benefit.  
For example, in fibromyalgia, some small studies suggest it may help with symptoms.  
It also seems to cause little harm.  

---

## Where Is Homeopathy Used?

Homeopathy is common in Europe and India.  
This is because it has been used for a long time.  
It has become part of the culture in these places.  

It is used to treat many conditions, including:  
- Allergies  
- Runny nose and sinus problems  
- Breathing issues  
- Digestive problems  
- Muscle and joint pain  
- Dizziness  

---

## Possible Side Effects

Homeopathy is usually safe and causes few side effects.  
Very rarely, a person may have an allergic or toxic reaction.  

Some studies have compared side effects of homeopathy and regular medicine.  
But more high-quality research is needed to compare them fairly.  

Do not assume homeopathic remedies are completely harmless.  
Even though most are so diluted they have no effect, some contain real medicine.  
These can cause side effects.  

Some people call dietary supplements “homeopathic” even when they are not.  
This can be confusing.  
Also, the FDA allows some plant-based medicines to be labeled as homeopathic if they go through a special process.  

---

### Key Points to Remember

- Do not assume homeopathic remedies are inactive.  
- Most are so diluted they have no effect.  
- But some contain real ingredients that can affect the body.  
- Always check what is in a remedy before using it.

# How the Body Processes Medicines

Your body changes medicines in a process called drug metabolism.

This happens mainly in the liver. The liver uses special proteins called enzymes to change medicines.

Some medicines are given in a form that is not active. The body turns them into an active form. These active forms are what help treat your condition.

The body may change a medicine into a substance called a metabolite. This metabolite might:
- Work the same way as the original medicine.
- Work differently.
- Stop working completely.

Some medicines are made into a form that is not active. The body then changes that form into a working version.

Metabolites can be changed again. This happens until the body can get rid of them.

The body removes medicines and their byproducts through the urine or bile.

## How the Liver Handles Medicines

The liver is the main place where medicines are changed. It uses a group of enzymes called cytochrome P-450 enzymes.

These enzymes control how fast many medicines are broken down.

The liver can only handle so much at once. If there is too much medicine in the blood, the enzymes can become overwhelmed.

## Things That Change How Medicines Are Processed

Many things can affect how well the liver enzymes work. These include:
- Other medicines.
- Foods.
- Supplements.

If something slows down the enzymes, the medicine stays in your body longer. This can make the medicine stronger and increase side effects.

If something speeds up the enzymes, the medicine breaks down faster. This can make the medicine less effective.

## Age and Drug Metabolism

Newborn babies have underdeveloped liver enzymes. This means they cannot process some medicines well.

Older adults also have slower enzyme activity. Like babies, they may need lower doses of medicine.

So both newborns and older adults often need smaller doses per pound of body weight than younger adults.

## Health Conditions and Drug Metabolism

Certain health problems can change how the liver works. These include:
- Liver disease.
- Kidney disease.
- Cystic fibrosis.

These conditions can make it harder for the body to process medicines.

## Genetics and Medicine Processing

People are born with different versions of the enzymes that break down medicines.

This means some people process certain medicines faster or slower than others.

For example, differences in genes can affect how well these medicines work:
- Clopidogrel (a blood thinner).
- Warfarin (a blood thinner).
- Omeprazole (a medicine for acid reflux).
- Codeine (a pain medicine).

Some people may have a higher risk of side effects from these medicines because of their genes.

## How Medicines Move in the Liver

Genes can also affect how medicines move into and out of the liver.

This can increase the risk of liver damage from certain medicines.

For example, some people may be more likely to get liver injury from statins (cholesterol medicines) because of how their body moves these drugs.

# Fibroids During Pregnancy

Fibroids are non-cancerous growths in the uterus.  
They are common and often do not cause any symptoms.  

During pregnancy, fibroids usually do not cause problems.  
But sometimes they can cause pain.  
This pain happens when the fibroid breaks down or changes.  

Fibroids can increase the chance of some pregnancy complications.  
These include:

- Labor starting too early  
- The baby not being in the right position for birth  
- The placenta covering the opening of the uterus (placenta previa)  
- The placenta coming loose too soon (placental abruption)  
- Losing the pregnancy early (miscarriage)  
- Heavy bleeding after delivery  

In rare cases, a fibroid can block part of the birth canal.  
This can make delivery harder.  

If you have very large fibroids, or if you have fibroids and have had a miscarriage before,  
talk to your doctor before getting pregnant.  
A check-up before pregnancy can help you plan for a healthier pregnancy.

# Eosinophilic Pneumonia

Eosinophilic pneumonia is a lung condition where a type of white blood cell called an eosinophil builds up in the lungs and often in the blood.

- Some health problems, medicines, chemicals, fungi, or parasites can cause this buildup.
- People may cough, wheeze, or feel short of breath. In some cases, breathing becomes so hard that it is life-threatening.
- Doctors use chest x-rays and blood tests to find the condition and figure out what is causing it. If parasites are suspected, extra tests are done.
- Steroids are usually given to reduce swelling and ease symptoms.

---

## What Are Eosinophils?

Eosinophils are a type of white blood cell. They help the body fight infections and play a role in allergic reactions. Their numbers go up during allergies and inflammation. This includes asthma, which often happens with some types of eosinophilic pneumonia.

Eosinophilic pneumonia is not like regular pneumonia. It is not caused by bacteria, viruses, or fungi in the tiny air sacs of the lungs. But the air sacs and airways can fill with eosinophils. In some cases, the walls of blood vessels in the lungs can also be affected. If asthma develops, mucus can build up and block the airways.

---

## Löffler Syndrome

Löffler syndrome is a mild form of eosinophilic pneumonia.

- It may cause no symptoms at all.
- Or it may cause a dry cough, wheezing, or mild shortness of breath.
- Sometimes a fever is present.
- Doctors diagnose it using a chest x-ray and blood tests that show high levels of eosinophils.
- It is often linked to a worm infection, especially with roundworms like *Ascaris lumbricoides*.
- In some people, no cause is found.
- The condition usually gets better on its own within one month.
- Doctors may give steroids to reduce symptoms and swelling.

---

## What Causes Eosinophilic Pneumonia?

The exact reason eosinophils gather in the lungs is not fully known. But it may be an allergic reaction. Often, the trigger is not found. Still, some known causes include:

- Cigarette smoke (only in acute cases)
- Certain medicines:
  - Penicillin
  - Aminosalicylic acid
  - Carbamazepine
  - Tryptophan
  - Naproxen
  - Isoniazid
  - Nitrofurantoin
  - Phenytoin
  - Sulfonamides (like sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim)
- Chemical fumes, such as from cocaine or nickel vapor
- Fungi, especially *Aspergillus fumigatus*
- Parasites, especially roundworms
- Other body-wide diseases, such as eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis

---

## Symptoms of Eosinophilic Pneumonia

Symptoms can be mild or very serious. They can come on quickly or develop slowly.

### Acute Eosinophilic Pneumonia

- Comes on fast, over hours or days.
- Causes fever, chest pain that gets worse when breathing deeply, shortness of breath, and cough.
- You may feel generally unwell.
- Oxygen levels in the blood can drop quickly.
- Without treatment, it can lead to sudden breathing failure in a few hours or days.

### Löffler Syndrome

- May not cause any symptoms.
- Or it may cause mild breathing problems like coughing, wheezing, or shortness of breath.
- Most people get better quickly.

### Chronic Eosinophilic Pneumonia

- Develops slowly over days or weeks.
- Can become serious over time.
- May go away on its own, but often comes back.
- Can get worse over weeks or months.
- Without treatment, it can lead to life-threatening shortness of breath.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to diagnose eosinophilic pneumonia.

### Chest X-ray
- Used first to look at the lungs.
- In acute cases, the x-ray usually shows changes.
- In chronic cases, the x-ray can help confirm the diagnosis.

### CT Scan of the Chest
- Often needed for a clear picture.
- Helps in diagnosing both acute and chronic forms.

### Blood Tests
- Check how many eosinophils are in the blood.
- In acute cases, the count may be normal.
- In chronic cases, the count is often very high—up to 10 to 15 times normal.

### Bronchoscopy
- A thin tube is passed into the lungs.
- Fluid is collected from the air sacs.
- A lab checks the fluid under a microscope.
- It usually shows clumps of eosinophils.

### Other Tests
- Stool tests may be done to check for worms or other parasites.
- Tests may also look for fungal infections.

### Pulmonary Function Tests
- Measure how well the lungs work.
- Check how much air the lungs can hold.
- Check how well air moves in and out.
- Check how well oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged.
- These tests help confirm the diagnosis.

---

## How Is It Treated?

### Steroids
- Steroids (like prednisone) are the main treatment.
- They reduce swelling and help the lungs work better.

### Acute Eosinophilic Pneumonia
- Steroids are usually needed.
- Most people get better quickly with treatment.

### Chronic Eosinophilic Pneumonia
- Steroids may be needed for many months or even years.
- Treatment may need to continue for a long time to prevent relapses.

### If You Have Wheezing
- Treatments used for asthma are also used.
- These help open the airways.

### If Parasites Are the Cause
- Specific medicines are given to kill the worms or other parasites.

### If a Medicine Is the Cause
- The medicine is stopped if possible.
- This can help the condition improve.

---

**Note:** This condition is not the same as regular pneumonia. It is not caused by infection. It is caused by an overactive immune response in the lungs.

# Vitamin E Deficiency

## What Is Vitamin E?

Vitamin E is a group of related substances found in food. The most important one is called alpha-tocopherol. Other forms include beta-, gamma-, and delta-tocopherols, and tocotrienols. These substances help protect your body’s cells from damage.

Vitamin E works as an antioxidant. This means it helps stop harmful chemical reactions in your body’s fats. These reactions can harm cell membranes.

Good sources of vitamin E include vegetable oils, nuts, seeds, and some green leafy vegetables.

## Who Gets Vitamin E Deficiency?

In countries where people do not have enough to eat, vitamin E deficiency is common. It happens because people do not get enough vitamin E in their food.

In other countries, most people get enough vitamin E. When deficiency happens, it is usually because the body cannot absorb fats properly.

## Causes of Vitamin E Deficiency

- Not eating enough vitamin E-rich foods.
- Problems with fat absorption in the gut. This can happen with:
  - Abetalipoproteinemia (a rare genetic disease).
  - Chronic liver or bile duct disease.
  - Pancreatitis (inflammation of the pancreas).
  - Short bowel syndrome (a condition where part of the intestine is missing or not working).
  - Cystic fibrosis (a genetic disease affecting the lungs and digestive system).
- A rare genetic problem that affects how the liver handles vitamin E, even if fat absorption is normal.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main signs of vitamin E deficiency are:

- Mild anemia (low red blood cell count).
- Nerve problems, such as unsteadiness, numbness, or weakness.

In children with abetalipoproteinemia, nerve and eye problems get worse over time. These issues often start in the first 20 years of life.

In preterm babies, vitamin E deficiency may lead to:
- Eye damage (retinopathy of prematurity).
- Bleeding in the brain (intraventricular or subependymal hemorrhage).
- Weak muscles.

In children with long-term liver disease or cystic fibrosis, vitamin E deficiency can cause:
- Trouble walking steadily (spinocerebellar ataxia).
- Loss of reflexes.
- Loss of feeling in hands and feet.
- Trouble feeling vibrations or knowing where limbs are.
- Weak eye muscles (ophthalmoplegia).
- Drooping eyelids (ptosis).
- Slurred speech (dysarthria).

In adults with fat absorption problems, nerve issues are rare. This is because adults store large amounts of vitamin E in body fat.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors check for vitamin E deficiency by measuring levels in the blood.

The best test is the ratio of alpha-tocopherol to total lipids (fats) in the blood. A low ratio means vitamin E deficiency.

A normal alpha-tocopherol level in adults is between 5 and 20 micrograms per milliliter (mcg/mL).  
If the level is below 5 mcg/mL, it suggests deficiency.

If a person has high fat levels in the blood, the ratio test is more accurate than the level alone.

In people with abetalipoproteinemia, vitamin E levels are usually undetectable.

A test that checks how red blood cells break down under stress can suggest deficiency. But this test is not specific and is not used alone.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment is vitamin E supplements.

- For most people: Take oral vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol) daily.
- For people with nerve problems or fat absorption issues: Higher doses are needed.
- For severe cases, such as abetalipoproteinemia, high-dose injections may be needed.

Mixed tocopherols (a mix of alpha-, beta-, and gamma-tocopherols) can also be used.

## Can It Be Prevented?

- Full-term babies get enough vitamin E from breast milk or infant formula.
- Preterm babies may need extra vitamin E, but only if advised by a doctor.

## Important Facts

- Vitamin E deficiency is usually due to poor diet in food-insecure areas.
- In other areas, it is usually due to fat absorption problems.
- The main problems are mild anemia and nerve issues.
- If someone has risk factors and symptoms, doctors should test their vitamin E level.
- Treatment is vitamin E supplements.

## Supplements: Do They Help?

- High-dose vitamin E supplements do not prevent cancer or heart disease.
- The US Preventive Services Task Force advises against taking high-dose vitamin E for these reasons.
- There is no strong proof that vitamin E slows down Alzheimer’s disease.
- One study found that vitamin E supplements may increase the risk of prostate cancer.
- It is unclear if vitamin E helps with tardive dyskinesia (a movement disorder).

## Units of Measurement

- Many products list vitamin E in international units (IU).
- Doctors now recommend using milligrams of alpha-tocopherol instead.

# How the Body Fights Infection

If your body had no way to fight infections, germs would quickly take over. These defenses only work when your body is alive and healthy. After death, the body starts to break down because the defenses stop working.

Your body has two main ways to fight germs:  
- Natural barriers  
- The immune system  

(See also: Lines of Defense)

---

## Natural Barriers That Keep Germs Out

Your skin is the first line of defense. It blocks germs unless it is broken. A cut, insect bite, or burn can let germs in.

Mucous membranes line parts of your body like your mouth, nose, vagina, and eyelids. These membranes are covered in fluids that fight germs. For example, your eyes are protected by tears. Tears contain an enzyme called lysozyme. This enzyme kills bacteria and helps keep your eyes safe.

Your airways filter the air you breathe. The inside of your nose and air passages are coated with mucus. When you breathe in, germs stick to the mucus. Tiny hairlike structures (called cilia) move the mucus up and out of your airways. You either cough it up or blow it out of your nose.

Your digestive tract has strong defenses. Stomach acid kills many germs. Pancreatic enzymes and bile also help destroy germs. The movement of your intestines (called peristalsis) pushes food through your gut. When you go to the bathroom, waste and any germs are removed. The lining of your intestines also sheds old cells. This helps wash away harmful germs.

Your urinary tract has defenses too. The urethra is the tube that carries urine out of your body. In men, the urethra is long. This makes it hard for germs to reach the bladder. In women, the urethra is shorter. This means germs can sometimes get into the bladder. But when you urinate, the flow flushes out any germs that made it in.

The vagina is normally acidic. This acid stops harmful bacteria from growing. It also helps keep helpful bacteria in balance.

---

## How the Blood Helps Fight Infection

When germs get past the body’s barriers, the blood steps in. It sends more white blood cells to the infected area.

Two types of white blood cells are especially important:  
- Neutrophils  
- Monocytes  

Neutrophils arrive first. They eat and destroy germs. If the infection lasts, monocytes arrive next. They also eat germs and help clean up dead tissue.

The bone marrow makes these white blood cells. When an infection starts, the body releases more white blood cells from the bone marrow into the blood. The blood carries them to the site of infection.

Another type of white blood cell, called eosinophils, increases during allergies and some parasite infections. But it does not usually rise during bacterial infections.

Some serious infections—like typhoid fever, viral infections, or overwhelming bacterial infections—can actually lower the number of white blood cells. This weakens the body’s ability to fight.

---

## What Happens During Inflammation

Any injury, including a germ invasion, causes inflammation. Inflammation is the body’s way of responding to damage.

When tissue is hurt, it releases chemicals. These chemicals do several things:  
- They block off the damaged area  
- They send immune cells to attack germs  
- They help remove dead or damaged tissue  
- They start the healing process  

Inflammation may not stop a large number of germs.

When inflammation happens:  
- Blood flow increases to the area  
- This makes the area red and warm  
- Blood vessel walls become leaky  
- Fluid and white blood cells move into the tissue  
- The tissue swells because of extra fluid  

White blood cells attack the germs. They also release more chemicals that keep the inflammation going.

Some chemicals cause tiny blood vessels to clot. This slows the spread of germs and their toxins.

The chemicals from inflammation also affect nerves. This causes pain. They also cause common symptoms like chills, fever, and muscle aches.

---

## How the Immune System Responds

When an infection starts, your immune system kicks in. It makes special tools to target the specific germ.

These tools include:  
- Killer T cells: a type of white blood cell that finds and kills germs  
- Antibodies: proteins that lock onto germs  

Antibodies stop germs from moving. They can kill germs directly. Or they help other white blood cells find and destroy the germs.

How well your immune system works depends partly on your genes. Some people are naturally better at fighting certain infections.

---

## What Is Fever?

Fever is a normal response to infection or injury. Your body temperature goes up to help fight the infection. Even though it feels uncomfortable, fever helps your body defend itself.

A part of your brain called the hypothalamus controls your body temperature. During fever, the hypothalamus resets the body’s thermostat to a higher level.

To raise your temperature:  
- Blood moves from your skin to deeper inside your body  
- This reduces heat loss  
- You may shiver (chills) to make more heat  

Your body keeps raising heat until your blood reaches the brain at the new, higher temperature. Then it stays at that level.

Later, when the infection is under control, the brain resets the thermostat back to normal. Your body then cools down by sweating and sending blood to the skin.

Some people cannot raise their temperature during infection. This includes very young children, older adults, and people with alcohol use disorder. In severe infections, these people may actually get a drop in body temperature instead of a fever.

# Pleural Biopsy

A pleural biopsy takes a small sample of the lining around the lungs.  
This test helps find out if there is cancer or an infection.  

It is used when fluid builds up in the space around the lungs (called a pleural effusion).  
If a test called thoracentesis does not give a clear answer, a biopsy may be needed.  

This test works better for finding tuberculosis than for finding cancer.  
Newer lab tests and better tools for looking at fluid have made biopsies less common.  

Only a doctor trained in this test should do it.  
The patient must be able to follow instructions.  
The patient must also have normal blood clotting.  

The biopsy is done the same way as thoracentesis.  
It can be done at the bedside.  
No special preparation is needed.  

The doctor takes at least three samples from the same spot on the skin.  
The needle is moved to three different positions: 3 o’clock, 6 o’clock, and 9 o’clock.  
This helps get enough tissue for testing.  

After the biopsy, a chest x-ray is needed.  
There is a higher risk of complications than with thoracentesis.  
The most common risks are air in the chest (pneumothorax) and blood in the chest (hemothorax).

# Other Spotted Fevers

Other spotted fevers are illnesses caused by tiny bacteria called rickettsiae. These bacteria are passed to people through tick bites. The diseases are similar to Rocky Mountain spotted fever but usually less severe.

## What Causes Other Spotted Fevers?

- A tick that carries the bacteria bites a person.
- The bacteria live only inside the cells of other living things.
- The bite causes a small sore that turns into a black scab.
- Nearby lymph nodes may swell.
- A red rash usually appears a few days after the fever starts.

## Types of Spotted Fevers

These are the main types:

- African tick bite fever (also called African tick typhus)
- Mediterranean spotted fever (also called boutonneuse fever)
- North Asian tick-borne rickettsiosis
- Queensland tick typhus
- Rickettsialpox
- Rickettsia parkeri rickettsiosis

These diseases can happen in the United States and other parts of the world. They are most common in spring and summer. This is when adult ticks are active and people spend more time outdoors. In warm areas, they can happen any time of year.

Mediterranean spotted fever can happen all year in the Mediterranean region. This is because it is spread by the brown dog tick, which can live indoors.

## Symptoms

Symptoms usually start 5 to 7 days after a tick bite.

- You get a fever, feel tired, have muscle aches, and get headaches.
- Your eyes may look red.
- You feel generally unwell.
- A small sore with a black scab forms at the bite site.
- Nearby lymph nodes may swell.
- About 4 days after the fever starts, a red rash appears on your forearms.
- The rash spreads to most of your body, including your palms and soles.
- The fever usually lasts more than a week.

If treated early, these infections rarely cause serious harm or death. Older adults and people who are already sick are more likely to have problems.

## How Doctors Diagnose These Infections

Doctors look at your symptoms and your history of tick exposure.

They may do:

- A skin biopsy: A small sample of the rash is taken and tested.
- A blood test: This checks for antibodies to the bacteria.

To confirm the diagnosis, doctors often need to do two blood tests. One is done when you first get sick. A second is done 1 to 3 weeks later. If the antibody level goes up, it means you have the infection.

The first blood test alone is not enough. It cannot give a clear answer right away.

## Treatment

- Doctors treat these infections with antibiotics.
- The most common antibiotic is doxycycline.
- Treatment usually lasts 5 days.

Doctors often start the antibiotic right away if they suspect a spotted fever. This is true even if test results are not yet back. Early treatment works best.

## Prevention

The best way to avoid these infections is to prevent tick bites.

### How to Prevent Tick Bites

- Stay on trails and paths.
- Tuck your pants into your boots or socks.
- Wear long-sleeved shirts.
- Use repellent with DEET on your skin.
- Apply permethrin to your clothes. It kills ticks on contact.

**Important:** Use DEET with care in very young children. Some cases of poisoning have been reported.

**Check yourself and others often.** Look for ticks, especially in hairy areas and on children. Do this after being outdoors in tick-prone areas.

### How to Remove a Tick

- Do not crush the tick between your fingers.
- Do not use petroleum jelly, matches, or other irritants. These do not work and can be dangerous.
- Use a small pair of tweezers.
- Grasp the tick’s head close to the skin.
- Pull it straight out slowly and steadily.
- Clean the bite area with alcohol.

### Reducing Ticks in Your Environment

There is no way to completely remove ticks from an area. But you can make it less likely for ticks to live there.

- Remove wood piles, leaf litter, and tall grasses around your home.
- Clear brush and weeds, especially near play areas.
- Mice and other animals carry ticks. They like to hide in piles of leaves, wood, and tall grass.

By cleaning up these areas, you make it harder for mice to live there. This helps reduce the number of ticks.
