# How the Baby Is Positioned Before Birth

During pregnancy, the baby can lie in many different ways inside the mother’s womb. The baby may be head down or head up. The baby may face the mother’s back or face her front. Early in pregnancy, the baby moves around a lot. But as the pregnancy nears its end, the baby grows larger and has less room to move. The baby usually stays in one position by the time labor begins.

How the baby is positioned affects how the birth will go. Some positions make delivery easier. Others make it harder. In some cases, a cesarean delivery is needed.

Doctors use special terms to describe the baby’s position. These terms help doctors plan for labor and delivery.

---

## Key Terms for Baby’s Position

### Presentation
This is the part of the baby’s body that comes out first during birth.  
- Most often, the baby’s head comes out first.  
- Sometimes, the baby’s bottom (buttocks) comes out first. This is called a breech presentation.  
- Less often, the baby’s shoulder or face comes out first.

### Position
This describes which way the baby is facing.  
- The back of the baby’s head is called the occiput.  
- If the baby is facing the mother’s back, it is called occiput anterior. This is the best position for birth.  
- If the baby is facing the mother’s front, it is called occiput posterior. This is less common and can make birth harder.

### Lie
This is the angle of the baby’s body in the womb.  
- The normal lie is head to toe, with the baby’s spine lined up with the mother’s spine. This is called a longitudinal lie.  
- Sometimes the baby lies sideways. This is called a transverse lie.  
- Sometimes the baby lies at an angle. This is called an oblique lie.

---

## The Best Position for Birth

The easiest and safest position for birth is:

- The baby’s head is down (vertex presentation).  
- The baby is facing the mother’s back (occiput anterior position).  
- The baby’s spine is lined up with the mother’s spine (longitudinal lie).  
- The baby’s neck is bent forward.  
- The baby’s chin is tucked to its chest.  
- The baby’s arms are folded across the chest.

If the baby is in a different position, birth may be harder. A normal vaginal birth may not be possible.

---

## Why the Baby’s Position Can Change

Some things can cause the baby to be in a position that makes birth harder. These include:

- The baby is too big for the mother’s pelvis.  
- The shape of the mother’s uterus is unusual.  
- The mother has growths in the uterus, such as fibroids.  
- The baby has a birth defect.  
- There is more than one baby (multiple pregnancy).

---

## Common Variations in Baby’s Position

### Occiput Posterior Position (Back to Front)
- The baby is head down, but the face is toward the mother’s front.  
- This is common and not dangerous.  
- But it can make labor longer and more painful.  
- The baby’s neck may be straight instead of bent. This makes the head wider.  
- The baby’s head may not fit through the birth canal easily.  
- In some cases, a vacuum device or forceps may be used to help deliver the baby.  
- A cesarean delivery may be needed.

### Breech Presentation (Bottom First)
- The baby’s bottom or feet come out first.  
- This is riskier than head-first delivery.  
- The baby’s hips and bottom are smaller than the head.  
- If the hips come out first, the head may not fit through the birth canal.  
- The baby’s neck may bend backward. This makes the head wider.  
- The baby’s body may come out, but the head gets stuck.  
- When the head is stuck, pressure can squeeze the umbilical cord.  
- This cuts off oxygen to the baby.  
- Brain damage from lack of oxygen is more likely in breech babies.

**Cesarean delivery is usually recommended** for breech babies.  
- This is especially true for first-time mothers.  
- The mother’s tissues have not been stretched before, so delivery is harder.  
- A cesarean is safer unless the doctor is very experienced with breech births.  
- Or if the hospital does not have the tools to do a safe cesarean.

**Breech presentation is more likely if:**

- Labor starts too early (preterm labor).  
- There is more than one baby.  
- The uterus is shaped oddly.  
- The mother has fibroids.  
- The baby has a birth defect.

---

### Turning the Baby Before Birth

Sometimes, doctors can turn the baby so it is head down before labor starts.  
- This is called an external cephalic version.  
- The doctor presses on the mother’s belly to gently turn the baby.  
- This is usually done at 37 or 38 weeks of pregnancy.  
- Sometimes, medicine is given to stop contractions during the procedure.  
- The medicine may be terbutaline.

---

### Face Presentation (Face First)
- The baby’s neck is bent back.  
- The baby’s face comes out first.  
- This is rare.  
- Most babies change to a head-first position before or during labor.  
- If the baby stays in this position, a cesarean delivery is usually needed.

### Brow Presentation (Brow First)
- The baby’s neck is bent back a little.  
- The baby’s forehead comes out first.  
- This is also rare.  
- Most babies change to a head-first position.  
- If not, a cesarean delivery is usually recommended.

### Transverse Lie (Side to Side)
- The baby lies across the birth canal.  
- The shoulder comes out first.  
- A cesarean delivery is needed.  
- The only exception is if the baby is the second twin.  
- In that case, the doctor may turn the baby and deliver it through the vagina.

# Finger Dislocations

Most finger dislocations happen at the middle joint of the finger.  
They usually happen when the finger is bent too far backward.  
This type of injury often pushes the bone out the back of the joint.

Finger dislocations can happen in different ways:  
- The bone can move to the back of the joint (dorsal).  
- The bone can move to the side (lateral).  
- The bone can move to the palm side (volar).  

These injuries can tear the ligaments that hold the joint in place.  
The ligaments are strong bands that connect bones and keep joints stable.

Most dislocations cause a visible change in the finger’s shape.  
You will likely feel pain and notice swelling.

To check for a dislocation, doctors take X-rays.  
They take three types of X-rays:  
- Front to back (anteroposterior)  
- Side (lateral)  
- Diagonal (oblique)  

For the side view, the injured finger must be kept apart from the others.  
This helps show the joint clearly.

Most dislocations are fixed without surgery.  
The doctor straightens the finger back into place.  
Before this, they numb the finger with a local anesthetic.  
This is called a digital nerve block.

After the finger is back in place, the doctor checks how stable it is.  
They do this by gently pushing on the sides of the joint.  
This is called stress testing.  
It helps find out if the ligaments are still strong.

## Key Points

- Finger dislocations can happen in the back, side, or palm side of the joint.  
- They can tear the ligaments that support the joint.  
- The finger often looks crooked or out of place.  
- X-rays are needed to confirm the injury.  
- Take three types of X-rays: front to back, side, and diagonal.  
- Keep the injured finger separate from the others in the side view.  
- Most dislocations are fixed by hand after numbing the finger.  
- After fixing the dislocation, check the joint stability with stress testing.

# What You Need to Know About the Thyroid Gland

## What Is the Thyroid Gland?

- The thyroid is a small gland in the front of your neck.
- It is about 2 inches wide and sits just under the skin.
- It has two sides (lobes) connected in the middle. This shape looks like a bow tie.
- Normally, you cannot see or feel the thyroid.
- If it gets bigger, you may notice a lump or bulge in your neck. This is called a goiter. It can appear below or beside the Adam’s apple.

## What Does the Thyroid Do?

- The thyroid makes hormones that control how fast your body’s chemical processes work.
- These hormones affect many important body functions, including:
  - Heart rate
  - How fast you burn calories
  - Skin health
  - Growth
  - Body heat
  - Fertility
  - Digestion

## How the Thyroid Works

- The thyroid makes two main hormones: T4 and T3.
- T4 is the main hormone made by the thyroid. It does not work very strongly on its own.
- Most of the T4 is changed into T3 in the liver and other tissues.
- T3 is the active hormone. It speeds up your body’s metabolism.
- The body controls how much T4 turns into T3 based on your needs and health.
- Most of the T4 and T3 in your blood is attached to a protein called thyroxine-binding globulin.
- Only the small amount of hormone that is not attached (free hormone) is active.
- When your body uses the free hormone, more hormone is released from the protein to replace it.

### Iodine Is Needed to Make Thyroid Hormones

- The thyroid needs iodine to make hormones.
- Iodine comes from food and water.
- The thyroid takes up iodine and turns it into hormones.
- When hormones are used, some iodine is released back into the body.
- The thyroid recycles this iodine to make more hormones.
- Too much iodine in the blood can actually reduce how much hormone the thyroid makes.

### The Thyroid Also Makes Calcitonin

- The thyroid also makes a hormone called calcitonin.
- This hormone may help keep bones strong by helping the body use calcium.

## How the Body Controls Thyroid Hormones

- The brain controls thyroid hormone levels through a chain of signals.
- First, the hypothalamus in the brain sends a signal to the pituitary gland.
- The pituitary gland then releases a hormone called TSH.
- TSH tells the thyroid to make more or less thyroid hormone.
- If your body needs more thyroid hormone, the pituitary releases more TSH.
- If your body has enough thyroid hormone, the pituitary releases less TSH.
- This system keeps your hormone levels balanced.

## Changes in the Thyroid as You Age

- Aging has only a small effect on the thyroid.
- The thyroid gland gets smaller and moves lower in the neck as you get older.
- The level of T3 hormone may drop slightly.
- But your body’s basic functions usually stay about the same.
- Still, thyroid problems become more common with age.
- Two main problems are:
  - Hyperthyroidism (too much thyroid hormone)
  - Hypothyroidism (too little thyroid hormone)
- These problems can cause symptoms that look like normal aging.
- They can also be mistaken for other health issues.
- These problems can make older adults feel very unwell and struggle with daily tasks.
- Because of this, it is important to recognize and treat them early.

### Should Older Adults Be Screened?

- Some experts suggest testing the TSH level every year or every few years in people over 70.
- But many medical groups say this is not needed for healthy people with no symptoms.
- They warn that testing can lead to over-treatment of small, harmless changes in blood tests.
- However, all newborns are tested for low thyroid function (congenital hypothyroidism).
- This is important because untreated low thyroid function can cause serious brain and organ problems in babies.

## How Doctors Test the Thyroid

### Step 1: Physical Exam

- The doctor will look at your neck and feel it.
- They check for swelling or lumps in the thyroid.

### Step 2: Blood Tests

- Blood tests measure how well the thyroid is working.
- Doctors usually check:
  - TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone)
  - T4 (thyroxine)
  - T3 (triiodothyronine)

#### TSH Test

- TSH is the best first test for thyroid problems.
- High TSH means the thyroid is underactive (hypothyroidism).
- Low TSH means the thyroid is overactive (hyperthyroidism).
- In rare cases, the pituitary gland may not work right. Then TSH levels may not show the true thyroid status.

#### T4 and T3 Tests

- Doctors often check both total and free levels of T4 and T3.
- Total T4 and T3 include both the hormone attached to protein and the free hormone.
- The free hormone is the active one.
- If the protein level is abnormal, total hormone levels can be misleading.
- So doctors may only check free T4 and free T3 in some cases.

#### When Protein Levels Are Abnormal

- Low protein levels can happen in:
  - Kidney disease
  - Liver disease
  - Low protein intake
  - Use of anabolic steroids
- High protein levels can happen in:
  - Pregnancy
  - Birth control pills or other estrogen use
  - Early hepatitis

### Step 3: Ultrasound

- If the doctor feels a lump in the thyroid, they may order an ultrasound.
- This test uses sound waves to:
  - Show the size of the thyroid
  - Check if a lump is solid or filled with fluid
  - Look for calcium in the lump
  - See how many blood vessels are in the area

### Step 4: Radioactive Iodine Uptake Test

- A small amount of radioactive material (like iodine or technetium) is injected into the blood.
- The thyroid takes up the material.
- A special camera detects the radiation and makes a picture of the thyroid.
- This test shows:
  - If the thyroid is working normally
  - If part of the thyroid is overactive or underactive

### Step 5: Antibody Test

- If the doctor suspects an autoimmune disease, they may test for antibodies.
- These are immune system proteins that attack the thyroid.

### Step 6: Biopsy

- If thyroid cancer is suspected, a small sample of thyroid tissue is taken.
- A thin needle is used to collect the sample.
- The sample is studied under a microscope.
- Ultrasound helps the doctor find the best spot to take the sample.

### Step 7: Calcitonin Test

- If medullary thyroid cancer is suspected, doctors check blood levels of calcitonin.
- This type of cancer always makes calcitonin.

## Summary

- The thyroid controls how fast your body works.
- It needs iodine to make hormones.
- It also makes a hormone that helps keep bones strong.
- The brain controls thyroid hormone levels through a chain of signals.
- Blood tests are the main way to check thyroid function.
- Ultrasound and other scans help find lumps or cancer.
- Screening for thyroid problems is not needed for all older adults without symptoms.
- But all newborns are tested to catch low thyroid function early.

# Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC)

Primary sclerosing cholangitis is a condition that causes inflammation, scarring, and narrowing of the tubes that carry bile from the liver to the intestines.  
The exact cause is unknown.  
Most people with PSC also have a bowel condition called inflammatory bowel disease.  
Ulcerative colitis is the most common type.  
About 80 percent of people with PSC have this bowel disease.  
Other health problems linked to PSC include autoimmune diseases, connective tissue disorders, and weak immune systems.  
These can lead to unusual infections.

Fatigue and itching come on slowly and get worse over time.  
Diagnosis is done using imaging tests of the bile ducts.  
The most common test is magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography, or MRCP.  
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, or ERCP, is used less often because it is more invasive.  
When the disease is advanced, liver transplantation may be needed.

## What Causes PSC?

We do not know what starts PSC.  
But it often happens in people who have inflammatory bowel disease.  
About 5 percent of people with ulcerative colitis will develop PSC.  
About 1 percent of people with Crohn disease will develop PSC.  
Some people with PSC have certain antibodies in their blood.  
These include antinuclear antibodies and pANCA.  
This suggests the body’s immune system may be attacking the bile ducts.  
T cells, a type of immune cell, seem to play a role in damaging the ducts.  
This points to a problem with how the immune system works.  
Some people with PSC have a family history of the disease.  
Certain genes, like HLAB8 and HLADR3, are more common in people with PSC.  
These genes are also linked to other autoimmune conditions.  
A trigger, such as a bacterial infection or injury to the bile ducts, may start the disease in people who are already at risk.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The disease often starts with tiredness and itching.  
These symptoms get worse over time.  
Up to 40 percent of people have other symptoms.  
These include belly pain, itchy skin, diarrhea, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), and fever.  
Some people may have fatty stools and low levels of fat-soluble vitamins.  
Persistent jaundice means the disease is getting worse.  
About 75 percent of people with PSC develop gallstones or stones in the bile ducts.  
Some people have no symptoms at first.  
They may only notice problems when the liver is already damaged.  
They may have an enlarged liver and spleen.  
Or they may have cirrhosis, which is scarring of the liver.  
PSC slowly gets worse over time.  
In the final stage, the liver fails.  
This can cause fluid buildup in the belly (ascites), high pressure in the liver’s blood vessels (portal hypertension), and brain problems from toxins (portosystemic encephalopathy).  
Bleeding from swollen veins in the esophagus (esophageal varices) can also happen.

Even though PSC and inflammatory bowel disease often occur together, they do not always follow the same course.  
Ulcerative colitis may appear years before PSC.  
When both conditions are present, the bowel disease often stays mild.  
Removing the colon (colectomy) does not change the course of PSC.  
Having both PSC and inflammatory bowel disease increases the risk of colorectal cancer.  
This risk stays even after a liver transplant.  
About 10 to 15 percent of people with PSC develop cancer of the bile ducts (cholangiocarcinoma).

## How Is PSC Diagnosed?

PSC is suspected when liver tests show unusual results.  
This is more likely if the person also has inflammatory bowel disease.  
The liver test pattern is called cholestatic.  
This means alkaline phosphatase and GGT levels are high.  
Aminotransferase levels are usually normal or only slightly raised.  
Gamma globulin and IgM levels are often high.  
Antinuclear antibodies and pANCA are usually positive.  
Antimitochondrial antibodies are negative.  
This helps rule out another liver disease called primary biliary cholangitis.

The first imaging test is usually an ultrasound of the belly.  
This checks for blockages outside the liver.  
Ultrasound or CT scans can show swollen bile ducts.  
But only cholangiography can confirm PSC.  
Cholangiography shows multiple narrowings and widenings in both the liver and outside the liver.  
MRCP is the first choice for this test.  
It is non-invasive and safe.  
ERCP is used only if MRCP is not clear or if treatment is needed.  
ERCP is more invasive and carries more risk.

A liver biopsy is not usually needed.  
But if done, it shows thickened bile ducts, scarring around the ducts, inflammation, and loss of ducts.  
As the disease gets worse, scarring spreads and leads to secondary biliary cirrhosis.

All adults with PSC should have imaging of the belly every 6 to 12 months.  
This includes ultrasound, CT, or MRI/MRCP.  
The goal is to check for gallbladder cancer and bile duct cancer.  
Blood tests for CA 19-9 should be done regularly.  
This marker can help detect bile duct cancer early.

All people with PSC should have a colonoscopy with biopsies.  
This is true even if they do not have inflammatory bowel disease.  
If they do have IBD, they should have a colonoscopy every year.  
This is because the risk of colorectal cancer is higher.

## How Is PSC Treated?

There is no cure for PSC.  
But treatment can help manage symptoms and complications.

People with no symptoms usually only need regular checkups.  
This includes physical exams and liver tests every six months.  
They should also have imaging and CA 19-9 blood tests every 6 to 12 months.  
Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) can help reduce itching and improve liver test results.  
But it does not improve survival.  
For people with long-term bile flow problems or cirrhosis, treatment focuses on managing symptoms.  
This includes treating infections and supporting liver function.

If a person gets bacterial infection in the bile ducts (bacterial cholangitis), they need antibiotics.  
They may also need ERCP to clear the blockage.  
ERCP can also be used to treat a major narrowing in the bile duct.  
This is called a dominant stricture.  
It happens in up to 45 percent of people.  
During ERCP, doctors can take samples to check for cancer.  
They may use brush cytology and FISH testing to look for cancer cells.  
Stents can be placed to keep the duct open and relieve symptoms.

Liver transplantation is the only treatment that can improve life expectancy.  
It can also cure PSC.  
Transplant is recommended for people with repeated bile duct infections.  
It is also needed for serious complications of liver failure.  
These include fluid in the belly that won’t go away, brain problems from liver failure, and bleeding from swollen veins in the esophagus.  
Transplant may also be considered for people with bile duct cancer, if they are good candidates.

## Key Points

- Most people with PSC have inflammatory bowel disease.  
  Ulcerative colitis is the most common type.  
  Many also have certain antibodies in their blood.

- Think about PSC if a person has unexplained liver test changes.  
  This is especially true if they have inflammatory bowel disease.

- Start with an ultrasound to rule out blockages outside the liver.  
  Then do MRCP to confirm the diagnosis.  
  ERCP is used only if needed for treatment.

- Watch people with PSC closely.  
  Do regular liver tests.  
  Screen for gallbladder and bile duct cancer.  
  Treat symptoms and complications as they arise.  
  For example, use ERCP to treat major strictures.

- Consider liver transplantation if a person has repeated infections or serious liver failure.

# What Are Hereditary Periodic Fever Syndromes?

These are rare conditions you are born with. They cause repeated episodes of fever and other symptoms. The symptoms are not caused by common childhood infections or other known illnesses.

## Most Common Syndrome

- **Familial Mediterranean fever** is the most common type across all ages.

## A Similar but Not Inherited Condition

- **PFAPA syndrome** causes fever episodes. It is not passed down through families.  
  Symptoms include fever, mouth sores, sore throat, and swollen glands in the neck.

## Other Less Common Syndromes

### 1. Hereditary Cryopyrin-Associated Periodic Syndromes (Cryopyrinopathies)

This group includes:
- Familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome (FCAS)
- Muckle-Wells syndrome (MWS)
- Neonatal-onset multisystem autoinflammatory disease (NOMID)

These conditions cause:
- Fever
- Rash
- Joint pain

Cold weather can trigger these symptoms.  
Medicines that change how the immune system works may help. These include:
- Anakinra
- Rilonacept
- Canakinumab

### 2. Hyper-IgD Syndrome

This condition causes:
- Fever
- Belly pain
- Headache
- Joint pain
- Rash
- Swollen lymph nodes

During attacks, the following may help:
- Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
- Corticosteroids
- Anakinra

To prevent future attacks, doctors may prescribe:
- Anakinra
- Canakinumab

### 3. Tumor Necrosis Factor Receptor–Associated Periodic Syndrome (TRAPS)

This condition causes:
- Fever
- Muscle pain and swelling in arms and legs
- Belly pain
- Joint pain
- Rash

For mild attacks, NSAIDs may help.  
For regular attacks, most people need prednisone, a type of steroid medicine.  
To prevent attacks, doctors may use:
- Anakinra
- Canakinumab

### 4. PAPA Syndrome (Pyogenic Arthritis, Pyoderma Gangrenosum, and Acne)

This condition causes:
- Fever
- Swollen, painful joints
- Skin ulcers
- Acne

By the time a person reaches puberty, joint problems often get better.  
Skin issues usually remain the main problem.

Medicines that may help include:
- Anakinra
- Etanercept
- Adalimumab
- Infliximab

Acne is treated with:
- The antibiotic tetracycline
- Or isotretinoin

## When Do Symptoms Start?

Most people first notice symptoms during childhood.  
Fewer than 1 in 10 people start having symptoms after age 18.  
Between attacks, people feel normal and healthy.  
Attacks come and go over time.

# Traveler’s Diarrhea

Traveler’s diarrhea is an upset stomach and bowel problem that many people get when traveling. It is usually caused by bacteria in the local water. The main symptoms are vomiting and loose stools. Doctors usually diagnose it by looking at your symptoms. Treatment focuses on replacing lost fluids and sometimes using antibiotics for more serious cases.

---

## What Causes Traveler’s Diarrhea?

Up to 70 out of 100 travelers get traveler’s diarrhea if they travel for more than two weeks. The risk depends on where you go and the time of year.

The most common cause is a type of bacteria called *Escherichia coli*, or *E. coli*. This bacteria is often found in water that is not properly cleaned. It is common in countries with limited water treatment. People traveling to these places are more likely to get sick.

Other common causes include:
- *Campylobacter jejuni*
- *Shigella*
- *Salmonella*
- Another type of *E. coli* called enteroaggregative *E. coli*

Viruses can also cause traveler’s diarrhea. One virus, called norovirus, has caused big outbreaks on cruise ships.

You can get sick from both food and water. Even if you avoid drinking local water, you can still get infected. For example:
- Using a toothbrush that was rinsed with local water
- Drinking bottled drinks with ice made from local water
- Eating food that was washed with local water or handled poorly

People who take medicines that reduce stomach acid are more likely to get a severe case. These medicines include antacids, H2 blockers, and proton pump inhibitors.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may feel sick to your stomach, vomit, have stomach cramps, and have loose or watery stools. These symptoms usually start 12 to 72 hours after eating or drinking something contaminated.

The illness can be mild or severe. Some people also get a fever or body aches. Blood in the stool is rare.

Most cases are mild and go away on their own. But you can become dehydrated, especially in hot weather.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose traveler’s diarrhea by talking to you and checking your symptoms. You do not usually need lab tests.

But if you have:
- A high fever
- Severe stomach pain
- Blood in your stool

Then you should see a doctor right away. These signs may mean a more serious illness.

---

## How Is It Treated?

The most important step is to replace lost fluids. Drink water, broth, or oral rehydration solutions. This helps prevent dehydration.

You may also use an antidiarrheal medicine like loperamide. This helps slow down your bowel movements.

For children under 12 years old, the dose of loperamide depends on their weight. Adults can also use diphenoxylate/atropine as an alternative.

**Do not use antidiarrheal medicines if:**
- You have a fever
- You have blood in your stool
- You are a child under 2 years old

These medicines can make some infections worse.

Do not use a medicine called iodochlorhydroxyquin. It can cause nerve damage.

---

### Key Tips for Treatment

- Antidiarrheal medicines are not safe for people with fever or bloody stools.
- They are also not safe for children under 2 years old.
- For mild diarrhea, antibiotics are not needed.
- For moderate to severe diarrhea (three or more loose stools in 8 hours), antibiotics are often used.
- If you have vomiting, stomach cramps, fever, or blood in your stool, antibiotics are more likely to help.

**For adults:**
- Ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin are common choices.
- But some areas now have bacteria that resist these drugs, especially *Campylobacter* infections.
- Alternatives include azithromycin or rifaximin.

**For children and pregnant women:**
- Azithromycin is the preferred antibiotic.

---

## How Can You Prevent It?

The best way to avoid traveler’s diarrhea is to be careful about what you eat and drink.

Eat only:
- Food that is cooked and still hot
- Fruits you can peel yourself
- Carbonated drinks in sealed bottles

Avoid:
- Tap water
- Ice made from local water
- Uncooked vegetables
- Salsa or other raw foods left out in the open
- Buffets and fast food restaurants (they carry higher risk)
- Any food washed with tap water

Street food and food from unclean places are risky.

---

### Who Should Take Preventive Medicine?

Some people are at higher risk and may need preventive medicine. This includes people with:
- Weakened immune systems (like those with HIV or inflammatory bowel disease)
- Organ transplants
- Severe heart or kidney disease

For these people, a medicine called rifaximin can be used to prevent diarrhea. It is a type of antibiotic that stays in the gut and is not absorbed into the body.

Fluoroquinolone antibiotics are not used for prevention. They can cause serious side effects like tendon damage and nerve problems.

Some travelers may consider bismuth subsalicylate as a non-antibiotic option. It may help reduce the risk of diarrhea.

---

## Summary of Key Points

- Traveler’s diarrhea is most often caused by *E. coli* in contaminated water.
- Viruses, parasites, and other bacteria can also cause it.
- Doctors usually diagnose it based on symptoms. Tests are not needed unless you have fever, severe pain, or blood in your stool.
- Treatment is fluid replacement and usually an antidiarrheal medicine like loperamide.
- Do not use antidiarrheal medicines if you have a fever, blood in your stool, or are a child under 2 years old.
- For severe cases, antibiotics are used. Adults get fluoroquinolones. Children and pregnant women get azithromycin.
- Prevention is the best approach. Be careful about food and water.
- Preventive antibiotics are not used for most travelers. They are only used for people with serious health conditions.

---

## More Information

The following English-language resources may be helpful. Note that *The Manual* is not responsible for the content of these websites.

- Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: _Preparing international travelers for travelers’ diarrhea_
- Expert panel: _Guidelines for the prevention and treatment of travelers' diarrhea_ (2017)

# Problems with Eggs and Fertility

Women may have trouble getting pregnant if they have few eggs or if their eggs are not working well.

- A woman is born with all the eggs she will ever have. Her ovaries hold these eggs.
- No new eggs are made after birth.
- The number and quality of eggs can start to drop as early as age 30.
- The drop happens faster after age 40.
- But age is not the only reason for fewer or lower-quality eggs. Problems in the ovaries can also cause this.

## What Is Primary Ovarian Insufficiency?

Some women have a condition called primary ovarian insufficiency. This means their eggs decrease in number and quality at a younger age than normal. It is also sometimes called premature menopause.

- This condition can cause irregular periods or no periods at all.
- It can make it harder to get pregnant.

## How Doctors Check for Egg Problems

Doctors use two main tests to check for problems with eggs:

1. **Blood tests**  
   - These check hormone levels in the blood.
   - Doctors test for follicle-stimulating hormone and estrogen.
   - These hormones help control when eggs are released.

2. **Ultrasound scan**  
   - A special ultrasound is done using a device placed inside the vagina.
   - This is called transvaginal ultrasound.
   - It lets doctors see and count the small fluid-filled pockets in the ovaries. These pockets hold the eggs.

### What the Tests Show

- A low level of a hormone called antimüllerian hormone (AMH) means there are fewer eggs.
- A low number of fluid-filled pockets seen on ultrasound also means fewer eggs.
- Fewer eggs make it harder to get pregnant through IVF, but pregnancy is still possible.

### Who Should Be Tested?

Doctors may suggest testing for egg problems in women who:

- Are 35 years old or older
- Have had surgery on their ovaries
- Did not respond well to fertility medicines that help eggs grow and be released

## Treatment for Egg Problems

Treatment depends on a woman’s age and her personal situation.

- If a woman is under 42, doctors may try medicines to help eggs grow and be released.
  - These include clomiphene, letrozole, and human gonadotropins.
  - These medicines are also used to treat other ovulation problems.

- If a woman is over 42, or if her eggs are very low in number or quality, using eggs from another woman may be an option.
  - This is called egg donation.
  - It can help women who otherwise could not get pregnant.

### Important Note

Even if test results are not normal, pregnancy may still be possible. Each woman’s situation is different. Doctors will work with her to find the best treatment.

# Toxic and Nutritional Optic Neuropathies

This condition affects the optic nerve. It causes blurry or dim vision. The problem happens in the part of the optic nerve near the eye. It is caused by toxins, poor nutrition, or unknown reasons. The main symptom is loss of vision without pain.

## What Causes This Condition?

This condition usually affects both eyes at the same time. It can happen when the body does not get enough nutrients. Low levels of certain vitamins, like vitamin B1, vitamin B12, or folate, can cause it. This is more common in people who have had weight-loss surgery or who have a problem with alcohol use.

True vision loss from smoking is very rare. Other health problems linked to poor nutrition can also lead to this condition. For example, Strachan syndrome causes nerve problems and skin issues. Low protein and low antioxidants may also increase the risk.

Many chemicals can harm the optic nerve. These include lead, methanol, chloramphenicol, digoxin, ethambutol, and many others.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Vision becomes blurry or dim over days or weeks. A small blind spot in the center of vision slowly gets bigger. It may grow to cover the point you look at and the blind spot in your eye. This is called a centrocecal scotoma.

Color vision may be lost even when the overall vision is only slightly affected. In rare cases, methanol poisoning can cause total blindness. But most other causes lead to serious loss of central vision, not total blindness.

The back of the eye (retina) usually looks normal. But over time, the optic nerve may look pale, especially on the side toward the temple.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors make the diagnosis based on your history and eye tests. They will ask about your diet, past surgeries, and exposure to harmful substances.

A visual field test shows the pattern of vision loss. This test often shows a specific type of blind spot that affects both eyes.

Blood tests may be done to check for lead, methanol, or low levels of vitamins and other nutrients. Tests may also check for other possible toxins.

## How Is It Treated?

The first step is to treat the cause.

Stop exposure to any harmful substance right away. This includes stopping alcohol, illegal drugs, or any medicine that may be causing the problem.

If lead poisoning is the cause, a treatment called chelation therapy is used. This helps remove lead from the body.

For methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning, treatments include dialysis, fomepizole, or ethanol. These help stop the damage from the poison.

If poor nutrition is the cause, giving vitamin B1, vitamin B12, folate, or other needed nutrients can help. This works best if started before vision loss becomes severe.

Low-vision aids can help with daily tasks. These include magnifiers, large-print books, and talking watches.

## What Is the Outlook?

If the cause is found and treated early, vision may improve. But if the optic nerve has already shrunk, vision usually does not come back.

## Key Points

- This condition causes blurry vision. It is caused by toxins, poor nutrition, or certain medicines.
- It is more common in people with alcohol use disorder or those who had weight-loss surgery.
- Vision loss usually happens slowly and affects the center of your vision.
- Doctors diagnose it by reviewing your history and doing eye tests.
- The most important step is to treat the cause. This may mean stopping a harmful substance or improving your diet.

# Low Blood Fat Levels (Hypolipidemia)

Low blood fat levels mean your blood has less fat than normal.  
This is called hypolipidemia.  
It happens when your total cholesterol is below 120 milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL) or your LDL cholesterol is below 50 mg/dL.

## What Causes Low Blood Fat Levels?

Low fat levels can come from two main causes:

- **Primary cause**: A rare inherited condition you are born with.
- **Secondary cause**: Another health problem you have.

Some rare genetic conditions cause low fat levels.  
These conditions can lead to serious health issues.  
Other times, low fat levels are a sign of a different illness.

## Signs and Symptoms

Most people with low fat levels do not have symptoms.  
But in some cases, low fat levels can cause:

- Poor growth
- Fatty, oily, smelly stools that float in water (called steatorrhea)
- Vision problems that can lead to blindness
- Trouble with balance and coordination
- Learning or thinking problems

These symptoms often start in infancy or early childhood.

## Possible Underlying Health Problems

Low cholesterol levels may point to another health issue.  
These include:

- Anemia (low red blood cells)
- Cancer
- Long-term infections like hepatitis C
- Problems absorbing food from the gut (malabsorption)
- Overactive thyroid gland (hyperthyroidism)
- Not getting enough food or nutrients (undernutrition)

If blood tests show very low cholesterol, your doctor may do more tests.  
The goal is to find the cause and treat it.

## Rare Genetic Conditions

Some rare inherited conditions cause very low fat levels.  
These can lead to serious health problems.  
But some people with a certain gene change (in the PCSK9 gene) have low fat levels with no serious problems.  
No treatment is needed for them.

---

### Abetalipoproteinemia (Bassen-Kornzweig Syndrome)

This is a rare inherited condition.  
The body cannot make certain fats that carry cholesterol and vitamins through the blood.  
These fats are called chylomicrons and VLDL.  
Because of this, the body cannot absorb fat and fat-soluble vitamins properly.

**Symptoms start in infancy.**  
They include:

- Poor growth
- Oily, foul-smelling, floating stools
- Vision loss (similar to retinitis pigmentosa)
- Loss of balance and coordination (ataxia)
- Learning or thinking problems

**Diagnosis:**

- Blood tests to check fat levels
- A small sample of the intestine (biopsy)
- Genetic testing

**Treatment:**

- Very high doses of vitamin E to protect the brain and nerves
- Supplements of dietary fat
- Vitamins A, D, and K

There is no cure.  
But treatment can slow down nerve damage.

---

### Chylomicron Retention Disease (Anderson Disease)

This is another rare inherited condition.  
The body cannot make chylomicrons.  
This leads to poor fat absorption.

**Symptoms in babies:**

- Trouble absorbing fat
- Oily, smelly stools
- Poor weight gain and growth
- Nervous system problems like poor coordination and learning issues

**Diagnosis:**

- Blood tests to check fat levels
- A biopsy of the intestine if levels are very low, especially after eating

**Treatment:**

- Supplements of dietary fat
- Vitamins A, D, E, and K

---

### Hypobetalipoproteinemia

This condition causes very low LDL cholesterol.  
Most people with it have no symptoms.  
No treatment is needed.

In the most severe form, there is almost no LDL cholesterol.  
Symptoms are similar to abetalipoproteinemia.

**Diagnosis:**

- Blood tests to check fat levels
- Family history helps confirm the diagnosis

**Treatment (for the severe form):**

- Supplements of vitamins A, D, E, and K
- Extra fat in the diet

This treatment is similar to that for abetalipoproteinemia.

# Dental, Mask, and Eye Barotrauma

Barotrauma happens when pressure changes in the body cause damage to tissues. This can happen during deep-water diving. It can affect the spaces around teeth, the area behind a face mask, or under hard contact lenses.

## Dental Barotrauma

Pain or damage to a tooth can happen when you go down or come up during a dive. This happens if there is an infection in a tooth root or a filling near the tooth. The pressure in the air space around the tooth changes fast. This can hurt the tooth. The tooth may hurt when you tap it with a tongue blade.

## Mask Barotrauma

This happens if you do not equalize the pressure inside your face mask during descent. You must blow air from your nose into the mask to do this. If you do not, a vacuum forms behind the mask. This can cause pain, bleeding in the eyes, and bruising on the skin covered by the mask. Bleeding behind the eye is rare.

If bleeding behind the eye is suspected:
- A full eye exam is done.
- This includes checking vision, eye movement, and pressure inside the eye.
- A head CT scan may be needed.

To prevent this, always blow air from your nose into the mask during descent.

## Eye Barotrauma

This can happen if small air bubbles get trapped behind hard contact lenses. The bubbles can hurt the eye. Symptoms include eye pain, blurry vision, and seeing halos around lights. A doctor should check your eyes to rule out other causes.

You cannot equalize pressure behind goggles. This can cause bleeding around the eye. Do not wear goggles when diving. Use a face mask instead.

## Treatment

### For Mild Symptoms
- Use pain medicine for mild tooth pain.
- Use pain medicine for small bruises on the face or around the eyes.

### For Severe Symptoms
- If tooth pain is severe, or if eye or face pain does not go away with pain medicine:
  - See a dentist.
  - See an eye doctor.
- Get help from a specialist for further care.

# Muscle Problems at Birth

Some babies are born without certain muscles or groups of muscles.  
Some muscles may also be underdeveloped.  

These problems are called birth defects.  
Birth defects are physical differences that are present when a baby is born.  
The word "congenital" means "present at birth."

Muscle problems can happen on their own.  
They can also be part of a larger condition called a syndrome.

---

## Poland Syndrome and Chest Muscle Problems

The large chest muscle (called the pectoralis major) may be small or missing.  
This can happen alone.  
It can also happen with other issues, such as hand problems, breast changes, or nipple differences.  
This condition is called Poland syndrome.

The exact cause of Poland syndrome is not known.

---

## Prune-Belly Syndrome

Some layers of the muscles in the belly may be missing at birth.  
This is called prune-belly syndrome.  
When these muscles are missing, the belly skin looks wrinkled.  
In baby boys, the testicles may not move down into the scrotum.  
This is called cryptorchidism.  
Some babies also have problems with the urinary tract.

The cause of prune-belly syndrome is not clear.

---

## How Muscle Problems Are Diagnosed

### Before Birth
Doctors can sometimes see muscle problems during a prenatal ultrasound.  
An ultrasound uses sound waves to create pictures of the baby inside the mother.

### After Birth
Doctors check the baby’s body during a physical exam.  
They look for signs of missing or underdeveloped muscles.

### Genetic Testing
Some muscle problems are linked to changes in genes.  
A geneticist is a doctor who studies genes and how traits are passed from parents to children.  
A blood test can check for gene or chromosome changes.  
This test helps doctors find out if a genetic condition is causing the problem.  
It also helps rule out other possible causes.

---

## How Muscle Problems Are Treated

Treatment depends on how serious the muscle problem is.  
Some babies may need surgery to fix the issue.  
This type of surgery is called reconstructive surgery.

If a gene problem is found, families may benefit from genetic counseling.  
Counseling helps families understand the condition.  
It also helps them make informed choices about future pregnancies.

# Nasal Congestion and Runny Nose

Nasal congestion and a runny nose often happen together. But sometimes one happens without the other.

## What Causes Nasal Congestion and Runny Nose?

The most common causes are:

- Cold or flu (upper respiratory infection)
- Allergies

### Common Causes and Their Signs

**Acute sinus infection**  
- Thick, yellow or green mucus, often from one side  
- Red or inflamed nasal lining  
- Bad taste in the mouth, pain in the face or head (especially when bending), or tenderness over the cheek or forehead  
- Doctors usually diagnose this with a history and physical exam  
- A special scan (CT scan) may be needed if you have diabetes, a weak immune system, or signs of a serious illness

**Allergic rhinitis (allergy-related runny nose)**  
- Clear, watery mucus  
- Frequent sneezing  
- Itchy, watery eyes  
- Pale, swollen nasal lining, especially in the lower parts  
- Symptoms often come and go with the season or when you are around triggers like pollen, dust, or pet dander  
- Diagnosis is based on your history and physical exam  
- Skin or blood tests can help find what you are allergic to

**Atrophic rhinitis (chronic thinning of nasal lining)**  
- Long-term runny nose  
- Dry, thin, and hard nasal lining  
- Open nasal passages  
- Crusts in the nose  
- Bad smell from the nose  
- Diagnosis is made by physical exam  
- A small tissue sample (biopsy) may be taken to check the lining

**Overuse of nasal decongestant sprays**  
- Congestion comes back after the spray wears off  
- Pale, very swollen nasal lining  
- Diagnosis is based on your history and physical exam  
- This is called rhinitis medicamentosa

**Nasal foreign body (object stuck in the nose)**  
- One-sided, bad-smelling, sometimes bloody discharge  
- This mostly happens in children  
- Diagnosis is based on history and physical exam

**Vasomotor rhinitis**  
- Recurring watery discharge  
- Sneezing  
- Red, swollen nasal lining  
- No clear trigger  
- Diagnosis is based on history and physical exam

**Viral upper respiratory infection (common cold)**  
- Watery to thick mucus  
- Sore throat  
- Feeling tired  
- Red nasal lining  
- Diagnosis is based on history and physical exam

> **Note:** Cold and dry air can make congestion worse.  
> Acute sinus infection is less common.  
> A foreign object in the nose is rare but mostly seen in children.

### Important Warning About Decongestants

Using nasal decongestant sprays for more than 3 to 5 days can cause rebound congestion.  
The congestion comes back stronger when the spray wears off.  
This can lead to a cycle of using more spray, which makes the problem worse.  
This condition is called rhinitis medicamentosa.  
It can last for weeks or months.  
People often think the original problem is still there, but it is actually from overusing the spray.

## How Doctors Evaluate These Problems

Doctors start by asking about your symptoms and doing a physical exam.  
They may use tests like skin or blood tests to check for allergies.  
A scan (CT) may be needed in some cases, especially if you have other health issues.

## How These Problems Are Treated

Treatment depends on the cause.  
Always treat the underlying problem when possible.

### For Cold or Flu (Viral Infection)

- Use a humidifier to add moisture to the air  
- Use saltwater spray or rinse your nose with saline  
- Hypertonic saline (stronger saltwater) can help reduce swelling  
- Use second-generation antihistamines like cetirizine or fexofenadine if needed  
- First-generation antihistamines like diphenhydramine can cause drowsiness  
- They may also cause confusion, nervousness, or even agitation in some people  
- These medicines should be used with care, especially in older adults

### For Allergies

- Use second-generation antihistamines like cetirizine or fexofenadine  
- These cause fewer side effects than older types  
- Use nasal steroid sprays like fluticasone (two sprays in each nostril daily)  
- These help reduce swelling and mucus

### For Chronic Sinus Infection with Polyps

- Start with nasal steroid sprays  
- Add antibiotics like amoxicillin-clavulanate if needed  
- See separate sections for more on chronic sinus infection and nasal polyps

### About Decongestants

- Topical (spray) and oral (pill) decongestants can help for a short time  
- But they should not be used long-term  
- Long-term use can cause rebound congestion  
- Oral decongestants can raise blood pressure and heart rate  
- They can be dangerous for people with heart or blood pressure problems

### Special Advice for Children

- Do not use antihistamines in children under 2 years old  
- Do not use decongestants in children under 6 years old

## Special Considerations for Older Adults

- First-generation antihistamines like diphenhydramine can make you drowsy  
- They can also cause confusion, trouble peeing, and increase the risk of falling  
- Use lower doses in older adults  
- Adrenergic medicines (like decongestants) should be used at the lowest effective dose  
- This helps avoid high blood pressure episodes

## Key Points

- Most cases of nasal congestion and runny nose are caused by colds or allergies.  
- In children, think about a foreign object in the nose.  
- Watch out for rebound congestion from overusing nasal decongestant sprays.

# How Cancer Is Treated

Cancer treatment is very complex. It takes a team of many different health care providers to help a person with cancer.

The team includes:
- Doctors such as primary care doctors, gynecologists, surgeons, and specialists in cancer (oncologists).
- Nurses, radiation therapists, physical therapists, social workers, and pharmacists.

Your treatment plan is made just for you. It takes into account:
- The type of cancer.
- Where the cancer is in your body.
- What kind of cells the cancer has.
- How big the cancer is and how far it has spread (this is called the stage).
- How abnormal the cancer cells look compared to normal cells (this is called the grade).
- The genetic makeup of the cancer.
- Your own health, age, and personal preferences.

Doctors also think about:
- How likely the treatment is to cure the cancer.
- If the cancer cannot be cured, how long the treatment might help you live.
- How the treatment will affect your symptoms.
- The side effects you might have.
- What you want for your care.

You want the best possible outcome. You want to live as long as possible with a good quality of life. But you also need to know the risks of treatment. Talk with all your doctors about your wishes. Be part of the decisions about your care. You can write down your wishes in advance. This is called an advance directive.

When cancer is first found, the main goal is to remove the cancer completely if possible. This may be done with:
- Surgery.
- Radiation therapy.
- Chemotherapy.
- Stem cell transplants (also called hematopoietic cell transplantation).
- Other cancer treatments.

Sometimes, treatment also aims to kill cancer cells in other parts of the body, even if doctors cannot see them there.

Because cancer treatments are complex, doctors use treatment plans called protocols. These plans help make sure you get safe and effective care. Protocols are based on results from scientific studies.

Doctors often test new treatments in clinical trials. In a clinical trial, they compare new treatments to standard ones. This helps them find out if the new treatment works better. Many people with cancer are invited to join a clinical trial. But not everyone can take part.

# Problems After Tooth Removal

Problems after tooth removal are serious issues. They need quick care. These problems include:

- Swelling and pain  
  Your face may swell. You may feel pain in the area where the tooth was removed.

- Bleeding  
  You may bleed more than normal after the tooth is out. This can last for several hours.

- Alveolitis  
  This is a painful condition. It happens when the blood clot in the tooth socket breaks down too soon. The bone and nerves in the socket become exposed. This causes strong pain.

- Osteomyelitis  
  This is an infection in the jawbone. It can happen after tooth removal. It causes pain, swelling, and fever. It needs strong treatment with antibiotics.

- Osteonecrosis of the jaw  
  This is a rare but serious problem. The jawbone does not heal properly. It can happen after tooth removal, especially in people who take certain medicines or have other health issues. The bone may become exposed and die. This can cause pain and infection.

# Bipolar Disorder

Bipolar disorder is a mental health condition where a person has strong mood swings. These swings go from deep sadness to extreme highs. The condition used to be called manic-depressive disorder.

## What Happens in Bipolar Disorder?

- A person may have times of feeling very low and sad. These are called depressive episodes.
- They may also have times of feeling very high, energetic, and overly confident. These are called manic episodes.
- Some people have a milder form of mania called hypomania.
- The mood swings can happen one after another, or they may happen at different times.
- Between episodes, a person may feel normal.

## How Common Is It?

- About 4 out of every 100 people in the United States have bipolar disorder.
- It affects men and women equally.
- Most people first notice symptoms in their teens, 20s, or 30s.
- Bipolar disorder in children is very rare.

## Types of Bipolar Disorder

There are two main types:

### Bipolar I Disorder
- A person has had at least one full manic episode.
- This episode is serious enough to stop normal daily life or includes delusions (false beliefs).
- Most people with this type also have depressive episodes.

### Bipolar II Disorder
- A person has had at least one major depressive episode.
- They also have at least one hypomanic episode (a milder form of mania).
- They have never had a full manic episode.

Some people have mood swings that are not severe enough to meet the full rules for Bipolar I or II. These may be called:
- Unspecified bipolar disorder
- Cyclothymic disorder

## What Causes Bipolar Disorder?

The exact cause is not known. But several things may play a role:

- Family history: If a close family member has bipolar disorder, you are more likely to get it.
- Brain chemistry: The brain uses chemicals called neurotransmitters to send messages. In people with bipolar disorder, these chemicals may not work properly.
- Stress: A major life event may trigger an episode, but it does not cause the disorder.
- Other medical conditions: Some illnesses can cause symptoms like mania.
- Medicines and drugs: Certain medicines and illegal drugs can cause mania.

### Conditions That Can Cause Mania

| Condition | Examples |
|--------|--------|
| Brain or nervous system problems | Brain tumors, head injuries, stroke, seizures, multiple sclerosis |
| Autoimmune diseases | Rheumatic fever, lupus |
| Infections | AIDS, encephalitis, flu, late-stage syphilis |
| Hormone problems | Overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism) |
| Medicines and drugs | Amphetamines, cocaine, corticosteroids, some antidepressants, levodopa, bromocriptine |

## Symptoms of Bipolar Disorder

### Depressive Episodes
- Feelings of deep sadness or emptiness
- Loss of interest in things you used to enjoy
- Slow thinking and slow movement
- Sleep more than usual or have trouble sleeping
- Changes in appetite — eat more or less than usual
- Weight gain or weight loss
- Feel hopeless, guilty, or worthless
- Trouble focusing or making decisions

Some people also have psychotic symptoms during depression. This means they may hear voices or see things that are not there. They may believe things that are not true, like they are a famous person or being followed.

### Manic Episodes
- Feel extremely happy, excited, or irritable
- Have a lot of energy
- Need very little sleep
- Talk faster than usual
- Thoughts race from one idea to another
- Easily distracted
- Act without thinking about the results
- Take big risks — like spending money recklessly, gambling, or having unsafe sex
- May dress or act in a wild or flashy way
- May not realize they are unwell

Mania often ends suddenly. It usually lasts at least one week.

### Manic Psychosis
This is a very serious form of mania. People may:
- Have strong false beliefs (delusions), like being a religious figure
- Feel they are being chased or punished
- Act wildly — run around, shout, sing, or swear
- Lose all sense of control
- Become extremely tired from the activity

This needs emergency treatment.

### Hypomania
- Feel cheerful and full of energy
- Need less sleep
- Think and act quickly
- May feel creative and confident

Some people enjoy this time. They feel productive and happy. But others may:
- Get easily distracted
- Get angry quickly
- Make promises they can’t keep
- Start many projects but never finish them
- Change moods fast
- Feel bothered by their own behavior or by how others react

### Mixed Episodes
- Feel sad and depressed while also feeling very energetic and excited
- May cry while feeling happy
- May have racing thoughts while feeling down
- May go to bed sad and wake up feeling high and full of energy

The risk of suicide is especially high during mixed episodes.

## How Is Bipolar Disorder Diagnosed?

Doctors use a careful evaluation to make a diagnosis. They look at:
- The pattern of mood changes
- How long symptoms last
- How much they affect daily life

They may:
- Ask about your symptoms and how they affect you
- Talk to family or friends to get a full picture
- Use a short questionnaire to help check for bipolar disorder
- Ask if you have thoughts about suicide
- Check your medicines to see if any could cause symptoms
- Do blood or urine tests to rule out other health problems (like thyroid issues or drug use)

## How Is Bipolar Disorder Treated?

Treatment usually includes a mix of:
- Medications
- Psychotherapy (talk therapy)
- Education and support

### Medications

#### Mood Stabilizers
- **Lithium** helps reduce both mania and depression.
- It can also help prevent future mood swings.
- It takes 4 to 10 days to start working.
- A faster-acting medicine is often used at first to control mania.
- People with a family history of bipolar disorder are more likely to respond to lithium.

**Side Effects of Lithium**
- Drowsiness
- Confusion
- Shaking (tremors)
- Muscle twitching
- Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea
- Thirst and needing to urinate more
- Weight gain
- Worsening of acne or psoriasis

These side effects often go away when the dose is adjusted. If they are too bad, the medicine may need to be stopped.

**Lithium Toxicity**
This happens when there is too much lithium in the blood. It can cause:
- Severe headaches
- Confusion
- Drowsiness
- Seizures
- Irregular heartbeat

Toxicity is more likely in:
- Older adults
- People with kidney problems
- People who have lost a lot of salt (from vomiting, diarrhea, or diuretics)
- Women who are pregnant or trying to get pregnant

Lithium can cause birth defects. Women who are pregnant or may become pregnant should not take it.

#### Antiseizure Medications
- **Valproate** and **carbamazepine** help stabilize mood.
- They are used for mania or mixed episodes.
- They do not harm the kidneys.
- But carbamazepine can lower red and white blood cell counts.
- Valproate can harm the liver (especially in children) or the pancreas (rarely).
- These problems can be caught early with regular doctor visits.

**Valproate and Pregnancy**
- Not recommended for women who are pregnant or could become pregnant.
- It may cause birth defects in the baby’s brain or spine (neural tube defects).
- It may also raise the risk of attention problems, ADHD, or autism in the child.

#### Lamotrigine
- Helps control mood swings and treat depression.
- Can cause a serious rash.
- Rarely, the rash becomes Stevens-Johnson syndrome — a life-threatening condition.
- Watch for:
  - New rash (especially near the rectum or genitals)
  - Fever
  - Swollen glands
  - Sores in the mouth or eyes
  - Swelling of lips or tongue
- Report any of these right away.
- The dose is started low and increased slowly over weeks.
- If you stop taking it for 3 days or more, you must restart the slow dose schedule.

#### Antipsychotic Medications
These are used for sudden mania. They work fast and have fewer serious side effects than older medicines.

Examples:
- Aripiprazole
- Lurasidone
- Olanzapine
- Quetiapine
- Risperidone
- Ziprasidone
- Cariprazine
- Lumateperone

**For Bipolar Depression**
Some antipsychotics are the best choice. They may be used with an antidepressant.

**Long-Term Side Effects of Antipsychotics**
- Weight gain
- Metabolic syndrome — a group of problems including:
  - Belly fat
  - High blood sugar
  - High blood pressure
  - Bad cholesterol levels
- Risk is lower with aripiprazole and ziprasidone.
- Some antipsychotics can be used during pregnancy, except risperidone, which may slightly increase birth defect risk.

#### Antidepressants
- Used only for short periods and with mood stabilizers or antipsychotics.
- Not used alone because they can trigger mania.

### Other Treatments

#### Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT)
- Used when other treatments do not work.
- Helps with severe depression or mania.
- It is safe and effective.
