# Histrionic Personality Disorder (HPD)

This condition is marked by a long-term pattern of being overly emotional and always wanting attention.  
It is diagnosed based on specific signs and symptoms.  
Treatment usually involves talking therapy focused on emotions and past experiences.

(See also: Overview of Personality Disorders.)

## What People with Histrionic Personality Disorder Do

People with this disorder often use their looks or behavior to get attention.  
They may act in ways that are too sexual or provocative, even in places like work or school.  
They do not have a strong sense of who they are.  
They easily follow others’ opinions and may act in a submissive way to keep people’s attention.

The condition affects less than 2 out of every 100 people in the general population.  
It affects men and women about equally.  
Earlier reports saying it was more common in women may have been wrong because those studies only looked at people in hospitals.

## Other Conditions That Often Happen with HPD

Many people with HPD also have other mental health issues.  
These include other personality disorders such as antisocial, borderline, and narcissistic types.  
Some also have somatic symptom disorder. This means they have physical symptoms that cause distress, but no clear medical cause.  
This may be why they go to a doctor.  
They may also have major depression, long-term low mood, or conversion disorder.

## Signs and Symptoms of HPD

People with HPD always want to be the center of attention.  
They feel sad or upset when they are not noticed.  
They are usually full of energy, dramatic, excited, and flirtatious.  
They often charm new people they meet.

They often dress or act in ways that are too sexual or attention-grabbing.  
This happens not just with romantic interests, but in many situations.  
They spend a lot of time thinking about how they look.  
They may show emotions that seem fake or change too fast.  
They talk in a dramatic way, but often do not give real facts or details.

They are easily influenced by others and by what is popular right now.  
They tend to trust people too much, especially those in power.  
They believe these people can fix all their problems.  
They often think their relationships are closer than they really are.  
They like new things and get bored easily.  
This can lead them to change jobs or friends often.  
They struggle to wait for rewards.  
They act to get what they want right away.

It can be hard for them to form deep emotional or sexual connections.  
They may unknowingly act out roles, like being a victim.  
They may use charm or emotional tricks to control a partner.  
At the same time, they become very dependent on that partner.

## How HPD Is Diagnosed

The diagnosis is based on the *Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders*, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR).

To be diagnosed, a person must show a long-term pattern of being overly emotional and seeking attention.  
They must have at least five of the following signs:

- They feel uncomfortable when they are not the center of attention.  
- They act in ways that are too sexually seductive or provocative.  
- Their emotions change quickly and seem shallow.  
- They use their looks to draw attention to themselves.  
- They speak in a vague, dramatic way without clear facts.  
- They act in a theatrical or exaggerated way.  
- They are easily influenced by others or by situations.  
- They see relationships as closer than they really are.

These signs must have started in early adulthood.

## How HPD Is Treated

The main treatment is psychodynamic psychotherapy.  
This type of therapy helps people understand their emotions and past experiences.  
It is not clear how well other types of therapy work for this condition.  
Medicines are not known to help directly with HPD.

In therapy, the therapist helps the person talk more and act less dramatically.  
The goal is to help them express themselves in a calmer, more honest way.  
The therapist also helps the person see how their dramatic behavior is a way to get attention and feel better about themselves.

# High Potassium in the Blood (Hyperkalemia)

High potassium in the blood is called hyperkalemia.

Potassium is a mineral your body needs to keep nerves and muscles working right. But too much potassium can be dangerous.

## What Causes High Potassium?

Many things can raise potassium levels. Most of the time, it happens when the kidneys do not remove enough potassium from the body.

Common causes include:

- Kidney problems that stop the kidneys from working well
- Certain medicines that affect kidney function
- Eating too many foods high in potassium
- Treatments that give extra potassium

The most common cause of mild high potassium is medicines that reduce blood flow to the kidneys or stop them from removing potassium.

Kidney failure can cause very high potassium levels. A condition called Addison disease can also cause high potassium.

Sometimes, a sudden release of potassium from body cells can cause a dangerous rise in blood potassium. This can happen after:

- Severe burns
- Crush injuries
- Diabetic ketoacidosis
- Metabolic acidosis
- Muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis)
- Certain medicines like beta-blockers
- Cancer chemotherapy
- Long, hard exercise

A normal diet with potassium-rich foods like beans, leafy greens, potatoes, fish, and bananas usually does not cause high potassium. Healthy kidneys can remove extra potassium.

### List of Causes

| Cause | Examples |
|------|----------|
| Kidneys not removing potassium | Kidney failure, Addison disease, low aldosterone |
| Medicines that block potassium removal | ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, eplerenone, triamterene, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, trimethoprim |
| Medicines that cause potassium to move out of cells | Beta-blockers, chemotherapy |
| Conditions that release potassium from cells | Severe burns, crush injuries, diabetes, acidosis, muscle breakdown |
| Extra potassium intake | Potassium-rich foods, IV treatments, potassium supplements |

## What Are the Symptoms?

Mild high potassium often causes no symptoms.

Some people may feel muscle weakness. In a rare condition called hyperkalemic familial periodic paralysis, weakness can turn into full paralysis.

When potassium levels get higher, the heart may beat abnormally. If levels are very high, the heart can stop.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors find high potassium through blood tests. It is often found by accident during routine testing.

An electrocardiogram (ECG) may show changes in the heart’s rhythm. This helps confirm the diagnosis.

To find the cause, doctors:

- Ask about your medical history
- Review your medicines
- Check blood tests for signs of diabetes, acidosis, muscle damage, or kidney problems

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on how high the potassium level is.

### For Mild Cases

- Cut back on high-potassium foods
- Stop medicines that raise potassium
- If kidneys are working, a diuretic may be used to help remove extra potassium

A medicine called sodium polystyrene sulfonate can be taken by mouth or as an enema. It pulls potassium from the gut and removes it in stool. But it can cause too much sodium to stay in the body. It is only used for short time.

Patiromer is another medicine that removes potassium from the gut. It can be used for longer periods. It helps people who need medicines that usually raise potassium, like ACE inhibitors.

Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate also binds potassium in the gut. It lowers blood potassium over several hours.

### For Moderate to Severe Cases

High potassium must be lowered fast. The heart is watched closely during treatment.

- Calcium is given through a vein to protect the heart. It does not lower potassium.
- Insulin and glucose are given to move potassium from blood into cells.
- Albuterol, a medicine used for asthma, can be inhaled to help lower potassium.

If these treatments do not work, or if you have kidney failure, dialysis may be needed. Dialysis removes extra potassium from the blood.

# Seizure Disorders During Pregnancy

Seizure disorders can make it harder to get pregnant. Some medicines for seizures can also reduce how well birth control pills work. This can lead to an unplanned pregnancy.

During pregnancy, your dose of seizure medicine may need to go up. This helps keep the medicine at the right level in your body. If you get enough rest and your medicine levels stay in the right range, seizures usually do not get worse. Most pregnancies go well. But there is a slightly higher chance of:

- High blood pressure in the mother (preeclampsia)  
- The baby not growing as expected  
- The baby being stillborn  

Uncontrolled seizures during pregnancy are more dangerous than taking seizure medicine. So the main goal of treatment is to stop seizures. It is best to talk with a neurologist before getting pregnant. This helps make sure your seizures are under control before you become pregnant. Your doctor should use the lowest possible dose of medicine and the fewest different medicines.

Babies of women with seizure disorders are more likely to be born with birth defects. About 6 to 8 out of 100 babies have a birth defect. This is higher than the 2 to 3 out of 100 in the general population. The risk of learning problems may also be higher. These risks may come from the seizure disorder itself or from the medicines used.

Some seizure medicines taken during pregnancy can increase the risk of bleeding in the newborn. This is called hemorrhagic disease of the newborn. This risk is higher with certain medicines like phenytoin, carbamazepine, and phenobarbital. But this problem is rare if you take prenatal vitamins with vitamin D during pregnancy and your baby gets vitamin K right after birth.

Phenytoin is usually the best choice. Phenobarbital may help reduce jaundice in newborns. Jaundice is a common yellowing of the skin and eyes in babies. Phenobarbital may help by boosting the baby’s liver function.

All seizure medicines increase the need for extra folic acid. You should take 4 milligrams of folic acid every day. It is best to start this before you become pregnant. Taking folic acid before pregnancy helps lower the risk of serious birth defects in the baby’s spine and brain.

Most women can have a vaginal birth. But if you have repeated seizures during labor, a cesarean birth may be needed.

After giving birth, your medicine levels can change quickly. It is important to check your medicine levels often during this time.

# Herpes Simplex Keratitis

Herpes simplex keratitis is an eye infection that affects the cornea.  
The cornea is the clear front part of the eye.  
It is caused by the herpes simplex virus.  
This virus also causes cold sores.  

The infection can come back many times.  
Each time it comes back, it can hurt the cornea.  
It may cause less feeling in the eye.  
It can also cause scarring on the cornea.  
In some cases, it can lead to vision loss.

## Symptoms

Common symptoms include:  
- Eye pain  
- Tearing  
- Redness  
- A feeling like something is in your eye  
- Pain when looking at bright light  

In rare cases, the cornea swells.  
This makes vision blurry.  
The more often the infection returns, the more damage it can cause.  
Repeated infections can lead to deep sores on the cornea.  
They can also cause permanent scars.  
Blood vessels may grow into the cornea.  
The surface of the eye may become numb.

Over time, repeated infections can cause serious vision problems.  
These problems can be permanent.

## How the Virus Works

The herpes simplex virus never leaves your body after the first infection.  
It stays in your nerves in a quiet, inactive state.  
Sometimes, the virus wakes up again.  
When it does, it can cause another infection.

The first infection usually happens in children.  
It causes mild swelling of the cornea and the clear membrane over the white of the eye.  
This is called keratoconjunctivitis.  
The first infection often gets better on its own.  
The virus then hides in the nerve roots.

Certain things can wake up the virus:  
- Strong light (from the sun or from eye surgery lasers)  
- Fever  
- Menstruation  
- Serious physical stress (like burns or broken bones)  
- Weak immune system  
- Using corticosteroid medicines (these are hormones that reduce swelling)

When the virus comes back, it can cause more serious eye problems.  
This can lead to temporary or permanent vision loss.

Herpes simplex keratitis is a leading cause of blindness around the world.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors look at your eye closely.  
They use a special tool called a slit lamp.  
This tool lets them see the eye in great detail.

They may put drops in your eye.  
These drops contain a yellow-green dye called fluorescein.  
The dye sticks to damaged areas of the cornea.  
It turns them bright green.  
This makes it easier for the doctor to see the damage.

Sometimes, the doctor takes a small sample from the eye.  
They test this sample to find the virus.  
They may use a viral culture or a nucleic acid amplification test.  

A viral culture grows the virus in a lab.  
This helps confirm the infection.  
A nucleic acid amplification test looks for the virus’s DNA or RNA.  
This test makes tiny amounts of genetic material easier to find.

## How It Is Treated

Treatment should start as soon as possible.  
The goal is to stop the virus and prevent more damage.

Doctors may prescribe antiviral eye drops.  
Examples include trifluridine or ganciclovir.  
They may also prescribe antiviral pills or medicine given through a vein.  
Examples include acyclovir or valacyclovir.

Acyclovir can be taken by mouth or given through a vein.  
Valacyclovir is taken by mouth.  
These medicines can also be used to prevent frequent outbreaks.  
This is called suppressive therapy.  
They are often used if past infections have threatened your vision.

If you have kidney problems, your doctor may need to change your dose.

For deep infections with strong swelling, doctors may use corticosteroid eye drops.  
These help reduce swelling and inflammation.

Drops that widen the pupil can help.  
Examples include cyclopentolate, atropine, or scopolamine.  
These drops can ease pain and discomfort.

In some cases, an eye doctor (called an ophthalmologist) may gently clean the cornea.  
They use a soft cotton swab to remove dead or infected cells.  
This can help the eye heal faster.

# Vesicant Chemical Warfare Agents

Vesicants are dangerous chemicals that cause blisters on the skin and eyes. They include:

- Mustards, such as sulfur mustard and nitrogen mustards  
- Lewisite  
- Phosgene oxime (this chemical causes hives and tissue damage. It is not a true blister agent, but it is grouped with blister agents)

These chemicals also harm the breathing system.  
Sulfur mustard mainly affects the large airways.  
Phosgene oxime affects the small airways and the tiny air sacs in the lungs.  
Lewisite affects both the large and small airways.

Sulfur mustard may smell like mustard, garlic, horseradish, or asphalt.  
Lewisite may smell like geraniums.  
Phosgene oxime causes a strong, irritating smell.  
But these smells are not reliable. People notice them differently. You cannot trust smell to tell if these chemicals are present.

---

## How Vesicant Chemicals Cause Harm

**Sulfur mustard and nitrogen mustard**  
These chemicals damage many parts of cells, including DNA. They also trigger inflammation in the body.  
They cause similar harm to the skin, eyes, and airways.  
At very high levels, they weaken the bone marrow, which makes blood cells.  
Damage to the bottom layer of the skin causes the top layer to separate or break off.  
At high doses, the skin may die and fall off.  
The fluid in blisters does not contain active sulfur mustard.  
In the lungs, these chemicals cause the lining of the large airways to peel off. This can form thick, false membranes.  
At high doses, fluid can build up in the lungs. This is called pulmonary edema.  
These chemicals can also cause nausea. This is likely due to effects on the nervous system.  
Low blood cell counts from bone marrow damage can lead to serious infections one or two weeks after exposure.  
Long-term problems may include eye damage, such as ongoing eye irritation. They may also increase the risk of skin and lung cancer.

**Lewisite**  
Lewisite causes skin damage similar to sulfur mustard. But it works in a different way.  
It affects chemicals in the body that protect cells. It also blocks an important enzyme.  
In the lungs, the arsenic part of Lewisite causes fluid to leak from blood vessels. This leads to fluid buildup in the lungs.  
High doses can cause a dangerous drop in blood pressure. This is called Lewisite shock.  
Unlike mustards, Lewisite does not weaken the immune system.

**Phosgene oxime**  
This chemical causes hives first. Then it causes tissue death.  
The exact way it causes damage is not fully known.

---

## Symptoms and Signs of Exposure

**Mustard compounds**  
Skin pain starts strong and gets worse over time.  
Redness and blisters appear after a delay.  
The delay depends on the amount of exposure. It is usually several hours, but can be up to 36 hours.  
Blisters from sulfur mustard may look like a string of pearls around a center that does not blister. That center is too damaged to form blisters.  
Blisters from nitrogen mustard are less likely to form this pattern.  
Blisters can grow large and hang down.  
Eye pain and irritation happen before skin symptoms. But they still take hours to appear.  
The eye’s clear front part may become cloudy.  
In the lungs, symptoms include coughing, tightness in the throat, hoarseness, wheezing, and a high-pitched breathing sound.  
These lung symptoms also appear after a delay. The delay depends on the dose.  
Chest tightness and trouble breathing can happen with severe exposure.  
Nausea may occur after moderate to high exposure.

**Lewisite**  
Skin pain starts within a minute of contact.  
Redness shows up in 15 to 30 minutes.  
Blisters form after several hours.  
They usually start in the center of the red area and spread outward.  
Pain is usually not as bad as with mustard. It often gets better once blisters form.  
Inhalation causes irritation in the nose, throat, and large airways. This leads to coughing, sneezing, and wheezing.  
After a few hours, symptoms like chest tightness and shortness of breath appear.

**Phosgene oxime**  
Skin contact causes sharp, stinging pain within 5 to 20 seconds.  
The skin turns pale at first. Then it turns gray with a red edge.  
Between 5 and 30 minutes, swelling forms a raised bump (urticaria).  
Over the next 7 days, the skin turns dark brown and then black. This is due to dead tissue.  
The damage can go deep into the skin and muscle.  
If not removed by surgery, the wound can last more than 6 months.  
In the lungs, even a small amount can cause fluid buildup.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Exposure

**Clinical Evaluation**  
If pain starts right after exposure, Lewisite or phosgene oxime is likely.  
The fast start of skin changes points to phosgene oxime.  
If pain starts hours later, sulfur mustard is more likely.  
Doctors can confirm exposure with lab tests. These tests look for breakdown products or chemical changes in DNA or proteins.  
But these tests are only available at special labs.

**Blood Tests**  
People exposed to mustard compounds should have blood tests every day for the first two weeks.  
This checks for low white blood cell counts and low lymphocyte counts.

---

## How to Treat Exposure

**Decontamination (Cleaning the Body)**  
Clean the skin as soon as possible.  
Use a special lotion called RSDL. It contains:  
- A potassium salt of 2,3-butanedione monoxime (DAM)  
- DAM itself  
- A solvent called polyethylene glycol monomethyl ether (MPEG)  
- Water  

If RSDL is not available, a 0.5% solution of sodium hypochlorite (bleach) can be used. It works less well but still helps.  
Physical cleaning, like wiping or rinsing, can also help.  
Soap and water, or high-flow, low-pressure water, can be used in emergencies for large groups.  
Eyes and open wounds should be flushed with sterile saline.

**Skin Care**  
Treat skin injuries like burns.  
But use less fluid than for thermal burns.  
Vesicant exposure causes less fluid loss than burns.  
So, use less fluid than the standard burn formulas (Brooke or Parkland).  
Keep the skin clean to prevent infection.  
Apply antibiotic ointment to the edges of the eyelids to stop them from sticking together.

**Breathing Support**  
If the lungs are affected, support breathing as needed.  
This includes keeping the airway open and helping with breathing.  
See the section on pulmonary chemical agents for more details.

**Nausea Treatment**  
Nausea from these chemicals comes from nerve system effects.  
It can be treated with atropine.  
Dose: 0.1 to 1.3 milligrams given through a vein every 1 to 2 hours as needed.

**Bone Marrow Damage**  
If the bone marrow is damaged, the patient must be protected from infection.  
This is called reverse isolation.  
Medicines that help the bone marrow make blood cells (colony-stimulating factors) may be used.

# Scleritis

Scleritis is a serious and damaging inflammation of the white part of the eye. This condition can harm your vision.

## Who Is Most Likely to Get Scleritis?

- Scleritis is most common in women between the ages of 30 and 50.
- It can happen in people who have a bodywide inflammatory disease.

## What Causes Scleritis?

- Some people with scleritis also have a systemic rheumatic disease. These include:
  - Rheumatoid arthritis
  - Systemic lupus erythematosus
  - Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
  - Polyarteritis nodosa
  - Relapsing polychondritis
- Some people have an autoimmune disorder. This means the body’s defense system mistakenly attacks its own tissues.
- In a few cases, an infection causes scleritis.
- In about half of all cases, the cause is unknown.

## What Are the Symptoms?

- You feel a deep, constant, and severe pain in the eye.
- The pain can be so bad it keeps you from sleeping or eating.
- The eye feels tender.
- Your eye waters more than usual.
- Bright light hurts your eye.
- The eye turns a purplish red color over part or all of the surface.

Rarely, the inflammation becomes so strong it can cause a hole in the eye. This is called necrotizing scleritis. It can lead to losing the eye. People with necrotizing scleritis often have a systemic rheumatic disease.

## How Is Scleritis Diagnosed?

- Your doctor will ask about your symptoms.
- They will look at your eye using a special microscope called a slit-lamp.
- If the problem is in the back of the eye, your doctor may use an ultrasound or a CT scan to see it better.
- In rare cases, your doctor may take a small sample from the eye to test for infection.

## How Is Scleritis Treated?

- Most people start with a medicine called a corticosteroid taken by mouth. Prednisone is one example.
- For mild cases, a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) may be enough.
- If the inflammation comes back, you may need to take corticosteroids for a longer time.
- If you need high doses of corticosteroids or have necrotizing scleritis with a systemic rheumatic disease, your doctor may give you an immunosuppressant medicine. These include:
  - Methotrexate
  - Cyclophosphamide
  - Rituximab
- If there is a risk of a hole forming in the eye, surgery may be needed to repair it.

## What Is the Outlook?

- Some people with scleritis lose some of their sharpness of vision.
- Early treatment can help protect your sight.

# Health Issues in Teens

Teens go through a big change from childhood to adulthood. This time brings fast body growth and big changes in thinking, feelings, and relationships. These changes can help teens stay healthy. But they can also bring health risks.

## Common Health Problems in Teens

The top causes of death and serious illness in teens in the United States are accidents. These include car crashes, gun injuries, and drug overdoses.

Some teens also face injuries on purpose. This includes violence like murder or suicide. Head injuries, such as concussions, can happen during sports or other activities.

Using drugs or alcohol is a serious health problem. It can hurt a teen’s body and mind now and later in life. Teaching teens about health, stopping problems before they start, checking for issues early, and finding problems quickly are all important.

Mental health problems are common during the teen years. The pandemic and the changes it brought—like school closures and disrupted routines—hurt many teens’ mental health.

As teens grow, they start to think about their sexuality. They may feel pressure from friends or others. Some common concerns include:

- Figuring out who they are attracted to
- Learning how to build healthy relationships
- Using protection during sex
- Preventing sexually transmitted infections
- Avoiding pregnancy
- Dealing with sexual abuse or other trauma
- Exploring their gender identity

Most teens are healthy. But some teens have long-term health problems. Being overweight is common and can lead to other health issues like diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol.

Medical advances mean more teens survive serious health problems they had as children.

About 4 out of 10 teens in the United States have a long-term health condition. Examples include asthma, diabetes, and inflammatory bowel disease.

Cancer is rare in teens. But when it does happen, the most common types are:

- Leukemia
- Lymphoma
- Bone cancers
- Soft-tissue cancers (like rhabdomyosarcoma)
- Brain and spinal cord tumors
- Thyroid cancer

# Hemoglobin C, S-C, and E Diseases

These are inherited conditions. They happen when a person gets abnormal genes from their parents. These genes change the hemoglobin in red blood cells. Hemoglobin carries oxygen in the blood. The abnormal hemoglobin causes red blood cells to break down faster than normal. This leads to long-term anemia.

(See also: Overview of Anemia and Sickle Cell Disease.)

---

## Hemoglobin C Disease

- This condition mostly affects people with African or Black American ancestry.
- About 2 to 3 out of every 100 people with African or Black American ancestry in the U.S. carry one copy of the abnormal gene.
- A person must get two copies of the abnormal gene—one from each parent—to have the disease.
- Most people with this disease have few or mild symptoms.
- Anemia can be mild or more severe.
- Some people have an enlarged spleen or mild yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice).
- People with this disease do not have the painful episodes (crises) seen in sickle cell disease.
- Gallstones are a common problem in people with this disease.

---

## Hemoglobin S-C Disease

- This is a type of sickle cell disease.
- It happens when a person has one abnormal gene for sickle cell disease and one abnormal gene for hemoglobin C disease.
- This condition is more common than hemoglobin C disease.
- Symptoms are similar to sickle cell anemia, but painful episodes and serious health problems happen less often.
- These problems may also start later in life.
- Some people develop kidney problems.
- Others may have an enlarged spleen.
- Bleeding in the back of the eye (retinal hemorrhage) can occur.
- Damage to the hip joint may also happen.

---

## Hemoglobin E Disease

- This condition mainly affects people with Southeast Asian ancestry.
- It causes mild anemia.
- It does not cause the painful episodes or other serious problems seen in sickle cell disease or hemoglobin C disease.

---

## How These Diseases Are Diagnosed

Doctors use blood tests to find these conditions.

- A doctor takes a blood sample and looks at it under a microscope.
- The red blood cells may have unusual shapes.
- Other changes in the blood can also be seen.

Another test called hemoglobin electrophoresis is also used.

- This test uses electricity to separate the different types of hemoglobin in the blood.
- It helps find abnormal hemoglobin.
- A second test, called high-performance liquid chromatography, may also be done.
- This test helps tell the different types of hemoglobin apart.

---

## How These Diseases Are Treated

Treatment depends on the symptoms and how bad they are.

- Some people do not need any treatment.
- People with hemoglobin C disease usually do not need treatment.
- In rare cases, they may need blood transfusions.
- When treatment is needed for hemoglobin S-C disease, it is similar to treatment for sickle cell disease.
- Most people with hemoglobin E disease do not need treatment.
- In severe cases, regular blood transfusions may be needed.
- In some cases, the spleen may need to be removed.

# Excoriation (Skin-Picking) Disorder

This condition means a person keeps picking at their own skin.  
The picking causes open sores or damage to the skin.  

People with this disorder pick at their skin again and again.  
They do not pick because they think their skin looks bad or is unhealthy.  
Some pick at skin that looks fine.  
Others pick at small problems like calluses, pimples, or scabs.  

Some people pick without really thinking about it.  
Others know they are doing it.  
The picking is not caused by fears about how they look.  
This is different from a condition called body dysmorphic disorder.  

Before picking, some people feel tense or anxious.  
Picking helps them feel better.  
They may also feel a sense of relief or satisfaction after picking.  

Skin picking often starts during the teenage years.  
But it can start at any age.  
About 3 out of every 100 people have this disorder.  
Most of them are women.  

---

## What to Look For: Symptoms and Signs

The skin picking usually lasts a long time.  
It can get worse or better over time if not treated.  
The places where people pick can change.  
No two people pick in the same way.  

Some people have many scars.  
Others only pick at a few spots.  
Many try to hide the marks with clothes or makeup.  

Some people follow certain routines when they pick.  
They may search for a specific scab to pull.  
They may want to pull it off in a certain way.  
They might use their fingers or tools.  
Some even bite or swallow the scab after pulling it off.  

People with this disorder often try to stop picking.  
They want to pick less or stop completely.  
But they cannot do it, even when they try.  

They may feel embarrassed or ashamed.  
They may not want others to see the marks.  
They often avoid social events.  
They usually do not pick in front of others, except maybe family.  

This can hurt their work or school life.  
It can also affect their relationships.  

Some people pick at the skin of others.  
Many also do other repetitive behaviors.  
These include pulling out their hair or biting their nails.  

If the picking is very bad, it can cause serious problems.  
These include scars, infections, heavy bleeding, or even blood poisoning.  

Many people with this disorder also have other mental health issues.  
These can include obsessive-compulsive disorder or depression.  

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

To be diagnosed, a person must meet these three main points:

- They have visible skin damage from picking.  
  (Some people hide the marks with clothes or makeup.)  
- They keep trying to stop or cut down on picking.  
- The picking causes them serious distress or problems in daily life.  

The distress can come from feeling ashamed.  
It can come from not being able to control the behavior.  
It can also come from how the skin looks after picking.  

---

## How Is It Treated?

The best treatment is a type of talk therapy.  
It is designed to help with skin picking.  
One proven method is called habit reversal training.  

This therapy includes:

- **Awareness training**: Learning to notice when you are about to pick.  
  You may keep a diary or track your triggers.  
- **Stimulus control**: Changing your environment to avoid triggers.  
  For example, avoid places or situations that make you want to pick.  
- **Competing response training**: Learning a new behavior to do instead.  
  Examples: clench your fist, knit, or sit on your hands.  

Medicines may also help.  
SSRIs or clomipramine can help with anxiety or depression.  
They may also reduce skin picking, though the evidence is limited.  

Another type of medicine, called a glutamate modulator, may help.  
These include *N* - acetylcysteine and memantine.  
Small studies show they can reduce symptoms.  
But we need more research to know if they are safe and effective long-term.  

---

## Key Points

- Skin picking is not about how you look.  
  It is often linked to tension or anxiety.  
  Picking gives a sense of relief or pleasure.  

- People with this disorder want to stop.  
  But they cannot, even when they try.  

- The picking causes visible damage to the skin.  

- Treatment includes therapy that targets skin picking.  
  Habit reversal training is one of the most effective types.  

- Medicines like SSRIs, clomipramine, *N* - acetylcysteine, or memantine may help.  
  They are used along with therapy.  

- Early treatment can improve quality of life.  
  Support and understanding from others are important.

# Chest Wall Tumors

Tumors in the chest wall can be cancer or not cancer.  
They grow in the ribs, chest muscles, connective tissues, or nerves.  
These tumors can affect how the lungs work.

You can find more about lung tumors in the section on "Overview of Lung Tumors."

Chest wall tumors can start in the chest wall.  
Or they can spread (move) to the chest wall from a cancer in another part of the body.  
About half of all chest wall tumors are not cancer.

## Noncancerous Tumors

The most common noncancerous chest wall tumors are:
- Osteochondroma
- Chondroma
- Fibrous dysplasia

## Cancerous Tumors

Many types of cancer can affect the chest wall.  
More than half of these cancers come from other parts of the body.  
They spread to the chest wall from organs like the breast or lung.  
Some cancers grow directly into the chest wall from nearby areas.

The most common cancer that starts in the chest wall is a sarcoma.

Chondrosarcoma is the most common type of primary chest wall sarcoma.  
It starts in the cartilage of the front ribs.  
It can also start in the breastbone, shoulder blade, or collarbone, but less often.

Bone cancers include:
- Osteosarcoma
- Small-cell cancers like Ewing sarcoma or Askin tumor

Soft-tissue cancers that start in the chest wall include:
- Fibrosarcoma (including desmoids and neurofibrosarcoma)
- Malignant fibrous histiocytoma

Other rare primary cancers in the chest wall are:
- Chondroblastoma
- Osteoblastoma
- Melanoma
- Lymphoma
- Rhabdomyosarcoma
- Lymphangiosarcoma
- Multiple myeloma
- Plasmacytoma

## Symptoms

A lump in the chest wall may be the only sign if the tumor is in soft tissue.  
Some people have a fever.  
Pain usually does not happen until the tumor is large or advanced.  
Tumors in bone or cartilage often cause pain.

## Diagnosis

Doctors use imaging tests to find and study chest wall tumors.  
These tests include:
- Chest x-ray
- Computed tomography (CT) scan
- Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
- Positron emission tomography (PET)–CT scan

Imaging helps doctors see where the tumor started.  
It also shows if the tumor is in the chest wall or came from another part of the body.

A biopsy is often done.  
This means taking a small sample of the tumor.  
The sample is checked under a microscope to confirm the diagnosis.

Sometimes a chest wall tumor is found by accident during imaging for another reason.

## Treatment

Most chest wall tumors are removed with surgery.  
If part of the chest wall is removed, doctors rebuild it.  
They may use tissue from another part of the body.

In some cases, treatment includes:
- Chemotherapy (medicine to kill cancer cells)
- Radiation therapy (high-energy beams to destroy cancer cells)

These treatments may be used alone or together with surgery.

## Outlook

The outlook depends on the type of cancer, how abnormal the cells look, and how far the cancer has spread.  
Because these tumors are rare, there is not much data on how they usually progress.  
As with most cancers, early-stage disease has a better outcome.

# Anxiety in Children and Teens

Anxiety is a strong feeling of fear, worry, or dread. It can make it hard to do normal things. When anxiety is too strong for the situation, it may be a disorder.

Anxiety can cause physical symptoms. These include stomachaches, headaches, trouble sleeping, and nausea.

Doctors diagnose anxiety by talking with the child and family. They look at the child’s history and behavior.

Treatment often includes therapy and sometimes medicine.

---

## Normal Fears Are Common

It is normal for children to feel anxious at times. These fears are part of growing up.

- Toddlers often get scared when separated from their mom, especially in new places.
- Many 3- and 4-year-olds are afraid of the dark, monsters, bugs, or spiders.
- Shy kids may feel nervous when meeting new people or trying new things.
- Older children often worry about getting hurt or dying.
- Teens may feel anxious when speaking in front of classmates.

These feelings are not a sign of a disorder. But if anxiety gets so strong that it stops a child from doing everyday things, causes great distress, or leads to avoiding situations, it may be an anxiety disorder.

---

## How Common Are Anxiety Disorders?

- About 3 out of every 100 children aged 6 have an anxiety disorder.
- About 5 out of every 100 teenage boys have an anxiety disorder.
- About 10 out of every 100 teenage girls have an anxiety disorder.

Children with anxiety are more likely later in life to:
- Feel sad or depressed
- Have thoughts about hurting themselves
- Use drugs or alcohol
- Struggle in school

---

## Types of Anxiety Disorders in Children and Teens

- Agoraphobia – fear of being in places where escape might be hard
- Generalized anxiety disorder – constant worry about many things
- Panic disorder – sudden, intense fear with physical symptoms
- Separation anxiety disorder – extreme fear of being away from parents
- Social anxiety disorder – fear of being judged or embarrassed in social situations
- Specific phobias – intense fear of one thing, like dogs, heights, or thunder

---

## What Causes Anxiety?

Scientists believe anxiety comes from problems in parts of the brain that control emotions and fear.

In mice, changes in a brain chemical called serotonin during early life led to anxious behavior.

Anxiety in children is linked to both genes and life experiences. No single gene causes it. Many small genetic differences may play a role.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, anxiety in youth doubled, especially in girls. Mental health visits for anxiety went up by 43%.

Even after accounting for age, gender, and past anxiety, researchers found that:
- Poor connection with a caregiver
- Poor sleep habits
- Too much screen time

were strong signs of anxiety during the pandemic.

Parents who are anxious often have anxious children. An anxious parent can make a child’s anxiety worse. Even normal children find it hard to stay calm around an anxious parent. Children with a family history of anxiety have an even harder time.

In up to 30% of cases, treating both the parent and child together helps.

---

## Signs and Symptoms

The most common sign of anxiety in children is refusing to go to school.

“School refusal” is now used instead of “school phobia.” Most children who refuse school are not afraid of school itself.

They may have:
- Separation anxiety
- Social anxiety
- Panic attacks
- A specific fear (like of dogs or thunder)
- Or a mix of these

Bullying at school is also a possibility and should be checked.

Some children can talk about their fear. For example:
- “I’m scared I’ll never see you again.” (Separation anxiety)
- “I’m scared the kids will laugh at me.” (Social anxiety)

But most children do not talk about their fear. Instead, they say they feel sick. They may say:
- “I have a stomachache.”
- “I have a headache.”
- “I can’t sleep.”

These physical symptoms are real. Anxiety can cause them. Many children with ongoing stomachaches or headaches actually have an anxiety disorder.

Long-term studies show that children with frequent physical complaints often have anxiety.

---

## How Is Anxiety Diagnosed?

Doctors use a mental health evaluation to diagnose anxiety.

They follow the guidelines in the *Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders*, Fifth Edition (DSM-5-TR).

A full history of the child’s life and family helps confirm the diagnosis.

Doctors may use screening tools to help find anxiety. These are free and reliable:
- SCARED (Screen for Child Anxiety-Related Emotional Disorders)
- SCAS (Spence Children’s Anxiety Scale)
- PAS (Preschool Anxiety Scale)
- GAD-7 (General Anxiety Disorder-7)

Physical symptoms from anxiety can make diagnosis harder. Doctors often test for physical illness first before deciding it is anxiety.

---

## How Is Anxiety Treated?

Treatment includes:
- Behavioral therapy
- Family support
- Medicine (in some cases)

### Behavioral Therapy (CBT)

This is the main treatment. It uses exposure and response prevention.

In this therapy:
- The child slowly faces the thing they fear.
- The therapist helps them stay in the situation without avoiding it.
- Over time, the fear gets smaller.

This works best when the therapist knows child development and can tailor the treatment to the child.

For mild cases, therapy alone is often enough.

For more severe cases, or when therapy is hard to access, medicine may be needed.

### Medicine

Most children start with a type of medicine called an SSRI. These are safe and effective for long-term use.

SSRIs include:
- Citalopram
- Escitalopram
- Fluoxetine
- Fluvoxamine
- Paroxetine
- Sertraline

Other medicines may be used:
- SNRIs (like duloxetine) – less common
- Tricyclic antidepressants – used in some cases
- Benzodiazepines – only for short-term use, like before a medical test

Benzodiazepines with a short effect (like lorazepam) are best for quick relief.

Buspirone is safe for children but has not been proven better than a placebo in studies.

Some children may have side effects from medicine. These can include:
- Upset stomach
- Diarrhea
- Trouble sleeping
- Weight gain
- Agitation or restlessness
- Feeling overly active or impulsive

These side effects are usually mild. Lowering the dose or switching medicine often helps.

Rarely, side effects can be serious, like increased thoughts about suicide or aggression.

Because of this, children on medicine must be watched closely.

### Medicine Dose Table

| Medicine | Used For | Starting Dose | Dose Range | Notes |
|--------|--------|-------------|----------|------|
| Citalopram | OCD | 10 mg | 10–40 mg/day | For children 7 and older |
| Duloxetine | Generalized anxiety | 30 mg | 30–120 mg/day | Can raise blood pressure |
| Escitalopram | Depression | 10 mg | 10–20 mg/day | For children 12 and older |
| Fluoxetine | OCD, anxiety, depression | 10 mg | 10–60 mg/day | Long-lasting |
| Fluvoxamine | Anxiety, OCD | 25 mg | 50–200 mg/day | Take in two doses if over 50 mg |
| Paroxetine | OCD | 10 mg | 10–60 mg/day | Can cause weight gain |
| Sertraline | OCD, anxiety | 25 mg | 25–200 mg/day | For children 6 and older |
| Venlafaxine (immediate) | Depression | 12.5 mg | 12.5 mg twice a day to 25 mg three times a day | Limited data, possible risk |
| Venlafaxine (extended) | Generalized anxiety | 37.5 mg | 37.5–225 mg once a day | For children 7 and older |

**Important Notes:**
- All these medicines are used for anxiety, OCD, and depression.
- Some are FDA-approved for certain uses. Others are not, because not enough studies have been done.
- No SSRI is clearly better than another.
- Doses are a guide. Doctors adjust based on the child.
- When stopping medicine, reduce slowly over weeks.
- Behavioral side effects (like agitation) are common but usually mild.
- Rarely, side effects can be serious (like aggression or suicidal thoughts).
- Children on these medicines must be watched closely.

### Genetic Testing

Some children have genes that affect how their body processes medicine.

Testing for these genes can help doctors pick the right medicine and dose.

For example:
- Some people break down medicine too fast or too slow.
- This affects how well the medicine works and how likely side effects are.

The CPIC guidelines help doctors use test results.

Ethnic background affects these genes:
- 7–15% of White people lack a key gene
- 2% of Asian and African American people lack it
- 10% of White people and 50% of Asian people have a gene variant that slows medicine breakdown

New genetic tests are improving, but they are not yet standard.

### Drug Interactions

Fluoxetine and paroxetine can affect how other medicines work. They can slow down the breakdown of:
- Blood pressure medicines
- Clonidine
- Lidocaine

Doctors must know about all medicines a child takes.

---

## Prognosis (Outlook)

How well a child does depends on:
- How severe the anxiety

# Coordination Disorders

Coordination disorders happen when the cerebellum does not work properly.  
The cerebellum is the part of the brain that helps control movement and balance.  
When it does not work right, people lose their ability to move smoothly and stay steady.

## What Causes Coordination Disorders?

The most common cause is long-term, heavy drinking of alcohol.  
This can permanently damage the cerebellum.

Other common causes include:
- Stroke
- Multiple sclerosis

Less common causes include:
- An underactive thyroid gland
- Low levels of vitamin E
- Brain tumors
- Certain inherited conditions, like Friedreich ataxia
- Rarely, some cancers (such as breast, ovarian, or lung cancer) can cause the body’s immune system to attack the cerebellum. This is called subacute cerebellar degeneration.

In children, brain tumors are a possible cause.

Some medicines and harmful substances can also cause coordination problems.  
These include:
- Antiseizure medicines (like phenytoin), especially at high doses or over long periods
- Alcohol
- Carbon monoxide
- Heavy metals like mercury or lead
- Lithium
- Sedatives (like benzodiazepines) in high doses

If the medicine or substance is stopped, the problem may go away.

---

## Symptoms of Coordination Disorders

When coordination is lost, people have trouble controlling their arms and legs.  
They may walk with wide, unsteady steps.  
They may sway or stagger when they walk.

They may also:
- Reach too far when trying to grab something (this is called dysmetria)
- Speak in a slurred or uneven way (this is called dysarthria)
- Speak in a slow, choppy way with pauses at the start of words (this is called scanning speech)
- Have eyes that move quickly back and forth when looking at something (this is called nystagmus)
- Shake when trying to move a limb (this is called tremor)

Muscle tone may become weak.

### Friedreich Ataxia

This is a hereditary condition.  
You must inherit one faulty gene from each parent to get it.

It gets worse over time.  
Most people start having trouble walking between ages 5 and 15.  
Then arm movements become unsteady, and speech becomes hard to understand.

Many children with this condition are born with:
- A clubfoot
- A curved spine (scoliosis)

They lose the ability to feel vibrations or know where their limbs are.  
They also lose reflexes.  
Their thinking may get worse over time.  
Tremors are usually mild.

Heart problems often develop and get worse.  
By their late 20s, most people need a wheelchair.  
Death often happens in middle age due to heart problems or irregular heartbeats.

### Spinocerebellar Ataxias (SCAs)

These are inherited conditions.  
Only one faulty gene from one parent is enough to cause the disorder.

There are many types.  
SCA type 3 (also called Machado-Joseph disease) is the most common worldwide.

These conditions get worse over time and are often fatal.

Symptoms vary by type, but most include:
- Poor sensation (less feeling of pain, touch, or vibration)
- Weak muscles
- Restless legs
- Loss of coordination
- Problems with balance, speech, and eye movements

Some types only cause coordination problems.

SCAs often cause intention tremors (shaking when trying to reach for something).  
Some people have symptoms like Parkinson’s disease, such as stiff muscles and tremors.

People with SCA type 3 may also have:
- Trouble moving their eyes
- Twitching in the face or tongue
- Bulging eyes
- Long-lasting, painful muscle contractions (dystonia)

---

## How Are Coordination Disorders Diagnosed?

Doctors start by asking about symptoms and family history.  
They check for conditions that could cause the symptoms.

A physical exam is done, including a neurologic exam.

A brain scan called magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is usually done.

Genetic testing may be done if there is a family history of similar problems.

---

## How Are Coordination Disorders Treated?

If the cause can be fixed, doctors will treat it.

For example:
- If alcohol is the cause, stop drinking.
- If a medicine is the cause, lower the dose or stop taking it.
- If the cause is low thyroid function or low vitamin E, these can be treated with medicine or supplements.
- If a brain tumor is the cause, surgery may help.

There is no cure for inherited conditions like Friedreich ataxia or spinocerebellar ataxias.  
But treatment can help with symptoms.

A medicine called riluzole may help improve coordination for a short time.

Physical therapy helps people improve balance, posture, and movement.  
Therapists teach exercises that can help people walk better and do daily tasks more easily.

Occupational therapists can suggest tools to help with walking, eating, and other daily activities.

Speech therapy can help with slurred speech and other communication problems.

# Pain Behind the Inner Ankle: Tibialis Posterior Tendinosis and Tenosynovitis

Pain behind the inner ankle bone is often caused by problems with the tibialis posterior tendon. This tendon runs behind the inner ankle bone. Two common issues are:

- **Tendinosis**: The tendon breaks down over time.
- **Tenosynovitis**: The sheath around the tendon becomes inflamed.

## What Causes These Problems?

The tendon can wear out because of long-term foot problems. These include:

- Feet that roll too far inward (over-pronation), especially in people who are overweight.
- A foot that tilts outward at the heel (hindfoot valgus).
- Long-term inflammation of the tendon sheath.
- A stiff foot condition called tarsal coalition. This can cause a flat foot and stop the tendon from working properly.

Inflammation in the tendon sheath can start suddenly. It may be caused by diseases like rheumatoid arthritis or gout.

## What Are the Symptoms?

At first, you may feel pain behind the inner ankle now and then. Over time, the pain gets worse. You may also have swelling and trouble standing, walking, or standing on your toes.

If the tendon tears (often from long-term tendinosis), the arch of your foot may suddenly fall. Pain can then spread to the bottom of your foot.

In long-term tendinosis without a tear, the arch slowly drops. The Achilles tendon pulls differently. This causes the heel to tilt outward. This change can lead to joint damage in the foot and eventually arthritis.

In later stages, the ankle joint can also develop arthritis because of the heel tilt.

With tenosynovitis, the pain comes on quickly. The tendon may feel thick and swollen as it wraps around the inner ankle bone.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tools to find the cause of your pain.

### Clinical Exam
Your doctor will check your foot and ankle. They may press on the tendon while you point your foot down and turn it inward. This often causes pain.

You may not be able to stand on your toes. This can mean the tendon is torn or not working well.

Swelling and tenderness behind the inner ankle suggest tenosynovitis.

A flat foot with a bulge on the inside of the ankle and toes that point outward (too many toes sign) suggests a serious tendon problem. This may mean the tendon is torn and needs testing.

### X-rays
X-rays help rule out other causes of inner ankle pain. These can include extra bones, like an accessory navicular bone.

X-rays can also show if the foot arch has collapsed. They show joint misalignment in the foot. The heel bone tilts outward. The angle of the heel bone and the ankle bone changes.

### MRI or Ultrasound
These scans can show fluid around the tendon. This means there is inflammation (tenosynovitis).

They can also show how much the tendon is damaged, torn, or worn down.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on how bad the problem is.

### Surgery
If the tendon is completely torn, surgery is needed to restore normal foot function. This is especially important for young, active people with a sudden tear.

### Non-Surgical Treatments
For less severe cases, doctors recommend:

- **Orthotics**: Special shoe inserts with a deeper heel cup and a wedge on the inner side. These help take pressure off the tendon.
- **Braces**: Custom braces that wrap around the foot and lower leg. They add stability and support.

### Injections
Corticosteroid injections can make tendon damage worse. They are not recommended.

### For Tenosynovitis
Rest and strong anti-inflammatory medicine are needed. This helps reduce swelling and pain.

# Skin-Picking Disorder

People with skin-picking disorder keep picking at their skin. This can hurt the skin and cause open sores or scars.

- They may feel tense or anxious just before picking.
- Picking can make that tension go away.
- Doctors diagnose the disorder when:
  - The skin is damaged from picking.
  - The person tries to stop but cannot.
  - The behavior causes strong distress or makes daily life harder.

## What Happens in Skin-Picking Disorder?

People pick at their skin again and again. They do not do it to fix a spot they think looks bad. They are not trying to remove a blemish or treat a skin problem.

Some people pick at healthy skin. Others pick at calluses, pimples, or scabs.

- Skin picking often starts during the teenage years.
- It can start at other times too.
- About 1 to 2 out of every 100 people have this disorder.
- Most people with it are women.

## Signs and Symptoms

The way people pick and where they pick varies.

- Some have many sores or scars.
- Others have only a few.
- The spots they pick at can change over time.

Some people pick without thinking. Others are fully aware of what they are doing.

- They do not pick because they are worried about how they look.
- But they often feel tense before picking.
- Picking gives them a sense of relief or satisfaction afterward.

Many people have routines around picking.

- They may search for a certain kind of scab.
- They may pull it off in a specific way—using fingers or tools like tweezers.
- Some bite or swallow the scab after pulling it off.

Many people with this disorder also do other repetitive body-focused habits. These include:

- Pulling out their hair
- Biting their nails
- Chewing the inside of their cheek
- Picking at the skin of others

People often feel embarrassed or ashamed.

- They may hide their skin damage.
- They avoid social situations where others might see the damage.
- They usually only pick in private, except in front of family.
- They may cover the damage with clothes or makeup.
- They feel upset about not being able to stop.
- They try many times to cut down or stop, but they cannot.

If done too much, skin picking can lead to:

- Scars
- Infections
- Heavy bleeding
- A serious blood infection (septicemia)

Many people with this disorder also have other mental health problems, such as:

- Obsessive-compulsive disorder
- Hair-pulling disorder
- Depression

Symptoms can come and go in intensity. But they often last for years or even a lifetime.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor or mental health professional will ask about your symptoms.

They use clear rules to decide if you have skin-picking disorder.

You must have:

- Picked at your skin so much that it caused damage.
- Tried many times to stop or reduce picking.
- Felt very upset or had trouble doing daily tasks because of the picking.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment includes therapy and sometimes medicine.

### Therapy: Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT)

CBT, especially a type called habit-reversal therapy, is the best treatment.

In this therapy, you learn to:

- Pay more attention to when you pick at your skin.
- Notice what triggers the picking.
- Use new habits to stop yourself. For example:
  - Clench your fist.
  - Knit.
  - Sit on your hands.

These new habits replace the picking.

### Medicine

Some medicines may help reduce symptoms.

- *N* - acetylcysteine (NAC) and memantine work on brain chemicals linked to the disorder. They may help reduce picking.
- Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (a type of antidepressant) can help.
- Clomipramine (another type of antidepressant) may also help.

These medicines can also improve symptoms of other conditions, such as:

- Depression
- Anxiety

Medicine works best when used with therapy.

# Respiratory Alkalosis

Respiratory alkalosis happens when your breathing becomes too fast or too deep. This causes carbon dioxide levels in your blood to drop. When carbon dioxide drops, your blood becomes more alkaline (less acidic). Your body may try to fix this with other changes, such as lowering bicarbonate levels.

This condition can happen suddenly (acute) or over time (chronic). The chronic form usually causes no symptoms. The acute form can cause dizziness, fainting, confusion, tingling in the hands and lips, and muscle cramps.

## What Causes Respiratory Alkalosis?

You breathe faster or deeper than normal when your body needs more oxygen. This can happen because of:

- Low oxygen levels in the blood (such as at high altitudes)
- Metabolic acidosis (a condition where your blood is too acidic)
- Fever or higher body demands for energy
- Pain or strong anxiety
- Brain problems like stroke or seizures

In many serious illnesses, fast breathing is a normal response. But sometimes, breathing gets too fast without a clear reason.

## How Does It Work in the Body?

When you breathe too fast, you blow off too much carbon dioxide. This changes the balance in your blood.

- In the short term (minutes), your body starts to adjust.
- Over the next two to three days, your kidneys help by reducing acid in your urine.

This helps bring your blood pH back toward normal.

## What Are the Symptoms?

### Acute Respiratory Alkalosis
You may feel:
- Dizzy or lightheaded
- Confused
- Tingling in your fingers, toes, or around your mouth
- Muscle cramps
- Fainting

The main sign is fast or deep breathing. In severe cases, you may have muscle spasms in your hands and feet. This happens because low carbon dioxide levels cause calcium to move into your cells, lowering the amount of active calcium in your blood.

### Chronic Respiratory Alkalosis
This form usually causes no symptoms. Some people report:
- Trouble sleeping
- Memory problems
- Changes in mood or personality

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use two main tests:
- Arterial blood gas (ABG): This measures oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH in your blood.
- Blood tests: These check your electrolyte levels, such as calcium, potassium, and phosphate.

If your blood oxygen level is low, your doctor will look for the cause. A high alveolar-arterial oxygen difference also suggests a problem.

Your doctor will review your medical history and do a physical exam. But even if you have no low oxygen, you may still have a serious condition like a blood clot in the lungs (pulmonary embolism). So, do not assume anxiety is the cause unless other serious problems are ruled out.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment focuses on fixing the underlying cause. For example:
- Treat fever
- Manage pain
- Treat lung or heart problems
- Address anxiety or stress

Respiratory alkalosis itself is not dangerous. You do not need to lower your blood pH. In fact, trying to do so by breathing into a paper bag can be harmful. It may reduce oxygen levels in your blood. It can also hide a serious condition like metabolic acidosis.

## Key Points

- Respiratory alkalosis means you are breathing too fast or too deeply.
- Fast breathing often happens in response to low oxygen, fever, acidosis, pain, or anxiety.
- Do not assume anxiety is the cause unless other serious conditions are ruled out.
- Treat the root problem. You do not need to treat the alkalosis itself.
- Breathing into a paper bag is not safe and can cause harm.

# Arginine Vasopressin Resistance

This condition means your kidneys do not respond to a hormone called vasopressin. As a result, your kidneys make a lot of urine that is very watery. Your body cannot keep the water it needs.

## What Causes This Condition?

Some people are born with this problem. It is passed down through families. It usually affects boys more than girls. Girls can carry the gene and pass it to their sons.

Other people develop this problem later in life. It can be caused by certain medicines. Lithium is one example. It is a medicine used to treat some mental health conditions.

It can also happen if the kidneys are damaged by other health problems. These include:
- Polycystic kidney disease
- Sickle cell anemia
- Medullary sponge kidney
- Severe kidney infections
- Amyloidosis
- Sjögren syndrome
- Some types of cancer, such as sarcoma or myeloma

High levels of calcium or low levels of potassium in the blood can also make the kidneys less able to respond to vasopressin.

Sometimes, doctors do not know the cause.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You will feel very thirsty all the time. You will pass a lot of urine. The urine will be very clear and thin.

You may pass between 1 and 6 gallons (3 to 20 liters) of urine each day.

If the condition is inherited, symptoms usually start right after birth. Babies cannot tell you when they are thirsty. They may become very dehydrated. They may have a fever, vomit, or have seizures.

Older adults with dementia may also become dehydrated. They may not know they are thirsty or may not be able to ask for water.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use blood and urine tests to check for this condition.

The tests show:
- High levels of sodium in the blood
- Very dilute urine

A water deprivation test may also be done. This test checks how your body handles water when you do not drink for a while.

## How Is It Treated?

You must drink enough water to stay hydrated. Drink water as soon as you feel thirsty.

Babies, young children, and very sick older adults need help drinking water often. If you drink enough water, you will not become dehydrated. But going several hours without water can lead to serious dehydration.

A low-salt and low-protein diet may help reduce how much urine you make.

Medicines can also help. These include:
- Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
- Thiazide diuretics

These medicines work in different ways. They help your kidneys keep more water and salt. This reduces the amount of urine you pass.

## What Is the Outlook?

If the condition is found early and treated, the outlook is good.

Infants with this condition can grow and develop normally if they get treatment right away.

If the condition is not treated quickly, brain damage can happen. This can lead to lifelong learning problems.

Frequent dehydration can also slow down physical growth.

If the condition is not inherited, fixing the underlying cause often helps the kidneys work normally again.
