# Urinary Stones

Urinary stones are hard pieces that form in the urinary system. They can cause pain, nausea, vomiting, blood in the urine, and chills or fever if there is an infection.

Doctors find stones using imaging tests, usually a CT scan without contrast. Treatment includes pain medicine, antibiotics if there is an infection, medicines to help pass the stone, and sometimes minor surgery. Surgery options include shock wave treatment or removing the stone with a small scope.

## How Common Are Urinary Stones?

About 1 to 2 out of every 100 adults in the United States get a urinary stone each year.  
About 1 in every 1,000 adults is hospitalized each year because of a stone.  
By age 70, up to 1 in 5 men and 1 in 10 women will have had a stone.

Stones can be tiny or as big as a few centimeters. A very large stone, called a staghorn stone, can fill the entire kidney drainage system.

---

## What Causes Urinary Stones?

Some health problems raise the risk of stones. These include:

- High levels of calcium or uric acid in the urine.
- Low levels of citrate in the urine.
- Conditions like overactive parathyroid glands, kidney problems, gout, or type 2 diabetes.

Diet also plays a role. Eating too much salt or not drinking enough water can make stones more likely.

### Types of Stones and Their Causes

Most stones are made of calcium, especially calcium oxalate.  
Here is how common each type is:

| Stone Type | Percentage | Common Causes |
|------------|------------|----------------|
| Calcium oxalate | 40–80% | High calcium in urine, low citrate, overactive parathyroid glands, kidney problems |
| Calcium phosphate | 18–24% | High calcium in urine, overactive parathyroid glands, low citrate, kidney problems |
| Cystine | 1–2% | A rare inherited condition called cystinuria |
| Magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) | 5–15% | Urinary tract infection with certain bacteria |
| Uric acid | 5–10% | Urine that is too acidic, high uric acid levels |

Note: Some stones are made of more than one type. This is why the total adds up to more than 100%.

---

## Calcium Stones

The most common cause of calcium stones is high calcium in the urine, even when blood calcium is normal. This is called hypercalciuria.

- It runs in families. About half of men and three-quarters of women with calcium stones have this condition.
- Urine calcium is high: over 250 mg per day in men, over 200 mg per day in women.

Low citrate in the urine also increases risk. Citrate helps stop calcium from forming stones.  
Low citrate is found in about 40 to 50% of people with calcium stones.

Other causes of high calcium in urine include:
- Kidney problems (renal tubular acidosis)
- Overactive parathyroid glands (in up to 5% of cases)
- Rare conditions like sarcoidosis, too much vitamin D, overactive thyroid, cancer, or a rare liver disease

High levels of oxalate in the urine (hyperoxaluria) can also cause calcium oxalate stones.  
This can happen because of:
- Eating too many oxalate-rich foods (spinach, rhubarb, nuts, tea, cocoa, pepper)
- Digestive problems (like Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, or after weight-loss surgery)
- A rare inherited condition

Other risk factors:
- Taking more than 2,000 mg of vitamin C daily
- Eating a low-calcium diet (this may let more oxalate get into the blood)
- Mildly high uric acid in the urine (from eating too much meat, fish, or poultry)

---

## Uric Acid Stones

These stones form when the urine is too acidic (pH below 5.5).  
They can also form if there is very high uric acid in the urine.

Uric acid stones may be the only type in the stone, or they may start a stone that later includes calcium.

---

## Cystine Stones

These only happen in people with a rare inherited condition called cystinuria.  
The body cannot reabsorb cystine, so it builds up in the urine and forms stones.

---

## Struvite Stones (Infection Stones)

These stones form only when there is a urinary tract infection with certain bacteria.  
These bacteria break down urea in the urine, making it more alkaline. This allows stones to grow.

These stones must be removed completely because they are infected.  
They are more common in women than men.

---

## Other Rare Causes

Some medicines or chemicals can cause stones. These include:
- Indinavir (a medicine for HIV)
- Melamine (a chemical found in some contaminated food)
- Triamterene (a blood pressure medicine)
- Xanthine (a rare metabolic condition)

---

## How Do Stones Cause Problems?

Stones can stay in the kidney or move into the ureter (the tube from kidney to bladder).  
When a stone moves, it can block urine flow. This causes pain and swelling.

Common blockage sites:
- Where the kidney meets the ureter
- Where the ureter crosses the pelvic bones
- Where the ureter enters the bladder

Larger stones (over 5 mm) are more likely to get stuck.  
Stones 5 mm or smaller often pass on their own.

Even a partial blockage reduces how well the kidney filters waste.  
This effect can last a short time after the stone passes.

If the blockage lasts too long, kidney function can get worse.  
But permanent damage usually only happens after about 28 days of full blockage.

Infections can develop if a stone stays in place for a long time.  
But most calcium stones do not cause infection.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many people with stones in the kidney have no symptoms.  
Symptoms usually start when the stone moves into the ureter.

The most common symptom is severe pain. This is called renal colic.

- The pain is sharp and intense.
- It comes in waves and lasts 20 to 60 minutes.
- It may come and go.
- It often starts in the side or back, just below the ribs.
- It can spread to the lower belly or groin.

Other symptoms:
- Nausea and vomiting
- Blood in the urine (visible or only seen under a microscope)
- Needing to urinate often or urgently
- Pain when urinating
- Fever, cloudy urine, or foul-smelling urine (if there is an infection)

On exam, a person with a stone may:
- Be very uncomfortable
- Sweat a lot
- Be pale
- Move around a lot, unable to stay still
- Have tenderness when the doctor presses on the side of the back (costovertebral angle tenderness)
- Not have signs of belly infection (like muscle tightness or pain when pressing and releasing)

Some people first notice a stone when they pass blood in the urine or see small stones in the toilet.

---

## How Are Stones Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tools to find stones.

### First, they check for other possible causes of pain.

Other conditions that can feel similar:
- Appendicitis – pain starts in the lower right belly, gets worse with movement
- Diverticulitis – pain in the lower left belly, often with fever
- Ectopic pregnancy – in women, pain in the lower belly with missed periods
- Pelvic inflammatory disease – in women, pain with vaginal discharge or bleeding
- Gallbladder disease – pain in the upper right belly, often with a positive Murphy sign
- Bowel blockage – pain in both sides of the belly, constipation, no gas
- Pancreatitis – constant pain in the upper belly, often radiates to the back

A tear in the aorta (a major blood vessel) can also cause kidney pain and blood in the urine. This is more common in older adults.

### Tests to Confirm a Stone

- **Urinalysis** – checks for blood, infection, and crystals in the urine.
- **Imaging** – usually a CT scan without contrast. This shows the stone clearly.
- **Stone analysis** – if the stone is passed, it can be tested to see what it is made of.

---

## How Are Stones Treated?

### Immediate Care

- Pain relief with medicine.
- Medicines to help the stone pass (like tamsulosin).
- Antibiotics if there is an infection.

### For Stones That Don’t Pass

- Surgery may be needed.
- Options include shock wave treatment or using a small scope to remove the stone.

### For Infection Stones

- Antibiotics that match the bacteria causing the infection.
- The stone must be removed completely.
- If the infection cannot be cured, long-term antibiotics may be needed.
- A medicine called acetohydroxamic acid can help prevent new stones.

---

## How to Prevent Future Stones

After passing one stone, the chance of getting another is:
- 11% within 2 years
- 39% within 15 years

### General Prevention Steps

- Drink plenty of fluids. Aim for 8 to 10 ten-ounce glasses (about 300 ml each) per day.
- For people with stones, aim to make at least 2.5 liters of urine each day.
- Collect and test the passed stone.
- Test the urine for stone-forming substances.
- Review

# Byssinosis

Byssinosis is a lung condition that causes the airways to narrow. It feels like asthma. It happens when people breathe in dust from raw cotton, flax, or hemp.

## What Causes Byssinosis?

People who work in textile factories are most at risk. They may be exposed to dust from raw cotton, flax, or hemp. This dust can come from unprocessed fibers.

The dust contains tiny particles. Some of these particles carry a toxin made by bacteria. This toxin can cause the airways to narrow in some people.

Over time, repeated exposure can lead to long-term lung problems. These include chronic bronchitis and a slow loss of lung function.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may feel tightness in your chest. You may also have trouble breathing or wheeze. These symptoms usually start on the first day of work after a break, like after a weekend or vacation.

The symptoms often get better as you keep working during the week. They may go away completely by the end of the workweek.

This pattern—worse at the start of the workweek and better later—is different from regular asthma.

Workers who are exposed for many years may develop a mix of asthma and chronic lung disease. This condition is called obstructive lung disease.

## How Is Byssinosis Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your work history. They ask if you have been around cotton, flax, or hemp dust.

They also do lung function tests. These tests measure how well your lungs work. The test is done at the start and end of the workday. If your lung function drops during the day, it may mean you have byssinosis.

Workers in the textile industry should have regular lung tests. This helps catch the problem early.

## How Is Byssinosis Treated?

The best treatment is to stop or reduce exposure to dust.

Medications that open the airways can help. These are the same medicines used for asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

You can reduce dust in the workplace by:
- Wetting the raw materials
- Improving ventilation
- Using exhaust hoods to pull dust away

For some jobs, wearing a respirator or dust mask is needed.

If symptoms continue or lung tests show serious blockage, you should move to a job with less dust.

## How Can Byssinosis Be Prevented?

The best way to prevent byssinosis is to control dust at work.

Use tools and methods that reduce dust. Examples include wetting the fibers and using exhaust fans.

Wear protective gear like respirators or dust masks when needed.

These steps can protect your lungs and keep you healthy.

# Liver Cysts

Liver cysts are often found by chance during imaging tests like ultrasound or CT scans of the belly.  
Most of these cysts do not cause any symptoms.  
They do not harm your health and usually do not need treatment.  

A rare condition called polycystic liver disease is present from birth.  
It often happens together with polycystic kidney disease and can affect other organs.  
This condition causes the liver to grow larger over time.  
In some cases, the liver becomes very large.  
Even with this growth, the liver still works well.  
High pressure in the blood vessels of the liver (portal hypertension) is very rare.  

Sometimes, a very large cyst can press on nearby organs.  
This can cause pain or other symptoms.  
If this happens, treatment may be needed.  
Options include draining the cyst or connecting it to the belly cavity (cyst marsupialization).  
But the cysts often come back after treatment.  
In rare cases, symptoms are severe enough to consider a liver transplant.  

## Other Types of Liver Cysts

### Hydatid Cysts  
These cysts are caused by a type of tapeworm called *Echinococcus granulosus*.  
People get infected by accidentally swallowing worm eggs.  
This usually happens when they touch the stool of infected animals like dogs or sheep.  

### Caroli Disease  
This is a rare inherited condition.  
It causes some parts of the liver’s bile ducts to become widened and cyst-like.  
It often causes problems in adulthood.  
Symptoms can include bile duct stones, infections in the bile ducts (cholangitis), and in rare cases, cancer of the bile ducts (cholangiocarcinoma).  

### Cystadenoma  
This is a rare type of tumor that can cause pain or loss of appetite.  
It can be seen on an ultrasound scan.  
Treatment usually involves removing the cyst.  

### Cystadenocarcinoma  
This is a rare cancer.  
It may develop from a cystadenoma that turns cancerous.  
It often has several lobes or parts.  
Treatment involves removing the affected part of the liver.  

### Other True Cystic Tumors  
These are very rare and not commonly seen.

# Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis

This is a serious eye condition. It causes swelling and sores on the cornea. The cornea is the clear front part of the eye.

It often happens in people with certain long-term body-wide diseases that affect the immune system. These include rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and relapsing polychondritis.

## Symptoms

- Your vision may become blurry.
- Bright light may hurt your eyes.
- You may feel like something is stuck in your eye.

The sore is usually on the edge of the cornea. It is often shaped like an oval.

## What Causes It

In many cases, the body’s own immune system attacks the cornea. This is called an autoimmune reaction.

In other cases, an infection may cause the problem. This could be from bacteria, fungi, or a virus like herpes simplex.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors look at your eye. They check for the sore on the cornea.

They also look at your medical history. They want to know if you have a long-term disease that affects connective tissue.

If they think an infection is the cause, they take a small sample from the sore and the eyelid. They send this sample to a lab. There, they grow the sample to find the germ causing the problem.

## How It Is Treated

Doctors treat the sore and the underlying disease.

They give medicines that calm down the immune system. These include:

- Methotrexate
- Cyclophosphamide
- Rituximab
- Etanercept

These medicines can be taken by mouth or given through a vein.

Doctors may also use a special glue to cover the sore. Then they place a special contact lens over it. This helps reduce swelling and protect the eye.

In some cases, surgery is needed. A partial corneal transplant may be done. This means replacing part of the damaged cornea with healthy tissue from a donor.

## Outlook

Without treatment, about 4 out of 10 people with this condition die within 10 years. Most of these deaths are due to heart problems.

With treatment, only about 1 in 10 people die within 10 years.

The eye problem itself does not cause death. The danger comes from the long-term disease affecting the whole body.

# Meningococcal Vaccine

Meningococcal disease in the United States is most often caused by three types of bacteria: serogroups B, C, and Y.  
From 2006 to 2015, serogroup B caused about 36% of cases.  
Serogroup Y caused about 29% of cases.  
Serogroup C caused about 23% of cases.  
Serogroups A and W cause disease in other parts of the world.  
Vaccines are available for some, but not all, of these types.

(See also: Overview of Immunization.)

---

## Types of Meningococcal Vaccines

There are six meningococcal vaccines available in the United States.

### For serogroups A, C, W, and Y (quadrivalent vaccines):

- MenACWY-CRM  
- MenACWY-TT  

### For serogroup B (monovalent vaccines):

- MenB-4C (3-strain)  
- MenB-FHbp (4-strain)  

### For serogroups A, B, C, W, and Y (pentavalent vaccines):

- MenACWY-TT/MenB-FHbp (5-strain)  
- MenACWY-CRM/MenB-FHbp (5-strain)  

---

## Who Should Get the Meningococcal Vaccine?

### Quadrivalent vaccine (MenACWY)

This vaccine is a routine shot for teens.  
It is best given at age 11 or 12.  
A booster dose is needed at age 16.  
It is also recommended for younger children who are at high risk of infection.

This vaccine is also recommended for adults who are at higher risk of meningococcal disease. These include people who:

- Do not have a spleen, or have a spleen that does not work well (this includes people with sickle cell disease)  
- Have HIV  
- Have a problem with their immune system (specifically, low levels of certain proteins called complement)  
- Take certain medicines that affect the immune system (like eculizumab or ravulizumab)  
- Work in a lab where they often handle the meningococcal bacteria  
- Are joining the military  
- Are traveling to or living in areas where meningococcal disease is common  
- Are starting college and live in a dormitory, if they are 21 years old or younger and have not had a dose on or after their 16th birthday  
- Have been exposed to a meningococcal disease outbreak caused by a vaccine-preventable type

If a first-year college student aged 21 or younger got only one dose before their 16th birthday, they should get a booster before starting college.

All teens aged 11 to 18 should get the MenACWY vaccine, including those with HIV.

MenACWY is the preferred vaccine for people aged 11 to 55.  
It is also preferred for adults over 55 who were vaccinated before and still need more shots.  
It is also preferred for adults over 55 who have not had the vaccine before and need just one dose (such as travelers).

People over 55 who are at high risk and were vaccinated before should get a booster every 5 years.

### MenB vaccines (MenB-4C or MenB-FHbp)

These vaccines are for people aged 10 and older who have certain high-risk conditions. These include:

- No spleen or a spleen that does not work well  
- Low levels of certain immune system proteins  
- Taking eculizumab or ravulizumab  
- Working in a lab with regular exposure to the meningococcal bacteria  
- Living in an area with a serogroup B outbreak

The CDC does not recommend MenB vaccines for all teens.  
But doctors may choose to give it to anyone aged 16 to 23, especially those aged 16 to 18.  
Booster shots are not usually needed.

### Pentavalent vaccines (MenACWY-TT/MenB-FHbp and MenACWY-CRM/MenB-FHbp)

These vaccines protect against five types: A, B, C, W, and Y.  
They are for people aged 10 to 25.  
They are especially recommended for healthy teens and young adults aged 16 to 23 when both MenACWY and MenB vaccines are needed.  
They are also recommended for some people aged 10 and older who are at high risk, such as those with:

- Long-term problems with their immune system  
- Taking immune-suppressing medicines  
- No spleen or a spleen that does not work well  

The rules for MenACWY-CRM/MenB-FHbp are the same as for MenACWY-TT/MenB-FHbp.

---

## Who Should Not Get the Meningococcal Vaccine?

### Do not get the vaccine if you:

- Had a serious allergic reaction (like anaphylaxis) to a previous dose  
- Had a serious allergic reaction to any part of the vaccine  

### Be careful before getting the vaccine if you:

- Are sick with a moderate or severe illness (with or without fever)  
  - Wait until you feel better if possible  
- Are a preterm baby (only for MenACWY vaccine)  
- Are pregnant (only for MenB vaccine)  
- Are allergic to latex (only for MenB-4C vaccine)  

Pregnant people at high risk of serogroup A, C, W, or Y disease can get the MenACWY vaccine.  
Pregnant people should delay MenB vaccine unless they are at high risk of serogroup B disease and the benefits outweigh the risks.

Children with no spleen or a spleen that does not work well should not get MenACWY and pneumococcal conjugate vaccine at the same time.  
Wait at least 4 weeks between these two shots.

---

## How the Vaccine Is Given

People aged 10 and older can get the MenB vaccine at the same time as the MenACWY vaccine.  
But give them in different parts of the body if possible.  
If both vaccines are needed on the same day, a single pentavalent vaccine (MenACWY/MenB) can be used instead of two separate shots.

---

## Side Effects of the Vaccine

Side effects are usually mild.  
They may include:

- Pain or redness at the injection site  
- Fever  
- Headache  
- Feeling tired  

For more details on side effects, check the vaccine’s prescribing information.

# What Are Idiopathic Interstitial Pneumonias?

Idiopathic interstitial pneumonias are lung diseases with no known cause. They all affect the lungs in similar ways. The word *idiopathic* means the cause is unknown.

These diseases are not infections. Even though the word *pneumonia* is used, they are not caused by germs like colds or flu.

There are eight main types. They happen less often in this order:

- Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis  
- Desquamative interstitial pneumonia  
- Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia  
- Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia  
- Respiratory bronchiolitis–associated interstitial lung disease  
- Acute interstitial pneumonia  
- Lymphoid interstitial pneumonia  
- Idiopathic pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis  

All types cause the same main symptoms:  
- Cough  
- Trouble breathing  
- Thick or rounded fingertips (called clubbing)

A doctor may hear crackling sounds when listening to your lungs with a stethoscope.

Even though symptoms are similar, the diseases are different. They can develop at different speeds. They respond to different treatments. And some are much more serious than others.

---

## Comparing the Types of Idiopathic Interstitial Pneumonias

| Disease | Who Gets It Most Often | How Many Smoke? | Treatment | What to Expect |
|--------|--------------------------|------------------|-----------|----------------|
| Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis | Men over 50 | More than 60% | Pulmonary rehab, antifibrotic drugs, lung transplant | 50 to 70 out of 100 people die within 5 years |
| Desquamative interstitial pneumonia | Men aged 30 to 50 | More than 90% | Stop smoking, steroids | 70 out of 100 people live 10 years or more |
| Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia | Women aged 40 to 60 | Fewer than 30% | Steroids, sometimes other immune drugs | Survival is usually better than for pulmonary fibrosis |
| Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia | People aged 50 to 60 (any age) | Fewer than 50% | Steroids | More than 90 out of 100 people live 5 years or more |
| Respiratory bronchiolitis–associated interstitial lung disease | People aged 30 to 50 (slightly more men) | More than 90% | Stop smoking, steroids | Death is rare if you stop smoking |
| Acute interstitial pneumonia | Any age | Unknown | Machine breathing support, sometimes steroids | More than 50 out of 100 people die in less than 6 months |
| Lymphoid interstitial pneumonia | Mostly women of any age | Unknown | Steroids | Hard to predict how long someone will live |
| Idiopathic pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis | Any age (average age 57) | Usually non-smokers | Treatment not clear (may help with steroids) | 25 to 60 out of 100 people live 5 years or more |

> *Note: Listed in order of how often they occur.*

---

## How Doctors Diagnose These Diseases

Doctors use several tools to find out what is wrong.

- A chest CT scan is the most important test. It shows detailed pictures of the lungs.
- If the CT scan does not give a clear answer, a small piece of lung tissue may be taken for testing. This is called a lung biopsy.
- The biopsy is usually done during surgery using a thin tube with a camera called a thoracoscope.
- Blood tests are done to check for other health problems.
- An ECG or echocardiogram may be done to see if the heart is affected by lung disease.

---

## How These Diseases Are Treated

- **Stopping smoking is always recommended.** Smoking makes the disease worse faster.
- Treatment depends on the type of disease.
- Some people get steroids. These are medicines that reduce swelling and inflammation.
- Some people get antifibrotic drugs. These slow down scarring in the lungs.
- In some cases, a lung transplant may be needed.

Your doctor will choose the best treatment based on your type of disease, your health, and how fast it is getting worse.

# Specific Phobias

A specific phobia is a strong, ongoing fear of a particular thing or situation.  
This fear is much stronger than what most people would feel.  
It causes serious anxiety and leads people to avoid the thing or situation.  

The exact cause of phobias is not known.  
Doctors diagnose phobias by talking to the person and learning about their symptoms.  
The main treatment is exposure therapy.  
Some people also benefit from hypnosis or relaxation techniques.  

---

## What Is a Specific Phobia?

You have a specific phobia if you feel extreme fear or anxiety about a certain object or situation.  
This fear is not reasonable given the real danger.  
You usually try to avoid the thing or situation.  
If you cannot avoid it, your anxiety comes on very quickly.  
In some cases, the anxiety can become so strong it leads to a panic attack.  
Most people with a phobia know their fear is too strong.  

Specific phobias are the most common type of anxiety disorder.  
Common examples include:  
- Fear of animals (like spiders or dogs)  
- Fear of heights  
- Fear of thunderstorms  

About 8 out of every 100 women and 3 out of every 100 men have a specific phobia in any one year.  

Some phobias cause little trouble.  
For example, a city person who fears snakes may not be bothered unless they go hiking in a forest.  
Other phobias can cause serious problems.  
For example, someone who works in a tall building may fear elevators.  
This can make it hard to do their job.  

A rare type of phobia involves fear of blood, needles, or injury.  
When these people are exposed to the feared thing, they may faint.  
This happens because their body’s automatic response slows the heart and lowers blood pressure.  

Phobias can also affect health care.  
For example, a fear of needles may stop someone from getting blood tests or vaccines.  

---

## Symptoms of Specific Phobias

You feel strong fear or anxiety when you face a specific object or situation.  
You then try to avoid that object or situation.  

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Specific Phobias

Doctors use the DSM-5-TR to diagnose specific phobias.  
To meet the diagnosis, you must have:  

- A strong fear or anxiety that lasts at least six months.  
- The fear or anxiety starts right away when you face the object or situation.  
- You actively avoid the object or situation.  
- Your fear is much stronger than the actual danger.  
- The fear, anxiety, or avoidance causes serious distress or makes daily life hard.  

Doctors will not diagnose a specific phobia if another mental health condition better explains the symptoms.  
Many people with a specific phobia also have other mental health issues.  
These can include:  
- Other anxiety disorders  
- Depression  
- Bipolar disorder  
- Substance use problems  
- Somatic symptom disorders  
- Personality disorders, especially dependent personality disorder  

---

## Treatment for Specific Phobias

The most effective treatment is exposure therapy.  
This means slowly and safely facing the feared object or situation.  
You do this in small steps, with support.  
This helps your mind learn that the thing is not as dangerous as you think.  

Relaxation techniques or breathing exercises can help reduce anxiety.  
Hypnosis may also be used in some cases.  

In rare cases, doctors may prescribe a short-term medicine.  
This could be a benzodiazepine or a beta-blocker.  
These are used only when needed and for a short time.  

---

## Prognosis (Outlook)

If left untreated, the outcome depends on the phobia.  
Some fears are easy to avoid.  
For example, you can avoid caves or snakes if you live in the city.  
Other fears are harder to avoid.  
For example, bridges and thunderstorms are common in daily life.  
This makes it harder to live without fear.

# Nonspecific Interstitial Pneumonia

This is a type of lung disease that causes inflammation and scarring in the lungs. It mostly affects women who do not smoke and are under the age of 50.

## Who Gets This Condition?

- Most people with this condition are women between 40 and 50 years old.
- Most do not have a clear cause or risk factor.
- In some cases, it can happen in people with certain autoimmune diseases, such as:
  - Systemic sclerosis
  - Polymyositis
  - Dermatomyositis
- It can also occur in people with lung damage from certain medicines.
- It may also happen in people with hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms develop slowly over months or years. They include:

- A dry cough
- Trouble breathing, especially during activity
- A low-grade fever
- Feeling tired or unwell

High fever, weight loss, or other serious signs of illness are rare.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find out if you have this condition.

### Imaging Tests
- A chest X-ray may be done first.
- A chest CT scan gives more detailed pictures of the lungs.

### Lung Function Tests
- These tests measure how well your lungs work.
- Most people have less lung capacity than normal.
- Blood oxygen levels are often low at rest and drop further during exercise.

### Bronchoscopy and Lung Washings
- Doctors may use a thin tube to look into the lungs.
- They wash part of the lung with a saltwater solution.
- They collect the fluid and test it.
- In more than half of people, the fluid has more of a certain type of white blood cell called lymphocytes than normal.

### Lung Biopsy
- A small sample of lung tissue is taken.
- This is often needed to confirm the diagnosis.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment usually includes:

- Steroids (also called glucocorticoids or corticosteroids)
- Other medicines that reduce immune system activity (immunosuppressants)

These medicines often help improve symptoms and slow disease progression.

### Prognosis (Outlook)
- People with mild disease often live at least 10 years after diagnosis.
- The outlook is worse for people with more severe disease.
- Survival depends on how bad the condition is when it is found.

# Daptomycin

Daptomycin is an antibiotic. It works in a special way to kill bacteria.

It attaches to the outer layer of bacterial cells. This causes the cell to lose important chemicals. The cell can no longer make DNA, RNA, or proteins. The cell dies quickly.

## When Daptomycin Is Used

Daptomycin works against many types of bacteria. It is especially useful for:

- Gram-positive bacteria
- Bacteria that are resistant to other antibiotics

It is mainly used to treat infections caused by:

- Methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus* (MRSA)
- Vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE)

Some of these bacteria can become resistant during treatment. This may lead to a return of the infection or a long-lasting infection.

Daptomycin is not good for treating pneumonia. It does not work well in the lungs. This is because it sticks to a natural substance in the lungs called pulmonary surfactant. This reduces its ability to fight infection in the air sacs of the lungs.

## Who Should Not Use Daptomycin

Do not use daptomycin if you have had an allergic reaction to it before.

## Using Daptomycin During Pregnancy and Breastfeeding

Studies in animals did not show harm to unborn babies. But there is not much information about its use in pregnant women. The amount that passes to the baby through the placenta is not known.

If you are pregnant and have a serious infection, your doctor may still decide that daptomycin is safe to use.

Daptomycin passes into breast milk. But very little of it is absorbed by the baby’s body. We do not know if it affects the baby.

## Side Effects of Daptomycin

Side effects can include:

- Eosinophilic pneumonia (a type of lung inflammation)
- Muscle problems

Long-term use may cause a type of lung problem called organizing pneumonia. This can happen because daptomycin builds up in the lungs. It sticks to a natural substance in the lungs.

Muscle problems from daptomycin are usually reversible. They are rare when the medicine is taken once a day. But serious muscle damage has been reported.

Taking daptomycin with certain other medicines, like statins, may increase the risk of muscle damage.

## How to Take Daptomycin

Daptomycin is given through a vein once a day.

Over 90 percent of the medicine stays in the blood and binds to proteins.

Your dose may need to be changed if you have kidney problems.

Because daptomycin can cause muscle pain or weakness, your doctor will check your muscles. They will ask about symptoms and test your blood for a muscle enzyme called creatine kinase. This test is done once a week.

# Understanding Mood Disorders

Mood disorders are mental health conditions that cause long periods of extreme sadness or extreme happiness. These feelings go beyond normal ups and downs.

Sadness and happiness are normal parts of life. But in mood disorders, the feelings are much stronger and last longer.

### Sadness

Sadness happens when you lose something important. It can come from losing a loved one, a breakup, a job, or a big disappointment. Grief is a normal reaction to loss. Most people feel sad after a loss, but their sadness gets better over time.

Some people have sadness that lasts a long time and gets worse. This is called prolonged grief disorder. It is more likely in people who are already at risk for mood disorders.

### Did You Know...

- Many people say they feel down when they see a doctor.
- But only a small number have a serious mood disorder.

### Happiness and Mania

Happiness is a good feeling when something positive happens. Mania is not the same as normal happiness. It is a very intense and unusual state.

Mania can feel like extreme joy to someone who has a mood disorder. But it often comes with:
- Feeling very excited
- Acting very energetic
- Talking very fast
- Having racing thoughts
- Not needing much sleep
- Feeling overly confident or important
- Doing risky things without thinking

These symptoms can make it hard to work, study, or keep relationships. Mania is not just being happy. It can cause serious problems.

### When Is It a Mood Disorder?

A mood disorder is diagnosed when:
- The sadness or happiness is much stronger than usual
- Other symptoms are present
- Daily life is affected — at work, school, or with family and friends

### Types of Mood Disorders

**Unipolar Disorder**  
This means only depression happens. It includes:
- Major depressive disorder
- Persistent depressive disorder
- Premenstrual dysphoric disorder
- Depression caused by drugs or medicine

**Bipolar Disorder**  
This means a person has both depression and mania (or a milder form called hypomania). These mood swings happen over time.  
Mania without depression is very rare.

### How Common Are Mood Disorders?

- About 30% of people who see a doctor say they feel depressed.
- But fewer than 10% have a serious depression that needs treatment.
- Nearly 4 out of every 100 people in the United States have bipolar disorder.

### Mood Disorders in Young People

Children and teens can also have mood disorders. These can affect their school, friendships, and family life.

### Risks of Untreated Mood Disorders

If not treated, mood disorders can lead to:
- Trouble doing daily tasks
- Problems in relationships
- Loss of appetite
- Extreme anxiety
- Alcohol misuse
- Suicidal thoughts or actions

Up to 15 out of every 100 people with untreated depression may die by suicide. This is a serious concern.

# Burkitt Lymphoma – Simple Explanation

Burkitt lymphoma is a fast-growing type of cancer that starts in a type of white blood cell called a B cell. It can happen in children and adults. There are three main types: one that is common in parts of Africa, one that happens randomly in other places, and one that occurs in people with weak immune systems.

## Types of Burkitt Lymphoma

**Endemic Burkitt lymphoma**  
This type is most common in central Africa. It often causes swelling in the jaw or face. It is also seen in about 30% of childhood lymphoma cases in the United States.

**Sporadic Burkitt lymphoma**  
This type is not linked to a specific region. It usually starts in the belly area, especially near the lower part of the small intestine or the tissue that holds the intestines in place. The tumor can block the bowel. It can also spread to other organs like the brain or other solid organs. In adults, the cancer may be widespread and affect the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. The brain and spinal fluid may be involved at the start of the disease or when it comes back.

**Immunodeficiency-related Burkitt lymphoma**  
This type mostly affects people with HIV. It can also happen in people who have had a bone marrow or organ transplant, or who have other conditions that weaken the immune system. In people with HIV, this cancer is considered a sign of advanced disease (AIDS).

## What the Cancer Looks Like

Burkitt lymphoma is the fastest-growing cancer in humans. The cancer cells divide very quickly. A sample of the tumor shows many cells dividing, and the cells are all the same type. The tissue looks like a night sky full of stars because of many small, normal cells that have eaten dead cancer cells.

The cancer shows up very brightly on a special scan called an FDG-PET scan. This is because the cancer cells use a lot of energy.

A key change in the cancer’s DNA is a swap between two genes: one on chromosome 8 and one on chromosome 14. This swap turns on a gene that makes the cancer grow fast.

This cancer is strongly linked to Epstein-Barr virus in the African form. But it is not clear if the virus actually causes the cancer.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

To diagnose Burkitt lymphoma, doctors take a sample of the tumor. This is usually done with a biopsy of a lymph node or from another area where the cancer is suspected, such as the bone marrow.

Sometimes, a small camera is used through a tiny cut in the belly (laparoscopy) to see the cancer and take a sample. This can also help treat the cancer in some cases.

Because the cancer grows so fast, testing must be done quickly. The main test is an FDG-PET/CT scan. If this is not available, a CT scan of the chest, belly, and pelvis is used instead.

All patients also need:
- A bone marrow biopsy
- A test of the fluid around the brain and spinal cord (cerebrospinal fluid)
- Blood tests, including one to check lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), a marker of how much cancer is present

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment must start right away because the cancer grows so fast.

For children and adults under 60 years old, the main treatment is a strong chemotherapy plan. It uses a mix of drugs: cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, methotrexate, ifosfamide, etoposide, and cytarabine. This is given in alternating cycles. Rituximab, a drug that targets cancer cells, is added to the treatment.

For some people under 60 and many over 60, a different treatment plan is used. It includes rituximab, etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, and doxorubicin. This is called dose-adjusted R-EPOCH.

All patients who do not have cancer in the brain or spinal fluid need treatment to prevent it. This is called CNS prophylaxis. It may include drugs given into the bloodstream or directly into the spinal fluid.

When treatment starts, the cancer cells die quickly. This can cause a serious problem called tumor lysis syndrome. This happens when the dead cells release chemicals into the blood. To prevent this:
- Patients get fluids through a vein (IV)
- They take medicine to lower uric acid levels (allopurinol, sometimes with rasburicase)
- Their urine is made more alkaline (if not too much phosphate is in the blood)
- Doctors check blood levels of potassium, phosphorus, and calcium closely

Rasburicase should not be used in people with G6PD deficiency. It can cause a dangerous drop in red blood cells in these patients.

Some patients may need dialysis if their potassium levels get too high.

If a patient has a bowel blockage from the tumor, and the tumor is fully removed during surgery, treatment is still needed. But fewer rounds of chemotherapy may be required.

At the end of treatment, doctors check to make sure the cancer is gone. This is done with a PET scan or a CT scan and a bone marrow test.

## Prognosis (Outlook)

If the cancer does not respond to the first treatment, or if it comes back within the first year, the outlook is poor. In these cases, doctors may suggest stronger treatment or a clinical trial.

# Understanding Acid-Base Balance in the Body

Your blood must stay within a normal range of acidity or alkalinity to keep you healthy. This balance is called acid-base balance.

The level of acidity or alkalinity is measured on a scale from 0 to 14.  
A number of 7 is neutral.  
Blood is normally slightly alkaline.  
The normal range for blood pH is between 7.35 and 7.45.  
Most of the time, blood pH stays close to 7.40.

Doctors check acid-base balance by testing blood for:
- pH level  
- Carbon dioxide levels (this is an acid)  
- Bicarbonate levels (this is a base)

---

## What Makes Blood More Acidic?

Blood becomes more acidic when:
- The body makes more acid than usual  
- The body takes in more acid than normal  
- The body cannot remove acid well enough  

Or when:
- The body loses too much base (alkaline substance)  
- The body makes less base than normal  
- The body removes base too quickly  

---

## What Makes Blood More Alkaline?

Blood becomes more alkaline when:
- The body has less acid than normal  
- The body has more base than normal  

---

## How the Body Controls Acid-Base Balance

The body keeps blood pH stable using three main systems:

1. **Lungs**  
2. **Kidneys**  
3. **Chemical buffer systems**

### Lungs Help Control pH

Carbon dioxide is a mild acid.  
It is made when your body uses oxygen and nutrients.  
All your cells make carbon dioxide all the time.  
It moves from the cells into the blood.  
The blood carries it to the lungs.  
The lungs then remove it when you breathe out.

If carbon dioxide builds up in the blood, the blood becomes more acidic.  
The brain controls how fast and how deep you breathe.  
When you breathe faster and deeper, you blow off more carbon dioxide.  
This helps raise the blood pH.  
The lungs can adjust blood pH in just minutes.

### Kidneys Help Control pH

The kidneys can remove extra acid or base from the body.  
They do this through urine.  
The kidneys can change how much acid or base they remove.  
But this takes time.  
It usually takes several days to make a change.

### Buffer Systems Help Prevent Sudden Shifts

Your body has natural chemical systems called buffer systems.  
These are pairs of weak acids and weak bases.  
They help stop pH from changing too fast.  
They work by shifting the balance between acid and base.

The most important buffer in the blood uses:
- Carbonic acid (a weak acid made from carbon dioxide in the blood)  
- Bicarbonate (a weak base that works with carbonic acid)

These two work together to keep blood pH steady.

---

## Types of Acid-Base Problems

There are two main types of acid-base problems:

### Acidosis
- Blood has too much acid  
- Or too little base  
- Blood pH goes down (becomes more acidic)

### Alkalosis
- Blood has too much base  
- Or too little acid  
- Blood pH goes up (becomes more alkaline)

Acidosis and alkalosis are not diseases.  
They are signs that something else is wrong in the body.  
They help doctors find serious health problems.

These problems are grouped by cause:

- **Metabolic** (related to the kidneys or body chemistry)  
- **Respiratory** (related to breathing or lungs)

---

### Metabolic Acidosis and Alkalosis

These happen when:
- The body makes too much acid or too little base  
- The kidneys do not remove acid or base properly

Examples:
- Metabolic acidosis: Diabetic ketoacidosis (a serious condition in people with diabetes)
- Metabolic alkalosis: Losing stomach acid from long-term vomiting

---

### Respiratory Acidosis and Alkalosis

These happen when:
- Breathing is too slow or too shallow (leads to acid buildup)
- Breathing is too fast or too deep (leads to acid loss)

Examples:
- Respiratory acidosis: Severe chronic lung disease
- Respiratory alkalosis: Fast breathing from anxiety

---

## The Body’s Response to Imbalance

When acid-base balance is off, the body tries to fix it automatically.

- The lungs help fix problems from kidney or chemical issues.  
- The kidneys help fix problems from breathing issues.

In most cases, these systems bring blood pH back to normal.

But if the pH is still far from normal, it means the body cannot keep up.  
This is a warning sign.  
Doctors must act fast to find and treat the root cause.

---

### Summary of Common Problems and the Body’s Response

| Problem | Cause | Initial Blood pH | Body’s Fix | Effect on pH |
|--------|-------|------------------|------------|--------------|
| Metabolic acidosis | High acid in diabetes (ketoacidosis) | Too low | Breathe faster to get rid of carbon dioxide | Rises toward normal |
| Respiratory acidosis | Poor breathing from lung disease | Too low | Kidneys remove more acid in urine | Rises toward normal |
| Metabolic alkalosis | Losing stomach acid from vomiting | Too high | Breathe slower to keep carbon dioxide | Falls toward normal |
| Respiratory alkalosis | Fast breathing from anxiety | Too high | Kidneys remove more base in urine | Falls toward normal |

---

If your blood pH is not normal, it means your body is under stress.  
Doctors use this information to find the cause and treat it.

# Mediastinoscopy and Mediastinotomy

These are two medical procedures used to look at or take tissue from the area between the lungs. This area is called the mediastinum.

## What Are These Procedures?

**Mediastinoscopy** is a test where a thin tube with a camera is put into the chest through a small cut in the neck. This lets doctors see the lymph nodes and tissues in the middle of the chest.

**Mediastinotomy** is a surgery that opens the chest to give direct access to the mediastinum. It is used when the area is hard to reach with the camera method.

These two procedures work together. Mediastinotomy can reach some lymph nodes that mediastinoscopy cannot.

## Why Are These Procedures Done?

Doctors use these tests to:

- Check for swollen lymph nodes or growths in the chest
- Help stage certain cancers, such as lung cancer or esophageal cancer

Newer tests like PET scans and endobronchial ultrasound have reduced the need for these procedures in many cases.

## When Are These Procedures Not Safe?

These tests should not be done if you have:

- A bulge in the main artery (aortic aneurysm)
- Had open heart surgery through the breastbone before
- Had radiation treatment to the chest in the past
- Swelling in the large vein in the chest (superior vena cava syndrome)
- A breathing tube in the windpipe (tracheostomy)

## How Are These Procedures Done?

Both are done in an operating room by a surgeon. You will be asleep under general anesthesia.

**For mediastinoscopy:**
- A small cut is made in the neck, just above the breastbone.
- The soft tissue is gently moved aside until the windpipe is reached.
- A thin tube with a camera is inserted to see the lymph nodes near the windpipe and the area below it.
- The camera can reach the nodes on the sides of the windpipe, the area where the windpipe splits, the azygous vein, and the nodes under the windpipe.

**For anterior mediastinotomy (Chamberlain procedure):**
- A cut is made in the chest, just left of the breastbone, between the second and third ribs.
- This gives direct access to the front part of the chest and the lymph nodes near the aorta and lungs.
- This area is often checked when there is a cancer in the upper left lung.

## Possible Risks and Complications

These risks are rare. They happen in less than 1 out of every 100 people.

- Bleeding
- Fluid buildup in the chest due to injury to a major lymph vessel (chylothorax)
- A tear in the esophagus
- Infection
- Air in the chest cavity (pneumothorax)
- Voice changes or loss of voice due to nerve damage in the throat

These risks are small compared to the benefits of getting accurate information about your health.

# Cutis Laxa

Cutis laxa is a rare condition that affects the body’s connective tissue. This tissue helps hold the body together and gives it strength and flexibility.

## What Causes Cutis Laxa?

- Most cases are caused by a faulty gene passed down through families.
- In rare cases, it can start after a serious illness or an allergic reaction.
- Some people are born with it. Others develop it later in life.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main sign is skin that stretches easily and hangs in loose folds.

- The skin may look loose from birth.
- Or it may become loose over time.
- The face is often most affected. This can make a person look older than they are.
- The nose may look hooked.

Other problems can happen in the body’s internal organs:

- Blood may leak backward through heart valves.
- Bulges can form in the belly wall (called hernias).
- The air sacs in the lungs can break down (a condition called emphysema).
- Heart, lung, or digestive problems may also occur.
- Some people have learning difficulties.

Symptoms can appear at any age:

- In babies, symptoms may be present at birth.
- In children or teens, symptoms often start after a serious illness with fever or inflammation.
- In adults, symptoms may appear slowly or suddenly, often linked to other health issues.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor will look at the skin and check for signs of the condition.

- A small sample of skin may be taken and examined under a microscope. This is called a biopsy.
- Tests like an echocardiogram (a heart ultrasound) or a chest x-ray may be done to check the heart and lungs.
- People with a family history of cutis laxa or those who developed it young should consider genetic testing.

Genetic testing can help predict:
- If a person might pass the condition to their children.
- If other organs besides the skin might be affected.

## What Is the Outlook?

- If the heart, lungs, blood vessels, or intestines are severely affected, the condition can be life-threatening.
- The severity varies from person to person.

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure for cutis laxa.

- Plastic surgery can improve how the skin looks.
- But the results may not last long.
- Other health problems, like heart or lung issues, are treated as needed.
- Physical therapy may help improve skin tone in some cases.
