# How Medicines Are Tested for Safety and Effectiveness

## What Is Drug Development?

Drug development is the process of finding or making new medicines. Scientists test these medicines to see if they work and if they are safe.

All medicines can cause harm as well as help. Safety depends on how much of the medicine is needed to work and how much can cause serious side effects.

The difference between the usual dose and the dose that causes serious harm is called the margin of safety. A wide margin is best. But sometimes, doctors must use medicines with a narrow margin when the illness is serious or no other options exist.

## Safe and Effective Medicines

The best medicines are both effective and safe.

**Penicillin** is a good example. It works well against many infections. Even in large doses, it is very safe for most people. The only exception is people who are allergic to it.

**Barbiturates** were once used to help people sleep. But they are rarely used today. They can slow breathing too much. They can also cause dangerously low blood pressure. Taking too much can be deadly.

Newer sleep medicines like **temazepam** and **zolpidem** are now preferred. They are safer than barbiturates because they have a wider margin of safety.

## Some Medicines Are Risky, But Needed

It is not always possible to make a medicine that is both very effective and very safe.

Some medicines are still used even though they have a narrow margin of safety.

**Warfarin** is one example. It is a blood thinner. It helps prevent dangerous blood clots. But it can also cause too much bleeding.

Doctors use warfarin when the risk of a blood clot is greater than the risk of bleeding.

People who take warfarin must have regular blood tests. This helps doctors adjust the dose. The goal is to prevent clots without causing dangerous bleeding.

## How to Stay Safe While Taking Medicines

To make your treatment as safe and effective as possible:

- Tell your doctor or nurse about your full medical history.
- List all medicines you take, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements.
- Include any herbal products or dietary supplements you use.
- Share any other health details that might matter.

Ask your doctor, nurse, or pharmacist to explain:

- What the treatment is meant to do.
- What side effects or problems might happen.
- How much you can help make decisions about your care.

## Useful Resources

These websites may help you learn more:

- **The Center for Information and Study on Clinical Research Participation (CISCRP)**  
  A nonprofit group that teaches patients, doctors, and others about clinical research.

- **ClinicalTrials.gov**  
  A global database of clinical studies. It lists research projects funded by governments and private groups.

## How New Medicines Are Made

Many medicines in use today were found by accident. Scientists saw a possible effect in a substance. Then they tested it in animals and people.

Today, many medicines are made on purpose in labs.

Scientists study how diseases change the body at the chemical and cell level. Then they design new compounds to fix or stop these changes.

When a new compound shows promise, scientists change its structure many times. The goal is to make it work better and be safer.

The ideal medicine:

- Works only where it is needed. It does not affect other parts of the body. This means fewer side effects.
- Works well even in small doses. This is helpful for hard-to-treat conditions.
- Can be taken by mouth. It is absorbed well from the stomach and intestines.
- Stays active in the body long enough to work. One dose per day is often enough. Short-acting medicines may be better for short-term problems.

## Dosing: One Size Does Not Fit All

Standard doses are set during drug testing. But people react differently to medicines.

Many things affect how a medicine works in a person:

- Age
- Weight
- Genes
- Other health conditions

Doctors must consider all these factors when choosing the right dose for you.

## What Is a Placebo?

A placebo is a fake medicine. It looks like a real pill but has no active ingredient. It may be made of sugar or starch.

Some people who take a placebo feel better. Others may feel worse, even though the pill has no medicine in it.

This is called the **placebo effect**.

There are two reasons this happens:

1. **Coincidence** – Many health problems get better on their own. A person may feel better after taking a placebo, but it was not the pill that helped.
2. **Expectation** – If you believe a medicine will work, your body may respond. This can make you feel better, even if the medicine does nothing.

The placebo effect mainly affects symptoms, not the disease itself.

For example:
- A placebo will not heal a broken bone.
- But it may make pain feel less.

Not everyone responds to placebos. And no one can predict who will.

## Testing New Medicines

When scientists test a new medicine, they compare it to a placebo.

This is because even fake medicine can make people feel better.

In a typical test:
- Half the people get the real medicine.
- The other half get a placebo that looks the same.

Ideally, neither the patients nor the researchers know who gets which. This is called a **double-blind study**.

After the study, scientists compare results.

The real medicine must work significantly better than the placebo to be approved.

In some studies, up to half the people taking the placebo get better. This makes it hard to prove a new medicine works.

## Weighing the Benefits and Risks

Every medicine can cause harm as well as help.

Before prescribing a medicine, doctors weigh the possible harm against the expected benefit.

A medicine should only be used if the benefits are greater than the risks.

Doctors also consider what happens if the medicine is not used.

The risks and benefits cannot be calculated exactly. They are based on judgment.

### Minor Illnesses

For small problems like colds, muscle pain, or occasional headaches:

- Only very low risk of side effects is acceptable.
- Over-the-counter medicines are usually safe and effective.
- These medicines have a wide safety margin. This means the dose that works is far below the dose that causes serious harm.

### Serious or Life-Threatening Illnesses

For serious conditions like heart attacks, strokes, cancer, or organ transplant rejection:

- A higher risk of serious side effects is often acceptable.
- The benefit of treating the illness may outweigh the risk.

### Personal Choices

People have different views on risk and quality of life.

For example:
- Some people are willing to accept side effects from cancer treatment if it gives them a small chance to live longer.
- Others may not want to take a medicine that has a 1 in 50 chance of causing serious bleeding, even if it helps.

Everyone must decide what level of risk they are willing to accept. Your doctor can help you understand your options.

# Infections During Pregnancy

Infections during pregnancy are common. Most are not serious. But some can harm the mother or the baby. For this reason, all pregnant women are tested for certain infections during routine checkups. If you have signs of an infection, you should see your doctor right away. Getting treated early can prevent problems.

Some infections can cause serious health issues in a baby. These include:
- Baby born with syphilis
- Baby born with cytomegalovirus
- Baby born with rubella
- Baby born with toxoplasmosis
- Baby born with herpes
- Baby born with hepatitis B

## Syphilis

The number of babies born with syphilis has gone up a lot in the United States. In 2012, there were 335 cases. By 2021, that number had risen to 2,865. That is a 755% increase.

All pregnant women should be tested for syphilis at their first prenatal visit. Depending on how common syphilis is in your area, you may need to be tested 2 to 3 more times during your pregnancy.

If you are diagnosed with syphilis, you will be treated with antibiotics. This treatment can prevent the baby from getting syphilis.

## HIV

HIV can pass from mother to baby during pregnancy or during childbirth. Without treatment, about 1 in 4 to 1 in 3 babies will get HIV.

In countries with good medical care, most pregnant women with HIV take strong HIV medicines during pregnancy. This treatment lowers the chance of passing HIV to the baby to less than 1%.

Your doctor will check your HIV level at 36 weeks. Based on the result, they will decide if you should have a vaginal birth or a cesarean section.

## Listeriosis

Pregnant women are more likely to get listeriosis than others. It is caused by eating food that has a type of bacteria called *Listeria monocytogenes*.

Listeriosis often causes stomach upset. It usually happens in the third trimester. It can spread from the mother to the baby through the placenta.

Listeriosis increases the risk of:
- Losing the baby early (spontaneous abortion)
- Going into labor too early (preterm labor)
- Losing the baby before birth (stillbirth)

The baby can also get infected during delivery. Treatment is with penicillin antibiotics.

## Infections of the Genital Area

Infections in the vagina or cervix can cause problems for the mother or baby. These include:
- Bacterial vaginosis: Can lead to early labor or infection in the womb
- Chlamydia: Can cause early loss of pregnancy, early labor, stillbirth, eye infection, or lung infection in the baby
- Gonorrhea: Can cause early labor, low birth weight, or eye infection in the baby
- Rupture of the membranes before labor starts
- Early labor

These infections are tested for during regular prenatal visits. They are also tested if you have symptoms.

## Genital Herpes

Herpes can pass to the baby during delivery. The baby may get very sick. This can include seizures or other serious health problems.

If you have visible sores around the vagina, vulva, or perineum, or if you have warning signs of an outbreak before labor, a cesarean section is usually recommended.

If you have no sores and no warning signs, even if you have had herpes before, the risk is low. You can have a vaginal birth.

All women with a history of herpes should have a pelvic exam early in labor. This checks for active sores.

If no sores are found, you can have a vaginal birth.

## Treatment for Herpes

Antiviral medicines like acyclovir or valacyclovir are safe to use during pregnancy.

If you have an active herpes outbreak during pregnancy, you should take acyclovir or valacyclovir.

Women with a history of herpes should start taking antiviral medicine at 36 weeks of pregnancy. This helps prevent an outbreak near delivery.

## Key Points

- Most infections during pregnancy, like urinary tract infections or colds, are not serious.
- But some infections can cause serious harm to the mother or baby.
- Infections that can cause birth defects or long-term health problems in a baby include:
  - Cytomegalovirus
  - Herpes simplex virus
  - Rubella
  - Toxoplasmosis
  - Hepatitis B
  - Syphilis
- Antibiotics should only be used during pregnancy if there is clear proof of a bacterial infection.
- The benefits of treatment must be greater than any possible risks.
- The risk of harm from medicine can change depending on the stage of pregnancy.

# Liver Fluke Infections

Some types of flukes can infect the liver.

## How People Get Infected

- People get infected by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish.
- They can also get infected by eating dried, salt-cured, wine-soaked, or pickled freshwater fish.
- Eating watercress or other water plants that are contaminated can also cause infection.
- The contamination comes from water that has been polluted with animal waste from sheep or cattle.

The flukes are in the form of tiny cysts. These cysts contain immature flukes called larvae.

- When you eat the fish or plants, the cysts break open in your intestines.
- The larvae come out and travel to your liver and bile ducts.
- The bile duct is the tube that carries bile from your liver to your intestines.

## Types of Flukes That Cause Liver Infections

- *Clonorchis sinensis* – causes clonorchiasis. This is also called the Chinese liver fluke.
- *Opisthorchis viverrini* and *Opisthorchis felineus* – cause an infection similar to clonorchiasis. These are found in Southeast Asia and Europe.
- *Fasciola hepatica* – causes fascioliasis. This is also called the common liver fluke or sheep liver fluke.

These flukes are parasites. They live in the body and feed off the host.

- Liver fluke infections are common in parts of Europe, Africa, eastern and central Asia, and South America.
- They are rare in the United States.

## How the Flukes Spread

The life cycle of flukes is long and complex.

### For *Clonorchis sinensis* and *Opisthorchis*:
- Eggs pass out in the stool.
- They get into freshwater and hatch into tiny swimming larvae.
- These larvae infect snails.
- The snails release more larvae that swim and attach to freshwater fish or shrimp.
- The larvae form cysts in the fish or shrimp.
- When people eat the fish or shrimp, the cycle starts again.

### For *Fasciola hepatica* and *Fasciola gigantica*:
- Eggs pass out in the stool.
- They hatch in water and infect snails.
- The snails release swimming larvae.
- These larvae attach to watercress and other water plants.
- When people eat the plants, they swallow the cysts.
- The larvae come out in the intestines and move to the liver and bile ducts.

## Symptoms of Liver Fluke Infections

Some people have no symptoms at all.

Others may have:
- Fever
- Chills
- Belly pain or discomfort
- Swelling in the liver
- Nausea or vomiting
- Hives (itchy red spots on the skin)

*Fasciola* flukes are more likely to cause these early symptoms.

Over time, if the flukes block the bile ducts:
- The skin and eyes may turn yellow (this is called jaundice).
- You may feel itchy.
- You may have diarrhea.
- You may lose weight.

The flukes can also damage the liver. This can cause scarring (fibrosis).

Other possible problems include:
- Infection in the bile ducts
- Gallstones
- Pancreatitis (inflammation of the pancreas)

In rare cases, flukes can travel to other parts of the body, such as the intestines, lungs, skin, or throat.

Years after infection, some people develop cancer of the bile ducts. This is called cholangiocarcinoma.

- This cancer has been seen in some Vietnam veterans.
- They may have eaten raw or undercooked freshwater fish while serving in Southeast Asia.
- It is not certain if the fluke infection caused the cancer.

## How Doctors Diagnose the Infection

Doctors use several methods to find out if you have a fluke infection.

### Stool Test
- They check your stool for fluke eggs.
- Finding eggs confirms the infection.
- But it can be hard to find eggs, especially early in the infection.

### Blood Tests
- Blood tests can check for antibodies.
- Antibodies are proteins your body makes to fight infections.
- These tests can show an infection even before eggs appear in the stool.
- Doctors also check for high levels of a type of white blood cell called eosinophils.
- This type of cell often increases during a fluke infection.

### Imaging Tests
- Doctors may use ultrasound, CT scan, MRI, or other imaging tests.
- These help check for damage to the liver and bile ducts.
- In some cases, doctors can see adult flukes in the bile ducts using a thin tube with a camera (endoscope).

## Treatment

Fluke infections are treated with medicine.

### Medicines
- **Praziquantel** or **albendazole** – used for clonorchiasis.
- **Triclabendazole** – used for fascioliasis.
- **Nitazoxanide** – may be used for fascioliasis in some cases.

These medicines kill the flukes in your body.

### Surgery
- If the flukes block the bile ducts, surgery may be needed.
- The goal is to remove the blockage and clear the flukes.

## Prevention

You can prevent liver fluke infections by taking simple steps.

- Always cook freshwater fish or shrimp thoroughly.
- Do not eat raw, dried, salt-cured, or pickled freshwater fish or shrimp from areas where flukes are common.
- Do not eat raw watercress or other water plants in areas where sheep or cattle are infected with *Fasciola*.
- Wash your hands and vegetables well, especially if you are in a high-risk area.

By following these steps, you can greatly reduce your risk of getting a liver fluke infection.

# What Is the Lymphatic System?

Blood vessels called capillaries leak a fluid called plasma. This fluid carries some white blood cells. It moves out of the capillaries into the spaces between your body’s cells.

Most of this fluid goes back into the blood vessels. Some of it is used by your body’s cells. The balance of pressure in the blood and tissues controls this process.

Some fluid, along with certain cells and waste material, enters the lymphatic system. This waste can come from infections, inflammation, or cancer.

The lymphatic system is like a network of thin tubes. It moves fluid around your body. These tubes are similar to veins but are not connected to the heart.

Small lymph vessels join together to form larger ones. These larger vessels carry fluid to two main ducts. One duct empties into the large vein near your heart. The other duct does the same on the right side of your body.

Like veins, lymph vessels have one-way valves. These valves stop the fluid from flowing backward. They help keep the fluid moving toward the heart.

Unlike blood, which the heart pumps, lymph moves when your muscles contract. When you move, your muscles squeeze the lymph vessels. This pushes the fluid forward.

Before the lymph returns to the main blood system, it passes through lymph nodes.

Lymph nodes act like filters. They trap harmful material. This includes cancer cells, germs, and other foreign particles.

Lymph nodes are also part of your body’s defense system. They contain special immune cells. These cells are ready to fight any threats that come in with the lymph.

There are two main types of lymph nodes:

- **Superficial nodes**: These are close to the skin. You can find them all over your body. They are most common in the neck, under your arms, and in your groin.
- **Deep nodes**: These are inside your body. They are found in the chest and belly areas.

The lymphatic system helps keep your body clean and protected. It removes waste and helps your body fight disease.

# Niacin Deficiency

Niacin deficiency is rare in countries where people have enough to eat.  
Many people with this deficiency also lack protein, riboflavin (a B vitamin), and vitamin B6.

## What Causes Niacin Deficiency?

Niacin deficiency happens when your diet does not have enough niacin or tryptophan.  
Tryptophan is an amino acid found in some foods.  
Your body can turn tryptophan into niacin, so low tryptophan can cause the same problems as low niacin.

Pellagra is the name for the illness caused by niacin deficiency.  
It affects the skin, the digestive system, and the brain.

You are more likely to get pellagra if:
- You eat mostly maize (corn) as your main food.
- Maize is not treated with alkali (like in tortillas). This treatment helps your body absorb niacin from maize.
- The diet is low in niacin and tryptophan, especially in spring and summer when maize products are common.

Pellagra can also happen if you have:
- Hartnup disease – a rare inherited condition that stops your body from absorbing tryptophan.
- Carcinoid syndrome – a rare condition where your body does not turn tryptophan into niacin.

Other causes of niacin deficiency include:
- Long-term alcohol use
- Severe diarrhea
- Liver disease (cirrhosis)
- Taking the antibiotic isoniazid for a long time

## What Are the Symptoms?

The first sign is a dark red rash that looks like a sunburn.  
It gets worse when you are in the sun.  
The rash appears in specific places:
- On the arms and hands (like gloves)
- On the feet and lower legs (like boots)
- Around the neck (like a necklace)
- On the face in a butterfly shape

The skin may stay red and become brown and scaly over time.

Your digestive system is also affected.  
Your tongue and mouth may become red and swollen.  
You may feel a burning sensation in your mouth or throat.  
Sores can form in your mouth.  
You may produce more saliva than usual.

Other digestive symptoms include:
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Belly pain
- Constipation
- Diarrhea (sometimes with blood)

Later, you may feel very tired.  
You may have trouble sleeping.  
You may feel unmotivated or lose interest in things.

Brain problems can develop.  
You may feel confused or forget things.  
You may have hallucinations.  
You may act very excited, very sad, or very happy.  
You may become delirious or feel that people are trying to harm you.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your diet and your symptoms.  
They may test your urine to check for a by-product of niacin.  
This test is not always available.

The diagnosis is confirmed if your symptoms improve when you take niacin supplements.

## How Is It Treated?

You take niacin supplements by mouth.  
The most common form used is nicotinamide.  
It works well and does not cause skin flushing, itching, burning, or tingling.

The other form, nicotinic acid, can cause these side effects.  
So nicotinamide is preferred.

You may also need supplements of other B vitamins.  
This is because people with niacin deficiency often lack other nutrients too.

Eating a balanced diet is very important.  
Good sources of niacin include:
- Dried yeast
- Liver
- Red meat
- Poultry
- Fish
- Beans and other legumes
- Whole grains and enriched breads and cereals

Foods rich in tryptophan, like milk and dairy products, can help.  
Your body can turn tryptophan into niacin, so these foods can make up for low niacin intake.

## What Is Niacin?

Niacin is a B vitamin.  
It helps your body turn food into energy.  
It helps your cells work properly.

The word "niacin" can mean:
- Nicotinic acid
- Nicotinamide
- Or both forms together

Both forms are important for health.

# How Children Grow and Develop

Children grow and develop in many areas. These areas include moving their bodies, using their hands, talking, thinking, getting along with others, and managing their feelings.

These areas are often described separately. But they are closely linked. A child may do well in one area but be slower in another.

Doctors and researchers have studied how children grow. They know the average age when most children reach certain milestones. But every child is different. Some reach milestones earlier. Others take more time. This is normal.

## Key Milestones in Development

Here are some common things children do at different ages.

### Birth to 6 Weeks
- Sleeps most of the time.
- Sucks on a nipple or pacifier.
- Clears their airway when breathing.
- Cries when they are uncomfortable or bothered.
- Turns their head toward sounds and voices.
- Looks at faces.

### 4 Weeks
- Brings hands to their eyes and mouth.
- Lifts their head when lying on their stomach.
- Moves their head from side to side.
- Follows a moving object about 15 centimeters above their face.
- Reacts to sounds (startles, cries, or quiets down).
- Turns toward familiar voices.
- Focuses on a face.

### 6 Weeks
- Looks at things in front of them.
- Smiles when someone talks to them.
- Pays more attention to their surroundings.
- Their head lags when pulled up to sit.

### 3 Months
- Holds their head steady when sitting.
- Lifts their head 45 degrees when lying on their stomach.
- Opens and closes their hands.
- Pushes down with their feet when placed on a flat surface.
- Swings at and reaches for dangling toys.
- Follows a moving object from one side to the other.
- Watches faces closely.
- Smiles at the sound of a caregiver’s voice.
- Makes sounds like “cooing.”

### 5 to 6 Months
- Holds their head steady when upright.
- Sits with help.
- Rolls over from back to front or front to back.
- Reaches for things.
- Recognizes people from a distance.
- Listens carefully to human voices.
- Smiles without being prompted.
- Makes happy sounds like “squeals.”
- Babbles to toys.

### 7 Months
- Sits without help.
- Bears some weight on their legs when held upright.
- Passes toys from one hand to the other.
- Holds their own bottle.
- Looks for toys they drop.
- Responds when their name is called.
- Understands “no.”
- Combines vowels and consonants in babbling.
- Moves excitedly when they expect to play.
- Plays peekaboo.

### 9 Months
- Sits well without support.
- Crawls or creeps on hands and knees.
- Pulls themselves up to stand while holding on.
- Works to get a toy that is out of reach.
- Gets into a sitting position from lying on their stomach.
- Stands while holding on to someone or something.
- Says “Mama” or “Dada” without meaning it yet.

### 12 Months
- Walks while holding onto furniture or another person.
- May take 1 or 2 steps without help.
- Stands for a few seconds at a time.
- Says “Dada” or “Mama” to the right person.
- Drinks from a cup.
- Claps hands and waves goodbye.
- Speaks several words.

### 18 Months
- Walks well.
- Climbs stairs while holding on.
- Draws a straight line.
- Builds a tower of 4 blocks.
- Turns several pages in a book at once.
- Speaks about 10 words.
- Pulls toys on strings.
- Eats some food by themselves.

### 2 to 2.5 Years
- Runs well and with balance.
- Climbs on furniture.
- Jumps.
- Goes up and down stairs without help.
- Uses a spoon well.
- Turns one page at a time in a book.
- Builds a tower of 7 blocks.
- Opens doors.
- Makes scribbles in circles.
- Puts on simple clothes.
- Says short phrases like “I want juice.”
- Says they need to use the toilet.

### 3 Years
- Walks with a mature style.
- Rides a tricycle.
- Favors one hand over the other.
- Counts to 10 and uses plural words like “cats.”
- Recognizes at least 3 colors.
- Asks many questions.
- Eats by themselves.
- Can use the toilet on their own (in about half of children).

### 4 Years
- Goes up and down stairs using alternate feet.
- Throws a ball overhand.
- Hops on one foot.
- Copies a cross.
- Dresses themselves.
- Washes hands and face.

### 5 Years
- Skips.
- Catches a ball that bounces.
- Copies a triangle.
- Draws a person with 6 parts (head, body, arms, legs, etc.).
- Knows 4 colors.
- Dresses and undresses without help.

### 6 Years
- Walks in a straight line from heel to toe.
- Writes their name.

> **Note:** The order of these milestones is usually the same. But the time when a child reaches them can vary. The ages listed are averages.

## What Affects How Children Grow

A child’s growth is shaped by many things. These include:
- What they eat.
- How much they are played with and talked to.
- Whether they are sick.
- Their feelings and emotions.

Genes also play a role. But the environment matters just as much.

Parents, teachers, and doctors watch how children grow every day. There are tools to help track development more closely. One common tool is the Denver Developmental Screening Test II. It checks many areas of growth. It shows the average age for each milestone. It also shows the normal range of when children reach them.

## How Children Move

Moving includes big movements (like walking and climbing) and small movements (like picking up small toys or drawing).

This kind of growth is continuous. It depends on:
- Family patterns.
- Health and activity levels.
- Any medical conditions like cerebral palsy, intellectual disability, or muscular dystrophy.

Most children walk at 12 months. They climb stairs with help at 18 months. They run well by age 2. But the exact age varies from child to child.

You cannot speed up a child’s movement skills by pushing them harder. They grow at their own pace.

## How Children Learn to Talk

Children understand words before they can speak. A child who says few words may still understand a lot.

Delayed speech does not always mean other delays. But if a child has trouble both understanding and speaking, they may have other developmental issues.

Always check hearing if a child is slow to talk. Most children with speech delays have normal intelligence.

Some children speak early. These children often have above-average intelligence.

Speech starts with sounds like “cooing.” Then babies make sounds like “ba-ba-ba.” By 12 months, most children say “Dada” and “Mama” correctly. By 18 months, they use several words. By age 2, they say short phrases like “I want milk.”

By age 3, most children can have a simple conversation. By age 4, they can tell short stories. By age 5, they may know thousands of words.

Even before 18 months, children enjoy being read to. By age 5, they can recite the alphabet and recognize simple words.

These skills are the foundation for learning to read. Most children begin to read by age 6 or 7. But this varies a lot.

## How Children Think and Learn

Thinking and learning grow over time. Good care in early life helps children think and feel better.

Reading to children, giving them fun activities, and showing love all help their brain and emotional growth.

Doctors and teachers watch how children use language, ask questions, and solve problems. As children talk more, it becomes easier to understand their thinking.

When children start school, they are tested often as part of learning.

### Age 2
- Understands time in general terms.
- Thinks everything in the past happened “yesterday.”
- Thinks everything in the future will happen “tomorrow.”
- Has a strong imagination.
- Cannot always tell the difference between pretend and real.

### Age 4
- Understands that a day has morning, afternoon, and night.
- Knows about the seasons.

### Age 7
- Can think about more than one thing at once.
- Understands that a tall, thin cup can hold the same amount as a short, wide one.
- Knows that medicine can taste bad but help them feel better.
- Knows that a parent can be angry but still love them.
- Can see things from another person’s point of view.
- Learns to take turns in games and conversations.
- Follows game rules.
- Uses observation and different views to solve problems.

## How Children Feel and Behave

Feelings and behavior depend on a child’s age and their natural mood.

Every child has a different temperament. Some are cheerful and easy to care for. They adapt well to new things. Others are more cautious and have irregular routines. They may react negatively to change. Some fall in between.

Doctors and parents watch how children act with others. When children start talking, it becomes easier to understand their feelings.

### Crying
- Crying is how babies communicate.
- They cry when hungry, uncomfortable, or upset.
- Crying peaks at 6 weeks (about 3 hours a day).
- It drops to about 1 hour a day

# Intestinal Lymphangiectasia

This is a rare condition. It happens when the small tubes that carry fluid from the intestines (called lymph vessels) are not working right. This stops the body from absorbing protein and fat properly.

## What Causes It?

- Some children are born with lymph vessels that are not formed correctly.
- In others, the flow of fluid gets blocked later in life.
- Blockages can happen because of:
  - Inflammation of the pancreas (pancreatitis)
  - Tumors
  - A stiff sac around the heart (constrictive pericarditis)

When the flow is blocked, fluid leaks back into the intestines. This stops the body from taking in fat and protein.

## Symptoms

- Swelling in one or both legs
- Diarrhea
- Nausea or vomiting
- Stools that are oily or greasy
- Belly pain
- Children may grow more slowly than expected

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use tests to find out if you have this condition.

- **Biopsy**: A small piece of tissue is taken from the small intestine. This is done using a thin, flexible tube with a camera and a tiny tool. The tissue is looked at under a microscope.
- **Contrast lymphangiography**: A special liquid is injected into the lymph vessels in the foot. X-rays are then taken to see how the fluid moves. This can show if the lymph vessels in the intestines are abnormal.
- Blood tests are also done. These check for low levels of:
  - Protein
  - Cholesterol
  - White blood cells

Low protein levels can cause swelling in the body.

## How Is It Treated?

The treatment depends on the cause.

- If another condition is causing the problem, that condition is treated first.
- A low-fat, high-protein diet helps reduce symptoms.
- Supplements are often needed. These include:
  - Calcium
  - Vitamins
  - Medium-chain triglycerides (a type of fat that enters the blood directly, not through the lymph system)
- In some cases, surgery may be needed to fix the blocked lymph vessels or parts of the intestines.

Treating the cause and making diet changes can help improve health and reduce symptoms.

# Osteoporosis

Osteoporosis is a condition where bones become weak and more likely to break.  
It happens when bones lose too much of their strength and density over time.  
Weak bones can break from small injuries or even everyday actions like bending or coughing.  
Common places for breaks include the spine, wrist, and hip.  
These breaks are called fragility fractures.

You can find out if you have osteoporosis with a special scan called a DXA scan.  
Or, your doctor may diagnose it if you have a fragility fracture, even if the scan is normal.

Preventing and treating osteoporosis includes:  
- Changing lifestyle habits that increase risk  
- Taking calcium and vitamin D supplements if needed  
- Doing exercises that strengthen bones and muscles  
- Improving balance to avoid falls  
- Using medicines to protect bones or help make new bone

---

## How Osteoporosis Develops

Bones are always changing.  
Old bone is removed and new bone is made.  
This process is balanced in healthy people.  
Two types of cells do this work:  
- Osteoblasts build new bone  
- Osteoclasts break down old bone  

Hormones like parathyroid hormone, estrogen, and vitamin D help control this balance.  
Other body chemicals also play a role.

Most people reach their strongest bones around age 30.  
Men usually have stronger bones than women.  
After age 30, bone strength stays steady for about 10 years.  
Then, bone loss begins to speed up.

In women, bone loss gets faster after menopause.  
It can be about 2 percent per year for about 10 years.  
After that, the loss slows down.

Osteoporosis affects both types of bone:  
- Cortical bone (the hard outer layer)  
- Trabecular bone (the spongy inner part)  

Both types become thinner and more porous.  
Trabecular bone weakens faster because it is more porous and changes more quickly.  
But both types of loss make bones fragile.

---

## Types of Osteoporosis

Osteoporosis can happen on its own, with no clear cause.  
This is called primary osteoporosis.  
It can also happen because of another health problem or medicine.  
This is called secondary osteoporosis.  
The places where bones break are similar in both types.

---

## Things That Increase Your Risk

If you are not active for long periods, your bones lose strength.  
Being very thin or having a low body mass index increases your risk.  
Not getting enough calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, or vitamin D in your diet can harm your bones.  
Having too much acid in your body (from diet or disease) also weakens bones.  
Smoking and heavy drinking hurt bone health.  
If a parent had a hip fracture, you are more likely to get osteoporosis.  
If you have already had a fragility fracture, you are more likely to have another one.

Some groups have been thought to be at higher risk, such as non-Hispanic White and Asian women.  
But this may not be true for everyone.  
Social factors like income, access to care, and living conditions play a big role.  
So, doctors should use risk tools that fit your background, not just your race or ethnicity.

---

## Signs and Symptoms

Most people with osteoporosis do not feel any symptoms until they break a bone.  
Breaks in the arms, legs, or hips usually cause pain.  
But most spine breaks do not cause pain at first.  
About two out of three spine breaks are silent.  
Some people may have long-term back pain from other causes like arthritis.

If a spine break causes pain, it starts suddenly.  
The pain is usually in the back and does not spread to other areas.  
It gets worse when you stand or walk.  
You may feel tenderness in your spine.  
The pain usually starts to get better in about a week.  
But some people have pain that lasts for months or never goes away.  
If this happens, your doctor should check for more breaks or other spine problems like infection or cancer.

Over time, several spine breaks can cause a hunched back.  
This is called a dowager’s hump.  
The neck may curve forward more than normal.  
The spine muscles and ligaments get stressed.  
This can cause dull, aching pain, especially in the lower back.  
The hunched shape can make it harder to breathe.  
It can also make you feel full quickly because the chest and belly are squeezed.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Osteoporosis

Doctors use two main ways to diagnose osteoporosis:

1. **DXA scan** – This is the most common test.  
   It measures how dense your bones are.  
   It is quick, painless, and uses a low level of radiation.

2. **Fragility fracture** – If you break a bone from a minor fall or even no fall at all, you may have osteoporosis.  
   This includes breaks in the spine, hip, upper arm, or wrist.

X-rays can show weak bones, but they are not enough to confirm osteoporosis.  
A DXA scan is needed for a clear diagnosis.

---

## Treating Osteoporosis

The main goals of treatment are to:  
- Keep your bones strong  
- Prevent future breaks  
- Reduce pain  
- Help you stay active and independent

Medicines can slow down bone loss.  
But you still need to get enough calcium and vitamin D.  
You also need to stay active with weight-bearing exercises.  
And you should avoid smoking and limit alcohol.

Your doctor may suggest medicines such as:  
- **Bisphosphonates** – These slow down bone loss  
- **Hormone replacement therapy** – Helps women after menopause  
- **Selective estrogen receptor modulators** – Protect bones without the risks of hormone therapy  
- **Denosumab** – A shot that stops bone breakdown  
- **Teriparatide and abaloparatide** – These are medicines that help build new bone  
- **Romosozumab** – A shot that both protects bone and helps make new bone

Your doctor will choose the best medicine based on your health and risk.

---

## Preventing Osteoporosis

Prevention has two main goals:  
- Keep your bones strong  
- Avoid fractures

These steps are important for:  
- Women after menopause  
- Men over age 70  
- People with low bone density (osteopenia)  
- People who already have osteoporosis  
- People on long-term steroid medicine or certain cancer drugs  
- People with other health problems that weaken bones

Everyone should:  
- Eat enough calcium and vitamin D  
- Do weight-bearing exercises like walking, dancing, or lifting light weights  
- Avoid smoking  
- Limit alcohol  
- Take steps to prevent falls (like removing loose rugs, using grab bars, and wearing good shoes)

If you have osteopenia and are at high risk for a fracture, your doctor may suggest medicine.  
This includes people with a high FRAX score or those on steroids or cancer drugs.

Teaching people about bone health is very important.  
Everyone should know how to keep their bones strong.

---

## Key Points

- Bone strength peaks around age 30.  
- After menopause, women lose bone at a faster rate—about 2 percent per year for 10 years.  
- Most cases of osteoporosis happen without a clear cause.  
- If you break a bone from a small fall or no fall at all, you may have osteoporosis.  
- Check bone density with a DXA scan if you are:  
  - A woman over 65  
  - A woman between menopause and age 65 with risk factors  
  - A man or woman of any age with a fragility fracture  
  - Someone with signs of weak bones on imaging  
  - Someone at risk for secondary bone loss  
- Test for other causes of bone loss if your bone density is very low, your bones are getting weaker, you break a bone while on treatment, or your doctor suspects another problem.  
- To prevent or treat osteoporosis:  
  - Get enough calcium and vitamin D (through food or supplements)  
  - Stay active with weight-bearing exercise  
  - Avoid smoking and limit alcohol  
  - Take steps to prevent falls  
- Medicines include:  
  - Drugs that slow bone loss (like bisphosphonates, denosumab, or hormone therapy)  
  - Drugs that build new bone (like teriparatide, abaloparatide, or romosozumab)  
- Follow up with DXA scans as your doctor recommends to check how well treatment is working.

# Hemangiomas

Hemangiomas are lumps caused by too many blood vessels growing in one spot.  
They can appear on the skin or inside the body.  
They often look red or purple.

(See also: _Overview of Skin Growths_ and _Overview of Growths and Malformations of the Vessels_.)

## Hemangiomas in Babies (Also Called Strawberry Hemangiomas)

These are the most common type of growth in babies.  
About 5 to 10 out of every 100 babies get one by their first birthday.  
They usually appear soon after birth.  
They grow fast during the first year of life.  
After 12 to 18 months, they start to shrink.  
Most go away completely within 3 to 5 years.

These growths form under or in the skin.  
They make the skin bulge out.  
The surface is usually bright red.  
If the growth is deep, it may look bluish.  
Most deep hemangiomas are between a quarter inch and 2 inches wide.  
Some can be much larger.  
Over half happen on the head or neck.  
Sometimes they grow inside organs, like the liver. (See: _Hemangiomas of the Liver_)

These growths do not hurt.  
But they can sometimes break open and bleed.  
If a hemangioma is near the eye, it can grow big enough to block vision.  
If not treated, this can cause permanent vision loss.  
Hemangiomas near the nose or throat can block breathing.

If a doctor thinks the growth is blocking the nose, throat, or another important part, they may order a special scan called an MRI.

Most hemangiomas in babies go away on their own.  
So doctors usually do not treat them at first.  
They only treat them if:  
- The growth is getting bigger very fast  
- It is blocking vision or breathing  
- It has broken open and is bleeding  
- It causes worry about how it looks

When treatment is needed, doctors may use:  
- Steroid medicine applied to the skin, injected, or taken by mouth  
- Laser treatment  
- A medicine called propranolol, applied to the skin or taken by mouth

If the growth has broken open, treatment includes:  
- Wet compresses  
- Creams or ointments for the wound  
- Special bandages

Surgery is usually not needed.  
Most hemangiomas go away on their own.  
Leaving them alone causes less scarring.  
For older children, when the growth has shrunk the most, surgery may help improve the skin’s look.

# Watery Eyes

Watery eyes happen when your eyes make too many tears or when tears do not drain properly.  
This can make your eyes feel wet or cause tears to roll down your face.

## How Tears Normally Work

Your eyes make tears in a gland near your eyebrow.  
Tears flow out through small openings in your upper and lower eyelids.  
From there, tears move through tiny tubes into a small sac and then down a duct into your nose.  
If this drainage system gets blocked, tears can build up.  
A blocked tear duct can lead to fluid staying in the sac.  
This can cause an infection in the sac.  
An infection in the sac can sometimes spread to the eye socket.

## What Causes Watery Eyes

The most common causes are:

- A cold or upper respiratory infection  
- Allergies

Sometimes, your eyes make too many tears.  
Other times, the tear drainage system does not work well.  
In many people, both problems happen at the same time.

## How Doctors Check Watery Eyes

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms.  
They will look at your eyes and face.  
They may check for allergies, infections, or foreign objects.  
Tests like imaging or nasal exams are not usually needed.  
But they may be used if surgery is being considered or if there is a possible abscess.

## How Watery Eyes Are Treated

If allergies are the cause, treatment focuses on the allergies.  
If there is an infection, it is treated with medicine.  
If a foreign object is in the eye, it is removed.

If your eyes feel dry, using artificial tears can help.  
This may reduce the reflex tearing that happens when your eyes are dry.  
This is true even though it seems strange.

For babies with blocked tear ducts, the problem often gets better on its own.  
For babies under one year old, gently pressing on the tear sac several times a day may help.  
If the blockage lasts past one year, a doctor may need to open the duct.  
This is done under general anesthesia.

For adults with blocked tear ducts, flushing the duct with fluid may help.  
This is done if other treatments do not work.  
If the blockage keeps coming back, surgery may be needed.  
This surgery creates a new path from the tear sac to the nose.

If the small drainage tubes are narrow or blocked, stretching them usually fixes the problem.  
If the blockage is severe and causes ongoing issues, a small tube can be placed.  
This tube goes from the inside corner of the eye to the nose.

## Older Adults and Watery Eyes

In older adults, the most common cause of watery eyes with no clear reason is narrowing of the tear duct.  
This happens with age.  
But doctors also check for tumors, especially if the problem starts suddenly or gets worse.

## Key Facts

- If your eyes feel dry and watery, dry eyes are likely the cause.  
- If tears run down your cheek, a blocked tear duct is likely.  
- Tests are not usually needed.  
- They may be used if surgery is planned or to check for an abscess.

# Your Medical Privacy Rights

Health care providers must protect your personal medical information. They must do this in ways that match your wishes.

For example, your doctor should talk to you in private. You might prefer that your doctor call you on your cell phone instead of your home phone.

Even close family members cannot always get your medical details. This is true even if they mean well.

Everyone has the right to keep their medical information private unless they say it is okay to share it.

## What Is HIPAA?

A federal law called the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, or HIPAA, applies to most health care providers.

HIPAA includes a rule called the Privacy Rule. This rule sets clear standards for how your personal health information is handled.

### Your Rights Under HIPAA

- You can usually see your medical records.
- You can ask for copies of your records.
- You can ask to fix mistakes in your records.
- If someone is legally allowed to make health care choices for you, they can also see your records.
- Health care providers must tell you how they protect your privacy.
- Providers can share your medical information only with other health care workers who need it to treat you or handle payment.
- Providers cannot use your medical information for marketing.
- Providers must take steps to keep your conversations private.
- You can file a complaint if you think your privacy was violated. You can do this:
  - Directly with the health care provider.
  - With the privacy officer at the health care facility.
  - With the Office for Civil Rights in the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

### Sharing Information with Family or Friends

HIPAA does not stop doctors from talking with other health care workers or with family and friends who are involved in your care.

Doctors can share information with your spouse, family, friends, or others you name.

If you are able to make your own health care decisions, your doctor can talk with your family or friends if:
- You agree.
- You are present and do not object when asked.

If you are not able to speak for yourself, or if it is not possible to ask you (for example, during an emergency), your doctor can still share information with family or friends if they believe it is in your best interest.

### When Health Care Providers Must Share Information

Sometimes, the law requires health care providers to share certain information. This usually happens when someone else might be in danger.

For example:
- Certain serious infections like COVID-19, HIV, syphilis, and tuberculosis must be reported to local or state health departments.
- Signs of child abuse, adult abuse, or elder abuse must be reported to child or adult protective services.
- In some states, conditions like dementia or recent seizures must be reported to the Department of Motor Vehicles if they could affect your ability to drive safely.
- During public health emergencies like the COVID-19 pandemic, health care providers can share information with health information exchanges and public health agencies to help protect the public.

# Pheochromocytoma – Simple Explanation

A pheochromocytoma is a rare tumor that comes from special cells in the adrenal glands. These cells make chemicals called catecholamines. The tumor can cause high blood pressure. This high blood pressure may happen all the time or come and go in sudden attacks.

## Where Pheochromocytomas Are Found

Most of these tumors are in the adrenal glands. About 90% are in the center of the adrenal gland, called the adrenal medulla.

Some pheochromocytomas are not in the adrenal glands. They can be found in other parts of the body that come from the same type of cells. These include:
- Along the main blood vessel in the belly (aorta)
- In the neck, near the carotid artery
- Near the base of the spine, where the aorta splits
- In the bladder or other parts of the urinary system
- In the brain
- In the sac around the heart
- In certain skin growths (dermoid cysts)

## Who Gets Pheochromocytoma?

- It affects men and women equally.
- In about 10% of cases, both adrenal glands have a tumor. This is more common in children, where up to 20% have tumors on both sides.
- Less than 10% of adrenal tumors are cancerous.
- About 30% of tumors outside the adrenal glands are cancerous.
- Most people are between 20 and 40 years old when they are diagnosed.
- Nearly half of all cases are linked to inherited gene changes.

Tumors outside the adrenal glands are more likely to spread and become cancerous.

## What Do These Tumors Look Like?

- They can be any size, but most are about 2 to 2.5 inches across (5 to 6 cm).
- They can weigh between 2 to 7 ounces (50 to 200 grams).
- Some are very large, even weighing several kilograms.
- Most are not felt during a physical exam.
- Rarely, a large tumor can press on nearby organs and cause symptoms.

A tumor is considered non-cancerous if it has not grown through its outer layer and has not spread to other parts of the body. But even tumors that look harmless can come back or spread. Larger tumors are more likely to be cancerous or return after treatment.

## Related Conditions

Pheochromocytoma can be part of certain inherited conditions:
- Multiple endocrine neoplasia types 2A and 2B – these include other hormone tumors in the thyroid and parathyroid glands.
- Neurofibromatosis – a rare condition that can include pheochromocytoma in about 1% of cases.
- von Hippel-Lindau disease – this can include pheochromocytoma, tumors in the brain, and kidney cancer.

Some families with pheochromocytoma or tumors in the neck (carotid body tumors) have changes in genes that affect how cells make energy.

## Symptoms and Signs

High blood pressure is the most common symptom. It may be steady or come in sudden attacks. About 45% of people have these sudden spikes.

Other common symptoms include:
- Fast heartbeat
- Sweating a lot
- Dizziness when standing up
- Fast breathing
- Cold, sweaty skin
- Severe headaches
- Chest pain
- Feeling your heart race
- Nausea and vomiting
- Pain in the upper belly
- Blurred or double vision
- Trouble breathing
- Tingling or numbness
- Constipation
- A strong feeling of fear or danger

Sudden attacks can be triggered by:
- Touching the tumor
- Standing up quickly
- Pressing on the belly
- Going under anesthesia
- Strong emotions
- Taking certain medicines (like beta-blockers without alpha-blockers)
- Urinating (if the tumor is in the bladder)

In older adults, unexplained weight loss with long-term high blood pressure may be a sign.

A physical exam is usually normal unless done during a sudden attack. The heart and eyes may not show as much damage as expected from high blood pressure. But people with pheochromocytoma are more likely to have heart or brain problems than others with similar blood pressure.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

If a doctor suspects pheochromocytoma, they will test your blood or urine for high levels of catecholamine chemicals.

The best tests are:
- Blood test for free metanephrines
- Urine test for metanephrines over 24 hours

If these tests are positive, imaging tests are done to find the tumor. These include:
- CT scan
- MRI scan

A special scan using a radioactive substance (Gallium-68 dotatate-PET) may also be used.

## How Is It Treated?

The main treatment is surgery to remove the tumor. But surgery is delayed until blood pressure is under control.

### Blood Pressure Control Before Surgery

You will take two types of medicine:
- Alpha-blockers (like phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin)
- Beta-blockers (like propranolol)

**Important:** You must start with alpha-blockers first. If you take beta-blockers before alpha-blockers, your blood pressure can get worse.

The goal is to keep blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg. It usually takes 10 to 14 days for the body to adjust.

### Surgery

- Most tumors can be removed using a minimally invasive method (laparoscopy).
- Blood pressure must be watched all the time during surgery.
- Fluid levels in your body must be carefully managed.
- Anesthesia is started with a safe medicine and continued with inhaled drugs (like enflurane or isoflurane).
- If blood pressure spikes during surgery, doctors can give:
  - Phentolamine (injected into a vein)
  - Nitroprusside (infused into a vein)
- Fast heartbeats are treated with propranolol or esmolol.
- If muscle relaxants are needed, doctors choose ones that do not cause allergic reactions.

**Do not use atropine before surgery.** It can make blood pressure worse.

### Before Surgery

- A blood transfusion (1 to 2 units) may be given to prepare for blood loss.
- If your blood pressure is well controlled, eat more salt to help increase blood volume.
- If blood pressure drops too low during surgery, a medicine called norepinephrine may be given through a drip.
- In some cases, hydrocortisone (a steroid) may help if low blood pressure does not improve with fluids.

### If Both Adrenal Glands Are Affected

If both adrenal glands have tumors (as in some inherited conditions), you will get hydrocortisone (100 mg twice a day through a vein) before and during surgery. This prevents a serious hormone shortage.

Sometimes, doctors can remove only part of the adrenal gland to keep some hormone function.

## Treatment for Cancerous or Spreading Tumors

If the tumor is cancerous and has spread, treatment focuses on controlling symptoms and slowing growth.

Medicines used include:
- Alpha-blockers and beta-blockers to control blood pressure.
- I-131 MIBG or lutetium-177 dotatate – these can help relieve symptoms in some patients.
- Metyrosine – this medicine helps reduce the amount of harmful chemicals made by the tumor.
- Radiation therapy – can help ease bone pain from spread.
- Chemotherapy – rarely helps, but one common option is a mix of three drugs: cyclophosphamide, vincristine, and dacarbazine.
- Temozolomide – a newer chemotherapy drug that may help.
- Sunitinib or cabozantinib – targeted drugs that may slow tumor growth.
- Belzutifan – a drug used in von Hippel-Lindau disease. It is being tested for cancerous pheochromocytoma.

## Key Points

- High blood pressure may be steady or come in sudden attacks.
- Diagnosis is confirmed by testing blood or urine for high levels of catecholamine chemicals.
- Imaging tests (like CT or MRI) are used to find the tumor.
- You will take alpha-blockers and then beta-blockers before surgery.
- Genetic testing is important to guide long-term care and check family members for risk.

# Decompression Sickness

Decompression sickness happens when nitrogen gas forms bubbles in your blood and body tissues. This occurs when pressure drops too quickly after being underwater or in a pressurized environment.

## What Causes Decompression Sickness?

Air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen. When you dive deep, the pressure increases. You breathe in more air molecules than you would at the surface. Your body uses oxygen right away. But nitrogen does not get used up. It builds up in your blood and tissues.

As you come up from a dive, the pressure around you drops. The extra nitrogen in your body cannot leave your body fast enough. It turns into gas bubbles. These bubbles can cause harm.

The bubbles can:
- Damage tissues
- Block blood vessels
- Cause blood clots
- Trigger inflammation

This leads to pain and other symptoms.

## Who Is at Risk?

Some people are more likely to get decompression sickness. Risk increases with:

- Heart problems like a hole in the heart
- Cold water
- Not drinking enough water
- Flying soon after diving
- Physical effort during or after a dive
- Being tired
- Diving deeper
- Staying underwater longer
- Being overweight
- Getting older
- Coming up too fast
- Not following safe diving rules

Nitrogen stays in your body for at least 12 hours after a dive. If you dive again in the same day, your risk goes up. Flying within 12 to 24 hours after diving adds more risk. The air pressure in airplanes is lower than on the ground. This can make bubbles grow and cause problems.

Fatty tissues, like those in the brain and spine, hold nitrogen well. So these areas are more likely to be affected.

## Types of Decompression Sickness

There are two main types:

**Type I** – Mild. It mainly affects joints, skin, and lymph vessels.  
**Type II** – Serious. It can affect the brain, spine, lungs, and heart. It can be life-threatening.

## Symptoms

Symptoms usually do not appear right away. Half of people feel symptoms within 1 hour. But 90% feel them within 6 hours.

### Early Symptoms
- Feeling tired
- Not wanting to eat
- Headache
- General feeling of being unwell

### Type I (Mild) Symptoms
- Pain in joints (arms, legs, back)
- Muscle pain
- Itching
- Skin rash or blotchy skin
- Swelling in arms, chest, or belly
- Extreme tiredness

This type is not life-threatening. But it can be a warning sign of worse problems.

### Type II (Severe) Symptoms

**Spinal Cord Problems**
- Numbness or tingling in arms or legs
- Weakness that gets worse over hours
- Paralysis (can become permanent)
- Trouble urinating or controlling bowel movements
- Back or belly pain

**Brain Problems**
- Headache
- Confusion
- Trouble speaking
- Double vision

Loss of consciousness is rare.

**Inner Ear Problems**
- Dizziness (feeling like you are spinning)
- Ringing in the ears
- Hearing loss

**Lung Problems**
- Cough
- Chest pain
- Getting worse at breathing (called "the chokes")
- In rare cases, shock or death

### Late Effects

**Dysbaric Osteonecrosis**
- Bone tissue dies, especially in the shoulder or hip
- Causes long-term pain and joint damage
- Often leads to arthritis
- May not cause symptoms at first
- Can take months or years to get worse
- Usually seen in deep-sea workers or technical divers
- Joint replacement may be needed if damage is severe

**Permanent Nerve Damage**
- Partial paralysis
- Can happen if treatment is delayed or not given
- Some people improve with repeated oxygen treatments in a high-pressure chamber

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your symptoms and when they started. They ask about your dive.

Tests like CT scans or MRI scans may show brain or spine problems. But these tests are not always needed. Treatment starts right away unless the diagnosis is unclear or you are stable.

MRI scans are the best way to find bone damage from decompression sickness.

## How Is It Treated?

Most people get better completely.

### Oxygen
- All people with symptoms should breathe 100% oxygen through a tight-fitting mask.
- This helps reduce bubble size and eases symptoms.

### Recompression Therapy
- This is treatment in a high-pressure chamber.
- It helps blood flow and oxygen reach damaged tissues.
- Pressure is lowered slowly, with breaks, so bubbles can leave the body safely.
- Even mild symptoms need this treatment because symptoms can return or get worse in the first 24 hours.

### When to Start Treatment
- The sooner treatment starts, the better.
- If you are flying, the lower pressure in the plane can make symptoms worse.
- But getting treatment quickly is more important than avoiding a flight.
- Experts say it is safer to fly in a pressurized plane or at low altitude if the plane is not pressurized.

### How Long Treatment Works
- Recompression therapy can help up to 48 hours or longer after diving.
- Do not wait. Get treatment even if you must travel far.
- While waiting, breathe oxygen and drink fluids.

Delaying treatment increases the risk of permanent injury.

## How to Prevent Decompression Sickness

You can lower your risk by following safe diving practices.

### Safe Diving Rules
- Limit how deep and how long you dive.
- Stay within no-stop limits (no need for decompression stops).
- If you go deeper, take planned stops during your ascent.
- Use a dive table or a dive computer to track your depth and time.

### Dive Computers
- These devices track your dive in real time.
- They tell you when to stop and how long to stay at each stop.
- Many divers use them to stay safe.

### Safety Stop
- After every dive, make a 3- to 5-minute stop at about 15 feet (4.5 meters) below the surface.
- This helps release extra nitrogen.

### Important Notes
- These steps do not remove all risk.
- Some people still get decompression sickness even after no-stop dives.
- Dive tables and computers do not account for all personal risks.
- Some people do not follow the rules.

### After Diving
- Wait at least 12 to 24 hours after diving before flying or going to a high altitude.
- This is especially important after several days of diving.

### After Recovering
- If you had decompression sickness, do not dive again until a doctor says it is safe.
- If you had symptoms even after following the rules, get a full medical check-up before diving again.
- Your doctor may check for heart problems or other hidden risks.

## Did You Know?

Flying within 12 to 24 hours after diving increases your risk of decompression sickness.

# Chromium

Chromium is a mineral your body needs in small amounts.  
It helps insulin work better.  
Insulin is a hormone that helps your body use sugar from food for energy.

Good food sources of chromium include:
- Carrots  
- Potatoes  
- Broccoli  
- Whole grains  
- Molasses  

Some supplements contain chromium combined with a substance called picolinate.  
Picolinate comes from another amino acid called tryptophan.  
This form may help your body absorb chromium more easily.

## What People Say About Chromium

Some people claim that chromium picolinate can:
- Help with weight loss  
- Build muscle  
- Reduce body fat  
- Lower cholesterol and triglycerides  
- Improve insulin function  

But low levels of chromium can harm insulin.  
Still, there is not strong proof that taking chromium supplements helps people with diabetes.  
There is also no clear proof it improves body fat, muscle, or blood fat levels.

## What the Research Shows

Scientists are not sure if chromium supplements help.  
Studies give mixed results.

A 2002 review of 20 studies found no clear benefit of chromium for blood sugar or insulin in people without diabetes.  
For people with diabetes, the results were unclear.

A later review of 14 studies on people with type 2 diabetes looked at meaningful results.  
These included:
- Hemoglobin A1C below 7%  
- A drop of 0.5% or more in hemoglobin A1C  

Only 3 of the 14 studies showed A1C below 7%.  
Only 5 of the 14 showed a drop of 0.5% or more.  
This means the benefit is very small.

Another review of 28 studies found a small drop in blood sugar and A1C.  
But the studies used different doses and types of chromium.  
This makes it hard to trust the results.

A 2019 review of people with overweight or obesity found a small drop in:
- Weight  
- Body mass index  
- Body fat  

The effect was noticeable but not large.  
Experts are not sure if this change is meaningful for health.

A Cochrane review of 14 studies on overweight or obese adults found a small weight loss.  
But the overall evidence does not support using chromium for this purpose.

More high-quality studies are needed.  
These studies should:
- Check people’s starting chromium levels  
- Use the same form of chromium  
- Focus on people at risk for health problems  
- Track what people eat

## Side Effects of Chromium

Taking up to 1000 micrograms of chromium per day is safe for most people.  
Some forms may cause stomach upset or ulcers.  
Rare cases of kidney or liver problems have been reported.  
People with kidney or liver disease should avoid chromium supplements.  
Chromium can also reduce how well your body absorbs iron.

## Drug Interactions

Chromium can lower blood sugar when taken with:
- Insulin  
- Sulfonylureas  

It does not seem to affect blood sugar when taken with metformin.

Chromium may lower levels of levothyroxine, a medicine for low thyroid.  
People on this medicine may need a dose change if they take chromium.

Because chromium binds to ferritin (a protein that stores iron), it may cause iron deficiency.

# Problems with Blood Vessels in the Liver

The liver gets the oxygen and nutrients it needs from two main blood vessels:

- The portal vein  
- The hepatic artery

The portal vein brings about two thirds of the blood. This blood comes from the intestines and carries nutrients and some oxygen. The hepatic artery brings the other one third. This blood is rich in oxygen and comes from the heart. It gives the liver about half of its oxygen.

Having two blood sources helps protect the liver. If one blood vessel is damaged, the liver can often keep working because it still gets blood from the other source.

## How Blood Moves Through the Liver

Blood leaves the liver through the hepatic veins. This blood is a mix of blood from both the portal vein and the hepatic artery. The hepatic veins carry blood to the inferior vena cava. This is the largest vein in the body. The inferior vena cava sends blood from the lower body to the heart.

## What Happens When Blood Flow Is Poor

Problems with blood vessels in the liver usually happen when blood does not flow well—either into the liver or out of it.

If blood cannot leave the liver, it builds up inside. This causes congestion. The liver may become enlarged. If blood cannot get into the liver, liver cells do not get enough oxygen and nutrients. This condition is called ischemia.

In ischemic cholangiopathy, the bile ducts do not get enough blood. Bile ducts carry bile from the liver to the intestines.

### Did You Know?

Unlike other organs, the liver gets more than half of its blood from a vein. Most other organs get blood from arteries.

## Causes of Poor Blood Flow

Poor blood flow can happen because of:

- Heart failure  
- Conditions that make blood more likely to clot

When blood clots form, they can block blood vessels. This can slow or stop blood flow.

Common conditions include:

- **Budd-Chiari syndrome**: Blood clots block the veins that carry blood out of the liver.  
- **Portal vein thrombosis**: A blood clot blocks or narrows the portal vein. This is the vessel that brings blood from the intestines to the liver.  
- **Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome** (formerly called veno-occlusive disease): Tiny blood vessels inside the liver become blocked.

# After Gallbladder Removal: Ongoing Belly Problems

Some people still have belly problems after gallbladder removal surgery. This is called postcholecystectomy syndrome.

- It happens in 5 to 40 out of every 100 people after surgery.
- The problem may be pain or other symptoms that feel like gallbladder issues.
- It can also be new symptoms caused by the surgery.

The gallbladder stores bile, a fluid that helps digest fat. Removing it usually does not cause major problems with the bile system.

But in about 1 out of 10 people, the muscle at the end of the bile tube (called the sphincter of Oddi) does not work right. This can cause pain or changes in pressure in the bile system. It can also make the belly more sensitive.

## Common Symptoms

- Upset stomach or general belly discomfort.
- Not true gallbladder pain (like sharp, crampy pain in the upper right side).
- Some people get diarrhea because too much bile reaches the colon.

Diarrhea often goes away on its own. But if it does not, medicine that binds bile acids may help.

## Causes of Ongoing Symptoms

- Narrowing of the bile tube opening (called papillary stenosis). This is rare. It can happen after injury, inflammation, or past pancreatitis.
- A stone left behind in the bile duct.
- Pancreatitis (inflammation of the pancreas).
- Acid from the stomach coming back up into the esophagus (gastroesophageal reflux).

## How Doctors Diagnose the Problem

Doctors look for both biliary and non-biliary causes of pain.

If the pain feels like gallbladder pain, the doctor will:

- Check blood tests for liver and pancreas function.
- Do imaging tests of the liver and bile system.

Specific tests include:

- Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with pressure testing (manometry).
- A scan that tracks bile flow through the system.

These tests help find problems with the sphincter of Oddi.

- High liver test results suggest a problem with the bile part of the sphincter.
- High pancreas enzyme levels suggest a problem with the pancreatic part.

The best way to find a sphincter problem is manometry during ERCP. But this test can cause pancreatitis in up to 1 out of 4 people.

- A pressure test that shows high pressure during pain is a sign of a problem.
- A slow movement of bile from the liver to the intestine on a scan also suggests a problem.

Papillary stenosis is diagnosed when a person has:
- Repeated episodes of biliary pain.
- Abnormal liver or pancreas blood test results.

## How Doctors Treat the Problem

- In some cases, a procedure called endoscopic sphincterotomy helps.
- This cuts the muscle around the bile tube opening. It can ease pain from sphincter problems, especially if there is narrowing (papillary stenosis).

Doctors may use ERCP and manometry to treat pain. But if no clear problem is found, this treatment does not help.

- If no clear cause is found, doctors treat the symptoms instead.
- This may include medicines, diet changes, or other supportive care.

# Pilonidal Disease

Pilonidal disease happens when a hair grows into the skin at the top of the crack between your buttocks.

## What Causes Pilonidal Disease?

- Hairs near the buttocks can get pushed into the skin.
- This can create a small hole or pocket under the skin.
- The pocket may hold hair and other debris.
- This pocket is called a pilonidal cyst.

Some people have no symptoms. Others may feel pain or have swelling.

## Symptoms

If the cyst gets infected, you may notice:
- Pain in the area
- Redness
- Swelling
- Pus draining from the skin

An infected cyst is called a pilonidal abscess. It can be very painful.

A pilonidal sinus happens when the cyst opens under the skin and forms a tunnel. This can lead to a long-lasting wound that keeps draining.

## Who Gets Pilonidal Disease?

- It is most common in young, hairy, White men.
- It can also happen in women.

The exact cause is not known. But it may happen when a hair irritates the skin and grows in.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor checks the area. They look for small holes near the infected spot. These holes are called pits.

This helps the doctor tell pilonidal disease apart from other skin infections.

## How Is It Treated?

### For a Pilonidal Abscess
- A doctor must cut into the abscess and drain the pus.
- Antibiotics are usually not needed.

### For a Pilonidal Cyst or Sinus
- The cyst or tunnel must be removed in surgery.
- This helps prevent future infections.

### For Larger Cysts
- A flap procedure may be needed.
- In this surgery, the doctor moves healthy skin and sometimes muscle from nearby areas.
- This covers the area where the cyst was removed.

This helps the wound heal better and lowers the chance of it coming back.

# Ehrlichiosis and Anaplasmosis

Ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis are infections caused by bacteria.  
These bacteria are similar to the ones that cause rickettsial diseases.  
The main cause of ehrlichiosis is a bacterium called *Ehrlichia chaffeensis*.  
The main cause of anaplasmosis is a bacterium called *Anaplasma phagocytophilum*.  
Both infections are spread to people through tick bites.  
Symptoms are like those of Rocky Mountain spotted fever.  
But a rash is much less common with ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis.  
Illness starts suddenly with fever, chills, headache, and feeling very tired.

---

## Where These Infections Happen

*Ehrlichia chaffeensis* causes a type of ehrlichiosis called human monocytic ehrlichiosis.  
Most cases happen in the southeastern and south central United States.  
This is where the lone star tick lives.  
This tick spreads the bacteria.

*Anaplasma phagocytophilum* causes human granulocytic anaplasmosis.  
This infection is found in the Northeast, mid-Atlantic, upper Midwest, and West Coast of the United States.  
It is spread by ixodid ticks.  
These same ticks also spread Lyme disease, babesiosis, and Powassan virus.  
A single tick bite can sometimes pass more than one infection.  
There have been rare cases where anaplasmosis was passed through blood transfusions from people who had no symptoms or were just getting sick.

> **Important:** Lyme disease, babesiosis, and Powassan virus are spread by the same ticks and in the same areas as anaplasmosis.  
> So, a tick bite can give you more than one infection at once.

---

## How the Infections Affect the Body

The two infections affect different types of white blood cells.  
Ehrlichiosis mainly affects monocytes.  
Anaplasmosis mainly affects granulocytes.  
This difference leads to only small differences in symptoms.

---

## Symptoms and Signs

Most people with ehrlichiosis or anaplasmosis get sick suddenly.  
Symptoms are like the flu.  
They include fever, chills, muscle aches, tiredness, nausea, vomiting, cough, headache, and general weakness.  
Symptoms usually start about 12 days after a tick bite.  
Some people have no symptoms at all.

A rash is rare in anaplasmosis.  
But some people with ehrlichiosis do get a rash.  
The rash may appear on the chest, arms, or legs.

In severe cases, these infections can cause:
- Serious blood clotting problems
- Failure of multiple organs
- Seizures
- Coma

People with weakened immune systems are at higher risk.  
This includes people taking medicines that lower immunity, such as steroids or cancer drugs.  
It also includes people with HIV or those who have had their spleen removed.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose These Infections

Doctors use a test called PCR on a blood sample.  
This test finds the bacteria’s genetic material.  
It is more accurate and faster than older blood tests.  
Older tests need two blood samples taken weeks apart to show a change in antibody levels.  
PCR can give results faster.

Doctors may also look at blood under a microscope.  
They can sometimes see tiny clumps inside white blood cells.  
These clumps are more common in anaplasmosis.

Blood and liver tests can show problems.  
These may include low white blood cell counts, low platelet counts, and high liver enzyme levels.

---

## How These Infections Are Treated

The best treatment is doxycycline.  
Start treatment as soon as possible, even before test results come back.  
Early treatment works very well.  
Delaying treatment can lead to serious problems.  
In some cases, it can lead to death.

Take doxycycline until you feel better and have no fever for 24 to 48 hours.  
But you must take it for at least 7 days.

If you cannot take doxycycline, your doctor can help you slowly build up tolerance.  
This is called desensitization.

Some people worry that doxycycline can stain children’s teeth.  
But the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says that short courses (5 to 10 days) are safe for children under 8.  
Research shows this short treatment does not harm tooth color or strength.

Chloramphenicol does not work for these infections.  
Do not use it.

Some people still feel tired, have headaches, or feel weak for weeks after treatment.  
This is normal and usually gets better over time.

---

## How to Prevent These Infections

There is no vaccine for ehrlichiosis or anaplasmosis.  
But you can protect yourself from tick bites.

### Ways to Avoid Tick Bites

- Stay on trails and paths.  
- Tuck your pants into your boots or socks.  
- Wear long-sleeved shirts.  
- Use insect repellent with DEET on your skin.  
- Apply permethrin to your clothes. This kills ticks on contact.

> **Warning:** Use DEET carefully in very young children.  
> Some cases of poisoning have been reported in babies and toddlers.

Check your body often for ticks.  
Pay special attention to hairy areas like the scalp, armpits, and groin.  
Check children carefully.

If you find a tick, remove it gently.  
Do not crush it between your fingers.  
Crushing it can spread the infection.

Use a small pair of tweezers.  
Grasp the tick near its head.  
Pull it straight out slowly and steadily.  
Do not twist or squeeze the body.

After removal, clean the bite area with alcohol.

Do not use petroleum jelly, a hot match, or other irritants.  
These methods do not work and can make things worse.

There is no way to completely remove ticks from large areas.  
But you can reduce tick numbers by controlling small animals like mice and deer.

---

## Key Points

- Ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis are tick-borne infections.  
- They are related to rickettsial diseases.  
- Symptoms are like the flu and start suddenly.  
- A rash is rare in anaplasmosis.  
- Severe cases can lead to serious problems like organ failure or coma.  
- Use PCR testing on blood for the fastest and most accurate diagnosis.  
- Start treatment with doxycycline as soon as possible.  
- Doxycycline is safe for children under 8 when used for a short time.
