# Earache

Earache usually affects only one ear. Some people also have fluid coming from the ear. A few people may also have trouble hearing.

## How the Ear Works

The ear is a complex system. It includes parts inside the ear and nearby areas like the nose, sinuses, throat, and jaw joint. These areas share nerves with the ear. So pain in one area can feel like it is in the ear.

## What Causes Earache?

### Acute Earache (lasts less than 2 weeks)

The most common causes are:

- **Middle ear infection** – Fluid builds up behind the eardrum. This causes pressure and pain. The eardrum may bulge. It can also burst and release pus or blood.
- **Outer ear infection** – The outer ear canal becomes inflamed and painful. Itching is common.
- **Sudden pressure change** – This happens during airplane flights or scuba diving. The tube that connects the middle ear to the back of the nose (eustachian tube) gets blocked. Pressure builds up and hurts the eardrum.

Middle ear infections can lead to hearing loss. The eardrum cannot move normally when fluid is behind it. In rare cases, the infection spreads to the bone behind the ear (mastoid bone). This is called mastoiditis.

People with diabetes, HIV, cancer treatment, or kidney disease are at higher risk for a serious outer ear infection called necrotizing otitis externa.

### Chronic Earache (lasts more than 2 to 3 weeks)

Common causes include:

- **Jaw joint problems (TMJ)** – Pain gets worse when you chew or open your mouth wide.
- **Long-term eustachian tube problems** – The tube does not work well. This causes pressure and fullness.
- **Long-term outer ear infection** – The ear canal stays inflamed and itchy.
- **Migraines** – These can cause ear pain, even if the ear looks normal.

Less common causes include throat or voice box problems. These can cause pain that feels like it is in the ear. This is called referred pain.

## When to See a Doctor

See a doctor right away if you have:

- Diabetes
- A weak immune system (from HIV or cancer treatment)
- Chronic kidney disease
- Redness or swelling behind the ear
- Swelling at the opening of the ear canal
- Fluid draining from the ear
- Fever
- Ear pain that wakes you from sleep
- Chronic pain with other symptoms like hoarseness, trouble swallowing, or blocked nose

If the only warning sign is long-term pain, you can wait about a week. But if you have sudden, severe pain, see a doctor within a few days.

## What the Doctor Will Do

The doctor will ask about your symptoms and health history. Then they will examine your ears, nose, and throat.

They will use a special tool called an otoscope or microscope to look inside your ear. This helps them see if there is an infection or other problem.

If the ear looks normal, the pain may come from another area. The doctor may check your jaw, throat, or voice box. They may use a thin, flexible tube with a camera (endoscope) to look inside your nose and throat.

Tests may be needed if the cause is not clear. These can include:

- Hearing tests (audiogram)
- Imaging scans like CT or MRI
- Biopsy (taking a small sample of tissue) if cancer is suspected

## Common Causes and What to Expect

| Cause | Typical Signs | How It’s Diagnosed |
|------|----------------|---------------------|
| Middle ear infection | Pain, fullness, muffled hearing, popping sounds | Doctor’s exam, sometimes hearing test |
| Pressure change (barotrauma) | Sharp pain, blood near eardrum | Doctor’s exam, hearing test if needed |
| Mastoiditis | Swelling behind ear, fever, ear discharge | Doctor’s exam, sometimes CT scan |
| Outer ear infection | Itching, pain, swelling, pus in ear canal | Doctor’s exam, CT scan if severe |
| Earwax blockage or foreign object | Visible blockage, often in children | Doctor’s exam |
| Injury to ear | Pain after trying to clean ear | Doctor’s exam |
| Cancer in throat, voice box, or nose | Long-term pain, history of smoking or drinking, swollen neck glands | MRI, endoscopy, biopsy |
| Tonsil infection | Pain when swallowing, red throat, trouble breathing | Doctor’s exam, sometimes culture |
| Migraine | Recurring headaches, normal ear exam | Doctor’s history and exam |
| Nerve pain (e.g., glossopharyngeal nerve) | Sharp, sudden pain lasting less than a second | Doctor’s exam, MRI if needed |
| Jaw joint (TMJ) problems | Pain when chewing, jaw feels stiff | Doctor’s exam, sometimes CT or MRI |

Note: Not all people have every symptom listed. Some have hearing loss with ear infections. A normal ear exam does not rule out problems in nearby areas.

## Treatment

The best treatment is fixing the cause.

For pain relief:

- Take a pain medicine like ibuprofen or acetaminophen.
- For severe outer ear infections, stronger pain medicine (like oxycodone or hydrocodone) may be needed for a few days.

For severe outer ear infections:

- The doctor may remove pus or fluid from the ear.
- A small foam plug (wick) may be placed in the ear canal. It holds medicine (antibiotics or steroids) in place.

Ear drops with pain relief are not very helpful. They should not be used if you think the eardrum is torn. Always check with a doctor before using any ear drops.

## Important Tips

- Never use cotton swabs or any object to clean inside your ear.
- Cotton swabs are only meant for the outer part of the ear.
- Do not flush your ears unless a doctor tells you to.
- Never use a water irrigator, self-cleaning kit, or video endoscope in your ear.

## Key Points

- Most earaches come from infections in the middle or outer ear.
- But jaw problems and migraines are also common causes of ear pain.
- A doctor’s exam is usually enough to find the cause.
- If the ear looks normal, the problem may be in nearby areas like the jaw, throat, or nose.

# Cogan Syndrome

Cogan syndrome is a rare disease where the body’s immune system attacks the eye and inner ear.

It mostly affects young adults. Most people with this condition are between 14 and 47 years old.

The exact cause is not fully known. But it seems the immune system mistakenly targets parts of the eye and inner ear.

Some people also develop serious inflammation of blood vessels. This can affect the aorta, the main blood vessel from the heart. This can be life-threatening.

## Symptoms and Signs

The first symptoms usually involve the eyes, the balance and hearing system, or both.

By five months after symptoms start, most people have problems with both eyes and hearing/balance.

Other common symptoms include fever, headache, joint pain, and muscle pain.

## Diagnosis

If Cogan syndrome is suspected, see an eye doctor and an ear, nose, and throat doctor right away.

Doctors make the diagnosis based on symptoms and test results.

They will check for other possible causes of eye inflammation, such as syphilis, Lyme disease, or Epstein-Barr virus infection. Blood tests help rule these out.

Some people with Cogan syndrome have certain antibodies in their blood. These include antibodies linked to inner ear damage, hearing loss, and blood vessel inflammation.

Imaging tests like CT or MRI may be done. These can show swelling or changes in the inner ear. But sometimes the scans look normal.

## Treatment

Treatment starts with eye drops that contain a steroid medicine. This helps reduce eye inflammation.

If the disease is not treated, it can lead to scarring of the cornea and permanent vision loss.

With treatment, the chance of lasting hearing loss is about 50%.

For mild eye problems like cornea inflammation, eye drops with prednisolone acetate 1% are used. Apply one drop four times a day. You can increase to once every hour while awake, for two to three weeks.

For deeper eye inflammation or to protect hearing and balance, a daily oral steroid medicine (prednisone) is started as soon as possible. The dose is based on body weight. It is taken once a day for two to six months.

If the disease does not respond well to steroids, doctors may add other medicines. These include cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, cyclosporine, infliximab, or rituximab.

## Key Points

- Cogan syndrome is rare. It mainly affects the eyes and the inner ear.
- In some cases, it causes dangerous inflammation of the aorta.
- Without treatment, it can lead to permanent vision and hearing loss.
- See an eye doctor and an ear, nose, and throat doctor right away if this condition is suspected.
- Treatment usually includes steroid eye drops and oral steroids.

# Arteriovenous Fistula

An arteriovenous fistula is an abnormal connection between an artery and a vein.

## What Are Arteries and Veins?

- Arteries carry blood with oxygen and nutrients from the heart to the rest of the body.
- Veins carry blood back to the heart from the rest of the body.
- Capillaries are tiny blood vessels that connect arteries and veins.
- Capillaries have very thin walls. This lets oxygen and nutrients pass into body tissues.
- Waste products from tissues pass into the blood through capillaries.

Normally, blood flows from arteries into capillaries and then into veins.  
An arteriovenous fistula lets blood flow directly from an artery into a vein.  
This skips the capillaries.

## Types of Arteriovenous Fistulas

Fistulas can be:

- **Congenital**: Present at birth.
- **Acquired**: Develops after birth.

Congenital fistulas are rare.  
Acquired fistulas usually happen after an injury.  
The injury often damages both an artery and a nearby vein.  
This can happen from a knife wound or a bullet.  
The fistula may appear right away or hours later.  
If blood leaks into nearby tissues, the area can swell fast.

## Why Are Some Fistulas Created on Purpose?

Some medical treatments need repeated access to a vein.  
One example is kidney dialysis.  
Each treatment requires a needle in a vein.  
Over time, repeated needle use can damage the vein.  
The vein may become inflamed, clot, or scar.  
This can make future treatments hard.

To prevent this, doctors may create a small fistula on purpose.  
They connect an artery and a vein in the arm.  
This makes the vein stronger and wider.  
It is easier to insert a needle.  
Blood flows faster through the vein.  
Faster flow means less chance of clotting.

These planned fistulas are small.  
They do not cause heart problems.  
They can be closed when no longer needed.

## Symptoms of an Arteriovenous Fistula

### Congenital Fistulas Near the Skin

- The area may look swollen.
- It may feel warm to the touch.

### Large Acquired Fistulas (Not Treated)

- A lot of blood flows under high pressure from artery to vein.
- Veins are not built to handle this pressure.
- Veins stretch and bulge. They may look like varicose veins.
- Blood flows more easily into the veins than it should.
- This can lower blood pressure.
- Low blood pressure may cause:
  - Tiredness
  - Dizziness
  - Rarely, fainting

To make up for low blood pressure, the heart pumps harder and faster.  
This extra work can strain the heart.  
Over time, this may lead to heart failure.  
Symptoms of heart failure include:
- Shortness of breath
- Swelling in the legs

Rarely, a large fistula can take too much blood from the arm or leg.  
This is called steal syndrome.  
It can cause:
- Numbness
- Pain
- Cramps
- Skin turns blue or gray
- In severe cases, skin sores

On dark skin, color changes may be hard to see.

## How Is a Fistula Diagnosed?

Doctors use imaging tests to find and check a fistula.

### Listening with a Stethoscope

- A doctor may hear a loud, machine-like sound over a large fistula.
- This sound is called a machinery murmur.

### Ultrasound

- Doppler ultrasound is the most common test.
- It shows blood flow and confirms the fistula.
- It helps doctors see how big the problem is.

### For Deep Fistulas

- If the fistula is deep in the body (like near the aorta or vena cava), doctors may use:
  - Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA)
  - Computed tomography (CT) angiography

### Angiography

- Used when treatment is needed.
- A special liquid (contrast agent) is injected into a blood vessel.
- This liquid makes the fistula show up better on x-rays.
- Doctors use the images to plan the best treatment.

## How Is a Fistula Treated?

### Congenital Fistulas

- Only treated if they cause symptoms.
- Doctors use a procedure called endovascular treatment.
- A thin tube (catheter) is inserted into a vein.
- Coils or plugs are placed into the fistula to block blood flow.
- This must be done by a skilled vascular surgeon.
- Fistulas near the eye, brain, or other important areas are harder to treat.

### Acquired Fistulas

- Usually have one large connection.
- Surgery is the main treatment.
- The surgeon cuts the abnormal connection.
- The holes in the artery and vein are sewn closed.
- Surgery should happen as soon as possible after diagnosis.

# What Is an Echocardiogram?

An echocardiogram is a test that uses sound waves to create pictures of your heart.  
It shows the heart’s size, shape, and movement.  
It also shows how well the heart valves work.  
The test can show the large blood vessels near the heart.

## What the Test Can Show

The test checks the thickness of the heart walls.  
It can find if the walls are too thick or too thin.  
It shows how the heart moves when it beats.  
It can help find areas of the heart that are not getting enough blood.  
It can also show if part of the heart has been damaged by a heart attack.

## How It Helps Doctors

The test measures how well the main pumping chamber of the heart works.  
It checks how the heart fills with blood between beats.  
This helps doctors find certain heart problems, such as:  
- Thickened heart muscle  
- Heart muscle that does not relax properly  
- Severe heart failure  
- A stiff lining around the heart

## What Else It Can Detect

The test looks at the heart valves.  
It can find clumps of bacteria on the valves.  
It can find blood clots inside the heart.  
It gives a rough idea of the pressure in the lungs.  
It also gives a rough idea of the pressure in the large vein near the heart.

## The 4-Chamber View

This is one of the main pictures taken during the test.  
It shows four parts of the heart:  
- The two upper chambers  
- The two lower chambers  
This view helps doctors see the heart’s structure and how it works.

# Religion and Spirituality in Older Adults

Religion and spirituality are related but not the same.  
Religion often involves organized groups, regular meetings, and set traditions.  
Spirituality is about personal beliefs, feelings, and a search for deeper meaning.  
It does not need to be tied to a church or group.  
Spirituality can include thoughts, emotions, and actions related to the soul or the sacred.

Religion often includes rules and expectations.  
Spirituality has fewer rules.  
Some people do not follow any religion but still feel spiritual.  
In the United States, 18 out of every 100 adults aged 65 and older have no religious ties.  
This is less than the 27 out of 100 adults in the general population.  
About 6 to 10 out of every 100 older adults are atheists.  
They do not rely on religion or spirituality to find meaning in life.

Older adults are more likely to take part in religious activities than any other age group.  
About half go to religious services once a week or more.  
For many older adults, their religious community is the main source of support outside the family.  
Being part of a religious group is the most common kind of volunteer activity.  
It is more common than all other volunteer activities combined.

## Benefits of Religion and Spirituality

People who are religious often report better physical and mental health.  
Some believe that God’s help explains these benefits.  
But experts do not know if religion causes better health or if healthier people are more likely to join religious groups.  
If religion helps, it is not clear why.  
Many possible reasons have been suggested, such as better mental health, healthy habits, and strong social ties.

Religion can help with mental health in several ways:

- It can help people stay positive and hopeful about life and illness.  
  This hope can lead to better recovery and health results.  
- It can give people a sense of purpose.  
  This sense of purpose can improve how they care for themselves and how they relate to family and friends.  
- It can help people deal with illness and disability.  

Many older adults say religion is the most important thing that helps them handle health problems and life stress.  
For example, staying hopeful can help people keep trying to get better, even when they are sick.

Some studies show that older adults who are very religious and use faith to cope are less likely to feel depressed or anxious.  
They also report greater happiness and well-being.  
Even how people see their own disability can change.  
One study of older women with hip fractures found that the most religious women had less depression.  
They were also able to walk farther when they left the hospital than those who were less religious.

People who are active in religious groups often stay healthier and more independent.  
Some religious groups encourage healthy habits.  
For example, Mormons and Seventh-Day Adventists avoid smoking and heavy drinking.  
Members of these groups are less likely to have substance problems.  
They also tend to live longer than the average person.

Religious beliefs often help build strong communities.  
More social contact helps older adults get sick care earlier.  
It also helps them follow their treatment plans.  
People in their religious communities often check in on each other.  
They ask about health and medical care.  
This support helps prevent older adults from ignoring their own needs.

Religious faith can also help caregivers.  
Studies show that caregivers of older adults with serious illnesses like dementia or cancer feel better mentally when they use religious coping.  
This includes prayer, faith, and support from their religious community.

## Possible Downsides of Religion and Spirituality

Religion is not always helpful.  
It can sometimes cause problems.  
For example, it may lead to too much guilt, rigid thinking, or anxiety.  
People with certain mental health conditions may have religious thoughts that are extreme or unrealistic.  
This can happen in people with obsessive-compulsive disorder, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, or other serious mental health issues.

Some people feel deeply hurt when they are not accepted by a religious group.  
This can happen because of gender identity or sexual orientation.  
They may feel rejected and lost.

Some religious groups discourage medical care.  
They may refuse lifesaving treatments.  
Examples include blood transfusions, antibiotics for serious infections, and insulin for diabetes.  
Instead, they may rely only on prayer, chanting, or lighting candles.  
This can be dangerous.  
Some strict religious groups isolate older adults from family and friends.  
This can lead to loneliness and poor health.

## How Health Care Providers Can Help

Health care providers may talk to older adults about religion and spirituality.  
These beliefs can affect a person’s health and well-being.  
Knowing about a person’s beliefs helps doctors give better care in some cases.

Talk about religion or spirituality when:

- A person is very sick, under great stress, or near the end of life and brings up religious topics.  
- A person says they are religious and that faith helps them cope with illness.  
- A person’s religious beliefs are clearly affecting their health or health choices.

When doctors understand a person’s spiritual needs, they can help connect them to support.  
This might include spiritual counseling, support groups, religious activities, or social contact through a faith community.

Doctors may ask:

- Is your faith an important part of your life?  
- How does your faith affect how you take care of yourself?  
- What are your most important ways of coping with stress or illness?

If a person wants to use religious or spiritual resources, doctors can ask:

- Are there any barriers to using these resources?  
- Can I help you find a way around those barriers?

For example, doctors may suggest transportation help for older adults who cannot get to religious services on their own.

Sometimes older adults feel more comfortable talking to a religious leader than to a mental health professional.  
Clergy members who are trained in counseling can be very helpful.  
They can also help people get community support.  
For example, they may visit after a hospital stay, bring meals, or help with rides.

# Problems with Nerve-to-Muscle Signals

Problems with nerve-to-muscle signals happen at the connection point between nerves and muscles.  
These problems often cause muscle weakness that comes and goes.  
They do not cause numbness or tingling.

(See also: Overview of Peripheral Nervous System Disorders.)

These problems can happen in different ways:

- The muscle side of the connection does not work well.  
  Example: Myasthenia gravis.

- The nerve does not release enough of a chemical called acetylcholine.  
  Example: Botulism.

- A chemical in the space between the nerve and muscle breaks down acetylcholine too fast.  
  This can happen due to certain medicines or toxic chemicals.

The most common problem of this kind is myasthenia gravis.

Some conditions that mainly affect other parts of the body can also cause muscle symptoms.  
Examples include stiff-person syndrome and Isaacs syndrome.

# Interstitial Keratitis

Interstitial keratitis is a serious eye problem. It causes swelling in the middle part of the cornea. The cornea is the clear front part of the eye. This condition often happens after an eye infection.

## What Are the Symptoms?

- Your eyes may water more than usual.
- You may feel pain in one or both eyes.
- Your vision may become blurry.
- Bright light may hurt your eyes more than normal.

In some cases, especially when caused by syphilis, the cornea can become cloudy. This can lead to lasting vision loss.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will check your eyes carefully. They may use a special tool called a slit lamp. This tool lets them see the eye in detail.

They will also do blood tests. These tests help rule out other diseases. They check for infections like syphilis, Lyme disease, and Epstein-Barr virus.

If your blood tests are normal but you still have symptoms, your doctor may check for a rare condition called Cogan syndrome.

## What Causes It?

This condition is rare in the United States. Most cases happen in children or teens. The most common cause is congenital syphilis — a type of syphilis passed from mother to baby during pregnancy.

Other causes include:
- Cogan syndrome
- Lyme disease
- Epstein-Barr virus
- Syphilis caught later in life
- Herpes simplex virus
- Chickenpox virus (varicella-zoster)
- Tuberculosis

## How Is It Treated?

The main treatment is to fix the underlying infection. For example, antibiotics treat syphilis or Lyme disease.

Sometimes, doctors prescribe corticosteroid eye drops. These drops help reduce swelling and inflammation in the cornea.

Treating the root cause often helps the eye heal. But early treatment is important to prevent lasting damage to your vision.

# POEMS Syndrome

POEMS syndrome is a rare condition that affects many parts of the body.  
It is not caused by the immune system attacking the body.  
It is linked to a problem with blood cells called plasma cells.  
These cells make abnormal proteins that can cause harm.  
Other substances in the blood, such as cytokines and VEGF, are also too high.

## Symptoms and Signs

People with POEMS syndrome may have:

- Weakness or numbness in the arms and legs (nerve damage)  
- Enlarged organs, such as the liver or spleen  
- Low levels of hormones from the adrenal glands (Addison disease)  
- Type 2 diabetes  
- Overactive parathyroid glands  
- Low sex hormone levels (in men and women)  
- Swollen lymph nodes  
- Abnormal proteins in the blood (monoclonal gammopathy)  
- Bone damage with holes in the bones  
- Skin changes like dark spots, thick skin, extra hair, or small red growths  
- Swelling in the legs or belly (edema or ascites)  
- Fluid around the lungs (pleural effusion)  
- Swelling in the optic nerve (papilledema)  
- Fever  

About 1 in 7 people with POEMS syndrome also have Castleman disease.  
This is a condition where lymph nodes grow too large.  
Some types of Castleman disease are linked to HIV or another virus.

## How Doctors Diagnose POEMS Syndrome

Doctors look at a person’s symptoms, physical exam, and test results.  
There is no single test for POEMS syndrome.  
To make the diagnosis, a person must meet all of the following:

### Must have both:
- Nerve damage (polyneuropathy)  
- Evidence of abnormal plasma cells in the blood or bone marrow  

### At least one of these:
- Castleman disease  
- High levels of a substance called VEGF in the blood  
- Bone damage with hard, dense spots on X-rays  

### At least one of these:
- Hormone problems not related to diabetes or low thyroid  
- Fluid buildup in the body (like swelling in the legs or belly)  
- Enlarged organs  
- Swelling in the optic nerve  
- Skin changes  
- High platelet or red blood cell counts  

## Treatment

Treatment depends on how far the disease has spread.

- If the disease is in one small area, radiation therapy may be used.  
- If the disease is widespread, including in the bone marrow, chemotherapy is used.  
- In some cases, chemotherapy is followed by a stem cell transplant.  
- This type of transplant uses the person’s own blood stem cells.  

The five-year survival rate for people with POEMS syndrome is about 60%.

# Paracentesis

Paracentesis is a medical procedure. A doctor uses a needle to remove fluid from the belly.

The belly normally holds only a small amount of fluid. But sometimes extra fluid builds up. This is called ascites.

Fluid can build up in the belly if you have liver disease, heart failure, a hole in the stomach or intestines, cancer, or a damaged spleen.

Doctors use paracentesis for two main reasons:

- To help find the cause of the fluid buildup. They take a small sample of fluid to test in a lab.
- To relieve pressure and swelling in the belly. They remove a large amount of fluid to make you feel better.

Before the procedure:

- The doctor checks your belly with a physical exam.
- They may use an ultrasound scan to see where the fluid is.

Next:

- The doctor cleans a spot on your skin, usually just below your belly button.
- They numb the area with a small amount of medicine to reduce pain.
- Then they gently push a needle through your skin and muscles into the fluid.

The needle can be used to:

- Draw out a small amount of fluid for testing.
- Or connect to a thin tube to remove up to several quarts of fluid to reduce swelling.

Possible risks include:

- Fluid leaking out through the small hole in the skin.
- Bleeding at the site.
- Very rarely, the needle may accidentally poke a hole in the stomach or intestines. This is called perforation of the digestive tract.

# Birth Injuries

Sometimes, the process of labor and delivery can cause physical harm to a newborn.  
The number of babies who get injured during birth is going down.  
This is because more births are now done by cesarean section instead of difficult vaginal deliveries.  
Cesarean sections are used more often than vacuum deliveries or forceps deliveries.  

Some babies are more likely to be injured during birth.  
This includes babies who are large for their due date.  
Large babies are more common when the mother has diabetes during pregnancy.  
Babies who are not head-down at birth (like breech or other abnormal positions) are also at higher risk.  
This risk is even greater for first-time mothers.

---

## Facial Nerve Injury in Newborns

The facial nerve is the most commonly injured nerve in newborns.  
Forceps used during delivery can press on the nerve.  
But some injuries happen before birth.  
This can happen if the baby’s head presses against the mother’s bones or a fibroid tumor in the uterus.  

The injury usually happens near or past the point where the nerve leaves the skull.  
It causes one side of the face to look different, especially when the baby cries.  
The side with the injury cannot move.  
Sometimes only one branch of the nerve is hurt, most often the one that controls the lower jaw.  

Another reason for a face that looks uneven is a jaw that is shaped differently.  
This happens when the baby’s jaw is pressed on in the womb.  
In this case, the nerves are fine.  
Both sides of the face can still move.  
The top and bottom teeth do not line up properly.  
This is different from a facial nerve injury.  

A rare birth defect can cause one side of the smile to be weak.  
This is due to missing a small muscle on one side of the mouth.  
This condition does not cause health problems.  
But it must be told apart from a facial nerve injury.  

No tests or special treatment are needed for facial nerve injuries or jaw shape differences.  
These problems usually go away on their own by 2 to 3 months of age.

---

## Brachial Plexus Injuries in Newborns

The brachial plexus is a group of nerves that control movement in the arm.  
These nerves can be injured during delivery.  
This often happens when the baby’s neck is pulled sideways.  
This can occur during shoulder dystocia, breech delivery, or when the baby’s head is pulled too far back.  

The injury can be mild or severe.  
It can be a stretch, bleeding inside the nerve, a tear, or a complete pull-off of the nerve from the spinal cord.  
Other injuries may happen at the same time, such as broken collarbone or upper arm, or shoulder or neck joint problems.  
Some injuries are caused by pressure in the womb.  

The injury can affect:

- The upper nerves (C5 to C7): This affects the shoulder and elbow.  
- The lower nerves (C8 to T1): This affects the forearm and hand.  
- All nerves: This affects the whole arm and may also affect nerves that control sweating and blood flow.  

Where and how the nerve is damaged affects the outcome.

### Erb Palsy

Erb palsy is a common injury to the upper nerves.  
It causes the shoulder to stay pulled in and turned inward.  
The forearm stays turned in (pronated).  
The biceps reflex may be missing.  
The Moro reflex (startle reflex) may be weaker on one side.  
The diaphragm on the same side may not work well.  
This is due to injury to the phrenic nerve.  

Treatment is usually supportive.  
Physical therapy helps the arm move and stay in the right position.  
The arm is gently held across the baby’s chest to prevent over-movement.  
Gentle stretching exercises are done every day starting at one week of age.  
These help prevent stiff joints.

### Klumpke Palsy

Klumpke palsy is rare.  
It affects the lower nerves.  
It causes weakness or no movement in the hand and wrist.  
The baby may not be able to grip.  
The biceps reflex is still normal.  
The nerve that controls sweating and eye movement (T1) is often injured.  
This causes Horner syndrome: a small pupil, droopy eyelid, and no sweating on one side of the face.  

Treatment is usually just gentle movement of the hand and wrist.  
No other treatment is needed.

### Both Erb and Klumpke Palsy

These injuries rarely cause loss of feeling.  
If feeling is lost, it may mean the nerve is torn or pulled off.  
Most babies improve quickly.  
But some may still have problems.  

If the problem does not get better in 1 or 2 weeks, physical or occupational therapy is recommended.  
If there is no improvement after 1 or 2 months, the baby may have long-term problems.  
A specialist should be seen.  
This may include a pediatric neurologist or orthopedist at a children’s hospital.  
Surgery may be needed to repair the nerve with a graft.

### Injury to the Whole Nerve Group

This is less common.  
It causes the whole arm to be limp and not move.  
Reflexes are missing.  
Sensation is often lost.  
Horner syndrome may be present.  

If the baby shows signs of spinal cord injury (like weak legs or a Babinski reflex), an MRI is needed.  
This helps find the exact problem.

---

## Phrenic Nerve Injuries in Newborns

Most phrenic nerve injuries happen with brachial plexus injuries.  
The injury is usually on one side.  
It is caused by pulling on the head and neck during delivery.  

The baby has trouble breathing.  
Breathing sounds are quieter on the injured side.  

Treatment is supportive.  
The baby may need continuous positive airway pressure or a breathing machine.  

About one-third of babies get better on their own within the first month.  
If the baby does not improve, surgery to fix the diaphragm may be needed.

---

## Other Nerve Injuries in Newborns

Injuries to other nerves (like radial, sciatic, or obturator nerves) are rare.  
They are not usually caused by labor and delivery.  
They are more often due to a local injury, such as a shot near the sciatic nerve.  

Treatment includes keeping the muscles that are not working in a relaxed position.  
Surgery to fix the nerve is rarely needed.  

Most of these injuries heal completely.

---

## Spinal Cord Injuries in Newborns

Spinal cord injuries are rare.  
They can range from mild to severe.  
They often involve bleeding in the cord.  
Complete severing of the cord is very rare.  

The injury usually happens during breech delivery.  
It is caused by pulling too hard on the baby’s spine.  
It can also happen if the baby’s neck is bent too far back in the womb.  
This is called the “flying fetus” position.  
The injury usually affects the lower neck (C5 to C7).  

If the injury is higher, it can be fatal.  
This is because breathing stops.  
Sometimes a click or snap is heard at birth.  

At first, the baby has no movement or feeling below the injury.  
The body is limp.  
Later, some movement or feeling may return.  
Spasticity (tight muscles) develops in days or weeks.  

Breathing is still possible because the phrenic nerve is not damaged.  
This nerve starts higher in the neck (C3 to C5).  

If the injury is complete, the muscles between the ribs and the belly stop working.  
The baby cannot control the bladder or bowel.  
Sensation and sweating are lost below the injury.  
This can cause body temperature to change with the environment.  

An MRI of the neck can show the injury.  
It can also rule out treatable causes like tumors or blood clots.  
The fluid around the brain and spinal cord is often bloody.  

Treatment includes:

- Care to prevent skin sores  
- Quick treatment of lung and urinary infections  
- Regular checks to catch kidney problems early  

With good care, most babies live for many years.  
The main causes of death are repeated pneumonia and kidney failure.

---

## Head Injuries in Newborns

Head injuries are the most common birth-related injury.  
Most are minor.  
But serious injuries can happen.

---

## Brain Bleeding in Newborns

Bleeding in or around the brain can happen in any newborn.  
It is more common in premature babies.  

Common causes include:

- Lack of oxygen  
- Changes in blood pressure  
- Poor blood flow followed by sudden return of flow  
- Pressure on the baby’s head during labor  

The germinal matrix is a soft area in the brain that is very sensitive to bleeding.  
This area is present in premature babies.  
It makes brain bleeding more likely.  
Bleeding is also more likely if the baby has a blood disorder.  
Examples include vitamin K deficiency, hemophilia, or a condition where blood clots form too easily.

Bleeding can happen in different parts of the brain.  
Small bleeds in the space around the brain, the falx, or the tentorium are often found by accident in babies who died from other causes.  
Larger bleeds in the brain, under the brain’s covering, or in the brain tissue or ventricles are less common but more serious.

### Signs of Brain Bleeding

A baby with brain bleeding may show:

- Pauses in breathing  
- Seizures  
- Lethargy (very sleepy or inactive)

# Postpartum Depression

Postpartum depression is a serious mood problem that can happen in the first year after giving birth. It lasts more than two weeks and makes you feel very sad. It also makes you lose interest in things you used to enjoy.

## What Is Postpartum Depression?

- It is not the same as the "baby blues."
- The baby blues are mild mood swings or sadness that go away in a few days.
- Postpartum depression lasts longer and is much stronger.
- It can stop you from doing everyday tasks, like caring for your baby or yourself.

About 7 out of every 100 women get postpartum depression. In rare cases, a more serious condition called **postpartum psychosis** can happen.

## Who Is at Risk?

Some women are more likely to get postpartum depression. These include women who:

- Have had depression before
- Had depression during pregnancy
- Had postpartum depression in a past pregnancy
- Have had mood changes linked to their period or birth control pills
- Have a close family member with depression
- Are under a lot of stress (like money problems, relationship issues, or parenting alone)
- Do not have support from a partner or family
- Had a difficult pregnancy (like a premature baby or a baby with health problems)
- Feel conflicted about the pregnancy (for example, if it was unplanned or they thought about ending it)
- Have trouble breastfeeding

Hormone changes after birth and not getting enough sleep may also play a role. Some women may have a gene that makes them more likely to get postpartum depression.

If you had depression before pregnancy, tell your doctor or midwife. This increases your chance of getting postpartum depression.

## Symptoms of Postpartum Depression

Symptoms usually start in the first three months after birth. But they can start later. They may come on slowly or suddenly.

Common symptoms include:

- Feeling very sad
- Crying often and not being able to stop
- Mood swings
- Feeling angry or irritable
- Losing interest in your baby or other activities
- Feeling too tired to do anything
- Trouble sleeping (sleeping too much or too little)
- Headaches or body pain
- Losing interest in sex
- Feeling anxious or having panic attacks
- Eating too little or eating too much
- Trouble doing normal tasks
- Worrying too much about the baby
- Feeling like you are not good enough as a mother
- Feeling guilty about your feelings
- Thinking about hurting yourself or the baby

You may not feel close to your baby. This can affect your baby’s emotional, social, and thinking development.

Partners can also become depressed. When a parent is depressed, it can cause stress in the family.

Without treatment, postpartum depression can last for months or even years. About 1 in 3 or 4 women who have had it will have it again.

### Postpartum Psychosis (Rare)

This is a very serious condition. It can include:

- Thoughts of harming yourself or the baby
- Seeing or hearing things that are not there (hallucinations)
- Strange or confused behavior

If you or someone you know has these symptoms, get help right away.

## How to Prevent or Manage the Baby Blues

The baby blues are normal and usually go away in a few days. But you can help yourself feel better by:

- Resting as much as you can. Nap when your baby naps.
- Focusing on what matters most: caring for your baby and yourself.
- Not trying to do everything perfectly. It’s okay if your house is not spotless.
- Asking for help from your partner, family, or friends.
- Sharing baby care and housework with your partner.
- Talking to someone about how you feel—your partner, family, or friends.
- Getting dressed and showering every day.
- Going outside often—run errands, meet friends, or take a walk.
- Arranging for someone to watch the baby so you can have time alone or with your partner.
- Talking with other new moms about your feelings. You are not alone.
- Remembering that tiredness, trouble focusing, and doubts about being a mom are common. These feelings usually pass.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask you questions and check your symptoms. They may use a special questionnaire during your post-birth check-up.

If you are depressed, your doctor may do blood tests. This helps rule out other health problems, like a thyroid issue.

You should see your doctor if:

- You feel sad for more than two weeks
- You have trouble doing your usual activities
- You have thoughts about hurting yourself or your baby

Family and friends should talk to you if they notice changes in your mood. Encourage you to see a doctor.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment works best when it includes both therapy and medicine.

### Medicines

Two medicines are approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for postpartum depression:

- **Brexanolone**: Given through a vein (IV) in a hospital. It is given over several hours.
- **Zuranolone**: Taken by mouth as a pill.

Other antidepressants may also be used.

### Therapy

Talk therapy helps you understand your feelings. It teaches you how to cope with stress and change negative thoughts.

### Postpartum Psychosis Treatment

If you have postpartum psychosis, you may need to stay in the hospital. A special unit may allow your baby to stay with you. You may need antipsychotic medicine and antidepressants.

### Breastfeeding and Medicines

If you are breastfeeding, talk to your doctor before taking any medicine. Most antidepressants are safe to use while breastfeeding. Your doctor can help you choose a medicine that is safe for you and your baby.

# Problems with Blood Vessels in the Liver

The liver gets its blood from two sources.  
One source is the portal vein. It brings blood full of nutrients and some oxygen. This supplies about two-thirds of the liver’s blood.  
The other source is the hepatic artery. It brings blood that is very rich in oxygen. This supplies the rest of the liver’s blood.  

The hepatic veins carry blood away from the liver. They empty into a large vein called the inferior vena cava.  

When more blood flows through the portal vein, less blood flows through the hepatic artery. When less blood flows through the portal vein, more blood flows through the hepatic artery. This is called the hepatic arterial buffer response.  
This system helps protect the liver from damage if blood flow drops, especially in healthy people.

---

## How Blood Flows to and from the Liver

Even though the liver has two blood supplies, it can still be damaged by:

- Not enough blood flow  
- Poor drainage of blood out of the liver  
- Specific problems in the blood vessels  

---

### Not Enough Blood Flow (Ischemia)

Ischemia means the liver does not get enough blood.  
This can happen if blood flow drops, oxygen levels fall, or the liver is working too hard.  
It can be caused by any or all of these.  

- If the whole liver gets too little blood, it can cause ischemic hepatitis.  
- If only part of the liver gets too little blood, it can cause liver tissue death (hepatic infarction) or damage to the bile ducts (ischemic cholangiopathy).  
- Hepatic infarction is usually due to a problem in the hepatic artery.

---

### Poor Blood Drainage from the Liver

If blood cannot leave the liver properly, it can build up and cause damage.  
This can happen because of:

- A blockage in the veins  
- Heart problems, especially on the right side of the heart  

When the heart does not pump well, blood backs up in the liver. This is called congestive hepatopathy.

Blockages can happen in different places:

- In the large veins inside the liver or outside the liver (this is called Budd-Chiari syndrome)  
- In the tiny veins inside the liver (called terminal hepatic venules and sinusoids)  
- This condition is now called sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (formerly called veno-occlusive disease)  

Often, more than one area is blocked.  

The most common cause of widespread blockage inside the liver is cirrhosis.  

When blood cannot drain well, the liver becomes swollen.  
This causes:

- Swelling of the liver (hepatomegaly)  
- High pressure in the portal vein (portal hypertension)  
- Less blood flow through the portal vein  
- Fluid buildup in the belly (ascites)  
- Enlarged spleen (splenomegaly)  

The symptoms of a blockage in one small area depend on where it is.

---

### Specific Problems in Liver Blood Vessels

Problems can happen in the hepatic artery, hepatic vein, or portal vein.

#### Hepatic Artery Problems

- The artery can become blocked.  
- Rarely, a bulge can form in the artery wall. This is called an aneurysm.  
- In a condition called peliosis hepatis, blood-filled spaces form inside the liver’s tiny blood vessels. These spaces are like small cysts.

#### Hepatic Vein Problems

- These can cause blockages in the veins.  
- The blockage can be in one small area or spread across the liver.

#### Portal Vein Problems

- Almost all portal vein problems block blood flow through the portal vein.  
- This leads to high pressure in the portal vein (portal hypertension).  

Blockages can happen in two places:

**Outside the liver (extrahepatic):**  
- Portal vein thrombosis (a blood clot in the portal vein)  
- This can be caused by:  
  - A condition that makes blood more likely to clot  
  - Infection in the vein wall (like pylephlebitis or omphalitis)  
  - A nearby problem, such as pancreatitis or a tumor  
  - A birth defect where the portal vein is missing or too narrow  

**Inside the liver (intrahepatic):**  
- Small blood vessels in the liver can become blocked.  
- This can happen in:  
  - Schistosomiasis (a parasitic infection)  
  - Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC)  
  - Sarcoidosis (a condition that causes small lumps in organs)  
  - Noncirrhotic portal hypertension (high pressure in the portal vein without cirrhosis)

# Polypeptides

Polypeptides are a type of antibiotic. They help treat certain kinds of infections.

The main polypeptides are:
- Bacitracin
- Colistin (also called colistimethate, colistin, or polymyxin E)
- Polymyxin B

Most bacteria have a protective outer layer called a cell wall.  
Bacitracin stops bacteria from building this wall.  
Colistin and polymyxin B damage the membrane just under the wall in some bacteria.  
When the membrane is damaged, the bacteria die.

## How Polypeptides Are Used

**Bacitracin** is used mainly for mild skin infections caused by *Staphylococcus aureus*.  
It is applied directly to the skin.  
It is not given by injection.

**Colistin and polymyxin B** can harm the kidneys.  
They are only used for serious infections when other antibiotics do not work.  
They are given through a vein (by injection).  
In some cases, colistin can be inhaled using a special machine called a nebulizer.

## Common Uses and Side Effects

| Medication | Common Uses | Some Possible Side Effects |
|-----------|-------------|----------------------------|
| Bacitracin | Skin, ear, or eye infections | Can cause skin irritation or rash |
| Colistin | Serious infections that resist other antibiotics; sometimes used in the bladder | Can harm kidneys and nerves (when given by injection) |
| Polymyxin B | Serious infections that resist other antibiotics; sometimes used in the bladder | Can harm kidneys and nerves (when given by injection) |

Polypeptide antibiotics are usually applied to the skin, ears, or eyes.  
Colistin and polymyxin B are only given by injection when no safer options exist.  
Bacitracin is never given by injection.

## Use During Pregnancy and Breastfeeding

**Bacitracin** is applied to the skin.  
Very little of it gets into the bloodstream.  
So, it is thought to be safe for the baby during pregnancy and breastfeeding.  
But there is not enough proof to be certain.  
The same is true for polymyxin B and colistin when used on the skin.

**Polymyxin B and colistin** given by injection during pregnancy should only be used if the benefits of treatment are greater than the risks.  
In animal studies, polymyxin B did not harm the fetus.  
But no good studies have been done in pregnant women.  
In animal studies, colistin did harm the fetus.

It is not known if it is safe to use polymyxin B or colistin by injection while breastfeeding.

# What Are Inherited Disorders of Metabolism?

Most inherited disorders of metabolism are caused by changes in genes. These changes affect enzymes. Enzymes help the body break down food and make needed substances.

When enzymes do not work right, two problems can happen:

- Harmful substances build up in the body.
- The body does not make enough of the substances it needs.

There are hundreds of these disorders. Each one is rare on its own. But together, they are not uncommon.

Doctors group these disorders by the type of substance they affect. For example:

- Problems with amino acids (the building blocks of protein)
- Problems with carbohydrates (sugars and starches)
- Problems with fats (fatty acids)
- Problems with purines and pyrimidines (parts of DNA and RNA)

All states in the United States test every newborn for certain inherited metabolic disorders. This is called newborn screening. The tests look for:

- Phenylketonuria
- Tyrosinemia
- Biotinidase deficiency
- Homocystinuria
- Maple syrup urine disease
- Galactosemia

Many states also screen for more conditions. These include disorders of fatty acid breakdown and other organic acid problems.

For detailed information about each condition, see the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics’ newborn screening ACT sheets and algorithms.

This article does not cover metabolic disorders that mainly affect adults. It also does not cover disorders that affect just one organ, such as Wilson disease or congenital adrenal hyperplasia. It also does not cover common inherited conditions like cystic fibrosis or hemochromatosis. For inherited disorders of lipoprotein metabolism, see the table on Genetic (Primary) Dyslipidemias.
