# Joint Tumors

Tumors in joints are rare. They usually happen only if a tumor in the bone or soft tissue is close to a joint.

Two conditions can affect the lining of the joint:
- Synovial chondromatosis
- Tenosynovial giant cell tumor

Both of these are not cancer. But they can seriously damage the joint.

These conditions usually affect just one joint. The knee or hip is most often affected. They can cause pain and fluid to build up in the joint.

## How Doctors Diagnose These Conditions

Doctors use imaging tests to look at the joint. These include:
- X-rays
- Computed tomography (CT) scans
- Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)

To be sure of the diagnosis, doctors take a small sample of tissue from the joint lining. They look at it under a microscope. This is called a biopsy.

## Treatment for Both Conditions

The main treatment is surgery to remove the abnormal lining of the joint. This surgery is called a synovectomy.

---

## Tenosynovial Giant Cell Tumor

This condition causes the joint lining to swell and grow abnormally. The overgrown lining harms the cartilage and bone around the joint.

The lining also makes extra fluid. This fluid can cause pain and swelling. Sometimes the fluid is bloody. Over time, this can lead to arthritis.

This condition usually affects only one joint.

### Treatment

Surgery is the usual treatment. But the condition often comes back after surgery.

A medicine called pexidartinib can help slow the tumor’s growth. It is taken by mouth. It is only used if:
- Symptoms are very bad
- Surgery did not help

Pexidartinib is only available in the United States at cancer centers. It is part of a special program by the drug maker to manage risks.

This medicine can cause serious liver damage. In rare cases, it can be deadly.

---

## Synovial Chondromatosis

In this condition, cells in the joint lining change into cells that make cartilage. These cells form clumps of cartilage.

The clumps break off and float in the joint space. They are often as small as a grain of rice. These loose pieces can cause pain and swelling.

This condition rarely turns into cancer.

### Diagnosis

Doctors use imaging tests to find the problem. MRI is the best test because it can find the smallest loose pieces.

Larger pieces can be seen on X-rays or CT scans. This is because they harden into bone over time.

### Treatment

If symptoms are bad, doctors remove the loose pieces and the abnormal lining. This is done with surgery.

The condition often comes back after treatment. Surgery is the usual way to treat it.

# What Are Eosinophilic Lung Diseases?

Eosinophilic lung diseases are a group of conditions where a type of white blood cell called an eosinophil builds up in the lungs. These cells are normally rare in the lungs. When they increase, they can cause inflammation and damage.

Eosinophils are found in the tiny air sacs of the lungs, in the lung tissue, or both. Many people with these diseases also have high levels of eosinophils in their blood. This is called blood eosinophilia. It means more than 500 eosinophils per microliter of blood.

## Possible Causes

Some known causes include:

- Allergic reactions to a fungus called *Aspergillus* (allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis).
- Side effects from certain medicines, such as some antibiotics or the seizure drug phenytoin.
- Infections, especially from parasitic worms (helminths).
- Breathing in harmful substances, like cocaine or other illegal drugs.
- Other body-wide diseases, such as eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

In many cases, doctors do not know the exact cause.

## Two Main Types with Unknown Cause

The two most common types with no known cause are:

- Acute eosinophilic pneumonia – comes on quickly and can be serious.
- Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia – develops slowly and lasts for months or longer.

Another condition called hypereosinophilic syndrome affects many organs in the body. It is discussed in other medical resources.

Löffler syndrome is a condition where lung changes appear and disappear quickly. It is linked to high blood eosinophils.

## How Doctors Diagnose These Diseases

Doctors use several tools to make a diagnosis:

- A chest X-ray or a CT scan of the chest.
- Blood tests to check for high levels of eosinophils.
- A sample of fluid from the lungs (bronchoalveolar lavage) to look for eosinophils.
- A lung tissue sample (biopsy) if needed.

A diagnosis is made when:

- The chest scan shows cloudy or patchy areas in the lungs.
- Blood, lung fluid, or lung tissue has more than 500 eosinophils per microliter of blood.

But sometimes, the blood test is normal even if eosinophils are in the lungs. So a normal blood test does not rule out the disease.

## Important Facts About Eosinophils

- Eosinophils are very sensitive to steroid medicines (glucocorticoids).
- After taking steroids, eosinophils can disappear from the blood within hours.
- This can make it hard to diagnose the disease if steroids were taken before testing.

Eosinophils live mostly in tissues, not in the blood. They are hundreds of times more common in tissues than in blood.

They are most active in areas where the body meets the outside world, like the lungs, gut, and lower urinary tract.

Healthy lungs do not have eosinophils. So if they are found in lung tissue or in fluid from the lungs, it means something is wrong.

If more than 10% of the cells in lung fluid are eosinophils, this is a sign of disease.

When lung scans show cloudy areas and blood tests show high eosinophils, doctors may call it PIE syndrome. PIE stands for pulmonary infiltrates with eosinophilia.

# Exhibitionistic Disorder – Simple Explanation

## What Is Exhibitionism?

Some people feel strong sexual excitement when they show their private parts to others.  
This is called exhibitionism.  

When this behavior causes serious problems, it is called exhibitionistic disorder.  

Not everyone who has these thoughts or feelings has a disorder.  
A disorder is diagnosed only when the behavior causes distress or harm.

## When Is It a Disorder?

Doctors diagnose exhibitionistic disorder when:

- A person feels very upset or troubled by their urges.  
- The urges make it hard to work, keep relationships, or live a normal life.  
- The person acts on their urges with someone who did not agree to it.

## Who Is Affected?

- Most people with exhibitionistic urges are men.  
- Women with this behavior are rare.  
- The behavior usually starts in the teenage years.  
- It can also start earlier or later in life.  
- Many exhibitionists are married, but their marriages are often difficult.

## How Common Is It?

- About 2 to 4 out of every 100 men may have exhibitionistic disorder.  
- It is much less common in women.  
- About 3 out of every 10 men arrested for sex crimes are exhibitionists.  
- Between 20% and 50% of these men are arrested again later.

## What Happens During an Episode?

- The person usually shows their private parts to someone who did not expect it.  
- The person is often a woman or a child.  
- The goal is not to have sex.  
- The person wants to surprise, shock, or impress the other person.  
- Actual sex is almost never the goal.  
- This is not the same as rape.

## Other Forms of Exhibitionism

Some people want others to watch them during sex.  
But they only do this with people who agree.  
Examples include making adult films or working in adult entertainment.  

These people are usually not upset by their desires.  
They do not have a mental health problem.

## Why Do Some People Have This Disorder?

- Some exhibitionists also have other mental health issues.  
- These can include antisocial personality disorder or conduct disorder.  
- These conditions make it hard to follow rules or care about others.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor will ask questions and check symptoms.  
The diagnosis is based on standard mental health guidelines.

To be diagnosed, a person must:

- Have strong sexual urges to show their private parts or be watched during sex.  
- Have these urges for at least 6 months.  
- Feel very upset or have trouble in daily life because of them.  
- Or have acted on the urges with someone who did not agree.

The doctor will also note if the person is aroused by children or adults.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment usually starts after the person is arrested.  
It includes:

- Talking therapy (psychotherapy)  
- Support groups  
- Certain antidepressants

### Medications

- Doctors often use a type of antidepressant called SSRIs.  
- These help reduce strong urges and improve mood.

If SSRIs do not work, other medicines may be used.  
These medicines lower sex drive and reduce male hormones like testosterone.

Examples include:
- Leuprolide  
- Medroxyprogesterone acetate

Before using these medicines, the person must understand the risks and agree to use them.  
Doctors will check blood regularly to watch for side effects.  
Tests may include:
- Liver function tests  
- Bone density scans  
- Blood tests to check hormone levels

These checks help keep the person safe while on the medicine.

## Important Notes

- Showing private parts to strangers for sexual excitement is rare in women.  
- Women may show their bodies in other ways, like wearing tight or revealing clothes.  
- This is not a mental health problem.  
- It is not the same as exhibitionistic disorder.

- Most people with exhibitionistic urges do not have a disorder.  
- A disorder only exists when the behavior causes harm or distress.

# Prosthetic Joint Infection

A prosthetic joint can become infected. This can lead to serious illness, long-term problems, or even death.  
Infection may happen soon after surgery or months or years later.  
Symptoms include pain, swelling, and trouble moving the joint.  
Diagnosing the infection can be hard. It often takes several tests.  
Treatment usually includes long-term antibiotics and surgery to clean the joint.

---

## What Causes Prosthetic Joint Infection?

Infections are more common in artificial joints than in natural ones.  
Most infections happen when bacteria get into the joint during surgery.  
They can also come from other infections in the body, such as skin sores, lung infections, urinary tract infections, or infections from medical devices.  
In rare cases, infections can come from dental work or falls.

Most infections happen within the first year after surgery.  
In the first few months, the most common cause is a type of bacteria called *Staphylococcus aureus*.  
This bacteria causes about half of all early infections.  
Other causes include mixed bacteria, gram-negative bacteria, and anaerobic bacteria.  
A bacteria called *Cutibacterium acnes* often causes infections in shoulder joints.  
It can take up to two weeks of special testing to find this bacteria.  
Fungal infections like *Candida* can also affect prosthetic joints, but this is very rare.

---

## Who Is at Risk?

Some people are more likely to get an infection after joint surgery.  
These include people with:

- Weakened immune systems (from medicines like prednisone or biologic drugs)
- Rheumatoid arthritis
- Diabetes
- Cancer
- Kidney disease
- Obesity

Surgery-related risks include:

- Having had joint surgery before
- A past infection at the surgery site
- Long surgery time
- Problems after surgery, such as bleeding or wound opening
- Having *Staphylococcus aureus* in the blood after surgery

---

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on how long it has been since surgery.  
Doctors divide infections into three types: early, delayed, and late.

### Early Infection (within 3 months after surgery)
- Symptoms come on suddenly.
- The joint is painful, swollen, and red.
- You may have fever or chills.
- This type of infection usually comes from the surgery itself.

### Delayed Infection (3 to 12 months after surgery)
- There may be a wound that keeps draining fluid.
- The joint feels warm, swollen, and painful.
- This infection likely started during or right after surgery.

### Late Infection (more than 12 months after surgery)
- The joint suddenly becomes painful, tender, and red.
- The joint was working well before.
- This type of infection usually comes from another infection in the body, like a urinary tract infection or pneumonia.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

No single test can always confirm the infection.  
Doctors use a mix of tests to make a diagnosis.

### Key Tests:
- **Joint fluid test**: A needle is used to draw fluid from the joint.  
  This fluid is tested for white blood cells and bacteria.  
  In early infection, the white blood cell count is usually over 10,000 per microliter.  
  In delayed or late infection, it is usually over 3,000 per microliter.  
  A high number of a certain type of white blood cell (polymorphonuclear neutrophils) suggests infection.  
  A test called alpha-defensin can also help show infection.

- **Blood tests**:  
  C-reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and D-dimer may be high.

- **Imaging tests**:  
  X-rays may show loosening of the joint or bone changes.  
  But these changes are not always clear.  
  Bone scans and white blood cell scans can help find infection, but they are not always accurate right after surgery.

- **Tissue samples**:  
  Tissue around the joint can be tested during surgery for bacteria and signs of infection.

### Definitive Diagnosis:
- If two separate samples from the joint grow the same bacteria, it confirms infection.  
- If there is a visible track from the skin to the joint prosthesis, this also confirms infection.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment is long and complex. It usually includes surgery and antibiotics.

### Surgery Steps:
- The surgeon opens the joint and removes the artificial joint.
- All infected tissue, dead tissue, and old cement are cleaned out.
- The surgeon may place a temporary spacer made with antibiotics to keep the joint space open.
- A new joint is implanted later, usually 2 to 4 months after the first surgery.

### Antibiotics:
- Long-term antibiotics are needed in all cases.
- Treatment starts right after surgery, based on the bacteria found in the joint.
- Initial antibiotics cover common bacteria, including methicillin-resistant staph and gram-negative bacteria.
- The treatment plan is adjusted once test results are back.

### Special Case: *Staphylococcus aureus* Infection
- A 6-week course of strong antibiotics is used.
- Rifampin is added to help the medicine reach deep into the infection site (called biofilm).
- After the 6 weeks, treatment continues with rifampin and another oral antibiotic (like levofloxacin or ciprofloxacin) for:
  - 3 months if the joint is in the hip
  - 6 months if the joint is in the knee

### Success Rate:
- With proper treatment, about 80% of patients are infection-free after 5 years.

### Rare Cases:
- If the infection is severe and there is not enough healthy bone, the joint may be removed and the bones fused together.

---

## How Can It Be Prevented?

- Antibiotics before dental work are not usually needed unless you have other health risks.  
  Check with your doctor or the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons for guidelines.

- Antibiotics may be needed before certain urologic procedures (like kidney stone treatment) because they can cause bacteria in the blood.

- Some hospitals test for *Staphylococcus aureus* in the nose before surgery.  
  If the test is positive, patients use a special ointment (mupirocin) in the nose to remove the bacteria before surgery.

---

## Key Points

- Watch for a joint that is warm, red, swollen, or painful.  
  This is most likely to happen within the first year after surgery.

- If you have joint pain that does not go away, get a joint fluid test.  
  This is the most useful test.  
  X-rays and blood tests are not always helpful.

- Treatment must include surgery to clean the joint and long-term antibiotics.

- If the infection is caused by *Staphylococcus aureus*, add rifampin to the antibiotics to help fight the infection better.

# Low Calcium in the Blood (Hypocalcemia)

Calcium is a mineral your body needs to stay healthy. It helps your muscles, nerves, and heart work properly. Most of your calcium is stored in your bones. A small amount circulates in your blood.

When the amount of calcium in your blood drops too low, it is called hypocalcemia.

## What Causes Low Blood Calcium?

Low blood calcium can happen for many reasons. Some common causes include:

- Damage to the parathyroid glands during thyroid surgery.
- The body not responding to normal levels of parathyroid hormone.
- Being born without parathyroid glands (as in DiGeorge syndrome).
- Low levels of magnesium in the blood.
- Not getting enough vitamin D from food or sunlight.
- Kidney problems that cause too much calcium to leave the body in urine.
- Not eating enough calcium-rich foods.
- Digestive problems that stop the body from absorbing calcium.
- Pancreatitis (inflammation of the pancreas).
- Some medicines, such as:
  - Antibiotics like rifampin.
  - Seizure medicines like phenytoin and phenobarbital.
  - Bone-strengthening drugs like alendronate, ibandronate, risedronate, and zoledronic acid.
  - Calcitonin.
  - Chloroquine.
  - Steroids (also called glucocorticoids or corticosteroids).

## What Are the Symptoms?

Low calcium may not cause any symptoms at first. But over time, you might notice:

- Dry, scaly skin.
- Weak, brittle nails.
- Coarse or thinning hair.
- Muscle cramps, especially in the back and legs.
- Confusion or trouble remembering things.
- Feeling sad or depressed.
- Hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there).
- Tingling in the lips, fingers, or feet.
- Muscle aches and spasms.
- Tight or stiff muscles (tetany).
- Trouble breathing due to muscle spasms in the throat.
- Seizures.
- Irregular heartbeats.

These symptoms usually go away when calcium levels return to normal.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors often find low calcium during a routine blood test.

To check for hypocalcemia, they measure:

- Total calcium in the blood.
- Albumin (a protein in the blood).
- Kidney function.
- Magnesium levels.
- Phosphate levels.
- Parathyroid hormone levels.
- Vitamin D levels.

They may also test for other substances to find the cause.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause and how low your calcium level is.

- If your calcium is only slightly low, you may take calcium pills by mouth.
- If your calcium is very low or you have symptoms, you may get calcium through a vein (IV).
- Vitamin D supplements help your body absorb calcium better.
- If you have a condition like hypoparathyroidism, your doctor may give you a man-made form of parathyroid hormone.

If a medicine is causing the low calcium, your doctor may change your medicine.

Treating the underlying cause — such as fixing kidney problems or correcting vitamin D deficiency — can also help restore normal calcium levels.

# Hereditary Spastic Paraplegia

Hereditary spastic paraplegia is a group of rare genetic conditions.  
It causes increasing stiffness and weakness in the legs.  
The problem gets worse over time.  
Some people also have learning difficulties, seizures, or other health issues.

The condition runs in families.  
It is caused by changes in certain genes.  
Scientists have found more than 80 different gene changes linked to this condition.  
For many types, the exact gene change is still unknown.

In all forms, the nerve pathways from the brain to the spinal cord break down.  
The back part of the spinal cord and some other nerve pathways may also be affected.  
In some cases, the nerve cells in the front of the spinal cord are lost.

The condition can start at any age.  
It may begin in infancy or in older adulthood.  
It affects both men and women.

---

## Symptoms and Signs

The main symptoms are stiff and weak legs.  
Walking becomes harder over time.  
The legs may jerk when touched.  
The knee and ankle reflexes are very strong.  
The foot may point downward when the foot is tapped.  
Bladder problems are common.  
Urgent need to urinate is often one of the first signs.  
Feeling in the legs is usually normal.  
But some people may have trouble feeling vibrations in the feet.  
The arms are usually not affected.  
The symptoms are not limited to one part of the spine.

Some types cause other problems in the nervous system.  
These can include:  
- Trouble with balance and coordination  
- Vision problems  
- Movement issues not related to spasticity  
- Loss of vision  
- Eye damage  
- Hearing loss  
- Learning difficulties or memory problems  
- Seizures  
- Nerve damage in the arms and legs  
- Unusual body features such as a very large or small head, short height, or unusual facial shape

---

## How It Is Diagnosed

Doctors look at your medical history and do a physical exam.  
They may also do genetic testing.

A family history of similar symptoms is a clue.  
The doctor will check for signs of leg stiffness and weakness.  
They will rule out other possible causes.  
If the cause is unclear, genetic testing may help.  
Talking with a genetic counselor is a good idea.

---

## How It Is Treated

There is no cure.  
Treatment focuses on relieving symptoms.

Medicines can help reduce leg stiffness.  
Common choices include:  
- Baclofen  
- Tizanidine  
Other options are:  
- Diazepam  
- Clonazepam  
- Dantrolene  
- Botulinum toxin (types A or B)

For bladder problems, medicines like oxybutynin may help.

Physical therapy and regular exercise are important.  
They help keep you mobile.  
They improve muscle strength and flexibility.  
They reduce tiredness and help prevent muscle spasms.  
Some people find it helpful to use splints, a cane, or crutches.

---

## Key Facts

- In all types, the nerve pathways from the brain to the spine break down.  
- The back and side parts of the spinal cord may also be affected.  
- People have stiff legs and trouble walking.  
- Reflexes are very strong.  
- The foot points down when tapped.  
- Some types cause other nervous system problems.  
- Think about hereditary spastic paraplegia if you have a family history and leg stiffness.  
- Rule out other causes.  
- If the diagnosis is unclear, consider genetic testing.  
- Treat symptoms.  
- Use medicines like baclofen or tizanidine for stiffness.  
- Use physical therapy to stay active and strong.

# Dissociative Identity Disorder

This condition used to be called multiple personality disorder.  
It means that one person has two or more separate identities.  
These identities take turns being in control of the person’s thoughts, feelings, and actions.  

Each identity may speak, act, or feel differently from the others.  
The person may not remember things that most people would easily recall.  
This includes everyday events, personal details, or past trauma.  

## What Causes This Disorder?

Most people with this disorder had very stressful or traumatic experiences as children.  
Between 70% and 100% of people with this disorder were physically, sexually, or emotionally abused.  
Some were neglected.  
Others had a major loss, like the death of a parent, or faced serious illness or stress.  

As children grow, they learn to combine all their experiences into one clear sense of self.  
But if a child is abused by a parent or caregiver, this process can break down.  
The child may separate painful memories, feelings, and thoughts into different parts of themselves.  

When caregivers are unpredictable—sometimes kind, sometimes cruel—this can make the child feel betrayed.  
This is called betrayal trauma.  
It can make it harder for the child to trust or feel safe.  

To cope, the child may mentally escape.  
They may “leave” their body or mind to avoid pain.  
Each time this happens, a new identity may form.  

But if a child is protected and comforted by caring adults, this disorder is less likely to develop.  

Brain research shows that people with this disorder often have a smaller hippocampus.  
This is a part of the brain that helps store and recall memories.  
High levels of stress hormones like cortisol from trauma may cause this change.  

## What Are the Symptoms?

This disorder lasts a long time.  
It can make life very hard, but many people still live full, creative, and productive lives.  

### In the Possession Form:
- Others can see that the person is acting very differently.  
- The person may speak or behave as if someone else is inside them.  
- Their voice, mood, or behavior changes suddenly and clearly.  

### In the Nonpossession Form:
- Others may not notice the change right away.  
- The person may feel disconnected from themselves.  
- They may feel like they are watching themselves from outside.  
- They may think, feel, speak, or act in ways they do not control.  
- Their likes and dislikes—like food, clothes, or hobbies—may change suddenly.  

Some people feel their body is not their own.  
They may feel like a child or like someone of the opposite sex.  
They may talk about themselves using “we” or “he,” “she,” or “they.”  

Some identities know things that others do not.  
Some identities can see and talk to each other inside the mind.  
For example, one identity may know what another one is doing.  
But the other identity may not know the first one exists.  

This can make life confusing.  
People may not know what their other identities are doing.  
They may not remember their own actions.  

Because the identities talk to each other, people may hear voices.  
These voices may be part of an inner conversation.  
Or they may speak directly to the person.  
Sometimes more than one voice speaks at once.  
This can be very confusing.  

The identities may also break into daily life.  
For example, at work, an angry identity might suddenly shout at a coworker.  

### Memory Problems:
- People may not remember parts of their childhood or teenage years.  
- They may forget simple daily tasks, like how to use a computer.  
- They may find things they did but have no memory of doing.  
- They may wake up in a place they do not remember going to.  
- They may find strange handwriting or objects they do not recognize.  
- They may be told they said or did things they cannot remember.  

People with this disorder often have other symptoms.  
These can look like symptoms of other mental health problems or physical illnesses.  
For example:  
- They may have frequent headaches or body pain.  
- They may feel sad, anxious, or hopeless.  
- They may hurt themselves on purpose.  
- They may use drugs or alcohol to cope.  
- They may think about or try to end their life.  
- They may have trouble with sex.  

Many people with this disorder have been abused.  
They may go back to dangerous situations or stay in them.  
They are at risk of being hurt again.  

They may also have other types of hallucinations.  
They may see, feel, smell, or taste things that are not there.  
These often happen during flashbacks.  
This can make doctors think the person has a psychotic disorder like schizophrenia.  

But there is a key difference:  
- People with dissociative identity disorder feel the voices or sensations come from inside their head.  
- They may feel like another identity is using their body.  
- People with schizophrenia usually believe the voices come from outside.  

Most people try to hide their symptoms.  
They may feel ashamed or afraid of being judged.  

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose this disorder based on a person’s history and symptoms.  

To be diagnosed, a person must:  
- Have two or more identities that take turns being in control.  
- Have memory gaps for everyday events, personal details, or trauma.  
- Feel very upset by these symptoms.  
- Have trouble functioning at work, school, or in relationships.  

Doctors do a full mental health interview.  
They use special questionnaires to check for this disorder.  
They also rule out other mental health problems.  

A physical exam and blood tests may be done.  
This helps rule out medical conditions that could cause similar symptoms.  

Sometimes, doctors use hypnosis or a calming medicine through a vein.  
This helps the person relax and talk more openly.  
It can help bring out hidden identities or memories.  

People may be asked to keep a journal between visits.  
This helps doctors see patterns and track changes.  

Doctors may also try to talk to other identities.  
They may ask the person to speak to the part of the mind that did something they do not remember.  

Doctors can usually tell if the disorder is real.  
People who fake it often:  
- Focus only on well-known symptoms.  
- Create identities that sound like movie characters.  
- Seem to enjoy having the disorder.  

People with real dissociative identity disorder usually want to hide it.  
Doctors can check for lies by comparing stories from different sources.  

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment has three main parts:  
- Support and care  
- Psychotherapy (talk therapy)  
- Sometimes, hypnosis or guided imagery  

The main goal is to help the different identities work together.  
In some cases, the goal is to merge them into one identity.  
But this is not always possible.  
If not, the goal is to help the identities live together in peace.  

Medicines can help with other problems like anxiety or depression.  
But medicines do not treat the core disorder.  

### Psychotherapy is the main treatment.  
It is long and hard.  
It can bring up painful memories and emotions.  
People may have emotional breakdowns during therapy.  

Some people need to stay in the hospital for a while.  
This gives them safety and support during tough times.  
It helps them face painful memories.  

Good therapy includes:  
- Helping the person calm strong emotions.  
- Building trust between the different identities.  
- Working through past trauma.  
- Protecting the person from further harm.  
- Building a strong, safe relationship with the therapist.  

Many people with this disorder can be hypnotized easily.  
Therapists may use hypnosis to help them:  
- Calm down.  
- See past events in a new way.  
- Slowly face painful memories.  
- Talk to other identities.  
- Control when identities switch.  

## What Is the Outlook?

This disorder does not go away on its own.  
Some symptoms may come and go, but the condition stays.  

Recovery depends on:  
- How severe the symptoms are.  
- How long and how good the treatment is.  

People who have other serious mental health problems do worse.  
Those who struggle to live a normal life or still feel attached to their abusers also do worse.  
They may need longer treatment, and it may be less effective.

# Metabolic Alkalosis – Simple Explanation

Metabolic alkalosis means your blood has too much bicarbonate. This makes your blood more alkaline than normal. It can happen when you lose acid from your body or take in too much base. It can also happen if your kidneys keep too much bicarbonate instead of getting rid of it.

This condition often happens with low levels of potassium in your blood. It can also be linked to low blood volume or certain kidney problems.

---

## What Causes Metabolic Alkalosis?

The most common causes are:

- **Vomiting for a long time** – This removes acid from your stomach.
- **Using diuretics (water pills)** – These increase urine output and can cause loss of important salts.
- **Low blood volume (hypovolemia)** – This can happen from dehydration or blood loss.
- **Low potassium levels (hypokalemia)** – This can both cause and result from alkalosis.

Your kidneys must keep holding on to bicarbonate for the alkalosis to continue. If your kidneys were working normally, they would get rid of extra bicarbonate.

Other causes include:

- Taking too much calcium or bicarbonate (like in some antacids).
- After a period of low oxygen (like in severe lung disease).
- After recovering from a serious acid buildup in the body.
- Losing salt and water through sweat (common in people with cystic fibrosis).
- Losing stomach acid through vomiting or a tube in the nose.
- Rare kidney diseases like Bartter syndrome or Gitelman syndrome.
- Too much aldosterone (a hormone that affects salt and water balance).
- Using licorice or products with licorice extract.
- Using certain antibiotics.
- Using laxatives too much.
- Rebuilding your body after starvation.

---

## Types of Metabolic Alkalosis

There are two main types:

### 1. Chloride-Responsive Alkalosis
- Happens when you lose chloride (a type of salt) from your body.
- Common causes: Vomiting, diuretics, or sweat loss.
- This type often gets better with IV fluids that contain salt (sodium chloride).
- The kidneys start to release bicarbonate again when chloride levels go back to normal.

### 2. Chloride-Unresponsive Alkalosis
- Happens when your body makes too much aldosterone or has other hormone problems.
- Often linked to low potassium and low magnesium.
- This type does **not** get better with salt fluids alone.
- You usually need to fix the potassium and magnesium levels and treat the root cause.

Sometimes both types happen at the same time. For example, someone on high-dose diuretics may have low potassium and low chloride, but also have volume overload.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Mild cases may not cause any symptoms. Symptoms usually appear when the condition is more serious.

Symptoms can include:

- Headache
- Feeling tired or weak
- Muscle cramps or spasms (tetany)
- Confusion or trouble thinking clearly
- Seizures (in rare cases)

Low potassium can cause muscle weakness. Low calcium in the blood (due to alkalosis) can make nerves and muscles overreact.

These imbalances can also make heart problems worse, such as chest pain or irregular heartbeats.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose metabolic alkalosis using:

- **Arterial blood gas test** – This measures the pH and bicarbonate levels in your blood.
- **Blood tests for electrolytes** – These check levels of sodium, potassium, chloride, calcium, and magnesium.

Your doctor will also look at your medical history and do a physical exam.

To find the cause, your doctor may test your urine:

- If your urine has **low chloride**, it suggests chloride-responsive alkalosis (like from vomiting or diuretics).
- If your urine has **high chloride**, it suggests chloride-unresponsive alkalosis (like from hormone problems).

Your doctor may also check:

- Urine potassium levels
- Whether you have high blood pressure

These help decide if the cause is related to hormones, kidney disease, or other conditions.

---

## How Is It Treated?

The main goal is to treat the underlying cause.

### For Chloride-Responsive Alkalosis:
- Give IV fluids with salt (0.9% saline).
- The fluid helps replace lost salt and water.
- The kidneys start to release bicarbonate again.
- The rate of fluid is adjusted based on how much you are losing in urine and sweat.

### For Chloride-Unresponsive Alkalosis:
- Treat the root cause (like hormone problems or kidney disease).
- Give potassium and magnesium supplements.
- Use special diuretics that do not remove potassium.
- Do not rely only on fluids with salt.

### For Severe Cases (pH over 7.6):
- If the blood is very alkaline, faster treatment is needed.
- Hemodialysis (a type of kidney machine) may be used if you have kidney failure or too much fluid.
- Acetazolamide (a medicine) can help your kidneys get rid of bicarbonate.
  - It can also cause loss of potassium and phosphate, so your levels must be watched.
- In rare cases, hydrochloric acid may be given through a central IV line.
  - This is only used if dialysis is not possible.
  - It must be given carefully and with close monitoring.

---

## Key Points to Remember

- Metabolic alkalosis means your blood has too much bicarbonate.
- It often happens from losing acid (like from vomiting) or using diuretics.
- Low potassium and low blood volume are common triggers.
- The kidneys must keep holding on to bicarbonate for the condition to last.
- There are two types: chloride-responsive and chloride-unresponsive.
- Chloride-responsive alkalosis often gets better with IV salt fluids.
- Chloride-unresponsive alkalosis needs treatment of the root cause and often potassium/magnesium supplements.
- Always treat the underlying condition, not just the alkalosis.
- Severe cases may need special medicines or dialysis.

If you have symptoms like confusion, muscle cramps, or heart issues, see a doctor right away.

# Narcissistic Personality Disorder – Simple Explanation

This is a mental health condition. It affects how a person thinks, feels, and relates to others.

## What It Means

People with this condition often feel they are better than others. They need constant praise. They struggle to understand how others feel.

They may:
- Think they are more talented or important than they really are.
- Talk about their achievements in a big way.
- Put down others to feel better about themselves.

## How It Shows Up

People with this condition:
- Want to be admired all the time.
- Believe they deserve special treatment.
- Try to get ahead by using others.
- Have a hard time seeing things from another person’s point of view.
- Feel jealous when others succeed.
- Act proud or dismissive toward others.

They often dream about being famous, powerful, or loved in a perfect way. They want to be around only people they see as “special” or “great.”

Their self-worth depends on what others think of them. This makes their self-esteem very fragile. They pay close attention to how people react to them.

They do not handle criticism well. Even small criticism can make them feel hurt, angry, or defeated. They may:
- Get angry or act mean.
- Fight back hard.
- Pull away or pretend to agree, just to protect their image.

They may avoid situations where they might fail.

## How Common Is It?

About 2 out of every 100 people have this condition. It is more common in men than in women.

## Other Conditions Often Seen With It

Many people with this condition also have other mental health issues, such as:
- Depression
- Anorexia nervosa (a serious eating disorder)
- Substance use problems (especially with cocaine)
- Another personality disorder, such as histrionic, borderline, antisocial, or paranoid

## What Causes It?

No single cause is known. Experts believe both genes and life experiences play a role.

One idea is that early childhood experiences matter. For example:
- A child may have been praised too much for small things.
- Or the child may have been criticized harshly or ignored.
- This can make it hard to build a strong sense of self.

Some people with this condition have real talents. They grow up used to getting praise. So they link their self-worth to being admired.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor or mental health professional makes the diagnosis.

They use a standard guide called the *Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders*, 5th edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR).

To be diagnosed, a person must show at least five of these signs:
- They think they are more important or talented than they really are.
- They spend a lot of time dreaming about being powerful, famous, or perfect.
- They believe they are special and should only be around other “top” people.
- They need constant admiration.
- They feel they deserve special treatment.
- They take advantage of others to get what they want.
- They have trouble understanding how others feel.
- They are jealous of others and think others are jealous of them.
- They act proud, arrogant, or look down on others.

These patterns must have started in early adulthood.

## How Is It Treated?

The main treatment is talk therapy (psychotherapy).

### Types of Therapy That Can Help

**Psychodynamic therapy**  
This helps people understand deep feelings and past experiences that affect their thoughts and actions.

**Mentalization-based treatment**  
This helps people think about:
- What they are feeling and why.
- What others might be feeling and why.

**Transference-focused psychotherapy**  
This focuses on how the person relates to the therapist. It helps them see how they act with others in real life.

**Cognitive-behavioral therapy**  
This helps people change unhelpful thoughts and behaviors.  
Some people with this condition respond well to this type of therapy, especially if they are motivated by the desire to be praised.

## Key Points

- This condition is not about being confident or proud.
- It is about deep patterns of thinking and feeling that cause problems in life.
- Therapy can help, but it takes time and effort.
- Support from a trusted therapist is important.
- Recovery is possible with the right help.

# Paranoid Personality Disorder (PPD)

This condition is marked by a long-term pattern of distrust and suspicion toward others. People with this disorder often believe others mean them harm, even when there is no real reason to think so.

Diagnosis is based on specific symptoms and how they affect daily life. Treatment usually involves talk therapy and sometimes medicine.

> *Note: This overview is part of a larger guide on personality disorders.*

---

## What It Feels Like

People with paranoid personality disorder do not trust others. They believe others want to hurt, trick, or take advantage of them — even when there is no proof.

They often feel like they are being attacked, even when no attack happens. They keep believing their fears, even if there is little or no evidence.

They may think others have deeply wronged them in the past. They stay alert for any sign of insult, disrespect, or betrayal. They look for hidden meanings in what people say or do.

For example, they might see a kind offer as a sign that they are not capable of doing something on their own.

If they feel hurt or insulted, they do not forgive easily. They often respond with anger or try to fight back. Because they do not trust others, they want to be independent and in control.

They avoid sharing personal thoughts with others. They fear that secrets will be used against them. They doubt the loyalty of friends. They may question their partner’s actions and motives constantly. They can be very jealous.

These beliefs make it hard to build close relationships. When people react negatively, they see it as proof that their fears are true.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors use a guide called the *Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders*, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR).

To be diagnosed, a person must show a long-term pattern of distrust and suspicion. They must have at least four of the following signs:

- They suspect others are trying to harm, cheat, or use them — even without good reason.
- They constantly doubt whether friends or coworkers are honest or reliable.
- They avoid sharing personal information because they fear it will be used against them.
- They see bad or threatening meaning in harmless comments or events.
- They hold onto grudges after being insulted, hurt, or slighted.
- They quickly feel attacked or insulted and react with anger or retaliation.
- They often suspect their partner is being unfaithful — even without proof.

These symptoms must have started in early adulthood.

---

## How It Is Treated

Treatment focuses on talk therapy and, sometimes, medicine.

### Talk Therapy (Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy)

This type of therapy helps people understand their thoughts and beliefs. It teaches them to question their suspicions and respond in healthier ways.

Building trust with the therapist is hard. But if the therapist shows they understand the person’s fears, even a little, it can help build a stronger connection.

This connection can help the person take part in therapy or agree to take medicine.

### Medicine

No medicine is proven to cure this disorder.

But some medicines may help with specific symptoms:

- Antidepressants can help with sadness or low mood.
- Atypical antipsychotics may reduce anxiety and fear.

These medicines are not a cure. They are used only when needed and under close care.

There are no strong studies showing that these medicines work well for this condition. But some people find them helpful for managing symptoms.

---

## Important Notes

- This disorder often happens with other mental health problems.
- Common co-occurring conditions include:
  - Schizophrenia
  - Anxiety disorders (like fear of social situations)
  - Posttraumatic stress disorder
  - Alcohol problems
  - Other personality disorders (like borderline personality disorder)

- The condition is more common in men than women.
- It may run in families.
- Childhood abuse — emotional or physical — may increase the risk.

---

## Summary

Paranoid personality disorder means a person constantly fears others mean them harm. They struggle to trust, form close bonds, or feel safe.

Treatment is possible. Therapy helps people learn to manage their fears. Medicine may help with anxiety or mood issues.

The key is building a strong, respectful relationship with a trusted professional. This can open the door to healing.

# Eye Problems at Birth

Some babies are born with eyes that are missing, not fully formed, or shaped differently than normal.

These problems are called birth defects. They happen before a baby is born. The word "congenital" means "present at birth."

## Types of Eye Birth Defects

- **Hypertelorism**: Eyes that are too far apart. This can happen with other birth defects that occur together.
- **Hypotelorism**: Eyes that are too close together.
- **Coloboma**: A missing piece of tissue in the eye. This can affect the eyelid, colored part of the eye, retina, or the nerve that sends vision to the brain. It can happen in one or both eyes.
- **Microphthalmia**: One or both eyes are smaller than normal.
- **Anophthalmia**: One or both eyes are completely missing. This can happen with more than 50 different birth defect conditions.

Some of these eye problems are caused by changes in genes. Others can be caused by the mother using certain medicines, alcohol, or illegal drugs during pregnancy. Infections during pregnancy can also play a role.

A child with an eye birth defect often has other birth defects. These may affect the face or the brain.

## Photos of Eye Birth Defects

**Hypertelorism**  
The eyes are too far apart. This person also has a small upper jaw.

**Coloboma**  
The eyes have a gap in the colored part. The pupils are large and reach down to the bottom of the colored part.

**Microphthalmia**  
Both eyes are small. The left eye is smaller than the right.

**Anophthalmia**  
One eye is missing. The ear on that side is shaped differently. The right side of the face is smaller than the left.

## How Doctors Diagnose Eye Birth Defects

Before birth:  
- Doctors can sometimes see eye problems during an ultrasound scan.  
- A blood test may be done to check the baby’s DNA.  
- Amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling can be used to get a sample of the baby’s DNA for testing.

After birth:  
- A doctor checks the baby’s eyes during a physical exam.  
- A geneticist may be involved. This is a doctor who studies genes and how traits pass from parents to children.  
- A blood test can check for gene or chromosome problems.  
- This testing helps find the cause. It can also rule out other possible causes.  
- If a genetic condition is found, families can get genetic counseling to learn more.

## How Doctors Treat Eye Birth Defects

- Surgery is the main treatment.  
- A pediatric ophthalmologist should examine the child. This is a doctor who treats eye problems in children.  
- Doctors use different types of surgery to help correct the eye shape or position.  
- The goal is to improve how the eyes look and work.

# Problems with Sperm

Sperm problems can mean there are too few sperm, no sperm at all, or sperm that do not work well. These problems can happen in how sperm are made or how they are released.

Doctors check for sperm problems with a semen test and sometimes genetic tests.

The best treatment for most men is a type of fertility treatment called in vitro fertilization with intracytoplasmic sperm injection.

(See also: Overview of Infertility.)

---

## How Sperm Are Made

Sperm are made all the time. It takes about 72 to 74 days for a sperm cell to fully grow.

The body makes sperm best at a temperature of 34 degrees Celsius. This is slightly cooler than normal body temperature.

Inside the testicles, special cells called Sertoli cells help sperm grow. Other cells called Leydig cells make testosterone, which is needed for sperm production.

The seminal vesicles make a sugar called fructose. This sugar helps sperm get energy. The fructose is released into the semen through the tubes that carry sperm.

---

## What Can Go Wrong with Sperm

Sperm problems can cause:

- Too few sperm (called oligozoospermia)
- No sperm at all (called azoospermia)
- Sperm that do not move well
- Sperm with unusual shapes

---

## What Causes Sperm Problems

Sperm problems can come from many causes. These include:

- Injuries or infections in the testicles or reproductive system
- Hormone imbalances
- Genetic conditions
- Certain medicines or lifestyle habits like smoking or heavy drinking
- Exposure to heat, radiation, or toxins

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Sperm Problems

Doctors start with a semen analysis. This test checks how many sperm are in the semen and how well they move.

Sometimes, doctors also do genetic testing to look for inherited causes.

When a couple cannot get pregnant, the man should always be tested for sperm problems.

The doctor will ask about past health issues. They will check the size of each testicle. Normal size is 20 to 25 milliliters.

A semen sample is needed for testing. The man must give a sample after 2 to 5 days of no sex.

---

## How Sperm Problems Are Treated

If there is an infection, the doctor will give antibiotics.

If there is a hormone imbalance, the doctor may treat it.

For men with low sperm counts (10 to 20 million per milliliter) and no hormone problems, the medicine clomiphene citrate may help.

- Clomiphene is taken as a pill once a day.
- It is taken for 25 days each month.
- The treatment lasts 3 to 4 months.

Clomiphene may help increase sperm count. But it is not clear if it helps sperm move better or have a normal shape. There is no proof it increases the chance of pregnancy.

If sperm count is below 10 million per milliliter, or if clomiphene does not work, the best treatment is usually in vitro fertilization with intracytoplasmic sperm injection.

- In this treatment, a single sperm is injected directly into a single egg.
- The fertilized egg is then placed in the woman’s womb.
- This method works well even when sperm counts are very low.

Today, doctors rarely do special tests to see if sperm can enter an egg. This is because intracytoplasmic sperm injection is so effective.

Another option is intrauterine insemination.

- The man’s sperm is cleaned and prepared.
- The prepared sperm is placed directly into the woman’s womb.
- This is done at the time of ovulation.

Pregnancy often happens within six treatment cycles. But this method is only partly effective.

Even with low sperm numbers or poor sperm quality, pregnancy is still possible.

To improve chances, doctors may:

- Help the woman’s ovaries release more eggs (called controlled ovarian stimulation)
- Use artificial insemination
- Use in vitro fertilization or intracytoplasmic sperm injection

Specialists can often get sperm from the testicles using a simple surgery. This is useful for men who have no sperm in their semen.

If a man cannot make enough healthy sperm, a couple may choose to use donor sperm.

- Donor sperm is frozen for at least 6 months.
- After that, the donor is tested again for infections.
- This lowers the risk of passing on diseases like HIV or other sexually transmitted infections.

In the United States, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says:

- If a donor has had Zika virus, or has lived in or traveled to an area with Zika, they must wait 3 months before giving sperm.

---

## Key Points

- Problems making sperm or problems releasing sperm can lead to low sperm count or poor sperm quality.
- Doctors start with a semen test. They may also do genetic testing.
- Treatments include fixing underlying health issues, using clomiphene citrate, or using in vitro fertilization with intracytoplasmic sperm injection.

# Intimacy and Older Adults

Intimacy means feeling close to another person.  
It comes from knowing someone well and sharing time together.  
Intimacy can be emotional, social, or physical.  
Physical intimacy includes touching, hugging, kissing, and sex.

You do not lose the need for closeness as you get older.  
There is no age when being close to someone is wrong or inappropriate.  
But health problems and changes that come with aging can make it harder to be intimate.  
Aging can also change how you show closeness.

Some reasons why physical intimacy may fade include:

- **Losing a partner**  
  This is the most common reason older adults lose intimacy.  
  When a partner dies or is no longer around, it can be hard to start a new close relationship.

- **Health problems**  
  Many health issues become more common with age.  
  These can make physical closeness harder.  
  For example, poor blood flow or diabetes can cause trouble getting or keeping an erection.  
  Arthritis can make movement painful and hard.  
  Pain, medicine side effects, and worry about health can reduce interest in sex.  
  Memory problems or dementia can make it hard to understand or agree to intimacy.  
  Caring for a partner can also be stressful.  
  This stress can make it hard to feel close.

- **Medicines**  
  Older adults often take medicines for high blood pressure or brain health.  
  Some of these medicines can cause side effects like less interest in sex or trouble with erections.

- **Body changes from aging**  
  Hormone levels drop with age.  
  This can make sex uncomfortable or harder.  
  The inside of the vagina may become thinner and drier.  
  Men may feel less interest in sex because of lower testosterone.

- **Not talking about changes**  
  Some older adults feel shy or embarrassed about body changes.  
  They may not want to talk about wrinkles, sagging skin, or other changes.  
  They may also avoid talking to their partner or doctor about problems with intimacy.

- **Different expectations**  
  One partner may want to be close in a physical way.  
  The other may not.  
  This difference can cause tension.

- **Lack of privacy**  
  People who live with family or in care homes may not have private space.  
  Privacy is needed for physical intimacy.

- **Choosing other ways to be close**  
  After many years together, couples often change how they show love.  
  They may not have sex as often.  
  Some stop altogether.  
  But many couples naturally turn to other ways to stay close.  
  These include holding hands, hugging, kissing, giving massages, or saying kind words.

Even so, many older adults still enjoy a good sex life.  
Being close to someone can help prevent sadness and loneliness.  
It can also boost confidence and improve physical health.

If an older adult has a new sex partner, they should use protection.  
More older adults are getting sexually transmitted infections.  
This includes HIV.  
These infections can happen at any age.  
Protection is important for everyone.

# Sleep Problems in Children

Most children have sleep issues from time to time. These problems usually go away on their own and do not need treatment.

(See also: Overview of Behavioral Problems in Children.)

---

## Normal Sleep

By six months old, about two out of every three babies can sleep through the night without waking up.

As children grow, they may wake up at night. This often happens when they are sick or when their daily routine changes.

As children get older, their sleep becomes more complex. They spend more time in a type of sleep called REM sleep. This is the stage where dreams happen.

At the start of the night, children spend more time in deep, quiet sleep. Later in the night, they spend more time in REM sleep.

This means that some sleep problems happen early in the night, while others happen later.

Knowing if a problem is due to sleep or to being awake helps doctors decide how to help.

Some children who have sleep issues in early childhood may later develop headaches like migraines.

If a child sleeps in the same bed as a parent or caregiver, it is important to ask if the parent sees this as a problem. Different families have different ideas about how children should sleep.

The American Academy of Pediatrics says babies should sleep in the same room as their parents, but not in the same bed. This may lower the risk of sudden unexpected infant death.

---

## Nightmares

Nightmares are scary dreams that happen during REM sleep.

A child who has a nightmare may wake up completely. They can remember the dream clearly.

Nightmares are not usually a sign of a serious problem. But if they happen often, they may need attention.

Nightmares can happen more often when a child is stressed. They can also happen after watching a scary movie or TV show.

If nightmares happen often, parents can keep a diary. They can write down what the child did during the day, especially close to bedtime. This may help find a cause.

---

## Night Terrors and Sleepwalking

Night terrors happen during deep, non-REM sleep. They usually happen in the first few hours after a child falls asleep.

They are most common in children between the ages of 3 and 8.

During a night terror, a child may scream. They may look very scared. Their heart beats fast and they breathe quickly.

The child does not notice their parents. They may move around wildly. They do not respond to comfort.

They may talk, but they cannot answer questions. After a few minutes, they usually fall back to sleep.

The child will not remember the event later. This is different from nightmares.

Night terrors can be very upsetting because the child seems to be in great distress.

About one in three children who have night terrors also sleepwalk. Sleepwalking means getting out of bed and walking around while still asleep.

About 13 out of every 100 children have at least one sleepwalking episode. The most common age is around 10.

Night terrors and sleepwalking usually stop on their own. Some children may have them for years.

Most children do not need treatment. But if the problem continues into teenage years or adulthood, or if it is very severe, treatment may be needed.

For some children, medicine like a sedative or certain antidepressants may help with night terrors.

There is some evidence that children with leg movements during sleep may improve with iron supplements. This is true even if they do not have low iron levels.

If a child snores and moves around a lot while sleeping, a doctor should check for sleep apnea.

---

## Resistance to Going to Bed

Children between 1 and 2 years old often resist bedtime. This is usually because they feel anxious when separated from their parents.

Older children may resist bedtime to feel in control of their environment.

Young children may cry when left alone in bed. They may get out of bed and go to find their parents.

Another common reason for bedtime resistance is a late bedtime. If a child stays up late and sleeps late for several nights, their body clock shifts. This makes it harder to fall asleep at the usual time.

To fix this, parents should move bedtime a few minutes earlier each night. This helps reset the body clock.

If needed, a short-term use of a nonprescription sleep aid like melatonin or an antihistamine can help.

Staying in the room for a long time to comfort the child can make bedtime resistance worse. So can taking the child out of bed.

These actions teach the child that they can get attention by waking up.

To help, a parent can sit quietly in the hallway where the child can see them. The parent stays there until the child stays in bed.

This helps the child learn to fall asleep on their own. They also learn that getting out of bed is not allowed.

The parent will not read more stories or play games. But they are still nearby.

Over time, the child calms down and falls asleep.

Giving the child a special object like a stuffed animal can help. A small night-light or white noise machine can also be comforting.

Some parents use a “sleep pass.” The child can turn it in once to get out of bed.

If a child is used to falling asleep while touching a parent, the parent can slowly reduce contact. Start by holding the child fully. Then move to just touching a hand. Then sit next to the bed. Then stay in the room for longer periods.

Once the child is used to falling asleep with a parent nearby, the parent can leave the room for longer and longer.

---

## Waking Up During the Night

Everyone wakes up several times each night. Most people fall back to sleep without help.

Children may wake up often after a move, illness, or stressful event.

Long afternoon naps or playing too much before bed can make sleep problems worse.

Letting a child sleep with parents after waking up can make the problem worse.

Playing with the child, feeding them, or scolding them at night also makes things worse.

The best way is to gently return the child to bed. A simple “It is okay” or “You are safe” is often enough.

A bedtime routine helps. This can include reading a short story, holding a favorite toy or blanket, and using a small night-light (for children over 3 years old).

To help the child stay asleep, the sleep environment should be the same as when they fell asleep.

Parents should keep the same routine every night. This helps the child know what to expect.

If the child is healthy, letting them cry for a few minutes may help them calm down and fall back to sleep.

But if crying goes on for too long, parents may feel the need to give in. This can undo progress.

Some parents of children aged 3 to 10 use a red light/green light clock. The green light means it is okay to stay in bed. The red light means it is not time to get up.

---

## Other Sleep Issues

Some children have restless legs. This means their legs feel uncomfortable and they want to move them. This can disturb sleep.

A few children who move around a lot and snore may have sleep apnea. This is when breathing is blocked during sleep.

Children with restless legs may benefit from iron supplements, even if they do not have low iron levels.

If a child snores and moves around a lot while sleeping, a doctor should check for sleep apnea.

# Common Health Issues in Newborns

Newborns can have health problems that start:

- Before birth, while the baby is still growing in the womb  
- During labor and delivery  
- After birth  

About 1 in 10 newborns need special care after birth. This can happen because the baby was born too early, had trouble adjusting to life outside the womb, had low blood sugar, struggled to breathe, had an infection, or had another health issue. Special care is often given in a **neonatal intensive care unit**, or NICU.

---

## How Old Was the Baby at Birth?

Doctors measure how old a baby is by counting the weeks of pregnancy. This is called **gestational age**. A baby’s gestational age tells us how developed the baby was at birth.

Doctors figure out the gestational age by counting from the first day of the mother’s last period. They may adjust this date using early pregnancy ultrasounds, which show how big the baby is. Ultrasounds done later in pregnancy are less accurate for this.

The due date is set at 40 weeks. But only a few babies are born on that exact day. Most are born a few weeks before or after.

Babies are grouped by gestational age:

- **Preterm**: Born before 37 weeks  
- **Full term**: Born between 37 and 41 weeks  
- **Postterm**: Born at 42 weeks or later  

Doctors also check the baby’s body features to confirm how old the baby was at birth.

---

## Problems That Start Before Birth

Some health problems in newborns begin before birth. These can come from the mother’s health or from the baby’s own condition.

Good **prenatal care** can help prevent or catch many problems early. Expectant mothers can help their baby stay healthy by:

- Taking prenatal vitamins, especially folate (start before pregnancy)  
- Getting regular checkups during pregnancy  
- Eating a healthy diet and staying at a healthy weight  

If a woman has a health condition before or during pregnancy, it can affect the baby. She should talk to her doctor about the risks and benefits of any treatment.

### Health Conditions That Can Affect the Baby

- **Diabetes**: If not well controlled, it can cause birth defects or lead to a baby who is too small or too large. Babies of mothers with diabetes may have low blood sugar after birth. This needs quick treatment.  
- **Epilepsy (seizure disorder)**: Some seizure medicines can harm the baby. But uncontrolled seizures can also be dangerous. Women should talk to their doctor about whether to keep, change, or stop their medicine during pregnancy.  
- **High blood pressure, heart disease, or kidney disease**: These can slow the baby’s growth and cause other problems. Women should discuss their medicines with their doctor.  
- **Preeclampsia**: This is a serious condition that causes very high blood pressure during pregnancy. It can harm the mother’s organs and the placenta. It may cause the placenta to separate early. This can lead to early delivery. A severe form, called **eclampsia**, causes seizures.  
- **Asthma**: If well controlled, it usually does not harm the baby. But severe attacks can lower oxygen levels, which can hurt the baby. Treatment is needed to protect both mother and baby.  
- **Thyroid disease**:  
  - Low thyroid hormone (hypothyroidism) can cause brain damage in the baby if not treated soon after birth.  
  - High thyroid hormone (hyperthyroidism) can make the baby’s thyroid too active.  
  - All newborns in the U.S. are tested for thyroid problems.  
- **Sickle cell disease**: Pregnant people with this condition may have more pain crises. If one or both parents carry the gene, the baby may have sickle cell disease. Testing before pregnancy can show the risk. The disease can be found in the fetus during pregnancy, but it does not start until months after birth. All newborns in most U.S. states are tested for it.  
- **Lupus (an autoimmune disease)**: This increases the risk of miscarriage, early birth, and a slow heart rate in the baby.  

### Medications, Smoking, Alcohol, and Drugs

- **Medications during pregnancy**: Some medicines are needed to keep the mother healthy. But others can harm the baby. Always talk to your doctor before starting, stopping, or changing any medicine — including over-the-counter drugs and supplements.  
- **Insulin**: If not taken as directed, it can harm the baby.  
- **Antidepressants**: Some can be risky. Discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor.  
- **Antiseizure medicines**: These can cause harm. But stopping them can be dangerous too. Work with your doctor.  
- **Smoking or second-hand smoke**: This slows the baby’s growth. Avoid all tobacco.  
- **Alcohol**: This is very dangerous. It can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, poor growth, early birth, birth defects, and **fetal alcohol syndrome**. This condition causes lifelong brain and behavior problems. There is no safe amount of alcohol during pregnancy.  
- **Opioids** (like prescription painkillers or illegal drugs such as heroin, oxycodone, fentanyl): These can harm the baby’s growth and cause withdrawal symptoms in the newborn. These symptoms can start hours to days after birth.  
  - People with opioid addiction may use methadone or buprenorphine to treat it. These medicines are safe during pregnancy when used under medical care.  
  - Babies born to mothers on these medicines may need longer treatment for withdrawal.  
- **Cocaine**: This increases the risk of poor growth and early birth. It can cause the placenta to separate early (placental abruption), which can lead to stillbirth or brain damage. Cocaine narrows blood vessels and can cause strokes or organ damage in the baby.  

### Birth Defects and Genetic Problems

Some babies are born with birth defects or genetic issues. These can affect any part of the body.  
- **Prenatal ultrasounds** and **fetal genetic tests** can find many of these problems before birth.

---

## Problems That Happen After Birth

Some newborns, especially those born too early, develop health problems after birth. These can affect the lungs, blood, hormones, gut, liver, or other body systems.

### Lung and Breathing Problems
- Apnea of prematurity  
- Bronchopulmonary dysplasia  
- Meconium aspiration syndrome  
- Persistent pulmonary hypertension  
- Pneumothorax (air in the space around the lungs)  
- Respiratory distress syndrome  
- Transient tachypnea (fast breathing that goes away quickly)

### Blood Problems
- Anemia (low red blood cells)  
- Hemolytic disease (red blood cells break down too fast)  
- Polycythemia (too many red blood cells)

### Hormone Problems
- Hyperthyroidism (too much thyroid hormone)  
- Hypothyroidism (too little thyroid hormone)  
- Hyperglycemia (high blood sugar)  
- Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar)

### Gut and Liver Problems
- Cholestasis (liver problem)  
- Jaundice (yellow skin or eyes)  
- Meconium ileus (blockage in the intestines)  
- Meconium plug syndrome  
- Necrotizing enterocolitis (serious gut infection)

### Other Problems
- **Retinopathy of prematurity**: A condition that affects the eyes of some preterm babies.

---

## How Are Problems Found?

### Before Birth
- Ultrasounds  
- Blood tests  
- Sometimes other imaging tests  

### After Birth
- Physical exam  
- Blood tests  
- X-rays  
- Ultrasounds  
- Other tests if needed  

Some problems are found before birth if the mother gets regular prenatal care. Others are found after birth.

Finding problems early helps parents and doctors plan for care. For example, if a baby has a serious birth defect, parents can plan to deliver in a hospital with a NICU.

### Ultrasound
Doctors use ultrasound during pregnancy to:
- Check the baby’s growth and development  
- Confirm how far along the pregnancy is  
- Find out if there are twins or more  
- Detect some birth defects  
- Find out the baby’s sex  

Ultrasound is not perfect. Some babies are born with problems that were not seen on the scan.

### Blood Tests During Pregnancy
These tests can find genetic or other problems in the baby. They are usually done in the first or second trimester.

- **cfDNA test**: Looks at tiny pieces of the baby’s DNA in the mother’s blood. It can detect conditions like Down syndrome, trisomy 18, and some other genetic issues.  
- **Other blood tests**: Measure hormone and protein levels. These can show if the baby has Down syndrome, trisomy 18, spina bifida, or other issues.

If the ultrasound or blood tests suggest a problem, doctors may do more tests:

- **Amniocentesis**: A needle takes fluid from the amniotic sac around the baby.  
- **Chorionic villus sampling (CVS)**: A needle takes a small sample from the placenta.  
- **Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling (cordocentesis)**: A needle takes blood from the umbilical cord.  

Some parents choose these tests even without screening, especially if they are at higher risk due to age or family history.

### Fetal Echocardiography
This is a special ultrasound of the baby’s heart. It helps find heart defects.

# Mesothelioma – Simple Explanation

Mesothelioma is a rare and serious type of cancer. It starts in the thin layer of tissue that covers the lungs, belly, or heart. Most cases are caused by exposure to asbestos.

## What Is Asbestos?

Asbestos is a group of natural minerals. It was used in many products because it resists heat and holds its shape. It was used in buildings, ships, car brakes, and some fabrics.

There are two main types:
- **Serpentine** – includes chrysotile
- **Amphibole** – includes amosite, crocidolite, tremolite, anthophyllite, and actinolite

All types of asbestos can cause mesothelioma. But some types are more likely to cause it than others. Amphibole fibers are more dangerous than serpentine.

## How Does Asbestos Cause Mesothelioma?

- The risk goes up with how much asbestos a person is exposed to.
- But even small amounts of asbestos can cause mesothelioma.
- It can take 30 to 50 years after exposure for the cancer to appear.

## Who Gets Mesothelioma?

- Most cases were in men who worked with asbestos in factories, shipyards, or construction.
- Over time, fewer men have gotten the disease.
- More women are now being diagnosed, likely because of secondhand exposure.

### How People Can Be Exposed

- **Workplace exposure** – in jobs like construction, mining, or manufacturing.
- **Take-home exposure** – when workers bring asbestos dust home on clothes or skin.
- **Environmental exposure** – living near areas with natural asbestos in the ground.

Some places with high rates of mesothelioma due to natural asbestos:
- Cappadocia, Turkey – erionite
- Mediterranean areas – tremolite
- Rural parts of southwestern China – crocidolite
- New Caledonia – antigorite
- Libby, Montana – Libby asbestos

- **Talcum powder** that is contaminated with asbestos has also been linked to mesothelioma.
- Other possible causes include other types of mineral fibers, radiation therapy for lymphoma, and a virus called SV40.
- Smoking does not increase the risk.

## Where Does Mesothelioma Happen?

- About 90% of cases start in the lining around the lungs (pleura).
- Most of the rest start in the lining of the belly (peritoneum).
- Rarely, it can start in the lining around the heart (pericardium) or in the testicles (tunica vaginalis).

## Types of Mesothelioma

There are two main types based on how the cells look under a microscope:
- **Epithelioid** – the most common type. It makes up at least 60% of cases.
- **Sarcomatoid** – less common and more aggressive.

## Symptoms of Mesothelioma

Most people notice:
- Trouble breathing
- Chest pain that does not go away
- A long-lasting cough
- Losing weight without trying

Other signs may include:
- Fluid building up in the chest (pleural effusion) – often on one side and sometimes bloody
- Pain that spreads to the shoulder or arm
- Hoarseness
- Trouble swallowing
- Swelling in the belly (ascites)

These symptoms usually appear only after the cancer has grown.

## How Is Mesothelioma Diagnosed?

Diagnosis can be hard. Doctors use several tools:

### Imaging Tests
- **Chest X-ray** – shows thickened lining, fluid, or loss of lung volume.
- **CT scan** – gives a clearer picture of the tumor and how far it has spread.
- **PET-CT or MRI** – may help find more areas of disease.

### Biopsy
- A sample of tissue is needed to confirm the diagnosis.
- Pleural fluid (fluid from the chest) is checked, but it often does not show cancer.
- A biopsy of the pleura is usually needed.

### Lab Tests
- The tissue is looked at under a microscope.
- Special tests (immunohistochemistry) help confirm it is mesothelioma and not another cancer.

There is no recommended screening test for mesothelioma, even for people with past asbestos exposure.

## Staging

Doctors use CT and MRI scans to stage the cancer. This helps them understand how far it has spread. MRI is especially helpful for seeing how deeply the tumor has grown.

## Treatment of Mesothelioma

There is no cure. Treatment focuses on helping you feel better and live longer.

### Supportive Care
- **Thoracentesis** – removing fluid from the chest to ease breathing.
- **Pleurodesis** – sealing the space around the lung to prevent fluid from building up again.
- **Pain control** – medicine to manage pain.

### Surgery
- Only possible in early-stage cases.
- In later stages, surgery may be used to remove as much tumor as possible, but it does not always help survival.

### Radiation Therapy
- Used to shrink tumors.
- Helps relieve pain and other symptoms.

### Chemotherapy
- Uses drugs to slow cancer growth.
- Common drugs include platinum-based medicines and folate blockers.
- It helps some people live longer, but the effect is small.

### Immunotherapy
- Uses medicines that help the body’s immune system fight cancer.
- Examples: tremelimumab, pembrolizumab, nivolumab, ipilimumab.
- Often used with chemotherapy.
- Can slow cancer growth and improve short-term survival.
- But it does not lead to long-term survival for most people.

Palliative care is a key part of treatment. It focuses on comfort, quality of life, and managing symptoms.

## Prognosis (Outlook)

- Mesothelioma is almost always fatal.
- Median survival is 6 to 18 months, depending on the stage and type.
- People with epithelioid mesothelioma tend to live longer than those with sarcomatoid mesothelioma.
- Other factors like blood tests or tumor markers do not help predict survival well.

## Key Points

- Mesothelioma is a rare, aggressive cancer that is almost always deadly.
- About 10% of people live 5 years after diagnosis.
- The vast majority of cases are linked to asbestos exposure.
- Exposure can happen at work, at home (from clothes), or in the environment.
- Treatment focuses on relieving symptoms and improving quality of life.
- New treatments like immunotherapy offer some hope, but long-term survival remains low.

# Bullous Keratopathy

Bullous keratopathy is a condition that causes blisters to form on the cornea.  
The cornea is the clear front part of the eye.  
These blisters are filled with fluid.

## Symptoms

The blisters can cause:
- Pain when looking at bright lights.
- Blurry or cloudy vision.
- A feeling like something is stuck in your eye.

The blisters can break open.  
When they do, the pain can be very strong.  
Broken blisters can make vision worse.

Symptoms are often worse when you first wake up.  
This is because your eyes stay closed at night.  
Moisture builds up and the cornea swells more.

As the day goes on, your eye dries out.  
The swelling goes down.  
So your symptoms often get better during the day.

## Who Gets It

Bullous keratopathy is most common in older adults.  
It can happen on its own.  
It can also run in families.  
Sometimes it happens after eye surgery, such as cataract surgery.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Your doctor will look at your eye closely.  
They will use a special tool called a slit lamp.  
This tool lets the doctor see the eye in detail.

The doctor may put in a few drops of a yellow-green dye.  
This dye is called fluorescein.  
It sticks to damaged parts of the cornea.  
This makes the damage easier to see.

The doctor will look for swelling and blisters on the cornea.  
The look of the cornea helps confirm the diagnosis.

## Treatment

Bullous keratopathy is treated by an eye doctor who specializes in eye diseases.  
This type of doctor is called an ophthalmologist.

Treatment options include:

- **Salty eye drops**  
  These drops help pull extra fluid out of the cornea.  
  They are also called hypertonic saline.

- **Salty ointments**  
  These are used at night.  
  They also help remove fluid from the cornea.

- **Medications to lower eye pressure**  
  These may be needed if pressure in the eye is high.

- **Soft contact lenses**  
  These can be worn for a short time.  
  They act like a bandage on the cornea.  
  They help reduce pain and discomfort.

- **Corneal transplantation**  
  This is surgery to replace the damaged cornea.  
  It is done if vision is poor or pain is severe and does not go away.
