# Tongue Injury

Tongue injury is the most common reason people feel pain or discomfort in the tongue.

The tongue has many nerves that sense pain and touch. This makes it more sensitive than most other parts of the body.

People often bite their tongue by accident. These bites usually heal fast.

A sharp or broken tooth or dental filling can hurt the tongue badly. The tongue is a soft and delicate tissue, so it can be damaged easily.

Injuries from things like gunshots or stab wounds are serious. They can hurt both the tongue and other parts of the face. For more information, see the section on facial injuries.

Shallow cuts on the tongue usually heal in a few days. Deeper cuts usually heal within three weeks.

When a doctor treats a cut on the tongue, they must decide if stitches are really needed. Many tongue cuts heal well without stitches. 

Also, it is hard for many people to keep their mouth open and their tongue still during stitching. This often means they need medicine to relax or go to sleep during the procedure.

# Rash in Babies and Young Children

A rash is a common problem in babies and young children. Most rashes are not serious.

---

## What Causes a Rash?

Rashes can happen for many reasons. Some causes include:

- Infections (from viruses, fungi, or bacteria)
- Skin irritation from diapers or soaps
- Allergies to food, medicine, or things on the skin
- Skin conditions like eczema
- Rare but serious illnesses

Some rashes are caused by viruses. These can include chickenpox, measles, and fifth disease. These are now rare because of vaccines. But they can still happen in children who are not vaccinated.

Other rashes come from fungi, like *Candida*, which can grow in the diaper area or in the mouth.

Some rashes are due to allergic reactions. These can happen after using a new soap, lotion, or medicine.

A few rashes are signs of very serious health problems. These include:

- Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
- Meningococcemia (a dangerous blood infection)
- Kawasaki disease
- Stevens-Johnson syndrome

---

## Common Types of Rashes

### Diaper Rash
- Red, irritated skin in the diaper area
- Can be caused by irritation or by a fungus called *Candida*
- *Candida* rash looks like red patches with small white spots around the edges
- Sometimes there are white, fluffy patches on the tongue

### Cradle Cap
- Thick, yellow, crusty patches on the scalp
- Often has red, inflamed skin underneath
- Common in newborns

### Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis)
- Red, dry, itchy patches on the skin
- Often starts on the face in babies
- Can spread to the neck, scalp, and arms and legs
- Can be linked to a family history of allergies

### Molluscum Contagiosum
- Small, firm, round bumps
- Color: pearly or pink
- Often have a small dent in the center
- Usually not itchy or painful
- Can appear in groups
- More severe in children with weak immune systems, like those with HIV

### Hives (Urticaria)
- Raised, red, itchy patches
- They come and go quickly
- Can appear anywhere on the body
- Often linked to an allergy

### Heat Rash (Miliaria)
- Tiny red bumps or small blisters
- Happens in hot, humid weather
- Common in young babies

### Neonatal Acne
- Small red bumps on the face
- Sometimes with white dots in the center
- Appears 2 to 4 weeks after birth
- Can last up to 18 months

### Erythema Toxicum
- Flat red spots with a small white bump in the middle
- Seen in up to half of all newborns
- Usually goes away in 7 to 14 days

### Pityriasis Rosea
- Starts with one large oval patch on the chest or back
- After 7 to 14 days, more patches appear
- Often shaped like a Christmas tree
- Itchy in some children

### Contact Dermatitis
- Red, itchy skin that may blister
- Often follows contact with something new, like a new soap, plant, or temporary tattoo
- A black "henna" tattoo can cause this
- The rash may follow the shape of the tattoo

### Fifth Disease (Erythema Infectiosum)
- Bright red cheeks, like slapped cheeks
- Rash spreads to arms, legs, and trunk
- May be itchy
- Often starts with a mild fever or tiredness

### Chickenpox
- Red dots that turn into itchy blisters
- Blisters go through stages: red spot → bump → blister → crust
- Starts on the face, scalp, and body
- Can also appear on the hands, feet, and inside the mouth

### Measles
- Red rash that starts on the face and spreads down the body
- Often has white spots inside the mouth (Koplik spots)
- High fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes

### Scarlet Fever
- Red, rough rash that starts on the chest and spreads
- Skin feels like sandpaper
- White patch around the mouth
- Red lines in skin folds (Pastia lines)
- Strawberry tongue (red and bumpy)
- Peeling skin on hands, feet, and groin after a few days

### Impetigo
- Painless sores near the nose or mouth
- Sores leak fluid and form a honey-colored crust
- Can also appear as fluid-filled blisters on arms, legs, or trunk

### Lyme Disease
- A red rash that grows larger over time
- Often has a clear center, like a bullseye
- May be linked to a tick bite
- Can cause fatigue, headache, joint pain

### Roseola
- High fever for 4 to 5 days
- Rash appears suddenly when the fever goes down
- Red or pink spots on the body

### Rubella (German Measles)
- Light pink rash that starts on the face and spreads
- Lasts up to 3 days
- Swollen glands behind the ears and neck
- Mild fever

### Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome
- Widespread red, painful skin
- Blisters form and break easily
- Skin peels off in large sheets
- Not usually on the mouth or genitals
- Most common in children under 5

### Kawasaki Disease
- High fever for more than 5 days
- Red eyes, red cracked lips, strawberry tongue
- Swollen hands and feet
- Swollen lymph nodes in the neck
- Rash that can look like hives, target spots, or purple patches
- Later, skin peels on fingers and toes

### Hemolytic-Uremic Syndrome
- Tiny purple spots (petechiae) on the skin
- Pale skin
- Often follows a stomach bug with bloody diarrhea
- Little or no urine
- High blood pressure
- Blood tests show low platelets and damaged red blood cells

### Milia
- Tiny, white, pearly bumps on a newborn’s face
- Harmless and go away on their own

### Erythema Multiforme
- Target-shaped rashes with a red ring, pale center, and outer red ring
- Can appear on arms, legs, or body
- May cause itching or sores in the mouth

---

## How Is a Rash Diagnosed?

Doctors look at the rash and ask questions. They may:

- Check the child’s medical history
- Ask about recent illnesses, medicines, or new products
- Look at the rash closely
- Take a skin scraping to test for fungus
- Do blood tests or urine tests if needed
- Use a special test to check for certain infections

Most rashes can be diagnosed with a simple exam. No tests are needed for many common rashes.

---

## How Is a Rash Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause.

### For Diaper Rash
- Change diapers often
- Clean the area gently with mild soap and water
- Let the skin dry before putting on a new diaper
- Use a cream with zinc oxide or vitamins A and D to protect the skin

### For Fungal Infections (like *Candida*)
- Use an antifungal cream
- Keep the area clean and dry

### For Eczema
- Use moisturizer often
- Avoid harsh soaps
- Use prescribed creams if needed

### For Viral Rashes
- No specific treatment
- Keep the child comfortable
- Use medicine for fever or itching if needed

### For Hives
- Use an antihistamine to reduce itching
- Avoid known triggers

### For Allergic Reactions
- Stop using the product that caused the rash
- Use antihistamines or steroid creams if needed

### For Serious Rashes (like Stevens-Johnson syndrome or Kawasaki disease)
- Need hospital care
- May need IV medicine and close monitoring

---

## Medicines for Itching

Antihistamines can help with itching. Common ones include:

- Diphenhydramine
- Hydroxyzine
- Cetirizine
- Loratadine

These can cause:
- Dry mouth
- Drowsiness
- Dizziness
- Nausea or vomiting
- Restlessness or mood changes in some children
- Trouble peeing
- Blurred vision
- Confusion

Talk to your doctor before giving any medicine to a child.

---

## Key Points

- Most rashes in children are not serious.
- A doctor can usually tell what is wrong by looking at the rash and asking questions.
- If a child has a rash and also seems very sick, with fever, poor feeding, or trouble breathing, see a doctor right away.
- Do not use strong creams or medicines without talking to a doctor.

# Malignant External Otitis

This is a serious infection of the outer ear. It spreads to nearby bones and tissues, including the bone behind the ear, the middle ear, and the inner ear.

It mostly affects older adults. It is more likely if you have a weak immune system or diabetes. The infection usually starts in the outer ear. It is often caused by a type of bacteria called *Pseudomonas*. Another bacteria, MRSA, can also cause this infection.

Even though the name says "malignant," this is not cancer. It is a severe infection.

## Symptoms

You may have strong ear pain. The pain often gets worse at night.  
You may have a bad-smelling fluid coming from your ear.  
You may see pus or dirty material in your ear canal.  
You may have trouble hearing.  
In serious cases, the infection can affect nerves in your face and head. This can cause weakness or paralysis in the face.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors use several tests to confirm the diagnosis.

- A CT scan gives a detailed picture of the bones and tissues in and around the ear.  
- A sample of the fluid from your ear is sent to a lab. This is called a culture. It helps find the bacteria causing the infection.  
- A small piece of tissue from the ear canal is taken. This is called a biopsy. It helps rule out cancer.

## Treatment

Treatment usually lasts six weeks. It includes:

- Strong antibiotics given through a vein (IV).  
- Ear drops or dressings that contain two medicines: ciprofloxacin (an antibiotic) and dexamethasone (a medicine that reduces swelling).  
- In some cases, treatment in a high-pressure oxygen chamber (hyperbaric oxygen therapy).  
- Careful control of diabetes.  
- Stopping any medicine that weakens your immune system, if possible.  
- Regular cleanings of the ear canal. Dead skin and infected tissue are removed during office visits.

If the infection is mild, you may take strong antibiotics by mouth instead of through a vein.  
If the infection has damaged a lot of bone, you may need antibiotics for longer than six weeks.

Surgery is rarely needed. But regular cleanings of the ear canal are important until the infection is gone.

# DNA Changes and Genetic Differences

Some genetic changes do not follow normal patterns of inheritance. This can happen when genes or chromosomes are changed. But not all changes are harmful. Some are very common and do not cause problems.

## Important Facts

- A gene change that looks like it was passed down from a parent can actually happen for the first time in a child. This means brothers or sisters do not have a higher chance of having the same change.
- Some health problems show up in patches on the body. This can happen because only some cells have the gene change. This is called mosaicism.
- When pieces of chromosomes swap places, it may not cause any symptoms. But sometimes it can lead to certain cancers, Down syndrome, miscarriages, or birth defects in children.
- Some inherited health problems get worse over time. They may also start earlier in life with each new generation. This can happen with certain conditions that involve repeated gene patterns.

# Feeding Your Baby with a Bottle

Babies in the hospital usually get fed soon after birth. After that, feed them whenever they seem hungry.  

In the first week, your baby will drink between half an ounce and two ounces per feeding. By the second week, they will drink three to four ounces about six to eight times a day.  

Let your baby decide how much to drink. Do not push them to finish every bottle. They will eat as much as they need when they are hungry.  

As your baby grows, they will drink more at each feeding. By the third or fourth month, they may drink up to six to eight ounces at a time.  

## How to Hold Your Baby During Feeding

Hold your baby in a semi-reclining or sitting position.  

Never let your baby feed while lying flat on their back. This can cause milk to go into the nose or the tubes that connect the middle ear to the throat.  

Older babies who can hold their own bottle should not be allowed to sleep with the bottle. Milk or juice left in the mouth can harm their teeth and cause cavities.  

## Types of Baby Formula

You can buy baby formula in three forms:  
- Ready-to-use bottles (sterile and ready to feed)  
- Concentrated liquid (must be mixed with water)  
- Powder (must be mixed with water)  

All formulas are made to give your baby the right mix of nutrients, energy, and vitamins. Some contain iron. All formula-fed babies should get iron-fortified formula. This helps prevent a condition called iron deficiency anemia.  

### Important Note  
All formula-fed babies should be given iron-fortified formula to prevent iron deficiency anemia.  

## Preparing Formula

If you use concentrated formula or powder, follow the mixing instructions exactly.  

Use water that has fluoride in it to mix the formula.  

Most formulas are made from cow’s milk. But some babies cannot handle cow’s milk. If your baby has trouble with regular formula, your doctor may suggest:  
- A soy-based formula  
- A hydrolyzed formula (where the proteins are broken down)  
- An amino acid formula (for babies who cannot handle hydrolyzed formula)  

There is no long-term health difference between babies fed standard formula and those fed special formulas.  

Do not give plain cow’s milk to babies under one year old. It is not safe for them.  

## Keeping Formula Safe

To protect your baby from germs, always use clean, sterile containers.  

Disposable plastic liners for bottles do not need to be sterilized.  

Sterilize bottle nipples by:  
- Running them through the dishwasher  
- Boiling them in water for five minutes  

## Warming the Formula

Warm the formula to body temperature before feeding.  

Place the filled bottle (or formula container with liner) in a bowl of warm water. Let it warm up.  

Do not use a microwave. It can heat the formula unevenly and make it dangerously hot.  

To check the temperature:  
- Shake the bottle gently  
- Put a few drops on the inside of your wrist  
- The formula should feel neither warm nor cold  

If it feels hot, it could burn your baby’s mouth.  

## Choosing the Right Nipple

The size of the nipple hole matters.  

When you hold the bottle upside down, the formula should drip slowly.  

As your baby grows, they will drink more. Older babies need a larger nipple hole to drink faster.

# Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)

Chronic granulomatous disease is a rare condition where the body’s white blood cells cannot fight certain infections well.  
This happens because the white blood cells do not make strong chemicals that kill bacteria and fungi.  
The disease is caused by problems in the way white blood cells work.  

Most people with CGD are boys.  
This is because the most common form is passed down through the mother’s genes.  
In other cases, both parents must pass on a faulty gene for a child to get the disease.  

The main genes involved are *gp91phox*, *p22phox*, *p47phox*, and *p67phox*.  
When these genes are not working right, the white blood cells cannot make hydrogen peroxide or other strong chemicals.  
This means bacteria and fungi can survive in the body even if the white blood cells can still grab them.  

---

## Symptoms of Chronic Granulomatous Disease

The disease often starts in early childhood.  
Some people do not show symptoms until their early teens.  
The most common sign is repeated abscesses.  
These are painful, pus-filled lumps that keep coming back.  

The most common germs that cause infections are bacteria and fungi that make a chemical called catalase.  
Examples include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Escherichia coli*, *Serratia*, *Klebsiella*, *Pseudomonas*, and *Aspergillus*.  
*Aspergillus* infections are the most dangerous and can be deadly.  

Other signs include:  
- Swelling in the lungs, liver, lymph nodes, or intestines  
- Blockages in the digestive or urinary system  
- Swollen lymph nodes that drain pus  
- Enlarged liver and spleen  
- Lung infections like pneumonia  
- Low red blood cell count (anemia)  
- High levels of certain immune proteins (hypergammaglobulinemia)  
- High rate of inflammation in the blood (elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate)  

Some people also have:  
- Skin sores or ulcers  
- Mouth sores  
- Bone infections  
- Problems with growth  

Girls who carry the faulty gene may not have symptoms.  
But some may have joint pain, mouth ulcers, eye problems, or skin that burns easily in sunlight.  

---

## How Is CGD Diagnosed?

A blood test checks how well white blood cells make strong chemicals.  
This test is called a flow cytometric oxidative burst assay.  
It uses a dye called DHR or NBT to see if the cells can make the needed chemicals.  

This test can also find female carriers of the disease.  
In carriers, the test shows two types of white blood cells: normal and abnormal.  

Genetic testing can confirm the faulty gene.  
But it is not needed to make the diagnosis.  
Siblings of a person with CGD are often tested using the same blood test.  

Blood tests may also show anemia and high inflammation levels.  

---

## How Is CGD Treated?

Treatment is lifelong and aims to prevent infections and manage complications.  

**Antibiotics** are given every day to prevent bacterial infections.  
The most common medicine is sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim, taken twice a day.  

**Antifungal medicines** are also used every day to prevent fungal infections.  
If a fungal infection happens even once, antifungals are started.  
Good choices include itraconazole, voriconazole, and posaconazole.  

**Interferon gamma** is a medicine that helps the immune system work better.  
It can reduce the number and severity of infections.  
It is usually given as part of daily treatment.  

For serious infections, **granulocyte transfusions** may be needed.  
These are transfusions of white blood cells from a donor.  
They can save lives during severe infections.  

Some people need **immunosuppressive medicines** to control swelling and inflammation that is not caused by infection.  
This is common in conditions like inflammatory bowel disease.  

**Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation** is a possible cure.  
It works best when done from a sibling who has matching genes.  
The transplant is usually successful if the person gets chemotherapy first to prepare the body.  

**Gene therapy** is being studied.  
It may one day offer a cure, but it is not yet widely available.  

---

## Key Points

- Think about CGD if a child has repeated abscesses, especially in early childhood or early teens.  
- The infection-causing germs are often bacteria or fungi that make catalase.  
- Use a blood test to check if white blood cells can make strong chemicals.  
- This test also helps find female carriers.  
- Treat most people with daily antibiotics, antifungals, and interferon gamma.  
- For serious infections, give granulocyte transfusions.  
- Consider stem cell transplant in suitable cases.

# Prolactinoma

A prolactinoma is a noncancerous growth in the pituitary gland. The pituitary gland is a small organ at the base of the brain. It helps control many body functions.

This type of tumor comes from special cells in the pituitary gland. These cells make a hormone called prolactin.

## What Causes Prolactinoma?

Prolactinomas cause the body to make too much prolactin. This is called hyperprolactinemia.

Too much prolactin can lead to:
- Unusual milk production from the breasts (galactorrhea)
- Trouble getting pregnant (infertility)
- In women: missing periods or having them less often
- In men: low sex drive and trouble getting or keeping an erection

## What Are the Symptoms?

The most common symptom is milk coming from the breasts when not pregnant or breastfeeding. This can happen in both women and men.

Other symptoms include:
- Women: No periods, dry vagina, pain during sex, less interest in sex, and extra hair on the face or body
- Men: Low sex drive, trouble getting an erection, and low levels of testosterone

If the tumor is large, it can press on nearby nerves. This may cause:
- Headaches
- Loss of vision in parts of the eyes

Low levels of estrogen in women and low levels of testosterone in men can increase the risk of weak bones (osteoporosis).

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect a prolactinoma if:
- A woman has no periods or unexpected milk from her breasts
- A man has low sex drive, low testosterone, or milk from his breasts

To confirm the diagnosis:
- A blood test checks the level of prolactin
- A high level of prolactin suggests a prolactinoma

Imaging tests like MRI or CT scans are used to look for a tumor in the pituitary area.

Even if no tumor shows up on the scan, a prolactinoma may still be the cause. The tumor might be too small to see.

If the tumor is large, an eye doctor checks vision to see if it is affected.

## What Causes High Prolactin Levels?

The most common cause is a prolactinoma.

Other causes include:
- Certain medicines:
  - Some drugs for mental health (phenothiazines)
  - Some blood pressure medicines (like methyldopa and verapamil)
  - Opioid pain medicines
  - Birth control pills
- Medical conditions outside the pituitary gland:
  - Underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism)
  - Chronic kidney disease
  - Liver disease
  - Some lung cancers

Tumors near the pituitary gland that do not make prolactin can also raise levels. They do this by pressing on the stalk that connects the pituitary to the brain. This stops a natural brain chemical called dopamine from reaching the pituitary. Dopamine normally helps lower prolactin.

## How Is It Treated?

### Medication

Medicines that act like dopamine are the first treatment. These are called dopamine agonists.

Examples: bromocriptine and cabergoline.

These medicines:
- Are taken by mouth
- Lower prolactin levels
- Help stop milk production
- Restore menstrual periods in women
- Improve sex drive and erections in men
- Increase estrogen and testosterone levels
- Can help restore fertility
- Shrink the tumor
- Improve vision problems

The medicines work only as long as you take them. But some people can stop them safely later.

### When Is Treatment Needed?

Treatment is not always needed if:
- The tumor is small
- Prolactin levels are not very high
- You have no symptoms
- Women: periods are regular, not trying to get pregnant, and not bothered by milk production
- Men: testosterone is normal

For women with small tumors who do not want to get pregnant and are not on medication, doctors may give estrogen or birth control pills. This helps with symptoms like vaginal dryness. But these treatments do not shrink the tumor.

Doctors recommend checking with an MRI or CT scan every year for at least two years. This makes sure the tumor is not growing.

### Surgery

Surgery is not usually the first choice. Medication is safer and easier.

Surgery may be needed if:
- The tumor is large
- Medication does not work
- You cannot tolerate the medicine
- You have vision or nerve problems

Before surgery, doctors may give dopamine agonists to shrink the tumor. After surgery, they may still be needed because surgery alone often does not cure the tumor.

In some cases, the tumor shrinks so much that you can stop the medicine. This is more likely if the tumor was small or if a woman has had a baby.

### Radiation Therapy

Radiation is used only if:
- Medicine and surgery do not work
- The tumor keeps growing

It is a treatment option for other pituitary tumors too.

## Important Notes

- Dopamine agonists are safe when used at the doses for prolactinoma.
- High doses used for Parkinson’s disease have been linked to heart valve problems. But studies show no such risk at the lower doses used for prolactinoma.

## Summary

- Prolactinoma is a noncancerous tumor in the pituitary gland.
- It causes too much prolactin.
- Symptoms include milk from the breasts, missed periods, low sex drive, and fertility problems.
- Diagnosis is based on blood tests and imaging.
- Treatment starts with medicine that lowers prolactin.
- Surgery or radiation may be needed if medicine does not work.
- Regular follow-up is important to check tumor size.

# Chronic Cholecystitis

Chronic cholecystitis means long-term inflammation of the gallbladder.  
It is almost always caused by gallstones.  

(See also: How the Bile System Works.)

This condition usually starts with repeated episodes of sudden gallbladder pain.  
These episodes can happen even if the gallbladder is not severely inflamed.  
Over time, the gallbladder can become scarred and shrink.  
In some cases, the gallbladder becomes hard and full of calcium.  
This is called a porcelain gallbladder.

---

## Symptoms and Signs

Gallstones can block the tube that carries bile out of the gallbladder.  
This blockage causes recurring sharp pain in the upper right side of the belly.  
This pain is called biliary colic.  
The pain may come and go.  
It does not always mean the gallbladder is badly inflamed.  
The amount of pain does not match how much inflammation is present.  
You may feel tenderness in the upper belly.  
But you usually do not have a fever.  
If you have a fever, it may mean you now have acute cholecystitis.  
Once the pain starts, it often returns again and again.

---

## How It Is Diagnosed

Your doctor will look at your symptoms and medical history.  
If you have repeated episodes of biliary colic and gallstones, this suggests chronic cholecystitis.  
An ultrasound scan can show gallstones.  
It can also show if the gallbladder is small and scarred.  
The diagnosis is confirmed if you have a history of repeated pain and ultrasound shows gallstones.  
Another test called cholescintigraphy can show if the gallbladder is not working.  
But this test is not as reliable as ultrasound.

---

## Treatment

The best treatment is surgery to remove the gallbladder.  
This is called laparoscopic cholecystectomy.  
It is done using small cuts and a camera.  
This surgery helps prevent future pain and other problems.  
It is especially important if you have a porcelain gallbladder.  
This type of gallbladder has a higher risk of becoming cancerous.

# Tests for Acid and Reflux Problems

These tests help doctors find out if stomach acid is coming up into the tube that connects your throat to your stomach. This tube is called the esophagus.

The tests check for acid reflux. Acid reflux happens when stomach acid moves up into the esophagus. This can cause heartburn and other symptoms.

There are two main types of tests: one uses a thin tube, and the other uses a small wireless device.

---

## Test with a Thin Tube (Catheter)

A doctor gently puts a thin plastic tube through your nose and down into your esophagus. The tube stays in place for 24 hours.

The tube has one or more sensors. These sensors measure how acidic the inside of your esophagus is. They can detect when acid from your stomach moves up into your esophagus.

Wires from the tube send the data to a small recorder that you wear on your belt or around your neck.

You will keep a diary for 24 hours. You will write down:
- When you eat or drink
- When you feel symptoms like heartburn or chest pain
- When you go to sleep or wake up

Your doctor will compare your diary with the data from the tube. This helps them see if your symptoms match times when acid was in your esophagus.

Some newer tubes can also detect any liquid that comes up from your stomach, even if it is not acidic. This is called impedance testing. These tubes can measure both acid and nonacid reflux.

---

## Wireless Test

A doctor uses a small camera (called an endoscope) to place a tiny wireless capsule on the lower part of your esophagus. The endoscope goes through your mouth.

The capsule stays in place for 48 to 72 hours. It measures acid levels in your esophagus and sends the results to a receiver you wear.

You do not have a tube in your nose during this test. This makes it more comfortable for many people.

You will keep a diary of your symptoms, meals, and sleep during the test. Your doctor will use this to see if your symptoms happened when acid was present.

The capsule does not need to be removed. It usually falls off on its own within a week. It passes out of your body in your stool. You do not need to find it or return it.

---

## What to Expect

- You must not eat or drink after midnight before the test.
- After the device is placed, you can go home and eat and drink normally.
- The test usually lasts 24 hours, but can go up to 72 hours.
- Complications are very rare.

These tests help doctors understand what is causing your symptoms and how to treat them.

# Postterm Infants

A postterm infant is born at 42 weeks or later in pregnancy.

These babies may have health problems such as:
- Not getting enough oxygen around birth (perinatal asphyxia)
- Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia)
- Breathing in meconium (meconium aspiration syndrome)

## What Causes a Postterm Birth?

The exact reason is often unknown. But if a mother has had a postterm baby before, she is more likely to have another one.

Some rare conditions can cause postterm birth. These include:
- Brain problems in the baby (like anencephaly)
- Underdeveloped adrenal glands
- A genetic condition affecting the adrenal glands (congenital adrenal hyperplasia)
- A skin condition called x-linked ichthyosis that also affects the placenta

## How Do Postterm Infants Develop Problems?

In most pregnancies, the baby keeps growing until birth. But in some cases, the placenta starts to break down as the pregnancy goes on. This can lead to:
- Scarring in the placenta
- Damage to the tiny blood vessels in the placenta

When this happens, the baby does not get enough food or oxygen from the mother. This causes the baby to become thin and undernourished. The baby’s body stores of sugar (glycogen) are low. There is also less amniotic fluid.

Babies with this problem are called dysmature. They may be small for their gestational age. This issue is most common in pregnancies that go past 41 to 42 weeks.

## What Do Postterm Infants Look Like?

Postterm babies often look alert and mature. But they have:
- Less soft tissue, especially under the skin
- Dry, peeling skin
- Loose skin on arms and legs
- Long fingernails and toenails

The baby’s nails, skin, and umbilical cord may be stained green or brown from meconium passed in the womb.

## How Is a Postterm Infant Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose a postterm infant by:
- Checking the baby’s gestational age
- Doing a physical exam

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists defines pregnancy stages as:

- Early term: 37 weeks and 0 days to 38 weeks and 6 days
- Full term: 39 weeks and 0 days to 40 weeks and 6 days
- Late term: 41 weeks and 0 days to 41 weeks and 6 days
- Postterm: 42 weeks and 0 days or later

## How Are Postterm Infants Treated?

### Treating Health Problems

Better care during pregnancy has reduced the number of babies born after 41 weeks. This has also lowered the number of babies with meconium aspiration syndrome.

Postterm and dysmature babies are at risk for low blood sugar. They must be checked often and treated if needed.

### For Babies with Low Oxygen at Birth

If a baby had low oxygen at birth, treatment depends on how serious the problem is. For babies born at 36 weeks or later, cooling therapy (therapeutic hypothermia) may help if:
- The baby had severe acidosis at birth
- The baby had a low Apgar score at 5 minutes or later
- The baby needed long resuscitation

### For Babies with Meconium in the Lungs

Suctioning the baby’s airway right after birth does not reduce the risk of meconium aspiration. This is true even if the fluid is thick or the baby seems active.

Doctors should only suction the airway if the baby needs help breathing or if there is a blockage from meconium.

Babies with meconium in the lungs may need help breathing. Some may need:
- High-frequency ventilation (a special kind of breathing support)
- Sedation (medicine to help the baby stay calm)

Surfactant medicine helps the lungs work better. It does not lower the death rate, but it reduces the need for ECMO. So doctors often use it in babies with serious breathing problems.

ECMO is a life-support machine for the heart and lungs. It is not available in all hospitals. But many hospitals can send the baby to a center that has ECMO.

ECMO is usually used for babies who are 34 weeks or older and who still have severe breathing problems after other treatments.

### For Babies with High Blood Pressure in the Lungs

Persistent pulmonary hypertension means the blood pressure in the lungs stays high. This makes it hard for the baby to get oxygen.

Treatment includes:
- Supportive care (like oxygen and breathing support)
- Inhaled nitric oxide or other medicines to open the blood vessels in the lungs

# Transvestic Disorder – Simple Explanation

## What Is Transvestic Disorder?

Transvestic disorder means a person often feels strong sexual excitement from wearing clothes of the opposite sex. This causes serious distress or makes daily life hard.

- Most people who wear clothes of the opposite sex do **not** have a mental health problem.
- Doctors only call it a disorder if the person feels very upset or cannot do normal things because of this desire.
- The person may spend a lot of time or money on cross-dressing, which harms their work, family, or friendships.

## What Is Cross-Dressing?

Cross-dressing means wearing clothes usually worn by the opposite sex.

- Men often wear women’s clothes. Women sometimes wear men’s clothes, but this is much less common.
- The clothing itself is the focus of the sexual excitement. This is called a fetish.
- This is not the same as gender dysphoria. People with gender dysphoria feel they are the wrong sex and want to change their body. Cross-dressers do not feel this way most of the time.

### Important Notes:
- The word “transvestite” is outdated and can be offensive. Use “cross-dresser” instead.
- Cross-dressing is not a mental illness by itself.
- It happens in both straight and gay men. It is rare in women.
- Nonbinary people who wear clothes of a different gender are not usually cross-dressing for sexual reasons.

## Why Do People Cross-Dress?

- Some men start in late childhood. At first, they feel strong sexual excitement when wearing women’s clothes.
- Others do it to feel calm, relax, or explore a different side of themselves.
- Some men may feel more gender dysphoria when stressed or after a loss.

## Life Changes Over Time

- Some men who cross-dressed as teens or young adults later develop a strong sense of being the opposite gender.
- These men may want to change their body using hormones or surgery.

## Relationships and Cross-Dressing

- If a partner agrees, cross-dressing can be part of a healthy sexual relationship.
- If a partner does not agree, the person may feel anxious, sad, guilty, or ashamed.
- This can lead to a cycle:  
  - They throw away their women’s clothes.  
  - Then they buy more clothes, wigs, and makeup.  
  - Then they feel guilty again and throw them away.

## How Is Transvestic Disorder Diagnosed?

A doctor checks for this disorder using standard mental health rules.

The diagnosis is made when:

- A person has repeated, strong sexual feelings about cross-dressing.
- These feelings lead to strong distress or problems in daily life.
- The problem has lasted at least six months.

### Doctors Also Note:
- If the person is aroused by the idea of being the opposite sex (called autogynephilia).
- If the person is aroused by the clothing itself (called a fetish).

## Treatment Options

- **Support groups** help many people feel less alone and more accepted.
- **Therapy** can help if needed. It focuses on self-acceptance and managing behaviors that cause problems.
- There are **no medicines** that reliably help with this condition.
- Some people seek help because their partner is upset, or because it affects their job or social life.
- Others are referred by courts or seek help for other issues like depression or substance use.

## Key Points

- Cross-dressing is not a mental illness.
- Most people who cross-dress do not have a disorder.
- Only when it causes serious distress or problems is it called transvestic disorder.
- Support and therapy can help people live well with their feelings.
- No medicine works well for this condition.

# Taenia asiatica (Asian Tapeworm) Infection

This infection is only found in Asia.  
It is very similar to another tapeworm infection called *T. saginata*, but the main animal that carries it is pigs, not cattle.

## Where the Infection Occurs

The infection happens mostly in China, Taiwan, Indonesia, Thailand, South Korea, India, and nearby countries.

## How People Get Infected

Pigs carry the tapeworm larvae.  
People get infected by eating raw or undercooked pork that has these larvae.  
Once inside the human body, the larvae grow into adult tapeworms in the small intestine.  
The adult worms can be 4 to 8 meters long.

## Symptoms

Most people with the adult tapeworm have no symptoms.  
Some may have mild stomach problems.  
You might see small, white segments of the worm in your stool.

## Diagnosis

Doctors check your stool for worm eggs or segments.  
They may also take a swab from around your anus to look for eggs.  
The eggs of *T. asiatica* look the same as those of other tapeworms.  
To tell them apart, doctors can use special lab tests that look at the worm’s DNA.

## Treatment

The main medicine used is praziquantel.  
In some countries outside the United States, niclosamide is used instead.  
After treatment, you should have your stool checked again at 1 month and 3 months to make sure the infection is gone.

## Prevention

Cook whole cuts of pork to at least 63 degrees Celsius (145 degrees Fahrenheit).  
Use a food thermometer to check the temperature.  
Let the meat rest for 3 minutes before cutting or eating.  
Ground pork must be cooked to at least 71 degrees Celsius (160 degrees Fahrenheit).  
No resting time is needed for ground meat.  
Always cook pork thoroughly to avoid infection.

# Cranberry

Cranberries are a type of fruit.  
You can eat them whole.  
You can also find them in foods like jellies and juices.  
Cranberry supplements come in pill form.

## What People Use Cranberry For

Many people take cranberry to help stop urinary tract infections from coming back.  
Some also use it to ease symptoms of urinary tract infections.  
A few people drink cranberry juice to lower fever.  
Some believe it may help treat certain stomach cancers caused by a bacteria called *Helicobacter pylori*.  
Some say cranberry helps protect the body’s cells.  
This is because it may act as an antioxidant.  
Antioxidants help protect cells from damage caused by harmful molecules called free radicals.  
These molecules are made naturally in the body during normal cell activity.

## What Science Says About Cranberry

In 2020, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration said that makers of cranberry supplements can say their product may help reduce the chance of repeat urinary tract infections in healthy women.  
But the FDA also said the science behind this is weak and not clear.  
Some studies show that cranberry juice or extract may help prevent urinary tract infections from coming back over the next 12 months.  
But the benefit is small.  
Cranberry does not treat an active urinary tract infection.  
The results from studies are mixed.  
Natural, unsweetened cranberry juice contains compounds called anthocyanidins.  
These help stop the bacteria *Escherichia coli* from sticking to the walls of the urinary tract.  
This bacteria is the most common cause of urinary tract infections.  
There is no proof that cranberry helps lower fever.  
There is also no proof that it helps treat cancer.

## Side Effects of Cranberry

No serious side effects are known.  
But most store-bought cranberry juices are very sweet.  
This added sugar can be a problem for people with diabetes.  
People with diabetes should only drink cranberry juice if it is unsweetened or sweetened with artificial sweeteners.  
To avoid extra sugar, people can choose cranberry pills instead of juice or other foods.

If you have kidney stones, talk to your doctor before using cranberry products.

## Drug Interactions

Cranberry can increase the risk of bleeding if taken with warfarin.  
Warfarin is a medicine that prevents blood from clotting.  
People on warfarin should avoid cranberry products.  
Cranberry may also make other medicines stronger.  
This includes atorvastatin, a drug used to lower cholesterol.  
It may also make nifedipine stronger.  
Nifedipine is a medicine used to lower blood pressure.

## Recommendations

If you have repeated urinary tract infections, you may want to try cranberry to help lower your risk.  
But always talk to your doctor first.  
This is especially important if you take other medicines.  
Your doctor can help you avoid possible side effects or drug interactions.

## More Information

The following English-language resource may be helpful.

National Institutes of Health's National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health: *Cranberry*

# Erythrasma

Erythrasma is a skin infection caused by a type of bacteria called *Corynebacterium minutissimum*.  
It often affects people with diabetes.  
It is also more common in warm, humid climates.  

The infection usually shows up in skin folds.  
These include the groin, under the arms, under the breasts, in the belly folds, and around the anus.  
It is most common in overweight middle-aged women and people with diabetes.  

## What Erythrasma Looks Like

On the feet, it often appears between the third and fourth toes.  
It causes the skin to peel, crack, and become soft and wet.  

In the groin area, it looks like pink or brown patches.  
The edges of the patches are sharp and clear.  
The skin has a fine, flaky surface.  

The same type of rash can also appear in other skin folds.  
This includes under the arms, under the breasts, in the belly folds, and around the anus.  

## How Doctors Diagnose Erythrasma

Doctors often diagnose erythrasma just by looking at the skin.  
A special black light called a Wood light can help.  
Under this light, the infected skin glows a bright coral-red color.  
This happens because the bacteria make a substance called porphyrin.  

A skin scraping test can also help.  
The test shows no fungal threads.  
This helps rule out a fungal infection like ringworm.  

## Differentiating Erythrasma from Other Conditions

Sometimes, erythrasma can look like other skin problems.  
For example, it may look like ringworm or a skin irritation called intertrigo.  

In the area around the anus, it can be confused with a bacterial infection caused by strep bacteria.  
This strep infection causes pain and bright red skin.  
It does not glow under the Wood light.  
A swab test can confirm if strep bacteria are present.  

## How Erythrasma Is Treated

For mild cases, use a topical antibiotic cream or ointment.  
Effective options include:  
- Erythromycin  
- Clindamycin  
- Mupirocin  
- Fusidic acid  
- Benzoyl peroxide  

For more widespread infections, take an oral antibiotic.  
Options include:  
- One single dose of clarithromycin 1 gram  
- Or erythromycin 250 milligrams four times a day for 14 days  

## Important Notes

Erythrasma often comes back after treatment.  
If your doctor cannot use a Wood light or skin scraping test to tell the difference between bacteria and fungus,  
they may suggest using a cream that treats both.  
This means a product that works against both bacteria and fungus.  

Always follow your doctor’s instructions.  
Do not stop treatment early, even if the skin looks better.

# What Are Bacteria?

Bacteria are tiny, single-celled living things.  
They are some of the oldest life forms on Earth.  
There are millions of different types of bacteria.  
They live in almost every place on the planet.  

Bacteria can be found in soil, in seawater, and deep underground.  
Some even survive in radioactive waste.  
Many bacteria live on and inside people and animals.  
They live on the skin, in the mouth, in the airways, and in the digestive, reproductive, and urinary systems.  

Most of these bacteria do not harm us.  
They are called resident flora.  
There are as many of these bacteria in our bodies as there are cells in our body.  
Many of them are helpful.  
For example, they help us digest food.  
They also stop harmful bacteria from growing.  

Only a few types of bacteria cause illness.  
These are called pathogens.  
Sometimes, the helpful bacteria in our body can cause disease if something changes.  
For example, if the body’s natural barriers are damaged.  

Bacteria cause disease in several ways.  
They can make poisons.  
They can invade body tissues.  
Or they can do both.  
Some bacteria cause inflammation.  
This can harm the heart, lungs, nerves, kidneys, or gut.  
Some bacteria, like *Helicobacter pylori*, raise the risk of cancer.  

Some bacteria can be used as weapons.  
These include the bacteria that cause anthrax, botulism, plague, and tularemia.

---

## How Scientists Classify Bacteria

Scientists group bacteria in several ways.

### Scientific Names  
Each type of bacteria has a scientific name.  
The name has two parts: the genus and the species.  
For example, *Clostridium botulinum* is the name for the bacterium that causes botulism.  
Within a species, there are different strains.  
Strains can differ in their genes and chemicals.  
Some medicines work only on certain strains.

### Staining  
Scientists use special dyes to color bacteria.  
This helps them see the bacteria under a microscope.  
The most common method is called Gram staining.  
Bacteria that turn blue are called gram-positive.  
Bacteria that turn red are called gram-negative.  
The difference comes from their cell walls.  
Gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria cause different infections.  
They also respond to different antibiotics.  
There are other staining methods besides Gram staining.

### Shape  
All bacteria fall into one of three basic shapes:  
- Spheres (called cocci)  
- Rods (called bacilli)  
- Spirals or corkscrew shapes (called spirochetes)

### Need for Oxygen  
Bacteria are also grouped by whether they need oxygen to live.  
Bacteria that need oxygen are called aerobes.  
Bacteria that do not need oxygen and can be harmed by it are called anaerobes.  
Some bacteria, called facultative bacteria, can live with or without oxygen.

### Genetic Makeup  
Special tests can look at the genes of bacteria.  
This helps scientists understand differences between types.

---

## Bacteria in the Human Body

The human body holds hundreds of different types of bacteria.  
There are trillions of individual bacteria in total.  

Most of them live in these places:  
- On the skin and teeth  
- Between the teeth and gums  
- In the lining of the nose, throat, intestines, and vagina  

The types of bacteria vary by location.  
This is because each place has a different environment.  

Many of these bacteria are anaerobes.  
This means they do not need oxygen to live.  
Usually, they do not cause disease.  
In fact, many help us.  
For example, they help break down food in the gut.  

But if the lining of the body is damaged, these bacteria can cause problems.  
They can enter tissues that are normally protected.  
These tissues have no way to fight the bacteria.  
The bacteria can then infect nearby areas.  
This includes the sinuses, middle ear, lungs, brain, abdomen, pelvis, and skin.  
They can also enter the bloodstream and spread through the body.

---

## Bacterial Infections

Doctors group infections based on the type of bacteria causing them.  
For example, they may classify infections as gram-negative or gram-positive.  
This matters because different antibiotics work for each type.

These include:  
- Brucellosis  
- Campylobacter infections  
- Cat-scratch disease  
- Cholera  
- *Escherichia coli* infections  
- Gonorrhea

- Plague  
- *Pseudomonas* infections  
- *Salmonella* infections  
- Shigellosis  
- Typhoid fever  
- Tularemia

### Gram-Positive Infections  
These include:  
- Anthrax  
- *Clostridioides difficile*-induced colitis

### Infections by Oxygen Needs  
Some bacteria need oxygen to grow.  
These are called aerobes.  
Others do not need oxygen.  
These are called anaerobes.  

**Anaerobic infections** include:

## Treating Bacterial Infections

Many antibiotics are available to treat bacterial infections.  
But more bacteria are becoming resistant to antibiotics.  
This is a serious problem.

---

## How Bacteria Protect Themselves

Bacteria have many ways to defend themselves.

Some bacteria make a sticky layer called a biofilm.  
This layer helps them stick to surfaces.  
For example, bacteria in the mouth form a biofilm on teeth.  
This is called dental plaque.  
The plaque traps food.  
The bacteria use the food to grow.  
This process may cause tooth decay.  
Biofilms also protect bacteria from antibiotics.  
This makes infections harder to treat.  
For example, bacteria in artificial joints or heart valves can hide in biofilms.

Some bacteria have a protective capsule around them.  
This capsule stops white blood cells from eating the bacteria.  
Bacteria with a capsule are called encapsulated.

Gram-negative bacteria have an outer membrane.  
This membrane protects them from some antibiotics.  
If the membrane breaks, it releases harmful substances called endotoxins.  
These toxins make infections worse.

Some bacteria can form spores.  
Spores are inactive, tough forms of bacteria.  
They can survive in dry or nutrient-poor conditions.  
When conditions improve, the spore turns back into an active bacterium.

Bacteria have long, thin tails called flagella.  
These help them move.  
Bacteria without flagella cannot move on their own.

Some bacteria are naturally resistant to certain antibiotics.  
Others become resistant by gaining genes from other bacteria.  
Or their genes can change on their own.  

For example, soon after penicillin was first used in the 1940s, some *Staphylococcus aureus* bacteria gained genes that made penicillin useless.  
These resistant bacteria survived when penicillin was used.  
The non-resistant ones died.  
The resistant ones multiplied and became more common.

Scientists then made a new drug called methicillin.  
It worked against the penicillin-resistant bacteria.  
But soon, some *Staphylococcus aureus* bacteria gained genes to resist methicillin too.  
These are now called MRSA (methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus*).

The genes for resistance can pass to future generations.  
They can even pass to other types of bacteria.

The more antibiotics are used, the more likely resistance becomes.  
Experts say doctors should only prescribe antibiotics when needed.  
They should use them for the shortest time possible.  
Antibiotics should only be used for real bacterial infections.  
They should not be used for viral infections like colds or the flu.  

Giving antibiotics to people who do not have a bacterial infection does not help them.  
It only helps resistant bacteria grow.  
It also increases the risk of side effects like allergic reactions and diarrhea.  

Because antibiotics have been used so much and often wrongly, many bacteria are now resistant.  
New antibiotics are not being developed fast enough.

---

Hospitals are a major concern.  
Antibiotics are used often in hospitals.  
People and visitors can spread bacteria if they do not wash hands or follow hygiene rules.  
Many patients in hospitals have weak immune systems.  
This makes them more likely to get infected.

# How the Body Keeps Acid and Base Levels in Balance

The body makes acid all the time as it carries out normal processes. It also makes a small amount of base.  
Too much acid can harm the body’s cells and stop them from working properly.  
The body must keep the amount of acid in the blood very steady.  

The normal level of acid in the blood is between 37 and 43 nanoequivalents per liter.  
This is the same as 37 to 43 nanomoles per liter.  
The normal pH of blood is between 7.37 and 7.43.  
pH measures how acidic or basic the blood is.  
The ideal level is 40 nanoequivalents per liter and a pH of 7.40.  
If the body’s systems that control acid and base go wrong, it can lead to serious health problems.

Acid-base balance is closely linked to fluid balance and the balance of minerals in the body.  
Problems in one system often affect the other.

## Where Acid Comes From in the Body

The main source of acid in the body comes from breaking down food, especially carbohydrates and fats.  

Every day, the body makes 15,000 to 20,000 millimoles of carbon dioxide.  
Carbon dioxide is not an acid by itself.  
But in the blood, an enzyme helps it mix with water to form carbonic acid.  
Carbonic acid quickly breaks down into hydrogen ions (which are acid) and bicarbonate.  

The hydrogen ions attach to a protein in red blood cells called hemoglobin.  
When the blood reaches the lungs, the hydrogen ions are released.  
There, another enzyme helps turn the hydrogen ions and bicarbonate back into water and carbon dioxide.  
The water is removed by the kidneys.  
The carbon dioxide is breathed out.

Other sources of acid in the body include:

- When the body does not fully break down glucose or fats, it makes lactic acid and ketoacids.  
- When the body breaks down certain amino acids that contain sulfur, it makes sulfuric acid.  
- When the body breaks down certain amino acids that carry a positive charge, it makes acid.  
- When the body breaks down phosphate from food, it makes acid.  

This type of acid is called “fixed” or “metabolic” acid.  
It cannot be removed through the lungs.  
So the kidneys must neutralize it or get rid of it.

## Where Base Comes From in the Body

Most of the base in the body comes from:

- Breaking down certain amino acids that carry a negative charge, like glutamate and aspartate.  
- Breaking down certain organic acids like lactate and citrate. This process makes bicarbonate, which acts as base.

## How the Body Keeps Acid and Base in Balance

The body uses three main systems to keep acid and base levels steady:

- **Chemical buffers** – These are chemicals in the blood that act fast to soak up extra acid or base.  
- **Lungs** – The lungs help control acid by breathing out carbon dioxide.  
- **Kidneys** – The kidneys remove acid and make new bicarbonate to replace what was used.

# Amino Acid Metabolism Disorders

Amino acid metabolism disorders are inherited conditions. They happen when the body cannot process amino acids properly.

These conditions are passed from parents to children through genes. Genes are the instructions in your body that tell it how to work.

In most cases, both parents carry one copy of a faulty gene. But neither parent shows symptoms. The child must get two faulty copies—one from each parent—for the disorder to appear.

Some of these disorders are X-linked. This means only one faulty gene is needed to cause the condition in boys. Girls usually do not get the disorder because they have two X chromosomes.

Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. Your body uses them for many jobs. Some amino acids your body makes on its own. Others come from the food you eat.

These disorders can happen in two ways:
- The body cannot break down amino acids properly.
- The body cannot move amino acids into cells where they are needed.

Common types of amino acid metabolism disorders include:
- Branched-chain amino acid metabolism disorders
- Homocystinuria
- Phenylketonuria
- Tyrosinemia
- Hartnup disease

# Ascariasis (Roundworm Infection)

## What Is Ascariasis?

Ascariasis is an infection caused by a type of large roundworm. The most common worm is *Ascaris lumbricoides*. A similar worm, *Ascaris suum*, can also infect people. This worm mainly affects pigs but can spread to humans.

The infection spreads when people swallow worm eggs. These eggs come from human or pig feces. The eggs can get on food, water, or soil. They can also get on hands after touching dirty surfaces.

## Where Does It Happen?

This infection is most common in tropical and warm areas. It happens where sanitation is poor. This means no clean toilets, dirty water, or soil that is contaminated with feces.

Globally, about 819 million people have this infection. It is most common in school-aged children.

In the United States, most cases are seen in refugees, immigrants, or travelers who came from areas where the infection is common.

## How Does the Infection Spread?

You get infected by swallowing worm eggs. This can happen by:

- Eating food or drinking water that has been contaminated.
- Touching dirty soil and then putting your hands in your mouth.
- Handling pigs that are infected.
- Eating raw or undercooked vegetables or fruits that were grown in soil with pig or human feces.

## What Happens in the Body?

When you swallow the eggs, they hatch in your small intestine. The tiny worms that come out then travel through your body.

First, they move through the wall of your intestine. They go through your liver, heart, and into your lungs. In the lungs, they grow a little and cause coughing or wheezing.

Then, they climb up your airways and are swallowed again. They return to your small intestine. There, they grow into adult worms. The adult worms live in your intestines for about 1 to 2 years.

Adult female worms can be 8 to 14 inches long. Adult males are 6 to 12 inches long.

The whole process takes about 2 to 3 months.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Some people have no symptoms, especially if they have only a few worms.

### Early Symptoms (When Worms Are in the Lungs)

- Cough
- Wheezing
- Shortness of breath
- Sometimes coughing up blood

These symptoms happen when the worms are moving through the lungs. They usually go away after a few weeks.

People who live in areas where this infection is common often get some protection after their first exposure. Their body learns to fight the worms better.

### Later Symptoms (When Adult Worms Are in the Intestines)

- Belly pain or cramps
- Nausea or vomiting
- Loss of appetite
- Weight loss or poor growth in children

If there are many worms, they can block the intestines. This can cause severe pain, vomiting, and constipation.

Sometimes, a single worm can block the tube that carries bile from the liver to the gut. Or it can block the tube that carries digestive juice from the pancreas. This can cause:

- Severe belly pain
- Fever
- Jaundice (yellow skin or eyes)

In rare cases, worms can cause liver abscesses or infection in the belly cavity.

Fever from other illnesses or certain medicines can cause worms to move abnormally in the body.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look for signs of the infection in:

- Stool samples – They check for worm eggs under a microscope.
- Seeing adult worms – Sometimes, worms come out through the nose, mouth, or rectum. You might see them in your stool.
- Sputum – If worms are in the lungs, they may show up in coughed-up mucus.
- X-rays or scans – These can show worms blocking the intestines or other organs.

A blood test may show high levels of a certain type of white blood cell called eosinophils. This happens when worms are moving through the lungs. This condition is called Löffler syndrome.

## How Is It Treated?

All cases of ascariasis should be treated.

### Medicines for Most People

- Albendazole
- Mebendazole
- Ivermectin

These medicines kill the worms in the intestines.

### For Pregnant Women

- Pyrantel pamoate is the best choice.

Benzimidazole medicines (like albendazole and mebendazole) may harm a baby if used during pregnancy. Doctors only use them if the risk of not treating the infection is higher.

### Special Care Needed

Before using ivermectin, doctors must check if you have another infection called loiasis. This is common in parts of central Africa. Ivermectin can cause serious side effects in people with high levels of loiasis worms.

### For Severe Cases

If worms block the intestines, bile ducts, or pancreas, surgery or a procedure using a scope may be needed to remove them.

### For Lung Symptoms

If worms are in the lungs, treatment focuses on relieving symptoms. This may include:

- Inhalers to open the airways
- Steroid medicines to reduce swelling

Antiparasitic medicines are usually not used for lung symptoms alone.

## How Can It Be Prevented?

Good hygiene and clean sanitation are key.

### Do These Things to Stay Safe:

- Wash your hands well with soap and water:
  - Before eating or preparing food.
  - After using the toilet.
  - After touching soil or animals.
- Wash, peel, or cook all raw fruits and vegetables before eating.
- Do not eat raw or unwashed vegetables in areas where human or pig feces are used as fertilizer.
- Always use a toilet with proper sewage disposal.
- Do not defecate in the open.

## Key Facts

- Ascariasis is the most common worm infection in the world.
- Eggs hatch in the small intestine.
- The worms travel to the lungs, then back to the intestines to grow into adults.
- Worms in the lungs can cause cough and wheezing.
- A large group of worms can block the intestines.
- A single worm can block the bile or pancreatic ducts.
- Diagnosis is done by checking stool for eggs or seeing worms in the nose, mouth, or rectum.
- Treatment is with medicine like albendazole, mebendazole, ivermectin, or pyrantel pamoate (for pregnant women).
- Blockages may need surgery or a scope to remove the worms.

# What the Skin Does and How It Works

The skin is the body’s largest organ.  
It does many important jobs.  

## What the Skin Does

- It protects your body from injury.  
- It helps keep your body at the right temperature.  
- It keeps water and important chemicals inside your body.  
- It feels pain and pleasure.  
- It helps make vitamin D when you are in sunlight.  

The skin keeps your body’s important parts safe.  
It holds in nutrients and keeps harmful things out.  
It also blocks the sun’s harmful rays.  

Your skin is unique to you.  
Your skin color, texture, and lines help make you look different from others.  

If the skin does not work well or changes in appearance, it can hurt your health.  
This can affect both your body and your mind.  

## Skin Problems

Some skin problems only affect the skin.  
But sometimes, skin changes can be a sign of a bigger health issue.  

Doctors often need to check for other diseases when someone has a skin problem.  
They may do blood tests or other lab tests to look for a deeper cause.  

## The Three Layers of the Skin

The skin has three main layers:  
1. The outer layer – called the epidermis  
2. The middle layer – called the dermis  
3. The bottom layer – called the fat layer or subcutaneous layer  

Each layer has its own job.  

### The Epidermis – The Outer Layer

The epidermis is thin but strong.  
It is the top layer of your skin.  

Most of the cells in the epidermis are called keratinocytes.  
These cells start in the deepest part of the epidermis, called the basal layer.  

New keratinocytes move slowly up toward the surface.  
When they reach the top, they are shed.  
New cells push up from below to take their place.  

The very top part of the epidermis is called the stratum corneum.  
This layer is waterproof.  
When it is not damaged, it stops most germs like bacteria and viruses from getting in.  

The epidermis also protects your muscles, nerves, blood vessels, and organs from harm.  
In areas that need more protection, like your palms and soles, this layer is thicker.  

In the basal layer, there are special cells called melanocytes.  
These make melanin, a pigment that gives skin its color.  

Melanin’s main job is to block the sun’s harmful rays.  
Too much sun can damage your DNA.  
This damage can lead to skin cancer.  

The epidermis also has Langerhans cells.  
These are part of your body’s defense system.  
They help find foreign invaders and fight infections.  
But they can also cause skin allergies.  

### The Dermis – The Middle Layer

The dermis is thick and strong.  
It is made of tough, stretchy fibers.  
Most of it is collagen.  
A small part is elastin, which helps the skin stretch and bounce back.  

The dermis holds many important parts:  
- Nerve endings  
- Sweat glands  
- Oil glands (called sebaceous glands)  
- Hair follicles  
- Blood vessels  

#### Nerve Endings

Nerve endings feel pain, touch, pressure, and temperature.  
Some areas have more nerve endings than others.  
For example, your fingertips and toes are very sensitive.  

#### Sweat Glands

Sweat glands make sweat when you are hot or stressed.  
Sweat is mostly water and salt.  
As it dries on your skin, it cools you down.  

Some sweat glands, like those in your armpits and groin, make a thicker, oily sweat.  
When bacteria on the skin break down this sweat, it causes body odor.  

#### Oil Glands

Oil glands make sebum.  
Sebum is an oily substance.  
It keeps your skin soft and moist.  
It also helps block germs and other harmful things.  

#### Hair Follicles

Hair follicles grow all the hair on your body.  
Hair helps with your looks.  
It also helps control body temperature.  
It protects your skin from injury.  
It also helps you feel things better.  

Some hair follicles have stem cells.  
These cells can help repair damaged skin.  

#### Blood Vessels

Blood vessels in the dermis bring food and oxygen to the skin.  
They also help control your body temperature.  

When you are hot, blood vessels widen.  
More blood flows near the skin surface.  
This lets heat escape.  

When you are cold, blood vessels narrow.  
This keeps heat inside your body.  

The number of nerve endings, sweat glands, oil glands, hair follicles, and blood vessels changes from one part of the body to another.  
For example, your head has many hair follicles.  
Your feet soles have none.  

### The Fat Layer – The Bottom Layer

Below the dermis is a layer of fat.  
This layer helps protect your body from heat and cold.  
It also cushions your body.  
It stores energy for later use.  

The fat is made of living cells called fat cells.  
These cells are held together by tough tissue.  

The fat layer can be very thin, like on your eyelids.  
Or it can be thick, like on the belly or buttocks in some people.

# Melatonin

Melatonin is a natural substance made in your body. It helps control your sleep schedule. Your body makes melatonin in a small gland in your brain called the pineal gland.

Most melatonin sold today is made in a lab. It is not taken from animals. In some countries, melatonin is treated like a medicine and is regulated as such.

## What Is Melatonin Used For?

Melatonin is used to help with short-term sleep problems. This includes trouble sleeping after long flights (jet lag) and trouble falling asleep (insomnia).

Doctors are also studying melatonin for other uses. These include:
- Helping people with seasonal mood changes (seasonal affective disorder).
- Helping people who work night shifts to sleep better.
- Helping people with early Alzheimer disease to reset their sleep schedule.

There is no standard dose. Most people take between 0.5 and 5 milligrams. Take it by mouth about one hour before your usual bedtime. Use it on the day of travel and for 2 to 4 nights after you arrive.

Melatonin is also used to help reduce anxiety before and after surgery. Many people feel anxious before surgery. About 8 out of 10 people report feeling anxious.

## What Does the Research Say?

Some studies show melatonin helps reduce jet lag, especially when traveling east across 2 to 5 time zones.

A review of 19 studies found that melatonin helps people fall asleep faster by about 7 minutes. It also helps people sleep longer by about 8 minutes. Sleep quality also improves.

Another review found melatonin helps:
- People with insomnia fall asleep faster.
- People with delayed sleep schedules (like night owls) get back on track.
- Blind people who have no regular sleep pattern.

A third review found melatonin helps people with sleep problems caused by not getting enough sleep. It helps them fall asleep faster and sleep longer. But it does not improve how well they sleep through the night.

A Cochrane review found that melatonin may help night shift workers sleep longer. It may add about 24 minutes of daytime sleep and 17 minutes of nighttime sleep. But the evidence is not strong.

For children and adults with brain or mental health conditions, the evidence is weaker. But one review of 19 studies found melatonin helped children with developmental delays sleep better. It helped them fall asleep faster, sleep longer, and wake up less during the night.

A 2015 Cochrane review found melatonin helps reduce anxiety before surgery. But results after surgery were mixed. Some people felt better, others did not.

Melatonin may also help with sundowning. Sundowning is when people with dementia become confused or agitated in the late afternoon or evening.

A review of 7 studies found melatonin may improve sleep quality in people with Alzheimer disease.

Melatonin levels can vary widely between different products. One bottle may have much more or much less than the label says.

## Side Effects

Some people have side effects from melatonin. These include:
- Headache
- Dizziness
- Nausea
- Feeling sleepy during the day
- Temporary low mood

Melatonin may make depression worse in some people.

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine advises against using melatonin in older adults with dementia. There is not enough strong evidence to show it is safe or helpful.

One report says melatonin may be safe for older adults in the short term. But we do not know what happens with long-term use.

Older adults may feel the effects of melatonin longer than younger people. This can cause drowsiness during the day. More research is needed to understand the safety of melatonin in older adults and those with dementia.

Children may accidentally take melatonin. This happens because it is easy to find at home and is often used by families.

## Drug Interactions

Melatonin can interact with other medicines. These interactions can be serious.

- Melatonin may increase the risk of bleeding if you take warfarin (a blood thinner).
- Melatonin may reduce the effect of seizure medicines. This could raise the risk of seizures.
- Melatonin may make other sleep medicines (like benzodiazepines) stronger. This can cause more drowsiness.
- Melatonin may make the side effects of methamphetamine worse.
- Some medicines increase melatonin levels. These include:
  - Fluvoxamine (an antidepressant)
  - Estrogen (used in hormone therapy)
  - Quinolone antibiotics (like ciprofloxacin)
- Some medicines decrease melatonin levels. These include:
  - Carbamazepine (a seizure medicine)
  - Rifampin (an antibiotic)

Always check with your doctor before using melatonin if you take any other medicines.

For more information, visit the National Institutes of Health website. They have a page on melatonin as a dietary supplement.
