# Clubfoot and Other Foot Problems Present at Birth

Clubfoot is a condition that affects the foot from birth. It causes the foot to point downward and turn inward.

The heel tilts inward toward the middle of the body.  
The front part of the foot bends inward, away from the leg’s center line.  
This makes the foot look twisted.

Other foot problems that babies can be born with include:

- **Metatarsus adductus**: The front part of the foot curves inward.  
- **Metatarsus varus**: The front part of the foot turns inward and upward.  
- **Talipes calcaneovalgus**: The foot points upward and outward.  
- **Pes planus**: The foot has a flat arch.  
- **Flexible flat feet**: The foot is flat but can move normally.  
- **Tarsal coalition**: Two or more bones in the foot are joined together.  

These conditions are part of a group of birth-related bone and muscle problems.

# Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD)

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a rare brain disease. It causes mental decline, muscle jerks, and trouble walking. A rare form of the disease comes from eating beef from infected cows.

## What Causes CJD?

CJD happens when a normal protein in the brain changes shape and becomes harmful. This harmful protein builds up in the brain over time. It damages brain cells and causes them to die.

There are three main types of CJD:

### Sporadic CJD
- This is the most common type.
- It happens by chance, with no known cause.
- It affects about 1 to 2 people per million each year.
- Most people with this type are over 40, usually around age 65.
- It makes up about 85% of all cases.

### Familial CJD
- This type runs in families.
- It is caused by a faulty gene passed from parent to child.
- Only one copy of the faulty gene is needed to cause the disease.
- It makes up 5% to 15% of cases.
- It often starts at a younger age than sporadic CJD and can last longer.

### Acquired CJD
- This type is rare and makes up less than 1% of cases.
- It can happen in two ways:
  - Eating beef from cows with mad cow disease (called variant CJD).
  - Getting a medical treatment with contaminated tools or tissues (called iatrogenic CJD).

CJD is **not** spread through casual contact or even close personal contact like hugging or kissing.

## Variant CJD (vCJD)

Variant CJD is caused by eating beef from cows with mad cow disease.

- It usually starts in people around age 30 or younger.
- It is much younger than the usual age for other types of CJD.

### How Many Cases Have There Been?

As of May 2022:
- Worldwide: 233 cases
- United Kingdom: 178 cases
- Other countries: 55 cases

Even though many people in the United Kingdom ate contaminated beef for years, the number of cases is low. This is because:
- Sick cows were killed.
- Beef processing rules were changed.
- Cattle are now regularly tested for mad cow disease.

Since 2011, only 2 new cases have been found in the United Kingdom.

In the United States, 4 cases have been found. In Canada, 2 cases have been found. None of these people got the disease in North America.

### Hidden Risk

About 1 in 2,000 people in the United Kingdom carry the abnormal prion protein linked to vCJD. They have no symptoms. But if they donate blood or have surgery, they could pass the disease to others.

To reduce this risk:
- Blood donors are screened for possible exposure to vCJD.
- This risk is already very low outside of France and the United Kingdom.

Mad cow disease has been found in a few cattle in North America:
- 6 in the United States
- 20 in Canada

> **Did You Know?**  
> The human form of mad cow disease (variant CJD) has affected only 233 people worldwide.

## CJD from Medical Procedures

CJD can also be passed during medical treatments. This is called iatrogenic CJD.

It can happen if:
- A cornea or brain tissue from a person with CJD is transplanted.
- Brain surgery is done with tools that were used on a person with CJD.
- A medicine made from human brain tissue is used.
- A blood transfusion comes from a person with variant CJD.

Standard cleaning and sterilizing do **not** kill prions. But special cleaning methods with bleach or other strong disinfectants can destroy them.

### Past Cases

- Some people got CJD from growth hormone made from human pituitary glands.
- These hormones are now made in labs using genetic engineering, so they are safe.
- Only 3 people got vCJD from blood transfusions and showed symptoms.
- One other person got infected but did not get sick.
- All cases came from donors with the variant form.
- The last case was reported in 2007.
- The blood was given between 1996 and 1999.

## Symptoms of CJD

Symptoms start slowly and get worse quickly.

### Early Symptoms
- Memory problems
- Confusion
- Trouble thinking clearly

These symptoms are like those of Alzheimer’s disease. But in variant CJD, the first signs are often:
- Anxiety
- Depression
- Other mental health changes

### Later Symptoms
- Involuntary muscle jerks (called myoclonus)
- Trouble walking (staggering, like being drunk)
- Loss of balance and coordination
- Slow movements
- Unusual body positions (twisting of arms or legs)
- Muscle jerks when stretched
- Hallucinations
- Seizures

People may:
- Startle easily
- Jump at loud noises
- React strongly to sudden sounds
- Feel tired and sleepy
- Have trouble sleeping

The muscles that control breathing and coughing weaken. This raises the risk of pneumonia.

Vision may become blurry or dim.

The disease gets worse fast. Most people with CJD die within 6 to 12 months. About 20% live a year or longer.

People with variant CJD usually live about 18 months.

Pneumonia is the most common cause of death.

Some people may not show symptoms for 10 to 20 years after getting variant CJD.

## How Is CJD Diagnosed?

Diagnosing CJD is hard because other diseases can cause similar symptoms.

Doctors look for:
- Rapid mental decline
- Muscle jerks
- Unsteady walking
- No other treatable cause

Tests used include:

### Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
- Shows changes in the brain.
- Can detect signs of variant CJD.

### Spinal Tap (Lumbar Puncture)
- A small sample of fluid from around the spine is taken.
- This fluid is tested for prions.
- It can find CJD early and more accurately than other tests.
- A urine test can also help find variant CJD.

### Electroencephalography (EEG)
- Measures brain activity.
- Shows a pattern that happens in about 65% of people with CJD.
- But this pattern may not show up early in the disease.

### Brain Biopsy or Autopsy
- A brain sample is not usually needed while a person is alive.
- After death, a brain exam is the only way to confirm CJD and find the exact type.

## Treatment for CJD

There is no cure for CJD. The disease always leads to death.

But doctors can help ease symptoms with medicine.

Medicines that may help:
- Valproate: reduces muscle jerks
- Clonazepam: helps with muscle jerks and anxiety
- Sedatives or antipsychotic drugs: calm people who are anxious or confused

Support for the patient and family is very important. Options include:
- Hospice care
- Respite care (short-term relief for caregivers)
- Long-term care

The **CJD Foundation** offers support and information. They can help with:
- Caregiver tips
- Phone and video support groups

## How to Prevent CJD

Since there is no cure, stopping the spread of CJD is key. Only acquired CJD can be prevented.

### For Health Care Workers
- Wear gloves and face masks when handling body fluids or tissues.
- Use special cleaning methods for tools and materials.
- Do not use human pituitary hormones. Use lab-made growth hormone instead.
- Do not accept blood, corneas, or other tissues from people who may have been exposed to CJD.

### For Public Health
- Test cattle regularly for mad cow disease.
- Kill infected cows.
- Control what animals eat. Do not feed animal parts to animals that people eat.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture checks a sample of cattle each month for mad cow disease.

# What Is Undernutrition?

Undernutrition is a type of poor nutrition.  
It happens when the body does not get enough food or the right kinds of food.  
Malnutrition also includes eating too much food.  

Undernutrition can happen if:
- A person does not eat enough food.
- The body cannot absorb nutrients from food.
- The body cannot use nutrients properly.
- A person loses nutrients due to diarrhea.
- The body needs more nutrients than usual, such as during fast growth, illness, or disease like cancer or infection.

When undernutrition lasts a long time, it is called chronic undernutrition.  
It happens when a person does not get enough calories or key nutrients over many weeks or months.  

Undernutrition develops in stages.  
It can start slowly, such as when a person loses their appetite.  
It can also happen very fast, like in some cases of advanced cancer.  

The first signs are changes in the body’s nutrient levels.  
Then, cells begin to change inside the body.  
Finally, symptoms appear.  

Doctors diagnose undernutrition by:
- Asking about your health and eating habits.
- Doing a physical exam.
- Measuring body composition (like fat and muscle).
- Sometimes doing blood tests (for example, checking albumin levels).

---

## How Common Is Undernutrition?

The number of people who are undernourished has been rising since 2014.  
In 2023, nearly 735 million people, or 9.2% of the world’s population, were undernourished.  
This is 122 million more than in 2019, before the pandemic.  

Most of these people live in countries where food is hard to get.  
In Africa, the rate of undernutrition rose from 19.4% in 2021 to 19.7% in 2022.  
In Asia, the rate dropped from 8.8% in 2021 to 8.5% in 2022.  
That means more than 12 million fewer people were undernourished in Asia.  
But even with this drop, the number is still 58 million higher than before the pandemic.  

By 2030, nearly 600 million people may be chronically undernourished.  
This number would be 23 million lower if the war in Ukraine had not happened.  
It would be 119 million lower if neither the pandemic nor the war in Ukraine had occurred.

---

## What Increases the Risk of Undernutrition?

Undernutrition is caused by many factors, including:
- Poverty.
- War and conflict.
- Political instability.
- Overcrowded or unsafe living conditions.
- Spread of infectious diseases.
- Global health crises like pandemics.
- Rapid urban growth.

Some life stages are especially risky for undernutrition.  
This includes:
- Babies and young children.
- Teenagers.
- Pregnant women.
- Women who are breastfeeding.
- Older adults.

These times involve fast growth or higher nutrient needs.  
So, not getting enough food can cause serious harm.

---

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on the type of undernutrition.  
For example:
- Lack of protein and energy can cause weakness and weight loss.
- Missing certain vitamins can cause skin problems, tiredness, or poor vision.

Symptoms can be different for each person.

---

## How Is Undernutrition Diagnosed?

Doctors check for undernutrition by:
- Talking to you about your health and what you eat.
- Examining your body.
- Measuring your body fat, muscle, and weight.
- Doing blood tests if needed.

There are suggested guidelines for diagnosis.  
But not all doctors use the same rules yet.

---

# Hip Dislocations

A hip dislocation happens when the ball at the top of the thighbone comes out of the hip socket.

- The hip joint is usually damaged by a strong force hitting a bent knee.
- This often happens in car crashes when the knee hits the dashboard.
- People with a hip dislocation often have other injuries too.
- The hip hurts a lot. Most people cannot move their leg.
- Doctors check the hip and take x-rays to confirm the injury.
- Doctors can usually put the hip back in place without surgery.
- They give medicine to help reduce pain and make the process easier.

## How Hip Dislocations Happen

Most hip dislocations happen when the thighbone is pushed backward. This usually occurs when the knee and hip are bent, such as when sitting. Common causes include:

- Car crashes where the knee hits the dashboard.
- Falling from a high place, like a ladder.
- Contact sports such as football or rugby.
- In older adults, even a small force can cause a dislocation.

The same force that dislocates the hip can also break bones or injure other parts of the body. For example:

- The pelvis, knee, or leg may be broken.
- The back or head may be injured.

When the hip is dislocated, the bones may break. Nerves can be damaged, including the sciatic nerve. This can cause numbness in the foot or ankle. The blood supply to the top of the thighbone may be cut off. This can cause the bone tissue to die. This condition is called osteonecrosis.

An artificial hip joint can also become dislocated. This can happen after an injury. It can also happen during normal daily activities, even when crossing your legs.

## Signs and Symptoms

- The hip is very painful.
- You cannot move your leg.
- If the thighbone is pushed backward, the leg looks shorter and turns inward.
- If the thighbone is pushed forward, the leg turns outward. It may look shorter, but not as much as when pushed backward.
- If nerves are damaged, parts of the foot or ankle may feel numb.

## How Doctors Diagnose a Dislocated Hip

- Doctors examine the hip.
- They take x-rays to confirm the dislocation and check for broken bones.

If you think your hip is dislocated, do not move. Call emergency services. Get taken to the hospital by ambulance.

## Treatment for a Dislocated Hip

- Doctors will put the hip back in place (called reduction).
- You may need to rest in bed for a short time.
- Physical therapy is often needed.

If the hip dislocation is the only injury or the most serious one, doctors will fix it as soon as possible. Delaying treatment increases the risk of bone damage.

Before the procedure, you may get:
- A sedative (given through a vein).
- A pain reliever.
- A muscle relaxant.
- You may stay awake, or you may get a general anesthetic (you fall asleep).
- Or you may get a spinal anesthetic (numbs you from the waist down).

There are different ways to put the hip back in place. One method is called the Captain Morgan technique.

### Captain Morgan Technique

- You lie on your back on a hard surface, like a board on the floor.
- Your hips are held down with a sheet or belt.
- A doctor gently bends your knee and moves it so it is over the hip joint.
- The doctor places their knee under yours and lifts up while pushing down on your ankle.

After the hip is back in place, a CT scan is done. This checks for broken bones or loose pieces of bone or cartilage in the joint.

- If there are no broken bones or loose pieces, most people go home with crutches.
- You can touch the injured foot to the floor for balance.
- But you must not put any weight on it.
- You will need follow-up visits with an orthopedic doctor.
- You should not put weight on your foot until your doctor says it is safe.

Most people can walk without crutches in about one week. Some people may need crutches longer, or in rare cases, forever.

Bed rest is not recommended. It increases the risk of blood clots.

If you have other injuries, surgery may be needed to fix them.

After surgery, a physical therapist will gently move your joint. This is called passive exercise. They may use a machine that moves the joint slowly and continuously.

# Bipolar Disorders

Bipolar disorders involve strong mood swings. These swings go from high energy and excitement to deep sadness and low energy. Some people have more high-energy episodes. Others have more low-energy episodes.

No one knows exactly what causes bipolar disorder. But family history, brain chemicals, and life stress may play a role.

Doctors diagnose bipolar disorder by talking to the person and learning about their symptoms.

Treatment usually includes medicine to balance mood. Sometimes therapy helps too.

## When Does Bipolar Disorder Start?

Bipolar disorder often begins in the teenage years, twenties, or thirties.  
About 2 out of every 100 people will have this condition in their lifetime.

## Types of Bipolar Disorder

There are several types of bipolar disorder:

- **Bipolar I disorder**: A person has at least one full manic episode. This means they feel extremely high energy, act recklessly, or have false beliefs. They often have depressive episodes too. Men and women are equally likely to have this type.

- **Bipolar II disorder**: A person has major depression and at least one hypomanic episode. Hypomania is a milder form of mania. It does not include delusions or serious problems in daily life. This type is more common in women.

- **Substance- or medication-induced bipolar disorder**: Mood swings happen after using certain drugs or medicines. Examples include cocaine, amphetamines, steroids, or some antidepressants.

- **Bipolar disorder due to another medical condition**: A health problem causes mood swings. Examples include Cushing syndrome or brain injury. The mood changes are not just from confusion or illness.

- **Unspecified bipolar disorder**: A person has clear signs of bipolar disorder but does not meet the full criteria for any other type.

## Cyclothymic Disorder

In cyclothymic disorder, a person has long periods of mild highs and mild lows. These do not meet the full criteria for mania or major depression. The pattern lasts for more than two years.

---

## What Causes Bipolar Disorder?

The exact cause is not known. But:

- Family history matters. If a close family member has it, you are more likely to get it.
- Brain chemicals like serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine may not work properly.
- Stressful life events can trigger symptoms. But it is not clear if stress causes the disorder or just makes it worse.

Some medicines and substances can make symptoms worse. These include:

- Cocaine
- Amphetamines (like Adderall)
- Alcohol
- Steroids (like prednisone)
- Some antidepressants (like tricyclics)

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Bipolar disorder starts with a sudden change in mood. It can be a high (mania or hypomania) or a low (depression). Then the person may feel better for a while. But the symptoms often come back.

- Remissions (times when symptoms go away) are often complete. But some people still feel some symptoms.
- Some people struggle to work or keep relationships.
- Relapses are new episodes with stronger symptoms. These can be manic, depressive, hypomanic, or a mix.

Episodes can last from a few weeks to several months.  
Depressive episodes usually last longer than manic or hypomanic ones.

The time between episodes varies.  
Some people have only a few episodes in their life.  
Others have four or more episodes in one year. This is called rapid cycling.

Most people do not switch back and forth between mania and depression in every cycle.  
In most cases, one type of episode happens more often.

Some people with bipolar disorder try to end their life.  
The risk of suicide is much higher than in the general population—20 to 30 times higher.

---

## How Is Bipolar Disorder Diagnosed?

Doctors use the *Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders*, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR) to make a diagnosis.

Tests are done to rule out other causes:

- Blood tests for thyroid function (T4 and TSH) to check for overactive thyroid.
- Drug tests (in blood or urine) to check for stimulant use.
- Routine blood tests to rule out other medical problems.

### Diagnosing Bipolar I Disorder

A person must have had at least one full manic episode.  
They must also have had periods of remission and relapse.  
The manic episode may have been followed by or preceded by a hypomanic or depressive episode.

### Diagnosing Bipolar II Disorder

A person must have had at least one hypomanic episode and one major depressive episode.  
The symptoms must be serious enough to affect work, school, or relationships.  
They may need hospital care to stay safe.

Some people come in with depression. But they may have had past episodes of high energy or risky behavior.  
They may not mention these unless asked directly.

Doctors may use a tool called the Mood Disorder Questionnaire to help find hidden signs.

All patients should be asked gently but clearly about thoughts of suicide, plans, or actions.

### Other Conditions That Can Look Like Bipolar Disorder

Some other conditions can cause similar symptoms:

- Stimulant use (like cocaine or amphetamines)
- Steroid use
- Dopamine agonist medicines
- Overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism)
- Tumor in the adrenal gland (pheochromocytoma)

People with overactive thyroid often have other physical signs.  
But a simple blood test can check thyroid levels.

People with pheochromocytoma often have very high blood pressure.  
If blood pressure is normal, this test is not needed.

Other rare medical problems can cause mania.  
Depression can also be a symptom of many other health issues.

A review of drug use and drug testing can help find the cause.  
But even if a drug triggered an episode, doctors must look for mood symptoms that are not due to the drug.

Some people with schizoaffective disorder have manic episodes. But they also have lasting psychotic symptoms (like hallucinations or delusions).

People with bipolar disorder may also have anxiety problems. These include fear of social situations, panic attacks, or obsessive thoughts. This can make diagnosis harder.

---

## How Is Bipolar Disorder Treated?

Treatment usually has three steps:

1. **Acute phase**: To calm down the first serious symptoms.
2. **Continuation phase**: To reach full recovery.
3. **Maintenance phase**: To stay well and prevent future episodes.

Most people with hypomania can be treated at home.  
But severe mania or depression often need hospital care.

### Medicines

Common medicines include:

- Lithium
- Certain antiseizure medicines (like valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine)
- Second-generation antipsychotics (like aripiprazole, lurasidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, ziprasidone, cariprazine)

These medicines help balance mood.

### Therapy and Support

Talking with a therapist can help.  
Support from family and friends is also important.

---

## Key Points

- Bipolar disorder is a cycle of mood changes. It can include mania and depression (Bipolar I) or hypomania and depression (Bipolar II).
- It can make it hard to work or get along with others.  
  The risk of suicide is high.  
  But mild highs (hypomania) can sometimes help. They may bring more energy, creativity, confidence, or better social skills.
- The length and number of mood cycles vary.  
  Some people have only a few episodes in life.  
  Others have four or more episodes in one year (rapid cycling).
- Most people have one type of episode more often.  
  Few switch back and forth between mania and depression in every cycle.
- Diagnosis is based on symptoms.  
  But doctors must check for drug use and other medical problems like overactive thyroid or pheochromocytoma.
- Treatment depends on the symptoms and how severe they are.  
  It usually includes mood stabilizers (like lithium, valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine) and/or second-generation antipsychotics (like aripiprazole, lurasidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, ziprasidone, cariprazine).

# Amebic Keratitis

Amebic keratitis is a rare eye infection. It affects the clear front part of the eye called the cornea. It is caused by a tiny, single-celled organism called *Acanthamoeba*. This organism is not a worm or a virus. It is a type of parasite that lives in water and soil.

Most people who get this infection wear contact lenses.

## What Happens in Amebic Keratitis?

- The infection causes painful sores on the cornea.
- Vision becomes blurry or cloudy.
- The eye turns red.
- The eye may water more than usual.
- You may feel like something is in your eye.
- Bright light hurts your eye.

The sores usually affect only one eye. In rare cases, both eyes can be affected.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors need to check the cornea to find out if you have this infection.

- They take a small sample of tissue from the cornea.
- They look at the sample under a microscope.
- They grow the organism in a lab to confirm the infection.
- They also do a test called PCR to check for the ameba’s DNA.

These tests help the doctor know for sure that the infection is caused by *Acanthamoeba*.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment must start right away. The earlier it starts, the better the chance of recovery.

- An eye doctor (ophthalmologist) will treat the infection.
- If the sores are shallow, the doctor may gently remove damaged tissue with a cotton swab.
- You will get strong antibiotic eye drops. The most common ones are:
  - Chlorhexidine
  - Polyhexamethylene biguanide
  - Propamidine
  - Hexamidine

You will need to use the eye drops every 1 to 2 hours for the first 3 days. After that, the number of drops will slowly decrease as your eye heals.

Treatment usually lasts 6 to 12 months. Do not stop treatment early. If you do, the infection may come back.

Steroid eye drops should not be used. They can make the infection worse.

In rare cases, if the infection does not respond to medicine, the doctor may do surgery to replace the damaged cornea with a healthy one. This is called a corneal transplant.

## How Can You Prevent Amebic Keratitis?

If you wear contact lenses, follow these steps to lower your risk:

- Always clean and store your lenses as your eye doctor or the manufacturer says.
- Wash your hands well before touching your lenses.
- Use fresh contact lens solution every time.
- Never reuse old solution.
- Never add new solution to old solution.
- Never use tap water or homemade solutions to clean or store your lenses.
- Do not wear your lenses while swimming, in hot tubs, or when bathing.
- Do not sleep with your lenses in, even if you are awake.

Soft contact lenses (except daily disposable ones) and certain types of contact lens solutions are linked to a higher risk. Some solutions have been recalled because they were not safe.

## More Information

For more details, visit the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) website:
- [About Acanthamoeba Infections](https://www.cdc.gov/parasites/acanthamoeba/)

# Superficial Punctate Keratitis

This condition means the surface of the eye is inflamed. It shows up as small, scattered spots on the clear front part of the eye. The cause can be many different things.

## Symptoms

You may notice:
- Red eyes
- Tears or watery eyes
- Pain from bright light
- A feeling like something is in your eye
- Slight blurring of vision

## How It Is Diagnosed

A doctor uses a special light called a slit lamp to look at your eye. The spots on the cornea will show up when a special dye is used.

## Common Causes

The condition can be caused by:
- Viral eye infection (most often from adenovirus)
- Swollen eyelids (blepharitis)
- Dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca)
- A serious eye infection called trachoma
- Chemical burns to the eye
- Too much exposure to ultraviolet light (like from welding, sunlamps, or snow glare)
- Wearing contact lenses too long
- Some medicines taken by mouth (like adenine arabinoside)
- Eye drops that are harmful (either the medicine or the preservative in the drop)
- Weakness on one side of the face (like Bell palsy)

## Treatment by Cause

- **Viral eye infection**: The eye problem usually gets better on its own in about three weeks.
- **Blepharitis, dry eyes, or trachoma**: These need specific treatment.
- **Overwearing contact lenses**: Stop wearing the lenses. Use an antibiotic ointment four times a day. Do not cover the eye with a patch. This can cause a serious infection.
- **Eye drops that are causing harm**: Stop using the drop. Talk to your doctor about a safer option.
- **Face nerve weakness (like Bell palsy)**: This may cause the eye to not close well. The eye needs special care to stay protected.

If you wear contact lenses and get this condition, see your doctor the next day.

## Ultraviolet Keratitis (UV Eye Burn)

UV light can burn the surface of the eye. This is called ultraviolet keratitis.

### Common Causes
- Looking at a welding arc without protection
- Electric sparks from high-voltage equipment
- Sunlamps used for tanning
- Sunlight bouncing off snow at high altitudes

The higher you go, the stronger the UV light gets. Snow reflects most of the UV light, which can cause a burn.

### Symptoms

Symptoms do not start right away. They usually appear 8 to 12 hours after exposure. They last 1 to 2 days. You may have:
- Pain in the eye
- Watery eyes
- Redness
- Swollen eyelids
- Trouble with bright light
- Headache
- A feeling like something is in your eye
- Blurry vision

Permanent vision loss is very rare.

### Diagnosis

Your doctor will ask about your exposure. They will check your eye and see the small spots. They will also make sure there is no foreign object or infection.

### Treatment

- Use an antibiotic ointment (like bacitracin or erythromycin) every 8 hours.
- Sometimes a drop that relaxes the eye muscle (like cyclopentolate) is used every 4 hours.
- For strong pain, take acetaminophen every 4 hours for up to 24 hours.
- The eye surface heals on its own in 1 to 2 days.
- See your doctor again in 24 hours.

### Prevention

Wear dark glasses or a welder’s helmet that blocks UV light when working with bright lights or in snowy areas.

# Carbapenems

Carbapenems are a type of antibiotic. They belong to a group called beta-lactam antibiotics. These antibiotics have a special chemical shape called a beta-lactam ring.

Other antibiotics in this group include cephalosporins, monobactams, and penicillins.

Carbapenems work against many different kinds of bacteria. They are especially useful for treating infections caused by bacteria that do not respond to other antibiotics.

## Types of Carbapenems

The following are examples of carbapenems:

- Ertapenem  
- Imipenem  
- Meropenem  
- Tebipenem  

These medicines are given through an injection into a vein. They are not taken as pills.

Doctors often use carbapenems together with another type of antibiotic called an aminoglycoside. Using both together can make the treatment more effective.

Imipenem is always given with another medicine called cilastatin. Sometimes, it is also given with a medicine called relebactam. These two medicines are not antibiotics. They help protect imipenem so it stays in the body longer and works better.

## How Carbapenems Work

Bacteria have a tough outer layer called a cell wall. This layer protects them. Like other beta-lactam antibiotics, carbapenems stop bacteria from building this cell wall. Without a cell wall, the bacteria die.

## Allergic Reactions

Some people who are allergic to penicillin may also have an allergic reaction to carbapenems. This is rare. But if you have ever had a bad reaction to penicillin, tell your doctor.

## Common Uses and Side Effects

Here is a table showing the main uses and possible side effects of each carbapenem.

### Carbapenems

| Medicine | Common Uses | Possible Side Effects |
|--------|-------------|------------------------|
| Ertapenem | Infections like sepsis, pneumonia, abdominal infections, and urinary tract infections | Rarely causes seizures (very low risk) |
| Imipenem with cilastatin | Infections like sepsis, pneumonia, abdominal infections, and urinary tract infections | Can cause seizures (slightly higher risk than other carbapenems) |
| Imipenem with cilastatin and relebactam | Infections caused by bacteria that resist other antibiotics | Can cause seizures (slightly higher risk) |
| Meropenem | Infections like sepsis, pneumonia, abdominal infections, and urinary tract infections | Can cause seizures (slightly higher risk) |
| Meropenem with vaborbactam | Infections caused by bacteria that resist other antibiotics | Can cause seizures (slightly higher risk) |
| Tebipenem | Infections like urinary tract infections and abdominal infections | Rarely causes seizures |

> **Note:** Ertapenem is not used for infections caused by *Pseudomonas* or *enterococcal* bacteria.

## Using Carbapenems During Pregnancy

In some animal studies, certain carbapenems caused harm to unborn babies. But this has not been seen in all animals or with all carbapenems. There is not enough safety data in pregnant women. So, doctors only use carbapenems during pregnancy if no safer antibiotic is available.

## Using Carbapenems While Breastfeeding

Small amounts of carbapenems can pass into breast milk. But we do not have enough information to say for sure if this is safe for babies.

It is possible that carbapenems could affect the healthy bacteria in a baby’s gut. This might lead to digestive problems.

If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, talk to your doctor before using any carbapenem.

# Herpangina

Herpangina is a viral illness that causes fever and sores in the back of the mouth. It is caused by certain types of enteroviruses, especially group A coxsackieviruses. These viruses lead to small blisters and open sores in the back part of the throat.

Herpangina often spreads in outbreaks. It most often affects babies and children.

## Symptoms of Herpangina

The illness starts suddenly. You may have a high fever, a sore throat, a headache, and lose your appetite. Some people also have neck pain. Babies may drool more than usual or throw up.

Within two days of the first symptoms, small grayish spots appear in the back of the mouth. These spots are about the size of a pinhead. They turn into small blisters surrounded by redness. The blisters usually show up on the tonsil pillars. They can also appear on the soft part of the roof of the mouth, the tonsils, the uvula, or the tongue.

Over the next 24 hours, the blisters break open and become shallow sores. These sores are usually less than half a centimeter across. They heal within one to seven days.

You may have trouble swallowing. You might drool more. You may refuse to eat or drink. This can lead to dehydration. But serious problems from herpangina are rare.

After you recover, you will be protected against the same virus. But you can get herpangina again from a different type of enterovirus.

## How Doctors Diagnose Herpangina

Doctors diagnose herpangina by asking about your symptoms and looking at your mouth.

The sores in the back of the mouth are a key clue. They look different from other mouth sores.

Testing is not usually needed. But if needed, doctors can:

- Test the sores for the virus using a lab test called reverse transcriptase–polymerase chain reaction.
- Try to grow the virus from the sores in a lab (this is less common).
- Check blood to see if your body is making more antibodies against the virus.

Other mouth sores can look similar. But they are different:

- Recurrent aphthous ulcers usually do not appear in the back of the throat. They also do not come with fever or other body-wide symptoms.
- Herpetic stomatitis causes larger, longer-lasting sores. These sores are more common in the front of the mouth.
- Coxsackievirus A10 causes a similar illness. But instead of blisters and sores, it causes small white or yellowish bumps in the throat.

## How Herpangina Is Treated

There is no cure for herpangina. Treatment focuses on making you feel better.

You can take pain medicine to reduce pain and fever. Use mouth rinses or gels to soothe the sores. Drink plenty of fluids to stay hydrated. Offer cool, soft foods if you can eat.

Good hand hygiene is important. Wash your hands often, especially after changing diapers or handling stool. Avoid touching open sores or saliva. This helps stop the virus from spreading to others.

# What Causes Skin Color?

Skin color comes from a substance called melanin.  
Melanin gives color to your skin, hair, and eyes.  
The more melanin you have, the darker your skin appears.  
The less melanin you have, the lighter your skin appears.  

If you had no melanin at all, your skin would be very pale white.  
It might show a pink color because of blood under the skin.  

People with light skin make very little melanin.  
People with dark skin make a moderate amount.  
People with very dark skin make the most melanin.  

Some people have a condition called albinism.  
They have little or no melanin.  
Their skin, hair, and eyes are very light.  

Usually, melanin is spread evenly across the skin.  
But sometimes, small areas have more melanin than others.  
These areas can appear as spots or patches.  

Examples of such spots include:  
- Freckles  
- Age spots (also called lentigines)  
- Melasma  

Melanin is made by special cells called melanocytes.  
These cells live in the deepest part of the outer layer of the skin.  
This layer is called the basal layer.  
After making melanin, the cells pass it to nearby skin cells.  

---

## Skin Color Changes: Common Problems

Some skin conditions cause changes in color.  
These changes can affect large areas of skin.  
Or they can affect only small, specific areas.  

There are three main types of skin color changes:  
- Depigmentation  
- Hypopigmentation  
- Hyperpigmentation  

### Depigmentation  
This means the skin loses all its color.  
The skin becomes white.  
A common condition that causes this is vitiligo.  

### Hypopigmentation  
This means the skin has less melanin than normal.  
The skin looks lighter than it should.  
It may be lighter than nearby skin that is not affected.  

Widespread hypopigmentation happens in albinism.  
Other causes include:  
- Past skin injuries, such as blisters, ulcers, burns, or chemical exposure  
- Skin infections that have healed  
- Inflammatory skin conditions that have healed, like atopic dermatitis or psoriasis  
- Rare inherited conditions  

### Hyperpigmentation  
This means the skin has more melanin than normal.  
The skin becomes darker.  
Sometimes the color is not just darker, but different from normal skin.  

Common causes include:  
- Skin inflammation from any cause  
- Certain medicines or chemicals  
- Sun exposure  
- Skin cancer

# What Are Paraphilias and Paraphilic Disorders?

Paraphilic disorders are repeated, strong sexual thoughts, urges, or actions that cause serious problems. These include sexual feelings about things like objects, children, or people who do not agree to sex. They may also involve pain, shame, or control. These behaviors can hurt others or cause serious harm.

Some people have unusual sexual interests. These are called paraphilias. But not all unusual interests are a disorder. A paraphilia only becomes a disorder if it causes serious distress or harm.

A paraphilic disorder is diagnosed when both of these are true:

- The sexual thoughts or urges are strong and keep happening.
- The person feels great distress or has serious problems in life. This can include problems at work, with relationships, or with mental health. Or the behavior could hurt someone else.

People with a paraphilic disorder often struggle to have healthy, loving, and equal relationships with a partner who agrees to be involved. They may also have other emotional or personal problems.

The pattern of unusual sexual feelings usually starts before puberty. Three possible reasons may explain this:

- Early anxiety or emotional pain can stop normal sexual development.
- A person may learn to feel sexual pleasure in unusual ways. This can happen after a strong sexual experience in childhood.
- The sexual feelings may become linked to certain symbols or habits. For example, a person may become aroused by a certain object because it was linked to a past sexual feeling.

It is not clear if all paraphilias come from these mental or emotional causes. Some research shows that brain differences may play a role in some cases, such as in people who are attracted to children.

In most cultures, paraphilias are more common in men. Scientists do not fully understand why this is, but biology may be part of the reason.

Many different paraphilias have been described. But most are rare. The most common ones are:

- Voyeuristic disorder: Getting sexual pleasure from watching others without their knowledge.
- Exhibitionistic disorder: Getting sexual pleasure from showing one’s body to others without their consent.
- Frotteuristic disorder: Getting sexual pleasure from touching or rubbing against someone without their consent.
- Sexual masochism disorder: Getting sexual pleasure from being hurt or humiliated.
- Sexual sadism disorder: Getting sexual pleasure from hurting or humiliating another person.
- Pedophilic disorder: Having strong sexual urges toward children.
- Fetishistic disorder: Getting sexual pleasure from non-living things, like clothes or shoes.
- Transvestic disorder: Getting sexual pleasure from wearing clothes of the opposite gender.

Some of these behaviors are against the law. If someone is caught, they can go to prison. They may also have to register as a sex offender for life.

Some people with these disorders also have serious personality problems. For example, they may be aggressive, lack empathy, or have a strong sense of self-importance. These issues make treatment harder.

It is common for one person to have more than one paraphilic disorder.

Doctors who treat these disorders have guidelines to help them decide when to use medicine.

# Teeth Grinding

Teeth grinding is when you tightly press or rub your teeth together.

You can grind your teeth while you are awake or while you are asleep.  
Grinding your teeth over time can wear down and damage them.  
The damage is often worse if you have acid reflux or sleep apnea.  
Artificial teeth made of gold, porcelain, or both can crack or break.  
If porcelain is on the chewing surface, the tooth across from it may wear down instead.  
Some people also get headaches or pain in the jaw, neck, or face.  
This pain comes from the jaw muscles tightening over and over.

Most people who grind their teeth do not mean to.  
The grinding happens without you knowing.  
It is usually worst when you are asleep.  
Even though you are asleep, your jaw can press down with a force of up to 250 pounds.  
This happens because your body does not have a built-in warning system to stop you.  
You may not notice you are grinding your teeth.  
But family members often hear the sound or see it happen.

## How to Treat Teeth Grinding

**When you are awake:**  
Try to stop clenching your teeth on purpose.  
Be aware of when you are doing it.  
Try to relax your jaw.

**When you are asleep:**  
Wear a plastic mouth guard at night.  
This guard fits between your upper and lower teeth.  
It stops your teeth from rubbing together.  
If your grinding is very bad, your dentist may suggest wearing the guard during the day too.  
This helps protect your teeth and reminds you not to clench your jaw.

Most guards are made by a dentist.  
The dentist shapes them to fit your mouth.  
For some people, a simpler guard is enough.  
These are sold over the counter.  
You can shape them at home with hot water.  
They are like the guards athletes wear.  
But you should see a dentist before using one.  
This makes sure it is safe and right for you.

## More Information

The following website may help you learn more about oral health:

**MouthHealthy.org**  
This site gives clear advice on keeping your mouth healthy.  
It covers what to eat, how to choose toothpaste and toothbrushes, and how to find a dentist.  
It also shows which products have the American Dental Association’s seal of approval.

# What Is Iron Overload?

Iron is a mineral your body needs to stay healthy.  
Your body carefully controls how much iron it takes in from food.  
It also recycles iron from old red blood cells.  

You lose a small amount of iron every day.  
This happens when skin and digestive tract cells naturally die and fall off.  
Even a normal diet has only a little iron.  
Most people do not get too much iron.  

But some people can get too much iron.  
This is called iron overload.  
It can happen for several reasons:

- A genetic condition that causes the body to absorb too much iron (called hemochromatosis).  
- Getting many blood transfusions over time.  
- Taking too many iron supplements or pills.  
- Breaking down red blood cells too quickly.  

Women lose iron during their monthly periods.  
Because of this, women who still have periods rarely develop iron overload symptoms.  
Most women only start to see symptoms after menopause.  

When the body takes in more iron than it can use, the extra iron builds up in body tissues.  
If too much iron collects in certain organs, it can cause problems.  
These organs include the pancreas, the reproductive organs, the pituitary gland, the liver, and the heart.  

If someone takes a very large amount of iron at once—like by overdosing on iron pills—it can be life-threatening.  
This is called iron poisoning.  
It can severely damage the stomach and intestines, the liver, the heart, and the brain.  
Iron poisoning can lead to death.  

There is a type of iron overload seen in some people in sub-Saharan Africa.  
It is linked to drinking a fermented drink that is high in iron.  
Scientists think a genetic factor may play a role.  
But so far, no specific gene has been found to cause this condition.

# Transthoracic Needle Biopsy

This test takes a small sample of tissue from the chest using a needle. The sample is checked under a microscope to find out what is causing a problem.

## Why This Test Is Done

Your doctor may recommend this test to check:

- A lump or spot in the outer part of the lung
- Abnormal areas in the center of the chest (mediastinum) or lining of the lungs (pleura)
- Lung infections that do not clear up, especially if another test called bronchoscopy cannot be used or did not give a clear answer

When the test is done using a CT scan for guidance and a trained lab expert is present, it can correctly identify cancer in about 90 to 95 out of 100 cases.

## When This Test Should Not Be Done

This test is not safe for some people. It should not be done if:

### Absolute Reasons to Avoid the Test

- Low platelet count (less than 50,000 per microliter of blood)
- Blood clotting problems that cannot be fixed
- A bleeding disorder

### Possible Reasons to Avoid the Test

- Large air pockets in the lungs (bullous lung disease) – this raises the risk of a collapsed lung
- Having had one lung removed on the other side – this makes it harder to handle a collapsed lung
- Severe, uncontrolled coughing – this raises the risk of a collapsed lung
- Being on a breathing machine – this raises the risk of a collapsed lung
- High blood pressure in the lungs (pulmonary hypertension)

If you have had a lung removed on the other side, the test should be delayed or avoided. A collapsed lung could be very dangerous for you.

Do not do this test on:
- Hydatid cysts (a type of parasitic infection in the lung)
- Lung abscesses (pockets of infection and pus)
- Blood vessel problems in the lung

## How the Test Is Done

A doctor who specializes in imaging, usually a radiologist, performs the test. A lab expert may also be in the room.

The area is cleaned and numbed with local anesthesia. You will lie on your side or back. The doctor uses imaging to guide the needle.

- A CT scan is used most often.
- Ultrasound may be used if the problem is near the lining of the lung.

You will be asked to hold your breath while the needle is placed into the area of concern.

The doctor may use saline (salt water) to help collect the sample. Two or three samples are taken.

The samples are sent to a lab for testing. They are checked for cancer, infection, or other causes.

After the test, a chest X-ray or real-time X-ray (fluoroscopy) is done to check for:
- A collapsed lung
- Bleeding

## Possible Problems After the Test

After the test, you may have:

- A collapsed lung (pneumothorax) – this happens in 10 to 17 out of 100 people
- Coughing up blood (hemoptysis) – this happens in 1 to 10 out of 100 people
- Bleeding inside the lung tissue
- Air in the bloodstream (air embolism) – rare
- Air under the skin (subcutaneous emphysema) – rare

Most of these problems are mild and can be treated. Some may need extra care.

# Juvenile Angiofibromas

Juvenile angiofibroma is a rare, noncancerous growth.  
It forms in the back of the nose.  
It grows in the same area where the adenoids are.  

## What Happens Inside the Throat

This tumor mostly affects teenage boys.  
It has many blood vessels inside it.  
It can grow slowly.  
It may spread to the area around the brain.  
It can also grow into the eye sockets.  

## Signs and Symptoms

The tumor often causes a blocked nose.  
It can cause headaches.  
It may lead to nosebleeds.  
These nosebleeds can be very heavy.  
The face might swell.  
One eye may bulge out.  
A lump may stick out from the nose.  
The nose may change shape.  
If the tumor grows slowly, you may not notice any symptoms at first.  

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors look at your symptoms to suspect the problem.  
To confirm the diagnosis, they use imaging tests.  
They usually do a CT scan and an MRI.  
A CT scan uses x-rays to make detailed pictures of the inside of the body.  
An MRI uses magnets and radio waves to create detailed images.  
Doctors may also do an angiography.  
This test takes x-rays of the blood vessels.  
A special dye is injected into a vein to make the blood vessels show up clearly.  
This helps doctors see the blood supply to the tumor.  
It also allows them to block the blood vessels before surgery.  
Blocking the blood vessels helps reduce bleeding during surgery.  

## How It Is Treated

The main treatment is surgery to remove the tumor.  
The surgeon removes the tumor through the nose.  
Sometimes, radiation therapy is used too.  
Radiation therapy uses high-energy beams to kill tumor cells.  
It is used when surgery cannot remove the entire tumor.  
It is also used if the tumor comes back after surgery.

# Massage Therapy

Massage therapy is a treatment that uses hands to press, rub, and move the body’s soft tissues. This includes muscles, tendons, and connective tissue.

The main goals of massage therapy are to:
- Reduce pain
- Ease tight muscles
- Lower stress levels

Many people find that massage helps with common health issues. It may help with:

- Headaches
- Pain from surgery, long-term conditions, or injuries
- Pain related to serious illness or end-of-life care
- Pelvic pain
- Pain during labor
- Burns
- Symptoms in people with dementia
- Fibromyalgia (a condition that causes widespread pain)
- Feelings of anxiety or depression
- Symptoms in people with cancer, such as pain, tiredness, stress, and swelling
- Sleep, growth, weight gain, and digestion in premature babies
- Quality of life, stress, and immune health in people with HIV/AIDS
- Movement and non-movement symptoms in people with Parkinson’s disease

Massage is not safe for everyone. People with low blood platelets or bleeding problems may get bruises or bleeding from massage. Therapists must be careful not to press on bones that are weak from osteoporosis or cancer that has spread. 

Always talk to your doctor before starting massage therapy if you have a health condition.

(For more information, see: Overview of Integrative, Complementary, and Alternative Medicine.)

# Blepharospasm

Blepharospasm means the muscles around your eye twitch or spasm uncontrollably.

Doctors do not always know what causes it.  
It is more common in women than in men.  
It sometimes runs in families.  
It can also be linked to other eye problems.  
These include:  
- Eyelashes that grow inward  
- Something stuck in the eye  
- Dry eyes  

It can also be linked to nerve problems, such as Parkinson disease.

## Symptoms

You may blink too much or close your eyes without meaning to.  
In serious cases, you may not be able to open your eyes at all.  
Fatigue, bright light, and stress can make the spasms worse.

## What Helps

If the spasms are mild, try simple things like:  
- Singing  
- Humming  
- Touching your eyelid  
- Chewing gum  

If these do not help, your doctor may suggest an injection.  
The injection uses a medicine called botulinum toxin A.  
It is given into the eye muscles.  
This can stop or reduce the spasms.

Other helpful steps include:  
- Taking medicine to ease anxiety  
- Wearing sunglasses to reduce light sensitivity  

If the injection does not work and your symptoms are severe, surgery may be an option.  
The surgery cuts the muscles in the eyelid to reduce the spasms.

# What Are Vascular Bleeding Disorders?

Bleeding can happen if there are problems with:

- Platelets  
- Blood clotting factors  
- Blood vessels  

This overview focuses on bleeding caused by problems with blood vessels.

## What Happens in Vascular Bleeding Disorders?

When blood vessels are weak or damaged, small spots or bruises can appear on the skin or inside the mouth and nose. These are called:

- **Petechiae**: Tiny spots less than 2 millimeters across.  
- **Purpura**: Larger spots between 2 and 10 millimeters across.  
- **Ecchymoses**: Even bigger bruises, over 10 millimeters across.  

These marks are usually not serious. They often look like small red or purple dots or patches.  

The most common cause of these marks is a problem with the blood vessels themselves.  

One exception is **hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia**. This condition can cause serious bleeding, unlike most other vascular bleeding disorders.

## Causes of Vascular Bleeding Disorders

Some rare inherited conditions weaken the blood vessels. These include:

- **Ehlers-Danlos syndrome** – a condition where the body does not make enough strong connective tissue around blood vessels.  
- **Pseudoxanthoma elasticum** – a rare disease that affects the elastic fibers in blood vessels.  
- **Osteogenesis imperfecta** – a disorder that causes weak bones and fragile blood vessels.  
- **Marfan syndrome** – a condition that affects connective tissue throughout the body, including blood vessels.  

In these conditions, the blood vessels are weak because they lack strong support from collagen.

## Other Causes of Bleeding

- **Scurvy** – a disease caused by a lack of vitamin C. It can lead to bleeding from weak blood vessels.  
- **Immunoglobulin A–associated vasculitis** – a condition where the immune system attacks small blood vessels. It is common in children and can cause bleeding and rashes.

## How Are These Disorders Diagnosed?

Most people with vascular bleeding disorders have normal results on standard blood tests for clotting.  

Doctors usually diagnose these conditions by looking at symptoms and medical history.  

In some cases, special tests may be needed. For example:

- Blood tests to check for abnormal proteins (immunoglobulins) in certain rare blood disorders.

## How Are These Disorders Treated?

Treatment aims to stop bleeding when it happens and to support the body.

- Some people need blood transfusions if they lose a lot of blood.  
- Many people need iron supplements. This is because repeated bleeding from the nose, mouth, or gut can lead to low iron levels.  
- Iron supplements help replace lost iron and treat iron deficiency anemia.  

Always follow your doctor’s advice for treatment.

# Pain in the Remaining Limb After Amputation

After an amputation, about 60 out of 100 people have pain in the remaining part of the limb. This pain can make daily tasks hard. It can also lower your quality of life and slow down your recovery. You should get this pain checked and treated right away. Some causes can be serious.

## What Is Phantom Limb Sensation?

Phantom limb sensation means you feel your missing limb is still there. This feeling is not painful. It can help you know where your limb was. It is not the same as phantom limb pain.

## What Is Persistent Residual Limb Pain?

Persistent residual limb pain is a long-term problem. It is different from phantom limb pain and phantom limb sensation.

## Common Causes of Residual Limb Pain

- Pain from surgery
- Skin infection
- Deep infection in the bone or deeper tissues
- Pressure sores, with or without broken skin
- Nerve tissue growing too much (called a neuroma)
- Nerve damage (neuropathy)
- Bone spurs
- Poor blood flow to the limb (ischemia)
- Phantom limb pain
- Complex regional pain syndrome

## Check for Infection

Look closely at your remaining limb. Watch for signs of infection. These include redness, swelling, warmth, pus, or open sores. If you see any of these, see your doctor.

Even if you do not see clear signs of infection, see your doctor if:
- The pain is sudden and very strong
- You have a fever

Your doctor may clean the area. They may flush it with a special solution. Dead skin may be removed. A bandage will be applied. You may need antibiotics. In some cases, surgery is needed.

## Pain from the Surgical Wound

Pain from the surgery usually goes away as the wound heals. This takes about 3 to 6 months. If pain lasts longer, it may be due to infection or a prosthesis that does not fit well.

Treatment depends on the cause. You may need to stop wearing the prosthesis until the wound heals. You may also need painkillers. Your doctor may adjust the prosthesis.

## Nerve Damage Pain (Neuropathic Pain)

Nerve damage pain is common after amputation. It often feels like shooting or burning. It usually starts within 7 days after surgery. It can go away on its own. But it often lasts a long time.

The pain can be constant and severe. Or it can come and go. Nerves may have been hurt during the injury or cut during surgery.

Treatments include:
- Counseling or therapy
- Physical methods (like heat or cold)
- Antidepressants
- Antiseizure medicines

## Painful Neuromas

A neuroma is a noncancerous growth of nerve tissue. It can form where a nerve was cut during surgery or trauma. It can cause sharp, electric-like, tingling, stabbing, or prickly pain.

This pain usually does not happen in the missing limb. But it can. Other signs include:
- Strange feelings without touching the area
- Unpleasant sensations when the muscles in the remaining limb tighten
- Pain when the skin is lightly touched

The longer the neuroma is irritated—by wearing the prosthesis or moving the muscles—the longer it takes to heal.

Your doctor may use MRI or ultrasound to confirm the diagnosis. In severe cases, surgery may be needed.

## Poor Blood Flow

Some people who had amputation due to poor blood flow (like peripheral arterial disease) may still have poor blood flow in the remaining limb. This can be hard to spot.

## Pain Without a Clear Medical Cause

If no medical problem is found, try this:
- Gently massage the area
- Lightly tap the area
- Keep the limb raised

This may help reduce pain. If this does not work, try mild painkillers like ibuprofen or acetaminophen.

If pain continues, see a pain management specialist.

## Pain in Other Parts of the Body

Sometimes pain shows up in other limbs, hips, spine, shoulders, or neck. This can happen because the prosthesis changes how you walk or stand. It can also come from repeating the same movements.

To help prevent or ease this pain:
- Do regular stretching exercises
- Do strength-building exercises

A physical therapist can help you create a safe and effective exercise plan.

---

## Phantom Limb Pain

Most people feel pain in the missing limb at some point. The pain is real. But it feels like it is coming from a limb that is no longer there.

This pain usually starts within days after surgery. But it can start months or even years later.

The pain can feel like:
- Tingling
- Shooting
- Stabbing
- Throbbing
- Burning
- Aching
- Pinching
- Clamping
- Squeezing

Phantom limb pain is often worse right after surgery. It usually gets better over time. Many people feel it more when not wearing the prosthesis—like at night.

Using both spinal and general anesthesia during surgery may lower the chance of this pain.

Treatments that may help:
- Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS)
- Acupuncture
- Spinal cord stimulation

---

## Phantom Limb Sensation

Most people feel their missing limb is still there. This is phantom limb sensation. It is not painful. It is different from phantom limb pain.

This sensation can be a problem, especially with lower limb amputations. For example, you may think your leg is still there when you get up at night. You may try to step with it. This can cause a fall or injury.

---

## Persistent Residual Limb Pain

Some people with a traditional prosthesis have ongoing pain. This is often due to constant rubbing, sweating, or pressure sores. This can lead to:
- Less control over the prosthesis
- Less ability to do daily tasks
- Less independence
- Lower quality of life

Persistent pain can also:
- Disrupt sleep
- Increase stress
- Worsen mental health (like anxiety, depression, or substance use)

Some people may benefit from a different type of prosthesis. This is called transcutaneous osseointegration. It involves surgically placing a metal anchor into the bone of the remaining limb. This anchor holds the prosthesis directly to the bone. It can reduce pain and improve function.

# Coal Worker Pneumoconiosis

This condition is caused by breathing in dust from coal mining. The dust comes from drilling, blasting, crushing coal, and the machines used to mine it.

Dust exposure in coal mines varies. This leads to different levels of illness among miners.

The disease can cause few or no symptoms. Or it can lead to serious lung damage and trouble breathing.

Many coal miners also get chronic lung problems like chronic bronchitis or COPD.

## What You Need to Know

- The disease is called coal worker pneumoconiosis.
- It is a type of lung disease that affects the tissue between the air sacs.
- It can be:
  - Simple pneumoconiosis
  - Complicated pneumoconiosis (also called progressive massive fibrosis)

### Simple Pneumoconiosis

- Small round spots show up on lung scans.
- These spots are usually in the upper parts of the lungs.
- Most people with this form do not have symptoms.
- Lung function is usually normal.

### Complicated Pneumoconiosis (Progressive Massive Fibrosis)

- The small spots grow together into larger masses.
- These masses usually form in the upper back part of the lungs.
- People with this form often have coughing, shortness of breath, and other symptoms.

## History of the Disease

After the Coal Mine Health and Safety Act passed in 1969, cases of this disease went down in the United States.

But since the late 1990s, the disease has come back — especially the severe form.

This rise is likely due to more exposure to silica dust.

Possible reasons include:
- Workers ignoring safety rules.
- Coal dust that contains more silica.
- Miners having to cut through more rock to reach coal.
- Use of powerful machines that make finer, more dangerous dust.

## What Causes the Disease?

- Long-term breathing in of coal dust (usually 10 years or more).
- The total amount of dust you breathe in is the biggest risk factor.
- The amount of silica in the dust also increases the risk of serious disease.
- Underground miners are at higher risk.
- Miners who cut or drill coal are more likely to get the disease.

## How the Disease Develops

- Coal dust contains silica and other materials.
- The body’s immune cells try to clean up the dust.
- These cells die and cause inflammation and scarring.
- This leads to small spots (called macules and nodules) in the lungs.
- The spots can grow and damage nearby lung tissue.

- Over time, the spots can join together into large scar masses.
- This is called progressive massive fibrosis.
- The risk of this serious form goes up with more silica exposure.
- The disease can keep getting worse even after you stop working in coal mines.

## Symptoms and Signs

- Symptoms can be mild or very severe.
- Common symptoms include:
  - Shortness of breath
  - Cough
  - Making more mucus
- Symptoms often start slowly and get worse over time.
- The disease can keep progressing even after you stop working in coal mines.
- In severe cases, it can lead to end-stage lung disease.

## How It Is Diagnosed

Diagnosis is based on:
- Your work history in coal mining
- Results from a chest scan (x-ray or CT)
- Lung function tests

### Chest Scans

- A chest x-ray or CT scan can show small, round spots in the lungs.
- These spots are signs of simple pneumoconiosis.
- A CT scan is better than an x-ray at finding early signs of serious disease.
- It can also show emphysema, cancer, and early signs of large scar masses.

### Lung Function Tests

- These tests measure how well your lungs work.
- They can show:
  - Obstructive problems (airflow blocked)
  - Restrictive problems (lungs can’t expand fully)
  - Or a mix of both
- A common finding is reduced ability to move oxygen into the blood.
- Problems can show up even if the scan looks normal.

## How It Is Treated

- Stop further exposure to coal dust.
- Supportive care to manage symptoms.

### For Advanced Disease

- Workers with severe disease, especially progressive massive fibrosis, should not return to mining.
- For early or mild cases, job loss is a concern. Doctors weigh this when deciding if you should stop working.

### Treatment Focus

- Treat symptoms and related lung problems.
- No treatment is needed for early, mild, or symptom-free disease.
- If you have COPD, treatment for COPD may help.

### For Severe Cases

- If you have low oxygen levels or high blood pressure in the lungs, you may need oxygen therapy.
- Pulmonary rehabilitation helps you do daily tasks better.
- Lung transplant may be an option for those with severe breathing failure.

### Ongoing Care

- The disease can still get worse after you stop working.
- Regular checkups are important for former miners.
- These checkups can catch new or worsening lung changes.

### Other Important Steps

- Quit smoking. This helps protect your lungs.
- Get tested for tuberculosis.
- Stay up to date on vaccines for:
  - Pneumonia
  - Flu
  - COVID-19

## How to Prevent the Disease

- The best way to prevent it is to reduce or remove dust exposure.
- Engineering controls (like better ventilation and dust suppression) are the most effective way to reduce dust.
- Even with rules in place, dust exposure still happens in mines.
- This leads to ongoing cases, including severe ones.

### Masks

- Dust masks offer only limited protection.
- They should be used with other safety measures, not alone.

### Health Checks

- Regular health checks for current miners can find disease early.

## Key Points

- Breathing in coal dust (which also contains silica) causes lung damage.
- It can lead to coal worker pneumoconiosis and COPD.
- It may get worse over time and lead to end-stage lung disease.
- Diagnosis is based on work history, chest scans, and lung function tests.
- Treatment focuses on reducing further exposure and managing symptoms.
- Regular health checks help find disease early.
- Preventive steps include reducing dust, quitting smoking, testing for TB, and getting vaccines.

# Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA)

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis is a group of childhood diseases. It starts before age 16. It causes long-term or repeated swelling and pain in the joints.

This condition can also affect other parts of the body. These include the eyes, skin, and internal organs.

## What You Need to Know

- JIA is not the same as adult rheumatoid arthritis in most children.
- A few children do have a type that is like adult rheumatoid arthritis.
- The exact cause is unknown.
- JIA is not passed down through families, but genes may play a role.
- JIA is not caused by an infection.

## Types of JIA

There are several types of JIA. Doctors decide which type a child has based on symptoms and test results.

### Oligoarticular JIA
- This is the most common type.
- It usually affects young girls.
- Only 4 or fewer joints are involved in the first 6 months.
- The knee is the most often affected joint.

### Polyarticular JIA
- This is the second most common type.
- It starts in late childhood.
- 5 or more joints are affected.
- It has two types: one with no rheumatoid factor and one with it.
- Rheumatoid factor is a substance in the blood linked to certain autoimmune diseases.
- Children with the rheumatoid factor-positive type often have symptoms like adults with rheumatoid arthritis.
- The same joint on both sides of the body may be affected (like both knees or both hands).
- Small joints in the hands and feet are often involved.

### Enthesitis-Related Arthritis
- This type causes joint pain and swelling where tendons and ligaments attach to bones.
- It often affects joints on one side of the lower body (like the hip, knee, ankle, or foot).
- It is more common in older boys.
- Some boys may also have joint pain in the lower spine.

### Psoriatic JIA
- This type often affects young girls, but can also affect older boys and girls equally.
- Some children have psoriasis, a skin disease with scaly patches.
- Others have a family history of psoriasis.

### Undifferentiated JIA
- This label is used when a child has JIA but does not fit clearly into any one type.
- Or when a child fits more than one type.

### Systemic JIA (Still Disease)
- This type causes joint pain and swelling.
- It also causes symptoms outside the joints.
- These include high fever, rash, swollen lymph nodes, and inflammation around the heart and lungs.

## Symptoms of JIA

JIA causes problems in the joints and sometimes in the eyes or skin.

### Joint Symptoms
- Joints may feel stiff when a child wakes up.
- Joints may swell and feel warm.
- Pain may come later, but it can be mild even with a lot of swelling.
- Pain often gets worse when the joint moves.
- A child may not want to walk or may limp.
- Some children have no pain at all.
- If not treated, joint pain can last for years.

### Enthesitis Symptoms
- Tenderness in the pelvis, hip bone, spine, kneecap, shin, Achilles tendon, or bottom of the foot.

### Eye Problems
- Eye inflammation can happen with any type of JIA.
- It is most common in oligoarticular JIA.
- It is rare in rheumatoid factor-positive polyarticular JIA and systemic JIA.
- The most common eye problem is inflammation of the iris (iridocyclitis).
- This usually causes no pain or redness.
- It may cause blurry vision or uneven pupils.
- If not treated, it can lead to scarring, cataracts, glaucoma, or permanent vision loss.
- Rarely, children with enthesitis-related arthritis may have red, painful eyes and sensitivity to light.

### Skin Problems
- Skin issues mainly happen in psoriatic JIA and systemic JIA.
- Children with psoriatic JIA may have rough, scaly skin patches.
- Fingers and toes may swell.
- Nails may have pits or come loose from the finger.

### Systemic JIA Symptoms
- A fever that comes every day and is highest in the afternoon or evening.
- The fever can reach 102.2 degrees Fahrenheit or higher.
- The fever may last for weeks.
- A child may feel tired and irritable.
- A rash appears in short bursts, often with fever.
- The rash is flat, pink or salmon-colored, and has clear centers.
- It mainly appears on the trunk and upper legs or arms.
- The rash may not appear in the same spot each time.

### Other Systemic Symptoms
- The liver, spleen, or lymph nodes may swell.
- Inflammation can affect the lining of the heart (pericarditis) or lungs (pleuritis).
- Inflammation inside the lungs can cause chest pain.
- Fluid may build up around the heart, lungs, or other organs.

## Complications of JIA

- JIA can slow down a child’s growth.
- If the jaw is affected, the chin may become small.
- Joints can become deformed if JIA is not treated.
- Even with treatment, long-term inflammation can damage joints over time.

## How Doctors Diagnose JIA

Diagnosis is based on:
- The child’s symptoms.
- A physical exam.

There is no single test that confirms JIA. But blood tests help doctors understand the type.

### Blood Tests
- Full blood count.
- Rheumatoid factor.
- Antinuclear antibodies.
- Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies.
- HLA-B27 antigen.

Most children with systemic JIA do not have rheumatoid factor or antinuclear antibodies.

Other tests may include:
- Ferritin.
- C-reactive protein (CRP).
- Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR).

High levels of CRP and ESR mean there is inflammation in the body.

### Eye Exams
- Children with antinuclear antibodies are at higher risk for eye inflammation.
- All children with JIA need regular eye checks, even if they have no symptoms.
- Children with oligoarticular or polyarticular JIA and antinuclear antibodies should see an eye doctor every 3 months.
- Those without antinuclear antibodies should see an eye doctor every 6 months.
- Children with systemic JIA should have an eye exam once or twice a year.

### X-rays
- Doctors may take X-rays to check for changes in bones or joints.

## Treatment of JIA

Treatment aims to reduce pain, stop joint damage, and help the child live a normal life.

### Medications

**Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drugs (DMARDs)**
- These drugs slow down the disease.
- They help prevent joint damage.
- Examples:
  - Methotrexate – fights inflammation.
  - Etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab – block a protein that causes inflammation.
  - Anakinra, canakinumab – block another inflammation-causing protein.
  - Tocilizumab – blocks a different inflammation protein.
  - Tofacitinib, upadacitinib – block an enzyme involved in inflammation.
  - Abatacept – blocks immune cells that cause inflammation.

**Corticosteroids**
- Doctors may inject them directly into a painful joint.
- Oral corticosteroids (like prednisone) are used only when needed.
- They are avoided if possible because they can cause side effects.
- If used, the lowest dose is given to reduce risks.
- Side effects can include slowed growth, weak bones (osteoporosis), cataracts, and bone death (osteonecrosis).

**Eye Treatment**
- Eye drops with steroids reduce inflammation.
- Eye drops that widen the pupil help prevent damage.
- If eye drops are not enough, methotrexate or other biologic drugs may be used.
- Surgery may be needed if the eye is damaged.

**NSAIDs (Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs)**
- These include naproxen and ibuprofen.
- They help reduce pain and swelling.
- They are most helpful for enthesitis-related arthritis.
- But they do not stop the disease from getting worse.

### Physical and Occupational Therapy
- Physical therapy helps improve movement, flexibility, and strength.
- Occupational therapy helps with daily tasks like writing or dressing.

## Outlook for Children with JIA

- About half of children go into remission (no symptoms) within 5 years of treatment.
- With early treatment, most children can live active, normal lives.
- Children with rheumatoid factor-positive polyarticular JIA tend to have a harder time.
