# Getting Ready for a Limb Prosthesis

If your doctor plans to remove a limb, there are steps you can take before surgery to help you recover better. It is important to learn about the process early. This includes understanding why the surgery is needed and what happens before, during, and after the surgery. You and your family should know what to expect from the time you go into the hospital until you get your prosthesis and learn to live with it.

Learning about the process helps you stay focused and committed. It also helps your family support you better. Talking with someone who has had a limb removed can be very helpful. They can share their own experiences and give you hope.

## Getting Ready Before Surgery

Before surgery, your care team will do a few important things:

- They will check how well you can move and do daily tasks.
- They will plan your care before and after surgery.
- They will help you start an exercise program.

Your doctor, prosthetist, and physical therapist will use your current abilities and your personal goals to make a plan. This plan will guide your recovery.

No matter your age or how you feel now, start exercising as soon as possible before surgery. Keep exercising after surgery too. A physical therapist will teach you exercises to build strength, improve flexibility, and keep your joints moving well. The stronger and more flexible you are, the more you can do with or without your prosthesis.

If you think you will have trouble doing everyday tasks like dressing or cooking, an occupational therapist can help. They will teach you ways to do these tasks safely and easily.

## After Surgery and Before Getting Your Prosthesis

After surgery, your main goals are to:

- Keep your remaining limb safe from injury (like bumps or falls).
- Reduce swelling.
- Help the wound heal.
- Stay strong and keep your heart and lungs healthy.
- Keep your joints moving well.

There are many types of bandages and wraps to protect your limb and reduce swelling. Controlling swelling helps blood flow, speeds up healing, and can reduce pain. This includes pain that feels like it is still in the limb even though it is gone—this is called phantom limb pain.

A physical therapist will work with you before you leave the hospital and after you go home. They will help you learn to stand, walk, and move safely. You may practice using parallel bars, a walker, crutches, or a wheelchair. You will also learn how to get in and out of bed, chairs, and the shower.

Your prosthetist will see you once a week. They will check how your limb is healing. They will decide when your limb is ready for a temporary prosthesis. This usually happens when the swelling has gone down and your limb size is stable.

# Liver Scarring (Fibrosis)

## What Is Liver Fibrosis?

Liver fibrosis means too much scar tissue forms in the liver.  
This happens when the liver tries to heal after damage.  
The liver makes scar tissue instead of new healthy cells.  
Fibrosis does not cause symptoms on its own.  
But if it gets worse, it can lead to a serious condition called cirrhosis.

## How Fibrosis Develops

The liver can heal after a single injury.  
For example, after a bad case of hepatitis, the liver often repairs itself.  
But if the liver is damaged over and over, or for a long time, healing goes wrong.  
Instead of making healthy cells, the liver makes scar tissue.  
This scar tissue builds up and harms the liver’s structure.  
Fibrosis can happen faster if there is a blockage in the tubes that carry bile.

## What Happens When Fibrosis Gets Worse?

Scar tissue does not work like normal liver cells.  
It does not help the liver do its job.  
Scar tissue can block blood flow through the liver.  
When blood flow is poor, liver cells do not get enough oxygen and nutrients.  
This causes more liver cells to die.  
More scar tissue forms as a result.  
Blood pressure in the main vein from the intestines to the liver (called the portal vein) rises.  
This is called portal hypertension.

Over time, the scar tissue spreads and destroys the liver’s normal shape.  
The liver can no longer make new cells or work properly.  
This advanced scarring is called cirrhosis.

## Can Fibrosis Be Reversed?

Yes, fibrosis can improve if the cause is found early and treated.  
But if damage continues for months or years, the scarring becomes permanent.  
Once cirrhosis develops, the damage is usually not reversible.

## Causes of Liver Fibrosis

Many things can harm the liver and cause fibrosis.  
Some common causes in the United States are:

- Drinking too much alcohol over a long time  
- Chronic hepatitis C virus infection  
- Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH)  
  - This is a type of fatty liver that is not caused by alcohol  
  - It often happens in people with extra body weight, diabetes or prediabetes, or high blood fats and cholesterol  
  - This group of health problems is called metabolic syndrome

Other causes include:

- Genetic conditions that affect how the body uses food and chemicals  
  - Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency  
  - Hemochromatosis (too much iron in the body)  
  - Wilson disease (too much copper in the body)  
- Viral infections like hepatitis B or C  
- Autoimmune diseases where the body attacks its own liver or bile ducts  
  - Autoimmune hepatitis  
  - Primary biliary cholangitis  
  - Primary sclerosing cholangitis  
- Problems with blood flow to or from the liver  
  - Budd-Chiari syndrome (a blood clot blocks blood leaving the liver)  
  - Heart failure  
  - Portal vein thrombosis (a blood clot blocks the main vein to the liver)  
  - Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (blockage of small liver veins)  
  - This can be caused by certain herbal products like some rooibos teas  
- Certain medicines and substances  
  - Alcohol  
  - Amiodarone (a heart medicine)  
  - Chlorpromazine (a mental health medicine)  
  - Corticosteroids (like prednisone)  
  - Isoniazid (a medicine for tuberculosis)  
  - Methotrexate (a medicine for cancer and autoimmune diseases)  
  - Methyldopa (a blood pressure medicine)  
  - Oxyphenisatin (a medicine for cough)  
  - Tolbutamide (a diabetes medicine)  
  - Most medicines are processed in the liver. Some can harm the liver.  
  - Doctors may check liver blood tests while people take these medicines.  
- Other rare conditions  
  - Congenital hepatic fibrosis (a condition present at birth that affects the liver, gallbladder, and kidneys)  
  - Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH) – fat builds up in the liver and can lead to scarring

## Symptoms of Liver Fibrosis

Fibrosis itself does not cause symptoms.  
Symptoms come from the condition causing the damage.  
Or they come from cirrhosis, if fibrosis gets worse.  
Cirrhosis can cause problems like swelling in the legs, fluid in the belly, or bleeding from veins in the esophagus.

## How Doctors Diagnose Liver Fibrosis

Doctors look for signs of liver damage when:

- A person has a condition known to harm the liver  
- A person takes a medicine that can harm the liver  
- Routine blood tests show liver problems

To confirm fibrosis and check how bad it is, doctors may use:

- Blood tests  
- Imaging tests (like ultrasound, CT scan, or MRI)  
- Liver biopsy (a small sample of liver tissue is taken)  
- Specialized tests that measure how stiff the liver is

### Blood Tests

Some blood tests can help tell if fibrosis is mild or moderate to severe.  
These tests help doctors predict how the disease may progress, especially in people with chronic hepatitis.

### Imaging Tests

Ultrasound, CT scans, and MRI can show signs of advanced liver damage.  
They may show an enlarged spleen or swollen veins in the esophagus (called varices).  
But these tests often miss early or mild fibrosis.

### Liver Biopsy

A liver biopsy is the most accurate way to see and measure fibrosis.  
It can also help find the cause of liver damage.  
Doctors use it to stage the disease and check how well treatment is working.  
But it is invasive and can cause side effects.  
So doctors often try blood tests and imaging first.

### Specialized Imaging Tests

Newer tests can measure how stiff the liver is.  
The stiffer the liver, the more scar tissue is likely present.  
These tests use sound waves and are not invasive.  
They include:

- Transient elastography (FibroScan)  
- Magnetic resonance elastography (MRE)  
- Acoustic radiation force impulse imaging (ARFI)

These tests give a number for liver stiffness.  
This makes results more reliable than regular ultrasound, which depends on the skill of the person doing it.  
These tests are also used to check how much fat is in the liver.

Doctors may use a mix of blood tests and imaging tests to get the best picture of fibrosis.

## Treatment of Liver Fibrosis

The main goal is to treat the cause of liver damage.  
This can stop or slow scarring.  
In some cases, it can even improve the liver.

Treatment options include:

- Antiviral medicines for chronic hepatitis B or C  
- Stopping alcohol use if alcohol is the cause  
- Medicines to remove excess iron (in hemochromatosis) or copper (in Wilson disease)  
- Stopping any medicine or supplement that harms the liver  
- Removing or opening a blocked bile duct  
- Losing weight and controlling blood sugar and cholesterol levels in people with MASH

There is no medicine yet that safely and effectively stops scar tissue from forming.  
But researchers are testing new drugs.  
Some studies suggest that milk thistle or coffee may help protect the liver.  
But there is not enough strong evidence to recommend them as treatment.

# What Is Iron Overload?

Most adults lose about 1 milligram of iron each day. This happens when skin and gut cells naturally shed. Women who have periods lose an extra 0.5 to 1 milligram of iron each day during their menstrual cycle.

The body gets iron from the food we eat. A typical American diet has between 10 and 20 milligrams of iron per day. The body absorbs only what it needs.

The body controls how much iron it absorbs. It does this based on how much iron it already has stored. Usually, the amount of iron absorbed matches the body’s needs.

But the body has no natural way to get rid of extra iron. So if you take in more iron than your body needs, or if you get repeated blood transfusions, the extra iron builds up in your body. It then gets stored in tissues.

## Types of Iron Buildup

- **Hemosiderosis** means iron builds up in small, scattered areas. This usually does not harm the body.
- **Hemochromatosis** means iron builds up throughout the body. This can damage tissues and organs.

## Causes of Iron Overload

Iron overload can happen in two main ways:

1. **Hereditary hemochromatosis** – A genetic condition. It affects how the body handles iron. It is passed down through families.
2. **Secondary hemochromatosis** – This is not inherited. It happens because of:
   - Taking too much iron in supplements or food.
   - Absorbing too much iron from food.
   - Getting many blood transfusions over time.

## Where Iron Builds Up and What It Can Cause

Too much iron mainly harms these organs:
- The pancreas
- The reproductive organs (ovaries or testicles)
- The pituitary gland (a small gland in the brain)
- The liver
- The heart

Damage to these organs can lead to serious health problems.

## African Iron Overload

This condition is most common in parts of sub-Saharan Africa. It often affects people who drink a type of fermented drink that is high in iron.

Scientists think genes may play a role in this condition. But so far, no specific gene has been found to cause it.

> **Note:** For more information, see the topics on *Iron Poisoning* and *Idiopathic Pulmonary Hemosiderosis*.

# Heart Imaging Using Radioactive Tracers

This test uses a small amount of a special radioactive substance to take pictures of your heart. It helps doctors find the cause of chest pain.

## How the Test Works

- A tiny amount of a radioactive substance, called a tracer, is given through a vein.
- The tracer gives off gamma rays that a special camera can detect.
- A computer turns the camera’s data into images showing how much tracer each part of the heart takes up.
- The amount of radiation you get is very small and safe.

## Why This Test Is Done

- It helps find the cause of chest pain when doctors are not sure what is wrong.
- It shows how well blood flows to the heart muscle.
- It checks if blood flow to the heart has improved after heart surgery.
- It helps predict how well a person may do after a heart attack.

## How the Test Is Done

- Different tracers are used depending on what the doctor suspects.
- For checking blood flow, two common tracers are technetium-99m sestamibi and thallium-201.
- You will do an exercise stress test. This means you walk on a treadmill or ride a stationary bike.
- The test is done while you are exercising. The heart muscle that gets enough blood takes up more tracer. The heart muscle with poor blood flow takes up less tracer and shows up lighter on the image.
- If you cannot exercise, you will get a medicine through a vein. Medicines like dipyridamole or adenosine make blood flow increase in the heart like it does during exercise.

After the first scan, you will rest for a few hours. Then you will have a second scan. Doctors compare the two images.

- Areas that look different during exercise but normal at rest may have blocked arteries. This problem can often be fixed.
- Areas that look bad both during exercise and at rest may be scarred from a past heart attack. This damage is permanent.

## Types of Imaging

### SPECT (Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography)

- SPECT takes many pictures from different angles.
- It creates detailed cross-sections of the heart.
- It can show 3D views of the heart.
- It gives more detail about blood flow and heart function than regular imaging.
- But it uses more radiation than regular imaging.

### MUGA (Multiple Gated Acquisition)

- MUGA shows how well the heart pumps blood.
- It is not used often because echocardiography (ultrasound of the heart) gives the same information.
- Echocardiography does not use radiation.

## After the Test

- The radioactive tracer stays in your body for a few days.
- You might set off radiation alarms at airport security.
- If you plan to travel by plane or by car, train, or boat across borders, ask your doctor for a note.
- This note will explain that you had a radionuclide imaging test.
- Security staff may ask for proof to avoid delays.

# Positron Emission Tomography (PET)

PET is a type of imaging test that uses a special radioactive substance to show how the body is working.

The test uses a substance that contains a radioactive material. This material gives off tiny particles called positrons. When a positron meets an electron in the body, it creates two small bursts of energy. These bursts travel in opposite directions, 180 degrees apart.

A scanner with detectors around the body catches these bursts. The scanner uses the data to find where the radioactive material is. It then makes color pictures of the area.

Because PET uses radioactive material that the body uses in normal processes, it can show how tissues are working. The test can show how active a part of the body is. A number called the standard uptake value, or SUV, shows how much of the substance the tissue took up. Higher SUV numbers mean the tissue is more active. The color on the image gets brighter with higher SUV numbers.

## The Most Common Substance Used in PET

The most common substance used in PET scans is:

* Fluorine-18 labeled deoxyglucose, also called FDG

FDG is similar to sugar. The body takes it up the same way it takes up sugar. The more active a tissue is, the more FDG it takes up. Doctors calculate a patient’s SUV by dividing the amount of FDG in the body by the patient’s weight.

## What PET Is Used For

PET scans help doctors in several ways:

- **Cancer**: To find out how far cancer has spread. To check specific types of cancer. To see if treatment is working.
- **Heart problems**: To check if heart muscle is still alive. To find areas of the heart that are not working well but may recover.
- **Brain issues**: To help diagnose dementia. To study seizures and other brain conditions.

## Different Types of PET

Images used in this guide are provided by Hakan Ilaslan, MD.

## Downsides of PET

- The radiation dose from a PET scan is about 7 millisieverts.
- A PET scan with CT (PET-CT) gives a higher dose, between 5 and 18 millisieverts.

Making FDG requires a special machine called a cyclotron. FDG breaks down quickly — it lasts only about 110 minutes. This means it must be made and used fast. The scan must be done soon after the substance is made.

Because of the need for special equipment, short shelf life, and fast timing, PET scans are expensive and hard to get. This limits how many places can offer the test.

# Perforation of the Digestive Tract

Any hollow part of the digestive system can tear open. This tear lets digestive contents leak out. This can cause a serious infection in the blood. It can also be deadly. Surgery must happen right away.

## What Happens When There Is a Perforation?

When a hole forms in the digestive tract, food, digestive juices, or other contents can leak into the belly (or into the chest if the esophagus is torn). These substances are very irritating. They also contain bacteria. This causes strong inflammation and infection. Without treatment, this infection usually leads to death.

## Common Causes of a Perforation

The cause depends on where the tear happens. But any part of the digestive system can be affected.

- **Swallowed objects** usually pass through the body without problems. But sometimes they get stuck and cause a tear.
- **Objects pushed into the rectum** can tear the rectum or colon.
- **Injury** can happen anywhere along the digestive tract.
- **Forceful vomiting** can tear the esophagus.
- **Medical procedures** can cause tears. For example, using a scope, balloon, or thin tube during a test can cause a tear.
- **Swallowing strong poisons** like battery acid or lye can damage the esophagus or stomach.
- **Peptic ulcers** can lead to a tear in the stomach or first part of the small intestine. This can happen even if the person never had ulcer symptoms before.
- **Blockages** in the intestine can cut off blood flow. This can cause a tear.
- **Appendicitis** or **Meckel diverticulitis** can lead to a tear.
- **Colon blockages** often come from cancer or hard stool.
- **Diverticulitis** is more likely in people on immune-suppressing medicines like prednisone. These people may not feel many symptoms.
- **Inflammatory bowel diseases** like ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease can cause tears.
- **Toxic megacolon** is when the large intestine swells badly. This can lead to a tear.
- **Gallbladder problems** can cause a tear. This can happen during gallbladder surgery or a liver test. It can also happen if the gallbladder becomes inflamed.

## Signs and Symptoms

- Sudden, severe pain in the chest or belly.
- Pain that may spread to the shoulder.
- Belly that feels tender and hard when touched.
- Fast heartbeat.
- Sweating.
- Feeling very sick.
- Nausea.
- Vomiting.
- Loss of appetite.

If the tear happens in the small or large intestine, symptoms may not be very strong. This is because the leak may be trapped in a small area. The symptoms may seem like a worsening of another problem, such as diverticulitis or appendicitis.

## How Doctors Diagnose a Perforation

- Doctors take **x-rays** of the chest and belly.
- Sometimes, doctors do a **CT scan** of the belly.

The x-rays can show air that has leaked from the digestive system. This is a clear sign of a tear. A CT scan can help confirm the diagnosis if the x-ray is not clear.

## Treatment

- Immediate surgery.
- Fluids and antibiotics given through a vein.

If a tear is found, surgery is needed right away. The surgeon will close the hole and clean the belly. The type of surgery depends on where the tear is and what caused it.

Before surgery, the patient gets fluids and antibiotics through a vein. This helps fight infection and keeps the body stable.

Sometimes, a thin tube is placed through the nose into the stomach. This tube removes stomach juices. It helps prevent more fluid from leaking out. It also reduces pressure in the bowel.

# Understanding Sexuality

Sexuality involves the body, mind, and emotions. It is a big part of how people connect with others.

Different cultures have different ideas about what is acceptable when it comes to sex. These ideas can be very different from one place to another.

Health care providers should not judge people for their sexual choices. This is true as long as the choices are between adults who agree to them and do not cause harm.

There is no single medical rule that says what is “normal” or “abnormal” in sex. Everyone’s experience is different.

But if a person feels upset or stressed about their sex life, or if it causes problems in a relationship, help is available. If sex causes harm to anyone, treatment should be considered.

# What You Need to Know About Antibiotics

Antibiotics are medicines that fight bacterial infections.  
They do not work against viruses.  
They also do not help with most other types of infections.

Antibiotics either kill bacteria or stop them from multiplying.  
This gives your body’s natural defenses a chance to clear the infection.

---

## How Doctors Choose Antibiotics

Doctors pick antibiotics based on the type of bacteria likely causing the infection.  
Sometimes, they start with a broad-spectrum antibiotic.  
This kind works against many different bacteria while waiting for test results.

Test results can take a day or two.  
So, doctors often begin treatment with an antibiotic that likely works for the most common bacteria.

When test results come back, doctors may switch to a different antibiotic if needed.

Not all antibiotics that work in the lab will work in your body.  
Your body’s ability to use the medicine depends on:

- How well your body absorbs the drug (if you take it by mouth)  
- How much of the drug reaches the infected area  
- How fast your body removes the drug

These things can vary from person to person.  
They depend on your age, other health conditions, and other medicines you take.

Doctors also think about:

- How serious the infection is  
- How strong your immune system is  
- Possible side effects of the antibiotic  
- Risk of allergic reactions  
- Cost of the medicine  
- How easy it is to follow the treatment plan

Some people find it hard to take medicine many times a day.  
Some must take it before or after meals.  
This can make it harder to finish the full course.

---

## When More Than One Antibiotic Is Needed

Doctors may use two or more antibiotics together when:

- The infection is very serious, especially early on  
- The bacteria can quickly become resistant to one antibiotic  
- The infection is caused by more than one type of bacteria  
- Each type needs a different antibiotic

---

## Antibiotic Resistance

Bacteria change over time.  
When antibiotics are used too much or not taken correctly, some bacteria survive.  
These bacteria can become resistant.  
This means the antibiotic no longer works.

For example, a type of bacteria called *Staphylococcus aureus* once responded well to penicillin.  
But over time, it developed a way to break down penicillin.  
Doctors made a new version of penicillin.  
But the bacteria changed again and became resistant to that version too.

Other bacteria have also become resistant.

You can help stop resistance by:

- Knowing antibiotics do not treat viral infections like colds or the flu  
- Taking antibiotics exactly as your doctor tells you  
- Finishing the full course, even if you feel better

> **Did You Know?**  
> If a virus is causing your illness, antibiotics will not help.  
> They can also make bacteria stronger over time.

---

## How Antibiotics Are Taken

For serious infections or when you cannot keep food or liquids down, antibiotics are given through a needle.  
This is usually into a vein, but sometimes into a muscle.

Once you are stable, you may switch to taking antibiotics by mouth.

For milder infections, you can often start with oral antibiotics.

---

### Special Considerations for Older Adults

Doctors may give older adults a lower dose of antibiotics.  
Kidneys work less well with age.  
This means the body may not clear the medicine as fast.  
This increases the risk of side effects.

Doctors also check:

- What other medicines you are taking  
- Whether the treatment plan is too complicated  
- If you have family or caregivers to help you

You must take antibiotics until all the bacteria are gone.  
This may take days after your symptoms go away.  
Stopping early can cause the infection to come back.

A doctor, nurse, or pharmacist can explain:

- How to take your medicine  
- What side effects to watch for

Some antibiotics must be taken on an empty stomach.  
Others should be taken with food.

**Metronidazole** causes a bad reaction if you drink alcohol.  
Some antibiotics can interact with other medicines.  
This can reduce their effect or increase side effects.

Some antibiotics make your skin more sensitive to sunlight.

---

## Preventing Infections with Antibiotics

Doctors sometimes give antibiotics to prevent infections.  
This is called prophylaxis.

Examples include:

- Giving antibiotics to people who have been near someone with meningitis  
- Giving antibiotics before dental or surgery procedures to people with artificial heart valves  
- Giving antibiotics before major surgery that could lead to infection

Doctors only give preventive antibiotics for a short time.  
This helps avoid resistance and side effects.

People with weak immune systems—like those with cancer, HIV/AIDS, or leukemia—may need long-term antibiotics.  
They are more likely to get serious infections.

---

## Antibiotics During Pregnancy and Breastfeeding

Doctors use antibiotics during pregnancy only when needed.  
Some are safer than others.

Safe options include:

- Penicillins  
- Cephalosporins  
- Erythromycin

Most antibiotics pass into breast milk.  
They can affect your baby.  
In some cases, you may need to stop breastfeeding or avoid the medicine.

If you are pregnant or breastfeeding and get an infection, talk to your doctor.  
They will help you weigh the benefits and risks.

---

## Antibiotics at Home

Most antibiotics are taken by mouth.  
But some infections—like bone or heart infections—may need antibiotics given through a vein (IV) for weeks.

If you are well enough and have no other health issues, IV antibiotics can be given at home.

Short IV catheters (used in hospitals) last only a few days.  
For long-term treatment, a special catheter is used.  
It can be placed in:

- A large vein in the neck or chest (central catheter)  
- A small vein in the arm, threaded into a large vein (PICC line)

Some people and their families can learn to use the IV system at home.  
Others need a nurse to come and give each dose.

You will be closely watched to make sure the medicine is given right and to catch any problems early.

---

### Signs of a Catheter Infection

Watch for:

- Pain, redness, or pus at the site where the needle goes in  
- Chills or fever (even if the site looks fine)

These could mean an infection is starting.

---

## Side Effects of Antibiotics

Common side effects include:

- Upset stomach  
- Diarrhea  
- Vaginal yeast infections (in women)

Some side effects are serious.  
They can affect your kidneys, liver, or bone marrow.  
Blood tests may be done to check for damage.

### *Clostridioides difficile* – Induced Colitis

Some antibiotics can cause a serious bowel problem called *Clostridioides difficile* – induced colitis.  
This happens when the medicine kills good gut bacteria.  
The harmful *C. diff* bacteria then grow out of control.

This type of colitis is more likely with:

- Cephalosporins  
- Clindamycin  
- Fluoroquinolones  
- Penicillins

It can be life-threatening, especially in older adults.  
It is hard to treat and may need special medicine.

---

## Allergic Reactions to Antibiotics

Antibiotics can cause allergic reactions.  
Mild reactions include:

- Itchy rash  
- Slight wheezing

Severe reactions (anaphylaxis) are life-threatening.  
They can include:

- Swelling in the throat  
- Trouble breathing  
- Low blood pressure

Tell your doctor or nurse if you are allergic to any antibiotic.  
Describe what happened before.

Not all side effects are allergies.  
For example, upset stomach is not always an allergy.

If you are allergic to one antibiotic, you should not take that drug or similar ones.  
This is because allergic reactions can be deadly.

If you only had mild side effects before, you can usually take other antibiotics.  
Your doctor can help decide what is safe.

> **Important:** Always tell your healthcare provider about any past reaction to antibiotics.

# Sporotrichosis

Sporotrichosis is a skin infection caused by a type of mold called *Sporothrix schenckii*.  
It usually does not affect the lungs or spread through the blood.  
The main signs are lumps in the skin that move along the lymph system.  
These lumps can break open and form sores or abscesses.  

The infection is diagnosed by growing the fungus in a lab.  
Treatment is with a medicine called itraconazole or, in severe cases, amphotericin B.  

---

## Where the Mold Lives

The mold *Sporothrix schenckii* grows on rose bushes, barberry bushes, moss, and other garden mulches.  
People who work with plants are most at risk.  
This includes gardeners, farmers, foresters, and people who work with wood.  
Infection usually happens after a small cut or scrape from contaminated plant material.  
Unlike other similar fungi, this mold is not usually breathed in.  
It enters the body through broken skin.  

The mold changes shape depending on the temperature.  
In the body (at 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit), it grows as a yeast.  
In cooler environments (like soil or moss), it grows as a thread-like fungus.  

---

## What the Infection Looks Like

The most common form is called lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis.  
It usually starts on one hand or arm.  
But it can happen anywhere on the body.  
It may also start on the feet or face if those areas were exposed.  

The first sign is a small, painless bump under the skin.  
Sometimes it starts as a small, raised spot.  
Over time, the bump may grow and become hard.  
It can die and break open, forming an ulcer.  

A few days or weeks later, nearby lymph nodes begin to swell.  
They form a chain of soft, movable lumps under the skin.  
If not treated, the skin over the lumps turns red.  
It may break down and form an abscess or open sore.  
Bacteria can then enter and cause a secondary infection.  

People with this infection usually do not feel sick.  
They do not have fever, chills, or other signs of a serious illness.  

---

## Pictures of the Infection

- A small bump or lump under the skin may appear first.  
- The lump can break open and become an ulcer.  
- The infection spreads along the lymph system.  
- Without treatment, redness, sores, and abscesses can spread.  
- In severe cases, a bacterial infection can make things worse.  
- Lumps may appear in a line along the arm or hand.  

*(Images from doctorfungus.org and the CDC Public Health Image Library.)*

---

## How Long the Infection Lasts

Lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis is slow to heal.  
It can last for months or even years.  
It is rarely life-threatening.  
But it can become dangerous if bacteria infect the open sores and spread through the body.  

In rare cases, the infection spreads through the blood.  
This can affect joints, bones, or organs like the liver, spleen, kidneys, or brain.  
It can also affect the genitals.  
This is more likely in people with weak immune systems.  
This includes people with alcohol use disorder or other health problems.  

Very rarely, the mold is breathed in.  
This can cause a long-lasting lung infection.  
It often shows up as patches or holes in the lungs.  
This is most common in people who already have lung disease.  

---

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors look at the symptoms and ask about exposure.  
For example, did the person work with plants, soil, or mulch?  

The typical pattern of lumps along the arm can look like other infections.  
Other causes include tuberculosis, certain types of bacteria, and parasites.  

The best way to confirm the diagnosis is to take a sample from the skin or lump.  
The sample is sent to a lab to grow the fungus.  
This is the only way to be sure.  

The mold is hard to see in tissue samples, even with special stains.  
There is no blood test to check for this infection.  

---

## How It Is Treated

The main treatment is a pill called itraconazole.  
You take one 200 milligram pill once a day.  
You keep taking it for 2 to 4 weeks after all the sores are gone.  
This usually takes 3 to 6 months.  

For severe infections, doctors use a stronger medicine called amphotericin B.  
This is given through a vein once a day.  
After the infection starts to improve, the treatment switches to itraconazole.  
The total treatment time is about 12 months.  

People with HIV or AIDS may need to take itraconazole for life.  
This is to prevent the infection from coming back, especially if it affects the brain or spreads through the body.  
Another medicine, posaconazole, may also help in some cases.  

---

## More Information

For more details, visit the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website.  
They have information on how to avoid the infection and who is at risk.

# Imaging Tests for the Liver and Gallbladder

These tests help doctors see the liver, gallbladder, and bile ducts. They include:

- Ultrasound  
- Computed tomography (CT)  
- Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)  
- Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)  
- Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography  
- Operative cholangiography  
- Radionuclide scanning  
- Simple x-rays  

(See also: Overview of the Liver and Gallbladder.)

---

## Ultrasound

Ultrasound uses sound waves to make pictures of the liver, gallbladder, and bile ducts.

It works well for finding lumps or tumors in parts of the liver.  
It is not as good at showing problems that affect the whole liver, like severe scarring or too much fat in the liver.

Ultrasound is the cheapest and safest way to look at the gallbladder and bile ducts.

Doctors can use ultrasound to find gallstones in the gallbladder.  
It can also help tell if yellow skin or eyes (jaundice) are caused by blocked bile ducts or by liver cells not working right.

If the bile ducts look wider than normal on ultrasound, this usually means there is a blockage.

Ultrasound can guide doctors when they insert a needle into the liver to take a small tissue sample for testing.

A special type of ultrasound called Doppler ultrasound shows blood moving through blood vessels in the liver.

It can find blockages in the liver’s blood vessels, especially the portal vein.  
This vein carries blood from the intestines to the liver.

Doppler ultrasound can also show high blood pressure in the portal vein, a condition called portal hypertension.

Another type, endoscopic ultrasound, uses a small probe on the end of a flexible tube.  
The tube goes through the mouth, down the throat, and into the stomach and first part of the small intestine.  
This brings the probe close to the liver and nearby organs.

---

## Computed Tomography (CT)

CT scans give very clear pictures of the liver and its blood vessels.

They are especially good at finding tumors.  
They can also show infections (abscesses) and liver problems that affect the whole liver, like fatty liver.

---

## Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)

MRI can find certain liver problems that affect the entire liver, such as too much iron in the liver (hemochromatosis) or fatty liver disease.

MRI shows how blood flows through the liver.  
This helps doctors see problems with blood vessels.

MRI is also useful for finding tumors.

A special MRI technique called magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) makes detailed pictures of the bile ducts and nearby areas.

MRCP images are as clear as those from more invasive tests that use contrast dye injected into the bile and pancreatic ducts.

Unlike CT, MRI does not use x-rays.  
But MRI is more expensive and takes longer than CT.

---

## Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)

ERCP uses a flexible tube called an endoscope.  
The doctor passes the tube through the mouth, down the throat, and into the stomach and first part of the small intestine (duodenum).

A thin tube is then passed through the endoscope into the bile and pancreatic ducts.

A special dye is injected into these ducts.  
X-rays are taken at the same time to show the ducts clearly.

ERCP is sometimes used just to look at the ducts.  
But doctors usually prefer MRCP when it is available.  
MRCP is just as good and safer.

The big advantage of ERCP is that doctors can do treatments during the test.

For example, they can remove a stone stuck in a bile duct.  
Or they can place a tube (stent) to bypass a blockage caused by swelling or cancer.

Complications from ERCP happen in about 1 out of every 100 people.  
If a treatment is done during ERCP, the risk of complications goes up.

---

## Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography

This test uses a long needle.  
The doctor inserts the needle through the skin and into the liver.  
An ultrasound helps guide the needle to the right spot.

A special dye is then injected into a bile duct in the liver.  
X-rays show the bile ducts clearly, especially any blockages.

This test is used more often to treat problems or take tissue samples than just to take pictures.

It can cause serious side effects like bleeding or internal injury.  
So it is not the first choice.  
It is only used when other methods are not possible.

---

## Operative Cholangiography

This test is done during gallbladder surgery.

A special dye is injected directly into the bile ducts.  
X-rays are taken right away to show the ducts clearly.

This test is only used when other, less invasive tests do not give enough information.

---

## Radionuclide (Radioisotope) Scanning

This test uses a small amount of a radioactive substance.  
It is given through a vein in the arm.

The substance collects in the liver.  
A special camera detects the radiation and makes a picture.

This is called a liver scan.

Another type, called cholescintigraphy (or hepatobiliary scan), tracks how a radioactive substance moves from the liver to the gallbladder and then through the bile ducts into the small intestine.

The test is done after fasting.  
It can show if the tube connecting the gallbladder to the main bile duct is blocked.

A blocked tube means the gallbladder is inflamed. This condition is called cholecystitis.

---

## X-rays of the Abdomen

Simple x-rays of the belly usually do not show problems with the liver, gallbladder, or bile ducts.

# What Is Edema?

Edema means swelling in the soft parts of the body. It happens when extra fluid builds up in the spaces between cells.

The fluid is mostly water. But if there is an infection or a blockage in the lymph system, the fluid can also contain proteins and white blood cells.

Edema can affect the whole body or just one area. For example, it can happen in one arm or leg, or only in the face.

Sometimes the swelling comes on fast. A person might say their leg suddenly got bigger. More often, the swelling grows slowly. It may start with gaining weight, puffy eyes in the morning, or shoes feeling tight by the end of the day. The swelling can get very bad before someone sees a doctor.

---

## Swelling in the Legs

Swelling in the legs is common. It often shows up in the feet and lower legs when a person is walking or standing.

If someone is in bed, swelling may appear in the buttocks, genitals, or back of the thighs.

Women who lie on one side for long periods may get swelling in the breast on that side.

When the lymph system is blocked, swelling happens in the part of the body beyond the blockage.

---

## Why Does Edema Happen?

Edema happens when fluid moves from blood vessels into the tissues. Or it can happen when the body does not remove fluid from the tissues well.

This can be caused by:

- High pressure in blood vessels
- Low levels of protein in the blood
- Blood vessel walls that are leaky
- A blocked lymph system

When fluid leaves the blood vessels, the blood volume drops. This triggers the body to hold on to salt and water. This helps keep blood volume normal.

But holding on to salt and water can lead to more fluid buildup. This is called fluid overload.

Too much salt in the diet can make this worse.

In some cases, edema happens because the blood does not pull fluid back from the tissues well. This can happen when the blood has low protein levels. This can be due to:

- Kidney disease (especially nephrotic syndrome)
- Problems with the gut that cause protein loss
- Liver disease
- Not eating enough

When blood vessel walls are damaged, they let more fluid out. This can happen during infections or due to toxins or inflammation.

In angioedema, certain chemicals in the body cause sudden swelling under the skin or in the mouth and throat.

The lymph system helps remove extra fluid, proteins, and white blood cells from the tissues. If this system is blocked, these substances build up and cause swelling.

---

## What Causes Edema?

### Generalized Edema (Affects the Whole Body)

The most common causes are:

- Heart failure
- Liver failure
- Kidney problems (especially nephrotic syndrome)

### Localized Edema (Affects One Area)

The most common causes are:

- Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or other vein problems
- Infection
- Angioedema
- Blocked lymph system
- Chronic venous insufficiency (a long-term vein problem)

Chronic venous insufficiency can affect one or both legs.

---

### Common Causes of Edema – By Type

| Cause | Signs and Symptoms | How It’s Diagnosed |
|------|---------------------|--------------------|
| **Right heart failure** (or heart problems on the right side) | Swelling in the legs, ankles, or feet. Swelling is even and gets worse when standing. No pain. May have trouble breathing when active, need to sit up to breathe, or wake up at night gasping. | Chest X-ray, ECG, echocardiogram |
| **Pregnancy or before your period** | Mild swelling in the legs, feet, or hands. Swelling is even and not painful. | Based on your history |
| **Medicines** (like minoxidil, NSAIDs, birth control pills, some blood pressure drugs) | Mild, even swelling in the legs or feet. No pain. | Based on your history |
| **Too much IV fluid** (from medical treatment) | Mild, even swelling in the legs or feet. | Based on your history and medical records |
| **Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)** | Swelling in one leg, usually the lower leg. Swelling is painful. The leg may feel warm and look red. | Ultrasound, D-dimer test |
| **Chronic venous insufficiency** | Long-term swelling in one or both legs. Skin may turn brown. Legs may feel heavy. Sores can form. | Based on symptoms and physical exam |
| **Tumor or pregnancy pressing on a vein** | Swelling that grows slowly. If the main vein in the chest is blocked, face may look red, neck veins may bulge, and pulses above the blockage may be missing. | Physical exam. Ultrasound or CT scan if needed |
| **Not moving for long** (like being in bed or on a long flight) | Swelling in both legs. No pain. | Based on your history |
| **Nephrotic syndrome** | Swelling all over the body. Belly may swell with fluid. Eyes may be puffy. | Urine test for protein, blood test for albumin |
| **Protein-losing gut disease** | Severe diarrhea. | Tests to find the cause. May need endoscopy or stool tests |
| **Liver disease or poor nutrition** | Swelling all over. Belly may swell with fluid. | Blood tests, liver function tests, physical exam |
| **Angioedema** (allergic, hereditary, or unknown cause) | Sudden swelling in one area. Often the face, lips, mouth, hands, or genitals. Swelling is not even. Not linked to gravity. | Based on symptoms |
| **Burns, chemicals, toxins, or injury** | Swelling in one spot. Skin may be red. | Based on history |
| **Severe infection (sepsis)** | Fever, fast heartbeat, signs of infection. Swelling is painless and even. | Blood cultures, imaging tests |
| **Skin infection (like cellulitis)** | Red or dark skin, painful, tender. Swelling is not as spread out as in DVT. | Physical exam, cultures, sometimes ultrasound |
| **Lymph system blockage** (after surgery, radiation, or birth defect) | Swelling starts in one area. May start as pitting (leaves a dent when pressed). Later, tissue may harden. | Based on history, physical exam |
| **Lymphatic filariasis** (a tropical disease) | Swelling in one area. Often affects the genitals. | Blood test to check for parasites |

> **Note:** Most people with swelling all over the body need:
> - Blood count
> - Blood tests for electrolytes, kidney function, liver function
> - Blood protein test
> - Urine test to check for protein

> Low blood protein often leads to more fluid buildup in the body.

---

## How Is Edema Checked?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and medical history.

They will do a physical exam.

They may order tests based on what they suspect.

---

## How Is Edema Treated?

The main goal is to treat the cause.

### Diet and Lifestyle

- Reduce salt in your diet. This helps reduce fluid buildup.
- Avoid adding salt when cooking or at the table.
- Avoid processed or packaged foods, which often have hidden salt.
- People with advanced liver disease or kidney disease may need to limit salt to 1 gram per day.
- Use salt substitutes with potassium if needed. But be careful if you take certain medicines or have kidney problems. Too much potassium can be dangerous.

### Medicines

- Diuretics (water pills) help the body get rid of extra fluid.
- Loop diuretics and thiazide diuretics are often used.
- But do not take diuretics just to make swelling go away. They are for treating the cause.
- Some diuretics cause the body to lose potassium. This can be dangerous.
- Potassium-sparing diuretics (like amiloride, triamterene, spironolactone, eplerenone) help keep potassium levels normal.
- These can be used alone or with other diuretics.
- An ACE inhibitor and thiazide combination also helps prevent potassium loss.

### Newer Diabetes Medicines

- SGLT2 inhibitors (like canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) help lower blood sugar.
- They also help the body get rid of extra fluid.
- They do not harm electrolyte levels.
- These medicines can help people with heart failure or kidney disease, even if they do not have diabetes.

---

## Special Care for Older Adults

Older people need extra care when treating edema.

- Start with low doses of medicine.
- Check how you feel when the dose changes.
- Watch for dizziness when standing up (orthostatic hypotension), especially if taking diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or beta-blockers.
- Check potassium levels often. Too low or too high can be dangerous.
- Do not stop taking calcium channel blockers just because your feet swell. This side effect is usually harmless.
- Weigh yourself every day. This helps track if your condition is improving or getting worse.

---

## Key Points

- Edema means swelling in the body.
- It can happen all over or just in one area.
- The most common causes of body-wide swelling are heart, liver, or kidney disease.
- Not all swelling is serious. The danger depends on the cause.
- If swelling comes on suddenly, see a doctor right away.

# Superficial Punctate Keratitis

This is an eye condition where small groups of cells on the surface of the cornea die. The cornea is the clear front part of the eye.

## What You Might Notice

- Your eyes may feel sore or painful.
- They may water more than usual.
- Bright light may hurt your eyes.
- Your vision might be a little blurry.
- You may feel like there is something in your eye, like sand or grit.
- Your eyes may look red and bloodshot.

## What Causes It

The condition can be caused by:

- A virus
- Inflammation of the eyelids (blepharitis)
- Dry eyes
- A bacterial infection (including trachoma)
- Chemicals splashed into the eye
- Too much exposure to ultraviolet light (from sunlight, sunlamps, or welding)
- Wearing contact lenses for too long
- Some medicines taken by mouth or through a vein
- An allergy to eye drops
- Bell palsy (a condition that causes weakness on one side of the face)

## When Symptoms Appear

- If UV light caused the problem, symptoms usually start several hours after exposure. They last 1 to 2 days.
- If a virus is the cause, the lymph node in front of the ear on the same side may swell and feel tender.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

- The doctor will ask about your symptoms.
- They will check if you were exposed to any known causes.
- They will use a special microscope called a slit lamp to look closely at your eye.
- They may put in eye drops with a yellow-green dye called fluorescein.
- This dye sticks to damaged areas of the cornea and makes them easier to see.

## How It Is Treated

Treatment depends on the cause.

- Most people get better completely.
- If a virus is the cause (but not herpes simplex or shingles), no treatment is needed. Most people feel better in about 3 weeks.
  - You should take steps to stop the virus from spreading to others.
- If a bacterial infection or long-term contact lens use is the cause, the doctor will prescribe antibiotics.
  - You must stop wearing contact lenses until the eye heals.
- If dry eyes are the cause, using eye ointments or artificial tears helps.
  - Artificial tears are eye drops that act like natural tears. They add moisture to the eye.
- If UV light caused the problem, an antibiotic ointment and a drop that widens the pupil may help relieve symptoms.
- If a medicine or eye drop caused the problem, you must stop using it right away.

# What Are Personality Disorders?

Personality disorders are long-term patterns of thinking, feeling, reacting, and relating to others. These patterns cause serious problems in daily life. They can make it hard to keep a job or have healthy relationships. They also cause distress for the person and for those around them.

These patterns are not just occasional mood swings. They are deeply rooted and do not change easily. They usually start in late teens or early adulthood. Sometimes signs show up earlier, in childhood.

Most people with personality disorders do not seek help because they are uncomfortable with their own thoughts or feelings. Instead, they come in because their behavior causes big problems in their lives. For example, they may lose jobs, break up with partners, or get into legal trouble.

They often do not realize their own behavior is the cause of these problems. This makes treatment harder. Clinicians must help them understand that their personality traits are behind their struggles.

## What Are Personality Traits?

Personality traits are the usual ways a person thinks, feels, and acts. They stay fairly stable over time. For example, some people are naturally calm. Others are always alert and active.

## When Do Traits Become a Disorder?

When these traits become too strong, too rigid, and too harmful, they become a personality disorder. The person has trouble working, being close to others, or managing emotions.

These problems cause real pain. They affect the person’s life and the lives of people around them.

## How Common Are Personality Disorders?

About 9 out of every 100 people in the general population have a personality disorder. In mental health clinics and hospitals, up to half of patients have one.

There are no clear differences by gender, race, or income level for most types. But there are some differences:

- Men are much more likely than women to have antisocial personality disorder.
- Women are more likely than men to have borderline personality disorder — but only in clinics, not in the general population.

## What Causes Personality Disorders?

Genes play a big role. About half of the risk comes from genetics. The other half comes from life experiences.

This means personality disorders are not just bad choices or weak character. They are not caused only by a bad childhood or poor parenting.

## How Much Do They Cost?

Personality disorders cost a lot in health care and lost work time. The costs are higher than for depression or anxiety.

## The 10 Types of Personality Disorders

The DSM-5-TR lists 10 types. They are grouped into three clusters based on similar traits. But these groups are not very useful in real life.

### Cluster A: Odd or Eccentric

These people seem strange or unusual.

- **Paranoid**: Always suspicious. They think others are out to harm them.
- **Schizoid**: Not interested in people. They prefer to be alone.
- **Schizotypal**: Strange beliefs or odd behavior. They may talk in unusual ways.

### Cluster B: Dramatic, Emotional, or Erratic

These people act in intense or unpredictable ways.

- **Antisocial**: Does not care about rules or other people. Lies, manipulates, or breaks laws for personal gain.
- **Borderline**: Feels empty inside. Relationships are unstable. Emotions swing fast and hard.
- **Histrionic**: Always wants attention. Acts overly dramatic or emotional.
- **Narcissistic**: Thinks they are better than others. Needs constant praise. Does not care about others’ feelings.

### Cluster C: Anxious or Fearful

These people are worried and avoidant.

- **Avoidant**: Afraid of rejection. Avoids people and social situations.
- **Dependent**: Needs others to make decisions. Feels helpless without support.
- **Obsessive-compulsive**: Needs everything to be perfect. Rigid and stubborn.

## What Are the Signs?

Personality disorders show up in two main areas:

### Problems with Self-Identity

- Their view of themselves changes a lot. One day they feel kind. The next day they feel cruel.
- Their values, goals, and appearance do not match. For example, they act holy in church but rude and loud elsewhere.

### Problems with Relationships

- They struggle to form or keep close relationships.
- They do not understand or care about others’ feelings.
- They may act in ways that confuse, frustrate, or hurt others.

They may not know where they end and others begin. Their self-worth may be too high or too low.

They may be poor parents. Their behavior can harm their children and partners, causing emotional or physical problems.

Most people with personality disorders do not see how their actions affect others.

## How Are They Diagnosed?

Diagnosis is based on the DSM-5-TR. This is a guide used by mental health professionals.

Many people with personality disorders are not diagnosed. They often come in for other problems, like depression or anxiety.

To diagnose a personality disorder, a clinician looks for:

- A long-term pattern of behavior that is rigid and inflexible.
- The pattern must affect at least two of these areas:
  - How a person sees themselves, others, and events.
  - How they feel and express emotions.
  - How they relate to others.
  - How they control their impulses.
- The pattern must cause serious distress or problems in work, school, or relationships.
- The pattern must have started in adolescence or early adulthood.
- Other causes must be ruled out. These include other mental health issues, drug use, or brain injury.

For people under 18, the pattern must last at least one year. But antisocial personality disorder cannot be diagnosed before age 18.

Because people with personality disorders often do not see their own role in problems, doctors may talk to family, friends, or past therapists to get the full picture.

## How Are They Treated?

### Psychotherapy Is the Main Treatment

- Therapy is the best way to help.
- Both individual and group therapy work well.
- The person must want to change and be willing to work on it.

### Medications Can Help with Specific Symptoms

- Medications do not treat the core disorder.
- But they can help with symptoms like anxiety, anger, or depression.
- They are used only when needed.

### Treatment by Type

| Disorder | Best Therapy | Medications |
|--------|--------------|------------|
| **Antisocial** | Cognitive-behavioral therapy, Contingency management | Antidepressants (SSRIs), Mood stabilizers (lithium, valproate) |
| **Avoidant** | Psychodynamic therapy, Supportive therapy, Cognitive-behavioral therapy | Antidepressants (MAOIs, SSRIs), Anti-anxiety drugs |
| **Borderline** | Dialectical behavior therapy, Mentalization-based therapy, Transference-focused therapy, Schema-focused therapy, Systems training | Mood stabilizers (lamotrigine, topiramate), Atypical antipsychotics, Antidepressants (limited effect) |
| **Dependent** | Psychodynamic therapy, Cognitive-behavioral therapy | Antidepressants (MAOIs, SSRIs) |
| **Histrionic** | Psychodynamic therapy | No medication needed |
| **Narcissistic** | Psychodynamic therapy, Mentalization-based therapy, Transference-focused therapy | No medication needed |
| **Obsessive-compulsive** | Psychodynamic therapy, Cognitive-behavioral therapy | Antidepressants (SSRIs) |
| **Paranoid** | Supportive therapy, Cognitive-behavioral therapy | Antidepressants, Atypical antipsychotics |
| **Schizoid** | Supportive therapy, Social skills training | No medication needed |
| **Schizotypal** | Supportive therapy, Social skills training, Cognitive-behavioral therapy | Atypical antipsychotics |

> **Note**: There is debate about whether antisocial personality disorder can be treated. Some experts believe it is hard to change.

> **Important**: Avoid benzodiazepines and stimulants. They can make symptoms worse.

## Key Points

- Personality disorders are long-term patterns of thinking and behaving that cause serious problems.
- People often do not realize their own behavior is the problem. They must see this to get better.
- Therapy is the main treatment. It helps people change their thoughts and actions.
- Medications help only with specific symptoms like anxiety, anger, or depression.
- Personality disorders do not go away quickly. But many improve over time.

# Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn (PPHN)

This is a serious condition in newborn babies. The small blood vessels in the lungs stay tight after birth. This blocks blood flow to the lungs. As a result, the baby does not get enough oxygen.

## What Happens in PPHN?

- The baby’s lungs do not get enough blood after birth.
- This means the baby’s blood does not get enough oxygen.
- The baby may have trouble breathing.
- This condition mostly affects full-term or late-term babies.

## Signs and Symptoms

Some babies show signs right after birth. Others develop symptoms in the first one or two days.

- Breathing is fast and hard.
- The skin or lips may look blue, gray, or pale.
- In babies with darker skin, the lips, gums, or inside of the eyelids may look blue, gray, or white.
- The lower part of the body may be bluer than the upper part.
- Some babies have low blood pressure.
- Their pulses may be weak.
- Their skin may look pale, gray, or patchy.

## Causes

The blood vessels in the lungs do not open up after birth. This causes high pressure in the lung blood vessels. Blood flow to the lungs stays low. The baby’s blood does not get enough oxygen.

Common causes include:

- Trouble during delivery (like meconium in the lungs)
- Lung problems such as respiratory distress syndrome
- Low oxygen levels before, during, or after birth
- Infections in the mother or baby (sepsis or pneumonia)
- Problems with the placenta
- A hole in the diaphragm (congenital diaphragmatic hernia)
- A collapsed lung
- Lungs that are not fully developed
- Heart issues caused by certain medicines the mother took during pregnancy (like high doses of aspirin or ibuprofen)

## How Doctors Diagnose PPHN

Doctors suspect PPHN if the baby:

- Has trouble breathing
- Has blue lips or skin
- Does not get better when given extra oxygen
- Has symptoms that change with activity or stress

Tests used to confirm the diagnosis:

- **Echocardiogram**: A special ultrasound of the heart and blood flow. This shows how blood moves through the heart and lungs.
- **Chest x-ray**: May show signs of lung problems like pneumonia or a diaphragm hernia.
- **Blood tests**: To check for infection (sepsis).

## Treatment

Treatment aims to open the blood vessels in the lungs and get more oxygen into the blood.

- **Oxygen**: Given through small prongs in the nose or a face mask.
- In severe cases, a **ventilator** (a breathing machine) may be used. It helps the baby breathe and delivers 100% oxygen.
- **Nitric oxide gas**: Added to the oxygen. It helps open the lung blood vessels.
- **Medications**: Given through a vein or by mouth to help widen the blood vessels.
- **ECMO (Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation)**: Used only in the most serious cases. A machine takes over the work of the lungs. It adds oxygen to the blood and removes carbon dioxide. The baby’s lungs can rest while the blood vessels slowly open.

Other treatments may include:

- Fluids to keep the baby hydrated
- Sedatives to calm the baby
- Muscle relaxants
- Antibiotics if there is an infection
- Medicines for heart problems

## Outlook

- PPHN can be deadly in some babies, depending on the cause.
- Some babies who survive may have long-term issues, such as:
  - Delayed development
  - Hearing problems
  - Ongoing lung problems

Early treatment improves the chances of a good outcome.

# Cerebellar Disorders

Cerebellar disorders can happen for many reasons.  
Some people are born with them.  
Others develop them later in life.  
Common causes include genetic conditions, brain problems present at birth, and damage from illness or injury.

The main symptom is usually ataxia.  
Ataxia means trouble with muscle coordination.  
People with ataxia may stumble or have shaky movements.

Symptoms can vary.  
They depend on the cause and which part of the brain is affected.

Doctors diagnose cerebellar disorders by:  
- Talking to the patient and family.  
- Doing a physical exam.  
- Using imaging tests, like MRI scans.  
- Sometimes doing genetic tests if there is a family history.

Treatment depends on the cause.  
If the cause can be fixed, doctors will try to treat it.  
For example, some health problems like low thyroid or celiac disease can be treated.  
Some brain issues, like tumors or fluid buildup, may need surgery.

But most of the time, the cause cannot be fixed.  
So treatment focuses on helping the person live better.

## What the Cerebellum Does

The cerebellum is a part of the brain.  
It has three main areas.  
Each area controls different movements.

### 1. Archicerebellum (Vestibulocerebellum)
- This part is in the back middle of the brain.  
- It helps you stay balanced.  
- It also helps control eye, head, and neck movements.  
- It works closely with the balance system in the inner ear.

### 2. Midline Vermis
- This is the central part of the cerebellum.  
- It helps control movements of the trunk and legs.  
- If this area is damaged, a person may have trouble standing or walking straight.

### 3. Lateral Hemispheres
- These are the outer sides of the cerebellum.  
- They help with fast, precise movements of the arms and hands.  
- For example, they help with writing, buttoning clothes, or catching a ball.

Scientists now believe the cerebellum also helps with some thinking and learning tasks.  
This includes memory and problem solving.

## Key Signs of Cerebellar Disorders

The most common sign is ataxia.  
But other movement problems can happen too.

Here are the main signs:

- **Ataxia**  
  Walking unsteady, like swaying or staggering.  
  Steps are wide apart.

- **Decomposition of movement**  
  Trouble doing small, smooth steps in a sequence.  
  For example, trouble with tasks like brushing teeth or tying shoelaces.

- **Dysarthria**  
  Hard to speak clearly.  
  Words may slur or sound slow.

- **Dysdiadochokinesia**  
  Trouble doing fast, alternating movements.  
  For example, quickly turning your hand over and back.

- **Dysmetria**  
  Trouble reaching a target.  
  You may miss the mark or go too far.

- **Hypotonia**  
  Muscles feel weak or floppy.  
  They do not hold tension well.

- **Nystagmus**  
  Eyes move in a jerky, uncontrolled way.  
  The fast movement is toward the side of the brain problem.

- **Scanning speech**  
  Speech is slow.  
  You pause at the start of words or syllables.

- **Tremor**  
  Shaking in a limb when reaching for something (intention tremor).  
  Or shaking when holding a position (postural tremor).  
  The shaking is slow and large.

## Causes of Cerebellar Disorders

The most common cause is damage from long-term heavy drinking.  
This is called alcoholic cerebellar degeneration.

Other causes include:
- Genetic conditions passed down in families.
- Infections.
- Stroke.
- Brain tumors.
- Autoimmune diseases.
- Exposure to toxins.

## How Doctors Diagnose Cerebellar Disorders

Doctors start by asking about symptoms and family history.  
They check for other health problems that could affect the brain.

They usually do an MRI scan.  
This shows the brain in detail.  
It helps find damage or structural problems.

If there is a family history of similar problems, doctors may do genetic testing.

## How Cerebellar Disorders Are Treated

If the cause can be treated, doctors will do so.  
For example:
- Low thyroid levels can be fixed with medicine.
- Celiac disease can be managed with diet.
- Tumors or fluid buildup in the brain may need surgery.

But most causes cannot be cured.  
So treatment focuses on helping the person manage daily life.

Supportive treatments include:
- Physical therapy to improve balance and coordination.
- Exercises to help with walking and standing.
- Devices like canes, walkers, or special utensils to help with eating and dressing.
- Speech therapy for slurred speech.

Medicines may help some people:
- Riluzole, taken twice a day, may help reduce ataxia for a short time.
- Amantadine might help with movement in some cases.  
  But there is not enough strong evidence to say it works for everyone.

In most cases, treatment is about improving quality of life.  
It is not about curing the condition.

# Gastrinoma

A gastrinoma is a type of tumor that comes from cells in the pancreas or the first part of the small intestine. It makes too much of a hormone called gastrin. This hormone tells the stomach to make too much acid. Too much acid can cause ulcers in the stomach or intestines.

- Gastrinomas are usually small and grow slowly.
- About half of them are cancerous.
- They are a type of pancreatic endocrine tumor.
- Sometimes they happen as part of a genetic condition called multiple endocrine neoplasia.

## What Happens When You Have a Gastrinoma?

The extra gastrin causes the stomach to make far too much acid. This can lead to a condition called Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. This syndrome causes ulcers or ulcer-like symptoms even if no ulcer is present.

### Common Symptoms

- Belly pain
- Blood in the stool
- Diarrhea

### Serious Problems (If Not Treated)

- Heavy bleeding in the stool
- Vomiting blood
- Feeling dizzy or fainting from blood loss
- Severe belly pain if the digestive tract bursts
- Severe constipation, belly pain, and vomiting if the digestive tract is blocked

These serious problems can be life-threatening.

## How Is a Gastrinoma Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect a gastrinoma if a person has many ulcers or ulcers that do not get better with normal treatment.

### Tests Used

- **Blood tests**: These check for high levels of gastrin in the blood. This is the most reliable test.
- **Imaging tests**: These help find the tumor. Examples include:
  - CT scan of the belly
  - Scintigraphy (a type of scan using a special dye)
  - Endoscopic ultrasound (a scope with a camera and sound waves)
  - PET scan
  - Arteriography (an X-ray after dye is injected into an artery)

These tumors are hard to find because they are usually small.

## How Is a Gastrinoma Treated?

Treatment depends on the size, location, and whether the tumor is cancerous.

### Medications

- High doses of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) help reduce stomach acid. These are acid-reducing medicines.
- If PPIs do not work well enough, a medicine called octreotide can be given as an injection. It helps lower gastrin levels and reduce symptoms.

### Surgery

- If there is only one tumor and the person does not have multiple endocrine neoplasia, surgery is often done to remove it.
- About 1 in 5 people are cured by surgery.

### Chemotherapy

- If the tumor is cancerous and has spread to other parts of the body, chemotherapy is used.
- This treatment can help reduce symptoms by shrinking the tumor and lowering gastrin levels.

## What Is the Outlook for People with Gastrinoma?

- If the tumor is completely removed by surgery, more than 90 out of 100 people live 5 to 10 years.
- If the tumor is not fully removed, about 43 out of 100 people live 5 years.
- About 25 out of 100 people live 10 years.

Early diagnosis and treatment improve the chances of a good outcome.

# Green Tea

Green tea comes from the dried leaves of the *Camellia sinensis* plant. This plant is an evergreen shrub that grows in Asia. The same plant is used to make regular tea. But green tea is different because it is not fermented. Instead, the leaves are steamed. This keeps the natural green color and some of the plant’s natural chemicals.

You can drink green tea as a hot drink. You can also take it in tablet or capsule form. These products are made from concentrated green tea extracts.

Green tea has many natural chemicals. Some of these may help protect your body from damage. Scientists think they may help prevent cancer. But more research is needed to be sure.

Green tea contains:
- Polyphenols
- Catechins
- Caffeine

Green tea has less caffeine than coffee. Many green tea products are also made without caffeine.

---

## What People Say About Green Tea

Some people believe green tea helps with many health problems. But most of these claims are not strongly supported by science.

Common claims include:
- Helps with weight loss
- Lowers cholesterol
- Prevents heart disease
- Helps with memory
- Eases joint pain from osteoarthritis
- Helps with menopause symptoms
- May help you live longer
- Helps prevent cancer
- Boosts mental alertness (because of caffeine)
- Treats genital warts

Only a few of these claims have strong scientific proof.

---

## What Science Says About Green Tea

Green tea is one of the most studied supplements. But the evidence for health benefits from drinking green tea is still limited.

### Genital Warts
One type of green tea extract is approved for treating genital warts. These warts are caused by a virus called human papillomavirus.

The extract is called sinecatechins. It is sold under the brand names Veregen and Polyphenon E.

Studies show this treatment works well and is safe. It helps clear warts on the skin and around the anus.

A review of three studies found that a 10% or 15% green tea extract helped treat external anogenital warts.

Another study found this treatment costs less than traditional medicines.

### Weight and Obesity
Some studies show green tea supplements may help with weight and body fat. But results are not strong or consistent.

### Cancer Prevention
There is not enough clear evidence that green tea prevents cancer.

One study found that men who drank about 7 cups of green tea a day had a lower risk of prostate cancer. But this does not prove green tea caused the lower risk.

Other studies have found mixed results. More research is needed.

### Heart Health
A large review of 39 studies found that people who drink tea regularly have lower risks of heart problems.

The study found:
- 4% lower risk of dying from heart disease
- 4% lower risk of stroke
- 2% lower risk of heart events
- 1.5% lower risk of dying from any cause

The benefits were stronger in older adults. But the studies were not all the same. This makes it hard to be sure.

### Limitations of the Research
Most studies have problems. They are small or not well designed. Most were done in countries where people drink green tea every day. Other lifestyle or genetic factors may also explain better health. So we cannot be sure green tea is the real cause.

More large, high-quality studies are needed before we can say for sure what green tea can do.

---

## Side Effects of Green Tea

Most side effects come from caffeine. They include:
- Trouble sleeping
- Feeling anxious
- Fast heartbeat
- Shaking hands

Pregnant women should avoid too much caffeine.

### Liver Problems
Rarely, green tea can cause liver problems. This is more likely with supplements than with drinking tea.

A review of studies found a few people had mild liver issues after taking green tea extracts. These problems usually went away.

The United States Pharmacopeia (USP) says that taking green tea on an empty stomach may increase the risk. This is because the body absorbs more of the active chemicals when the stomach is empty.

Products with a USP verification label say:
- Do not drink brewed green tea on an empty stomach.
- See a doctor if you have symptoms like yellow skin, dark urine, or stomach pain.

The risk of liver damage from drinking green tea on an empty stomach has not been studied enough.

---

## Green Tea and Medicines

Green tea can interact with some medicines. Always talk to your doctor before using green tea if you take medicine.

### Warfarin (a blood thinner)
Green tea has vitamin K. This can reduce how well warfarin works. This may increase your risk of blood clots.

### Lithium (for mood disorders)
If you stop drinking green tea suddenly, lithium levels in your blood may rise. This can cause side effects.

### Beta Blockers (like nadolol)
Green tea may lower the amount of this medicine in your blood. This could make it less effective.

### Statins (for high cholesterol)
Green tea may lower levels of some statins, like atorvastatin and rosuvastatin. This could reduce their effect.

### Iron and Folic Acid
Green tea can reduce how well your body absorbs iron and folic acid. This may lead to low iron levels or anemia.

---
