# Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA)

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis is a group of childhood diseases. It starts before age 16. It causes long-term or repeated swelling and pain in the joints.

## What Is JIA?

- JIA is not the same as adult rheumatoid arthritis.
- Some types of JIA can cause fever, a rash, swollen lymph nodes, or affect the heart.
- The exact cause is unknown.
- JIA is not caused by an infection.
- It is not passed down through families, but genes may play a small role in raising the risk.

## Types of JIA

There are several types. Each type has different signs. Doctors decide which type a child has based on symptoms and test results.

### Oligoarticular JIA
- This is the most common type.
- It usually affects young girls.
- Only 4 or fewer joints are affected in the first 6 months.
- The knee is the most often affected joint.

### Polyarticular JIA
- This is the second most common type.
- It starts in late childhood.
- 5 or more joints are affected.
- It has two types:
  - Rheumatoid factor negative
  - Rheumatoid factor positive
- Rheumatoid factor is a substance in the blood. High levels are linked to rheumatoid arthritis.
- Children with rheumatoid factor positive JIA often have symptoms like adults with rheumatoid arthritis.
- The same joint on both sides of the body is often affected (like both knees or both hands).
- Small joints in the hands and feet are often involved.

### Enthesitis-Related Arthritis
- This type causes joint pain and swelling where tendons and ligaments attach to bones.
- It often affects joints on one side of the lower body (like the hip, knee, ankle, or foot).
- It is more common in older boys.
- Some boys may also get arthritis in the lower spine.

### Psoriatic JIA
- This type often affects young girls, but can also affect older boys and girls equally.
- Some children have psoriasis (a skin disease with scaly patches).
- Others have a family history of psoriasis.

### Undifferentiated JIA
- This label is used when a child has JIA but does not fit clearly into one type.
- Or when a child fits more than one type.

### Systemic JIA (Still Disease)
- This type causes joint pain and swelling.
- It also causes symptoms outside the joints.
- These include high fever, rash, swollen lymph nodes, and inflammation around the heart and lungs.

## Symptoms of JIA

JIA can cause problems in the joints, eyes, skin, or all three.

### Joint Symptoms
- Joints may feel stiff when a child wakes up.
- Joints may swell and feel warm.
- Pain may come later, but it can be mild even with a lot of swelling.
- Pain often gets worse when the joint is moved.
- A child may walk less or limp.
- Some children have no pain at all.
- If not treated, joint pain can last for years.

### Enthesitis Symptoms
- Tenderness in the pelvis, hip bone, spine, kneecap, shin, Achilles tendon, or bottom of the foot.

### Eye Problems
- Eye inflammation (iridocyclitis) can happen with any type of JIA.
- It is most common in oligoarticular JIA.
- It is rare in rheumatoid factor-positive polyarticular JIA and systemic JIA.
- The inflammation affects the iris (the colored part of the eye).
- It often causes no pain or redness.
- It may cause blurry vision or uneven pupils.
- If not treated, it can lead to scarring, cataracts, glaucoma, or permanent vision loss.
- Rarely, children with enthesitis-related arthritis may have red, painful eyes and sensitivity to light.

### Skin Problems
- Skin issues mainly happen in psoriatic JIA and systemic JIA.
- Children with psoriatic JIA may have rough, scaly skin patches.
- Fingers or toes may swell.
- Nails may have pits or come loose from the finger.

### Systemic JIA Symptoms
- A rash appears as flat, pink or salmon-colored patches.
- The rash has clear centers.
- It mainly appears on the trunk and upper legs or arms.
- It comes and goes, often in the evening with fever.
- It may not appear in the same spot each time.
- High fever happens every day.
- The fever is usually highest in the afternoon or evening.
- It can reach 102.2 degrees Fahrenheit (39 degrees Celsius) or higher.
- The fever may last for weeks.
- A child may feel tired and irritable.
- The liver, spleen, or lymph nodes may swell.
- Inflammation can affect the lining of the heart (pericarditis) or lungs (pleuritis).
- It can also cause fluid to build up around the heart, lungs, or other organs.
- This can cause chest pain.

## Complications of JIA

- JIA can slow down a child’s growth.
- If the jaw is affected, the chin may become small.
- Joints can become deformed if JIA is not treated.
- Even with treatment, long-term inflammation can damage joints over time.

## How Is JIA Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose JIA based on:
- The child’s symptoms
- A physical exam

There is no single test that confirms JIA. But blood tests help doctors understand the type.

### Blood Tests
- Full blood count
- Rheumatoid factor
- Antinuclear antibodies
- Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies
- HLA-B27 antigen

Most children with systemic JIA do not have rheumatoid factor or antinuclear antibodies.

Other tests may include:
- Ferritin
- C-reactive protein (CRP)
- Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)

High levels of CRP and ESR mean there is inflammation in the body.

Children with antinuclear antibodies are at higher risk for eye problems. They must see an eye doctor regularly, even if they have no symptoms.

- Children with oligoarticular or polyarticular JIA and antinuclear antibodies: eye exam every 3 months.
- Children with oligoarticular or polyarticular JIA but no antinuclear antibodies: eye exam every 6 months.
- Children with systemic JIA: eye exam once or twice a year.

X-rays may be taken to check for changes in bones or joints.

## How Is JIA Treated?

Treatment aims to reduce pain, stop joint damage, and help the child live a normal life.

### Medications

**Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drugs (DMARDs)**
- These drugs slow down the disease.
- They help prevent joint damage.
- Examples:
  - Methotrexate – fights inflammation
  - Etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab – block a protein that causes inflammation
  - Anakinra, canakinumab – block another inflammation-causing protein
  - Tocilizumab – blocks a different inflammation protein
  - Tofacitinib, upadacitinib – block an enzyme involved in inflammation
  - Abatacept – blocks immune cells that cause inflammation

**Corticosteroids**
- Doctors may inject them directly into a painful joint.
- Oral corticosteroids (like prednisone) are used only when needed.
- They are avoided if possible because they can cause side effects.
- If used, the lowest dose is given to reduce risks.
- Risks include slowed growth, weak bones (osteoporosis), cataracts, and bone death (osteonecrosis).

**Eye Treatment**
- Iridocyclitis is treated with steroid eye drops to reduce swelling.
- Eye drops that widen the pupil are also used to prevent damage.
- If eye drops are not enough, methotrexate or other DMARDs may be used.
- Surgery may be needed if the eye is damaged.

**NSAIDs (Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs)**
- These include medicines like naproxen and ibuprofen.
- They help reduce pain and swelling.
- They are most helpful for enthesitis-related arthritis.
- But they do not stop the disease from getting worse.

### Other Treatments
- Physical therapy helps improve movement, flexibility, and strength.
- Occupational therapy helps with daily tasks like writing or dressing.

## Outlook for Children with JIA

- About half of children have periods with no symptoms (remissions) within 5 years of starting treatment.
- With early treatment, most children can live active, normal lives.
- Children with rheumatoid factor-positive polyarticular JIA tend to have a harder time.

This site offers clear, helpful information about JIA in children. It covers types of arthritis, living with the condition, and how to move from pediatric care to adult care.

# Preoperative Evaluation

You are having surgery. Before the surgery, a team of doctors will check your health. This is called a preoperative evaluation.

The anesthesiology team often does this check. They help plan your anesthesia. Your surgeon may also send you to a general doctor (internist) for a medical check. This is to make sure you are ready for surgery.

The main goal is to find any health problems. This helps lower the risk of problems during or after surgery. The team looks at your past health issues. They check how these might affect your surgery.

They use this check to decide if you need extra steps before surgery. For example, you might need more tests or special care during surgery. In some cases, your surgery may be delayed. This gives time to better control health issues like high blood pressure or diabetes.

If you are at high risk for major surgery, the team may change your surgery plan. They might choose a less invasive method. This can lower your risk.

A general doctor or a specialist may do the check. Specialists include heart doctors, lung doctors, and others. They help manage your long-term health problems. They also help prevent and treat problems after surgery, such as heart or lung issues, or infections.

Sometimes, a mental health doctor is needed. This is to check if you can make decisions about your care. It can also help if you have mental health issues that could affect your surgery or recovery.

## Older Adults

Older adults may get better care with a team of experts. This team may include doctors who specialize in older adults, social workers, mental health therapists, and physical therapists. This team works together to help you prepare for surgery and recover.

## Emergency Surgery

If your surgery is not planned, the team must act fast. They look at how urgent the surgery is. They also check your health risks.

For emergency surgery, there is not enough time for a full check. But the team will still review your medical history as quickly as possible. They pay special attention to allergies. They also look for things that raise your risk, such as blood thinners or bleeding problems. They also check if you had bad reactions to anesthesia before.

## High-Risk Surgeries

Some surgeries carry a higher risk. These include:

- Heart or lung surgery  
- Liver surgery  
- Belly surgeries that take a long time or may cause heavy bleeding (like Whipple surgery, aortic surgery, or retroperitoneal surgery)  
- Open surgery on the prostate  
- Major joint surgeries (like hip replacement)

If you are having elective surgery, especially one that may cause heavy bleeding, you may want to consider saving your own blood. This is called autologous donation. You give your own blood before surgery. It can be used if you need a transfusion.

But there are risks. You might become anemic. You might have to wait for your blood counts to return to normal. This could delay your surgery.

This practice was more common in the past. But it is used less now. This is because blood transfusions are safer than they used to be.

Emergency surgery is riskier than the same surgery done on a planned schedule.

## Your Personal Risk

Your personal health risks affect how likely you are to have problems after surgery. Doctors use special tools to estimate this risk. These tools are based on research and are proven to work.

One example is the ACS NSQIP Surgical Risk Calculator. It helps predict possible problems after surgery.

Using these tools helps doctors compare results fairly. It also helps you and your family make better choices. You can understand the risks and benefits. This leads to better informed consent.

# Voyeuristic Disorder – Simple Explanation

## What Is Voyeurism?

- Some people get sexually excited by watching others who do not know they are being watched.
- This can happen when someone is getting undressed, naked, or having sex.
- The excitement comes from watching, not from having sex with the person.

## What Is Voyeuristic Disorder?

- Voyeuristic disorder happens when watching others without their knowledge causes serious problems.
- It is not just about having thoughts or urges.
- It is a problem if:
  - You feel very upset by your urges.
  - You cannot do your job, take care of your family, or enjoy time with friends.
  - You act on your urges with someone who did not agree.

## Key Facts

- Most people who watch others without permission do not have a disorder.
- Doctors only diagnose voyeuristic disorder when the behavior causes serious distress or harm.
- The disorder is more common in men than in women. For every woman with the disorder, 2 to 3 men have it.
- Many people with this disorder have been arrested. This is how most of what we know about it comes from.

## How Common Is It?

- Voyeurism is one of the most common types of sexual disorders.
- It often starts during teenage years or early adulthood.
- Some level of this behavior is common, especially in boys and men.
- It is becoming more common in women too.
- Watching sexual content online is not voyeurism. That is different because the people in the videos know they are being filmed and have agreed.

## New Risks: Video Voyeurism

- Small cameras and phone cameras make it easier to secretly film people.
- Filming someone without their permission while they are undressing or having sex is a crime in most countries.
- This kind of secret filming is growing in number and is illegal.

## What Happens When Voyeurism Becomes a Disorder?

- People with the disorder spend a lot of time looking for chances to watch others.
- They may ignore work, family, or other responsibilities.
- Watching becomes a main way to get sexual pleasure.
- It can take up many hours each day.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor checks for voyeuristic disorder using standard mental health rules. They look for:

- Repeated and strong sexual excitement from watching someone who does not know they are being watched.
- This excitement leads to:
  - Strong feelings of distress.
  - Trouble doing normal daily tasks.
  - Acting on urges with someone who did not agree.
- The problem has lasted for at least six months.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment usually starts after someone is arrested. It includes:

- Talking therapy (psychotherapy) to help change thoughts and behaviors.
- Support groups where people share experiences and get help.
- Medicines called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). These are a type of antidepressant that can help reduce urges.

### For Severe Cases

- If the main medicines do not work, doctors may use other drugs.
- These drugs lower the body’s level of testosterone.
- Lower testosterone reduces sexual desire.
- Examples: leuprolide and medroxyprogesterone acetate.

### Important Notes About Medication

- You must agree to take these medicines. This is called informed consent.
- Doctors check your health regularly.
- Tests include:
  - Blood tests to check liver health.
  - Blood tests to check testosterone levels.
  - Bone density tests to check bone strength.

These medicines are not used lightly. They are only for serious cases and are closely watched.

# Chronic Eosinophilic Pneumonia

This is a rare lung condition. It happens when too many of a certain type of white blood cell called eosinophils build up in the lungs over time.

## What Are the Symptoms?

People with this condition often have:
- A dry cough that lasts for months.
- Fever.
- Getting more and more short of breath.
- Wheezing.
- Night sweats.

Some people also have asthma or other allergies. These can come before or at the same time as the lung symptoms.

If the condition comes back, you may lose weight. This is due to long-term inflammation in the body.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to diagnose this condition. They first rule out infections and other diseases.

### Imaging Tests
- A chest X-ray may show cloudy areas in the outer parts of the lungs, especially in the middle and upper zones.
- These areas look like the opposite of fluid in the lungs (called pulmonary edema).
- This pattern is very common in this condition, but not everyone has it.
- A high-resolution CT scan of the chest can show similar changes. The cloudy areas may be on one side or both.

### Blood Tests
- A complete blood count checks for high levels of eosinophils in the blood.
- A count over 500 eosinophils per microliter is common.
- Other blood signs include high inflammation markers (like ESR or CRP), low iron levels, and low red blood cell counts.
- High levels of IgE (a type of antibody linked to allergies) are also common.

### Lung Fluid Test
- Doctors may do a bronchoscopy to collect fluid from the lungs.
- If more than 40% of the cells in this fluid are eosinophils, it strongly suggests this condition.

### Lung Function Tests
- These tests check how well your lungs work.
- Results may show blocked airways, stiff lungs, or a mix of both.
- The ability to move oxygen into the blood may be reduced.

## How Is It Treated?

This condition responds very well to steroid medicines.

### Main Treatment
- You will take oral steroids like prednisone.
- The dose starts high and is slowly lowered over time.
- Most people feel much better within two days.
- Symptoms and lung scans usually return to normal within two weeks. Almost everyone is fully recovered by one month.

### Long-Term Care
- Some people have a return of symptoms after stopping treatment.
- Others get worse when the steroid dose is lowered.
- Relapses can happen months or even years later.
- For this reason, some people need low-dose steroids for years.

### Inhaled Steroids
- Inhaled steroids (like fluticasone or beclomethasone) can help.
- They are used twice a day, at a dose of 500 to 750 micrograms each time.
- They can reduce the need for oral steroids.

### Monitoring
- Your doctor may check your blood tests during treatment.
- These include eosinophil counts, inflammation markers, and IgE levels.
- But not everyone has abnormal results.

## What Is the Outlook?

- Most people get better and stay well with treatment.
- Relapses do not mean the disease is worse or harder to treat.
- People still respond well to steroids when symptoms return.
- Some may have mild, lasting changes in lung function.
- But these changes usually do not cause serious problems.
- In rare cases, long-term untreated inflammation can cause scarring in the lungs.
- However, this is very uncommon and rarely leads to serious illness or death.

# Nephrotic Syndrome – Simple Explanation

Nephrotic syndrome is a kidney problem. It happens when the tiny filters in your kidneys (called glomeruli) get damaged. These filters normally keep important proteins in your blood. When they are damaged, too much protein leaks into your urine.

When protein leaves your blood, your body loses important nutrients. This can cause fluid to build up in your body. You may notice swelling in your face, hands, feet, or belly. You may also feel tired and unwell.

---

## What Causes Nephrotic Syndrome?

Nephrotic syndrome can happen for many reasons. Some causes are:

- **Kidney problems** that start in the kidneys (called primary causes).
- **Other health issues** that affect the kidneys (called secondary causes).

### Common Causes

#### Diseases
- **Diabetes** – This is one of the most common causes.
- **Lupus** – An autoimmune disease that can damage the kidneys.
- **Infections** – Such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, or HIV.
- **Cancer** – Especially lymphoma, leukemia, or solid tumors.
- **Amyloidosis** – A rare condition where abnormal proteins build up in organs.
- **Kidney inflammation** – Called glomerulonephritis.
- **Obesity** – Can increase the risk.
- **Preeclampsia** – A serious condition during pregnancy.
- **Parasite infections** – Like schistosomiasis or malaria.
- **Blood vessel diseases** – Such as IgA vasculitis or granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

#### Medicines and Drugs
- **Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)** – Like ibuprofen or naproxen.
- **Gold** – Used in some older treatments.
- **Heroin** – A dangerous illegal drug.
- **Penicillamine** – A medicine used for some conditions.

#### Allergies
- Insect bites.
- Poison ivy or poison oak.
- Pollen.

Some types of nephrotic syndrome are passed down in families (hereditary).

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Early signs include:

- Not feeling hungry.
- Feeling generally unwell.
- Swelling in the face, especially around the eyes.
- Swelling in the hands, feet, or belly.
- Belly swelling due to fluid buildup (called ascites).
- Fluid around the lungs, which can cause shortness of breath.
- Swelling in the genitals (labia or scrotum).
- Frothy or bubbly urine.

### How Swelling Moves in the Body

- When you lie down at night, fluid collects in your face and eyelids.
- When you stand or sit during the day, fluid moves to your legs and ankles.

Swelling can hide muscle loss that is happening at the same time.

### Other Possible Problems

- **Low blood pressure** – Common in children. It may drop when standing up (called orthostatic hypotension).
- **Shock** – Rare, but serious.
- **High or low blood pressure** – Adults may have any of these.
- **Less urine** – This can happen if blood volume drops.
- **Kidney failure** – Can happen suddenly or slowly. It means the kidneys stop working well.

### Nutrition and Health Effects

- Nutrients are lost in the urine.
- Children may grow more slowly.
- Bones may weaken because calcium is lost.
- You may have low vitamin D, which harms bones.
- Hair and nails may become weak or break easily.
- Some people lose hair.
- White lines may appear across the fingernails (reason unknown).

### Infections

- The lining of the belly (peritoneum) can become inflamed or infected.
- Infections from bacteria that are usually harmless can happen more often.
- This happens because the body loses infection-fighting proteins in the urine.

### Blood Clots

- Blood is more likely to clot, especially in the veins of the kidneys.
- In rare cases, blood may not clot when it should, leading to bleeding.

High blood pressure with heart or brain problems is more likely if you have diabetes or lupus.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find out if you have nephrotic syndrome.

### Tests Used

- **Urine test** – Checks how much protein is in your urine.
  - A 24-hour urine collection is best, but hard for many people.
  - A single urine sample can also be used to check the protein-to-creatinine ratio.
- **Blood tests** – Check for:
  - Low albumin (a key protein in blood).
  - High fats (lipids) in the blood.
  - High or low levels of blood clotting proteins.
  - Anemia (low red blood cells).
  - Signs of infection or autoimmune disease.
- **Imaging tests** – Like ultrasound or CT scan of the kidneys.
- **Kidney biopsy** – A small sample of kidney tissue is taken to see the damage and find the cause.

Doctors also check for:
- Past infections.
- Autoimmune diseases (where the body attacks itself).
- Cancer – especially in older adults or those who have lost weight.

---

## Types of Kidney Problems That Cause Nephrotic Syndrome

| Condition | Who It Affects | What Happens | Prognosis (Outlook) |
|--------|----------------|--------------|---------------------|
| **Congenital nephrotic syndrome** (Finnish type) | Babies at birth | Rare inherited disease. Very low albumin. | Does not respond to steroids. Often needs dialysis and kidney transplant. |
| **Diffuse mesangial sclerosis** | Children | Similar to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. | Same as above. Needs transplant. |
| **Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis** | Teens and young adults | Damages kidney filters. More common in Black men. | Poor outcome. Two-thirds develop kidney failure within 15 years. |
| **Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis** | Children or adults | Caused by immune system problems. | If caused by treatable disease (like lupus or hepatitis), some improvement possible. Unknown cause = worse outcome. |
| **Membranous nephropathy** | Adults | Serious kidney disease. | One-third get better on their own. One-third develop kidney failure. One-third keep protein in urine. |
| **Mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis** | All ages | Mild to moderate damage. | Half respond to steroids. 10–30% develop kidney failure. Relapses may respond to other drugs. |
| **Minimal change disease** | Children (most common), also adults | Mild kidney damage. | Good outlook. Over 80% go into remission with treatment. |

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause and how bad the damage is.

### Treat the Underlying Cause
- If caused by an infection, treat the infection.
- If caused by medicine, stop the medicine (if safe).
- If caused by cancer or lupus, treat that condition.

### Medicines
- **ACE inhibitors or ARBs** – These help protect the kidneys and reduce protein in urine. Examples: enalapril, lisinopril, losartan, valsartan.
- **Diuretics** – Help remove extra fluid from the body.
- **Statins** – Lower fat levels in the blood.
- **Corticosteroids** – Used for some types, like minimal change disease.
- **Immunosuppressants** – Used if the immune system is attacking the kidneys.
- **Anticoagulants** – Prevent blood clots.

### Diet and Lifestyle
- Limit salt (sodium) in your food.
- Eat a healthy diet with enough protein.
- Stay active, if possible.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

The long-term result depends on:

- What caused the problem.
- Your age.
- The type and amount of kidney damage.

### Good Outcomes
- If the cause is treatable (like an infection, cancer, or medicine), symptoms may go away completely.
- This happens in about half of children, but less often in adults.
- If the cause responds to steroids, the disease may stop getting worse. In rare cases, it may improve.

### Poor Outcomes
- If caused by HIV, the disease often gets worse quickly. Kidney failure can happen in 3–4 months.
- Babies born with nephrotic syndrome rarely live past their first birthday. Some survive with dialysis or a kidney transplant.

### Chronic Kidney Disease
- If caused by lupus or diabetes, medicines may help control protein in urine.
- But some people still develop chronic kidney disease.
- This can lead to kidney failure within a few years.

---

## How Can It Be Prevented?

The best way to prevent worsening kidney damage is to use certain medicines early.

- **ACE inhibitors** (like enalapril, benazepril, lisinopril) or **ARBs** (like losartan, valsartan, candesartan).
- These are used in people with diabetes or lupus who have mild or moderate protein in urine.
- Starting these medicines early can slow kidney damage and keep protein levels from rising.

---

# Anemia During Pregnancy

Anemia during pregnancy is a serious health issue.  
About 37 out of every 100 pregnant women worldwide have anemia.  
Rates are higher in low-income and lower-middle-income countries.  
In the United States, anemia is more common in Black and Pacific Islander women.  
It is less common in Asian and White women.

Anemia during pregnancy can harm both mother and baby.  
It can lead to early delivery, serious bleeding from the placenta, or needing intensive care.  
It can also cause stillbirth, slow growth in the baby, or problems with brain development.

## What Happens to Blood During Pregnancy?

Your body makes more blood during pregnancy.  
Red blood cells increase by 15% to 25%.  
But your blood plasma (the liquid part) increases even more—by 40% to 50%.  
This causes a normal drop in blood concentration, called hemodilution.  
This is not a problem. It is a normal change.

Your body still carries enough oxygen.  
Your blood’s ability to carry oxygen stays normal.  
After delivery, your blood levels go back to normal quickly.  
This happens because blood from the placenta flows back into your body.

Anemia affects up to one third of women in the third trimester.  
The most common causes are:
- Not enough iron
- Not enough folate

Bleeding during or just after delivery is a common cause of iron deficiency.

## Signs and Symptoms of Anemia

Early on, you may not feel any symptoms.  
If you do, they may include tiredness, weakness, dizziness, or shortness of breath when active.  
You might also look pale.  
If anemia is severe, you may have a fast heartbeat or low blood pressure.

If your baby is not growing well, your doctor may check for anemia.

## How Is Anemia Diagnosed?

Your doctor will do a blood test called a complete blood count (CBC).  
This test checks your hemoglobin and hematocrit levels.

The following levels mean you have anemia during pregnancy:

- **First trimester:** Hemoglobin below 11 grams per deciliter or hematocrit below 33%
- **Second trimester:** Hemoglobin below 10.5 grams per deciliter or hematocrit below 32%
- **Third trimester:** Hemoglobin below 11 grams per deciliter or hematocrit below 33%

After the CBC, your doctor will look at the size of your red blood cells.  
This is called the mean corpuscular volume (MCV).  
Based on this, they will decide what tests to do next.

### If Red Blood Cells Are Small (Microcytic Anemia)

This often means iron deficiency.  
Your doctor will check your iron levels and ferritin (a protein that stores iron).  
They may also test for hemoglobin problems like sickle cell disease.

If tests are unclear or treatment does not help, a blood specialist may be needed.

### If Red Blood Cells Are Large (Macrocytic Anemia)

This often means low folate or low vitamin B12.  
Your doctor will check your folate and vitamin B12 levels.

### If There Are Mixed Causes

Your doctor will test for both iron and folate problems.

### Common Types of Anemia and Their Features

| Type of Anemia | Blood Cell Shape | Key Features |
|----------------|------------------|------------|
| Blood loss (acute) | Normal size, some immature cells | May see abnormal white blood cells and platelets |
| Blood loss (chronic) | Same as iron deficiency | Same as iron deficiency |
| Folate deficiency | Same as vitamin B12 deficiency | Low folate in blood; low red blood cell folate |
| Hereditary spherocytosis | Small, round cells | High red blood cell count; fragile red blood cells |
| Warm antibody hemolytic anemia | Small, round cells | High red blood cell count; positive test for antibodies |
| Hemolysis (red blood cells breaking down) | Normal size | High reticulocyte count; high bilirubin; low haptoglobin |
| Chronic disease (infection, cancer, etc.) | Normal size early, then small | Normal or high iron stores; low iron in blood |
| Iron deficiency | Small, uneven size | Low iron, low ferritin, high iron-binding capacity |
| Marrow failure | Normal or large | Low blood cell counts; bone marrow may not work |
| Marrow replacement (e.g., cancer, fibrosis) | Uneven shape, teardrop cells | May see abnormal cells in bone marrow |
| Cold agglutinin disease | Large cells | Cells clump when cold; may follow infection |
| Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria | Low white and platelet counts | Dark urine in the morning; blood clots |
| Sickle cell disease | Uneven shape, sickle-shaped cells | Common in people of African ancestry; pain crises |
| Sideroblastic anemia | Often small, some large | Ringed cells in bone marrow; may respond to vitamin B6 |
| Thalassemia | Small cells, target-shaped | High Hb A2 and Hb F; common in Mediterranean people |
| Vitamin B12 deficiency | Large, oval cells | High white blood cell count; high methylmalonic acid |

Note:  
- Hb = hemoglobin  
- RBC = red blood cell  
- WBC = white blood cell  
- CBC = complete blood count  
- CNS = brain and nervous system  
- GI = stomach and intestines

## How Is Anemia Treated?

The goal is to fix the cause of anemia.  
Blood transfusions may be needed in severe cases.

### When Is a Blood Transfusion Needed?

- If your hemoglobin drops below 6 grams per deciliter  
- If you have severe symptoms like dizziness, weakness, or trouble breathing  
- If your baby is in danger

The decision is not based only on hemoglobin.  
It also depends on your symptoms and how you feel.

### Preparing for Delivery

If you have anemia, your doctor will plan ahead.  
They will prepare for possible blood loss during delivery.  
They will also consider if you can receive a blood transfusion.  
For example, some people (like Jehovah’s Witnesses) do not accept blood transfusions.

### Key Points

- The normal increase in blood volume during pregnancy causes a mild drop in blood concentration.  
  This is normal and does not harm you or your baby.
- The most common causes of real anemia are low iron and low folate.
- Anemia can lead to serious problems for both mother and baby.
- All pregnant women should take low-dose iron supplements in the first trimester to prevent anemia.
- Treat the cause of anemia if possible.  
  But if your hemoglobin is below 6 grams per deciliter or you have severe symptoms, a blood transfusion is usually needed.

---

## Iron Deficiency Anemia in Pregnancy

Iron deficiency anemia is the most common type of anemia in pregnancy.  
It happens when your body does not have enough iron.

### Why Does This Happen?

- You do not eat enough iron-rich foods.
- You lose iron every month during your period.
- You lost blood in a past pregnancy.

### How Is It Diagnosed?

- Hematocrit is 30% or lower.
- Red blood cells are small.
- Blood tests show low iron and low ferritin.
- Iron-binding capacity is high.

### How Is It Treated?

- Oral iron pills every day or every other day.
- Some women need iron through a vein (IV iron) if pills do not work or cause side effects.

Most prenatal vitamins have 27 mg of iron.  
But if you have anemia, you may need more—like 325 mg of ferrous sulfate (which gives 65 mg of elemental iron).

If you have stomach upset or constipation, you can take iron every other day.

About 20% of women do not absorb enough iron from pills or cannot tolerate them.  
These women need IV iron.

Your doctor will check your hemoglobin and hematocrit weekly to see if treatment is working.

If iron pills do not help, you may also be low in folate.

### What About the Baby?

Babies born to mothers with iron deficiency usually have normal blood counts at birth.  
But they have low iron stores.  
They will need iron supplements early in life.

### Prevention

All pregnant women should take low-dose iron supplements in the first trimester.  
If your hemoglobin is below 11.5 grams per deciliter at the start of pregnancy, you may need extra iron.  
This is because your blood will become more diluted as pregnancy progresses.

---

## Folate Deficiency Anemia in Pregnancy

Folate deficiency can cause serious birth defects.  
It increases the risk of neural tube defects (like spina bifida).  
It may also raise the risk of fetal alcohol syndrome.

### How Common Is It?

Folate deficiency affects 0.5% to 1.5% of pregnant women.  
It can cause large red blood cells and anemia.

### Symptoms

- Rarely, severe anemia or sore tongue (glossitis)

### How Is It Diagnosed?

- Blood test shows large red blood cells.
- High red blood cell distribution width (RDW).
- Low folate in blood.

### How Is It Treated?

- Take 1 milligram of folic acid once a day by mouth.

Severe cases may need a bone marrow test and more treatment.

# Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD)

Borderline personality disorder is a mental health condition that affects how a person feels about themselves, relates to others, and handles emotions.

## What It Feels Like

- People with BPD often fear being left alone.
- They may feel empty inside, especially when no one is around to care for them.
- They may feel like they do not exist when they are alone.
- They react strongly to small signs of rejection or being ignored.

## How It Shows Up

- They may change how they feel about people quickly. One moment they love someone. The next, they hate them.
- They may idealize a person at first. Then they suddenly think the person does not care and treat them badly.
- Their mood can shift fast. These changes usually last only a few hours, not days.
- They may act on impulse in ways that hurt them. Examples include reckless driving, unsafe sex, binge eating, or spending too much money.
- They may hurt themselves on purpose. This includes cutting or burning their skin.
- They may threaten or attempt suicide. These acts are often not meant to end life. They are a way to cope with pain or to get help.
- They may sabotage their own success. For example, they might quit school just before finishing or ruin a good relationship.
- They may feel paranoid or disconnected from themselves during times of stress. This can include feeling unreal or detached from their body.

## Why It Happens

- Some people may be born with a tendency to react strongly to stress.
- BPD sometimes runs in families. This suggests genes may play a role.
- Many people with BPD had tough experiences as children. These include abuse, being separated from caregivers, or losing a parent.
- These early experiences can make it hard to trust others or feel safe in relationships.

## Other Mental Health Issues

People with BPD often have other mental health problems. These include:

- Depression
- Anxiety (like panic attacks)
- Posttraumatic stress disorder
- Eating disorders
- Substance use problems

## How It Is Diagnosed

A doctor or mental health professional makes the diagnosis after a careful evaluation.

To be diagnosed with BPD, a person must show at least five of the following:

- They try very hard to avoid being abandoned, even if the threat is not real.
- Their relationships are intense and unstable. They may love someone one day and hate them the next.
- They often change how they see themselves. This can include changing goals, values, or friends.
- They act impulsively in at least two ways that could cause harm. Examples: unsafe sex, binge eating, reckless driving.
- They have repeated suicide-related behaviors. This includes threats, attempts, or self-harm.
- Their mood changes quickly. These changes usually last only a few hours.
- They feel empty inside most of the time.
- They get angry in ways that are out of proportion to the situation.
- They have brief episodes of paranoia or feeling disconnected from themselves when stressed.

These symptoms must have started by early adulthood.

## How It Is Treated

Treatment helps people feel better and live more stable lives.

### Psychotherapy (Talk Therapy)

- This is the main treatment for BPD.
- It helps people understand their emotions and behaviors.
- It teaches better ways to handle stress and relationships.
- It can reduce self-harm and suicidal thoughts.
- It helps people feel more in control of their lives.

### Medications

- Medicines are not a cure for BPD.
- But they can help with specific symptoms like depression, anxiety, or mood swings.
- Doctors may prescribe them to support therapy.

### Treating Other Conditions

- It is important to treat other mental health issues at the same time.
- For example, treating depression or anxiety can improve overall progress.

## Outlook

- In most people, BPD symptoms get much better over time.
- Many people no longer meet the full criteria for BPD after several years.
- However, getting better does not always mean they can keep a job or have stable relationships.
- Treatment helps people function better and feel more in control.
- While symptoms improve more than daily functioning, many people still face challenges in work and relationships.

With the right support, people with BPD can lead meaningful and productive lives.

# Trachoma

Trachoma is an eye infection caused by a germ called *Chlamydia trachomatis*.  
It causes long-term inflammation of the eye.  
The condition comes and goes over time.  
It is the top cause of blindness that can be prevented.  

## Who Gets Trachoma?

Trachoma is common in poor areas of North Africa, the Middle East, India, Australia, and Southeast Asia.  
About 1.9 million people have it.  
It causes about 1.4% of all blindness worldwide.  
The germ that causes trachoma is *Chlamydia trachomatis*, especially types A, B, Ba, and C.  

In the United States, trachoma is rare.  
It happens now and then in American Indian communities and among immigrants.  
It mostly affects children under 10 years old.  
Older children and adults are less likely to get it.  
This is because they have stronger immunity and better hygiene.  

Trachoma spreads easily in the early stages.  
It spreads through:  
- Touching the eye with a dirty hand  
- Eye-to-eye contact  
- Flies that land on the eye  
- Sharing towels, clothes, or makeup that are dirty  

## Symptoms and Signs

Trachoma usually affects both eyes.  
The World Health Organization uses five stages to describe it.  

**Stage 1: Trachomatous inflammation–follicular (TF)**  
- You see 5 or more small bumps (follicles) on the upper eyelid inside.  

**Stage 2: Trachomatous inflammation–intense (TI)**  
- The inside of the upper eyelid is thick and swollen.  
- The swelling covers more than half of the normal blood vessels.  

**Stage 3: Trachomatous scarring (TS)**  
- The inside of the upper eyelid has scars.  

**Stage 4: Trachomatous trichiasis (TT)**  
- At least one eyelash rubs against the eye.  

**Stage 5: Corneal opacity (CO)**  
- The clear front part of the eye (cornea) has a cloudy spot over the pupil.  

Pictures show:  
- Small bumps and redness in the upper eyelid.  
- Scarring on the eyelid and cornea.  
- A cloudy cornea and an eyelash rubbing the eye.  

In rare cases, the eye can heal on its own.  
The blood vessels in the cornea may go away.  
The eye can become clear again.  
With treatment, the inside of the eyelid becomes smooth and pale.  

Repeated infections cause long-term swelling.  
This leads to scarring.  
Scarring pulls the eyelid inward.  
This causes eyelashes to rub the eye.  
Over time, this can scar the cornea.  
This can lead to blindness.  

In one study in Egypt, 6.5% of adults had eyelashes rubbing the eye.  
Of these, 13% had poor vision.  
8% were blind.  

## How Is Trachoma Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose trachoma by looking at the eyes.  
Testing is not always available in poor areas.  

Signs that help doctors make the diagnosis include:  
- Small bumps on the inside of the upper eyelid  
- Thick, swollen eyelid lining  
- Scarring on the eyelid  
- Cloudy growth on the cornea  

A lab test can find the germ *Chlamydia trachomatis*.  
Tests include:  
- Growing the germ in a lab  
- Using a DNA test (NAAT)  
- Using a special stain to see the germ  

These tests are best when the diagnosis is unclear.  
They help confirm the disease and stop it from getting worse.  

In early trachoma, a lab test can show tiny spots inside eye cells.  
These spots are called inclusion bodies.  
They help tell trachoma apart from other eye infections.  

Other eye problems can look like trachoma.  
But they have different symptoms.  
For example:  
- Palpebral vernal conjunctivitis has flat, white bumps.  
- It does not have inclusion bodies.  
- It has a different pattern of symptoms.  

## How Is Trachoma Treated?

Treatment depends on the stage.  

**Antibiotics**  
- For mild cases, use eye ointment.  
- For more serious cases, take a pill.  

**Surgery**  
- If the eyelid is twisted and lashes rub the eye, surgery can fix it.  
- If the cornea is cloudy and blocks vision, surgery may help.  

**The SAFE Program**  
The World Health Organization recommends a full plan called SAFE:  
- **S**urgery for eyelid problems  
- **A**ntibiotics to kill the germ  
- **F**acial cleanliness to stop spread  
- **E**nvironmental improvement to reduce flies and dirty water  

**For mild inflammation (TF):**  
- Use eye ointment.  
- Apply tetracycline 1% ointment to both eyes twice a day for 6 weeks.  

**For severe inflammation (TI):**  
- Use eye ointment.  
- Or take a pill.  

**For scarring (TS):**  
- No treatment is needed unless it leads to trichiasis.  

**For severe cases (TT or CO):**  
- Surgery is needed.  
- If the cornea is cloudy, a corneal transplant may restore vision.  
- But this surgery is hard to do in poor areas.  
- It needs strong aftercare to prevent infection and rejection.  
- So it is not always possible.  

**Pills for treatment:**  
- A single dose of azithromycin is 78% to 95% effective.  
- The dose is 20 milligrams per kilogram of body weight.  
- The maximum dose is 1 gram.  
- This medicine also helps reduce child deaths.  
- Other options:  
  - Erythromycin: 500 milligrams twice a day for 14 days  
  - Doxycycline: 100 milligrams twice a day for 10 days  
- Do not use doxycycline in pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers, or children under 8.  

## Key Points

- Trachoma is a long-term eye infection caused by a germ.  
- It is common in children under 10 in poor areas.  
- It starts with red, swollen eyes.  
- It can lead to scarring, eyelashes rubbing the eye, and blindness.  
- It is the top cause of preventable blindness.  
- Doctors usually diagnose it by looking at the eyes.  
- Lab tests can confirm it when available.  
- Treatment is with eye ointment or pills.  
- In poor areas, the best way to stop trachoma is the SAFE program: surgery, antibiotics, clean faces, and better living conditions.

# Tapeworm Infection

Tapeworms are parasites that live in the intestines. They can make you sick. You usually get them by eating raw or undercooked meat or fish. You can also get them from food or water that has been touched by human stool.

## Types of Tapeworms

There are several types of tapeworms that can infect people:

- **Beef tapeworm** – found in undercooked beef  
- **Pork tapeworm** – found in undercooked pork  
- **Asian tapeworm** – found in pork in Asia  
- **Fish tapeworm** – found in raw or undercooked freshwater fish  
- **Dwarf tapeworm** – very small; found in food or water with human stool

Dogs can carry other tapeworms. These can also infect people and cause cysts in the liver or other organs.

## How Tapeworms Work

Tapeworms have three parts:

- The **head** attaches to the inside of the intestine  
- The **neck** can grow new parts  
- The **body** is made of many segments. Each segment can hold eggs

If the head and neck are not removed, the worm can grow back.

## How You Get Infected

### Pork, Beef, and Fish Tapeworms

1. You eat raw or undercooked meat or fish that has tiny cysts in it.  
2. The cysts break open in your intestine.  
3. The tapeworm grows and attaches to the wall of your intestine.  
4. The worm makes new segments. These segments contain eggs.  
5. The segments or eggs come out in your stool.  
6. If pigs, cows, or fish eat the eggs, the eggs hatch and form cysts in their muscles.  
7. If you eat that meat or fish, the cycle starts again.

### Dwarf Tapeworm

- You swallow the eggs, not cysts.  
- The eggs come from food, water, or surfaces touched by infected people.  
- You can also get them from eating bugs like fleas or beetles in grain.  
- The eggs grow into adult worms in your intestine.  
- The worms lay eggs that come out in your stool.  
- You can swallow your own eggs and get infected again. This is called autoinfection.

## What Happens in the Body

### Intestinal Infection

Most people with adult tapeworms in the intestine feel fine.  
Some people have:

- Belly pain  
- Diarrhea  
- Weight loss  
- Nausea or vomiting  
- Loss of appetite  

You might see a piece of the worm in your stool. It looks like a ribbon.

The fish tapeworm can cause anemia. It takes vitamin B12 from your body. This vitamin is needed to make healthy blood.

### Cysticercosis

This happens when pork tapeworm eggs get into your body and form cysts in your brain, muscles, or other organs.

You can get cysts in your brain if you swallow pork tapeworm eggs. This can happen if:

- You eat food or drink water with human stool on it  
- You touch something with eggs on it and then touch your mouth  
- You swallow eggs from your own stool (autoinfection)

The eggs turn into tiny larvae. These travel through your blood. They can end up in your brain, muscles, or other tissues. There they form cysts.

Cysts in the brain can cause:

- Headaches  
- Seizures  
- Confusion  
- Memory problems  
- Muscle weakness  
- Paralysis  
- Blindness (if cysts form in the eyes)

These symptoms can appear years after the first infection. They happen when the cysts start to break down and cause swelling.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

### For Intestinal Infection

- A doctor checks your stool for worm segments or eggs.

### For Cysticercosis

- A CT scan or MRI can show cysts in the brain or other parts of the body.  
- Blood tests can check for signs of infection.  
- Sometimes, a doctor can feel a hard lump under the skin.

## How It Is Treated

### Intestinal Infection

- A single dose of medicine called praziquantel kills the worm.  
- For dwarf tapeworm, a medicine called nitazoxanide may be used instead.

### Cysticercosis

- If cysts are in the brain, treatment depends on symptoms and where the cysts are.  
- Corticosteroids (like prednisone) reduce swelling and inflammation.  
- Antiseizure medicine is used if you have seizures.  
- Antiparasitic medicine (like albendazole or praziquantel) can kill living cysts. But it is only used after symptoms are under control.  
- Corticosteroids are also given with antiparasitic medicine to prevent swelling from dying cysts.  
- These medicines are not used for cysts in the eye or spinal cord. They can cause serious swelling and damage.  
- Surgery may be needed if cysts block fluid around the brain or spinal cord. It may also be needed if cysts are causing serious problems in the eye or spine.

## How to Prevent Tapeworm Infection

### Cook Meat and Fish Thoroughly

- Cook whole cuts of meat to over 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63 degrees Celsius) for at least 3 minutes.  
- Let the meat rest for 3 minutes after cooking before cutting or eating.  
- Cook ground meat to at least 160 degrees Fahrenheit (71 degrees Celsius).  
- Do not let ground meat rest.  
- Cook freshwater fish to 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63 degrees Celsius).  
- Do not eat raw fish (like sushi).  
- Freezing fish can also kill the parasite. Use one of these methods:

  - Freeze at -4 degrees Fahrenheit (-20 degrees Celsius) or colder for 7 days  
  - Freeze at -31 degrees Fahrenheit (-35 degrees Celsius) or colder until solid, then keep at that temperature for 15 hours  
  - Freeze at -31 degrees Fahrenheit (-35 degrees Celsius) or colder until solid, then keep at -4 degrees Fahrenheit (-20 degrees Celsius) or colder for 24 hours

- Smoking or drying fish does not kill the parasite.

### Check Meat and Fish

- Trained inspectors can find cysts in meat.  
- Only eat meat that has been checked.

### Handle Waste Safely

- Treat human waste properly.  
- This breaks the cycle of infection and helps stop beef and pork tapeworms from spreading.

### Avoid Contaminated Food and Water

- Wash, peel, or cook all raw fruits and vegetables before eating.  
- Use clean water.  
- Wash your hands with soap and warm water after using the toilet, changing diapers, or handling animals.  
- Wash your hands before preparing food.

## Key Facts

- Tapeworms can grow up to 30 feet long.  
- Most people with intestinal tapeworms feel no symptoms.  
- Cysts in the brain can cause serious health problems.  
- Cooking food well and washing hands are the best ways to stay safe.

# Swelling in the Remaining Limb After Amputation

Swelling can still happen in the remaining limb even after it has fully healed. This usually takes 18 to 24 months after the amputation.

A prosthesis that fits well is the best way to keep the size and shape of the remaining limb steady.

When you are not wearing your prosthesis, you can reduce swelling by using:

- Elastic bandages
- Compression sleeves made of stretchy material
- A soft, cushioning layer that goes between your limb and the prosthesis

It also helps to stay active and eat healthy. Regular exercise or physical therapy can help keep your muscles strong.

If the surgery preserved some movement in the muscles near the amputation site, swelling is usually less of a problem.

In hot and humid weather, the remaining limb may swell and sweat. This can make it hard to put on the prosthesis.

To help, try this:
- Take a shower, or soak the limb in cold water for 3 to 5 minutes.
- Dry it completely right away.
- Put the prosthesis on as soon as it is dry.

After wearing the prosthesis for 5 to 15 minutes, take it off and put it back on right away. This helps your limb settle into the right position inside the socket.

If cold water is not available, try this instead:
- Wrap the limb with an elastic bandage.
- Or wear the cushioning layer (viscoelastic interface).
- Keep the limb raised for 20 minutes or longer.

Even though vacuum suction systems (which use a pump to hold the prosthesis in place) might seem like they could cause swelling, they do not when the socket fits perfectly.

# Renal Glucosuria

Glucose, or sugar, appears in the urine even when blood sugar levels are normal or low.

This is different from diabetes, where high blood sugar causes sugar to appear in the urine.

In healthy people, the kidneys filter sugar from the blood. Then, the kidneys return almost all of it back into the blood.

In people with renal glucosuria, the kidneys do not reabsorb sugar properly. This means some sugar passes into the urine even when blood sugar is normal.

The problem comes from a defect in the kidney’s tubule cells. These cells are responsible for returning sugar to the blood.

Some cases of renal glucosuria are inherited. They may happen on their own or as part of a larger kidney condition called Fanconi syndrome.

Other cases are caused by certain medicines or diseases that harm the kidney tubules.

Most people with renal glucosuria have no symptoms. The condition does not cause serious health problems.

Doctors find this condition during a routine urine test. The test shows sugar in the urine, but blood tests show normal sugar levels.

No treatment is needed. The condition does not require medicine or special care.

# Optic Neuritis

Optic neuritis is swelling and irritation of the nerve that sends vision signals from your eye to your brain.  
It usually affects only one eye.  
The main symptoms are eye pain and vision loss.  
The pain often gets worse when you move your eye.  
Vision loss can be mild or complete.  
It usually gets worse over a few days.

Most people get better on their own without treatment.  
But doctors will look for the cause and treat it if needed.

---

## What Causes Optic Neuritis?

Optic neuritis is the most common problem with the optic nerve in people under 50.  
The most common cause is a condition called multiple sclerosis.  
This is a disease where the body’s immune system attacks the covering of nerves.  
Optic neuritis can be the first sign of multiple sclerosis.  
It can come back in the same eye or the other eye later.

Other causes include:

- **Neuromyelitis optica (NMO)** – a rare immune disease that attacks the optic nerve and spinal cord.  
- **MOG antibody disease (MOGAD)** – another immune condition that affects the optic nerve and spinal cord.  
- **Infections** – such as viral brain infections (especially in children), sinus infections, meningitis, tuberculosis, syphilis, and HIV.  
- **Cancer spread** – if cancer spreads to the optic nerve.  
- **Lupus** – a long-term immune system disease.  
- **Toxins and medicines** – like lead, methanol, quinine, arsenic, ethambutol, and some antibiotics.  
  These can damage the optic nerve but are not true optic neuritis.  
- **Certain medicines** – such as TNF-alpha inhibitors and immune checkpoint inhibitors.  
  These can cause optic neuritis in some people.  
- **Rare causes** – like vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia) and other autoimmune diseases.  
- In many cases, doctors cannot find a cause, even after testing. This is called idiopathic.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main symptom is a sudden loss of vision.  
It often gets worse over a few days.  
Vision loss can be small or affect the whole eye.  
Some people lose vision in the center of their eye or in a small area near the center.

Most people feel pain in the eye.  
The pain usually gets worse when you move your eye.

Other signs include:

- Blurry or poor vision.  
- Trouble seeing colors.  
  Color vision problems often appear even when vision is only slightly blurry.  
- A difference in how the pupils react to light.  
  This is called an afferent pupillary defect.  
  It happens when one eye is more affected than the other.

In about two out of three people, the nerve swelling is behind the eye.  
This means the nerve head at the back of the eye looks normal.  
In the rest, the nerve head looks red and swollen.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors start by asking about your symptoms and doing a physical exam.  
They will check your vision, eye movement, and how your pupils react to light.

An MRI scan is usually needed.  
This is the best test to see if the optic nerve is inflamed.  
A gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the brain and eye area is recommended.  
It shows if the nerve is swollen and inflamed.

The MRI can also help find the cause.  
For example:

- It can show signs of multiple sclerosis.  
- It can help diagnose NMO or MOGAD.  
- In NMO and MOGAD, the nerve often shows more swelling than in multiple sclerosis.  
- The MRI may show brain lesions in people with multiple sclerosis.  
- It can also show if the spinal cord is involved.  
  This is common in NMO and MOGAD, but less so in multiple sclerosis.

If you have symptoms that suggest spinal cord problems, your doctor may also scan your spine.

### Tips for Doctors

- Do a gadolinium-enhanced MRI if a young person has eye pain with movement and vision loss.  
- Do a spinal MRI if you suspect multiple sclerosis, NMO, or MOGAD.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Corticosteroids (steroid medicines) may be used.  
They are most helpful if multiple sclerosis or NMO is suspected.  
A common treatment is:

- 1000 milligrams of methylprednisolone given through a vein once a day for 3 days.  
- Then, 1 milligram of prednisone per kilogram of body weight by mouth once a day for 11 days.

This can help you get better faster.  
But in the end, your vision will likely be just as good if you do not take steroids.

Steroids do not help people with multiple sclerosis or unknown causes in the long run.  
But they may help in rare cases like NMO or MOGAD.

Taking low-dose oral prednisone alone does not help vision.  
It may even increase the chance of another attack.

If the optic nerve does not improve after steroids, doctors may use plasma exchange.  
This is a treatment that removes harmful substances from the blood.  
It is often used for NMO attacks.  
It may also be used for severe cases from other causes.

Other helpful tools include:

- Magnifiers  
- Large-print books or devices  
- Talking watches or clocks  

These can help if vision does not fully return.

If you have multiple sclerosis, you should take medicines to slow the disease.  
If you have NMO, you need special medicines for that condition.  
People with MOGAD who have repeated attacks may need long-term treatment to control the immune system.

Important: Do not give certain multiple sclerosis medicines to people with NMO or MOGAD.  
These medicines can make their condition worse.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Most people with typical optic neuritis get better on their own.  
Vision usually improves over 2 to 3 months.  
But the long-term outcome depends on the cause.

If you have multiple sclerosis, NMO, or MOGAD, you are more likely to have another attack.  
This can happen in the same eye or the other eye.  
Vision recovery may be worse, especially with NMO.

An MRI can help predict if you are likely to develop multiple sclerosis later.

---

## Key Points

- Optic neuritis is the most common optic nerve problem in people under 50.  
- The most common causes are multiple sclerosis, NMO, and MOGAD.  
- Other causes include infections, medicines, toxins, and rare diseases.  
- Symptoms include eye pain, vision loss, trouble seeing colors, and a pupil reaction difference.  
- Get a gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the brain and eyes.  
- If spinal cord symptoms are present, get a spinal MRI.  
- Steroids and other treatments may help, especially if multiple sclerosis or NMO is suspected.  
- Plasma exchange is used for severe cases or NMO attacks.  
- Do not use certain multiple sclerosis medicines in people with NMO or MOGAD.

# Secondary Thrombocythemia

Secondary thrombocythemia means you have too many platelets in your blood. This happens because of another health problem. It rarely causes serious blood clots or bleeding.

## What Are Platelets?

Platelets are small parts in your blood. They help stop bleeding by forming clots. Your body makes platelets in the bone marrow. Special cells called megakaryocytes make them.

When you have thrombocythemia, your body makes too many platelets.

There are two main types:

- **Primary (essential) thrombocythemia**: A problem with the platelet-making cells themselves.
- **Secondary thrombocythemia**: A normal platelet-making process that is overactive because of another illness.

When high platelet counts are caused by another condition, it is called secondary thrombocythemia. It is not a type of blood cancer called a myeloproliferative neoplasm.

## Common Causes

Secondary thrombocythemia can be caused by:

- Bleeding
- Having your spleen removed
- Surgery
- Injury or trauma
- Infections
- Rheumatoid arthritis
- Inflammatory bowel disease
- Other long-term inflammatory conditions
- Some types of cancer
- Early breakdown of red blood cells (hemolysis)
- Low iron levels (iron deficiency)
- Sarcoidosis

## Symptoms

Most people with secondary thrombocythemia do not feel any symptoms from the high platelet count. The symptoms you feel are usually from the main health problem, not the extra platelets.

## Clotting and Bleeding Risks

You might think more platelets mean more blood clots. But this is rare in secondary thrombocythemia unless you also have serious artery disease.

Some people with primary thrombocythemia have a higher risk of bleeding. This is not a concern with secondary thrombocythemia.

## Diagnosis

Doctors check for secondary thrombocythemia when a person has a high platelet count and a clear reason for it.

To find the cause, doctors may do:

- Blood tests
- Genetic tests (in some cases)
- A bone marrow biopsy (rarely needed)
- Imaging tests like X-rays or scans (if needed)

These tests help rule out primary thrombocythemia and find the real cause.

## Treatment

Treatment focuses on fixing the underlying condition. Once the cause is treated, your platelet count usually returns to normal.

# Eating Habits in Children

Children’s eating habits can vary a lot. Some changes are normal for their age. Others may be signs of serious problems.

Some children may have eating disorders. These include:
- Not eating enough and becoming very thin (anorexia nervosa).
- Eating a lot and then trying to get rid of the food (bulimia nervosa).
- Eating large amounts of food in a short time, often when not hungry (binge eating).

Eating problems can also lead to being overweight or obese. (See also: Obesity in Adolescents.)

Parents often worry about their child’s eating. They may worry:
- The child is not eating enough.
- The child is eating too much.
- The child only eats certain foods.
- The child refuses to eat some foods. (This is sometimes called ARFID.)
- The child acts in strange ways at mealtimes, like giving food to a pet or dropping food on the floor.

To understand the problem, doctors will ask about:
- How often the issue happens.
- How long it has been going on.
- How serious it is.

The child’s growth is checked. The doctor measures:
- Height or length.
- Weight.

These numbers are plotted on growth charts. These charts show how a child grows compared to others of the same age and sex. The World Health Organization has charts for babies and young children up to age two. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has charts for children older than two.

When parents see that their child is growing normally, they often feel less worried.

A child should be checked for an eating disorder if:
- They keep talking about their body or weight.
- Their weight stops going up when it should grow.
- Their weight starts going up much faster than before.

If a child is always worried about how they look, it may be a sign of body dysmorphic disorder. This is when someone sees flaws in their body that others do not see.

Most eating problems do not last long. They do not harm a child’s growth or development. If a child looks healthy and is growing at a steady rate, parents can be reassured. They should avoid forcing food or arguing about eating. Too much pressure can actually lead to eating problems later.

If parents are worried that a child is not eating certain foods or not eating enough, forcing food will not help. It can make things worse. The child may:
- Feel upset.
- Hold food in their mouth.
- Spit food out.
- Throw up.

Instead, parents should:
- Sit with the child at the table during meals.
- Turn off the TV and put away phones or tablets.
- Do not use food to show love or punishment.
- Remove food after 20 to 30 minutes, no matter what was eaten.
- Let the child help clean up any food that is dropped on the floor.

Also, limit snacks to one in the morning and one in the afternoon. These steps usually help the child’s appetite match their real needs. They help restore a healthy relationship with food.

# Substance Use in Teens

Teens may not use substances at all. Some try them once or twice. Others develop serious problems with substance use. Even trying a substance once can cause harm. It can lead to accidents, fights, unsafe sex, or overdose.

Teens who use substances are more likely to get sexually transmitted infections. They are also more likely to develop a serious substance use problem later.

Teens are especially sensitive to the effects of drugs and alcohol. Using them during the teen years can lead to long-term problems. These include mental health issues, failing in school, trouble functioning as an adult, and a higher chance of addiction.

In many places, using substances feels like a normal part of growing up. Teens often want to take risks and seek excitement. This makes substance use common as teens get older. Most teens will try alcohol before they finish high school.

But using substances again and again is much less common. Even using once in a while is dangerous. Adults should not ignore or allow this behavior. What parents do and say about alcohol, tobacco, and other substances matters a lot.

The types of substances teens use and how strong they are depend on where they live and who they are. In the United States, the risk of harm has gone up. This is because stronger, more addictive, and more dangerous products are now easy to get. These include prescription opioids, strong cannabis, nicotine vaping, fentanyl, and e-cigarettes.

One serious short-term risk is overdose. An overdose happens when someone takes too much of a drug, medicine, or alcohol at once. It can be deadly. Overdose rates among teens in the U.S. are rising. This is because of more fentanyl on the streets.

Fentanyl is much stronger than morphine or heroin. Even a tiny amount can cause a fatal overdose. Teens who buy fake pills or other drugs may not know they contain fentanyl. They are at serious risk without realizing it.

The pandemic had mixed effects on teen substance use. During lockdowns, fewer teens started using substances. But for those who already used them, use increased. Some used more to cope with stress and loneliness.

The most common substances teens use in the U.S. are alcohol, nicotine (in tobacco or vaping), and cannabis.

---

## Alcohol Use in Teens

Alcohol is the most commonly used substance among teens. A long-term study called the Monitoring the Future Survey tracks teen drug use in the U.S.

In 2023, the survey found:
- 46% of 12th graders had used alcohol in the past year.
- 33% had been drunk in the past year.
- 24.3% had used alcohol in the past 30 days.
- 10% had drunk more than five drinks in a row in the past two weeks.

Heavy drinking is common. Nearly 90% of all alcohol teens drink is consumed during binge drinking.

A binge is when someone drinks enough to raise their blood alcohol level to 80 milligrams per deciliter. This can happen with as few as three drinks in two hours for younger girls. But teens often drink from bottles or pour their own drinks. So their “drink” may be much larger than a standard adult drink.

Binge drinking puts teens at risk of accidents, injuries, unsafe sex, and other serious problems. Teens should not drink alcohol.

Some media show drinking as normal, cool, or even helpful for stress or sadness. But parents can make a big difference. They can set clear rules, stick to them, and talk openly about drinking. If parents drink too much, teens may think that is okay.

Some teens who try alcohol go on to develop a serious problem with alcohol. Risk factors include starting young and having a family history of alcohol problems. Teens with a family member who has a drinking problem should know they are at higher risk. They should talk to a health care provider for support.

---

## Tobacco Use in Teens

Most adult smokers started when they were teens. Teens who try cigarettes before age 13 are more likely to keep smoking as adults.

Tobacco products that burn include cigarettes, cigars, and hookahs. Use of these products dropped sharply in the 1990s and 2000s. The trend continues downward.

In 2023, the survey found:
- About 2.9% of 12th graders used cigarettes in the past 30 days.
- This is down from 28.3% in 1991.
- Only about 0.7% of 12th graders smoked every day.

Risk factors for teen smoking include:
- Parents who smoke
- Friends or role models (like celebrities) who smoke
- Using e-cigarettes (this increases the chance of smoking regular cigarettes)
- Using alcohol or other drugs
- Mental health issues or learning problems
- Poor school performance
- Easy access to cigarettes
- Low self-esteem

Pipe smoking is rare in the U.S. The number of people over 12 who smoke cigars has also dropped.

Teens may also use tobacco in other ways. About 2.5% of 12th graders use smokeless tobacco. This includes chewing tobacco, dipping tobacco (dip), or snuff (inhaled into the nose).

Parents can help prevent teen tobacco use by:
- Not smoking or using smokeless tobacco themselves
- Talking openly about the dangers
- Helping teens who already use tobacco to quit, including getting medical help if needed

---

## Electronic Cigarettes (Vaping)

E-cigarettes are battery-powered devices that heat a liquid into a vapor. Teens inhale the vapor. The liquid usually contains nicotine or THC (the main ingredient in cannabis). Both nicotine and THC are addictive.

E-cigarettes first came out as a tool for adults who wanted to quit smoking. They were not popular with teens at first. But now, they are designed to look cool and are very popular with teens, especially those from middle- and upper-income families.

In 2017, 11% of 12th graders used e-cigarettes. By 2019, that number rose to 25.5%. In 2023, it dropped to 16.9%. But 22.1% of 12th graders said they had tried e-cigarettes at least once.

E-cigarettes cause health problems different from smoking. But they can still harm the lungs. Some users have had sudden, severe, or long-lasting lung injuries. In the worst cases, these injuries can be deadly.

E-cigarettes can deliver very high levels of nicotine and THC. These are highly addictive. They can also be toxic. Secondhand vapor from e-cigarettes can expose others to nicotine and other harmful chemicals.

E-cigarettes are now the most common way teens first come into contact with nicotine. But we do not yet know how they affect the rate of adult smoking. The long-term health risks of e-cigarettes are still unknown.

---

## Cannabis (Marijuana)

In 2023, 18.4% of 12th graders used cannabis in the past year. This is down from 22.3% in 2019. About 36.5% of 12th graders said they had used cannabis at least once in their life.

Cannabis use passed tobacco use for the first time in 2010.

The biggest increase in use is in vaping THC. In 2017, 4.9% of 12th graders used THC vaping. By 2019, that rose to 14%. In 2023, it was 13.7%.

---

## Other Substances

Use of substances other than alcohol, nicotine, and cannabis is less common.

In 2023, the survey found these percentages of 12th graders who had used these substances at least once:
- Inhalants (like glue or aerosols): 6.3%
- Hallucinogens (like LSD, PCP, mescaline, mushrooms): 6.6%
- Cocaine: 1.3%
- Methamphetamines (nonprescription): 0.6%
- Heroin: 0.2%

Commonly misused prescription drugs include:
- Opioid painkillers
- Anti-anxiety medicines
- Sleeping pills
- Stimulants (like those used to treat ADHD, such as methylphenidate)

Commonly misused over-the-counter (OTC) medicines include cough and cold medicines with dextromethorphan. These are easy to get and many teens think they are safe.

Some young teens try illegal drugs as early as age 12. Many who experiment with OTC, prescription, or other drugs go on to develop serious substance use problems.

Anabolic steroids are more common among athletes. But non-athletes use them too. In teens, steroid use can cause growth plates in bones to close too early. This leads to shorter adult height. Other side effects affect both teens and adults.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Substance Use in Teens

Doctors use several tools to check for substance use in teens.

- A regular health check-up that includes private questions about substance use
- Screening tools that ask about use of tobacco, alcohol, and other substances
- Sometimes, a drug test

Doctors may ask about:
- How often the teen uses substances
- How much they use
- When they started

Screening tools are short and can be filled out by the teen or given by a doctor. They help doctors decide if a teen has a substance use problem or is at risk.

Drug tests can help, but they have limits:
- A test may be negative even if the teen used drugs, if the drug is no longer in their system
- Some drugs are not

# Tay-Sachs Disease and Sandhoff Disease

Tay-Sachs disease and Sandhoff disease are rare genetic conditions.  
They affect how the body breaks down certain fats in the brain.  
Both diseases cause serious brain problems and lead to early death.

Gangliosides are fats that are normally found in brain cells.  
Two types, GM1 and GM2, can build up in the body when the system that breaks them down does not work.  
This buildup causes damage to the brain and nervous system.  
There are two main types of GM2 gangliosidosis.  
Each type can be caused by many different gene changes.

For more details, see the table titled *Some Sphingolipidoses*.

You can also read about how doctors evaluate patients with suspected inherited metabolic disorders.

---

## Tay-Sachs Disease

A lack of a specific enzyme called hexosaminidase A causes GM2 to build up in the brain.  
This disease is passed down through families in an autosomal recessive pattern.  
This means a child must inherit one faulty gene from each parent to get the disease.  
About 1 in 27 adults of Eastern European Jewish descent carry a common faulty gene.  
Other groups, such as some French-Canadian and Cajun families, also have higher rates of certain gene changes.  
If both parents are carriers, there is a 25 percent chance their child will have the disease.

Children with Tay-Sachs usually develop normally for the first 6 months.  
After that, they stop reaching milestones like sitting or crawling.  
Their thinking and movement skills get worse over time.  
They may have seizures, lose mental abilities, become paralyzed, and die by age 5.

A red spot in the center of the eye is common.  
This is called a cherry-red macular spot.

![Cherry-red macular spot](https://www.sciencephoto.com/image/1020807/530w/ralph-c-eagle-jr-science-photo-library)  
*Image: Ralph C. Eagle, Jr./Science Photo Library*

Doctors diagnose Tay-Sachs based on symptoms and tests.  
DNA testing and enzyme tests can confirm the diagnosis.  
For more on testing for inherited metabolic disorders, see the related section.

There is no cure for Tay-Sachs.  
Care focuses on finding carriers before they have children.  
This is done through testing for enzyme levels and gene changes.  
Couples who are both carriers can get genetic counseling to understand their risks.

---

## Sandhoff Disease

This disease is similar to Tay-Sachs but more severe.  
It happens when two enzymes, hexosaminidase A and B, are missing.  
Symptoms start around 6 months of age.  
They include worsening brain function, blindness, a cherry-red macular spot, and extreme sensitivity to sound (hyperacusis).

Sandhoff disease looks very much like Tay-Sachs in how it progresses, how it is diagnosed, and how it is managed.  
But there are key differences:  
- The liver and bones are affected.  
- There is no link to any specific ethnic group.

---
