# Shoulder Dislocations

A shoulder dislocation happens when the ball at the top of the upper arm bone (humerus) comes out of the shoulder socket (glenoid fossa). Most often, the ball moves forward.

Shoulder dislocations are the most common type of major joint dislocation.

There are three main types of shoulder dislocations:
- Forward (anterior)
- Backward (posterior)
- Downward (inferior)

---

## Forward Shoulder Dislocations

Over 95 out of 100 shoulder dislocations happen forward. This usually occurs when the arm is raised and twisted outward.

Possible injuries that can happen with a forward dislocation include:
- Damage to the nerves that control arm movement
- Tears in the rotator cuff (the group of muscles and tendons that hold the shoulder together)
- A break in the upper part of the arm bone (greater tuberosity)
- Injury to the axillary nerve (this can cause numbness on the side of the shoulder)

People over 30 years old are more likely to have repeated dislocations.

The shoulder looks different. The bony tip of the shoulder (acromion) sticks out more. The elbow is held slightly away from the body. The ball of the arm bone is pushed forward and down. It cannot be felt in its normal spot. The person will not want to move the arm. They may have weakness or numbness in the arm or hand, especially if the axillary nerve is injured.

### Diagnosis

X-rays are needed to confirm a forward dislocation. The best views are:
- A true front-to-back (anteroposterior) x-ray
- An axillary (side) x-ray

These x-rays show the ball of the arm bone is no longer in the socket.

### Treatment

Most forward dislocations are treated with closed reduction. This means the doctor puts the ball back into the socket without surgery.

This is usually done using:
- Local numbing medicine (injected into the joint)
- Or sedation to help the patient relax

Common methods include:
- Traction-countertraction
- External rotation (like the Hennepin technique)
- Scapular manipulation
- Cunningham (massage) technique
- Davos (autoreduction) technique
- Stimson (dangling weights) technique
- FARES (fast, reliable, and safe) technique

No one method works best for everyone. The doctor picks the best method based on how the patient is lying or sitting.

Some methods can be done without sedation. These include:
- Hennepin
- Scapular manipulation
- Cunningham
- FARES

But they take time. The muscles need to relax. The patient must stay calm and focus on relaxing.

Other things to consider:
- If the arm cannot be moved toward the body, do not use the Cunningham or external rotation methods.
- If the arm is stuck out to the side, use the FARES, Stimson, or scapular manipulation method.
- If the arm is pushed down, use traction-countertraction.
- If the patient is pregnant and cannot lie on their stomach, avoid the Stimson method.

After the shoulder is back in place, the arm is put in a sling and swathe right away. This holds the arm still.

For people over 40, keep the sling on for 5 to 7 days. Then start gentle movement early. This helps prevent stiffness (frozen shoulder).

### How the Methods Work

#### Traction-Countertraction
- The patient lies on a stretcher with wheels locked.
- One person pulls on a folded sheet wrapped around the chest.
- Another person pulls the injured arm down and out at a 45-degree angle.
- Once the arm is free, a small pull on the upper arm may help.
- This method works well for forward dislocations.

#### Hennepin Technique (External Rotation)
- The patient lies on their back or sits up.
- The arm is bent at the elbow and pulled in toward the body.
- The arm is slowly turned outward over 5 to 10 minutes.
- This gives time for muscle spasms to calm down.
- The shoulder often goes back into place at 70 to 110 degrees of outward turn.
- This method works in about 80 to 90 out of 100 cases.

#### Scapular Manipulation
- The patient stands or lies face down.
- The elbow is bent to 90 degrees.
- The arm is slowly turned outward.
- An assistant gently pulls on the arm.
- The doctor moves the shoulder blade so the bottom tip moves toward the spine.
- This can be used with other methods, like the Stimson technique.

#### Cunningham Technique (Massage)
- The patient sits up.
- The doctor sits beside them.
- The patient’s hand rests on the doctor’s shoulder.
- The elbow is bent and held close to the body.
- The doctor places their hand in the bend of the patient’s elbow.
- The doctor gently massages the biceps, middle of the shoulder muscle, and upper back muscles.
- The patient is told to relax, not tense up.
- The patient should sit straight and pull their shoulders back.
- The shoulder often slips back into place within minutes.

#### Davos (Autoreduction) Technique
- The patient sits with one knee bent.
- The elbows are close to the thighs.
- The hands are clasped in front of the leg and tied together with an elastic band.
- The band also ties the hands to the upper leg.
- This lets the patient relax without holding the position.
- The doctor sits on the patient’s foot.
- The patient is told to tilt their head back and shrug their shoulders.
- This pulls on the shoulder and helps it go back into place.
- The patient uses their own body weight to reduce the dislocation.

#### Stimson Technique (Dangling Weights)
- The patient lies face down.
- The injured arm hangs off the edge of the bed.
- Weights are attached to the wrist.
- After about 30 minutes, the muscles relax enough for the shoulder to go back into place.
- This method is not used if the patient is pregnant or very overweight.
- It can be combined with scapular manipulation to speed up the process.

#### FARES Technique
- The patient lies on their back.
- The elbow is straight.
- The forearm is in a neutral position.
- The doctor pulls gently on the arm and moves it up and down in small, quick motions (2 to 3 times per second).
- This helps the muscles relax.
- The arm is slowly raised up to 90 degrees.
- Then the palm is turned up.
- The arm is turned outward while the up-and-down motion continues.
- The shoulder usually goes back into place at about 120 degrees of arm lift.

---

## Backward Shoulder Dislocations

Backward dislocations are rare and often missed.

They are often caused by:
- Seizures
- Electric shock
- Electroconvulsive therapy without muscle relaxants

### Signs to Watch For
- Shoulder pain
- Arm held close to the body
- Inability to turn the arm outward
- X-rays show no obvious problem

The arm may look normal. The elbow is bent. The arm is turned inward. When the elbow is bent, the arm cannot be turned outward.

If the arm cannot be turned outward, get an x-ray. If the x-ray shows no fracture or dislocation, think about a backward dislocation.

A clue on the front x-ray is the “light bulb” or “ice cream cone” sign. The ball of the arm bone looks round instead of oval. The bony parts on the side of the bone are not visible.

Bony injuries happen in about 65 out of 100 backward dislocations.

The best x-ray to confirm this is the Y view (trans-scapular Y view). This view is needed to rule out a backward dislocation.

On the Y view:
- Lines drawn through the shoulder tip, the coracoid bone, and the body of the shoulder blade should meet in the center of the socket.
- If the ball of the arm bone is behind the socket, it is a backward dislocation.

### Treatment
- Reduction is often done with gentle pulling (longitudinal traction).
- This is similar to the traction-countertraction method used for forward dislocations.

---

## Downward Shoulder Dislocations

Downward dislocations (called luxatio erecta) are rare. They are easy to spot.

The arm is held straight up over the head. The forearm rests on the head. The arm looks shorter. The ball of the arm bone can often be felt in the armpit.

The joint capsule is torn. The rotator cuff may be damaged. The brachial artery is injured in less than 5 out of 100 cases. The axillary nerve or another nerve is often damaged, but feeling and movement usually return after the shoulder is put back in place.

### Diagnosis
X-rays confirm the diagnosis.

### Treatment
- The doctor uses traction-countertraction on the raised arm.
- Closed reduction (without surgery) usually works.
- If the ball gets stuck in a tear in the lower part of the joint capsule (called a buttonhole deformity), surgery is needed.

--- 

**Note:** Always get x-rays before trying to put the shoulder back in place. Never try to reduce a dislocation without checking the bones first.

# Tuberous Sclerosis Complex

Tuberous sclerosis complex is a genetic condition that causes unusual growths in the brain, skin, and other organs. These growths are usually not cancer. The condition is present from birth, but symptoms may not appear right away.

## What Causes Tuberous Sclerosis Complex?

- A change in a gene causes this condition.
- Most cases happen because of a new gene change that is not inherited.
- In rare cases, a parent with the condition can pass it to a child.
- The chance of passing it on is 50 percent if a parent has the condition.
- The condition affects about 1 in every 6,000 children.

## How the Condition Affects the Body

Tuberous sclerosis complex can affect many parts of the body:

- **Brain**: Can cause seizures, learning problems, delayed development, autism, or behavior issues.
- **Skin**: Can cause patches, bumps, or growths that may be visible.
- **Heart**: Tumors can form before birth but often go away on their own.
- **Kidneys**: Tumors or cysts can form later in life. These may cause high blood pressure or pain.
- **Lungs**: Some women develop growths in the lungs, especially during teenage years.
- **Eyes**: Small growths can form in the back of the eye. These may affect vision if they are in the center.

## Symptoms of Tuberous Sclerosis Complex

Symptoms vary widely. Some people have mild signs. Others have serious problems.

### Brain and Nervous System

- Seizures are common. The first sign may be infantile spasms.
- Some children have trouble learning or speaking.
- Some have delayed motor skills, like walking or using hands.
- Some have autism or behavior problems such as being very active or aggressive.
- Some have intellectual disability.

### Skin Changes

- Light-colored patches shaped like leaves (ash-leaf spots) may appear in infancy or early childhood.
- Rough, bumpy patches (shagreen patches) often appear on the back. They may be present at birth or develop later.
- Brown spots like coffee with milk (café-au-lait spots) can appear.
- Red bumps made of blood vessels and tissue (angiofibromas) grow on the face during childhood.
- Small fleshy bumps (fibromas) can grow around or under fingernails and toenails (Koenen tumors). These can appear at any time during childhood or early adulthood.

### Heart

- Benign tumors (rhabdomyomas) can form before birth.
- These tumors may cause heart problems in newborns.
- Most go away over time and do not cause problems later in life.

### Teeth

- Some children have teeth with small pits or holes.

### Eyes

- Small growths can form on the retina.
- If the growths are near the center of the eye, vision may be affected.

### Kidneys

- Tumors or cysts can form at any age.
- These may cause high blood pressure, pain in the belly, or blood in the urine.

### Lungs

- Solid growths (nodules) can form in the lungs, especially in teenage girls.
- This condition is called lymphangioleiomyomatosis.

## How Doctors Diagnose the Condition

Doctors use a set of known rules to help diagnose tuberous sclerosis complex. They look for certain signs and symptoms.

### What Doctors Do

- Do a full physical exam.
- Check for seizures, skin changes, or delays in development.
- Use imaging tests:
  - MRI scan of the brain.
  - Ultrasound of the kidneys or abdomen.
  - CT scan of the chest (for women 18 and older).
  - Echocardiogram to check the heart.
- Do an eye exam to check for growths in the back of the eye.
- Sometimes do genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis.

### When Diagnosis Happens

- Sometimes the condition is found before birth during a routine ultrasound.
- If a baby has heart or brain tumors, doctors may suspect the condition.
- Genetic testing may be done if:
  - A person has symptoms but the diagnosis is unclear.
  - A family member has the condition, but the person does not yet show symptoms.
  - A pregnancy is being tested for the condition.

## How the Condition Is Treated

There is no cure. Treatment focuses on managing symptoms and preventing complications.

### For Seizures

- Doctors may prescribe antiseizure medicines.
- If medicines do not work, surgery may be an option.
- Surgery can remove a tumor or a small part of the brain that causes seizures.

### For High Blood Pressure

- Doctors may prescribe blood pressure medicines.
- If kidney tumors are causing the problem, surgery may be needed.

### For Behavior Problems

- Parents and teachers can use behavior strategies like time-outs and consistent rewards.
- In some cases, medicine may help.

### For Developmental Delays

- Special education programs can help.
- Physical therapy, occupational therapy, or speech therapy may be needed.

### For Skin Growth

- Dermabrasion (rubbing the skin to remove the top layer) can help.
- Lasers can remove bumps on the face.

### For Tumors

- A medicine called everolimus or sirolimus can shrink tumors.
- These medicines can help shrink brain and heart tumors, facial growths, and kidney tumors.
- Sirolimus can also be applied to the skin to treat facial bumps.
- These medicines are also used to treat some cancers and to prevent organ rejection after transplant.

### Monitoring Over Time

Because the condition lasts a lifetime, regular checkups are needed.

- MRI of the head every few years.
- Ultrasound or MRI of the kidneys to check for tumors.
- CT scan of the chest for women 18 and older.
- Echocardiogram to check the heart.
- Regular testing of thinking and learning skills in children to help plan school and support.

## Prognosis (Outlook)

- If symptoms are mild, most children grow up to live long, full lives.
- If symptoms are severe, some children may have serious disabilities.
- Still, most children continue to improve over time.
- Life expectancy is usually normal.

## Genetic Counseling

- Families should talk to a genetic counselor if they are thinking about having children.
- This helps them understand the chance of passing the condition to a child.

# Congenital Knee Dislocation

Some babies are born with a knee that is out of place.

(See also: Overview of Congenital Musculoskeletal Anomalies.)

A knee that is dislocated forward and bent too far back is rare at birth. This needs urgent medical check-up. The doctor will check for damage to blood vessels. This condition can happen with Larsen syndrome. Larsen syndrome includes multiple joint dislocations (like elbows, hips, and knees), clubfoot, and a unique face shape. The face may have a large forehead, a flat nose bridge, and eyes that are far apart. It can also happen with arthrogryposis.

The dislocation may be due to weak or unbalanced muscles. This can happen if the baby has myelodysplasia or arthrogryposis. It may also be caused by the baby’s position in the womb. Often, the hip on the same side is also dislocated.

When the doctor checks the baby, the leg is straight. The baby cannot bend the knee much.

The doctor may order imaging tests. These include X-rays, MRI scans, or CT scans of the knee.

If the baby is otherwise healthy, treatment starts right away. The doctor will gently move the knee into a bent position every day. The baby will wear a splint to keep the knee bent. This treatment usually leads to a knee that works well.

# Anti-Glomerular Basement Membrane Disease

This is a rare condition where the body’s immune system attacks its own lungs and kidneys. It is also known as Goodpasture syndrome.

## What Happens in This Disease?

- The immune system normally fights infections.
- In this disease, the immune system makes mistakes.
- It attacks parts of the lungs and kidneys as if they were harmful invaders.
- This causes bleeding in the lungs and damage to the kidneys.
- The damage can get worse quickly and may lead to serious health problems.

## Symptoms

You may notice these signs:

- Coughing up blood
- Blood in your urine
- Feeling very tired
- Shortness of breath
- Fever
- Unplanned weight loss
- Swelling in your legs

Some people feel weak and look pale. This can be due to anemia, which happens when you lose too much blood.

Lung symptoms can appear weeks or even years before kidney problems start.

In severe cases, breathing becomes very hard. The skin may turn blue, gray, or very pale. This means the body is not getting enough oxygen. Without treatment, this can be life-threatening.

You can lose a lot of blood from the lungs. At the same time, your kidneys can stop working fast.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find out if you have this disease:

- **Chest imaging** – A scan of your chest to check for bleeding in the lungs.
- **Bronchoscopy** – A thin tube is gently put into your lungs. Fluid is used to wash out the air sacs. This helps check for blood and other signs.
- **Urine test** – Checks for blood and protein in your urine.
- **Blood tests** – Look for signs of anemia and the specific antibodies that cause this disease.
- **Kidney biopsy** – A small sample of kidney tissue is taken. It is checked under a microscope. The test shows the antibodies in a clear pattern.

These tests help confirm the diagnosis.

## Treatment

This disease needs fast treatment to prevent permanent damage.

### Main Treatments:

- **Plasma exchange** – A machine removes harmful antibodies from your blood. This helps stop the damage.
- **Steroids** – Strong medicines that calm down the immune system. They are given through a vein.
- **Cyclophosphamide** – A medicine that also reduces immune system activity. It is given through a vein.
- **Rituximab** – An alternative medicine that also calms the immune system.

Starting treatment early can help protect your lungs and kidneys.

### If Kidneys Are Damaged:

- You may need **dialysis** – a machine that takes over kidney function.
- In some cases, a **kidney transplant** may be needed.

### Supportive Care:

- You may need oxygen to breathe easier.
- A breathing machine (mechanical ventilator) may be used if breathing becomes very hard.
- Blood transfusions may be needed if you have lost a lot of blood.

## Outlook

- The disease can get worse very fast.
- If treatment starts before lung or kidney failure happens, the outcome is much better.
- Delaying treatment can be deadly.

## More Information

For more details, you can visit:

**National Kidney Foundation: Goodpasture's Syndrome**

# How Medicines Affect Older Adults

## What Is Pharmacodynamics?

Pharmacodynamics is how a medicine affects your body. It looks at the body’s reaction to the medicine. This includes how the medicine binds to receptors, how the body responds after the medicine binds, and any chemical changes that happen.

In older adults, the same amount of medicine in the body can have a stronger or weaker effect than in younger people. This is because of changes in how medicines interact with the body. These changes can come from aging, health problems, or damage to organs.

It can be hard to tell if a medicine’s effect is due to how the body handles the medicine (pharmacokinetics) or how the body reacts to it (pharmacodynamics). This is especially true when the reaction is stronger than expected.

## Risks of Anticholinergic Medicines

Older adults are more sensitive to medicines that block a certain nerve signal called acetylcholine. These are called anticholinergic medicines.

Many common medicines have this effect. Examples include:
- Some antidepressants (like tricyclics)
- Sleepy antihistamines (like those in allergy or cold medicines)
- Medicines for bladder control
- Some antipsychotic drugs
- Some drugs for Parkinson’s disease
- Many over-the-counter cold and allergy remedies

### Side Effects in Older Adults

Older adults, especially those with memory problems, are more likely to have side effects in the brain and nervous system. These can include:
- More confusion
- Feeling very sleepy

Other common side effects include:
- Trouble passing stool (constipation)
- Trouble urinating (especially in men with an enlarged prostate)
- Blurry vision
- Dizziness when standing up (orthostatic hypotension)
- Dry mouth

Even small doses of these medicines can raise the risk of heatstroke. This is because they stop the body from sweating properly.

### What You Should Do

When possible, older adults should avoid medicines with anticholinergic effects. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist about whether your medicines could cause these problems. There may be safer choices available.

# Knee Pain in the Front

Pain in the front of the knee is common. It often happens when you run or walk. The pain can get worse over time.

## What Causes Front Knee Pain?

Your kneecap is a small bone at the front of your knee. It moves up and down when you bend your knee. If the muscles around your knee are weak, your kneecap may not move properly. This can cause pain.

Common causes include:

- Weak muscles in the front of your thigh
- Feet that roll inward too much when you walk or run (called excessive pronation)
- Tight muscles or tendons in your legs
- A kneecap that sits too high or too low in the knee joint
- Muscles around the kneecap that attach in the wrong place
- Tight hamstrings (back of the thigh) or Achilles tendon (back of the ankle)

## Runner’s Knee

Runner’s knee is a common cause of front knee pain. It happens when the muscles in your thigh are weak. This lets your kneecap move sideways. It rubs against the thighbone in a way that causes pain.

At first, you may only feel pain when running downhill. Later, even walking or going down steps can hurt.

## Foot Rolling Inward

If your feet roll inward too much when you walk or run, it can pull your kneecap outward. This causes it to rub against the thighbone. This rubbing leads to pain and wear on the knee.

## How Doctors Diagnose Knee Pain

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms. They will check your knee and leg. They may order tests if needed.

- Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) gives a detailed picture of the knee.
- Arthroscopy lets the doctor look inside the knee using a small camera.

These tests help find the exact cause of the pain.

## How to Treat Knee Pain

### Rest

Stop running or any activity that causes pain. Wait until the pain is gone before you start again.

### Ice and Pain Relief

Use ice on the knee for 15 to 20 minutes several times a day. This helps reduce swelling and pain.

You can take nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen to help with pain and swelling. Use them only as directed.

### Support

A knee sleeve or elastic bandage can help support the knee while it heals.

### Exercise

Do gentle exercises to keep your body strong and fit. These are safe for your knee:

- Ride a stationary bike with the seat high, low resistance, and few repetitions
- Swim or do water exercises

These help keep your heart and muscles strong without stressing the knee.

### Strengthening and Balancing Exercises

Do exercises to strengthen the muscles in the front and back of your thigh. This helps your kneecap move properly.

- Strengthen your quadriceps (front thigh muscles)
- Stretch and strengthen your hamstrings (back thigh muscles)

Stretching before exercise may help prevent injury. It helps balance the forces on your knee.

### Shoe Inserts

If your feet roll inward too much, shoe inserts (orthotics) can help. They support your arch and correct your foot position. This reduces pressure on your knee.

## Summary

- Weak thigh muscles can cause front knee pain.
- Feet that roll inward too much can also cause pain.
- Pain often starts when running downhill. It can later happen with walking.
- Rest, ice, and pain medicine help reduce symptoms.
- Exercise helps strengthen and balance the muscles around the knee.
- Shoe inserts can help if your feet roll inward.
- Doctors may use MRI or arthroscopy to find the cause.

Always talk to your doctor before starting any new exercise or treatment.

# Saw Palmetto

Saw palmetto comes from the berries of a small palm tree.  
The berries contain active ingredients that may affect hormones.  
These ingredients may block a chemical that changes testosterone into another hormone called dihydrotestosterone.  
The berries can be made into a tea.  
They can also be turned into tablets, capsules, or liquid supplements.  
Most studies have used a special extract made with a chemical called hexane.  
This extract is mostly made of fatty acids and plant sterols.

## What People Use Saw Palmetto For

Many men take saw palmetto to help with symptoms of an enlarged prostate.  
These symptoms include needing to urinate often, especially at night.  
Some people also say it helps with hair growth.  
Others claim it increases sperm, makes breasts larger, or boosts sex drive.  
But there is no strong proof that any of these claims are true.

## What the Science Says

There is no proof that saw palmetto can shrink an enlarged prostate.  
Tests like ultrasound or MRI show no change in prostate size.  
Studies on urinary symptoms give mixed results.  
One large study with 369 men found no better results with saw palmetto than with a fake treatment.  
A review of 32 studies found no improvement in urine flow or prostate size.  
Another review of 27 studies found some small benefit in nighttime urination and urine flow.  
But a later review of 27 studies found no real difference in symptoms or quality of life.  
A 2020 review of 4 studies found saw palmetto worked about as well as a common medicine for prostate problems.  
However, a 2021 review of 22 studies found no meaningful benefit.  
Another 2021 review of 27 studies found no benefit for urinary symptoms.  
Overall, results from studies are not clear.  
The Canadian Urological Association does not recommend saw palmetto for prostate problems.

One small study found that men who took saw palmetto for two months before surgery had shorter surgery times and better recovery.

A review of 5 small studies and 2 group studies found some improvement in hair quality, hair count, and hair thickness.  
But more large, high-quality studies are needed to confirm this.

There is no proof that saw palmetto increases sperm, breast size, or sex drive.

## Side Effects

Some people may get a headache or diarrhea.  
Serious side effects are rare.  
One man had serious liver damage after taking saw palmetto.  
Another man had sudden pancreatitis, which may have been linked to the supplement.  
Women who are pregnant or could become pregnant should not take saw palmetto.  
This is because it may affect hormones.  
Different brands of saw palmetto have different amounts of active ingredients.  
This can affect how safe or effective the product is.

## Drug Interactions

No clear interactions have been found between saw palmetto and medicines.  
But people on blood thinners like warfarin should be careful.  
There is a possible risk of liver damage or bleeding.  
Saw palmetto may reduce the effect of birth control pills or hormone replacement therapy.  
This is because it may affect hormone levels.

## More Information

For more details, visit the National Institutes of Health website:  
[National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health: Saw Palmetto](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/saw-palmetto)

# Ear Infection (Acute)

An ear infection is a sickness caused by germs. It happens in the middle part of the ear.

## What Causes Ear Infections?

- Germs like bacteria or viruses cause the infection.
- Ear infections often happen after a cold or allergies.
- Babies and young children get them most often.
- This is because their ear tubes are still growing and do not work well yet.

## Who Is at Risk?

You are more likely to get an ear infection if:
- You live in a home where people smoke.
- Many family members have had ear infections.
- You live in a place with dirty air.
- You are fed from a bottle instead of being breastfed.
- You go to a day care center.

## What Are the Symptoms?

- The ear hurts.
- The eardrum looks red and swollen.
- You may have trouble hearing.
- Babies may cry more than usual or have trouble sleeping.
- Young children may have a fever, feel sick to their stomach, or have diarrhea.
- The eardrum can burst. If it does, pus may come out of the ear. This can ease the pain.

If the infection spreads, you may have:
- A very bad headache.
- Trouble thinking clearly.
- Confusion.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor checks your ear with a small light tool called an otoscope.
- They look at the eardrum.
- If there is fluid behind the eardrum, it may mean an infection.

## How Is It Treated?

### Pain Relief
- Use acetaminophen or ibuprofen to ease pain.
- These medicines help with pain and fever.

### Antibiotics
- Not everyone needs antibiotics.
- Some doctors give antibiotics to all patients with ear infections.
- Others only give them if:
  - The child is under 6 months old.
  - The symptoms are very bad.
  - The symptoms do not get better after 3 days.
  - The child has had many ear infections before.

For children aged 6 to 23 months with a mild infection in one ear:
- Doctors may start with no antibiotics.
- If the child feels worse or does not improve in 2 to 3 days, antibiotics are given.

### Decongestants and Antihistamines
- These help people with allergies.
- They do not help with colds.
- They are not safe for children under 2 years old.
- They can cause serious side effects in young children.

### Surgery for Severe Cases
If the pain is very bad, the fever is high, and the eardrum is bulging:
- A doctor may make a small hole in the eardrum.
- This lets fluid drain out.
- The hole usually heals on its own.

### Tubes in the Eardrum
- Some children get repeated ear infections.
- A doctor may put small tubes in the eardrum.
- These tubes help air flow and keep fluid from building up.
- The tubes stay in for 6 to 12 months.
- Most come out on their own.
- If they do not, a doctor removes them.
- If the hole does not close, surgery may be needed.

After the tubes are in:
- Children can wash their hair.
- They can swim, but some doctors say to use earplugs when going underwater.

If fluid comes out of the ear, call the doctor.

## How to Prevent Ear Infections

- Get routine childhood vaccines.
  - These protect against pneumococcal bacteria.
  - These protect against *Haemophilus influenzae* type B.
  - These protect against the flu.
- Do not let babies sleep with a bottle.
  - This can let liquid flow into the ear.
- Do not smoke around children.
  - Secondhand smoke increases the risk.

If you have repeated ear infections, tubes in the eardrum can help prevent them.

# Parapsoriasis

Parapsoriasis is a group of skin conditions.  
The skin shows flat or slightly raised patches that are scaly.  
The patches are usually not itchy or painful.  
The condition is not the same as psoriasis.  
It is called parapsoriasis because the patches can look a little like psoriasis.

There are two main types:

- **Small-plaque parapsoriasis**: This type is usually harmless.  
- **Large-plaque parapsoriasis**: This type can turn into a type of skin cancer called cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.

Small-plaque parapsoriasis may turn into skin cancer in about 10 out of every 100 people each decade.  
Large-plaque parapsoriasis may turn into skin cancer in about 35 out of every 100 people each decade.  
Regular checkups and skin tests can help catch any changes early.

---

## What Does Parapsoriasis Look Like?

The patches are thin and scaly.  
They are dull pink in color.  
They may look slightly wrinkled or thin.  
They are not thick or silvery like psoriasis patches.

- Small-plaque parapsoriasis: Each patch is less than 5 centimeters across.  
- Large-plaque parapsoriasis: Each patch is more than 5 centimeters across.

Sometimes, the patches form finger-like shapes along the sides of the body.  
This happens more often in small-plaque parapsoriasis.  
Even if these finger-like patches are large, they rarely turn into cancer.

---

## How Is Parapsoriasis Diagnosed?

Doctors look at the skin to make a diagnosis.  
They check the size, shape, and color of the patches.  
They also look at where the patches are on the body.

A skin biopsy may be done if there is any concern about skin cancer.  
The biopsy helps rule out a serious condition called cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.

Tests can check for abnormal cells.  
These tests include genetic and molecular testing.  
They help find if there is a clone of abnormal T-cells.

### Possible Conditions That Can Look Like Small-Plaque Parapsoriasis:

- Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma  
- Nummular dermatitis (a type of eczema)  
- Pityriasis rosea  
- Secondary syphilis  
- Guttate psoriasis  
- Pityriasis lichenoides chronica

It is very important to rule out skin cancer.  
Early skin cancer can look just like small-plaque parapsoriasis.  
A skin biopsy can help tell the difference.

### Possible Conditions That Can Look Like Large-Plaque Parapsoriasis:

- Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma  
- Psoriasis  
- Contact dermatitis (a rash from skin contact with an irritant)

---

## How Is Parapsoriasis Treated?

### For Small-Plaque Parapsoriasis:
- Treatment is not always needed.  
- If symptoms bother you, you can use moisturizers.  
- You can also use special ointments made from tar.  
- Topical steroids (cream or ointment) may help.  
- Light therapy (phototherapy) can be used.  
- A mix of treatments may be used.

### For Large-Plaque Parapsoriasis:
- Light therapy with narrowband UVB light is the main treatment.  
- Topical steroids (cream or ointment) may also be used.

---

## What Is the Outlook for Parapsoriasis?

The course of the disease is hard to predict.  
Some people stay the same for years.  
Others may develop skin cancer.

Regular visits to your doctor are important.  
Your doctor may take skin samples (biopsies) over time.  
This helps track any changes.

---

## Key Facts

- Parapsoriasis causes thin, scaly, dull pink patches.  
- The patches look slightly wrinkled or thin.  
- Patches smaller than 5 centimeters are usually harmless.  
- Patches larger than 5 centimeters may turn into skin cancer in about 10% of people each decade.  
- Diagnosis is based on how the skin looks.  
- A skin biopsy may be needed to rule out skin cancer.  
- Small-plaque parapsoriasis is treated only if needed.  
- Large-plaque parapsoriasis is treated with light therapy or topical steroids.

# Anorectal Fistula

An anorectal fistula is an abnormal tunnel that starts inside the anus or rectum. It usually leads to the skin near the anus. In rare cases, it can connect to another organ, like the vagina.

## What Causes an Anorectal Fistula?

- Most fistulas start in a small gland inside the anus or rectum.
- They often happen after an abscess (a pocket of infection) in the area has drained.
- Some people get fistulas after an injury to the anus or rectum.
- Fistulas are more common in people with Crohn disease or tuberculosis.
- They can also happen in people with diverticulitis or certain cancers.
- In babies, a fistula is usually present at birth. It is more common in boys than in girls.
- Fistulas between the rectum and vagina (called rectovaginal fistulas) can happen after childbirth injuries, radiation therapy, cancer, or Crohn disease.

## What Are the Symptoms?

- A painful lump near the anus.
- Pus or blood draining from the skin near the anus.
- Swelling or redness in the area.
- A feeling of pressure or discomfort.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor will examine the area. They may use special tools to look inside.

- The doctor may use a small tube called an anoscope to look inside the rectum.
- A longer scope called a sigmoidoscope can help find the internal opening of the fistula.
- If needed, a colonoscopy may be done to check for Crohn disease or cancer.
- A probe may be gently inserted to feel the path of the fistula and find its depth and direction.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the type of fistula and the person’s health.

- Surgery is often used. The most common type is a fistulotomy, where the tunnel is opened and allowed to heal from the inside.
- In some cases, the doctor may cut part of the muscle around the anus (the sphincter). Cutting too much can lead to trouble controlling bowel movements.
- Other options include:
  - Advancement flaps: Using tissue from the rectum or anus to cover the fistula opening.
  - Biologic plugs: A patch made from natural tissue to close the tunnel.
  - Fibrin glue: A sticky substance injected into the fistula to seal it.
- For people with Crohn disease or ongoing diarrhea, surgery is usually avoided. Healing may be slow, and there is a risk of losing control of bowel movements.
- Medicines used to treat Crohn disease can help close the fistula without surgery.

## Important Notes

- Early treatment can prevent complications.
- Always follow your doctor’s advice.
- If you have symptoms, see a doctor as soon as possible.

# Pseudomonas and Related Infections

*Pseudomonas aeruginosa* and similar bacteria are germs that often cause serious infections in hospitals. They mostly affect people who are already sick or weak. This includes people with severe burns, those on breathing machines, those with low white blood cell counts, or those who are very ill for a long time.

These infections can happen in many parts of the body. They are usually serious. Doctors diagnose them by growing the germ in a lab. Choosing the right antibiotic is important. The germ may resist many antibiotics, so testing is needed to find the best one.

---

## Where Pseudomonas Comes From

Pseudomonas germs are found almost everywhere, especially in wet places.

In people, *P. aeruginosa* is the most common type that causes illness. But other similar germs can also cause infections. These include *P. paucimobilis*, *P. putida*, *P. fluorescens*, *P. stutzeri*, *P. mendocina*, and *P. acidovorans*. 

Some other germs once thought to be Pseudomonas are now known to be different. These include *Burkholderia cepacia* and *Stenotrophomonas maltophilia*. Both can cause serious infections in hospitals.

Another germ, *B. pseudomallei*, used to be called *Pseudomonas pseudomallei*. It causes a disease called melioidosis. This disease mainly happens in southeast Asia and northern Australia.

*P. aeruginosa* can sometimes be found in the underarms or around the anus of healthy people. It is rarely found in stool unless someone is taking antibiotics. In hospitals, it often lives in sinks, antiseptic liquids, and urine collection containers.

Healthcare workers can pass the germ to patients if they do not follow strict infection control rules. This is especially true in burn units and newborn intensive care units.

---

## What Illnesses Pseudomonas Can Cause

Most *P. aeruginosa* infections happen in people who are in the hospital. They are most common in people who have low white blood cell counts, are very weak, or have a weak immune system.

This germ is a frequent cause of infections in intensive care units. People with advanced HIV or cystic fibrosis can also get infected in the community, not just in hospitals.

Pseudomonas can infect many parts of the body. These include the skin, tissues under the skin, bones, ears, eyes, urinary tract, lungs, and heart valves.

The part of the body that gets infected depends on how the germ entered the body and how sick the person is.

In hospitalized patients, the first sign may be a severe bloodstream infection caused by a gram-negative germ.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Pseudomonas Infections

Doctors diagnose these infections by growing the germ in a lab. They take samples from the infected area. This can include blood, fluid from a wound, urine, spinal fluid, or eye discharge.

They also test the germ to see which antibiotics will work best.

If the infection is in a local area, the wound may smell like fresh-cut grass. The pus may look green.

---

## How Pseudomonas Infections Are Treated

Treatment depends on where the infection is and how serious it is. The right antibiotic is chosen based on test results.

---

## Key Facts

- Most *P. aeruginosa* infections happen in hospitals. They are most common in people who are weak, very ill, or have a weak immune system.
- People with cystic fibrosis or advanced HIV can get these infections outside of hospitals.
- Infections can happen in many parts of the body. The site depends on how the germ entered the body. For example:
  - Skin infections often happen in people with burns.
  - Lung infections are common in people on breathing machines.
  - Urinary tract infections can happen after bladder procedures or blockages.
- A severe bloodstream infection can develop quickly in sick patients.
- Skin infections like folliculitis, ear infections, or eye ulcers can happen in healthy people.
- Diagnosis is done by growing the germ from a sample.
- Systemic infections are treated with strong antibiotics given through a vein. One common choice is an antibiotic that works against Pseudomonas, such as a specific type of penicillin or a fluoroquinolone.

# Adjustment Disorders

Adjustment disorders happen when a person has strong emotional or behavior problems after a stressful event.

These problems are a reaction to something that caused stress. They are common. Between 5% and 20% of people who visit a mental health clinic have this condition.

The stressor can be one event, like losing a job.  
It can be several events, like money problems followed by a breakup.  
It can also be ongoing stress, like caring for a family member who is disabled.  

The stress can affect one person, a whole family, or a large group.  
Even positive life changes, like becoming a parent, can cause this disorder.

The death of someone close can trigger an adjustment disorder.  
But doctors must consider how people in different cultures usually grieve.  
They only diagnose a disorder if the grief is much worse than expected.  
Or if it is better described as prolonged grief disorder.

When a doctor checks for an adjustment disorder, they ask:

- Is the reaction linked to a specific stressor?  
- Does the reaction cause serious distress?  
- Does it make daily life hard? For example, at work, with friends, or in family life?

## Symptoms of Adjustment Disorder

Symptoms usually start soon after the stressful event.  
They usually go away within 6 months after the stress ends.

Common symptoms include:

- Feeling sad or low  
- Feeling anxious or worried  
- Acting out in ways that are not normal for you  

Most people have a mix of these symptoms.  
Some people only have one main symptom. For example, feeling very nervous after being attacked.

There is a higher risk of suicide attempts and suicide in people with this disorder.

## How Doctors Diagnose Adjustment Disorder

A doctor will talk to you and use standard mental health guidelines.

To be diagnosed, you must have:

- Emotional or behavior problems within 3 months of a stressor  
- Problems that are serious enough to cause real distress or trouble in daily life  

The distress must be much worse than what most people would feel in the same situation.  
Doctors consider your culture and background when making this judgment.

Adjustment disorders often happen with other mental health problems.  
These can include obsessive-compulsive disorder, personality disorders, or bipolar disorder.

## Treatment for Adjustment Disorder

Treatment includes:

- Taking care of yourself  
- Talking with a therapist  
- Sometimes using medicine for specific symptoms  

It is important to get a full evaluation and treatment.  
But there is not much strong evidence about which treatment works best.

Many types of therapy have helped people. These include:

- Short-term therapy  
- Cognitive-behavioral therapy  
- Supportive therapy  

Therapy often focuses on one issue, like grief or trauma.

Help is more likely to work if you feel safe.  
You also need to take care of yourself every day.

Being in a stable family, part of a healthy community, or working with a therapist who understands trauma can help you heal.

Most people get better over time with support from friends and family.

Medicine may help with symptoms like:

- Trouble sleeping  
- Anxiety  
- Depression  

## Self-Care After a Crisis or Trauma

Self-care is very important during and after a hard time.  
It has three main parts: safety, physical health, and mindfulness.

### Personal Safety

Safety is the most important first step.  
After a single traumatic event, you can process it better if you feel safe.  
But safety is harder to achieve during ongoing crises, like abuse, war, or a pandemic.  
In these cases, talk to experts about how to stay as safe as possible.

### Physical Health

Trauma can harm your body.  
Try to keep a regular routine for:

- Eating healthy food  
- Sleeping well  
- Moving your body (exercise)  

Avoid using medicines or substances that slow you down or make you high.  
This includes some anxiety medicines and alcohol.  
Use them only if needed and only as directed.

### Mindfulness

A mindful approach helps reduce stress, boredom, anger, sadness, and loneliness.

If possible, follow a normal daily routine. For example:

- Get up at the same time each day  
- Shower and get dressed  
- Go outside and walk  
- Eat meals at regular times  

Do things you enjoy. Try old hobbies or start new ones.  
For example:

- Draw a picture  
- Watch a movie  
- Cook a meal  

Staying involved with family and community matters, even if it is hard.  
It helps you feel connected.

Limit time spent on news.  
Instead, focus on activities that feel good and take your mind off the stress.  
For example:

- Read a book  
- Do a puzzle  

## Therapy and Medication

There is not much strong proof that therapy works for adjustment disorders.  
But when it is used, it can help in general.  
It can also focus on specific problems, like grief, trauma, or big life changes.

There is also not much strong proof that medicine helps.  
But some antidepressants called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) have helped people with anxiety or depression that happen with adjustment disorders.

# Leg Amputation Rehabilitation

## Before Surgery

Your doctor will explain what your recovery will involve after surgery.  
You may need help with your emotions and mental health.  
A team of health professionals will work with you to decide if you need a prosthesis or a wheelchair.  

## Getting Strong and Walking Again

Rehabilitation helps you learn to walk again.  
It includes exercises to build strength and improve balance.  
You will stretch your hip and knee.  
You will strengthen all your limbs.  
You will learn how to use your prosthesis.  

Walking after a below-the-knee amputation uses 10 to 40% more energy.  
Walking after an above-the-knee amputation uses 60 to 100% more energy.  
Because of this, you may need special exercises to build endurance.  

Start rehab as soon as you are stable after surgery.  
This helps prevent new health problems.  
Older patients should start standing and balancing with support bars as soon as possible.  

## Preventing Joint Stiffness

Stiffness in the hip or knee can happen fast.  
This makes it hard to fit and use a prosthesis.  
An extension brace made by an occupational therapist can help prevent this.  

## Caring for the Remaining Limb

Your physical therapist will teach you how to care for your remaining limb.  
You will learn how to spot early signs of skin problems.  

## Preparing the Limb for a Prosthesis

Preparing the limb means getting it ready to use a prosthesis.  
This includes skin care, physical therapy, and managing pain.  
These steps help your limb shrink naturally.  
This shrinking is needed before a prosthesis can fit well.  

Within days, your limb may shrink a lot.  
An elastic shrinker or bandages worn all day can help shape the limb.  
They also help prevent swelling.  

- A shrinker is easy to put on.  
- Bandages give better control over pressure and where it is applied.  
- Bandages need skill to apply.  
- They must be reapplied if they come loose.  

## Using a Temporary Prosthesis

Using a temporary prosthesis early helps in these ways:  
- You can stay active.  
- Your limb shrinks faster.  
- You avoid joint stiffness.  
- You may feel less phantom limb pain.  

The socket of the prosthesis must fit snugly.  
Modern tools make this possible.  
There are temporary prostheses with adjustable sockets.  

With a temporary prosthesis, you can:  
- Practice walking on support bars.  
- Move to walking with crutches or a cane.  
- Work toward using a permanent prosthesis.  

## Getting a Permanent Prosthesis

The final prosthesis should be light and safe for you.  
It must meet your needs and lifestyle.  

If the prosthesis is made before your limb stops shrinking, it may not fit well.  
So, doctors usually wait a few weeks after surgery.  
This gives your limb time to shrink fully.  

For most older adults with a below-the-knee amputation:  
- A prosthesis that rests on the patellar tendon is best.  
- It has a solid ankle with a cushioned heel.  
- It uses a suprapatellar cuff to stay in place.  

A prosthesis with a thigh corset and waist belt is not usually used.  
It is heavy and hard to manage.  

For people with an above-the-knee amputation:  
- There are different knee options.  
- The choice depends on your skills and how active you are.  
- Newer models have computer-controlled knees and ankles.  
- These let you adjust your movement as needed.  

## Possible Problems After Amputation

### Pain in the Remaining Limb

This is the most common problem.  
Common causes include:  

- A prosthesis that does not fit well.  
  This is the most common cause.  
- A nerve lump (neuroma).  
  This lump can often be felt.  
  Treatments include:  
  - Ultrasound therapy.  
  - Injections of medicine into the lump or nearby area.  
  - Cold treatment.  
  - Tight bandaging all day.  
  - Surgery if other treatments do not work.  
- A bony growth at the end of the bone.  
  This can be seen on an X-ray.  
  The only real treatment is surgery to remove it.  

### Phantom Limb Sensation

Some people feel their missing leg is still there.  
You may feel tingling or movement.  
This is normal after amputation.  
It can last months or years.  
It usually goes away on its own.  

- You may feel only part of the missing limb.  
- Often, the foot is the last part to feel.  
- This feeling is not dangerous.  
- But you might try to stand on both legs.  
- This can cause falls, especially at night when you get up to use the bathroom.  

### Phantom Limb Pain

This is less common.  
It can be very painful and hard to treat.  
It is more likely if you had pain before surgery.  
It is also more likely if pain was not well controlled during or after surgery.  

Treatments that may help include:  
- Moving both legs at the same time.  
- Massaging the remaining limb.  
- Tapping the limb with your fingers.  
- Using a vibrating device.  
- Ultrasound therapy.  
- Medicines like gabapentin.  

### Skin Breakdown

This happens when the prosthesis rubs or presses too hard on the skin.  
Moisture can build up between the limb and the prosthesis.  
This can lead to sores.  

Skin breakdown is a sign the prosthesis needs adjusting.  
It must be treated right away.  

Early signs:  
- Redness of the skin.  
- Then cuts, blisters, or open sores.  
- The prosthesis becomes painful to wear.  
- Infection can start.  

Ways to prevent or delay skin breakdown:  
- Make sure the prosthesis fits well.  
- Keep your weight steady.  
  Even small weight changes can affect fit.  
- Eat healthy food and drink plenty of water.  
  This helps control weight and keeps skin healthy.  
- If you have diabetes, keep your blood sugar under control.  
  This helps blood flow to the skin.  
- If you use a lower-limb prosthesis, wear shoes with similar heel height.  
  This helps keep your body balanced.  

Even with a good fit, problems can still happen.  
Your limb changes shape and size during the day.  
This depends on your activity, what you eat, and the weather.  

To keep a good fit:  
- Try a thicker or thinner liner or sock.  
- Use a liner with a sock.  
- Add or remove thin socks.  

But even with these changes, your limb may still change too much.  
If you see redness, soreness, or blisters:  
- See your doctor or prosthetist right away.  
- Avoid wearing the prosthesis until it is fixed.  

(See also: Loosening of the Prosthesis)

# Genetic Counseling and Genetic Testing Before Pregnancy

## What Are Genetic Disorders?

Genetic disorders happen when there is a problem with one or more genes or chromosomes.  
Some of these problems are passed down from parents to children.  
Others happen by chance during the formation of a baby’s cells.

- **Hereditary disorders** are passed from one generation to the next.  
- **Spontaneous disorders** happen when a gene or chromosome is damaged by chance, medicine, chemicals, or radiation. This can happen in the sperm, egg, or early embryo.

## Talk to Your Doctor Before Pregnancy

If you are thinking about having a baby, talk to your doctor or a genetic counselor.  
This helps you understand your chances of having a baby with a genetic problem.

### Things that can raise your risk include:
- Being older (especially the mother over 35 or the father over 50).
- A family history of birth defects or genetic problems.
- A past miscarriage or stillbirth.
- A previous baby with a birth defect.
- A chromosomal problem in one of the parents.

Genetic testing is offered to all pregnant women.  
It is especially important if your risk is higher than average.

## What You Can Do Before Pregnancy

Talking to your doctor before getting pregnant is a good time to learn how to lower your risk of birth defects.

- **Take folic acid every day.** This helps prevent serious brain and spine problems like spina bifida.  
  Folic acid is in most prenatal vitamins.
- **Avoid harmful medicines, alcohol, drugs, and radiation.** These can harm the baby’s development.

## Types of Genetic Problems

All your body’s cells contain DNA.  
Genes are parts of DNA that tell your body how to make proteins.  
Chromosomes are structures that hold your genes.

Genetic problems can come from:
- One gene being faulty.
- Many genes being faulty.
- A part of a chromosome being missing, extra, or changed.

### How Common Are These Problems?
- 0.5% of babies have a chromosome problem.
- 1% have a single-gene problem.
- 1% have a problem caused by several genes.

### Chromosome Problems

Chromosome problems happen in about 1 in 200 babies born in the United States.  
They can cause a baby to die before birth or be born with serious health issues.

- **Down syndrome** is the most common chromosome problem in babies born alive.
- The risk of having a baby with Down syndrome goes up with the mother’s age.

#### Risk by Mother’s Age:
| Age of Woman | Risk of Chromosome Problem |
|--------------|----------------------------|
| 20           | 0.2%                       |
| 30           | 0.3%                       |
| 35           | 0.6%                       |
| 40           | 1.6%                       |
| 45           | 5.4%                       |
| 49           | 15%                        |

> Note: This table only includes problems seen with standard tests. Smaller problems (called submicroscopic) are not included.

#### Factors That Increase Risk:
- **Mother’s age:** Risk rises sharply after age 35.
- **Father’s age:** Men over 50 may have a higher risk.
- **Family history:** If a past baby had a chromosome problem, future babies may be at higher risk.
- **Previous birth defects or stillbirths:** About 15% of babies with birth defects and 8–16% of stillborn babies have a chromosome problem.
- **Recurrent miscarriages:** Chromosome problems cause 50–80% of early miscarriages. If you have had 2 or more miscarriages, your chromosomes should be checked.
- **One parent has a chromosome problem:** Even if the parent is healthy, they can pass on a chromosome issue.

### Small Chromosome Problems

Some chromosome problems are too small to see under a microscope.  
These are called submicroscopic abnormalities.

- A tiny piece of a chromosome may be missing (microdeletion).
- A tiny extra piece may be present (microduplication).

These problems are found in about 6% of children with birth defects.  
Special tests called chromosomal microarray tests can find them.

### Single-Gene Disorders

These happen when one gene has a change (mutation) that causes disease.

- **Dominant genes:** Only one bad copy is needed to cause a problem.
- **Recessive genes:** Two bad copies are needed to cause a problem.

#### Sex and Inheritance

There are 23 pairs of chromosomes.  
One pair, the X and Y, decides a baby’s sex.

- Women have two X chromosomes.
- Men have one X and one Y.

If a bad gene is on the X chromosome, it is called an X-linked disorder.

- **Boys** have only one X chromosome. If it has a bad gene, they will have the disorder—even if it is recessive.
- **Girls** need two bad X genes to have the disorder if it is recessive. If it is dominant, one bad gene is enough.

If the parents are closely related (like cousins), they are more likely to share the same bad gene.  
This raises the risk of recessive disorders.

### Inheritance Patterns

| Inheritance Type | Chance of Child Having the Disorder | Chance of Being a Carrier |
|------------------|-------------------------------------|----------------------------|
| Autosomal dominant | 50% for boys and girls | 0% |
| Autosomal recessive (both parents carriers) | 25% for boys and girls | 50% for boys and girls |
| X-linked dominant (mother has gene) | 50% for girls; usually not for boys | 0% |
| X-linked recessive (mother has gene) | 50% for boys; 50% for girls | 100% for girls if father has gene |

> **Carriers** have one bad gene but do not have symptoms.

## Neural Tube Defects

These are birth defects of the brain or spine.  
They happen when the neural tube (which becomes the brain and spine) does not close properly.

Examples:
- **Spina bifida:** The spine does not close completely. The spinal cord may be exposed.
- **Anencephaly:** Part of the brain and skull are missing.

### Causes
- A mix of genes and other factors.
- Low levels of folic acid in the mother’s diet.
- Exposure to certain medicines or chemicals.
- In rare cases, a single gene or chromosome problem.

### Risk Factors
- A family history of spina bifida or anencephaly.
- A past baby with one of these problems.
- A mother with low folic acid levels.

### Prevention
- Take folic acid every day before and during pregnancy.
- Folic acid is in most prenatal vitamins.

If your risk of a neural tube defect is 1% or higher, your doctor may suggest tests like amniocentesis or ultrasound.

## Other Birth Defects

Some birth defects, like cleft lip or cleft palate, happen when:
- A baby has a faulty gene.
- The baby is exposed to harmful substances like alcohol or illegal drugs.

The gene makes the baby more likely to have a problem.  
But the problem usually only happens if the baby is exposed to a harmful substance.

Many heart problems and other common birth defects follow this pattern.

## Family History Review

Your doctor will ask about your family’s health.  
This helps find if you are at higher risk.

They will ask about:
- Health problems in family members.
- Cause of death in family members.
- Health of parents, siblings, children, aunts, uncles, and grandparents.
- Past miscarriages, stillbirths, or babies who died soon after birth.
- Babies born with birth defects.
- Whether the parents are related (like cousins).
- Ethnic or racial background (some groups have higher risks for certain disorders).

Usually, three generations of family history are needed.  
If the history is complex, more distant relatives may be included.

Your doctor may look at medical records of relatives if needed.

## Genetic Carrier Screening

Carriers have a bad gene but do not have symptoms.  
They can pass the gene to their children.

Most carriers have a recessive gene.  
This means both parents must pass on a bad gene for the child to have the disorder.

### Who Should Be Screened?

Screening is offered to people at higher risk.  
But some doctors now screen all couples, no matter their background.

# Linezolid and Tedizolid

Linezolid and tedizolid are antibiotics. They are used to treat serious bacterial infections.

Both medicines belong to a group called oxazolidinone antibiotics. These medicines work by stopping bacteria from growing.

---

## Linezolid

Linezolid treats infections caused by certain types of bacteria. These include:

- Streptococci
- Enterococci, including those that do not respond to vancomycin (called VRE)
- Staphylococci, including MRSA and other strains that resist other antibiotics
- Mycobacteria, including the bacteria that cause tuberculosis
- Anaerobic bacteria, such as Fusobacterium, Prevotella, Porphyromonas, Bacteroides, and peptostreptococci

You should not take linezolid if you have ever had an allergic reaction to it.

Do not take linezolid if you are using a medicine called a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI). These are used to treat depression and other conditions.

Studies in animals show linezolid may harm a developing baby. There are no large, well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Use linezolid during pregnancy only if your doctor believes the benefits outweigh the risks to the baby.

It is not known if linezolid passes into breast milk. It is also not known if it is safe to use while breastfeeding.

Side effects of linezolid can include:

- Low blood cell counts (this usually goes away when you stop the medicine)
- Nerve damage in the hands and feet (this may be permanent)
- Vision problems (this usually goes away when you stop the medicine)
- Serotonin syndrome (a serious reaction that can happen if you take certain other medicines)
- Build-up of lactic acid in the blood (this usually goes away when you stop the medicine)

Low blood cell counts happen in about 3 out of every 100 people. The risk is higher in newborns and young children. This side effect is more likely if you take linezolid for more than two weeks. Your doctor will check your blood every week if you are on this medicine for longer than two weeks.

Nerve damage and vision problems can happen if you take linezolid for a long time. If you are on long-term treatment, your doctor will check you closely for these problems.

---

## Tedizolid

Tedizolid is another oxazolidinone antibiotic. It works against many of the same bacteria as linezolid.

Tedizolid may also work against some bacteria that no longer respond to linezolid.

In clinical trials, tedizolid caused fewer cases of serotonin syndrome and low platelet counts than linezolid.

Like linezolid, tedizolid can cause low white blood cell counts. Do not use this medicine if you have a low white blood cell count (less than 1,000 cells per microliter) and another safe option is available.

Animal studies show tedizolid may harm a developing baby. There are no large, well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Use tedizolid during pregnancy only if your doctor believes the benefits outweigh the risks to the baby.

It is not known if tedizolid passes into breast milk. It is also not known if it is safe to use while breastfeeding.

---

You may find the following resource helpful:

**FDA Adverse Events Reporting System (FAERS)**  
This is a database that allows users to search for reports of side effects from medicines.
