# Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders – Simple Explanation

These are mental health conditions where a person focuses too much on physical symptoms. This focus causes serious distress or makes daily life hard.

Most mental health problems show up as unusual thoughts, feelings, or behaviors. But in somatic symptom disorders, emotional or mental issues show up as physical symptoms. This is called somatization.

The person’s main worry is about physical problems like pain, tiredness, weakness, nausea, or other body sensations. They may or may not have a real physical illness. But if they do, their reaction is much stronger than it should be.

It’s normal to feel upset when you are not well. But people with these disorders react in extreme ways. Their thoughts, feelings, and actions about their symptoms are much stronger than usual. This can cause serious problems in their life.

To be a disorder and not just a normal reaction, the response must:
- Cause a lot of distress.
- Make it hard to do everyday tasks.
- Sometimes cause problems for others.

The exact type of disorder depends on how the person reacts. Here are the main types:

### Somatic Symptom Disorder
- The person is deeply worried about their physical symptoms.
- They think about the symptoms all the time.
- They go to doctors often, even when tests show nothing serious.

### Illness Anxiety Disorder
- The person is very afraid they have a serious illness.
- They worry about getting sick, even when they feel fine.
- This used to be called hypochondria.

### Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder
- The person has symptoms that look like a brain or nerve problem.
- Examples: trouble walking, shaking, or losing feeling.
- But tests show no real nerve or brain damage.

### Psychological Factors Affecting Other Medical Conditions
- A person’s thoughts or emotions make a real physical illness worse.
- For example, stress or fear can make pain or sickness last longer.

### Factitious Disorders
- The person makes up symptoms on themselves or on someone else.
- They do this even when there is no clear reason, like getting time off work.
- This can happen to themselves or to another person.

People with these disorders often go to doctors for help. They do not usually go to a mental health professional, even though the problem is mental.

These disorders can also happen in children.

Treatment depends on the type of disorder. But most people benefit from talk therapy.

---

## How the Mind and Body Work Together

The mind and body are closely linked. They affect each other in many ways.

- Stress from life problems can make physical illnesses worse. This includes diabetes, heart disease, and asthma.
- Mental stress can make physical symptoms last longer or feel worse.
  - For example, someone who is anxious or sad may feel sicker when they are injured or ill.
- Stress can cause physical symptoms even when there is no illness.
  - A child may have stomach pain because they are scared about school.
  - An adult may get a headache when under emotional pressure.
- What a person thinks can change how a disease progresses.
  - For example, someone with high blood pressure may deny they have it.
  - This can reduce their fear, but it may also stop them from taking medicine.
  - Not taking medicine can make the condition worse.
- A serious or long-term physical illness can lead to depression.
  - Depression can make the physical illness harder to manage.
- Brain diseases like Alzheimer’s can change a person’s mood or thinking.
- When physical symptoms come from stress or emotions, it can be hard for doctors to find the cause.
  - Tests may be needed to rule out real physical problems.

# Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD)

Mixed connective tissue disease is a rare condition. It combines symptoms from three other autoimmune diseases: systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis. It is linked to very high levels of a specific antibody in the blood. This antibody targets a protein called ribonucleoprotein.

The disease can affect many parts of the body. Common problems include swollen hands, cold fingers that turn white or blue (Raynaud syndrome), joint pain, muscle weakness, trouble swallowing, and lung problems.

Doctors diagnose MCTD by looking at symptoms, blood tests, and ruling out other similar diseases. Treatment depends on how severe the disease is and which organs are affected. Most people need corticosteroids and other medicines that reduce immune system activity.

MCTD can happen in any race and around the world. It is most common in teenagers and young adults. Women are much more likely to get it than men.

The exact cause is not known. In some people, MCTD later turns into one of the three main diseases it overlaps with. Because of this, some doctors are not sure if MCTD is a separate disease.

---

## Symptoms and Signs of MCTD

Raynaud syndrome often appears first. It can happen years before other symptoms. The first signs may look like early lupus, scleroderma, polymyositis, or even rheumatoid arthritis.

Many people start with no clear diagnosis. Their symptoms may change over time. They may develop more widespread problems.

Swelling in the hands is common at first. But not everyone has it. Skin changes can include painful red patches on the skin (chilblains), raised red spots (discoid lesions), and a butterfly-shaped rash across the cheeks (malar rash), like in lupus.

Some people develop thick, tight skin like in scleroderma. Others may get sores or dead skin on the fingertips.

Almost everyone has joint pain. About three out of four people also have joint swelling. The joint swelling is often not deforming. But some people develop joint damage and bent fingers, similar to what happens in rheumatoid arthritis.

Muscle weakness is common. It usually affects the arms and legs. This weakness often comes with high levels of certain muscle enzymes in the blood.

Digestive problems are also common. These include trouble moving food through the stomach and intestines, similar to what happens in scleroderma.

Kidney problems happen in about one in four people. The most common type is called membranous nephropathy. It is usually mild. Severe kidney damage is rare in MCTD.

Lung problems affect up to three out of four people. The most common issues are fluid around the lungs (pleural effusions) and scarring in the lungs (interstitial lung disease). Pulmonary hypertension (high blood pressure in the lungs) is a serious problem. It can lead to death. It happens in up to 13% of people.

Inflammation of the lining around the heart (pericarditis) is common. Severe heart muscle inflammation (myocarditis) is rare but can happen. It can lead to heart failure.

Some people develop dry eyes and dry mouth. This is called Sjögren syndrome.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose MCTD

Doctors look for signs of MCTD when a person has symptoms from more than one autoimmune disease. They may suspect MCTD if someone has signs of lupus, scleroderma, or polymyositis at the same time.

The first tests are for antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and antibodies to U1 ribonucleoprotein (RNP). Almost all people with MCTD have high levels of ANA. The test shows a speckled pattern. Antibodies to U1 RNP are also present, and usually at very high levels.

Doctors also test for antibodies linked to lupus. These include anti-Sm and anti-double-stranded DNA. In MCTD, these are usually negative. This helps rule out lupus.

Having high levels of anti-RNP antibodies alone is not enough to diagnose MCTD. The person must also have typical symptoms.

Rheumatoid factor is often positive. Blood tests for inflammation (like ESR and CRP) are often high.

Lung problems are common. Doctors check for pulmonary hypertension using lung function tests and heart ultrasound (echocardiography), just like in scleroderma.

To check for muscle disease, doctors may use blood tests for muscle enzymes, MRI, nerve tests, or a small muscle biopsy.

---

## How MCTD Is Treated

For mild symptoms, doctors may prescribe nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or antimalarial medicines like hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine. Sometimes low-dose corticosteroids are used.

For moderate to severe disease, doctors use corticosteroids and other medicines that lower immune system activity. These include methotrexate, azathioprine, and mycophenolate mofetil.

For Raynaud syndrome, doctors often prescribe calcium channel blockers like nifedipine. In some cases, they may also use phosphodiesterase inhibitors like tadalafil. These medicines are adjusted based on blood pressure and how well they work.

Treatment is based on the main symptoms. If the disease looks like lupus, treatment follows lupus guidelines. If it looks like scleroderma or myositis, treatment follows those disease plans.

Early treatment with corticosteroids works well for most people with moderate to severe disease. But if the person has signs of scleroderma, doctors use the lowest possible dose of corticosteroids. This is to avoid a serious kidney problem called scleroderma renal crisis.

For severe organ damage, higher doses of corticosteroids are needed. For example, oral prednisone at 1 milligram per kilogram of body weight per day. Additional immunosuppressants are also used.

If the main problem is muscle disease (myositis) or skin thickening (systemic sclerosis), treatment follows the standard plan for those conditions.

All patients should be watched closely for heart disease. Long-term use of corticosteroids can weaken bones. Patients should take medicine to prevent osteoporosis.

If a person takes multiple immune-suppressing medicines, they are at higher risk for infections. They should get preventive treatment for certain infections, like *Pneumocystis jirovecii*. They should also get vaccines for common infections, including pneumonia, flu, and COVID-19.

Some experts recommend checking for pulmonary hypertension every 1 to 2 years. This is done with lung function tests and heart ultrasound, especially if symptoms are present.

---

## Outlook for People with MCTD

Most people with MCTD live for at least 10 years after diagnosis. The 10-year survival rate is about 96%.

But the outlook depends on which symptoms are most severe. People with strong signs of scleroderma or muscle disease tend to have a worse outcome.

People with MCTD are at higher risk for heart disease, including hardening of the arteries (atherosclerosis).

Causes of death include pulmonary hypertension, kidney failure, heart attack, bowel rupture, serious infections, and brain bleeding.

Some people go into long-term remission. They may stay well for years without needing treatment.

---

## Key Points

- MCTD includes symptoms from lupus, scleroderma, and/or polymyositis.
- Blood tests show high levels of ANA and anti-RNP antibodies. Tests for anti-Sm and anti-DNA antibodies are negative.
- Always check for pulmonary hypertension.
- Mild disease: treat with NSAIDs or antimalarials.
- Moderate to severe disease: treat with corticosteroids and other immune-suppressing medicines.

# Tarsal Tunnel Syndrome

Tarsal tunnel syndrome causes pain in the ankle, foot, or toes.  
It happens when a nerve in the foot gets squeezed or damaged.  
This nerve runs from the back of the calf, through a narrow space near the heel, and into the bottom of the foot.

## What Causes Tarsal Tunnel Syndrome?

Swelling in the tissues around the nerve can press on it.  
This pressure causes pain and discomfort.  
Several conditions can lead to this swelling:

- A broken ankle  
- Swelling in the ankle from heart or kidney problems  
- An underactive thyroid gland  
- Inflammation from gout or rheumatoid arthritis  
- Poor foot posture, such as when the ankle rolls too far inward  

## Symptoms

The most common symptom is pain.  
It often feels like a burning or tingling sensation.  
The pain usually starts when you stand or walk.  
It may get worse when wearing certain shoes.  
The pain is often on the inside of the ankle.  
It can spread to the heel, arch, or toes.  
Rest usually helps ease the pain.  
Over time, the pain may happen even when you are not moving.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors start by examining your foot.  
They may tap the area just below the ankle bone.  
If this causes tingling in the foot or toes, it may be a sign of tarsal tunnel syndrome.  
This is called the Tinel sign.

Sometimes, doctors use nerve tests to check how well the nerve is working.  
These tests help find the cause or how bad the nerve damage is.  
An MRI scan may also be done.  
This shows the soft tissues around the nerve.  
It helps rule out other causes of pain.

## Treatment

Treatment depends on how bad the pain is.

**Injections**  
A doctor may inject a medicine into the area near the nerve.  
This medicine reduces swelling and eases pain.  
It often includes a steroid and a numbing medicine.

**Medicines**  
Pain relievers like ibuprofen or similar drugs may help at first.  
They can reduce swelling and ease discomfort.

**Support Devices**  
Wrapping the foot or using special shoe inserts (called orthoses) can help.  
These devices support the foot and reduce pressure on the nerve.

**Surgery**  
If other treatments do not help, surgery may be needed.  
The goal is to release the pressure on the nerve.  
This can relieve long-term pain.

Always talk to your doctor about your symptoms and treatment options.

# Autoimmune Disorders

Your immune system usually protects you from germs and infections.  
In autoimmune disorders, your immune system makes a mistake.  
It attacks your own body instead of foreign invaders.  

This happens when your immune system makes antibodies against your own body parts.  
These body parts are called autoantigens.  

There are different ways this attack can cause harm.  

## Types of Immune Reactions in Autoimmune Disorders

### Type II Reaction  
Your immune system puts antibodies on your own cells.  
This is like marking a foreign object for destruction.  
The body then destroys these marked cells.  
This can damage tissues and organs.  

### Type III Reaction  
Antibodies and antigens stick together in the blood.  
These clumps can get stuck in small blood vessels.  
This causes inflammation and tissue damage.  

### Type IV Reaction  
Special immune cells called T cells attack your body.  
This type of reaction is slower than others.  
It leads to damage in tissues over time.  

## Type I Reaction – Not Related to Autoimmune Disorders  
Type I reactions happen quickly.  
They involve a type of antibody called IgE.  
They are linked to allergies, not autoimmune diseases.  
For example, they cause hives, asthma, or severe allergic reactions.  

## Common Autoimmune Disorders  
The following conditions are examples of autoimmune disorders:  

- **Autoimmune hemolytic anemia** – The body destroys its own red blood cells.  
- **Bullous pemphigoid** – Blisters form on the skin.  
- **Cutaneous lupus erythematosus** – A skin condition that causes rashes and sores.  
- **Diabetes mellitus, type 1** – The body attacks insulin-making cells in the pancreas.  
- **Goodpasture syndrome** – The body attacks the kidneys and lungs.  
- **Graves disease** – The thyroid gland becomes overactive.  
- **Hashimoto thyroiditis** – The thyroid gland becomes underactive.  
- **Multiple sclerosis** – The immune system damages nerves in the brain and spinal cord.  
- **Myasthenia gravis** – The body attacks muscles, causing weakness.  
- **Pemphigus vulgaris** – Blisters form on the skin and inside the mouth.  
- **Pernicious anemia** – The body cannot absorb vitamin B12, leading to anemia.  
- **Rheumatoid arthritis** – The immune system attacks the joints, causing pain and swelling.  
- **Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)** – A serious condition that can affect many organs.  
- **Vasculitis** – Inflammation of blood vessels.  

## Who Is Most Affected?  
Women are more likely than men to develop autoimmune disorders.

# Rashes in Children

A rash means the skin looks or feels different than normal.

Rashes can happen for many reasons. These include:
- Things that irritate the skin
- Allergies
- Certain medicines
- Infections caused by bacteria, fungi, or viruses

Types of rashes include:
- Red spots or patches
- White or yellow flakes on the skin
- Small bumps, pimples, or lumps under the skin

Some rashes cause itching. Others may hurt or feel sore. Some rashes do not cause any discomfort at all.

If a rash needs treatment, it can often be helped by:
- Gentle soaps or cleansers
- Moisturizing creams or ointments
- Antibiotic or steroid creams
- Medicines to reduce itching

Rashes in babies and young children are usually not serious. They can come from many different causes. These include:
- Irritating substances on the skin
- Certain medicines
- Allergic reactions
- Skin conditions that cause swelling or inflammation

## Common Rashes in Babies and Young Children

Here are some of the most common types of rashes in young children:

- **Diaper rash** – Red, irritated skin in the diaper area. It is often caused by wet or dirty diapers.
- **Cradle cap** – Scaly patches on the scalp. It is not itchy and does not hurt.
- **Eczema** – Dry, itchy, red skin. It is also called atopic dermatitis.
- **Rashes from viruses** – Some viruses cause a rash. These rashes often go away on their own.

# Continuous Blood Filtration and Dialysis

These treatments clean the blood without stopping. They help people whose kidneys are not working well. This is different from other kidney treatments that happen in short sessions.

## Why These Treatments Are Used

These methods are best for people with sudden kidney failure who are very sick. They are used when:
- The person’s blood pressure is unstable.
- The person needs a lot of fluids, such as during severe illness or shock.
- The person is getting strong medicines through a drip.

These treatments remove large amounts of fluid slowly. This helps avoid sudden drops in blood pressure. This is a big problem with other types of dialysis that happen in short bursts.

## How Continuous Hemofiltration Works

In this method, water and waste move out of the blood through a special filter. This is called convection. The fluid that comes out is thrown away. The patient must get replacement fluids with the right balance of water and salts.

A dialysis machine can be added to the filter to remove more waste.

There are two types of this treatment:

### Arteriovenous (AV) Method

- A tube is placed into an artery in the leg (femoral artery).
- Blood flows from the artery to the filter and back into a vein in the same leg.
- The pressure from the artery pushes the blood through the system.
- This method does not need a pump.
- It works best when blood pressure is normal.
- It may not work well if blood pressure is low.

### Continuous Venovenous (CVV) Method

- A pump moves blood from a large vein (in the leg, chest, or neck).
- Blood goes through the filter and returns to the same vein.
- A special double-lumen tube is used to draw blood in and return it.
- The pump gives better control over blood flow and fluid removal.
- It is safer for people with low blood pressure.
- Only one vein needs to be used.

## Which Method Is Better?

- The AV method is simpler but may not work well in very sick patients.
- The CVV method gives better control and is safer for unstable patients.
- There is no clear proof that one method is better than the other overall.

## Preventing Blood Clots

Both methods need medicine to stop blood from clotting in the machine.

Most often, doctors use regional citrate anticoagulation. This means:
- Citrate is added to the blood before it goes into the filter.
- Citrate stops the blood from clotting by binding calcium.
- Calcium is added back into the blood before it returns to the body.

This method avoids the risks of using heparin throughout the body.

But not everyone can use citrate. People with sudden liver failure cannot use it. Their liver cannot break down citrate well. This can lead to a dangerous buildup of citrate in the body.

# Osteogenesis Imperfecta

Osteogenesis imperfecta is a genetic condition that causes bones to be weak and break easily.  
It is passed down through families.  
The condition affects how bones form in the body.

## What Causes Osteogenesis Imperfecta?

The body makes a protein called collagen that helps build strong bones.  
In people with this condition, the genes that help make collagen do not work properly.  
This leads to weak bones that break easily.

## Types of Osteogenesis Imperfecta

There are four main types: Type I, Type II, Type III, and Type IV.  
There are also rarer forms.

### Type I
- This is the mildest form.  
- Some children only have blue-colored whites of the eyes.  
- They may have joint pain or loose joints.  
- They may break bones during childhood.  
- Most people with this type live normal lives.

### Type II
- This is the most serious form.  
- Babies are born with many broken bones.  
- The skull is very soft and may not protect the brain during birth.  
- Arms and legs are short.  
- The eyes may have a blue tint.  
- Most babies with this type do not survive past birth or die within days or weeks.

### Type III
- This is the most severe form that does not cause death.  
- Children are very short.  
- The spine curves abnormally.  
- Bones break easily, even from small injuries.  
- This often happens when children start walking.  
- The head is large and the face is small.  
- The chest may be shaped oddly.  
- The color of the eyes can vary.

### Type IV
- This type varies in how serious it is.  
- Bones break easily during childhood, before puberty.  
- The eyes are usually white, not blue.  
- Children are short.  
- Treatment can help.  
- Most children live into adulthood.

## Symptoms

- Most people with this condition have bones that break easily.  
- About half to two-thirds of people have hearing loss.  
- The whites of the eyes may look blue.  
  - This happens because the eye tissue is thinner than normal.  
  - The blue color shows through from the veins underneath.  
- Some children have weak or discolored teeth.  
  - This is called dentinogenesis imperfecta.  
  - It depends on the type of osteogenesis imperfecta.  
- Some children may develop heart or lung problems.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

### Before Birth
- An ultrasound scan can sometimes show signs of the most severe form.  
- This can happen during pregnancy.

### After Birth
- Doctors look at symptoms and do a physical exam.  
- If the diagnosis is unclear, they may take a small skin sample.  
  - This is checked under a microscope.  
  - They look at certain cells that help build connective tissue.  
- Blood tests can check for changes in genes.  
- X-rays can show bone problems.  
  - Bones may look thin or broken in unusual ways.  
- Hearing tests (audiometry) are done often during childhood.

## Treatment

There is no cure, but treatments can help manage symptoms.

### Medicines
- **Growth hormone** injections can help children grow taller and build stronger bones.  
  - This works best for Types I and IV.  
- **Bisphosphonates** help strengthen bones.  
  - They reduce pain and the number of fractures.  
  - They can be given through a vein (pamidronate) or taken as a pill (alendronate).  
- **Denosumab** is another medicine that helps prevent bone loss.  
  - It may help some people with osteogenesis imperfecta.  
- **Vitamin D** helps the body use calcium and phosphorus to build strong bones.  
  - If levels are low, doctors give vitamin D supplements.

### Broken Bones
- Treatment is similar to that for other children.  
- But broken bones may not heal properly.  
- They can become bent or stop growing.  
- This can lead to permanent short stature.  
- Metal rods may be placed inside bones to keep them straight.

### Therapy
- **Physical therapy** helps improve movement and strength.  
- It can help prevent fractures.  
- **Occupational therapy** helps with daily tasks.  
- Avoiding even small injuries is important.

### Hearing Loss
- Some children with hearing loss may benefit from a cochlear implant.  
  - This device sends sound signals to the inner ear.  
  - It helps some people hear better.

## More Information

The following English-language resource may be helpful:

**Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI) Foundation**  
This group offers support, education, and research information about osteogenesis imperfecta.

# Radiation Therapy for Cancer – Simple Explanation

Radiation therapy uses high-energy rays to treat cancer. It can cure some cancers on its own. It can also work better when used with other treatments like surgery or chemotherapy.

This treatment works best for cancers that:
- Are sensitive to radiation.
- Are in one place and not spread.
- Can be fully covered by the radiation beam.

Using radiation before surgery or chemotherapy can help shrink the tumor. This may make surgery easier and less extensive. Using radiation after surgery or chemotherapy can help kill any remaining cancer cells.

Even if a cure is not possible, radiation can still help. It can improve quality of life by easing symptoms. For example:

- **Brain tumors**: Helps you stay active longer and prevents nerve problems.
- **Cancers pressing on the spine**: Stops nerve damage from getting worse.
- **Superior vena cava syndrome**: Opens up a blocked blood vessel in the chest.
- **Painful bone areas**: Often reduces pain.

Radiation kills cancer cells, but it can also harm nearby healthy cells. Doctors must balance the benefits against the risks.

The results of radiation depend on several things:
- What kind of radiation is used (like photons, electrons, protons, or radioactive materials).
- How much radiation is given.
- How often it is given and how the total dose is split over time.
- How sensitive the cancer is to radiation.

Cancer cells are more likely to be damaged than normal cells. This is because cancer cells grow and use energy faster. Healthy cells can usually repair themselves better.

Key points when using radiation therapy:
- The amount of radiation and how often it is given.
- How the dose is split into smaller parts (called fractionation).
- How well the radiation can be aimed at the cancer.
- How much area needs to be treated.
- The shape and direction of the radiation beams.
- How the radiation dose is spread across the body.

Treatment plans are made to hurt cancer cells as much as possible while protecting healthy tissue.

## How Radiation Therapy Is Given

Each treatment session starts with careful positioning of the patient. To keep the same position each time, doctors may make a custom mold or mask from foam or plastic. Lasers help guide the setup.

Most treatment plans follow a schedule:
- **For symptom relief (palliative care)**: Larger doses each day over several weeks.
- **For cure (curative treatment)**: Smaller daily doses, five days a week, for six to eight weeks.

## Types of Radiation Therapy

There are several types:

- **External beam radiation**: Radiation comes from outside the body, aimed at the cancer.
- **Stereotactic radiation therapy**: Very precise, high-dose radiation given in a few sessions.
- **Conformal radiation therapy**: Radiation is shaped to match the tumor’s shape.
- **Brachytherapy**: Radioactive material is placed inside or near the tumor.
- **Systemic radionuclides**: Radioactive substances are given by mouth or injection to travel through the body and target cancer cells.

## Side Effects of Radiation Therapy

Radiation can harm any normal tissue that lies between the machine and the cancer.

### Short-term side effects (acute effects)
These depend on the area being treated. They may include:
- Feeling tired or weak.
- Feeling very tired (fatigue).
- Sore mouth or throat.
- Skin changes like redness, itching, or peeling.
- Swelling or soreness in the esophagus (food pipe).
- Lung irritation (pneumonitis).
- Liver irritation (hepatitis).
- Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or a strong urge to pass stool.
- Urinary problems like needing to go often, urgency, or pain when urinating.
- Lower blood cell counts (bone marrow suppression).

# Infection of the Esophagus

The esophagus is the tube that carries food from your throat to your stomach.

Infection in the esophagus usually happens in people whose body defenses are weak. These defenses normally keep infections from happening.

The main causes of esophagus infection are:
- A yeast called *Candida albicans*
- Herpes simplex virus
- Cytomegalovirus

Your body has several ways to protect the esophagus from infection. These include:
- Saliva
- Normal movement of the esophagus (contractions)
- Immune system cells

In healthy people, these defenses work well. But some people are at higher risk because their defenses are weak. This includes people who:
- Have HIV
- Have had an organ transplant
- Have alcohol use disorder
- Have diabetes
- Have a weak or damaged immune system
- Are underweight or not getting enough nutrition
- Have cancer
- Have problems with how the esophagus moves

Swallowing or inhaling corticosteroid medicines can also raise the risk of infection.

*Candida* infection can happen in any of these people.

Herpes simplex virus and cytomegalovirus infections mainly affect people with HIV or those who have had an organ transplant and are taking medicines to weaken their immune system.

> **Did You Know?**  
> Saliva helps protect the esophagus from infection.

---

## Symptoms of Esophagus Infection

The most common symptom is pain when you swallow.  
Some people also have trouble swallowing.

The infection can cause sores (ulcers) in the esophagus.  
It can also cause irritation and swelling of the esophagus, called esophagitis.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Esophagus Infection

Doctors often use a thin, flexible tube with a camera to look inside the esophagus. This is called endoscopy.

During the test, the doctor may take a small piece of tissue for testing. This is called a biopsy.

If you have a *Candida* infection, the doctor may see white patches in your mouth. This is called thrush.  
But people with herpes simplex virus or cytomegalovirus infections usually do not have any signs in the mouth.

---

## Treatment for Esophagus Infection

### For *Candida* Infection
You will be given an antifungal medicine.  
The most common is fluconazole.  
It can be taken as a pill.  
If you cannot swallow pills, it can be given through a vein.

### For Herpes Simplex Virus Infection
You will be given an antiviral medicine.  
Options include acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir.  
These can be taken by mouth or given through a vein.

### For Cytomegalovirus Infection
You will be given an antiviral medicine.  
Options include ganciclovir (given through a vein) or valganciclovir (taken as a pill).

# Trigeminal Neuralgia

Trigeminal neuralgia causes sudden, severe, sharp pain in the face.  
It happens when the fifth nerve in the head (called the trigeminal nerve) does not work properly.  
The pain can feel like a stabbing shock.  
It usually lasts just a few seconds to two minutes.  
But it can come back many times in a day—up to 100 times.  

This condition mostly affects adults.  
It is more common in older adults.  
Women are more likely to get it than men.  

---

## What Causes Trigeminal Neuralgia?

Most often, a blood vessel near the brain presses on the trigeminal nerve.  
This pressure can happen at the nerve’s starting point in the brain.  
The most common blood vessels involved are the anterior inferior cerebellar artery or a widened basilar artery.  

Less often, a vein pressing on the nerve causes the problem.  

Other, less common causes include:  
- A tumor near the nerve  
- An abnormal blood vessel connection (arteriovenous malformation)  
- A bulging blood vessel (aneurysm)  
- A scar from multiple sclerosis in the brain stem  

These other causes often come with other symptoms, like numbness or weakness.  
That helps doctors tell them apart from typical trigeminal neuralgia.  

Sometimes, other conditions like multiple sclerosis can cause similar pain.  
But doctors may still call it trigeminal neuralgia if the pain matches.  

The exact reason for the pain is not fully known.  
One idea is that pressure on the nerve damages its protective covering.  
This damage may cause the nerve to send wrong signals.  
These signals can cause sudden, intense pain.  

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The pain happens in one or more areas of the face.  
It most often affects the middle part of the face (the maxillary area).  
The pain is sudden and sharp.  
It can be so strong it makes it hard to do normal things.  

The pain often starts when something touches a sensitive spot on the face.  
Examples include:  
- Chewing food  
- Brushing your teeth  
- Smiling  
- Touching your face  

Only one side of the face is usually affected.  
Lying on that side can be very painful.  

There are no other signs of nerve damage.  
For example, your face does not feel numb or weak.  

If you do have numbness or weakness, it may mean another problem is causing the pain.  
In that case, a brain scan (MRI) is needed.  

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose trigeminal neuralgia by talking to you and doing a physical exam.  
The pattern of pain is often a clear sign.  

Other conditions can cause facial pain.  
Doctors check for differences:  

- **Chronic paroxysmal hemicrania**: Pain lasts longer—5 to 8 minutes.  
  It gets much better with a medicine called indomethacin.  

- **Postherpetic pain**: This pain is constant, not sudden.  
  It follows a past rash from shingles.  
  It often affects the eye area.  

- **Migraine**: Pain lasts longer and feels like a throbbing ache.  
  It is not sudden and sharp like trigeminal neuralgia.  

- **Sinus infection or tooth pain**: These often come with other signs.  
  Examples include a runny nose, fever, or tooth sensitivity.  

A normal exam means the nerve is working normally.  
If the exam shows numbness or weakness, another problem may be present.  
Then, a brain scan (MRI) is needed.  

---

## How Is It Treated?

Most people start with a medicine called carbamazepine.  
It is an antiseizure drug that helps calm the nerve.  
The dose is slowly increased until it works.  
This medicine often helps for a long time.  

If carbamazepine does not work or causes side effects, other medicines may be tried.  
These include:  
- Oxcarbazepine  
- Lamotrigine  
- Gabapentin  
- Baclofen  
- Phenytoin  
- Amitriptyline  

These are all taken by mouth.  

A nerve block can give short-term relief.  
It involves injecting medicine near the nerve.  

Botulinum toxin (Botox) can be injected into the skin at the pain spot.  
It may help if medicines do not work.  
But there is not much strong evidence yet.  

If the pain is still bad, more serious treatments may be needed.  
These include:  
- Surgery to relieve pressure on the nerve  
- Procedures that damage the nerve to stop pain signals  

These treatments can help, but the pain may come back.  
Sometimes, the new pain is worse than before.  

Some treatments can cause numbness in the face.  
This is called "painful numbness" or anesthesia dolorosa.  
It happens in about 4 out of 100 people after one type of surgery.  

### Types of Surgery

**Microvascular decompression (Jannetta procedure):**  
A small pad is placed between the nerve and the blood vessel.  
This stops the vessel from pressing on the nerve.  
This surgery often works well.  
But in about 15 out of 100 people, the pain comes back.  

**Gamma knife radiosurgery:**  
A focused beam of radiation is aimed at the nerve.  
This stops pain signals from reaching the brain.  

**Percutaneous procedures:**  
A needle is guided to the nerve through the skin.  
Then, a small injury is made to the nerve.  
This can be done with heat, chemicals, or a balloon.  

**Nerve cutting:**  
In rare cases, the nerve is cut between the brain and the face.  
This is only done when all other options fail.  

---

## Key Points

- Trigeminal neuralgia is usually caused by a blood vessel pressing on the trigeminal nerve.  
- The pain is sudden, sharp, and often comes in quick bursts.  
- It is often a clear sign of this condition.  
- Start treatment with carbamazepine. It works well for many people.  
- If carbamazepine does not help or causes side effects, try another medicine.  
  Options include oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, gabapentin, baclofen, or pregabalin.  
- If pain remains severe, consider Botox, surgery, or nerve damage procedures.  
- These treatments may help, but pain can return.  
- Sometimes, the new pain is worse than before.

# What Are Specific Phobias?

A specific phobia is a strong, ongoing fear of a certain thing, situation, or place. This fear is much stronger than what most people would feel.

- The fear can make daily life hard.
- People often avoid the thing they fear.
- The fear is not based on real danger.

## How Common Are Specific Phobias?

- About 8 out of every 100 women have a specific phobia each year.
- About 3 out of every 100 men have a specific phobia each year.
- Many people have more than one phobia.

## Common Types of Specific Phobias

Here are some of the most common fears:

- Fear of animals (like spiders, snakes, or mice)
- Fear of heights
- Fear of thunder and lightning
- Fear of flying
- Fear of needles or shots
- Fear of being in small, closed spaces
- Fear of bridges
- Fear of water
- Fear of public speaking
- Fear of the number thirteen
- Fear of blood or injury
- Fear of ghosts
- Fear of passing gas in public

Some fears are rare. There are over 500 named phobias, but most are very uncommon.

## How Do Specific Phobias Affect People?

- People with a phobia feel strong fear when they face the thing they fear.
- They may avoid the situation or object completely.
- They may stay in the situation but feel very upset.
- Some people have panic attacks when they face their fear.
- Even though they feel this way, they know their fear is too strong.

### Some Phobias Cause Little Trouble

- A city person who fears snakes may never meet one.
- So the fear does not affect their daily life.

### Some Phobias Cause Big Problems

- A city person who fears elevators may need to take many stairs to get to work.
- They may miss important meetings just to avoid the elevator.
- This can hurt their job or personal life.

## How Are Specific Phobias Diagnosed?

A doctor or mental health professional checks for a specific phobia by asking questions and using standard guidelines.

You may have a specific phobia if:

- Your fear has lasted at least six months.
- You fear a specific thing or situation.
- The fear starts right away when you face the thing.
- You avoid the thing or situation.
- The fear is much stronger than the real danger.
- The fear causes serious stress or makes life hard.

Doctors also check to rule out other mental health problems, such as:

- Fear of being in public places (agoraphobia)
- Fear of social situations (social anxiety)
- Problems from past trauma (stress disorder)

It is possible to have a specific phobia and another mental health condition at the same time. These can include:

- Other anxiety problems
- Depression
- Bipolar disorder
- Substance use problems
- Physical symptoms with no clear cause (somatic symptom disorder)
- Certain personality types, especially dependent personality disorder

## How Are Specific Phobias Treated?

The best treatment is **exposure therapy**.

### What Is Exposure Therapy?

- It is a type of talk therapy.
- You face your fear slowly and safely.
- You do this in your mind or in real life.
- You learn to stay calm during the process.

### How Does It Work?

- You start with a small step.
- You keep going step by step.
- You learn to feel less afraid over time.
- A therapist can help guide you.
- You can also do it on your own.

### Examples of Exposure Therapy

- Fear of blood or needles:
  - First, just walk by a doctor’s office.
  - Next, sit in the exam room without getting a shot.
  - Then, let a needle come close to your skin.
  - Finally, allow a blood draw.

- Fear of flying:
  - Start by looking at pictures of airplanes.
  - Then, visit an airport.
  - Next, go on a short flight.

Exposure therapy works for more than 90% of people who do it regularly. It is usually the only treatment needed.

### Other Treatments

- **Relaxation and breathing techniques** help you stay calm during exposure.
- **Medications** are not usually helpful for curing phobias.
- A short-term medicine like a benzodiazepine may help some people with flying phobias.
  - It does not cure the fear.
  - It helps the person get on the plane.
- A beta-blocker like propranolol may help before public speaking.
  - It helps with physical symptoms like shaking or a fast heartbeat.

Medications are not a long-term fix. They are only used in special cases.

## When Is Treatment Needed?

- If the thing you fear is easy to avoid, you may not need treatment.
  - Example: A fear of bats or caves.
- If the thing you fear is common, treatment is often needed.
  - Example: Fear of thunderstorms, elevators, or public speaking.

For more details, visit the National Institute of Mental Health website.  
This site has general facts about specific phobias, including how common they are.

# Understanding Capacity and Incapacity in Health Care

In the past, the United States treated "incapacity" as a medical issue. "Incompetency" was seen as a legal issue. Today, most states use the word "incapacity" instead of "incompetency." The two terms are often used the same way. But in health care, it is more helpful to think about two types of capacity:

- Clinical incapacity  
- Legal incapacity

## What Is Clinical Capacity?

Clinical capacity means a person can understand health care information.  
It means they can think through choices.  
It means they can make a decision based on that information.  
A doctor checks for clinical capacity.

## What Is Legal Capacity?

Legal capacity means a person has the right to make health care decisions.  
A court decides if someone has legal capacity.  
Only a court can say a person lacks legal capacity.

## What Happens When Someone Has Capacity?

If a person has both clinical and legal capacity, they can make their own health care choices.  
They can accept or refuse treatment.  
They can refuse care that doctors say is needed.  
Even if refusing care leads to death, they still have the right to choose.

## What Happens When Someone Lacks Capacity?

If a person lacks both clinical and legal capacity, they cannot make health care decisions.  
No one can make those decisions for them unless a court has given someone else that power.

## What If a Person Lacks Clinical Capacity But Has a Preference?

If a doctor says a person lacks clinical capacity, but the person still says what they want, the doctor must respect that wish.  
The doctor can ignore the person’s preference only if a court says the person lacks legal capacity.  
The court must agree before anyone can override the person’s choice.

# Liddle Syndrome

Liddle syndrome is a rare inherited condition. It affects how the kidneys handle salt and water.

The kidneys remove potassium from the body. But in this condition, they keep too much salt and water. This causes high blood pressure.

## How It Is Passed Down

The gene that causes Liddle syndrome is dominant. This means a child has a 50% chance of getting the faulty gene if one parent has the condition.

## Symptoms

Not everyone with Liddle syndrome has symptoms. When symptoms do appear, they often start in childhood or young adulthood.

Common signs include:
- High blood pressure
- Low levels of potassium in the blood
- High levels of bicarbonate in the blood

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors use several tests to diagnose Liddle syndrome:

- They check blood pressure, especially in young people with high blood pressure.
- They do blood and urine tests.
- They find low sodium in the urine.
- They find low levels of two hormones: renin and aldosterone. These hormones help control salt and blood pressure.

Genetic testing may also be done to confirm the diagnosis.

## How It Is Treated

Liddle syndrome is treated with specific medicines. These medicines help the body get rid of extra salt and keep more potassium.

The most common medicines are:
- Triamterene
- Amiloride

These medicines lower blood pressure effectively. They also help balance potassium levels.

The outlook is very good. With treatment, most people live normal, healthy lives.

# What You Need to Know About Antibacterial Medications Antibacterial medications are medicines that fight bacterial infections. They come from bacteria or mold. Some are made in labs from scratch. The word "antibiotic" usually means the same thing as "antibacterial medication." But technically, "antibiotic" only refers to medicines made from bacteria or mold. These medicines work in different ways. They can stop bacteria from building their outer shell. They can make holes in the bacteria’s outer layer. They can block the bacteria’s ability to make proteins. They can also interfere with DNA and other key processes in the bacteria. For example, they can stop the bacteria from making folic acid, which it needs to grow. Some medicines can affect how antibiotics work. They can raise or lower the levels of other medicines in the blood. This is especially important for medicines that have a narrow safety range. That means the amount that works is very close to the amount that can cause harm. Also, some medicines can change how much antibiotic is in the body. ## How Antibiotics Work: Blocking Protein Production Many antibiotics work by stopping bacteria from making proteins. This stops the bacteria from growing and spreading. There are many types of antibiotics. They are grouped by how they look and how they work. Even if two antibiotics are in the same group, they may act differently. They may also work against different kinds of bacteria. ## When to Use Antibiotics Use antibiotics only when a doctor confirms a bacterial infection. Do not use them for viral infections. Do not use them for fever with no clear cause. Using antibiotics when not needed can cause harm. It can also harm the good bacteria in your body. It can also lead to bacteria that no longer respond to antibiotics. In 2019, antibiotic-resistant infections caused nearly 5 million deaths worldwide. Misusing antibiotics is a major reason for this problem. For more information, visit the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention or the World Health Organization. Some infections need surgery. For example, abscesses or infections with a foreign object (like a device or implant) often need surgery. Antibiotics alone will not fix these. Doctors should use the narrowest-spectrum antibiotic possible. This means the medicine that targets only the bacteria causing the infection. They should also use it for the shortest time needed. (See also: Antibiotics in Newborn Babies.) ## How Bacteria Become Resistant to Antibiotics Some bacteria are naturally resistant to certain antibiotics. Others become resistant through changes in their genes. These changes can happen by chance or by picking up resistance genes from other bacteria. There are several ways bacteria can pass resistance genes to each other: - **Transformation**: A bacterium takes in DNA from another dead bacterium. - **Transduction**: A virus that infects bacteria carries resistance genes from one bacterium to another. - **Conjugation**: Two bacteria connect and share genetic material. This material can be plasmids or transposons. - Plasmids are small pieces of DNA that can copy themselves. - Transposons are small pieces of DNA that can move around inside a bacterium. Plasmids and transposons can spread resistance genes quickly. When antibiotics are used, they kill the bacteria that are not resistant. This leaves behind the resistant ones. The resistant bacteria then grow and multiply. This happens not just with harmful bacteria, but also with the good bacteria in your body. These resistant good bacteria can pass their resistance genes to harmful bacteria. ## Common Ways Bacteria Resist Antibiotics | How Resistance Happens | Example | |------------------------|--------| | Bacteria become less able to let antibiotics in | A type of *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* loses a pore in its outer layer. This makes it resistant to imipenem. | | Bacteria make enzymes that destroy antibiotics | *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, and *Escherichia coli* make enzymes that break down penicillin. | | Bacteria change the target of the antibiotic | In methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus* (MRSA), the bacteria change the protein that penicillin binds to. | | Bacteria change their ribosomes to avoid antibiotics | In some *Staphylococcus aureus*, the ribosome changes so macrolides, clindamycin, and quinupristin no longer work. | | Bacteria change their cell wall to avoid antibiotics | In some *Enterococcus faecium*, the cell wall changes so vancomycin cannot bind. | | Bacteria change their DNA enzyme to avoid antibiotics | In fluoroquinolone-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus*, the DNA enzyme changes so the antibiotic no longer works. | | Bacteria pump antibiotics out faster | *Staphylococcus aureus* can pump out tetracycline, macrolides, clindamycin, or fluoroquinolones faster. | | Bacteria find a way around the antibiotic | Some bacteria can use nutrients from the environment instead of making them. This lets them survive even when the antibiotic blocks their normal process.
Or, they make extra copies of the target protein. This reduces the effect of the antibiotic.
This happens in some bacteria exposed to trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. | **MLSB** means macrolide, lincoside, and streptogramin B — three types of antibiotics.

# Mechanical Ventilation

A mechanical ventilator is a machine that helps you breathe. It moves air in and out of your lungs.

Some people with serious breathing problems need a ventilator to stay alive. The machine can help when your lungs are too weak or damaged to work on their own.

## How Mechanical Ventilation Works

Doctors usually put a thin plastic tube into your nose or mouth and down into your windpipe. This tube connects to the ventilator.

If you need the ventilator for more than a few days, your doctor may make a small cut in your neck and put the tube directly into your windpipe. This is called a tracheostomy. It is safer and more comfortable for long-term use.

The ventilator pushes air into your lungs even if you are not breathing on your own.

Different types of ventilators and settings are used based on your condition. The machine can give you pure oxygen or a mix of oxygen and air.

## Alternatives to Mechanical Ventilation

Some people do not need full help from a machine. Instead, they can wear a tight-fitting mask over the nose or both the nose and mouth.

The mask delivers air under pressure. This helps your own breathing and stops your breathing muscles from getting too tired.

This method is called bilevel positive airway pressure or CPAP. It can help about half of people with breathing failure avoid needing a tracheostomy.

For people whose breathing problems come from weak muscles, using this mask at night can help. Resting at night lets the muscles recover. This makes it easier to breathe during the day.

## Risks of Mechanical Ventilation

Too much pressure or too much air can hurt your lungs. It can stretch the tiny air sacs in your lungs too much. These air sacs can burst. Air can then leak around your lung and cause it to collapse. This is called pneumothorax.

To prevent this, doctors carefully control how much air and pressure the ventilator gives.

But if the pressure and air volume are too low, not enough air moves in and out. This can cause carbon dioxide to build up in your blood. It can also cause small airways and air sacs to close.

Doctors check your breathing often. They adjust the ventilator settings to find the right balance.

Even though most people on a ventilator need extra oxygen, too much oxygen can harm your lungs. Doctors check your oxygen levels to make sure you get just the right amount.

People on a ventilator, especially those with a tube in the windpipe, may feel restless or anxious. Doctors can give medicine to calm you down. These medicines include propofol, lorazepam, midazolam, morphine, or fentanyl. They can also help ease shortness of breath.

When you have a tube in your windpipe, bacteria from your nose and mouth can get into your lungs. This can cause a serious infection. Doctors must find and treat these infections fast.

People on a ventilator cannot eat normally. If you need the ventilator for more than a few days, you will get nutrition through a tube placed in your stomach. This is called tube feeding.

## Stopping Mechanical Ventilation

As you get better, your doctors will slowly reduce the help your lungs get from the ventilator.

They may turn the ventilator off for short times to see if your lungs can work on their own.

These tests are done carefully. If you have trouble breathing, the ventilator can be turned back on right away.

# Necrotizing Enterocolitis

Necrotizing enterocolitis is a serious condition that affects the intestines of newborn babies.  
It mainly happens in babies who are born too early or who are very sick.  
The condition causes damage to the lining of the intestine, and sometimes deeper layers.  
It is the most common serious intestinal problem in newborns.  

## Who Gets Necrotizing Enterocolitis?

Most babies who get this condition are born too early.  
About 85 percent of these babies weigh less than 1.5 kilograms at birth.  
Or they are born before 32 weeks of pregnancy.  
Between 6 percent and 15 percent of babies in the neonatal intensive care unit get this condition.  

## What Causes Necrotizing Enterocolitis?

The exact cause is not fully known.  
But the intestines of very young babies are not fully developed.  
This makes them more likely to get sick.  
Poor blood flow to the intestines can damage the lining.  
This damage lets bacteria from the gut get into the intestinal wall.  
This can lead to infection and tissue death.  

Babies who are fed breast milk (chest milk) are less likely to get this condition.  
Once feeding starts, bacteria in the gut can grow quickly.  
If the intestinal wall is damaged, bacteria can pass through.  
This can cause gas to build up in the intestinal wall or in blood vessels.  

Some medicines can change the balance of bacteria in the gut.  
This includes antibiotics and medicines that reduce stomach acid.  
These changes may increase the risk of necrotizing enterocolitis.  

Low blood flow to the intestines can happen for many reasons.  
It can happen during a low-oxygen event.  
It can also happen during blood transfusions, sepsis, or when using formulas that are too strong.  
Babies with heart problems may also have poor blood flow to the intestines.  
This can lead to the condition, even if the baby is full term.  

Sometimes, several babies in the same hospital unit get this condition at once.  
This is called an outbreak.  
Some outbreaks are linked to certain bacteria like *Klebsiella*, *Escherichia coli*, *Pseudomonas*, *Clostridioides difficile*, or coagulase-negative staphylococci.  
But often, no specific germ is found.  

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

Babies may have trouble feeding.  
They may bring up blood or greenish fluid from the stomach after feeding.  
This can get worse and lead to vomiting green bile.  
The belly may become swollen and hard.  
The skin on the belly may turn red or dark.  
The baby may pass blood in the stool.  

The baby may seem very tired or weak.  
Their body temperature may go up or down.  
They may have more pauses in breathing.  
They may also have signs of a serious infection.  

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look for blood in the stool.  
They take X-rays of the belly.  
They may use ultrasound to look at the intestines.  
They also do blood tests and check for bacteria in the blood.  

Blood in the stool is a warning sign.  
Early X-rays may not show much.  
But if a loop of intestine stays swollen and does not change on repeat X-rays, it is a red flag.  

Two signs on X-ray are very important:  
- Gas in the wall of the intestine (called pneumatosis intestinalis).  
- Gas in the blood vessels of the liver (called portal vein gas).  

If there is gas in the space around the intestines (pneumoperitoneum), it means the intestine has burst.  
This is an emergency and needs surgery right away.  

Doctors use a system to stage the condition:  

- **Stage 1 (suspected):** Mild signs like poor feeding or blood in the stool.  
- **Stage 2 (confirmed):** More serious signs, such as worsening belly swelling or low blood pressure.  
- **Stage 3 (advanced):** Severe signs, including shock, bowel perforation, or gas in the belly cavity.  

Blood tests check for infection and inflammation.  
They also help guide antibiotic treatment.  

A similar condition called spontaneous intestinal perforation can look like advanced necrotizing enterocolitis.  
But it is different.  
It happens in very early babies.  
It is more localized and does not cause the same widespread inflammation.  

Ultrasound is used more often now.  
It can show thickened bowel walls, gas in the wall, and blood flow.  
But it depends on the skill of the person doing the scan.  
X-rays are still the most common tool.  

## How Is It Treated?

The baby stops getting feedings by mouth.  
A tube is placed through the nose into the stomach to remove fluid and air.  
The baby gets fluids through a vein.  
They also get nutrition through a vein.  
They are given strong antibiotics to fight infection.  
If there is an infection, the baby is kept in isolation.  

Some babies need surgery.  
Surgery removes dead or damaged parts of the intestine.  
It also treats a burst intestine.  
In some cases, a tube is placed through the skin to drain fluid.  

The chance of death is about 25 percent in all confirmed cases.  
It goes up to 35 percent if surgery is needed.  
For babies who weigh less than 1 kilogram at birth, the death rate is about 40 percent.  
Early and strong support, plus careful timing of surgery, gives the best chance of survival.  

## How Can It Be Prevented?

Babies at risk should be fed human milk if possible.  
Start with small amounts and slowly increase.  
Use a clear feeding plan.  
If human milk is not available, use preterm formula.  

Avoid strong formulas, certain medicines, or contrast dyes.  
Treat anemia, low oxygen levels, and high red blood cell counts quickly.  
Try to avoid antibiotics and medicines that reduce stomach acid when possible.  

Probiotics (good bacteria) may help prevent the condition.  
Examples include *Bifidus infantis* and *Lactobacillus acidophilus*.  
But we still need more research to know the best dose and which types to use.  

If a pregnant person is at risk of giving birth too early, steroids may be given.  
This can help protect the baby’s intestines and reduce the risk of necrotizing enterocolitis.  

## Key Facts

- Necrotizing enterocolitis is damage to the intestines.  
- It mostly happens in premature or sick newborns after feeding starts.  
- Complications include a burst intestine and infection in the belly.  
- Infection in the blood happens in 24 to 42 percent of cases.  
- About 23 percent of babies with this condition do not survive.  

- Early signs: trouble feeding, blood or green fluid in stomach after feeding.  
- Later signs: green vomit, swollen or discolored belly, blood in stool.  

- Diagnosis is based on X-rays of the belly.  

- Supportive care (fluids, suction, antibiotics, IV nutrition) works in 50 to 75 percent of cases.  

- Surgery is needed in about 25 to 50 percent of babies.

# Female Genital Birth Defects

Some girls are born with problems in how their genitals develop. These problems can affect the labia, vagina, cervix, or uterus.

- Some birth defects happen because of hormone problems during pregnancy.
- Others are caused by changes in the baby’s genes or chromosomes.
- Exposure to certain medicines or chemicals during pregnancy can also cause problems.
- Sometimes, a birth defect affects more than one part of the body.

Doctors find out what is wrong by doing tests. These may include imaging tests and blood tests.

Many girls need surgery to fix the problem.

---

## What Causes These Birth Defects?

In the early stages of pregnancy, all babies start with the same kind of tissue for their sex organs. Whether this tissue becomes male or female depends on several things.

One key thing is the sex chromosomes. Girls usually have two X chromosomes. Boys have one X and one Y chromosome.

If a baby has a Y chromosome, the body starts making testes. These make a male hormone called testosterone. This hormone tells the body to form male parts like the penis and scrotum.

If there is no Y chromosome, the body does not make testosterone. The body then forms female parts like the clitoris, labia, and separate openings for urine and the vagina.

Other hormones made by the baby also help shape the genitals.

Sometimes, a girl is born with too much testosterone or testosterone-like substances. This can cause her genitals to look more like a boy’s.

Other causes of genital birth defects include:

- Problems with the sex chromosomes
- Missing or faulty genes (the body’s instruction manual)
- Exposure to certain medicines, drugs, or hormones during pregnancy

Sometimes, the same problem that causes a genital defect also causes a problem in another organ.

Girls with genital defects may have trouble peeing. Later in life, they may have trouble having sex, trouble getting pregnant, or emotional and social challenges.

---

## Types of Female Genital Birth Defects

Common types include:

- Imperforate hymen
- Labial adhesions
- Extra genital organs (duplication)
- Genital organs joined together (fusion)
- Missing or short vagina (vaginal agenesis)

### Labial Adhesions

The labia are the outer lips around the vaginal opening. Sometimes these lips stick together. This is called labial adhesions.

- This usually happens in young girls, often around age 2.
- It can happen earlier or later.
- Most of the time, it does not cause any symptoms.
- It often goes away on its own.

When symptoms do happen, it is usually because urine gets trapped in the vagina. This can cause irritation, infections, or leaking.

If the adhesions cause symptoms, doctors may use a cream with estrogen to help separate them.

In some cases, doctors may gently open the adhesions in the office or in surgery.

Even if there are no symptoms, doctors often recommend surgery before puberty. This is so that menstrual blood can flow out properly.

Labial adhesions often come back. To help prevent this, girls may use a cream several times a day to protect the area.

### Imperforate Hymen

The hymen is a thin membrane at the opening of the vagina. In most girls, it has a small opening. But some girls are born with a hymen that completely blocks the opening. This is called an imperforate hymen.

- The vaginal opening is closed.
- Vaginal fluids cannot get out.
- If not fixed early, the problem may not be noticed until a girl starts her period.
- Then, menstrual blood gets trapped and causes pain in the belly.

Girls with this condition have a small surgery to open the hymen.

### Extra Genital Organs (Duplication)

Some girls are born with extra parts. For example, they may have two vaginas, two cervixes, or two uteruses.

- Sometimes, one organ is split into two parts by extra tissue (like a wall in the vagina or uterus).
- These problems may be found at birth, but often they are not noticed until later.
- Problems may show up during periods, when trying to get pregnant, or during pregnancy.

Some of these issues do not need treatment. Others need surgery to fix.

### Genital Organs Joined Together (Fusion)

In rare cases, a girl is born with her anus, vagina, and urethra joined together into one opening.

- Minor cases may not need treatment.
- Severe cases need surgery to separate the parts.

---

## Missing or Short Vagina (Vaginal Agenesis)

Sometimes, a girl is born without a vagina or with only a short one. The lower part of the vagina may form, but the upper part does not.

- The cervix and uterus may also not develop.
- This condition is called vaginal agenesis, mullerian agenesis, or MRKH syndrome.

These problems are not always found at birth. The outside parts, like the labia and lower vagina, often look normal.

- Girls usually do not get diagnosed until puberty.
- They develop breasts and pubic hair, but they never get their period.
- Sometimes, the uterus is small or blocked by tissue, so blood cannot flow out. This causes pain.

Girls with vaginal agenesis may also have other problems, such as:

- Missing one kidney
- Bone problems
- Problems with the wall of the belly

No treatment is needed right away unless there is pain from trapped menstrual blood.

When a girl is ready, she can start treatment using a vaginal dilator.

- A vaginal dilator is a smooth plastic rod, like a tampon.
- She inserts it and uses it regularly over time.
- This slowly stretches the vaginal canal.

---

## How Are These Defects Diagnosed?

Doctors use several methods to find out what is wrong.

### Physical Exam

- The doctor checks the baby’s genitals.
- They also look for other birth defects.

### Imaging Tests

- An ultrasound uses sound waves to make pictures of the inside of the body.
- An MRI uses magnets and radio waves to make detailed pictures.
- These tests help doctors see if the vagina, cervix, uterus, and ovaries are present.

Sometimes, doctors use a thin tube with a camera (a hysteroscope or cystoscope) to look inside the vagina.

If the results are unclear, doctors may do a laparoscopy.

- This is a small surgery.
- A camera is inserted through a tiny cut in the belly.
- It lets doctors see inside the abdomen.

### Blood Tests

- These tests check the baby’s chromosomes.
- They also measure hormone levels.

---

## How Are These Defects Treated?

### Surgery

- Most girls with genital defects need surgery to fix the problem.
- Some small problems do not need surgery.

Surgery can help with:

- Opening blocked areas
- Separating joined parts
- Creating a working vagina

The goal is to help the girl live a healthy, normal life. This includes being able to pee normally, have sex, and, if possible, get pregnant.

# Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition Disease (CPPD)

This condition happens when calcium crystals build up in and around your joints. These crystals can cause joint problems. The condition is also called pseudogout or acute CPP crystal arthritis.

## What Happens in CPPD?

- Calcium crystals form in your joints or nearby tissues.
- The symptoms can be mild or very strong.
- You may have sudden, painful joint flares. These flares feel like gout but can last longer and be harder to treat.
- You may also have long-term joint damage. This damage can be serious and look like severe wear and tear.
- Some people have no symptoms at all. Their joints look abnormal on X-rays, but they feel fine.

## How Common Is It?

- This condition becomes more common as you get older.
- It often shows up in the knee, wrist, hip, finger joints, spine, and the area between the pelvic bones.
- Men and women are affected about equally.

## Do You Need Treatment If You Have No Symptoms?

- No. Finding calcium crystals on an X-ray or scan does not mean you need treatment.
- The crystals do not cause harm if you do not have pain or swelling.
- But the crystals can make osteoarthritis worse over time.

## What Causes CPPD?

- In most cases, the cause is unknown.
- Some people get it because of other health problems, such as:
  - Low magnesium levels
  - Overactive parathyroid glands
  - Gout
  - Iron overload (hemochromatosis)
  - Rare bone diseases
  - Certain genetic conditions
  - Past joint injury or surgery
- Some cases run in families. If a parent has it, their children may get it too.
- A protein called ANK helps move chemicals that lead to crystal formation. Too much of this protein can cause more crystals.

## What Are the Symptoms?

- You may have sudden joint pain and swelling. This often happens in the knee, wrist, or other large joints.
- The pain can feel like gout, but it may last longer and be harder to treat.
- Some people have no pain between flares. Others have ongoing mild pain in many joints.
- This pattern usually lasts for life.
- In rare cases, the neck can be affected. This causes severe neck pain and stiffness. It can look like other serious conditions, such as:
  - Polymyalgia rheumatica
  - Giant cell arteritis
  - Spinal infection
  - Meningitis

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- A doctor will look at fluid from your joint.
- The fluid is checked under a microscope.
- If rhombus-shaped or rod-shaped crystals are found, and they do not shine brightly under special light, it is likely CPPD.
- The joint fluid will also show signs of inflammation.
- Other causes of joint pain must be ruled out, such as infection or gout.
- Infection is ruled out with a lab test of the fluid.
- Gout is ruled out by checking for uric acid crystals. You can have both gout and CPPD at the same time.
- If joint fluid cannot be taken, imaging tests like X-rays or ultrasound may help.
  - These can show calcium deposits in cartilage.
  - But these signs do not rule out gout or infection.
- If you are young and have frequent flares, your doctor may test your blood.
  - Tests may include:
    - Calcium levels
    - Parathyroid hormone
    - Magnesium levels
    - Liver and bone enzymes
    - Iron levels

## How Is It Treated?

### For Acute Flares (Sudden Pain and Swelling)

- **Steroid injections** into the joint can help. For example, 40 milligrams of a steroid like prednisolone acetate in the knee.
- **Pain relievers** like indomethacin or naproxen can stop flares.
- **Colchicine** taken by mouth (0.6 mg once or twice a day) can help prevent future flares.
- **Oral steroids** like prednisone or methylprednisolone work well, especially if you cannot take NSAIDs or colchicine.
- If other treatments do not work, a medicine called anakinra (an IL-1 blocker) may help.

### For Long-Term Care

- There is no treatment that removes the crystals.
- Managing symptoms is the main goal.
- You may need long-term care to control pain and swelling.

## What Is the Outlook?

- Each flare usually gets better with treatment.
- But some people have ongoing joint problems.
- In rare cases, joint damage can be severe. It may look like the damage seen in nerve-related joint disease (Charcot joints).
- Unlike gout, there is no treatment that removes the crystals or stops their buildup.

## Key Points

- Finding calcium crystals on an X-ray does not mean you need treatment if you have no symptoms.
- CPPD often affects the knee, wrist, hip, spine, and pelvic area.
- It can feel like gout, rheumatoid arthritis, or osteoarthritis.
- To diagnose it, doctors look for specific crystals in joint fluid.
- They must also rule out infection and gout.
- For sudden pain, treatment options include:
  - Steroid injections into the joint
  - Oral pain relievers (NSAIDs)
  - Colchicine
  - Oral steroids
  - Anakinra (in some cases)

# Chondroitin Sulfate

Chondroitin sulfate is a natural substance found in cartilage.  
It comes from shark or cow cartilage.  
It can also be made in a lab.  
It is often used with another substance called glucosamine.

## What Is It Used For?

People take chondroitin sulfate to help with joint pain from osteoarthritis.  
It is most often used with glucosamine.

## What Does Science Say?

Studies show that chondroitin sulfate alone does not help much.  
But when taken with glucosamine, it may help in some cases.  

It might:
- Reduce joint pain
- Improve how well your joints move
- Help you take less of your regular pain medicine

One large study looked at people with knee osteoarthritis.  
It tested glucosamine, chondroitin sulfate, and the two together.  
The study found no big improvement in pain for most people.  
But some people with moderate to severe knee pain did feel better with the combination.  
More research is needed to confirm these results.

Experts do not agree on whether chondroitin sulfate works.  
The American College of Rheumatology says it should not be used for hip or knee osteoarthritis.  
They say it might help a little for hand osteoarthritis, but only in some cases.  
The European Society of Clinical and Economic Aspects of Osteoarthritis says pharmaceutical-grade chondroitin sulfate can help with hand osteoarthritis.

## Side Effects

Chondroitin sulfate is safe for most people.  
It does not cause serious side effects.  
Some people have stomach pain, nausea, or other digestive issues.  

If the chondroitin sulfate is not made in a lab (pharmaceutical grade), it could carry infections.  
These include bacteria, viruses, or prions.  
Prions are very rare and dangerous proteins that can cause brain disease.

## Drug Interactions

Chondroitin sulfate may increase the risk of bleeding if taken with blood thinners.  
This includes warfarin and other similar medicines.  
People on blood thinners should not take chondroitin sulfate.

## Recommendations

Chondroitin sulfate with glucosamine might help a little with knee osteoarthritis.  
But any benefit is likely small.  
Current treatment guidelines do not recommend using chondroitin and glucosamine for osteoarthritis.

Chondroitin sulfate is generally safe.  
But people taking blood thinners like warfarin should avoid it.

The following English-language resource may be helpful.
