# Bladder Cancer – Simple Explanation

Bladder cancer most often starts in the cells that line the inside of the bladder. These are called transitional cells, and the cancer is also known as urothelial carcinoma.

## Who Gets Bladder Cancer?

- In the United States, about 83,000 new cases are found each year. Around 17,000 people die from it each year.
- It is the fourth most common cancer in men. It is less common in women.
- Men are about three times more likely than women to get it.
- It is more common in White people than in Black people.
- The risk goes up with age.

## What Causes Bladder Cancer?

The main risk factors are:

- **Smoking** – This is the biggest cause. It leads to more than half of all new cases.
- **Long-term use of a certain cancer medicine** – Cyclophosphamide, used in some cancer treatments, can raise the risk.
- **Long-term irritation of the bladder** – This can happen from:
  - A parasite infection called schistosomiasis.
  - Having a catheter in the bladder for a long time.
  - Bladder stones.
- **Exposure to certain chemicals** – These include:
  - Chemicals used in the dye, rubber, electric, cable, paint, and textile industries.
  - Aromatic amines, like naphthylamine, used in making dyes.
  - Other industrial chemicals and hydrocarbons.

## Types of Bladder Cancer

There are three main types:

- **Transitional cell carcinoma (urothelial carcinoma)** – This is the most common type. It makes up over 90% of all bladder cancers.
  - Most of these grow like small bumps (papillary tumors) and stay near the surface.
  - Some are flat and grow deeper. These are more dangerous and can spread early.
- **Squamous cell carcinoma** – This is less common. It usually happens in people with long-term bladder infections or irritation.
- **Adenocarcinoma** – This is rare. It can start in the bladder or spread from cancer in the bowel.

## How Often Does Bladder Cancer Come Back?

- In more than 4 out of 10 people, the cancer returns in the same or another part of the bladder.
- The risk is higher if:
  - The tumor is large.
  - The tumor is not well-formed (poorly differentiated).
  - There are many tumors.

Bladder cancer often spreads to the lymph nodes, lungs, liver, or bones.

Carcinoma in situ is a high-grade cancer that does not grow into the bladder wall. It is flat and often found in many places at once. It tends to come back.

## Symptoms of Bladder Cancer

Most people first notice:
- Blood in the urine (hematuria). This can be visible or only seen under a microscope.
- Some people have anemia. Blood in the urine may be found when testing for anemia.
- Urinary symptoms like:
  - Burning when peeing.
  - Needing to pee often.
  - A strong urge to pee.
- Some people have pus in the urine (pyuria).
- In later stages, pelvic pain may occur. A lump in the pelvis may be felt.

## How Is Bladder Cancer Diagnosed?

Diagnosis starts with symptoms. If you have blood in your urine, your doctor will do tests.

### Tests Used:
- **Cystoscopy** – A thin tube with a camera is passed through the urethra into the bladder. This lets the doctor see inside the bladder.
- **Biopsy** – If the doctor sees anything abnormal, a small sample of tissue is taken for testing.
- **Urine cytology** – A lab checks your urine for cancer cells.
- **Imaging tests** – These help see if the cancer has spread. They include:
  - CT urogram (a special CT scan of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder).
  - Renal ultrasound (an image of the kidneys using sound waves).
- **Urinary antigen tests** – These are not used often. They may be used if cancer is suspected but urine tests are normal.

### Advanced Testing:
- A special type of cystoscopy using blue light after a medicine is put into the bladder can help find cancer better. This can improve early detection and reduce future recurrences.
- If the cancer is deep in the bladder wall, more tests are needed:
  - Blood tests.
  - CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis.
  - Chest X-ray.
  - MRI (in some cases) to see the bladder and nearby tissues.

### Staging the Cancer:
Doctors use the TNM system to describe the cancer:
- **T** = How far the tumor has grown into the bladder wall.
- **N** = Whether the cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes.
- **M** = Whether the cancer has spread to distant parts of the body.

#### Stages of Bladder Cancer:
| Stage | Tumor | Lymph Nodes | Distant Spread |
|-------|-------|-------------|----------------|
| 0a    | Small, noninvasive tumor | No spread | No spread |
| 0is   | Flat, high-grade tumor | No spread | No spread |
| I     | Tumor in the inner layer | No spread | No spread |
| II    | Tumor in the muscle layer | No spread | No spread |
| IIIA  | Tumor outside the bladder | No spread | No spread |
| OR    | Any tumor | Spread to one node | No spread |
| IIIB  | Any tumor | Spread to two or more nodes | No spread |
| IVA   | Tumor in nearby organs | Any spread | No spread |
| OR    | Any tumor | Any spread | Spread to distant nodes |
| IVB   | Any tumor | Any spread | Spread to other organs |

#### What the T, N, and M Mean:
- **T0a**: Tumor is small and not growing into the bladder wall.
- **T0is**: Flat tumor, not growing into the wall.
- **T1**: Tumor has grown into the connective tissue under the lining.
- **T2**: Tumor has grown into the muscle layer.
  - **T2a**: Grows into the inner half of the muscle.
  - **T2b**: Grows into the outer half of the muscle.
- **T3**: Tumor has grown into the tissue around the bladder.
  - **T3a**: Tiny spread seen only under a microscope.
  - **T3b**: Larger spread seen without a microscope.
- **T4**: Tumor has grown into nearby organs.
  - **T4a**: Grows into the prostate, uterus, vagina, or seminal vesicles.
  - **T4b**: Grows into the pelvic or abdominal wall.
- **N0**: No cancer in lymph nodes.
- **N1**: Cancer in one node in the pelvis.
- **N2**: Cancer in two or more nodes in the pelvis.
- **N3**: Cancer in a common iliac node.
- **M0**: No distant spread.
- **M1a**: Cancer in nodes far from the pelvis.
- **M1b**: Cancer in organs like the lungs, liver, or bones.

## How Is Bladder Cancer Treated?

Treatment depends on how deep the cancer is in the bladder wall.

### For Nonmuscle-Invasive Cancer (Stage Ta, Tis, T1):
- The tumor is removed using a thin tool passed through the urethra (transurethral resection).
- The area is burned with electricity (fulguration).
- After surgery, medicine is put directly into the bladder (intravesical instillation).
  - This can be chemotherapy or immunotherapy.
- These treatments help prevent the cancer from coming back.

### For Muscle-Invasive Cancer (Stage T2 or higher):
- First, chemotherapy is given before surgery (neoadjuvant chemotherapy).
  - This uses a medicine called cisplatin-based chemo.
- Then, surgery is done to remove the entire bladder (radical cystectomy).
  - A new way to pass urine is created (urinary diversion).
- In some cases, radiation therapy and chemotherapy are used instead of surgery.

## Prognosis (Outlook)

- **Nonmuscle-invasive cancers**:
  - These often come back.
  - Low-grade and small tumors rarely cause death.
  - High-grade or larger tumors can grow deeper and become more serious.
  - Carcinoma in situ is aggressive and should be treated like a high-grade cancer.

- **Muscle-invasive cancer**:
  - About half of people live at least 5 years after diagnosis.
  - Neoadjuvant chemotherapy helps improve survival in some people.

- **Squamous cell and adenocarcinoma**:
  - These types are often found late and grow deeply.
  - The outlook is poor.

## Key Points

- Over 90% of bladder cancers are transitional (urothelial) cell carcinomas.
- Think of bladder cancer if you have blood in your urine, especially if you are a middle-aged or older man.
- Diagnosis is done with cystoscopy and biopsy. Imaging is used if the cancer is deep.
- Superficial cancers are removed through the urethra and treated with medicine in the bladder.
- If the cancer has grown into the muscle, treatment usually includes chemotherapy before surgery or radiation with chemotherapy.
- Early detection and treatment improve outcomes.

# Perichondritis

Perichondritis is an infection or swelling in the tissue that covers the cartilage of the outer ear. This outer ear is also called the pinna or auricle.

## What Can Cause Perichondritis?

- Injuries to the ear  
- Burns to the ear  
- Insect bites on the ear  
- Ear piercings that go through the cartilage  
- Ear surgery  
- A boil on the ear  
- Infections spreading from the surface of the outer ear  

Perichondritis is more likely to happen in people who have:

- Long-term inflammation in the body (such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis)  
- A weak immune system  
- Diabetes  

## Symptoms of Perichondritis

The first signs are:

- Redness on the ear  
- Pain in the ear  
- Swelling of the ear  
- Fever  

Pus builds up between the cartilage and the layer of tissue around it. This layer is called the perichondrium.  

If the pus stays trapped, it can cut off blood flow to the cartilage. Without blood, the cartilage can die. This can lead to a deformed ear. This shape is often called cauliflower ear.  

Perichondritis can cause serious damage. It can come back. It can last for a long time.

## Treatment of Perichondritis

Doctors treat perichondritis with:

- Antibiotics (medicine to fight infection)  
- Corticosteroids (medicine to reduce swelling)  
- Removal of foreign objects, like earrings or splinters  
- Warm compresses  
- Pain relief medicine  

### Antibiotics

Doctors prescribe antibiotics by mouth. One common type is ciprofloxacin. The right antibiotic depends on how bad the infection is and which bacteria are causing it.

### Removing Foreign Objects

If there is a piercing or a splinter in the ear, doctors will remove it.

### Draining Pus

If there is a collection of pus (called an abscess), doctors will make a small cut to drain it. This lets blood flow back to the cartilage. A small tube may stay in place for one to three days to keep the area draining.

### Healing the Ear

Doctors may sew the tissue around the cartilage back in place. This helps the ear heal properly and prevents a deformed shape.

### Pain Relief

Pain medicine is also given to help you feel better.

# Kawasaki Disease – Simple Explanation

Kawasaki disease is a serious illness that affects children. It causes inflammation in blood vessels, especially the ones that supply blood to the heart. It mostly happens in children between 1 and 5 years old.

This disease can lead to serious heart problems if not treated early. It is the most common cause of heart disease in children in the United States.

---

## What Causes Kawasaki Disease?

We do not know exactly what causes Kawasaki disease. But it may be linked to an infection that triggers a strong reaction in the body’s immune system. Some children may be more likely to get it because of their genes.

It is more common in children of Japanese or Korean descent. But it can happen in any child, anywhere in the world.

About 4,000 to 5,500 children in the United States get it each year. Boys are more likely than girls to get it. Most cases happen in children under 5 years old, with the highest number between 6 and 24 months.

The disease can happen at any time of year, but it is more common in spring and winter. It does not spread from one child to another.

There is no way to prevent it. About 2 out of every 100 children who get it may have it again, months or years later.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The illness happens in three stages: acute, subacute, and convalescent.

### Acute Phase (First 1–2 weeks)

- A high fever that lasts at least 5 days. The fever is usually over 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit (38.0 degrees Celsius).
- The child may be irritable, tired, or have belly pain.
- Red eyes that are not swollen or filled with pus.
- A rash that starts on the chest and back. It may look like hives, measles, or a sunburn. It often gets worse in the area around the bottom.
- Lips that are red, dry, or cracked. The tongue may look red and bumpy, like a strawberry.
- Swelling and redness in the hands and feet. The skin may feel tight and hard. The nails may turn white in the middle.
- Swollen lymph nodes in the neck. At least one node is at least 1.5 centimeters wide.

The fever ends when this stage ends.

### Subacute Phase (About Day 25)

- Skin peeling from the fingers, toes, palms, soles, and around the bottom. The skin may come off in large pieces.
- Joint pain or swelling in large joints like knees or elbows. This happens in about one-third of children.
- Blood tests show high platelets (a type of blood cell that helps clot). This happens in the second or third week.
- Heart problems may start now. These can include heart rhythm issues, heart muscle swelling, or fluid around the heart.

### Convalescent Phase (Weeks 6 to 8)

- All symptoms slowly go away.
- The child starts to feel better and return to normal.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose Kawasaki disease based on symptoms. The child must have a fever for at least 5 days and at least 4 of the following 5 signs:

1. Red eyes (no pus).
2. Changes in the lips, mouth, or tongue (red, dry, cracked, or strawberry-like).
3. Swelling or redness in the hands and feet, or peeling skin.
4. A rash on the body, especially the chest and back.
5. Swollen lymph nodes in the neck (at least one node is 1.5 cm or larger).

Some children, especially babies under 1 year, may not have all 4 signs. But they can still get serious heart problems. These children are said to have “atypical” or “incomplete” Kawasaki disease.

If a child has had a fever for 5 days and at least 2 of the 5 signs, doctors may still suspect Kawasaki disease and test for it.

### Tests That Are Done

- Blood tests to check for infection and inflammation.
- Urine test.
- Chest X-ray.
- Electrocardiogram (ECG) to check heart rhythm.
- Echocardiogram (ultrasound of the heart) to look for heart problems.

These tests help rule out other illnesses that can look like Kawasaki disease, such as:
- Scarlet fever
- Measles
- Staphylococcal infection
- Drug reactions
- Juvenile arthritis

A rare condition called MIS-C (multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children) can look like Kawasaki disease. It is linked to a past infection with the virus that causes COVID-19. Children with MIS-C often have more stomach pain, vomiting, and headaches than children with Kawasaki disease.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment must start as soon as possible, ideally within 10 days of the fever starting.

### Main Treatments

- **IV immune globulin (IVIG)**: A special medicine given through a vein. It helps calm the immune system. It is given in one dose over 10 to 12 hours.
- **High-dose aspirin**: Given by mouth. It helps reduce fever, swelling, and blood clots.

These treatments work best when started early. They help stop the illness from getting worse and lower the risk of heart damage.

### What Happens After the Fever Goes Down?

- The aspirin dose is lowered after the child has been fever-free for 4 to 5 days.
- Low-dose aspirin is continued for at least 8 weeks. This helps prevent blood clots.
- The child must have repeat heart tests (echocardiograms) to check for heart problems.

### When Is Aspirin Stopped?

- If the heart is normal and blood tests show no signs of inflammation, aspirin can be stopped after 8 weeks.
- If the child has heart problems, aspirin is continued for life.
- Children with large heart artery bulges (giant aneurysms) may need extra medicines to prevent blood clots. These include warfarin or other blood thinners.

### What If the Child Does Not Get Better?

Some children do not respond to the first treatment. They may still have a fever. In these cases, doctors may give:
- A second dose of IVIG
- Steroid medicine
- Infliximab (a medicine that reduces inflammation)

These treatments are done with help from a heart doctor and a specialist in childhood immune diseases.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

With proper treatment, most children get better completely.

- The chance of dying from Kawasaki disease is very low—about 1 in 600.
- Most deaths are due to heart problems, and they can happen suddenly.
- Without treatment, up to 20% of children develop heart artery bulges.
- With treatment, this drops to less than 5%.

### Long-Term Outlook

- About two-thirds of heart artery bulges go away within a year.
- Some may leave behind narrowed blood vessels. We do not yet know if this causes future heart problems.
- Giant heart artery bulges are less likely to go away. These children need regular heart checkups and special care.

---

## Key Points

- Kawasaki disease is a serious illness that causes blood vessel inflammation in children.
- It is the most common cause of heart disease in children.
- It causes fever, rash, red eyes, mouth changes, swollen hands and feet, and swollen neck glands.
- Some children have fewer symptoms but still get heart problems.
- Diagnosis is based on symptoms and heart tests.
- Early treatment with IVIG and high-dose aspirin helps stop the illness and prevents heart damage.
- Children need long-term heart follow-up, especially if they had heart artery problems.
- Most children recover fully if treated early.

# Behavioral Problems in Children – Simple Explanation

Children learn many skills as they grow. Some skills, like controlling when they pee or poop, depend on how mature their brain and nerves are. Other skills, like behaving well at home or school, come from a mix of physical health, thinking ability, emotions, personality, and how they get along with parents, caregivers, and teachers.

Some behaviors, like sucking a thumb, help children cope with stress. Other behaviors come from how parents raise their children.

When behaviors become too hard to manage, they can hurt a child’s relationships and slow down their emotional, social, and learning growth. Common examples include:

- Problems with eating
- Holding their breath until they turn blue (breath-holding spells)
- Not wanting to go to school
- Trouble sleeping
- Tantrums
- Aggressive or violent actions

Many of these behaviors are normal parts of growing up.

Some problems, like wetting the bed, are mild and go away on their own as the child gets older. Others, like those linked to attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, may need ongoing help.

---

## Behaviors That Come from Stress

Every child deals with stress in their own way. Some common stress responses are:

- Sucking a thumb or finger
- Biting nails
- Banging their head or rocking their body

### Thumb Sucking

Sucking a thumb or pacifier is normal in babies and young children. Most stop by age 1 or 2. Some keep it up into school age.

It’s okay for a child to suck their thumb when they are stressed. But if a child still does it after age 5, it can change the shape of the roof of the mouth and cause crooked teeth. It can also lead to teasing from other kids.

If a child keeps sucking their thumb past age 5, a doctor or mental health expert may need to check on it.

Most children stop on their own. Parents should only step in if the dentist says so or if the habit causes social problems.

To help a child stop, parents can:

- Gently explain why it’s better to stop
- Wait until the child shows they want to stop
- Use kind reminders, like putting a colored bandage or a star on the thumb
- Try a plastic guard or a safe bitter taste on the nail

But never force the child. These tools should only be used with the child’s agreement.

### Nail Biting and Picking

Biting or picking nails is common in young children. It often goes away as they grow older. It may be linked to stress or worry.

If a child wants to stop, they can learn to do something else instead, like twirling a pencil.

A reward system works well. Give small rewards when the child avoids biting or picking.

### Head Banging and Rocking

Head banging and body rocking are common in healthy babies and toddlers. It may look scary, but the child is not hurt and often seems calm or happy during it.

Most children stop these behaviors between 18 months and 2 years. But some older children and teens may still do them.

Children with autism or other brain development issues may also do these things. But they usually have other signs that make the condition clear.

These behaviors rarely cause injury. But to be safe:

- Move the crib away from the wall
- Remove wheels or add padding under the crib
- Put soft padding on the crib bars

---

## How Parenting Affects Behavior

Praise and rewards help children act well. But sometimes, parents only pay attention when a child misbehaves. This can make the bad behavior worse.

Most children would rather get attention for misbehavior than no attention at all. So, parents should set aside special time each day to enjoy fun, calm moments with their child.

This helps reduce bad behavior.

### Problems in the Parent-Child Relationship

Some parent-child problems start in the first few months of life. They can happen because of:

- A tough pregnancy or birth
- Trouble breastfeeding
- A parent feeling sad or low after the baby is born (postpartum depression)
- Stress between parents
- Not enough support from family or friends
- Money problems, job stress, or housing issues
- A parenting style that does not build a strong bond

The first months of parenting are hard. Babies do not sleep through the night until they are 3 to 4 months old. This can make parents feel tired and overwhelmed.

If the parent-child bond is weak, the child may not grow well mentally or socially. They may not gain weight or grow as they should.

A doctor or nurse can help. They can talk about the baby’s personality and offer tips for parenting. This helps parents feel better and set realistic goals.

Parents may feel guilty or conflicted. These feelings are normal. With support, they can rebuild a healthy relationship with their child.

If the bond stays weak, the child may have more problems later.

### Unrealistic Expectations

Parents sometimes think a child should act older than they are. For example, expecting a 2-year-old to clean up toys without help may seem like a behavior problem. But this is normal for that age.

Other normal 2-year-old behaviors, like saying “no” or not following rules, are not bad. They are part of learning independence.

### A Cycle of Bad Behavior

Sometimes, a child acts out because they are upset. The parent gets angry and yells or punishes the child. The child then acts worse. The parent yells more. This cycle keeps going.

This can happen when a child is stubborn, rude, or aggressive instead of crying. The parent responds with scolding, yelling, or spanking.

It can also happen when a child is scared or clingy. The parent then becomes too protective or too lenient.

This cycle can be broken by:

- Ignoring behavior that does not hurt others, like tantrums or refusing to eat
- Distracting the child with a fun activity
- Rewarding good behavior when it happens

For behavior that cannot be ignored, try:

- Distracting the child
- Using a time-out

---

## How to Discipline Children

Discipline is not just punishment. It means giving clear, fair, and age-appropriate rules. It helps children know what to expect.

It is easier and better for both parents and children to reward good behavior than to punish bad behavior.

Older children and teens may act out as they try to become more independent. They may test rules or avoid being watched.

Parents should learn to tell the difference between serious problems and normal mistakes.

---

## How to Help a Child Change Behavior

The goal is to help the child want to change. This takes consistent effort from parents. When parents change their actions, the child’s behavior often improves.

It is best to act early. The longer a behavior lasts, the harder it is to change.

Sometimes, parents only need reassurance that the behavior is normal. Or they may just need a few simple tips.

### Simple Tips for Parents

- Spend 15 to 20 minutes each day doing something fun with your child
- Notice and praise good behavior (“catch the child being good”)
- Spend time away from the child so they learn to be calm and independent

### Other Helpful Strategies

- Find out what triggers bad behavior
- Watch for things that accidentally reward bad behavior (like attention)
- Clearly say what behavior is okay and what is not
- Set consistent rules and limits
- Keep track of how well the child follows the rules
- Give rewards for good choices
- Give consequences for bad choices
- Focus on the behavior, not the child (“That was not okay” instead of “You are bad”)
- Stay calm when enforcing rules
- Spend more time doing positive things together

Experts recommend healthy discipline methods, such as:

- Praising good behavior
- Setting clear limits
- Redirecting the child to a better activity
- Planning for the future

They do **not** recommend:

- Spanking
- Hitting
- Slapping
- Threatening
- Insulting
- Humiliating
- Shaming

If a behavior does not improve in 3 to 4 months, a doctor may suggest seeing a mental health professional.

---

## Time-Out: A Simple Tool

Time-out works best when the child knows their behavior was wrong. It also works when the child sees not getting attention as a punishment.

Most children understand this by age 2.

### How to Use Time-Out

- Choose a quiet, simple place with no toys, TV, or screens
- Do not use the child’s bedroom
- The place should not be dark or scary

Use time-out when the child misbehaves in a way that leads to time-out.

Before starting:

- Briefly explain what the child did wrong
- Tell them to go to the time-out spot
- If needed, gently guide them there

Time in time-out:

- Stay for 1 minute for each year of age (maximum 5 minutes)
- The child must stay on their own. Do not force them
- Do not use physical restraint

If the child gets up early:

- Bring them back to the spot
- Restart the timer
- Do not talk or make eye contact

When time is up:

- Ask the child why they were in time-out
- If they forget, remind them briefly
- Do not make them say sorry unless they understand

After time-out:

- Immediately praise good behavior
- Help the child move to a new activity far from the problem area

### What If the Child Gets Worse During Time-Out?

If the child acts out more during time-out:

- Calmly explain why time-out was used
- Say you want to give attention for good behavior, not bad
- Redirect to a better activity

# Fourth Cranial Nerve Palsy

This condition affects a nerve that controls one of the eye muscles. The muscle involved is called the superior oblique. When this nerve is damaged, the muscle does not work well. This makes it hard to move the eye up and down, especially when looking inward.

Most of the time, doctors do not know the exact cause. This is called idiopathic. But some known causes include:

- A head injury, even if it was not serious. This can affect one or both eyes.
- A small blood vessel blockage, often in people with diabetes.

Rarely, the cause is something more serious, such as:
- A bulging blood vessel (aneurysm)
- A tumor in the brain (like a tentorial meningioma or pinealoma)
- Multiple sclerosis

Some people are born with this problem. It may appear as a misaligned eye from birth.

The condition can affect one eye or both eyes. When the superior oblique muscle is weak, the eye cannot turn inward properly. This causes double vision. One image appears above and slightly to the side of the other. This makes tasks like going down stairs very hard, because you need to look down and inward.

Tilting your head to the side opposite the weak eye can help. This position reduces or removes the double vision.

During an exam, the doctor may find only small problems with eye movement. These may not be easy to see, but they cause symptoms. To find the cause, the doctor may order a CT scan or an MRI.

## How Is It Treated?

There are a few treatment options:

- Eye exercises to help improve eye movement and coordination.
- Special glasses with prisms. These help align the images so you see clearly.
- Surgery, if the problem does not get better on its own.

Eye exercises or prism glasses may help you see clearly again. If the weakness does not improve over time, surgery may be needed to fix the eye alignment.

# Mental Health in Teens

Mental health affects how you feel, think, and act every day.  
It helps you handle stress, get along with others, and make good choices.  
Good mental health is important at every age, including during the teen years.

Mental health problems happen when someone feels, thinks, or acts in ways that cause trouble.  
These problems are more common in teens than at any other time in childhood.  
Doctors and nurses check teens for these issues during regular health visits.

If a teen has a mental health problem, a doctor will give clear advice.  
If needed, the teen may be referred to a mental health specialist for help.

---

## Common Mental Health Issues in Teens

### Depression
Many teens feel sad or worried at times.  
These feelings are normal and usually pass.  
But if sadness lasts a long time and starts to hurt school, friendships, or home life, it may be depression.  
Doctors can help with treatment, which may include medicine or therapy.  
The pandemic made things harder for many teens.  
This led to more cases of sadness and worry.

### Anxiety
Feeling nervous or afraid is common in teens.  
But if anxiety gets in the way of daily life, it may be a disorder.  
Treatment can help.  
This may include talking with a therapist or taking medicine.

### Suicide
Suicide is the third most common cause of death in teens aged 14 to 18.  
Some teens have thoughts about ending their life.  
These thoughts are called suicidal thoughts.  
If a teen talks about suicide, get help right away.  
Parents should not try to judge how serious the situation is.  
A mental health professional must evaluate the teen.

### Mood and Behavior Problems
Teens may develop mood disorders like bipolar disorder.  
They may also have behavior problems such as oppositional defiant disorder or conduct disorder.  
Therapy is the main treatment.  
Parents are also given support and advice.

### Physical Symptoms
Teens with anxiety or mood disorders may feel tired all the time.  
They may have dizziness, headaches, stomach pain, or chest pain.  
These physical symptoms are real and can be part of a mental health issue.

### Eating Disorders
Eating disorders are common in girls but can also happen in boys.  
They can be very serious and even life-threatening.  
Teens often hide their behaviors and changes in weight.  
Treatment works best when a team of experts is involved.  
This team includes mental health professionals.

### Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
ADHD is the most common mental health issue in children.  
It often continues into the teen years and adulthood.  
But teens who have trouble focusing may actually have depression or a learning problem.  
ADHD is often treated with stimulant medicine like amphetamine or methylphenidate.  
These medicines do not increase the risk of drug abuse.  
In fact, they may lower the risk.  
Some teens pretend to have ADHD to get medicine.  
They may use it to study better or for fun.  
This is not safe and can cause harm.

### Thought Disorders (Psychosis)
Some teens have trouble telling the difference between real events and imagination.  
This is called psychosis.  
It often starts in the teen years or early adulthood.  
Examples include schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder.  
The first time a teen has psychosis is called a psychotic break.  
Substance use, especially cannabis (marijuana), can trigger psychosis.  
Edible forms of cannabis are especially risky.  
Some teens who have a psychotic episode from cannabis go on to have long-term mental health issues.  
Treatment includes medicine and therapy.

---

## Social Media and Mental Health

Social media has changed how teens talk to each other and learn.  
For some, it is a place to be creative and connect with friends.  
For teens who are LGBTQIA, social media can be a safe space.  
It helps them find support and connect with others like them.  

But too much time on social media is linked to poor mental health.  
This may be because it takes time away from sleep, school, exercise, and real-life friendships.  
Spending too much time online can make teens feel worse over time.

If you or someone you know is struggling, help is available.

This service offers free, private support for teens in crisis.  
You can call or text 988 to talk to someone who can help.  
This is a safe and confidential way to get support.

# How the Thyroid Gland Works

## The Thyroid Gland and Its Hormones

The thyroid gland sits in the front of your neck, just below the voice box.  
It has two sides connected by a thin bridge.  

The gland makes two main hormones:  
- Tetraiodothyronine (also called thyroxine or T4)  
- Triiodothyronine (also called T3)  

These hormones travel through your blood to every part of your body.  
They enter your cells and affect how your body uses energy.  

Thyroid hormones are very important for brain and body growth in babies and young children.  
They also help your body use proteins, sugars, and fats for energy at all ages.  

T4 has very little effect on your body.  
But it stays in your blood for a long time—about 8 days.  
This makes it a storage form for T3.  

Most of the T4 in your body turns into T3.  
T3 is the active hormone that your cells use.  
Some T4 also turns into a form called reverse T3.  
This form does not do anything in your body.  
Reverse T3 levels go up in some illnesses.  

Another type of cell in the thyroid makes a hormone called calcitonin.  
This hormone is released when your blood calcium is too high.  
It helps lower calcium levels in your blood.  

## How the Thyroid Makes and Releases Hormones

To make thyroid hormones, your body needs iodine.  
You get iodine from food and water.  

Your thyroid takes up iodine from your blood.  
It turns iodine into a form that can be used in hormone-making.  
This process happens inside special cells in the thyroid.  

These cells surround a space filled with a thick fluid called colloid.  
The colloid contains a large protein called thyroglobulin.  
This protein holds many building blocks called tyrosine.  

Iodine attaches to tyrosine in the colloid.  
One iodine makes monoiodotyrosine.  
Two iodines make diiodotyrosine.  

Then, two iodinated tyrosine molecules join together:  
- Two diiodotyrosine molecules make T4  
- One diiodotyrosine and one monoiodotyrosine make T3  

T3 and T4 stay inside the colloid until the thyroid cells take them back in.  
Once inside the cells, the hormones are cut free from the thyroglobulin.  

Free T3 and free T4 are then released into your bloodstream.  
They travel through your blood attached to proteins.  

The main protein that carries them is called thyroxine-binding globulin.  
It binds tightly to T3 and T4, but there is not much of it.  
It carries about 75% of the thyroid hormones in your blood.  

Other proteins also carry thyroid hormones:  
- Thyroxine-binding prealbumin (also called transthyretin) binds tightly to T4, but there is not much of it.  
- Albumin binds weakly to T3 and T4, but there is a lot of it.  

Only a tiny amount of thyroid hormones is free in your blood:  
- About 0.3% of T3 is free  
- About 0.03% of T4 is free  

Only the free hormones can enter your cells and do their job.  

All steps in making and releasing T3 and T4 are controlled by a hormone called TSH.  
TSH is made by the pituitary gland in your brain.  

The pituitary gland listens to your blood levels of free T3 and T4.  
If these levels are high, the pituitary makes less TSH.  
If levels are low, the pituitary makes more TSH.  

This is called a feedback loop.  
It keeps your thyroid hormones at a healthy level.  

TSH is also influenced by another brain hormone called TRH.  
TRH is made in the part of your brain that controls hormones.  
We do not fully understand how TRH is made and released.  
But we know that high thyroid hormone levels can reduce TRH production.  

Most of the T3 in your blood is made outside the thyroid.  
It comes from T4 being changed in other tissues.  
Only about 1 in 5 of the T3 in your blood comes directly from the thyroid.  

## Testing Thyroid Function

### Checking for Thyroid Problems

In many places, all newborn babies are tested for thyroid problems.  
This is to find congenital hypothyroidism.  
If not treated, this condition can harm brain and body development.  

For healthy adults with no symptoms, routine testing is not needed.  
This includes pregnant women who have no known risk factors.  
There is not enough proof that testing helps in these cases.  

If you have risk factors for thyroid disease, your doctor may test your TSH level.  
This test is the best way to check for both overactive and underactive thyroid.  

In older adults, TSH levels often go up with age.  
Some experts suggest testing every year after age 70.  
But higher TSH does not always mean disease.  
Treating older adults with slightly high TSH may do more harm than good.  
In some cases, treatment leads to over-treatment.  
This may happen in up to 40% of people.  
So, it is not clear if treating mild thyroid changes in older adults helps.  

### Radioactive Iodine Tests and Imaging

A test can measure how much iodine your thyroid takes up.  
You swallow a small amount of radioactive iodine or get it through a vein.  
A scanner then measures how much of the iodine your thyroid absorbs.  

The best type of radioactive iodine for this test is iodine-123.  
It gives a clear picture and exposes you to very little radiation.  
This is much safer than iodine-131.  

Your iodine intake affects the test result.  
If you eat too much iodine, your thyroid may take up less.  

This test helps doctors tell the difference between types of overactive thyroid:  
- In Graves’ disease, the thyroid takes up a lot of iodine.  
- In thyroiditis, the thyroid takes up little iodine.  

The test can also help plan treatment with iodine-131 for overactive thyroid.  

Imaging can be done after giving a radioactive substance.  
This can be iodine-123 or a different substance called technetium 99m pertechnetate.  
A special camera makes a picture of how the thyroid takes up the substance.  

Areas that take up more than normal are called "hot" spots.  
Areas that take up less are called "cold" spots.  

Most hot nodules are not cancer.  
But cold nodules have a higher chance of being cancer.  
About 1 in 10 to 20 cold nodules may be cancer.  
Hot nodules are almost never cancer.

# Urethral Cancer

Cancer of the urethra is rare.  
It usually happens in people over the age of fifty.  
It can affect both men and women.  
It is the only cancer of the urinary system that is more common in women.

Some types of human papillomavirus can cause urethral cancer in certain people.  
In most cases, the cause is not known.

## Symptoms

In women, the first sign is often blood in the urine.  
The blood may be so small that you cannot see it.  
A lab test is needed to find it.  
In other cases, the urine may look red.  

In both men and women, the flow of urine may slow down.  
Urinating may become hard or painful.  
Some women may notice a small growth near the opening of the urethra.  
This growth may bleed easily and could be cancer.

## Diagnosis

Doctors use a thin tube with a camera to look inside the urethra.  
This test is called cystourethroscopy.  
A small sample of tissue is taken during the test.  
This sample is checked under a microscope to confirm cancer.

## Treatment

Treatment options include:  
- Radiation therapy  
- Surgery to remove the urethra  
- Surgery to remove the urethra and bladder  
- A mix of radiation and surgery  

The outcome depends on where the cancer is and how far it has spread.

# Skin Vessel Problems

Skin vessel problems are changes in the blood vessels under the skin. They can appear at birth or later in life.

## Types of Skin Vessel Problems

### Problems That Appear Later in Life
Some skin vessel problems develop after birth. These include:
- **Pyogenic granuloma**: A small, red bump that bleeds easily. It often appears on the skin or gums.
- **Spider angioma**: A small red spot with thin lines spreading out like a spider’s legs. It often shows up on the face or chest.
- **Cherry angioma**: A small, bright red spot that grows larger over time. It is common in adults.

### Problems Present at Birth
Some skin vessel problems are present when a baby is born. These are called vascular birthmarks.

### Types of Vascular Birthmarks
Vascular birthmarks are either:
- **Vascular tumors**: These grow quickly at first, then slow down and may go away on their own. An example is infantile hemangioma.
- **Vascular malformations**: These are not tumors. They are present at birth and do not go away. They grow as the child grows.

### What Are Vascular Malformations?
Vascular malformations are birth defects in how blood vessels form. They last a lifetime and stay in one place. Types include:
- **Capillary malformations**: Red or pink patches on the skin. A common example is nevus flammeus (also called a port-wine stain).
- **Venous malformations**: Soft, blue or purple lumps under the skin. They may get bigger when the person is active or lying down.
- **Arteriovenous malformations**: Abnormal connections between arteries and veins. These can cause a pulsing lump. A type is called a cirsoid aneurysm.
- **Lymphatic malformations**: Fluid-filled sacs under the skin. They can feel soft and may grow over time.

# Tapeworm Infection

Tapeworms are parasites that live in the intestines. They can make you sick. You usually get them by eating raw or undercooked meat or fish. You can also get them from food or water that has been touched by human stool.

## Types of Tapeworms

There are several types of tapeworms that can infect people:

- **Beef tapeworm** – found in undercooked beef
- **Pork tapeworm** – found in undercooked pork
- **Asian tapeworm** – found in pork in Asia
- **Fish tapeworm** – found in raw or undercooked freshwater fish
- **Dwarf tapeworm** – very small; found in food or water with human stool

Dogs can carry other tapeworms. These can also infect people and cause cysts in the liver or other organs.

## How Tapeworms Work

Tapeworms have three parts:

- The **head** attaches to the inside of the intestine.
- The **neck** can grow new parts.
- The **body** is made of many segments. Each segment can hold eggs.

If the head and neck are not removed, the worm can grow back.

## How You Get Infected

### Pork, Beef, and Fish Tapeworms

1. You eat raw or undercooked meat or fish that has tiny cysts in it.
2. The cysts break open in your intestine.
3. The tapeworm grows and attaches to the wall of your intestine.
4. It starts making new segments with eggs.
5. The segments or eggs come out in your stool.
6. If pigs, cows, or fish eat the eggs, the eggs turn into larvae in their bodies.
7. The cycle starts again when someone eats the infected meat or fish.

### Dwarf Tapeworm

- You swallow the eggs, not cysts.
- The eggs come from human stool.
- You can get them from food, water, or by touching something that has been contaminated.
- You can also get them from eating insects like fleas or beetles in grain.
- The eggs grow into adult worms in your intestine.
- The worms lay eggs that come out in your stool.
- If you swallow the eggs again, you can get a new infection without ever leaving your body. This is called autoinfection.

## What Happens in the Body

### Intestinal Infection

Most people with adult tapeworms in their intestines feel fine. But some may have:

- Belly pain
- Diarrhea
- Weight loss
- Feeling a piece of worm come out of the anus
- Seeing a ribbon-like worm in the stool

The dwarf tapeworm is more likely to cause nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite.

The fish tapeworm can cause anemia. It takes vitamin B12 from your body. This vitamin is needed to make healthy blood cells.

### Cysticercosis

This happens when pork tapeworm eggs get into your body and form cysts in your brain, muscles, or other organs.

You can get cysticercosis if:

- You eat food or water with pork tapeworm eggs
- You touch something with the eggs and then touch your mouth
- You swallow eggs from your own stool (autoinfection)

The eggs hatch in your intestine. The larvae travel through your blood to your brain, muscles, liver, lungs, or skin. There, they form cysts.

Cysts in the brain can cause:

- Headaches
- Seizures
- Confusion
- Other brain problems

Cysts in the eyes can cause blindness. Cysts in the spinal cord can cause muscle weakness or paralysis.

Symptoms may not show up for years. They appear when the cysts start to break down and cause swelling.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

### For Intestinal Infection

- A doctor checks your stool for worm segments or eggs.

### For Cysticercosis

- A CT scan or MRI can show cysts in the brain or other parts of the body.
- Blood tests can check for antibodies. These are proteins your body makes to fight infections.
- Sometimes, hard lumps under the skin can be felt.

## How It Is Treated

### Intestinal Infection

- A single dose of medicine called praziquantel kills the worm.
- For dwarf tapeworm, another medicine called nitazoxanide may be used.

### Cysticercosis

- If cysts are in the brain, treatment depends on symptoms and where the cysts are.
- Corticosteroids (like prednisone) reduce swelling and inflammation.
- Antiseizure medicines are used if you have seizures.
- Antiparasitic medicines (like albendazole or praziquantel) can kill living cysts in the brain.
- But these medicines are only used after symptoms are under control.
- Corticosteroids are also given with antiparasitic drugs to prevent bad reactions from dying cysts.
- These medicines are not used for cysts in the eye or spinal cord. They can cause serious swelling and damage.

Surgery may be needed if:

- Cysts block the flow of fluid around the brain or spinal cord
- Cysts cause serious problems in the eye or spinal cord

## How to Prevent Tapeworm Infection

### Cook Meat and Fish Thoroughly

- Cook whole cuts of meat to over 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63 degrees Celsius) for at least 3 minutes.
- Let the meat rest for 3 minutes after cooking before eating.
- Cook ground meat to at least 160 degrees Fahrenheit (71 degrees Celsius).
- Do not use a rest period for ground meat.

### Cook or Freeze Freshwater Fish

- Never eat freshwater fish raw (like sushi).
- Cook it to 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63 degrees Celsius).
- Or freeze it properly to kill the parasite.

**Freezing methods that work:**

- At -4 degrees Fahrenheit (-20 degrees Celsius) or colder for 7 days
- At -31 degrees Fahrenheit (-35 degrees Celsius) or colder until solid, then keep at that temperature for 15 hours
- At -31 degrees Fahrenheit (-35 degrees Celsius) or colder until solid, then keep at -4 degrees Fahrenheit (-20 degrees Celsius) or colder for 24 hours

Smoking and drying do not kill the tapeworm.

### Check Meat and Fish

- Trained inspectors can find cysts in meat.
- Cysts are visible in infected meat.

### Handle Waste Carefully

- Treat human waste properly.
- This breaks the cycle of infection and helps stop beef and pork tapeworms from spreading.

### Avoid Contaminated Food and Water

- Wash, peel, or cook all raw fruits and vegetables before eating.
- Use safe water when traveling.
- Wash your hands with soap and warm water after using the toilet, changing diapers, or before handling food.

These steps can help you avoid getting tapeworms.

# How Doctors Diagnose Infections

Infections are caused by tiny living things like bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites.

Doctors look at your symptoms, do a physical exam, and consider your risk factors to decide if you have an infection.

First, they must figure out if your symptoms are due to an infection or another health problem.

For example, a cough and trouble breathing could mean pneumonia. But it could also mean asthma or heart failure. A chest x-ray can help doctors tell the difference.

Once they confirm an infection, doctors need to find out which specific germ is causing it.

Many different germs can cause the same illness. For example, pneumonia can be caused by viruses, bacteria, or, rarely, fungi.

The treatment depends on the germ. So it is important to know exactly which one is causing the problem.

There are many types of lab tests to find germs. These tests use samples from your body, such as blood, urine, sputum, or tissue.

The lab may:

- Use special dyes to color the sample and look at it under a microscope  
- Grow the germ in a lab dish or tube (this is called culturing)  
- Test for antibodies your body made to fight the germ  
- Test for antigens, which are parts of the germ that trigger your immune system  
- Look for the germ’s genetic material, like DNA or RNA  

No single test can find every germ. Some tests work well for one germ but not for another.

Doctors choose the best test based on which germs they think are most likely.

Sometimes, doctors do several tests in a certain order. Each test helps narrow down the possibilities.

If the right test is not done, doctors might miss the cause of the infection.

Once the germ is found, doctors can test which medicines will work best against it. This helps them start the right treatment faster.

---

## Where the Lab Gets the Sample

The lab takes a sample from the part of your body that likely has the germ.

Common samples include:

- Blood  
- Sputum (mucus from deep in the lungs)  
- Urine  
- Stool (bowel movement)  
- Tissue (a small piece of skin or organ)  
- Cerebrospinal fluid (fluid around the brain and spinal cord)  
- Mucus from the nose, throat, or genital area  

Some samples, like sputum, stool, and mucus, normally have many harmless bacteria. Doctors must tell the difference between harmless bacteria and the ones causing your illness.

Other samples, like blood, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid, should not have any germs. If germs are found in these samples, it is a sign of infection.

But only if the skin was cleaned well before the sample was taken. Otherwise, germs from the skin could get into the sample and give a false result.

---

## Looking at the Sample Under a Microscope

Sometimes, doctors can see the germ just by looking at the sample under a microscope.

Most samples are treated with special dyes (stains) to make the germs stand out.

Some germs have a unique size, shape, and color when stained. This helps doctors identify them.

But many germs look very similar under a microscope. So they cannot always be told apart.

Also, there must be enough germs, and they must be big enough to see. Viruses are too small to see with a regular microscope.

For bacteria, doctors often use a stain called Gram stain.

- **Gram-positive bacteria** turn blue  
- **Gram-negative bacteria** turn red  

This helps doctors pick the right antibiotic. Gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria respond to different types of antibiotics.

Other stains can be used depending on the germ doctors suspect. Fungi can also be stained.

---

## Growing the Germ in the Lab (Culture)

Many samples have too few germs to see or test. So doctors try to grow the germ in the lab until there are enough to study.

This process is called culture.

The sample is placed on a sterile dish or in a tube with food that helps germs grow.

Different foods are used depending on which germ is suspected.

Doctors may add substances to stop unwanted germs from growing.

Many germs, like those that cause urinary tract infections or strep throat, grow easily in culture.

Some germs, like the one that causes syphilis, cannot be grown at all.

Others, like the bacteria that cause tuberculosis, can be grown but take weeks.

Some viruses can be grown, but many cannot.

After the germ grows, doctors test it to identify it and see which medicines will work.

---

## Testing How Well Medicines Work Against the Germ

Doctors know which medicines usually work against certain germs. But germs can become resistant to medicines over time.

So doctors test the germ to see which medicines work best.

This is called susceptibility testing.

They use a culture to grow the germ. Then they add different medicines to see which ones kill the germ.

They also test how sensitive the germ is to a medicine.

This tells them if a small or large amount of medicine is needed to kill the germ.

If a large amount is needed, doctors usually do not use that medicine.

Sometimes, doctors use genetic testing to find genes that make the germ resistant to certain medicines.

For example, MRSA (a type of staph infection) can be found by testing for a gene called *mecA*.

But lab results do not always match what happens in your body.

Your body’s response to medicine depends on:

- How strong your immune system is  
- Your age  
- Other health problems you may have  
- How your body absorbs and processes the medicine  

---

## Testing for Antibodies or Antigens

Some germs, like the one that causes syphilis, cannot be grown in the lab.

For these, doctors use special tests called immunologic tests.

These tests look for:

- Antibodies  
- Antigens  

### Antibody Tests

Antibodies are proteins your body makes to fight infection.

They are made by white blood cells when they meet a germ.

It takes several days to weeks for your body to make enough antibodies to be detected.

Antibodies are made for a specific germ. So if you have antibodies to a germ, you have been exposed to it.

But antibodies can stay in your blood long after the infection is gone.

So finding antibodies does not always mean you are still infected.

Doctors may test for several antibodies, depending on what they suspect.

They often check how much antibody is in your blood.

To do this, they dilute your blood sample in half many times until the test no longer shows antibodies.

The more times they can dilute it and still get a positive result, the more antibodies were in your blood.

Because it takes time to make antibodies, early tests may be negative.

So doctors may take a sample right after you get sick and then another one weeks later.

If the antibody level goes up between the two tests, it means you have a current or recent infection.

---

### Antigen Tests

Antigens are parts of a germ that trigger your immune system.

Every germ has unique antigens on its surface or inside.

If a test finds a specific antigen, it means that germ is present.

Antigen tests find the germ directly. So doctors can diagnose an infection quickly.

They do not have to wait for your body to make antibodies.

These tests are also useful for people whose immune system is weak, such as those who had a bone marrow transplant or have advanced HIV.

To do an antigen test, doctors mix your sample with a special antibody that targets the suspected germ.

If the germ is in your sample, its antigens will stick to the test antibody.

Different methods can detect this match.

If the test is positive, the germ is likely causing your illness.

---

## Testing for the Germ’s Genetic Material

Tests that look for a germ’s genetic material are called nucleic acid–based tests.

These tests are used when a germ is hard to grow or identify by other methods.

Genetic material includes DNA or RNA.

Each germ has unique pieces of DNA or RNA.

Finding these pieces means the germ is present.

One common test is called PCR. It makes many copies of a gene from the germ. This makes it easier to find.

Each genetic test is for only one specific germ.

For example, a test for hepatitis C virus will only detect that virus.

These tests are only done when doctors already suspect a certain infection.

Most of these tests only check if the germ is present (qualitative testing).

But for some infections, like HIV and hepatitis C, doctors can also measure how much genetic material is in your body (quantitative testing).

This helps them know how serious the infection is.

It also helps track how well treatment is working.

Some genetic tests can check for genes that make a germ resistant to medicine.

But these tests are not perfect.

Not all resistance genes are known.

So the test might miss some resistance.

These tests are also expensive and not available everywhere.

They are only used for a few types of germs.

---

## Other Tests to Identify Germs

Some tests look at other features of germs that are not related to their genetic material.

These are called non-nucleic acid–based identification tests.

For example, doctors may test:

- What food the germ can grow on or grows best in  
- What enzymes the germ makes (enzymes help the germ infect cells or spread)  
- Other substances in the germ, like proteins or fatty acids  

These tests help doctors identify the germ more precisely.

# Problems with Blood Clotting

Blood that does not stop flowing when it should can be a sign of a problem. This can happen if:

- Your blood clotting system is not working right.
- Your platelets are not working well.
- Your blood vessels are damaged.

Some clotting problems are passed down in families. Others develop later in life.

## Causes of Clotting Problems That Develop Later in Life

The most common reasons for clotting problems that develop later in life are:

- The body makes substances that stop blood from clotting.
- A serious condition called disseminated intravascular coagulation, or DIC.
- Liver disease.
- Not getting enough vitamin K.

When the liver is very damaged, it can no longer make the proteins needed to form blood clots. All of these clotting proteins are made in the liver. When the liver is not working well, two blood tests — the prothrombin time and the partial thromboplastin time — will show longer times. This means blood is taking longer to clot.

In some cases, very bad liver disease can also cause too much breakdown of clots. This happens because the liver does not make enough of a protein called alpha 2-antiplasmin, which normally helps stop clots from breaking down too soon.

## Inherited Clotting Problems

The most common inherited problem with blood clotting is:

- von Willebrand disease

The most common inherited clotting disorders are:

- Hemophilia A and hemophilia B

## Testing for Clotting Problems

If a clotting problem is suspected, your doctor will order lab tests. The first tests usually include:

- Prothrombin time (PT)
- Partial thromboplastin time (PTT)
- Complete blood count (CBC) with platelet count
- A blood smear to look at blood cells under a microscope

These tests help narrow down what might be wrong. They also help guide any further testing that may be needed.

# Understanding Skin Reactions from the Immune System

Your body’s immune system helps protect you from harmful invaders like germs, foreign substances, and cancer cells.  
It does this by causing inflammation to fight off the threat.  
This response usually helps your body heal.  

But sometimes, the immune system overreacts.  
It may attack healthy tissues by mistake.  
This can cause strong inflammation and damage to the body.  
These unusual immune responses are called hypersensitivity reactions.  
Some of these reactions are known as allergies.  
Allergies happen when the body reacts strongly to something that is usually harmless.

## Skin Problems from Immune System Reactions

The skin can be affected by these immune system reactions.  
This can lead to several types of skin disorders, including:

- Drug rashes  
- Erythema multiforme  
- Erythema nodosum  
- Granuloma annulare  
- Panniculitis  
- Pyoderma gangrenosum  
- Stevens-Johnson syndrome  
- Toxic epidermal necrolysis  

The skin may change in color or texture.  
A rash means the skin looks red, swollen, or has bumps.  
Many rashes cause itching.  
This often happens after an allergic reaction.  
But some rashes hurt instead of itch.  
Others do not cause any feeling at all.

### What Triggers These Skin Reactions?

An immune reaction can be set off by:

- An infection  
- Something you touch or eat  
- A medicine you take  
- A drug you use illegally  

But in many cases, doctors do not know what causes the reaction.

Some rashes are more common in children.  
Others almost always happen in adults.

## Not All Skin Problems Come from the Immune System

Some skin issues are not caused by the immune system.  
They happen when something directly harms the skin.  
These things can cause itching or a rash, such as:

- Certain chemicals  
- Ingredients in lotions or makeup  
- Some medicines or illegal drugs  
- Body fluids like sweat or urine  
- Sunlight (ultraviolet light)  
- Heat or cold  
- Rubbing or friction  

## How Doctors Diagnose These Skin Problems

Doctors often start by looking at the rash.  
The way the rash looks can help them make a diagnosis.  

Blood tests are not usually helpful.  
They rarely show what caused the rash.  

If the rash does not go away or gets worse, the doctor may do a skin biopsy.  
This means they take a small sample of the skin with a blade.  
They then look at it under a microscope to check for signs of disease.

## How These Skin Problems Are Treated

Treatment depends on what is causing the rash.

If a medicine is the cause, stopping it may be enough.  
Avoiding a known irritant can also help.

If an infection is involved, treatment depends on the type:

- Bacterial infections are treated with antibiotics.  
- Viral infections may be treated with antiviral medicines.

Other treatments can help with symptoms:

- Creams or ointments applied to the skin can reduce itching or swelling.  
- Pills taken by mouth, like antihistamines, can help with itching.

For more serious skin reactions, doctors may use:

- Corticosteroids to reduce swelling and inflammation.  
- Immunosuppressants to calm down an overactive immune system.  

These medicines help the body stop attacking itself.

# Ureteral Anomalies

Ureteral anomalies often happen with kidney problems. But they can also happen on their own.

## Possible Problems

These issues can cause:
- Blockage in the tube that carries urine from the kidney to the bladder
- Backflow of urine from the bladder to the kidney
- Urinary tract infections
- Kidney stones (from urine building up)
- Incontinence (leaking urine) if the ureter opens in the wrong place

## How Doctors Find These Problems

Doctors may see signs of a problem before birth. A routine ultrasound during pregnancy can show swelling in the baby’s kidneys or urinary system.

After birth, a doctor might find a problem during a physical exam. For example:
- A visible lump in the belly
- A ureter opening in the wrong place (like in the vagina or near the opening of the penis)

Doctors also look for these signs in children:
- A kidney infection (pyelonephritis)
- Repeated urinary tract infections
- Girls who keep leaking urine
- Boys who keep getting infections in the testicles (orchitis)

To check for these problems, doctors use:
- Ultrasound of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder before and after urinating
- A special X-ray test called voiding cystourethrogram
- Sometimes, an MRI scan to see the ureter and kidney more clearly

## Treatment

Most ureteral anomalies need surgery. The type of surgery depends on the problem.

---

## Ectopic Ureteral Orifices

A ureter can open in the wrong place. This can happen with one ureter or two. The opening may be:
- On the side wall of the bladder
- Near the bottom of the bladder
- In the bladder neck
- In the female urethra, past the muscle that controls urine flow (this causes constant leaking)
- In the reproductive organs (prostate or seminal vesicles in boys, uterus or vagina in girls)
- Outside the body

If the opening is on the side, it often causes backflow of urine. If it is lower down, it often causes blockage and leaking.

Surgery is needed if there is blockage or leaking. Sometimes surgery is also needed for backflow.

---

## Retrocaval Ureter

Sometimes the large vein in the belly (the vena cava) forms in a way that causes the ureter to pass behind it. This usually happens on the right side. It can also happen on the left side if the baby’s blood vessels developed differently.

This can block the flow of urine. If the blockage is serious, surgery is needed.

The surgery involves cutting the ureter and reconnecting it in front of the vein or pelvic blood vessel.

---

## Ureter Duplication Anomalies

One or both ureters can be split into two tubes. This can happen with the kidney’s collection system also splitting.

In complete duplication:
- The upper part of the kidney sends urine through a ureter that opens lower in the bladder
- The lower part of the kidney tends to send urine backward
- The upper part tends to get blocked when there is a problem

Other issues can happen:
- One or both openings are too narrow
- Backflow of urine into the lower ureter
- A small balloon-like swelling (ureterocele)

Surgery may be needed if there is blockage, backflow, or leaking.

Incomplete duplication rarely causes problems.

---

## Ureteral Stenosis

The ureter can become narrow at any point. The most common places are:
- Where the ureter meets the kidney (ureteropelvic junction)
- Where the ureter meets the bladder (ureterovesical junction)

This narrowing can cause:
- Infection
- Blood in the urine
- Blockage

In many children, the narrowing gets better as they grow.

If the ureter is very wide and causes problems, surgery may be needed. This can include:
- Reshaping the ureter and reattaching it
- Repairing the area where the ureter meets the kidney

Surgery can be done through open surgery, laparoscopy, or robotic tools.

---

## Ureterocele

A ureterocele is when the end of the ureter bulges into the bladder. This can block urine flow.

This can lead to:
- Swelling of the ureter
- Swelling of the kidney
- Infection
- Kidney stones (rarely)
- Poor kidney function

Treatment options:
- A small cut through the urethra to open the blocked area
- Open surgery to fix the problem

If the ureterocele is in the upper part of a duplicated ureter, the doctor checks how well that part of the kidney works. If it is not working well or is badly formed, removing that part of the kidney and ureter may be better than trying to fix the blockage.

Another option is to connect the ureter to the other ureter so urine can go around the blockage.

In rare cases, the ureterocele pushes out past the bladder opening. This can block urine from leaving the bladder. In girls, this may look like a small lump between the labia.

# Preparing for a Limb Prosthesis

Losing a limb is hard. It affects your body and how you see yourself. Doctors want you and your family to understand what is happening. They explain why the surgery is needed. They also explain what will happen before, during, and after the surgery. They talk about the steps to get a prosthesis. People who know what to expect and understand the challenges are more likely to stay strong and do well. Doctors and prosthetists often connect you with someone who has had an amputation and has adjusted well.

## Before the Surgery

Before surgery, your surgeon, prosthetist, and physical therapist meet with you. They talk about your goals and what is realistic. They create a plan for your recovery. This includes:

- A check of your current abilities and what you want to do
- A plan for before surgery
- A plan for after surgery

The better your health before surgery, the better your recovery will be. You should eat healthy food. You should manage any health problems like diabetes, heart disease, or lung disease. You should stop smoking.

No matter your age or how you feel now, you should start exercising before surgery. Keep exercising after surgery. A physical therapist will teach you exercises to build strength, stay flexible, and keep your joints moving. The stronger and more flexible you are, the more you can do with or without a prosthesis. If you think you will have trouble doing daily tasks, an occupational therapist can help.

## After the Surgery

After surgery, your care team and you work together to set goals. These goals are to:

- Keep the remaining part of your limb safe from injury
- Control swelling
- Help the limb heal
- Keep your strength, heart health, and joint movement

Your limb needs time to heal. Treatments like massage, tapping, vibration, and slowly putting weight on the limb can help reduce sensitivity. There are many types of bandages and wraps to protect your limb and control swelling. Good swelling control helps blood flow, speeds healing, and reduces pain. This includes pain that feels like it is still in the missing limb. Eating healthy food is still important after surgery.

A physical therapist will work with you before and after you leave the hospital. You will learn to stand, walk with support, use a walker or crutches, or use a wheelchair. You will also learn how to do daily tasks like getting in and out of bed, bathing, and dressing.

Your prosthetist checks your healing every week. They watch for signs that you are ready for a temporary prosthesis.

When your limb has healed and the size is stable—usually 6 to 10 weeks after surgery, but longer if there are problems—you will get a temporary prosthesis. This is not a final device. It helps you slowly get used to putting weight on the limb. It also lets the team change parts as you improve. The socket of the temporary prosthesis may need to be adjusted several times.

Starting a prosthesis early helps in many ways. It can help you accept the loss, feel better about your body, reduce phantom limb pain, and improve your overall health.

Your limb will keep changing in size and shape for 12 to 18 months after surgery. After that time, when the changes slow down, you will get a final prosthesis. You will still use the temporary one while you get used to the final one. The final prosthesis has better parts. It uses the same joints and limbs that worked best during the temporary phase. But your limb size will still change a little every day and over time. How much it changes varies from person to person. Sometimes this can cause problems.

During fitting, you learn how to use your prosthesis. This takes several visits. The goal is to feel comfortable and stable.

For people with an upper limb prosthesis:  
Once you are comfortable and stable, the prosthetist adjusts the joints and parts to help you do more. Your therapist will teach you exercises to strengthen and keep your remaining arm flexible. They will also teach you how to use the prosthesis for daily tasks.

For people with a lower limb prosthesis:  
Once your limb feels comfortable and stable, the prosthetist adds a hip, knee, ankle, or foot. This helps you stand and walk straight. You will start walking in parallel bars. As you improve, the prosthetist changes or adjusts the joints and parts to help you walk better.

If you are struggling emotionally with losing your limb or using a prosthesis, counseling or therapy can help.

# Ankylosing Spondylitis – Simple Explanation

Ankylosing spondylitis is a long-term condition that causes inflammation in the spine and other joints. It can also affect the heart, eyes, and lungs. It often starts in young adults, especially men.

## Who Gets It?

- It is about 3 times more common in men than in women.
- Most people get it between the ages of 20 and 40.
- It runs in families. If a close family member has it, your risk is much higher.
- A gene called HLA-B27 is linked to the disease. Most white people with the disease have this gene. But many people without the disease also have it.
- Even if you have the gene, you may not get the disease. This means other factors, like the environment, also play a role.

## Types of Ankylosing Spondylitis

There are different types based on where the disease affects the body:

- **Axial ankylosing spondylitis**: The spine and pelvis are mainly affected. Imaging shows inflammation in the sacroiliac joints.
- **Nonradiographic ankylosing spondylitis**: Symptoms are like axial ankylosing spondylitis, but X-rays do not show joint damage.
- **Peripheral ankylosing spondylitis**: The disease mainly affects arms, legs, or hands and feet.

## Symptoms

The most common symptom is back pain that:

- Starts at night and wakes you up.
- Gets better with movement.
- Is stiff in the morning and lasts for more than 30 minutes.
- Comes back over time.

Other symptoms include:

- A bent-forward posture.
- Trouble breathing deeply because the chest cannot expand.
- Pain in the heels or knees (tendon pain).
- Swollen fingers or toes (called dactylitis).
- Eye pain, redness, or blurry vision (anterior uveitis).
- Fatigue, loss of appetite, weight loss, or low blood count.

In later stages, the spine may become stiff and fused. This can make it hard to stand straight. It can also affect lung function and make lying flat difficult.

Some people may also have:

- Heart problems like a leaky aortic valve or irregular heartbeat.
- Lung issues such as scarring or infection in the upper lung.
- Bowel problems like mild colitis.
- Skin rashes or psoriasis (in some cases).

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Diagnosis is based on:

- Your symptoms.
- Physical exam.
- Imaging tests (X-rays or MRI).
- Blood tests.

### Key Signs to Watch For

You should be checked for ankylosing spondylitis if you have:

- Back pain at night that improves with movement.
- Morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes.
- A family history of the disease.
- Eye pain or swelling.
- Heel or knee pain.
- Swollen fingers or toes.

### Tests Used

- **Blood tests**: Check for signs of inflammation (like ESR and CRP). They also check for the HLA-B27 gene.
- **X-rays**: Look for joint damage in the spine and pelvis.
- **MRI**: Can show early signs of inflammation before X-rays do. It is used when symptoms are strong but X-rays are normal.
- **ASAS criteria**: A set of rules used to help doctors diagnose the disease, especially early on.

### What the Tests Show

- Early X-ray changes: Small areas of bone damage, then thickening or narrowing of the joints.
- Later X-ray changes: The spine may look like a bamboo stick due to fused bones.
- MRI shows swelling in the bone marrow and early joint damage before X-rays can see it.

Note: X-rays may not show changes for years. MRI can find problems earlier, but it is not always needed for every patient.

## Treatment

The goal of treatment is to:

- Reduce pain.
- Keep joints flexible.
- Prevent long-term damage.

### Medicines

- **NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs)**: These are the first treatment. They help reduce pain and swelling. Use the lowest dose that works. Do not stop suddenly.
- **TNF inhibitors** (like etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab): These are very effective for back pain and inflammation. They are often used if NSAIDs do not work well.
  - For people with eye problems, adalimumab or infliximab are preferred.
- **IL-17 inhibitors** (like secukinumab, ixekizumab): Used if TNF inhibitors do not help. They reduce inflammation and joint symptoms.
  - Side effects: Skin rash, colds, fungal infections, stomach upset, shingles, or worse bowel symptoms.
- **JAK inhibitors** (like upadacitinib, tofacitinib): Used only if other treatments fail. They carry risks like heart problems, blood clots, and cancer. So they are used carefully.

### Other Treatments

- **Exercise**: Daily movement is essential. It helps keep the spine and joints flexible.
  - Try exercises that stretch and strengthen the back and chest muscles.
  - Lying on your stomach and pushing up with your arms can help keep the back straight.
- **Posture training**: Helps prevent a bent-forward posture.
- **Smoking**: Should be avoided. It harms the lungs and can make the disease worse.
- **Corticosteroid injections**: Can help if one joint is very painful. These are given directly into the joint, often guided by imaging.
- **Surgery**: If the hips become severely damaged, joint replacement surgery can help reduce pain and improve movement.

### Eye Problems

- If you have eye pain or redness, use eye drops and dilating drops (as prescribed).
- For repeated eye problems, TNF inhibitors (like adalimumab or infliximab) are often the best treatment.

## Prognosis

Most people with ankylosing spondylitis can live full, active lives with proper treatment.

- The disease often comes in flare-ups, then quiet periods.
- With good care, many people have little or no disability.
- In some cases, the disease gets worse over time and causes serious stiffness or deformity.

### Poor Prognosis Signs

- High levels of inflammation in blood tests.
- Hip joint problems.
- No improvement with NSAIDs.
- Eye or heart problems.
- Lung disease.

## Key Points

- Ankylosing spondylitis affects the spine, joints, eyes, heart, and lungs.
- It usually starts with back pain at night and morning stiffness.
- Diagnosis uses imaging, blood tests, and symptoms.
- NSAIDs are the first treatment.
- If NSAIDs do not work, TNF or IL-17 inhibitors are used.
- Exercise and good posture are very important.
- Smoking should be avoided.
- Eye problems need prompt treatment.
