# Drug Interactions

Your body may react to a medicine in a way that is not expected. This can happen when the medicine interacts with:

- Another medicine you are taking  
- Food, drinks, or supplements you use  
- A health problem you already have  

These interactions are usually not good. They can cause harm. They may:

- Make a medicine stronger than it should be. This can lead to side effects or poisoning.  
- Make a medicine weaker than it should be. This can mean the medicine does not work.  

---

## Medicine and Medicine Interactions

Medicine and medicine interactions can happen with both prescription and over-the-counter medicines. There are three main types:  
- Taking two medicines that do the same thing  
- Taking two medicines that work against each other  
- One medicine changing how the body handles another medicine  

### Taking Two Medicines That Do the Same Thing

If you take two medicines that have the same effect, you may get too much of that effect. This is called duplication.  

For example:  
- A cold medicine and a sleep aid may both contain diphenhydramine.  
- A cold medicine and a pain reliever may both contain acetaminophen.  

This kind of duplication is common. It often happens when you take medicines that have many ingredients. It also happens when different brands have the same active ingredient.  

You can avoid this by:  
- Knowing what is in each medicine you take  
- Checking every new medicine before you use it  

For example:  
- Many prescription pain medicines contain an opioid and acetaminophen.  
- If you do not know this, you might take an over-the-counter acetaminophen for extra pain relief. This can lead to too much acetaminophen in your body. This can cause serious liver damage.  

You are more likely to have this problem if you see more than one doctor. Or if you get prescriptions from more than one pharmacy. Doctors may not know what other medicines you are taking.  

For example:  
- If two doctors both prescribe a sleep aid, you may feel very sleepy.  
- If one doctor prescribes a sleep aid and another prescribes an anxiety medicine that also causes drowsiness, you may feel dizzy or very tired.  

To reduce this risk:  
- Tell every doctor about all medicines you take  
- Use only one pharmacy for all your prescriptions  
- Keep a written list of all your medicines  
- Bring this list to every doctor visit  
- Do not take old medicines (like a sleeping pill or pain reliever) without asking your doctor or pharmacist first  

### Taking Two Medicines That Work Against Each Other

When two medicines work against each other, one or both may not work as well.  

For example:  
- Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), like ibuprofen, can make your body keep salt and water.  
- Diuretics, like hydrochlorothiazide or furosemide, help your body get rid of extra salt and water.  
- If you take both, the NSAID may reduce how well the diuretic works.  

Another example:  
- Beta-blockers, like propranolol, are used for high blood pressure and heart disease.  
- Albuterol is used for asthma.  
- Both medicines affect the same part of the body (beta-2 receptors).  
- One blocks the receptor. The other turns it on.  
- If you take both, they may cancel each other out.  

### One Medicine Changing How the Body Handles Another

One medicine can change how your body absorbs, moves, breaks down, or removes another medicine.  

For example:  
- Acid-blocking medicines, like H2 blockers or proton pump inhibitors, make your stomach less acidic.  
- This can reduce how well some medicines are absorbed.  
- For example, ketoconazole (a medicine for fungal infections) may not work well if taken with acid blockers.  

Many medicines are broken down by liver enzymes. Some medicines can change how active these enzymes are.  

For example:  
- Barbiturates, like phenobarbital, make liver enzymes more active.  
- This can make warfarin (a blood thinner) break down faster.  
- Warfarin may not work as well.  
- This increases the risk of blood clots.  

Another example:  
- Antibiotics like erythromycin and ciprofloxacin make liver enzymes less active.  
- This can make warfarin stay in your body longer.  
- This increases the risk of bleeding.  

When you take warfarin and another medicine that affects liver enzymes:  
- Your doctor will check your blood more often  
- Your warfarin dose may be changed  
- The dose will be adjusted again when you stop the other medicine  

Smoking can also affect liver enzymes.  
- Chemicals in cigarette smoke make some liver enzymes more active.  
- This can make some medicines less effective.  
- For example, theophylline (a medicine for breathing problems) may not work as well if you smoke.  

Some medicines can change how your kidneys remove other medicines.  

For example:  
- Large amounts of vitamin C make your urine more acidic.  
- This can change how fast some medicines leave your body.  
- Acidic medicines like aspirin may stay in your body longer.  
- Basic medicines like pseudoephedrine may leave your body faster.  

Doctors and pharmacists use books and computer programs to check for possible interactions.  
- Most pharmacies use computer systems to check for drug interactions.  
- These systems help prevent dangerous combinations.

## Medicine and Food, Drink, or Supplements Interactions

Food, drinks, and supplements can change how medicines work.  

Medicines you take by mouth must pass through your stomach and intestines to be absorbed.  
- Food in your stomach can slow or stop a medicine from being absorbed.  
- You can avoid this by taking the medicine 1 hour before or 2 hours after eating.  

### Dietary Supplements

Dietary supplements include vitamins, minerals, herbs, and amino acids.  
- They are sold as food, not as medicine.  
- They are not tested as thoroughly as medicines.  
- But they can still interact with medicines.  

Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you take any supplements.  
- This helps avoid harmful interactions.  

### Alcohol

Even though alcohol is not a food, it affects your body.  
- It can interact with many medicines.  

For example:  
- Taking alcohol with metronidazole (an antibiotic) can cause:  
  - Flushing (red face)  
  - Headache  
  - Fast heartbeat  
  - Nausea and vomiting  

Ask your doctor or pharmacist about alcohol and your medicines.

# Assisted Reproductive Technologies (ARTs)

ARTs are medical treatments that help people get pregnant by working with sperm, eggs, or embryos in a lab.

These treatments are used when medicine alone does not work or is unlikely to work.

ARTs are more likely to succeed in women under the age of 35.

ARTs can lead to more than one baby, such as twins or triplets. But this is less common than when only fertility medicines are used.

Sometimes, during IVF, doctors can test an embryo for genetic problems before placing it in the uterus. This is called preimplantation genetic testing.

> **Did You Know?**  
> During IVF, doctors can test an embryo for genetic problems before it is placed in the uterus.

---

## Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection

This method is used when:

- The man has serious sperm problems.
- Other methods are unlikely to work.

A doctor puts just one sperm directly into an egg. This helps the egg become fertilized.

This is often done as part of IVF.

There is a slightly higher chance of birth defects after this procedure. This may happen because:

- The process can harm the egg, sperm, or embryo.
- If the sperm comes from a man with an abnormal Y chromosome, the baby boy may have problems with his reproductive organs. These problems are often like those of the father.
- Most birth defects linked to this method affect the reproductive organs.

---

## Using Donated Eggs or Sperm

Sometimes, fertility treatments do not work after several tries. In these cases, some people choose to use donated eggs or sperm.

The donor can be someone the couple knows. Or the donor can be anonymous.

### Using Donated Eggs

- The egg donor goes through the first steps of IVF.
- In the lab, the donor’s eggs are mixed with the sperm of the man who wants to be a father.
- The fertilized eggs are then placed in the uterus of the woman who wants to carry the baby.

### Using Donated Sperm

- Sperm from anonymous donors is frozen and stored in sperm banks.
- During treatment, the donor sperm is mixed with the woman’s eggs in a lab dish.
- The fertilized eggs are then placed in the woman’s uterus.

---

## Using a Gestational Carrier

Some women cannot carry a pregnancy because of a problem with their uterus or a serious health condition.

A gestational carrier can carry the baby for them.

- The gestational carrier carries the baby in her uterus.
- But she is not the genetic mother. The baby’s egg comes from the woman who wants to be a mother.
- The fertilized eggs from the couple are placed in the carrier’s uterus.

### Surrogacy vs. Gestational Carrier

- A surrogate is different. In surrogacy, the surrogate provides the egg. So she is the baby’s genetic mother.
- Surrogacy is less common because it can cause emotional and legal challenges.
- Being a gestational carrier or a surrogate is illegal in many countries.

# Problems with the Cornea

If you have a red eye and also have any of the following, it may be a problem with the cornea, not just simple eye irritation:

- Only one eye is affected  
- You feel pain, like something is in your eye, or a dull ache  
- Light hurts your eye (this is called photophobia)  
- Your vision is not as clear as usual  

## Types of Corneal Problems

Here are some common conditions that affect the cornea:

- **Bullous keratopathy**: The cornea swells and forms blisters.  
- **Cogan syndrome**: A rare condition that causes eye inflammation and hearing or balance problems.  
- **Corneal ulcer**: A sore on the surface of the cornea. It can be caused by infection or injury.  
- **Herpes simplex keratitis**: An eye infection caused by the herpes simplex virus. It can cause sores on the cornea.  
- **Herpes zoster ophthalmicus**: A rash and eye problem caused by the shingles virus. It can affect the eye.  
- **Interstitial keratitis**: Inflammation deep in the cornea. It can cause blurry vision.  
- **Keratoconjunctivitis sicca**: Dry eyes. The eyes do not make enough tears.  
- **Keratoconus**: The cornea becomes thin and cone-shaped. This changes how light enters the eye.  
- **Keratomalacia**: A rare condition where the cornea softens and can break down. It is often due to vitamin A deficiency.  
- **Peripheral ulcerative keratitis**: Sores on the outer edge of the cornea. It can be linked to autoimmune diseases.  
- **Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis**: Small bumps on the cornea or white part of the eye. Often linked to infection or allergy.  
- **Superficial punctate keratitis**: Tiny spots of damage on the surface of the cornea. Can be caused by dryness, injury, or infection.  
- **Corneal transplantation**: A surgery to replace a damaged cornea with a healthy one from a donor. This is a treatment option.

## How Doctors Check the Cornea

To look at the cornea, doctors may:

- Use a special dye called fluorescein. This makes any damage on the cornea easier to see.  
- Use a slit lamp. This is a special microscope that lets the doctor see the eye in detail.  
- Do tests to check for bacteria, viruses, or other germs if needed.

If you have symptoms of a corneal problem—like pain, a red eye, or blurry vision—see an eye doctor right away. You should be referred to an ophthalmologist for proper care.

### Key Tips

- If someone has a red eye with pain, a feeling like something is in the eye, or blurry vision, do a slit-lamp exam and use fluorescein dye.  
- These tests help find problems with the cornea early.

# How Single-Gene Disorders Are Passed Down

## What Are Genes and Chromosomes?

Genes are small parts of DNA. They tell your body how to make proteins. Proteins help your body work properly.

Chromosomes are long strands of DNA. Each chromosome holds many genes. Most cells in your body have 23 pairs of chromosomes. That is 46 chromosomes in total.

There are 22 pairs of nonsex chromosomes. These are called autosomes. There is also 1 pair of sex chromosomes. These determine if a baby will be a boy or a girl.

Each pair has one chromosome from your mother and one from your father.

## How Sex Is Determined

A boy has one X chromosome and one Y chromosome. The X comes from his mother. The Y comes from his father.

A girl has two X chromosomes. One X comes from her mother. The other X comes from her father.

## How Traits Are Passed Down

Traits are features that come from genes. Examples include eye color or blood type.

Traits can be:

- **Dominant** – You only need one copy of the gene to have the trait.
- **Recessive** – You need two copies of the gene to have the trait.
- **Codominant** – Both versions of the gene show up at the same time.

### Dominant Traits

If you have one copy of a dominant gene, you will have the trait. You do not need a second copy.

### Recessive Traits

For a recessive trait to appear, you must have two copies of the abnormal gene. One from each parent.

People with only one copy of a recessive gene do not have the disorder. But they can pass the gene to their children. These people are called carriers.

### Codominant Traits

With codominant traits, both versions of the gene are active. For example, blood type A and blood type B are both expressed if you have one gene for each. This gives you blood type AB.

## X-Linked Genes

Some genes are on the X chromosome. These are called X-linked genes.

Males have only one X chromosome. So, if they have an abnormal gene on the X chromosome, it will show up. There is no second X to balance it out.

Females have two X chromosomes. If one X has an abnormal gene, the other X often keeps the gene from causing a problem.

## Penetrance and Expressivity

These two terms explain how a gene affects a person.

### Penetrance

Penetrance is how often a gene leads to a visible trait.

- If 100% of people with the gene show the trait, it is fully penetrant.
- If only some people with the gene show the trait, it is incompletely penetrant.

Even if a person does not show the trait, they can still pass the gene to their children.

Penetrance can change with age. It can also vary from person to person.

### Expressivity

Expressivity is how strongly the trait shows up in a person.

Some people may have a very strong form of the trait. Others may have only mild signs. Some may have no signs at all.

Many things can affect expressivity. These include other genes, exposure to harmful substances, and age.

## Inheritance Patterns

Some genetic disorders follow clear patterns. These patterns depend on whether the gene is dominant or recessive, and whether it is on a sex chromosome or not.

### Autosomal Dominant Disorders

These are caused by a dominant gene on a nonsex chromosome.

- If one parent has the disorder and the other does not, each child has a 50% chance of getting it.
- People without the disorder usually do not carry the gene.
- Males and females are equally likely to be affected.
- Most people with the disorder have a parent with the disorder. But sometimes the parent does not know they have it.
- Sometimes the disorder starts with a new mutation in the child.

Examples: Marfan syndrome, Huntington disease.

### Autosomal Recessive Disorders

These are caused by a recessive gene on a nonsex chromosome.

- To have the disorder, a person must get one abnormal gene from each parent.
- Both parents are usually healthy but carry one abnormal gene each.
- If both parents carry the gene, each child has:
  - A 25% chance of having the disorder.
  - A 25% chance of having two normal genes.
  - A 50% chance of being a carrier (no symptoms, but can pass the gene on).

- If one parent has the disorder and the other is a carrier, half the children will have the disorder. The other half will be carriers.
- If one parent has the disorder and the other has no abnormal gene, none of the children will have the disorder. But all will be carriers.
- If a person does not have the disorder, but their siblings do, and their parents do not, they have a 66% chance of being a carrier.

Examples: Cystic fibrosis.

### X-Linked Dominant Disorders

These are caused by a dominant gene on the X chromosome.

- An affected father passes the gene to all his daughters. He does not pass it to his sons (sons get the Y chromosome).
- An affected mother with one abnormal gene passes the gene to about half her children, no matter the sex.
- An affected mother with two abnormal genes passes the gene to all her children.
- Many X-linked dominant disorders are more serious in males. Some are so severe that affected males do not survive.
- More females than males are affected. This is especially true if the disorder kills males before birth or early in life.

Examples: Familial rickets, hereditary nephritis (Alport syndrome).

- In hereditary rickets, females have milder bone problems than males.
- In hereditary nephritis, females often have no symptoms. Males usually develop kidney failure in early adulthood.

### X-Linked Recessive Disorders

These are caused by a recessive gene on the X chromosome.

- Almost all people with the disorder are male.
- A male with the disorder passes the gene to all his daughters. They become carriers.
- He does not pass the gene to his sons (sons get the Y chromosome).
- A female carrier usually does not have the disorder. But she can pass the gene to her children.
  - Each son has a 50% chance of getting the abnormal gene and having the disorder.
  - Each daughter has a 50% chance of being a carrier. She has a 50% chance of getting two normal genes.

Examples: Red-green color blindness, hemophilia.

- Red-green color blindness affects about 1 in 10 males. It is rare in females.
- Males get the gene from their mother. The mother usually has normal vision but carries the gene.
- Fathers cannot pass the gene to sons. They pass the Y chromosome instead.
- Daughters of color-blind fathers are always carriers. They rarely have the disorder.

Hemophilia is a serious condition. It causes heavy bleeding from small injuries.

## Sex-Limited Traits

Some traits only appear in one sex. This is not because the gene is on the X chromosome. It is because of hormones and other body differences.

For example, male-pattern baldness is a dominant trait. But it rarely shows up in women. When it does, it usually happens after menopause.

## Mitochondrial Disorders

Mitochondria are tiny parts inside your cells. They make energy for the cell.

Each mitochondrion has its own small piece of DNA. This DNA holds some genes that help the mitochondrion work.

Some rare diseases come from abnormal genes in mitochondrial DNA.

Examples:
- Leber hereditary optic neuropathy – causes sudden vision loss in both eyes. Often starts in the teens.
- A disorder that causes type 2 diabetes and hearing loss.

### How Mitochondrial Genes Are Passed Down

- Mitochondrial DNA comes only from the mother.
- A mother with a mitochondrial gene problem can pass it to all her children.
- A father with the problem does not pass it to any of his children.

But not all mitochondrial disorders come from mitochondrial DNA. Some come from genes in the cell’s main DNA (in the nucleus). In those cases, the father’s genes can play a role.

### Why It’s Hard to Predict

Mitochondrial DNA can vary from cell to cell. One cell may have many abnormal genes. Another cell may have few or none.

So, two people with the same abnormal gene may have very different symptoms.

This makes diagnosis hard. It also makes genetic testing and counseling difficult. It is hard to predict how a disease will affect a person.

# Strabismus

Strabismus means the eyes are not lined up properly. One eye may look in a different direction than the other. This can happen all the time or only sometimes.

If left untreated, about half of children with strabismus will lose some vision in one eye. This is called amblyopia. It happens when the brain stops using the eye that is not looking straight.

## Types of Strabismus

There are different kinds of strabismus. They are named based on how the eye moves and when the problem shows up.

### How the Eye Moves

- **Eso**: The eye turns toward the nose.
- **Exo**: The eye turns toward the temple (side of the head).
- **Hyper**: The eye turns upward.
- **Hypo**: The eye turns downward.

### Types of Misalignment

- A **tropia** is a visible eye turn. You can see it when both eyes are open.
- A **phoria** is a hidden eye turn. It only shows up when one eye is covered.
- A **comitant deviation** means the eye turn is the same in all directions.
- An **incomitant deviation** means the eye turn changes depending on where the child looks.

## What Causes Strabismus?

Most cases are due to:
- Problems with how the eyes focus (refractive error)
- Weakness or imbalance in the eye muscles

Rare causes include:
- Eye tumors (like retinoblastoma)
- Brain or nerve problems
- Serious eye defects

### Infantile Strabismus
This type appears in the first 6 months of life. It is not always present at birth, so "infantile" is a better term than "congenital."

Risk factors include:
- A family history of strabismus or lazy eye
- Genetic conditions like Down syndrome or facial birth defects
- Exposure to drugs or alcohol before birth
- Medicines taken during pregnancy
- Premature birth or low birth weight
- Brain or nerve problems like cerebral palsy
- Birth defects in the eyes

### Acquired Strabismus
This type starts after 6 months of age. It can happen suddenly or slowly.

Causes include:
- High farsightedness (hyperopia)
- Tumors in the eye
- Head injuries
- Brain or nerve problems (like increased pressure in the brain, cerebral palsy, spina bifida, or nerve damage)
- Infections (like encephalitis or meningitis)
- Eye injuries or defects

### Specific Types

**Esotropia** (eye turns inward)
- Often appears in infancy and has no known cause.
- Can happen in older children due to farsightedness.
- Can also happen if one eye has poor vision (like from cataracts or nerve problems).
- Rarely, it is caused by a problem with the sixth cranial nerve.
- It can be part of a syndrome, like Duane syndrome or Möbius syndrome.

**Exotropia** (eye turns outward)
- Usually happens only sometimes and has no clear cause.
- Can be constant and caused by nerve problems, like damage to the third cranial nerve.

**Hypertropia** (eye turns upward)
- Often caused by a problem with the fourth cranial nerve.
- Can happen at birth or after head injury.

**Hypotropia** (eye turns downward)
- Often caused by physical blockage in the eye socket (like from a broken bone).
- Can also be caused by thyroid eye disease (Graves ophthalmopathy).
- Rarely, it is due to nerve damage or tight eye muscles.

## Signs and Symptoms

- Phorias usually do not cause symptoms. If they do, the child may have eye strain.
- Tropias can cause:
  - Head tilting to help see better
  - Double vision
  - Lazy eye (amblyopia) in the eye that is not used

## How Is Strabismus Diagnosed?

Doctors check for strabismus during regular child checkups.

### What the Doctor Does

- Asks about family history of lazy eye or crossed eyes.
- Asks if someone noticed the eye turn, when it started, how often it happens, and if the child prefers using one eye.
- Checks vision in each eye.
- Tests how the pupils react to light.
- Checks how well the eyes move in all directions.
- Uses a special light to look inside the eye (slit-lamp exam) to check for cataracts.
- Looks at the back of the eye (fundus exam) to check for tumors or other problems.
- Examines the nerves in the head and face.

### Tests Used

**Corneal light reflex test**
- The child looks at a light.
- The doctor checks where the light reflects on the eye.
- If the eyes are aligned, the light reflects in the same spot on both eyes.
- If one eye turns inward, the light reflects toward the nose.
- If one eye turns outward, the light reflects toward the temple.

This test is good for screening but may miss small eye turns.

**Cover test**
- The child looks at an object.
- The doctor covers one eye and watches the other.
- If the uncovered eye moves to fixate, the eyes are not aligned.
- The test is repeated with the other eye.

**Alternate cover test**
- The doctor quickly covers and uncovers each eye.
- If the eye moves when uncovered, it means there is a hidden eye turn.
- In exotropia, the eye moves inward when uncovered.
- In esotropia, the eye moves outward when uncovered.

**Prism test**
- Prisms are used to measure how much the eye turns.
- The doctor adds prisms until the eye no longer needs to move to fixate.
- The strength of the prism shows how big the eye turn is.
- The unit used is the prism diopter. One prism diopter means the eye is off by 1 centimeter at a distance of 1 meter.

### Pseudostrabismus
This is when the eyes look crossed, but they are actually straight. It happens in babies with a wide nose or skin folds over the inner eye. The light reflex and cover tests are normal. This is not real strabismus.

### Imaging and Testing
- Brain scans may be needed if a nerve problem is suspected.
- Genetic testing may help if there is a birth defect.

## How Is Strabismus Treated?

Treatment has two main goals:
1. Fix lazy eye (amblyopia) first.
2. Then fix the eye alignment.

### Treating Lazy Eye (Amblyopia)

- **Patching**: Cover the stronger eye with a patch. This forces the weaker eye to work.
- **Atropine drops**: Put drops in the stronger eye to blur its vision. This helps the weaker eye get stronger.

Patching does not fix the eye turn. It only helps the weak eye see better.

### Correcting Vision Problems

- Glasses or contact lenses help if the child is very farsighted.
- This is especially important for children with accommodative esotropia.

### Eye Exercises

- These can help with some cases of intermittent exotropia (eye turns outward sometimes).
- They are only used for convergence insufficiency.

### Surgery

- Surgery is done if glasses, patches, or exercises do not fix the eye alignment.
- The surgeon changes the eye muscles by loosening or tightening them.
- Most often, the muscles on the sides of the eyes are adjusted.
- Surgery is usually done on both eyes.
- It is done in a hospital or clinic and the child goes home the same day.
- Success rates are over 80%.
- About 1 in 5 children need another surgery later.
- Possible side effects:
  - Eye turn is too much (overcorrection) or not enough (undercorrection)
  - Eye turn comes back later in life
  - Infection (rare)
  - Too much bleeding (rare)
  - Loss of vision (very rare)

## Prognosis

Do not assume strabismus will go away on its own. If not treated early, it can cause permanent vision loss.

- The best time to treat is before age 8.
- After age 8, the brain is fully developed and treatment is less effective.
- All children should have regular eye checks during preschool years.

## Key Points

- Strabismus means the eyes are not lined up. It affects about 3 out of every 100 children.
- About half of these children will lose vision in one eye if not treated.
- Most cases are due to focusing problems or weak eye muscles.
- Rarely, it is caused by serious conditions like eye tumors or nerve damage.
- Vision loss can be permanent if treatment is delayed.
- The eyes can be checked during regular child visits.
- Treatment depends on the cause. Surgery may be needed to fix the eye alignment.

# X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia

This is a rare condition that is passed down through families. It affects the body’s ability to fight infections. It is caused by a change in a gene on the X chromosome. This gene helps the body make a type of white blood cell called B cells.

B cells make antibodies. Antibodies help protect the body from infections. In this condition, the body makes no B cells. So it also makes very little or no antibodies.

## What Happens in This Condition

- Babies are protected from infections for the first 6 months of life by antibodies they get from their mother.
- After about 6 months, these antibodies fade away.
- Then, the baby starts to get frequent coughs and infections in the nose, ears, skin, sinuses, and lungs.
- These infections are often caused by bacteria like pneumococci, streptococci, and *Haemophilus*.
- Some rare infections can affect the brain.
- The tonsils are very small. Lymph nodes do not grow normally because B cells are missing.
- The condition increases the risk of joint infections, long-term lung damage, and some types of cancer.

With early diagnosis and treatment, most people live a normal life span. But brain infections can be serious and may shorten life.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors use blood tests to check:
- How many B cells are in the blood.
- How much antibody is in the blood.

Genetic testing may be done to confirm the diagnosis. It is not always needed. But it is helpful for family members who may carry the gene.

If a family member has this condition, prenatal testing may be offered during future pregnancies. This testing checks the baby’s genes before birth.

## How It Is Treated

There is no cure yet. But treatment helps prevent serious infections.

**Immune globulin**
- This is a medicine made from antibodies taken from healthy people.
- It replaces the missing antibodies in the body.
- It is given for life.
- It can be given through a vein (IV) or under the skin (subcutaneous).

**Antibiotics**
- These are used to treat bacterial infections right away.
- Some people take antibiotics every day to prevent infections.

**Vaccines**
- People with this condition should not get live vaccines.
- These include:
  - Rotavirus vaccine
  - Measles-mumps-rubella vaccine
  - Chickenpox vaccine
  - One type of shingles vaccine
  - BCG vaccine
  - Flu vaccine given as a nasal spray

These vaccines contain live but weakened viruses or bacteria. They can cause serious illness in people with weak immune systems.

Even with treatment, many people still get long-term infections in the sinuses and lungs.

**New Treatments Being Studied**
- Doctors are testing new treatments like stem cell transplants and gene therapy.
- These are not yet standard care but may help in the future.

# Common Hand Problems

Hand problems can cause pain, swelling, or trouble moving your hand. Some common issues include:

- Bumps or lumps under the skin (called ganglia)
- Infections in the hand
- A condition where the small bone in the wrist dies due to poor blood flow (Kienböck disease)
- Nerve problems that cause tingling, numbness, or weakness
- Swelling in the tendons that move the fingers (noninfectious tenosynovitis)
- Wear and tear in the joints (osteoarthritis)

Other hand problems include:
- Complex regional pain syndrome (a type of long-lasting pain after an injury)
- Hand injuries

## Bones in the Hand

The hand has many small bones. They help you grip, pinch, and move your fingers.

## How Doctors Check Hand Problems

Doctors often find the cause of hand problems by asking about your symptoms and doing a physical exam.

They will ask:
- When the problem started
- What makes it better or worse
- If you have any other health issues

They will check:
- How well you can move your hand and fingers
- If there is swelling, redness, or tenderness
- If you feel numbness or tingling
- How strong your grip is

In many cases, this is enough to know what is wrong.

# Lipomas

Lipomas are soft lumps under the skin made of fat.  
They are usually round or oval in shape.

## What Lipomas Look Like

- They feel smooth and soft.  
- Some feel firmer or harder.  
- The skin over the lump looks normal.  
- They can appear anywhere on the body.  
- They are most common on the forearms, chest, back, and neck.  

Lipomas are very common.  
They are more likely to happen in women than in men.  
Some people have just one lipoma.  
Others have many lipomas.  

Having many lipomas can run in families.  
It can be part of a genetic condition called familiar multiple lipomatosis.

## Do Lipomas Cause Problems?

Most lipomas do not cause any issues.  
But sometimes they can be tender or painful.  
They rarely cause pain or discomfort.

## How Are Lipomas Diagnosed?

A doctor can usually tell a lipoma is a lipoma just by looking at it and feeling it.  
No special tests are needed in most cases.  

Lipomas are not cancer.  
They almost never turn into cancer.  

If a lipoma changes in size, shape, or color, or if it is large, your doctor may take a small sample of tissue.  
This is called a biopsy.  
The sample is checked under a microscope to make sure it is not cancer.

## How Are Lipomas Treated?

Most lipomas do not need treatment.  
If a lipoma bothers you, you can have it removed.  

Removal options include:  
- Surgery: Cutting out the lipoma.  
- Liposuction: Using a suction device to remove the fat.  

Both methods are safe and effective.

# Chest Injuries After Trauma

Chest injuries are a major cause of death from trauma in the United States.  
About one in four trauma deaths are due to chest injuries.  
Many of these injuries are life-threatening in the first minutes or hours after the injury.  
Most of these problems can be treated right away at the patient’s bedside.  
No advanced surgery is needed for many of these treatments.

---

## What Causes Chest Injuries?

Chest injuries can happen from blunt force or penetrating wounds.  
Blunt force means a hard impact, like from a car crash or fall.  
Penetrating wounds mean something sharp goes into the chest, like a knife or bullet.

Common serious chest injuries include:

- Damage to the large blood vessel (aorta) in the chest
- Injury to the heart from a blunt blow
- Fluid buildup around the heart (cardiac tamponade)
- A section of the chest wall that breaks and moves abnormally (flail chest)
- Blood in the space around the lung (hemothorax)
- Air in the space around the lung (pneumothorax)
  - Traumatic pneumothorax: air gets into the chest from injury
  - Open pneumothorax: air enters through a hole in the chest wall
  - Tension pneumothorax: air builds up under pressure and pushes on the heart and lungs
- Bruising of the lung tissue (pulmonary contusion)

Many people have both blood and air in the chest space at the same time.  
This is called hemopneumothorax.

Bone injuries are common.  
The most often broken bones are the ribs and collarbone.  
The breastbone and shoulder blade can also break.  
The tube that carries food from the mouth to the stomach (esophagus) can be injured.  
The muscle that separates the chest from the abdomen (diaphragm) can also be damaged.

Because the diaphragm can rise as high as the nipple line when you breathe out,  
a wound in the chest at or below the nipple level can also injure the organs inside the belly.

---

## How Chest Injuries Cause Problems

Most serious problems from chest injuries happen because they affect breathing or blood flow, or both.

### Breathing Problems

Breathing can be affected by:

- Direct damage to the lungs or air passages
- Changes in how the chest moves during breathing

Injuries that damage the lungs or airways include:

- Pulmonary contusion: bruising of the lung tissue
- Tracheobronchial disruption: tearing of the windpipe or main airways

Injuries that change how the chest moves include:

- Hemothorax: blood in the space around the lung
- Pneumothorax: air in the space around the lung
- Flail chest: a section of the chest wall breaks and moves in the wrong direction

When the lung, airway, or esophagus is torn, air can leak into the soft tissues of the chest or neck.  
This is called subcutaneous emphysema.  
Air can also get into the center of the chest (mediastinum), called pneumomediastinum.

The air itself is not usually dangerous.  
The real problem is the injury that caused the air leak.

Tension pneumothorax is very serious.  
It makes breathing harder and also stops blood from returning to the heart.

Pulmonary contusion causes poor oxygen exchange.  
This happens because blood and fluid build up in the lung tissue.

### Blood Flow Problems

Blood flow can be affected by:

- Bleeding
- Less blood returning to the heart
- Direct injury to the heart

Bleeding, such as in hemothorax, can be very heavy.  
This can lead to shock.  
A large amount of blood in the chest space also makes breathing harder.

Less blood returning to the heart can cause low blood pressure.  
This can happen when pressure builds up inside the chest (tension pneumothorax)  
or inside the sac around the heart (cardiac tamponade).

Blunt injury to the heart can damage the heart muscle or heart valves.  
This can lead to heart failure or abnormal heart rhythms.

---

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

Common symptoms include:

- Pain in the chest
- Pain that gets worse when you breathe in
- Shortness of breath

Common physical findings include:

- Tenderness when the chest is touched
- Bruising on the chest
- Trouble breathing
- Low blood pressure or shock

Swollen neck veins can happen in tension pneumothorax or cardiac tamponade.  
This only occurs if the body still has enough fluid in the blood vessels.

Decreased breath sounds can mean:

- Air in the chest space (pneumothorax)
- Blood in the chest space (hemothorax)

When you tap on the chest:

- A dull sound means blood is present (hemothorax)
- A very hollow sound means air is present (pneumothorax)

In tension pneumothorax, the windpipe may shift away from the injured side.

In flail chest, a section of the chest wall moves the wrong way.  
It moves inward when you breathe in and outward when you breathe out.  
This section can often be felt when touched.

Subcutaneous emphysema feels like a crackling or crunching when touched.  
It may be in one small area or spread over a large part of the chest or neck.  
Pneumothorax is the most common cause.  
If the crackling is widespread, it may mean a serious injury to the windpipe or upper airway.

Air in the center of the chest can cause a crunching sound that matches the heartbeat.  
This is called Hamman sign.  
It suggests pneumomediastinum.  
It often means there is a tear in the windpipe or airway.  
Rarely, it can mean the esophagus is injured.

---

## How Are Chest Injuries Diagnosed?

Diagnosis starts with:

- A detailed history of the injury
- A physical exam

A chest X-ray is usually done next.

Sometimes other imaging tests are needed, such as:

- CT scan
- Ultrasound
- Tests to look at the aorta

---

## How Are Chest Injuries Treated?

Treatment has two parts:

1. Supportive care to keep the patient stable
2. Specific treatment for each injury

Some life-threatening injuries must be treated right away, even before imaging is done.

### Immediate Treatments at the Bedside

- **Tension pneumothorax with breathing trouble**:  
  A needle is inserted into the chest to release trapped air.  
  Or a finger is used to open a small hole in the chest wall (finger thoracostomy).

- **Breathing trouble or shock with decreased breath sounds and suspected hemothorax**:  
  A tube is placed into the chest to drain blood (tube thoracostomy).

- **Breathing trouble with open pneumothorax**:  
  A dressing that covers the wound but allows air to escape is placed first.  
  Then a chest tube is inserted.

- **Breathing trouble with flail chest**:  
  The patient is placed on a breathing machine (mechanical ventilation).

- **Shock with suspected cardiac tamponade**:  
  A needle is used to drain fluid from around the heart (pericardiocentesis).

- **Suspected low blood volume (hypovolemic shock)**:  
  Fluids are given through a vein.  
  Blood products are used if available.

### Immediate Surgery (Resuscitative Thoracotomy)

This surgery may be considered only if:

- The doctor is trained and experienced in it
- The patient has one of the following:

  - A penetrating chest injury and needed CPR for less than 15 minutes
  - A penetrating injury not in the chest but needed CPR for less than 5 minutes
  - A blunt injury (like from a car crash) and needed CPR for less than 10 minutes
  - Blood pressure stays below 60 mm Hg despite treatment, due to suspected tamponade, bleeding, or air in the blood vessels

> **Important Note**:  
> If a patient has breathing trouble or shock and decreased breath sounds,  
> a chest tube can be placed before imaging is done.  
> This can save time and lives.

> **Warning**:  
> Resuscitative thoracotomy should not be done if none of the above conditions are met.  
> The procedure carries serious risks, such as spreading infections or harming the doctor.  
> It is also very costly.

### Specific Injury Treatments

Each injury is treated based on its type and severity.

Supportive care usually includes:

- Pain relief medicine
- Extra oxygen through a mask or tube
- Breathing machine (mechanical ventilation) if needed

# Microcephaly

Microcephaly means a baby is born with a head that is much smaller than normal.  
This usually happens because the brain is small or did not develop properly.

## What Causes Microcephaly?

Many different things can cause microcephaly. These include:

- Problems with genes or chromosomes  
- Infections during pregnancy (like rubella, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, syphilis, or Zika virus)  
- Not getting enough oxygen before or during birth  
- Exposure to harmful substances like alcohol, drugs, or toxins during pregnancy  
- Poor nutrition in the mother during pregnancy  
- Birth defects in the brain  
- A family history of small head size (this is usually mild and does not cause serious problems)

Some cases happen by chance. Others run in families.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The symptoms depend on how much the brain is affected.

Babies with severe microcephaly may have:

- Seizures  
- Trouble reaching development milestones (like sitting up, walking, or talking)  
- Problems feeding  
- Hearing or vision problems  
- Trouble moving or keeping balance  
- High energy levels or trouble focusing  
- Learning difficulties or intellectual disabilities

Some babies with mild microcephaly may not have any symptoms.

## How Is Microcephaly Diagnosed?

Doctors can find out if a baby has microcephaly before or after birth.

**Before birth:**  
A routine ultrasound test done in the second or third trimester can sometimes show a small head size.

**After birth:**  
Doctors measure the baby’s head around the widest part.  
They compare this to standard growth charts for babies of the same age, sex, and background.

If the head is much smaller than expected, the baby may have microcephaly.  
Sometimes, the head starts out normal but does not grow as it should.

Doctors also check the head size of the parents.  
A slightly small head can run in families and not be a problem.

If microcephaly is found, doctors may do:

- A brain scan using CT or MRI to look for brain problems  
- Blood tests to check for infections or genetic issues  
- A visit with a geneticist (a doctor who studies genes and how traits are passed down)

A blood test from the baby may be used to look for gene or chromosome problems.

## How Is Microcephaly Treated?

There is no cure for microcephaly.  
It is a lifelong condition.

But doctors can treat the symptoms.  
For example:

- Seizures can be managed with medicine  
- Feeding problems can be helped with special feeding methods  
- Physical therapy can help with movement and balance  
- Speech and learning support can help with communication and thinking skills

Early help is very important.  
Early intervention programs can make a big difference in a child’s development.

If the small head size runs in the family and the child has no other problems, treatment is usually not needed.

## Follow-Up Care

Regular check-ups with a team of doctors are important.  
This team may include pediatricians, neurologists, therapists, and geneticists.

These visits help track the child’s growth and development.  
They also help catch any new problems early.

## More Information

The following organization offers helpful support and information:

**March of Dimes**  
This group supports pregnant people and babies.  
They provide advice on how to stay healthy during pregnancy.  
They also work to prevent premature birth and infant deaths.

# Crying in Children

All babies and young children cry to show they need something.  
Crying is their only way to talk before they can speak.  
Most crying happens because a child is hungry, uncomfortable, or lonely.  
For example, a wet diaper or a need for a hug can cause crying.  
When their needs are met, the crying stops.  
This kind of crying is normal.  
It usually gets better after the baby is 3 months old.  
But if a child keeps crying even after you try to meet their basic needs, or if the crying lasts longer than usual, it may need more attention.

## Why Children Cry

Most crying has no serious medical cause.  
Less than 5 out of every 100 cases have a medical problem.  
About 95 out of every 100 cases are not due to a medical issue.  
One common reason for crying with no clear cause is colic.  
Colic means a baby cries a lot for no obvious reason.  
It usually happens in babies who are 4 months old or younger.  
The baby cries for at least 3 hours a day.  
This happens on 3 or more days each week.  
It lasts for more than 3 weeks.  
There is no illness or injury causing the crying.

## Checking on a Crying Child

If your child is crying a lot, it is important to look for a cause.  
Check if the baby is hungry, has a dirty diaper, or is too hot or cold.  
Look for signs of pain, such as a fever, vomiting, or trouble breathing.  
If the baby seems healthy and the crying does not stop, talk to a doctor.  
The doctor will check for any medical problems.  
If no medical issue is found, the crying is likely due to normal development.

## Helping a Crying Child

If a medical problem is found, treat it as directed by a doctor.  
If no medical cause is found, support for parents is very important.  
Babies often calm down when they are held close.  
Swaddling a baby in the first month can help reduce crying.  
Holding your baby can make the crying stop faster.  
If you feel overwhelmed or frustrated, it is okay to take a break.  
Put your baby in a safe place, like a crib, for a few minutes.  
This helps you stay calm and safe.  
Letting parents know it is okay to take a break can help prevent harm.  
Offering help and support services can also help parents who feel stressed.  
This can prevent future problems.

## Key Points

Crying is a normal part of growing up.  
It is most common in the first 3 months of life.  
Crying that lasts a long time may be due to a medical issue.  
But most crying is not caused by illness.  
Less than 5% of crying has a medical cause.  
Parents often feel upset when their baby cries a lot.  
Support and understanding can help both the baby and the parent.

# Pyruvate Metabolism Disorders

These are rare health problems that affect how the body uses energy from food. They happen when the body cannot properly break down a substance called pyruvate.

Pyruvate comes from the food we eat, especially carbohydrates and proteins. It helps make energy for our cells.

When pyruvate does not break down properly, it causes a buildup of lactic acid in the body. This can lead to serious health issues.

These disorders are passed from parents to children through genes. Both parents must pass on a faulty gene for the child to have the disorder.

## What Happens in These Disorders?

- A missing or faulty enzyme stops the body from processing pyruvate.
- This leads to low energy and too much lactic acid in the blood.
- The brain and muscles are often affected.
- Symptoms can start at any age, from infancy to adulthood.

## Common Symptoms

- Seizures
- Weak muscles
- Trouble walking or balancing
- Learning difficulties or intellectual disability
- Poor growth or failure to thrive

Illnesses and physical activity can make symptoms worse. They may lead to very high levels of lactic acid, which can be dangerous.

## How Are These Disorders Diagnosed?

Doctors can check for these disorders using:

- A skin sample to test enzyme activity
- A blood test to look at DNA
- Sometimes both tests

## Can These Disorders Be Prevented or Treated?

- There is no cure for most of these disorders.
- Some children may improve with special diets.
- Some may benefit from vitamin supplements, like thiamin.

Genetic testing can help parents understand their risk of having a child with one of these disorders.

---

## Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Deficiency

This disorder happens when the body lacks a group of enzymes needed to process pyruvate.

### Symptoms

- Some babies are born with brain problems.
- Others seem normal at birth but develop symptoms later.
- These include weak muscles, seizures, poor coordination, and balance issues.
- Many children have learning problems.

### Treatment

- There is no cure.
- Some children do better on a diet high in fat and low in carbohydrates.
- Vitamin thiamin may help some children.

---

## Pyruvate Carboxylase Deficiency

This is a very rare disorder. It happens when the body lacks an enzyme called pyruvate carboxylase.

### What Happens

- The body cannot make enough glucose from pyruvate.
- Lactic acid and ketones build up in the blood.
- This can be life-threatening.

### Symptoms

- Many children do not survive infancy.
- Survivors may have:
  - Delayed development
  - Seizures
  - Poor growth
  - Learning problems

Some children have milder symptoms.

### Treatment

- There is no cure.
- A special diet and thiamin supplements may help reduce symptoms in some cases.

---

# Galactosemia

Galactosemia is a rare condition you are born with. It happens when your body does not have enough of certain enzymes. These enzymes help change a sugar called galactose into another sugar called glucose.

The condition can cause several health problems. These include:
- Liver problems
- Kidney problems
- Learning and memory issues
- Cloudy lenses in the eyes (cataracts)
- Early loss of fertility in women

## How Is Galactosemia Diagnosed?

Doctors may suspect galactosemia based on symptoms. They then do tests to confirm it.

The main tests are:
- Blood tests to check galactose levels
- Tests on red blood cells to check enzyme activity
- DNA tests to look for gene changes

A simple urine test can also help. It checks for certain sugars in the urine. If galactose or a related sugar is found, it may point to galactosemia.

In the United States, all newborn babies are tested for galactosemia. This is part of routine newborn screening. The test checks for a missing enzyme called galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase.

## How Is Galactosemia Treated?

The main treatment is to stop eating any food that contains galactose.

Galactose is found in:
- Milk and dairy products (like cheese, yogurt, and butter)
- Breast milk
- Some infant formulas made from milk
- Many processed foods (as a sweetener)

You must follow a strict lactose-free diet. Lactose is a sugar that breaks down into galactose. Avoiding it helps prevent serious short-term harm. It can also improve some symptoms, like cataracts.

But even with a good diet, some people still have learning and thinking problems. These may not get better with treatment.

Some people with a specific type of galactosemia need a small amount of galactose. This is because galactose helps make a substance called UDP-galactose. This substance is needed for many body processes.

People on a special diet often need extra calcium and vitamins to stay healthy.

This is a free online database. It gives detailed information about genes, how they work, and where they are located in the body.

# Tigecycline

Tigecycline is a type of antibiotic. It belongs to a group called glycylcyclines. These are similar to another group of antibiotics called tetracyclines.

This medicine stops bacteria from making proteins. Without these proteins, bacteria cannot grow or multiply.

Tigecycline works against many bacteria that are hard to treat. This includes bacteria that do not respond to tetracyclines.

But studies show that people using tigecycline are more likely to die than those using other antibiotics. Because of this, doctors only use tigecycline when no other treatment options are available.

Tigecycline is given through a vein (IV). It is not taken by mouth.

---

## What is tigecycline used for?

- Complicated infections in the belly (abdomen)
- Complicated skin infections
- Pneumonia (lung infection)

It works against certain bacteria, including:
- *Escherichia coli*
- *Staphylococcus aureus*, including strains that are resistant to methicillin (like MRSA)
- Bacteria that live without much oxygen (anaerobes)

---

## Possible side effects

- Upset stomach
- Nausea or vomiting
- Diarrhea
- Increased sensitivity to sunlight
- Permanent tooth discoloration in unborn babies if used late in pregnancy
- Possible harm to bone and tooth development in unborn babies
- Higher risk of death compared to other antibiotics

Because of the higher risk of death, tigecycline is only used when no other antibiotics will work.

---

## Using tigecycline during pregnancy

Tigecycline can harm the baby’s teeth and bones if taken during pregnancy. It should not be used unless absolutely necessary.

---

## Using tigecycline while breastfeeding

It is not known if tigecycline passes into breast milk. It is also not known if it could harm a nursing baby. Talk to your doctor before using this medicine while breastfeeding.

# Tropical Sprue

Tropical sprue is a rare condition that affects how the body absorbs nutrients.  
It is likely caused by an infection in the small intestine.  
It leads to poor absorption of food and a type of anemia called megaloblastic anemia.  

The condition is most common in the Caribbean, southern India, and Southeast Asia.  
It affects both local people and travelers.  
It is rare in travelers who stay less than one month in these areas.  

Doctors think tropical sprue is caused by long-term infection with certain harmful bacteria in the small intestine.  
The disease is now very rare in the United States.  
Its rate has dropped over time, possibly because more people use antibiotics for traveler’s diarrhea.  

## Symptoms of Tropical Sprue

At first, people may have sudden diarrhea, fever, and feel very tired.  
After that, symptoms become milder but last longer.  
These include ongoing diarrhea, nausea, loss of appetite, stomach cramps, and constant tiredness.  

Stools may be pale, bulky, greasy, and smell very bad.  
This is called steatorrhea.  

Over time, the body loses important nutrients.  
Low levels of folate and vitamin B12 are common.  
Vitamin B2 deficiency can also happen.  
Anemia often develops because of low folate, low B12, or low iron.  

Other signs include losing weight, sore tongue, mouth sores, and swelling in the legs or feet.  

## How Doctors Diagnose Tropical Sprue

Doctors suspect tropical sprue in people who live in or have visited tropical areas and have anemia and symptoms of poor nutrient absorption.  

The best test is an endoscopy.  
This means a doctor uses a thin tube with a camera to look at the small intestine.  
A small sample of tissue (biopsy) is taken during the test.  

The tissue shows damage to the lining of the small intestine.  
The tiny finger-like parts (villi) are flattened.  
There are also signs of long-term inflammation.  

Doctors must rule out other causes, such as celiac disease or parasite infections.  
In tropical sprue, blood tests for celiac disease are negative.  

Blood tests check for anemia, low protein, low calcium, and low levels of iron, folate, and vitamin B12.  
A barium X-ray of the small intestine may show thickened folds, widened areas, and patchy barium patterns.  
A D-xylose test shows poor sugar absorption in over 90% of cases.  
But these tests are not needed to confirm the diagnosis.  

## Treatment of Tropical Sprue

Treatment lasts up to six months.  
The main medicine is tetracycline.  
Doxycycline can be used instead if needed.  

Folate is given by mouth for the first month.  
Vitamin B12 is given by injection for several weeks.  

Anemia improves quickly.  
Most people feel much better within days.  

Other missing nutrients are replaced as needed.  

If there is no improvement after four weeks, another condition may be present.  
The disease can come back after treatment, even if it seemed to be cured.

# Galactosemia

Galactosemia is a condition where a sugar called galactose builds up in the blood. This happens because the body lacks a needed enzyme to break down galactose. Galactose is part of a larger sugar called lactose, which is found in milk. When galactose builds up, it can harm the liver, kidneys, and eyes.

The condition is passed from parents to children through genes. Both parents must carry a copy of the faulty gene for a child to be affected. Most of the time, neither parent has symptoms.

## What Causes Galactosemia?

- A child gets galactosemia when both parents pass on a faulty gene.
- The faulty gene means the body cannot make a needed enzyme.
- Without this enzyme, galactose builds up in the blood.
- High levels of galactose can damage the liver, kidneys, and eyes.

## Symptoms of Galactosemia

Newborns with galactosemia may look healthy at first. But within days or weeks of drinking breast milk or formula, they may:

- Lose their appetite
- Vomit often
- Have yellow skin and eyes (this is called jaundice)
- Have diarrhea
- Stop growing normally

The condition can also affect the immune system. This makes infections more likely.

Many children develop cataracts. These are clouded lenses in the eyes. Girls may have problems with their ovaries. Most cannot get pregnant without help. Boys are not affected in this way.

If treatment is delayed, children may stay small. They may also have learning problems or not survive.

## How Is Galactosemia Diagnosed?

Doctors use two main tests:

- A blood test checks for high levels of galactose.
- A urine test checks for extra galactose.

All babies in the United States are tested for galactosemia shortly after birth. This is part of routine newborn screening.

If a parent has a child or sibling with galactosemia, they can get tested before having a child. This helps them know their risk.

A person who carries the faulty gene but does not have symptoms is called a carrier.

## How Is Galactosemia Treated?

The main treatment is to remove galactose from the diet.

- No milk or milk products are allowed.
- Babies are switched to a soy-based formula after diagnosis.
- Galactose is also found in small amounts in some fruits, vegetables, and seaweed. But doctors do not recommend avoiding these foods.
- Galactose is used as a sweetener in many processed foods. People with galactosemia must avoid these.

People with galactosemia must follow this diet for life.

Many people also need to take calcium and vitamin supplements to stay healthy.

## What Is the Outlook for People with Galactosemia?

If galactosemia is found at birth and treated early:

- The liver and kidneys usually stay healthy.
- Brain development starts out normal.

But even with good treatment, many children still face challenges:

- They may have a lower IQ than their siblings.
- They often have trouble with speech.
- They may have balance problems during their teenage years.
