# Osteosclerosis

Osteosclerosis is a type of bone disease where bones become too hard and dense.  
This happens because the body’s bone-breaking cells do not work properly.  
The bones grow too thick and strong, which can squeeze the space inside the bones where blood cells are made.  
When this space gets too small, it can lead to low blood cell counts.

This condition is part of a group of rare inherited diseases called osteopetroses.  
These diseases are passed down through families.  
They happen when the cells that break down old bone do not work right.  
This causes bones to become abnormally dense and misshapen.

---

## Osteopetrosis with Delayed Symptoms (Albers-Schönberg Disease)

This form of osteopetrosis causes bones to become too dense.  
It is caused by a problem in a gene called *CLCN7*.  
This gene helps bone-breaking cells work properly.  
The disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant way.  
This means only one parent needs to pass on the faulty gene.

Symptoms usually appear in childhood, teenage years, or young adulthood.  
It is less severe than the early-onset form.  
It affects about 1 in 20,000 people.  
It occurs in all parts of the world and across different ethnic groups.

Some people have no symptoms at all.  
Their health is usually normal.  
But some may develop facial weakness or hearing loss.  
This happens when extra bone presses on nerves in the skull.

Extra bone can also block the space inside bones where blood cells are made.  
This can lead to low blood cell counts.  
This can range from mild anemia to severe low counts of all blood cells (pancytopenia).

When the body tries to make more blood cells, it may do so in the liver and spleen.  
This causes these organs to grow larger.  
This can make anemia worse over time.

Bones look normal at birth.  
But over time, they become denser.  
Doctors often find the condition by accident during X-rays for other reasons.  
The bone changes are widespread but not even.  
The skull becomes very thick.  
The sinuses may be blocked.

The ends of the spine become thick and show a pattern called the **rugby-shirt appearance**.  
This is a horizontal banding look on X-rays.

Other problems can include broken bones, curved spine, hip joint damage, and bone infections in the jaw or elsewhere.

Some people need blood transfusions or surgery to remove the spleen to treat anemia.

---

## Osteopetrosis with Early Symptoms

This is a serious form of the disease.  
It appears at birth or in early infancy.  
It is inherited in an autosomal recessive way.  
This means both parents must pass on a faulty gene.

It is caused by a mutation in the *TCIRG1* gene.  
This gene is important for bone-breaking cells.  
The disease is rare, affecting about 1 in 250,000 people.

The bone-breaking cells do not work.  
This causes bone to grow too thick and block the space for blood cell production.  
This leads to severe low blood cell counts.

The disease is often life-threatening.  
Most children do not survive past their first year.

Early signs include poor growth, low weight, and not gaining weight as expected.  
They may bruise easily or bleed abnormally.  
They often have anemia.

Later, they may develop weakness in the nerves that control facial muscles, eye movement, and facial sensation.  
The liver and spleen may grow larger.

The main cause of death is bone marrow failure.  
This means the body cannot make enough blood cells.  
This leads to severe anemia, serious infections, or dangerous bleeding.

Doctors suspect this disease when a child has dense bones, anemia, unusual bleeding, frequent infections, and poor growth.

X-rays show bones are much denser than normal.  
Long bones show horizontal bands and lines.  
The ends of long bones, especially the upper arm and thigh bones, become shaped like bottles (flask-shaped).  
Bones inside bones (called endobones) form in the spine, pelvis, and long bones.  
The skull becomes thick.  
The spine shows the **rugby-shirt appearance**.

The best treatment is a bone marrow transplant.  
This has worked well in many cases.  
Some patients also respond to prednisone or interferon gamma.

---

## Osteopetrosis with Kidney Problems (Guibaud-Vainsel Syndrome; Marble Brain Disease)

This rare form of osteopetrosis causes bone and brain to become too dense.  
It also causes kidney problems.

It is inherited in an autosomal recessive way.  
It is caused by a mutation in the gene for carbonic anhydrase II.

This disease causes weakness, short stature, and poor growth.  
It leads to low weight and slow development.

Doctors diagnose it by seeing dense bones on X-rays.  
They also see calcium deposits in the brain.  
The kidneys do not work right.  
This is called renal tubular acidosis.  
Red blood cells have low levels of carbonic anhydrase.

A bone marrow transplant can fix the bone problems.  
But it does not help the kidney issues.

Treatment focuses on replacing lost salts and fluids.  
Patients take bicarbonate and other supplements to balance their body chemistry.

---

## Pyknodysostosis

Pyknodysostosis is a rare inherited disease.  
It is caused by a faulty *CTSK* gene.  
This gene makes a protein called cathepsin K.  
This protein helps break down bone.

People with this disease have bones that are dense but weak.  
They break easily.  
They are short in height.  
They have a small face, a receding chin, and misshapen teeth.

The disease is inherited in an autosomal recessive way.  
This means both parents must pass on a faulty gene.

Short stature becomes clear in early childhood.  
Adults are usually 150 cm (5 feet) or shorter.  
The skull is large.  
Hands and feet are short and wide.  
The tips of the fingers are short and thick.  
Nails are weak and deformed.  
Baby teeth do not fall out on time.

The whites of the eyes are blue.  
This is because the tissue under the eye is thin.  
The blood vessels show through.

The skull bones do not close properly.  
The soft spot on the head stays open.  
Bone breaks are common.

Doctors suspect pyknodysostosis when they see blue eyes, short height, and unusual bone features.

X-rays show dense bones.  
But they do not show the lines or bone-in-bone patterns seen in other forms.  
The face bones are underdeveloped.  
The jaw angle is wide.  
The collarbones are thin and may not form fully.  
The tips of the fingers are underdeveloped.

Growth hormone therapy may help improve height.  
Plastic surgery can fix serious facial and jaw problems.

# Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA)

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis is a group of childhood diseases. It starts before age 16. It causes long-term or repeated swelling and pain in the joints.

This condition can also affect other parts of the body. These include the eyes, skin, and internal organs.

## What You Need to Know

- JIA is not the same as adult rheumatoid arthritis in most children.
- A few children do have a type that is like adult rheumatoid arthritis.
- The exact cause is unknown.
- JIA is not passed down through families, but genes may play a role.
- JIA is not caused by an infection.

## Types of JIA

There are several types of JIA. Doctors decide which type a child has based on symptoms and test results.

### Oligoarticular JIA
- This is the most common type.
- It usually affects young girls.
- Only 4 or fewer joints are involved in the first 6 months.
- The knee is the most often affected joint.

### Polyarticular JIA
- This is the second most common type.
- It starts in late childhood.
- 5 or more joints are affected.
- It has two types: one with no rheumatoid factor and one with it.
- Rheumatoid factor is a substance in the blood linked to certain autoimmune diseases.
- Children with the rheumatoid factor-positive type often have symptoms like adults with rheumatoid arthritis.
- The same joint on both sides of the body may be affected (like both knees or both hands).
- Small joints in the hands and feet are often involved.

### Enthesitis-Related Arthritis
- This type causes joint pain and swelling where tendons and ligaments attach to bones.
- It often affects joints on one side of the lower body (like the hip, knee, ankle, or foot).
- It is more common in older boys.
- Some boys may also have joint pain in the lower spine.

### Psoriatic JIA
- This type often affects young girls, but can also affect older boys and girls equally.
- Some children have psoriasis, a skin disease with scaly patches.
- Others have a family history of psoriasis.

### Undifferentiated JIA
- This label is used when a child has JIA but does not fit clearly into any one type.
- Or when a child fits more than one type.

### Systemic JIA (Still Disease)
- This type causes joint pain and swelling.
- It also causes symptoms outside the joints.
- These include high fever, rash, swollen lymph nodes, and inflammation around the heart and lungs.

## Symptoms of JIA

JIA causes problems in the joints and sometimes in the eyes or skin.

### Joint Symptoms
- Joints may feel stiff when a child wakes up.
- Joints may swell and feel warm.
- Pain may come later, but it can be mild even with a lot of swelling.
- Pain often gets worse when the joint moves.
- A child may not want to walk or may limp.
- Some children have no pain at all.
- If not treated, joint pain can last for years.

### Enthesitis Symptoms
- Tenderness in the pelvis, hip bone, spine, kneecap, shin, Achilles tendon, or bottom of the foot.

### Eye Problems
- Eye inflammation can happen with any type of JIA.
- It is most common in oligoarticular JIA.
- It is rare in rheumatoid factor-positive polyarticular JIA and systemic JIA.
- The most common eye problem is inflammation of the iris (iridocyclitis).
- This usually causes no pain or redness.
- It may cause blurry vision or uneven pupils.
- If not treated, it can lead to scarring, cataracts, glaucoma, or permanent vision loss.
- Rarely, children with enthesitis-related arthritis may have red, painful eyes and sensitivity to light.

### Skin Problems
- Skin issues mainly happen in psoriatic JIA and systemic JIA.
- Children with psoriatic JIA may have rough, scaly skin patches.
- Fingers and toes may swell.
- Nails may have pits or come loose from the finger.

### Systemic JIA Symptoms
- A fever that comes every day and is highest in the afternoon or evening.
- The fever can reach 102.2 degrees Fahrenheit or higher.
- The fever may last for weeks.
- A child may feel tired and irritable.
- A rash appears in short bursts, often with fever.
- The rash is flat, pink or salmon-colored, and has clear centers.
- It mainly appears on the trunk and upper legs or arms.
- The rash may not appear in the same spot each time.

### Other Systemic Symptoms
- The liver, spleen, or lymph nodes may swell.
- Inflammation can affect the lining of the heart (pericarditis) or lungs (pleuritis).
- Inflammation inside the lungs can cause chest pain.
- Fluid may build up around the heart, lungs, or other organs.

## Complications of JIA

- JIA can slow down a child’s growth.
- If the jaw is affected, the chin may become small.
- Joints can become deformed if JIA is not treated.
- Even with treatment, long-term inflammation can damage joints over time.

## How Doctors Diagnose JIA

Diagnosis is based on:
- The child’s symptoms.
- A physical exam.

There is no single test that confirms JIA. But blood tests help doctors understand the type.

### Blood Tests
- Full blood count.
- Rheumatoid factor.
- Antinuclear antibodies.
- Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies.
- HLA-B27 antigen.

Most children with systemic JIA do not have rheumatoid factor or antinuclear antibodies.

Other tests may include:
- Ferritin.
- C-reactive protein (CRP).
- Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR).

High levels of CRP and ESR mean there is inflammation in the body.

### Eye Exams
- Children with antinuclear antibodies are at higher risk for eye inflammation.
- All children with JIA need regular eye checks, even if they have no symptoms.
- Children with oligoarticular or polyarticular JIA and antinuclear antibodies should see an eye doctor every 3 months.
- Those without antinuclear antibodies should see an eye doctor every 6 months.
- Children with systemic JIA should have an eye exam once or twice a year.

### X-rays
- Doctors may take X-rays to check for changes in bones or joints.

## Treatment of JIA

Treatment aims to reduce pain, stop joint damage, and help the child live a normal life.

### Medications

**Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drugs (DMARDs)**
- These drugs slow down the disease.
- They help prevent joint damage.
- Examples:
  - Methotrexate – fights inflammation.
  - Etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab – block a protein that causes inflammation.
  - Anakinra, canakinumab – block another inflammation-causing protein.
  - Tocilizumab – blocks a different inflammation protein.
  - Tofacitinib, upadacitinib – block an enzyme involved in inflammation.
  - Abatacept – blocks immune cells that cause inflammation.

**Corticosteroids**
- Doctors may inject them directly into a painful joint.
- Oral corticosteroids (like prednisone) are used only when needed.
- They are avoided if possible because they can cause side effects.
- If used, the lowest dose is given to reduce risks.
- Side effects can include slowed growth, weak bones (osteoporosis), cataracts, and bone death (osteonecrosis).

**Eye Treatment**
- Eye drops with steroids reduce inflammation.
- Eye drops that widen the pupil help prevent damage.
- If eye drops are not enough, methotrexate or other biologic drugs may be used.
- Surgery may be needed if the eye is damaged.

**NSAIDs (Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs)**
- These include naproxen and ibuprofen.
- They help reduce pain and swelling.
- They are most helpful for enthesitis-related arthritis.
- But they do not stop the disease from getting worse.

### Physical and Occupational Therapy
- Physical therapy helps improve movement, flexibility, and strength.
- Occupational therapy helps with daily tasks like writing or dressing.

## Outlook for Children with JIA

- About half of children go into remission (no symptoms) within 5 years of treatment.
- With early treatment, most children can live active, normal lives.
- Children with rheumatoid factor-positive polyarticular JIA tend to have a harder time.

**The Arthritis Foundation: Juvenile Arthritis**  
This site offers clear, helpful information about JIA in children. It covers types of arthritis, living with the condition, and how to move from pediatric care to adult care.

# Holy Basil

Holy basil is a plant that grows in India and nearby areas. It is also called tulsi. It is similar to the basil you use in cooking.

The plant has many natural chemicals. These include camphor, eucalyptol, eugenol, alpha and beta bisabolene, and beta caryophyllene. These chemicals may help fight bacteria and viruses. One of them, eugenol, may also help prevent cancer. More research is needed to confirm this.

## What People Say About Holy Basil

Some people believe holy basil helps the body handle stress. It is called an adaptogen. It may help with:

- Feeling less anxious or stressed  
- Lowering blood sugar in people with diabetes  
- Lowering cholesterol levels  
- Fighting off infections from bacteria or viruses  
- Healing wounds faster  
- Reducing swelling and pain

Most people can take holy basil by mouth for up to 8 weeks without harm. We do not know if it is safe to take longer than 8 weeks.

## What the Research Shows

There are not many strong studies in people that prove holy basil works for any health problem.

One study with 100 adults found that those who took holy basil felt less stressed and slept better than those who took a fake treatment (placebo).

Another small study with 40 people found that holy basil helped lower blood sugar after fasting and after eating.

A third study followed 60 people with diabetes for 90 days. One group took a diabetes medicine alone. The other group took the same medicine plus holy basil. The group that took both had better blood sugar control and better long-term blood sugar levels.

## Side Effects

Holy basil can cause stomach upset. Some people may feel sick to their stomach or have diarrhea.

It may not be safe for women who are pregnant or trying to get pregnant. In animal studies, large amounts of holy basil made it harder for a baby to grow in the womb. It also made pregnancies shorter. We do not know if this happens in people. Anyone trying to get pregnant should avoid holy basil.

We do not know if it is safe for women who are breastfeeding. No studies have looked at this.

Holy basil may lower thyroid hormone levels. This could make hypothyroidism worse.

It may also slow down blood clotting. This could increase the risk of bleeding during or after surgery.

## Interactions with Medicines

Holy basil may reduce how well thyroid hormone medicines work.

Because it slows blood clotting, it may increase the risk of bleeding in people who take blood thinners or medicines that stop blood cells from clumping.

Animal studies suggest holy basil may make barbiturates (a type of sleep medicine) stronger. This could make you more sleepy.

# What You Need to Know About Parasitic Infections

Parasites are tiny living things that live inside or on a person. They need a host to survive. The host is the person or animal the parasite lives in or on.

## Where Parasitic Infections Happen

- Parasitic infections are more common in places with dirty water and poor toilets.
- In places with clean water and good toilets, infections can still happen in people who travel from areas with poor sanitation.
- People with weak immune systems are also more likely to get these infections.

## How Parasites Get Into the Body

Parasites usually enter through the mouth or the skin.

- If they enter through the mouth, they are swallowed. They can stay in the gut or move into other parts of the body.
- Some parasites can go through the skin. This can happen when walking barefoot on dirty soil or swimming in contaminated water.

## Types of Parasites

There are three main types of parasites that affect people:

### 1. Protozoa
- These are tiny one-celled organisms.
- They live inside the body.
- They multiply by splitting into two.
- Examples: *Giardia*, *Entamoeba histolytica*, and *Plasmodium*.
- *Plasmodium* causes malaria, which spreads through mosquito bites.

### 2. Worms (Helminths)
- These are larger and made of many cells.
- They have organs like a real animal.
- They live inside the body.
- They lay eggs or make baby worms in the environment.
- Some need another animal (like a snail or pig) to grow before they can infect a person.
- Examples: hookworms, tapeworms, and flukes.

### 3. External Parasites (Ectoparasites)
- These live on or in the skin.
- They have organs and can move around.
- They lay eggs on or in the skin.
- Examples: lice, ticks, mites, bedbugs, and fleas.
- Ticks can cause Lyme disease and Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
- Mites cause scabies.
- Fleas can cause cat-scratch disease and plague.

## Where Infections Are Most Common

- Parasitic infections are more common in tropical and warm areas.
- Intestinal parasites are often linked to poor sanitation.
- People visiting these areas can get infected without knowing it.
- Doctors may not think of a parasite when someone returns home with symptoms.

In the United States and other wealthy countries, infections are more common in:
- Immigrants from areas with poor sanitation
- Travelers returning from such areas
- People with weak immune systems (like those with HIV or on certain medicines)

Some parasites are also found in the U.S., such as:
- Pinworms
- Trichomoniasis (a sexually transmitted infection)
- Toxoplasmosis
- Giardiasis and cryptosporidiosis (intestinal infections)

## How Parasites Spread

### Through the Mouth (Fecal-Oral Route)
This is one of the most common ways parasites spread.

- Feces (poop) from an infected person or animal can carry parasites.
- If someone touches something contaminated with this feces and then puts their fingers in their mouth, they can get sick.
- This can happen when:
  - Hands are not washed after using the toilet.
  - Food is touched by someone with dirty hands.
  - Water is drunk that has been polluted with sewage.
  - Raw shellfish (like oysters) are eaten from dirty water.
  - Fruits and vegetables are eaten that were washed in dirty water or grown in dirty soil.
  - Undercooked meat is eaten.
  - Mouth-to-anus contact happens during sex.
  - Swimming in pools, lakes, or oceans that have sewage in them.

### Through the Skin
Some parasites can go through the skin:
- Hookworms can enter through bare feet on dirty soil.
- Flukes (like schistosomes) can enter when swimming or bathing in contaminated water.

### Through Insect Bites
Insects can carry parasites from one person to another. These insects are called vectors.
- Mosquitoes carry the parasite that causes malaria.
- Blackflies carry the parasite that causes river blindness.

### Other Ways
Rarely, parasites can spread through:
- Blood transfusions
- Organ or bone marrow transplants
- Sharing needles
- From a pregnant person to their unborn baby

## How Doctors Diagnose Parasitic Infections

Doctors suspect a parasite if:
- A person has symptoms like stomach pain, diarrhea, or fever.
- The person lives in or has traveled to a place with poor sanitation.

To confirm the infection, doctors may test:
- Stool (poop)
- Blood
- Urine
- Sputum (phlegm)
- Skin or tissue samples

Tests may include:
- Looking at samples under a microscope.
- Testing for parasite proteins (antigen tests).
- Testing for parasite DNA.
- Checking for antibodies in the blood (proteins the body makes to fight infection).

Sometimes, doctors take a small piece of tissue (a biopsy) from the gut or skin to look for parasites. They may need to take several samples and test them more than once to find the parasite.

## How Parasitic Infections Are Treated

- Some infections go away on their own without treatment.
- Most infections are treated with antiparasitic medicines.
- These medicines kill parasites or reduce their numbers so symptoms go away.
- Some antibiotics and antifungal medicines also work against certain parasites.
- No one medicine works for all parasites.
- Some infections do not have a good treatment.

## How to Prevent Parasitic Infections

### Vaccines
- Only one parasite has a vaccine: malaria.
- The World Health Organization has two malaria vaccines: RTS,S and R21.
- Research is ongoing to make vaccines for other parasites like leishmaniasis, schistosomiasis, and hookworm.

### Travelers at Risk
- Immigrants returning to their home countries are at higher risk.
- They may have less immunity.
- They may not take health steps before travel.
- They often visit places with more disease than tourists.

### General Prevention Tips

Good hygiene and clean habits help prevent infection.

#### Wash Your Hands Often
- After using the toilet.
- After changing a diaper or cleaning a child.
- Before, during, and after cooking food.
- Before eating.
- Before and after caring for a sick person.
- Before and after treating a cut or wound.
- After touching animals or animal waste.

#### Keep Food and Water Safe
- Avoid drinking tap water in areas with poor sanitation.
- Drink only bottled, boiled, or filtered water.
- Do not swallow water when swimming in pools, lakes, or oceans.
- Even clear water can have parasites.
- Ice can carry disease if it is made from dirty water.

**Traveler’s Rule: Cook it, boil it, peel it, or forget it.**
- Do not eat:
  - Raw or undercooked meat, fish, shellfish, or eggs.
  - Unwashed fruits and vegetables.
  - Unpasteurized milk or fruit juice.
- Safe to eat raw: fruits with thick peels (like bananas) if you wash the outside before peeling.

#### Avoid Insect Bites
- Use insect sprays (like permethrin or pyrethrum) in homes.
- Use screens on doors and windows.
- Use air conditioning.
- Sleep under mosquito netting treated with insecticide.
- Use repellent with DEET on skin.
- Wear long pants and long sleeves, especially at night.
- Treat clothes with permethrin.

#### Take Malaria Medicine Before Travel
- If you are going to a place where malaria is common, take antimalarial medicine before, during, and after your trip.

# Congenital Gastrointestinal Anomalies – Simple Explanation

Most babies born with a problem in their digestive system have a blockage in the intestines.  
This blockage shows up soon after birth.  
Signs include trouble feeding, a swollen belly, vomiting, and not passing gas or stool.  
These signs usually appear at birth or within the first one or two days of life.

Some of these problems have a good chance of recovery.  
For example, malrotation often has a positive outcome.  
Other problems, like congenital diaphragmatic hernia, are more serious.  
About one in four babies with this condition does not survive.

## What Is Atresia?

Atresia means a part of the digestive tract did not form properly.  
It may have started to form but then stopped growing.  
Or it may have formed and then been damaged inside the womb.  
This damage can happen if blood flow to the area was cut off.

The most common types are:
- Esophageal atresia (a problem in the tube from the mouth to the stomach)
- Atresia in the middle part of the small intestine (jejunum and ileum)
- Atresia in the first part of the small intestine (duodenum)

## Immediate Care for the Baby

The baby needs quick treatment.  
A tube is placed through the nose into the stomach.  
This tube removes air and fluid from the stomach.  
It helps prevent vomiting.  
Vomiting can lead to lung infection.  
It also helps stop the belly from swelling more.  
A swollen belly can make breathing harder.

The baby must be taken to a special hospital for newborns who need surgery.  
This is very important.  
The baby’s body temperature must be kept stable.  
Low blood sugar must be prevented.  
The baby needs fluids with sugar and salts through a vein.  
This helps prevent dehydration and keeps the body’s chemistry balanced.  
The baby must also be protected from infections.  
These steps help the baby be ready for surgery.

## Other Health Problems May Be Present

Many babies with a digestive problem also have issues in other organs.  
For example:
- About 1 in 5 babies with gastroschisis have another problem.
- About half of babies with diaphragmatic hernia or anorectal malformation have another issue.
- Up to 7 in 10 babies with omphalocele have another problem.

So doctors check for problems in the brain, heart, and kidneys.

## Problems in the Upper Digestive Tract

Problems in the esophagus, stomach, or first part of the small intestine (duodenum) can be suspected if a prenatal ultrasound shows too much amniotic fluid.  
This happens because the baby cannot swallow and absorb the fluid normally.

After birth, once the baby is stable, a tube is passed through the nose into the stomach.  
If a lot of fluid comes out, especially if it looks green or yellow, it suggests a blockage in the upper digestive tract.  
If the tube cannot go into the stomach, it may mean the esophagus is not connected properly.

Once the baby is stable, X-rays are taken to get a clearer picture.

## Problems in the Middle and Lower Digestive Tract

Blockages in the middle and lower intestines can be caused by:
- Atresia in the jejunum or ileum
- Malrotation (when the intestines are twisted)
- Meconium ileus (a blockage caused by thick stool)

Blockages in the large intestine are usually due to:
- Meconium plug syndrome (a blockage caused by a hard plug of stool)
- Colonic atresia (a missing section in the large intestine)
- Anal atresia (a missing or blocked anus)

In many cases, there is no history of too much amniotic fluid.  
This is because the baby can still absorb some fluid before the blockage.

Most babies with these problems show symptoms in the first few days of life.  
They have trouble feeding, a swollen belly, and vomit.  
The vomit may be green or look like stool.  
They may pass a small amount of meconium at first, but then stop passing stool.

Malrotation, intestinal duplication, and Hirschsprung disease can show up at different times.  
They may appear in the first few days or even years later.  
Hirschsprung disease can also cause a hole in the large intestine in newborns.

## How Doctors Diagnose and Treat

The baby must not eat or drink anything by mouth.  
A tube is placed through the nose into the stomach.  
This prevents more swelling and stops vomit from being breathed into the lungs.  
The baby’s fluid and salt levels must be corrected.  
An X-ray of the belly is done.

A contrast enema (a special X-ray using a liquid) can help show the problem.  
It can also help clear the blockage in some cases, like meconium plug syndrome or meconium ileus.  
If Hirschsprung disease is suspected, a small sample of rectal tissue must be taken for testing.

## Problems with the Belly Wall

Some babies are born with a hole in the belly wall.  
This allows the intestines or other organs to push out through the opening.  
Examples include:
- Omphalocele (organs push out through the belly button area)
- Gastroschisis (organs push out through a hole near the belly button)

## Diaphragmatic Hernia

This is a hole in the diaphragm.  
The diaphragm is the muscle that separates the chest from the belly.  
When the hole is present, organs from the belly can move into the chest.  
This includes the intestines, stomach, and liver.  
This can stop the lungs from growing properly.  
This condition is serious and needs urgent care.

## Meckel Diverticulum

This is a small pouch that forms in the small intestine.  
It is a leftover from the umbilical cord.  
It is found in less than 1 to 3 out of every 100 people.  
Most people with this pouch have no symptoms.  
But in a few, it can cause a blockage or bleeding in the intestines.

# Secondary Iron Overload

Secondary iron overload means too much iron builds up in the body. This can happen for several reasons.

- People take too many iron supplements.
- People get many blood transfusions.
- The body cannot make healthy red blood cells. This leads to too many red blood cells breaking down.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people with mild iron overload feel no symptoms.  
Some people feel weak and tired.  
In rare cases, too much iron can damage organs.  
Damage can affect the heart, liver, or glands that make hormones.

Symptoms of serious iron overload include:
- Scarring of the liver (cirrhosis)
- Diabetes
- Skin that looks bronze or dark
- Trouble getting or keeping an erection
- Heart problems (rare)
- Joint pain
- Higher chance of liver cancer
- Trouble getting pregnant (infertility)
- An underactive thyroid gland (hypothyroidism)

## What Causes It?

Iron overload can happen in people with certain health problems:

- Inherited blood disorders like sickle cell disease, thalassemia, or sideroblastic anemias.
- Conditions where red blood cells break down too fast (hemolytic anemias), such as hereditary spherocytosis or pyruvate kinase deficiency.
- A condition called myelodysplasia, where red blood cells do not form properly.

In these cases, the body may absorb more iron than it needs. But it cannot use all the iron because it cannot make enough healthy red blood cells. This causes iron to build up.

Iron can also build up from:
- Taking too much iron medicine for too long.
- Getting many blood transfusions.

Men and women after menopause usually do not need iron supplements. If they take them, they may get too much iron. But this usually does not cause serious harm.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use blood tests to check for iron overload.  
They test for:
- Iron levels in the blood.
- Ferritin, a protein that stores iron.
- Transferrin, a protein that carries iron in the blood.

Sometimes doctors use:
- A liver MRI scan to see how much iron is in the liver.
- A liver biopsy (a small sample of liver tissue) to check for damage.

## How Is It Treated?

The goal is to lower the amount of iron in the body.

Some people can have blood removed (phlebotomy).  
But many people with secondary iron overload also have anemia.  
Removing blood would make anemia worse.  
So most people get iron chelation therapy instead.

Iron chelation therapy uses medicine to bind to extra iron and help the body get rid of it.

Medicines used include:
- Deferasirox (taken by mouth).
- Deferiprone (taken by mouth).
- Deferoxamine (given through a needle under the skin or into a vein).

Sometimes doctors give deferasirox and deferiprone together.

Oral chelation medicines (by mouth) work well to lower iron levels.  
Side effects may include:
- Stomach pain.
- Diarrhea.
- Skin rash.

These medicines can also harm the liver or kidneys.  
So blood tests are done regularly to check how well these organs are working.

Deferoxamine is given as an infusion, usually overnight.  
Side effects may include:
- Upset stomach.
- Low blood pressure.
- Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis).

Long-term use may cause hearing or vision problems.

## More Information

The following English-language resource may be helpful.  
Note: The Manual is not responsible for the content on this site.

**Iron Disorders Institute**  
This group gives information about conditions that cause too much or too little iron.  
It includes details on testing and tips for living with these conditions.

# Prolactinoma

A prolactinoma is a noncancerous growth in the pituitary gland.  
The pituitary gland is a small organ at the base of the brain.  
It helps control many body functions, including hormone levels.

The most common symptom of a prolactinoma is galactorrhea.  
Galactorrhea means milk comes from the breast without being pregnant or breastfeeding.  
This can happen in both men and women, but it is more common in women.

## What Causes a Prolactinoma?

Prolactinomas are made of cells called lactotrophs.  
These cells make a hormone called prolactin.  
Prolactin helps the body make milk after childbirth.

Prolactin levels are usually kept low by a brain chemical called dopamine.  
When dopamine is low, prolactin levels go up.  
This can lead to a prolactinoma.

Most prolactinomas are small (less than 10 millimeters).  
These are called microadenomas.  
Some are larger (more than 10 millimeters).  
These are called macroadenomas.

In women, most prolactinomas are small when found.  
In men, they are often larger and more likely to cause symptoms.

Other things can raise prolactin levels too.  
These include:
- Certain medicines (like some antipsychotics, blood pressure drugs, and painkillers)
- Low thyroid function (hypothyroidism)
- Kidney problems
- Breast stimulation
- Pregnancy
- Stress
- Head injuries
- Tumors in the brain
- Liver disease
- Chest injuries or scars
- Some types of cancer (like lung or kidney cancer)

## What Are the Symptoms?

### In Women:
- Milk leaking from the breast without being pregnant or breastfeeding
- Missed or irregular periods
- Less interest in sex
- Pain during sex
- Dryness in the vagina

Some women may still have normal estrogen levels.  
But high prolactin can stop the body from releasing other hormones needed for ovulation.

Some women may also have signs of too much male hormone, like extra body hair.

### In Men:
- Headaches
- Vision problems (like blurred or double vision)
- Low sex drive
- Trouble getting or keeping an erection

Men often have larger tumors when they are first diagnosed.  
This can cause more serious symptoms.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

To find out if you have a prolactinoma, your doctor will:
- Check your blood for prolactin levels
- Test your thyroid function (TSH and T4)
- Do a brain scan (MRI or CT)

High prolactin levels (usually more than 5 times normal) suggest a prolactinoma.  
The higher the level, the more likely it is a tumor.

A brain scan can show if there is a tumor in the pituitary gland.  
MRI with contrast is the best test for small tumors.  
CT scans can be used if MRI is not possible.

Your doctor may also check:
- Hormone levels for sex and fertility
- Vision, especially if the tumor is large

A trial of medicine can help confirm the diagnosis.  
If the tumor shrinks and prolactin drops, it is likely a prolactinoma.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on:
- Your sex
- The size of the tumor
- Your symptoms
- The cause of high prolactin

### First Step: Medicine
- Most people start with a medicine called a dopamine agonist.
- This medicine lowers prolactin and often shrinks the tumor.
- Common medicines include cabergoline and bromocriptine.

### For Larger Tumors (Macroadenomas):
- Medicine is still the first choice.
- If the medicine does not work well, surgery may be needed.
- Radiation therapy is an option if surgery is not possible and medicine fails.

### For Small Tumors (Microadenomas):
- Medicine is used only if symptoms are bothersome.
- If there are no symptoms, your doctor may just watch the tumor over time.

## Key Points

- The most common sign of a prolactinoma is milk leaking from the breast.
- The most common cause of milk leaking is a pituitary tumor.
- Many other conditions and medicines can also cause milk leakage.
- Blood tests and brain scans are needed to find the cause.
- For small tumors, medicine is used only if symptoms are troubling.
- For large tumors, medicine is the first treatment. Surgery or radiation may be needed if medicine does not work.

# Mouth, Nose, and Throat Cancers – Simple Explanation

## What Are These Cancers?

- Each year, more than 70,000 people in the United States get cancer in the mouth, nose, or throat.
- These cancers are more common in men than in women.
- This is partly because more men smoke than women.
- Men are also more likely to have a certain virus called human papillomavirus (HPV) in the mouth or throat.
- Most people with these cancers are between 50 and 70 years old.
- But cancers caused by HPV often happen in younger people.

Doctors often talk about these cancers together because they are similar in many ways.

## What Causes These Cancers?

- Over 90% of these cancers start in flat cells that line the inside of the mouth, nose, or throat. These are called squamous cells.
- Most people with these cancers use tobacco or drink alcohol, or both.
- Some cancers are caused by viruses.
  - HPV can cause cancer in the mouth and throat.
  - The Epstein-Barr virus can cause cancer in the upper part of the throat (nasopharynx).

## Where Do These Cancers Usually Start?

The most common places are:

- The voice box (larynx)
- Inside the mouth, including:
  - The tongue
  - The bottom of the mouth
  - The hard roof of the mouth (hard palate)
- The middle part of the throat (oropharynx), including:
  - The back wall of the mouth
  - The base of the tongue
  - The tonsils
  - The soft roof of the mouth (soft palate)

Less common places include:

- The hollow spaces in the bones around the nose (paranasal sinuses)
- The inside of the nose (nasal cavity and passages)
- The upper throat (nasopharynx)
- The lower part of the throat (hypopharynx)
- The salivary glands

For information about thyroid cancer or skin cancer, see those topics.  
For cancers in the bones, such as the jawbone, see the section on bone cancers.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on where the cancer is. Common signs include:

- A hoarse voice that does not go away
- A lump in the neck
- A sore or growth in the mouth that does not heal
- Trouble swallowing
- Weight loss due to difficulty eating
- Red or white patches in the mouth (these can be early signs)

## How Are These Cancers Diagnosed?

Doctors use several steps to find and confirm cancer.

### Step 1: Physical Exam
- A doctor or dentist checks the mouth, nose, and throat during a routine visit.
- Some cancers can be seen or felt even before symptoms appear.

### Step 2: Endoscopy
- If symptoms are present, the doctor uses a thin, flexible tube with a camera (called an endoscope) to look deeper into the mouth, nose, and throat.

### Step 3: Biopsy
- A small sample of tissue is taken from the suspicious area.
- This is done with a needle or a small cut using a scalpel.
- The tissue is checked under a microscope to see if cancer is present.

### Step 4: Staging Tests
- These tests show how far the cancer has spread.
- Doctors use staging to plan the best treatment.
- Staging looks at:
  - The size of the tumor
  - How deeply it has grown into nearby tissues
  - Whether it has spread to lymph nodes in the neck
  - Whether it has spread to other parts of the body (called metastasis)

Stages range from I (least advanced) to IV (most advanced).

### Imaging Tests
- Common tests include:
  - CT scan (computed tomography)
  - MRI scan (magnetic resonance imaging)
  - Sometimes a PET scan (positron emission tomography)
- For oropharyngeal cancer, doctors also check the person’s HPV status.

## What Is the Outlook?

- The outcome depends on the type, location, cause, and stage of the cancer.
- Early diagnosis and treatment lead to better results.
- People with HPV-related mouth and throat cancers tend to do better than those whose cancer was caused by smoking or drinking alcohol.

## How Can These Cancers Be Prevented?

- Stop using tobacco in any form (cigarettes, cigars, chewing tobacco).
- Limit alcohol use.
- Removing these risks helps prevent cancer from coming back after treatment.
- Vaccines against HPV can help prevent some types of mouth and throat cancers.

## How Are These Cancers Treated?

Treatment depends on the cancer’s stage, location, and other factors. A team of specialists works together to plan care.

### Main Treatments
- Surgery
- Radiation therapy
- Sometimes chemotherapy

### Key Points:
- Surgery and radiation are the most common treatments.
- Chemotherapy is not usually the first treatment, but it may be added to other treatments.
- Palliative care is important for managing symptoms and improving quality of life.

### Palliative Care
- This is care focused on relieving pain and other problems.
- It helps people feel better, even if the cancer cannot be cured.
- Specialists work on:
  - Pain relief
  - Difficulty eating
  - Choking on mucus or saliva
- Palliative care may include:
  - Surgery
  - Radiation
  - Chemotherapy
- For example, if a tumor causes pain but cannot be removed, radiation can shrink it and reduce pain.

# Hydrocephalus (Enlarged Head)

Hydrocephalus means too much fluid builds up in the brain.  
This extra fluid can make the brain’s empty spaces grow larger.  
It can also raise pressure inside the skull.

## What Causes Hydrocephalus?

Hydrocephalus can be present at birth or happen after birth.  
It has two main types:

- **Obstructive hydrocephalus**: A block stops fluid from flowing where it should.
- **Communicating hydrocephalus**: The body cannot absorb the fluid properly.

Scientists have found many genes linked to hydrocephalus.  
Some of these genes also cause other brain problems.  
For example:
- Mutations in the *SLC12A6* and *SLC12A7* genes often cause both hydrocephalus and a brain defect called schizencephaly.
- These changes are passed down through families in an autosomal dominant pattern.
- Mutations in *LICAM1* and *AP1S2* are linked to the X chromosome.
- Mutations in *CCDC88C* and *MPDZ* are inherited in an autosomal recessive way.

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

The symptoms depend on whether pressure in the skull is high.

### In Babies:
- They may cry in a high-pitched way.
- They may be very fussy or irritable.
- They may vomit often.
- They may seem very sleepy or hard to wake.
- Their eyes may not line up properly (strabismus).
- The soft spot on their head (fontanelle) may bulge out.

### In Older Children:
- They may say they have a headache.
- They may have trouble seeing clearly.
- They may have both problems.

A swollen optic nerve (papilledema) is a late sign.  
If this is not seen, it does not mean hydrocephalus is not present.

Long-term hydrocephalus can lead to:
- Early puberty in girls.
- Trouble learning, focusing, remembering, or thinking clearly.
- Seizures.
- Vision loss.
- Problems with planning, organizing, and solving problems.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

### Before Birth:
- A routine ultrasound scan can find hydrocephalus.

### After Birth:
- If a baby’s head is growing too fast, doctors may suspect hydrocephalus.
- The soft spot on the head may bulge.
- The skull bones may be far apart.

Other conditions can cause a large head too.  
These include:
- Bleeding in the brain (subdural hematoma).
- Fluid-filled brain cysts (porencephalic cysts).
- Brain tumors.

Some large heads are due to brain diseases like Alexander disease or Canavan disease.  
Others are just a normal, inherited trait with extra fluid around a healthy brain.

To confirm hydrocephalus, doctors use imaging tests:
- **Ultrasound** for newborns and young babies (if the soft spot is still open).
- **CT scan** or **MRI** for older babies and children.

Once diagnosed, doctors use CT or ultrasound to check if the condition is getting worse.  
If a child has seizures, an EEG (brain wave test) may help.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on how serious the condition is and whether it is getting worse.

### Mild Cases:
- Doctors may just watch and check the head size and brain scans over time.
- In some cases, they may remove fluid from the brain with a needle (ventricular tap) or through the lower back (lumbar puncture).
- This can help lower pressure temporarily.
- These methods may also help reverse hydrocephalus caused by bleeding in the brain.

### Severe or Growing Cases:
- A shunt is usually needed.
- A shunt is a tube that drains extra fluid from the brain to another part of the body.
- Most shunts go from the brain to the belly (peritoneal cavity).
- Some go to the heart (right atrium), but this is rare.

When a shunt is placed in a baby whose soft spot is closed, the brain can shrink fast.  
This can cause bleeding under the skull.  
If the soft spot is still open, the skull can shrink too.  
So doctors often recommend placing the shunt before the soft spot closes.

### Another Option: Third Ventriculostomy
- A small hole is made in the brain using a camera (endoscope).
- This lets fluid flow out of the brain’s center into the space around the brain.
- This procedure is often done with removal of part of the fluid-making tissue (choroid plexus).
- It is becoming more common in the United States.
- It is helpful in places where follow-up care is hard to get.
- It may be enough treatment for some types of hydrocephalus, like those caused by a narrow passage in the brain.

### Temporary Shunt:
- A shunt to the space just under the scalp (subgaleal space) may be used in babies.
- This is only for short-term use.
- It may help avoid a permanent shunt.

### Can Shunts Be Removed?
- Some children grow out of needing a shunt.
- But doctors rarely remove shunts because of the risk of bleeding and brain injury.

### Fetal Surgery?
- Surgery on a baby in the womb to fix hydrocephalus has not worked well so far.

## Key Points

- Hydrocephalus is usually caused by a block in fluid flow.  
  It can also happen if the body cannot absorb the fluid.

- If the condition starts before the skull bones close, the head will grow larger.  
  The soft spot may bulge.

- Symptoms mostly appear when pressure in the skull is high.  
  Babies may cry loudly, be irritable, vomit, be sleepy, or have crossed eyes.

- Doctors use ultrasound before birth and in newborns.  
  They use CT or MRI for older children.

- Treatment depends on the cause, how bad it is, and whether it is getting worse.  
  Options include watching, removing fluid, or placing a shunt.

# Pressure on the Spinal Cord

Pressure on the spinal cord can cause back or neck pain, tingling, weak muscles, and other problems.

The spinal cord runs through the spine. It sends signals between your brain and the rest of your body. When pressure builds on the spinal cord, it can stop these signals. This can lead to serious symptoms.

## What Can Cause Pressure on the Spinal Cord?

Pressure can come from:

- Broken or shifted bones in the spine  
- Blood buildup (hematoma)  
- Pus from an infection (abscess)  
- Tumors (cancer or non-cancer)  
- A disk in the spine that has torn or bulged (herniated disk)  

Some of these causes happen fast. Others build up slowly over time.

### Fast-Onset Pressure (Minutes to Days)

This type of pressure often comes from:

- A sudden injury, like a fall or car crash  
- A broken or dislocated bone  
- A blood clot (hematoma)  
- A disk that has torn or bulged  

Sometimes bones that are weak from cancer or osteoporosis break with little or no injury. This can cause sudden pressure.

### Slow-Onset Pressure (Months to Years)

This type of pressure builds over time. Causes include:

- Wear and tear in the neck (cervical spondylosis)  
- Slow-growing tumors  

## Symptoms of Pressure on the Spinal Cord

### Mild Pressure

You may feel:

- Pain in your back or neck  
- Slight weakness in your arms or legs  
- Tingling or numbness  
- Changes in how your skin feels  
- Trouble getting or keeping an erection (in men)  

If the lower back is affected, pain may go down one or both legs. If the neck is affected, pain may go down the arms. The area may be tender to touch. You might lose reflexes or have trouble urinating.

### Severe Pressure

You may have:

- Strong muscle weakness  
- Numbness in your arms or legs  
- Trouble urinating or passing stool  
- Loss of bladder or bowel control  

If all signals stop, you may become paralyzed. If the neck is affected, you might have trouble breathing.

Once symptoms start, they can get worse quickly. This can happen in minutes, hours, or days.

## How Doctors Diagnose Pressure on the Spinal Cord

You need to see a doctor right away if you have these symptoms.

### Step 1: Physical Exam

Your doctor will check your:

- Strength in your arms and legs  
- Sensation (feeling) in your skin  
- Reflexes  
- Bladder and bowel control  

Based on your symptoms, your doctor can guess where the pressure is in your spine.

### Step 2: Imaging Tests

You will likely have one of these tests:

- **MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging):** This gives a clear picture of the spinal cord and surrounding tissues. It is the best test for finding pressure.
- **Myelography with CT scan:** If MRI is not available, this test is used. It involves a spinal tap to inject a special dye into the space around the spinal cord. Then a CT scan is done to see if the spinal cord is blocked.

These tests can show:

- Broken or shifted bones  
- Herniated disks  
- Blood clots  
- Abscesses  
- Tumors  
- Areas of swelling  

If the cause is a broken bone from an injury, X-rays may also be taken. They are fast and help doctors see the bones clearly.

### Step 3: Confirming the Cause

If a mass is found but its cause is unclear, your doctor may:

- Take a small sample of tissue (biopsy) to test  
- Use a needle guided by CT scan to get the sample  
- Or do surgery to get the sample  

This helps confirm if the mass is cancer or something else.

## How Doctors Treat Pressure on the Spinal Cord

Treatment depends on the cause. But in most cases, surgery is needed.

### Immediate Treatment

If you have partial or recent loss of function, treatment must start right away. Acting fast can prevent permanent damage.

### Surgery

Surgery is done when:

- Symptoms are getting worse  
- A biopsy is needed  
- The spine is unstable  
- A tumor is present or returns after treatment  
- An abscess or blood clot is suspected  

Surgery can remove the pressure. It may also involve placing rods, screws, or pins to stabilize the spine.

### Medicines

- **Corticosteroids (like dexamethasone or methylprednisolone):** These are given through a vein. They reduce swelling around the spinal cord. This helps relieve pressure. They are used right away for tumors, abscesses, or hematomas.

### Treatment by Cause

#### If a Tumor Is the Cause

- High-dose corticosteroids are given first  
- Then surgery to remove the tumor  
- Radiation therapy may follow, or be used instead of surgery  

#### If an Abscess Is the Cause

- A neurosurgeon drains the pus as soon as possible  
- Antibiotics are given to fight infection  
- If symptoms are mild, a needle may be used to drain the pus instead of surgery  

#### If a Blood Clot (Hematoma) Is the Cause

- The blood is drained through surgery  
- If you have a bleeding disorder or take blood thinners, you get medicine to reverse the effect  
- You may also get a blood transfusion to help stop bleeding  

## Important Notes

- Pressure on the spinal cord is a medical emergency.  
- Early treatment can save function and prevent permanent damage.  
- Always seek medical help right away if you have back or neck pain with weakness, numbness, or bladder/bowel problems.

# Tibial Torsion

The shin bone (tibia) can be twisted when a baby is born. This twist can go in two directions: outward (called external torsion) or inward (called internal torsion).

## External Tibial Torsion

This type of twist is normal as a child grows. At birth, the shin bone is straight. By adulthood, it naturally twists outward by about 20 degrees. This twist usually does not cause any problems.

## Internal Tibial Torsion

Most babies are born with some inward twist of the shin bone. This often gets better as the child grows. But if the twist is very strong, it may be a sign of a nerve or muscle problem. It can also happen in a condition called Blount disease.

A strong inward twist can cause a child to walk with toes pointing inward. It may also lead to bowlegs.

## How Doctors Check for Tibial Torsion

Doctors measure the twist using simple steps:

- The child lies on their stomach.
- The knees are bent to 90 degrees.
- The doctor measures the angle between the foot and the thigh.

In most children, the foot points about 10 degrees outward compared to the thigh. This measurement can also be done while the child sits. The doctor draws a line between the bony bumps on each side of the ankle.

## Treatment

In most cases, the shin bone straightens on its own by age 5 or 6. No treatment is needed.

If the twist is very severe, the child may need special support. This can include:

- Orthotics (special shoe inserts)
- A cast
- Leg braces

These help guide the bone into a better position as the child grows.

# Pleural Effusion – Simple Explanation

Pleural effusion means fluid builds up in the space between the two layers of the thin membrane that covers the lungs.

This fluid normally stays very thin. But when too much builds up, it can cause problems.

---

## What Causes Pleural Effusion?

Many different health issues can cause fluid to build up in the space around the lungs. Some common causes include:

- Heart failure  
- Cancer  
- Pneumonia  
- Blood clots in the lung (pulmonary embolus)  
- Recent heart surgery, like bypass surgery  
- Injury to the chest  
- Liver disease (cirrhosis)  
- Kidney failure  
- Autoimmune diseases like lupus or rheumatoid arthritis  
- Pancreatitis (inflammation of the pancreas)  
- Tuberculosis  
- Nephrotic syndrome (a kidney problem that causes protein in the urine and high blood pressure)  
- Peritoneal dialysis (a treatment for kidney failure)  
- Some medicines, such as hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, phenytoin, chlorpromazine, methysergide, interleukin-2, nitrofurantoin, bromocriptine, dantrolene, and procarbazine

---

## Types of Fluid in the Pleural Space

The kind of fluid can help doctors find the cause.

- **Watery fluid (transudate):** Often caused by heart failure or liver disease.  
- **Fluid rich in protein (exudate):** Often caused by infection, cancer, or viral illness.

Other rare types of fluid include:

- **Blood in the pleural space (hemothorax):** Usually from a chest injury. Rarely, a blood vessel can burst without injury, or a bulging aorta (aortic aneurysm) can leak blood into the space.  
- **Pus in the pleural space (empyema):** Happens when pneumonia or a lung abscess spreads into the space. It can also happen after chest wounds, chest surgery, a tear in the esophagus, or an abdominal abscess.  
- **Milky fluid (chylothorax):** Caused by injury or blockage of the main chest lymph duct (thoracic duct), often due to a tumor.

---

## Symptoms of Pleural Effusion

Many people have no symptoms at all.

The most common symptoms are:

- Trouble breathing  
- Chest pain

### Chest Pain

The chest pain is often sharp and gets worse when you breathe deeply or cough. It is called pleuritic pain.

- The pain is usually felt in the chest wall, right where the lung or pleura is inflamed or infected.
- Sometimes the pain is felt in the upper belly, neck, or shoulder. This is called referred pain.

Pleuritic pain can also be caused by other conditions, such as:
- Pneumonia  
- Broken ribs  
- Blood clots in the lung  
- Viral infections  
- Pancreatitis  
- Rheumatoid arthritis  
- Lupus

As fluid builds up, the pain may go away. But the fluid can make it hard for the lungs to expand, which causes shortness of breath.

---

## How Is Pleural Effusion Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find out if you have pleural effusion and what is causing it.

### 1. Chest X-ray
- Shows if fluid is in the pleural space.
- Small amounts of fluid may not show up.

### 2. Ultrasound of the Chest
- Helps find small amounts of fluid that a chest x-ray might miss.

### 3. Thoracentesis
- A doctor uses a needle to take a sample of the fluid.
- The fluid is checked for:
  - How it looks (clear, cloudy, bloody)
  - Chemical makeup
  - Presence of bacteria (including tuberculosis)
  - Number and type of cells
  - Cancer cells

### 4. CT Scan (Computed Tomography)
- Gives a clearer picture of the lungs and fluid.
- Can show pneumonia, tumors, abscesses, or other problems.
- Sometimes a special dye is used (CT angiography) to check blood vessels for clots.

### 5. Thoracoscopy
- A doctor inserts a small camera into the chest to look at the pleural space.
- May be done if the cause is still unclear.
- A small tissue sample (biopsy) may be taken from the pleura or lung.

Sometimes, even after all tests, doctors cannot find the cause.

---

## How Is Pleural Effusion Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause and how much fluid is present.

### Small Effusions (No Symptoms)
- No treatment may be needed.
- The underlying condition must still be treated.
- Pain relief medicine may be given until the fluid goes away.

### Larger Effusions (Causing Shortness of Breath)
- Fluid must be drained to relieve symptoms.
- Drainage often helps breathing right away.

#### Drainage Methods

**Thoracentesis:**
- A thin needle is used to remove fluid.
- The area between two lower ribs is numbed.
- A small tube (catheter) may be guided over the needle to reduce the risk of lung injury.
- This method is often used for diagnosis, but can also drain enough fluid to help breathing.

**Chest Tube:**
- Used for large amounts of fluid.
- A thin tube is inserted between two ribs after numbing the area.
- The tube is connected to a drainage system that keeps air out.
- A chest x-ray checks the tube’s position.
- If the tube is blocked or bent, drainage may not work.
- Thick or clotted fluid may not drain well.

#### If the Effusion Is Caused by Pneumonia
- Antibiotics are needed.
- A fluid sample is taken for testing.
- If the fluid is pus or has certain signs, a chest tube is used to drain it.
- If scar tissue has formed and divided the fluid into pockets, drainage is harder.
- Doctors may use:
  - Fibrinolytic medicines (to break up clots)
  - Dornase alfa (to thin thick fluid)
- These medicines can help drainage and may avoid surgery.

#### If Surgery Is Needed
- Two options:
  - **Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS):** A camera and tools are used through small cuts.
  - **Thoracotomy:** A larger cut is made in the chest.
- During surgery, thick scar tissue on the lung is removed so the lung can expand fully.

#### If the Effusion Is Caused by Cancer
- Fluid often comes back quickly.
- Draining the fluid and giving cancer medicine may help stop more fluid from building up.
- A small tube can stay in the chest for regular drainage into special bottles.
- If fluid keeps coming back, doctors may seal the pleural space (pleurodesis).
  - All fluid is drained first.
  - A medicine (like doxycycline, bleomycin, or talc) is put into the space.
  - This causes the two layers of the pleura to stick together.
  - No space is left for more fluid.
- Pleurodesis can also be done using a camera (thoracoscopy).

#### If the Effusion Is Caused by Chylothorax (Milky Fluid)
- The goal is to stop the leak in the lymph duct.
- Treatment may include:
  - Surgery
  - Chemotherapy
  - Radiation therapy
- These are used if a tumor is blocking the duct.

---

## Summary

- Pleural effusion means fluid builds up around the lungs.
- It can be caused by many conditions, including heart failure, infection, cancer, and injury.
- Symptoms include shortness of breath and chest pain.
- Diagnosis uses x-rays, ultrasound, fluid tests, and sometimes CT scans or surgery.
- Treatment depends on the cause and amount of fluid.
- Small effusions may not need treatment.
- Larger ones are drained with a needle or chest tube.
- Special treatments like pleurodesis or surgery may be needed for cancer or persistent fluid.

Always treat the underlying cause.

# Hammer Toe Deformity

A hammer toe is a condition where a toe bends upward at the middle joint. This causes the toe to look like a hammer. It usually affects the second toe, but other smaller toes can be involved too.

## What Causes Hammer Toe?

The main cause is an imbalance in the tendons that move the toe. These tendons pull too hard on one side, which forces the toe out of place. This imbalance can happen because of:

- A past injury to the foot or toe  
- A family history of foot problems  
- Having long toes  
- A bunion (a bony bump on the big toe)  
- Certain health conditions like rheumatoid arthritis or nerve problems (such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease)

When the toe bends too much, it can become stiff and stay in a bent position. Over time, this can cause the toe to rub against the inside of the shoe. This rubbing leads to pain and skin problems.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may feel pain when wearing shoes, especially shoes with a narrow or shallow front. The pain often comes from:

- Corns on the top of the toe, especially at the middle joint  
- Calluses on the bottom of the foot near the ball of the foot  
- Swelling or soreness under the corns (called bursas)  
- Pain in the ball of the foot, known as metatarsalgia

As the toe gets stiffer, it changes how you walk. This can put extra pressure on the ball of the foot. This pressure can make the toe bend more and cause more pain.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will look at your foot and toes. They will check how the joints move and if there is any swelling or pain. They may also take X-rays while you stand. These X-rays help show how bad the bend is and if the toe joint is loose or out of place.

## How Is It Treated?

Most people can manage hammer toe with simple steps:

- **Wear roomy shoes** with a wide toe box. This gives your toes space to lie flat.  
- **Use toe splints or tape** to gently hold the toe in a straighter position. This can help reduce pain and pressure.  
- **Use toe pads** from the pharmacy. These pads protect the top of the toe from rubbing against the shoe.  
- **Try orthotics** (custom shoe inserts). These can help reduce pressure on the ball of the foot. Some have a pad under the ball of the foot to ease pain.

If these steps do not help, surgery may be needed. Surgery can straighten the toe and relieve pain. It is usually done when the toe is stiff and painful, and other treatments have not worked.

## Key Points

- Hammer toe is a bent toe that often starts in the second toe.  
- It is caused by tendon imbalance, injury, genetics, or other health issues.  
- Pain comes from rubbing, corns, calluses, and pressure on the foot.  
- Wearing the right shoes and using pads or splints can help.  
- X-rays help the doctor see how bad the bend is.  
- Surgery is an option if pain does not go away with other treatments.

# Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID)

Common variable immunodeficiency is a long-term health condition. It affects the body’s ability to fight infections. People with this condition have very low levels of antibodies. Antibodies are proteins that help protect the body from infections. The number of B cells is usually normal. B cells are a type of white blood cell that makes antibodies. But these B cells do not work properly. They do not mature and cannot make the needed antibodies.

This condition is a primary immunodeficiency. That means it is present from birth, even if symptoms appear later. Most people are diagnosed between the ages of 20 and 40. But it can show up earlier or later in life.

In some people, T cells also do not work well. T cells are another type of white blood cell that helps control the immune system.

## Symptoms of CVID

People with CVID often get repeated infections in the sinuses and lungs. These include pneumonia. They may have a long-lasting cough. Some cough up blood. They may also have trouble breathing.

Diarrhea is common. The body may not absorb nutrients well from food. The spleen may become larger than normal.

Over time, repeated lung infections can cause a condition called bronchiectasis. This means the airways in the lungs become widened. This makes it harder to clear mucus and move air in and out of the lungs.

Some people develop autoimmune disorders. In these conditions, the immune system attacks the body’s own tissues. Examples include:
- Low blood platelets (immune thrombocytopenia)
- Destruction of red blood cells (autoimmune hemolytic anemia)
- Low vitamin B12 levels due to lack of stomach acid (pernicious anemia)
- Addison disease (affecting the adrenal glands)
- Thyroiditis (inflammation of the thyroid gland)
- Rheumatoid arthritis (joint inflammation)

About 1 in 10 people with CVID develop stomach cancer or lymphoma. These cancers can be serious.

## Causes of CVID

The exact cause is not always known. Some cases are due to inherited gene changes. But most cases happen without a family history. The gene changes occur by chance.

## Diagnosis of CVID

Doctors suspect CVID when a person has frequent infections and other typical symptoms.

Blood tests are used to check:
- The level of antibodies (immunoglobulins)
- How well the body makes antibodies after receiving vaccines

If CVID is confirmed, yearly tests are done to check for other problems. These include:
- Blood tests
- Lung function tests (spirometry) to measure how much air you can breathe in and out
- Imaging tests like CT scans to look at the lungs and other organs

## Treatment of CVID

There is no cure for CVID. But treatment helps manage symptoms and prevent complications.

### Immune Globulin Therapy

This treatment gives the missing antibodies. It is given for life.

- It can be injected into a vein once a month.
- Or it can be injected under the skin once a week or once a month.

This helps protect against infections.

### Antibiotics

Antibiotics are used to treat infections quickly when they happen.

Sometimes, people take antibiotics every day to prevent infections.

### Autoimmune Disorders

If an autoimmune disorder develops, treatment depends on the condition. Medicines may be used to calm down the immune system. These include:
- Rituximab
- Etanercept
- Infliximab
- Corticosteroids

These medicines help reduce damage caused by the immune system attacking the body.

## Outlook

Most people with CVID live a normal life span. But if serious problems like lymphoma or hard-to-treat autoimmune diseases develop, life span may be shorter.
