# Shoulder Dislocation

A shoulder dislocation happens when the ball at the top of the upper arm bone comes out of the socket in the shoulder blade.

- The ball usually moves forward out of the socket.
- The shoulder may look crooked or out of place.
- It is usually very painful.
- Doctors can often tell if the shoulder is dislocated by looking and feeling it.
- X-rays are taken to confirm the diagnosis and to check for broken bones.

Most people can have the shoulder put back in place without surgery. Doctors may give medicine to help with pain and to relax the muscles during the procedure.

## Common Causes

The shoulder is the most common large joint to dislocate.  
In over 95 out of 100 cases, the upper arm bone moves forward.  
Sometimes it moves backward or downward.

- Backward dislocations often happen during a seizure or an electric shock, like from lightning.
- Downward dislocations are rare. People with this type usually hold their arm over their head, with the forearm resting on the head.

The bone may come all the way out — this is called a complete dislocation.  
Or it may only come partway out — this is called a partial dislocation.

A strong force can cause a dislocation. This can happen when the shoulder is pulled, pushed, or twisted suddenly.  
Common causes include:
- Sports injuries (like blocking a basketball shot)
- Car crashes
- Falls

When the shoulder dislocates, nearby tissues can be damaged. This includes:
- Ligaments
- Tendons
- Blood vessels
- Nerves

Sometimes the top of the arm bone breaks, especially in people over 45.

If the injury is serious, or if someone under 30 dislocates their shoulder more than once (for example, by playing sports), the shoulder may become unstable. This makes it more likely to dislocate again.

## Symptoms

- The shoulder may look out of place or misshapen.
- The area around the joint may be swollen or bruised.
- Pain is usually severe.
- People cannot move their arm away from their body.
- The muscle on top of the shoulder may feel numb.

The sudden injury can cause muscle spasms. These spasms can make the pain worse.

## How Doctors Diagnose a Dislocated Shoulder

- Doctors will ask how the injury happened.
- They will check how bad the pain is and whether the arm can move.
- They will examine the shoulder.
- X-rays are usually taken to confirm the dislocation and to check for broken bones.

Doctors must know if any bones are broken before trying to put the shoulder back in place.

## What to Do If You Think Your Shoulder Is Dislocated

- See a doctor right away.
- Do not try to push the shoulder back in place yourself.
- This can cause more damage.
- Keep the arm still. Use a sling or splint if possible.
- Apply ice to help reduce pain and swelling.

## Treatment

The main goal is to put the shoulder back in the correct position. This is called reduction.

Before the procedure:
- People may get medicine to help with pain.
- They may get a shot of numbing medicine into the joint.
- They stay awake during the process.

There are several ways to put the shoulder back in place. Each method uses different movements.

### 1. Traction-Countertraction
- The person lies down on a firm surface.
- One person holds the chest with a folded sheet to keep the body still.
- Another person pulls the injured arm down and out.
- This helps guide the ball back into the socket.

### 2. External Rotation (Hennepin Technique)
- The arm is bent at the elbow.
- The person slowly turns the arm away from the body.
- This helps the joint slip back into place.

### 3. Shoulder Blade Manipulation
- The person can sit or lie down.
- The doctor moves the bottom tip of the shoulder blade toward the spine.
- An assistant gently pulls, rotates, and presses on the arm.

### 4. Cunningham (Massage) Technique
- The doctor sits across from the person.
- The person places their hand on the doctor’s shoulder.
- The doctor massages the upper arm and shoulder muscles.
- The person is told to relax and shrug their shoulders back, trying to touch the shoulder blades together.
- The massage helps the muscles relax so the shoulder can go back in place.

### 5. Davos (Autoreduction) Technique
- The person sits on a bed.
- They bend the knee on the same side as the injured shoulder.
- They place that foot on the bed.
- They clasp their hands in front of the knee, with elbows close to the thigh.
- An elastic band ties the hands together and to the knee.
- The doctor sits on the person’s foot.
- The person leans their head back.
- This pressure helps push the shoulder back into place.

### 6. Stimson (Dangling Weights) Technique
- The person lies face down on a bed.
- The injured arm hangs over the edge of the bed.
- Weights are attached to the wrist.
- After about 30 minutes, the muscles relax enough for the shoulder to move back in place.

### 7. FARES (Fast and Reliable) Technique
- The person lies on their back.
- The elbow is straight, and the arm is by the side.
- The doctor holds the hand or wrist.
- The doctor slowly moves the arm away from the body.
- At the same time, the doctor moves the arm up and down in small, slow motions.
- This movement helps the muscles relax.

## After the Shoulder Is Put Back

- The joint is immediately held still with a sling and swathe.
- A swathe is a band that wraps around the chest and arm to keep the arm close to the body.
- For people over 40, the sling and swathe are used for a shorter time than for younger people.
- This helps prevent stiffness and other problems, like frozen shoulder.

Sling and Swathe  
A sling supports the arm. A swathe keeps the arm close to the body. Together, they help the shoulder heal.

# How the Body Processes Medicines

The liver is the main place in the body where medicines are changed.  
This process is called drug metabolism.

Most of the time, metabolism makes a medicine less active.  
But sometimes, the changed form of the medicine is still active.  
In some cases, the changed form is even stronger than the original medicine.

A medicine that starts out inactive or weakly active is called a prodrug.  
This type of medicine is made to turn into its active form in the body.  
It is designed to deliver the active part more effectively.

Medicines can be changed in several ways:  
- By adding or removing oxygen (oxidation or reduction)  
- By breaking a bond with water (hydrolysis)  
- By adding water (hydration)  
- By joining with natural body substances (conjugation)  
- By combining two parts (condensation)  
- By changing the shape of the molecule (isomerization)

The goal of all these changes is to make the medicine easier to get rid of from the body.

The enzymes that do these changes are found in many parts of the body.  
But they are most common in the liver.

People process medicines at different rates.  
Some people break down a medicine so fast that it does not stay in the body long enough to work.  
Others break it down so slowly that normal doses can cause harm.

Your rate of medicine breakdown depends on:  
- Your genes  
- Other health problems, especially long-term liver issues or serious heart failure  
- Other medicines you are taking, especially those that speed up or slow down the process

Most medicines go through two main steps to be changed.

### Phase I: Making a New or Changed Part  
This step adds or changes a small part of the medicine.  
It does not join the medicine to another substance.  
Examples: adding oxygen, removing oxygen, or breaking a bond with water.

### Phase II: Joining with a Natural Substance  
This step joins the medicine to a natural substance in the body.  
Common joining partners include:  
- Glucuronic acid  
- Sulfate  
- Glycine  

This step is called a synthetic reaction because it builds a new molecule.

The results of Phase II are more water-friendly.  
This means they are easier for the kidneys to remove in urine.  
They are also easier for the liver to remove in bile.

Some medicines only go through Phase I.  
Others only go through Phase II.  
The phase numbers do not mean the steps always happen in order.  
They describe the type of change, not the sequence.

### How Medicines Move in the Liver

The liver has special transporters that help move medicines around.  
These transporters are found in liver cells.  
They help control how medicines are processed and removed.

There are two main types:

- **Influx transporters** bring medicines into the liver cells.  
- **Efflux transporters** move medicines out of the liver cells.  
  They send medicines into the blood or into bile for removal.

Some people have genetic differences that affect how these transporters work.  
This can change how much medicine stays in the body.  
It can also increase the risk of side effects or liver damage.

For example, some people with certain gene types have higher levels of statins in their blood.  
This makes them more likely to get muscle pain or weakness when taking statins for high cholesterol.

(See also: Overview of How Medicines Work in the Body.)

# Elbow Dislocations

An elbow dislocation happens when the bottom of the upper arm bone no longer fits with the tops of the two forearm bones.  

The dislocation can be complete. That means the bones are completely out of place.  
It can also be partial. That means the bones still touch in some way.  
A partial dislocation is called a subluxation.

Most elbow dislocations happen when someone falls on an arm that is straight.  
These injuries can also cause broken bones, nerve damage, or damage to a blood vessel.

Elbow dislocations are fairly common.  
But it takes a lot of force to completely dislocate an elbow.  
Partial dislocations (subluxations) are common in toddlers.  
They can happen with much less force.  
Subluxations are rare in babies, older children, and adults.

X-rays can show if the elbow is dislocated.

(See also: Overview of Dislocations.)

---

## How a Dislocated Elbow Is Treated

Most people with a dislocated elbow need a doctor to put the bones back in place.  
This is called reduction.

The treatment usually includes:

- A medicine to help you relax and another to reduce pain.  
- Lying down on your back.  
- Bending the elbow.  
- Gently turning the forearm so the palm faces up.  
- Holding the upper arm steady.  
- Pulling the wrist upward until the joint snaps back into place.

After the joint is back in place, the doctor checks it for stability.  
An X-ray is taken to make sure no bones are broken.  
Then the elbow is usually held still with a splint for up to one week.  
This helps the pain and swelling go down.

After the splint is removed, gentle movement exercises begin.  
A sling is worn for two to three weeks to protect the elbow.

---

## Radial Head Subluxation (Nursemaid’s Elbow)

Radial head subluxation is a partial dislocation of the elbow.  
It happens when the top of one forearm bone (the radius) slips out of its normal position.

This injury is common in toddlers.  
It often happens when a caregiver pulls a child forward or grabs the child by the wrist.

The only sign may be that the child refuses to use the injured arm.

Doctors suspect this injury based on how the injury happened, the child’s symptoms, and a physical exam.

Doctors can usually fix the problem without surgery.  
No sedatives or pain medicine are needed.

This injury usually happens in children who are about 2 to 3 years old.  
At this age, the top of the radius bone is small.  
It can slip through the ligaments that hold the elbow together.  
This can happen when a parent or caregiver pulls a child forward or grabs the wrist during a fall.  
Many caregivers do not remember doing this.

As children grow, the top of the radius gets bigger.  
It becomes too large to slip through the ligaments easily.

The elbow may only be slightly tender.  
Toddlers often cannot explain how they feel.  
So the only sign may be that they do not move the arm.  
The arm may hang down by the side.  
It may turn slightly inward.  
Or the child may hold the arm bent against their body.

Parents or caregivers should not try to move the arm.

Toddlers may cry when the injury happens.  
But they often calm down quickly.  
They may act normal, except they do not use the injured arm.

### When to See a Doctor

If a toddler shows signs of elbow subluxation, take them to a doctor.  
If the elbow has popped back into place, the child will be able to move it normally.  
If the child still cannot move the elbow, they need to see a doctor.

Doctors make the diagnosis based on the story of how the injury happened, the symptoms, and the physical exam.

X-rays are not needed.  
They do not show this injury.

### How to Prevent This Injury

To help prevent radial head subluxation:

- Do not suddenly jerk a toddler’s hand, wrist, or forearm.  
- Do not lift a toddler by one arm, wrist, or hand.  
- Do not swing a child by the hand or forearm.  
- Lift toddlers from under their arms or from both arms.

### How Doctors Fix the Injury

Doctors usually put the bone back in place.  
This is called reduction.  
No sedatives or pain medicine are usually needed.  
You might hear a soft pop or click when the bone moves back.  
The child may start using the arm again in 10 to 20 minutes.

If the child does not move the arm, the doctor may take an X-ray.  
If the child can move the arm, no X-ray or splint is needed.

If the child still has pain after 24 hours, or still cannot use the arm, the joint may not be fully in place.  
Or there may be a broken bone.  
In that case, the child should see a doctor again.

### Recovery

Most toddlers recover fully after treatment.  
But 20 to 40 percent of them will have this injury again.

# Older Adults Living Alone

In the United States in 2023, about 16.2 million older adults lived alone.  
This includes 5.7 million older men and 10.5 million older women.  
More older people live alone as they get older.  
For example, about 42 out of every 100 women aged 75 and older live alone.

Men are more likely to die before their wives.  
Widowed or divorced men are more likely to marry again than women are.  
In 2023, 68 out of every 100 older men were married.  
Only 47 out of every 100 older women were married.  
About 29 out of every 100 older women were widows.  
There are more than three times as many widows (9 million) as widowers (2.9 million).  
Still, more than half (59%) of adults aged 65 and older who live in the community live with their spouse or partner.

Older adults who live alone are more likely to have low income, especially as they grow older.  
Many feel lonely.  
About 1 in 4 older adults aged 65 and over are considered socially isolated.  
If they have health problems or vision or hearing issues, new or worsening symptoms may go unnoticed.  
Some have trouble following their treatment plans.  
Some do not cook full, balanced meals because they have physical limits and because eating is often a social activity.  
This can lead to poor nutrition.

Even with these challenges, most older adults who live alone want to stay independent.  
Many are afraid of becoming too dependent on others.  
They may feel lonely, but still prefer to live alone.  
Doctors can help by encouraging regular physical activity and social contact.  
Doctors should also connect patients with social services to support these goals.

It is harder for people who live alone to get help during recovery from illness.  
Doctors should make sure home care is available.  
They should also suggest extra services when needed.  
A medical alert device—either automatic or one the person can press—can give peace of mind.  
It lets the person know help is available if they need it.

Since the start of the _COVID-19_ pandemic, many local mental health and social care groups have improved their use of technology.  
They now offer more virtual check-ins and remote support.

# Sever Disease

Sever disease is a common cause of heel pain in growing children. It happens when the growth plate in the heel bone becomes inflamed.

## What Is Sever Disease?

- Sever disease is a type of injury that affects the growth plate in the heel bone.
- The growth plate is a soft area of developing bone. It helps the bone grow longer.
- As children grow, the growth plate eventually turns into solid bone.
- The heel bone usually becomes solid by the time a child is 15 years old.

## Where Is the Heel Bone?

- The heel bone is at the back of the foot.
- It is the part of the foot that touches the ground when you stand.

## Why Does Sever Disease Happen?

- Sever disease happens during puberty, when children grow quickly.
- During a growth spurt, bones, muscles, and tendons grow at different speeds.
- The calf muscles and Achilles tendon can become tight.
- These tight muscles pull on the growth plate in the heel.
- This pulling can cause injury, swelling, and pain.

Children who are active in sports are more likely to get Sever disease. This is especially true if they wear shoes that do not raise the heel, like track shoes or soccer cleats.

## What Are the Symptoms?

- Pain in the back of the heel, especially on the sides.
- Pain gets worse when standing on tiptoes or running.
- The heel may feel warm or look red.
- Some children limp or avoid putting weight on the affected foot.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- Doctors look at the child’s symptoms to make a diagnosis.
- X-rays are not used to diagnose Sever disease.
- But X-rays can help rule out other problems like stress fractures or bone cysts.

## How Is Sever Disease Treated?

### Stretching Exercises

- Stretching the calf muscles and Achilles tendon helps prevent and relieve pain.
- Do these stretches before and after sports.

**Seated Stretch:**
- Sit on the floor with one leg straight.
- Loop an elastic band around the ball of the foot.
- Gently pull the band toward you until you feel a stretch in the foot and calf.
- Hold for 15 to 30 seconds. Repeat 2 to 3 times.

**Standing Stretch:**
- Stand facing a wall.
- Place one foot behind the other.
- Keep the back leg straight and the heel on the ground.
- Lean forward until you feel a stretch in the calf.
- Hold for 15 to 30 seconds. Repeat 2 to 3 times.

> Watch the video: *Standing Gastrocnemius Stretch* for a demonstration.

### Heel Support Devices

- **Heel cups** go inside shoes. They cushion the heel and reduce pressure.
- **Heel pads** raise the heel slightly. This reduces the pull on the Achilles tendon.
- **Night splints** are worn while sleeping. They keep the calf muscles stretched and help maintain flexibility.

### Rest and Care at Home

- Rest the foot. Avoid activities that cause pain.
- Apply ice to the heel for 15 to 20 minutes several times a day.
- Reduce or stop sports and other high-impact activities.

### Casts

- A cast may be used if the pain is severe or does not improve.
- The cast keeps the foot still. This helps reduce pain and stretches the calf muscles.

### Medications

- Doctors may prescribe ibuprofen or other pain relievers to reduce pain and swelling.
- Always follow the doctor’s instructions when using medicine.

## Outlook

- Symptoms can last several months.
- Most children get better with time and proper care.
- Sever disease does not cause long-term problems.
- Once the growth plate closes, the pain usually goes away for good.

# Problems That Can Happen During a Blood Transfusion

## Most Common Problems
- Fever, chills, and shaking (called febrile nonhemolytic reactions)

## Serious Problems (Can Be Life-Threatening)
- **Acute hemolytic reaction**: Happens when the blood type of the donor does not match the patient’s. This is the most dangerous type.
- **Graft-versus-host disease**: A rare but serious condition where donor immune cells attack the patient’s body.
- **Transfusion-associated circulatory overload**: Too much fluid in the bloodstream. This can strain the heart and lungs.
- **Transfusion-related acute lung injury**: A sudden lung problem that causes breathing trouble.

## Other Possible Problems
- Allergic reactions (like rash or itching)
- Changes in how well red blood cells carry oxygen
- Delayed hemolytic reactions (can happen days after transfusion)
- Infections (from the donated blood)
- Post-transfusion purpura (a rare condition that causes easy bruising and bleeding)

## What to Do If a Reaction Happens
- Watch for symptoms during and after the transfusion.
- Common signs include:
  - Chills
  - Shaking
  - Fever
  - Trouble breathing
  - Dizziness
  - Hives
  - Itching
  - Pain in the back or side

If you have any of these symptoms (except for mild itching or hives in one small area), stop the transfusion right away.

- Keep the IV line open with normal saline.
- Do not restart the blood unit.
- Do not begin a new blood unit until the cause is found.
- Send the rest of the blood bag and blood samples (both clotted and anticoagulated) to the blood bank for testing.

If more blood is needed right away, use type O Rh-negative red blood cells. This type is safe for most people in emergencies.

## How Hemolysis Happens
Hemolysis means red blood cells break apart. This can happen during or after a transfusion.

Causes include:
- Blood type mismatch (especially ABO or Rh)
- Antibodies in the patient’s blood that attack donor red blood cells
- Damaged red blood cells (for example, from being too warm or mixed with weak fluids)

The most serious cases happen when the donor’s blood type does not match the patient’s. The patient’s body attacks the donor’s red blood cells.

Types of hemolytic reactions:
- **Acute**: Happens within 24 hours
- **Delayed**: Happens 1 to 14 days after the transfusion

# Shoulder Sprains

A shoulder sprain happens when the ligaments in your shoulder are torn.  
Ligaments are strong bands that connect bones to each other.  

- The ligaments can be partly torn or completely torn.  
- Shoulder sprains are common, especially in athletes.  
- Sports like football, rugby, wrestling, alpine skiing, and jet skiing often lead to these injuries.  

## What Causes Shoulder Sprains?

Most sprains happen after a fall onto the shoulder.  
Sometimes, a fall onto an outstretched arm can also cause a sprain.  

The shoulder joint is held together by ligaments.  
These ligaments connect the collarbone to two bony parts of the shoulder blade:  
- One on the front of the shoulder blade (called the acromion).  
- One on the back of the shoulder blade (called the coracoid process).  

The most common sprain affects the ligament on the front of the shoulder.  
But any of the ligaments can be injured.  

If the ligament connecting the collarbone to the coracoid process is completely or almost completely torn, the collarbone pulls away from the shoulder blade.  
This is called a shoulder separation.  

## Symptoms of Shoulder Sprains

- The shoulder hurts.  
- The area feels tender to the touch.  

## How Doctors Diagnose Shoulder Sprains

Doctors use X-rays to check the injury.  
They take X-rays of both shoulders to compare them.  

The X-rays show how far apart the bones are.  
This helps the doctor decide how bad the sprain is.  

Based on the X-ray results, doctors divide sprains into types:  

- **Type I**: The injury is mild. The bones stay in their normal position.  
- **Type II**: The bones are partly out of place. This is called subluxation.  
- **Types III to VI**: The bones are completely separated. These are called shoulder separations.  

## Treatment for Shoulder Sprains

Treatment depends on how severe the sprain is.  

### For Mild to Moderate Sprains (Types I and II)

- The shoulder is put in a sling to rest.  
- Gentle movement exercises start early.  
- These exercises help keep the shoulder from getting stiff.  

### For Severe Sprains (Types III to VI)

- Surgery may be needed.  
- This is often the case with shoulder separations.  

## Note About Rotator Cuff Injuries

The rotator cuff is a group of muscles that help keep the upper arm bone in the shoulder socket.  
These muscles can get pinched, inflamed, or torn.  
This is not a sprain.  
It is a different type of injury.  
It is called a rotator cuff injury.

# Cephalosporins – Simple Explanation

Cephalosporins are a type of antibiotic. They kill bacteria by stopping the bacteria from building their outer shell. This shell is needed for the bacteria to survive.

There are many types of cephalosporins. They are grouped into generations. Each generation works against different kinds of bacteria.

---

## Types of Cephalosporins

Here are the main cephalosporins and how they are given:

### First Generation
- Cefadroxil – taken by mouth
- Cefazolin – given through a vein or muscle
- Cephalexin – taken by mouth
- Cephradine – taken by mouth

### Second Generation
- Cefaclor – taken by mouth
- Cefotetan – given through a vein
- Cefoxitin – given through a vein
- Cefprozil – taken by mouth
- Cefuroxime – taken by mouth or given through a vein

### Third Generation
- Cefdinir – taken by mouth
- Cefditoren – taken by mouth
- Cefixime – taken by mouth
- Cefoperazone/sulbactam – given through a vein (not available in the United States)
- Cefotaxime – given through a vein
- Cefpodoxime – taken by mouth
- Ceftazidime – given through a vein
- Ceftazidime/avibactam – given through a vein
- Ceftibuten – taken by mouth
- Ceftriaxone – given through a vein

### Fourth Generation
- Cefepime – given through a vein

### Cephalosporins That Work Against MRSA
- Ceftaroline/fosamil – given through a vein
- Ceftobiprole/medocaril – given through a vein

### Other Cephalosporins
- Cefiderocol – given through a vein
- Ceftolozane/tazobactam – given through a vein

> Note: Cefotetan and cefoxitin are also called cephamycins.

> MRSA means methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus*. This is a type of tough bacteria that does not respond to many antibiotics.

---

## How Cephalosporins Work in the Body

Cephalosporins spread well through most body fluids and tissues. This includes areas with swelling or infection.

The only cephalosporins that reach high enough levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord are:
- Ceftriaxone
- Cefotaxime
- Ceftazidime
- Cefepime

These are the only ones used to treat infections of the brain and spinal cord (meningitis).

Cephalosporins do not get into the inside of cells well. They also do not reach high levels in the fluid inside the eye (vitreous humor).

Most cephalosporins leave the body through the kidneys. If your kidneys are not working well, your dose may need to be lowered.

Two cephalosporins—cefoperazone and ceftriaxone—leave the body through the liver and bile. These do not need dose changes for kidney problems.

---

## When Cephalosporins Are Used

Cephalosporins kill many types of bacteria, including:
- Gram-positive bacteria
- Gram-negative bacteria

### How Generations Differ
- First-generation cephalosporins work best against gram-positive bacteria.
- Later generations work better against gram-negative bacteria.
- Ceftaroline and ceftobiprole are special. They work against MRSA.

### What Cephalosporins Do Not Work Against
- Enterococci (a type of bacteria)
- Methicillin-resistant staphylococci (except ceftaroline and ceftobiprole)
- Anaerobic gram-negative bacteria (except cefotetan and cefoxitin)

---

## Who Should Not Take Cephalosporins

Do not take cephalosporins if you had a serious allergic reaction to another cephalosporin.

Allergic reactions to penicillin do not always mean you will react to cephalosporins. Only about 2 out of 100 people with a penicillin allergy will react to cephalosporins.

The risk depends on the specific drug. Third- and fourth-generation cephalosporins, and those with different chemical structures than the penicillin you reacted to, are very safe.

Cefazolin has a unique structure and is especially safe for people with penicillin allergies.

Still, if you have had a serious allergic reaction to any antibiotic, your doctor will be careful when giving you a cephalosporin.

---

### Special Warning About Ceftriaxone

Ceftriaxone must not be given with calcium-containing IV fluids in babies under 28 days old. This can cause dangerous clumps to form in the lungs and kidneys. There have been fatal cases in newborns.

Even in older patients, ceftriaxone and calcium-containing IV fluids should not be mixed or given close together—within 48 hours—even through different IV lines.

No studies have looked at the risk of ceftriaxone and oral calcium supplements.

Ceftriaxone should also not be given to premature babies with high levels of bilirubin. This is because the drug can push bilirubin out of the blood, which may lead to brain damage (kernicterus).

---

## Cephalosporins During Pregnancy and Breastfeeding

Cephalosporins are generally considered safe during pregnancy. No studies have shown harm to the baby. But more detailed studies have not been done.

Cephalosporins can pass into breast milk. They may change the baby’s gut bacteria. Because of this, doctors often advise against using them while breastfeeding.

---

## Side Effects of Cephalosporins

Common side effects include:
- Allergic reactions (rash is most common)
- Diarrhea caused by *Clostridioides difficile* (a serious type of gut infection)
- Low white blood cell count
- Low platelet count
- A positive Coombs test (this can happen, but severe anemia is rare)

### Allergic Reactions
Rash is common. But serious reactions like hives or anaphylaxis are rare.

You can usually take cephalosporins if you had a delayed rash from penicillin. But always check with your doctor.

### Other Side Effects
- Pain at the injection site (if given by muscle)
- Swelling or irritation in the vein (if given through a vein)

### Cefotetan Specific Risks
- If you drink alcohol while taking cefotetan, you may get nausea and vomiting. This is like the reaction seen with disulfiram.
- Cefotetan can make blood clotting tests show abnormal results. This effect goes away with vitamin K.

--- 

Always follow your doctor’s instructions when taking cephalosporins. Tell your doctor about all your medical conditions and allergies.

# Pelvic Fractures

A pelvic fracture means one or more bones in the pelvis are broken.  
The break can be small, like a chip of bone.  
It can also be a serious break from a strong force, like in a car crash.  
In older adults, even a small fall can cause a break if the bones are weak.

## What the Pelvis Is

The pelvis is the ring of bones at the bottom of your body.  
It holds your upper body up when you stand.  
It protects your bladder, bowel, and reproductive organs.  
It connects your spine to your legs.

The pelvis is made of three bones:
- The ilium — the top and largest bone, in the back
- The pubis — the middle bone, in the front
- The ischium — the bottom bone, in the back

These bones form a socket for the top of your thighbone.  
Together, the thighbone and pelvis make the hip joint.  
The pelvis connects to the tailbone (sacrum) at the base of your spine.  
Strong ligaments hold the bones together.  
Muscles in your thigh attach to the pelvis with tendons.

## How Pelvic Fractures Happen

In young adults, serious pelvic fractures often happen in:
- High-speed car crashes
- Motorcycle crashes
- Falls from a height
- Being hit by a car while walking

These injuries can cause heavy bleeding inside the body.  
The bleeding can be life-threatening, even if the skin is not broken.  
Low blood pressure (called shock) can happen.  
Nerves and nearby organs like the bladder, intestines, or reproductive organs can be damaged.  
These fractures are usually unstable — the bones are not held together well.

In older adults, bones can become weak from osteoporosis.  
A fall — even a small one — can break part of the pelvis.  
This can happen when getting out of the bathtub, going down steps, or even standing on flat ground.

A type of fracture called an avulsion fracture often happens in teens, especially athletes.  
It occurs when a muscle pulls a small piece of bone away.  
This usually happens when the hamstring muscles (in the back of the thigh) contract suddenly.  
The pull breaks off a piece of the ischium, near the base of the buttocks.

## Signs and Symptoms

Most pelvic fractures cause strong pain in the groin.  
The pain can be bad even when lying down or sitting.  
Walking makes the pain much worse.  
Some people can still walk, but it is very painful.

The area may be swollen and bruised.  
People often keep their leg bent in a certain way to avoid more pain.

If the fracture is severe and unstable, the pain is extreme.  
You cannot walk at all.  
But some small fractures hurt less.

If other parts of the body are injured, you may have other symptoms:
- Blood in your urine
- Trouble urinating
- Incontinence (can’t control your urine)
- Bleeding from the rectum or vagina

If the hip joint socket is damaged, you may have long-term disability.

Severe bleeding or damage to other organs can be deadly.

## How Doctors Diagnose Pelvic Fractures

If you think you have a pelvic injury, go to the emergency room.  
If you were in a serious accident, you will likely be taken by ambulance.

Doctors suspect a pelvic fracture if:
- You have groin pain
- You had a major injury

They will do:
- X-rays — to see if any bones are broken
- Computed tomography (CT scan) — to get a clearer picture of all the broken pieces and to check for other injuries

Doctors also do a physical exam to check for other injuries.  
This includes:
- A neurologic exam — to check nerve function
- A digital rectal exam — to check the rectum
- A pelvic exam — for women

They will also test your urine.  
If they think the urinary tract is injured, they may do a CT scan or another imaging test.

## How Pelvic Fractures Are Treated

### Minor, Stable Fractures

- You may only need pain medicine.
- You can usually walk with help.
- You should get up and move as soon as possible.
- Bed rest should be short. Long bed rest can cause weakness and stiffness.

Pain medicine helps you walk.  
Walking does not make the injury worse.  
Most people can walk short distances without a walker within a week.  
By 1 to 2 months, most can walk without help and with only mild pain.

### Severe, Unstable Fractures

- The pelvis must be held still to heal.
- Emergency workers often wrap the pelvis with cloth or a special binder to stabilize it.
- Doctors may use an external fixator — a metal frame attached to the outside of the body with screws through the skin.  
  This holds the bones in place until they can be fixed more permanently.

Later, surgery is usually done to:
- Line up the broken bones
- Use metal plates and screws to hold them together (called open reduction with internal fixation, or ORIF)

After the pelvis is stable, you are encouraged to walk as soon as possible.  
Sometimes surgery is done right away, without using an external fixator.

### If Bleeding Continues

If bleeding does not stop, doctors may do one of two things:

**Embolization**  
- A thin tube (catheter) is inserted into a blood vessel.
- It is guided to the bleeding vessel.
- Tiny coils or a gel-like material are injected to block the blood flow and stop the bleeding.

**Pelvic Packing**  
- Surgery is done to place material around the injured organs in the pelvis.
- The material soaks up blood and presses on blood vessels to slow or stop bleeding.
- After a few days, when bleeding stops, another surgery removes the packing.
- Then, the pelvis is repaired with surgery (ORIF).

### Other Injuries

Any other injuries are treated as needed.

# Problems with the Voice Box

The voice box is a part of your throat. It holds your vocal folds, which are also called vocal cords. The voice box lets air pass into your windpipe and lungs. It also helps you speak.

## Common Voice Box Problems

These are some of the most common issues that can affect the voice box:

- Non-cancerous growths in the voice box  
- Sores on the voice box caused by rubbing or pressure  
- Swelling of the voice box (often from infection or overuse)  
- A fluid-filled sac in the voice box  
- Narrowing of the windpipe and voice box  
- Cancerous growths in the voice box  
- A condition where the voice box muscles move abnormally  
- One or both vocal folds stop moving  
- Small growths on the vocal folds, such as polyps, nodules, or small sores  

Other problems that can affect the voice box include:

- Croup – a sudden swelling in the voice box and windpipe, often in children  
- Epiglottitis – a serious swelling of the flap that covers the windpipe  
- Laryngomalacia – a condition where the voice box is soft and collapses when breathing in, often seen in babies  

If something is stuck in the throat, the Heimlich maneuver can help remove it. See the section on clearing the upper airway for more details.

## How the Voice Box Works

The vocal folds are shaped like a V. When you breathe in, they open to let air in. When you swallow or speak, they close tightly.

When the vocal folds are healthy, they move smoothly and make a clear voice. If they are damaged, your voice may sound hoarse, weak, shaky, or strained.

## When to See a Doctor

If your voice changes and does not go back to normal after two weeks or more, you should see a doctor. This is especially important if you are older.

Even though voices naturally change with age – becoming softer or rougher – sudden or big changes should not be ignored. These could be signs of a serious problem.

## How Doctors Check the Voice Box

Doctors use several methods to look at the voice box. They may:

- Look at your neck from the outside  
- Feel the neck with their hands  
- Use a small mirror in your mouth to see the voice box  
- Use a thin, flexible tube with a camera (flexible laryngoscopy)  
- Use a rigid scope with a camera (rigid transoral laryngoscopy)  
- Do a full exam under general anesthesia (this gives the clearest view)

The last method is used when a detailed look is needed. It allows doctors to:

- See the underside of the vocal folds  
- Check how well the folds move when they are not working properly  
- Take a small sample of tissue for testing (biopsy)

## What Doctors Look For

During the exam, doctors check:

- The shape and movement of the vocal folds  
- The epiglottis (the flap that covers the windpipe)  
- The false vocal folds  
- The arytenoids (small parts at the back of the voice box)  
- The area below the voice box (subglottic region)  
- The sides of the throat (pyriform sinuses)

They also record your voice, especially if surgery is planned.

## Important Notes

- Always take steps to avoid catching or spreading infections.  
- If you are having surgery, your voice will be checked and recorded before the procedure.  
- A mirror in the back of your mouth can help doctors see the vocal folds. They can check for issues like sores, growths, paralysis, or cancer.  
- Paralysis can affect one side of the voice box or both sides.  

If you notice any lasting change in your voice, get it checked. Early care can help prevent serious problems.

# Bone Tumors That Spread from Other Cancers

Cancer that starts in one part of the body can spread to the bones. This is called metastatic bone tumor.

## Which Cancers Are Most Likely to Spread to Bones?

The following cancers often spread to the bones:
- Breast cancer
- Lung cancer
- Prostate cancer
- Kidney cancer
- Thyroid cancer
- Colon cancer

Breast cancer is the most common type to spread to bones. But any cancer can eventually spread to bones. Cancer can affect any bone. However, it rarely spreads to bones below the middle of the forearm or the middle of the calf. When it does, it is usually from lung or kidney cancer.

## Symptoms of Metastatic Bone Tumors

The main symptom is bone pain. The pain may be mild at first. It often gets worse over time. It can happen when you are resting or at night.

The tumor weakens the bone over time. This makes the bone more likely to break during normal daily activities. This kind of break is called a pathologic fracture.

Sometimes, the first sign of cancer is a broken bone. Or you may have pain in more than one place. This can happen if there are several tumors in different bones.

## How Doctors Diagnose Metastatic Bone Tumors

If you have cancer and now have bone pain or swelling, your doctor will check for metastatic bone tumors.

Your doctor will ask about your health history. They will do a physical exam. Blood tests may be done.

Imaging tests help find the problem. These include:
- X-rays
- Bone scans
- MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)
- CT (computed tomography)
- PET-CT (a scan that combines PET and CT)

A bone scan uses a small amount of radioactive material. It shows the whole skeleton at once. It can find tumors that do not show up on regular x-rays.

MRI and CT give detailed pictures of one area. PET-CT is often used to look at tumors.

Sometimes, a small sample of tissue is taken from the bone. This is called a biopsy. The sample is checked under a microscope. This can help doctors find where the original cancer started.

If the original cancer is not yet known, doctors will test for it. For example:
- A chest x-ray or CT scan may look for lung cancer.
- A mammogram may check for breast cancer.

## Treatment of Metastatic Bone Tumors

Treatment depends on the type of cancer that spread to the bone.

Some cancers respond to radiation therapy. Some respond to chemotherapy. Some respond to both. Some do not respond to either. Radiation therapy usually works best.

### Radiation Therapy
This uses high-energy beams to kill cancer cells. It helps reduce pain and slow bone damage.

### Surgery
Surgery may be done to:
- Fix broken bones
- Prevent future breaks
- Remove tumors

For broken bones, doctors may:
- Put a metal rod inside the bone
- Use plates and screws to hold the bone in place
- Remove the damaged bone and rebuild the limb

If only one tumor is left in the bone, and the original cancer was removed long ago, doctors may remove the tumor. They may rebuild the bone with metal or bone grafts. This surgery is often combined with radiation or chemotherapy. This does not usually cure the cancer. But it can improve your quality of life. It can also help you move better and look more normal.

### Preventing Bone Loss
Cancer can cause bone to weaken and break. To prevent this:
- Radiation therapy can help
- Medicines like bisphosphonates or denosumab can stop bone loss

These treatments work best when started early, before pain or serious bone damage happens.

### Back Pain Relief
If the spine is affected, two procedures may help:
- **Kyphoplasty**: A balloon is placed in the broken bone. It is inflated to lift the bone back into place. Then bone cement is injected to hold it.
- **Vertebroplasty**: Bone cement is injected directly into the broken bone. No balloon is used.

These help relieve pain and prevent further collapse.

If the tumor is at risk of pressing on the spinal cord, surgery may be needed. This can prevent serious problems like leg weakness or paralysis.

## Multiple Myeloma and Bone Tumors

Multiple myeloma is a type of cancer that starts in the bone marrow. The bone marrow is the soft tissue inside bones that makes blood cells.

Even though it affects the bone, multiple myeloma is not a true bone tumor. It is a cancer of the blood-forming system.

It is the most common type of cancer that starts in the bone marrow. It mostly affects older adults.

The cancer cells in the bone marrow make substances that destroy bone. This causes bone loss. The loss can be widespread. Or it may appear as small holes in the bone.

Multiple myeloma can affect one bone or many bones. Pain may happen in one spot or in several places.

If only one bone is affected, it is called **plasmacytoma**.  
If many bones are affected, or the bone marrow is widely involved, it is called multiple myeloma.

### Diagnosis of Multiple Myeloma

A bone biopsy may be done if the bone is damaged. This checks for cancer cells.

If the biopsy suggests multiple myeloma, doctors will take a sample of bone marrow. They will examine it under a microscope.

Blood tests are also done.

Doctors may take x-rays of the whole body. This is called a skeletal survey.

MRI or PET-CT may be used to look closely at areas with pain.

### Treatment of Multiple Myeloma

Treatment is complex. It may include:
- Chemotherapy
- Radiation therapy
- Sometimes surgery

The goal is to control the cancer, reduce pain, and help you live better.

# Cocaine

Cocaine is a drug that affects the brain and body.  
It makes you feel very alert and happy.  
It is also known as a stimulant and a mood booster.

## What Happens When You Use Cocaine

Using too much cocaine can cause serious health problems.  
You may feel extreme fear or panic.  
You might have symptoms like those seen in schizophrenia.  
You could have seizures.  
Your body temperature may rise very high.  
Your blood pressure may go up.  
Your heart may beat too fast or irregularly.  
You could have a stroke.  
You might get a tear in the main artery of your body.  
You could have poor blood flow to your intestines.  
You might have a heart attack.

## How to Treat Cocaine Overdose

Doctors treat cocaine overdose with supportive care.  
They give medicine through a vein to calm you down.  
This helps if you are very anxious, have high blood pressure, or are having seizures.  
They use cooling methods if your body temperature is too high.  
There is no specific antidote for cocaine overdose.

## What Happens When You Stop Using Cocaine

When you stop using cocaine after heavy use, you may feel very down.  
You may have trouble focusing.  
You may feel very sleepy.  
This is called cocaine washout syndrome.

## Who Uses Cocaine?

Most people who use cocaine do so only occasionally.  
They use it for fun, not every day.  
About one in four users have a problem with cocaine.  
They use it too much or cannot stop, even when it harms them.  
Use of cocaine among teens has gone down slightly since 2011.

## How Cocaine Is Used

Cocaine comes in different forms.  
The most common way is to inhale it through the nose.  
Some people smoke it.  
Others inject it into a vein.  
Smoking is the most common method in the United States.

To smoke cocaine, people turn the powder into a rock-like form.  
This is called crack cocaine.  
They mix the powder with baking soda, water, and heat.  
The mixture forms a solid that can be heated and inhaled.  
It is not burned.  
The high comes on very fast.  
The feeling is as strong as when cocaine is injected.

## How Cocaine Affects the Body

Cocaine comes from the leaves of the coca plant.  
It works by changing how brain chemicals work.  
It stops the brain from reabsorbing certain chemicals.  
These chemicals are norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin.  
This leads to a rush of energy and pleasure.

The increase in dopamine is what makes the high feel good.  
This feeling makes people want to use cocaine again.  
This can lead to addiction.

The increase in norepinephrine causes physical effects.  
Your heart beats faster.  
Your blood pressure goes up.  
Your pupils get bigger.  
You sweat more.  
Your body temperature rises.

Cocaine also blocks nerve signals.  
This is why it can numb pain.  
It can also cause dangerous heart rhythms.  
Cocaine causes blood vessels to tighten.  
This can reduce blood flow to many organs.  
This can lead to serious problems.  
These include heart attacks, strokes, tears in the main artery, poor blood flow to the intestines, and kidney damage.

## How Fast Does Cocaine Work?

The speed of the high depends on how you use it.

- **Intravenous injection (into a vein):** Effects start right away.  
  Peak effect in 3 to 5 minutes.  
  Lasts about 15 to 20 minutes.

- **Smoking (crack):** Effects start right away.  
  Peak effect in 3 to 5 minutes.  
  Lasts about 15 to 20 minutes.

- **Snorting (through the nose):** Effects start in 3 to 5 minutes.  
  Peak effect in 20 to 30 minutes.  
  Lasts about 45 to 90 minutes.

- **Swallowing (oral use):** Effects start in 10 minutes.  
  Peak effect in about 60 minutes.  
  Lasts about 90 minutes.

Because the high does not last long, heavy users may take more every 10 to 15 minutes.

## Signs and Symptoms of Cocaine Use

You may notice these signs if someone is using cocaine:  
- Fast heartbeat  
- High blood pressure  
- Sweating  
- Dilated pupils  
- High body temperature  
- Anxiety or panic  
- Restlessness  
- Trouble sleeping  
- Mood swings  
- Poor concentration  
- Increased appetite after stopping use

## How Is Cocaine Use Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose cocaine use based on symptoms.  
They do not test blood or urine levels.  
But most standard drug tests check for a breakdown product of cocaine.  
This is called benzoylecgonine.  
It can be found in urine for several days after use.

## How Is Cocaine Use Treated?

Treatment focuses on managing symptoms.  
Doctors give medicine through a vein to calm you down.  
This is usually a type of medicine called a benzodiazepine.  
It helps with anxiety, high blood pressure, and seizures.

Do not use beta-blocker medicines.  
They can make things worse.

If your body temperature is too high, doctors will cool you down.  
They may use cooling blankets or cold fluids.

## Help and Support

If you or someone you know is struggling with cocaine use, help is available.

- **Cocaine Anonymous World Services, Inc.**  
  A group of people who help each other stop using cocaine.  
  They meet regularly and share experiences.  
  They offer support and hope.

- **Findtreatment.gov**  
  A website that lists licensed treatment providers in the United States.  
  It helps you find help for substance use problems.

# Dermatofibromas

Dermatofibromas are small, firm bumps under the skin.  
They range in color from red to brown.  
They form when too much collagen builds up under the skin.  
Collagen is a natural protein made by cells called fibroblasts.  
These cells live in the soft tissue just below the skin.

## Who Gets Dermatofibromas?

- They are common in adults.  
- Women are more likely to get them than men.  
- Most people have only one bump.  
- Some people get many bumps.  
- Bumps usually appear on the thighs or legs.  
- Most bumps are smaller than half an inch (less than 1 centimeter across).

## What Causes Dermatofibromas?

A specific gene change may cause these bumps to form.  
The exact reason is not fully known.  
They are not caused by anything you did or did not do.

## Do Dermatofibromas Cause Problems?

- Most dermatofibromas do not cause any symptoms.  
- Some may itch.  
- A bump may break open (ulcerate) if it gets scratched or bumped.  
- This usually happens after a small injury.

## Do You Need Treatment?

- Most dermatofibromas do not need treatment.  
- They are harmless and do not turn into cancer.  
- You only need treatment if the bump bothers you.  
- Treatment is needed if the bump grows larger.  
- A doctor can remove the bump with surgery.  
- The procedure is simple and done in a doctor’s office or clinic.

# How DNA and RNA Tests Help Find Infections

These tests look for unique parts of the genetic material from a germ. This genetic material can be DNA or RNA.

The test can work with the original amount of genetic material. Or, it can make more copies of the material in the lab to make it easier to find.

These tests are now common in hospitals and clinics. They give fast results. This helps doctors start the right treatment quickly. It also means patients do not need to take broad-spectrum antibiotics for too long.

The tests are very accurate. They can find even small amounts of a germ. They work for all types of germs. Results come fast.

Each test usually checks for just one germ. So doctors must know which germs are possible. They must choose the right test based on the patient’s symptoms.

Newer tests can check for many germs at once. These are called multiplex tests. One test can find and tell apart two or more germs.

These tests are used to find dangerous germs like those used in biological attacks. They also help find germs that cause lung, gut, or brain infections.

The tests can find both viruses and non-virus germs. Doctors order them based on the patient’s symptoms. For example, if someone has a cough, a fever, or a headache.

Multiplex tests are just as accurate as tests for one germ. But they usually only say “yes” or “no” — not how much of the germ is present. This can make results harder to understand in some cases.

Most of these tests only tell if a germ is present. But for some infections, there are ways to measure how much of the germ is in the body. This includes:

- Hepatitis B  
- Hepatitis C  
- HIV  
- Cytomegalovirus  
- Human T-lymphotropic virus  

Measuring the amount of germ can help with diagnosis. It also helps track how well treatment is working.

# Bad Breath

Bad breath means your breath has a bad smell that lasts or keeps coming back.

## Other Smells in the Breath

Some health problems cause odors in the breath. But these smells are usually mild and not the same as bad breath.

- **Liver failure** can make your breath smell like mice. It is musty, sweet, and sometimes like rotten eggs.
- **Kidney failure** makes your breath smell like urine or ammonia.
- **Uncontrolled diabetes** can make your breath smell like nail polish remover. This is because of a chemical called acetone.

## What Causes Bad Breath?

Most bad breath comes from problems in the mouth.

### Common Causes

- **Gum disease** (like gingivitis or periodontitis)
- Bacteria on the back of the tongue
- Certain foods and drinks, like garlic, onions, and alcohol
- Smoking

Bacteria in the mouth break down leftover food. This creates bad smells. These bacteria grow more in people with gum disease or poor oral hygiene.

Gum disease causes swelling and damage to the gums and the parts that hold teeth in place. It is caused by certain bacteria that build up in deep pockets around the teeth. These bacteria can also grow on the back of the tongue, even if you do not have gum disease.

Low saliva flow can also help bacteria grow. This can happen because of some health problems or certain medicines. (This is called dry mouth.)

After you eat, some food smells travel from your blood to your lungs. Then they come out when you breathe. This can make your breath smell bad. For example, garlic can still smell bad on your breath 2 to 3 hours after you eat it—even after it is gone from your mouth and stomach. Brushing and flossing will not remove this smell.

Smokers are more likely to have bad breath than non-smokers.

### Less Common Causes

- Infections in the sinuses or lungs
- Cancers in the nose, mouth, or throat
- A small object stuck in the nose (more common in children)
- Imagined bad breath (called psychogenic halitosis)

Many people think stomach problems cause bad breath. But this is rare. The tube from your throat to your stomach (esophagus) usually stays closed. So, stomach smells do not usually come up into the mouth.

However, in rare cases:
- A small pouch in the esophagus (called Zenker diverticulum) can trap food. The food can rot and cause a bad smell.
- Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) can cause bad breath.
- Stomach cancer can also cause bad breath.

### Imagined Bad Breath

Some people believe their breath smells bad when it does not. This is called psychogenic halitosis. It can happen in people who worry too much about their body or have serious mental health issues like schizophrenia. Some people with obsessive thoughts feel constantly dirty and think their breath smells bad.

## What to Look For: Causes and Features

| Cause | Common Signs | How It Is Checked |
|------|--------------|-------------------|
| Bacteria on the back of the tongue | Bad smell from tongue scrapings | Doctor or dentist exam |
| Gum disease (gingivitis, periodontitis) | Swollen or bleeding gums, loose teeth | Dentist exam |
| Mouth cancer | Often found during a routine exam | Biopsy, CT scan, or MRI |
| Foreign object in the nose | Pus or blood from the nose | Doctor exam, sometimes imaging |
| Nasal or throat cancer | Trouble swallowing | Doctor exam |
| Lung infections (like abscess or bronchiectasis) | Cough with blood or phlegm, fever | Chest X-ray, sputum test, CT, or bronchoscopy |
| Sinus infection | Pus from nose, face pain, headache | Doctor exam, sometimes CT |
| Zenker diverticulum | Food coming back up when lying down | Barium swallow test |
| GERD | Spitting up food when lying down or bending over | Barium swallow test |
| Foods or drinks (garlic, onions, alcohol, tobacco) | Smell matches what was eaten or drunk | History and exam |
| Imagined bad breath | Others do not notice the smell | Doctor exam, sometimes psychologist visit |

> **Note:** The smell from a foreign object or sinus infection is usually stronger from the nose than the mouth.

> **CT** = scan using X-rays and computers  
> **MRI** = scan using magnets and radio waves  
> **Biopsy** = taking a small tissue sample for testing

## When to See a Doctor or Dentist

Bad breath rarely needs urgent care. But you should see a doctor or dentist if:

- You have warning signs like a lump, trouble swallowing, or a bad smell from the nose.
- The bad breath does not go away after good oral care.
- You are worried about it.

Your doctor will ask about your health and habits. They will check your mouth, nose, and throat.

They may suggest you stop eating or drinking something that might cause the smell. Then see if the smell goes away.

Some doctors use special tools to test for bad breath. But these are not needed for most people.

## How to Treat Bad Breath

### Treat the Cause

- Stop eating garlic, onions, and other strong-smelling foods.
- Stop smoking.
- If you have gum disease, see a dentist for cleaning and treatment.
- If you have a foreign object in your nose, a doctor can remove it.

### Improve Your Oral Care

- Brush your teeth twice a day.
- Floss every day.
- Brush or scrape the top and back of your tongue.
- Use a tongue scraper or your toothbrush.

### Mouthwashes and Sprays

- Many mouthwashes and sprays claim to help.
- But their effects usually last less than 20 minutes.
- People recovering from alcohol addiction should use mouthwashes without alcohol.

### Mental Health and Bad Breath

- If you think your breath smells bad but others do not, you may have psychogenic halitosis.
- A mental health professional can help.

## Special Tips for Older Adults

- Older adults often take medicines that cause dry mouth.
- Dry mouth makes it harder to keep your mouth clean.
- This can lead to bad breath.
- Oral cancer is also more common in older adults.
- But bad breath is not more common just because you are older.

## Key Facts

- Most bad breath comes from bacteria in the mouth breaking down food.
- Good home care means brushing, flossing, and cleaning your tongue.
- Mouthwashes help only for a short time.
- Problems outside the mouth can cause bad breath. But doctors can often spot them during an exam.

- How to pick safe dental products (look for the American Dental Association’s seal)
- How to find a dentist

# Sprained Thumb Ligament

A sprain of the ligament on the inside of the thumb is common. It can be painful and make it hard to use the thumb.

## What Happens

The ligament connects the base of the thumb bone to the main thumb bone. It helps keep the thumb stable.

Most injuries happen when the thumb bends too far to the side. This often occurs when someone falls on their hand while holding a ski pole.

Sometimes, the ligament tears off a small piece of bone where it attaches.

## Symptoms

- Pain on the inside of the thumb joint
- Tenderness when you press on that spot
- The joint may feel weak or unstable over time

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors use two main tests:

**Stress test**  
The doctor holds the thumb steady and gently pulls the tip of the thumb to the side. This checks how loose the joint feels.  
Some people need a numbing shot before the test.  
The doctor compares both thumbs to see if one is looser than the other.

**X-rays**  
X-rays are taken to check for a broken bone.  
The most common view is front to back and side.  
Sometimes, special stress X-rays are taken.  
Most of the time, the X-rays look normal because there is no break.

## How It’s Treated

**Non-surgical treatment (most common)**  
- Wear a thumb spica splint for several weeks.  
- After a few weeks, take the splint off to do gentle strengthening exercises.  
- Put the splint back on after exercising.  
- Repeat this cycle for 2 to 3 more weeks.

**Surgery (if needed)**  
Surgery may be needed if the joint stays unstable.  
After surgery, a cast is worn for 6 to 8 weeks.

## Thumb Spica Splint

This is a special splint that holds the thumb and wrist in place. It helps the ligament heal.

# Birth Control: Simple Facts

Birth control stops pregnancy. It works in three main ways:

- It stops the ovaries from releasing an egg.
- It stops a sperm from joining an egg.
- It stops a fertilized egg from attaching to the lining of the uterus.

---

## How Well Does Birth Control Work?

No method is 100% effective. But some work much better than others.

Effectiveness depends on two things:

- **Perfect use**: When you follow all instructions exactly.
- **Typical use**: When you use the method as most people do — which may include mistakes.

For example:
- Birth control pills work very well if you take them every day.
- But if you forget a few pills, the protection drops.
- An IUD (intrauterine device) is placed once and works for years. You don’t need to do anything after that. So typical use and perfect use are almost the same.

Over time, people often get better at using a method. So the gap between perfect and typical use usually gets smaller.

---

### How Effective Are Different Methods?

Here is how many women get pregnant in the first year of using each method.

| Method | Pregnant with Perfect Use | Pregnant with Typical Use |
|--------|----------------------------|----------------------------|
| Birth control pill | 0.3% | 9% |
| Skin patch | 0.3% | 9% |
| Vaginal ring | 0.3% | 9% |
| Progestin shot | 0.2% | 6% |
| Implant under skin | 0.05% | Same as perfect use |
| Hormonal IUD | 0.2–0.6% | Same as perfect use |
| Male condom | 2% | 18% |
| Female condom | 5% | 21% |
| Diaphragm with spermicide | 6% | 12% |
| Cervical cap with spermicide | 10–13% | 8% (higher if you’ve had a baby) |
| Contraceptive gel | 7% | 14% |
| Contraceptive sponge | 9% (no baby), 20% (with baby) | 12% (no baby), 24% (with baby) |
| Spermicide alone | 18% | 28% |
| Copper IUD | 0.6% | Same as perfect use |
| Fertility awareness (rhythm) | 4% or more | 24% |
| Withdrawal (pulling out) | 4% | 22% |

> **Note**: Without any birth control, about 85 out of 100 women will get pregnant in one year of regular sex.

---

## What Are the Pros and Cons of Each Method?

Each method has benefits and downsides. Your choice depends on:

- How reliable you need it to be.
- What fits your lifestyle.
- Your health and personal preferences.

---

### Hormonal Methods

#### Birth Control Implant (under the skin)
- A small rod is placed in your arm. It lasts 3 to 5 years.
- You only need to visit a doctor once every few years.
- Side effects: Irregular periods, headaches, weight gain.
- Not for people with certain health issues.
- A small cut is needed to remove it.

#### Progestin Shot (like Depo-Provera)
- A shot every 12 weeks (3 months).
- Side effects: Irregular bleeding, weight gain, mood changes, lower bone density over time.
- It lowers the risk of uterine cancer, pelvic infections, and iron deficiency.

#### Hormonal IUD (Levonorgestrel-releasing)
- Inserted by a doctor. Lasts 3, 5, or 8 years.
- Side effects: Irregular bleeding or no periods. Rarely, the IUD can poke through the uterus.
- Sometimes the IUD comes out on its own.

#### Birth Control Pills (Combination: estrogen + progestin)
- Take one pill every day for 3 weeks, then a placebo pill for 1 week.
- Side effects: Spotting, nausea, bloating, higher blood pressure, breast tenderness, headaches, weight gain.
- Higher risk of blood clots.
- Not safe for women 35 or older who smoke.
- Helps reduce cramps, mood swings, acne, and abnormal bleeding.
- Lowers risk of osteoporosis and some cancers (like endometrial and ovarian).

#### Birth Control Pills (Progestin-only)
- Take one pill every day at the same time.
- Side effects: Irregular bleeding, no periods, headaches, weight gain.
- No risk of blood clots.

#### Skin Patch
- Stick a new patch on your skin every week for 3 weeks, then take a week off.
- Side effects: Like pills. Skin irritation at the patch site.
- Same health limits as pills.
- You may need backup birth control the first week.

#### Vaginal Ring
- Insert a ring once every 3 weeks. Leave it in for 3 weeks, then take it out for 1 week.
- Some women leave it in for 4 or 5 weeks.
- Side effects: Like pills, but less spotting.
- Same health limits as pills.
- If the ring comes out, put it back in within 3 hours — no backup needed.

---

### Barrier Methods

#### Cervical Cap
- Put in up to 40 hours before sex.
- Must stay in for at least 6 hours after sex, but no longer than 48 hours.
- Side effects: Allergy, irritation.
- Cannot be used during your period.

#### Male Condom
- Put on before sex. Remove carefully after.
- Disposable. Buy at stores.
- Side effects: Allergy, skin irritation.
- Only latex condoms protect against all STIs, including HIV.
- Synthetic condoms (polyurethane, polyisoprene, silicone) offer some protection but are thinner and more likely to break.
- Must be used correctly every time.
- Needs cooperation from your partner.

#### Female Condom
- Inserted into the vagina before sex.
- Penis goes into the condom.
- Disposable. Buy at stores.
- Side effects: Allergy, irritation.
- Less effective than male condoms.

#### Contraceptive Gel
- Use within 1 hour before sex.
- Side effects: Burning, itching, yeast infections, UTIs.

#### Contraceptive Sponge
- Put in before sex. Works for 24 hours.
- Must stay in for at least 6 hours after sex.
- Throw away after one use.
- Side effects: Allergy, dryness, irritation.
- Hard to remove. Must be taken out within 30 hours.
- Less effective than a diaphragm.

#### Diaphragm with Spermicide
- Put in up to 2 hours before sex.
- Must stay in for at least 6 to 8 hours, up to 24 hours.
- A doctor fits it. Check fit yearly or after childbirth.
- SILCS diaphragm is one size and does not need fitting.
- Spermicide can be messy.
- Side effects: Allergy, irritation, UTIs.
- Add more spermicide before each sex act.

#### Spermicide Alone
- Put in vagina 10 to 30 minutes before sex.
- Side effects: Burning, irritation, rash, UTIs.
- Not strong enough alone. Often used with other methods.

---

### Other Methods

#### Copper IUD
- Inserted by a doctor. Lasts 10 years.
- Side effects: Bleeding, cramps. Rarely, the IUD can poke through the uterus.
- Sometimes it comes out on its own.

#### Fertility Awareness (Rhythm Method)
- Track your fertile days using:
  - A calendar.
  - Check your cervical mucus daily.
  - Check mucus + temperature + other signs.
- No side effects.
- Needs daily tracking and avoiding sex during fertile days.
- Less effective if your cycle is irregular.

#### Withdrawal (Pulling Out)
- Man pulls out before he ejaculates.
- Needs strong self-control and timing.
- Not very effective.
- Sperm can leak out before ejaculation.
- Man may not pull out in time.

---

## Emergency Birth Control

If you have unprotected sex, emergency birth control can help prevent pregnancy.

- It is not meant for regular use.
- It works best if taken as soon as possible after sex.
- It does not protect against STIs.

---

## Key Points

- **Condoms are the only method that protect against STIs**, including HIV.
- Use condoms even if you use another method.
- No method is perfect. But some are much more reliable than others.
- Your health, lifestyle, and preferences help decide the best method for you.
- Talk to your doctor to find the right choice.
