# Sick Sinus Syndrome

Sick sinus syndrome means the heart’s natural pacemaker is not working well.  
This causes the heart to beat too slowly.  
The slow heart rate is not normal for the body’s needs.

Some people have no symptoms.  
Others may feel weak or tired.  
They may have trouble doing physical activity.  
They might feel their heart racing or fluttering.  
Some people pass out.

Doctors diagnose sick sinus syndrome using an electrocardiogram, or ECG.  
This test records the heart’s electrical activity.

If you have symptoms, you will likely need a pacemaker.  
A pacemaker is a small device that helps the heart beat at a normal rate.

---

## Types of Sick Sinus Syndrome

The condition can show up in several ways:

- The heart beats too slowly all the time.
- The heart alternates between slow and fast rhythms.
- The heart stops beating for a few seconds.
- The heart’s natural signal gets blocked before it reaches the upper chambers.
- The heart cannot speed up during exercise.

---

## Who Gets Sick Sinus Syndrome?

This condition mostly affects older adults.  
It is more common in people with other heart problems.  
It also happens more often in people with diabetes.

In the brady-tachy type, the heart beats too slowly at times.  
At other times, it beats too fast.  
The most common fast rhythm is atrial fibrillation.

---

## What Happens in the Heart?

### Sinus Pause
The heart’s natural pacemaker stops working for a few seconds.  
On an ECG, this shows as missing heartbeats.  
The pause can last seconds to minutes.  
After the pause, another part of the heart takes over.  
This keeps the heart beating.  
But if the pause is too long, you may feel dizzy or pass out.

### SA Exit Block
The heart’s natural pacemaker sends a signal.  
But the signal does not reach the upper chambers of the heart.  
This is called SA exit block.

- **First-degree SA block**: The signal is just slow.  
  The ECG looks normal.  
  No symptoms.

- **Type I second-degree SA block**: The signal gets slower and then stops.  
  The ECG shows a pattern where the time between beats gets shorter.  
  Then a beat is missing.  
  The pause is shorter than two normal beats.

- **Type II second-degree SA block**: The signal stops without slowing first.  
  The pause is a multiple of the normal beat interval.  
  Usually, it is twice as long.  
  The ECG shows grouped beats.

- **Third-degree SA block**: The signal never gets through.  
  No normal P waves appear on the ECG.  
  It looks like the heart has stopped.

### Chronotropic Incompetence
This means the heart cannot speed up during exercise.  
It is diagnosed when the heart rate does not reach 80% of the expected maximum.  
The expected maximum is 220 minus your age.

---

## What Causes Sick Sinus Syndrome?

The most common cause is aging.  
The heart’s natural pacemaker becomes scarred and weak.  
This is called fibrosis.  
Sometimes, other parts of the heart’s electrical system also become damaged.

Other causes include:

- Sleep apnea
- Certain medicines
- Overactive vagus nerve
- Heart disease from poor blood flow
- Inflammation or infection of the heart
- Build-up of abnormal substances in the heart

---

## Symptoms and Signs

Many people have no symptoms.  
When symptoms do occur, they are due to a slow heart rate.  
In the brady-tachy type, symptoms can also come from a fast heart rate.  
Or from a pause in the heart’s rhythm after a fast rhythm stops.  
This pause can cause dizziness or passing out.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests:

- **ECG**: Checks the heart’s rhythm.
- **Thyroid test**: Checks for low thyroid function.
- **Wearable ECG monitor**: Records heart rhythm over 24 hours or longer.
- **Exercise test**: Checks if the heart can speed up during activity.
- **Implantable monitor**: A small device placed under the skin.  
  It records heart rhythm for months.  
  Used if symptoms are rare.
- **Electrophysiology study**: A special test done during a heart catheter procedure.  
  Used only if the cause of passing out is unclear.

A slow, irregular pulse may suggest sick sinus syndrome.  
The ECG confirms the diagnosis.  
Some people come in with atrial fibrillation.  
The true problem may only show up after the heart returns to normal rhythm.  
Then, a pause in the heart’s rhythm appears.

The goal is to link your symptoms to a slow heart rhythm.

If your doctor suspects another condition, they may test for:

- Low thyroid function (with a blood test)
- Sleep apnea (with a sleep study)
- Poor heart response to exercise (with an exercise test)
- Heart structure problems (with an echocardiogram)

If symptoms happen very rarely, a long-term monitor may be needed.

---

## How Is It Treated?

The main treatment is a pacemaker.  
This device helps keep the heart beating at a normal rate.

If you have symptoms and no other treatable cause, you will need a pacemaker.

Using a pacemaker that works with the upper chambers (atrial or AV) lowers the risk of atrial fibrillation.  
A dual-chamber pacemaker is better than one that only works in the lower chambers.  
It also helps if you later develop another heart rhythm problem.

After getting a pacemaker, some people still have fast heart rhythms.  
Medicines can help prevent these.

In rare cases, two medicines may be used to raise the heart rate:

- Theophylline
- Hydralazine

These are only used in healthy, younger people with slow heart rate and symptoms.  
They are not used often.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

The heart’s natural pacemaker usually gets worse over time.  
The long-term outlook is mixed.

- About 4 out of 100 people die each year.  
  This is mostly due to other heart problems.
- About 5 out of 100 people develop atrial fibrillation each year.  
  This raises the risk of heart failure and stroke.

---

## Key Points

- Sick sinus syndrome causes the heart to beat too slowly.
- You may have no symptoms.  
  Or you may feel weak, tired, dizzy, or pass out.
- In the brady-tachy type, you may also have fast heartbeats or pauses after a fast rhythm stops.
- Diagnosis is based on ECG and heart rhythm monitoring.
- If you have symptoms, treatment is a pacemaker.

# Domestic Violence

Domestic violence is when someone hurts or controls another person they live with. This can happen between partners, family members, or other people in the same home.

It includes:
- Physical harm (like hitting, pushing, or choking)
- Sexual abuse
- Emotional or mental abuse (like threats, insults, or controlling behavior)

## Who Can Be Affected

Domestic violence can happen to anyone. It affects:
- Children
- Adults
- Older adults

It can happen between:
- Partners (current or former)
- Parents and children
- Grandparents and grandchildren
- Siblings
- Other adults or teens in the home

It happens across all ages, races, cultures, religions, sexual orientations, genders, jobs, and income levels.

## How Common Is It?

Women are more likely than men to be victims of domestic violence.

In 2021:
- 34% of women killed in murder or manslaughter cases were killed by a partner.
- Only 6% of men killed in such cases were killed by a partner.

About:
- 47% of women
- 44% of men

Have experienced stalking, physical violence, or sexual violence from a partner at some point.

In the United States, domestic violence happens at similar rates among people of all sexual orientations and gender identities.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, abuse increased in many countries. Reasons include:
- Stress from losing jobs
- Being stuck at home with no way to escape
- Difficulty reaching shelters or safe places

### Did You Know...

- Domestic violence can happen to anyone.
- An abuser may try to control the victim by:
  - Taking away money
  - Stopping contact with friends or family
  - Monitoring phone calls, emails, or social media

## Terms Used to Describe People Who Have Been Abused

Different words are used to describe people who have been abused. These include:
- **Victim** – a word used by police and courts. It is often used for someone who is still being abused or has recently been abused.
- **Survivor** – a word often used for someone who has gone through abuse and is now recovering.

Healthcare providers should ask people which word they prefer.

## Effects of Domestic Violence

### Physical Injuries

People who are abused may have:
- Bruises
- Black eyes
- Cuts or scratches
- Broken bones
- Lost teeth
- Burns

These injuries can make it hard to work. This can lead to loss of income.

Injuries can also cause shame. Victims may hide from family and friends.

### Unexplained Health Problems

Some people have symptoms with no clear cause. These can include:
- Headaches
- Belly or pelvic pain
- Feeling very tired

### Sexual Health and Pregnancy

Abuse can lead to:
- Sexually transmitted infections (STIs)
- Problems during pregnancy

### Moving Often

Victims may need to move many times to stay safe. This is expensive and stressful.

### Death

In the worst cases, domestic violence leads to death.

### Mental Health

Abuse can cause:
- Depression
- Anxiety
- Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
- Eating disorders
- Alcohol or drug problems

The more severe the abuse, the worse the mental health issues tend to be.

Abuse can also make existing mental health problems worse.

### Emotional and Psychological Abuse

Even if physical violence stops, emotional abuse often continues. This can include:
- Constant criticism
- Threats
- Isolation
- Control over daily life

This kind of abuse can hurt just as much—or more—than physical harm.

## Children Who See Domestic Violence

Children who see abuse at home can be deeply affected.

One study found:
- 11% of children in the U.S. see some form of family violence in a year.
- 26% see such violence at some point in their lives.

Children may show signs like:
- Being very anxious or crying often
- Being afraid all the time
- Trouble sleeping
- Trouble focusing at school
- Feeling sad or anxious
- Pulling away from others
- Missing school or doing poorly in school
- Acting out or being aggressive toward others

Some children blame themselves for the violence.

Older children may run away from home.

In homes with abuse, children are more likely to be hurt physically.

## How Doctors Check for Abuse

Doctors may suspect abuse if:
- A person has injuries that don’t match their story
- They have strange or unexplained symptoms
- Their behavior or their partner’s behavior seems unusual

A person may also say they are being abused.

Doctors may ask:
- Do you feel safe at home?
- Do you feel safe in your relationship?

Many experts say all patients should be asked about abuse, even if they don’t seem to be at risk.

### When Is It Not Safe to Go Home?

Doctors may worry about safety if:
- The person has said they want to leave the relationship
- The violence is getting worse (like choking or more frequent attacks)
- The partner has access to guns or other weapons
- The partner has threatened to kill or hurt the person

### Documenting Abuse

If abuse is confirmed, doctors may:
- Take photos of injuries
- Write down details of the abuse

This record can help in legal cases. Rules about reporting abuse vary by state and by the type of healthcare worker.

## How to Stay Safe

### Safety Is the Top Priority

Abuse is never okay. Help is available no matter what a person decides to do.

### What to Do During an Attack

If violence happens:
- Try to get to a safe place
- Avoid areas where you can be trapped
- Stay away from places with weapons (like the kitchen)

Call emergency services or the police right away.

Leave the home if you can.

### Get Medical Help

Have all injuries treated. Take photos of them. Keep the records.

Teach children:
- Not to get in the middle of fights
- How and when to call for help

### Make a Safety Plan

A safety plan helps you stay safe if you decide to leave or stay.

Your plan should include:
- Safe places to go (like a friend’s house, shelter, or family member’s home)
- People you can call for help
- Ways to leave the house (like going on a fake errand or walking the dog)
- How to get money (like hiding cash, opening a secret bank account, or getting a credit card)
- Copies of important documents (like birth certificates, ID cards, insurance cards, bank numbers)
- A packed bag with clothes, documents, and essentials—hidden in case you need to leave fast

### Leaving the Relationship

Sometimes, the only safe choice is to leave for good. Abuse often gets worse over time, especially with very aggressive people.

Even if physical violence stops, emotional abuse may continue.

Leaving is hard. People may stay because:
- They are afraid of what the abuser will do
- They depend on the abuser for money or help

### Danger After Deciding to Leave

The risk of serious harm or death is highest after a person tells their partner they want to leave.

At this time, take extra steps to stay safe:
- Get a restraining order (a court order that tells the abuser to stay away)
- Note: A restraining order does not guarantee safety, but it can help

## Help Is Available

In the United States, you can get help from:
- Shelters for people who have been abused
- Support groups
- The courts
- A national hotline: 1-800-799-SAFE (or 1-800-787-3224 for TTY)

The National Domestic Violence Hotline also offers online chat. This is useful if you can’t speak safely.

You should seek help even if the abuse is not severe. Getting help does not always mean trouble for the abuser.

### Using Technology Safely

If you are using a phone or computer that the abuser can check, be careful. There are ways to use technology safely. Information is available online.

## More Resources

The following websites may help. The Manual is not responsible for their content.

- **Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)**: Intimate Partner Violence  
  This site has facts, prevention tips, and data on abuse, sexual violence, and stalking in the U.S.

- **Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)**: Sexual Violence Resources  
  This site includes information on sexual violence, mental health after disasters, rape prevention, and sex trafficking.

# What Are Systemic Rheumatic Diseases?

Systemic rheumatic diseases are a group of long-term conditions that affect the body’s immune system. They cause inflammation in many parts of the body. These diseases include:

- Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies  
- Eosinophilic fasciitis  
- Mixed connective tissue disease  
- Relapsing polychondritis  
- Sjögren syndrome  
- Systemic lupus erythematosus  
- Systemic sclerosis  
- Inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis and spondyloarthropathies  
- Vasculitis, such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis  

The details of inflammatory arthritis and vasculitis are covered in other sections.

We do not fully understand what causes these diseases. But researchers are learning more about how they develop. This helps doctors create better treatments.

Most people with these diseases have a higher chance of developing hardening of the arteries. This condition can lead to heart attacks or strokes. Treating the underlying disease can lower this risk.

People who take moderate doses of corticosteroids and another medicine that weakens the immune system should take steps to prevent certain infections. These steps include:

- Taking medicine to prevent *Pneumocystis jirovecii* pneumonia  
- Getting vaccines for common infections like pneumococcal pneumonia, the flu, and COVID-19  

Corticosteroids can also make bones weaker. This increases the risk of osteoporosis. People on these medicines should talk to their doctor about ways to protect their bones.

# Stiff-Person Syndrome

Stiff-person syndrome causes muscles to become stiff over time.  
The stiffness gets worse slowly.  

## Who Gets Stiff-Person Syndrome?

This condition is more common in women.  
It often happens in people with type 1 diabetes.  
It can also happen in people with certain autoimmune diseases.  
Some people with certain cancers get it too.  
These cancers include breast cancer, lung cancer, kidney cancer, thyroid cancer, colon cancer, and Hodgkin lymphoma.

## What Causes Stiff-Person Syndrome?

In most cases, the body makes antibodies that attack its own nerves.  
These antibodies target nerve cells in the spinal cord.  
These nerve cells help control muscle movement.  
The most common antibody attacks an enzyme called glutamic acid decarboxylase.  
This enzyme helps make a chemical that stops nerves from overstimulating muscles.  
When the enzyme is damaged, nerves send too many signals to muscles.  
This causes muscles to stay tight and stiff.  

Sometimes, doctors do not know what causes the condition.

## Symptoms

Muscles in the middle of the body and the belly become stiff first.  
These muscles also grow larger over time.  
Muscles in the arms and legs are affected later.  
The stiffness gets worse over time.  
It can lead to serious disability.  
The whole body can become stiff.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your symptoms to suspect stiff-person syndrome.  
They use tests to confirm the diagnosis.  

**Electromyography**  
This test checks how well nerves and muscles work.  
It measures electrical activity in muscles.  

**Blood tests**  
These tests check for specific antibodies in the blood.  
Many people with stiff-person syndrome have these antibodies.  

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment focuses on easing symptoms.  

**Diazepam**  
This is a sedative.  
It helps relax muscles.  
It works best for most people.  

**Baclofen**  
This is a muscle relaxant.  
It may help if diazepam does not work.  
But there is not much strong evidence that it helps.  

**Immune globulin**  
This is a solution made from blood of many healthy donors.  
It contains many different antibodies.  
It is given through a vein.  
It can help for up to a year.  

**Corticosteroids**  
These medicines reduce inflammation.  
They can help, but they are not used often.  
Long-term use can cause serious side effects.  

**Rituximab**  
This medicine changes how the immune system works.  
It is used if other treatments do not help.  

**Plasma exchange**  
This is a process that filters harmful substances from the blood.  
It removes the abnormal antibodies.  
It is used if other treatments do not work.  

Treatment plans are made based on your symptoms and how well you respond to medicine.  
There is no cure, but treatment can improve quality of life.

# Corneal Transplant

A corneal transplant replaces part or all of the cornea. This surgery is done for several reasons:

- To fix a damaged cornea, such as one that has a hole in it.
- To ease severe pain that does not get better with other treatments.
- To treat a serious eye problem that does not respond to medicine.
- To improve vision when the cornea is scarred, cloudy, or misshapen.

## How Well Does a Corneal Transplant Work?

The chance that the transplant will last a long time depends on the reason for the surgery:

- **Keratoconus**, scars from injury, early bullous keratopathy, and Fuchs dystrophy: about 90% success rate.
- More advanced bullous keratopathy or old viral infections: 70% to 90% success rate.
- Active eye infection: about 50% success rate.
- Chemical burns: about 14% success rate.

Some people get better vision faster after a type of transplant called DMEK. Most people see their best after about 2 months with DMEK. More people reach 20/20 vision with DMEK than with other types.

The cornea has a low chance of being rejected because it has no blood vessels. The eye also has a special way of handling immune responses. This helps the body accept the new tissue. Steroid eye drops, shots, or pills are used to prevent rejection.

## Limbal Stem Cell Transplant

This surgery replaces stem cells at the edge of the cornea. These stem cells make new surface cells for the cornea.

The stem cells are damaged by:

- Severe chemical burns.
- Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
- Wearing contact lenses too long.

When these stem cells are damaged, the cornea cannot heal. This can lead to open sores, infection, scarring, or even a hole in the eye.

A regular corneal transplant only replaces the center of the cornea. It does not fix the edge where the stem cells live. So, a stem cell transplant is needed to restore the cornea’s ability to heal.

Stem cells can come from:

- The other healthy eye of the same person.
- A donor eye after death.

The surgeon removes the damaged cells from the edge of the cornea. Then, healthy donor tissue is placed in the same spot and stitched in place. If donor tissue is used, the patient must take medicine to prevent rejection.

## Key Facts

- Corneal transplants are used for many conditions, including:
  - Bullous keratopathy
  - Keratoconus
  - Infections of the cornea
  - Chemical burns
  - Corneal dystrophies

- The transplant can replace:
  - The full thickness of the cornea.
  - Just the middle layer (stroma).
  - Just the back layer (endothelium).
  - Or the stem cells at the edge.

- No tissue matching is usually needed.
- After surgery, patients use antibiotic and steroid eye drops.
- Patients must protect their eyes with shields or glasses.

- DMEK is a type of transplant that:
  - Has the lowest risk of rejection.
  - Gives the best chance of 20/20 vision.
  - Can lead to full vision improvement in as little as 2 months.

# Urethral Stricture

A urethral stricture is a scar that makes the tube that carries urine from the bladder out of the body narrower than normal.

This condition can happen:

- From birth
- After an injury
- After an infection

Most often, a stricture comes from a past injury. Infections, such as sexually transmitted infections, are now a rare cause. In many cases, doctors do not know what caused the stricture.

## The Urethra

[Video showing the urethra]

## Symptoms of Urethral Stricture

If the urethra is only slightly narrowed, you may notice:

- A weaker stream of urine
- A split or double stream of urine

If the urethra is very narrow, urine may not pass at all. Pressure builds up behind the blockage. This can cause small pouches to form in the tissue around the urethra. These pouches are called diverticula.

When you do not empty your bladder fully or often enough, you are more likely to get a urinary tract infection.

## How Doctors Diagnose a Urethral Stricture

Doctors use two main tests:

- **Retrograde urethrography**: A special x-ray is taken after a liquid that shows up on x-rays is put into the urethra.
- **Cystoscopy**: A thin, flexible tube with a camera is passed into the urethra. The doctor uses a numbing gel first to make the procedure more comfortable.

These tests help the doctor see the inside of the urethra and find the narrow spot.

## Treatment for Urethral Stricture

The goal of treatment is to open up the narrowed part of the urethra.

Doctors use two main methods:

- **Dilation**: The urethra is numbed. Then, a special tool is gently pushed into the urethra to stretch the narrow area.
- **Urethrotomy**: A small knife or laser is used through a tool passed into the urethra. The doctor cuts the scar tissue to open the passage.

Sometimes, scar tissue forms again after treatment. This can cause the stricture to come back.

If the stricture returns, surgery may be needed. The surgeon removes the scar tissue. In some cases, the urethra is rebuilt using tissue from another part of the body. This surgery is called urethroplasty.

# Injuries to the Knee’s Straightening System

The knee’s straightening system includes the quadriceps tendon, the patellar tendon, the kneecap (patella), and the tibial tubercle (a bump on the shinbone). These injuries usually need surgery to fix.

(See also: Overview of Sprains and Other Soft-Tissue Injuries.)

To straighten the knee, the muscles in the front of the thigh (quadriceps) pull on the kneecap through the quadriceps tendon. The kneecap then connects to the shinbone through the patellar tendon. If the knee bends suddenly while the thigh muscles are tight, these parts can get damaged.

Types of injuries include:
- Tears in the quadriceps tendon
- Tears in the patellar tendon
- Breaks in the kneecap
- Breaks in the tibial tubercle

In healthy people, it takes a lot of force to injure these parts. The tendons are usually strong enough that the kneecap breaks before the tendon tears. But some people are more likely to tear a tendon. These include people who:
- Are older
- Have osteoarthritis
- Take certain medicines (like fluoroquinolone antibiotics or corticosteroids)
- Have diabetes
- Are overweight
- Have overactive parathyroid glands
- Have nerve damage in the limbs (polyneuropathy)
- Abuse anabolic steroids

In these people, even a small injury—like stepping down from a step—can cause a tendon tear. The quadriceps tendon is more often injured than the patellar tendon, especially in older adults.

## Symptoms and Signs

The injured area is painful and swollen.

If the tendon is completely torn, the person cannot:
- Stand on the injured leg
- Lift the injured leg straight while lying on their back
- Straighten the knee while sitting

Long-term problems are common. These can include limited movement and weak muscles.

## How Doctors Diagnose the Injury

Doctors use several tools to find the problem:

- A physical exam
- X-rays
- MRI scans

During the exam, doctors look for signs of injury:
- Quadriceps tendon tear: The kneecap sits lower than normal.
- Patellar tendon tear: The kneecap sits higher than normal.
- Kneecap break: There may be a gap between the broken pieces.

Swelling can hide these signs. This can make the injury look like a ligament problem with blood in the joint. If a person has knee pain and swelling after an injury, doctors ask them to:
- Sit and try to straighten the injured leg
- Lie on their back and lift the injured leg straight

**Important:** Always check if the person can actively straighten the knee when there is knee pain and swelling after an injury.

X-rays are done for everyone. They can show if the kneecap is too high or too low. They often show a broken kneecap or a shift in position. But sometimes the x-ray looks normal. An MRI scan gives a clearer picture and confirms the diagnosis.

## Treatment

All these injuries need surgery to repair.

# Kienböck Disease

Kienböck disease happens when the lunate bone in your wrist dies because it does not get enough blood. This is also called osteonecrosis.

You can find more about hand problems in the overview of hand disorders.

The lunate bone is one of the small bones in your wrist.

## Bones in the Wrist

The wrist has many small bones. They sit between the bones of your forearm and the bones of your hand.

### What the Wrist Bones Do

- They help your hand move.
- They support your hand when you use it.

## Who Gets Kienböck Disease?

Kienböck disease is not common.  
Doctors do not know exactly why the blood flow to the lunate bone stops.  
Most people do not remember hurting their wrist.  
It most often affects men between 20 and 45 years old.  
It usually happens in the hand they use most.  
It is more common in people who do heavy physical work.

## Symptoms of Kienböck Disease

- Pain starts slowly in the middle of the wrist, where the lunate bone is.
- The pain gets worse over time.
- Swelling may appear on top of the wrist.
- The wrist may feel stiff.
- In 1 out of 10 people, both wrists are affected.

## How Doctors Diagnose Kienböck Disease

Doctors use imaging tests to find the problem early.

- Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can show the problem before it shows up on other tests.
- Computed tomography (CT) can also help find early signs.
- X-rays are used later to confirm the diagnosis.

## How Kienböck Disease Is Treated

Surgery is the main treatment.

- Doctors may change the length of bones near the lunate to reduce pressure.
- They may do a bone graft to try to bring back blood flow to the lunate bone.
- They may also use a blood vessel graft to improve blood supply.
- If the lunate bone has collapsed, doctors may remove some wrist bones or join bones together with surgery. This is called arthrodesis. It helps reduce pain.

Non-surgical treatments, like medicine or physical therapy, have not worked well.  
But a wrist splint may help ease pain in very mild cases.

# How to Prevent Injuries in Older Adults

Older adults are more likely to get hurt.  
Doctors should check each older patient for injury risks.  

They should talk to the patient and their family about how to stay safe.  
This includes simple steps to avoid falls and other injuries.  

Everyone involved should know what actions to take.  
The goal is to help older adults stay healthy and independent.

# Too Much Vitamin E

Too much vitamin E is rare. But very high doses can cause problems.

## What Can Happen with Too Much Vitamin E

- High doses of vitamin E can make you bleed more easily.  
- This risk is higher if you are already taking medicine to prevent blood clots, such as warfarin.  
- Some people who take very high doses may feel weak in the muscles.  
- They may also feel tired, sick to their stomach, or have diarrhea.  
- Most adults can take large amounts of vitamin E for months or years without harm.  

## How Doctors Know You Have Too Much Vitamin E

- Doctors look at your symptoms.  
- They ask if you are taking vitamin E supplements.  
- They may check your blood to see how well it clots.  

## How to Treat Too Much Vitamin E

- Stop taking vitamin E supplements.  
- If you are bleeding, your doctor may give you vitamin K.  
- Vitamin K helps your blood clot.  
- Once you stop the supplements, your symptoms usually go away.  

## What Is Vitamin E?

- Vitamin E is a nutrient that helps protect your body’s cells.  
- It fights harmful chemicals made during normal body processes.  
- These chemicals can damage cells over time.  
- Vitamin E is found in foods like vegetable oils, nuts, seeds, green leafy vegetables, and wheat germ.  
- It dissolves in fat, so it is best absorbed when eaten with some fat.  

## Do Vitamin E Supplements Help Prevent Disease?

- Many people take vitamin E supplements to stay healthy.  
- But there is no strong proof that vitamin E prevents cancer.  
- It does not prevent heart disease or blood vessel problems.  
- It does not slow down Alzheimer disease, even in high doses.  
- It does not lower the risk of prostate cancer.  
- It is not clear if vitamin E helps with tardive dyskinesia.  
- Tardive dyskinesia is a side effect of some mental health medicines.  
- It causes uncontrolled movements of the mouth, tongue, arms, or legs.  
- It is also not clear if vitamin E increases or decreases the risk of stroke.  

## Key Points

- Vitamin E is safe when taken in normal amounts from food.  
- High doses from supplements can cause harm.  
- Always talk to your doctor before taking vitamin E or any other supplement.

# Licorice

Licorice is a plant root that tastes very sweet. It comes from a shrub called *Glycyrrhiza glabra*. People use it in medicine as a capsule, tablet, or liquid. Most licorice candy in the United States does not come from this plant. It is made with artificial flavors instead.

The main active part of natural licorice is called glycyrrhizin. Some people are sensitive to glycyrrhizin. For them, there are special licorice products with much less glycyrrhizin. These are called deglycyrrhizinated licorice.

## What People Use Licorice For

People take licorice to:
- Stop coughs
- Soothe a sore throat
- Ease an upset stomach

Some people use it on the skin to help with mouth sores or skin irritation like eczema.

Licorice is also said to help with:
- Stomach ulcers
- Liver problems caused by hepatitis C or other liver diseases

## What the Research Shows

Some studies show that licorice, when used with other herbs, can help with:
- Bloating and discomfort in the stomach (functional dyspepsia)
- Irritable bowel syndrome

But there are not enough good studies to know if licorice alone helps with stomach ulcers or liver problems.

One review of five small studies found that using licorice on the throat before surgery helped prevent sore throats after surgery. It also helped reduce coughing after surgery.

Another study gave people with mouth sores a mix of licorice and a medicine called diphenhydramine. These people healed faster than those who only took diphenhydramine.

A third study gave people with long-term cough a licorice lozenge. It helped reduce their cough symptoms.

Licorice has also been used to help ease symptoms in people with Parkinson disease, but more research is needed.

## Side Effects of Licorice

At normal amounts, licorice is safe for most people. But high doses can cause problems.

High doses of real licorice (more than one ounce per day) or glycyrrhizin can:
- Cause the body to hold on to salt and water
- Raise blood pressure
- Lower potassium levels in the blood

Low potassium can be dangerous. It can cause heart problems. This is especially risky for people who:
- Have heart disease
- Take digoxin
- Take diuretics (water pills)

These people should not take licorice.

A large review of studies found that people who eat licorice often over time may have higher blood pressure.

Licorice may also affect pregnancy. It can act like some hormones. It may raise the risk of early birth. It may also affect the baby’s stress system. Pregnant women should avoid licorice.

## Drug Interactions

Licorice can interact with some medicines. It may:
- Make warfarin less effective. This increases the risk of blood clots.
- Change potassium levels. This can affect digoxin and other heart medicines.
- Reduce the effect of blood pressure medicines. This is because licorice causes the body to keep more salt and water.
- Change how some cancer medicines (paclitaxel and cisplatin) work.
- Increase the side effects of steroid medicines.
- Change how estrogen medicines work.
- Act like a type of antidepressant called an MAO inhibitor. This may make side effects worse if you take antidepressants.

Always talk to your doctor before using licorice if you take any medicine.
