# Symptoms of Cancer

Cancer starts as a small group of abnormal cells. At first, it causes no symptoms.

As the cancer grows, it can press on or spread into nearby tissues. This can cause problems in that area.

Some cancers make substances or cause reactions in the body. These can cause symptoms in parts of the body far from the cancer.

Sometimes, a blood test done for another reason finds something wrong. For example, a colon cancer might be found when a blood test shows low red blood cells (anemia).

Cancer can hurt nearby tissues by pressing on them or growing into them. This pressure or growth can cause pain.

Pressure can also stop tissues from working normally. For example:
- A bladder cancer or a cancer in the belly may press on the tube that carries urine from the kidney to the bladder. This can block urine flow.
- A lung cancer may block air in part of the lung. This can cause part of the lung to collapse. It also raises the risk of infection.

If cancer grows in a space with room to expand, like the wall of the large intestine or the inside of the lung, it may not cause symptoms until it is large.

But if cancer grows in a tight space, like on a vocal cord, it can cause symptoms early. For example, it may cause hoarseness even when small.

If cancer spreads to another part of the body, it can cause the same problems—like pressure or irritation—in that new area. This means the symptoms may be different.

Cancers that grow near the lining of the lungs (pleura) or the sac around the heart (pericardium) often cause fluid to build up. This fluid can collect around those organs.

Too much fluid can make it hard to breathe. It can also make the heart work poorly.

---

## Some Complications of Cancer

| Complication | What Happens |
|--------------|--------------|
| **Cardiac tamponade** | Fluid builds up around the heart. This pressure stops the heart from pumping well. It can cause chest pain and shortness of breath. This happens when cancer irritates the sac around the heart. |
| **Pleural effusion** | Fluid builds up around the lungs. This makes it hard to breathe. |
| **Superior vena cava syndrome** | A cancer blocks the large vein that carries blood from the upper body to the heart. This causes swelling in the face, neck, and upper chest. |
| **Spinal cord compression** | Cancer presses on the spinal cord or nerves. This can cause pain and loss of control over the bladder or bowels. The longer the pressure lasts, the harder it is to recover normal function. |
| **Brain dysfunction** | Cancer in the brain (primary) or cancer that spread to the brain (metastasis) can cause confusion, drowsiness, restlessness, headaches, vision problems, strange feelings, weakness, nausea, vomiting, or seizures. |
| **Bleeding** | Cancer can break down normal tissue and blood vessels. It can also grow fragile blood vessels inside the tumor. This can cause bleeding. |

---

## Pain

Many cancers do not cause pain at first. But some cancers, like brain tumors, can cause pain early. For example:
- Brain tumors may cause headaches.
- Cancers in the head, neck, or esophagus may cause painful swallowing.

As cancer grows, the first sign is often a mild ache. This pain can get worse over time.

Pain can happen when the cancer presses on or damages nerves or other body parts.

Not all cancers cause strong pain. And the lack of pain does not mean the cancer is not growing or spreading.

---

## Bleeding

Early on, a cancer may bleed a little. Its blood vessels are weak and can break easily.

As the cancer grows, it may invade nearby blood vessels. This can cause more bleeding.

The bleeding may be so small it is not noticed. Or it may only show up in tests. This often happens in early colon cancer.

In later stages, bleeding can be serious. It can be heavy and even life-threatening.

Where the cancer is affects where the bleeding happens:
- Cancer in the digestive tract can cause blood in the stool.
- Cancer in the urinary tract can cause blood in the urine.
- Other cancers can bleed inside the body.
- Bleeding in the lungs can cause coughing up blood.

---

## Blood Clots

Some cancers make substances that cause blood to clot too much. This mainly happens in the veins of the legs (deep vein thrombosis).

A blood clot in the leg can break loose. It can travel to the lung and block blood flow. This is called a pulmonary embolism. It can be deadly.

Too much clotting is common in people with cancers of the pancreas, lung, or other solid tumors. It also happens in people with brain tumors.

---

## Weight Loss and Fatigue

Many people with cancer lose weight and feel very tired. These problems often get worse as the cancer grows.

Some people lose weight even if they are eating well. Others lose their appetite. They may feel sick when they eat or have trouble swallowing. They can become very thin.

People with advanced cancer are often extremely tired. If they develop anemia, even light activity can make them feel tired or short of breath.

---

## Swollen Lymph Nodes

When cancer starts to spread, it often moves first to nearby lymph nodes. These nodes can become swollen.

The swollen nodes are usually not painful. They may feel hard or rubbery.

They may move easily at first. But if the cancer spreads further, they can stick to nearby tissues or to each other.

---

## Neurologic and Muscular Symptoms

Cancer can grow into or press on nerves or the spinal cord. This can cause:
- Pain
- Weakness
- Tingling or numbness

If cancer grows in the brain, symptoms can be hard to describe. They may include:
- Confusion
- Dizziness
- Headaches
- Nausea
- Vision changes
- Seizures

Some nerve and muscle problems are part of a paraneoplastic syndrome. This is when the body’s immune system reacts to cancer in a way that harms nerves or other organs.

---

## Respiratory Symptoms

Cancer can press on or block the airways in the lungs. This can cause:
- Shortness of breath
- Cough
- Pneumonia

Shortness of breath can also happen if:
- A large amount of fluid builds up around the lungs (pleural effusion)
- There is bleeding in the lungs
- The person has anemia

# Neuro-Ophthalmologic and Cranial Nerve Disorders – Simple Explanation

This guide explains problems with nerves that control the eyes, face, and other parts of the head and neck. These issues can affect vision, eye movement, facial muscles, and more.

---

## What Are These Disorders?

Some nerves in the head and neck are called cranial nerves. They control many important functions, including:

- Eye movement
- Vision
- Pupil size
- Facial expressions
- Chewing
- Swallowing
- Speaking
- Hearing
- Balance
- Smell
- Taste

When one or more of these nerves do not work properly, it can cause symptoms like:

- Blurry or lost vision
- Double vision
- Drooping eyelid
- Eye that does not move well
- Face weakness
- Trouble swallowing
- Dizziness
- Loss of smell or taste

These problems are called **cranial nerve disorders** or **neuro-ophthalmologic disorders**. Some conditions affect both.

---

## How the Nerves Work

Each cranial nerve has a specific job. Here is a simple list of the 12 cranial nerves and what they do:

| Nerve | Main Job |
|------|--------|
| I (Olfactory) | Smell |
| II (Optic) | Vision |
| III (Oculomotor) | Moves the eye up, down, and inward. Lifts the eyelid. Controls pupil size. |
| IV (Trochlear) | Moves the eye down and inward. |
| V (Trigeminal) | Sensation in the face, teeth, and mouth. Controls chewing. |
| VI (Abducens) | Moves the eye outward. |
| VII (Facial) | Controls facial expressions. Helps with tears and saliva. Controls taste on front two-thirds of the tongue. |
| VIII (Vestibulocochlear) | Hearing and balance. |
| IX (Glossopharyngeal) | Sensation in the throat and back of the tongue. Controls swallowing. Helps regulate blood pressure. |
| X (Vagus) | Controls voice, swallowing, heart rate, and digestion. |
| XI (Accessory) | Turns the head and shrugs the shoulders. |
| XII (Hypoglossal) | Moves the tongue. |

---

## Common Problems and Their Causes

### 1. **Smell Problems (Nerve I)**
- **Symptoms**: Can’t smell things.
- **Causes**: Head injury, colds, allergies, brain diseases like Alzheimer’s or Parkinson’s, sinus infections, or tumors.

### 2. **Vision Problems (Nerve II)**
- **Symptoms**: Sudden loss of vision in one eye, blind spots, or temporary blindness.
- **Causes**: Blocked blood vessels in the eye, diabetes, high blood pressure, inflammation, or nerve damage from infection or autoimmune disease.

### 3. **Eye Movement Problems (Nerves III, IV, VI)**
- **Symptoms**: Double vision, eye that won’t move, droopy eyelid.
- **Causes**:
  - Aneurysm (a weak spot in a blood vessel)
  - Stroke or diabetes
  - Head injury
  - Tumors
  - Multiple sclerosis
  - Infections

### 4. **Facial Weakness (Nerve VII)**
- **Symptoms**: One side of the face droops, trouble smiling, drooling, dry eye, or taste changes.
- **Causes**: Bell’s palsy, stroke, injury, infection (like shingles), or tumors.

### 5. **Hearing and Balance Problems (Nerve VIII)**
- **Symptoms**: Ringing in the ears, dizziness, feeling unbalanced, hearing loss.
- **Causes**: Inner ear infection, Meniere’s disease, aging, head injury, or tumors.

### 6. **Swallowing and Voice Problems (Nerves IX and X)**
- **Symptoms**: Trouble swallowing, hoarse voice, choking on liquids.
- **Causes**: Stroke, tumor, infection, or nerve damage.

### 7. **Tongue Problems (Nerve XII)**
- **Symptoms**: Tongue twitches, shrinks, or moves poorly.
- **Causes**: Stroke, brain tumor, nerve injury, or motor neuron disease.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose These Problems

Doctors use a step-by-step approach:

### 1. **Ask About Symptoms**
- When did the problem start?
- What makes it better or worse?
- Are there other symptoms like headache, fever, or weakness?

### 2. **Examine the Eyes and Nerves**
- Check vision and eye movements.
- Look at the pupils (size, shape, response to light).
- Test facial strength and movement.
- Check hearing, balance, and swallowing.

### 3. **Use Imaging Tests**
- **CT scan** or **MRI** of the brain and head to look for tumors, stroke, or swelling.

### 4. **Special Tests**
- **Swinging flashlight test**: Checks for pupil problems.
- **Eye movement tracking**: Watches how the eyes follow a moving object.

---

## Pupil Problems – What to Look For

Pupils should be the same size and react quickly to light.

| Finding | Possible Cause |
|--------|----------------|
| One pupil larger than the other, but no other symptoms | Normal variation |
| One pupil stays large, doesn’t react to light, but reacts to focusing | Nerve damage from syphilis |
| Both pupils small | Opioid use, glaucoma drops |
| Both pupils large, but still react to light | Stress, drug use (like cocaine), thyroid issues |
| Both pupils large and don’t react to light | Eye drops used during exam, or brain injury |
| One pupil large and doesn’t react to light | Damage to the optic nerve or eye |
| One pupil large and doesn’t react to light, but reacts to focusing | Third nerve damage (often from aneurysm or stroke) |
| One pupil large and slow to react, but reacts to focusing | Tonic pupil (Adie’s pupil) – usually harmless, happens in young women |

> **Note**: A doctor can test if a large pupil is from eye drops or brain injury by putting a special drop in the eye. If the pupil does not shrink, it was likely caused by eye drops.

---

## Eye Movement Problems – What to Watch For

- **Double vision** can mean a nerve or brain problem.
- If double vision goes away when you close one eye, it is likely due to eye movement issues.
- If double vision stays when one eye is closed, it may be a problem inside the eye.

### Common Eye Movement Issues

| Problem | What It Looks Like | Possible Cause |
|-------|-------------------|----------------|
| Can’t move eye to one side | Eyes don’t move together | Stroke, tumor, multiple sclerosis |
| Can’t move eyes up or down | Eyes stuck in one position | Brainstem stroke, tumor, Parkinson’s disease |
| One eye turns down and out | Eye doesn’t move inward or up | Fourth nerve palsy (often from injury or diabetes) |
| Eyes move in jerky waves | Involuntary eye movements | Inner ear problem, stroke, brain injury, or medication side effect |
| Eyes jerk rapidly in one direction | Fast eye movements | Brain injury, stroke, or drug use |

---

## Treatment

Treatment depends on the cause.

- **If caused by infection**: Antibiotics or antiviral medicine.
- **If caused by inflammation**: Steroids or other anti-inflammatory drugs.
- **If caused by a tumor**: Surgery, radiation, or chemotherapy.
- **If caused by diabetes or high blood pressure**: Control blood sugar and blood pressure.
- **If caused by a stroke**: Treat the stroke and prevent future ones.
- **If caused by nerve compression**: Surgery may help.

Some conditions improve on their own over time. Others need long-term care.

---

## When to See a Doctor

See a doctor right away if you have:
- Sudden vision loss
- Double vision that does not go away
- Face drooping
- Trouble speaking or swallowing
- Severe headache with vision changes
- Dizziness or loss of balance

Early treatment can prevent serious problems.

---

> **Note**: This information is for general understanding. Always talk to your doctor for diagnosis and treatment.

# Delivery Using a Vacuum or Forceps

Sometimes, a baby needs help coming out during birth. Doctors may use a vacuum extractor or forceps to assist.

## What Is a Vacuum Extractor?

- A vacuum extractor has a soft cup made of rubber-like material.
- The cup is placed on the baby’s head.
- A vacuum creates suction to hold the cup in place.
- The doctor gently pulls on the device while you push to help deliver the baby.

If the vacuum does not work, the doctor will do a cesarean birth instead.

### Possible Risks of Vacuum Extraction

- The baby’s scalp may have a bruise.
- The baby may have small bleeding in the eyes (called retinal hemorrhage).
- The baby may be more likely to have shoulder dystocia, especially if the baby is large.
- The baby may develop jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes).

## What Are Forceps?

- Forceps are metal tools with curved, rounded ends.
- They are placed around the baby’s head.
- The doctor uses them to gently guide the baby out during pushing.

### Possible Risks of Forceps

- The baby may have a bruise on the head.
- The area between the vagina and anus (called the perineum) may tear.

## When Are These Tools Used?

A vacuum or forceps may be used if:

- The baby is not getting enough oxygen.
- The mother is too tired to push effectively.
- Labor is taking too long.
- The mother has a health condition, such as a heart or brain problem, that makes pushing hard unsafe.

## How It Works

- The doctor places the forceps around the baby’s head or attaches the vacuum cup to the head.
- As you push, the doctor gently pulls to help guide the baby out.
- The process is done carefully to protect both mother and baby.

# Lung Abscess

A lung abscess is a serious infection in the lung. It forms a pocket of pus inside the lung tissue. This pocket is surrounded by damaged tissue and filled with fluid and dead cells.

Most lung abscesses happen when a person breathes in saliva or other fluids from the mouth. This is more likely to happen if the person has trouble swallowing or is not fully awake. This can occur after drinking too much alcohol, using drugs, or being under anesthesia.

## What Causes a Lung Abscess?

The most common cause is breathing in mouth fluids. This often happens in people with poor dental health or gum disease.

Other causes include:
- A blockage in the airway, such as from a tumor or a foreign object.
- Infection spreading from nearby areas, like an abscess under the diaphragm or in the chest.
- Infection traveling through the blood from another part of the body. This is less common.

Some people are more at risk:
- Older adults.
- People with brain or nerve problems that affect swallowing.
- People who are very sick or have weak immune systems.

In rare cases, lung abscesses can be caused by:
- Infections from IV drug use.
- A serious heart infection (endocarditis).
- Certain bacteria like *Staphylococcus aureus*.
- Fungal infections or tuberculosis.
- Parasites, such as those from a rare type of amoeba.

## How Does a Lung Abscess Develop?

Bacteria from the mouth enter the lungs. They cause inflammation and damage to lung tissue. Over time, the damaged tissue dies and forms a hole filled with pus.

The abscess may break open into a breathing tube. The pus then comes up through the mouth when the person coughs. This can cause a bad smell or taste in the mouth.

In some cases, the infection spreads to the space around the lung. This causes a condition called empyema, where pus builds up in the chest.

In rare cases, the infection destroys large parts of the lung. This is called pulmonary gangrene. It is very serious and can be life-threatening.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on the type of bacteria and how fast the infection develops.

**For abscesses caused by mouth bacteria (anaerobes):**
- Cough that brings up thick, foul-smelling mucus.
- Fever and chills.
- Night sweats.
- Weight loss over time.
- Feeling tired and not wanting to eat.
- Fingers may become rounded and club-shaped.
- Coughing up blood.
- Pain in the chest that gets worse when breathing.

**For abscesses caused by other bacteria (aerobes):**
- Symptoms come on quickly, over hours or days.
- They feel like a bad case of pneumonia.
- No bad smell in the mucus.
- May affect areas of the lung that are not usually dependent (like the top parts).

**Other signs:**
- A fever of 38 degrees Celsius or higher.
- Breathing sounds that are different when listening with a stethoscope.
- Crackling sounds in the lungs.
- A dull sound when tapping the chest.
- Signs of gum disease or poor dental health.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect a lung abscess in people who:
- Have risk factors like poor swallowing, altered consciousness, or weak immunity.
- Have symptoms like a long-lasting cough, fever, and weight loss.

The main test is a chest X-ray. It can show a hole in the lung filled with air and fluid.

If the X-ray is unclear, a CT scan may be done. This gives a more detailed picture. It helps find blockages, rule out cancer, or check for complications like empyema.

Tests may include:
- Sputum (mucus) sample tested for bacteria.
- Blood tests to check for infection.
- Sputum tests for fungi or tuberculosis if needed.
- A bronchoscopy (a thin tube with a camera) to look inside the airways. This helps rule out cancer or foreign objects.
- Fluid from around the lung may be tested if there is an empyema.

If a person has many abscesses in the lungs, doctors may check the heart for infection. This is done with an ultrasound of the heart.

## How Is It Treated?

Most people need antibiotics. The type depends on the likely bacteria.

**First-line treatment:**
- A combination of two antibiotics: one that works against anaerobic bacteria and one that covers other common bacteria.
- Example: ampicillin and sulbactam.

**Alternatives:**
- A carbapenem antibiotic (like imipenem/cilastatin).
- A mix of metronidazole and ceftriaxone.
- For people allergic to penicillin: moxifloxacin or a mix of levofloxacin and metronidazole.

**For MRSA infections:**
- Linezolid or vancomycin are the best choices.

**For gram-negative bacteria:**
- The antibiotic plan may be changed to target the specific bacteria found in tests.

**Oral vs. IV antibiotics:**
- People who are not very sick can start on oral antibiotics.
- Those who are very ill get IV antibiotics at first.
- Once the fever goes down and the person feels better, IV antibiotics can be switched to oral ones.

**Treatment length:**
- Usually 3 to 6 weeks or longer.
- The longer the treatment, the larger the abscess.
- Treatment continues until the X-ray shows the abscess has fully healed or left a small, stable scar.

**Drainage or surgery:**
- If the abscess does not get better with antibiotics, drainage may be needed.
- A tube can be placed through the skin into the abscess (percutaneous drainage).
- A bronchoscope can guide a tube into the abscess from inside the airway.
- Surgery may be needed in about 10% of cases, especially if:
  - The abscess does not respond to antibiotics.
  - The lung tissue is severely damaged (pulmonary gangrene).
  - There is an empyema that needs drainage.

**Surgery options:**
- Removing part of the lung (lobectomy) is most common.
- Smaller areas may need only a segmental resection.
- In severe cases, the whole lung may need to be removed.

**What is not recommended anymore:**
- Chest physical therapy and postural drainage are no longer used. They can spread the infection to other parts of the lung.

## When to Re-evaluate

If a person does not get better after 7 to 10 days of antibiotics, doctors should check for:
- A resistant or unusual type of bacteria.
- A blockage in the airway.
- A non-infectious cause of the hole in the lung (like cancer).

A CT scan and bronchoscopy may be needed to find the cause.

## Key Points

- Most lung abscesses are caused by breathing in mouth fluids, especially in people who are not fully awake or have trouble swallowing.
- The most common bacteria come from the mouth and are anaerobic.
- Look for a lung abscess in people with long-term cough, fever, weight loss, and a history of risk factors.
- Start treatment with antibiotics.
- If no improvement after 7 to 10 days, check for resistant bacteria, blockages, or other causes.
- Drain empyemas and consider surgery for abscesses that do not respond to medicine or for severe lung damage.

# Holes in the Heart: Atrial and Ventricular Septal Defects

Holes in the heart are common birth defects. They happen when the wall between the heart’s left and right sides does not close completely.

## What Are Atrial and Ventricular Septal Defects?

- An **atrial septal defect** (ASD) is a hole between the two upper chambers of the heart.
- A **ventricular septal defect** (VSD) is a hole between the two lower chambers of the heart.

These holes let blood flow where it should not go. This makes the heart work harder and less efficiently.

## How Do These Holes Affect the Heart?

- Blood that has already picked up oxygen from the lungs can go through the hole and back to the lungs.
- This is not useful. It wastes energy and makes the heart and lungs work too hard.
- Over time, this can cause problems like high blood pressure in the lungs or heart failure.

## Types of Holes

- Some atrial septal defects are just a normal hole that did not close after birth. This is called a **patent foramen ovale**.
- Most of these close on their own in the first few years of life.
- About one in four adults still has this hole. It usually does not cause problems.
- A true hole between the upper chambers (true ASD) rarely closes on its own.
- Ventricular septal defects can be in different places in the lower heart wall.
- Some small VSDs, especially those in the muscle wall, may close on their own.
- Others do not close and may need treatment.

## Symptoms

### Atrial Septal Defects

- Most children with ASD have no symptoms.
- Some may grow more slowly than other children.
- In young adults or middle age, untreated large ASDs can cause:
  - Trouble breathing during exercise
  - Feeling tired
  - Fast or irregular heartbeat
  - Stroke
  - High blood pressure in the lungs
- Even small ASDs can get worse over time as the heart stiffens and pushes more blood through the hole.

### Ventricular Septal Defects

- Small VSDs may only cause a heart murmur. The child may feel fine.
- Larger VSDs often cause symptoms in babies between 4 and 8 weeks old.
  - Fast breathing
  - Trouble feeding
  - Sweating while eating
  - Slow weight gain
- These signs mean the baby may be developing heart failure.
- Untreated large VSDs can lead to:
  - Frequent lung infections
  - Permanent high blood pressure in the lungs
  - Heart failure
  - Shorter life span
- If the hole is near the aortic valve, it can cause the valve to leak.
  - This is called **aortic regurgitation**.
  - Leaking blood back into the heart can cause heart failure.
  - Even a small VSD near the aortic valve may need closing if it causes leaking.

## How Are These Defects Diagnosed?

Doctors often find a hole when they hear a heart murmur during a check-up.

- A **heart murmur** is a sound made by blood flowing through the heart in an unusual way.
- To confirm the diagnosis, doctors use **echocardiography**.
  - This is a special ultrasound of the heart.
  - It shows the size, location, and shape of the hole.
  - It also checks if the heart chambers are enlarged.
  - It can find other heart problems at the same time.
- An **electrocardiogram** (ECG) may be done.
  - It checks the heart’s electrical activity.
  - It can show if a heart chamber is enlarged.
- A **chest x-ray** may show if the heart is bigger than normal.

## How Are These Defects Treated?

Treatment depends on the size of the hole, where it is, and whether it causes symptoms.

### Atrial Septal Defects

- Most children with small ASDs do not need medicine.
- If the hole is still open after age 2 or 3, and it is not small, doctors usually recommend closing it.
- This helps prevent future problems.
- Small ASDs in the center of the upper heart wall can be closed using a catheter.
  - A thin tube is inserted into a vein in the groin.
  - It is guided up to the heart.
  - A closure device is sent through the tube and placed over the hole.
  - The device expands and seals the hole.
- Large ASDs or those near the edges of the heart need surgery.
  - A patch is used to close the hole.
- After the hole is closed:
  - Children need antibiotics before dental visits or certain surgeries for 6 months.
  - This prevents a serious heart infection called **endocarditis**.
  - After 6 months, antibiotics are no longer needed unless there is a leftover hole.

### Ventricular Septal Defects

- Small VSDs often need no treatment.
- If the hole is near the aortic valve and causes leaking, surgery is usually needed.
  - The hole is closed.
  - The valve may be repaired or replaced.
- Babies with large VSDs and symptoms may first be treated with medicine.
  - **Furosemide** helps remove extra fluid from the body.
  - **Digoxin** helps the heart pump better.
  - **ACE inhibitors** relax blood vessels and make it easier for the heart to pump.
- These medicines help the baby feel better and give time for the hole to close.
- If symptoms do not improve or the hole does not get smaller, surgery is needed.
- Some VSDs can be closed with a catheter device.
  - But this is less common than with ASDs.
- After surgery:
  - Children need antibiotics before dental visits or certain surgeries for 6 months.
  - If a small hole remains, antibiotics may be needed for life.
  - This prevents **endocarditis**, a serious heart infection.

## More Information

The following resources may help parents and caregivers:

- [American Heart Association: Common Heart Defects](https://www.heart.org)  
  Learn about common heart birth defects and what to expect.

- [American Heart Association: Infective Endocarditis](https://www.heart.org)  
  Understand how to prevent serious heart infections and when antibiotics are needed.

# Uterine Inversion

Uterine inversion is a rare but serious problem that can happen after childbirth.  
The uterus turns inside out and pushes into the vagina.  
In some cases, it can push all the way out of the body.  
This can cause heavy bleeding or low blood pressure.  
It can even be life-threatening for the mother.

The most common cause is pulling too hard on the umbilical cord while trying to deliver the placenta.  
Other factors that can increase the risk include:  
- Pushing too hard on the top of the uterus during delivery  
- A weak or relaxed uterus  
- A placenta that is stuck too tightly to the uterus (called placenta accreta)

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose uterine inversion by doing a physical exam.  
The mother may have heavy bleeding after delivery.  
She may also feel dizzy or weak from low blood pressure.  
When the doctor checks the belly, the top of the uterus may not be felt where it should be.  
Or it may feel lower than normal.  
The top of the uterus may be seen at the opening of the vagina or even outside the body.

## How Is It Treated?

This is an emergency.  
Doctors must act quickly to fix it.  
They should call for help from other medical staff who are trained in childbirth emergencies.  
An anesthesiologist or operating room team may also be needed.

The main treatment is manual reduction.  
The doctor will push the uterus back into its normal position.  
This is done by placing fingers inside the vagina and pushing up on the inside of the uterus.  
The doctor may also press on the belly to help.  
If the placenta is still attached, the uterus must be put back in place before removing the placenta.

The procedure can be painful.  
So the mother may need pain medicine or sedation.  
In some cases, general anesthesia is used.  
Medicines like terbutaline or nitroglycerin may also be given to help relax the uterus.

Once the uterus is back in place, the mother will get a medicine called oxytocin.  
This helps the uterus stay firm and reduces the risk of bleeding or the uterus turning inside out again.

If manual attempts fail, surgery may be needed.  
A laparotomy (an incision in the belly) may be required.  
This allows the doctor to use both vaginal and abdominal methods to reposition the uterus.

# What Is Integrative, Complementary, and Alternative Medicine?

This guide explains integrative, complementary, and alternative medicine in simple terms.

---

## What Are These Types of Medicine?

Integrative, complementary, and alternative medicine (often called CAM) include healing practices that are not part of standard Western medicine. Many of these practices come from ancient traditions in places like China, India, Africa, and the Americas.

These terms are often used together, but they mean different things:

- **Complementary medicine** means using non-traditional methods *alongside* standard medical care.
- **Alternative medicine** means using non-traditional methods *instead of* standard medical care.
- **Integrative medicine** means combining safe and effective traditional and non-traditional treatments. It focuses on your whole health—body, mind, and spirit—and your personal needs.

---

## How Do Conventional and Integrative Medicine Differ?

There are key differences between how conventional medicine and integrative medicine view health and illness.

### Definition of Health

- **Conventional medicine** sees health as the absence of disease or injury.
- **Integrative medicine** sees health as balance and strength in your body, mind, and spirit.

### Definition of Illness

- **Conventional medicine** sees illness as a problem in a specific organ or body process.
- **Integrative medicine** sees illness as a sign of imbalance in your body, mind, or spirit.

### Life Force

- **Conventional medicine** believes all body functions come from known physical and chemical processes.
- **Integrative medicine** believes in a life energy (called *qi* in Chinese medicine) that flows through the body and supports health.

### Consciousness

- **Conventional medicine** believes thoughts and feelings come only from brain activity.
- **Integrative medicine** believes consciousness may go beyond the brain and can help in healing.

### Treatment Methods

- **Conventional medicine** uses only treatments proven by strong scientific research. These include medicines, surgery, physical therapy, diet changes, and lifestyle changes.
- **Integrative medicine** uses proven conventional treatments and also includes natural healing methods. These may include breathing exercises, meditation, herbal products, and bodywork.

### Use of Scientific Evidence

- **Conventional medicine** relies only on strong scientific proof.
- **Integrative medicine** uses scientific proof when available. It also considers long-term use and traditional beliefs, especially for low-risk practices.

---

## How Common Are These Practices?

Many people use complementary and alternative medicine.

- Up to 38% of adults have used CAM at some point.
- About 12% of children have used CAM.
- A 2012 national survey found the most common CAM practices were:

  - Deep breathing exercises (11%)
  - Yoga, tai chi, and qi gong (10%)
  - Manual therapy (like chiropractic or osteopathy) (8%)
  - Meditation (8%)
  - Yoga (6.1%)

Other practices are less common:

  - Homeopathy (2.2%)
  - Naturopathy (0.4%)
  - Energy healing (0.5%)

Also, over half of adults (57.6%) used at least one dietary supplement in the past month.

---

## Are These Therapies Effective and Safe?

### Research on CAM

In 1992, the U.S. government created a research office to study alternative therapies. It later became the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).

Many CAM therapies have been studied. Some are proven to help with certain health problems. Others have not been proven effective.

Some therapies are used for many conditions, even when there is no strong proof they work for those uses.

A lack of strong research does not mean a therapy is useless. But it does mean we do not yet know if it works.

### Why Is Research Hard?

Studying CAM is not easy. Here are some reasons:

- Few research funds are available for CAM.
- Some CAM advocates lack training in scientific research.
- CAM products are not held to the same strict rules as medicines.
- Companies make less money from CAM than from drugs or medical devices.

### Challenges in Designing Studies

- **Placebos** are hard to create for physical treatments. For example, it is hard to make a fake acupuncture needle that feels real.
- **Blinding** is difficult. Practitioners often know if they are giving real treatment. This can affect results.
- **Standardization** is hard. Different people use different methods. Herbal products vary in strength and ingredients.

Despite these challenges, some good studies have been done. For example, one study used a fake acupuncture needle (with no real needle) to compare with real acupuncture. This helped test the real effect of the treatment.

To be considered effective, a therapy must work better than a placebo or no treatment.

### Funding and Profit

CAM is a big business. Yet, it gets less research funding than conventional medicine. This is not because it is not profitable. It is because drug and device companies make much more money.

---

## Safety of CAM Therapies

### The Biggest Risk

The greatest danger of CAM is using it instead of proven medical treatment for serious diseases like cancer or heart disease.

If you have a life-threatening illness, do not stop your doctor’s treatment to try an unproven therapy.

### Safe CAM Practices

Some CAM therapies are safe and may be better than conventional options for some people:

- Meditation for stress or pain
- Acupuncture for nausea or pain
- Yoga for balance and flexibility
- Ginger tea for upset stomach

These can be used before or instead of stronger medicines like opioids.

### Possible Dangers

Some CAM therapies can be harmful:

- **Dietary supplements** are not regulated like medicines. They may contain unsafe ingredients or interact with your prescription drugs.
- Supplements made in other countries may have harmful contaminants or hidden drugs.
- Physical treatments like spinal manipulation can cause injury if done wrong.
- Some herbal products can harm your liver or kidneys.

### Unknown Risks

For many CAM therapies, we do not know if they are safe or harmful. In some cases, harm has been shown. But people who promote these therapies often do not report the risks.

---

## Key Takeaways

- Integrative medicine combines safe, proven treatments from both conventional and non-conventional sources.
- Always talk to your doctor before trying any CAM therapy.
- Never stop your doctor’s treatment to use an unproven therapy for a serious illness.
- Some CAM therapies are safe and helpful. Others may be risky.
- Scientific research is the best way to know if a therapy works.

---

## For More Information

You can learn more from the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).  
This is a U.S. government website that provides reliable information on CAM.

# Sulfonamides – Simple Explanation

Sulfonamides are a type of medicine that fights bacteria. They stop bacteria from growing and multiplying. They do this by blocking a key step in how bacteria make a vital substance called folate. Folate helps bacteria make DNA and build new cells.

Humans do not make folate. We get it from food. So these medicines affect bacteria more than they affect people.

---

## How Sulfonamides Work

Sulfonamides block a part of the process that bacteria use to make folate. Without folate, bacteria cannot grow or multiply.

This is why they are called "bacteriostatic" – they stop bacteria from growing, but do not kill them directly.

---

## Types of Sulfonamides

These are the most common sulfonamides:

- Mafenide  
- Sulfacetamide  
- Sulfadiazine  
- Sulfadoxine  
- Sulfamethizole  
- Sulfamethoxazole  
- Sulfanilamide  
- Sulfasalazine  
- Sulfisoxazole  

Some of these are available as single medicines you can take by mouth:

- Sulfisoxazole  
- Sulfamethizole  
- Sulfasalazine  

Sulfamethoxazole is often combined with another medicine called trimethoprim. This combination is sold as one pill.

Sulfadoxine is also combined with another medicine called pyrimethamine. This combination is used by mouth.

---

## Topical Sulfonamides (Applied to Skin or Mucous Membranes)

These are used on the skin or in the eyes or vagina:

- Silver sulfadiazine and mafenide burn cream – for burns  
- Sulfanilamide vaginal cream and suppositories – for vaginal infections  
- Sulfacetamide eye drops or ointment – for eye infections

---

## How the Body Handles Sulfonamides

- Most sulfonamides are well absorbed when taken by mouth.  
- They are also absorbed through the skin when used on burns.  
- The medicine spreads through the body.  
- The liver breaks down most of the drug.  
- The kidneys remove the rest from the body.  
- Sulfonamides can bind to a protein in the blood called albumin. This may affect how bilirubin (a waste product) is handled.

---

## When Sulfonamides Are Used

Sulfonamides work against:

- Many types of bacteria, both gram-positive and gram-negative  
- The parasites that cause malaria (*Plasmodium*)  
- The parasite that causes toxoplasmosis (*Toxoplasma*)

Sulfasalazine is used by mouth to treat inflammatory bowel disease, such as ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s disease.

Sulfonamides are often used with other antibiotics. They are used for:

- Nocardiosis (a rare bacterial infection)  
- Urinary tract infections  
- Malaria that does not respond to chloroquine

Topical sulfonamides are used for:

- Burns – silver sulfadiazine and mafenide cream  
- Vaginal infections – sulfanilamide cream or suppositories  
- Eye infections – sulfacetamide eye drops or ointment

---

## When Not to Use Sulfonamides

Do not use sulfonamides if:

- You have had an allergic reaction to them before  
- You have a condition called porphyria

Sulfonamides do not work for strep throat caused by group A streptococci. They should not be used to treat this infection.

---

## Use During Pregnancy and Breastfeeding

- Studies in animals show some risk to the baby.  
- There are not enough safe studies in pregnant women.  
- Use near the end of pregnancy or while breastfeeding is not safe.  
- These medicines should not be used in babies under 2 months old, except in special cases.

If used near the end of pregnancy or in newborns, sulfonamides can raise levels of a substance called unconjugated bilirubin in the blood. This can lead to a serious brain condition called **kernicterus**.

Sulfonamides pass into breast milk. This may harm a nursing baby.

---

## Side Effects of Sulfonamides

Side effects can happen with oral or topical use. They include:

- Skin rashes, hives, or severe skin reactions like Stevens-Johnson syndrome  
- Swelling under the skin (angioedema)  
- Fever, joint pain, or body aches (serum sickness)  
- Blood disorders such as low white blood cells, low platelets, or anemia  
- In people with G6PD deficiency, a type of anemia can occur  
- Liver problems (hepatitis)  
- Low thyroid function (hypothyroidism)  
- Worsening of lupus symptoms  
- Worsening of porphyria  
- Nervous system effects like headache or trouble sleeping  
- Increased sensitivity to sunlight (photosensitivity)

Some people may get kidney problems. This can happen if the medicine forms crystals in the urine.

Sulfasalazine can reduce how much folate (folic acid) the body absorbs. This may lead to folate deficiency, especially in people with inflammatory bowel disease who already have poor absorption. This risk is higher if diet is low in folate.

Mafenide can cause a condition called metabolic acidosis. This happens because it blocks an enzyme in the body that helps balance acid and base.

---

## Dosing and Safety Tips

- Drink plenty of fluids to prevent kidney problems. Aim for at least 1200 to 1500 milliliters of urine per day.  
- If kidney function is poor, your doctor may check blood levels.  
- For sulfamethoxazole, blood levels should not go above 120 micrograms per milliliter.

Sulfonamides can affect other medicines:

- They can make sulfonylureas (diabetes pills) too strong, leading to low blood sugar  
- They can increase side effects of phenytoin (a seizure medicine)  
- They can make blood thinners (like warfarin) more powerful

---

> **Note:** Always follow your doctor’s instructions. Do not stop or change your medicine without talking to your healthcare provider.

# Heavy Chain Diseases

Heavy chain diseases are a type of cancer that starts in plasma cells. Plasma cells are a kind of white blood cell. They normally help the body fight infections by making antibodies.

When one plasma cell grows out of control, it makes many copies of itself. These copies are all the same. They make a single type of abnormal protein. This protein is called a monoclonal antibody. It is also known as an M-protein.

People with a lot of M-protein often have lower levels of normal antibodies. This makes it harder to fight infections.

Antibodies are made of two types of parts: light chains and heavy chains. Normal antibodies have both. In heavy chain diseases, the cancer cells make only heavy chains. They do not make the matching light chains.

There are five main types of antibodies: IgM, IgG, IgA, IgE, and IgD. Each type has its own kind of heavy chain. In heavy chain diseases, the cancer cells make only one kind of abnormal heavy chain.

The three main types of heavy chain disease are:

- Alpha (from IgA)
- Gamma (from IgG)
- Mu (from IgM)

---

## Alpha Heavy Chain Disease

Alpha heavy chain disease mostly affects younger adults from Middle Eastern or Mediterranean backgrounds.

The cancer cells often spread into the wall of the intestines. This can stop the body from absorbing nutrients from food. This problem is called malabsorption.

Symptoms include:
- Severe diarrhea
- Weight loss

A rare form affects the lungs and airways.

To diagnose this disease, doctors do blood tests. These include:
- Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP): This test checks for abnormal proteins in the blood.
- Immunofixation: A more detailed test that identifies specific proteins.
- Tests to measure levels of immunoglobulins (antibodies).

Urine tests may also be needed. In some cases, a small sample of intestine tissue is taken and examined under a microscope. This is called a biopsy.

This disease often gets worse quickly. Some people live only 1 to 2 years after diagnosis.

Treatment may help slow the disease or put it into remission. Options include:
- Cyclophosphamide (a chemotherapy drug)
- Prednisone (a corticosteroid)
- Antibiotics

---

## Gamma Heavy Chain Disease

Gamma heavy chain disease mostly affects older men.

Some people have no symptoms at all. Others may have other immune system problems, such as:
- Rheumatoid arthritis
- Sjögren syndrome
- Lupus

The cancer cells can spread into the bone marrow. This can cause:
- Frequent infections
- Fever and chills
- Low white blood cell count
- Fatigue and weakness due to anemia

The cancer can also make the liver and spleen larger.

To diagnose this disease, doctors do blood and urine tests.

People with symptoms may get treatment with:
- Chemotherapy drugs
- Corticosteroids
- Radiation therapy

But the disease often progresses fast. About half of people with this disease die within about one year.

---

## Mu Heavy Chain Disease

Mu heavy chain disease is the rarest of the three main types. It mostly affects people over age 50.

It can cause:
- Enlarged liver
- Enlarged spleen
- Swollen lymph nodes in the abdomen
- Bone fractures
- Amyloidosis (a condition where abnormal proteins build up in organs)

To diagnose this disease, doctors do:
- Blood tests
- Urine tests
- Bone marrow exam (a sample of bone marrow is taken and tested)

Treatment usually includes:
- Chemotherapy drugs
- Corticosteroids

Survival time and response to treatment vary widely from person to person.

# Chagas Disease – Simple Explanation

## What Is Chagas Disease?

Chagas disease is an infection caused by a tiny parasite called *Trypanosoma cruzi*.  
This parasite can make people very sick.  

The most common way people get infected is from a bite by a kissing bug.  
Kissing bugs are also called triatominae or assassin bugs.  

Less often, people get infected by:  
- Drinking sugar cane juice or eating food that has been touched by infected bugs or their poop.  
- Getting a blood transfusion from an infected person.  
- Receiving an organ transplant from an infected donor.  
- A mother passing the infection to her baby during pregnancy.  

Animals like dogs, opossums, armadillos, rats, and raccoons can carry the parasite.  
They can spread it to bugs, which then spread it to people.  

Kissing bugs live in many parts of North, Central, and South America.  

Around 6 to 8 million people worldwide have a long-term (chronic) infection.  
Most of them live in Latin America, where the disease is still common in 21 countries.  
But the number of new cases is going down because of better homes, safer blood, and bug control.  

In Latin America, about 1.13 million women of childbearing age have the infection.  
Each year, 1 to 5 out of every 100 babies born to these women get infected.  
This means at least 15,000 babies are born with Chagas disease every year.  

In the United States, about 288,000 people had the infection between 2014 and 2018.  
Most of them got it while living in areas where the disease is common.  
Some cases in the U.S. are from local bugs. These have been found in Arizona, Arkansas, California, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Tennessee, and Texas.  
About 40,000 women of childbearing age in the U.S. have Chagas disease.  

---

## How Does the Infection Spread?

A kissing bug bites a person or animal that has the parasite.  
The bug then bites another person.  
While biting, the bug poops on the skin.  
The parasite in the poop can get into the body through the bite wound, or through the eyes or mouth.  

The parasite enters the body and starts to grow inside cells.  
It moves through the blood and can affect the heart, muscles, and nerves.  

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Chagas disease has three stages:  
1. **Acute stage** – happens soon after infection.  
2. **Chronic indeterminate stage** – no symptoms, but the parasite is still in the body.  
3. **Chronic stage** – symptoms appear years later.  

### Acute Stage
- A red, swollen area may appear at the bite site.  
- One eye may swell up.  
- Fever, tiredness, body aches, and swollen glands may follow.  
- The liver and spleen may get bigger.  

These symptoms often go away on their own.  
But the parasite stays in the body.  

### Chronic Indeterminate Stage
- Most people have no symptoms.  
- The infection stays quiet for years.  
- Some people stay this way forever.  
- Others go on to the next stage.  

### Chronic Stage
- After many years, some people develop serious problems.  
- Heart problems are most common.  
  - The heart may beat irregularly.  
  - The heart muscle can weaken.  
- Less often, people get:  
  - A swollen esophagus (megaesophagus), making it hard to swallow.  
  - A swollen colon (megacolon), causing severe constipation.  

People with weak immune systems, like those with advanced HIV, may get skin sores or brain problems.  

---

## How Is Chagas Disease Diagnosed?

### For Acute Infection
- A doctor can see the parasite in a blood sample under a microscope.  
- A blood smear (thin or thick) is used.  
- If needed, a sample from the heart or lymph node can be tested.  
- A PCR test can also be used. This test finds the parasite’s DNA. It works best when there are many parasites in the blood.  

### For Chronic Infection
- Blood tests look for antibodies. These are proteins the body makes to fight the parasite.  
- Two different blood tests are needed to confirm the diagnosis.  
- If the first test is positive, a second test checks for the same antibodies using a different method.  
- In the U.S., a test called TESA immunoblot is often used.  
- A positive result on two different tests means the person has Chagas disease.  

### Special Cases
- PCR tests are used for babies born to infected mothers.  
- They are also used if someone got infected through blood, a transplant, or lab exposure.  
- In some areas, doctors use a method called xenodiagnosis. This means they feed a lab-raised bug a blood sample and then check the bug’s gut for the parasite.  

### When to Test the Heart or Gut
- If a person has symptoms of heart problems, an echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) is done.  
- If no symptoms, but the person has a confirmed infection, a chest X-ray, ECG, and rhythm strip are done.  
- If a person has trouble swallowing or other gut issues, tests like a barium swallow or endoscopy are used.  

---

## How Is Chagas Disease Treated?

### Antiparasitic Drugs
Two medicines can kill the parasite:  
- Benznidazole  
- Nifurtimox  

These drugs work best when used early.  
They are most effective in children and young adults.  

#### Who Should Get Treatment?
- Anyone with acute Chagas disease.  
- Babies born with the infection.  
- People with a reactivated infection (like those with HIV).  
- Children up to age 18 with chronic infection.  
- Adults aged 18 to 50 who do not have serious heart or gut damage.  

#### When Treatment Is Not Used
- For people over age 50, treatment is decided case by case. The risks and benefits are weighed.  
- For people with advanced heart or gut disease, the drugs are not helpful.  
  - They do not fix heart damage or gut problems that have already started.  

#### Benefits of Early Treatment
- Kills the parasite faster.  
- Shortens the illness.  
- Lowers the chance of death.  
- Reduces the risk of long-term heart or gut problems.  

#### Side Effects
- **Benznidazole**:  
  - Skin rash or allergic reaction.  
  - Loss of appetite.  
  - Weight loss.  
  - Nerve problems (numbness or tingling in hands and feet).  
  - Trouble sleeping.  

- **Nifurtimox**:  
  - Loss of appetite.  
  - Nausea and vomiting.  
  - Weight loss.  
  - Nerve problems.  
  - Headache, dizziness, and feeling off-balance.  

Benznidazole is usually easier to take than nifurtimox.  
It is taken for a shorter time.  
Side effects are more common in older adults.  

#### Who Should Not Take These Drugs?
- People with severe liver or kidney disease.  
- Pregnant women or those who are breastfeeding.  
  - Treatment is usually delayed until after delivery.  
  - If the baby is infected, treatment starts after birth.  

---

## How Can Chagas Disease Be Prevented?

### Stop Bugs from Living in Homes
- Use plaster to fill cracks in walls.  
- Replace thatched roofs with metal or tile.  
- Spray homes with long-lasting insecticides.  

### Avoid Infection When Traveling
- Do not sleep in mud or adobe houses.  
- If you must sleep in one, use a bed net.  

### Avoid Unsafe Food and Drinks
- Do not drink fresh sugar cane juice unless you are sure it is safe.  
- Avoid food that might have been touched by bugs or their poop.  

### Prevent Congenital Infection
- Test women of childbearing age who are at risk.  
- Treat them before pregnancy to prevent passing the infection to the baby.  

### Safe Blood and Organs
- In many countries, blood and organ donors are tested.  
- In the United States, all blood and organ donors have been tested since 2006.  
- This stops infections from blood transfusions or transplants.  

---

## Key Points

- Chagas disease is caused by a parasite called *Trypanosoma cruzi*.  
- It is spread mainly by kissing bugs.  
- It is common in Latin America, but also found in the U.S. and other places.  
- Most people have no symptoms at first.  
- Some people develop serious heart or gut problems years later.  
- Diagnosis uses blood tests, parasite checks, or PCR tests.  
- Two medicines, benznidazole and nifurtimox, can kill the parasite.  
- Treatment works best early, especially in children.  
- These drugs do not fix heart or gut damage that has already happened.  
- Supportive care includes heart medicine, pacemakers, surgery, and other treatments.  
- Prevention includes protecting homes from bugs, avoiding unsafe food, and testing blood and organs.

# Intravenous Feeding

Intravenous feeding gives nutrients directly into the blood through a vein. It is used when a person cannot get enough nutrition through their digestive system.

The nutrients go into the bloodstream through a tube called a central venous catheter. This tube is placed into a large vein, such as the one under the collarbone.

This type of feeding is needed when the digestive system is not working or must rest. It may be used for people with:

- Severe problems absorbing food
- Certain stages of ulcerative colitis
- A blockage in the intestine
- Birth defects of the digestive system
- Long-term diarrhea in children, no matter the cause
- Short bowel syndrome after surgery to remove part of the small intestine

If the digestive system works but still needs help, doctors usually use tube feeding instead. Tube feeding sends food through a tube into the stomach or small intestine.

Compared to tube feeding, intravenous feeding has more risks and costs more. It also does not keep the digestive system as strong.

Intravenous feeding can be done at home or in the hospital.

---

## How Intravenous Feeding Works

A special liquid is given through a central venous catheter. The catheter is placed into a large vein, like the subclavian vein under the collarbone.

To place the catheter:

- A needle is put through the skin into the vein.
- A thin wire is passed through the needle.
- The needle is removed.
- The catheter is moved over the wire into the vein.
- The wire is taken out.

An ultrasound may be used to guide the placement. An X-ray is often done afterward to check the position.

The catheter may be placed in the neck if it is only used during a hospital stay.

Once in place, the nutrient solution flows into the bloodstream. The body uses the nutrients from the solution.

Because the catheter stays in place for a long time, there is a risk of infection. To lower this risk, health care workers follow strict clean rules:

- They clean the skin before placing the catheter.
- They change the tubing and filter every day.
- They change the dressing over the catheter every other day.
- They use the catheter only for feeding, not for other medicines.

---

## Watching the Patient During Feeding

A team of health care workers checks the patient’s progress. This team may include a doctor, dietitian, pharmacist, and nurse.

They check:

- Body weight
- Blood cell counts
- Levels of electrolytes (like sodium and potassium)
- Blood sugar (glucose)
- Urea (a waste product the kidneys remove)
- Protein levels
- Liver function
- How much fluid the person drinks
- How much urine the person makes

They also do a full nutrition check. This includes measuring body mass index (BMI) and body composition. The check is done as often as needed.

People who are very ill need more frequent checks. People who are stable and getting feeding at home need fewer checks.

If feeding is done at home, the patient and caregivers learn how to:

- Care for the catheter and skin around it
- Give the feeding solution
- Handle the bags
- Spot signs of problems, like infection

Nurses visit the home regularly to check for issues.

---

## What Is in the Feeding Solution?

The feeding solution is made to fit the person’s needs. The nutrition team adjusts it based on:

- The person’s health
- Lab test results
- Age
- Other medical conditions

They can change the amounts of:

- Water
- Protein
- Fats
- Electrolytes (like sodium and potassium)
- Vitamins
- Minerals
- Essential amino acids (parts of protein)
- Essential fatty acids (parts of fat)

If a hospital cannot make a custom solution, a standard one is used. This one works for most people.

The team also considers:

- For people with heart, liver, or kidney problems: Less fluid
- For people with diabetes: More fat, less sugar
- For newborns: Less sugar
- For people with obesity: Sometimes fewer calories

---

## Possible Problems with Intravenous Feeding

Intravenous feeding can cause several problems. Some are due to the catheter. Some come from the solution. Some causes are not known.

### Problems During Catheter Insertion

- A blood vessel, nerve, or lung may be hurt during placement.

### Infections

- The skin is cut to place the catheter. This opens a path for germs.
- Infections can spread to the blood. This can lead to a serious illness called sepsis.
- Using clean, sterile tools and methods helps prevent infections.

### Blood Clots

- A clot may form in the vein where the catheter is placed.

### Blood Sugar Problems

- Blood sugar can get too high (hyperglycemia) or too low (hypoglycemia).
- These are common.
- Blood tests check sugar levels.
- The solution is adjusted as needed.
- Sugar levels are checked often.

### Vitamin and Mineral Deficiencies

- Rarely, the body may lack certain vitamins or minerals.
- Blood tests check for this.
- The solution is changed to fix the problem.

### Water Imbalance

- Too much water (overhydration) can cause fluid to build up in the lungs. This makes breathing hard.
- Too little water causes dehydration.
- Doctors check weight and urine output.
- Blood tests check urea levels. High levels may mean dehydration.
- The right amount of water is calculated before feeding starts. It is adjusted as needed.

### Problems from Fat in the Solution

- Some people have trouble with fat in the solution.
- Symptoms include:
  - Trouble breathing
  - Allergic reactions
  - Nausea
  - Headache
  - Back pain
  - Sweating
  - Dizziness
- Fat levels in the blood may rise, especially in people with kidney or liver problems.
- Later, the liver or spleen may get bigger.
- People may bleed or bruise more easily.
- They may get infections more often.
- Premature babies with lung problems are at higher risk.
- Doctors may slow or stop the fat solution to prevent or reduce these issues.

### Liver Problems

- Liver problems can happen at any age, but are most common in babies, especially premature ones.
- The liver is not fully developed in newborns.
- Blood tests check liver enzyme levels to see how well the liver is working.
- A solution with fish oil may help.
- If the liver is swollen and painful, calorie intake is lowered.
- In babies, ammonia can build up in the blood.
- High ammonia can cause:
  - Feeling slow or tired
  - Seizures
  - Muscle twitches
- Giving a special amino acid (arginine) can fix this.

### Bone Problems

- If feeding lasts more than 3 months, bones may weaken.
- This can lead to osteoporosis or osteomalacia (a softening of bones due to low vitamin D).
- These conditions can cause severe pain in the joints, legs, and back.

### Gallbladder Problems

- The gallbladder may not work well during intravenous feeding.
- This can cause substances like cholesterol to build up.
- This may lead to gallstones or sludge.
- Stones can block a duct and cause inflammation (cholecystitis).
- To help the gallbladder work:
  - More fat is added to the solution.
  - Sugar is not given for several hours each day.
  - This helps the gallbladder contract and move things along.
- Eating by mouth or using a tube in the nose may also help.
- Medicines like metronidazole, ursodeoxycholic acid, phenobarbital, or cholecystokinin may be used to help the gallbladder work better.

# Monitoring and Testing the Critical Care Patient

Patients in critical care are watched closely. Some checks are done by hand, like looking at the patient and feeling their pulse. These checks happen only when needed and depend on how sick the patient is. Other checks are done all the time using special machines. These machines need trained staff to run them. Most machines will sound an alarm if something is wrong.

Every intensive care unit must follow strict rules for checking alarms.

## What is Checked?

Common checks include:
- Body temperature
- Blood pressure
- Heart rate
- Breathing rate
- How much fluid the patient takes in and how much they lose
- Daily weight
- Pressure inside the skull (in some cases)

Blood pressure can be checked with a machine that wraps around the arm. Or, a small tube (arterial catheter) can be placed in an artery to check blood pressure all the time. A small sensor on the skin can also check how much oxygen is in the blood.

## Blood Tests

Taking blood from patients is common in the ICU. It helps find problems early. But drawing blood can hurt, damage veins, and cause low blood counts.

To make blood draws easier, doctors may place a special tube (central venous catheter or arterial catheter) in a large vein or artery. This lets them take blood without using a new needle each time. But these tubes can cause problems, so the risks are weighed carefully.

Most patients get blood tests every day. These include:
- Electrolytes (like sodium and potassium)
- Complete blood count (CBC)

Other tests may be done as needed:
- Magnesium, phosphate, and ionized calcium levels
- Liver tests and blood clotting tests if the patient is on total parenteral nutrition
- Blood cultures if the patient has a fever
- Repeat CBCs if there is a chance of bleeding

### Point-of-Care Testing

Some blood tests are done right at the patient’s bedside using small, easy-to-use machines. These are common in the ICU, emergency room, and operating room.

Tests done this way include:
- Blood sugar
- Blood chemistry
- Arterial blood gases (ABGs)
- Complete blood count (CBC)
- Heart markers
- Blood clotting tests

These tests take less than two minutes and need only a tiny amount of blood—less than half a milliliter.

## Heart Monitoring

Most patients in critical care have their heart activity watched with a 3-lead system. Small pads on the chest send signals to a central monitor. A small radio device on the patient sends the data.

The system sounds an alarm if the heart rate or rhythm is abnormal. It also saves the heart’s electrical pattern for later review.

Some advanced heart monitors check for signs of poor blood flow to the heart. These include:
- Continuous ST segment monitoring
- Heart rate variability

A loss of normal heart rate changes may mean the heart is under stress. It can also signal a higher risk of death.

## Pulmonary Artery Catheter (PAC) Monitoring

A pulmonary artery catheter (also called a Swan-Ganz catheter) is a thin tube with a balloon at the tip. It is placed through a large vein, goes through the heart, and ends in the lung artery.

The tube has several openings. It can measure pressure, inject fluids, or check oxygen levels in the blood. Some versions have a sensor to measure oxygen in the blood returning from the heart.

Doctors use this catheter to estimate:
- How well the heart pumps (cardiac output)
- How full the heart is (preload)

Preload is often guessed from the pressure in the lung artery. But a more accurate way is to measure the volume of blood in the heart at the end of a beat. This uses a fast-response thermometer that works with the heart’s rhythm.

Despite being used for years, this catheter has not been shown to help patients live longer. In fact, it may increase the risk of death. This may be due to complications from the tube or mistakes in reading the results.

Still, some doctors believe the catheter can help when used with other test results. A pattern of change over time is more important than one single abnormal number.

### When Might a PAC Be Used?

- Severe heart valve problems
- Fluid around the heart (cardiac tamponade)
- Complicated heart failure
- Complicated heart attack
- A hole in the heart wall after a heart attack

- Low blood pressure that does not improve (shock)
- Need for medicines to support the heart

- After heart surgery
- After surgery in patients with serious heart disease
- For patients with serious lung problems, such as:
  - Large blood clots in the lungs (pulmonary embolism)
  - High blood pressure in the lungs (pulmonary hypertension)

## Noninvasive Heart Output Monitoring

Other ways to check how well the heart is pumping do not need a pulmonary artery catheter. These include:
- Ultrasound at the bedside
- Esophageal Doppler (a probe in the throat)
- Thoracic bioimpedance (measuring electrical resistance in the chest)

These methods avoid the risks of the catheter. But none is yet as accurate as the pulmonary artery catheter.

## Brain Pressure Monitoring

Measuring pressure inside the skull is standard for patients with serious head injuries. It is also used in some other brain conditions, such as:
- Hydrocephalus (fluid buildup in the brain)
- Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (high pressure in the brain with no clear cause)
- After surgery or bleeding in brain blood vessels (arteriovenous malformations)

Normal pressure inside the skull is 5 to 15 mm Hg. Doctors aim to keep the pressure in the brain high enough to keep blood flowing to the brain. This is called cerebral perfusion pressure. It is calculated by subtracting the skull pressure from the average blood pressure. The goal is to keep this number above 60 mm Hg.

### Types of Brain Pressure Monitors

1. **Extraventricular drain (EVD)**  
   - A tube is placed through the skull into a fluid-filled space in the brain.  
   - It can measure pressure and drain extra fluid to lower pressure.  
   - It is the most useful method but also the most invasive.  
   - It has the highest risk of infection.  
   - It is hard to place.  
   - It can get blocked if the brain swells a lot.

2. **Intraparenchymal monitor**  
   - A small sensor is placed directly into brain tissue.  
   - This is the most commonly used type.

3. **Subarachnoid bolt**  
   - A sensor is placed between the brain and its covering.

4. **Subdural bolt**  
   - A sensor is placed under the brain’s covering.

5. **Epidural bolt**  
   - A sensor is placed between the skull and the brain’s covering.

All brain pressure monitors should be removed or replaced after 5 to 7 days. This helps prevent infection.

## Near Infrared Spectroscopy (NIRS)

NIRS is a noninvasive way to check how well tissues are getting oxygen. A sensor is placed on the skin over the area being checked.

It measures the activity of tiny parts in cells (mitochondria) that use oxygen. This tells how well blood is flowing to the tissue.

NIRS can help:
- Find early signs of compartment syndrome (swelling in a muscle area)
- Spot poor blood flow after a tissue transplant
- Monitor blood flow after leg bypass surgery
- Check how well a patient is recovering after major injury or surgery (by measuring stomach acid levels)

This tool gives real-time data and helps guide care.

# Anal Atresia

Anal atresia is a birth defect. It means the opening at the end of the bowel is missing or covered by a thin layer of skin. This condition can happen alone or with other problems in the rectum, urethra, or vagina.

## What Is the Anus and Rectum?

- The anus is the opening at the end of the digestive system. It lets stool leave the body.
- The rectum is the part of the large intestine that holds stool before it is passed out.

In anal atresia, the skin may cover the spot where the anus should be. The skin can be thick or just a thin membrane. The opening may be too narrow or completely missing.

## Types of Problems

Anal atresia is part of a group of conditions called anorectal malformations. These can include:
- A narrow anus or rectum.
- Fistulas — abnormal tubes that connect the anus to other parts of the body. These can go to the urethra, the area between the urethra and anus (perineum), the vagina, or rarely the bladder.

## What Causes It?

Doctors do not know why this happens. It occurs when the intestines do not form correctly during pregnancy.

## Other Birth Defects

Many babies with anal atresia also have other birth defects. These can include:
- Spine problems.
- Heart problems.
- Kidney problems.
- Limb problems.
- Tracheoesophageal fistula (an abnormal connection between the windpipe and the food pipe).
- Esophageal atresia (a blocked food pipe).

## Symptoms

Babies with anal atresia cannot pass stool normally after birth. If not treated, a blockage in the intestines will develop. This is called intestinal obstruction.

Symptoms of intestinal obstruction in babies include:
- Belly pain.
- Crying and irritability.
- Vomiting.
- A swollen belly.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors check the baby’s anus right after birth. They look for any signs of a missing or blocked opening.

They also use imaging tests:
- X-rays show the position of the rectum and any fistulas.
- Ultrasound helps doctors see the type of malformation and check for other problems.

## How Is It Treated?

Surgery is needed to fix the problem.

### Types of Surgery

There are two main types of surgery:
1. **Temporary surgery** – This is done first in some cases.
2. **Permanent surgery** – This is done later to fully fix the problem.

### Temporary Surgery: Colostomy

A colostomy is a temporary surgery. It creates a new opening in the belly for stool to pass out.

Here’s how it works:
- The surgeon cuts the large intestine (colon).
- The healthy part of the colon is brought through the belly wall.
- It is stitched to the skin, creating a new opening.
- Stool now passes through this opening into a plastic bag attached to the skin.

This allows the lower part of the bowel to rest and heal. The colostomy stays in place until the baby is older and strong enough for the final repair.

### Final Surgery

When the baby is ready, the surgeon closes the colostomy. The two ends of the colon are joined back together. This lets stool pass normally through the anus again.

After the final surgery, most babies can pass stool through the anus and live normal lives. Some may need extra help with bowel control later on. But with care and follow-up, most do well.

# Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (Eye Shingles)

This is a reactivation of the same virus that causes chickenpox. It affects the eye and the skin on one side of the face. The virus stays in your body after chickenpox. It can come back later as shingles.

## What Causes It?

After you have chickenpox, the virus hides in your nerve cells. Your immune system keeps it under control. When your immune system weakens, the virus can wake up. This can happen with age, illness, or certain medicines that lower your immunity.

If you have a rash on the tip of your nose and shingles on your forehead, you are much more likely to have eye problems. About half of people with this type of shingles will have eye involvement.

The virus spreads through direct contact with open sores or through the air from droplets. It can spread to others who have never had chickenpox.

## Symptoms and Signs

You may feel pain or tingling in your forehead before the rash appears.

During the illness, you may have:
- A painful rash on one side of your forehead or eyelid
- Swelling of the eyelid
- Redness in the white part of the eye
- A cloudy or swollen cornea (the front part of the eye)
- Severe eye pain
- Trouble with bright light (light hurts your eyes)

These symptoms can be very serious and may lead to long-term eye damage.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look for:
- A rash on the forehead, eyelid, or tip of the nose
- Eye problems on the same side of the face

The rash usually does not cross the middle of your face. It only appears on one side.

Even if the rash has not yet reached the eye, you should see an eye doctor right away. The virus can spread to the eye without obvious signs.

Tests like skin swabs or blood tests are only done if the rash looks unusual or the diagnosis is unclear.

## How Is It Treated?

You must start treatment as soon as possible.

**Oral antiviral medicine** (like acyclovir, famciclovir, or valacyclovir) helps reduce eye damage. These medicines work best when started within 72 hours of the rash appearing.

If you have swelling inside the eye (uveitis) or corneal problems (keratitis), you may need **eye drops with steroids** (like prednisolone acetate).

Your doctor will also use eye drops to keep your pupil open. This helps prevent pain and scarring. Common drops are atropine 1% or scopolamine 0.25%. You use one drop three times a day.

Your eye pressure must be checked often. If it goes up too high, it can damage your eye. Treatment is needed if pressure rises.

Some doctors may use short-term, high-dose oral steroids to prevent long-term nerve pain in people over 60 who are otherwise healthy. But this is still debated.

For long-term nerve pain (postherpetic neuralgia), medicines like gabapentin or certain antidepressants can help.

## How Can It Be Prevented?

All healthy adults aged 50 and older should get the **recombinant herpes zoster vaccine**, even if they have had shingles before or had the older shingles vaccine.

This vaccine reduces the chance of getting shingles by:
- About 97% for adults aged 50 to 69
- About 90% for adults aged 70 and older

It is the best way to prevent this condition.

## Key Points

- The eye is affected in about half of cases of shingles on the forehead.
- Eye problems like corneal swelling or inflammation can be serious and may cause lasting vision issues.
- A typical rash on the forehead or nose is usually enough to make the diagnosis.
- Treatment includes oral antiviral medicine, eye drops with steroids, and pupil-dilating drops.
- All healthy adults aged 50 and older should get the recombinant herpes zoster vaccine.

# Ketamine and PCP

Ketamine and PCP are drugs that are similar in chemistry.  
They are used in medicine to help people go to sleep during surgery.  
But some people use them for fun, even though this is dangerous.

## How People Use Ketamine and PCP

Ketamine comes as a powder or a liquid.  
The powder can be snorted or swallowed.  
The liquid can be injected into a vein, into a muscle, or under the skin.

PCP, also known as angel dust, is usually smoked.  
People sprinkle it on plants like parsley, mint, tobacco, or marijuana.  
Some street names for PCP are "wet" and "fry."  
It can also be snorted or swallowed.

## What Happens When Someone Uses Ketamine or PCP

At first, the person may feel happy and light-headed.  
This feeling is often followed by sudden anxiety.  
With higher doses, the person may feel confused about their body, surroundings, or time.  
They may feel like they are not real or disconnected from themselves.  
This is called depersonalization.  
They may also feel cut off from the world around them.  
This is called dissociation.

At even higher doses, the person may see things that are not there (hallucinations).  
They may have strong fears or false beliefs (paranoid delusions).  
The feeling of being disconnected from reality becomes stronger.  
Ketamine users often call this extreme experience a "k-hole."  
The person may become aggressive or violent.  
They may lose control of their movements.  
Their muscles may shake or twitch.

Very high doses can cause serious health problems.  
These include:  
- A very high body temperature (dangerously high fever)  
- A fast heartbeat  
- Unusual sexual behavior  
- Very high blood pressure  
- Seizures  
- Loss of consciousness (coma)  
- In rare cases, death

## How Doctors Diagnose Use of Ketamine or PCP

Doctors look at the person’s history of drug use.  
They also check for symptoms that match ketamine or PCP use.  
Standard urine tests do not find ketamine.  
Special lab tests are needed to confirm ketamine use.  
These tests are called gas chromatography and mass spectroscopy.

## How Doctors Treat Ketamine or PCP Use

The best treatment is a calm, safe environment.  
The person should be watched closely until they are fully awake.  
Reassurance helps calm them down.  
Sometimes, doctors give sedatives to help with agitation or seizures.  
Most people come back to normal within 45 minutes to several hours.
