It offers tools to find treatment, a free help line, training for health workers, and reports on drug use.

# What Are Plasma Cell Disorders?

Plasma cell disorders are conditions where abnormal plasma cells grow too quickly in the bone marrow. These disorders can range from mild to serious. They are not fully understood, but they involve a single type of plasma cell multiplying out of control.

## How Plasma Cell Disorders Work

Plasma cells come from B cells. B cells start in the bone marrow and then move to other parts of the body like the lymph nodes, spleen, and gut. There, they become mature and can respond to specific germs or threats.

When a B cell meets the right germ, it turns into a plasma cell. Each plasma cell makes one kind of antibody. This antibody has:

- Two identical heavy chains (types: gamma, mu, alpha, delta, or epsilon)
- Two identical light chains (types: kappa or lambda)

The body normally makes a little extra light chain. It is normal to pass small amounts of these in the urine each day.

In plasma cell disorders, one type of plasma cell grows too much. This causes high levels of a single type of antibody in the blood. This abnormal antibody is called an M-protein.

M-proteins can be made of:
- Both heavy and light chains
- Only heavy chains
- Only light chains

## Problems Caused by Plasma Cell Disorders

Too many abnormal plasma cells and M-proteins can cause health problems:

- **Kidney damage**: Some M-proteins harm the kidneys. High calcium levels (from bone breakdown) can also hurt the kidneys.
- **Weak immunity**: The body makes fewer normal antibodies. This makes infections more likely.
- **Bleeding**: M-proteins can stop platelets from working. They can also block blood clotting and thicken the blood.
- **Amyloidosis**: M-proteins can form harmful deposits in organs. These deposits often affect the heart and kidneys.
- **Bone problems**: The abnormal cells can invade the bones. This leads to weak bones, high calcium levels, anemia, or low blood counts.

Some people have no symptoms at all. Others have serious illness. The most common serious form is multiple myeloma.

## Types of Plasma Cell Disorders

| Type | Symptoms | Description | Examples |
|------|----------|-------------|----------|
| Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance | No symptoms, slow change | Seen in healthy people or those with other diseases | Linked to B-cell cancers like chronic lymphocytic leukemia, multiple myeloma, or some solid tumors |
| | | Linked to long-term infections or inflammation | Chronic cholecystitis, osteomyelitis, rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculosis |
| | | Seen with other health issues | Familial high cholesterol, Gaucher disease, Kaposi sarcoma, liver disease, myasthenia gravis, pernicious anemia, hyperthyroidism |
| Smoldering multiple myeloma | No symptoms, slowly getting worse | High levels of M-protein in blood or many abnormal plasma cells in bone marrow | No signs of kidney damage, anemia, bone disease, or high calcium |
| Multiple myeloma | Symptoms, getting worse | High levels of IgG, IgA, or light chains in blood or urine | Often causes bone pain, anemia, kidney issues, and infections |
| Macroglobulinemia | Symptoms, getting worse | High levels of IgM in blood | Causes thick blood and nerve problems |
| Nonhereditary primary systemic amyloidosis | Symptoms, getting worse | M-proteins form harmful deposits in organs | Most often affects heart and kidneys |
| Heavy chain diseases | Symptoms, getting worse | M-proteins made only of heavy chains | IgG, IgA, IgM, or IgD types; some are not cancerous |
| Transient plasma cell disorders | May or may not have symptoms | Short-term condition | Linked to drug allergies (like sulfonamides, phenytoin, penicillin), viral infections, or after heart or organ transplant surgery |

**Note**: Smoldering multiple myeloma means:
- M-protein in blood is 3 grams per deciliter or higher
- Or 10% to 59% of the bone marrow is made of abnormal plasma cells
- But no signs of kidney damage, anemia, bone disease, or high calcium

## How Doctors Diagnose These Disorders

Doctors may suspect a plasma cell disorder if a person has:
- Bone pain or fractures
- Kidney problems
- Low blood counts (anemia)

Or if a routine blood or urine test shows high protein levels.

To check for the disorder, doctors use:
- **Electrophoresis**: This test finds abnormal proteins in blood or urine.
- **Immunofixation electrophoresis**: This test identifies the exact type of abnormal protein (heavy or light chains).

These tests help confirm the diagnosis and guide treatment.

# Uterine Rupture

Uterine rupture means the uterus tears open. This can happen in the later stages of pregnancy or during labor. It is most common in women who have had surgery on their uterus before, such as a previous cesarean birth.

When the uterus ruptures, the baby may float freely in the mother’s belly.

This condition is very rare. But it is a serious emergency that needs immediate care.

The rupture can happen before labor starts or during labor.

These things increase the chance of a rupture:

- A past cesarean birth, especially if labor is started with medicine instead of starting on its own.
- Any past surgery on the uterus.
- The uterus is stretched too much. This can happen if there is too much fluid around the baby or if there are more than one baby.
- The baby is not in the right position for birth and needs to be turned.

Signs of a ruptured uterus include:

- Severe, ongoing pain in the belly.
- The baby’s heart rate drops too low.

To check if the uterus has ruptured, doctors may make a cut in the belly. This lets them see the uterus directly. This surgery is called a laparotomy.

The baby must be delivered right away by cesarean birth.

The uterus is then fixed with surgery. In some cases, the entire uterus must be removed. This is called a hysterectomy.

# Acute Ear Infection (Otitis Media)

An acute ear infection is an infection in the middle part of the ear. It is usually caused by a virus or bacteria. It often happens when a person has a cold or another upper respiratory infection.

## Who Gets It?

- Ear infections are most common in babies and young children.
- The peak age is between 3 months and 3 years.
- At this age, the tube that connects the middle ear to the back of the nose (called the eustachian tube) is not fully developed.
- This tube is more flat and does not open and close well, which makes it easier for fluid and infection to build up.

## What Causes It?

- Most ear infections start with a virus.
- A virus can lead to a second infection with bacteria.
- In newborns, the most common bacteria are *Escherichia coli* and *Staphylococcus aureus*.
- In older babies and children under 14 years, the most common bacteria are:
  - *Streptococcus pneumoniae*
  - *Moraxella catarrhalis*
  - *Haemophilus influenzae* (not the type that causes flu)
- In adults over 14 years, the most common bacteria are:
  - *Streptococcus pneumoniae*
  - Group A strep
  - *Staphylococcus aureus*
  - *Haemophilus influenzae*

## Symptoms

The main symptom is an earache. Other signs include:
- Hearing loss
- Fever
- Nausea or vomiting
- Diarrhea (especially in young children)
- Trouble sleeping
- Being fussy or irritable (in babies who cannot talk)

A doctor can check the ear with a special tool called an otoscope. The eardrum may look red, swollen, and pushed outward. When air is blown into the ear, the eardrum should move. If it does not move well, this suggests fluid is trapped behind it.

If the eardrum breaks open, fluid may drain from the ear. This often brings quick relief from pain.

In rare cases, the infection can spread to the brain. Signs of this include:
- Severe headache
- Confusion
- Weakness on one side of the body

If the infection spreads to nearby nerves, it can cause:
- Facial weakness or paralysis
- Dizziness

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor makes the diagnosis by:
- Asking about symptoms
- Checking the ear with an otoscope
- Testing how well the eardrum moves using a puff of air (called pneumatic otoscopy)

Most of the time, no lab tests are needed. Fluid from the ear is only tested if a doctor removes it during a small procedure.

## How Is It Treated?

### Pain Relief

- Everyone with an ear infection should get pain medicine.
- For children, use acetaminophen or ibuprofen.
- Dose should be based on the child’s weight.
- For babies who cannot talk, look for signs of pain like:
  - Pulling or rubbing the ear
  - Crying a lot
  - Being fussy

Topical ear drops (drops for the ear) may help some people feel better for a short time. But they do not work well for long. They should not be used if the eardrum is broken.

### Antibiotics

- Most ear infections go away on their own.
- About 8 out of 10 cases get better without antibiotics.
- But antibiotics can help symptoms get better faster.
- They may also lower the risk of lasting hearing problems or serious complications.

Doctors now use antibiotics more carefully because some bacteria are becoming resistant.

Antibiotics are usually recommended for:
- Babies under 6 months old
- Children with severe symptoms (like high fever or bad pain)
- Children with both ears affected
- Children who have had many ear infections before

For older children with mild symptoms, doctors may suggest waiting 48 to 72 hours. If the child does not improve, antibiotics are started. A prescription can be given at the first visit if follow-up is planned.

### Antibiotics Used

| Antibiotic | When It’s Used |
|------------|----------------|
| Amoxicillin | First choice for most children |
| Amoxicillin with clavulanate | For infections that did not get better with amoxicillin |
| Cefdinir, cefuroxime, cefpodoxime | For children allergic to penicillin |
| Ceftriaxone | Given by injection if the child cannot take pills or is very sick |
| Clindamycin | Used only if other options are not safe or effective |

- Treatment usually lasts 10 days for children under 2 years.
- For older children, treatment is usually 7 days.
- All antibiotics are taken by mouth unless otherwise needed.

### When Surgery Is Needed

A doctor may do a small procedure called myringotomy if:
- The eardrum is bulging badly
- Pain is severe and does not go away
- The child has high fever, vomiting, or diarrhea

During this procedure, a small cut is made in the eardrum to drain fluid. This helps relieve pressure and pain.

If the facial nerve is affected (causing facial weakness), the patient must see a specialist right away. A tube may be placed in the ear to help drain fluid and prevent future infections.

## How to Prevent Ear Infections

- Make sure children get all recommended vaccines:
  - Pneumococcal vaccine
  - Hib vaccine (for *Haemophilus influenzae* type B)
  - Flu vaccine
- Do not let babies sleep with a bottle.
- Keep the home smoke-free.
- Do not use antibiotics to prevent ear infections in children who have them often.

Tympanostomy tubes (small tubes placed in the ear) can help prevent repeated ear infections and fluid buildup.

## Key Points

- Give pain medicine to everyone with an ear infection.
- Use antibiotics only when needed. The decision depends on:
  - Age of the child
  - How sick the child is
  - Whether follow-up care can be arranged
- Do not use decongestants or antihistamines for children.
- Adults may use nasal sprays or pills to help with congestion, but only for a few days.
- Antihistamines are only for adults with allergies.

# Understanding Chromosome and Gene Disorders

## What Are Chromosomes?

Chromosomes are tiny structures inside your cells.  
They hold your genes.  
Each chromosome looks like a long, twisted string.  
It has two arms: a short arm and a long arm.  
The short arm is called the "p" arm.  
The long arm is called the "q" arm.  
The two arms are joined at a spot called the centromere.  
The ends of each arm are called telomeres.  

## What Are Genes?

Genes are small parts of DNA.  
They carry instructions to make proteins.  
Proteins help your body work properly.  
Every normal cell in your body has 46 chromosomes.  
These come in 23 pairs.  
Sperm and egg cells have only 23 chromosomes—just one from each pair.  
Each chromosome holds hundreds to thousands of genes.  

## What Are the Sex Chromosomes?

One of the 23 pairs of chromosomes is the sex chromosome.  
There are two types: X and Y.  
Females usually have two X chromosomes (XX).  
Males usually have one X and one Y chromosome (XY).  

## What Is DNA?

DNA is the material that holds your genetic code.  
It is found in the nucleus of your cells and in tiny parts of the cell called mitochondria.  
Most cells have 23 pairs of chromosomes in the nucleus.  
Each chromosome holds many genes.  
A gene is a section of DNA that tells your body how to make a protein or a type of RNA.  
DNA looks like a spiral staircase.  
It has two long strands that twist around each other.  
The steps of the staircase are made of four building blocks called bases.  
The bases are adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine.  
Adenine always pairs with thymine.  
Guanine always pairs with cytosine.  
These pairs are held together by weak bonds called hydrogen bonds.  
A gene is a sequence of these base pairs.  
Every three bases in a row tell the body to make one amino acid.  
Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins.  

## Problems with Chromosomes

Chromosome problems can happen in any chromosome.  
They can affect the number of chromosomes or the shape of the chromosomes.  

### Types of Chromosome Problems

**Number Problems**  
Sometimes a person has too many or too few chromosomes.  
Having one extra chromosome is called trisomy.  
Having two extra chromosomes is called tetrasomy.  
Not having a full chromosome is called monosomy.  
Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome.  
Trisomy 13 and trisomy 18 also cause serious health problems.  
These conditions affect both boys and girls.  
Doctors can see these problems under a microscope using a test called karyotyping.  

**Age and Risk**  
The older a pregnant person is, the higher the chance the baby will have a chromosome problem.  
This risk is not linked to the father’s age.  
The father’s age only slightly increases the risk.  

**Structure Problems**  
Sometimes part of a chromosome is broken or changed.  
Parts of chromosomes can be missing.  
This is called a deletion.  
Parts can also be extra.  
This is called a duplication.  
Sometimes a piece of one chromosome joins to another chromosome.  
This is called a translocation.  
These changes are too small to see under a microscope.  
Special tests are needed to find them.  

### How These Problems Affect Health

Some chromosome problems cause a pregnancy to end early.  
Others cause health issues such as:  
- Learning difficulties  
- Short height  
- Seizures  
- Heart problems  
- A cleft palate (a gap in the roof of the mouth)  

## Problems with Genes

Changes in just a few base pairs in a gene can create a new version of that gene.  
This is called a gene variant.  
These changes do not affect the shape of chromosomes.  
So, they cannot be seen in a karyotype test.  
Special genetic tests are needed to find them.  

### What Can Gene Variants Cause?

Some gene variants cause no health problems.  
Some cause mild issues.  
Others cause serious diseases.  
Examples include:  
- Sickle cell anemia  
- Cystic fibrosis  
- Muscular dystrophy  

Scientists are learning more about how specific gene changes cause diseases in children.  

### How Do Gene Variants Happen?

Most gene variants appear on their own.  
They are not passed down from parents.  
Some things in the environment can damage genes.  
These things are called mutagens.  
Examples of mutagens are:  
- Radiation  
- Ultraviolet light  
- Certain medicines  
- Certain chemicals  

These can cause some cancers and birth defects.  

### Can Gene Variants Be Passed to Children?

A gene variant in a sperm or egg can be passed to a child.  
A gene variant in other body cells does not affect the sperm or egg.  
So, it is not passed to the next generation.  
If a child inherits two copies of a bad gene, they may get a serious disease.  
Examples include:  
- Cystic fibrosis  
- Tay-Sachs disease  

Sometimes, a disease can happen even if a person has only one bad copy of a gene.  

## Testing for Chromosome and Gene Problems

Doctors can test your chromosomes and genes.  
They use a sample of blood.  
They can also use cells from the inside of your cheek.  

### Testing During Pregnancy

During pregnancy, doctors can test the baby’s chromosomes and genes.  
They can collect cells using two methods:  
- Amniocentesis: A needle takes fluid from the amniotic sac.  
- Chorionic villus sampling: A small sample is taken from the placenta.  

These tests can find some chromosome and gene problems.  
If a problem is found, more tests may be done to check for specific birth defects.  

### Noninvasive Prenatal Screening (NIPS)

This test uses a blood sample from the pregnant person.  
It checks for small amounts of the baby’s DNA in the mother’s blood.  
It can show if the baby has a higher chance of:  
- Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)  
- Trisomy 13  
- Trisomy 18  
- Some other genetic disorders  

If the test shows a higher risk, doctors usually recommend more testing.  

## Preventing Chromosome and Gene Problems

Chromosome and gene problems cannot be fixed.  
But some birth defects can be prevented.  

### How to Reduce Risk

- Pregnant women can take folic acid (also called folate).  
  This helps prevent neural tube defects.  
- Parents can be tested to see if they carry a gene for certain genetic disorders.  
- Babies made through in vitro fertilization (IVF) can be tested before being placed in the womb.  
  This is called preimplantation genetic diagnosis.  
  It helps avoid passing on serious genetic problems.

# Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL)

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a type of blood cancer.  
It happens when a certain kind of white blood cell, called a B lymphocyte, becomes abnormal.  
These abnormal cells build up slowly over time.  
They collect in the blood, bone marrow, spleen, and lymph nodes.

Many people with CLL do not have symptoms at first.  
When symptoms do appear, they can include:  
- Swollen lymph nodes  
- A swollen spleen  
- A swollen liver  
- Feeling tired  
- Fever  
- Night sweats  
- Losing weight without trying  
- Feeling full quickly after eating small amounts

Doctors diagnose CLL by testing a blood sample.  
They use a test called flow cytometry to look at the blood cells.  
This test checks for specific markers on the surface of the cells.  
It helps confirm that the cells are abnormal and come from the same original cell.

Treatment usually starts only when symptoms appear.  
It may include chemotherapy and medicines that help the immune system fight the cancer.  
Newer treatments are now available.  
These include targeted drugs that block specific signals in the cancer cells.  
Examples are drugs that stop Bruton tyrosine kinase (Btk) and Bcl-2.  
These drugs may be used with or without chemotherapy.

CLL is the most common type of leukemia in Western countries.  
In the United States in 2023, about 19,000 new cases were expected.  
About 4,500 people died from CLL that year.  
Almost all cases and deaths happened in adults.  
The average age of someone with CLL is 70 years.  
It is very rare in children.

The chance of getting CLL in a lifetime is about 1 in 175 for both men and women.  
The exact cause is not known.  
But some cases seem to run in families.  
CLL is rare in Japan and China.  
People of Japanese descent in the United States do not have a higher risk.  
This suggests that genes play a role.  
CLL is more common in people with Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry.

## How CLL Develops

In CLL, a type of B cell that has a marker called CD5 becomes cancerous.  
These cells keep getting activated because of changes in their genes.  
This leads to a condition called monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (MBL).  
Over time, more gene changes happen.  
This turns the MBL into full-blown CLL.

The abnormal cells start in the bone marrow.  
They then spread to lymph nodes and other lymph tissue.  
This can cause the spleen and liver to grow larger.  
It can also cause general symptoms like tiredness, fever, night sweats, and weight loss.

As the disease gets worse, the bone marrow cannot make enough healthy blood cells.  
This leads to:  
- Low red blood cells (anemia)  
- Low white blood cells (neutropenia)  
- Low platelets (thrombocytopenia)  
- Less antibody production

Many people with CLL have low levels of antibodies.  
This makes them more likely to get infections.  
About two out of three people with CLL have this problem.  
They are also more likely to develop autoimmune problems.  
These include:  
- Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (the body attacks its own red blood cells)  
- Autoimmune thrombocytopenia (the body attacks its own platelets)

In rare cases, CLL can change into a more aggressive cancer.  
It can turn into a type called B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia.  
It can also turn into a high-grade non-Hodgkin lymphoma.  
This change is called Richter’s transformation.  
It happens in about 2% to 10% of CLL cases.

## Symptoms and Signs of CLL

Most people do not feel sick at first.  
Symptoms come on slowly and are not specific.  
They can include:  
- Feeling tired  
- Weakness  
- Loss of appetite  
- Weight loss  
- Fever  
- Night sweats  

More than half of people with CLL have swollen lymph nodes.  
These can be in the neck, under the arms, or in the groin.  
They may be in one area or all over the body.  
A swollen spleen or liver is less common than swollen lymph nodes.  
Skin problems from CLL are rare.

## How Doctors Diagnose CLL

Doctors use several tests to diagnose CLL:

- A complete blood count (CBC)  
- A blood smear to look at the cells under a microscope  
- Flow cytometry to test the blood cells  
- Immunophenotyping to check for specific markers

The diagnosis starts when a blood test shows more than 5,000 lymphocytes per microliter of blood.  
This is a high number.  
Flow cytometry confirms that the lymphocytes are all from the same original cell.  
This means they are clonal.

The abnormal cells must have certain markers:  
- CD5  
- CD19  
- CD20  
- CD23  
- Kappa or lambda light chains

If a person has fewer than 5,000 lymphocytes per microliter but still has clonal cells, they are diagnosed with monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (MBL).  
About 1% to 2% of people with MBL develop CLL each year.

A bone marrow test is not needed to diagnose CLL.  
But if done, it usually shows more than 30% abnormal cells.

Other findings at diagnosis can include:  
- Low antibody levels (in about 15% of cases)  
- High levels of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)  
- High uric acid  
- High liver enzymes  
- Rarely, high calcium levels

Doctors also do genetic tests on the blood.  
These help predict how the disease may progress.

There are two main ways to stage CLL:  
- The Rai system  
- The Binet system

Neither system can predict how fast the disease will get worse.  
Imaging tests like CT scans are not needed for the first diagnosis.

### Rai Staging System

- **Stage 0**: High lymphocyte count in blood and more than 30% abnormal cells in bone marrow  
- **Stage I**: Stage 0 plus swollen lymph nodes  
- **Stage II**: Stage 0 plus a swollen liver or spleen  
- **Stage III**: Stage 0 plus anemia (low red blood cells)  
- **Stage IV**: Stage 0 plus low platelets

### Binet Staging System

- **Stage A**: High lymphocyte count and more than 30% abnormal cells in bone marrow  
  - Hemoglobin at least 10 grams per deciliter  
  - Platelets at least 100,000 per microliter  
  - Two or fewer areas affected (lymph nodes, liver, spleen)  
- **Stage B**: Same as Stage A, but three to five areas affected  
- **Stage C**: Same as A or B, but low hemoglobin or low platelets

## Treating CLL

There is no cure for CLL with current treatments.  
The goal is to control symptoms and improve quality of life.  
Treatment is not started right away.  
It begins only when one of the following happens:

- Symptoms appear that are caused by CLL  
- The lymphocyte count increases by at least 50% in two months  
- The lymphocyte count doubles in less than six months

Symptoms that may need treatment include:  
- Fever, night sweats, extreme tiredness, or weight loss  
- A very large spleen, liver, or lymph nodes  
- Frequent infections  
- Severe anemia or low platelets

### Treatment Options

- **Chemoimmunotherapy**: A mix of chemotherapy and immune system drugs  
- **Targeted therapy**: Drugs that attack specific parts of cancer cells  
- **Radiation therapy**: Used only in rare cases, such as for very large lymph nodes

### Supportive Care

This helps manage side effects and complications:

- Blood transfusions for anemia  
- Platelet transfusions if bleeding is a problem  
- Antibiotics, antifungals, or antivirals for infections

Because people with CLL often have low white blood cells and low antibodies, infections can be serious.  
Antibiotics should kill bacteria, not just slow them down.  
People with low antibodies and frequent infections may benefit from regular infusions of gamma globulin.

## Outlook for People with CLL

The course of CLL varies widely.  
Some people live 2 years.  
Others live more than 20 years.  
The average survival is about 10 years.

People with early-stage disease (Rai stages 0 to II) may live 5 to 20 years without treatment.

Other factors that affect outlook include:

- How fast the lymphocyte count doubles  
- Specific gene changes in the cancer cells

If the lymphocyte count doubles in less than 12 months, the disease is more aggressive.

High-risk gene changes include:  
- Missing part of chromosome 17 (del(17p))  
- Missing part of chromosome 11 (del(11q))  

Other poor prognostic signs are:  
- Unmutated immunoglobulin heavy chain gene  
- CD38 protein on the cell surface  
- High levels of ZAP-70 protein

## Key Points

- CLL is a slow-growing blood cancer that affects older adults.  
- It is the most common type of leukemia in Western countries.  
- The disease course varies greatly from person to person.  
- Treatment is not started until symptoms

# Adult Day Care for Older Adults

Adult day care helps older adults stay healthy and active during the day. It is not the same as a nursing home. People go to these centers for a few hours each day, several days a week.

## What Day Care Centers Offer

These centers provide different kinds of support:

- Help with health problems
- Care to keep a person’s health stable
- Fun and social activities
- Mental health support, like group therapy

Family caregivers can bring an older adult to a day care center for a few hours. This gives the caregiver a break. This break is called **respite care**. It can help families avoid moving the older adult into a nursing home.

## How Many Programs Are There?

In the United States, there are about 4,100 adult day care programs. There are more than 15,300 nursing homes.

Most day care programs are small. They serve about 20 people at a time. But together, these programs help more than 200,000 older adults every day.

## Types of Day Care Programs

### Day Hospitals

- These are for people recovering from serious health events.
- Examples: stroke, broken bones, or losing a limb.
- They offer advanced tests, treatments, and rehab.
- People go home at night.
- A doctor or hospital may send someone here.
- Care is usually short-term — from 6 weeks to 6 months.
- These programs are expensive because there are many staff members for each person.

### Maintenance Programs

- These offer light medical care, like checking blood pressure or watching for health changes.
- They include physical exercise and help with daily tasks.
- The goal is to keep the person strong and independent.
- They help prevent health problems from getting worse.
- They also offer activities to boost mood and reduce loneliness.
- These programs can last for years.
- They are less expensive than day hospitals.

### Social Programs

- These focus on mental health and social connection.
- They offer counseling and group therapy.
- They include games and activities to keep the mind sharp.
- They help people adapt to memory loss or other changes.
- They may feel like a senior center or a mental health clinic.
- They serve older adults with dementia or mental health issues.

## How Are These Services Paid For?

Medicare does not pay for adult day care.

Most programs are funded by:

- The Older Americans Act (this helps older adults stay independent)
- Medicaid waiver programs (for low-income people)
- Long-term care insurance
- Personal savings or family funds

These programs are not free. Families need to check what options are available in their area.

# What Is a Cardiomyopathy?

A cardiomyopathy is a problem with the heart muscle. It is not the same as other heart problems like blocked arteries, valve issues, or birth defects of the heart.

There are three main types of cardiomyopathy:

- Dilated
- Hypertrophic
- Restrictive

### Ischemic Cardiomyopathy

Sometimes, a weak heart muscle happens after severe heart artery disease. This is called ischemic cardiomyopathy. It is not one of the three main types. It is caused by poor blood flow to the heart muscle, not by a direct problem with the muscle itself.

### What Symptoms Can You Have?

Symptoms often come from heart failure. These include:

- Trouble breathing
- Swelling in the legs or belly
- Feeling very tired

The type of symptoms depends on how the heart is not working right. Some people have:

- Problems pumping blood (systolic dysfunction)
- Problems filling with blood (diastolic dysfunction)
- Or both

Some people also have:

- Chest pain
- Fainting
- Irregular heartbeats
- Sudden death (in rare cases)

### How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find out what type of cardiomyopathy you have. These include:

- A review of your family health history
- Blood tests
- An electrocardiogram (ECG) to check the heart’s electrical activity
- A chest X-ray to see the heart size
- An echocardiogram (echo) to look at heart structure and movement
- A cardiac MRI for more detail
- In some cases, a small sample of heart tissue (biopsy) may be taken

Other tests may be done to find the cause.

### Treatment Depends on the Type

Treatment varies based on the type and cause of the cardiomyopathy. The table below shows the main features and treatments for each type.

---

## Types of Cardiomyopathy and How They Are Treated

### Dilated Cardiomyopathy

- **What is wrong?** The heart muscle is weak and does not pump well.
- **Symptoms:** Heart failure in both left and right sides of the heart. Can lead to sudden death. The heart is often enlarged. You may hear extra heart sounds. The heart valves may leak.
- **ECG:** Shows changes in the heart’s electrical pattern. May show abnormal Q waves or blockages.
- **Echo:** The heart chambers are big and do not move well. The heart’s pumping ability is low. Blood clots may form. Valves may leak.
- **X-ray:** The heart is enlarged. Fluid may build up in the lungs.
- **Heart pressure:** Pressure in the heart is normal or high. The heart pumps less blood.
- **Outlook:** About 20% of people die in the first year. After that, about 10% die each year.
- **Treatment:** 
  - Diuretics to reduce swelling
  - Medicines to lower blood pressure and help the heart work better
  - Beta-blockers to slow the heart rate
  - Spironolactone or eplerenone to protect the heart
  - Digoxin to help the heart pump
  - An implantable defibrillator (ICD) to prevent sudden death
  - Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) to help the heart beat better
  - Blood thinners to prevent clots

---

### Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy

- **What is wrong?** The heart muscle is too thick. It can block blood flow out of the heart. The heart may not fill properly.
- **Symptoms:** Trouble breathing during activity, chest pain, fainting, sudden death. A loud heart murmur may be heard. The pulse may feel strong and fast.
- **ECG:** Shows thick heart muscle. May show signs of poor blood flow. Deep Q waves may appear.
- **Echo:** The heart muscle is thick. The heart may pump normally or poorly. The mitral valve may move forward during contraction. The heart may have a pressure blockage.
- **X-ray:** The heart may be slightly enlarged or normal.
- **Heart pressure:** Pressure in the heart is high. There may be a blockage in blood flow out of the heart. The heart may pump less blood.
- **Outlook:** About 1% of people die suddenly each year.
- **Treatment:** 
  - Beta-blockers to slow the heart
  - Verapamil to relax the heart muscle
  - Disopyramide to reduce blockage
  - Mavacamten to reduce muscle thickness
  - Surgery to remove part of the thick muscle (septal myotomy)
  - Alcohol injection into a heart artery to reduce muscle thickness
  - A combination of these treatments may be used

---

### Restrictive Cardiomyopathy

- **What is wrong?** The heart muscle is stiff. It does not fill with blood properly.
- **Symptoms:** Trouble breathing and tiredness during activity. Heart failure may affect the left or right side. The heart valves may leak.
- **ECG:** Shows thick heart muscle or low electrical signals.
- **Echo:** The heart walls are thick. The heart chamber may be small. The heart does not fill well.
- **X-ray:** The heart may be slightly enlarged or normal.
- **Heart pressure:** Pressure in the heart is high. The filling pattern is abnormal. The heart may pump less blood.
- **Outlook:** About 70% of people die within five years.
- **Treatment:** 
  - Phlebotomy (removing blood) if caused by iron overload
  - Surgery to remove part of the inner heart lining (endocardial resection)
  - Hydroxyurea to treat high levels of certain white blood cells

---

### Key Terms Explained

- **ECG:** A test that records the heart’s electrical activity.
- **Echo:** An ultrasound of the heart that shows how it moves and pumps.
- **Cardiac MRI:** A detailed scan of the heart using magnets and radio waves.
- **ICD:** A small device placed under the skin to stop dangerous heart rhythms.
- **CRT:** A special pacemaker that helps both sides of the heart beat together.
- **Beta-blockers:** Medicines that slow the heart rate and reduce strain.
- **ACE inhibitors:** Medicines that lower blood pressure and help the heart.
- **ARNI:** A newer medicine that works like ACE inhibitors but with better results.
- **SGLT2 inhibitors:** Medicines that help the heart and kidneys work better.
- **Spironolactone / Eplerenone:** Medicines that reduce fluid and protect the heart.
- **Digoxin:** A medicine that helps the heart pump better.
- **Phlebotomy:** Removing blood to reduce iron levels.
- **Hydroxyurea:** A medicine used to lower high white blood cell counts.

---

# Anticholinergic Chemical-Warfare Agents

There are many types of chemical-warfare agents. Each one affects the body in different ways.

"Anticholinergic" means a substance that blocks the action of a natural chemical called acetylcholine.  
Acetylcholine helps nerves send signals to muscles and other nerves.  
When acetylcholine is blocked, some nerves stop working normally.

Doctors use some anticholinergic drugs to treat nerve agent poisoning.  
But these same drugs can also be used as weapons.  
These weapons are called incapacitating agents.  
They are meant to stop people from working or fighting.  
They do not usually cause serious harm or death.

One such agent is called BZ.  
BZ is a solid chemical.  
It can stay in the environment for 3 to 4 weeks.  
It can be spread as a fine mist in the air.  
If people breathe in this mist, they can become sick.  
BZ can also be put on surfaces.  
It can then be absorbed through the skin.

---

## Symptoms of Exposure to BZ

People exposed to BZ may have:

- Dry mouth and dry skin  
- Pupils that are larger than normal  
- Blurry vision  
- Fast heartbeat  
- High body temperature (this can be dangerous)  
- Feeling very tired or weak  
- Seeing or hearing things that are not real (hallucinations)

The hallucinations are usually clear and easy to describe.  
For example:  
- Hearing voices of people they know  
- Seeing imaginary TV shows  
- Pretending to share cigarettes with someone who is not there  
- Seeing strange shapes or patterns

They may also speak unclearly.  
They often pick at their clothes or skin.  
They may become very drowsy or fall into a deep sleep.  
This can last from hours to several days.  
Most people slowly get better over time.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose BZ Exposure

Doctors look at the symptoms a person has.  
They ask about recent exposure to chemicals or drugs.  
There is no lab test that can confirm BZ exposure.  
Doctors suspect BZ if a person has the right symptoms and did not take a medicine known to cause these effects.

---

## How Doctors Treat BZ Exposure

Doctors focus on three main things:

1. **Lower high body temperature**  
   If a person’s body temperature is too high, doctors must cool them down.  
   This is important to prevent serious harm.

2. **Treat agitation and hallucinations**  
   Some people become very upset or act out.  
   Doctors may give a medicine called physostigmine.  
   This helps calm them down and reduces hallucinations.

3. **Keep people safe**  
   People exposed to BZ may be quiet at first.  
   But they can become disruptive.  
   They may need to be gently restrained to keep them from hurting themselves or others.

# Chronic Fatigue Syndrome

Chronic fatigue syndrome, also called myalgic encephalomyelitis or ME/CFS, is a serious health condition. It causes extreme tiredness that does not go away. This tiredness is not caused by a known physical or mental health problem. Doctors find no clear signs of illness during exams or lab tests.

## What You Need to Know

- The tiredness lasts for at least 6 months in a row.
- Some people first feel sick after an illness that feels like a virus.
- There is no single cure. But treatments can help ease symptoms.

Even though many people say they are often tired, only a small number actually have chronic fatigue syndrome. About 1 in 200 people have it. It mostly affects adults between the ages of 20 and 50. Women are more likely to have it than men. But it can happen to anyone, including children.

People with this condition are not faking their symptoms. The tiredness and other problems are real and can be very hard to live with.

## What Causes Chronic Fatigue Syndrome?

Scientists still do not know the exact cause. Some think it may come from a mix of factors. These could include:

- A family history of the condition
- Infections from viruses or bacteria
- Exposure to toxins
- Stress or trauma

There is no proof yet that one single cause exists. But the symptoms are real for each person who has them.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people with chronic fatigue syndrome were doing well at work, school, or in daily life—until the illness started. It often begins suddenly, sometimes after a stressful event.

The main symptom is extreme tiredness. This tiredness:

- Lasts at least 6 months
- Makes it hard to do normal daily tasks
- Is still there when you wake up
- Gets worse with physical activity or stress

You may feel tired all day long. But your muscles are not weak. Your joints and nerves also work normally.

Some people first feel sick after an illness that feels like a virus. They may have a fever, a runny nose, or swollen glands. But many people do not have any illness before the tiredness starts.

Other possible symptoms include:

- Trouble focusing or remembering things
- Poor sleep that does not help you feel rested
- Sore throat
- Headaches
- Joint pain
- Muscle pain
- Belly pain

Depression is common, especially when symptoms are getting worse.

These symptoms are similar to those of fibromyalgia, another condition that causes pain and fatigue.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

There is no lab test that can confirm chronic fatigue syndrome. Doctors must first rule out other possible causes.

They may do blood tests or other checks to make sure you do not have:

- Anemia (low red blood cells)
- Imbalanced body chemicals (electrolyte problems)
- Kidney problems
- Autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis
- Sleep problems
- Thyroid or adrenal gland issues

They also check if your symptoms are caused by medicine.

A diagnosis of chronic fatigue syndrome is only made if no other cause is found.

In 2015, a group of experts recommended a new name: **systemic exertion intolerance disease**, or SEID. They also made clearer rules for diagnosis. To be diagnosed, a person must have:

1. A big drop in daily activity levels that lasts more than 6 months.
   - The tiredness is new or clearly started at a certain time.
   - It is not from overdoing things.
   - Rest does not fix it.
2. Symptoms get worse after physical activity.
3. Sleep does not feel refreshing.

Plus, at least one of these must also be present:

- Trouble thinking clearly
- Feeling dizzy or light-headed when standing up
   - This goes away when lying down

Doctors will ask how often and how badly these symptoms happen. If they do not happen at least half the time with moderate, strong, or severe intensity, the diagnosis may not be correct.

These rules help doctors talk clearly about the condition. But when treating a person, doctors focus more on that person’s actual symptoms than on the rules.

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure. But some treatments can help.

- **Cognitive-behavioral therapy** helps people change how they think and act. It can improve daily life.
- **Graded exercise** means slowly increasing physical activity. It may help some people feel better over time.
- **Medicines** may be used for pain, sleep problems, or depression if needed.

Most people get better over time. But it can take years. Not all symptoms go away completely.

Recovery is often better when people focus on what they *can* do, rather than what they have lost.

Treating specific problems like pain, poor sleep, or depression is important.

Cognitive-behavioral therapy and graded exercise may help some people. They are worth trying if you are open to them.

# Beta-Oxidation Cycle Disorders

These are rare inherited conditions. They affect how the body breaks down fats for energy.

Most of these disorders show up when a person has not eaten for a while. Symptoms include low blood sugar and a buildup of acid in the body. Some people also develop heart problems or muscle weakness.

These disorders are part of a larger group of conditions that affect how the body uses fats and glycerol.

For more information, see:
- How to approach a patient with a suspected inherited metabolic disorder
- How to test for inherited metabolic disorders

---

## How the Body Breaks Down Fats

The body uses a process called beta-oxidation to turn fats into energy. This process happens in small steps. Each step uses four different enzymes. These enzymes work on fats of different lengths: very long, long, medium, or short.

All of these disorders are passed down through families in an autosomal recessive pattern. This means a child must inherit one faulty gene from each parent to have the condition.

---

## Fatty Acid Transport and Mitochondrial Oxidation Disorders

Below is a list of specific disorders. Each one affects a different part of fat breakdown.

### Systemic Primary Carnitine Deficiency
- **Problem:** The body cannot move carnitine into cells.
- **Signs:** Low carnitine in blood, high levels in urine.  
- **Symptoms:** Low blood sugar without ketones, trouble fasting, weak muscles, breathing problems, seizures, heart issues, delayed development.
- **Treatment:** Carnitine supplements.

### Long-Chain Fatty Acid Transport Deficiency
- **Problem:** Fats cannot enter the mitochondria to be broken down.
- **Signs:** Normal or low carnitine; high levels of long-chain fat-carnitine in blood during illness.
- **Symptoms:** Sudden liver failure, high ammonia in blood, brain problems.
- **Treatment:** Liver transplant may be needed.

### Carnitine Palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I) Deficiency
- **Problem:** A key enzyme is missing.
- **Signs:** Normal or high carnitine; no extra acid in urine.
- **Symptoms:** Can’t fast, low blood sugar without ketones, large liver, seizures, coma, high muscle enzyme levels.
- **Treatment:** Avoid fasting. Eat often. Use glucose during attacks. Replace long-chain fats with medium-chain fats.

### Carnitine/Acylcarnitine Translocase Deficiency
- **Problem:** Carnitine cannot move across the mitochondrial membrane.
- **Signs:** Low total carnitine; most is bound to long-chain fats; high C16 carnitine.
- **Symptoms:**  
  - In newborns: Low blood sugar, coma, vomiting, weak muscles, heart problems, irregular heartbeat.  
  - In mild form: Recurring low blood sugar, no heart issues.
- **Treatment:** Avoid fasting. Eat often. Use carnitine if levels are low. Use glucose during attacks.

### Carnitine Palmitoyltransferase II (CPT-II) Deficiency
- **Problem:** A key enzyme is missing.
- **Signs:** High C16 carnitine. In severe cases, low carnitine with most bound to fats.
- **Symptoms:**  
  - Classic form: Muscle pain and weakness after exercise, fasting, illness, or stress.  
  - Severe form: Symptoms in newborns or infants: low blood sugar, heart problems, irregular heartbeat, large liver, coma, seizures.
- **Treatment:** Avoid fasting. Eat often. Use carnitine if needed. Use glucose during attacks.

### Very Long-Chain Acyl-CoA Dehydrogenase (VLCAD) Deficiency
- **Problem:** A key enzyme is missing.
- **Signs:** High levels of long-chain fats in blood and urine.
- **Symptoms:**  
  - Type C: Heart rhythm problems, thickened heart muscle, sudden death.  
  - Type H: Low blood sugar, brain issues, mild acid buildup, mild liver swelling, high ammonia, high liver enzymes.
- **Treatment:** Avoid fasting. Eat more carbs. Use carnitine. Use medium-chain fats. Use glucose during attacks.

### Long-Chain 3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA Dehydrogenase (LCHAD) Deficiency
- **Problem:** A key enzyme is missing.
- **Signs:** High levels of long-chain hydroxy acids and their carnitine forms.
- **Symptoms:** Low blood sugar after fasting, muscle breakdown after exercise, heart problems, liver disease, eye damage, and a serious pregnancy condition called HELLP syndrome in mothers.
- **Treatment:** Avoid fasting. Eat more carbs. Use carnitine. Use medium-chain fats. Use glucose during attacks. For eye damage, docosahexanoic acid may help.

### Mitochondrial Trifunctional Protein (TFP) Deficiency
- **Problem:** A large enzyme complex is missing.
- **Signs:** Similar to LCHAD deficiency.
- **Symptoms:** Liver failure, heart problems, low blood sugar, muscle weakness, sudden death.
- **Treatment:** Same as for LCHAD deficiency.

### Medium-Chain Acyl-CoA Dehydrogenase (MCAD) Deficiency
- **Problem:** A key enzyme is missing.
- **Signs:** High levels of medium-chain fats in blood and urine. Low free carnitine.
- **Symptoms:** Low blood sugar after fasting, vomiting, large liver, tiredness, coma, sudden infant death, or a condition like Reye’s syndrome.
- **Treatment:** Avoid fasting. Eat often, including at bedtime. Eat more carbs. Use carnitine. Use glucose during attacks.

### Short-Chain Acyl-CoA Dehydrogenase (SCAD) Deficiency
- **Problem:** A key enzyme is missing.
- **Signs:** In newborns: Ethylmalonic acid in urine. In chronic form: Low carnitine in muscles.
- **Symptoms:**  
  - Newborns: Acid buildup, vomiting, poor growth, delayed development.  
  - Chronic form: Muscle weakness that gets worse over time.
- **Treatment:** Avoid fasting.

### Glutaric Aciduria Type II
- **Problem:** A key electron transfer system is broken. This affects fat and some amino acid breakdown.
- **Signs:** High levels of many acids in urine and blood. Low carnitine. High sarcosine in blood.
- **Symptoms:** Low blood sugar after fasting, acid buildup, sudden death, brain problems, muscle weakness, possible liver or heart issues.
- **Treatment:** Avoid fasting. Eat often. Use carnitine. Use riboflavin. Use glucose during attacks.

### Short-Chain 3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA Dehydrogenase (SCHAD) Deficiency
- **Problem:** A key enzyme is missing.
- **Signs:** High levels of certain acids in urine.
- **Symptoms:** Muscle breakdown, ketones in urine, low blood sugar, brain issues, heart problems.
- **Treatment:** Avoid fasting.

### Short/Medium-Chain 3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA Dehydrogenase (S/MCHAD) Deficiency
- **Problem:** A key enzyme is missing.
- **Signs:** High levels of specific fats and their carnitine forms.
- **Symptoms:** Liver failure, brain problems.
- **Treatment:** Avoid fasting.

### Medium-Chain 3-Ketoacyl-CoA Thiolase (MCKAT) Deficiency
- **Problem:** A key enzyme is missing.
- **Signs:** Lactic acid in urine, ketones in blood, high levels of medium-chain acids in urine.
- **Symptoms:** Can’t fast, vomiting, dehydration, acid buildup, liver problems, muscle breakdown.
- **Treatment:** Avoid fasting.

### 2,4-Dienoyl-CoA Reductase Deficiency
- **Problem:** A key enzyme is missing.
- **Signs:** High lysine in blood, low carnitine, high levels of a specific fat-carnitine in blood and urine.
- **Symptoms:** Weak muscles at birth, breathing problems due to acid buildup.
- **Treatment:** Not yet clear.

> **Note:** For full genetic and location details, see the Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) database.

> **HELLP** means hemolysis (broken-down red blood cells), high liver enzymes, and low platelets.

---

## Medium-Chain Acyl-CoA Dehydrogenase Deficiency (MCADD)

This is the most common disorder in this group.

Symptoms usually start after 2 to 3 months of age. They happen after fasting, even as short as 12 hours.

People with MCADD may have:
- Vomiting
- Extreme tiredness
- Seizures
- Coma
- Death (sometimes mistaken for sudden infant death)

During attacks:
- Blood sugar is low
- Ammonia is high
- Ketones are lower than expected
- Acid buildup in the body may occur, but often later

### Diagnosis
- Test blood for medium-chain fat-carnitine levels
- Test urine for certain acids
- Test skin cells for enzyme activity
- DNA testing can confirm the diagnosis

MCADD is now part of newborn screening in all U.S. states.

### Treatment During Attacks
- Give 10% glucose through a vein
- Give fluids at 1.5 times normal rate
- Some doctors also use carnitine

### Prevention
- Eat a diet low in fat and high in carbohydrates
- Avoid long periods without food
- Use cornstarch at night to help prevent low blood sugar

# Medulloblastoma in Children

Medulloblastoma is a fast-growing brain cancer. It starts in the cerebellum. The cerebellum is the part of the brain that helps with balance and coordination.

All medulloblastomas are cancerous. They are one of the most common types of brain cancer in children.

## Who Gets Medulloblastoma?

Medulloblastoma most often affects children between 3 and 4 years old or between 8 and 10 years old. But it can happen in babies and teens too.

The exact cause is not known. In rare cases, it may be linked to inherited conditions like Gorlin syndrome or Turcot syndrome.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The tumor can cause pressure inside the skull. It can also affect how the cerebellum works.

Symptoms may include:
- Frequent vomiting
- Headaches
- Feeling very tired or sluggish
- Nausea
- Trouble walking or staying balanced
- Clumsiness
- Seeing double

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find and confirm medulloblastoma.

### Imaging Test
An MRI scan is done. A special dye (contrast agent) is used to make the brain and tumor easier to see.

### Tissue Sample
A small piece of the tumor is taken during surgery. This is called a biopsy. The tissue is looked at under a microscope. Special tests may be done to check the tumor’s genes.

Often, the whole tumor is removed during surgery. The removed tissue is sent to a lab for testing.

### Spinal Tap
A spinal tap checks for cancer cells in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord. This helps find out if the cancer has spread.

### Follow-Up MRI
After surgery, another MRI is done. This shows if any tumor remains.

### Risk Level
Doctors use test results to decide if the cancer is average risk or high risk.

**Average risk means:**
- The surgeon removed almost all of the tumor.
- The cancer has not spread to the spinal fluid, other parts of the brain, or the body.

**High risk means:**
- A large part of the tumor could not be removed.
- The cancer has spread to the spinal fluid, other parts of the brain, or other areas of the body.

New genetic tests on the tumor can also help predict how well a child will do.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment usually includes:
- Surgery to remove the tumor
- Chemotherapy (medicine to kill cancer cells)
- Radiation therapy (high-energy beams to destroy cancer cells)

For children under 3 years old, doctors may avoid radiation therapy. This is to protect the developing brain. These children are treated with surgery and chemotherapy only.

Some children may get a stem cell transplant using their own stem cells. This is done to help the body recover after strong treatment.

## What Is the Outlook?

The chance of recovery depends on the child’s age and the risk level of the tumor.

### Children older than 3 years:
- If the tumor is average risk: about 8 out of 10 children survive cancer-free for 5 years.
- If the tumor is high risk: about 6 to 7 out of 10 children survive cancer-free for 5 years.

### Children 3 years old or younger:
- The outlook is harder to predict.
- About 4 out of 10 children have cancer that has already spread at diagnosis.
- Radiation therapy is often delayed or not used. This is to avoid brain damage.
- Children who survive may have serious long-term problems. These can include:
  - Trouble learning
  - Memory problems
  - Difficulty making decisions
  - Slower mental development

Some types of medulloblastoma have a very good outcome. Up to 10 out of 10 children survive in these cases.

# Broken Thigh Bone

A broken thigh bone usually happens from a strong impact. It is easy to see when it is broken. The main treatment is to stabilize the bone right away and then fix it with surgery.

(See also: Overview of Broken Bones.)

## How a Thigh Bone Breaks

Most breaks happen from a hard hit to the leg. This often happens in car crashes or when a car hits a person walking. The knee is usually bent at the time. Other serious injuries often happen at the same time, like a broken pelvis.

## What to Look For

When the thigh bone breaks, you will see:
- Swelling
- The leg looks bent or twisted
- The leg may be shorter than the other one
- The leg feels unstable

You can lose up to 1.5 liters of blood for each break. This is a lot of blood. Losing this much blood can lead to shock, especially if the injury came from a hard hit and other injuries are present.

## How Doctors Diagnose a Broken Thigh Bone

Doctors use X-rays to confirm the break.

They take two X-rays: one from the front and one from the side. These pictures show the break clearly.

If the break came from a very strong force, doctors will also take X-rays of the hip. This checks for a break in the upper part of the thigh bone. They will also check the knee carefully.

Image courtesy of Danielle Campagne, MD.

## How a Broken Thigh Bone Is Treated

### Step 1: Stabilize the Leg Right Away

The first step is to put a splint on the leg. A special traction splint is often used. These include the Hare traction splint or the Sager traction splint. These splints gently pull on the leg to keep it in place.

Do not use a traction splint if the shin bone is also broken. This could make the injury worse.

### Step 2: Surgery to Fix the Bone

After the leg is stabilized, surgery is done. The surgeon will realign the bone and hold it in place with metal rods or plates. This is called open reduction with internal fixation, or ORIF.

## Key Facts

- A broken thigh bone usually comes from a strong force. It is not hard to spot.
- You can lose up to 1.5 liters of blood for each break.
- If the thigh bone is broken, always check the hip and knee with X-rays.
- Put a splint on the leg as soon as possible after the injury.

# Biofeedback

Biofeedback is a way to help your body and mind work together better.  
It is a type of mind-body therapy.  
It helps you learn to control body functions that usually happen without your awareness.

Electronic devices measure things like your heart rate, blood pressure, and muscle tension.  
These devices send the information to you in real time.  
You can see or hear this information on a screen or through sounds.

A trained therapist can help you understand what the information means.  
You can then learn how to change your body’s responses.  
This can help reduce problems like pain, stress, trouble sleeping, and headaches.

There are different types of biofeedback.  
Some focus on heart rate.  
Others track brain activity.  
This is called neurofeedback.

---

## What Biofeedback Can Help With

Biofeedback is often used to help with:
- Pain, including headaches  
- Stress and anxiety  
- Trouble sleeping (insomnia)  
- Pelvic floor problems, such as leaking urine

Heart rate variability biofeedback may also help:
- Improve performance in sports  
- Support people with mental health or brain-related conditions, such as ADHD or brain injury

Neurofeedback may help improve thinking skills and is used to treat ADHD.

# Liver Damage Caused by Medicines

Many medicines can cause small changes in liver blood tests. These changes often do not cause symptoms.  
Common medicines like statins are known to cause this.  
But serious liver damage—such as yellow skin or eyes, belly pain, or severe itching—is very rare.  
Serious liver damage can also mean the liver cannot make important proteins. This can show up as a long blood clotting time or low protein levels in the blood.

Stopping statins is not needed for people with long-term liver problems.  
Using statins in people with liver disease is just as safe as in people without liver disease.  
Statins may even help slow down liver scarring.  
They can help people with fatty liver disease linked to poor metabolism.  
This includes conditions called MASLD and MASH.  
These conditions are linked to weight, blood sugar, and high cholesterol.  
Experts say people with MASLD have a higher risk of heart disease and stroke.  
But they are not at higher risk for serious liver damage from statins.  
Doctors can safely use statins to treat high cholesterol in people with MASLD, MASH, or liver scarring from MASH.  
In people with advanced liver scarring and poor liver function, statins can still be used—but only at low doses.  
This should only happen after a careful check of risks and benefits.

The term "drug-induced liver injury" can mean any liver problem from a medicine.  
It can also mean only serious liver problems.  
This includes harm from herbal products, plants, and supplements as well as regular medicines.

## How Medicines Can Harm the Liver

The way medicines hurt the liver depends on the medicine.  
In many cases, we do not fully understand how this happens.  
Some medicines can:  
- Stick to liver cells and cause the body’s immune system to attack them.  
- Block normal liver cell processes.  
- Stop the liver from moving substances in and out of cells.  
- Trigger cell death.  
- Damage the energy centers inside liver cells.

We do not fully understand all the risk factors for liver injury from medicines.  
Some risks may apply to certain medicines but not others.  
Examples include:  
- Being 18 years old or older: This increases risk with some antibiotics and tuberculosis medicines.  
- Being overweight or having diabetes: This can make liver injury worse and more likely with some medicines.  
- Having liver disease already: This raises the risk of liver injury from medicines like methotrexate or tuberculosis drugs.  
- Drinking alcohol or smoking: The link to liver injury is not clear.  
- Certain gene differences: Some people have gene changes that make them more likely to have liver injury from many medicines. One such gene is called PTPN22.

## How Doctors Diagnose Liver Injury from Medicines

Doctors look for patterns in blood test results.  
They rule out other causes of liver problems.  
Symptoms can range from feeling tired, sick to your stomach, or not hungry.  
Or they can include yellow skin or eyes, poor liver function, or confusion.  
Finding liver injury early improves the chance of recovery.

To diagnose liver injury from a medicine, doctors need:  
- A possible harmful medicine.  
- A typical pattern of abnormal liver blood tests linked to that medicine.  
- The injury started around the time the medicine was taken.  
- Liver tests improve after stopping the medicine.  

The LiverTox database can help find out if a medicine might cause liver injury.  
This free online tool is run by the National Institutes of Health.  
It gives details on:  
- How likely a medicine is to cause liver injury.  
- The type of injury it causes.  
- How long it takes for injury to appear.  
- How long recovery may take.  
- Real patient cases linked to the medicine.

There is no single test to confirm liver injury from a medicine.  
Doctors must rule out other causes.  
These include:  
- Viral infections (like hepatitis).  
- Problems with the bile ducts.  
- Alcohol use.  
- Autoimmune diseases.  
- Metabolic conditions.

Doctors often define serious liver injury as having at least one of these:  
- Liver enzyme levels more than five times the normal high limit.  
- Alkaline phosphatase more than two times the normal high limit.  
- These results must happen twice, at least 24 hours apart.  
- Bilirubin level above 2.5 milligrams per deciliter, with high liver enzymes or alkaline phosphatase.  
- A blood clotting time longer than 1.5, with high liver enzymes or alkaline phosphatase.

Never give a medicine again if it is suspected of causing liver injury.  
In the United States, doctors should report suspected cases to:  
- The FDA’s MedWatch program.  
- The Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network (DILIN).  
This research group is funded by the National Institutes of Health.  
You can find more about joining their study at their website.

### Key Tips
- Never give a medicine again if it might have caused liver injury.

## How Doctors Treat Liver Injury from Medicines

The most important step is to stop the medicine.  
Stopping early usually leads to full recovery.  
In severe cases, a liver specialist should be consulted.  
This is especially true if the person has yellow skin, poor liver function, or confusion.  
In rare cases, a liver transplant may be needed.  

There are antidotes for only a few types of liver injury:  
- N-acetylcysteine helps with acetaminophen overdose.  
- Silymarin or penicillin can help with poisoning from a certain mushroom.  

Sometimes, steroids can help in rare cases:  
- When the injury is linked to a severe skin rash and body-wide symptoms (DRESS syndrome).  
- When the injury looks like an autoimmune disease, such as from minocycline or certain cancer medicines.

## How to Prevent Liver Injury from Medicines

Preventing liver injury starts when medicines are being tested.  
But safety in small studies does not guarantee safety in large use.  
After a medicine is approved, the FDA now requires ongoing monitoring.  
This helps catch liver problems that were not seen before.  
The LiverTox database is a helpful tool for this.

Checking liver blood tests regularly does not prevent liver injury.  
Using genetic testing may help doctors choose safer medicines for some people.  
This can avoid harm in those who are more sensitive.

## Summary of Key Facts

- Most medicines cause only small, harmless changes in liver blood tests.  
- Serious liver damage from medicines is rare.  
- Risk factors include being 18 or older, being overweight, having diabetes, or certain gene differences.  
- Liver injury from medicines can be predictable (linked to dose) or unpredictable (not linked to dose).  
- The injury can be:  
  - Hepatocellular (liver cell damage).  
  - Cholestatic (bile flow blocked—usually less serious).  
  - Mixed (both types).  
- To confirm the diagnosis, doctors must rule out other causes of liver disease.  
- Never give a medicine again if it is suspected of causing liver injury.

# Epiretinal Membrane

An epiretinal membrane is a thin layer of scar tissue that forms on the retina.  
The retina is the part of the eye that senses light and sends images to the brain.  
This membrane can tighten and pull on the retina.  
When this happens, the retina gets wrinkled.  
A wrinkled retina can cause blurry or distorted vision.

This condition usually happens after age fifty.  
It is most common in people over seventy-five.

Some things that can lead to this problem include:
- Damage to the retina from diabetes
- Inflammation inside the eye
- A tear or detachment of the retina
- Injury to the eye

In many cases, doctors do not know what causes the membrane to form.

## What You Should Know About the Retina and Optic Nerve

[Video available]

## Symptoms of Epiretinal Membrane

You may notice:
- Blurry vision
- Distorted vision (straight lines may look wavy)
- A feeling that you are looking through plastic wrap or cellophane

These symptoms often get worse slowly over time.

## How Doctors Diagnose Epiretinal Membrane

Your doctor will examine the back of your eye using a special light and lens called an ophthalmoscope.  
They may also use imaging tests to get a clearer picture.  
These tests can include:
- Color photography of the eye
- Fluorescein angiography (a test that uses a special dye to see blood flow in the eye)
- Optical coherence tomography (a scan that shows detailed images of the retina)

These tests help confirm the diagnosis.

## Treatment for Epiretinal Membrane

Most people do not need treatment.  
If your vision is blurry or distorted and it bothers you, surgery may help.  
The surgery is called a vitrectomy with membrane peel.  
It removes the gel-like substance inside the eye and the scar tissue on the retina.  
The surgery is done in an operating room.  
You will be awake but numb.  
It usually takes about thirty minutes.
