# Alport Syndrome

Alport syndrome is a rare condition that affects the kidneys, ears, and eyes.  
It is caused by a change in a gene that helps build a type of protein called type IV collagen.  
This protein is important for the structure of tiny filters in the kidneys, the inner ear, and the eye.  
When the protein is not made correctly, these organs can become damaged over time.

The condition often runs in families.  
It can be passed down in different ways:  
- Most often, it is passed through the X chromosome (X-linked).  
- Less often, it is passed through both parents (autosomal recessive).  
- Very rarely, it is passed through one parent (autosomal dominant).

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main symptoms affect the kidneys, ears, and eyes.

### Kidney Problems
- Blood in the urine (hematuria) is usually the first sign.  
- This blood may be too small to see with the naked eye (microscopic).  
- Over time, some people may see blood in their urine (gross hematuria).  
- Protein in the urine (proteinuria) may also occur.  
- High blood pressure (hypertension) can develop.  
- Kidney function slowly gets worse.  
- Most men with the X-linked form develop chronic kidney disease between ages 20 and 30.  
- Some men and people with other forms may not have kidney problems until after age 30 or even later.

### Hearing Loss
- Hearing loss is common, especially for high-pitched sounds.  
- It often starts in childhood or early teens.  
- It may not be noticed at first.  
- It can get worse over time.

### Eye Problems
- Cataracts (cloudy lenses) are the most common eye issue.  
- Some people have a cone-shaped bulge in the front of the lens (anterior lenticonus).  
- Others may have a round-shaped lens (spherophakia), which can cause the lens to move out of place.  
- Some people have eye movement problems (nystagmus).  
- A few may develop retinitis pigmentosa, which can lead to vision loss or blindness.  
- Eye problems usually appear in the late teens or early twenties.

### Other Symptoms
- Some people may have nerve problems (polyneuropathy) or low blood platelets (thrombocytopenia).  
- These are rare.

### Differences Between Men and Women
- Men are usually more severely affected.  
- Women who carry the gene may have mild kidney problems or no symptoms at all.  
- Their kidney function usually stays normal for longer.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect Alport syndrome if a person has:
- Blood in the urine.  
- Hearing or vision problems.  
- A family history of kidney disease.

To confirm the diagnosis, doctors may do:

- **Blood test** to check kidney function.  
- **Urine test** to look for blood, protein, and other signs of kidney damage.  
- **Kidney biopsy** – a small sample of kidney tissue is taken and examined.  
- **Skin biopsy** – a small sample of skin is taken, especially if there is a family history.  
- **Genetic testing** – to look for changes in the COL4A3, COL4A4, or COL4A5 genes.  
- **Special microscope tests** – electron microscopy to see the tiny structure of kidney filters.

The kidney tissue may show:
- Thick and thin areas in the filter layer.  
- A pattern that looks like a basket weave.  
- Scarring in the kidney and around the tubes.

These changes help tell Alport syndrome apart from other similar conditions.

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure for Alport syndrome.  
But treatment can help slow kidney damage and manage symptoms.

### Kidney Care
- Treatment is similar to that for other types of chronic kidney disease.  
- Early use of medicines called ACE inhibitors or ARBs can slow kidney damage.  
- These medicines help lower blood pressure and reduce protein in the urine.  
- People should follow a healthy diet and avoid things that harm the kidneys.

### Kidney Transplant
- A kidney transplant can be successful.  
- But in some men, the new kidney may be attacked by the body’s immune system.  
- This is a rare condition called anti-glomerular basement membrane disease.  
- It usually only happens in men who have Alport syndrome.

### Hearing and Eye Care
- Hearing aids can help with hearing loss.  
- Eye problems are managed with regular checkups and treatment as needed.

### Genetic Counseling
- Families should talk to a genetic counselor.  
- This helps them understand how the condition is passed down and what it means for future children.

## Key Points

- Think about Alport syndrome if someone has blood in the urine and also has hearing or vision problems, or a family history of kidney disease.  
- Confirm the diagnosis with a kidney or skin biopsy and special tests for type IV collagen.  
- Genetic testing can also help confirm the diagnosis.  
- Treat kidney disease early with medicines and lifestyle changes.  
- Consider kidney transplant if kidney function fails.  
- Supportive care helps with hearing and eye issues.  
- Genetic counseling is important for families.

# Care Providers for Older Adults: What You Need to Know

Older adults often need help from more than one health care provider. Each type of provider has special skills. Working together, they give better care. Knowing what each provider does can help you get the best care possible.

---

## Doctors

Older adults may see different kinds of doctors. These include:

- Family doctors who care for people of all ages.
- Internal medicine doctors who focus on adult health.
- Specialists like heart doctors (cardiologists) or cancer doctors (onncologists).
- Surgeons who perform operations.

Sometimes, several doctors work together in one office. This makes it easier to share information and reduces the need to travel to many places.

### Geriatricians

A geriatrician is a doctor who focuses on older adults. Most are internal medicine doctors or family doctors who have extra training.

They may be your main doctor or come in for a short time to give advice.

Geriatricians know how aging changes the body. They can tell if a symptom is from a health problem or just from getting older.

They look at more than just physical health. They also consider your emotions, your home life, and your ability to do daily tasks.

Their main goal is to help you stay as independent and healthy as possible. They manage multiple health issues at once, especially long-term conditions like diabetes or heart disease.

You may benefit from seeing a geriatrician if you:

- Are very weak or frail.
- Have many health problems.
- See many different doctors.
- Take many medicines and worry about side effects.

---

## Nurses

Nurses work in many places: doctor’s offices, hospitals, nursing homes, senior centers, or in your home.

They help keep your care organized. They talk to your doctors, you, and your family to make sure everyone is on the same page.

Nurses are often available when you have questions about your health or treatment.

They teach you how to stay healthy. This includes advice on eating well, staying safe, managing stress, sleeping well, and exercising.

They also:

- Check your blood pressure, pulse, and temperature.
- Take blood samples.
- Give treatments and medicines.
- Teach you how to care for yourself at home.
- Ask about your health history and your living situation.

### Registered Nurses (RNs)

RNs give most of the care for older adults. They supervise other staff like licensed practical nurses and nurses’ aides.

RNs can do physical exams and notice changes that need a doctor’s attention. They can give medicines as directed by a doctor.

### Licensed Practical Nurses (LPNs)

LPNs do many tasks but always under the care of an RN.

### Geriatric Nurse Specialists

These nurses have extra training in caring for older adults. They help with complex health needs.

---

## Nurse Practitioners (NPs)

Nurse practitioners are registered nurses with extra training. They can:

- Diagnose health problems.
- Prescribe medicines.
- Order tests.

Some NPs focus on older adults. These are called adult-gerontological nurse practitioners.

Family nurse practitioners also care for older adults, but with less focus on aging-related issues.

---

## Physician Assistants (PAs)

PAs work under a doctor’s direction. They do many of the same things as doctors and nurse practitioners.

Their duties include:

- Asking about your health history.
- Doing physical exams.
- Ordering tests.
- Helping plan your treatment.
- Assisting in surgery.
- Giving shots and stitching wounds.
- Explaining your treatment plan and how to care for yourself (like diet and exercise).

PAs work in hospitals, nursing homes, and in people’s homes. Some specialize in caring for older adults.

---

## Pharmacists

Pharmacists do more than just give out medicine. They also:

- Check your prescriptions to make sure the right medicine is being used.
- Make sure you are not taking medicines that could be dangerous for older adults.
- Explain how much to take and how often.
- Keep a record of all your medicines and refills.
- Watch for harmful interactions between medicines.

In hospitals, pharmacists help with medication reconciliation. This means they make a full list of all your current medicines. They compare this list to your medical records to catch mistakes.

Medication reconciliation should happen every time your care changes—like when you go from hospital to home.

Some pharmacists specialize in older adults. They are called consultant pharmacists or senior care pharmacists. They often work in nursing homes.

---

## Dietitians

Dietitians check if you are getting enough good food. They look at your diet and your health.

If you are not eating well, they give clear advice on what to eat and how to prepare meals.

Many older adults, especially those in nursing homes, do not get enough food. A dietitian can help improve your nutrition.

---

## Therapists

Different therapists help with different problems.

### Physical Therapists

They help people who have trouble moving. This includes walking, standing up, sitting down, getting in and out of bed, lifting, or bending.

They work with people who have had a stroke, lost a limb, or had hip surgery.

They use exercises, heat, ultrasound, and special positioning to help you feel better and move more easily.

### Occupational Therapists

They help people do daily tasks. This includes dressing, bathing, working, and other everyday activities.

They find ways to make these tasks easier and safer.

### Speech Therapists

They help people who have trouble speaking or understanding language.

They also help people who have trouble swallowing, especially after a stroke.

---

## Social Workers

Social workers help with big steps in care. They help you:

- Leave the hospital.
- Move from one care facility to another.
- Fill out insurance and government forms.

They find services you can get at home or in your community. They often help arrange these services.

They also check how you are doing with your care and support.

They may bring family members together to talk about health decisions.

Many social workers help people with anxiety, depression, or stress from illness or disability.

Some are specially trained to work with older adults. They can decide if you need more help or supervision.

---

## Nurses’ Aides

Nurses’ aides work in hospitals, nursing homes, and other care facilities. They follow instructions from nurses.

They are trained to:

- Take your temperature.
- Check your pulse and blood pressure.

They also help with basic daily tasks like:

- Bathing.
- Dressing.
- Eating.

They may respond to call lights or bells when someone needs help.

---

## Home Health Aides

Home health aides help with housework. They may:

- Cook meals.
- Do laundry.
- Clean the house.

They help keep your home safe and comfortable.

---

## Medical Ethicists

Medical ethicists help when there is a disagreement about care.

For example, a family and doctors may disagree about whether to keep a treatment that is not working.

Medical ethicists are trained in ethics. They can be doctors, nurses, lawyers, or other experts.

Some hospitals have a medical ethicist or a team to help with tough decisions.

# Tests for Infections Using the Immune System

These tests look for signs of infection by checking how your body’s immune system responds.

They use one of two things:

- A piece of the germ (called an antigen) to find if your body has made antibodies against it.
- A special antibody to find if the germ is still in your body.

How the sample is handled depends on the test.  
If the test will not be done right away, keep the sample cold.  
Refrigerate it or freeze it.  
This stops bacteria from growing and keeps the sample safe.

# Mental Health Problems in Children and Teens

Many mental health problems start during childhood or the teen years. Some of the most common ones include:

- Depression  
- Anxiety  
- Eating problems  

Some conditions, like autism, only begin in childhood.

Schizophrenia and similar serious mental health issues are rare in children. When they do happen, they usually start during the middle of the teen years or early adulthood. Some people may first show signs in their mid-30s.

Up to 1 in 5 children and teens may have a mental health problem that affects their daily life. The chance of having a mental health problem goes up as a child gets older. About 3 in 10 teens aged 13 to 17 may have two or more mental health problems.

Events like the COVID-19 pandemic can disrupt routines and relationships. This can make even strong, healthy children and teens more likely to develop mental health issues.

Most mental health symptoms are like feelings that every child has at times. These include sadness, anger, fear, excitement, pulling away from others, or feeling lonely.

The key difference is how strong the feeling is. If a feeling is so strong it stops a child from doing normal things like going to school, playing with friends, or sleeping well, it may be a sign of a mental health problem. It may also mean the child is suffering a lot.

Doctors use clear rules and their experience to decide when a feeling is more than just a normal part of growing up.

---

### Did You Know...

The difference between a normal feeling and a mental health problem is whether the feeling is so strong it:

- Overwhelms the child  
- Stops the child from doing everyday activities  
- Causes the child to suffer  

---

## Types of Mental Health Problems

### Behavioral Issues

These problems mainly affect how a child acts. The child does not mean to cause trouble. But their behavior can upset others, like teachers, friends, or family.

Common types include:

- Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) – the most common one  
- Oppositional defiant disorder  
- Conduct disorder – less common  

### Developmental Disorders

These affect both mental health and how a child grows and learns. They often start in early childhood.

Types include:

- Autism spectrum disorder  
- Rett syndrome  
- Fragile X syndrome  
- DiGeorge syndrome  
- Mitochondrial disorders  

Autism spectrum disorder can mean:

- Trouble making and keeping friendships  
- Very narrow interests  
- Delayed or unusual speech and language  
- Some children also have learning challenges  

Rett syndrome is a genetic condition. It causes similar problems, like trouble talking and connecting with others.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Mental Health Problems

Doctors use several steps to check for mental health problems in children and teens.

They may:

- Talk with the child or teen  
- Talk with parents and teachers  
- Watch how the child acts during the visit  
- Use questionnaires about symptoms  

There is no single test that can prove a mental health problem. Doctors make their decision based on what they see and hear.

Sometimes, doctors send the child to a mental health specialist. These experts are trained to diagnose and treat mental health issues in young people.

The specialist may use special tools to learn more about the child’s thoughts, feelings, and behavior.

Doctors may also do blood tests. These tests can help check for certain genetic conditions, such as:

- Fragile X syndrome  
- Rett syndrome  
- DiGeorge syndrome

# Phlyctenular Keratoconjunctivitis

This condition causes inflammation in the clear front part of the eye (cornea) and the white part of the eye (conjunctiva). It happens when the eye reacts strongly to bacteria.

## What Causes It?

- The main cause is a reaction to bacteria, especially staphylococci.
- Other possible causes include tuberculosis, chlamydia, and other germs.
- It is more common in children.
- Many people with this condition also have eyelid inflammation, called blepharitis.

## What Are the Symptoms?

- Small yellow or gray bumps (called phlyctenules) appear at the edge of the cornea, on the cornea, or on the white part of the eye.
- These bumps last from a few days to two weeks.
- On the white part of the eye, the bumps may break open but heal without leaving a mark.
- If the cornea is affected, you may have:
  - Lots of tears.
  - Pain from bright light.
  - Blurry vision.
  - Aching in the eye.
  - A feeling like something is in your eye.
- The condition can come back often, especially if there is a new infection.
- Repeated episodes can cause cloudiness in the cornea and new blood vessels to grow. This can lead to poor vision.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- Doctors can usually diagnose it by looking at the eye.
- If there is a chance of tuberculosis, testing for TB may be needed, especially in high-risk patients.

## How Is It Treated?

- For cases not caused by tuberculosis:
  - Use eye drops that contain both a steroid and an antibiotic.
  - These drops reduce pain quickly, often within hours.
  - They help prevent scarring and vision loss.
- If you have oily eyelid inflammation (seborrheic blepharitis):
  - Clean your eyelids with special scrubs.
  - This can help stop the condition from coming back.

# Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder

This is not the same as obsessive-compulsive disorder.  
It is a mental health condition.  
It causes a long-term pattern of being overly focused on order, perfection, and control.  
This focus makes it hard to finish tasks.  
It also makes it hard to be flexible or work well with others.

## What It Feels Like

People with this disorder need to be in control.  
They must do things their way.  
They want everything to be perfect.  
They often feel they must do things exactly right.

They may do things alone.  
They do not trust others to help.  
They think others will do things wrong.

This condition is fairly common.  
It affects between 4 and 8 out of every 100 people in the United States.  
It is more common in men.

Some traits run in families.  
These include being overly careful, having a narrow range of emotions, and needing things to be perfect.  
These traits may increase the risk of this disorder.

## Other Conditions Often Present

Many people with this disorder also have other mental health issues.  
These may include:

- A mood disorder like major depression or long-term depression  
- An anxiety disorder  
- Obsessive-compulsive disorder  
- A problem with alcohol use

## How It Is Different from OCD

Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder is not the same as obsessive-compulsive disorder.

People with OCD have unwanted thoughts that cause strong anxiety.  
They feel driven to do certain actions, like washing hands many times or checking doors.  
They often feel upset by these thoughts and actions.

People with obsessive-compulsive personality disorder do not have these thoughts or rituals.  
They do not feel anxious about their behavior.  
They believe their way of doing things is necessary.  
They think it leads to better results.

## Common Signs and Symptoms

People with this disorder are focused on order, perfection, and control.  
They pay close attention to rules, small details, schedules, and lists.  
They want everything done in a strict way.

This focus makes it hard to be flexible.  
It makes it hard to work with others.  
It can stop them from finishing tasks.

They may check for mistakes over and over.  
They spend too much time on small details.  
They leave the most important work until the end.  
They delay finishing tasks because they want everything perfect.

They do not notice how their behavior affects others.  
When focused on one task, they ignore other parts of life.

They do not like to give tasks to others.  
They want others to do things exactly as they say.  
They get upset if someone suggests a different way.  
They may refuse help even when they are behind.

They are very serious about work.  
They work hard not because they need money.  
They care more about being perfect than about earning money.

Because they focus so much on work, they miss out on fun and relationships.  
They may say they have no time to relax or see friends.  
They may cancel vacations or bring work on trips.  
They do not want to waste time.

When they do spend time with others, it is often in a planned activity.  
Sports or organized events are common.  
Hobbies are treated like work.  
They must be done perfectly and with effort.

They plan far ahead.  
They do not like changes.  
Their strict ways can frustrate coworkers and friends.

They do not show affection easily.  
They may seem stiff or formal.  
They wait until they think of the perfect thing to say.  
They focus on logic and facts.  
They do not like emotional or expressive behavior.

They are strict about right and wrong.  
They apply their rules to themselves and others.  
They are hard on themselves and others.

They respect authority.  
They demand that rules be followed exactly.  
They do not make exceptions, even when there is a good reason.

They find it hard to throw away old or broken things.  
Even items with no value are hard to let go of.

They are careful with money.  
They save money in case of emergencies.  
They do not like spending it.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors use a standard guide called the DSM-5-TR.  
This guide lists the signs and symptoms of mental health conditions.

To be diagnosed, a person must show at least four of the following:

- They are focused on details, rules, schedules, organization, and lists.  
- They try to do things perfectly, but this stops them from finishing tasks.  
- They are extremely focused on work and productivity.  
  This causes them to ignore fun and friends.  
- They are overly strict about right and wrong.  
  They are hard on themselves and others.  
- They keep old or useless items, even if they have no value.  
- They do not like to give tasks to others.  
  They only accept help if others do things exactly as they want.  
- They are very careful with money.  
  They save it for possible future problems.  
- They are rigid and stubborn.

These patterns must have started in early adulthood.

## How It Is Treated

Treatment can help.  
But the person’s need for control can make treatment hard.

Two types of therapy may help:

- **Psychodynamic therapy** – Helps people understand their thoughts and feelings.  
  It looks at how past experiences affect current behavior.  
- **Cognitive-behavioral therapy** – Helps people change unhelpful thinking and behavior patterns.

Some antidepressant medicines may also help.  
These are called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs.  
They can improve mood and reduce anxiety.

Treatment takes time.  
It works best when the person is willing to try new ways of thinking and acting.

# What You Need to Eat for Good Health

Good nutrition helps you stay at a healthy weight. It also gives you energy for physical and mental tasks.

Your body uses energy every day. How much energy you need depends on your age, sex, weight, and how active you are.

If you eat more calories than your body uses, you gain weight.  
If you eat fewer calories than your body uses, you lose weight.

You also need certain nutrients every day. These include protein, vitamins, and minerals.  
How much you need depends on your age, sex, weight, and how active you are.

Every five years, experts from the National Academy of Sciences and the U.S. Department of Agriculture update the **Dietary Reference Intakes**. These are guidelines for how much of each nutrient you should eat.  
They include recommendations for protein, energy, and some vitamins and minerals.

For nutrients we know less about, experts give safe and helpful daily amounts based on the best available science.

Pregnant women and babies have special food needs.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture created **MyPlate**.  
It helps people plan healthy meals.  
The advice is tailored to your age, sex, and how active you are.

---

## Recommended Daily Food Amounts for a 40-Year-Old with Moderate Activity

These numbers are for a man who is 5 feet 10 inches tall and weighs 150 pounds.  
They are for a woman who is 5 feet 6 inches tall and weighs 130 pounds.  
Your actual needs may be different based on your height, weight, and activity level.

**Daily Food Group Targets**

| Food Group | Men | Women |
|-----------|-----|-------|
| Grains | 9 ounces | 6 ounces |
| Vegetables | 3.5 cups | 2.5 cups |
| Fruits | 2 cups | 2 cups |
| Dairy | 3 cups | 3 cups |
| Protein | 6.5 ounces | 5.5 ounces |
| Oils | 6 teaspoons | 5 teaspoons |
| Total Calories | 2,600 | 2,000 |

**Notes:**

- **Grains:** At least half should be whole grains.  
  One ounce of grains equals:  
  - 1 slice of bread  
  - 1 cup of ready-to-eat cereal  
  - ½ cup of cooked rice, pasta, or cereal

- **Vegetables:** Eat a variety. Include:  
  - Beans and peas  
  - Dark green veggies (like broccoli, spinach, lettuce)  
  - Orange veggies (like carrots, sweet potatoes, winter squash)  
  - Starchy veggies (like corn, potatoes)  
  - Other veggies (like asparagus, cauliflower, mushrooms, tomatoes)  
  One cup of vegetables equals:  
  - 1 cup of raw or cooked veggies  
  - 1 cup of vegetable juice  
  - 2 cups of raw leafy greens

- **Fruits:** One cup of fruit equals:  
  - 1 cup of fresh or frozen fruit  
  - ½ cup of dried fruit  
  Fruit juice does not count toward your daily fruit goal.

- **Dairy:** One cup of dairy equals:  
  - 1 cup (8 ounces) of milk, yogurt, or soy milk  
  - 1.5 ounces of natural cheese  
  - 2 ounces of processed cheese  
  Choose low-fat or fat-free milk, yogurt, or cottage cheese.

- **Protein:** This includes:  
  - Meat, poultry, fish  
  - Beans, peas, eggs  
  - Processed soy foods (like tofu)  
  - Nuts and seeds  
  One ounce of protein equals:  
  - 1 ounce of meat, poultry, or fish  
  - ¼ cup of cooked beans  
  - 1 egg  
  - 1 tablespoon of peanut butter  
  - ½ ounce of nuts or seeds  
  Choose lean or low-fat meats.  
  Most experts suggest limiting red meat and processed meats.

- **Oils:** Use oils that are liquid at room temperature, like olive oil or canola oil.

- **Calories:** These numbers are general estimates.  
  Everyone’s calorie needs are different.  
  The best way to find your true needs is to watch how your weight changes when you change your eating habits.

- **Activity Level:** Moderate activity means 30 to 60 minutes a day of brisk walking, jogging, biking, dancing, or yard work.

## As You Age, You May Need Less Food

As you get older, you usually become less active.  
This means your body burns fewer calories.  
So you may need fewer calories than when you were younger.

These tips apply to adults and children:

- Eat a healthy pattern of food at every stage of life.  
- Pick foods you like. Make your meals fit your culture, budget, and lifestyle.  
- Focus on healthy foods from each food group. Stay within your daily calorie goal.  
- Limit foods and drinks with added sugar, saturated fat, and salt.  
- Limit alcohol.

## Stay Hydrated

Drinking enough fluids is important for your health.  
Water is the best choice.

- Fat should make up 20% to 35% of your total daily calories.  
- Less than 7% of your calories should come from saturated fat.  
- Too much saturated fat can lead to clogged arteries.  
- Replacing saturated fats with healthy fats (like those in fish, nuts, and vegetable oils) can lower your risk of heart disease.

Most people do not need vitamin or mineral supplements.

# Small Intestine Transplant

A small intestine transplant is when a healthy small intestine from a recently deceased person is placed into someone whose small intestine does not work well. This helps the person get enough nutrition.

Sometimes, the transplant includes other organs like the liver, stomach, or pancreas.

## Why a Small Intestine Transplant Is Needed

You might need this transplant if:

- Your small intestine cannot absorb nutrients properly.
- Part of your small intestine had to be removed due to injury or disease.
- You have many tumors, long-term infections, or other blockages in your intestine.
- You rely on feeding through a vein (called total parenteral nutrition), but your body can no longer handle it. This can happen if you develop liver problems or frequent infections.

Transplants are less common now. New treatments and better care mean fewer people need them.

After three years, more than half of the transplanted intestines are still working. About 65 out of every 100 people who get a transplant are still alive after three years.

## Before the Transplant

Both the donor and the person getting the transplant go through a screening process. This checks that the organ is healthy and that the person receiving it is strong enough for the surgery.

## The Transplant Surgery

The surgeon removes the damaged part of your small intestine. They then connect a healthy small intestine from the donor to your digestive system.

Blood vessels from your body are connected to the blood vessels of the new intestine. The new intestine is also linked to the rest of your digestive tract.

A small opening is made in your belly wall. This is called an ileostomy. It lets doctors check how well the new intestine is working. It also helps them spot problems early.

Waste from your body will pass through this opening into a pouch outside your body. This opening can usually be closed later, once the new intestine is working well.

## Possible Problems After the Transplant

Transplants can cause several issues. The new intestine is especially at risk for infection and rejection.

### Rejection

Your body’s immune system may see the new intestine as foreign and attack it. This is called rejection.

Even if the donor and recipient have similar tissue types, rejection can still happen. Medicines are needed to stop this.

Rejection happens in about 30 to 50 out of every 100 people within the first year. Signs include:

- Diarrhea
- Fever
- Belly pain or cramps

Doctors use a small camera (endoscope) to look inside your intestine. They do this often at first—sometimes once a week. Later, they check less often, like every few weeks or months.

### Graft-versus-Host Disease

The small intestine has a lot of immune cells. Sometimes, these cells from the new intestine attack your body. This is called graft-versus-host disease.

### Other Problems

- The new intestine may not get enough blood. If this happens, surgery is needed to remove the tissue.
- Some people may develop a type of blood cancer called lymphoma over time.

# Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis

This condition is a serious problem with the clear front part of the eye (the cornea). It causes swelling and a sore that can damage vision.

It often happens in people who have long-term or active rheumatic diseases. These are conditions that affect the body’s immune system and cause inflammation in joints, blood vessels, and other tissues.

Common symptoms include:
- Blurry or poor vision
- Pain from bright light
- A feeling like something is in the eye

The edge of the cornea becomes cloudy. This happens because white blood cells move into the area. The cloudiness appears first. Then, a sore (ulcer) forms soon after.

This is different from an infection. Infections usually start with a scratch on the surface of the eye. Then the area gets cloudy. In this condition, the cloudiness comes first.

It is very important to rule out infection. Doctors will take samples from the sore and the eyelid edges to test for bacteria, fungus, or herpes virus.

Without treatment, this condition can be life-threatening. In the past, about 40 to 50 out of 100 people with this condition died within 10 years. Most deaths were from heart attacks. Now, with better treatments, the death rate is much lower.

All patients with this condition should see an eye doctor right away.

Treatment includes:
- Strong medicines that calm the immune system, such as cyclophosphamide, rituximab, etanercept, or other similar drugs
- These medicines help stop the eye damage, treat dangerous blood vessel inflammation, and control the underlying disease
- Local treatments to reduce swelling and protect the eye, such as special glue or soft contact lenses that act like a bandage
- Surgery to repair the eye, such as a patch graft
- Medicines that may help slow down tissue damage, such as tetracycline (taken by mouth) or a 20% solution of N-acetylcysteine (applied to the eye)

Early treatment improves the chance of saving vision and staying healthy.

# Liver Damage Caused by Medicines

Many medicines can affect how your liver works. Some can harm your liver. Some can do both.

## Statins and Liver Health

Statins are medicines used to lower high cholesterol. They can raise liver enzyme levels. This can cause mild liver damage. But most people do not feel any symptoms.

Doctors often still prescribe statins to people with long-term liver problems. These include:

- Fatty liver disease linked to metabolism issues (formerly called nonalcoholic fatty liver disease)
- Inflamed fatty liver (formerly called nonalcoholic steatohepatitis)
- Liver scarring from long-term damage (cirrhosis due to inflammation)

Why? Because the benefits of using statins to lower cholesterol outweigh the risks. Statins are no more dangerous for people with liver disease than for others.

But doctors do not prescribe statins, or give lower doses, to people with advanced liver disease. This is when the liver can no longer do its job well.

## When Liver Damage Causes Symptoms

Very few medicines cause noticeable symptoms. These include:

- Yellow skin or eyes (jaundice)
- Belly pain
- Itching
- Easy bruising or bleeding

## What Is Drug-Induced Liver Injury?

Doctors use the term drug-induced liver injury (DILI) for any liver damage caused by medicines. This includes damage from:

- Prescription and over-the-counter medicines
- Illegal drugs
- Herbal remedies
- Plant-based supplements
- Energy drinks
- Hormones
- Antibiotics

## Types of Liver Damage from Medicines

Some medicines cause liver damage in a predictable way. This happens soon after you take the medicine. The damage depends on how much you take. In the United States, this is often due to too much acetaminophen (like Tylenol). It can lead to sudden jaundice or liver failure.

Other medicines cause liver damage in an unpredictable way. This may happen days, weeks, or even months after you take the medicine. The amount you take does not matter. This kind of damage is rare but can be serious.

## Herbal Remedies and the Liver

Some herbal products can harm your liver. The liver is especially at risk because it processes everything you swallow.

### Pyrrolizidine Alkaloids

Many herbs contain a substance called pyrrolizidine alkaloids. These can damage the liver. Examples include:

- Borage
- Comfrey
- Some Chinese herbs: *zi cao*, *kuan dong hua*, *qian li guang*, *pei lan*

Some teas also contain these harmful substances. Milk, honey, and cereals can be contaminated without you knowing.

If you take small amounts over time, liver damage can build up slowly. If you take a large amount, damage can happen fast.

Pyrrolizidine alkaloids can block blood flow from the liver. This can cause:

- Belly pain
- Vomiting
- Swelling in the belly and legs

Over time, this can lead to liver scarring (cirrhosis), liver failure, or even death.

### Other Herbs That Can Harm the Liver

Other herbs linked to liver damage include:

- *Atractylis gummifera*
- *Camellia sinensis* (used in green and black tea)
- Celandine
- Chaparral
- *Garcinia cambogia* (a weight-loss supplement)
- Green tea extract
- Germander
- *jin bu huan*
- Kava
- *ma huang* (also called *Ephedra*)
- Mistletoe
- Pennyroyal oil
- *syo-saiko-to* (a mix of herbs)

Liver doctors recommend avoiding all herbal supplements. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration does not test these products for safety. Many can cause liver damage or even liver failure—even in healthy people.

## Who Is at Higher Risk?

You may be more likely to have liver damage from medicines if you:

- Are 18 years old or older
- Are overweight or have diabetes
- Already have liver disease
- Have a family history that makes you more sensitive to certain medicines

It is not clear how alcohol or smoking affect this risk.

## How Doctors Classify Liver Damage

Doctors group liver damage by:

- How the medicine harms the liver
- Which liver cells are affected
- What blood test results show

For example:

- Some medicines directly harm liver cells (called hepatocellular damage)
- Some block the flow of bile from the liver (called cholestatic damage)
- Some cause both types of damage

## Symptoms of Liver Damage from Medicines

Symptoms can be mild or severe. They include:

- Feeling tired
- Feeling unwell
- Nausea
- Itching
- Loss of appetite
- Yellow skin or eyes (jaundice)
- A swollen liver
- Pain in the upper right side of the belly
- Confusion
- Being less alert
- Disorientation

## How Doctors Diagnose Liver Damage from Medicines

Doctors use:

- A full health review
- Blood tests to check liver function

After stopping the medicine, doctors repeat the blood tests. If liver enzyme levels go down, it supports the idea that the medicine caused the damage.

## How Doctors Treat Liver Damage from Medicines

The main treatment is to stop the medicine causing the problem.

Some medicines have antidotes. For example:

- *N* - acetylcysteine can treat acetaminophen overdose.

In some cases, doctors may use corticosteroids.

If the liver damage is very serious, a liver transplant may be needed.

Most people get better after stopping the harmful medicine. Doctors may also give medicine to help with symptoms like itching.

## How to Prevent Liver Damage from Medicines

For some medicines that can harm the liver (like statins), doctors may check your blood regularly. This helps catch liver problems early and may prevent serious damage.

For most medicines, blood tests are not done routinely.

# High Calcium in the Blood

High calcium in the blood is when the level of calcium in your blood is too high.  
This is called hypercalcemia.  
It is diagnosed when the total calcium in your blood is more than 10.4 milligrams per deciliter.  
Or when the ionized calcium (the active form) is more than 5.2 milligrams per deciliter.  

The most common causes are:  
- Overactive parathyroid glands  
- Too much vitamin D  
- Cancer  

Some people with high calcium have no symptoms.  
Others may have:  
- Needing to urinate often  
- Constipation  
- Weak muscles  
- Confusion  
- In severe cases, coma  

High calcium can harm the kidneys.  
It can cause kidney stones.  
It can also lead to kidney damage over time.  
In very high levels, it can cause heart rhythm problems.  
It can even lead to shock, kidney failure, or death.  

## What Causes High Calcium?

Many things can cause high calcium.  
The most common are:  
- Overactive parathyroid glands  
- Cancer  

Other causes include:  
- Cancer that has spread to the bones  
- Diseases that cause inflammation in the body, like sarcoidosis or tuberculosis  
- Too much vitamin A or vitamin D  
- Taking certain medicines, such as lithium or theophylline  
- Taking too much calcium or vitamin D supplements  
- A condition called milk-alkali syndrome  
- Immobilization, like being in a cast for a long time  
- Bone diseases such as Paget disease or osteoporosis  
- Rare genetic conditions  

Some lab tests can give a false high reading.  
This can happen if the blood sample was not handled properly.  
Or if the person has high levels of protein in the blood.  
Always check the ionized calcium if you suspect high calcium but the total level is normal.  

## How High Calcium Affects the Body

High calcium can slow down the kidneys.  
This leads to more urine and more thirst.  
It can also cause nausea, vomiting, and stomach pain.  
It can make you lose your appetite.  

When calcium levels are very high, you may feel confused.  
You may become restless or have mood swings.  
You may fall into a deep sleep or even go into a coma.  

High calcium can weaken your muscles.  
It can also cause heart rhythm problems.  
This is more likely if you are taking digoxin, a medicine for heart problems.  

## How Doctors Diagnose High Calcium

Doctors check your blood to measure calcium levels.  
They may also test for:  
- Parathyroid hormone  
- Vitamin D levels  
- Kidney function (creatinine and blood urea nitrogen)  
- Electrolytes (like potassium and phosphate)  
- Alkaline phosphatase (a liver and bone enzyme)  
- Protein levels in the blood  

They may do a chest X-ray.  
They may also test your urine to see how much calcium is being lost.  

The severity of high calcium is based on the level:  
- Mild: 10.5 to 11.9 mg/dL  
- Moderate: 12.0 to 13.9 mg/dL  
- Severe: over 14.0 mg/dL  

If your blood protein is high, it can make calcium look higher than it is.  
If your protein is low, it can hide true high calcium.  
So doctors often check ionized calcium when protein levels are abnormal.  

## How High Calcium Is Treated

Treatment depends on how high the calcium is and what is causing it.  

### For Mild Cases (calcium under 11.5 mg/dL)  
- Drink more fluids  
- Take oral phosphate (a medicine that helps lower calcium)  
- If you have no kidney problems and mild symptoms, this may be enough  

### For Moderate Cases (calcium 11.5 to 18 mg/dL)  
- Get fluids through a vein (IV saline)  
- Use a diuretic medicine (like furosemide) to help your kidneys remove extra calcium  
- Use bisphosphonates (medicines that stop bone from breaking down)  
- Sometimes use corticosteroids or calcitonin  

### For Severe Cases (calcium over 18 mg/dL)  
- Use hemodialysis (a machine that filters the blood)  
- This is needed when calcium is very high and other treatments are not working fast enough  

### For Overactive Parathyroid Glands  
- Surgery to remove the overactive parathyroid gland(s)  
- This is often needed if the condition is getting worse or causing symptoms  

### For Secondary Hyperparathyroidism (often in people on dialysis)  
- Limit phosphate in your diet  
- Take phosphate binders (like calcium carbonate or sevelamer) with meals  
- Use vitamin D analogs carefully  
- Sometimes use cinacalcet (a medicine that lowers parathyroid hormone)  
- In some cases, surgery may be needed  

## Main Ways to Lower Calcium

Doctors use four main methods:  
1. Reduce how much calcium your gut absorbs  
2. Help your kidneys get rid of more calcium  
3. Stop bones from releasing calcium  
4. Remove calcium from the blood using dialysis  

## Key Points

- The most common causes of high calcium are overactive parathyroid glands and cancer.  
- Symptoms include frequent urination, constipation, loss of appetite, muscle weakness, confusion, and kidney stones.  
- Always check ionized calcium if protein levels are abnormal.  
- For mild cases, use oral phosphate or IV fluids with a diuretic.  
- For moderate cases, add bisphosphonates, corticosteroids, or calcitonin.  
- For severe cases, hemodialysis may be needed.  
- Surgery is often used for overactive parathyroid glands.  
- For secondary hyperparathyroidism, control phosphate, use binders, and consider vitamin D analogs or cinacalcet.

# Bulimia Nervosa

Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder. It involves eating large amounts of food quickly, followed by actions to undo the effects of overeating.

## What Happens in Bulimia Nervosa?

- A person eats a very large amount of food in a short time.
- After eating, they try to get rid of the food or prevent weight gain.
- Common ways to compensate include vomiting, using laxatives, fasting, or exercising too much.
- The person often feels out of control during the binge.
- Binges usually happen in secret and are linked to stress or strong emotions.
- People often eat sweet, high-fat foods like ice cream or cake.
- The amount of food eaten can be very high—sometimes thousands of calories.
- Binges can happen several times a day.

### Feelings and Physical Signs

- People with bulimia often feel deep shame or guilt after binging.
- They may have scars on their knuckles from pushing their fingers down their throat to make themselves vomit.
- Vomiting can damage teeth and cause swollen glands in the cheeks.
- Vomiting can also lower potassium levels in the blood. This can cause heart problems.
- In rare cases, vomiting can cause the stomach or esophagus to tear. This is life-threatening.
- Some people take water pills (diuretics) to feel less bloated.

### How It Differs from Other Disorders

- Unlike anorexia nervosa, people with bulimia often have a normal or near-normal weight.
- Unlike binge-eating disorder, people with bulimia try to undo the effects of overeating.
- People with bulimia are often more aware of their behavior and feel bad about it.
- They are more likely to talk to a doctor or trusted person about their struggles.

## Who Gets Bulimia Nervosa?

- It mostly affects teens and young adults.
- It is more common in women than in men.
- About 1 in 200 women and 1 in 1,000 men will have bulimia at some point in their lives.
- It is more common in cultures that value thinness.
- It is also more common in people who do activities that focus on body shape or weight, like gymnastics or ballet.

## What Causes Bulimia Nervosa?

- Genetics play a role. It can run in families.
- Social pressure to be thin can contribute.
- Low self-esteem and strong focus on body shape and weight are common.

## Symptoms of Bulimia Nervosa

- Eating large amounts of food in a short time, even when not hungry.
- Feeling out of control during the binge.
- Eating in secret.
- Feeling extreme guilt or shame after eating.
- Using vomiting, laxatives, fasting, or over-exercising to control weight.
- Constantly thinking about weight and body shape.
- Self-worth tied to body size and shape.
- Mood swings, anxiety, and depression.
- Impulsive behavior.
- Problems with alcohol or drug use.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor will ask about your eating habits and feelings. They will look for signs of bulimia.

Diagnosis is based on:

- Binge eating at least once a week for 3 months or longer.
- Feeling out of control during or after a binge.
- Using vomiting, laxatives, fasting, or over-exercising to compensate.
- Being very worried about weight gain.
- Seeing your self-worth as tied to your weight and body shape.

The doctor may also check for:

- Big changes in weight over time.
- Swollen glands in the cheeks.
- Scars on the knuckles.
- Worn-down tooth enamel.
- Low potassium levels in a blood test.

## Treatment for Bulimia Nervosa

Treatment helps people stop bingeing and purging. It also improves mood and self-worth.

### 1. Therapy

**Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)**  
This is the most common and effective treatment.

- Helps people change harmful thoughts and behaviors.
- Teaches regular, flexible eating habits.
- Reduces obsession with weight and body shape.
- Done in weekly or bi-weekly sessions for 4 to 5 months.
- Works for 30 to 50% of people.
- Some people stop therapy early or do not improve.
- Those who improve usually stay better over time.

**Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT)**  
An option if CBT is not available.

- Focuses on improving relationships and communication.
- Helps solve personal problems that may be linked to the eating disorder.
- Does not tell people what to do or interpret their behavior.
- Does not directly treat the eating habits.

### 2. Medication

- A type of antidepressant called a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) can help.
- It reduces the number of binges and vomiting.
- Works best when used with therapy.
- Also helps with anxiety and depression, which are common in people with bulimia.
- Long-term benefits are not fully known.

## Support and Resources

The following organizations offer help and information in English:

- **National Eating Disorders Association (NEDA)**
- **National Association of Anorexia Nervosa and Associated Disorders (ANAD)**
- **National Institutes of Mental Health (NIMH), Eating Disorders**

# What You Need to Know About Idiopathic Interstitial Pneumonias

Idiopathic interstitial pneumonias (IIPs) are a group of lung diseases with unknown causes.  
They all affect the tissue between the air sacs in the lungs.  
These diseases cause shortness of breath and show similar patterns on lung scans.  
Doctors tell them apart by looking at lung tissue under a microscope.  

There are 8 main types of IIPs.  
They are listed here in order of how often they occur:  

- Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)  
- Desquamative interstitial pneumonia (DIP)  
- Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP)  
- Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP)  
- Respiratory bronchiolitis–associated interstitial lung disease (RBILD)  
- Acute interstitial pneumonia (AIP)  
- Lymphoid interstitial pneumonia (LIP)  
- Idiopathic pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis (IPPFE)  

All types cause some swelling and scarring in the lungs.  
All lead to shortness of breath.  
All show abnormal patterns on high-resolution CT scans.  
All can be confirmed with a lung biopsy.  

The type matters because each one has different symptoms.  
Each responds differently to treatment.  
Some types may not be easy to classify.  
This can happen if test results do not match or if the lung tissue is not clear.  
Some medicines, like steroids, can change test results.  
This can make it harder to know which type a person has.

---

## Key Features of Each Type

| Type | Most Common People | How It Starts | Chest X-ray | CT Scan Findings | Other Conditions That Look Similar |
|------|--------------------|----------------|-------------|------------------|-----------------------------------|
| **Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)** | Men over 50, especially smokers | Slow, lasting over a year | Scarring in lower lungs, small lungs | Scarring and honeycomb-like areas in lower lungs | Asbestos exposure, rheumatoid arthritis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis |
| **Desquamative interstitial pneumonia (DIP)** | Men aged 30–50, almost all smokers | Weeks to years | Cloudy areas in lower lungs | Cloudy areas and lines in lower lungs | Hypersensitivity pneumonitis, pneumonia, RBILD, sarcoidosis |
| **Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP)** | Women aged 40–60, usually non-smokers | Months to years | Cloudy and line-like areas | Symmetric lines and cloudy areas in lower lungs | Rheumatic diseases, COP, DIP, IPF, hypersensitivity pneumonitis |
| **Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP)** | People aged 50–60, less than half smoke | Less than 3 months | Patchy cloudy areas in both lungs | Patchy cloudy areas, nodules, or ring-shaped cloudy spots | Lung cancer, chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, lymphoma, infection, vasculitis |
| **Respiratory bronchiolitis–associated interstitial lung disease (RBILD)** | Men aged 30–50, almost all smokers | Weeks to months | Thickened airway walls, cloudy areas | Thickened airway walls, small nodules, cloudy areas | DIP, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, infection, NSIP |
| **Acute interstitial pneumonia (AIP)** | Any age | Starts suddenly, in 1–2 weeks | Widespread cloudy areas | Widespread cloudy areas, some areas spared | Acute eosinophilic pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome, pneumonia, fluid in lungs |
| **Lymphoid interstitial pneumonia (LIP)** | Mostly women, any age | Lasts over a year | Lines and small spots in lungs | Small spots, cloudy areas, thickened lines, thin-walled cysts | Amyloidosis, Langerhans cell disease, cancer spread, sarcoidosis, rheumatic diseases |
| **Idiopathic pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis (IPPFE)** | No gender preference, average age 57 | Lasts over a year | Thickened lining at top of lungs | Dense scarring near lung surface, lung shrinkage | Asbestos exposure, drug side effects, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, NSIP, radiation, rheumatic diseases |

---

## Symptoms and Signs

Most people with IIPs have:  
- A dry cough  
- Trouble breathing when walking or doing light activity  

Other signs include:  
- Breathing faster than normal  
- Less movement in the chest when breathing  
- Crackling sounds at the bottom of the lungs when breathing in  
- Fingers that are rounded and wider than normal (clubbing)  

Some people also have symptoms of other diseases, such as:  
- Fever  
- Weight loss  
- Feeling tired  
- Muscle pain  
- Joint pain  

These can happen with conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, or vasculitis.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose IIPs

Doctors use several tools to find the right diagnosis.  

### Step 1: Ask About Your Health History  
They will ask:  
- How long have you had symptoms?  
- Do you have any signs of autoimmune disease?  
- Has anyone in your family had lung problems?  
- Have you ever smoked or used drugs?  
- What do you do for work?  
- What chemicals or dusts have you been around?  

They will list your jobs and exposures in order.  
They will check how much and how long you were exposed.  
They will also ask if you used protective gear.

### Step 2: Chest X-ray  
This is usually abnormal.  
But it does not show which type of IIP you have.

### Step 3: Pulmonary Function Tests  
These tests measure how well your lungs work.  
They show if your lungs are stiff and can’t hold much air.  
They also check if your blood has low oxygen levels, especially during activity.

### Step 4: High-Resolution CT Scan (HRCT)  
This is the most important test.  
It shows the inside of your lungs in detail.  
It helps tell the difference between lung tissue disease and air sac disease.  
It can find other problems like cancer, emphysema, or swollen lymph nodes.  
The scan should be done while you lie on your back and then on your front.  
It should also include breathing out slowly to check small airways.

### Step 5: Blood Tests  
These are done if your doctor suspects an autoimmune disease or exposure to toxins.  
Tests may include:  
- Antinuclear antibodies  
- Rheumatoid factor  
- Specific antibodies for rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, scleroderma, and myositis  

### Step 6: Bronchoscopy and Biopsy  
A thin tube is passed through your mouth or nose into your lungs.  
A small sample of lung tissue is taken.  
This helps rule out infections or sarcoidosis.  
But it usually does not give enough tissue to diagnose IIPs.  
It can help narrow down the cause.

### Step 7: Cryobiopsy  
This is a newer method.  
The lung tissue is frozen just before it is removed.  
It gives more tissue than a bronchoscopy biopsy.  
But less than a surgical biopsy.  
It carries risks like bleeding or a collapsed lung.  
It may be used instead of surgery in centers with experience.

### Step 8: Surgical Lung Biopsy  
This is needed if the history and CT scan are not clear.  
It is done using a small camera and tools through small cuts in the chest (VATS).  
Multiple samples are taken.  
This gives the best chance to know the exact type of IIP.

---

## Treatment for Each Type

Treatment depends on the type of IIP.  
Smoking must stop in all cases.  
This helps slow disease and prevents other lung problems.

### Supportive Care
Many people need:  
- Oxygen at home  
- Pulmonary rehabilitation (a program to help you breathe better and stay active)  

Care may involve doctors from different fields.  
This is especially true if you have heart problems from lung disease.

### Medicines by Type

| Type | Treatment | Prognosis |
|------|----------|----------|
| **Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)** | Pirfenidone or nintedanib (to slow lung damage) | 50–70% die within 5 years |
| **Desquamative interstitial pneumonia (DIP)** | Stop smoking, steroids | 70% survive 10 years |
| **Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP)** | Steroids, sometimes other immune drugs | Survival is usually better than IPF; very good in some cases |
| **Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP)** | Steroids | Over 90% survive 5 years |
| **Respiratory bronchiolitis–associated interstitial lung disease (RBILD)** | Stop smoking, steroids | Rare deaths if you quit smoking |
| **Acute interstitial pneumonia (AIP)** | Supportive care, breathing machine, steroids | Over 50% die in less than 6 months |
| **Lymphoid interstitial pneumonia (LIP)** | Steroids | Survival is not well known |
| **Idiopathic pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis (IPPFE)** | Steroids (treatment not clear) | 25–60% survive 5 years |

### Lung Transplant
This may be an option for people with severe, end-stage disease.

# Bicuspid Aortic Valve

A bicuspid aortic valve is a heart valve that has two flaps instead of the usual three.

The aortic valve opens with each heartbeat. It lets blood flow from the heart to the rest of the body. A normal valve has three flaps.

This condition is the most common heart problem present at birth.

When the valve has only two flaps, it may not open all the way. This is called aortic stenosis. It may also not close tightly. This lets blood leak back into the heart instead of going to the body. This is called aortic regurgitation.

A bicuspid aortic valve is the most common cause of aortic stenosis.

People with this condition also have a higher risk of a widened aorta. They are also more likely to get an infection in the heart valve. This infection is called infective endocarditis.

Some people with a bicuspid aortic valve have no symptoms as babies, children, or teens. Problems often start in adulthood.

Symptoms depend on the complications that develop.

If you have an infection in the heart valve, you may have a fever.

If the valve does not open well or does not close properly, you may feel tired. You may also have shortness of breath. You might faint. You may notice your heart beating fast or irregularly. You could also have chest pain.

Doctors may suspect a bicuspid aortic valve if they hear unusual sounds when listening to your heart with a stethoscope. These sounds include a murmur or a clicking noise.

To confirm the diagnosis, you will need an echocardiogram. This test uses sound waves to create a picture of the heart.

If the valve does not work well, it may need repair or replacement.

Aortic stenosis can sometimes be treated with a balloon during a heart catheter procedure. The balloon is used to open the valve.

If the aorta gets too wide, surgery may be needed to replace part of it.

This condition often runs in families. If you have a close relative with a bicuspid aortic valve, that person’s family members should be checked with an echocardiogram.
