# Adjustment Disorders

Adjustment disorders happen when a person has strong emotional or behavior problems after a stressful event.  
The stressor can be one big event, like losing a job.  
It can also be many smaller events, like money troubles or repeated relationship problems.  
It might be a normal life change, such as becoming a parent.  
Or it could be a long-term challenge, like caring for a family member who is disabled.

The stressor can affect just one person.  
It can also affect a whole family or a large group of people.

Losing someone close can lead to an adjustment disorder.  
But doctors must consider how people in different cultures normally react to loss.  
They only diagnose an adjustment disorder if the reaction is much worse than expected.  
They also check if it might be better described as prolonged grief.

## Symptoms of Adjustment Disorder

Symptoms usually start within a few days after the stressful event.  
They usually go away within six months after the stress ends.  
There are three main types of symptoms:  
- Feeling sad or low  
- Feeling anxious or worried  
- Acting out in ways that are not like your usual self

Some people have one type of symptom that stands out.  
For example, someone might feel very nervous after being attacked.  
Another person might act angry or aggressive after a divorce.  
Most people have a mix of these symptoms.

Adjustment disorder symptoms are not as strict as those for acute stress disorder or posttraumatic stress disorder.  
This makes it a common diagnosis in both hospital and clinic settings.  
Some doctors think of it as a mild condition.  
But it can still cause serious pain and make daily life hard.

People with adjustment disorder are more likely to try to harm themselves or die by suicide.  
This is important to know and take seriously.

## How Doctors Diagnose Adjustment Disorder

Doctors use the *Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders*, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR) to make the diagnosis.  
To qualify, a person must meet all of these criteria:

- They have emotional or behavior problems within three months of a stressful event.  
- The problems cause serious distress.  
  - The distress is much worse than what most people would feel in the same situation.  
  - The doctor considers culture and personal background.  
- The problems make it hard to function in daily life.  
  - This includes work, school, relationships, or other important areas.

Doctors must rule out other conditions like posttraumatic stress disorder or acute stress disorder.  
These disorders have different time frames and more specific symptoms.

Adjustment disorder often happens with other mental health conditions.  
For example, a person might have both adjustment disorder and obsessive-compulsive disorder.  
In such cases, both diagnoses are usually made.  
But if a person has sadness after a stressful event, the doctor must decide if it is better to diagnose major depression instead.

The term "adjustment disorder" has sometimes been used too loosely.  
It has been used for any vague or mild mental health issue.  
To fix this, the DSM-5-TR now places adjustment disorder in the trauma section.  
This reminds doctors that symptoms must follow a stressor.  
Still, the symptoms can vary widely.  
Some people have anxiety, others have sadness, and some act out.  
This mix of symptoms makes the diagnosis common but harder to treat.

## Treatment for Adjustment Disorder

Recovery is easier when a person is safe and supported.  
It is hard to heal if the stress keeps happening.  
It is also harder if the person lives in a dangerous or unstable environment.

Having a strong family and healthy social connections helps.  
Most people get better over time with support from friends and family.

Treatment options include:

- **Self-care**: Taking care of your body and mind.  
  This includes eating well, sleeping enough, and staying active.  
  It also means avoiding alcohol and drugs.

- **Psychotherapy**: Talking with a mental health professional.  
  This can help you understand your feelings and learn coping skills.  
  It can also help you improve relationships and solve problems.

- **Medications**: Sometimes doctors prescribe medicine.  
  This is usually for severe anxiety or depression.  
  But there is not much strong evidence that medicine works well for adjustment disorder.

There is not enough clear research to show that therapy or medicine always helps.  
But many people still find them useful.  
The best support often comes from people who care about you.

# Noncancerous Tumors in the Esophagus

Noncancerous tumors in the esophagus are rare.  
The esophagus is the tube that carries food from your throat to your stomach.  
Some of these tumors can make it hard to swallow.  
In rare cases, they can cause sores or bleeding.  
Most of the time, these tumors are not dangerous.  
They are more of a nuisance than a serious health threat.

## Most Common Type of Noncancerous Tumor

The most common type is called a leiomyoma.  
It starts in the smooth muscle of the esophagus.  
Leiomyomas usually appear in people between the ages of 30 and 60.

## Other Types of Noncancerous Tumors

Other types are much rarer.  
Some grow from connective tissue. These are called fibrovascular polyps.  
Others grow from nerve tissue. These are called schwannomas.

## How Doctors Diagnose These Tumors

Doctors use two main tests to find these tumors:

- **Upper endoscopy**: A doctor uses a thin, flexible tube with a camera to look inside the esophagus.  
- **Barium swallow**: The person drinks a liquid that shows up on x-rays. X-rays are taken as the person swallows.

If the tumor is seen, the doctor may take a small sample of tissue during the endoscopy.  
This helps confirm the diagnosis.

In some cases, doctors may also do a CT scan.  
This gives a detailed picture of the inside of the body.

## How Doctors Treat These Tumors

Treatment is usually not needed right away.  
It is only recommended if symptoms start or the tumor grows larger.

Most leiomyomas are small and do not cause problems.  
But a few grow big enough to block the esophagus.  
This can cause difficulty swallowing or pain.  
Pain relievers can help for a short time.  
But only surgery can fix the problem permanently.

Other rare noncancerous tumors can turn into cancer over time.  
Because of this risk, doctors usually remove them when found.

# Diphyllobothriasis (Fish Tapeworm Infection)

This is an infection caused by a type of tapeworm that lives in the intestines.  
The most common tapeworm is called *D. latum*.  
It can grow up to 10 meters long—this is very long for a worm that lives in the human body.  

You get this infection by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish.  
The tapeworms start as tiny eggs in human poop.  
These eggs hatch in freshwater and turn into small swimming larvae.  
Tiny crustaceans eat the larvae.  
Then, fish eat the crustaceans.  
The larvae grow inside the fish and become dangerous to humans.  

Other types of tapeworms can also infect people this way.  
But they are not as common as *D. latum*.  

This infection happens all over the world.  
It is more common in places with cold lakes that are polluted with sewage.  
In the United States and northern Europe, it mostly affects people who eat raw or undercooked freshwater fish.  
Modern sewage treatment has made this infection less common.

---

## Symptoms and Signs

Most people do not have any symptoms.  
Some may feel mild stomach pain, have diarrhea, or lose weight.  

The tapeworm can take vitamin B12 from your food.  
This can lead to low vitamin B12 levels.  
Low vitamin B12 can cause a type of anemia called megaloblastic anemia.  

In rare cases, a heavy infection can block the intestines.  
It can also cause problems in the gallbladder.  
This happens when parts of the tapeworm move into these areas.

---

## How It Is Diagnosed

A doctor will check your stool under a microscope.  
They look for the worm’s eggs or pieces of the worm.  
The eggs have a special lid, which helps identify them.  

A blood test checks for anemia.  
This test checks if you have megaloblastic anemia.

---

## How It Is Treated

You take one dose of a medicine called praziquantel by mouth.  
This medicine kills the tapeworm.  

If praziquantel is not available, a different medicine called niclosamide can be used.  
This medicine is not sold in the United States.  

After treatment, you need to give another stool sample one month later.  
This checks if the worm is gone.  

If you have anemia from low vitamin B12, you may need vitamin B12 supplements.  
These help fix the anemia.

---

## How to Prevent It

Always cook freshwater fish well.  
The fish should reach an internal temperature of at least 63 degrees Celsius (145 degrees Fahrenheit).  

You can also freeze the fish to kill the tapeworm.  
Use one of these freezing methods:

- Freeze at -20 degrees Celsius (-4 degrees Fahrenheit) or colder for 7 full days.  
- Freeze at -35 degrees Celsius (-31 degrees Fahrenheit) or colder until solid.  
  Then keep it at that temperature for 15 hours.  
- Freeze at -35 degrees Celsius (-31 degrees Fahrenheit) or colder until solid.  
  Then move it to a freezer at -20 degrees Celsius (-4 degrees Fahrenheit) or colder.  
  Keep it there for 24 hours.  

These steps kill the tapeworm larvae in the fish.

# Hirschsprung Disease

Hirschsprung disease is a birth defect. It means a baby is born with a part of the large intestine that lacks the nerves needed to make the intestine move. This can block the flow of stool.

## What Happens in Hirschsprung Disease?

- The large intestine needs nerves to push stool toward the anus.
- In this condition, a section of the intestine does not have these nerves.
- Without the nerves, that part of the intestine cannot move.
- Stool builds up behind the blocked section.
- This can cause serious swelling and infection in the intestine.

## Symptoms

Most babies with Hirschsprung disease show signs in the first few days of life. But some children may not have symptoms until later.

**Newborns may have:**
- No bowel movement (meconium) in the first 48 hours.
- A swollen belly.
- Vomiting.
- Poor weight gain and slow growth.

**Babies with infection in the intestine (enterocolitis):**
- Sudden fever.
- Swollen belly.
- Explosive, sometimes bloody diarrhea.

**Older babies and children may have:**
- Refusing to eat.
- No urge to have a bowel movement.
- Severe constipation.

## Causes

- The nerves in the intestine do not form properly during pregnancy.
- Some cases are linked to changes in genes.
- The condition can run in families.
- Some children with Hirschsprung disease also have other birth defects.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors use several tests to confirm the diagnosis.

**Barium enema:**
- A liquid called barium is put into the rectum.
- Air is added to help outline the intestines.
- X-rays are taken to see the shape and flow of the bowel.
- This test is not done if the baby has signs of infection.

**Rectal biopsy:**
- A small piece of tissue is taken from the rectum.
- It is checked under a microscope to look for missing nerves.

**Manometry:**
- A small tube measures pressure inside the rectum.
- This helps check how well the rectum works.

**Blood tests:**
- These may be done to check for gene changes linked to the disease.

## Treatment

Surgery is the main treatment.

**Surgery:**
- The part of the intestine without nerves is removed.
- The healthy part is connected to the rectum and anus.
- The timing of surgery depends on how much of the intestine is affected.

**For severe cases:**
- Surgery must be done quickly to prevent life-threatening infection.

**If infection occurs (enterocolitis):**
- The child is admitted to the hospital.
- They get fluids and antibiotics through a vein.
- A tube is passed through the nose into the stomach or intestine to remove gas and fluid.
- A second tube is placed in the rectum to help relieve pressure.
- The doctor may wash out the rectum with salt water to clear out built-up stool.
- Surgery is done later to remove the non-working part of the intestine.

## Important Notes

- Early diagnosis and treatment help prevent serious problems.
- Without treatment, the condition can lead to infection, poor growth, and other health issues.
- Most children do well after surgery and can live normal lives.

# Stillbirth

Stillbirth means a baby dies in the womb after 20 weeks of pregnancy.  
Some places define it as after 28 weeks.  
The baby does not survive to be born.  

Every year, about 2 million babies die before birth around the world.  
If a woman has had a stillbirth before, her next pregnancy has a higher chance of a stillbirth too.

---

## What Causes Stillbirth?

A stillbirth can happen because of problems with the mother, the placenta, or the baby.

### Problems from the Mother
- High blood pressure during pregnancy (preeclampsia or eclampsia)
- Serious injury or trauma
- Blood clotting problems that develop during pregnancy
- Uncontrolled diabetes
- Thyroid problems
- Being very overweight (body mass index of 40 or higher)
- Using drugs or alcohol
- Smoking
- Serious infections (sepsis)
- Being Black (this increases risk)
- Being a teenager or over 35 years old

### Problems with the Placenta
- The placenta tears away from the uterus too early (placental abruption)
- Infection in the fluid around the baby (chorioamnionitis)
- Blood loss from the baby into the mother’s bloodstream (fetomaternal hemorrhage)
- In twin pregnancies, one baby gives too much blood to the other (twin-twin transfusion)
- The umbilical cord gets tangled, squeezed, or slips through the birth canal before the baby (prolapse or knots)
- Poor blood flow from the mother to the placenta
- The baby’s blood vessels are in front of the baby’s head (vasa previa)

### Problems with the Baby
- Abnormal chromosomes (like Down syndrome)
- A single gene problem
- Major birth defects (especially in the heart or brain)
- Low platelets due to the mother’s immune system attacking the baby’s blood cells
- Anemia in the baby from the mother’s immune system or from a genetic condition
- Fluid buildup in the baby’s body (nonimmune hydrops fetalis)
- Being in a multiple pregnancy (twins, triplets, etc.)
- Infection in the womb

---

## How Is Stillbirth Diagnosed?

A stillbirth is diagnosed when a doctor confirms the baby has no heartbeat and is not moving.

### What the Doctor Checks
- The mother’s medical history and physical exam
- Tests to find the cause

### Tests to Find the Cause
- A careful look at the baby after death (size, weight, appearance, head size)
- A detailed examination of the baby’s body (autopsy)
- Tests on the baby’s chromosomes (karyotype and microarray)
- A close look at the placenta
- Blood tests for the mother:
  - Complete blood count (to check for anemia or infection)
  - Kleihauer-Betke test (to check for blood loss from baby to mother)
  - Tests for blood clotting problems (like antiphospholipid antibodies)
  - Thyroid function test (TSH, and if needed, free T4)
  - Blood sugar test (HbA1C) to check for diabetes
  - Infection tests (TORCH: toxoplasmosis, parvovirus, rubella, CMV, herpes)
  - Syphilis test (RPR)
  - Drug screening

### Genetic Blood Clotting Tests
- Testing for inherited blood clotting problems is not usually done.
- It may be considered only if:
  - The placenta shows serious damage
  - The baby did not grow well in the womb
  - The mother or family has a history of blood clots

Most of the time, doctors cannot find the exact cause of stillbirth.

---

## How Is Stillbirth Treated?

The main goals are to deliver the baby safely and support the mother and family.

### Delivering the Baby
- Sometimes the body starts labor on its own.
- If not, the uterus must be emptied using medicine (like oxytocin) or surgery.
- For surgery, the cervix is opened first with special dilators. Misoprostol may be used to help.
- The method depends on how far along the pregnancy is.

### Cleaning the Uterus
- After delivery, the doctor may need to gently clean out the uterus.
- This is called curettage.
- It is more likely needed if the stillbirth happened early in pregnancy.
- Leftover tissue can cause infection or bleeding.

### Blood Clotting Problems
- If the mother develops a serious blood clotting issue (DIC), she will need blood or blood products right away.
- This is more likely if delivery is delayed.

### After Delivery
- Care after stillbirth is similar to care after a live birth.
- The mother is watched for bleeding, infection, and other issues.

### Emotional Support
- Parents feel deep sadness and grief.
- Emotional support is very important.
- Counseling may help some families.
- Doctors should talk about risks in future pregnancies based on what might have caused the stillbirth.

---

## Key Points

- Stillbirth means a baby dies in the womb after 20 weeks of pregnancy.  
  Some places use 28 weeks as the cutoff.
- Many things can cause stillbirth: problems with the mother, placenta, or baby.
- Delaying delivery can lead to a serious blood clotting problem (DIC).
- Tests can help find the cause, but often no cause is found.
- The uterus must be emptied using medicine or surgery.
- Parents need emotional support and care after the loss.

# Stridor

Stridor is a loud, gasping sound when breathing in. It happens when part of the throat, voice box, or windpipe is partly blocked.

The sound is caused by air rushing through a narrowed airway. It is usually loud enough to hear from a distance.

## In Children

Common causes include:
- **Croup** – a viral infection that swells the voice box and windpipe.
- A **foreign object** inhaled into the airway, like a small toy or food.
- **Infection of the epiglottis** – a rare but serious condition where the flap at the back of the throat becomes infected and swollen.

## In Adults

Common causes include:
- A **tumor** in the head or neck area.
- An **abscess** – a pocket of pus caused by infection.
- Swelling (edema) in the upper airway.
- **Vocal cord paralysis or dysfunction** – when the voice box does not work properly.
- A **foreign object** inhaled into the airway (less common).
- **Infection of the epiglottis** – rare but serious.

## When to Seek Help

If stridor happens when a person is at rest and they feel short of breath, it is a medical emergency. This needs immediate care.

## How It Is Treated

If a tumor in the voice box or windpipe is blocking the airway, it can cause stridor. This is especially true with cancers like laryngeal cancer.

When both vocal cords are paralyzed, the space between them becomes very small. This makes it hard to breathe, even with light activity. The breathing sound becomes harsh and high-pitched.

Brief episodes of stridor can happen if a person accidentally inhales food or water into the lungs. This can cause the voice box to tighten.

If a foreign object is suspected and the person is not in a hospital, someone trained can help. For example, in an adult, the **Heimlich maneuver** can be used to push the object out.

## Medical Care

If a person with stridor is in a hospital or emergency room, doctors may insert a tube through the mouth or nose into the windpipe. This is called **tracheal intubation**. It helps air reach the lungs and prevents choking.

In some cases, a small cut is made in the neck to place a tube directly into the windpipe. This is called a **tracheostomy**.

During intubation, the doctor can see the airway directly. This often helps find the cause of the stridor.

If intubation is not done, doctors may use a thin, flexible tube with a camera. They pass it through the nose and into the throat. This test is called **nasopharyngeal laryngoscopy**. It lets the doctor see the upper airway and make a diagnosis.

# Tooth Decay (Cavities)

Tooth decay is also called a cavity.  
It happens when the hard parts of your tooth break down.  
At first, you may not feel any pain.  
Symptoms like tooth pain usually show up later.

## What Causes Tooth Decay?

Tooth decay is caused by a mix of things.  
It starts with a sticky film on your teeth called plaque.  
Plaque builds up every day after you eat or drink.  
It contains bacteria, dead cells, and food bits.  
Some bacteria in plaque eat sugar and make acid.  
This acid wears down your tooth enamel.  
The bacteria *Streptococcus mutans* are especially bad at causing decay.  
Some types of this bacteria are worse than others.  
After about 72 hours, plaque hardens into tartar.  
Tartar is tough and can’t be removed by brushing alone.

## What Are the Signs of Tooth Decay?

Early decay only affects the outer layer of the tooth.  
It does not cause pain at first.  
When decay reaches the inner layer of the tooth, you may feel pain.  
You might feel it when eating or drinking something hot, cold, or sweet.  
Later, you may feel pain when chewing or tapping the tooth.  
If the decay reaches the nerve inside the tooth, the pain can be sharp and long-lasting.

## How Is Tooth Decay Diagnosed?

Your dentist checks your teeth with their eyes and a small probe.  
They may take X-rays of your teeth.  
Sometimes they use special tools to find early decay.  
These tools can detect changes in how electricity flows, how light reflects, or how light passes through the tooth.  
But X-rays are still the most useful tool.  
They help find decay that is hidden, deep, or under old fillings.

## How Is Tooth Decay Treated?

If the decay is small and only in the outer layer, your dentist may try to fix it without drilling.  
They may recommend better brushing, flossing, and fluoride treatments.  
If the decay has reached the inner part of the tooth, your dentist will remove the damaged area.  
They will then fill the hole with a material like metal, plastic, or glass.  
In some cases, the nerve is damaged.  
Then you may need a root canal and a crown to save the tooth.

## How Can You Prevent Tooth Decay?

You can prevent most tooth decay with simple daily habits.  
Brush your teeth at least twice a day.  
Floss between your teeth every day.  
Use fluoride toothpaste.  
Get regular cleanings from your dentist.  
Avoid sugary drinks and snacks.  
Eat more foods that help your teeth, like milk, cheese, and vegetables.

### Brushing Tips

- Brush for at least 2 minutes.  
- Use an electric toothbrush or a soft manual brush.  
- Brushing for 3 to 4 minutes with a manual brush is enough.  
- Don’t use too much toothpaste.  
- Avoid toothpastes that are very rough or abrasive.  
- Focus on the area near the gums. This is the most important spot to clean.  
- It’s often missed, so take extra care.

### Flossing Tips

- Slide the floss between each tooth.  
- Curve it around the side of each tooth.  
- Move it up and down 3 times.  
- Go just below the gum line.  
- Use thin or waxed floss if your teeth are very close together.  
- Water flossers can help if you have trouble using regular floss.

### Fluoride Helps Prevent Decay

- Fluoride makes your tooth enamel stronger.  
- It helps repair early damage and resist acid.  
- Use fluoride toothpaste every day, no matter your age.  
- If your tap water does not have enough fluoride, your child may need fluoride supplements.  
- These are available as drops, tablets, gels, or toothpaste.  
- Tablets should be swished in the mouth before swallowing.  
- The right dose depends on your child’s age, diet, and how much fluoride is in the water.  
- Too much fluoride can cause white spots or streaks on teeth.  
- This is called dental fluorosis.  
- Young children often swallow toothpaste.  
- Use toothpaste made for kids. It has less fluoride.

### Sealants Help Protect Deep Grooves

- Some teeth have deep grooves.  
- These grooves can trap food and bacteria.  
- Fluoride alone does not protect these areas well.  
- Sealants are a special plastic coating.  
- They stick to the grooves and block food and bacteria.  
- This helps stop decay from starting.

### More Help If Decay Keeps Happening

If you keep getting cavities, your dentist may suggest stronger steps.  
They may recommend a mouth rinse with chlorhexidine.  
Use it for 60 seconds, twice a day, for 2 weeks.  
This helps reduce harmful bacteria in plaque.  
It may help good bacteria grow back.  
But we are not sure how well this works.  
Your dentist may also suggest chewing gum or hard candy with xylitol.  
Use it 3 times a day for 5 minutes.  
Xylitol stops harmful bacteria from growing.  
You may also be told to use a high-fluoride toothpaste at night.  
Or use a custom fluoride tray at night.

### For Pregnant Women

If you had many cavities before, you may pass harmful bacteria to your baby.  
This can lead to early tooth decay in your child.  
To help prevent this:  
- Eat less sugar.  
- Brush your teeth twice a day with fluoride toothpaste.  
- Floss every day.  
- If you can’t do this, use xylitol from the time your baby is born.  
- Keep using it until you stop sharing food with your child.

### For Babies

If your baby has teeth, do not give them a bottle at bedtime.  
Only give water in the bottle.  
Avoid milk, juice, or formula at night.  
These can cause decay.

## Key Facts

- Tooth decay is caused by acid made by bacteria in plaque.  
- Risk factors include weak teeth, dry mouth, acidic saliva, eating sugary foods often, and not getting enough fluoride.  
- Early decay in the outer layer can sometimes be fixed with better brushing, flossing, and fluoride.  
- Decay that reaches the inner tooth needs drilling and filling.  
- Prevention means brushing, flossing, and cleanings every 6 to 12 months.  
- Fluoride is key. Use it in toothpaste. If your water lacks fluoride, children may need supplements.

# Scorpion Stings

Most scorpion stings in North America are not serious.  
They usually cause pain, a little swelling, soreness, and warmth at the spot where the scorpion stung.

But one scorpion, called the bark scorpion, is more dangerous.  
It lives in parts of Arizona, New Mexico, and on the California side of the Colorado River.  
Its sting hurts more than other scorpion stings.  
It can cause numbness or a tingling feeling around the sting area.

Children are more likely to have serious symptoms.  
These include:
- Strange movements of the head, eyes, or neck
- More saliva than normal
- Sweating
- Feeling restless or unable to stay still

Some people may have strong, sudden muscle twitches or jerks.  
Their blood pressure can rise very high.  
They may also have trouble breathing.

---

## What to Do for a Scorpion Sting

### For most stings:
- No special treatment is needed.
- Put an ice cube on the sting.  
  Wrap the ice in plastic and a thin cloth first.  
  This helps reduce pain.
- Use a cream or ointment that has an antihistamine, a numbing medicine, a steroid, or a mix of these.  
  It can help with pain and swelling.

### For bark scorpion stings with serious symptoms:
- Doctors may give medicine through a vein to calm the person down.
- They may also give medicine to lower very high blood pressure.
- A special medicine called antivenom can quickly ease symptoms.  
  But it can cause a serious allergic reaction in some people.
- This antivenom is only available in the United States.  
  It is only used when symptoms are very severe.

### In other parts of the world:
In places like Turkey, the Middle East, and India, scorpions are more dangerous.  
Doctors treat stings with medicines to ease symptoms and prevent problems.  
If breathing becomes very hard due to high blood pressure, special medicines may be needed.  
Antivenoms for specific scorpion poisons are available.  
They are used only in the most serious cases.

# Tularemia – Simple Explanation

Tularemia is a serious illness caused by a germ called *Francisella tularensis*. It can feel like a severe flu. The illness can affect the skin, lymph nodes, lungs, or other parts of the body. It does not spread from person to person.

## How You Can Get Tularemia

You can get tularemia in several ways:

- Eating or drinking food or water that is contaminated.
- Being bitten by an infected tick, deer fly, or flea.
- Breathing in tiny particles of the germ from the air.
- Touching infected animal tissue, such as a rabbit or hare, with bare hands.

The germ can enter your body through tiny breaks in the skin, even if the skin looks normal.

## Types of Tularemia

There are seven main types. The symptoms depend on how you were exposed.

| Type | How Common | What Happens |
|------|-------------|--------------|
| Ulceroglandular | Most common | A sore on the hand or finger. Swollen lymph nodes nearby. |
| Typhoidal | Common | Fever, chills, and body aches. No clear sore or wound. |
| Oculoglandular | Uncommon | Swollen eye and nearby lymph nodes. Often from touching the eye with a dirty hand. |
| Glandular | Rare | Swollen lymph nodes. No sore. Often linked to eating contaminated food. |
| Pneumonic | Uncommon | Lung infection. May cause coughing up blood. Can happen on its own or after another type. |
| Oropharyngeal | Rare | Sore throat and swollen neck glands. Caused by eating or drinking contaminated food or water. |
| Septicemic | Rare | Severe illness. Low blood pressure, trouble breathing, and organ failure. |

The germ can spread through the blood to other organs like the lungs, liver, kidneys, heart, or brain.

## Two Main Types of the Germ

- **Type A**: More dangerous. Found in rabbits, hares, and rodents in the United States and Canada.
- **Type B**: Less severe. Found in rodents and water animals in North America, Europe, and Asia.

## Who Gets Tularemia?

People most at risk are:
- Hunters
- Butchers
- Farmers
- Fur workers

In winter, most cases come from handling infected rabbits or hares.  
In summer, cases often come from tick bites or handling other infected animals or birds.

Rarely, people get it from:
- Eating undercooked infected meat.
- Drinking dirty water.
- Mowing grass in areas where the germ is common.

In the western United States, ticks, deer flies, horse flies, and contact with infected animals are common causes.

No one has ever passed tularemia to another person.  
Lab workers are at higher risk because the germ is easy to catch during normal lab work.

## Tularemia and Bioterrorism

Tularemia is considered a possible bioterrorism threat. Just 10 germs inhaled as a mist can cause serious lung infection.

## What Happens in the Body

In severe cases, small areas of dead tissue form in the body. These can be found in:
- Skin sores
- Lymph nodes
- Liver
- Spleen
- Kidneys
- Lungs
- Heart
- Brain

These spots are white-yellow and range from 1 mm to 8 cm wide.  
The illness causes strong sickness, but no poison from the germ has been found.

## Symptoms of Tularemia

Symptoms start suddenly, usually 1 to 10 days after exposure. Most often, they start 2 to 4 days after exposure.

Early symptoms:
- High fever (39.5 to 40 degrees Celsius)
- Headache
- Chills
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Extreme tiredness

Later, you may have:
- Repeated chills
- Heavy sweating
- Weakness

The type of symptoms depends on how you were exposed.

Within 1 to 2 days after exposure:
- A red bump appears at the site of infection (on the hand, arm, eye, or mouth).
- The bump turns into a pus-filled sore.
- The sore opens and forms a clean, shallow crater with clear fluid.

Sores are usually one on the arms or hands. But in the mouth or eyes, there may be more than one. Only one eye is usually affected.

Lymph nodes near the sore swell up. They may fill with pus and drain.

By day 5, many people feel like they have typhoid fever. Some develop pneumonia. A few may become confused or delirious.

## How Doctors Diagnose Tularemia

Diagnosis is based on:
- Your history of exposure (rabbits, ticks, animals, etc.)
- Sudden symptoms
- A skin sore and swollen lymph nodes

Doctors may do:
- Blood tests
- Swab tests from sores or sputum
- Antibody tests (done twice, 2 weeks apart)
- PCR test (a fast test to find the germ)

A rise in antibodies or a high antibody level confirms the diagnosis.

Some people with brucellosis may have similar test results, but usually at lower levels.

The germ is very dangerous. Samples must be handled with care. Labs with high safety levels should do testing.

## Treatment for Tularemia

The best treatment for moderate to severe cases is:
- **Streptomycin** or **Gentamicin**

These are given by injection into the muscle or vein.

**Streptomycin:**
- Adults: 10 mg per kg every 12 hours for 7 to 10 days (max 2 grams per day)
- Children: 15 to 20 mg per kg every 12 hours for 7 to 10 days (max 2 grams per day)

**Gentamicin:**
- Adults: 1.7 mg per kg every 8 hours for 7 to 10 days
- Children: 1.7 mg per kg every 8 hours or 2.5 mg per kg every 12 hours for 7 to 10 days

Gentamicin is often used instead of streptomycin because it is safer and less likely to harm hearing.

**Other options for mild to moderate cases:**
- **Ciprofloxacin**: 500 mg by mouth every 12 hours for 10 to 14 days
- **Doxycycline**: 100 mg by mouth every 12 hours for 14 to 21 days

**Chloramphenicol** is only used for meningitis. It is not preferred because safer options exist.

**If the brain is infected (meningitis):**
- Adults: Streptomycin or gentamicin + ciprofloxacin, doxycycline, or chloramphenicol
- Children: Gentamicin + ciprofloxacin or doxycycline

All treatments last 14 to 21 days.

In emergencies, if injections are not possible, oral doxycycline or ciprofloxacin can be used. But relapses can happen.

## Care for Skin Sores

- Keep sores wet with saline (salt water) dressings.
- This helps reduce swelling and pain in nearby lymph nodes.

Surgery to drain large abscesses is rarely needed unless treatment is delayed.

## Eye Infections

- Use warm salt water compresses.
- Wear dark glasses to reduce light sensitivity.
- In severe cases, eye drops (homatropine) may help.

## Pain Relief

Headaches are common. Over-the-counter pain medicine usually helps.

## Outlook (Prognosis)

- With treatment, almost no one dies.
- Without treatment, about 6% of people with the most common type (ulceroglandular) die.
- For more serious types (typhoidal, septicemic, pneumonic), death rates can be as high as 50% without treatment.
- Death usually happens from severe infection, pneumonia, brain infection, or belly infection.

Relapses can happen if treatment is not complete.

One infection gives you long-term protection.

## How to Prevent Tularemia

- Wear tick-proof clothing and use repellent when in areas where ticks live.
- Check your body for ticks after being outdoors.
- Remove ticks right away.

When handling rabbits, hares, or rodents:
- Wear gloves and a face mask.
- The germ can be on the animal or in tick poop on its fur.

Always cook wild birds and game meat thoroughly.

Disinfect water that might be dirty.

There is no vaccine available now. One is being reviewed by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

**After a high-risk exposure** (like a lab accident or bioterrorism event):
- Take doxycycline or ciprofloxacin by mouth for 14 days.

## Key Points

- The germ *Francisella tularensis* is very infectious.
- In North America, rabbits, hares, and rodents are the main carriers.
- You can get it from animals, ticks, contaminated food or water, or breathing in germs.
- Symptoms include high fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, and extreme tiredness.
- Skin sores and swollen lymph nodes are common. Pneumonia can also happen.
- Diagnosis uses blood tests, swabs, antibody tests, and PCR.
- Treatment is with streptomycin or gentamicin. Other antibiotics are used for milder cases or brain infection.
- Prevent it by avoiding ticks, wearing gloves when handling animals, and cooking meat well.

# Understanding Chest Injuries

Chest injuries often affect the ribs, upper belly, lungs, blood vessels, heart, chest muscles, soft tissues, and breastbone. Sometimes the food pipe, collarbone, or shoulder blade are also hurt.

In the United States, chest injuries lead to about one in four deaths from serious trauma. Many of these life-threatening injuries can be treated or stabilized in the emergency room. Surgery is not always needed right away.

---

## What Causes Chest Injuries?

Chest injuries can happen from a strong blow, like in car crashes, falls, or sports accidents. They can also happen when something sharp pierces the chest, such as a bullet or knife.

Chest injuries are often serious or life-threatening. They can make it hard to breathe or cause major blood loss. Some injuries damage the ribs and chest muscles so much that the lungs cannot expand properly.

When the lungs are damaged, they cannot do their main job: take in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide from the body.

Heavy bleeding inside the chest can also cause problems. Blood in the chest wall can make breathing harder. Injuries to the heart can stop it from pumping blood well.

Common and serious chest injuries include:

- Injury to the heart from a blunt force  
- Blood building up around the heart (called cardiac tamponade)  
- Blood in the space between the lung and chest wall (called hemothorax)  
- Bruising of the lung tissue (called pulmonary contusion)  
- Broken ribs  
- A tear in the main artery leaving the heart (called aortic injury)  
- Air trapped between the lung and chest wall (called traumatic pneumothorax, or a collapsed lung)

> **Did You Know?**  
> Simple treatments—like putting in a needle or tube—can save lives in some chest injuries.

---

## Signs and Symptoms of Chest Injuries

The injured area is usually sore or painful. The pain gets worse when you breathe in. The chest may be bruised. Some people feel short of breath.

If the injury is severe, you may feel very out of breath, sleepy, or confused. Your skin might feel cold, wet, or bluish. These signs can happen when the lungs stop working well (called respiratory failure) or when you go into shock.

Shock means your blood pressure drops dangerously low. You may feel your heart racing.

Other symptoms depend on the type of injury. For example:

- In a pneumothorax, air can build up under the skin. The skin feels like it is crackling and makes a crackling sound when touched.
- If blood or fluid builds up around the heart (cardiac tamponade), the neck veins may look swollen.
- In tension pneumothorax, the pressure in the chest increases quickly. This can be life-threatening.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Chest Injuries

### A Doctor’s Evaluation

Most chest injuries are easy to see. But only a doctor can tell how serious they are.

The doctor listens to your lungs with a stethoscope. They check your neck and chest for signs of injury. If you are struggling to breathe, the doctor puts a small device on your finger to check how much oxygen is in your blood.

Sometimes, a blood test checks oxygen and carbon dioxide levels.

### Imaging Tests

A chest x-ray is almost always done. It can show:

- Air in the space between the lung and chest wall  
- Blood in the space between the lung and chest wall  
- Broken collarbones  
- Some broken ribs

But a quick ultrasound test is often needed too. This is called E-FAST (Extended Focused Assessment With Sonography in Trauma). It is used in emergency rooms and trauma centers to check the heart and lungs fast.

If doctors suspect a tear in the main artery from the heart (aorta), they may do:

- A CT scan  
- An ultrasound  
- A special x-ray of the aorta (called aortography)

Blood tests and an electrocardiogram (ECG) may also be done.

---

## How Chest Injuries Are Treated

### Support for Breathing and Blood Flow

All chest injuries need quick attention. The first goal is to help you breathe and keep blood flowing.

You may get extra oxygen through nasal prongs, a face mask, or a breathing tube. You may also get fluids through a vein. In some cases, you may need a blood transfusion.

People with serious chest injuries are usually admitted to the hospital.

Pain relief medicine is given to help with pain.

### Specific Treatments for Each Injury

For some injuries, a tube is placed into the chest. This is called a chest tube or thoracostomy.

The tube drains blood if there is blood in the chest (hemothorax). It removes air if air is trapped (pneumothorax). This helps the lung re-expand.

The procedure is usually done with local anesthesia, so you are awake but the area is numb.

# Hashimoto Thyroiditis

Hashimoto thyroiditis is a long-term condition where the body’s immune system attacks the thyroid gland.  
This causes swelling in the thyroid and can lead to low thyroid hormone levels.  

The main signs are a painless swelling in the front of the neck and symptoms of low thyroid function.  
These symptoms include tiredness, feeling cold, and gaining weight without trying.  

Some people may have symptoms of too much thyroid hormone instead.  
This can happen during the early stages when the inflamed thyroid releases stored hormones.  
It can also happen if a person has both Hashimoto thyroiditis and Graves’ disease at the same time.  

## What Causes Hashimoto Thyroiditis?

This condition is the most common cause of low thyroid function in North America.  
It is much more common in women than in men.  
The risk goes up with age.  
It is also more common in people with certain genetic conditions, such as Down syndrome, Turner syndrome, and Klinefelter syndrome.  

Many people with Hashimoto thyroiditis have a family history of thyroid problems.  

This condition often happens with other autoimmune diseases.  
These include:  
- Addison disease (a problem with the adrenal glands)  
- Type 1 diabetes  
- Low parathyroid hormone levels  
- Vitiligo (loss of skin color in patches)  
- Premature graying of hair  
- Pernicious anemia (a type of vitamin B12 deficiency)  
- Rheumatoid arthritis  
- Lupus  
- Sjögren syndrome  
- Celiac disease  
- A rare condition called type 2 polyglandular deficiency syndrome (Schmidt syndrome), which includes Addison disease, low thyroid function, and sometimes type 1 diabetes  

There may also be a higher chance of thyroid tumors.  
In rare cases, this can lead to thyroid lymphoma.  

Under the microscope, the thyroid shows many immune cells and scar tissue.  

## Symptoms and Signs

You may notice a swelling in the front of your neck.  
It may feel like a lump or a feeling of fullness in the throat.  

When a doctor checks your neck, they will feel a thyroid that is not tender.  
It may feel smooth or lumpy.  
It is usually firm and rubbery, not soft like a normal thyroid.  

Most people have symptoms of low thyroid function.  
These include:  
- Feeling very tired  
- Feeling cold even when others are warm  
- Gaining weight without changing your diet or activity  

Some people may have symptoms of high thyroid function.  
These include:  
- Feeling hot  
- Losing weight without trying  

These symptoms can happen during the early, inflamed stage of the disease.  
They can also happen if you have both Hashimoto thyroiditis and Graves’ disease.  

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will do blood tests to check your thyroid function.  
They will check:  
- Thyroxine (T4) – a thyroid hormone  
- Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) – a hormone from the pituitary gland that tells the thyroid to make more hormones  
- Thyroid autoantibodies – these are immune system proteins that attack the thyroid  

In the early stages, your T4 and TSH levels may be normal.  
But your thyroid peroxidase antibodies will be high.  
You may also have high antithyroglobulin antibodies, though this is less common.  

If your doctor feels a lump in your thyroid, they may order an ultrasound.  
This test uses sound waves to create a picture of the thyroid.  

The ultrasound often shows:  
- Uneven texture in the thyroid tissue  
- Dark areas (hypoechoic) with thin lines (septations)  
- Small dark spots (micronodules)  
- Less blood flow in the gland  

Your doctor may test for other autoimmune diseases only if you have symptoms of them.  
Or if you have a strong family history of autoimmune thyroid disease or other autoimmune conditions.  

## How Is It Treated?

Most people need to take thyroid hormone medicine every day for the rest of their lives.  
The most common medicine is levothyroxine.  
It is taken as a pill once a day.  

The usual dose is between 75 and 150 micrograms per day.  
Your doctor will adjust the dose based on your blood tests.  

In some people, low thyroid function goes away on its own.  
But this is rare.  
Most people need lifelong treatment.  

## Key Points

- Hashimoto thyroiditis is an immune system attack on the thyroid gland.  
- People with this condition often have other autoimmune diseases.  
- Early on, thyroid hormone and TSH levels are normal.  
- Later, thyroid hormone drops and TSH goes up.  
- This leads to symptoms of low thyroid function.  
- High levels of thyroid peroxidase antibodies are a key sign.  
- Most people need to take thyroid hormone medicine for life.

# Female Genital Mutilation – Simple Explanation

Female genital mutilation is a harmful practice in some cultures. It means cutting or removing part or all of a girl’s outer genitals.

## What Are the Female External Genitals?

The outer parts of a girl’s genitals include:
- The clitoris: a small, sensitive bump that feels pleasure during touch.
- The labia: two folds of skin that protect the inside of the genitals.
- The hymen: a thin piece of tissue that partly covers the opening of the vagina.

## Where Is This Practice Done?

This practice happens in some parts of Africa, especially in the north and center. It also occurs in some areas of the Middle East and other places around the world.

In some cultures, people believe this practice helps with cleanliness, makes a girl more likely to have children, keeps her faithful, or makes men more satisfied during sex. Some believe it is needed for a girl to get married.

But more and more people are speaking out against it. Religious leaders and community members are helping to stop the practice. It is becoming less common in some areas.

## What Are the Risks?

There are no health benefits to this practice. It causes serious harm.

- Most girls are cut when they are about 7 years old.
- The cutting is done without pain relief (no anesthesia).

## The Four Main Types

The World Health Organization lists four main types:

- **Clitoridectomy**: Removing part or all of the clitoris and the skin around it.
- **Excision**: Removing the clitoris and the small inner lips. Sometimes the larger outer lips are removed too.
- **Infibulation**: Cutting and sewing the outer lips together, leaving only a small hole for urine and menstrual blood. The clitoris may be removed too.
- **Other**: Any other harmful cutting or burning of the genitals for nonmedical reasons. This includes pricking, piercing, cutting, scraping, or burning the area.

## Health Problems After Mutilation

Cutting the genitals can cause:
- Heavy bleeding.
- Infections, including tetanus (a serious bacterial infection).
- Scarring.
- Pain when urinating or having sex.
- Recurring infections in the bladder or reproductive system.

Women who have been infibulated may have trouble during childbirth. They can bleed heavily or suffer serious injury to the pelvic area.

Many women also face emotional and mental health problems. These can include anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress.

## Care and Support

Women who have been infibulated need care from health workers who understand their culture and background.

Some women choose to have a procedure called deinfibulation. This means opening the stitched area. It is often done before having sex or before giving birth.

This procedure should be done by a trained specialist. It is important to get care from someone with experience in this type of treatment.

# How Some Medicines Work

Some medicines work without changing how cells behave.  
They also do not attach to receptors in the body.

For example, most antacids help reduce stomach acid.  
They do this through simple chemical reactions.  
Antacids are basic substances.  
They react with stomach acid to form neutral salts.  
This reduces the acid level in the stomach.

Another example is cholestyramine.  
It is used to treat high cholesterol.  
Its main job is to bind bile acids in the gut.  
It does not enter the bloodstream.  
It works only in the digestive system.

# Velopharyngeal Insufficiency

## What Is It?

Velopharyngeal insufficiency means the back of the roof of the mouth does not close tightly enough. This causes air to leak through the nose when speaking. The result is a voice that sounds too nasal.

## How Does It Work?

The soft part of the roof of the mouth (the soft palate) and the sides and back of the throat form a seal during speech and swallowing. This seal keeps air and food from going into the nose.

When the seal is weak or incomplete, air escapes through the nose. This makes the voice sound too nasal. This is called a hypernasal voice.

## What Causes It?

- A cleft palate (a split in the roof of the mouth) from birth.
- A soft palate that is too short.
- Surgery to remove the tonsils or adenoids.
- Weak throat muscles due to nerve or brain problems, such as:
  - Cerebral palsy
  - Stroke
  - Brain tumors
- Tumors in the roof of the mouth

## What Are the Symptoms?

- A voice that sounds too nasal.
- Trouble making clear speech sounds.
- In severe cases, food or liquids come back through the nose when eating or drinking.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look for signs of speech problems. To confirm the diagnosis, they may:

- Use a thin, flexible tube with a camera (called a fiberoptic nasoendoscope) to look inside the nose and throat.
- Take moving x-rays while you swallow different foods. The foods are mixed with barium, a substance that shows up white on x-rays. This helps doctors see how the throat moves.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment options include:

- Speech therapy to help improve speech.
- A special device worn in the mouth (called a palatal lift prosthesis) to help close the gap.
- Surgery to fix the structure of the soft palate or throat.

Treatment depends on the cause and how severe the problem is.

# Retropharyngeal Abscess

A retropharyngeal abscess is a serious infection behind the throat. It is most common in young children. It can cause a severe sore throat, high fever, stiff neck, and noisy or difficult breathing.

This infection starts in small glands (lymph nodes) at the back of the throat. These glands are near the spine. The infection can come from a throat infection, sinus infection, infected adenoids, or a nose infection.

Children between 1 and 8 years old are most at risk. This is because their lymph nodes in this area shrink after age 4 or 5. Adults can get this infection after swallowing a sharp object or after a medical procedure in the throat.

Common bacteria that cause this infection include *Streptococcus* and *Staphylococcus*. Other bacteria like *Bacteroides* and *Fusobacterium* can also cause it. In some adults and children, HIV or tuberculosis bacteria may be involved.

## Serious Risks

This infection can lead to very serious problems. These include:
- Blockage of the airway
- Life-threatening infection in the blood (septic shock)
- The abscess bursting into the airway, which can cause pneumonia or choking
- Infection spreading to the chest (mediastinitis)
- Bleeding from a major neck blood vessel (carotid artery)
- Blood clots in the neck veins (Lemierre syndrome)

## Symptoms and Signs

In children, symptoms often start after a cold or upper respiratory infection. In adults, they may follow swallowing a foreign object or a medical procedure.

Children may have:
- Pain when swallowing
- Trouble swallowing
- High fever
- Swollen neck glands
- Stiff neck
- Noisy or high-pitched breathing
- Difficulty breathing
- Loud snoring at night
- Head tilted to one side

Adults often have severe neck pain. But they are less likely to have noisy breathing.

The back of the throat may look swollen on one side.

## How It Is Diagnosed

Doctors suspect this infection in people with:
- A very bad sore throat with no clear cause
- Stiff neck
- Noisy or difficult breathing

### X-ray
A special X-ray of the neck can show:
- Swelling behind the spine
- Changes in the normal curve of the neck
- Air in soft tissues behind the spine
- Damage to the spine bone

### CT Scan
A CT scan gives a clearer picture. It helps confirm the diagnosis. It can show if the infection is just swelling or a full abscess. It also shows how big the abscess is and how far it has spread.

## How It Is Treated

Treatment includes antibiotics, surgery to drain the abscess, and breathing support.

### Antibiotics
Doctors use strong antibiotics. Common ones include ceftriaxone and clindamycin. These are given through a vein.

In some children with a small abscess, antibiotics alone may be enough. But most patients need surgery.

### Surgery
Most patients need surgery to drain the abscess. A doctor makes a small cut in the back of the throat. This lets the pus out.

### Breathing Support
Before surgery, a tube is placed into the windpipe to help with breathing. This tube stays in place for 24 to 48 hours after surgery.

Treatment plans are based on past experience and observations. They are not always backed by large studies.

# Swollen Lips and Tongue

Swelling in the lips or tongue can happen suddenly. It is often due to an allergic reaction.

Allergies can be caused by:
- Certain foods or drinks
- Some medicines
- Illegal drugs
- Chemicals or irritants
- Lipstick
- Airborne substances like pollen or smoke

In many cases, doctors cannot find the exact cause of the swelling.

A rare condition called hereditary angioedema can cause repeated episodes of swelling. Other causes include:
- Skin rash called erythema multiforme
- Sunburn
- Cold or dry weather
- Injury or trauma

Swelling in the lips alone is not usually dangerous. But if the swelling is due to angioedema, it can spread to the mouth, throat, or airways. This can block breathing and become life-threatening quickly.

Treatment depends on what is causing the swelling.

If you know the cause, avoiding it helps. The swelling usually goes down once the trigger is removed.

For allergic swelling, a doctor may prescribe a cream with steroids. This helps reduce swelling and inflammation.

In some cases, surgery may be done to remove extra lip tissue. This is only if the swelling affects appearance and does not go away.

If the tongue swells, it can make it hard to speak or swallow. This needs quick medical attention.

Always seek help if you have trouble breathing, swallowing, or speaking. These are signs of a serious problem.

# Risks of Medical Radiation

Radiation from medical tests can be a concern. Here is what you need to know in simple terms.

## What Is Ionizing Radiation?

Ionizing radiation comes from:
- High-energy waves like X-rays and gamma rays.
- Tiny particles such as alpha particles, beta particles, and neutrons.

This type of radiation comes from:
- Radioactive materials.
- Medical machines like X-ray and radiation therapy devices.

## How Much Radiation Do Medical Tests Give?

Most medical tests that use radiation give a small amount. These include:
- X-rays
- CT scans
- Nuclear scans

These small amounts are usually safe. But even small amounts of radiation can cause harm over time. There is no safe level that is completely risk-free. So doctors always try to use the lowest possible dose.

## How Is Radiation Measured?

Doctors use different ways to measure radiation exposure:

- **Absorbed dose** tells us how much radiation a body part takes in. It is measured in gray or milligray. (Older units were called rad. One milligray equals 0.1 rad.)

- **Equivalent dose** adjusts the absorbed dose based on the type of radiation. It is measured in sievert or millisievert. (Older units were rem. One millisievert equals 0.1 rem.) For X-rays and CT scans, the adjustment factor is 1.

- **Effective dose** gives a better idea of overall risk. It takes into account how sensitive different body parts are. For example, reproductive organs are more sensitive than skin. This number is also in sievert or millisievert. Younger people get a higher effective dose for the same test.

The effective dose helps doctors compare risks between different tests. It also helps set safety limits for people who work with radiation.

## Other Sources of Radiation

Medical imaging is not the only source of radiation. You are also exposed to radiation from:
- Cosmic rays from space
- Natural radioactive materials in the ground and air

This background radiation is higher at high altitudes. For example:
- A coast-to-coast airplane flight gives about 0.01 to 0.03 millisievert.
- The average person in the United States gets about 3 millisievert per year from background sources.
- People living in high-altitude areas like Colorado or New Mexico get about 1.5 millisievert more per year.

## Typical Radiation Doses from Medical Tests

Here are average radiation doses from common tests:

| Test | Average Effective Dose (millisievert) |
|------|-------------------------------|
| DEXA bone scan | 0.001 |
| Chest X-ray (one view) | 0.02 |
| Chest X-ray (two views) | 0.1 |
| Lower back X-ray (one view) | 1.5 |
| Hand or foot X-ray (one view) | 0.001 |
| Abdomen X-ray (one view) | 0.7 |
| Barium enema | 6 |
| Upper GI with barium | 6 |
| Mammogram (screening) | 0.21 |
| CT scan of head | 2 |
| CT scan of chest | 6.1 |
| CT scan of abdomen and pelvis | 7.7 |
| Coronary angiogram | 7 |
| Coronary angiogram with treatment | 15 |
| Lung perfusion scan | 2 |
| PET scan (no CT) | 7 |
| Bone scan | 6.3 |
| Liver and gallbladder scan | 2.1 to 3.1 |
| Heart scan with technetium | 9.4 to 12.8 |

> Note: Doses can vary depending on the machine, the patient, and the hospital.

## When Is Radiation Risk Higher?

Some people are more sensitive to radiation. Risks are higher when:
- You are pregnant.
- You are a baby or young child.
- You are a young woman getting a mammogram.

## Trends in Radiation Use

From 2006 to 2016, the amount of radiation from medical tests in the U.S. went down by 15% to 20%.  
- In 2006, the average person got 2.92 millisievert per year.  
- In 2016, that dropped to 2.16 millisievert per year.

## Newer CT Scanners and Safer Scans

Modern CT scanners (multidetector CT) use more radiation than older ones. They can use 40% to 70% more radiation per scan.

But new technology is helping reduce this:
- Automatic settings that adjust the dose.
- Better image processing that needs less radiation.
- New scanner detectors.

These advances mean lower doses for the same quality images.

## Programs to Reduce Radiation

Two programs help protect patients:
- **Image Gently** – for children.
- **Image Wisely** – for adults.

These programs give doctors and hospitals tools and training to use less radiation when doing imaging tests.

## Key Takeaways

- All radiation carries some risk, even small amounts.
- Doctors aim to use the lowest possible dose.
- Children, pregnant women, and young adults are more sensitive.
- New technology is making scans safer.
- You can ask your doctor about the risks and benefits of any test.

# Watching the Baby’s Heartbeat During Labor and Delivery

Doctors check the baby’s heartbeat during labor. This helps them see if the baby is doing well.

As soon as a woman comes to the hospital to give birth, a doctor or nurse starts checking the baby’s heartbeat. They do this either at regular times or all the time.

Checking the heartbeat is the easiest way to see if the baby is getting enough oxygen.

If the baby’s heartbeat is too fast or too slow, or if it changes in a bad way during contractions, it may mean the baby is in trouble.

## How the Heartbeat Is Monitored

There are two main ways to check the baby’s heartbeat.

### External Monitoring

A doctor or nurse uses a special stethoscope called a fetoscope. Or they use a handheld device that sends and receives sound waves. This device goes on the mother’s belly to check the baby’s heartbeat at set times.

Another device can stay on the mother’s belly to check the heartbeat all the time. This is called electronic fetal monitoring. It also tracks the mother’s contractions.

### Internal Monitoring

A small round sensor is placed on the baby’s head. The sensor is attached to a wire and put through the vagina. This method is used only if there is a risk of problems during labor. It is also used if the external device cannot get a clear signal.

This method can only be used after the water breaks. That means the sac around the baby has opened and fluid has leaked out.

### Nonstress Test

When continuous monitoring starts, doctors often do a nonstress test. This checks the baby’s heartbeat for 20 to 40 minutes.

The test looks for certain patterns. Results are either:

- **Reassuring** – the baby is doing well.
- **Nonreassuring** – the baby may be in trouble.

If the result is nonreassuring, doctors do more tests to check the baby’s health.

### Biophysical Profile

A biophysical profile uses ultrasound to make real-time pictures of the baby. Doctors watch the baby for up to 30 minutes.

They check:

- The baby’s heartbeat
- How much amniotic fluid is around the baby
- Whether the baby is breathing
- How much the baby is moving

Each of these is scored. The total score can be up to 10.

### What Happens Next

Based on the results of these tests, doctors decide:

- If it is safe to keep going with labor.
- If a cesarean delivery is needed to deliver the baby safely.

# Arterial Gas Embolism – Simple Explanation

This condition happens when air bubbles get into the blood vessels that carry blood to the body’s organs. These bubbles can block blood flow. This can stop oxygen from reaching important organs. It is a serious and dangerous problem.

## What Causes Arterial Gas Embolism?

Air bubbles can enter the blood in several ways:

- If a diver holds their breath while coming up from deep water, the air in their lungs can expand and burst the lung tissue. This lets air into the blood.
- In rare cases, air bubbles form in the blood during decompression sickness.
- Air can move from the veins into the arteries if there is a hole in the heart or a problem in the lungs. This is more dangerous if the person has a heart defect.

Even small amounts of air in the veins can cause serious problems if there is a hole in the heart. The air can then reach the brain and cause a stroke.

Air in the veins that does not reach the arteries is less dangerous. But large amounts can cause lung problems, such as fluid in the lungs. This is called "chokes."

## Who Is at Risk?

This can happen to people in high-pressure environments, such as deep-sea divers. It can also happen during:

- Surgery, especially brain or ear, nose, and throat surgery
- Use of breathing machines (mechanical ventilation)
- Use of tubes in blood vessels (intravascular catheters)
- Injuries to the neck or chest that let air into the blood

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms can start within minutes after a diver comes to the surface. They can happen even after a shallow dive.

Common symptoms include:

- Sudden confusion or loss of awareness
- Weakness on one side of the body
- Trouble moving or feeling parts of the body
- Seizures
- Passing out
- Not breathing
- Low blood pressure or shock
- Death can happen quickly

Other signs may include:

- Damage to the lungs (pulmonary barotrauma)
- Symptoms of decompression sickness (type II)

Air bubbles can also affect other organs. This can cause:

- Heart problems (like irregular heartbeat or heart attack)
- Kidney problems (blood in the urine, protein in the urine, kidney failure)
- Skin changes (blue or pale spots on the skin, pale tongue)
- Spinal cord problems
- Problems in the digestive system

## Important Warning

If a diver passes out right after coming up from a dive, it is very likely due to arterial gas embolism. This is a medical emergency. Treatment must start right away.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors make the diagnosis based on the person’s history and physical exam. They do not need imaging tests to confirm it.

Imaging tests are not usually helpful. They can delay treatment. But in some cases, doctors may use them if the diagnosis is unclear.

Imaging tests that may show air in the body include:

- Echocardiography: shows air in the heart
- Chest CT: shows lung injury or bleeding
- Head CT: may show air in blood vessels or brain swelling
- Abdominal CT: may show air in blood vessels in the intestines

Note: Air in the blood vessels may not always show up on imaging. A normal scan does not rule out the condition.

Doctors also check for other causes of passing out, such as carbon monoxide poisoning from bad air in a scuba tank.

Sometimes decompression sickness can cause similar symptoms. The two conditions can look alike, but they are different.

## How Are They Different?

| Feature | Arterial Gas Embolism | Decompression Sickness |
|--------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **Main Symptoms** | Sudden loss of consciousness, often with seizures | Pain (especially in joints), brain or nerve problems, breathing trouble (chokes) |
| **When Symptoms Start** | Right after surfacing, even from a shallow dive | Usually starts over an hour after surfacing. Can happen up to 24 hours later |
| **Cause** | Holding breath while coming up, or lung injury | Too fast a return to normal pressure after being under pressure |
| **How It Happens** | Air from lungs enters blood and blocks brain vessels | Gas bubbles form in blood and tissues when pressure drops too fast |

## What Is the Emergency Treatment?

If you suspect arterial gas embolism, act fast.

### Immediate Steps:
- Give 100% oxygen through a tight-fitting mask.
- Keep the person lying flat. This helps blood pressure stay stable.
- If the person is unconscious and cannot protect their airway, place them on their side. This helps prevent choking on vomit.
- Do not use the left-side-down or head-down positions. These are not helpful and are no longer recommended.
- Start CPR or use a breathing machine if needed.
- Give fluids through a vein if the person is not awake. If they are awake, give fluids by mouth.

### Transport to a Recompression Chamber:
- Get the person to a recompression chamber as soon as possible.
- This is the most important treatment. It uses high pressure to shrink the air bubbles and help the body absorb them.
- Do not delay transport for imaging or other tests.

### Air Travel:
- Air travel may be okay if it saves time.
- The patient must be breathing 100% oxygen before flying.
- Some air ambulances keep the cabin at sea level pressure. These are safe to use.

## What About Medicines?

- **Lidocaine** (given through a vein) may help improve brain recovery. This is based on animal studies, not human trials.
- Do not use routine positioning like left-side-down or head-down. These do not help and can cause harm.

## Key Points to Remember

- If someone has brain symptoms within minutes of surfacing from a dive, think arterial gas embolism.
- Do not rule it out just because imaging tests look normal.
- Do not do routine imaging to look for air in the blood.
- Start 100% oxygen right away.
- Get the person to a recompression chamber as fast as possible.

## Where to Get Help

If you need urgent help, call:

- **Divers Alert Network**: 24-hour hotline – 919-684-9111
- **Duke Dive Medicine**: Doctor-to-doctor consultation – 919-684-8111
- **Undersea and Hyperbaric Medical Society**: Scientific and medical information on diving and high-pressure medicine. Visit their website or read their journal *Undersea and Hyperbaric Medicine*.

# Compressive Optic Neuropathy

This condition happens when something, often a tumor, presses on the nerve that carries vision from your eye to your brain.

## What Causes It?

Many things can cause this problem. They include:
- Tumors inside the eye socket
- Tumors in the brain, like pituitary tumors
- Swelling from inflammation, such as orbital pseudotumor
- Other health issues, like thyroid eye disease

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main symptom is a slow, painless loss of vision. It usually starts in one eye and gets worse over time. Most people notice trouble seeing things in the center of their vision.

But if the pressure is on a part of the nerve where the two eyes’ nerves cross (called the optic chiasm), it can cause loss of side vision in both eyes. This often happens with tumors in the pituitary gland.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor will check your vision and look at your optic nerve. An eye doctor (optometrist or ophthalmologist) will test your vision and take pictures of the nerve inside your eye.

The nerve may look swollen, pale, or normal. But the key test is imaging. A magnetic resonance imaging scan (MRI) of the brain and eye area is needed. This scan helps find any mass or tumor pressing on the nerve.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on what is causing the pressure.

- Surgery is often needed to remove the mass or make it smaller.
- For some tumors, radiation therapy is used instead or in addition to surgery.
- After surgery, some people see an improvement in their vision.

Early treatment can help protect your vision. If you notice any slow, painless vision loss, see a doctor right away.

# What Is Vasculitis? Vasculitis means inflammation of blood vessels. This inflammation can damage the walls of blood vessels. When blood vessels are damaged, blood flow to tissues can slow down or stop. This can cause tissue damage or death. Vasculitis can affect any blood vessel. This includes arteries, arterioles, veins, venules, and capillaries. It can also cause inflammation in organs. But organ inflammation is not always caused by vasculitis. The symptoms of vasculitis depend on: - Which blood vessels are affected - Where the vessels are in the body - How much organ damage has happened - How much inflammation is outside the blood vessels --- ## What Causes Vasculitis? There are two main types: - Primary vasculitis - Secondary vasculitis **Primary vasculitis** has no known cause. It happens on its own. **Secondary vasculitis** is caused by something else. This can include: - Infections - Certain medicines - Toxins - Other autoimmune diseases (like lupus or relapsing polychondritis) - Cancer --- ## How Does Vasculitis Work in the Body? When a blood vessel is inflamed, doctors look at the tissue under a microscope. They check for: - Damage to the vessel wall - Types and locations of immune cells in the wall - How much damage there is - Whether there is dead tissue (necrosis) - Signs of healing, like thickening or scarring The type of immune cells seen can help identify the kind of vasculitis. For example: - In new injuries, white blood cells called polymorphonuclear leukocytes are common. - In older injuries, lymphocytes are more common. Inflammation can affect part of a vessel or the whole vessel. At the site of inflammation, the vessel wall may have swelling, dead cells, or scarring. In muscular arteries, the inner layer of the vessel wall often breaks down. Some types of vasculitis include giant cells in the vessel wall. In diseases like granulomatosis with polyangiitis or Kawasaki disease, the main problem is not just vessel inflammation. There is also strong inflammation in the organ tissue itself. **Leukocytoclastic vasculitis** is a term used for small blood vessel problems in the skin. It means white blood cells break down and leave behind small pieces of cell nuclei. This happens all the way through the vessel wall. The inflammation is not granulomatous (no large clumps of immune cells). Early on, polymorphonuclear leukocytes are most common. Later, lymphocytes take over. As the inflammation goes away, the vessel wall may thicken and scar. This can narrow the inside of the vessel. A narrowed vessel reduces blood flow. This can cause tissue damage or death. --- ### Clues from a Biopsy That Help Diagnose Vasculitis | What the Biopsy Shows | Possible Diagnosis | |------------------------|--------------------| | Inflammation with lymphocytes, macrophages, and giant cells, but no dead tissue | Giant cell arteritis
