# Nipple Discharge

Fluid that comes out of one or both nipples is called nipple discharge. Each breast has 15 to 20 milk ducts. The discharge can come from one or more of these ducts.

(See also: Overview of Breast Disorders.)

Nipple discharge can happen normally in the last weeks of pregnancy and after childbirth. This is because the body makes breast milk. Discharge can also happen in women who are not pregnant or breastfeeding, especially during their childbearing years. This can happen if the nipples are touched or rubbed. But in men, any nipple discharge is always a sign of a problem.

A normal discharge is usually thin, cloudy, whitish, or almost clear. It can also be gray, green, yellow, or brown. A discharge that is bloody is not normal.

Abnormal discharges can look different depending on the cause. They may come with other signs, such as:
- Skin that looks dimpled
- Swelling
- Redness
- Crusting
- Sores
- A nipple that pulls inward and does not come back out when touched

If fluid comes from only one breast without any touching or squeezing, it is not normal.

## What Can Cause Nipple Discharge?

Many different conditions can cause nipple discharge.

If the discharge comes from one milk duct or one breast, it is likely due to a problem in that breast. This could be a noncancerous (benign) tumor. It could also be cancer, but this is less common.

If the discharge comes from both breasts or from several ducts in one breast, it is more likely due to a problem outside the breast. This could be a hormone imbalance or a side effect of certain medicines.

Most of the time, the cause is a noncancerous condition in the milk ducts. These include:

- A small, noncancerous tumor in a milk duct (called an intraductal papilloma)
- Milk ducts that are wider than normal (called mammary duct ectasia)
- Fibrocystic changes (this means breast pain, fluid-filled sacs, and lumpy breasts)
- A breast infection or abscess

An intraductal papilloma is the most common cause of nipple discharge. It is also the most common cause of a bloody discharge when there is no lump in the breast.

Some conditions cause breast milk to be made even when a woman is not pregnant or breastfeeding. These conditions often raise the level of a hormone called prolactin. Some medicines can also raise prolactin levels and cause discharge.

Cancer causes less than 10% of all cases.

## When to See a Doctor

You should see a doctor if your nipple discharge:
- Comes with a lump you can feel
- Is bloody or pink
- Comes from only one breast
- Happens without touching or squeezing the nipple (this is called spontaneous discharge)
- Happens in women aged 40 or older
- Happens in a boy or man

If the discharge lasts more than one menstrual cycle, or if any of these warning signs are present, see a doctor. Waiting a week or two is usually safe unless you have signs of infection. These signs include redness, swelling, or pus. If you have these, see a doctor within 1 or 2 days.

## How Doctors Evaluate Nipple Discharge

Doctors start by asking questions about your symptoms and medical history. Then they do a physical exam of your breasts.

What they find during the exam often helps point to the cause. They may also order tests.

They will ask:
- Does the discharge come from one breast or both?
- What color is the discharge?
- How long has it been happening?
- Does it happen only when you touch the nipple, or does it happen on its own?
- Do you have a lump or breast pain?
- Have you had any health problems that raise prolactin levels?
- Are you taking any medicines that could cause this?

During the exam, the doctor checks for lumps. If the discharge does not come on its own, they gently press around the nipple to see if it appears.

They also check the lymph nodes in your armpits and above your collarbone for swelling.

### Common Causes and Their Features

| Cause | Typical Signs | Tests Needed |
|------|----------------|--------------|
| **Intraductal papilloma** (noncancerous tumor in a milk duct) | Bloody or pink discharge from one breast | Ultrasound. May need mammogram, MRI, or ductogram. Biopsy if cancer is still possible. |
| **Mammary duct ectasia** (widened milk ducts) | Bloody, pink, or colored discharge (gray, milky, or thick) from one or both breasts | Same as for intraductal papilloma |
| **Fibrocystic changes** (lumpy, painful breasts) | A rubbery, tender lump (often before menopause). May have pale yellow, green, or white discharge. History of breast lumps | Same as for intraductal papilloma |
| **Breast infection or abscess** | Sudden pain, redness, warmth, swelling. May have fever. A tender lump and foul-smelling pus | Breast exam. If no improvement, testing like for intraductal papilloma |
| **Breast cancer** | Nipple discharge (often bloody or pink). May have a lump, skin changes, or swollen lymph nodes | Same as for intraductal papilloma |
| **High prolactin levels** (hormone that causes milk production) | Milky discharge (not bloody), usually from both breasts. No lumps. May have missed periods or irregular periods | Blood tests for prolactin and thyroid-stimulating hormone. Review of medicines. If levels are high, brain MRI |
| **Hypothyroidism** (underactive thyroid) | Feeling cold, tired, constipated, or gaining weight | Blood tests. Review of medicines. If needed, brain MRI |
| **Pituitary or brain problems** | Hormone issues, vision changes, headaches, or infertility | Blood tests. Brain MRI if needed |
| **Kidney or liver disease** | Swelling in the belly (ascites), yellow skin (jaundice) | Blood tests. Review of medicines. Brain MRI if needed |
| **Certain medicines** | Includes opioids, birth control pills, some stomach medicines (like cimetidine, metoclopramide), some antidepressants, and some blood pressure medicines | Blood tests. Review of medicines. Brain MRI if needed |

> **Note:** Ranitidine (a medicine for stomach issues) has been removed from the market in the U.S. and many other countries. It was taken off because it contained a substance that may cause cancer.

> **MRI** = magnetic resonance imaging.  
> **CT** = computed tomography.  
> **Cytology** = looking at fluid under a microscope for cancer cells.

If doctors think a hormone problem is the cause, they do blood tests to check prolactin and thyroid-stimulating hormone levels.

If a brain or pituitary problem is suspected, they may do an MRI or CT scan of the head.

If the discharge is not clearly bloody, they test it to see if it has any blood. If blood is found, they examine the fluid under a microscope to check for cancer cells.

If you can feel a lump, they do an ultrasound or mammogram. The testing is the same as for any breast lump.

If a cyst (fluid-filled sac) is found, they drain it. The fluid is tested. If it is bloody, it is checked for cancer cells.

If the lump is solid, they do a mammogram, then a biopsy.

If no lump is felt but cancer is still a concern, or if test results are unclear, they do a mammogram.

If ultrasound, mammogram, or aspiration (draining fluid) show abnormal results, a biopsy is done.

If no cause is found with ultrasound or mammogram, and the discharge comes from one duct and happens on its own, doctors may do a special X-ray called a ductogram. They inject a contrast dye into the duct and take X-rays. This helps find or rule out cancer.

If no lump is felt and the mammogram is normal, cancer is very unlikely.

Sometimes, even after all tests, the cause is not found.

## When to See a Doctor

See a doctor who specializes in breast health if you have:
- A lump in your breast
- A bloody or pink discharge
- A spontaneous discharge from one breast
- A past abnormal result from a mammogram or ultrasound

## Treatment

If a cause is found, it is treated.

If a noncancerous tumor or condition is causing the discharge from one breast, the doctor may remove the milk duct that is leaking. This is a minor surgery. It uses local anesthesia and does not require staying in the hospital overnight.

## Key Points

- Most nipple discharges are not caused by cancer.
- If the discharge comes from both breasts or many ducts and is not bloody, it is usually due to a noncancerous hormone problem.
- If the discharge comes from only one breast and is bloody or pink, cancer is possible — especially in women aged 40 or older.
- The tests you need — blood tests, imaging, or both — depend on what the doctor suspects is the cause.

# PAPA Syndrome

PAPA syndrome is a rare condition that affects the skin and joints.  
It runs in families and can be passed from parent to child.  

## What Causes PAPA Syndrome?

A change in a gene called *PSTPIP1* causes PAPA syndrome.  
This gene is on chromosome 15.  
The changed gene makes a protein that does not work properly.  
This faulty protein sticks too tightly to another protein called pyrin.  
When pyrin is stuck, it cannot calm down inflammation in the body.  
This leads to too much activity in immune cells called neutrophils.  
These cells cause swelling and damage in joints and skin.  

Some people with this gene change have similar but slightly different symptoms.  
These include:  
- PAPASH: skin sores, acne, swollen glands, and joint pain  
- PASH: skin sores, acne, and swollen glands, but no joint pain  

## Symptoms of PAPA Syndrome

Joint pain usually starts before age 10.  
The joint pain can get worse over time.  
Even small injuries, like a bump or fall, can trigger joint pain.  
The joint pain may go away by the time a person reaches puberty.  

Skin sores are common.  
They often appear where the skin has been hurt, like at a vaccination site.  
The sores have a deep hole in the middle.  
The edges of the sore look like they are curling under.  
The sores do not heal well and can leave scars.  

Acne is also common.  
It shows up as large, deep pimples.  
If not treated, the acne can cause permanent scars.  

## How Is PAPA Syndrome Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your symptoms and family history.  
They may take a small sample of skin from a sore to check it.  
The skin sample will show signs of inflammation and many white blood cells.  
A blood test can check for changes in the *PSTPIP1* gene.  
This test can help confirm the diagnosis.  

## How Is PAPA Syndrome Treated?

Medicines that reduce inflammation can help.  
These include:  
- Etanercept  
- Adalimumab  
- Infliximab  

These medicines block a substance called tumor necrosis factor.  
Another medicine called anakinra may also help.  

For acne:  
- Oral tetracycline is a common treatment.  
- Isotretinoin is used if the acne is severe.  

These medicines can help clear the skin and prevent scarring.  

Early treatment can reduce pain, prevent joint damage, and improve skin health.

# Whipple Disease

Whipple disease is a rare illness caused by a bacterial infection.  
The bacteria damage the small intestine, which stops it from absorbing nutrients properly.  
This problem is called malabsorption.  
The infection can also spread to other parts of the body.

## Who Gets Whipple Disease?

Whipple disease is rare in the United States.  
It mostly affects white people over age thirty.  
It is more common in people over age sixty.  
In some parts of the world, the disease is more common.

## What Causes Whipple Disease?

The disease is caused by a bacteria called *Tropheryma whipplei*.  
This bacteria usually starts in the small intestine.  
But it can also spread to other organs, such as the heart, lungs, brain, joints, and eyes.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The four main symptoms are:

- Painful and swollen joints  
- Diarrhea  
- Belly pain  
- Losing weight without trying  

Other common symptoms include:

- Fever  
- Not feeling hungry  
- Feeling tired and weak  
- Coughing  
- Pain when breathing  
- Fluid building up in the space around the lungs (called pleural effusion)  
- Swollen lymph nodes  

Some people notice their skin gets darker.  
The heart can become infected.  
If the brain is affected, a person may feel confused, have memory problems, or have uncontrolled eye movements.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose Whipple disease by looking at tissue from the small intestine.  
They use a thin, flexible tube with a light and camera (called an endoscope) to take a small sample of tissue.  
This is called a biopsy.  
They may also take a sample from an enlarged lymph node.  
The tissue is then checked under a microscope to find the bacteria.

## How Is It Treated?

If not treated, Whipple disease gets worse over time and can be deadly.  
The disease can be cured with antibiotics.  

Treatment usually starts with strong antibiotics given through a vein.  
These include ceftriaxone or penicillin.  
This phase lasts two to four weeks.  

After that, the person takes antibiotics by mouth for at least twelve months.  
These may be sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim, or a mix of doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine.  

Symptoms often improve quickly after starting treatment.  
But even if the symptoms go away, the disease can come back.  
That is why long-term treatment is needed.

# Weakness

Weakness means you have less strength in your muscles.  
Many people use the word "weakness" when they feel tired or have trouble moving, even if their muscles are strong.  
True weakness means your muscles are not working as well as they should.

Weakness can affect just a few muscles or many muscles.  
It can start suddenly or get worse slowly over time.  
Other symptoms may appear depending on what is causing the weakness.  
For example, weakness in certain muscles can make it hard to move your eyes, speak clearly, swallow, or breathe.

---

## What Causes Weakness?

Your brain sends signals through nerves to your muscles to make them move.  
If any part of this system is damaged, weakness can happen.

The main places where problems can cause weakness are:

- The brain (upper motor neurons)
- The spinal cord (lower motor neurons)
- The nerves outside the spinal cord (peripheral nerves)
- The connection between nerves and muscles (neuromuscular junction)
- The muscles themselves

Each of these areas has different signs when it is not working right.

### Problems in the Brain (Upper Motor Neuron Issues)
- Muscles become stiff and tight (spasticity).
- Reflexes are too strong (hyperreflexia).
- The big toe points up when the foot is touched (Babinski reflex). This is a sign of brain or spinal cord damage.
- In some cases, muscles may be weak and floppy at first, especially after a sudden injury like a spinal cord cut.
- Weakness usually affects the arms in a way that makes it hard to straighten them, and the legs in a way that makes it hard to bend them.

### Problems in the Spinal Cord or Nerves (Lower Motor Neuron Issues)
- Muscles become soft and loose (flaccidity).
- Reflexes are weak or missing (hyporeflexia).
- Muscles may twitch (fasciculations).
- Over time, muscles shrink (atrophy).

### Problems in the Longest Nerves (Peripheral Polyneuropathies)
- Weakness is worse in the feet and hands than in the arms and legs.
- Reflexes are weak.
- Numbness or tingling often happens in the same areas (like gloves or socks).
- This pattern is common in diabetes, alcohol use, or nerve damage from medicines.

### Problems at the Nerve-Muscle Connection (Neuromuscular Junction)
- The most common problem here is **myasthenia gravis**.
- Weakness gets worse with activity and improves with rest.
- It often affects the eyes, face, throat, and breathing.

### Problems in the Muscles (Myopathies)
- Weakness is most noticeable in large muscles, like those in the hips and shoulders.
- This can happen with long-term illness, poor nutrition, or certain medicines.
- Some muscle diseases are inherited.

---

## What Can Cause Weakness?

### Focal Weakness (Affects One Side or One Area)
- **Stroke** – the most common cause of sudden weakness on one side of the body.
- **Nerve damage** from injury, pressure, or disease (like carpal tunnel or Bell’s palsy).
- **Herniated disk** in the spine pressing on a nerve.
- **Spinal cord compression** from arthritis, tumors, or injury.
- **Multiple sclerosis** – a disease that affects the brain and spinal cord.
- **Temporary weakness** can happen after a seizure (Todd’s paralysis), or from a brief lack of blood flow (transient ischemic attack).
- A rare cause is **periodic paralysis**, which is linked to changes in potassium levels.

### Generalized Weakness (Affects the Whole Body)
- **Not moving enough** – being sick or inactive can cause muscles to shrink.
- **Long time in the hospital** – especially in intensive care – can cause muscle and nerve damage.
- **Common muscle diseases** – like those from alcohol, low potassium, or steroid medicines.

---

## How Doctors Find the Cause

Doctors look at your symptoms and do a physical exam.  
They check for:

- Is it real muscle weakness or just tiredness?
- Where is the weakness?
- Are reflexes normal, too strong, or too weak?
- Are muscles stiff, floppy, or shrinking?
- Is there numbness or tingling?

Based on these findings, they can guess where the problem is.

### Tests That May Be Used
- **Brain and spine imaging** – like MRI or CT scans.
- **Nerve tests** – to check how well nerves send signals.
- **Blood tests** – to check for infections, vitamin levels, hormone problems, or toxins.
- **Spinal fluid test** – if an infection or autoimmune disease is suspected.
- **Muscle biopsy** – to look at muscle tissue under a microscope.
- **Genetic testing** – for inherited muscle or nerve diseases.

---

## How Is Weakness Treated?

- The cause of weakness is treated directly.
- If weakness is severe and affects breathing, a machine may be needed to help you breathe.
- Physical therapy and occupational therapy help people move better and stay independent, no matter what caused the weakness.

---

## Special Considerations for Older Adults

- It is normal to have slightly weaker reflexes as you age.
- But if one side is much weaker than the other, or reflexes are missing, this is not normal.
- Older adults lose muscle mass naturally (sarcopenia).
- Just a few days of not moving can cause serious muscle loss.
- Older adults take more medicines, and some medicines can cause muscle or nerve problems.
- Feeling too weak to walk can have many causes:
  - Muscle weakness (from stroke, medicine, spine issues, or inactivity)
  - Fluid in the brain (hydrocephalus)
  - Parkinson’s disease
  - Painful joints
  - Loss of balance or coordination from aging nerves, brain, or vision

Doctors should check for causes that can be fixed.  
Physical therapy helps most older adults, no matter what caused the weakness.

---

## Key Points

- Real muscle weakness is different from feeling tired.
- If you feel tired but your exam is normal, the cause might be chronic fatigue, anemia, low thyroid, depression, or a medicine side effect.
- If you have true weakness, doctors first check if the problem is in the brain, spinal cord, nerves, nerve-muscle connection, or muscles.
- Strong reflexes and stiff muscles suggest a brain or spinal cord problem. An MRI is usually needed.
- Weak reflexes, soft muscles, shrinking muscles, and twitching suggest a nerve or muscle problem.
- Weakness in the hands and feet with numbness suggests nerve damage.
- Trouble climbing stairs, standing up, or lifting arms suggests a muscle problem.
- Physical therapy helps improve strength and function in most cases.

# Hepatic Granulomas – Simple Explanation

Hepatic granulomas are small clumps of cells that form in the liver. They happen when the body’s immune system reacts to something it sees as a threat.

These clumps can form because of certain health problems or certain medicines.

## What Causes Hepatic Granulomas?

Granulomas form when immune cells gather in the liver. This can happen to fight an infection or react to a medicine.

Common causes include:

- Some medicines
- Infections that affect the whole body, such as tuberculosis or schistosomiasis
- Liver damage caused by medicines (drug-induced liver injury)
- Types of lymphoma, like Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin lymphoma
- Inflammatory diseases, such as sarcoidosis

Granulomas can also appear in some liver diseases, like primary biliary cholangitis, but this is less common.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most of the time, granulomas do not cause any symptoms.

The liver may become slightly larger. Some people may develop mild jaundice. Jaundice means the skin and the whites of the eyes turn yellow.

If symptoms do appear, they are usually due to the condition that caused the granulomas.

For example:
- Granulomas from sarcoidosis often go away on their own.
- They may stay for years without causing any problems.

**Idiopathic granulomatous hepatitis** is a rare condition with no known cause. It causes:
- Granulomas in the liver
- Fever
- Muscle aches
- Tiredness

These symptoms may come and go over many years.

## How Are Granulomas Diagnosed?

Doctors will ask about:
- Medicines you are taking
- Illegal drug use
- Other health problems that could cause granulomas

They will do blood tests to check how well the liver is working.

They may also use imaging tests, such as:
- Ultrasound
- CT scan
- MRI

These tests can show if there are clumps in the liver. But they may not give a clear answer.

If needed, doctors may do a **liver biopsy**. This means they take a tiny sample of liver tissue with a needle. They then look at it under a microscope to confirm the diagnosis.

Other tests, like cultures, may be done to find the exact cause.

## How Are Granulomas Treated?

The main goal is to treat the underlying cause.

- If a medicine is causing the problem, stopping it often makes the granulomas go away.
- If an infection is the cause, treating the infection usually clears the granulomas.

For sarcoidosis, doctors may use corticosteroids. But it is not clear if these medicines stop the disease from getting worse.

# Sympathetic Ophthalmia

This is a rare eye condition. It causes swelling and inflammation in the middle layer of the eye. It can happen after an eye injury or eye surgery.

The condition is very rare. It happens in about 2 to 5 out of every 1,000 people who have a serious eye wound. It also happens in about 1 out of every 1,000 people after eye surgery.

The body’s immune system may attack the eye by mistake. This happens because the immune system sees parts of the eye as foreign. This is the same kind of reaction seen in another eye disease called Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease.

Symptoms usually start 2 to 12 weeks after the injury or surgery. But in some cases, symptoms can appear as early as 1 week or as late as 30 years later.

Symptoms can affect any part of the eye. Common signs include:
- Seeing floaters (small dark spots or lines in your vision)
- Blurry or weak vision

Other common problems include:
- Fluid building up under the retina
- Swelling in the layer behind the retina (choroid)

Doctors diagnose this condition by looking at your eye and reviewing your symptoms. They do not rely on lab tests or scans.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment usually starts with oral corticosteroids. These are pills that reduce swelling and inflammation. A common example is prednisone. The usual dose is 1 milligram per kilogram of body weight, taken once a day.

After the swelling goes down, you will likely need to take another medicine for a long time. This second medicine helps control the immune system. It is not a steroid.

In some serious cases, doctors may suggest removing the injured eye. This is called enucleation. It should be considered only if:
- The injured eye has no chance of regaining vision
- The surgery is done within 2 weeks of losing vision

Removing the injured eye can lower the risk of the other eye becoming inflamed. This is only done when the injured eye cannot be saved.

# Bone Density Problems in Children

Bone density problems affect how strong and dense a child’s bones are. Weak bones break easily. They can also grow in unusual ways.

- These problems happen when the body does not recycle old bone cells properly.
- Common signs include bones that do not grow right and bones that break easily.
- Doctors check for these problems using symptoms, x-rays, and sometimes blood tests.
- Treatments like medicine and surgery can help with some of the issues.

Bone density measures how much mineral is in the bone. Bones that are too hard or too soft are more likely to break.

Some bone density problems come from faulty genes. These genes can be passed from parent to child. Other causes include poor diet, hormone problems, or other health conditions.

Bone density problems are split into two types: low bone density and high bone density.

(See also: Overview of Bone Disorders in Children.)

---

## Low Bone Density in Children

Children’s bones are always growing and changing. Old bone is removed and new bone is made. This keeps bones strong.

In children with low bone density, this balance is broken. It can be due to a specific cause or because the child is not moving much. The result is less bone mass and weaker bones.

Weaker bones become thinner and more likely to break. This can happen in the spine or in long bones like the arms and legs. These problems can slow down growth, make movement hard, and affect overall development.

The main low bone density problems in children are:
- Osteogenesis imperfecta
- Osteoporosis
- Rickets

Causes of low bone density include:
- Poor diet
- Low vitamin D levels
- Faulty genes
- Low levels of hormones like growth hormone, estrogen, or testosterone
- Health issues like celiac disease or chronic kidney disease
- Some medicines, such as steroids

To check for low bone density, doctors use a test called a DXA scan. This scan uses two types of x-rays on the spine and hip. These are the areas most likely to break.

The scan compares the child’s bone density to that of a healthy child of the same age, sex, and size. The result is called a Z-score. A lower Z-score means weaker bones. A score of –2.0 or lower means the child has low bone density.

Doctors treat the root cause when possible. Lifestyle changes and medicine can also help.

---

## High Bone Density in Children (Osteopetroses)

High bone density problems are called osteopetroses. These are rare and inherited. They happen because of faulty genes.

Bones are made of cells that grow, live, and then get removed. This is a natural recycling process. In osteopetrosis, the body does not remove old bone cells. This causes bones to become too thick and dense.

Even though the bones are dense, they are actually weak and brittle. The shape of the bones can also change. The dense bone takes up space inside the bone. This leaves less room for bone marrow, where blood cells are made.

When bone marrow is crowded, the body may not make enough blood cells. This can lead to anemia (low red blood cells) and low platelets (which help stop bleeding). The spleen may also become overactive and destroy too many red blood cells.

Osteopetroses can be mild or very serious. Some children show signs at birth (early onset). Others may not have symptoms until later in life (delayed onset).

Most types of osteopetroses cause similar problems:
- Bones grow poorly
- Bones become thick but break easily
- Blood cell production drops, leading to infection or bleeding
- Bleeding often happens after small injuries, like nosebleeds from picking the nose or bleeding gums from brushing teeth

Extra bone in the skull can cause pressure inside the head. This can press on nerves. It may lead to facial weakness, vision loss, or hearing loss. It can also change the shape of the face and teeth.

Bones in the fingers, feet, arms, legs, spine, and pelvis can be affected.

### How Doctors Diagnose Osteopetrosis

Doctors use:
- X-rays
- Blood tests
- Genetic tests

X-rays show bones that are very dense or oddly shaped. Sometimes, doctors find osteopetrosis by accident when taking x-rays for another reason.

Blood tests can show:
- Low red blood cells (anemia)
- Low platelets (thrombocytopenia)

Genetic tests help confirm the diagnosis by finding the faulty genes that affect bone cell function.

### How Doctors Treat Osteopetrosis

Treatments include:
- Steroids (like prednisone)
- Stem cell transplantation
- Surgery

Steroids help reduce the formation of new bone cells. They also help remove old bone cells. This can make bones stronger. Steroids may also ease bone pain and improve muscle strength.

Stem cell transplantation can cure some babies with early-onset osteopetrosis. But it does not fix kidney problems that may already be present.

If nerves in the skull are pressed, surgery may be needed to relieve pressure. Surgery may also be used to reduce pressure inside the skull. Plastic surgery can fix serious face or jaw shape problems.

Orthodontic care may be needed to fix crooked teeth.

Minor fractures are treated with a cast or a traction device. Major fractures (where bones are broken apart or need to stay still) may need surgery.

Anemia and low platelets are treated with blood transfusions.

In rare cases, if the spleen is overactive, removing it can help with both anemia and bleeding.

Infections are treated with antibiotics.

Without treatment, early-onset osteopetrosis is often fatal in infancy or early childhood. Death usually comes from anemia, infection, or severe bleeding.

Late-onset osteopetrosis is usually mild and does not cause serious problems.

# Low Blood Sugar in Newborn Babies

Low blood sugar in newborns is called neonatal hypoglycemia. It happens when a baby’s blood sugar drops too low. This can be dangerous if not treated quickly.

## What Is Low Blood Sugar?

Doctors define low blood sugar differently depending on the baby.  
- For a full-term baby who shows symptoms, it is below 40 milligrams per deciliter.  
- For a full-term baby without symptoms, it is below 45 milligrams per deciliter.  
- For a premature baby in the first two days, it is below 30 milligrams per deciliter.

## Who Is at Risk?

Some babies are more likely to have low blood sugar. These include:  
- Babies born too early (premature).  
- Babies who are smaller than expected for their due date.  
- Babies whose mothers had diabetes during pregnancy.  
- Babies who had trouble getting enough oxygen around birth.

## Why Does It Happen?

The most common reasons are:  
- The baby’s body does not have enough stored sugar (glycogen).  
- The baby does not start feeding soon enough.  
- The baby makes too much insulin, which lowers blood sugar.

## What Are the Signs?

Many babies do not show any signs.  
But if blood sugar stays low for too long, the baby may show:  
- Fast heartbeat.  
- Blue color in the lips or skin.  
- Seizures.  
- Pauses in breathing.  
- Weakness or extreme tiredness.  
- Poor feeding.  
- Low body temperature.  
- Fast breathing.  
- Low muscle tone.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect low blood sugar based on symptoms.  
But they must check the baby’s blood sugar to be sure.  
A quick test is done using a drop of blood from the baby’s heel.  
If the result is low, a second test using blood from a vein confirms it.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on how low the blood sugar is and how sick the baby is.

### Early Feeding
Most babies with risk factors should start feeding early and often.  
This gives them sugar from milk or formula.  
This helps prevent low blood sugar.

### IV Glucose
If the baby’s blood sugar is very low, they may need glucose through a vein.  
A special sugar solution (dextrose) is given slowly through a needle in the vein.  
The amount and speed of the drip are adjusted based on blood sugar checks.

### Glucagon Shot
If it is hard to start an IV, a shot of glucagon can raise blood sugar fast.  
This works for 2 to 3 hours.  
But it does not work well if the baby has no stored sugar.

### Steroid Medicine
If the baby does not respond to high levels of glucose, a steroid medicine may help.  
It is given through the IV every 6 hours.

### Check for Other Problems
If the low blood sugar does not get better, doctors look for other causes.  
These may include infection, hormone problems, or rare genetic conditions.

## What Is the Outlook?

The baby’s long-term health depends on the cause of the low blood sugar.  
Most babies recover fully if treated early.

## Key Points

- Premature or small babies often have low sugar stores.  
  They need to be fed early and often to stay healthy.

- Babies of mothers with diabetes are born with extra insulin.  
  This can cause low blood sugar after birth, when the mother’s sugar is no longer available.

- Signs of low blood sugar include sweating, fast heartbeat, tiredness, poor feeding, low body temperature, seizures, or coma.

- Preventive treatment is given to:  
  - Babies of mothers with diabetes.  
  - Extremely premature babies.  
  - Babies with breathing problems.

- If blood sugar drops to 50 milligrams per deciliter or lower:  
  - Start feeding by mouth right away.  
  - Or give a sugar solution through the IV.  
  - Give 2 milliliters of 10% to 12.5% sugar solution per kilogram of body weight over 10 minutes.  
  - Then keep giving more sugar through the IV or by feeding.  
  - Check blood sugar often to adjust the treatment.

- Always reduce the IV sugar slowly.  
  Stopping it suddenly can cause blood sugar to drop again.

# Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO)

SIBO happens when there are too many bacteria in the small intestine.  
This can cause problems with absorbing nutrients.  
It can lead to low levels of vitamins, poor fat absorption, and weight loss.

SIBO is a type of malabsorption disorder.  
This means your body cannot take in enough nutrients from food.

Normally, the small intestine has very few bacteria.  
The number is less than 100,000 bacteria per milliliter.  
Most of these are harmless types of bacteria.

Your body keeps this number low with help from:  
- Normal movement of food through the gut  
- Stomach acid  
- Mucus in the gut  
- A special immune protein in the gut  
- A healthy valve between the small and large intestine

## What Causes SIBO?

**Changes in the shape of the gut** can cause food to get stuck.  
This gives bacteria time to grow too much.  
Conditions that cause this include:  
- Diverticulosis (small pouches in the small intestine)  
- Surgery that creates a "blind loop" (a section of intestine that food cannot pass through)  
- After stomach surgery, especially Billroth II  
- Narrowing of the intestine (strictures)  
- Partial blockage of the intestine

### What Is Billroth II Surgery?

This surgery removes part of the stomach.  
It connects the remaining stomach to the small intestine.  
There are two parts to the small intestine after this surgery:  
- The afferent limb: the part that gets bile and pancreatic juice from the liver and pancreas  
- The efferent limb: the part that gets food from the stomach

**Problems with gut movement** can also cause SIBO.  
This happens in people with:  
- Nerve damage from diabetes  
- Systemic sclerosis (a condition that makes tissues stiff)  
- Amyloidosis (a rare disease where abnormal proteins build up)  
- Low thyroid function  
- A condition called intestinal pseudo-obstruction (the gut acts like it is blocked, even when it is not)

Some older adults develop SIBO due to low stomach acid or unknown causes of poor gut movement.

## How SIBO Works in the Body

The most common bacteria in SIBO are:  
- Streptococci  
- Bacteroides  
- Escherichia  
- Lactobacillus  
- Klebsiella  
- Aeromonas

These extra bacteria eat your food.  
They take in carbohydrates and vitamin B12.  
This can lead to low energy and vitamin B12 deficiency.  
But they also make folate, so folate deficiency is rare.

The bacteria break down bile salts.  
Bile helps your body absorb fat.  
When bile is broken down, fat cannot be absorbed.  
This causes fat in the stool (called steatorrhea).

Severe overgrowth can also damage the lining of the intestine.  
This damage can cause diarrhea.

## Symptoms of SIBO

The most common symptom is bloating.  
Other symptoms include:  
- Belly pain or discomfort  
- Diarrhea  
- Passing more gas than usual  
Some people have severe diarrhea or fatty, oily stools.

## How Is SIBO Diagnosed?

Doctors use several methods to diagnose SIBO:

### Breath Tests
- A glucose-hydrogen breath test or a lactulose-hydrogen breath test is often used.  
- You drink a special liquid and breathe into a tube over time.  
- The test checks for hydrogen or methane gas in your breath.  
- These gases come from bacteria in the small intestine.

Before the test:  
- Do not take antibiotics for 4 weeks.  
- Do not take medicines that speed up gut movement or laxatives for at least 1 week.

A positive test means:  
- Hydrogen goes up by more than 20 parts per million in the first 90 minutes  
- Or methane goes up by more than 10 parts per million at any time

### Intestinal Fluid Culture
- This is the most accurate test.  
- A doctor uses a scope to take a sample of fluid from the small intestine.  
- The sample is tested for bacteria.  
- A count of more than 1,000 bacteria per milliliter means SIBO.

This test needs an endoscopy.

### Imaging Tests
- If surgery is not the cause, imaging tests can help find structural problems.  
- These include:  
  - Upper GI series with small-bowel follow-through  
  - CT enterography  
  - Magnetic resonance enterography

Some doctors use a trial of antibiotics to help diagnose SIBO.  
But this is not the best way.  
Bacteria overgrowth can look like other gut diseases.  
Also, antibiotics can make diarrhea worse.

## How Is SIBO Treated?

### Antibiotics
- Treatment usually lasts 10 to 14 days.  
- The antibiotics must work against both aerobic and anaerobic bacteria.  
- Common choices include:  
  - Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid  
  - Cephalexin  
  - Sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim  
  - Metronidazole  
  - Rifaximin alone, or with neomycin  
    - Neomycin is added if methane is found in the breath test  
  - Ciprofloxacin

If symptoms come back, treatment may be repeated in cycles.  
The antibiotic may be changed based on lab results.  
But changing antibiotics can be hard because many types of bacteria are present.

### Diet Changes
- Bacteria mainly eat carbohydrates.  
- A diet high in fat and low in carbohydrates and fiber can help.  
- This limits food for the bacteria.

### Fix Underlying Problems
- Treat any condition that caused SIBO.  
- Correct vitamin deficiencies, especially vitamin B12.

## Key Points

- Changes in gut shape or poor gut movement can cause food to stay in the small intestine.  
  This lets bacteria grow too much.  
- Bacteria break down bile, which stops fat from being absorbed.  
- Diagnosis uses breath tests or a sample of fluid from the small intestine.  
- Treatment includes antibiotics and a high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet.

# Garlic

Garlic is a plant used in cooking and for health purposes.  
When you cut or crush a garlic clove, a substance called allicin forms.  
Allicin gives garlic its strong smell and is linked to its health benefits.

The active parts of garlic break down when the garlic is crushed.  
This means different garlic products have different amounts of active ingredients.  
Aged garlic extract, made from garlic that has aged for at least 20 months, keeps its active ingredients more stable.  
Taking aged garlic extract may give the most health benefits and cause fewer side effects.

## What People Say Garlic Can Do

Garlic may help reduce how easily blood clots form.  
It can stop some bacteria and other tiny germs from growing.  
Some people believe garlic can:

- Lower bad cholesterol (LDL)
- Reduce the risk of certain cancers, especially in the stomach and intestines
- Lower blood sugar levels
- Help prevent the common cold
- Help treat fatty liver disease that is not caused by alcohol

## What Science Says About Garlic

The strongest proof is that aged garlic extract can slightly lower blood pressure.  
This effect is seen with higher doses.

Garlic’s effect on cholesterol is mixed.  
But a 2013 review of many studies found that garlic lowers total cholesterol and bad cholesterol (LDL).  
This drop may help reduce the risk of heart attacks and other heart problems.

A 2023 review of 12 studies found garlic may improve good cholesterol (HDL) and slow down hardening of the arteries.

There is little or no strong evidence that garlic prevents cancer.

A review of 7 studies found garlic may help lower blood sugar when the body is fasting (not eating).

Most studies used aged garlic extract.  
Some garlic products made to have no smell may not be active.  
More research is needed on these products.

## Side Effects of Garlic

Garlic usually does not cause serious harm.  
But it can make your breath, body odor, and breast milk smell like garlic.  
Eating too much garlic can cause nausea and a burning feeling in the mouth, throat, or stomach.

## Drug Interactions with Garlic

Small amounts of garlic in food are unlikely to cause problems.  
But large amounts in supplements may interact with certain medicines.

Garlic may increase the risk of bleeding if you take blood-thinning medicines like warfarin.  
Do not use garlic supplements or eat large amounts of garlic for two weeks before surgery or a dental procedure.

Garlic may reduce how well some HIV medicines work, such as saquinavir.  
It may also make blood sugar-lowering medicines too strong, leading to low blood sugar.

Garlic can add to the effects of blood pressure medicines.  
This may lower blood pressure too much.

Garlic may raise levels of tacrolimus, a medicine used after organ transplants.  
This can lead to liver damage.  
Animal studies show garlic may lower levels of isoniazid, a medicine used to treat tuberculosis.

## When to Talk to Your Doctor

Garlic may help lower blood pressure, bad cholesterol, and blood sugar.  
This may reduce the risk of heart problems.

Garlic is generally safe.  
But talk to your doctor before taking garlic supplements if you:

- Have diabetes
- Have HIV
- Take blood thinners
- Take blood pressure medicines
- Take medicines to prevent organ transplant rejection
- Take medicines for diseases like tuberculosis

# Fascioliasis – Simple Explanation

Fascioliasis is an infection caused by flatworms called liver flukes.  
The two main types are *Fasciola hepatica* and *Fasciola gigantica*.  
These worms live in the liver and bile ducts of animals like sheep and cattle.  
People can get infected by eating watercress or other plants that grow in water and are dirty with animal waste.

## How People Get Infected

- The worms start in the dung of infected animals like sheep or cattle.  
- Tiny snails eat the worm eggs in the dung.  
- The worms grow inside the snails.  
- Then they leave the snails and attach to plants like watercress.  
- If a person eats these plants without washing them well, the worms can enter the body.  
- This kind of infection is rare in the United States.  
- It is more common in parts of Europe, the Middle East, Africa, China, and South America.

## What the Worms Do in the Body

- After eating contaminated plants, the worms travel through the stomach and intestines.  
- They move through the belly wall and into the liver.  
- They grow and move around in the liver for about 3 to 4 months.  
- Then they go into the bile ducts and become adult worms.  
- The adult worms lay eggs.  
- The eggs pass into the intestines and come out in the stool.

## Symptoms of Fascioliasis

### Early Stage (Acute Infection)

- Belly pain  
- Swollen liver  
- Nausea and vomiting  
- Fever that comes and goes  
- Itchy skin rash (hives)  
- Feeling tired and weak  
- Losing weight  
- High number of a certain type of white blood cell (eosinophilia) – this is common

### Later Stage (Chronic Infection)

- Some people have no symptoms at all.  
- Others may have belly pain that comes and goes.  
- The infection can cause gallstones (cholelithiasis).  
- It can lead to infection in the bile ducts (cholangitis).  
- It can block the flow of bile, causing yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice).  
- It can cause inflammation of the pancreas (pancreatitis).  
- This stage usually starts 6 months after infection and can last 10 years or more.

### Severe Cases

- Heavy infections can cause scarring in the bile ducts (sclerosing cholangitis).  
- They can also cause liver scarring (biliary cirrhosis).  
- The worms can sometimes travel to other parts of the body, like the intestines or lungs.

### Rare Case: Halzoun

- In some parts of the Middle East, people get sick after eating raw liver from infected animals.  
- This is called halzoun.  
- It causes sore throat, swelling in the throat, trouble swallowing, and trouble breathing.  
- The exact cause is not fully known. Other germs may also be involved.

## How Doctors Diagnose Fascioliasis

Doctors look for signs and symptoms and ask about your diet and travel history.

### Tests Used

- **Stool test**: Look for worm eggs in the stool.  
- **Duodenal aspirate**: A sample taken from the small intestine during a test called endoscopy.  
- **Bile test**: A sample taken from the bile ducts during endoscopy.  
- **Blood test (serology)**: Checks for antibodies to the worm. This is very helpful early in infection, before eggs appear.  
- **Imaging tests**: Ultrasound, CT scan, MRI, or ERCP (a special X-ray of the bile and pancreatic ducts) can show problems in the liver and bile ducts.

### Important Notes About Testing

- Worm eggs are hard to see in the stool, especially in *F. gigantica* infections.  
- Blood tests can find the infection even when eggs are not in the stool.  
- Blood tests are useful in early infection (before eggs are made) and in long-term infections (when eggs are rare).  
- After treatment, antibodies go away in 6 to 12 months.  
- In some places, eating infected animal liver can cause false positive results.  
- To avoid this, people should not eat liver for several days before a stool test.

## How Fascioliasis Is Treated

### First Choice Treatment

- **Triclabendazole** is the best medicine.  
- It is taken as two doses, 12 hours apart.  
- It must be taken with food.  
- It works well in people 6 years and older.

### Alternative Treatment

- **Nitazoxanide** may help.  
- It is taken twice a day for 7 days.  
- But there is not much strong evidence yet.

### What Not to Use

- **Praziquantel** does not work well for this infection.  
- It is not recommended.

### Special Cases

- In some people, doctors may use a procedure called ERCP to remove adult worms from the bile ducts.  
- This can help reduce symptoms and worm numbers.

## How to Prevent Fascioliasis

- Do not eat watercress or other freshwater plants unless you are sure they are clean.  
- Wash all plants well before eating.  
- Avoid eating raw liver from animals in areas where the worm is common.  
- If someone in your family has this infection, others should be checked too.

## Summary

- Fascioliasis is caused by eating dirty water plants.  
- It can cause belly pain, liver problems, and other symptoms.  
- Diagnosis uses stool tests, blood tests, and imaging.  
- Triclabendazole is the best treatment.  
- Prevention means avoiding raw or unwashed plants from risky areas.

# Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10)

Coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, is a substance your body makes naturally.  
It helps your cells make energy.  
It also acts as an antioxidant.  
Antioxidants help protect your cells from damage.

Free radicals are harmful by-products of normal cell activity.  
They can harm your cells over time.  
CoQ10 helps reduce this damage.

People who are older or have long-term health problems may have lower levels of CoQ10.  
These health problems include heart disease, cancer, Parkinson disease, diabetes, HIV, and muscle disorders.  
But we do not know if low CoQ10 levels cause these conditions.

You can get CoQ10 from food.  
Good sources include meat, fish, and vegetable oils.  
A man-made version of CoQ10 is also available as a dietary supplement.

---

## What People Say About CoQ10

Some people believe CoQ10 helps with:

- Skin appearance  
- Exercise performance  
- Fertility  
- Brain and lung health  
- Migraine headaches  

It is also said to help people with:

- Diabetes  
- Heart failure  
- Nerve diseases like Parkinson disease  

CoQ10 may also protect the heart from damage caused by certain cancer drugs.  
These drugs include doxorubicin and daunorubicin.  
Some people also say CoQ10 helps reduce muscle pain from statin drugs.  
Statin drugs are used to lower cholesterol.

---

## What the Research Shows

Scientists have studied CoQ10 because people with some diseases have low levels.  
They want to know if taking CoQ10 supplements helps.

The results are not clear.  
Some early studies suggest CoQ10 may help, but more research is needed.

A 2014 review of 7 studies found no strong evidence for or against CoQ10 for heart failure.  
A 2017 review of 14 studies found that people taking CoQ10 could exercise more and lived longer than those on a placebo.  
A 2022 study found some improvement in symptoms for people with certain types of heart failure.

CoQ10 may help protect the heart from damage caused by doxorubicin and daunorubicin.  
This has been seen in several studies.

CoQ10 has also been studied for muscle problems like soreness, cramps, and weakness.  
This includes muscle issues caused by statin drugs.  
But we do not yet know if it works well for these problems.

---

## Side Effects of CoQ10

Side effects are rare.  
But some people have reported:

- Stomach pain  
- Nausea  
- Heartburn  
- Diarrhea  
- Vomiting  
- Dizziness  
- Light sensitivity  
- Irritability  
- Headache  
- Itchy skin  
- Rash  
- Loss of appetite  
- Tiredness  
- Flu-like symptoms

If you have any of these, stop taking CoQ10 and talk to your doctor.

---

## Drug Interactions

CoQ10 may interact with some medicines.  
This includes:

- Blood pressure medicines  
- Certain chemotherapy drugs  

CoQ10 may reduce how well warfarin works.  
Warfarin is a blood thinner.  
If you take warfarin, CoQ10 could increase your risk of blood clots.  
Always talk to your doctor before starting CoQ10 if you take warfarin.

---

## Recommendations

CoQ10 may help protect the heart from damage caused by certain cancer drugs.  
It may also help people with heart disease.  
It appears to be safe for most people.

If you take warfarin, talk to your doctor before using CoQ10.

---

# Religion and Spirituality in Older Adults

## What Is Religion and Spirituality?

Religion and spirituality are similar but not the same.  
Religion is often tied to a specific group or church.  
It has rules, routines, and regular activities like going to services.  
Spirituality is about personal feelings and thoughts.  
It is about finding meaning, purpose, or connection to something greater.  
Spirituality does not need to be part of a group or organized religion.  
It can include thoughts about the soul or a search for what is sacred.

Religion often includes rules and responsibilities.  
Spirituality has fewer rules.  
Some people do not follow any religion but still feel spiritual.  

In the United States, 18 out of every 100 adults aged 65 and older do not belong to any religion.  
But 27 out of every 100 adults overall do not belong to any religion.  

Most studies focus on religion, not spirituality.  
These studies look at things like:  
- How often people go to religious services  
- How often people pray or read religious texts  
- How people use religion to cope with hard times  
- How deeply people believe in their faith  

For most older adults in the United States, religion plays a big part in daily life.  
About half of older adults go to religious services at least once a week.  

Older adults are more likely to take part in religious activities than any other age group.  
For many older adults, their religious community is the biggest source of support outside their family.  
Being part of a religious group is the most common way older adults take part in volunteer work.  
This is more common than all other types of volunteer work combined.

## How Religion and Spirituality Can Help

Religion is linked to better physical and mental health.  
Some people believe that God helps make them healthier.  
But experts do not know if religion causes better health.  
Or if healthier people are just more likely to join religious groups.  

If religion helps, it may be because of:  
- Feeling better emotionally  
- Being encouraged to live a healthy lifestyle  
- Getting support from others in the religious group  

These benefits are real and important.

## When Religion and Spirituality Can Cause Harm

Religion is not always helpful.  
Strong religious beliefs can lead to too much guilt.  
They can make people feel rigid or anxious.  
Some people with mental health conditions may become overly focused on religious ideas.  
This can happen in people with:  
- Obsessive-compulsive disorder  
- Bipolar disorder  
- Schizophrenia  
- Other serious mental health issues  

Some religious groups do not allow certain medical treatments.  
They may refuse care that could save a life.  
Examples include:  
- Blood transfusions  
- Treatment for serious infections  
- Insulin for diabetes  

Instead, they may rely only on religious acts like:  
- Praying  
- Chanting  
- Lighting candles  

Some strict religious groups may cut off older adults from family members who do not share their beliefs.  
They may also isolate them from the wider community.  
This can lead to loneliness and sadness.

## How Health Care Professionals Can Help

Talking with older patients about their beliefs is important.  
Their religious or spiritual views can affect their health.  
It is okay for health care providers to ask about religion in certain situations.  
These include when:  
- A patient is very sick or under great stress  
- A patient is near the end of life and brings up religion  
- A patient says religion helps them cope with illness  
- A patient’s religious beliefs are clearly affecting their health or choices  

Older adults often have spiritual needs.  
These needs are different from mental health needs.  
But they can overlap.  
Finding out about a patient’s spiritual needs helps doctors and nurses:  
- Connect them with spiritual counselors  
- Help them join support groups  
- Encourage them to take part in religious activities  
- Build social connections through their faith community  

Understanding a patient’s beliefs leads to better care.

# Anemia During Pregnancy

Anemia means you have too few red blood cells in your blood.

This happens in up to one in three pregnant women during the last three months of pregnancy.

The most common reasons for anemia are:
- Not having enough iron in your body
- Not having enough folate (also called folic acid) in your body

If you have a hereditary anemia, such as sickle cell disease, hemoglobin S-C disease, or certain types of thalassemia, your pregnancy may be more risky.

If your race, ethnicity, or family history puts you at higher risk for these conditions, your doctor will do blood tests before delivery to check for them.

Your doctor may also do tests on the baby during pregnancy to see if the baby has these conditions.

## Signs of Anemia During Pregnancy

When you have anemia, your blood can’t carry as much oxygen as it should.

At first, you may not feel any symptoms. Or you may feel tired, weak, or dizzy.

You may look pale.

If anemia is severe, your pulse may be fast and weak. You may pass out. Your blood pressure may drop.

If anemia continues, it can cause problems such as:
- The baby not getting enough oxygen. This can harm the baby’s growth, especially the brain.
- You feeling very tired and short of breath.
- A higher chance of going into labor too early.
- A higher chance of getting an infection after delivery.
- Bleeding during labor and delivery can make your anemia worse.

## How Anemia Is Found

Your doctor will check for anemia with a blood test.

This test is usually done at your first visit after you find out you are pregnant.

## How Anemia Is Treated

Treatment depends on what is causing the anemia.

If you have severe symptoms or the baby is having problems, you may need a blood transfusion.

Your doctor will decide if you need a transfusion based on:
- How bad your symptoms are, such as dizziness, weakness, or tiredness.
- If anemia is making it hard to breathe or is affecting your heart rate.
- If the baby’s heart rate is not normal.

## Anemia from Low Iron or Low Folate

**Low iron** causes anemia in about 95 out of 100 pregnant women.

This happens because:
- You are not eating enough iron-rich foods.
- You lose iron each month during your period.
- You lost blood in a past pregnancy.

Women normally lose about the same amount of iron each month during their period as they take in through food. So, your body does not store much iron.

During pregnancy, your baby needs twice as much iron as usual. This makes it easy to become low in iron. This can lead to anemia.

**Low folate** can also cause anemia during pregnancy.

If you do not have enough folate, your baby has a higher chance of being born with a birth defect of the brain or spine. This is called a neural tube defect. An example is spina bifida.

Blood tests can confirm if you have low iron or low folate.

Anemia can usually be prevented or treated by taking iron and folate supplements during pregnancy.

If you are low in iron, your baby will usually be given iron supplements after birth.

Taking folate before you get pregnant and during pregnancy lowers the risk of your baby having a neural tube defect.

## Sickle Cell Disease

Sickle cell disease causes anemia and also raises the risk of other problems during pregnancy.

These include:
- Infections: such as pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and infections in the uterus.
- High blood pressure: About one in three women with sickle cell disease get high blood pressure during pregnancy.
- Heart failure.
- Blood clots in the lungs: This can be life threatening.
- Problems with the baby: The baby may grow slowly or be smaller than expected for the stage of pregnancy. The baby may be born too early, before 37 weeks.
- Sickle cell crisis: This is a sudden, severe pain attack. It can happen during pregnancy, just like at any other time.

The worse your sickle cell disease is before pregnancy, the higher the risk of health problems for you and your baby. The risk of the baby dying during pregnancy is also higher.

Sickle cell disease usually gets worse as your pregnancy continues.

Regular blood transfusions can help prevent sickle cell crises. But they can also cause your body to reject future transfusions. This is called alloimmunization. It can be life threatening.

Transfusions during pregnancy do not lower the risks for the baby.

So, doctors only use transfusions if:
- Your anemia causes serious symptoms, heart failure, or a severe bacterial infection.
- You have serious problems during labor and delivery, such as heavy bleeding or a blood infection (sepsis).

If you have a sickle cell crisis, you will be treated the same way as if you were not pregnant.

You will be admitted to the hospital. You will get fluids through a vein, oxygen, and pain relief medicine.

If your anemia is very bad, you will get a blood transfusion.

# Cerebral Palsy (CP)

Cerebral palsy is a group of conditions that affect movement and posture.  
It does not get worse over time.  
It starts before a child turns two years old.  
It happens because of problems in the brain that develop before birth or in the first few weeks after birth.  

The brain controls how muscles work.  
When the brain is damaged, muscles may not work the way they should.  
This can cause stiff muscles, weak muscles, or uncontrolled movements.  

Cerebral palsy is not one single disease.  
It is a group of related conditions with different causes and symptoms.  
If movement problems start after age two, it is not called cerebral palsy.  

## How Common Is Cerebral Palsy?

About 2 out of every 1,000 babies born have cerebral palsy.  
Babies who are born too early or who weigh very little at birth are more likely to have it.  
For example:  
- Babies born weighing between 1,000 and 1,499 grams have a rate of 59 out of 1,000.  
- Babies born before 28 weeks of pregnancy have a rate of 112 out of 1,000.  

## What Causes Cerebral Palsy?

There is often more than one cause.  
It can happen because of problems before birth, during birth, or in the first few weeks after birth.  

Common causes include:  
- Being born too early (premature birth)  
- Low birth weight  
- Problems in the womb, such as infections or poor blood flow  
- Lack of oxygen during birth (called perinatal asphyxia)  
- Stroke in the newborn period  
- Brain infections like meningitis  
- High levels of bilirubin in the blood (a condition once called kernicterus)  
- Severe illness or injury in early childhood, such as sepsis or dehydration  

Some children with cerebral palsy have changes in their genes.  
These changes can be found in more than 30% of cases using special genetic tests.  

## Types of Cerebral Palsy

Different types affect different parts of the body.  
The type depends on where the brain was damaged and how the muscles are affected.  

Examples:  
- **Spastic diplegia**: Stiffness in both legs. Often seen in babies born too early.  
- **Spastic hemiplegia**: Stiffness on one side of the body. Often caused by a stroke in a full-term baby.  
- **Spastic quadriplegia**: Stiffness in all four limbs. Often linked to lack of oxygen at birth or being small for gestational age.  
- **Dyskinetic CP**: Uncontrolled, writhing movements. Can follow lack of oxygen or high bilirubin levels.  
- **Ataxic CP**: Poor balance and coordination. Often due to problems in the part of the brain that controls balance.  

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

Most children with cerebral palsy show signs early in life.  
They may not meet normal motor milestones.  
For example, they may not roll over, sit up, crawl, or walk at the usual age.  

Other signs include:  
- Stiff or floppy muscles  
- Overactive reflexes  
- Unusual movement patterns  
- Holding limbs in odd positions  

Many children with cerebral palsy also have other issues, such as:  
- Trouble speaking or understanding language  
- Hearing or vision problems  
- Seizures  
- Pain  
- Hip problems  
- Drooling  
- Eye misalignment (strabismus)  
- Hearing loss or trouble looking up (especially in children with past bilirubin problems)  

Some children with spastic diplegia or hemiplegia have normal intelligence.  
Children with more severe types, like quadriplegia, may have learning difficulties.  

## How Is Cerebral Palsy Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose cerebral palsy based on:  
- A detailed medical history  
- A physical exam  
- Brain imaging tests  

The most useful test is a brain MRI.  
It can show brain damage or abnormal development.  
CT scans and cranial ultrasounds may also be used, especially in premature babies.  

Doctors may also test for genetic or metabolic disorders.  
These tests help rule out other possible causes.  

Diagnosis can happen as early as 5 months of age in high-risk babies.  
High-risk babies include those who:  
- Were born too early  
- Had low birth weight  
- Had a stroke or brain bleeding  
- Had signs of brain injury at birth  
- Had severe jaundice  
- Had meningitis  
- Had seizures in the newborn period  
- Have very stiff or very floppy muscles  
- Have abnormal reflexes  

About half of children with cerebral palsy also have seizures.  
An EEG (a test that measures brain activity) can help manage seizures.  

All children with cerebral palsy should be checked for vision and hearing problems.  

## How Is Cerebral Palsy Treated?

There is no cure, but treatment can help improve movement and daily life.  
Treatment starts early and is tailored to each child’s needs.  

### Physical and Occupational Therapy  
These are the main treatments.  
They help children:  
- Stretch tight muscles  
- Build strength  
- Learn to move better  
- Do everyday tasks like dressing and eating  

Therapy is often combined with other treatments.  

### Braces and Splints  
These help keep limbs in better positions.  
They can prevent joint problems and improve walking.  

### Constraint Therapy  
This means limiting the use of a stronger limb to help the weaker one get stronger.  

### Medications  
Some medicines help reduce muscle stiffness.  
They include:  
- Baclofen (taken by mouth)  
- Diazepam (a type of benzodiazepine)  
- Tizanidine  
- Dantrolene (used less often)  

These are often used for children with stiffness in many muscles.  

### Botulinum Toxin Injections  
This is a medicine injected into tight muscles.  
It helps relax them.  
It works best for small areas, like one leg or arm.  

### Intrathecal Baclofen  
This is a medicine delivered through a pump and tube in the spine.  
It is used for children with severe stiffness that does not improve with oral medicine.  

### Surgery  
Surgery may help in severe cases.  
Examples:  
- Releasing tight tendons or muscles  
- Realigning bones or joints  
- Selective dorsal rhizotomy (a surgery to reduce leg stiffness in some children with good thinking skills)  

### Assistive Devices  
These include walkers, wheelchairs, communication tools, and special eating utensils.  
They help children move, talk, and do daily tasks.  

Children with mild learning issues can join regular school classes.  
They can also take part in adapted sports and activities.  
Speech training or other communication tools may help children who have trouble speaking.  

Teaching daily living skills helps children become more independent.  
It also helps families feel less stressed.  

Many children need lifelong support.  
Some programs help children with cerebral palsy transition into adult life.  

## What Is the Outlook?

Most children with cerebral palsy live into adulthood.  
Some may have shorter lives if they have serious problems with feeding or breathing.  
This can happen if they cannot swallow well and choke on food or liquids.  
This increases the risk of lung infections.  

Severe movement problems or learning difficulties can also raise the risk of early death.  

But death rates are going down worldwide.  
Better care and treatments are helping children live longer and healthier lives.  

With the right support, many children with spastic diplegia or hemiplegia can live nearly normal lives.  

## Can Cerebral Palsy Be Prevented?

Yes, some cases can be prevented.  

Before birth:  
- Giving corticosteroids to mothers at risk of early delivery helps protect the baby’s brain.  
- Giving magnesium sulfate to mothers before early delivery also helps protect the baby’s brain.  

After birth:  
- Giving caffeine to premature babies helps protect the brain.  
- Cooling the baby’s body (therapeutic hypothermia) helps protect the brain after a lack of oxygen at birth.  

These treatments are now standard in many newborn intensive care units.  

## Key Points

- Cerebral palsy is a group of conditions that affect movement and posture.  
- It does not get worse over time.  
- It starts before age two.  
- It is caused by brain damage before, during, or shortly after birth.  
- Common causes include prematurity, low birth weight, lack of oxygen, stroke, infections, and genetic issues.  
- Symptoms include stiff or floppy muscles, poor movement control, and delayed motor skills.  
- Other problems like seizures, learning issues, vision or hearing loss, and pain may also occur.  
- Diagnosis is based on history, physical exam, and brain imaging (like MRI).  
- Treatment includes physical and occupational therapy, braces, medicine, injections, surgery, and assistive devices.  
- Early treatment helps children reach their full potential.  
- Many children with mild forms can live nearly normal lives.  
- Prevention is possible in some cases through medicines and cooling therapy for high-risk babies.

# Glucagonoma

A glucagonoma is a rare type of tumor in the pancreas. It makes too much of a hormone called glucagon. This hormone raises blood sugar levels. It also causes a unique skin rash.

## What Causes Glucagonoma?

- The tumor starts in special cells in the pancreas that normally make glucagon.
- Glucagon helps the body raise blood sugar when it gets too low.
- In a glucagonoma, the body makes too much glucagon all the time.
- This leads to high blood sugar and a specific rash.

## Who Gets Glucagonoma?

- Most people are around 50 years old when symptoms start.
- About 8 out of 10 people with this condition are women.
- A small number of people have a genetic condition called multiple endocrine neoplasia.

## Symptoms

High levels of glucagon cause symptoms like those of diabetes. These include:

- Losing weight without trying.
- Urinating more than usual.
- Feeling very thirsty.

In addition, many people with glucagonoma have:

- A long-lasting rash that is brownish-red in color. This is called necrolytic migratory erythema.
- The rash usually starts in the groin and spreads to the buttocks, arms, hands, legs, and feet.
- The skin may peel or scale.
- The tongue may look smooth, shiny, and bright red-orange.
- People with darker skin may notice their skin turns redder or darker.
- Cracks may appear at the corners of the mouth.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use blood tests and imaging scans to find a glucagonoma.

**Blood tests:**
- They check for high levels of glucagon in the blood.

**Imaging tests:**
- A CT scan of the belly is done first.
- Then, an endoscopic ultrasound is used to look closely at the pancreas.
- If the CT scan does not show the tumor, doctors may use MRI or PET scans.

## How Is It Treated?

The main goal is to remove the tumor.

**Surgery:**
- If possible, doctors remove the tumor completely.
- This often cures the rash and stops all symptoms.

**Chemotherapy:**
- If the tumor cannot be removed or has spread, chemotherapy may be used.
- It can lower glucagon levels and ease symptoms.
- But it does not help people live longer.

**Medicines:**
- Octreotide or lanreotide can lower glucagon levels.
- These medicines may clear up the rash and help you eat better, which can help you gain weight.
- However, they can also raise blood sugar even more.

**Other treatments for the rash:**
- Zinc can be taken by mouth, applied as a cream, or given through a vein.
- Sometimes, doctors give amino acids or fatty acids through a vein to help the rash.

## Outlook

- Most glucagonomas are cancerous, but they grow slowly.
- Many people live 15 years or more after diagnosis.
- Early treatment improves the chances of a good outcome.

# What Are Tubulointerstitial Diseases?

Tubulointerstitial diseases affect the tiny tubes and the surrounding tissue in the kidneys. These conditions can cause damage to the kidney’s filtering system.

The damage may start in the small tubes of the kidney. If it gets worse or lasts a long time, the whole kidney can be affected. This can lead to poor kidney function or even kidney failure.

There are several main types of tubulointerstitial diseases:

- **Acute tubular necrosis**: This is sudden damage to the kidney tubes. It often happens after a serious illness or injury.
- **Acute or chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis**: This is inflammation in the kidney tubes and nearby tissue. It can happen suddenly or over a long time.
- **Contrast nephropathy**: This is a type of acute tubular necrosis caused by a special dye used in some X-ray tests.
- **Analgesic nephropathy**: This is long-term kidney damage from overusing certain pain medicines.
- **Reflux nephropathy**: This happens when urine flows backward into the kidneys, causing damage over time.
- **Myeloma kidney**: This is kidney damage caused by a type of blood cancer.

Some tubulointerstitial diseases are also caused by:

- Problems with the body’s chemistry (metabolic issues).
- Exposure to harmful substances (toxins).

## How These Diseases Develop

The kidneys get a lot of blood flow — more than any other organ. This means they are exposed to high levels of chemicals and toxins.

The kidneys filter blood very fast. This brings toxins into the kidney tubes at a rate 50 times higher than in other organs.

When the kidneys make concentrated urine, the inside of the tubes can be exposed to chemicals at levels 300 to 1,000 times higher than in the blood.

The tiny, hair-like parts on the surface of the kidney tubes give them a huge area to absorb substances.

The kidney uses a system that helps concentrate urine. This makes the fluid in the kidney’s inner part up to four times more concentrated than blood.

Certain things can make kidney cells more likely to be damaged by toxins:

- The kidney moves medicines out of the blood and away from protective proteins. This can make the medicines more harmful.
- Some chemicals enter the inside of kidney cells and reach their inner parts. This increases the risk of damage.
- Some toxins stick to certain parts of cells. They can get in easily but leave slowly. This is common with heavy metals.
- Changes in the body’s acidity or alkalinity can affect how chemicals move in and out of cells.
- Blocking certain pathways in the kidney can reduce how much toxin reaches the tissue. For example, some medicines that increase urine flow can lower the amount of toxin in the kidney.

The kidneys use a lot of energy. They need high levels of oxygen and sugar to work. Because of this, they are especially sensitive to toxins that harm energy production in cells.
