# Medications for Bipolar Disorder

Bipolar disorder can be hard to treat. No medicine works for everyone. All medicines can cause side effects. Some medicines can interact with others. Your doctor will choose the best medicine based on what worked for you before. If you have not tried any medicine before, your doctor will look at your health history and how bad your symptoms are.

## Choosing the Right Medicine

### For Severe Mania with Psychosis
If you are very out of control and at risk of hurting yourself or others, you may need a strong medicine to calm you down quickly. A second-generation antipsychotic medicine is often used. It may be given with a short-term medicine like lorazepam or clonazepam to help you relax.

### For Less Severe Mania or Depression
If your symptoms are not life-threatening, lithium is often a good first choice. It works for both mania and depression. But it takes time to work—usually 4 to 10 days. If you have strong symptoms, your doctor may also give you another medicine like an antiseizure drug or a second-generation antipsychotic to help fast.

### For Bipolar Depression
The best evidence shows that these medicines can help with depression:
- Quetiapine
- Cariprazine
- Lumateperone
- Lurasidone  
Or a combination of fluoxetine and olanzapine.

## Keeping Symptoms Under Control Long-Term

Once your symptoms go away, you should keep taking a mood stabilizer. This is especially true if you have bipolar I disorder. This means you have had at least one full manic episode.

If your symptoms come back during treatment, your doctor will check if you are taking your medicine as directed. If you are not, your doctor will ask why. Maybe the medicine causes side effects. Maybe the dose is too high. Your doctor may change the medicine or the dose to make it easier to take.

---

## Lithium

Lithium helps reduce mood swings in bipolar disorder. It does not change normal mood. People with a family history of bipolar disorder are more likely to respond well to lithium.

Lithium is less likely to work well if you have:
- Mixed states (both mania and depression at the same time)
- Rapid cycling (4 or more mood episodes in a year)
- Anxiety
- Substance use problems
- A brain or nervous system condition

### How Lithium Is Used
Lithium is usually given in a tablet form called lithium carbonate. Your doctor will adjust the dose based on blood tests, how you feel, and how well it works.

Higher doses help prevent mania but do not help with depression. Higher doses also cause more side effects.

- Young people often need higher doses because their kidneys work well.
- Older people often need lower doses.

### Side Effects of Lithium
Common mild side effects include:
- Shaking hands (fine tremor)
- Muscle twitches
- Nausea
- Diarrhea
- Drinking a lot of water
- Urinating often
- Gaining weight (partly from drinking sugary drinks)

These side effects often go away over time. They may improve if:
- The dose is lowered slightly
- The dose is split into 3 smaller doses a day
- A slow-release form is used

Once your dose is stable, take the full dose at night, after dinner. This may help you stick to your medicine schedule and may protect your kidneys.

If hand shaking is severe, a beta-blocker like atenolol can help. But some beta-blockers (like propranolol) can make depression worse.

### Lithium Poisoning (Toxicity)
Lithium poisoning can happen if levels in your blood get too high. Early signs include:
- Severe shaking
- Headache
- Vomiting
- Confusion

If not treated, it can lead to:
- Drowsiness
- Seizures
- Heart rhythm problems

You are more likely to get lithium poisoning if you:
- Are older
- Have kidney problems
- Are losing salt (from fever, vomiting, diarrhea, or diuretics)

Medicines like thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors, and most NSAIDs (except aspirin) can raise lithium levels. Always tell your doctor about all medicines you take.

Check lithium blood levels every 6 months. Check them again when your dose changes.

### Long-Term Side Effects
Lithium can cause long-term problems, including:
- Low thyroid function (hypothyroidism), especially if you have a family history
- High calcium levels (hypercalcemia) and overactive parathyroid glands (hyperparathyroidism)
- Kidney damage after 15 or more years of use

To catch problems early:
- Test thyroid function when you start lithium and once a year if you have a family history of thyroid issues. Test every other year if you do not.
- Test thyroid function if you feel tired, gain weight, or your mood swings return.
- Test kidney function (BUN and creatinine) at the start, then 2–3 times in the first 6 months, then once or twice a year.
- Test calcium and parathyroid hormone levels once a year.

Use the lowest dose that works. This lowers the risk of kidney damage.

---

## Antiseizure Medicines

Some antiseizure medicines also help stabilize mood. These include:
- Valproate
- Carbamazepine
- Lamotrigine

### Valproate
- Used for mania and mixed states.
- Dose is adjusted based on blood levels.
- A higher starting dose (based on weight) may help you feel better faster.
- Side effects: nausea, headache, drowsiness, dizziness, weight gain.
- Rare but serious side effects: liver damage and pancreatitis.

### Carbamazepine
- Used for mania and mixed states.
- Do not start with a high dose. Increase slowly.
- Side effects: nausea, dizziness, drowsiness, unsteadiness.
- Rare but serious side effects: low blood cell counts (aplastic anemia and agranulocytosis).

### Lamotrigine
- Used for mood swings and depression.
- Dose depends on other medicines you take:
  - Lower dose if you take valproate
  - Higher dose if you take carbamazepine
- Can cause a rash. Rarely, it can cause a serious skin reaction called Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
- This risk is higher if the dose is increased too fast.

**Watch for these warning signs:**
- New rash or hives
- Fever
- Swollen glands
- Sores in the mouth or eyes
- Swelling of lips or tongue

If you see any of these, stop the medicine and call your doctor right away.

---

## Antipsychotic Medicines

These medicines are used to treat mania and psychosis. They are also used to help mood stabilizers work better after the worst symptoms are gone.

Common second-generation antipsychotics include:
- Aripiprazole
- Cariprazine
- Lurasidone
- Olanzapine
- Quetiapine
- Risperidone
- Ziprasidone

### Side Effects
All of these medicines can cause:
- Movement problems (extrapyramidal side effects)
- Restlessness (akathisia)

The risk is lower with more sedating medicines like quetiapine and olanzapine.

Other long-term side effects include:
- Weight gain
- Metabolic syndrome (extra belly fat, high blood sugar, high cholesterol, insulin resistance)

The risk is lower with less sedating medicines: lurasidone, ziprasidone, and aripiprazole.

### For Very Severe Cases
If you are extremely active and not eating or drinking well, your doctor may give an antipsychotic by injection (IM). This is used with other treatments like lithium or an antiseizure medicine.

---

## Antidepressants

Antidepressants like SSRIs (e.g., sertraline) may be added if your depression is very severe. But they are not usually used alone for bipolar depression. They can sometimes trigger mania.

There is some evidence that sertraline may be safe and helpful for bipolar II depression when used alone.

Some small studies suggest tranylcypromine may work better than other antidepressants for bipolar depression.

---

## Medicines During Pregnancy

### Lithium
- Lithium use during pregnancy increases the risk of heart defects in the baby (especially Ebstein anomaly).
- The absolute risk is low.
- The risk of any birth defect is about 2 times higher than normal.
- This risk is similar to carbamazepine and lamotrigine.
- It is much lower than the risk with valproate.

### Valproate
- Valproate greatly increases the risk of birth defects.
- Risk of neural tube defects (like spina bifida) is 2 to 7 times higher than with other antiseizure medicines.
- It also increases the risk of:
  - Heart defects
  - Genital or urinary problems
  - Bone or joint issues
  - Cleft lip or palate
- Children of mothers who took valproate during pregnancy often have lower IQ scores.
- The risk is higher with higher doses.
- Valproate also increases the risk of attention problems and autism in children.

**Valproate should not be used during pregnancy.**

### Other Medicines
- First-generation antipsychotics and tricyclic antidepressants do not appear to cause harm during early pregnancy.
- Second-generation antipsychotics seem safe, except possibly risperidone.
- SSRIs appear to have a low risk of birth defects.

# Chest Physical Therapy

Chest physical therapy helps clear mucus from the lungs. It uses physical methods like tapping, positioning, and shaking.

Healthcare providers use different methods to treat lung problems. These include:

- Moving the body into certain positions to drain mucus
- Using suction to remove mucus from the airways
- Doing breathing exercises to keep the lungs open

The right method depends on the person’s illness and overall health.

(See also: Pulmonary Rehabilitation.)

---

## Positioning to Drain Mucus

In this method, the person lies in a special position. The body is tilted so mucus can drain out of the lungs. A therapist may gently clap the chest or back with a cupped hand. This is called chest percussion. It helps loosen mucus so it can be coughed up.

A therapist may also use a machine that vibrates the chest. Or they may use a special vest that shakes the chest at a high speed. This helps break up mucus. The therapist can teach a family member how to use the machine or vest at home.

These methods are used for people who make a lot of mucus. This includes people with:

- Cystic fibrosis
- Bronchiectasis (airways that are permanently widened)
- Sometimes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)

They are also used when a person cannot cough up mucus well. This may happen in older adults, people with weak muscles, or those recovering from surgery, injury, or serious illness.

Do not use this method if:

- The person cannot stay in the required position
- The person just vomited blood
- The person recently broke a rib or spine bone
- The person has severe bone thinning (osteoporosis)
- The person is at high risk of bleeding

This method is not helpful if the lung problem does not cause extra mucus.

---

## Suctioning

A healthcare provider or trained family member can use suctioning to remove mucus from the airways.

A thin plastic tube is gently put through the nose and moved a few inches into the windpipe. A soft vacuum pulls out mucus that cannot be coughed up.

Suctioning is used when:

- A person has a tracheostomy (a hole in the neck for breathing)
- A breathing tube is in place (through the nose or mouth into the windpipe)
- The person is on a ventilator (a machine that helps with breathing)

---

## Breathing Exercises

These exercises help people take deep breaths. This keeps the tiny air sacs in the lungs open. This prevents them from collapsing.

These exercises do not make the lungs stronger. But they help lower the risk of lung problems after surgery. This is especially true for heavy smokers and people with lung disease.

They are also helpful for people with COPD who do not move much. They are also useful for people who have just stopped using a ventilator.

### Incentive Spirometer

This is a small device that helps people take deep breaths. It has a tube and a plastic chamber with a ball inside.

The person breathes in deeply through the tube. The ball rises with each breath. The goal is to do 5 to 10 deep breaths every hour while awake.

This device is used often in hospitals before and after surgery.

But studies show that guided breathing exercises by a nurse or therapist work better than doing them alone with the device.

### Pursed-Lip Breathing

This is a breathing pattern that helps people with COPD. It is useful when the lungs become too full during:

- Airway narrowing
- Panic attacks
- Exercise

People are taught to breathe out slowly through tightly closed lips, as if they are whistling. This keeps the airways open and prevents them from collapsing.

This exercise is safe and causes no harm. Some people start doing it on their own without being taught.

### Bending Forward While Breathing

Some people find it easier to do pursed-lip breathing while bending forward.

To do this:

- Stand with arms and hands stretched out
- Rest your body on a table or similar surface
- Lean forward slightly

This position can make breathing easier.

# Pulmonary Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (PLCH)

This is a lung disease that mainly affects young adults who smoke. It happens when certain immune cells in the lungs grow too much and build up in the air sacs and small airways. These cells are called Langerhans cells. The exact cause is not known, but smoking plays a big role.

## What Causes PLCH?

- The disease mostly affects white people between the ages of 20 and 40.
- Almost all people with PLCH are current or former smokers.
- It is very rare in other groups.
- The body may react to cigarette smoke by sending more of these cells to the lungs.
- The cells grow in a way that is not normal. They are not cancer, but they can cause lung damage.

## Symptoms of PLCH

Common symptoms include:
- Trouble breathing, especially when active
- A dry cough that does not produce mucus
- Feeling tired all the time
- Fever
- Losing weight without trying
- Sharp chest pain that gets worse when you breathe deeply

Some people have no symptoms at all. Their disease is found by chance during a chest X-ray done for another reason.

A sudden lung collapse (called pneumothorax) is common in PLCH. This can cause sudden, sharp chest pain and shortness of breath.

Other signs of the disease outside the lungs can include:
- Bone pain from small holes in the bones (bone cysts)
- A skin rash
- Passing a lot of urine (due to a hormone problem)

These extra-lung symptoms happen in up to 15 out of 100 people with PLCH. Sometimes they are the first signs of the disease.

Physical exams often show normal results. But if the disease gets worse, you may develop high blood pressure in the lungs (pulmonary hypertension).

## How Is PLCH Diagnosed?

Diagnosis uses several tools:

### Chest X-ray
- Shows small, round spots in the upper and middle parts of both lungs.
- The lower parts of the lungs are often clear.
- The pattern can look like chronic lung disease or another rare lung condition.

### High-Resolution CT Scan (HRCT)
- This is the best test to confirm PLCH.
- It shows cysts and nodules in the upper and middle lung areas.
- The cysts often have strange shapes.
- It also shows thickening in the lung tissue between air sacs.

### Pulmonary Function Tests
- These measure how well your lungs work.
- Results can be normal, or show problems with airflow, lung volume, or oxygen transfer.
- Most people have lower oxygen transfer ability (low DLCO).
- Exercise may make it harder to get enough oxygen.

### Bronchoscopy and Biopsy
- Used when the diagnosis is unclear.
- A small sample of lung tissue is taken through a tube in the windpipe.
- The sample is checked under a microscope.
- Finding more than 5% of CD1a-positive cells in lung washings is a strong sign of PLCH.
- The cells stain positive for CD1a, S-100 protein, and langerin.
- The tissue shows clusters of Langerhans cells and other immune cells in nodules that may look star-shaped.

## Treatment for PLCH

### Stop Smoking
- This is the most important step.
- Quitting smoking can lead to symptom improvement in up to one-third of patients.
- It also helps prevent the disease from getting worse.

### Steroid Medicine (Glucocorticoids)
- Doctors often give these medicines, especially if the disease is active or affects other organs.
- But there is no strong proof that they help in most cases.
- They may be used for a short time to reduce inflammation.

### Other Medicines
- Some patients get medicines that slow down cell growth (cytotoxic drugs).
- Examples include cladribine, cytarabine, and vinblastine.
- These are used when the disease is severe or does not respond to steroids.

### Lung Transplant
- This may be an option for people who are otherwise healthy but have severe lung damage.
- It can cure the lung problem if the person stops smoking.
- If the person starts smoking again, the disease can return in the new lung.

## Prognosis (Outlook)

- Many people with mild disease get better on their own or with treatment.
- Most people live more than 10 years after diagnosis.
- The 5-year survival rate is about 74%.

### Signs That the Disease May Get Worse
- You keep smoking
- You are very young or very old
- The disease affects more than one organ
- You still have symptoms like fatigue or fever
- Your chest X-ray shows many cysts
- Your lung function tests show poor oxygen transfer
- Your lung volume is high and airflow is blocked
- You need long-term steroid treatment

### Causes of Death
- Breathing failure due to lung damage
- Cancer, especially lung cancer

People with PLCH have a higher risk of cancer because of smoking.

## Key Points

- PLCH is a lung disease where abnormal immune cells grow in the air sacs and small airways.
- Think of PLCH in people aged 20 to 40 who smoke and have a chest X-ray showing spots and cysts in the upper lungs.
- Confirm the diagnosis with a high-resolution CT scan. If needed, a lung biopsy can help.
- The most important treatment is quitting smoking.
- Consider steroid medicine and other drugs if the disease is active.
- If the disease continues after quitting smoking, lung transplant may be an option.

# How the Body Gets Rid of Drugs

Your body removes drugs over time. This process is called drug elimination.

All drugs leave the body eventually. Some drugs are changed in the body before they are removed. Others leave the body without being changed.

Most drugs, especially those that dissolve in water, are removed through the kidneys. The kidneys filter waste from the blood and send it out in urine. So, how well your kidneys work affects how your body handles drugs.

Some drugs are removed through the bile. The bile is a fluid made by the liver and stored in the gallbladder. It helps digest food.

---

## How Drugs Leave Through Urine

Several things affect how well the kidneys remove drugs:

- The drug must dissolve in water.
- The drug should not stick too tightly to proteins in the blood.
- The acidity of the urine matters. This can change with diet, other medicines, or kidney problems.

Doctors can change the acidity of urine to help remove certain drugs faster. For example, in cases of drug overdose, they may give sodium bicarbonate (a type of antacid) or ammonium chloride to make the urine more alkaline or acidic. This speeds up the removal of the drug.

The kidneys’ ability to remove drugs also depends on:

- How fast urine flows out of the kidneys.
- How much blood flows through the kidneys.
- The overall health of the kidneys.

Many conditions can harm kidney function. These include:

- High blood pressure
- Diabetes
- Repeated kidney infections
- Exposure to harmful chemicals
- Normal aging

As you get older, your kidneys work less well. For example, an 85-year-old person’s kidneys remove drugs about half as well as a 35-year-old person’s.

When kidney function is poor, a normal dose of a drug may be too high. This can cause side effects. So, doctors often lower the dose for people with weak kidneys.

Doctors use several methods to check kidney function:

- Age can give a rough idea.
- Blood tests can measure creatinine, a waste product.
- Urine tests can also help.
- They use these results to calculate creatinine clearance. This number shows how well the kidneys are filtering waste.

---

## How Drugs Leave Through Bile

Some drugs pass through the liver and go into the bile without being changed. Others are changed in the liver before being sent into the bile.

The bile then moves into the intestines. From there:

- Some drugs leave the body in stool (poop).
- Some are absorbed back into the blood and circulate again.

If the liver is not working well, the body may not remove certain drugs properly. This may require a lower dose.

Unlike kidney function, there is no simple test to predict how well the liver will process and remove drugs.

---

## Other Ways Drugs Leave the Body

Some drugs leave the body through:

- Saliva
- Sweat
- Breast milk
- Breath

Most drugs leave in very small amounts through these routes.

The only time drug excretion in breast milk matters is when the drug could affect a nursing baby. (See: Medications and Substances That Should Not Be Taken While Breastfeeding.)

Drugs breathed out in the air are mainly inhaled anesthetics. These are removed from the body through the lungs when you breathe out.

# Parts of a Prosthetic Limb

A prosthetic limb replaces a missing arm or leg. It has four main parts.

## Interface  
This is the part that connects to your body. It fits over the end of your limb. It helps the prosthesis stay in place and feel comfortable.

## Suspension  
This keeps the prosthesis from falling off. It holds the device tightly to your body. It uses suction, straps, or a special socket to stay secure.

## Structural Components  
These are the inner parts that give the prosthesis its shape and strength. They include the frame and joints. They let the limb move and support your weight.

## Cover  
This is the outer layer. It looks like real skin. It covers the inner parts. It can be custom made to match your skin color and style.

# How Your Mind Can Affect Your Physical Health

Sometimes, your thoughts, feelings, or actions can make a physical illness worse. This is called psychological factors affecting other medical conditions.

This diagnosis is used when your mental state or behavior harms your health in a way that makes a medical problem worse.

## How Your Mind Can Affect Your Body

Your attitudes and behaviors can make any health problem worse. This includes conditions like:
- Diabetes
- Heart disease
- Migraine headaches
- Chronic pain

For example:
- Extreme stress can make your heart work too hard for a short time.
- Long-term stress from work can raise your blood pressure over time.
- Poor habits or ignoring your health can lead to serious problems, like needing hospital care or going to the emergency room.

These issues can increase your risk of getting sicker, dying, or becoming disabled.

## What Can Make a Medical Condition Worse?

The following behaviors can harm your health:
- Believing your symptoms are not serious
- Refusing to accept that you need treatment
- Not following your doctor’s treatment plan
- Skipping recommended tests

A doctor may diagnose this condition if it is clear that your mental state or behavior is making your illness progress more slowly or become more severe.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment focuses on helping you understand how your mind and behavior affect your body. It includes:
- Education about how stress, emotions, and habits can impact your health
- Talking therapy (also called psychotherapy) to help you change harmful thoughts and behaviors

# Vaginal Bleeding During Early Pregnancy

About one in five pregnant women have vaginal bleeding in the first 20 weeks of pregnancy.  
Half of these cases end in a miscarriage.  

Vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy can also lead to other serious problems, such as:  
- Baby being born too early  
- Baby being born with low weight  
- Baby being stillborn  
- Baby dying shortly after birth  

## What Can Cause Vaginal Bleeding?

Many different conditions can cause vaginal bleeding during early pregnancy.  
Some are related to the pregnancy. Others are not.  

The most dangerous cause is an ectopic pregnancy.  
This happens when the baby grows outside the uterus, usually in a fallopian tube.  
If the tube bursts, it can cause heavy bleeding inside the belly.  
This can lead to shock and needs emergency care.  

A rare but serious cause is a ruptured corpus luteum cyst.  
This is a fluid-filled sac on the ovary.  
If it breaks, it can cause bleeding inside the belly and lead to shock.  

The most common cause is a miscarriage.  
There are different types:  
- Threatened miscarriage: bleeding with or without cramps, but the cervix stays closed  
- Inevitable miscarriage: bleeding and cramps, and the cervix opens  
- Incomplete miscarriage: bleeding and cramps, and some pregnancy tissue stays in the uterus  
- Complete miscarriage: bleeding stops, and the uterus returns to normal size  
- Missed miscarriage: no symptoms, but the baby has stopped growing  

### Common Causes of Vaginal Bleeding in Early Pregnancy

| Cause | Signs and Symptoms | How It Is Diagnosed |
|-------|--------------------|---------------------|
| **Ectopic pregnancy** | Bleeding, sudden sharp pain in the belly or pelvis, no fetal heartbeat, possible dizziness or fainting | Blood test for pregnancy hormone (beta-hCG), blood count, pelvic ultrasound, sometimes surgery |
| **Threatened miscarriage** | Bleeding, cramps, cervix still closed | Blood test, blood count, ultrasound, listen to baby’s heartbeat |
| **Inevitable miscarriage** | Bleeding, cramps, cervix open | Same as threatened miscarriage |
| **Incomplete miscarriage** | Bleeding, cramps, tissue seen or felt in the cervix | Same as threatened miscarriage |
| **Complete miscarriage** | Light bleeding, history of heavy bleeding, mild cramps, cervix closed | Same as threatened miscarriage |
| **Septic miscarriage** | Fever, chills, constant pain, foul-smelling discharge, bleeding | Same as threatened miscarriage, plus tests for infections |
| **Gestational trophoblastic disease (hydatidiform mole)** | Bleeding, very large uterus, high blood pressure, severe nausea, passing grape-like tissue | Same as threatened miscarriage, plus blood tests, chest X-ray |
| **Ruptured corpus luteum cyst** | Sudden pain, bleeding, nausea or vomiting | Same as ectopic pregnancy |
| **Trauma** | History of injury, like a car crash or sexual assault | Blood test, ultrasound, imaging tests, questions about safety |
| **Vaginitis** | Light bleeding, unusual discharge | Tests for infection |
| **Cervicitis** | Mucus or pus from cervix, light bleeding, pain during sex or pelvic pain | Tests for infections |
| **Cervical polyp** | Light bleeding, no pain | Exam shows a small growth on the cervix, biopsy may be done |

> **Note:** All pregnant women with bleeding should have their vital signs checked.  
> A physical exam is needed.  
> The baby’s heartbeat should be checked with a monitor or ultrasound.  

## How Is It Evaluated?

If you are pregnant and have vaginal bleeding, you must be seen right away.  
Some causes can lead to life-threatening bleeding.  

You should get blood tests and an ultrasound.  
Your blood type should be checked.  
IV access should be set up early in case you need blood.  

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause.  

- **Ectopic pregnancy (ruptured):** Emergency surgery  
- **Ectopic pregnancy (not ruptured):** Medicine (methotrexate) or surgery  
- **Threatened or inevitable miscarriage:** Watch and wait if stable  
- **Incomplete or missed miscarriage:** Remove tissue from the uterus  
- **Complete miscarriage:** Follow-up care with your doctor  
- **Septic miscarriage:** IV antibiotics and urgent removal of tissue  
- **Other causes:** Treat the specific condition (e.g., infection, polyp)  

If you have Rh-negative blood and are bleeding or have an ectopic pregnancy, you must get a shot called Rho(D) immune globulin.  
This prevents your body from making harmful antibodies against your baby’s blood.  

## Key Points

- Always think about ectopic pregnancy if you have bleeding in early pregnancy.  
  Symptoms can be mild or severe.  
- The most common cause of bleeding is a miscarriage.  
- All women with bleeding in early pregnancy should have their blood type checked.  
  If you are Rh-negative, you need a shot to protect future pregnancies.

# Chromium

Chromium is a mineral your body needs in small amounts. It helps insulin work properly.

## Where You Get Chromium

- Most people get enough chromium from their food.
- Good food sources include whole grains, carrots, potatoes, broccoli, and molasses.

## Chromium Supplements

- Chromium is often combined with a substance called picolinate in supplements. This is called chromium picolinate.
- Some people believe this form helps the body absorb chromium better.

## How Chromium Works

- In the body, chromium helps insulin do its job.
- It may help lower blood sugar levels.
- Some studies show that taking up to 1,000 micrograms of chromium per day is safe.

## What Chromium Is Said to Do

Some people use chromium picolinate for:
- Losing weight
- Building muscle
- Reducing body fat
- Lowering bad cholesterol (LDL)
- Raising good cholesterol (HDL)

It is also used for:
- Diabetes
- High cholesterol
- Polycystic ovary syndrome (a condition where women have enlarged ovaries with fluid-filled sacs)
- Other health issues

But there is no strong scientific proof that chromium helps with most of these conditions.

## What the Research Shows

- Chromium deficiency can make insulin work poorly.
- But taking chromium supplements does not help most people with diabetes.
- There may be a very small effect on weight loss.
- One review of studies found a small drop in weight in people with obesity or being overweight.
- However, researchers said there is no clear reason to use chromium for this.
- There is no proof that chromium helps with body fat, cholesterol, or triglyceride levels.

## Side Effects

- Chromium supplements can reduce how well your body absorbs iron.
- Some forms of chromium can cause stomach upset or ulcers.
- Rarely, chromium has been linked to kidney or liver damage.
- People with kidney or liver problems should not take chromium.
- Some studies suggest chromium might damage chromosomes. This could mean it may cause cancer, but more research is needed.

## Safe Amounts

- The highest safe amount of chromium is not known.
- But daily doses up to 1,000 micrograms have been shown to be safe in studies.

## Drug Interactions

- Chromium may lower blood sugar, especially when taken with insulin or certain diabetes pills (sulfonylureas).
- It does not seem to affect blood sugar when taken with metformin.
- Taking chromium at the same time as levothyroxine (a thyroid medicine) may reduce how much of the thyroid medicine your body absorbs.
- This may mean you need a different dose of your thyroid medicine if you take chromium.

## Recommendations

- The use of chromium as a supplement is not recommended.
- Even though it may cause a small drop in blood sugar or weight, the risks may outweigh the benefits.
- The American Diabetes Association does not recommend chromium to lower blood sugar.
- Chromium supplements are usually safe at doses up to 1,000 micrograms per day.
- But there is little benefit to justify the small risk of side effects.
- Do not take chromium if you have:
  - Kidney or liver problems
  - Iron deficiency

# IPEX Syndrome

IPEX syndrome is a rare and serious condition. It affects the body’s immune system and causes it to attack healthy tissues.

This condition is caused by a change in a gene called *FOXP3*. This gene helps control a type of immune cell called regulatory T cells. When the gene is not working right, these cells do not work properly. This leads to the immune system attacking the body.

The main signs of IPEX syndrome include:
- Swollen lymph nodes and spleen
- Type 1 diabetes
- Severe skin rash (eczema)
- Allergies to foods
- Frequent infections
- Long-term diarrhea
- Poor growth and weight gain

Most children show symptoms in the first few months of life. But some may not show signs until later in childhood.

Doctors suspect IPEX syndrome based on the symptoms. A genetic test can confirm the diagnosis.

If a child has IPEX syndrome, family members should consider genetic testing. This helps find out if other children in the family are at risk.

## Treatment for IPEX Syndrome

Without treatment, most children with IPEX syndrome do not survive past their first year.

A treatment called hematopoietic stem cell transplantation can help. This treatment replaces the faulty immune system with a healthy one from a donor.

After this treatment, many children see improvement in their autoimmune symptoms. Some also have fewer new autoimmune problems.

Doctors are still studying the long-term results of this treatment in children with IPEX syndrome. Follow-up care is important.

# Symptoms of Cancer

Cancer starts as a small group of abnormal cells. At first, it causes no symptoms.

As the cancer grows, it can press on or spread into nearby tissues. This can cause problems in that area.

Some cancers make substances or cause reactions in the body. These can cause symptoms in parts of the body far from the cancer.

Sometimes, a blood test done for another reason shows something wrong. For example, colon cancer can cause low red blood cell counts, which shows up as anemia on a routine blood test.

Cancer can hurt nearby tissues by pressing on them or growing into them. This pressure or growth can cause pain.

Pressure can also stop tissues from working normally. For example:

- A bladder cancer or a cancer in a lymph node in the belly can press on the tube that carries urine from the kidney to the bladder. This can block urine flow.
- A lung cancer can block air from reaching part of the lung. This can cause part of the lung to collapse. It also raises the risk of infection.

Cancer in open areas, like the inside of the large intestine or the lung, may not cause symptoms until it is large. But cancer in tight spaces, like on a vocal cord, can cause symptoms early. For example, it may cause hoarseness even when small.

If cancer spreads to other parts of the body, it can cause the same problems—pressure or irritation—in the new location. This means the symptoms can be different.

Cancer that affects the lining around the lungs (pleura) or the sac around the heart (pericardium) often causes fluid to build up. Too much fluid can make breathing hard or stop the heart from pumping well.

---

## Some Complications of Cancer

| Complication | What Happens |
|--------------|--------------|
| **Cardiac tamponade** | Fluid builds up around the heart. This pressure stops the heart from pumping blood properly. It can cause chest pain and shortness of breath. This happens when cancer irritates the sac around the heart. |
| **Pleural effusion** | Fluid builds up around the lungs. This makes it hard to breathe. |
| **Superior vena cava syndrome** | A cancer blocks the large vein that returns blood from the upper body to the heart. This causes swelling in the face, neck, and upper chest. |
| **Spinal cord compression** | Cancer presses on the spinal cord or nerves. This can cause back pain and loss of control over the bladder or bowels. The longer the pressure lasts, the harder it is to recover normal function. |
| **Brain dysfunction** | Cancer in the brain—either starting there or spreading from elsewhere—can cause confusion, drowsiness, restlessness, headaches, vision changes, strange feelings, weakness, nausea, vomiting, or seizures. |
| **Bleeding** | Cancer can break down normal tissue and blood vessels. It can also grow fragile blood vessels inside the tumor. This can cause bleeding. |

---

## Pain

Many cancers do not cause pain at first. But some cancers, like brain tumors, can cause headaches early on. Cancers in the head, neck, or esophagus may cause pain when swallowing.

As cancer grows, the first sign is often a mild ache. This pain can get worse over time.

Pain happens when the cancer presses on or damages nerves or other body parts.

Not all cancers cause strong pain. And not feeling pain does not mean the cancer is not growing or spreading.

---

## Bleeding

Early on, a cancer may bleed a little because its blood vessels are weak.

As the cancer grows, it can invade nearby blood vessels. This can cause bleeding.

The bleeding may be so small it is not noticed. Or it may only show up in tests. This often happens in early colon cancer.

In later stages, bleeding can be serious. It can be heavy and even life-threatening.

Where the cancer is affects where the bleeding happens:

- Cancer in the digestive tract can cause blood in the stool.
- Cancer in the urinary tract can cause blood in the urine.
- Other cancers can bleed inside the body.
- Bleeding in the lungs can cause coughing up blood.

---

## Blood Clots

Some cancers make substances that cause blood to clot too much. This mostly happens in the veins of the legs.

A blood clot in a leg vein can break loose. It can travel to the lungs and block a blood vessel. This is called a pulmonary embolism. It can be deadly.

Too much clotting is common in people with pancreatic cancer, lung cancer, other solid tumors, and brain tumors.

---

## Weight Loss and Fatigue

Many people with cancer lose weight and feel very tired. These problems often get worse as the cancer grows.

Some people lose weight even if they are eating well. Others lose their appetite. They may feel sick when they eat or have trouble swallowing. They can become very thin.

People with advanced cancer are often extremely tired. If they also have anemia, even light activity can make them feel tired or short of breath.

---

## Swollen Lymph Nodes

When cancer starts to spread, it often moves first to nearby lymph nodes. These nodes can swell.

The swollen nodes are usually not painful. They may feel hard or rubbery.

They may move easily at first. But if the cancer is more advanced, they can stick to nearby tissues or to each other.

---

## Neurologic and Muscular Symptoms

Cancer can grow into or press on nerves or the spinal cord. This can cause:

- Pain
- Weakness
- Tingling or numbness

If cancer grows in the brain, symptoms can be hard to describe. They may include:

- Confusion
- Dizziness
- Headaches
- Nausea
- Vision changes
- Seizures

Some nerve and muscle problems are part of a paraneoplastic syndrome. This is when the body’s immune system reacts to cancer in a way that harms nerves or other tissues.

---

## Respiratory Symptoms

Cancer can press on or block the airways in the lungs. This can cause:

- Shortness of breath
- Cough
- Pneumonia

Shortness of breath can also happen if:

- A large amount of fluid builds up around the lungs (pleural effusion)
- There is bleeding in the lungs
- The person has anemia

# Respite Care

Family members often help care for older adults who are sick or disabled. This help can keep the older person at home longer. But caring for someone at home for a long time can be hard on the caregiver’s body and mind.

Respite care gives the main caregiver a break. Another person takes over the care for a short time. This gives the main caregiver time to rest, run errands, or just take care of themselves.

In the United States, more than half of the states offer respite care programs. These programs can happen in different places:

- At the older person’s home. This can be done by a respite care agency or a home health care agency.
- In the community. This includes adult day care centers, local respite care groups, or special facilities just for short-term care.
- In a long-term care facility. This might be a board-and-care home or a nursing home.
- In a hospital.

The length of respite care can vary. Some programs allow up to 28 days of care in one year.

Most of these programs are small. They usually have about 21 beds. They can be set up in apartments, motels, shelters for people without homes, or assisted living homes.

Support for these programs comes from many sources. This includes hospitals, government agencies, and private groups. The exact help available depends on the state.

(See also: Overview of Geriatric Care.)

# What You Need to Know About Antibiotics

Antibiotics are medicines that fight bacterial infections.  
They do not work against viruses.  
They also do not help with most other types of infections.

Antibiotics either kill bacteria or stop them from multiplying.  
This gives your body’s natural defenses a chance to clear the infection.

---

## How Doctors Choose Antibiotics

Doctors pick antibiotics based on the type of bacteria likely causing the infection.  
Sometimes, they start with a broad-spectrum antibiotic.  
This kind works against many different bacteria while waiting for test results.

Test results can take a day or two.  
If the infection is serious, doctors may start treatment right away.  
They choose an antibiotic that likely works against the most common bacteria.

When test results come back, doctors may switch to a different antibiotic if needed.

An antibiotic that works in a lab may not work in a person.  
This depends on:

- How well the medicine gets into the blood  
- How much reaches the infected area  
- How fast the body removes the medicine

These things can vary from person to person.  
Other medicines, health conditions, and age can affect how the antibiotic works.

Doctors also think about:

- How serious the infection is  
- How strong your immune system is  
- Possible side effects  
- Allergies or past bad reactions  
- The cost of the medicine  
- How easy it is to take the medicine as prescribed

Some people find it hard to take medicine on a strict schedule.  
For example, if you must take it many times a day or only at certain times (like before or after meals), it can be tough to follow through.

---

## When More Than One Antibiotic Is Needed

Doctors may use two or more antibiotics together when:

- The infection is very serious, especially early on  
- The bacteria can quickly become resistant to one antibiotic  
- The infection is caused by more than one type of bacteria  
- Each type needs a different antibiotic

---

## Antibiotic Resistance

Bacteria change over time.  
When antibiotics are used too much or not taken correctly, some bacteria survive.  
These bacteria can become resistant.  
This means the antibiotic no longer works.

For example, once, penicillin worked well against *Staphylococcus aureus*, a common cause of skin infections.  
But over time, the bacteria made an enzyme that broke down penicillin.  
Doctors made a new version of penicillin, but the bacteria adapted again.  
Now, many strains of this bacteria are resistant.

Other bacteria have also become resistant.

You can help stop resistance by:

- Knowing antibiotics do not treat viruses (like colds or the flu)  
- Taking antibiotics exactly as told  
- Using the right dose, number of times per day, and number of days  
- Finishing the full course, even if you feel better

> **Did You Know?**  
> Taking antibiotics for a virus does nothing.  
> It can also make bacteria stronger and harder to treat later.

---

## How Antibiotics Are Taken

For serious infections or when you can’t keep food or liquids down, antibiotics are given by injection.  
This is usually into a vein, but sometimes into a muscle.  
Once the infection is under control, you may switch to pills.

For milder infections, you can often start with pills.

### Special Considerations for Older Adults

Doctors may give a lower dose to older adults.  
Kidneys slow down with age.  
This means antibiotics stay in the body longer and can cause more side effects.

Doctors also check:

- What other medicines you are taking  
- If the treatment plan is too complicated  
- If you have family or caregivers to help

You must take antibiotics until all the bacteria are gone.  
This may take days after symptoms go away.  
Stopping early can let the infection come back.

A doctor, nurse, or pharmacist can explain:

- How to take the medicine  
- What side effects to watch for

Some antibiotics must be taken on an empty stomach.  
Others should be taken with food.  
For example, metronidazole causes bad reactions if you drink alcohol.  
Some antibiotics can interact with other medicines.  
This can reduce their effect or increase side effects.

Some antibiotics make your skin more sensitive to sunlight.

---

## Using Antibiotics to Prevent Infections

Doctors sometimes give antibiotics to prevent infections.  
This is called prophylaxis.

Examples include:

- Giving antibiotics to people who have been near someone with meningitis  
- Giving antibiotics before dental or surgery to people with artificial heart valves  
- Giving antibiotics before major surgery (like joint or intestinal surgery)

Doctors only give preventive antibiotics for a short time.  
This helps avoid resistance and side effects.

People with weak immune systems may need long-term antibiotics.  
This includes people with leukemia, cancer patients on chemotherapy, or people with HIV/AIDS.

---

## Antibiotics During Pregnancy and Breastfeeding

Doctors use antibiotics during pregnancy only when needed.  
Some are safer than others.

Safe options include:

- Penicillins  
- Cephalosporins  
- Erythromycin

Most antibiotics pass into breast milk.  
They can affect your baby.  
In some cases, you may need to stop breastfeeding or avoid the medicine.

If you are pregnant or breastfeeding and get an infection, talk to your doctor.  
Discuss the risks and benefits of treatment.

---

## Home Antibiotic Treatment

Most antibiotics are taken by mouth.  
But some infections—like bone infections (osteomyelitis) or heart infections (endocarditis)—may need IV antibiotics for weeks.

If you are well enough and have no other health issues, you can get IV antibiotics at home.

Short IV catheters (used in hospitals) last only a few days.  
For long treatment, a special catheter is used.  
It can be placed in:

- A large vein in the neck or chest (central catheter)  
- A small vein in the arm, threaded into a large vein (PICC line)

Some people and their families can learn to use the IV system at home.  
Others need a nurse to come and give each dose.

You will be closely watched for:

- Problems with the catheter site  
- Signs of infection in the blood

---

## Signs of a Catheter Infection

Watch for:

- Pain, redness, or pus at the catheter site  
- Chills or fever (even if the site looks fine)

If you see any of these, contact your doctor right away.

---

## Common Side Effects of Antibiotics

Side effects include:

- Upset stomach  
- Diarrhea  
- Vaginal yeast infections (in women)

Some side effects are serious.  
They can harm the kidneys, liver, bone marrow, or other organs.  
Blood tests may be done to check for damage.

---

## Severe Side Effect: *Clostridioides difficile* Colitis

Some antibiotics cause a serious bowel problem called *Clostridioides difficile* –induced colitis.

This happens when antibiotics kill good gut bacteria.  
The *C. diff* bacteria grow out of control and make toxins.  
This causes severe inflammation in the large intestine.

It is more common with certain antibiotics:

- Cephalosporins  
- Clindamycin  
- Fluoroquinolones  
- Penicillins

This condition can be life-threatening, especially in older adults.  
It is hard to treat and may need special medicine.

---

## Allergic Reactions to Antibiotics

Antibiotics can cause allergic reactions.

Mild reactions may include:

- Itchy rash  
- Slight wheezing

Severe reactions (anaphylaxis) are life-threatening.  
They can include:

- Swelling in the throat  
- Trouble breathing  
- Low blood pressure

Tell your doctor or nurse if you are allergic to any antibiotic.  
Describe your past reaction.

Not all bad reactions are allergies.  
For example, upset stomach or diarrhea may be side effects, not allergies.

If you are allergic to one antibiotic, you should avoid that drug and similar ones.  
Allergic reactions can be dangerous.

If you only had mild side effects before, you may still be able to take the same or similar antibiotics.

Healthcare providers can help decide if a reaction is serious or not.

# Mallory-Weiss Syndrome

This condition happens when the lining of the lower part of the food pipe (esophagus) or the upper part of the stomach tears.  
The tear is caused by forceful vomiting, dry heaving, or severe hiccups.  

It was first seen in people who drink too much alcohol.  
But anyone who vomits hard can get this tear.  
It causes about 5 to 10 out of every 100 cases of bleeding in the upper part of the digestive system.  

Some people feel pain in the lower chest.  

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor will ask about your symptoms.  
You may have vomited without blood, but then later vomited blood.  
If the bleeding is small and you feel stable, the doctor may wait before testing.  
Some people can go home without further tests.  

If the bleeding continues or the history is unclear, you will need tests.  
The main test is called upper endoscopy.  
This uses a thin tube with a camera to look inside the esophagus and stomach.  

The endoscopy can also treat the tear.  
A small clip can be placed on the tear to stop the bleeding.  

---

## How Is It Treated?

Most tears stop bleeding on their own.  
About 1 in 10 people have serious bleeding.  
These people need treatment such as blood transfusions or endoscopic procedures.  

Endoscopic treatments include:  
- Placing a clip on the tear.  
- Injecting a medicine like epinephrine or alcohol into the area.  
- Using heat (electrocautery) to seal the tear.  

In rare cases, doctors may use a special procedure during angiography.  
This involves giving medicine directly into a blood vessel to stop the bleeding.  

Surgery is very rarely needed.

# What Are Prion Diseases?

Prion diseases are very rare brain disorders. They are always serious and always fatal. There is no cure.

These diseases happen when a normal protein in the body changes into a harmful form. This harmful form is called a prion.

Before scientists learned about prions, they thought diseases like Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease were caused by viruses. But prions are not viruses. They are much smaller. Prions are not alive. They do not have DNA or any kind of genetic material.

The normal protein is called PrP C. It is found in all body cells, but mostly in the brain. In prion diseases, PrP C changes shape. It becomes a bad version called PrP Sc. This bad version is also called a prion.

The bad prion does not break down easily. It builds up slowly in the brain. It also causes nearby normal proteins to change into bad ones. This process keeps going. When enough bad prions build up, brain damage happens.

Once a protein becomes a prion, it never turns back into a normal protein.

The brain damage caused by prions creates tiny holes in brain tissue. The brain looks like a sponge under a microscope. This is why these diseases are called spongiform encephalopathies.

Over time, brain cells stop working and die. This leads to serious problems with thinking, movement, and behavior.

## Types of Prion Diseases

There are three main types of prion diseases:

### Sporadic Prion Diseases

These happen without any known cause. They are the most common type.

About 85 to 90 out of every 100 human prion disease cases are sporadic.

There are three types of sporadic prion disease:

- Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease  
- Fatal insomnia  
- Variably protease-sensitive prionopathy  

Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is the most common. It affects about 1 or 2 people per million each year worldwide.

Scientists do not know exactly how the first prion forms in sporadic cases. But they think a mistake in the body’s normal cell processes may cause a normal protein to change shape on its own.

### Familial Prion Diseases

These run in families. They are caused by a change in a gene that controls the PrP C protein.

This gene change makes the normal protein more likely to turn into a prion.

More than 50 different gene changes are known. Each one can cause a different type of prion disease.

These diseases are passed down in an autosomal dominant pattern. This means:

- The gene is not on the sex chromosomes (X or Y).
- Only one copy of the changed gene — from either parent — is enough to cause the disease.

The main types of familial prion disease are:

- Familial Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease  
- Fatal familial insomnia  
- Gerstmann-Sträussler-Scheinker disease  

A newer type has been found. It causes diarrhea and nerve problems in the body years before brain symptoms appear. It is called prion disease associated with diarrhea and autonomic neuropathy.

### Acquired Prion Diseases

These are rare. They happen when a person comes into contact with a prion from outside the body.

They can happen when:

- A person eats beef from cattle infected with prions (this causes variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease)
- A person receives a transplant of infected brain tissue or organ
- A person gets an injection of a prion-contaminated hormone
- A person has brain surgery using tools that were not properly cleaned
- A person receives a blood transfusion from someone with a prion disease (very rare)

Kuru is another acquired prion disease. It used to affect people in Papua New Guinea who practiced ritual cannibalism.

There is no evidence that prion diseases can spread through normal contact like hugging, touching, or being near someone with the disease.

## Prion Diseases in Animals

Prion diseases affect many animals, including:

- Sheep  
- Goats  
- Cattle  
- Elk  
- Deer  
- Minks  
- Cats  
- Camels  

These diseases can spread between animals when:

- An animal eats meat from an infected animal  
- An animal touches body fluids or waste from an infected animal  
- An animal walks on soil that has been contaminated by infected animals  
- An animal lives near infected animals  

Animals with prion diseases slowly lose coordination. They act strangely. Their brain function gets worse over time.

Scrapie is the name of the prion disease in sheep. It is called scrapie because infected sheep rub against fences or trees and tear off their wool.

Chronic wasting disease affects elk and deer. It is a big concern in parts of the United States, South Korea, Canada, Norway, Finland, and Sweden. People who hunt, butcher, or eat deer or elk from these areas may be at risk.

But so far, there are no confirmed cases of chronic wasting disease or scrapie causing disease in people.

Mad cow disease (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) is the name for the prion disease in cattle. The name comes from the way infected cows act — they become restless and agitated.

Scientists believe mad cow disease started when cattle were fed parts from infected sheep.

Eating beef from infected cattle can cause a rare form of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in people. This is called variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

It is sometimes called the human version of mad cow disease.

Variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is different from other forms of the disease:

- It causes different changes in brain tissue (seen under a microscope)
- The first symptoms are often mental health issues like anxiety or depression
- It does not start with memory loss or loss of balance like other forms

This disease was very rare. As of May 7, 2022:

- 178 cases were reported in the United Kingdom  
- 55 cases were reported in other countries  
- Total: 233 cases worldwide  

In the United Kingdom, the number of new cases peaked in 2000. Since then, the number has gone down steadily.

In the United States, only 4 cases have been found. All of them likely happened outside the country.

## Treatment of Prion Diseases

There is no cure for prion diseases. All of them are fatal.

Most people live only a few months to a few years after symptoms start.

Treatment focuses on making the person as comfortable as possible. It helps relieve symptoms.

Caregivers can use helpful strategies to support people with dementia caused by prion disease. (See sidebar: Creating a Beneficial Environment for People With Dementia.)

People with prion disease should talk about their wishes for medical care at the end of life. This is called making advance directives.

Hospice care is recommended for people with prion disease.

Family members who may have inherited a prion disease can get genetic counseling to understand their risk.

## Prevention of Prion Diseases

To stay safe:

- Do not eat meat from animals known or suspected to have prion disease.

Health care workers can prevent the spread of prion diseases by:

- Cleaning medical tools properly after use
- Using safe methods when handling infected tissues
- Protecting themselves when working with contaminated materials

# Hirschsprung Disease – Simple Explanation

Hirschsprung disease is a birth defect that affects the lower part of the bowel. It happens when nerves do not grow properly in part of the intestine. This causes a blockage because the bowel cannot move stool normally.

## What Causes Hirschsprung Disease?

The nerves in the bowel do not form correctly during pregnancy. This is due to a problem with nerve cells that should move from the back of the body into the bowel. When these cells do not reach the bowel, that part has no nerves. This is called aganglionosis.

This condition is linked to genes. More than 40 genes have been found to play a role. In some cases, one gene change causes the disease. In others, several gene changes are involved. Some children with Hirschsprung disease also have other birth defects, such as Down syndrome.

About 20 to 30 out of every 100 children with this disease have another birth defect. Some of these include:
- Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (Haddad syndrome)
- Waardenburg syndrome
- Bardet-Biedl syndrome
- Goldberg-Shprintzen syndrome
- Cartilage-hair hypoplasia

Boys are more likely to have Hirschsprung disease than girls. But if the whole colon is affected, boys and girls are equally likely to be affected.

## How Common Is It?

Hirschsprung disease affects about 1 in every 5,000 newborns.

## Where Does It Happen?

Most often, the problem is in the last part of the colon. In about 75% of cases, only the lower part is affected. In 3 to 10% of cases, the whole colon is involved. In rare cases, both the large and small intestines are affected. The part without nerves is always one continuous section.

## What Happens in the Bowel?

The part of the bowel without nerves cannot relax or move stool. This causes a constant muscle spasm. The stool builds up behind the blockage. The part of the bowel in front of the blockage gets very big and swollen. This is called dilation.

The blockage is always in one place. There are no skipped areas.

## Symptoms and Signs

### Babies (Newborns)

Most babies pass their first stool (meconium) within 24 hours of birth. Babies with Hirschsprung disease often do not pass meconium for more than 48 hours.

Symptoms in babies include:
- Not passing stool
- Swollen belly
- Vomiting
- Poor weight gain or slow growth

Some babies with a very short affected area may only have mild or occasional constipation. They may even have loose stools between times. This can delay diagnosis.

Some babies develop a serious bowel infection called Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis.

### Older Babies and Children

Symptoms may include:
- Not wanting to eat
- Constipation
- No urge to have a bowel movement
- A doctor finds an empty rectum during a check-up
- When the finger is removed, a large amount of stool comes out suddenly (called the "blast sign")

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Diagnosis should happen as soon as possible. The longer it is delayed, the higher the risk of a serious infection called Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis.

### Tests Used

1. **Barium enema**  
   - A special X-ray of the bowel using a liquid called barium.  
   - The test shows a clear change in size between the normal part of the bowel and the narrow, blocked part.  
   - The test should be done without any cleaning of the bowel first. If the bowel is cleaned, the results may be wrong.  
   - A follow-up X-ray 24 hours after the test is helpful. If the bowel still has barium, Hirschsprung disease is likely.

2. **Rectal biopsy**  
   - A small sample of tissue is taken from the rectum.  
   - This is the only way to confirm the diagnosis.  
   - The sample is checked for nerve cells. In Hirschsprung disease, these cells are missing.  
   - Special stains can help show nerve patterns.

3. **Rectal manometry**  
   - A small balloon is gently put into the rectum.  
   - The test checks if the muscle around the anus relaxes properly.  
   - In Hirschsprung disease, the muscle does not relax. This is a key sign.

### Important Note:
Do not do a barium enema if a child has signs of Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis. It can cause the bowel to burst.

## Treatment

The only treatment is surgery.

### What Surgery Does

The surgeon removes the part of the bowel that has no nerves. Then, the healthy part of the bowel is connected directly to the anus. The muscles around the anus are kept intact.

### Types of Surgery

- **Short-segment disease (only a small part affected):**  
  One surgery is done right away, or after waiting 1 to 3 months.

- **Long-segment disease (large part of colon affected):**  
  Two surgeries are needed.  
  - First, a colostomy is made. This lets stool leave the body through an opening in the belly. This helps the bowel rest and grow.  
  - Later, the second surgery removes the blocked part and connects the healthy bowel to the anus.

### Surgery Methods

- Open surgery (traditional method)  
- Laparoscopic surgery (smaller cuts, less pain, faster recovery)  

Both methods work well. Laparoscopic surgery often means shorter hospital stays and faster return to normal feeding.

### After Surgery

Most children do well after surgery. But some still have problems like:
- Constipation
- Bowel blockages
- Trouble moving stool

These issues may need ongoing care.

## Hirschsprung-Associated Enterocolitis (A Serious Complication)

This is a life-threatening infection of the bowel. It can happen in children with Hirschsprung disease.

### What Happens?

- The bowel becomes very swollen and stretched.
- The bowel wall becomes thin.
- Bacteria grow too much in the bowel.
- Bacteria can leak into the blood, causing sepsis and shock.

This can happen quickly and can be deadly. But with fast treatment, most children survive.

### Who Is at Risk?

- Most often happens in the first few months of life, before surgery.
- Can also happen after surgery, especially in the first year.
- Children with Down syndrome are at higher risk after surgery.

### Signs of Enterocolitis

- Fever (or unstable body temperature in newborns)
- Swollen belly
- Diarrhea (may be bloody or explosive)
- Later, no bowel movements

### What to Do If This Happens

- Do not do a barium enema. It can cause the bowel to burst.
- Immediate treatment includes:
  - Stop feeding the bowel (bowel rest)
  - Give fluids through a tube
  - Use tubes in the nose and rectum to remove gas and fluid
  - Give strong antibiotics that work against many types of bacteria, including anaerobes

Some doctors may gently clean the bowel with rectal irrigation. But this must be done carefully to avoid increasing pressure and causing a burst.

### Surgery for Enterocolitis

- If the child has not had surgery yet, surgery is needed.
- If the bowel has burst or is dead, surgery is urgent.
- In stable children, surgery can be done instead of making a stoma (like a colostomy).
- For very sick children, a stoma may still be the best first step.

## Key Points

- Hirschsprung disease is a birth defect where part of the bowel lacks nerves.
- It causes a blockage in the lower bowel.
- Babies often do not pass stool in the first 48 hours of life.
- Symptoms include a swollen belly, vomiting, and constipation.
- Diagnosis uses X-rays, rectal biopsy, and muscle function tests.
- Surgery is the only treatment. It removes the blocked part and connects healthy bowel to the anus.
- A serious infection called Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis can happen. It needs fast treatment.
- Most children do well after surgery, but some may have ongoing bowel problems.

# Infections During Pregnancy

Most infections during pregnancy, like bladder or lung infections, do not cause serious harm.  
But some infections can pass to the baby before or during birth.  
These can cause serious problems.  
They may lead to hearing loss, miscarriage, stillbirth, or early birth.

## Sexually Transmitted Infections

Some sexually transmitted infections can harm the baby. Here’s what you need to know:

- **Chlamydia** can cause early breaking of the water bag or early labor.  
  It can also give the baby an eye infection after birth.

- **Gonorrhea** can also cause eye infections in newborns.

- **Syphilis** can pass from mother to baby through the placenta.  
  It can cause birth defects, stillbirth, or serious health issues in the baby.  
  All pregnant women are tested for syphilis early in pregnancy.  
  Treatment during pregnancy usually cures both mother and baby.

- **HIV** can pass to the baby in about one out of four pregnancies if the mother is not treated.  
  Women with HIV should take antiretroviral medicines, especially during pregnancy.  
  For some women, a planned cesarean birth can lower the risk of passing HIV to the baby.

- **Genital herpes** can pass to the baby during a vaginal birth.  
  Babies with herpes can get a dangerous brain infection called herpes encephalitis.  
  The infection can also harm other organs, cause seizures, sores in the mouth and skin, brain damage, or even death.  
  If you have had herpes before, your doctor may give you medicine late in pregnancy to prevent an outbreak at delivery.  
  If you have symptoms or sores in the genital area late in pregnancy, your doctor will test you for herpes.  
  If the test is positive, you will likely be advised to have a cesarean birth.

- **Zika virus** can cause the baby to be born with a small head.  
  A small head means the brain did not grow properly.  
  Zika can also cause eye problems in the baby.  
  The virus spreads through mosquito bites.  
  It can also spread through sex, blood transfusions, or from mother to baby during pregnancy or birth.

## Other Infections That Can Cause Problems

Some other infections can also harm the baby:

- **Rubella** (German measles) can cause poor growth before birth, cataracts, heart defects, hearing loss, or delayed development.

- **Cytomegalovirus** can cross the placenta and harm the baby’s liver and brain.  
  The baby may not grow as expected.

- **Chickenpox** (varicella) raises the risk of miscarriage.  
  It can damage the baby’s eyes, cause limb defects, blindness, or intellectual disability.  
  The baby’s head may be smaller than normal.

- **Toxoplasmosis** is a parasite infection.  
  It can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, or serious birth defects.

- **Listeriosis** is a bacterial infection.  
  It raises the risk of early labor, miscarriage, or stillbirth.  
  The baby may be born with the infection, but symptoms may not show for weeks.

- **Bacterial vaginosis** (a vaginal infection) can lead to early labor or early breaking of the water bag.

- **Urinary tract infections** can also raise the risk of early labor or early breaking of the water bag.

- **Hepatitis** can spread through sex, but it often spreads in other ways.  
  It is not usually seen as a sexually transmitted infection.  
  Hepatitis in a pregnant woman can raise the risk of early birth.  
  It can also pass to the baby during delivery and cause health problems.

## Treating Infections During Pregnancy

Doctors decide whether to treat infections with medicine by weighing the risks and benefits.

They look at the risks of the infection and the risks of the medicine.

Some antibiotics are safe during pregnancy. These include:
- Penicillins
- Cephalosporins
- Macrolides (like erythromycin)

Other antibiotics, such as tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones, can harm the baby.  
Always check with your doctor before taking any medicine.

Most antiviral medicines are safe during pregnancy.  
But talk to your doctor before starting any new medicine.

Doctors also ask: Will treatment help?  
For example, if you have bacterial vaginosis but no symptoms and your pregnancy is low-risk, treating it may not help.

# Paget Disease of the Breast

Paget disease of the breast is a rare type of breast cancer.  
It starts in the milk ducts under the nipple and spreads to the skin of the nipple and areola.  
The skin looks red, scaly, and may ooze or crust.  
It often looks like a skin rash, but it is not a rash.  

This disease usually affects only one breast.  
It is not the same as Paget disease of the bones, which is a different condition.

## What Causes Paget Disease of the Breast?

The disease happens when cancer cells from inside the breast move to the skin of the nipple and areola.  
The cancer usually starts in the milk ducts.  
In many cases, the cancer has already spread to other parts of the body when the disease is found.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor will take a small sample of the skin (a biopsy) to check for cancer.  
The skin changes look like a skin infection, but they do not get better with creams or ointments.  
The rash is sharp and clear at the edges.  
It only affects one side.  

Because this is a sign of breast cancer, the doctor will do more tests.  
These may include a physical exam, imaging tests like a mammogram or ultrasound, and other checks for cancer in the body.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on whether there is a hidden breast cancer under the skin.  

If there is a breast cancer, treatment is the same as for other breast cancers.  
This may include surgery to remove the cancer.  
The nipple and areola are usually removed.  
Sometimes, the whole breast is removed.  

If no cancer is found in the breast, the doctor may still remove the nipple and areola.  
After that, radiation therapy may be used.  

For Paget disease in other areas (like the groin or around the anus), treatment options include:  
- Surgery  
- Creams applied to the skin (like 5-fluorouracil or imiquimod)  
- Light therapy (photodynamic therapy)  
- Radiation therapy  
- Laser treatment  

A full check-up is needed to make sure there is no cancer inside the body, such as in the bladder, rectum, or anus.  
This is because some cases of extramammary Paget disease come from cancer in these areas.

# Pica

Pica is a condition where a person regularly eats things that are not food.

- People with pica often eat things like paper, clay, dirt, or hair.
- In most cases, eating these things does not cause harm.
- But sometimes, it can lead to serious problems.

## What Can Go Wrong

Some things people with pica eat can cause health issues. These include:

- Low levels of iron or zinc in the body
- Trouble passing stool (constipation)
- Blockages in the stomach or intestines
- Poisoning from lead (for example, from eating paint chips)
- Infections from parasites (if dirt is eaten)

## Who Gets Pica?

- Pica is not diagnosed in children under 2 years old. At that age, it is normal for kids to put things in their mouths.
- Some people eat nonfood items during pregnancy.
- Pica can also happen in people with low iron levels.
- It is more common in people with certain mental health conditions, such as autism, intellectual disability, or schizophrenia.
- Pica is not the same as self-harm or pretending to be sick.

## Cultural Practices

In some places, eating nonfood items is part of a tradition. For example, some people in the Georgia Piedmont eat clay as part of their culture. This is not considered pica if it is part of a cultural practice.

## How Doctors Diagnose Pica

Doctors look for signs of pica using these steps:

- They ask about what the person has been eating.
- They check if the person has been eating nonfood items for at least one month.
- They do not diagnose pica in children under 2 years old.
- They do not diagnose pica if eating nonfood items is part of a cultural tradition.

If pica is suspected, doctors may:

- Check the person’s weight and overall health.
- Run blood tests to check for lead or low iron.
- Do stool tests to check for parasites.
- Take X-rays to look for blockages in the digestive system.

## How Pica Is Treated

There is no standard treatment for pica. But some options may help:

- Behavioral therapy can help people stop eating nonfood items and learn better habits.
- Doctors treat any health problems that come from pica.
  - For example, low iron or zinc levels are treated with supplements.
  - Blockages in the digestive system may need surgery.

Pica often goes away on its own, especially in children. It can last for several months.

# Goldenseal

Goldenseal is a plant that is in danger of disappearing in the United States. It is related to the buttercup plant. The main active parts of goldenseal are hydrastine and berberine. These parts can kill germs. Goldenseal comes in liquid, tablet, and capsule forms. The products are made to have a set amount of the active parts.

## What People Use Goldenseal For

Some people use goldenseal to clean sores in the mouth. They also use it for red, sore eyes and irritated skin. Some use it as a wash inside the vagina for infections. It is often mixed with echinacea to help with colds. Some people also use it to help with an upset stomach or diarrhea.

## What the Research Shows

There is no strong proof that goldenseal alone helps with colds.  
Two small but well-done studies found that berberine, the main active part in goldenseal, helped reduce diarrhea caused by cholera.  
Berberine also helped reduce symptoms in people with diarrhea that comes and goes with irritable bowel syndrome.  
There are very few recent large studies that test goldenseal in people.  

Some research shows that berberine may help people with diabetes. It can lower blood sugar levels before eating and after eating. It can also lower a long-term blood sugar measure called hemoglobin A1C.  
A review of 28 studies found that berberine worked better when used with diabetes medicines than when used alone.  
But its effect gets weaker after 90 days of use. It also works less well in people over 60 years old.

For high cholesterol, a review of 16 studies found that berberine lowered total cholesterol and bad cholesterol (LDL). It also lowered triglycerides and raised good cholesterol (HDL).  
But the results from these studies were very different. The quality of the studies was not always strong.

Berberine has also been used to help with weight loss. A review of 12 studies found that people taking berberine lost weight. They also had lower body mass index, smaller waist size, and lower levels of a marker linked to inflammation.

## Side Effects of Goldenseal

Goldenseal can cause side effects. These include nausea, feeling anxious, stomach pain, and strong contractions in the uterus. It can also cause yellowing of the skin in newborn babies.  
Taking too much goldenseal can cause seizures and breathing problems. It may also affect how the heart beats.  
Women who are pregnant or breastfeeding should not take goldenseal.  
Newborn babies should not take it.  
People with seizure disorders or blood clotting problems should avoid it.  
A lab study found that berberine in goldenseal may damage DNA. This could raise the risk of cancer.

## Drug Interactions

Goldenseal may interact with warfarin, a blood thinner.  
Berberine may make heparin, another blood thinner, stronger.  
Berberine can block certain liver enzymes. This can raise the levels of some medicines in the blood. These include:  
- Midazolam  
- Omeprazole  
- Dextromethorphan  
- Losartan  
- Tacrolimus  
- Caffeine  

Goldenseal may raise the levels of cyclosporine, a medicine used after organ transplants.  
It may lower the levels of metformin, a common diabetes medicine. This could make blood sugar harder to control.  
The berberine in goldenseal may also make other diabetes medicines work stronger, which could cause low blood sugar.
