# Pneumococcal Vaccine

This vaccine helps protect you from serious infections caused by a type of bacteria called *Streptococcus pneumoniae*. These infections can include ear infections, sinus infections, pneumonia, blood infections, and meningitis.

---

## Types of Pneumococcal Vaccines

There are more than 90 types of this bacteria. The vaccines protect against the types most likely to cause serious illness.

There are two main types of vaccines: conjugate and polysaccharide.

- **PCV13** protects against 13 types of the bacteria.  
  It is no longer used in the United States for routine use in children. It may be used in some adults 65 years and older who do not have a weak immune system.

- **PCV15** protects against 15 types of the bacteria.

- **PCV20** protects against 20 types of the bacteria.

- **PCV21** protects against 21 types of the bacteria.

- **PPSV23** protects against 23 types of the bacteria.

All of these vaccines contain small, harmless parts of the bacteria. These parts cannot cause infection. But they help your body learn how to fight the real bacteria if you are ever exposed.

---

## Who Should Get the Vaccine and When

All conjugate vaccines (PCV13, PCV15, PCV20, PCV21) are given as an injection into a muscle.

The PPSV23 vaccine is given under the skin or into a muscle.

Your age and health condition will decide which vaccine you need and when.

### Children

Pneumococcal vaccine is a routine shot for all children.

Children get four doses:
- At 2 months old
- At 4 months old
- At 6 months old
- At 12 to 15 months old

Most children get either PCV15 or PCV20.

Some children with a weak immune system may get PPSV23 instead.

Children under 5 years old should get all four doses.

Children ages 5 to 18 who have not had the vaccine do not need it unless they have certain health problems. These include:
- Long-term heart or lung disease
- Diabetes
- A leak of spinal fluid
- A cochlear implant
- A weak immune system

### Adults Ages 19 to 49

You should get a pneumococcal vaccine if you:
- Have certain health conditions or risk factors
- Have never had a conjugate vaccine
- Do not know your vaccination history

You can get:
- One dose of PCV20
- One dose of PCV21
- One dose of PCV15, followed by one dose of PPSV23

**Health conditions and risk factors include:**
- Chronic kidney disease or nephrotic syndrome
- A leak of spinal fluid
- A weak immune system (from HIV, leukemia, lymphoma, advanced cancer, or medicines that lower immunity)
- A spleen that does not work well (such as in sickle cell disease)
- A cochlear implant
- Long-term heart, lung, or liver disease (including asthma and emphysema)
- Diabetes
- Alcohol use disorder
- Smoking cigarettes

### Adults Ages 50 and Older

If you have never had a conjugate vaccine or do not know your history, you should get:
- One dose of PCV20
- One dose of PCV21
- One dose of PCV15, followed by one dose of PPSV23

### Timing Between Vaccines

For people 50 and under:
- Wait at least 1 year after PCV15 before getting PPSV23.
- In some cases, such as for people with a weak immune system, a cochlear implant, or a spinal fluid leak, you can wait as little as 8 weeks.

### Adults Ages 65 and Older

You may get PCV13 only after talking with your doctor. This is only if you have no health problems or risk factors.

All adults 65 and older should get one dose of PPSV23.

If you get PCV13, wait at least 1 year before getting PPSV23.

---

## Who Should Not Get the Vaccine

Do not get the vaccine if you:
- Had a serious allergic reaction (like anaphylaxis) to any part of PCV13, PCV15, PCV20, or PCV21
- Had a serious allergic reaction to any vaccine that contains diphtheria toxoid (such as DTaP)

Do not get PPSV23 if you:
- Had a serious allergic reaction to any part of PPSV23
- Had a serious reaction to a previous dose of PPSV23

If you are sick with a fever or a temporary illness, your doctor may wait to give the vaccine until you feel better.

---

## Side Effects

Common side effects include:
- Pain or redness at the injection site
- Fever
- Feeling irritable
- Feeling sleepy
- Loss of appetite
- Vomiting

For more details about side effects, check the vaccine package insert.

# After Your Surgery

Care after surgery starts right after your operation. It continues in the recovery area and through your hospital stay and any follow-up visits.

## What the Care Team Will Watch For

- **Breathing and airway**: They will make sure you can breathe well and your airway stays open.
- **Fluids and blood pressure**: They will check your fluid levels and blood pressure to keep them in a safe range.
- **Blood clots**: They will take steps to prevent dangerous blood clots in your legs or lungs.
- **Pain**: They will help you manage any pain you feel.
- **Mental alertness**: They will check how clear your mind is and how well you are thinking.
- **Wound healing**: They will watch your surgical wound to make sure it is healing properly.

## Other Common Issues

- **Nausea and vomiting**: Some people feel sick to their stomach after surgery. Medicines can help.
- **Urinary retention**: Some people have trouble urinating after surgery. A tube may be needed temporarily.
- **Constipation**: You may have trouble having a bowel movement. This is common after surgery and can be managed with diet and medicine.

## Special Care for People with Diabetes

If you have diabetes, your blood sugar will be checked often. They will use a small needle to test your finger every one to four hours. This will continue until you are awake and eating normally. Keeping your blood sugar under control helps you heal better and reduces risks.

# Trimethoprim and Sulfamethoxazole

Trimethoprim is an antibiotic. It can be taken alone or with another antibiotic called sulfamethoxazole.

The combination of trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole is stronger than either drug alone. This makes it more effective at fighting certain infections.

This medicine works by stopping bacteria from making a type of folic acid they need to survive.

## What It Is Used For

Trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole are used to treat:

- Infections caused by bacteria that do not respond to other antibiotics
- Infections caused by methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus* (MRSA)
- Chronic prostate infections (prostatitis)
- Bladder infections in women
- Recurring urinary tract infections in women and children
- Intestinal infections caused by bacteria like *Escherichia coli* (E. coli)
- Pneumonia caused by a fungus called *Pneumocystis jirovecii*

Trimethoprim alone is used for:

- Prostate infections
- Urinary tract infections in people who are allergic to sulfamethoxazole

## Possible Side Effects

Common side effects include:

- Upset stomach
- Vomiting
- Diarrhea
- Skin rashes or other allergic reactions

Less common side effects:

- Crystals in the urine (rare)
- Lower levels of white blood cells and platelets
- Increased sensitivity to sunlight
- Higher risk of bleeding if taken with warfarin
- Kidney problems in people with poor kidney function

Trimethoprim has similar side effects to sulfamethoxazole, but they happen less often.

## Use During Pregnancy

Do not take trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole during the first three months of pregnancy. This medicine may cause serious birth defects, such as spina bifida.

Do not use this medicine during pregnancy or in newborns. It can cause jaundice and brain damage in the baby.

## Use While Breastfeeding

Avoid using trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole while breastfeeding. Sulfamethoxazole passes into breast milk.

Trimethoprim is usually safe to use while breastfeeding.

# Vestibular Schwannoma (Acoustic Neuroma)

A vestibular schwannoma is a noncancerous growth on a nerve that helps with hearing and balance. It grows slowly and usually affects only one side of the head.

## What Causes It?

- The tumor starts in the eighth cranial nerve, which controls hearing and balance.
- It most often begins in the part of the nerve that handles balance.
- In rare cases, people with a genetic condition called neurofibromatosis type 2 get tumors on both sides of the head.

## How the Tumor Grows

- The tumor starts inside a small canal near the inner ear.
- As it grows, it pushes into the space behind the brainstem.
- It can press on nearby nerves, including those for facial movement, facial sensation, and other brain functions.

## Symptoms

The most common symptom is hearing loss in one ear. This may come on slowly or suddenly. It can also come and go.

Other early signs include:
- Ringing in one ear (tinnitus)
- Dizziness or feeling unsteady
- A full or blocked feeling in the ear
- Headaches
- Ear pain
- Sharp facial pain (trigeminal neuralgia)
- Numbness or weakness in the face

## How It Is Diagnosed

Doctors use several tests to find a vestibular schwannoma.

### First Test: Hearing Test (Audiogram)
- This test checks how well you hear different sounds.
- It often shows hearing loss that is worse on one side.
- It may also show that you have trouble understanding speech, even if the sound is loud enough.

### Imaging Test: MRI with Contrast
- A special MRI scan with a dye (gadolinium) is the best way to see the tumor.
- The scan can show the size and exact location of the growth.
- Sometimes, the tumor is found by accident during an MRI done for another reason.

### Other Tests
- **Tympanometry**: Checks how the eardrum moves. It may show a change in the reflex response.
- **Auditory brain stem response test**: Measures how fast signals travel from the ear to the brain. Delays or missing signals can point to a tumor.
- **Caloric testing**: Checks balance function. It often shows weak response on the side with the tumor.

## Treatment Options

Treatment depends on the size of the tumor, your symptoms, your hearing, and your overall health.

### Watch and Wait
- Small tumors that are not growing and do not cause symptoms do not need treatment.
- Doctors may check with repeat MRI scans every 6 to 12 months.
- Treatment starts only if the tumor grows or causes new problems.

### Surgery
- Surgery removes the tumor.
- The type of surgery depends on your hearing and the tumor size.
- If you still have useful hearing, surgeons may use a method that tries to keep your hearing.
- If hearing is already gone, a different surgery may be used that goes through the inner ear.

### Radiation Therapy
- This uses focused beams of radiation to stop the tumor from growing.
- It is often used for older patients, those with small tumors, or those who cannot have surgery.
- It is not a cure, but it can stop the tumor from getting bigger.

## Key Facts

- Most vestibular schwannomas affect only one side of the head.
- People with neurofibromatosis type 2 may have tumors on both sides.
- The main signs are hearing loss, ringing in the ear, and dizziness.
- Larger tumors or those causing symptoms are treated with surgery or radiation.
- Small, harmless tumors that are not growing can be watched over time with regular MRI scans.

# Tapeworm Infection – Simple Explanation

Tapeworms are parasites that live in the intestines. They can make you sick. You usually get them by eating raw or undercooked meat or fish that has the worm in it. You can also get them from food or water that has been touched by human poop.

---

## Types of Tapeworms

There are several types of tapeworms that can infect people:

- **Beef tapeworm** – Found in undercooked beef.
- **Pork tapeworm** – Found in undercooked pork.
- **Asian tapeworm** – Found in pork in parts of Asia.
- **Fish tapeworm** – Found in raw or undercooked freshwater fish.
- **Dwarf tapeworm** – Very small. You get it by swallowing tiny eggs from dirty food or water.

---

## How Tapeworms Work

Tapeworms have three main parts:

- The **head** – This part sticks to the inside of your intestine.
- The **neck** – This can grow new parts of the worm.
- The **body** – Made of many segments. Each segment can hold eggs.

If the head and neck are not fully removed, the worm can grow back.

---

## How You Get Infected

### Pork, Beef, and Fish Tapeworms

1. You eat raw or undercooked meat or fish that has tiny worm cysts in it.
2. The cysts break open in your gut and turn into adult worms.
3. The adult worms attach to your intestine and grow long.
4. They make new segments full of eggs.
5. The eggs leave your body in your stool.
6. If the stool gets into the environment, pigs, cows, or fish can eat the eggs.
7. The eggs turn into larvae in the animal’s body.
8. The cycle starts again when someone eats the infected meat or fish.

### Dwarf Tapeworm

- You swallow the tiny eggs from food, water, or surfaces touched by infected people.
- The eggs hatch in your gut and grow into adult worms.
- The worms lay eggs that come out in your stool.
- You can swallow your own eggs and get infected again. This is called **autoinfection**.
- This can lead to many worms in your body, which can cause more symptoms.

---

## What Happens in the Body

### Intestinal Tapeworms

Most people with adult tapeworms in their intestines feel fine. But some may have:

- Belly pain
- Diarrhea
- Weight loss
- Feeling a piece of worm come out of the anus
- Seeing worm parts in the stool

The dwarf tapeworm is more likely to cause nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite.

The fish tapeworm can cause **anemia**. It takes vitamin B12 from your body. This vitamin is needed to make healthy blood cells.

### Cysticercosis

This happens when you swallow pork tapeworm eggs. The eggs turn into larvae that travel through your body and form cysts in places like the brain, muscles, liver, lungs, or eyes.

Cysts in the brain can cause:

- Headaches
- Seizures
- Confusion
- Memory problems
- Muscle weakness
- Paralysis
- Blindness (if cysts form in the eyes)

These symptoms can show up years after the original infection. They happen when the cysts break down and cause swelling and irritation.

---

## How Doctors Find the Infection

### For Intestinal Tapeworms

- A doctor checks your stool for worm segments or eggs.

### For Cysticercosis

- A CT scan or MRI can show cysts in the brain or other parts of the body.
- Blood tests can check for signs of infection.
- Sometimes, a doctor can feel hard lumps under the skin.

---

## How It’s Treated

### For Tapeworms in the Intestine

- A single dose of medicine called **praziquantel** kills the worm.
- For dwarf tapeworms, a different medicine called **nitazoxanide** may be used.

### For Cysticercosis (Cysts in the Brain or Body)

- If cysts are in the brain and causing symptoms, doctors may give:
  - **Corticosteroids** to reduce swelling and inflammation.
  - **Antiparasitic medicine** like albendazole or praziquantel to kill the cysts.
- These medicines are only used after symptoms are under control.
- Corticosteroids are also given with the antiparasitic medicine to prevent bad reactions from dying cysts.
- If seizures happen, antiseizure medicine is also given.

**Important:** Antiparasitic medicines are not used for cysts in the eye or spinal cord. They can cause serious swelling and damage.

- Surgery may be needed if:
  - Cysts block the flow of fluid around the brain or spinal cord.
  - Cysts are causing serious problems in the eye or spinal cord.

---

## How to Prevent Tapeworms

### Cook Meat and Fish Thoroughly

- Cook whole cuts of meat to **145 degrees Fahrenheit (63 degrees Celsius)** for at least 3 minutes.
- Let the meat rest for 3 minutes after cooking before eating.
- Cook ground meat to **160 degrees Fahrenheit (71 degrees Celsius)**.
- Do not use a rest time for ground meat.

### Cook or Freeze Freshwater Fish

- Never eat freshwater fish raw (like in sushi).
- Cook it to **145 degrees Fahrenheit (63 degrees Celsius)**.
- Or freeze it properly to kill the worm:

  - At **-4 degrees Fahrenheit (-20 degrees Celsius)** for 7 days.
  - At **-31 degrees Fahrenheit (-35 degrees Celsius)** until solid, then keep at that temperature for 15 hours.
  - At **-31 degrees Fahrenheit (-35 degrees Celsius)** until solid, then keep at **-4 degrees Fahrenheit (-20 degrees Celsius)** for 24 hours.

- Smoking or drying fish does **not** kill the worm.

### Check Meat and Fish

- Trained inspectors can spot cysts in meat. This helps stop infected meat from being sold.

### Handle Waste Safely

- Properly treat human waste to stop the cycle of infection.
- This helps prevent beef and pork tapeworms, including cysticercosis.

### Avoid Dirty Food and Water

- Wash, peel, or cook all raw fruits and vegetables before eating, especially when traveling.
- Wash your hands with soap and warm water after using the toilet, changing diapers, or handling dirty items.
- Avoid eating grains that might have bugs like fleas or beetles.

---

## Key Facts

- Tapeworms can grow up to 30 feet long.
- Most people with intestinal tapeworms feel no symptoms.
- The dwarf tapeworm is more likely to cause stomach problems.
- Cysts in the brain can cause serious health issues years later.
- Cooking meat and fish well is the best way to stay safe.
- Good hygiene and clean water are key to preventing infection.

# Tests for Skin Problems

Sometimes, a doctor needs more than just a look and a talk to figure out what is wrong with your skin. These tests help when the cause is not clear.

Here are common tests:

- Patch testing  
- Skin biopsy  
- Skin scrapings  
- Wood light exam  
- Tzanck test  
- Diascopy  

(See also: Evaluation of the Dermatologic Patient.)

---

## Skin Biopsy

A skin biopsy takes a small sample of skin to check for disease. There are three main types:

### Punch Biopsy
A small, round tool (about 4 millimeters wide) is used to remove a deeper piece of skin. The sample is cut off at the base.

### Shave Biopsy
A razor or scalpel is used to cut off a thin layer of skin. This works best for skin problems near the surface. If there is bleeding, the doctor uses a special solution or heat to stop it.

### Wedge Excision
A larger or deeper piece of skin is cut out with a scalpel. The cut is then closed with stitches.

Pigmented spots (dark spots) are sometimes removed to check how deep they go. If they are too shallow, the doctor may not get a clear answer. For many small skin tumors, removing the whole growth with a small border of normal skin can both diagnose and cure the problem.

---

## Skin Scrapings

Skin scrapings help find fungal infections and scabies.

### For Fungal Infections
The doctor takes a small piece of flaky skin from the edge of the rash. This is placed on a glass slide. A drop of a special liquid (potassium hydroxide) is added. If the test shows thread-like growths or yeast, it means you have a fungal infection like ringworm or yeast infection.

### For Scabies
The doctor scrapes skin from a suspected burrow (tiny tunnel under the skin). The sample is placed under a cover slip with oil. If mites, their waste, or eggs are seen, scabies is confirmed. But a negative result does not rule out scabies. Some people have scabies even if the test is negative.

---

## Wood Light Exam

A Wood light is a special black light. It helps doctors see skin problems better.

It can show the exact edges of a dark spot before surgery. It can also tell the difference between:
- Skin that has lost color (hypopigmentation) — this does not glow
- Skin that has no pigment at all (depigmentation), like in vitiligo — this glows a pale white

Other things that glow under the light:
- Erythrasma (a bacterial skin infection) glows bright orange-red
- Some types of scalp ringworm (tinea capitis) caused by *Microsporum canis* or *M. audouinii* glow bright green
  - Note: Most scalp ringworm in the U.S. is caused by *Trichophyton* species, which do not glow
- Early signs of a *Pseudomonas* skin infection (like in burns) may show green glow

---

## Tzanck Test

This test checks for certain viral infections, like cold sores (herpes simplex) or shingles (herpes zoster). It works best when you have active, unbroken blisters.

The doctor removes the top of the blister with a sharp blade. Then, the base is gently scraped with a small blade. The sample is put on a slide and stained. If the lab sees large cells with many nuclei, it means you have a herpes virus infection.

This test cannot tell the difference between herpes simplex and herpes zoster.

Photo courtesy of Joe Miller via the Public Health Image Library of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

---

## Diascopy

Diascopy helps doctors tell if redness in the skin is due to blood in small blood vessels (inflammation) or due to bleeding under the skin (like tiny red spots).

The doctor presses a glass slide firmly against the skin. If the redness fades (blanches), it is due to blood in the vessels. If the redness stays, it is due to bleeding under the skin.

Diascopy can also help find sarcoidosis in the skin. When tested, the skin turns a color like apple jelly.

# Who Makes Medical Decisions When Someone Can’t?

If a person cannot make their own health care choices, someone else must step in. This person is called a surrogate decision maker.

If there is no written health care power of attorney and no court-appointed guardian, health care teams usually turn to the person’s closest family member or a close friend. This is called a default surrogate decision maker.

Most states allow this. But the rules vary by state. Some states list who can decide in a certain order. Others let a close friend act as the decision maker. (See also: Overview of Legal and Ethical Issues in Health Care.)

---

## For Adults

In most states, the order for who can make decisions is:

- Spouse or domestic partner  
- Adult child  
- Parent  
- Sibling  
- Other relatives (if needed)

More states now also allow a close friend to make decisions if no family member is available.

If several people have the same rank—like three adult children—everyone should agree. But if they cannot agree, some states allow a majority vote. Some states let one person be chosen to speak for the group.

Doctors prefer to follow the person who understands the medical situation and truly wants what is best for the patient.

If there is a disagreement among decision makers, it can slow down or block care.

People with no family or close friends in the hospital are more likely to get a court-appointed guardian or conservator.

If it is unclear who should decide, doctors may ask the hospital’s ethics team or a lawyer for help.

In states without clear rules, doctors still rely on family members. But legal confusion or family fights can delay or stop treatment.

---

## For Children

Children under 18 years old usually cannot give legal consent for medical care.

For most medical decisions, a parent or legal guardian must give permission.

A parent’s decision can only be overruled by a court if it is seen as neglect or abuse.

There are two main exceptions:

1. **Emancipated minors** – These are young people who live on their own and manage their own lives. They can give consent for all medical care.
2. **Certain treatments** – In most states, minors can consent to care for:
   - Sexually transmitted infections
   - Birth control
   - Abortion
   - Drug or substance use treatment
   - Mental health care

Each state has its own rules. So the exact rights depend on where the person lives.

---

## How to Make Medical Decisions

The goal is to include the patient in decisions as much as possible.

All decision makers—whether chosen by the patient, by a court, or by default—must follow the patient’s known wishes and values.

Health care teams must respect these wishes and values too.

If the patient’s wishes are not known, the decision maker must act in the patient’s best interest.

Health care providers do not have to offer treatments that are not medically sound or go against accepted medical standards.

If a doctor personally disagrees with a treatment but it is still considered acceptable by medical standards, the doctor must try to find another doctor or hospital that will provide it. In most states, this is required by law.

---

### Steps to Make a Good Decision

When you are making a medical decision for someone, start by learning the facts from the health care team. Ask about:

- The diagnosis (what is wrong)
- The prognosis (what to expect)
- The treatment options

When facing a tough choice, ask yourself:

- Will this treatment or test really help? How?
- Are the risks or side effects worse than the benefits?
- Is there a chance of getting better? What will life be like after?
- What is the main goal of this treatment? Does it match what the patient wants?

# Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GISTs)

Gastrointestinal stromal tumors are rare growths in the digestive system.  
They start in special cells in the wall of the gut.  
These cells are called interstitial cells of Cajal.  

Most GISTs are found during an endoscopy.  
The main treatment is surgery to remove the tumor.  

GISTs are a type of soft-tissue cancer.  
They are the most common kind of cancer in the digestive tract.  
About 4,000 to 6,000 new cases happen each year in the United States.  

GISTs are caused by changes in certain genes.  
The most common change is in the *C-KIT* gene.  
Some GISTs are caused by a change in the *PDGFRA* gene.  
A few happen after radiation treatment to the belly for another cancer.  
The rest have other rare gene changes. These are called wild-type GISTs.  

In one study:  
- 51% of GISTs were in the stomach.  
- 36% were in the small intestine.  
- A few were in the esophagus, colon, or rectum.  

Most people with GISTs are between 50 and 60 years old.  

Some people get GISTs because of a genetic condition.  
The two most common are:  
- Neurofibromatosis type 1  
- Familial SDH deficiency (also called Carney-Stratakis syndrome)  

GISTs often grow slowly.  
But they can behave in many different ways.  
Some are harmless. Others can spread and become dangerous.  

How dangerous a GIST is depends on:  
- Where it is in the digestive system  
- How big it is  
- How fast the cells are dividing (called the mitotic rate)  

Small tumors in the stomach with slow cell growth have the best outcomes.  
Tumors smaller than 2 centimeters have a very low chance of spreading.  
They are often watched instead of treated right away.  

Symptoms depend on where the tumor is.  
Common symptoms include:  
- Bleeding in the stomach or intestines  
- Upset stomach or heartburn  
- Blockage in the digestive system  

Many GISTs are found by accident.  
They show up on scans done for another reason.  

---

## How GISTs Are Diagnosed

### Endoscopy

Doctors usually find GISTs during an endoscopy.  
This is a test that uses a thin tube with a camera to look inside the stomach and intestines.  
A small sample of tissue (biopsy) is taken.  
An endoscopic ultrasound may also be done to check the size and depth of the tumor.  

### Lab Tests

Special lab tests are done on the tissue sample.  
If the cells stain positive for CD117 (also called C-KIT) or DOG-1, it confirms the diagnosis of GIST.  

### Imaging

After diagnosis, all patients need a full scan.  
This includes a CT scan of the chest, belly, and pelvis.  
This helps check if the cancer has spread.  

---

## How GISTs Are Treated

### Surgery

For early-stage GISTs, surgery is the main treatment.  
The goal is to remove the tumor completely.  

For advanced cases, surgery may still be an option.  
This depends on:  
- How much the liver is affected  
- How big the tumor is  
- Whether it can be safely removed  

### Medicine After Surgery

Some patients get medicine after surgery.  
This is called adjuvant therapy.  
It helps lower the risk of the cancer coming back.  

Imatinib is the most common medicine used.  
It works best for tumors that have the CD117 protein.  

Imatinib is usually given for 3 years after surgery.  
Some studies suggest longer treatment may help, but more research is needed.  

### Shrinking Tumors Before Surgery

Imatinib can also be used before surgery.  
It helps shrink tumors that are hard to remove.  
This makes surgery easier or possible when it wasn’t before.  

### For Tumors That Do Not Respond to Imatinib

If the cancer does not respond to imatinib, other medicines can be used.  
These include sunitinib and regorafenib.  

### Special Case: PDGFRA Exon 18 Mutations

For patients with a specific gene change in the PDGFRA gene (including D842V), avapritinib is the best first-choice medicine.  
It works better than other options for this type of tumor.

# Swan-Neck Deformity

Swan-neck deformity is a problem with how the fingers bend. It affects the joints in a specific way:

- The joint at the base of the finger bends inward.
- The middle joint of the finger straightens out.
- The outermost joint of the finger bends inward.

This shape looks like a swan’s neck, which is how the condition got its name.

## What Causes Swan-Neck Deformity?

The most common cause is rheumatoid arthritis. Other causes include:

- A mallet finger that was not treated.
- Loose ligaments or a weak fibrous plate in the hand.
- Muscle spasms in the hand due to nerve damage.
- Other types of arthritis.
- A torn finger tendon.
- A broken finger bone that healed in the wrong position.

Over time, the finger may become stiff. Normal bending may become impossible. This can make daily tasks hard and cause serious disability.

## How It Differs from Other Finger Problems

Some conditions cause fingers to bend in unusual ways. Here’s how swan-neck deformity is different:

- In **swan-neck deformity**:  
  - The base joint bends in.  
  - The middle joint straightens out.  
  - The tip joint bends in.

- In **boutonnière deformity**:  
  - The middle joint bends toward the palm.  
  - The tip joint bends away from the palm.

## The Thumb and Swan-Neck Deformity

True swan-neck deformity does not affect the thumb. The thumb has fewer joints than the other fingers, so it does not develop this exact pattern.

But there is a related condition called **duck-bill deformity**, also known as Z-type or 90-degree deformity. In this case:

- The top joint of the thumb is overstraightened.
- The base joint of the thumb bends inward.
- The two joints form a 90-degree angle.

If both duck-bill deformity and swan-neck deformity happen at the same time, it becomes very hard to pinch things between the thumb and fingers.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

A doctor will look at your hand and fingers. They will check how the joints move. They may ask about your medical history and any past injuries.

## How It Is Treated

Treatment depends on the cause and how bad the deformity is.

### 1. Treat the Underlying Cause
If the problem comes from arthritis or another illness, treating that condition can help slow or stop the deformity.

### 2. Use Finger Splints
For mild cases, a doctor may recommend a ring splint. This is a small device that holds the finger in the right position. It helps correct the shape while still letting you use your hand.

### 3. Surgery
Surgery may be needed if the deformity is severe or if it stops you from using your hand well.

- The surgeon can realign the joints so they work better.
- In some cases, they may fuse the joints together. This means the joint no longer moves, but it becomes stable and strong.
- Fusing the thumb or finger joints in a good position can greatly improve your ability to pinch and grip things.

Surgery is usually considered when other treatments do not help.

# What Is Domestic Violence?

Domestic violence happens between people who live together. This includes partners, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings.

It can be physical, sexual, or emotional abuse. It can also happen between current or former partners.

This is also called intimate partner violence.

---

## How Common Is Domestic Violence?

Domestic violence is very common.

In the United States between 2003 and 2012, it made up 21% of all violent crime. Intimate partner violence alone made up 15%.

Globally, a woman or girl is killed by someone in her own family every 11 minutes. In 2020, 47,000 women and girls were killed by a partner or family member.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, abuse became more common. Stress from losing jobs and being stuck at home made things worse. Many people who were abused could not go to shelters or other safe places.

A major U.S. study found that:
- 47 out of every 100 women and 44 out of every 100 men have been stalked, hit, or sexually assaulted by a partner at some point in their lives.
- Women are more likely to suffer serious physical harm or forced sex.

Abuse happens across all ages, races, and cultures. It affects lesbian, bisexual, gay, and transgender people just as much as others.

Women are more likely to be killed by a partner than men are. In 2021, 34% of women killed in murders were killed by a partner. Only 6% of men killed in murders were killed by a partner.

If the abuser has a gun, the risk of death is much higher.

---

## Types of Abuse

### Physical Abuse

This is the most visible kind of abuse. It includes:
- Hitting, slapping, kicking, punching
- Breaking bones
- Pulling hair
- Pushing or twisting arms
- Denying food or sleep
- Using weapons like guns or knives to threaten or hurt

### Sexual Assault

This happens when someone forces or pressures another person into sex without their clear yes.

Many women who are hit by their partner are also sexually assaulted.

Sexual assault includes:
- Unwanted touching, grabbing, or kissing
- Forced sex
- Any sexual act without consent

It often uses threats or force.

### Psychological Abuse

This is very common. It can happen before or at the same time as physical abuse.

It is any behavior that harms a person’s mind or emotions. It is meant to control or break down the victim.

Examples include:
- Using harsh or cruel words
- Isolating the person from friends and family
- Controlling money and finances

The abuser may:
- Humiliate or insult the victim in private or in public
- Make the victim doubt their own feelings, thoughts, or memory (this is called gaslighting)
- Make the victim feel guilty or responsible for the abuse

The abuser may:
- Stop the victim from seeing friends or family
- Block phone calls, texts, emails, or letters
- Make the victim believe no one will help
- Use jealousy to justify control
- Stop the victim from going to the doctor

The abuser may also control money. This can mean:
- The victim depends on the abuser for all money
- The abuser hides financial information
- The abuser stops the victim from working

After an attack, the abuser may say sorry and promise to change. But the abuse usually continues. Often, it gets worse.

The violence comes in sudden, unpredictable bursts. This makes victims live in constant fear of the next attack.

### Stalking

Stalking is repeated, unwanted contact that makes someone feel afraid.

It can include:
- Unwanted phone calls, texts, or social media messages
- Sending gifts, flowers, or letters
- Watching, following, or spying on the person
- Showing up at the person’s home, job, or school

Abusers may use technology to:
- Post videos or messages about the victim
- Track the victim’s location
- Monitor their phone or computer without their knowledge
- Humiliate, punish, or threaten them

---

## What Do We Call People Who Have Been Abused?

Different words are used depending on the situation.

- “Victim” is a term used by police and courts. It is often used for someone who is still being abused or has just stopped being abused.
- “Survivor” is a term used by many people who have gone through abuse and are healing.

Healthcare providers should ask patients which word they prefer.

---

## How Does Domestic Violence Affect People?

### Physical Effects

People who are abused may be hurt. Injuries can include:
- Bruises
- Black eyes
- Cuts, scratches
- Broken bones
- Lost teeth
- Burns

These injuries can make it hard to work. This can lead to loss of income.

Injuries and the abuse itself can make people feel ashamed. They may hide from family and friends.

They may have to move often to stay safe. This is expensive and stressful.

In some cases, the abuser kills the victim.

### Mental Health Effects

Many survivors develop mental health problems. These can include:
- Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
- Drug or alcohol problems
- Anxiety
- Depression

Physical abuse is linked to more serious mental health issues.

Even if the hitting stops, emotional abuse often continues. This reminds the victim that they could be hurt again at any time.

Many survivors say emotional abuse hurts more than physical abuse.

---

## Children Who See Abuse

Children who see abuse at home are deeply affected.

In the U.S.:
- 11% of children are exposed to some form of family violence each year.
- 26% see abuse at some point in their lives.

Children may show signs like:
- Being very anxious or crying a lot
- Being afraid all the time
- Having trouble sleeping
- Not being able to focus
- Feeling sad or anxious
- Withdrawing from others
- Doing poorly in school
- Skipping school
- Getting into fights with other kids
- Acting out because they think violence is normal

Some children blame themselves for the abuse.

Older children may run away from home.

The abuser may also hurt the children directly.

In homes with abuse, children are much more likely to be physically hurt.

---

## How Do Doctors Find Out About Abuse?

Doctors may suspect abuse when:
- A patient has injuries that do not match the story
- The patient’s symptoms do not make sense
- The partner refuses to leave the room
- The patient seems afraid or nervous

Sometimes, the patient tells the doctor directly.

Doctors should ask all patients about their relationships. This is called screening.

They should also ask if it is safe for the patient to go home.

It is not safe if:
- The patient has said they want to leave the relationship (this is the most common reason for murder)
- The violence is getting worse (for example, being choked)
- The abuser has a gun
- The abuser has threatened to kill or hurt the patient

If abuse is suspected, doctors should give information about help services.

If abuse is confirmed, doctors may need to take photos of injuries. These can be used in court.

Laws about reporting abuse vary by state and by the type of doctor.

---

## How Can We Help?

### Safety Is the Top Priority

If violence happens:
- Try to move away from places where you can be trapped or where weapons are kept (like the kitchen).
- If possible, call emergency services or the police.
- Leave the home if you can.
- Get medical care for injuries.
- Take photos of any injuries.
- Teach children how to stay safe and how to call for help.

### Make a Safety Plan

A safety plan helps you stay safe. It should include:
- A safe place to go (like a friend’s house or shelter)
- How to get away quickly
- How to get money
- A way to contact help

Keep copies of important documents hidden. These include:
- Children’s birth certificates
- Social security cards
- Insurance cards
- Bank account numbers

Keep an overnight bag packed and hidden. This helps you leave fast if needed.

### Leaving the Relationship

Sometimes, the only safe choice is to leave the relationship for good.

Abuse often continues. Even if the hitting stops, emotional abuse may not.

Leaving is hard. Many people stay because:
- They fear the abuser will hurt them or their children
- They depend on the abuser for money or housing

The risk of serious harm or death is highest right after someone decides to leave.

At this time, take extra steps to stay safe:
- Get a restraining order or protection order
- Note that these orders do not guarantee safety, but they can help

---

## Help Is Available

In the United States, help is available through:
- Shelters for survivors (including LGBTQ+ people)
- Support groups
- The courts
- A national hotline: 1-800-799-SAFE (or 1-800-787-3224 for TTY)
- Online chat services through the National Domestic Violence Helpline

You can get help even if you are not sure what to do.

---

## Key Points

- Domestic violence includes hitting, sexual assault, and emotional abuse between people who live together.
- It can cause physical injuries, mental health problems, isolation, job loss, money problems, and even death.
- Staying safe is the most important thing. Have a plan to leave if needed.
- Abuse often continues. In many cases, leaving the relationship permanently is the only safe choice.
- Leaving takes planning and extra care to stay safe.
