# Idiopathic Pleuroparenchymal Fibroelastosis

This is a rare lung disease. It causes scarring in the upper parts of the lungs. The disease gets worse slowly over time. It has no known cause. Doctors call it "idiopathic," which means the cause is unknown.

## What Causes This Disease?

We do not know what causes this disease. But some people with it have had many lung infections. Doctors think genes or the body’s immune system may play a role.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people first notice symptoms around age 49. Men and women are equally affected.

Common symptoms include:
- Frequent lung infections
- Trouble breathing, especially when active
- A dry cough that does not go away

Some people also develop a collapsed lung. This is called pneumothorax.

As the disease gets worse, the chest can become shorter and flatter. This is due to scarring in the upper lungs.

People with advanced disease often lose weight and become underweight.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use a special type of CT scan called high-resolution CT to look at the lungs. This scan shows thickening in the upper lung areas and near the outer lining of the lungs.

The scan may also show:
- Areas of lung tissue that are solid (consolidation)
- Widened airways (bronchiectasis)
- Small air-filled spaces (cysts) near the lung surface

In some cases, a lung biopsy is needed. This means taking a small sample of lung tissue to examine under a microscope.

The biopsy shows:
- Thick, stiff tissue inside the tiny air sacs
- Extra elastic fibers in the lung walls
- Thickening of the outer lining of the lung (visceral pleura)

Sometimes, other types of lung scarring are also found in the lower lungs.

## How Is It Treated?

There is no proven best treatment. But some people get help from steroid medicines like prednisone. These reduce swelling and may slow the disease.

For people with severe symptoms, two medicines used for other lung scarring diseases may help. These are nintedanib and pirfenidone. They may slow the loss of lung function.

In advanced cases, surgery to remove scarred lung areas is not common. But lung transplantation may be an option for some people. This is considered when breathing problems become life-threatening.

## What Is the Outlook?

The disease usually gets worse over time. Most people will see their lung function decline.

Survival rates vary. About 25 to 60 out of 100 people are still alive five years after diagnosis. This depends on how early the disease is found and how fast it progresses.

# Esophageal Pouches (Diverticula)

An esophageal pouch is an abnormal bulge or pocket in the food pipe.  
These pouches are rare.  
They can sometimes cause trouble swallowing or make you spit up food.  
Spitting up food means the food comes back up without feeling sick or forcing it up with your stomach muscles.

## What Causes Esophageal Pouches?

The cause depends on the type of pouch.  
All types are likely linked to poor coordination when swallowing.  
Many are linked to problems with how the muscles in the food pipe move.  
These muscle problems can include esophageal spasm or achalasia.

## Types of Esophageal Pouches

### Zenker Diverticulum (Pharyngeal Diverticulum)

This pouch forms in the throat, just above the muscle that controls the top of the food pipe.  
It may happen when the throat muscles do not relax at the right time.  
Food can get trapped in the pouch.  
When you bend over or lie down, the food may come back up.  
This can cause you to inhale food into your lungs while sleeping.  
Inhaling food can lead to a lung infection called aspiration pneumonia.  
In rare cases, the pouch grows large enough to cause trouble swallowing.  
It may also cause a visible lump in the neck.

### Midesophageal Diverticula (Traction Diverticula)

This pouch forms in the middle part of the food pipe.  
It is usually caused by inflammation outside the food pipe in the chest.  
The inflammation pulls on the food pipe and creates a pouch.  
It can also be caused by muscle movement problems in the food pipe.  
Most of the time, this pouch does not cause symptoms.  
But the muscle problem behind it might cause symptoms.

### Epiphrenic Diverticula

This pouch forms just above the diaphragm.  
The diaphragm is the muscle that separates the chest from the belly.  
It usually happens with a muscle movement problem, such as achalasia or esophageal spasm.  
This pouch rarely causes symptoms.  
But the muscle problem behind it might.

## How Are Esophageal Pouches Diagnosed?

Doctors use two main tests to find esophageal pouches.

**Barium swallow x-ray**  
You drink a liquid that contains barium.  
This liquid coats the inside of your food pipe.  
X-rays are then taken.  
The barium makes the food pipe and any pouches show up clearly.  
Sometimes the test is recorded on video so doctors can watch it later.

**Upper endoscopy**  
Doctors use a thin, flexible tube with a camera on the end.  
They pass this tube through your mouth and into your food pipe.  
This lets them see the inside of the food pipe and check for pouches.

## How Are Esophageal Pouches Treated?

Most people with esophageal pouches do not need treatment.  
The pouches do not cause problems and do not need to be removed.

If the pouch is large or causes serious symptoms, surgery may be needed.  
The pouch can be removed during surgery.

If the pouch is linked to a muscle movement problem, the muscle issue must also be treated.  
For example, if a Zenker diverticulum is caused by a tight throat muscle, the doctor can cut that muscle during surgery.  
This is called a myotomy.  
Cutting the muscle helps the food pipe work better.

# Acute Eosinophilic Pneumonia

This is a serious lung condition that comes on quickly. It happens when a type of white blood cell called an eosinophil builds up in the lungs. The lungs become inflamed and filled with fluid. This can make it hard to breathe.

Most people get better if they get treatment right away. But the condition can get worse fast. Some people need help breathing with a machine.

## What Causes It?

The exact cause is not always known. But it may be a reaction to something in the air. This could include:

- Smoke from cigarettes or other sources
- Dust from deserts or construction sites
- Fumes from chemicals or cleaning products
- Certain medicines
- Infections

Some people have had asthma or allergies before. This may make them more likely to get the condition.

In many cases, no clear cause is found. When this happens, doctors call it idiopathic.

## Who Gets It?

This condition is rare. It can happen at any age. But it most often affects people between 20 and 40 years old. Men are more likely to get it than women.

One study found about 9 cases per 100,000 people each year among U.S. military personnel.

## Symptoms

The illness starts suddenly and lasts less than a week. Symptoms include:

- A dry cough that does not bring up mucus
- Trouble breathing
- Feeling very tired
- Muscle aches
- Night sweats
- Sharp chest pain that gets worse when you breathe in

## Signs a Doctor Might Find

A doctor may notice:

- Fast breathing
- High fever (over 101.3 degrees Fahrenheit)
- Low oxygen levels in the blood
- Crackling sounds in the lungs when listening with a stethoscope
- Wheezing when breathing out

The condition can get worse very fast. Some people need a breathing machine to survive. In rare cases, blood pressure drops too low, which is dangerous.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

There is no single test for this condition. Doctors rule out other causes first. They use several tests to make a diagnosis.

### Tests Used

- **Chest X-ray**: May show blurry areas in the lungs. These can look like fine lines or cloudiness. Some people have fluid around the lungs.
- **CT scan of the chest**: This gives a clearer picture. It always shows patchy, cloudy areas in both lungs. The pattern is random and not in one spot.
- **Blood test**: This checks for signs of infection or inflammation. Eosinophils may be high, but not always. Other markers like ESR and IgE can also be high, but these are not specific to this condition.
- **Pleural fluid test**: If there is fluid around the lungs, doctors test it. It often has many eosinophils and a high pH.
- **Bronchoscopy**: A thin tube is passed into the lungs. A small amount of fluid is washed out and tested. This fluid usually has more than 25% eosinophils.
- **Lung biopsy**: This is only done if the person does not get better with treatment. Or if an infection is still possible after other tests.

### Important Note

This condition is a diagnosis of exclusion. That means doctors must rule out other causes first. These include:

- Reactions to medicines or toxins
- Parasite infections
- Fungal infections
- Autoimmune diseases like eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
- A rare blood disorder called hypereosinophilic syndrome
- Cancer

The diagnosis is suspected when a person has sudden pneumonia symptoms. They get worse fast. They do not get better with antibiotics.

## Treatment

Most people need treatment. Some may get better on their own, but this is rare.

### Main Treatment

- **Steroid medicine**: This is the main treatment. It is given as a pill or through a vein. 
  - For mild cases: High-dose oral prednisone.
  - For severe cases: Intravenous methylprednisolone.

Steroids work fast. Most people feel better within 1 to 2 days.

### Breathing Support

- **Mechanical ventilation**: This is used if oxygen levels are too low. A breathing machine helps the person breathe until the lungs recover.

### Recovery

- Most people recover fully in 4 to 8 weeks.
- Symptoms go away quickly after starting steroids.
- The lungs take longer to clear on scans. X-rays and CT scans may still show changes even after the person feels well.
- Fluid around the lungs takes longer to go away than the cloudy areas in the lungs.

## Outlook

The outlook is usually good if treatment starts early. Most people recover completely. The condition does not come back in most cases. It is not the same as chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, which can return over time.

# Respiratory Failure

Respiratory failure means your blood does not have enough oxygen or has too much carbon dioxide. This can be life-threatening.

## What Is Respiratory Failure?

- Your blood may have too little oxygen.
- Or your blood may have too much carbon dioxide.
- Both problems can make you very sick.

### Types of Respiratory Failure

**Acute respiratory failure** happens suddenly. It can happen to people with long-term lung problems when their condition gets worse fast. It can also happen to healthy people who suddenly develop serious lung disease.

An example of sudden lung disease is acute respiratory distress syndrome.

**Chronic respiratory failure** is a long-term breathing problem. It often happens in people with long-standing lung diseases like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

---

## Causes of Respiratory Failure

Almost any problem that affects your breathing or lungs can lead to respiratory failure. There are two main types:

1. **Low oxygen in the blood** (hypoxemic respiratory failure)
2. **High carbon dioxide in the blood** (hypercarbic respiratory failure)

Some people have both problems at the same time.

### What Can Cause Respiratory Failure?

| Problem | Possible Causes |
|--------|----------------|
| **Chest wall issues** | A chest injury, surgery scars, severe obesity, or scoliosis (a curved spine) |
| **Lung tissue damage** | Acute respiratory distress syndrome, pneumonia, fluid in the lungs (from heart or kidney problems), lung scarring, radiation, sarcoidosis, or cancer |
| **Airway blockage** | Asthma, bronchiectasis, bronchiolitis, COPD, cystic fibrosis, or a foreign object in the airway |
| **Weak breathing muscles** | ALS, stroke, Guillain-Barré syndrome, muscular dystrophy, myasthenia gravis, polio, polymyositis, or spinal cord injury |
| **Poor breathing drive** | Alcohol or drug overdose, certain medications, low thyroid hormone, obesity, or sleep apnea |

### Low Oxygen (Hypoxemic) Respiratory Failure

This often happens when the lungs cannot take in oxygen properly. Causes include:

- Severe pneumonia
- Fluid in the lungs (from heart or kidney problems)
- Lung scarring
- Acute respiratory distress syndrome
- A blood clot in a lung artery (pulmonary embolism)

In pulmonary embolism, the lungs get oxygen from the air, but blood cannot flow through the affected area. So oxygen cannot be picked up by the blood.

### High Carbon Dioxide (Hypercarbic) Respiratory Failure

This happens when you cannot breathe well enough to remove carbon dioxide. Causes include:

- Low thyroid hormone (hypothyroidism)
- Sleep apnea
- Overdose of opioids or alcohol
- Blocked or narrowed airways
- Injury to the chest or lungs
- Weak chest muscles
- Nerve or muscle problems that affect breathing

Low thyroid hormone, sleep apnea, and drug or alcohol overdose reduce your body’s natural urge to breathe.

Airway blockage can come from asthma, COPD, or a foreign object like a coin or toy.

Injury to the chest or lungs, or weak chest muscles (as in ALS, myasthenia gravis, or Guillain-Barré syndrome), can stop you from breathing deeply or often enough.

If your breathing drive is weak, you may not get enough oxygen. But this is not called hypoxemic respiratory failure unless your lungs are also damaged.

High carbon dioxide makes your blood more acidic. This can harm your body’s chemistry and cause serious problems.

> **Did You Know?**  
> As people age, their lungs do not work as well. This makes older adults more likely to have severe symptoms if they get pneumonia.

---

## Symptoms of Respiratory Failure

Both low oxygen and high carbon dioxide cause similar symptoms:

- You feel very short of breath.
- Your skin may turn blue (cyanosis) if you have light skin.
- If you have dark skin, your lips, around your eyes, or under your nails may look gray or white.
- You may feel confused or very sleepy.

If your body can still sense the need to breathe, you may breathe fast and deep to get rid of carbon dioxide. But if your lungs are too weak, this does not help.

Over time, your brain and heart may stop working properly. This can lead to:

- Extreme drowsiness
- Loss of consciousness
- Irregular heartbeats (arrhythmias)

These problems can be deadly.

### Symptoms That Vary by Cause

- If you took too much alcohol or medicine, you may be very sleepy, breathe slowly, and fall into a coma.
- A child who swallowed a small object may suddenly gasp and struggle to breathe.

---

## How Is Respiratory Failure Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find out if you have respiratory failure.

### Tests Used

- **Pulse oximetry**: A small sensor on your finger or ear measures how much oxygen is in your blood. No blood is drawn.
- **Arterial blood gas test**: A small blood sample is taken from an artery. This test shows how much oxygen and carbon dioxide are in your blood.
- **Chest x-ray**: This shows the condition of your lungs.
- Other tests: May be needed to find the cause.

Doctors may suspect respiratory failure based on your symptoms and what they see during the exam.

---

## How Is Respiratory Failure Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause and how severe the problem is.

### Main Treatments

- **Oxygen therapy**: Extra oxygen is given to raise blood oxygen levels.
- **Mechanical ventilation**: A machine helps you breathe when your lungs are too weak.
- **Treat the underlying cause**: For example, antibiotics for infection, or medicines to open airways.

### Oxygen Therapy

- Oxygen is given through small prongs in the nose (nasal cannula).
- Or through a face mask.
- The amount is adjusted over time. Doctors start with more oxygen than needed and reduce it as you improve.

### Mechanical Ventilation

This helps move air in and out of the lungs. It lowers carbon dioxide levels.

There are two types:

- **Noninvasive ventilation**: A mask covers your nose or mouth. Air is pushed in by a machine.
- **Invasive ventilation**: A tube is placed into your windpipe. Air is pushed in by a machine.

Doctors usually try the noninvasive method first. But if it does not work, invasive ventilation is used.

Most people need both oxygen and some form of mechanical ventilation.

### Treating the Underlying Cause

- Antibiotics are used for bacterial pneumonia.
- Bronchodilators help open airways in asthma.
- Other medicines may be used to reduce swelling, treat blood clots, or manage other issues.

People with acute respiratory failure are usually treated in an intensive care unit (ICU). This is a special hospital unit for very sick patients.

# Cancer During Pregnancy

Cancer during pregnancy needs treatment right away. Do not wait until after the baby is born.

Treatment is usually the same as for women who are not pregnant. But there are some differences for rectal cancer and gynecologic cancers.

The baby’s cells grow very fast during early pregnancy. These fast-growing cells are like cancer cells. This makes them very sensitive to cancer drugs.

Many cancer drugs can harm the baby. This includes drugs like busulfan, chlorambucil, cyclophosphamide, 6-mercaptopurine, and methotrexate.

Methotrexate is especially risky. If a woman takes it in the first three months of pregnancy, the baby may not survive. If the pregnancy continues, the baby may be born with serious birth defects.

Even though many women go on to have healthy babies after cancer treatment, some choose to end the pregnancy. This is because of the risk of harm to the baby from treatment.

Cancer care during pregnancy or after childbirth needs a team of experts. This team includes cancer doctors and doctors who specialize in high-risk pregnancies.

It is very important that the woman understands her options. She should talk with her doctors and make decisions together with them. This helps her choose the best path for her and her baby.

# Eosinophilic Pneumonia

Eosinophilic pneumonia is a lung condition where a type of white blood cell called an eosinophil builds up in the lungs and often in the blood.

- Some health problems, medicines, chemicals, fungi, or parasites can cause this buildup.
- People may cough, wheeze, or feel short of breath. In some cases, breathing becomes so hard that it is life-threatening.
- Doctors use chest x-rays and blood tests to find the condition and figure out what is causing it, especially if a parasite might be the cause.
- Steroids are usually given to reduce swelling and ease symptoms.

---

## What Are Eosinophils?

Eosinophils are a kind of white blood cell. They help the body fight infections and play a role in allergic reactions. Their numbers go up during allergies and inflammation. This includes asthma, which often happens with some types of eosinophilic pneumonia.

Eosinophilic pneumonia is not like regular pneumonia. It is not caused by bacteria, viruses, or fungi in the tiny air sacs of the lungs. But the air sacs and airways can fill with eosinophils. The walls of blood vessels in the lungs may also be affected. If asthma develops, the airways can get blocked with mucus.

---

## Löffler Syndrome

Löffler syndrome is a mild form of eosinophilic pneumonia.

- It may cause no symptoms at all.
- Or it may cause a dry cough, wheezing, or a low fever.
- A chest x-ray and blood test are needed to confirm the diagnosis.
- It is often linked to a worm infection, especially by a type of roundworm called *Ascaris lumbricoides*.
- In some people, no cause is found.
- Most people get better within one month.
- Doctors may give steroids to reduce symptoms and swelling.

---

## What Causes Eosinophilic Pneumonia?

The exact reason why eosinophils gather in the lungs is not fully known. But it may be due to an allergic reaction. Often, the trigger is not found. Still, some known causes include:

- Cigarette smoke (only in acute cases)
- Certain medicines:
  - Penicillin
  - Aminosalicylic acid
  - Carbamazepine
  - Tryptophan
  - Naproxen
  - Isoniazid
  - Nitrofurantoin
  - Phenytoin
  - Sulfonamides (like sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim)
- Chemical fumes, such as from cocaine or nickel vapor
- Fungi, especially *Aspergillus fumigatus*
- Parasites, especially roundworms
- Other body-wide diseases, such as eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis

---

## Symptoms of Eosinophilic Pneumonia

Symptoms can be mild or very serious. They can come on quickly or develop slowly.

### Acute Eosinophilic Pneumonia

- Comes on fast, over hours or days.
- Causes fever, chest pain that hurts when breathing deeply, shortness of breath, cough, and feeling unwell.
- Blood oxygen levels can drop quickly.
- Without treatment, it can lead to sudden breathing failure in a few hours or days.

### Löffler Syndrome

- May not cause any symptoms.
- Or it may cause mild breathing problems like coughing, wheezing, or shortness of breath.
- Most people recover fast.

### Chronic Eosinophilic Pneumonia

- Develops slowly over days or weeks.
- Can get worse over time.
- May go away on its own, but often comes back.
- Can become very serious if not treated.
- Can lead to life-threatening shortness of breath.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to diagnose eosinophilic pneumonia.

### Chest X-ray
- Used first to look at the lungs.
- In acute cases, the x-ray usually shows changes.
- In chronic cases, the x-ray can help with the diagnosis.

### CT Scan of the Chest
- Often needed to get a clearer picture.
- Helps confirm the diagnosis in both acute and chronic cases.

### Blood Tests
- Check how many eosinophils are in the blood.
- In acute cases, the count may be normal.
- In chronic cases, the count is often very high—up to 10 to 15 times normal.

### Bronchoscopy
- A thin tube is passed into the lungs.
- Fluid is collected from the air sacs.
- A lab checks the fluid under a microscope.
- It usually shows clumps of eosinophils.

### Other Tests
- Stool tests may be done to check for worms or other parasites.
- Tests may also look for fungal infections.

### Lung Function Tests
- Measure how well the lungs hold air and move air in and out.
- Check how well the lungs exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide.
- Help show how much the lungs are affected.

---

## How Is It Treated?

### Steroids
- Steroids (like prednisone) are the main treatment.
- They reduce swelling and help the lungs work better.

### Acute Eosinophilic Pneumonia
- Steroids are usually needed.
- Most people get better quickly with treatment.

### Chronic Eosinophilic Pneumonia
- Steroids may be needed for many months or even years.
- Treatment may need to continue for a long time to prevent relapses.

### If Asthma Develops
- Treatments used for asthma are also given.
- These help open the airways and ease wheezing.

### If Parasites Are the Cause
- Specific medicines are used to kill the worms or other parasites.

### If a Medicine Is the Cause
- The medicine is stopped if possible.
- This can help the condition improve.

## Using Steroid Injections in the Foot and Ankle

Steroid injections should be used only when needed.  
They are best for swelling and pain from certain conditions like gout or rheumatoid arthritis.

### Where to Inject

The tarsus, ankle, back of the heel, and top of the toes have little padding between the skin and bone.

- Skin to lose color  
- Skin to thin  
- Sores or ulcers

- The heel pad  
- The space inside the ankle bones

# Coal Worker Pneumoconiosis

This is a lung disease caused by breathing in coal mining dust over many years.

## Types of the Disease

There are two main types:

- **Simple pneumoconiosis**  
  Dust builds up around small airways in the lungs. Most people with this type do not have breathing problems.

- **Complicated pneumoconiosis (also called progressive massive fibrosis)**  
  This is a more serious form. Large scars form in the lungs. These scars can keep getting worse even after a person stops working in coal mines.  
  In recent years, young miners in the eastern United States have developed these large scars quickly.

Scarring can damage lung tissue and blood vessels. This makes it harder to breathe.

## Why the Disease Is Getting More Common

After the Coal Mine Health and Safety Act of 1969, cases of this disease went down in the United States.  
But since the late 1990s, cases have increased again — especially severe cases.

This rise is likely due to more exposure to silica.  
Silica is a type of rock dust found in coal mines.  
Possible reasons for more silica exposure include:

- Workers not following safety rules  
- Coal dust that contains more silica  
- Mining deeper underground, which means cutting through more rock  
- Using powerful machines that make finer, more dangerous dust

## What Causes the Disease

- You get this disease from breathing in coal mining dust for a long time.  
  This usually takes 10 years or more.

- The more dust you breathe in, the higher your risk.

- The amount of crystalline silica in the dust also increases the risk of serious disease.

- Miners who work underground, near where coal is cut, or who use cutting or drilling tools are at higher risk.

## Symptoms

Common symptoms include:

- Coughing  
- Trouble breathing  
- Coughing up mucus

The disease can get worse even after you stop working in coal mines.  
Progressive massive fibrosis can lead to very severe lung damage.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors look for signs of the disease using:

- A history of working in coal mines  
- Chest x-rays or CT scans

If a person has worked in coal mines for many years and the scan shows typical spots in the lungs, the doctor may diagnose coal worker pneumoconiosis.

## How the Disease Is Treated

- **Stop further exposure to coal dust**  
  People with advanced disease, like progressive massive fibrosis, should not return to coal mining.

- **Treat symptoms**  
  If you have no symptoms, you do not need treatment.

  If you have trouble breathing, treatment may help. This can include medicines used for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

- **Oxygen therapy**  
  People with severe symptoms may need extra oxygen to breathe easier.

- **Pulmonary rehabilitation**  
  This program helps you do daily tasks more easily. It includes exercise and education.

- **Lung transplant**  
  This may be needed for people with the most severe cases.

- **Stop smoking**  
  If you smoke, quitting helps protect your lungs. (See Smoking Cessation.)

- **Check for other problems**  
  Regular checkups help catch infections like tuberculosis early.

- **Get vaccines**  
  Miners should get:
  - Pneumococcal vaccine  
  - Annual flu shot  
  - COVID-19 vaccine

These vaccines help prevent infections that can be harder to fight when lungs are already damaged.

## How to Prevent the Disease

- **Reduce dust at work**  
  Use water sprays to keep dust down. Use good ventilation systems.

- **Wear a proper respirator**  
  A mask that filters the air can help protect your lungs.

- **Get regular chest x-rays**  
  Doctors often recommend screening for coal workers.  
  This helps find the disease early.

- **Limit exposure if disease is found**  
  If you are diagnosed, avoid more coal dust to slow the disease.

Early detection and action can help protect your lungs for longer.

# How Medicines Work in Older Adults

Medicines behave differently in older adults. This is because the body changes with age. These changes affect how the body handles medicines.

## What Happens to Medicines in the Body?

The body does four main things to medicines:

- **Absorption**: How well the medicine gets into the bloodstream.
- **Distribution**: How the medicine spreads through the body.
- **Metabolism**: How the body breaks down the medicine.
- **Excretion**: How the body removes the medicine.

## Changes with Age

As people get older, these four steps can change. Some changes are more important than others.

- The body breaks down many medicines more slowly.
- The body also removes many medicines more slowly.

Because of this, older adults may need lower doses of some medicines.

## Risks of Slow Changes

When a medicine builds up in the body, it can cause side effects. This buildup takes time.

- It can take 5 to 6 half-lives for a medicine to reach a steady level in the body.
- A half-life is how long it takes for the body to remove half of the medicine.

So, side effects may not show up right away. They can appear days or even weeks after starting a new medicine.

## Example: Certain Sleeping Pills

Some medicines used for sleep or anxiety (like diazepam, flurazepam, and chlordiazepoxide) stay in the body for a long time in older adults.

- Their half-life can be up to 96 hours.
- This means it takes up to 4 days for the body to remove half of the medicine.
- Side effects like drowsiness, confusion, or falls may not appear until days or weeks after starting the medicine.

## Key Points

- Older adults may need lower doses of some medicines.
- Side effects can take time to appear.
- Always talk to your doctor before starting or stopping any medicine.
- Report any new symptoms, especially dizziness, confusion, or falls.

# Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome

This is a serious heart problem that a baby is born with. The left side of the heart does not grow properly. This includes the left lower chamber, the valves, and the main blood vessel leaving the heart.

Babies with this condition also have two extra openings in the heart:
- A hole between the two upper chambers (called an atrial septal defect).
- A blood vessel that normally closes after birth but stays open (called a patent ductus arteriosus).

## What Happens in This Condition

The left side of the heart is too small to pump enough blood to the body. This causes heart failure soon after birth. Without treatment, the baby will not survive.

The small left side of the heart cannot hold all the blood coming from the lungs. Some of this blood is pushed into the right side of the heart through the hole. Blood from the body (low in oxygen) mixes with blood from the lungs (high in oxygen). This makes the blood less effective at delivering oxygen to the body.

The baby depends on the ductus arteriosus to get blood to the body. This is a special blood vessel that is normal in a fetus but usually closes after birth. If it closes, the baby will not survive unless it is kept open with medicine.

## Symptoms

Symptoms appear when the ductus arteriosus starts to close. This usually happens in the first 24 to 48 hours after birth.

Signs of heart failure and shock include:
- Fast breathing
- Trouble breathing
- Weak pulse
- Pale or bluish skin
- Cold body
- Lethargy (very sleepy or weak)
- Fewer wet diapers

If blood flow to the body drops, the heart, brain, and other vital organs do not get enough blood. Without quick treatment, the baby will die.

## How It Is Diagnosed

Doctors use a special ultrasound of the heart called echocardiography to confirm the diagnosis.

Many babies are found to have this problem before birth. A routine ultrasound during pregnancy may show the issue. A fetal echocardiogram can also detect it.

If a baby shows signs of heart failure after birth, doctors suspect this condition. They confirm it with an emergency echocardiogram.

Other tests may include:
- A chest x-ray
- An electrocardiogram (ECG)
- In rare cases, a cardiac catheterization

## How It Is Treated

Treatment starts right after birth. It includes:
- A medicine called a prostaglandin to keep the ductus arteriosus open
- A series of surgeries over 2 to 3 years
- In some cases, a heart transplant

### Medicine to Keep the Ductus Open

Most babies with this condition are diagnosed before birth. Doctors start giving the prostaglandin medicine right after birth, even before symptoms appear.

The baby is treated in a special care unit for newborns or for children with heart problems.

The medicine is given through a vein. It keeps the ductus open so blood can still reach the body.

Babies who are very sick often need help breathing. They are placed on a machine called a ventilator.

Some babies also need medicine to help the heart pump better.

### Surgery

Surgery is needed within the first few weeks of life. It is done in three stages over 2 to 3 years.

#### Stage 1: Norwood Procedure
- Done in the first few weeks of life.
- The right side of the heart is used to pump blood to the body.
- A new connection is made to help blood flow to the body.

#### Stage 2: Glenn Procedure
- Done when the baby is 3 to 6 months old.
- Blood from the upper body goes directly to the lungs.
- This bypasses the heart.

#### Stage 3: Fontan Procedure
- Done when the child is 18 to 36 months old.
- Blood from the lower body goes directly to the lungs.
- This means all blood returning to the heart bypasses the heart on its way to the lungs.

### Heart Transplant

In some hospitals, a heart transplant is the first choice.

The baby must stay on prostaglandin medicine until a donor heart is found.

But donor hearts are very rare. About 20% of babies die while waiting for a transplant.

Survival rates after transplant are similar to survival rates after the three-stage surgery.

Because donor hearts are hard to find and surgery has improved, most hospitals recommend the three-stage surgery.

After a transplant, the child must take medicine for life to stop the body from rejecting the new heart. These medicines are called immunosuppressants.

These medicines can:
- Make the child more likely to get infections
- Increase the risk of some types of tumors
- Damage the blood vessels of the new heart

If the blood vessels are damaged, the only treatment is another transplant.

### Other Medicines

Some children need antibiotics before dental visits or certain surgeries. These help prevent a serious heart infection called endocarditis.

Most children need medicine to prevent blood clots. This may include:
- Aspirin
- Warfarin
- Enoxaparin

Many children also need other medicines to help their hearts work well.

# What Are Skilled Nursing Facilities?

Skilled nursing facilities (also called nursing homes) are licensed by each state. They must meet federal rules to be approved for Medicare.

These facilities care for people who need medical help. Most residents are 65 years or older. But younger people with serious disabilities may also live there.

## What Services Do Nursing Homes Offer?

Nursical homes provide many types of care. These include:

- **Skilled nursing care**: This is care that a doctor orders. Only registered nurses or licensed vocational nurses can give this care.
- **Rehabilitation services**: These help people recover after an illness or injury. They include physical therapy, speech therapy, and occupational therapy.
- **Custodial care**: This means help with daily living. It includes meals, bathing, dressing, and using the bathroom.
- **Social services**: These help with emotional and mental health needs. They also help with family visits and community connections.
- **Medicine services**: Staff give medicines as needed and manage drug schedules.
- **Diet services**: Meals are planned to meet each person’s health needs.

## Types of Care in Nursing Homes

Many nursing homes offer short-term care after a serious illness or injury. Examples include:

- A broken hip
- A heart attack
- A stroke

This short-term care may include intense therapy or close nursing care.

Nursing homes can be part of a hospital. Or they can be separate buildings. Some are linked to hospitals. Others are not.

Almost all nursing homes offer long-term care. Many also offer extra services like:

- Day care for older adults
- Respite care (short breaks for family caregivers)

## Is a Nursing Home Always Needed?

No. If a person can get help at home or in a community setting, a nursing home may not be needed.

Options include:

- Independent housing for older adults
- Board-and-care homes
- Assisted living
- Life-care communities

The decision depends on how much care a person needs. It also depends on what the nursing home can offer.

## Who Lives in Nursing Homes?

More people are choosing to stay in their own homes or in community settings. This is partly because of:

- More assisted living homes
- More home health care
- More help from family and friends

Still, many older adults will spend some time in a nursing home. But only 5 to 10 out of every 100 older adults live in a nursing home for several years.

The chance of needing a nursing home goes up with age. It also goes up if a person:

- Has many long-term health problems
- Cannot move well
- Has memory issues (like dementia)
- Cannot care for themselves
- Lives alone
- Has no family or friends to help
- Is poor
- Is a woman

Even though many older adults need help, more than twice as many who need help live in the community than in nursing homes.

Many older adults in the community have no family to help. Focusing on their health needs can improve their lives and help them stay out of nursing homes.

## What Are the Risks and Benefits of Living in a Nursing Home?

### Benefits

- A daily routine that helps with structure
- Chances to meet and talk with others
- Help with eating healthy foods
- Regular exercise and fun activities
- Access to nurses and doctors
- Help with taking medicines correctly

### Risks

- Being unable to leave the facility easily
- Few visitors
- Being ignored when you speak up
- Abuse (this can be physical, like pinching or slapping, or hidden, like using too many medicines or restraints)
- Getting weaker over time
- Losing weight or not eating well
- Skin sores (pressure injuries)
- Incontinence (not being able to control bladder or bowels)
- Constipation
- Infections
- Depression
- Taking too many medicines

Some of these problems can be prevented with good care.

## What Are the Rules for Nursing Homes?

To get paid by Medicare, a nursing home must meet strict rules. These include:

- A registered nurse must be on site for 8 hours a day, 7 days a week
- A registered nurse or licensed practical nurse must be on site 24 hours a day, 7 days a week
- Enough certified nursing assistants to care for all residents at all times
- A full-time social worker if the home has more than 120 beds
- A medical director and a licensed administrator
- A qualified recreation therapist
- A rehabilitation therapist
- A dietitian
- Doctors, pharmacists, dentists, and chaplains must be available when needed (but not always on site)

In 2024, the federal government set new rules. These require nursing homes to have a minimum number of staff. The rules will be rolled out over three years.

## Extra Services in Nursing Homes

Some nursing homes offer more services, such as:

- Specialized care for people with Alzheimer’s or cancer
- Eye, ear, nose, and throat care
- Mental health care
- Neurological care
- Psychiatric or psychological care
- IV medicine
- Feeding tubes
- Long-term oxygen or breathing machines
- Special events and activities
- Personal services like haircuts or makeup (usually paid by the resident)

## How Many Nursing Homes Are There?

- About 15,300 certified nursing homes in the U.S. (2020)
- About 1.6 million beds
- About 1.3 million people live in nursing homes (2020)

## Who Qualifies for Medicare Coverage?

To get Medicare to pay for nursing home care, a person must:

- Need daily skilled nursing care or daily therapy
- Have been in the hospital for at least 3 days before moving in
- Enter the nursing home within 30 days of leaving the hospital

Some plans can waive the 3-day hospital stay rule.

## What Are the Risks of Going to a Nursing Home?

Older adults are more likely to go to a nursing home if they:

- Are older
- Live alone
- Cannot care for themselves
- Cannot walk well
- Have memory problems (like dementia)
- Have incontinence
- Have no family or friends to help
- Are poor
- Are women

## How Is Care Supervised?

A doctor must check in on every new resident. After that, a nurse practitioner or physician assistant can take over.

They must visit the resident:

- At least once every 30 days for the first 90 days
- At least once every 60 days after that

Some states require visits every 30 days.

Nurse practitioners can manage care on their own in some states.

During visits, the provider checks the person’s health. They review medicines and order tests if needed. All findings must be written in the person’s file.

Some doctors, nurse practitioners, and physician assistants work only in nursing homes. They help train staff and improve care.

Nurse practitioners can give antibiotics, check IV lines, clean suction tubes, and manage breathing machines. This can help avoid hospital visits.

Many doctors work with nurse practitioners and physician assistants to give better care.

## Preventing Abuse

Doctors, nurses, and other staff must watch for signs of abuse or neglect.

If abuse is suspected, staff must act. There are public systems to report abuse. Nursing homes can be fined or shut down for poor care.

## Who Checks on Nursing Homes?

The federal and state governments are responsible for making sure nursing homes are safe.

Inspectors check on homes by:

- Looking at health outcomes
- Watching how care is given
- Talking to residents and staff
- Reviewing medical records

The COVID-19 pandemic showed that many nursing homes had serious problems. This led to stronger rules.

Now, staff get more training in infection control. Some states require full-time infection control experts.

In 2022, a national group studied nursing home care. They made 8 key recommendations:

1. Give care that is personal, fair, and focused on health, safety, and quality of life.
2. Train and support staff well. Pay them fairly.
3. Be open about how money is spent and how homes are run.
4. Create a better system for paying for care.
5. Build a stronger system to check care quality.
6. Measure quality often and improve it continuously.
7. Use health technology in all nursing homes.

These changes are needed to protect older adults.

## What Happens If Someone Needs Hospital Care?

If a nursing home resident must go to the hospital, the nursing home doctor should work with the hospital doctor.

Hospital stays are avoided when possible. They can cause infections and other problems.

When a person is sent to the hospital, their medical records, advance directives, and POLST forms must go with them.

A nurse from the nursing home should call the hospital nurse. This call should explain:

- The person’s diagnosis
- Why they are being transferred
- Their usual level of function and mental health
- What medicines they take
- Their advance directives

When the person returns, the hospital nurse should call the nursing home nurse.

Many nursing homes use an SBAR form (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) to make sure all key information is shared.

## How Much Does Nursing Home Care Cost?

Nursing home care is very expensive.

In 2016, the average cost was:

- $225 per day for a semi-private room ($6,844 per month)
- $253 per day for a private room ($7,698 per month)

Costs have risen over time:

- $21 billion in 1980
- $70 billion in 2000
- $121.9 billion in 2005

# Hyper-IgM Syndrome

Hyper-IgM syndrome is a condition where the body does not make enough of certain infection-fighting proteins. This makes it harder to stay healthy.

- People with this condition often get frequent infections in the sinuses and lungs.
- The body makes normal or high levels of one type of protein called IgM.
- But the body makes too little or none of the other types of infection-fighting proteins.

This lack of key proteins means the body cannot fight off infections well.

## What Causes Hyper-Ig-M Syndrome?

This is a primary immune problem. It is present from birth and not caused by another illness.

It can be passed down in two main ways:

- **X-linked form**: A change in a gene on the X chromosome. This usually affects boys.
- **Autosomal recessive form**: A child must inherit a changed gene from each parent. This can affect boys and girls.

Most cases are X-linked.

The symptoms can vary depending on which gene is affected.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look for signs of frequent infections. They then do blood tests to check the levels of infection-fighting proteins.

- High or normal IgM levels.
- Low or missing levels of other proteins.

If the blood test results suggest the condition, doctors may do a genetic test to confirm it.

Pregnant women with a family history of this condition may choose to have a test during pregnancy to see if the baby has the gene change.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment helps protect the body from infections.

- **Immune globulin**: This is a medicine made from blood of healthy people. It gives the body extra infection-fighting proteins. It is given through a vein, usually every few weeks.
- **Antibiotics**: Some people take a daily antibiotic to prevent a specific lung infection called *Pneumocystis jirovecii*.
- **Stem cell transplant**: If a matching donor is available, such as a brother or sister, this may be done. It can cure the condition in some cases.

# Creatine

Creatine is a substance that comes in different forms. The most common form is called creatine monohydrate. This form is sold as a dietary supplement.

When you take creatine, your body turns it into a compound called phosphocreatine. This happens after you eat or take the supplement.

Phosphocreatine is stored in your muscles. It helps your muscles make energy quickly during short bursts of activity, like sprinting or lifting weights. It does this by giving a phosphate group to a molecule called ADP. This process makes ATP, which is the main energy source for your muscles.

Your body makes phosphocreatine on its own. It does this in the liver using three building blocks: arginine, glycine, and methionine.

You can also get creatine from food. Good sources include milk, steak, and some types of fish.

---

## What People Say About Creatine

Some people believe creatine helps them perform better during physical activity. It may also help reduce muscle tiredness.

There is growing interest in creatine. It is used not only by healthy people but also by older adults who want to build stronger muscles. It may also help with recovery after exercise and lower the risk of injury.

---

## What the Research Shows

Some studies show that creatine helps people do more work during short, intense activities. Examples include sprinting, rowing, and weightlifting.

One small study followed 22 active adults for six weeks. It found that taking creatine during strength training helped improve muscle strength.

Creatine has proven benefits for certain medical conditions:

- Muscle phosphorylase deficiency (also known as glycogen storage disease type V or McArdle disease)
- A rare eye condition called gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina

Early research also suggests creatine might help with Parkinson disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), but more studies are needed.

Many clinical trials have shown that creatine is safe for most people. It may also help increase muscle mass. Benefits have been seen in several groups:

- Healthy people: stronger muscles and more muscle mass
- People with muscle diseases: better muscle strength
- People with knee osteoarthritis: better movement and improved quality of life

---

## Possible Side Effects

Creatine may cause weight gain. This is likely due to increased muscle mass.

It can also make blood tests show higher levels of creatinine. This is not always a sign of kidney problems, but it can be confusing.

Some people report mild side effects, including:

- Upset stomach
- Headaches
- Feeling dehydrated
- Mood changes like irritability or aggression
- Swelling (edema)
- Imbalance in body salts (electrolytes)
- Muscle cramps

These side effects are not common and usually mild.

---

## Medicines and Creatine

No strong evidence shows that creatine interacts with other medicines.

However, taking creatine may increase the risk of kidney problems if you are also using certain medicines. These include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen or naproxen.

Caffeine may reduce the benefits of creatine. It can interfere with how well creatine helps your muscles make energy.

# What Phosphate Does in the Body

Phosphorus is a natural element your body needs.  
In your body, phosphorus mostly joins with oxygen to form a substance called phosphate.  

Phosphate is one of the body’s electrolytes.  
Electrolytes are minerals that carry an electric charge when they are in body fluids like blood.  
Most of the phosphate in your body does not carry a charge.  

About 85 percent of your body’s phosphate is stored in your bones.  
The rest is mostly inside your cells.  
Inside cells, phosphate helps make energy.  

Phosphate is essential for building strong bones and teeth.  
It also helps make important parts of your cells.  
These include energy sources, cell membranes, and DNA.  
DNA holds your genetic information.  

You get phosphate from the foods you eat.  
Foods high in phosphate include milk, egg yolks, chocolate, and soft drinks.  
Adults need about 700 milligrams of phosphate each day to keep levels normal in the blood.  

Your body removes extra phosphate through urine.  
Sometimes, phosphate leaves the body in stool.  
The amount in stool depends on how much phosphate your body did not absorb from food.  

The level of phosphate in your blood can be:  
- Too high (called hyperphosphatemia)  
- Too low (called hypophosphatemia)

# Help for Older Drivers Who Are Having Trouble Driving

If an older person has serious health or physical problems that affect driving, and they choose to stop or limit driving, doctors and other health care providers can offer support.  

If a health check finds problems that can be fixed, and the older person agrees they have these problems but still wants to drive, the doctor can offer treatment to help improve their condition.

Most health care providers are not trained to create or carry out a full plan to help someone get back to safe driving. In these cases, it is best to refer the person to a specialist.  

If the problems cannot be fixed enough to allow safe driving, the doctor may need to take the lead in helping the person stop driving.

(See also: Overview of the Older Driver.)

---

## Getting Help to Stay Safe on the Road

Some older drivers may benefit from a refresher driving course, such as the one offered by the American Association of Retired Persons.  

But most older drivers need help from an occupational therapist who specializes in driving. These experts are called driving rehabilitation specialists.  

You can find a driving rehabilitation specialist by contacting local rehabilitation centers, the Association for Driver Rehabilitation Specialists, or the American Occupational Therapy Association.

These specialists do a full check of the person’s abilities. This includes tests of vision, movement, and thinking skills. They also do on-road evaluations.  

During the on-road test, the specialist rides in the car with the older driver. They watch how the driver handles real traffic situations.  

The car used for the test must have special features. For example, it should have a brake on the passenger side so the specialist can take control if needed.

After the full evaluation, the specialist gives clear advice about whether the person can drive safely. They can also help by:

- Creating a personal plan to improve strength, thinking, and awareness in daily life  
- Recommending special equipment for the car (like a spinner knob for one-handed steering, or hand controls for the gas and brake)  
- Teaching the person how to use the equipment  
- Checking how well the plan is working  
- Sharing feedback with the driver, family, and doctor about whether driving is still safe  
- Offering advice on other ways to get around, like public transit or ride services  

In most states, insurance does not cover the cost of a driving rehabilitation evaluation. The person must pay for it themselves.  

If there is no specialist nearby or the cost is too high, the doctor can refer the person to a local occupational therapist who works with older adults.  

Another option is to contact the state’s driver licensing office. They can retest vision, give a written test, and do a road test.

---

## Stopping Driving

Sometimes older drivers do not realize they have problems. Or they may deny that their abilities have changed.  

If treatment does not help, the doctor may need to take action.  

The doctor should talk with the older person and their family about:

- Safety risks on the road  
- The need to stop driving  
- How the person will get around without a car  
- What other transportation options are available  

The doctor must weigh the benefits of stopping driving against the risks.  

Stopping driving can improve safety for the person, other drivers, and pedestrians.  

But it can also lead to loneliness, less activity, lower quality of life, and depression.  

For people with moderate or severe dementia, stopping driving is almost always the right choice. The safety benefits far outweigh the downsides.

Talk with the person and family about other ways to get around. Options vary by community.  

Use these national resources for up to-date information:

- National Aging and Disability Transportation Center  
- Alzheimer’s Association: Dementia and Driving guide  
- Eldercare Locator  

Family members can find helpful tips online about how to talk with an older driver about stopping or limiting driving.  

Examples include:
- The Hartford’s “At the Crossroads: Family Conversations About Alzheimer’s Disease, Dementia & Driving”  
- AARP’s “We Need to Talk”  
- Alzheimer’s Association: “Having the Conversation”

Newer transportation options, like on-demand ride services through apps, may help.  

But the older person must be able to use these services on their own.  

Often, the same problems that make driving unsafe also make it hard to schedule or use ride services.  

In many cases, a family member or friend must help.  

It helps if several people take turns. This way, the older person can keep going to appointments, social events, and other activities.  

Having reliable transportation helps prevent isolation, inactivity, and depression.

Losing the ability to drive can be very hard emotionally. It can feel like losing independence.  

If no transportation is available and daily activities are affected, the person may need to move in with a family member.  

Or they may need to move to an assisted-living facility or retirement community.

---

## Reporting Concerns to the State

If a doctor believes a person’s health problems make driving unsafe, they must follow their state’s rules for reporting.  

Rules vary by state.  

All states allow doctors to report concerns voluntarily.  

Some states require doctors to report if they think a person is not safe to drive.  

In most states, doctors are protected. Their name is kept private, or they are immune from legal action.  

It may help to talk with a lawyer when setting up reporting rules at a clinic or hospital.

Before reporting, the doctor should talk directly with the older person and their family.  

They should explain why driving is no longer safe.  

They should also explain why reporting is required.  

The goal is to help the person understand and cooperate with driving restrictions.

In some cases, a doctor must report even if the patient does not want to.  

This can hurt the relationship with the patient.  

But if a doctor does not report and someone gets hurt, the doctor could be held legally responsible.

In the United States, only the Department of Motor Vehicles can take away a driver’s license.  

Doctors and other health care providers do not have this power.  

It is important to make this clear to the older person and their family.  

Rules about driver’s licenses for older adults differ from country to country.

# Early Puberty

Early puberty means a child’s body starts changing into an adult’s body too soon.  
This is also called precocious puberty.  
It usually starts before age 8 in girls or before age 9 in boys.  

The cause is often unknown.  
But sometimes it is due to a problem in the brain, like a tumor or other abnormal growth.  

Signs of early puberty include:  
- A sudden growth spurt  
- Early growth of pubic hair and underarm hair  

Doctors diagnose early puberty using:  
- X-rays of the hand and wrist to check bone age  
- Blood tests to measure hormone levels  
- Imaging tests like MRI or ultrasound to look for tumors or brain problems  

Treatment depends on the type of early puberty.  
It may include hormone medicine to slow down the changes.

---

## What Is Normal Puberty?

Puberty is the time when a child’s body changes into an adult’s body.  
These changes allow a person to have children later in life.  

Puberty starts when the brain sends a signal to the pituitary gland.  
The pituitary gland then releases hormones that tell the sex glands to grow.  
In boys, the sex glands are the testicles.  
In girls, the sex glands are the ovaries.  

The sex glands make sex hormones.  
These hormones cause the body to change in ways that mark puberty.  

### For Boys:
- The testicles and scrotum get bigger first  
- Then the penis grows longer  
- Next, pubic and underarm hair appear  
- Puberty usually starts between ages 9 and 14  

### For Girls:
- The first sign is usually breast growth  
- Then pubic and underarm hair start to grow  
- Puberty usually starts between ages 8 and 13  

### How Long Does Puberty Last?
- For girls: about 4 years  
- For boys: about 4 to 6 years  

The timing and speed of changes vary from child to child.  

During puberty, the adrenal glands also start working.  
They make hormones that cause pubic and underarm hair to grow.  
These adrenal hormones are not the same as the main puberty hormones.  

In the United States, puberty is starting earlier than in the past.  
This is especially true for girls.  
Higher body weight is linked to earlier breast development.  
This trend is connected to the rise in childhood obesity.  

Race and ethnicity also affect when puberty starts.  
Black and Hispanic girls tend to start puberty earlier than White girls.

---

## Types of Early Puberty

There are three types of early puberty:

1. Central precocious puberty  
2. Peripheral precocious puberty  
3. Incomplete puberty  

Each type has different causes and symptoms.

### Central Precocious Puberty

This is the most common type.  
It is 5 to 10 times more common in girls than in boys.  

In this type, the brain starts sending signals too early.  
The pituitary gland releases hormones that make the ovaries or testicles grow.  
Once the sex glands grow, they make sex hormones like estrogen or testosterone.  
These hormones cause normal puberty changes, but they start too soon.  

**In boys:**  
- Testicles get bigger  
- Penis grows longer  
- Pubic and underarm hair appear  
- The body takes on a more masculine look  

**In girls:**  
- Breasts grow  
- Pubic and underarm hair appear  
- Menstruation may start  

Both boys and girls grow quickly in height.  
But this fast growth ends early.  
As a result, children with early puberty often end up shorter as adults than they would have been otherwise.  

In most girls, no cause is found.  
But sometimes a tumor or brain problem causes it.  
In boys, brain problems are more likely to be the cause.  

Some rare conditions are linked to this type, such as:  
- Neurofibromatosis (a condition where soft growths form on nerves under the skin)  

Certain medical treatments, like surgery, radiation, or chemotherapy, can also trigger this type.  
Children with a family history of early puberty are more likely to get it.

### Peripheral Precocious Puberty

This type is much less common.  

In this case, the sex hormones estrogen or testosterone are made without help from the pituitary gland.  
Instead, a tumor or other problem in the adrenal gland, ovary, or testicle causes the hormone to be made.  

The testicles or ovaries do not grow or mature.  
But the body still shows signs of puberty.  

The changes depend on which hormone is made, not the child’s sex.  

- If estrogen is made:  
  - Boys and girls may grow breast tissue  
- If androgens (male-like hormones) are made:  
  - Both boys and girls may get pubic and underarm hair  
  - Both may get adult body odor and acne  
  - In boys, the penis may grow larger, but the testicles stay small  

### Incomplete Puberty

Some children show only a few signs of puberty.  
They may have early breast growth or early pubic hair, but no other changes.  

For example:  
- Some girls have breast growth in the first two years of life.  
  - But their hormone levels are normal.  
- Some children get pubic hair between ages 6 and 8.  
  - They may also get adult body odor and acne.  
  - The changes happen slowly.  

These early changes are not caused by a serious illness.  
Most children do not go on to have full early puberty.  

Early pubic hair happens because the adrenal glands make more androgen hormones.  
But the main puberty hormones (gonadotropins and estrogen) stay normal.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Early Puberty

Doctors use several tests to find the cause of early puberty.

### X-ray of the Hand and Wrist
- This shows how mature the bones are.  
- It helps doctors estimate the child’s bone age.  
- If the bones look older than they should, more tests are needed.

### Blood Tests
- These check hormone levels.  
- High levels of certain hormones may point to a tumor or other problem.

### Imaging Tests
- Ultrasound of the pelvis and adrenal glands checks for tumors.  
- MRI of the brain checks for brain tumors or structural problems in the hypothalamus or pituitary gland.

### Genetic Testing
- Doctors may do this if a family member has had early puberty.

---

## How Early Puberty Is Treated

### Treat the Cause
- If a tumor or cyst is found, doctors may remove it.  
- This can stop the early puberty.

### Hormone Medicine
- If no treatable cause is found, medicine may be used.  
- The goal is to slow down puberty.  
- This helps the child grow to a normal adult height.  
- It also helps reduce stress or worry from being different from peers.

**For Central Precocious Puberty:**
- Synthetic hormone injections stop the body from making sex hormones.  
- Injections are given once a month, every 3 months, or every 6 months.  
- A small implant under the skin can also deliver the hormone once a year.

**For Peripheral Precocious Puberty:**
- Medicine blocks the effects of the sex hormones.  
- This stops the body from showing signs of puberty.

### When Treatment Is Not Needed
- If a child only has early pubic or underarm hair, treatment is usually not needed.  
- But regular checkups are important to watch for later changes.  
- Girls who have breast growth before age 2 should be checked if it continues past age 2.

# Urethral Cancer

Urethral cancer is very rare. It can happen in both men and women. There are different types. The most common types are squamous cell cancer and transitional cell cancer. Sometimes it is adenocarcinoma.

Most people with this cancer are 50 years old or older. Some types of human papillomavirus may play a role in causing it. Tumors in the urethra often grow into nearby tissues early. This means the cancer is often advanced by the time it is found. The first places the cancer spreads to are usually the lymph nodes in the groin or pelvis.

## Symptoms and Signs

Most women notice blood in their urine. They may also have trouble passing urine or feel like they cannot empty their bladder. Many women have had frequent urges to urinate or a condition called urethral syndrome. This means the muscles in the pelvic area are overly sensitive.

Most men have symptoms of a narrowed urethra. This is called urethral stricture. Only a few men notice blood in their urine or see a bloody discharge. In some cases, if the cancer is very advanced, a lump can be felt.

## Diagnosis

Doctors suspect urethral cancer based on symptoms. They confirm the diagnosis with a procedure called cystourethroscopy. This uses a thin tube with a camera to look inside the urethra and bladder. The doctor may also do an exam under anesthesia. This means they check the area while the patient is asleep. For women, this may include a pelvic exam and taking a small tissue sample from the vagina.

A biopsy may be needed. This helps tell the difference between cancer, a prolapsed organ, or a small growth called a caruncle. Imaging tests like CT or MRI help show how far the cancer has spread.

## Treatment

Treatment depends on the size and location of the tumor.

For small, early-stage tumors in the front part of the urethra, treatment options include:
- Surgery to remove the tumor
- Radiation therapy (either inside the body or from outside)
- Using heat or electricity to destroy the tumor (fulguration)
- Laser treatment

For larger tumors or those that go deep into tissue, or for tumors in the back part of the urethra, treatment is more complex. It usually includes:
- Major surgery to remove the cancer
- A new way to pass urine (urinary diversion)
- Chemotherapy
- Radiation therapy

The surgery may involve removing lymph nodes from the pelvis and groin. In some cases, part of the pubic bone is also removed.

## Prognosis

The outlook depends on where the cancer is and how deep it has grown.

- If the cancer is in the front part of the urethra, more than 60 out of 100 people live at least 5 years after diagnosis.
- If the cancer is in the back part of the urethra, only 10 to 20 out of 100 people live at least 5 years.

More than half of people who are treated still have the cancer come back.

# Kidney Problems During Pregnancy

Pregnancy usually does not make a kidney problem worse.  
The main reason kidney problems get worse is if a woman has high blood pressure that is not well managed.  

If you have a kidney problem during pregnancy, you are more likely to develop high blood pressure.  
One type of high blood pressure that can happen during pregnancy is called preeclampsia.  

If you had a kidney problem before getting pregnant, your baby may not grow as much as expected.  
This is called being small for gestational age.  
You are also more likely to have a stillbirth.  
If your kidney problem is very severe, you may not be able to carry your baby to full term.  

Doctors will check your kidney function and blood pressure often.  
They will also check how your baby is growing.  

If your kidney problem is serious, you may need to stay in the hospital after 28 weeks of pregnancy.  
This helps you get enough rest.  
It also helps doctors keep your blood pressure under control.  
And it allows them to watch your baby closely.  

Women who have had a kidney transplant can usually have a healthy baby if all of the following are true:  
- The transplant has been in place for at least 2 years.  
- Your kidneys are working normally.  
- You have not had any episodes of rejection.  
- Your blood pressure is normal.  

Women who need regular hemodialysis (a treatment to clean the blood when kidneys fail) face a higher risk of pregnancy problems.  
These include miscarriage, stillbirth, early birth, and preeclampsia.  
But thanks to better dialysis treatments, up to 90 percent of babies born to these women survive.  

Most women with kidney problems need to deliver before their due date.  
This is often because of preeclampsia or because the baby is not growing well.  

Doctors may take a small sample of the fluid around the baby.  
This is called amniocentesis.  
It helps them check if the baby’s lungs are ready to work.  
This tells them when it is safe to deliver the baby.  

A cesarean delivery (C-section) is often needed.  
But sometimes, a vaginal birth is possible.

# Spinal Cord Infarction (Simplified)

This condition happens when blood flow to the spinal cord stops. It usually starts because a blood vessel outside the spine is damaged.

## What Causes It?

The spinal cord needs blood to stay healthy.  
The main blood supply comes from three arteries: two on the back and one on the front.  
The front artery gets most of its blood from a few small branches.  
One large branch, called the artery of Adamkiewicz, supplies the lower part of the spine.  
These branches come from the aorta, the main blood vessel in the body.

Because there are not many backup blood vessels, some parts of the spinal cord are at higher risk.  
The middle to lower chest area is especially vulnerable.  
Damage to the blood vessels outside the spine is the most common cause.  
This can happen from hardening of the arteries, a tear in the aorta, or during surgery when the aorta is clamped.  
Blood clots inside the spinal arteries are rare.  
A disease called polyarteritis nodosa can also cause it, but this is very uncommon.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The first sign is sudden, severe back pain.  
The pain often feels like a tight band around the chest or abdomen.  
Within minutes, both legs and sometimes arms become weak and floppy.  
You may lose feeling, especially to pain and temperature.  
Touch, position, and vibration sense are often still there.  
This pattern is called anterior cord syndrome.

If the damaged area is small and in the center of the spinal cord, you may have central cord syndrome instead.  
This means you lose more function in the arms than the legs, or have more problems with fine movements.

Some people get better over the first few days.  
But many are left with lasting weakness or numbness.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect spinal cord infarction when someone has sudden back pain and quickly develops weakness and numbness.

The best test is an MRI scan.  
It shows the spinal cord and can confirm if an area is damaged from lack of blood.

If an MRI is not available, a CT myelogram may be done.  
This test helps rule out other causes like a blood clot, herniated disc, tumor, or infection.

Other conditions can look similar, such as acute transverse myelitis, spinal cord compression, or demyelinating diseases.  
But those usually develop more slowly.  
MRI and spinal fluid tests help rule them out.

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure for spinal cord infarction.  
Treatment focuses on helping the person feel better and stay safe.

Supportive care includes:  
- Pain relief  
- Physical therapy  
- Help with bladder and bowel control  
- Prevention of complications like pressure sores or blood clots

If the cause is known, such as aortic dissection or polyarteritis nodosa, doctors may treat that condition.  
But in most cases, there is no specific treatment for the infarction itself.

## Key Points

- Spinal cord infarction is most often caused by damage to blood vessels outside the spine.  
- It causes sudden back pain, followed quickly by weakness and numbness in both legs.  
- Pain and temperature sensation are more affected than touch, position, or vibration.  
- A central cord syndrome can also happen.  
- MRI is the best test to confirm the diagnosis.  
- If the cause can be treated, doctors will try.  
- Otherwise, care is focused on support and recovery.

# Exercise for Older Adults

Most people over 65 do not get enough exercise.  
But regular exercise can help you live longer and feel better.  

Exercise can improve:  
- How long you live  
- Your energy and strength  
- Your mood  
- How well you can move and stretch  
- How well you sleep  
- Your thinking and memory  

Many older adults do not know how hard to exercise.  
They also do not know how much they can safely do.  

Exercise is one of the safest and most helpful things you can do for your health.  
As you age, your body naturally loses strength and stamina.  
This makes exercise even more important for older adults.  
You can still gain big health benefits from starting exercise later in life.  

Simple strength training helps with everyday tasks.  
For example:  
- Climbing stairs  
- Bathing  
- Getting dressed  
- Cooking meals  
- Shopping for groceries  

The biggest health gains come when inactive people start moving.  
This is especially true for aerobic exercise.  

Muscles get weaker as you age.  
Weak muscles make daily tasks harder.  
Strength training can build more muscle.  
More muscle means you can do tasks with less effort.  
It also means your heart and lungs do not have to work as hard.  

Stronger leg muscles help you walk faster and climb stairs more easily.  
Older adults who exercise are more likely to recover well if they get very sick.  

Not everyone can exercise safely.  
Some heart problems, uncontrolled high blood pressure, or uncontrolled diabetes can make exercise risky.  
Arthritis or other joint problems can make movement painful.  

But most older adults can still exercise.  
Some may need a special plan.  
Some may need to work with a doctor, physical therapist, or certified trainer.  

Stop exercising and call a doctor if you feel:  
- Chest pain  
- Dizziness  
- Fast or irregular heartbeats  

Before starting any exercise program, see your doctor.  
Your doctor will check for heart problems or other issues that could limit exercise.  

An electrocardiogram (ECG) is usually not needed.  
It is only used if your doctor finds a possible problem during the exam.  

Stress testing is usually not needed.  
It is only recommended for people who are not active and plan to do intense exercise.  
This is especially true if your doctor suspects diabetes, lung disease, or heart disease.  

## Your Exercise Plan

A good exercise plan for older adults includes:  
- Aerobic activity  
- Strength training  
- Flexibility and balance exercises  

Your doctor or an exercise expert can help you create a plan that covers all these areas.  

### Aerobic Activity

Aerobic exercise means moving your body in a way that gets your heart pumping.  
Examples: walking, swimming, cycling.  

Older adults should do aerobic activity for the same amount of time as younger adults.  
But the intensity should be lower.  

During exercise, you should be able to talk comfortably.  
If you cannot talk, you are working too hard.  

If you have no health problems that limit exercise, you can slowly increase your effort.  
You can aim for a target heart rate based on your age.  
(See the table for usual maximum and target heart rates.)  

Some older adults need to build strength first.  
They may not be able to do aerobic exercise until they are stronger.  

### Strength Training

Strength training builds muscle.  
It works the same way for older adults as for younger ones.  

Start with light resistance.  
Examples:  
- Resistance bands  
- Light dumbbells (2 pounds or 1 kilogram)  
- Standing up from a chair  

Do 12 to 20 repetitions per set.  
Use heavier weights and fewer reps only if needed.  
This increases the risk of injury without clear benefits for most older adults.  

### Flexibility

Stretch major muscle groups at least 3 times a week.  
Best time: after exercise, when muscles are warm and loose.  

### Balance Training

Balance training means doing exercises that challenge your stability.  
Examples: standing on one foot, using a balance board.  

Some people use balance training to prevent falls.  
But it may not help much.  
Skills learned on a balance board do not always carry over to real-life situations.  

Also, balance training can cause falls.  
For most older adults, strength and flexibility training are better at preventing falls.  

These exercises:  
- Build stronger muscles around your joints  
- Help you stand and walk more steadily  
- Help you stay upright if you start to fall  
- Help you recover faster if you do fall  

Stronger muscles and better flexibility mean you can handle falls better and heal faster.

# Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID)

This condition means a person eats very little or avoids certain foods. It is not about being unhappy with your body shape or size. That is different from anorexia or bulimia.

ARFID usually starts in childhood. Most often, it begins between the ages of eleven and thirteen. But it can start at any age. We do not know exactly what causes it. It may be linked to genes and life experiences. These can include trauma, anxiety, autism, or other developmental challenges.

At first, ARFID can look like normal picky eating. Some children refuse to eat certain foods. They may not like the color, texture, or smell of food. But normal picky eating usually only affects a few foods. The child still eats enough. Their appetite, growth, and development stay healthy.

People with ARFID avoid or limit food for many reasons. Some lose interest in eating. Others fear eating will cause harm. For example, they may fear choking or vomiting. They may avoid foods because of how they look, feel, or smell.

## Symptoms of ARFID

A person with ARFID avoids food so much that they have at least one of the following:

- They lose a lot of weight.
- Children do not grow as they should.
- They lack important nutrients in their body.
- They need a feeding tube or special supplements to get nutrition.
- Their daily life is seriously affected. For example, they cannot join family meals or spend time with friends when food is involved.

Low nutrition can be dangerous. It can even be life-threatening. Social life can also suffer. People may avoid events where food is served.

## How Doctors Diagnose ARFID

Doctors use a mental health evaluation to diagnose ARFID. They follow strict guidelines from the *Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders*, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR).

To diagnose ARFID, the person must have:

- A serious lack of food intake.
- This lack causes weight loss, poor growth in children, serious nutrient shortages, need for feeding tubes or supplements, or major problems in daily life.
- The lack of food is not due to not having food available.
- It is not part of a cultural practice like fasting for religious reasons.
- It is not caused by a medical illness or its treatment, such as chemotherapy.
- It is not caused by another eating disorder, especially anorexia.

There is no sign that the person has a distorted view of their body size or shape.

Sometimes, a person with a medical condition eats less than normal. But if they keep eating very little for much longer than expected, and need special help to eat more, they may be diagnosed with ARFID.

When someone first sees a doctor, the doctor checks for other health problems. These include medical illnesses, depression, schizophrenia, or other eating disorders. The doctor must rule out these causes before diagnosing ARFID.

## How ARFID Is Treated

Two main treatments are used:

- Cognitive behavioral therapy
- Family-based treatment

Both help people eat more normally. They also help reduce fear and anxiety around food.

## Key Points

- ARFID can cause serious weight loss.
- It can lead to life-threatening nutrient shortages.
- It can make daily life very hard, especially around food and social events.
- Diagnosis depends on clear rules. Doctors must rule out other conditions like anorexia or bulimia.
- Treatment works best with cognitive behavioral therapy or family-based therapy.

# Kidney Cancer

Most solid kidney tumors are cancer. But tumors filled only with fluid (called cysts) are usually not cancer.

Almost all kidney cancers are a type called renal cell carcinoma. Another type, called Wilms tumor, mainly affects children.
