# Circadian Rhythm Sleep Disorders

Your body has an internal clock. It tells you when to sleep and when to wake up. This clock follows the natural cycle of light and dark during the day and night.

Sometimes, this internal clock does not match the outside world. When that happens, you may have trouble sleeping or waking at normal times. This is called a circadian rhythm sleep disorder.

## What Causes These Problems?

### Internal Causes
- Brain damage from infection, stroke, injury, or Alzheimer’s disease.
- Your body does not respond well to changes in light and dark.

### External Causes
- Traveling across many time zones (jet lag).
- Working night or rotating shifts.
- Going to bed and waking up at different times every day.
- Being in bed for long periods without moving.
- Being blind or not getting enough sunlight.
- Taking certain medicines or illegal drugs.

People in hospitals often have sleep problems. They are woken up at night. They also do not get enough sunlight during the day. This can make their sleep schedule go off track.

## Types of Circadian Rhythm Sleep Disorders

### Jet Lag Disorder
This happens after fast travel across several time zones. Your body clock is out of sync with the new time zone.

### Shift Work Disorder
This affects people who work night or rotating shifts. The severity depends on:
- How often your shift changes.
- How much your shift times change.
- Whether your shift is earlier or later than usual.
- How many nights you work in a row.
- How long your shift lasts.

It is better to work the same night or evening shift every time. You should also keep the same bedtime on days off. But even then, noise and light during the day can make it hard to sleep. Many workers also shorten their sleep or change their sleep times to spend time with family or friends.

### Delayed Sleep Phase Disorder
You go to sleep very late and wake up very late. For example, you might fall asleep at 3 AM and wake up at 10 AM or later. This is more common in teens and young adults. You cannot fall asleep earlier, even if you try.

### Advanced Sleep Phase Disorder
You go to sleep very early and wake up very early. You cannot stay awake later, even if you try. This is more common in older adults.

### Non–24-Hour Sleep-Wake Syndrome
Your sleep and wake times shift later by 1 to 2 hours each day. Your body clock is longer than 24 hours. This is rare. It mostly happens in people who are totally blind.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may feel very sleepy during the day. You may have trouble focusing, thinking clearly, or doing your normal tasks.

You might use alcohol, sleeping pills, or stimulants to help you sleep or stay awake.

Symptoms get worse when:
- You change your sleep schedule often (like frequent travel or shift changes).
- You have to go to sleep earlier (such as when flying east).

If the cause is outside your body, other rhythms in your body are also affected. These include body temperature and hormone levels. You may feel:
- Unwell.
- Irritable.
- Nauseous.
- Sad or low.
- Sleepy.

You may also have a higher risk of heart and metabolic problems.

If the cause is fixed, your symptoms usually go away in a few days. In older adults, it may take weeks or months.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms. You may be asked to keep a sleep log for several weeks. This means writing down when you go to bed and when you wake up.

A sleep lab test is rarely needed.

## How Is It Treated?

### Change Your Habits

Good sleep habits can help you get back on track.

#### Follow a Regular Sleep-Wake Schedule
- Go to bed at the same time every night.
- Get up at the same time every morning—even on weekends and vacations.
- Do not spend too much time in bed.

#### Have a Nighttime Routine
- Do the same things every night before bed. Examples: listen to soft music, brush your teeth, wash your face, set your alarm.
- Avoid bright lights before bed.
- Do not use your phone, computer, or TV for a few hours before bed.

#### Make Your Bedroom Sleep-Friendly
- Keep the room dark, quiet, and at a comfortable temperature.
- Use earplugs, a white-noise machine, or a fan to block noise.
- Use heavy curtains or a sleep mask to block light.
- If you wake up at night, avoid bright lights.

#### Use Pillows for Comfort
- Place a pillow between your knees or under your waist.
- If you have back pain, try lying on your side with a pillow between your knees.
- Or lie on your back with a pillow under your knees.

#### Use Your Bed Only for Sleep and Sex
- Do not eat, read, watch TV, work, or use your phone in bed.

#### Get Up If You Can’t Sleep
- If you are still awake after 20 minutes, get up.
- Go to another room and do something quiet.
- Return to bed only when you feel sleepy.

#### Exercise Regularly
- Exercise helps you fall asleep naturally.
- But avoid exercise within 5 hours of bedtime. It can make you too alert.

#### Relax Before Bed
- Stress and worry keep you awake.
- Try reading, taking a warm bath, or using relaxation techniques.
- Examples: imagining peaceful scenes, tensing and relaxing your muscles, slow breathing.
- Set aside time during the day to think about your worries. This helps you leave them behind at bedtime.

#### Avoid Stimulating Activities Before Bed
- Do not watch exciting shows, play intense games, or work on hard tasks in the hour before bed.

#### Avoid Things That Hurt Sleep
- Alcohol, caffeine (coffee, tea, soda, chocolate), nicotine (cigarettes, patches), appetite suppressants, and diuretics can all hurt sleep.
- Do not have caffeine within 12 hours of bedtime.
- Drinking a lot of alcohol in the evening can cause you to wake up too early.
- Quitting smoking may help.

#### Eat a Light Snack If Needed
- Hunger can keep you awake.
- A small warm snack may help, unless you have acid reflux.
- Stop eating at least a few hours before bed.
- Avoid heavy meals close to bedtime. They can cause heartburn and make sleep harder.

#### Avoid Anxiety-Triggering Behaviors
- Turn your clock away so you cannot see the time.
- Do not watch the clock while in bed.

#### Get Bright Light During the Day
- Light during the day helps your body clock match the day-night cycle.
- For jet lag: spend time in sunlight, especially in the morning, after you arrive at your destination.
- For shift workers: get bright light (sunlight or artificial) when you are awake.
- Wear sunglasses on the way home to reduce light exposure before bedtime. But do not wear them if they make you drowsy while driving.
- When shift workers sleep, make the room as dark and quiet as possible. Use sleep masks and white-noise machines.

#### Use Light Therapy Based on Your Problem
- Morning light helps people with delayed sleep phase disorder.
- Evening light helps people with advanced sleep phase disorder.

#### Gradually Shift Your Schedule
- Before traveling, slowly move your sleep and wake times to match your destination.
- Start this change well before your trip.

### Medications

If habits alone do not help, your doctor may suggest medicine.

#### Short-Acting Sleep Aids
- These help you fall asleep faster.
- They are for short-term use only.

#### Brain-Stimulating Drugs (like modafinil)
- These help you stay awake during the day.
- They are used for shift workers or people with sleepiness during the day.

> Note: These medicines do not fix your body clock faster. They only help with sleep or alertness.

#### Melatonin
- This hormone helps reduce jet lag and shift work problems.
- It can help your body adjust to new times.

#### Tasimelteon
- This medicine works like melatonin.
- It helps blind people with non–24-hour sleep-wake syndrome.
- It increases nighttime sleep and reduces daytime sleep.
- Take it by mouth every night before bed.
- Side effects: headaches and strange dreams or nightmares.

> Always talk to your doctor before starting any medicine.

# Immersion Pulmonary Edema – Simple Explanation

## What Is Immersion Pulmonary Edema?

Immersion pulmonary edema is a sudden buildup of fluid in the lungs.  
It usually happens to divers while they are at the surface or early in a dive.  
It can also happen to swimmers during intense open water swimming.

This condition is not caused by pressure changes in the lungs or by decompression sickness.  
It happens when blood shifts from the body’s limbs into the blood vessels in the lungs.  
This causes too much pressure in the lung blood vessels.  
The pressure forces fluid into the lung tissue.

## Who Is at Risk?

You are more likely to get this if you:
- Swim or dive in cold water.
- Have high blood pressure.
- Have lung problems.
- Have heart problems, especially those affecting how the heart pumps or relaxes.

This includes conditions like valve problems in the heart, heart muscle disease, or other heart issues.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may feel very short of breath.  
This usually happens while you are underwater.  
You will likely come up to the surface quickly.  
You may start coughing.  
You might cough up frothy, bubbly mucus.  
Your lungs may make crackling sounds when you breathe.  
Your lips or fingertips may turn blue.  
You may feel dizzy or weak.

Low oxygen levels in your blood are common.  
This can be life-threatening if not treated.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A chest X-ray will show fluid in the lungs.  
A lung ultrasound done at the scene can also help find fluid.  
Heart tests usually show normal heart function and normal heart arteries.  
But some people have heart wall movement problems, valve issues, or heart muscle disease.  
An echocardiogram can check for problems with how the heart relaxes.

## How Is It Treated?

You will need oxygen right away.  
This helps raise your blood oxygen level.  
Sometimes, a breathing treatment with a medicine that opens the airways is used.  
Most people get better with these steps.  
Diuretics (water pills) are rarely needed.  
In severe cases, a breathing machine may be required.  
Recompression therapy is not needed and should not be used.

## How Can It Be Prevented?

People who have had this problem should be checked for:
- High blood pressure.
- Valve problems in the heart.
- Heart muscle disease.
- Lung problems.

Doctors should also check for silent heart disease, even if you have no symptoms.  
This condition can come back in people who are at risk.  
Before returning to diving or competitive swimming, you must be fully evaluated.  
Any treatable risk factors should be fixed first.

## More Help and Information

The following resources can help if you need more information:

**Divers Alert Network**  
24-hour emergency hotline: 919-684-9111

**Duke Dive Medicine**  
Doctors can talk to other doctors: 919-684-8111

# Growth Hormone Deficiency in Children

## What Is Growth Hormone Deficiency?

Growth hormone deficiency means the body does not make enough growth hormone.  
This hormone helps children grow taller and develop physically.  
It is made by a small gland at the base of the brain called the pituitary gland.  

This condition is the most common problem with the pituitary gland.  
It causes slow growth and short height.  

Other symptoms depend on the child’s age and why the deficiency started.  

Most of the time, doctors do not know the cause.  
But sometimes it is due to a birth defect, brain tumor, or injury.  

## The Pituitary Gland: The Body’s Control Center

The pituitary gland is about the size of a pea.  
It sits at the bottom of the brain.  
It makes many hormones that control other glands in the body.  

Because it controls so many other glands, it is often called the master gland.  

Each hormone it makes affects a specific part of the body.  
For example:  
- Growth hormone affects muscles and bones.  
- Thyroid-stimulating hormone affects the thyroid gland.  
- Adrenocorticotropic hormone affects the adrenal glands.  
- Oxytocin affects the uterus and breasts.  
- Prolactin affects the breasts.  

Some hormones are made in the brain’s hypothalamus.  
They are stored in the pituitary and released when needed.  

## What Happens When Growth Hormone Is Low?

If the pituitary gland does not make enough growth hormone, a child grows slowly.  
They may be much shorter than other children their age.  

Sometimes, a child with low growth hormone also has low levels of other pituitary hormones.  
This is called hypopituitarism.  
It can affect the thyroid, adrenal glands, ovaries, or testes.  

## What Is Short Stature?

Short stature means a child is shorter than 97 out of 100 children their age.  
Doctors use growth charts to track height and weight over time.  

Many children are short because their parents are short.  
Some grow late, but still reach a normal height.  

Other causes of short stature include:  
- Poor nutrition  
- Chronic health problems like thyroid disease, heart disease, lung disease, kidney disease, or intestinal issues  
- Genetic conditions such as Turner syndrome or skeletal dysplasia  

## Causes of Growth Hormone Deficiency

In most cases, the cause is unknown.  
But about 1 in 4 cases has a clear reason.  
These include:  
- A problem with a gene  
- Brain problems, tumors, infections like meningitis, or head injuries  
- Radiation treatment to the brain  
- A lung disease called histiocytosis  

## Symptoms of Growth Hormone Deficiency

Children grow very slowly.  
Before age 4, they grow less than 2.5 inches (6 centimeters) per year.  
From age 4 to 8, they grow less than 2 inches (5 centimeters) per year.  
Before puberty, they grow less than 1.5 inches (4 centimeters) per year.  

Most children with this condition are short but have normal body proportions.  
Some may get their baby teeth later than usual.  

Newborns with this condition may have:  
- Low blood sugar  
- Yellow skin (jaundice)  
- A small penis in boys  
- Face problems like a cleft palate  

Some children do not start puberty on time.  
They may gain weight faster than they grow taller.  
This can lead to being overweight.  

They may also have symptoms of other hormone problems, such as low thyroid function.  

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several steps to diagnose growth hormone deficiency.  

### Step 1: Check Growth and Medical History  
Doctors measure the child’s height and weight.  
They compare these to standard growth charts.  
They also ask about past health problems that could slow growth.  

### Step 2: X-rays of the Hand  
A hand x-ray shows how far the bones have developed.  
This is called bone age.  
Children with growth hormone deficiency often have delayed bone age.  
This can also happen in other conditions like low thyroid function or late puberty.  

### Step 3: Blood Tests  
Growth hormone levels in the blood change all day.  
So a single blood test is not reliable.  

Instead, doctors test for other substances in the blood that grow when growth hormone is present.  
These include:  
- Insulin-like growth factor 1  
- Insulin-like growth factor binding protein 3  

But these levels can be affected by other health issues.  
So doctors may test for:  
- Low thyroid function  
- Celiac disease  
- Poor nutrition  

### Step 4: Genetic Testing  
If a doctor suspects a genetic condition, they may do genetic testing.  
This is common if the child has signs of Turner syndrome or other known syndromes.  

### Step 5: Brain Imaging  
If the doctor thinks there is a problem in the brain, they may order an MRI.  
This scan checks for tumors or other brain issues.  

### Step 6: Stimulation Test  
If no other cause is found and growth is very slow, doctors do a stimulation test.  
They give medicine to make the body release growth hormone.  
Then they check blood levels over several hours.  
This helps confirm if the pituitary gland is not working right.  

## How Is It Treated?

The main treatment is growth hormone replacement.  
The child gets daily or weekly injections of synthetic growth hormone.  

The treatment continues until:  
- The child reaches a height that is acceptable  
- The child grows less than 1 inch (2.5 centimeters) in a year  

In the first year of treatment, many children grow 4 to 5 inches (10 to 12 centimeters).  
But results vary from child to child.  

### Side Effects of Treatment  
Most children do not have serious side effects.  
Some may have mild swelling in the hands or feet.  
This usually goes away quickly.  

Rarely, more serious side effects can happen:  
- Increased pressure in the brain (idiopathic intracranial hypertension)  
- Pain in the hip or knee, or limping (slipped capital femoral epiphysis)  

### Using Growth Hormone for Short Stature Without Deficiency  
Some children are short but have normal growth hormone levels.  
Doctors may still give growth hormone to help them grow taller.  
But this is controversial.  

Many doctors do not support this use.  
They believe short stature is not a disease unless it is caused by a medical problem.  

Growth hormone only works before the bones stop growing.  
Once growth stops, it will not help.  

## Treating Underlying Causes

If a brain tumor is found, surgery may be an option.  
But surgery can damage the pituitary gland.  
This can lead to hypopituitarism.  

If the child lacks other hormones, they will need hormone replacement therapy.  
This treatment helps the body work normally.

# Sprains and Other Soft-Tissue Injuries – Simple Explanation

## What Are Sprains and Other Soft-Tissue Injuries?

A sprain is a tear in a ligament.  
A ligament connects bone to bone.  
A strain is a tear in a muscle.  
A tendon connects muscle to bone.  
Tears can also happen in tendons.

Other injuries that affect the muscles, bones, and joints include:
- Broken bones (fractures)
- Joints that come out of place (dislocations) or move partially out (subluxations)

These types of injuries are common.  
They can happen in any part of the body.  
The arms, legs, spine, and pelvis can all be injured.

Injuries can happen on their own.  
They can also happen with other serious injuries, like in a car crash or a fall from a height.

Most injuries come from blunt force.  
This means a hard hit or impact.  
But sharp injuries, like from a knife or bullet, can also damage muscles, bones, and joints.

---

## How Are These Injuries Diagnosed?

### Step 1: Talk to the Patient and Do a Physical Exam

Doctors will ask about how the injury happened.  
They will check the injured area.  
They will also check the joints above and below the injury.

Most sprains, strains, and tendon injuries can be diagnosed this way.  
No special tests are always needed.

### Step 2: Check for Serious Injuries

If the injury came from a high-speed car crash or a fall from a height, doctors will check the whole body.  
They will look for life-threatening injuries first.  
They may need to start treatment right away.

### Step 3: Use X-rays When Needed

X-rays help find broken bones.  
They are not needed for all injuries.  
For example, most ankle sprains do not need an X-ray.

### Step 4: Use MRI for Soft-Tissue Injuries

An MRI scan can show tears in ligaments, tendons, and muscles.  
It gives a clear picture of soft tissues.

---

## How Are These Injuries Treated?

### Treat Serious Injuries First

If there is a dislocation, the joint must be put back in place.  
This is called reduction.  
Pain relief (analgesia) is given.  
The injured area is splinted to keep it stable.

### Use RICE or PRICE for Most Injuries

RICE means:
- Rest: Do not use the injured area.
- Ice: Put a cold pack on it for 15 to 20 minutes at a time.
- Compression: Wrap it with a bandage to reduce swelling.
- Elevation: Raise the injured part above heart level.

PRICE adds:
- Protection: Use a brace or support to keep the area safe.

This treatment helps reduce pain and swelling.

### Immobilization

Most injuries need the area to be kept still.  
This helps the tissues heal.

### Surgery

Some injuries need surgery.  
This is usually for severe tears or when the joint is unstable.

---

## Special Considerations for Older Adults

Older people are more likely to get these injuries because:

- They fall more often.  
- Age can reduce balance and body awareness.  
- Some medicines can make balance worse.  
- Blood pressure can drop when standing up, causing dizziness.

Older people also have weaker reflexes.  
This makes it harder to protect themselves during a fall.

### Goals of Treatment in Older Adults

The main goal is to get back to normal daily activities as fast as possible.

Immobilizing a joint for too long can cause problems.  
These include:
- Stiffness
- Tightened muscles
- Loss of muscle strength

### What Helps Recovery?

- Start moving again as soon as possible.  
- Do physical therapy exercises.  
- These help restore movement and strength.

Other health problems, like arthritis, can slow healing.  
They must be managed at the same time.

---

## Key Points to Remember

- Compartment syndrome and loss of blood flow are rare with sprains and strains.  
  But they can be life-threatening if they happen.

- Always check for broken bones and dislocations.  
  Also check for injuries to ligaments, tendons, and muscles.  
  Sometimes, the full exam is delayed until a fracture is ruled out.

- Pain in one joint may come from a problem in a nearby joint.  
  For example, shoulder pain can come from a problem at the collarbone joint.  
  Always check the joints above and below the injured area.

- X-rays are not needed for many injuries.  
  For example, most ankle sprains do not need an X-ray.

- MRI scans are useful for seeing soft-tissue injuries.

- Treat serious injuries right away.  
  Stabilize unstable injuries with a splint.  
  Treat pain as soon as possible.

- Most minor injuries are treated with PRICE: protection, rest, ice, compression, elevation.

- Give patients clear, written instructions on how to care for casts or bandages.

- Encourage all patients to do their exercises.  
  This is especially important for older adults.  
  Exercises help keep joints moving and muscles strong.

# Barotrauma

Barotrauma is injury to body tissues caused by changes in pressure. This happens when air inside parts of your body gets squeezed or expands.

## What Can Be Affected

- Lungs  
- Belly and digestive system  
- Face under a face mask  
- Eyes  
- Ears  
- Sinuses (air pockets in the bones around your nose)

## Symptoms by Area

- **Lungs**: Trouble breathing, chest pain  
- **Face mask**: Red, bloodshot eyes  
- **Ears**: Dizziness, ear pain  
- **Sinuses**: Face pain, nosebleed

## When Risk Is Highest

The biggest risk happens when you go from the surface down to about 33 feet (10 meters) underwater.

## How to Prevent Barotrauma

- **For lungs**: Breathe normally while coming up. Never hold your breath.
- **For face mask**: Blow air from your nose into the mask as you go down.
- **For ears and sinuses**: Yawn, swallow, or pinch your nose and try to blow gently. Use a nasal decongestant before diving if you have a stuffy nose.

## Why It Happens

Water pressure increases as you go deeper. Your body fluids do not get squeezed because they are mostly liquid. But air in your lungs, sinuses, ears, or inside a face mask can get squeezed or expand.

When pressure drops during ascent, air expands. If you do not let air out, it can stretch or burst tissues.

## Most Serious Type: Lung Injury

Lung barotrauma is the most dangerous type.

- You breathe in more air at depth because pressure squeezes it.
- As you rise, the air in your lungs expands.
- If you hold your breath, the air has nowhere to go.
- The lungs can overinflate and burst.

When the lungs burst:
- Air can leak into the space between the lungs and chest wall. This can cause the lung to collapse.
- Air can get into the tissues around the heart.
- Air can enter the skin under the neck and chest.
- Air can enter blood vessels.

Air in blood vessels can travel to other parts of the body. This can block blood flow and cause serious harm.

### Common Cause

Holding your breath while rising from a dive. This often happens when you run out of air and panic.

Even a short rise of just 4 feet (1 meter) can cause this if you hold your breath.

Lung injury can also happen in a pool if you breathe in air at 3 to 4 feet below the surface and do not exhale while coming up.

People with lung disease, such as asthma, are at higher risk.

### COVID-19 and Diving Risk

Some people who had even mild symptoms of COVID-19—like chest pain, fast heartbeat, cough, or trouble breathing—may have lung damage. This increases the risk of lung injury while diving.

Anyone with such symptoms should get checked by a doctor before diving again.

## Symptoms of Barotrauma

Symptoms usually start near the surface during descent or ascent.

### Lung Injuries

- Chest pain  
- Trouble breathing  
- Coughing up blood or frothy spit  
- Air trapped under the skin of the neck or chest can make a crackling sound when touched  
- Voice may sound hoarse if nerves are pressed

### Face Mask Injury

- Eyes look red and bloodshot  
- Vision is usually not affected  
- Rarely, bleeding behind the eyes can cause vision loss  
- Face may look bruised

### Ear Injury

- Pain in the ear during descent  
- The eardrum bulges inward  
- If pressure builds too much, the eardrum can burst  
- Cold water rushes into the ear  
- Dizziness, spinning feeling, confusion, nausea, or vomiting  
- These symptoms can be dangerous and may lead to drowning  
- Dizziness fades as the water warms up  
- Hearing may be reduced  
- Infection can develop later, causing pain and ear discharge  
- Inner ear damage can cause sudden hearing loss, ringing in the ears, or dizziness

### Sinus Injury

- Face pain and headaches during descent  
- Feeling of stuffiness in the face or nose  
- Nosebleed during ascent  
- Rarely, skin over the cheek becomes very sensitive or vision is affected

### Tooth Pain

- Pressure in air spaces near teeth or fillings can cause toothache  
- Can damage teeth

### Eye Injury

- Small air bubbles can get trapped behind hard contact lenses  
- This can hurt the eyes  
- Causes soreness, blurry vision, or halos around lights

### Belly and Digestive System

- Swallowing air while diving can cause bloating, cramps, pain, burping, or gas  
- These usually go away on their own  
- Rarely, the stomach or intestine can burst  
- This causes severe pain and serious illness

## How Doctors Diagnose Barotrauma

Doctors look at your symptoms and your diving history.

They may do tests depending on the injury:
- Chest X-ray for lung problems  
- Hearing or vision tests for ear or eye injuries

## How Barotrauma Is Treated

### Lung Injuries

- **Collapsed lung (pneumothorax)**: A tube is placed in the chest to let air out and help the lung re-expand.
- **Air in chest tissues (pneumomediastinum)**: Rest and extra oxygen.
- **Air under the skin (subcutaneous emphysema)**: Rest and extra oxygen.

### Ear and Sinus Injuries

- Use nasal decongestants (like oxymetazoline spray) or pills.
- If healing is slow, a doctor may prescribe steroid medicine (spray or pills).
- If you have major hearing loss, ringing in the ears, or severe dizziness, see a doctor right away.
- Inner ear injury may need surgery to prevent permanent damage.

### Ruptured Eardrum

- Usually heals on its own.
- If infection develops, antibiotics (pills or ear drops) are needed.
- A tear between middle and inner ear may need surgery to prevent lasting damage.

### Stomach or Intestine Rupture

- Requires surgery to fix.

## How to Prevent Barotrauma

- **Lungs**: Always breathe out slowly while coming up. Even in a pool, if you breathe in air at depth, let it out as you rise.
- **Sinuses and ears**: Use decongestants if you have a stuffy nose. Yawn or swallow with your nose pinched to open the eustachian tube.
- **Face mask**: Blow air from your nose into the mask to keep pressure balanced.

### Do Not Use

- Earplugs: They trap air and stop pressure from equalizing.
- Eye goggles: They trap air and cannot be adjusted.
- Tight-fitting wet suit hoods: They must be vented so air can move in and out.

### Before Diving

- If you have asthma or other lung problems, get checked by a doctor first.
- If you had any symptoms of COVID-19, get cleared by a doctor before diving.

# Merkel Cell Carcinoma

Merkel cell carcinoma is a rare and serious type of skin cancer.  
It mostly affects older white people.  
It can also affect younger people who have weak immune systems.  

The average age when people are diagnosed is about 75 years.  
The cancer grows quickly and can spread to other parts of the body.  

## What Causes Merkel Cell Carcinoma?

- Long-term exposure to sunlight (ultraviolet light)  
- Infection with a certain virus called the Merkel cell polyomavirus  
- Having another type of cancer, such as multiple myeloma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, or melanoma  

## What Does It Look Like?

The cancer often shows up as a lump on the skin.  
The lump is usually firm and shiny.  
It may be the color of the skin or look bluish-red.  
It feels like a small, hard bump.  

The most common signs are:  
- It grows very fast  
- It does not hurt or feel tender  

The cancer most often appears on skin that gets a lot of sun.  
This includes the face and arms.  

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor will take a small sample of the lump.  
This is called a biopsy.  
The sample is checked in a lab to confirm if it is cancer.  

Most people already have cancer that has spread when they are first diagnosed.  
This makes the outlook less favorable.  

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on how far the cancer has spread.  
This is called staging.  

Common treatments include:  
- Surgery to remove the tumor and a wide area around it  
- Radiation therapy after surgery to kill any remaining cancer cells  
- Removal of nearby lymph nodes if the cancer has spread there  

For cancer that has spread or comes back after treatment:  
- Immunotherapy drugs like avelumab, pembrolizumab, or retifanlimab may be used  
- These drugs help the body’s immune system fight the cancer  
- Chemotherapy may also be used in some cases  

## How Can It Be Prevented?

Since sunlight plays a role in causing this cancer, it is important to protect your skin.  

**Stay out of the sun when it is strongest:**  
- Seek shade during the day  
- Avoid being outside between 10 in the morning and 4 in the afternoon  
- Do not use tanning beds or sunbathe  

**Wear protective clothing:**  
- Long-sleeved shirts  
- Long pants  
- Hats with wide brims  

**Use sunscreen every day:**  
- Choose a sunscreen with at least SPF 30  
- Make sure it protects against both UVA and UVB rays  
- Apply it as directed  
- Reapply every two hours  
- Reapply after swimming or sweating  
- Do not use sunscreen to stay in the sun longer than safe

# What Is a Blood Transfusion?

A blood transfusion moves blood or part of blood from a healthy person to someone who is sick.  
The goal is to help the blood carry more oxygen.  
It also helps replace lost blood and fix problems with blood clotting.

In the United States, about 15 million people get blood transfusions each year.  
Common reasons for needing a transfusion include:

- Serious injuries  
- Surgery  
- Cancer treatments like leukemia  
- Other blood disorders such as sickle cell disease and thalassemia  

The Food and Drug Administration, or FDA, makes sure blood is collected, moved, and stored safely.  
These rules protect both the person giving blood and the person receiving it.  
State and local health groups, and groups like the American Red Cross and AABB, also follow strict safety rules.  
Because of these rules, giving and receiving blood is very safe.

Still, there are some risks for the person getting the blood.  
These include:

- Allergic reactions  
- Fever and chills  
- Too much blood in the body  
- Infections from bacteria or viruses  

The chance of getting AIDS, hepatitis, or other infections from a transfusion is very small.  
Doctors only give transfusions when there is no other choice.  
Before a transfusion (unless it is an emergency), doctors explain the risks.  
They ask the patient to sign a form showing they understand the risks and agree to the transfusion.  
This is called informed consent.

Sometimes, people who give blood may feel unwell afterward.  
Side effects can include dizziness, low blood pressure, nausea, or tingling, numbness, or bruising where the needle went in.

---

## Blood Types

Everyone has a blood type.  
Your blood type depends on certain markers on the surface of your red blood cells.  
These markers are called antigens.  
The main antigens are A and B.  
Another important marker is the Rh factor.

There are four main blood types:

- Type A: Has A antigens, but not B antigens  
- Type B: Has B antigens, but not A antigens  
- Type AB: Has both A and B antigens  
- Type O: Has neither A nor B antigens  

Blood can also be Rh-positive or Rh-negative.  
Rh-positive means the Rh factor is on the red blood cells.  
Rh-negative means it is not.  
About 85 out of 100 people are Rh-positive.  
About 15 out of 100 are Rh-negative.

If your blood lacks A or B antigens, your body naturally makes antibodies against them.  
For example:

- People with type A blood have antibodies against B  
- People with type O blood have antibodies against both A and B  

There are other blood group antigens besides A and B.  
But your body does not make antibodies against them unless you are exposed to them through a transfusion.

Some blood types are more common than others.  
In the United States, the most common types are:

- O-positive  
- A-positive  
- B-positive  
- O-negative  
- A-negative  

Less common types include:

- AB-positive  
- B-negative  
- AB-negative  

---

## Matching Blood Types

The safest transfusion happens when the donor’s blood type matches the patient’s blood type and Rh status.  
This is called compatibility.  
Before a transfusion, blood banks test both the donor’s and the patient’s blood.  
This test is called a type and cross-match.  
It helps prevent dangerous or life-threatening reactions.

The patient’s blood is also checked for antibodies that could react with the donor’s blood.

In an emergency, anyone can get type O red blood cells.  
So people with type O blood are called universal donors.  
People with type AB blood can receive red blood cells from any donor.  
They are called universal recipients.

People with Rh-negative blood must usually get Rh-negative blood.  
This is true unless it is a life-threatening emergency.  
People with Rh-positive blood can get either Rh-positive or Rh-negative blood.

# Chondroitin Sulfate

Chondroitin sulfate is a natural substance found in cartilage.  
Cartilage is the tough, flexible tissue that covers the ends of bones in joints.  
It helps joints move smoothly and absorb shock.  

Chondroitin sulfate comes from shark or cow cartilage.  
It can also be made in a lab.  
The exact makeup of chondroitin sulfate can vary between products.  
It is often used together with another supplement called glucosamine.

---

## What People Use Chondroitin Sulfate For

People take chondroitin sulfate to help with joint pain from osteoarthritis.  
Osteoarthritis is a condition where the cartilage in joints wears down over time.  
This causes pain, stiffness, and swelling in the joints.  

Studies show that chondroitin sulfate alone does not help much.  
But when taken with glucosamine, it may help reduce joint pain.  
It may also help you move your joints more easily.  
Some people may be able to take less of their regular pain medicine.  
These benefits may happen if you take the supplement every day for 6 to 24 months.  
We do not know if it helps after longer than 2 years.  
The reason it works is not yet clear.

---

## What the Research Says

Research on chondroitin sulfate gives mixed results.  

The Glucosamine / Chondroitin Arthritis Intervention Trial (GAIT) was a large study.  
It looked at glucosamine, chondroitin sulfate, and both together.  
The study found no overall pain relief in people with knee osteoarthritis.  
But a closer look at a smaller group showed some benefit.  
This group had moderate to severe knee pain.  

Before GAIT, only small studies had looked at chondroitin sulfate.  
These earlier studies gave unclear results.  

A review of 43 studies found only small pain relief in the short term.  
But quality of life may improve.  
Another review of 18 studies found that chondroitin sulfate reduced pain and improved joint function.  

One reason for the mixed results may be the quality of the supplements.  
Some chondroitin sulfate products sold as food supplements are not pure.  
They may not have the right amount of active ingredient.  
A different study used a high-quality, pharmaceutical-grade version.  
This version worked better than a placebo.  
It worked as well as a common pain medicine called celecoxib.  

The type of osteoarthritis and its cause can also affect how well chondroitin sulfate works.  
This makes it hard to predict who will benefit.

---

## What Experts Recommend

The American College of Rheumatology does not recommend chondroitin sulfate for knee or hip osteoarthritis.  
They do suggest it may be helpful for hand osteoarthritis, but only with caution.  

The European Society of Clinical and Economic Aspects of Osteoarthritis (ESCEO) recommends using pharmaceutical-grade chondroitin sulfate.  
This means a high-quality product with a known level of purity.

---

## Side Effects

Chondroitin sulfate is generally safe.  
No serious side effects have been reported.  

Common side effects include:  
- Upset stomach  
- Nausea  
- Bloating  
- Diarrhea  

These side effects are usually mild and go away on their own.

---

## Risks from Animal Sources

Chondroitin sulfate from animals may carry risks.  
Shark or cow cartilage may contain viruses, bacteria, or other harmful germs.  
These can cause illness.  
This risk is lower with lab-made or high-quality pharmaceutical products.

---

## Drug Interactions

Chondroitin sulfate may affect blood-thinning medicine.  
It may make warfarin work stronger.  
This increases the risk of bleeding.  
If you take warfarin, talk to your doctor before using chondroitin sulfate.

# Birth Defects in the Digestive Tract

A birth defect means a problem that is present when a baby is born. These problems can affect any part of the digestive system. The digestive system includes the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum, and anus.

## Types of Digestive Tract Birth Defects

Some common birth defects in the digestive tract include:

- **Abdominal wall defects** – The belly wall does not close properly. This can cause organs to stick out. Examples are omphalocele and gastroschisis.
- **Anal atresia** – The opening at the end of the rectum is missing or blocked.
- **Biliary atresia** – The tubes that carry bile from the liver to the intestines are blocked or missing. Bile helps digest food.
- **Diaphragmatic hernia** – A hole in the muscle that separates the chest from the belly. This lets belly organs move into the chest.
- **Esophageal atresia and tracheoesophageal fistula** – The tube from the mouth to the stomach (esophagus) is not connected properly. Sometimes it connects to the windpipe by mistake.
- **Hirschsprung disease** – The nerves in the intestines do not form correctly. This stops food from moving through the intestines.
- **Intestinal malrotation** – The intestines do not twist into the right position during development. This can cause blockages.

In many cases, an organ is not fully formed or is in the wrong place. This can cause a narrowing or blockage in the digestive tract. Blockages can happen in the esophagus, intestines, rectum, or anus. Sometimes a part of the digestive tract does not form at all. Or it forms and then gets damaged in the womb. The muscles around the belly may be weak or have holes. This can happen in abdominal wall defects and diaphragmatic hernia. In Hirschsprung disease, the nerves that control the intestines do not develop.

## Symptoms of Digestive Tract Birth Defects

Symptoms depend on the type of defect and where it is in the body.

Babies may have:
- Belly pain
- Swollen belly
- Vomiting
- Trouble feeding
- Poor weight gain

Some babies develop a yellow color in the skin and the whites of the eyes. This is called jaundice.

## How Doctors Diagnose Digestive Tract Birth Defects

Doctors use imaging tests to find birth defects.

Most defects can be seen before birth using a routine prenatal ultrasound.

After birth, doctors may use x-rays of the chest or belly. Ultrasound may also be used to find and locate the problem.

Other tests may be needed, such as:
- Blood tests
- Biopsies – a small piece of tissue is taken and looked at under a microscope

Genetic testing may be done if other test results or symptoms suggest a genetic cause.

## How Doctors Treat Digestive Tract Birth Defects

Surgery is the main treatment for most digestive tract birth defects.

Doctors usually perform surgery to open blockages. They also repair holes in the belly wall. In some cases, more than one surgery is needed. The goal is to restore normal digestion and prevent complications.

# Quinupristin and Dalfopristin – Simple Explanation

Quinupristin and dalfopristin are two antibiotics that work together to stop bacteria from making proteins. Without these proteins, bacteria cannot grow or survive.

These two medicines are always given together in a fixed ratio: 70% dalfopristin and 30% quinupristin.

This combination kills certain bacteria more effectively than either medicine alone. It works well against:

- Streptococci and staphylococci, including strains that do not respond to other antibiotics
- Some types of anaerobic bacteria (bacteria that grow without oxygen)
- *Clostridium perfringens*
- *Peptostreptococcus* species
- Some unusual lung infection-causing bacteria, such as:
  - *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*
  - *Chlamydophila pneumoniae*
  - *Legionella pneumophila*

The combination also stops *Enterococcus faecium* from growing. This includes strains that are resistant to vancomycin, a common antibiotic. However, it does not work against *Enterococcus faecalis*.

### How It Is Given

This medicine is given through a central IV line (a special tube placed in a large vein in the chest). It should not be given through a regular IV in a hand or arm. Giving it this way helps prevent swelling, pain, and damage to the smaller veins.

### Side Effects

- Up to 3 out of 10 people get muscle pain. This can be strong and may last for a while.
- Some people develop high levels of bilirubin in their blood. This can cause yellowing of the skin or eyes. It is usually not serious but should be checked.

### Dose Adjustments

- If your liver is not working well, your doctor may lower your dose.
- If your kidneys are not working well, you do not need a lower dose.

### Important Safety Warning

Quinupristin and dalfopristin can affect how other medicines work. They may slow down the breakdown of certain drugs in the body. This includes medicines that are processed by a system called cytochrome P-450 3A4. Always tell your doctor about all the medicines you are taking.

# Sudden Cardiac Death in Athletes

Every year, 1 to 3 out of every 100,000 young athletes who seem healthy suddenly die during or right after exercise. This is called sudden cardiac death. Boys are more likely to have this happen than girls. In the United States, basketball and football players are at higher risk. In Europe, soccer players are at higher risk.

## What Causes Sudden Cardiac Death in Athletes?

The reasons for sudden death during exercise are different in young athletes than in older ones. But in all athletes, asthma, heatstroke, and using performance-enhancing or recreational drugs can trigger a dangerous heart rhythm.

### In Young Athletes

Most young athletes who die suddenly have no visible heart problems. But some have a heart that is too thick. This is called hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. It can cause a dangerous heart rhythm.

Some young people are born with heart problems. These include long QT syndrome and Brugada syndrome. These conditions can cause sudden death during exercise.

Sometimes, a young person has a heart that is larger than normal but has no symptoms. This is called dilated cardiomyopathy. It can lead to sudden death during or after hard exercise.

A viral infection can cause swelling in the heart muscle. This is called myocarditis. It can make the heart larger and cause dangerous heart rhythms, such as ventricular tachycardia. This can lead to sudden death.

Some young athletes have a coronary artery that runs through the heart muscle instead of on top of it. During exercise, this can get squeezed. This cuts off blood flow to the heart and may cause sudden death.

Some young people have a genetic condition like Marfan syndrome. This weakens the wall of the main artery from the heart. This can cause a tear or a bulge in the artery. If it bursts, it causes massive bleeding and sudden death.

Rarely, a young, thin athlete can have a sudden heart rhythm problem after a hard hit to the chest. This is called commotio cordis. It can happen even if the person has no heart problem. The hit is often from a fast-moving ball, like a baseball, hockey puck, or lacrosse ball. It can also happen from a collision with another player.

### In Older Athletes

In older athletes, the most common cause is coronary artery disease. This is when the blood vessels to the heart become narrow or blocked.

Sometimes, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or heart valve disease causes sudden death. Some causes that affect young athletes can also affect older ones.

## Signs of Sudden Cardiac Death in Athletes

Some athletes feel dizzy or faint before they collapse. Some feel short of breath. But many do not notice these signs. They may not report them. The first sign is often that the person suddenly stops breathing and falls to the ground.

## How to Treat Sudden Cardiac Death in Athletes

### Immediate Care

If someone stops breathing and collapses, act right away.

- Start cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). This is chest compressions and rescue breaths.
- Use an automated external defibrillator (AED) if one is nearby.

CPR and AED use should continue in the emergency room. If the person survives, doctors will treat the cause of the abnormal heart rhythm.

Sometimes, doctors place an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator. This is a small device placed under the skin. It checks the heart rhythm all the time. If the rhythm becomes dangerous, it sends a shock to fix it.

### How an AED Works

An AED is a device that can detect and fix a dangerous heart rhythm called ventricular fibrillation. This rhythm stops the heart from pumping blood. It causes cardiac arrest.

AEDs are simple to use. Many groups offer short training sessions. These usually take just a few hours. You can still use an AED even if you have not taken a class.

Each AED has clear instructions. They are printed on the device. Most AEDs also give voice instructions step by step.

AEDs are found in many public places. These include stadiums, airports, and concert halls.

People who are at high risk for ventricular fibrillation may want to buy an AED for home. Family members should be trained to use it.
