# Diving Injuries: Simple Explanation

Diving deep underwater can be dangerous. It can lead to serious harm or even death. One main cause is the effect of compressed air on the body.

In the United States, more than 1,300 people go to the emergency room each year because of diving injuries. For every 1,000 of these visits, about 47 people die.

The same types of injuries can happen to workers in tunnels or caissons. These are watertight structures used in construction. Workers use pressurized air to keep water out of the work area.

The deeper you go underwater, the higher the pressure. This pressure comes from the weight of the water above you plus the air pressure at the surface. 

At 10 meters (33 feet) deep, the water pressure equals the normal air pressure at sea level. That pressure is about 1.03 kilograms per square centimeter, or 14.7 pounds per square inch. This is also called 1 atmosphere absolute, or 1 ATA. So at 10 meters, the total pressure is 2 ATA.

For every additional 10 meters you go down, the pressure increases by another 1 ATA.

When pressure changes, the amount of gas in your body changes too. Gases in your body shrink when pressure goes up. They expand when pressure goes down. This change can hurt your body tissues. This kind of injury is called barotrauma.

As pressure increases, more gas dissolves into your blood. This can cause harm directly. For example, too much nitrogen can make you feel dizzy or confused. Too much oxygen can damage your lungs or brain.

When you come up from deep water, the pressure drops. The extra gas in your blood or tissues can form bubbles. These bubbles can block blood flow or damage organs. This condition is called decompression sickness.

Sometimes, a bubble of air can get into an artery. This is called arterial gas embolism. It can happen if a lung is damaged by pressure changes. It can also happen during decompression.

The term "decompression illness" includes both decompression sickness and arterial gas embolism.

Some health problems make it more likely that you will have symptoms when you dive. These symptoms can be so bad that you lose your balance or become confused. This can lead to drowning.

If you or someone you know has a diving injury, call the Divers Alert Network at 919-684-9111 for emergencies. For other questions, call 919-684-2948.

Doctors can get expert advice from Duke Dive Medicine at 919-684-8111.

Other water dangers, like drowning and hypothermia, are covered in separate guides.

# Vestibular Schwannoma (Acoustic Neuroma)

A vestibular schwannoma is a noncancerous growth. It starts in the cells that cover the nerve for balance. These cells are called Schwann cells.

## How the Ears Work

The vestibular schwannoma begins in the part of the nerve that helps you stay balanced. This nerve is called the vestibulocochlear nerve. It has two parts.

One part carries sound signals to the brain. This is the hearing part.  
The other part helps with balance. This is the balance part.

The tumor grows slowly. It presses on the hearing nerve. This causes hearing loss in one ear. The hearing loss usually gets worse over time.

(For more about how the inner ear works, see "Overview of the Inner Ear.")

## Symptoms

Early signs of a vestibular schwannoma include:

- Hearing loss in one ear that gets worse slowly  
- Ringing or noise in the ear (called tinnitus)  
- Headaches  
- A feeling of fullness or pressure in the ear  
- Ear pain  
- Feeling unsteady when turning quickly  

Sometimes hearing loss happens all at once. The amount of hearing loss can vary.

If the tumor gets bigger, it can press on other nerves in the brain. This can cause:

- Weakness on one side of the face (face drooping)  
- Pain or numbness in the face  

## Diagnosis

Doctors use two main tests to find a vestibular schwannoma:

1. **Hearing test** – This checks how well you hear. It is called an audiogram.  
2. **MRI scan** – This is a detailed picture of the brain and nerves. A special type called gadolinium-enhanced MRI is best for finding the tumor.

If the hearing test shows loss in only one ear, doctors will do an MRI.

Other tests may include:

- **Tympanometry** – This checks how well sound moves through the eardrum and middle ear.  
- **Auditory brain stem response test** – This measures how the brain responds to sound.

## Treatment

Not all vestibular schwannomas need treatment.

If the tumor is small and not growing, and if it is not causing symptoms, doctors may just watch it. This is called watchful waiting.

If the tumor starts to grow or causes symptoms, treatment is needed. Options include:

- **Surgery** – The tumor is removed. Surgeons use a microscope to protect the facial nerve. In some cases, hearing can be saved.  
- **Radiation therapy** – This uses very precise beams of energy to stop the tumor from growing. The most common method is called stereotactic radiation therapy. It targets only the tumor and leaves nearby nerves safe.

The choice between surgery and radiation depends on:

- Your age  
- Your overall health  
- How much hearing you still have  
- The size of the tumor  

Your doctor will help you decide which treatment is best for you.

# Peliosis Hepatis

Peliosis hepatis is a condition where small, blood-filled spaces form in the liver.  
These spaces are not true cysts.  
They are usually not painful and do not cause symptoms.  

The spaces can be a few millimeters to about 3 centimeters across.  
Most do not have a lining of cells.  
They are surrounded by normal liver cells.  
Some have a lining made of endothelial cells.  
These areas are often linked to widened blood vessels in the liver.  

The exact cause is not fully known.  
It may happen when the lining of small liver blood vessels gets damaged.  

This condition is linked to certain medicines and substances.  
These include:  
- Anabolic steroids  
- Birth control pills  
- Steroid medicines like prednisone  
- Tamoxifen  
- Vinyl chloride (a chemical used in plastics)  
- High doses of vitamin A  
- Azathioprine (used after kidney transplants)  

Most people with peliosis hepatis do not feel sick.  
But in rare cases, the blood-filled spaces can burst.  
This can cause serious bleeding.  
In very rare cases, it can lead to death.  

Some people develop clear signs of liver problems.  
These signs include:  
- Yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice)  
- A larger than normal liver (hepatomegaly)  
- Liver failure  

Some cases are found by accident.  
This happens when a person has imaging tests for other reasons.  
For example, if liver blood tests are slightly off, a doctor may order a scan.  
Ultrasound or CT scans can show the blood-filled spaces.  

Most people with this condition do not need treatment.  
The condition often does not get worse.  
Doctors may just watch it over time.

# Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Syndromes (MEN)

Multiple endocrine neoplasia syndromes are rare conditions passed down through families. They cause several hormone-making glands to grow too much or form tumors. These tumors can be noncancerous or cancerous.

- These syndromes are caused by changes in genes.  
- The condition often runs in families.  
- There are four main types: MEN type 1, MEN type 2A, MEN type 2B, and MEN type 4.  
- Symptoms depend on which glands are affected.  
- Genetic tests can confirm the diagnosis and find out which family members have the condition.  
- There is no cure. But doctors treat each problem as it appears, using surgery or medicine.  

The problems can start in infancy or develop at any time during life.

Tumors and overgrown glands often make too much hormone.  
Tumors can appear in more than one gland at once. But they usually show up one at a time, over time.

---

## Types of MEN Syndromes

There are four main types: MEN 1, MEN 2A, MEN 2B, and MEN 4. They can sometimes overlap.

### MEN Type 1

People with MEN type 1 often have problems in these glands:

- Parathyroid glands (small glands near the thyroid in the neck)  
- Pancreas  
- Pituitary gland (a small gland at the base of the brain)  
- Adrenal glands (less often affected)

Almost everyone with MEN type 1 has tumors in the parathyroid glands.  
Most of these tumors are not cancer. But they make too much parathyroid hormone.  
This raises calcium levels in the blood. High calcium can lead to kidney stones.

Many people with MEN type 1 also get tumors in the pancreas.  
These are called islet cell tumors.  
They form in the hormone-making cells of the pancreas.

- Over 50% of these tumors make too much gastrin.  
- Gastrin makes the stomach make too much acid.  
- This can cause peptic ulcers.  
- Ulcers may bleed, break through the stomach wall, or block the stomach.  
- High acid levels can also stop the pancreas from working right.  
- This leads to diarrhea and fatty, smelly stools.

Some islet cell tumors make too much insulin.  
This causes very low blood sugar, especially if the person has not eaten.  
This is called hypoglycemia.

Other tumors make different hormones.  
One example is vasoactive intestinal polypeptide.  
This causes severe diarrhea and can lead to dehydration.

Some islet cell tumors do not make any hormones.

Some of these tumors are cancerous.  
They can spread to other parts of the body.  
But in people with MEN type 1, these cancers tend to grow slowly.

Some people with MEN type 1 get tumors in the pituitary gland.  
These tumors can make too much prolactin.  
This causes menstrual problems in women.  
It can also cause breast milk to leak in women who are not breastfeeding.  
In men, it can cause low sex drive and erectile dysfunction.

Other pituitary tumors make too much growth hormone.  
In adults, this causes acromegaly.  
In children, it causes gigantism.

A small number of pituitary tumors make corticotropin.  
This overstimulates the adrenal glands.  
The adrenal glands then make too much steroid hormone.  
This causes Cushing syndrome.

Some pituitary tumors do not make any hormones.  
But they can press on nearby brain areas.  
This can cause headaches, vision problems, or reduced hormone production.

Some people with MEN type 1 get overgrown or tumor-like growths in the adrenal glands.  
These are usually not cancer.  
But in rare cases, they can become cancerous.

A few people get neuroendocrine tumors.  
Some also get harmless fatty lumps under the skin called lipomas.

Women with MEN type 1 may have a higher risk of breast cancer.

---

### MEN Type 2A

People with MEN type 2A often have problems in these glands:

- Thyroid gland  
- Adrenal glands  
- Parathyroid glands  

Almost everyone with MEN type 2A gets medullary thyroid cancer.  
This is a type of thyroid cancer that is serious and often fatal if not treated.

About half get tumors in the adrenal glands.  
These are called pheochromocytomas.  
They make hormones that raise blood pressure.  
This high blood pressure can come and go, or be constant.  
It is often very high.

Some people with MEN type 2A have overactive parathyroid glands.  
This raises calcium levels in the blood.  
This can lead to kidney stones.  
Kidney stones are more common in people with MEN syndromes than in others.

A few people with MEN type 2A get a skin condition called cutaneous lichen amyloidosis.  
This causes itchy skin.

A small number have Hirschsprung disease.  
This is a condition where the intestines do not empty properly.

---

### MEN Type 2B

People with MEN type 2B often have:

- Medullary thyroid cancer  
- Pheochromocytomas  
- Growths around nerves (neuromas)

Many people with MEN type 2B have no family history of the condition.  
This means the gene change happened for the first time in that person.

Medullary thyroid cancer in MEN type 2B starts very early in life.  
It has been found in babies as young as 3 months.

These tumors grow faster and spread more quickly than those in MEN type 2A.

Almost everyone with MEN type 2B gets neuromas.  
These are small, shiny bumps on the lips, tongue, and inside the mouth.  
They can also appear on the eyelids and on the clear parts of the eyes.

The lips and eyelids may become thick.  
The lips may turn inside out.

Digestive problems are common.  
People may have constipation or diarrhea.  
In some cases, the colon becomes enlarged and stretched.  
This is called megacolon.  
These problems are likely due to neuromas growing on nerves in the intestines.

Spinal problems are common.  
The spine may curve abnormally.  
Bones in the skull, feet, and thighs may also be affected.

Most people with MEN type 2B have long arms and legs.  
They have loose joints and appear thin.  
These features are similar to those seen in Marfan syndrome.

---

### MEN Type 4

MEN type 4 is like MEN type 1.  
But it is caused by a different gene.  
It is much rarer.

People with MEN type 4 get tumors in:

- Parathyroid glands  
- Pancreas  
- Pituitary gland  

In MEN type 4, usually only one parathyroid gland is affected.  
In MEN type 1, several parathyroid glands are affected.

People with MEN type 4 do not get the same skin changes as people with MEN type 1.

---

## Conditions That Occur With Each MEN Type

| Condition | MEN 1 | MEN 2A | MEN 2B | MEN 4 |
|---------|-------|--------|--------|-------|
| High parathyroid hormone | 95% or more | 10–20% | — | 55–80% |
| Pancreas tumors | 30–80% | — | — | 15–25% |
| Pituitary tumors | 15–42% | — | — | 30–45% |
| Medullary thyroid cancer | — | More than 95% | More than 95% | — |
| Pheochromocytoma | — | 40–50% | 50% | — |
| Adrenal cortex tumors | 33% | — | — | — |
| Neuromas on mucous membranes | — | — | Almost 100% | — |
| Body features like Marfan syndrome | — | — | Almost 100% | — |
| Neuroendocrine tumors | 10–15% | — | — | 5% |
| Lipomas (fatty lumps under skin) | Up to 35% | — | — | — |
| Angiomas or collagenomas (skin growths) | 70–85% | — | — | — |

- A lipoma is a harmless fatty lump under the skin.  
- An angioma is a harmless growth of small blood vessels.  
- A collagenoma is a harmless growth of connective tissue in the skin.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose MEN Syndromes

Doctors use several tests:

- **Genetic tests** – These check for the gene changes linked to each type of MEN.  
- **Blood and urine tests** – These check hormone levels.  
- **Imaging tests** – These help find tumors. Examples include ultrasound, CT scans, MRI scans, and PET scans.

Genetic testing is done in people who have a typical tumor.  
It is also done in family members of people already diagnosed.

Screening family members is very important.  
About half of children of people with MEN inherit the condition.  
In rare cases, a person with MEN may have normal genetic test results.

Blood and urine tests help find high hormone levels.

Imaging tests help doctors see where tumors are located.

---

## How Doctors Treat MEN Syndromes

There is no overall cure.  
Doctors treat each problem as it appears

# Head and Neck Tumors – Simple Explanation

## What Are Head and Neck Tumors?

Each year, more than 70,000 people in the United States develop cancer in the head or neck area.

### Most Common Places for These Cancers

- **Larynx** – This includes the upper part, middle part, and lower part of the voice box.
- **Mouth** – This includes the tongue, the floor of the mouth, the hard roof of the mouth, the inside of the cheeks, and the gums.
- **Oropharynx** – This includes the back and sides of the throat, the base of the tongue, the tonsils, and the soft part of the roof of the mouth.

### Less Common Places

- Nasopharynx (behind the nose)
- Nose and sinuses
- Hypopharynx (lower part of the throat)
- Salivary glands

### Other Types of Tumors in the Head and Neck Area

- Tumors inside the brain (in adults and children)
- Thyroid cancer
- Tumors in the eye socket
- Cancers of the retina (the back of the eye)
- Vestibular schwannoma (a tumor on a nerve near the ear)
- Skin cancers on the head and neck

### Who Gets These Cancers?

- The chance of getting head and neck cancer goes up with age.
- Most people are between 50 and 70 years old.
- But more younger people are getting these cancers, especially oropharyngeal cancer caused by a virus called human papillomavirus (HPV).
- Men are more likely than women to get these cancers. This is partly because more men have smoked in the past. It is also because men are more likely to have HPV in the mouth.

---

## What Causes Head and Neck Cancers?

Most people with head and neck cancer have a history of smoking or drinking alcohol, or both.

- People who smoke and drink heavily have a much higher risk of a type of cancer called squamous cell carcinoma.
- Other possible causes include:
  - Using smokeless tobacco (like snuff or chewing tobacco)
  - Getting too much sun on the lips
  - Having X-rays of the head or neck in the past
  - Certain viral infections
  - Poorly fitting dental plates or dentures
  - Long-term yeast infection in the mouth (candidiasis)
  - Not keeping the mouth clean

In some parts of Asia, oral cancer is more common. This may be because people chew a mixture called betel quid (also called paan).

- Sunlight and tobacco use are the main causes of squamous cell cancer on the lower lip.

### Human Papillomavirus (HPV)

- HPV is linked to head and neck cancers, especially in the oropharynx.
- The rise in HPV-related cancers has increased the number of oropharyngeal cancers, even though smoking rates have gone down.
- HPV causes cancer in a different way than smoking does.

### Epstein-Barr Virus

- This virus is linked to nasopharyngeal cancer.
- Blood tests can check for certain proteins from this virus. These tests may help predict if the cancer comes back after treatment.

---

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

The symptoms depend on where the tumor is and how big it is.

### Early Signs

- A painless lump in the neck
- A sore in the mouth that does not heal
- A visible spot or patch in the mouth (like white or red patches)
- Hoarseness that lasts more than a few weeks
- Trouble swallowing

### Later Symptoms

- Pain
- Tingling or numbness
- Weakness in the face or neck muscles
- Trouble opening the mouth wide
- Bad breath
- Ear pain (this is often not from the ear, but from a tumor nearby)

Weight loss is common. This happens because eating becomes hard or painful.

---

## How Are These Cancers Diagnosed?

### Step 1: Medical History and Physical Exam

- A doctor will ask about your symptoms and habits (like smoking or drinking).
- A full exam will be done, including a careful look at your mouth and throat.

### Step 2: Biopsy

- A small sample of tissue is taken to check for cancer.
- For a neck lump, a thin needle is used to take a sample (fine-needle aspiration). This is safe and does not affect future treatment.
- For mouth sores, a small piece of tissue is removed (incisional biopsy) or a brush is used to collect cells (brush biopsy).
- For tumors in the throat, nose, or voice box, a scope is used to take a sample during an endoscopy.

### Step 3: Imaging Tests

- CT scans, MRI scans, or PET scans help show how big the tumor is and if it has spread.
- These tests check if the cancer has reached nearby tissues or lymph nodes in the neck.

---

## How Are These Cancers Staged?

Staging tells doctors how far the cancer has spread. It helps guide treatment.

### The TNM System

- **T** – How big the main tumor is and how far it has grown.
- **N** – Whether the cancer has spread to lymph nodes in the neck, and how many.
- **M** – Whether the cancer has spread to other parts of the body.

For oropharyngeal cancer, the HPV status is also important.

### Two Types of Staging

- **Clinical staging (cTNM)** – Based on exams and tests done before surgery.
- **Pathologic staging (pTNM)** – Based on what doctors see during surgery and what the lab finds.

### Extranodal Extension

- This means the cancer has grown outside the lymph node into nearby tissue.
- Doctors can see this during a physical exam and with imaging.
- In the lab, they can confirm it by looking at the tissue under a microscope.

---

## How Are These Cancers Treated?

The main treatments are surgery, radiation therapy, and sometimes chemotherapy.

### Surgery and Radiation

- These are the main treatments.
- They can be used alone or together.
- They may also be used with chemotherapy.

### Choosing the Right Treatment

- Many head and neck cancers respond well to either surgery or radiation.
- The choice often depends on the patient’s preference and the location of the tumor.

### When Surgery Is Better

- For early-stage cancer in the mouth, surgery is often better than radiation.
- Radiation can damage the jawbone over time, leading to serious problems.

### Endoscopic Surgery

- This is a type of surgery done through the nose or mouth using a scope.
- It is often used for tumors in the voice box.
- A laser is used to cut the tumor.
- It has fewer side effects than open surgery and gives good cure rates.

### Radiation Therapy

- If radiation is used, it is aimed at the tumor and sometimes both sides of the neck.
- Whether to treat the lymph nodes depends on the tumor site, type, and risk of spread.
- Early-stage tumors may not need lymph node treatment.
- Tumors in areas with many lymph nodes (like the oropharynx) usually need lymph node treatment, even if small.
- Tumors in areas with fewer lymph nodes (like the larynx) usually do not need it for early-stage disease.
- Intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) targets the cancer more precisely. This helps reduce side effects.

### Advanced Cancers (Stages III and IV)

- These cancers often need a mix of treatments: surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy.
- If the cancer has spread into bone or cartilage, surgery is usually needed.
- After surgery, radiation may be given to the neck if there are high-risk features, such as cancer in multiple lymph nodes or cancer that has spread outside the lymph node.
- Radiation after surgery is preferred over radiation before surgery. This is because radiation can slow healing.

### Adding Chemotherapy

- Chemotherapy with radiation after surgery improves cancer control and survival.
- But it can cause serious side effects, like worse swallowing and low blood counts.
- The decision to add chemotherapy must be carefully weighed.

### Chemotherapy with Radiation (for Advanced Cancer)

- For advanced squamous cell cancer without bone spread, chemotherapy and radiation are often used together.
- This approach can save the voice box and other organs.
- But it doubles the risk of severe side effects, especially trouble swallowing.
- Radiation alone may be used for very sick patients who cannot handle chemotherapy or surgery.

### Chemotherapy as a Main Treatment?

- Chemotherapy is rarely used alone to cure head and neck cancer.
- It is used only for certain cancers that respond well to it, like Burkitt lymphoma.
- It is also used when cancer has spread widely (like to the liver or lungs).
- Drugs like cisplatin, fluorouracil, bleomycin, and methotrexate can shrink tumors and relieve pain.
- The effect is often good at first, but the cancer usually comes back.
- Targeted drugs like cetuximab can be used instead of chemotherapy for some patients.

### Team-Based Care Is Key

- Treating head and neck cancer is complex.
- A team of specialists should plan treatment together.
- This team includes:
  - Ear, nose, and throat doctors
  - Surgeons (including plastic and reconstructive surgeons)
  - Radiation and medical oncologists
  - Speech and language therapists
  - Dentists
  - Nutritionists

### Reconstructive Surgery

- After surgery, some patients need help rebuilding the mouth, throat, or face.
- Surgeons use tissue from other parts of the body to do this.
- Common donor sites include:
  - Fibula (from the lower leg) – used to rebuild the jaw
  - Radial forearm

# Cogan Syndrome

Cogan syndrome is a rare condition where the body’s immune system attacks its own tissues. This can cause swelling in the eyes, ears, and blood vessels.

## What Happens in Cogan Syndrome?

- The immune system normally fights infections.
- In Cogan syndrome, it mistakenly attacks healthy parts of the body.
- This can lead to swelling in the eyes, ears, and blood vessels.
- When blood vessels are affected, it can cause a serious condition called aortitis. This can be life-threatening.

## How Cogan Syndrome Affects the Eye

- The cornea is the clear front part of the eye.
- It covers the iris and pupil.
- It protects the inside of the eye and helps focus light onto the retina.
- The cornea is made of cells, protein, and fluid.
- It looks soft but is as strong as a fingernail.
- It is very sensitive to touch.

## Symptoms of Cogan Syndrome

### Eye Symptoms
- Eye pain
- Blurry or worse vision
- Trouble with bright light
- Red eyes

### Ear Symptoms
- Hearing loss
- Ringing in the ears
- Dizziness or spinning feeling (vertigo)
- A feeling of fullness or pressure in the ears

### Blood Vessel Symptoms
- Heart murmurs (unusual sounds when the heart beats)
- Pain in the legs or arms when walking or exercising (claudication)

## How Doctors Diagnose Cogan Syndrome

- Doctors look at your symptoms and medical history.
- They do a detailed eye exam using a special tool called a slit lamp.
  - This tool lets the doctor see the eye in great detail.
- Blood tests are done to rule out other diseases with similar symptoms.
  - These include syphilis, Lyme disease, and Epstein-Barr virus.
- Imaging tests like CT scans or MRI scans may be done.
  - These help check for swelling in blood vessels or other problems.

## How Cogan Syndrome Is Treated

- Steroid eye drops are used first.
  - These help reduce swelling in the cornea.
- If the eye drops do not help, or if the swelling is deep, or if the ears or blood vessels are involved, oral steroids are used.
  - These are pills taken by mouth.
- In some cases, other medicines are used.
  - These include cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, cyclosporine, rituximab, or infliximab.
  - These medicines help control the immune system.

## Important Notes

- Early treatment is key to preventing serious damage.
- Regular follow-up with a doctor is needed.
- If you have symptoms like eye pain, hearing loss, or dizziness, see a doctor right away.

# Body Odor (Bromhidrosis)

Body odor that is strong or unusual can happen when bacteria and yeast break down sweat and dead skin cells on your skin.

## What Causes Body Odor?

- **Apocrine sweat** comes from special glands. It has fats and is not smelly at first. But when bacteria on your skin break it down, it creates a strong smell.
- **Eccrine sweat** is the kind you sweat when you are hot or nervous. It is mostly water and does not usually smell bad.
- Sometimes, eccrine sweat can make body odor worse. This happens when bacteria break down a protein in the skin called keratin. This type of body odor can also come from eating certain foods like curry, garlic, onions, or alcohol. Some medicines, like penicillin, can also cause it.

There is a strong link between body odor and the type of earwax a person has. If your earwax is wet or sticky, you are more likely to have strong body odor. This is tied to a small change in a gene called *ABCC11*.

## How to Treat Body Odor

You can try several ways to reduce body odor and sweating:

- Wash your underarms with an antiseptic soap for a few days. You can also use antibacterial creams with clindamycin or erythromycin.
- Shave the hair in your armpits. Hair can trap sweat and bacteria, so removing it may help reduce smell.
- Change sweaty clothes right away. This stops bacteria from growing.
- Use deodorants to cover up bad smells.
- Use antiperspirants to reduce how much you sweat.

Other treatments like Botox, microwave devices, lasers, or surgery may help some people. But results vary. The best choice depends on what you are comfortable with, how well you tolerate side effects, and whether you are willing to repeat the treatment.

# Drug Rashes

A drug rash is a skin reaction caused by a medicine.

## What Causes Drug Rashes?

Most drug rashes happen because the body’s immune system reacts to a medicine. This is called an allergic reaction. But some rashes are not allergic.

Some medicines can cause a rash even if they are not applied to the skin. They can be taken by mouth or given through a needle.

The body can become sensitive to a medicine after just one dose. Or it may take many doses. Once sensitive, the body reacts again when the medicine is taken.

Some rashes happen without an allergic reaction. For example:
- Corticosteroids and lithium can cause a rash that looks like acne.
- Blood thinners can cause bruising under the skin.

Some medicines make the skin more sensitive to sunlight. This is called photosensitivity. The rash does not appear right away. It shows up after sun exposure while taking the medicine.

Other serious rashes linked to medicines include:
- Stevens-Johnson syndrome
- Toxic epidermal necrolysis
- Erythema nodosum

## What Do Drug Rashes Look Like?

A rash means changes in the skin. This can be redness, bumps, swelling, blisters, or peeling.

Rashes can be:
- Itchy
- Painful
- Or cause no symptoms at all

Rashes can appear suddenly after taking a medicine. Or they may show up hours, days, or even weeks later.

Rashes can be mild or very serious. They may cover a small area or affect the whole body.

Some rashes cause:
- Red, purple, blue, or gray skin color
- Sores in the mouth

People with an allergic rash may also have:
- Hives (raised, itchy patches)
- Runny nose
- Watery eyes
- Wheezing
- Low blood pressure

Hives are very itchy. Other rashes may itch only a little or not at all.

## How Are Drug Rashes Diagnosed?

Doctors look at all medicines a person is taking. This includes:
- Prescription drugs
- Over-the-counter medicines
- Eye drops
- Nose drops
- Suppositories
- Herbal products

Doctors check when the rash started. They look for a link to when a medicine was first taken.

The medicine most likely to be the cause is stopped. If the rash goes away, it was likely the medicine.

Sometimes, all medicines must be stopped except those needed to stay alive. Then, medicines are added back one at a time. This helps find the cause. But this method can be dangerous if the person had a severe reaction before.

In some cases, doctors do a patch test. They place small amounts of possible causes on the skin to see if a reaction happens.

If the rash is serious or unusual, a doctor may take a small skin sample. This is called a skin biopsy. The sample is checked under a microscope.

## How Are Drug Rashes Treated?

The main treatment is to stop the medicine causing the rash.

For mild rashes:
- Antihistamines (by mouth) can help with itching.
- Corticosteroid creams can reduce swelling and itching.

For severe rashes:
- Epinephrine (given by injection) is used if there is trouble breathing or low blood pressure.
- Antihistamines and corticosteroids may also be given.
- Hospital care may be needed.

Most rashes go away once the medicine is stopped.

If the rash is very itchy, use antihistamines or corticosteroid creams as needed.

Severe allergic reactions (called anaphylaxis) need immediate treatment. This includes:
- Epinephrine (injected)
- An antihistamine
- A corticosteroid

These treatments help prevent serious problems.

# Hemosiderosis

Hemosiderosis means too much iron builds up in certain parts of the body.  
This buildup usually does not harm the tissue.  

## What Causes Hemosiderosis?

### Bleeding in an Organ
- If there is bleeding inside an organ, iron from the blood leaks out.  
- The iron stays in that organ and can build up over time.  
- This can lead to large amounts of iron stored in the organ.  
- Even though the iron is stored, the body cannot use it again.  
- This can still lead to low iron levels in the blood.  
- Low iron levels can cause anemia.  

### Long-Term Inflammation
- Conditions like fatty liver disease linked to metabolism problems and metabolic syndrome can cause this.  
- These conditions may lead to extra iron in the liver and spleen.  
- Doctors can see this with an MRI scan of the belly.  
- A liver sample may show iron in liver cells and in the body’s cleaning cells.  

### Lungs Affected
- The lungs can also collect extra iron.  
- This usually happens when there is repeated bleeding in the lungs.  
- Causes include:  
  - Goodpasture syndrome (a rare immune disease).  
  - Long-term high blood pressure in the lungs.  
  - Lung scarring (pulmonary fibrosis).  
  - Severe narrowing of the heart’s mitral valve (mitral stenosis).  

### Kidneys Affected
- The kidneys can also collect iron.  
- This happens when red blood cells break apart inside blood vessels.  
- The broken-down hemoglobin passes into the kidneys.  
- Iron from the hemoglobin builds up in the kidney tissue.  
- The kidney tissue does not get damaged.  
- But heavy iron loss in the urine can lead to low iron levels in the body.  
- This can cause anemia.

# Brain Death

Brain death means the brain has stopped working completely.  
It will never start again on its own.  
No medical treatment can bring it back.  

When brain death happens, a person cannot breathe on their own.  
They cannot keep other body functions going.  
They have no awareness.  
They cannot think or feel anything.  

Artificial support, like a breathing machine or medicines, can keep the heart beating and lungs working for a short time.  
But even with this help, the body will eventually stop working.  
Nothing can keep the heart beating forever once brain death occurs.  

Doctors use strict rules to confirm brain death.  
No treatment can help someone who is brain dead.  
Once brain death is confirmed, the person is legally dead.  

In the past, brain death was not a concern.  
When the brain stopped, the body stopped too.  
The person would stop breathing and the heart would stop.  
Now, machines can keep breathing and the heart beating even when the brain is completely dead.  
But the body will still fail over time.  

## How Doctors Diagnose Brain Death

Doctors follow clear steps to make sure brain death is real.  
They check for any treatable problems that could look like brain death.  
They also check for conditions that could cause a deep coma.  

The doctor will:  
- Check all reflexes. For example, they touch the back of the throat.  
  A person who is brain dead will not react.  
- Shine a light into the eyes.  
  A brain-dead person will not blink or move their eyes.  
- Take the person off the breathing machine.  
  A brain-dead person will not try to breathe.  

Some conditions can look like brain death but are treatable.  
These include:  
- Very low body temperature  
- Very low blood pressure  
- Low blood sugar  
- Low sodium in the blood  
- Too much sedative medicine  

Brain death is **not** diagnosed if:  
- The person can breathe on their own  
- The person can wake up  
- The person is not in a coma  
- Any reflexes are still present  

Doctors should talk to the family or close loved ones as soon as they start the evaluation.  
They usually repeat the tests 6 to 24 hours later to be sure.  

To confirm brain death, all of these must be true:  
- All treatable problems are ruled out  
- A full brain and nervous system exam is done  
- All required tests are completed  

For adults:  
- At least one full check is needed  
- A second check is recommended  

For children:  
- Some states say doctors should do two exams  
- These exams must be at least 48 hours apart  

Sometimes, the first test is unclear.  
Or the exam cannot be finished.  
In these cases, doctors may use special tests to help confirm brain death.  
This is especially important if organ donation is planned.  

Tests that can help:  
- **Electroencephalography (EEG):** This records brain activity.  
  A brain-dead person shows no brain waves.  

- **Imaging tests:** These check blood flow to the brain.  
  No blood flows to the brain when a person is brain dead.  
  Types of imaging tests include:  
  - Positron emission tomography (PET)  
  - Angiography  
  - CT angiography  
  - Single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT)  
    (This uses a special substance to show blood flow)  
  - Doppler ultrasonography  
    (This uses sound waves to check blood flow in the brain)  

## What Happens After Brain Death Is Confirmed

No one who meets the brain death criteria ever recovers.  
Once confirmed, the person is dead.  

Life support is turned off after brain death is confirmed.  
Family members may choose to be with the person at this time.  

They should know that:  
- One or more limbs may move when breathing support is stopped  
- The person may even sit up briefly  
  (This is called the Lazarus sign)  

These movements are not signs of life.  
They are caused by reflexes in the spinal cord.  
They do not mean the person is still alive.  
The person is still brain dead.

# What Is Rehabilitation?

Rehabilitation helps people recover after they lose the ability to do normal activities. It also helps reduce pain.

Loss of function can happen after:
- A broken bone
- Losing a limb
- A stroke
- Brain injury from an accident
- A sports injury
- Long-term joint or muscle problems like arthritis
- Spinal cord injury
- Heart or lung problems
- Chronic pain
- Being inactive for a long time (such as after surgery or illness)

Rehabilitation may include:
- Occupational therapy – helps you do daily tasks like dressing or cooking
- Physical therapy – helps you move better and build strength
- Speech therapy – helps if you have trouble talking or swallowing
- Counseling – helps with feelings like sadness or stress
- Social services – helps with money, housing, or other needs
- Medicines – such as pills or shots to help with muscle tightness
- Pain relief – using medicines or other treatments

Some people aim to get back to full health and do everything they did before. Others focus on doing as many daily tasks as possible.

How well someone improves depends on:
- The type of injury or illness
- How motivated they are

Older people, those with serious injuries, poor health, or weak muscles may improve more slowly. Low motivation, depression, lack of support from family or friends, and money problems can also slow progress.

## Where Does Rehabilitation Happen?

Rehabilitation can start in a hospital. But the most intense care usually happens in a special rehabilitation hospital or unit. These are best for people who:
- Have a good chance to recover
- Can handle at least three hours of therapy each day

Nursing homes often offer less intense programs. These last longer and are better for people who:
- Are older
- Are frail
- Cannot handle long or hard therapy sessions

Outpatient clinics or home visits offer even less frequent care. But some outpatient programs are still very intense – several hours a day, up to five days a week.

Home visits may be right for people who:
- Are stable but have serious problems
- Cannot go to a clinic because of distance or no transport

Home therapy is often used after:
- Knee replacement surgery
- Trouble walking after a fall
- Being unable to leave home due to long-term illness

## A Team Approach Works Best

Disability can cause many problems. These include:
- Feeling sad or hopeless
- Losing motivation to get better
- Money worries

Because of this, people often need:
- Mental health support
- Help from social workers or counselors
- Support for family members

Family members may need help learning how to support the patient and adjust to changes.

## Rehabilitation for Older Adults

Older people often need rehabilitation after:
- A stroke
- A heart attack
- A broken hip
- Losing a limb

Older adults are also more likely to be out of shape before they get sick or injured.

Even older adults with memory problems can benefit from rehabilitation. Age alone is not a reason to delay or skip rehab.

But older adults may recover more slowly because of:
- Not being active
- Getting tired easily
- Depression or dementia
- Weak muscles
- Stiff joints
- Poor balance
- Trouble moving or staying steady

Special programs for older adults are best. These programs:
- Focus on what older people want to achieve
- Match their needs
- Help them avoid feeling discouraged by comparing themselves to younger people

Some programs are made for specific issues, like recovering after hip surgery. People in these groups can:
- Work together
- Support each other
- Practice skills together
- Stay motivated

# Idiopathic Pleuroparenchymal Fibroelastosis (IPPF)

This is a rare lung disease. It causes scarring in the lungs. The disease gets worse slowly over time.

## What Are the Symptoms?

- You may get lung infections often.
- You may feel short of breath, especially when you walk or do light activity.
- You may have a dry cough that does not go away.
- Some people have a collapsed lung. This is called pneumothorax.

## Who Gets This Disease?

- Men and women are affected about equally.
- It can happen at any age.
- The average age when symptoms start is around 57 years.
- Most people with this disease do not smoke.

## What Causes It?

- Doctors do not know the exact cause.
- Experts think repeated lung infections may play a role.
- Some believe genes or the body’s immune system may also be involved.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- A special type of chest scan called a CT scan is needed.
- Sometimes, a small sample of lung tissue is taken to confirm the diagnosis. This is called a lung biopsy.

## How Is It Treated?

- There is no proven treatment for this disease.
- Doctors sometimes use steroids. These are medicines that reduce swelling. They help in other lung diseases like this one, but it is not clear if they help in this condition.
- Some doctors try medicines that slow down lung scarring. These are called antifibrotic medicines. Examples are nintedanib and pirfenidone.
- In severe cases, a lung transplant may be considered.

## What Is the Outlook?

- The disease gets worse in most people.
- After five years, between 25% and 60% of people are still alive. This varies from person to person.

# Chest Wall Tumors

Tumors in the chest wall can be non-cancerous or cancerous.  
They can affect how the lungs work.

### Types of Chest Wall Tumors

- About 5% of all chest tumors start in the chest wall.  
- Only 1 to 2% of all primary tumors begin in the chest wall.  
- Nearly half of these tumors are not cancer.

#### Most Common Non-Cancerous Tumors

- Osteochondroma  
- Chondroma  
- Fibrous dysplasia

#### Most Common Cancerous Tumors

- More than half of cancerous chest wall tumors come from other parts of the body.  
- Some spread to the chest wall from nearby areas like the breast, lung, lining of the lungs, or the center of the chest.

The most common cancerous tumors that start in the chest wall are:

- Sarcomas:  
  - About 45% start in soft tissues.  
  - About 55% start in cartilage or bone.

Chondrosarcomas are the most common type of sarcoma in the chest wall.  
They usually start in the front part of the ribs.  
They can also start in the breastbone, shoulder blade, or collarbone, but less often.

Bone tumors include:
- Osteosarcoma  
- Small-cell cancers like Ewing sarcoma and Askin tumor

Soft-tissue cancers include:
- Fibrosarcomas (including desmoids and neurofibrosarcomas)  
- Malignant fibrous histiocytomas

Other rare primary tumors:
- Chondroblastomas  
- Osteoblastomas  
- Melanomas  
- Lymphomas  
- Rhabdomyosarcomas  
- Lymphangiosarcomas  
- Multiple myeloma  
- Plasmacytomas

---

## Symptoms and Signs

- Soft-tissue tumors often show up as a lump in the chest.  
- They may not cause other symptoms.  
- Many are found by chance during imaging tests done for another reason.  
- Some people have a fever.  
- Most do not feel pain until the tumor is large or advanced.

- Tumors in cartilage or bone often cause pain.  
- Pain is a common early sign for these types.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Chest Wall Tumors

### Imaging Tests

- Chest x-ray  
- CT scan  
- MRI  
- Sometimes PET-CT scan

These tests help find the tumor’s size, location, and whether it started in the chest wall or spread from elsewhere.

### Biopsy

- A small sample of the tumor is taken.  
- A pathologist checks the sample under a microscope.  
- This confirms the diagnosis and tells if the tumor is cancerous.

---

## Treatment

### Surgery

- Most chest wall tumors are treated with surgery to remove the tumor.  
- After surgery, the chest wall is rebuilt.  
- Rebuilding often uses skin and muscle from another part of the body.  
- Sometimes artificial materials are used.

- Surgery is not done if there is fluid in the space around the lungs caused by cancer (malignant pleural effusion).

### Chemotherapy and Radiation Therapy

- For multiple myeloma or isolated plasmacytoma:  
  - Chemotherapy and radiation are the main treatments.

- For small-cell cancers like Ewing sarcoma and Askin tumor:  
  - Treatment includes chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery.

- For tumors that spread to the chest wall from other organs:  
  - Surgery may be done only if other treatments do not relieve symptoms.  
  - This is to improve comfort, not to cure.

---

## Prognosis (Outlook)

- The outlook depends on the type of cancer, how abnormal the cells look, and how far the cancer has spread.  
- It is hard to give firm answers because these tumors are rare.  
- Sarcomas have been studied the most.  
- For primary chest wall sarcomas, about 17% of people are still alive five years after diagnosis.  
- People with early-stage disease tend to do better.

---

## Key Points

- Nearly half of chest wall tumors are not cancer.  
- Less than half of cancerous chest wall tumors start in the chest wall.  
- Think about this diagnosis if someone has a chest lump or unexplained chest wall pain, with or without fever.  
- Diagnosis starts with imaging tests, followed by a biopsy.  
- Most are treated with surgery and chest wall repair.  
- Surgery is not done if there is cancer-related fluid around the lungs.  
- Some people also need chemotherapy or radiation therapy.

# Glycopeptides and Lipoglycopeptides – Simple Explanation

These medicines are antibiotics. They treat serious infections caused by certain types of bacteria.

## What Infections Do They Treat?

These antibiotics work against gram-positive bacteria. These are a type of bacteria that can cause serious infections. They are often used when other antibiotics do not work.

## The Medicines

The following are examples of glycopeptides and lipoglycopeptides:

- Dalbavancin  
- Oritavancin  
- Teicoplanin  
- Telavancin  
- Vancomycin  

Most of these medicines are given through a vein. One, vancomycin, can also be taken by mouth.

## How Do They Work?

Bacteria have a hard outer layer called a cell wall. This layer protects them. These antibiotics stop the bacteria from building this wall. Without a cell wall, the bacteria die.

## Common Uses and Side Effects

Here is a list of the medicines, what they are used for, and possible side effects.

### Dalbavancin
- Used for serious skin infections caused by certain bacteria, including MRSA.
- Side effects may include:
  - Upset stomach
  - A strange metal taste in the mouth
  - Foam in the urine
  - Redness, warmth, and itching on the face, neck, and shoulders

### Oritavancin
- Used for serious skin infections caused by certain bacteria, including MRSA.
- Side effects may include:
  - Upset stomach
  - A strange metal taste in the mouth
  - Foam in the urine
  - Headache
  - Redness, warmth, and itching on the face, neck, and shoulders

### Teicoplanin
- Used for serious infections, including those caused by MRSA.
- Also used to treat a type of severe diarrhea caused by *Clostridioides difficile*.
- Side effects may include:
  - Kidney damage
  - Hearing problems or loss of hearing
  - Lower levels of platelets and white blood cells
  - Redness, warmth, and itching on the face, neck, and shoulders

### Telavancin
- Used for serious infections, including those caused by MRSA.
- Side effects may include:
  - Upset stomach
  - A strange metal taste in the mouth
  - Foam in the urine
  - Kidney damage
  - Dizziness
  - Lower levels of platelets
  - Redness, warmth, and itching on the face, neck, and shoulders

### Vancomycin
- Used for serious infections, including those caused by MRSA.
- Also used to treat *Clostridioides difficile* diarrhea when taken by mouth.
- Side effects may include:
  - Redness, warmth, and itching on the face, neck, and shoulders
  - Kidney damage
  - Hearing problems
  - Lower levels of white blood cells and platelets

> **Note:** All these medicines are usually given through a vein, except vancomycin, which can also be taken by mouth.

> **Note:** Redness, warmth, and itching on the face, neck, and shoulders are often caused by the speed of the infusion. Slowing down the injection can help relieve these symptoms.

## Using These Medicines During Pregnancy

These medicines are not usually recommended during pregnancy. But sometimes, the benefits of using them may be greater than the risks.

For example, vancomycin taken by mouth may be used to treat *Clostridioides difficile* diarrhea in pregnant women.

Always talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant.

## Using These Medicines While Breastfeeding

It is not recommended to use these medicines while breastfeeding. They may pass into breast milk and could harm the baby.

Talk to your doctor if you are breastfeeding and need treatment.

# Coarctation of the Aorta

Coarctation of the aorta is a narrowing in the main blood vessel that carries blood from the heart to the rest of the body.  
This narrowing makes it harder for blood to flow through.  
It causes high blood pressure in the arms and upper body.  
It can also make the heart work too hard.  
If the narrowing is severe, blood flow to the belly and legs may be too low.

Symptoms depend on how bad the narrowing is.  
Some people have headaches, chest pain, cold arms or legs, or feel tired.  
Some may have pain in the legs when walking.  
In babies, the condition can cause sudden serious illness.  
This includes low blood pressure, poor kidney function, and a dangerous chemical imbalance in the blood.  
In rare cases, it can lead to heart failure or shock.

A doctor may hear a soft whooshing sound (called a bruit) when listening to the chest.  
This sound comes from blood rushing through the narrowed area.

Doctors diagnose this condition using imaging tests.  
These include an echocardiogram, CT scan, or MRI scan.  
The test shows the shape and flow of blood in the aorta.

Treatment depends on age and how serious the condition is.  
Babies with symptoms get a medicine called prostaglandin E1.  
This keeps a natural blood vessel open so blood can flow better.  
For high blood pressure, doctors may prescribe beta-blockers.  
Surgery is often used in babies and young children.  
In older children and teens, doctors may use a balloon to widen the narrowed area.  
Sometimes a small metal tube (a stent) is placed to keep the area open.

This condition is found in 6 to 8 out of every 100 babies born with heart problems.  
It is more common in people with Turner syndrome.  
It affects boys more than girls, about 2 boys for every 1 girl.

---

## How Coarctation of the Aorta Works

The narrowing usually happens just past the left arm artery, near where a special blood vessel (the ductus arteriosus) used to connect the heart and lungs before birth.  
This duct closes after birth.  
Before it closes, most blood can go around the narrow spot through the duct.  
This helps the baby survive even with the narrowing.

The narrowing can happen alone or with other heart problems.  
These include a bicuspid aortic valve, a hole in the heart, or a narrowed aortic valve.  
It can also be linked to weak spots in brain arteries, called berry aneurysms.

There are two main problems caused by the narrowing:

- High pressure in the blood vessels above the narrowing.  
- Low blood flow in the blood vessels below the narrowing.

High pressure makes the heart’s left side thicken and work harder.  
This can lead to high blood pressure in the arms and brain.

Low blood flow affects the belly organs and legs.  
Poor blood flow to the intestines raises the risk of serious infection.

Over time, the body creates new blood vessels to help carry blood around the narrow spot.  
These new vessels come from the chest, upper back, and under the arms.

If not treated, this condition can lead to serious problems later in life.  
These include heart failure, infections of the heart, bleeding in the brain, brain damage from high blood pressure, and heart disease.  
There is also a higher risk of a tear in the aorta or a rupture.  
This risk is higher during pregnancy.  
The most common place for a tear or rupture is the part of the aorta just after the heart.

Recent studies suggest the main cause of these problems is not the narrowing itself.  
It is more likely due to a bicuspid aortic valve and related aorta problems.

---

## Signs and Symptoms

In newborns, severe narrowing can cause sudden illness in the first week of life.  
This includes low blood pressure, poor kidney function, and a dangerous chemical imbalance in the blood.  
These signs can look like sepsis or other serious conditions.  
Babies with severe narrowing often get very sick right after the ductus arteriosus closes.

Mild cases may not cause any symptoms in babies.  
As children grow, they may feel tired, have headaches, chest pain, or leg pain when walking.  
High blood pressure in the arms is common.  
But heart failure is rare after the first few months of life.

In adults, rare cases can involve a burst brain aneurysm.  
This can cause bleeding in the brain or around it.

On physical exam, doctors check blood pressure and pulses in all four limbs.  
They often find strong pulses and high blood pressure in the arms.  
Pulses in the legs are weak or slow to appear.  
Blood pressure in the legs is low or hard to measure.  
The left arm may also have lower pressure and weaker pulses, but still higher than the legs.

A doctor may hear a murmur (a whooshing sound) during the heartbeat.  
This murmur is often heard at the upper left side of the chest, under the left arm, or in the upper back.  
It is usually a grade 2 to 3 out of 6.  
If the person also has a bicuspid aortic valve, a click sound may be heard at the heart’s apex.  
Dilated new blood vessels can cause a continuous murmur between the ribs.

Girls with this condition may have Turner syndrome.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors use several tools to diagnose coarctation:

- A chest X-ray  
- An ECG (electrocardiogram)  
- An echocardiogram, CT scan, or MRI scan

The diagnosis starts with checking blood pressure and pulses in all four limbs.  
This helps spot a difference between the arms and legs.  
A chest X-ray may show a “3” shape in the upper chest.  
This is a clue to the narrowing.  
The heart size is normal unless heart failure is present.  
Over time, the new blood vessels can wear down the ribs, causing notches.  
But this sign is rare before age five.

An ECG often shows thickening of the heart’s left side.  
But it can also be normal.  
In newborns with severe narrowing, the right side of the heart may be thickened instead.  
This is because the baby’s blood flow is shifted to the right side before birth.

---

## How It Is Treated

For babies with symptoms, doctors give prostaglandin E1.  
This medicine keeps the ductus arteriosus open so blood can flow better.

For high blood pressure, doctors may prescribe beta-blockers.

Surgery is the usual treatment for babies, young children, and infants.  
In older children and teens, doctors may use a balloon to stretch the narrowed area.  
Sometimes a stent is placed to keep it open.

Babies with mild narrowing and no signs of poor blood flow in the legs are watched closely.  
Treatment is delayed until a safe time for surgery or repair.

---

## Key Points

- Coarctation of the aorta is a narrowing in the main blood vessel from the heart.  
- It usually happens just past the left arm artery.  
- It causes high blood pressure in the arms and low blood flow in the legs and belly.  
- Severe cases can cause serious illness in newborns.  
- Mild cases may not show symptoms until later in life.  
- A blood pressure difference between arms and legs is common.  
- Pulse strength is stronger in the arms than in the legs.  
- A whooshing sound (murmur) is often heard in the upper back.  
- Babies with symptoms get prostaglandin E1 to keep a blood vessel open.  
- The condition is fixed with surgery or balloon treatment.

---

# Centipede and Millipede Bites

## What They Look Like

Centipedes and millipedes both have long bodies made of many small sections.  
Each section of a millipede has two pairs of legs.  
Each section of a centipede has only one pair of legs.  
The legs of a centipede are on the sides of its body.  
The legs of a millipede are directly under its body.  
From the side, a centipede looks flatter.  
A millipede looks rounder.

## Centipede Bites

Some large centipedes can bite.  
Their bite can hurt a lot.  
The area around the bite may swell and turn red.  
These symptoms usually go away in two days or less.  
For pain relief, place an ice cube wrapped in plastic and a thin cloth on the bite.  
This can help reduce pain.

## Millipede Contact

Millipedes do not bite.  
But they can release a liquid that irritates the skin.  
This liquid can cause burning and itching.  
If the liquid gets in your eye, it can cause redness, swelling, and pain.  
Wash the area with plenty of soap and water right away.  
If your skin still feels bad, use a cream that reduces swelling.  
If the liquid gets in your eye, flush it with water right away.  
Do not rub your eye.  
Get medical help if symptoms do not improve.

# How to Treat Pain and Swelling

This guide explains how to treat pain and swelling. The goal is to help you move better and use your muscles and joints more smoothly.

## What Treatments Are Used?

These treatments do not use medicine. They include:

- Exercise
- Heat
- Cold
- Electrical stimulation
- Neck pulling (cervical traction)
- Massage
- Acupuncture

These treatments help with many problems in muscles, tendons, and ligaments.

Your doctor or therapist will choose the best treatment based on your needs and what feels right for you. These treatments are usually used along with other care, not alone.

They are often used before and after exercise. They are part of a full plan to help you get better.

## What Should Be Written Down?

When your provider gives you a treatment plan, they should write down:

- Your diagnosis (what is wrong)
- The type of treatment (for example, ultrasound or a hot pack)
- Where the treatment goes (for example, right shoulder or lower back)
- How often it is done (for example, once a day or every other day)
- How long it lasts (for example, 10 days or one week)

## When to Use Each Treatment

Here is a list of when each treatment may help.

### Heat

Use heat for:
- Joint pain
- Arthritis (inflammation in joints)
- Back pain
- Fibromyalgia (widespread pain)
- Muscle tightness
- Muscle pain
- Nerve pain
- Sprains and strains
- Tendon swelling
- Neck injuries from whiplash

### Ultrasound

Use ultrasound for:
- Bone injuries
- Bursitis (swelling in fluid-filled sacs)
- Complex regional pain syndrome (long-term pain after injury)
- Stiff joints
- Osteoarthritis
- Tendon inflammation

### Low-Level Laser (Cold Laser)

Use low-level laser for:
- Sprains and strains
- Muscle tightness
- Pain in muscle and connective tissue

### Cold

Use cold for:
- Swelling (in the first few days after injury)
- Lower back pain
- Muscle tightness
- Muscle and connective tissue pain
- Pain from injury

### Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation (TENS)

Use TENS for:
- Pain in muscles and bones
- Nerve pain
- Poor blood flow in the legs

### Cervical Traction

Use neck pulling for:
- Neck pain from nerve pressure
- Long-term neck pain from joint wear
- Neck twist (torticollis)
- Neck injuries from whiplash

### Massage

Use massage for:
- Pain after limb loss
- Cerebral palsy
- Tight tissues
- Fibromyalgia
- Paralysis on one side of the body
- Injuries to soft tissues (like joint injuries, sprains, strains)
- Lower back pain
- Muscle and connective tissue pain

### Acupuncture

Use acupuncture for:
- Long-term pain
- Injuries to muscles and bones (new or old)
- Arthritis that causes swelling or joint damage

> **Note:** Acupuncture is used with other treatments, not alone.

# Menstrual Cramps

Menstrual cramps are pain in the lower belly. They can happen a few days before your period, during your period, or just after. The pain is usually worst about one day after your period starts. It often gets better after 2 or 3 days.

The pain can feel like a cramp, a dull ache, or a sharp, throbbing pain. It may come and go. Sometimes the pain spreads to your lower back or legs.

Many women also have other symptoms. These can include:
- Headaches
- Feeling sick to your stomach (nausea), sometimes with vomiting
- Constipation or diarrhea
- Needing to pee more often

Some women also have symptoms of premenstrual syndrome. These include:
- Feeling irritable or nervous
- Feeling down or sad
- Feeling tired
- Swelling in the belly

These symptoms can last through part or all of your period.

Menstrual cramps can make it hard to do normal daily activities. About 30% or more of women are affected this way. Some women miss school or work because of the pain. Women with bad cramps are more likely to have long-term pelvic pain or other long-term pain problems.

---

## What Causes Menstrual Cramps?

There are two main types of menstrual cramps:

### 1. Primary Dysmenorrhea
This type has no clear cause. It usually starts during the teenage years. It often gets better with age and after having a baby. This is the most common type.

### 2. Secondary Dysmenorrhea
This type is caused by another health problem in the reproductive system. It usually starts in adulthood. It can also start earlier if there is a birth defect in the reproductive organs.

Experts think that primary dysmenorrhea is caused by a substance called prostaglandin. This substance is released during your period. High levels of prostaglandin can make your uterus tighten like it does during labor. This can reduce blood flow to the uterus and cause pain. Prostaglandin also makes the nerves in the uterus more sensitive to pain.

Stress or anxiety may also make the pain worse.

---

### Risk Factors for Severe Cramps

You are more likely to have bad cramps if you:
- Started your periods early
- Have long or heavy periods
- Have never been pregnant
- Are under 30 years old
- Have depression, anxiety, or high stress
- Smoke or drink too much alcohol
- Have a family history of bad cramps

Cramps often get better with age and after your first pregnancy.

---

### Common Causes of Secondary Dysmenorrhea

These are the most common causes of cramps due to a health problem:

#### Endometriosis
Tissue that normally lines the inside of the uterus grows outside the uterus. This is the most common cause of secondary cramps.

#### Adenomyosis
Tissue from the lining of the uterus grows into the wall of the uterus. This makes the uterus swell and become painful during your period.

#### Fibroids
These are noncancerous growths made of muscle and fibrous tissue. They grow inside the uterus.

#### Cervical Stenosis
The opening from the vagina into the uterus is narrow or blocked.

Other less common causes include:
- Cysts or tumors in the ovaries
- Use of an intrauterine device (IUD)
- Pelvic inflammatory disease
- Scar tissue in the uterus
- Birth defects in the vagina, cervix, or uterus

Copper IUDs often make periods more painful. IUDs that release a hormone called progestin usually do not cause pain.

In some women, the opening in the cervix is too narrow. This can happen after a treatment for a precancerous condition in the cervix.

---

## How Doctors Evaluate Menstrual Cramps

Doctors usually diagnose menstrual cramps when a woman says she has regular, painful periods. They then check if the cramps are due to a health problem or not.

You should see a doctor right away if you have any of these warning signs:
- Severe pain that started suddenly or is new
- Pain that never goes away
- Fever
- A thick, pus-like discharge from the vagina
- Sharp pain that gets worse when you touch your belly or move

If you do not have warning signs but your cramps are worse than usual or last longer than normal, see a doctor within a few days.

Other women with cramps should also call their doctor. The doctor will decide how soon you need to be seen based on your symptoms, age, and health history.

The doctor will ask about:
- When your periods started
- How long your periods last
- How heavy they are
- How often they come
- If your periods are regular
- If you have spotting between periods
- When your cramps happen in relation to your period

They will also ask:
- When your cramps started
- If you have other symptoms, like pain not linked to your period
- How bad the pain is
- What helps or makes it worse (including pain medicine)
- How the pain affects your daily life
- If you have pain during sex or trouble getting pregnant

The doctor will also ask about:
- Other health problems
- Medicines you take (like birth control pills)
- Any past surgeries that could cause pelvic pain (like a procedure to remove the lining of the uterus)

---

### Physical Exam

The doctor will do a pelvic exam. They will check for:
- Abnormal discharge
- Tenderness in the pelvic area
- Enlarged uterus
- Cervical polyps
- Fibroids

They will also gently press on your belly to check for sore spots. This can help find serious inflammation in the belly.

---

### Tests to Find the Cause

To rule out serious causes, doctors may do:

- A pregnancy test (for all women of childbearing age)
- An ultrasound of the pelvis (to check for fibroids, polyps, endometriosis, adenomyosis, or growths in the ovaries)

If pelvic inflammatory disease is suspected, the doctor will take a sample from the cervix. They will check it under a microscope and send it to a lab.

If the first tests are unclear and symptoms continue, more tests may be needed:

- Hysterosalpingography (X-rays after a special dye is put into the uterus and tubes)
- Sonohysterography (ultrasound after fluid is put into the uterus)
- Hysteroscopy (a thin tube is used to look inside the uterus)
- MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)
- Laparoscopy (a small camera is used to look inside the pelvis)

---

### How the Tests Work

- **Hysterosalpingography:** A special dye is put into the uterus and tubes. X-rays are taken to see if there are blockages or problems.
- **Sonohysterography:** Fluid is put into the uterus through a thin tube. Then an ultrasound is done. The fluid helps show any problems.
- **Hysteroscopy:** A thin tube with a camera is passed through the vagina and cervix into the uterus. This lets the doctor see inside the uterus.
- **Laparoscopy:** A small camera is put through a tiny cut near the belly button. It lets the doctor see the uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, and other organs in the pelvis.

---

## How Menstrual Cramps Are Treated

### 1. Treat the Underlying Cause
If cramps are caused by a health problem, that problem is treated if possible.

- A narrow cervix can be widened with surgery. But this often only helps for a short time.
- Fibroids or misplaced tissue (from endometriosis) can be removed with surgery.

### 2. For Primary Dysmenorrhea (No Clear Cause)
If there is no treatable condition, you can try:
- Moist heat on the lower belly
- Abdominal massage
- Getting enough sleep and rest
- Exercising regularly

Some women try:
- A low-fat diet
- Supplements like omega-3 fatty acids, flaxseed, magnesium, vitamin B1, vitamin E, or zinc

There is not strong proof these help. But they are usually safe. Talk to your doctor before trying them.

---

### 3. Pain Relief Medicine

If cramps are painful, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can help. Examples include:
- Ibuprofen
- Naproxen
- Mefenamic acid

Start taking these 24 to 48 hours before your period starts. Keep taking them for 1 or 2 days after your period begins.

If NSAIDs do not help, your doctor may suggest:
- Birth control pills that contain both progestin and estrogen
- Birth control pills with only progestin (if you cannot take estrogen)

These pills stop the ovaries from releasing an egg each month.

---

### 4. Other Hormone Treatments

If birth control pills or NSAIDs do not help, other options include:
- Progestin pills (like levonorgestrel, etonogestrel, medroxyprogesterone, or micronized progesterone)
- GnRH agonists (like leuprolide or nafarelin)
- GnRH antagonists (like elagolix)
- A progestin-releasing IUD
- Danazol (a synthetic male hormone)

GnRH drugs help with cramps from endometriosis. Danazol is not used often because it can cause many side effects.

# Bruxism

Bruxism means clenching or grinding your teeth.

You can grind or clench your teeth while you are awake. You can also do it while you are sleeping.

Some people with bruxism have headaches, neck pain, or jaw pain. The strongest grinding and clenching usually happens when you are asleep.

You might not know you are grinding your teeth. But someone close to you might hear it or notice it.

Grinding your teeth can wear down the hard outer layer of your teeth. It can also damage dental crowns made of metal or ceramic. Over time, your teeth may become loose.

Bruxism is caused by many things. Known risk factors include sleep problems and emotional stress, such as anxiety.

Tooth damage is often worse in people who also have acid reflux or sleep apnea. Doctors are still learning how sleep apnea and bruxism are connected.

## How to Treat Bruxism

Try to stop clenching or grinding your teeth when you are awake. Be aware of the habit and make a conscious effort to relax your jaw.

Wear a plastic mouth guard at night. This device fits between your upper and lower teeth. It stops them from touching each other.

If your symptoms are severe, you may also wear the guard during the day.

Most guards are made just for you by a dentist. They are custom-fitted to your mouth.

If your only problem is tooth wear, you can buy a store-bought guard. These are soft and can be shaped at home with warm water. But first, see a dentist. They will check how much wear you have. They will also decide if a store-bought guard is good enough.

For short-term help, a doctor may prescribe a mild medicine to reduce anxiety. Benzodiazepines are one type. But do not use these medicines for a long time.

(See also: Myofascial Pain Syndrome.)

# Pseudohypoaldosteronism Type I – Simple Explanation

This is a rare inherited condition. It affects how the kidneys work. The kidneys do not handle salt and water properly. This leads to low blood pressure.

## Types of Pseudohypoaldosteronism

There are two main types:

- **Type I**: This type has two subtypes. Both cause low blood pressure.
- **Type II**: This is very rare and is not covered here.

## What Causes Type I?

Two different gene changes can cause this condition. These changes stop the body from responding to a hormone called aldosterone. Aldosterone helps the body keep sodium and water. Without it, the body loses too much sodium and water.

The two subtypes differ in how much salt is lost:

- In one subtype, salt is lost only through the kidneys.
- In the other, more serious subtype, salt is also lost through sweat and other body parts.

## Symptoms

### Severe Form

Children with the severe form may have symptoms like those of cystic fibrosis. These include:

- Frequent lung or breathing infections
- Dehydration, which can cause nausea and vomiting
- Feeling tired all the time
- Weak muscles
- Low blood pressure, which can cause dizziness or fainting
- A rash with tiny red bumps, caused by salt loss through sweat

### Less Severe Form

This form may cause only low blood pressure. Some children grow out of the condition as they get older.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors use several tests:

- They check blood pressure.
- They test blood and urine to measure sodium and potassium levels.
- They also test blood for hormones that control sodium and blood pressure, such as renin and aldosterone.
- Genetic testing may be done to confirm the diagnosis.

## How It Is Treated

Treatment focuses on replacing lost salt and water:

- Eat more salt in your diet. Salt contains sodium.
- Sometimes, a medicine called fludrocortisone is needed. This helps the kidneys keep sodium and water in the body.

Treatment is the same for both subtypes. Eating more salt is the main step. Medicine may be needed in more serious cases.
