# Kidney Problems During Pregnancy

Kidney issues do not usually get worse during pregnancy.  
Most kidney problems stay the same unless a woman has high blood pressure that is not under control.  

If a woman has serious kidney problems before getting pregnant, she may not be able to carry the baby to full term.  
Serious kidney problems are defined as:  
- Blood creatinine level above 3 milligrams per deciliter (or above 270 micromoles per liter)  
- Blood urea nitrogen level above 30 milligrams per deciliter (or above 10.5 millimoles of urea per liter)  

When a pregnant woman has poor kidney function, it can lead to:  
- The baby growing more slowly than normal  
- The baby being stillborn  

After a kidney transplant, many women can have a full-term pregnancy without problems if all of the following are true:  
- The new kidney has been in place for more than 2 years  
- Kidney function is normal  
- There have been no episodes of the body rejecting the new kidney  
- Blood pressure is normal  

Treating kidney problems during pregnancy needs close care from a kidney specialist.  
Your blood pressure and weight will be checked every two weeks.  
Blood tests for urea and creatinine, plus a test to measure how well the kidneys filter waste, will be done often.  
The frequency depends on how serious the kidney problem is and how fast it is changing.  

Furosemide (a water pill) is only used when needed to lower blood pressure or reduce swelling.  
Some women need other medicines to control blood pressure.  

Women with severe kidney problems may need to stay in the hospital after 28 weeks of pregnancy.  
This is to rest in bed, keep blood pressure under control, and monitor the baby closely.  
If tests show the baby is doing well, the pregnancy can continue.  

Most women with kidney problems will need to deliver before the due date.  
This is because of risks like preeclampsia, slow baby growth, or poor blood flow to the baby.  
Sometimes, a test called amniocentesis is done to check if the baby’s lungs are mature.  
If the test shows the lungs are mature, delivery may be planned.  
A ratio of lecithin to sphingomyelin above 2 to 1, or the presence of a certain substance called phosphatidylglycerol, means the lungs are ready.  

Cesarean birth is common.  
But vaginal birth may be possible if the cervix is ready and there are no other reasons to avoid it.  

## Important Facts

- Women with serious kidney problems before pregnancy usually cannot carry the baby to full term.  
- If you are pregnant and have kidney problems, your blood pressure and weight will be checked every two weeks.  
- Blood tests for kidney function will be done often, based on how serious your condition is.  
- Work closely with a kidney doctor when managing kidney issues during pregnancy.  
- Delivery is often needed before the due date.  
- Better dialysis treatments have helped people with end-stage kidney disease live longer and have babies.  
- But these women still face a higher risk of complications during pregnancy.

# Stem Cell Transplant

This is a medical treatment that helps people with serious blood problems. It involves taking special cells called stem cells from a healthy person and putting them into someone who is sick.

## What Are Stem Cells?

Stem cells are special cells that can turn into many different types of cells in the body. They can become blood cells, nerve cells, muscle cells, heart cells, and skin cells.

Some stem cells can become any kind of cell. Others are already on their way to becoming a certain type, like a nerve cell.

Stem cells grow and divide. They stay as stem cells until they get a signal to change into a specific type of cell. Once they start changing, they keep getting more specialized. Eventually, they can only become one kind of cell.

Scientists hope to use stem cells to fix or replace damaged cells. This could help treat diseases like Parkinson’s disease, diabetes, and spinal injuries. They are trying to find ways to turn stem cells into the exact type of cell that is missing or damaged.

Scientists can get stem cells from several sources:

- **Embryos**: These come from early-stage babies made during fertility treatments. Some embryos are not used. Scientists can take stem cells from these unused embryos. But this is controversial because the embryo can no longer grow into a baby. Still, these stem cells are very powerful and can become many different cell types.

- **Fetuses**: After 8 weeks of development, an embryo is called a fetus. Scientists can get stem cells from fetuses that were lost through miscarriage or abortion.

- **Umbilical cord blood**: After a baby is born, blood from the umbilical cord and placenta can be collected. This blood has stem cells that can make different types of blood cells.

- **Bone marrow from children or adults**: The bone marrow in the body contains stem cells. These can only make blood cells. This is the most common source for transplants.

- **Induced pluripotent stem cells**: Scientists can take adult cells, like skin or blood cells, and change them so they act like stem cells. This is done by changing their genes. This method is still being studied and is not yet widely used.

## When Is a Stem Cell Transplant Used?

Stem cell transplants are mainly used to treat serious blood diseases. These include:

- Leukemia
- Certain types of lymphoma, including Hodgkin lymphoma
- Aplastic anemia
- Thalassemia
- Sickle cell disease

They may also be used for some inherited conditions that affect metabolism or the immune system. Examples include chronic granulomatous disease.

Stem cell transplants are sometimes used after high-dose chemotherapy or radiation therapy. These treatments can destroy the bone marrow, which makes blood cells. The transplant helps rebuild the bone marrow.

In rare cases, the transplant may be used to replace bone marrow damaged by cancer treatments for breast cancer or neuroblastoma (a cancer that often affects children).

Doctors are also studying whether stem cell transplants can help treat autoimmune diseases like multiple sclerosis.

Outcomes vary:

- About 30 to 40 out of 100 people with lymphoma are cancer-free after treatment, including stem cell transplant.
- About 20 to 50 out of 100 people with leukemia are cancer-free after treatment.
- The transplant can help people with multiple myeloma live longer.
- It is not very helpful for breast cancer.

## How Is the Transplant Done?

There are two main types of stem cell transplants:

- **Autologous transplant**: The person uses their own stem cells.
- **Allogeneic transplant**: The person uses stem cells from a donor.

### If Using Your Own Cells

If you are getting your own stem cells, doctors collect them before you start chemotherapy or radiation. These treatments can harm stem cells.

After your treatment, the collected stem cells are put back into your body.

### If Using a Donor’s Cells

If the stem cells come from a donor, you will get medicine to weaken your immune system. This helps prevent your body from rejecting the new cells.

Before the transplant, you will get strong drugs and radiation. This kills your old bone marrow so the new stem cells can grow.

## How Are Stem Cells Collected?

### From Blood

Stem cells can be taken from blood in an outpatient procedure.

First, the donor takes medicine for a few days. This medicine helps move more stem cells into the blood.

Then, blood is taken from one arm through a tube. It goes through a machine that removes the stem cells. The rest of the blood is returned through a tube in the other arm.

This process takes 2 to 4 hours. It is done several times over a few days until enough stem cells are collected.

The stem cells can be frozen and saved for later use.

### From Bone Marrow

For bone marrow collection, the donor is given medicine to make them sleep (anesthesia).

Doctors use a needle to take marrow from the hip bone. This takes about 1 hour.

### How the Transplant Is Given

The stem cells are put into your vein through a tube. This takes 1 to 2 hours.

The stem cells travel to your bones. There, they start to grow and make new blood cells.

## After the Transplant

You will stay in the hospital for 1 to 2 months.

You will need regular checkups after you go home. Most people need at least 1 year to fully recover.

You will get medicine to prevent problems. These include:

- Drugs that help your body make more blood cells, especially white blood cells that fight infection
- Antibiotics and other medicines to lower the risk of infection

## Risks and Complications

Stem cell transplants are risky. The treatment destroys your white blood cells. This makes you very likely to get an infection for 2 to 3 weeks. This is until the new stem cells start making enough white blood cells.

To reduce infection risk:

- You may stay in a special room with no visitors.
- Anyone entering the room must wear a mask and gown.
- Everyone must wash their hands well.

### Graft-versus-Host Disease

If the stem cells come from a donor, the new cells may attack your body. This is called graft-versus-host disease.

This can be serious. It causes death in 20 to 40 out of 100 people who get it.

To prevent this, you will get medicine to weaken your immune system (immunosuppressants).

### Does the Disease Come Back?

Whether the original illness returns depends on:

- What the original disease was
- How bad it was
- What type of transplant you had

The disease comes back in:

- 40 to 75 out of 100 people who get their own stem cells
- 10 to 40 out of 100 people who get stem cells from a donor

# Tarsal Tunnel Syndrome

This condition causes pain along a nerve in the inside of the ankle. It happens when the nerve gets squeezed in a narrow space.

## What Is the Nerve?

The nerve that runs through the ankle is called the posterior tibial nerve. It passes through a tight tunnel made of bone and tough tissue. At the ankle, this nerve splits into two smaller nerves that go to the bottom of the foot.

Tarsal tunnel syndrome means the nerve is pressed inside this tunnel. But doctors sometimes use the term for any pain in this nerve, even if the cause is not pressure.

## What Can Cause This Problem?

- Swelling in the tendons that bend the foot
- Foot problems like flat feet
- Joint disease such as rheumatoid arthritis
- Scar tissue from past injuries
- Fluid-filled lumps (ganglion cysts)
- Foot or ankle shape changes
- Swelling from poor blood flow in the ankle
- Low thyroid levels (hypothyroidism) can cause similar symptoms

## Symptoms

- Pain behind the inside ankle bone
- Burning or tingling in the bottom of the foot
- Pain that may move from the heel to the toes
- Pain gets worse when standing or walking
- In later stages, pain can happen even when sitting or resting

This is different from plantar fasciitis, which usually hurts most when you first stand up.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will check your foot and ankle. They may tap or press on the nerve behind the ankle bone. If you feel tingling in the foot, that is a sign of nerve irritation.

Tests can help confirm the diagnosis:
- Nerve function tests (electrodiagnostic tests)
- MRI scan to look for lumps or swelling near the nerve

A positive test result, along with your symptoms and physical exam, makes the diagnosis likely.

If heel or arch pain lasts more than six months, it may mean the nerve is trapped.

Your doctor will also look for the cause of any swelling near the nerve.

## Treatment

Treatment depends on the cause and how bad the symptoms are.

### Non-surgical Options
- Wear a brace or special shoe insert that keeps the foot turned inward
- Use tape to hold the foot in a neutral or slightly inward position
- Raise the heel of the shoe to reduce pressure on the nerve
- Take nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) to reduce pain and swelling
- Injections of steroid and numbing medicine into the area if swelling or scar tissue is the cause

### Surgery
If symptoms do not improve with other treatments, surgery may be needed. The goal is to open the tunnel and relieve pressure on the nerve.

Surgery is usually considered when symptoms are severe and long-lasting.

# Pancreatic Islet Cell Transplantation

This treatment helps people with severe diabetes. It involves taking special cells from a donor’s pancreas and putting them into a person whose body no longer makes enough insulin.

## What Are Islet Cells?

Islet cells are the part of the pancreas that make insulin. Insulin helps control blood sugar levels. When the pancreas stops making enough insulin, blood sugar can get too high. This can cause serious health problems.

Some people with severe diabetes may benefit from this transplant. It can help them live with less need for insulin shots.

## How the Transplant Works

Doctors take the pancreas from someone who recently died. They separate the islet cells from the rest of the pancreas. Then, they inject these cells into a vein that leads to the liver.

The islet cells travel to the liver and settle in small blood vessels there. Once there, they can start making insulin again.

Sometimes, one transplant is not enough. A person may need more than one injection. This means more than one donor may be needed.

To prevent the body from attacking the new cells, patients take medicines that calm the immune system. These are called immunosuppressants. They help stop rejection.

## Special Case: Using Your Own Cells

Some people have their pancreas removed because of a serious condition called chronic pancreatitis. After the surgery, they often develop diabetes.

In these cases, doctors can take the islet cells from the person’s own pancreas before removing it. They save these cells and put them back into the body later. This is called autologous transplantation.

Because the cells come from the person’s own body, the immune system does not attack them. So, no immunosuppressant medicines are needed.

## Possible Problems

Even if the donor and recipient have similar tissue types, the body may still reject the new cells. The immune system sees the new cells as foreign and attacks them.

Rejection can be mild or very serious. In serious cases, the new cells may stop working.

Doctors check for rejection by testing blood. They look at:
- Levels of certain digestive enzymes from the pancreas
- Blood sugar levels
- A protein called hemoglobin A1C (this shows average blood sugar over time)

Other problems can happen during or after the procedure. These include:
- Bleeding
- Blood clots in the portal vein (the vein that carries blood to the liver)

## Important Notes

- About 75% of people who get an islet cell transplant no longer need insulin one year after the procedure.
- Some may stay off insulin for many years.
- But we do not yet know if this benefit lasts a long time for everyone.

# Tumor Necrosis Factor Receptor–Associated Periodic Syndrome (TRAPS)

TRAPS is a rare genetic condition that causes repeated episodes of fever and muscle pain. It runs in families and is passed down from parent to child.

## What Causes TRAPS?

TRAPS is caused by a change in a gene called *TNFR1*. This gene helps make a protein that controls inflammation. When the gene is changed, the protein does not fold correctly. It gets stuck inside the cell and causes the body to make too much inflammation.

This buildup of faulty protein triggers a stress response in the cell. The cell tries to fix the problem, but this process creates harmful chemicals. These chemicals cause swelling and pain in the body.

## Symptoms of TRAPS

Most people with TRAPS start having symptoms before age ten.

Each flare-up usually lasts between 7 and 21 days, with an average of 10 days.

The main signs during a flare-up are:
- High fever
- Muscle pain that moves from one place to another
- Swelling in the arms or legs
- Red, tender skin over the swollen area

Other possible symptoms include:
- Headaches
- Belly pain
- Diarrhea or constipation
- Nausea
- Eye pain or redness
- Swelling around the eyes
- Joint pain
- Skin rash
- Pain in the testicles (in males)

Some males may also develop a hernia in the groin area.

Flare-ups can happen without any clear reason. But some people report that stress, injury, or infection can trigger them.

About 1 in 10 people with TRAPS develop kidney damage from a condition called amyloidosis. This usually happens around age 43.

## How Is TRAPS Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose TRAPS based on:
- Your medical history
- A physical exam
- Genetic testing

Doctors look for certain signs to help make the diagnosis:
- A family history of similar symptoms
- Long fever episodes
- Swelling around the eyes
- Rash that moves from one place to another
- Muscle pain
- No sore throat or mouth sores

These signs are helpful, but not all people have every one. The test for these signs is accurate in 87 out of 100 cases and correctly rules out TRAPS in 92 out of 100 cases.

During a flare-up, blood tests may show:
- High white blood cell count
- High levels of inflammation markers
- Increased levels of certain proteins

All people with TRAPS should have regular urine tests to check for protein. This helps catch kidney problems early.

## How Is TRAPS Treated?

For mild flare-ups, short-term use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen may help.

For more severe flare-ups, doctors often prescribe corticosteroids such as prednisone. These drugs reduce inflammation quickly.

But over time, some people need higher doses. This can make flare-ups last longer and happen more often.

To prevent flare-ups, doctors may prescribe:
- Anakinra once daily
- Canakinumab every 4 weeks

These medicines work by blocking a key part of the body’s inflammation system.

Etanercept is another option, but it helps only some people. It is usually used if the other medicines do not work well.

## Outlook

With proper treatment, most people with TRAPS can live normal lives.

If kidney damage from amyloidosis occurs, the outlook is less positive. Early detection and treatment are key to preventing serious problems.

Regular check-ups and monitoring are important for long-term health.

# What Are Hereditary Periodic Fever Syndromes?

These are rare conditions you are born with. They cause repeated episodes of fever and other symptoms. These symptoms are not caused by common childhood infections or other known illnesses.

## Most Common Syndrome

- **Familial Mediterranean fever** is the most common type across all ages.

## A Similar Condition (Not Hereditary)

- **PFAPA syndrome** causes fever episodes. It also causes mouth sores, sore throat, and swollen glands in the neck. This condition is not passed down through families.

## Other Less Common Syndromes

### 1. Hereditary Cryopyrin-Associated Periodic Syndromes (Cryopyrinopathies)

This group includes:
- Familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome (FCAS)
- Muckle-Wells syndrome (MWS)
- Neonatal-onset multisystem autoinflammatory disease (NOMID)

**What happens:**
- You get fever, a rash, and joint pain.
- Cold weather can trigger these attacks.

**How it is treated:**
- Medicines like anakinra, rilonacept, or canakinumab can help.
- These medicines change how your immune system works.

---

### 2. Hyper-IgD Syndrome

**What happens:**
- You have fever, belly pain, headaches, joint pain, a rash, and swollen lymph nodes.

**How it is treated:**
- During attacks, medicines like NSAIDs, corticosteroids, or anakinra can ease symptoms.
- To prevent future attacks, anakinra or canakinumab may be used.

---

### 3. Tumor Necrosis Factor Receptor–Associated Periodic Syndrome (TRAPS)

**What happens:**
- You have repeated attacks of fever, muscle pain, and swelling in arms and legs.
- You may also have belly pain, joint pain, and a rash.

**How it is treated:**
- Mild attacks may be helped by NSAIDs.
- Most attacks need prednisone, a type of corticosteroid.
- Anakinra or canakinumab may be used to prevent attacks.

---

### 4. PAPA Syndrome (Pyogenic Arthritis, Pyoderma Gangrenosum, and Acne)

**What happens:**
- You get fever, swollen and painful joints, skin ulcers, and severe acne.
- By the time you reach puberty, joint problems often get better.
- Skin issues become the main problem.

**How it is treated:**
- Medicines like anakinra, etanercept, adalimumab, or infliximab may help.
- Acne is treated with the antibiotic tetracycline or with isotretinoin.

---

## When Do Symptoms Start?

- Most people first notice symptoms during childhood.
- Fewer than 1 in 10 people start having symptoms after age 18.
- You feel normal between attacks.
- Attacks come and go over time.

# Hemifacial Spasm

Hemifacial spasm is a condition that causes one side of the face to twitch or spasm.  
The spasms happen without pain.  
They are caused by abnormal electrical signals in the facial nerve.  
These signals come from the facial nerve or the part of the brain that controls it.

The most common cause is a blood vessel pressing on the facial nerve.  
The pressure makes the nerve send out extra electrical signals.  
This is similar to what happens in trigeminal neuralgia.

The twitching usually starts in the eyelid.  
It may then spread to the cheek and mouth.  
At first, the twitching may only happen sometimes.  
Over time, it can become constant.

An MRI scan can often show the blood vessel pressing on the nerve.  
But doctors usually diagnose the condition based on your symptoms.  
Other conditions can cause similar twitching.  
These include seizures in one part of the brain, eyelid spasms, and tics.

The best treatment is injecting a medicine called botulinum toxin into the twitching muscles.  
There are two types: botulinum toxin type A and botulinum toxin type B.  
This treatment helps relax the muscles and reduces the twitching.

Some treatments used for trigeminal neuralgia can also help.  
These include:  
- Medicines that stop nerve signals (antiseizure drugs)  
- A muscle relaxer called baclofen  
- A medicine that helps with nerve pain and mood (amitriptyline)  
- Surgery to move the blood vessel away from the nerve (microvascular decompression)

# Hepatopulmonary Syndrome

Hepatopulmonary syndrome is a condition that causes low oxygen levels in the blood. It happens in people who have liver disease.

The problem comes from changes in the tiny blood vessels in the lungs. These changes make it hard for the blood to get enough oxygen.

## What Happens in the Lungs

- The small blood vessels in the lungs become wider than normal.
- More blood than usual flows through the lungs.
- The blood moves through the lungs too quickly. This gives it less time to pick up oxygen.
- Some blood vessels connect in the wrong way. Oxygen-rich blood mixes with oxygen-poor blood.
- The blood that leaves the lungs and goes to the rest of the body has less oxygen than it should.

## Symptoms

- You may feel short of breath, especially when sitting up.
- Lying down often makes breathing easier.
- Your blood oxygen level drops when you sit up.
- Most people also have signs of long-term liver disease.
- You may see small red or brown spots on your skin. These are called spider angiomas.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors look for hepatopulmonary syndrome in people with liver disease who suddenly feel short of breath.

They check your blood oxygen level using a small sensor on your finger. This test is called pulse oximetry.

They may also take blood samples:
- One while you breathe normal air.
- One after you breathe extra oxygen.

They may use special tests to confirm the diagnosis:
- A contrast echocardiogram: A special liquid is injected into a vein. Bubbles in the liquid travel through the heart and lungs. If there are abnormal blood vessel connections, the bubbles appear in the heart sooner than normal.
- A nuclear lung scan: A safe radioactive substance is injected. It moves through the lungs. If blood flows too fast or in the wrong places, the scan will show it.

## Treatment

- The main treatment is extra oxygen through a mask or tubes.
- If the liver disease improves, the lung problem may get better.
- In many cases, a liver transplant can fix the problem.

# Paget Disease of Bone – Simple Explanation

## What Is Paget Disease of Bone?

Paget disease of bone is a long-term condition that affects the bones. It causes some parts of the bone to break down and rebuild too quickly. This leads to bone that is weaker than normal, even though it may be larger or thicker.

The disease often causes no symptoms. When symptoms do appear, they come on slowly. They may include bone pain, joint stiffness, tiredness, or changes in bone shape.

Doctors usually find the disease by looking at X-rays. Treatment helps relieve symptoms and may include medicines, especially bisphosphonates.

## Who Gets Paget Disease?

About 2 to 3 out of every 100 adults over age 55 in the United States have this disease. Men are slightly more likely to get it than women.

The chance of having the disease goes up with age. But overall, fewer people are being diagnosed now than in the past.

The disease is most common in the United Kingdom and parts of Europe like Spain, France, and Italy. It is also seen in countries settled by people from Europe, such as Australia, New Zealand, the United States, and Canada.

It is rare in Scandinavia and Asia.

## What Causes Paget Disease?

About 1 in 10 people with Paget disease have a change in a gene called *SQSTM1*. This gene change makes bone cells called osteoclasts work too hard. Osteoclasts break down old bone.

Other gene changes in the RANK pathway can also cause the disease. This pathway helps control how osteoclasts form and work.

Some doctors think a virus might play a role. For example, a type of virus called measles has been linked to the disease. This is because some bone cells in people with Paget disease look like cells infected with a virus under a microscope.

But this idea is still debated. It is possible that a virus triggers the disease in people who are already at risk due to their genes.

## How Does Paget Disease Work in the Body?

Any bone can be affected, but the most common ones are:

- The pelvis
- The thigh bone (femur)
- The skull

Less often affected bones include the shin bone (tibia), spine bones (vertebrae), collarbone (clavicle), and upper arm bone (humerus).

In affected areas, bone breaks down and rebuilds too fast. The bone becomes very active and has more blood vessels than normal.

The cells that break down bone (osteoclasts) become large and have many nuclei. The cells that build new bone (osteoblasts) also work too hard. This leads to thick, rough bone structure.

Even though the bone gets bigger and harder in some places, it is actually weaker. This can lead to fractures, bending, or deformities.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people with Paget disease have no symptoms.

When symptoms do happen, they come on slowly. They may include:

- A deep, aching pain in the bones
- Stiffness in joints
- Feeling tired
- Changes in bone shape

Bone pain can be bad, especially at night. It may also come from pressure on nerves or from joint wear and tear (osteoarthritis).

If the skull is affected, you might see:

- A larger skull, especially in the front and sides
- Swollen veins on the scalp
- Hearing loss in one or both ears

Other possible symptoms include dizziness, headaches, and hearing problems.

Bowing of long bones or joint damage from osteoarthritis can cause visible changes in shape.

A broken bone without a clear cause may be the first sign of the disease.

If you have new or worsening pain in a bone that has Paget disease, it could be a sign of a rare cancer called osteosarcoma. This needs to be checked.

## How Is Paget Disease Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tools to diagnose Paget disease:

- X-rays of the bones
- Blood tests to check bone activity
- A bone scan to see how much of the skeleton is affected

You should be tested for Paget disease if you have:

- Unexplained bone pain or bone shape changes
- Abnormal findings on an X-ray
- High levels of a liver enzyme called alkaline phosphatase in blood tests, especially if other liver tests are normal

If Paget disease is suspected, your doctor will order:

- X-rays
- Blood tests for alkaline phosphatase, vitamin D, kidney function, calcium, and phosphate

Key blood test results:

- Alkaline phosphatase is often high (this shows bone is very active)
- Gamma-glutamyl-transpeptidase (GGT) and 5'-nucleotidase are usually normal
- Phosphate levels are usually normal
- Calcium is usually normal, but may be high if you are not moving much

If calcium is high, your doctor will check for another condition called hyperparathyroidism.

If the alkaline phosphatase is not high, or if it’s unclear whether the high level comes from bone or liver, a special test for bone-specific alkaline phosphatase can be done.

Other blood tests can show if bone turnover is high. These include PINP and CTX.

Before starting treatment with bisphosphonates, your doctor will check:

- Vitamin D level (low levels increase risk of side effects)
- Kidney function (if it is poor, bisphosphonates are not safe)

### Confirming the Diagnosis

X-rays are needed to confirm the diagnosis. Typical signs on X-rays include:

- Thickened bone
- Coarse, bumpy patterns in the bone
- Bone that is larger than normal
- Bending (bowing) of the thigh or shin bones

If the X-ray or blood test results are unclear, a bone scan using a special dye can show how much of the skeleton is involved.

If there is any doubt, a small sample of bone (biopsy) may be taken to rule out cancer.

If you already have Paget disease and your symptoms get worse, your doctor may order:

- CT scan
- MRI scan
- Biopsy

These tests help check for rare cancers like osteosarcoma or giant cell tumor of bone.

## Important Tips

- If you have high alkaline phosphatase but normal GGT, think about Paget disease, especially if you are over 55.

## How Is Paget Disease Treated?

Treatment depends on whether you have symptoms or signs of active disease.

### For Symptoms and Problems

- Pain relief with painkillers or NSAIDs (like ibuprofen)
- Devices like braces or shoe inserts to help with walking problems
- Surgery may be needed for severe joint damage (like hip or knee replacement) or nerve pressure in the spine

### For Active Disease

- Bisphosphonates are the main treatment. These medicines slow down bone breakdown.
- Zoledronic acid is the preferred medicine. It is given as a one-time infusion into a vein.

### When No Treatment Is Needed

- If the disease is only in one spot and you have no symptoms, treatment may not be needed.

### General Advice

- Stay active and keep weight on your bones. Avoid long periods of bed rest.

## What Is the Outlook?

Most people with Paget disease live normal lives. The disease does not shorten life span.

But common problems include:

- Joint pain from osteoarthritis
- Bone pain
- Bone deformities
- Broken bones

Zoledronic acid helps relieve bone pain in most people. It also brings bone activity back to normal in over 90% of patients.

We do not have strong proof that treatment stops long-term problems like joint damage or bone bending. But untreated disease does get worse over time. Bones can become more deformed, and bone breakdown can spread.

## Key Points

- Paget disease affects bone growth and breakdown. It is common in older adults.
- It often causes no symptoms, but can lead to pain, joint problems, broken bones, nerve pressure, or rare cancers.
- Diagnosis is usually based on X-rays showing thickened, bumpy, or enlarged bones.
- The first treatment is bisphosphonates, especially zoledronic acid.

# Short Bowel Syndrome

Short bowel syndrome happens when a large part of the small intestine is removed. This makes it hard for the body to absorb food and fluids. As a result, people often have diarrhea and do not get enough nutrition.

## What Causes Short Bowel Syndrome?

The small intestine is usually removed because of serious health problems. Common reasons include:

- Crohn disease  
- A blood vessel blockage in the intestine (mesenteric infarction)  
- Damage from radiation therapy  
- Intestinal cancer  
- A twisted loop of intestine (volvulus)  
- Birth defects  
- In babies, a condition called necrotizing enterocolitis  

Most of the time, the problem starts when more than two-thirds of the small intestine is removed.

## How the Small Intestine Works

The small intestine is about 12 to 21 feet long. It is where most of the body’s food and nutrients are absorbed.

- If the middle part of the small intestine is removed, the last part may grow stronger and take over some of the work.  
- If more than about 3 feet of the last part (ileum) is removed, the body usually cannot adapt.  
- Without enough small intestine, the body cannot absorb fats, proteins, or many vitamins.  
- If the end of the small intestine is gone, the body cannot absorb bile acids. These help digest food.  
- Without bile acids, the colon gets too much of them. This causes diarrhea.  
- The body also cannot absorb vitamin B12 if the end of the small intestine is missing.

Diarrhea usually starts right after surgery. Later, people may become underweight and develop vitamin deficiencies, such as low vitamin B12.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose short bowel syndrome by:

- Reviewing your surgery history  
- Checking your symptoms  
- Doing a physical exam  

## How Is It Treated?

### Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN)

After surgery, you will get fluids and nutrients through a vein. This is called TPN. It gives you all the nutrients your body needs, including proteins, fats, carbs, vitamins, and minerals.

- You will get TPN right after surgery, especially if diarrhea is severe.  
- As you get better and pass less stool, you will slowly start drinking fluids and eating food.  
- If you have less than 3 feet of small intestine left, you may need TPN for life.  
- Some people can eventually eat food by mouth.  

### Diet Tips

- Eat more fat and protein, and less carbohydrate.  
- Eat small meals often instead of large ones.  
- This helps your body absorb more nutrients.

### Medicines

- **Loperamide** – Take this 1 hour before meals if you have diarrhea after eating.  
- **Cholestyramine** – Take this with meals to help reduce diarrhea caused by bile acid problems.  
- **Teduglutide or apraglutide** – These are injections for people 1 year and older who need TPN. They may help reduce how much TPN you need.  
- **Proton pump inhibitors** – These medicines reduce stomach acid. Most people with this condition have too much acid.  
- **Vitamin B12 shots** – Some people need a shot once a month.

### Supplements

Most people need extra vitamins, calcium, and magnesium.

### Intestinal Transplant

If your body does not adapt and you cannot handle long-term TPN, a small intestine transplant may be an option.

## Key Facts

- Surgery that removes most of the small intestine can cause diarrhea and poor nutrition.  
- If you have less than 3 feet of small intestine left, you may need to be fed through a vein.  
- If you have more intestine left, you may be able to eat some food by mouth.  
- Most people need extra medicines, vitamins, and supplements.

# What You Need to Know About Enterovirus Infections

## What Are Enteroviruses?

Enteroviruses are a group of viruses. They are small and made of RNA.  
They are closely related to the viruses that cause the common cold.  
There are more than 100 types of enteroviruses.  
These include polioviruses, coxsackieviruses, echoviruses, and others.

These viruses can cause many different illnesses.  
They are found all over the world.

## How Do People Get Infected?

Enteroviruses spread in several ways:  
- Through contact with stool (poop).  
- Through respiratory secretions (like mucus from the nose or cough).  
- Through skin or mouth sores.  

The most common way is through the mouth after touching something contaminated.  
Less often, the virus spreads through direct contact with sores on the skin or mouth.

In some serious cases, the virus can be found in the blood or spinal fluid.  
This happens when the infection spreads to the brain or other organs.

In temperate climates, these viruses are most active in summer and fall.  
Infections are more common during these seasons.

If a pregnant woman gets infected late in pregnancy, the virus can pass to the baby.  
This can cause a severe infection in newborns.  
The baby may develop widespread illness affecting many organs.  
This includes liver problems, brain infection, heart issues, and lung disease.  
This type of infection can be life-threatening.

## Who Is at Risk?

A healthy immune system helps fight off enterovirus infections.  
People with weak immune systems are more likely to have serious or long-lasting infections.

Specifically, people with low levels of antibodies are at higher risk.  
This includes people with:  
- Agammaglobulinemia (a rare condition where the body makes no antibodies).  
- Hypogammaglobulinemia (a condition where the body makes too few antibodies).  
- Those taking certain medicines that weaken B cells (like rituximab).

These people can develop chronic infections.  
They may have ongoing brain infections, muscle problems, or liver disease.

People with other types of immune problems usually do not get long-term enterovirus infections.

## What Illnesses Can Enteroviruses Cause?

Enteroviruses can cause many different symptoms.  
Some illnesses are caused almost only by these viruses.

### Illnesses Caused Almost Only by Enteroviruses:
- Epidemic pleurodynia (severe chest pain)
- Hand-foot-and-mouth disease
- Herpangina (sore throat with mouth sores)
- Poliomyelitis (polio)
- Acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) – a rare condition that causes sudden muscle weakness

### Other Conditions Linked to Enteroviruses:
- Aseptic meningitis (infection of the brain lining)
- Meningitis with rash
- Eye infections with bleeding (hemorrhagic conjunctivitis)
- Heart and lining of the heart inflammation (myopericarditis)
- Skin rashes
- Respiratory illness (like cough, fever, runny nose)

| Meningitis with rash | Coxsackieviruses A9, B4; Echoviruses 4, 16; Enterovirus A71 |
| Hemorrhagic conjunctivitis | Enterovirus D70; Coxsackievirus A24 |
| Epidemic pleurodynia | Coxsackieviruses B1–6 |
| Hand-foot-and-mouth disease | Coxsackieviruses A6, 9, 16, B2–5; Enterovirus A71 |
| Herpangina | Coxsackieviruses A2, 4–6, 8, 10; possibly B3 |

| Respiratory illness | Echoviruses 4, 8, 9, 11, 20; Coxsackieviruses A21, 24, B1, B3–5; Enterovirus D68 |

## How Are Enterovirus Infections Diagnosed?

Doctors often diagnose enterovirus infections based on symptoms and a physical exam.

To confirm the virus, doctors may use a test called RT-PCR.  
This test looks for viral genetic material in samples.

Samples can come from:
- Blood
- Spinal fluid (fluid around the brain and spinal cord)
- Stool
- Mucus from the nose or throat
- Sores on the skin or mouth

The test is most important when:
- A person has brain infection (like aseptic meningitis).
- A person has acute flaccid myelitis (AFM).
- A newborn has a severe infection.
- A person with weak immunity has a long-term infection.

Some common lab tests for respiratory viruses cannot tell the difference between rhinoviruses and enteroviruses.  
They may also miss some enterovirus types.  
To get a clear answer, doctors may need to do more detailed testing.

## How Are Enterovirus Infections Treated?

There is no specific medicine to kill enteroviruses.  
Treatment focuses on helping the body feel better.

This includes:
- Rest
- Drinking plenty of fluids
- Pain relief
- Fever reducers

For people with weak immune systems, such as those with agammaglobulinemia, doctors may give intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG).  
This is a treatment made from donated blood.  
It contains antibodies that help fight infections.

IVIG can reduce the risk of long-term infection.  
It may also be used to treat a new infection in these patients.

# Shoulder Dystocia – Simple Explanation

Shoulder dystocia happens during childbirth when the baby’s shoulder gets stuck behind the mother’s pelvic bone. This can happen after the baby’s head has already come out.

The baby’s head may pull back slightly into the birth canal. The baby cannot breathe because the birth canal presses on the chest and the umbilical cord. This can lower the baby’s oxygen levels. It can also lead to injury or even death if not handled quickly.

Shoulder dystocia is rare. But it is more likely if any of the following are true:

- The baby is very large
- Labor is hard, long, or happens too fast
- A vacuum device or forceps is used to help deliver the baby
- The mother is overweight or obese
- The mother has diabetes
- The mother has had a previous baby with shoulder dystocia

When shoulder dystocia happens, the doctor acts fast to free the baby’s shoulder. This helps deliver the baby through the vagina.

The doctor may make a small cut in the mother’s vagina. This is called an episiotomy. It helps open the birth canal more and makes delivery easier.

If the baby still cannot be delivered this way, the doctor may gently push the baby back into the birth canal. Then, a cesarean delivery may be done to deliver the baby safely.

Shoulder dystocia can cause serious problems for the baby. These include:

- Broken bones
- Injury to the brachial plexus (a group of nerves that control movement in the arms and hands)

The mother may also have problems after delivery, such as:

- Heavy bleeding
- Tears in the area between the vagina and the anus
- Injury to muscles in the genital area
- Injury to nerves in the groin
- Separation of the bones in the front of the pelvis (pubic bones)

# Riboflavin Deficiency

Riboflavin deficiency often happens at the same time as other B vitamin deficiencies.  
It can cause a sore throat.  
It may lead to sores on the lips and inside the mouth.  
The tongue can become sore and look red or swollen.  
Eyes may become red and irritated.  
Skin can become dry, flaky, and greasy, especially around the nose, ears, eyelids, and genitals.  
Some people develop anemia, where the blood does not carry enough oxygen.

Doctors usually diagnose this condition by looking at symptoms.  
Treatment is usually riboflavin supplements taken by mouth.  
In some cases, riboflavin is given through a shot.

Riboflavin helps the body turn food into energy.  
It plays a key role in how the body uses carbohydrates and proteins.  
Riboflavin is very safe. Even high doses do not cause harm.

Good sources of riboflavin include milk, cheese, liver, meat, eggs, and enriched cereals.

---

## What Causes Riboflavin Deficiency?

**Primary deficiency** happens when you do not get enough riboflavin in your diet.  
This can occur if you eat too few fortified cereals, milk, or animal-based foods.

**Secondary deficiency** happens when your body cannot absorb or use riboflavin properly.  
This can be due to:  
- Long-term diarrhea  
- Problems absorbing nutrients from food  
- Liver disease  
- Kidney dialysis (hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis)  
- Long-term use of certain sleeping pills (barbiturates)  
- Heavy alcohol use

---

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

The most common signs are:  
- Cracks or sores at the corners of the mouth  
- Sores on the lips  
- Skin around the mouth becomes soft and wet  
- The tongue turns bright red or magenta  

These sores can get infected with a yeast called *Candida albicans*.  
This causes white patches in the mouth, often called perlèche.

Skin problems include:  
- Red, scaly, and oily patches on the face, ears, eyelids, and genitals  
- These areas may itch or feel sore

In rare cases, the eye’s clear front part (cornea) can develop new blood vessels.  
This can cause tearing and sensitivity to light.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look for the typical signs and symptoms.  
They also check if you have other B vitamin deficiencies.

Diagnosis can be confirmed in two ways:  
- A trial of riboflavin supplements. If symptoms improve, the diagnosis is likely.  
- A urine test to measure how much riboflavin your body is passing out.

The skin and mouth changes are not unique to riboflavin deficiency.  
But if you have these signs and other B vitamin problems, riboflavin deficiency should be considered.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Take riboflavin supplements by mouth.  
The usual dose is 5 to 30 milligrams once a day, split into smaller doses.  
Keep taking it until you feel better.

Also take other water-soluble vitamins, such as B1, B2, B3, B6, B12, and vitamin C.

In some cases, riboflavin is given through a shot.  
This is done as part of a multivitamin injection.

---

## Key Points

- Riboflavin deficiency causes skin and mouth problems.  
- Common signs include sores at the corners of the mouth and on the lips.  
- The tongue may look red and swollen.  
- Skin can become flaky and greasy, especially on the face and around the genitals.  

- Think about riboflavin deficiency if you have these symptoms and other B vitamin problems.  
- Confirm it with a trial of riboflavin supplements or a urine test.  

- Treat it with riboflavin and other water-soluble vitamins.  
- Most people get better with treatment.

# Problems With Sperm

A man may have trouble getting a woman pregnant if his sperm are too few, move too slowly, have unusual shapes, or if sperm cannot pass out of the body.

## What Can Cause Sperm Problems?

Too much heat in the testes can harm sperm. This can happen from:
- Wearing tight underwear or pants
- Sitting for long periods
- Hot baths or saunas
- Certain medical conditions
- Injuries to the testes
- Some medicines or harmful chemicals

Some health problems can also affect sperm:
- Undescended testes (testes that did not move into the scrotum before birth)
- Varicocele (swollen veins in the scrotum)
- Infections like mumps that affect the testes
- Hormone imbalances
- Genetic conditions such as cystic fibrosis or Klinefelter syndrome
- Tumors in the testes
- Diabetes
- Nerve or brain disorders

Certain medicines and substances can reduce sperm:
- Alcohol, especially in large amounts
- Anabolic steroids (like testosterone)
- Some cancer drugs (chemotherapy)
- Medicines for gout, ulcers, or high blood pressure
- Antidepressants
- Recreational drugs like cocaine, heroin, or amphetamines
- Some antibiotics
- Exposure to pesticides, lead, or other toxins

Some men are born without certain parts of the reproductive system. This can stop sperm from leaving the body. These parts include:
- The tubes that carry sperm (vasa deferentia)
- The glands that feed sperm (seminal vesicles)
- The area where sperm mature (epididymides)

In some men, sperm go backward into the bladder instead of out through the penis. This is called retrograde ejaculation.

## How Are Sperm Problems Diagnosed?

Doctors check for sperm problems when a couple cannot get pregnant after trying for a year.

### Step 1: Medical History and Exam
The doctor will ask about:
- Past illnesses or surgeries
- Medicines you take
- Exposure to harmful chemicals
- Lifestyle habits (like smoking, drinking, or drug use)

The doctor will also check your body for:
- Undescended testes
- Swelling or lumps in the scrotum
- Signs of hormone problems

### Step 2: Semen Analysis
This is the main test for male fertility.

You will be asked to avoid ejaculation for 2 to 3 days before the test. This helps make sure your sample has as many sperm as possible.

You will give a sample by masturbating into a clean container. This is usually done at the clinic.

If you cannot give a sample this way, special condoms without sperm-killing chemicals can be used during sex.

You may need to give more than one sample, at least a week apart. This gives a better picture of your sperm health.

The lab checks:
- How much semen you produce
- The color and texture of the semen
- How many sperm are in the sample
- How well the sperm move
- Whether the sperm have normal shapes

A low sperm count does not always mean infertility. But very low or no sperm can be a sign of a serious problem.

### Step 3: Hormone Tests
If the sperm count is very low, your doctor may test your blood for:
- Testosterone
- Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
- Luteinizing hormone (LH)
- Prolactin

High prolactin levels may mean a tumor in the brain or a side effect of medicine.

### Step 4: Genetic Testing
If there are no sperm or very few, genetic testing may be done. This can check for:
- Chromosome problems
- The gene for cystic fibrosis
- Other genetic issues

A blood sample or other tissue can be used for testing.

### Step 5: Other Tests
If needed, doctors may do:
- A test to see if sperm are in your urine after ejaculation (to check for retrograde ejaculation)
- A test to see if your sperm can attach to and enter an egg
- A test to check for antibodies that attack sperm

These tests are not always helpful. Their value is still being studied.

## How Are Sperm Problems Treated?

### Treat the Underlying Cause
If possible, the cause is treated:
- Varicoceles can be fixed with surgery. This may help sperm count, but results are not certain.
- Infections are treated with antibiotics.
- Hormone imbalances may be treated with medicine.

### Medicines to Boost Sperm
Clomiphene is a medicine sometimes used to help men make more sperm. It is also used in women to help them ovulate.

But clomiphene does not clearly improve sperm movement or shape. It has not been proven to increase fertility.

### Assisted Reproductive Technologies
If sperm count is low or clomiphene does not work, other treatments are often needed.

#### In Vitro Fertilization (IVF) with Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection (ICSI)
This is the most effective option.

- A few sperm are found in the testes using a small sample (biopsy).
- One healthy sperm is injected directly into an egg.
- The fertilized egg is grown in a lab.
- The embryo is placed in the woman’s uterus.

This method works even if there are very few or no sperm in the semen.

#### Intrauterine Insemination (IUI)
This is less invasive and cheaper than IVF.

- The healthiest sperm are separated from the rest of the semen.
- These sperm are placed directly into the woman’s uterus.
- This is done around the time of ovulation.

Pregnancy often happens within six tries if it is going to happen.

### Donor Sperm
If no sperm can be found, donor sperm may be used.

In the United States, fresh donor sperm is not used because of infection risks.

Instead:
- Donor sperm is frozen for at least 6 months.
- The donor is tested again after freezing.
- Only if the test is still negative is the sperm used.

If a donor has had the Zika virus or has lived in an area with Zika, they must wait 3 months before donating.

### Support for the Partner
The woman may also get treatment to help her make more eggs. This is done with hormones called human gonadotropins.

This increases the chance of pregnancy during IVF or IUI.

## Key Points

- Heat harms sperm. Avoid hot baths, tight clothes, and long sitting.
- Some medicines and drugs can lower sperm count.
- Anabolic steroids can shrink the testes and stop sperm production.
- Retrograde ejaculation means sperm go into the bladder instead of out the penis.
- A semen test is the main way to check sperm health.
- Hormone and genetic tests may be needed if sperm are missing or very low.
- IVF with ICSI is the most effective treatment for low sperm count.
- Donor sperm is safe when properly tested and frozen.
- The woman may also get medicine to help her make more eggs.

# Other Carbohydrate Metabolism Disorders

## Phosphoenolpyruvate Carboxykinase Deficiency

This condition affects how the body makes glucose.  
It slows down a key process called gluconeogenesis.  
This leads to symptoms like low blood sugar and poor growth.  
The signs are similar to some liver problems caused by glycogen storage diseases.  
But unlike those diseases, the liver does not build up extra glycogen.

## Other Enzyme Deficiencies

Some people are born with missing or weak enzymes in the pathways that break down sugar.  
This can affect energy production and red blood cell health.  

**Pyruvate kinase deficiency**  
This is a common enzyme problem in the glycolytic pathway.  
It can cause anemia.  
Red blood cells break down too quickly.  
This is called hemolytic anemia.

**Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency**  
This enzyme helps protect red blood cells.  
When it is missing or not working well, red blood cells can break down under stress.  
This also leads to hemolytic anemia.  
Triggers include certain infections, medicines, or foods.

**Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome**  
This condition is linked to a weak enzyme called transketolase.  
Transketolase is needed in a sugar-processing pathway.  
This enzyme needs vitamin B1 (thiamin) to work.  
A lack of vitamin B1 can cause this enzyme to fail.  
This leads to brain problems, confusion, memory loss, and eye movement issues.

# Tapeworm Infection

Tapeworms are parasites that live in the intestines. They can make you sick. You usually get them by eating raw or undercooked meat or fish. You can also get them from food or water that has been touched by human stool.

## Types of Tapeworms

There are several types of tapeworms that can infect people:

- **Beef tapeworm** – found in undercooked beef
- **Pork tapeworm** – found in undercooked pork
- **Asian tapeworm** – found in pork in Asia
- **Fish tapeworm** – found in raw or undercooked freshwater fish
- **Dwarf tapeworm** – very small; found in food or water with human stool

Dogs can carry other tapeworms. These can also infect people and cause cysts in the liver or other organs.

## How Tapeworms Work

Tapeworms have three parts:

- The **head** attaches to the wall of the intestine.
- The **neck** can grow new parts.
- The **body** is made of many segments. Each segment can hold eggs.

If the head and neck are not removed, the worm can grow back.

## How You Get Infected

### Pork, Beef, and Fish Tapeworms

- You get infected by eating raw or undercooked meat or fish that has tiny cysts.
- The cysts grow into adult worms in your intestine.
- The worms lay eggs. These eggs pass out in your stool.
- If the stool gets into the environment, animals like pigs or fish can eat it.
- The eggs grow into larvae in the animal’s body.
- When you eat the animal’s meat, you get the tapeworm.

### Dwarf Tapeworm

- You get infected by eating eggs, not cysts.
- The eggs come from human stool.
- You can swallow the eggs from food, water, or dirty hands.
- You might also eat infected insects like fleas or beetles in grain.
- The eggs grow into adult worms in your intestine.
- The worms lay eggs that pass out in your stool.
- You can swallow your own eggs and get infected again. This is called autoinfection.

## What Happens in the Body

### Intestinal Infection

- Most people with adult tapeworms in the intestine feel fine.
- Some people have stomach pain, diarrhea, or lose weight.
- You might see a piece of worm in your stool.
- The dwarf tapeworm is more likely to cause nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite.

### Cysticercosis

- This happens when pork tapeworm eggs get into your body.
- The eggs grow into cysts in your brain, muscles, or other organs.
- The cysts can stay in your body for years.
- When the cysts break down, they cause swelling and damage.
- This can lead to headaches, seizures, confusion, or other serious problems.
- Cysts in the brain can cause long-term brain damage.
- Cysts in the eyes can cause blindness.
- Cysts in the spinal cord can cause muscle weakness or paralysis.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

- For intestinal infection: A doctor checks your stool for worm segments or eggs.
- For cysticercosis: A doctor uses imaging tests like CT or MRI scans to find cysts in the brain or other parts of the body.
- Blood tests can also help find signs of infection.

## How It Is Treated

### Intestinal Infection

- A single dose of medicine called praziquantel kills the worm.
- For dwarf tapeworm, a different medicine called nitazoxanide may be used.

### Cysticercosis

- If cysts are in the brain, treatment depends on symptoms and where the cysts are.
- Corticosteroids (like prednisone) reduce swelling and inflammation.
- Antiparasitic medicines (like albendazole or praziquantel) can kill living cysts.
- These medicines are only used after symptoms are under control.
- They are always given with corticosteroids to prevent swelling from dying cysts.
- Antiparasitic medicines are not used for cysts in the eye or spinal cord. They can cause serious harm.
- Surgery may be needed if cysts block fluid flow around the brain or spinal cord.
- Surgery may also be needed if cysts cause eye or spinal cord problems.

## How to Prevent Infection

### Cooking Meat and Fish

- Cook whole cuts of meat to at least 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63 degrees Celsius) for 3 minutes or more.
- Let the meat rest for 3 minutes after cooking before eating.
- Cook ground meat to at least 160 degrees Fahrenheit (71 degrees Celsius).
- Do not eat raw freshwater fish.
- Cook fish to at least 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63 degrees Celsius).
- Or freeze fish properly before eating.

### Freezing Fish to Kill Cysts

- Freeze at -4 degrees Fahrenheit (-20 degrees Celsius) or colder for 7 days.
- Freeze at -31 degrees Fahrenheit (-35 degrees Celsius) or colder until solid, then keep frozen for 15 hours.
- Freeze at -31 degrees Fahrenheit (-35 degrees Celsius) or colder until solid, then keep frozen at -4 degrees Fahrenheit (-20 degrees Celsius) or colder for 24 hours.

**Note:** Smoking or drying fish does not kill the tapeworm.

### Other Prevention Tips

- Have meat and fish checked by trained inspectors. Cysts can be seen in infected meat.
- Treat human waste properly. This breaks the cycle of infection.
- Wash your hands with soap and warm water after using the toilet, after changing diapers, and before handling food.
- When traveling, wash, peel, or cook all raw fruits and vegetables with clean water.
- Avoid food and water that might be dirty with human stool.
- Avoid eating grain that might have insects like fleas or beetles.

## Key Facts

- Tapeworms can grow up to 30 feet long.
- You can get infected by eating raw or undercooked meat or fish.
- The dwarf tapeworm is small but can cause serious symptoms.
- Cysts in the brain can cause seizures, headaches, and confusion.
- Treatment depends on where the infection is and how serious it is.
- Cooking food well and washing hands are the best ways to stay safe.

# Aortic Disruption After Chest Injury

This condition happens when the main blood vessel from the heart (the aorta) is damaged by a sudden, strong force to the chest. The damage can be a full tear or a partial tear.

## How It Happens

- **Blunt injury** (like in a car crash) often causes this. The body stops suddenly, but the aorta keeps moving. This can tear the vessel.
- **Penetrating injury** (like a stab or gunshot) can also cause this. The wound goes through the center of the chest (the mediastinum), often between the nipples or near the shoulder blades.

## What Happens in the Body

- A full tear in the aorta leads to fast blood loss and death.
- A partial tear may not bleed out right away. The outer layer of the aorta may stay intact and hold the blood in.
- But even a partial tear can cause a blood collection in the chest area (a hematoma).
- Most partial tears happen near a small ligament that connects the aorta to the pulmonary artery.

## What People Feel and Show

- Most people have chest pain.
- Some may have:
  - Weak or missing pulse in one arm.
  - A loud, harsh heart sound heard in the chest or between the shoulder blades.
  - A hoarse voice.
  - Weak pulses or low blood pressure in the legs compared to the arms.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors suspect this injury if:
- The person had a serious fall, car crash, or other high-force chest injury.
- The chest X-ray shows signs of possible aortic damage.

### Signs on a Chest X-ray

- A wider-than-normal shadow in the center of the chest.
- A broken first or second rib.
- The aorta’s normal curve is not visible.
- The windpipe or food pipe is pushed to the right.
- The left main airway is pushed down.
- A small area of fluid or air at the top of the left lung.
- Blood or air in the space around the lung (hemothorax, pneumothorax).
- Bruising in the lung tissue (pulmonary contusion).

> Note: Some of these signs may not show up right away. Some people have no signs on the X-ray even if they have a tear.

Because the X-ray is not always clear, many doctors recommend imaging the aorta in all patients with a serious deceleration injury—even if the X-ray looks normal.

### Best Tests to Check the Aorta

- **CT angiography**: This is the most common test. It is fast, widely available, and gives clear pictures of the aorta.
- **Aortography**: This is very accurate but is more invasive. It takes longer and has more risks. It is used less often now.
- **Transesophageal echocardiography**: This is not used as a first test. But it may be used during surgery if the patient is already under anesthesia. It can find injuries that a CT scan might miss.

## How It Is Treated

### Step 1: Stabilize the Patient

- Give fluids to help blood pressure.
- Lower the heart rate and blood pressure to reduce stress on the aorta. This is done with a medicine like esmolol (a beta-blocker).
- Goal: Heart rate below 90 beats per minute and blood pressure below 120 mm Hg.
- Avoid coughing or gagging during procedures like intubation (putting in a breathing tube) or placing a stomach tube. Use medicine like lidocaine to prevent this.

### Step 2: Repair the Aorta

- **Endovascular stent placement** is now the preferred method. A stent is a small tube placed inside the aorta to fix the tear. It is done through a blood vessel in the leg.
- This method is less risky than open surgery.
- Doctors can delay the repair to treat other serious injuries first.

## Key Points

- Think about a partial aortic tear in anyone with a major chest injury from a sudden stop (like a car crash).
- Chest X-rays often show signs, but they can be missing or unclear. Better tests include CT angiography and aortography.
- Control heart rate and blood pressure with medicine.
- Use a stent to fix the aorta. This is the standard treatment today.

# Hair-Pulling Disorder (Trichotillomania)

This condition causes people to pull out their hair again and again. This leads to noticeable hair loss.

## What Happens in Hair-Pulling Disorder?

- People with this disorder pull their hair for reasons other than looks. They are not trying to fix their appearance.
- They usually pull hair from the scalp, eyebrows, or eyelashes. But they may pull hair from any part of the body.
- The pulling often starts just before or after puberty.
- About 1 to 2 out of every 100 people have this disorder.
- It is more common in women than in men.

## How Does It Feel?

- Some people feel tense or anxious just before pulling their hair.
- Pulling the hair can make that tension go away.
- After pulling, they may feel a sense of relief or satisfaction.
- Some people do it without thinking. Others are very aware of what they are doing.

## What Else Might Happen?

- People may do other repetitive actions. These can include picking at their skin, biting their nails, chewing their cheeks, or doing other similar things.
- Some people also have depression.
- They may feel embarrassed or ashamed of their hair loss.
- They may hide the hair loss with wigs, scarves, or hats.
- Some pull hair from many different spots to hide the loss.
- They often avoid social situations where others might see the hair loss.
- They usually do not pull hair in front of others, except maybe family members.
- They feel upset about not being able to stop pulling.
- They try many times to stop or cut down, but they cannot.

Some people pull hair from other people, pets, or from fabric like clothing, blankets, or curtains.

## What Are the Signs?

- The amount of hair pulled and the places where it is pulled vary from person to person.
- Some people have bald patches.
- Eyebrows or eyelashes may be missing.
- Others just have thinning hair.
- People may change where they pull hair from over time.

## Risks of Swallowing Hair

- Some people swallow the hair they pull out.
- Swallowed hair can build up in the stomach or intestines.
- This can form a hard lump called a trichobezoar.
- A trichobezoar can cause:
  - Feeling full too soon after eating
  - Nausea
  - Vomiting
  - Belly pain
  - Other digestive problems

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor will look at your symptoms. They will check if you have:

- Pulled out enough hair to cause visible hair loss
- Tried many times to stop or reduce pulling, but could not
- Felt very upset or stressed because of the pulling
- Had trouble doing normal daily activities because of it

If all these signs are present, the doctor may diagnose hair-pulling disorder.

## How Is It Treated?

### Therapy

- The best first treatment is a type of talk therapy called cognitive-behavioral therapy.
- A specific form of this therapy, called habit-reversal therapy, is most often used.
- In this therapy, you learn to:
  - Pay more attention to when you are pulling your hair
  - Notice the situations that make you want to pull
  - Use new habits to stop yourself, like:
    - Clenching your fist
    - Knitting
    - Sitting on your hands

### Medications

- Sometimes doctors prescribe medicine to help.
- *N* - Acetylcysteine (NAC) and memantine may help reduce hair pulling. They work on brain chemicals involved in habits.
- Antidepressants like selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) or clomipramine may help if you also have symptoms of depression or anxiety.

## Important Notes

- Symptoms can get better or worse over time.
- The disorder can last for years or even a lifetime.
- Early treatment can help reduce symptoms and improve quality of life.
- You are not alone. Many people have this condition and get better with help.

# Nitrofurantoin

Nitrofurantoin is an antibiotic. It kills bacteria. The exact way it works is not fully known.

You can only take nitrofurantoin by mouth. It comes in pills or capsules.

---

## How Nitrofurantoin Works in the Body

After you take one dose, the amount of medicine in your blood stays very low.  
But the amount in your urine is high enough to treat a bladder infection.  
This means it works well in the urinary tract but not in the rest of the body.

---

## When Is Nitrofurantoin Used?

Nitrofurantoin works against many common bacteria that cause bladder infections. These include:

- *Escherichia coli*  
- *Staphylococcus saprophyticus*  
- *Enterococcus faecalis*

Other bacteria like *Enterococcus* (including those resistant to vancomycin), *Klebsiella*, and *Enterobacter* are often not affected. But nitrofurantoin may still help treat simple bladder infections caused by these.

Most strains of *Proteus*, *Providencia*, *Morganella*, *Serratia*, *Acinetobacter*, and *Pseudomonas* are resistant to nitrofurantoin.  
There is no resistance cross-over with other types of antibiotics.

Nitrofurantoin is used only for:

- Treating or preventing simple bladder infections (cystitis)  
- Helping women who get bladder infections often by reducing how many times they happen

It is **not** used for kidney infections (pyelonephritis) or serious infections in the body.  
This is because the medicine does not reach high levels in the blood or tissues.

---

## When Should You Not Take Nitrofurantoin?

Do not take nitrofurantoin if you:

- Have had an allergic reaction to it before  
- Are less than one month old  
- Are at term (38 to 42 weeks pregnant), in labor, or about to give birth  
- Have a condition called glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PD deficiency)  
- Have serious kidney problems

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration says not to use nitrofurantoin if your kidney function is low (creatinine clearance below 60 mL per minute).  
But research shows that short-term use is usually safe and works well in people with kidney function as low as 30 mL per minute.  
Still, people with kidney problems are more likely to have side effects.

---

## Using Nitrofurantoin During Pregnancy and Breastfeeding

Animal studies have not shown harm to unborn babies.  
There are no large, well-controlled studies in pregnant women.  
But nitrofurantoin is generally considered safe during all three trimesters of pregnancy.

However, it should **not** be used at term (38 to 42 weeks) or during labor or delivery.  
This is because it can harm the red blood cells of newborns.  
It may cause a type of anemia called hemolytic anemia.

Nitrofurantoin passes into breast milk.  
It should be avoided during the first month of breastfeeding if possible.  
This is to lower the risk of hemolytic anemia, especially in babies with high levels of bilirubin.

---

## Side Effects of Nitrofurantoin

Common side effects include:

- Nausea  
- Vomiting  

These are less likely with a special form called macrocrystalline.

Other possible side effects:

- Fever and rash  
- Lung problems (like shortness of breath, cough, or lung scarring)  
- Nerve problems (tingling, numbness, or weakness in hands and feet)  
- Anemia (low red blood cells)  
- Liver problems

Lung issues can happen suddenly (with fever and high levels of a certain white blood cell) or slowly over time.  
Nerve problems can get worse if you keep taking the medicine, especially if you have kidney problems.

Low white blood cell count and liver damage (either sudden or long-term) have been reported.  
Anemia can happen in people with G6PD deficiency and in babies under one month old.

Long-term use (more than 6 months) increases the risk of serious lung and liver problems.

# Strabismus

Strabismus means one eye is not looking at the same place as the other eye.  
This can happen all the time or only sometimes.  
If not treated, strabismus can lead to weak vision in one eye.  
It can also cause permanent vision loss.

## What Is Strabismus?

- Strabismus is when the eyes do not line up together.  
- One eye may turn inward, outward, up, or down.  
- The misalignment can be constant or come and go.  
- It can be mild or severe.

## Causes of Strabismus

Strabismus can start in the first few months of life or later.  
The cause depends on the child’s age.

**For babies under 6 months:**
- A family history of strabismus increases the risk.  
- Genetic conditions like Down syndrome can cause it.  
- Certain medicines or alcohol taken by the mother during pregnancy can affect the baby’s eyes.  
- Being born too early (premature) is a risk.  
- Birth defects in the eyes can cause strabismus.  
- Conditions like cerebral palsy are linked to it.

**For children 6 months and older:**
- Too much farsightedness (a type of vision problem) is a common cause.  
- The muscles that move the eyes may not work evenly.  
- If one eye has very poor vision, the brain may stop using it. This can cause the eyes to misalign.  
- Serious eye problems like cataracts can cause strabismus.  
- Eye cancer (retinoblastoma) can also be a cause.  
- Brain or nerve problems such as high pressure in the skull, cerebral palsy, spina bifida, or weak nerves that control eye movement can lead to strabismus.  
- Head injuries or brain infections (like encephalitis) may cause it.  
- A broken eye socket can block eye movement and cause strabismus.

## Types of Strabismus

There are different types of strabismus:

- **Esotropia (cross-eye):** One eye turns inward.  
- **Exotropia (walleye):** One eye turns outward.  
- **Hypertropia:** One eye turns upward.  
- **Hypotropia:** One eye turns downward.

Some people have a small, hidden misalignment called a **phoria**.  
The brain fixes this automatically.  
It usually does not cause symptoms.  
But if the misalignment is large, it can cause double vision.

A **tropia** is a visible, constant eye turn.  
An eye that turns sometimes but not always is called an intermittent tropia.

## Symptoms of Strabismus

Parents may notice:
- The child squints or covers one eye.  
- The eyes do not move together.  
- The eyes look like they are not lined up.

Phorias usually do not cause symptoms.  
If they do, the child may feel eye strain.

Tropias can cause:
- Loss of vision in one eye (especially in young children).  
- Double vision (in older children).  
- Tilting the head or twisting the neck to see better.

## How Is Strabismus Diagnosed?

Doctors check the eyes during regular visits.  
This should start when the child is a few months old.

For babies:
- A doctor shines a light into the eyes.  
- The light should reflect from the same spot on each pupil.

For older children:
- The doctor asks the child to look at objects or letters.  
- One eye is covered at a time.  
- Tests check how well the eyes line up.

All children with strabismus need to see an eye doctor who specializes in eye problems (an ophthalmologist).

Sometimes doctors use imaging tests like CT scans or MRI scans.  
These check the brain or spine.  
Blood tests may be done to check for genetic conditions.

> **Did You Know?**  
> Children as young as 3 can have their vision checked.

## Treatment of Strabismus

Treatment depends on the cause and type of strabismus.  
The first goal is to fix any vision problems.

### Treating Weak Vision (Amblyopia)
- If one eye has weaker vision, the child must use it more.  
- A patch is placed over the stronger eye.  
- Or eye drops are used to blur the vision in the stronger eye.  
- This helps the weaker eye get stronger.  
- Patching does not fix the eye turn. It only helps vision.

### Correcting Vision Problems
- If the child is farsighted, glasses or contact lenses are prescribed.  
- These help the eyes work together better.

### Eye Exercises
- Some children with intermittent exotropia (eye turns outward) can improve with eye exercises.

### Surgery
- If glasses, patches, or exercises do not work well, surgery may be needed.  
- The surgeon adjusts the eye muscles by loosening or tightening them.  
- The child usually goes home the same day.  
- Surgery can have side effects:  
  - The eye may be turned too much (overcorrection).  
  - The eye may not be turned enough (undercorrection).  
  - The eye turn may come back later.  
- Rarely, infection, too much bleeding, or vision loss can happen.

## Outlook for Strabismus

- Do not wait to see if strabismus will go away on its own.  
- If weak vision (amblyopia) is not treated early, it can cause permanent vision loss.  
- Treatment works best before age 8.  
- After age 8, the brain is fully developed. Treatment is less effective.  
- All children should have regular vision checks during preschool years.

### Success of Surgery
- More than 80% of children have good results after surgery.  
- About 1 in 5 children need another surgery later.

## More Information

The following resource may help:

**Children's Eye Foundation of AAPOS**  
Practical information on preventing eye problems, spotting them early, research, and education to protect children’s vision.
