# Lymphatic Filariasis – Simple Explanation

Lymphatic filariasis is a disease caused by tiny worms that live in the body’s lymph system.  
The worms are called *Wuchereria bancrofti*, *Brugia malayi*, and *Brugia timori*.  
These worms are a type of roundworm known as filarial worms.

## How the Disease Spreads

Mosquitoes spread the disease.  
When an infected mosquito bites a person, it puts worm larvae into the skin.  
The larvae travel to the lymph system, where they grow into adult worms.  
Adult female worms can be 3 to 4 inches long.  
They produce millions of tiny worm larvae called microfilariae.  
These microfilariae live in the blood and lymph fluid.  
When another mosquito bites an infected person, it picks up the microfilariae.  
Inside the mosquito, the microfilariae grow into new larvae.  
The mosquito then passes these larvae to the next person it bites.

## What the Disease Does to the Body

The adult worms cause most of the symptoms.  
The tiny larvae do not cause symptoms and go away when people leave the area where the disease is common.

Early signs include:
- Fever
- Swollen lymph nodes in the armpits or groin
- Pain in the legs or groin

These episodes last 4 to 7 days.  
Sometimes pus builds up in a leg and drains through the skin, leaving a scar.

The worms block the lymph vessels.  
This makes it harder for the body to fight off infections.  
Bacteria can get into the skin and tissues more easily.  
This leads to more infections and swelling.

Symptoms often come and go.  
They are worse in people who are not used to living in areas where the disease is common.

Over time, the blocked lymph vessels widen.  
Most people have no symptoms.  
But in some, the swelling becomes permanent.  
This is called lymphedema.

Lymphedema usually affects the legs.  
It can also affect the arms, breasts, or genitals.  
The swelling happens because:
- The worms stop lymph fluid from draining properly.
- Fluid builds up in the tissues.
- The immune system reacts to the worms, causing inflammation and swelling.

Lymphedema makes the skin soft and spongy.  
If you press on it, the skin stays indented for a while. This is called pitting.  
Over time, the skin can become hard and thick. This is called elephantiasis.  
Elephantiasis often affects the legs. It can also affect the arms or the scrotum.

People with lymphatic filariasis often get skin infections.  
These can be bacterial or fungal.  
They cause pain and make swelling worse.  
They also increase the risk of elephantiasis.

Some people have:
- Mild joint pain
- Blood in the urine

In rare cases, the microfilariae travel to the lungs.  
This causes a condition called tropical pulmonary eosinophilia.  
Symptoms include:
- Low-grade fever
- Shortness of breath
- Coughing
- Wheezing

If the infection lasts, scar tissue can form in the lungs.

## How Doctors Diagnose the Disease

Doctors look for the worm larvae in blood or tissue samples.  
They use a microscope to check the samples.  
They may also use ultrasound to see adult worms moving in the lymph vessels.

Blood tests can check for:
- Antibodies: proteins the body makes to fight infection
- Antigens: substances made by the worms that trigger the immune system

But blood tests are not always helpful.  
They cannot tell the difference between this worm and other similar worms.  
They also cannot tell if the infection is current or past.

## How the Disease Is Treated

The main medicine is diethylcarbamazine.  
It is taken by mouth for 1 or 12 days.  
It kills the tiny worm larvae and some adult worms.

Doctors may also give:
- Doxycycline
- Albendazole

Before giving diethylcarbamazine, doctors check for other worm infections like loiasis and onchocerciasis.  
Diethylcarbamazine can cause serious side effects if these other infections are present.

### For Long-Term Swelling (Chronic Lymphedema)

- Keep the skin clean and dry.
- Avoid cuts, scrapes, and injuries.
- Wash any small wounds right away.
- Wrap the swollen limb with elastic bandages.
- Keep the limb raised when possible.

These steps help prevent infections and reduce swelling.

### For Severe Swelling (Elephantiasis)

Surgery may be needed if swelling is very bad.  
Surgery can help improve fluid drainage in the lymph system.

### For Skin Infections

Antibiotics are given by mouth.  
They help stop infections and may prevent more swelling.

### For Lung Problems

Diethylcarbamazine is taken for 14 to 21 days.  
But the infection comes back in about 1 out of 4 people.  
If it returns, treatment must be repeated.

## How to Prevent the Disease

To avoid mosquito bites:
- Use insect repellent on skin
- Wear long-sleeved shirts and long pants
- Wear clothes treated with permethrin (an insecticide)
- Sleep under mosquito netting

In areas where the disease is common, the World Health Organization runs a program to stop the spread.  
It gives medicine to large groups of people every year.  
This medicine lowers the number of worm larvae in the blood.  
This makes it harder for mosquitoes to spread the disease.  

As of 2023, over 657 million people in 39 countries needed this preventive treatment.

# Dacryostenosis (Narrowing of the Tear Drainage System)

## What Is Dacryostenosis?

Dacryostenosis means the tear drainage tube is blocked or narrowed.  
This causes too many tears to build up in the eye.  
The tube that carries tears from the eye to the nose is called the nasolacrimal duct.  
When this tube is blocked, tears cannot drain properly.

## Types of Dacryostenosis

There are two main types:  
- **Congenital** – present at birth  
- **Acquired** – develops later in life

### Congenital Dacryostenosis

Some babies are born with a narrow or blocked tear duct.  
The most common reason is a thin membrane at the end of the duct that does not open fully.  
This membrane is called the valve of Hasner.  
Symptoms usually start after two weeks of age.  
Most often, they begin between 3 and 12 weeks.  
Symptoms include:  
- Constant tearing  
- Thick, pus-like discharge from the eye  
- Redness or swelling in the inner corner of the eye  
- Eye infections that keep coming back (chronic conjunctivitis)

Many babies get better on their own by 6 to 9 months of age.  
If the blockage does not clear by age 1, treatment may be needed.

### Acquired Dacryostenosis

This type happens later in life.  
The most common cause is aging.  
The tear duct slowly narrows over time.  
Other causes include:  
- Past injuries to the nose or face  
- Surgery on the sinuses  
- Certain long-term health problems:  
  - Sarcoidosis  
  - Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (a rare disease that causes inflammation in blood vessels)  
- Tumors in the sinuses (especially in the upper jaw or between the eyes)  
- Small stones in the tear duct (called dacryoliths)

### Punctal or Canalicular Stenosis

This is a blockage in the tiny opening or small tube near the inner corner of the eye.  
Causes include:  
- Long-term eye infections, especially from herpes simplex virus  
- Some types of chemotherapy  
- Bad reactions to certain eye drops (especially echothiophate iodide)  
- Autoimmune skin diseases:  
  - Mucous membrane pemphigoid  
  - Lichen planus  
- Radiation treatment to the face or eye area

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose dacryostenosis by looking at symptoms and doing a physical exam.  
They may test the tear duct by flushing it with salt water.  
Sometimes they add a special dye (fluorescein) to the water.  
If the fluid comes back out the eye or nose, it means the duct is blocked.  
This is called reflux.

## How Is It Treated?

### For Congenital Dacryostenosis

- Most babies get better without treatment by 9 months of age.  
- Before age 1, parents can gently press on the tear sac 4 to 5 times a day.  
  - This may help open the blocked duct.  
- If the blockage lasts past age 1, a doctor may need to probe the duct.  
  - This is done under general anesthesia.  
- If the blockage keeps coming back, a small tube may be placed in the duct.  
  - This tube stays in place for a few months to keep the duct open.

### For Acquired Dacryostenosis

- First, doctors try to treat the cause.  
  - For example, treat an infection or manage a chronic disease.  
- If the cause cannot be treated or if treatment does not work, surgery may be needed.  
- A common surgery is called dacryocystorhinostomy.  
  - This creates a new path from the tear sac to the inside of the nose.  
  - This lets tears drain again.

### For Punctal or Canalicular Stenosis

- If the blockage is mild, stretching the opening (dilation) often fixes it.  
- If the blockage is severe and causes ongoing problems, surgery may be needed.  
- A small tube made of glass (called a Jones tube) can be placed.  
  - It goes from the inner corner of the eye into the nose.  
  - This tube lets tears drain properly.  
- The surgery to place this tube is called conjunctivo-dacryocystorhinostomy (C-DCR).

## Key Points

- Dacryostenosis can be present at birth or develop later in life.  
- The main symptom is too many tears.  
- If flushing the tear duct causes fluid to come back out, it confirms the blockage.  
- In babies, symptoms often go away by 9 months.  
  - Gentle pressure on the tear sac may help.  
- In adults, the cause of the blockage should be treated if possible.  
- Surgery may be needed if symptoms do not improve with other treatments.

# Connective Tissue Disorders in Children

Connective tissue is the strong, fibrous material that holds the body together. It gives shape and support to many parts of the body.  
Muscles, bones, cartilage, ligaments, and tendons are mostly made of connective tissue.  
This tissue is also found in the skin and inside organs.  
The type of connective tissue and the cells it contains depend on where it is in the body.  
Connective tissue is strong. It can handle weight and stretching.

There are more than 200 conditions that affect connective tissue.  
The following are some of the disorders discussed here:  
- Chondromalacia patellae  
- Cutis laxa  
- Ehlers-Danlos syndromes  
- Infrapatellar tendinitis  
- Marfan syndrome  
- Nail-patella syndrome  
- Osteochondrodysplasias  
- Osteogenesis imperfecta  
- Pseudoxanthoma elasticum  

Some of these conditions have no known cause.  
Others are passed down through families.  
Certain inherited conditions cause connective tissue to form in the wrong way.  
Most inherited connective tissue disorders start in childhood.  
These conditions last a lifetime.

## How Doctors Diagnose These Disorders

Doctors use several tools to make a diagnosis.

**A doctor’s evaluation**  
The doctor will ask about symptoms and check the child’s body.  
They will look for signs of connective tissue problems.

**X-rays**  
X-rays can show if bones are shaped abnormally.  
This may point to a connective tissue disorder.

**Biopsy**  
A small sample of tissue is taken for testing.  
This is usually done with a local anesthetic to numb the area.  
The sample is looked at under a microscope to check for problems.

**Genetic testing**  
A blood sample is tested to look at the child’s genes.  
This can help find inherited disorders.

# Growth and Weight Faltering in Children

This condition means a child is not growing or gaining weight as they should. It used to be called "failure to thrive," but that term is no longer used. Now, doctors call it "growth and weight faltering."

## What Causes Growth and Weight Faltering?

The main cause is not getting enough good food. This can happen for three reasons:

- A medical problem in the child’s body.
- Problems in the child’s home or family life.
- A mix of both medical and family problems.

Most children have a mix of both causes.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use growth charts to track a child’s height, weight, and head size. These charts show if a child is growing normally.

- Weight is the best sign of whether a child is getting enough food.
- A body mass index, or BMI, that is very low also shows poor nutrition.
- If a child’s weight drops below their usual level, but their height stays the same, it likely means they are not eating enough calories.
- If both height and weight drop, it may mean a serious health problem or long-term illness.
- A small head size usually shows very severe or long-lasting malnutrition. The brain grows first, so head size stays normal until the problem is serious.

Children with this condition may:
- Be smaller than other children their age.
- Be fussy or cry a lot.
- Be tired or sleepy.
- Have trouble with bowel movements (constipation).
- Be slow to sit, stand, or walk.
- Have trouble learning or playing with others.
- In older children, puberty may start late.

Doctors will:
- Check the child’s growth over time.
- Ask about the child’s diet and feeding habits.
- Look at the family and home life.
- Do blood tests and other exams if needed.

A child’s growth chart can help point to the cause. If both weight and height drop at the same time, it may mean a medical problem. But no single test can always tell the difference between a medical problem and a family problem.

Doctors often work as a team. This team may include:
- A doctor
- A nurse
- A social worker
- A dietitian
- A child development expert
- A mental health professional

The child’s feeding behavior is watched closely. This can happen in the hospital or at home.

If a child does not gain weight even after being seen in the clinic, they may need to stay in the hospital. This allows doctors to watch feeding closely and do tests quickly.

In the hospital, doctors watch how the child acts around people. Some children with this condition:
- Are very alert and watchful.
- Avoid close contact with people.
- Prefer to play with toys or objects instead of people.

Even though this condition is often due to neglect, doctors must still check for signs of abuse.

A child’s development is tested. If needed, more detailed testing is done.

If a child starts gaining weight well in the hospital with proper feeding, it suggests the problem is not medical but related to the home environment.

## Working With Families

It is important to include the child’s caregivers in the process. This helps them feel capable and not blamed.

- Caregivers should be allowed to visit the child often during hospital stays.
- Staff should welcome them and help them feed the child.
- Staff should give toys and ideas to help caregivers play with the child.

Doctors should check if caregivers can meet the child’s needs. If there is concern about neglect or abuse, it must be reported.

But often, the family just needs help. For example:
- Extra food assistance
- Better child care
- Parenting classes

## What to Ask About When Taking a History

### Growth Charts
- Look at the child’s growth over time.
- Do not diagnose based on one number. Use the trend over time.

### Diet History (for 3 days)
- How often does the child eat?
- What do they eat?
- For babies: How is formula made? How much is given? Is breast milk enough?
- Check the bottle nipple and flow rate.
- Watch the caregiver feed the baby. Does the baby tire easily? This could mean a heart or lung problem.
- Does the baby spit up a lot? This can happen if the baby is fed too fast or if the bottle is propped up. Propping bottles is not safe.

A caregiver who seems uninterested may be depressed or overwhelmed.

For older children:
- Keep a food diary.
- Ask about food allergies or problems with swallowing.
- Ask if the child has a poor appetite.
- Ask if the child only eats certain foods or textures.
- Ask about medicines that might reduce appetite.

### Bowel and Bladder Habits
- Unusual urine or stool.
- Frequent vomiting.
- These signs may mean a kidney, gut, or stomach problem.

### Medical and Birth History
- Was the baby born early or small?
- Has the child had delays in development?
- Has the child had long-term or repeated infections?
- Has the child had heart, lung, brain, or kidney problems?
- Has the child been sick or in the hospital?
- Could the child have a food allergy?

For older children and teens:
- Ask about anxiety, depression, or eating disorders.

### Family History
- How tall are the parents and siblings?
- Does anyone in the family have a condition that affects growth (like cystic fibrosis)?
- Has a caregiver had a recent illness or mental health problem that made it hard to care for the child?

### Social History
- Who lives in the home?
- Is the home stable? Do they have a fridge, stove, and clean water?
- Is there enough food at home?
- Did the family want the child? Do they accept the child?
- Are there big stressors? (Job loss, moving, divorce, death, etc.)
- Are there cultural or special diets the family follows?

## How Is It Treated?

The main goal is to give the child enough good food and support.

- A healthy diet with extra calories is needed for catch-up growth.
- The child may need extra help from doctors, nurses, dietitians, and social workers.
- Any medical problem must be treated right away.

Even if a child gains weight in the hospital, it does not always mean the cause is not medical. All children grow when they get enough food.

But sometimes, children with nonorganic faltering lose weight in the hospital. This shows the problem is complex.

For children with medical problems, treat the illness quickly.

For children with nonorganic or mixed problems:
- Give education and emotional support.
- Long-term help is often needed.
- The care team may not be able to provide all the help. They will refer the family to community services.
- Caregivers should understand why referrals are made.
- They should be involved in choosing which services to use.

If the child is in a hospital far from home, the doctor who sent the child should be consulted about local services.

Before the child goes home:
- Hold a planning meeting with hospital staff, community workers, and the child’s doctor.
- Clearly define who is responsible for what.
- Share this plan with everyone.
- Invite the caregivers to a meeting to meet the community workers, ask questions, and set up follow-up visits.

In some cases, a child must live with a foster family. Most children return to their birth parents later. But only when the parents can care for the child well. This is not based on time, but on ability.

## What Is the Outlook?

- If the cause is a medical problem, the outcome depends on the illness.
- For children over 1 year old with nonorganic faltering, most get back to a healthy weight with proper care.
- Children who have this problem before age 1 are at high risk for learning delays, especially in speaking and math.
- The risk is highest if the problem starts before 6 months, when the brain grows fastest.

## Key Points

- Growth and weight faltering means a child is not growing or gaining weight as expected.
- It can be caused by a medical problem, a family problem, or both.
- A medical problem might include issues like poor digestion or a rare metabolic disease.
- A family problem might include poverty, neglect, or stress.
- Doctors should watch how caregivers feed the child.
- Hospital care may be needed to check the child, see how they respond to feeding, and bring in a feeding team if needed.

## More Information

These resources may help:

- **World Health Organization**: Growth charts for children 0 to 2 years
- **Centers for Disease Control and Prevention**: Growth charts for children 2 years and older

# Lumbar Spinal Stenosis

Lumbar spinal stenosis means the space around the nerves in the lower back has become too narrow. This narrowing presses on the nerves. The nerves run from the lower back down into the legs.

## What Causes Lumbar Spinal Stenosis?

- Osteoarthritis can cause the bones and joints in the spine to grow larger and press on the nerves.
- Injuries to the spine can lead to swelling or bone changes that narrow the space.
- Spondylolisthesis happens when one bone in the spine slips forward over the one below it.
- Spondylolysis is a crack or weakness in a bone in the spine.
- Paget disease of bone is a rare condition that causes bones to grow abnormally.

Some people are born with a narrow spinal canal. This can lead to stenosis later in life.

## The Spine and Nerves

The spine is made of a column of bones called vertebrae. These bones protect the spinal cord. The spinal cord runs through the center of the spine.

Between the vertebrae are soft discs. These discs act like cushions and help the spine bend and move.

Nerves come out of the spinal cord between the vertebrae. Each nerve splits into two parts: one part sends signals from the brain to muscles, and the other brings signals from the body to the brain.

At the bottom of the spinal cord, a bundle of nerves continues down. This bundle is called the cauda equina. It looks like a horse’s tail. It controls movement and feeling in the legs, and it helps control the bladder and bowels.

When the spinal canal narrows, the nerves can get squeezed. This causes pain and other symptoms.

## Symptoms of Lumbar Spinal Stenosis

Symptoms can vary. They depend on which nerves are affected.

You may feel:
- Pain in the lower back.
- Pain that travels down one or both legs.
- A tingling or pins-and-needles feeling in the legs or feet.
- Weakness in the legs or feet.
- Reduced reflexes in the legs or feet.

The pain often gets worse when you stand up straight or walk. It may also get worse when you walk downhill or lean back.

The pain often gets better when you:
- Sit down.
- Bend forward (like leaning on a shopping cart).
- Walk uphill.

Some people find relief when they push a shopping cart or use a rolling walker. This is because bending forward opens up the space in the spine.

In rare cases, sudden pressure on the nerves can cause a serious problem called cauda equina syndrome. This can cause:
- Loss of bladder or bowel control.
- Paralysis in one leg.
- Loss of feeling in the groin or around the buttocks.

If you have any of these symptoms, get medical help right away.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and do a physical exam. They will check your strength, reflexes, and sensation.

If your symptoms last more than six weeks, or if you have weakness or numbness, your doctor may order tests.

These tests can include:
- **MRI (magnetic resonance imaging):** This creates detailed pictures of the spine and nerves.
- **CT scan (computed tomography):** This also shows the bones and soft tissues in the spine.
- **Nerve tests:** These check how well the nerves and muscles are working. They include nerve conduction studies and electromyography.

These tests help the doctor find where the narrowing is and how much damage has occurred.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment aims to reduce pain and improve movement.

### Non-Surgical Treatments

- Rest for one to two days may help ease pain.
- Avoid long periods of bed rest. It can weaken your core muscles and make pain worse.
- Sleep on a medium-firm mattress.
  - If you sleep on your back, place a pillow under your knees.
  - If you sleep on your side, use a pillow to keep your head in a neutral position. Place another pillow between your knees and bend your hips and knees slightly if it helps.
  - You can sleep on your stomach if it feels comfortable.

- Use cold packs (like ice) or heat (like a heating pad) to ease pain.
- Take over-the-counter pain medicines such as acetaminophen or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
- Some people benefit from medicines that help with nerve pain. These include:
  - Gabapentin
  - Certain antiseizure medicines
  - Some antidepressants

- If pain is severe or does not improve, your doctor may give a corticosteroid injection into the space around the spinal cord (epidural space). This can reduce swelling and relieve pain.

- Physical therapy can help. Stretching the hamstrings (the muscles in the back of the thighs) after warming up may reduce muscle spasms.

### Surgery

If pain does not improve with other treatments, surgery may be needed.

Two common surgeries are:

- **Lumbar laminectomy:** The doctor removes part of the bone (lamina) that covers the spinal cord. This opens up the space and takes pressure off the nerves. The surgery is done through a small cut in the lower back. The muscles are gently moved aside. The bone is removed, and the nerves are freed.

- **Lumbar laminotomy:** The doctor makes a small hole in the lamina instead of removing it. This also relieves pressure on the nerves.

Sometimes, if several bones are involved, the doctor may join two bones together using a bone graft. This is called fusion.

Both surgeries can be done through very small cuts. This helps you recover faster.

## Summary

- Lumbar spinal stenosis is a narrowing of the space in the lower back that holds the nerves.
- It causes pain, numbness, or weakness in the legs.
- It is common in older adults but can also affect younger people.
- Causes include arthritis, injury, and spine misalignment.
- Symptoms often get worse when standing or walking and improve when bending forward.
- Diagnosis uses physical exams and imaging tests.
- Treatment starts with pain relief and physical therapy.
- Surgery is an option if other treatments do not work.

If you have sudden loss of bladder or bowel control, leg weakness, or numbness in the groin, seek medical help right away.

# Macrolides

Macrolides are a type of antibiotic. They stop bacteria from growing. They do this by blocking a part of the bacteria’s protein-making system.

## How Macrolides Work

- Macrolides bind to a part of the bacteria’s protein-making machine.
- This stops the bacteria from making the proteins they need to survive.
- The bacteria cannot grow or multiply.

## Types of Macrolides

| Medicine | How It Is Taken |
|--------|----------------|
| Azithromycin | By mouth or through a vein |
| Clarithromycin | By mouth |
| Erythromycin | By mouth or through a vein |
| Fidaxomicin | By mouth |

## How the Body Handles Macrolides

- Macrolides are not well absorbed when taken by mouth.
- Fidaxomicin is not absorbed into the blood. It only works in the gut.
- Food affects how well some macrolides are absorbed:
  - Extended-release clarithromycin: More is absorbed when taken with food.
  - Immediate-release clarithromycin: Food does not change absorption.
  - Azithromycin and erythromycin: Less is absorbed when taken with food.
  - Fidaxomicin: Food has little effect.
- Once in the body, macrolides spread into body fluids, except the fluid around the brain and spinal cord.
- They build up in certain immune cells.
- Most of the drug leaves the body through the bile (a fluid made by the liver).

## When Macrolides Are Used

Macrolides (except fidaxomicin) are effective against many types of bacteria, including:

- Some common bacteria that cause pneumonia and skin infections
- *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* (a cause of walking pneumonia)
- *Chlamydia trachomatis* (a cause of sexually transmitted infections)
- *Chlamydophila pneumoniae* (a cause of lung infections)
- *Legionella* (a cause of Legionnaires’ disease)
- *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* (a cause of diphtheria)
- *Campylobacter* (a cause of food poisoning)
- *Treponema pallidum* (a cause of syphilis)
- *Cutibacterium acnes* (a cause of acne)
- *Borrelia burgdorferi* (a cause of Lyme disease)
- *Haemophilus influenzae* (a cause of ear and lung infections)
- *Mycobacterium avium* complex (a type of lung infection in people with weak immune systems)

- *Bacteroides fragilis* is not affected by macrolides.
- Clarithromycin and azithromycin work better against *Haemophilus influenzae* than other macrolides.
- Clarithromycin and azithromycin also work against *Mycobacterium avium* complex.

### Common Uses

- Macrolides are often used when penicillin cannot be used for:
  - Group A strep infections
  - Pneumococcal infections
- But some of these bacteria are now resistant to macrolides.
- Macrolides are often used for lung infections when the cause is not clear, especially if it is a type of bacteria that does not respond to other antibiotics.
- They are not used to treat meningitis (infection of the brain and spinal cord fluid).

### Fidaxomicin

- Fidaxomicin only works against *Clostridioides difficile* (a cause of severe diarrhea).
- It does not work against most other bacteria.
- It is not absorbed into the blood.
- It is used only for *C. difficile* infection.

## Other Uses of Macrolides

| Medicine | Use | Notes |
|--------|-----|-------|
| Macrolides (except fidaxomicin) | Infections from *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, *Legionella*, or *Bordetella pertussis* | First-choice antibiotics |
| Macrolides (except fidaxomicin) | Removing *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* from carriers | First-choice antibiotics |
| Azithromycin | Brain infection caused by *Toxoplasma* | Used with other antibiotics |
| Azithromycin | Babesiosis (a tick-borne illness) | Used with other antibiotics |
| Azithromycin | *Chlamydia trachomatis* infections (in the urethra or cervix) | First-choice treatment |
| Clarithromycin and azithromycin | *Mycobacterium avium* complex and other similar infections | Part of a combination treatment |
| Erythromycin | Mild skin infections | First-choice for some cases |
| Erythromycin | Acne | Also used as a cream or gel |
| Erythromycin | Bowel prep before surgery | Taken by mouth, used with another antibiotic |

## When Not to Use Macrolides

- Do not use macrolides if you have had an allergic reaction to them.
- Do not take macrolides with:
  - Astemizole
  - Cisapride
  - Pimozide
  - Terfenadine
- These combinations can cause serious heart rhythm problems.
- This risk is highest with clarithromycin and erythromycin.
- These drugs slow down how the body breaks down other medicines, which can lead to dangerous side effects.

## Using Macrolides During Pregnancy and Breastfeeding

- Animal studies show no harm to the baby from erythromycin or azithromycin.
- Some studies found a slightly higher chance of heart problems in babies if the mother took erythromycin early in pregnancy.
- But other studies did not find this risk.
- Erythromycin is considered safer than azithromycin because it has been used more widely.
- Clarithromycin has shown some risk in animal studies. It should not be used during pregnancy unless no other option exists.
- Erythromycin is safe to use while breastfeeding.
- The safety of other macrolides during breastfeeding is not known.
- Fidaxomicin has not shown harm in animal studies.
- It is not absorbed into the blood, so it is unlikely to harm a baby during pregnancy or breastfeeding.

## Side Effects of Macrolides

### Common Side Effects

- **Gastrointestinal (GI) issues**:
  - Nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, diarrhea
  - Most common with erythromycin
  - Less common with clarithromycin and azithromycin
  - Taking the medicine with food may help reduce these problems
- **Hearing and balance issues**:
  - Erythromycin can cause ringing in the ears, dizziness, or temporary hearing loss
- **Liver problems**:
  - Erythromycin estolate can cause jaundice (yellowing of the skin or eyes)
  - This usually appears after 10 days of use, mainly in adults
  - It can happen sooner if you have taken erythromycin before
- **Pain at injection site**:
  - Erythromycin should not be given by injection (IM) because it causes severe pain
  - IV use can cause pain or inflammation in the vein
- **Allergic reactions**:
  - Rare

### Special Risks

- Erythromycin should be avoided in newborns unless no other option is available.
  - It can cause a serious stomach blockage in babies (hypertrophic pyloric stenosis).
  - Other macrolides are less likely to cause this.
- Erythromycin can cause dangerous heart rhythm problems (QT prolongation).
  - This risk is higher in women, people with heart problems, or those with low levels of potassium or magnesium.
  - It is also higher if you are taking another medicine that affects the heart rhythm.
- Clarithromycin and azithromycin can also cause heart rhythm changes, but they are less likely to cause serious problems.

### Fidaxomicin

- Does not cause jaundice or heart rhythm problems.
- Because it is not absorbed into the blood, it does not harm other organs.
- Side effects are mainly limited to the gut.

## Dosing and Drug Interactions

- **Azithromycin**:
  - No dose change is needed for kidney problems.
- **Erythromycin and clarithromycin**:
  - These drugs can affect how other medicines are broken down in the liver.
  - This can lead to serious side effects.
  - Azithromycin is least likely to cause these interactions.

### Dangerous Interactions

- **Warfarin** (a blood thinner): Can increase bleeding risk.
- **Lovastatin and simvastatin** (cholesterol drugs): Can cause muscle damage.
- **Midazolam and triazolam** (sleep or anxiety drugs): Can cause extreme drowsiness.
- **Theophylline** (lung medicine): Can cause nausea, vomiting, or seizures.
- **Tacrolimus, cyclosporine, and ergot alkaloids** (immune drugs and migraine treatments): Can build up to dangerous levels in the blood.

- **Fidaxomicin**:
  - Does not interact with most common medicines.
  - No major drug interaction concerns.

# Leprosy – Simple Explanation

Leprosy is a long-term infection caused by bacteria. The most common bacteria are *Mycobacterium leprae* and *Mycobacterium lepromatosis*.  
It mainly harms the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, the skin, the testes, the eyes, and the lining of the nose and throat.

## What Leprosy Looks Like

- Leprosy can be mild or severe.
- Mild cases affect only one or a few areas of the skin.
- Severe cases affect many skin areas and can damage many organs.
- You may see rashes or bumps on the skin.
- The skin may feel numb in some areas.
- Muscles may become weak.

## How Doctors Diagnose Leprosy

- Doctors look at your symptoms.
- They may take a small sample of skin and check it under a microscope. This is called a biopsy.
- The test confirms if you have leprosy.
- The bacteria do not grow in lab tests, so those tests are not helpful.
- Blood tests are not very useful because they do not always show the infection.

## How Leprosy Spreads

- Leprosy can spread from person to person through droplets from the nose or mouth.
- You can get it by breathing in these droplets or touching them.
- But most people who come in contact with the bacteria do not get sick.
- About half of people with leprosy likely got it from close, long-term contact with someone who has it.
- Casual contact, like a handshake, does not spread the disease.
- You cannot catch leprosy just by touching someone who has it.
- Health care workers often work with people who have leprosy and do not get sick.

> **Did You Know?**  
> Leprosy is not easily spread.  
> Armadillos are the only other known source of the bacteria, besides people. Other animals or the environment might also carry it.

## Types of Leprosy

Leprosy is grouped in two ways.

### Based on How Many Skin Areas Are Affected

- **Paucibacillary:** Fewer than 5 skin areas are affected. No bacteria are found in skin samples.
- **Multibacillary:** 6 or more skin areas are affected. Bacteria are found in skin samples.

### Based on Symptoms and How the Disease Behaves

- **Tuberculoid:** Few skin areas are affected. The disease is mild, less common, and less likely to spread.
- **Lepromatous:** Many skin areas are affected. The disease is more serious, more common, and more likely to spread.
- **Borderline:** Shows signs of both tuberculoid and lepromatous leprosy.

The type of leprosy you have affects:
- How well you will do over time.
- What problems you might face.
- How long you need to take antibiotics.

## Symptoms of Leprosy

The bacteria grow very slowly.  
Symptoms usually do not start for at least 1 year after infection.  
On average, symptoms appear 5 to 7 years after infection.  
They can take up to 20 to 30 years to show.

Leprosy mainly affects the skin and nerves outside the brain and spinal cord.

### Tuberculoid Leprosy

- One or a few flat, lighter patches appear on the skin.
- The edges of the patches are raised and clear.
- The skin in these areas feels numb because the nerves are damaged.

### Lepromatous Leprosy

- Many small or large bumps appear on the skin.
- More areas of the body feel numb than in tuberculoid leprosy.
- Some muscles become weak.
- The skin, nose, testes, kidneys, and other organs may be affected.
- Men may develop larger breasts.
- Eyebrows and eyelashes may fall out.

### Borderline Leprosy

- Shows signs of both tuberculoid and lepromatous leprosy.
- Without treatment, it may get better and act more like tuberculoid leprosy.
- Or it may get worse and act more like lepromatous leprosy.

## Serious Problems from Leprosy

Nerve damage is the most serious issue.

- You may lose the ability to feel pain or temperature.
- You might burn or cut yourself without knowing it.
- Repeated injuries can lead to loss of fingers or toes.
- Nerve damage can cause muscle weakness.
- Fingers may curl inward like claws.
- Feet may become too weak to lift. This is called foot drop.
- Nerves may swell and feel thick under the skin.

### Other Body Parts Affected

- **Feet:** Sores on the soles can make walking painful.
- **Nose:** Damage can cause a stuffy nose, nosebleeds, and eventually a collapsed nose.
- **Eyes:** Damage can lead to glaucoma or blindness.
- **Sexual function:** Men with lepromatous leprosy may have trouble getting an erection or may become infertile. The infection can lower testosterone and sperm production.
- **Kidneys:** The kidneys may not work well. In serious cases, kidney failure can happen.

## Leprosy Reactions

Even after treatment, the body’s immune system can react to the bacteria.  
These reactions cause:
- Fever
- Swelling and redness in the skin
- Pain in the nerves
- Swollen lymph nodes, joints, testes, kidneys, liver, or eyes
- Open sores on the skin
- More nerve damage

Mild skin swelling does not need treatment.

## Where Leprosy Is Found

- Worldwide, the number of cases is going down.
- In 2020, about 130,000 new cases were reported.
- Most cases (73%) were in India, Brazil, and Indonesia.
- In the United States, 159 new cases were reported in 2020.
- Most U.S. cases happen in people who lived in or came from countries where leprosy is common.
- Over 70% of U.S. cases were in six states: California, Florida, Hawaii, New York, Texas, and Louisiana.
- Many of these cases were in people who had contact with nine-banded armadillos. These animals carry the leprosy bacteria.

## Who Gets Leprosy?

- Leprosy can happen at any age.
- Older age increases the risk.
- Most cases happen in people aged 5 to 15 years or over 30 years.

## Why Most People Don’t Get Leprosy

- Most people who are infected with the leprosy bacteria do not get sick.
- Their immune system fights off the infection.
- People who do get leprosy may have genes that make them more likely to get sick after exposure.

## How to Prevent Leprosy

- Leprosy is not easily spread.
- The only form that can spread is untreated lepromatous leprosy.
- Once treatment starts, the disease cannot be passed on.

To help prevent leprosy:

- Avoid contact with nose or mouth fluids from someone with leprosy.
- Avoid touching armadillos.
- People who live with someone who has leprosy and are over 2 years old can get a single dose of the antibiotic rifampicin as a preventive measure.
  - This is only given after doctors check for leprosy and tuberculosis.
  - It is not given if there are other health problems that would make the drug unsafe.

The BCG vaccine, used for tuberculosis, gives some protection against leprosy.  
But it is not used just to prevent leprosy.

## Treating Leprosy

- Antibiotics stop the disease from getting worse.
- But they cannot fix nerve damage or deformities.
- Early treatment is very important.

### Why Multiple Antibiotics?

- Using just one antibiotic can lead to drug resistance.
- Doctors use more than one drug to stop this.

### How Long Do You Take Antibiotics?

- The bacteria are hard to kill.
- Treatment lasts 6 to 12 months, sometimes up to 2 years.

### Types of Antibiotics

#### For Multibacillary Leprosy

- **United States:** Adults take dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine every day for 24 months.
- **Other countries:** Adults take rifampin and clofazimine once a month under a doctor’s care. They take dapsone and clofazimine every day at home. This lasts 12 months.

#### For Paucibacillary Leprosy

- **United States:** Adults take rifampin and dapsone every day for 12 months.
- **Other countries:** Adults take rifampin once a month with supervision. They take dapsone every day on their own. This lasts 6 months.

### Details on Each Drug

- **Dapsone**
  - Cheap and safe for most people.
  - Can cause allergic rashes or low red blood cell count (anemia).

- **Rifampin**
  - More expensive but stronger than dapsone.
  - Can harm the liver.
  - May cause flu-like symptoms.
  - Rarely causes kidney failure.

- **Clofazimine**
  - Very safe.
  - Main side effect: skin color changes. This may last for months.

### Treating Leprosy Reactions

- Doctors use oral corticosteroids (like prednisone) to treat reactions.
- Mild skin swelling does not need treatment.

# Intimacy and Older Adults

Intimacy means feeling close to another person. It comes from knowing each other well and sharing experiences. Intimacy can be emotional, social, or physical. Physical intimacy includes touching, hugging, kissing, or sex.

You do not lose the need for closeness as you get older. There is no age when being close to someone is wrong or inappropriate. But aging can make it harder to be intimate. Health problems, changes in your body, and life changes can affect your ability to connect with a partner.

Here are some reasons why physical intimacy may be harder for older adults:

- **Losing a partner:** Many older adults lose their partner through death or separation. This is the most common reason for less physical intimacy.
- **Health problems:** Conditions like heart disease, diabetes, or arthritis can make sex difficult. These problems can cause pain, reduce movement, or lead to trouble getting or keeping an erection. Medicines for these conditions can also reduce interest in sex. Pain, worry, and side effects from illness can lower your desire for closeness.
- **Cognitive issues:** If someone has serious memory problems, it can be hard to give clear consent or feel comfortable during sex. This can be stressful for the partner, especially if they are also the caregiver.
- **Medicines:** Older adults often take many medicines. Some of these, like blood pressure drugs or mental health medicines, can reduce sex drive or cause erection problems.
- **Body changes:** As you age, your body changes. Hormone levels drop. This can cause dryness in the vagina or make sex painful. Men may feel less interest in sex as their testosterone drops.
- **Not talking about changes:** Some older adults feel shy or embarrassed about body changes. They may not talk to their partner or doctor about problems. But doctors can help with solutions.
- **Different expectations:** One partner may want to be close in a physical way. The other may not. This can cause tension.
- **No privacy:** If you live with family or in a care home, you may not have a private space. Privacy is important for physical intimacy.
- **New ways to be close:** Some couples choose to show love in other ways. They may enjoy hugging, holding hands, kissing, or saying kind words. These can still bring deep connection.

Still, many older adults stay close to their partners. Physical intimacy can help prevent sadness and loneliness. It can also boost confidence and improve health.

If you start a new relationship later in life, use protection during sex. Sexually transmitted infections, including HIV, can happen at any age. Talk to your doctor about safe sex.

Many older adults who live alone find comfort in pets. Caring for a pet can give you a sense of purpose. It can also help you feel less alone and more connected to someone.

# Mucous Membrane Pemphigoid

This is a group of rare, long-term conditions.  
The body’s immune system attacks the lining of the mouth, eyes, and other moist areas of the body.  
This causes blisters that come and go over time.  
Blisters can lead to scarring and ongoing health problems.

## What It Looks Like

- Blisters are raised and filled with fluid.  
- They are at least 10 millimeters wide.  
- The most common areas affected are the mouth and eyes.  
- Other areas like the nose, throat, genitals, and skin (especially on the head and upper body) can also be involved.  
- Older adults are most likely to get this condition.  
- Women are more likely than men to be affected.

## What Causes It

- The immune system makes antibodies that attack parts of the skin and mucous membranes.  
- These antibodies target proteins in the basement membrane.  
- This layer is deep under the surface of the skin and mucous membranes.  
- The condition is different from bullous pemphigoid because the attack happens deeper in the tissue.  
- Specific proteins targeted include BPAG2, laminin-332, and type VII collagen.  
- Antibodies to beta-4 integrin are found in widespread and eye forms.  
- Antibodies to alpha-6 integrin are found in mouth cases.

## How It Is Diagnosed

- A small sample of skin or mucous membrane is taken for testing.  
- This is called a skin biopsy.  
- A special test called direct immunofluorescence is done on the sample.  
- This test shows if antibodies are stuck to the basement membrane.  
- The test often shows a line of antibodies along the base of the skin.  
- These antibodies can be of types IgG, IgA, or C3.  
- Blood tests for antibodies are often negative or show very low levels.

## How It Is Treated

### For Mild Cases

- Topical corticosteroids (creams or ointments) are used on the affected areas.  
- Injections of corticosteroids into the blisters may also help.  
- A combination of two medicines is often used:  
  - Doxycycline, taken by mouth twice a day.  
  - Nicotinamide, taken by mouth three times a day.  
- These medicines help reduce inflammation and stop the immune system from attacking.

### For Severe Cases

- Stronger treatment is needed.  
- This may include medicines that lower the activity of the immune system.  
- Options include:  
  - Dapsone  
  - Prednisone  
  - High-dose prednisone with other immunosuppressants  
    - Rituximab  
    - Azathioprine  
    - Mycophenolate  
    - Cyclophosphamide  
- Intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) may also be used.  
- These treatments are given to control the disease and prevent serious damage.

## What the Future Holds

- The condition gets worse slowly over time.  
- It rarely goes away on its own.  
- Treatment helps, but it may not stop all damage.  
- Serious problems can happen depending on the area affected:  
  - Eye damage or blindness  
  - Damage to the airway (windpipe)  
  - Narrowing of the throat, esophagus, or genital area  
- People with antibodies against laminin-332 have a higher risk of internal cancers.  
- If this type is suspected, doctors should check for cancer based on age and sex.

## Key Points

- Mucous membrane pemphigoid is a rare, long-term condition.  
- It causes blisters on moist areas like the mouth and eyes.  
- Blisters can lead to scarring and lasting problems.  
- Diagnosis is done with a skin biopsy and a special test.  
- Mild cases are treated with corticosteroid creams and a combination of doxycycline and nicotinamide.  
- Severe cases need stronger medicines that reduce immune system activity.  
- Regular checks are important, especially for cancer risk in certain types.

# Lung Abscess

A lung abscess is a pocket of pus in the lung. It is surrounded by swollen, irritated tissue. It is caused by an infection.

## What Causes a Lung Abscess?

Most lung abscesses are caused by bacteria that live in the mouth or throat. These bacteria get into the lungs when a person breathes them in.

Poor gum health (periodontal disease) often leads to these bacteria.

The body usually protects the lungs. A strong cough helps clear out harmful germs. But if a person is very sleepy, unconscious, or under the influence of drugs, alcohol, or medicine, they may not cough well. This lets bacteria enter the lungs and cause infection.

People with weak immune systems may get lung abscesses from unusual germs. These can include fungi or the bacteria that cause tuberculosis.

Other bacteria that can cause abscesses include streptococci and staphylococci. One type, called MRSA, is very hard to treat.

Blockages in the airways can also cause abscesses. If a tumor or a foreign object blocks the air passages, mucus builds up behind it. Bacteria can grow in this mucus. The blockage stops the mucus from being coughed up.

Sometimes, bacteria or infected blood clots travel through the blood to the lungs. This can cause abscesses in many places in both lungs. This is most common in people who inject drugs using dirty needles.

Over time, some abscesses burst into an airway. This causes a large amount of thick, smelly mucus to be coughed up. After bursting, a hole remains in the lung. This hole fills with fluid and air.

In some cases, the abscess bursts into the space between the lungs and the chest wall. This space fills with pus. This condition is called empyema.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms often start slowly. But they can come on fast, depending on the cause.

Early signs include:

- Feeling very tired  
- Losing your appetite  
- Sweating a lot at night  
- Fever and chills  
- A cough that brings up mucus  

The mucus may smell bad. This is because the bacteria come from the mouth or throat, which often have strong odors. The mucus may also have streaks of blood.

You may have bad breath. You may also feel pain in your chest when you breathe. This happens if the lining around the lungs is inflamed.

Many people have these symptoms for weeks or months before seeing a doctor. These are called chronic abscesses. They cause weight loss, daily fever, and night sweats.

Abscesses caused by staphylococci or MRSA can be deadly within days. Sometimes, they can be fatal in just hours.

## How Is a Lung Abscess Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find a lung abscess.

### Chest X-ray
This is the most common test. It usually shows a hole in the lung filled with fluid and air. But other problems, like cancer or lung cysts, can look the same on an x-ray.

### Chest CT Scan
If the x-ray is unclear, a CT scan gives a more detailed picture. It can show small abscesses that an x-ray might miss.

### Lab Tests
Doctors may test your sputum (mucus from your lungs). They try to grow the bacteria in a lab. They also look at the sample under a microscope.

Blood tests can also help. Doctors may grow bacteria from your blood.

If there is pus in the space around the lungs (empyema), they will take a sample and send it to the lab.

### Bronchoscopy
This test uses a thin tube with a camera to look inside the airways. It may be used if:

- Antibiotics are not working  
- A tumor or blockage is suspected  
- The immune system is weak  

If the immune system is weak, the cause may be a rare germ. These germs need special treatment. Finding them early is important.

## How Is a Lung Abscess Treated?

### Antibiotics
Most people need antibiotics. These are usually given through a vein (IV) at first. Once you feel better and your fever is gone, you switch to pills.

Treatment lasts until symptoms go away and a chest x-ray shows the abscess is gone. This usually takes 3 to 6 weeks. Some people need longer treatment, depending on the cause and how well they respond.

### Surgery or Drainage
If the abscess is caused by a tumor or a foreign object, doctors may use a bronchoscope to remove the blockage.

If the abscess does not respond to antibiotics, or if there is an empyema, a tube may be placed into the chest. This tube drains the pus.

The tube can be placed using a bronchoscope or through surgery.

In rare cases, infected lung tissue must be removed. This may mean removing part of a lung or even an entire lung.

### Outlook
Most people recover fully. But treatment is harder if:

- The person is very weak  
- The immune system does not work well  
- A tumor blocks the airway  

Early treatment improves the chances of a full recovery.

# How to Prevent Mental and Social Problems in Older Adults

Depression is common in older adults.  
It is important to check for signs of depression.  
Several simple tests can help find depression.  
Examples include the Geriatric Depression Scale, the Hamilton Depression Scale, and the PHQ-9.  
These tests are easy to use.  
Some do not need a doctor to give them.  

If an older adult feels lonely or left out, help from a social worker can make a difference.  
This help can include finding ways to meet people and stay connected.  
Staying connected can improve health and may even help someone live longer.  

If someone is depressed, they should get help.  
This help can include talking with a counselor or taking medicine.  

Feeling good about yourself helps you stay healthy.  
Older adults should keep doing things that give them a sense of purpose.  
They should stay active in hobbies and social events.  
They should stay in touch with family, friends, or community groups.  

Simple actions can help build a sense of belonging.  
For example, getting a pet can bring comfort.  
Helping with chores at home gives a feeling of usefulness.  
Volunteering time to help others can also improve mood and well-being.  
These activities can help prevent mental health issues and reduce the risk of physical problems.

# Polyglandular Deficiency Syndromes

These are rare inherited conditions. They cause several hormone-producing glands to stop working properly.

Hormone-producing glands make chemicals that control body functions. In this condition, the body’s immune system attacks its own glands by mistake. This is called an autoimmune reaction. Genes and outside factors like viruses, diet, or certain medicines may play a role.

There are three main types:

## Type 1 (APECED)

- This type usually starts in childhood.
- The parathyroid glands and adrenal glands may not work well.
- People often get long-lasting yeast infections, especially in the mouth, skin, or genitals. These infections can be the first sign of the problem.
- Yeast infections are common in children under 5 years old.
- Other autoimmune problems may also occur, such as:
  - Thyroid disease
  - Diabetes
  - Liver problems (autoimmune hepatitis)
  - Digestive issues that make it hard to absorb nutrients (malabsorption)

## Type 2 (Schmidt Syndrome)

- This type usually starts in adults, especially women.
- The adrenal glands and thyroid glands may not work well.
- Sometimes the thyroid gland becomes overactive instead.
- Diabetes can also develop.

## Type 3

- This type is like Type 2.
- But the adrenal glands stay normal.
- Only the thyroid gland may be affected.

## Symptoms

Symptoms depend on which glands are not working.

**Underactive adrenal glands:**
- Feeling weak
- Loss of appetite
- Vomiting
- Dark patches on the skin
- In serious cases: very low blood pressure, which can be life-threatening if not treated

**Underactive thyroid gland:**
- Gaining weight
- Constipation
- Dry hair and dry skin
- Feeling cold easily

**Underactive parathyroid glands:**
- Tingling around the mouth
- Cramps in hands and feet
- Seizures

## Diagnosis

Doctors look for signs and symptoms. They confirm the diagnosis with blood tests.

- Blood tests check hormone levels.
- If the immune system is attacking the glands, the blood may show specific antibodies.
- Because other glands may fail years later, doctors do regular blood tests to catch new problems early.
- Since these conditions can run in families, doctors may test relatives for the same gene changes.

## Treatment

Treatment focuses on replacing missing hormones.

- Hormone replacement therapy is used for any gland that is not working.
- Treating multiple hormone problems can be more complex than treating one.
- People with frequent yeast infections may need long-term antifungal medicine.
- In some cases, medicines that calm the immune system (immunosuppressants) are used to reduce the body’s attack on its own glands.

# Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA)

This is a rare disease that affects blood vessels. It mainly harms small and medium-sized blood vessels. The disease causes swelling and damage in tissues. It often starts with long-term asthma or allergies. It can affect many organs, including the lungs, skin, nerves, heart, kidneys, and digestive system.

The disease has three main stages. These stages can happen in any order. They can also overlap. Not everyone goes through all three stages.

---

## What Causes EGPA?

We do not know the exact cause of EGPA.  
It may be linked to an overactive immune system.  
The immune system may attack the body’s own tissues.  
This can happen after long-term asthma or allergies.  
Some people with EGPA have a type of antibody called ANCA.  
This antibody is found in about 30% to 40% of cases.

---

## Symptoms and Signs

### Stage 1: Allergy and Asthma Phase
- This stage can last for years.  
- People have ongoing asthma.  
- They may also have nasal allergies or nasal polyps.  
- Asthma often starts in adulthood.  
- It can be severe and hard to control.

### Stage 2: Eosinophil Surge Phase
- The blood has too many eosinophils.  
- Eosinophils are a type of white blood cell.  
- They can damage tissues when they are too active.  
- This stage may cause lung problems like coughing, shortness of breath, or chest pain.  
- It can also cause stomach pain, nausea, or diarrhea.

### Stage 3: Vasculitis Phase
- Blood vessels become inflamed and damaged.  
- This can lead to serious health problems.  
- Symptoms include fever, tiredness, weight loss, and general weakness.  
- This stage can be life-threatening.

---

### How EGPA Affects Different Parts of the Body

#### Lungs and Breathing
- Most people have asthma.  
- Some have patchy areas in the lungs seen on X-ray.  
- These areas come and go.  
- Shortness of breath is common.

#### Nerves
- Nerve problems are very common.  
- Many people have pain, numbness, or weakness in their arms or legs.  
- This is called mononeuritis multiplex.  
- It affects multiple nerves at once.  
- Brain problems are rare but can happen.  
- They may include confusion, seizures, or trouble moving one side of the body.

#### Skin
- About half of people get skin changes.  
- Small lumps or red spots appear on the arms and legs.  
- These lumps are caused by inflammation under the skin.  
- Some people get purple spots from damaged blood vessels.

#### Joints and Muscles
- Joint pain or muscle pain is common.  
- Some people have joint swelling or stiffness.

#### Heart
- Heart problems are serious and can be deadly.  
- The heart muscle can become inflamed.  
- This can lead to heart failure.  
- Blood vessels in the heart can become blocked.  
- This may cause a heart attack.  
- The heart lining can also become thick and stiff.  
- This is called endomyocardial fibrosis.

#### Digestive System
- Up to one-third of people have stomach or bowel symptoms.  
- These include belly pain, diarrhea, or bleeding.  
- Some people have inflammation in the gut.  
- Others have poor blood flow to the intestines.

#### Kidneys
- Kidneys are less often affected than in other similar diseases.  
- When they are affected, the damage is usually mild.  
- The kidneys may show signs of inflammation.  
- This is seen in a small number of cases.

> **Note:** If the kidneys, heart, or nerves are affected, the outlook is worse.

---

## How Is EGPA Diagnosed?

Diagnosis is based on symptoms, blood tests, and sometimes a biopsy.

### Key Steps in Diagnosis

- **Blood tests** check for high levels of eosinophils.  
- **Chest X-ray** may show patchy areas in the lungs.  
- **Urinalysis** checks for kidney problems.  
- **Echocardiogram** (a heart ultrasound) is done for all patients at diagnosis.  
- It is repeated if heart symptoms develop.  
- **Biopsy** of affected tissue (like lung or skin) is often needed to confirm the diagnosis.

### Diagnostic Criteria (2022 Guidelines)

Doctors use a scoring system to help diagnose EGPA.  
You get points for certain signs and test results.

| Sign or Test | Points |
|--------------|--------|
| Asthma | +3 |
| Nasal polyps | +3 |
| Nerve problems (like numbness or weakness) | +1 |
| High eosinophils in blood (over 10%) | +5 |
| Biopsy shows blood vessel damage with eosinophils | +2 |
| Positive ANCA test (specific type) | –3 |
| Blood in urine | –1 |

- A score of **6 or higher** means EGPA is likely.  
- This test is very accurate.  
- It correctly identifies EGPA in 85% of cases.  
- It rules out other diseases in 99% of cases.

> **Note:** Blood tests and X-rays alone cannot confirm EGPA.  
> A biopsy is often needed.

---

## How Is EGPA Treated?

Treatment must be started early.  
The goal is to stop the disease and prevent organ damage.

### Main Treatment: Steroids and Immunosuppressants

- **Corticosteroids** (like prednisone) are the first treatment.  
- They reduce inflammation.  
- But steroids alone are not enough for long-term control.  
- Doctors add another medicine to help stop the disease.

### Other Medicines Used

- **Rituximab** – Helps reduce immune system activity.  
  - Shown to help many patients go into remission.  
  - Helps reduce the need for steroids.  
  - Used when the disease is active or severe.

- **Cyclophosphamide** – Used for serious cases.  
  - Especially helpful for heart problems.  
  - Heart damage is the main cause of death in EGPA.

- **Mepolizumab** – A newer medicine that targets a specific immune signal.  
  - Works well for people with asthma or lung issues.  
  - Helps prevent flares.  
  - Not proven to help those with serious heart or nerve problems.

- **Benralizumab** – Another medicine that blocks the same immune signal.  
  - Works as well as mepolizumab.  
  - Also helps reduce long-term steroid use.

> **Note:** The choice of medicine depends on which organs are affected and how severe the disease is.

---

## Key Points

- EGPA is a rare disease that affects blood vessels.  
- It often starts with asthma or allergies.  
- It has three stages: allergy/asthma, high eosinophils, and serious blood vessel damage.  
- The stages can happen in any order.  
- Heart or nerve problems are serious and mean a worse outcome.  
- Diagnosis uses symptoms, blood tests, and sometimes a biopsy.  
- All patients should have a heart ultrasound at diagnosis.  
- Treatment includes steroids and other immune-suppressing medicines.  
- Rituximab is a strong option for many patients.  
- Mepolizumab or benralizumab may help those with lung or asthma symptoms but not serious organ damage.

# Glomerulonephritis

Glomerulonephritis is a condition that affects the tiny filters in your kidneys. These filters are called glomeruli. They help clean your blood by removing waste and extra fluid. When the filters get damaged, your body can swell up, your blood pressure may rise, and your urine may look red or dark.

## What Causes Glomerulonephritis?

Glomerulonephritis can happen for many reasons. It may be caused by:

- Infections, like strep throat or skin infections
- Inherited genetic problems
- Autoimmune diseases, where your body attacks its own tissues

It can also be caused by other health issues that affect parts of the body beyond the kidneys.

### Types of Glomerulonephritis

There are two main types:

- **Acute glomerulonephritis**: This develops quickly, often after an infection.
- **Chronic glomerulonephritis**: This builds up slowly over time.

In rare cases, acute glomerulonephritis can get worse fast. This is called rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. It can destroy most of the kidney filters and lead to kidney failure.

### Common Causes

#### Infections
- Strep throat or skin infections with streptococcus bacteria
- Other bacterial infections (like staph or pneumococcus)
- Viral infections (such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, or HIV)
- Parasite infections (like malaria)

When glomerulonephritis follows an infection, it is called **postinfectious glomerulonephritis**.

#### Blood Vessel Inflammation (Vasculitis)
- Cryoglobulinemia
- Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
- Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
- Microscopic polyangiitis

#### Immune System Problems
- Lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus)
- Goodpasture syndrome

#### Other Causes
- Hereditary nephritis (a genetic condition passed down in families)
- Certain medicines, such as some chemotherapy drugs, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, lithium, and others

## Symptoms

### Acute Glomerulonephritis
Many people have no symptoms at first. If symptoms do appear, they may include:

- Swelling in the face, eyelids, or legs
- Less urine than normal
- Dark or red-colored urine
- High blood pressure
- Feeling tired, dizzy, or confused
- Nausea or a general feeling of being unwell (especially in older adults)

### Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis
This type comes on fast. Early signs include:

- Weakness and fatigue
- Fever
- Loss of appetite
- Nausea, vomiting, or stomach pain
- Joint pain

About half of people have flu-like symptoms a month before kidney failure starts. They may have swelling and make very little urine. High blood pressure is rare and usually mild.

### Chronic Glomerulonephritis
This type often has no symptoms at first. It may go unnoticed for years. Later, you might notice:

- Swelling
- High blood pressure
- Itching
- Poor appetite
- Nausea
- Tiredness
- Trouble breathing

If the disease gets worse, it can lead to kidney failure.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find out if you have glomerulonephritis.

### Tests Used
- **Blood tests**: Check for waste buildup in the blood (like urea and creatinine).
- **Urine tests**: Look for blood and protein in the urine.
- **Kidney biopsy**: A small sample of kidney tissue is taken to check for damage. This is done using a needle guided by ultrasound or CT scan.
- **Imaging tests**: Like ultrasound or CT scans to see the size and shape of the kidneys.

### What the Tests Show
- Blood tests may show anemia (low red blood cells).
- Urine tests may show casts — clumps of cells that form when the kidney filters are damaged.
- A kidney biopsy helps confirm the diagnosis and find the cause.
- In advanced cases, the kidneys may be small and scarred. This makes a biopsy less useful.

### Finding the Cause
- If an infection is suspected, doctors may test your throat or blood for signs of bacteria or viruses.
- If an autoimmune disease is suspected, blood tests check for abnormal antibodies and immune system activity.

Some people with no symptoms but who still have blood and protein in their urine may be diagnosed with:
- **IgA nephropathy**: A common type that can stay mild or get worse over time.
- **Alport syndrome**: A rare inherited condition that can cause kidney failure, hearing loss, and vision problems.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause and type of glomerulonephritis.

### General Steps
- Treat the underlying cause if possible.
- Eat less salt and protein until your kidneys improve.
- Take diuretics to help remove extra fluid.
- Control high blood pressure.

### Acute Glomerulonephritis
- No specific treatment is needed in most cases.
- If a bacterial infection is still present, antibiotics are used.
- Antimalarial drugs may help if malaria is the cause.
- Antibiotics do not help if the infection happened weeks ago.

### Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis
This needs fast treatment to prevent kidney failure.

- High-dose corticosteroids (given through a vein) are used for about a week, then taken by mouth.
- Medicines like cyclophosphamide or rituximab may be used to calm the immune system.
- Plasma exchange may be done to remove harmful antibodies from the blood.
- The sooner treatment starts, the better the chance of saving kidney function.
- Dialysis may be needed if kidney failure happens.
- Kidney transplant is possible, but the disease can return in the new kidney.

### Chronic Glomerulonephritis
- ACE inhibitors or ARBs are often used. These help lower blood pressure and reduce protein in the urine.
- Reducing salt and protein in your diet can slow kidney damage.
- Controlling blood pressure is very important.
- If kidney failure happens, treatment options include dialysis or kidney transplant.

## Outlook (Prognosis)

### Acute Glomerulonephritis
- Most children recover fully.
- About 1% of children and 10% of adults develop long-term kidney problems.

### Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis
- Early treatment can save kidney function.
- But many people do not notice symptoms early. By the time they see a doctor, kidney failure has already started.
- Up to 90% of people with this type end up needing dialysis.
- The outlook is worse if the cause is unknown or if the person is older.

### Chronic Glomerulonephritis
- Some people never get worse.
- Others slowly lose kidney function over time.
- In some cases, it leads to kidney failure.

### Specific Conditions

| Condition | What It Is | Prognosis |
|--------|------------|----------|
| **Fibrillary glomerulonephritis** | Rare disease where abnormal proteins build up in the kidneys. Can cause kidney failure. | Poor. Half of people lose kidney function within 4 years. Treatment with steroids or immune drugs may help, but it’s not clear. |
| **IgA nephropathy** | Most common type worldwide. Caused by immune complexes in the kidneys. | Usually progresses slowly. Kidney failure can happen after 10 years. Children tend to do better. |
| **Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis** | Uncommon type. Often linked to infections or other diseases. | If the cause is found and treated (like malaria or multiple myeloma), some improvement is possible. If the cause is unknown, the outcome is worse. |
| **Primary rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis** | Fast-moving damage to kidney filters. Needs a biopsy to diagnose. | Poor. Without treatment, 90% develop kidney failure within 6 months. Better if the cause can be treated. |
