# Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD)

Age-related macular degeneration is the most common cause of lasting vision loss in older adults.  
It affects the center of the vision.  
This condition is more common in White people.

## What Causes AMD?

You are more likely to get AMD if you:
- Are older
- Have a family member with AMD
- Have certain gene changes
- Smoke
- Have heart disease
- Have high blood pressure
- Are overweight
- Spend a lot of time in the sun
- Eat few foods with omega-3 fatty acids or dark green leafy vegetables

## How AMD Affects the Eye

There are two types of AMD:

### Dry AMD
- This is the most common type.  
- It starts slowly and gets worse over time.  
- It affects about 85 out of 100 people with AMD.  
- The layer under the retina (called the retinal pigment epithelium) becomes damaged.  
- This layer helps keep the light-sensitive cells in the retina healthy.  
- Waste from these cells builds up and forms small yellow spots called drusen.  
- In later stages, parts of the retina shrink and stop working. This is called geographic atrophy.  
- There is no swelling, bleeding, or scar tissue under the center of the retina.

### Wet AMD
- This type is less common but causes more serious vision loss.  
- It affects about 15 out of 100 people with AMD.  
- Abnormal blood vessels grow under the retina.  
- These vessels can leak fluid or blood.  
- This causes swelling, bleeding, or a bump under the center of the retina.  
- Over time, untreated wet AMD leads to a scar under the center of the retina.  
- Even though only 15% of people have wet AMD, it causes 80 to 90% of severe vision loss from AMD.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may notice:
- Blurry or distorted center vision  
- Straight lines look wavy  
- Dark or empty spots in the center of your vision  
- Colors seem less bright  
- Trouble reading or recognizing faces

## How Is AMD Diagnosed?

Your eye doctor will check your eyes using:
- A special eye exam with a bright light (dilated funduscopic exam)  
- A photo of the back of your eye (color fundus photography)  
- A test that uses a special dye to see blood vessels (fluorescein angiography)  
- A scan that shows detailed layers of the retina (optical coherence tomography)

The doctor may use an Amsler grid to check for vision changes.  
This is a grid of lines that helps spot blurriness or missing areas in your vision.

If the doctor sees signs of wet AMD, they will do more tests.  
These tests help show:
- Where abnormal blood vessels are  
- How much damage has happened  
- How well treatment is working

## How Is AMD Treated?

### For Dry AMD
- Take daily eye health supplements if you are at high risk.  
- These include vitamins and minerals like zinc, vitamin C, vitamin E, and lutein.  
- Supplements may slow the disease in some people.  
- There is no treatment to reverse dry AMD.

### For Wet AMD
- Get injections into the eye with medicine that stops abnormal blood vessels from growing.  
- This medicine is called anti-VEGF.  
- Injections are done in the doctor’s office.  
- Some people get a small device placed in the eye to deliver medicine over time.  
- Laser treatment may be used in some cases.  
- Another treatment called photodynamic therapy may be used in special cases.

### Supportive Care
- Use low-vision aids like magnifiers or special glasses.  
- Make changes at home to help with daily tasks.  
- Work with a vision specialist to stay independent.

## Key Facts to Remember

- AMD is the top cause of lasting vision loss in older adults.  
- It is more common in White people.  
- Most cases start as dry AMD.  
- Even though dry AMD is more common, wet AMD causes most serious vision loss.  
- Dry AMD shows up as drusen, thinning of the retina, and changes in the retinal pigment layer.  
- Wet AMD shows up as swelling, bleeding, a bump under the retina, or a gray-green area under the center of the eye.  
- If your doctor sees AMD during an eye exam, do a photo, dye test, and scan.  
- Give supplements to people with high-risk dry AMD or wet AMD in only one eye.  
- Treat wet AMD with anti-VEGF injections or laser therapy.  
- In some cases, use photodynamic therapy or laser treatment.

# Chancroid

Chancroid is a sexually transmitted infection caused by a type of bacteria called *Haemophilus ducreyi*.  
It causes painful sores on the genitals or in the mouth.  

This infection is rare in the United States and other high-income countries.  
It is more common in parts of Asia, Africa, and the Caribbean.  

People with chancroid are more likely to get HIV.  
They are also more likely to spread HIV to others.  

The bacteria can cause sores in places other than the genitals.  
These include the mouth, breasts, inner thighs, and fingers.  

---

## Symptoms of Chancroid

Symptoms usually start 3 to 7 days after infection.  
Small, painful blisters appear on the genitals or near the anus.  
These blisters break open quickly and turn into open sores.  
The sores are shallow and have ragged edges.  
The sores can grow larger and join together.  
In some cases, the sores go deep and damage nearby tissue.  

Lymph nodes in the groin may swell and become very tender.  
This is called a bubo.  
One or more buboes may form a large lump.  
Sometimes, a bubo turns into an abscess.  
An abscess is a collection of pus.  
The skin over the abscess may turn red and shiny.  
It may break open and drain pus onto the skin.  

Sores can also appear in the mouth or on other parts of the skin.  

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Chancroid

Doctors look at your symptoms and ask about your health history.  
They may test a sample of fluid or pus from a sore or bubo.  

One test is called nucleic acid amplification testing, or NAAT.  
This test looks for the bacteria’s genetic material.  
It can find very small amounts of the bacteria.  
This test is very accurate.  

If NAAT is not available, doctors may try to grow the bacteria in a lab.  
This is called a culture.  
But this method is not always successful, even if the bacteria are present.  
So doctors often rely on symptoms and your risk of exposure.  

People with chancroid are at high risk for syphilis and HIV.  
If tests for these infections come back negative, doctors recommend retesting in 3 months.  

---

## Treatment for Chancroid

Chancroid is treated with antibiotics.  
You can take antibiotics by mouth or get them as an injection.  

Effective oral antibiotics include:  
- Azithromycin  
- Ciprofloxacin  
- Erythromycin  

An effective injection is:  
- Ceftriaxone  

If buboes are painful, doctors may make a small cut to drain the pus.  
This is only done if you are also taking antibiotics.  

If your sex partner had sex with you in the 10 days before your symptoms started, they should be checked and treated.  
This is true even if they do not have symptoms.  

---

## How to Prevent Chancroid

You can lower your risk of chancroid and other sexually transmitted infections by:  

- Using a condom every time you have oral, anal, or genital sex.  
- Limiting the number of sex partners.  
- Avoiding sex with people who have many partners or who do not use protection.  
- Choosing to have sex only with one partner (mutual monogamy).  
- Choosing not to have sex (abstinence).  
- Getting vaccinated if a vaccine is available for the infection.  
- Getting tested and treated quickly if you think you are infected.  
- Telling your past and current sex partners if you are diagnosed with an STI.  
- Helping them get tested and treated.

# Sexual Masochism Disorder – Simple Explanation

## What Is Sexual Masochism?

Some people get sexually excited when they are humiliated, beaten, tied up, or made to suffer in some way. This is called sexual masochism.

If a person has strong, repeated urges to be humiliated or hurt during sex, and this causes them serious distress or problems in daily life, they may have a condition called sexual masochism disorder.

## What Is a Paraphilia?

Sexual masochism is a type of paraphilia. A paraphilia means having strong sexual interests that are not common. But most people with these interests do not have a mental health problem. A diagnosis is only made if the behavior causes real harm or distress.

To be diagnosed, the behavior must have been happening for at least six months.

## Who Has These Interests?

Most people who enjoy masochistic activities know about their interest. They often talk openly about it.

The term BDSM stands for bondage, domination, sadism, and masochism. It describes a range of sexual activities. This includes people who enjoy these activities but do not have a mental health problem.

## How Common Is This?

We do not know exactly how many people have sexual masochism disorder.

One survey in Australia from 2001 to 2002 found that:
- 2.2% of men said they took part in BDSM activities in the past year.
- 1.3% of women said the same.

## Is This Normal?

Many people have fantasies or play games involving humiliation or pain. These are usually between adults who agree to do them. The activities are often planned and safe.

Most people who play these games know it is pretend. They use a “safe word” to stop if things get too intense. This helps keep everyone safe.

But some people push the limits. They may stop using their safe word. This can lead to serious injury or even death.

## How Do People Act on These Feelings?

Some people do these things alone. Examples include:
- Tying themselves up
- Piercing their skin
- Giving themselves electric shocks
- Burning their skin
- Stopping breathing during masturbation (called asphyxiophilia)

Others do these things with a partner. The partner may be a sexual sadist. Activities with a partner can include:
- Being tied up
- Being blindfolded
- Being spanked
- Being whipped
- Being humiliated by being urinated or defecated on
- Being forced to wear clothes of the opposite gender
- Being forced into a sexual act
- Being partially choked, usually at the moment of orgasm

## How Is the Disorder Diagnosed?

The DSM-5-TR (a guide used by doctors) says a person has sexual masochism disorder if they meet all of these criteria:

- They have strong, repeated sexual excitement from being humiliated, beaten, tied up, or made to suffer.
- These thoughts, urges, or actions cause serious distress or problems at work, in relationships, or in other important areas of life.
- The problem has lasted for at least six months.

The doctor will also note:
- If the person has asphyxiophilia (sexual excitement from stopping breathing).
- If the person lives in a place where it is hard to act on these urges (like a hospital or prison).
- If the person has been free of symptoms for at least five years and is no longer troubled or impaired.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment is only needed if the person is suffering or having problems in life.

Two main treatments may help:
- Cognitive-behavioral therapy: This helps people understand their thoughts and change harmful behaviors.
- Antiandrogen medicine: This lowers sex drive. It is used only in specific cases.

There are not many large studies on treatment. But for those who need help, a mix of therapy and medicine seems to work best.

# Vaginal Bleeding During Early Pregnancy

About 20 to 30 out of every 100 women have vaginal bleeding in the first 20 weeks of pregnancy.  
Some of these women have a problem with the pregnancy.  
But many women with light bleeding or spotting go on to have a healthy baby.  

In about half of women who bleed, the pregnancy ends in a miscarriage.  
If a miscarriage does not happen right away, other problems can still occur.  
These include a baby with a low birth weight.  
Or the baby may be born too early.  
Or the baby may die during or shortly after birth.  
In rare cases, heavy bleeding can cause blood pressure to drop too low.  
This can lead to shock, which is dangerous.  

Still, many women with light bleeding go on to have a healthy pregnancy and delivery.

## What Causes Vaginal Bleeding in Early Pregnancy?

Vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy can come from problems related to the pregnancy.  
It can also come from other causes.

### Most Common Cause: Miscarriage

The most common cause of bleeding is a miscarriage.  
A miscarriage is when a pregnancy ends on its own.  
Bleeding may mean a miscarriage is possible.  
But sometimes the bleeding stops and the pregnancy continues.  

When a miscarriage happens, it usually occurs in stages.  
First, there is bleeding.  
Then cramping starts.  
The cramps can be strong.  
The bleeding may get heavier.  
The woman then passes the pregnancy tissue from her body.  
She may see tissue come out of the vagina.

Sometimes a miscarriage happens without any symptoms.  
It may only be found during a regular checkup.  
This is called a missed abortion.  

If you think you are having a miscarriage, contact your doctor.  
Some women can go through a miscarriage at home.  
But if the pain is severe or the bleeding is heavy, you need medical help.  
You may need medicine or a procedure to make sure the pregnancy ends safely.

### Most Dangerous Cause: Ectopic Pregnancy

The most serious cause of bleeding is an ectopic pregnancy.  
This is when the pregnancy grows outside the uterus.  
It often grows in a fallopian tube.  
But it can also grow in the ovary, cervix, or a scar from a past cesarean section.  

An ectopic pregnancy cannot survive.  
As it grows, it can burst the tube or other area.  
This causes severe pain and heavy bleeding.  
It can be life-threatening.  

If an ectopic pregnancy is found, treatment is needed.  
This may be medicine or surgery to end the pregnancy.

### Other Possible Causes

A rare but serious cause is a ruptured corpus luteum cyst.  
After an egg is released from the ovary, the empty sac may fill with blood or fluid instead of breaking down.  
This can cause bleeding.

## Risk Factors

### For Miscarriage:
- Age over 35
- Having had one or more miscarriages before
- Smoking cigarettes
- Using illegal drugs like cocaine
- Drinking alcohol
- Having fibroids, scars, or an unusual shape in the uterus

### For Ectopic Pregnancy:
- A past ectopic pregnancy (this is the biggest risk)
- Past abdominal surgery, especially sterilization surgery
- Problems with the fallopian tubes
- Using an intrauterine device (IUD) now
- Getting pregnant through in vitro fertilization
- History of sexually transmitted infections or pelvic infections
- Using birth control pills with estrogen and progestin
- Smoking
- Having fertility problems
- Past miscarriage or abortion

## How Doctors Evaluate Bleeding

Doctors first check if the bleeding is caused by an ectopic pregnancy.

### Warning Signs – See a Doctor Right Away:
- Fainting, feeling dizzy, or a fast heartbeat
- Losing a lot of blood
- Blood with clots or tissue
- Severe pain in the belly that gets worse when you move
- Fever, chills, or a thick, pus-like vaginal discharge

### No Warning Signs? See a Doctor Within 48 to 72 Hours.

Doctors will ask about your symptoms and medical history.  
This includes past pregnancies, miscarriages, abortions, and risk factors.

They will do a physical exam.  
They check for fever and signs of heavy blood loss.  
They look for a fast heartbeat or low blood pressure.

They do a pelvic exam.  
They check if the cervix is starting to open.  
This can mean the pregnancy is passing.  
If any tissue is found, it is removed and sent to a lab for testing.

They gently press on your belly to see if it hurts.

### Tests Doctors May Do:
- A pregnancy test using a urine sample
- Blood tests to check hormone levels (hCG)
- A complete blood count (CBC) if bleeding is heavy
- Ultrasound of the pelvis

Doctors may use a handheld device placed on your belly to check for a baby’s heartbeat.

If a home pregnancy test shows pregnancy, but it hasn’t been confirmed by a doctor, they will do a test using your urine.

Once pregnancy is confirmed, doctors do:
- Blood type and Rh status (positive or negative)
- Ultrasound
- Blood tests to measure hCG

### Why Rh Status Matters

If you have Rh-negative blood, you need a special shot if you have bleeding.  
This shot is called Rho(D) immune globulin.  
It prevents your body from making antibodies that could harm future babies.

If you lose more than about one cup of blood, doctors may do a CBC or other tests.  
This checks for blood clotting problems or the need for a blood transfusion.

### Ultrasound

Doctors usually use a probe placed inside the vagina for ultrasound.  
This can show if the pregnancy is in the uterus.  
It can also show a baby’s heartbeat after about 6 weeks.

If no heartbeat is seen after 6 weeks, a miscarriage is likely.  
If a heartbeat is seen, a miscarriage is less likely, but still possible.

Ultrasound can also show:
- Leftover tissue in the uterus after a miscarriage
- An ectopic pregnancy (if it is in a certain spot and big enough)
- A molar pregnancy (an abnormal growth of placental tissue)

### hCG Blood Tests

Measuring hCG levels helps doctors understand what is happening.  
It helps tell a normal pregnancy from an ectopic one.  
If an ectopic pregnancy is suspected, hCG levels are checked often.  
Ultrasound may be repeated as needed.

### Emergency: Ruptured Ectopic Pregnancy

If a ruptured ectopic pregnancy is likely, this is an emergency.  
Doctors may need to do surgery right away.  
They may even operate before doing blood tests or ultrasound.

They usually make a small cut near the belly button.  
They insert a thin tube with a camera (laparoscope) to look inside.  
This is called laparoscopy.

Sometimes they make a larger cut in the lower belly.  
This is called laparotomy.

## Treatment for Vaginal Bleeding

Doctors used to recommend bed rest if a miscarriage seemed possible.  
But there is no proof that bed rest helps.  
Still, doctors often suggest avoiding sex.  
There is no clear proof that sex causes miscarriage.

### If Bleeding Is Heavy or Dangerous:
- A large tube is placed in a vein to give blood quickly
- Surgery is done right away if an ectopic pregnancy has ruptured

### If Bleeding Is Caused by a Specific Problem:
- That problem is treated, if possible

## Key Points

- The most common cause of bleeding in early pregnancy is a miscarriage.
- The most serious cause is an ectopic pregnancy.
- See a doctor right away if you have a fast heartbeat, faint, or feel dizzy.
- Blood tests check if you are Rh-negative or Rh-positive.
- If you are Rh-negative and have bleeding, you need a shot to protect future babies.

# Narcolepsy – Simple Explanation

Narcolepsy is a long-term sleep disorder. It causes extreme tiredness during the day. It can also cause sudden muscle weakness. This weakness happens when you feel strong emotions like laughter or anger.

Other symptoms include:
- Being unable to move for a short time when falling asleep or waking up (sleep paralysis).
- Seeing or hearing things that are not real when falling asleep or waking up (hallucinations).
- Trouble sleeping at night.

## What Causes Narcolepsy?

The exact cause is not known. But research shows it may be due to the body attacking certain brain cells. These cells make a chemical called hypocretin. This chemical helps keep you awake.

Narcolepsy is linked to certain genes. But it is not passed down through families. Most people with narcolepsy do not have a family history of the condition.

Environmental factors, like infections, may trigger the disease in people who are at risk.

## Types of Narcolepsy

There are two types:

**Type 1**  
- You have low levels of hypocretin in your brain.
- You have cataplexy (sudden muscle weakness).
- You may also have sleep paralysis and hallucinations.

**Type 2**  
- You have normal levels of hypocretin.
- You do not have cataplexy.
- The main symptom is extreme daytime sleepiness.

Type 2 is more common than Type 1.

## Symptoms of Narcolepsy

The main symptoms are:
- Extreme tiredness during the day.
- Sudden muscle weakness (cataplexy).
- Hallucinations when falling asleep or waking up.
- Sleep paralysis.
- Poor sleep at night.

Up to 15 out of 100 people with narcolepsy have all five symptoms.

Symptoms usually start in teens or young adults. They can begin after an illness, stress, or lack of sleep. Once it starts, narcolepsy lasts a lifetime. But it does not shorten your life.

## How Is Narcolepsy Diagnosed?

Diagnosis takes time. It often takes about 10 years from when symptoms start to get a correct diagnosis.

Doctors use two tests:
1. **Polysomnography** – You sleep overnight in a lab. Machines record your brain activity, eye movements, heart rate, and muscle activity.
2. **Multiple sleep latency testing (MSLT)** – You take short naps during the day. The test measures how fast you fall asleep and whether you go into REM sleep quickly.

A diagnosis of narcolepsy is made if:
- You fall asleep in less than 8 minutes on average during the day.
- You enter REM sleep during at least two of the five nap tests.
- Or you enter REM sleep during one nap test and also during the overnight sleep study.

If you have cataplexy, you likely have Type 1 narcolepsy. If you do not have cataplexy, you likely have Type 2.

The maintenance of wakefulness test is not used to diagnose narcolepsy. But it can help check if treatment is working.

Other conditions can cause extreme daytime sleepiness. These include:
- Brain tumors or swelling.
- Low thyroid function.
- Low or high blood sugar.
- Anemia.
- Kidney or liver problems.
- High carbon dioxide levels in the blood.
- Seizure disorders.
- Infections like flu or sleeping sickness (from a tsetse fly bite).

Your doctor will check for these if narcolepsy is not the cause.

## Treatment for Narcolepsy

Not everyone needs treatment. If symptoms are mild, you may not need medicine.

But if symptoms are bothersome, treatment can help. The goal is to reduce daytime sleepiness and prevent muscle weakness.

### General Tips
- Get enough sleep at night.
- Take short naps (less than 30 minutes) at the same time every day, usually in the afternoon.
- Avoid triggers for cataplexy, such as strong emotions like laughter, anger, or fear.

### Treatment by Type

**For Type 1 Narcolepsy**
- Use oxybates or pitolisant to treat cataplexy.
- If daytime sleepiness remains, add modafinil.

**For Type 2 Narcolepsy**
- Start with modafinil for daytime sleepiness.
- If modafinil does not work well, try solriamfetol.
- Pitolisant can also be used for daytime sleepiness.

### Medicines

**Modafinil**
- Helps you stay awake during the day.
- Taken once in the morning. Sometimes a second small dose at noon helps.
- Works best when started at a low dose and slowly increased.
- Side effects: nausea, headache. These often go away with time.
- Can make birth control pills less effective.
- Rarely causes serious skin rashes. Stop the medicine if this happens.
- Should not be used during pregnancy. It can cause serious birth defects.

**Armodafinil**
- Similar to modafinil but lasts longer.
- Taken once in the morning.
- Same side effects and warnings as modafinil.

**Solriamfetol**
- Helps with daytime sleepiness.
- Does not help with cataplexy.
- Taken once a day in the morning.
- Works well for people with narcolepsy or sleep apnea.
- Dose may need to be adjusted if you have kidney problems.
- Not safe for people with end-stage kidney disease.
- Side effects: insomnia, headache, nausea, loss of appetite, diarrhea.
- Does not affect birth control pills.

**Pitolisant**
- Helps with both daytime sleepiness and cataplexy.
- Taken once a day when you wake up.
- Dose can be increased over time.
- Dose may need to be adjusted if you have kidney or liver problems.
- Not safe for people with end-stage kidney disease.
- Side effects: headache, irritability, anxiety, nausea.
- Makes birth control pills less effective.
- Can affect heart rhythm. Your doctor may check your heart with an EKG.

**Oxybates**
- Treats both daytime sleepiness and cataplexy.
- Available in three forms: high-sodium or low-sodium, taken once or twice a night.
- Taken at bedtime. A second dose is taken 2.5 to 4 hours later (if using twice-daily form).
- Side effects: headache, nausea, dizziness, stuffy nose, sleepiness, vomiting, bedwetting, sleepwalking.
- Can be misused or lead to dependence. It is a controlled substance.
- Not safe for people with a rare genetic condition (succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency).
- Use with caution if you have lung problems, high blood pressure, or heart failure.

**Older Medicines (Tricyclic Antidepressants and SSRIs)**
- These were used in the past to treat cataplexy and hallucinations.
- But there is not enough proof they work well.
- Only used if newer medicines do not help.

**Stimulant Medicines (Methylphenidate, Amphetamines)**
- Used only if other medicines do not work or cannot be used.
- These include methamphetamine and dextroamphetamine.
- Taken once a day in long-acting form.
- Side effects: agitation, high blood pressure, fast heartbeat, heart attack, changes in appetite, mood swings (like mania).
- High risk of abuse.
- If you are over 40, your doctor may do a heart test before starting these medicines.

## Key Points

- Narcolepsy may be caused by the body attacking brain cells that make hypocretin.
- Main symptoms: extreme daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, hallucinations, sleep paralysis, and poor nighttime sleep.
- Diagnosis needs two tests: overnight sleep study and daytime nap test.
- Daytime sleepiness usually improves with modafinil or similar medicines.
- Cataplexy usually improves with pitolisant or oxybates.

# Chamomile

Chamomile is a type of plant that looks like a daisy.  
It contains natural substances that may have health benefits.  
Two main types are used in supplements: *Matricaria chamomilla* and *Chamaemelum nobile*.

## How People Use Chamomile

You can take chamomile in several ways:
- Drink it as a tea
- Take it in a capsule
- Use it as a skin cream or lotion
- Breathe in the scent (aromatherapy)

Many people drink chamomile tea to feel calmer and less anxious.

## What People Use Chamomile For

People take chamomile to:
- Feel less anxious or down
- Sleep better
- Reduce swelling
- Lower a fever
- Ease stomach problems like diarrhea, heartburn, or an upset stomach

Some people use chamomile on the skin to soothe irritation.  
This includes rashes from eczema, poison ivy, diaper rash, or chickenpox.  
It may also help with ear or eye infections.  
It can ease pain in the stomach, back, or muscles.

Parents sometimes use chamomile for babies and children with:
- Colic (severe crying)
- Croup (a coughing illness)
- Fever

Some people believe chamomile can help prevent cancer or heart disease.  
But there is not enough proof to support this.

## What Science Says About Chamomile

Research on chamomile is limited.  
Some studies suggest it may help a little with sleep and mild anxiety or depression.  
But the effects are small and not strong enough to be certain.

## Side Effects of Chamomile

Chamomile is safe for most people.  
The most common side effect is an allergic reaction.  
This is more likely if you are allergic to ragweed or sunflowers.  
Allergic reactions can cause:
- Itchy eyes
- Sneezing
- Runny nose
- Skin rash or irritation

In rare cases, a serious allergic reaction can happen.  
This can be life-threatening and needs emergency care.

## Medicines That May Interact with Chamomile

Chamomile can affect some medicines.  
It may make them stronger or weaker.  
Talk to your doctor before using chamomile if you take:
- Blood thinners (like warfarin)
- Sleep aids or sedatives (including alcohol)
- Iron supplements
- Tamoxifen (a cancer medicine)
- Hormone replacement therapy
- Birth control pills that contain estrogen

Chamomile may increase the effects of blood thinners and sedatives.  
It may also reduce how well some other medicines work.

## Advice on Using Chamomile

Chamomile may help with mild anxiety, low mood, and sleep.  
But the benefits are small.  
It seems to be safe for most people when used in normal amounts.

Talk to your doctor before using chamomile if you take any of the following:
- Blood thinners
- Sleep medicines
- Iron supplements
- Tamoxifen
- Hormone replacement therapy
- Birth control pills with estrogen

For more details, visit the National Institutes of Health’s National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health website.  
This is a trusted source in English.

# Placenta Previa

## What Is Placenta Previa?

The placenta is a special organ that grows in the uterus during pregnancy. It gives the baby oxygen and nutrients.  
Placenta previa happens when the placenta sits low in the uterus.  
It covers part or all of the opening to the birth canal. This opening is called the internal cervical os.  
If the placenta is near the opening but does not cover it, this is called a low-lying placenta.  
This condition is more common early in pregnancy.  
As the uterus grows, the placenta often moves up and away from the opening.  
This usually happens by 28 weeks of pregnancy.

## Symptoms of Placenta Previa

Most women with placenta previa do not have any symptoms.  
The condition is often found during a routine ultrasound in the second trimester.  
The main symptom is sudden, painless bleeding from the vagina.  
The bleeding can be light or very heavy.  
Heavy bleeding can lead to shock.  
Bleeding can start as early as 16 weeks of pregnancy.  
Some women also feel contractions when bleeding happens.  
The bleeding comes from the mother’s blood vessels.  
It does not come from the baby.

## How Is Placenta Previa Diagnosed?

All women who have vaginal bleeding after 20 weeks of pregnancy should be checked for placenta previa.  
A pelvic exam should not be done if placenta previa is suspected.  
This is because a pelvic exam can cause sudden, dangerous bleeding.  
A speculum exam (looking at the cervix with a tool) is safe.  
The best way to check for placenta previa is with an ultrasound.  
A transvaginal ultrasound gives the clearest picture.  
This test is safe and accurate.  
It helps tell the difference between placenta previa and placental abruption.  
Placental abruption causes pain and tenderness in the belly.  
But the two conditions can look similar.  
So ultrasound is needed to be sure.

> **Important:** If you have vaginal bleeding in the second or third trimester, get an ultrasound before any pelvic exam.

All women with suspected placenta previa should have their baby’s heart rate checked.  
This helps make sure the baby is doing well.

## How Is Placenta Previa Treated?

If you have a first episode of bleeding before 36 weeks, you will likely need to stay in the hospital.  
You will be told to rest and avoid activities that raise pressure in your belly.  
This means staying off your feet most of the day.  
You should also avoid sex.  
Sex can cause contractions and lead to bleeding.  
If the bleeding stops, you may be allowed to go home.  
You can slowly return to normal activity.

If you have a second episode of bleeding, you will likely be readmitted.  
You may stay in the hospital until delivery.  
Your care will be based on your health and your baby’s health.

If early delivery is likely before 34 weeks, your doctor may give you medicine to help your baby’s lungs mature.  
This medicine is called corticosteroids.  
It can also be given between 34 and 36 weeks if you have not had it before.  
This helps protect your baby if born early.

Delivery is planned at 36 to 37 weeks and six days if both you and your baby are stable.  
You do not need to wait for proof that your baby’s lungs are ready.  
This timing helps reduce risks.

You will need a cesarean delivery (C-section) if:
- You are bleeding heavily or the bleeding is not stopping.
- The baby’s heart rate is not normal.
- You are feeling weak, dizzy, or have low blood pressure.

A C-section is the safest way to deliver when the placenta covers the birth canal.

In rare cases, a vaginal birth may be possible if:
- The placenta is near the opening but not covering it.
- The edge of the placenta is 1.5 to 2 centimeters from the opening.
- You and your doctor agree it is safe after discussing the risks and benefits.

If you have severe bleeding, you may go into shock.  
This is a serious condition.  
It needs quick treatment.  
If you have Rh-negative blood, you will get a shot to prevent problems in future pregnancies.  
This shot is called Rho(D) immune globulin.

## Key Points

- Placenta previa means the placenta covers or is near the opening of the birth canal.
- It often causes sudden, painless vaginal bleeding in the second or third trimester.
- Placental abruption usually causes belly pain. But the two can look similar.
- Always check for placenta previa with ultrasound before doing a pelvic exam if you have bleeding after 20 weeks.
- For a first episode of bleeding before 36 weeks, stay in the hospital, rest, and avoid sex.
- Give corticosteroids to help the baby’s lungs if delivery may happen before 34 weeks, or between 34 and 36 weeks if not given before.
- Deliver by C-section if you or your baby are unstable.
- If you and your baby are stable, deliver between 36 and 37 weeks and six days.

# Misuse of Anxiety and Sleep Medications

These medicines are prescribed to help with anxiety or trouble sleeping. But they can be misused. This can lead to addiction and a substance use disorder.

## What These Medications Are

Medicines for anxiety (antianxiety drugs) and sleep (sedatives or sleep aids) include:
- Benzodiazepines (like diazepam and lorazepam)
- Barbiturates
- Zolpidem
- Eszopiclone
- Other similar drugs

Each medicine works differently. Each also has a different risk of causing dependence and tolerance.

Dependence means your body needs the drug to feel normal. Tolerance means you need more of the drug to get the same effect.

You are dependent if you feel sick when you stop taking the drug.  
You have a substance use disorder if you keep using the drug even when it causes problems.

Most people who become dependent started using these drugs for a real medical reason.  
Dependence can start in as little as two weeks of daily use.

---

## Signs and Symptoms of Overuse

These medicines slow down your brain and body. They can cause:

- Slurred speech  
- Poor balance or coordination  
- Confusion  

These effects get worse if you also drink alcohol.

Older adults may have stronger side effects. These can include:
- Dizziness  
- Disorientation  
- Delirium  
- Loss of balance  
- Falls that can break bones, especially the hip

Higher doses can cause:
- Stupor (you can only be woken up with great effort)  
- Very slow and shallow breathing  
- Death (especially with barbiturates)

Some people also have:
- Memory problems  
- Poor judgment  
- Trouble focusing  
- Strong mood swings  
- Slow speech  
- Difficulty thinking or understanding others  
- Involuntary eye movements (eyes moving without control)

Withdrawal symptoms can start within 12 to 24 hours after stopping.  
The type and severity depend on the drug and how much you took.

---

## Withdrawal Symptoms

If you have used benzodiazepines for more than a few days, you may feel you cannot sleep without them.  
When you stop, you may feel:
- Anxiety or nervousness at bedtime  
- Trouble sleeping  
- Bad dreams  
- Irritability when you wake up  

More serious withdrawal symptoms can include:
- Fast heartbeat  
- Fast breathing  
- Confusion  
- Seizures  

Barbiturate withdrawal can be very dangerous.  
Stopping suddenly after long-term use can cause a severe reaction. This is similar to alcohol withdrawal.

Other serious effects include:
- Dehydration  
- Delirium  
- Severe insomnia  
- Confusion  
- Hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there)

Because of the risk, people are usually treated in the hospital during withdrawal.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose the Problem

Doctors usually ask what medicines you took.  
They may also talk to friends or family.

If you are sleepy or confused, doctors check for other causes. These can include:
- Low blood sugar  
- Head injury  

Some drug tests can find benzodiazepines and barbiturates.  
But finding the drug does not always mean it caused the symptoms.  
Most hospitals cannot measure how much of the drug is in your blood.

---

## How Doctors Treat the Problem

### Overdose Treatment

If someone takes too much of these medicines, they need emergency care.  
An overdose of barbiturates is just as dangerous as one of benzodiazepines.

If breathing, heart, or blood pressure is affected, the person must be hospitalized.  
They may be placed in an intensive care unit for close monitoring.

Supportive care includes:
- Fluids through a vein  
- Medicines to raise blood pressure if needed  
- A breathing machine (ventilator) if breathing is weak

### Antidote for Benzodiazepines

A medicine called flumazenil can reverse a serious benzodiazepine overdose.  
But it can cause withdrawal symptoms and seizures in people who have used benzodiazepines for a long time.  
Because of this risk, doctors do not use flumazenil unless absolutely necessary.

### Treatment for Barbiturate Overdose

Doctors can give sodium bicarbonate through a vein.  
This helps the body get rid of barbiturates through urine.

---

## Withdrawal Treatment

People with mild withdrawal symptoms need support.  
This includes counseling and help to stay away from the drug.

People with severe withdrawal need hospital care.  
They may be in an intensive care unit.  
They are given small doses of the same medicine through a vein.  
The dose is slowly lowered over days or weeks.  
Then the medicine is stopped.

Sometimes, doctors switch to a similar medicine that is easier to stop.  
Even with good treatment, it may take a month or more to feel normal again.

---

# Bulimia Nervosa – Simple Explanation

Bulimia nervosa is a serious mental health condition. It involves cycles of eating large amounts of food quickly, followed by actions to prevent weight gain.

## What Happens in Bulimia Nervosa?

- People with bulimia have repeated episodes of binge eating.
- A binge means eating a very large amount of food in a short time.
- They feel they cannot stop eating during a binge.
- After a binge, they try to get rid of the food or calories.
- Common ways to do this include:
  - Making themselves throw up.
  - Using laxatives or water pills.
  - Not eating for long periods.
  - Exercising too much.

These episodes happen at least once a week for three months or more.

## Who Gets Bulimia Nervosa?

- It affects about 0.5% of women and 0.1% of men over their lifetime.
- People with bulimia are often very worried about their body shape and weight.
- They are usually at a normal weight or above. They do not lose a lot of weight like people with anorexia.

## What Triggers Bulimia?

- It is more common in cultures that value being very thin.
- Sports or activities that focus on body shape or weight (like gymnastics or ballet) can increase the risk.

## Signs and Symptoms

- Binge eating often happens in secret.
- People eat fast and eat much more than most people would in the same time.
- They often choose sweet or high-fat foods like ice cream or cake.
- Binges can happen several times a day.
- Stress often triggers a binge.
- After eating, they feel guilty or ashamed.
- They may try to hide their behavior.

## Physical Signs of Bulimia

- Swollen glands in the face (salivary glands).
- Scars on the back of the hands from using fingers to make themselves throw up.
- Teeth that are worn down or damaged.
- Sore throat or pain when swallowing.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- A doctor or mental health expert will talk to the person about their eating habits and feelings.
- They may do blood tests to check for problems with body chemicals like potassium.
- The diagnosis is based on clear patterns of behavior over time.

### Criteria for Diagnosis (DSM-5-TR):

- Binge eating at least once a week for 3 months.
- Using actions like vomiting or fasting to control weight at least once a week for 3 months.
- Feeling that body shape and weight are too important in how they see themselves.

## Treatment Options

Bulimia can be treated. The best results come from combining therapy and medicine.

### 1. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)

- This is the most effective treatment.
- It usually takes 4 to 5 months with 16 to 20 sessions.
- It can be done one-on-one or in a group.
- CBT helps people:
  - Want to change their behavior.
  - Eat in a regular, healthy way.
  - Stop being overly focused on weight and body shape.
  - Avoid relapse.

- About 35% to 50% of people stop bingeing and purging after CBT.
- Many others improve, but some do not finish treatment or do not respond.

### 2. Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT)

- This helps people fix problems in their relationships.
- It does not focus directly on food or weight.
- It is a good option if CBT is not available.

### 3. Medication – SSRIs

- These are antidepressants that also help with bulimia.
- They reduce the number of binges and vomiting.
- They are not enough on their own. They work best with therapy.
- Fluoxetine is the most commonly used SSRI for bulimia.
- The dose is higher than what is used for depression alone.
- SSRIs also help with anxiety and depression, which often go with bulimia.

## Complications

- Repeated vomiting can damage teeth and the throat.
- Low potassium levels (hypokalemia) can happen. This can be dangerous.
- Rare but serious risks include:
  - A tear in the esophagus or stomach.
  - Heart problems.

## Key Points

- Bulimia nervosa means repeated binge eating followed by actions to avoid weight gain.
- People with bulimia are usually not underweight.
- Vomiting can damage teeth and the throat.
- Low potassium levels can occur and be serious.
- Heart problems are rare but possible.
- Treatment works best with cognitive behavioral therapy and sometimes an SSRI.

# What Is Botulism?

Botulism is a rare but serious illness. It happens when a powerful poison gets into your body. This poison comes from a type of bacteria called *Clostridium botulinum*. These bacteria live in soil, water, and dust.

The poison can cause muscle weakness or paralysis. It can be deadly if not treated quickly.

---

## How Does Botulism Happen?

The bacteria *Clostridium botulinum* make a poison. This poison is the strongest known poison. It stops nerves from sending signals to muscles. Without these signals, muscles cannot move.

The bacteria do not need oxygen to survive. They are called anaerobes.

The poison blocks a chemical called acetylcholine. This chemical tells muscles to contract. When the signal stops, muscles go limp.

In very small amounts, the same poison is used to treat muscle spasms and reduce wrinkles. But only doctors should use it.

---

## Types of Botulism

There are several types of botulism. The most common are:

- **Foodborne botulism** – from eating contaminated food  
- **Wound botulism** – from a wound infected with the bacteria  
- **Infant botulism** – affects babies under one year old  
- **Adult intestinal toxemia botulism** – rare, happens when the bacteria grow in the intestines of older children and adults

---

### Foodborne Botulism

This happens when you eat food that has the botulism poison in it.

The poison comes from bacteria that grow in food. These bacteria are often in soil and water. They can get into food during canning or storage.

The most common sources are:

- Home-canned foods, especially low-acid ones like green beans, asparagus, beets, and corn  
- Garlic or herbs stored in oil  
- Canned tomatoes  
- Baked potatoes wrapped in foil and left out too long  
- Home-canned or fermented fish  

Sometimes, store-bought foods cause botulism. This happens in about 10% of cases. Common sources include vegetables, fish, fruits, and condiments like salsa.

Refrigerating food does not stop the bacteria from making poison. Some toxins can grow at refrigerator temperatures.

---

### Wound Botulism

This happens when the bacteria get into a wound. They grow in the wound and make poison.

This can happen if:

- You inject drugs with dirty needles  
- You use contaminated heroin  
- You have a deep cut or burn that gets infected  

The poison then enters your blood and spreads through your body.

---

### Infant Botulism

This affects babies under one year old.

Babies can get the bacteria from swallowing soil or honey. The bacteria grow in their intestines and make poison.

Honey should never be given to babies under one year old.

---

### Adult Intestinal Toxemia Botulism

This is rare. It happens when the bacteria grow in the intestines of older children and adults.

It is more likely in people who:

- Have had stomach or intestine surgery  
- Have inflammatory bowel disease  
- Have been on antibiotics for a long time  

The cause is not always clear.

---

## Symptoms of Botulism

All types of botulism cause similar symptoms. They start slowly and get worse over time.

Common early signs:

- Dry mouth  
- Trouble swallowing or talking  
- Blurred or double vision  
- Drooping eyelids  
- Eyes that do not react to light  
- Slurred speech  

Later symptoms:

- Weakness in arms and legs  
- Trouble breathing  
- Muscle paralysis  

The mind stays clear. You can think normally, but your muscles do not work.

Because swallowing is hard, food or saliva can go into the lungs. This can cause choking or pneumonia.

Muscle weakness usually starts in the face and head. Then it moves to the arms, legs, and breathing muscles.

If breathing muscles stop working, you can die without help.

---

### When Do Symptoms Start?

- **Foodborne botulism**: Symptoms usually start 18 to 36 hours after eating the bad food. But they can start as early as 4 hours or as late as 8 days.  
  The more poison you eat, the faster you get sick.  
  Early signs are often nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, and diarrhea. Later, people often become constipated.

- **Wound botulism**: No digestive symptoms. Symptoms start slowly and get worse over days.

---

## How Is Botulism Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect botulism based on symptoms. But other illnesses can look similar.

To confirm the diagnosis, doctors may:

- Test food, blood, or stool for the poison  
- Do an electromyography (EMG) test  
  - This checks how muscles respond to electrical signals  
  - In botulism, muscles react abnormally

For **foodborne botulism**, doctors look for a common food source. If several people got sick after eating the same food, it is more likely.

For **wound botulism**, doctors check for a wound. They may look for signs of drug use.

The diagnosis is confirmed if the poison is found in blood or stool, or if the bacteria are found in a wound sample.

Sometimes, it is hard to tell if the illness came from food or a wound.

---

## How Is Botulism Treated?

Botulism is a medical emergency. Go to the hospital right away.

Treatment includes:

- **Antitoxin** – a medicine that blocks the poison  
  - Given as soon as possible after symptoms start  
  - Most helpful if given within 72 hours  
  - Works best in adults and older children  
  - Not used in babies under one year old  
  - A special antitoxin is used for infant botulism  
  - Some people have serious allergic reactions to the antitoxin  
  - Others may get a reaction called serum sickness

- **Activated charcoal** – if the poison was eaten  
  - Helps remove poison from the stomach before it is absorbed

- **Mechanical ventilator** – a machine that helps you breathe  
  - Used if breathing muscles fail  
  - This has reduced deaths from botulism to less than 10%

- **Feeding tube** – if you cannot swallow  
  - A thin tube goes through the nose and into the stomach  
  - Food is given through the tube

- **Wound care** – for wound botulism  
  - The wound is cleaned well  
  - Dead tissue is removed  
  - Antibiotics like penicillin or metronidazole are given through a vein

Recovery can take months. Some people feel tired and short of breath for years. Physical therapy may help.

You do not become immune after one case. You can get botulism again.

---

## How to Prevent Botulism

You can prevent most cases by handling food safely.

### Safe Food Handling Tips

- Cook food at 176 degrees Fahrenheit (79.9 degrees Celsius) for 30 minutes. This destroys the poison.
- Never eat food from cans that are swollen, leaking, or smell bad.
- Throw away any canned food that looks or smells spoiled.
- Follow safe home-canning instructions from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
- Refrigerate homemade garlic or herb oils. Throw them away after 4 days.
- Keep baked potatoes wrapped in foil hot until served. Do not leave them at room temperature.
- If you are unsure about a can, test it before opening:
  - Put a few drops of water on the spot to be punctured.
  - If water is pushed out when you open the can, the can is bad. Throw it away.
- When in doubt, throw it out. It is safer than risking illness.

### Handling Contaminated Food

- Do not touch contaminated food with bare hands.
- Wash hands well after handling suspect food.
- Dispose of contaminated food carefully.

### Preventing Wound Botulism

- Clean all wounds right away.
- Do not inject drugs with dirty needles.
- Seek medical help if a wound becomes infected.

---

The following resources can help:

# Knee Pain

Knee pain is a common issue. It affects many athletes and people who are not athletes.

## What Causes Knee Pain?

Many things can cause pain in or around the knee, especially in runners. These include:

- The kneecap moves out of place when you bend your knee.
- The cartilage under the kneecap softens. This is called runner’s knee.
- Tears in the meniscus (the cushioning tissue in the knee).
- A fold in the lining inside the knee becomes inflamed.
- The fat pad under the kneecap becomes irritated.
- A small crack in the shin bone. This is called a stress fracture.
- The leg bones are not lined up properly.
- The tendon below the kneecap becomes inflamed. This is called jumper’s knee.
- Pain from the lower back or hip can feel like it is coming from the knee.
- Problems with the feet, such as rolling the foot inward too much when walking or running, can cause knee pain.

## How Is Knee Pain Diagnosed?

Doctors use two main tools to find the cause of knee pain:

- A detailed conversation about your symptoms and training.
- A physical exam of your legs and knees.

Your doctor will ask about when your pain started. They will also ask what makes it worse. They will check your whole leg, from your hip to your foot.

Certain signs can point to specific problems:

- If your knee locks or catches, you may have a torn meniscus.
- If your knee feels unstable or gives way when you turn, you may have a ligament injury or a kneecap that moves out of place.

Pain in the front of the knee after running, especially uphill, may be due to soft cartilage under the kneecap. Pain and stiffness after sitting for a while is also a sign. This is called the movie sign.

Pressing on the kneecap while bending the knee can cause pain if the cartilage is damaged.

If pain gets worse when you put weight on the leg, it may be a stress fracture.

## How Is Knee Pain Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause of the pain.

### General Treatments

- Strengthening exercises for the front thigh muscles (quadriceps).
- Sometimes, using pads, supports, or braces.
- Pain relievers like ibuprofen or naproxen.

### Specific Treatments

- For soft cartilage under the kneecap (runner’s knee):
  - Exercises to strengthen the front thigh muscles.
  - Exercises to balance the back thigh muscles.
  - Arch supports in your shoes if your feet roll inward too much.
  - Pain relievers if needed.

- For a kneecap that moves out of place:
  - Use of special pads or braces.
  - This is especially helpful in sports like basketball or tennis that require quick changes in direction.

- If your feet roll inward too much and no other cause is found:
  - Custom shoe inserts (orthotics) may help.

- For a stress fracture:
  - Stop all weight-bearing activities.
  - Rest until the bone heals.

- For internal knee problems like meniscus tears:
  - Surgery may be needed.

---

# Goldenseal

Goldenseal is a plant that is now rare and at risk of disappearing. It is related to the buttercup family. The plant contains two main active ingredients: beta-hydrastine and berberine. These ingredients can kill germs. Berberine may also help with diarrhea. You can buy goldenseal as a liquid, tablet, or capsule.

## What People Use Goldenseal For

Some people use goldenseal as a cleaning wash for mouth sores, sore or swollen eyes, cuts, and irritated skin. It is also used as a vaginal wash for infections. It is often mixed with echinacea to help with colds. Some people take it to ease stomach problems or diarrhea. Because berberine may lower blood sugar, some people use goldenseal to help control their blood sugar levels.

## What Research Shows

There is no strong proof that goldenseal helps with colds. However, studies show that berberine alone can reduce diarrhea, including diarrhea linked to irritable bowel syndrome. Early research suggests that berberine may help people with diabetes by lowering blood sugar levels before meals and after eating. It may also lower long-term blood sugar levels, as shown by a test called HbA1C. Berberine may also help lower cholesterol, blood pressure, and body weight.

## Side Effects of Goldenseal

Goldenseal can cause many side effects. These include stomach upset, anxiety, and contractions of the uterus. It may cause jaundice in newborn babies. Taking too much goldenseal can lead to seizures, trouble breathing, and heart problems. 

Do not take goldenseal if you are:
- Pregnant or breastfeeding
- A newborn baby
- Have a history of seizures
- Have a problem with blood clotting

Berberine may harm DNA in some cells. Scientists do not yet know what this means for people.

## Drug Interactions

Goldenseal can make blood-thinning medicines, like warfarin, stronger. This increases the risk of bleeding. It can also change how the liver handles certain medicines. This may cause other problems.

For example:
- Goldenseal may raise levels of blood pressure medicines. This could make blood pressure too low.
- Berberine may stop one blood pressure medicine, losartan, from working as well.
- Goldenseal may raise levels of cyclosporine, a medicine used after organ transplants.
- Goldenseal may lower levels of metformin, a common diabetes medicine. This could make blood sugar harder to control.
- Berberine may increase the effect of other diabetes medicines, which could cause blood sugar to drop too low.

## Recommendations

Goldenseal can cause serious side effects and dangerous drug interactions. The possible health benefits are small and can usually be achieved with safer, proven medicines. Because of this, goldenseal is not recommended. Pregnant or breastfeeding women should not take it.

# Injury to the Outer Ear

The outer part of the ear (also called the pinna or auricle) can get hurt in several ways.
