# Pancreas Transplant

A pancreas transplant is a surgery to put a healthy pancreas into someone whose pancreas no longer makes enough insulin. This usually happens when a person has severe diabetes.

The new pancreas comes from a person who recently died. In rare cases, part of a pancreas can come from a living donor.

## Why a Pancreas Transplant Is Done

The transplant is done for people with diabetes when their body cannot make enough insulin. After the transplant:

- More than 80% of people have normal blood sugar levels.
- Most no longer need insulin shots.

But they must take medicine to stop their body from rejecting the new organ. These medicines can cause infections and other side effects.

Insulin shots are safe and work well for most people with diabetes. So, being free of insulin is not enough reason to have a pancreas transplant.

A pancreas transplant is usually only done if:

- The person also has kidney failure.
- Blood sugar levels are hard to control.
- The person does not feel when blood sugar drops too low.

Low blood sugar that lasts too long can damage the brain and other organs.

Because diabetes often harms the kidneys, many people who need a pancreas transplant also need a kidney transplant. Over 90% of people who get a pancreas transplant also get a kidney transplant at the same time.

Having both transplants at once is safe. The surgery and recovery are similar to having just one transplant.

A pancreas transplant may help people who still have high blood sugar even when taking insulin. It may also help those who have dangerous low blood sugar after insulin.

Sometimes, only the insulin-making cells from the pancreas are transplanted. This is called pancreatic islet cell transplantation.

More than 95% of people live at least one year after the transplant.

## Screening Before the Transplant

Both the donor and the person getting the transplant go through screening.

This checks that the organ is healthy and that the person is well enough for the surgery.

### Who Can Be a Donor?

A donor is usually someone who:

- Recently died.
- Was between 10 and 55 years old.
- Did not have a problem with alcohol.
- Did not have prediabetes or diabetes.

If both a pancreas and a kidney are being transplanted, they must come from the same donor.

A living person can donate part of their pancreas, but this is rare. It carries serious risks for the donor.

## The Transplant Surgery

There are three main types of pancreas transplant:

- Pancreas and kidney at the same time (simultaneous transplant).
- Kidney first, then pancreas later (pancreas-after-kidney).
- Pancreas only (pancreas-alone).

The surgery is major. It requires a large cut in the belly and general anesthesia. The person’s own pancreas stays in place.

The surgery usually takes about 3 hours. Most people stay in the hospital for 1 to 3 weeks.

Medicine to stop the body from rejecting the new organ (called immunosuppressants) starts the same day as the surgery. These medicines help prevent rejection.

## Possible Problems After the Transplant

A transplant can cause complications. These may include:

- Infections.
- Rejection of the new organ.
- Side effects from the medicines.
- Bleeding or blood clots.
- Problems with the new pancreas not working right.

These risks are carefully managed by the medical team.

# Manometry

Manometry measures pressure inside parts of the digestive system.

A thin tube with sensors is passed through the mouth or anus into the digestive tract. The tube measures pressure in the area being studied.

This test is usually done when other tests show no structural problems. It helps find issues with how the digestive system moves food.

Manometry is used in the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, sphincter of Oddi, and rectum.

The test is safe. Side effects are rare. Some people feel mild discomfort. You must not eat or drink after midnight before the test.

An added test called impedance planimetry can give more information when used with manometry.

---

## Anorectal Manometry

This test checks the muscles around the anus and how well the rectum senses pressure.

It helps diagnose problems in people with bowel leakage or constipation.

It can help find Hirschsprung disease and issues with passing stool.

It can also help train patients with bowel leakage using biofeedback.

A small balloon is placed in the rectum during the test. Air is added to the balloon to check how the rectum responds.

The balloon expulsion test is often done at the same time. It checks how well a person can push out the balloon. This gives a clear measure of how well the rectum works.

---

## Barostat

A barostat is a device that measures how well the digestive tract stretches and adjusts.

It has a small balloon made of plastic and a small electronic control unit.

The control unit adds or removes air from the balloon to keep pressure steady.

This device is mainly used in research studies. It helps doctors understand how people feel pain or discomfort in the gut. It is often used in people with long-term digestive problems that have no clear cause.

---

## Esophageal Manometry

This test checks how well the esophagus works.

It is used for people with trouble swallowing, heartburn, food coming back up, or chest pain.

The test measures pressure in the upper and lower esophagus. It checks how well the muscles squeeze food down. It also finds abnormal muscle movements.

It can help diagnose conditions like achalasia, distal spasm, systemic sclerosis, and problems with the lower esophageal sphincter.

It is also used before certain treatments. For example, before surgery to prevent acid reflux or before a procedure to open a tight esophagus.

High-resolution manometry can be used with impedance planimetry. This lets doctors see how food moves through the esophagus during swallowing.

---

## Gastroduodenal Manometry

This test measures pressure in the lower stomach, the first part of the small intestine, and the upper part of the small intestine.

Sensors are placed in these areas. Pressure is recorded for 5 to 24 hours. The test is done when the stomach is empty and after eating.

It is used for people who have symptoms of poor digestion but whose stomach emptying tests were normal. It is also used when treatments have not worked.

The test helps find out if symptoms come from a muscle problem (weak or strong contractions) or a nerve problem (irregular timing of contractions).

# Dacryocystitis

Dacryocystitis is an infection in the tear sac.  
This happens when the tube that carries tears from the eye to the nose becomes blocked.  

The tear sac is a small space where tears collect.  
Tears flow from the eye into this sac.  
From there, they drain into the nose through a small tube called the nasolacrimal duct.  

When this tube is blocked, tears can’t drain properly.  
This can lead to infection in the tear sac.  

---

## How Tears Work

Tears are made in glands near the eyes.  
They keep the eyes wet and clean.  
They flow from the eye into the tear sac.  
Then they move through the nasolacrimal duct into the nose.  

---

## Types of Dacryocystitis

Dacryocystitis can happen suddenly (acute).  
It can also last for a long time (chronic).  

---

## Symptoms

### Acute Dacryocystitis

The area near the tear sac becomes painful, red, and swollen.  
The skin around the eye may turn red and water.  
Pus may leak from the eye.  
Pressing on the tear sac may push thick fluid out through the small opening at the inner corner of the eyelid.  
This opening is called the punctum.  
Because tears can’t drain, the eye waters more than normal.  
Some people also get a fever.  
In rare cases, a pocket of pus forms under the skin.  
This can break open and drain through the skin.  

### Chronic Dacryocystitis

The skin over the tear sac may bulge.  
Pressing on the area may not hurt.  
But a thick, pus-like fluid often comes out of the punctum.  
People with this condition often have long-term pink eye (chronic conjunctivitis).  

---

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Doctors look at your symptoms.  
They examine your eye and the area near the nose.  
They may press on the tear sac to see if fluid comes out.  
They do not usually need special tests.  

---

## Treatment

### For Acute Dacryocystitis

You will take antibiotics by mouth.  
If the infection is severe or you have a fever, you may need antibiotics through a vein.  
Apply warm, damp cloths to the area several times a day.  
This helps reduce swelling and pain.  
After the infection clears, surgery is usually needed.  
The surgery creates a new path for tears to drain into the nose.  
This prevents future infections.  

### For Chronic Dacryocystitis

Surgery is the main treatment.  
It is called dacryocystorhinostomy, or DCR.  
This surgery creates a new drainage route for tears.  
It helps stop the infection from coming back.  

Early surgery can help clear the infection faster.  
It also lowers the chance of future problems.

# What Is Malabsorption?

Malabsorption means your body does not take in enough nutrients from the food you eat.  
This can happen because of problems in digestion, absorption, or moving nutrients through the body.

Malabsorption can affect:
- Large nutrients like proteins, carbs, and fats.
- Small nutrients like vitamins and minerals.  
Or it can affect both.

When this happens, your body loses too many nutrients in your stool.  
This leads to poor nutrition and health problems.  
It can also cause stomach and bowel symptoms.

Malabsorption can be:
- **Global**: You cannot absorb most nutrients.
- **Partial (isolated)**: You only have trouble with certain nutrients.

---

## How Malabsorption Works

Your body breaks down food and takes in nutrients in three main steps:

1. **Food is broken down in the gut**  
   Enzymes in your gut break down fats, proteins, and carbs.  
   Bile helps fats mix with water so they can be digested.

2. **Nutrients are taken in through the gut lining**  
   Enzymes on the surface of the gut lining finish breaking down food.  
   The small pieces are then pulled into the body.

3. **Nutrients travel through the body’s lymph system**  
   Fats and some other nutrients move through small tubes called lymph vessels.

If any of these steps fail, you may have malabsorption.  
But if the first step fails, it is more accurate to call it **maldigestion**, not malabsorption.

---

## What Causes Malabsorption?

Many things can cause malabsorption. Here are the main causes:

### Problems with Mixing or Moving Food
- After certain stomach surgeries (like Billroth II gastrectomy).
- A connection between the stomach and colon (gastrocolic fistula).
- A surgery that connects the stomach to the small intestine (gastroenterostomy).

### Not Enough Digestive Enzymes or Bile
- Autoimmune damage to the stomach lining.
- Blockage in the bile ducts.
- Liver disease like cirrhosis.
- Chronic pancreatitis.
- Medicines that remove bile acids (like cholestyramine).
- Cystic fibrosis.
- Lactose intolerance (lack of lactase enzyme).
- Pancreatic cancer.
- Removal of part of the pancreas.
- Lack of sucrase-isomaltase (an enzyme for sugar digestion).

### Problems with the Gut Environment
- Slow or fast movement of food through the small intestine (due to diabetes, scleroderma, or thyroid problems).
- Overgrowth of bacteria in the small intestine (SIBO), which can happen after surgery or in people with diverticula.
- Too much acid in the small intestine (as in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome).

### Damage to the Gut Lining
- Acute infections (bacterial, viral, or parasitic) can harm the tiny finger-like parts of the gut (villi and microvilli).
- Alcohol can damage the gut lining.
- Some antibiotics (like neomycin) can harm the gut.

- Chronic damage to the gut lining can be caused by:
  - Amyloidosis (a rare disease where abnormal proteins build up).
  - Celiac disease (an immune reaction to gluten).
  - Crohn disease (a type of inflammatory bowel disease).
  - Poor blood flow to the gut (ischemia).
  - Radiation damage to the gut.
  - Tropical sprue (a condition in tropical areas).
  - Whipple disease (a rare bacterial infection).
  - Having had a large part of the small intestine removed (short bowel syndrome).
  - Weight-loss surgery (jejunoileal bypass).
  - Lymphoma or tuberculosis blocking the lymph vessels.

### Problems with Nutrient Transport
- Abetalipoproteinemia (a rare genetic disorder that stops fat transport).
- Addison disease (a hormone problem).
- Lack of intrinsic factor (needed for vitamin B12 absorption, as in pernicious anemia).
- Lymphangiectasia (swollen lymph vessels in the gut).

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

When your body does not absorb nutrients, you may have:
- Diarrhea (loose, watery stools).
- Fatty stools (steatorrhea).
- Bloating and gas in the belly.
- Weight loss, even if you eat enough.

### Fatty Stools (Steatorrhea)
- This happens when more than 7 grams of fat pass out in your stool each day.
- The stool is pale, greasy, and smells very bad.
- It floats in the toilet.

### Symptoms from Missing Nutrients
Missing certain vitamins or minerals causes specific problems:

| Symptom | Missing Nutrient |
|--------|------------------|
| Pale, small red blood cells (anemia) | Iron |
| Large red blood cells (anemia) | Vitamin B12, folate |
| Easy bruising or bleeding | Vitamins K and C |
| Muscle cramps in hands and feet | Calcium, magnesium |
| Swelling in the body (edema) | Protein |
| Sore or red tongue | B vitamins (B1, B2, B3, B6, B12), folate, niacin, iron |
| Trouble seeing in low light | Vitamin A |
| Pain in bones, weak bones, broken bones | Potassium, magnesium, calcium, vitamin D |
| Numbness or tingling in hands and feet | B vitamins (B1, B6, B12) |
| Missed periods | Undernutrition (common in young women with celiac disease) |

---

## How Is Malabsorption Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your symptoms and medical history.  
They may do tests to confirm the problem and find the cause.

### Step 1: Look at Your History
- Do you have long-term diarrhea?
- Have you lost weight even though you eat?
- Do you have anemia?

These signs make doctors suspect malabsorption.

### Step 2: Check for Common Causes
- If you had many episodes of pancreatitis, it may be chronic pancreatitis.
- If you have diarrhea that gets worse after eating gluten, it may be celiac disease.
- If you have yellow skin or eyes (jaundice), it may be liver disease or pancreatic cancer.
- If diarrhea starts 30 to 90 minutes after eating carbs, you may lack a sugar-digesting enzyme (like lactase).

### Step 3: Blood Tests
These tests help check for nutrient shortages and general health:
- Complete blood count (CBC)
- Red blood cell size and shape
- Iron levels (ferritin)
- Vitamin B12 and folate levels
- Calcium
- Albumin (a protein made by the liver)
- Cholesterol
- Blood clotting time (prothrombin time)

These results can point to a possible cause.

### Step 4: Stool Test
A test to measure fat in your stool can confirm malabsorption if it’s unclear.

### Step 5: Further Tests
Based on the results, doctors may use:
- Endoscopy (a camera to look inside the gut).
- Imaging tests (like X-rays with contrast).
- Other special tests.

---

### Key Clues from Blood Tests

- **Large red blood cells (macrocytic anemia)**  
  Check vitamin B12 and folate levels.  
  Low B12 can happen in pernicious anemia, chronic pancreatitis, SIBO, or ileal disease.  
  Low B12 with high folate may mean SIBO — because gut bacteria use B12 and make folate.

- **Small red blood cells (microcytic anemia)**  
  This usually means low iron.  
  This can happen in celiac disease.

- **Low albumin**  
  This can mean poor nutrition, liver disease, or protein loss.

- **Low carotene (a form of vitamin A)**  
  If you eat enough vitamin A but still have low levels, it may mean malabsorption.

---

## Summary

Malabsorption means your body does not absorb enough nutrients from food.  
It can affect many nutrients or just one.  
It causes diarrhea, fatty stools, weight loss, and vitamin or mineral shortages.

Common causes include:
- Gut infections.
- Surgery.
- Diseases like celiac disease, Crohn disease, or pancreatitis.
- Bile or enzyme problems.
- Bacterial overgrowth in the small intestine.

Diagnosis starts with your symptoms and history.  
Blood and stool tests help confirm the problem.  
Further tests find the exact cause.

Early diagnosis and treatment can prevent serious health issues.

# Essential Thrombocythemia

Essential thrombocythemia is a condition where the body makes too many platelets. Platelets help blood to clot. When there are too many, they can cause blood clots or bleeding.

## What Happens in This Condition?

- The bone marrow makes too many blood cells.
- Platelets are made in the bone marrow by special cells called megakaryocytes.
- In this condition, these cells grow too fast and make too many platelets.
- This can lead to blood clots or bleeding.

There are two types:
- **Primary (essential)**: The problem is in the platelet-making cells.
- **Secondary**: Another illness causes the body to make more platelets than normal.

This condition usually affects people over age fifty. But younger people, especially young women, can also get it.

The cause is often a change in a gene. The most common genes involved are JAK2, CALR, and MPL. These changes make certain proteins work too hard. This leads to overproduction of blood cells.

## Possible Complications

Complications are rare but can be serious.

**Blood clots** can form in any blood vessel. They can block:
- Veins in the legs (deep vein thrombosis)
- Blood vessels in the brain (stroke)
- Blood vessels in the heart (heart attack)
- Blood vessels in the lungs (pulmonary embolism)

Clots in tiny blood vessels can affect the eyes, brain, or skin.

**Bleeding** can also happen. Even though more platelets are present, very high numbers can actually cause bleeding. This is because the extra platelets do not work properly.

## Symptoms

Some people have no symptoms. Others may have:

- Burning, red, or discolored hands and feet
- Cold fingertips
- Tingling or strange feelings in fingers, hands, or feet
- Chest pain
- Blurry vision or seeing spots
- Headaches
- Feeling weak
- Dizziness
- Mild bleeding, such as nosebleeds, easy bruising, bleeding gums, or blood in the stomach or intestines

The spleen may get bigger, but this is rare. It is more common in women.

Older adults with other health problems like diabetes or high blood pressure are at higher risk for serious clotting problems, such as stroke or heart attack.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests:

- **Blood tests**: Check the number of platelets and other blood cells.
- **Genetic tests**: Look for changes in the JAK2, CALR, or MPL genes.
- **Bone marrow biopsy**: Sometimes needed. A small sample of bone marrow is taken and examined under a microscope.

Doctors look for signs of other conditions that could cause high platelets. This helps them tell essential thrombocythemia apart from secondary thrombocythemia.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on symptoms and risks.

**Aspirin**:
- Helps reduce pain and warmth in hands and feet.
- Lowers the chance of blood clots.
- Not safe if you are bleeding heavily.

**Medications to lower platelet count**:
- These drugs slow down the overproduction of platelets.
- Common ones include: ruxolitinib, anagrelide, interferon-alpha, and hydroxyurea.
- These are used when clots or bleeding happen, not just because the platelet count is high.

**Plateletpheresis**:
- A procedure used in emergencies.
- Blood is taken out, platelets are removed, and the rest is returned.
- It works fast but only for a short time.
- Not a long-term fix.

## Outlook

Most people with this condition live a normal life span.

Some people may later develop other blood disorders:
- Polycythemia vera (more common in women)
- Myelofibrosis (more common in men)

# Liddle Syndrome

Liddle syndrome is a rare genetic condition. It causes high blood pressure and other health problems. It runs in families and is passed down from parents to children.

## What Happens in Liddle Syndrome?

The kidneys do not work properly. They lose too much potassium and keep too much sodium and water. This leads to high blood pressure. The problem comes from a part of the kidney called the epithelial sodium channel. This channel lets too much sodium into the body. It also causes the body to lose too much potassium.

This condition is not the same as other causes of high blood pressure. It acts like a condition called primary aldosteronism. But the body makes normal or low levels of two hormones: renin and aldosterone.

People with Liddle syndrome often get symptoms before age 35. They may have:
- High blood pressure
- Swelling from fluid buildup
- Low potassium levels in the blood
- Blood that is too alkaline (not acidic enough)

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find Liddle syndrome. These include:
- A urine test to check sodium levels
- Blood tests to check renin and aldosterone levels

A diagnosis is likely if:
- A young person has high blood pressure
- There is a family history of high blood pressure
- Urine sodium is low (less than 20 milliequivalents per liter)
- Blood renin and aldosterone levels are low
- The person gets better with certain medicines

A genetic test can confirm the diagnosis. This test looks for changes in the genes that control the sodium channel.

## How Is It Treated?

The best treatment uses medicines that block the overactive sodium channel. These are called potassium-sparing diuretics. They help the body get rid of extra sodium and water without losing potassium.

The two main medicines are:
- Triamterene: 100 to 200 milligrams by mouth, twice a day
- Amiloride: 5 to 20 milligrams by mouth, once a day

These medicines work by closing the sodium channels in the kidneys. This helps lower blood pressure and corrects potassium loss.

Spironolactone does not help. It is not effective for this condition.

## More Information

The following resource may be helpful:
- **GTR: Genetic Testing Registry**  
  This is a central website with information about genetic tests. It explains what each test is for, how reliable it is, and how useful it is. Tests are grouped by type, such as human tests or tests for diseases.

# Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia

This condition affects how your eyes move side to side. It happens when the nerves in the brain stem that connect eye movement control centers get damaged.

## What Happens

- Your eyes can still move up and down normally.
- Your eyes cannot move smoothly side to side.
- The eye on the damaged side cannot turn inward toward your nose.
- The eye on the damaged side can still turn outward.

## One-and-a-Half Syndrome

This is a more severe form of the same problem. It happens when the damage affects both the nerve fibers and the brain center that controls side-to-side eye movement.

- When you try to look to either side, the eye on the damaged side stays still in the middle.
- The other eye can turn outward but cannot turn inward.
- Up and down movements are still normal.

## Symptoms

- You may see double when looking to the side.
- You usually do not see double when looking straight ahead.

## Common Causes

### In older adults:
- A stroke. Usually only one eye is affected.

### In younger people:
- Multiple sclerosis. Both eyes are often affected.

### Other causes:
- Lyme disease
- Neurosyphilis (a type of syphilis that affects the nervous system)
- Brain tumors
- Head injuries
- Poor nutrition, such as in Wernicke encephalopathy
- Certain medicines, including:
  - Antipsychotic drugs (like phenothiazines)
  - Opioid painkillers
  - Tricyclic antidepressants

## How the Eyes Move

- The nerves that help both eyes move together side to side are damaged.
- These nerves connect parts of the brain that control the third, fourth, and sixth cranial nerves (which control eye movement).

## Important Note About Eye Movement

- Even if your eyes cannot turn inward when looking sideways, they can still turn inward when you focus on something close, like your finger.

## Treatment and Outlook

- The treatment and how well you recover depend on what caused the problem.
- If the cause is a stroke, recovery may be slow and incomplete.
- If the cause is multiple sclerosis, symptoms may come and go.
- Treating the underlying cause can help improve or stabilize your eye movement.

Always talk to your doctor about your symptoms and treatment options.

# What You Need to Know About Filarial Worm Infections

Filarial worms are small, thread-shaped parasites that live in the bodies of animals and people.  
Only a few types of these worms can infect humans.  

The adult worms live in the lymph system or under the skin.  
Female worms give birth to live young called microfilariae.  
These young worms travel through the blood or move through body tissues.  

When a mosquito or fly bites a person, it can swallow these microfilariae.  
Inside the insect, the microfilariae grow into a form that can infect a new person.  
The insect passes the infection to the next person when it bites.  

All filarial worms have similar life cycles.  
The main difference is where the adult worms live in the body.  

## Types of Filarial Infections

### Infections Under the Skin (Subcutaneous Filariasis)

- **Loiasis** is caused by a worm called *Loa loa*.  
  This worm lives under the skin and can sometimes move across the eye.  
  It is found mainly in parts of Africa.

- **Onchocerciasis** (also called river blindness) is caused by *Onchocerca volvulus*.  
  The worms live under the skin and can cause serious eye problems.  
  It is common in parts of Africa and Latin America.

### Infections in the Lymph System (Lymphatic Filariasis)

- **Bancroftian filariasis** and **Brugian filariasis** are caused by three types of worms:  
  *Wuchereria bancrofti*, *Brugia malayi*, and *Brugia timori*.  
  These worms live in the lymph system.  
  They can cause swelling in the arms, legs, or genitals.

### Other Types of Filarial Infections

- **Mansonellosis** is caused by three types of worms:  
  - *Mansonella perstans* lives in the lining of the chest, heart, or belly.  
  - *Mansonella ozzardi* lives under the skin.  
  - *Mansonella streptocerca* lives in the top layer of the skin.  
  These infections often cause mild or no symptoms.

- **Dirofilariasis** is caused by *Dirofilaria immitis*, a worm that normally infects dogs.  
  In people, the worm larvae may be found in the lungs.  
  Rarely, they can be found in the eyes, brain, or testicles.  
  But they do not grow into adult worms in humans.

## Testing for Filarial Infections

Some special labs can test blood for signs of filarial infection.  
These tests can find infections caused by *Wuchereria*, *Brugia*, *Onchocerca*, and *Mansonella* worms.  

The tests are very good at detecting the infection.  
But they cannot tell which specific worm is causing the problem.  
They also cannot say if the infection is active or happened in the past.  

This makes the test less helpful for people who live in areas where these worms are common.  
But it is still useful for travelers who have symptoms.

# Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE)

This is a bone problem that happens when the top part of the thighbone slips off the neck of the thighbone. It occurs at the growth plate near the hip joint.

- The growth plate is a soft area of cartilage near the end of a bone.  
- Children’s bones grow from these growth plates.  
- This condition usually starts during early teenage years.  
- It is more common in boys.  
- Being overweight is a major risk factor.  
- Many children who get it in one hip will later get it in the other hip.

## What Happens in SCFE?

The head of the thighbone (the ball part of the hip joint) slips off the neck of the bone. This happens at the upper growth plate near the hip. The growth plate weakens over time. When this happens, the bone can slip out of place.

The exact cause is not known. But it may be linked to:
- Injury to the hip
- Hip shape problems
- Being overweight
- Inflammation in the body
- Hormone changes during puberty
- Low thyroid hormone levels

When the bone slips, it can cut off blood flow to the top of the thighbone. Without blood, the bone can break down and collapse.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The first sign is often stiffness or mild pain in the hip.  
The pain may feel like it is in the knee or thigh instead.  
Rest helps ease the pain.  
Walking or moving the hip makes the pain worse.  
Later, a limp appears.  
Hip pain spreads down the inside of the thigh to the knee.  
The affected leg turns outward.

## How Is SCFE Diagnosed?

Doctors use imaging tests to check for the problem.

- X-rays of both hips are taken.  
- The x-ray of the affected hip shows the head of the thighbone has slipped.  
- If the x-ray looks normal but symptoms are still present, doctors may use an MRI or ultrasound.  
- These tests can show early signs of slippage that x-rays miss.

Early diagnosis is very important.  
The sooner treatment starts, the better the outcome.

## How Is SCFE Treated?

Surgery is almost always needed.

- The surgeon puts the bone back in place.  
- Metal screws are used to hold the bone in the correct position.  
- The screws keep the bone from slipping again.  
- The child must not put weight on the affected leg until after surgery and healing.

After surgery, the child will need to follow the doctor’s instructions carefully.  
Recovery takes time.  
Most children can return to normal activities with proper care.

# Glucagonoma

A glucagonoma is a rare tumor in the pancreas. It starts in cells that make a hormone called glucagon. This tumor causes high blood sugar and a specific skin rash.

## What Causes Glucagonoma?

The pancreas normally makes glucagon when blood sugar drops. Glucagon tells the liver to release stored sugar. This raises blood sugar levels.

Glucagonomas are a type of pancreatic tumor. They come from the alpha cells in the pancreas. These tumors grow slowly. Many are cancerous. Most people live 15 years or more after diagnosis.

The average age when symptoms start is 50. Most patients are women. A few people have a genetic condition called multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1.

## Symptoms and Signs

Glucagonomas cause symptoms like those of diabetes. These include:

- High blood sugar
- Weight loss
- Feeling weak or tired
- Low levels of certain amino acids in the blood
- Low levels of fats in the blood
- Anemia (low red blood cells)

The most unique sign is a skin rash. It often appears on the arms, legs, or buttocks. The rash may look red, scaly, and peel. It can move from one area to another. This is called necrolytic migratory erythema.

Other signs include:
- A smooth, shiny, red tongue
- Cracked lips (cheilitis)

## How Is Glucagonoma Diagnosed?

Doctors check for high levels of glucagon in the blood. Most patients have levels over 1,000 picograms per milliliter. Normal levels are below 200 picograms per milliliter.

But high levels can also happen with kidney problems, severe stress, pancreatitis, or fasting. So doctors must link high levels to symptoms.

To find the tumor, doctors use imaging tests:
- Abdominal CT scan
- Endoscopic ultrasound

If the CT scan does not show the tumor, MRI or PET scans may help.

People with the skin rash often have low levels of:
- Amino acids
- Zinc
- Essential fatty acids

## How Is Glucagonoma Treated?

### Surgery
If the tumor is small and has not spread, surgery is the best option. Removing the tumor can fix all symptoms.

### Chemotherapy
If the tumor has spread or cannot be removed, chemotherapy is used. The most common treatment is a mix of two drugs:
- Streptozocin
- Doxorubicin

This treatment can:
- Lower glucagon levels
- Reduce symptoms
- Help about half of patients

But it does not usually extend life.

New treatments being studied include:
- Temozolomide-based drugs
- Everolimus
- Sunitinib
- Cabozantinib

### Octreotide or Lanreotide
These are injections that help lower glucagon production. They can:
- Improve the skin rash
- Help with appetite and weight loss

But they may also lower insulin levels. This can make blood sugar harder to control.

Patients who respond well may switch to a long-acting version. This is given as a shot once a month.

People on these injections may also need to take pancreatic enzyme supplements. The injections can reduce the pancreas’s ability to make digestive enzymes.

### Zinc and Nutrition
Zinc applied to the skin, taken by mouth, or given through a vein may help the rash go away. But the rash can also improve with simple hydration or IV fluids with amino acids or fatty acids.

This suggests the rash is not just due to zinc deficiency. It may be caused by a lack of other nutrients.

## Summary

- Glucagonoma is a rare tumor in the pancreas.
- It causes high blood sugar and a specific skin rash.
- Diagnosis is based on high glucagon levels and imaging tests.
- Surgery is the best treatment if the tumor is localized.
- Chemotherapy helps control symptoms if the tumor has spread.
- Octreotide can reduce glucagon and improve the rash.
- Nutrition support, including zinc, amino acids, and fatty acids, may help the skin.

Always talk to your doctor about the best treatment plan for your situation.

# Intestinal Fluke Infections

Some types of flukes can infect the intestines.

Flukes are tiny, flat worms that live inside the body. They are parasites, which means they depend on a host to survive. There are many types of flukes. Each type usually infects a different part of the body. The flukes that affect the intestines include:

- *Fasciolopsis buski*, which causes a condition called fasciolopsiasis  
- *Heterophyes heterophyes*, which causes a condition called heterophyiasis  

These infections are most common in Egypt, the Middle East, and parts of Asia and the Indian subcontinent.

## How People Get Infected

The life cycle of flukes is complicated. People get infected when they:

- Drink water that is dirty with fluke eggs  
- Eat raw or undercooked aquatic plants, like water chestnuts  
- Eat raw, undercooked, or salted freshwater fish that carry fluke larvae  

The larvae are inside tiny cysts in the food or water. Once inside the body, the larvae grow into adult flukes in the intestines.

## What Happens in the Body

Most people with intestinal fluke infections have no symptoms or only mild ones. These may include:

- Upset stomach  
- Feeling sick to the stomach (nausea)  

If the infection is serious, symptoms can include:

- Belly pain  
- Diarrhea  
- Fever  

In some cases, the flukes can stop food from being properly absorbed into the body. This is called malabsorption.  
In rare cases, the flukes can block the intestines. This is called intestinal obstruction.

## How Doctors Diagnose the Infection

Doctors look for fluke eggs or sometimes adult flukes in a sample of stool.  
They may also do blood tests or imaging tests like X-rays or scans if they suspect complications.

## How the Infection Is Treated

The infection is treated with a medicine called praziquantel.  
This medicine kills the flukes.

## More Information

For more details, visit the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website.  
They have information about fasciolopsiasis.

# Stress Testing – Simple Explanation

This test checks how well your heart works under stress. It helps find problems with blood flow to the heart.

## What Happens During the Test?

- Your heart is watched using an ECG (a machine that records heart activity).
- You may also have imaging tests like pictures of your heart.
- The test makes your heart work harder. This can be done by:
  - Walking on a treadmill.
  - Using medicine to increase heart rate if you cannot exercise.
- Your heart rate goes up to about 85% of what is normal for your age.
- Or, the test stops if you feel symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, or dizziness.

## Why Is This Test Done?

- To check for blockages in the heart’s blood vessels (coronary artery disease).
- To see how serious the disease is if you already have it.
- To check how well treatment is working if you have known heart disease.

## How Does It Compare to Other Tests?

- Stress testing is safer and cheaper than cardiac catheterization (a more invasive test).
- It can show if blood flow to the heart is poor during stress.
- But it is not always accurate if you are unlikely to have heart disease.
- It can help decide if a blockage seen on another test is actually causing problems.
- A normal result does not mean you will never have a heart attack. Some blockages can break open and cause a heart attack even if the test is normal.

## Risks of the Test

- Very rare, but serious risks include heart attack or sudden death.
- These happen in about 1 out of every 5,000 people tested.

## When Should You Not Have This Test?

### Do not do this test if you have any of these conditions:

- A recent heart attack (within the last 48 hours).
- Unstable chest pain that is not under control.
- A tear in the large blood vessel from the heart (aortic dissection) if it is new.
- Severe narrowing of the aortic valve if you have symptoms.
- Serious irregular heartbeats that cause symptoms or low blood pressure.
- Heart failure that is getting worse.
- Active inflammation of the heart muscle (myocarditis).
- Active inflammation of the sac around the heart (pericarditis).
- A blood clot in the lung (pulmonary embolism) if it is recent.
- A blood clot in the lung tissue (pulmonary infarction) if it is recent.

### Be careful if you have any of these conditions:

- High-degree heart block (a problem with the heart’s electrical system).
- Slow heart rate that is not normal.
- Imbalance in body chemicals like potassium or sodium.
- High blood pressure (systolic over 200 mm Hg or diastolic over 110 mm Hg).
- A thickened heart muscle that blocks blood flow (hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy).
- Trouble exercising due to physical or mental health issues.
- Moderate or severe narrowing of any heart valve.
- Narrowing in the main artery to the heart (left main coronary artery).
- Other serious illnesses.
- Fast or irregular heartbeats.

## How Is the Test Done?

### Before the Test

- Do not eat or drink anything (except water) for 4 to 6 hours before the test.
- If you are getting medicine to stress your heart, avoid:
  - Coffee
  - Tea
  - Chocolate
  - Energy drinks
  - Caffeinated sodas
  - Some medicines like aminophylline or theophylline
- Avoid these for 24 hours before the test. They can make the test less accurate.

### Two Ways to Increase Heart Demand

1. **Exercise** – You walk on a treadmill or ride a stationary bike.
2. **Medicine** – If you cannot exercise, you get medicine through a vein to make your heart beat faster.

## How Is Ischemia Detected?

After stress, your doctor may use one or more of these tests to see if your heart is getting enough blood:

- **ECG** – Records the heart’s electrical activity.
- **Radionuclide perfusion imaging** – Uses a small amount of radioactive material to take pictures of blood flow in the heart.
- **Echocardiography** – Uses sound waves to make moving pictures of the heart. It shows how well the heart pumps and if any parts are not working well.

# Sexual Sadism Disorder

## What Is Sexual Sadism?

Some people feel sexual excitement when they cause pain or suffering to another person. This is called sexual sadism.

When this behavior causes serious problems, harms someone, or happens without the other person’s agreement, it is called sexual sadism disorder.

## What Is a Paraphilia?

Sexual sadism is a type of paraphilia. A paraphilia means having strong sexual urges that are not common. Most people with these urges do not have a disorder.

## Sadism in Healthy Relationships

It is normal for some couples to play out mild forms of dominance and submission during sex. For example:

- Using soft ropes or scarves to pretend to tie someone up.
- Light spanking during sex.

These activities are only done when both people agree. They are part of a fun, safe game. No one is truly hurt or humiliated.

In these cases, one partner may enjoy being controlled or mildly hurt. This is called sexual masochism. Both partners know it is pretend. They set clear limits and stop if anyone feels uncomfortable.

## When Sadism Becomes a Problem

Sexual sadism disorder happens when:

- The person feels upset or ashamed about their actions.
- Their behavior stops them from living a normal life.
- They cause serious harm to someone else.
- The other person did not agree to what happened.
- The behavior has lasted for at least six months.

If someone causes harm without consent, this is a crime. It often continues until the person is caught.

## Sadism and Other Crimes

Sexual sadism is not the same as rape. Rape is about power and force. Sadism is about getting sexual pleasure from hurting someone.

- Less than 10% of people who commit rape have sexual sadism.
- Between 37% and 75% of people who commit sexual murders have sexual sadism.

## Danger in Certain People

Sexual sadism is more dangerous in people who also have antisocial personality disorder. These people often break rules, lie, and do not care about others’ feelings or safety.

## Treatment Options

There is some evidence that treatment can help. This includes:

- Cognitive-behavioral therapy. This helps people change harmful thoughts and behaviors.
- Antiandrogen medicines. These reduce the effects of testosterone, which can lower sexual urges.

If a person also has antisocial personality disorder, treatment is less likely to work.

# Infections Caused by Proteeae Bacteria

Proteeae are bacteria that normally live in the intestines. They can cause infections when the balance of good bacteria in the body is disrupted by antibiotics.

There are at least three types of Proteeae bacteria:

- *Proteus*: Includes *P. mirabilis*, *P. vulgaris*, and *P. myxofaciens*
- *Morganella*: Includes *M. morganii*
- *Providencia*: Includes *P. rettgeri*, *P. alcalifaciens*, and *P. stuartii*

*P. mirabilis* causes the most infections in people.

These bacteria are normally found in the intestines, soil, and water. They can also be found in open wounds, ear infections (in the outer, middle, or inner ear), and in mucus from the lungs. This is especially common in people who have taken antibiotics for a long time.

In some cases, these bacteria can enter the bloodstream. They can also cause serious infections in the ears, the area behind the ear bones (mastoid sinuses), the belly cavity (peritoneal cavity), and the urinary tract.

People with long-term urinary tract infections or with kidney or bladder stones are more likely to get these infections. *Proteus* bacteria make a substance called urease. This breaks down a waste product in urine called urea. This makes the urine more alkaline (less acidic). Alkaline urine can lead to the formation of certain types of kidney stones made of magnesium, ammonium, and phosphate.

*P. mirabilis* usually responds well to several antibiotics, including:

- Ampicillin
- Carbenicillin
- Ticarcillin
- Piperacillin
- Cephalosporins
- Fluoroquinolones
- Aminoglycosides

But it does not respond to:

- Tetracyclines
- Nitrofurantoin

Some strains of *P. mirabilis* are resistant to many antibiotics. These are called multidrug-resistant bacteria. They are becoming a growing concern.

Other types of Proteeae that test positive for indole (including *P. vulgaris*, *M. morganii*, and *P. rettgeri*) are often harder to treat. However, they usually still respond to:

- Fluoroquinolones
- Carbapenems
- Piperacillin with tazobactam
- Third-generation cephalosporins
- Cefixime

# Genes and Chromosomes

## What Are Genes and Chromosomes?

- Genes are small parts of DNA. They hold the instructions to make proteins or certain types of RNA.
- Chromosomes are structures inside cells. They carry a person’s genes.
- Genes are found inside chromosomes.
- Chromosomes are located in the center of the cell, called the nucleus.
- One chromosome can hold hundreds or even thousands of genes.
- Every normal human cell has 23 pairs of chromosomes. That makes 46 chromosomes in total.
- A trait is a feature that comes from your genes. Examples include eye color or height.
- Most traits are shaped by more than one gene.
- Some traits come from changes in genes. These changes can be passed down from parents. Or they can happen for the first time in a person.

## What Are Proteins?

- Proteins are very important in the body.
- They build muscles, skin, and other body parts.
- Proteins also make enzymes.
- Enzymes are special proteins that help control chemical reactions in the body.
- The body makes thousands of different enzymes.
- The kind and amount of proteins your body makes affect how your body looks and works.
- Genes control how proteins are made. Genes are found on chromosomes.

## The Genome, Genotype, and Phenotype

- The **genome** is the full set of DNA in a person.
- In humans, the genome includes 23 pairs of chromosomes in the cell nucleus and in the mitochondria.
- The **genotype** is the specific version of a gene or all your genes.
- The **phenotype** is your actual body structure and how it works.
- Your phenotype shows what your genes do. Not all genes are used all the time.
- Whether a gene is used depends on many things. These include your genes, your environment, and other unknown factors.

## What Is a Karyotype?

- A karyotype is a full set of a person’s chromosomes.
- It can also be a picture made in a lab. The picture shows chromosomes from one cell, arranged in order.
- Doctors use karyotypes to check for problems with chromosome number or shape.

## How Many Genes Do Humans Have?

- Humans have about 20,000 to 25,000 genes.
- Genes are made of DNA.
- DNA holds the code to make a protein or an RNA molecule.
- Genes come in different sizes. The size depends on the protein or RNA they make.

## The Structure of DNA

- DNA looks like a long spiral staircase.
- It is made of two strands twisted together. The steps are made of four types of building blocks called bases.
- The bases are: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G), and cytosine (C).
- A always pairs with T. G always pairs with C.
- Each DNA molecule is tightly coiled inside a chromosome.
- A gene is a section of DNA. It is made of a sequence of bases.
- Every three bases form a code for one amino acid.
- Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins.

## How Proteins Are Made

- Proteins are made of long chains of amino acids.
- There are 20 different amino acids.
- Some amino acids must come from food. Others are made by the body.
- As the chain grows, it folds into a unique 3D shape.
- The shape of the protein determines what it does.
- The order of amino acids decides the shape.
- Different sequences make different proteins.
- Some proteins have more than one folded chain.
- The instructions to make proteins are stored in DNA.

## How DNA Codes for Proteins

- The order of the bases (A, T, G, C) in DNA holds the code.
- The code is written in groups of three bases.
- Each group of three bases tells the body to add one amino acid.
- For example:
  - GCT means add the amino acid alanine.
  - GTT means add the amino acid valine.
- The order of amino acids in a protein comes from the order of base triplets in the gene.
- Turning DNA code into a protein happens in two steps: transcription and translation.

### Transcription

- Transcription copies the DNA code into a molecule called RNA.
- RNA is similar to DNA, but it uses a base called uracil (U) instead of thymine (T).
- The DNA double helix opens up.
- One strand of DNA acts as a template.
- A matching RNA strand forms.
- This RNA is called messenger RNA (mRNA).
- The mRNA leaves the nucleus and goes into the main part of the cell, called the cytoplasm.
- There, it attaches to a ribosome. Ribosomes are tiny machines that build proteins.

### Translation

- Translation uses the mRNA code to build a protein.
- The ribosome reads the mRNA code.
- It tells the ribosome which amino acids to link together.
- A smaller type of RNA, called transfer RNA (tRNA), brings each amino acid to the ribosome.
- Each tRNA carries one amino acid.
- The ribosome links the amino acids into a chain.
- The chain folds into a 3D shape with help from other molecules called chaperones.

## Why Do Cells Look and Act Differently?

- The body has many types of cells: heart cells, liver cells, muscle cells, and more.
- These cells look and work differently.
- But all cells come from one fertilized egg.
- So, all cells have the same DNA.
- Cells become different because different genes are turned on or off in different cells.
- The timing and location of gene use are also written in the DNA.
- Gene use depends on the type of tissue, a person’s age, chemical signals, and other factors.
- Scientists are learning more about how genes are controlled. But many details are still unknown.

## How Genes Control Each Other

- Genes have chemical markers that show where to start and stop making proteins.
- Other chemicals around DNA can block or allow gene activity.
- A type of RNA called antisense RNA can bind to mRNA and stop protein production.

## How Cells Make Copies of DNA

- Cells divide to make two new cells.
- Each new cell needs a full set of DNA.
- So, the DNA in the original cell must copy itself.
- This copying process is called replication.
- The DNA double helix unwinds and splits in two.
- Each strand acts as a template.
- New bases attach to the old ones: A with T, G with C.
- After copying, two identical DNA molecules exist.

### Proofreading and Repair

- Cells have a built-in check system to catch mistakes.
- If a base is wrong, the cell can fix it.
- But with so many base pairs and complex processes, errors can still happen.
- Errors can be caused by radiation, medicines, viruses, or no clear reason.
- Small changes in DNA are common and usually harmless.
- If a mistake is copied in future cell divisions, it is called a mutation.

## Inherited Mutations

- Inherited mutations can be passed from parent to child.
- Only mutations in sperm or egg cells can be inherited.
- Mutations in other cells affect only the cells that come from them.
- For example, a mutation in a skin cell can lead to skin cancer. But it is not passed to children.

## Types of Mutations

- Mutations can be rare or common.
- Most harmful mutations are rare.
- When a mutation affects more than 1% of a population, it is called a polymorphism.
  - Example: blood types A, B, AB, and O are polymorphisms.
- Most polymorphisms do not change how a person looks or works.
- Mutations can affect small or large parts of DNA.
- The effect depends on the size and location of the change.
- A mutation may:
  - Do nothing.
  - Change the amino acid in a protein.
  - Reduce the amount of protein made.
- If a protein has a different amino acid sequence, it may not work right.
- A missing or broken protein can cause serious harm or even death.
  - Example: In phenylketonuria, a gene mutation stops the body from making a key enzyme.
  - This causes a harmful buildup of a substance called phenylalanine.
  - This buildup can cause severe brain damage.

### Rare Cases: Helpful Mutations

- Sometimes a mutation helps a person survive.
- Example: The sickle cell gene.
  - If a person has two copies, they get sickle cell disease.
  - If a person has one copy, they are a carrier.
  - Carriers have some protection against malaria.
- The protection helps them survive in areas where malaria is common.
- But sickle cell disease causes serious health problems and can shorten life.

## Natural Selection and Evolution

- Natural selection means that harmful mutations are less likely to be passed on.
- Helpful mutations are more likely to be passed on.
- Over time, helpful mutations become more common in a population.
- The slow changes in a population over time are called evolution.
- These changes come from mutations and natural selection.

### Did You Know?

- Not all gene changes are bad.
- The sickle cell gene can protect against malaria.
- This is why the gene is still around in some populations.

## What Are Chromosomes?

- A chromosome is a long strand of DNA with many genes.
- Genes on a chromosome are in a specific order.
- Each gene has a fixed spot on the chromosome. This spot is called a locus.
- The version of a gene at the same spot on both chromosomes of a pair is called an allele.
- Chromosomes also contain other chemicals that affect how genes work.

# Birth Defects in the Digestive Tract

A birth defect means a problem that is present when a baby is born. These problems can affect any part of the digestive system. The digestive system includes the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum, and anus.

## Types of Digestive Tract Birth Defects

Some common birth defects in the digestive tract include:

- **Abdominal wall defects** – The belly wall does not close properly. This can cause organs to stick out. Examples are omphalocele and gastroschisis.
- **Anal atresia** – The opening at the end of the rectum is missing or blocked.
- **Biliary atresia** – The tubes that carry bile from the liver to the intestines are blocked or missing. Bile helps digest food.
- **Diaphragmatic hernia** – A hole in the muscle that separates the chest from the belly. This lets belly organs move into the chest.
- **Esophageal atresia and tracheoesophageal fistula** – The tube from the mouth to the stomach (esophagus) is not connected properly. Sometimes it connects to the windpipe by mistake.
- **Hirschsprung disease** – The nerves in the large intestine do not form correctly. This stops food from moving through the bowel.
- **Intestinal malrotation** – The intestines do not twist into the right position during development. This can cause blockages.

In many cases, an organ is not fully formed or is in the wrong place. This can cause a narrowing or blockage in the digestive tract. Blockages can happen in the esophagus, intestines, rectum, or anus. Sometimes a part of the digestive tract does not form at all. Or it starts to form but is damaged by a problem in the womb. The muscles around the belly may be weak or have holes. This happens in abdominal wall defects and diaphragmatic hernia. In Hirschsprung disease, the nerves that control the intestines do not develop.

## Symptoms of Digestive Tract Birth Defects

Symptoms depend on the type of defect and where it is in the body.

Babies may have:
- Belly pain
- A swollen belly
- Vomiting
- Trouble feeding
- Poor weight gain

Some babies develop a yellow color in the skin and the whites of the eyes. This is called jaundice.

## How Doctors Diagnose Digestive Tract Birth Defects

Doctors use imaging tests to find birth defects.

Most defects can be seen before birth using a routine prenatal ultrasound.

After birth, doctors may use x-rays of the chest or belly. Ultrasound may also be used to find and locate the problem.

Other tests may include:
- Blood tests to check for signs of illness or liver problems.
- Biopsies – a small piece of tissue is taken and looked at under a microscope.

Genetic testing may be done if needed. This depends on the results of other tests and the baby’s symptoms.

## How Doctors Treat Digestive Tract Birth Defects

Surgery is the main treatment for most digestive tract birth defects.

Doctors usually operate to open up blockages. They also repair holes in the belly wall. In some cases, more than one surgery is needed. The goal is to restore normal digestion and help the baby grow and thrive.

# Ataxia-Telangiectasia

Ataxia-telangiectasia is a rare genetic condition.  
It affects how the body repairs damaged DNA.  
This problem leads to weak immune systems.  
It also causes problems with movement and balance.  
The condition causes small, visible blood vessels to appear on the skin and eyes.  
People with this condition often get repeated infections in the sinuses and lungs.

## What Causes Ataxia-Telangiectasia?

A person must inherit two faulty copies of a gene—one from each parent.  
The gene is called ATM.  
It makes a protein that helps find and fix damaged DNA.  
When this gene is faulty, the body cannot repair DNA properly.  
This leads to immune system problems and nerve damage.

## Symptoms and Signs

The first sign is often trouble walking.  
This usually starts when a child is learning to walk.  
The walking problems get worse over time.  
Speech becomes hard to understand.  
The body may move in uncontrolled ways.  
Eye movements may become shaky.  
Muscles weaken and shrink.

Tiny red blood vessels appear on the skin and eyes.  
These usually show up between ages 4 and 6.  
They are most common on the eyes, ears, inner elbows, back of the knees, and sides of the neck.

People with this condition get repeated infections in the nose, sinuses, and lungs.  
These infections can lead to pneumonia.  
They can also cause permanent lung damage.

Some people develop hormone problems.  
This can include issues with the ovaries or testicles.  
Some develop diabetes.

The risk of cancer is much higher than normal.  
Common cancers include leukemia, lymphoma, brain tumors, and stomach cancer.  
Cancer can happen after age 10.  
The risk is about 1 in 100 people each year.  
But the risk stays high throughout life.  
Cancer can happen at any age.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors check for signs of the condition using blood tests and exams.  
They test for low levels of immunoglobulin A.  
They also test for high levels of a protein called alpha-1 fetoprotein.  
A complete blood count checks for low white blood cell counts.

If a person has ataxia and telangiectasias, the diagnosis is likely.  
Low IgA levels are found in about 80% of people with this condition.  
High alpha-1 fetoprotein levels are also common.

A test of the chromosomes may show breaks.  
This shows a problem with DNA repair.

The diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing.  
This test looks for two faulty copies of the ATM gene.  
Parents and siblings can be tested to see if they carry one faulty copy.  
Carriers usually do not have symptoms.  
But they may have a higher risk of cancer.

Newborn screening for immune problems can sometimes find this condition.  
About half of babies with this condition are born with low T cells.

Family members of someone with this condition should get genetic counseling.  
They can choose to be tested to see if they carry the faulty gene.

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure.  
Treatment focuses on helping the person stay healthy.  
Doctors may give antibiotics to prevent infections.  
They may also give immune globulin to help the immune system.

One small study found that a drug called amantadine helped with movement a little.  
But it does not stop the nerve damage.  
The nerve problems get worse over time.  
Most people die by age 30 from complications.

Researchers are testing new treatments.  
These include new types of medicine called antisense oligonucleotides.  
Another option being studied is nicotinamide riboside.

If cancer develops, chemotherapy is often used.

## Key Facts

- The condition causes both immune system and nerve problems.  
- Trouble walking is often the first sign.  
- It usually starts when a child begins to walk.  
- There is no treatment that stops the nerve damage.  
- Most people live into their 30s, but the condition is life-threatening.

# Substance- or Medication-Induced Psychotic Disorder

This condition causes people to see things that are not there (hallucinations) or to believe things that are not true (delusions). These symptoms happen because of a substance or medicine. They can also happen when someone stops using a substance after long-term use. The person does not have confusion or disorientation (which is called delirium).

## What Causes This?

Many different substances can cause this kind of psychosis. These include:
- Alcohol
- Amphetamines (like methamphetamine)
- Cannabis (marijuana)
- Cocaine
- Hallucinogens (like LSD or psilocybin)
- Opioids (like heroin or prescription painkillers)
- PCP (phencyclidine)
- Sedatives (like benzodiazepines or sleeping pills)

For a diagnosis to be made, the hallucinations or delusions must be worse or last longer than what is normal during regular use or withdrawal from the substance.

## How Long Do Symptoms Last?

In most cases, the symptoms go away once the substance leaves the body. But for some substances, the symptoms can last a long time. For example:
- Amphetamine use can cause psychosis that lasts for weeks.
- Cocaine use can cause psychosis that lasts for weeks.
- PCP use can cause psychosis that lasts for weeks.

## How Is It Treated?

- A calm, quiet place helps the person feel safer.
- A doctor may give a benzodiazepine (a medicine that calms the nervous system) or an antipsychotic (a medicine that helps with hallucinations and delusions).
- Stopping the substance and taking medicine often helps the symptoms go away.
- For some medicines like LSD, quiet observation may be all that is needed. No medicine is usually required.

## Follow-Up Care Is Important

After treatment, it is very important to see a doctor again. This helps:
- Treat any ongoing problem with substance use.
- Check if the symptoms are an early sign of schizophrenia or a similar mental health condition.

Do not ignore these symptoms. Getting help early can make a big difference.

# Dacryocystitis

Dacryocystitis is an infection in the tear sac.  
It can sometimes lead to a pocket of pus forming in the area.  
The most common causes are bacteria called staphylococcus or streptococcus.  
These infections usually happen when the tube that carries tears from the eye to the nose becomes blocked.

## How Tears Work

Tears are made by two main glands in the eye.  
One is the main tear gland.  
The other is a group of smaller glands.  
The main tear gland makes extra tears when the eye is irritated.  
For example, it makes more tears when something gets in your eye or when you cut an onion.  
The smaller glands keep your eye wet all the time.

Tears start at tiny openings in the inner corner of the eye.  
These openings are called puncta.  
From there, tears flow through small tubes called canaliculi.  
Then they move through a larger tube called the nasolacrimal duct.  
This duct carries tears into the nose.

# Lung Conditions Linked to Smoking

Two rare lung conditions are linked to smoking:  
- Respiratory bronchiolitis-associated interstitial lung disease  
- Desquamative interstitial pneumonia  

Both cause long-term lung inflammation. They mostly affect people who currently smoke or used to smoke.

These conditions are types of idiopathic interstitial pneumonia. They are very similar. Some doctors believe they may be the same disease. But desquamative interstitial pneumonia tends to be more serious.

Most people with these conditions are between 30 and 50 years old. Men are more likely to get them than women—about two men for every one woman.

## Symptoms

Some people have a cough.  
Most people feel short of breath even when doing light activities, like walking a short distance.

## How Doctors Diagnose

Doctors use several tests to check for these conditions.

**Chest CT scan**  
This scan shows detailed images of the lungs. It can show changes not seen on a regular chest x-ray.  
A chest x-ray may show little or no change. This is different from another lung disease called idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, which shows more clear changes on x-ray.

**Pulmonary function test**  
This test measures how well your lungs work.  
It shows that your lungs hold less air than normal.

**Blood test**  
A small sample of blood is tested.  
It shows that your blood has less oxygen than it should.

**Lung biopsy**  
Doctors often need to take a small sample of lung tissue to confirm the diagnosis.  
This is done during a minor surgery.

## Treatment

**Stop smoking**  
Stopping smoking is the most important step.  
It greatly improves the chances of getting better.  
Even if symptoms are mild, quitting smoking helps.

Doctors do not always know how these conditions will progress. But the outlook is good if you stop smoking.

**Medicines**  
Some doctors give steroid medicines. These are also called glucocorticoids or corticosteroids.  
Other doctors may use medicines that reduce immune system activity. Examples include azathioprine or cyclophosphamide.  
These medicines are used because they help in other lung diseases.  
But there is no clear proof they help with these two conditions.  
More research is needed.

# Staying Active as You Age

Most people over the age of 65 do not get enough physical activity.  
This is true even though being active has clear health benefits.

Being active helps you:
- Live longer  
- Feel better every day  
- Have more energy and strength  
- Sleep better  
- Move more easily  
- Improve how your body uses insulin  
- Keep your bones strong (especially if you do weight-bearing activities like walking or lifting)  
- Possibly improve your memory and thinking skills  

Many older adults do not know how hard they should exercise.  
They also do not realize how much they can still do.

Exercise is one of the safest and most helpful things you can do for your health.  
As you age, your body naturally loses strength and stamina.  
This makes exercise even more important for older adults.  
It is never too late to start.  
Even beginning exercise later in life brings real benefits.

Simple strength training helps you do everyday tasks.  
Examples include carrying groceries, getting up from a chair, or climbing stairs.  
Many older adults need help to start a safe and steady exercise plan.

The biggest health gains come when people who have been inactive start moving.  
This is especially true for aerobic activities like walking, swimming, or cycling.

Muscle strength naturally declines with age.  
When you lose strength, it becomes harder to do daily tasks.  
For example:
- Nearly half of women over 65 cannot lift 10 pounds.  
- More than half of women over 75 cannot lift 10 pounds.

Strength training can increase muscle size by 25% to 100% or more.  
This means you can do daily activities with less effort.  
It also means your heart and lungs do not have to work as hard.  
Stronger leg muscles help you walk faster and climb stairs more easily.  

Older adults in care homes who have more muscle mass:
- Keep their body’s balance of nutrients better  
- Stay healthier during illness  
- Have a better chance of recovery if they get very sick

# Lymphangiomas

Lymphangiomas are non-cancerous lumps that form under the skin.  
They happen when lymph vessels get enlarged.  
Lymph vessels carry a clear fluid that helps the body fight infection.  

These lumps are rare.  
They usually show up in babies or young children, before age two.  
They can be very small or grow large enough to change the shape of the body.  

Lymphangiomas most often appear in the head and neck area.  
They can also appear in the armpit or in the chest, between the lungs.  

The lumps do not cause itching or pain.  
They are not cancer.  
Most are yellowish or tan in color.  
Some are reddish or purple.  

If a lymphangioma is cut or broken open, it may leak clear fluid or fluid with a little blood.  

Doctors diagnose lymphangiomas by looking at the lump and using a special scan called magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI.  

Most lymphangiomas do not need treatment.  
If the lump is large and causes problems, doctors may use a treatment called sclerotherapy.  
This treatment involves injecting a special solution into the lump to shrink it.  
This method is often used for varicose veins and spider veins.  

Surgery to remove a lymphangioma is usually not helpful.  
The lumps grow deep under the skin and spread out.  
They often come back after surgery.

# Blastomycosis

Blastomycosis is a lung infection caused by breathing in tiny spores from a fungus called *Blastomyces dermatitidis*.  
The fungus lives in soil, especially in areas near rivers.  
It grows as a mold in warm, moist soil that has animal waste or decaying plant material.  

Once in the lungs, the spores turn into yeast cells.  
These yeast cells can cause a lung infection.  
In some people, the infection spreads through the blood to other parts of the body.  

The most common place the infection spreads to is the skin.  
It can also spread to the bones, joints, brain, prostate, testicles, kidneys, and other organs.  

## Where Blastomycosis Is Found

Blastomycosis is most common in parts of North America.  
These include:  
- The Ohio and Mississippi River valleys  
- The northern Midwest  
- Upstate New York  
- Southern Canada  

It is rare in the Middle East and Africa.  

Anyone can get blastomycosis, even healthy people.  
But it is more serious in people with weak immune systems.  
It is less common than other fungal infections like histoplasmosis or coccidioidomycosis.  

## Symptoms

Many people with blastomycosis have no symptoms.  
Others may have:  
- Cough  
- Fever  
- Chest pain  
- Shortness of breath  
- Weight loss  
- Night sweats  

Skin sores can appear.  
They may look like sores from other infections, such as tuberculosis or a skin cancer.  
Sores can also appear in the mouth or nose.  

If the infection spreads to the brain, it can cause headaches, confusion, or seizures.  

## How Doctors Diagnose Blastomycosis

Doctors suspect blastomycosis when a person has lung symptoms and lives in an area where the fungus is common.  

A chest x-ray may show signs of pneumonia.  
The x-ray can show patchy areas in the lungs, often starting near the center.  
These signs can look like other lung infections, such as bacterial pneumonia, tuberculosis, or cancer.  

To confirm the diagnosis, doctors may take a sample from the lungs, skin, or other infected area.  
They send this sample to a lab to grow the fungus.  
This is called a culture.  

The lab must be warned if blastomycosis is suspected.  
The fungus can be dangerous to lab workers.  

A lab test can also look at the fungus under a microscope.  
The fungus has a unique shape.  
It looks like large round cells with a wide base.  
This shape helps doctors make a diagnosis.  

A blood or urine test can also detect the fungus.  
But this test can sometimes give a false positive if you have another fungal infection.  

A special test called PCR can also help find the fungus.  
This test looks for the fungus’s genetic material.  

## Treatment

Treatment depends on how serious the infection is.  

### For Mild to Moderate Infection

If you have mild to moderate symptoms and do not need to stay in the hospital, your doctor will likely prescribe itraconazole.  
You take it by mouth.  
The dose is:  
- 200 milligrams three times a day for 3 days  
- Then 200 milligrams once a day or twice a day for 6 to 12 months  

Fluconazole may be used if you cannot take itraconazole.  
But it is not as strong.  
The dose is 400 to 800 milligrams once a day.  

### For Severe or Life-Threatening Infection

If you are very sick, you will get amphotericin B through a vein.  
This medicine is given in a hospital.  
The dose is 3 to 5 milligrams per kilogram of body weight once a day.  
Or, a different form of amphotericin B may be used at 0.7 to 1.0 milligrams per kilogram once a day.  

You will get this for 1 to 2 weeks, or until you start to feel better.  

Once you improve, your doctor will switch you to itraconazole.  
The dose is:  
- 200 milligrams three times a day for 3 days  
- Then 200 milligrams twice a day for at least 12 months  

### Special Cases

People with brain infection, pregnant women, and those with weak immune systems should get amphotericin B.  
The best form is a liposomal version.  
It is given the same way as for severe cases.  

Other medicines like voriconazole, isavuconazonium, and posaconazole can work against the fungus.  
But we do not yet know how well they work in real patients.  

## Key Points

- Blastomycosis starts in the lungs after breathing in fungus spores.  
- It can spread to the skin and other organs.  
- It is most common in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys and around the Great Lakes.  
- Diagnosis is made by testing samples from the lungs, skin, or blood.  
- A chest x-ray can show signs of lung infection.  
- For mild cases, itraconazole is the main treatment.  
- For severe cases, amphotericin B is used first.  
- Most people get better with treatment.  
- Without treatment, the disease can slowly get worse.
