# Smuggling Drugs in the Body

Some people hide illegal drugs inside their body to get them across borders or past security checks. They may swallow drug packets or put them in body openings like the rectum or vagina.

- If a packet breaks open, it can cause a drug overdose.
- An overdose can lead to serious health problems.
- The risks depend on the type of drug, how much is inside, and how the packet is made.

---

## Body Packing

Body packing means swallowing many drug packets. This usually involves high-value drugs like heroin or cocaine. These drugs come from other countries.

The drugs are wrapped in layers of plastic, latex, or condoms. Sometimes they are covered with wax to make them harder to detect.

After swallowing the packets, people may take medicine to slow down their digestion. This helps keep the packets in place until they can be removed.

Some people swallow hundreds of packets in one trip.

If a packet breaks:
- The drug can enter the body quickly.
- This can cause a dangerous overdose.
- The packet can block or damage the intestines.
- If the intestine tears, its contents can leak into the belly. This causes a serious infection called peritonitis.

Symptoms of an overdose from a broken packet depend on the drug. They may include:
- Seizures that keep coming back
- Very high blood pressure
- Extremely high body temperature
- Trouble breathing
- Loss of consciousness (coma)

---

## Body Stuffing

Body stuffing is similar to body packing. But it happens in a hurry—usually to avoid being caught.

People swallow drug packets quickly. Sometimes they hide packets in the rectum or vagina.

The amount of drugs is usually smaller than in body packing. But the packets are less secure. This makes an overdose more likely.

---

## How Doctors Find Hidden Drugs

Doctors may suspect body packing or stuffing if:
- A person recently traveled to another country.
- A person is newly in jail or prison.
- A person is unconscious or having seizures with no clear cause.

Doctors check for hidden drugs by:
- Doing a physical exam of the rectum and vagina (body cavity search).
- Using imaging tests like x-rays or CT scans.

A plain x-ray can sometimes show drug packets in the gut. But a CT scan is the best test to find them.

---

## How Doctors Treat People Who Have Hidden Drugs

### If Someone Has Overdose Symptoms

Doctors treat the symptoms right away. This may include:
- Helping the person breathe.
- Supporting blood pressure.
- Giving medicine to stop seizures.

If the drug is known, doctors may use a specific antidote. But this is not always available.

### If the Packets Are Still Intact

Doctors often use a treatment called whole-bowel irrigation. This means flushing the digestive system with a special liquid. It helps move the packets out through the stool.

### If a Packet Breaks Open

If a packet breaks, doctors act fast to remove all the drug packets. They may use:
- Surgery.
- An endoscope (a thin tube with a camera that goes into the gut).

These removal methods take time. But they are needed because:
- A large amount of pure drug is released when a packet breaks.
- This can cause a deadly overdose.

People with a blocked or torn intestine need emergency surgery.

### Activated Charcoal

Doctors may give activated charcoal to help absorb the drug. But this is dangerous if there is a blockage or tear in the intestine.

### Removing Packets from the Rectum or Vagina

Doctors can often remove packets from the rectum or vagina by hand, using a gloved finger.

---

## Monitoring and Follow-Up

People who have no symptoms should be watched closely. They must pass all the packets in their stool.

Doctors may use whole-bowel irrigation to help move the packets out faster.

If a person shows signs of drug poisoning or overdose, doctors may do an endoscopy to remove the packets early.

# Heart Imaging Using Radioactive Tracers

This test uses a special camera to take pictures of your heart after you receive a small amount of a radioactive substance. The test helps doctors check how well your heart is working.

## Why This Test Is Done

Doctors use this test to look at:
- Problems with heart valves
- Weakness in the heart muscle
- Heart problems you were born with
- Blockages in the blood vessels of the heart
- Other heart conditions

The amount of radiation from this test is about the same as a CT scan. But because the radioactive material stays in your body for a short time, you might set off airport security alarms for a few days after the test.

---

## SPECT Imaging

SPECT is the most common type of heart imaging in the United States. It uses a rotating camera to make 3D pictures of the heart.

- The test takes about 10 minutes or less.
- Doctors compare pictures taken when your heart is under stress and after it has rested.
- They can see:
  - Damage in the lower or back part of the heart
  - Small areas of heart tissue that are dead or damaged
  - Which blood vessel is blocked or narrowed
- The test can also measure how much heart muscle is damaged and how much is still healthy. This helps predict your long-term health.

---

## Blood Flow to the Heart

In this test, a radioactive substance is given through a vein. It goes into the heart muscle in proportion to blood flow.

- Areas with less substance show up as darker spots. These areas may not be getting enough blood.
- This can mean the heart muscle is not getting enough oxygen, either during stress or at rest.

### False Results

Sometimes, the image can be misleading. This is called attenuation.

- Soft tissue, like breast tissue in women, can block the signal and make it look like there is heart damage when there isn’t.
- The diaphragm and belly organs can also block the signal, especially in men.
- This problem is more common with one type of radioactive substance (technetium-99m) than with another (thallium-201).

---

## Finding Dead Heart Tissue

This test uses special tracers that collect in damaged heart tissue.

- The tracers used are Tc-99m pyrophosphate and antimyosin (a substance made from antibodies).
- The heart shows up on the scan 12 to 24 hours after a heart attack.
- The signal stays positive for about one week.
- It may stay positive longer if the heart damage continues or if a bulge forms in the heart wall (aneurysm).

This test is rarely used today because:
- Other tests (like blood tests) are easier and cheaper.
- It only shows the size of the damaged area, not how well you will do in the future.

### New Use for Tc-99m Pyrophosphate

Now, this test is used to check for a rare heart condition called **transthyretin amyloidosis**.

- This is a disease where abnormal proteins build up in the heart and other tissues.
- The heart tissue in this condition strongly takes up Tc-99m pyrophosphate.
- If blood and urine tests do not show signs of another type of amyloidosis (which can also affect the heart), and you have no recent heart attack, a high heart uptake on the scan means you likely have transthyretin amyloidosis.
- This can help avoid the need for a heart biopsy.

---

## Checking Heart Pumping Function

This test measures how well your heart pumps blood.

### How It Works

- A radioactive substance is attached to your red blood cells.
- These cells are then injected into a vein.
- The camera tracks the blood as it moves through the heart.

There are two main types of this test:

### First-Transit Study

- The camera records 8 to 10 heartbeats as the tracer moves through the heart.
- It is fast and simple.
- Best for checking right heart function and detecting blood flow between heart chambers (shunts).

### MUGA Scan

- The camera takes pictures in sync with your heartbeat (using ECG).
- It takes 5 to 10 minutes.
- The computer puts together many small images to make a movie-like view of the beating heart.

### What MUGA Can Measure

- How well each part of the heart moves
- How much blood the heart pumps out with each beat (ejection fraction)
- How fast the heart fills and pumps
- The size of the heart chambers
- How much blood is flowing through the left and right sides of the heart

Ejection fraction is the most commonly used measure.

### When MUGA Is Used

- To check heart function at rest or after exercise
- To monitor patients on chemotherapy drugs that can harm the heart (like doxorubicin)
- To see how well treatments like angioplasty, bypass surgery, or clot-busting drugs are working

### Risks and Limitations

- The test is very safe at rest.
- It is not used often now because echocardiography (ultrasound of the heart) is cheaper, does not use radiation, and gives similar results.
- Irregular heartbeats (arrhythmias) can make the test harder to do. This is because the camera needs regular heartbeats to work properly.

# Histrionic Personality Disorder

This is a mental health condition. It involves long-term patterns of being overly emotional and needing attention.

## What It Feels Like

- People with this condition always want to be the center of attention.
- They often act in ways that are overly dramatic or flirtatious.
- They may dress in ways that are too sexy or provocative, even in places like work or school.
- They can feel upset or sad when they are not the focus of attention.
- Their emotions can change very fast. One moment they are happy, the next they are sad or angry.
- They may act in exaggerated ways to get attention. They speak with strong feelings but often lack real details.
- They may try to control others by being seductive or using strong emotions.
- They often depend heavily on others, especially romantic partners.
- They may pretend to be a victim or play a role to get attention.
- They believe their relationships are deeper than they really are.
- They get bored easily and may change jobs or friends often.
- They want quick rewards and do not like waiting.
- They are easily influenced by others and by what is popular right now.
- They tend to trust people too much, especially those in authority.

## How It Is Diagnosed

Doctors use a standard guide called the DSM-5-TR to diagnose mental health conditions.

To be diagnosed with histrionic personality disorder, a person must show at least five of the following:

- They feel uncomfortable when they are not the center of attention.
- They act in ways that are sexually seductive or provocative, even when it is not appropriate.
- Their emotions change quickly and seem shallow to others.
- They use their looks to get attention.
- Their speech is vague and lacks details.
- They express emotions in a dramatic or exaggerated way.
- They are easily influenced by others or by situations.
- They think their relationships are more close than they really are.

These patterns must have started in early adulthood.

## How It Is Treated

- The main treatment is talk therapy.
- There is not much research on how well medicine or cognitive-behavioral therapy work for this condition.
- Psychodynamic therapy may help. This kind of therapy focuses on deep feelings and past experiences.
- The therapist may first help the person talk more instead of acting out.
- This helps the person understand themselves better.
- Over time, the therapist helps the person see that dramatic behavior does not help them get real attention or feel better.
- The goal is to help the person communicate in a more honest and calm way.

# Late-Term and Postterm Pregnancy

A pregnancy is called **late-term** if it lasts from 41 weeks and 0 days to 41 weeks and 6 days.  
It is called **postterm** if it lasts 42 weeks or more.

You should check the baby’s health starting at 41 weeks.  
Labor should be started if the pregnancy reaches 41 weeks, especially if the cervix is ready.  
It is strongly recommended to start labor after 42 weeks, but no later than 42 weeks and 6 days.

## How to Know How Far Along the Pregnancy Is

Knowing the exact length of the pregnancy is very important.  
If your periods are regular, your due date is based on the first day of your last period.  
If you are not sure about your due date, or if your period dates do not match, an ultrasound scan early in pregnancy (before 20 weeks) can help.

## Risks of a Late-Term or Postterm Pregnancy

A pregnancy that goes past the due date can be risky for both you and your baby.  
These risks include:

- Low levels of amniotic fluid (the fluid around the baby)
- The baby passing stool (meconium) in the womb
- The baby being very large, which can lead to:
  - Shoulder injury during birth
  - Injury to you or the baby
  - Severe tearing of the vaginal area
  - Need for assisted delivery (using forceps or vacuum)
  - Need for cesarean delivery
- Heavy bleeding after delivery
- A condition called **postmaturity syndrome**, where the baby is not getting enough nutrients and oxygen
- Seizures in the newborn
- Stillbirth or death of the baby shortly after birth

## What Is Postmaturity?

Postmaturity means the baby has stayed in the womb too long.  
The placenta can no longer support the baby’s growth and health.  
Signs of postmaturity include:

- Dry, peeling skin
- Long fingernails and toenails
- Lots of scalp hair
- Deep lines on the palms and soles
- Little body fat
- Skin that looks green or yellow from meconium

The baby may also be at risk for **meconium aspiration syndrome**, where the baby breathes in meconium after birth.

## Checking the Baby’s Health

Starting at 41 weeks, your doctor may check the baby’s health using one of these tests:

- **Nonstress test**: Checks the baby’s heart rate when the baby moves
- **Modified biophysical profile**: Combines the nonstress test with a check of the amniotic fluid level
- **Full biophysical profile**: Checks the amniotic fluid level and the baby’s movement, muscle tone, breathing, and heart rate

## How to Manage Late-Term and Postterm Pregnancy

### Inducing Labor

Labor can be started at 41 weeks if the cervix is ready.  
It is strongly recommended to start labor after 42 weeks, but no later than 42 weeks and 6 days.

### Cesarean Delivery

A cesarean delivery is not needed just because the pregnancy is late-term or postterm.  
But it may be needed for other reasons, such as:

- The baby is in a breech position (bottom or feet first)
- The baby’s heart rate is abnormal
- Labor stops or does not progress
- You have a medical condition that makes vaginal birth unsafe

## Key Points

- Knowing the correct due date is very important.  
  If your period dates are unclear, an early ultrasound (before 20 weeks) can help.

- Start checking the baby’s health at 41 weeks.  
  This can include a nonstress test or a biophysical profile.

- If the baby is in distress or there is low amniotic fluid, delivery is needed.

- Consider starting labor between 41 and 42 weeks.  
  It is recommended to start labor after 42 weeks, but no later than 42 weeks and 6 days.

# Ascariasis

Ascariasis is an infection caused by a type of roundworm. The most common worm is *Ascaris lumbricoides*. A similar worm, *Ascaris suum*, can also cause the infection in people, but it mainly infects pigs.

## How People Get Infected

- People get infected by swallowing roundworm eggs.
- The eggs usually come from food that touched soil contaminated with human or pig poop.
- You can also get infected by touching dirty soil and then putting your hands in your mouth.
- The eggs can live in soil for years. They are very tough and hard to kill.

## What Happens in the Body

- Once swallowed, the eggs hatch in the intestines.
- The tiny worms (larvae) travel through the wall of the intestines.
- They move through the body’s fluid system and into the lungs.
- In the lungs, they grow a little and then move up into the throat.
- You swallow them again, and they go back to the intestines.
- There, they grow into adult worms. This takes about 2 to 3 months.
- The adult worms live in the intestines for 1 to 2 years.
- The female worms lay eggs that come out in the stool.
- The eggs can survive in soil and start the cycle again.

## Size and Life of the Worms

- Adult female worms are 8 to 14 inches long (20 to 35 centimeters).
- Adult male worms are 6 to 12 inches long (15 to 30 centimeters).
- They live in the intestines for 1 to 2 years.

## Symptoms

- Many people have no symptoms at all.
- Some people may have fever, cough, wheezing, or cough up blood.
- A large number of worms can cause stomach cramps, nausea, and vomiting.
- In severe cases, worms can block the intestines or tubes that carry bile from the liver to the gut.
- Blockages can cause severe pain, swelling in the belly, and vomiting.
- Sometimes worms move into the mouth or nose. They may come out in vomit or stool. This can be very upsetting.
- Children with many worms may not grow or gain weight normally. This is called undernutrition.

## How Doctors Diagnose It

- Doctors check a stool sample for worm eggs or adult worms.
- Sometimes worms are seen in the stool, or they come out of the mouth or nose.
- Rarely, larvae are found in phlegm.
- If a CT scan or ultrasound is done for another reason, doctors may see the worms.
- A chest x-ray can show lung problems caused by the worms moving through the lungs.

## Treatment

- Doctors use medicines to kill worms. These are called anthelmintics.
- Common medicines are albendazole, mebendazole, or ivermectin. They are taken by mouth.
- These medicines are not safe during pregnancy. They can harm the baby.
- Pregnant women are given pyrantel pamoate instead.
- If a safe medicine is not available, doctors must weigh the risks and benefits.
- If you have lived in central Africa, doctors check for another worm called *Loa loa* before giving ivermectin. This is because ivermectin can cause serious brain swelling in people with both worms.
- For mild infections, doctors may give nitazoxanide. It is taken by mouth and treats intestinal parasites.
- If worms block the intestines, treatment may include medicine, surgery, or using a thin tube (endoscope) to remove the worms through the mouth.
- If the lungs are affected, doctors treat symptoms. They may use medicines to open the airways and reduce swelling. They do not usually use worm-killing medicine for lung problems.

## Prevention

- Wash your hands well with soap and water before eating or handling food.
- Wash your hands after touching pigs or working in soil.
- Wash, peel, or cook all raw fruits and vegetables before eating.
- This is especially important if the food was grown in areas where human or pig poop is used as fertilizer.
- Do not go to the bathroom outside unless you are in a proper toilet with safe sewage disposal.
- Good sewage systems help stop the spread of this infection.

## Did You Know?

- About 819 million people worldwide have ascariasis.
- It is most common in school-aged children.
- The infection is rare in places with good sanitation.
- In the United States, it mostly affects refugees, immigrants, and travelers from areas where the infection is common.

(See also: Overview of Parasitic Infections.)

# Blockage of Blood Vessels from the Abdominal Aorta

Blood vessels that branch off from the abdominal aorta can become blocked. This can happen due to hardening of the arteries, a condition called fibromuscular dysplasia, or other causes. When this occurs, organs may not get enough blood. This can lead to pain, tissue damage, or organ failure.

Doctors use imaging tests to find the blockage. Treatment depends on how sudden the blockage is and which vessel is affected. Options include removing the blockage, opening the vessel with a balloon, or using surgery to reroute blood flow.

## Types of Blockage

Blockages can happen suddenly or over time.

- **Sudden blockage** can be caused by a blood clot, a piece of plaque breaking off, or a tear in the artery wall.
- **Slow blockage** is often due to hardening of the arteries, fibromuscular dysplasia, or pressure from a tumor or other mass.

Common places where blockages occur include:
- The superior mesenteric artery (supplies blood to the intestines)
- The celiac axis (supplies blood to the liver, spleen, and stomach)
- The renal arteries (supply blood to the kidneys)
- The aortic bifurcation (where the aorta splits into the two main leg arteries)

Blockage of the celiac axis is more common in women, though doctors do not know why.

## Symptoms and Signs

Symptoms depend on how fast the blockage happens and which blood vessel is affected.

### Sudden Blockage of the Intestine’s Blood Supply
- Severe belly pain that feels worse than what the exam shows.
- This is called acute mesenteric occlusion.
- The pain is often widespread and intense.
- It can lead to death of intestinal tissue if not treated quickly.

### Slow Blockage of the Intestine’s Blood Supply
- This is called chronic mesenteric vascular insufficiency.
- It often does not cause symptoms unless both the superior mesenteric artery and celiac axis are badly narrowed.
- The body can use other blood vessels to help supply blood to the intestines.
- Pain usually starts 30 minutes to one hour after eating.
- The pain is steady, severe, and often around the belly button.
- It may go away with a nitroglycerin tablet under the tongue.
- People become afraid to eat because of the pain.
- They often lose a lot of weight.
- In rare cases, the body does not absorb food well, which adds to weight loss.
- Other signs may include a whooshing sound in the belly, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, or black stools.

### Sudden Blockage of the Celiac Axis
- Can cause damage to the liver or spleen.

### Sudden Blockage of a Kidney Artery
- Causes sudden pain in the side or back.
- Blood may appear in the urine.
- This can be mistaken for kidney stones.

### Slow Blockage of a Kidney Artery
- May not cause any symptoms.
- Can cause new or hard-to-control high blood pressure.
- May lead to other problems from poor kidney function.

### Sudden Blockage at the Bottom of the Aorta
- Causes sudden pain in the legs, even when resting.
- Legs may look pale or cold.
- You may not be able to move the legs.
- Pulse in the legs may be missing.
- This is similar to acute peripheral arterial occlusion.

### Slow Blockage at the Bottom of the Aorta
- Causes pain in the legs or buttocks when walking.
- This is called intermittent claudication.
- Can also cause trouble getting or keeping an erection (Leriche syndrome).
- The pulse in the legs may be weak or missing.
- The ankle-brachial index (a test comparing blood pressure in the arms and legs) will be abnormal.
- One leg may be at risk of serious damage.

## How Doctors Diagnose the Problem

Doctors start by asking about your symptoms and doing a physical exam.

They then use imaging tests to confirm the blockage. These include:
- Duplex ultrasound
- CT angiography
- Magnetic resonance angiography
- Conventional angiography

## How Doctors Treat the Problem

### For Sudden Blockages
- This is a medical emergency.
- Treatment includes removing the clot (embolectomy) or opening the vessel with a balloon (angioplasty).
- A stent may be placed to keep the vessel open.
- If the first treatments fail, surgery may be needed to reroute blood flow or remove damaged intestine.

### For Slow Blockages
- If symptoms are bad, treatment may include surgery or angioplasty.
- Doctors also recommend lifestyle changes and medicines to lower risk.
- For blockages in the arteries to the intestines, eating small meals and avoiding large meals may help.
- If symptoms are severe, surgery can reroute blood flow from the aorta to the intestines.
- Grafts used in surgery stay open in about 89% of cases.
- For older patients or those not fit for surgery, angioplasty with a stent may work well.
- Symptoms can improve quickly, and weight may return.
- For kidney artery blockages, treatment starts with blood pressure medicines.
- If blood pressure stays high or kidney function gets worse, angioplasty with a stent or surgery may be needed.
- For blockages at the bottom of the aorta, urgent embolectomy is often done through the groin.
- For long-term claudication, surgery can place a graft to bypass the blockage.
- Angioplasty is an option for some patients.

## Key Points

- Blockages in the blood vessels from the abdominal aorta can happen suddenly or over time.
- Symptoms depend on how fast the blockage happens and which vessel is blocked.
- Diagnosis starts with your history and physical exam. Imaging tests confirm the blockage.
- Sudden blockages need emergency treatment with clot removal, balloon opening, or surgery.
- Slow blockages are treated with medicines, lifestyle changes, and sometimes surgery or angioplasty.

# Birth Defects in the Digestive Tract

A birth defect means a problem that is present when a baby is born. These problems can affect any part of the digestive system. The digestive system includes the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum, and anus.

## Types of Digestive Tract Birth Defects

Some common birth defects in the digestive tract include:

- **Abdominal wall defects** – The belly wall does not close properly. This can cause organs to stick out. Examples are omphalocele and gastroschisis.
- **Anal atresia** – The opening at the end of the rectum is missing or blocked.
- **Biliary atresia** – The tubes that carry bile from the liver to the intestines are blocked or missing. Bile helps digest food.
- **Diaphragmatic hernia** – A hole in the muscle that separates the chest from the belly. This lets belly organs move into the chest.
- **Esophageal atresia and tracheoesophageal fistula** – The tube from the mouth to the stomach (esophagus) is not connected properly. Sometimes it connects to the windpipe by mistake.
- **Hirschsprung disease** – The nerves in the intestines do not form correctly. This causes blockages.
- **Intestinal malrotation** – The intestines do not twist into the right position during development. This can cause blockages.

In many cases, an organ is not fully formed or is in the wrong place. This can cause narrowing or blockage in the digestive tract. Blockages can happen in the esophagus, intestines, rectum, or anus.

Sometimes, a part of the digestive tract does not form at all. Or it starts to form but is damaged by a problem in the womb before birth.

The muscles around the belly may be weak or have holes. This happens in abdominal wall defects and diaphragmatic hernia.

The nerves that control the intestines may not develop. This is what happens in Hirschsprung disease.

## Symptoms of Digestive Tract Birth Defects

Symptoms depend on the type of defect and where it is in the body.

Babies may have:
- Belly pain
- Swollen belly
- Vomiting
- Trouble feeding
- Poor weight gain

Some babies develop a yellow color in the skin and the whites of the eyes. This is called jaundice.

## How Doctors Diagnose Digestive Tract Birth Defects

Doctors use imaging tests to find birth defects.

Most defects can be seen before birth using a routine prenatal ultrasound.

After birth, doctors may use x-rays of the chest or belly. Ultrasound may also be used to find and locate the problem.

Other tests may include:
- Blood tests to check for signs of illness or liver problems.
- Biopsies – a small piece of tissue is taken and looked at under a microscope.

Genetic testing may be done if needed. This helps find if the defect is linked to a genetic condition.

## Treatment of Digestive Tract Birth Defects

Most digestive tract birth defects need surgery.

Surgery is used to:
- Open up blockages in the digestive tract.
- Repair holes in the belly wall.
- Fix organs that are in the wrong place.

Surgery is often needed soon after birth to help the baby eat and grow normally.

# Physical Therapy

Physical therapy helps you move better. It focuses on your joints and muscles. It can help you stand, balance, walk, and climb stairs.

It can also help you after you lose a leg. Physical therapy teaches you how to use a prosthesis. It helps you move safely and with more strength.

Another type of therapy is called occupational therapy. This helps you with daily tasks. It focuses on small movements in your hands and arms. It helps you do things like dress yourself, eat, and write.

# Ehrlichiosis and Anaplasmosis

Ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis are infections caused by bacteria spread by ticks.  
They cause fever, chills, body aches, headaches, tiredness, and sometimes a rash.  
Anaplasmosis is less likely to cause a rash than ehrlichiosis.

## How the Infections Spread

The bacteria that cause these diseases live inside white blood cells.  
They cannot survive outside the body.  
These infections are passed to people through tick bites.  
They are most common from spring to late fall, when ticks are active.

Different ticks carry each disease:
- Ehrlichiosis: Lone star tick
- Anaplasmosis: Deer tick

Lyme disease and babesiosis are also spread by deer ticks.  
So a person can get more than one infection from a single tick bite.

The bacteria can also spread through blood transfusions or organ transplants.  
A few people have gotten anaplasmosis after receiving blood from someone who had the infection but showed no symptoms.

## Where These Infections Occur

Ehrlichiosis is most common in the southeastern and south central United States.  
Anaplasmosis is found in the Northeast, mid-Atlantic states, upper Midwest, and West Coast.  
It also occurs in parts of Europe.

## Symptoms

Symptoms usually start about 12 days after a tick bite.  
They come on suddenly and include:
- Fever
- Chills
- Muscle aches
- Weakness
- Nausea or vomiting
- Cough
- Headache
- Feeling unwell

Some people with ehrlichiosis get a rash on the arms, legs, or torso.  
This is rare in anaplasmosis.  
Some people have no symptoms at all.

In severe cases, these infections can cause:
- Blood clots throughout the body
- Failure of multiple organs
- Seizures
- Coma

People with weak immune systems are at higher risk for serious illness.  
This includes people with HIV or those taking certain medicines like steroids.  
Death is rare but more likely in people with weak immune systems or those who do not get treatment quickly.

## How Doctors Diagnose the Infections

Doctors use blood tests to check for signs of infection.  
These tests may show:
- Low white blood cell count
- Low platelet count
- High liver enzyme levels
- Problems with blood clotting

These results can happen in many other illnesses too.  
So they are not enough to confirm the diagnosis.

A test called PCR can find the bacteria’s DNA in the blood.  
It works quickly and helps doctors make a fast diagnosis.

Blood tests for antibodies to the bacteria can help.  
But they usually do not show positive results until several weeks after the illness starts.

## Treatment

Doctors usually start treatment right away if a person has symptoms and has been in tick-infested areas.  
Waiting for test results can be dangerous.

The main treatment is an antibiotic called doxycycline.  
It is a type of tetracycline.  
Most people get better quickly when treatment starts early.

People take doxycycline until they feel better and have no fever for 24 to 48 hours.  
But they must take it for at least 7 days.

Even though long-term use of some tetracyclines can stain teeth in children under 8, a short course of doxycycline (5 to 10 days) is safe for children of all ages.  
It does not harm tooth development.

Some people still feel weak or have headaches for weeks after treatment.

## Prevention

The best way to avoid these infections is to prevent tick bites.

### Ways to Avoid Tick Bites

- Stay on trails and paths.
- Tuck your pants into your boots or socks.
- Wear long-sleeved shirts.
- Use insect repellent with DEET on your skin.
- Apply permethrin to clothing. It kills ticks on contact.

Use DEET with care in very young children.  
Toxic reactions have been reported.

Check yourself, your family, and your pets often for ticks.  
Pay special attention to hairy areas like the scalp, behind the ears, and under the arms.

### How to Remove Ticks

- Do not crush the tick between your fingers.
- Do not use petroleum jelly, matches, or other irritants.
- These methods do not work and can increase the risk of infection.

To remove a tick:
- Use fine tweezers or a tick remover.
- Grasp the tick close to the skin.
- Pull it straight out slowly and steadily.
- Clean the bite area with alcohol.

### Reducing Ticks in Your Environment

There is no way to completely remove ticks from an area.  
But you can make your yard less attractive to the animals that carry ticks.

- Remove wood piles and leaf litter.
- Cut back tall grass and brush.
- Keep play areas clear of clutter.

Mice and other small animals like to hide in these places.  
They carry ticks.  
By cleaning up your yard, you reduce the number of ticks around your home.

# Neonatal Hypocalcemia (Low Calcium in Newborns)

Low calcium in the blood is called hypocalcemia.  
It happens when a baby’s blood calcium level is too low.  

For full-term babies, this means a total calcium level below 8 milligrams per deciliter.  
For premature babies, it means a total calcium level below 7 milligrams per deciliter.  
Ionized calcium (the active form) below 3.0 to 4.4 milligrams per deciliter also counts as low.  

Low calcium can cause problems with the nervous system.  
Symptoms include weak muscles, slow breathing, and muscle spasms.  
Some babies may have seizures or stop breathing.  

Treatment means giving calcium through a vein or by mouth.  

---

## Types of Neonatal Hypocalcemia

There are two main types:  

**Early-onset hypocalcemia**  
This happens in the first two days of life.  

**Late-onset hypocalcemia**  
This happens after three days of life. It is rare.  

Some babies born with a condition called DiGeorge syndrome may have both early and late hypocalcemia.  
This is because their parathyroid glands did not form properly.  

---

## Symptoms and Signs

Symptoms usually only appear when calcium levels are very low.  
This means total calcium below 7 milligrams per deciliter.  
Or ionized calcium below 3.0 milligrams per deciliter.  

Signs include:  
- Weak muscles (hypotonia)  
- Fast heart rate (tachycardia)  
- Fast breathing (tachypnea)  
- Stopping breathing (apnea)  
- Poor feeding  
- Shaking or jitteriness  
- Muscle spasms (tetany)  
- Seizures  

These same signs can also happen with low blood sugar or opioid withdrawal.  
So doctors must check carefully to find the real cause.  

---

## How It Is Diagnosed

Doctors diagnose low calcium by testing the baby’s blood.  
They measure either total calcium or ionized calcium.  
Ionized calcium is more accurate because it does not change with protein levels or blood pH.  

An electrocardiogram (ECG) may also help.  
If the QT interval is too long, it can suggest low calcium.  

Other tests may include:  
- Parathyroid hormone level  
- Magnesium level  
- Phosphorus level  
- Vitamin D level  

These help find the cause of the low calcium.  

---

## Treatment

### Early-Onset Hypocalcemia (First 2 Days)

Treatment is intravenous (IV) calcium gluconate.  
This is a calcium solution given through a vein.  

- Give 10% calcium gluconate slowly over 30 minutes.  
- Do not give it too fast. Too fast can slow the heart rate.  
- Watch the baby’s heart rate during the infusion.  
- Check the IV site often.  
- If calcium leaks into the skin, it can cause pain, redness, swelling, or tissue death.  
- In rare cases, it can damage nerves, like the radial nerve at the wrist.  

After the first dose:  
- Mix calcium gluconate into the baby’s IV fluids.  
- Start with 400 milligrams per kilogram of body weight per day.  
- Increase the dose to 800 milligrams per kilogram per day if needed.  
- This helps keep calcium levels normal.  

When the baby starts feeding by mouth:  
- Add the same daily dose of calcium gluconate to the baby’s formula.  
- Mix the 10% calcium gluconate solution into the day’s formula.  
- This is usually needed for only a few days.  

### Late-Onset Hypocalcemia (After 3 Days)

Treatment is different.  
It is not IV calcium.  

- Add calcitriol (a form of vitamin D) or extra calcium to the baby’s formula.  
- Keep doing this until calcium levels stay normal.  
- Use a low-mineral formula, especially one low in phosphate.  
- This type of formula is often used for babies with kidney problems.  

Note:  
- Some oral calcium supplements have a lot of sugar.  
- This can cause diarrhea in premature babies.  

---

## Key Points

- Neonatal hypocalcemia most often happens in the first two days of life.  
- It is more common in premature babies, small babies, babies of mothers with diabetes or overactive parathyroid glands, and babies who had trouble during birth.  
- Babies may have weak muscles, fast heart rate, fast breathing, breathing pauses, poor feeding, shaking, muscle spasms, or seizures.  
- Diagnosis is done by testing blood calcium levels.  
- Always check blood sugar to rule out low blood sugar.  
- Treat early-onset hypocalcemia with IV calcium, then switch to oral calcium for a few days.

# Coarctation of the Aorta – Simple Explanation

Coarctation of the aorta is a condition where part of the main blood vessel from the heart is too narrow. This vessel is called the aorta. It carries oxygen-rich blood from the heart to the rest of the body.

## What Happens in Coarctation?

- The aorta narrows in one spot.
- The heart must work harder to push blood through the narrow part.
- This can lead to less blood flow to the lower half of the body, including the legs, kidneys, and belly organs.

## Who Gets It?

- Some babies are born with this condition. It is a type of heart birth defect.
- The narrowing usually happens just after where a special blood vessel called the ductus arteriosus connects to the aorta.
- The ductus arteriosus is open before birth and in the first few days of life. It lets blood bypass the narrow part of the aorta.

## Symptoms

### In Babies

- Mild cases: May have no symptoms at all.
- Moderate cases: May breathe fast or with effort. They may have a fast heartbeat. They may not feed well. Their skin may look pale or gray. They may have fewer wet diapers. They may be irritable or very sleepy.

- Severe cases: Symptoms often start a few days after birth, when the ductus arteriosus closes.
  - Blood flow to the lower body drops suddenly.
  - This can cause sudden heart failure and very low blood pressure.
  - These babies become very ill quickly.

### In Older Children

- Most older children have no symptoms.
- Some may have headaches or nosebleeds because of high blood pressure in the upper body.
- Some may get leg pain when they exercise. This happens because the legs do not get enough blood.

## Why It’s a Problem

- Without treatment, severe coarctation can be deadly in newborns.
- Over time, even mild cases can strain the heart. The heart may grow larger and weaker.
- High blood pressure can develop.
- The child is at higher risk for serious heart infections.
- The child may also have other heart problems, such as a narrow aortic valve or holes in the heart.

## How It’s Diagnosed

- A doctor may hear a heart murmur during a check-up.
- A heart murmur is a sound made by blood flowing through a narrow or abnormal area.
- The doctor may notice that blood pressure is high in the arms but low in the legs.
- The pulses in the legs may be weak or hard to feel.

Tests used to confirm the diagnosis:

- **Echocardiography**: Uses sound waves to create a moving picture of the heart. This shows the narrowing.
- **CT scan or MRI**: These may be used if more detail is needed.
- **Electrocardiogram (ECG)**: Checks the heart’s electrical activity.
- **Chest x-ray**: Can show if the heart is enlarged.

## How It’s Treated

Treatment depends on how severe the narrowing is and what symptoms the child has.

### For Babies with Severe Symptoms

- They need emergency care.
- A medicine called a prostaglandin is given. This keeps the ductus arteriosus open. This helps blood flow to the lower body.
- Other medicines may be used to help the heart pump better.
- Emergency surgery is often needed to fix the narrowing.

### Surgery Options

- The narrow part of the aorta is cut out. The healthy ends are sewn together.
- A patch is used to widen the narrow area. The patch may come from a nearby blood vessel (the subclavian artery).

### For Mild Cases or Older Children

- If there are no symptoms, the condition may not be found until later in childhood.
- A doctor may notice high blood pressure in the arms and weak pulses in the legs.
- Surgery or balloon angioplasty can fix the problem.

**Balloon angioplasty**:
- A thin tube (catheter) is guided into the narrowed aorta through a blood vessel in the arm or leg.
- A small balloon at the tip of the tube is inflated. This pushes the walls of the aorta apart and opens the narrow spot.
- Sometimes, a small metal tube (stent) is placed to keep the aorta open.

### After Surgery

- Some children develop scar tissue at the repair site.
- This scar tissue can narrow the aorta again.
- Balloon angioplasty, with or without a stent, is often very effective for this.

### Preventing Infection

- After repair, children need antibiotics before:
  - Dental visits.
  - Certain surgeries, like those on the lungs or throat.
- This is to prevent a serious infection of the heart called endocarditis.
- Antibiotics are needed for 6 months after the repair.

  This site explains common heart problems in children. It is helpful for parents and caregivers.

- **American Heart Association: Infective Endocarditis**  
  This site explains heart infections and when antibiotics are needed. It is helpful for parents and caregivers.

# Pain During Periods

Pain during your period is called dysmenorrhea.  
This pain usually starts just before your period or when it begins.  
It often gets worse within the first day or two of your period.  
The pain usually goes away after two to three days.  

The pain can feel like cramps.  
It can also feel like a dull ache, a sharp pain, or a throbbing pain.  
Sometimes the pain spreads to your lower back or legs.  

Other common symptoms include:  
- Headaches  
- Feeling sick to your stomach  
- Constipation or diarrhea  
- Lower back pain  
- Needing to urinate more often  

Vomiting can happen, but it is not common.  

Sometimes the pain comes with other signs of premenstrual syndrome.  
You might also have heavy bleeding.  
You may pass large blood clots during your period.  

About 30% or more of women say the pain is bad enough to stop them from doing normal things.  
Some women miss school or work because of the pain.  
Women with painful periods are more likely to have long-term pelvic pain.  
They are also more likely to have other types of long-term pain.  

## What Causes Pain During Periods?

There are two main types of painful periods:  

**Primary dysmenorrhea**  
- This is the most common type.  
- There is no clear physical cause.  
- It usually starts in the teens or early 20s.  
- It is not linked to any disease or problem in the reproductive organs.  

**Secondary dysmenorrhea**  
- This type is caused by another health problem in the pelvis.  
- It often starts later in life, after years of normal periods.  
- Common causes include:  
  - Endometriosis (tissue like the lining of the uterus grows outside the uterus)  
  - Adenomyosis (the lining of the uterus grows into the muscle wall of the uterus)  
  - Fibroids (non-cancerous growths in the uterus)  
  - Cervical stenosis (a narrow opening in the cervix)  

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms.  
They will do a physical exam, including a pelvic exam.  
They may also use a transvaginal ultrasound.  
This is a scan that uses sound waves to look at the inside of your pelvis.  
It helps check for any problems like fibroids or endometriosis.  

## How Is It Treated?

There are several ways to treat painful periods.  

**Medicines**  
- Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are the first choice.  
  - These include ibuprofen or naproxen.  
  - They help reduce pain and inflammation.  
  - They work by blocking a substance in the body that causes pain.  
- Hormonal birth control is often used.  
  - This includes pills, patches, or rings that contain estrogen and progestin.  
  - These can reduce or stop your period.  
  - They can also reduce pain.  
- Other hormone treatments that stop ovulation or reduce bleeding may help.  

**Treating the Underlying Cause**  
- If a problem like fibroids or endometriosis is found, it can be treated.  
- For example, surgery may be used to remove fibroids.  
- In some cases, a doctor may treat the cause with medicine or surgery.  

**Lifestyle and Other Approaches**  
- Exercise may help ease pain.  
- Hypnosis has been tried by some women.  
- These methods are not proven to work, but they are safe and low risk.  

**Surgery or Nerve Treatment**  
- Surgery or nerve treatment is only used if other treatments do not work.  
- It may be an option for women who want a permanent solution.  

## Guidelines

The following are official medical guidelines for treating painful periods:  
- American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG): Dysmenorrhea and Endometriosis in the Adolescent (2018, reaffirmed 2021)  
- ACOG: Management of Acute Obstructive Uterovaginal Anomalies (2019, reaffirmed 2021)  

## Key Facts

- Dysmenorrhea means pain during or just before your period.  
- The pain often starts 1 to 3 days before your period.  
- Most cases are primary — there is no clear cause.  
- Secondary pain is caused by a health problem in the pelvis.  
- Common causes include endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, and a narrow cervix.  
- Diagnosis includes talking to your doctor, a pelvic exam, and usually an ultrasound.  
- First treatment is usually an NSAID or hormonal birth control.  
- Other hormone treatments that stop ovulation or reduce bleeding may help.  
- Exercise and hypnosis are safe and low risk, but not proven to work.  
- Surgery or nerve treatment is only used if other treatments fail or if you want a permanent fix.

# Tornwaldt Cyst

A Tornwaldt cyst is a rare, noncancerous lump. It forms in the back of the nose, near the throat. This area is called the nasopharynx.

The cyst can get infected. When it does, it may cause bad taste and smell in the mouth. It can also block the tube that connects the middle ear to the back of the nose. This blockage can lead to ear pain or pressure. You may also have a sore throat.

## Where Is the Nasopharynx?

The nasopharynx is the space behind the nose. It starts at the back of the nasal passages. It goes up to the area just above the soft part of the roof of the mouth. This is where the nose and throat meet.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use a thin, flexible tube with a camera to look inside your nose. This tool is called a nasopharyngoscope. They pass it through your nose to see the back of your throat.

To confirm the diagnosis, doctors may order imaging tests. These include a CT scan or an MRI. These tests create detailed pictures of the inside of your head and neck.

## How Is It Treated?

There are two main treatment options.

**Surgery to remove the cyst**  
Doctors can remove the entire cyst. This is done in an operating room.

**Marsupialization**  
This is a different kind of surgery. Doctors make a small cut in the cyst. They then fold the edges of the cut back and sew them in place. This creates a permanent opening. The cyst can now drain on its own. This method helps prevent future buildup.

Both procedures are done in a hospital. You may need general anesthesia. This means you will be asleep during the surgery.

# Cachexia in Cancer – Simple Explanation

Cachexia is when the body loses both fat and muscle. It happens in many serious health conditions. It is common in people with advanced or spreading cancer, especially when treatment is not working.

Some cancers cause severe cachexia. These include cancers of the pancreas and stomach. People with these cancers may lose 10 to 20 percent of their body weight. Men often lose more weight from cancer than women do. The size of the tumor or how far it has spread does not predict how bad the weight loss will be. Cachexia makes it harder to respond to chemotherapy. It also leads to poor physical function and a higher risk of death.

## What Causes Cachexia?

Cachexia is not caused by not eating enough. It is not just hunger. The real problem is that the body breaks down muscle and fat faster than it can rebuild them. The body makes less protein and breaks down more. This happens because of certain chemicals in the body. These chemicals are called cytokines. Tumor cells and the body’s own cells make them. Key cytokines include tumor necrosis factor-alpha, interleukin-1 beta, and interleukin-6. Another process, the ATP-ubiquitin-protease pathway, also plays a role.

## How to Recognize Cachexia

Cachexia is easy to see. The main sign is weight loss. You can see it in the face. The muscles in the temples (temporalis) shrink. This gives the face a hollow look, known as Hippocratic facies. Losing fat under the skin makes pressure sores more likely on bony parts of the body, like the hips and heels.

## Treating Cachexia in Cancer

The best way to treat cachexia is to treat the cancer. If the cancer is controlled or cured, the weight loss often stops.

Giving extra food is important. The goal is to give the right amount of calories for the person’s age, size, and activity level. Extra calories are often given. But any weight gain is usually small. It mostly comes from fat, not muscle. This does not improve strength or life expectancy. For most people with cancer and cachexia, extra calories are not helpful.

If a person cannot eat enough food, tube feeding or IV nutrition may be used. But this is only for rare cases when eating is not possible.

Other treatments may help some people.

- **Corticosteroids** can make a person feel better and increase appetite. But they do not help much with weight gain.
- **Cannabinoids** (like marijuana or dronabinol) increase appetite. But they do not lead to weight gain.
- **Progestogens**, such as megestrol acetate, taken as a pill (40 milligrams two or three times a day), can increase both appetite and body weight.
- **Androgenic steroids** are sometimes used. But they can harm the liver. They may also make some cancers, like prostate cancer, grow faster.

New medicines that target the chemicals involved in cachexia are being studied.

# Blockage of Blood Flow to the Spinal Cord

The spinal cord needs a steady flow of blood to stay healthy.  
Blood carries oxygen to the spinal cord.  
If an artery that supplies blood to the spinal cord gets blocked, the cord cannot get enough oxygen.  
Without oxygen, parts of the spinal cord can die. This is called infarction.

## What Causes the Blockage?

- Hardening of the aorta (a large blood vessel) due to fatty buildup.  
- A tear in the wall of the aorta.  
- Surgery or other medical procedures on the aorta in the belly.  
- A blood clot that forms in the heart and travels through the blood to the spinal cord.  
- Inflammation of blood vessels, such as a rare condition called polyarteritis nodosa.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The first sign is often sudden, sharp pain in the back.  
The pain may spread around the chest or rib area.  
Soon after, muscle weakness appears.  
You may lose the ability to feel heat, cold, or pain in parts of the body below the blocked area.  
In some cases, paralysis can happen quickly.

If the front part of the spinal cord loses blood flow:  
- The legs may become numb and weak.  
- You may not be able to move your legs.  

But some feelings stay normal because the back part of the spinal cord gets blood from other sources.  
These include:  
- The sense of touch.  
- The ability to feel vibrations.  
- The ability to know where your limbs are without looking.

Symptoms may improve a little over the first few days.  
But if the blood flow is not restored, the damage is usually permanent.

Other problems can happen:  
- Pressure sores from lying in one position too long.  
- Trouble breathing.  
- Problems with bladder control.  
- Problems with bowel control.  
- Sexual problems.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect this condition based on symptoms.  
They usually use imaging tests to confirm the diagnosis.

- **Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)**: This test shows detailed images of the spinal cord. It is the most common test used.  
- **Myelography with CT scan**: If MRI is not available, this test is used instead. It helps rule out other causes of similar symptoms.

Sometimes a **spinal tap** is done.  
This test checks the fluid around the spinal cord.  
It helps rule out other conditions like transverse myelitis.

An **angiography** test can show if an artery to the spinal cord is blocked.  
But this test is not usually needed.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause.

- If the cause can be treated, doctors will try to fix it.  
  For example:  
  - Repairing a tear in the aorta.  
  - Treating inflammation of blood vessels.

- If the cause cannot be fixed, treatment focuses on managing symptoms and preventing complications.

### Preventing Complications

- **Pressure sores**: These can form if you stay in one position too long.  
  - Change position often.  
  - Use special cushions or mattresses.

- **Breathing problems**:  
  - Do deep breathing exercises.  
  - Use postural drainage (lying in certain positions to help clear mucus).  
  - Use suctioning (a small tube to gently clear mucus from the airway).

- **Bladder problems**:  
  - A catheter is often needed.  
  - This tube drains urine from the bladder.  
  - It helps prevent the bladder from swelling and getting damaged.

- **Physical therapy**: Helps keep muscles strong and improve movement.  
- **Occupational therapy**: Helps you do daily tasks despite weakness or paralysis.

## Important Notes

- Spinal cord damage from this condition is usually permanent.  
- Early treatment can help reduce long-term problems.  
- Ongoing care is needed to manage symptoms and prevent further issues.

# Ketamine and PCP

Ketamine and phencyclidine (PCP) are strong drugs that affect the brain.  
They are used as anesthetics in medicine but are also used illegally.  
These drugs can cause serious side effects when misused.

## What These Drugs Are

Ketamine and PCP are chemically similar.  
They are both used to make people feel detached from their body and surroundings.  
They are sometimes mixed with other drugs to pass them off as different substances.  
For example, they may be sold as LSD or other hallucinogens.

Ketamine comes as a liquid or a powder.  
When used illegally, people usually sniff the powder.  
Some people swallow it.  
The liquid form is injected into a vein, muscle, or under the skin.  
In hospitals, doctors use ketamine to calm patients, control pain, and treat depression.

PCP is no longer made legally.  
It is now made illegally and sold on the street.  
It is often called "angel dust."  
It may be mixed with herbs, marijuana, or tobacco before being sold.

## What Happens When You Use These Drugs

At low doses, ketamine or PCP can make you feel very happy and excited.  
This feeling is often followed by sudden anxiety or mood swings.

At higher doses, you may feel disconnected from your body and mind.  
You may not respond to people or things around you.  
You might become aggressive, unsteady on your feet, or have trouble speaking.  
Your muscles may become stiff.  
Your eyes may move quickly back and forth.  
Your reflexes may be too strong.  
You might have sudden jerking movements.

Very high doses can cause serious problems.  
These include:  
- A dangerous buildup of acid in the blood  
- High body temperature  
- Fast heartbeat  
- Very high blood pressure  
- Seizures  
- Coma  

Death is rare but possible.

Even at normal medical doses, ketamine can cause a brief spasm in the throat.  
This can make it hard to breathe for a short time.

Most effects go away quickly.  
Most people return to normal within 45 minutes to a few hours.

## Recovery Problems

Some people have a hard time coming back to normal after using these drugs.  
This is called an "emergence reaction."  
It can cause strange behavior, confusion, or hallucinations.  
You might see vivid dreams or feel like you are floating.  
Some of these symptoms can last for weeks.

## Dependence and Withdrawal

Animal studies show that PCP can lead to physical dependence.  
People who use ketamine may become mentally dependent.  
This means they feel a strong need to keep using it.

Some people who stop using ketamine have withdrawal symptoms.  
These include:  
- Anxiety  
- Sweating  
- Fast or irregular heartbeat  

Long-term ketamine users may have problems with their bladder.  
They may feel pain when urinating, need to go often, or pass blood in their urine.  
Frequent use of ketamine may also harm long-term memory.

## How Doctors Diagnose Use

Doctors usually diagnose ketamine or PCP use based on symptoms.  
Some labs can test urine for PCP.  
But standard drug tests do not detect ketamine.  
If ketamine use must be confirmed, special tests are needed.  
These tests are called gas chromatography and mass spectroscopy.

## How Doctors Treat Use

People who use these drugs should be in a quiet, calm place.  
They should be watched closely.  
If they become very agitated or have seizures, doctors may give a medicine called a benzodiazepine.  
This helps calm them down.  
Most people do not need more treatment.

# Platelet Dysfunction

Platelets are small parts of blood that help stop bleeding. They are made in the bone marrow and travel in the blood. When you get a cut, platelets gather at the site to form a clot and stop the bleeding.

The normal number of platelets in the blood is between 140,000 and 440,000 per microliter.  
If the number drops below 50,000, you may bleed more than normal after a small injury.  
If the number falls below 10,000 to 20,000, you may bleed without any injury at all.

When platelets do not work right, you may bleed too much. This can happen after a small cut or even without any injury.

Platelet dysfunction can be caused by:
- A problem with the platelets themselves
- Something outside the body that affects how platelets work

---

## Types of Platelet Dysfunction

### Inherited Platelet Disorders

Some people are born with platelet problems. The most common inherited condition is von Willebrand disease.

Other rare inherited disorders include:
- Glanzmann disease
- Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
- Chédiak-Higashi syndrome
- Bernard-Soulier syndrome

Some of these conditions also cause skin problems, weak immune systems, or kidney issues.

### Acquired Platelet Disorders

These are not inherited. They develop later in life. They are usually caused by:
- Certain medicines
- Certain diseases

#### Common Medicines That Affect Platelets
- Aspirin
- Other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen
- Antiplatelet medicines such as clopidogrel

These medicines are often used to prevent heart attacks and strokes. But they can make bleeding more likely.

#### Diseases That Can Affect Platelets
- Liver disease (cirrhosis)
- Multiple myeloma
- Kidney disease
- Lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus)

Some people also develop platelet problems after open-heart surgery that uses a heart-lung machine.

---

## Symptoms of Platelet Dysfunction

Symptoms depend on how bad the problem is and what caused it.

### Signs of Inherited Platelet Problems
- Easy bruising
- Bleeding that lasts longer than normal after small injuries
- Heavy bleeding after dental work or minor surgery
- Boys may bleed a lot after circumcision
- Women may notice very heavy menstrual periods

### Other Common Signs
- Tiny red, purple, or brown spots on the skin (called petechiae)
- Bruises that appear after minor bumps or no injury at all

**Petechiae** are small spots. They can show up on the skin or inside the mouth.

**Ecchymoses** are large purple bruises. They often appear on the legs.

---

## How Doctors Diagnose Platelet Dysfunction

Doctors use blood tests to check for platelet problems.

### First Test: Complete Blood Count (CBC)
This test checks how many platelets you have.  
If the count is low, it may explain your bleeding.  
If the count is normal, the problem may be that the platelets are not working right.

### Other Tests
If the cause is not clear, doctors may do more tests:
- Prothrombin time (PT) and partial thromboplastin time (PTT)  
  These measure how long it takes your blood to clot.
- Platelet function tests  
  A blood sample is tested to see how well platelets respond to triggers.

Abnormal results can help doctors find the cause of the problem.

---

## Treatment of Platelet Dysfunction

### If a Medicine Is the Cause
Stop taking the medicine if possible.  
This often fixes the problem.

### If You Have an Inherited Disorder
- Avoid medicines that make bleeding worse
- If you have serious bleeding, you may need:
  - A platelet transfusion
  - A medicine called desmopressin to help reduce bleeding

### To Prevent Bleeding
- A medicine called tranexamic acid can help stop bleeding during:
  - Minor medical procedures
  - Heavy menstrual periods

This medicine helps blood clot better.

### Treating the Underlying Disease
If a disease is causing the problem, treating that disease can help.  
For example, dialysis may help if kidney failure is the cause.

---

**Note:** Always talk to your doctor before stopping or starting any medicine.

# What Is Transplantation?

Transplantation means moving tissue or an organ from one person to another. The tissue can come from:

- The patient’s own body (autografts). Examples: bone, bone marrow, or skin.
- A genetically identical donor (isografts). This only happens between identical twins.
- A donor who is not genetically identical (allografts or homografts). This is the most common type.
- A donor from a different species (xenografts or heterografts). This is very rare.

The transplanted material can be:

- Cells. For example: blood-forming stem cells, immune cells, or insulin-making cells from the pancreas.
- Parts of an organ. For example: a lobe of the lung or a section of the liver.
- A whole organ. For example: heart, kidney, hand, face, or uterus.
- Tissues. For example: corneas or complex tissue grafts.

The transplant can go into the normal place (orthotopic). For example, a heart goes into the chest. Or it can go into a different place (heterotopic). For example, a kidney may be placed in the lower belly.

Most transplants are done to fix a failing organ. This helps the body work better and can save lives. But some transplants, like hands, faces, or uteruses, do not save life. They improve quality of life. These procedures carry big risks from surgery and from medicines that weaken the immune system. Still, some of these are now standard care, even though they are rare and complex.

Most transplants use organs from:

- Living donors who are related to the patient.
- Living donors who are not related.
- People who have died.

Living donors are often used for kidney and blood stem cell transplants. They are used less often for liver parts. They are very rarely used for pancreas or lung transplants.

Organs from people who have died (whether they were still breathing or not) help meet demand. But there are still far more people needing transplants than there are organs. The number of people on waiting lists keeps growing.

Scientists are studying the use of animal organs, like hearts, kidneys, and livers, for human transplants. Progress has been made. But major problems remain. The body often rejects these organs. Also, animal organs do not work the same way as human ones.

---

## Before the Transplant

Before a transplant is done, doctors check the patient carefully. They look at health, lifestyle, and other factors. This helps predict if the transplant will work.

Donors are also checked. They get medical tests, mental health reviews, and lab work. These tests look for infections and other risks.

---

## After the Transplant

After the transplant, patients take medicines to stop the body from attacking the new organ. These medicines are called immunosuppressants.

These medicines are key to making transplants work. But they also weaken the body’s ability to fight infections. They can cause other problems, like cancer, heart disease, or serious infections that can be deadly.

Patients usually need to take these medicines for life. At first, they take high doses. A few weeks after surgery, the dose is lowered. Later, a small daily dose may be enough—unless the body starts rejecting the organ.

Doctors are studying ways to lower the dose even more. They are also researching how to train the body to accept the new organ without long-term medicine.

---

## Possible Problems After Transplant

After a transplant, patients may face:

- Rejection: The body attacks the new organ.
- Infections: The immune system is weak, so infections are more likely.
- Kidney problems: The new organ or the medicines can harm kidney function.
- Cancer: Weakened immunity raises cancer risk.
- Hardening of the arteries: This can lead to heart disease.

# Canaliculitis

Canaliculitis is an infection that causes swelling in a small tube near the inner corner of your eyelid. This tube helps drain tears from your eye into a small sac.

Each eye has two of these tubes. One is for the upper eyelid. The other is for the lower eyelid.

## Symptoms

You may notice:
- Tears that keep falling down your face
- A discharge from your eye
- A red eye
- Mild pain or tenderness

The redness and soreness are usually strongest on the side of the eyelid closest to your nose.

These symptoms can look like those of another condition called dacryocystitis.

## Where Tears Come From

Tears are made in glands near your eyes. They flow across the surface of your eye and then drain through small tubes into a tear sac. From there, they go into your nose.

## How Doctors Diagnose Canaliculitis

Doctors diagnose canaliculitis by:
- Asking about your symptoms
- Examining your eye

During the exam, the doctor may press on the area near your nose. If there is an infection, a cloudy or thick material may come out of the small tube.

## How Canaliculitis Is Treated

Treatment usually includes:
- Removing infected material
- Cleaning the tube with a special solution
- Using warm compresses
- Using antibiotic eye drops

An ophthalmologist is a doctor who specializes in eye care. They can remove the infected material from the tube. They may also flush the tube with an antibiotic solution to clear the infection.

After this, you should:
- Use warm compresses several times a day
- Put in antibiotic eye drops as directed

In some cases, surgery is needed. The surgery, called canaliculotomy, removes any blockage in the tube. This surgery usually cures the problem.

## How to Use Eye Drops and Eye Ointments

To use eye drops:
- Lean your head back and look up
- Gently pull down your lower eyelid with your clean finger
- Make a small pocket
- Put the drop into the pocket, not directly on the eye
- Close your eye and blink a few times

To use eye ointment:
- Lean your head back and look up
- Gently pull down your lower eyelid with your clean finger
- Make a small pocket
- Put a small strip of ointment into the pocket
- Close your eye and blink a few times

This helps spread the medicine over your eye.

# Protein-Energy Undernutrition (PEU)

Protein-energy undernutrition (PEU) happens when the body does not get enough energy from food. This is mainly due to a lack of protein, but also includes shortages of other nutrients. It can happen suddenly, like during starvation, or slowly over time. The condition can be mild, moderate, or severe. It affects many parts of the body. People with PEU often have low levels of many vitamins and minerals.

PEU is common in older adults who live in care homes. It also affects people with diseases that reduce appetite or make it hard to digest food. In places where food is hard to get, children are most at risk. They do not get enough calories or protein.

---

## How PEU Is Classified and What Causes It

PEU is split into three levels: mild, moderate, and severe. Doctors use a person’s weight compared to what is normal for their height or length to decide the level.

- **Mild PEU**: Weight is 85% to 90% of normal.
- **Moderate PEU**: Weight is 75% to 85% of normal.
- **Severe PEU**: Weight is less than 75% of normal.

There are two main types:

- **Primary PEU**: Happens when a person does not eat enough food.
- **Secondary PEU**: Happens when a disease or medicine stops the body from using nutrients properly.

---

## How PEU Affects the Body

When the body lacks energy, it slows down its metabolism. At first, it burns fat for energy. Later, it starts breaking down muscle and organs. This causes weight loss and weakness.

The liver and intestines lose the most weight. The heart and kidneys lose some. The brain is least affected.

---

## What People with PEU May Experience

People with moderate PEU often feel tired, weak, and irritable. They may have trouble thinking clearly. They may not want to work or do normal activities.

Digestion problems are common. Some people cannot digest lactose (a sugar in milk). This can cause diarrhea. The intestines may not make enough digestive enzymes.

Sex organs shrink. Women may stop having periods. Men and women may lose interest in sex.

Fat and muscle waste away. In severe cases, weight loss can reach 50% in adults. In children, it can be even worse.

In adults, the body looks very thin. Bones stick out. The skin becomes dry, thin, pale, and cold. Hair becomes dry and falls out. Wounds heal slowly. Older people are more likely to break hips or get pressure sores.

In serious cases, the heart gets smaller. The pulse slows. Blood pressure drops. Breathing becomes shallow. Body temperature falls. This can lead to death.

Other signs include swelling (edema), anemia, yellow skin (jaundice), and small red spots under the skin (petechiae). Liver, kidney, or heart failure can happen.

---

### Marasmus (in infants)

This is a type of PEU in babies. It causes extreme hunger, weight loss, and slow growth. The baby loses fat and muscle. The ribs and face look very bony. The skin hangs loose and thin.

### Kwashiorkor

This type causes swelling in the legs and around the eyes. This happens because the blood lacks a protein called albumin. The belly sticks out because the stomach muscles are weak, the intestines are full, the liver is big, and fluid builds up in the belly (ascites).

The skin becomes dry, wrinkled, and cracked. It may turn darker or lighter. It can break easily. Hair becomes thin, reddish-brown, or gray. Hair on the scalp falls out. Eyelashes may grow longer. If the child goes in and out of starvation and good nutrition, the hair can look like a striped flag.

Children with this condition may seem quiet but become upset when held.

### Total Starvation

If a person eats nothing for 8 to 12 weeks, they will die. In this case, some symptoms of PEU do not have time to appear.

---

## How PEU Is Diagnosed

Doctors start by asking about the person’s diet and health history.

To check how bad the condition is, they measure:

- Body mass index (BMI)
- Blood levels of albumin
- White blood cell count
- CD4 count (a type of immune cell)
- Blood level of transferrin

To check for complications, they test:

- Complete blood count
- Electrolytes (like sodium, potassium)
- Blood urea nitrogen
- Blood sugar
- Calcium, magnesium, and phosphate

If the diet history shows poor eating, the diagnosis is clear. But if not, blood tests are needed.

Doctors also look at the body. They measure height and weight. They check fat and muscle levels. BMI is calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by height in meters squared.

Blood tests help confirm the diagnosis, especially if the case is unclear. Many blood values are abnormal in PEU. For example:

- Hormones, vitamins, and fats are low.
- Prealbumin, insulin-like growth factor-1, and retinol-binding protein are low.
- Urine tests can show how much muscle is being broken down.

A skin test can check immune strength. A small amount of a common antigen is injected under the skin. The size of the bump shows how well the immune system is working.

If the cause of PEU is not clear, doctors may test for inflammation. They check C-reactive protein or soluble interleukin-2 receptor. These can show if there is an infection, cancer, or other serious illness.

Other tests may be done to find hidden infections. These include:

- Stool tests for parasites
- Urine tests
- Blood cultures
- Chest x-ray
- Tuberculin test

People with PEU may not show normal signs of infection. So these tests are important.

---

## How PEU Is Treated

Most people with mild or moderate PEU can be treated at home. They should eat a balanced diet. If they cannot eat solid food, they can use liquid food supplements. These are usually made without lactose.

If diarrhea continues, it may mean the person cannot digest lactose. In this case, yogurt-based formulas are better than milk-based ones. Yogurt is easier to digest.

People should also take a multivitamin.

For severe PEU or long-term starvation, hospital care is needed. The first step is to fix fluid and electrolyte problems. Infections must be treated.

A recent study found that children may benefit from antibiotics to prevent infections.

Next, the body needs nutrients. These are given by mouth if possible. If not, a feeding tube is used. A nasogastric tube goes through the nose into the stomach. A gastrostomy tube goes through the belly into the stomach (this is called enteral nutrition).

If the gut cannot absorb nutrients, nutrients are given through a vein (this is called parenteral nutrition).

As the person gets better, they may need extra vitamins and minerals. Doctors often recommend twice the normal daily amount until full recovery.

---

## Prognosis (Outlook)

The outlook depends on how severe the PEU is and how quickly treatment starts.

If not treated, severe PEU can lead to organ failure and death.

---

## Key Points

- PEU can happen because a person does not eat enough, or because a disease stops the body from using food properly.
- In severe cases, the body loses fat and then vital organs. Immunity weakens. Organs slow down. This can lead to multiple organ failure.
- To check the severity, doctors use BMI, blood albumin, white blood cell count, CD4 count, and transferrin levels.
- To find complications, doctors test blood for complete blood count, electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, glucose, calcium, magnesium, and phosphate.
- For mild PEU, a balanced diet is best. Avoid lactose if diarrhea continues.
- For severe PEU, hospital care is needed. The person must get a controlled diet. Fluid and electrolyte problems must be fixed. Infections must be treated.
- A serious risk during treatment is refeeding syndrome. This can cause fluid buildup, low electrolytes, high blood sugar, heart rhythm problems, and diarrhea.

# Nitrofurantoin

Nitrofurantoin is a medicine that fights certain types of bacterial infections.  
It is only used to treat or prevent simple bladder infections.  

Doctors do not fully understand how it works.  
But it stops bacteria from growing and doing harm.  

You take nitrofurantoin by mouth.  
You swallow the pills with water.  

## What It Is Used For

- Treating bladder infections that are not serious  
- Preventing bladder infections in people who get them often  

## Possible Side Effects

- Upset stomach or throwing up  
- Numbness or tingling in the hands or feet  
- Allergic reactions, such as rash or swelling  

## Who Should Not Take Nitrofurantoin

- People with poor kidney function  
- People with a blood disorder called glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PD deficiency)  
  - This condition can make red blood cells weak and break easily  
  - Nitrofurantoin can make this worse and cause anemia (too few red blood cells)  

## During Pregnancy

- Do not take nitrofurantoin near the time of delivery  
- Do not take it during labor or birth  
- It can harm the baby’s red blood cells  
- This can lead to a type of anemia called hemolytic anemia  

## During Breastfeeding

- Do not take nitrofurantoin in the first month after giving birth  
- It may pass into breast milk and affect the baby
