# Multiple Pregnancy

A multiple pregnancy means there is more than one baby in the uterus.

In the United States in 2021:
- There were 31 twin births for every 1,000 total births.
- There were 80 births of triplets or more for every 100,000 total births.

Twin pregnancy rates vary by region:
- Highest in Africa.
- Middle in the United States, Europe, and Australasia.
- Lowest in Asia and South America.

## What Increases the Chance of a Multiple Pregnancy?

You are more likely to have more than one baby if:
- You used fertility treatments like in vitro fertilization.
- You or a close family member has had a multiple pregnancy before.
- You have had more than one baby before.
- You are overweight or obese.
- You are 65 inches (164 centimeters) or taller.
- You are 35 years old or older.

## How Is a Multiple Pregnancy Diagnosed?

Your doctor may suspect a multiple pregnancy if your uterus is larger than expected for how far along you are.

An ultrasound scan confirms the diagnosis. It also shows whether each baby has its own sac and outer membrane.

- If babies share the outer membrane, they are called monochorionic twins.
- If babies share both the outer and inner membranes, they are called monoamniotic twins.

Babies who share membranes are at higher risk for a condition called twin-twin transfusion syndrome. This can cause uneven growth and fluid levels between the babies.

## How Is a Multiple Pregnancy Managed?

Your care during pregnancy focuses on watching the babies’ growth and spotting any problems early.

### Routine Tests
- Testing for gestational diabetes is the same as for single pregnancies.
- Checking for preeclampsia is the same as for single pregnancies.

### Extra Monitoring for Multiple Pregnancies
- Ultrasounds in the second trimester to check for a short cervix.
- Starting at 32 weeks, regular checks of the babies’ health. These may include:
  - Nonstress test.
  - Biophysical profile.

### Preventive Treatments (if needed)
Talk to your doctor about whether these may help:
- **Aspirin** to lower the risk of preeclampsia.
- **Cerclage**, **vaginal progesterone**, or **tocolytics** to help prevent early delivery.
- **Corticosteroids** and **magnesium sulfate** to help protect the babies if they are born early.

### Delivery Method
- For twins, vaginal birth is preferred if the first baby is head-down.
- Cesarean delivery is used if:
  - The first baby is not head-down.
  - There are three or more babies.
  - There is a medical need to deliver quickly for the safety of the mother or babies.

## Key Points

Multiple pregnancies come with higher risks for both mother and babies. These include:
- Gestational diabetes.
- Preeclampsia.
- Early delivery.
- Poor growth of one or more babies.
- Heavy bleeding after delivery.
- Stillbirth or baby death soon after birth.

- If your uterus is larger than expected, get an ultrasound to check for more than one baby.

- Watch the babies’ growth and check for problems by:
  - Testing for diabetes.
  - Checking for preeclampsia.
  - Doing regular ultrasounds in the second trimester to check the cervix.
  - Starting fetal checks at 32 weeks (like nonstress tests or biophysical profiles).

- Talk to your doctor about preventive treatments if needed:
  - Aspirin for preeclampsia.
  - Cerclage, vaginal progesterone, or tocolytics for early delivery.
  - Corticosteroids and magnesium sulfate for babies born early.

- Vaginal birth is preferred for twins if the first baby is head-down.

- Use cesarean delivery if the first baby is not head-down, if there are three or more babies, or if there is a medical reason to deliver quickly.

# Elbow Dislocations

An elbow dislocation happens when the lower end of the upper arm bone no longer fits with the tops of the two forearm bones.  

The dislocation can be complete. This means the bones are completely out of place and do not touch.  
It can also be partial. This means part of the bones still touch. A partial dislocation is called a subluxation.

Most elbow dislocations happen when someone falls on an arm that is straight.  
These injuries can also cause broken bones, nerve damage, or damage to a blood vessel.

Elbow dislocations are fairly common.  
But it usually takes a lot of force to completely dislocate an elbow.  
Partial dislocations (subluxations) are common in toddlers.  
They can happen with much less force.  
Subluxations are rare in babies, older children, and adults.

X-rays can show if the elbow is dislocated.

(See also: Overview of Dislocations.)

---

## How a Dislocated Elbow Is Treated

Most people with a dislocated elbow need a doctor to put the bones back in place. This is called reduction.

The treatment usually includes:

- A medicine to help you relax and another to reduce pain.  
- Lying down on your back.  
- Bending the elbow and gently turning the forearm so the palm faces up.  
- Holding the upper arm steady.  
- Pulling the wrist upward until the bones go back into place.

After the joint is put back, the doctor checks it for stability.  
An X-ray is taken to make sure no bones are broken.  
Then the elbow is usually held still with a splint for up to one week.  
This helps the pain and swelling go down.

After the splint is removed, gentle movement exercises begin.  
A sling is worn for two to three weeks to protect the elbow.

---

## Radial Head Subluxation (Nursemaid’s Elbow)

This is a partial dislocation of the elbow.  
It happens when the top of one forearm bone (the radius) slips out of its normal position.

This injury is common in toddlers.  
It often happens when a caregiver pulls a child forward or grabs the child by the wrist.

The only sign may be that the child refuses to use the injured arm.

Doctors suspect this injury based on how the injury happened, the child’s symptoms, and a physical exam.

Doctors can usually fix the problem without surgery.  
No sedatives or pain medicine are needed.

This injury mostly happens in children who are about 2 to 3 years old.  
At this age, the top of the radius bone is small.  
It can slip through the ligaments that hold the elbow together.  
This can happen when a parent or caregiver pulls a child forward or grabs the wrist during a fall.  
Many caregivers do not remember doing this.

As children grow, the top of the radius gets bigger.  
It becomes too large to slip through the ligaments.  
So the injury usually stops happening after age 4 or 5.

The elbow may only be slightly tender.  
Toddlers often cannot explain how they feel.  
So the only sign may be that they do not move the arm.  
The arm may hang down by the side.  
It may turn slightly inward.  
Or the child may hold the arm bent against their body.

Parents or caregivers should not try to move the arm.

Toddlers may cry when the injury happens.  
But they often calm down quickly.  
They may act normal, except they do not use the injured arm.

### When to See a Doctor

If a toddler has symptoms that suggest a subluxation, take them to a doctor.  
If the elbow has popped back into place, the child will be able to move it normally.  
If the child still cannot move the elbow, they need to see a doctor.

Doctors make the diagnosis based on the story of how the injury happened, the symptoms, and the physical exam.

X-rays are not needed because the injury does not show up on X-rays.

### How to Prevent This Injury

Parents and caregivers should:

- Never suddenly jerk a toddler’s hand, wrist, or forearm.  
- Never lift a toddler by one arm, wrist, or hand.  
- Never swing a child by the hand or forearm.  
- Instead, lift the child from under the arms or from both arms.

### How Doctors Fix the Injury

Doctors usually put the bone back in place. This is called reduction.  
No sedatives or pain medicine are usually needed.  
You might hear a soft pop or click when the bone slips back.  
The child may start using the arm again in 10 to 20 minutes.

If the child moves the elbow, no X-ray or splint is needed.

If the child still has pain after 24 hours or still cannot use the arm, the bone may not be fully in place.  
Or there may be a broken bone.  
In this case, the child should see a doctor again.

### Recovery

Most toddlers recover fully after treatment.  
But 20 to 40 percent of them will have the same injury again.

# Understanding Birth Control You might choose to use birth control for many reasons. These can include your personal life, health, family plans, or financial situation. Birth control helps you avoid getting pregnant. It can be used for a short time or for life. If you do get pregnant when you did not mean to, you may consider ending the pregnancy. This is called an abortion. # Childhood Cancer: Simple Facts

## How Common Is Childhood Cancer?

In the United States, more children and teens are being diagnosed with cancer than in the past.  
In 2024, about 10,000 children from birth to 14 years old are expected to be diagnosed with cancer.  
About 5,300 teens aged 15 to 19 are also expected to be diagnosed.  

Even though more children are getting cancer, fewer are dying.  
From 1970 to 2020, death rates dropped by 70% in children and 64% in teens.  

Cancer is still a leading cause of death in children.  
In children aged 1 to 14, cancer is the second most common cause of death.  
Accidents are the most common cause.  
In teens aged 15 to 19, cancer is the fourth most common cause of death.  

## Types of Cancer in Children and Teens

Some cancers that happen in children can also happen in adults.  
These include:

- **Leukemia** – the most common childhood cancer. It makes up about 28% of all childhood cancers.  
- **Brain and nervous system tumors** – found in about 25% of cases.  
- **Lymphomas** – found in about 12% of cases.  
- **Bone cancers** like osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma – found in about 4% of cases.  

Some cancers only happen in children and teens.  
These include:

- Neuroblastoma  
- Retinoblastoma  
- Rhabdomyosarcoma  
- Wilms tumor  

Unlike many adult cancers, childhood cancers are often curable.  
About 85 out of 100 children and teens with cancer live at least 5 years after diagnosis.  
In 2020, about 500,000 adults in the United States were living who had cancer as children.  

## Side Effects of Cancer Treatment

Doctors use several treatments to fight cancer in children.  
These include:

- Surgery  
- Chemotherapy (medicine to kill cancer cells)  
- Stem cell transplants  
- Radiation therapy (using high-energy beams to destroy cancer cells)  

Newer treatments are also being used:

- **Immunotherapy** – helps the body’s own immune system fight cancer.  
- **Targeted therapy** – uses medicine that attacks specific changes in cancer cells.  

Because children are still growing, these treatments can cause side effects that adults do not usually get.  
For example:

- A limb treated with radiation may not grow to full size.  
- Radiation to the brain may affect learning and thinking skills.  

Children who survive cancer may face long-term health problems later in life.  
These can include:

- Trouble having children (infertility)  
- Poor growth  
- Delayed or no puberty  
- Heart or other organ damage  
- A second cancer (this happens in 3 to 12 out of 100 survivors)  
- Mental health or social challenges  
- Learning or brain problems  

The chance of a second cancer depends on:

- The type of first cancer  
- Whether radiation therapy was used  
- The type of chemotherapy given  

Because of these risks, children with cancer should be treated at centers that specialize in childhood cancer care.  

## The Care Team for Children with Cancer

Being diagnosed with cancer is hard on the child and the whole family.  
Treatment can be intense and long.  
It may be hard to keep a normal routine.  
Children may need to stay in the hospital often.  
They may also need to go to the doctor’s office or clinic for treatment.  

Parents often feel stressed.  
They may struggle to work, care for other children, and meet the needs of their child with cancer.  
This is even harder if treatment is far from home.  

### Did You Know?

Even though more children are being diagnosed with cancer, more are surviving than ever before.  

### A Good Care Team Makes a Big Difference

Children with cancer need a team of experts who know how to treat childhood cancer.  
These experts are called pediatric doctors.  
They focus on babies, children, and teens.  

A strong care team usually includes:

- Pediatric cancer doctors (oncologists and radiation oncologists)  
- A pediatric oncology nurse – a registered nurse who cares for children with cancer and teaches families  
- A pediatric surgeon – who removes or takes a sample of tumors  
- A pediatric radiologist – who reads imaging tests like X-rays and MRIs for children  
- A pathologist – who checks tissue samples to confirm the cancer type  
- The child’s regular doctor (pediatrician)  
- A child life specialist – who helps children and families cope with hospital stays and illness  
- A social worker – who offers emotional support and helps with money and insurance issues  
- A teacher – who works with the child, school, and doctors to keep education on track  
- A school liaison – who helps the family and child connect with the school  
- A psychologist – who supports the mental health of the child, siblings, and parents  
- A parent advocate – another parent who has been through this and can guide families  

All children newly diagnosed with cancer should be seen by a genetics team.  
This team checks for gene changes that can raise cancer risk or affect treatment.

The following resources can help families.  
These are in English.

# Rhodiola

The plant known as rhodiola has the scientific name *Rhodiola rosea*.  
People in Eastern and Northern Europe and parts of Asia have used the root and underground stem of this plant for centuries in traditional medicine.  
It is also called arctic root, golden root, orpin rose, rose root, rosewort, and Siberian golden root.  
The root and stem are dried and mixed with alcohol to make medicine.

Doses of rhodiola supplements can vary widely.  
There is not enough reliable evidence to know the best dose.  
The amount listed on store-bought products may not be accurate.

## What People Say Rhodiola Can Do

Some people believe rhodiola helps the body handle stress and return to normal function.  
This idea is called being an "adaptogen."  
Rhodiola is said to help with:

- Symptoms of altitude sickness  
- Better learning and memory  
- More energy  
- Better performance in sports and exercise  
- Lower cholesterol levels  
- Less depression  
- Less tiredness  
- Slowing down aging

## What Research Shows About Rhodiola

There are no strong studies in people that prove rhodiola works for any health problem.

Some small studies suggest rhodiola may help with exercise and sports performance.  
One review looked at 13 studies with 263 people.  
Short-term use helped with endurance and how hard exercise felt.  
Long-term use helped with short bursts of power but not with long endurance.  
Another review found that higher doses of rhodiola helped with sprinting and strength training in both trained and untrained people.  
But the studies used different doses and lengths of time.  
More research is needed.

One small study with 89 people found that rhodiola helped with mild to moderate depression after 42 days.  
Another study with 57 people compared rhodiola to sertraline (a common antidepressant) and a placebo.  
Both rhodiola and sertraline helped with depression.  
There was no big difference between them.  
But rhodiola worked less well than sertraline when compared to the placebo.  
Rhodiola also caused fewer side effects.

Rhodiola may help when used with another antidepressant called an SSRI.  
However, two major medical groups — the World Federation of Societies of Biological Psychiatry and the Canadian Network for Mood and Anxiety Treatments — do not recommend rhodiola alone or with other treatments for major depression.

Rhodiola has also been used to help manage stress.

## Possible Side Effects of Rhodiola

Rhodiola may cause:

- Dizziness  
- Dry mouth  
- Too much saliva  
- A sudden episode of mania (a high mood with racing thoughts and risky behavior) — this was seen in one person who took rhodiola as an exercise supplement

## Drug Interactions with Rhodiola

Rhodiola may interact with certain medicines.  
It can raise your heart rate when taken with some antidepressants.  
It may cause serotonin syndrome if taken with other drugs that affect serotonin.  
Serotonin syndrome is a serious condition with symptoms like confusion, fast heartbeat, and muscle stiffness.

Rhodiola may lower blood sugar.  
This could be dangerous if you take medicine for high blood sugar.

Rhodiola may lower blood pressure.  
This could be a problem if you already have low blood pressure or take blood pressure medicine.

Rhodiola may increase the effect of warfarin, a blood thinner.  
This could raise the risk of bleeding.

Rhodiola has anti-inflammatory effects.  
If you take other anti-inflammatory medicines, the effects may add up and cause side effects.

Rhodiola may reduce how well immunosuppressant drugs work.  
These drugs are used to calm the immune system after organ transplants or for autoimmune diseases.

(See also: *Some Possible Dietary Supplement–Medication Interactions*)

# Brain Infections: Simple Explanation

Infections in the brain can come from viruses, bacteria, fungi, or, less often, tiny organisms called protozoa or parasites.  
Another type of brain problem, called spongiform encephalopathy, is caused by strange proteins known as prions.

The brain and spinal cord are part of the central nervous system.  
When the brain gets infected, the spinal cord is often affected too.  
The brain and spinal cord are usually well protected from infections.  
But if they do get infected, the results can be very serious.

Infections can cause swelling in the brain. This is called encephalitis.  
Viruses are the most common cause of encephalitis.  
Infections can also cause swelling in the layers of tissue that cover the brain and spinal cord. This is called meningitis.  
Bacterial meningitis often spreads into the brain, leading to encephalitis.  
Viral infections that cause encephalitis often also cause meningitis.  
When both the brain and the covering layers are infected, doctors call it meningoencephalitis.  
But if the main problem is in the covering layers, it is usually called meningitis.  
If the main problem is in the brain, it is usually called encephalitis.

In most cases of encephalitis or meningitis, the infection is not just in one spot.  
It can spread across the whole brain or along the entire spinal cord.

In some cases, the infection stays in one place.  
It forms a pocket of pus.  
This is called an abscess if it is inside the brain.  
It is called an empyema if it is in a space between the brain’s covering layers or in the lungs.

- **Empyemas** form in natural spaces in the body.  
  For example, they can form between the layers that cover the brain or in the lungs.

- **Abscesses** look like boils.  
  They can form anywhere in the body, including inside the brain.

Fungi, such as aspergilli, protozoa like Toxoplasma gondii, and parasites like Taenia solium (a type of pork tapeworm) can cause cysts in the brain.  
These cysts are clusters of tiny organisms surrounded by a protective wall.

Sometimes, a brain infection, a vaccine, cancer, or another illness can cause the body’s immune system to react wrongly.  
The immune system then attacks healthy brain cells.  
This is called an autoimmune reaction.  
It leads to brain swelling.  
This condition is known as postinfectious encephalitis.

Bacteria and other germs can reach the brain and spinal cord in several ways:

- They can travel through the bloodstream.  
- They can enter the brain directly from outside the body.  
  For example, through a broken skull or during brain surgery.  
- They can spread from nearby infected areas.  
  For example, from the sinuses or the middle ear.

# Tapeworm Infections – Simple Explanation

## What Are Tapeworms?

Tapeworms are flat, parasitic worms that live in the intestines of animals and people.  
They are not worms you can see with the naked eye.  
They grow inside the body and take nutrients from the food you eat.

The four main types of tapeworms that infect people are:

- *Taenia saginata* – the beef tapeworm  
- *Taenia solium* – the pork tapeworm  
- *Hymenolepis nana* – the dwarf tapeworm  
- *Diphyllobothrium latum* – the fish tapeworm  

Other tapeworms can also infect people.  
These include species that cause sparganosis, coenurosis, and echinococcosis.

Tapeworms spread through food.  
They can also spread when people swallow tiny eggs from contaminated soil or surfaces.

## How Tapeworms Live and Spread

All tapeworms go through three stages: eggs, larvae, and adults.

- Adult tapeworms live in the intestines of final hosts.  
- Final hosts are animals that eat other animals. Humans are one of these hosts.  
- The adult worms do not have a mouth or stomach.  
- They absorb food directly from the intestines of their host.

Tapeworms have three main parts:

- The **scolex** (head) – this is how the worm sticks to the inside of the intestine.  
- The **neck** – this part can grow new segments.  
- The **proglottids** (segments) – these are the body parts behind the neck.  
  - New segments grow near the neck.  
  - As they move down the worm, they become mature.  
  - Mature segments contain eggs and are called gravid segments.  
  - Each mature segment has one ovary and many eggs.

The life cycle works like this:

1. Adult tapeworms in the intestines lay eggs.  
2. The eggs leave the body in stool.  
3. The eggs get into the environment, like soil or water.  
4. An animal (the intermediate host) eats the eggs.  
5. The eggs hatch into larvae inside that animal.  
6. The larvae travel through the blood and form cysts in muscles or organs.  
7. A final host (like a human) eats the infected animal’s meat.  
8. The cysts break open in the intestines.  
9. The larvae grow into adult tapeworms.  
10. The cycle starts again.

Some tapeworms, like *Taenia solium*, can cause problems in people who eat the eggs.  
In this case, the eggs turn into larvae that travel through the body and form cysts in tissues like the brain, muscles, or eyes.

## Who Gets Infected?

- People get *Taenia saginata* (beef tapeworm) by eating undercooked beef.  
- People get *Diphyllobothrium latum* (fish tapeworm) by eating raw or undercooked fish.  
- People get *Hymenolepis nana* (dwarf tapeworm) by swallowing eggs from contaminated surfaces.  
- People get *Taenia solium* (pork tapeworm) in two ways:  
  - By eating undercooked pork (then they become the final host).  
  - By swallowing eggs (then they become the intermediate host).  
- People get *Echinococcus* species by swallowing eggs from dog feces.  
- *Taenia asiatica* is like *Taenia saginata*, but it is linked to eating pork in Asia.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most adult tapeworms do not cause symptoms.  
They live quietly in the intestines and do not make people feel sick.

But some infections can cause problems:

- Heavy infections with *Hymenolepis nana* can cause stomach pain, diarrhea, and weight loss.  
- Infections with *Diphyllobothrium latum* can lead to low vitamin B12 levels.  
- Low vitamin B12 can cause anemia, which makes people feel weak and tired.

Larvae are more dangerous than adult worms.  
They can grow in places outside the intestines, such as the brain, liver, lungs, eyes, or muscles.

When larvae grow in the brain, they can cause seizures, headaches, or even death.  
This is called cysticercosis when caused by *Taenia solium*.  
*Echinococcus granulosus* causes cystic hydatid disease.  
*Echinococcus multilocularis* causes alveolar disease.

Other rare tapeworms can also infect people.  
They can form lumps under the skin or in muscles.  
Some can even affect the brain or eyes.

## How Are Tapeworm Infections Diagnosed?

- For adult tapeworms:  
  A doctor checks a stool sample under a microscope.  
  They look for eggs or segments of the worm.

- For larval infections:  
  Doctors use imaging tests like CT scans or MRI scans.  
  These show where the larvae are in the body.  
  Blood tests may also help confirm the infection.

## How Are Tapeworm Infections Treated?

- For adult tapeworms in the intestines:  
  Medicines called anthelmintics kill the worms.  
  The most common medicine is praziquantel.  
  Another medicine, niclosamide, is also effective but not available in the United States.  
  Nitazoxanide is used for *Hymenolepis nana* infections.

- For larvae in the body (like in the brain or organs):  
  Some infections respond to medicine like albendazole or praziquantel.  
  Others need surgery to remove the cysts.

## How Can You Prevent Tapeworm Infections?

- Cook meat well.  
  - Pork, beef, lamb, game meat, and fish must be cooked to safe temperatures.  
  - Use a food thermometer to check.

- Freeze meat for a long time.  
  - This kills some tapeworms, especially in fish.

- Deworm pets regularly.  
  - Dogs and cats can carry tapeworm eggs.  
  - Keep their feces away from food and water.

- Do not let pets eat dead animals.  
  - This stops them from getting infected and spreading eggs.

- Keep rodents, fleas, and grain beetles out of your home.  
  - These can carry tapeworm eggs.

- Check meat before buying.  
  - Look for signs of infection during meat inspection.

- Treat human waste safely.  
  - Use toilets and proper sewage systems.  
  - Do not use human feces as fertilizer.

- Do not rely on smoking or drying meat.  
  - These methods do not kill tapeworms.

## Key Points

- Tapeworms live in the intestines and take nutrients from your food.  
- Most adult tapeworms do not cause symptoms.  
- Larvae can cause serious illness if they grow in the brain, eyes, or other organs.  
- Diagnosis depends on stool tests or imaging.  
- Medicines can treat most infections.  
- Prevention is the best way to stay safe.  
- Always cook meat well and keep your environment clean.

# Meckel Diverticulum

A Meckel diverticulum is a small pouch that sticks out from the wall of the small intestine.  
It is present at birth in some children.  
It is a rare variation of normal intestinal structure.

## What You Need to Know

- Most children with a Meckel diverticulum have no symptoms.  
- Some children may have painless bleeding from the rectum.  
- The pouch can become infected or cause other problems.  
- Boys are more likely than girls to have complications.  

## Possible Problems

You can live your whole life without knowing you have a Meckel diverticulum.  
But sometimes it causes serious issues.  

Common problems include:

- **Bleeding**  
- **Blockage** (obstruction)  
- **Inflammation** (diverticulitis)  
- **A hole** (perforation)  
- **Tumors**  

More than half of all Meckel diverticula contain tissue like stomach or pancreas tissue.  
If stomach tissue is present, it can make acid.  
This acid can cause ulcers and bleeding in nearby parts of the intestine.  
Bleeding is most common in children under 5 years old.

Blockage can happen at any age.  
It is more common in older children and adults.  
In young children, blockage often happens when the pouch folds into itself.  
This is called intussusception.

The pouch can also become inflamed.  
This is called diverticulitis.  
It can happen at any age, but it is most common in older children.

If the pouch develops a hole, it can cause a serious infection in the belly.  
This is called peritonitis.  
It causes severe pain and needs urgent care.

Tumors in the pouch are rare.  
They mostly happen in adults.  
One type is called a carcinoid tumor.

## Symptoms

Most children with a Meckel diverticulum feel fine.  
Many adults only find out about it during surgery for another reason.

The most common symptom in children under 5 is painless bleeding from the rectum.  
This bleeding comes from ulcers in the small intestine.  
The ulcers are caused by acid from the pouch.

The stool may look:
- Bright red  
- Brick-colored  
- Like currant jelly (a mix of blood and mucus)  
- Black (if blood has broken down)

Bleeding is usually not severe.  
But in rare cases, it can be serious enough to need emergency surgery.

In all age groups, a blockage causes:
- Cramping belly pain  
- Nausea  
- Vomiting

Diverticulitis causes:
- Severe belly pain  
- Tenderness in the belly  
- Vomiting  
- Symptoms that look like appendicitis

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Diagnosing a Meckel diverticulum can be hard.

If a child is bleeding from the rectum, doctors may do a **Meckel scan**.  
This test uses a small amount of a safe radioactive substance.  
It is given through a vein.  
The substance collects in the pouch.  
A special camera then shows where it is.

Other tests that can help:
- **Video capsule endoscopy**: The child swallows a small camera.  
  It takes pictures as it moves through the intestines.  
  It can find sources of bleeding.

- **Enteroscopy**: A thin, flexible tube with a camera is gently passed into the small intestine.  
  It lets doctors see inside and check for problems.

For belly pain, doctors often use **computed tomography (CT)**.  
This scan gives detailed pictures of the belly.  
It can show the pouch and other causes of pain.  
Doctors may also take regular x-rays of the belly.

## Treatment

No treatment is needed if the pouch causes no symptoms.

But if the pouch is bleeding, causing a blockage, or causing ongoing pain, surgery is needed.  
Surgery removes the pouch.

Diverticulitis usually also needs surgery.

If a doctor finds a Meckel diverticulum during another surgery, they may remove it.  
This is to prevent future problems.

# Varices

Varices are enlarged veins in the lower part of the food pipe (esophagus) or the upper part of the stomach.  
They happen when blood pressure in the liver’s main blood vessel (portal vein) is too high.  
This high pressure is usually caused by scarring in the liver, known as cirrhosis.  

Varices can burst and cause very heavy bleeding.  
But they do not cause other symptoms before they bleed.  

## How Varices Are Found

Doctors use a thin, flexible tube with a camera (called an endoscope) to look inside the esophagus and stomach.  
This test is called upper endoscopy.  
It is the best way to see varices and check if they are likely to bleed.  

Sometimes, other causes of bleeding in the stomach or intestines are found during the same test.  
In fact, up to one-third of people with liver disease who bleed from the upper gut have a different cause, not varices.  

## What Happens When Varices Bleed

Bleeding from varices is sudden and often very heavy.  
It usually does not hurt.  
You may vomit blood, or the blood may come out in the stool.  
You might feel dizzy, weak, or have a fast heartbeat.  
These are signs of shock.  

Bleeding from the lower esophagus is most common.  
Bleeding from the stomach area (gastric varices) can be sudden, but it often happens slowly over time.  

If you have liver disease, bleeding can also lead to confusion or changes in thinking.  
This is called portosystemic encephalopathy.  

## How Varices Are Treated

### Immediate Care

- Doctors will help you breathe and keep your blood pressure up.  
- You may need fluids through a tube in your vein.  
- You may need blood transfusions if you have lost a lot of blood.  

### Endoscopic Banding

- The main treatment is endoscopic banding.  
- A doctor uses the endoscope to place small rubber bands around the varices.  
- This stops the bleeding and helps prevent it from happening again.  
- Injection therapy (sclerotherapy) is used only if banding is not possible.  

### Medicine

- A medicine called octreotide is given through a vein.  
- It helps reduce blood flow to the liver and lowers pressure in the portal vein.  
- It is given as a shot first, then as a continuous drip for 3 to 5 days.  
- Octreotide works better than older medicines and has fewer side effects.  

### Antibiotics

- People with liver disease and bleeding are at risk for infection.  
- Doctors give antibiotics like norfloxacin or ceftriaxone to prevent infection.  

### Other Treatments

- If bleeding continues, a special procedure called TIPS may be needed.  
- TIPS is done by a radiologist.  
- A small tube (stent) is placed inside the liver to create a new path for blood to flow.  
- This lowers pressure in the portal vein and stops bleeding.  
- The size of the stent is very important.  
  - Too big: can cause brain problems.  
  - Too small: may block up over time.  

- A Sengstaken-Blakemore tube is a tube with balloons that can be used to stop bleeding temporarily.  
- It is not used as the first treatment because it is uncomfortable and can cause harm.  
- It may be used only if you are waiting for a TIPS or surgery.  
- The tube is put through the nose and into the stomach.  
- One balloon is inflated in the stomach and pulled tight.  
- If that does not stop the bleeding, a second balloon in the esophagus is inflated.  
- This can cause pain, damage to the esophagus, or breathing problems.  
- So, you will likely need a breathing tube and sedation.  

- Metal stents that expand in the esophagus can also be used to stop bleeding.  

- For some people, a liver transplant can fix the problem.  
- But this is only an option if you are already on the transplant waiting list.  

### What to Do If You Are on Beta-Blockers

- If you take a medicine like propranolol to prevent variceal bleeding, stop it if you are bleeding and your blood pressure is low.  

## Long-Term Outlook

- About 4 out of 10 people stop bleeding on their own.  
- Between 15% and 25% of people die within 6 weeks of bleeding.  
- After 5 years, death rates range from 20% to 80%, depending on how bad the liver disease is.  
- People with very poor liver function are more likely to die from bleeding.  
- People with better liver function usually survive.  

- If you survive the first bleed, you are at high risk of bleeding again.  
- Regular endoscopy or medicine (like banding or beta-blockers) can lower this risk.  
- Rebleeding rates vary from 5% to 60%, depending on treatment.  
- But these treatments do not always improve long-term survival.  
- This is because the liver disease itself is the main problem.  

## Key Points

- Varices are the most common cause of serious bleeding in people with liver disease.  
- But they are not the only cause.  
- The severity of liver disease is the biggest factor in whether you survive a bleed.  
- Endoscopy is used to both diagnose and treat varices.  
- Banding is the preferred treatment.  
- The chance of bleeding again is between 5% and 40%, depending on treatment.

# Aztreonam

Aztreonam is a type of antibiotic. It is the only antibiotic in a group called monobactams. Monobactams are a type of beta-lactam antibiotic. Beta-lactam antibiotics include penicillins, cephalosporins, and carbapenems.

Aztreonam is often used to treat infections in people who are allergic to other beta-lactam antibiotics. It is also used with other antibiotics to treat bacteria that are hard to kill.

Most bacteria have a strong outer layer called a cell wall. This layer protects the bacteria. Aztreonam stops bacteria from building this cell wall. Without a cell wall, the bacteria die.

## What Aztreonam Is Used For

- Infections caused by gram-negative bacteria

## Possible Side Effects

- Pain or swelling where the injection is given
- Diarrhea
- Nausea or vomiting
- Skin rash

## Important Notes

- Aztreonam can usually be used in people who are allergic to penicillins, cephalosporins, or carbapenems.
- Do not use aztreonam if you have a severe allergy to ceftazidime or cefiderocol.
- Aztreonam must be given by injection. It is not taken as a pill.

## Using Aztreonam During Pregnancy

- Use aztreonam during pregnancy only if your doctor says the benefits of treatment are greater than any possible risks.
- Animal studies have not shown harm to unborn babies.
- There are no well-designed studies in pregnant women.

## Using Aztreonam While Breastfeeding

- It is generally safe to use aztreonam while breastfeeding.

# Disorders of Pyruvate Metabolism

Your body breaks down sugar to make energy. One part of this process is called pyruvate metabolism. If this process does not work right, it can cause too much lactic acid in the blood. This condition is called lactic acidosis. It can also cause problems in the brain and nervous system.

Pyruvate is a key part of how your body uses sugar for energy. Disorders of pyruvate metabolism are a type of sugar metabolism disorder.

For more information on how doctors check for inherited metabolic disorders, see: *Approach to the Patient With a Suspected Inherited Disorder of Metabolism*.

---

## Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Deficiency

A group of enzymes called pyruvate dehydrogenase helps turn pyruvate into a substance that feeds into the body’s main energy-making system. When this enzyme group does not work well, pyruvate builds up. This leads to high levels of lactic acid in the blood.

This condition can be passed down in two ways:
- Through the X chromosome (X-linked)
- Or through both parents (autosomal recessive)

Symptoms can vary widely in how serious they are. Common signs include:
- High levels of lactic acid in the blood
- Brain problems that are present at birth or develop after birth
- Cysts in parts of the brain, including the outer layer, brain stem, and deep brain areas
- Trouble with balance and coordination (ataxia)
- Delayed development in thinking and movement (psychomotor retardation)

To diagnose this condition, doctors may test skin cells in a lab. They may also do genetic testing. Both tests can confirm the diagnosis.

There is no cure for this condition. But some people get better with:
- A diet low in carbohydrates
- A ketogenic diet (high fat, low carb)
- Extra vitamin B1 (thiamin)

---

## Pyruvate Carboxylase Deficiency

This condition affects an enzyme called pyruvate carboxylase. This enzyme helps make new sugar from other substances. It is important for keeping blood sugar levels stable.

There are three types of this deficiency:
- Type A: Appears in infancy
- Type B: Severe form that shows up at birth
- Type C: Milder form that comes and goes

This condition can be:
- Primary: Caused by a gene problem
- Secondary: Caused by another inherited metabolic disorder

All types are inherited from both parents (autosomal recessive). All types cause lactic acidosis.

The primary form is rare. It happens in fewer than 1 in 250,000 babies. But it may be more common in some American Indian groups.

Common symptoms include:
- Delayed development
- Seizures
- Poor growth and weight gain (failure to thrive)

Lab tests may show:
- High levels of ammonia in the blood
- High lactic acid
- High ketones in the blood (ketoacidosis)
- High levels of certain amino acids in the blood (lysine, citrulline, alanine, proline)
- More alpha-ketoglutarate in the urine

Type B also causes:
- Enlarged liver (hepatomegaly)
- Signs of nerve damage in the legs
- Unusual movements

People with Type C usually have normal or only slightly delayed brain development. They may have episodes of acidosis in the blood, but not all the time.

Secondary deficiency can look similar. It may cause:
- Poor growth
- Seizures
- Other abnormal substances in the urine (organic aciduria)

To diagnose this condition, doctors test skin cells in a lab or do genetic testing.

There is no cure. But some people feel better with:
- Special diets
- Extra vitamin B1 (thiamin)

Most children with Type A die in infancy or early childhood.

Most babies with Type B die within the first three months of life.

# Hydrocephalus

Hydrocephalus means too much fluid builds up in the brain. This fluid is called cerebrospinal fluid. It normally flows through the brain and is absorbed into the blood. When the fluid cannot drain, it builds up and causes pressure in the brain.

This buildup can lead to a larger head and problems with development.

## What Causes Hydrocephalus?

- The fluid may not drain because of a birth defect.
- Bleeding inside the brain can block the flow. This is more common in babies born too early.
- A brain tumor can block the fluid’s path.
- Some gene problems can also cause hydrocephalus.

Hydrocephalus can be present at birth or develop after birth.

## Signs and Symptoms

### In Babies
- The head grows too fast and becomes larger than normal.
- The soft spots on the head (fontanelles) bulge out.
- The baby may be very fussy or sleepy.
- The baby may cry in a high-pitched way.
- The baby may vomit often.
- The baby may have seizures.
- The eyes may not move together. This can make the child look cross-eyed.

### In Older Children
- Headaches.
- Vision problems.

If not treated, hydrocephalus can stop a child from developing normally. Some children may have learning problems, intellectual delays, seizures, or early puberty (in girls). Some may lose vision.

Other children grow up with normal thinking and learning skills.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

### Before Birth
- A routine ultrasound scan during pregnancy can find hydrocephalus.

### After Birth
- Doctors check the baby’s head size and soft spots during a physical exam.
- If they suspect hydrocephalus, they do an ultrasound of the head.
- In older babies and children, doctors use CT scans, MRI scans, or head ultrasounds to confirm the diagnosis.

After diagnosis, doctors do regular imaging tests to check if the fluid buildup is getting worse.

## How Is It Treated?

The goal is to keep pressure in the brain at a safe level.

### Temporary Relief
- Doctors can remove some fluid from the spine with a needle. This is called a spinal tap.
- This helps lower pressure until a long-term solution is put in place.

### Long-Term Treatment

#### Shunt
- A shunt is a small tube placed in the brain.
- It redirects fluid from the brain to another part of the body, usually the belly.
- The tube has a valve that opens when pressure gets too high.
- The shunt is placed in the brain and runs under the skin to the belly. This is called a ventriculoperitoneal shunt, or VP shunt.
- Most children need the shunt for life.
- Shunts are rarely removed, even as children grow older. Removing them can cause serious harm.

#### Ventriculostomy
- In some cases, doctors make a small opening in the brain.
- This lets fluid drain into the normal space around the brain.
- The fluid can then be absorbed as it should.
- If the opening does not work well, a shunt may still be needed.

### After Treatment
- Doctors measure the child’s head size regularly.
- They check how the child is growing and learning.
- Imaging tests like CT or MRI are done over time to make sure the treatment is working.

### Problems with Shunts
- Shunts can get infected. If this happens, the child gets antibiotics. The shunt is usually removed and replaced.
- Shunts can break or get blocked. This stops them from working.
- Doctors use X-rays and brain scans to check if the shunt is working.
- If the shunt fails, it is removed and replaced.

# Atypical Fibroxanthoma

Atypical fibroxanthoma is a type of skin cancer. It is a slow-growing tumor that starts in the skin.

(See also: Overview of Skin Cancer.)

This type of skin cancer is rare. It mostly affects older adults. It usually appears on the head or neck.

The skin changes look like other types of skin cancer. They may be pink or red. They can be tender or not heal over time. They often start as small bumps or lumps.

To diagnose this condition, a doctor takes a small sample of the skin. This is called a biopsy. A lab checks the sample under a microscope.

The best treatment is to remove the tumor. The doctor cuts out the growth. In some cases, a special surgery called Mohs surgery is used. This method removes the tumor layer by layer. The doctor checks each layer under a microscope right away. This keeps healthy skin around the tumor. The surgery continues until no cancer cells are found.

It is very rare for this cancer to spread to other parts of the body.
