## How to Prevent Atypical Fibroxanthoma

This skin cancer is linked to too much sun exposure. To lower your risk, follow these steps:

- **Stay out of the sun when it is strongest.**  
  Avoid being outside between 10 in the morning and 4 in the afternoon.  
  Seek shade when you are outside.

- **Do not use tanning beds.**  
  Tanning beds give off harmful rays that can cause skin cancer.

- **Wear protective clothing.**  
  Wear long-sleeved shirts, long pants, and hats with wide brims.

- **Use sunscreen every day.**  
  Choose a sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher.  
  Make sure it protects against both UVA and UVB rays.  
  Apply it before going outside.  
  Reapply every 2 hours.  
  Reapply after swimming or sweating.  
  Do not use sunscreen to stay in the sun longer.

# Liver Blood Tests

These tests use a blood sample to check how well your liver is working. They are not painful and do not require surgery.

## What These Tests Can Show

- They can find if your liver is inflamed, damaged, or not working right.
- They help show how serious the liver problem is.
- They track how your liver disease changes over time.
- They help doctors see how well treatment is working.
- They help doctors make a more accurate diagnosis.

## Common Liver Tests

These tests measure levels of certain substances in your blood. The liver makes or uses these substances.

### Enzymes and Substances Measured

- **Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)** – This enzyme shows liver damage.
- **Albumin** – This protein is made by the liver. Low levels mean the liver is not working well.
- **Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)** – This enzyme can be high if bile flow is blocked.
- **Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)** – This substance can be high in some liver cancers.
- **Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)** – This enzyme shows liver damage.
- **Bilirubin** – This is a waste product from old blood cells. High levels can mean liver problems.
- **Gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT)** – This enzyme can be high if the liver is damaged or if you drink alcohol.
- **Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)** – This enzyme can be high in many conditions, including liver issues.
- **5’-Nucleotidase** – This enzyme can be high if bile flow is blocked.

Some of these levels can be high even if your liver is not the problem. Other health issues can cause this.

## Blood Clotting Tests

The liver makes proteins that help your blood clot. Two tests check this:

- **Prothrombin Time (PT)** – This measures how long it takes your blood to clot.
- **International Normalized Ratio (INR)** – This is a standard way to report PT results.

If your PT or INR is high, it means your blood takes longer to clot. This can mean your liver is not making enough clotting proteins. A rising PT or INR can mean your liver is getting worse and may be failing.

## Next Steps

If your liver test results are not normal, your doctor will:

- Ask about your medical history.
- May order imaging tests like an ultrasound or CT scan.
- May do a liver biopsy (a small sample of liver tissue) to learn more.

These steps help find the cause of the liver problem.

# Fatigue

Fatigue means feeling too tired to start or keep going with daily activities. It comes with a strong need to rest.

It is normal to feel tired after hard work, long stress, or not getting enough sleep.

Fatigue often happens with other symptoms. But sometimes it is the only symptom people notice. Even then, it is one of the most common complaints.

We can group fatigue by how long it lasts:

- **Recent fatigue**: lasts less than one month  
- **Prolonged fatigue**: lasts from one to six months  
- **Chronic fatigue**: lasts more than six months  

One type of chronic fatigue is called **myalgic encephalomyelitis** or **chronic fatigue syndrome**. Another name for this condition is **systemic exertion intolerance disease**.

Some people who had **COVID-19** still feel tired weeks or even months later. This is known as **post-COVID-19 syndrome**, **long COVID**, or **long-haul COVID**. These symptoms are very similar to those of **postviral fatigue** and **chronic fatigue syndrome**.

Sometimes people describe other problems as fatigue. A careful talk with your doctor can help tell the difference:

- **Weakness** means muscles do not work well, even when you try your hardest. This can happen with nerve or muscle diseases. For example, **myasthenia gravis** and **Eaton-Lambert syndrome** can cause weakness that feels like fatigue.
- **Shortness of breath** when you move can make you feel tired. This often happens with heart or lung problems. Your doctor can find out if this is the real cause by asking questions about your breathing.
- **Somnolence** means feeling an extreme need to sleep during the day. It can happen if you do not sleep well at night. Yawning a lot or falling asleep during the day is common. Most people can tell the difference between feeling tired and feeling sleepy. But poor sleep—especially not getting deep sleep—can cause muscle aches and tiredness. Many people with fatigue also have trouble sleeping. So it can be hard to tell the difference.

---

## What Causes Fatigue?

Many serious and minor illnesses can cause fatigue. But often, other symptoms like pain, cough, fever, or yellow skin show up first. This section focuses on conditions where fatigue is the main or only symptom.

### Common causes of recent fatigue (less than one month):

- Side effects from medicine  
- Low blood count (anemia)  
- Stress or depression  

### Common causes of prolonged fatigue (one to six months):

- Diabetes  
- Underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism)  
- Sleep problems, like sleep apnea  
- Cancer  

### Common causes of chronic fatigue (more than six months):

- Myalgic encephalomyelitis / chronic fatigue syndrome / systemic exertion intolerance disease  
- Postviral fatigue syndrome  
- Mental health issues, like depression  
- Certain medicines  

---

### Things that often make fatigue worse (especially long-term or ongoing fatigue):

| Category | Examples |
|--------|--------|
| Chronic health problems | Chronic kidney disease, giant cell arteritis, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus |
| Medicines or drugs | Antidepressants, older antihistamines, blood pressure medicines, cocaine withdrawal (usually causes short-term fatigue), diuretics that lower potassium, muscle relaxers, recreational drugs, sleeping pills |
| Hormone problems | Low adrenal function, diabetes, overactive thyroid (especially in older adults), underactive thyroid, low pituitary function |
| Infections | Cytomegalovirus, heart infection (endocarditis), fungal lung infections, hepatitis, HIV, mononucleosis, parasites, tuberculosis, SARS, COVID-19 |
| Mental health issues | Anxiety, depression, drug use, panic attacks, somatization disorder |
| Conditions with unclear causes | Myalgic encephalomyelitis / chronic fatigue syndrome / systemic exertion intolerance disease, fibromyalgia, unexplained fatigue |
| Other causes | Anemia, cancer, lack of fitness, pregnancy, poor nutrition, high calcium levels, multiple sclerosis, injury or trauma (including abuse) |

> Note: Most of the conditions listed above do not usually cause long-term fatigue.

---

## How Doctors Check for Fatigue

Fatigue is hard to measure. Everyone feels it differently. There is no test that can prove fatigue or show how bad it is.

Doctors rely on your story and a physical exam. They look for signs of other health problems. These may include infections, hormone issues, joint or muscle diseases, anemia, or depression. These clues help decide which tests to do.

---

## How Fatigue Is Treated

The best way to reduce fatigue is to treat the cause.

People with **myalgic encephalomyelitis / chronic fatigue syndrome / systemic exertion intolerance disease** and those with unexplained chronic fatigue are treated the same way.

Tell patients clearly that the exact cause is still unknown. But treatment works better when doctors are kind, patient, and take the problem seriously.

There are no medicines approved specifically for this condition. But that does not mean future treatments will not work.

Non-drug treatments include:

- Physical therapy, such as slowly increasing activity (graded exercise therapy)  
- Talking therapy, like cognitive-behavioral therapy  
- Improving sleep habits  
- Managing pain  

The goal is to help people return to work and stay active in daily life.

---

## Important for Older Adults

Fatigue is often the first sign of illness in older adults. Do not think it is just part of getting older.

For example, the first sign of **pneumonia** in an older person may be tiredness—not cough or chest pain.  
Fatigue can also be the first sign of **giant cell arteritis**.

If an older adult suddenly feels very tired, it could mean a serious illness. It is important to find the cause quickly.

---

## Key Points

- Fatigue is very common.  
- When fatigue comes from a medical problem, it usually gets worse with activity and better with rest.  
- Blood tests and other tests often do not help unless there are clear signs of illness.  
- Treating long-term fatigue works better when doctors are patient and understanding.

# Vitamin K Deficiency

## What Is Vitamin K?

Vitamin K is a nutrient your body needs to make proteins that help blood clot. It also helps keep bones strong.

Vitamin K comes in two forms:
- **Phylloquinone**: Found in plants. You get this from food. It works better when eaten with fat. It is safe and not harmful.
- **Menaquinone**: Made by bacteria in your gut. Your body makes only a small amount. Some supplements use this form.

Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin. This means it dissolves in fat and is best absorbed when eaten with some fat.

Good sources of vitamin K include:
- Green leafy vegetables like collard greens, spinach, and kale
- Soybean oil and canola oil

## Who Is at Risk?

### Newborns
Newborns are at high risk for vitamin K deficiency. This is because:
- Only a small amount of vitamin K passes from mother to baby during pregnancy.
- A newborn’s gut has not yet developed the bacteria that make vitamin K.
- Breast milk has very little vitamin K.

Because of this, all newborns should get a vitamin K injection shortly after birth. This protects them from serious bleeding.

Babies who are breastfed and did not get the injection are at higher risk. So are babies with:
- Problems that stop fat from being absorbed (like blocked bile ducts or cystic fibrosis)
- Liver problems
- A mother who took certain medicines during pregnancy, such as:
  - Antiseizure drugs (like phenytoin)
  - Blood thinners (anticoagulants)
  - Some antibiotics

Infant formula contains vitamin K, so formula-fed babies are less likely to be deficient.

### Healthy Adults
Vitamin K deficiency is rare in healthy adults. Most people get enough from their diet and from bacteria in the gut.

## What Happens If You Lack Vitamin K?

The main problem is bleeding. This can happen in many places:
- Under the skin (bruises)
- From the nose
- From a cut or wound
- In the stomach or intestines
- In the urine or stool
- Stools may look black and sticky

In newborns, bleeding in or around the brain can be life-threatening.

Vitamin K deficiency can also weaken bones over time.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect vitamin K deficiency if you are bleeding and have a condition that increases your risk.

To confirm the diagnosis, they may do:
- Blood tests to see how fast your blood clots
- A test to measure the level of vitamin K in your blood

Your diet and any medicines you take also help the doctor understand the results.

## How Is It Treated?

### For Newborns
All newborns should get a vitamin K injection in the muscle right after birth. This prevents serious bleeding, especially in the brain.

### For People with Deficiency
- Vitamin K can be taken by mouth or given as an injection under the skin.
- If a medicine is causing the deficiency, your doctor may change the dose or add extra vitamin K.

## Causes of Vitamin K Deficiency

You may not get enough vitamin K if:
- You do not eat enough foods with vitamin K
- You eat very little fat (since vitamin K needs fat to be absorbed)
- You have a condition that stops fat from being absorbed, such as:
  - Blocked bile ducts
  - Cystic fibrosis
- You take certain medicines, including:
  - Antiseizure drugs
  - Some antibiotics
- You use large amounts of mineral oil (which can stop vitamin K from being absorbed)

## Important Notes

- **Warfarin and other blood thinners** can make bleeding worse if you are low in vitamin K. These medicines are used to prevent dangerous blood clots in people who:
  - Are bedridden
  - Are recovering from surgery
  - Have an irregular heartbeat (called atrial fibrillation)

- People on warfarin need regular blood tests to check how fast their blood clots.

## Did You Know?

Newborns are at risk for vitamin K deficiency because they do not get enough vitamin K before birth and cannot make their own yet. A simple injection after birth prevents serious problems.

# Unexplained Infertility

Infertility is called unexplained when:

- The man’s sperm is normal.  
- The woman’s eggs are healthy.  
- The woman releases an egg each month (ovulation).  
- The fallopian tubes are open and working.  
- The uterus is healthy.

Some doctors think we should keep looking for other causes even if all these tests are normal.  
Other doctors agree with this definition and say it is okay to start treatment right away.

---

## Treating Unexplained Infertility

There are two main treatments:

1. Controlled ovarian stimulation (COS)  
2. In vitro fertilization (IVF)

### Controlled Ovarian Stimulation (COS)

This treatment helps you get pregnant faster. It makes your body release more than one egg in a cycle. This is called superovulation.

But this can lead to more than one baby. Having more than one baby carries higher risks for both mother and babies.

How COS works:

- You take a medicine called letrozole or clomiphene.  
- You also get a shot of hCG to trigger ovulation.  
- This is done for up to 3 menstrual cycles.  
- You have an insemination (sperm placed in the uterus) within 2 days of the hCG shot.

If this does not work, your doctor may switch to stronger medicines called gonadotropins.  
These contain hormones that help eggs grow. They are used with hCG to trigger ovulation.  
Then, you have an insemination.

Some doctors start with gonadotropins instead of clomiphene or letrozole.

You may also need a progesterone medicine during the second half of your cycle. This helps the embryo attach to the uterus.

The dose of gonadotropins depends on your age and how many eggs your body can make.

Because of the risk of multiple babies, many doctors now skip COS and go straight to IVF.

---

## What Is the Chance of Getting Pregnant?

If you do not get pregnant after trying clomiphene and hCG, your chance of success is about 65% whether you go straight to IVF or try gonadotropins with insemination first.

But there are important differences:

- Going straight to IVF after clomiphene and hCG leads to pregnancy faster.  
- Going straight to IVF also means fewer high-order multiple pregnancies (three or more babies).  
- This is especially important for women over age 38.

For women over 38, IVF is often the best next step. It leads to pregnancy faster and costs less than continuing with COS.

# Unexplained Infertility

Infertility is unexplained when:

- The man’s sperm is normal.  
- The woman’s eggs are healthy.  
- The woman ovulates normally.  
- The fallopian tubes are open.  
- The uterus is healthy.

This means doctors cannot find a clear reason why a couple cannot get pregnant.

---

## Treatment for Unexplained Infertility

If no cause is found, doctors may suggest a treatment called **controlled ovarian stimulation**.

This treatment can help a woman get pregnant faster. It may also lead to more than one baby.

### How Controlled Ovarian Stimulation Works

1. The woman takes a medicine called **clomiphene**.  
   - This medicine helps several eggs grow and mature.  
2. She also gets a shot of **hCG**.  
   - This shot triggers the release of the mature eggs.  
3. This treatment is done for up to three months.  
4. A few days after the hCG shot, the man’s sperm is placed directly into the woman’s uterus.  
   - This is called **intrauterine insemination**.  
   - It helps sperm reach the egg more easily.

If this treatment does not lead to pregnancy, the doctor may suggest:

- A stronger fertility medicine called **human gonadotropins**.  
  - This medicine helps the ovaries grow more eggs.  
- Then, another hCG shot to release the eggs.  
- Then, another intrauterine insemination.

But there is a risk of having more than one baby.  
Because of this risk, many doctors skip controlled ovarian stimulation and go straight to **in vitro fertilization**.

---

## What to Expect: Prognosis

- About 65 out of 100 women with unexplained infertility will get pregnant, no matter which treatment they try.  
- But women get pregnant faster when they go straight to **in vitro fertilization** after clomiphene fails.  
- They are also less likely to have a pregnancy with three or more babies.

So, if clomiphene and intrauterine insemination do not work, the next step is often **in vitro fertilization**.

### Age Matters

- Women over age 38 with unexplained infertility may get pregnant faster if they go straight to in vitro fertilization.  
- Waiting to try other treatments may delay pregnancy.

# Consent and Making Decisions for Someone Else

Sometimes, a patient needs medical treatment right away.  
The patient may not be able to make their own decisions.  
If no one authorized to decide for them is nearby, doctors can act based on a rule called presumed consent.  

This rule means doctors assume the patient would agree to life-saving treatment if they could speak for themselves.  

In all other cases, doctors must get clear permission from the patient or their legal decision-maker before starting treatment.

# Chest Imaging

Imaging tests help doctors see inside the chest. These tests can show problems with the lungs, heart, or other parts of the chest.

## Types of Chest Imaging

The following tests are used to look at the chest:

- X-rays  
- Computed tomography (CT)  
- CT angiography  
- Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)  
- Ultrasonography  
- Nuclear lung scanning  
- Pulmonary artery angiography  
- Positron emission tomography (PET)  

(See also: *Medical History and Physical Examination for Lung Disorders*, *Overview of the Respiratory System*, and *Overview of Imaging Tests*.)

Most of these tests use radiation. MRI and ultrasonography do not use radiation.

Doctors often start with a chest x-ray when they suspect a lung or heart problem. Other tests are used when more detail is needed.

---

## Chest X-Rays

A chest x-ray is usually taken from the back to the front. A side view is often taken too. Sometimes the person must stand or lie in a different position so the doctor can see a certain area of the lungs.

X-rays show the shape and size of the heart and major blood vessels. They can often find serious problems in the lungs, nearby areas, or the chest wall.

For example, x-rays can show:
- Pneumonia  
- Lung tumors  
- Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)  
- A collapsed lung (atelectasis)  
- Air in the space around the lungs (pneumothorax)  
- Fluid in the space around the lungs (pleural effusion)

X-rays usually do not show the exact cause of a problem. But they help doctors decide which other tests to do.

---

## Computed Tomography (CT) of the Chest

CT scans use x-rays and a computer to create detailed pictures of the chest. They show more detail than a regular x-ray.

The CT machine takes many x-ray images from different angles. A computer puts them together to make cross-sections and other views.

A special dye (called a contrast agent) may be given through a vein or by mouth. This helps highlight certain areas and makes problems easier to see.

Two special types of CT are:
- High-resolution CT: gives more detail about lung problems.  
- Helical (spiral) CT: creates 3D images.

Most CT scans are done after the person takes a deep breath. Sometimes, scans are done after a deep breath and again after a full breath out. This helps doctors see small airways better.

---

## CT Angiography of the Chest

CT angiography uses a contrast agent injected into a vein in the arm. It creates clear pictures of blood vessels in the chest.

This test is often used to check for blood clots in the pulmonary artery (the main blood vessel from the heart to the lungs). This condition is called pulmonary embolism.

CT angiography is usually preferred over nuclear lung scanning for this purpose.

But it may not be safe for people with:
- Kidney disease (the contrast agent can make it worse)  
- Allergies to the contrast agent

---

## Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of the Chest

MRI uses magnets and radio waves to make very detailed pictures. It does not use radiation.

MRI is especially helpful when doctors suspect a blood vessel problem in the chest, such as a bulge in the aorta (aortic aneurysm).

MRI takes longer and costs more than CT. It is not as good as CT for seeing lung problems.

Because of this, MRI is not often used for chest imaging.

---

## Ultrasonography of the Chest

Ultrasonography uses sound waves to create a picture of the inside of the body.

It is often used to find fluid in the space around the lungs (pleural space). It can also guide a needle when removing fluid.

Doctors may do bedside ultrasound to check for a collapsed lung (pneumothorax).

Another type, called endobronchial ultrasonography (EBUS), is used with a bronchoscope. This helps doctors take a tissue sample from the lungs to check for cancer. The ultrasound probe is on the bronchoscope, so it can see inside the airways.

---

## Nuclear Lung Scanning

Nuclear lung scanning can help find blood clots in the lungs (pulmonary emboli). But CT angiography is now used more often.

Nuclear lung scanning may still be used when:
- A person has kidney disease (the contrast agent in CT can make it worse)  
- A person has an allergy to the contrast agent used in CT  
- A person is being checked before lung surgery for lung cancer or severe COPD

The test helps doctors see how well the remaining lungs work after surgery.

A lung ventilation/perfusion scan is two tests in one:
- A perfusion scan: checks blood flow in the lungs  
- A ventilation scan: checks how well air moves in the lungs

The tests are usually done together but can be done separately.

For the perfusion scan:
- A small amount of radioactive material is injected into a vein.  
- It travels to the lungs and shows the blood supply.

For the ventilation scan:
- The person breathes in a harmless gas with a tiny amount of radioactive material.  
- The gas spreads through the small air sacs in the lungs.  
- The scanner shows where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged.

Doctors compare the two scans. If blood flow is blocked but air moves normally, it may mean a blood clot is present.

---

## Pulmonary Artery Angiography

This test checks the blood vessels in the lungs. A thin tube (catheter) is guided through a vein, into the heart, and then into the pulmonary artery.

A contrast agent is injected through the tube. X-rays are taken as the contrast moves through the blood vessels.

This test shows the inside of the blood vessels clearly.

It was once the most accurate way to find blood clots in the lungs (pulmonary embolism). But it is now rarely used because it is more invasive.

CT angiography is safer and gives similar results. So, it is usually preferred.

---

## Positron Emission Tomography (PET)

PET scans are used when cancer is suspected.

Cancer cells use more energy than normal cells. PET scans detect this difference.

A special sugar (glucose) is linked to a radioactive substance. This is injected into a vein.

The sugar collects in fast-growing tissues, like cancer. These areas show up on the scan.

Benign (noncancerous) growths do not collect enough sugar to show up.

PET scans are often done with a CT scan. This gives two types of information:
- CT shows the structure of the lungs  
- PET shows which areas are very active (possibly cancer)

This helps doctors find and stage lung cancer.

# Tetracyclines

Tetracyclines are a type of antibiotic.  
They stop bacteria from growing.  
They do this by blocking the bacteria’s ability to make proteins.  
This helps your body fight off infections.

## Types of Tetracyclines

The main tetracyclines are:

- Doxycycline  
- Eravacycline (only given through a vein)  
- Minocycline  
- Omadacycline (a newer type)  
- Tetracycline  

## How Tetracyclines Work in the Body

Most of the medicine is absorbed into your blood when you take it by mouth.  
About 60 to 80 percent of tetracycline is absorbed.  
More than 90 percent of doxycycline and minocycline are absorbed.  

But certain minerals can block absorption.  
These include aluminum, calcium, magnesium, and iron.  
So do not take tetracyclines with antacids or many vitamin and mineral supplements.  

Tetracycline and omadacycline should be taken with a full glass of water.  
Take them on an empty stomach.  
Food can reduce how much of the medicine your body absorbs.  
This effect is less strong with doxycycline and minocycline.  

The medicine spreads through most parts of your body.  
It builds up in the bile (a fluid made by the liver).  
But it does not reach high levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord.  
Minocycline is the only one that reaches high levels in tears and saliva.  

How the medicine leaves your body depends on the type:  
- Tetracycline and minocycline are mostly removed through the kidneys.  
- Doxycycline, eravacycline, and omadacycline are mostly removed through the intestines.  

## When Tetracyclines Are Used

Tetracyclines can treat infections caused by:

- Rickettsia (like those that cause Rocky Mountain spotted fever)  
- Spirochetes (such as the bacteria that cause Lyme disease and syphilis)  
- Helicobacter pylori (a cause of stomach ulcers)  
- Vibrio (like the bacteria that cause cholera)  
- Yersinia pestis (the cause of plague)  
- Francisella tularensis (the cause of tularemia)  
- Brucella (a cause of brucellosis)  
- Bacillus anthracis (the cause of anthrax)  
- Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium falciparum (types of malaria)  
- Mycoplasma  
- Chlamydia and Chlamydophila  

Some strains of staph bacteria that are resistant to other antibiotics can also be treated.  
But some pneumococcal bacteria, strep bacteria, and gonorrhea bacteria are resistant.  

For most infections, any tetracycline can be used.  
Minocycline has been studied the most for treating resistant staph infections.  

**Doxycycline is usually the best choice** for:

- Infections from rickettsia or Anaplasma  
- Infections from Chlamydia or Chlamydophila  
- Infections from Ehrlichia  
- Infections from Mycoplasma  
- Infections from Vibrio  
- Flare-ups of chronic bronchitis  
- Lyme disease  
- Brucellosis  
- Anthrax  
- Plague  
- Tularemia  
- Granuloma inguinale  
- Syphilis  
- Preventing malaria caused by a type that resists chloroquine  

## Who Should Not Take Tetracyclines

Do not take tetracyclines if you have had an allergic reaction to them.  

Doctors used to avoid giving tetracyclines to children under 8 years old.  
This was because of concerns about tooth staining.  
But recent studies show that short-term use of doxycycline (less than 21 days) does not cause tooth staining.  
So most experts now agree that short-term doxycycline is safe for children of all ages.  

One study looked at children under 8 who took doxycycline for suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever.  
These children did not have more tooth problems than children who did not take the medicine.  

## Using Tetracyclines During Pregnancy and Breastfeeding

Tetracyclines were avoided during pregnancy.  
This was because they can build up in the baby’s bones and teeth.  
But short courses of doxycycline (up to 10 days) do not seem to raise the risk of tooth discoloration.  

Still, pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid tetracyclines if safer options are available.  

Taking high doses during pregnancy can cause serious liver damage.  
This is more likely if you are given the medicine through a vein.  
It is also more likely if you have kidney problems or a kidney infection.  

## Side Effects of Tetracyclines

Common side effects include:

- Upset stomach  
- Nausea  
- Vomiting  
- Diarrhea  
- Yeast infections (such as in the mouth or vagina)  
- Skin that burns easily in sunlight (photosensitivity)  

If you do not drink enough water when taking tetracyclines, the medicine can irritate your esophagus.  
This can cause pain or damage.  

Tooth and bone problems can happen in children under 8.  
These include:  
- Yellow, brown, or gray tooth staining  
- Weak tooth enamel  
- Abnormal bone growth  

But these problems are not seen with short-term doxycycline use.  

In babies, tetracyclines can cause increased pressure in the brain.  
This can lead to a bulging soft spot on the head.  

High levels of the medicine in the blood can cause liver failure.  
This is more likely during pregnancy.  
It can happen with high doses or if your kidneys are not working well.  

Minocycline can cause balance problems and dizziness.  
This can make it hard to use.  
It has also been linked to rare autoimmune diseases.  
These include lupus and a condition called polyarteritis nodosa.  
These conditions may go away when you stop the medicine.  

Minocycline can also cause a serious reaction called DRESS.  
This includes:  
- Fever  
- Rash  
- Swollen glands  
- Liver problems  
- Abnormal white blood cells  
- High levels of a certain type of white blood cell (eosinophils)  
- Low platelet count  

Tetracyclines (except doxycycline) can make kidney problems worse in people with kidney disease.  
Doxycycline is less likely to cause this because it leaves the body through the intestines, not the kidneys.  

Expired tetracycline pills can break down.  
If you take them, they can cause a rare kidney problem called Fanconi syndrome.  
Always throw away medicine after the expiration date.  

## Dosing and Special Considerations

- Doxycycline, eravacycline, and omadacycline do not need dose changes if your kidneys are not working well.  
- Tetracycline and minocycline do need dose changes if your kidneys are not working well.  

Tetracyclines can make birth control pills less effective.  
They can also increase the risk of bleeding if you are taking blood thinners.

# Understanding Kidney and Urinary Tract Problems

If you have symptoms that might be linked to your kidneys or urinary tract, your doctor will start by learning about your health. They will ask you questions and do a physical exam. Sometimes, they will also need to run tests to find the cause.

## What Your Doctor Will Ask

Your doctor will talk to you about your health. They will ask about:

- Your symptoms
- Any past health problems you have had
- All medicines you take, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements
- Use of alcohol, tobacco, or other drugs
- Allergies you have
- Health issues that run in your family

They will also ask about your urinary habits, such as:

- How much you urinate
- How often you go to the bathroom
- When you urinate (day or night)
- If urination hurts or burns
- If you see blood in your urine
- If you leak urine (incontinence)
- If it is hard to start urinating
- If your bladder feels full even after you urinate
- If you have had past urinary tract infections
- If you have had any procedures or surgeries on your urinary tract
- If you have pain in your side, lower back, belly, or near your genitals (like the groin or labia)

They may also ask about your diet and what you eat and drink, and when. For example, some foods and medicines can change the color of your urine. If you wake up at night to urinate, your doctor may want to know how much and what kind of drinks you have, and when.

## What Your Doctor Will Check

After the interview, your doctor will do a physical exam.

They may gently press on your side or lower back. If this causes pain, it could mean your kidney is swollen or infected.

If you have trouble urinating and your lower belly feels full, your doctor may press on your lower belly and tap it. A dull sound may mean your bladder is full and swollen.

In men, your doctor will check your genitals. They will look at your testicles to make sure they are not swollen, tender, or in the wrong place. They will also do a rectal exam to check your prostate. If the prostate is enlarged, it can block urine flow.

In women, your doctor may do a pelvic exam. This helps check if irritation or inflammation in the vagina or other genital areas is causing your symptoms.

Your doctor will also look at your skin. Some skin changes can be signs of kidney disease. They will listen to your heart and lungs with a stethoscope. Unusual sounds may point to a kidney problem. If your doctor thinks you have long-term kidney disease, they will check if you feel tired, sleepy, or confused.

## Tests and Procedures

After the exam, your doctor will likely ask for a urine sample. This helps check for infection or other problems.

If an infection is suspected, the lab will try to grow bacteria from the urine. This is called a urine culture.

If your doctor thinks there is a blockage or a problem inside your urinary tract, they may order imaging tests. These can include X-rays, ultrasounds, or scans.

To check how well your kidneys are working, your doctor will test your blood and urine. These are called kidney function tests.

Sometimes, your doctor may need to look inside your bladder using a thin tube with a camera. This is called cystoscopy.

They may also take a small sample of cells from your urine, kidney, or prostate. This is called a biopsy. It helps find the cause of the problem.

# Foreign Objects in the Digestive System

People sometimes swallow objects by accident or on purpose.  
Most objects pass through the digestive system without problems.  
But some objects get stuck.  
When this happens, they can cause symptoms or serious issues.

Imaging tests like X-rays help doctors decide what to do.  
But there is no single rule for when to use these tests.  
Most stuck objects can be removed using a scope.  
This is a thin tube with a camera that goes into the body.  
Surgery is needed only in rare cases.  
The time to remove the object depends on what it is.

Objects can get stuck in different parts of the digestive system:

- In the throat (esophagus)  
- In the stomach (including clumps of undigested food called bezoars)  
- In the intestines  
- In the rectum (the last part of the bowel)

Most cases happen in children.  
Some adults swallow objects on purpose.  
This is more common in people in prison or those with mental health conditions.  
Older adults, people with dentures, or those who have had too much alcohol may accidentally swallow large pieces of food.  
Meat is a common problem because it can get stuck in the throat.  
Some people swallow drug-filled balloons, bottles, or packages to hide drugs.  
This is called body packing or body stuffing.  
If the package breaks, the drugs can leak into the body.  
This can cause a drug overdose.

## Risks of Swallowing Objects

Swallowing objects can lead to serious problems.  
These include:

- Blockage in the digestive system  
- A hole in the digestive tract  
- Sores in the lining of the digestive system  
- Bleeding  
- An abnormal connection between two parts of the body (fistula)  
- Infection in the blood (bacteremia)

# Drug-Induced Lung Problems

Drug-induced lung problems are not one single illness. Many different medicines can cause lung issues in people who do not have other lung diseases. The kind of lung problem depends on the medicine. Most of these problems are thought to be caused by an allergic reaction. Older adults often have more serious problems.

If the issue is not an allergic reaction, the severity often depends on how much of the drug you take and how long you take it.

## What Symptoms Might You Have?

The symptoms depend on the medicine. You might have:

- A cough
- Wheezing
- Trouble breathing
- Other lung symptoms

Symptoms can appear in two ways:

- Slowly, over weeks or months
- All at once, and become very bad quickly

## How Is It Diagnosed and Treated?

The main step is to stop taking the medicine. Then, your doctor watches to see if your symptoms get better. If they do, the medicine was likely the cause.

Your doctor will choose the safest medicine possible for your condition. They will pick a drug that is least likely to harm your lungs.

## Testing Before Starting Certain Medicines

Doctors may do lung tests or take pictures of your lungs before you start certain medicines. This is especially true for cancer medicines or radiation therapy. These treatments can harm the lungs.

But we do not yet know if these tests help predict or catch lung problems early. The benefits of screening are still unclear.

(See also: Overview of Interstitial Lung Diseases.)

# Caring for a Very Sick Patient

Critical care medicine focuses on patients who are extremely ill.  
These patients need the most intensive care.  
They are best treated in a special unit called an intensive care unit.  
An intensive care unit has doctors and nurses who are specially trained.  

Some hospitals have separate units for certain types of patients.  
For example, some units care for patients after heart surgery.  
Others care for patients who had organ transplants.  
Some units are for patients with serious injuries, brain problems, or surgery complications.  
There are also units for children and newborns.  

The intensive care unit has more nurses per patient than other hospital units.  
This allows for constant care and close monitoring.  
Nurses check vital signs often.  
They watch for changes and act quickly.  

Patients in the intensive care unit need support to stay as healthy as possible.  
They need enough food and fluids.  
Doctors and nurses work to prevent infections.  
They also treat or prevent stomach problems like ulcers and inflammation.  
They take steps to prevent blood clots in the lungs.  

About 15 to 25 out of every 100 patients who go to the intensive care unit do not survive.  
When a patient is dying, doctors and nurses focus on comfort.  
They help reduce pain and suffering.  
They make sure the patient feels respected and treated with dignity.

# Air Pollution and Health

Air pollution can cause illness. It can also make existing health problems worse.

## What Air Pollution Does to the Body

- Some air pollutants make the airways smaller.
- This can cause coughing, wheezing, and trouble breathing.
- Air pollution can trigger asthma attacks.
- It can make chronic obstructive pulmonary disease worse.
- It increases the risk of lung infections and lung cancer.
- It raises the risk of heart attacks, heart disease, and stroke.
- People who live near busy roads are more likely to have health problems from air pollution.

## Main Types of Air Pollutants

- **Nitrogen dioxide** comes from burning fuels like gasoline and oil.
- **Ozone** forms when sunlight reacts with nitrogen dioxide and other chemicals. It is the main part of smog.
- **Carbon monoxide** is made when fuels do not burn completely.
- **Particulate matter** is tiny solid or liquid bits in the air. These can come from smoke, traffic, and construction.
- **Sulfur oxides** come from burning fuels that contain sulfur.

## Where Air Pollution Comes From

- Outdoor pollution can get inside homes.
- Indoor pollution comes from:
  - Smoking.
  - Cooking with gas or wood.
  - Building or remodeling.
  - Burning wood, animal waste, or crops for heat and cooking. This is common in some countries.

## Air Quality Rules in the U.S.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency sets rules for clean air. These rules cover:
- Nitrogen oxides
- Ozone
- Sulfur oxides
- Carbon monoxide
- Lead
- Particulate matter

These are called the "criteria pollutants."

## How Each Pollutant Affects Health

### Ozone
- Ozone is a strong irritant in the air.
- It is worst in hot, sunny weather, especially in the late morning and early afternoon.
- Short exposure can cause:
  - Shortness of breath
  - Chest pain
  - Airways that react too strongly
- Children who play outside on high-ozone days are more likely to develop asthma.

### Sulfur Oxides
- These come from burning fossil fuels.
- They can irritate the airways.
- They may increase the risk of chronic bronchitis.
- They can also make airways narrower.

### Nitrogen Oxides
- Most come from car and truck exhaust.
- They can irritate the airways.
- They may trigger asthma.

### Carbon Monoxide
- It comes from incomplete burning of fuels.
- It blocks oxygen from reaching body tissues.
- It binds to hemoglobin, the part of blood that carries oxygen.
- Very high levels are rare outdoors.

### Lead
- Lead has been removed from gasoline.
- This has greatly reduced lead in the air in the United States.

### Particulate Matter
- This is a mix of tiny solid and liquid particles.
- Sources include:
  - Diesel engines
  - Smokestacks
  - Construction sites
- These particles can cause inflammation in the lungs and throughout the body.
- Wildfire smoke is a major source.
- Smoke from fires can affect people hundreds of miles away.
- Particulate pollution increases death rates from all causes, especially heart and lung diseases.

### Wildfire Smoke
- Wildfire smoke adds particulate matter to the air.
- It also contains:
  - Carbon dioxide
  - Water vapor
  - Carbon monoxide
  - Hydrocarbons
  - Nitrogen oxides
  - Small amounts of minerals

### Nanoparticles
- The nanotechnology industry makes very small particles.
- These particles are smaller than 100 nanometers.
- A human hair is about 100,000 nanometers wide.
- So, it would take 1,000 of these tiny particles to match the width of one hair.
- Some of these tiny particles are linked to worse breathing problems in people with asthma.

## How Doctors Diagnose Air Pollution Illness

- Doctors ask about your health history and your exposure to pollution.
- They check your lung function with special tests.
- They ask people with asthma or COPD if their symptoms get worse when air quality is poor.
- Tests often cannot tell if pollution is the exact cause.
- If many people in the same area get sick at the same time, it may point to pollution as the cause.

## How Air Pollution Illness Is Treated

- The main treatment is to avoid more pollution.
- Medicines can help relieve symptoms.
- For example, asthma medicines that open the airways can help with coughing and shortness of breath.

## How to Prevent Air Pollution Problems

- Air pollution is a leading cause of death worldwide.
- Reducing exposure to outdoor pollution helps prevent both short-term and long-term health problems.

### Check the Air Quality Every Day

- Air pollution levels change by place and weather.
- Ozone is highest on hot, sunny days, especially in the afternoon.
- The Air Quality Index (AQI) tells you how clean or dirty the air is.
- You can use the AQI to decide if it is safe to be outside.

### Use the Air Quality Index to Stay Safe

| AQI Value | Health Risk Level | What to Do |
|-----------|-------------------|------------|
| 0–50      | Good              | Normal activities are safe. |
| 51–100    | Moderate          | If you are sensitive, limit long outdoor activities. |
| 101–150   | Unhealthy for sensitive groups | Children, older adults, and people with heart or lung disease should stay indoors. |
| 151–200   | Unhealthy         | Everyone should limit outdoor time. |
| 201–300   | Very unhealthy    | Avoid all outdoor activity. |
| 301–500   | Hazardous         | Stay indoors. Close windows. Use air purifiers. |

**Note:** The AQI measures five pollutants:
- Ozone
- Particulate matter
- Carbon monoxide
- Sulfur dioxide
- Nitrogen dioxide

**Sensitive groups** include:
- People with lung or heart disease
- Children
- Older adults

### Ways to Reduce Your Risk

- On bad air days, avoid heavy outdoor exercise.
- Stay indoors in clean, filtered spaces.
- Use high-efficiency air filters (HEPA filters).
- Stop smoking indoors.
- Cook with clean fuels and keep windows open when cooking.
- Improve air flow in your home.

## More Help

For up-to-date air quality information in your area, visit:

**Air Now**  
A free service from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency  
[www.AirNow.gov](https://www.AirNow.gov)

# Guided Imagery

Guided imagery is a way to use your mind to help your body feel better. It is part of mind-body medicine. This means it uses your thoughts and feelings to support your physical health.

You use mental pictures to help you relax. You can do this on your own or with help from a guide. The pictures can include sights, sounds, smells, tastes, or feelings.

This method can help before a medical test or treatment. It may also help your body heal and stay healthy. For example, it might help your body’s natural defenses work better.

---

## When People Use Guided Imagery

Guided imagery works best when used with other calming methods. These include:
- Relaxing your muscles
- Breathing slowly and deeply
- Using hypnotherapy (a type of deep relaxation)

People use this method to:
- Reduce pain, especially those with fibromyalgia (a condition that causes long-term body pain)
- Feel better during cancer treatment
- Sleep better
- Handle stress and anxiety
- Recover from trauma, such as being in an intensive care unit

Studies show that guided imagery can help people feel more in control and improve their daily life. It is safe and well accepted by most patients.

# Mechanical Ventilation

A mechanical ventilator is a machine that helps you breathe. It moves air in and out of your lungs.

Some people with serious breathing problems need a ventilator to stay alive. The machine can take over breathing when your lungs are too weak.

## How Mechanical Ventilation Works

Doctors usually put a thin plastic tube into your nose or mouth and down into your windpipe. This tube connects to the ventilator.

If you need the ventilator for more than a few days, doctors may make a small cut in your neck. They then place the tube directly into your windpipe. This is called a tracheostomy. It is safer and more comfortable for long-term use.

The tube connects to the ventilator. The machine can push air into your lungs even if you are not breathing on your own.

Different types of ventilators and settings are used. The right one depends on your condition. The machine can give you pure oxygen or a mix of oxygen and air.

## Alternatives to Mechanical Ventilation

Some people do not need full help from a machine. Instead, they can wear a tight-fitting mask over the nose or both nose and mouth.

The mask delivers air under pressure. This helps your own breathing and stops your breathing muscles from getting too tired.

This method is called bilevel positive airway pressure or CPAP. It can help about half of people with breathing failure avoid needing a tracheostomy.

For people whose breathing problems come from weak muscles, using this mask at night can help. Resting at night lets the muscles recover. This makes it easier to breathe during the day.

## Risks of Mechanical Ventilation

Too much pressure or too much air can hurt your lungs. It can stretch the tiny air sacs in your lungs too much. These air sacs can burst. Air may then leak around the lung and cause it to collapse. This is called pneumothorax.

To prevent this, doctors carefully control how much air and pressure the machine uses.

But if the pressure and air volume are too low, not enough air moves in and out. This can cause carbon dioxide to build up in your blood. It can also cause small airways and air sacs to close.

Doctors check your breathing often. They adjust the machine to find the right balance.

Even though most people on a ventilator need extra oxygen, too much oxygen can harm the lungs. Doctors check your oxygen level to make sure you get just the right amount.

People on a ventilator, especially those with a tube in the windpipe, may feel restless or anxious. Doctors can give medicine to calm you down. These include drugs like propofol, lorazepam, and midazolam. Opioids like morphine or fentanyl may also be used. These medicines can also ease the feeling of breathlessness.

When you have a tube in your windpipe, germs from your nose and mouth can get into your lungs. This can cause a serious lung infection. Doctors must find and treat these infections fast.

People on a ventilator cannot eat normally. If you need the ventilator for more than a few days, you will get nutrition through a tube placed in your stomach. This is called tube feeding.

## Stopping Mechanical Ventilation

As you get better, doctors will slowly reduce the help your lungs get from the machine.

They may turn the ventilator off for short times. This tests whether your lungs can work on their own.

These tests are done carefully. If you have trouble breathing, the machine can be turned back on right away.

# Meckel Diverticulum – Simple Explanation

## What Is Meckel Diverticulum?

Meckel diverticulum is a small pouch that forms in the small intestine.  
It is present from birth.  
It happens in about 2 out of every 100 people.  
It forms when a small tube in the fetus does not close completely.  
This tube connected the intestine to the yolk sac during early development.  

The pouch sticks out from the side of the small intestine that does not have blood vessels attached.  
It has all the same layers as the normal intestine.  
This makes it a "true" diverticulum.  

In some people, the pouch contains tissue that does not belong there.  
This can be stomach tissue or pancreas tissue.  
Stomach tissue can make acid.  
This acid can cause sores in the nearby intestine.  

## Why It Matters

Most people with this pouch never have any problems.  
But in some, it can cause serious issues.  
These include:  
- Bleeding from the intestine  
- Blockage in the intestine  
- Inflammation (called diverticulitis)  
- A hole in the intestine (perforation)  
- Rarely, tumors  

Men are more likely than women to have problems with this pouch.  

## Problems and How They Show Up

### Bleeding
- Most common in children under 5 years old.  
- The acid from stomach tissue in the pouch can damage the nearby intestine.  
- This causes bleeding.  
- The blood may come out as bright red from the rectum.  
- The bleeding is often not severe.  
- Adults may bleed too, but the blood usually turns black (melena).  

### Blockage
- Can happen at any age.  
- More common in older children and adults.  
- In children, the pouch can fold into itself. This is called intussusception.  
- Other causes include scar tissue, twisted intestine, foreign objects, tumors, or getting stuck in a hernia.  
- Symptoms include cramping belly pain, nausea, and vomiting.  

### Inflammation (Diverticulitis)
- Can happen at any age.  
- Most common in older children.  
- Causes belly pain and tenderness.  
- The pain is often near the belly button.  
- It feels similar to appendicitis.  
- Other symptoms include vomiting.  

### Perforation
- The pouch can tear.  
- This lets intestinal contents leak into the belly.  
- This causes a serious infection called peritonitis.  

### Tumors
- Very rare.  
- Mostly seen in adults.  
- Can be tumors from the gut or pancreas.  

## How Doctors Diagnose It

Diagnosis depends on the symptoms.  

### If You Are Bleeding
- A special scan using a small amount of radioactive material (Meckel scan) can find the pouch.  
- This scan works well in children with bleeding.  
- It finds the pouch in 85 to 97 out of 100 cases.  
- But it only works if the pouch has stomach tissue.  
- If the pouch has no stomach tissue, the scan will not show it.  
- A capsule endoscopy (a small camera you swallow) or a scope can also help find the source of bleeding.  

### If You Have Belly Pain
- A CT scan with contrast (a special dye) is often used.  
- If you have vomiting and cramping, X-rays of the belly may be done.  
- These help find a blockage.  

### Sometimes, It’s Found by Accident
- Doctors may find the pouch during surgery for another problem.  
- For example, when they think you have appendicitis but the appendix looks normal.  
- In that case, they check for a Meckel diverticulum.  

## How It’s Treated

Surgery is the main treatment.  

### If There Is a Blockage
- Surgery is needed right away.  

### If There Is Bleeding
- If the area around the pouch is hard or thick, the surgeon removes the pouch and the hard part of the intestine.  
- If the area is not hard, only the pouch is removed.  

### If There Is Inflammation (Diverticulitis)
- Surgery is usually needed to remove the pouch.  

### If the Pouch Is Found by Chance
- If the pouch is small and causes no symptoms, it may not need to be removed.  
- But some surgeons remove it in children and young adults, even if it causes no problems.  
- In older adults, surgeons may remove it if it feels thick when touched.  
- A thick pouch may have abnormal tissue inside.  
- This raises the risk of future problems.  

## Key Points

- Meckel diverticulum is a small pouch in the small intestine.  
- It is present from birth and affects about 2% of people.  
- Most people never have symptoms.  
- In some, it can cause bleeding, blockage, or inflammation.  
- Less than a quarter of these pouches have stomach tissue.  
- That tissue can make acid and cause ulcers and bleeding.  
- Diverticulitis can feel just like appendicitis.  
- Tests depend on your symptoms.  
- A Meckel scan is very good at finding the pouch in children with bleeding.  
- Surgery is needed for any pouch that causes symptoms.

# Growths and Malformations of the Blood Vessels

These are lumps or changes in the skin caused by blood or lymph vessels that are not normal. They often show up as red or purple marks on the skin.

## What You Need to Know

- Some of these growths are present at birth or appear soon after.
- They are often called birthmarks.
- Most of these growths go away on their own over time.
- Doctors can usually tell what kind of growth it is just by looking at it.
- A skin sample (biopsy) is rarely needed.

## Types of Growth or Malformation

- **Hemangiomas**: Fast-growing lumps that often appear in the first few weeks of life. They may shrink and fade over time.
- **Port-wine stains**: Flat, red or purple marks that are present at birth. They do not go away on their own.
- **Lymphangiomas**: Swellings caused by abnormal lymph vessels. They often appear as soft lumps under the skin.
- **Pyogenic granulomas**: Small, red, raised bumps that bleed easily. They often appear after an injury.
- **Spider angiomas**: Small red spots with thin lines spreading out like spider legs. They are often linked to liver problems.
- **Cherry angiomas**: Small, bright red spots that grow with age. They are harmless.

## When Treatment Is Needed

- Not all growths need treatment.
- Treatment may be needed if the growth causes problems.
- Problems can include pain, bleeding, or trouble with vision, breathing, or eating.
- Treatment options include medicine, laser therapy, or surgery.

## Important Notes

- Most babies with these growths do not have serious health issues.
- If a growth is large, in a sensitive area, or growing fast, see a doctor.
- Early care can help prevent long-term problems.

# Myotonic Dystrophy

Myotonic dystrophy is a genetic muscle disease. It is one of the most common types of muscle disease that starts in adulthood. There are two main types. Both types affect muscles you control on purpose. Type 1 also affects muscles you do not control on purpose.

The disease usually starts in the teenage years or early adulthood. Symptoms include muscle stiffness, muscle weakness, and loss of muscle size. The weakness often starts in the hands, feet, and face. Some people develop a droopy eyelid. Heart problems can also occur. Other possible issues include learning difficulties, cataracts, hormone problems, and early balding in men and women.

People with Type 1 may also have trouble swallowing or constipation. Women with Type 1 may have problems during childbirth because of weak muscles in the uterus.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your symptoms, when they started, and your family history. A DNA test confirms the diagnosis. This test checks for changes in your genes.

## How Is It Treated?

Medicines can help with muscle stiffness. These are called membrane-stabilizing medicines. The most effective one is mexiletine. Others include lamotrigine, carbamazepine, and phenytoin.

Mexiletine works well for muscle stiffness that affects daily life. But it can cause heart rhythm problems in some people. It should not be used if you already have serious heart rhythm issues. Always talk to a heart doctor before starting this medicine, especially if your heart test was abnormal.

There is no medicine to treat muscle weakness. This weakness is what usually causes major disability. As the disease gets worse, many people need braces to help with footdrop.

## What Is the Outlook?

Most people with myotonic dystrophy live into their 50s. The main causes of death are heart problems and breathing issues. People who get serious heart problems or severe muscle weakness at a young age are at higher risk of dying early.

# What Is the Autonomic Nervous System?

The autonomic nervous system controls many body functions without you having to think about them.  
It helps manage blood pressure, breathing rate, body temperature, digestion, and more.  

This system works automatically. You do not need to make a conscious effort to use it.  

Disorders of this system can affect any part of the body.  
Some of these problems can get better. Others may get worse over time.

---

## What Makes Up the Autonomic Nervous System?

The autonomic nervous system sends signals to your internal organs.  
These include your heart, lungs, stomach, intestines, liver, kidneys, bladder, sweat glands, salivary glands, and more.  

It has two main parts:  
- The sympathetic nervous system  
- The parasympathetic nervous system  

These two parts work together to keep your body balanced.  
One part can speed up a body process. The other can slow it down.  

A nerve signal travels through two nerve cells to reach an organ.  
The first cell is in the brain stem or spinal cord.  
It connects to a second cell in a group of nerve cells called a ganglion.  
From there, nerve fibers go to the organs.  

The ganglia for the sympathetic system are near the spinal cord.  
The ganglia for the parasympathetic system are close to or inside the organs they control.

---

## What Does the Autonomic Nervous System Do?

This system controls many automatic body functions, such as:  
- Blood pressure  
- Heart rate and breathing rate  
- Body temperature  
- Digestion  
- How your body uses energy (metabolism)  
- Balance of water and minerals like sodium and calcium  
- Production of saliva, sweat, and tears  
- Urination  
- Bowel movements  
- Sexual response  

Some organs are mainly controlled by one system.  
Other organs are influenced by both systems.  
For example, the sympathetic system raises blood pressure.  
The parasympathetic system lowers it.  

Together, they help your body respond to different situations.

---

### The Sympathetic Nervous System

This system prepares your body for stress or danger.  
It is often called the "fight or flight" system.  

It does the following:  
- Increases heart rate and makes the heart beat harder  
- Opens up the airways so you can breathe easier  
- Releases stored energy from the liver  
- Increases your body’s energy use at rest  
- Makes your muscles stronger  
- Makes your palms sweat  
- Makes your pupils widen  
- Makes your hair stand up  
- Slows down digestion and urination  

These changes help you react quickly in an emergency.

---

### The Parasympathetic Nervous System

This system helps your body rest and recover.  
It works during normal, calm situations.  

It does the following:  
- Slows the heart rate  
- Lowers blood pressure  
- Helps the digestive system break down food  
- Helps the body get rid of waste  
- Uses energy from food to repair and rebuild tissues  

This system helps your body conserve energy and stay balanced.

---

Both the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems are involved in sexual activity.  
Other parts of the nervous system also play a role.  
These include the nerves that control movement and sensation in the skin.

---

## Chemical Messengers in the Autonomic System

Two main chemicals carry messages in this system:  
- Acetylcholine  
- Norepinephrine  

Nerve fibers that release acetylcholine are called cholinergic fibers.  
Nerve fibers that release norepinephrine are called adrenergic fibers.  

Acetylcholine usually has effects linked to the parasympathetic system.  
Norepinephrine usually has effects linked to the sympathetic system.  

But acetylcholine can also cause some sympathetic effects.  
For example, it can trigger sweating or make your hair stand up.

---

## What Causes Autonomic Disorders?

Autonomic disorders happen when the nerves or brain areas that control these functions are damaged.  
They can also happen without a clear cause.

Common causes include:  
- Diabetes  
- Nerve problems in the arms and legs (peripheral nerve disorders)  
- Aging  
- Parkinson disease  

Less common causes include:  
- Autonomic neuropathies  
- Multiple system atrophy  
- Pure autonomic failure  
- Spinal cord injuries or diseases  
- Problems at the connection between nerves and muscles, such as botulism or Lambert-Eaton syndrome  
- Certain viral infections, including COVID-19  
- Injury to neck nerves, such as from surgery  
- Some medications

---

## What Are the Symptoms of Autonomic Disorders?

Many people feel dizzy or lightheaded when standing up.  
This is due to a sudden drop in blood pressure (called orthostatic hypotension).  

Other symptoms include:  
- Dizziness  
- Blurred vision  
- Head pressure  
- Fast or irregular heartbeat  
- Shaking or trembling  
- Nausea  
- Trouble breathing  
- Fainting (rarely)

Some people sweat less or not at all.  
This makes it hard to cool down in hot weather.  

The eyes and mouth may feel dry.  

After eating, some people feel full too soon.  
Others may vomit because food stays in the stomach too long (called gastroparesis).  

Some people leak urine (urinary incontinence).  
This often happens because the bladder is overactive.  
Others have trouble emptying their bladder (urine retention).  
This happens when the bladder is too weak.

Constipation may occur.  
Some people lose control of bowel movements.

The pupils may not react normally to light.  
They may not get bigger in the dark or smaller in bright light.

In men, trouble getting or keeping an erection (erectile dysfunction) can be an early sign.

---

## How Are Autonomic Disorders Diagnosed?

Doctors start by asking about your symptoms and doing a physical exam.  

They check for signs like orthostatic hypotension.  
They measure your blood pressure and heart rate while you are lying down, sitting, and standing.  
When you stand up, blood can pool in your legs.  
This lowers blood pressure.  
In healthy people, the heart quickly adjusts.  
If your heart rate and blood pressure change too much or last too long, you may have a problem.

Doctors may ask you to do a Valsalva maneuver.  
This means you try to blow out hard without letting air escape through your nose or mouth.  
It is like straining during a bowel movement.  
They watch how your heart rate and blood pressure respond.

A tilt table test may be done.  
You lie flat on a table that tilts upright.  
Your blood pressure and heart rate are measured before, during, and after the tilt.  
This helps see how your body reacts to position changes.

The Valsalva maneuver and tilt table test together help doctors tell if the problem is in the autonomic nervous system.

Doctors also check your pupils.  
They shine a light into your eyes to see how they react.

Sweat testing is also used.  
One type uses small electrodes on your legs and arms.  
These deliver a small amount of acetylcholine to stimulate sweat glands.  
Then, they measure how much sweat is produced.  
You may feel a mild burning sensation.

In the thermoregulatory sweat test, a powder is put on your skin.  
You enter a warm, enclosed room to make you sweat.  
The powder changes color where you sweat.  
Doctors use the pattern to find out where the problem lies.

Other tests may check reflexes.  
Blood tests or imaging scans may be done to find the cause.

---

## How Are Autonomic Disorders Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause.  
If another condition is causing the problem, it is treated first.  
If no cause is found, treatment focuses on relieving symptoms.

### For Low Blood Pressure When Standing (Orthostatic Hypotension)

- Raise the head of your bed by about 4 inches (10 centimeters)  
- Stand up slowly  
- Wear compression stockings or an abdominal binder  
- Drink more fluids and eat more salt (if approved by your doctor)  
- Medications may help:  
  - Fludrocortisone: helps the body keep salt and fluid, which raises blood pressure  
  - Midodrine or droxidopa: make small blood vessels tighten, which raises blood pressure  
  These medicines are taken by mouth.

### For Reduced or No Sweating

- Avoid hot environments  
- Stay cool  
- Use fans or air conditioning

### For Urinary Incontinence (Leaking Urine)

- Medications can help relax an overactive bladder:  
  - Oxybutynin  
  - Mirabegron  
  - Tamsulosin  
  - Tolterodine  
  These are taken by mouth.

### For Urine Retention (Trouble Emptying the Bladder)

- You can learn to insert a catheter (a thin tube) into your bladder through the urethra.  
  - Do this several times a day.  
  - Remove it after the bladder is empty.  
- Bethanechol can help the bladder contract better and empty more completely.

### For Constipation

- Eat more fiber (like bran or psyllium)  
- Use stool softeners (like docusate, lactulose, or polyethylene glycol)  
- If needed, use enemas

### For Erectile Dysfunction

- Medications can help:  
  - Sildenafil  
  - Tadalafil  
  - Vardenafil  
  These are taken by mouth.

# Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL)

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most common type of cancer in children. It can also happen in adults of any age.

This disease starts when blood cells in the bone marrow grow out of control. The abnormal cells are called blasts. They build up in the blood and replace healthy blood cells. This can cause problems in the brain and spinal cord (called the central nervous system). It can also affect the testes.

## Who Gets ALL?

- In the United States, over 6,500 new cases of ALL are expected each year.
- About 1,400 people die from ALL each year.
- Most cases happen in children, especially between ages 2 and 5.
- A second group of cases happens in adults over age 50.
- ALL is the most common cancer in children under 15.
- It makes up about 20% of all adult leukemia cases.
- The chance of getting ALL in a lifetime is about 1 in 1,000 for both men and women.
- Hispanic people have a higher chance of getting ALL than other groups. This may be linked to a certain gene.

## What Causes ALL?

ALL starts when blood stem cells in the bone marrow get damaged by changes in their genes. These changes cause the cells to grow too fast and not die when they should. The damaged cells take over the bone marrow and stop healthy blood cells from forming.

## Types of ALL

There are two main types of ALL:

- **B-ALL**: The abnormal cells come from B-lymphocytes.
- **T-ALL**: The abnormal cells come from T-lymphocytes.

The disease can act like leukemia if the abnormal cells are in the blood and bone marrow. It can act like lymphoma if the cells spread to other parts of the body, like the lymph nodes, liver, or spleen.

The World Health Organization uses a system that looks at the genes, cell shape, and protein markers on the cells. This helps doctors predict how the disease will behave and what treatment will work best.

## Symptoms of ALL

Symptoms can start suddenly and last only days or weeks.

The main symptoms come from low levels of healthy blood cells:

### Low Red Blood Cells (Anemia)
- Feeling tired or weak
- Pale skin
- Feeling unwell
- Shortness of breath when active
- Fast heartbeat
- Chest pain during activity

### Low Platelets (Thrombocytopenia)
- Easy bruising
- Tiny red or purple spots on the skin (petechiae)
- Bleeding from the nose or gums
- Heavy periods
- Bleeding in the urine or stomach (rare)
- Sudden bleeding in the brain or belly (rare but serious)

### Low White Blood Cells (Granulocytopenia or Neutropenia)
- Frequent or severe infections
- Fever
- Infections caused by bacteria, fungi, or viruses

### Spread of Cancer to Other Areas
- Swollen liver, spleen, or lymph nodes
- Bone or joint pain (common in children)
- Headaches
- Vision or hearing problems
- Confusion or changes in thinking
- Weakness on one side of the body (like a stroke)
- Numbness or tingling

## How Is ALL Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to find out if someone has ALL.

### Blood Tests
- A complete blood count (CBC) checks the number of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.
- A blood smear looks at the shape and size of blood cells under a microscope.
- If the blood shows many abnormal cells, it may mean leukemia.

### Bone Marrow Test
- A small sample of bone marrow is taken from the hip bone.
- This is the most important test to confirm ALL.
- Doctors look for at least 20% abnormal blast cells in the marrow.

If bone marrow is not available, doctors can use blood tests to make the diagnosis.

### Special Lab Tests
- These tests help tell ALL apart from other types of leukemia.
- They check for specific proteins on the surface of the cells (immunophenotyping).
- They look for certain genes or chromosomes (cytogenetics).
- They test for an enzyme called TdT, which is found in lymphoid cells.

### Common Gene Changes in ALL

| Gene Change | Seen In | Prognosis |
|------------|--------|----------|
| t(9;22) / BCR-ABL1 (Ph+ ALL) | Adults | Poor |
| High hyperdiploidy (51–65 chromosomes) | Children | Good |
| Hypodiploidy (< 46 chromosomes) | Adults and children | Poor |
| t(12;21) / TEL-AML1 | Children | Good |

Other rare gene changes include:
- t(v;11q23) / MLL rearranged (common in infants)
- t(1;19) / E2A-PBX1
- t(5;14) / IL3-IGH
- t(8;14), t(8;22), t(2;8) / C-MYC rearranged

Some cases look like Ph+ ALL but do not have the Philadelphia chromosome. These are called *BCR-ABL1-like* and are harder to treat.

### Other Lab Findings
- High levels of uric acid, phosphate, potassium, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) may mean tumor lysis syndrome. This happens when cancer cells die quickly and release their contents into the blood.
- High liver enzymes or creatinine levels may show organ damage.
- Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) can happen.
- People with Ph+ ALL or MLL rearrangements often have very high white blood cell counts.

### Imaging Tests
- A CT scan of the head is done if there are brain symptoms.
- A CT scan of the chest and belly checks for swollen lymph nodes, a mass in the chest, or enlarged liver or spleen.
- An echocardiogram or MUGA scan checks heart function before treatment with certain chemotherapy drugs that can harm the heart.

## How Is ALL Treated?

Treatment depends on the person’s age, health, and the type of ALL.

### Main Treatments
- **Chemotherapy**: A mix of drugs given over time to kill cancer cells.
- **CNS Prophylaxis**: Medicine put into the spinal fluid (intrathecal) and sometimes steroids to prevent cancer in the brain and spinal cord.
- **CNS Radiation**: Used only if cancer has spread to the brain.
- **Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (TKIs)**: Used for Ph+ ALL. These drugs target a specific protein made by the abnormal gene.
- **Stem Cell Transplant**: Used in high-risk cases or after relapse.
- **Immunotherapy**: Uses the body’s immune system to fight cancer.
- **Supportive Care**: Treats side effects like infections, low blood counts, and pain.

### Treatment Phases
- **Induction**: First 9 to 12 months. Uses strong chemotherapy to kill most cancer cells and bring the disease into remission.
- **Consolidation**: Follows induction. Uses more chemotherapy to kill any remaining cancer cells.
- **Maintenance**: Lasts 2.5 to 3 years. Uses lower doses of drugs to keep the cancer from coming back.

## Prognosis (Outlook)

The chance of recovery depends on many factors.

### Good Prognosis Means:
- Age 3 to 9 years
- Low white blood cell count at diagnosis
- Certain gene changes: high hyperdiploidy, t(1;19), or t(12;21)
- No cancer in the brain or spinal cord at diagnosis

### Poor Prognosis Means:
- Certain gene changes: hypodiploidy, near triploidy, t(v;11q23), t(5;14), t(8;14), t(8;22), t(2;8), or Ph+ ALL
- High white blood cell count
- Older age in adults
- *BCR-ABL1-like* gene pattern

### Survival Rates
- **Children**: Over 80% survive at least 5 years. Most are cured.
- **Adults**: Less than 50% survive long-term.

### Why Adults Do Worse Than Children
- Adults often cannot handle strong chemotherapy as well.
- They are more likely to have other health problems.
- Their cancer cells are more likely to resist treatment.
- They may miss appointments or doses of medicine.
- They are less likely to get treatment plans used for children.

Doctors often give stronger treatment to people with poor outlooks. The risks of side effects are balanced against the risk of dying from the disease.

## Key Points

- ALL is the most common cancer in children but can also affect adults.
- The brain and spinal cord are often involved. Most patients get medicine into the spinal fluid and steroids. Some also get radiation to the brain.
- Children have a very good chance of being cured — over 80% survive 5 years or more.
- Adults have a lower chance of long-term survival — less than 50%.
- If the cancer comes back, repeat chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or stem cell transplant may help.
