# Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy (CIDP)

CIDP is a long-term condition that affects nerves in the arms, legs, and other parts of the body.  
It causes muscle weakness that gets worse over time.  
The weakness lasts for more than 8 weeks.  

This condition is similar to Guillain-Barré syndrome.  
But in CIDP, the symptoms get worse slowly over many weeks or months.  
In Guillain-Barré, symptoms usually get worse in just a few days or weeks.

## What Causes CIDP?

CIDP happens when the body’s immune system attacks the protective covering around nerves.  
This covering is called the myelin sheath.  
The myelin sheath helps nerve signals travel fast and clear.  
When it is damaged, nerve signals slow down or stop.  
This causes weakness and other nerve problems.

## How Nerves Work

Most nerves in the body are wrapped in layers of fat called myelin.  
This is like insulation on an electrical wire.  
It helps nerve signals move quickly and correctly.  
When the myelin is damaged, the nerve cannot send signals well.  
This is called demyelination.

## Symptoms of CIDP

The main symptom is muscle weakness.  
It usually starts in the legs and moves up the body.  
Weakness may get worse slowly.  
Or it may come and go.  
It can improve, then get worse again.

Numbness or tingling may happen, but it is less common than weakness.  
Reflexes are often missing.  
For example, your knee jerk reflex may not work.

People with CIDP usually have fewer problems with blood pressure and heart rhythm than people with Guillain-Barré.  
The weakness may affect one side of the body more than the other.  
It often gets worse more slowly than in Guillain-Barré.

## How Doctors Diagnose CIDP

Doctors look at your symptoms and medical history.  
They may do tests to confirm the diagnosis.

- **Electromyography (EMG)**: This test checks how well nerves and muscles work.  
- **Nerve conduction studies**: These measure how fast nerve signals travel.  
- **Spinal tap (lumbar puncture)**: A small amount of fluid is taken from the lower back.  
  This fluid surrounds the brain and spinal cord.  
  Doctors check it for signs of nerve damage.

In rare cases, a small piece of nerve may be removed for testing.  
This is called a nerve biopsy.  
It helps confirm if the myelin is damaged.

## Treatment for CIDP

Treatment aims to reduce nerve damage and improve strength.  
It may take months or years.

### Immune Globulin

This is a solution made from blood donated by many people.  
It contains antibodies that help calm the immune system.  
It can be given through a vein or under the skin.  
It helps relieve symptoms.  
It has fewer side effects than steroids.  
It is easier to use than plasma exchange.  
But its benefits may not last as long after treatment ends.

### Corticosteroids

These are medicines that reduce swelling and calm the immune system.  
Examples include dexamethasone and methylprednisolone.  
They can be taken by mouth or given through a vein.  
They help some people with CIDP.  
But they can cause side effects with long-term use.

### Medications That Suppress the Immune System

These medicines slow down the immune system.  
They are used if other treatments do not work.  
Examples include azathioprine and monoclonal antibodies.  
Monoclonal antibodies are man-made antibodies.  
They target specific parts of the immune system to stop it from attacking nerves.

### Plasma Exchange

This is a treatment that filters harmful substances from the blood.  
It removes antibodies that attack the myelin sheath.  
It is used if CIDP is severe or does not respond to other treatments.  
It is done in a hospital and requires several sessions.

## Long-Term Care

People with CIDP often need treatment for many months or even years.  
Regular checkups are important.  
Treatment can help you stay active and improve your quality of life.

# Chest Physiotherapy

Chest physiotherapy helps clear mucus from the lungs. It uses physical techniques done by a trained person. These techniques include tapping on the chest, changing body position, and shaking the chest gently.

The goal is to help move mucus out of the airways. This is important when a person cannot cough well enough to clear thick or large amounts of mucus.

This treatment is used when coughing alone is not enough. It is helpful for people with certain lung conditions, such as:

- **Bronchiectasis**  
  This is a condition where the airways in the lungs are damaged and widened. It can happen in people with or without cystic fibrosis.

- **COPD** (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease)  
  This includes long-term lung problems like emphysema and chronic bronchitis. It may be used in some cases when mucus builds up.

- **Cystic fibrosis**  
  A genetic condition that causes thick mucus to build up in the lungs and other organs.

- **Neuromuscular disorders**  
  Conditions that affect the nerves and muscles involved in breathing. These can make it hard to cough effectively.

- **Pneumonia in lower parts of the lungs**  
  When infection causes mucus to collect in the lower areas of the lungs, especially when lying down.

These techniques are not for everyone. A doctor or lung specialist decides if chest physiotherapy is right for a person.

# Contraception and Pregnancy in Teens

Many teens have sex. But not all teens know enough about birth control, pregnancy, or sexually transmitted infections. Teens may act on impulse. They may not plan ahead. Some teens use alcohol or drugs, which makes it less likely they will use birth control or condoms.

(See also: Introduction to Health Care Issues in Teens.)

---

## Birth Control for Teens

Teens can use the same birth control methods as adults. But the biggest problem is getting access to birth control and using it correctly every time.

Male condoms are the most common type of birth control teens use. But some teens think condoms reduce pleasure. Others feel uncomfortable talking to a partner about using condoms. Some teens do not feel strong enough to ask their partner to use a condom during sex.

Girls may forget to take birth control pills every day. Or they may stop taking them. They may not switch to another method of birth control.

Longer-lasting options can work well for some teens. These include:
- Intrauterine devices (IUDs): Small devices placed in the uterus that last for years.
- Hormonal injections: Shots given every 3 months or longer.
- Implants: Small rods placed under the skin that last several years.

All of these can be very effective.

Teens should talk with a doctor or nurse about birth control and safe sex. Some schools and health groups also offer counseling and birth control. Most teens can get birth control from their regular doctor or a specialist. In the United States, each state has its own rules about privacy for teens getting this care.

---

## Pregnancy in Teens

Being pregnant can be very stressful for a teen.

Pregnant teens and their partners often leave school or job training. This can make it harder to earn money later. It can also hurt self-confidence or cause problems in relationships.

Pregnant teens are less likely than adult women to get early and regular prenatal care. This can lead to worse health for both the teen and the baby.

For the teen, this can mean:
- Giving birth too early (preterm birth).
- Anemia: Not having enough healthy red blood cells.
- Preeclampsia: High blood pressure and protein in the urine. This can harm the baby.

For the baby, this can mean:
- Low birth weight.
- Infection.
- Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).

The risks are even higher for very young teens, such as those aged 10 to 13.

A pregnant teen can choose to:
- Continue the pregnancy.
- End the pregnancy (abortion).

If she continues, she can raise the baby alone or with the baby’s father. She may get help from family. Or she can choose to give the baby up for adoption.

All of these choices can be hard to handle emotionally. Counseling can help both the teen and her partner. Counseling should also teach about birth control after the baby is born.

Parents may react in many ways when their teen becomes pregnant, gets someone pregnant, or is in a relationship with someone who is pregnant. Reactions can include worry, excitement, sadness, disappointment, or anger.

It is important for parents to show support. They should be willing to help their teen make choices. Open talks about abortion, adoption, and parenting are key. These are tough decisions. Teens should not have to face them alone.

# Neuropathic Pain – Simple Explanation

Neuropathic pain comes from damage or problems in the nerves. It is not caused by injury to skin, muscles, or bones. Instead, it happens when the nerves themselves are hurt or not working right.

This kind of pain can feel very different from normal pain. It often feels like burning, tingling, or sharp shooting pain. The pain may be worse than what you would expect from the injury. Sometimes, even light touch or a breeze can feel painful.

---

## What Causes Neuropathic Pain?

Neuropathic pain can happen after any injury to the nervous system. This includes nerves in the arms, legs, or spine. It can also happen after a stroke, spinal cord injury, or nerve damage from disease.

Some common causes include:
- Nerve damage from diabetes
- Nerve damage from chemotherapy
- Nerve injury after surgery
- Shingles (a viral infection)
- Injury from trauma or accidents
- Conditions like multiple sclerosis

In some cases, the nerves send pain signals even when there is no injury. This is called **deafferentation pain**. It can happen after an amputation (phantom limb pain) or after nerve damage from shingles (postherpetic neuralgia).

Sometimes, the body’s stress system (sympathetic nervous system) becomes overactive. This can make the pain worse. This is called **sympathetically maintained pain**. It is often seen in complex regional pain syndrome.

---

## Symptoms and Signs

You may feel:
- Burning, tingling, or electric-like pain
- Pain from light touch (like a soft brush)
- Pain that feels deep and aching
- Pain that spreads beyond the original area

You may avoid moving the painful area. This can lead to:
- Weak muscles
- Stiff joints
- Bone loss
- Less movement over time

The pain often lasts a long time. It can continue even after the original injury has healed. This is because the nervous system has changed and become more sensitive.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and do a physical exam. They will look for signs of nerve damage.

Key clues include:
- Pain that is much worse than expected for the injury
- Burning or tingling pain
- Pain that spreads beyond the injured area
- Pain that feels like it comes from a different place

Tests may be done to check nerve function. These can include:
- Nerve conduction studies
- Electromyography (EMG)
- Imaging tests like MRI

If the pain gets better after a nerve block, it may be due to the sympathetic nervous system.

---

## How Is It Treated?

There is no single cure. Treatment usually uses several methods together. The goal is to reduce pain and help you live better.

### Medications

Some medicines work well for nerve pain. These are not the usual painkillers like acetaminophen or ibuprofen.

**First-line treatments:**
- Tricyclic antidepressants (like amitriptyline, nortriptyline)
- Antiseizure drugs (like gabapentin, pregabalin)
- SNRIs (like duloxetine, venlafaxine)

These medicines help calm overactive nerves. They are often used at lower doses than for depression.

**Second-line treatments:**
- Topical creams or patches (like lidocaine or capsaicin)
- These are applied directly to the skin

**Third-line treatment:**
- Opioid painkillers (like oxycodone or morphine)
- These are not usually the best choice. They can cause addiction and side effects.

### Other Treatments

- **Physical therapy** – Helps you move safely and reduces pain sensitivity
- **Psychological support** – Anxiety and depression can make pain worse. Treating these helps.
- **Neuromodulation** – Devices that send small electrical signals to nerves. Examples:
  - Spinal cord stimulation
  - Nerve stimulation (peripheral or dorsal root ganglion)
- **Nerve blocks or ablation** – Injections or procedures to stop nerve signals
- **Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS)** – A small device that sends gentle electrical pulses to the skin

### Special Treatments

- **Capsaicin patch (8%)** – A strong cream applied once by a doctor. It causes a burning feeling at first, but can help for up to 3 months.
- **Lidocaine patches** – Help reduce pain and can be used with capsaicin to reduce irritation.

---

## Important Notes

- **Medicines are not a cure.** They aim to reduce pain so it is easier to live with.
- **Start slowly.** Doctors often begin with one medicine and add others if needed.
- **Side effects matter.** Some medicines can cause drowsiness, dry mouth, or heart problems. Your doctor will watch for these.
- **Not all medicines work for everyone.** You may need to try a few before finding one that helps.
- **Mental health is part of treatment.** Depression and anxiety can make pain worse. They should be treated too.

---

## When to See a Specialist

If your pain does not improve with standard treatments, a pain clinic may help. These clinics use a team approach. They offer many treatments together, including medicine, therapy, and nerve stimulation.

---

## Key Points

- Neuropathic pain comes from nerve damage, not from injury to skin or muscle.
- It often feels like burning, tingling, or sharp pain.
- Pain may be worse than expected and spread beyond the injury site.
- Treatment uses many methods: medicine, therapy, nerve stimulation, and mental health support.
- Early treatment helps prevent long-term problems like muscle loss and joint stiffness.
- Work with your doctor to find the best plan for you.

# Vipoma

A vipoma is a rare kind of tumor in the pancreas.  
It makes a hormone called vasoactive intestinal peptide.  
This hormone causes severe watery diarrhea.

## What Causes Vipoma?

- The tumor starts in cells in the pancreas that make the hormone VIP.
- More than half of these tumors are cancer.
- In a small number of people, vipoma is part of a larger condition called multiple endocrine neoplasia.

## Symptoms of Vipoma

The main symptom is very bad, watery diarrhea.  
Some people have diarrhea every day.  
They can pass 1 to 3 quarts (1,000 to 3,000 milliliters) of stool each day.  
This much diarrhea can lead to dehydration.

The diarrhea takes away important salts from the body.  
This can cause low potassium in the blood.  
It can also make the blood too acidic.

Low potassium and acid in the blood can cause:
- Feeling tired or weak
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Stomach cramps
- Flushing (redness and warmth in the face)

## How Is Vipoma Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your symptoms and do blood tests.  
They check for high levels of the hormone VIP in your blood.  
If VIP levels are high, you will need imaging tests to find the tumor.

Imaging tests include:
- Endoscopic ultrasound (a special ultrasound done through the throat)
- PET scan (a scan that shows active tumors)
- Octreotide scintigraphy (a scan using a special dye)
- Arteriography (an X-ray after a dye is injected into an artery)

## How Is Vipoma Treated?

### Step 1: Replace Lost Fluids and Salts

You will need fluids and salts through a vein (IV).  
This helps prevent dehydration and balances your body’s chemicals.  
You may also need bicarbonate to correct acid in the blood.  
The diarrhea keeps draining fluids and salts, so replacement must continue.

### Step 2: Use Medication to Control Diarrhea

The medicine octreotide or lanreotide usually helps stop the diarrhea.  
You may need high doses to get results.

### Step 3: Surgery

Surgery to remove the tumor can cure about half of people whose tumor has not spread.  
For people with spread cancer, surgery may help ease symptoms for a time.

### Step 4: Chemotherapy

Chemotherapy can reduce diarrhea and shrink the tumor.  
But it does not cure the disease.

# Mandibular Dislocation

Mandibular dislocation is a dental emergency that needs quick care.

## What Causes It?

- Some people get this problem more than once.
- It often happens when the mouth opens very wide.
- Common triggers include biting into a large sandwich with hard bread, yawning widely, or during a dental visit.
- People who get this problem may have looser jaw joints than most.
- Injury can cause it, but this is less common.

## What Are the Symptoms?

- The mouth stays wide open.
- The person cannot close their mouth.
- Pain comes from trying to close the mouth.
- If the jaw line tilts to one side, the dislocation is on that side.

## Treatment Options

- A local numbing medicine (like lidocaine) may help relax the jaw muscles.
- This is not used often.
- A doctor or dentist may need to push the jaw back into place.
- Medicine like diazepam or midazolam with fentanyl can help relax muscles.
- This is usually not needed.

## How Long It Takes to Heal

- The longer the jaw stays out of place, the harder it is to fix.
- The more likely it is to happen again.

## How to Put the Jaw Back in Place

- The patient’s head is held steady.
- The doctor or dentist puts their thumbs on the jaw, just behind the back teeth or on the lower teeth.
- The fingers go under the jaw.
- The patient is told to open wide, like yawning.
- The doctor pushes down on the back teeth and up on the chin at the same time.
- This helps the jaw move back into place.

## After the Jaw Is Fixed

- A special bandage called a Barton bandage may be used for 2 to 3 days.
- The patient must not open the mouth wide for at least 6 weeks.
- To avoid yawning too wide, place a fist under the chin.
- Cut food into small pieces.
- If the jaw keeps coming out and other treatments do not work, see a specialist.
- Surgery may be an option in rare cases.
- The surgeon can tighten the ligaments around the jaw joint.
- Or, they can remove part of the bone in the joint to prevent dislocation.

## Barton Bandage

- This bandage wraps around the head and jaw.
- It supports the jaw from below and in front.

# Scrotal Pain

Pain in the scrotum can happen to boys and men of any age.  
The scrotum is the skin bag that holds the testicles.  
The testicles are very sensitive. Even a small injury can cause pain.

---

## What Causes Scrotal Pain?

Pain can come from the testicles or from nearby areas like the groin or belly.

### Common Causes of Sudden Pain

**Testicular torsion**  
This happens when a testicle twists on its cord.  
Twisting cuts off blood flow.  
This causes sudden, severe pain.  
It can lead to loss of the testicle if not treated fast.  
It is most common in newborns and boys after puberty.  
It can also happen in adult men.

**Torsion of the testicular appendage**  
This is a small piece of leftover tissue attached to the testicle.  
It can twist and block blood flow.  
This causes pain.  
It is most common in boys aged 7 to 14.

**Epididymitis**  
This is swelling and irritation of the tube on top of the testicle.  
This tube stores and helps sperm mature.  
It is the most common cause of scrotal pain in adult men.  
It is often caused by an infection.  
The infection is usually from a sexually transmitted disease.  
Sometimes there is no infection.  
In those cases, doctors think urine may flow backward into the tube.  
This can happen after heavy lifting or straining.

### Less Common Causes

- A hernia in the groin (a bulge where part of the intestine pushes through a weak spot)  
- Infection of the testicle (orchitis), often from a virus like mumps  
- Pain from a problem in the belly, such as a kidney stone or appendicitis  
- Injury to the groin or testicles  
- A ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (a serious blood vessel problem)  
- Fournier gangrene — a rare but dangerous infection in the area between the genitals and anus  
- Testicular cancer — this rarely causes pain

---

## When to See a Doctor

Seek medical help right away if you have:

- Sudden, very bad pain in the scrotum  
- Swelling in the scrotum or groin that does not go down when pressed  
- Swelling with severe pain or vomiting  
- Blisters or red, black, or dark spots on the scrotum or near the anus  
- Signs of serious illness: high fever, trouble breathing, heavy sweating, dizziness, or confusion

If you have any of these warning signs, go to a doctor or emergency room right away.  
Some causes can lead to loss of a testicle or other serious problems.

If you do not have warning signs, see a doctor within 1 or 2 days.

---

## What the Doctor Will Do

The doctor will ask questions and do a physical exam.

### Questions the Doctor May Ask

- Where is the pain?  
- How long has it been there?  
- Have you had any injury to the groin?  
- Do you have a history of sexual activity?  
- Are you having trouble urinating? (For example, burning or discharge)  
- Do you have any other health problems that could cause pain in the groin?

### What the Doctor Will Check

- The genitals and scrotum  
- The groin area  
- The belly  
- Signs of other problems that might cause pain in the scrotum

The doctor will look for conditions that need urgent treatment.  
The type of pain and the person’s age can help point to the cause.

---

### Common Causes and Their Features

| Cause | Typical Signs | Tests Needed |
|------|----------------|--------------|
| **Testicular torsion** | Sudden, severe pain in one testicle. The testicle may be higher than the other. | Ultrasound |
| **Torsion of testicular appendage** | Pain that builds over days. Usually in the top part of the testicle. Sometimes mild swelling. | Ultrasound |
| **Epididymitis or epididymo-orchitis** | Pain in the tube or testicle. May have frequent urination, burning when peeing, or discharge. May happen after heavy lifting. Swelling in the scrotum. | Urine test, urine culture, STI tests |
| **Injury** | Pain after a blow to the groin. Swelling in the scrotum. | Ultrasound |
| **Inguinal hernia** | A soft, balloon-like bulge in the groin. Gets bigger when standing or straining. May go back in when lying down. Pain if it gets stuck. | Doctor’s exam |
| **Pain from another area (referred pain)** | No swelling or problems found in the scrotum. Pain may come from kidney stones, appendicitis, a tumor, or nerve pressure. | Depends on symptoms |
| **Orchitis (testicle infection)** | Pain in the scrotum and belly. Nausea. Fever. Swelling and redness. | Blood tests to check for virus antibodies |
| **Fournier gangrene** | Severe pain. Looks very sick. Fever. Confusion, trouble breathing, sweating, dizziness. Redness, blisters, or dead skin in the genital area. | Doctor’s exam, sometimes imaging |

> Note: These signs are common but not always present.

---

## Tests and Diagnosis

The doctor decides which tests are needed based on the history and exam.

### Common Tests

- **Urinalysis and urine culture** – to check for infection  
- **STI tests** – to check for sexually transmitted infections  
- **Color Doppler ultrasound** – to check blood flow in the testicles. Used if torsion is suspected

If the doctor strongly suspects testicular torsion, they may go straight to surgery.  
Waiting for tests could cause permanent damage.

---

## Treatment

The best treatment is fixing the cause.

- **Testicular torsion** – needs surgery right away  
- **Strangulated hernia** – needs surgery  
- **Fournier gangrene** – needs emergency surgery and antibiotics

For pain relief, doctors may give:

- Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (like ibuprofen)  
- Opioids (strong painkillers) for severe pain

---

## Special Notes for Older Men

- Testicular torsion is rare in older men.  
- When it does happen, symptoms may be different. This makes it harder to diagnose.  
- Epididymitis and orchitis are more common in older men.  
- Sexually transmitted infections are less likely to cause epididymitis in older men.  
- Other causes of pain in older men include:  
  - Inguinal hernia  
  - A hole in the colon (perforation)  
  - Kidney stones (renal colic)

---

## Key Points

- In boys and young men with sudden scrotal pain, testicular torsion is the first thing doctors think about.  
- In adult men, epididymitis is the most common cause of scrotal pain.  
- If a doctor suspects testicular torsion, they may do surgery right away instead of waiting for tests.  
- Pain in the scrotum can sometimes come from a problem in the belly, like a kidney stone or appendicitis.

Teeth can be lost for several reasons.

Sometimes, teeth must be removed if treatment does not work.

# Bone Density Problems in Children

Bone density problems affect how strong and dense a child’s bones are. Weak bones break easily. They can also grow in unusual ways.

- These problems happen when the body does not recycle old bone cells properly.
- Common signs include bones that do not grow right and bones that break easily.
- Doctors check for these problems by looking at symptoms, doing x-rays, and sometimes running blood tests.
- Treatments like medicine and surgery can help reduce some of the problems.

Bone density measures how much mineral is in the bone. Bones that are too hard or too soft are more likely to break.

Some bone density problems come from faulty genes. These genes can be passed from parent to child. Other causes include poor diet, hormone issues, or other health problems.

Bone density problems are split into two types: those that cause bones to be too weak (low density) and those that cause bones to be too thick (high density).

(See also: Overview of Bone Disorders in Children)

---

## Weak Bones in Children

Children’s bones are always growing and changing. Old bone is removed and new bone is made. This keeps bones strong.

In children with weak bones, this process is broken. It can be due to a specific cause or because the child is not moving much. The result is less bone mass and poor bone structure.

This makes bones thinner, weaker, and more likely to break. Breaks can happen in the spine or in long bones like the arms and legs. These problems can slow down growth, make movement hard, and affect overall development.

The main types of weak bone problems in children are:
- Osteogenesis imperfecta
- Osteoporosis
- Rickets

Causes of weak bones include:
- Poor diet
- Low vitamin D levels
- Faulty genes
- Low levels of hormones like growth hormone, estrogen, or testosterone
- Health issues like celiac disease or chronic kidney disease
- Some medicines, such as steroids

To check for weak bones, doctors use a test called a DXA scan. This scan uses two types of x-rays on the spine and hip. These are the areas most likely to break.

The scan compares the two x-ray readings to find out how dense the bone is. The result is a Z-score. This score compares the child’s bone density to that of a healthy child of the same age, sex, and size.

A Z-score of –2.0 or lower means the bones are too weak.

Doctors treat the root cause when possible. Lifestyle changes and medicine can also help.

---

## Thick Bones in Children (Osteopetroses)

Thick bone problems are called osteopetroses. These are rare, inherited conditions caused by faulty genes.

Bones are made of cells that grow, live, and then get removed. This is a natural recycling process. In osteopetroses, the body does not remove old bone cells. This causes bones to become too thick and change shape.

Even though the bones are denser, they are actually weaker, brittle, and more likely to break. The thick bone also takes up space where bone marrow should be. Bone marrow makes blood cells.

When bone marrow is crowded out, the body may not make enough blood cells. This can lead to anemia (low red blood cells) and low platelets (which help stop bleeding). The spleen may also become overactive and destroy too many red blood cells.

Osteopetroses can be mild or very serious. Some children show signs at birth (early onset). Others may not have symptoms until later in life (delayed onset).

Most types of osteopetroses cause similar problems:
- Bones grow poorly
- Bones get thicker and break easily
- Blood cell production drops because there is less bone marrow
- This can lead to infections or bleeding
- Bleeding often happens after small injuries, like nosebleeds from picking the nose or gum bleeding after brushing teeth

Extra bone in the skull can cause pressure inside the head. This can press on nerves and lead to:
- Facial paralysis
- Loss of vision or hearing
- Changes in face shape and teeth

Bones in the fingers, toes, arms, legs, spine, and pelvis can also be affected.

### How Doctors Diagnose Osteopetroses

Doctors use:
- X-rays
- Blood tests
- Genetic tests

X-rays show bones that are very dense or oddly shaped.

Sometimes, doctors find osteopetrosis by accident. This happens when a child has an x-ray for another reason and the bones look too dense.

Blood tests can show:
- Low red blood cells (anemia)
- Low platelets (thrombocytopenia)

Genetic tests help confirm the diagnosis by finding the faulty genes that affect bone cell function.

### How Doctors Treat Osteopetroses

Treatments include:
- Steroids (like prednisone)
- Stem cell transplantation
- Surgery
- Blood transfusions
- Antibiotics
- Orthodontic care

Steroids help reduce the formation of new bone cells. They may also speed up the removal of old bone cells. This can make bones stronger. Steroids can also ease bone pain and improve muscle strength.

Stem cell transplantation can cure some babies with early-onset osteopetrosis. But it may not fix kidney problems that are already present.

If nerves in the skull are pressed by bone, surgery may be needed to relieve the pressure. Surgery can also help if pressure builds up inside the skull. Plastic surgery may be used to fix serious face or jaw changes.

Teeth that are misaligned may need orthodontic treatment.

Minor bone breaks are usually treated with a cast or a traction device.

Major breaks—where bones are separated or not moving properly—may need surgery.

Anemia and low platelets are treated with blood transfusions.

In rare cases, if the spleen is overactive, removing it can help with both anemia and bleeding.

Infections are treated with antibiotics.

Without treatment, early-onset osteopetrosis is often fatal in infancy or early childhood. Death usually comes from severe anemia, infection, or bleeding.

Late-onset osteopetrosis is usually mild and does not cause serious problems.

# Metastatic Bone Tumors

Cancer from any part of the body can spread to the bones. But the most common cancers that spread to bones come from solid organs. These include:

- Breast
- Lung
- Prostate
- Kidney
- Thyroid
- Colon

In men, prostate cancer is the most common type. In women, breast cancer is the most common. Lung cancer causes the most cancer deaths in both men and women.

Breast cancer is the most common cancer to spread to bones. Any bone can be affected. But bone spread rarely happens below the middle of the forearm or the middle of the calf. When it does happen in these areas, it is most often from lung or kidney cancer.

The American Cancer Society says that more women will get breast cancer than men and women together will get lung cancer. But more people will die from lung cancer than from breast cancer or prostate cancer.

In hospitals that treat bone problems from cancer, breast cancer is the most common reason for surgery. People with breast cancer that has spread to bones often live longer than people with other types of cancer that have spread to bones. They may live longer before the cancer spreads to the lungs, liver, or brain.

## Symptoms and Signs of Metastatic Bone Tumors

The most common symptom is bone pain. But some people have no symptoms at all. The pain may appear before a doctor knows about the original cancer. Or it may show up in someone who already knows they have cancer.

## How Doctors Find Metastatic Bone Tumors When the Original Cancer Is Unknown

Doctors start with:

- A full health history
- A physical exam
- Blood tests (complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, protein tests, and prostate-specific antigen test for men)

They then take an X-ray of the entire bone area.

Next, they use advanced imaging:

- CT scan of the chest, belly, and pelvis

They also do a whole-body bone scan using a special radioactive material (technetium-99m). This scan helps find other places where cancer may have spread.

If needed, they take a small sample of the bone (biopsy) to confirm where the cancer started.

Doctors think about metastatic bone tumors in anyone over 40 who has unexplained bone pain. This is especially true if the person:

- Has a history of cancer
- Has pain or abnormal findings in more than one bone area
- Has imaging results that suggest cancer has spread to other parts of the body

Different cancers affect bones in different ways:

- Prostate cancer usually causes bone to grow too much (blastic)
- Lung cancer usually causes bone to break down (lytic)
- Breast cancer can cause either bone growth or bone breakdown

If cancer spread to bones is suspected, doctors often do a whole-body scan using a radioactive substance (radionuclide scan) or a PET/CT scan. These tests are better than X-rays at finding early or hidden bone spread. They can check the whole body.

If a scan shows multiple spots of cancer in the bones, doctors will suspect metastases. Even if there is only one spot, they still suspect cancer spread — especially if the person has known cancer. But a single spot may not be cancer spread. This is more likely if the original cancer was slow-growing or if a long time has passed since treatment.

For this reason, doctors often recommend a biopsy to confirm the diagnosis.

To find the original cancer in someone with a bone lesion, doctors do:

- A full health history and physical exam
- A CT scan of the chest, belly, and pelvis
- Blood tests

This approach finds the original cancer in over 85% of cases.

The diagnosis is confirmed with a bone biopsy. This is usually done using imaging guidance to get a small sample of the bone. Special stains on the sample can help guess the original cancer type.

Sometimes, even after all these tests, doctors still cannot find the original cancer. In these cases, they may do more tests. These can include another PET/CT scan or endoscopy (looking inside the body with a camera).

## Treatment of Metastatic Bone Tumors

Treatment depends on the type of cancer and how it affects the bone.

Radiation therapy is often used for:

- Painful bone areas
- Large bone areas that are growing
- Areas at risk of breaking

Surgery may be needed to:

- Stabilize a bone that is likely to break
- Remove a badly damaged bone
- Replace the bone with a joint implant if needed

For painful broken bones in the spine, doctors may use a minimally invasive procedure. They inject a special cement into the bone (kyphoplasty or vertebraplasty). This helps relieve pain and strengthens the bone.

Treatment depends on the type of cancer. Radiation therapy is often used with certain medicines. These include chemotherapy or hormone therapy.

Radiation therapy helps stop bone damage. It is used early to prevent pain, fractures, and hard-to-treat problems. Medicines that stop bone breakdown (like bisphosphonates or denosumab) also help slow damage.

Some cancers respond better to radiation than others. Breast cancer, prostate cancer, and multiple myeloma often heal well after radiation. Lung cancer and kidney cancer do not respond as well.

Because of this, doctors may choose more aggressive surgery for cancers that do not respond well to radiation.

If the bone is badly damaged and at risk of breaking, surgery may be needed. This can include using metal rods or plates to fix the bone. Or the damaged bone may be removed and replaced with an artificial joint.

In rare cases, if the cancer has only spread to a few bones and the original cancer was treated long ago, doctors may try to remove the cancer completely. This is called en bloc excision. It may be combined with radiation or chemotherapy. This approach can sometimes cure the disease.

Kyphoplasty or vertebraplasty helps relieve pain and stabilize broken spine bones. These are minimally invasive procedures. They are becoming more common for treating bone spread in the pelvis and limbs.

## Multiple Myeloma Bone Tumors

Multiple myeloma is the most common type of cancer that starts in the bone. It mostly affects older adults.

Even though it starts in the bone, it is actually a blood cancer. It begins in the bone marrow. It is not a true bone tumor, but it causes serious bone damage.

Multiple myeloma is a type of cancer that grows from plasma cells. These are a kind of white blood cell.

Doctors diagnose it with:

- Blood and urine tests to check for abnormal proteins (monoclonal spike)
- A bone marrow biopsy to confirm the diagnosis

The cancer usually starts in many places in the body. But sometimes it starts in just one spot. This is called a plasmacytoma.

Unlike other cancers that spread to bones, multiple myeloma does not show up well on a bone scan. Doctors use full-body X-rays (skeletal surveys) instead.

These X-rays usually show clear, round holes in the bone (punched-out lesions) or thinning of the bone.

Some bone lesions from multiple myeloma respond very well to radiation therapy.

## Key Points

- Breast, lung, prostate, and kidney cancers are the most common sources of bone spread.
- Bone spread should be suspected in people with known cancer, pain in more than one bone, or imaging that shows spread.
- A new bone lesion in someone with known cancer may need a biopsy. This checks if it is cancer spread or a new cancer.
- Radiation therapy, bisphosphonates, and denosumab are often used to slow bone damage.
- Broken bones from cancer may need surgery to fix or replace the damaged bone.

# Holy Basil

## What Is Holy Basil?

- The scientific name for holy basil is *Ocimum tenuiflorum*.
- In Hindu culture, it is called tulsi, which means "the incomparable one."
- It is also known as Thai basil or brush-leaf tea.
- This plant comes from India but grows in Australia, West Africa, and parts of the Middle East.
- People have used holy basil in traditional medicine for over 3,000 years.
- Hindus consider it sacred. They often grow it near temples and shrines.
- Medicines are made from the leaves, stems, and seeds of the plant.
- Some people use holy basil in cooking. It has a strong, bitter, spicy taste. It is sometimes called "hot basil" in recipes.
- You can buy holy basil as a dietary supplement in pill or capsule form.
- The essential oil is made from the leaves and flowers of the plant.

## What Do People Say Holy Basil Can Do?

Some people believe holy basil helps the body handle stress. This is called being an "adaptogen."  
They say it may help with:

- Feeling less anxious or stressed
- Lowering blood sugar in people with diabetes
- Reducing cholesterol levels
- Fighting off bacteria and viruses
- Healing wounds faster
- Reducing swelling and pain

## What Does Science Say?

There is not enough strong evidence to prove that holy basil helps with any of these health problems.

Most studies on holy basil are small or poorly designed.  
Some animal studies show possible benefits, but these results have not been tested in people.

For example, animal studies suggest holy basil seed oil might:

- Help prevent stomach ulcers and heart problems caused by stress
- Slow the growth of cancer cells and help animals with cancer live longer
- Reduce anxiety
- Help prevent tooth plaque and gum disease when used in mouthwash

But these results do not prove the same effects happen in humans.

Some small studies in people suggest holy basil might:

- Help reduce anxiety and the sadness that comes with it
- Lower blood sugar levels
- Ease stress symptoms like trouble sleeping, feeling tired, or forgetting things
- Improve breathing and reduce asthma attacks
- Boost the body’s ability to fight viral infections
- Reduce swelling and joint pain

These findings are promising, but more large, well-designed studies are needed.

## Side Effects

- Holy basil is likely safe for most people when taken by mouth for up to 8 weeks.
- Some people may get nausea or diarrhea.
- It is not known if it is safe to take for longer than 8 weeks.
- It may not be safe for women who are pregnant or trying to get pregnant.  
  In animal studies, large doses of holy basil made it harder for a pregnancy to start or last.
  It is not known if this happens in people.
- It is not known if holy basil is safe for women who are breastfeeding.
- Holy basil may lower thyroid hormone levels. This could make hypothyroidism worse.
- It may increase the risk of bleeding during and after surgery.  
  This is because it may slow down blood clotting.

## Drug Interactions

Holy basil may slow blood clotting.  
If you take it with medicines that also slow clotting, you may bruise or bleed more easily.  
These medicines include:

- Aspirin
- Clopidogrel
- Dalteparin
- Heparin
- Warfarin

In animal studies, holy basil may make certain sedatives stronger.  
This could make you drowsy or sleepy.

Holy basil may lower blood sugar.  
If you take it with diabetes medicines like insulin or sulfonylureas (such as glimepiride), you may get too low blood sugar.  
This is called hypoglycemia.

## Recommendations

- Holy basil is not recommended.  
  There is not enough strong proof that it helps with any health condition.
- It is probably safe for most people, but take care if you:
  - Are pregnant or trying to become pregnant
  - Are breastfeeding
  - Have type 2 diabetes
  - Have hypothyroidism
  - Are having surgery

- If you take medicines that slow blood clotting or lower blood sugar, talk to your doctor before using holy basil.

# Desquamative Interstitial Pneumonia (DIP)

Desquamative interstitial pneumonia is a long-term lung problem. It causes inflammation in the lungs. This condition mostly affects people who currently smoke or used to smoke.

It is a type of lung disease with no known cause. Most adults with this condition are smokers. They usually develop symptoms in their 30s or 40s.

The disease affects the lung tissue evenly. The tiny air sacs in the lungs are filled with certain immune cells. The walls of the air sacs are lined with large, round cells. There is a moderate buildup of immune cells in the walls between the air sacs. These include lymphocytes, plasma cells, and sometimes eosinophils. If there is scarring, it is mild.

The most noticeable sign is many dark-colored immune cells in the small air sacs. When doctors first saw this, they thought these cells were dead lung cells. But they are actually immune cells. Scarring that looks like a honeycomb is rare.

Similar but milder changes are seen in another lung condition linked to smoking. This condition is called respiratory bronchiolitis–associated interstitial lung disease. Because of these similarities, doctors think DIP and this other condition may be different forms of the same disease caused by smoking.

## Symptoms

People with DIP slowly get worse over time.  
They feel short of breath during normal activities.  
They have a dry cough that does not bring up mucus.

## How Doctors Diagnose DIP

### High-Resolution CT Scan (HRCT)
This scan gives detailed pictures of the lungs.  
It often shows cloudy areas in the lower parts of the lungs.  
These cloudy areas are called ground-glass opacities.  
They can be in many places or spread throughout the lungs.  
Small air-filled spaces (cysts) may appear, especially in cloudy areas.  
Irregular lines and web-like patterns are common.  
But they are not the main feature.  
Honeycombing may be seen in some patients.  
It is rare and usually limited to small areas.

### Chest X-ray
This test may show blurry patches in the lower lungs.  
It does not show honeycombing.  
In up to 1 in 5 patients, the chest x-ray can look normal.

### Surgical Lung Biopsy
Sometimes doctors need to take a small sample of lung tissue.  
This helps confirm the diagnosis when other tests are unclear.

## Treatment

### Stop Smoking
Stopping smoking is the most important step.  
About 3 out of 4 patients improve after quitting.  
This is the best way to help the lungs heal.

### Medicines
If symptoms do not improve after quitting, doctors may try steroid medicines.  
They may also use other medicines that affect the immune system.  
But there is not much strong evidence to guide these choices.

## Outlook

The long-term outlook is good.  
About 7 out of 10 people are still alive 10 years after diagnosis.

# Liver Tumors: Simple Explanation

Liver tumors can be noncancerous or cancerous.

## Cancerous Liver Tumors

Cancerous tumors in the liver are of two types:

- **Primary tumors**: These start in the liver.
- **Metastatic tumors**: These spread to the liver from another part of the body.

## The Liver

[Video about the liver]

## Noncancerous Liver Tumors

Noncancerous liver tumors are common. Most do not cause any symptoms.

In rare cases, they can cause:
- Pain in the upper right side of the belly.
- The liver to get bigger.
- Bleeding into the belly.

Types of noncancerous liver tumors include:
- Hemangiomas (benign blood vessel growths)
- Hepatic cysts (fluid-filled sacs)
- Hepatic granulomas (small areas of inflammation)
- Most hepatocellular adenomas (noncancerous liver cell growths)

Most of these tumors are found by chance during imaging tests done for other reasons. These tests include:
- Ultrasound
- CT scan
- MRI

The liver usually works normally even with a noncancerous tumor. Blood tests to check liver health are often normal.

Treatment is not always needed. Your doctor will decide based on your situation.

### Did You Know...

Most noncancerous liver tumors are found by accident. This happens when a scan is done for another health issue.

[Lab test: Liver Function Tests]

## Liver Cysts

Cysts are fluid-filled sacs that can form in the liver.

Most liver cysts do not cause any problems. They are found by chance during imaging tests.

Sometimes, very large cysts can press on nearby organs. This can cause pain.

If a cyst causes pain or other issues, your doctor may drain the fluid. This can be done through the skin with a needle. Sometimes, a small cut is needed.

Cysts often come back after drainage. If they keep coming back and affect your daily life, your doctor may suggest a liver transplant. But this is very rare.

Some people are born with many liver cysts. This is called polycystic liver disease. These people often have cysts in other organs too, especially the kidneys. This is called polycystic kidney disease.

The liver may get bigger, but it usually still works well.

# Testicular Cancer – Simple Explanation

Testicular cancer starts as a lump in the scrotum. This lump is usually not painful. It can be found by a man during a self-check. Most men find it themselves after noticing a change.

## How Common Is It?

In the United States, about 9,760 new cases are found each year. About 500 men die from it each year.  
Testicular cancer is the most common solid cancer in men between the ages of 15 and 35.  
It is much more common in men who were born with one or both testicles not in the scrotum (a condition called cryptorchidism).  
If surgery is done before age 10 to move the testicle into the scrotum, the risk goes down.  
Cancer can also develop in the other testicle, even if it is in the right place.  
The exact cause of testicular cancer is not known.

## What Causes It?

Most testicular cancers start in cells that are meant to become sperm.  
There are two main types:  
- Seminomas – make up about 40% of cases  
- Nonseminomas – make up about 60% of cases  

Nonseminomas include several types:  
- Teratomas  
- Embryonal carcinomas  
- Endodermal sinus tumors (also called yolk sac tumors)  
- Choriocarcinomas  

Some tumors have more than one type. For example, a teratocarcinoma has both teratoma and embryonal carcinoma.  
Cancer in the hormone-making cells of the testicle is very rare.

## Can It Spread?

Even if the cancer seems to be only in the testicle, it may have already spread to lymph nodes or other organs.  
For nonseminomas, almost 30% of men will have the cancer come back after surgery if they get no further treatment.  
Choriocarcinoma is the type most likely to spread. Teratoma is the least likely.

## Other Scrotal Lumps

Lumps in the epididymis, spermatic cord, or testicular attachments are usually not cancer.  
They are often benign (not cancer) growths like fibromas, fibroadenomas, adenomatoid tumors, or lipomas.  
Sarcomas (a rare type of cancer) can happen, but mostly in children.

---

## Symptoms and Signs

Most men notice a lump in the scrotum.  
The lump is usually painless. Some men feel a dull ache.  
In rare cases, bleeding inside the tumor causes sudden pain and tenderness.  
Some men find the lump after minor injury to the scrotum.  
If the cancer has spread widely, symptoms may include:  
- Belly pain  
- Lower back pain  
- Headaches or confusion  
- Trouble breathing  
- Chest pain  

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

### Step 1: Ultrasound
An ultrasound of the scrotum helps find the source of the lump.  
It can show if the lump is in the testicle or outside it.

### Step 2: Check for Cancer
If the lump is in the testicle, the next step is to do a chest x-ray and blood tests.  
Blood tests check for three markers:  
- AFP (alpha-fetoprotein)  
- Beta-HCG (human chorionic gonadotropin)  
- LDH (lactate dehydrogenase)  

These markers can help tell if the lump is cancer or not. But they are not 100% certain.

### Step 3: Surgery
If cancer is likely, the testicle and its cord are removed through a cut in the groin. This is called a radical inguinal orchiectomy.  
The cord is clamped before the testicle is touched. This helps stop cancer from spreading.

### Step 4: Staging
After surgery, more tests are done to see if the cancer has spread.  
These include CT scans of the belly, pelvis, and chest.  
The cancer is then staged using the TNM system:  
- T = size and spread of the main tumor  
- N = whether cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes  
- M = whether cancer has spread to distant organs  

Blood marker levels are also used in staging.  
The levels are labeled S0, S1, S2, or S3.  
S0 means normal levels.  
S3 means very high levels.

---

## Treatment

The main treatment is surgery to remove the testicle.  
This surgery gives important information about the cancer.  
It helps doctors plan the next steps.

After surgery, treatment depends on the type and stage of cancer.

### For Seminomas:
- Some men need radiation therapy to the lymph nodes in the belly.  
- Others may need chemotherapy.  
- Some men are watched closely with no further treatment (active surveillance).

### For Nonseminomas:
- Chemotherapy is often used.  
- Surgery may be done to remove lymph nodes in the belly (retroperitoneal lymph node dissection).  
- Some men are watched closely with no further treatment.

### Other Options:
- A man can get a fake testicle (prosthesis) during surgery.  
- Saline-filled prostheses are available. Silicone ones are not common due to safety concerns.  
- Men who want to have children in the future can save sperm before treatment.

---

## Prognosis (Outlook)

Testicular cancer has a very good chance of being cured.  
The 5-year survival rate is over 95% for men with cancer that is only in the testicle.  
It is also high for men with small spread to the lymph nodes in the belly.  
For men with cancer that has spread to the lungs or other organs, survival rates vary.  
But even men with advanced cancer can be cured.

---

## Key Points

- Testicular cancer is the most common solid cancer in men aged 15 to 35.  
- It is often curable, especially seminoma.  
- If you find a lump in your scrotum, see a doctor right away.  
- Ultrasound can confirm if the lump is in the testicle.  
- If it is, do a chest x-ray and blood tests for AFP, beta-HCG, and LDH.  
- The main treatment is surgery to remove the testicle.  
- After surgery, treatment may include chemotherapy, radiation, surgery to remove lymph nodes, or close monitoring.

# Substance Use Disorders

A substance use disorder means a person keeps using a drug even when it causes problems in their life.

This can happen with many types of drugs. The most common ones fall into ten main groups.

## The Ten Drug Groups Linked to Substance Use Problems

- Alcohol  
- Medicines that calm the mind or help you sleep (like benzodiazepines)  
- Caffeine (found in coffee, tea, and soda)  
- Cannabis (including marijuana and synthetic forms)  
- Hallucinogens (like LSD, PCP, magic mushrooms, and MDMA)  
- Inhalants (such as glue, paint thinner, and aerosol sprays)  
- Opioids (like fentanyl, morphine, and oxycodone)  
- Stimulants (like amphetamines and cocaine)  
- Tobacco (including cigarettes and vaping products)  
- Other substances (like anabolic steroids and other commonly misused drugs)

Each drug has its own effects. The way someone feels when they use it, and what happens when they stop, depends on the drug.

The word "substance use disorder" is better than older terms like "addiction," "abuse," or "dependence." It is clearer and less judgmental.

Using illegal drugs is against the law. But that does not always mean someone has a substance use disorder.

Even legal drugs can cause problems. Alcohol, prescription medicines, and marijuana (in many places) can all lead to a substance use disorder.

Problems from drug use affect people from all walks of life. They do not depend on income, education, or job.

People have used drugs for fun, for religion, to feel more spiritual, or to perform better at work or sports.

Some people use drugs only now and then. They take small amounts. They do not get sick or feel bad when they stop. They do not need more over time.

These drugs are often called recreational. They include opium, alcohol, nicotine, marijuana, caffeine, hallucinogenic mushrooms, and cocaine.

Many of these drugs come from plants. They are not highly concentrated. They contain mild mind-altering chemicals.

People can take these drugs by mouth, by breathing them in, or by injecting them.

## How Drugs Affect the Body and Mind

All these drugs affect the brain’s reward system. They make people feel good. This feeling can be so strong that people crave the drug.

They may stop doing normal things to get and use the drug.

Drugs also cause physical changes. These include:

- Intoxication  
- Withdrawal  
- Mental health problems caused by the drug

### Intoxication

Intoxication is the immediate effect of using a drug.

It changes how a person thinks, feels, and acts.

It can make someone feel very happy, excited, or calm. It can also make them sleepy.

Many drugs hurt physical coordination. This can lead to falls or car crashes.

Some drugs make people more aggressive. This can lead to fights.

Using too much of a drug (an overdose) can be dangerous. It can cause serious harm or even death.

**Tolerance** means you need more of the drug to feel the same effect.

People can build up a high tolerance to opioids and alcohol.

### Withdrawal

Withdrawal happens when someone stops using a drug or cuts back a lot.

It causes uncomfortable symptoms. The symptoms depend on the drug.

Some withdrawals, like from alcohol or barbiturates, can be life-threatening.

Most people know that using more of the drug will make the withdrawal symptoms go away.

Withdrawal happens based on the drug and how long it was used. It does not matter if the person has a substance use disorder, uses the drug recreationally, or if it is illegal.

Even when taken as prescribed for a short time, some drugs like opioids, sedatives, and stimulants can cause withdrawal.

People who have withdrawal symptoms were once called "physically dependent." But this word sounds bad. Doctors now avoid it.

## What Causes Substance Use Disorders?

Most people start by trying a drug once. Then they use it sometimes. Later, they may use it more often. Some go on to develop a substance use disorder.

This path is complex. It depends on the drug, the person, and the situation.

Some drugs are more likely than others to cause problems. This depends on:

- How the drug is used  
- How strongly it affects the brain’s reward system  
- How fast it works  
- How quickly it causes tolerance or withdrawal

Drugs that are easy to get, like alcohol and tobacco, are often used first.

As people keep using a drug, they may start to see less danger in it. They may use more or try other drugs.

People’s views on risk can change based on what others do and what the law says.

After surgery or illness, doctors often prescribe opioids for pain.

If people do not use all the medicine, the leftover pills may end up in the hands of others who want to use them.

Because this is a growing problem, many doctors now:

- Use non-addictive pain medicines (like acetaminophen or ibuprofen) when possible  
- Prescribe smaller amounts of opioids  
- Tell patients how to store or safely throw away leftover pills  
- Support programs that let people return unused medicine

Some people are more likely to develop a substance use disorder because of their personal traits.

### Personal Traits

Some people have less self-control. They may take more risks or seek new experiences.

These traits may raise the risk of a substance use disorder.

But there is no strong proof of an "addictive personality." That idea is not well supported by science.

### Life Circumstances and Other Health Problems

Certain situations and health issues raise the risk.

- People who feel sad, lonely, or disconnected from others may use drugs to feel better. This can lead to more use and eventually a disorder.  
- People with other mental health problems—like anxiety, depression, schizophrenia, ADHD, or personality disorders—are more likely to develop a substance use disorder.  
- People with long-term pain often need opioids. Some of them later develop a substance use disorder.  
- But for many, non-opioid medicines and other treatments do not help enough.

Substance use disorders come from many causes. Some are genetic. Others come from life experiences that affect how genes work.

Research has not found clear differences in brain chemistry between people who do and do not develop a substance use disorder.

Culture and social life play a big role.

- Seeing parents or older siblings use drugs increases the chance a person will start.  
- Friends have a strong influence, especially on teens.  
- People trying to quit find it harder if they are around others who still use drugs.

Doctors can make things worse by giving out too many mind-altering drugs to relieve stress.

Media and society often push the idea that drugs should fix all problems.

## How Doctors Diagnose Substance Use Disorders

Doctors use several tools to find out if someone has a substance use disorder.

- A personal conversation with the doctor  
- Blood, urine, or hair tests (in some cases)

Some people come in asking for help to stop using a drug.

Others hide their use. They may not know it is a problem.

Family, friends, or coworkers may notice changes in mood or behavior.

Doctors may find signs during a check-up. For example:

- Needle marks on the skin (tiny dark dots from repeated injections)  
- Scars or sores from injecting drugs  
- Liver damage from heavy drinking

Some people get very sick from using too much of a drug. They may need emergency care.

Doctors also use questionnaires to check for substance use problems.

Tests on urine, blood, or hair can show if someone has used drugs.

## How Substance Use Disorders Are Treated

Treatment depends on the drug and the person’s situation.

Most treatments include:

- Counseling  
- Sometimes medicine to help with cravings or withdrawal  
- Support from family and friends  
- Support groups

Substance use disorders are common. They are causing more deaths.

To help, many groups now run harm-reduction programs.

These programs offer:

- Education  
- Counseling  
- Help finding treatment  
- National phone lines

Sharing needles spreads diseases like HIV and hepatitis.

To stop this, some programs give out clean needles and syringes.

This helps prevent infections. It also saves money for society.

## Screening for Substance Use Disorders

Doctors should check for substance use during regular health visits.

This should not wait until a doctor suspects a problem.

Screening helps catch issues early. It allows help before problems get worse.

It also avoids making people feel ashamed or afraid to speak up.

During a good screening, the doctor asks about:

- Alcohol use  
- Tobacco or nicotine use  
- Cannabis use  
- Prescription medicine use  
- Illegal drug use

The doctor may use a formal test. Or they may just ask one simple question:

“How many times in the past year have you used an illegal drug or used a prescription medicine in a way it was not meant to be used?”

If the answers raise concern, the doctor checks:

- How serious the use is  
- How much it affects daily life  
- If there are other mental health issues

Then, the doctor may refer the person to a specialist.

## How to Prevent Substance Use Disorders

Some substance use disorders can be prevented.

Early action helps. Doctors can help by:

- Screening for risk factors  
- Using age-appropriate prevention strategies

This is especially important during teenage years. That is when most people start using drugs. The brain is also more sensitive to addiction at this age.

Doctors check for:

- Family history of substance use  
- Past trauma  
- Other mental health issues  
- Early behavior problems

Then they may offer:

- Education about risks  
- Skills to manage emotions and behavior  
- Family support programs

Patients and families should learn about overdose risks—especially when opioids are prescribed.

# Congenital Muscular Anomalies

Some muscles or groups of muscles may not form properly at birth.  
Some muscles may be missing completely.  
Some muscles may be underdeveloped.

These problems can happen on their own.  
They can also be part of a larger condition that affects many parts of the body.

## Poland Syndrome

One common issue is when the large chest muscle on one side of the body is missing or underdeveloped.  
This often happens on the right side.  
It can also affect the hand on the same side.  
The breast and nipple on that side may be small or missing.  
This condition is called Poland syndrome.

Poland syndrome can sometimes happen with another condition called Möbius syndrome.  
Möbius syndrome causes weakness or paralysis in the nerves that control facial movement and eye movement.  
It can also affect the nerves that control the tongue and throat.  
Some children with Möbius syndrome may also have autism spectrum disorder.

## Prune-Belly Syndrome

In prune-belly syndrome, the muscles in the belly wall are missing or underdeveloped.  
More than one layer of these muscles may be affected.  
This condition often comes with serious problems in the kidneys and bladder.  
The kidneys may become swollen due to blocked urine flow.  
This is called hydronephrosis.

This condition is more common in boys.  
Boys with this condition often have undescended testicles on both sides.  
Other problems can include foot deformities and issues with the rectum.  
The outlook is not always good, even if doctors treat the urine blockage early.

## Testing and Diagnosis

Doctors may use special tests to look for genetic causes.  
These include chromosomal microarray analysis.  
They may also test for specific genes or use broader gene panels.  
If these tests do not give a clear answer, doctors may suggest whole exome sequencing.

## Treatment

Treatment depends on how severe the muscle problem is.  
Some people need little or no treatment.  
Others may need surgery to rebuild or repair the affected muscles.

# Relaxation Techniques

Relaxation techniques are ways to calm your mind and body. They are part of a group of practices called mind-body medicine.

These techniques help your body relax. They can:

- Slow down your body’s stress response
- Lower your blood pressure
- Ease tight muscles
- Slow down your body’s energy use
- Change the patterns of activity in your brain

Relaxation therapy can help reduce anxiety. It may also help with certain types of pain. Some research shows it can help with depression too.

Many studies on relaxation therapy are small. They also do not always follow strong research methods.

You can use relaxation techniques along with other practices. These include:

- Meditation
- Guided imagery
- Hypnotherapy

# Gastrointestinal Neuroendocrine Tumors and Carcinoid Syndrome

Carcinoid syndrome is a group of symptoms that can happen in some people with certain types of tumors.  
These tumors are called neuroendocrine tumors.  
They are usually found in the intestines and have spread to other parts of the body.  
The main symptoms are flushing of the skin, stomach cramps, and diarrhea.  
Over time, some people may develop heart problems on the right side of the heart.  

The symptoms happen because the tumor releases certain chemicals into the blood.  
These chemicals include serotonin, histamine, bradykinin, prostaglandins, and other hormones.  
The body breaks down serotonin into a substance called 5-HIAA.  
This substance can be measured in the urine to help diagnose the condition.  

Treatment focuses on controlling symptoms.  
Medicines like octreotide and lanreotide can help reduce flushing and diarrhea.  
Surgery may help if the tumor is found early and has not spread.  
If the tumor has spread to the liver, removing as much of it as possible may help ease symptoms.  
Chemotherapy may be used in some cases, but it is not always effective.  

---

## What Causes Carcinoid Syndrome?

Some tumors in the body make hormones and other chemicals.  
These are called neuroendocrine tumors.  
Most cases of carcinoid syndrome come from tumors in the small intestine.  
These tumors make a chemical called serotonin.  

The syndrome usually only appears when the tumor has spread to the liver.  
This is because the liver normally breaks down serotonin before it reaches the rest of the body.  
When the tumor spreads to the liver, the chemicals escape into the bloodstream.  
This causes the symptoms.  

Carcinoid syndrome can also happen if the tumor is in the appendix, rectum, pancreas, lungs, or ovaries.  
Rarely, other types of cancer, like lung cancer or thyroid cancer, can cause the same symptoms.  

---

## How Does Carcinoid Syndrome Work?

Serotonin causes diarrhea, stomach cramps, and poor absorption of food.  
Histamine and bradykinin cause flushing of the skin.  
These chemicals affect blood vessels and make them widen.  

Other chemicals made by the tumor may also play a role.  
But we do not yet fully understand how they work.  
Some people with the syndrome also have high levels of certain hormones.  

Over time, some people develop thickened heart valves on the right side of the heart.  
This can lead to heart problems like shortness of breath or swelling.  
Left-sided heart problems are rare because the lungs destroy serotonin before it reaches that side.  

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The most common early sign is flushing.  
This is a sudden redness and warmth in the face and neck.  
It can be triggered by stress, hot drinks, food, or alcohol.  
The skin may turn pale, red, or even purple.  

Stomach cramps and frequent diarrhea are common.  
These can be the main problem for many people.  
Some may also have trouble absorbing nutrients from food.  

Heart problems may cause a heart murmur.  
Some people have wheezing or breathing issues.  
Others may have low sex drive or trouble getting an erection.  
Very rarely, a condition called pellagra can occur.  
This is due to a lack of vitamin B3, which happens when the body uses too much tryptophan to make serotonin.  

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect carcinoid syndrome based on symptoms.  
They confirm it with two main tests.  

The first test checks for 5-HIAA in the urine.  
This is a breakdown product of serotonin.  
You must avoid certain foods for three days before the test.  
These include bananas, tomatoes, plums, avocados, pineapples, eggplant, and walnuts.  
Some medicines also interfere with the test.  
These include guaifenesin, methocarbamol, and phenothiazines.  
You must stop taking them before the test.  

On the third day, you collect all your urine for 24 hours.  
A normal result is less than 10 milligrams per day.  
People with carcinoid syndrome usually have more than 50 milligrams per day.  

The second test checks for chromogranin A in the blood.  
This is a protein that is often high in people with neuroendocrine tumors.  
Using both tests together gives a more accurate result.  

In the past, doctors used special tests to trigger flushing.  
These included calcium, alcohol, or other substances.  
They are rarely used now because they can cause serious side effects.  

---

## How Is It Treated?

The first treatment is usually a medicine called octreotide or lanreotide.  
These are called somatostatin analogs.  
They help reduce flushing and diarrhea.  
They work by blocking the release of many hormones from the tumor.  
They do not always lower 5-HIAA levels, but they still help with symptoms.  

Long-acting versions of these medicines are very effective.  
They are the main treatment for most people.  

If diarrhea continues despite these medicines, a drug called telotristat etiprate may help.  
It works by reducing the amount of serotonin made in the body.  

Surgery can cure the condition if the tumor has not spread.  
If the tumor has spread to the liver, removing as much of it as possible may help.  
This is called debulking.  
It can ease symptoms and may help you live longer.  

Other treatments for liver tumors include:  
- Transarterial chemoembolization (TACE)  
- Bland embolization  
- Radioembolization with yttrium-90 microspheres  
- Radiofrequency ablation  

New treatments are also being used.  
These include everolimus, which slows tumor growth.  
Another is peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) with a substance called 177-lutetium.  
This treatment targets the tumor directly.  

Radiation therapy does not work well.  
The liver does not tolerate radiation well.  

Chemotherapy is not very effective.  
A combination of three drugs—streptozotocin, 5-fluorouracil, and cyclophosphamide—may be used in some cases.  
But it is only for people with more aggressive tumors.  
Even then, the benefits last only a short time.  

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Neuroendocrine tumors grow slowly.  
Even if they have spread, many people live 10 to 15 years or more.  
The outlook depends on where the tumor started, how fast it grows, and how far it has spread.  

---

## Key Points

- Only some neuroendocrine tumors cause carcinoid syndrome.  
- The main chemicals involved are serotonin and histamine.  
- Serotonin causes diarrhea and stomach cramps.  
- Histamine causes flushing.  
- Diagnosis is done by testing urine for 5-HIAA and blood for chromogranin A.  
- Medicines like octreotide and lanreotide help control symptoms.  
- Surgery can cure the condition if the tumor has not spread.  
- For liver spread, removing part of the tumor may help ease symptoms and extend life.  
- Treatments like ablation, embolization, and radioembolization can also help.  
- Standard chemotherapy and radiation do not work well.  
- New treatments like everolimus and PRRT with 177-lutetium may be helpful.

# Macrophage Activation Syndrome

Macrophage activation syndrome is a serious and dangerous condition. It happens when the body’s immune system goes into overdrive. This can lead to life-threatening problems.

It often occurs in people with certain long-term autoimmune diseases. These include:
- Juvenile idiopathic arthritis, especially the systemic type
- Systemic lupus erythematosus
- Adult-onset Still disease

It affects about 1 in 10 children with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

---

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

You may see these signs if someone has macrophage activation syndrome:

- A very high fever that does not go down
- Swollen liver and spleen
- Swollen lymph nodes all over the body
- A rash that does not go away
- Bleeding problems, such as easy bruising or nosebleeds
- Brain problems, like seizures or loss of consciousness
- Low blood pressure and shock

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look for this condition when a person with a long-term autoimmune disease suddenly gets very sick.

Diagnosis is based on:
- The person’s medical history
- A physical exam
- Blood tests

Doctors must suspect this condition early. It can be hard to tell apart from a flare-up of the original disease.

Some signs help doctors tell the difference:
- Fever that never stops (in contrast to the fever pattern in juvenile idiopathic arthritis)
- A rash that stays for days (not just a short-lived rash)
- Bleeding problems
- Seizures or coma
- Shock

Even though the body is very inflamed, the blood test for inflammation (ESR) may be low. This is because the body has low levels of a protein called fibrinogen.

To help confirm the diagnosis in children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis, doctors use these blood test rules:
- Ferritin level above 684 nanograms per milliliter (or 684 micrograms per liter)
- Plus at least two of the following:
  - Platelets below 181,000 per microliter
  - Liver enzyme (AST) above 48 units per liter
  - Triglycerides above 156 milligrams per deciliter
  - Fibrinogen below 360 milligrams per deciliter

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause and how sick the person is.

The main treatment is high-dose corticosteroids. These are strong anti-inflammatory medicines.

Other medicines may also be used, including:
- Cyclosporine
- Medicines that block IL-1 (a type of immune signal)
- Janus kinase inhibitors
- Emapalumab (a medicine that targets immune cells)

Doctors often treat the underlying disease at the same time. If that works well, the macrophage activation syndrome may improve.

There is no single agreed-upon treatment plan. Doctors decide based on the patient’s condition.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Macrophage activation syndrome can be deadly. It can cause multiple organs to fail.

The condition is serious and needs fast treatment. Early diagnosis and care improve the chances of survival.

# Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10)

Coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, is a substance your body makes naturally.  
It helps your cells make energy.  
It also acts as an antioxidant, which means it helps protect your cells from damage.

CoQ10 levels tend to drop as people get older.  
They may also be lower in people with long-term health problems.  
These include heart disease, cancer, Parkinson disease, diabetes, HIV, and muscle diseases.

We do not know if low CoQ10 levels cause these health problems.  
But eating meat, fish, and vegetable oils gives you more CoQ10.

---

## What People Say About CoQ10

Some people believe CoQ10 helps with many health issues.  
They say it works because it fights cell damage and helps your body make energy.

Specific claims include:
- Helping the immune system fight cancer.
- Reducing the need for insulin in people with diabetes.
- Slowing the worsening of Parkinson disease.
- Helping treat heart failure.
- Protecting the heart from damage caused by some cancer drugs.

One of the biggest claims is that CoQ10 improves blood vessel health.  
This may help prevent heart disease.

Some early studies show possible benefits.  
But the results are not clear.  
More research is needed to know if CoQ10 really helps.

---

## What the Research Shows

A 2012 review of five small studies found that CoQ10 improved blood vessel function.  
This was measured by how well blood vessels opened and closed.

A 2013 review of small studies found that CoQ10 may help people with heart failure feel better.  
But the studies were too small and short to be certain.

A 2014 study of 420 people with heart failure found that CoQ10 was safe.  
It helped reduce symptoms.  
It also lowered the risk of serious heart problems when used with standard heart treatments.

A 2021 review of 11 studies found moderate evidence that CoQ10 may reduce deaths and hospital stays for heart failure.  
But the evidence was not strong enough to say for sure that CoQ10 helps.

A 2017 review of 14 studies found that people taking CoQ10 had better exercise ability and lower death rates than those on placebo.  
Another study of 216 people with heart failure found that a form of CoQ10 called ubiquinol helped improve energy levels, heart function, and symptoms.  
It also lowered a blood marker linked to heart failure.

There is also debate about whether CoQ10 helps with muscle pain from statin drugs.  
Some studies show it helps.  
Others do not.  
A 2018 review found that people on CoQ10 had less pain, weakness, cramps, and tiredness than those on placebo.  
But the studies were different in design, so results are not fully reliable.

---

## Side Effects of CoQ10

CoQ10 is generally safe.  
But some people report side effects.  
These include:
- Loss of appetite
- Upset stomach
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Dizziness
- Sensitivity to light
- Irritability
- Headaches
- Itching
- Skin rash
- Tiredness
- Flu-like symptoms

These side effects are rare and usually mild.

---

## Drug Interactions

CoQ10 may affect how some medicines work.

It may reduce the effect of warfarin, a blood thinner.  
This could increase the risk of blood clots.

CoQ10 may also interact with some blood pressure medicines and certain cancer treatments.

Always talk to your doctor before taking CoQ10 if you are on any medicine.
