# How Doctors Identify Infections Without Using Genetic Tests

When a germ is found in a lab culture, doctors need to figure out exactly what kind of germ it is. Knowing the germ helps decide the right treatment and whether the patient needs special isolation.

This type of testing does not look at the germ’s genes. Instead, it checks the germ’s physical traits and how it acts. These include how the germ grows, what it looks like, and what chemicals it can use.

### What Doctors Look For

- The size, color, and shape of the germ’s growth on culture plates.
- The results of a Gram stain test. This test shows if the germ is one of two main types based on its cell wall.

These clues help doctors pick the next steps in testing.

### How Testing Works

Doctors use many different tests. Each test checks a specific trait of the germ. For example:

- Can the germ use certain food sources to grow?
- Does it make certain enzymes, like catalase or coagulase?

Tests are done one after another. The result of each test tells the doctor which test to do next. The order of tests can vary from one lab to another.

### Types of Tests Used

These are the main ways doctors identify germs without using genetic tests:

- **Manual methods**: Lab staff do the tests by hand.
- **Automated systems**: Machines run the tests and give results.
- **Serologic assays**: These tests look for specific proteins in the germ.
- **Chromatographic methods**: These separate chemicals in the germ to identify it.
- **Mass spectrometry**: This measures the weight of proteins in the germ to find its type.

### Ready-Made Test Kits

Some test kits come with many tests in one package. They can be used at the same time with just one sample. These kits can work for a wide range of germs.

- They are very accurate.
- But they can take several days to give a final answer.

# Ginkgo

Ginkgo is a supplement made from the leaves of the ginkgo tree.  
This tree is often planted in the United States for its appearance.  
It is the only surviving member of its plant family.  

The active parts of ginkgo come from chemicals in the leaves.  
These chemicals are called terpene ginkgolides and flavonoids.  

The fruit of the ginkgo tree smells very bad.  
It is not used in ginkgo supplements.  
Touching the fruit’s soft part can cause serious skin irritation.  
Raw ginkgo seeds are dangerous.  
They can cause seizures and, in large amounts, can be deadly.  
Cooked ginkgo seeds are eaten in some Asian countries.  
You can find them in Asian grocery stores in the United States.  
But cooked seeds do not have the same chemicals as the leaves.  
So they do not help with health conditions like memory or circulation.

---

## What Ginkgo Is Used For

Some people use ginkgo to help with leg pain when walking.  
This pain happens when blood flow to the legs is poor.  
Ginkgo may help people walk a little farther without pain.  
But exercise and a medicine called cilostazol may work better.  

Ginkgo has been used for many years to help people with memory problems.  
It is also used for memory loss, anxiety, ringing in the ears, age-related eye damage, and altitude sickness.  
It may help protect the kidneys from damage caused by a medicine called cyclosporine.  
It is also used to help with sudden altitude sickness.  
Some people use it along with other medicines to help control type 2 diabetes.

---

## What the Research Shows

Ginkgo may help blood vessels work better.  
A major review from 2013 looked at 14 studies with 739 people.  
It found that ginkgo helped people walk a little longer without pain.  
But the benefit was small.  

Early studies said ginkgo could slow down mental decline in people with mild to moderate memory problems.  
But later, larger studies found no clear benefit.  
Ginkgo did not slow down dementia or Alzheimer’s disease in older adults.  

One review of 12 smaller studies found that high doses of ginkgo (over 200 mg per day) for at least 5 months may help with thinking, daily tasks, and how people feel overall.  
But the evidence was weak.  

Another review looked at 18 studies with 1,642 people with Alzheimer’s disease.  
It found that combining ginkgo with a medicine called donepezil may improve some thinking skills and daily living.  
But more research is needed.

Some early studies said ginkgo might help with ringing in the ears.  
But a review of 4 studies with 1,543 people found no real benefit.  

A review of ginkgo for preventing altitude sickness showed a possible small benefit.  
But the data was not strong enough to prove it works.  

Newer studies suggest ginkgo may help people with type 2 diabetes.  
When taken with a common diabetes medicine called metformin, ginkgo lowered blood sugar and a long-term blood sugar measure.  

---

## Side Effects

Ginkgo can cause nausea, stomach upset, headaches, dizziness, or a fast heartbeat.  
Pregnant women should not use ginkgo.  
It may cause early labor or heavy bleeding during childbirth.  
Stop taking ginkgo at least two weeks before surgery.  
It may increase the risk of bleeding during or after surgery.  

Some low-quality ginkgo products may be mixed with other substances.  
These include rutin and quercetin.  
They are added to make the product look better, even if it is not real ginkgo.

---

## Interactions with Medicines

Ginkgo can interact with certain medicines.  
It may increase the risk of bleeding when taken with aspirin, other pain medicines like ibuprofen, or blood thinners like warfarin.  
It may also reduce how well seizure medicines work.  
Ginkgo may cause a serious condition called serotonin syndrome if taken with certain antidepressants.  
This is especially true if the antidepressant is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor.  

Always talk to your doctor before using ginkgo if you take any medicines.

# Nonspecific Interstitial Pneumonia (NSIP)

Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia is a lung disease. It is not caused by a known factor. It mostly affects women between the ages of 40 and 50.

People with this condition often have a cough and trouble breathing. These symptoms can last for months or even years.

The disease is not as common as another lung condition called idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

Some people with NSIP also have other health problems. These include certain autoimmune diseases like systemic sclerosis or inflammatory myositis. It can also happen after taking certain medicines or from exposure to allergens in the air (hypersensitivity pneumonitis).

## Symptoms

You may have a cough that does not go away.  
You may feel short of breath, especially when walking or doing light activity.  
You may feel tired or have a low fever.  
These symptoms usually come on slowly and get worse over time.

## How Doctors Diagnose NSIP

Doctors look at your symptoms and test your lungs.  
They use a special type of CT scan called high-resolution CT.  
They also need a sample of lung tissue from a surgical lung biopsy.

A chest X-ray may show blurry areas in the lower parts of the lungs.  
The high-resolution CT scan shows patchy cloudy areas in both lungs.  
It may also show thickened lines and slightly widened airways.  
The condition usually affects the lower parts of the lungs.  
The area just under the lung lining may be spared.  
Honeycombing (a sign of advanced scarring) is rare.

A fluid sample from the lungs (bronchoalveolar lavage) may show more lymphocytes.  
But this finding is not unique to NSIP and can happen in other lung diseases.

A lung biopsy is needed to confirm the diagnosis.  
The biopsy shows inflammation and scarring in the lungs.  
The scarring is even in time — it is not patchy in a mixed way like in other lung diseases.  
But the changes can still be patchy, with some areas of normal lung in between.

## Treatment

Most people with NSIP improve with medicine.  
The main treatment is a steroid medicine called glucocorticoids.  
Some people also need other medicines that reduce immune system activity.  
These include azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, or cyclophosphamide.

Treatment helps many people feel better and live longer.

## Prognosis (Outlook)

The long-term outlook depends on how much scarring is seen in the lung tissue.  
If the biopsy shows mostly inflammation and little scarring, most people live at least 10 years.  
If the biopsy shows a lot of scarring, the outlook is worse.

## Key Points

- NSIP is rare.  
- Most people with NSIP are women aged 40 to 50.  
- There is no known cause in most cases.  
- Rule out other conditions first. These include autoimmune diseases like systemic sclerosis or myositis.  
- Also rule out lung damage from medicines or from breathing in allergens.  
- Treat with steroid medicine, and sometimes other immune-suppressing medicines.  
- The more scarring seen in the lung tissue, the worse the long-term outcome.

# Dermatitis Herpetiformis

Dermatitis herpetiformis is a skin condition that causes severe itching. It is a long-term condition. It happens because the body’s immune system attacks the skin. It is strongly linked to celiac disease.

The skin rash often appears in groups. It looks like small red bumps, blisters, or raised patches. The rash usually appears on the elbows, knees, back, buttocks, and back of the head. The rash is often the same on both sides of the body.

The rash is very itchy and can burn. The skin is fragile, so blisters often break quickly. This makes it hard to see intact blisters during a doctor’s exam.

Some people may have sores in the mouth. But these are usually not painful. Certain medicines that contain iodine can make the rash worse.

## Who Gets Dermatitis Herpetiformis?

This condition most often starts in adults between the ages of 30 and 40. But it can also happen in children and older adults. It is rare in Black and Asian people.

Almost everyone with dermatitis herpetiformis also has celiac disease. But many do not have stomach or bowel symptoms. About 1 in 6 to 1 in 4 people with celiac disease will develop this skin rash.

People with this condition may also be more likely to have other autoimmune diseases. These include thyroid problems, anemia from lack of vitamin B12, and type 1 diabetes. There is also a higher risk of a type of bowel cancer called small-bowel lymphoma.

A protein called IgA builds up in the skin. This causes inflammation and attracts white blood cells. A strict gluten-free diet can remove this buildup.

The name “herpetiformis” means the rash looks like clusters, similar to herpes. But it is not caused by the herpes virus.

## Symptoms and Signs

The rash can start suddenly or slowly. It usually appears on the outside of the elbows, knees, back, buttocks, and back of the head.

The rash is very itchy and can burn. Because the skin is so sensitive, blisters often break before you see them. This makes it hard to find intact blisters during a doctor’s visit.

Sores in the mouth can happen. But they usually do not cause pain.

Medicines that contain iodine can make the rash worse.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Diagnosis is based on two main tests:

- A skin biopsy: A small sample of skin is taken from a rash and from nearby normal skin.
- Direct immunofluorescence: This test checks for IgA protein deposits in the skin.

This test is very accurate. It finds the condition in 90 to 95 out of 100 people who have it. It is also very specific — it rarely gives a false positive.

All people with dermatitis herpetiformis should be tested for celiac disease. Blood tests can help confirm the diagnosis. These include:

- IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody
- IgA anti-epidermal transglutaminase antibody
- IgA anti-endomysial antibody

These tests also help track how the disease is doing over time.

## How Is It Treated?

### Dapsone

Dapsone is the most common medicine used. It works very well. Most people feel much better within 1 to 3 days.

- Adults start with 25 to 50 milligrams once a day.
- Children start with 0.5 milligrams per kilogram of body weight once a day.

If symptoms improve, the dose stays the same. If not, the dose can be increased every week, up to 400 milligrams a day for adults.

Most people need between 50 and 150 milligrams a day.

Dapsone can cause serious side effects. The most common is a type of anemia called hemolytic anemia. This risk is highest after one month of treatment. It is higher in people with a condition called glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency.

Before starting dapsone, people should be tested for this deficiency.

Other possible side effects include:
- Methemoglobinemia (a blood problem that reduces oxygen in the blood)
- Liver problems
- Low white blood cell count
- A rare condition called dapsone syndrome (liver problems and swollen lymph nodes)
- Nerve problems that affect movement

### Sulfapyridine

Sulfapyridine is an option for people who cannot take dapsone.

- Dose: 500 milligrams three times a day.
- It can be increased up to 2000 milligrams three times a day if needed.

Sulfapyridine can also cause low white blood cell count.

### Blood Tests

All patients on dapsone or sulfapyridine must have regular blood tests.

- A full blood count is done before starting treatment.
- Then weekly for the first 4 weeks.
- Then every 2 to 3 weeks for the next 8 weeks.
- After that, every 12 to 16 weeks.

### Gluten-Free Diet

Everyone with dermatitis herpetiformis must follow a strict gluten-free diet.

Gluten is a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye. It must be avoided completely.

After the rash is under control, most people can stop taking medicine. They can stay well with just the diet.

It may take months or years to stop medicine safely.

Following the diet strictly for 5 to 10 years lowers the risk of bowel cancer.

## Key Points

- Almost everyone with dermatitis herpetiformis has celiac disease, even if they have no stomach or bowel symptoms.
- They are at higher risk for a type of bowel cancer called small-bowel lymphoma.
- The rash is so itchy and the skin is so fragile that blisters often break before you see them.
- Diagnosis must be confirmed with a skin biopsy and special testing.
- Dapsone or sulfapyridine is used first to control the rash.
- Long-term control is best achieved with a strict gluten-free diet. This can allow stopping medicine over time.

# Do-Not-Resuscitate (DNR) Orders and Portable Medical Orders

## What is a DNR Order?

A DNR order tells doctors and nurses not to do CPR if your heart stops.  
CPR is a set of emergency actions to restart a stopped heart.  
This order helps avoid painful and often unsuccessful treatments at the end of life.

## When Is a DNR Order Used?

Doctors talk with patients about CPR when they are very ill.  
They explain what CPR involves and what the likely results are.  
They ask patients what kind of care they want.  
If a patient cannot speak for themselves, a family member or trusted person can decide.  
That person should follow the patient’s past wishes.  
If no wishes are known, the decision should be what is best for the patient.

## Why Are Living Wills Not Enough?

Living wills and health care powers of attorney are not always available in emergencies.  
They may not be found when needed.  
First responders must start life support unless they see a valid DNR order or a portable medical order.

## What Is a Portable Medical Order?

A portable medical order is a form that follows you across care settings.  
It shows your wishes for end-of-life care.  
It is used by people with serious, long-term illness.  
It helps make sure your care matches your goals.

## Common Names for These Programs

In the United States, these programs are called by different names.  
The most common name is **POLST** (Provider Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment).  
Other names include:  
- MOLST (Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)  
- POST (Physician Orders for Scope of Treatment)  
- MOST (Medical Orders for Scope of Treatment)  
- COLST (Clinical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)  
- TPOPP (Transportable Physician Orders for Patient Preferences)  

All of these programs work the same way.  
They use different forms and rules in each state.

## Who Qualifies for a Portable Medical Order?

You may qualify if your doctor thinks you could die within the next year or two.  
This does not mean you will die soon.  
It means your illness is serious and likely to get worse.

## How Does the Process Work?

Health care providers talk with you or your family about your health and your care goals.  
You discuss what kind of treatment you want.  
You may want full treatment to get better.  
Or you may want only comfort care to feel better and stay peaceful.  
You may want limited treatment in between.  
The form includes your choices about CPR, feeding, hydration, and other key care decisions.

## Why Are These Orders Important?

These orders follow you wherever you go.  
They are used in hospitals, nursing homes, and at home.  
They help doctors and nurses give you the care you want.  
They help avoid confusion and unwanted treatments.

## Where Can You Find More Information?

POLST or similar programs are available in every U.S. state.  
You can learn more at the national POLST website:  
[www.polst.org](https://www.polst.org)

# Clonorchiasis

Clonorchiasis is an infection caused by a type of parasitic worm called *Clonorchis sinensis*.  
This worm lives in the bile ducts of the liver.  
The infection happens when you eat raw or undercooked freshwater fish.  
It can also happen from eating raw or undercooked shrimp.

Most people with this infection do not have any symptoms.  
When symptoms do occur, they may include:  
- Pain in the upper right side of the belly  
- Trouble digesting food  
- Feeling tired  
- Diarrhea

## How the Infection Spreads

The worm’s life cycle starts in freshwater snails.  
The worm’s eggs pass out in the stool.  
Snails eat the eggs and become infected.  
From the snails, tiny swimming larvae (called cercariae) come out.  
These larvae infect freshwater fish and shrimp.  
The worms then form a resting stage (called metacercariae) inside the fish or shrimp.  
When you eat the fish or shrimp raw, undercooked, pickled, dried, salted, or soaked in wine, the worms come out in your intestines.  
They travel up to the bile ducts in the liver.  
They grow into adult worms in about one month.  
Adult worms can live in the body for 25 years or more.  
They grow to be about 10 to 25 millimeters long and 3 to 5 millimeters wide.

Some people who served in Vietnam during the war still show signs of past exposure to this worm, even decades later.  
But no worms were found in their stool tests.

## What Symptoms You Might Have

Most people have only a few worms and feel fine.  
Symptoms usually happen when there are many worms or the infection lasts a long time.  
The symptoms come from:  
- Inflammation in the bile ducts  
- Blockage of the ducts  
- Damage to the lining of the ducts  
- Toxins made by the worms  
- Infections caused by bacteria

In the early stage, heavy infections can cause:  
- Fever  
- Chills  
- Pain in the upper belly  
- A swollen liver that hurts when touched  
- Mild yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice)  
- High levels of a type of white blood cell called eosinophils

Later, diarrhea may appear.  
These symptoms usually last 2 to 4 weeks.

In long-term, heavy infections, the liver can become damaged.  
The liver tissue may shrink and scar.  
Scarring can block the bile ducts.  
This can cause jaundice.

Other serious problems can happen, including:  
- Infection in the bile ducts (suppurative cholangitis)  
- Gallstones (cholelithiasis)  
- Inflammation of the gallbladder (cholecystitis)  
- Inflammation of the pancreas (pancreatitis)  
- Cancer of the bile ducts (cholangiocarcinoma)

Some Vietnam veterans who developed bile duct cancer may have been infected with this worm or a similar one while serving in Southeast Asia.  
Bile duct cancer is more common in people from Asia and in older men.

## How Doctors Diagnose Clonorchiasis

Doctors look for worm eggs in your stool.  
They may also check your duodenal fluid (fluid from the first part of the small intestine).  
This test is called feces ova and parasite examination.

Eggs usually show up in the stool 3 to 4 weeks after infection.  
The eggs look very similar to those of another worm called *Opisthorchis*.  
If the bile ducts are blocked, eggs may not appear in the stool.  
This is because eggs are usually passed through bile into the intestines.

Other tests may help but are not enough to confirm the infection.  
Blood tests may show:  
- High levels of a liver enzyme called alkaline phosphatase  
- High levels of bilirubin  
- High levels of eosinophils  
- High levels of a type of antibody called IgE

High eosinophils help doctors tell this infection apart from viral hepatitis.

Imaging tests can show damage in the liver and bile ducts.  
These include:  
- Abdominal X-rays (may show calcium deposits in the liver)  
- Ultrasound  
- CT scan  
- MRI  
- Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)  
- Cholangiography

Ultrasound screening for scarring around the bile ducts is useful in high-risk people.  
This includes men over 50 who live in or come from areas where the worm is common.  
Early detection can improve survival if cancer develops.

In rare cases, doctors find adult worms in tissue samples from surgery.  
They may also see worms in the stool after treatment with medicine.

Special tests like blood tests for antibodies (ELISA) or DNA tests (PCR) can detect the worm.  
But these tests are not widely available.

## How Clonorchiasis Is Treated

Two medicines are used to treat this infection:  
- Praziquantel  
- Albendazole

**Praziquantel**  
- Take it by mouth, three times a day for two days.  
- It works very well against the worm.  
- It is the only medicine recommended by the World Health Organization for global use.

**Albendazole**  
- Take it by mouth, once a day for seven days.  
- It works about as well as praziquantel.  
- But studies on it are small and not very strong.  
- In the United States, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says it can be used as an alternative.

Another medicine called tribendimidine may be helpful.  
It works as well as praziquantel and causes fewer stomach problems.  
But it is not widely available outside China.

If the bile ducts are blocked, surgery may be needed.

## How to Prevent Clonorchiasis

Do not eat raw or undercooked freshwater fish or shrimp.  
Always cook them thoroughly.  
Do not eat fish or shrimp that are:  
- Dried  
- Pickled  
- Salted  
- Soaked in wine

This is especially important if you live in or have been to areas where the worm is common.  
These areas include:  
- China  
- Japan  
- South Korea  
- Northern Vietnam  
- Taiwan  
- Parts of Russia

In some areas, treating large groups of people with praziquantel has reduced the number of infections.

If someone in your family has this infection, other family members should be tested.  
They should have a stool test to check for worm eggs.  
They should also have a blood test to check for high levels of eosinophils.

# Multiple Mononeuropathy

Multiple mononeuropathy means that more than one nerve in the body is affected.  
This can cause numbness, tingling, or weakness in the areas served by those nerves.

## What Causes It?

This condition is often due to other health problems, such as:

- Autoimmune diseases like polyarteritis nodosa, lupus, vasculitis, Sjögren syndrome, and rheumatoid arthritis  
- Sarcoidosis (a condition where small lumps form in organs)  
- Metabolic problems like diabetes and amyloidosis  
- Infections such as Lyme disease, HIV, and leprosy  

Note: Diabetes usually causes a different kind of nerve problem. It mainly affects nerves in the feet and hands, causing numbness and weakness in both legs and arms.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Each affected nerve causes symptoms in its own area.  
You may feel pain, weakness, or strange sensations like tingling or burning.  

If only motor nerves are involved, you may notice weakness without pain.  
If only sensory nerves are involved, you may feel numbness or odd sensations without weakness.  

The problem often starts on one side of the body.  
It may affect nerves all at once or over time.  
If many nerves are involved, the symptoms can look like a widespread nerve problem.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will check your symptoms and do a physical exam.  
Some signs are very clear and point directly to multiple mononeuropathy.  

If the signs are not clear, your doctor may order tests.  
These tests measure how well your nerves and muscles are working.  
They help confirm the diagnosis, find where the problem is, check how bad it is, and predict how well you might recover.

## How Is It Treated?

The main goal is to treat the underlying cause.  
For example, if an autoimmune disease is the cause, treatment will focus on that condition.  
Treating the root cause can help improve nerve function and reduce symptoms.

# Enlarged Spleen

An enlarged spleen is called splenomegaly.

The spleen is a small organ in the upper left part of your belly. It helps filter blood and fight infections.

Splenomegaly is almost always caused by another health problem.

## Common Causes of an Enlarged Spleen

In temperate climates (like in North America and Europe), the most common causes are:

- Autoimmune diseases such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis  
- Liver scarring (cirrhosis) that raises pressure in the blood vessels of the liver  
- Anemia caused by the breakdown of red blood cells (hemolytic anemias)  
- Infections like hepatitis or mononucleosis  
- Diseases that cause abnormal substances to build up in the spleen, such as:  
  - Fatty liver disease linked to metabolic issues  
  - Sarcoidosis (a condition where small lumps form in organs)  
  - Amyloidosis (a rare disease where abnormal proteins build up)  
  - Hemochromatosis (too much iron in the body)  
  - Gaucher disease (a rare inherited disorder)  
- Blood cancers such as lymphomas, especially those linked to hepatitis B or C  
- Blood disorders like myeloproliferative neoplasms  
- Chronic myeloid leukemia

In tropical regions, the most common causes are:

- Infections such as malaria, visceral leishmaniasis, and schistosomiasis

If the spleen is very large (measurable 8 centimeters below the rib cage), the cause is often:

- Chronic lymphocytic leukemia  
- Chronic myeloid leukemia  
- Gaucher disease  
- Hairy cell leukemia  
- Non-Hodgkin lymphoma  
- Polycythemia vera  
- Primary myelofibrosis

## Problems from an Enlarged Spleen

An enlarged spleen can cause low blood counts. This is called hypersplenism.

Hypersplenism means the spleen removes too many blood cells. This can lead to:

- Low red blood cells (anemia)  
- Low white blood cells (increased infection risk)  
- Low platelets (increased bleeding risk)

## How Doctors Evaluate an Enlarged Spleen

Doctors will look for the cause of the enlarged spleen. They may do:

- Blood tests  
- Imaging tests like ultrasound or CT scan  
- In some cases, a biopsy (removing a small sample of spleen tissue)

If no clear cause is found, doctors will check for infections.

## How an Enlarged Spleen Is Treated

Treatment focuses on the underlying cause.

If the spleen is enlarged but you have no symptoms, no treatment is needed.

But if you have:

- Severe low blood counts (hypersplenism)  
- Feeling full too quickly because the spleen presses on the stomach  

Then treatment may be needed. Options include:

- Treating the root cause (like curing an infection or managing anemia)  
- Removing the spleen (splenectomy) in serious cases

## Important Things to Know

- An enlarged spleen is almost always due to another health problem.  
- If no cause is found, check for infections.  
- If you have no symptoms and an enlarged spleen, you do not need treatment.  
- But you should avoid contact sports and heavy weight-lifting. This lowers the risk of the spleen tearing or rupturing.

# Sclerosing Cholangitis

Sclerosing cholangitis is a long-term liver condition.  
It affects the tubes that carry bile from the liver to the intestines.  
These tubes become inflamed, scarred, and narrowed.  
The damage happens in parts of the liver and outside the liver.  

Over time, the bile tubes can close off completely.  
This can lead to liver scarring.  
It may also cause liver failure.  
In some cases, it can lead to a type of cancer called cholangiocarcinoma.

## Types of Sclerosing Cholangitis

There are two main types:  
- **Primary sclerosing cholangitis**: This happens without a clear cause.  
- **Secondary sclerosing cholangitis**: This is caused by other health problems.  

Secondary cases can be due to:  
- Weak immune systems in children (from birth).  
- Weak immune systems in adults (such as in AIDS).  
- Infections like cytomegalovirus or Cryptosporidium.  
- A rare condition called histiocytosis X.  
- Certain medicines, such as floxuridine given through an artery in the liver.  

Both types cause the same kind of damage.  
They lead to inflammation and scarring in the bile tubes.  

Other things can also cause bile tube narrowing.  
These include:  
- Gallstones in the bile duct.  
- Scarring after surgery on the bile ducts.  
- Damage from poor blood flow during liver transplant surgery.  
- Birth defects in the bile ducts.  
- Bile duct cancer.  
- Infections from parasites.

## How It Is Diagnosed

Doctors use imaging tests to see the bile ducts.  
These tests can show narrowing or swelling.  
Common tests include:  
- Ultrasound.  
- Cholangiography (a special X-ray of the bile ducts).

## How It Is Treated

Treatment aims to open blocked bile ducts.  
Doctors may stretch the narrow parts and place a small tube (stent) to keep them open.  
If an infection is causing the problem, doctors treat the infection.  
For example, if the cause is HIV, they treat the HIV.  
The goal is to slow down liver damage and improve symptoms.

# Blepharospasm

Blepharospasm means the muscles around your eye twitch or spasm.  
This causes your eyes to blink or close without your control.  

Doctors do not always know what causes blepharospasm.  
It happens more often in women than in men.  
It can run in families.  

In rare cases, blepharospasm is caused by other health problems.  
These include eye issues like:  
- Eyelashes that grow inward and irritate the eye  
- A foreign object in the cornea (the front part of the eye)  
- Dry eye disease  

It can also be linked to brain or nerve conditions such as Parkinson disease.  

## Symptoms

You may blink your eyes without meaning to.  
Your eyes may close completely, even when you want to keep them open.  
In serious cases, you may not be able to open your eyes at all.  
Fatigue, bright light, and stress can make the spasms worse.  

## Treatment

The most common treatment is a shot of botulinum toxin type A.  
This is injected into the muscles around the eye.  
The shot helps relax the muscles and reduce spasms.  
Most people need more than one shot over time.  

Medicines that reduce anxiety may help some people.  

Surgery to remove part of the eyelid muscles can work.  
But it is only used if the shot does not help.  
Surgery has risks and possible side effects.  

Wearing sunglasses can help if bright light makes your eyes worse.  
Some people find short-term relief by doing simple actions like:  
- Touching their face  
- Covering their eyes  
- Singing  
- Yawning  

These actions may calm the muscle spasms for a short time.

# PFAPA Syndrome

PFAPA stands for periodic fevers with mouth sores, sore throat, and swollen glands.  
It is the most common type of recurring fever in children.  
It usually starts between the ages of 2 and 5 years.  
Boys are more likely to have it than girls.  
It can also happen in adults, but this is rare.

## What Happens During an Episode

Fever comes in regular cycles.  
Each episode lasts 3 to 6 days.  
Episodes happen about every 3 to 4 weeks.  
Between episodes, the child feels completely well.  
Growth stays normal.

During an episode, a child may have:
- High fever
- Sore throat
- Mouth sores (small, painful ulcers)
- Swollen glands in the neck
- Feeling tired
- Chills
- Belly pain (sometimes)
- Joint pain (sometimes)
- Headache (sometimes)

The child is healthy and active between episodes.  
No other symptoms like diarrhea, rash, or cough appear.

## How Doctors Diagnose PFAPA

Doctors diagnose PFAPA based on the child’s symptoms and history.  
There is no single test for it.  
The diagnosis is made when all of these are true:

- At least three episodes of fever
- Each episode lasts up to 5 days
- Episodes happen at regular times
- Each episode includes a sore throat plus swollen glands or mouth sores
- The child feels completely well between episodes
- Growth is normal

Blood tests show higher levels of inflammation during a fever.  
But levels return to normal between episodes.  
If the child has low white blood cells, diarrhea, rash, or cough, it may not be PFAPA.  
These signs point to a different illness.

One condition to rule out is cyclic neutropenia.  
This is a rare blood disorder that causes low white blood cells and fever.

## How PFAPA Is Treated

Treatment is not always needed.  
It depends on how often the fevers happen and how bad they are.

### Options for Treatment

- **Glucocorticoids** (like prednisone or betamethasone)  
  A single dose at the start of a fever can stop the episode in a few hours.  
  This is called abortive treatment.

- **Cimetidine**  
  This medicine may help reduce how often episodes happen.  
  It is taken every day.

- **Colchicine**  
  This medicine may also help prevent episodes.  
  It is taken every day.

- **Tonsillectomy**  
  Surgery to remove the tonsils is rarely needed.  
  It may help in some children who have very frequent or severe episodes.

### Other Medicines for Hard-to-Treat Cases

In rare cases, doctors may try:
- Anakinra
- Canakinumab  
These are newer medicines.  
They have helped some children who did not respond to other treatments.

## Long-Term Outlook

Most children grow out of PFAPA by their teenage years.  
There are no lasting health problems.  
The condition does not cause long-term damage.

# Care Goals for Older Adults

Before starting a treatment or a major test, doctors and nurses should think carefully about the possible risks and benefits. They must also consider what matters most to the patient.

Ask these questions:

- How will this treatment or test change the patient’s daily life?
- Do the choices match what the patient wants for their care?

## Possible Risks

These are possible downsides of treatment or testing:

- Death
- Health problems that last a long time, like extreme tiredness or being unable to do normal activities
- Pain or discomfort
- Trouble fitting the treatment into daily life
- High cost
- Need for more tests or treatments later

## Possible Benefits

These are possible good outcomes:

- Getting better completely
- Living longer
- Slowing down how fast a disease gets worse
- Being able to do more things on your own
- Feeling better with fewer symptoms
- Avoiding future health problems

When a treatment is very likely to help and very unlikely to cause harm, the choice is usually clear. But when a treatment might help in some ways and hurt in others, it’s important to know what matters most to the patient.

For example, strong cancer treatment may help a person live longer. But it can also cause serious side effects like constant nausea, vomiting, or painful sores in the mouth. These side effects can make life harder. In this case, the patient’s choice about whether to focus on living longer or living better helps decide the best path.

Different treatments can also affect quality of life in different ways. For example, surgery and medicine may both treat severe chest pain or joint pain. But one may work better, while the other causes more side effects. The patient’s personal preferences matter.

Health care providers should explain what each treatment can do. They should use simple words and match the explanation to the patient’s understanding. This helps patients make choices that fit their own values.

When predicting how a treatment will affect a person, doctors should look at the patient’s health and body, not just their age. Age alone does not decide what treatment is best.

But life expectancy does matter. For example, if a person is not expected to live long, aggressive treatment for a slow-growing cancer may not help. They may not live long enough to see the benefit.

Still, quality of life is important no matter how long a person is expected to live. So, treatments that can improve daily life—like joint replacement or heart surgery—should not be ruled out just because life expectancy is short.

Also, if a treatment is no longer helpful or causes more harm than good, it may be time to stop it. For example, a medicine to lower cholesterol may not be needed for someone in hospice care.

In the end, care should focus on helping the patient live as well as possible. It should match what the patient wants and values.

# Medical Check-Up for Older Drivers

A medical check-up for older drivers looks at health problems and medicines that could affect driving. Some health issues can slowly reduce your ability to drive. Others can happen suddenly and make you lose awareness. These include vision loss, seizures, or fainting.

Talk to your doctor about national guidelines for checking if older people can still drive safely. (See "More Information" for helpful resources.)

---

## Medicines and Driving

Older adults often take many medicines for different health issues. Some medicines affect the brain or nervous system. These can cause drowsiness, confusion, or slow reactions. They can make driving unsafe.

Many of these medicines have been shown to hurt driving skills in real tests or driving simulators. They also raise the chance of a car crash.

Do not stop taking these medicines suddenly. Stopping too fast can be dangerous. Always talk to your doctor or pharmacist before making any changes.

Some medicines that can increase driving risk include:

- Antihistamines (like those for allergies)
- Benzodiazepines (used for anxiety or sleep)
- Opioids (used for pain)
- Anticholinergics (used for bladder or stomach issues)
- Hypnotics (sleeping pills)
- Blood pressure medicines
- Tricyclic antidepressants

These can cause drowsiness, low blood pressure, or irregular heartbeats.

- Antiparkinson medicines like pramipexole or ropinirole can cause sudden sleep attacks.
- Anti-nausea medicines and muscle relaxants can change how you feel or see things.
- Seizure medicines can cause drowsiness. Your doctor may need to switch you to a safer option.

When starting a new medicine that could affect your vision, body movement, or thinking, do not drive for several days. Wait until your body adjusts and you feel safe.

If you must take a medicine that can affect driving, choose the one that causes the least harm. Use the lowest dose that still works.

---

## Falls and Driving

Falls and car crashes often have the same causes. These include poor vision, weak muscles, or trouble thinking clearly.

If you have fallen in the past, you are more likely to have a car crash. A history of falls means you should be checked for problems with movement, vision, or thinking.

(See "Functional Assessment of the Older Driver" for more details.)

---

## Heart Problems and Driving

Heart problems can make driving unsafe. This is especially true if the problem causes fainting or loss of awareness.

After heart surgery, stents, or a pacemaker, you should not drive for a short time. The length of time depends on your recovery and your doctor’s advice.

Heart problems can cause long-term brain issues or sudden problems like dizziness, fainting, or drowsiness.

If you have severe heart failure, such as trouble breathing even at rest or while driving, do not drive. Wait until you can be tested in real traffic and your doctor says it is safe.

---

## Nervous System Problems and Driving

Nervous system problems raise the risk of car crashes. These include:

### Stroke or Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)

- After one TIA, wait at least one month before driving.
- After a stroke or repeated TIAs, wait 3 to 6 months with no new events.
- You must be cleared by a neurologist or your regular doctor.
- A physical exam should check how any lasting damage affects driving.
- If you still have vision, movement, or thinking problems, ask for help from a driving specialist.

### Seizures

Rules for driving after seizures vary by state. Most require being seizure-free for at least 6 months.

About 70% of people with seizures can control them with medicine. But seizures can return if you stop the medicine or skip doses.

Check your state’s rules. The Epilepsy Foundation has a database with this information. Talk to your neurologist too.

### Alzheimer’s Disease or Other Dementias

These conditions slowly get worse. They affect memory, thinking, and the skills needed to drive.

Watch for new driving mistakes. These may be signs of mental changes. Tests that measure thinking skills can help decide if you need a driving test or should stop driving.

The American Academy of Neurology has guidelines on driving and dementia.

Some states require doctors to report serious memory or thinking problems to the motor vehicle office.

### Other Nervous System Conditions

Conditions like Parkinson’s disease or multiple sclerosis can cause disability. Check your abilities regularly. An on-road driving test may be needed.

---

## Diabetes and Driving

Diabetes can be risky while driving. Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) can cause confusion, dizziness, or loss of awareness.

If you have had a low blood sugar event that made you lose consciousness, do not drive for 3 months. Or wait until your doctor checks what caused it and how to prevent it.

Well-controlled diabetes does not raise crash risk.

Diabetes can also cause nerve damage, eye problems, or both. These can hurt your ability to see or feel while driving.

High blood sugar can also cause brain fog. Do not drive until your blood sugar is under control and your symptoms improve.

---

## Sleep Problems and Driving

Sleep problems, especially obstructive sleep apnea, can cause drowsiness. This increases the risk of crashes.

Do not drive until your sleep problem is treated.

Using a CPAP machine (a device that helps you breathe while sleeping) has been shown to improve driving skills in tests. It also lowers crash rates.

---

## More Information

The following resources may help you or your doctor:

- **National Highway Traffic Safety Administration**: *Clinician's Guide to Assessing and Counseling Older Drivers, 4th edition*  
- **Austroads**: *Assessing Fitness to Drive* – A guide from Australia with medical rules for driving licenses  
- **Epilepsy Foundation**: *State Driving Laws Database* – A U.S. tool with rules for people with epilepsy

# Hymenolepis nana Infection (Dwarf Tapeworm)

This is a type of tapeworm that lives in the intestines.  
It is one of the most common tapeworms that infect people.  
It does not need another animal to complete its life cycle.  
The infection is treated with medicine called praziquantel or niclosamide.

The worm is very small.  
It is only 15 to 40 millimeters long.  
Unlike other tapeworms, it can live and grow in just one host.  
It can also complete its life cycle inside the same person.  
The worm’s young stage stays in the wall of the gut.  
The worm lives for only 4 to 6 weeks.

This infection is more common in people who live in poor conditions.  
It is especially common in children.  
It is more likely when hygiene is poor.  
It is also more common when fleas are around.

There are three ways a person can get infected:

- **Indirect two-host cycle**:  
  Rodents (like rats) are the main hosts.  
  Insects such as fleas or grain beetles eat droppings from infected rodents.  
  People can get infected by eating these infected insects.

- **Human-to-human cycle**:  
  Eggs pass from one person to another.  
  This can happen through contact, especially if someone touches their anus and then touches food or another person.

- **Internal autoinfection**:  
  Eggs hatch inside the gut.  
  They start a new generation without leaving the body.  
  This can lead to many worms and more serious symptoms.

## Symptoms of Infection

Many people have no symptoms.  
But heavy infections can cause:  
- Crampy belly pain  
- Diarrhea  
- Loss of appetite  
- Itching around the anus  
- General feelings of being unwell

Sometimes this infection is mistaken for pinworm infection.

## How It Is Diagnosed

A doctor checks a stool sample under a microscope.  
They look for worm eggs or parts of the worm.  
Finding eggs in the stool confirms the infection.

## How It Is Treated

The best medicine is praziquantel.  
It is taken as a single dose.  
The dose is 25 milligrams per kilogram of body weight.  
It is taken by mouth.

Other options include nitazoxanide and niclosamide.  
Niclosamide is not available in the United States.

**For nitazoxanide:**

- For people over 11 years old:  
  500 milligrams by mouth, twice a day for 3 days.

- For children aged 4 to 11 years:  
  200 milligrams by mouth, twice a day for 3 days.

- For children aged 1 to 4 years:  
  100 milligrams by mouth, twice a day for 3 days.

**For niclosamide:**

- For adults:  
  2 grams by mouth, once a day for 7 days.

- For children over 34 kilograms:  
  1.5 grams on day one, then 1 gram once a day for 6 more days.

- For children 11 to 34 kilograms:  
  1 gram on day one, then 500 milligrams once a day for 6 more days.

One month after finishing treatment, a stool sample should be tested again.  
This checks if the infection is gone.

For more information, visit the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website.  
Look up: Parasites – Hymenolepiasis (also known as *Hymenolepis nana* infection).

# Acute Cholecystitis – Simple Explanation

## What Is Acute Cholecystitis?

Acute cholecystitis is a sudden swelling and irritation of the gallbladder.  
It usually happens when a gallstone blocks the tube that carries bile out of the gallbladder.  
This blockage causes pain and swelling in the upper right side of the belly.  
The condition can also lead to fever, chills, nausea, and vomiting.

## What Causes It?

Most people with acute cholecystitis have gallstones.  
In fact, more than 95 out of 100 people with this condition have gallstones.  
When a stone gets stuck in the tube leading from the gallbladder, bile builds up.  
This buildup causes the gallbladder to become inflamed.

The blocked gallbladder starts to leak chemicals that cause more swelling.  
The lining of the gallbladder also makes extra fluid.  
This fluid makes the gallbladder swell even more.  
The swelling leads to more pain and damage.  
If not treated, the gallbladder can die or burst.

Bacteria can also get into the gallbladder and make the infection worse.  
This creates a cycle of swelling, fluid buildup, and damage.

If the swelling comes and goes over time, the gallbladder can become scarred and weak.  
It stops working well and can no longer store or release bile properly.  
This is called chronic cholecystitis.

---

## Symptoms and Signs

Most people have had similar pain before.  
The pain is in the upper right side of the belly.  
It feels like a sharp or dull ache.  
It lasts longer than six hours and is worse than the pain from gallstones alone.

You may feel sick to your stomach and throw up.  
The area over the gallbladder is tender when touched.  
You may also have a low fever.

In older adults, the symptoms can be different.  
They may not have a fever.  
They may just feel weak, tired, or lose their appetite.  
They may also feel sick to their stomach or vomit.

Most people start to feel better in 2 to 3 days.  
About 85 out of 100 people get better within a week—even without treatment.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your symptoms and do a physical exam.  
They may use imaging tests to confirm the diagnosis.

### Ultrasound of the Abdomen

This is the best test to find gallstones.  
It can also show if the gallbladder is swollen or inflamed.  
The test can detect tenderness in the area of the gallbladder.  
This is called the ultrasonographic Murphy sign.

### Cholescintigraphy (HIDA Scan)

This test is used if the ultrasound is unclear.  
It helps check if the tube from the gallbladder is blocked.  
A special dye is used to see if bile can flow out of the gallbladder.

False results can happen if you are very ill, on IV nutrition, or have liver disease.  
A past surgery on the bile duct or certain medicines can also cause false results.  
To avoid this, doctors may give a medicine called morphine to help the test work better.

### CT Scan of the Abdomen

This test is used to check for serious problems.  
It can show if the gallbladder has burst or if the pancreas is inflamed.

### Blood Tests

Blood tests are not enough to diagnose the condition.  
But they can show signs of infection or liver issues.  
White blood cell counts are often high.  
Liver tests may be slightly raised.  
If bilirubin or alkaline phosphatase is high, it may mean the liver is affected.  
If the enzyme lipase is more than three times normal, it may mean a stone is blocking the bile duct.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment includes:

- Getting fluids through a vein (IV)
- Pain relief medicine
- Antibiotics to fight possible infection

### Cholecystectomy (Gallbladder Removal)

This is the best long-term solution.  
It cures the problem and stops future pain.  
It is usually done as soon as possible—within 24 to 48 hours—when safe.

It is best done early in these cases:
- The diagnosis is clear and the person is healthy enough for surgery.
- The person is older or has diabetes. These people are more likely to have serious infections.
- The gallbladder is full of pus (empyema), damaged (gangrene), or has burst.
- There are no gallstones (acalculous cholecystitis).

If the person has serious health problems like heart or lung disease, surgery may be delayed.  
Treatment is first focused on stabilizing the person’s health.  
If the condition improves, surgery can be done at least six weeks later.  
Delaying surgery increases the risk of another attack.

### Percutaneous Cholecystostomy

This is a tube placed through the skin into the gallbladder.  
It drains out the bile and reduces pressure.  
It is used for people who are too sick for surgery.  
This includes very old people, those with severe liver disease, or those in intensive care.

---

## Key Points

- More than 95 out of 100 people with acute cholecystitis have gallstones.
- In older adults, symptoms may be vague. They may feel weak, tired, or lose their appetite. Fever may not be present.
- About 85 out of 100 people get better on their own within a week. But 10 out of 100 develop serious problems like a burst gallbladder.
- Ultrasound is the best test to find gallstones. If unclear, a HIDA scan can help.
- Treatment includes IV fluids, pain medicine, and antibiotics.  
- Surgery to remove the gallbladder is the best cure when possible.

# Chelation Therapy – Simple Explanation

Chelation therapy is a treatment that uses a special drug to remove certain metals or minerals from the blood.

This treatment is used in conventional medicine to treat poisoning from lead and other heavy metals.

Some people believe that too much of certain metals in the body may lead to health problems. These include:

- Dementia  
- Heart and blood vessel disease  
- Kidney disease  

One type of chelation therapy uses a drug called EDTA. Some people suggest this drug can remove calcium from the body. They believe this might help treat a condition where blood vessels become narrow and hard, called atherosclerosis.

But after more than fifty years of research, scientists have not found a clear way that chelation therapy could help with heart disease or prevent heart attacks or strokes.

In 2012, a large study called TACT looked at chelation therapy in people who had had a heart attack. The study found a small benefit when looking at all outcomes together. But there was no clear benefit for individual results like death, heart attacks, or hospital visits.

The study had some problems in how it was done. So, it did not settle the debate about whether chelation therapy works.

Later, researchers looked at the data again. They found that people with diabetes and poor blood flow in their legs had better results with chelation therapy. They had fewer deaths and fewer serious heart problems.

Another review of 38 studies found that chelation therapy might help prevent another heart problem in people who already had one. But the evidence is not strong or clear.

## Risks of Chelation Therapy

Chelation therapy can cause serious side effects. These include:

- Low calcium levels in the blood. This can be dangerous.
- Pain, redness, or swelling at the site where the drug is given.
- Fever, nausea, or vomiting.
- Damage to the kidneys.
- Delay in getting better treatments that are proven to work.
- In rare cases, death.

Always talk to your doctor before trying chelation therapy. It is not a proven treatment for heart disease. It can be risky.

# Hyper-IgD Syndrome

Hyper-IgD syndrome is a rare condition that runs in families. It causes repeated episodes of chills and fever. These episodes usually start in the first year of life. Each episode lasts about 4 to 6 days. They can be triggered by things like vaccines or minor injuries.

Doctors diagnose this condition based on symptoms and tests. A blood test checks the level of a protein called IgD. If the level is over 100 units per liter, it may point to Hyper-IgD syndrome. But some people with the condition have normal IgD levels.

Another test checks for a substance called mevalonic acid in the urine. High levels during an attack help confirm the diagnosis. Genetic testing can also be done, but it does not always find the problem. In about a quarter of cases, the test is negative even when the person has the condition.

This condition is more common in children with Dutch, French, or other Northern European roots. It is caused by changes in a gene that makes an enzyme called mevalonate kinase. This enzyme helps make cholesterol. When it does not work right, it may lead to less production of proteins that calm inflammation. This may explain the symptoms.

## Symptoms and Signs

Common symptoms include:
- Chills
- Fever
- Belly pain
- Vomiting
- Diarrhea
- Headaches
- Joint pain

Signs seen by doctors include:
- Swollen glands in the neck
- Enlarged spleen
- Joint swelling or pain
- Skin rashes (red spots or patches)
- Small purple spots on the skin
- Sores in the mouth or genital area

## Diagnosis

Doctors look at the patient’s history and do a physical exam. They also check:
- Blood levels of IgD
- White blood cell count
- Markers of inflammation in the blood
- Urine levels of mevalonic acid during an attack

Genetic testing is available but may not find the problem in some people.

## Treatment

To prevent attacks:
- Use anakinra once a day
- Use canakinumab every 4 weeks

These medicines are proven to reduce the number of attacks.

To treat symptoms during an attack:
- Use nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
- Use corticosteroids
- Use anakinra on an as-needed basis

NSAIDs and corticosteroids can help ease pain and fever. Using anakinra when symptoms start has also worked well in some cases.

People with this condition will likely have repeated fever episodes throughout life. But after adolescence, the attacks often become less frequent.

# What Is Vitiligo?

Vitiligo is a skin condition where the skin loses its color in patches.  
These patches can be small or large.  
The skin loses pigment because the cells that make color (melanocytes) are missing or not working.  

We do not know exactly what causes vitiligo.  
But it may be linked to genes and the body’s immune system.  
Some people with vitiligo also have other autoimmune conditions.  

## What Causes Vitiligo?

The exact cause is not known.  
But the skin loses its color because the pigment-making cells are damaged or missing.  
Possible reasons include:  
- The body’s immune system attacking the pigment cells.  
- The pigment cells not surviving well.  
- A problem with the pigment cells from the start.  

Vitiligo can run in families.  
It can also appear suddenly in people with no family history.  
Some people with vitiligo have antibodies that attack pigment.  
Up to one in three people with vitiligo also have other autoimmune conditions.  
These include:  
- Problems with the thyroid gland.  
- Addison disease.  
- Type 1 diabetes.  
- Pernicious anemia.  

The strongest links are with two thyroid conditions:  
- Graves disease.  
- Hashimoto thyroiditis.  

In rare cases, vitiligo starts after a skin injury.  
This includes sunburn or a cut.  
Some chemicals in household cleaners or dyes can also trigger it.  
Some people say stress made their vitiligo worse.  

Certain cancer treatments, like those for melanoma, can cause vitiligo as a side effect.  
These treatments boost the immune system.  
That can lead to the immune system attacking pigment cells.  

## What Does Vitiligo Look Like?

The skin loses color in patches.  
These patches are usually smooth and have clear edges.  
They often appear on both sides of the body in the same places.  

Types of vitiligo:  
- **Focal**: One or a few small patches.  
- **Segmental**: Affects one side or area of the body, like one arm or leg.  
- **Generalized**: Affects many parts of the body.  
- **Universal**: Nearly all skin loses color.  

Common spots include:  
- Around the mouth, eyes, and nose.  
- Fingers and hands.  
- Wrists, elbows, knees, and shins.  
- Ankles, armpits, groin, belly button, and nipples.  

The skin may look very different from the rest of the body.  
This can be hard to live with, especially for people with darker skin.  
Hair in the affected areas often turns white.  

## How Is Vitiligo Diagnosed?

A doctor can usually tell if you have vitiligo by looking at your skin.  
The patches are easy to see, especially on darker skin.  

A special light called a Wood light can help.  
It makes the pale patches stand out more.  
The skin looks chalk white under this light.  

Other skin conditions can look like vitiligo.  
These include:  
- Skin that lost color after a rash or injury.  
- A rare inherited condition called piebaldism.  
- Scleroderma (thickened skin).  
- Leprosy (a bacterial infection).  
- Lichen sclerosus.  
- Pityriasis alba.  
- Skin damage from chemicals.  
- Skin changes from melanoma.  

Your doctor may do blood tests if needed.  
These can check for:  
- Anemia.  
- Diabetes.  
- Thyroid problems.  
- Autoimmune antibodies.  

## How Is Vitiligo Treated?

There is no cure for vitiligo.  
But treatments can help the skin regain color.  
Some people choose not to treat it.  
Others want to improve the look of their skin.  

### Protect Your Skin from Sun

All areas without color are very sensitive to sun.  
They can burn easily.  
Always cover them with clothing or use sunscreen.  

### Cover the Patches

Small patches can be covered with makeup.  
This helps hide the color loss.  

### Treat the Skin to Regain Color

For larger areas, treatment aims to bring back skin color.  
There is no one best treatment.  
Doctors choose based on your skin, the size of patches, and your health.  

**Topical corticosteroids**  
These are creams or ointments that reduce inflammation.  
They can help restore color.  
But long-term use can thin the skin or cause lighter spots.  

**Calcipotriene**  
This is a cream that helps skin cells grow.  
It is often used with a corticosteroid.  
This mix works better than either alone.  

**Calcineurin inhibitors**  
These are creams like tacrolimus and pimecrolimus.  
They are good for sensitive areas like the face and groin.  
They do not thin the skin like steroids can.  

**Narrowband UVB light therapy**  
This is a type of light treatment.  
It is often the first choice for widespread vitiligo.  
It helps many people regain color.  
It is safe for most people.  
But it may slightly raise the risk of skin cancer over time.  
Regular skin checks are a good idea.  

**Excimer laser**  
This is a focused light beam.  
It works well for small, stubborn patches.  
It is not used for large areas.  

**Oral corticosteroids**  
These are pills.  
They are used only for a short time if vitiligo is spreading fast.  
They stop the spread but do not restore color.  
They are often used with light therapy to help color come back.  

**Surgery**  
Surgery is only for people with stable vitiligo.  
It means the patches are not getting bigger.  
Surgery options include:  
- **Skin grafting**: Taking healthy skin and placing it on the pale areas.  
- **Tattooing**: Using ink to color the skin.  
Tattooing works well for hard-to-treat spots like lips, nipples, and fingertips.  

### Depigmentation (Bleaching)

If most of your skin has lost color, you may choose to make the rest of your skin lighter.  
This creates a more even look.  
A cream called monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone is used.  
It is applied twice a day.  

This treatment is only for people with very widespread vitiligo.  
It is permanent.  
You will lose all skin color.  
This means you will always be at higher risk for sun damage.  
This includes:  
- Skin cancer.  
- Premature aging of the skin.  

The cream can irritate the skin.  
Always test a small area first.  
It may take more than a year to see results.  

### New Treatments: JAK Inhibitors

A new type of medicine called a JAK inhibitor is now available.  
Ruxolitinib is a cream that helps restore color.  
It works by calming the immune system.  

Another JAK inhibitor, tofacitinib, is being studied.  
But color may return after stopping the medicine.  

## Key Points

- Vitiligo may be linked to genes or autoimmune problems.  
- It can appear in small spots, on one side of the body, or cover most of the skin.  
- A doctor can usually diagnose it by looking at your skin.  
- Blood tests may help check for other health issues.  
- Treatments include creams, light therapy, surgery, or bleaching.  
- New medicines like ruxolitinib are now available.  
- Treatment choices depend on your skin, your health, and your goals.

# How Fertilization Happens and How the Baby Grows

Sperm travel from the vagina through the cervix and into the uterus. They then move into the fallopian tubes.

In the ovaries, small sacs called follicles grow. One follicle becomes dominant and releases an egg. This is called ovulation.

The egg moves into the fallopian tube through the finger-like ends of the tube. It then travels through the tube and into the uterus.

A single sperm enters the egg. When this happens, the egg becomes a fertilized egg. This usually happens in the fallopian tube.

## How Eggs and Sperm Are Made

The body makes eggs and sperm through a process called gametogenesis.

In women, this process is called oogenesis. In men, it is called spermatogenesis.

Both processes start with cells that have two sets of chromosomes. These cells divide and change to become mature eggs or sperm. Each mature egg or sperm has only one set of chromosomes.

Usually, one sperm fertilizes one egg. But sometimes, two eggs are released at the same time. If each egg is fertilized by a different sperm, this leads to twins. These are called fraternal twins.

It is rare for more than two eggs to be released and fertilized. This can lead to triplets, quadruplets, or more. But this does not happen often.

Sometimes, more than one sperm enters a single egg. This causes a problem. The fertilized egg will not develop normally.

## When Ovulation Happens

For women with a 28-day cycle, ovulation usually happens about 14 days after the first day of their period.

At ovulation, the mucus in the cervix becomes thinner. This helps sperm move faster through the cervix and into the uterus.

Sperm can live in the female reproductive tract for up to 3 days after sex.

## How the Fertilized Egg Grows

The fertilized egg is called a zygote. It has two sets of chromosomes — one from the mother and one from the father.

The zygote starts to divide as it moves through the fallopian tube toward the uterus.

It keeps dividing and grows into a ball of cells with a hollow center. This is called a blastocyst.

The outer layer of the blastocyst is one cell thick. But one side, called the embryonic pole, is three to four cells thick.

About 6 days after fertilization, the blastocyst attaches to the lining of the uterus. This is called implantation.

The embryonic pole is the first part to attach. This part will become the baby.

# Behçet Disease – Simple Explanation

Behçet disease is a long-term condition that causes inflammation in blood vessels. It can affect many parts of the body. The disease comes and goes over time, with flare-ups and periods of improvement.

## What Happens in Behçet Disease?

The disease causes swelling in blood vessels. This can lead to serious problems. It often starts with painful sores in the mouth and genitals. It can also cause skin sores and eye problems.

Some of the most serious issues include:
- Loss of vision
- Brain and nerve problems
- Blood clots in veins
- Bulging blood vessels (aneurysms) in arteries

## Who Gets Behçet Disease?

The disease affects men and women about equally. But men often have more severe symptoms. It usually starts in the twenties. It can also happen in children, but this is rare.

The disease is most common in areas along an old trade route from the Mediterranean to China. It is very rare in the United States.

## What Causes Behçet Disease?

The exact cause is not known. Experts think the immune system may be overactive. Some believe infections or genes play a role.

A gene called *HLA-B51* increases the risk. This gene is common in people from Europe, the Middle East, and East Asia. It is rare or absent in people from Africa, Oceania, and South America.

## Symptoms and Signs

Common symptoms include:
- Recurrent mouth sores (like canker sores)
- Eye problems (redness, pain, blurry vision)
- Genital sores (on the penis or scrotum in men, on the vulva in women)
- Skin sores (red, tender lumps under the skin)

Some people also have:
- Joint pain
- Headaches
- Nerve problems (like numbness or weakness)

## How Is It Diagnosed?

There is no single test for Behçet disease. Doctors make the diagnosis based on symptoms and physical exams.

The main rule for diagnosis is:
- At least three mouth sores in one year
- Plus two of the following:
  - Recurrent genital sores
  - Eye problems (especially uveitis or retinal swelling)
  - Skin sores
  - A positive pathergy test

A pathergy test means a small needle is stuck into the skin of the forearm. If a red, swollen bump with a small pus-filled spot appears within 24 to 48 hours, the test is positive.

Blood tests may be done to check for signs of inflammation. These tests often show:
- High levels of certain proteins
- High white blood cell count

But these results are not unique to Behçet disease.

## Treatment

Treatment depends on the symptoms and how severe they are.

### For Mouth and Genital Sores, Skin Sores
- Colchicine
- Apremilast
- Corticosteroids (topical or oral)
- Dapsone
- Azathioprine
- TNF inhibitors (like infliximab or adalimumab)
- Interferon alfa
- Thalidomide

### For Eye Problems
- Azathioprine
- Methotrexate
- Cyclosporine
- TNF inhibitors

### For Severe Brain or Life-Threatening Disease
- TNF inhibitors
- Cyclophosphamide

Topical corticosteroids can help with eye pain and mouth sores. But they do not stop future flare-ups. In rare cases, high-dose oral steroids (like prednisone) may help with severe eye or brain problems.

TNF inhibitors are very helpful. They can reduce the number of flare-ups. They work well for eye and gut problems. Infliximab acts quickly.

Immunosuppressants (like TNF inhibitors) help prevent blood clots in veins. It is not clear if blood thinners help. Blood thinners are not safe if you have a bulging artery.

## Prognosis (Outlook)

Behçet disease often comes and goes. It can improve over time. Many people go into remission.

The outlook is worse for:
- Young men
- People with the *HLA-B51* gene
- People who have frequent flare-ups
- People with artery problems (like blood clots or bulging vessels)

Early symptoms often include mouth sores, skin sores, and eye problems. Brain and large blood vessel issues usually appear later.

In rare cases, the disease can be deadly. This usually happens due to brain, blood vessel, or gut problems.

## Key Points

- Behçet disease causes inflammation in blood vessels.
- It often starts with mouth and genital sores.
- Eye problems, skin sores, and nerve issues are common.
- Diagnosis is based on symptoms and a special test (pathergy).
- The disease can be serious, especially in young men.
- Treatment depends on the symptoms.
- TNF inhibitors and other strong medicines help prevent serious damage.
- Some people get better over time. Others have ongoing problems.

# Understanding Gestational Age

Gestational age tells us how far along a baby is in the womb. It helps doctors predict if a baby might have health problems after birth. The main factor in a baby’s health at birth is how mature the organs are. This depends on how many weeks the baby has been developing.

## How Gestational Age Is Measured

Doctors usually count gestational age from the first day of the mother’s last normal period. This is the standard method used by all doctors who care for pregnant women and newborns.

But this method is not always exact. Ovulation and conception happen about two weeks after the start of the last period. So, the count starts two weeks before the baby actually formed.

If a woman has irregular periods, the last period method can be even less accurate.

### Embryologic Age

Embryologic age is the time from the actual day of conception to birth. It is usually two weeks less than gestational age.

A woman can guess the day of conception by tracking her body temperature or using home tests for ovulation. But the only way to know the exact day of conception is if the baby was made using fertility treatments like IVF.

## Other Ways to Estimate Gestational Age

Doctors can also use these methods to estimate how far along a pregnancy is:

- The date of ovulation or conception
- Fetal ultrasound (an image of the baby in the womb)
- Physical exam of the baby after birth using the **new Ballard score**

## Estimating the Due Date

The **due date** is the day a baby is expected to be born.

You can find the due date in several ways:

- Add 266 days to the date of conception.
- Add 280 days (40 weeks) to the first day of the last period. This works best for women with regular 28-day cycles.
- If the cycle is not 28 days long, add 280 days to the first day of the last period, then add or subtract the difference in days.

If a woman has regular periods, her menstrual history is a good way to find the due date.

### Ultrasound in Early Pregnancy

If the due date is not clear, ultrasound in the first trimester gives the most accurate estimate. This is especially helpful if the woman does not know when her last period was or if her periods are irregular.

Doctors compare the due date from the last period with the due date from the first ultrasound. If they differ, the ultrasound date may be used instead.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) says to use the ultrasound date if it differs from the last period date by:

- Up to 8 weeks and 6 days: more than 5 days
- 9 to 15 weeks and 6 days: more than 7 days
- 16 to 21 weeks and 6 days: more than 10 days
- 22 to 27 weeks and 6 days: more than 14 days
- 28 weeks or more: more than 21 days

Doctors only use the first ultrasound to adjust the due date. They do not change the due date based on later ultrasounds.

Ultrasound is less accurate later in pregnancy. So, second and third trimester ultrasounds are rarely used to change the due date. If a change is needed, a specialist in fetal ultrasound should be consulted.

To improve accuracy in later pregnancy, doctors can use more than one measurement, such as the baby’s head size and thigh bone length.

## Checking the Baby After Birth

Doctors can also estimate gestational age by examining the baby after birth. This uses the **new Ballard score**.

The new Ballard score is a tool that looks at the baby’s physical features and muscle tone. It is more accurate than the old version and works for very early babies.

The score is only accurate within about two weeks. It can overestimate the age of a baby born too early. It can also underestimate the age of a baby who is small for their age.

Doctors use the new Ballard score only when there is no clear due date from the mother’s history. Or when the due date from the mother’s history does not match the baby’s physical exam.

The new Ballard score can be used up to 4 days after birth. In practice, it is usually done within the first 24 hours.

The muscle tone part of the score stays more stable over time. The physical features change quickly after birth.

But illness or medicines given during labor (like magnesium sulfate) can affect the muscle tone part of the score.

## How Babies Are Grouped by Gestational Age

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists groups babies by how far along they are at birth:

- **Preterm**: less than 37 weeks
- **Late preterm**: 34 to 36 weeks and 6 days
- **Early term**: 37 weeks and 0 days to 38 weeks and 6 days
- **Full term**: 39 weeks and 0 days to 40 weeks and 6 days
- **Late term**: 41 weeks and 0 days to 41 weeks and 6 days
- **Postterm**: 42 weeks or more

The World Health Organization (WHO) breaks down preterm babies into more groups:

- **Extremely preterm**: less than 28 weeks
- **Very preterm**: 28 weeks and 0 days to 31 weeks and 6 days
- **Moderate preterm**: 32 weeks and 0 days to 33 weeks and 6 days

# Kidney Damage from Heavy Metals

Heavy metals and other harmful substances can harm the kidneys.

This type of kidney problem affects the small tubes and the spaces between them in the kidneys.

Common heavy metals that can cause this include lead, cadmium, and copper.

The condition is a type of long-term kidney inflammation called chronic interstitial nephritis.

# Nasal Foreign Bodies

Foreign objects in the nose happen sometimes in young children, people with learning difficulties, or those with mental health conditions.

Common items pushed into the nose include:
- Cotton
- Paper
- Small stones
- Beads
- Beans
- Seeds
- Nuts
- Insects
- Magnets
- Button batteries

Button batteries are especially dangerous. They can cause serious chemical burns inside the nose.

If an object stays in the nose for a long time, mineral salts can build up around it. This makes the object hard and turns it into a rhinolith.

You should suspect a foreign object in the nose if:
- One side of the nose has a bad smell
- There is blood in the discharge
- The discharge is thick and yellow or green

Often, someone else sees the object being pushed into the nose. Or, a doctor can see it using a special tool called a nasal speculum.

It is important to remove the object quickly and carefully. If not, it can lead to:
- Infection
- A hole in the nose
- Heavy nosebleeds

This is especially urgent for button batteries. They must be removed right away.

In many cases, a doctor can remove the object in the office. Tools used include:
- A nasal speculum
- Hartmann nasal forceps

Other tools that have worked well include:
- Wire loop or hook curettes
- Suction catheters
- Balloon catheters

Before removal, a numbing medicine and a medicine that shrinks blood vessels (lidocaine and epinephrine) can be sprayed into the nose. This helps the doctor see better and makes removal easier.

If the object is round and slippery, do not push it deeper. Instead, use a blunt probe with a bent tip. Slide it behind the object and pull it forward.

Sometimes, general anesthesia is needed. This is true if:
- A rhinolith has formed
- The object might move up into the back of the nose and block the airway

After the object is removed, the doctor checks the nose for any leftover pieces.

Washing the nose with salt water (saline irrigation) helps clear out any remaining debris. It also lowers the risk of infection.

Antibiotics are usually not needed after the object is removed.

# Isaacs Syndrome

Isaacs syndrome is a rare condition that affects the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord.  
It causes muscles to twitch constantly.  
This condition is caused by the body’s immune system attacking the nerves.

It is also known as neuromyotonia.  
It is linked to problems with potassium channels in the nerves.  
In some cases, it is connected to cancer.  
It can also happen with other health issues like myasthenia gravis, thyroid disease, vitamin B12 deficiency, celiac disease, or connective tissue disorders.  
In rare cases, it can be passed down through families.

The exact cause is not known.  
Doctors believe the problem starts in the peripheral nerves.  
The twitching stops when a drug called curare is used.  
But the twitching continues during general anesthesia.

## Symptoms

The most common symptoms affect the arms and legs.  
The main sign is constant muscle twitching.  
People describe this as a "bag of worms" moving under the skin.  
Other symptoms include:  
- Small, quick muscle twitches (fasciculations)  
- Spasms in the hands and feet  
- Muscle cramps that come and go  
- Stiff muscles  
- Sweating more than normal  
- Muscles that do not relax after a strong effort (pseudomyotonia)

## Diagnosis

Doctors diagnose Isaacs syndrome by:  
- Talking with the patient and doing a physical exam  
- Testing nerve function  
- Doing an electromyography (EMG) test

Nerve tests show extra electrical activity after a nerve is stimulated.  
EMG tests show:  
- Twitching in individual muscle fibers  
- Continuous muscle activity  
- Abnormal electrical patterns in muscles  
- Cramp-like activity  
These findings are strongest in the hands and feet.

Blood tests are done to check for specific antibodies.  
These include:  
- Antibodies to Caspr2  
- Antibodies to calcium channels in muscles  
- Antibodies to gluten (gliadin)  
- Antibodies to an enzyme called GAD  
- Antibodies to acetylcholine receptors in muscles  
- Antibodies to potassium channels in nerves

About 20% of people with Caspr2 antibodies have a tumor in the thymus gland.  
Many also have other types of solid tumors.  
Imaging tests like CT or MRI scans of the chest can help find these tumors.

## Treatment

Treatment focuses on reducing symptoms.  
Medications can help calm the nerves and reduce twitching.  
These include:  
- Carbamazepine  
- Phenytoin  
- Gabapentin  
- Valproate  
- Lamotrigine  
- Mexiletine (used less often)  
- Clonazepam  
- Rituximab (used in some cases)

Plasma exchange is often helpful.  
It removes harmful antibodies from the blood.  
Intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) can also help, though it is less effective than plasma exchange.  
These treatments are often used with:  
- Prednisone (a steroid medicine)  
- Azathioprine (a medicine that reduces immune system activity)

## Key Points
