- The toes may become bent or misshapen.
- The bunion may hurt, but not always — even if it is large.
- Bunions can lead to joint pain over time.
- They can make walking harder and increase the risk of falling.

---

## What Causes Bunions?

Several things can raise your risk of getting a bunion:

- You may inherit a foot shape that makes bunions more likely.
- Some people have weak connective tissue in their feet.
- Certain health conditions can increase risk, such as:
  - Rheumatoid arthritis
  - Diabetes
  - Poor blood flow in the legs
- A short Achilles tendon or short calf muscles can also play a role.
- Flat feet or splayfoot (a foot that spreads out) can contribute.

Even though tight shoes are often blamed, they are not the main cause. But they can make bunions worse. High heels and pointed shoes put extra pressure on the toes.

Some people wear tight shoes every day and never get bunions. Others wear comfortable shoes and still develop them.

---

## How Common Are Bunions?

Bunions are much more common in women than in men. This may be because women often have weaker foot tissue and wear tighter shoes.

About one in three people over age 65 has a bunion to some degree.

---

## How Can You Prevent Bunions?

To help prevent bunions:

- Wear flat, comfortable shoes with plenty of room for your toes.
- Make sure your shoes are wide enough at the front.
- Walk barefoot when possible to keep your foot muscles strong.
- Let your feet and toes move naturally.
- Some doctors suggest using special shoe inserts (insoles). But there is not enough proof that they work.

---

## How Is a Bunion Diagnosed?

Your doctor will check your foot in several ways:

- They will look at the shape of your big toe and the joint at its base.
- They will see how your toes are lined up.
- They will check how well your foot and toes move.
- They will examine your legs and feet while you stand, walk, and sit.
- They will look at your skin for redness, swelling, or sores.
- They will ask about your pain and how it affects daily life.
- An X-ray of your foot while standing helps show the angle of the big toe and the joint.

Bunions can be mild or severe. The doctor measures the angle between the big toe and the foot bone to decide how bad it is.

> **Important:** A small bump is not always a problem. Many people have mild bunions that never cause pain.

---

## How Is a Bunion Treated?

Bunions can get worse over time. But you only need treatment if they cause pain or trouble.

Your treatment depends on:

- How bad the pain is
- The type of bunion
- Other health issues you may have, such as diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, or poor blood flow

Try these first:

### Splints

- These are worn at night to keep the big toe in a better position.
- They may help reduce pain and slow the bunion from getting worse.
- They cannot fix the shape of the foot.
- They are not proven to work well.

### Good Shoes

- Wear flat shoes with a wide toe box.
- Make sure your toes are not squeezed.
- Use bunion pads if the joint hurts.
- If the ball of your foot hurts, use shoe inserts or special shoes with a rocker bottom.
- Walking barefoot when safe helps keep foot muscles strong.

### Physiotherapy

- You can do simple foot exercises to stretch and strengthen the muscles.
- These may help with pain and movement.

### Painkillers

- You can take non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) as tablets or ointments.
- Tablets should only be used for a short time due to possible side effects.

> **Important:** Studies show that these treatments give only small relief. There is not strong proof that they work well.

### Surgery

- Surgery is an option if pain is severe and other treatments do not help.
- It is the only way to fix the bone alignment.
- Surgery can reduce pain and improve foot shape.
- But it does not always work completely.
- It can have side effects, such as swelling, stiffness, or numbness.
- Healing takes time.

For more detailed information about when surgery is needed, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

# Hydrocele

A hydrocele is a buildup of fluid in the scrotum. It usually does not cause pain. This page explains how hydroceles form and why it’s important to get them checked.

---

## Quick Facts

- A hydrocele means too much fluid has built up in the scrotum.
- Most hydroceles do not hurt.
- There are two types: one you are born with (congenital), and one that develops later in life (acquired).
- In most cases, doctors do not know what causes a hydrocele. This is called “idiopathic.”
- These fluid buildups grow slowly over time.
- Most hydroceles are harmless and do not need treatment unless they cause symptoms.
- Rarely, a hydrocele can be caused by a hernia, injury, infection, testicle twisting, or a tumor.
- If a hydrocele does not go away on its own, surgery may be needed.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical care. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Hydrocele?

A hydrocele is extra fluid in the sac that holds the testicles. This sac is called the scrotum.

The fluid can also collect in the tube behind the testicle (epididymis) or in the cord that connects the testicle to the body (spermatic cord). Most of the time, this fluid buildup does not cause pain.

Hydroceles can happen at any age. When they develop later in life, they are called “acquired” hydroceles. Some people are born with them, which is called a “congenital” hydrocele.

Congenital hydroceles often go away on their own within the first few months after birth. The fluid usually drains out naturally.

Acquired hydroceles often appear with no clear cause. These are usually not dangerous and do not need treatment. But if they cause discomfort, treatment can help.

In rare cases, a hydrocele forms after an injury, infection, or hernia. These types usually need treatment.

> **Warning:** A very large hydrocele can twist the testicle. This can block blood flow. If blood flow stops, the testicle can be damaged or die. This is an emergency. Seek medical help right away.

---

## What Are the Signs of a Hydrocele?

Most people notice a swelling in the scrotum. The swelling feels firm and bouncy, but it is usually not painful. Larger hydroceles may cause a dull ache or discomfort when moving.

In babies with a congenital hydrocele:
- The swelling gets bigger when the baby cries or is held upright.
- The swelling gets smaller when the baby lies down.

---

## What Causes a Hydrocele?

### Congenital Hydroceles

These happen during pregnancy. The testicles start in the belly, near the kidneys. They move down into the scrotum through a small tube called the inguinal canal.

As they move, they bring a small piece of the inner lining of the belly (peritoneum) with them. This lining forms a protective covering around the testicles.

If this process is not complete, a small hole can remain. Fluid from the belly can leak through this hole into the scrotum.

This is more likely if:
- One or both testicles did not move into the scrotum (undescended testicles).
- The bladder did not form properly (bladder exstrophy).
- The baby has a connective tissue disorder.
- The baby is born too early (premature).

### Acquired Hydroceles

These develop later in life. Most have no known cause and are called “idiopathic.” They are common and usually not serious.

Some acquired hydroceles are caused by:
- A hernia in the groin.
- Injury from an accident or surgery.
- Infection in the testicles or nearby areas.
- Twisting of the testicle (torsion).
- A tumor in the scrotum.

---

## How Common Are Hydroceles?

- About 90 out of 100 boys are born with a small hole in the lining of the belly.
- In 20 out of 100 of these babies, the hole stays open for the first 5 months.
- This increases the chance of a hydrocele.
- Not all babies with the hole will get a hydrocele.
- Most hydroceles in babies happen on the right side of the scrotum.

It is hard to know how many boys get a hydrocele during puberty.  
About 1 in every 100 adult men has a hydrocele.

---

## How Is a Hydrocele Diagnosed?

A doctor will first feel the scrotum. They will check the size and feel of the swelling. They will also ask about past injuries or health problems.

An ultrasound scan is usually done to confirm the diagnosis. This uses sound waves to create a picture of the inside of the scrotum.

The exam and ultrasound help rule out other problems, such as:
- Varicose veins in the scrotum (varicocele).
- Twisted testicle (testicular torsion).
- Testicular cancer.

Blood or urine tests may also be done to help rule out cancer.

---

## How Is a Hydrocele Treated?

Treatment depends on the type and cause of the hydrocele.

### Congenital Hydroceles

- Most go away on their own within the first two years.
- If the hydrocele is large or does not shrink, surgery may be needed.
- The surgery closes the hole in the belly lining. It is done through a small cut in the groin.

### Acquired Hydroceles

- Some go away on their own.
- If they do not, surgery may be recommended.
- The surgeon makes a small cut in the scrotum.
- They remove the fluid and sew the sac closed to prevent more fluid from collecting.

### Other Treatments

- **Aspiration:** A needle is used to drain the fluid. This is rarely done because the fluid often comes back and there is a risk of infection.
- **Sclerotherapy:** A medicine is injected to shrink the sac. This is very rare and not commonly used.

---

## What to Expect After Surgery

- Some boys and men can go home the same day.
- Older men, premature babies, and those with large hydroceles may stay in the hospital for a few days.

### Care After Surgery

- Keep the scrotum raised for 2 to 3 days to reduce swelling.
- Use a cool, damp cloth to help with swelling.
- Use special scrotal supports. These are available at pharmacies. They are small cushions or stretchy bands that go around the thigh.
- These supports help the testicles lie flat. This improves blood flow and helps healing.
- Wear a protective support (like a padded cup or pouch) when walking for 2 to 4 weeks after surgery.
- Avoid heavy lifting, sports, and physical activity during recovery.
- Wait before having sex. Talk to your doctor about when it is safe to resume.

> Always follow your doctor’s advice after surgery.

# Chickenpox (Varicella)

Chickenpox is a common illness in children. It is caused by a virus. Most children between the ages of 2 and 10 get it. The illness causes a very itchy rash with red blisters and a mild fever. While it is uncomfortable, it rarely causes serious problems in healthy children.

## Quick Facts

- Chickenpox is a very contagious virus. It mostly affects children.
- The main signs are a very itchy rash with red blisters and a mild fever.
- Chickenpox is much less common now than in the past. Most children are now vaccinated.
- A person can spread the virus one to two days before the rash appears.
- In healthy children, chickenpox is usually not serious.
- It can be dangerous for newborn babies, adults, and people with weak immune systems.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Chickenpox?

Chickenpox is caused by a virus. It spreads easily from person to person. It mostly affects children. The main symptoms are a very itchy rash with red blisters and a mild fever. Thanks to vaccination, fewer children now get chickenpox than before.

A person can spread the virus before the rash shows up. Good hygiene and taking precautions can help stop the virus from spreading.

In healthy children, chickenpox is usually not serious. But it can be dangerous for newborn babies, adults, and people with weak immune systems.

## What Are the Symptoms?

At first, a person with chickenpox may feel tired, have a headache, or feel sore all over. They may also have a fever.

Then, a rash appears. It usually starts on the face and chest. Later, it spreads to the scalp, arms, and legs.

In some cases, the rash can also appear in the mouth or on the genitals. The worst part is the intense itching. It can make sleep hard.

Adults with chickenpox may not get the same rash as children. Their rash may be less widespread.

Fever usually lasts 3 to 5 days. It rarely goes above 39 degrees Celsius.

The rash starts as small red spots. These turn into blisters filled with clear fluid. Over time, the fluid becomes cloudy.

After a few days, the blisters dry up and form scabs. The scabs fall off after a short time.

Most blisters heal within 3 to 5 days. Because blisters are at different stages at the same time, the rash can look like a “starry sky.”

The number of blisters varies from person to person.

## What Causes Chickenpox?

Chickenpox is caused by the varicella-zoster virus. This virus belongs to a group of viruses called herpes viruses.

The virus spreads through tiny droplets in the air. These droplets come from the breath, coughs, sneezes, or speech of an infected person.

The fluid inside the blisters is also contagious. If the blisters are scratched or burst, the virus can spread to other parts of the body or to other people.

Almost any contact with an infected person can lead to infection. Only people who have had chickenpox before or who are vaccinated are protected.

## How Common Is Chickenpox?

Most cases happen in children between 2 and 10 years old. Teens and adults who never had chickenpox or were not vaccinated can also get it.

In Germany, the Standing Committee on Vaccination (STIKO) has recommended the chickenpox vaccine since 2004. Most parents now follow this advice. As a result, chickenpox is much less common than it used to be.

Before 2004, about 750,000 people got chickenpox each year in Germany. In 2020, only 11,300 cases were reported — about half as many as the year before. Over 90% of those infected had not been vaccinated.

Even though it is less common, chickenpox is still one of the most common childhood illnesses.

## How Does the Illness Progress?

After infection, symptoms usually appear after about two weeks. But they can start as early as one week later.

In rare cases, it can take up to three weeks for symptoms to show.

In children, chickenpox usually clears up in about two weeks. Adults often have a more severe illness. Their symptoms last longer and are worse. They also have a higher risk of complications.

Once a person has had chickenpox, they are usually protected for life. They are very unlikely to get it again.

## How Can Chickenpox Be Prevented?

The STIKO recommends vaccination for people who have not had chickenpox, including:

- Children aged 11 months and older
- Teens
- Women planning to become pregnant
- People with certain health conditions, such as severe eczema

In Germany, public health insurance covers the cost of the vaccine. Two doses are needed. They are given at least 4 to 6 weeks apart.

If you have never had chickenpox and are exposed to someone with it, you can still get the vaccine. It must be given within five days of contact. This can prevent the illness or make symptoms milder.

Pregnant women cannot get the vaccine. But if they are at risk, they can get special antibodies to fight the virus. This is called passive immunization. It can also be given to newborns if their mother gets chickenpox shortly before or after birth.

In rare cases, a vaccinated person can still get chickenpox. But their symptoms are usually milder, and they are less likely to have complications.

Chickenpox is a reportable disease in Germany. Doctors must tell the local health department if someone has it or is suspected of having it. The health department may then contact the family to say the child must stay home until no longer contagious.

People who can still spread the virus should avoid close contact with others. This is especially important around pregnant women and people at high risk of serious illness.

For more information on how to avoid chickenpox, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

## How Is Chickenpox Diagnosed?

Doctors can usually tell if someone has chickenpox just by looking at the rash. They may take a blood test or a sample from a blister if the illness is not going as expected.

A blood test can show if a person has had chickenpox before. This is useful for pregnant women or others who need to know their immune status.

## How Is Chickenpox Treated?

Most people only need treatment for symptoms. If the illness is severe or the person is at risk of complications, the doctor may prescribe antiviral medicine.

To relieve itching, doctors often recommend lotions, gels, or powders. These may contain zinc, tannins, menthol, or polidocanol. Sometimes, oral medicine like antihistamines is used to reduce itching. But their effectiveness for chickenpox has not been fully proven.

Fever and body aches can be treated with pain relievers that contain paracetamol. Do not use ibuprofen for children with chickenpox.

Children and teens should only take medicines with acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) if a doctor prescribes it. And only in rare cases. This medicine can cause a rare but serious condition called Reye’s syndrome in young people.

## Other Important Things to Know

The itching from chickenpox can be very strong. It is hard not to scratch. But scratching should be avoided. The fluid in the blisters is contagious. Scratching can also leave scars.

Keep fingernails short to help prevent scratching. For babies and young children, use cotton mittens. This makes it harder to scratch.

Wear loose, soft clothes made of smooth fabric. This helps avoid further skin irritation.

Showering is better than taking a long bath. The skin absorbs less water. After washing, dry the skin gently by patting it — do not rub.

# Type 2 Diabetes

Type 2 diabetes means your blood has too much sugar.  
This happens because your body’s cells do not respond well to insulin.  
Insulin is a hormone that helps your cells take in sugar from the blood.  
When cells do not respond properly, sugar stays in the blood.  

Some people with type 2 diabetes only need to change their diet.  
They may also need to lose a little weight and move more.  
These changes can help control blood sugar levels.  

Others need medicine, such as tablets or insulin shots.  
Medicine helps keep blood sugar in a healthy range.  

---

## Quick Facts

- Type 2 diabetes is a long-term condition that affects how your body uses sugar.  
- Your pancreas makes insulin, but your body does not use it well.  
- If not treated, blood sugar stays high all the time.  
- Being overweight and not moving enough can raise your risk.  
- Changing your lifestyle can help lower blood sugar, even if you do not have diabetes yet.  

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

---

## What Is Type 2 Diabetes?

Type 2 diabetes is a condition where sugar builds up in the blood.  
Your body makes insulin, but your cells do not use it properly.  
This is called insulin resistance.  

It often starts in adults, which is why it was once called “adult-onset diabetes.”  
It is much more common than type 1 diabetes.  
About 9 out of 10 people with diabetes have type 2.  

Some people can manage their diabetes with small changes.  
Others need medicine every day.  
Knowing how the disease works helps you take better care of yourself.

---

## What Are the Signs of Type 2 Diabetes?

High blood sugar can build up slowly.  
At first, you may not notice any symptoms.  
Over time, you might feel:

- Very thirsty  
- Needing to pee more often  
- Tired all the time  
- Feeling sick to your stomach  
- Dizzy or unsteady  

If blood sugar gets very high, you could lose consciousness.  
This is a serious condition called diabetic coma.  
It needs emergency care.

---

## Why Does Type 2 Diabetes Happen?

Your body needs sugar for energy.  
Insulin helps move sugar from the blood into your cells.  
The pancreas makes insulin and releases it when blood sugar rises.  

In type 2 diabetes, the pancreas still makes insulin.  
But your cells do not respond to it well.  
This means sugar stays in the blood.  
Too much sugar in the blood is called high blood sugar or hyperglycemia.

---

## What Raises Your Risk?

You are more likely to get type 2 diabetes if you:

- Are overweight  
- Do not get enough physical activity  
- Smoke  
- Eat a diet high in fat and sugar and low in fiber  
- Take certain medicines that affect sugar levels  
- Have a family history of diabetes  

Some of these risks you can change. Others you cannot.

---

## How Does Type 2 Diabetes Progress?

If blood sugar stays high for a long time, it can damage blood vessels.  
This increases the risk of heart attack, stroke, and poor blood flow in the legs and feet.  

High blood pressure makes this risk even higher.  
Small blood vessels in the eyes, nerves, and kidneys can also be damaged.  
This can lead to:

- Blurred vision or vision loss  
- Numbness or tingling in hands and feet  
- Kidney problems  

Poor blood flow and nerve damage can cause a condition called “diabetic foot.”  
You may not feel pain in your feet.  
A small cut or bruise can turn into a serious wound.  
Wounds heal slowly because blood flow is poor.

---

## How Can You Prevent Type 2 Diabetes?

You can lower your risk by making healthy choices.  

- Eat a balanced diet with more vegetables, whole grains, and less sugar and fat.  
- Be physically active every day. Walking is a great start.  
- If you are overweight, losing even a small amount of weight helps.  

Changing your lifestyle can delay diabetes for years.  
It is not yet clear if it can stop it completely.

---

## How Is Type 2 Diabetes Diagnosed?

Type 2 diabetes often develops slowly.  
You may not have symptoms at first.  
It is often found during a routine check-up.  

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and health history.  
They will do a physical exam and test your blood sugar.  

You may need to give blood samples before meals and at different times of the day.  
A lab will test the blood.  

The HbA1c test shows your average blood sugar over the past two to three months.  

If blood sugar is very high, sugar may also show up in your urine.  
You can buy simple test strips at pharmacies to check urine at home.

---

## How Is Type 2 Diabetes Treated?

Treatment depends on your age, health, other conditions, and personal goals.  

Lifestyle changes can make a big difference.  
Losing weight and moving more can help your body use insulin better.  
This lowers blood sugar.  

Quitting smoking also helps protect your heart and blood vessels.  

Some people can control their diabetes with lifestyle changes alone.  
Others need medicine.  

Medicines include:

- Tablets that lower blood sugar  
- Insulin shots  
- Incretin mimetics – medicines that help your body make more insulin  

Some people take tablets and insulin together.  
Common medicines are metformin, gliptins, and sulfonylurea.  

For more information, visit **gesundheitsinformation.de**.

---

## How Can You Manage Type 2 Diabetes Every Day?

You can reduce the need for medicine by making healthy choices.  

- Try to lose even a small amount of weight.  
- Walk more. Take the stairs. Park farther from the store.  
- These small changes can help your blood sugar.  

If lifestyle changes are not enough, medicine is needed.  
You must take it every day, even if you feel fine.  

It can be hard to accept taking medicine for life.  
You may not feel sick, and you may not notice the benefits right away.  

But treating diabetes early helps protect your health.  
Understanding the disease makes it easier to see treatment as part of daily life.

---

## What Else Should You Know?

No matter what treatment you use, it is important to understand your condition.  
You can take an active role in your care.  

Talk to your doctor and other health experts.  
They can help with:

- Diabetes education  
- Nutrition advice  
- Foot care (podiatrist)  

You can also join a disease management program.  
These programs offer training, support, and care from diabetes specialists.  
They help you live well with diabetes.

# Goiter

A goiter is when the thyroid gland in your neck gets bigger.  
Doctors also call this condition a "struma."  
The most common reason is not getting enough iodine in your diet.  
Doctors can treat a goiter with medicine, surgery, or radiation therapy.

---

## Quick Facts

- A goiter means the thyroid gland is enlarged.  
- Many people do not notice the swelling at first. It often grows slowly over years.  
- The main cause is a lack of iodine in food.  
- Sometimes the whole thyroid grows bigger.  
- Other times, one or more lumps (called nodules) form in the gland.  
- A goiter can make the thyroid make too little or too much hormone.  
- Most goiters are not dangerous. They can be treated in different ways.  

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Goiter?

A goiter is a swollen thyroid gland.  
The thyroid is a small gland in the front of your neck.  
It makes hormones that help your body use energy, grow, and develop.  
It also helps your body reach puberty and keeps many body functions working right.

Your thyroid needs iodine to make hormones.  
Your body cannot make iodine on its own.  
You must get it from food.  
If you do not eat enough iodine, your thyroid may grow larger to try to make more hormones.

Iodine deficiency is the most common cause of goiter.  
In Germany, about 30 out of 100 adults and 44 out of 100 children do not get enough iodine.

Goiters can look different.  
The treatment depends on what caused the swelling.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people with a goiter do not feel any symptoms.  
The gland grows slowly, so you may not notice it.  
Many people find out they have a goiter during a routine doctor visit.

Some people have a thyroid that makes too little or too much hormone.  
But some people with a goiter have normal hormone levels.

Doctors can check hormone levels with a blood test.

If your thyroid makes too little hormone, you may feel tired, cold, or have trouble with constipation.  
You might also feel sluggish or gain weight.

When a goiter is linked to low hormone levels, it is often due to iodine deficiency or long-term inflammation of the thyroid.

Less often, a goiter causes symptoms of too much hormone.  
These include losing weight without trying, sweating a lot, or feeling restless.

---

## What Causes a Goiter?

The most common cause is not getting enough iodine in your food.  
Iodine is a trace element your body needs.  
Your body cannot make it, so you must get it from food.

In Central Europe, the soil has little iodine.  
This means plants and animals raised there have low iodine levels.  
For many years, Germany was considered a region with low iodine levels.  
But things have improved. Now, salt is often fortified with iodine, and many foods are made with added iodine.

Rarely, a goiter is caused by thyroid diseases.  
For example, Hashimoto’s thyroiditis or Basedow’s disease.  
In these conditions, your immune system attacks your thyroid.  
This can lead to hormone problems.

It is very rare for a goiter to be caused by a tumor.

---

## How Common Are Goiters?

Goiters are common in Germany.  
The chance of getting one goes up as you get older.  
About 18 out of 100 people aged 31 to 45 have a goiter.  
This number rises to about 24 out of 100 people aged 46 to 65.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

The thyroid usually grows slowly.  
The swelling does not hurt.  
You may not see or feel it until it becomes large.

There are different types of goiter:

- **Diffuse goiter:** The whole thyroid grows evenly and feels smooth. No lumps are present.  
- **Nodular goiter:** Lumps (nodules) form in the gland. These can be felt and seen.  

Some nodules make too much hormone. These are called "hot" nodules.  
Other nodules do not make any hormone. These are called "cold" nodules.

Goiters can affect hormone production in different ways.  
Some allow normal hormone levels.  
Others cause too much or too little hormone.

---

## How Can You Prevent a Goiter?

To avoid iodine deficiency and goiter, eat iodine-rich foods every day.

The German Nutrition Society recommends:

- 200 micrograms of iodine per day for people aged 13 to 50.  
- Less iodine is needed for younger and older people.  
- Pregnant and breastfeeding women need more iodine.

### Natural Sources of Iodine and Iodized Salt

- Fish like pollack, cod, and plaice are good sources.  
- Shellfish also contain iodine.  
- Eat seafood once or twice a week.  
- Use iodized salt when cooking.  
- Choose food products that contain iodized salt.  
- Dairy products and eggs have small amounts of iodine.  
- Organic foods often have less iodine.

> **Important:** The amount of iodine in iodized salt is legally controlled. It is safe and does not cause too much intake.  
> People with thyroid problems do not need to avoid iodized salt.

### Iodine in Vegetarian or Vegan Diets

- Most plant foods have very little iodine.  
- Some seaweed used in sushi has iodine.  
- But do not eat too much dried seaweed. It can have too much iodine.  
- Increase your intake of foods made with iodized salt.  
- Talk to your doctor before taking iodine supplements.

### Iodine for Pregnant and Breastfeeding Women

- Iodine is very important for your baby’s brain development.  
- During pregnancy, you need 230 micrograms of iodine per day.  
- During breastfeeding, you need 260 micrograms per day.  
- Ask your doctor if you should take an iodine supplement.

---

## How Is a Goiter Diagnosed?

You might find a goiter yourself.  
Or your doctor might find it during a regular check-up.

An ultrasound scan is the best way to confirm a goiter.  
It shows the size of the gland and whether there are lumps.

A blood test can check your hormone levels.  
It measures TSH, which is a hormone made by the brain to tell the thyroid to make more hormones.

- High TSH means your thyroid is not making enough hormones.  
- Low TSH means your thyroid is making too many hormones.

The blood test can also check for antibodies.  
These can show if your immune system is attacking your thyroid.

If cancer is suspected, your doctor may take a small sample of tissue.  
This is called a biopsy.  
A thin needle is used to collect a tiny piece of the thyroid for testing.

In some cases, an MRI or CT scan may be done.  
These scans give detailed pictures of the thyroid.  
They help doctors see the size and exact location of the goiter.

---

## How Is a Goiter Treated?

Most goiters are not harmful.  
Treatment depends on the size of the goiter and whether it is growing.

Your doctor may choose one of these options:

- **Medicine:** To help control hormone levels or shrink the gland.  
- **Surgery:** To remove part or all of the thyroid gland.  
- **Radiotherapy:** Using radioactive iodine to shrink the gland.

Your doctor will decide the best treatment based on your situation.

# Asthma

Asthma is a condition that makes it hard to breathe. It happens when the airways in the lungs become narrow. This can cause sudden attacks. During an attack, a person may feel short of breath, wheeze, or cough.

Most people with asthma start having symptoms as children. But asthma can begin at any age. With the right treatment, most people can live a normal life with few or no symptoms.

---

## Quick Facts

- In Germany, about 4 out of every 100 children and 6 out of every 100 adults have asthma.
- Doctors divide asthma into two types: allergic and non-allergic. The type depends on what causes the symptoms.
- Symptoms often come on suddenly. They may happen at night.
- Asthma does not always get worse over time.
- With good treatment, most people can live without many symptoms.
- Treatment includes medicine and healthy habits like regular exercise.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat asthma on your own.

---

## What Is Asthma?

Asthma is a long-term condition that affects the airways. The airways can become narrow and swollen. This makes breathing difficult.

During an asthma attack, you may:
- Wheeze (make a whistling sound when breathing)
- Cough
- Feel short of breath

Without treatment, your body may not get enough oxygen. This can reduce your energy and fitness.

Asthma does not always get worse. With proper care, most people can live with few or no symptoms. Over time, you will learn what helps you and what to avoid.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

In children, asthma often shows up as:
- Coughing
- Wheezing or whistling when breathing

Teenagers and adults may also have:
- Trouble breathing, especially during an attack
- Shortness of breath when exercising
- Noisy breathing (wheezing, rattling, or whistling)
- A tight feeling in the chest
- A strong urge to cough

Symptoms usually come in sudden attacks. An attack may start with mild breathing trouble. It can quickly get worse. Many people have attacks at night. This can leave them tired and sleepy the next day.

---

## What Increases the Risk of Asthma?

Some people are more likely to get asthma. Risk factors include:
- A family history of allergies, eczema, or hay fever
- Being born with a low birth weight
- Being a boy (boys are more likely to have asthma than girls)
- Parents who smoke

---

## What Causes Asthma?

In people with asthma, the immune system reacts too strongly to certain triggers. But the immune system only reacts if a trigger reaches the airways.

There are two main types of asthma:

### Allergic Asthma (Extrinsic Asthma)
This type is caused by things you breathe in from the outside. Common triggers include:
- Tobacco smoke (from smoking or secondhand smoke)
- Pollen from plants
- Pet dander (tiny bits of skin or fur from animals)
- Dust mite droppings
- Certain foods
- Cold air
- Perfumes
- Car exhaust
- Some chemicals

If you have allergic asthma, you may react to one or more of these.

### Non-Allergic Asthma (Intrinsic Asthma)
This type is not caused by outside allergens. Instead, it is triggered by things inside the body. These include:
- Infections in the airways (from bacteria or viruses)
- Stress or strong emotions
- Physical exercise
- Certain painkillers like acetylsalicylic acid (also known as aspirin) and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)

No matter the cause, asthma affects the lungs in the same way:
- Immune cells in the airway lining become active
- The muscles around the airways tighten
- The lining of the airways swells
- Thick mucus builds up

When all these happen together, the airways become too narrow. This causes an asthma attack.

---

## How Common Is Asthma?

Asthma can start at any age. But most people first notice symptoms as children or teens. In Germany, about 4 out of every 100 children and 6 out of every 100 adults have asthma.

Asthma is the most common long-term illness in children.

---

## What Is the Outlook for People with Asthma?

Asthma affects people differently. Some children grow out of it. They have few or no symptoms as adults. Others continue to have symptoms. In some cases, symptoms get worse.

It is important to find out what triggers your asthma. Then, try to avoid those triggers.

Your outlook depends on:
- Getting treatment early
- Taking your medicine as prescribed
- Doing healthy things like exercise
- Using breathing techniques

Asthma often happens in people who already have allergies. These can include hay fever, eye irritation (conjunctivitis), or eczema. Symptoms may change with the season or other factors. Sometimes they go away for a while.

---

## How Is Asthma Diagnosed?

Many health problems can cause breathing issues. So doctors use several tests to confirm asthma.

The diagnosis process includes:
- A detailed talk with your doctor. You will discuss your medical history, lifestyle, and symptoms.
- A physical exam. The doctor checks your lungs, heart, and blood circulation.
- Lung function tests:
  - Spirometry: measures how much air you can breathe in and out.
  - Peak flow measurement: measures how fast you can blow air out.

If the results are unclear, your doctor may do more tests. These could include allergy tests or tests of your airways.

For more information on symptoms and diagnosis, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## How Is Asthma Treated?

The goal of treatment is to reduce symptoms and prevent attacks. The aim is to live as normal a life as possible.

There are safe medicines that work well and have few side effects. These medicines are safe to use during pregnancy. Your doctor will help you choose the right one.

There are two main types of asthma medicine:

### 1. Fast-Acting Medicine (Relievers)
- Used only when symptoms appear
- Works quickly to open the airways
- Good for mild asthma

### 2. Daily Medicine (Controllers)
- Taken every day, even when you feel fine
- Helps reduce swelling and inflammation in the airways
- Needed for more severe asthma

If your asthma is mild, you may only need relievers. But if your airways are always inflamed, you need daily medicine to stay in control.

Other helpful steps include:
- Regular exercise
- Learning special breathing techniques
- Getting vaccinated against the flu and pneumococcal bacteria

> **Important:** Try to avoid triggers when possible. Know if your triggers are pets, dust, or cold air. But if you take your medicine correctly, you may not need to worry too much about triggers.

---

## What Is Life Like with Asthma?

Asthma can affect many parts of daily life. Nighttime attacks can leave you tired and unable to focus during the day. You may also feel less fit.

It takes time to learn how to manage asthma. This is true for you and your family. The more you know, the better you can support each other.

> **Important:** Knowing your condition helps you act fast during an attack. This can prevent emergencies and avoid hospital visits.

---

## What Support Is Available?

You can get help from:
- Your doctor
- A specialist in lung health (pulmonologist)
- Rehabilitation clinics that offer asthma training

Asthma training teaches you:
- How asthma works and how it is treated
- How to spot early signs of an attack
- How to avoid triggers
- What to do in an emergency

You can also join an asthma support group. These groups meet regularly. They let people with asthma, and their families, share experiences and help each other.

To find a group near you, visit the website of the **National Contact and Information Point for Encouraging and Supporting Self-Help Groups (NAKOS)**.

# Chronic Itching (Pruritus)

Itchy skin that lasts a long time can be very hard to live with.  
Scratching gives only a short break from the itch.  
But scratching too much damages the skin.  
This damage makes the itch worse.  
This creates a cycle: itch leads to scratch, scratch leads to more itch.

The cause of the itch can be hard to find.  
Because of this, treatment can take time.  
Sometimes, the cause is not clear even after many tests.

---

## Quick Facts

- When you feel an itch, your body wants to scratch it.  
- Scratching too much harms the skin.  
- Damaged skin causes more itching.  
- This creates a cycle that is hard to break.  
- Dry skin and skin diseases are not the only causes.  
- Problems with nerves, liver, or kidneys can also cause itching.  
- Sometimes, no clear cause can be found.  
- Good skin care can help.  
- But treatment may take weeks or months.  
- Finding the right mix of treatments can take time.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Chronic Itching?

Chronic itching means your skin itches for more than 6 weeks.  
You may feel the urge to scratch often.  
The itch can happen in one spot or all over your body.  
It can make daily life very hard.

Many things can cause itching.  
Some are skin problems.  
Others are health issues inside the body.

If doctors find and treat the cause, the itching often goes away.  
But sometimes, the itching stays even after the cause is treated.  
In these cases, the itching becomes a condition on its own.

Even though many things can cause itching, the treatment is often similar.

Doctors may use creams or ointments.  
They may also prescribe pills.  
Light therapy (phototherapy) can help some people.  
Talking with a therapist (psychotherapy) may also help.

It can take several weeks to find the right treatment plan.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main symptom is a strong need to scratch.  
Scratching gives quick relief.  
But the relief only lasts a short time.  
So your brain tells you to scratch again when the itch returns.

Over time, scratching too much can change your skin.  
These changes include:

- Red, raw, or bleeding skin  
- Open sores, scabs, thickened skin, lumps, or scars  
- Light or dark patches on the skin

If the itching started from a skin disease, the original problem may no longer be visible.  
This is because scratch marks cover it up.

If bacteria get into the damaged skin, it can become inflamed.

Chronic itching can affect your mood and daily life.  
You may have trouble sleeping.  
You might feel sad, anxious, or stressed.  
You may feel self-conscious around others because of visible marks or scars.

---

## What Causes Chronic Itching?

Scientists now know that itching is not just a mild pain.  
Special nerves in the skin send itch signals to the brain.

Skin cells, nerve cells, and blood cells can release chemicals that cause itching.  
If these nerves are extra sensitive, even a small itch can feel very strong.

When you scratch, it hurts a little.  
This pain makes the itch feel less for a moment.  
Your brain sees this as a good thing.  
So it tells you to scratch again.  
This creates the scratch-itch cycle.

Many health problems can cause chronic itching.  
These include:

- Skin diseases like eczema, psoriasis, or hives  
- Dry skin, especially in older adults  
- Diabetes or an overactive thyroid  
- Infections from viruses or parasites (like shingles, HIV, scabies, or head lice)  
- Rarely, cancer — especially blood cancers or liver tumors  
- Long-term kidney or liver disease  
- Nerve problems or brain disorders (like nerve damage)  
- Mental health issues like obsessive-compulsive disorder  
- Side effects from some medicines (like certain antidepressants or antibiotics)  
- Skin problems that only happen during pregnancy

Sometimes, more than one cause is present.  
But even after many tests, doctors may not find the cause.

---

## How Common Is Chronic Itching?

About 14 out of every 100 people in Germany have chronic itching.  
One in three people who see a doctor report itching.  
This is even more common in older adults.  
Up to two out of every three older adults have chronic itching.  
Women are more likely to have it than men.

---

## How Is Chronic Itching Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask you questions about your itching.  
They may use a written questionnaire to help.

Important questions include:

- When did the itching start?  
- Where does it happen? How bad is it? How long does it last?  
- What did your skin look like before you scratched it?  
- Do you have any allergies?  
- What medicines are you taking?  
- Do you have other symptoms? Any health problems?  
- Are people close to you also itchy?  
- Does anything make the itch worse? Does it happen at certain times?  
- Has your diet changed recently?  
- Did you get new furniture or a pet?  
- Do any family members have similar symptoms?  
- How is the itching affecting your life?  
- Is it causing sleep problems or anxiety?

> **Tip:** Keeping a diary of your itching can help your doctor understand it better.

Your doctor will also examine your skin.  
If they suspect a specific health problem, they may order tests.  
These can include blood tests, ultrasound, or MRI scans.

They may also take a small sample of skin or fluid from the affected area.

---

## How Is Chronic Itching Treated?

Finding the cause can take time.  
Treatment does not work right away.  
It may take weeks or months to see improvement.  
You must keep using the treatment even if it feels slow.

Treatment has two goals:  
1. Fix the underlying cause if possible.  
2. Reduce the itching itself.

### General Care for Your Skin

- Do not take hot showers or baths too often.  
- Use lukewarm water.  
- Use gentle soap.  
- Use moisturizing creams or lotions every day.  
- Dry your skin gently after washing.  
- Keep your home cool and humid.  
- Wear soft, loose clothing.  
- Avoid wool, rough fabrics, and strong cleaning products.  
- Use bandages that hold in moisture. These protect your skin from new scratches.  
- Try to reduce stress.  
- Relaxation methods like yoga or acupuncture may help.

### Creams and Ointments for the Skin

- Use cooling lotions with ingredients like urea, menthol, camphor, or numbing agents.  
- Anti-inflammatory creams can help.  
- Capsaicin (from chili peppers) can reduce pain and improve blood flow.  
- Light therapy (phototherapy) may help if the itching comes from a skin disease or internal condition.  
  This uses special ultraviolet light on the skin.

### Pills and Medicines

- Antihistamines can help with itching from allergies.  
- Some medicines for depression or seizures can also reduce itching.  
- Other medicines can change how pain signals travel or affect your immune system.

There is no single medicine that works for everyone.  
You may need to try several before finding what helps.  
Each person must work with their doctor to find the best option.

### Therapy for the Mind

Therapy can help you change the habit of scratching.  
It teaches you how to manage the urge to scratch.  
Stress management and training programs can improve your daily life.

# Stomach Ulcer

A stomach ulcer is a sore in the lining of the stomach. It usually happens because of a bacterial infection or long-term use of certain painkillers.

Most stomach ulcers can be treated successfully. This page explains the common signs, possible problems, and how doctors treat them.

---

## Quick Facts

- The most common causes are an infection with *Helicobacter pylori* bacteria or using painkillers for a long time.
- Ulcers from painkillers often do not cause symptoms until they lead to serious problems like bleeding.
- In rare cases, a stomach ulcer can cause a hole in the stomach wall.
- Common symptoms include pain in the upper belly, feeling full too soon, loss of appetite, nausea, and vomiting.
- The chance of getting a stomach ulcer goes up with age.
- Doctors usually diagnose a stomach ulcer with a gastroscopy and a small tissue sample.
- Treatment usually includes medicine to reduce stomach acid and, if needed, antibiotics.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## Possible Problems

If a stomach ulcer is not found and treated, it can lead to serious issues.

The most common problem is bleeding.  
See a doctor right away if you notice:

- Stool that is black or very dark
- Vomiting blood (red or black)
- Signs of anemia, such as extreme tiredness, shortness of breath when active, or pale skin

Frequent vomiting after eating is another warning sign.  
This can happen if scar tissue forms near the opening between the stomach and the intestines. The scar can narrow the opening, so food cannot pass through easily.

In very rare cases, a stomach ulcer can cause a hole in the stomach wall.  
This causes sudden, severe pain. It is life-threatening.  
If you think this might be happening, call emergency services (112) right away.

---

## What Is a Stomach Ulcer?

A stomach ulcer is a deep sore in the inner lining of the stomach.  
It happens when the stomach’s protective layer is damaged.

The most common cause is an infection with *Helicobacter pylori* bacteria.  
Another common cause is using non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) regularly.

The risk of getting a stomach ulcer increases with age.

The main symptom is pain in the upper belly.  
To find out if you have a stomach ulcer, doctors usually do a gastroscopy and take a small tissue sample.

Treatment usually includes medicine to reduce stomach acid and, if needed, antibiotics.

If left untreated, a stomach ulcer can lead to serious problems.

---

## Symptoms of a Stomach Ulcer

Many people with stomach ulcers have no symptoms at all.  
This is especially true if the ulcer was caused by painkillers.

When symptoms do appear, they are often vague and not unique to ulcers.  
They can include:

- A feeling of pressure or fullness in the upper belly
- Not wanting to eat
- Nausea, sometimes with vomiting
- Bloating, gas, or irregular bowel movements
- Heartburn or acid coming up from the stomach
- Pain in the upper belly — this may happen after eating, not before

---

## How Does a Stomach Ulcer Develop?

The two main causes are:

1. Infection with *Helicobacter pylori* bacteria  
2. Long-term use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)

*Helicobacter pylori* bacteria can grow in the stomach lining.  
They damage the lining and make the stomach produce more acid.  
This weakens the stomach’s natural protection.

Common NSAIDs include:
- Acetylsalicylic acid (like aspirin)
- Ibuprofen
- Naproxen
- Diclofenac

These medicines stop the body from making a hormone called prostaglandin.  
Prostaglandin helps protect the stomach lining from acid.  
Without it, the stomach lining is more likely to be damaged by acid and bacteria.

Sometimes, both causes happen together.

> **Note:** Taking NSAIDs with cortisone medicine can make stomach damage worse.

---

## How Can You Prevent a Stomach Ulcer?

There is no strong scientific proof that food, smoking, or stress cause stomach ulcers.  
But if you notice that greasy food, alcohol, or stress make your symptoms worse, try to avoid those triggers.

Using painkillers regularly can increase your risk.  
Your doctor may suggest taking medicine to reduce stomach acid at the same time.

Talk to your doctor about your personal risk and whether you need extra protection for your stomach.

---

## How Is a Stomach Ulcer Diagnosed?

If your doctor suspects a stomach ulcer, they will:

1. Feel your belly with their hands to check for tenderness.
2. Perform a gastroscopy — a thin tube with a camera is passed through your mouth into your stomach.
3. Take a small tissue sample (biopsy) during the test.

The sample is checked for:
- *Helicobacter pylori* bacteria
- Signs of infection
- Changes that look like cancer

---

## How Is a Stomach Ulcer Treated?

Some stomach ulcers heal on their own in 2 to 3 months.  
But they often come back without treatment.

Treatment depends on the results of the gastroscopy and biopsy.

### If no bacteria or cancer is found:
- Doctors prescribe proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), such as omeprazole or pantoprazole.
- These reduce stomach acid.
- You take the medicine for 4 to 8 weeks.

### If the ulcer is caused by NSAIDs:
- Stop using the painkiller if possible.
- Switch to a different painkiller if needed.
- Avoid smoking and alcohol, or take a break from them.

### If the ulcer is caused by *Helicobacter pylori*:
- You get two different antibiotics plus a proton pump inhibitor (called triple therapy).
- This treatment lasts 1 to 2 weeks.

In some cases, doctors may use four medicines: three antibiotics and a proton pump inhibitor (quadruple therapy).  
This is used if the bacteria are resistant to common antibiotics.

After treatment, your doctor will check if the bacteria are gone.  
This usually happens about 4 weeks after finishing the antibiotics.

They may do a special breath test (13C breath test) to check for the bacteria.

If the test is still positive, you will get another round of antibiotics and acid-reducing medicine.

### If there is severe bleeding:
- Doctors treat the ulcer with a minimally invasive procedure (endoscopy).
- This involves a small cut in the belly wall.
- In some cases, open surgery may be needed.

--- 

Always follow your doctor’s advice. Do not stop or change your treatment without talking to them.

# Gallstones

Gallstones are hard pieces that form from thickened bile.  
They can cause sudden, sharp pain in the upper belly.  
Some people have gallstones but never feel any pain.  

This article explains how gallstones form and how they are treated.  

---

## Quick Facts

- Gallstones are hard pieces of thickened bile.  
- They can cause sudden, sharp pain in the upper belly.  
- Many people with gallstones do not have any symptoms.  
- Women and older adults are more likely to get gallstones.  
- Doctors usually find gallstones with an ultrasound scan.  
- Removing the gallbladder is one of the most common surgeries in Germany.  
- Surgery is only recommended if symptoms keep coming back or if there are serious problems.  

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Are Gallstones?

Gallstones are hard pieces that form in the gallbladder or bile ducts.  

The gallbladder is a small, pear-shaped organ under the liver on the right side of the belly.  

The liver makes about one liter of bile every day.  
Bile helps the body digest fats.  
After eating, most bile flows directly into the small intestine.  
Between meals, the rest of the bile is stored in the gallbladder.  
There, it becomes thicker.  

In Germany, many people have gallbladder surgery each year.  
About 170,000 people have this surgery every year.  
Most do so because gallstones are causing pain or other health problems.  

But many gallstones do not cause any trouble.  
If you have no pain, treatment is usually not needed.  
Sometimes, doctors remove gallstones stuck in the bile ducts.  
Or they remove the entire gallbladder.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many people with gallstones feel no symptoms at all.  
About 2 to 4 out of 100 people with gallstones will have noticeable symptoms within one year.  
Of those who already had symptoms, about half will have them again within two years.  

The most common symptom is sudden, severe pain in the upper belly.  
This is called a gallbladder attack or colic.  

The pain happens when the gallbladder squeezes, but the bile cannot flow out because a stone blocks the way.  
The pain comes in waves.  
It can spread to the back or the right shoulder.  
It usually lasts less than an hour and goes away completely within a few hours.  

Other possible symptoms include:  
- Burping  
- Gas  
- Nausea  
- Vomiting  
- A feeling of fullness or bloating  

Bile duct stones can also cause yellowing of the skin and eyes.  
This is called jaundice.  
It happens when bile cannot leave the body.  
The bile pigment bilirubin builds up in the blood.  
This causes the skin and eyes to turn yellow.  
Urine may become dark.  
Stool may become pale or bright in color.  

Jaundice happens when the bile duct stays blocked for too long.  
The body cannot get rid of bilirubin, which comes from broken-down red blood cells.

---

## What Causes Gallstones?

Bile is made of water and other substances.  
Some of these substances do not dissolve well in water.  
When they clump together, they can form gallstones.  

The exact reason why this happens is not fully known.  
But it may be due to an imbalance in the bile.  
For example, too much cholesterol in the bile can lead to stones.  

Most gallstones are made of cholesterol.  
Some are made of pigment.  
Pigment stones are made of calcium and bilirubin.  

Gallstones usually form in the gallbladder.  
But they can also form in the bile ducts.  
Most bile duct stones start in the gallbladder and move into the main bile duct.  

When stones are in the gallbladder, it is called cholecystolithiasis.  
When they are in the bile ducts, it is called choledocholithiasis.

---

## What Increases the Risk of Gallstones?

You are more likely to get gallstones if you:  

- Are over 40 years old  
- Have family members with gallstones  
- Are a woman (hormones may play a role)  
- Are pregnant  
- Take birth control pills or hormone therapy during menopause  
- Have a gallbladder that does not work well  
- Have had a large part of the small intestine removed  
- Have diabetes  
- Have liver disease caused by long-term alcohol use or other problems  
- Are overweight  
- Lose a lot of weight quickly (for example, after weight-loss surgery)  
- Use special high-calorie liquid supplements or tube feeding  
- Have a condition that causes red blood cells to break down too fast (hemolysis)

---

## How Common Are Gallstones?

About 5 to 25 out of every 100 people have gallstones.  
They are more common in women and older adults.  
Most people with gallstones do not have any symptoms.

---

## How Do Gallstones Develop?

If you have typical symptoms, the risk of complications increases.  
Complications can include:  
- Inflammation of the gallbladder  
- Inflammation of the pancreas  
- Rarely, a blockage in the intestine  

About 0.2 out of every 100 people with gallstones will have a complication each year.

---

## How Are Gallstones Diagnosed?

Many people find out they have gallstones by accident.  
For example, an ultrasound scan done for another reason may show them.  

If you have symptoms, your doctor will ask about your pain and do an exam.  
An ultrasound scan of the belly is usually the first test.  
It is simple and shows the gallbladder and bile ducts clearly.  

In most cases, this is enough to make a diagnosis.  
But sometimes, other tests are needed to rule out other causes.  

Diagnosing stones in the bile ducts is harder.  
Ultrasound may not show them well.  

In such cases, doctors may use:  
- **Endoscopic retrograde cholangiography (ERC):**  
  A thin tube is passed through the mouth, down the throat, and into the stomach and small intestine.  
  A dye is injected into the bile duct.  
  X-rays then show the stones.  
  If stones are found, they can be removed during the same test.  

- **Magnetic resonance cholangiography (MRC):**  
  This creates detailed images of the bile ducts using magnets.  
  It does not use radiation.  
  No tube is needed.  
  But stones cannot be removed during this test.  
  A separate surgery is needed if removal is required.  

- **Endoscopic ultrasound:**  
  A small ultrasound device is placed on the end of a tube.  
  It gives very clear images of the bile ducts.  
  It does not use radiation.  
  But stones cannot be removed during this test.

---

## How Are Gallstones Treated?

If gallstones cause no symptoms, treatment is usually not needed.  
Many people live with gallstones for years without any problems.  
All treatments carry risks.  
Surgery always has some risk.

To ease pain from a gallbladder attack:  
- Painkillers can help.  
- Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), like ibuprofen, are especially effective.  
- These work better than other pain medicines.  
- Medicines can also help with bloating or nausea.  

Medicines to dissolve gallstones are rarely used.  
They take a long time and often do not work.

The only way to prevent future attacks is to remove the gallbladder.  
Whether to do this depends on:  
- How often the pain comes back  
- How bad the pain is  
- The risk of complications  

If you have a condition called a porcelain gallbladder, surgery is usually recommended.  
This is a rare condition where the gallbladder wall becomes hard and full of calcium.  
It increases the risk of gallbladder cancer.  
Even if you have no symptoms, doctors often suggest removing the gallbladder as a safety step.

For more information on treatment options, including the pros and cons of surgery and how life changes after gallbladder removal, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

# Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma

Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma is a type of cancer that starts in the lymphatic system.  
It is also sometimes called lymph node cancer.  
There are about 30 different types of this disease.  
This article explains what these lymphomas are.  
It also covers how doctors diagnose and treat them.

---

## Quick Facts

- Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma is a cancer in the lymphatic system.  
- The lymphatic system includes lymph nodes, the spleen, and the tonsils.  
- Lymph tissue is also found in other parts of the body, like the stomach, intestines, and skin.  
- The cancer starts in white blood cells called lymphocytes.  
- These cancer cells often grow in lymph nodes.  
- They can also spread to other organs like the liver.  
- Some lymphomas grow slowly. Others grow very fast.  
- The exact type of lymphoma determines the best treatment.  

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

---

## What Is Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma?

Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma is a cancer that begins in the lymphatic system.  
The lymphatic system helps the body fight infections.  
It includes lymph nodes, the spleen, and the tonsils.  
But it also has tissue in places like the stomach, bowel, and skin.

The cancer comes from white blood cells called mature lymphocytes.  
These cells multiply out of control and form tumors.  
The word “lymphoma” means “swelling of the lymph nodes.”  
When this swelling is caused by cancer, doctors call it a malignant lymphoma.

---

### Hodgkin’s vs. Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma

Doctors used to divide lymph cancers into two groups:

- Hodgkin’s lymphoma, which has a special type of cancer cell.  
- All other lymph cancers, which are now called non-Hodgkin’s lymphomas.

There are about 30 different types of non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma.  
Doctors no longer use this term officially for classification.  
But it is still widely used in everyday medical practice.

---

### Types of Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma

Since the 1970s, doctors have grouped non-Hodgkin’s lymphomas into two main types:

- **Slow-growing (indolent)** lymphomas  
- **Fast-growing (aggressive)** lymphomas

Examples of slow-growing types include:

- Follicular lymphoma  
- Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)

An example of a fast-growing type is:

- Diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL)

Most non-Hodgkin’s lymphomas start in B-lymphocytes.  
These are a type of white blood cell.  
Doctors call these B-cell lymphomas.

Some lymphomas start in T-lymphocytes or natural killer cells.  
These are called T-cell or NK-cell lymphomas.

> **Important:** Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is actually a type of non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma.  
> It starts in mature B-cells in the lymphatic system.  
> Unlike other lymphomas, the cancer cells often show up in the blood.

When doctors say “leukemia,” they usually mean cancer from immature white blood cells in the bone marrow.  
An example is acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).

---

## What Symptoms Can Occur?

People with non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma often first notice swollen lymph nodes.  
These lumps are usually painless.  
They often appear in the neck, under the arms, or in the groin.  
Sometimes several areas are swollen at once.

The lymph nodes may also be inside the body.  
For example, in the chest or stomach.  
These cannot be felt from the outside.

In rare cases, the lymphoma can affect the brain or spinal cord.  
This is called central nervous system involvement.

Other possible symptoms include:

- Fever that does not go away  
- Heavy night sweats  
- Losing weight without trying  
- A dry cough or pressure in the chest  
- Stomach pain  
- An enlarged liver or spleen  
- Back pain  
- Frequent infections

No symptom is unique to non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma.  
These signs can also happen with infections or other illnesses.  
If symptoms last for weeks or months, see a doctor.  
Your general practitioner can help figure out what is causing the problem.  
They may refer you to a specialist for further tests.

---

## What Causes Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma?

Cancer starts when a single cell changes its DNA.  
This change causes the cell to grow and divide uncontrollably.  
In non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, this happens in a lymphocyte.

For most people, doctors do not know why this happens.  
It likely takes several factors to trigger the disease.

Some things may increase the risk:

- Radiation therapy or chemotherapy  
- Infection with the Helicobacter pylori bacterium (linked to stomach lymphoma)  
- Infection with the Epstein-Barr virus (linked to Burkitt lymphoma)

> **Important:** In Germany, if you were exposed to the chemical benzene at work, your lymphatic disease may be recognized as an occupational illness.

---

## How Common Is It?

Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma is rare compared to breast or prostate cancer.  
It is more common in older adults than in younger people.

The most common types are:

- Diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL)  
- Multiple myeloma  
- Follicular lymphoma  
- Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)

Less common types include:

- Marginal zone lymphoma (including MALT lymphoma)  
- Mantle cell lymphoma  
- Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia  
- Burkitt lymphoma

---

## How Does It Progress?

The course of the disease depends on the type of lymphoma.

### Aggressive Lymphomas

These grow quickly over weeks or months.  
They often respond well to strong treatment.  
Many people can be cured with proper therapy.

### Indolent (Slow-Growing) Lymphomas

These grow slowly over years or even decades.  
People may not need treatment right away.  
Treatment is usually started only when symptoms appear.  
These lymphomas cannot usually be cured.  
But treatment can keep them under control for a long time.  
Many people live normal lives for many years.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

If a doctor suspects non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, they will take a sample of tissue.  
This is usually a whole lymph node or a suspicious area.  
They send the sample to a lab for detailed testing.  
This helps identify the exact type of lymphoma.

### Staging: Finding Out How Far It Has Spread

After the type is known, doctors check how much the cancer has spread.  
This is called staging.  
It helps plan the best treatment.

Staging tests may include:

- A detailed medical history  
- A physical exam  
- Blood tests  
- Imaging scans (like CT or PET scans)  
- A bone marrow test (if needed)  
- A test of the fluid around the brain and spinal cord (if needed)

All these results help doctors decide on the best treatment.

### Checking Overall Health

Before treatment starts, doctors check your heart, lungs, and thyroid.  
This helps them know if you can handle the planned therapy.  
If you have other health problems, they may adjust the treatment.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the type of lymphoma.  
It also depends on how far it has spread.  
Your age and general health matter too.

### Chemotherapy

This is a common treatment.  
It uses drugs to slow down or stop cell growth.  
These drugs are called cytostatics.  
They are often combined with antibodies that target lymphoma cells.  
This is called immunochemotherapy.

### New Treatments

Scientists are testing new drugs and therapies.  
Some of these are already approved and used successfully.  
They are designed to target specific types of lymphoma.

> **Important:** Surgery is not used to cure non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma.  
> The cancer usually affects the whole body, even if only one lymph node is swollen.  
> Doctors only remove a lymph node to get a sample for diagnosis.

For more information on chemotherapy and side effects, visit the website of the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## After Treatment: What Happens Next?

After treatment ends, you will need regular check-ups.  
The schedule depends on the type of lymphoma and the treatment you had.

These check-ups help:

- Find a return of the cancer early  
- Spot long-term side effects of treatment

You will be seen regularly at first.  
Then the visits become less frequent over time.  
During each visit, the doctor will:

- Ask about your symptoms  
- Do a physical exam  
- Check your blood  
- Possibly do imaging tests

Talk to your treating doctor about how often you need to come back.  
And which tests are needed.

If the lymphoma cannot be cured, regular check-ups help catch problems early.  
You and your doctor can discuss new treatment options and support.  
The goal is to keep your quality of life as high as possible.

---

## Life With Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma

Many people want to stay active during treatment.  
Here are some ways to help manage the illness and its effects:
