# Dust Mite Allergy

Dust mite allergies often start in childhood or during the teenage years.  
The symptoms are not caused by dust itself.  
They are caused by tiny particles in the waste of dust mites.  
These particles spread through the air when dust moves around.

## Quick Facts

- The real cause of the allergy is not dust. It is tiny bits in dust mite waste.
- Most people first get this allergy before age 20.
- No home is free of dust mites. They live in beds, carpets, rugs, couches, and curtains.
- When allergy symptoms affect the nose and sinuses, it is called allergic rhinitis.
- Medicine like tablets and nasal sprays can help reduce symptoms.
- A treatment called hyposensitization can help reduce symptoms over time.
- This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is a Dust Mite Allergy?

Your body reacts strongly to tiny particles in dust mite waste.  
These particles are not in the dust itself.  
They are in the droppings of dust mites.  
When dust moves around, it carries these tiny waste particles through the air.

Dust mites live in many homes.  
They are found in beds, carpets, rugs, couches, and curtains.  
Because dust mites are everywhere, people with this allergy often have symptoms all year long.

If the allergy affects the nose and sinuses, it is called allergic rhinitis.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may sneeze a lot.  
Your nose may run or feel blocked.  
You might feel tired or weak if symptoms are bad.  
Your eyes may water or itch.  
Your eyelids may swell.

You might also have asthma-like symptoms.  
These include coughing, wheezing, and trouble breathing.

Dust mite allergy symptoms are usually milder than hay fever.  
But they happen all year, not just in one season.  
Symptoms are often worse at night and in the morning.  
This is because dust mites live in mattresses, pillows, and bedding.

## What Causes a Dust Mite Allergy?

Your body overreacts to things that are usually harmless.  
These things are called allergens.  
In this case, the allergens are in dust mite waste.

When your body first meets the allergen, it makes special proteins called antibodies.  
These antibodies attach to certain cells in your body.  
If you meet the allergen again, those cells react fast.  
They release chemicals like histamine.  
These chemicals cause allergy symptoms such as sneezing or itchy eyes.

It is hard to avoid dust.  
When dust moves, it floats in the air.  
You can breathe in the dust and the allergens on it.

Some people are more likely to get allergies if they have family members with allergies.  
Air pollution and cigarette smoke can also increase the risk.

## How Common Is This Allergy?

About 1 in 4 people in countries like Germany have allergic rhinitis.  
Most people develop it before age 20.

Dust mite allergies often start in childhood or teenage years.  
They usually last a lifetime.

If allergic rhinitis goes on for years, it can lead to asthma.  
This is called the “allergic march.”  
It means the allergy starts in the nose and later affects the lungs.

Sometimes, people with dust mite allergies also become allergic to certain foods.  
This is called cross-reactivity.  
It is less common with dust mite allergies than with hay fever.  
But some people with dust mite allergies may also react to shellfish, mussels, crabs, or snails.

Severe symptoms can lead to other problems.  
For example, sinus infections are more likely.  
Allergic rhinitis can also make your nose and throat more sensitive.  
This means irritants like smoke or dry air can cause symptoms.

## How Can You Prevent Symptoms?

The best way to prevent symptoms is to reduce contact with dust mites.  
You can’t remove them completely, but you can lower their numbers.

In the bedroom, try these steps:

- Wipe the floor with a damp cloth.
- Use covers that block dust mites on your mattress and pillows.
- Remove items that collect dust, like heavy curtains and soft furniture.
- Wash bedding in hot water — at least 60 degrees Celsius.

Dust mites like warm, damp places.  
Keep your bedroom cool — between 18 and 20 degrees Celsius.  
Open windows often to let in fresh air.

Avoid using humidifiers and houseplants in the bedroom.  
They make the air more humid, which helps dust mites grow.

You can also use sprays that kill dust mites.  
These sprays contain special chemicals that target mites and ticks.  
Spray them on mattress covers or bedding.

It is not clear how well special air filters work for dust mites.

## How Is the Allergy Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and your health history.  
They may do a skin test.  
This is called a skin prick test.

The doctor puts small drops of different allergens on your forearm.  
Then they gently prick the skin.  
If the skin turns red and swells like a mosquito bite, you are allergic to that substance.

You might also need a blood test.  
Or a provocation test.  
In this test, the doctor puts a small amount of allergen into your nose or eyes.  
If your nose swells, you sneeze, or your nose runs, you are likely allergic.

## How Is the Allergy Treated?

Several types of medicine can help with symptoms:

- Antihistamines
- Corticosteroids
- Chromones (also called mast cell stabilizers)
- Leukotriene receptor antagonists
- Decongestant nasal drops or sprays

There are also non-drug options:

- Saline (salt water) nasal sprays
- Nasal washes (also called nasal irrigation)

These can help ease symptoms.  
But they usually do not work as well as medicine.

A long-term treatment called allergen-specific immunotherapy can help.  
It is also called desensitization.  
It works like a vaccine.  
You get small, regular doses of the allergen.  
This can be done by injection under the skin or by placing drops under the tongue.

This treatment lasts at least three to five years.  
It can reduce your body’s reaction to dust mites over time.

For more details about this treatment, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

## More Information

You can find more about dust mite allergies at: [allergieinformationsdienst.de](https://www.allergieinformationsdienst.de) (in German)

# Osteoarthritis

Osteoarthritis is a condition where the cushioning material between bones in a joint wears down.  
It often happens as people get older.  
The main signs are joint pain and stiffness.  
This article explains the symptoms, how it gets worse over time, and how it is treated.

---

## Quick Facts

- In the early stages, pain only happens when you put weight on the joint.  
- As the condition gets worse, the pain increases. It can make daily tasks harder.  
- Anyone can get osteoarthritis, no matter their age.  
- Many people develop it as part of getting older.  
- The most common signs are pain and stiffness in the joints.  
- Staying active and moving regularly is important, even if you have osteoarthritis.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor.  
> Do not use this to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Osteoarthritis?

Osteoarthritis happens when the soft tissue between bones, called cartilage, gets thinner and rougher.  
Over time, the joint becomes stiff and painful.  
This makes movement harder.

Some joint wear is normal with age.  
But osteoarthritis can also start in middle age.  
The most common types are:

- Osteoarthritis in the knee  
- Osteoarthritis in the hip  
- Osteoarthritis in the fingers  
- Osteoarthritis in the spine joints (also called facet syndrome)

---

## What Are the Signs?

The first sign is pain when you press on or use the joint.  
Running or jumping can cause sharp pain in the knees or hips.  
If you feel pain even when resting, the condition is likely advanced.

In later stages, joints feel stiff after sitting or lying down for a long time.  
You may feel pain when you first get up in the morning.  
This pain usually goes away after a few minutes of moving around.  
If the pain does not improve after 30 minutes, it may be due to a different condition, like rheumatoid arthritis.

---

## What Causes Osteoarthritis?

Bones meet at joints.  
Cartilage acts like a cushion between them.  
This cartilage takes a lot of pressure but can repair itself a little.  
Special cells in the cartilage get their nutrients from joint fluid, not from blood.  
When you move, the joint fluid is squeezed out and fresh fluid flows in, like a sponge.

Even with this repair process, cartilage wears down over time.  
This is a normal part of aging.  
But only about one in four people with visible joint damage on an x-ray actually have symptoms.

If the cartilage wears away completely, the bones rub against each other.  
This causes pain and limits movement.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

The biggest risk factor is age.  
About 1 in 10 people aged 30 to 40 have osteoarthritis.  
By age 60 to 70, about 4 in 10 people have it.

Some things can make joint wear faster:

- A family history of joint problems  
- Playing high-impact sports like football or handball  
- Working in jobs that require frequent kneeling, squatting, or lifting heavy things  
- Injuries to the knee, such as a torn ligament or damaged meniscus  
- Problems in the joints, like hip issues  
- Being overweight

---

## How Does It Get Worse?

Many people live normal lives with osteoarthritis.  
They manage pain for years.  
But the condition can get worse quickly in some people.

Pain and limited movement often happen when bone grows abnormally.  
These extra bone growths are called bone spurs.  
In advanced cases, you may hear or feel bones rubbing together.  
This causes constant pain and joint noises.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose osteoarthritis based on symptoms.  
An x-ray can show a narrow space between bones.  
This is a clear sign of joint damage.  
If the x-ray shows this, no further tests are needed.

If symptoms are unclear, doctors may do blood tests or an MRI.  
These help rule out other conditions, like rheumatoid arthritis.

---

## How Is It Treated?

The most important treatment is staying active.  
Not moving can weaken muscles and make cartilage wear faster.  
There is no cure yet.  
But staying active keeps your body strong and flexible.  
This is especially helpful if your knee or hip is affected.

Pain relief treatments are available.  
The type depends on which joint is affected.

Only a few treatments have strong scientific proof of helping.  
The most effective ones are:

- Physical therapy and movement exercises  
- Rehabilitation programs  
- Painkillers

People who are overweight and have knee or hip osteoarthritis should try to lose weight.  
This reduces pressure on the joints.

For finger or wrist osteoarthritis, occupational therapy can help.  
It teaches you how to avoid movements that hurt your joints.  
Tools like special pens, bottle openers, or gripping aids can make daily tasks easier.

Walking sticks or joint supports (splints) can help with knee or hip pain.

When the joint is severely damaged, surgery may be an option.  
A doctor can replace the worn joint with an artificial one.  
This is called joint replacement surgery.

---

## Important Note on Other Treatments

Many treatments are offered for osteoarthritis.  
But their effectiveness has not been proven by science.  
These include:

- Acupuncture  
- Arthroscopy (a type of joint surgery)  
- Herbal remedies  
- Dietary supplements  
- Ultrasound therapy  
- TENS (a device that sends small electric pulses to relieve pain)

Always talk to your doctor before trying these.

---

For more information on painkillers for osteoarthritis, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

# Breast Cancer

Breast cancer is the most common type of cancer in women in Germany.  
About 69,000 women are diagnosed each year.  
A small number of men also get breast cancer — around 700 to 800 each year.  
This article explains the risks, how it is found, how it is treated, and what happens after treatment.

---

## Quick Facts

- Breast cancer is very common in women. It is rare in men.
- The chance of getting breast cancer goes up with age.
- Germany has a free breast cancer screening program for women.
- Doctors divide breast cancer into types. Each type is treated differently.
- Breast cancer can often be cured if found early.
- Even if the cancer is advanced or has spread, many treatment options are still available. These can slow the disease and help people live well.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for talking to a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Breast Cancer?

The most common type of breast cancer is called mammary carcinoma.  
It starts in the milk-producing tissue of the breast.  
This cancer can grow in different ways.  
Some types grow because of hormones. Others do not depend on hormones.

The earliest form is called ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS).  
In DCIS, abnormal cells are in the milk ducts.  
They have not spread into nearby tissue or other parts of the body.

---

## Living with Breast Cancer

Treatment for breast cancer can last five years or longer — especially if the cancer is hormone-sensitive.  
Many women are able to keep doing their normal daily activities during treatment.  
Some women feel limited for a long time, though.

Women who have survived breast cancer do not need to limit themselves.  
Staying active and doing regular exercise can help prevent problems.  
Exercise may also lower the chance of the cancer coming back.

---

## Signs of Breast Cancer

Possible signs include:

- A lump you can feel in the breast
- A nipple that turns inward (retracted)
- Fluid coming from the nipple
- A breast that is red, warm, and stays that way for a long time — even after antibiotics

Small tumors often do not cause any symptoms.  
But they can be found during cancer screening.

If you notice any of these changes, see your doctor.  
Early checks can help find the cause and start treatment if needed.

> **Important:** Men should also see a doctor if they notice any breast changes.

---

## Causes and Risk Factors

Doctors do not know exactly what causes breast cancer in most people.  
But some things make it more likely.

- Age is the biggest risk factor. The chance goes up as you get older.
- Some women have a family history of breast cancer.
- Changes in certain genes — like BRCA1 and BRCA2 — greatly increase the risk.
- Radiation to the chest during childhood or teenage years can raise the risk.  
  This can happen when treating a type of lymph node cancer called Hodgkin’s lymphoma.
- Dense breast tissue or certain non-cancerous breast conditions slightly increase the risk.
- Hormone-related factors also play a role. These include:
  - Starting your period before age 12
  - Going through menopause after age 55
  - Using hormone replacement therapy for a long time after menopause

---

## How Breast Cancer Grows and Spreads

Breast cancer treatment has improved a lot in recent years.  
The earlier it is found, the better the chance of recovery.

Some types of breast cancer that need hormones to grow can come back more than 10 years after treatment.  
If this happens, treatment can be started again.

If the cancer is advanced or has spread to other organs, a full cure is usually not possible.  
But many treatments are available. These can help people live long and meaningful lives.

---

## Can Breast Cancer Be Prevented?

A healthy lifestyle may lower your risk.  
This includes:

- Keeping a healthy weight
- Eating a balanced and varied diet
- Drinking little or no alcohol
- Not smoking
- Doing regular physical activity

There is no medicine approved in Germany to prevent breast cancer.

If you have a high genetic risk, you may choose to have surgery to reduce your risk.  
You may also be checked more often so that cancer can be found early.

---

## Early Detection: How It Works

All women aged 30 and over can have a yearly check-up with a gynecologist.  
The doctor will check the breasts and nearby lymph nodes.  
They will also teach you how to check your own breasts.

Women aged 50 to 75 can take part in mammography screening every two years.  
This uses low-dose X-rays to look at the breast.  
Participation is optional.

### If You Have a Family History of Breast Cancer

Women at high risk due to genes can join a special screening program.  
These programs are offered by centers for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.

The Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center explains how mammograms and other tests work.  
It also covers the benefits and possible downsides. (Available in German.)

The Joint Federal Committee (G-BA) has published a patient brochure with more details.  
It helps you decide whether to take part in mammography screening.

---

## How Is Breast Cancer Diagnosed?

If a doctor suspects breast cancer, they will:

- Do a mammogram
- Perform an ultrasound scan
- Sometimes use magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)

If cancer is still suspected, they take a small sample of tissue from the breast.  
This is called a biopsy.  
A specialist doctor (pathologist) examines the sample to confirm or rule out cancer.

### If Cancer Is Confirmed

After a diagnosis, doctors look closely at the cancer to plan treatment.  
They check:

- **Receptor status:** Whether the cancer cells have receptors for estrogen and progesterone.  
  They also check for HER2 receptors.
- **How the tumor looks compared to normal breast tissue**
- **How fast the cancer cells are dividing**
- **Whether nearby lymph nodes are affected:**  
  Doctors often take a sample from the first few lymph nodes that drain fluid from the tumor.  
  These are usually in the armpit. This is called a sentinel lymph node biopsy.
- **Gene expression tests:** These help decide if chemotherapy is needed.

For more information on these tests, visit the website of the Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center. (In German.)

---

## How Is Breast Cancer Treated?

There are many treatment options.  
Doctors often use more than one type.  
The choice depends on the cancer type and how far it has spread.

Treatments are either local (targeting the breast) or systemic (affecting the whole body).

> **Important:** Men with breast cancer are treated much like women — even though there are fewer studies on this.

### Local Treatments: Surgery and Radiation

Surgery is the main treatment for early-stage breast cancer.

- **Breast-conserving surgery:** Only the tumor and a small area around it are removed.  
  The rest of the breast stays. After surgery, radiation is usually given to kill any remaining cancer cells.
- **Mastectomy:** The entire breast tissue is removed.  
  Surgeons can rebuild the breast using implants or tissue from another part of the body.

Sometimes the lymph nodes in the armpit are treated with radiation.  
If many cancer cells are found in the lymph nodes, surgery is needed to remove them.  
Radiation alone is not enough in these cases.

### Systemic Treatments: Affecting the Whole Body

Almost all breast cancer patients get treatments that work throughout the body.  
These help prevent the cancer from coming back.  
They can be given before surgery (neoadjuvant) or after (adjuvant).

Common treatments include:

- **Chemotherapy:** Used when the cancer does not respond to hormones or grows fast.  
  It is often given before surgery to see if the tumor shrinks.
- **Hormone therapy (endocrine therapy):** Used for cancers with hormone receptors.  
  - Before menopause: Tamoxifen is used.  
  - After menopause: Aromatase inhibitors are used.  
  These are usually given after surgery.
- **HER2-targeted therapy:** Used when cancer cells have too many HER2 receptors.  
  This type of cancer grows fast. Treatment includes special antibodies, often with chemotherapy.
- **Bone-stabilizing drugs:** Such as bisphosphonates.  
  These help prevent cancer from spreading to the bones.

### What Is Post-Neoadjuvant Treatment?

If cancer is still present at the time of surgery, another round of chemotherapy or targeted therapy may be given.  
This is called post-neoadjuvant treatment.

### Advanced or Metastatic Cancer

If the cancer is advanced or has spread to other organs, treatment focuses on:

- Slowing the disease
- Managing symptoms
- Keeping quality of life as high as possible

For more details on treatments, side effects, and results, visit the website of the Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center. (In German.)

---

## Rehab and Aftercare

Breast cancer treatment can be hard on the body and mind.  
Common physical issues include:

- Trouble moving the arm or shoulder
- Swelling in the arm (lymphedema)
- Feeling anxious, sad, or lacking energy

Rehab helps with these problems.  
It may include:

- Physical movement and exercises
- Lymphedema therapy
- Nutrition advice
- Relaxation techniques

### What Happens During Aftercare?

Doctors check regularly for:

- Side effects from treatment
- Signs of cancer returning

They also check both breasts at regular times.  
This helps catch any local relapse early.

# Impetigo: What You Need to Know

Impetigo is a skin infection that causes itching and sometimes pain.  
It mostly affects young children.  
The infection is caused by bacteria.  
Doctors often use antibiotics to treat it.

---

## Quick Facts

- Impetigo is also called school sores.  
- It affects the outer layer of the skin.  
- It is very common in children.  
- The first signs often show up around the mouth and nose.  
- In Europe, about 2 out of every 100 children get treated for it each year.  
- Antibiotic creams are often used to treat it.  

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself or your child.

---

## What Is Impetigo?

Impetigo is a skin infection caused by bacteria.  
It is very contagious.  
Children with impetigo must stay home from school or daycare.  
They can return only after about 24 hours of antibiotic treatment.  
Without treatment, the infection can stay contagious for weeks.

---

## What Does Impetigo Look Like?

The first signs are usually an itchy red rash.  
The rash often starts around the mouth or nose.  
It may have small blisters filled with fluid.  
These blisters break easily and form yellow crusts.  
The crusts fall off after a while and leave no scars.  
The arms and legs can also be affected.

In rare cases, larger blisters form.  
These do not break right away.  
This type is called bullous impetigo.  
It can appear on the neck, chest, armpits, or diaper area.  
Some people also have a fever or swollen glands.

---

## What Causes Impetigo?

Impetigo is caused by bacteria, usually strep or staph.  
These bacteria can enter the skin through small cuts, scrapes, rashes, or insect bites.  
The infection spreads through direct skin contact.  
It can also spread by touching objects that an infected person has touched.

---

## How Common Is Impetigo?

Impetigo is the most common skin infection in children.  
In Europe, about 2 out of every 100 children are treated for it each year.

---

## How Does Impetigo Start?

The rash usually appears 2 to 10 days after infection.  
Most cases go away on their own in about three weeks.  
But some can last longer.  
The person remains contagious until the infection is gone.

Without treatment, the infection can spread deeper into the skin.  
Having had impetigo does not protect you from getting it again.

---

## How Can You Prevent Impetigo?

Good hygiene helps prevent impetigo.  
Wash hands often with soap.  
Do this before eating and after using the toilet or playing outside.  
There are no special rules for adults or children to avoid impetigo in daily life.

If someone in the family has impetigo, take extra care:

- Wash hands often, even at home.  
- Do not touch the rash.  
- Use your own towel.  
- Wash underwear, clothes, towels, and bedding at 60 degrees Celsius or higher.

---

## How Is Impetigo Diagnosed?

Doctors can usually tell it’s impetigo just by looking at the skin.  
They usually do not need to take a swab or do other tests.  
But they may do a test if they are unsure if it’s something else, like a fungal infection.

---

## How Is Impetigo Treated?

If the rash is small, doctors may suggest using antiseptic creams or solutions.  
But it is not clear if these help much.

Antibiotic creams are proven to work.  
To avoid spreading the bacteria, use a wooden stick or wear gloves when applying the cream.

Antibiotic tablets are only used if the rash covers a large area or affects many parts of the body.  
Tablets can cause side effects.  
Common ones include nausea and diarrhea.

If blisters break, the area can become inflamed.  
To stop a child from scratching, keep their fingernails short.

For more tips on healing faster, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

---

## What Else Should You Know?

Impetigo is a reportable illness.  
This means you must stay away from others if you think you have it.  
Children must not go to school or daycare.  
They should not play with other children.

Parents and guardians must tell the local health authority if a child has or might have impetigo.

You can return to normal activities only when a doctor says you are no longer contagious.  
If you are on antibiotics, this is usually about 24 hours after starting treatment.  
Without treatment, the infection stops being contagious only when it heals on its own.

# Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS)

Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) is a common condition that affects women during their childbearing years. It happens when a woman’s body makes too many male hormones. This can cause problems with her periods and fertility.

This guide explains what PCOS is, how it shows up, what causes it, and how it can be treated.

---

## What Is PCOS?

PCOS is a hormone problem. It affects how the ovaries work.

The ovaries are the organs that release eggs for pregnancy. They also make female hormones like estrogen and progesterone.

In PCOS, the ovaries make too much of a male hormone called testosterone.

This hormone imbalance can stop the ovaries from working properly. It can also stop a woman from releasing an egg each month.

Small fluid-filled sacs (called cysts) can form on the ovaries. These are not true cysts but are harmless. They show up on ultrasound scans.

---

## What Are the Signs of PCOS?

The most common signs of PCOS include:

- Irregular or missing periods
- Excess body hair in places like the face, chest, back, or pubic area (this is called hirsutism)
- Acne
- Weight gain or trouble losing weight
- Thinning hair on the scalp
- A deeper voice
- A larger clitoris (in rare cases)

Some women have all of these signs. Others may have only a few. Some women have no symptoms at all.

---

## What Causes PCOS?

Doctors do not yet know the exact cause of PCOS.

But it may run in families. This means some women may be more likely to get it if other women in their family have it.

---

## What Makes PCOS Worse?

Many women with PCOS are overweight. About half to four out of every five women with PCOS are overweight.

Being overweight can make PCOS worse. It can also lead to insulin resistance.

Insulin resistance means the body does not use insulin well. Insulin helps control blood sugar.

When insulin does not work properly, blood sugar levels rise. This can lead to type 2 diabetes.

High blood sugar also causes the body to make more male hormones. This makes PCOS symptoms worse.

---

## How Common Is PCOS?

PCOS affects about 8 to 13 out of every 100 women of childbearing age.

Many women with PCOS do not know they have it. Up to 7 out of 10 women with PCOS are not diagnosed.

---

## What Problems Can PCOS Cause?

PCOS can lead to both physical and emotional health issues.

Physical problems include:

- Trouble getting pregnant
- Higher risk of heart disease
- Higher risk of type 2 diabetes
- Problems during pregnancy, such as miscarriage or high blood pressure

Emotional problems can include:

- Depression
- Anxiety
- Eating disorders

These issues can affect a woman’s quality of life.

---

## How Is PCOS Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tests to diagnose PCOS.

They look for:

- Irregular or missing periods over time
- High levels of male hormones in the blood
- Excess body hair (hirsutism)
- Cysts on the ovaries seen on an ultrasound scan

A blood test checks hormone levels. An ultrasound scan shows the ovaries and any cyst-like sacs.

A diagnosis is made when a woman has at least two of these signs.

---

## How Is PCOS Treated?

There is no single cure for PCOS. But doctors treat the symptoms.

Treatment depends on whether a woman wants to get pregnant.

---

### If You Are Not Trying to Get Pregnant

Doctors may prescribe birth control pills. These help:

- Regulate the menstrual cycle
- Lower male hormone levels
- Reduce unwanted body hair

Birth control pills also lower the risk of endometrial cancer. This is a type of cancer in the lining of the uterus. It can happen if a woman does not have periods for a long time.

If birth control pills are not an option, doctors may prescribe a medicine called metformin. This helps:

- Lower blood sugar
- Improve insulin sensitivity
- Reduce male hormone levels

Lifestyle changes also help. These include:

- Losing weight
- Eating healthier foods
- Exercising regularly

Even a small weight loss can improve symptoms and restore regular periods.

---

### If You Are Trying to Get Pregnant

Women with PCOS who want to get pregnant are given medicines that help the ovaries release an egg.

These medicines are called ovulation inducers.

Losing weight before starting these medicines can improve the chances of getting pregnant.

---

## Where Can You Get Support?

Living with PCOS can be hard. You are not alone.

Self-help groups offer:

- Information about PCOS
- Advice from others who have it
- A chance to share your experiences

You can find a self-help group through the **National Contact and Information Point for Encouraging and Supporting Self-Help Groups (NAKOS)** website.

---

**Important Note:** This information is for general knowledge only. It is not a substitute for medical advice. Always talk to a doctor if you think you might have PCOS. Do not try to diagnose or treat yourself.

# Tonsillitis

Tonsillitis causes a sore throat, trouble swallowing, tiredness, and fever.  
If it keeps coming back, it can be very hard to live with.  
In rare cases, it can lead to serious problems.

## Quick Facts

- Tonsillitis makes your throat sore.  
- Your tonsils (the lumps on each side of the back of your throat) become swollen and may have a yellowish coating.  
- Most cases go away in one to two weeks.  
- Painkillers can help ease the pain and fever.  
- Antibiotics may be used if a bacteria is causing the infection.  
- Getting tonsillitis many times is tough, but serious problems are rare.  
- Surgery to remove the tonsils may be an option if you get sick often.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor.  
> Do not use this to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Tonsillitis?

A sore throat is usually caused by a virus, like the common cold.  
The virus can spread to your tonsils and cause infection.  
Bacterial infections of the tonsils happen less often.  
It can be hard to tell if a virus or bacteria is causing the problem.  
Tonsillitis is more common in children and teens than in adults.  
It often starts suddenly and usually gets better in one to two weeks.  
Some people get it many times a year.  
Recurring infections can be very hard to deal with.  
But serious problems are rare.

It is important to know that tonsillitis is not the same as having large tonsils.  
Large tonsils (called tonsillar hyperplasia) can happen without infection.  
They can affect the tonsils at the back of the throat or the pharyngeal tonsils near the nose.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may have:

- A sore throat  
- Trouble swallowing  
- Swollen, dark red tonsils with a yellow coating  
- Fever over 38 degrees Celsius (100.4 degrees Fahrenheit)  
- Headache  
- Feeling tired or weak  
- Bad breath  
- Loss of appetite  
- Swollen and painful glands in the neck

If a virus is the cause, you may also have:

- Coughing  
- Sneezing  
- Runny nose

If the infection is mainly in the tonsils, it is called tonsillitis.  
If the infection is in the throat, it is called pharyngitis (commonly known as a sore throat).

In children, tonsillitis can also cause:

- Belly pain  
- Nausea  
- Vomiting

## What Causes Tonsillitis?

Most germs spread through tiny droplets in the air.  
When someone talks, coughs, or sneezes, they release droplets.  
These droplets can be breathed in by others and cause infection.

The most common bacteria causing tonsillitis are certain types of streptococci.  
Not everyone who carries these bacteria gets sick.  
Tonsillitis can also happen with other illnesses, such as:

- Scarlet fever (a bacterial illness)  
- Glandular fever (also called mononucleosis, a viral illness)

## How Does It Progress?

Most cases of tonsillitis get better in one to two weeks.  
Fever usually goes down first.  
The sore throat and swollen tonsils may last longer.

Serious problems are rare.  
The most common issue is a pus-filled pocket near the tonsil.  
This is called a peritonsillar abscess.  
It can happen with bacterial tonsillitis.  
It may go away on its own.  
But it can spread to nearby tissues in the neck or chest.  
In very rare cases, it can lead to sepsis (a dangerous blood infection).  
This is why it is important to treat the abscess.

Symptoms of a peritonsillar abscess include:

- Pain on one side of the throat or in one ear  
- Trouble swallowing or speaking

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask:

- Is the sore throat caused by tonsillitis?  
- How bad is the infection?  
- Is it caused by bacteria?  
- Do you need antibiotics?  
- Are you at risk for complications?

The doctor will look at your throat and ask about your symptoms.  
A bacterial infection often shows:

- Swollen, coated tonsils  
- Fever  
- No cough

A rapid test can check for a specific type of streptococci.  
This test uses a swab from your tonsils.  
Results come in minutes.  
But it is not always correct.  
A more accurate test sends the swab to a lab.  
This takes one to two days.

Blood tests are rarely needed unless the doctor suspects another illness.

## How Is It Treated?

The goal is to ease symptoms and avoid problems.

Medicines used for acute tonsillitis include:

- Painkillers and fever reducers, such as ibuprofen or paracetamol  
- Antibiotics, if a bacteria is causing the infection

Antibiotics can shorten the illness.  
After one dose, you are no longer contagious.  
They lower the risk of complications, though these are rare.  
But antibiotics do not help much with symptoms.  
They can also cause side effects.  
Many people choose not to take them.

To feel better, some people use:

- Cough drops  
- Gargling with salt water  
- Drinking warm tea  
- A warm compress on the neck

If tonsillitis keeps coming back, treatment may include:

- Painkillers  
- Antibiotics  
- Surgery to remove the tonsils

> **Important:** If surgery is recommended, it may help to get a second opinion.  
> Talk to another doctor or hospital.

The decision aids from **gesundheitsinformation.de** can help you decide whether surgery is right for you or your child.  
These tools are available for both children and adults.

# Uterine Polyps

Uterine polyps are small growths inside the lining of the uterus.  
They often cause light bleeding between periods or after menopause.  
Most uterine polyps are not cancer and do not cause harm.  
You only need to remove them if they cause symptoms or make it hard to get pregnant.

---

## Quick Facts

- Uterine polyps grow in the inner lining of the uterus.  
- The most common sign is bleeding between periods or after menopause.  
- Some women have no symptoms at all.  
- Polyps can make it harder to get pregnant.  
- They are more common as women get older.  
- A doctor will take a small sample of the polyp to check for cancer.  
- Surgery is not always needed.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Are Uterine Polyps?

Uterine polyps are growths in the inner lining of the uterus.  
They are usually not cancer.  
They can be as small as a few millimeters or as large as a few centimeters.  
They are more common in women after menopause.  
The exact cause is not known.

Bleeding between periods or after menopause can be a sign of a polyp.  
But some polyps do not cause any symptoms.  
In some cases, polyps are found when a woman sees a doctor because she cannot get pregnant.

Sometimes, doctors remove polyps to help with fertility.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main symptoms are:

- Light bleeding between periods  
- Bleeding after menopause  
- Bleeding after sex  

About 75 out of 100 women with polyps have some kind of bleeding.  
The amount of blood is usually small.  
But some women have a thicker discharge that may look like mucus or pus.

Some women have no symptoms at all.  
Polyps may be found by chance during a check-up for infertility.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

Uterine polyps are rare in young women.  
They become more common with age, especially after menopause.  
Hormones may play a role.

You are more likely to get polyps if you:

- Are overweight or obese  
- Have high blood pressure  
- Take a medicine called tamoxifen (used to treat breast cancer)

---

## How Are They Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and medical history.  
They may ask:

- If you have irregular bleeding  
- If you are taking tamoxifen  
- If you are on hormone replacement therapy  
- If you are having trouble getting pregnant  

Polyps on the cervix can sometimes be felt during a pelvic exam.  
But polyps inside the uterus need special tests.

Two common tests are:

- **Vaginal ultrasound:** A small probe is placed in the vagina to take pictures of the uterus.  
- **Hysteroscopy:** A thin tube with a camera is inserted through the vagina into the uterus.  
  This lets the doctor see inside the uterus.  
  Polyps can be removed during this test.

To be sure the polyp is not cancer, the removed tissue is checked under a microscope.

---

## How Are They Treated?

Polyps can only be removed with surgery.  
If you have no symptoms and the polyp is found by chance, surgery is not always needed—especially before menopause.  
But regular check-ups are important to catch any changes early.

Surgery may be recommended if:

- There is a higher chance the polyp could become cancer  
- The polyp is very large  
- You have more than one polyp  
- The polyp sticks out into the cervix  
- You want to get pregnant but are having trouble

If a polyp causes symptoms, it should be removed.

Most polyps are removed during a hysteroscopy.  
The doctor uses a thin tube with a camera and light to see inside the uterus.  
Small tools can be passed through the tube to cut and remove the polyp.  
The camera helps guide the doctor during the procedure.  
This surgery is usually simple and safe.

# Hepatitis B – Simple Explanation

Hepatitis B is an infection that causes swelling and damage in the liver. It is caused by a virus called the hepatitis B virus. The virus spreads through contact with infected blood or body fluids.

This guide explains what hepatitis B is, how it spreads, what symptoms it causes, how it is treated, and how to prevent it.

---

## Quick Facts

- Hepatitis B is an infection that inflames the liver.
- In Germany, most cases spread through sexual contact.
- Most adults with acute hepatitis B feel better in a few weeks. Over 90 percent recover fully without problems.
- If the infection lasts a long time, it can lead to serious liver damage or liver cancer.
- Everyone should get the hepatitis B vaccine. It is especially important for babies, young children, and adults at higher risk.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Hepatitis B?

The word "hepatitis" comes from Greek. "Hepar" means liver. So hepatitis means liver inflammation.

There are several types of hepatitis. Doctors label them with letters from A to E.

Hepatitis B is caused by a virus. It was once called "serum hepatitis." The virus spreads through:

- Unprotected sex
- Blood contact (like sharing needles)
- From an infected mother to her baby during childbirth

Most people with hepatitis B feel only mild symptoms or none at all. The body often clears the virus on its own in a few weeks.

But in some people, the virus stays in the body for a long time. This is called a chronic infection. Chronic hepatitis B can lead to serious liver problems later, including liver cancer.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Not everyone has symptoms. Here’s how symptoms usually show up:

- One third of people have no symptoms at all.
- Another third have general feelings of being unwell.
- The last third develop jaundice.

### General symptoms include:
- Feeling very tired
- Not feeling hungry
- Nausea (feeling sick to your stomach)
- Pain in joints or muscles
- A slight fever

### Jaundice (icterus)
Jaundice means the whites of the eyes and the skin turn yellow. This happens because the liver is not working well.

When the liver is inflamed, it cannot process a substance called bilirubin properly. Bilirubin builds up in the blood and causes the yellow color.

Other signs of jaundice:
- Stool (poop) becomes lighter in color
- Urine (pee) becomes darker

---

## How Do People Get Infected?

The hepatitis B virus is found in blood and body fluids. These include:

- Blood
- Saliva
- Tears
- Sperm
- Vaginal fluid
- Colostrum (the first milk a mother produces)

The virus spreads through:

- Unprotected sex
- Sharing needles (for drugs)
- Getting tattoos or piercings with unsterile tools
- Accidental cuts or scratches with contaminated objects
- From mother to baby during birth

In Western countries, the most common way people get infected is through sex. This is especially true for people who have many sexual partners.

Blood transfusions used to be a common way the virus spread. But today, all blood is tested. So this is now very rare.

If a mother has hepatitis B, she can pass it to her baby during delivery. This is a major way the virus spreads worldwide. In Germany, this happens much less often.

---

## How Common Is Hepatitis B?

Hepatitis B is one of the most common infections in the world.

- At least 2 billion people have had hepatitis B at some point.
- About 3 percent of people worldwide carry the virus long-term.

The rate is highest in parts of Africa and East Asia. In Western Europe, less than 1 percent of people carry the virus. In Germany, the number is even lower.

The hepatitis B vaccine is given to babies at birth. This is helping to reduce the number of new cases in Germany.

---

## How Does the Infection Develop?

There are two types of hepatitis B infection: acute and chronic.

### Acute Infection

- Symptoms usually start 60 to 120 days after infection.
- It is hard to know where the infection came from because symptoms appear so long after exposure.
- Some people can spread the virus even before they feel sick.
- Some people develop jaundice a few days after getting sick. This goes away after several weeks.
- Over 90 percent of adults recover fully and are protected for life.
- In rare cases, the infection becomes very serious and can cause liver failure.

Even after recovery, tiny amounts of the virus can stay hidden in liver cells. The body’s immune system keeps it under control. But if the immune system weakens (for example, due to illness or medicine), the virus can become active again.

### Chronic Infection

- A chronic infection means the virus is still in the blood for more than six months.
- Doctors look for a part of the virus called HBs antigen to confirm this.
- Up to 10 percent of infected people develop a chronic infection.
- The virus can still spread to others if it is multiplying fast.

Chronic hepatitis B often causes no symptoms. It is often found by chance when blood tests show high liver values.

Some people may feel:
- Tired
- Not hungry
- Pain in muscles or joints

Sometimes, symptoms suddenly get worse. This is called a flare-up. It can feel like a new acute infection.

Over time, chronic hepatitis B can lead to:
- Scarring of the liver (cirrhosis)
- Liver cancer

### Hepatitis B and Hepatitis D Together

In rare cases, a person with hepatitis B also gets hepatitis D.

- Hepatitis D virus needs hepatitis B to survive and grow.
- Only people with hepatitis B can get hepatitis D.
- This double infection is usually worse than hepatitis B alone.
- It often leads to long-term, serious liver problems.

---

## How Can Hepatitis B Be Prevented?

The best way to prevent hepatitis B is vaccination.

### Vaccination for Babies and Children
- All babies should get the hepatitis B vaccine shortly after birth.
- The vaccine is given in several doses.
- Children who did not get the vaccine as babies should get it before puberty, and no later than age 18.

### Vaccination for Adults at Higher Risk
These adults should also get the vaccine:
- Doctors, nurses, and other healthcare workers
- People with weak immune systems
- People with HIV
- Dialysis patients
- People with liver damage
- People who have many sexual partners
- People who use drugs and share needles
- People living in close contact with someone who has chronic hepatitis B (like in families, shelters, mental health facilities, or prisons)

### Travel Vaccination
- If you are traveling to a country where hepatitis B is common, get the vaccine.
- Often, the hepatitis A and B vaccines are given together.

### Emergency Protection (Passive Immunization)
- If someone who is not vaccinated comes into contact with infected blood, they can get a shot of antibodies.
- This gives immediate protection.
- It works while the body builds its own immunity from the vaccine.
- This is used for newborns whose mothers have hepatitis B.
- The baby gets the vaccine and antibodies within 12 hours of birth.
- Without this, the baby has a very high chance of getting a lifelong infection.

Pregnant women with high levels of the virus should take antiviral medicine during the third trimester. This lowers the risk of passing the virus to the baby.

---

## How Is Hepatitis B Diagnosed?

Doctors use a blood test to check for:
- Parts of the hepatitis B virus
- Antibodies (the body’s response to the virus)

The test results help doctors know:
- If someone is currently infected
- If they had hepatitis B in the past
- If they are protected by vaccination

---

## How Is Hepatitis B Treated?

### Acute Infection
- Most people do not need special treatment.
- Rest and a healthy diet help.
- Eat more carbohydrates and less fat.
- Medicines can help with nausea and pain.
- Most people can recover at home.
- Only go to the hospital if the infection is severe.
- Antiviral medicine is only used if the liver is already damaged and at risk of failing.

### Chronic Infection
- Long-term treatment is usually needed.
- Medicines stop the virus from multiplying.
- These medicines are called nucleotide analogues and nucleoside analogues.
- They work by blocking the virus’s ability to copy itself.
- Another treatment is alpha-interferon. This is a protein that helps the immune system fight the virus.
- This treatment is given for a limited time.

---

## More About the Hepatitis B Vaccine

Want to know if you need the hepatitis B vaccine before traveling?

The Robert Koch Institute gives clear advice on travel vaccines and related topics. Visit their website for more information.

# Gum Inflammation and Tooth Support Problems

Gum problems are common. Most of the time, they are not serious and go away on their own. But if they do not get better, they can harm the parts that hold your teeth in place. This more serious condition is called periodontitis.

## Quick Facts

- Gingivitis usually does not cause big problems at first.
- But it can turn into periodontitis over time.
- Periodontitis can make your teeth loose.
- Cleaning your teeth well every day helps prevent gum problems.
- The earlier you find periodontitis, the better it can be treated.
- A dentist removes plaque and hard buildup during treatment.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Are Gingivitis and Periodontitis?

Gingivitis means your gums are inflamed. Many people get it from time to time. It usually does not hurt and does not cause big issues at first. But if it spreads, it can damage the tissues that support your teeth. When this happens, it is called periodontitis. This is a more serious problem. It can lead to loose teeth.

To avoid gingivitis, clean your teeth every day. Even if you already have periodontitis, good care helps stop it from getting worse. This is true during treatment and after.

## What Are the Signs?

Gingivitis often has no pain or obvious symptoms. But your gums may look red or swollen. They may bleed when you brush your teeth. Sometimes they bleed without any reason.

Periodontitis shows signs only when it is advanced. You may notice:
- Red or swollen gums
- Gums that bleed easily
- Teeth that feel sensitive
- Teeth that look longer than before
- Bad breath
- Pain when chewing

The gums pull away from the tooth. This creates small gaps called periodontal pockets. If the disease is severe, your teeth may shift, wiggle, or hurt when you chew.

## What Causes These Problems?

Most of the time, gum inflammation is caused by plaque. Plaque is a thin film of bacteria. It builds up where your teeth meet your gums. You can feel it with your tongue—it feels fuzzy.

The bacteria in plaque produce waste. This waste can irritate your gums and make them swell. Brushing your teeth properly removes plaque. Good daily care lowers your risk of gum problems.

Some things make gum disease more likely:
- Smoking
- Diabetes
- Hormone changes during pregnancy

Some medicines can cause your gums to grow too much. This makes cleaning harder and raises the risk of gum disease. These include:
- Drugs that weaken the immune system
- Medicines for heart and blood vessel problems

Some people are more likely to get gum disease than others.

## How Do These Conditions Develop?

Gingivitis can go away on its own. But if it stays, it can turn into periodontitis.

In periodontitis, the gaps between your teeth and gums grow deeper. They can be several millimeters deep. In some cases, they are over a centimeter deep. The deeper the gap, the harder it is to clean.

Plaque in these deep gaps cannot be removed by brushing. It can harden on the tooth root and neck. Once it hardens, only a dentist can remove it.

Hardened plaque under the gums is called calculus. Hardened plaque above the gums is called tartar.

Bacteria and tartar in the pockets cause more inflammation. In periodontitis, the infection attacks the tissues that hold your teeth. Later, it can damage the jawbone. This can expose the tooth root and loosen the teeth. Chewing becomes painful or hard. In the end, saving the tooth may no longer be possible.

The disease does not get better on its own. It moves in cycles. Some times, the damage gets worse. Other times, the tissue may heal a little. But without treatment, it will not improve.

## How Can You Prevent These Problems?

Plaque builds up fast. But you can remove it by brushing your teeth every day. Use interdental brushes or dental floss too. Children and teens can learn how to clean their teeth properly at the dentist. Public health insurance covers these training sessions until age 18.

If you do not remove plaque, your gums can become inflamed in just a few days. Plaque can also turn into tartar. You need a dentist to remove tartar. This is often part of a regular dental check-up. Public health insurance pays for this once a year.

People who need care or have a disability can have tartar removed twice a year. Their insurance also covers training on how to care for teeth and dentures.

Professional cleaning removes both soft and hard plaque. But you usually have to pay part of the cost yourself.

For more details on the benefits and downsides of professional cleaning, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

## How Are These Conditions Diagnosed?

Dentists check for gingivitis during regular visits. People with public health insurance can have two check-ups each year.

**Important:** Anyone with public health insurance can also have a special gum check-up every two years. This is called the Periodontal Screening Index, or PSI. The dentist uses a special tool to check each tooth for gum pockets. They also look for:
- Bleeding gums
- Tartar
- Receding gums
- Loose teeth

If periodontitis is suspected, the dentist may take X-rays. This shows whether the jawbone is already damaged.

## What Is the Treatment?

The earlier you find periodontitis, the better the treatment works. The goal is to stop the disease from getting worse. This helps prevent further damage and tooth loss.

Good daily care is key to successful treatment. If you have gingivitis or periodontitis, your dentist will teach you how to care for your teeth properly. Public health insurance covers this training as part of periodontitis treatment.

Before treatment starts, your dentist may suggest professional cleaning. You usually pay for this yourself.

To treat gingivitis, the dentist removes tartar. They may also fix or smooth out fillings or crowns that stick out. This makes it easier to clean the area.

If you have periodontitis, the dentist removes plaque and hard deposits below the gum line. If this is not enough, surgery may be needed. Surgery helps clean the root surface of the tooth.

# Erysipelas and Cellulitis

Bacteria can get into the body through broken or damaged skin.  
This can cause a skin infection.  
There are two main types: erysipelas and cellulitis.  

Erysipelas affects only the top layers of the skin.  
Cellulitis goes deeper into the skin and the tissue underneath.  
Both infections cause redness, swelling, and pain in the skin.  
Most people recover fully if treatment starts early.  
The feet and lower legs are the most common places for these infections.  

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor.  
> Do not use this to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Are Erysipelas and Cellulitis?

When the skin is cut, scratched, or damaged, bacteria can enter.  
This can lead to an infection.  

If the infection stays near the surface, it is usually erysipelas.  
Erysipelas is also known as “St. Anthony’s fire.”  
If the infection spreads deeper into the skin and tissue, it is called cellulitis.  
Cellulitis is sometimes called a phlegmonous infection or just “phlegmons.”  

Both infections can be treated successfully if caught early.  
Without treatment, they can lead to serious problems.  

The word “cellulitis” has nothing to do with “cellulite.”  
Cellulite is a harmless condition that makes the skin look lumpy.  

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

These infections happen when bacteria get into the skin and soft tissue.  
They can affect any part of the body, but most often the feet and lower legs.  

- **Facial erysipelas** means the infection is on the face.  
- **Hand cellulitis** can happen on the palm. It may spread in a V-shape between the thumb, wrist, and little finger.  

### Signs of Erysipelas:
- The skin becomes red, swollen, and painful.  
- The red area has clear, sharp edges.  
- The skin looks shiny and light red.  
- Red streaks may appear, showing the infection is spreading through the lymph vessels.  
- Blisters can form in severe cases.  
- Nearby lymph nodes may swell and hurt when touched.  
- Fever and feeling unwell often start when the skin turns red.  

### Signs of Cellulitis:
- The red area has blurry or unclear edges.  
- The skin color ranges from dark red to light purple.  
- The infection goes deeper into the skin and tissue.  
- It can spread along tendons and muscles.  
- Pus may form in some cases.  
- Swelling and pain are common.  
- Fever and feeling unwell can happen, especially in severe cases.  

### How to Tell the Difference:
- Erysipelas has a clear border and light red color.  
- Cellulitis has a fuzzy border and darker red or purple color.  

---

## What Causes These Infections?

- Erysipelas is often caused by streptococcus bacteria.  
- Cellulitis is usually caused by staphylococcus bacteria.  
- Sometimes both types of bacteria can cause either infection.  

Bacteria are more likely to enter if the skin is already damaged.  
This includes:  
- Skin conditions like eczema (neurodermatitis)  
- Impetigo (a skin infection with blisters and crusts)  
- Fungal infections like athlete’s foot  
- Cuts, scrapes, wounds, or open sores  

Infections can also start after:  
- Insect or animal bites  
- Needle pricks  
- Surgery  

Your risk goes up if your immune system is weak.  
This can happen if you take:  
- Cortisone medicine  
- Some cancer treatments  
- Medicines after an organ transplant  

Other risk factors include:  
- Diabetes  
- Being overweight  
- Poor lymph flow or blood circulation  
- Varicose veins (venous insufficiency)  
- Having had erysipelas or cellulitis before  

---

## How Can You Prevent These Infections?

Re-infection is common.  
About one in three people get it again, even after successful treatment.  

You can lower your risk by:  
- Treating skin problems like athlete’s foot or eczema early.  
- Keeping your feet clean and dry, especially if you have diabetes or poor circulation.  
- Taking good care of any cuts or wounds.  

If you keep getting infections, your doctor may suggest long-term antibiotics.  
These are taken every day for several months.  

For more details on prevention, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## How Are These Infections Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose erysipelas and cellulitis by:  
- Looking at the skin and its appearance  
- Asking about your symptoms  
- Reviewing your medical history and past injuries  

Tests are not usually needed.  
But your doctor may order tests if:  
- You were bitten by an animal  
- They suspect a specific type of germ is causing the infection  

---

## How Are These Infections Treated?

Antibiotics are used to treat both infections.  

- Mild cases: You take pills.  
- Severe cases: You get antibiotics through a drip in a vein.  
- If you need hospital care, you usually stay for about a week.  

The type of antibiotic depends on:  
- The kind of bacteria likely involved  
- How severe the infection is  

To track healing, the doctor may draw a line around the red area with a pen.  
This helps check if the redness is shrinking.  

To ease symptoms:  
- Keep the swollen area cool.  
- Use moist antiseptic wipes on the skin.  
- Take anti-inflammatory painkillers like ibuprofen.  
- These help with pain and fever.  

Most people feel better within a few days of starting treatment.

# Botulism

Botulism is a serious type of food poisoning. It is caused by a powerful poison called the botulinum nerve toxin. This poison comes from bacteria called *Clostridium*. The bacteria are found in soil, water, and some foods. Botulism is rare in Germany, with about 5 cases each year.

---

## What Is Botulism?

Botulism happens when a person eats food that contains the botulinum nerve toxin.  
The toxin is made by a type of bacteria called *Clostridium botulinum*.  
These bacteria grow in places with no oxygen, like sealed jars or cans.  
They form spores that can survive for years.  
When conditions are right, the spores grow into bacteria that make the toxin.

The botulinum nerve toxin is one of the strongest poisons known.  
Even a tiny amount can be deadly.

---

## Types of Botulism

There are several types of botulism:

- **Food-borne botulism**: Happens when you eat food that has the toxin. This is the most common type.  
  It often comes from home-preserved foods, sausages, or honey.

- **Wound botulism**: Happens when spores get into a wound. The bacteria grow in the wound and make the toxin.  
  This is more common in people who inject drugs.

- **Infant botulism**: Affects babies under one year old.  
  A baby’s stomach is not acidic enough to kill the spores.  
  Honey can carry spores that cause this type.

- **Inhalation botulism**: Happens when someone breathes in the toxin.  
  This is rare and mostly affects lab workers.

- **Iatrogenic botulism**: Happens when too much toxin is injected by mistake.  
  This can happen during medical or cosmetic treatments like Botox.

- **Rare forms**: In some adults with certain gut problems, the bacteria can grow in the intestines and cause botulism.

---

## Who Is at Risk?

Everyone can get botulism if they eat or touch the toxin.  
But some people are at higher risk:

- Babies under 12 months: Their stomachs are not strong enough to kill the bacteria.  
  Honey should never be given to babies under one year old.

- People who inject drugs: They can get wound botulism.

- People who make their own preserved foods:  
  Home-made sausages and canned foods are the most common cause of botulism in Germany.

---

## Symptoms of Botulism

Symptoms can start within hours or up to several days after eating the poisoned food.  
They depend on how much toxin was eaten and how long it has been in the body.

Common symptoms include:

- Dry mouth  
- Nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea  
- Eyes that do not focus well or see double  
- Trouble swallowing or speaking  
- Weakness in the arms, legs, or neck  
- Trouble breathing  
- Loss of the cough reflex, which can lead to lung infections like pneumonia  
- Constipation or blocked bowels

In babies, symptoms may also include:

- Weakness in the body  
- Floppy movements  
- Delayed development  
- Trouble sucking or feeding

---

## What Causes Botulism?

Botulism is caused by the botulinum nerve toxin.  
This toxin is made by *Clostridium botulinum* bacteria.  
The bacteria grow in low-oxygen environments, like sealed jars or cans.  
They form spores that can survive for years.  
When the spores grow, they make the toxin.

The bacteria and their spores are found in soil, water, and some foods.  
They are common worldwide.

**Fun fact**: *Clostridium botulinum* is related to *Clostridium tetani*, the bacteria that causes tetanus.  
Tetanus causes muscle spasms.  
Botulism causes paralysis.

---

## How Can You Prevent Botulism?

There is no vaccine for botulism.  
The best way to prevent it is to follow good food safety rules.

- Never eat food from bulging, damaged, or leaking cans.  
- Do not eat food from jars that look or smell bad.  
- Always cook home-preserved foods long enough to heat them all the way through.  
- Freezing does not kill the spores.  
- Reheat leftover meals to over 85 degrees Celsius for several minutes.

**Important**:  
- The toxin is destroyed at over 85 degrees Celsius.  
- The spores need over 120 degrees Celsius to die.  
- Moist heat (like boiling) works better than dry heat.

For more tips, see the consumer guide from the Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR).  
(Only available in German.)

---

## How Is Botulism Diagnosed?

Botulism symptoms can look like other illnesses at first.  
This makes early diagnosis hard.

Doctors will suspect botulism if:

- Several people who ate the same food get sick at the same time.  
- A person has signs of paralysis, especially in the eyes, throat, or breathing muscles.

To confirm the diagnosis, doctors send samples to a special lab.  
They test:

- Blood  
- Stomach contents or vomit  
- Stool (for babies and food-borne cases)  
- Wound swabs (for wound botulism)  
- Fluid from the lungs (for inhalation botulism)  
- Swabs from the nose (for inhalation botulism)

**Note**: The toxin can only be found in blood for up to 48 hours after eating.  
If food is still available, it can be tested for the toxin.

---

## How Is Botulism Treated?

Botulism is a medical emergency.  
All suspected cases must be treated in hospital, often in intensive care.

### Antitoxin Treatment

- Doctors give an antitoxin as soon as possible.  
- The antitoxin works only on toxin that is still in the blood.  
- It does not work once the toxin has entered nerve cells.  
- The antitoxin must be given within 48 hours of eating the poisoned food.

### Other Treatments

- **Gastric lavage**: A tube is used to wash out the stomach. This only works if done within 2 hours of eating.  
- **Laxatives or activated charcoal**: These can help if the intestines are not yet paralyzed.  
- **Bowel stimulants**: Used if constipation or bowel blockage happens.  
- **Cholinesterase inhibitors**: Help keep nerve signals working.  
- **Antibiotics**: Used for wound botulism. But they can release more toxin when bacteria die.  
  So, antibiotics are always given with an antitoxin.

### Recovery

The toxin stays in nerve cells for months.  
Nerve signals slowly return.  
Most people recover fully.  
Permanent damage is rare.

---

**Important Note**:  
This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.  
If you think you or someone else has botulism, go to the hospital right away.

# Metabolic Syndrome

Metabolic syndrome is a group of health problems that happen at the same time.  
It increases your risk of serious diseases like type 2 diabetes and heart problems.  
It often has no symptoms at first.  
You might not know you have it until it causes other health issues.

---

## What You Need to Know at a Glance

- Metabolic syndrome does not cause symptoms early on.  
- It is often found only after it leads to other health problems.  
- These problems can include heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, kidney damage, and fatty liver disease.  
- The exact cause is not fully known.  
- A lack of physical activity and poor eating habits are major contributors.  
- Carrying extra weight around your waist raises your risk.  
- The best way to prevent or treat it is to reach and keep a healthy body weight.  
- This means moving more and eating a balanced diet.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

---

## What Is Metabolic Syndrome?

Metabolic syndrome means you have several health issues at once.  
These include:

- Being severely overweight  
- High blood pressure  
- High blood sugar  
- High levels of triglycerides (a type of fat in the blood)  
- Low levels of HDL cholesterol (the “good” kind)

Having these problems together increases your risk of:

- Type 2 diabetes  
- Heart disease  
- Stroke  
- Other serious health problems

> **Important:** Carrying extra weight around your belly is especially dangerous.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Metabolic syndrome usually has no symptoms.  
You may not feel sick at all.  
The first sign might be a health problem that develops later.

For example:
- Heart problems  
- A heart attack  
- Type 2 diabetes

The most common warning sign is carrying too much weight around your waist.

---

## What Causes Metabolic Syndrome?

The exact cause is still unclear.  
But we know some things increase the risk:

- Being overweight, especially with belly fat  
- A family history of the condition  
- Not being physically active  
- Eating unhealthy foods

Excess fat, especially around the belly, harms your body’s normal processes.  
It can make your body less able to use insulin.  
This is called insulin resistance.

When this happens:
- Your body makes more insulin  
- You feel hungrier  
- You eat more  
- You gain more weight  
- This creates a cycle that is hard to break

Your body’s fat and sugar levels also change in unhealthy ways.

---

## What Increases Your Risk?

Many factors can raise your risk.  
Some you can change. Others you cannot.

**Risk factors include:**

- Belly fat  
- Not getting enough physical activity  
- A family history of metabolic syndrome  
- Not sleeping well (for example, due to sleep apnea)  
- Eating too many sugary or starchy foods  
- Drinking too many sugary drinks  
- Poor physical fitness

> **Good news:** Most of these risks can be reduced by making healthy lifestyle choices.

---

## How Common Is It?

In Germany:
- About 1 in 5 adults has metabolic syndrome.  
- Among people aged 50 to 70, up to 1 in 3 have it.  
- Men are slightly more likely than women to have it.

Also:
- 1 in 4 adults in Germany is severely overweight (obese).  
- This puts them at high risk for metabolic syndrome.

But even people with a normal weight can have metabolic syndrome if they carry fat around their belly.

---

## What Happens If You Have It?

Metabolic syndrome leads to other serious health problems.  
These include:

- Heart disease and blood vessel problems (like hardening of the arteries)  
- Higher risk of heart attack and stroke  
- Type 2 diabetes  
- Kidney damage (poor kidney function)  
- Fatty liver disease (not caused by alcohol)  
- Mental health issues like depression and Alzheimer’s disease

---

## How Can You Prevent It?

You can lower your risk by living a healthy lifestyle.  
This includes:

- Moving your body every day  
- Eating a balanced diet  
- Drinking little or no alcohol  
- Not smoking

The most important step is to maintain a healthy body weight.  
This means eating nutritious foods and staying active.

If you are unsure what to do, talk to your doctor.

---

## How Can It Be Detected Early?

In Germany, there is a free health check-up.  
It helps find risk factors early and stop the condition from developing.

- People aged 18 to 34 can have one check-up.  
- People aged 35 and older can have one every three years.

This check-up includes:
- A discussion about your health and habits  
- A physical exam  
- Blood tests

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose metabolic syndrome by checking for at least three of the following five signs:

1. **Severe overweight (obesity):** Measured by waist size  
   - Men: waist over 102 cm (40 inches)  
   - Women: waist over 88 cm (35 inches)

2. **High blood pressure:**  
   - At least 130/85 mmHg (systolic/diastolic)

3. **High blood sugar:**  
   - Fasting blood sugar of 100 mg/dl or higher

4. **High triglycerides:**  
   - 150 mg/dl or higher

5. **Low HDL cholesterol (“good” cholesterol):**  
   - Below 40 mg/dl in men  
   - Below 50 mg/dl in women

If you meet three or more of these, you may have metabolic syndrome.

---

## How Is It Treated?

The main treatment is to reduce your risk factors, especially your weight.  
This usually means making big changes in your daily habits.

### Lifestyle Changes

You should:

- Exercise for at least 30 minutes most days of the week  
- Eat more fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and healthy fats (like olive oil and nuts)  
- Avoid saturated fats and added sugar  
- Drink little or no alcohol  
- Stop smoking

A Mediterranean-style diet is a good example of a healthy eating pattern.

### Medication

If your blood pressure, blood sugar, or cholesterol levels are very high, your doctor may prescribe medicine.  
The decision depends on your personal health situation.

### Surgery

If you are severely overweight and lifestyle changes do not work, surgery may be an option.  
Types of surgery include:

- Gastric balloon: a device placed in the stomach to reduce hunger  
- Gastric bypass: surgery that makes the stomach smaller

These help you eat less and lose weight.  
Many people improve their health and reverse metabolic syndrome after surgery.

---

> **Always talk to your doctor** before starting any treatment or making big changes to your lifestyle.

# Prostate Stones

Prostate stones are small calcium deposits that form in a man’s prostate gland.  
They are very common in men over middle age.  
Most of the time, they do not cause any problems.  
If they do cause pain or trouble when urinating, treatment is possible.

---

## Quick Facts

- Prostate stones are small calcium deposits in the prostate gland.  
- They are common in men over middle age.  
- They usually do not cause symptoms.  
- Sometimes they cause a strong need to urinate, especially at night.  
- They can also cause pain in the lower back, pelvis, penis, or the area between the scrotum and anus.  
- If there is an infection, antibiotics can help.  
- If stones cause ongoing problems, they can be removed through the urethra using a thin surgical tool called an endoscope.  
- This same tool can also remove extra prostate tissue if the prostate is enlarged.  

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use this to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

---

## What Are Prostate Stones?

Prostate stones are tiny lumps made of calcium.  
They form inside the prostate gland.  
Men can have just one stone or many.  
They are usually between half a millimeter and five millimeters in size.  
That is about the size of a poppy seed or a millet seed.  

Do not confuse them with kidney stones.  
Kidney stones form in the kidneys, ureters, or bladder.  
Prostate stones are not the same.

Most men with prostate stones do not know they have them.  
They are often found by chance during a scan or test for another issue.  
But sometimes they cause symptoms.

---

## What Symptoms Can Prostate Stones Cause?

Some men with prostate stones have symptoms such as:

- A strong urge to urinate, especially at night.  
- Trouble starting to urinate or weak urine flow.  
- Pain in the lower back, pelvis, penis, or the area between the scrotum and anus.

Bacteria can grow inside prostate stones.  
This may lead to long-term inflammation of the prostate.  
This is called chronic prostatitis.  
It can also lead to urinary tract infections.

It is not clear if prostate stones cause erection problems or pain during ejaculation.  
So far, there is no proof of this link.

---

## How Do Prostate Stones Form?

Prostate stones are often made of calcium phosphate.  
This is the same type of mineral found in bones and teeth.

The exact cause of how they form is not fully known.  
But aging may play a role.  
There are two main ideas:

1. Prostate fluid may build up and then harden due to inflammation.  
2. A blockage in the prostate’s tubes may allow stones to form.

---

## How Common Are Prostate Stones?

Prostate stones are common in men over 50.  
But we do not have exact numbers on how many men have them.

They are often found when a man is tested for other prostate issues, such as:

- Benign prostate enlargement (BPH)  
- Chronic prostate inflammation  

The link between these conditions and prostate stones is not fully understood.

Calcium deposits in the prostate are also often seen in men with prostate cancer.

---

## How Are Prostate Stones Diagnosed?

Prostate stones are usually found by accident.  
For example, during a test for another problem.

Common ways to find them include:

- A transrectal ultrasound: a small probe is inserted into the rectum to take pictures.  
- A CT scan of the pelvis.  
- An X-ray of the kidneys and urinary tract.

These tests can clearly show the stones.

---

## How Are Prostate Stones Treated?

Most men do not need treatment.  
The body may naturally pass the stones in the urine.

But if the stones cause pain or trouble, treatment is available.

- If there is a bacterial infection, doctors give antibiotics.  
- If stones are large or cause ongoing inflammation, they can be removed through the urethra.  
- A thin surgical tool called an endoscope is used.  
- The tool is passed through the penis into the urethra.  
- The stones are removed, and extra prostate tissue is taken out if needed.  
- This procedure is called transurethral resection of the prostate, or TURP.

# Varicocele

A varicocele is a type of swollen vein in the scrotum. It is also called a varicose vein in the scrotum.

These veins are similar to varicose veins in the legs. They happen when blood builds up in the veins. This causes the veins to stay enlarged.

Varicoceles form in the veins that run along the spermatic cord. This cord carries blood from the testicles back to the body.

About 5 to 15 out of every 100 men have a varicocele. Most men do not have any symptoms.

Sometimes, a varicocele can cause:
- Swelling in the scrotum
- A feeling of tightness
- A dull, heavy, or dragging pain

A varicocele can also affect a man’s ability to have children. But many men with a varicocele can still have children.

---

## What is a varicocele?

Varicose veins are not only found in the legs. When they happen in the scrotum, doctors call them varicoceles.

They form in the veins along the spermatic cord. This cord carries blood from the testicles back to the body.

When blood builds up in these veins, they become permanently swollen. This is how a varicocele forms.

---

## What are the symptoms?

Most men with a varicocele do not feel any symptoms.

Some men may feel:
- Swelling in the scrotum
- A tight feeling
- A dull, heavy, or dragging pain

A varicocele can also lower fertility. It may make it harder for a man to have children. But this does not happen in all cases.

Many men with a varicocele can still have children.

---

## What causes a varicocele?

Several things can cause a varicocele.

In some men, the vein from the testicle joins the main vein in the pelvis at a sharp angle. This slows down blood flow. Blood can then build up in the scrotum. This leads to a varicocele.

This sharp angle happens more often on the left side. So varicoceles are more common on the left.

Some men are born with weak vein walls. This can also lead to varicoceles.

Valves in the veins help blood flow in one direction. If these valves do not work well, blood can pool in the veins.

A rare cause is a tumor pressing on the veins. This blocks blood flow and can cause a varicocele. When this happens, doctors call it a “symptomatic” varicocele.

---

## How common are varicoceles?

Varicoceles are most often found in teenage boys and young men between 15 and 25 years old.

Experts estimate that 5 to 15 out of every 100 men have a varicocele.

In about 9 out of 10 cases, the varicocele is on the left side.

---

## How is a varicocele diagnosed?

If the varicocele is large, a doctor can see or feel it during an exam.

Sometimes, the doctor presses on the stomach to push blood into the veins. This makes the varicocele easier to feel.

For smaller varicoceles, a doctor uses an ultrasound scan. This test uses sound waves to show the veins clearly.

---

## How are varicoceles treated?

Most varicoceles do not need treatment. They do not cause harm and do not affect health.

But if a man cannot have children and has a varicocele, treatment may help improve fertility.

The goal of treatment is to stop blood from flowing through the swollen vein. Blood then flows through healthy nearby veins.

There are three main treatment methods:

### 1. Embolization
A thin tube is inserted into a blood vessel in the leg. The doctor guides it to the swollen vein in the scrotum. Medicine or small metal coils are then released. These cause a blood clot to form and close off the vein.

### 2. Sclerotherapy
