A special medicine is injected into the swollen vein. This medicine damages the inside of the vein. The vein then sticks together and closes.

### 3. Surgery
The doctor cuts open the scrotum or groin. They tie off or clip the swollen vein. The blood is then rerouted through smaller, healthy veins.

### Possible side effects of treatment
Treatment can cause:
- Bleeding
- Infected wounds
- Nerve damage
- Swelling in the scrotum (called a hydrocele)

---

## Important note

This information is for general understanding only. It cannot replace a visit to a doctor. Do not use this to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a healthcare provider for medical advice.

# Ingrown Toenail (Onychocryptosis)

An ingrown toenail happens when the edge of the nail grows into the skin around it. This is most common on the big toe.

It can cause pain, redness, and swelling. If not treated, it may lead to infection.

You can often prevent this problem with good nail care.

---

## What Is an Ingrown Toenail?

The nail grows into the skin on one or both sides of the toe. This can hurt and cause inflammation.

The skin around the nail becomes red, swollen, and tender.

In medical terms, this is called unguis incarnatus or onychocryptosis.

---

## What Causes Ingrown Toenails?

Common causes include:

- Cutting the nails too short or rounding the corners
- Wearing shoes that are too tight
- Feet that sweat a lot
- Having naturally curved or thick toenails (a family trait)
- Being overweight
- Health conditions like diabetes
- Swelling in the feet due to heart, kidney, or vein problems
- Some cancer treatments

---

## How Common Are Ingrown Toenails?

About 20 out of every 100 people who see a doctor for foot pain have an ingrown toenail.

They are most common in teenagers and young adults. Sweaty feet from sports or puberty can increase the risk.

Older people also get them often. As we age, our nails get thicker and harder to cut. Feet also become less flexible, making care harder.

Conditions like diabetes are more common in older adults and can make ingrown toenails worse.

---

## How Does It Start?

An ingrown toenail usually hurts right away. Most people notice it early.

If you act quickly, you can often treat it at home. The pain and swelling usually go away without problems.

But if your immune system is weak, or if bacteria get into the area, the infection can spread.

This can cause pus, severe pain, and swelling under or around the nail.

You should see a doctor if:

- The pain gets worse
- The area swells more
- You have a high fever
- You feel very tired
- The infection spreads into the soft tissue (called a phlegmon)

---

## How Can You Prevent It?

Good foot care helps stop ingrown toenails.

- Cut your nails straight across. Do not round the corners.
- Keep the nails long enough so the edges sit flat on the skin.
- Wear shoes that give your toes room to move.
- Choose open-toed or breathable shoes to reduce sweating.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor can usually tell if you have an ingrown toenail just by looking at your toe.

They will ask about your symptoms and what might have caused it.

If there is a serious infection, they may order a blood test or other check.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on how bad the pain and swelling are.

### For mild cases:
- Soak your foot in warm, soapy water for 10 to 15 minutes.
- Dry your foot completely after soaking.
- Apply an antiseptic or anti-inflammatory cream or gel.
- Avoid putting pressure on the toe.
- Do not wear shoes right away after soaking.

You can also use special bandages or nail braces. These help the nail grow straight again. A podologist (foot care specialist) can provide these.

### When to see a doctor:
- If home care does not help
- If the area is very swollen or red
- If pus is coming from the toe
- If you have diabetes or poor circulation

In these cases, surgery may be needed. There are different types of surgery. Talk to your doctor to learn what is best for you.

For more information on home treatments, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## How Does It Affect Daily Life?

An ingrown toenail can make walking and standing painful.

To reduce pain:

- Wear open-toed shoes or sandals
- Use wide, soft socks
- Keep your foot free at night
- Do not let the bed cover press on the toe
- Hang the cover over the foot of the bed to create space

Some people have trouble caring for their feet. This can happen if they have joint pain or poor balance.

If you cannot get help from a family member or friend, you can get professional help.

### Options for foot care:

- **Pedicure salon (cosmetic foot care):**  
  They can trim nails and remove hard skin.  
  You pay for this yourself.

- **Podologist (medical foot care):**  
  Best for people with health issues like diabetes.  
  Some health insurance plans cover this care if the foot problem is linked to a medical condition.

Always talk to your doctor before starting any new foot care, especially if you have diabetes or poor circulation.

# Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS)

MERS is a lung infection caused by a virus called the MERS coronavirus.  
Most people get infected by being close to an infected dromedary camel.  
The disease mostly happens in countries on the Arabian Peninsula.  
It is very rare in Germany.

---

## Quick Facts

- MERS is caused by a virus called MERS-CoV.  
- The virus can infect both dromedary camels and people.  
- It mostly happens in countries on the Arabian Peninsula.  
- Many people with MERS have flu-like symptoms at first.  
- Some people have no symptoms at all.  
- About half of all diagnosed cases become serious.  
- Around one in three people with MERS die.  
- Serious illness is more common in older adults and people with long-term health problems.  
- There is no specific medicine to treat MERS.  
- Doctors focus on helping the patient feel better and supporting their body.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is MERS?

Middle East Respiratory Syndrome is a lung infection caused by the MERS-CoV virus.  
The virus was first found in 2012.  
It can make both humans and dromedary camels sick.  
The virus can pass between animals and people.  
In camels, the illness is very mild or not noticeable.  
Most cases have happened in countries on the Arabian Peninsula.  
The largest number of cases have been in Saudi Arabia.  
All cases outside this region are linked to travel there or contact with someone who has MERS.  
Unlike SARS or COVID-19, the World Health Organization does not see MERS as a global health threat.  
This is because it does not spread easily from person to person.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Some people infected with MERS have no symptoms.  
This is called an asymptomatic infection.  
If symptoms do appear, they usually start one to three weeks after infection.  
Most people first feel like they have the flu.  
Common flu-like symptoms include:  
- High fever  
- Chills  
- Body aches  
- Cough  
- Trouble breathing  

Some people also have stomach problems like:  
- Diarrhea  
- Nausea  
- Belly pain  

Over time, many people develop pneumonia.  
Some also get severe breathing problems or kidney failure.

---

## How Do People Get MERS?

MERS is caused by the MERS-CoV virus.  
The main way people get infected is through close contact with infected dromedary camels.  
Diseases that pass from animals to people are called zoonotic diseases.  
It is also possible to catch MERS from another person.  
But this rarely happens outside of hospitals.  
Most person-to-person cases happen in healthcare settings.  
Sometimes one infected person spreads the virus to many others. These are called super-spreader events.  
The exact way MERS spreads is not fully known.  
It may spread through touch or through tiny droplets in the air when someone coughs or sneezes.

---

## Who Is at Higher Risk for Severe MERS?

Older adults, especially those over 60, are more likely to get very sick.  
People with long-term health problems are also at higher risk.  
These include:  
- Diabetes  
- High blood pressure  
- Heart disease  
- Kidney disease

---

## How Common Is MERS?

Around 2,600 cases of MERS have been recorded worldwide.  
Most of these cases happened in countries on the Arabian Peninsula.  
Saudi Arabia has had the most cases.  
Nearly 900 people have died from MERS or its complications.  
If you have never been to the Arabian Peninsula and have not been near dromedary camels, your risk is very low.  
Germany has had only three confirmed cases.  
All three people had traveled to the Arabian Peninsula before getting sick.  
None of them spread the virus to anyone else in Germany.

---

## What Is the Outlook for MERS?

MERS can cause mild illness, serious illness, or no symptoms at all.  
Up to half of all diagnosed cases become moderate to severe.  
The older a person is, the more likely they are to have a serious case.  
Older people are also more likely to die from MERS.  
Common complications include:  
- Pneumonia  
- Severe breathing problems  
- Kidney failure  

Almost everyone with MERS needs to be in the hospital.  
Many need help breathing with a machine.  
About one in three patients die from MERS or its complications.

---

## How Can MERS Be Prevented?

There is no approved vaccine for MERS.  
This makes prevention steps very important.

### Avoid Contact with Dromedary Camels

- MERS often spreads from camels to people.  
- The World Health Organization advises people, especially those at higher risk, to avoid camels.  
- Do not drink raw camel milk.  
- Do not eat raw camel meat.

### Be Careful When Traveling to the Arabian Peninsula

- Wash your hands often.  
- Avoid close contact with people who have a cough or cold.

### Limit Contact and Practice Good Hygiene

- If you have MERS or think you might have it, stay at home.  
- Do not go to work, school, or public places.  
- Healthcare workers must wear gloves, goggles, and an FFP2 mask when treating patients.  
- They must follow strict hygiene rules.

---

## How Is MERS Diagnosed?

If you think you might have MERS — for example, after a trip to the Arabian Peninsula and then getting a lung infection — you should get tested.  
Your doctor will take a sample from your lungs.  
This sample goes to a lab.  
A PCR test checks for the virus’s genetic material in the sample.

---

## How Is MERS Treated?

There is no medicine that directly treats MERS.  
Scientists are still working on treatments.  
Right now, treatment focuses on relieving symptoms.  
This may include:  
- Oxygen therapy  
- Help with breathing using a machine in severe cases

# Pulmonary Embolism

A pulmonary embolism happens when a blood vessel in the lung gets blocked. This blockage is usually caused by a blood clot that travels from another part of the body, often the leg or pelvis. It is a serious emergency that needs immediate medical care.

---

## What You Need to Know at a Glance

- A pulmonary embolism blocks a blood vessel in the lung.
- The blockage is most often caused by a blood clot from the leg or pelvis.
- Common symptoms include:
  - Sudden shortness of breath
  - Chest pain, especially when breathing in or coughing
  - Coughing up blood
  - Dizziness or feeling faint
  - Fast or irregular heartbeat
  - Strong feelings of anxiety
- This is an emergency. If you or someone else has these symptoms, call emergency services right away at 112.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Pulmonary Embolism?

A pulmonary embolism occurs when a blood vessel in the lung becomes blocked. This usually happens when a blood clot moves through the bloodstream and gets stuck in a lung artery.

If a lung artery is blocked, blood cannot flow through it properly. This causes pressure to build up in the heart. Over time, this can weaken the heart and lead to life-threatening problems.

---

## How Do You Know If You Have a Pulmonary Embolism?

Small clots may cause no symptoms at all. Larger clots can cause serious symptoms, including:

- Sudden shortness of breath
- Sharp chest pain that gets worse when you breathe in or cough
- Coughing, sometimes with blood
- Dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting
- Fast or irregular heartbeat
- A strong sense of fear or panic

> **Act fast:** If you or someone else has these symptoms, call 112 immediately. Ask for an ambulance with an emergency doctor. Do not wait for a regular doctor on call.

---

## What Causes a Pulmonary Embolism?

When you get hurt and bleed, your body forms a blood clot to stop the bleeding. This is a normal and helpful process.

But sometimes, blood clots form inside blood vessels without any injury. If a clot blocks a blood vessel, it can cause serious problems like a heart attack, stroke, or pulmonary embolism.

This is rare in healthy people. But certain conditions can increase the risk:

- Certain genetic conditions
- Previous blood clots in the leg (deep vein thrombosis)
- Some cancers
- Heart problems like heart failure, heart attack, or irregular heartbeat
- Hormonal birth control pills or hormone therapy for menopause
- Recent surgery or injury

Most blood clots that cause a pulmonary embolism start in the veins of the legs. These clots can break loose and travel through the blood to the lungs.

In very rare cases, a pulmonary embolism can be caused by fat, air, or fluid from the amniotic sac during childbirth.

---

## What Increases the Risk of a Pulmonary Embolism?

The main risk factors include:

- Broken hip or leg
- Major surgery, such as knee or hip replacement
- Blood clotting disorders (like antiphospholipid syndrome)
- History of deep vein thrombosis
- Certain cancers
- Heart problems (heart failure, heart attack, or atrial fibrillation)
- Hormonal birth control with estrogen
- Menopause hormone therapy

Other factors that slightly raise the risk are:

- Being older
- Pregnancy
- Being overweight
- High blood pressure
- Diabetes
- Varicose veins
- Staying in bed for more than three days
- Lung infections, such as those caused by SARS-CoV-2 (the virus that causes COVID-19)

> **Important:** The risk is much higher if several of these factors are present at the same time.

---

## How Common Is a Pulmonary Embolism?

The risk goes up with age:

- About 1 in 1,000 people aged 40 to 50 get a pulmonary embolism each year.
- About 10 in 1,000 people aged 80 or older get it each year.

Men are more likely to get it than women.

---

## How Does a Pulmonary Embolism Progress?

The severity depends on how big the clot is and how many clots are in the lung. Your overall health also matters, especially how well your heart and lungs are working.

Most people’s hearts can still pump blood even with a clot in the lung. But if the heart is weak, it may not be able to push blood through the blocked vessels. This can cause low blood pressure and poor oxygen supply.

Low blood pressure is a sign that the condition is serious. Out of every 100 people with a pulmonary embolism:

- About 95 have normal blood pressure and a low risk of serious complications.
- About 5 have very low blood pressure and a high risk of serious or fatal outcomes.

If you have ongoing risk factors like cancer or blood clotting disorders, you may be at risk for another embolism.

---

## How Can You Prevent a Pulmonary Embolism?

After surgery or long periods of inactivity, doctors may prescribe medicine to prevent blood clots. This medicine can be taken as a pill or injected.

If you are recovering from surgery or injury and must stay in bed, it is important to get up and move as soon as possible.

Simple movements like wiggling your toes or feet can help keep blood flowing.

People at high risk of leg blood clots may wear compression stockings. These tight-fitting socks help push blood back toward the heart.

People who take blood-thinning medicine do not need compression stockings. These stockings are an option for people who cannot take blood-thinning medicine.

For more information on preventing future embolisms, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

---

## How Is a Pulmonary Embolism Diagnosed?

Symptoms like sudden chest pain or shortness of breath can also be signs of other serious conditions, such as a heart attack or pneumonia.

If you have these symptoms, call 112 right away. Do not wait.

If a pulmonary embolism is suspected, the doctor will ask questions and do a physical exam. A quick and accurate diagnosis is essential.

The hospital will perform several tests in sequence. These include:

- A blood test (D-dimer test)
- An electrocardiogram (ECG)
- An ultrasound scan of the heart and leg veins
- A CT scan of the lungs (called a CTPA)

These tests together help confirm the diagnosis.

---

## How Is a Pulmonary Embolism Treated?

Treatment depends on how stable the person’s circulation is and how severe the symptoms are.

### If the Circulation Is Stable

- You will likely stay in the hospital for a few days.
- You will be given blood-thinning medicine (anticoagulants).
- This medicine stops new clots from forming and prevents the existing clot from getting bigger.
- Your body will slowly break down the clot over time.

### If the Circulation Is Unstable

- You will be treated in intensive care.
- You will be closely monitored.
- You may need fluids through a drip, breathing support, or extra medicine.
- Blood-thinning medicine will start right away, even before the diagnosis is confirmed.

In some cases, doctors may use a treatment called thrombolysis. This uses special medicine delivered through a drip to break up the clot. This treatment is not safe for people at high risk of bleeding.

Another option is a catheter procedure. A thin tube is guided through a blood vessel to the blocked lung artery. Doctors can then deliver medicine directly to the clot or try to break it up.

### After Recovery

Once you have recovered, your doctor will likely recommend taking blood-thinning medicine for several months. In some cases, long-term treatment may be needed to prevent future clots.

For more information on treating pulmonary embolism with blood-thinning medicine, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

# Overactive Parathyroid Glands

Overactive parathyroid glands mean the glands make too much of a hormone called parathyroid hormone. This raises the amount of calcium in the blood. High calcium can harm bones, kidneys, and other parts of the body. It can also cause tiredness, mood changes, and stomach problems. Surgery often helps fix the problem.

---

## Quick Facts

- The parathyroid glands are small glands in the neck, behind the thyroid gland.
- They make a hormone that controls calcium levels in the body.
- Overactive parathyroid glands are one of the most common hormone problems.
- Too much parathyroid hormone raises blood calcium and lowers blood phosphate.
- Many people have no symptoms at first. Others have serious problems.
- A non-cancerous tumor on one gland is the most common cause.
- Other health issues, like long-term kidney problems, can also cause this condition.
- Surgery is often the best treatment.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Are Overactive Parathyroid Glands?

Overactive parathyroid glands mean the glands make too much parathyroid hormone. This is called hyperparathyroidism.

The parathyroid glands are small and sit behind the thyroid gland in the neck. They work on their own and are not part of the thyroid.

These glands help control how much calcium is in your blood. They do this by making parathyroid hormone.

When the glands are overactive, they make too much hormone. This causes the body to release more calcium from the bones. The kidneys cannot remove all of this extra calcium. So, calcium builds up in the blood.

At the same time, the body loses more phosphate through urine. This lowers the amount of phosphate in the blood.

About half of all people with this condition feel no symptoms. Others may have:

- Bone pain
- Kidney stones
- Tiredness
- Anxiety
- Depression

Most often, a non-cancerous tumor on one gland causes the problem. This is more common in women and becomes more likely with age.

Other health issues can also lead to overactive glands. For example, long-term kidney problems can cause this.

In many cases, surgery removes the overactive gland. This often cures the problem.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

A mild form of the condition may cause no symptoms. It might only be found during a routine blood test.

When symptoms do appear, they can include:

- Feeling very tired or weak
- Constipation, loss of appetite, or nausea
- Stomach or small intestine ulcers
- Gallstones
- Needing to urinate more often or feeling very thirsty
- Sharp pain in the side if you have kidney stones
- Bone or joint pain
- Broken bones in the spine or feet without a clear cause
- Itching
- Trouble sleeping, poor concentration, or memory problems
- Mood swings, anxiety, or depression
- High blood pressure
- Irregular heartbeat

---

## What Causes Overactive Parathyroid Glands?

There are three main types of this condition: primary, secondary, and tertiary.

### Primary Hyperparathyroidism

This is the most common type. It starts in the parathyroid glands themselves.

In most cases, one gland has a non-cancerous tumor. This tumor makes too much parathyroid hormone. The tumor is called an adenoma.

Sometimes, more than one gland is affected. The extra hormone causes high blood calcium and low blood phosphate.

### Secondary and Tertiary Hyperparathyroidism

These types are caused by other health problems.

If you have long-term bowel issues or kidney disease, your body may not get enough calcium. Your parathyroid glands try to fix this by making more hormone. This pulls more calcium from your bones.

Chronic kidney disease is a major cause. It disrupts the balance of minerals in your body. Over time, the glands grow larger and keep working too hard. This is called tertiary hyperparathyroidism.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

At first, symptoms may be mild or seem like other problems. Your doctor will ask about your health history and symptoms.

If overactive parathyroid glands are suspected, your doctor will do tests.

### Blood and Urine Tests

- High levels of parathyroid hormone in the blood are a strong sign.
- Calcium levels are often high. Phosphate levels are often low.
- Your doctor will also check your vitamin D levels, kidney function, and how much calcium is in your urine.

### Bone Density Test

A special X-ray checks your bones. It shows if the condition has already weakened your bones. The spine, hips, and forearms are usually checked.

### Imaging Before Surgery

If surgery is planned, your doctor will use imaging to find the problem gland.

- An ultrasound scan looks at the neck area.
- A scintigraphy scan helps locate a tumor and which gland is affected.
- High-resolution CT scans of the neck are also used more often now to plan surgery.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on how serious the condition is and whether it is primary or secondary.

### Treating Primary Hyperparathyroidism

This type is usually caused by a tumor on one gland.

The best treatment is surgery to remove the overactive gland. This is done under general anesthesia.

In many cases, only a small cut is needed. This is called minimally invasive surgery.

During surgery, the hormone level drops quickly. This confirms the surgery worked.

Sometimes, more than one gland needs to be removed. In rare cases, a small piece of healthy gland tissue is moved to the neck muscle or forearm. This helps keep some hormone production in the body.

Surgery often cures the problem. It also helps prevent future health issues.

If the condition is very mild and causes no symptoms, surgery may not be needed. Instead, your doctor will check your blood regularly to watch for changes.

### Treating Secondary Hyperparathyroidism

This type is caused by another illness, like long-term kidney disease.

The main treatment is to fix the underlying problem. This includes managing kidney health and balancing minerals in the body.

You may also need to take vitamin D and other supplements.

If the glands are very large, surgery may be an option. This means removing part or all of the overactive glands.

But there is not enough long-term research on how well surgery works for this type. So, each person must carefully consider the risks and benefits before deciding.

# Balanitis

Balanitis means inflammation of the head of the penis.  
It causes redness and pain in that area.  
The condition is often caused by a fungal infection.  
It can also be caused by bacteria passed during sex.  
Irritation from soap or an allergy to latex in condoms can also lead to balanitis.

## Quick Facts

- Balanitis is inflammation of the head of the penis.  
- If the foreskin is also inflamed, doctors call it balanoposthitis.  
- Common signs include redness and pain on the head of the penis.  
- Fungal infections are a common cause.  
- Bacteria from sexual contact can also cause it.  
- A buildup of smegma increases the risk.  
- Smegma is a mix of skin oil, dead skin cells, and bacteria.  
- Perfumed soaps or latex in condoms can irritate the skin or cause an allergic reaction.  
- Good, gentle hygiene can help prevent balanitis.  

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical care.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Balanitis?

Balanitis is a name doctors use for swelling and irritation of the head of the penis.  
It can be caused by bacteria, viruses, or yeast.  
It can also happen due to skin irritation.  
For example, using scented soap can irritate the skin.  
An allergic reaction to latex in condoms can also cause it.  
Keeping the area clean and gentle can help stop balanitis.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Redness and pain on the head of the penis may mean you have balanitis.  
Other signs include:  
- Itching  
- Swelling of the penis  
- Pain when peeing  
- Thick, white, or yellow fluid coming from the tip of the penis  
- Sores or patches on the skin  
- Trouble pulling back the foreskin

## What Causes Balanitis?

Poor hygiene can lead to balanitis.  
If you do not clean under the foreskin, smegma can build up.  
Smegma is a mix of skin oil, dead skin cells, and bacteria.  
This mix can grow germs and cause infection.  

Using scented soaps or harsh body washes can harm the skin’s natural protection.  
Over-washing can also cause problems.  

Fungi are a common cause.  
Bacteria from sexually transmitted infections can also cause it.  
Examples include the germs that cause gonorrhea and syphilis.  
Some types of human papillomavirus can also lead to balanitis.  

Allergic reactions to medicine or latex in condoms can cause inflammation.  
Other skin conditions like psoriasis or lichen sclerosus can also cause it.

## How Common Is Balanitis?

Balanitis is fairly common.  
About 12 to 20 out of every 100 men will have it at some point.  
It is more likely if you have phimosis.  
Phimosis means the foreskin is too tight to pull back easily.

## How Can I Prevent Balanitis?

Wash your penis regularly.  
If you are not circumcised, gently pull back the foreskin.  
Wash the head of the penis with warm water only.  
Do not scrub or pull hard.  
Do not use soap, body wash, shower gel, scrubs, or aftershave.  

Clean the area after sex or exercise.  
Sweat, sperm, or lubricant can collect and cause irritation.  

For young boys, change diapers often.  
Clean the head of the penis gently when changing.  
Do not force the foreskin back if it is stuck or tight.

## How Is Balanitis Diagnosed?

A doctor will look at the redness and skin changes on the head of the penis.  
They may take a sample to test for fungi or bacteria.  
This helps find the cause.  

Tests like blood or urine checks may be done.  
These can show if the infection has spread to the bladder or urinary tract.  
They can also check for conditions like diabetes.  

If you are uncircumcised, the doctor will check how easily the foreskin moves.  
This helps rule out phimosis.

## How Is Balanitis Treated?

Wash the area gently with clean, warm water two to three times a day.  
Dry it with a clean cotton swab or dry wipe.  

You can use warm baths with antiseptic (like octenidine) to help healing.  
These are called sitz baths.  
Compresses can also help.  

For pain, take ibuprofen or paracetamol.  

See a doctor if symptoms do not improve in a week.  
They can find the exact cause and recommend the right treatment.  

- If it is a yeast infection, use an antifungal cream.  
- If it is due to an allergy, use a cortisone cream.  
- If it is a bacterial infection, use an antibiotic cream.  
- In some cases, oral medicine may be needed.

## Who Should I Contact?

If you have redness, pain, or swelling on the head of the penis, see a urologist.  
They are doctors who specialize in the urinary and reproductive system.

# Hip Fractures

A hip fracture means the thigh bone (femur) is broken near the hip joint. This is common in older adults after a fall.

Most people with a hip fracture need surgery. In some cases, the damaged part of the hip is replaced with an artificial joint.

---

## Quick Facts

- Bones get weaker as we age. This makes falls more likely to cause breaks.
- Many falls happen when someone lands directly on their hip while standing.
- Surgery should happen within the first 24 hours. Pain medicine alone is not enough.
- Even with good treatment, many people still need help walking afterward.
- There is a higher risk of death in the first few months after surgery.
- The best way to prevent hip fractures is to strengthen bones and avoid falls.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Hip Fracture?

A hip fracture is a break in the upper part of the thigh bone, close to the hip joint.

More people are getting hip fractures as the population ages. This is often due to weak bones from a condition called osteoporosis — especially in women.

The most common break happens at the neck of the femur. This is the narrow part that connects the ball of the hip to the long shaft of the bone.

---

### How Is the Hip Joint Built?

The hip joint has a ball-shaped top of the thigh bone (femoral head) that fits into a socket in the pelvis.

The ball and socket are covered with smooth tissue. A strong capsule surrounds the joint.

A short, slanted neck connects the ball to the long shaft of the bone, which runs down to the knee.

Below the ball is a small bump called the lesser trochanter. On the side is a larger bump called the greater trochanter. These bumps are where muscles attach. The muscles help you walk and keep your pelvis level.

---

### Types of Hip Fractures

There are three main types, based on where the break happens:

- **Femoral neck fracture**: The break is inside the joint capsule.
- **Pertrochanteric fracture**: The break is between the two bony bumps (greater and lesser trochanters).
- **Subtrochanteric fracture**: The break is below both bony bumps.

---

## What Are the Signs of a Hip Fracture?

Pain is the main symptom. It usually happens right after the fall. The pain is in the hip, groin, buttock, or thigh. Sometimes it spreads to the knee.

One leg may look shorter than the other. The injured leg often turns outward.

You will not be able to put weight on the leg. You will not be able to stand up on your own.

In rare cases, the broken bone ends are tightly locked together. Then the pain may be mild, and you might still be able to walk.

If the break is outside the joint capsule, you may see a large bruise on the hip.

---

## What Causes a Hip Fracture?

Most hip fractures in older adults happen after a fall. The person lands directly on the hip.

Sometimes, a twist or sudden movement causes the break — for example, if the foot gets caught.

Older people fall for many reasons. Some causes include:

- Heart or blood vessel problems
- Poor eyesight
- Dizziness
- Side effects from medicine
- General weakness and poor balance

If bones are weak from osteoporosis, even a small fall from standing can break them.

Younger people usually break their hip from serious accidents — like falling from a height or a car crash.

---

## Who Is at Higher Risk?

The main risk factors are:

- Osteoporosis (weak bones)
- Increased chance of falling in older age

Other things that raise the risk of falling include:

- Heart or blood vessel disease
- Diabetes
- Overactive thyroid
- Poor vision
- Dizziness
- Certain medicines that cause dizziness or weaken bones

People who have had a hip fracture before are more likely to break a bone again.

---

## How Common Are Hip Fractures?

Hip fractures mostly happen in older adults.

In Germany, between 6 and 9 out of every 1,000 people aged 65 or older break a hip each year.

Women are affected about three times more often than men. This is because women often lose bone density after menopause. Hormonal changes make their bones weaker and more likely to break.

---

## What Is the Outlook After a Hip Fracture?

Femoral neck fractures are common. They can damage blood vessels that feed the top of the thigh bone.

If the blood supply is cut off, the bone head can die. This is called femoral head necrosis. The risk is higher if the broken pieces move out of place.

---

### Possible Complications

Even with good treatment, problems can still happen:

- Ongoing pain
- Broken bone pieces move apart
- The bone does not heal
- Trouble moving
- Difficulty walking (pelvis drops to one side)
- Infected bone

Older patients often stay in hospital longer. This can lead to:

- Blood clots in the legs (thrombosis)
- Pneumonia
- Urinary tract infections
- Wound healing problems
- Bedsores (decubitus)
- Confusion (delirium)

Many older people already have other health issues, like heart disease or dementia. These can affect recovery and increase the risk of complications.

That is why surgery should happen within 24 hours. Getting the patient moving quickly helps prevent these problems.

The risk of dying increases in the first few months after surgery. Only about half of older adults can walk without help after a hip fracture. One in five will need long-term care.

---

## How Can Hip Fractures Be Prevented?

Prevention focuses on stronger bones and fewer falls. Ways to help include:

- Exercise regularly, starting early in life
- Get tested for osteoporosis. If found, treat it with medicine like bisphosphonates
- Eat enough calcium and vitamin D
- Do not smoke
- Limit alcohol
- Do strength training
- Remove tripping hazards at home (like loose rugs or clutter)
- Treat health problems that increase fall risk

---

## How Is a Hip Fracture Diagnosed?

A simple X-ray usually shows the break. Doctors may compare it to an X-ray of the other hip.

If the X-ray is unclear, a CT scan may be used. An MRI is only used in rare cases.

These scans help doctors see the exact type of break. This helps them decide on the best surgery.

A physical exam checks for injuries in other parts of the body.

If the cause of the fall is not clear, doctors will investigate further after surgery.

---

## How Is a Hip Fracture Treated?

Most hip fractures need surgery as soon as possible. The goal is to fix the bone so the person can walk again.

Pain relief is given first, using medicine like tablets, injections, or nerve blocks.

The type of surgery depends on the fracture type and the patient’s age and activity level.

- **Screws** can hold the bone in place. This is usually for younger people.
- A **metal rod (nail)** can be inserted into the bone shaft.
- The damaged bone head may be removed and replaced with an **artificial hip joint**.

Doctors try to keep the natural hip joint in younger patients. In older patients, a replacement is often better.

---

### When Is Surgery Not Done?

Surgery is not always needed. It may be skipped in these cases:

- The bone pieces are tightly locked together and the person can walk with little pain. Screws may still be added to prevent future slipping.
- The person was already unable to walk or had dementia before the fall and is not in much pain.
- The person has other serious health problems that make surgery too risky.

---

### Other Treatments Used

- **Pain relief** is key. Medicine can be taken by mouth, injected, or given through a drip.
- To prevent blood clots in the legs, patients get medicine that thins the blood.
- Breathing exercises help prevent pneumonia.

---

## What Aftercare Is Needed?

After surgery, patients should start moving as soon as possible. This includes sitting up, standing, and doing physical exercises.

The type of movement allowed depends on the treatment. A doctor or nurse will explain what to avoid at first.

The main goal is to help the person walk again and regain independence.

For older adults, the broken bone is usually fixed with a nail or an artificial joint. This allows full weight on the leg.

After the hospital stay, follow-up care or rehabilitation is needed. For older patients, this is best done in a geriatric hospital.

If the reason for the fall was unclear, the hospital stay is a good time to find out and treat the cause.

# Diastasis Recti

Diastasis recti means the two main stomach muscles have moved apart.  
This often happens during pregnancy.  
It usually gets better on its own after childbirth.  
Special exercises can help prevent it or treat it.

---

## Quick Facts

- Diastasis recti is when the two stomach muscles separate in the middle.
- You may see a thin, vertical bulge down the center of your stomach.
- The most common causes are pregnancy or being very overweight.
- A doctor can check for it by feeling your stomach.
- Most people get better with physiotherapy or by losing weight.
- Surgery is rarely needed.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Diastasis Recti?

Your stomach has two strong muscles that run from your ribs down to your pelvis.  
They meet in the middle along a line called the "linea alba."  
This line is usually one to two centimeters wide.  
When pressure builds up inside your belly, the line can stretch.  
This creates a gap between the muscles.  
You can feel this gap with your fingers.  
You may also see a bulge in the middle of your stomach.

Pregnancy is the most common reason for this.  
The gap often closes on its own after giving birth.  
Exercises after childbirth can help speed up recovery.

---

## What Are the Signs?

You may notice a thin, vertical bulge in the middle of your stomach.  
It often shows up when you sit up or strain.  
The bulge may go away when you lie down.

You might feel a little pain in your stomach, pelvis, or hips.  
You may also find it harder to do certain physical activities.

---

## What Causes It?

The two stomach muscles pull apart at the center.  
This happens when pressure builds up inside the belly.  
Pregnancy is the most common cause.  
Being very overweight can also cause it.

Surgery in the stomach area can weaken the muscles.  
This may lead to diastasis recti.

---

## Who Is at Higher Risk?

Not all pregnant women get diastasis recti.  
But it is more likely if:

- You are carrying twins.
- You are slim but carrying a very large baby.
- You have had more than one baby.
- You had a cesarean section before.

Lifting heavy things during pregnancy can also raise your risk.

Outside of pregnancy, rapid weight gain or loss can increase your risk.  
It is also more common after stomach surgery.

---

## How Can You Prevent It?

During pregnancy, doing regular exercises can help keep your stomach muscles strong.  
These exercises can lower your risk of diastasis recti.

Work with a trained physiotherapist or midwife.  
They can teach you safe and effective moves.  
They can also check that you are doing them correctly.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor can check for diastasis recti during a simple exam.  
They will press on your stomach to feel for a gap between the muscles.

If you are very overweight, the doctor may use an ultrasound or CT scan.  
These tests give a clearer picture of what is happening inside.

> **Important:** Diastasis recti is not dangerous.  
> But it is still a good idea to see a doctor.  
> They can make sure you do not have a hernia.  
> A hernia may need surgery.

---

## How Is It Treated?

If it is caused by pregnancy, the gap usually closes on its own.  
Doing the right exercises after childbirth can help.  
Midwives and physiotherapists can show you safe exercises.  
They can also check that you are doing them right.

If diastasis recti is not caused by pregnancy, losing weight and doing physiotherapy often help.  
Exercises that strengthen your core, upper body, and balance are especially useful.

Surgery is only considered if:

- You have severe pain.
- The gap is very wide.
- Other treatments do not help.

> **Important:** Diastasis recti is seen as a cosmetic issue.  
> It is not a medical emergency.  
> Most health insurance plans do not pay for surgery to fix it.

# Atrial Fibrillation

Atrial fibrillation is a common heart rhythm problem. It causes the heart to beat in an irregular and often fast way. This can make you feel your heart pounding or racing. The condition is not an emergency, but it can lead to serious health issues over time.

## What You Need to Know at a Glance

- Atrial fibrillation is a type of irregular heartbeat.
- The heart beats too fast and in a chaotic way.
- This means the heart does not pump blood as well as it should.
- It is often caused by other long-term health problems like high blood pressure or heart disease.
- It increases your risk of stroke.
- There are several ways to manage symptoms and lower your stroke risk.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Atrial Fibrillation?

Your heart has a natural electrical system that tells it when to beat. In atrial fibrillation, this system goes wrong. The upper chambers of the heart (the atria) quiver instead of pumping blood properly. This causes the heart to beat fast and irregularly.

Because the heart is not pumping well, you may feel dizzy, weak, or faint. Some people feel a strong pounding in their chest. This is called palpitations.

Atrial fibrillation is usually caused by another health condition. The most common causes are high blood pressure and heart disease. In some cases, doctors cannot find a clear cause.

While atrial fibrillation is not dangerous right away, it can lead to long-term problems. These include stroke and weakening of the heart muscle.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The most common symptom is a noticeable pounding or racing heartbeat. This means your heart is beating faster and less regularly than normal. A normal resting heart rate is between 60 and 90 beats per minute. In atrial fibrillation, the rate can be much higher.

Other possible symptoms include:
- Feeling weak or dizzy
- Chest tightness
- Shortness of breath, especially during activity

But more than half of people with atrial fibrillation have no symptoms at all — or only mild ones — at first.

If you already have heart problems, such as heart failure, the symptoms may be worse. You may feel very tired or out of breath when you walk or do light exercise.

## What Causes Atrial Fibrillation?

Your heart beats because of electrical signals. These signals start in a small group of cells called the sinus node. This is like the heart’s natural pacemaker. The signals travel through the heart and make it contract in a steady rhythm.

In atrial fibrillation, the electrical signals become chaotic. They spread quickly through the upper chambers of the heart. The sinus node stops working properly. The upper chambers no longer pump blood in a regular way. Instead, they shake or quiver.

This means the lower chambers of the heart do not fill with blood as they should. They still pump blood to the body, but not as well or as regularly.

Common causes of atrial fibrillation include:
- High blood pressure
- Coronary heart disease
- Heart attack
- Heart failure (which can also be caused by atrial fibrillation)
- Heart valve problems
- Overactive thyroid gland
- Certain medications

In some people, no clear cause can be found.

## What Increases Your Risk?

Your chance of developing atrial fibrillation goes up as you get older. About 2 out of every 100 people have it. Among people over 65, about 8 out of every 100 have it.

You are more likely to get it if:
- A close family member (like a parent or sibling) has it
- You are a man
- You have fair skin

Other risk factors include:
- Drinking too much alcohol
- Smoking
- Having diabetes
- Being very overweight
- Having sleep apnea (a condition where breathing stops during sleep)

Some of these risks you can change, like smoking or weight.

## How Does Atrial Fibrillation Progress?

Atrial fibrillation often starts with short, occasional episodes. Over time, the episodes may last longer or become permanent.

There are four types, based on how long the episodes last:
- **Intermittent (paroxysmal):** The heart rhythm returns to normal on its own within 48 hours — sometimes up to 7 days. It may happen once or many times.
- **Persistent:** The irregular rhythm lasts more than 7 days.
- **Long-standing persistent:** The irregular rhythm lasts more than a year.
- **Permanent:** The heart rhythm does not return to normal, even with treatment.

But doctors often find it hard to classify the type. It can be unclear if someone had atrial fibrillation in the past or how long it has been going on.

### Long-Term Effects

Over time, atrial fibrillation can lead to other health problems:
- **Heart failure:** When the heart does not pump well, the rest of the heart must work harder. This can weaken the heart muscle over time. Existing heart failure may get worse.
- **Stroke:** Because the upper chambers do not pump blood well, blood can pool and form clots. If a clot travels to the brain, it can block a blood vessel and cause a stroke.

## How Is Atrial Fibrillation Diagnosed?

Atrial fibrillation does not always cause symptoms. It may be found by chance during a check-up for another condition.

To diagnose it, your doctor may:
- Ask about your symptoms, health history, family history, and lifestyle
- Check your heart rate and blood pressure
- Do an electrocardiogram (ECG): small sensors on your skin record the heart’s electrical activity. This test can confirm atrial fibrillation.
- Run a blood test: this checks your thyroid function. An overactive thyroid can cause atrial fibrillation.
- Use an echocardiogram: this is an ultrasound of the heart. It shows how well the heart is pumping and can detect valve problems.

Other tests may be done to check kidney and liver function. Some medicines used for atrial fibrillation are not safe if these organs are not working well.

## How Is Atrial Fibrillation Treated?

Treatment has two main goals:
1. To reduce or relieve symptoms
2. To lower the risk of stroke

### Treating Symptoms

There are two main ways to manage symptoms:

**Heart rate control:**  
- Medicines like beta blockers are used to slow the heart rate.  
- This reduces strain on the heart and helps ease symptoms like dizziness and fatigue.  
- The treatment does not fix the irregular rhythm — it just keeps the heart from beating too fast.

**Heart rhythm stabilization:**  
- This aims to restore a normal heart rhythm.  
- It is usually done in a hospital using electric shocks (called cardioversion).  
- Afterward, medicine or a procedure called catheter ablation is used to prevent the rhythm from returning.  
- Catheter ablation uses a thin tube (catheter) to destroy small areas of heart tissue that are causing the problem. This is done with heat or cold.

Rhythm stabilization helps if rate control does not work well. It can improve your quality of life and reduce symptoms like palpitations and dizziness.

### Preventing Stroke

People with atrial fibrillation are at higher risk of stroke. Your doctor will help you decide if you need medicine to prevent clots.

**Oral anticoagulants (blood thinners):**  
- These medicines reduce the risk of stroke by preventing blood clots.  
- But they also increase the risk of bleeding.  
- You and your doctor must weigh the benefits (stroke prevention) against the risks (bleeding).  
- A special tool can help you estimate your personal risk of stroke and bleeding.

For more information on stroke prevention and help choosing treatment, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

> **Important:** In some cases, blood thinners are not safe — for example, if you have a very high risk of bleeding. In such cases, a surgery may be an option. A small device called an occluder can be placed in the left atrial appendage to block blood clots. But this surgery is still being studied and can cause serious side effects.

### Treating Other Conditions

It is also important to treat any other health problems you have, such as high blood pressure or coronary heart disease. Managing these can help control atrial fibrillation.

## Other Useful Information

Most people do not notice their heart beating when it is working normally. But when atrial fibrillation happens, you may feel your heart is not beating right. This can be very worrying and make you want to see a doctor.

If you are diagnosed with atrial fibrillation, it is normal to feel anxious. But the condition can usually be managed well with treatment.

Support programs and training courses can help you learn:
- How to live with the condition every day
- How to take your medicine correctly

Many people still have questions. For example:
- Can I still play sports?
- Do I need to be more careful?

The good news is: yes, you can still be active. There is no medical reason to avoid physical activity. In fact, moderate exercise can improve your fitness and well-being. Studies show it does not make atrial fibrillation worse.

# Hand, Foot and Mouth Disease

This is a viral illness that mainly affects babies and children under 10 years old.  
It spreads easily but is usually not serious.  
Most people get better within a week or two.  
No lasting problems happen after recovery.

---

## Quick Facts

- This illness is caused by a virus.  
- It spreads very easily from person to person.  
- It mostly affects young children.  
- Most cases are mild and go away on their own.  
- The illness lasts about 7 to 10 days.  
- The first signs are fever, sore throat, and not wanting to eat.  
- Later, painful sores appear in the mouth.  
- A rash with red spots or blisters shows up on the hands and feet.  
- The rash is not itchy.  
- Children stay contagious as long as the rash is present.  
- They should stay home until the rash is gone.  
- Washing hands often helps stop the spread.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself or your child.

---

## What Is Hand, Foot and Mouth Disease?

Hand, foot and mouth disease is a viral infection.  
It causes a rash and blisters on the hands, feet, and inside the mouth.  
The virus spreads easily through body fluids.  
It mainly affects children under 10.  
Adults rarely get it.  
The illness is not the same as foot and mouth disease in animals.  
They are completely different diseases.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many people have no symptoms at all.  
This is especially true for adults.  

If symptoms do appear, they usually start with:

- A fever  
- A sore throat  
- Not feeling hungry  

One to two days after the fever starts:

- Painful sores or ulcers form in the mouth.  
- These often appear on the tongue, gums, or inside the cheeks.  

At the same time:

- A rash appears on the hands and feet.  
- It may also show up around the mouth.  
- The rash has small red spots.  
- Some spots turn into blisters.  
- The rash does not itch.  
- The rash lasts about 10 days.  
- Blisters may break open.  
- They then form a crust and heal without scars.

In rare cases:

- The rash appears on the bottom, genitals, knees, or elbows.  
- This rash can be itchy.

---

## How Do People Get Infected?

The illness is caused by a group of viruses called enteroviruses.  
These viruses spread easily.  
It takes 3 to 10 days after infection for symptoms to appear.

### How Do People Catch the Virus?

You can get infected by touching body fluids from an infected person.  
These fluids include:

- Mucus from the nose or throat  
- Saliva  
- Fluid from blisters  
- Stool (poop)

### How Is the Virus Spread?

The most common way is by touching something with the virus on it.  
Then touching your mouth.  
This is called “smear infection.”  
It can happen on:

- Door handles  
- Toys  
- Pacifiers  
- Other shared items  

You can also get infected by:

- Kissing someone who is sick  
- Changing a diaper without washing hands first  

The virus can also spread through the air when someone talks, coughs, or sneezes.  
This is called “droplet infection.”

> **Important:** The risk of catching the virus is highest while the rash is still present.  
> The risk drops after the rash heals.  
> Even after symptoms are gone, the virus can still be in the stool for weeks.

---

## How Common Is It?

Hand, foot and mouth disease is not a reportable illness in Germany.  
So we do not have exact numbers.  
Experts estimate that between 80,000 and 140,000 people get it each year.  
Most cases happen in late summer and early autumn.

---

## How Does the Illness Progress?

Most people get better in 7 to 10 days.  
No special treatment is needed.  
It is very rare to get the illness again after recovery.

In rare cases, the virus can spread to the brain or spinal cord.  
This can cause serious problems like:

- Brain inflammation (encephalitis)  
- Meningitis (inflammation of the brain lining)  
- Paralysis  

In some cases, fingernails or toenails fall off.  
But they grow back later.

### What Happens in Pregnant Women and Newborns?

Pregnant women usually have no symptoms or only mild ones.  
In very rare cases, a mother who is sick near delivery can pass the virus to her baby.  
This can happen if she has not built up immunity yet.

Most newborn infections are mild.  
But in rare cases, the virus spreads through the whole body.  
If it affects organs like the liver or heart, it can be life-threatening.

---

## How Can You Prevent It?

Good hygiene is the best way to stop the spread.  
There is no vaccine available in Germany.

### At Home

- Wash hands often with soap.  
- Especially after using the toilet or changing diapers.  
- Clean toys, door handles, and other surfaces regularly.  
- Avoid close contact with sick people.  
- Do not kiss or hug someone who is sick.  
- Do not share eating utensils or cups.  
- Use your own towel.

### In Kindergarten or School

- Keep sick children at home.  
- Children can return to school or kindergarten when:  
  - They feel well again  
  - The rash blisters have healed  
- No doctor’s note is needed.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors usually recognize the illness by the symptoms.  
They look at the rash and mouth sores.  

In severe cases, they may test:

- Stool samples  
- Throat swabs  
- Fluid from blisters  

These tests check for the virus’s genetic material using a PCR test.

If a child has symptoms like weakness or paralysis, doctors may test the fluid around the brain and spinal cord.

---

## How Is It Treated?

There is no medicine that kills the virus.  
Treatment focuses on making the person feel better.

- Make sure the child drinks enough fluids.  
  Even if the mouth hurts, they must stay hydrated.  
- Use pain relief like ibuprofen or paracetamol.  
- Use special mouthwashes to soothe mouth sores.  

See a doctor if:

- The child refuses to drink anything  
- The child is not drinking enough  
- Symptoms get worse

> **Important:** Never give children medicine with acetylsalicylic acid (ASA).  
> This ingredient can cause a rare but dangerous condition called Reye’s syndrome.

# Sinusitis

Sinusitis means inflammation in the sinuses.  
The sinuses are small air-filled spaces in the bones around your nose and face.  
When the lining of the nose is also inflamed, doctors call it rhinosinusitis.  
"Rhino" means nose. "Sinus" means cavity.

## Quick Facts

- Sinusitis is swelling in the sinuses.  
- There are two types: acute and chronic.  
- Common symptoms include a blocked nose, pressure in the face, and trouble smelling.  
- Pain in the forehead, jaw, eyes, or even teeth can happen.  
- Nasal sprays with cortisone can help reduce symptoms.  
- Pain relievers or rinsing the nose with salt water may also help.  
- Surgery is sometimes needed for long-term sinusitis.  

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Sinusitis?

Sinusitis is when the sinuses become inflamed.  
The sinuses are air-filled spaces in the skull.  
They connect to the nose and help drain mucus.  
They stretch from the forehead down to the upper teeth.  
Mucus from the sinuses flows out through the nose and throat.

Doctors divide sinusitis into two types:

- **Acute sinusitis** comes on quickly and usually goes away in a few weeks.  
- **Chronic sinusitis** lasts more than three months.  
  The lining of the nose stays swollen and inflamed.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Common symptoms include:

- A blocked or stuffy nose  
- Trouble breathing through the nose  
- Loss of smell  
- Pressure or pain in the face

Some people also have:

- A fever  
- Headaches

When the sinuses are inflamed, the lining swells.  
This blocks the flow of mucus.  
Mucus builds up and gets thick.  
If the mucus turns yellow or green, it may mean there is an infection.

Pain often happens in the forehead, jaw, or around the eyes.  
Sometimes the teeth hurt too.  
Leaning forward can make the pain worse.  
This often happens when you get out of bed.

The sense of smell may be weak or lost.

## What Causes Acute Sinusitis?

Acute sinusitis often starts after a cold or the flu.  
Colds are usually caused by viruses.  
Sometimes bacteria move in after the virus.

When viruses or bacteria cause the infection, the mucus lining swells.  
This makes it hard for mucus to drain.  
The mucus gets thicker and turns sticky.  
It often looks yellow or green.

## What Causes Chronic Sinusitis?

The cause of chronic sinusitis is often not clear.  
It is more common in people who:

- Have allergies  
- Have asthma  
- Have a crooked nasal septum (the wall inside the nose)  
- Are sensitive to acetylsalicylic acid (also known as aspirin)

## How Does Sinusitis Develop?

Acute sinusitis usually gets better in 1 to 2 weeks.  
If symptoms last longer than 3 months, it is called chronic sinusitis.

With chronic sinusitis, small growths called nasal polyps may form.  
These are soft, non-cancerous growths in the nose.  
They can block the nose and make it hard to breathe or smell.

> **Fun fact:** Enlarged tonsils in children are sometimes called polyps.  
> But nasal polyps are not the same thing.

In rare cases, sinusitis can spread to nearby areas.  
This can affect the eyes or brain.  
Signs of this include:

- High fever  
- Swelling around the eyes  
- Red, swollen skin near the eyes  
- Severe face pain  
- Pain when looking at light  
- Stiff neck

If you have any of these symptoms, see a doctor right away.

## How Is Sinusitis Diagnosed?

Your doctor will start by asking about your symptoms.  
They may ask if you have a blocked nose or trouble smelling.

They will gently press on your face to check for pain.  
They may use a small tube with a light (called an endoscope) to look inside your nose.  
This helps them see if the lining is swollen and what the mucus looks like.

In rare cases, they may take a sample of the mucus to test for germs.

If the diagnosis is unclear or there are signs of complications, imaging tests may be used.  
These can include:

- CT scan (a type of detailed X-ray)  
- Ultrasound

Usually, it is not needed to find out if the sinusitis is caused by a virus or bacteria.  
This does not change the treatment for acute sinusitis.

For chronic sinusitis, an allergy test may help.  
Allergies often go along with long-term sinus problems.

## How Is Sinusitis Treated?

Nasal sprays with cortisone can reduce swelling and ease symptoms.  
Decongestant sprays can help for a short time with acute sinusitis.  
But they should only be used for a few days.  
They are not safe for long-term use, especially in chronic cases.

Some people find relief by rinsing their nose with salt water.  
Inhaling steam may also help.

Antibiotics are rarely needed.  
They are only used if a bacterial infection is confirmed.

For severe chronic sinusitis, a new type of medicine called biologics may be an option.  
These are special drugs that reduce inflammation.

Surgery may help if other treatments do not work.  
The surgeon opens up narrow areas in the sinuses to improve drainage.

For more information on treating sinusitis, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

# Chronic Fatigue Syndrome

Chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) means extreme tiredness that does not go away, even after resting.  
It does not get better with sleep or rest.  
Even small amounts of physical or mental effort can make the symptoms worse.  
There is no cure for CFS.  
Treatment focuses on managing the symptoms.

---

## Quick Facts

- CFS means extreme tiredness that makes daily life very hard.  
- If muscle pain is also present, the condition is called myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME).  
- The condition is also known as systemic exertion intolerance disease (SEID).  
- Symptoms often get worse the day after any kind of effort.  
- People with CFS may have trouble sleeping, concentrating, and feel weak when standing up.  
- The exact cause is still unknown.  
- It is very important to find a doctor who understands the condition and can help.  
- Some symptoms can be treated with medicine.  
- There is no single medicine that cures CFS.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use this to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Chronic Fatigue Syndrome?

CFS is a long-term illness.  
It causes extreme tiredness that does not improve with rest.  
It makes it hard to do normal daily tasks.  
Even sleeping does not help.  

If muscle pain is also present, doctors may call it ME.  

CFS often starts after an infection, like a virus, bacteria, or parasite.  
If the symptoms last more than six months, it is called ME/CFS.  

CFS is not a mental illness.  
It is a physical condition.  
But living with it can lead to stress, anxiety, or depression.  
Early diagnosis and proper care can help prevent the condition from getting worse.

---

### How Is CFS Different from Normal Tiredness?

Some people with long-term health problems like cancer, arthritis, or multiple sclerosis feel very tired.  
This tiredness usually improves when their main illness is treated.  

For these people, moving around or doing light activity often helps.  

But for people with CFS, even small efforts make the tiredness worse.  
Only a small number of people who feel tired actually have CFS.  

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main symptom is extreme tiredness.  
It often starts after an infection, overexertion, or a stressful event.  

A key sign is that symptoms get worse the day after any effort.  
Doctors call this post-exertional malaise (PEM).  
It can last for days or even weeks.  

Some people with CFS are so tired they cannot get out of bed.  

Other common symptoms include:

- Trouble focusing or remembering things  
- Poor sleep or waking up not refreshed  
- Joint pain, muscle pain, or headaches  
- Stomach problems  
- Dizziness  
- Feeling weak when standing up  
- Being easily overwhelmed by stress  
- Sensitivity to light or loud sounds  
- Getting sick often  
- Allergies or trouble with certain foods  

Symptoms can change over time.  
They may get better for a while, then get worse again.

---

## What Causes CFS?

Scientists do not yet know exactly what causes CFS.  
Some think one thing triggers it.  
Others believe several factors must happen together.  

### Possible Triggers

- Viral infections  
- Problems with the immune system  
- Genetic factors  
- Exposure to toxins  
- Vaccinations  
- Accidents  
- Very stressful life events  

### What Doctors Have Found in People with CFS

Tests on people with CFS have shown:

- Higher levels of inflammation in the blood  
- More free radicals (harmful oxygen compounds) in the body  
- A leaky gut (the gut wall is more porous)  
- Antibodies that attack the body’s own nerve cells  
- Brain cells that do not work properly, leading to overstimulation  
- Imbalances in important body chemicals like serotonin and cortisol  

> **Important:** These findings can also happen in people without CFS.  
> They are not enough on their own to diagnose CFS.

---

## How Common Is CFS?

CFS can affect people of any age, including children.  
Most people are diagnosed between the ages of 30 and 40.  

Women are up to four times more likely to have CFS than men.  
In children, boys and girls are equally affected.  

There are no exact numbers of how many people have CFS.  
This is because different doctors use different rules to define the condition.  

---

## What Is the Outlook?

CFS affects people in different ways.  

- Up to one third of people get better within five years.  
- Even then, they often still need more rest than healthy people.  
- For others, symptoms last for years.  
- Symptoms can come and go without warning.  
- It is hard to predict when a good day or bad day will happen.  

- About half of people with CFS can return to work, either part-time or full-time.  
- Up to a quarter of people are too unwell to leave their bed or home for long periods.  
- Some need a wheelchair.  
- Some people with CFS need help with daily tasks.  

As the illness continues, many people develop depression or anxiety.  
They often feel pressure to do more than they can.  
Balancing what they want to do with their energy levels is a daily challenge.

---

## How Is CFS Diagnosed?

It is hard to tell CFS apart from other causes of tiredness.  
There is no single test to confirm CFS.  
Doctors must rule out other possible causes first.  

### Diagnosis Requirements

To be diagnosed with CFS, a person must have:

- Extreme tiredness that lasts more than six months  
- The tiredness cannot be explained by another illness  
- The person remembers when the tiredness started  
- Daily activities are much more limited than before  
- Physical or mental effort makes symptoms worse  
- Getting up from sitting or lying down causes dizziness or weakness  
- Rest, sleep, and breaks do not improve symptoms  

### Medical Tests

Doctors will:

- Check blood pressure while lying down, sitting, and standing  
- Run blood tests to check for other health problems  
- Order other tests to rule out hidden illnesses  

CFS is only diagnosed when no other cause is found.

---

## How Is CFS Treated?

There is no cure for CFS.  
But some treatments can help manage symptoms.

### Research on New Treatments

Scientists are testing medicines that:

- Fight viruses  
- Help balance the immune system  

One example is rintatolimod.  
It lowers inflammation and may help restore immune balance.  

Another idea is a stool transplant.  
This means putting healthy donor stool into the patient’s gut.  
But there is not enough proof yet to say it works.

### Treating Symptoms

Medicines can help with:

- Pain (like NSAIDs or opioids)  
- Sleep problems (sleeping pills)  
- Low energy (stimulants)  
- Anxiety or depression (certain antidepressants)  

> **Important:**  
> People with CFS often need lower doses of medicine.  
> Only the treating doctor should adjust the dose.  
> Take only the medicines that are truly needed.

### Physical Activity

Avoiding effort that makes symptoms worse is key.  
But gentle, tailored physical activity can help over time.  
How much activity is safe depends on the person.  
It must be carefully planned and not pushed too hard.

### Therapy and Support

- **Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)** helps people use their energy wisely.  
- Therapy can help people cope with the emotional impact of the illness.  
- Physiotherapy and occupational therapy help people move more easily and do daily tasks.  
- Relaxation, massage, acupuncture, yoga, tai chi, and meditation may also help.

### Diet

There are no strict diet rules.  
Experts recommend eating a balanced diet.  
Vitamins, omega-3 fatty acids, and other supplements have not been proven to help.

---

## Living with CFS Every Day

Getting a diagnosis is an important first step.  
It helps people name their condition and understand it.  

Even if tests show no problems, the symptoms are real.  
Family, friends, and doctors must recognize the illness.  

Many people with CFS used to be very active.  
Now they struggle with work, hobbies, and home tasks.  
This can be very hard to accept.  

Having a doctor who understands CFS is very helpful.  
They can guide the person in managing energy and daily life.

### Tips for Better Sleep

Good sleep habits can make a big difference.  

- Avoid coffee, especially in the afternoon  
- Do not nap after 3 p.m.  
- One hour before bed, do quiet activities only  
- Spread your tasks through the day to avoid overdoing it  
- Get natural light in the morning (outside or near a window)  
- Use earplugs or noise blockers if needed  
- Keep your bedroom dark at night  
- If you can’t sleep, try something calming  
- Eat a light snack with carbohydrates before bed  

---

## Where Can I Learn More?

Support groups help people with CFS and their families.  
They offer information, advice, and a chance to share experiences.  

You can find more information on:

- Websites of patient groups and university hospitals  
- The NAKOS database (National Contact and Information Point for Self-Help Groups)  
- The German Society for ME/CFS (Deutsche Gesellschaft für ME/CFS e.V.)  
- The Charité Fatigue Center (Charité Fatigue Centrum)

# Intestinal Pseudo-Obstruction (Paralytic Ileus)

Sometimes, the muscles in the intestines stop working properly. This can happen after surgery or during an illness. When this happens, food and fluids cannot move through the intestines as they should. This causes a blockage. The blockage leads to belly pain, a swollen belly, and nausea. Doctors work to get the intestines working again.

---

## Quick Facts

- Intestinal pseudo-obstruction is also called paralytic ileus or adynamic ileus. It means the intestines are not moving food properly.
- The muscles in the intestines are not working. This stops food from moving through the gut.
- Many things can cause this problem, such as surgery, infection, or inflammation in the belly.
- Common signs include belly pain, a swollen belly, nausea, vomiting, and constipation.
- Treatment focuses on emptying the bowels and helping the intestines start moving again.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical care. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Pseudo-Obstruction?

Pseudo-obstruction means the intestines are not working right. The muscles in the gut are not moving food forward. This causes a blockage, even though there is no physical blockage.

Normally, the muscles in the intestines squeeze and relax in a smooth way. This pushes food through the gut. It moves from the stomach to the rectum, where it leaves the body as waste.

When pseudo-obstruction happens, the muscle movements become weak or uncoordinated. Food, fluid, and gas build up in the intestines. The gut wall stretches and swells. The belly becomes bloated.

If the blockage is not treated, the gut wall can get damaged. Some parts of the gut may die.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms usually start slowly over a few days.

- First, you may feel mild belly pain.
- The pain gets worse over time.
- Your belly becomes swollen and hard.
- You may feel sick to your stomach.
- You may vomit.
- You may not pass stool (constipation).
- You may not be able to pass gas.

---

## What Causes Pseudo-Obstruction?

Pseudo-obstruction happens when the nerves or muscles in the gut do not work right. It is often caused by another illness or condition.

The exact reason is not always clear.

Possible causes include:

- Surgery, especially in the belly
- Serious injuries, like to the pelvis or spine
- Cancer
- Nervous system diseases, such as Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, or multiple sclerosis
- Problems with the liver or kidneys
- Diabetes
- Drinking too much alcohol
- Low levels of key minerals like potassium, calcium, or magnesium
- Poor blood flow to the intestines
- Some medicines, including strong painkillers (like opioids), certain antidepressants, or anesthesia

> **Interesting fact:** It is normal for the bowels to slow down after surgery. The body’s stress and the surgery itself can temporarily stop the intestines from working.

---

## Who Is at Higher Risk?

Some people are more likely to get pseudo-obstruction after surgery. This is especially true if:

- The surgery lasted a long time
- There were complications after surgery
- Strong painkillers were used during surgery
- You did not eat or drink right after surgery
- You had a feeding tube after surgery
- There was inflammation in the belly

---

## How Common Is It?

Pseudo-obstruction is fairly common after belly surgery. About 10% to 30% of people have a temporary slowdown in gut movement after surgery.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

- The small intestine usually starts working again within a few hours after surgery.
- The large intestine takes 2 to 3 days to return to normal.

If the problem lasts more than 3 to 5 days, it is called prolonged ileus. This means symptoms continue. Supportive care helps the intestines recover.

### Can Problems Happen?

Yes. If the gut stays blocked for more than 6 days, or if it becomes very swollen, serious problems can occur. These include:

- Infection in the lining of the belly (peritonitis)
- Poor blood flow to the intestines
- Death of some gut tissue (necrosis)

---

## How Can It Be Prevented?

You can lower your risk after surgery by:

- Getting up and walking as soon as possible
- Starting to eat and drink soon after surgery
- Chewing gum (this may help stimulate gut movement)

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and do a physical exam.

Signs of pseudo-obstruction include:

- A swollen belly
- No bowel movements
- No sounds from the intestines (when listening with a stethoscope)

Your doctor will take an x-ray of your belly. This shows if the intestines are swollen and blocked.

A CT scan or MRI may be done to rule out a physical blockage.

Blood tests check for:

- Signs of infection
- Poor blood flow
- Imbalances in minerals
- Problems with the liver or kidneys

---

## How Is It Treated?

First, doctors treat any underlying condition that may be causing the problem.

In the first 1 to 2 days, the main goal is to empty the bowels. Treatment includes:

- Stopping food and drink for a short time
- Giving fluids through a vein (IV) to prevent dehydration
- Using a tube through the nose into the stomach to remove trapped fluid and gas
- Giving an enema through the rectum to clear the bowels
- Walking and changing positions to help the intestines move

If these steps do not work, medicine may be used to help the intestines move. One common medicine is neostigmine. It can help, but it may cause side effects like low blood pressure or shaking.

If medicine does not work or cannot be used, a doctor may use a colonoscopy. A tube is passed through the anus into the colon to drain the contents.

Surgery is rarely needed. But it may be required if there is a risk of bleeding or if the gut tissue is dying.

# Intertrigo

Intertrigo is a skin problem that happens in skin folds. The skin becomes red, sore, and itchy. It may also leak fluid, burn, or crack. The main causes are moisture and rubbing.

---

## What You Need to Know

- Intertrigo happens in skin folds like the groin, under the arms, or under the breasts.
- It is also called intertriginous dermatitis.
- Moisture and rubbing cause the skin to become inflamed.
- Fungi or bacteria can infect the skin, making it worse.
- It is common in babies with diaper rash and in people who are bedridden.
- People with diabetes, those who are overweight, or those with weak immune systems are more likely to get it.
- Keep skin folds dry and avoid rubbing.
- Medicine like ointments can help if the skin is very inflamed.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Intertrigo?

Intertrigo is a rash that forms in skin folds. It happens when skin rubs together and stays wet. The skin becomes red, sore, and itchy. It can also get infected, especially by a yeast called Candida. In rare cases, bacteria can cause infection too.

It often affects:
- The groin and genital area
- The armpits
- The area under the breasts in women
- Any skin fold, really

Babies in diapers and older people who are bedridden are especially at risk. So are people who are overweight or have diabetes or a weak immune system.

Treatment focuses on keeping skin folds dry and reducing rubbing. Anti-inflammatory ointments may also help.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The skin in a fold becomes red and sore. It may:
- Itch
- Burn
- Leak fluid

Common places where it shows up:
- Groin
- Between the thighs
- Genital and buttock area
- Diaper area in babies (called diaper rash)
- Between the buttocks
- Under the breasts in women
- Under the arms
- In stomach folds, especially in people who are overweight

It can also appear:
- Between fingers or toes
- In the bends of knees or elbows
- In the belly button
- Behind the ears
- In neck folds of babies

If the rash does not heal, the skin may crack or peel.  
If infected, the skin may form scabs or pus-filled bumps.  
Sometimes, a bad smell can develop.

---

## What Causes Intertrigo?

Intertrigo is caused by rubbing and moisture in skin folds. The outer layer of skin gets damaged, which leads to inflammation.

Skin folds often have little air flow. Heat builds up, and sweat collects. This wet, warm environment helps yeast and bacteria grow. The yeast Candida is naturally on the skin, but it can cause problems when conditions are right.

Rubbing and moisture can also let bacteria grow.  
If the causes are not fixed, the rash can last a long time or keep coming back.  
With proper care, the rash usually clears up fast.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

Intertrigo can happen to anyone, even healthy people. For example, it can happen after long walks, runs, or bike rides.

But some things make it more likely:
- Hot, humid weather
- Sweating a lot
- Being overweight or obese
- Having diabetes
