- Smoking or drinking alcohol
- A weak immune system
- Wearing diapers
- Being bedridden
- Not being able to control your bladder (urinary incontinence)
- A family history of skin problems

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor can usually tell you have intertrigo just by looking at your skin.

They may:
- Gently scrape a small bit of skin
- Take a swab (a small sample) to test for fungus or bacteria
- In rare cases, take a small skin sample (biopsy) for testing

---

## How Is It Treated?

The main goal is to keep skin folds dry and reduce rubbing.

Try these steps:
- Wash skin folds every day with mild soap, especially after exercise.
- Dry the area well after washing. Use a soft towel or a hair dryer on cool.
- Use protective creams on sensitive skin.
- Wear clothes that pull sweat away from the skin, like cotton.
- Use special clothing for sports.
- Use antiperspirants or drying powders to reduce sweat.
- Put soft gauze or pads in sore folds when sweating a lot.
- Let the skin breathe as much as possible.

For mild cases, these steps are often enough.

If the skin is infected with fungus, your doctor will give you a cream to kill the fungus.  
If it is infected with bacteria, they will give you an antibiotic cream.

Your doctor may also prescribe a mild steroid cream to reduce swelling and itching.

# Zika Virus Infection

Zika virus is found in tropical and warm regions. It spreads mainly through mosquito bites. It can also spread through unprotected sex. Most people get better without serious problems. But if a woman is infected during pregnancy, the virus can harm the baby.

---

## Quick Facts

- Zika virus is found in tropical and warm countries.
- It spreads mostly through mosquito bites. It can also spread through unprotected sex.
- Most people have only mild symptoms, like a rash, headache, body aches, or a slight fever.
- If a pregnant woman gets infected, the virus can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, or birth defects in the baby.
- There is no specific medicine to treat Zika virus.
- There is no vaccine to prevent Zika virus.
- The best way to protect yourself is to avoid mosquito bites.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Zika Virus?

Zika virus is found in many tropical and warm countries. These include parts of North, Central, and South America, Southeast Asia, Africa, the Caribbean, and the Pacific Islands.

Most people get infected when a mosquito bites them. The virus can also spread through unprotected sex.

The illness is usually mild. Symptoms go away in a few days. But if a pregnant woman gets infected, the virus can pass to her unborn baby and cause serious harm.

> **Important:** Women who are pregnant or planning to become pregnant should talk to a doctor before traveling to tropical areas. There is no vaccine yet.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people with Zika virus have no symptoms. Others may have mild signs that appear 2 to 14 days after being bitten by an infected mosquito.

Common symptoms include:

- A red rash on the skin
- Headache
- Body aches (in arms, legs, or joints)
- Slight fever
- Eye irritation (red, watery eyes)

Some people feel pain behind the eyes. Rarely, people may have nausea, vomiting, or stomach pain.

Most symptoms go away in 2 to 7 days. But even after symptoms fade, a person can still pass the virus to others.

---

## How Does Zika Virus Spread?

Zika virus is part of a group of viruses that also cause yellow fever and dengue fever. It spreads mainly through bites from two types of mosquitoes:

- Yellow fever mosquito (Aedes aegypti)
- Asian tiger mosquito (Aedes albopictus)

These mosquitoes bite during the day and at dusk. They breed in standing water, like in rain barrels, flower pots, or old tires.

When a mosquito bites a person with Zika virus, it can pass the virus to the next person it bites.

Zika virus can also stay in sperm and vaginal fluids for a long time. This means it can spread through unprotected sex.

It is very rare, but the virus can also spread through blood transfusions.

If a pregnant woman gets infected, the virus can cross the placenta and reach the baby. The baby’s brain and nervous system are most at risk during the first and second trimesters of pregnancy.

---

## How Common Is Zika Virus?

The risk is highest in areas where there have been large outbreaks. This happened in Central and South America between 2015 and 2017.

Since 2016, Zika virus has been a disease that doctors must report to health authorities.

In Germany:
- 69 cases were reported in 2017
- 18 cases were reported in 2018

Almost all of these people got infected outside Germany.

The real number of infections is likely much higher. Many people have no symptoms and do not see a doctor.

For more details on how Zika virus spreads, see the leaflet from the German Federal Foreign Office (Auswärtiges Amt).

---

## What Can Happen After a Zika Virus Infection?

Most people recover fully and have no lasting problems.

But after large outbreaks, doctors have seen more cases of:

- Guillain-Barré syndrome (a rare nerve condition)
- Certain birth defects in babies born to infected mothers

These problems are likely caused by the virus.

### Guillain-Barré Syndrome

This is a rare condition where the body’s immune system attacks the nerves. It can cause weakness or full-body paralysis. It often starts after a viral infection, including Zika.

Most people recover over several weeks. But some may have long-term effects.

### Birth Defects in Babies

If a pregnant woman gets infected, the baby may be born with serious problems. These include:

- A very small head (microcephaly)
- A thin brain layer with hard spots (calcifications)
- Eye problems, like changes in the retina
- Joint problems that limit movement
- Stiff muscles that make movement hard

It is not possible to predict how a baby will develop after being exposed to Zika in the womb.

Some babies look normal at birth but develop problems later. Others have symptoms that go away over time. But conditions like microcephaly last a lifetime and cause serious challenges.

---

## How Can You Prevent Zika Virus?

There is no vaccine yet. The best way to stay safe is to avoid mosquito bites, especially in tropical areas.

The mosquitoes that carry Zika are active during the day and at dusk. They breed in standing water, like in buckets, plant saucers, or old tires. These places are often near homes.

To protect yourself:

- Wear long-sleeved shirts and long pants
- Spray your clothes with insect repellent that contains permethrin
- Use skin repellent with DEET or icaridin
- Stay in air-conditioned rooms
- Sleep under a mosquito net

> **Important:** If you have Zika virus or have been in a high-risk area, avoid mosquito bites for up to 3 weeks. This stops the virus from spreading to local mosquitoes.

Zika virus can also spread through sex. To protect a baby in a planned or unplanned pregnancy:

- Use condoms during sex while in a high-risk area
- After returning home:
  - Men should avoid unprotected sex for at least 3 months
  - Women should avoid unprotected sex for at least 2 months
  - In some cases, doctors recommend using condoms for up to 6 months

Zika virus can also be passed through blood. People who have been in high-risk areas should not donate blood for at least 4 weeks.

---

## How Is Zika Virus Diagnosed?

If you travel to a high-risk area and develop symptoms like fever, rash, or joint pain, see a doctor.

The doctor may take a blood or urine sample to test for the virus.

Even if your partner visited a high-risk area, you may still be infected. The virus can spread through sex.

Two tests are used:

- PCR test: Finds the virus’s genetic material in the blood or urine
- Antibody test: Looks for antibodies your body made to fight the virus

Pregnant women should be tested even if they have only mild symptoms. If Zika is suspected, regular ultrasounds can check the baby’s development.

Amniocentesis (testing the fluid around the baby) is not usually done.

---

## How Is Zika Virus Treated?

There is no medicine to kill the Zika virus. Treatment focuses on relieving symptoms:

- Rest in bed
- Drink plenty of fluids
- Take medicine to reduce pain or fever

If you have Zika, protect yourself from mosquito bites. This stops the virus from spreading to other people through mosquitoes.

If you have a fever after a trip to a tropical country, it could be dengue fever. Until dengue is ruled out, do not take medicine with acetylsalicylic acid (like aspirin).

Instead, use paracetamol for pain and fever.

> **Important:** Acetylsalicylic acid can cause serious bleeding when taken with some viral infections. In children, it can cause a rare but life-threatening condition called Reye’s syndrome.

# Athlete’s Foot

Athlete’s foot is a common skin problem. It can make your feet itchy. It can also cause cracks in the skin. In some cases, it can lead to a toenail infection. This page explains how athlete’s foot starts, how to stop it, and how to treat it.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Athlete’s Foot?

Athlete’s foot is a skin infection caused by a type of fungus. It often starts between the toes. The skin may become red, cracked, and itchy. It can also feel dry and flaky. The skin may turn white and feel thicker than normal.

You can treat athlete’s foot with over-the-counter creams, gels, or sprays. Keeping your feet dry helps prevent it.

---

## What Are the Signs?

The most common place for athlete’s foot is between the baby toe and the next toe. There, the skin may:

- Turn red  
- Crack open  
- Feel itchy  
- Become flaky  
- Look white and feel thick or swollen  

If the fungus spreads across the whole bottom of the foot, it is called **moccasin athlete’s foot**. This causes the soles, heels, and edges of the feet to become dry, flaky, and itchy. It can look like other skin problems, such as eczema.

In rare cases, athlete’s foot causes a sudden, strong inflammation. The skin becomes very red. Small pus-filled bumps (called pustules) may appear. The skin may feel tight and itchy.

---

## What Causes Athlete’s Foot?

Athlete’s foot is usually caused by a fungus that lives on the skin. These fungi like warm, damp places. They enter the skin through small cracks or injuries.

The fungus spreads in several ways:

- By touching infected skin flakes  
- By walking barefoot in shared areas like showers or pools  
- By sharing towels, socks, or shoes  

Fungal spores can also cause toenail infections. Feet are a favorite place for fungi because:

- The outer layer of foot skin has a lot of keratin – a protein fungi eat  
- Shoes often stay warm and moist  

You are more likely to get athlete’s foot if you:

- Have allergies  
- Sweat a lot on your feet  
- Have eczema (neurodermatitis)  
- Have a weak immune system (from serious illness or long-term medicine)  
- Have poor blood flow in your legs (for example, due to diabetes or blocked blood vessels)  
- Wear tight or non-breathable shoes (like safety boots or rubber boots)  
- Do sports like running or swimming  
- Have family members with athlete’s foot  

---

## How Common Is Athlete’s Foot?

Athlete’s foot is very common. Studies show that 3 to 15 out of every 100 people have it at some point. It is more common in older adults and in men.

---

## How Does Athlete’s Foot Develop?

Athlete’s foot does not go away on its own. If you do nothing, the fungus can spread. It may reach your toenails and cause a fungal nail infection.

Athlete’s foot rarely spreads to other parts of the body, like your hands. It is not dangerous for healthy people.

In very rare cases, a bacterial infection can develop if the fungus is severe.

---

## How Can You Prevent Athlete’s Foot?

No single method is proven to work 100%. But these steps can help reduce your risk:

- Dry your feet completely after showering, swimming, or bathing  
- Wear flip-flops in public showers, locker rooms, or around pools  
- Wear shoes that fit well and let your feet breathe  
- Take your shoes off often and change your socks every day  
- Never share towels, socks, or shoes  
- Wash towels, socks, and bedding at 60 degrees Celsius or higher  
- If you wash at lower temperatures, use a hygiene rinse or special laundry additive  

---

## How Is Athlete’s Foot Diagnosed?

A doctor will look at your feet and ask about your symptoms.

They may take a small skin sample to test. This helps rule out other skin problems. The sample is sent to a lab to check for fungus.

- Most test results are ready the next day  
- If the lab needs to grow the fungus to identify it exactly, results may take about three weeks  
- This kind of test is rarely needed  

---

## How Is Athlete’s Foot Treated?

You can buy antifungal sprays, gels, or creams at the pharmacy. These work by killing the fungus or stopping it from spreading.

- These treatments usually work well  
- In rare cases, they do not help  
- If that happens, your doctor may prescribe antifungal tablets  

There is no strong scientific proof that home remedies like herbal foot baths or tea tree oil work.

---

# Arteriosclerosis

Arteriosclerosis is a condition where the blood vessels harden and narrow.  
It is also called vascular calcification.  
It happens when fatty deposits build up inside the walls of arteries.  
This makes the arteries stiff and less flexible.  

Over time, this can lead to serious heart and blood vessel problems.

---

## Quick Facts

- Arteriosclerosis happens when fat and other substances build up on artery walls.  
- This causes the arteries to narrow and harden.  
- High cholesterol is a major cause. Other risks include high blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, being overweight, and family history.  
- The condition develops slowly. It often has no symptoms for many years.  
- It can lead to heart attacks, strokes, and other heart problems.  
- A healthy lifestyle, lowering cholesterol, and treating other health issues can reduce the risk of serious problems.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Arteriosclerosis?

Arteriosclerosis is a long-term condition that affects the arteries.  
Arteries carry blood from the heart to the rest of the body.  
In arteriosclerosis, the walls of the arteries become thick and stiff.  
This is often due to cholesterol and other substances building up inside the artery walls.  

When this happens, the body’s immune system responds.  
This causes inflammation in the artery walls.  
The buildup of cholesterol and other materials is called atherosclerosis.  
Atherosclerosis is a type of arteriosclerosis.

The condition grows slowly.  
It usually does not cause symptoms for years.  
But over time, it can lead to serious health problems.

People with arteriosclerosis are more likely to have a heart attack or stroke.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

In the early stages, arteriosclerosis does not cause any symptoms.  
You may not know you have it until it causes a serious problem.

The symptoms depend on which blood vessels are affected and what organs are not getting enough blood.

### Possible Health Problems and Their Signs

**If the heart’s blood vessels are affected:**

- The heart may not pump blood well. This is called heart failure.  
- You might feel tired or short of breath.  
- You may have chest pain or feel your heart beating fast or irregularly.  
- Simple tasks like walking up stairs or walking a few blocks can become hard.

**If the heart’s main blood vessels are narrowed:**

- This is called coronary heart disease.  
- You may feel chest pain or pressure when you exercise.  
- This pain is called angina.  
- If a blood clot blocks a narrowed artery completely, it can cause a heart attack.

**If the blood vessels in the legs are affected:**

- This is called peripheral artery disease.  
- You may feel pain in your legs when walking.  
- The pain usually goes away when you rest.  
- In severe cases, poor blood flow can lead to tissue damage.  
- In rare cases, this may require amputation of a leg.

**If the blood vessels in the kidneys are affected:**

- This can cause high blood pressure.  
- It can also lead to kidney damage or kidney failure.

---

## What Causes Arteriosclerosis?

High levels of certain types of cholesterol increase the risk.  
But other factors also play a role.

### What Is HDL Cholesterol?

HDL stands for high-density lipoprotein.  
It helps remove cholesterol from the blood and take it back to the liver.  
This helps protect the arteries.  

High HDL levels are good for your heart.  
Very high levels may not be helpful and could even be harmful.

### What Is LDL Cholesterol?

LDL stands for low-density lipoprotein.  
It carries cholesterol through the blood.  
High levels of LDL cholesterol are linked to a higher risk of heart disease.

Scientists now know that LDL cholesterol does not just sit on artery walls.  
Instead, it helps cause inflammation in the artery walls.  
This inflammation can lead to hardening and narrowing of the arteries.  
Over time, these areas can become calcified.

> **Important:** Cholesterol is needed by the body.  
> It helps make hormones and build cell walls.  
> The body makes its own cholesterol.  
> You do not need to get it from food.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

These factors raise your risk of arteriosclerosis:

- High LDL cholesterol  
- Low HDL cholesterol  
- High blood pressure  
- Diabetes  
- Smoking  
- Family history of heart disease  
- Being overweight or obese  
- High levels of inflammation in the body  
- Not getting enough physical activity

These risks can add up.  
Having more than one increases your chances of developing problems.

---

## Can You Prevent Arteriosclerosis?

Yes, you can lower your risk by making healthy choices.

The most important steps are:

- Eat a healthy diet  
- Exercise regularly  
- Do not smoke

A healthy lifestyle can help keep your arteries clear and your heart strong.

For more tips on heart health, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## Can Arteriosclerosis Be Found Early?

Yes, regular check-ups can help find early signs.

People with statutory health insurance can get a free health check-up every three years starting at age 35.  
People aged 18 to 34 can have one check-up.

These check-ups look for early signs of:

- Diabetes  
- Kidney problems  
- Heart and blood vessel diseases

The check-up includes a blood test.  
It checks your cholesterol, blood sugar, and other values.

---

## How Is Arteriosclerosis Diagnosed?

High cholesterol is a warning sign.  
But it is not enough to confirm arteriosclerosis.

Doctors use several tools to make a diagnosis:

- Blood tests to check cholesterol, blood sugar, and inflammation markers  
- Imaging tests such as ultrasound, CT scans, or MRI scans

### Checking Cholesterol Levels

Three types of cholesterol are measured:

- LDL cholesterol  
- HDL cholesterol  
- Total cholesterol: This shows how much cholesterol is in your blood overall

> **Important:** Doctors may also test for lipoprotein(a).  
> This is a type of cholesterol that increases heart disease risk.  
> It cannot be changed by diet. It needs medical treatment.

### What Are Normal Cholesterol Levels?

These levels are considered healthy for most people:

- Total cholesterol: below 200 mg/dL (5.2 mmol/L)  
- LDL cholesterol: below 100 mg/dL (2.6 mmol/L)  
- HDL cholesterol: above 40 mg/dL (1 mmol/L) for men, above 50 mg/dL (1.3 mmol/L) for women

> **Note:** Some experts think these numbers are too strict.  
> They say many people are labeled as “ill” even if they are healthy.  
> A study from 2010 found over half of Germans had high cholesterol by these standards.  
> But high cholesterol alone does not mean you have heart problems.  
> Other factors matter too.

---

## How Is Arteriosclerosis Treated?

There is no cure for arteriosclerosis.  
But treatment can slow it down and reduce the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

The goal is to bring your heart disease risk back to normal.

Treatment includes:

- Managing other health problems like high blood pressure and diabetes  
- Making healthy lifestyle changes  
- Taking medicine if needed  
- Surgery in severe cases

### Lifestyle Changes

These are key:

- Stop smoking  
- Eat a healthy diet with little animal fat  
- Exercise regularly  
- Lose weight if you are overweight

### Medication

If diet and exercise are not enough, medicine may be needed.

For people who have never had a heart attack or stroke, **statins** are the only medicine proven to help.

### Surgery

If the condition is advanced, surgery may be needed.

Options include:

- **Angioplasty:** A thin tube with a balloon is guided to the blocked artery.  
  The balloon is inflated to open the artery.  
  A small metal tube (stent) may be placed to keep it open.

- **Bypass surgery:** A healthy blood vessel from another part of the body or an artificial tube is used to go around the blocked area.  
  This restores blood flow.

---

## How Does Arteriosclerosis Affect Daily Life?

Arteriosclerosis and its complications are long-term conditions.  
They last for life.

But they do not have to control your life.

With good care and understanding, you can live well.

You do not need to make big changes all at once.  
Small, steady steps are better.

It is not your fault if you have arteriosclerosis.  
Lifestyle is just one of many factors.  
Genetics, age, and other health issues also play a role.

# Sprained Ankle

A sprained ankle happens when your foot rolls or twists. This often occurs while walking, jumping, or running. The twist stretches the ligaments too much. Small blood vessels can also break. This causes swelling and pain.

## Quick Facts

- When the ankle twists, the ligaments stretch. In bad cases, they can tear.
- The ankle swells and hurts.
- If you can walk right after the twist, your bone is likely not broken.
- If the ligaments are only slightly stretched, you can usually move your foot normally again in a few days.
- Most mild sprains heal in about two weeks.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is a Sprained Ankle?

When you twist your ankle, the ligaments that hold the bones together stretch too far. The tissue around the joint also gets hurt. The joint swells and hurts. This is called a sprain. Sprains are very common.

Ligaments are strong, stretchy bands that connect bones in a joint. The ankle has many bones and several ligaments that keep it stable.

## What Are the Signs of a Sprained Ankle?

Twisting the ankle stretches the ligaments. In the worst case, they can tear. Stretching also breaks small blood vessels. This causes swelling and pain.

If you can walk right after the twist, your bone is probably not broken. If the ligaments are only slightly stretched, your foot usually feels better in a few days. But even a mild sprain can hurt.

## What Causes a Sprained Ankle?

The ankle lets your foot move up, down, and side to side. It is easier to roll the foot inward than outward. Most sprains happen when the foot rolls inward. This often happens after a jump or a misstep.

The ligaments on the outside of the ankle are most often injured. These are called the lateral collateral ligaments. In rare cases, the ligaments on the inside of the ankle—called the medial collateral ligaments—can be stretched too.

**Important:** Some people have naturally weak ligaments. They are more likely to sprain their ankle. People with tight feet or weak muscles also have a higher risk.

Athletes get sprains more often. About one in four athletes will have a tear in the lateral ligaments. This is especially common in sports like volleyball, basketball, and football.

## How Does a Sprained Ankle Heal?

Most mild sprains heal in about two weeks. At that point, you can usually walk with little pain.

If the ligaments are torn, healing takes longer. It may take weeks before the ankle feels stable again. In serious cases, it can take two to three years to fully recover.

After a sprain, you are more likely to get another injury. This is especially true during sports that put heavy stress on the foot, like football or basketball.

About 1 to 2 out of every 10 people with a severe sprain will have a long-term unstable ankle. The joint still gives way easily even six months after the injury. These people often sprain their ankle again and again.

## How Can You Prevent a Sprained Ankle?

To protect your ankle during sports, some people wear a bandage or splint. Kinesiology tape is a common choice. It is a stretchy tape that moves with your body. It is meant to help muscles and nerves. But studies have not proven it works.

The best way to prevent repeated sprains is to do strengthening and balance exercises. These exercises help your ankle stay stable. You may need to do them for weeks or months.

One common tool is a balancing board. It tilts when you shift your weight. You practice standing on one leg. To stay balanced, your foot must react quickly. This strengthens the muscles and makes the ankle more stable.

## How Is a Sprained Ankle Diagnosed?

If you think you sprained your ankle, your doctor will ask about how it happened and what symptoms you have. They will examine your foot to check the injury.

If a broken bone is possible, your doctor may order an X-ray.

If your symptoms do not improve after a few days, there may be a ligament tear. In that case, your doctor may use an MRI scan. MRI gives a clear picture of the ligaments and soft tissues. It shows more detail than an X-ray.

## How Is a Sprained Ankle Treated?

A sprained ankle swells fast and hurts quickly. To reduce pain and swelling, do this right away:

- Raise your foot above heart level.
- Apply cold packs to the ankle.
- Use a compression bandage to gently press on the ankle.

These steps are usually enough for a mild sprain.

If needed, your doctor may use a splint, brace, or firm bandage to support the foot. If the ankle is very swollen, a cast may help for a short time.

Do not keep the foot still for too long. Start moving it as soon as you can. Early movement helps healing.

Surgery is rarely needed for a sprained ankle, even if the ligaments are torn.

For more details on treatment, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

# Thyroid Cancer – Simple Explanation

Thyroid cancer is rare. It can happen at any age. Most types grow slowly and do not cause symptoms early on. The main treatment is surgery. This article explains how thyroid cancer is diagnosed and treated.

---

## Quick Facts

- Lumps in the thyroid gland are common, but cancer is rare.
- There are different types of thyroid cancer. Some run in families.
- Surgery is the main treatment. After surgery, many people get radioactive iodine therapy.
- Chemotherapy is not usually used.
- Targeted therapy may be used for advanced or aggressive cases.
- After surgery, you will need to take thyroid hormone tablets for the rest of your life.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

---

## What Is Thyroid Cancer?

The thyroid gland sits in the front of your neck. It makes hormones that help your body work properly. These hormones control your energy, heart rate, and body temperature.

Thyroid cancer starts in the cells of this gland. There are four main types:

1. **Papillary thyroid cancer** – the most common type.
2. **Follicular thyroid cancer**.
3. **Anaplastic thyroid cancer** – rare and fast-growing.
4. **Medullary thyroid cancer** – starts in special cells called C cells. These cells help control calcium levels in your body.

In papillary and follicular cancers, the cancer cells look similar to normal thyroid cells under a microscope. These are called well-differentiated cancers.

In anaplastic cancer, the cells look very different from normal cells. These are called undifferentiated cancers and grow quickly.

Medullary thyroid cancer can run in families. It is linked to a genetic condition.

Because the thyroid is part of the body’s hormone system, thyroid cancer is also called an endocrine cancer.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Thyroid cancer may cause:

- A hoarse voice that does not go away.
- Trouble swallowing.
- Breathing problems.
- A dry cough that lasts and is not caused by a cold or infection.
- A lump or swelling in the front of your neck (near your Adam’s apple).
- Swollen lymph nodes in your neck.
- Neck pain that spreads to your ears.

These symptoms can also be caused by other conditions, like infections. If you have any of them, see a doctor.

---

## What Causes Thyroid Cancer?

We do not fully know what causes thyroid cancer.

The only clear environmental risk factor is exposure to radiation, especially to the neck. This can happen after radiation therapy or nuclear accidents, like Chernobyl or Fukushima.

Some people have a history of thyroid problems, such as a goiter (enlarged thyroid) or non-cancerous tumors. These increase the risk slightly, but the overall risk is still low in Germany.

Medullary thyroid cancer can be inherited. It is linked to a genetic change.

There is no strong proof that diet, lifestyle, or other environmental factors cause thyroid cancer. We also do not know why women are more often affected than men.

---

## How Common Is Thyroid Cancer?

About 5,700 new cases are diagnosed each year in Germany. Women are more likely to get it than men.

---

## How Is Thyroid Cancer Diagnosed?

Your doctor will start by asking about your symptoms and risk factors. They will feel your neck to check for lumps or swelling.

Blood tests will check:

- Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) – a hormone that controls thyroid activity.
- Calcitonin – a hormone made by C cells, important for calcium balance.

An ultrasound scan is the most important test. It shows the size, shape, and texture of the thyroid and nearby lymph nodes. It can show if a lump is solid or fluid-filled.

A nuclear medicine scan (scintigraphy) may be done if:

- The lump is larger than one centimeter.
- Your TSH level is low.

This scan shows how the lump uses iodine. It helps doctors decide if it might be cancer.

To confirm cancer, your doctor will take a small sample of cells from the lump. This is called a fine needle aspiration biopsy. A thin needle is used to remove cells. The cells are then checked under a microscope.

If cancer is confirmed, more tests are done to see how far it has spread. These include:

- Ultrasound of neck lymph nodes.
- Chest X-ray.
- Laryngoscopy – a test to check how your vocal cords move.

---

## How Is Thyroid Cancer Treated?

Treatment depends on the type of cancer and how far it has spread.

### Surgery

Surgery is the main treatment. The surgeon removes part or all of the thyroid gland. This is called a subtotal or total thyroidectomy.

If cancer has spread to lymph nodes, the doctor will remove those too.

### Radioactive Iodine Therapy

After surgery, some patients get radioactive iodine (I-131). This is a special kind of internal radiation.

The cancer cells (and healthy thyroid cells) take up the radioactive iodine. The radiation kills any remaining cancer cells.

If the entire thyroid is removed and radioactive iodine is used, there is no thyroid tissue left. So you must take thyroid hormone tablets (L-thyroxine) for life.

### Advanced or Spreading Cancer

If cancer has spread to other organs, treatment focuses on slowing the disease and improving quality of life. Cure is rare at this stage.

New treatments, like targeted therapy, are being used for aggressive or advanced cases. New drugs are being tested in clinical trials.

### Anaplastic Thyroid Cancer

This type grows very fast. Surgery is tried if possible. But it does not take up iodine, so radioactive iodine therapy does not work.

Instead, doctors may use a mix of radiation and chemotherapy, called radiochemotherapy. This is also used if surgery is not possible.

> **Important:** Anaplastic thyroid cancer needs fast treatment at a center with experience in this rare cancer.

---

## What Happens After Treatment?

Aftercare helps catch any return of cancer early. It also checks for long-term side effects.

You will have regular check-ups. The time between visits depends on your risk of cancer returning.

> **Important:** If you notice any new symptoms, see your doctor right away—even if it’s not your scheduled appointment.

At check-ups, your doctor will:

- Ask about symptoms.
- Examine your neck.
- Test your blood to check thyroid hormone levels. This ensures you are getting the right dose of L-thyroxine.

The tests you need later depend on your cancer type and your risk of relapse.

Common aftercare tests include:

- Ultrasound of the neck.
- Blood test for thyroglobulin (a protein made by thyroid cells). This is used if your thyroid was fully removed.
- Nuclear medicine scan with radioactive iodine (if your risk of relapse is high).

If cancer returns or spreads, more tests may be needed, such as:

- CT scan.
- X-ray.
- Ultrasound of the chest or abdomen.
- PET scan – this can show active cancer cells in the body.

---

## What Is Life Like After Treatment?

Life after treatment depends on the side effects of surgery and therapy.

### After Thyroid Removal

You will need to take thyroid hormone tablets every day for life. This is usually well-tolerated, but you need regular blood tests to check the dose.

### Possible Side Effects

- **Adrenal gland damage:** Surgery can affect calcium levels. You may need calcium supplements.
- **Vocal cord paralysis:** This can happen after surgery. It often improves over time, but sometimes it is permanent.
- **Radioactive iodine therapy:** This can slightly increase the risk of other cancers later in life.
- **Fertility issues in men:** High-dose radioactive iodine can stop sperm from maturing. Freezing sperm before treatment can help if you want children later.
- **Early menopause in women:** High doses of radioactive iodine may cause menopause to start earlier.

### Emotional and Social Support

Cancer can be hard on your mental health. Support is available.

- Counseling is often offered during hospital stays.
- Psycho-social cancer centers and trained psycho-oncologists can help.
- Self-help groups connect you with others who have similar experiences.

> **Need help finding support?** Use the website of the Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center to find local centers, therapists, or support groups.

---

## Where Can You Get Help?

There are no cancer centers in Germany officially certified by the German Cancer Society (DKG) specifically for thyroid cancer.

But good care comes from clinics where many specialists work together. These include:

- Surgeons.
- Doctors who treat cancer (oncologists).
- Radiation therapists.
- Nuclear medicine doctors.
- Endocrinologists (hormone doctors).
- Ear, nose, and throat doctors.

It is best to go to a center with experience in thyroid cancer.

You can find information on how to choose the right clinic on the website of the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

Some centers are certified for treating endocrine cancers. You can find them on the **OncoMap** website.

The German Society for General and Visceral Surgery (DGAV) certifies special centers for thyroid and adrenal surgery.

The European Neuroendocrine Tumor Society (ENETS) has certified several German centers as centers of excellence. Find them on the website of the **Neuroendocrine Tumors Network self-help organization**.
