# Acute Pancreatitis

## What Is Acute Pancreatitis?

The pancreas is a gland behind the stomach. It helps digest food and controls blood sugar. When the pancreas becomes inflamed suddenly, it is called acute pancreatitis.

This condition causes sudden, severe pain in the upper belly. The pain can spread to the back. It is often so bad that people go to the doctor right away.

Most people get better in 1 to 2 weeks. But some have lasting problems. About 3 out of every 100 people with this condition die from complications.

**Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main symptom is intense pain in the upper belly. The pain often goes into the back.

Other common signs include:
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- High fever
- Swollen belly
- Low blood pressure or dizziness

The pain is so strong that most people go to the hospital the same day they feel it.

---

## What Causes Acute Pancreatitis?

The most common cause is gallstones. These are hard pieces of material that form in the gallbladder. They can block the tube that carries digestive juice from the pancreas to the intestine.

When the tube is blocked, digestive juice builds up in the pancreas. This causes inflammation.

The second most common cause is heavy drinking over a long time. Scientists know this link, but they are still studying how alcohol causes the problem.

Other possible causes include:
- Certain medicines
- Viral infections
- Narrowing of the bile duct
- High levels of fat (triglycerides) in the blood
- High levels of calcium in the blood

In about 1 in 10 cases, doctors cannot find the exact cause.

---

## How Common Is It?

In Germany, about 55,000 people are treated in hospital each year for acute pancreatitis.

That is about 70 people per 100,000.

Most people who get this condition are over 45 years old. Men are slightly more likely to get it than women.

---

## How Does It Progress?

Most people (80%) get better in 1 to 2 weeks. But some still feel weak or have stomach pain and digestion issues after leaving the hospital.

About 20% of people develop serious problems. These can include infections, fluid buildup, or damage to organs. Recovery may take weeks or months.

About 3% of people die from complications.

If gallstones caused the problem, it can come back. Removing the gallbladder can prevent future attacks.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors start by asking about your symptoms and health history. They will check your belly for tenderness.

They will also test your blood. One key test measures a substance called lipase. This is made by the pancreas. If the level in your blood is very high, it means the pancreas is inflamed.

An ultrasound scan of the belly is usually done next. It can show:
- Swelling in the pancreas
- Gallstones
- Blockages in the ducts

Sometimes, more tests are needed:
- A CT scan can show how bad the inflammation is and if there are complications.
- An MRI can help find stones in the bile ducts.

Other conditions can cause similar symptoms. These include:
- A heart attack
- An inflamed gallbladder
- A hole in the stomach from an ulcer

If gallstones are found in the bile duct, a special test may be done. This uses a thin tube passed through the mouth into the intestine. It is called endoscopic ultrasound or ERC.

If acute pancreatitis is confirmed, you will be admitted to hospital the same day.

---

## How Is It Treated?

There is no direct treatment for the cause. The goal is to ease symptoms and let the pancreas heal.

You will get fluids through a drip (infusion) to prevent dehydration.

Pain relief is important. Strong painkillers, like opioids, are often needed. These can make you drowsy.

You will not eat solid food at first. This gives the pancreas a chance to rest.

You can start eating again when the pain goes down and you feel hungry. Most people can begin eating again after 2 days.

If you cannot eat normally, you may need a special liquid diet through a tube. This gives your body the nutrients it needs.

For more information, visit the website: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Hip Osteoarthritis (Coxarthrosis)

Hip osteoarthritis causes pain in the hip and groin when you move.  
It happens because the smooth, protective layer of cartilage in the hip joint wears down over time.  
This condition mostly affects people over the age of 45.

---

## Quick Facts

- Hip osteoarthritis usually starts slowly.  
- The main treatments are exercise and physical therapy.  
- It is caused by wear and tear on the cartilage in the hip joint.  
- The way it develops can be very different from person to person.  
- More women than men are affected by this condition.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Hip Osteoarthritis?

Hip osteoarthritis happens when the cartilage in the hip joint wears away.  
Cartilage is the smooth, cushioning material that covers the bones in the joint.  
When it thins, the bones rub against each other.  
This causes pain and makes the joint stiffer over time.  
Pain in the hip and groin during movement is often the first sign.  
Most people with this condition are over 45 years old.

The way the condition progresses varies widely.  
Some people have only mild symptoms that do not affect their daily life.  
Others may have a rapid worsening of symptoms that greatly impacts their quality of life.

Exercise and physical therapy are key treatments.  
Pain relief medicines called non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can help.  
Losing weight can also reduce pressure on the joint if you are very overweight.  
If the pain becomes severe and limits daily activities, joint replacement surgery may be an option.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

At first, pain usually only happens when you are active.  
It may go away after a short rest.  
The pain often comes on slowly and can last for months or years.

You may feel pain when climbing stairs, walking, or moving your leg sideways.  
Some people feel pain in the inner thigh, buttock, or even the knee.

Your hip may feel stiff in the morning or after sitting for a long time.  
This stiffness usually lasts no more than 30 minutes.  
If stiffness lasts longer than that, it may be a different condition, like rheumatoid arthritis.

Pain that happens when you are resting or at night usually means the condition is advanced.

---

## What Causes Hip Osteoarthritis?

In a healthy hip, the ball of the thigh bone and the socket in the pelvis are covered in cartilage.  
This cartilage acts like a cushion.  
It lets the bones move smoothly without rubbing.

When the cartilage wears down, it becomes soft and starts to tear.  
This leads to osteoarthritis, also known as joint degeneration.

Cartilage does not heal well on its own.  
Once damaged, it usually does not grow back.  
So, the damage is often permanent.

Many factors can increase the risk of developing hip osteoarthritis:

- A family history of joint problems  
- Being born with a misshapen hip (hip dysplasia)  
- Rare birth defects in the hip joint  
- Inflammatory joint diseases like rheumatoid arthritis  
- Past injuries to the hip, such as fractures or dislocations  
- Hip impingement – where extra bone causes pinching in the joint  
- Being overweight or obese  
- Jobs that involve heavy lifting or long hours of standing  
- Sports that put strong pressure on the hips, like football or handball

---

## How Common Is It?

In Germany, about 5 out of every 100 adults have hip osteoarthritis with symptoms.  
More women than men are affected.

---

## How Does It Develop?

As we age, the cartilage in our joints naturally wears down.  
The space between the bones gets smaller.  
This means the bones are less protected from pressure.  
The body tries to fix this by building extra bone.  
These new bone growths, called bone spurs or osteophytes, show up on X-rays.

These changes in the joint can happen slowly.  
The body may balance wear and repair for years.  
So, joint changes do not always cause pain or symptoms.

A large study in the Netherlands followed patients for five years.  
It found:

- 40% had mild, steady pain the whole time  
- 20% had moderate, steady pain  
- 25% had moderate pain that got worse over time  
- 15% had constant, severe pain

Pain can also come and go.  
Some people have flare-ups with strong pain, followed by times with little or no pain.  
Not everyone with joint damage needs surgery.  
Many people live well with the condition without needing an artificial joint.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose hip osteoarthritis based on your symptoms.  
A common sign is “start-up pain” – pain that happens after sitting or lying still, but goes away quickly when you move.

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms.  
They will want to know:

- How long you’ve had pain  
- When the pain happens  
- What the pain feels like  
- If it happens only when moving or also when resting  
- If your joints feel stiff in the morning  
- If you’ve had any past injuries

The doctor will also examine your hip.  
They will check how well it moves.  
They will look at your walking style.  
They will check if your pelvis is tilted or if your legs are different lengths.

Imaging tests like X-rays, ultrasounds, CT scans, or MRIs are not always helpful.  
Studies show that only 1 in 4 people with visible joint changes on an X-ray actually have pain.  
So, these tests often do not add useful information.

However, imaging or blood tests may be needed if your symptoms suggest another condition, such as rheumatoid arthritis or gout.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on how bad the pain is.  
Your doctor will also consider your overall health, job, and personal goals.

Recommended treatments include:

- Physical therapy with exercises to strengthen the hip and thigh muscles  
- Rehabilitation sports and movement programs  
- Functional training, aquarobics, and tai chi  
- Taking non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)  
- Losing weight if you are very overweight  
- Wearing flat, soft, and comfortable shoes

Many people with joint pain avoid exercise because they fear it will make things worse.  
But research shows the opposite.  
Strengthening, stretching, and endurance exercises reduce pain and improve joint function.  
These exercises can even delay the need for surgery.

For more information on how to strengthen your hips, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

Cortisone injections can help relieve pain for several weeks.  
They work best if only one joint is affected.  
They may be used if the joint is very inflamed and painful.  
They may also be used if other treatments have not worked.

But cortisone injections are not meant for long-term use.  
They can cause side effects.  
It is not clear if they help in the long run.

> **Important:** Injections into the hip joint can cause side effects.  
> In rare cases, they can cause serious problems.  
> They must be done by an experienced doctor.  
> Good hygiene is essential.  
> An ultrasound machine is needed to place the needle safely.  
> This helps avoid damage to nerves, blood vessels, or other structures.

If pain is severe and daily life is hard, even with medicine and exercise, an artificial hip joint may be needed.  
This is called total hip replacement (THR) or total hip arthroplasty (THA).  
It helps relieve symptoms in over 90% of people.

Many other treatments have not been proven effective. These include:

- Pain-relief creams  
- Painkillers like paracetamol  
- Duloxetine (used for depression or nerve pain)  
- Hyaluronic acid injections  
- Arthroscopy to smooth cartilage  
- Ultrasound, laser, or electrical therapy (TENS)  
- Heat treatments like diathermy  
- Gold implants  
- Low-dose X-ray therapy (orthovoltage radiation)  
- Dietary supplements (like chondroitin, glucosamine, or vitamins)  
- Herbal remedies (like rampion or stinging nettle)  
- Homeopathy  
- Special foods or food extracts (like soy or avocado)

---

## What Is Life Like with Hip Osteoarthritis?

Advanced hip osteoarthritis can make daily tasks harder.  
But many people learn to manage well over time.  
They may take more time to do chores or adjust how they do things.

Walking aids can help.  
These include walking sticks, walkers, or wheeled walkers.  
They reduce pressure on the hip joint.

Experts can help you choose and set up the right aid.  
These include:

- Physiotherapists  
- Occupational therapists  
- Doctors specializing in bones (orthopedics), joints (rheumatology), or older adults (geriatrics)

# Ringing in the Ears (Tinnitus)

Many people hear ringing, buzzing, or humming in their ears from time to time. This often happens after being in a loud place, like a concert. But some people hear these sounds all the time, even when there is no noise around. This constant noise in the ears is called tinnitus. It can make daily life very hard for some people.

---

## Quick Facts

- The sounds in the ears can come from many different reasons.
- These sounds are rarely a sign of a serious health problem.
- Between 5% and 15% of adults will have tinnitus that lasts for a long time at some point in their lives.
- Most of the time, tinnitus goes away on its own.
- Some people get tinnitus suddenly, but it usually lasts less than a minute.
- In some people, the sounds continue for longer.
- If tinnitus lasts more than three months, it is called chronic.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Tinnitus?

You may have heard a high-pitched sound in your ears after a loud concert. Or after working near loud machines. This kind of noise usually goes away by itself. These sounds are called tinnitus. They can happen for many reasons. But they are rarely a sign of a serious illness.

Sometimes tinnitus starts suddenly with no clear reason. But it usually does not last long. In some people, the sounds continue for days, weeks, or even longer. If tinnitus lasts more than three months, doctors call it chronic.

Most people with tinnitus have only mild symptoms. The noise is annoying, but they can still live their lives normally. But for some, the noise is so strong that it causes stress. It can make it hard to focus. It can also make it hard to sleep.

---

## What Do People With Tinnitus Experience?

The word tinnitus comes from Latin and means “ringing.” But people do not just hear ringing. They may hear whistling, buzzing, humming, hissing, clicking, or knocking sounds.

The noise can be in one ear or both ears. Some people feel the sound is inside their head. Others feel it is coming from outside. The noise can be constant or come and go. It can be very soft at times and then very loud.

Most people with tinnitus have normal hearing. Tinnitus can be linked to hearing loss, but it does not always happen.

---

## What Causes Tinnitus?

Tinnitus is often caused by loud noise. Loud sounds can damage tiny cells in the inner ear. These cells help you hear. Many people with tinnitus have been in loud places often. Or they had a sudden loud noise, like an explosion or gunshots. This is called acoustic trauma.

Other possible causes include:

- Earwax blocking the ear canal
- Long-term middle ear infections
- A hole in the eardrum
- Otosclerosis: a bone problem in the middle or inner ear that can cause hearing loss
- Ménière’s disease: a condition in the inner ear that causes tinnitus, dizziness, and hearing loss
- Problems with the jaw muscles or jaw joint

Some medicines can also cause tinnitus. This includes very high doses of aspirin. Always take medicine as directed.

For many people, doctors cannot find a clear cause. This is called primary or idiopathic tinnitus. The word “idiopathic” means the cause is unknown.

Scientists do not fully understand how loud noise leads to tinnitus. One idea is that damaged ear cells stop sending signals to the brain. Then, the brain’s hearing center becomes overactive. It starts making sounds on its own. This is similar to how some people feel pain in a missing limb.

Stress may play a role, but there is no clear proof. Relaxation techniques do not seem to directly help tinnitus.

---

## How Common Is Tinnitus?

Tinnitus is fairly common. About 5% to 15% of adults will have long-lasting tinnitus at some point in their lives. In 10% to 20% of these people, the tinnitus is so bad that it affects their daily life. These people may need treatment.

Tinnitus is most common in people over 50. But it can also happen in children, though this is rare.

---

## How Does Tinnitus Develop?

No one can predict how tinnitus will behave. If the cause is known and treatable, the tinnitus may go away quickly. If the cause is unclear, it may continue and become chronic.

Some people also become more sensitive to normal sounds. This can be uncomfortable in noisy places. This is called hyperacusis.

Chronic tinnitus can hurt quality of life. It can cause sleep problems and trouble focusing. Some people start avoiding social events. This can lead to loneliness or even depression.

But over time, the problems caused by tinnitus can also get better.

---

## How Can Tinnitus Be Prevented?

Protecting your ears from loud noise is the best way to prevent tinnitus. Avoid loud places when possible. If you must be in a loud place, wear earplugs or other hearing protection. This lowers your risk of getting tinnitus. It can also help prevent tinnitus from getting worse.

---

## How Is Tinnitus Diagnosed?

Your doctor will start by asking questions. They will want to know:

- What kind of sounds you hear
- When you hear them
- If you have other symptoms, like ear pain or pressure
- What medicines you take and how much

If the tinnitus is only in one ear and comes with other symptoms, it likely has a clear cause. This cause is often treatable.

After the talk, your doctor will check your ears and do a hearing test. You may also need a dental check-up. This helps rule out jaw problems.

Based on the results, your doctor will decide what type of tinnitus you have. There are four main types:

- **Subjective tinnitus:** Only you can hear the sound. This is the most common type. It is usually caused by problems in the hearing system or nerves.
- **Objective tinnitus:** Very rare. The doctor can also hear the sound with a stethoscope. It may come from blood vessels or muscle movements.
- **Primary tinnitus:** No clear cause can be found. This is also called idiopathic tinnitus.
- **Secondary tinnitus:** A clear cause is found, such as a hole in the eardrum or a blood vessel problem.
- **Acute tinnitus:** Lasts less than three months.
- **Chronic tinnitus:** Lasts more than three months.
- **Severity levels:** Some people have mild tinnitus that comes and goes. Others have constant, loud sounds that make life very hard. This can affect work, sleep, and focus.

---

## How Is Tinnitus Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause. If a medical condition is causing tinnitus, treating that condition may help. For example, if high blood pressure is the cause, lowering it may reduce the tinnitus.

But if no cause is found, treatment focuses on managing symptoms. The goal is to help you live well with tinnitus.

If you have hearing loss, a hearing aid may help. It can make the tinnitus less noticeable.

Many products are sold for tinnitus. These include herbal remedies, vitamins, and medicines like steroids or carbamazepine. But none of these have been proven to work. Some may even cause side effects.

The most effective treatment is **cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)**. This therapy helps people learn how to cope with tinnitus. It does not make the sounds go away. But it can improve your quality of life.

If tinnitus starts suddenly, doctors may give a drip (infusion) right away. This is often a salt solution. Sometimes a different fluid called hydroxyethyl starch (HES) is used. But studies show HES does not help. Worse, it can cause serious allergic reactions, like itching all over the body.

For more information on what treatments work and what do not, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

# Polyneuropathy

## What is polyneuropathy?

Your body has nerves outside your brain and spinal cord. These are called peripheral nerves.  
They help you feel things like touch, heat, and pressure.  
They also help you move your muscles and control your organs.  

When several of these nerves are damaged, it can cause symptoms like pain and tingling.  
Doctors call this condition polyneuropathy.  

Damage to these nerves can happen for many reasons.  
One common cause is poorly managed diabetes.  
Another is heavy drinking over a long time.  

Tingling, burning, or sharp pain in the feet is a common sign.  
You might also feel weak in your legs or have trouble walking steadily.  

The goal of treatment is to find and fix the cause if possible.  

---

## What are the signs of polyneuropathy?

Symptoms depend on which nerves are damaged.  

### If sensory nerves are affected (nerves that carry feelings):
- Tingling or a crawling feeling on the skin  
- Itching or numbness  
- Sharp or burning pain, even from light touch like clothes  
- A feeling of tightness or pressure  
- Feeling like you are walking on cotton  
- Less ability to feel heat, cold, or pain  
- Trouble walking in the dark  
- Sores on the feet that do not hurt  

### If motor nerves are affected (nerves that control movement):
- Weak muscles  
- Muscle cramps or twitching  
- Trouble moving your arms or legs  

### If nerves to organs are affected:
- Heart racing when sitting still  
- Dizziness or fainting when standing up  
- Constipation, bloating, or diarrhea  
- Trouble peeing or leaking urine  
- Sweating too much or not enough  
- Men may have trouble getting or keeping an erection  

---

## What causes polyneuropathy?

Many things can damage peripheral nerves.  

Some causes include:  
- Long-term diabetes  
- Heavy alcohol use  
- HIV infection over time  
- Severe kidney disease  
- Cancer  
- Autoimmune diseases like Guillain-Barré syndrome  
- Infections such as Lyme disease  
- An underactive thyroid  
- Certain cancer drugs and antibiotics  
- Low levels of vitamin B12  
- Rapid weight loss or weight-loss surgery  
- Drug or alcohol abuse  

In many older adults, doctors cannot find the exact cause.  

---

## How common is polyneuropathy?

About 3 out of every 100 people will get polyneuropathy in their lifetime.  

Diabetes is the most common cause.  
Nearly half of all people with diabetes will develop nerve damage.  

It is also common in people with long-term alcohol problems.  

---

## What is the outlook?

The course of polyneuropathy varies from person to person.  

If nerve damage is due to high blood sugar, it usually gets worse slowly.  
It often starts in the feet and then moves up to the hands.  

If alcohol is the cause, the damage gets worse with more drinking.  
The more alcohol you consume, the worse the symptoms become.  

If the cause is an immune problem or a genetic condition, the damage may progress steadily.  
Some people have sudden worsening followed by periods of stability.  

---

## How is polyneuropathy diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask you about your symptoms.  
They will want to know:  
- What symptoms you have  
- When they started  
- If only your hands and feet are affected  
- If symptoms are getting worse  
- If you have other health problems  
- What medicines you take  
- How much alcohol or drugs you use  
- About your sexual health and any sexually transmitted infections  

Your doctor will also do a physical exam.  
They will check:  
- How well you feel touch, heat, and pain  
- How well you walk and stand  
- If any muscles are weak or not working  
- How your reflexes respond  

To learn more about nerve damage, your doctor may use:  
- Electroneurography (ENoG): This measures how fast nerve signals travel  
- Electromyography (EMG): This checks how well muscles respond to nerve signals  

They may also test your blood, urine, or spinal fluid.  
They might take a small sample of tissue or do genetic testing.  
Imaging tests like ultrasound or MRI can also help.  

---

## How is polyneuropathy treated?

First, doctors treat the underlying cause.  
For example, they will help you control your blood sugar if diabetes is the problem.  
They will help you stop drinking alcohol if that is the cause.  

Treating the cause can improve symptoms.  
But it may not fully reverse the nerve damage.  

Pain relief is also important.  
Doctors often use antidepressants to help with nerve pain.  
These drugs work by changing how your body sends pain signals.  
They can help even if you do not have depression.  

Anticonvulsants are medicines used for seizures.  
They can also reduce nerve pain by calming overactive nerves.  

If these medicines do not help enough, stronger painkillers may be used.  
But these should only be used for a short time.  
They can be addictive and cause other problems.

# Presbyopia

Most people start to have trouble seeing things up close in their mid-forties.  
This is a normal part of aging.  
It is called presbyopia.  
There is no way to stop or reverse it.  
But you can manage the problem with help.

---

## Quick Facts

- Your close-up vision gets worse as you age.  
  This usually starts in your mid-forties.  
- The most common sign is trouble reading.  
- An eye doctor or optician can check for presbyopia.  
- You cannot cure presbyopia.  
  But glasses or contact lenses can help you see clearly again.  
- After about age 65, your vision usually stops getting worse.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Presbyopia?

Most people notice they need to hold books or phones farther away to read.  
They may need more light or feel tired after reading.  
This is presbyopia.  
It is also called age-related farsightedness.  
It happens because the eye’s lens loses flexibility over time.  
This makes it hard to focus on close-up objects.  
The good news is that you can fix the problem with reading glasses.

---

## Signs of Presbyopia

You may notice:
- Words look blurry when you read them.  
- You have to hold reading material farther away.  
- Reading for long periods feels tiring.  
- Your eyes feel sore or sting.  
- You get headaches after reading.

These problems are worse when you are tired or in dim light.

---

## What Causes Presbyopia?

Presbyopia is part of normal aging.  
The lens inside your eye changes over time.  
It becomes less flexible.  
This makes it harder to focus on close-up objects.  

The lens works by changing shape.  
When you look at something near, the lens gets thicker.  
When you look at something far, it gets thinner.  
This change is controlled by a small muscle around the lens.  

As you age:
- The lens becomes stiffer.  
- The muscle around the lens gets weaker.  
- The lens can no longer change shape well.  
This leads to trouble seeing up close.

---

## Who Is More Likely to Get Presbyopia?

Presbyopia usually starts in the mid-forties.  
But some people notice it earlier.  
Others notice it later.  
No one knows exactly why this happens.  

Certain health conditions may make it start sooner.  
These include:
- Diabetes  
- Heart disease  
- Multiple sclerosis  

There is no difference between men and women in when presbyopia starts.  
But women often get reading glasses earlier.  
This is not because they have presbyopia sooner.  
It is because they are more likely to act on the problem.

---

## How Does Presbyopia Change Over Time?

Even before you notice presbyopia, your lens slowly loses flexibility.  
Young children can see things clearly right in front of them.  
Most adults need to hold reading material about 35 centimeters away.  
After age 40, this distance gets longer.  
Most people need reading glasses by age 45.  
After about age 65, your vision usually stops getting worse.

People who are near-sighted (short-sighted) often have milder presbyopia.  
They may not need reading glasses until later.  
They can sometimes use their regular glasses for distance and remove them to read.

People who are far-sighted (long-sighted) often feel presbyopia more strongly.  
This is because their eyes already have trouble focusing on close-up objects.  
Presbyopia makes this worse.

---

## Can You Prevent Presbyopia?

Some people suggest eye exercises to prevent presbyopia.  
These are often sold online or in books.  
But these exercises cannot stop the lens from becoming less flexible.  
They cannot prevent presbyopia.  
The condition will still happen with age.

---

## How Is Presbyopia Diagnosed?

An eye doctor or optician can check for presbyopia.  
They use a machine called an auto-refractometer.  
This measures how your eyes focus light.  

Then they do a full eye test.  
They check your vision for both near and far distances.  
They test each eye one at a time.  
They cover one eye while testing the other.  

They use charts with letters, numbers, or broken rings.  
They may use a projector to show the test images.  

The strength of glasses or contact lenses is measured in diopters.  
This number tells you how much correction you need.

---

## How Can Presbyopia Be Treated?

There is no cure for presbyopia.  
But many treatments can help you see clearly again.

### Reading Glasses
- Ready-made reading glasses are easy to buy.  
- They are not always perfect.  
- They do not account for differences between your two eyes.  
- They do not help if you have astigmatism.

### Custom Reading Glasses
- Opticians make glasses based on your eye test results.  
- They take into account the space between your eyes.  
- They can correct for astigmatism or other issues.  
- These glasses are often thin.  
- You can look over the top to see things far away without removing them.

### Multifocal Lenses
These are good for people who already wear glasses.  
They have more than one lens power in one pair of glasses.

- **Bifocals:** Two lens areas.  
  The top part is for distance.  
  The bottom part is for reading.  
  There is a visible line between them.

- **Trifocals:** Three lens areas.  
  One for distance, one for middle distance, one for reading.  
  There are two visible lines.

- **Varifocals:** The most common type.  
  They have no visible lines.  
  The lens changes smoothly from one power to another.

### Contact Lenses
- Some people use contact lenses for presbyopia.  
- But glasses are often easier to use.  
- This is especially true if you don’t need vision correction all the time.

---

## Laser Treatment and Surgery

Some doctors suggest laser treatment.  
You may see ads for this in magazines or online.  
But laser treatment is not a good choice if you only have presbyopia.  

It may help you avoid reading glasses.  
But it can cause side effects.  
These include:
- Trouble seeing in three dimensions  
- Problems with distance vision  
- Overall vision getting worse  

Other surgeries, like replacing the lens or using a corneal inlay, are also options.  
But they carry risks.  
They may cause side effects.  
They only help you avoid glasses.  
They do not fix the underlying problem.

---

## More Information

For more details on how presbyopia can be corrected, visit:  
[gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Tetanus

Tetanus is a serious illness caused by a toxin from certain bacteria. It can be deadly. Thanks to vaccines, tetanus is now very rare in Germany.

## Quick Facts

- Tetanus bacteria live in soil all over the world.
- You get tetanus when these bacteria enter your body through a skin injury.
- Common symptoms include muscle spasms, especially in the face and back.
- Even with good medical care, 10 to 20 out of 100 people with tetanus still die.
- If medical care is not available, more people die.
- Vaccination is the best way to protect yourself.
- Tetanus is now very rare in Germany because of vaccination.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Tetanus?

Tetanus is also called "lockjaw" because muscles become stiff and tight.

The illness happens when toxins from tetanus bacteria enter the body. These toxins come from bacteria that get into a wound.

Vaccination stops tetanus. That is why the disease is so rare in Germany.

Tetanus is deadly, but with good intensive care, most people survive.

### Types of Tetanus

Doctors divide tetanus into three types:

- **Generalized tetanus**: affects the whole body.
- **Localized tetanus**: affects only the muscles near the wound.
- **Neonatal tetanus**: can happen in newborn babies if the mother is not protected.

> **Important:** Localized tetanus is very rare. There have been no cases of neonatal tetanus in Germany for many decades.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms usually appear between 3 days and 3 weeks after infection.

Common signs include:

- Sweating
- Fluctuating blood pressure
- Fast heartbeat
- Painful muscle spasms
- A fixed grin due to tight facial muscles
- Trouble opening the mouth (lockjaw)
- Stiff neck and back
- Difficulty swallowing
- Breathing problems

### Symptoms in Newborns

Newborns with tetanus cannot open their mouth well, so they cannot feed properly. They also have stiff muscles and sudden muscle spasms.

## How Do People Get Tetanus?

You can only get tetanus if a wound lets the bacteria enter your skin. This can happen from:

- A splinter
- A nail
- An animal bite
- Any deep or dirty injury

Tetanus cannot spread from person to person.

### What Causes Tetanus?

The bacteria that cause tetanus are called *Clostridium tetani*. They are found in soil and in horse manure.

These bacteria can form spores. Spores are tough forms that survive heat, disinfectants, and long periods in the ground.

When conditions improve, the spores turn back into active bacteria. They grow best in warm, oxygen-free environments.

The bacteria make toxins that make you sick. If they grow in a wound, the toxins travel along nerves to the spinal cord.

Normally, nerves in the spinal cord calm down muscle activity. But the tetanus toxins block this calming effect. This causes muscles to overreact. Even small stimuli can trigger strong muscle contractions and spasms.

## What Increases the Risk of Tetanus?

You are at higher risk if you have:

- Deep wounds
- Drug use
- Poor circulation
- Diabetes
- Long-term skin problems
- Dental infections

> **Important:** People who are not vaccinated or only partly vaccinated are at the highest risk.

## How Common Is Tetanus?

Tetanus bacteria are found in soil all over the world. They cannot be completely removed. So there is always some risk of infection.

### Tetanus in Germany

In recent years, only a few cases have been reported in Germany. Most were in older adults.

There have been no cases of tetanus in newborns in Germany for many decades. This is mainly because of vaccination.

### Tetanus Around the World

Tetanus is still common in warm, humid countries with low vaccination rates and poor medical care.

We do not know the exact number of cases. But we know how many people die each year:

- Between 48,000 and 80,000 people die from tetanus worldwide every year.
- Most deaths are newborns.
- In 2018, about 25,000 babies died from tetanus.
- In 1988, about 800,000 babies died from tetanus.

This shows that fewer babies are dying from tetanus now than before.

## How Does Tetanus Progress?

The course of the disease depends on the type and how much toxin enters the blood.

### Generalized Tetanus

This form does not happen in people who are fully vaccinated.

It causes the classic symptoms. The illness has several stages.

Severe spasms can affect both the front and back muscles of the spine. This can cause spinal fractures.

Later, the toxins affect nerves that control breathing and blood pressure. This leads to:

- Trouble breathing
- Blood pressure swings
- Sweating

Many deaths happen due to breathing or heart failure.

With modern intensive care, 80 to 90 out of 100 people survive.

### Localized Tetanus

This form can happen in people who are partly immune, such as those who were vaccinated a long time ago.

Symptoms are only in the muscles near the wound.

This form is usually not serious. But it can turn into the generalized form.

### Neonatal Tetanus

This happens if a mother is not vaccinated and the baby’s umbilical stump is not kept clean.

The bacteria enter through the stump after the cord is cut.

Symptoms appear within the first two weeks of life. They include:

- Stiff muscles
- Muscle spasms
- Weak sucking reflex

## How Can Tetanus Be Prevented?

The best way to prevent tetanus is to get vaccinated.

The German Standing Committee on Vaccination (STIKO) gives different recommendations for different groups.

### Vaccination for Babies and Children

Babies should get three doses of the vaccine:

- At 2 months
- At 4 months
- At 11 months

The vaccine is usually given together with other vaccines:

- Diphtheria
- Whooping cough
- Polio
- Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib)
- Hepatitis B

Booster shots are given:

- At age 5 to 6
- At age 9 to 16

### Vaccination for Adults

Unvaccinated adults can catch up using the same schedule as children.

Vaccinated adults should get a booster every 10 years.

Most adults get a combined vaccine that protects against:

- Diphtheria
- Or both diphtheria and whooping cough

For more information, visit the Robert Koch Institute website.

You can find:

- Answers to common questions about tetanus vaccination
- The latest STIKO recommendations
- A vaccination calendar in 21 languages
- A pocket-sized version of the recommendations

## How Is Tetanus Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose tetanus based on symptoms like:

- Lockjaw
- Muscle spasms in the face and back

An electrical test of the muscles (electromyography) can show increased muscle activity.

To confirm the diagnosis, doctors can test for the toxins in animals. But this is only done in rare cases and under special rules.

> **Important:** If you are fully vaccinated and up to date, you almost certainly cannot have tetanus. The disease can usually be ruled out in such cases.

## How Is Tetanus Treated?

Treatment has two goals: fight the bacteria and ease symptoms.

### Vaccination and Antibodies

If you have a wound and are not vaccinated or unsure about your vaccination status, you get:

- Tetanus antibodies (immunoglobulins) to neutralize the toxins (passive immunization)
- The regular tetanus vaccine to help your body make its own antibodies (active immunization)

If you are fully vaccinated and your last shot was recent, you do not need extra shots or antibodies.

### Wound Care

For deep or dirty wounds, a surgeon must clean the wound carefully. They remove dead or damaged tissue.

This stops the bacteria from multiplying and making more toxins.

### Antibiotics

Antibiotics do not destroy the toxins. But they stop the bacteria from making more toxins.

Patients are given antibiotics like metronidazole.

### Intensive Care

If symptoms are already present, patients are treated in an intensive care unit.

Doctors monitor breathing and heart function.

To prevent spasms, patients are kept in a quiet, calm environment.

They are given medicine to relax the muscles.

# False Croup

False croup is a swelling in the upper airways. It mostly happens in young children. The main signs are a cough that sounds like a dog barking, a raspy sound when breathing in, and a little trouble catching their breath.

## Quick Facts

- False croup is swelling in the upper airways.
- It mostly affects young children.
- Symptoms often start suddenly, usually in the evening or at night.
- Common signs include:
  - A barking cough
  - A raspy or whistling sound when breathing in
  - Hoarseness
  - A little shortness of breath
- Most children get better on their own within a few days.
- Call emergency services (112) if the child is struggling badly to breathe.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical care. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself or your child.

## What Is False Croup?

False croup is a condition in the airways. It usually happens in young children. When a child has a cold, the upper airways can become inflamed. If the voice box (larynx) swells up, this is called false croup.

The main symptoms are:
- A barking cough
- A raspy or whistling sound when breathing in
- Hoarseness
- A little shortness of breath

These symptoms usually go away on their own.

The name “false croup” helps to tell it apart from “true croup.” True croup is a serious bacterial infection called diphtheria. False croup is not that serious. The name also refers to where the swelling happens — in the upper airways, near the voice box.

Doctors call false croup *Laryngitis subglottica*. This means inflammation in the part of the voice box just below the vocal cords.

For more details, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

## What Are the Symptoms?

False croup often starts with a common cold. The child may have a runny nose and a mild fever. After a few days, the symptoms of false croup begin — usually at night or in the evening.

Common symptoms include:
- A cough that sounds like a dog barking
- A raspy or whistling sound when breathing in
- Hoarseness
- A little shortness of breath

The swelling in the voice box makes it harder to breathe. The child may breathe faster and deeper. Most children only feel a little short of breath. But this can be scary. When children are scared, they may cry. Crying can make breathing even harder.

## What Causes False Croup?

Most cases are caused by cold viruses. The most common is a virus called parainfluenza. This virus often causes a mild cold. But sometimes it causes the lining of the voice box to swell.

## How Common Is It?

False croup is most common in autumn and winter. It mostly affects children between 6 months and 3 years old. About 3 out of every 100 children in this age group get it each year. Adults rarely get false croup.

## How Does It Progress?

A child may first have a cold, a runny nose, and a mild fever. After a few days, they may suddenly develop false croup symptoms — often at night. Most children have mild symptoms. These usually go away on their own within 2 days.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Call emergency services (112) if the child is having a hard time breathing.

A sign that things are getting worse is if the skin between the ribs pulls in with each breath. This is called retractions. If the child is very short of breath, they may turn blue around the lips or face. They may also seem weak, tired, or not respond.

These signs can mean the airways are inflamed and narrowed. In rare cases, the flap that covers the windpipe (epiglottis) may be infected. A doctor may use a special tool to look inside the throat. This is called a laryngoscopy.

If a bacterial infection is suspected, the doctor may take a swab from the throat.

## How Is It Treated?

Stay calm. Your calmness helps your child stay calm too. Anxiety can make breathing harder.

Most children have mild symptoms. These go away on their own in a few days. No medicine is needed in these cases.

Some people say that fresh, cool, moist air helps. But there is no strong proof that this works.

If the child is very uncomfortable or not getting better, see a doctor. Take the child to the hospital if they are struggling to breathe.

The doctor will likely give a medicine called cortisone. This reduces swelling. It can be given as a tablet, suppository, injection, or spray. The child usually feels better within a few hours. This medicine is safe for short-term use and rarely causes side effects.

If the child is very short of breath, they may get adrenaline. This is breathed in through a nebulizer. Adrenaline helps shrink the blood vessels in the throat. The swelling usually goes down in about 30 minutes. Possible side effects are a faster heartbeat and higher blood pressure. These are not dangerous.

A child who is very short of breath will also get oxygen through a mask on the nose.

Stay calm. Be with your child. Comfort them. Your presence can help reduce their fear and make breathing easier.

# Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy

This condition affects the heart muscle. The heart wall becomes thicker than normal. This can make it harder for the heart to pump blood. If not found early, it can lead to serious problems. These include heart failure or sudden death. Finding it early and treating it is very important.

---

## Quick Facts

- Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) means the heart muscle gets thicker.
- The thickening mainly happens in the left lower chamber of the heart.
- Many people with HCM have no symptoms for years, especially young people.
- When symptoms do appear, they may include:
  - Trouble breathing during activity
  - Feeling very tired
  - Chest pain
  - Fainting, especially during or after exercise
  - Heart palpitations (feeling like the heart is racing or skipping)
- The main cause is often a genetic change passed down in families.
- HCM can lead to sudden cardiac arrest or heart failure.
- There is no cure, but treatment can help manage symptoms and reduce risks.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy?

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a condition you are usually born with. The heart muscle, especially in the left lower chamber, becomes thicker than normal. Doctors call this thickening “hypertrophy.”

The left lower chamber pumps oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the rest of the body through the main artery (aorta). This blood gives oxygen to all organs.

In about 7 out of 10 people with HCM, the thickened muscle blocks blood flow from the heart to the aorta. This is called **obstructive HCM**.

If there is no blockage, it is called **non-obstructive HCM**.

HCM affects about 2 in every 1,000 people worldwide.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many people with HCM feel no symptoms for years. Some may never have any.

When symptoms do appear, they often include:

- Shortness of breath during physical activity
- Feeling very tired
- Chest pain, especially during exercise
- Fainting or dizziness during or after activity
- Heart palpitations (feeling like the heart is fluttering or racing)

These symptoms can start at any age. But signs of heart failure usually show up in middle age. Women often develop symptoms later than men, but their symptoms may be worse.

The severity of symptoms does not always match how much blood flow is blocked. Some people with severe blockage have few symptoms. Others with no blockage can still have dangerous heart problems, like sudden cardiac arrest.

---

## What Causes HCM?

Most cases of HCM are caused by changes in genes. These changes are inherited from a parent. About 60% to 70% of people with HCM have a family member with the same condition.

In rare cases, HCM develops after another illness.

Sometimes, doctors cannot find a cause. When this happens, they call it **idiopathic HCM**.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

HCM is usually present from birth. But symptoms often do not appear until later in life. Many people live normal lives and never know they have it.

Some people do get worse over time. Their symptoms and risks can increase.

About 1% to 2% of people with HCM die each year from the condition or its complications. The most common causes of death are:

- Sudden cardiac arrest
- Heart failure
- Blood clots blocking blood vessels

Certain factors raise the risk of sudden death. These include:

- Fainting for no reason in the past 6 months
- A close family member died suddenly from HCM
- The heart wall is 30 millimeters thick or more
- Blood pressure does not rise during exercise
- Severe symptoms

---

## How Can HCM Be Found Early?

HCM often runs in families. If one person in a family has it, their parents, children, and siblings are usually offered screening.

The process includes:

- A doctor visit and physical exam
- An echocardiogram (ultrasound of the heart) to check for thickened muscle and blocked blood flow
- A genetic test, if needed, to look for gene changes

People already diagnosed with HCM should have a check-up every 1 to 3 years. This is true even if they feel fine. These visits help doctors track heart health and check for risks.

They also help decide if a person needs an **implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD)**.

An ICD is a small device placed under the skin. It monitors the heart rhythm. If the heart beats too fast or irregularly, the device sends a small electric shock to restore a normal rhythm. This can prevent sudden death.

---

## How Is HCM Diagnosed?

If HCM is suspected, a heart doctor (cardiologist) will do tests.

- **Echocardiogram (echo):** This ultrasound scan shows if the heart wall is thickened and if blood flow is blocked. It is usually enough to make a diagnosis.
- **Cardiac MRI:** This scan gives a more detailed image. It may be used if the echo is unclear.
- **Electrocardiogram (ECG):** This test checks for irregular heartbeats.

For more details on ECG and echo, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

If the tests are not clear, a **genetic test** may be done. It can find gene changes linked to HCM. If a change is found, doctors can test other family members to see if they are affected.

Not all gene changes can be found, though.

---

## How Is HCM Treated?

There is no cure for HCM. But many treatments can help with symptoms and lower risks.

If you have no symptoms, you may not need treatment. But doctors recommend light, regular exercise. Avoid intense sports like competitive football or boxing.

If you are overweight, losing weight can help.

When symptoms start, treatment options include:

### Medicines

- **Beta-blockers:** These slow the heart rate and help with chest pain and shortness of breath. They also help prevent irregular heartbeats.
- **Calcium channel blockers:** These work like beta-blockers. They also help blood flow improve.
- If these do not help, other medicines like diuretics may be used.

### Surgery

If blood flow is severely blocked and medicine does not help, surgery may be needed.

Heart surgeons can remove part of the thickened muscle. This opens up the path for blood to flow out of the heart.

For people at high risk of dangerous heart rhythms, an **ICD** is often recommended.

For more on ICDs, including how they work and what life is like with one, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

Some people need a **pacemaker** if other treatments do not work. A pacemaker helps the heart beat properly.

In rare cases, if the heart can no longer pump blood well, a **heart transplant** may be needed.

---

## What Is Life Like with HCM?

Many people with HCM live normal, active lives. A healthy lifestyle helps.

You should:

- Stay physically active with light to moderate exercise
- Eat a balanced diet
- Limit alcohol

But avoid overexerting yourself. Too much strain on the heart can be dangerous.

Avoid high-intensity sports like football, basketball, or wrestling.

You can safely do:

- Walking
- Skating
- Golf
- Skiing (if you are fit)
- Some ball sports (if approved by your doctor)

Talk to your heart doctor before starting any new activity.

Eat healthy foods. Watch portion sizes. Large meals can cause chest pain, especially if you have obstructive HCM.

--- 

> **Always follow your doctor’s advice.** Regular check-ups are key to staying healthy.

# Anemia

Anemia means your blood does not have enough healthy red blood cells.  
Red blood cells carry oxygen from your lungs to the rest of your body.  
When you have anemia, your body does not get enough oxygen.  

This can cause tiredness, weakness, and pale skin.  
You may also have trouble focusing or feel dizzy.  

Anemia is common.  
It often happens in older adults and in pregnant women.  
It can usually be treated well once the cause is found.

---

## What is anemia?

Anemia means your blood has too few red blood cells or too little hemoglobin.  
Hemoglobin is the part of red blood cells that carries oxygen.  
Without enough hemoglobin, your body does not get enough oxygen.  

One of the most common causes is not having enough iron in your body.  
Iron helps your body make hemoglobin.  
If you lack iron, your body cannot make enough hemoglobin.  

Older people often develop anemia.  
Their bodies make fewer red blood cells, and the ones they do make break down faster.

---

## What are the signs of anemia?

Common signs include:  
- Pale skin  
- Feeling tired all the time  
- Weakness  
- Dizziness or lightheadedness  
- Headaches  

Other possible signs are:  
- Trouble concentrating  
- Feeling short of breath when you walk or climb stairs  
- Chest pain  
- Fast or irregular heartbeat  
- Low blood pressure  
- Fainting  

---

## What causes anemia?

The most common cause is a lack of iron.  
Other causes include:  
- Not enough vitamin B12  
- Not enough folic acid  
- Long-term health problems like kidney disease  
- Blood cancers or bone marrow diseases  

### Why is iron important?

You get iron from the food you eat.  
Your body absorbs iron mainly in the small intestine.  
It then sends the iron to your bone marrow, where it is used to make hemoglobin.  

Hemoglobin is the part of red blood cells that carries oxygen.  
If your body lacks iron, it cannot make enough hemoglobin.  
This leads to less oxygen in your body.  

Your body stores extra iron, mostly in the liver.  
It can use this stored iron when needed.  

An iron deficiency can happen if:  
- You do not eat enough iron-rich foods  
- You have a condition that stops your gut from absorbing iron (like celiac disease)  
- You lose blood slowly over time (for example, from stomach ulcers, heavy periods, or bleeding in the digestive tract)  
- You have a long-term inflammatory disease (like rheumatoid arthritis or bowel disease)  
- You are born with a rare condition that causes iron deficiency  

**Important:** Some medicines can make stomach bleeding worse.  
These include painkillers for joint pain (like those for osteoarthritis) and blood thinners used for heart rhythm problems.

### Other causes of anemia

In some cases, red blood cells break down too fast.  
This is called hemolytic anemia.  
It can happen if the red blood cells are shaped wrong from birth or if the body breaks down hemoglobin too quickly.  

As people age, their bodies make fewer red blood cells.  
The ones they do make also break down faster.  
This can lead to anemia in older adults.  

Sometimes, doctors cannot find the cause of anemia.

---

## What increases the risk of anemia?

Pregnancy can cause temporary anemia.  
Your body needs to make more blood for your baby.  
By the end of pregnancy, your blood volume can increase by up to 50%.  
But your red blood cell count only goes up by about 25%.  
This can lead to anemia.

Women with heavy periods are more likely to become anemic.  
They lose more blood, which means they lose more iron.

As you get older, your risk of anemia goes up.  
This is partly because your body makes less testosterone.  
Testosterone helps your body make red blood cells.  
Both men and women make less testosterone as they age.

---

## How common is anemia?

In Germany, about 1 in 10 adults has anemia.  
Women are more likely to have it than men.  

Among people over 85 years old, about 1 in 4 has anemia.

---

## What happens if anemia is not treated?

Anemia usually develops slowly.  
Your body may adjust to having less oxygen over time.  
But untreated anemia can cause serious problems.  

It can increase the risk of blood clots.  
In people over 65, even mild anemia can reduce physical strength.  
It can also raise the risk of heart problems like heart failure or heart attack.

---

## How can anemia be prevented?

You need iron to make red blood cells.  
A balanced diet usually gives you enough iron.  

During pregnancy or while breastfeeding, you may need extra iron.  
A doctor may suggest an iron supplement.  
Women with heavy periods may also benefit from iron supplements.  
Always talk to a doctor before starting any supplement.

If you follow a vegan diet, be careful to eat enough iron and folic acid.  
Good sources include:  
- Nuts  
- Sprouts  
- Beans and lentils (pulses)  
- Green leafy vegetables like spinach  

For more information on iron-rich foods, visit **gesundheitsinformation.de**.

---

## How is anemia diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your health history.  
They will ask about:  
- What you eat  
- How much alcohol you drink  
- Any past or current illnesses  
- Any medicines you take  

Then, they will do blood tests.  
These tests check:  
- How much hemoglobin is in your blood  
- How many red blood cells you have  
- How much iron, vitamin B12, and folic acid are in your blood  

Other blood tests can check for kidney problems or inflammation.  
These conditions can cause anemia.  

If your iron levels are low but your diet is good, your doctor may check for:  
- Bowel inflammation  
- Small bleeding in the digestive tract  

In people over 65 with unexplained anemia, doctors may check for bone marrow problems.

---

## How is anemia treated?

First, the cause must be treated.  
If anemia is due to blood loss or long-term inflammation, those problems must be fixed.  

If it is caused by iron deficiency, a doctor may suggest seeing a nutritionist.  
They can help you plan meals that include more iron-rich foods.  

**Important:** Some drinks and foods block iron absorption.  
Do not drink black tea, coffee, or milk with iron supplements.  
Wait at least one hour after taking iron before drinking these.

For severe anemia caused by cancer or poor kidney function, doctors may use medicine to help the body make more red blood cells.  
If you lose a lot of blood, you may need a blood transfusion to replace lost red blood cells.

---

**Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.  
Always talk to a doctor if you think you may have anemia.

# Listeriosis – Simple Explanation

Listeriosis is an infection caused by a type of bacteria called *Listeria*.  
This bacteria is found in nature, in soil, water, and animals.  
It can get into food during production or processing.  
You can get listeriosis by eating food that has the bacteria on it.

Most people who get listeriosis have no symptoms or only mild ones.  
But it can be very dangerous for some people.  
These include unborn babies, newborns, older adults, and people with weak immune systems.

---

## What Is Listeriosis?

Listeriosis is a foodborne illness.  
That means it spreads through contaminated food.  
The main cause is a type of bacteria called *Listeria monocytogenes*.  
This bacteria is common in the environment.  
It can be found in soil, water, and animal feed.

In most cases, the infection is mild.  
But in some people, it can spread through the blood and cause serious problems.  
These include blood poisoning (sepsis) or brain infection (meningitis).

If you are sick, your doctor will give you antibiotics that work against listeria.  
These medicines help stop the bacteria from growing.

To stay safe, buy fresh food and eat it before the use-by date.  
This lowers your risk of getting sick.

---

## Who Is at Risk?

Some people are more likely to get a severe case of listeriosis.  
This includes:

- Unborn babies and newborns  
- Older adults (over 65 years)  
- People with long-term health problems like cancer or HIV  
- People who take medicine that weakens the immune system (like after an organ transplant)  
- People who take daily acid-reducing medicine for heartburn or stomach issues

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many people do not feel sick at all.  
Their body may carry the bacteria, but it does not cause harm.

Some people may have:
- Diarrhea
- A mild fever

The time between eating contaminated food and getting sick can be from a few hours to 14 days.  
For pregnant women, it can take even longer.

Pregnant women often feel only like they have the flu.  
But the infection can harm the unborn baby.

People with weak immune systems may have:
- High fever
- Muscle pain
- Diarrhea
- Vomiting

Newborn babies who get infected during birth or in the first few weeks may:
- Have blood poisoning (sepsis)
- Struggle to breathe
- Develop skin problems

---

## How Does Listeriosis Spread?

The most common way to get listeriosis is by eating food that has the bacteria on it.  
The bacteria can be in:
- Raw or undercooked meat and sausages
- Poultry
- Smoked fish (like salmon or trout)
- Cheese made from unpasteurized milk
- Unpasteurized milk
- Pre-packaged salads

Listeria can grow in the refrigerator.  
It grows faster at room temperature.  
So, it’s best to eat fresh food quickly after buying it.

If a pregnant woman gets infected, the bacteria can pass to the baby through the placenta.  
The baby can also get infected during birth or shortly after.

---

## How Common Is Listeriosis?

In Germany, between 200 and 800 people get listeriosis each year.  
The number changes from year to year.

About 1 in 10 cases happen in pregnant women or newborns.  
The rest mostly affect people over 50 or those with health conditions.  
Men are more likely to get sick than women.

---

## What Can Happen If You Get Listeriosis?

About 3 out of 10 people with listeriosis develop serious complications.  
These include:
- Blood poisoning (sepsis)
- Brain infection (meningitis)

These problems are more common in newborns and people with weak immune systems.

If the bacteria spread through the body, they can cause infections in:
- Joints
- Heart valves

An infection during pregnancy can lead to:
- Early birth
- Stillbirth

Listeriosis is rare, but it is the most deadly foodborne illness.  
About 7 out of 100 people with severe listeriosis die.

---

## How Can You Prevent Listeriosis?

Listeria can get into food during processing or packaging.  
To keep food safe, food companies in Germany and other EU countries test their products regularly for listeria.

The bacteria grow best in:
- Raw or cold meat
- Smoked fish
- Unpasteurized dairy products
- Pre-packaged salads

Even if food is vacuum-packed or stored in the fridge, listeria can still grow.  
It does not make food smell bad or look spoiled.  
So, you cannot tell if food is contaminated just by looking or smelling it.

To stay safe, people in high-risk groups should avoid:
- Raw or undercooked meat and sausages
- Raw, smoked, or marinated fish
- Soft or hard cheeses made from unpasteurized milk
- Pre-packaged salad leaves

Always eat fresh food quickly after buying it.  
Do not keep it in the fridge for too long.

For more tips on safe food handling, read the article:  
**Food hygiene – don’t give germs a chance**

For detailed advice, visit the website of the **Federal Institute for Risk Assessment**.

---

## How Is Listeriosis Diagnosed?

If your doctor suspects listeriosis, they will take a blood sample.  
They may also take a sample of fluid from around your spine (cerebrospinal fluid).

They might also test:
- Mucus
- Stool
- Vaginal discharge

These samples are sent to a lab to check for listeria.  
If the bacteria are found, the doctor must report the case to the local health authority.

The health authority will then investigate to find the source of the infection.

---

## How Is Listeriosis Treated?

Doctors treat listeriosis with two different antibiotics.  
These medicines either kill the bacteria or stop them from growing.

The treatment is not simple.  
The bacteria can hide inside your body’s cells and multiply there.  
To prevent the infection from coming back, treatment lasts at least 3 weeks.

If the brain or heart is affected, treatment may last up to 6 weeks.

Always follow your doctor’s instructions exactly.  
Do not stop taking the medicine early, even if you feel better.

# Aortic Dissection

A tear in the inner layer of the main artery (the aorta) lets blood rush into the wall of the artery. This causes the layers of the artery wall to split apart. This is called an aortic dissection.

If the tear happens near the heart, surgery is needed right away.

---

## Quick Facts

- An aortic dissection happens when blood gets into the wall of the aorta through a tear.
- The most common symptom is sudden, severe pain in the chest or back. It often feels like a ripping or tearing.
- Aortic dissection is rare.
- Most people who get it are men in middle age or older.
- If the tear is near the heart, surgery must be done quickly.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical care. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is an Aortic Dissection?

When blood pushes into the wall of the aorta through a tear, the layers of the artery can split apart. Doctors call this an aortic dissection.

The aorta has three layers. A tear in the inner layer lets blood enter the wall. This can cause the layers to separate.

This split often causes sudden, sharp pain in the chest or back.

Aortic dissection is rare but very serious. It can be life-threatening. If the tear is near the heart, surgery must happen as soon as possible.

> **Important:** An aortic dissection is not the same as a regular aneurysm. In a regular aneurysm, the artery bulges out but does not split open.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The most common symptom is sudden, severe pain in the chest or back. It often feels like a tear or stab.

Other symptoms depend on where the tear is. They can include:

- A weak or missing pulse in an arm, neck, or leg
- Fainting or feeling confused
- Numbness, pain, or weakness in the arms or legs
- A hoarse voice
- One eyelid drooping and one pupil smaller than the other
- Trouble breathing

---

## What Causes an Aortic Dissection?

A tear in the inner layer of the aorta starts the process. The aorta carries blood under high pressure. If the lining tears, blood rushes into the wall.

The aorta starts in the heart. It goes up, curves over, and then runs down through the chest and belly.

If the tear happens near the heart or in the upper part of the aorta, it is called a type A dissection. Blood can then travel down the aorta and cause a longer split.

If the tear happens only in the lower part of the aorta, it is called a type B dissection.

> **Important:** About two out of every three people with aortic dissection have type A. This type is more dangerous.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

Aortic dissection is rare. Most people who get it are men in middle or older age.

Some things make it more likely:

- High blood pressure
- Hardened arteries (arteriosclerosis)
- A sudden spike in blood pressure, such as during heavy lifting or using drugs like cocaine or ecstasy
- Genetic conditions that affect connective tissue, like Marfan syndrome or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
- A heart valve that is not normal (bicuspid aortic valve)
- A previous aneurysm in the aorta
- Past heart surgery or catheter procedures
- Inflammation in blood vessels (vasculitis)
- Pregnancy and childbirth (the link is not fully understood)

---

## How Does It Progress?

Most cases are an emergency. But some cases develop slowly or last a long time.

The outcome depends on where the tear is, how big it is, and what complications happen in the first few weeks.

If the aorta tears completely through, it causes internal bleeding. This is an emergency and can lead to shock.

If the tear is near the heart (type A), blood can leak into the sac around the heart. This puts pressure on the heart and stops it from working. This is called cardiac tamponade.

The aortic valve may not close properly. This lets blood flow backward into the heart. This can cause a heart attack.

The tear can block blood flow to major branches of the aorta. This can cause:

- A stroke if blood flow to the brain is blocked
- Kidney failure if blood flow to the kidneys is blocked
- Nerve damage or weakness in arms and legs if blood flow to the spinal cord or limbs is blocked

Type A dissections are very dangerous. Without surgery, about half of all patients die.

But if treatment starts quickly, about 8 out of 10 people survive.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Sudden, severe chest or back pain is a strong sign of aortic dissection.

Doctors will check for risk factors and do tests.

First, they rule out a heart attack, which causes similar pain. They usually do an electrocardiogram (ECG).

To confirm the diagnosis, doctors use imaging tests:

- **Echocardiography:** Uses sound waves to look at the heart and aorta. The probe may go down the throat.
- **Computed tomography (CT):** Uses X-rays to create detailed images. A special dye may be used to see blood vessels better. This is called CT angiography.
- **Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI):** Sometimes used instead of CT. It gives clear pictures of soft tissues.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Doctors always give medicine right away to relieve pain and lower blood pressure and heart rate. This reduces stress on the damaged artery.

Treatment depends on the type and location of the tear.

### Treating Type A Dissection

If the tear is near the heart, emergency surgery is needed. The sooner it happens, the better the chance of survival.

The surgery is open-heart surgery. The damaged part of the aorta is removed and replaced with a synthetic tube (a vascular prosthesis).

If the aortic valve is damaged, it is also replaced with a new one.

### Treating Type B Dissection

If only the lower part of the aorta is affected, medicine may be enough for mild cases.

The patient stays in the hospital for monitoring.

Surgery is only needed if:

- Pain and blood pressure stay high
- The aorta is getting bigger and may burst
- Other problems develop

In surgery, a small cut is made in the groin. A stent graft is guided through a thin tube (catheter) to the aorta and placed in the right spot.

---

## What Aftercare Is Needed?

After recovery, you must keep checking your blood pressure regularly.

You may need medicine to keep your blood pressure under control.

You should have regular checkups to watch for late problems or signs the dissection is spreading.

These checkups use:

- CT scans
- MRI scans
- Heart ultrasounds (echocardiograms)

Checkups start every 3 to 6 months after treatment. Later, they are done once a year.

# Psoriasis

Psoriasis is a long-term skin condition. It causes red, scaly patches on the skin. These patches often itch a lot. The condition comes and goes. It can be mild at times and severe at others. There is no cure, but treatments can help reduce symptoms.

---

## Quick Facts

- Psoriasis is not contagious. You cannot catch it from someone else.
- The main signs are red, flaky skin patches. These often itch.
- Psoriasis can affect more than just the skin. It can also affect joints and nails.
- There is no cure for psoriasis yet.
- Many treatments can help ease symptoms.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Psoriasis?

Psoriasis is a long-term skin problem. It causes red, scaly skin. The skin may also itch. It happens because the body’s immune system acts too strongly.

The condition can appear in many different ways. Some people have bad flare-ups. Others have only mild symptoms. Some have no symptoms for long periods.

For some people, psoriasis affects daily life a lot. Skin care and treatment can take time and effort. The visible skin changes can cause stress, low mood, or anxiety.

Psoriasis can also affect other parts of the body. It can cause joint pain and swelling. This is called psoriatic arthritis. It can also change the nails.

There are treatments that help. But there is no cure.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

There are different types of psoriasis. The most common is plaque psoriasis.

### Plaque Psoriasis

This type causes red patches on the skin. The patches are raised and covered in silvery scales. These raised areas are called plaques.

Plaques often appear on both sides of the body at the same time. For example, both elbows or both knees.

The skin may itch, especially during flare-ups. Scratching can make the skin worse. It can cause small cuts or sores.

Plaques can be small or very large. Some are less than one centimeter across. Others are over ten centimeters wide.

Some people only have a few plaques. Others have many. The most common places are the scalp, elbows, knees, and lower back.

Plaques can also appear behind the ears, on the hands, feet, or around the belly button.

The skin on hands and feet can become very dry and crack. This can hurt, especially when moving. Cracks can get worse when touching things like fruit or getting bumped.

Another form is nail psoriasis. This changes the nails. The nails may have small dents or pits. They can become thick or turn brownish-yellow. In some cases, the nail may come loose.

### Other Types of Psoriasis

**Inverse psoriasis** affects skin folds. These include the groin, under the arms, between the buttocks, under the breasts, or in the genital area. The skin in these areas stays moist and rubs a lot. So, the patches may not have scales. This can look like a fungal infection.

**Pustular psoriasis** causes small, pus-filled blisters. These blisters are not contagious. They can appear alone or with plaque psoriasis.

**Guttate psoriasis** is rare. It mostly affects children and young adults. It causes small, red spots all over the body. It often starts 1 to 2 weeks after a strep infection. It may go away on its own in a few weeks or months. But it can come back or turn into plaque psoriasis.

---

## What Causes Psoriasis?

The top layer of skin is made of skin cells. These cells grow and move to the surface. There, they die and fall off.

In healthy skin, this process takes about 4 weeks. In people with psoriasis, it takes only 4 days. The skin cells grow much faster. They pile up before they can fall off. This causes thick, flaky skin.

This happens because the immune system is overactive. It sends out too many chemical signals. These signals cause inflammation. They also make skin cells grow faster. The extra blood flow makes the skin look red.

---

## What Increases the Risk of Psoriasis?

Genetics play a big role. If one parent has psoriasis, the child has a 15% chance of getting it. If both parents have it, the chance rises to about 40%.

There is no test to predict if someone will get psoriasis. And there is no way to prevent it, based on current science.

---

## How Common Is Psoriasis?

Psoriasis affects about 2% of people. In Germany, that is more than 1.5 million people. It affects men and women equally.

It often starts before age 40. Many people first notice it in childhood or young adulthood. But some get it later, between ages 50 and 70.

Doctors sometimes divide psoriasis by age of first symptoms:
- Type 1: starts before age 40
- Type 2: starts between ages 50 and 70

---

## How Does Psoriasis Develop?

No one can predict how psoriasis will behave. It often comes in waves. Some days are bad. Other days are better. Some people have constant symptoms.

Certain things can trigger flare-ups. These include:
- Sunburn
- Hot showers or baths
- Harsh chemicals
- Minor skin injuries (like scratches, tattoos, or piercings)

Stress, infections, smoking, and drinking too much alcohol can also make flare-ups more likely.

Some medicines, like certain antimalarial drugs, may trigger psoriasis.

> **Important:** Psoriasis is an autoimmune disease. It can affect joints. About 1 in 4 people with psoriasis also get joint pain and swelling. This is called psoriatic arthritis. If you think you have joint problems, see a doctor. Early treatment helps protect your joints.

Psoriasis can also affect mental health. Some people feel sad or anxious. Therapy or counseling can help.

People with psoriasis are more likely to have heart and blood vessel problems. This may be because they are more likely to be overweight, have high blood pressure, diabetes, or unhealthy cholesterol levels. The immune system’s overactivity may also play a role.

They are also more likely to have long-term bowel problems like Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis.

---

## How Is Psoriasis Diagnosed?

A doctor will look at the skin. The typical red, scaly patches are a strong sign.

If the diagnosis is unclear, the doctor may take a small skin sample. This helps rule out other conditions.

For example, inverse psoriasis often looks like a fungal infection. A skin sample can confirm if it is psoriasis.

Nail psoriasis can look like a fungal nail infection. A nail sample can show if fungi are present. Both conditions can happen at the same time.

Doctors also check how bad the psoriasis is. They look at how much of the body is affected:

- Severe: more than 10% of skin affected
- Moderate: 5% to 10%
- Mild: less than 5%

Doctors may also call it moderate or severe if it affects the head, hands, nails, feet, genitals, or if it greatly affects daily life.

---

## How Is Psoriasis Treated?

There is no cure. But many treatments can help.

### Skin Care (Maintenance)

Use moisturizing ointments, creams, or lotions. This helps keep the skin soft and reduces flaking. Good care is helpful even when there are no symptoms.

### Creams and Ointments

Doctors often prescribe anti-inflammatory creams. These may contain cortisone or vitamin D3. They are applied directly to the skin. These work well for mild psoriasis.

More information is available at _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

### Light Therapy

This uses ultraviolet light (UV light). The light reduces skin inflammation and slows down fast-growing skin cells. It is often used with a medicine called psoralen, which makes the skin more sensitive to light.

This treatment is for people with moderate to severe psoriasis when creams are not enough.

### Pills and Injections

These medicines calm the immune system. They include:
- Methotrexate
- Fumaric acid esters
- Apremilast
- Ciclosporin
- Biologics (biological treatments)

These are used for moderate to severe psoriasis.

There is no strong proof that other treatments work. This includes:
- Plant-based products (like Oregon grape, birch bark, aloe vera)
- Fish oil or omega 3 supplements

These are not recommended by medical groups.

Some studies show that losing weight helps improve psoriasis in people who are overweight.

> **Important:** Some people say removing the tonsils helps. But there is no scientific proof that this cures or prevents psoriasis.

---

## What Is Life Like with Psoriasis?

Many people find psoriasis hard to live with. Daily care can take time. Balancing treatment with work, family, and free time is tough.

Itching often gets worse at night. This can make it hard to sleep. People often feel tired during the day.

Even though psoriasis is common, some people avoid others. Some think it is contagious. This can make simple things like getting a haircut stressful.

Worrying about how others react can lower quality of life. Some people start to avoid social situations.

Talking to others who have psoriasis can help. They understand the feelings, daily struggles, and challenges that others may not see.
