This is a guide to help you understand endometrial cancer. It explains what it is, what causes it, how it is found, treated, and what life after treatment might be like.

---

## What Is Endometrial Cancer?

Endometrial cancer starts in the lining of the uterus. This lining is called the endometrium.

The cancer grows when cells in the endometrium change and start multiplying too fast.

The cancer can grow into the inside of the uterus. It can also grow into the muscle layer of the uterus.

This type of cancer is also called womb cancer or uterine cancer. But these terms are not exact. The womb and uterus can be affected by other types of cancer too.

**Important:** Endometrial cancer is not the same as cervical cancer.

---

## What Are the Signs of Endometrial Cancer?

The most common sign is unusual bleeding from the vagina.

This includes:
- Bleeding after menopause
- Bleeding between periods
- Heavier or longer periods than normal, especially before menopause

Bleeding after menopause is a strong warning sign. Any vaginal bleeding after menopause should be checked by a doctor.

Not all bleeding after menopause is caused by cancer. Some causes are not serious. But it is still important to see a doctor right away.

In younger women, unusual bleeding is less likely to be cancer. But if the bleeding does not stop after treatment, or if it causes too much blood loss, a doctor will investigate.

---

## What Causes Endometrial Cancer?

Most cases happen because of changes in the body’s cells. These changes are in the DNA, which is the body’s instruction manual.

These changes cause normal cells to become cancer cells. They grow and multiply too fast.

Most of these changes happen by chance over time. But some people inherit gene changes that raise their risk.

About 5 out of 100 cases are due to inherited gene changes.

One example is Lynch Syndrome. People with this condition have a higher risk of endometrial cancer and bowel cancer.

Having a family history of bowel cancer, ovarian cancer, or kidney pelvis cancer also increases the risk.

---

## What Increases the Risk of Endometrial Cancer?

Certain things make it more likely to get endometrial cancer.

These include:
- Taking estrogen-only hormone therapy
- Being overweight — fat tissue makes estrogen
- Getting your last period (menopause) at a late age
- Getting your first period at a very young age

Other risk factors:
- Being older
- Having diabetes
- Taking tamoxifen for a long time (a medicine used for breast cancer)
- Having a condition called atypical endometrial hyperplasia — this is a precancerous change in the uterine lining

---

## How Common Is Endometrial Cancer?

Endometrial cancer is the most common cancer in the female reproductive system.

It is the fifth most common cancer in women in Germany.

About 11,000 women are diagnosed each year.

The average age at diagnosis is around 67.

---

## Can Endometrial Cancer Be Prevented?

You can lower your risk by staying active and exercising.

Exercise helps you keep a healthy weight. This is important because fat tissue makes estrogen.

Other things that may help prevent endometrial cancer:
- Taking a combination of estrogen and progesterone (gestagen) every day
- Taking the birth control pill
- Using a copper IUD or a levonorgestrel IUD
- Having a child later in life

**Important:** Not all of these things work for everyone. Even if you live a healthy life, you can still get cancer.

---

## Is There a National Screening Program?

No, Germany does not have a national screening program for endometrial cancer.

There is no simple test that can find the cancer early in women who have no symptoms.

But there are early warning signs. The most important one is unusual bleeding.

Because there is no screening, it is very important to see a gynecologist if you have any unusual bleeding.

Women at higher risk should talk to their doctor about what steps they can take.

---

## How Is Endometrial Cancer Diagnosed?

Your doctor will start by asking about your health and doing a physical exam.

Then you will have a vaginal ultrasound. This checks the thickness of the uterine lining.

If the lining is too thick, your doctor will do a hysteroscopy.

This is a procedure where a thin camera is used to look inside the uterus. It is done under anesthesia.

The doctor will check for any abnormal areas. They will take small tissue samples (biopsies) from suspicious spots.

After that, a curettage is done. This means the entire lining of the uterus is gently scraped off.

The tissue samples are sent to a lab.

Doctors will look at the tissue under a microscope. They may also do special tests on the cells.

If the tissue is cancerous, more tests are needed. These tests show how far the cancer has spread.

These tests include:
- MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)
- CT scan (computed tomography)
- Abdominal ultrasound
- Chest X-ray

For more details on these tests, visit the website of the Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center (in German).

---

## How Is Endometrial Cancer Treated?

You should go to a certified gynecological cancer center for treatment.

The treatment depends on the type and stage of the cancer.

But surgery is almost always the first step.

### Surgery

The surgeon removes the cancer as completely as possible.

This usually means removing:
- The uterus
- The cervix
- The ovaries
- The fallopian tubes (almost always)

If the cancer has spread, the doctor may also remove nearby lymph nodes or tissue in the pelvis and abdomen.

**Important:** Removing the uterus, ovaries, and fallopian tubes means you can no longer have children.

Younger women who want to have children should talk to their doctor. In some cases, surgery can be delayed to allow for pregnancy.

### Other Treatments After Surgery

Some patients need extra treatment after surgery to lower the risk of cancer returning.

This can include:
- Radiation therapy inside the vagina (brachytherapy)
- Radiation therapy to the pelvis from outside the body

If the cancer has spread to nearby tissues, lymph nodes, or other organs, chemotherapy may be used.

Chemotherapy is also used if the cancer has spread far in the body.

In some younger women with early-stage cancer, hormone therapy with progesterone (gestagen) may be used instead of surgery. This is only for very early cases.

The goal is to shrink the cancer and allow pregnancy later.

Even if the cancer cannot be cured, hormone therapy, chemotherapy, or immunotherapy can help slow it down.

Pain and bleeding can be treated with radiation or other methods.

For more information on treatments, side effects, and how to manage them, visit the website of the Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center (in German).

---

## What Happens After Treatment?

Treatment can be hard on your body and mind.

Medical rehabilitation (rehab) can help you recover.

Rehab programs are made for each person based on their health and needs.

Possible rehab options:
- Physical therapy, including pelvic floor exercises
- Sexual therapy to help with changes in sex life
- Psycho-oncological therapy to help with fears and worries

### Aftercare

After treatment ends, you will have regular check-ups.

These help find any return of cancer early. They also help catch long-term side effects.

Check-ups start often and then become less frequent over time.

You can go to the doctor sooner if you have new symptoms.

Aftercare includes:
- Talking about your health and any new symptoms
- Feeling the vagina and rectum
- A gynecological exam, including a look inside the vagina
- Ultrasound if needed

The exact tests depend on your personal situation and risk level.

If you have symptoms, your doctor may order imaging tests.

You should also talk about your mental health during these visits.

### If the Cancer Cannot Be Cured

Regular check-ups still help. They can catch problems early and help manage symptoms.

The goal is to keep your quality of life as good as possible for as long as possible.

---

## Life With and After Endometrial Cancer

It can be hard to return to normal life after cancer.

Cancer and its treatment can cause lasting effects.

Support is available and should be tailored to your needs.

Common issues after treatment:
- Pain, dryness, or narrowing in the vagina
- Emotional stress or anxiety
- Urinary incontinence (leaking urine)
- Swelling in the legs (lymphedema)

You may need to adjust to changes in your sex life. Vaginal dryness and pain are common.

But most side effects can be managed or even prevented with proper care.

Talk to your doctor about support options.

---

## Where to Get Help

Doctors from different fields work together to treat endometrial cancer.

Hospitals with special experience in treating gynecological cancers can be certified.

The German Cancer Society checks these centers regularly.

You can find certified centers on the OncoMAP website.

For more information on daily life and support, visit the website of the Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center (in German).

You can also contact the Cancer Information Service directly:
- Call free: 0800 420 30 40
- Email: krebsinformationsdienst@dkfz.de

# Broken Collarbone

A broken collarbone is a common injury. It often happens when you fall onto your shoulder. This can occur during sports or car accidents. Most people with a broken collarbone can go home after a doctor checks them. An X-ray is usually enough to confirm the break.

## Quick Facts

- The collarbone is a thin bone that runs from your breastbone to your shoulder blade.
- It is shaped like an S and usually breaks in the middle third.
- Young people often break their collarbone during sports or traffic accidents.
- The injury causes pain when you move your arm or press on the broken area.
- Swelling often appears above the bone.
- Treatment depends on how the bone is broken. Some people need a sling. Others need surgery.
- Most people can use their arm again without pain after 2 to 3 months.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical care. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is a Broken Collarbone?

The collarbone connects your breastbone to your shoulder blade. It is shaped like an S. Most breaks happen in the middle of the bone. Doctors also call this a fractured clavicle.

Most breaks happen when you fall on your shoulder. Young people often get this injury during sports or car crashes. Cyclists are especially at risk.

About 3 out of every 100 bone breaks involve the collarbone. It is common in children, young adults, and older adults.

If the bone moves a lot or damages nearby blood vessels or nerves, surgery is usually needed.

If the break is simple, a sling can help. The arm can usually move again without pain before long. But the bone takes 6 to 12 weeks to heal fully. Children may heal in just 3 to 6 weeks.

## What Are the Signs of a Broken Collarbone?

Common signs include:

- A loud snap or crack at the time of the injury.
- Sharp pain in one spot that gets worse when you move your arm.
- Swelling above the bone.
- The bone looks crooked or out of place.
- If the break is near the breastbone, the bone may stick out in front. This creates a visible bump.

In some cases, the bone can push under the breastbone and no longer be felt near the chest. This kind of break needs surgery right away. It can damage organs below the bone.

If the injury was very strong, it can hurt blood vessels, nerves, or even the lungs. If you have trouble breathing or feel dizzy, call emergency services at 112 or go to the emergency room immediately.

## What Causes a Broken Collarbone?

Falling on your shoulder is the most common cause. Young people often break their collarbone during sports or car accidents. Cyclists are especially likely to get this injury.

Less common causes include:

- A direct hit to the collarbone, such as in contact sports.
- Falling on an outstretched hand.

If the break is near the breastbone, it usually comes from a serious accident. It may also cause injuries to the lungs, ribs, neck, or other organs.

Another cause near the breastbone is overuse. This is called a stress fracture. It can happen from intense training in sports like rowing or gymnastics.

Older adults with weak bones (osteoporosis) can break their collarbone from a small fall. People with certain cancers or who are getting radiation therapy are also at higher risk.

## How Does a Broken Collarbone Heal?

Most collarbone breaks heal well. You can start gentle movement soon after the injury. The bone usually takes 6 to 12 weeks to heal. Children may heal in just 3 to 6 weeks.

After a serious accident, doctors focus on other injuries first.

If the arm is in a sling for a long time, muscles can weaken and joints can stiffen. It is important to start moving your arm early. A physiotherapist can guide you through safe exercises.

Sometimes a false joint forms. This is when the broken bone ends do not grow together. Instead, a soft tissue connection forms. This usually does not cause pain or problems. But if it causes pain or makes the bone shorter, surgery may help.

A bump can also form at the break site. In children, this bump often goes away on its own. In adults, it may stay and be visible under the skin. If the bump forms deeper, it can press on nerves and cause pain.

If the break is near the shoulder joint, pain from wear and tear may appear years later.

## How Is a Broken Collarbone Diagnosed?

Your doctor will examine your shoulder. They will feel the area and look for swelling or misalignment. The collarbone is close to the skin, so breaks are often visible.

An X-ray is done to see:

- Where the bone broke.
- How much the bone pieces moved.
- If the bone is shorter than before.
- If the bone broke into more than one piece.

If the injury was very severe, your doctor may order more tests. These can include:

- CT scan (a detailed X-ray).
- MRI (shows soft tissues like nerves and blood vessels).
- Ultrasound (checks blood flow).
- Nerve tests.

These tests help find damage to nearby tissues or bones.

## How Is a Broken Collarbone Treated?

Right after the injury, you can use cold packs or ice on the area for 20 to 30 minutes every 1 to 3 hours. This helps reduce pain and swelling. You can also take painkillers for a short time.

Treatment depends on the type of break. It can be non-surgical or surgical.

### Non-Surgical Treatment

- Use an arm sling to keep the arm still.
- Use a clavicula bandage. This is a special sling that goes across the back and holds both shoulders together.

### Surgical Treatment

- The bone is fixed with a metal plate and screws.
- Or a metal rod is placed inside the bone (medullary nail).

Surgery may be needed if:

- Blood vessels, nerves, skin, or nearby bones are damaged.
- The bone cannot be held still with a sling.
- The break is near a joint.
- The bone ends are far apart.
- The bone is shorter or broken into many pieces.

Your job or sport may also affect the decision. Talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits.

### Benefits of Surgery

- You can use your arm under full strain sooner than without surgery.
- The chance of a false joint is lower.
- Some studies show better shoulder movement after surgery. But the difference is small.
- Surgery usually prevents a visible bump on the bone. This gives a better appearance.

### Risks of Surgery

- The wound can become infected.
- Scars will form at the surgery site.
- Surgery can damage blood vessels or nerves.
- Problems can happen with anesthesia.
- The result may not be as expected.
- Metal plates or screws must be removed in a second surgery about a year later.
- You cannot use your arm fully for a while after the second surgery.

## What Follow-Up Care Is Needed?

To avoid long-term problems like weak muscles or stiff joints, start moving your arm early.

Move your wrist and elbow several times a day. A clavicula bandage allows light activities that do not cause pain.

Your doctor will check how well your shoulder moves. Once the sling is off, a physiotherapist will guide you through exercises to rebuild strength and movement.

Most people regain full shoulder movement within 6 to 12 weeks.

Even if you can move your arm without pain, avoid contact sports and heavy lifting for another 4 weeks. Children can wait 2 to 3 weeks.

Do not return to sports that stress the shoulder until 3 to 6 months after the injury. Only then can you safely restart training.

# Diabetes Insipidus

This condition happens when your body does not make enough of a key hormone. Or, it may make the hormone, but your kidneys do not respond to it. As a result, your kidneys cannot make concentrated urine. This leads to needing to urinate often and feeling very thirsty.

## Quick Facts

- Your kidneys cannot make concentrated urine.
- You urinate often and your urine is pale or clear.
- The problem comes from not enough of a hormone made in the brain, or the kidneys not reacting to it.
- Most people with this condition can be helped with medicine and a diet low in salt and protein.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Diabetes Insipidus?

Diabetes insipidus is a rare condition. It causes your body to pass large amounts of urine. You lose too much water through your kidneys. This makes you feel extremely thirsty.

Normally, your kidneys save water from the urine. This keeps your body from losing too much fluid. A hormone called antidiuretic hormone, or ADH, helps your kidneys do this. ADH comes from a small gland in your brain called the pituitary gland.

If your body does not make enough ADH, or your kidneys do not respond to it, you get diabetes insipidus.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Common signs of diabetes insipidus include:

- Always feeling very thirsty
- Urinating many times a day
- Urine that is pale or almost clear
- Waking up at night to urinate, which can disrupt sleep

In some cases, symptoms come on suddenly. In others, they grow slowly over months or years.

Other signs of dehydration (not having enough water in your body) may include:

- Feeling weak or tired
- Feeling slow or dull in your mind
- Muscle pain

## What Causes Diabetes Insipidus?

Your body uses a hormone called ADH to control water balance. This hormone is made in your brain. The pituitary gland releases it into your blood when needed. ADH tells your kidneys to save water from the urine.

If your brain does not make enough ADH, or stops making it, your kidneys cannot save water. You then pass large amounts of watery urine. This is called central diabetes insipidus. The cause is in the brain or central nervous system.

Sometimes, doctors do not know why ADH is missing. But certain health problems can cause it, such as:

- Serious head injuries
- Brain surgery
- Inflammation in the area of the pituitary gland. This may be due to your immune system attacking your own body.
- Tumors in the head or brain
- Inherited (genetic) conditions

There is also another type called renal or nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. In this case, your body makes enough ADH. But your kidneys do not respond to it.

Causes of this type include:

- Inherited problems with how the hormone signals the kidneys
- Some medicines, like lithium used for mental health conditions
- Kidney disease
- Imbalances in minerals, such as too little potassium or too much calcium in the blood

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use symptoms and lab tests to diagnose diabetes insipidus.

### Check Urine Output

If an adult makes more than 40 to 50 milliliters of urine per kilogram of body weight in 24 hours, it may be diabetes insipidus. For a 70-kilogram person, this is more than 2.8 to 3.5 liters of urine a day.

### Blood and Urine Tests

In diabetes insipidus:

- Your blood is too concentrated
- Your urine is too diluted

These results can be confirmed in a lab. Doctors also check your blood for salt levels. This helps find any mineral imbalances.

### Check Blood Sugar

If your blood and urine sugar levels are high, it is likely not diabetes insipidus. It may be a different type of diabetes.

### Special Tests

Four other tests help confirm the diagnosis:

**Thirst Test**  
You stop drinking fluids for several hours. If you still make large amounts of dilute urine, it suggests diabetes insipidus. This test must be done under medical supervision.

**Desmopressin Test**  
Doctors give you a medicine called desmopressin. It works like your body’s own ADH.  
- If your urine becomes more concentrated after the medicine, your kidneys are working fine. The problem is low ADH in the brain (central diabetes insipidus).  
- If the medicine does not help, the problem is in the kidneys (renal diabetes insipidus).

**Copeptin Blood Test**  
Copeptin is a protein linked to ADH production. High or low levels may help confirm the diagnosis.

**MRI Scan**  
This scan can show problems in the brain, such as tumors or inflammation in the pituitary gland area.

## How Is It Treated?

Staying well hydrated is key. Not drinking enough water can be dangerous, especially for children and older adults. A lack of water can lead to low blood pressure and shock.

If a cause is found, doctors may treat that directly. For example:

- Fixing a mineral imbalance
- Stopping a medicine that causes the problem

Treatment depends on the type of diabetes insipidus.

### Treating Central Diabetes Insipidus

You will be given desmopressin to replace the missing hormone. It comes in:

- A liquid to inject
- A spray for the nose
- A tablet to swallow

### Treating Renal Diabetes Insipidus

If kidney damage is the cause, you should eat less salt and protein. Medicines may also be needed. Some adults can manage mild cases by drinking more fluids. In babies, early treatment is very important. Repeated water shortages can harm development.

# Bowel Cancer

Bowel cancer is one of the most common types of cancer in Germany.  
It includes two main types: colon cancer and rectal cancer.  
This article explains the risks, screening, diagnosis, and treatment options.

---

## Quick Facts

- Bowel cancer is also called colorectal carcinoma.  
- It affects the large intestine (colon) or the last part of the intestine (rectum).  
- In the early stages, bowel cancer often causes no symptoms.  
- Germany has a free screening program for bowel cancer.  
- Some people have a higher risk because of family history or inherited genes.  
- Treatment usually includes surgery. Chemotherapy, radiation, or special drugs may also be used.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Bowel Cancer?

Bowel cancer happens when abnormal cells grow in the colon or rectum.  
These cells form tumors that can become cancerous over time.  
It does not include cancers of the small intestine or the anus.

Most cases start in the inner lining of the bowel.  
At first, small, non-cancerous growths called polyps form.  
These polyps can turn into cancer over several years.  
Most polyps are harmless, but some can become cancer.

> **Important:** Other rare cancers can grow in the intestines, such as GIST, MALT-lymphoma, or neuroendocrine tumors.  
> Doctors do not count these as bowel cancer.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many people with bowel cancer feel no symptoms at first.  
If symptoms do appear, they may include:

- Frequent gas, bloating, or a sudden need to go to the bathroom  
- Feeling full even after eating little  
- Nausea or vomiting  
- Changes in bowel habits, like constipation, diarrhea, or switching between both  
- Pain when passing stool or cramp-like pain in the belly  
- Blood in the stool (red or black)  
- Mucus in the stool  
- Stool that is very thin or smells bad

These symptoms can also happen with other, less serious bowel problems.  
If they last more than a few weeks, see a doctor.  
Your general practitioner can help find the cause and refer you to a specialist if needed.

---

## What Causes Bowel Cancer?

Bowel cancer starts when normal cells in the bowel change and grow out of control.  
These changes are due to damage in the cell’s DNA.  
This damage can happen by chance over time.  
It can also be passed down through families.

If bowel cancer runs in your family, even without a known genetic cause, your risk is higher.  
Close relatives of people with bowel cancer are more likely to get it too.

For more details on inherited and family-related bowel cancer, visit the website of the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## What Increases the Risk?

Besides family history, other factors raise your risk:

- Smoking  
- Being overweight  
- Not getting enough physical activity  
- Eating a diet low in fiber and high in red or processed meat  
- Drinking alcohol regularly  
- Having long-term bowel inflammation (like Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis)

---

## How Common Is Bowel Cancer?

In Germany, bowel cancer is one of the most common cancers.  
It is the third most common cancer in men and the second in women.

> **Important:** The risk goes up with age.  
> Men are usually diagnosed around age 72.  
> Women are usually diagnosed around age 76.

---

## How Can You Lower Your Risk?

There are two main ways to reduce your risk:

### Live a Healthy Lifestyle

Avoiding certain habits helps lower your risk. Experts recommend:

- Do not smoke  
- Limit alcohol  
- Stay physically active  
- Keep a healthy body weight  
- Eat more fiber-rich foods (like vegetables, fruits, and whole grains)  
- Eat less red meat and processed meat (like sausages and bacon)

> **Important:** Even healthy people can get bowel cancer.  
> But avoiding these risk factors can still reduce your personal risk.

### Remove Benign Tumors Early

A colonoscopy can find and remove non-cancerous growths (polyps) before they turn into cancer.  
This is a key way to prevent bowel cancer.

---

## Screening for Bowel Cancer in Germany

Germany offers free bowel cancer screening for people aged 50 and older.  
You will get a letter from your health insurance inviting you to take part.  
Screening is not mandatory. You can talk to your doctor about the benefits and risks.

There are two reliable screening methods:

1. **Colonoscopy** – The most accurate test.  
   A doctor uses a camera to look inside the bowel.  
   They can find and remove polyps during the same visit.

2. **Stool test** – Checks for hidden blood in the stool.  
   Blood may be a sign of cancer or polyps.

For more information on the pros and cons of each test, see the **patient brochures from the Joint Federal Committee (G-BA)** for men and women.

---

### Special Cases

- Over half of all people diagnosed with bowel cancer are over 70.  
- If you have a family history of bowel cancer, you may get it earlier — often before age 50.  
- If a close relative (parent, sibling, or child) had bowel cancer, talk to your doctor.  
- You may need a colonoscopy 10 years before the youngest age at which a family member was diagnosed.  
- Ask your doctor about this during your annual check-up.

You can also contact a center for hereditary bowel cancer.  
More information is available at the **German Consortium of Familial Bowel Cancer**.

> **Important:** If you have sudden symptoms like blood in your stool, see a doctor right away.  
> Do not wait for a screening appointment.

Want to learn more about screening? Visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## How Is Bowel Cancer Diagnosed?

The most important test is a **colonoscopy**.  
A doctor uses a camera to look at the inside of the bowel.  
They check for changes in the lining.  
If anything looks suspicious, they take a small tissue sample (biopsy).

The sample is sent to a lab.  
If the lab finds cancer, more tests are needed.

These tests help doctors understand how far the cancer has spread.  
They help plan the best treatment.  
Tests may include:

- Blood tests to check for cancer-related substances (tumor markers)  
- Ultrasound of the belly  
- X-ray of the chest  
- CT scan  
- PET scan

For **rectal cancer**, extra tests are needed:

- A physical exam of the rectum  
- A rigid tube exam (rectoscopy)  
- MRI scan of the pelvis  
- Sphincter muscle pressure test  
- Ultrasound of the rectum from inside

---

## How Is Bowel Cancer Treated?

Treatment depends on your health, the type of tumor, and test results.

### If the Cancer Has Not Spread

If the cancer is still in the bowel and has not spread to other organs, surgery is the main treatment.

- The surgeon removes the tumor and nearby tissue.  
- Lymph nodes near the tumor are also removed.  
- If all cancer is removed, recovery is possible.

**For colon cancer:**
- Most patients get chemotherapy after surgery.  
- This lowers the chance of cancer returning.  
- It also kills any remaining cancer cells.

**For rectal cancer:**
- Some patients get radiation and chemotherapy before surgery.  
- This can shrink the tumor.  
- It may help keep the sphincter muscle working.  
- In some cases, the tumor may disappear completely.  
- Doctors are still studying whether surgery is needed in these cases.

If surgery comes first, chemotherapy or radiation follows.

### If the Cancer Has Spread

If cancer has spread to other organs, surgery is only an option if:

- All cancer can be removed  
- Or if the bowel tumor is causing serious symptoms

If surgery is not possible, treatment includes:

- Chemotherapy, often with targeted drugs  
- Radiation therapy for bone pain caused by spread

---

## What Happens After Treatment?

### Medical Rehabilitation

Cancer treatment can be hard on your body and mind.  
Rehab helps you recover strength and adjust to life after treatment.

Rehab may include:

- Diet advice tailored to your needs  
- Support from a stoma nurse if you have a stoma  
- Counseling for anxiety or emotional stress

### Aftercare

After treatment, regular check-ups help catch a return of cancer early.  
You will be seen often at first, then less often over time.  
You can visit your doctor sooner if you have new symptoms.

Check-ups usually include:

- A physical exam  
- Blood tests for cancer markers  
- Ultrasound of the belly  
- Colonoscopy

People with colon cancer may need extra tests.

### If the Cancer Cannot Be Cured

Even if the cancer cannot be cured, care can help you feel better.  
Doctors focus on managing symptoms and improving your quality of life.

---

## Life After Bowel Cancer

Returning to normal life can be hard after cancer.  
Treatment can cause lasting effects.  
Everyone’s experience is different.

Common challenges include:

- Changes in eating habits  
- Incontinence (inability to control bowel movements)  
- Living with a stoma (an artificial opening in the belly for waste)

You may need time to adjust.  
Start with small steps to return to regular meals.  
Learn how to care for a stoma or manage incontinence.

For most people, life improves

# Cancer of Unknown Primary (CUP Syndrome)

This is a type of cancer where doctors find cancer in different parts of the body, but they cannot find the original tumor. This is why it is called CUP — cancer of unknown primary.

## What Is CUP Syndrome?

- Cancer usually starts in one organ. It then spreads to other parts of the body.
- In CUP syndrome, doctors find cancer in other areas, but they cannot find where it started.
- The cancer has already spread. This means it is at an advanced stage.
- The cancer cells broke away from the original tumor and traveled through the body.
- These spreading cancer cells form new tumors in places like the liver, lungs, bones, or lymph nodes.
- Sometimes, the cancer spreads to areas where it is not common, like the brain or skin.
- The cancer can appear in more than one organ at the same time.

### Where Does the Cancer Start?

- Doctors look for the original tumor, called the primary tumor.
- If they find it, the cancer is named after the organ it came from.
- If they cannot find it, even after thorough testing, the diagnosis is CUP syndrome.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms vary from person to person. They depend on where the cancer has spread.

There are no typical symptoms for CUP syndrome. But common signs of advanced cancer include:

- Swollen lymph nodes that feel hard, do not move, and are not painful.
- A swollen belly or lumps in the chest or stomach.
- Trouble breathing or pain in the chest or stomach.
- Bone pain.
- Constant tiredness, feeling weak, or no appetite.
- Losing weight without trying.

If you have any of these symptoms for more than a few days or weeks, see a doctor. This is especially important if they are not caused by an infection.

## What Causes CUP Syndrome?

The exact cause is not known. But we do know the cancer must have started somewhere.

Cancer begins when cells in the body change in a harmful way. These cells grow out of control and damage healthy tissue.

Cancer cells can break off from the original tumor. They travel through the blood or lymph system. They then form new tumors in other organs.

Why can’t doctors find the original tumor?

Experts have some ideas:

- The original tumor may be so small that it does not cause symptoms.
- It may have disappeared on its own, possibly because the body’s immune system fought it.
- The cancer may have spread very fast, so the original tumor never grew large enough to be seen.

## How Common Is CUP Syndrome?

- About 10,500 people in Germany are diagnosed with CUP syndrome each year.
- This is about 2 out of every 100 cancer cases.
- Most people with CUP syndrome are over 60 years old.
- It affects men and women about equally.

The number of CUP diagnoses is going down. This is likely because doctors are now better at finding the original tumor or identifying the type of cancer.

## How Does CUP Syndrome Progress?

The course of the disease varies from person to person.

It depends on:

- Where the cancer started.
- How fast it grows.
- Where it has spread.

Most people with CUP syndrome cannot be cured. The cancer often grows quickly.

But about 1 in 5 people have a better outlook. Their cancer cells show signs that point to a likely original organ. Doctors can then treat the cancer like a known type. These patients often live as long as people with the same cancer that started in a known organ.

## How Is CUP Syndrome Diagnosed?

When doctors find cancer in the body, they first check:

- How many tumors are present.
- How big they are.
- Where they are located.

They then try to find the original tumor. This can take time and patience.

### Step-by-Step Diagnosis

1. **Medical history**: The doctor asks about your health and symptoms.
2. **Physical exam**: The doctor checks your body for signs of cancer.
3. **Blood, urine, and stool tests**: These help check your overall health.
4. **Imaging scans**: These are the main tools used. They include:
   - CT scan of the chest, belly, and pelvis.
   - PET scan.
   - MRI scan.
   - Ultrasound of the breast or other areas.
   - Endoscopy (looking inside organs with a camera).
   - Transvaginal ultrasound (for women).
   - Scintigraphy (a special scan using a small amount of radioactive material).

Doctors also check for certain cancers that can look like CUP syndrome but are easier to treat. These include lymphoma and germ cell tumors.

They also test for signs of common cancers like breast or prostate cancer. This is done by measuring certain substances in the blood.

### Tissue Testing (Biopsy)

If the original tumor is still not found, doctors take a sample of the cancer tissue. This is called a biopsy.

The sample is examined under a microscope. Special stains are used to look for clues.

This helps doctors answer:

- Can the cancer be linked to a specific organ? (For example, lung, breast, bowel.)
- What type of cancer is it? (For example, carcinoma, melanoma, sarcoma, or lymphoma.)
- What kind of cancer is it? (For example, adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma.)

The goal is to either find the original tumor or get information that helps plan treatment.

If the original tumor cannot be found after all tests, the diagnosis is CUP syndrome.

## How Is CUP Syndrome Treated?

Most people with CUP syndrome get treatment to relieve symptoms and improve quality of life. Cure is rare.

Treatment is always personalized. It depends on:

- Your overall health.
- How fast the cancer is growing.
- Your personal wishes.

### Is the Original Tumor Found?

- **If the tumor is found**: It is no longer CUP syndrome. The cancer is treated based on the organ it came from. Prognosis is usually better.
- **If the tumor is suspected**: Doctors treat it as if it came from a specific organ. Prognosis is often better.
- **If the tumor cannot be found**: Most patients have cancer in several organs. Prognosis is worse. Treatment is usually palliative — meaning it aims to ease symptoms and improve comfort.

### How Far Has the Cancer Spread?

- **If cancer is in one place only**: Surgery or targeted radiation may be used. Surgery is only done if it can help cure the cancer or reduce symptoms. Radiation shrinks tumors and stops them from growing. It can also help relieve bone pain.

- **If cancer has spread to many organs**: Treatment must affect the whole body. This is called systemic therapy.

  - **Chemotherapy** is the most common treatment. Doctors choose drugs with the fewest side effects.
  - **Immunotherapy** may be used if the cancer cells show certain traits.
  - **Hormone therapy** may help if the cancer is sensitive to hormones.
  - **Targeted drugs** block specific processes that help cancer grow. These only work if the cancer has certain traits.

For more details on treatments and side effects, visit the German Cancer Research Center’s Cancer Information Service website (in German).

## What Happens After Treatment?

Treatment can be very hard on the body and mind.

Medical rehabilitation (rehab) helps you regain strength and cope with the effects of the disease and treatment.

Rehab is based on your personal history and your current abilities.

Psychological support is very helpful. It can help you deal with fear, anxiety, and stress.

### Aftercare

- If treatment was meant to cure the cancer, you will need close follow-up care.
- But most cases of CUP syndrome cannot be cured.
- Regular checkups help catch and treat symptoms early.
- The goal is to keep your quality of life as high as possible for as long as possible.

## What Changes After a CUP Diagnosis?

A cancer diagnosis is very stressful. This is especially true for CUP syndrome, where the original tumor may never be found.

The disease often progresses quickly. This leaves little time to adjust.

You will need to make many decisions with your doctor. You must weigh the risks and benefits of each treatment option.

You do not need to stay in the hospital all the time. Many treatments and checkups can be done in a doctor’s office or outpatient clinic.

Regular contact with your medical team is important. Cancer can change fast. Checkups are a chance to talk about:

- Pain.
- Nausea.
- Problems with eating or weight.
- Other troubling symptoms.

There is usually something that can help with these issues.

## Who Can Help You?

There is no official list of clinics that specialize in CUP syndrome in Germany.

But many university hospitals and large clinics have teams of specialists who work together to treat CUP.

Some major cancer centers have special outpatient clinics for CUP patients.

To find the right clinic, visit the German Cancer Research Center’s Cancer Information Service website (in German).

You can also contact professional groups. One example is the CUP Syndrome sub-group of the Working Group on Internal Oncology (AIO).

For help with daily life and support options, visit the same website.

For any questions about CUP syndrome, you can call the free helpline: **0800 420 30 40**  
Or email: **krebsinformationsdienst@dkfz.de**

# Corneal Irregularity (Astigmatism)

Astigmatism means your eye does not focus light properly onto the back of the eye.  
This causes blurry vision.  
The blurriness can happen whether you are looking at something close or far away.  
You can fix this problem with glasses, contact lenses, or sometimes surgery.

---

## Quick Facts

- Light does not land as a small dot on the back of your eye.  
  Instead, it lands as a line.  
  This makes the image look distorted and unclear.  
- Most often, the shape of the front part of the eye (the cornea) is uneven.  
  Sometimes, the lens inside the eye is also uneven.  
- Astigmatism is usually passed down in families.  
- It can affect how a child’s vision develops.  
- Vision is blurry both up close and at a distance.  
- Glasses or contact lenses can correct it.  
  Surgery, like laser treatment, can also help in some cases.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Astigmatism?

Your eye has a clear front part called the cornea.  
Sometimes, the cornea is not shaped like a perfect ball.  
The lens inside the eye can also be uneven.  
When this happens, light does not focus into a single point on the back of the eye.  
Instead, it forms lines.  
This makes the image look blurry.  
Astigmatism is also called corneal irregularity.  

The word “astigmatism” comes from Greek.  
It means “without points.”  
This condition is usually present from birth.  
It often happens together with nearsightedness or farsightedness.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

A very mild case may not cause any problems.  
You might not even notice it.  
But if it is more noticeable, you may see:

- Blurry or stretched-out images  
- Tired or sore eyes  
- Headaches  

A key sign of astigmatism is that both near and far vision are blurry.  
This is different from nearsightedness (where only far things are blurry) or farsightedness (where only close things are blurry).

---

## What Causes Astigmatism?

Most often, the cornea is not shaped evenly.  
The cornea helps bend light so it lands in the right spot.  
But if the cornea is more curved in one direction than another, light does not focus correctly.  

Think of a ball.  
A normal cornea is like a ball — curved the same in every direction.  
But if you gently press a ball from the sides, it becomes more oval.  
That shape causes light to focus into a line instead of a dot.  
This leads to a blurry image.

Most people are born with this shape.  
It usually does not change much over time.  
If one eye is more affected than the other, the brain may stop using the weaker eye.  
This can lead to weak vision in that eye, called amblyopia.

In some cases, astigmatism develops later in life.  
This can happen because of:

- Eye injuries  
- Scars on the cornea  
- A condition called keratoconus (where the cornea becomes thin and cone-shaped)  
- Eye surgery  

> **Interesting fact:** Reading or using screens does not cause astigmatism.  
> This is different from nearsightedness, which can be linked to screen use.

---

## How Common Is Astigmatism?

Many people have a slightly uneven cornea.  
So astigmatism is very common.  
In Germany, about one in three adults has some degree of astigmatism.  
It becomes more common with age.  
But many cases are mild.  
You may not need treatment if the blurriness is not bad.

---

## How Can Astigmatism Be Found Early?

It is important to find vision problems in children early.  
This helps avoid learning problems at school.  
But children often do not know they have a vision issue.  
They may not complain.

Since 2008, Germany has offered a special check-up for children at age three.  
This is called U7a.  
It is part of the regular health checks for kids.  
It helps find vision problems like astigmatism early.

---

## How Is Astigmatism Diagnosed?

Eye care professionals use several tests to check for astigmatism.

### Refraction Test (Subjective)

You look through a device called a phoropter.  
This has many lenses.  
You look at an eye chart and say which lenses make the image clearer.  
The doctor uses your answers to find the right correction.

### Refraction Test (Objective)

This test does not need your input.  
A machine measures how light bends in your eye.  
It uses infrared light to check how sharp the image is on the retina.  
For young children, doctors may use a method called skiascopy.  
They shine a light into the eye and watch how it reflects off the retina.  
This helps them figure out the type of vision problem.

> **Important:** For young children, eye drops are used to widen the pupils.  
> This helps get more accurate results.  
> The drops also relax the eye’s focusing muscles.

### Measuring the Cornea

Doctors can measure the shape of the cornea using:

- **Ophthalmometry:** A device measures the curve of the cornea.  
  It looks like a small microscope.  
- **Corneal topography:** A computer creates a detailed map of the cornea’s surface.  
  This is very useful for complex cases or before surgery.

---

## How Is Astigmatism Treated?

Most people with astigmatism wear glasses or contact lenses.  
These are special lenses called cylindrical lenses.  
They bend light differently in different directions.  
This helps fix the uneven shape of the cornea.

There are also surgery options.  
These depend on how bad the astigmatism is.  
The doctor will decide what is best.

Common surgical methods include:

- **Laser treatment:** A laser reshapes the cornea to make it more even.  
- **Artificial lenses:** A new lens is placed inside the eye to correct vision.

Surgery is usually only done in adults.  
In children, surgery is only considered if other treatments do not work.

# Animal Allergy

A runny nose or stuffy nose and sneezing when near an animal may mean you have an allergy.  
It is not the animal’s fur that causes the reaction.  
It is proteins found in the animal’s skin flakes, sweat, or spit.  

These proteins are called allergens.  
They can get into your body through your nose or mouth.  
They can also get on your skin when you touch the animal.  

## What You Should Know at a Glance

- The fur itself does not cause the allergy.  
- The real cause is proteins in the animal’s skin flakes, saliva, sweat, urine, or droppings.  
- These allergens can float in the air or stick to surfaces.  
- Most people get symptoms like a runny or blocked nose and sneezing.  
- Over time, this can lead to asthma.  
- You can develop an animal allergy even if you have never owned a pet.  

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

## What Is an Animal Allergy?

When you sneeze or have a runny nose around cats or dogs, you might think it’s the fur.  
But it’s not the fur.  
It’s the proteins in the animal’s skin flakes, sweat, oil, spit, urine, or droppings.  
These proteins are called allergens.  

The allergens stick to the animal’s fur.  
They also land on carpets, furniture, and other surfaces.  
Tiny particles with these proteins can float in the air.  
You can breathe them in or touch them.  

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people feel symptoms right after being near the animal.  
The most common symptoms affect the nose and breathing.  
They happen when you breathe in tiny particles with the allergens.  

Common symptoms include:  
- A runny nose  
- A blocked nose  
- Sneezing  

After several years, these symptoms can turn into asthma.  

Other possible symptoms:  
- Watery or itchy eyes  
- Skin rashes or hives (red, itchy spots)  

Skin rashes are less common.

## Which Animals Cause Allergies?

Many animals can cause allergies.  
The allergens spread in different ways.  

Here are the most common ones:  
- **Cats:** Allergens are in their saliva and skin flakes.  
- **Dogs:** Allergens are in their saliva and skin flakes.  
- **Guinea pigs:** Allergens are in their urine.  
- **Horses:** Allergens are in their hair.  
- **Birds:** Allergens are in their feathers and droppings.  

Farm animals like cows, sheep, and chickens can also cause allergies.  

Allergens can stay on clothes, mattresses, carpets, rugs, and furniture.  
This means you can have symptoms even when no animal is present.  

Cat allergens are especially strong.  
They can stay in a home for months or even years.  
So, if you are thinking about moving into a new home, ask if the previous owners had cats.

## How Can You Prevent an Animal Allergy?

Even if you do not have a pet, you can still develop an animal allergy.  
Some people have a cat allergy even if they have never owned a cat.  

For people who are more likely to develop allergies, getting a pet might cause symptoms for the first time.  

But living with animals might also help prevent allergies.  
Regular contact with animal allergens and germs may help the body’s immune system learn to react less strongly.  

However, we do not yet fully understand how living with animals affects allergy risk.  
The risk depends on the type of animal and how much contact you have.

## How Is an Animal Allergy Diagnosed?

Allergy symptoms can come from many causes.  
These include dust mites, pollen, and animals.  
A doctor can help find the real cause.  

Tests are used to check for allergies.  
Two common tests are:  

**Skin prick test:**  
- A doctor places small drops of possible allergens on your forearm.  
- The skin is lightly scratched at each spot.  
- If the skin turns red or itchy, you are allergic to that substance.  

**Blood test:**  
- A blood sample is taken.  
- The lab checks for antibodies to animal allergens.  

In some cases, a provocation test may be needed.  
- The doctor puts a small amount of allergen near your nose or eye.  
- The doctor watches for a reaction.  
- This test is done only under medical supervision.

## How Is an Animal Allergy Treated?

Medicine can help reduce symptoms.  
For a runny or blocked nose, you can use:  
- Nasal sprays  
- Allergy tablets  

For skin rashes, a doctor may prescribe a steroid cream.  

For more details on treatment options, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).  

**Immunotherapy (desensitization)** is another option.  
It is used for severe allergies, such as to cats.  
It helps your body get used to the allergen over time.  
It may be recommended if you cannot avoid the animal.

If you are allergic to a certain animal, avoid contact with it.  
Clean clothes and furniture thoroughly.  
In some cases, it may be best to remove furniture or give up your pet.  

The decision depends on:  
- How bad your symptoms are  
- What treatments are available  
- How important the animal is to you  

## More Information

For more details about animal allergies, visit:  
[allergieinformationsdienst.de](https://www.allergieinformationsdienst.de)

# Indigestion (Functional Dyspepsia)

Everyone has felt full, had a stomach ache, or felt sick to their stomach at some point.  
But if these feelings happen often over several months, you should see a doctor.  
Indigestion might be the reason.

---

## Quick Facts

- About 5 to 11 out of every 100 people have indigestion.  
- Common signs are feeling full quickly when eating, stomach pain, or heartburn.  
- Doctors do not yet know exactly what causes it.  
- Diagnosis is based on your symptoms and by checking for other possible illnesses.  
- There are many ways to treat it.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Indigestion?

Indigestion, also called “irritable stomach,” is one of the most common stomach problems.  
Doctors also call it “functional dyspepsia.”  

It affects the upper part of the belly.  
Symptoms can be different from person to person.  
They often include:  
- Feeling full too soon when eating  
- A heavy or full feeling after meals  
- Stomach pain or heartburn  

The exact cause is not known.  
Many things may play a role.  

There is no cure that fixes the root cause.  
But there are many treatments that can help.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms can be different for each person.  
They may also be vague or unclear.  

The most common symptoms are:  
- Feeling full after eating only a small amount  
- A feeling of fullness after meals  
- Stomach pain or heartburn  

Some people also feel sick to their stomach, vomit, or have heartburn.

---

## What Causes Indigestion?

Doctors do not fully understand what causes indigestion.  
But several factors may be involved:

- The stomach empties too slowly  
- The stomach is more sensitive to pain  
- An infection with a bacteria called *Helicobacter pylori*  
- An imbalance of good and bad bacteria in the upper gut  
- Mental health issues like long-term stress, anxiety, or depression  

---

## How Common Is Indigestion?

Indigestion is very common.  
In Germany, about 1 in 7 to 1 in 10 people have it.  
Women are more likely to have it than men.

---

## How Does Indigestion Develop?

Symptoms can come and go.  
You might feel fine for a while, then have a flare-up.  
The severity of symptoms can change during a flare-up.  

Some people have symptoms for months or even years.  
In about half of all cases, symptoms go away on their own after a few years — even without treatment.  
In others, symptoms continue for a long time.

---

## How Is Indigestion Diagnosed?

A doctor will diagnose indigestion if you have at least one of these symptoms for at least 3 months in a 6-month period:

- Feeling full too soon when eating  
- Feeling full after eating  
- Stomach pain or heartburn  

The doctor will also check for other possible causes, such as:

- A stomach ulcer or duodenal ulcer  
- Stomach cancer  
- Inflammation of the stomach lining (gastritis)  
- Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)  
- Certain medicines, like painkillers, that can irritate the stomach  

The doctor will ask about your health history and symptoms.  
They will do a physical exam and blood tests.  
In some cases, they may do a gastroscopy.  
This is a test where a thin tube with a camera is used to look inside the esophagus, stomach, and first part of the small intestine.  

If needed, a special breath test checks for *Helicobacter pylori* bacteria in the stomach.

---

## How Is Indigestion Treated?

If no *Helicobacter pylori* infection is found, the doctor may prescribe a medicine called a proton pump inhibitor (PPI).  
Examples include omeprazole or pantoprazole.  
These medicines reduce stomach acid and can ease stomach pain.

If *Helicobacter pylori* is found, treatment includes a mix of antibiotics and a PPI.  
This combination can clear the infection and help with symptoms.

Another option is H2 blockers.  
These medicines also lower stomach acid.

If these treatments do not help, the doctor may suggest:

- Antidepressants (even if you are not depressed)  
- Prokinetic agents (medicines that help the stomach move food better)

If medicines do not work, psychotherapy may help.  
This is talk therapy that can improve how you handle stress and emotions.

Diet changes can also help.  
Some people find relief by avoiding certain foods.  
Studies show that wheat, caffeine, and fatty foods can trigger symptoms in some people.

For more tips on managing indigestion, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

---

## How Does Indigestion Affect Daily Life?

You can take simple steps to help manage symptoms:

- Keep a symptom diary to track what you eat and when symptoms happen  
- Avoid foods or drinks that make symptoms worse  
- Eat regular meals  
- Avoid large portions  
- Chew your food well  
- Eat slowly  

Relaxation exercises, like deep breathing or gentle stretching, may also help.

It is reassuring to know that indigestion does not lead to serious health problems.  
If symptoms keep coming back, it helps to accept the condition.  
Over time, many people learn to live well with it.

# Bacterial Vaginosis

## What Is Bacterial Vaginosis?

Bacterial vaginosis happens when certain bacteria in the vagina grow too much.  
These bacteria are usually present in small amounts.  
When they grow too much, they can cause problems.  
This condition can lead to vaginal irritation and discomfort.  

It is one of the most common vaginal infections.  
About 5 out of every 100 women have it at some point.  
Many women do not notice any symptoms.  
The infection is not always serious, but it can cause unpleasant side effects.  

## What Are the Symptoms?

Half of all women with bacterial vaginosis do not have any symptoms.  
When symptoms do appear, the most common is a thin, grayish-white discharge.  
The discharge often has a strong fishy smell.  
The smell may get worse after sex or during your period.  

Itching, burning, or dryness in the vagina is not usually caused by bacterial vaginosis.  
These symptoms are more likely due to vaginal inflammation.  
Inflammation can make the area around the vagina red and swollen.  
It can also make it painful to pee or to have sex.  

## What Causes Bacterial Vaginosis?

The vagina normally has a mix of good bacteria.  
The most important are lactic acid bacteria.  
They help keep the vagina healthy and slightly acidic.  
This acidity helps stop harmful germs from growing.  

Bacterial vaginosis happens when the balance of bacteria changes.  
The number of lactic acid bacteria drops.  
Other bacteria grow too fast.  
One type of bacteria, called Gardnerella vaginalis, is often the main cause.  

## What Increases the Risk?

You are more likely to get bacterial vaginosis if:  
- You have new sexual partners often.  
- You use strong soaps or douches for cleaning the vagina.  
- You have hormonal changes, such as during pregnancy or menopause.  

These things can upset the natural balance of bacteria in the vagina.  

## How Common Is It?

Bacterial vaginosis is very common.  
About 5 out of every 100 women get it.  
In about one third of cases, the infection goes away on its own.  
If you have symptoms, treatment is usually needed.  

## What Can Happen If It’s Not Treated?

When the bacteria balance is off, other harmful germs can grow more easily.  
This can lead to vaginal inflammation.  
It can also cause infections in the uterus or the tubes that carry eggs from the ovaries to the womb.  

Bacterial vaginosis also increases your risk of getting a sexually transmitted infection.  
In pregnant women, it may raise the chance of:  
- Going into labor too early  
- Losing the baby before the due date  
- Having a baby born too early  

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor cannot always tell bacterial vaginosis just by looking at your symptoms.  
They will take a small sample of vaginal fluid during a check-up.  
This sample is tested to check the pH level and the types of bacteria present.  

Women with bacterial vaginosis usually have high levels of Gardnerella bacteria.  

## How Is It Treated?

If you have symptoms, your doctor will likely prescribe antibiotics.  
These can come as pills, vaginal suppositories, or creams.  
The treatment kills the overgrown bacteria.  

You do not need to treat your partner.  
The infection is not passed through sex, and treating the partner does not prevent it from coming back.  

Another option is using suppositories or capsules with live lactic acid bacteria.  
These help restore the healthy balance in the vagina.  
But there is not enough proof yet on how well they work.  

Some women try home remedies like:  
- Putting tampons soaked in tea tree oil in the vagina  
- Using natural yogurt in the vagina  

There is not enough research to know if these are safe or effective.  
Do not use them without talking to your doctor.  

For more information about bacterial vaginosis and treatment options, visit:  
[gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# West Nile Fever

West Nile fever is an illness caused by a virus spread by mosquitoes.  
It was once only seen in tropical areas.  
Now, it is also being found in Germany.  
This article explains how the virus spreads and how you can protect yourself.

---

## Quick Facts

- West Nile fever is caused by the West Nile virus.  
- The virus started in tropical areas.  
- Since 2019, cases have been found in Germany.  
- Most people get infected through mosquito bites.  
- Mosquitoes pass the virus from wild birds to people and animals.  
- Four out of five people who get infected do not feel sick.  
- One out of five people get flu-like symptoms.  
- Severe cases are rare but can harm the brain and nerves.  
- Severe cases can be life-threatening.  
- Good mosquito protection can stop infection.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is West Nile Fever?

West Nile fever is an infection that causes fever.  
It is caused by the West Nile virus.  
The virus spreads through mosquito bites.  
Most people have no symptoms or only mild ones.  
In rare cases, the virus attacks the brain and nerves.  
This can lead to serious health problems.

The West Nile virus was once only found in tropical regions.  
That is why it was called an “exotic” disease.  
Since the 1990s, it has spread to other parts of the world.  
The first cases in Germany were reported in 2019.  
Since then, more cases have been found each year.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many people infected with the virus do not feel sick at all.  
About one in five people get symptoms.  
These include fever, chills, headache, back pain, and tiredness.  
Some people also have eye pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.  
About half of those who get sick develop a rash.  
The rash starts on the upper body and spreads to the arms, legs, and head.  
It may be itchy.

A very small number of people get a serious form of the illness.  
This affects the brain and nerves.  
It happens in about one in 100 infected people.  
Symptoms of this serious form include:

- Weak muscles  
- Confusion  
- Paralysis  
- Trouble moving  
- Swelling in the eye nerves  
- Seizures

---

## How Is West Nile Fever Spread?

The virus spreads through mosquito bites.  
Mosquitoes get the virus from wild birds.  
They can then pass it to people and animals like horses and dogs.  
People who get infected do not spread the virus to others.  
The virus does not multiply enough in human blood to be passed on by mosquitoes.  
It is not spread through coughing, sneezing, or touching.

In Germany, most infections happen in late summer and early autumn.  
This is when mosquitoes are most active.  
In warmer areas, such as southern Europe, mosquitoes can spread the virus into November.

In rare cases, the virus can also spread through:

- Blood transfusions  
- Organ donations  
- Breast milk  
- From mother to baby during pregnancy

> **Important:** You cannot catch West Nile fever from touching, hugging, or shaking hands with an infected person or animal.

---

## Who Is at Higher Risk for Severe Illness?

People over the age of 50 are more likely to get very sick.  
Other risk factors include:

- Heart disease  
- Cancer  
- Kidney problems  
- Diabetes  
- A weak immune system  
- Heavy alcohol use

---

## How Common Is West Nile Fever?

The virus was once only in tropical areas.  
Now it is found in parts of Europe.  
It spreads often in southern France, northern Italy, and Greece.  
In 2020, 336 cases were reported in the European Union.  
38 of those people died.

Germany first reported cases in 2019.  
More cases have been found each year since.  
Experts believe the virus will keep spreading in Germany.  
Warmer weather makes it easier for mosquitoes to survive and spread the virus.

So far, the number of reported cases in Europe and Germany is low.  
But experts think only about 2% of all infections are found and reported.  
This is because most people have no symptoms or only mild ones.  
They do not go to the doctor.

Also, doctors in Germany often do not think of West Nile fever when someone has flu-like symptoms.  
So they rarely test for it.

---

## How Does the Illness Progress?

Ninety-nine out of 100 people have no or mild symptoms.  
Their nerves are not affected.  
They usually get better on their own.  
There are no long-term problems.

Of the people who get the serious form with brain damage, 5 to 10 percent die.  
Of those who survive, about half have long-term problems.  
These can include:

- Feeling tired  
- Weakness  
- Headaches  
- Balance issues  
- Memory problems

---

## How Can You Prevent Infection?

There is no vaccine for the West Nile virus.  
The best way to stay safe is to avoid mosquito bites.  
This is especially important in areas where the virus is common and during peak mosquito times.

To protect yourself:

- Wear long-sleeved shirts and long pants when outside  
- Use mosquito repellent with DEET or icaridin before going outdoors  
- Stay indoors in the evening  
- Keep windows and doors closed if they do not have insect screens  
- Install insect screens on windows and doors

> **Important:** Mosquitoes breed in standing water.  
> This includes bird baths, rain barrels, and flower pots.  
> Empty these containers at least once a week.  
> Avoid them if possible.

---

## How Is West Nile Fever Diagnosed?

If a doctor suspects West Nile fever, they will take a blood sample or a sample of cerebrospinal fluid.  
Cerebrospinal fluid is the fluid around the spinal cord.

Lab tests can find the virus’s genetic material or antibodies.  
The virus can only be found in the first few days after infection.  
Antibodies appear later and stay in the body for a long time.

---

## How Is West Nile Fever Treated?

There is no medicine that kills the West Nile virus.  
Treatment focuses on easing symptoms.  
This may include:

- Painkillers  
- Fever reducers like ibuprofen or paracetamol

Most people get better with these measures.  
They recover fully.

People with serious brain or nerve symptoms need intensive care.  
In very severe cases, a machine may be needed to help with breathing.

---

## Do People Need Rehabilitation After West Nile Fever?

About one in 100 people get very sick and need intensive care.  
The virus can damage nerve cells.  
After recovery, many of these people have lasting problems.  
These can include trouble walking, concentrating, or doing daily tasks.

To help regain skills or learn new ways to manage daily life, rehabilitation is available.  
This can include physical therapy, mental support, and training.

# Insect Venom Allergy

Most people can be stung or bitten by insects without serious problems.  
But for some people, insect stings or bites can cause very bad reactions.  
These reactions can sometimes be life-threatening.  

In people with this allergy, the body’s defense system overreacts to certain proteins in the insect’s venom.  

---

## Quick Facts

- Bee and wasp stings are the most common cause of allergic reactions.  
- The body’s defense system attacks parts of the venom.  
- The area around the sting can swell a lot.  
- Symptoms usually start right after the sting.  
- Sometimes symptoms appear hours later.  
- The reaction can affect the whole body. This is called an anaphylactic reaction.  
- About 2 out of every 100 people have symptoms beyond the sting site.  

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

---

## What Is an Insect Venom Allergy?

Most insect stings cause only mild pain, redness, and swelling.  
But in people with an insect venom allergy, a sting can cause serious symptoms.  
This happens because the body’s defense system reacts strongly to proteins in the venom.  

Scientists do not fully understand how this happens.  
The allergy does not appear after the first sting.  
A person can be stung many times over years without any problem.  
Over time, the body becomes sensitive to the venom.  
This is called sensitization.  
After that, even one sting can cause a strong reaction.

---

## How Does the Allergy Show Up?

The area around the sting swells a lot.  
The swelling is often more than 10 centimeters wide.  
It lasts longer than 24 hours.  
It can cause strong pain, itching, or a burning feeling.

Stings in the mouth or throat are especially dangerous.  
Swelling there can block the airway.  
This makes breathing hard.  
But serious breathing problems are rare.

Mild symptoms include:

- Raised, itchy red patches on the skin (hives)  
- Itching all over the body  
- Dizziness  
- Nausea  
- Stomach pain  
- Trouble swallowing  
- Feeling weak  
- Swelling in the face or hands  

Severe symptoms include:

- Trouble breathing  
- Low blood pressure  
- Fainting  
- Heart stoppage  

Most symptoms start right after the sting.  
But sometimes they appear hours later.

The whole body can be affected.  
This is called an anaphylactic reaction.  
It can be mild or very serious.  
Sometimes the symptoms go away at first, then come back within 8 hours.

> **Important:** An anaphylactic reaction is serious.  
> It can be treated quickly if action is taken right away.  
> People with this allergy should carry an emergency kit.  
> They can also store allergy details on their electronic medical card.

For more on anaphylaxis, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## What Causes the Allergy?

Some people are more likely to have allergies.  
But scientists do not know why some people develop an allergy to insect venom and others do not.

Bees and wasps are the most common causes.  
Knowing how these insects behave can help you avoid them.  
It also helps you react correctly if stung.

Bees usually cause stronger reactions than wasps.

Rarely, people react to:

- Hornet venom (usually if they are already allergic to wasps)  
- Bumblebee venom (usually if they are already allergic to bees)

In Germany, allergic reactions to midges, horseflies, or ants are very rare.  
They usually only happen at the bite site.

---

### Bees

- Active from spring to late summer  
- Usually calm unless they feel threatened  
- Leave their stinger in the skin after stinging  
- Often found near beehives and flowers

### Wasps

- Active from summer to late fall  
- More likely to become aggressive  
- Feel threatened by movement or blowing at them  
- Keep their stinger after stinging  
- Often seen near food and trash

---

## How Common Is This Allergy?

About 2 out of every 100 people have symptoms beyond the sting site.  

People who are stung more often are more likely to be affected.  
This includes:

- Beekeepers and their family members  
- People who sell baked goods or fruit  
- Farmers and others who work outdoors

---

## How Does the Allergy Develop?

Most allergic reactions to insect stings do not cause lasting harm.  

In Germany, about 20 deaths per year are linked to bee, wasp, or hornet stings.  
The real number may be higher.  
Some deaths are not recorded as allergy-related.

---

## How Can You Protect Yourself?

The best way is to avoid stings and bites.  
Here are some tips:

- Stay away from trash, beehives, and wasp nests  
- Do not swat at bees or wasps. They sting to defend themselves.  
- Move slowly and stay calm around them  
- Avoid eating outdoors when many insects are around  
- If eating outside, clean the table right after  
- Cover drinks and use straws  
- Wash your mouth and hands after eating  
- Wear long sleeves and pants to cover your skin  
- Keep windows closed during the day

---

## How Is the Allergy Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and the sting event.  
It can be hard to tell bees and wasps apart.  
The location and behavior of the insect help the doctor decide.

If symptoms spread beyond the sting site, you will need tests.  
These tests check if your immune system reacts to insect venom.

### Skin Test

- A small amount of venom is placed on the skin  
- The skin is gently scratched  
- The doctor watches for redness or itching

### Blood Test

- Checks if your body has made antibodies to the venom

### Provocation Test

- Not used often because it can cause serious reactions  
- Only done in special clinics under strict conditions  
- Involves slowly giving small amounts of venom and watching for reactions

---

## How Is the Allergy Treated?

Treatment depends on the symptoms and whether you have had hyposensitization.

### For Mild Symptoms

- Take an antihistamine tablet  
- Use a cortisone cream or pill if the skin reaction is strong

### For Severe Symptoms

- Use adrenaline (epinephrine) right away  
- Symptoms like trouble breathing, nausea, low blood pressure, or swelling in the mouth or throat need fast treatment

### Hyposensitization (Immunotherapy)

- This treatment can reduce or stop allergic reactions  
- It is given over time with small amounts of venom  
- It is usually very effective  
- It is recommended for people with a history of severe reactions

If you have an insect venom allergy, get an allergy passport from your doctor.  
Carry it with you at all times.

For more details on treatment, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## More Information

You can also find helpful information at:  
[allergieinformationsdienst.de](https://www.allergieinformationsdienst.de)

# Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS)

SARS is a serious lung infection. It is caused by a virus called the SARS coronavirus. It often leads to a severe illness in adults. In 2003, this virus caused a global outbreak. The outbreak ended within a few months. Since then, no new cases have been reported.

---

## Quick Facts

- SARS is a lung infection caused by the SARS coronavirus.
- It first appeared at the end of 2002 and spread to more than 30 countries in 2003.
- The outbreak ended in the summer of 2003.
- Early symptoms include fever, cough, joint pain, and feeling very tired.
- Later symptoms include shortness of breath and trouble breathing.
- People over 65 years old are most at risk of serious illness or death.
- Doctors must test for the virus in a lab to confirm a diagnosis.
- There is no specific medicine for SARS. Treatment focuses on helping the patient feel better and supporting breathing.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is SARS?

SARS stands for severe acute respiratory syndrome. It is a lung infection. It is similar to pneumonia. It is caused by a virus called SARS-CoV.

The virus first appeared in 2002. It spread quickly in 2003 and became a global outbreak. Cases were reported in many countries across Asia, Europe, and North America. Strict hygiene rules helped stop the outbreak within the same year.

No new cases of SARS-CoV have been found since 2004. In total, about 8,096 people were infected. Around 1 in 10 of them died.

**Fun Fact:** Many different coronaviruses exist in animals. Some are closely related to SARS-CoV. The virus that causes COVID-19 is called SARS-CoV-2. Because of this, the original SARS virus is now also called SARS-CoV-1.

---

## What Are the Symptoms of SARS?

It usually takes 2 to 7 days after infection for symptoms to appear. It is very rare for someone to be infected and not show any symptoms.

The most common symptom is a high fever. Other early signs include chills, cough, headache, joint pain, and extreme tiredness.

About 75 out of 100 people develop shortness of breath and trouble breathing as the illness gets worse. About 20 out of 100 people also have diarrhea during this stage.

---

## Where Does the SARS Virus Come From? How Is It Spread?

SARS is caused by the SARS coronavirus. Experts believe the virus started in wild animals and then spread to people. Diseases that jump from animals to humans are called zoonotic diseases.

People with SARS can pass the virus to others. They are most likely to spread it 6 to 11 days after symptoms start.

The virus spreads mainly through close contact with an infected person. It spreads through large droplets when someone coughs, sneezes, or talks. It can also spread through tiny airborne particles (aerosols). This is why many healthcare workers became infected.

It is possible to catch SARS by touching surfaces that have been contaminated with infected saliva or feces. But this is not the main way the virus spreads.

After infection, the virus multiplies in the body, especially in the lower airways and lungs. The body’s immune system tries to fight it. In some people, the immune system overreacts. This causes strong inflammation. It can damage the lungs and cause fluid to build up. This makes it hard to get enough oxygen from the air you breathe.

---

## Who Is at Higher Risk of Severe SARS?

Most SARS cases during the 2002–2003 outbreak were in adults. Children under 12 rarely got infected. When they did, their symptoms were mild.

Older people are more likely to get very sick or die from SARS. Other risk factors include:

- Diabetes
- Heart disease
- Lung disease

---

## What Is the Outlook for SARS?

Most people with SARS first had cold-like symptoms. Then they developed shortness of breath and breathing problems.

- One-third of patients got better within a week.
- The other two-thirds stayed sick for a second week.
- Some people got worse at the end of the second week.

About 20 out of 100 people needed intensive care.

Severe cases could lead to serious complications, such as:

- Bacterial or fungal infections (called superinfections)
- Blood poisoning (sepsis)
- Blood clots in blood vessels (thromboembolisms)
- Damage to the liver or kidneys
- High blood pressure in the lungs (pulmonary hypertension)
- Sudden lung failure

These complications often led to death. The average death rate was about 10%. It was much higher in older adults and people with other health problems.

---

## How Can SARS Spread Be Prevented?

You can reduce your risk of getting SARS by:

- Practicing good hygiene (like washing hands often)
- Keeping a safe distance from others
- Wearing a full surgical face mask in high-risk settings

During the 2003 outbreak, quickly finding infected people and isolating them was key to stopping the spread. These steps helped end the outbreak in a few months.

Scientists worked hard to develop a vaccine. But no vaccine has been approved yet.

---

## How Is SARS Diagnosed?

To diagnose SARS, doctors must find the virus in a lab. They collect samples from:

- The nose and throat (using a swab)
- Fluid from the airways
- Stool

These samples are tested using a PCR test. This test looks for the virus’s genetic material.

---

## How Is SARS Treated?

There is no medicine that kills the SARS virus. Treatment focuses on helping the patient feel better and supporting breathing.

Common treatments include:

- Oxygen therapy
- Ventilation (using a machine to help with breathing) for very ill patients

Doctors treat symptoms and support the body’s systems while the immune system fights the virus.

# Pneumonic Plague – Simple Explanation

Pneumonic plague is a serious infection caused by bacteria. It affects the lungs and can spread quickly from person to person.

It is not found in Germany or most of Europe. But it still happens in some parts of Africa, Asia, and America.

---

## Quick Facts

- Pneumonic plague is a dangerous bacterial infection.
