> **Note:** This article cannot replace a doctor’s visit. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Laryngeal Cancer?

Laryngeal cancer is a tumor that starts in the voice box. It can grow on, above, or below the vocal cords.

The voice box is in the front of your neck, halfway up. It helps you speak and keeps food and drink from going into your windpipe.

The voice box has three main parts:
- The vocal cords (where sound is made)
- The area above the vocal cords
- The area below the vocal cords

Cancer in the voice box is a type of head and neck cancer. About 3,200 people in Germany get it each year. Men are much more likely to get it than women.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on where the cancer is in the voice box.

- If the cancer is on the vocal cords, hoarseness is usually the first sign.
- If the cancer is above or below the vocal cords, symptoms may not appear early. Later signs include:
  - Trouble swallowing
  - Pain when swallowing
  - Feeling like something is stuck in your throat
  - Ear pain
  - Swelling in the neck
  - Breathing problems
  - Coughing up blood
  - Bad breath

If any of these symptoms last more than four weeks, see a doctor.

Your family doctor can check your symptoms and refer you to a specialist if needed.

---

## What Causes Laryngeal Cancer?

Laryngeal cancer starts when normal cells in the voice box change and grow out of control. These changes are due to genetic mutations. Most happen by chance over time.

But some things increase the risk:

- Smoking tobacco
- Drinking too much alcohol
- Breathing in asbestos dust
- Exposure to harmful chemicals like radiation, sulfuric acid, coal tar, or polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons
- Infection with certain types of human papillomavirus (HPV), especially HPV 16
- Pre-cancerous changes in the lining of the voice box, such as white or red patches

Smoking and drinking together are especially dangerous. Poor diet, like eating too much meat or fried food, may also raise the risk.

---

## How Does Laryngeal Cancer Spread?

Laryngeal cancer can start from pre-cancerous changes in the voice box lining. If these cells grow deeply and spread, they become cancer.

The cancer can spread to other parts of the body. It often spreads through the blood to the lungs. It can also spread to bones or the liver, but less often.

Tobacco and alcohol make it more likely that a person will get other cancers in the head and neck area, such as:
- Lung cancer
- Esophageal cancer
- Mouth or throat cancer

The spread depends on where the cancer starts:
- Tumors on the vocal cords rarely spread to lymph nodes early on.
- Tumors above or below the vocal cords often spread to neck lymph nodes early.

---

## How Can I Lower My Risk?

The best way to reduce your risk is to stop smoking and avoid heavy drinking.

---

## How Is Laryngeal Cancer Diagnosed?

If cancer is suspected, your doctor will ask about your symptoms, health history, and risk factors.

### Physical Exam and Biopsy

A specialist will examine your throat and voice box. If they see something suspicious, they will take a small tissue sample (a biopsy).

- The biopsy is done under general anesthesia.
- The sample is sent to a lab to be checked under a microscope.
- If cancer cells are found, you have laryngeal cancer.

If the suspicious area is small, the doctor may remove it completely during the exam. This avoids a second procedure.

Before the biopsy, your doctor may check how well your vocal cords work. This helps rule out deep tumors.

If the tumor is large and clearly cancerous, imaging scans are done before the biopsy.

### Imaging Scans

Scans help doctors see how far the cancer has spread. They check for:
- Spread to neck lymph nodes
- Spread to other organs
- Other tumors

Types of scans used:
- MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)
- CT (computed tomography)
- PET (positron emission tomography)
- Ultrasound of the neck and sometimes the belly

If the scans are unclear, a fine needle biopsy may be done. A thin needle takes cells from the lymph node for testing.

For more details on biopsies, visit the website of the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## How Is Laryngeal Cancer Treated?

Before treatment, you may get help from:
- A speech therapist
- A dentist
- A nutritionist

Treatment depends on:
- How advanced the cancer is
- Your overall health
- Your personal wishes
- Possible side effects

### Treating the Main Tumor

- Early-stage cancer can often be cured with surgery or radiation.
- Doctors usually only remove the whole voice box if the tumor is above the vocal cords. These tumors are rare but grow fast.
- Even in advanced cases, treatment can still cure the cancer.

**Surgery** removes the tumor. Often, the whole voice box must be removed.

**Radiation** is used after surgery to kill any remaining cancer cells. People at higher risk may also get chemotherapy with radiation.

If surgery is not possible or not wanted, doctors may use radiation and chemotherapy instead. Sometimes, antibody therapy is added.

> **Important:** If the voice box is removed, you will:
> - Lose your natural voice
> - Lose your normal sense of smell
> - Breathe through a hole in your neck (tracheostoma)

Talk to your doctor about the pros and cons of each treatment. Ask if it’s possible to keep your voice box.

### Treating Lymph Nodes in the Neck

Doctors often treat neck lymph nodes even if they look normal. Hidden cancer may already be there.

- If the cancer is on the vocal cords and early, treatment of lymph nodes is usually not needed.
- If lymph nodes are already swollen, surgery removes them. Other tissue may also be removed.
- If surgery is not possible or not wanted, radiation is used. Chemotherapy may be added.

### Treating Cancer That Cannot Be Cured

When the cancer cannot be cured, the goal is to slow it down and relieve symptoms.

Treatment options include:
- Chemotherapy
- Targeted therapy
- Immunotherapy
- Radiation
- Surgery (if helpful)

Supportive care is very important. This includes:
- Pain relief
- Nutrition advice
- Mental health support from a psycho-oncologist

For more information on treatment, side effects, and symptom relief, contact the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center**.

You can also email them or call the free number: **0800 420 30 40**.

---

## What Happens After Treatment?

Cancer treatment can be hard on your body and mind. Medical rehabilitation helps you recover.

Rehab programs are tailored to your needs. They may include:
- Voice therapy
- Speech and swallowing therapy
- Nutrition support
- Mental health care

### Follow-Up Care

After treatment, you will have regular check-ups. These help find:
- A return of cancer
- New cancers
- Long-term side effects

Check-ups include:
- Talking about your health and symptoms
- A full throat exam
- Feeling the neck and doing an ultrasound

Your doctor may also order:
- CT scans
- MRI scans
- PET/CT scans (if needed)

The check-up schedule starts with frequent visits, then becomes less often over time. You can come more often if you feel unwell.

If the cancer cannot be cured, follow-ups help catch serious symptoms early. The goal is to keep your quality of life as good as possible.

---

## What Changes Happen During or After Treatment?

Cancer and its treatment can change your daily life. Everyone copes differently.

Possible problems include:
- Loss of voice or trouble speaking
- Trouble swallowing
- Loss of smell
- Dry mouth
- Tooth or jaw problems
- Trouble chewing
- Swelling in the face or neck (lymphedema)

If your voice box was removed, you will need to learn new ways to speak. You will also need to care for the breathing hole in your neck (tracheostoma).

Talk to your doctor about support options. Self-help groups and patient organizations can also help.

---

## Who Can Help Me?

Laryngeal cancer is treated by a team of doctors. Some hospitals are certified for this type of care.

You can find certified centers on the **OncoMAP** website.

For more information on living with cancer and support options, visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

You can also contact them directly:
- Call the free number: **0800 420 30 40**
- Email: **krebsinformationsdienst@dkfz.de**

They are available to answer

# Heel Spurs

A heel spur is a bony growth that forms where a tendon attaches to the heel bone.  
It often does not cause any pain.  
But if the area becomes irritated from wear and tear, it can cause pain under the heel.

---

## Quick Facts

- As we age, tendons can harden and turn into bone. This is called ossification.  
- This usually happens where the bottom of the foot meets the heel bone.  
- Overusing the foot can cause small injuries and swelling at the tendon’s attachment point.  
- This swelling can lead to bone growth. Doctors call this condition plantar fasciitis.  
- The pain usually starts when pressure is applied to the heel.  
- It often happens in the morning when you first get out of bed.  
- It can also happen after sitting or resting for a long time.  
- Most people get better without surgery.  
- Healing can take months.  

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always see a doctor.

---

## What Is a Heel Spur?

A heel spur is a small piece of extra bone that forms where a tendon connects to the heel bone.  
This bone growth usually happens on the bottom of the heel.  
In rare cases, it can form where the Achilles tendon connects to the heel bone.  

The heel spur itself usually does not hurt.  
The pain comes from irritation of the soft tissue around it.  
This irritation is often caused by wear and tear on the plantar fascia.  

The plantar fascia is a strong band of tissue that runs along the bottom of the foot.  
It supports the arch of the foot.  
Every time you step, this band is stretched and pulled.  
If you put too much strain on it, tiny tears can happen.  

These tiny tears cause inflammation.  
This is called plantar fasciitis.  
It causes pain under the heel.  
About half of people with plantar fasciitis also have a heel spur.  

The pain can make walking difficult.  
It is common in long-distance runners and older adults.  
Heel pain can last a long time.  
It often comes back even after treatment.  
But surgery is rarely needed.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may have a heel spur without any pain at all.  
If you do feel pain, it is usually from plantar fasciitis.  
The pain is felt under the heel.  
It can be triggered by pressure on the heel.  
It may also hurt when you pull your toes upward with your hand.  

In some cases, the pain spreads into the lower leg.  
It is worst in the morning when you first get up.  
It often gets better as you walk more during the day.  
But it can return in the evening after standing for long periods.  
It can also get worse after carrying heavy loads.  

If the pain affects the whole heel, or if you feel tingling or numbness,  
it may not be from a heel spur.  
Other health problems could be causing the pain.  
You should see a doctor to find out why.

---

## What Causes a Heel Spur?

The arch of your foot is held up by muscles and a strong band of tissue called the plantar fascia.  
This band connects to the heel bone and the front part of the foot.  
When the tissue at the heel attachment point hardens and turns into bone, a heel spur forms.  

Plantar fasciitis is the main cause of heel pain.  
It happens when the tendon attachment point is overused.  
This causes tiny tears in the tissue.  
These small injuries lead to swelling and pain.  

Sometimes, a foot injury can cause the same damage.  
The body may respond by forming extra bone at the site of injury.

---

## How Common Is Heel Pain?

About 11 to 15 out of every 100 foot problems are caused by plantar fasciitis.  
This means about 10 out of every 100 people will have heel pain at some point in life.  
It is most common between the ages of 40 and 60.  
In about one third of these people, both heels are affected.  

Women are slightly more likely to get it than men.  
It is very common in runners.  
But people who stand or walk a lot at work are also at risk.  
Those who play sports like tennis on hard surfaces are more likely to develop heel pain too.

---

## How Long Does Heel Pain Last?

Heel pain can last from a few weeks to several months.  
Most people feel better within a year.  
Some may need to take breaks from work or sports.  
They may not be able to walk or stand for long periods.  
They may also need to avoid lifting heavy things.  

Only about 5 out of every 100 people need surgery.

---

## How Can Heel Spurs Be Prevented?

Runners can reduce their risk by:

- Wearing running shoes that cushion the impact when your foot hits the ground  
- Changing shoes regularly to avoid wear and tear  

They should also:

- Do stretching exercises often  
- Train less intensely  
- Run shorter distances  

These steps help protect the foot and reduce strain.

---

## How Are Heel Spurs Diagnosed?

A doctor can often tell if you have a heel spur just by examining your foot.  
No extra tests are usually needed.  

If the pain does not improve, the doctor may order tests:

- An X-ray can show the bone spur.  
- An ultrasound can check for swelling, thickening, or calcium deposits.  
- An MRI can find stress fractures or damage to cartilage.  
- Ultrasound can also check the condition of tendons and muscles.  

If the doctor suspects a connective tissue or joint disease,  
a blood test may be done.  

If nerve problems are suspected, a detailed nerve exam may be needed.

---

## How Are Heel Spurs Treated?

The heel spur itself will not go away.  
But the pain can be treated.  

Here are common treatments:

- Stop doing the activity that causes pain.  
- Apply ice to the heel after activity to reduce swelling.  
- Do stretching exercises for the foot and calf, especially before moving.  
- Use silicone heel pads to reduce pressure on the heel.  
- Avoid walking barefoot or wearing shoes with thin leather soles.  
- Wear shoes with cushioned soles, footbeds, or orthopedic insoles.  
  Insoles are especially helpful if your foot is misaligned.  
- Take painkillers for up to 2 to 3 weeks.  
  Do not take them longer than that.  
- Injections of anti-inflammatory medicine (like cortisone) and numbing medicine can help.  
  But too many injections can harm the tendons.  
- Use anti-inflammatory creams with a mild electric current.  
  This method is called iontophoresis.  
- Wear a foot splint at night if pain is worst in the morning.  
- Use special tape on the foot to support the arch.  
  This can help reduce pain at first.  

Surgery should only be considered if no other treatment helps after 6 to 12 months.  

> **Important:** Surgery does not always work.  
> It carries risks.  
> Always talk to your doctor before deciding on surgery.

---

## Other Treatments (Not Yet Proven)

Some treatments are used for persistent pain, but their benefits are not yet proven.  
These include:

- Shockwave therapy  
- Injections with your own blood or botulinum toxin (a substance made by bacteria)  
- Applying cortisone creams or herbal remedies  
- Low-dose X-rays  
- Freezing treatment (cryotherapy)  
- Laser therapy  
- Acupuncture-like treatment using needles (dry needling) to treat tight spots in the foot muscles  

Talk to your doctor before trying any of these.

# Ulcerative Colitis – Simple Explanation

Ulcerative colitis is a long-term condition that causes inflammation in the lining of the large intestine.  
It often comes and goes.  
Some people have no symptoms for weeks or months.  
Then symptoms return suddenly and can be very strong.

When symptoms are active, you may feel:
- Severe pain in the lower left side of your belly
- Frequent diarrhea, sometimes with blood or mucus
- High fever
- Weight loss

These symptoms can be so bad that daily life becomes hard.  
Some people need to go to the hospital during these flare-ups.  
But most people do not have symptoms all the time.  
Only a few have constant symptoms.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Ulcerative Colitis?

Ulcerative colitis is a long-term inflammation of the inner lining of the large intestine.  
It only affects the large intestine.  
It does not affect the small intestine.

This is different from Crohn’s disease, which can affect any part of the digestive system.

When the inflammation is only in the last part of the large intestine, doctors call it **proctitis**.

About 150,000 people in Germany have this condition.

---

## What Are the Signs?

During a flare-up, you may notice:
- Diarrhea with blood or mucus
- Needing to go to the bathroom many times a day
- Cramp-like pain in your lower belly
- Fever
- Swollen or painful joints, like hips or knees
- Red, sore eyes
- Skin rashes
- Sores in your mouth
- Losing weight without trying

Some of these symptoms come and go.  
Others happen again and again.

---

## What Causes It?

Doctors do not yet know the exact cause.  
But they believe the body’s immune system mistakenly attacks the lining of the intestine.  
This causes inflammation.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

You are more likely to get ulcerative colitis if:
- A close family member has it
- You are under a lot of stress
- You live in a certain environment
- You have another illness

It is not clear what triggers a flare-up.  
But stress, lifestyle, and other health problems may play a role.

---

## How Does It Progress?

Most people first get the disease as teenagers or young adults.  
The condition lasts for life.

Most people have flare-ups that come and go.  
Between flare-ups, symptoms may be mild or disappear completely.

If symptoms last a long time, you may not get enough nutrients.  
This can lead to poor health.

People with ulcerative colitis have a higher chance of getting bowel cancer.  
Doctors recommend regular colonoscopies to check for early signs.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Many conditions can cause similar symptoms.  
To be sure it is ulcerative colitis, doctors do several tests.

First, they ask you:
- What symptoms you have and when they started
- If any foods upset your stomach
- If you have had certain vaccines
- If you smoke
- If anyone in your family has ulcerative colitis

Then they may do:
- An ultrasound scan
- Blood tests
- A colonoscopy (a camera is used to look inside the colon)
- A small tissue sample is taken during the colonoscopy

They may repeat the colonoscopy after a few months to check progress.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Medicine is used to reduce inflammation during flare-ups.

The type of medicine depends on:
- How bad the symptoms are
- How much of the colon is affected

Common medicines include:
- 5-aminosalicylic acid (a medicine that reduces inflammation)
- Cortisone (a medicine that reduces swelling and pain)

If these medicines do not work well or cause bad side effects, your doctor may switch to a different type of medicine.

These are called **biological medicines** or **biologics**.  
They work by calming down the immune system.

Surgery may be needed if:
- Medicines stop working
- There are serious complications

For more information about biologics, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## Where Can I Get Help?

In Germany, many services support people with ulcerative colitis.  
You can find:
- Local self-help groups
- Advice centers

These services are organized differently in each region.

To find the right one for you, use the database at the **National Contact and Information Point for Supporting Self-Help Groups (NAKOS)**.  
You can find it online at: [nako.de](https://www.nako.de)

# Problems with Blood Clotting

Blood clotting problems can cause too much bleeding or too many blood clots.  
Some of these problems are mild and do not need treatment.  
Others can be serious and may need special care.  
In some cases, treatment involves using blood products.

---

## Quick Facts

- Blood clotting problems mean your blood does not clot the way it should.  
- This can lead to more bleeding than normal.  
- It can also cause blood clots to form too easily.  
- Common signs of bleeding include frequent nosebleeds, easy bruising, or very heavy periods.  
- Blood clots often show up as swelling, pain, or tightness in the legs.  
- Some clotting problems are present from birth.  
- Others develop later in life due to illness, medicine, or other health issues.  
- Mild cases usually do not need treatment.  
- More serious cases can be managed with medicine or blood products.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

---

## What Are Blood Clotting Problems?

Your blood normally clots when you are hurt.  
This helps stop bleeding.  
But with clotting problems, your blood may not clot properly.

There are two main types:

1. **Bleeding problems**  
   - Blood does not clot fast enough.  
   - You may bleed for longer than normal after a cut.  
   - You may get bruises easily.  
   - You may have heavy periods.  
   - You may bleed after minor surgery, like a tooth extraction.

2. **Clotting problems**  
   - Blood clots form too easily.  
   - This can lead to blood clots in the legs or other parts of the body.  
   - These clots can be dangerous.

---

## What Causes Blood Clotting Problems?

Many things can cause clotting problems.

### Some people are born with them  
- Certain clotting factors are missing or low.  
- This is called hemophilia.  
- It is passed down through families.

### Newborns  
- Babies are born with low levels of vitamin K.  
- This can cause bleeding.  
- Doctors give vitamin K to newborns to prevent this.

### Medicines  
- Blood thinners like heparin or phenprocoumon increase bleeding risk.  
- Painkillers with acetylsalicylic acid (like aspirin) can also cause bleeding.  
- Some birth control pills increase the risk of blood clots.

### Immune system issues  
- The body may make antibodies that attack platelets.  
- This lowers the number of platelets.  
- Fewer platelets mean more bleeding.  
- The cause of this is often unknown.

### Other health problems  
- Liver disease can reduce clotting factors.  
- Kidney disease can also affect clotting.  
- Cancer can lead to both bleeding and blood clots.

### Vitamin K deficiency  
- Vitamin K helps make clotting factors.  
- Babies need extra vitamin K at birth.  
- In adults, low vitamin K is rare and usually not a big problem.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Look for these signs:

- Nosebleeds that are hard to stop  
- Bleeding from the mouth or gums  
- Bruises that appear after small bumps  
- Tiny red or purple spots on the skin (especially on legs and ankles)  
- Cuts that bleed for a long time  
- Bleeding after minor surgery  
- Very heavy or long-lasting periods  
- Bruises or swelling in muscles or joints with no injury

Some people have too much clotting.  
This can cause:

- Pain and swelling in the legs  
- A feeling of tightness in the legs  
- Blood clots in the deep veins (called deep vein thrombosis)

---

## How Are Clotting Problems Diagnosed?

Doctors start by asking about your health history and symptoms.  
They want to know if you have bleeding or clotting issues.

A blood test is needed to confirm the diagnosis.  
The test checks:

- How long it takes your blood to clot  
- How many platelets you have  
- The shape and number of platelets

Depending on the results, more tests may be done.  
These can include:

- Measuring specific clotting factors  
- Testing how well platelets work  
- Genetic testing in some cases

Specialists in blood disorders (hematologists) often handle the diagnosis.  
But sometimes, the exact cause is not clear.

---

## How Are Clotting Problems Treated?

Mild clotting problems often do not need treatment.  
You may just need to avoid certain medicines.

For more serious cases, treatment options include:

- **Tranexamic acid** – helps stop or prevent bleeding  
- **Clotting factor injections** – used for people with hemophilia  
- **Vitamin K** – given to newborns at birth. Sometimes used in adults  
- **Blood thinners** – used to prevent clots in people with high clotting risk  
- **Compression stockings** – help prevent blood clots in the legs

Doctors weigh the risks and benefits of each treatment.  
Sometimes, treatment is only needed for a short time, such as before surgery or a dental procedure.

If bleeding is severe or long-lasting, you may need to go to the hospital.  
There, you may receive blood products or platelet transfusions.

# Allergies

An allergy happens when your body’s defense system overreacts to something that is actually harmless.  
This reaction can cause a range of symptoms.  
Common triggers include plant pollen and certain foods.  
There are several ways to manage allergies.

---

## Quick Facts

- An allergy happens when your body overreacts to a harmless substance (called an allergen).  
- Allergic reactions most often affect your nose, throat, lungs, skin, or eyes.  
- Some people inherit a tendency to develop allergies.  
- You can avoid some allergens, but others are hard to avoid completely.  
- In Germany, about one in three people will have an allergy at some point in their life.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is an Allergy?

An allergy happens when your body’s defense system reacts too strongly to a harmless substance.  
These substances are called allergens.  
Examples include plant pollen and certain foods.  

Symptoms can be mild or very severe.  
Some people have only small problems.  
Others may feel very unwell and have trouble doing daily activities.  
In rare cases, an allergic reaction can be life-threatening.

There are different ways to treat allergies.  
You can avoid some triggers, but others are hard to avoid.  
Common allergens include:

- Pollen from plants  
- Tiny bugs in house dust (dust mites)  
- Pet dander (skin flakes from cats, dogs, or farm animals)  
- Insect stings  
- Certain foods  
- Some medicines  
- Metals, perfumes, or other skin contact substances  
- Mold

> **Important:** Some people use the word “hypersensitivity” to describe allergies.  
> But not all hypersensitivities are allergies.  
> For example, lactose intolerance and celiac disease are not allergies.  
> They cause similar symptoms but work differently.  
> That is why it is important to see a doctor to find out what is really causing your symptoms.  
> Only then can you get the right treatment.

---

## What Are the Signs of an Allergy?

Common signs of an allergic reaction include:

- Sneezing  
- Itchy or runny nose  
- Blocked nose  
- Coughing  
- Trouble breathing  
- Watery eyes  
- Itching  
- Skin rashes  
- Swelling in the mouth or throat  
- Stomach pain, nausea, or diarrhea

Usually, symptoms appear in the part of the body that touched the allergen.  
For example, if you touch a plant that causes a rash, the rash will show up on your skin.

For more details on specific allergies, visit:  
[Food allergy](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)  
[Contact allergy](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)  
[Medication allergy](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)  
[Hay fever](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)  
[Insect venom allergy](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## What Causes an Allergy?

Several things can increase your chance of developing an allergy.

Your genes play a big role.  
Some people are born with a higher risk of allergies.  
This is called “atopy.”  
But genes alone do not cause allergies.  
Environmental factors also matter.

Exposure to air pollution or cigarette smoke can raise your risk.  
These factors may also lead to asthma or other health problems.

Substances like dust mites or food are not harmful to most people.  
But in people with allergies, they cause symptoms.

Why does this happen?  
When you have an allergy, your immune system mistakes a harmless protein (an allergen) for a dangerous germ.  
It then tries to fight it off.  
To do this, your body makes special proteins called IgE antibodies.

---

## How Common Are Allergies?

In Germany, about one in three people will develop an allergy at some point.  
Around 20 to 25 percent of children and teens have hay fever, asthma, or neurodermatitis.  
The number of people with allergies has gone up over the last 30 years.

---

## How Do Allergies Develop?

Most allergies start in childhood or teenage years.  
Many last a lifetime.  
But some improve as people get older.

Some food allergies, like those to milk or eggs, may go away over time.  
But peanut allergies usually do not go away.  
The type of allergen affects how the allergy progresses.

At first, symptoms may be mild.  
Over time, they can get worse.  
They may also lead to other health problems.

For example, long-term hay fever can lead to asthma.  
This is called the “allergic march” or “atopic march.”  
People with allergies are also more likely to get skin conditions like neurodermatitis.

> **Important:** Some allergens have similar proteins.  
> This means you might react to more than one substance.  
> For example, a pollen allergy can sometimes cause a reaction to certain fruits or vegetables.

---

## Can Allergies Be Prevented?

In many cases, allergies cannot be prevented.  
But some steps may lower the risk.

Babies who are breast-fed for the first six months are less likely to develop allergic asthma.  
But this does not seem to help much with other allergy symptoms like hay fever.

Cigarette smoke increases allergy risk.  
People who do not smoke and children raised in smoke-free homes are less likely to have allergies.

If you or your child is at high risk for allergies, think carefully before getting a cat.  
This can help avoid a cat allergy.  
But if your risk is low, having a pet is usually safe.

---

## How Is an Allergy Diagnosed?

Your doctor will first ask about your symptoms, your living situation, and your health history.  
Then, they may do special tests.

Allergy tests are done by doctors who specialize in allergies.  
These doctors include skin and lung specialists, ear, nose, and throat doctors, or pediatricians.

A skin prick test checks if you react to certain allergens.  
A small amount of the substance is placed on your skin.  
The doctor then lightly pricks the skin.  
If you are allergic, the area will swell and turn red.

An epicutaneous test (also called a patch test) is used for reactions that take longer to appear.  
The suspected allergen is placed on a patch.  
The patch is stuck to your back or arm.  
If you are allergic, the skin will become red, swollen, or itchy after 12 hours to three days.

Sometimes, a blood test is needed to check for allergy antibodies.  
In a provocation test, the doctor slowly exposes you to small amounts of allergens to see if a reaction happens.

For more information on allergy testing, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## How Is an Allergy Treated?

The first step is to avoid the allergen if possible.  
This works well for some triggers, like certain foods or chemicals.  
But it is hard to avoid things like pollen.  
For dust mite allergies, you can reduce dust in your home.

Medicines are often used to treat allergy symptoms.  
Common ones include:

- Antihistamines (tablets, nasal sprays, or shots)  
- Cortisone treatments (for nose, eyes, or skin)

Cortisone creams and ointments help with skin rashes and itching.

Another option is desensitization (also called immunotherapy).  
This helps your body get used to the allergen over time.  
It works like a vaccine.  
You get small, regular doses of the allergen.  
These are either injected under the skin or placed under the tongue.

This treatment is used for allergies to pollen, dust mites, and insect stings.  
It usually lasts at least three to five years.

There is no strong proof that plant-based remedies, homeopathy, or acupuncture help with allergies.

---

## What Else Should You Know?

If you have a severe allergy that could cause a life-threatening reaction, you can record this in your electronic medical data card.  
This is called the emergency data record.

For more on severe allergic reactions, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

Scientists are studying how the immune system and the environment interact.  
This research may lead to better ways to prevent and treat allergies.

For more on allergy research, visit: [allergieinformationsdienst.de](https://www.allergieinformationsdienst.de)

# Ovarian Cysts

Ovarian cysts are fluid-filled or tissue-filled sacs that form in the ovaries.  
They are usually harmless and often go away on their own.  
Most women with ovarian cysts do not have any symptoms.  
You do not need treatment if the cysts are small and not causing problems.

## Quick Facts

- Ovarian cysts are sacs filled with fluid or tissue.  
- They are usually about the size of a grape.  
- They are surrounded by a thin outer layer.  
- Most cysts disappear without treatment.  
- Hormonal changes during puberty or menopause often cause them.  
- Very few cysts are present from birth or caused by other rare conditions.  
- About 1 in 10 women will have an ovarian cyst at some point.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

## What Are Ovarian Cysts?

Ovarian cysts are sacs that grow in the ovaries.  
They are usually small and filled with fluid or tissue.  
They are covered by a thin outer layer.  
Most go away on their own within a few months.  
They rarely cause pain or other health problems.  
Surgery is only needed in very rare cases.  
Hormonal changes during puberty or menopause often cause them.  
Only a few cysts are present from birth or caused by other rare conditions.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most women with ovarian cysts feel no symptoms.  
Some may feel a dull ache in the lower belly.  
Very large cysts can press on the bladder or intestines.  
This can cause bloating, pressure, constipation, or pain when peeing.  
Cysts can affect your period.  
You might have heavier bleeding, missed periods, or spotting between periods.  
This happens if the cyst makes hormones that affect the lining of the womb.  
Cysts can burst.  
This can cause sudden pain, but it is usually not serious.  
A cyst can also cause the ovary to twist.  
This is called ovarian torsion.  
It causes sudden, sharp pain on one side of the lower belly.  
It can also cause nausea, vomiting, and a fast heartbeat.

## What Causes Ovarian Cysts?

Most cysts form during the normal process of egg development and release.  
These are called functional cysts.  
They can happen in one or both ovaries.  
They are most common during puberty or menopause.

The most common types of functional cysts are:

- **Follicular cysts:** A follicle (a small sac that holds an egg) does not release the egg.  
  It fills with fluid and becomes a cyst.

- **Corpus luteum cysts:** After an egg is released, the leftover follicle becomes the corpus luteum.  
  If blood collects inside it, it can turn into a cyst.  
  This cyst makes hormones like progesterone and estrogen.

- **Theca lutein cysts:** These are caused by fertility treatments.  
  The medicines used to help eggs mature can lead to cysts as a side effect.

**Chocolate cysts (endometriomas):**  
These are a special type of cyst.  
They contain old blood that looks like chocolate.  
They can form if you have endometriosis.

**Dermoid cysts:**  
These are not functional cysts.  
They can contain skin, hair, or oil glands.  
They form from a benign tumor.  
The oil they make cannot escape, so it builds up inside.  
These cysts can be present from birth.  
In rare cases, they can become cancerous.

**Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS):**  
This condition causes many small cysts in the ovaries.  
It happens when there are too many male hormones (androgens).  
This stops the eggs from maturing properly.

## How Long Do Ovarian Cysts Last?

Most cysts are 1 to 3 centimeters wide.  
They usually go away on their own within a few months.  
Very rarely do they grow large enough to cause serious pain.  
In rare cases, they can grow to 15 to 30 centimeters wide.

Ruptures are uncommon.  
If a cyst bursts, the fluid leaks into the belly.  
This can be painful but is usually not dangerous.

Large cysts can press on the bladder or intestines.  
This can cause bloating, pressure, constipation, or pain when peeing.  
Sometimes, bleeding happens.  
This may need surgery to stop.

If the ovary twists, it can cut off blood flow.  
This is very painful and dangerous.  
It can happen with large cysts, especially during sudden movements like playing sports.  
If this occurs, surgery is needed quickly to save the ovary.

## How Are Ovarian Cysts Diagnosed?

Doctors often find cysts by chance during a pelvic ultrasound.  
Some can be felt during a physical exam.

If a cyst is suspected, your doctor will ask about your symptoms.  
They may ask about changes in your period or pain.  
A blood test may be done.

Imaging tests like CT scans or a mirror exam (laparoscopy) are only needed in rare cases.  
These tests help check if the cyst could be cancer.  
Most cysts are not cancer, but they can look like tumors on scans.

For more information about whether ultrasounds are helpful, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

## How Are Ovarian Cysts Treated?

If you have no symptoms or only mild ones, you can wait and see.  
The cyst may go away on its own.  
Your doctor may suggest checking it every few months.  
Pain can be managed with painkillers like ibuprofen or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).

If the cyst grows, changes, or does not go away, your doctor may do a laparoscopy.  
This is a small surgery to look inside the belly.  
The cyst can be removed during the same procedure.  
But even after removal, cysts can come back.

Removing one or both ovaries is very rare.  
This may be needed if cancer is suspected.  
It may also be needed if the cyst is stuck in the tissue and cannot be removed safely.  
Doctors try to keep the ovaries if possible, especially if you want to have children.

> **Important:** Some doctors suggest using birth control pills to treat cysts.  
> But this does not work for functional cysts.  
> The pill stops ovulation by lowering hormone levels.  
> However, studies have not shown that it helps cysts go away faster.

# Spinal Fractures

Spinal fractures happen when one or more bones in the spine break. They often happen because of weak bones from a condition called osteoporosis. Less often, they happen after serious falls, car crashes, or sports injuries. This article explains the signs, how to prevent them, and what treatment and recovery involve.

---

## Quick Facts

- A spinal fracture can happen anywhere along the spine.
- The middle back (thoracic spine) and lower back (lumbar spine) are most often affected.
- Most spinal fractures are caused by osteoporosis.
- A few are caused by car crashes, falls, or sports injuries.
- If the spinal cord is damaged, it can cause weakness or paralysis in the legs. This is called paraplegia.
- The spine must be kept stable to protect the nerves.
- If the spinal cord is involved, surgery is needed right away.
- For less serious fractures, pain medicine and physical therapy are usually enough.
- The goal of treatment is to help you move well again and avoid long-term pain.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Spinal Fracture?

The spine is made of 33 small bones called vertebrae. These are grouped into five sections:

- Neck (cervical)
- Chest (thoracic)
- Lower back (lumbar)
- Sacrum (a fused group of bones at the base of the spine)
- Tailbone (coccyx)

Most vertebrae have a front part (vertebral body), a back part (vertebral arch), and bony projections. The hole in the center of each vertebra forms a tunnel when stacked. This tunnel is called the spinal canal.

The spinal canal holds the spinal cord. The spinal cord is a bundle of nerves that sends messages between your brain and the rest of your body.

Most spinal fractures happen because of weak bones from osteoporosis. Less often, they happen after a hard fall, car crash, or sports injury.

A fracture is **stable** if the spinal canal is not narrowed and the spinal cord is not damaged. There is no risk of nerve injury in stable fractures.

A fracture is **unstable** if the spinal cord is damaged or at risk of damage. This can lead to nerve problems.

Doctors decide how to treat a spinal fracture based on how serious it is and whether the spine is stable. The key question is: Is the spinal cord at risk?

> **Important:** After a serious accident, do not move the injured person unless absolutely necessary. Wait for medical help. Moving them too soon can cause more harm.

---

## What Are the Signs of a Spinal Fracture?

People with osteoporosis often have weak bones. This can lead to spinal fractures.

- About half of people with this type of fracture feel no pain at all.
- Others feel back pain. The pain is worse when standing or walking. It is better when lying down.
- It becomes hard to stand straight or keep balance.
- If several vertebrae are broken, the spine can shorten. This makes the person lose height.

Fractures in the neck (cervical spine) may show visible signs:

- Bones may be out of place.
- Swelling or bruising may appear.
- Severe neck pain can happen.
- Numbness, tingling, or weakness in the arms or legs may mean the spinal cord is damaged.

---

## What Causes Spinal Fractures?

The most common cause is **osteoporosis**. This is when bones lose strength and become porous. They break more easily.

In osteoporosis, spinal fractures often happen without a fall. They occur when a disk in the spine gets squeezed. These are called **compression fractures**.

Spinal fractures can also happen from strong force, such as:

- Car crashes
- Falling from a height
- High-impact sports

Common accidents that cause spinal fractures include:

- Car crashes or rollovers
- Falls from motorcycles or bicycles
- Skiing, horseback riding, or rock climbing accidents
- Falls from ladders or scaffolding at work

---

## What Increases the Risk of a Spinal Fracture?

Some people are more likely to break a spine bone. Risk factors include:

- Playing contact sports like wrestling or ice hockey
- Getting older – bone strength naturally decreases with age
- Having osteoporosis – bones become weak and break easily
- Having had a previous bone fracture
- Bone cancer
- Bone infections (like osteomyelitis)
- Overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism)
- Low estrogen levels after menopause in women
- Smoking
- Drinking too much alcohol
- Not getting enough vitamin D
- Long-term use of steroid medicines (like cortisone)
- Chemotherapy or radiation therapy

---

## How Common Are Spinal Fractures?

Compression fractures are common. They are mostly caused by osteoporosis.

Fractures from falls or accidents are less common. In about half of these cases, the middle or lower back is affected.

About one in four people with a spinal fracture also has another fracture. Often, this is in the neck.

---

## What Is the Outlook After a Spinal Fracture?

- Stable fractures (no spinal cord damage) usually heal on their own. Surgery is not needed.
- Up to 40% of people with serious spinal cord injury develop long-term nerve problems.
- The more severe the injury, the greater the chance of lasting symptoms.
- Early treatment helps with recovery, even if there is some weakness or numbness.
- Many people with partial paralysis get better. About 60 to 80% recover fully or partly.
- If the injury is severe, you may not be able to return to your old job.
- If the neck is injured, 5 to 10% of people die. This is more likely after a motorcycle or car crash.

---

## How Can Spinal Fractures Be Prevented?

You can reduce your risk by taking safety steps:

- Always wear seat belts in cars.
- Wear helmets and protective gear when riding bikes or playing risky sports.
- Use safety equipment when working on ladders or scaffolding.
- Wear a safety harness when climbing trees or mountains.

Staying active helps keep bones strong. Regular exercise builds muscle and supports the spine.

Eat a healthy, balanced diet. Avoid smoking and limit alcohol.

If you have osteoporosis, medicine can help prevent future fractures. For example, bisphosphonates slow down bone loss.

Older adults can prevent falls by:

- Removing loose rugs or clutter
- Installing grab bars in bathrooms
- Using walking aids if needed
- Reviewing medications with a doctor – some can cause dizziness

---

## How Are Spinal Fractures Diagnosed?

Doctors start with a physical exam. They check the spine by gently pressing on it to find pain or tenderness.

Imaging tests help confirm the diagnosis:

- A **CT scan** gives detailed pictures of the spine. It shows the exact location and type of fracture.
- An **MRI scan** shows soft tissues like the spinal cord, disks, and ligaments. It helps detect nerve or disk damage.

Doctors also do neurological tests. These check for numbness, weakness, or loss of movement. They help determine if the spinal cord is injured.

---

## How Are Spinal Fractures Treated?

If you have a serious injury, call emergency services right away (dial 112).

Until help arrives:

- Lie still.
- Do not move the person unless absolutely necessary.
- Do not carry or drag them.

Treatment aims to:

- Stabilize the spine
- Protect the spinal cord and nerves

Initial treatment includes:

- Rest in bed
- Pain relief medicine

Pain medicine helps prevent long-term back pain.

For mild fractures, treatment may include:

- Medication
- Physical therapy
- Occupational therapy
- Behavioral therapy

These help you start moving again safely and quickly.

If pain continues or movement is still limited, surgery may be needed.

Surgery is required immediately if:

- The spinal canal is narrowed
- The spinal cord is damaged

> **Important:** If the spinal cord is damaged, the injury may not be fully reversible. The person may have lasting physical or nerve problems.

---

## What Happens After Surgery?

After a stable fracture (no nerve damage), early rehab helps you return to daily life faster.

Rehab can start during hospital treatment.

The type of rehab depends on your mobility and injury level:

- Inpatient rehab: You stay at a facility.
- Outpatient rehab: You go to appointments and return home.

Rehab focuses on:

- Getting back normal posture and movement
- Physical therapy and exercise
- Occupational therapy to help with daily tasks
- Sports or movement training
- Psychological support

Rehab also teaches how to:

- Move safely in daily life
- Adjust your work environment to protect your back

For severe fractures with nerve damage or paralysis (paraplegia), early care at a specialized center is essential.

---

## What Aftercare Is Needed?

After surgery:

- Avoid heavy lifting or intense physical activity until the bones heal.
- Gradually increase activity as healing progresses.

Special follow-up programs help people return to work and normal life.

Most people return to work about three months after the injury.

These programs teach:

- How to change habits and lifestyle
- How to manage daily tasks safely
- How to stay on track with recovery

Hospital and rehab center staff can help with:

- Information about benefits and financial support
- What health insurance covers
- How to apply for help

> **Important:** If you have statutory health insurance and cannot care for yourself after surgery, you may get help at home. You may also qualify for transitional care. What is covered depends on your level of disability.

# Drop in Blood Pressure When Standing Up (Orthostatic Hypotension)

This condition happens when your blood pressure drops suddenly when you stand up from sitting or lying down. It can make you feel dizzy, weak, or even cause you to faint. There are different ways to treat it, depending on what is causing it and how bad the symptoms are.

---

## Quick Facts

- Orthostatic hypotension means your blood pressure drops when you stand up.
- It is most common in people over 65 years old.
- It can be caused by certain medicines or linked to long-term health problems like Parkinson’s disease, dementia, or diabetes.
- In some cases, doctors do not know the exact cause.
- Simple steps like standing up slowly or wearing support stockings can help.
- Medicine may be needed if symptoms are very bad.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Orthostatic Hypotension?

Orthostatic hypotension is a type of low blood pressure. It happens when your blood pressure drops quickly after you stand up from sitting or lying down. "Orthostatic" means standing upright.

When your blood pressure drops, you may feel dizzy, see blurry, or feel confused. In some cases, you may faint. These symptoms go away fast if you sit or lie down again. This can help you avoid passing out.

The drop in blood pressure can happen just once. Or it can happen again and again over time.

Most people who get this problem are over 65. They often have other health issues. They also take many different medicines. Some of these medicines can cause blood pressure to drop when standing up.

Simple steps can help reduce dizziness and other symptoms. Your doctor may also suggest medicine if needed.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may feel dizzy, sleepy, or even pass out for up to 30 minutes after standing up from sitting or lying down.

Older adults may also have a drop in blood pressure 15 to 90 minutes after eating. This is called postprandial hypotension.

As soon as you sit or lie down, you usually feel better.

Other possible symptoms include:
- Blurry or foggy vision
- Rarely, headaches or chest pain

---

## What Causes This Problem?

Your body normally keeps blood pressure steady when you stand up. But in orthostatic hypotension, this system does not work well.

Gravity pulls blood into your legs and belly when you stand. If your body does not respond fast enough, less blood reaches your brain. This causes symptoms.

This problem often happens with other long-term health conditions.

It is common in people with:
- Heart or blood vessel problems
- Nerve problems, such as Parkinson’s disease or some types of dementia
- Diabetes, which can damage nerves that control blood pressure

Some medicines can cause this issue. These include:
- Drugs for depression
- Blood pressure medicines, especially if taken for many years

Drinking too much alcohol or using certain drugs can also cause blood pressure to drop when standing.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Some people only have this problem once in a while. They may feel dizzy or faint a few times, but it does not happen often.

Others may pass out many times when standing. This can lead to falls and injuries.

If this happens more often, it can cause serious harm. It also increases the risk of accidents.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Talk to your family doctor if you have symptoms.

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and your health history. They will check your blood pressure and pulse while you are lying down, sitting, and standing up.

They will measure your blood pressure right after you stand and again about one minute later.

If needed, a specialist may do a tilt table test. You lie on a special table that slowly tilts you into a standing position. Your blood pressure and pulse are checked several times during the test.

---

## How Is It Treated?

If a medicine is causing the problem, your doctor may switch you to a different one.

You can take steps to reduce dizziness and fainting. These include:

- Stand up slowly, especially in the morning.
- Do simple leg exercises before standing, like tightening and relaxing your calf muscles.
- Avoid heavy activity in hot weather.
- Wear support stockings.
- Drink enough fluids every day.
- Eat less food high in carbohydrates, like potatoes, white bread, and white rice — especially if your blood pressure drops after eating.

If these steps do not help and your symptoms are very bad, your doctor may prescribe medicine.

One medicine used is fludrocortisone. It helps keep blood pressure stable by balancing water and salt in your body.

Possible side effects include:
- Swelling in the legs or ankles (fluid buildup)
- Weight gain
- Headaches
- Stomach ulcers

Always talk to your doctor before starting or stopping any medicine.

# Urticaria (Hives)

Urticaria, also called hives, is a skin problem. It causes itchy bumps on the skin. Sometimes it also causes painful swelling under the skin. This swelling is called angioedema. Both can happen at the same time.

Medicine can help reduce the symptoms. This page explains the signs, causes, how doctors diagnose it, and how it is treated.

---

## Quick Facts

- Urticaria can be short-term (acute) or long-term (chronic).
- Itchy bumps appear on the skin. These bumps can be small or join together to form larger areas.
- Sometimes, fluid builds up under the skin, causing painful swelling.
- Urticaria can be a warning sign of a serious allergic reaction. This is an emergency.
- Long-term urticaria is split into two types: one that happens without a clear cause, and one triggered by outside factors.
- Doctors usually prescribe allergy medicines called antihistamines.
- Urticaria can make daily life very hard.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Urticaria?

Urticaria is a skin condition. It causes itchy, raised bumps on the skin. These bumps are often the size of a coin. They can appear alone or join together.

Sometimes, the skin under the surface swells up. This is called angioedema. It can be painful and may happen at the same time as the bumps.

There are two main types:

- **Acute urticaria** lasts less than 6 weeks.
- **Chronic urticaria** lasts more than 6 weeks.

Chronic urticaria has two forms:

- **Spontaneous**: No clear cause can be found. This is also called idiopathic urticaria.
- **Induced**: Caused by outside triggers like cold, heat, pressure, or sunlight.

Chronic urticaria can be very stressful. It can affect work, sleep, and daily activities. Some people with chronic urticaria also feel sad or anxious.

Urticaria is not contagious. You cannot catch it from someone else.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

More than half of people with chronic spontaneous urticaria get both hives and swelling under the skin.

- About one in three get only hives.
- About one in ten get only swelling under the skin.

### Symptoms of Hives (Wheals)

- A raised bump appears. It can be any size.
- The bump is usually red around the edges.
- The skin itches. Sometimes it burns.
- The redness fades within 30 minutes to 24 hours.

### Symptoms of Angioedema

- A sudden, noticeable swelling appears.
- The area may be painful or itchy.
- The swelling goes down after about 72 hours.

---

## What Causes Urticaria?

The bumps and swelling happen because of a reaction in the immune system. Special cells called mast cells release a substance called histamine. This causes blood vessels to widen and leak fluid. This leads to redness and swelling.

### Causes of Acute Urticaria

- Infections like colds, rotavirus, or strep bacteria.
- Allergies to things like cow’s milk, bee stings, pollen, or animal fur.
- Some medicines, such as those for rheumatism or high blood pressure.
- In 30 to 50 percent of cases, no cause is found.

### Causes of Chronic Urticaria

- In 80 to 90 percent of cases, no cause is found. This is called idiopathic urticaria.
- In some cases, the body’s immune system attacks its own healthy tissue. This is called an autoimmune reaction.
- Antibodies called IgE can trigger mast cells to release more histamine.
- Other health issues may make urticaria worse. These include:
  - Stomach inflammation (gastritis)
  - Acid reflux
  - Inflammation of the gallbladder or bile ducts
  - Infections
  - Rarely, cancer

### Induced Urticaria

This is less common. It is caused by outside triggers, such as:
- Cold
- Heat
- Pressure (like tight clothes)
- Sunlight

---

## How Common Is Urticaria?

- Between 9% and 20% of people will get hives at some point in their lives.
- It can happen at any age, but most cases occur between ages 20 and 40.
- Up to 5% of people have long-term urticaria.
- Women are twice as likely as men to have long-term urticaria.
- Spontaneous chronic urticaria is two to three times more common than induced urticaria.

---

## How Does Urticaria Progress?

- If symptoms last less than 6 weeks, it is called acute urticaria.
- If symptoms last more than 6 weeks, it is called chronic urticaria.

---

## How Is Urticaria Diagnosed?

Doctors first rule out other similar conditions. These include:
- Urticarial vasculitis (a type of blood vessel inflammation)
- Medication allergy
- Contact dermatitis (skin reaction from touching something)
- Serious infections or inflammation

Doctors also ask how much the condition affects your daily life. They may use special questionnaires to find out.

### For Acute Urticaria

- No special tests are usually needed.
- The doctor will ask about:
  - How long the bumps or swelling have been there
  - If you or your family have had this before
  - If you have joint pain, stomach pain, or other symptoms
  - If you have any long-term health problems like rheumatoid arthritis or food allergies
  - If you take painkillers with acetylsalicylic acid (ASS)
  - If you take medicines for rheumatism or high blood pressure
  - If you recently went on holiday or have a stressful job
  - If you are under stress

### For Chronic Urticaria

- Additional tests may help find hidden causes.
- These can include blood tests or checks for infections or allergies.

---

## How Is Urticaria Treated?

The goal is to find and avoid triggers. The main goal is to reduce symptoms.

### Treatment for Acute Urticaria

- Doctors prescribe antihistamine tablets. These are allergy medicines that help stop itching and swelling.
- If symptoms are severe or antihistamines do not work, the doctor may:
  - Increase the dose
  - Use other medicines like corticosteroids (anti-inflammatory drugs)
  - Use special antibodies (biologic drugs)

### Treatment for Chronic Urticaria

- Doctors look for triggers. Some medicines can make symptoms worse.
  - Painkillers with acetylsalicylic acid (ASS)
  - Certain medicines for rheumatism or high blood pressure
- If these are the cause, the doctor can help you switch to safer options.

> **Important:** Acute urticaria with or without swelling can be a sign of a serious allergic reaction. This is an emergency. Seek help right away if you have trouble breathing, swelling in the face or throat, or feel dizzy.

---

## Where Can I Get Support?

You are not alone. Support groups can help you and your family.

- You can learn more about your condition.
- You can share your experiences.
- You can get advice from others who have similar problems.

Find a group through the **National Contact and Information Point for Encouraging and Supporting Self-Help Groups (NAKOS)** website.

---

## What Else Should I Know?

- Chronic urticaria should be treated by a skin doctor with experience in this condition.
- Ask the doctor’s office about their experience with urticaria.
- More information is available at **allergieinformationsdienst.de** (in German).

# Vaginal Prolapse and Uterine Prolapse

The muscles and connective tissue in the pelvic floor can become weak. This can cause the uterus, bladder, or rectum to drop down inside the pelvis. This is called a prolapse. It can be treated with pelvic floor exercises, special supports, or surgery.

---

## Quick Facts

- Many women have some weakness in the pelvic floor at some point in their lives.
- The uterus, bladder, or rectum can drop down if the pelvic floor is too weak to hold them up.
- About half of all women have mild pelvic floor weakness during their lives.
- Around 3 out of every 100 women have a prolapse that causes symptoms.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Vaginal Prolapse and Uterine Prolapse?

Normally, the muscles and connective tissue in the pelvis hold the organs in place. But in some women, these tissues weaken over time.

When this happens, the uterus, bladder, or rectum can drop down. In some cases, the vagina bulges out of the vaginal opening. In severe cases, the uterus may come out of the vagina. Doctors call this vaginal or uterine prolapse.

The most common type is bladder prolapse. This happens when the bladder pushes into the front wall of the vagina. But because the organs are connected, they often drop together.

Treatment usually starts with pelvic floor exercises. Some women use a silicone support called a pessary. Surgery is another option.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many women with mild pelvic floor weakness have no symptoms. But if the organs drop further, you may notice:

- A feeling of pressure or heaviness in the pelvis
- A sensation that something is pushing out
- Trouble controlling your bladder
- Needing to urinate more often
- Difficulty starting to urinate
- Aching or pulling pain in the lower belly
- Pain during sex
- Trouble having a bowel movement
- Back pain or lower back pain
- Sores or bleeding in the vagina

These symptoms often get worse when standing, walking, or pushing during a bowel movement. They usually improve when lying down.

When the vagina or uterus sticks out, it can be very distressing. It can affect your self-image and your sex life. Many women feel ashamed.

---

## What Causes Prolapse?

Prolapse happens when the pelvic floor muscles and connective tissue are too weak. This is called pelvic floor weakness.

Some women are born with weaker connective tissue. Other causes include:

- **Childbirth through the vagina:** This can stretch or damage the pelvic floor. Cesarean birth does not increase the risk.
- **Age:** As we get older, muscles and connective tissue lose strength. This makes the pelvic floor less stable.
- **Being very overweight:** Extra weight puts more pressure on the pelvic floor.

Other things that increase pressure on the pelvic floor may also contribute. These include:

- Lifting heavy objects often
- Long-term coughing (like from smoking or lung disease)
- Chronic constipation

But we do not yet have strong proof that these factors cause prolapse.

It is not clear if removing the uterus (hysterectomy) increases the risk. But doctors think the bladder and bowel may have less support after the uterus is removed. This could make them drop more easily.

---

## How Common Is Prolapse?

- About half of all women have some degree of pelvic floor weakness during their lives.
- Around 3 out of every 100 women have a prolapse that causes noticeable symptoms.

---

## How Does Prolapse Develop?

There are four stages of prolapse. The stage depends on how far the organs have dropped.

- **Stage 1:** The organs have dropped only a little.
- **Stage 2:** The organs have dropped to the opening of the vagina.
- **Stage 3:** The organs stick out of the vagina by up to one centimeter.
- **Stage 4:** The organs stick out a lot from the vagina.

Most prolapses are mild. Some mild cases may get better on their own over time. But some slowly get worse.

About half of women with mild prolapse (Stage 1 or 2) also have stress incontinence. This means they leak urine when they cough, sneeze, or exercise. The bladder can no longer hold urine under pressure.

In more severe cases (Stage 3 or 4), the organs may block the urethra. This makes it hard to empty the bladder completely.

---

## How Can Prolapse Be Prevented?

You can help protect your pelvic floor by:

- Doing pelvic floor exercises regularly
- Doing postnatal exercises after childbirth
- Avoiding heavy lifting or carrying
- Treating long-term coughs
- Treating constipation
- Losing weight if you are very overweight

But we do not yet have strong evidence that these steps actually prevent prolapse.

---

## How Is Prolapse Diagnosed?

You may see a doctor because of pelvic discomfort or bladder problems. A doctor can often see a severe prolapse during a physical exam.

To check for mild prolapse, the doctor will:

- Feel the organs from outside the body
- Examine the vagina using a speculum
- Press on the rectum to check the position of the organs in the back of the pelvis

These exams are usually enough to find a prolapse and see how bad it is.

The doctor may also do a cough stress test. You will be asked to cough hard while the doctor watches. If you leak urine, you have stress incontinence.

If you have trouble emptying your bladder, the doctor may do a post-void residual test. You will urinate first. Then the doctor will use an ultrasound to check if any urine is left in the bladder.

---

## How Is Prolapse Treated?

Treatment depends on your symptoms, not just how far the organs have dropped.

Your doctor will consider:

- What symptoms bother you the most
- Your age
- Whether you want to have children in the future
- Whether you want to keep your uterus
- Which organ is affected and how far it has dropped
- How well non-surgical treatments work
- Whether you have other health problems, like incontinence

Treatment options include:

- **Pelvic floor exercises:** These strengthen the muscles in the pelvic floor. They are also called Kegel exercises.
- **Therapeutic pessaries:** These are soft, shaped devices made of rubber or silicone. They are placed in the vagina to support the organs. Do not confuse these with birth control pessaries.
- **Surgery:** This lifts and holds the organs in place. In some cases, the uterus may be removed. But in most cases, the uterus stays.

Many women find relief with pelvic floor exercises or a pessary. If these do not help, or if symptoms get worse, surgery may be an option. The uterus is usually kept during surgery.

For help choosing the right treatment, you can use the decision aid from [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

# Ovarian Cancer – Simple Explanation

Ovarian cancer often has no symptoms in the early stages. By the time it is found, it is usually already advanced. The main treatment is surgery. This article explains how doctors find ovarian cancer and what treatments are available.

---

## Quick Facts

- Ovarian cancer is also called ovarian carcinoma.
- In the early stages, most women do not have any symptoms. The cancer is often found at a later stage.
- There are different types of ovarian cancer.
- Surgery is the main treatment. Most patients also get chemotherapy after surgery.
- For advanced cases, doctors may use targeted therapy.
- Radiation therapy is rarely used for ovarian cancer.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Ovarian Cancer?

Ovarian cancer is a type of cancer that starts in the ovaries. The ovaries are small organs in the female pelvis that produce eggs and hormones.

The ovaries are made of different types of tissue. Cancer can start in any of these tissues. That is why there are different kinds of ovarian cancer:

- About 90 to 100 out of every 100 ovarian cancers start in the outer layer of the ovary. These are called epithelial tumors.
- Some tumors are called borderline tumors. They are not clearly cancer or not cancer. They are watched closely.
- Less often, cancer can start in the supportive tissue of the ovary. These are called sex cord stromal tumors.
- Rarely, cancer can start directly from the egg cells. These are called germ-cell tumors.

> **Important:** Cancer of the lining of the abdomen (peritoneal cancer) and cancer of the fallopian tubes are treated the same way as ovarian cancer.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Ovarian cancer often grows without causing any symptoms. The tumor can grow large before it causes problems.

The following signs may mean ovarian cancer:

- Feeling full even after eating a small amount
- Swelling or bloating in the belly
- Unexplained belly pain or stomach discomfort
- Swelling in the belly or unexplained weight loss
- Needing to urinate more often than usual

These symptoms can also happen with non-cancerous conditions. But if they happen often or last for more than a few weeks, see a doctor. This is especially important for women over 50.

Your general doctor or gynecologist can check for possible causes. They may refer you for more tests if needed.

---

## What Causes Ovarian Cancer?

The risk of ovarian cancer goes up with age. Being overweight also increases the risk.

Hormones play a role too. Women who have never been pregnant or who have fertility problems may have a higher risk. Hormone therapy after menopause can also raise the risk.

But some things lower the risk:

- Having many children
- Breastfeeding for a long time
- Taking birth control pills
- Having your fallopian tubes sealed (a type of sterilization)

About 1 in 4 or 5 cases of ovarian cancer are linked to inherited genes. The most common genes involved are BRCA1 and BRCA2. These genes are linked to breast and ovarian cancer.

If close family members have had breast or ovarian cancer, your risk may be higher.

---

## Can Ovarian Cancer Be Screened For?

There is no official screening program for ovarian cancer in Germany.

Tests like vaginal ultrasounds and blood tests for tumor markers have not been proven to reduce deaths from ovarian cancer.

Experts do not recommend screening even for women with a family history of the disease.

---

## How Is Ovarian Cancer Diagnosed?

If a doctor suspects ovarian cancer, they will do several tests:

- Ask about your medical history, symptoms, and risk factors.
- Do a physical exam. The doctor will feel your belly and check your reproductive organs through the vagina.
- Use a mirror to look inside the pelvis.
- Do a vaginal ultrasound to see the ovaries.
- Use imaging tests like CT, MRI, or PET scans to see how far the cancer has spread.

The final diagnosis comes from surgery. The tumor is removed and examined under a microscope. This tells doctors if it is cancer and what type it is.

> **Important:** Most ovarian tumors are not cancer. Many young women get harmless cysts on their ovaries. Some cancers come from other parts of the body and spread to the ovaries. These are not ovarian cancer and are treated differently.

For more details on how tests work and what they can show, visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## How Is Ovarian Cancer Treated?

Doctors choose treatment based on:

- How far the cancer has spread
- The type of tumor
- Your overall health

The main treatment is surgery followed by chemotherapy. In early cases, surgery alone may be enough.

> **Important:** Surgery is not only for treatment. It is also used to find out the stage of the cancer. Doctors may talk about several treatment options before surgery, even if not all are used.

### Surgery

The goal is to remove as much of the tumor as possible.

- If the cancer is still only in the ovaries, it is called localized. Doctors check this during surgery.
- In about one in three women with localized cancer, hidden spread is found. This means the cancer is more advanced than first thought.
- In about 75 out of 100 cases, the cancer has already spread to other organs in the pelvis or belly, or to other parts of the body.

For advanced cases, surgeons aim to remove all visible cancer. They may also remove parts of the intestines or other organs if needed.

### Chemotherapy and Other Treatments

Most patients get chemotherapy after surgery. This uses medicine to slow down or stop cancer cell growth.

Other treatments include:

- **Targeted therapy:** Drugs that attack specific parts of cancer cells. Used in advanced cases.
- **Supportive care:** Treatments to ease symptoms and improve quality of life.

Radiation therapy is rarely used for ovarian cancer.

For more information on chemotherapy and other treatments, visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## What Happens After Treatment?

Rehabilitation helps you recover after treatment. It can help you regain strength and deal with side effects.

Rehab may include:

- Exercises to build strength
- Help with digestion and eating well
- Support for side effects like tiredness or nerve pain
- Counseling to help with emotional stress

---

## Aftercare and Monitoring

Cancer and its treatment can affect your body and mind. There is also a risk the cancer may come back.

Regular check-ups help find a return of cancer early. They also help catch long-term side effects of treatment.

Check-ups include:

- Talking about symptoms
- Physical exams
- Gynecological mirror exam
- Palpation of the belly
- Rectal exam
- Vaginal ultrasound

> **Important:** If you have any new or worrying symptoms, see your doctor right away—even if it’s not your scheduled appointment.

If the cancer cannot be cured, regular check-ups help manage symptoms early. Supportive care can help you live well for as long as possible.

---

## Life After Ovarian Cancer

Surgery for ovarian cancer is major. It is done under general anesthesia. Recovery can take weeks or months.

- You will have a large scar.
- Scar tissue (adhesions) can form inside the belly. These may cause pain or digestive issues.
- A hernia in the belly wall can develop later. This can cause pain or discomfort.

Removing both ovaries means you will go into early menopause. You may have hot flashes, mood swings, or other menopause symptoms. Talk to your doctor about hormone therapy if these are hard to handle.

Cancer and treatment can affect your sex life. Talking with your partner and your doctor can help.

Many women want to help their recovery. What helps depends on the person. Options include:

- Gentle exercise to fight tiredness
- Eating a healthy, balanced diet
- Talking to a psycho-oncologist if you feel overwhelmed by fear or anxiety

If the cancer is no longer curable, good care is very important. Doctors can help with:

- Fluid buildup in the belly (ascites)
- Pain
- Digestive problems
- Emotional support

This care helps you live well for as long as possible.

> **Need help?** You can find a psycho-oncologist, a self-help group, or a cancer support service through the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## Who Can Help With Information?

Ovarian cancer is treated by a team of doctors. Some hospitals are specially certified to treat this cancer.

The German Cancer Society checks hospitals to make sure they meet high standards. These are called certified gynecological cancer centers.

You can find a list of these centers on the **OncoMAP** website.

For more information about daily life, support, and coping, visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

You can also contact them directly:

- Freephone: 0800 420 30 40
- Email: krebsinformationsdienst@dkfz.de

# Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm

If part of the main blood vessel in your tummy stretches and bulges out, it is called an abdominal aortic aneurysm. This condition is more common in men than in women. Most of the time, it does not cause any problems. But if it bursts, it is a life-threatening emergency that needs immediate treatment.

---

## Quick Facts

- The main blood vessel in your tummy is called the aorta.
- If a section of the aorta in the tummy bulges out and grows larger than 3 centimeters, it is an aneurysm.
- Most aneurysms do not cause symptoms. You may not even know you have one.
- If the aneurysm bursts, it can cause sudden, severe pain and massive internal bleeding.
- The size of the aneurysm and your other health risks help doctors decide how likely it is to burst.
- About 2 out of every 100 men between the ages of 65 and 75 have this condition.
- Men over 65 can get a free screening test for this condition during their regular health check-up.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is an Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm?

An abdominal aortic aneurysm is a weak spot in the wall of the aorta. The aorta carries oxygen-rich blood from your heart to the rest of your body. The part of the aorta that runs through your tummy is called the abdominal aorta.

Normally, the abdominal aorta is about 2 centimeters wide. If one section becomes wider than 3 centimeters and bulges out, it is called an aneurysm.

Most aneurysms do not cause symptoms. They are often found by chance during other tests. But if the aneurysm keeps growing, it can burst. A burst aneurysm is a medical emergency and can be deadly.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people with an abdominal aortic aneurysm feel no symptoms at all. The condition often goes unnoticed.

If the aneurysm is large, you might feel:

- Pain in your back
- Pain in your belly
- Pain on the sides of your body

If the aneurysm bursts, you will feel sudden, severe pain in your back or side. The pain may spread to your groin. You may also feel dizzy, weak, or faint. You could lose consciousness. This is because a large amount of blood leaks into your belly. This is a life-threatening emergency.

---

## What Causes an Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm?

The wall of the aorta can weaken over time. This can happen because of aging. High blood pressure can also put extra stress on the blood vessel wall.

Smoking is a major risk factor. It damages the blood vessels and makes aneurysms more likely.

Once a weak spot starts to bulge, it often gets bigger over time. The larger it gets, the higher the risk of it bursting.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

Several things can raise your risk of developing an abdominal aortic aneurysm:

- **Age:** Most cases happen in people over 65.
- **Smoking:** This is the most important risk factor you can control.
- **High blood pressure:** This puts extra strain on blood vessels.
- **Coronary heart disease:** This increases your risk.
- **High blood fat levels:** High cholesterol and other fats in the blood can contribute.
- **Family history:** If a close relative had an aneurysm, your risk is higher.
- **Fair skin:** People with fair skin may be more likely to develop one.

Men are much more likely to have this condition than women.

---

## How Common Is It?

About 2 out of every 100 men between 65 and 75 years old have an abdominal aortic aneurysm. The chance increases with age.

Women are much less likely to have this condition.

---

## How Does It Develop?

Most aneurysms grow slowly and do not cause problems. Only some get large enough to be dangerous.

If the aneurysm grows too much, it can burst. When this happens, blood leaks into the belly. This is a life-threatening emergency.
