The risk of bursting is higher if:

- The aneurysm is growing fast
- The aneurysm is 5.5 centimeters or larger in diameter

For men with an aneurysm larger than 5.5 centimeters, there is a 3 to 6 percent chance it will burst within one year.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use ultrasound scans to check for an abdominal aortic aneurysm. This test is painless and uses sound waves to create images of the blood vessels.

The scan measures the width of the aorta. If it is wider than 3 centimeters, it is considered an aneurysm.

If you have symptoms like back pain or belly pain, your doctor may do an ultrasound to find the cause.

---

## Can Screening Find It Early?

Yes, screening with ultrasound can find an aneurysm before it causes any problems.

If a small aneurysm is found, doctors can check it regularly to see if it is growing. This helps prevent it from becoming large enough to burst.

Screening for men over 65 has been shown to reduce deaths from aneurysm rupture.

There is only one high-quality study on screening for women. It found no clear benefit for women.

> **Important:** Screening is not perfect. It can sometimes find an aneurysm that would never have caused harm. This is called overdiagnosis. It can lead to unnecessary surgery. Surgery itself carries risks. Some people feel very anxious after learning they have an aneurysm, even if it is small and not dangerous.

For more information, see the brochure from the Joint Federal Committee (B-GA).

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the size of the aneurysm, how fast it is growing, and your overall health.

- If the aneurysm is smaller than 5.5 centimeters, doctors usually just monitor it with regular check-ups.
- Smokers are strongly encouraged to quit. Smoking can make the aneurysm grow faster.
- If you have high blood pressure or high cholesterol, your doctor will recommend treatment to control these conditions.
- It is not yet clear if blood pressure or cholesterol medicines can slow the growth of an aneurysm or lower the risk of rupture.

If the risk of rupture is high, surgery is the only way to prevent it. There are two types of surgery:

1. **Open surgery:** A large cut is made in the belly. The damaged part of the aorta is removed. A strong artificial tube (graft) is sewn in its place.
2. **Endovascular repair:** A small cut is made in the groin. A thin tube (stent) is guided through the blood vessel to the aneurysm. It is placed inside the aneurysm to stop blood from flowing into it.

Both surgeries carry risks. They must be carefully considered. There is still a small chance the aneurysm could burst during or after surgery.

For more details on when surgery is needed, visit gesundheitsinformation.de.

---

## What Happens After Surgery?

Open surgery is a major operation. After surgery, rehabilitation helps you recover.

Rehabilitation helps you slowly return to your normal daily activities. It can improve your strength, energy, and overall well-being.

The goal is to reduce the negative effects of surgery and help you live a better life.

---

## Living with an Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm

Learning you have an aneurysm can bring mixed feelings.

Some people feel relieved. They are glad the problem was found early. Regular check-ups help them feel safe.

Others feel scared. They wish they had never known. The idea of a possible rupture can be very stressful.

Many people live with the knowledge that they are at risk. Even small pains in the belly or back can feel like a sign of danger. This can be frightening, even if the pain is not caused by the aneurysm.

Some people start avoiding physical activity. They become more cautious. They worry that exercise might cause the aneurysm to burst.

It is important to talk to your doctor about your fears. You can still live a full life with an aneurysm. Your doctor can help you understand your risks and make safe choices.

# Dunbar Syndrome

Dunbar syndrome is a rare condition.  
It can cause stomach pain that comes back often.  
This happens when a strong band of tissue presses on a large blood vessel in the belly.  
The blood vessel supplies blood to the stomach, liver, and small intestine.

---

## Quick Facts

- A band of tissue in the chest presses on a major blood vessel in the belly.  
- This condition is rare.  
- It happens more often in women than in men.  
- It usually affects people between the ages of 40 and 60.  
- It is more common in people with a slim build.  
- It can also happen in children.  
- Many people have no symptoms at all.  
- When symptoms do occur, stomach pain is the most common.  
- Pain often starts after eating.  
- Some people feel pain during or after physical activity.  
- Others have pain all the time, even when resting.  
- Doctors use special imaging tests to see the blood vessels and blood flow.  
- Surgery is the only treatment that works.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Dunbar Syndrome?

The celiac artery is a large blood vessel that sends blood to the upper belly organs.  
It includes the stomach, liver, and small intestine.  
A band of tissue called the median arcuate ligament sits near this artery.  
This ligament is part of the diaphragm, the muscle that helps you breathe.  
When the ligament presses on the celiac artery and causes pain, it is called Dunbar syndrome.  

Other names for this condition include:
- Median arcuate ligament syndrome
- Celiac artery compression syndrome
- Celiac axis syndrome
- Truncus coeliacus compression syndrome
- Harjola-Marable syndrome

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Stomach pain is the most common symptom.  
The pain can be mild or severe.  
It often starts after eating.  
Some people feel pain during or after exercise.  
Others have pain all the time, even when not moving.

Other possible symptoms include:
- Losing weight without trying
- Feeling sick to your stomach
- Vomiting
- Diarrhea
- Gurgling sounds from the stomach
- A feeling of pressure in the upper belly
- Food staying in the stomach longer than normal

---

## What Causes Dunbar Syndrome?

The median arcuate ligament connects the two sides of the diaphragm.  
It forms the front of the opening through which the aorta passes.  
Below this ligament, the celiac artery branches off from the aorta.  
This artery feeds blood to the stomach, liver, and small intestine.

The position of the ligament and artery can vary from person to person.  
In some people, the ligament sits too low.  
In rare cases, the celiac artery starts higher up on the aorta.  
Both of these differences can cause the ligament to press on the artery.

Most people do not have any problems.  
Other blood vessels can still supply blood to the belly organs.  
But in some people, the pressure causes symptoms.  

Doctors think another factor may be involved.  
A group of nerve cells called the celiac ganglion is near the celiac artery.  
This nerve group is part of a larger network that controls digestion.  
The ligament may also press on these nerves.  
This could be why some people feel pain even if the blood vessel is not fully blocked.

---

## How Common Is Dunbar Syndrome?

Dunbar syndrome is rare.  
It affects more women than men.  
It most often appears in adults between 40 and 60 years old.  
It is more common in people with a slender body type.  
It can also happen in children.

---

## What Is the Long-Term Outlook?

If the artery stays pressed on over time, it can change.  
The wall of the artery may thicken.  
This can lead to a partial or full blockage.  
Below the narrowed area, the artery may bulge out.  
This bulge is called an aneurysm.  
An aneurysm can be dangerous if it bursts.

---

## How Is Dunbar Syndrome Diagnosed?

The symptoms of Dunbar syndrome are similar to those of other stomach and digestive problems.  
These include issues with the stomach, intestines, gallbladder, or liver.  
Because many people have no symptoms, doctors first rule out other conditions.

Tests may include:
- Blood tests to check for signs of illness
- Ultrasound scans of the liver, pancreas, and gallbladder
- Endoscopy or gastroscopy to look inside the stomach
- Colonoscopy to examine the bowel

To see the blood vessels clearly, doctors use special imaging:
- Doppler ultrasound
- CT scan
- MRI scan

A Doppler ultrasound with a CT or MRI scan gives the most reliable results.

Another helpful test is a nerve block.  
A doctor injects a numbing medicine near the celiac ganglion.  
They use a CT scan to guide the needle.  
If the pain goes away after the injection, it suggests Dunbar syndrome.

---

## How Is Dunbar Syndrome Treated?

Medicine cannot fix the problem.  
Surgery is the only treatment that helps.

During surgery, the surgeon cuts the ligament to stop it from pressing on the artery.  
The celiac ganglion is often removed too.  
This nerve group may be involved in causing the pain.

The surgery is usually done using a small camera and tiny tools.  
This is called laparoscopic surgery or minimally invasive surgery.  
The surgeon makes small cuts in the belly.  
A thin tube with a light and camera is inserted.  
Small tools go through the same tube.  
This method causes less pain and faster healing.

If the artery is already damaged or blocked, cutting the ligament alone will not help.  
In these cases, the surgeon may:
- Stretch the narrowed part of the artery
- Use a new tube (a bypass) to go around the blocked section

Most people feel better right after surgery.  
A few people get no relief.  
In some, the pain returns after a while.  
This happens in about 1 in 10 people who improve after surgery.  
It may take several months for symptoms to fully go away.  
Sometimes symptoms return after a long time.

---

## What Happens After Surgery?

Most people stay in the hospital for 2 to 3 days after laparoscopic surgery.  
Recovery is usually quick.  
The cuts are small, so healing is faster.  
Most people can return to normal activities within a few weeks.

# Gastritis

Gastritis is a common condition. It happens when the lining of the stomach becomes inflamed. This lining protects the stomach from acid and harmful germs. When it gets damaged, it can become inflamed.

Most people with gastritis do not have serious problems. But some may feel unwell. The condition can be short-term or long-term.

---

## What is gastritis?

Gastritis means inflammation of the stomach lining.  
The stomach lining protects the stomach wall from acid and germs.  
When this lining is damaged, it can become inflamed.  
If the inflammation lasts a long time, it can harm the stomach wall.  
In some cases, it can lead to a stomach ulcer.

Gastritis often happens because of:
- An infection with a type of bacteria called *Helicobacter pylori*.
- Taking certain painkillers regularly, especially non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).

There are two main types:
- **Acute gastritis**: Comes on quickly and causes clear symptoms.
- **Chronic gastritis**: Develops slowly and may not cause any symptoms at first.

---

## What are the symptoms?

### Acute gastritis may cause:
- Stomach pain or discomfort.
- A feeling of fullness after eating small amounts.
- Bloating (a swollen belly).
- Excess gas.
- Heartburn (a burning feeling in the chest).
- Nausea, sometimes with vomiting.
- Burping (belching).
- Loss of appetite.

These symptoms usually go away on their own in a few days.

### Chronic gastritis:
- Often causes no symptoms at all.
- May only be found when a stomach ulcer causes problems.
- Can still cause the same symptoms as acute gastritis.

Some of these symptoms can also happen with other conditions, such as:
- Acid reflux.
- Indigestion.
- Irritable bowel syndrome.
- Stomach flu.

---

## What causes gastritis?

Gastritis happens when the stomach lining is damaged and then becomes inflamed.  
Here are the most common causes:

### 1. *Helicobacter pylori* infection
- This is a type of bacteria that lives in the stomach.
- It can damage the stomach lining and cause inflammation.
- Not everyone with the bacteria gets gastritis.
- In Germany, about 40 out of 100 people carry this bacteria.
- Only about 4 to 8 out of 100 of these people will develop gastritis or ulcers.

**How it spreads:**
- Through saliva (like kissing).
- Through vomit.
- Through stool (poop).
- Through contaminated water or food.
- Most infections happen in childhood, often within families.

### 2. Using NSAID painkillers
- NSAIDs include common painkillers like:
  - Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid).
  - Ibuprofen.
  - Diclofenac.
  - Naproxen.

- These drugs help reduce pain and swelling.
- They are safe for short-term use.
- But if taken every day for weeks or months, they can harm the stomach lining.

**Why they cause problems:**
- They block a natural substance called prostaglandin.
- Prostaglandin helps the stomach make mucus and neutralize acid.
- Without enough prostaglandin, the stomach lining is not protected.
- This can lead to inflammation or ulcers.

**Extra risk:**
- Taking NSAIDs with cortisone (a steroid medicine) increases the risk of stomach damage.

### 3. Other causes
- Smoking.
- Constant stress.
- Eating too much fatty, spicy, or sugary food.
- Drinking too much alcohol.
- Bile flowing backward from the small intestine into the stomach (bile reflux).

---

## How common is gastritis?

- About 1 in 5 people in Germany will have acute gastritis at some point in their life.
- The chance of getting it goes up with age.
- Women most often get it between ages 45 and 64.
- Men most often get it after age 65.

---

## How does gastritis develop?

- Most cases of gastritis heal well with time.
- If the stomach lining is not protected, it can get damaged.
- This damage can lead to a stomach ulcer.
- Ulcers can cause serious problems like bleeding.

With long-term (chronic) gastritis:
- The body may not make enough healthy red blood cells.
- This can lead to anemia (low blood count).
- In very rare cases, it can lead to stomach cancer.

---

## How is gastritis diagnosed?

Your doctor will:
- Ask about your symptoms.
- Check your medical history.
- Ask what medicines you are taking.
- Feel your belly to check for tenderness.

### Further tests may be needed:
- **Gastroscopy**: A thin tube with a camera (called a gastroscope) is passed through your mouth into your stomach.  
  - This lets the doctor see the inside of your stomach and duodenum.
  - They can look for redness, swelling, ulcers, or bleeding.
  - The test takes 5 to 10 minutes.

- **Tissue samples**: Small pieces of stomach lining may be taken during the gastroscopy.  
  - These are tested for:
    - *Helicobacter pylori* infection.
    - Cell changes that could be a sign of cancer.

- **Breath test**: This checks for *Helicobacter pylori* bacteria.  
  - You drink a special liquid and then blow into a bag.
  - The test checks for a gas produced by the bacteria.

- **Blood test or stool test**: These can also detect *Helicobacter pylori*.

---

## How is gastritis treated?

Treatment depends on:
- How severe the inflammation is.
- What symptoms you have.
- What caused the gastritis.

### Non-drug treatments

- Stop drinking alcohol and smoking.
- Eat simple, easy-to-digest foods like:
  - Crispbread.
  - Oatmeal.
- Avoid:
  - Coffee.
  - Fatty foods.
  - Spicy foods.
- Rest and take it easy.
- Some doctors suggest fasting or eating small meals for 1 to 2 days.  
  - But there is not enough proof yet that this helps.

- If stress seems to be a trigger:
  - Try to manage stress better.
  - Make time each day for relaxation.

### Drug treatments

If symptoms are bad or do not go away, your doctor may prescribe medicine.

**Acid-blocking medicines:**
- **Antacids** (like aluminum or magnesium hydroxide):  
  - They work right away to calm acid in the stomach.

- **Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs)** (like omeprazole or pantoprazole):  
  - They reduce acid production in the stomach.

- **H2 receptor antagonists** (like ranitidine or famotidine):  
  - They also reduce acid production.

**If caused by *Helicobacter pylori* infection:**
- You will get a PPI plus two or three antibiotics.
- This combination kills the bacteria and heals the stomach lining.

**If caused by NSAID painkillers:**
- Talk to your doctor about switching to a different painkiller.
- Or take an acid-blocking medicine at the same time as the NSAID.
- This can protect your stomach.
- Never stop or change your medicine without talking to your doctor.

---

**Important note:**  
This information is for general knowledge only.  
It cannot replace a visit to a doctor.  
Do not use this to diagnose or treat yourself.  
Always talk to a healthcare professional for advice.

# Parkinson’s Disease

Parkinson’s disease is a condition that affects the brain.  
It mainly happens in older adults.  
It makes movement harder.  
The exact cause is not yet known.

---

## Quick Facts

- Parkinson’s disease affects the nervous system.  
- It is most common in older people.  
- It slows down movement.  
- The disease can be managed well for many years.  
- It is also called Morbus Parkinson or shaking palsy.  
- Scientists have not yet found the full cause.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Parkinson’s Disease?

Parkinson’s disease is a brain condition.  
It mainly affects older people.  
It makes it harder to move.  
There is no cure.  
But many people live independently for years.  
The disease gets worse slowly.  
Medicines can help reduce symptoms.  
Most people are treated with drugs.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms can vary from person to person.  
Common signs include:

### Slowed or limited movement (akinesia)
- Walking becomes slow and hesitant.  
- Steps become short and shuffling.  
- Starting to walk is hard.  
- Stopping movement is difficult.  
- Arms do not swing when walking.  
- Tasks like tying shoes become harder.  
- The face looks less expressive.  
- Swallowing becomes harder.  
- Voice becomes quiet and flat.

### Stiff muscles (rigor)
- Arms, legs, and neck feel tight and stiff.  
- Movement is hard, even with help.  
- Muscles may not move at all.  
- Tension can cause pain.

### Shaking at rest
- Hands shake when not moving.  
- Writing becomes smaller and harder to read.  
- Shaking stops when moving.

Symptoms often start on one side of the body.  
Other possible symptoms:
- Problems with the bladder or bowels.  
- Low blood pressure.  
- Skin becomes oily.  
- Feelings of sadness or depression.

---

## What Causes Parkinson’s Disease?

There are different types.  
The most common type has no known cause.  
This is called idiopathic Parkinson’s.

A brain chemical called dopamine helps control movement.  
In Parkinson’s, brain cells that make dopamine are damaged.  
This damage stops the brain from sending clear signals to the muscles.  
As a result, movement becomes slow or uncoordinated.  
This can lead to balance problems.  
Balance issues raise the risk of falls and broken bones.

Some other conditions can cause similar symptoms.  
These include:
- Brain infections or tumors.  
- Certain medicines, especially mental health drugs.  
- Other brain diseases like dementia.

---

## How Common Is Parkinson’s Disease?

About 1 to 2 in every 1,000 people have Parkinson’s.  
It usually starts after age 50.  
After age 70, about 20 in 1,000 people are affected.  
Men are slightly more likely to get it than women.

---

## How Does the Disease Progress?

The disease develops differently in each person.  
It can take years before symptoms are noticed.  
Some early signs:
- Changes in handwriting.  
- Trouble with small hand movements.  
- Face looks less expressive.  
- Arms stop swinging while walking.  
- Loss of rhythm in movement.  
- Constipation.  
- Trouble sleeping.  
- Mood swings.  
- Loss of smell.

Symptoms usually get worse slowly.  
In the early stage, medicines can greatly reduce or even remove symptoms.

After 5 to 10 years, the disease keeps damaging brain cells.  
Medicines become less effective.  
Symptoms come and go.  
This is called “on” and “off” phases:
- “On” phase: movement is better.  
- “Off” phase: movement is very limited.

Later in the disease, new symptoms may appear:
- Arms hang loosely.  
- Lips smack.  
- Movements become jerky.  
- Speech problems.  
- Memory issues.  
- Bladder problems.  
- Hallucinations.  
- Depression.  
- Some people develop dementia.

In the late stage, people need help with daily tasks.  
They may need help with:
- Eating and drinking.  
- Standing up and walking.  
- Dressing.  
- Personal hygiene.

---

## How Is Parkinson’s Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose Parkinson’s through:
- A detailed talk about symptoms.  
- A physical exam.  
- Review of medical history.

Family and friends can help.  
They may notice changes that the person does not see.

The doctor checks:
- Reflexes.  
- Sensitivity to pain or pressure.  
- Joint movement.  
- Muscle strength and resistance.

### L-dopa test
- The patient takes a medicine called L-dopa.  
- If symptoms improve quickly, it suggests Parkinson’s.

In early stages, it can be hard to tell Parkinson’s from other conditions.  
Doctors may watch the person over time.  
They may order imaging tests like:
- CT scan.  
- MRI scan.  
These help rule out other causes.

---

## How Is Parkinson’s Treated?

### Early stage
- If symptoms are mild, treatment may not be needed yet.

### Medicines
- Drugs help replace or mimic dopamine.  
- They reduce symptoms.  
- But they do not stop the disease from getting worse.  
- Over time, the effect wears off.  
- Dosage and type of medicine may need to change.  
- A special pump can deliver medicine steadily.  
  - It puts medicine under the skin.  
  - Or it sends medicine into the small intestine.

### Deep brain stimulation
- A surgery places small wires in the brain.  
- These wires send electrical signals.  
- This helps control movement.  
- It is used when medicines are not enough.

### Physical therapy
- Limited movement leads to weaker muscles.  
- Physical therapy helps keep strength and movement.  
- Exercises and sports improve balance and coordination.

### Speech therapy
- If voice becomes quiet or speech unclear, therapy can help.

For more information on brain pacemakers, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## What Is Life Like with Parkinson’s?

Parkinson’s affects many parts of life:
- Work.  
- Relationships.  
- Family.  
- Hobbies.

In the early stage, life may not change much.  
But many people worry about becoming dependent on others.

It is possible to live well with Parkinson’s for years.  
It helps to plan ahead for future needs.

Staying active and connected to others is important.  
Good medical care and support from family and friends make a big difference.

It is important to:
- Know your limits.  
- Adjust your daily activities to your abilities.  
- Keep doing what you can.

To learn how others live with Parkinson’s, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Toxoplasmosis

Toxoplasmosis is caused by a tiny parasite called *Toxoplasma gondii*.  
About one in three people around the world carry this parasite.  
Most people do not know they have it.  
Only about 5 out of every 100 people get sick from it.  
When sickness does happen, it can be serious or even life-threatening in some cases.

This article explains:
- What causes toxoplasmosis
- How to avoid getting it
- How it is treated

> **Important note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## Quick Facts

- Around one third of people worldwide carry the parasite *Toxoplasma gondii*.
- Over 90% of infected people have no symptoms.
- Toxoplasmosis can be dangerous for people with weak immune systems.
- If a woman gets infected for the first time during pregnancy, it can harm the unborn baby. This can cause eye or brain damage.
- Babies born with toxoplasmosis may have serious health problems.

---

## What Is Toxoplasmosis?

Toxoplasmosis is a disease that spreads from animals to people.  
It is found all over the world.  
It is caused by a single-celled parasite called *Toxoplasma gondii*.  
The parasite lives inside the cells of its host.

All mammals can get infected.  
But only cats can pass the parasite on in their poop.  
Cats release a form of the parasite that is not yet infectious.  
This form becomes infectious in the environment within 48 hours.

People can get infected by:
- Touching soil or sand that has cat poop in it
- Eating fruits or vegetables that were not washed well
- Gardening without gloves

Once inside the body, the parasite moves into the intestines.  
It then spreads to other parts of the body.  
It forms long-term storage units called cysts.  
These cysts stay in the brain, eye, heart, and muscle tissue for life.

People can also get infected by eating raw or undercooked meat that has cysts in it.  
This includes pork, lamb, and poultry.

If a woman gets infected for the first time during pregnancy, the parasite can pass to the baby.  
This is called prenatal toxoplasmosis.

---

## What Are the Signs of Toxoplasmosis?

Most children and adults with healthy immune systems do not feel sick when infected.  
They may not know they are infected.

Only about 5% of people get flu-like symptoms.  
These include:
- Fever
- Headache
- Muscle pain
- Swollen glands in the neck and head

These symptoms usually go away on their own.  
After that, the parasite stays in the body but does not cause more problems.

In rare cases, the parasite can cause:
- Inflammation in the eye (retina)
- Inflammation in the brain (encephalitis)

These serious problems are more likely in people with weak immune systems.

Pregnant women who get infected for the first time during pregnancy can pass the parasite to their baby.  
This can lead to:
- Brain damage
- Eye damage
- Miscarriage

Women who were already infected before pregnancy cannot pass the parasite to their baby.

People with weak immune systems are at high risk.  
This includes people with AIDS and those who have had organ transplants.

When the parasite wakes up from its dormant state, it can cause serious illness in the brain, eyes, and other organs.

---

## How Common Is Toxoplasmosis?

About one third to half of all people carry the parasite.  
In Germany, the number of infected adults is rising by about 1% each year.  
More than 70% of people over 70 are infected.  
The infection rate is much higher in East Germany than in West Germany.

---

## How Can You Prevent Toxoplasmosis?

People with weak immune systems and pregnant women who are not yet infected should take extra care.

Here are ways to stay safe:

- Do not eat raw or undercooked meat.  
- Freeze meat at minus 21 degrees Celsius for at least 24 hours.  
- Or cook meat until the inside reaches at least 50 degrees Celsius for 20 minutes.  
- Wash all fruits and vegetables well before eating.  
- Always wash your hands before eating.  
- Wash your hands after handling raw meat.  
- Wash your hands after gardening, working in soil, or playing at a playground.  
- If you are pregnant and have a cat, feed it only canned or dry food.  
- Do not clean the cat’s litter box if you are pregnant or have a weak immune system.  
- If someone else must clean it, they should do so daily using hot water.

---

## How Is Toxoplasmosis Diagnosed?

If doctors suspect toxoplasmosis, they take blood samples.  
They may also test other body fluids.

Lab tests can show:
- If your body has ever fought the parasite
- If this is a new infection

Special lab methods can find the parasite’s genetic material.

If brain symptoms are present, doctors may do a brain scan with contrast dye.  
This helps rule out other diseases with similar symptoms.

If the eye is affected, an eye doctor uses special tools to look at the back of the eye.  
They can see signs of swelling, scarring, or damage.

---

## How Is Toxoplasmosis Treated?

Several medicines can stop the parasite from growing.  
Some antibiotics also work against the parasite.

Common treatments include:
- Spiramycin
- Pyrimethamine
- Sulfadiazine
- Clindamycin
- Atovaquone

These are used for:
- Active infections in people with weak immune systems
- Eye infections
- Pregnant women with a new infection
- Babies before or after birth

To protect the baby’s spinal cord, doctors also give a medicine called folinic acid.

For most people who get infected after birth and have no symptoms, no treatment is needed.  
Doctors just monitor them.

> **Important:** Folinic acid is not the same as folic acid.  
> Folic acid is a vitamin that helps during pregnancy.  
> Folinic acid is a different substance used as a medicine.

# Lactose Intolerance

Some people feel sick after drinking milk or eating dairy foods. They may have a bloated stomach, gas, stomach pain, or diarrhea. This happens because their body cannot handle milk sugar well. The medical name for this is lactose intolerance.

## Quick Facts

- Some people have digestive problems after drinking milk or eating dairy.
- This may be due to lactose intolerance. These people can only handle small amounts of milk sugar.
- About 5 to 15 percent of people in Europe have lactose intolerance. It is least common in Northern Europe.
- There is no cure for lactose intolerance. But you can avoid symptoms by changing your diet.
- **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Lactose Intolerance?

If you get stomach pain, gas, or diarrhea after drinking milk or eating dairy, you may have lactose intolerance. This means your body can only handle small amounts of lactose, the sugar in milk.

You might also have a reaction to milk for other reasons. That is why it is important to see a doctor before changing your diet. This is especially true for children, teens, and people who need more calcium.

**Important:** Lactose intolerance is not the same as a milk allergy.  
- People with lactose intolerance can often eat some milk or dairy without serious problems.  
- People with a milk allergy react strongly even to tiny amounts of milk.

## What Are the Symptoms?

If you cannot handle much lactose, symptoms usually start soon after eating or drinking milk or dairy.  
- Your stomach may feel bloated.  
- You may feel full.  
- You may have pain in your lower belly.  
- You may pass a lot of gas.  
- You may have diarrhea.  
- You may feel nauseous or even vomit.  
- Sometimes, you may also have constipation.

Symptoms can start as early as 30 minutes after eating. They are usually worst about one and a half to two hours later. But they can last longer.

## What Causes Lactose Intolerance?

Most cases of lactose intolerance are inherited. This is called primary lactose intolerance.

Babies are born to digest breast milk only. Their bodies make an enzyme called lactase. This enzyme breaks down the sugar in milk (lactose) in the small intestine. This allows the body to absorb the sugar.

After breastfeeding ends, the body naturally makes less lactase. Most people can still handle small amounts of lactose. But some people do not make enough lactase. So they cannot break down the lactose in milk and dairy.

If an adult eats more lactose than their body can break down, some lactose stays in the small intestine. It moves into the large intestine (colon). There, bacteria break it down. This process is called fermentation. It creates extra gas and other substances. These cause the symptoms.

How well someone can handle lactose varies from person to person. It depends on their genes.

For more details on causes, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

## How Common Is Lactose Intolerance?

Lactose intolerance is very common worldwide. But rates differ by region.

- In Europe, 5 to 15 percent of people have it. It is least common in Northern Europe.
- In Africa and East Asia, 65 to over 90 percent of adults have trouble with milk or dairy.
- Lactose intolerance is very rare in children under 5 years old.
- It usually starts during adolescence or adulthood.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

If you think you have lactose intolerance, see your family doctor. They may refer you to a specialist in digestive health.

The following tests can help diagnose lactose intolerance:

- **Diet or exclusion test:** You stop eating all milk and dairy for a while. Then you slowly add back a set amount of lactose. Your doctor watches how your body reacts.
- **Lactose tolerance test:** Your blood sugar level is checked before and after drinking a lactose solution. This shows if your body can break down and absorb lactose.
- **Breath test:** You drink a lactose solution. Then your doctor measures the amount of hydrogen in your breath. High levels mean lactose is not being digested.

Not all tests are needed. In Germany, the breath test is the most common.

**Important:** A test result alone is not enough. The doctor must see your symptoms during testing to confirm lactose intolerance.

## How Is It Treated?

Primary (inherited) lactose intolerance cannot be cured. But you can avoid symptoms by changing your diet.

Research shows the best way to reduce symptoms is to:
- Eat small amounts of lactose.
- Drink milk only with other foods.

Secondary lactose intolerance happens when another illness causes the problem. In these cases, treating the original illness is key. If the gut heals, symptoms often go away.

**Important:** Some people take supplements with lactase. These are man-made enzymes that help break down lactose. But studies have not proven they help with symptoms.  
- Probiotics are live good bacteria.  
- Prebiotics are fibers your body cannot digest.  
There is no clear proof that either helps people with lactose intolerance.

## Living with Lactose Intolerance

You can still eat a healthy, balanced diet without dairy. But you must make sure you get enough calcium.

Good sources of calcium include:
- Green vegetables like spinach and kale.
- Calcium-rich mineral water.
- Hard cheeses such as Parmesan and old Gouda. Many people with lactose intolerance can eat these without problems.

If you find it hard to avoid dairy, try this:
- Test how much lactose you can handle without symptoms.
- Then eat that amount, spread out over the day and with other foods.

In most cases, you do not need to cut out all lactose. The following amounts are usually okay, especially when eaten with other foods:
- Up to 12 grams of lactose in one meal (for example, 250 milliliters of milk).
- Up to 24 grams of lactose in one day (for example, 500 milliliters of milk).

People with severe symptoms often avoid all dairy. But this can be hard when eating away from home. Many ready-made meals and processed foods contain some lactose.

For tips on living with lactose intolerance and shopping, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

## Where Can I Learn More?

More information about lactose intolerance is available at _allergieinformationsdienst.de_ (in German).

# Acute Laryngitis

Laryngitis makes your voice hoarse. It can also cause a sore throat. In some cases, you may lose your voice completely. To help your voice heal and avoid further damage, it is very important to rest your voice until you feel better.

## Quick Facts

- Laryngitis means inflammation of the voicebox. It often causes hoarseness or loss of voice. It also causes pain in the throat and voicebox.
- The most common cause is a virus, like the flu. Sometimes a bacterial infection can also develop.
- The windpipe (trachea) can also become inflamed at the same time.
- If a small child has trouble breathing, call an emergency doctor right away.
- Most people get better within two weeks.
- Resting your voice is one of the most important things you can do to heal.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Laryngitis?

Laryngitis is swelling of the lining inside the voicebox. It often comes with swelling in the windpipe, called tracheitis.

Most cases are caused by a virus in the nose and throat. For example, a flu infection can lead to laryngitis.

The swelling usually goes away on its own.

### What Is the Voicebox and What Does It Do?

The voicebox is in the middle of your throat. It connects the throat to the windpipe.

Its main job is to protect your airways. It has a small flap (called the epiglottis) that closes when you swallow. This keeps food and drink from going into your windpipe.

The voicebox also holds the vocal cords. These are two bands of tissue that vibrate when you speak or sing.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main symptom is hoarseness. In some cases, you may not be able to speak at all.

Your throat may feel dry and scratchy. You might have a painful sore throat.

Other possible symptoms include:

- A burning feeling in the throat
- Pain when swallowing
- A dry cough
- Needing to clear your throat often
- Trouble breathing

Some people feel like there is a lump in their throat. Using your voice makes these symptoms worse. It can cause extra strain and stress.

Symptoms often start suddenly and get worse over a few days. You may also have other signs of a virus, such as fever, headache, or tiredness.

### Symptoms in Babies and Young Children

In babies and young children, laryngitis can cause swelling in the voicebox where it meets the windpipe. This leads to coughing fits and wheezing when breathing. This is called pseudocroup (false croup).

If the windpipe is also inflamed, you may see fever, trouble breathing, and general weakness.

**Important:** In children, the windpipe can swell quickly. This can cause serious breathing problems, wheezing, or choking. If this happens, call an emergency doctor right away.

## What Causes Laryngitis?

Laryngitis is usually caused by a virus in the nose and throat. The virus spreads to the voicebox.

Other causes include:

- Exposure to smoke, dust, or hot air
- Injury to the voicebox
- Problems with the vocal cords
- Bacterial infections

In rare cases, laryngitis is caused only by bacteria. This can happen with:

- Inflammation of the epiglottis
- Diphtheria (also called true croup)

## Who Is at Higher Risk?

You are more likely to get laryngitis if:

- You snore or have untreated sleep apnea (where breathing stops during sleep)
- You breathe through your mouth at night, which dries out the voicebox lining
- You smoke
- You use your voice a lot, such as singers, teachers, or actors
- You have a weak immune system due to a long-term health condition

## How Does Laryngitis Progress?

Symptoms usually start suddenly and get worse over several days.

Your voice may sound different. You may need to push harder to speak.

The swelling can spread to other areas, like the windpipe or throat. Doctors call this a spreading infection.

Most people recover in about two weeks. If symptoms last longer, you may have a second infection with bacteria on top of the virus.

## How Is Laryngitis Diagnosed?

If you think you have laryngitis, see your family doctor first.

The doctor will ask about your symptoms. They will want to know if you have:

- A dry cough
- Lost your voice
- Throat or neck pain
- Other complaints

To confirm the diagnosis, you may need a special exam called a laryngoscopy. This is done by an ear, nose, and throat doctor or a voice specialist.

The doctor uses a small camera (endoscope) to look inside your voicebox.

You should have this exam if hoarseness lasts more than 4 weeks.

If a bacterial infection is suspected, the doctor may take a swab from your throat. This is tested in a lab to find the cause.

## How Is Laryngitis Treated?

The most important step is to rest your voice. Try not to speak at all.

If you keep using your voice, healing may take longer or not happen fully.

### What If You Must Speak?

If you cannot avoid speaking, use your voice gently. Keep your voice quiet and relaxed. Do not shout or strain.

**Important:** Whispering is not good for your voice. It dries out the vocal cords and can make strain worse.

### Other Helpful Steps

- Drink plenty of fluids. Water, herbal teas, and clear broths help keep the voicebox moist.
- Avoid alcohol and nicotine. They can make inflammation worse.
- Use a humidifier or take steam inhalations. This helps soothe the throat.
- Add herbs like thyme, sage, or marshmallow to the steam. They can help.
- Use salt water for inhalation. It helps keep the vocal cords moist longer.
- Your doctor can prescribe an inhalation device. You can get it from a pharmacy.

If a bacterial infection is present, your doctor may prescribe antibiotics. These only work for bacterial infections, not viral ones.

# Food Allergy

Food allergies are not as common as many people think. Often, other causes are behind the symptoms. A careful check by a doctor can tell if you really have an allergy. If so, treatment can be targeted. This means you may not need to avoid certain foods unnecessarily. You might be able to eat them again.

---

## Quick Facts

- A food allergy happens when the body’s defense system wrongly sees a harmless food protein as a threat.
- Even a tiny amount of the food can cause a reaction.
- Symptoms can vary a lot and may affect different parts of the body.
- The inside of the mouth and throat may swell.
- Itching, red skin, and raised, itchy bumps (hives) are common.
- About 4 out of every 100 people in Germany have a food allergy.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Food Allergy?

If you have a food allergy, you always get the same symptoms after eating even a small amount of the food. These symptoms happen quickly.

But food allergies are less common than people believe. Other conditions can cause similar symptoms. That is why a proper diagnosis is important. A doctor can find out if you truly have an allergy. If not, you may be able to eat the food safely.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

A food allergy can cause symptoms after even a small bite. The symptoms can affect many parts of the body.

Common symptoms include:

- Swelling in the mouth or throat
- Itching
- Red, itchy skin or rashes
- Hives (raised, itchy bumps)
- Feeling sick to your stomach
- Belly pain, diarrhea, or other gut problems
- Trouble breathing

Symptoms usually start within 30 minutes. They can appear up to a few hours after eating.

In rare cases, a food allergy can cause a severe reaction called anaphylaxis. This can include:

- A sudden drop in blood pressure
- Fainting or loss of consciousness
- A rash or swelling on the face
- Swelling in the airways, which can make breathing hard

With fruit and vegetable allergies, symptoms are often mild, like a rash. Nuts and shellfish are more likely to cause serious reactions.

> **Important:** Other conditions can cause similar symptoms. These include:
> - Lactose intolerance (trouble digesting milk sugar)
> - Celiac disease (an immune reaction to gluten)
> - Sensitivity to food additives like glutamate
> - Stomach infections
> - Irritable bowel syndrome

If you think you have a food allergy, see your doctor. Only a doctor can tell what is really happening.

---

## What Causes a Food Allergy?

The body’s defense system reacts to certain food proteins as if they were dangerous germs.

Some people are born with a higher chance of having allergies. A food allergy can also happen if you are allergic to pollen. This is called cross-sensitivity. The proteins in some foods are very similar to pollen proteins.

For example:
- Birch pollen can cause reactions to apples, celery, nuts, or carrots.

But the exact cause of food allergies is still not fully known.

Common foods that cause allergies include:

- Peanuts, walnuts, hazelnuts
- Beans, lentils, and other pulses
- Cow’s milk, chicken eggs, soy, wheat
- Stone fruits (like peaches) and pome fruits (like apples)
- Vegetables such as celery or carrots
- Fish and shellfish
- Meat

> **Note:** Children most often react to nuts, milk, soy, wheat, and eggs. Adults more often react to nuts, soy, celery, or seafood. Most people with a food allergy react to one to three different foods.

---

## How Common Are Food Allergies?

About 4 out of every 100 people in Germany have a food allergy. It can start at any age. The course of the allergy varies a lot depending on the food and the person’s age.

It is hard to say how long an allergy will last. Some children outgrow allergies to milk, wheat, or soy. Their bodies learn to handle the food over time.

Allergies that start in adulthood, such as to fish or shellfish, usually last a lifetime. Nut allergies also often last for life.

About half of children with a food allergy later develop asthma or hay fever.

The more severe the symptoms, the more likely the allergy will last. Strong reactions in allergy tests also suggest the allergy will not go away.

---

## How Is a Food Allergy Diagnosed?

Doctors use tests to check if you have a food allergy.

**Skin prick test:**  
- Small amounts of possible allergens are placed on the forearm.  
- The skin is lightly scratched at each spot.  
- The doctor watches for redness or hives.  
- If the skin reacts, it may mean an allergy.

**Blood test:**  
- A blood sample is taken.  
- The lab checks for specific antibodies (like IgE) that the body makes against certain foods.  
- High levels may suggest an allergy.

But these tests alone are not enough. Doctors often do a **provocation test**.  
- You eat the suspected food under medical supervision.  
- The doctor watches for any reaction.

Other tools that help include:
- Keeping a daily food and symptom diary
- Trying an elimination diet (removing certain foods for a time)

---

## How Is a Food Allergy Treated?

The main rule is to avoid the food that causes the allergy.

For severe symptoms, medicine can help. But medicine is not used every day for food allergies.

The most serious reaction is called anaphylaxis. This affects the whole body. At least two organs are involved at once. For example:
- Skin and airways
- Gut and heart

If anaphylaxis happens, a special emergency kit is used. It contains medicine that can stop the reaction and prevent it from getting worse.

You can also store information about your severe allergy in the **emergency data section** of your **electronic health card**.

For more details on treatment, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## More Information

For more facts about food allergies in German, visit: [allergieinformationsdienst.de](https://www.allergieinformationsdienst.de)

# Antibody Deficiencies

Antibodies help your body fight infections.  
They are part of your immune system.  
If your body does not make enough antibodies, you may get sick more often.  
This article explains how doctors find out if someone has low antibody levels.  
It also explains how these conditions are treated.

---

## Quick Facts

- If your body does not make enough antibodies, you are more likely to get infections.  
- There are many types of antibody deficiencies.  
- Most are found in babies and young children.  
- Most last a lifetime and need ongoing care.  
- Doctors use blood tests to check for low antibody levels.  
- Treatment usually includes antibody replacement and antibiotics to prevent infections.  

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

---

## What Is an Antibody Deficiency?

Antibodies are proteins made by your body to fight germs.  
They attach to germs and help your immune system destroy them.  
Special white blood cells called B cells make these antibodies.  

Healthy people have five main types of antibodies:  
- IgA  
- IgD  
- IgE  
- IgG  
- IgM  

Each type has a different job.  
For example, IgA is found in mucus in the nose, throat, and gut.  
IgG and IgM are found in the blood.

If you have an antibody deficiency, your body makes too few antibodies.  
This weakens your immune system.  
You are more likely to get infections.

There are several types of antibody deficiencies:

- **Common variable immune deficiency (CVID):**  
  Your body makes too little IgG, IgA, and/or IgM.

- **X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA):**  
  Your body makes almost no antibodies at all.  
  This condition is present from birth.

- **Hyper IgM syndrome:**  
  Your body makes too little IgA and IgG.  
  But it makes normal or too much IgM.

- **Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy (THI):**  
  Babies and young children may have low antibody levels.  
  This is temporary and usually goes away as the immune system matures.

---

## What Are the Signs?

The main sign is getting infections more often than usual.  
You may get sick many times a year.  
Infections can happen in:

- The nose, throat, and lungs  
- The stomach and intestines  
- The skin  
- The urinary tract  
- The middle ear  

These infections may not go away easily.  
They may keep coming back.

---

## What Causes Antibody Deficiencies?

Some causes are temporary.  
For example, some babies have low antibody levels because their immune system is still developing.  
This usually gets better on its own.

Other causes are long-term.  
They happen because the body does not make enough B cells.  
Or the B cells do not work properly.  
This means they cannot make all five types of antibodies.

In some cases, the cause is in a person’s genes.  
For example, X-linked agammaglobulinemia is caused by a missing gene on the X chromosome.  
This gene is needed for B cells to grow and work.  
Since men have only one X chromosome, they are affected.  
Women have two X chromosomes.  
If one is faulty, the other can still work.  
So women usually do not get this condition.

In many cases, doctors do not know the exact cause.

---

## How Common Are Antibody Deficiencies?

Antibody deficiencies are the most common type of immune problem.  
About 1 in every 12,000 newborns has one.  

The most common type is common variable immune deficiency.  
It affects about 1 in 50,000 people.

Most antibody deficiencies affect men and women equally.  
The exception is X-linked agammaglobulinemia, which only affects boys and men.

---

## When Do They Start and How Do They Progress?

Some types show up in early childhood.  
Most are found in the first year of life.  

Common variable immune deficiency often shows up later.  
It is usually diagnosed during teenage years or early adulthood.

Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy usually goes away on its own.  
It happens when a baby’s immune system takes longer to mature.

Other types last a lifetime.  
They need regular treatment to prevent serious infections.  
For example, infections can lead to blood poisoning (sepsis).

In some cases, a stem cell transplant can cure the condition.  
This means the body gets healthy blood stem cells from a donor.  
If it works, the person can live a normal life.  
But the treatment is risky and not for everyone.

---

## How Do Doctors Diagnose It?

If you get sick often, your doctor may suspect an antibody deficiency.  

It is normal for young children to get sick up to 15 times a year.  
But adults should not get sick more than three times a year.  
More than that may be a sign of a problem.

To check for low antibodies, doctors do blood tests.  
These tests show how many antibodies you have.  
They also show which types are missing or low.

In some cases, doctors can find the exact gene problem.  
They do a genetic test to confirm the diagnosis.

> **Important:** Low antibodies can also be a sign of another illness.  
> Doctors must rule out other causes before making a final diagnosis.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Most people with antibody deficiencies get antibody replacement therapy.  
These antibodies come from healthy donors.  
They are taken from donated blood and plasma.

The treatment is given either under the skin or into a vein.  
It is done every few weeks.  

This treatment does not cure the condition.  
But it helps protect you from infections.  
It strengthens your immune system for a time.

Doctors may also give antibiotics to prevent bacterial infections.  
These medicines fight many types of bacteria.  
They are used only when a person is at high risk of serious infection.

For some types of antibody deficiency, a stem cell transplant may be an option.  
This can cure the condition.  
But it carries serious risks.  
It also requires a matching donor.  
You and your doctor must carefully weigh the risks and benefits.

---

## What Support Is Available?

Living with a lifelong antibody deficiency can be hard.  
It can affect your daily life, school, work, and relationships.

Support groups can help.  
They offer advice, emotional support, and information.  
You are not alone.

You can find support groups through the **National Contact and Information Point For Encouraging and Supporting Self-Help Groups (NAKOS)** website.  
This site has a database of self-help organizations.

# Boils and Carbuncles

## What Are Boils and Carbuncles?

- A boil is a painful, pus-filled lump under the skin.
- It starts in a hair root and spreads into the surrounding tissue.
- A boil looks like a large pimple but is deeper and much more painful.
- If several boils join together, they form a larger, more serious infection called a carbuncle.
- A carbuncle is deeper in the skin than a single boil and can cause fever and tiredness.
- Pimples, boils, abscesses, and carbuncles are all types of skin infections.
- They are caused by bacteria, especially a type called staphylococcus aureus.

## When to See a Doctor

- You should not squeeze a boil yourself, especially if it is on your face.
- Squeezing can push bacteria into your blood or lymph system.
- This can lead to serious problems like swollen lymph nodes or spreading infection.
- If you have a boil on your face, near your nose or upper lip, there is a small risk of the infection reaching your brain.
- This could cause meningitis or dangerous blood clots in the brain.
- People with weak immune systems are more likely to get boils.
- Conditions like diabetes, cancer, or long-term infections increase the risk.
- Allergies such as asthma, eczema, or eye allergies may also make you more likely to get boils.

## How Common Are Boils?

- About 3 out of every 100 people who see a doctor for a skin problem have a boil.
- Boils can appear suddenly or grow over several days.
- Most boils heal within a few weeks, either on their own or with treatment.
- A small scar may remain after healing.
- Sometimes the pus is absorbed by the body without coming out.

## What Do Boils Look Like?

- A boil starts as a red, painful lump.
- It can be as small as a cherry stone or as big as a walnut.
- The area feels warm and swollen.
- Pus may show through the skin as a yellowish spot.
- Boils most often appear on the face, neck, back of the neck, armpits, groin, buttocks, or thighs.
- If many boils join together, they form a carbuncle.
- Carbuncles are deeper and more serious than single boils.
- They can cause high fever, chills, and extreme tiredness.

## How Do Boils Develop?

- Bacteria enter the skin through a hair root or small cut.
- The body sends white blood cells to fight the infection.
- Dead cells and bacteria build up, forming pus.
- The pus collects in a pocket under the skin, creating an abscess.
- In some cases, boils can form after a bad insect bite or from a dirty needle.
- If the boil is squeezed or scratched, bacteria can spread through the body.
- Red streaks from the boil may mean the infection is moving through the lymph system.
- This is called lymphangitis.
- Swollen, painful lymph nodes near the boil are a sign of lymphadenitis.
- Some people mistake red streaks for blood poisoning, but this is rare.
- Blood poisoning (sepsis) only happens if a huge number of bacteria enter the blood at once.

## How Are Boils Diagnosed?

- Doctors can usually tell a boil by looking at it and asking about symptoms.
- If you get many boils, or if they keep coming back, your doctor may do tests.
- A sample of the pus may be sent to a lab to find the exact type of bacteria.
- This helps the doctor choose the right antibiotic.
- Blood tests may also be done to check if the infection has spread.
- Blood tests can also check for conditions like diabetes or other health problems that make infections more likely.

## How Are Boils Treated?

- A doctor will open the boil with a small cut.
- The pus is drained out.
- The wound is cleaned and a gauze strip is placed inside to soak up more pus.
- The wound stays open to heal from the inside out. No stitches are needed.
- Do not try to open a boil yourself, especially on your face.
- If the boil is still growing and not ready to burst, warm, moist cloths can help.
- A special drawing ointment may also help bring the boil to a head.
- Antibiotics are needed if:
  - The boil is large.
  - There are many boils.
  - A carbuncle has formed.
  - The infection is spreading.
- In hospitals, antibiotics may be given through a drip.
- For carbuncles, the doctor must cut it open to drain the pus.
- The wound is cleaned often with antiseptic solutions.

## When to Seek Help

- If you have a boil on your face, especially near your nose or upper lip, see a doctor right away.
- If you have a fever, chills, or feel very weak, get medical help.
- If the redness spreads or you see red streaks, go to a doctor.
- If boils keep coming back or appear in many places at once, this is called furunculosis.
- This may need special treatment and further testing.

> **Important Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Always talk to a doctor for diagnosis and treatment. Do not try to treat a boil yourself.

# Carpal Tunnel Syndrome

## What Is Carpal Tunnel Syndrome?

The carpal tunnel is a narrow passage in your wrist.  
It holds tendons and a nerve called the median nerve.  
This nerve controls feeling and movement in your thumb and first three fingers.

When the tissue inside the carpal tunnel swells, it can press on the median nerve.  
This pressure causes carpal tunnel syndrome.

You may feel numbness, tingling, or pain in your hand.  
These symptoms often come and go at first.  
They usually happen at night or in the early morning.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may feel:
- Numbness or tingling in your thumb, index finger, middle finger, and part of your ring finger.
- A feeling that your hand is “asleep.”
- Pain in your hand or wrist. The pain can go up your arm.
- Weakness in your hand. You may drop things more easily.

The symptoms often go away when you shake your hand.  
Both hands can be affected, but not always at the same time.

## What Causes Carpal Tunnel Syndrome?

No one knows exactly why the tissue in the carpal tunnel swells.  
But certain things may make it more likely:

- Doing the same hand or wrist movements over and over.
- Using tools that vibrate a lot, like a jackhammer.
- Having a wrist injury.
- Having certain health problems, such as:
  - Diabetes
  - Rheumatism
  - Tendon inflammation
- Being pregnant (extra fluid in the body can cause swelling)

In rare cases, sudden and severe symptoms happen.  
This is called acute carpal tunnel syndrome.  
It can be caused by injury, bleeding, or strong swelling in the wrist.

## How Common Is It?

Carpal tunnel syndrome is most common in people aged 40 to 70.  
It is very rare in children.

Women are more likely to get it than men.  
People who do heavy physical work are also more likely to get it.

About 3 out of every 1,000 people develop carpal tunnel syndrome each year.

## How Does It Develop?

Some people have mild symptoms that come and go for years.  
In about one third of cases, symptoms get better on their own within six months.

For others, symptoms last longer.  
In severe cases, the hand may feel numb all the time.  
The muscles at the base of the thumb can shrink.  
This can make it hard to hold things like a cup or glass.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms.  
They will check your hand and wrist.  
They will test your strength, feeling, and movement.

They may do special tests to see how well your nerves are working.  
These tests measure how fast electrical signals travel through the nerve.

Your doctor will also rule out other possible causes.  
For example, neck problems or other nerve diseases can cause similar symptoms.

## How Is It Treated?

### Mild to Moderate Cases

- Wear a wrist splint at night.  
  This keeps your wrist straight and stops it from bending.
- Avoid activities that make your symptoms worse.
- Try cortisone injections.  
  These can help reduce swelling and ease pain for a short time.

### Surgery

Surgery may be needed if symptoms are severe or do not improve.

During surgery, the doctor cuts the tight band of tissue across the wrist.  
This relieves pressure on the nerve.

Surgery can stop symptoms for good.  
But it is not always needed.  
It is usually only done when other treatments fail.

In rare cases of acute carpal tunnel syndrome, surgery is needed right away.

### Other Treatments

- **Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT):**  
  This uses sound waves to treat the area.  
  It may help some people.  
  But most health insurance plans do not cover it.

- **Ultrasound, magnetic fields, laser therapy, and acupuncture:**  
  These are sometimes suggested.  
  But there is no strong proof they work.

- **Painkillers:**  
  Over-the-counter medicines like ibuprofen can help with pain.  
  But they do not fix the root cause.

- **Vitamin B6:**  
  Some people take vitamin B6 supplements.  
  But studies show they do not help much.

## Important Notes

- This information is not a substitute for medical advice.
- Do not try to diagnose or treat yourself.
- Always talk to a doctor if you have hand numbness or pain.

For more details on surgery, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

# Styes and Chalazia (Swelling on the Eyelid)

A red, swollen eyelid or a small bump filled with pus on the edge of the eyelid may mean you have an eyelid problem. This is usually either a stye or a chalazion.

## Quick Facts

- The eyelid swells when a small gland near the eyelid edge becomes inflamed.
- A stye happens when a gland gets infected with bacteria.
- A chalazion happens when a gland gets blocked and cannot drain.
- Most cases go away without treatment.
- These problems can happen at any age.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Eyelid Inflammation?

When a gland near the edge of your eyelid becomes inflamed, your eyelid swells. This is called eyelid inflammation.

If bacteria get into the gland, it becomes painful and fills with pus. This is called a stye.

A chalazion grows more slowly. It is not caused by bacteria. It happens when oil from a gland gets stuck and cannot flow out. A chalazion is usually not painful. But it can last longer than a stye.

Styes and chalazia are common. They can happen to children and adults.

## How to Spot Eyelid Inflammation

Signs of eyelid inflammation include:
- A red and swollen eyelid.
- A bump about the size of a pea.
- The bump is usually near the eyelashes.

This is called inflammation of the eyelid edge.

With a stye:
- Pus collects in the center of the bump.
- You can often see a yellow spot in the middle.
- The bump hurts when you press on it.

With a chalazion:
- There is no pus.
- It is not painful.
- It may look unsightly.
- It often forms on the inside of the eyelid.

Both types can appear on the top or bottom eyelid.

## What Causes Styes and Chalazia?

A stye happens when bacteria get into a gland. The most common bacteria is staphylococcus.

You can get bacteria in your eyes if you touch them with dirty hands. This is especially true if you wear contact lenses. Always wash your hands before touching your eyes or lenses.

A stye can also happen if oil or sweat gets blocked. This can happen if you do not clean makeup off your eyelids well. The blockage can lead to infection.

Styes are more common in people with:
- Diabetes.
- A weak immune system.
- High stress.
- Hormone changes.
- Skin problems like rosacea.

A chalazion happens when a gland is blocked and stays inflamed. The oil cannot drain. Over time, hard tissue forms. Because no bacteria are involved, a chalazion does not contain pus.

## What Happens Next?

A stye appears fast and goes away fast. After about one week, the pus usually drains on its own. The swelling then goes down.

A chalazion grows slowly. It may go away on its own, but this can take weeks or even months. Sometimes it does not go away without treatment.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor can usually tell the difference between a stye and a chalazion just by looking.

The main clue is pain. If the bump hurts, it is likely a stye.

The doctor will use a special light to look closely at your eye and eyelid. They may also check your vision.

Since styes are usually caused by staphylococcus bacteria, a swab test is not needed. Tests like blood work or tissue checks are only done if the person has a weak immune system or if cancer is suspected.

## How Is It Treated?

Most styes and chalazia go away on their own. If they do not, a small procedure can help.

You can help healing by:
- Keeping the area clean.
- Avoiding touching your face or eyes.
- Washing your hands often.

For more tips on what to do if you have a stye, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

# Underactive Thyroid

An underactive thyroid means your thyroid gland does not make enough hormones. This slows down your body’s normal processes. You may feel tired, have a slow heartbeat, or have trouble with constipation. A blood test can confirm if you have this condition.

---

## Quick Facts

- When the thyroid gland does not make enough hormones, it is called an underactive thyroid.
- This condition slows down your metabolism.
- Common symptoms include tiredness, low energy, and constipation.
- The most common cause is a condition called Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.
- In adults, the condition often develops slowly and quietly.
- In older adults, symptoms may be mistaken for normal aging.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is an Underactive Thyroid?

Your thyroid gland makes hormones that control how your body uses energy. When it does not make enough of these hormones, your body slows down.

This slowdown can cause tiredness, low energy, and constipation.

Most cases happen because the thyroid gland is inflamed over a long time. The good news is that this condition can be treated with daily hormone tablets. These tablets replace the missing hormones and usually make symptoms go away.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

An underactive thyroid can affect many parts of your body. Symptoms can include:

### General Symptoms
- Feeling weak or tired
- Having a slow heartbeat

### Mental and Emotional Changes
- Trouble focusing or remembering things
- Feeling low or sad
- Feeling slow to react or speak

### Physical Changes
- Gaining a small to moderate amount of weight
- Constipation
- Dry skin and hair
- Hair falling out
- Voice becoming deeper and hoarse
- Tongue getting larger
- Face or body looking puffy
- Swelling in the neck (a goiter)
- Hearing problems
- Heavier or irregular periods
- Trouble getting or staying aroused (in men)

### Body-Wide Symptoms
- Muscle or joint pain
- Slow reflexes
- Feeling cold, even in warm rooms
- Tingling or numbness in hands or feet

Many of these symptoms can also happen for other reasons. In older adults, they may be seen as normal signs of aging. This can make it hard to notice the thyroid problem. For example, early signs of memory loss (like dementia) can look similar. That is why a blood test is needed to confirm the diagnosis.

---

## What Causes an Underactive Thyroid?

Several things can cause the thyroid to make too few hormones.

### 1. Inflammation of the Thyroid
The most common cause is Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. This is an autoimmune disease. Your body’s immune system attacks the thyroid gland by mistake. This causes long-term inflammation. Over time, the gland stops working well.

Infections can also cause thyroid inflammation.

### 2. Surgery or Radiation
Some people have part or all of their thyroid removed. This can happen when treating an overactive thyroid or thyroid cancer. Radiation treatment to the neck can also damage the thyroid. After these treatments, the thyroid may not make enough hormones. Sometimes, the problem shows up years later.

### 3. Not Enough Iodine
Iodine is a mineral your body needs to make thyroid hormones. You get it from food. If you do not get enough iodine over a long time, your thyroid may not work properly. But this is rare in countries like Germany.

### 4. Certain Medicines
Some medicines can stop the thyroid from working. For example:
- Lithium (used for mood disorders)
- Some drugs used to treat an overactive thyroid

If the dose is too high, these medicines can cause an underactive thyroid.

### 5. Being Born with It
In rare cases, a baby is born with an underactive thyroid. This can happen if the mother had very low iodine during pregnancy or if her immune system attacked the baby’s thyroid.

In all these cases, the thyroid gland itself is damaged. This is called **primary hypothyroidism**.

But sometimes, the problem is not in the thyroid. It can be in the brain. The pituitary gland or the hypothalamus in the brain control the thyroid. If they do not send the right signals, the thyroid may not work even if it is healthy. This is called **secondary or central hypothyroidism**.

---

## How Common Is It?

- About 5 out of every 100 people in Germany have an underactive thyroid.
- It is more common in women and older adults.
- About 1 in every 3,400 babies is born with this condition.

---

## How Does It Progress?

The way the condition develops depends on the cause.

Most adults have chronic thyroid inflammation. Over time, the gland slowly loses its ability to make hormones. At first, the remaining thyroid tissue can make more hormones to make up for the loss. So you may not notice any symptoms.

But as more tissue is damaged, the gland can no longer keep up. Then symptoms start to appear.

The missing hormones can be replaced with daily tablets. This brings your body back to normal. Most people feel much better after starting treatment.

In some cases, the thyroid can heal on its own — for example, if the inflammation goes away.

---

## Can It Be Prevented?

In Germany, iodine deficiency is now very rare. But you can still help prevent it by:

- Drinking milk or eating dairy products every day
- Eating fish from the sea regularly
- Using iodized salt
- Taking iodine supplements (if needed)

> **Important:** Too much iodine can also cause problems. It can lead to an overactive thyroid. This is very unlikely from food. But dried seaweed (like kelp) has extremely high levels. One serving can give you more than the daily safe limit.

Iodine supplements can also be risky if they contain more than 100 micrograms per day.

---

## Can It Be Detected Early?

Your thyroid is very important for babies and children. An underactive thyroid can harm their growth and brain development.

All newborn babies in Germany are tested for thyroid function. This is done with a simple blood test. The test checks for a hormone called TSH.

TSH is made by the pituitary gland. It tells the thyroid to make more hormones. If the thyroid is not working well, the pituitary makes more TSH. So a high TSH level can be an early sign of an underactive thyroid.

If TSH is high but you have no symptoms, this is called **latent hypothyroidism**.

There is no clear benefit to testing adults for this condition. So routine screening is not recommended.

> **Important:** A slightly high TSH level does not always mean you have an underactive thyroid. Many people with slightly high levels do not need treatment. Their levels may go back to normal on their own. Testing everyone could lead to unnecessary worry and treatment.

---

## How Is It Treated?

To diagnose an underactive thyroid, your doctor will:

1. Ask about your symptoms
2. Feel your neck to check the thyroid
3. Order a blood test to measure thyroid hormone and TSH levels

TSH is a signal from the brain to the thyroid. If the thyroid is not working well, the brain makes more TSH to try to fix it. A high TSH level is often the first sign of a problem.

But not everyone with a high TSH needs treatment. Only about 2 to 5 out of every 100 people with high TSH levels will develop symptoms that need treatment.

The risk is higher if:
- TSH levels are very high
- Antibodies are found in the blood
- You are a woman

---

## Treatment

The main treatment is daily tablets that replace the missing thyroid hormone. The medicine is called levothyroxine or L-thyroxine. It is the same hormone your body makes.

This treatment:
- Restores normal hormone levels
- Usually makes symptoms go away
- Can be taken for life or for a shorter time, depending on the cause

The dose is based on your body weight. It is adjusted after 2 to 3 months, because it takes that long for hormone levels to stabilize.

There are almost no side effects if the dose is correct.

### Latent Hypothyroidism
If your TSH is high but you have no symptoms, doctors may debate whether to start treatment. There is no clear answer yet.

For more information on when and how to treat an underactive thyroid, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Hearing Loss and Deafness in Adults

Hearing loss means you have trouble hearing sounds and understanding speech.  
If you cannot hear at all, or almost nothing, doctors call this deafness.  
Some people are born with hearing problems.  
Others develop them later in life.  
Most people start to lose their hearing as they get older.

---

## What Is Hearing Loss and Deafness?

Your ears pick up sound waves.  
They turn these waves into signals.  
Your brain then turns the signals into sounds and words.  
If you have hearing loss, you may miss parts of speech or sounds.  
If your hearing is almost gone, doctors call this deafness.

Some people are born with hearing problems.  
Others get them in childhood.  
But for most people, hearing loss starts as they age.  
This is called age-related hearing loss.  
It is also known as presbycusis.

Depending on how bad the hearing loss is, treatment can help.  
Options include hearing aids, ear surgery, or cochlear implants.  
These can improve your hearing and your daily life.

---

## How Does Hearing Loss or Deafness Show Up?

Hearing problems can affect one ear or both ears.  
They can be mild, moderate, severe, or profound.

- Mild hearing loss: You may not hear whispers.  
- Moderate hearing loss: You can only hear loud sounds.  
- Severe hearing loss: You can only hear very loud noises.  
- Profound hearing loss: You may only feel sounds as vibrations.  
  This is called deafness.

Other symptoms may include:  
- Ringing in the ears (tinnitus)  
- A feeling of pressure in the ear  
- Dizziness

---

## What Causes Hearing Loss and Deafness?

Many people lose their hearing as they grow older.  
Scientists do not yet fully understand why.  
But they believe aging, long-term noise exposure, and genetics play a role.

Loud noise can damage your ears.  
It can harm the eardrum, the middle ear, and especially the inner ear.  
Short-term exposure may cause temporary damage.  
But repeated or very loud noise can cause lasting harm.

Even regular exposure to loud noise can lead to long-term hearing loss.  
This is called noise-induced hearing loss.

---

## What Increases the Risk of Hearing Loss?

Besides noise, other things can raise your risk:

- Earwax blocking the ear canal  
- Long-term middle ear infections  
- Serious infections like meningitis  
- Sudden hearing loss  
- Otosclerosis (when tiny bones in the ear harden)

Less common causes include head injuries, side effects from some medicines, and tumors.

---

## How Common Is Hearing Loss in Adults?

The World Health Organization says about 430 million adults worldwide have hearing problems.  
More than 30 out of every 100 people over age 65 have hearing loss.  
Exact numbers for Germany are not yet available.

Experts believe 16 to 25 out of every 100 adults have some hearing loss.  
The number is higher in older adults.

---

## How Does Hearing Loss Develop?

Some people are born with hearing problems.  
Others develop them in childhood.  
But for most people, hearing loss starts later in life.

Age-related hearing loss usually affects both ears equally.  
It gets worse over time.

At first, you may only notice trouble hearing quiet sounds or high-pitched tones.  
You may also struggle to follow conversations in noisy places, like restaurants or buses.  
Hearing loss usually gets worse slowly over the years.

If hearing loss comes on suddenly or is caused by injury, it can happen fast or even right away.  
In some cases, hearing may come back.  
But in older people, it is usually permanent.

---

## How Can Hearing Loss Be Prevented?

If your job involves loud noise, like working with machines or aircraft, wear hearing protection.  
Workplaces have rules to protect your hearing.

In daily life, avoid listening to loud music through headphones.  
Use earplugs at loud events like concerts or nightclubs.  
Even short bursts of loud noise during home projects can harm your hearing.  
Wear proper protection when doing DIY work.

---

## How Is Hearing Loss Diagnosed?

An ear, nose, and throat doctor (ENT specialist) can check for hearing loss.

The doctor will look inside your ears with a special tool.  
They will check for infections or blockages.  
They will also ask you about when you first noticed the problem.  
They may ask if you have other symptoms.

You will likely take several hearing tests.  
These tests help find out what kind of hearing loss you have and how bad it is.

In some cases, the doctor may order a CT scan or an MRI scan.  
These scans help find the exact cause of the hearing loss.

---

## How Is Hearing Loss Treated?

If hearing loss is caused by a middle ear infection, it can often be cured.  
But in adults, especially older adults, hearing loss is often permanent.

Hearing aids are often used.  
They make quiet sounds louder and block out very loud sounds.  
They send sound into your inner ear.  
This helps you talk with others and enjoy social life.

If the tiny sensory cells in your ears are badly damaged, cochlear implants may help.  
These are small devices placed inside the ear.  
They send signals directly to the hearing nerve.

---

## What Helps Manage Hearing Loss and Deafness?

Hearing loss can make communication hard.  
You may talk less with others.  
Some people feel left out, lonely, or sad.  
Some develop anxiety or depression.

Others may not notice your hearing problem.  
They might think you are not paying attention, rude, or strange.  
In some cases, people may wrongly think you have dementia.

Family members also need to learn how to help.  
Communication problems can cause stress and frustration for both sides.

The first step is to accept that your hearing is not what it used to be.
