Then, see a doctor and talk about your options.

It takes time and effort to get used to hearing aids or cochlear implants.  
But using them can greatly improve your hearing and your life.

---

## Where Can You Get Help?

If you have trouble hearing, see your family doctor first.  
They can refer you to an ear, nose, and throat specialist.

Self-help groups connect you with others who face similar challenges.  
You can share feelings, advice, and tips.

You can find local self-help groups through the National Contact and Information Point for Encouraging and Supporting Self-Help Groups (NAKOS).  
Visit their website to search for services near you.

# Lung Cancer

Every year, about 57,000 people in Germany are diagnosed with lung cancer.  
It is the second most common cancer in men.  
It is the third most common cancer in women.  
This article explains the causes, how it is diagnosed, and what treatments are available.

---

## Quick Facts

- Lung cancer is also called bronchial carcinoma or lung carcinoma.
- In the early stages, lung cancer often causes no clear symptoms.
- Smoking is the biggest risk factor for lung cancer.
- Doctors divide lung cancer into two main types: non-small cell and small cell.
- For non-small cell lung cancer, treatment depends on how far the cancer has spread.
- For small cell lung cancer, chemotherapy is usually the main treatment, often combined with other therapies.

> **Important:** This article is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

---

## What Is Lung Cancer?

Lung cancer means a cancer that starts in the lung tissue.  
Doctors use the terms lung carcinoma or bronchial carcinoma to describe it.  
There are two main types: non-small cell and small cell lung cancer.

> **Note:** Not every tumor in the lungs is lung cancer.  
> Sometimes cancer from another part of the body spreads to the lungs.  
> This is called a lung metastasis.  
> It is treated differently than lung cancer that starts in the lungs.

---

## What Symptoms Can Lung Cancer Cause?

About 57,000 people in Germany get lung cancer each year.  
Most people only find out they have it when the cancer is already advanced.  
There are two main reasons for this:

1. Lung cancer often does not cause symptoms early on.
2. When symptoms do appear, they are not unique to lung cancer.

Common symptoms include:

- A cough that does not go away
- Trouble breathing or feeling short of breath
- Coughing up phlegm, or phlegm with blood
- Pain in the chest or lung area
- Feeling weak or very tired
- Losing weight without trying
- Bone pain
- Fever
- Headaches or other nervous system problems

Coughing and tiredness can also happen with other illnesses like bronchitis.  
If these symptoms last for several weeks, especially if you have risk factors for lung cancer, see a doctor.

Your general practitioner can help figure out what is causing your symptoms.  
They may refer you to a specialist for further tests.

---

## What Causes Lung Cancer?

Smoking is the biggest cause of lung cancer.  
About 9 out of 10 men and 8 out of 10 women with lung cancer have smoked for many years.

Tobacco smoke contains harmful substances called carcinogens.  
These can damage lung cells and lead to cancer.  
The longer and more you smoke, the higher your risk.

But not everyone with lung cancer has smoked.  
Other causes include:

- Certain types of radiation
- Harmful chemicals in the workplace
- Air pollution, including fine dust

You cannot avoid all of these risks.  
But quitting smoking now can greatly reduce your risk of getting lung cancer within a few years.

---

## How Can You Prevent Lung Cancer?

The best way to prevent lung cancer is not to smoke.  
If you already smoke, quitting now helps a lot.

Even if you do not smoke, being around secondhand smoke increases your risk.

Your risk goes up if:

- You have smoked for a long time
- You started smoking at a young age
- You smoke many cigarettes, cigars, or pipe tobacco each day
- You are often around people who smoke

A healthy lifestyle also helps prevent cancer in general.  
Key habits include:

- Eating a balanced diet
- Being physically active for at least 150 minutes per week (like brisk walking)

---

## Is There Lung Cancer Screening in Germany?

For common cancers like lung cancer, screening might seem helpful.  
But so far, there is no safe, reliable test for everyone.

Experts and government officials are working on a screening program for heavy, long-term smokers aged 50 to 75.  
The test would use low-dose CT scans of the chest.

To qualify as a heavy smoker, you must meet all three of these conditions:

- You have smoked for at least 25 years
- You stopped smoking less than 10 years ago
- You have smoked at least 15 pack years (number of packs per day × number of years smoked)

This program may take several more months to start.

For more information, visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## How Is Lung Cancer Diagnosed?

If lung cancer is suspected, doctors use several tests.

The first step is a basic diagnosis. It includes:

- Talking to the patient about symptoms, health history, and risk factors
- A physical exam
- Blood tests
- X-rays and CT scans of the chest
- A bronchoscopy

Your general practitioner can start the process.  
Specialists like radiologists or lung doctors take over for more tests.

During a bronchoscopy, doctors take small tissue samples from the lungs.  
These samples help confirm the diagnosis.  
They also check the type of cancer and whether it has special features.

If lung cancer is confirmed, doctors use imaging tests to see if it has spread.

For more details on testing, visit the **Cancer Information Service** website (in German).

---

## How Is Lung Cancer Treated?

Doctors choose the best treatment based on:

- How advanced the cancer is
- The type of tumor (non-small cell or small cell)
- The tumor’s special features
- The patient’s overall health
- The patient’s personal wishes

### Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer

- Surgery is possible in early stages. The goal is to remove the tumor completely.
- If surgery is not possible, radiation therapy may be used alone in very early cases.
- Surgery is rarely used for small cell lung cancer because it spreads fast.

Surgery is only considered if the patient is healthy enough.  
Many lung cancer patients are around 70 years old.  
They may have other health problems that make surgery risky.

Most people are diagnosed at a later stage, when the cancer has already spread.  
At this point, surgery or radiation cannot remove all the cancer.

Instead, drug treatments are the main option.  
These aim to slow the cancer and ease symptoms.

Treatment options for advanced non-small cell lung cancer include:

- **Chemotherapy:** Stops cancer cells from growing and dividing.
- **Targeted therapy:** Uses drugs that attack specific features on cancer cells. Healthy cells usually do not have these features.
- **Immunotherapy:** Helps the body’s own immune system fight cancer.
- **Supportive care:** Treatments to relieve symptoms and improve quality of life. This can include radiation therapy to shrink tumors and reduce pain.

### Small Cell Lung Cancer

If small cell lung cancer has spread, treatment usually includes:

- Chemotherapy
- Immunotherapy

These are used together to fight the cancer.

For more details on treatment options, visit the **Cancer Information Service** website (in German).

---

## After Treatment: What Is Rehabilitation?

Cancer treatment can be very hard on the body and mind.  
Rehabilitation helps patients recover strength and cope with side effects.

A rehab program is tailored to each person’s needs.  
It may include:

- Breathing exercises to help with shortness of breath after surgery
- Counseling to support mental health
- Advice on healthy eating
- Physical therapy and exercise
- Help to quit smoking

---

## Aftercare and Follow-Up Care

After treatment, regular checkups help detect:

- A return of the cancer
- Side effects from treatment that appear later

You will get a personal aftercare plan.  
You will be checked often at first, then less often over time.

You can also see your doctor sooner if you have new symptoms.

During checkups, doctors:

- Ask about your symptoms
- Do a physical exam
- Check your lung function
- May use CT scans of the chest or MRI scans of the brain

If the cancer cannot be cured, regular visits help catch problems early.  
The goal is to keep your quality of life as good as possible.

---

## Life with Lung Cancer

Many people with lung cancer want to stay active and in control.  
What helps depends on the individual.

Ways to cope better include:

- **Exercise:** Can reduce tiredness and weakness. Start slowly and adjust to your ability.
- **Healthy eating:** Helps prevent poor nutrition. A dietitian can help if needed.
- **Counseling:** Can help if anxiety or fear become overwhelming.

When the cancer can no longer be cured and is getting worse, good care is essential.  
Symptoms like coughing and shortness of breath can be managed.  
Support from doctors, nurses, and counselors helps maintain quality of life.

---

## Where Can You Get Help?

Lung cancer is treated by a team of doctors with different specialties.  
Some hospitals are certified for treating lung cancer.  
They meet strict quality standards.

You can find certified centers on the **OncoMAP** website.

The German Society for Thoracic Surgery certifies centers through **Doc-Cert AG**.

For information about daily life with lung cancer and support options, visit the **Cancer Information Service** website (in German).

You can also contact them directly:

- Call the free number: 0800 - 420 30 40
- Email: krebsinformationsdienst@dkfz.de

# Warts

Warts are small, harmless growths on the skin.  
They can appear anywhere on the body.  
They come in different shapes and sizes.  
Warts are caused by a virus.  
The virus spreads through direct skin contact.  
Warts are very common, especially in children and teens.  
They often show up after playing sports or using public showers or pools.

---

## Quick Facts

- Warts are not cancer.  
- They usually go away on their own in a few weeks or months.  
- Warts can appear on any part of the body.  
- They are caused by a virus and can spread to others.  
- Children and teens are most likely to get warts.  
- Treatments can help warts disappear faster.  

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Are Warts?

Warts are non-cancerous skin growths.  
They can grow on any part of the body.  
They are caused by a virus.  
The virus enters the skin through tiny cuts or scratches.  
Most people will get at least one wart in their life.  
Children and teens are most likely to get them.  
But adults can get them too.

Warts are usually harmless.  
They often go away without treatment.  
This can take weeks or months.  
Some people find warts unattractive.  
They may feel self-conscious or upset by their look.  
There are treatments that can help warts go away faster.  
But these treatments do not always work.

**Important:** There is another type of skin growth called senile warts.  
They are also harmless.  
But they are not caused by a virus.  
They do not spread.  
They are more common in older adults.  
They do not go away on their own.

---

## What Do Warts Look Like?

Warts usually do not hurt.  
But some can itch, feel tight, or press on the skin.  
Warts on the bottom of the feet can hurt when walking.  
Some warts have small dark spots.  
These spots are tiny blood vessels that have clotted.

Warts can appear alone or in groups.  
A group of warts can cover a large area of skin.

Here are the main types of warts:

### Plantar Warts (Verrucas)

- Found on the soles of the feet or heels.  
- Can be large.  
- They grow inward because of pressure from walking and standing.  
- They are often painful when walking.

### Common Warts

- Small, hard, rough, and scaly.  
- Size ranges from a pinhead to a pea.  
- Often found on fingers, around nails, or on feet.

### Flat Warts

- Small and slightly raised.  
- Only a few millimeters wide.  
- Light brown in color.  
- Most often on the face, especially the forehead and cheeks.  
- Also common on the hands and underarms.

### Mosaic Warts

- White and about the size of a pinhead.  
- Found on the balls of the feet or under the toes.  
- Can spread across the whole bottom of the foot.  
- Flatter than plantar warts.  
- Usually do not hurt when walking.

### Facial Warts (Digitate or Filiform Warts)

- Look like thin, finger-like or feather-like growths.  
- Often appear on the face.  
- Can be very noticeable and upsetting.

### Genital Warts (Anogenital Warts or Condylomas)

- Small, hard lumps with a rough surface.  
- Appear only in the genital or anal area.  
- Spread through sexual contact.  
- Need different treatment than other warts.

---

## What Causes Warts?

Warts are caused by a virus called human papillomavirus, or HPV.  
There are over 100 types of this virus.  
The virus gets into the skin through small cuts or tears.  
It makes skin cells grow too fast.  
This causes a thick, hard bump to form — a wart.

The virus spreads through:
- Touching a wart directly.  
- Sharing towels, razors, or shoes.  
- Being in damp or wet places like pools or showers.  
- The risk is higher if the skin is broken or wet.

---

## Who Is More Likely to Get Warts?

Some people are more likely to get warts.  
This includes:

- People who work in meat processing, like slaughterhouses or butchers.  
- Kids and teens who use shared showers after sports or swimming.  
- People who have family members with warts.  
- School children who are in class with someone who has warts.  
- People with weak immune systems. This includes those who had an organ transplant or have serious illnesses like cancer or AIDS.  
- People with skin conditions like neurodermatitis.

---

## How Common Are Warts?

Warts are very common in children and teens.  
Up to one in three kids and teens have warts.  
In adults, warts are much less common.  
Only about 3% to 5% of adults have them.

---

## How Do Warts Go Away?

For healthy people, warts are not dangerous.  
The body usually builds up a defense against the virus.  
Over time, the wart disappears on its own.  
How long this takes depends on the virus type and the person’s health.

Studies show:
- About half of children and teens with warts are clear after one year.  
- After two years, about 70% are clear.  
- Few studies exist on how long warts last in adults.

If your immune system is weak, warts may take much longer to go away.

---

## How Can You Prevent Warts?

You can help stop warts from spreading to others.  
You can also stop them from spreading on your own skin.

**To protect others:**
- Cover the wart with a waterproof bandage when swimming.  
- Do not share towels, shoes, gloves, or socks.  
- Wear shoes in public showers, pools, and changing rooms.  
- Do not touch warts.

**To stop warts from spreading on your own skin:**
- Do not scratch or pick at warts.  
- Wash your hands well after touching a wart.  
- Keep your feet dry.  
- Change your socks every day.  
- Do not use tools like pumice stones or files on warts.  
- If you use them on a wart, do not use them on other skin areas.

These tips are not proven by science.  
But they may help.  
Wart viruses are very contagious.  
It is hard to stop them completely.

---

## How Are Warts Treated?

You do not always need to treat a wart.  
Most go away on their own.  
But some can last for years.  
Some people want to get rid of warts because they are unsightly or upsetting.

There are two main treatments:

### Salicylic Acid

- Available in creams, liquids, or plasters.  
- You apply it to the wart several times a day.  
- It slowly removes the thickened skin.  
- Most products are sold without a prescription.  
- Treatment lasts several weeks.

### Freezing (Cryotherapy)

- Done by a doctor or dermatologist.  
- Uses very cold liquid nitrogen.  
- The cold kills the top layer of skin.  
- The wart is frozen several times, with a week or more between sessions.  
- The area may hurt briefly during freezing.  
- After treatment, the skin is red, swollen, and may blister.

Both treatments work for many people.  
But not all warts go away completely.  
Some virus may stay behind.  
This can cause a new wart later.

> **Important:** Other treatments exist.  
> But many have not been tested well.  
> Results are unclear.

**Special advice:**
- If you have nerve damage in your feet (like from diabetes), see a doctor before treating a wart.  
- Pregnant or breastfeeding women should avoid treating warts unless advised by a doctor.

For more detailed guidance on treating warts, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Prostatitis and Pelvic Pain Syndrome

Prostatitis means inflammation of the prostate. The prostate is a small gland in men that helps make semen. It sits below the bladder and surrounds part of the tube that carries urine out of the body.

Pain when peeing, in the penis, or in the area between the scrotum and anus is common with prostatitis. The cause is often not known. Sometimes bacteria cause it. Most men get better with medicine.

---

## Quick Facts

- About 1 in 6 men will have prostatitis at some point.
- It can happen suddenly (acute) or last a long time (chronic).
- Common signs are pain when peeing and trouble peeing.
- Doctors often cannot find the exact cause of the pain. In some cases, bacteria are to blame.
- If bacteria are the cause, antibiotics usually help.
- If no bacteria are found, doctors may give medicine to reduce swelling and ease pain.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Prostatitis?

The prostate is about the size of a chestnut. It sits below the bladder. It makes part of the fluid that carries sperm. Its muscles help control whether urine flows out through the penis or semen is released during ejaculation.

When the prostate becomes inflamed, it is called prostatitis. This condition is fairly common.

Because the prostate surrounds part of the tube that carries urine, swelling can cause pain when peeing. Other common signs include a weak urine stream and needing to pee often.

One cause of prostatitis is a bacterial infection. This is called bacterial prostatitis. It can be sudden or long-lasting.

If no bacteria are found, the condition is called abacterial prostatitis or pelvic pain syndrome. The exact cause of this type is still unclear.

How the condition is treated and how long it lasts depend on the type.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Pain when peeing is a common sign. It often feels like a burning sensation.

The urine stream may be weak. Some men feel they do not fully empty their bladder. This leads to needing to pee often.

Pain can also happen in the area between the scrotum and anus. It may also come after sex.

With sudden bacterial prostatitis, men often feel very sick. They may have a high fever, shivers, and feel unwell.

Chronic prostatitis and pelvic pain syndrome usually cause milder symptoms. There is no high fever or shivers. But men may have ongoing pain in the area between the scrotum and anus, in the testicles, or in the penis. A constant need to pee may also be a sign.

Some men also lose interest in sex or have trouble getting or keeping an erection.

---

## What Causes Prostatitis?

Most cases of prostatitis are caused by a type of bacteria called *Escherichia coli*. This bacteria normally lives in the intestines. It can sometimes move into the prostate.

Other causes include sexually transmitted infections like *chlamydia* or *gonorrhea* (also called the clap).

These germs can enter the prostate through the tube that carries urine (the urethra). In rare cases, they may enter through the bladder or the bloodstream.

In chronic bacterial prostatitis, the body’s defense system does not fully fight off the germs. This causes the problem to last longer. It can also take time to find the right antibiotic to treat the infection.

The cause of pelvic pain syndrome is still unknown. Doctors think it may be due to inflammation in other nearby organs spreading to the prostate. A wrongly acting immune system, long-term problems with emptying the bladder, or nerve irritation may also play a role.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

Men with weak immune systems are more likely to get prostatitis. This includes men who are getting chemotherapy.

Drinking a lot of alcohol or having diabetes can also weaken the immune system. This may raise the risk of bacterial infections like prostatitis.

An enlarged prostate may also make prostatitis more likely.

Surgery on the bladder or urethra increases the risk. For example, having a tube (catheter) put into the bladder can let bacteria grow on it. These bacteria can then move into the bladder and cause inflammation in the prostate.

---

## How Common Is Prostatitis?

Prostatitis is fairly common. Up to 16 out of every 100 men will have it at some point in life.

In about 5 to 10 out of every 100 cases, doctors can prove that bacteria caused the problem.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Most men with sudden prostatitis feel better within 6 months after treatment. About 60 to 80 out of every 100 men no longer have symptoms.

With chronic prostatitis or pelvic pain syndrome, symptoms last more than 6 months or may never go away. They can come back in waves.

The pain can be so strong that it affects daily life and lowers quality of life. Scientists still do not know why some men develop long-term problems while others do not.

> **Important:** If treatment is delayed or antibiotics are not taken correctly or for too short a time, the condition is more likely to become chronic.

---

## How Is Prostatitis Diagnosed?

If you think you have prostatitis, see your family doctor or a urologist.

The doctor will ask about your symptoms and medical history. Then they will do a physical exam.

They may insert a finger into your rectum to feel the prostate. This is called a digital rectal exam.

A urine sample is tested in a lab. The middle part of the urine stream (midstream urine) is usually used. This helps check for bacteria.

In some cases, a more detailed test called the “four-glass test” is used. This involves testing:
- The first urine of the day
- Midstream urine
- Urine after a prostate massage

The fluid released from the prostate during the massage (prostatic expressate) is also tested.

The urine samples are used to grow bacteria in a lab. This helps find the exact type of germ and choose the right antibiotic.

A blood test may also be done. High levels of certain markers can suggest prostatitis. One of these is PSA. This is a protein made only by prostate cells. When the prostate is irritated or inflamed, more PSA enters the blood.

In some cases, an ultrasound of the prostate is done. This is called a transrectal ultrasound. It is done from the anus. It helps check if the prostate is very big or if there are pus-filled areas (abscesses).

---

## How Is Prostatitis Treated?

If bacteria are causing the prostatitis, antibiotics that target the specific germ can help.

> **Important:** Take the full course of antibiotics exactly as the doctor prescribes. This helps prevent symptoms from returning and stops the condition from becoming chronic.

If the inflammation is severe, you have a high fever, or the infection has spread into the blood, you may need to go to the hospital.

In the hospital, antibiotics are given through a vein. This allows the medicine to work faster and in higher doses. This helps prevent a serious blood infection called sepsis.

For pelvic pain syndrome, doctors often use a mix of two types of medicine:
- Alpha blockers: These relax the muscles around the bladder and urethra. This helps urine flow more easily and reduces pain when peeing.
- Anti-inflammatory medicine: This reduces swelling and helps ease pain.

If you have trouble getting or keeping an erection, your doctor may suggest a medicine that improves blood flow to the penis.

# Pityriasis Versicolor (Tinea Versicolor)

Many people do not know that their patchy skin is caused by a fungus. The fungus grows too much and causes the skin changes. The rash is not dangerous. It does not spread to others. It can be treated.

---

## Quick Facts

- Tinea versicolor causes light or dark patches on the skin.
- It is caused by a yeast that lives on almost everyone’s skin.
- The condition is not dangerous and cannot be passed to others.
- Doctors do not yet know why the yeast grows too much in some people but not in others.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Pityriasis Versicolor?

Pityriasis versicolor causes patches on the skin. These patches can be lighter or darker than the rest of the skin. It is caused by a yeast that lives on most people’s skin. The condition is not contagious. It is usually harmless. It is also called tinea versicolor. In parts of South Asia, it is known as Peter Elam’s disease.

Most people can treat this condition with creams or shampoos applied to the skin.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may first notice small round or oval spots on your skin. Over time, these spots grow and join together into larger, uneven patches.

The patches often appear on the chest, neck, back, and arms. The face can also be affected, especially in children.

The color of the patches varies. Some are yellowish or brownish. Others are pink or reddish. On darker or tanned skin, the patches often look lighter. On fair skin, they may look darker than the surrounding skin.

The patches do not change much under a special black light. The skin may feel dry and flaky. Itching is rare. If it happens, it is usually mild.

---

## What Causes Pityriasis Versicolor?

A yeast fungus that lives on nearly everyone’s skin causes this condition. Doctors do not know why the fungus grows too much in some people and causes visible patches.

> **Important:** Poor hygiene does not cause this condition. It is not contagious.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

Certain things can make it more likely to get pityriasis versicolor:

- Living in a warm, humid climate
- Sweating a lot, such as during exercise or in hot weather
- Using oils or cosmetics that block the skin pores
- Having a family history of the condition

A weak immune system can also increase the risk. This can happen with certain cancers or when taking medicines that lower the body’s ability to fight infections.

---

## How Common Is It?

Pityriasis versicolor is common. In countries with a mild climate, about 1 in 100 people have it. In some tropical countries, up to 4 out of 10 people may have it.

Men and women are equally affected. Most people first notice it during their teenage years.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor can often tell you have pityriasis versicolor by looking at the patches on your upper body or arms.

To rule out other skin problems, the doctor may take a small sample of skin flakes using clear sticky tape. They will look at the sample under a microscope. This test usually shows the fungus clearly.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Cool or dry weather may help the patches fade. But the condition usually does not go away on its own.

You need to use special creams, lotions, or shampoos. These products kill or stop the growth of the fungus.

- Apply the cream or lotion directly to the affected skin.
- Wash your hair and scalp with a special shampoo. This helps stop the fungus from spreading.

Some products work quickly—just a few minutes. Others take several hours. Many people apply the cream at night and wash it off in the morning.

After treatment, it may take weeks or even months for the skin color to return to normal.

Tablets are rarely needed. Most people get better with topical treatments.

---

For more information, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Burnout

A life full of stress can push people to their limits. When someone feels completely drained, disconnected, and unable to handle daily demands, it is often called burnout. This happens when a person is constantly overwhelmed by work or personal life.

## Quick Facts

- Burnout is a term used for symptoms that come from being overworked all the time.
- Common signs include feeling tired, emotionally empty, and not able to do your usual tasks well.
- There is no official medical definition for burnout.
- Work stress leading to burnout is a common reason people take time off from work.
- Other health problems, like depression or anxiety, can cause similar symptoms.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Burnout?

The word "burnout" was first used in the 1970s in the United States. A psychologist named Herbert Freudenberger created it to describe the effects of extreme stress in jobs that help others. Doctors, nurses, and other caregivers often worked long hours and gave everything to their patients. Over time, they became so tired and worn out that they felt “burned out.”

Today, the term is used more broadly. Anyone can experience burnout — not just healthcare workers. It can affect people who are driven at work, celebrities, employees, students, or those managing a household.

Because there is no clear medical definition, it is hard to know exactly what burnout is. Doctors do not agree on how to diagnose it. And we do not know how many people actually have it.

## Signs of Burnout

All descriptions of burnout agree that the main symptoms come from ongoing stress. Stress can come from work, but it can also come from other areas, like caring for a sick family member.

There are three main signs of burnout:

### Feeling Completely Drained

People with burnout feel empty and exhausted. They have no energy left. They feel sad, tired, and worn out. They may also have physical problems like stomach pain or bowel issues.

### Losing Connection to Work

Work feels harder and more frustrating. People may start to pull away emotionally. They feel numb. They no longer care about their job, their work environment, or even their coworkers.

### Doing Less Well at Tasks

Burnout makes it hard to do everyday things at work, at home, or while caring for others. People feel negative about their tasks. They struggle to focus. They feel lazy, unmotivated, and lose their creativity.

## What Causes Burnout?

When life feels too heavy, it can lead to burnout. Work stress can cause both physical and mental problems. Some people reach a point where they feel empty, exhausted, and unable to cope.

Common causes include:

- Always feeling overworked.
- Feeling under-challenged or bored at work.
- Constant time pressure.
- Conflicts with coworkers or bosses.
- Putting others’ needs first and ignoring your own.

Work-related stress is a frequent reason people take sick leave.

## How Is Burnout Diagnosed?

Unlike depression or diabetes, burnout does not have a clear medical definition. It is not officially recognized as a medical condition. There is not enough research to fully understand it.

**Important:** The symptoms of burnout can also be caused by other health problems. These include:

- Depression
- Anxiety disorders
- Chronic fatigue syndrome

Certain physical illnesses or medications can also cause similar symptoms.

There are questionnaires people can use to check their own symptoms. But these tools are not reliable. They cannot clearly tell burnout apart from other conditions. Online tests are not trustworthy for diagnosing burnout.

## How Is Burnout Treated?

Improving work conditions can help. For example, changing work hours, reducing workload, or getting more support can make a big difference.

For people who are caring for a sick relative, getting help with daily tasks can ease the burden.

But first, it is important to rule out other health problems. For example, depression can cause:

- Extreme tiredness
- Feeling sad or low
- Trouble doing normal tasks

These symptoms are very similar to burnout. So it is easy to mistake one for the other.

If you think you have burnout, do not jump to conclusions. Getting the wrong diagnosis can lead to the wrong treatment.

For example, someone who is just tired from work might feel better after a long break. But someone with depression might get worse if they only take time off. People with depression usually need therapy or medicine — not just rest.

## More Information

To learn more about burnout — what it is and how it is different from depression — visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

# Tenosynovitis (Inflammation of the Tendon Sheath)

The protective covering around a tendon can become inflamed if the tendon is overused. Sometimes, the tendon itself also swells and becomes inflamed. This condition can cause severe pain and make movement very difficult. There are several treatment options if the symptoms do not go away on their own.

---

## Quick Facts

- Tendons connect muscles to bones. They help your body move and stay stable.
- A thin, protective layer called the synovium wraps around parts of tendons that move a lot.
- This layer is filled with fluid that helps the tendon slide smoothly.
- When the synovium becomes inflamed, it is called tenosynovitis (or tendovaginitis).
- Tenosynovitis often happens in the hands, arms, and feet.
- It is very important to limit movement in the affected area to help healing.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Tenosynovitis?

Tendons connect muscles to bones. They carry the power from muscles to move your body.

Some tendons have a protective covering made of connective tissue. This covering is called the synovium. It is filled with fluid that lets the tendon move easily with little friction.

If a tendon is used too much or too hard, the synovium can become inflamed and swollen. Sometimes, the tendon itself also swells.

Inflammation of the tendon sheath can cause sharp pain. It can also make movement very hard. This condition is most common in the hands, arms, and feet.

Most people get better within a few weeks if they rest the affected area.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Pain is the most common symptom. It usually gets worse when you move the area.

The area may also look swollen and feel tender to the touch.

As the inflammation gets worse, you may feel pain even when the area is at rest. For example, you might feel pain at night when lying down.

In some cases, the inflamed tissue can stick together. This makes movement feel rough or stiff.

You might feel a rubbing, grinding, or crackling sensation when you move.

In the fingers and wrists, the tendon can narrow. This can make it hard to move your fingers.

One common result is a condition called “trigger finger.” This happens when a finger bends but then gets stuck and won’t straighten. You may need to push it back into place.

Tenosynovitis can also irritate nearby nerves. This can cause numbness or tingling in the area.

---

## What Causes Tenosynovitis?

Most often, tenosynovitis is caused by doing movements that are new or repeated too often. These movements put too much stress on the tendons and their sheaths.

For example, walking or running long distances without training first can cause problems in the feet and lower legs. Wearing new or poorly fitting shoes can also cause strain.

Some jobs and hobbies raise the risk. Working at a computer for long hours or playing a musical instrument can stress the hands, wrists, and forearms.

Inflammation in the wrist often comes from repeatedly stretching the thumb away from the fingers. This happens often when using smartphones or lifting babies.

Certain health conditions also increase the risk. These include:
- Rheumatoid arthritis
- Gout
- Diabetes

Women who are pregnant or breastfeeding are also more likely to develop tenosynovitis.

---

## How Common Is Tenosynovitis?

Tenosynovitis is a common problem, especially in the hands and wrists. Women are more likely than men to get it.

About 2 to 3 out of every 100 people will develop “trigger finger” at some point in their lives.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor can usually tell if you have tenosynovitis with a short exam.

First, the doctor will ask you about your symptoms. Then, they will look at and gently press on the painful area.

They will also test which movements make the pain worse.

In most cases, no further tests are needed. But if the doctor suspects another illness is causing the problem, they may order tests.

These can include:
- Blood tests
- X-rays
- Ultrasound scans

Blood tests help check if the inflammation is caused by an infection.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Surgery is not usually needed for tenosynovitis.

The first step is to rest the affected area. This gives the tendon and sheath time to heal.

Once the pain goes away, avoid doing the same movements that caused the problem. This helps prevent it from coming back.

If the condition is caused by work, changing your setup can help. For example, switch to an ergonomic mouse or adjust your desk height.

Occupational therapists or doctors who specialize in work health can give advice on how to make changes.

If rest and changes don’t help, the doctor may inject medicine into the area. This includes a numbing medicine and a steroid called cortisone. These can reduce pain and swelling.

In rare cases, surgery may be needed. The surgeon removes or cuts the tight part of the sheath. This lets the tendon move freely again.

For more details on treatment options, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

# Senile Purpura

Senile purpura is a type of bruising that happens in older adults.  
It occurs without a strong bump or injury.  
The bruising is not dangerous.  
It goes away on its own after 1 to 3 weeks.  
It mostly shows up on skin that has had a lot of sun exposure over the years.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Senile Purpura?

Bruising in older adults is called senile purpura.  
It can happen after a light touch or a small bump.  
The skin changes with age, especially from sun damage.  
The skin gets thinner and less strong.  
The small blood vessels under the skin become weak.  
These weak blood vessels can break easily.  
This causes blood to leak under the skin, forming bruises.  
The bruises are not painful.  
They go away on their own.  
But they can come back.  
This can be upsetting for some people.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The bruises are often dark purple.  
They can be between 1 and 4 centimeters wide.  
They usually appear on the backs of the hands or lower arms.  
They can also show up on the legs, neck, or face.  
The skin around the bruise is often thin, dark, and stiff.  
The bruise does not hurt or itch.

---

## What Causes Senile Purpura?

Bruising happens even from small bumps.  
This is because the skin weakens with age.  
Sunlight is a major cause of this skin weakening.  
The small blood vessels in the skin become fragile.  
They leak more easily.  
This leads to bruising.  
The areas most exposed to the sun are most likely to get bruised.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

You are more likely to get senile purpura if you:

- Spend a lot of time in the sun without protection  
- Have fair skin  
- Are older

---

## How Common Is It?

The chance of getting senile purpura goes up with age.  
It is more common in people who have had a lot of sun exposure.  
About 12 out of 100 people over age 50 get it.  
Up to 30 out of 100 people over age 75 get it.

---

## How Does It Progress?

The bruise fades after 1 to 3 weeks.  
Sometimes a brown mark stays behind.  
There are no serious health problems linked to it.  
But the bruising can come back.  
This can be annoying.

---

## How Can It Be Prevented?

Be careful with your skin.  
Avoid bumps, even small ones.  
Be gentle during daily care like washing or dressing.  
Protect your skin from the sun.  
Wear long sleeves and pants when outside.  
Use sunscreen with a high protection factor (SPF 50 or higher).  
This helps block the sun’s harmful rays.  
These rays are a major cause of skin aging and bruising.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor checks the bruised skin.  
They ask about your health history.  
They may ask about past illnesses.  
This helps rule out other causes of bruising.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Senile purpura is harmless.  
It does not need special treatment.  
The bruises go away on their own.  
They do not hurt or itch.  
If your skin feels dry, use a moisturizer.

# Diabetic Neuropathy

Diabetic neuropathy happens when blood sugar stays too high for a long time.  
This can hurt the nerves, especially in the feet.  
When nerves are damaged, you may feel pain or lose feeling in your feet.  
Keeping blood sugar levels steady can help prevent this problem.

---

## Quick Facts

- Diabetic neuropathy is a common problem for people with diabetes.  
- High blood sugar over time slowly harms the nerves.  
- Other body changes linked to diabetes also play a role.  
- Common signs include pain, burning, tingling, or numbness in the feet.  
- Hands, lower arms, and lower legs can also be affected.  
- Nerve damage can also affect organs. This may cause stomach or heart problems.  
- There is no cure for diabetic neuropathy.  
- But you can prevent it or slow it down.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Diabetic Neuropathy?

Doctors use the term diabetic neuropathy to describe nerve problems caused by diabetes.  

The nerves outside the brain and spinal cord are affected. These are called peripheral nerves.  

These nerves help you feel touch, pain, and temperature. They also help your muscles move.  
When they are damaged, you may not feel things properly. This is called sensorimotor neuropathy.  
You might also have weakness or trouble moving.

Diabetic neuropathy can also affect the autonomic nerves.  
These nerves control organs like the stomach, heart, bladder, and sex organs.  
When these nerves are damaged, you may have problems with digestion, blood pressure, or bladder control.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

If the nerves in your feet are damaged, you may feel:

- Pain  
- Burning  
- Tingling  
- Numbness  

These symptoms often get worse at night.  
Even light touches, like a blanket or socks, can hurt.  
You may have trouble walking. You may fall more often.

If the nerves that control organs are damaged, you may have:

- Low blood pressure  
- Dizziness  
- Trouble swallowing  
- Nausea  
- Constipation  
- Diarrhea  
- Trouble emptying your bladder  
- Sweating too much  
- Erectile dysfunction in men

Almost half of people with diabetic neuropathy do not feel pain.  
But their nerves may still be damaged.  
They may walk unsteadily and fall more often.  
They may not notice cuts or sores on their feet because they do not feel pain.

> **Important:** Many people with diabetes learn to recognize low blood sugar by symptoms like sweating, shaking, or a fast heartbeat.  
> But this does not work for everyone. It is harder for people with nerve damage.

---

## What Causes Diabetic Neuropathy?

The main cause is high blood sugar over a long time.  
This slowly harms the nerves.

In people with type 2 diabetes, problems with fat and cholesterol in the body also increase the risk.

---

## How Common Is It?

Diabetic neuropathy is very common.  
About half of all people with type 1 or type 2 diabetes will develop it at some point.  
The longer you have diabetes, the higher the risk.  
Poor blood sugar control makes nerve damage more likely.

---

## What Can Go Wrong?

People with diabetic neuropathy are at risk for foot problems.  
Sores and infections can form.  
They may not feel pain, so injuries go unnoticed.  
This can lead to serious infections.

Nerve damage can also harm bones and joints in the feet.  
In severe cases, the foot may need to be removed.

---

## How Can You Prevent It?

The best ways to prevent diabetic neuropathy are:

- Keep blood sugar levels steady  
- Eat healthy foods  
- Exercise regularly  

Avoid smoking and drinking too much alcohol.  
These habits increase your risk of complications.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

People with diabetes should see their doctor regularly.  
Early checks can catch nerve damage before it gets worse.

Your doctor will ask about symptoms like pain or numbness.  
They will look at your hands and feet.  
They will check for:

- Dry or warm feet  
- Sores, cuts, or red patches  
- Infections or ulcers  

They will test your ability to feel light touches and vibrations.  
They will check your reflexes, like the reflex in your ankle.  
A weak reflex may mean nerve damage.  
They may also test your sensitivity to pain and cold.

Your doctor will ask about other symptoms like dizziness or stomach issues.

Sometimes, extra tests are needed.  
These may include blood tests or heart tests.  
They help rule out other causes.

---

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure for diabetic neuropathy.  
The goal is to slow it down and prevent serious problems like foot sores.

For people with type 1 diabetes, keeping blood sugar under control is key.  
This helps delay or prevent nerve damage.

For people with type 2 diabetes, eating well and staying active helps control blood sugar, blood pressure, cholesterol, and weight.

Pain is often treated with medicines used for depression or epilepsy.  
These medicines block pain signals to the brain.  
They can help reduce nerve pain.

> **Important:** Some people try other pain relief methods like TENS (electrical nerve stimulation) or acupuncture.  
> But there is not enough proof that these work for diabetic neuropathy.

---

## How Can You Live Better with Diabetic Neuropathy?

Check your feet every day.  
Look for:

- Dry or cracked skin  
- Cuts or sores  
- Redness between toes  
- Problems with nails  

Early detection helps prevent infections and ulcers.

If you cannot see your feet well, ask a family member to help.  
Or visit a foot specialist regularly.

Stay independent.  
Physical therapy can improve strength and balance.  
This helps prevent falls and injuries.

Occupational therapy can help you find ways to manage daily tasks.

Make your home safer.  
Install grab bars in the bathroom.  
Use night lights to see in the dark.

Hot water can burn you without you feeling it.  
Always test the water with your elbow before getting in the shower or bath.

# Slipped (Herniated) Disc

A slipped disc can cause serious pain. But it can also go unnoticed. Most people feel better within six weeks.

## Quick Facts

- Early signs may include sharp pain that runs down one leg and into the foot.
- You might also feel numbness or a tingling sensation.
- These symptoms often get better on their own after a few weeks.
- Staying active and managing pain helps during recovery.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is a Slipped Disc?

Back pain is common. But it is hard to know the exact cause. If you have pain that shoots down one leg and into your foot, it could be a slipped disc. This is also called a herniated disc. Most people feel better within six weeks.

Your spine has bones called vertebrae. Between these bones are spinal discs. These discs act like cushions. Each disc has a soft center and a tough outer layer.

A slipped disc happens when the soft center pushes out through the outer layer. This can press on nearby nerves. That pressure causes pain. But not every slipped disc causes pain.

## What Are the Symptoms?

A slipped disc can cause sudden, sharp pain in the lower back. A common sign is pain that runs down one leg and into the foot. This is called sciatica. It usually comes from a problem in the lower back.

If the problem is in the neck, the pain may go into the arms.

In rare cases, you might lose feeling in the buttocks. Or you might have trouble moving a leg. These signs can mean nerve damage. They need medical attention right away.

> **Important:** Studies show that many people have a slipped disc but feel no pain.  
> - In people aged 20 to 30, about 30 out of 100 had a slipped disc with no symptoms.  
> - In people aged 50 and older, about 40 out of 100 had a slipped disc with no symptoms.

## What Causes a Slipped Disc?

Spinal discs help absorb shock between the bones in your spine. When a disc can no longer handle the pressure, it can slip. The pain comes when the disc presses on a nerve.

Most slipped discs happen because of normal wear and tear over time. This is part of aging. Over the years, discs lose their strength. They dry out and crack. Very rarely, a fall or accident can cause a slipped disc.

Sciatica happens when disc material presses on a nerve in the lower back. These nerves connect to the sciatic nerve. The sciatic nerve runs down each leg. When it is irritated, it causes pain, tingling, or numbness.

Doctors describe three types of slipped discs:

- **Protrusion:** The disc bulges out, but the outer layer stays whole.
- **Prolapse:** The outer layer tears. Some disc material spills out, but it is still attached.
- **Sequestration:** The disc material breaks off and moves into the spinal canal. It is no longer connected to the disc.

> **Important:** Prolapses and sequestrations are more likely to cause leg pain than protrusions. The type matters for treatment and how the condition will progress.

## How Common Is a Slipped Disc?

About 3 out of every 100 people will have back pain from a slipped disc at some point in life. Slipped discs are more common in people over 30. Men are about twice as likely to have one as women.

## What Is the Outlook?

Pain can start suddenly and go away just as fast. Some people have long-term pain. Others have it come back again and again. Every case is different.

About 90 out of 100 people get better on their own within six weeks. The body may reabsorb some of the disc material. Or the material may move so it no longer presses on the nerve. If pain lasts longer than six weeks, it is unlikely to go away without treatment.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose a slipped disc by asking questions and doing a physical exam.

There is little need for complex tests. X-rays are not helpful. They often show disc problems in people who have no pain. Imaging tests can show a problem that is not really causing the pain. This can lead to unnecessary treatment that may do more harm than good.

Imaging tests like MRI are only needed if:

- You have weakness in one or both legs.
- You have trouble using your bladder or bowels.
- The pain is unbearable even with treatment.
- Back pain does not improve after four weeks.
- Leg pain does not improve after two weeks.
- Another condition, like a tumor, is suspected.

## How Is It Treated?

The main goal is to relieve pain and help you stay active. Staying active helps recovery. But treating pain does not make healing faster.

Even severe sciatica often gets better on its own. Surgery is rarely needed.

> **Important:** Surgery is needed if nerves are so damaged that you lose control of your bladder or bowels. Surgery may also be an option if severe sciatica lasts longer than six to twelve weeks, even with pain treatment.

For more information on when surgery is right, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

## What Rehabilitation Helps?

Rehabilitation is for people whose back pain is so bad they cannot work or do daily tasks.

Rehab programs may include:

- Back pain training classes.
- Strength training.
- Stretching and relaxation exercises.

These exercises aim to reduce pain and improve movement. They also strengthen the muscles in your core. Stronger core muscles help support your spine.

Rehab also helps you stay motivated to keep exercising. It teaches you how to manage pain in daily life.

> **Important:** Keep doing the exercises even after rehab ends. This helps keep your progress and prevents future pain.

# Bladder Infection (Cystitis)

A bladder infection, also called cystitis, is an infection in the lower part of the urinary system. It mainly affects women. The most common signs are a burning feeling when you pee and a strong need to go to the bathroom often.

Most bladder infections are caused by bacteria. They can usually be treated well.

---

## Quick Facts

- Cystitis mostly happens in women.
- Most cases are not serious and go away on their own.
- Antibiotics can help, but you don’t always need them.
- Some women get cystitis only once in a while. Others get it again and again.
- Having sex can raise your risk because it can push bacteria into the tube that carries urine out (the urethra).
- About 10 out of every 100 women have a bladder infection at least once a year.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Cystitis?

Cystitis is an infection in the bladder. People with this infection often feel the need to pee many times. They also feel a sharp, stinging pain when they pee.

The symptoms can be very uncomfortable. But the good news is that cystitis can usually be treated successfully.

Most simple infections go away without any problems. Antibiotics work well, but they are not always needed.

There is no proven way to stop cystitis completely. Many common tips for prevention have not been tested by science.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may feel a strong urge to pee, even if your bladder is not full.

You may also feel a burning or stinging pain when you pee.

Some women say it hurts the most when the bladder is almost empty.

The need to pee can come suddenly. You may rush to the bathroom, but only a small amount of urine comes out.

Some women have trouble holding in their urine. This can be very upsetting.

Your urine might look cloudy. It may also have a strong or unusual smell. Sometimes, you might see blood in your urine.

> **Warning:** If the infection is severe, you may feel weak, unwell, or irritable. You might have trouble sleeping. The pain could spread across your belly or into your back.

Sometimes, a urine test finds bacteria even if you have no symptoms. Doctors call this "asymptomatic bacteriuria." It is usually harmless and does not need treatment.

---

## What Causes Cystitis?

Cystitis happens when bacteria get into the bladder through the urethra. The bacteria then grow and cause inflammation in the bladder lining.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

- Having sex can increase your risk. It can push bacteria into the urethra.
- Spermicides (like creams or gels used during sex) and contraceptive diaphragms can also raise the risk.
- Pregnant women are more likely to get cystitis.
- People with certain health conditions are at higher risk, including:
  - Those with a urinary catheter
  - Those with a urological disease
  - Those with changes in the shape of their urinary tract
  - People with diabetes
  - People with multiple sclerosis
- Women who have had cystitis before are more likely to get it again.
- Cystitis is more common after menopause.

---

## How Common Is Cystitis?

Women get bladder infections much more often than men. This is because women have a shorter urethra. That makes it easier for bacteria to reach the bladder.

About 10 out of every 100 women have a bladder infection at least once a year. Half of these women will have another one within a year.

---

## How Does Cystitis Progress?

Cystitis is called "uncomplicated" if:

- The symptoms stay in the bladder and urethra.
- There are no other health problems that could make it worse.

Uncomplicated cystitis is easy to treat and usually gets better without problems.

Cystitis is called "complicated" if there is a higher risk of serious problems. This includes:

- Men
- People with a weak immune system
- People with damaged kidneys
- People with changes in their urinary tract

If bacteria can travel from the bladder to the kidneys, the infection can spread. This can cause a serious kidney infection called pyelonephritis.

If you have pain in your side (near your kidneys), a fever, nausea, or vomiting, you must see a doctor or go to the hospital right away.

These symptoms could mean you have a kidney infection. This is rare but can cause long-term damage if not treated quickly.

---

## Can Cystitis Be Prevented?

Sometimes, cystitis happens with no clear reason. If you get it often, you can try to notice what might be making it worse.

If you can’t avoid those triggers and you keep getting infections, your doctor may suggest medicine to prevent them.

This medicine must be taken regularly to work. It can also cause side effects.

---

## How Is Cystitis Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and medical history.

They may test your urine using a small strip. This can show if there are signs of infection.

If the symptoms are clear, you may not need more tests.

An ultrasound (a scan using sound waves) can check your kidneys and bladder. This is usually only done if the infection is complicated or keeps coming back.

X-rays or a cystoscopy may be done in rare cases. A cystoscopy is a test where a doctor puts a thin tube with a camera into the urethra and moves it into the bladder. This helps the doctor see if there is anything wrong with the inside of the bladder.

You can see your family doctor, gynecologist, or urologist for help.

---

## How Is Cystitis Treated?

For many women, cystitis is a one-time or rare problem. For others, it keeps coming back.

Antibiotics usually help relieve symptoms fast and shorten the illness. But you don’t always need them.

In about 30 to 50 out of 100 women, symptoms go away within a week even without antibiotics. Not using antibiotics does not usually lead to serious problems.

Talk to your doctor about whether antibiotics are right for you.

If you have a complicated case, you will need antibiotics.

For mild to moderate pain, you can use painkillers like paracetamol or ibuprofen. These can help until your body fights off the infection.

Some home remedies may help too:
- Drink plenty of fluids
- Use a warm heating pad on your lower belly

For more detailed information on treating cystitis, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)

You might sleep enough but still feel very tired during the day. This could be a sign of obstructive sleep apnea. Many people with this condition snore loudly. Their breathing stops or slows down while they sleep. They often do not notice these pauses in breathing.

These breathing problems can make daily life hard. They can affect your energy, mood, and health.

---

## Quick Facts

- Many people with sleep apnea snore and stop breathing at night. They usually do not know it is happening.
- Snoring alone is not dangerous. But if breathing stops, it is sleep apnea.
- Over time, sleep apnea can lead to serious health problems.
- It can make your life feel harder and less enjoyable.
- Sleep apnea happens when the muscles in the upper airway relax too much.
- About 3 out of 100 women and 5 out of 100 men have obstructive sleep apnea.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Sleep Apnea?

Some people with sleep apnea sleep long enough but still feel tired during the day. This happens because their breathing is blocked or slowed while they sleep. They may wake up briefly many times without realizing it. These short awakenings break their sleep. Over time, this can lead to health problems and lower quality of life.

---

## What Are the Signs of Sleep Apnea?

Common signs include:

- Feeling very tired all day
- Trouble focusing or remembering things
- Sweating a lot at night
- Waking up often during the night
- Waking up with a fast heartbeat or shortness of breath
- Waking up with a dry mouth
- Headaches in the morning
- Trouble keeping an erection (in men)

---

## What Causes Sleep Apnea?

Sleep apnea happens when the muscles in the throat relax too much. This makes the airway narrower or even close off. When this happens, you snore loudly when breathing in and out.

When breathing stops, your body gets less oxygen. Your blood pressure and heart rate drop. Your brain senses this and wakes you up briefly. These tiny awakenings are called "arousals." They stop you from getting deep, restful sleep.

You may not remember these awakenings. But they happen many times a night. This is why you feel tired during the day.

Certain things can make sleep apnea worse:

- Being overweight
- Having large tonsils
- A small lower jaw
- A small soft palate
- A tongue that sits too far back
- Blocked nasal passages
- Sleeping on your back
- Drinking too much alcohol
- Using sleeping pills or calming medicines

The chance of having sleep apnea goes up after age 45.

---

## How Common Is Sleep Apnea?

Experts estimate that:

- About 3 out of 100 women have obstructive sleep apnea.
- About 5 out of 100 men have obstructive sleep apnea.

---

## How Does Sleep Apnea Affect the Body?

People with severe sleep apnea often feel groggy and tired all day. They do not feel rested after sleep. Their mood may get worse. Some people with sleep apnea also develop depression.

Sleep apnea is linked to:

- High blood pressure
- Heart disease
- Stroke
- Irregular heartbeats

If breathing stops only a few times and for short periods, it may not cause problems. But if it happens often and lasts long, it can harm your health. If you have ongoing symptoms, talk to a doctor.

---

## How Is Sleep Apnea Diagnosed?

If your doctor suspects sleep apnea, they will:

- Ask about your symptoms and habits
- Do a physical exam

You may be given a small device to wear at home. It records:

- How you breathe
- Your heart rate
- Oxygen levels in your blood
- How much you snore
- Your body position while sleeping

If the results show problems, you may need to go to a sleep lab.

In the sleep lab, you spend one or more nights. Doctors use sensors and a video camera to monitor your sleep. This helps them see if you have sleep apnea.

---

## How Is Sleep Apnea Treated?

There are several ways to treat sleep apnea. The best treatment depends on your situation.

**Lifestyle changes:**
- Losing weight can help if you are overweight.

**Medical treatments:**
- Devices that help keep your airway open
- Special mouthpieces that move the jaw forward
- Positioning aids to stop you from sleeping on your back
- Surgery to fix blocked airways

**CPAP therapy (most effective for severe cases):**
- CPAP means continuous positive airway pressure.
- A machine pumps air into your airway at a steady pressure.
- You wear a mask over your nose or mouth while sleeping.
- The air pressure keeps your airway open.
- This stops breathing pauses.
- It can greatly reduce daytime tiredness.

CPAP works very well. But it takes time to get used to wearing the mask every night. Not everyone likes it at first. But many people find it helps a lot.

**Medication:**
- There is no medicine that treats sleep apnea well.
- No drug has been proven to work.

---

## What Is Life Like with Sleep Apnea?

Sleep apnea can make life hard. You may sleep poorly. You feel tired and foggy during the day. Some people fall asleep without meaning to. This is called a microsleep.

You may also have trouble focusing or remembering things.

Sleep apnea can affect your relationships. Your loud snoring can wake up your partner. They may feel tired and irritable too. The breathing pauses can also be scary for your partner.

You can get help to adjust to treatment:

- Attend a training course to learn how to use CPAP.
- Join a self-help group. Talking with others who have sleep apnea can help.
- Many cities in Germany have self-help groups for people with sleep apnea.

Be patient. It takes time to get used to treatment. But if you stick with it, your life can improve a lot.

For more help, visit the website **gesundheitsinformation.de**. It lists self-help groups and support services.

# Vulvar Cancer – Simple Explanation

Vulvar cancer is a type of cancer that affects the outside parts of a woman’s genitals. It used to mostly happen in older women. But now, more younger women are also getting it.

Many cases are caused by a virus called human papillomavirus, or HPV. A vaccine can help prevent this virus and lower the risk of cancer.

---

## Quick Facts

- Most early changes that can turn into vulvar cancer are caused by HPV.
- The HPV vaccine can stop these changes from happening.
- These early changes are becoming more common, especially in younger women.
- If the cancer is found early and the tumor is fully removed, recovery is likely.
- The outlook depends on whether the cancer has spread to the lymph nodes.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Vulvar Cancer?

Vulvar cancer starts in the outer parts of a woman’s reproductive system. This includes:

- The large lips (labia majora)
- The small lips (labia minora)
- The clitoris
- The area around the opening of the urethra
- The pubic mound (mons pubis)
- The area between the vagina and anus (perineum)

The cancer begins in the skin or lining of the vulva. It can start from abnormal tissue changes called precursors. Doctors use the term VIN for these changes.

Most of these precursors are caused by HPV. If not treated, they may stay the same, go away, or turn into cancer that grows into deeper tissue.

Some precursors are not linked to HPV. One rare type is called Paget’s disease of the vulva.

When cancer develops, the cells grow into the deeper layers of tissue under the skin and mucous membranes.

Most vulvar cancers in older women are not linked to HPV. But HPV-related cases are rising — especially in younger women.

> **Note:** Vulvar cancer is not the same as vaginal cancer. Vaginal cancer happens in the vagina, which is the tube that connects the vulva to the uterus.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

In the early stages, vulvar cancer often causes no symptoms. There is no single look that tells you it’s cancer.

But common early signs include:

- Itching in the genital area
- Pain
- A burning feeling
- Trouble passing urine
- Visible or felt changes in the vulva

Itching and trouble peeing can also happen with non-cancerous conditions. But if these symptoms last more than a few weeks, see a doctor.

Your general practitioner or gynecologist can check what is causing the problem. They can also order further tests if needed.

---

## What Causes Vulvar Cancer?

The main risk factor is infection with HPV in the genital area.

Women who have had HPV-related cancers in the cervix, vagina, or anus are more likely to develop vulvar changes.

People with weakened immune systems — for example, after an organ transplant or with HIV — are also at higher risk.

Other risk factors include:

- Smoking
- Long-term skin conditions like lichen sclerosus

---

## How Common Is It?

Vulvar cancer is the fourth most common cancer of the outer female genitals.

In 2020, about 3,100 new cases were reported in Germany.

Most cases happen in women over 70. But in recent years, more younger women have been diagnosed.

This rise is linked to increasing HPV infections.

---

## Can It Be Prevented?

Yes, the HPV vaccine can help prevent HPV infections and the precursors that can lead to vulvar cancer.

The vaccine is recommended for girls and boys between ages 9 and 14. Health insurance covers the cost up to age 17.

> **Important:** The vaccine does not protect against all types of HPV that can cause cancer. Even vaccinated women should watch for early warning signs.

For more information about the HPV vaccine, visit the website of the German Cancer Research Center (in German).

---

## Can We Screen for It?

Germany does not have a regular screening program for vulvar cancer.

But from age 20, women can get a free yearly gynecological exam. During this exam, the doctor checks the entire vulva for any changes.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor checks the vulva during a gynecological exam. They may use a magnifying glass to look closely.

If anything looks suspicious, the doctor takes a small tissue sample (a biopsy) to test in a lab.

If the cancer is advanced, the doctor may do imaging tests like:

- Ultrasound
- CT scan
- MRI scan

They may also check the bladder and rectum.

The doctor will also check if the cancer has spread to the lymph nodes in the groin or pelvis. This is important because more affected lymph nodes mean a worse outlook.

The doctor can feel the lymph nodes or use scans to see if they are enlarged.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment should be done at a specialist center with doctors who focus on cancer.

The treatment plan is decided together by the patient and the medical team. The doctor considers:

- The stage of the cancer
- The patient’s health
- The patient’s personal wishes

### Treating Precursors

- Mild precursors caused by HPV do not always need treatment. But the patient must agree and keep checking for new symptoms. The doctor will follow up regularly.
- For more serious HPV-related precursors, doctors often use a laser to remove the abnormal tissue.
- If there is no HPV link and the condition is Paget’s disease, surgery is used to remove the tissue.

### Treating Invasive Cancer

- If the cancer has grown into deeper tissue, the doctor removes the tumor completely. Plastic surgery may be used to rebuild the vulva.
- For large tumors, chemotherapy and radiation (called chemoradiotherapy) may be used first to shrink the tumor.
- If surgery is not possible or refused, chemoradiotherapy is an option.
- If the cancer has spread in the pelvis, chemoradiotherapy is the main treatment.
- If the cancer has reached nearby organs, parts of the bladder, rectum, or other organs may need to be removed.
- If cancer has spread to the lymph nodes, the doctor removes them first. Additional treatment like chemoradiotherapy or radiation may follow.

### Treating Spread to Other Organs

If the cancer has spread far away (metastasized), a full cure is usually not possible. But treatment can help relieve symptoms.

Chemotherapy may be used in some cases. The focus is on improving quality of life.

### Treating a Return of Cancer

If the cancer comes back after treatment, the doctor checks:

- What treatment was used before
- Is it a local return?
- Has it spread to other organs?
- How many lymph nodes are affected?

Treatment options include:

- Surgery to remove the new tumor
- Chemoradiotherapy or radiation if surgery is not possible
- Surgery, radiation, or chemotherapy for lymph node recurrence
- Same treatment as for initial diagnosis if cancer has spread far

For more details on treatments, side effects, and how to manage them, visit the website of the German Cancer Research Center (in German).

---

## Aftercare

After treatment, regular check-ups are important. They help with:

- Finding a return of cancer early
- Treating side effects
- Helping you live well

If you have a skin condition called lichen sclerosus, you will need lifelong follow-up care — even after treating precursors.

For the first 5 years, you will have several check-ups each year. After that, one check-up per year is enough.

Aftercare includes:

- Physical exams
- Imaging tests
- Biopsies of any suspicious areas

For more on what aftercare can and cannot do, and who leads it, visit the German Cancer Research Center’s website (in German).

---

## Life After Vulvar Cancer

The vulva is close to the bladder and rectum. Some women have trouble controlling urine or stool after treatment. This is called incontinence.

You can help with incontinence by:

- Doing pelvic floor exercises (a physiotherapist can teach you)
- Using pads or special underwear
- Using a catheter (a tube to drain urine) if needed

Other side effects can include:

- Changes in how the vulva looks
- A narrower vagina
- Inflammation of the lining
- Swelling from fluid buildup (lymphedema)

These can be managed with supportive care.

Cancer also affects mental health. Many women feel stressed, anxious, or sad. Psycho-oncologists can help you cope. Talking to a self-help group can also be useful.

### How Does Cancer Affect Sex Life?

Cancer and its treatment can change your sex life. You may lose interest in sex or have pain during sex.

This can be hard on you and your partner.

Talk to your doctor. A psycho-oncologist or a specialist in sexual health can help. There are also advice centers that offer support.

---

## Who Can You Contact for Help?

Cancer care involves doctors from many fields. Hospitals that treat gynecological cancers often have special certification.

The German Cancer Society checks these centers regularly.

You can find certified centers on the OncoMAP website.

For more help with daily life, support, and questions about cancer, visit the German Cancer Research Center’s Cancer Information Service (in German).

You can also call them for free at **0800 420 30 40** or email **krebsinformationsdienst@dkfz.de**.

# Crohn’s Disease

Crohn’s disease is a long-term condition that causes inflammation in the lining of the digestive system.  
It can make daily life very hard during flare-ups.  
But there are also times when symptoms go away or are mild.

---

## Quick Facts

- Crohn’s disease causes long-term inflammation in the digestive tract.  
- It often affects parts of the small intestine and the large intestine.  
- Most people first notice symptoms between the ages of 20 and 30.  
- Symptoms come and go. Some days are good. Other days are hard.  
- The exact cause is not known. But genes, the environment, and the immune system may play a role.  
- The disease can greatly affect a person’s quality of life.  
- There is no cure. But many medicines can help reduce symptoms.  

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Crohn’s Disease?

Crohn’s disease is a long-term inflammation of the digestive system.  
It can affect any part of the digestive tract — from the mouth to the anus.  
Unlike another condition called ulcerative colitis, Crohn’s can affect different parts of the gut that are not next to each other.  

The most common areas affected are the end of the small intestine and the beginning of the large intestine.  
Crohn’s disease damages not just the surface layer of the gut lining, but also deeper layers.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms can vary from person to person.  
They may happen alone or together.  

Common symptoms include:

- Cramping pain in the belly  
- Diarrhea that lasts four weeks or longer  
- Stool that may contain blood or mucus  
- Losing weight without trying  
- Feeling very tired  
- Having a high temperature (fever)

Less common problems include:

- Narrowing of the bowel (called stenosis)  
- Abnormal tunnels between the anus and the skin around it (called fistulas)

Crohn’s disease can also cause symptoms outside the gut, such as:

- Eye inflammation  
- Joint pain or swelling  
- Skin rashes

---

## What Causes Crohn’s Disease?

The disease starts when the body’s immune system attacks the lining of the gut.  
This causes inflammation.  
But doctors do not yet know why the immune system acts this way.

Research shows that some people are more likely to get Crohn’s because of their genes.  
Other possible causes include:

- Auto-immune problems  
- Environmental factors  
- Imbalance in the natural bacteria in the gut

---

## Who Is at Risk?

You are more likely to get Crohn’s disease if:

- A close family member has it  
- You have another inflammatory or auto-immune condition  
- You smoke  
- You have taken antibiotics often

---

## How Common Is It?

In Germany, between 100 and 200 out of every 100,000 people have Crohn’s disease.  
About 7 new cases appear every year for every 100,000 people.  
Most people first get symptoms between the ages of 20 and 30.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Crohn’s disease is a lifelong condition.  
There is no cure.  

But most people do not have constant symptoms.  
They have flare-ups followed by periods of feeling better or having only mild symptoms.  
During these quiet times, the inflammation goes down.

If symptoms last a long time, they can lead to:

- Poor nutrition  
- Anemia (low red blood cells)  
- Serious complications

People with Crohn’s disease also have a higher risk of bowel cancer.  
Doctors recommend regular colonoscopies to catch any problems early.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Many things can cause gut inflammation.  
These include infections, food intolerances, or other bowel diseases like ulcerative colitis.  
Doctors must rule out these causes before diagnosing Crohn’s.

The doctor will ask about:

- Your symptoms and when they started  
- Any food intolerances  
- Medicines you take  
- Whether you smoke  
- Family history of Crohn’s  
- Recent travel abroad

Then they will do:

- A blood test to check for anemia, high platelets, and signs of inflammation  
- A stool test to rule out infections

If Crohn’s is suspected, the doctor may suggest:

- A colonoscopy (to look at the large intestine)  
- An endoscopy (to look at the stomach and upper gut)  
- A tissue sample (biopsy) may be taken during these tests

In some cases, imaging tests like ultrasound or MRI are needed to see how bad the disease is.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on how severe the symptoms are and where in the body the disease is active.

Medicines are the main treatment.  
They can help control inflammation and reduce symptoms.  
New treatments have made a big difference in recent years.

Surgery may be needed in severe cases or if complications happen.  
This can include:

- Opening a narrowed part of the bowel  
- Removing a damaged section of the bowel

---

## How Can People Live with Crohn’s Disease?

Diet can help manage symptoms.  
Severe diarrhea can cause loss of important nutrients like potassium, calcium, iron, and zinc.  
Talk to your doctor about a healthy eating plan to prevent deficiencies.

Stop smoking.  
Smoking makes Crohn’s worse and increases the risk of flare-ups.

Get support for mental health.  
Stress, anxiety, and depression are common.  
Talking to a counselor or joining a support group can help.

**Important:**  
Some Crohn’s treatments weaken the immune system.  
This makes infections more likely.  
Stay up to date on vaccinations.  
Avoid people who are sick.  
Wash your hands often.

---

## Where Can I Find More Help?

In Germany, many groups and services offer support for people with Crohn’s disease.  
These include self-help groups and advice centers.
