## How Is CLL Diagnosed?

Diagnosis starts with signs like high white blood cell counts or swollen lymph nodes.

Your doctor will do three main things:

1. Ask about your medical history. They will want to know:
   - If you feel tired or weak
   - If you have had frequent infections
   - If you have had blood tests before
   - If anyone in your family has had blood or lymph node cancers

2. Do a physical exam. They will check:
   - Lymph nodes in the neck, armpits, and groin
   - The size of your spleen and liver
   - Signs of anemia or bleeding

3. Take a blood sample and test it thoroughly.

A bone marrow biopsy is not usually needed at first. But your doctor may order one later if your blood counts change unexpectedly or if treatment is not working.

Imaging tests like MRI or CT scans are not needed for the first diagnosis.

Doctors may take a sample from a swollen lymph node only in rare cases.

When treatment is planned, your doctor may do more tests, such as:

- Genetic tests on the cancer cells
- Special blood tests
- Ultrasound or CT scans of the chest, belly, or neck

---

## How Is CLL Treated?

Treatment depends on your symptoms, how far the disease has spread, and your overall health.

### Watch and Wait

If you have no symptoms and the disease is not growing fast, your doctor may suggest watching and waiting.

This means regular check-ups and blood tests. You do not need treatment yet.

Treatment starts when symptoms appear or the disease begins to progress.

The goal is to control the disease and improve your quality of life. This works well for many people over a long time.

But current treatments do not usually cure CLL.

### Drug Treatments

Most people with CLL are treated with medicines.

These include:

- **Targeted drugs**: These attack specific parts of the cancer cells.
- **Antibodies**: These are drugs that help the immune system find and destroy cancer cells.
- **Chemotherapy**: These drugs slow down or stop cell growth.

Your doctor will choose the right drugs and doses based on your health and risk level.

These medicines are often used together. They are given in cycles, with breaks in between.

Surgery or radiation therapy is rarely used.

### Stem Cell Transplant

In some cases, a stem cell transplant may be an option.

This is only for people who are otherwise healthy and have a high risk of the disease coming back.

The process involves:

- High-dose chemotherapy to destroy the cancer cells
- Replacing the bone marrow with healthy stem cells from a donor

This treatment can lead to a cure in some cases.

But it is very hard on the body. It has serious side effects.

It is not suitable for everyone.

---

## Aftercare After CLL Treatment

Aftercare is different for each person.

If you are in the “watch and wait” phase and have no symptoms, you will have regular check-ups and blood tests.

If you have had treatment, you will need follow-up care. This helps detect:

- A return of the disease (relapse)
- Side effects from treatment

The type and frequency of follow-up tests depend on:

- How far the disease had spread at diagnosis
- How likely it is to come back
- What treatment you had
- How well the disease responded
- Your overall health and any other medical conditions

---

## Living with CLL

Being diagnosed with CLL can be stressful for you and your family.

Symptoms like fatigue, frequent infections, and weakness can make daily life harder.

If you are working, you may need to change your job or reduce hours.

Older people may find it harder to manage everyday tasks.

The main goal of treatment is to reduce symptoms and help you live as normally as possible.

Many people want to take an active role in their recovery. Here are some helpful steps:

- **Exercise**: Light physical activity can help reduce tiredness and weakness. Start slowly and adjust to your energy level.
- **Eat well**: A balanced diet helps prevent poor nutrition. A dietitian can help if needed.
- **Talk to a counselor**: If you feel anxious or overwhelmed, psycho-oncological counseling can help.

---

## Where to Get Help and Information

In Germany, there is a network called the **Malignant Lymphomas Competence Network (KML)**.

This group includes doctors and researchers who specialize in lymphoma.

You can use the KML website to find hospitals or clinics that treat CLL.

CLL should be treated by a team of specialists. These include doctors who focus on blood and lymph system diseases.

Some hospitals are certified as centers for “hematological neoplasms.” They meet strict quality standards.

You can find these centers on the **OncoMAP** website. Choose “Hematological Neoplasms” in the search tool.

Note: Certification is not required by law. Some excellent clinics may not yet be certified.

For more information about living with CLL and support options, visit the **Cancer Information Service** of the German Cancer Research Center.

You can contact them by:

- Calling **0800 - 420 30 40** (free phone number)
- Sending an email to **krebsinformationsdienst

# Chlamydia

Chlamydia is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections.  
Many people with chlamydia do not feel sick.  
This means the infection can spread without anyone knowing.  
If left untreated, it can lead to infertility.  
Chlamydia is easy to treat with antibiotics.  
Using condoms can help prevent getting or spreading chlamydia.

---

## Quick Facts

- The germ that causes chlamydia is called *Chlamydia trachomatis*.  
- It causes pus-filled or sore inflammation in the reproductive organs.  
- If the infection spreads, it can cause infertility.  
- Some types of this germ can also infect the eyes and cause blindness.  
- The infection can also affect other parts of the body, like the intestines.  
- Antibiotics can cure chlamydia.  
- Condoms help reduce the risk of infection.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always see a doctor.

---

## What Is Chlamydia?

*Chlamydia trachomatis* is a type of germ that causes sexually transmitted infections.  
There are different types of this germ.  
In Germany, the most common type causes swelling and pus in the reproductive organs.  
It can sometimes lead to infertility.  
But many people with the infection do not have any symptoms.  
This means the germ can spread without anyone noticing.

In tropical countries, other types of this germ cause open sores around the genitals or repeated eye infections.  
These eye infections can lead to blindness.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

About 8 out of 10 women and half of all men with chlamydia have no symptoms.  
Those who do have symptoms may notice:

- Itching, pain, or a burning feeling when peeing or during sex  
- Thick, cloudy discharge from the vagina or penis  
- Sores in the rectum or throat, depending on the type of sex practiced

If the infection spreads, it can cause:

- Belly pain in women  
- Pain in the testicles in men  
- Infertility in both men and women  
- Long-term bowel problems

If a pregnant woman has chlamydia, the baby can get infected during birth.  
The baby may then develop:

- Eye infection (pus in the eye)  
- Ear infection  
- Rarely, pneumonia

Chlamydia can also lead to early birth or other pregnancy problems.

Some people develop joint or tendon pain after the main symptoms go away.

---

### Want to check your risk?

The **WIR – Walk In Ruhr Center for Sexual Health and Medicine** offers a free, anonymous online test to check your risk for chlamydia and other sexually transmitted diseases.

---

## How Is Chlamydia Spread?

Chlamydia is caused by the germ *Chlamydia trachomatis*.  
This germ only lives in humans.  
It spreads mainly through sexual contact.  
If a pregnant woman has chlamydia, the baby can get infected during childbirth.

If someone has an eye infection (conjunctivitis), the germ can spread through touch.  
This means you can pass it on by touching your eyes after touching infected areas.

---

## How Common Is Chlamydia?

Around 89 million new cases of genital chlamydia happen every year worldwide.  
These are the cases that cause pus and swelling in the reproductive organs.

---

## How Can You Prevent Chlamydia?

Using condoms during sex can help prevent chlamydia.  
Use them every time and use them correctly.  
This greatly lowers your risk.  
But condoms do not offer 100% protection.

If you think you might have chlamydia, see a doctor right away.  
Avoid sex until you have been tested and treated.

In Germany:

- All pregnant women are tested for chlamydia as part of their prenatal care.  
- This has been the case since 1995.  
- The test is also recommended before a pregnancy termination.

Since 2008, all women under 25 can get a free preventive test.  
If the test is positive, all sexual partners from the past 60 days should also be tested and treated if needed.

Men who suspect they have chlamydia can also get tested at no cost through public health insurance.

> **Important:** The only way to stop the spread of chlamydia is to treat everyone who is infected — even if they have no symptoms.  
> Even if a partner tests negative, doctors often recommend treating them anyway.

---

## How Is Chlamydia Diagnosed?

Doctors use different tests to find chlamydia.  
They may take swabs from the vagina, penis, rectum, or throat.  
They may also use urine, semen, or joint fluid samples.

The most accurate test looks for the germ’s genetic material.  
This is called PCR (polymerase chain reaction).  
It is a lab test that can detect even small amounts of the germ.

---

## How Is Chlamydia Treated?

Chlamydia is treated with antibiotics.  
It is very important to take the full dose and finish the entire course of medicine.  
This ensures the infection is fully gone.

You can get reinfected at any time if you have sex with someone who has chlamydia.

It is a good idea to get tested again at least 28 days after finishing treatment.

---

## Other Important Information

> **Note:** In Germany, chlamydia is only required to be reported to health authorities in the state of Saxony.

---

### Where to Get Help

- **Liebesleben** – A website by the Federal Centre for Health Education (BZgA).  
  It gives clear, helpful information about love, sex, and protection.

- **WIR – Walk In Ruhr Center for Sexual Health and Medicine**  
  Offers reliable information about chlamydia and other sexually transmitted diseases.

# Sleep Problems (Insomnia)

Sleep problems are common. But if you have trouble sleeping more than three nights a week for over a month, it may be a long-term sleep issue.

You should only take prescription sleep medicine for a short time.

---

## Quick Facts

- People need different amounts of sleep.
- If you sleep poorly more than three nights a week for over a month, you may have a chronic sleep problem.
- Stress, worries, and physical discomfort are the most common causes.
- Women and older adults are more likely to have sleep problems.
- Prescription sleep pills and sedatives, like benzodiazepines, should only be used for a short time.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Sleep Disorder?

Doctors call it a chronic sleep disorder (insomnia) when someone does not get good, restful sleep on more than three nights a week for over a month.

Another sign is that poor sleep is affecting your daily life. If this happens, talk to your doctor. They can help you find the cause and the best treatment.

---

## When Is It a Sleep Disorder?

You may have a sleep disorder if your sleep does not feel refreshing. This can happen when you:

- Take a long time to fall asleep.
- Wake up often during the night.
- Lie awake for long periods at night.
- Wake up too early and cannot fall back asleep.

> **Important:** Age does not decide whether you will have trouble sleeping. People of all ages can struggle with sleep.

---

## How Much Sleep Is Normal?

Everyone needs different amounts of sleep. Your age is one factor.

Here are general guidelines for how much sleep most people need each night:

- Children aged 6 and older: about 9 hours
- Adults: about 7 hours
- People over 80 years old: about 6 hours

Total sleep time starts when you fall asleep and ends when you are fully awake and out of bed. Any time you are awake during the night is not counted as sleep.

It is normal to take about 30 minutes to fall asleep after turning off the light. This is not a problem.

For more on normal sleep, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

---

## What Causes Sleep Problems?

Many things can make it hard to sleep well. Possible causes include:

- Loud noise
- Worry and stress
- Big life changes, like a breakup or serious illness
- Working night shifts
- Alcohol, drugs, or caffeine
- Grinding your teeth at night (bruxism)
- Sleep apnea – a condition where breathing stops and starts during sleep
- Physical symptoms like needing to pee at night, hot flashes, or pain
- Restless legs syndrome
- Some medicines, such as certain antidepressants (SSRIs) and drugs used to treat Parkinson’s disease

---

## How Common Are Sleep Problems?

Many people have trouble sleeping. About one in three people have difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep.

Sleep problems can happen at any age, even in young children. But they are more common in women and older adults.

---

## How Is a Sleep Disorder Diagnosed?

A sleep diary or a smartphone app can help find what is causing your sleep problems. Write down:

- When your sleep was poor.
- What happened the day before.

This helps spot patterns. Doctors may use your notes to understand how serious your sleep issues are.

Your doctor will ask about your health and habits. They may ask:

- Are you taking any medicine?
- Do you drink alcohol, use drugs, or drink caffeine? When?
- Are you under stress at work or in your personal life?
- Have you had any hard emotional experiences?
- Do you have any other health problems?

Your doctor will also do a physical exam. They may take a blood test to check for health issues that could be causing your sleep problems.

Some health problems linked to poor sleep include:

- Poor kidney function
- Thyroid problems
- Heart or lung disease
- Anxiety or depression

If your sleep problems are serious, you may need a sleep study. This is done in a sleep lab. You will be watched and recorded while you sleep. This helps doctors check if you get enough deep sleep and dream sleep. It can also show if you have a sleep disorder.

---

## How Are Sleep Problems Treated?

There are many products and methods for treating sleep problems. But not all have been proven to work well.

### Simple Lifestyle Changes

- Eat light meals before bedtime.
- Cut down on alcohol and coffee.
- Do not watch TV in bed.
- Only go to bed when you feel truly tired.

### Home Remedies

- Take a warm bath before bed.
- Drink a glass of warm milk.
- Try a calming herbal tea.

### Herbal Products

- Valerian and other herbal sleep aids may help some people.

### Relaxation Methods

- Progressive muscle relaxation
- Autogenic training
- Other relaxation techniques

### Exercise

- Walk in the evening.
- Try gentle activities like yoga, Tai Chi, or Qigong.

---

### Medical Treatments

Once a sleep disorder is diagnosed, your doctor may suggest:

- **Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT):** This helps you change thoughts and habits that keep you awake.
- **Melatonin medicine:** This boosts a natural hormone that helps control sleep. It is used when your sleep schedule is off, such as after shift work or jet lag.
- **Prescription sleep pills (benzodiazepines or Z-drugs):** These help you fall asleep, calm your mind, and reduce anxiety.

> **Important:** These sleep pills have many side effects. You may feel sleepy the next day. You might have trouble focusing or reacting quickly. Older adults are more likely to fall if they take these pills. These medicines can also be addictive. They should only be used for a short time.

For more help with sleep problems, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

# Anthrax

Anthrax is a serious infection caused by bacteria. It can spread from animals to people. People who work with animals, like farmers, foresters, and hunters, may be at higher risk if they touch sick animals.

## Quick Facts

- Anthrax is rare but dangerous.
- It is caused by a type of bacteria called *Bacillus anthracis*.
- The bacteria spread from animals to humans.
- People who work closely with animals are more likely to get infected.
- If not treated, some forms of anthrax can be deadly.
- Cutaneous anthrax (on the skin) heals on its own in 80 out of 100 cases without treatment.
- Antibiotics work well if treatment starts early.
- A vaccine is available only for people at high risk.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Anthrax?

Anthrax is a rare but serious infection caused by bacteria. The name comes from the Greek word for "coal" because the infected areas turn black. The bacteria are called *Bacillus anthracis*.

There are four types of anthrax:

- Skin anthrax (cutaneous)
- Lung anthrax (pulmonary)
- Gut anthrax (gastrointestinal)
- Injection anthrax

Skin anthrax is the most common. The other three types are very rare.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on which part of the body is infected.

### Skin Anthrax

- Small, pea-sized bumps appear at the site of infection.
- Most often on hands, arms, neck, or face.
- The bumps turn into blisters filled with fluid.
- Then they form a black scab (called an anthrax carbuncle).
- The sores do not hurt.

### Lung Anthrax

- Starts like a cold.
- After one to three days, symptoms get worse fast.
- High fever, severe breathing problems, and shock can follow.
- Can lead to blood poisoning and failure of the lungs and heart.

### Gut Anthrax

- Starts with stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite.
- Later, bloody diarrhea and swelling in the belly (peritonitis) occur.
- The toxins from the bacteria damage the digestive system.

### Injection Anthrax

- Swelling and pain around the injection site.
- Large areas of skin and tissue become inflamed.
- The nervous system and gut may also be affected.

### Anthrax Meningitis (a serious complication)

- All types of anthrax can lead to meningitis.
- Symptoms include severe headache, high fever, confusion, shaking, and muscle pain.
- The illness gets worse very fast.
- This form is almost always fatal.

## What Causes Anthrax?

All types of anthrax are caused by the same bacteria: *Bacillus anthracis*. These bacteria live as spores. Spores can survive for years in soil.

The bacteria make toxins that cause illness. People get infected through contact with sick animals or animal products. This kind of disease is called a zoonosis.

Animals most often infected include pigs, cattle, horses, sheep, and goats.

**Important:** People do not usually pass anthrax to each other. But it is possible to get infected by touching open wounds or skin fluid from an infected person.

### How Is Anthrax Spread?

#### Skin Anthrax

- You get it by touching infected animals or their products.
- Animals get infected from spores in the soil.
- People at risk include those who work with animal hides, bones, or tissues.
- Farmers, veterinarians, hunters, and foresters are at risk.
- Anthrax still happens in Europe, though it is rare.

#### Lung Anthrax

- You get it by breathing in spores.
- This usually happens when spores are released on purpose, like in a biological attack.
- Symptoms can take up to two months to appear.

#### Gut Anthrax

- You get it by eating meat from an infected animal.

#### Injection Anthrax

- You get it when a substance with spores is injected.
- This can happen when people use contaminated drugs like heroin.
- Contaminated needles can also spread the disease.

> The Robert Koch Institute offers helpful advice for people who use drugs.

## How Common Is Anthrax?

Anthrax is very rare. The last case of skin anthrax in Germany was in 1994. Since 2000, there have been several cases in Europe among people who use drugs. In 2012, four German drug users got anthrax.

The last outbreak in cattle in Germany was in 2012. In developing countries, anthrax is more common.

## How Can People at Risk Protect Themselves?

- Avoid touching sick animals or their products.
- Use protective gear when handling animal materials.
- A vaccine is available for people at high risk.

In Germany, a vaccine has been approved since 2013 for adults at high risk. The United States and the United Kingdom also offer the vaccine to certain groups, such as soldiers or lab workers.

## How Is Anthrax Diagnosed?

Diagnosis can be hard because symptoms are similar to other infections.

- Skin anthrax may look like other skin infections. But those usually hurt. Anthrax does not.
- Lung anthrax can look like flu or other lung infections.
- Gut anthrax can look like common stomach bugs.
- Injection anthrax can look like an abscess or tissue death.

To confirm anthrax, doctors take blood, swabs, or tissue samples. These samples must be tested in special labs with strict safety rules.

It is important to take blood samples before starting antibiotics. This helps the lab find the bacteria.

## How Is Anthrax Treated?

Antibiotics are used to treat anthrax. The type and length of treatment depend on the form and severity.

- Doctors should start antibiotics right away if anthrax is suspected.
- Waiting can be deadly.
- Early treatment leads to fast recovery.

Many antibiotics work against the bacteria. They are usually given through a drip (infusion). Sometimes more than one antibiotic is used.

- Severe cases may need intensive care.
- If the bacteria have made many toxins, antibiotics may not work.

For lung anthrax, doctors can use special antibodies to block the toxins. These are only approved in the United States.

Injection anthrax can destroy skin and tissue. Surgery may be needed to remove dead tissue. This may need to be done more than once.

## What Should You Do If You Are Near Someone with Anthrax?

The risk of catching anthrax from a person is very low. But it is possible if you touch contaminated clothes or wound fluid.

These steps help protect health workers:

- Wear gloves, protective gowns, face masks, and eye protection.
- Clean hands and surfaces with strong disinfectants that kill spores (like peracetic acid).
- Keep the infected person in a separate room if possible.

People who have been near an infected person do not need to stay home. But they should be watched closely for symptoms. They may be given antibiotics as a precaution.

**Important:** Anthrax must be reported to health authorities. If there is any sign of a biological attack, local health officials will take action.

# Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)

A deep vein thrombosis is a blood clot that forms in a deep vein, usually in the leg.  
It often causes pain, swelling, or redness in the leg.  
Some people have no symptoms at all.  
If you think you might have DVT, see a doctor right away.

---

## Quick Facts

- DVT often has no symptoms and can go away on its own.  
- If you are diagnosed with DVT, you will need treatment to prevent serious problems.  
- About 1 in every 1,000 people gets noticeable DVT each year.  
- This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Deep Vein Thrombosis?

A blood clot blocks a blood vessel.  
In DVT, the clot forms in a deep vein, usually in the lower leg.  
These veins run through the muscles and carry blood back to the heart.  
DVT often goes unnoticed.  
But it can cause pain, swelling, or warmth in the leg.  
If the clot breaks loose, it can travel to the lungs.  
This can cause a life-threatening condition called pulmonary embolism.  
After major surgery, such as hip or knee replacement, the risk of DVT goes up.  
To prevent this, doctors often give patients medicine to stop clots from forming.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Common signs of DVT include:  
- Pain in the leg or hip  
- Tenderness when you press on the leg  
- A feeling of tightness in the leg  
- Red or warm skin  
- Swelling in the leg  

Some people have no symptoms at all.  
If you notice any of these signs, see a doctor.

---

## What Causes DVT?

Blood clots can form when:  
- Blood moves too slowly through a vein  
- A person has a condition that makes their blood clot too easily  
- The wall of a blood vessel is damaged  

This can happen after:  
- Long periods in bed, such as after surgery or a serious injury  
- Being in the hospital for a long time  
- Having a blood clotting disorder (some people are born with this)  
- Major surgery or serious trauma  

These events can slow blood flow or damage blood vessels, which increases the risk of clots.

---

## What Increases the Risk of DVT?

Certain factors can raise your risk of DVT. These include:  
- Being over 60 years old  
- Having a close family member who had DVT  
- Having certain types of cancer  
- Having heart failure  
- Being severely overweight  
- Taking the birth control pill  
- Using hormone therapy for menopause  

Most of these factors only slightly increase your risk.  
But the risk goes up with age.

---

## How Common Is DVT?

About 1 in every 1,000 people develops noticeable DVT each year.  
The risk is higher in older people.  
Men are slightly more likely to get DVT than women.

---

## What Are the Possible Complications?

One common complication is called post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS).  
It can happen weeks or months after DVT.  
It occurs if the clot damages the vein walls or valves.  
This makes it hard for blood to flow back to the heart.  

Symptoms of PTS include:  
- A heavy, swollen leg  
- Pain in the leg  
- Discolored skin  
- Itching or a rash  
- In severe cases, open sores (chronic wounds) on the leg  

Wearing compression stockings can help reduce the risk of PTS.

---

## How Can DVT Be Prevented?

You can lower your risk of DVT by:  
- Getting up and moving as soon as possible after surgery or injury  
- Doing small movements like wiggling your toes or feet while in bed  
- Wearing compression stockings if you are at higher risk  
- Taking medicine that reduces blood clotting, if recommended by your doctor  

Compression stockings are tight-fitting socks.  
They press gently on the legs.  
This helps blood flow back to the heart and lowers the risk of clots.

Medicines that reduce clotting come in two forms:  
- Injections (like heparin or fondaparinux) – work within hours  
- Pills (like coumarins or direct oral anticoagulants) – work within hours or days  

Examples of oral medicines:  
- Phenprocoumon (sold under names like Marcumar or Marcoumar)  
- Apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, rivaroxaban  

If you cannot take blood-thinning medicine, a doctor may place a small metal filter in the large vein above the kidney.  
This filter catches clots before they reach the lungs.  
The procedure is done using a thin tube (catheter), similar to heart procedures.

To learn when prevention with injections is recommended, visit **gesundheitsinformation.de**.

---

## How Is DVT Diagnosed?

Doctors cannot be sure you have DVT just by looking at your symptoms.  
Pain, swelling, and redness can also be caused by other problems, such as:  
- Inflammation of surface veins  
- Varicose veins  
- Skin infection (erysipelas)  
- Narrowed leg arteries (peripheral artery disease)

To check for DVT, doctors usually start with a blood test called a D-dimer test.  
This test looks for substances released when blood clots break down.  
If the result is normal, DVT is very unlikely.  
If the result is abnormal, a Doppler ultrasound is done.  
This scan uses sound waves to check blood flow and vein health.  

If DVT is suspected, the ultrasound is done right away.  
In rare cases, a special X-ray of the veins (angiography) may be needed.  
This involves injecting a special dye into a vein to see if there are blockages.

---

## How Is DVT Treated?

DVT is usually treated in the hospital.  
Treatment starts with fast-acting medicine, such as heparin.  
This helps stop the clot from getting bigger.  

After the initial treatment, most people take anticoagulant tablets for at least three months.  
Some may need to take them longer.  
These pills help prevent new clots and help dissolve the existing one.

If you cannot take anticoagulant medicine, a doctor may place a small metal filter in the large vein above the kidney.  
This filter traps clots so they cannot reach the lungs.

To reduce the risk of long-term problems like a heavy leg or skin changes, wear compression stockings for up to two years.

# Encephalitis (Inflammation of the Brain)

Encephalitis means the brain is inflamed.  
It is most often caused by a virus.  
It can be mild or very serious.  
Some people recover fully. Others have lasting problems.  
Finding the exact cause is important for treatment.

---

## Quick Facts

- Encephalitis is the medical name for brain inflammation.  
- It is usually caused by a virus.  
- It can also happen when the body’s immune system attacks the brain by mistake.  
- The brain may not work properly.  
- Common symptoms include confusion, headache, fever, seizures, and drowsiness.  
- Behavior changes and memory problems are also common.  
- The illness can be mild or life-threatening.  
- If the cause is found, treatment can be more effective.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical care.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Encephalitis?

Encephalitis is swelling in the brain.  
When the brain and its covering (meninges) are both inflamed, it is called meningoencephalitis.

Most cases are caused by a virus.  
Herpes simplex virus is a common cause.

Sometimes, the immune system attacks the brain by mistake.  
This is called auto-immune encephalitis.

The brain may not work as it should.  
This can lead to confusion, seizures, or changes in behavior.  
Some people lose awareness of their surroundings.

The illness can be mild.  
But it can also be dangerous and cause lasting damage.

> **Critical:** If herpes simplex virus causes the encephalitis, treatment must start right away.  
> Early treatment greatly improves the chance of survival.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Common symptoms include:

- Confusion  
- Headache  
- Seizures  
- Drowsiness or trouble staying awake  
- Fever  

Other possible signs:

- Changes in mood or personality  
- Hallucinations  
- Trouble remembering things  
- Trouble speaking or understanding words  

Different viruses cause different symptoms:

- Herpes simplex virus often causes speech problems, like trouble finding words.  
- Arboviruses (spread by insects) often cause movement problems.  
- Enteroviruses often cause shaking, muscle twitches, movement issues, facial weakness, and fluid in the lungs.

Other possible symptoms:

- One side of the body may become weak or paralyzed.  
- Some nerves may become weak.  
- Numbness may occur in parts of the body.

In some cases, symptoms are so mild they are hard to notice.

Babies and young children show different signs:

- They may not feed well  
- They may seem very tired or sleepy  
- They may have fever or seizures  

---

## What Causes Encephalitis?

Encephalitis can be caused by:

- Viruses  
- Bacteria  
- Fungi  
- Parasites (like tiny worms or single-celled organisms)

When caused by an infection, it is called infectious encephalitis.

Sometimes, the immune system attacks the brain by mistake.  
This is called auto-immune encephalitis.  
The body makes antibodies that harm brain cells.

About 70 out of 100 cases are caused by viruses.  
Common viruses include:

- Herpes simplex virus (causes cold sores and genital herpes)  
- Enteroviruses (cause hand, foot, and mouth disease)  
- Epstein-Barr virus (causes glandular fever)  
- Cytomegalovirus (CMV)  
- Varicella-zoster virus (causes chickenpox and shingles)  
- Parechoviruses (cause breathing and stomach problems)  
- Influenza virus (causes flu)  
- Arboviruses (spread by ticks and mosquitoes)

Encephalitis can also be caused by:

- Measles  
- Mumps  
- Rubella  
- Rarely, SARS-CoV-2 (the virus that causes COVID-19)

Auto-immune encephalitis can sometimes be linked to cancer.

---

## How Common Is Encephalitis?

About 4 to 8 out of every 100,000 people get viral encephalitis each year.  
It affects young adults and older adults most often.  
In children, about 4 to 10 out of every 100,000 get it.  
It is most common in the first year of life.

Some types of encephalitis happen more often at certain times of year:

- Tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) is common in early summer.  
  Ticks carry the virus and are most active then.  
- Mosquito-borne encephalitis (like West Nile virus) also peaks in summer.

---

## What Are the Long-Term Effects?

Many people recover fully with no lasting problems.

About one in three people have long-term issues.  
These may include:

- Ongoing seizures  
- Trouble focusing or paying attention  
- Behavior changes  
- Memory problems  
- Trouble speaking or understanding language  

Some seizures do not respond well to medicine.

About 1 in 100 people remain severely disabled after recovery.  
They never fully regain full awareness.

Half of all children who get encephalitis have lasting problems.  
These may include:

- Delayed development  
- Learning difficulties  
- Behavioral issues  
- Problems with movement, vision, hearing, or bladder control  

The outcome depends on the virus.  
For example, herpes simplex virus encephalitis is very dangerous if not treated early.

---

## How Is Encephalitis Diagnosed?

Doctors need to find the cause to treat it properly.

They will ask about:

- Your general health  
- Medicines you take  
- Past vaccinations  
- Recent travel  

Certain symptoms can point to a specific cause:

- Skin rashes  
- Swollen glands  
- Memory or language problems  
- Specific movement issues  

Imaging tests help:

- CT scan or MRI scan can show brain swelling.  
- The location of the swelling may suggest the cause.

A sample of cerebrospinal fluid (liquor) is often taken.  
This fluid surrounds the brain and spinal cord.  
Doctors collect it from the lower back.

The fluid is tested for:

- Viruses or bacteria  
- Antibodies that fight specific infections  
- Autoantibodies (in auto-immune cases)

Blood tests can also show antibodies to certain infections.

If seizures are happening, an EEG (brain wave test) is done.

---

## How Is Encephalitis Treated?

For most viral infections, there is no specific medicine.  
Treatment focuses on easing symptoms.

One important exception: herpes simplex virus.  
This type can be deadly if not treated early.  
The medicine aciclovir can prevent serious damage.  
Doctors often give aciclovir right away—even before the cause is confirmed.

Aciclovir and similar drugs are also used for:

- Varicella-zoster virus (chickenpox/shingles)  
- Cytomegalovirus (CMV)

Seizures are treated with antiseizure medicine.

If behavior changes are severe, doctors may use short-term antipsychotic medicine.

For non-viral causes:

- If bacteria are suspected, antibiotics are given early.  
- For auto-immune encephalitis, high-dose steroids are used to reduce swelling.  
- Blood plasma exchange (plasmapheresis) may be used.  
- Immunosuppressive drugs may be given to calm the immune system and stop it from attacking the brain.

# COVID-19, Cold, and Flu – What You Need to Know

The symptoms of COVID-19, the flu, and the common cold are very similar. You cannot tell which illness you have just by looking at the symptoms. Testing is needed to know for sure.

---

## What Are These Illnesses?

- COVID-19, the flu, and the common cold are all infections that affect the nose, throat, and lungs.
- They are caused by different viruses.
- The common cold is usually caused by rhinoviruses or RSV.
- The flu is caused by influenza viruses.
- COVID-19 is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus.

---

## Common Symptoms

All three illnesses can cause:
- Sore throat
- Cough
- Runny or blocked nose
- Sneezing
- Itchy nose

A high temperature is more common with the flu and COVID-19 than with a cold.

---

## When to Stay Home

- If you have symptoms, stay home until you feel better.
- Stay home for about 3 to 5 days, or until your symptoms are much better.
- Avoid close contact with others while you are sick.

---

## When to See a Doctor

- If your symptoms are getting worse or are very strong, call your doctor.
- People at higher risk of serious illness should contact a doctor early.
- This includes older adults, pregnant people, and those with long-term health conditions.

---

## How Serious Can These Illnesses Be?

- The common cold is usually mild. It rarely causes serious problems in healthy people.
- The flu and COVID-19 can become serious. They can lead to pneumonia or other complications.
- In rare cases, people can have trouble breathing, need hospital care, or even die.
- Some people who had COVID-19 still feel unwell weeks or months later. This is called long COVID.

---

## How to Tell the Illnesses Apart

You cannot tell the difference between these illnesses just by symptoms.  
Rapid tests can help, but they are not always accurate.

- A rapid test may miss an infection if there is only a small amount of virus.
- If the test is positive and you have symptoms, it is likely correct.
- For a reliable result, a PCR test is needed.

---

## Symptoms of COVID-19

Common symptoms include:
- Cough
- Runny or blocked nose
- Sore throat
- Headache
- Body aches
- High temperature

Other possible symptoms:
- Feeling very tired
- Shortness of breath (hard to breathe)
- Nausea or stomach pain
- Diarrhea
- Eye irritation (red, watery eyes)
- Skin rash
- Swollen glands in the neck

An early sign of COVID-19 was loss of smell or taste. This is less common now, especially with the Omicron variant.

Omicron often causes milder symptoms. Most people feel better in 1 to 2 weeks.

But some people still get very sick. In rare cases, the illness can lead to lung failure or damage to other organs.

---

## Symptoms of the Flu

The flu often starts suddenly. You may feel very unwell all at once.

Common symptoms:
- High temperature
- Cough
- Sore throat
- Headache
- Body aches
- Feeling very weak

Other possible symptoms:
- Sweating
- Runny or blocked nose
- Nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea (less common)

The flu usually lasts 5 to 7 days. But cough and tiredness can last longer.

In rare cases, the flu can cause:
- Brain inflammation (encephalitis)
- Heart muscle inflammation
- Ear infections (especially in children)

Older adults may not have a high temperature. But they are more likely to get very sick.

Pregnant people and those with long-term health problems are also at higher risk.

---

## Why Do Flu Outbreaks Happen?

- Flu outbreaks happen most often in colder months, from autumn to spring.
- In Germany, outbreaks can last until May.
- Flu viruses spread more easily in cold, dry air.
- After you get the flu, you are protected for a while. But the virus changes often. So you can get it again.

During an outbreak:
- 5% to 20% of people may get sick.
- There can be sudden spikes when many people get sick at once.

Severe outbreaks can overwhelm hospitals. More people may need intensive care at the same time.

If flu, COVID-19, or other respiratory infections happen at the same time, hospitals can become very busy.

For more information on flu, visit: [www.bzga.de](https://www.bzga.de)

---

## Symptoms of the Common Cold

A cold usually causes:
- Runny or blocked nose
- Sneezing
- Cough
- Sore throat (sometimes)

High temperature is rare with a cold. Complications are also rare.

For more information, visit the Lung Information Service at the Helmholtz Center in Munich.

---

## How to Protect Yourself and Others

You can reduce your risk of catching or spreading these illnesses by:

- Opening windows often to let fresh air in
- Washing your hands often and thoroughly
- Covering your mouth and nose when you cough or sneeze (use your elbow or a tissue)
- Staying home when you are sick

**Wearing a mask indoors** can help:
- If you are sick and can’t avoid being around others
- If you are in a high-risk group

---

## Vaccines: Your Best Protection

Vaccines are one of the most effective ways to stay safe.

### Vaccines Against COVID-19

- They help prevent serious illness, hospitalization, and death.
- You can still get infected after vaccination, but symptoms are usually milder.
- The Standing Committee on Vaccination (STIKO) recommends:
  - All adults aged 18 and over should have basic immunity.
  - Some children and teens with health problems should also be vaccinated.
  - Booster shots are recommended for:
    - People aged 60 and over
    - People with certain health conditions
    - People in high-risk jobs

**Basic immunity** means you have been protected by at least three exposures to the virus. This can be:
- Three doses of the vaccine
- Or a mix of vaccine doses and infections

To get the best protection, at least one of the three exposures should be a vaccine dose.

### Vaccines Against the Flu

- Flu vaccines help prevent serious illness.
- STIKO recommends annual flu shots for:
  - All people aged 60 and over
  - People with long-term health conditions
  - Pregnant people in their second or third trimester
  - People in high-risk jobs

### Other Important Vaccines

- **Pneumococcal vaccine**: Recommended for:
  - All people aged 60 and over
  - People with certain health conditions
  - Children aged 2 to 24 months
- **RSV vaccine**: Recommended for:
  - People aged 75 and over
  - People in care homes or with serious health problems (sometimes from age 60)

You can get more than one vaccine at the same time. For example, you can get the flu and COVID-19 vaccines together.

---

## Where to Find More Information

- **infektionsschutz.de** – Official site for information on COVID-19 vaccines
- **impfen-info.de** – Information on flu, pneumococcal, and RSV vaccines
- **Corona-Impfcheck** – Online tool to check if you need a COVID-19 vaccine
- **Grippe-Impfcheck** – Tool to check if you need a flu vaccine
- **RSV-Impfcheck** – Tool to check if you need an RSV vaccine
- **Robert Koch Institute (RKI)** – Answers to common questions about all vaccines

This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor if you are unsure.

# Malaria

Malaria is a serious illness caused by a tiny parasite.  
It is mostly found in warm, tropical areas.  
People who travel to these areas can catch malaria.  
Most cases in travelers are the most dangerous type, called malaria tropica.  
If caught early, malaria can be treated and cured.  
If not treated, it can lead to death.

---

## Quick Facts

- Malaria is a tropical disease.  
- It is caused by a parasite that spreads through the bite of a certain mosquito.  
- There are different types of malaria. Each type is caused by a different kind of parasite.  
- Malaria can be deadly.  
- Children under five, older adults, and pregnant women are at highest risk.  
- People living in areas where malaria is common should take steps to protect themselves.  
  These steps include using mosquito nets and taking medicine to prevent infection.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always see a doctor.

---

## What Is Malaria?

Malaria is an illness caused by a tiny parasite called *Plasmodium*.  
This parasite is passed to people through the bite of a female Anopheles mosquito.  
The disease is found in almost all tropical and warm regions near the equator.  
It is present in about 90 countries across the world.  
It is not found in Australia.

Different types of malaria vary in how serious they are.  
Each type is caused by a different kind of *Plasmodium* parasite.

In Germany, over 75% of malaria cases are the most dangerous type: malaria tropica.  
People from Germany usually have no natural protection against this form.  
This makes prevention very important when visiting high-risk areas.

---

### What Are Airport Malaria and Suitcase Malaria?

**Airport malaria** is a rare case where a person gets malaria at an airport or on a plane.  
This happens when an infected mosquito is brought in on a flight.  
It can bite someone in the airport or nearby area.

**Suitcase malaria** happens when a mosquito is hidden in a traveler’s bag.  
The mosquito can bite the traveler or others after they return home.  
This is very rare but possible.

---

## What Are the Symptoms of Malaria?

The time between being bitten and getting sick is usually 7 to 40 days.  
In some cases, it can take months.

Early symptoms include:
- Fever
- Chills
- Headache
- Body aches
- Diarrhea
- Vomiting
- Feeling very unwell

These symptoms are often mistaken for the flu or stomach bug.

Other possible symptoms:
- Coughing
- Fast heartbeat
- Fast breathing

The fever pattern depends on the type of malaria.

---

### Malaria Tropica

This is the most dangerous form.  
Fever does not follow a regular pattern.  
Other symptoms may include:
- Muscle cramps
- Confusion
- Pale skin (anemia)
- Red spots on the skin
- Yellowing of the skin (jaundice)
- Trouble breathing

Without treatment, 2 out of 10 people with no immunity will die.

---

### Malaria Tertiana

This type causes fever every three days.  
The fever spikes, then drops.  
This is why it is called “three-day fever.”  
The fever attack lasts 3 to 4 hours.  
It is usually followed by heavy sweating.  
The fever goes back to normal after that.

This type is not usually deadly.

---

### Malaria Quartana

This is less common.  
Fever happens every four days.  
This is why it is called “four-day fever.”

It is not usually life-threatening.

---

### Knowlesi Malaria

This type is only found in Southeast Asia.  
It causes fever every day.  
It is just as dangerous as malaria tropica.

> **Important:** If you have been in a malaria area and develop a high fever,  
> get tested for malaria right away — no matter how the fever behaves.

---

## What Causes Malaria?

Malaria is caused by a tiny parasite called *Plasmodium*.  
Different types of this parasite cause different forms of malaria.

---

### How Do People Get Malaria?

The main way is through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito.  
A pregnant woman can pass the parasite to her unborn baby.  
This is rare, but it puts both mother and baby at risk.

The only other way malaria spreads is through blood.  
This is very rare.

> **Important:**  
> - People who have been in a malaria area cannot give blood for at least 6 months.  
> - People who have had malaria in the past can never donate blood.

---

### What Happens in the Body After Infection?

After being bitten, the parasite first multiplies in the liver.  
At this stage, you feel no symptoms.

Next, the parasite attacks red blood cells.  
It multiplies again inside these cells.  
After 2 to 3 days, the blood cells burst open.  
This releases more parasites into the blood.

The breaking of blood cells causes fever.  
As the number of parasites grows, the fever gets worse.

Infected blood cells can block small blood vessels.  
This causes more symptoms and serious problems.

---

## Who Is at Higher Risk?

Most people in Germany have no natural protection against malaria.  
This is because malaria is not found in Germany.

> **Important:**  
> - People who have had malaria before may have some protection for a time.  
> - A recent infection means a new one is less likely to cause serious illness.

Older adults, young children, and pregnant women are at highest risk of severe or deadly malaria.

About two-thirds of all malaria deaths happen in children under five.

---

### Malaria During Pregnancy

Malaria during pregnancy is very dangerous for both mother and baby.  
But preventive medicine is not safe to use during pregnancy.  
No medicine can guarantee it will not harm the baby.  
For this reason, pregnant women should avoid traveling to malaria areas until after their pregnancy.

---

## How Common Is Malaria?

Malaria is very common in certain parts of the world.  
Almost all cases in Germany are brought in by travelers.

---

### Malaria Around the World

- About 40% of the world’s population lives in areas where malaria is common.  
- Every year, 200 to 300 million people get malaria.  
- Around 600,000 people die from it each year.  
- Most deaths happen in children under five.

Over 90% of cases happen in African countries.  
Cases in Asia and South America have gone down in recent years.  
In the last few years, a few cases of malaria tertiana were found in southern Europe, like Spain and Greece.

---

### Malaria in Germany

All malaria cases in Germany are from people who traveled abroad.  
In recent years, between 300 and 1,000 cases were reported each year.  
Men and boys are infected more than twice as often as women and girls.

Most cases come from African countries.  
The most common countries are Cameroon, Nigeria, Ghana, and Togo.  
Outside Africa, most cases come from India.

> **Important:** Malaria is most common among people visiting relatives or friends in high-risk areas.

---

## How Does Malaria Progress?

The course of the disease depends on:
- Whether the person has had malaria before
- The type of malaria

---

### Malaria Tropica

This is the most dangerous type.  
Early symptoms include tiredness, headaches, body aches, diarrhea, and fever.

It can lead to serious complications, such as:
- Kidney failure
- Lung damage
- Enlarged spleen
- Enlarged liver
- Poor blood circulation
- Low red blood cell count
- Internal bleeding

The parasite can attack the brain. This is called cerebral malaria.  
Symptoms include seizures, confusion, and coma.

---

### Malaria Tertiana

This type rarely causes life-threatening problems.  
But symptoms can be severe.  
Fever comes every three days.  
It spikes quickly, then drops after 3 to 4 hours.  
The person sweats heavily during the drop.

After recovery, symptoms can return weeks or even years later.

---

### Malaria Quartana

This is less common.  
Fever happens every four days.  
It usually does not cause serious problems.  
Relapses can happen after recovery.

---

### Knowlesi Malaria

This causes daily fever attacks.  
It can be as serious as malaria tropica.

---

## How Can Malaria Be Prevented?

There is no vaccine to prevent malaria.  
This makes other steps very important.

If you plan to visit a malaria area, talk to a doctor before you go.  
They will help you choose the right prevention plan.

Prevention includes:
- Taking medicine to prevent malaria (prophylaxis)
- Using mosquito protection

---

### Medicine to Prevent Malaria

There are several types of medicine that can help prevent malaria.  
Your doctor will help you pick the best one for your trip.

You usually start taking the medicine a few days before your trip.  
You must keep taking it during your stay.  
You should continue for up to one week after returning home.

General rules:
- Strongly recommended for trips to high-risk countries.
- Not usually needed for low or medium-risk countries.  
  But it may be wise to carry emergency medicine if you are going to remote areas.

> **Important:**  
> - Emergency medicine should only be used if you have a fever and no doctor is available.  
> - See a doctor as soon as possible after using it.

# Spinal Stenosis

Spinal stenosis means the space around the spinal cord has become too narrow.  
This can press on the spinal cord, nerve roots, or blood vessels.  
When this happens, you may feel pain, numbness, or weakness.  
In some cases, it can even cause paralysis.  

Most people find relief with physical therapy and medicine.  
Surgery is an option if other treatments do not work.

---

## Quick Facts

- Spinal stenosis is when the spinal canal gets narrower.
- It most often affects the lower back (lumbar spine) or the neck (cervical spine).
- Symptoms can include pain, numbness, or weakness in the arms or legs.
- Dizziness can happen if the neck is affected.
- It is usually caused by wear and tear over time.
- Older people are more likely to get it than younger ones.
- Many people improve with physical therapy and pain relievers.
- If symptoms are severe or the spinal cord is damaged, surgery may be needed.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

---

## What Is Spinal Stenosis?

Spinal stenosis means the spinal canal has narrowed.  
This can squeeze the spinal cord or nerve roots.  

Your spine is made of bones called vertebrae.  
Each vertebra has a hole in the middle.  
When the holes line up, they form a tunnel called the spinal canal.  
The spinal cord runs through this tunnel.  
Nerves branch off from the spinal cord to the rest of the body.

Spinal stenosis most often happens in the lower back or neck.  
When it affects the lower back, it is called lumbar spinal stenosis.  
When it affects the neck, it is called cervical spinal stenosis.

Many older adults have spinal stenosis due to normal wear and tear.  
Not everyone with this condition has symptoms.  
But if the narrowing presses on nerves or blood vessels, it can cause problems.  
Then treatment is needed.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many people with spinal stenosis have no symptoms.  
Symptoms only appear if the narrowing is severe enough to press on nerves or blood vessels.

The symptoms depend on whether the neck or lower back is affected.

**If the neck is affected:**
- Neck pain that spreads to the arms.
- Dizziness.
- Numbness or weakness in the hands, arms, or legs.
- Over time, nerve damage can cause lasting numbness or weakness.

**If the lower back is affected:**
- Long-term lower back pain.
- Pain that spreads to the buttocks and legs.
- Pain gets worse when standing or walking.
- Pain eases when sitting or bending forward.
- Some people walk with a limp because of pain.
- Numbness or weakness in the legs.
- Problems with bladder or bowel control, such as leaking urine.

---

## What Causes Spinal Stenosis?

The most common cause is wear and tear on the spine.  
This happens slowly over time, especially with age.  
It is rare for someone to be born with spinal stenosis.

Injuries to the spine can also cause it.  
For example:
- Car accidents.
- Sports injuries, like diving into shallow water.
- Falls, especially in older adults.

Other possible causes include:
- Infections in the spine bones or discs.
- Long-term joint diseases like rheumatoid arthritis.
- Hormone problems, such as Cushing’s syndrome, which can weaken bones.
- Bone diseases like Paget’s disease, where bones grow too fast and become weak.

---

## How Common Is It?

We do not know the exact number of people with spinal stenosis.  
But it becomes more common as people get older.

Studies show that about 5 out of every 1,000 people aged 50 to 65 develop spinal stenosis.  
In people over 65, spinal stenosis is the most common reason for spine surgery.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

To diagnose spinal stenosis, your doctor will:
- Ask you about your symptoms.
- Do a physical exam.

During the exam, your doctor checks:
- If you have numbness or tingling.
- How well you can move and how flexible you are.
- How you walk.
- If certain movements cause pain.

To confirm the diagnosis, your doctor will likely order an MRI scan.  
An MRI shows detailed images of the spine.  
It helps find where and how much the spinal canal is narrowed.

If an MRI is not possible, a CT scan may be used instead.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause and how bad the symptoms are.  
Options include exercise, medicine, and surgery.

If there is no infection, tumor, or spinal cord injury, doctors usually start with non-surgical treatments.  
These may include:
- Gentle movement exercises and muscle strengthening.
- Pain relievers like ibuprofen or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
- Injections of numbing medicine and anti-inflammatory drugs into the spine.

If these treatments do not help, or if the spinal cord or nerves are damaged, surgery may be needed.

Surgery usually involves removing part of the bone or joint to make more space in the spinal canal.  
This reduces pressure on the nerves.  
This is called decompression surgery.

Because surgery can make the spine less stable, doctors often join two bones together at the same time.  
This is called fusion.  
But studies have not shown that fusion helps more than decompression alone.

Surgery should only be done when necessary.  
About 10 to 24 out of every 100 lower back surgeries for spinal stenosis lead to complications.  
Some of these complications can cause lasting problems.

> **Important:** Talk carefully with your doctor about the risks and benefits of surgery before deciding.

---

## How Long Does Recovery Take?

Recovery from spinal stenosis can take a long time.  
It is especially hard after surgery.

Good recovery depends on teamwork.  
A team of doctors, physical therapists, and occupational therapists should work together.

The more support and care you get, the better your chances of full recovery.

# Acidosis

Acidosis means the body’s balance of acids and bases is off.  
This makes the blood and tissues too acidic.  
The body needs a stable balance between acids and bases to work well.  
When you breathe, move, or eat, your body makes waste products that affect this balance.  

Your lungs and kidneys help remove these waste products.  
Your blood and tissues also have natural buffers.  
These buffers help fix small changes in acidity right away.  

If your lungs or kidneys are not working well, the balance can break.  
This leads to acidosis.  

The pH level of your blood shows how acidic or basic it is.  
A normal pH is between 7.35 and 7.45.  
If your pH drops below 7.35, your blood is too acidic.  
This is called acidosis.  

There are two main types:  
- Respiratory acidosis  
- Metabolic acidosis  

---

## What Are the Two Types of Acidosis?

**Respiratory acidosis** happens when you do not breathe well.  
You may breathe too slowly or too shallowly.  
This causes carbon dioxide to build up in your body.  

**Metabolic acidosis** happens when your body makes too many acids.  
It can also happen if your kidneys do not remove enough waste.  
This can be due to kidney failure, severe diarrhea, or poisoning.  

**Important:** Eating alkaline foods does not help fix acidosis.  
Food cannot change your body’s acid-base balance.  

---

## What Are the Symptoms of Acidosis?

Acidosis often causes symptoms only when it gets serious.  

### Symptoms of Respiratory Acidosis:
- Skin turns blue or gray  
- Hard time breathing  
- Feeling dizzy or weak  
- May pass out  
- Muscle twitches  
- Headaches  

These happen because your body is not getting enough oxygen.  
Too much carbon dioxide builds up in your blood.  

### Symptoms of Metabolic Acidosis:
- Breathing becomes deep and fast  
- Nausea  
- Vomiting  
- Diarrhea  
- Confusion  
- Trouble focusing  
- Anxiety  
- Restlessness  
- Nighttime headaches  
- Feeling strange or disoriented  
- Hallucinations  

These symptoms can also happen with other serious conditions like diabetes, kidney failure, or poisoning.  

---

## What Causes Acidosis?

Acidosis is usually caused by another health problem.  

### Causes of Respiratory Acidosis:
- Asthma  
- Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)  
- Emphysema  
- Chest injuries  
- Brain injury that affects breathing  

When breathing is weak, carbon dioxide builds up in the blood.  
This lowers the pH and makes the blood more acidic.  

### Causes of Metabolic Acidosis:
- Poisoning from alcohol or painkillers (like paracetamol or aspirin)  
- Severe diarrhea  
- Kidney failure  
- Blood poisoning (sepsis)  
- Heart attack  

### Special Case: Ketoacidosis
This is a type of metabolic acidosis.  
It can happen when diabetes is not well managed.  
It can also happen during extreme hunger, such as in anorexia or long fasting.  

---

## What Is the Outlook for Acidosis?

If acidosis is not treated, it can lead to serious problems.  
It may cause coma or even death.  

### In Respiratory Acidosis:
- Skin and lips turn blue or gray  
- Breathing gets harder  
- Heart rate increases  
- Blood pressure rises  
- You may feel weak or dizzy  

### In Metabolic Acidosis:
- Breathing becomes fast and deep  

But doctors can find acidosis early.  
They can start treatment right away.  
With proper care, most people recover.  

---

## How Can Acidosis Be Prevented?

You can lower your risk by managing certain health conditions.  

### If You Have Diabetes:
- Check your blood sugar often  
- Take your medicine as prescribed  
- Work with your doctor to adjust your treatment  

### If You Have Kidney Problems or COPD:
- Follow your doctor’s advice  
- Get regular checkups  
- Stay on your treatment plan  

Good management of these conditions helps prevent acidosis.  

---

## How Is Acidosis Diagnosed?

Doctors use a blood test to check for acidosis.  
This test is called a blood gas analysis.  

It measures:  
- The pH level of your blood  
- The amount of bicarbonate in your blood  
- The amount of carbon dioxide in your blood  

Bicarbonate helps balance acidity in your body.  

- If you have metabolic acidosis, your bicarbonate level is low.  
- If you have respiratory acidosis, your bicarbonate level is high.  
  This is because your body tries to fix the problem by making more bicarbonate.  

---

## How Is Acidosis Treated?

Doctors treat acidosis by fixing the cause.  

### For Respiratory Acidosis:
- Give oxygen to help you breathe better  
- Use medicine to open your airways (like bronchodilators)  
- If it is caused by an opioid overdose, use a drug called naloxone  
- Give bicarbonate to help balance the pH in your blood  

### For Metabolic Acidosis:
- Give bicarbonate to help balance the pH  
- Treat the root cause (like kidney failure, poisoning, or severe diarrhea)  

Treatment depends on the cause.  
Doctors act quickly to prevent serious harm.  

---

**Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical care.  
Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.  
Always talk to a doctor if you are worried about your health.

# Angina (Chest Pain from Heart Problems)

Angina is a sudden chest pain that happens when your heart does not get enough blood and oxygen. It often occurs during physical activity or times of stress.

The most common cause is narrowed heart arteries. This narrowing slows down blood flow to the heart muscle.

---

## Quick Facts

- Angina is usually caused by heart disease.
- Narrowed heart arteries can cause chest pain.
- Some people need surgery, depending on how bad the symptoms are.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Angina?

The word "angina" comes from Latin and means "tight chest." It happens when one or more of the heart’s blood vessels become narrow.

This narrowing is often due to a buildup of fat and other substances in the artery walls. This is called hardening of the arteries.

Physical activity or stress can trigger angina. Your heart needs more blood and oxygen during these times. But if the arteries are narrow, the heart does not get enough.

This causes sudden chest pain.

> **Important:** Chest pain can also be a sign of a heart attack. If you are unsure, call emergency services right away. In Germany, dial 112 and ask for an ambulance. Do not call a doctor on call.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Angina can feel different in different people. Some may feel only mild discomfort when climbing stairs. Others may feel sharp, strong pain in the chest.

The pain can spread to:

- The left arm
- The jaw
- The upper belly
- The back

In most cases, the pain goes away after a few minutes of rest. It usually starts during activity and stops when you stop moving.

If the pain happens while you are resting, it is more serious. This is called unstable angina. It can be a warning sign of a heart attack.

---

## What Causes Angina?

Angina is often the first sign of heart disease. It happens because of hardening of the arteries.

This process starts with small damage to the artery walls. Over time, fat, immune cells, and other materials build up. These buildups are called plaques.

When plaques form in the arteries that feed the heart, they narrow the blood flow.

The heart needs more blood and oxygen during activity. If the arteries are narrow, the heart cannot get enough. This causes pain.

When the pain only happens during activity and goes away at rest, it is called **stable angina**.

When the pain happens even when you are at rest, it is called **unstable angina**. This is a serious condition. It means the blood flow is severely blocked. It can lead to a heart attack.

A heart attack must be treated right away. If not, part of the heart muscle can die.

---

## What Increases the Risk of Angina?

These factors raise your risk:

- Smoking
- Being very overweight
- High cholesterol
- High blood pressure
- Type 2 diabetes

The risk goes up as you get older.

---

## How Does Angina Progress?

Doctors use a four-level system to describe how bad angina is:

- **Level 1:** Pain only during sudden or strong effort. Not during normal daily tasks like walking or climbing stairs.
- **Level 2:** Pain during heavy activity. Examples: running fast, walking uphill, walking upstairs after eating. Also during cold weather or stress.
- **Level 3:** Pain during light activity. Examples: walking at a normal pace, getting dressed.
- **Level 4:** Pain even when resting or doing very little.

> **Important:** The more severe the angina, the higher the risk of a heart attack or other heart problems.

---

## How Can Angina Be Prevented?

You can lower your risk by keeping your heart healthy:

- Do not smoke
- Stay physically active
- Keep a healthy weight
- Eat a balanced diet

It is not clear if vitamins or supplements help prevent heart disease.

For more tips on heart health, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## How Is Angina Diagnosed?

Chest pain can come from many causes. It may be from the muscles, bones, or lungs — not just the heart.

The main test for angina is an **electrocardiogram (ECG)**. It records the heart’s electrical activity. This test can be done while you are at rest or during exercise.

Doctors may also use an **ultrasound of the heart** (echocardiography) to see how well the heart is working.

Other tests may be needed. These depend on your age, symptoms, and other health conditions.

Since angina is caused by heart disease, your doctor will check for:

- Blood pressure
- Overall health
- Blood sugar levels (to check for type 2 diabetes)
- Other risk factors

---

## What Screening Is Available?

People with public health insurance can get a free health check-up:

- Once between ages 18 and 35
- Every three years after age 35

This check-up looks for:

- Heart and blood vessel problems
- Diabetes
- Kidney issues

It includes:

- Blood and urine tests
- Blood pressure measurement

---

## How Is Angina Treated?

For stable angina, medicine can help. Common medicines include:

- Beta blockers
- Calcium channel blockers
- Nitrates

These can reduce pain and help you feel better every day.

If medicine does not help enough, a doctor may use a thin tube (catheter) to open the narrowed artery.

If the artery is very blocked or if several arteries are affected, surgery may be needed. This is called a bypass.

In bypass surgery, a healthy blood vessel from another part of the body is used to go around the blocked artery. This helps blood flow to the heart.

Treating angina can also help prevent serious problems like:

- Heart attack
- Heart failure

To help prevent these, doctors recommend:

- Eating healthy
- Staying active
- Quitting smoking

Medicines can also help:

- Antiplatelet drugs to prevent blood clots
- Statins to protect blood vessels

For more information on treatment, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Bell’s Palsy (Facial Paralysis)

Bell’s palsy is a condition that causes sudden weakness or paralysis on one side of the face. It happens when the nerve that controls the facial muscles is damaged. In most cases, the nerve and muscles get better on their own.

---

## Quick Facts

- Bell’s palsy usually affects just one side of the face.
- The face may look droopy or stiff on the affected side.
- People often have trouble speaking clearly.
- Doctors do not know the cause in most cases.
- In about 1 out of every 4 people, the paralysis is due to another health problem.
- Most people get better within a year.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Bell’s Palsy?

Bell’s palsy means the muscles on one side of the face stop working properly. It happens when the facial nerve is damaged. This nerve controls the muscles used to smile, frown, raise eyebrows, and move the mouth.

The facial nerve splits into many smaller nerves. It also controls:
- Tear production
- Saliva production
- Taste on the front part of the tongue
- How loud sounds seem in the ear

When the nerve is damaged, people may:
- Not be able to close one eye
- Not be able to smile on one side
- Have trouble showing emotions with their face
- Feel numb or tingly in the face

These changes can be upsetting and hard to live with. Many people feel stressed or sad because of how they look.

In most cases, doctors do not know why the nerve was damaged. When the cause is unknown, they call it “idiopathic” — which means “of unknown cause.”

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The symptoms come on quickly — often within hours. They can be mild or very strong. Usually, only one side of the face is affected.

Common signs include:
- The face feels stiff or pulled to one side
- One eyebrow droops
- The cheek feels numb or tingles
- Pain in the ear
- Trouble tasting food
- Inability to close one eye or the corner of the mouth
- Sensitivity to loud sounds
- Dry mouth
- Dry eye

Some people also have trouble eating or drinking because they cannot move their mouth properly.

---

## What Causes Bell’s Palsy?

In 75 out of 100 cases, doctors do not know the cause. This is called idiopathic facial paralysis.

In the other 25 cases, the cause may be:
- A head injury or facial fracture
- Damage to other nerves
- Tumors in the brain or near the ear
- Viral infections, such as shingles (caused by the varicella zoster virus)
- Bacterial infections, like a middle ear infection
- Surgery that affects the facial nerve

In children, Bell’s palsy can happen during birth if forceps were used. It can also be caused by birth defects or genetic conditions.

---

## How Common Is It?

About 40 people in every 100,000 develop Bell’s palsy each year. Most cases happen in people aged 15 to 45.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Most people get better without treatment.  
- In 85 out of 100 cases, people recover fully or mostly within a few weeks.  
- In another 10 out of 100 cases, recovery happens within 3 to 6 months.

After one year:
- 71 out of 100 adults with Bell’s palsy recover fully.
- 95 out of 100 children recover fully.

In severe cases — for example, if the cause is a viral infection — some people may have lasting problems. These can include:
- Weakness in facial muscles
- Trouble making tears
- Dry eye

If the eye cannot close, the surface of the eye (the cornea) can dry out and get damaged.

Many people with Bell’s palsy also feel anxious or depressed. The change in appearance and daily struggles can be very hard to deal with.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will check how much movement you can still do with your face. You may be asked to:
- Close your eyes
- Raise your eyebrows
- Frown
- Smile or pucker your lips

The doctor will also:
- Look inside your ear for signs of infection
- Check your mouth for swelling

If another illness is suspected, blood tests or a spinal fluid test may be done. These can check for diseases like Lyme disease.

If the cause is unclear, your doctor may use:
- Electrical tests to check nerve function
- Imaging scans like CT or MRI to look at the brain and nerves

---

## How Is It Treated?

If Bell’s palsy is caused by another condition, treating that condition is the first step. For example:
- Antibiotics for bacterial infections
- Antiviral medicine for viral infections

For most people with unknown causes, symptoms go away on their own. But treatment with a steroid medicine like prednisolone for about one week can help speed up recovery. Steroids reduce swelling and inflammation.

In severe cases where the paralysis does not go away, other treatments may help:
- Transcutaneous nerve stimulation: small electric pulses are sent through the skin to help the nerve and muscles work again
- Surgery: in rare cases, surgery may help restore some function

If you cannot close your eye:
- Use artificial tears during the day
- Use eye ointment at night
- Wear a protective eye bandage while sleeping

---

## Living with Bell’s Palsy

If the condition lasts a long time or is permanent, you can learn ways to manage it every day.

You can take training courses with a professional instructor. These can teach you:
- How to protect your eye
- How to eat and drink safely
- How to speak more clearly

There are also special exercises and facial massages that can help:
- Rebuild muscle strength
- Improve facial expressions
- Help with speech

Therapists trained in facial rehabilitation can guide you through these steps. Support is available to help you live well with Bell’s palsy.

# Hemorrhoids (Piles)

Everyone has hemorrhoids. They are normal tissues in the lower part of the rectum, just inside the anus. These tissues are filled with blood vessels and act like cushions. They help the anus close tightly. This keeps stool from leaking out when you pass gas.

Hemorrhoids only cause problems when they get bigger. When they do, they are called enlarged hemorrhoids. Many people have this. About half of all adults over the age of thirty have enlarged hemorrhoids at some point.

---

## Quick Facts

- Hemorrhoids are normal parts of the body. They are soft cushions of tissue with blood vessels.
- Problems only happen if the hemorrhoids grow larger.
- Common symptoms include itching, a burning feeling, mucus leaking, or bright red blood during or after a bowel movement.
- Bleeding is usually painless and shows up as red blood on toilet paper or in the stool.
- Some people see soft lumps sticking out of the anus. These are prolapsed hemorrhoids.
- Hemorrhoids can be mistaken for skin tags. Skin tags are harmless flaps of skin around the anus and do not cause symptoms.
- Pain usually only happens if the condition is advanced or if there are other injuries, like small tears.
- Larger hemorrhoids can make sitting uncomfortable. You may feel like you still need to go to the toilet even after you’ve just gone.
- Mucus or stool may leak out by accident, especially when passing gas.
- The size of the hemorrhoids and how bad the symptoms are will decide the best treatment.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not try to diagnose or treat yourself. Always see a doctor.

---

## What Are Hemorrhoids?

Hemorrhoids are natural cushions of tissue in the anal canal. They are made of blood vessels and help the anus close properly. This stops stool from leaking out when you pass gas.

When people say they “have hemorrhoids,” they usually mean the cushions have become enlarged. This can cause symptoms like:

- Itching around the anus
- Bleeding during or after a bowel movement
- A feeling of fullness or pressure in the anal area

Doctors call this condition hemorrhoidal disease.

Many people feel embarrassed about this problem. They may not want to talk about it. Some are afraid of a physical exam or worried they have a serious illness. But most cases are not serious. Still, it is important to see a doctor. This helps you get the right treatment.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Hemorrhoids can cause several symptoms. These include:

- Itching around the anus
- A burning feeling in or around the anus
- Mucus leaking from the anus
- Painless bleeding during or right after a bowel movement

The bleeding is usually bright red. It can be seen on toilet paper or in the toilet bowl. If you see blood in your stool, you must see a doctor. Do not try to figure out the cause on your own.

Sometimes, enlarged hemorrhoids stick out of the anus. These are called prolapsed hemorrhoids. They look like soft lumps. They may go back inside on their own or need to be pushed back gently.

Hemorrhoids can be confused with skin tags. Skin tags are small, harmless pieces of extra skin around the anus. They do not cause symptoms.

Pain is rare unless the condition is very advanced. But pain can also come from other issues, like small tears in the skin.

Larger hemorrhoids often cause more problems. You may feel pressure or a lump in the anal area. Sitting can become painful. You may feel like you haven’t finished going to the toilet, even after you have.

In some cases, mucus or stool may leak out by accident. This is more likely when passing gas. Severe hemorrhoids can be very painful.

---

## What Causes Hemorrhoids?

The exact cause of enlarged hemorrhoids is not fully known. Scientists have not found clear answers yet.

It is likely that the tissues supporting the hemorrhoids weaken over time. This can happen as we age.

There may also be a family link. Some people may be more likely to get hemorrhoids because of their genes.

Certain things can increase the risk of developing hemorrhoids. These include:

- Hard or dry stool
- Long-term constipation
- Frequent diarrhea
- Pregnancy and childbirth
- Being overweight or obese

---

## How Common Are Hemorrhoids?

Hemorrhoids are very common. More than half of all adults will have symptoms at some point in their lives.

But many people do not go to the doctor. In Germany, about 4 out of every 100 adults visit a doctor each year because of enlarged hemorrhoids.

---

## How Do Hemorrhoids Progress?

It is hard to predict how hemorrhoids will change over time.

Some people with slightly enlarged hemorrhoids may feel better. Their symptoms may go away. But others may get worse.

Once hemorrhoids are enlarged, they usually do not shrink on their own.

Enlarged hemorrhoids can irritate the skin around the anus. This can lead to a condition called anal eczema. This means the skin is red, swollen, itchy, and may weep. Small blisters or scabs can form.

---

## How Are Hemorrhoids Diagnosed?

Some people are afraid of physical exams. They worry about pain. But most exams are not painful. They may feel uncomfortable or embarrassing, but they are routine for doctors.

At your first visit, your doctor will ask about your symptoms and your medical history.

Then, the doctor will look at your anus. They will check if it is inflamed. They will also see if any hemorrhoids are sticking out.
