Next, the doctor will do a rectal exam. They will gently insert a gloved, lubricated finger into the anus. This lets them feel the inside of the anal canal. They check the muscles and the lining of the anus.

If you have blood in your stool, your doctor may suggest a colonoscopy. This is a test that uses a camera to look inside your bowel.

If the doctor thinks you have enlarged hemorrhoids, they will likely do a proctoscopy. This is a quick test. It is usually not painful.

During a proctoscopy, the doctor uses a small tube to look at the inside of the rectum. The rectum must be empty before this test. You may be given laxatives, suppositories, or an enema to clear it out.

---

## How Are Hemorrhoids Treated?

The treatment depends on how big the hemorrhoids are and how bad the symptoms are.

If your hemorrhoids are only slightly enlarged, you may not need medicine. Simple changes can help:

- Avoid constipation
- Don’t strain when you go to the toilet
- Eat more fiber
- Drink plenty of water

Some people use creams, ointments, or sitz baths (shallow warm baths) to feel better. These may help with itching or discomfort. But not all of these treatments have been proven to work well in studies.

For more information on home remedies, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

If your symptoms are bothering you, see a doctor. Your family doctor or a proctologist can help. A proctologist is a doctor who specializes in problems of the colon, rectum, and anus.

Talk to your doctor about:

- Whether surgery might help
- What other treatments are available

Hemorrhoidal disease is divided into four grades:

- Grade 1: Mild
- Grade 2: Moderate
- Grade 3: Severe
- Grade 4: Very severe

Treatment options depend on the grade:

- **Grade 1 and Grade 2:** Sclerotherapy may be used. This means a special solution is injected into the hemorrhoid. It reduces blood flow and makes the tissue shrink.
- **Grade 2 and Grade 3:** Rubber band ligation may be used. A small rubber band is placed around the base of the hemorrhoid. This cuts off the blood supply. The hemorrhoid falls off after a few days.
- **Grade 3 or Grade 4:** Surgery may be needed. The enlarged tissue is removed. Different types of surgery can be used, depending on the size and location of the hemorrhoids.

# Salivary Stones

Salivary stones can block the flow of saliva. This causes pain and swelling in the salivary gland. The pain often happens when you eat. There are several ways to remove these stones.

---

## Quick Facts

- People have six large salivary glands. These glands connect to the mouth through small tubes called ducts.
- If a duct gets blocked by a stone, the gland swells up.
- Swelling and pain are most common when eating.
- The swelling may go away and come back. Or it may keep getting worse.
- Often, the stone can be pushed out by increasing saliva flow. This can be done with massage and sour foods.
- In some cases, surgery is needed.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Are Salivary Stones?

A salivary stone is a small, hard lump made from trapped saliva. It forms in the tube that carries saliva from a gland to the mouth. When the tube is blocked, saliva builds up. This causes pain and swelling.

There are three main salivary glands on each side of the face:

- The parotid gland (in front of the ears)
- The submandibular gland (under the jaw)
- The sublingual gland (under the tongue)

Most salivary stones form in the submandibular gland, and usually only on one side.

Stimulating saliva flow can help push the stone out. But sometimes, the stone must be removed with surgery.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Salivary stones are usually between 2 and 10 millimeters wide. That’s about the size of a pea. Some can grow up to three times that size, especially in the submandibular gland.

Stones can form in different parts of the duct. Sometimes, you can see them in the mouth. They are round or oval and white to yellowish. Even if you can’t see them, you may feel them.

Small stones often cause no symptoms. But if a stone grows big enough to block the duct, saliva can’t flow out. It backs up into the gland. This causes swelling and pain.

The pain usually starts when you eat. That’s when your body makes more saliva.

The swelling may go away and return after days or weeks. Or it may keep growing. Usually, only one side of the face is affected.

If the pain gets worse and the area turns red or feels hot, this may mean there is an infection.

---

## What Causes Salivary Stones?

Salivary glands make saliva. Saliva helps with chewing and digestion. It flows from the gland into the mouth through a tube.

If the tube gets narrow — from injury, swelling, or natural shape — saliva can build up. This may lead to stone formation.

Saliva changes in texture. It can be watery or thick and sticky. It also contains minerals and proteins. Scientists do not yet know exactly why liquid saliva turns into hard stones.

Tiny particles or bacteria can start the process. If saliva flows slowly and thickly, layers build up over time. The stone grows bigger. Eventually, it blocks the tube.

Stones are most common in the submandibular glands. These glands make thicker saliva. The tubes are long and go upward against gravity. This makes the saliva move slowly.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

Certain things make salivary stones more likely:

- Taking water pills (diuretics)
- Not drinking enough fluids
- Some medicines that cause dry mouth
- Health problems like:
  - Gout
  - Kidney stones
  - Long-term gum disease
  - Smoking

These factors can reduce saliva flow or change its texture, making stones more likely.

---

## How Common Are They?

Fewer than 1 in 100 people will have a salivary stone that causes symptoms in their lifetime.

Men are more likely than women to get them. Children rarely do.

Most people who get salivary stones are between 30 and 60 years old.

Three out of four people with salivary stones have just one stone.

Stones affect both sides of the face equally. It is rare for both sides to be affected at the same time.

---

## Possible Complications

When saliva is blocked, the gland can become inflamed. This is more common in older adults.

Most cases of gland inflammation can be treated with antibiotics. But sometimes, pus builds up. This is called an abscess.

If the blockage lasts a long time, the gland may stop working properly. Saliva production may drop permanently.

If the blockage is removed early, the gland often recovers.

---

## How Are They Diagnosed?

Doctors start by looking in your mouth and feeling your glands and ducts.

An ultrasound scan is often the best way to find the stone and see where it is.

During the exam, doctors may give you a sour candy or powder. This makes your mouth produce more saliva. This helps show if the duct is blocked.

In some cases, doctors may use an MRI or CT scan.

They can also use a thin, flexible tool to look directly into the duct. This is called a salivary duct endoscopy. The good thing is, treatment can be done during the same visit.

Another test is called salivary gland scintigraphy. A small amount of a safe radioactive substance is put into the blood. This lets doctors watch how the glands make and release saliva.

---

## How Are They Treated?

The best treatment depends on the size and location of the stone.

If a stone is found by chance and causes no problems, it may not need treatment right away.

If the stone is causing pain or swelling, the first steps are:

- Eat sour foods like lemon drops or chew sour gum. This increases saliva flow and may push the stone out.
- Drink plenty of fluids. This helps keep saliva flowing.
- Doctors may gently massage the gland toward the duct opening. They may also widen the duct opening slightly.
- If there is an infection, doctors will prescribe antibiotics and pain medicine.

In many cases, the symptoms go away with these steps.

If the stone still blocks the duct, other treatments are available:

- A very thin tool called a micro-endoscope can be used to find and remove the stone. Sometimes, a small cut is made to open the duct more.
- Shock waves can break the stone into tiny pieces. The waves come from outside the body or from inside the duct using a scope.
- Surgery may be needed. This can be done through a small cut in the skin or through the mouth. Doctors always try to save the gland. Only in rare cases is the whole gland removed.

# Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo

Dizziness can happen when the balance system in your inner ear does not work properly. This condition is called benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. It is not dangerous, but it can be very uncomfortable.

---

## Quick Facts

- This condition causes sudden attacks of dizziness.
- It happens when tiny particles move inside the balance system of your inner ear.
- Most people get better on their own within a few weeks.
- A special movement exercise can help if symptoms do not go away.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo?

When you feel like everything is spinning around you, that is called vertigo. This can happen when you are standing, walking, or lying down. The spinning feeling can last a few seconds to several minutes.

This type of vertigo is often caused by a problem in the balance system inside your inner ear. Certain head movements can set off the dizziness. The condition is easy to recognize and treat. It is not serious, even though it feels unpleasant.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

During an attack, you feel like you are spinning, like being on a merry-go-round. The dizziness usually starts when you move your head in certain ways. These include:

- Nodding your head or turning it side to side
- Bending forward
- Lying down
- Rolling over in bed
- Sitting up from lying down

The dizziness usually lasts only a few seconds to five minutes. It does not last all the time.

You might feel sick to your stomach during or after the attack. Vomiting can happen, but it is rare.

---

## What Causes This Condition?

The cause is loose particles in the fluid-filled tubes of the inner ear. These tubes are part of your balance system. They help your body know when your head moves.

The particles are usually tiny calcium stones called otoliths. They are found at the back of one of the tubes. When you move your head, the loose stones shift. They touch the sensitive cells in the tube. This sends wrong signals to your brain. Your brain gets confused because the signals do not match what your eyes and body feel. That causes dizziness.

Other causes of dizziness can include ear infections, head injuries, poor blood flow, or being in bed for a long time.

---

## How Common Is This Condition?

About 2 out of every 100 people will have this condition at some point in their life. Women are twice as likely to get it as men. It most often affects people between the ages of 40 and 70.

The dizziness comes in short bursts. Once the particles settle or are broken down by the body, the condition usually goes away. About half of people feel better within three months.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors can usually tell if you have this condition based on your symptoms and medical history. They will ask if the dizziness happens in attacks, if it comes and goes, and if certain movements trigger it.

To confirm the diagnosis, doctors use a test called the Hallpike test. In this test, the doctor helps you move your head and body in a specific way. If this causes dizziness, it confirms the condition.

During the dizziness attack, your eyes may make quick jerking movements. These are called nystagmus. Special glasses called Frenzel goggles can help the doctor see these eye movements.

---

## How Is It Treated?

In many cases, no treatment is needed. The condition often gets better on its own.

A treatment called canalith repositioning can help. This is a series of head and body movements. They guide the loose particles to a place where they no longer cause dizziness. A doctor will help you do these movements. There are also versions you can do at home.

If you feel sick, medicine can help. This is only needed in some cases. For severe dizziness, short-term medicine can reduce the spinning feeling.

For more information, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

---

## What Are the Effects?

Dizziness can be upsetting, especially if you are not sure what is causing it.

Older adults are at higher risk of falling during an attack. Some people may avoid moving or doing normal activities because they fear another attack. This can limit daily life.

# Hemophilia

Hemophilia is also called “bleeder’s disease.”  
It is a condition that makes it hard for blood to clot.  
This means cuts take longer to stop bleeding.  
It can also cause bleeding inside the body.

---

## Quick Facts

- Hemophilia makes blood clot more slowly than normal.  
- Cuts heal slowly. Internal bleeding can happen without a clear cause.  
- Most people with hemophilia inherit it from their parents.  
- Treatment can be given when needed or on a regular schedule.  
- People with mild hemophilia often have no symptoms every day.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Hemophilia?

People with hemophilia have trouble forming blood clots.  
Their blood takes longer to stop bleeding.  
This is why it is called “bleeder’s disease.”

Bleeding can happen inside the body.  
This may happen after a fall or injury.  
Sometimes, there is no clear reason for the bleeding.  
Internal bleeding can harm joints, muscles, or organs.

Hemophilia is a group of related conditions.  
The two most common types are hemophilia A and hemophilia B.  
Both happen because the body lacks a special protein that helps blood clot.  
- People with hemophilia A are missing clotting factor VIII.  
- People with hemophilia B are missing clotting factor IX.  
Hemophilia A is more common.

---

## Signs of Hemophilia

There are three levels of severity:

### Mild Hemophilia
- Most people have no daily symptoms.  
- Bleeding problems may only show up during surgery or after a deep cut.  
- Often noticed in teenage years or adulthood.

### Moderate Hemophilia
- Bleeding happens sometimes, usually after an injury or surgery.  
- Bleeding without a clear cause is rare.

### Severe Hemophilia
- Bleeding often happens for no clear reason.  
- Common in joints like the knee, ankle, elbow, shoulder, hip, or hand.  
- Muscles in arms and legs are often affected.  
- Bleeding in the belly, throat, or brain is very dangerous.

> **Important:** Severe hemophilia is often noticed in babies or young children.  
> They bruise very easily.  
> As they start walking, they may begin to bleed into joints and muscles.

Bleeding in joints causes pain.  
The joint swells and hurts when moved.  
It may also become inflamed.

---

## What Causes Hemophilia?

Hemophilia is usually inherited.  
It is caused by a missing clotting factor in the blood.  
This is usually due to a faulty gene.

Most people have two copies of each gene.  
The genes for clotting factors are on the X chromosome.  
Women have two X chromosomes.  
Men have one X and one Y chromosome.

If a woman has one faulty gene, the other normal gene often prevents problems.  
It is very rare for both genes to be faulty in women.

But if a man has a faulty gene, he has no backup.  
So he will likely have hemophilia.  
This is why hemophilia is more common in men.

---

## How Common Is Hemophilia?

About 2 out of every 10,000 men have hemophilia.  
In Germany, around 10,000 men have the condition.  
About 3,000 to 5,000 of them have the severe form.

---

## How Does Hemophilia Progress?

If a joint has bled before, it is more likely to bleed again.  
Repeated bleeding can damage the joint.  
It can become stiff and deformed over time. This is called hemarthrosis.

In advanced cases, movement may become very hard.  
Some people may need a wheelchair or other mobility aid.

Bleeding into muscles increases pressure.  
This can damage nearby nerves, blood vessels, and tissues.

Bleeding in the brain is rare but serious.  
It can affect thinking, concentration, and balance.  
Severe brain bleeding can be life-threatening.

Other internal bleeding is also dangerous:  
- Bleeding in the mouth or throat can make breathing hard.  
- Bleeding in the belly can cause heavy blood loss.  
- Bleeding in vital organs can damage them.

---

## How Is Hemophilia Treated?

Treatment replaces the missing clotting factor with injections.

### On-Demand Treatment
This means getting the clotting factor only when needed.  
For example:
- To stop bleeding that is already happening.  
- Before surgery.  
- Before tooth removal.

### Preventive Treatment
This is used for people with severe hemophilia.  
The missing clotting factor is given regularly.  
It is injected into a vein every few days.  
This helps reduce the chance of bleeding.

Many people with hemophilia learn to give themselves the injection.  
With training and practice, it becomes easier.

> **Important:**  
> Other medicines are used only for mild hemophilia.  
> These include:
> - Tranexamic acid  
> - Desmopressin  
>  
> Desmopressin helps release stored clotting factors from blood vessels.

Painkillers may also be used for pain.  
Use painkillers that do not affect blood clotting.  
For example, ibuprofen is safe.  
But do not use acetylsalicylic acid (like in Aspirin).  
It increases the risk of bleeding.

For more details on preventive treatment, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

---

## Life with Hemophilia

Hemophilia used to limit what people could do.  
Today, treatment allows most people to live full lives.  
They can do most activities — as long as they avoid high-risk sports or jobs.

This includes:
- Contact sports  
- Mountain biking  
- Skiing  
- Manual labor jobs

The ability to do these things depends on:
- How likely the person is to bleed  
- How well treatment works

Exercise helps strengthen muscles.  
It improves flexibility, balance, and body awareness.  
This can help prevent injuries that cause bleeding.

Even with treatment, living with hemophilia takes effort.  
Learning to give injections takes time and practice.

Children with severe hemophilia often learn early how to manage their condition.  
They know what to do when bleeding starts.

It helps to:
- Tell family and caregivers about the condition  
- Carry an emergency ID card at all times  
- Store medical details in the emergency data section of the electronic medical card

---

## Additional Support and Information

Germany has special hemophilia centers.  
These centers focus on treating hemophilia.  
They also offer emotional and social support for:
- Children  
- Teenagers  
- Parents  
- Adults

Since 2019, people with hemophilia can use a special outpatient care service called ASV.  
This service brings together different specialists in one place.  
The team includes:
- Doctors in internal medicine  
- Orthopedic specialists  
- Experts in blood clotting disorders (transfusion medicine)

Children and teens also see a pediatrician trained in hemophilia.

You can find a list of all ASV centers on the ASV service center website.

People with hemophilia can also get help from:
- Support groups  
- Information centers  

These groups offer advice, connection, and understanding.

# Back Pain and Lower Back Pain

Back pain in the lower part of the back is very common.  
The good news is that it is usually not serious.  
Most people feel better within a few days or weeks.  
The best way to prevent back pain is to stay active and exercise regularly.

---

## Quick Facts

- There is almost never just one reason for back pain.  
- There are two main types: nonspecific and specific.  
- Nonspecific back pain is not dangerous.  
- Most people get better without treatment in a few days or weeks.  
- Tests like X-rays, scans, or shots are rarely needed for nonspecific back pain.  
- About one in three people have back pain again within a year.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor.  
> Do not use this to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Back Pain?

Lower back pain is very common.  
It usually starts suddenly and goes away on its own.  
It is important to keep moving when you have back pain.  
Do not stay in bed for long.  
Avoid resting too much or holding your body in a stiff way.  
These things can slow down recovery.

There is almost never a single cause for back pain.  
Nonspecific back pain is not a sign of injury.  
This is true even if the pain comes back or lasts a long time.

But long-term pain can affect your daily life and mood.

For nonspecific back pain, tests, medicine, injections, or surgery are rarely helpful.  
They can cause harm and are only used in rare cases.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Pain in the lower back — between your hips and the bottom of your ribs — is called lower back pain.  
You may feel muscle tightness.  
You might also find it hard to move or bend.

Sudden, sharp pain in the lower back is called lumbago.

The pain can spread down one or both legs.  
If the pain goes past the knee or into the foot, it is called sciatica.  
The most common cause of sciatica is a slipped disc.

Back pain and leg pain can happen at the same time.  
But they do not always come from the same cause.  
If your leg pain is worse than your back pain,  
or if it follows a nerve path,  
or if you feel tingling or numbness,  
then sciatica is likely the cause.

---

## What Causes Back Pain?

There are two main types of back pain:  
- Nonspecific (no clear cause)  
- Specific (a clear cause can be found)

Most back pain is nonspecific.  
It can be linked to:

- Not moving enough or weak core muscles  
- Sitting too long, like at a desk  
- Doing one-sided or heavy work  
- Muscle tension from poor posture or strain  
- Stress, anxiety, money worries, family problems, or depression  
- Changes in how your body feels pain  
- Family history of back pain

Specific back pain has a clear cause.  
Examples include:

- Narrowing of the spine  
- A slipped disc  
- A broken bone in the spine (often from weak bones due to osteoporosis)  
- A rare condition called Bechterew’s disease

Because the cause is clear in specific cases, treatment may be different.

---

## How Long Does Back Pain Last?

Most back pain goes away in a few days or weeks — even without treatment.  
But many people have it again.  
About one in three people have back pain again within a year.

Chronic back pain lasts for months.  
It can be:

- Severe at times, mild at others  
- Mild but always there  
- Severe and constant

It is hard to predict how long the pain will last.

---

## How Can You Prevent Back Pain?

The best way to prevent back pain is regular exercise.  
Strengthening your core muscles helps.  
Do strength and stability exercises.  
Try to move several times a week.

Studies show that core exercises can cut back pain by half.

For more information on why movement helps, visit **gesundheitsinformation.de**.

---

## How Is Back Pain Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask questions.  
They may ask:

- Is this your first time with back pain?  
- Is it coming back?  
- Where exactly is the pain?  
- Does it happen when you move or when you rest?

They will also ask about:

- Recent accidents  
- Medicines you take (like cortisone)  
- Other health problems  
- Tingling, numbness, or weakness  
- Any signs of paralysis  
- Stress or mental health issues

During the exam, the doctor will:

- Feel your muscles for tightness or pain  
- Test your reflexes  
- Check how well you can move

Most of the time, this is enough.  
Doctors do not need X-rays, CT scans, or MRIs for nonspecific back pain.

Why?  
Because these tests can show small changes that are not really the cause of pain.  
This can lead to wrong treatment or fear.

Imaging may be needed if:

- There is a clear reason to suspect a serious problem  
- Symptoms do not get better after six weeks  
- They get worse over time

---

## How Is Back Pain Treated?

Acute back pain usually gets better on its own.  
But staying active helps it go away faster than staying in bed.

Simple steps that help:

- Use heat — like a hot water bottle or heating pad  
- Take painkillers like ibuprofen for a short time only

If the pain is very bad:

- Avoid lifting heavy things  
- Be careful when bending  
- Try the psoas position: lie on your back with your legs raised so your upper and lower legs form a 90-degree angle

But do not stay in bed for long.  
Keep moving as much as you can.

Do your daily tasks.  
Avoid sitting still for long periods — like at a desk.  
Even light walking can help reduce pain.

For ongoing or repeated back pain, the best thing you can do is stay active.  
Do not let pain stop you from doing things you enjoy.

Studies show that exercise is the most effective treatment for long-term back pain.  
The longer you stay inactive, the longer the pain lasts.

Other helpful tools:

- Mindfulness training  
- Relaxation exercises (like Jacobson’s method)

For chronic pain, cognitive behavioral therapy or multidisciplinary pain programs can help.  
These teach you how to manage pain by changing thoughts and habits.

---

## What Is Back Pain Rehabilitation?

If back pain keeps you from working, rehabilitation may help.  
It can be done at home or in a clinic.

The goal is to reduce pain and help you return to your normal life.  
Rehabilitation is not only for people at risk of long-term work disability.

A rehab program usually includes:

- Doctors  
- Physical therapists  
- Psychologists  

They work together to help you get better.

# Osteoporosis

Osteoporosis means your bones become weaker and less dense.  
This makes your bones more likely to break.  
It is normal for bones to lose strength as you get older.  
But osteoporosis makes this happen faster.  
It is more common in older people.

---

## Quick Facts

- Bones naturally lose strength with age.  
- Osteoporosis speeds up this loss.  
- Weak bones are more likely to break.  
- But other things also affect your risk of breaking a bone.  
- Women start losing bone mass earlier than men.  
- To help protect your bones, stay active, spend time outside, eat foods with calcium, and do not smoke.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Osteoporosis?

As you age, your bones naturally lose some strength.  
But in some people, this loss happens much faster.  
When bone strength drops too low, it is called osteoporosis.

Older people are most at risk.  
Women begin losing bone mass earlier than men.

People with osteoporosis are more likely to break a bone.  
In older adults, broken bones heal more slowly.  
A break can lead to serious health problems.

But bone strength alone does not tell the whole story.  
Even if your bones are weak, you should still stay active.  
Movement helps keep your bones and muscles strong.  
It also improves balance and helps you avoid falls.  
Falls are the most common cause of broken bones in older people.

You can take steps to keep your bones strong.  
These actions help prevent osteoporosis:

- Stay physically active  
- Spend time outdoors  
- Eat foods rich in calcium  
- Do not smoke

Your age and other personal risks will help decide if medicine to strengthen bones is right for you.

---

## What Are the Signs of Osteoporosis?

Often, the first sign of osteoporosis is a broken bone.  
Sometimes, you may notice your spine is slightly bent.  
This can make you lose a small amount of height.

In later stages, the spine may curve forward.  
This can cause a hump in the upper back.

This happens because the bones in the spine break.  
These breaks can cause back pain.  
But many people do not feel any pain at all.

Other common break sites include the wrist, upper arm, pelvis, and hip.  
Breaks in the neck of the thigh bone (femoral neck) are especially serious.  
These often happen in people over 80.  
They can lead to long-term care needs.

---

## What Causes Osteoporosis?

Your skeleton supports your body and protects your organs.  
It works with muscles, tendons, ligaments, and joints to let you move.

Inside your bones is a network of tiny fibers called trabeculae.  
When these fibers break down, bones become weaker.  
The spaces between them grow larger.  
This lowers bone density.

But how weak your bones become also depends on their shape, structure, and mineral content.

Bone strength peaks around age 15 in girls and 20 in boys.  
After age 30, bone mass slowly decreases.

In women, bone loss speeds up around age 50.  
Before menopause, female hormones (estrogen) help protect bones.  
After menopause, estrogen levels drop.  
This removes the protection and bone loss increases.

Doctors divide osteoporosis into two types:

- **Primary osteoporosis**: No other cause is found.  
- **Secondary osteoporosis**: Caused by another illness or long-term use of certain medicines.

---

## What Increases Your Risk?

Some risk factors cannot be changed.  
Others you can control.

Main risk factors include:

- Being older  
- Being a woman  
- Being underweight for your height  
- Having had a broken bone before  
- Not getting enough calcium  
- Not getting enough vitamin D  
- Not being active  
- Family history of osteoporosis  
- Smoking  
- Drinking too much alcohol  
- Taking cortisone medicine for a long time

---

## How Common Is Osteoporosis?

We do not know the exact number of people in Germany with osteoporosis.  
We also do not know how many bone breaks it causes.

One large study found:

- About 10% of men aged 70 had been told they have osteoporosis.  
- About 20% of women aged 70 had been told they have osteoporosis.

Around 30% of hip, spine, and wrist breaks are linked to very weak bones.

Not everyone with weak bones will break a bone.  
But hip breaks are especially serious.

Most hip breaks happen in people over 80.  
About 1% to 2% of people in this age group break the neck of the thigh bone each year.

---

## How Can You Prevent Osteoporosis?

You can take steps to protect your bones:

- Eat foods rich in calcium.  
  Good sources include milk, cheese, yogurt, leafy green vegetables, and some mineral waters.  
- Stay active.  
  Exercise strengthens bones and muscles.  
  It also improves balance and coordination.  
  This lowers your risk of falling.  
- Do not smoke.  
- Get enough vitamin D.  
  Your body makes vitamin D when your skin is exposed to sunlight.

More information on calcium-rich foods is available at _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

Studies show that calcium and vitamin D supplements do not help most people.  
In fact, they may increase the risk of kidney stones.  
So, health groups do not recommend taking these supplements regularly to prevent broken bones.

Supplements may help people who are in care or not very mobile.  
They often spend little time in the sun and are less active.

A break in the neck of the thigh bone can be very serious.  
Older people may never fully recover from this type of break.  
While osteoporosis increases the risk, falls are the main cause.  
So, preventing falls is key.

Some medicines can increase your risk of falling.  
Talk to your doctor about your medicines.  
Ask if any are necessary.  
It helps to write down your medicines before the visit.

For more tips on staying active and getting vitamin D, go to _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

---

## How Can Osteoporosis Be Found Early?

Some doctors offer a bone density test (osteodensitometry) as a private service.  
But women under 65 with no risk factors do not need this test.  
It may even do harm if you start avoiding movement out of fear of breaking a bone.

Your health insurance will pay for the test if there is a medical reason.  
This includes:

- A broken bone that may be due to weak bones  
- Long-term use of cortisone medicine  
- Planning to start medicine for osteoporosis

There is no clear evidence that testing young women, women with no risk factors, or men is helpful.

---

## How Is Osteoporosis Diagnosed?

Osteoporosis is sometimes found by accident.  
For example, an X-ray of the upper body for another reason may show a broken spine.

It may also be found after a bone breaks from a minor fall.  
For example, falling from standing height.  
In such cases, a doctor can often diagnose osteoporosis after a conversation and physical exam.

If you have not broken a bone yet, osteoporosis is not a disease.  
It is a risk factor for breaking bones.

A bone density test can show if your bones are weak.  
It uses a special X-ray to measure how much mineral is in your bones.

The result is given as a T-score:

- A T-score from 0 to -1 is normal  
- A T-score from -1 to -2.5 means bone density is lower than normal (called osteopenia)  
- A T-score of -2.5 or lower means osteoporosis

But bone density tests alone cannot predict your risk of breaking a bone.  
Other factors matter too.  
These include the shape of your bones, how strong they are, and your overall health.

---

## How Is Osteoporosis Treated?

If you have osteoporosis, staying active and eating enough calcium and vitamin D is important.

### Medicine for Osteoporosis

Some medicines can help slow bone loss or help bones grow back.

The most common type is called bisphosphonates.  
They are usually used if you have already broken a bone or are at high risk.

This includes people with very low bone density or many risk factors.

If you choose medicine, you usually take it for several years.

People with only a small increase in risk or only slightly weak bones should carefully think about the benefits and risks before starting medicine.

More information on treatment is available at _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

> **Important:** Hormone treatments (like those used for menopause symptoms) can reduce the risk of broken bones.  
> But long-term use increases the risk of heart disease and breast cancer.  
> Because of this, hormone treatment is only used in special cases.  
> You should carefully weigh the benefits and risks.

### Surgery for Spine Breaks

If the bones in your spine break due to osteoporosis, two treatments may be offered:

- **Vertebroplasty**: Injecting bone cement into the broken bone  
- **Kyphoplasty**: A similar procedure with a balloon to lift the bone first

Studies show most people do not benefit from these treatments.  
They may help if you have severe pain.  
But the risks can be serious.

If your doctor suggests this treatment, you have the right to a free second opinion.

The decision aid on _gesundheitsinformation.de_ can help

# Keratoconus

Keratoconus is an eye condition. The cornea, which is the clear front part of the eye, becomes thinner and starts to bulge outward. This bulge looks like a cone. As the cornea changes shape, your vision gets worse over time.

This article explains how doctors find keratoconus and what treatments are available.

---

## Quick Facts

- Keratoconus causes the cornea to become thin and bulge into a cone shape.
- It usually starts in one eye during the teenage years or early adulthood.
- Over time, the other eye may also be affected.
- Vision gets worse as the disease progresses.
- Most people can manage their vision with contact lenses.
- If needed, there are treatments to slow or stop the cornea from changing shape.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Keratoconus?

Keratoconus is a rare eye condition. It is not caused by infection. The cornea becomes thinner and changes shape. Normally, the cornea is smooth and curved like a dome. In keratoconus, it bulges outward in a cone shape.

The condition often starts in one eye. But over time, both eyes are usually affected. The disease can get worse slowly or in sudden steps. Vision keeps getting worse until it usually stops around age 40.

To help with poor vision, most people wear glasses or contact lenses. In some cases, a simple surgery done in a doctor’s office can slow down or stop the worsening of vision.

The exact cause of keratoconus is not known. But some things may make it more likely to happen.

---

## What Are the Signs of Keratoconus?

Early signs include:

- Blurry or distorted vision
- Trouble seeing in bright light
- Vision that changes often

You may need new glasses or contact lenses often. This is because your eyes keep changing.

One eye is often worse than the other. Some people are very sensitive to light.

In later stages, you might see changes in the eye. These can include:

- Thin yellow or brown lines on the edge of the cornea
- A greenish or brownish ring around the cornea

In advanced cases, the lower eyelid may look like it has a cone shape. This can be seen without a special tool.

---

## What Increases the Risk of Keratoconus?

The exact cause is unknown. But these factors may raise the risk:

- Repeated injuries to the cornea, such as from rubbing your eyes too hard
- Wearing hard contact lenses that do not fit well
- A family history of keratoconus — about 6 to 8 out of 100 people with the disease have a relative with it
- Allergies
- Certain connective tissue disorders

People with Down’s Syndrome are more likely to develop keratoconus.

---

## How Common Is Keratoconus?

Keratoconus is one of the most common problems affecting the cornea. About 1 in every 2,000 people develops it each year.

---

## When Does Keratoconus Start?

For men, it usually begins in the teenage years.  
For women, it often starts in their early 20s.

It is rare for keratoconus to start later in life. But it can happen during pregnancy or menopause due to hormone changes.

The disease usually stops getting worse around age 40.  
It often affects both eyes. But one eye may be much worse than the other. In some cases, one eye may stay healthy.

---

## How Is Keratoconus Diagnosed?

A regular eye exam may not catch keratoconus early. It can look like astigmatism, which is a common eye problem.

If your vision keeps changing even with glasses or contact lenses, your doctor may do a special test.

They use tools like:

- Corneal topography – a scan that maps the shape of the cornea
- Optical coherence tomography – a scan that shows the thickness and structure of the cornea

These tests help doctors see if the cornea is thinning or changing shape. They can also spot early signs of damage or cloudiness.

---

## How Is Keratoconus Treated?

Treatment depends on how far the disease has progressed.

If the condition is stable and not getting worse, the main goal is to correct your vision.

If the condition is getting worse quickly, the goal is to stop it from getting worse.

### Early Treatment

- Glasses or contact lenses can help improve vision.
- Hard (rigid) contact lenses often give the clearest vision. But not everyone can wear them comfortably.
- If hard lenses are not tolerated, doctors may suggest hybrid lenses or scleral lenses. These are special types of contact lenses.

### Stopping Progression

A treatment called UV-riboflavin crosslinking can stop the cornea from bulging further.

Here’s how it works:

- The doctor numbs your eye with drops.
- They gently remove the very top layer of the cornea.
- They apply a special liquid (containing vitamin B2) to the eye.
- Then they shine a special UV light on the eye.

This process strengthens the cornea’s inner structure. It helps prevent further thinning and bulging.

This treatment does not fix blurry vision. But it can stop the condition from getting worse. It works best when used early.

### Advanced Cases

If the cornea becomes too thin, crosslinking is no longer an option.

In severe cases, a corneal transplant may be needed.

This means replacing part or all of the damaged cornea with healthy tissue from a donor. This surgery is called keratoplasty.

---

## What Should You Do in Daily Life?

If you have keratoconus:

- Try not to rub your eyes. This can make the cornea worse.
- If your eyes feel dry or irritated, use eye drops to keep them moist.
- If you have hay fever or other allergies that bother your eyes, take medicine as directed by your doctor.

Taking care of your eyes every day can help protect your vision.

# Concussion in Adults

A concussion is a mild brain injury. It usually does not cause lasting harm. This guide explains the main signs and how to care for yourself after a concussion.

---

## Quick Facts

- Most concussions happen after a blow to the head.
- Common signs include headache, dizziness, feeling confused, or trouble remembering things.
- If someone has strong symptoms, call an emergency doctor right away.
- Symptoms usually show up right after the injury or within 48 hours.
- Medicine can help with headaches.
- Rest is very important. Take it easy for 1 to 2 days after the injury.
- Most people do not have long-term problems after a concussion.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical care. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Concussion?

A concussion often happens during accidents. These can occur at work, at home, or while playing sports or doing other physical activities.

The brain controls your body. It is very sensitive and protected inside the skull. Fluid around the brain acts like a cushion.

When the head hits something hard, the brain can bump into the inside of the skull. This can cause a concussion.

Some people have a cut or bruise on the head. Others do not. Common signs include:
- A short loss of consciousness
- Feeling dazed or foggy
- Headache
- Trouble remembering things

> **Important:** If someone loses consciousness, cannot remember events, keeps vomiting, or feels very dizzy, get emergency help right away.

---

## What Are the Signs of a Concussion?

Symptoms usually appear right after the injury or within 24 to 48 hours.

You may have:
- Headache
- Feeling dazed or slow
- Dizziness
- Nausea or vomiting
- Trouble hearing
- Blurry or double vision

Memory problems are common. You might not remember:
- How you got hurt
- What happened just before or after the injury

You might also:
- Pass out briefly
- Act confused, sleepy, or disoriented
- Have trouble sleeping
- Struggle to focus

---

## What Causes a Concussion?

The brain is protected by the skull and cushioning fluid. This fluid helps prevent small bumps from causing harm.

But a strong hit to the head can push the brain into the skull. The fluid cannot stop this impact. This causes a concussion.

---

## Who Is at Risk?

Most head injuries happen by accident. They often happen during sports or physical activities like:
- Skiing
- Cycling
- Playing contact sports

People who play sports like ice hockey are more likely to get head injuries.

---

## How Common Are Concussions?

Concussions are very common. In Germany, about 320,000 people have a brain injury each year. About 91 out of 100 of these are concussions.

---

## How Does a Concussion Develop?

Symptoms usually start right after the injury or within 1 to 2 days. Most people feel better in a few days.

If symptoms are serious, you may need to stay in the hospital for monitoring. Rest is key.

Most people recover fully. But some people still have symptoms like:
- Headaches
- Feeling tired
- Anxiety
- Trouble remembering things

This is more likely in people who play sports where the head gets hit often.

To avoid long-term problems, always rest after a concussion—even if it seems mild.

> **Important:** Most symptoms should go away within 14 to 21 days. If they last longer, see your doctor again.

---

## How Is a Concussion Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your injury and check your health.

They will look for:
- Memory problems
- Vision issues
- Weakness or trouble moving
- Changes in alertness

They may use a CT scan only if symptoms are serious or if there is a risk of complications.

---

## How Is a Concussion Treated?

Most mild concussions do not need special treatment.

You can take medicine for:
- Severe headache
- Nausea

Rest is essential. For 1 to 2 days, avoid:
- Physical activity
- Reading
- Watching screens
- Talking in a loud or stressful way

Lying down can help. After rest, slowly return to normal activities. Start with light tasks that do not cause symptoms.

> **Important:** If you have any of these signs, call an emergency doctor:
- Loss of consciousness
- Memory gaps
- Vomiting again and again
- Severe dizziness

In many cases, you will need to stay in the hospital for 24 hours. This lets doctors act fast if there is bleeding in the brain or pressure building up.

# Menstrual Cramps

Periods are a normal part of being a woman. But severe cramps do not have to be part of your monthly cycle. Most women can find relief from strong pain. If your cramps are very bad or getting worse, see a doctor.

---

## Quick Facts

- Many girls and women feel cramps or pain in the lower belly during their period.
- There are two types of menstrual cramps: primary and secondary.
- Cramps can stay in the lower belly. Or they can spread to the back and legs.
- Some women also feel sick to their stomach, throw up, have diarrhea, or get headaches.
- One in ten women has pain so bad that they cannot do normal activities for one to three days each month.
- Severe cramps can usually be treated well.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Are Menstrual Cramps?

Menstrual cramps are pain in the lower belly during your period. Doctors call this condition dysmenorrhea.  
Many women have some cramps during their period.  
But severe pain is not normal. It can usually be treated.  
If your pain is strong or getting worse, see a doctor to find out why.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

- Cramps in the lower belly.
- Pain that spreads to the back or legs.
- Feeling sick to your stomach.
- Vomiting.
- Diarrhea.
- Headaches.
- Feeling generally unwell.

Women with heavy periods often have more pain.

---

## What Causes Menstrual Cramps?

Every month, the lining of the uterus gets thicker. This is in case a baby is growing.  
If no baby grows, the top layer of the lining breaks off. It leaves the body as blood and tissue during your period.

During your period, the uterus squeezes and relaxes. These movements help push the lining out.  
Some women feel nothing. Others feel strong cramps.

There are two types of cramps:

### Primary Cramps

These are caused by strong muscle contractions in the uterus.  
A substance called prostaglandin causes the uterus to squeeze.  
Some women make too much prostaglandin. Others are more sensitive to it.  
This leads to stronger cramps.  
Younger women, especially under 30, are more likely to have these cramps.  
Women with heavy periods also often have them.  
Stress and family history may play a role.

### Secondary Cramps

These are caused by other health issues.  
They often start after a woman has had periods for several years.  
Possible causes include:
- Benign (non-cancerous) growths in the uterus, like fibroids or polyps.
- Endometriosis: when tissue like the uterine lining grows outside the uterus.
- A copper IUD (a type of birth control device).

These cramps can happen even when you are not on your period.

---

## How Common Are Menstrual Cramps?

Most girls and women have some pain during their period.  
One in ten women has pain so bad that it stops them from doing normal things for one to three days each month.

Pain is usually worse in women under 20.  
It often gets better a few years after the first period.  
Many women also feel less pain after having their first child.

Secondary cramps usually start later. They can happen even when you are not on your period.

---

## How Are Menstrual Cramps Treated?

There are many ways to ease cramps. Some advice from doctors and other women may seem different.

### Medicine

- Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), like ibuprofen or naproxen, can help.
- These drugs reduce prostaglandin levels. This eases cramps.
- Most women can take them safely.
- Some may get an upset stomach.

### Hormonal Birth Control

- Birth control pills, hormonal IUDs, or other hormonal methods can help.
- They make the uterine lining thinner.
- This means less bleeding and shorter periods. Some women have no bleeding at all.
- Side effects can include headaches, nausea, or a higher risk of blood clots.
- Talk to your gynecologist about which option is best for you.

### Heat

- Heat plasters or wraps can help ease pain.
- Warm baths, hot water bottles, or saunas may also help.

### Exercise

- Light exercise like walking, yoga, or aerobics may reduce pain.
- It can also help with mood and stress.

### Other Treatments

- Acupuncture, supplements, and herbal remedies have not been proven to work.
- Studies on them were not strong or gave mixed results.

### Mental Health Support

- Some women find the pain so stressful that they need help with their mental health.
- Counseling, relaxation techniques, and mindfulness can help manage pain and stress.

### Surgery

- If cramps are caused by fibroids or endometriosis, surgery may be an option.

For more details on medicine and treatment, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

---

## How Can Women Cope in Daily Life?

Many people do not take menstrual cramps seriously.  
Some women think they must suffer in silence. They believe pain is just part of having a period.

But pain that stops you from working, studying, or doing daily tasks is not normal.  
You do not have to accept it.

It helps to:
- Talk to your partner, family, or friends about your pain.
- See a doctor to get help.
- Find a treatment that works for you.

You may need to slow down during your period.  
Try:
- Postponing tough tasks.
- Using relaxation techniques.
- Breathing exercises.
- Yoga or tai chi.
- Light walking or exercise.
- Warm baths or hot water bottles.

If you miss work often because of pain, you may feel guilty.  
But support from loved ones can help.  
Understanding and care from family, friends, and coworkers make a big difference.

# Thrombophilia

Thrombophilia means your blood is more likely to form clots than normal.  
These clots can block blood vessels.  
Blocked blood vessels can be dangerous and even life-threatening.  
Treatment aims to dissolve clots that are already there.  
It also aims to stop new clots from forming.

## Quick Facts

- People with thrombophilia are more likely to get blood clots.  
- Blood clots can block blood flow in veins or arteries.  
- Thrombophilia can be inherited (you are born with it).  
- It can also develop later in life (acquired).  
- Doctors often use anti-clotting medicine and compression stockings.  
- These help prevent or treat clots.  
- Certain things raise the risk of clots. These include:  
  - Surgery under general anesthesia  
  - Injuries that keep you from moving  
  - Cancer  
  - Birth control pills that contain estrogen  
  - Pregnancy  
  - Infections, such as from the SARS-CoV-2 virus

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Thrombophilia?

Thrombophilia is a condition where the body’s blood clotting system does not work properly.  
It makes blood clots more likely to form.  
This can lead to clots in veins or arteries (called thromboses or embolisms).  
The blood may clot too easily, even when there is no injury.

### Why Does Blood Clotting Matter?

Clotting is important when you are hurt.  
It helps stop bleeding and helps wounds heal.  
For example, if you cut your skin, your blood clots to close the wound.  
When you are not hurt, your body has natural substances that stop clots from forming.  
These keep your blood flowing smoothly.

### What Happens in Thrombophilia?

In people with thrombophilia, the balance between clotting and anti-clotting factors is off.  
This means blood can clot even when it should not.  
This increases the chance of clots forming in blood vessels.

### Who Can Help?

You should see a doctor who specializes in:  
- Internal medicine  
- Vascular medicine (angiology)  
- Blood clotting disorders (hemostaseology)

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many people with thrombophilia have no symptoms.  
But if you have repeated blood clots, especially at a young age, it may be a sign of thrombophilia.  
The most common problems are:  
- Blood clots in the deep veins of the leg  
- A clot in the lungs (pulmonary embolism)

If blood clots run in your family, you may have inherited thrombophilia.  
You should also consider thrombophilia if clots happen without a clear cause.  
Or if clots form in unusual places in the body.

### Signs of a Deep Vein Clot in the Leg

- Pain in the leg muscles  
- Swelling in one leg  
- Tenderness in the leg  
- A tight or heavy feeling in the leg  
- Skin that looks dark or bluish

### Signs of a Pulmonary Embolism

- Sudden shortness of breath  
- Chest pain that gets worse when you breathe  
- Fast heartbeat  
- Low blood pressure  
- Coughing up blood  
- Fainting

## What Causes Thrombophilia?

Thrombophilia can be present from birth or develop later in life.

### Inherited Thrombophilia

This type is passed down through families.  
It comes from changes in your DNA.  
The most common types are:  
- Factor V Leiden mutation  
- Prothrombin mutation  

These changes are found in 2 to 5 percent of people.  
But most people with these changes never develop a blood clot.

Some people are born with low levels of natural anti-clotting substances.  
These include:  
- Antithrombin  
- Protein C  
- Protein S  

Low levels of these increase the risk of clots.  
These deficiencies are rare in the general population.  
They are found in less than 5 percent of people who have had a clot.  
A very low level of any of these greatly increases the risk of clots.

### Acquired Thrombophilia

This type develops later in life due to other health problems.  
Some people develop antibodies that attack their own clotting system.  
One example is antiphospholipid antibodies.  
These can cause clots in veins or arteries.  
They also raise the risk of miscarriage and early birth.

## What Are the Long-Term Effects?

Many people with thrombophilia do not know they have it.  
Most clots dissolve on their own without causing harm.  
But sometimes clots block blood flow and cause symptoms.

### What Happens When a Clot Forms?

If a clot forms in a deep leg vein, it slows blood flow back to the heart.  
This causes fluid to build up in the leg tissues.  
You may feel pain, swelling, or tightness in the leg.

A fresh clot can break loose.  
It can travel through the bloodstream.  
It moves through the heart and into the lungs.  
There, it can block a blood vessel.  
This is called a pulmonary embolism.  
A severe pulmonary embolism can be fatal.

## How Is Thrombophilia Diagnosed?

If you have a blood clot at a young age, or without a clear reason, thrombophilia may be the cause.  
Your doctor will ask about your medical history and do a physical exam.  
They will look for risk factors.

### When Is Testing Worth It?

Your doctor may suggest testing if:  
- You or a close family member has had repeated clots  
- Clots happen without a clear cause  
- Clots form in unusual places  

Testing can include blood tests or genetic tests.  
But these tests only help if the results change your treatment plan.  
Talk to your doctor before testing.  
Sometimes, your doctor can decide on the best treatment without testing.

## How Is Thrombophilia Treated?

If you have thrombophilia, staying active helps reduce your risk of clots.  
Exercise improves blood flow and lowers the chance of clots.

If you are at high risk for clots — for example, after surgery or after an injury — your doctor may prescribe anti-clotting medicine.  
This helps prevent clots from forming.

Women with a higher risk of clots should talk to their gynecologist.  
They may want to switch to a birth control pill that does not contain estrogen.  
These pills do not increase the risk of blood clots.

# Endometriosis

Endometriosis is a common condition that affects many women.  
It happens when tissue like the lining inside the uterus grows outside the uterus.  
This tissue acts like the uterine lining during the menstrual cycle.  
It grows, breaks down, and bleeds — but the blood has no way to leave the body.  
This can cause pain, inflammation, and scar tissue.  

Some women have no symptoms.  
Others have severe pain, especially during their period.  
Endometriosis can also make it harder to get pregnant.  
The pain may spread to the lower back, legs, or pelvis.  
It can feel like cramps, and may come with nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.  

There is no cure for endometriosis.  
But treatments can help reduce or stop the pain.  
Symptoms often go away after menopause.  

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

---

## What Is Endometriosis?

Endometriosis is one of the most common health issues in women.  
It happens when tissue like the uterine lining grows in other parts of the body.  
These patches of tissue are called endometrial lesions.  
They grow and bleed each month, just like the uterine lining.  
But the blood and tissue cannot leave the body.  
This causes irritation, swelling, and pain.  

Over time, this can lead to scar tissue and cysts.  
Cysts are fluid-filled sacs in the tissue.  
The condition can affect fertility.  

Many women think their pain is just normal period cramps.  
They may wait years before getting help.  
Diagnosis can be delayed because symptoms are often ignored.  

There is no single test for endometriosis.  
Doctors must rule out other causes of pain.  
Treatment should match each woman’s needs and how severe her symptoms are.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main symptom is pelvic pain.  
It often starts around the time of your period.  
Pain during or after sex can also be a sign.  
The pain can be mild or very strong.  
It may spread to the lower back, hips, or legs.  
Some women feel cramping, nausea, or stomach upset.  

Where the tissue grows affects the symptoms.  
For example, if it grows near the bowel, it may cause pain when going to the toilet.  
If it affects the bladder, it may cause pain when urinating.  

Severe endometriosis can make daily life very hard.  
It can affect work, school, relationships, and hobbies.  
Some women feel disconnected from their own bodies.  
Chronic pain can lead to tiredness, mood changes, or depression.  

---

## What Causes Endometriosis?

Each month, the lining of the uterus grows and then sheds if no pregnancy happens.  
This is your period.  

In endometriosis, tissue like this grows outside the uterus.  
It also grows and bleeds each month.  
But the blood and tissue stay trapped in the body.  
In most women, the body breaks down this leftover tissue without harm.  
In some women, the body does not clear it well.  
This leads to inflammation, scarring, and cysts.  

The exact cause is still unknown.  
But hormones, the immune system, and family history may play a role.  
The body usually stops tissue from growing in the wrong places.  
In endometriosis, this system does not work properly.  

---

## How Common Is It?

Endometriosis is very common.  
But we do not know the exact number of women affected.  
Many women have no symptoms or only mild ones.  
Up to half of women with severe period pain may have endometriosis.  

---

## How Does It Progress?

Endometriosis usually affects women during their childbearing years.  
It stops when periods end at menopause.  

In mild cases, symptoms may stay the same or even get better.  
In other women, symptoms get worse over time.  
We cannot predict how it will progress.  

The tissue patches can grow larger.  
Cysts can form, especially on the ovaries.  
These are called endometriomas.  
If cysts and scar tissue form on the ovaries or fallopian tubes, it can make pregnancy harder.  

Most women with endometriosis can still get pregnant.  
But severe cases can cause infertility.  
It is not clear if mild endometriosis affects fertility.  

Endometriosis is almost always non-cancerous.  
It is extremely rare for it to turn into cancer.  

---

## What Are the Possible Consequences?

Severe endometriosis can affect many parts of life.  
Pain can make it hard to work, study, or enjoy activities.  
Some women miss school or work because of pain.  

Pain during sex can harm relationships.  
Chronic pain can cause fatigue, irritability, or sadness.  
Some women develop depression.  

It can be hard to plan a family.  
Some women may not be able to have children.  
This can be emotionally difficult for women and their partners.  

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Pelvic pain has many possible causes.  
Endometriosis is often diagnosed only after other causes are ruled out.  
It may be found when a woman has trouble getting pregnant.  

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms.  
They will do a physical exam and a gynecological check-up.  
If needed, they may recommend a laparoscopy.  
This is a small surgery where a doctor looks inside the abdomen.  
They can see endometrial lesions, scars, or cysts.  

Some women are diagnosed by chance.  
They go to the doctor for another reason, like not being able to get pregnant.  

Once diagnosed, most women feel relief.  
They know the condition is not cancer.  
Treatment can often reduce or stop the pain.  

---

## How Is It Treated?

There are several ways to manage endometriosis.  
Treatment depends on your symptoms, age, and whether you want to get pregnant.  

**Pain relief:**  
Painkillers can help with pain.  
They do not treat the cause.  

**Hormone treatments:**  
These can slow or stop the growth of endometrial tissue.  
They include birth control pills, hormone patches, or injections.  
They may stop periods or make them lighter.  

**Surgery:**  
This may be needed if the bowel, bladder, or other organs are affected.  
The goal is to remove all visible endometrial tissue.  
But new tissue can grow back after surgery.  

A decision aid from **gesundheitsinformation.de** can help you choose the right treatment.  

---

## What Is Rehabilitation Like?

After surgery or if symptoms continue, rehabilitation may help.  
Some clinics offer special programs for women with endometriosis.  
There are also certified endometriosis centers.  

These centers have teams of trained health professionals.  
They offer care tailored to your symptoms and life situation.  
They may include doctors, nurses, physiotherapists, and counselors.  

Rehabilitation can help you manage pain, improve your mood, and return to daily life.  

---

## What Is Life Like with Endometriosis?

Endometriosis can affect your relationships, family plans, and self-image.  
It can be hard to feel confident in your body.  
You may need to make changes in your daily routine.  

Good information helps you make choices.  
This includes choosing the right treatment and organizing your life.  
You can learn how to reduce pain and keep doing the things you enjoy.  

Doctors who know endometriosis well can give better care.  
They should understand both the physical and emotional impact.  
They should also know how it affects your social life.  

You are not alone.  
Stories from women with endometriosis and resources for partners are available at **gesundheitsinformation.de**.

# Tight Foreskin (Phimosis)

It is normal for baby boys to be born with a tight foreskin.  
The foreskin protects the sensitive head of the penis from rubbing, drying out, and germs.  
This tightness usually goes away on its own within the first few years of life.  
If it does not go away, treatment may be needed.

---

## Quick Facts

- A tight foreskin means the foreskin cannot be pulled back over the head of the penis.  
- It may cause pain when trying to pull it back.  
- About 96 out of 100 boys are born with a tight foreskin.  
- Most boys grow out of it without any treatment.  
- If treatment is needed, a doctor often prescribes a special ointment with cortisone.  
- This ointment is used for several weeks and usually works well.  

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself or your child.

---

## What Is a Tight Foreskin?

Some parents worry if they cannot pull back their baby’s foreskin.  
This is normal. Almost all baby boys are born with a tight foreskin.  
Sometimes, the foreskin sticks to the head of the penis.  
This is called adhesion.  
It is a natural protection for the sensitive head of the penis.  
It helps prevent irritation, drying, and infections in the first months of life.

The adhesion usually breaks on its own over time.  
The foreskin slowly becomes looser.  
It becomes easier to pull back without pain.  
Treatment is only needed if the foreskin stays tight after several years.

---

## What Are the Signs of a Tight Foreskin?

A tight foreskin is present if:
- The foreskin cannot be pulled back at all.  
- Pulling it back causes pain.  
- A balloon-like swelling appears under the foreskin when urinating.  
  This happens because urine gets trapped.  
  It is not dangerous and usually goes away on its own.

A tight foreskin usually does not cause problems in childhood.  
It may cause issues in older boys and men.  
Problems can include:
- Pain  
- Swelling  
- Redness  
- Inflammation  

These problems often happen during an erection.  
The penis gets bigger and harder.  
If the foreskin is too tight, it may not fit over the head.  
This can cause pain during masturbation or sex.

---

## What Causes a Tight Foreskin?

There are two main types:

**Primary phimosis:**  
This is when the foreskin stays tight after birth.  
It does not go away on its own.  
The exact cause is not known.

**Secondary phimosis:**  
This happens after scarring.  
Scarring can come from:
- Skin conditions  
- Repeated infections  
- Injuries  

For example, pulling the foreskin back too hard as a child can cause small tears.  
These tears can scar and lead to a tight foreskin later.

---

## How Common Is This?

- About 96 out of 100 boys are born with a tight foreskin.  
- By age seven, about half of boys still have a tight foreskin.  
- By age ten, about one in three boys still have it.  
- By the end of puberty, only about one in 100 boys still has primary phimosis.  
- The number of cases of secondary phimosis is not known.

---

## What Can Happen If It Is Not Treated?

A tight foreskin can lead to problems in older boys and men.  
They may have trouble cleaning under the foreskin.  
This can lead to bacteria or fungi building up.  
This may cause inflammation of the head of the penis or the foreskin.

Trying to force the foreskin back can cause small tears or injuries.  
In rare cases, this can lead to a serious condition called **paraphimosis**.  
This happens when the foreskin gets stuck behind the head of the penis.  
It can cut off blood flow.  
The tissue can die if not treated right away.

> **This is an emergency.**  
> Get medical help immediately.

Another rare problem is urine backing up in the urinary tract.  
This can happen if the foreskin becomes inflamed and swollen.  
The child may not be able to pee or only pees a little.  
If not treated quickly, the urine can go all the way back to the kidneys.  
This can damage the kidneys.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Parents often notice the foreskin cannot be pulled back in babies.  
Older children or teens usually notice it themselves.  
The doctor will ask questions and examine the penis.  
They will check if the tightness has been there since birth.  
They will also look for signs of scarring or skin conditions.  
The treatment plan depends on the cause and the child’s age.

---

## How Is It Treated?

- A tight foreskin in babies is normal.  
- No treatment is needed.  
- Do not try to force the foreskin back.  
  This can hurt the child and cause scarring.  
  Scarring can lead to a worse problem later.  
- Clean the outside of the penis with warm water and mild soap.  
  This is enough for hygiene.

If the foreskin stays tight and causes pain, see a doctor.  
The doctor will check if treatment is needed.

For children, the usual treatment is a cortisone ointment.  
It is applied to the foreskin every day.  
Treatment lasts several weeks.  
It usually works well.

If the ointment does not help, surgery may be an option.  
This is called circumcision.  
It is a common and safe procedure.

Surgery is recommended if:
- The foreskin keeps getting inflamed  
- The tightness is due to scarring  
- The foreskin gets stuck behind the head (paraphimosis)

Children have surgery under general anesthesia.  
Teens and adults may have it under local anesthesia.

For more information, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Cauliflower Ear

Cauliflower ear is a permanent change in the shape of the outer ear.  
It happens when the ear gets a hard blow and a bruise forms inside.  
If the bruise is not treated quickly, the ear can become lumpy and misshapen.  
The new shape looks like a piece of cauliflower.

This condition is common in people who play contact sports or practice martial arts.  
It can be avoided if the injury is treated right away.

---

## What Is Cauliflower Ear?

The outer ear is made of soft cartilage covered by skin.  
When the ear gets hit hard, the blood vessels can break.  
Blood then collects between the cartilage and the tissue around it.  
This is called a bruise or hematoma.

If the bruise is not treated, the cartilage loses its blood supply.  
Without blood, the cartilage can die and shrink.  
The body then replaces the damaged tissue with thick, hard scar tissue.  
This new tissue grows in lumps and folds.  
The ear becomes swollen and bumpy.

Wearing protective headgear can help prevent this injury.  
Cauliflower ear is mostly a cosmetic issue.  
Some people feel self-conscious about the look of their ear.  
Infections or tears in the ear are very rare.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The most obvious sign is a swollen, lumpy, and misshapen ear.  
Other signs may include:

- Pain in the ear  
- A red or bluish color on the ear  
- Swelling from fluid buildup

These symptoms usually appear soon after the injury.

---

## How Does It Happen?

Cauliflower ear usually starts with a strong hit to the ear.  
It is common in sports like rugby, wrestling, boxing, and martial arts.  
The impact damages the tissue around the cartilage.  
Blood leaks into the space between the cartilage and the covering layer.  
This causes a bruise to form.

If the bruise is not treated, the body starts to repair the area.  
It first builds soft tissue.  
Later, it forms new cartilage.  
This new growth changes the shape of the ear.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor will ask about the injury.  
They will want to know if you hit your ear recently.  
They will look at your ear for swelling, bruising, or changes in shape.  
They may also check for pain or tenderness.

In some cases, the doctor may order an ultrasound or a CT scan.  
These tests help rule out other injuries, like broken bones.

---

## How Is It Treated?

The best way to prevent cauliflower ear is to treat the bruise fast.  
If you injure your ear, do this right away:

- Apply cold to the area to reduce swelling.  
- Use a bandage to gently press on the ear.  
- Take pain medicine if needed.

A doctor can drain the blood from a small bruise using a needle.  
This is done with a local anesthetic to numb the area.

For larger bruises or ones that have been there for more than two days, surgery may be needed.  
The doctor will remove the blood and clots under local anesthetic.  
They will help the tissue around the cartilage reattach.  
This restores blood flow to the cartilage.

After surgery, a compression bandage is used.  
It holds the tissue in place.  
It also stops more blood from collecting and forming a new bruise.

---

**Important Note:**  
This information is not a substitute for medical care.  
Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.  
Always see a doctor if you injure your ear.

# Long COVID – What You Need to Know

Some people have health problems that last for weeks or months after having a COVID-19 infection. This is called long COVID.

## Quick Facts

- After a COVID-19 infection, some people have ongoing health issues.
- If symptoms last more than four weeks after infection, or if new symptoms appear at that time, it is called long COVID.
- If symptoms last more than 12 weeks, it is called post-COVID condition or post-COVID syndrome.
- There is no single set of symptoms for long COVID. The symptoms must not be explained by any other health problem.
- Many people with long COVID feel very tired and lack energy.
- People who had a severe case of COVID-19 are more likely to get long COVID than those with mild cases.
- Treatment focuses on easing symptoms and helping people live better.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Long COVID?

When someone gets infected with the virus that causes COVID-19, they may have health problems weeks or months later. This can happen after other infections too, like the flu.

If symptoms last more than four weeks after infection, or if new symptoms show up at that time, it is called long COVID. If symptoms last longer than 12 weeks and are either constant or keep coming back, it is called post-COVID condition.

The term “long COVID” includes both cases lasting 4 to 12 weeks and those lasting longer than 12 weeks. So we will use “long COVID” throughout this text.

Research shows that people who had a severe case of COVID-19 are more likely to develop long COVID. But even people with mild or no symptoms can develop long-term problems.

Long COVID can affect adults, children, and teens. It seems to be less common in children and teens. But we still know less about long-term effects in young people. More research is needed.

There is no standard pattern of symptoms for long COVID. People report many different physical and mental health issues. These problems can be so bad that they make daily life hard, affect work, and reduce quality of life.

To help people feel better and regain strength, early and proper medical care is very important.

---

## What Are the Symptoms of Long COVID?

Symptoms vary from person to person. They can happen alone or together. They may last for different times and range from mild to severe.

### Common Symptoms

- Feeling weak, tired, and unable to do normal activities
- Trouble focusing, memory problems (often called “brain fog”)
- Ongoing cough or shortness of breath

### Other Possible Symptoms

- Muscle weakness or pain
- Trouble sleeping or not feeling rested
- Feelings of sadness, low mood, or anxiety
- Loss or change in sense of smell or taste

Some people have lasting damage to their lungs or kidneys after a COVID-19 infection. Others may develop new health problems, such as:

- Heart or blood vessel diseases
- Diabetes
- Autoimmune diseases (where the body attacks itself)
- Nervous system problems

> **Important:** Many people with long COVID have much less energy than before. Some develop a condition called chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS), also known as myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME). With ME/CFS, even small physical or mental effort can make symptoms worse. This is called exertion intolerance.

---

## What Causes Long COVID?

We do not yet fully understand what causes long COVID. Experts believe several things may play a role, either alone or together.

Possible causes include:

- **Virus staying in the body:** Small parts of the virus may remain after the infection. These could cause ongoing inflammation.
- **Immune system overreaction:** The body’s defense system might attack its own tissues by mistake. This could lead to long-term symptoms.
- **Reactivation of another virus:** The Epstein Barr virus (EBV) can stay in the body for life. A weakened immune system after COVID-19 might reactivate it. This could trigger long COVID.
- **Tiny blood clots:** Some people with long COVID may have small clots in tiny blood vessels. These could block blood flow and cause damage.

---

## How Common Is Long COVID?

We do not yet know exactly how many people get long COVID. Studies have given different numbers because they used different methods and definitions.

Early studies (2020–2021) estimated that 6% to 15% of people had long COVID. More recent studies suggest it is less common. One large study from 2022 found that only 1% to just under 5% of people still had daily symptoms 12 weeks after infection.

The risk may depend on the virus variant. Long COVID seems less common after Omicron infection than with earlier versions.

Vaccination also seems to lower the risk of long COVID. But more research is needed to confirm this.

---

## What Increases the Risk of Long COVID?

Certain factors may raise your chance of getting long COVID:

- Being female
- Having a severe case of COVID-19
- Having certain pre-existing health conditions

Young adults appear to be more affected than children, teens, or older adults.

---

## What Is the Outlook for Long COVID?

Most people see their symptoms improve within a few months. But those who were hospitalized for severe COVID-19 tend to take longer to recover.

> **Good to know:** Long COVID has only been studied since 2020. Many questions remain. Scientists are still learning about causes, risk factors, and treatments.

For the latest research, visit the **Long COVID Initiative** website run by the Federal Ministry of Health.

---

## How Can I Prevent Long COVID?

The best way to avoid long COVID is to prevent getting infected with the virus that causes COVID-19.

Getting fully vaccinated against COVID-19 may also reduce the risk and severity of long COVID.

Vaccination might help people who already had COVID-19 and are now showing long-term symptoms. But this has not been proven yet.

You can check your immunity level using the **“Corona-Impfcheck”** tool from the Federal Center for Health Education.

More information about vaccination is available at **www.infektionsschutz.de**.

> **Interesting fact:** In rare cases, people report symptoms like long COVID after getting a vaccine. This is sometimes called “post-vac syndrome.” There is no clear evidence yet. For more info, visit the **Long COVID Initiative** website.

---

## How Is Long COVID Diagnosed?

There is no single test for long COVID. Doctors must rule out other possible causes first.

Diagnosis is based on symptoms and medical history. It can be hard because:

- Symptoms vary widely
- No lab test can confirm long COVID
- Some people had no symptoms during the original infection
- Some did not get tested at the time

### Step-by-Step Diagnosis

If you think you have long COVID, see your family doctor or pediatrician (for children or teens).

The doctor will ask:

- What symptoms you had during the original illness
- What symptoms you still have now
- If any new health problems have developed
