- If any symptoms were worse after the infection

They will also ask how your symptoms affect your daily life, work, and mental health.

They may check for signs of depression or anxiety.

Depending on your symptoms, the doctor may order:

- Blood tests
- Heart tests (ECG)
- X-rays

> **Important:** A specialist may be needed to check for organ damage or rule out other illnesses. Special clinics for long COVID are available in hospitals.

For help finding a clinic or support, call the **Long COVID Initiative phone line** or visit their website.

---

## How Is Long COVID Treated?

There is no cure for long COVID. Treatment focuses on easing symptoms and improving quality of life.

### Treatment Options

- Regular check-ups with a doctor
- Physical therapy (to improve strength and breathing)
- Occupational therapy (to help with daily tasks and thinking)
- Speech and language therapy (for speaking or swallowing issues)
- Psychotherapy (to support mental health)
- Pain management
- Nutrition advice
- Medication for specific symptoms

> **Good to know:** Many people with long COVID feel extremely tired. Some get worse after even light activity — this is called a “crash.” Learning to pace yourself can help. Pacing means planning your activities to use your energy carefully and avoid overdoing things.

It is also important to learn how to manage your illness in daily life. Trained professionals can give you personalized advice.

---

## What Rehabilitation Options Are Available?

Rehabilitation by a team of specialists can help you regain strength and energy.

Rehab can be done:

- In a hospital (inpatient)
- At a clinic (outpatient)

Depending on your needs, you may also get help with returning to work or daily routines.

Costs may be covered by health insurance, pension funds, or other providers.

Use the **rehab responsibility navigator** from the Federal Association for Rehabilitation to find out who pays.

For more information, visit:

- The **German pension insurance organization** (Deutsche Rentenversicherung)
- The **Federal Ministry for Labor and Social Affairs**

### Long COVID as an Occupational Disease

In some cases, long COVID may be recognized as an occupational disease or accident. If you think this applies to you, contact your insurance provider to ask about rehabilitation support.

## Where Can I Get Support for Daily Life?

Self-help groups offer a place to share experiences, get advice, and learn from others with long COVID.

# Macular Degeneration

Your eyesight usually gets worse as you get older. Some diseases can make this worse. One of these is macular degeneration. It makes things look blurry and twisted when you look at them directly. Reading becomes harder.

## Quick Facts

- Macular degeneration is a long-term condition. It starts because of a problem in how the body uses energy.
- It usually affects both eyes.
- It mainly harms your ability to see clearly in the center of your vision.
- Doctors do not yet know the exact cause.
- It is more common in older people.  
  - About 1 in 100 people aged 65 to 75 have it.  
  - Between 10 and 20 out of 100 people over 85 have it.
- Macular degeneration does not usually cause total blindness.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Macular Degeneration?

As you age, your eyesight naturally gets worse. Some diseases can make this worse. One of these is macular degeneration.

Macular degeneration is a long-term condition. It starts in the center of the retina. This part is called the macula. The macula helps you see fine details. It helps you read, drive, and recognize faces.

There are two types: dry and wet.  
- Dry macular degeneration is more common. It gets worse slowly.  
- Wet macular degeneration causes vision loss faster.  

There is no cure for either type.  
But treatment for the wet form can help. It can stop vision loss. In some cases, it can even improve vision. Treatment can slow down the disease.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Macular degeneration slowly harms your central vision. This is the part of your sight that lets you see things clearly when you look straight at them.

The macula is in the center of the back of your eye. It helps you do daily tasks like reading and recognizing people.

When the macula is damaged, things you look at directly may look blurry or bent.  
In later stages, you may not see things in the center of your vision at all.  
But you may still see things at the edges of your vision. You just can’t make them out clearly.

## What Causes Macular Degeneration?

Doctors do not yet know the exact cause of macular degeneration.  
It may be linked to problems in the cells that sense light in the retina.

Your body makes waste during normal cell activity. Normally, your body breaks this down. But sometimes, it does not. This waste builds up under the retina. These deposits are called drusen. They look yellow. They stop the retina from getting enough nutrients.

The type of macular degeneration affects how it develops:

- In dry macular degeneration, the light-sensitive cells in the retina die. The area under the retina may also change color.
- In wet macular degeneration, the body tries to fix the damage by growing new blood vessels under the retina. These new vessels are weak. They can leak blood and fluid into the retina. This harms the cells. The new blood vessels can also push the retina up.

If you have a close family member with macular degeneration, you are more likely to get it.  
Smoking increases your risk. It also makes the disease appear earlier.  
It is not yet clear if being in strong sunlight without eye protection raises your risk.

## How Common Is Macular Degeneration?

Most people develop macular degeneration as they age.  
- About 1 in 100 people aged 65 to 75 have it.  
- Between 10 and 20 out of 100 people over 85 have it.

Dry macular degeneration is more common than the wet form.

## How Does It Progress?

Macular degeneration can develop in different ways. It usually goes through these stages:

- **Early stage:** You have medium-sized drusen. No color changes. No vision problems.
- **Intermediate stage:** You have large drusen or color changes. Some people have mild vision problems.
- **Late stage:** You have dry or wet macular degeneration. Vision is clearly affected.

The type of macular degeneration affects how fast it gets worse.  
- Dry macular degeneration gets worse slowly. Vision problems happen less often.  
- Wet macular degeneration is usually found in the late stage. It can get worse quickly.

The size of the drusen affects how fast vision problems appear in the late stage.

> **Important:** Dry macular degeneration can turn into wet macular degeneration.  
> If wet macular degeneration is not treated, it can get worse fast.  
> Getting treatment early can stop or slow it down.

Macular degeneration does not usually cause total blindness.  
In advanced cases, you may lose the ability to read or recognize faces.  
But even if both eyes are affected, most people can still move around.  
If your vision is very poor, you may be considered legally blind.  
You may then qualify for special support and benefits.

## Can It Be Prevented?

Not smoking lowers your risk of macular degeneration.  
Smokers have a higher risk.

Some people take dietary supplements like beta carotene, vitamins, zinc, omega-3 fatty acids, or ginkgo biloba.  
But studies have not proven these help prevent macular degeneration.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will first check your symptoms. They will also rule out other eye problems.

They will use a special microscope with a bright light to look at the front and middle parts of your eye.

To see the back of your eye, your doctor will put drops in your eyes. These make your pupils wider. This lets them see the retina better.

You will also do vision tests. These check how well you see in the center of your vision.

To confirm the diagnosis and plan treatment, your doctor may do more tests.

If wet macular degeneration is suspected, they may do a fluorescein angiography.  
A safe dye is injected into your arm. It travels to the blood vessels in your retina. A special camera takes pictures of the blood vessels. This shows if there are leaks or abnormal vessels.

Another test uses a laser to measure the thickness of the retina. This is called optical coherence tomography, or OCT.  
It can show if fluid has built up.  
OCT helps doctors track the disease over time. It also helps them adjust treatment.

## How Is It Treated?

There is no effective treatment for dry macular degeneration yet.

For wet macular degeneration, there are four main treatments:

- Medication  
- Laser treatment  
- Surgery  
- Other options

### Medication

This is the most important treatment.  
Doctors use drugs called VEGF inhibitors.  
VEGF is a substance that helps grow new blood vessels.  
The drugs block VEGF. They are injected into the eye.  
This stops new blood vessels from forming.  
The treatment does not cure macular degeneration.  
But it can stop it from getting worse. In some cases, vision may even improve.

### Laser Treatment

This uses a strong beam of light to burn and destroy abnormal blood vessels.  
It is only used in a few people with wet macular degeneration.  
It is less effective than medication. It also has more side effects.

### Surgery

In rare cases, when other treatments do not work, surgery may be used to treat the new blood vessels.

### Other Options

Studies have not proven that supplements like vitamin C, vitamin E, zinc, copper, lutein, zeaxanthin, or beta carotene prevent macular degeneration.  
But for people with large drusen, these supplements may help slow the disease when used with certain medicines.

For more information on treating macular degeneration, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

# Wisdom Teeth

## What Are Wisdom Teeth?

Wisdom teeth are the last teeth in each row of teeth. They sit at the very back of your mouth.

Most people do not fully develop their wisdom teeth until they are between 18 and 24 years old.

These teeth only break through the gums once they are fully grown. Some people never get their wisdom teeth to come through at all.

Many people feel pain or discomfort from their wisdom teeth. This happens because there is often not enough room in the mouth for them.

Wisdom teeth are leftover from our ancestors. They had bigger jaws and needed more teeth to chew tough food.

Today, most people have smaller jaws. This means there is not enough space for wisdom teeth. But not all wisdom teeth cause problems.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for a doctor’s visit. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## Do All People Have Wisdom Teeth?

Most people have four wisdom teeth — two in the top jaw and two in the bottom jaw.

But not everyone gets all four. In about 8 out of 10 young adults, at least one wisdom tooth stays inside the jaw.

Sometimes, a wisdom tooth only comes partway through the gum. The top part (crown) may still be covered by gum tissue.

---

## What Problems Can Wisdom Teeth Cause?

If a wisdom tooth does not come through fully, it can cause pain, swelling, or gum infections.

It can also push against nearby teeth. This may damage those teeth.

The area around a partially erupted tooth can trap food and bacteria. This raises the risk of tooth decay.

Even when wisdom teeth do come through, they can cause issues. They may grow in at an angle. They can push other teeth out of place.

They may also cause inflammation or other problems.

---

## How Do Dentists Decide If Wisdom Teeth Are a Problem?

If you think your wisdom teeth are causing trouble, see your dentist.

The dentist will ask you about your symptoms. They will look inside your mouth and check your jaw.

They will take an X-ray. This shows the exact position of the wisdom teeth and how they are growing.

With this information, the dentist can decide if the wisdom teeth are likely to cause problems.

---

## How Are Problematic Wisdom Teeth Treated?

If wisdom teeth are causing pain or other issues, they are usually removed.

The type of treatment depends on whether the tooth has broken through the gum or is still inside the jaw.

If the tooth is still under the gum, surgery may be needed.

In the past, dentists often removed wisdom teeth even if they were not causing any problems.

Today, dentists only recommend removal if there is a clear problem or a likely future problem.

For more details about when wisdom teeth should be removed, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

# Lacrimal Duct Diseases

This article explains problems with the tear system. It covers blocked tear ducts and inflamed tear glands. You will learn about symptoms and treatments.

---

## Quick Facts

- Doctors call a blocked tear duct **dacryostenosis**.
- When the tear duct is blocked, tears cannot drain into the nose properly.
- About 6 out of every 100 babies are born with a blocked tear duct.
- Most babies get better within a few months if they get treatment, especially gentle massage.
- Inflammation of the tear gland is called **dacryoadenitis**.
- Causes can be bacteria, viruses, or other illnesses. Sometimes the cause is unknown.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Are Lacrimal Duct Diseases?

The tear system helps keep your eyes wet and clean. It includes:

- The **tear gland** – sits above your eye, makes tears.
- **Tear points** – small openings in each eyelid that collect tears.
- **Tear ducts** – tubes that carry tears from the eye to the nose.
- The **tear sac** – a small pouch that holds tears before they go into the nose.

Problems can happen in this system. They can be:

- Present at birth – called **congenital lacrimal duct obstruction**.
- Caused by infection – like bacteria or viruses.
- Due to injury or a foreign object blocking the duct.
- With no clear cause – called **idiopathic**.

About 6% of babies are born with a blocked tear duct. But some people develop it later in life, often after an infection.

A tear gland infection can happen after an eye infection. It can also be linked to other illnesses, like glandular fever (caused by the Epstein-Barr virus).

> **Important:** Acute (sudden) tear gland inflammation usually hurts. Chronic (long-term) inflammation usually does not hurt.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on the cause and where the problem is.

### Signs of a Blocked Tear Duct (Born with It)

- Eyes water all the time.
- A small bump near the inner corner of the eye may appear.
- Pressing on the bump may push out a clear or cloudy fluid.

> **Important:** A blocked tear duct can lead to an infection in the tear sac. This is called **dacryocystitis**. It causes pain, swelling, and fever. In babies, this is an emergency. It needs fast treatment.

### Signs of an Acute Tear Gland Infection

- Redness and swelling on the outer side of the upper eyelid.
- The eyelid may droop.
- Pus may form if bacteria are the cause.
- Tears flow constantly.
- Scabs may form on the eyelid.
- Swollen lymph nodes near the ear.
- Fever and feeling unwell.
- Often, there is also **conjunctivitis** (pink eye).

### Signs of a Chronic Tear Gland Infection

- A slow-growing lump on one or both upper outer eyelids.
- No pain.
- The lump grows over weeks or months.

---

## What Causes These Problems?

The cause depends on whether the duct is blocked or the gland is inflamed.

### Why Babies Are Born with a Blocked Tear Duct

- A thin membrane blocks the tear duct near the nose.
- This is called **Hasner’s fold**.
- It should open after birth, but sometimes it does not.
- This stops tears from draining into the nose.

### Why the Tear Gland Gets Inflamed (Acute)

- Usually caused by a virus or bacteria.
- Germs can enter through the eye, skin, or a small cut.
- Some infections spread through the blood.
- Common causes:
  - Influenza virus
  - Epstein-Barr virus (glandular fever)
  - Mumps virus
  - Chickenpox virus (varicella zoster)
  - Certain bacteria
  - Rarely, some fungi

### Why the Tear Gland Gets Inflamed Over Time (Chronic)

- Often linked to other long-term health problems, such as:
  - Sarcoidosis (a lung disease)
  - Wegener’s disease (a blood vessel disease)
  - Crohn’s disease (a gut disease)
- In many cases, doctors cannot find a clear cause.

---

## How Common Are These Problems?

- About 6% of babies are born with a blocked tear duct.
- This is the most common reason for constant watery eyes in babies and young children.
- Tear gland infections are rare.
- They mostly happen in children, teens, and young adults.
- Chronic tear gland inflammation is more common in women.
- This is because women are more likely to have autoimmune diseases.

---

## How Are These Problems Diagnosed?

Doctors can often spot the problem during a simple exam.

### For a Blocked Tear Duct in Babies

- Parents tell the doctor about watery eyes.
- The doctor checks the eyes and rules out other eye issues.
- A test called the **Schirmer’s test** may be used.
  - A small paper strip is placed under the eyelid.
  - It measures how many tears are made.
- If needed, the doctor may use a tiny needle to check if fluid is stuck in the duct.

### For Tear Gland Inflammation

- If the swelling is due to a virus, no extra tests are usually needed.
- Doctors may do more tests if:
  - The cause is unclear.
  - They are not sure if it is a tear gland problem or something else.
  - Treatment is not working.
  - The person is older.
  - Both eyes are affected.

Tests may include:

- Blood tests to check for signs of autoimmune disease.
- MRI scans to see if the gland is enlarged or changed.
- A biopsy – a small tissue sample is taken and tested.

---

## How Are These Problems Treated?

Treatment depends on the type of problem.

### Treating a Blocked Tear Duct in Babies

- Keep the eye clean.
- Gently massage the tear duct area several times a day.
- Parents can learn how to do this from a doctor.
- Most babies get better within weeks or months.

- If pus builds up, it means bacteria are growing.
  - The doctor will prescribe antibiotics.
  - These kill the bacteria.

- If the blockage lasts past six months:
  - The doctor may use a thin probe or needle to flush the duct.
  - This clears the blockage.

- If massage, medicine, and flushing do not work:
  - Surgery may be needed.
  - The doctor makes a new path from the tear sac to the nose.
  - This lets tears drain even if the duct is still blocked.

### Treating an Acute Tear Gland Infection

- If caused by a virus: the infection usually gets better on its own in 4 to 6 weeks.
- If caused by bacteria: take antibiotics.
  - These kill the bacteria.
- If a pus-filled lump (abscess) forms:
  - A small surgery may be needed to drain it.
- Doctors may prescribe corticosteroids.
  - These reduce swelling and inflammation.

### Treating a Chronic Tear Gland Infection

- The inflammation is often linked to another long-term illness.
- Treating the main illness helps the tear gland problem.
- Corticosteroids are used to reduce swelling.
  - These are anti-inflammatory medicines.

> **Always follow your doctor’s advice. Do not start or stop treatment without talking to a healthcare provider.**

# Schizophrenia – Simple Explanation

Schizophrenia is a mental health condition. It causes changes in how a person sees reality. These changes happen in episodes or phases.

During these phases, a person may:
- Believe things that are not true (delusions).
- Hear voices that others do not hear.
- Feel like someone is watching them or controlling their thoughts.

These episodes can be very upsetting. They can make it hard to think clearly or act normally.

---

## What Is Schizophrenia?

Schizophrenia means “split mind.” But this does not mean a person has two personalities.

It is a common misunderstanding. People with schizophrenia do not split into two people. Their personality stays the same.

Instead, they go through times when their thinking and feelings are very different from what is real. They may act strangely or stop talking in a clear way.

These episodes are usually temporary. Some people only have one episode in their life. Others have many episodes over time.

The exact cause of schizophrenia is not known. But doctors believe it comes from a mix of factors.

---

## Symptoms of Schizophrenia

There are different types of schizophrenia. They are based on the main symptoms a person has.

### Paranoid Schizophrenia
- The person has strong false beliefs (delusions).
- They may hear voices or feel watched or controlled.
- This is the most common type.
- It usually starts between ages 25 and 35.

### Residual Schizophrenia
- The person has ongoing symptoms after a major episode.
- They may feel very tired, slow, or sad.
- They may have trouble focusing or remembering things.

### Disorganized (Hebephrenic) Schizophrenia
- The person’s emotions do not match the situation.
- They may laugh when something is sad or cry when something is funny.
- Their thoughts and actions are confused or strange.
- This usually starts between ages 15 and 25.

### Catatonic Schizophrenia
- This is rare.
- The person may move too much for no reason.
- Or they may not move at all, even when asked.
- They may make strange faces.
- It usually starts between ages 15 and 25.

---

### Early Signs of a Psychotic Episode

Before a full episode, people may notice changes weeks or months earlier. These can include:
- Feeling stressed or restless.
- Trouble sleeping.
- Difficulty concentrating.
- Memory problems.
- Feeling like someone is watching or controlling them.
- Mild hearing voices or strange thoughts.

Some people also start to care less about their appearance. They may pull away from friends and family.

---

## What Causes Schizophrenia?

Doctors do not know the exact cause. But several things may increase the risk:

- A family history of schizophrenia. If a parent or sibling has it, the risk is higher.
- About 12 out of every 100 children with a parent who has schizophrenia will also develop it.
- Changes in the brain.
- Long-term sleep problems (insomnia).
- Using drugs like cannabis or amphetamines.
- Traumatic events (like abuse or accidents).
- High levels of stress.
- Problems during pregnancy or early childhood development.

Major life changes — like divorce, moving, or starting a new job — can also trigger an episode.

A home life with constant criticism or strict rules may also raise the risk.

---

## How Common Is Schizophrenia?

About 5 out of every 1,000 people will develop schizophrenia in their lifetime.

Men are slightly more likely to get it than women.

It is more common in people who are socially isolated or single. But being alone or poor is often a result of the illness, not the cause.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

The first episode usually happens between ages 15 and 35.

Some people have warning signs for years before the first episode. These can include:
- Feeling down or depressed.
- Mood swings.
- Feeling unsure about themselves.
- Trouble focusing.
- Anxiety.
- Problems at school or work.

Many people in early stages stop taking care of their appearance. They may also avoid friends and family.

### How Often Do Episodes Happen?

- About 1 in 4 people with schizophrenia only have one episode.
- About 60 out of 100 people have another episode within two years of the first.
- An episode can last weeks or months.

Even after symptoms go away, the person may still feel shaken. They may struggle with confidence or feel damaged by what happened.

Some people return to normal life quickly. Others need long-term support.

### Life Expectancy

People with schizophrenia live about 15 years less than others.

This is often due to:
- More frequent use of alcohol, nicotine, or drugs.
- Higher risk of infections, heart disease, or diabetes.

These health problems can come from lifestyle choices or side effects of medication.

But if the illness is treated well, life expectancy improves.

About 5 out of every 100 people with schizophrenia die by suicide. This is more common in young men who are having their first episode or in those with long-term severe illness.

High-risk times include:
- When symptoms are not treated.
- Right after leaving the hospital.

---

## How Is Schizophrenia Diagnosed?

A doctor will only diagnose schizophrenia if symptoms last for more than one month.

They pay more attention to:
- False beliefs (delusions).
- Hearing voices that are not real.

They pay less attention to:
- Confused speech.
- Unexplained restlessness.
- Hallucinations that are not voices.

To make a diagnosis, doctors:
- Talk to the person.
- Talk to family or close friends.
- Watch how the person acts.

They also do physical and brain checks to rule out other causes.

Other conditions can cause similar symptoms, such as:
- Brain disorders.
- Alcohol or drug use.
- Depression.
- Anxiety disorders.

It can be hard to tell the difference between normal teenage behavior and early signs of schizophrenia.

Because of this, a specialist psychiatrist must carefully evaluate the person.

---

## How Is Schizophrenia Treated?

Treatment should focus on the person’s needs. But this is harder during the first episode.

Once the episode ends, treatment can be planned together with the person.

Fast and effective treatment improves the chances of recovery.

### Treatment and Support Options

- **Support from family and friends:** Emotional help, daily support, and stability.
- **Medication:** Antipsychotic drugs can reduce symptoms and lower the chance of future episodes. But they can cause side effects.
- **Psychotherapy:** Helps reduce symptoms and improve coping. Types include:
  - Cognitive behavioral therapy.
  - Family therapy.
  - This can help even during a crisis.
- **Psychoeducation:** Teaches the person and their family about the illness, treatment, and how to manage it. It also offers a chance to share experiences with others.
- **Sociotherapy:** Helps people return to work, school, or social life. It can also reduce symptoms.

For more information on medication and therapy, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

### Hospital Treatment for Severe Episodes

Some people need to stay in a hospital during a serious episode.

They may not realize they are unwell. They may refuse help.

In rare cases, doctors can admit them to hospital against their will. This is only allowed if:
- They are at serious risk to themselves (like suicidal thoughts).
- Or they are a danger to others (like violent behavior).
- And no other way to keep them safe exists.

### Treatment Agreements

People with schizophrenia can make a plan with doctors in advance.

This plan can say:
- What to do if they have another episode.
- How medication should be given.
- How to handle hospital admission if needed.
- What kind of support they want.

It is also a good idea to write:
- An advance health care directive (living will).
- A lasting power of attorney for health and welfare.

These documents say who can make decisions if the person cannot.

---

## Where Can I Get Help?

If you or someone you know may have schizophrenia, start with the family doctor.

The **Telefonseelsorge** crisis hotline offers free support for people in crisis. They can help connect you to other services.

Other support services are also available.

To find a therapist:
- Visit the website of the **Federal Association of Psychotherapists**.
- Use their therapist search tool.

To find a specialist doctor:
- Contact the **appointment service centers** of the Associations of Statutory Health Insurance Physicians.

These centers can help you make an appointment with a psychiatrist or psychotherapist.

# Severe Menstrual Bleeding

Some women feel very tired, unwell, or in pain during their period. Heavy bleeding is often the cause. This kind of bleeding can be treated with medicine or surgery.

## Quick Facts

- About 10 out of every 100 women have very heavy periods.
- Medicine or surgery can help reduce heavy bleeding.
- Losing too much blood during your period can lead to low iron levels. This can cause anemia.
- The most common reason for heavy bleeding is that the womb does not tighten properly.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Severe Menstrual Bleeding?

Many women have cramps, pain, or heavy bleeding during their period. If you need to change your pad or tampon every 1 to 2 hours, or if your menstrual cup needs emptying every few hours, your bleeding may be heavier than normal.

If the bleeding makes daily life hard or leaves you weak, it is called severe menstrual bleeding. Doctors call this *hypermenorrhea*.

About 10 out of 100 women have this condition. If your period lasts longer than 5 to 7 days, it is called prolonged bleeding, or *menorrhagia*. These two often happen together because they have the same cause.

Some women manage heavy bleeding on their own. But if it causes low iron or is too disruptive, treatment can help. Medicine or surgery are options.

---

## What Are the Signs of Severe Menstrual Bleeding?

On average, a woman loses about 60 milliliters of blood during her period. That is about one and a half shot glasses.

Most women need to change their pad or tampon every 4 hours. But this varies. Some days may be heavier than others.

If you lose more than 80 milliliters of blood in total during your period, doctors consider it severe.

Watch for these signs:

- You need to change your pad or tampon every 1 to 2 hours.
- You have to empty your menstrual cup every few hours.
- You feel weak, tired, or sluggish during your period.
- Your period blood has large, thick clots.

---

## What Causes Severe Menstrual Bleeding?

Some girls are born with heavy periods. But most women start having heavy bleeding later in life.

Hormonal changes, such as those around menopause, can also make bleeding worse.

The most common cause is that the womb does not tighten properly. Normally, the womb tightens to push out the lining. This helps stop bleeding from lasting too long.

But if the womb does not tighten well, bleeding can become heavy.

Fibroids and polyps can block the womb from tightening.

- Fibroids grow in the muscle wall of the womb.
- Polyps grow in the lining of the womb (called the endometrium).
- A contraceptive coil (IUD) can also interfere with the womb’s ability to tighten.

Other causes include growths on the womb or infections in the womb or fallopian tubes. In some cases, doctors cannot find a clear cause.

---

## What Problems Can Severe Bleeding Cause?

Losing too much blood during your period can lead to low iron levels. Iron is needed to make red blood cells.

When iron is low, your body cannot make enough red blood cells. This can lead to anemia.

Red blood cells carry oxygen to your organs. If you have too few, your organs do not get enough oxygen. This causes:

- Feeling weak or tired
- Pale skin
- Cold hands

With more severe anemia, you may also feel short of breath or have a fast heartbeat, especially when you move.

---

## How Is Severe Menstrual Bleeding Diagnosed?

Doctors first want to know how much blood you are losing. They cannot measure it exactly, but they can estimate it.

You can help by tracking:

- How many pads or tampons you use each day
- How often you empty your menstrual cup

Keep a record for one or two months. This helps your doctor understand the problem.

Your doctor will examine your womb. They will feel it and use an ultrasound scan.

In some cases, a hysteroscopy is needed. This means a small camera is gently put into the womb to look inside.

A blood test checks for anemia. It also checks hormone levels that affect your period and womb lining.

Your doctor will also ask about your health history. This includes:

- Other medical conditions
- Family health history
- Medicines you take
- Weight issues
- Stress or mental health

All of this helps find the cause.

---

## How Is Severe Menstrual Bleeding Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause.

- Fibroids, polyps, or other growths can be removed with surgery.
- Many women first try medicine to reduce bleeding.
- Some painkillers can help reduce bleeding a little.

Hormonal birth control, like the pill or a hormonal IUD, can help. These stop the womb lining from growing too much.

If symptoms are very bad and you do not want to have children, your doctor may suggest:

- Removing or shrinking the womb lining (called endometrial resection or ablation)
- Removing the entire womb (hysterectomy)

A hysterectomy is major surgery. It is only done when other treatments do not work.

> **Important:** If you do not have anemia and your bleeding does not affect your life, treatment may not be needed.

Before choosing treatment, talk to your doctor. Learn about the benefits and risks of medicine and surgery.

Your choice depends on whether you want to have children in the future.

- The pill and hormonal IUD stop you from getting pregnant while you use them.
- After a hysterectomy, you can never get pregnant.

The decision aid from [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de) can help you choose the right treatment.

---

## How Does Severe Menstrual Bleeding Affect Daily Life?

Many women feel tired and foggy during and right after their period.

If symptoms are very bad, daily tasks become hard. This includes work, housework, or caring for children.

Even fun activities like going out with friends or doing hobbies can feel stressful.

You may need to change pads, tampons, or your menstrual cup many times at night. This can break your sleep.

You may also have strong stomach pain.

Heavy bleeding is not just hard on the body. It can also be embarrassing.

It can be uncomfortable during sex. Some women feel scared by how much blood they lose.

> **Important:** Some people, even doctors, may not take heavy periods seriously. But you do not have to suffer through this.

Rest when you can. Seek medical help. Find a treatment that works for you.

Menstruation is a normal part of life. But if heavy bleeding harms your well-being, help is available. You can feel better and live more comfortably.

# Zinc Deficiency

Zinc is a mineral your body needs to stay healthy.  
Your body cannot make zinc.  
You must get it from the food you eat.

A balanced diet usually gives you enough zinc.  
But some people may not get enough.  
This can happen if you eat a very limited diet.  
It can also happen if you have long-term bowel problems.

---

## Quick Facts

- Zinc is a vital mineral.  
- You must get zinc from food.  
- Most people get enough zinc from their daily meals.  
- Not eating enough zinc-rich foods can cause a deficiency.  
- Long-term bowel diseases can also cause a deficiency.  
- Some medicines can affect zinc levels.  
- Symptoms may include skin changes, more infections, diarrhea, hair loss, and slow growth in children.  
- If you are low in zinc, your doctor may recommend a zinc supplement.  
- Always talk to your doctor before starting any supplement.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Zinc Deficiency?

Zinc helps your body grow.  
It helps your cells divide and heal wounds.  
It supports your immune system.  
It also helps your body process fats and sugars.

Good sources of zinc include:
- Red meat
- Seafood
- Dairy products
- Whole grains
- Nuts like cashews
- Legumes like lentils

Your small intestine absorbs zinc from food.  
It then moves into your blood and tissues.

A zinc deficiency can happen if:
- You do not eat enough zinc-rich foods.
- Your gut cannot absorb zinc well. This can happen with long-term bowel diseases.
- You lose too much fluid. This can happen with severe diarrhea.

Severe zinc deficiency is rare in Germany and other parts of Europe.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Mild zinc deficiency can cause:
- Weaker immunity (more frequent colds or infections)
- Trouble tasting or smelling food
- Night blindness (trouble seeing in low light)
- Dry skin or mild skin irritation
- Changes in your nails

Severe deficiency causes more serious symptoms:
- Red, flaky skin with blisters around the mouth, anus, elbows, knees, knuckles, and ankles
- More frequent infections
- Diarrhea
- Hair loss
- Slow growth in children
- Wounds that heal slowly
- Feeling tired all the time
- Sensitivity to light
- Loss of appetite

> **Important:** Some babies are born with a rare condition called congenital acrodermatitis enteropathica.  
> These babies cannot absorb zinc properly, even while breastfeeding.  
> Symptoms usually appear between 4 and 6 weeks after stopping breast milk.

---

## What Causes Zinc Deficiency?

You may not get enough zinc if:
- You follow a very restrictive diet.
- You eat mostly plant-based foods without variety.
- You eat a lot of legumes, nuts, or whole grains. These contain phytate, which blocks zinc absorption.

Long-term bowel diseases like ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s disease can stop your gut from absorbing zinc.

Other causes include:
- Severe diarrhea (you lose zinc in your stool)
- Drinking too much alcohol (your body gets rid of more zinc in urine)
- Some medicines, such as certain antibiotics and diuretics (water pills)

A rare genetic condition called congenital acrodermatitis enteropathica stops the gut from absorbing zinc.

---

## How Can You Prevent Zinc Deficiency?

Zinc is especially important during pregnancy, infancy, and childhood.  
But you do not need to take a supplement unless your doctor says so.

Breast milk, baby food, and a balanced diet usually provide enough zinc.

If you follow a vegan diet:
- Eat plenty of zinc-rich plant foods.
- Good choices include whole grains, legumes, nuts, soy products, and wheat or rye germ.

> **Important:** Whole grains and legumes contain phytate, which reduces zinc absorption.  
> But you can reduce phytate by:
> - Soaking the food before cooking
> - Germinating (sprouting) the seeds or grains
> - Fermenting (like in sourdough bread)

These steps help your body absorb more zinc.

---

## How Is Zinc Deficiency Diagnosed?

If you have symptoms of zinc deficiency, your doctor may test your blood.

But blood tests are not always clear.  
Zinc levels can be normal even if you are low in zinc.  
Also, zinc levels drop during infections — even if you are not actually deficient.

So, your doctor will look at your symptoms and medical history, not just the test result.

---

## How Is Zinc Deficiency Treated?

If your doctor confirms a zinc deficiency, they may prescribe a zinc supplement.

You may also get a supplement if your doctor suspects a deficiency.

You take the supplement every day for several weeks.  
The length of treatment depends on how bad the deficiency is and what caused it.

Most people feel better within 1 to 2 weeks of starting treatment.

For people with congenital acrodermatitis enteropathica:
- Zinc tablets are the main treatment.
- They must take the supplement for life.
- This is because their body cannot absorb zinc properly.

# Trigeminal Neuralgia

Trigeminal neuralgia causes sudden, severe pain on one side of the face.  
Simple actions like sneezing, chewing, or a cold breeze can set off the pain.  
Medicine, surgery, or radiation therapy can help reduce the pain.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical care.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Trigeminal Neuralgia?

Trigeminal neuralgia means you have sharp, intense pain on one side of your face.  
The pain comes from irritation of a nerve in your face called the trigeminal nerve.  
This nerve sends signals about touch and pain from your face to your brain.

The trigeminal nerve covers these areas:  
- The forehead and eyes  
- The upper and lower jaws  
- The lips and cheeks  

The pain only happens on one side of the face.  
You may have times with no pain, followed by times when the pain comes back often.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

You feel sudden, sharp pain in your face.  
The pain usually hits the middle and lower parts of your face.  
It often feels worst around the jaw and cheeks.

You may go through periods with no pain.  
Then, the pain returns again and again.  
Over time, the pain attacks may happen closer together.  
Some people also feel a constant dull ache.

The pain may come with a headache.  
Other signs include:  
- Red eyes  
- Small pupils  
- Watery eyes  
- A stuffy or runny nose  
- Swollen eyelid  
- Drooping eyelid

---

## What Causes Trigeminal Neuralgia?

In most cases, a blood vessel near the nerve presses on it.  
This pressure damages the nerve’s protective covering.  
When this happens, the nerve sends pain signals even when it shouldn’t.

This is called **classic** or **primary** trigeminal neuralgia.

Sometimes, another health problem causes the nerve to be irritated.  
This is called **secondary** or **symptomatic** trigeminal neuralgia.  
Causes include:  
- Multiple sclerosis  
- Tumors pressing on the nerve  
- Diseases that affect connective tissue  
- Birth defects in blood vessels

If doctors cannot find a cause for the pain, it is called **idiopathic** trigeminal neuralgia.

Pain attacks can happen at random.  
They can also be triggered by:  
- Touching your face  
- Chewing  
- Brushing your teeth  
- A cool breeze

Many people first see a dentist because they think the pain is from a tooth.  
The nerve that controls feeling in the jaw is often the one affected.

---

## How Common Is It?

Trigeminal neuralgia is rare.  
It affects between 4 and 27 people out of every 100,000 each year.  
It is more common in women than in men.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Trigeminal neuralgia comes in waves.  
You may have long periods with no pain.  
Then, you may have frequent attacks.  
It is hard to predict when an attack will happen.

Some people have daily attacks for weeks or months.  
Then, they may have a long break with no pain.  
Over time, attacks often become more frequent.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms.  
They will want to know how long the pain lasts and how often it happens.  
They will also ask what triggers the pain.

Your doctor will check your face for sensitivity.  
They may do other physical tests.  
In most cases, this is enough to make a diagnosis.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Trigeminal neuralgia can be treated well with medicine, surgery, or radiation.

Regular painkillers like aspirin, ibuprofen, or paracetamol do not work.  
The pain attacks are too short.  
Even strong pain medicines like opioids do not help.

For longer pain episodes, special IV treatments may help reduce symptoms.

Long-term treatment is often needed to prevent attacks.  
Medicines used for epilepsy are usually the best choice.

The most common medicines are:  
- Carbamazepine  
- Oxcarbazepine  

These medicines reduce the number of pain attacks.  
Your doctor will slowly increase the dose until it works well.  
They will also watch for side effects.

Other treatment options include:

### Microvascular Decompression
- A surgeon separates the nerve from the blood vessel pressing on it.  
- This reduces pressure on the nerve.  
- It is a good option if a blood vessel is causing the problem.

### Neuroablation
- Doctors destroy parts of the nerve using heat, pressure, or alcohol.  
- This stops the nerve from sending pain signals.

### Gamma Knife Radiation
- A focused beam of radiation treats the nerve.  
- It changes the nerve so it no longer sends pain signals to the brain.

Surgery is only used if medicine does not work or causes bad side effects.  
Your doctor will discuss the best option for you.

# Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)

A transient ischemic attack, or TIA, often happens before a stroke. It occurs when part of the brain does not get enough blood. This can cause sudden problems like weakness, trouble seeing, or difficulty speaking.

## Quick Facts

- A TIA is a medical emergency. You must get help right away.
- It often warns that a stroke may happen soon.
- Symptoms come on suddenly and include severe headache, weakness on one side of the body, trouble seeing, and slurred speech.
- Most TIAs are caused by a small blood clot that blocks a blood vessel in the brain.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is a TIA?

A TIA happens when blood flow to part of the brain stops for a short time. The brain does not get the oxygen it needs. This can cause sudden symptoms.

**Important:** A TIA can be a warning sign that a stroke may happen soon.

## What Are the Signs of a TIA?

The symptoms of a TIA are like those of a stroke. But they go away within 24 hours.

Common signs include:

- Sudden, severe headache
- Weakness or numbness in one arm or leg
- Trouble seeing in one or both eyes
- Slurred or unclear speech

These symptoms may last only a few minutes or a few hours. Then they disappear completely.

**Important:** In a TIA, the blood clot breaks up quickly. The brain is not damaged. But the event still needs urgent care.

For more details about stroke symptoms, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

## What Causes a TIA?

A TIA is usually caused by a blood clot. The clot blocks a blood vessel in the brain. This stops blood from reaching part of the brain.

This is the same thing that happens in a stroke. But in a TIA, the clot dissolves on its own. The brain recovers without lasting harm.

## How Is a TIA Diagnosed?

TIA symptoms are very similar to stroke symptoms. Because of this, a TIA is treated as an emergency.

If you or someone else has any of these symptoms, call emergency services immediately. Do not wait to see if the symptoms go away.

The emergency team will do quick tests. If possible, the person will be taken to a hospital that specializes in stroke care. There, doctors will run more tests. They will find the cause and start treatment right away.

## How Is a TIA Treated?

When symptoms first appear, doctors do not know if it is a TIA or a stroke. So they treat it the same way as a stroke.

Treatment depends on what the tests show. Doctors will monitor the person closely. They will also check for risks of future strokes and take steps to prevent them.

# Rabies – Simple Explanation

Rabies is a deadly virus that spreads when an infected animal bites a person.  
It attacks the brain and spinal cord.  
There is no cure once symptoms start.  
But it can be prevented if you act quickly after a bite.

Germany does not have rabies anymore.  
The disease is still common in parts of Asia and Africa.  
Most cases happen because of bites from stray dogs.  
If you travel to these areas, you can get a vaccine to protect yourself.

If you are bitten by an animal, get medical help right away.  
Even if you feel fine, you must act fast.  
The sooner you get treatment, the better your chance of staying safe.

---

## What Is Rabies?

Rabies is a disease that can pass from animals to people.  
It is caused by a virus.  
The virus spreads through the saliva of an infected animal.  
Most people get it from a bite.  
The bite must break the skin.  
The virus can also enter through open cuts or scratches if they touch the animal’s saliva.

Rabies is rare in Germany.  
The last case in Germany was in 2007.  
That person was bitten by a stray dog while visiting North Africa.

---

## Where Does Rabies Happen?

Rabies is still found in many countries.  
It is most common in parts of Asia and Africa.  
In most of Europe, rabies has been stopped in wild and pet animals.  
Germany was officially declared free of rabies in 2008.

But you can still get rabies if you bring home a pet from a country where rabies is common.  
The animal might be infected even if it looks healthy.

---

## How Common Is Rabies?

Rabies is a serious disease that must be reported to health authorities.  
In Germany, the last case was in 2007.  
Globally, about 60,000 people die from rabies every year.  
This number may be higher because many cases are not reported.  
Most deaths happen in Asia and Africa.

---

## How Is Rabies Spread?

Rabies spreads when an infected animal bites a person.  
The virus is in the animal’s saliva.  
It enters the body through broken skin or open wounds.  
Bats, foxes, monkeys, and stray dogs are the most common carriers.  
Rabies can also spread through contact with infected saliva on open wounds.

It is very rare for rabies to spread from person to person.  
It does not spread through the air, water, or casual contact.

### What Happens in the Body?

After a bite, the virus stays at the wound site for a while.  
Then it moves along the nerves toward the brain and spinal cord.  
Once it reaches the brain, it multiplies fast.  
This causes serious brain problems.  
The virus then spreads to other parts of the body.  
Deep bites can let the virus enter the blood faster.  
This leads to symptoms appearing sooner.

---

## How Can You Prevent Rabies?

Stay away from stray dogs and wild animals like bats, foxes, and monkeys.  
These animals may seem friendly, but they can be dangerous.  
Wild animals often lose their fear of people when they are sick with rabies.  
Be extra careful around them.

### Can You Get a Rabies Vaccine?

Yes.  
If you are traveling to a country where rabies is common, you can get a preventive vaccine.  
This is called a pre-exposure vaccine.  
It helps your body react faster if you are bitten later.

In Germany, the official recommendation is three doses of the vaccine.  
The World Health Organization says two doses are enough for healthy people.  
Both schedules are available in Germany after talking to a doctor.

**Important:**  
If you are already vaccinated and get bitten, you still need more shots.  
The first vaccine helps your body respond faster.  
A second set of shots after the bite can stop the disease from starting.

---

## What Should You Do If You Are Bitten Abroad?

Go to a doctor right away.  
Do not wait.  
The doctor will check:

- What kind of animal bit you?  
  Only mammals can carry rabies.
- Where did the bite happen?  
  If the country is rabies-free, the risk is low.
- How did the contact happen?  
  A bite is more dangerous than just touching the animal.
- Have you been vaccinated before?  
  This changes the treatment plan.
- Has any treatment already started?  
  This affects what comes next.

If rabies is possible, start the vaccine right away.  
Do not wait for test results.  
The vaccine works best when given early.  
It can prevent the disease from developing.

### Wound Care Is Also Important

Clean the wound immediately.  
Wash it well with soap and water.  
Use running water for at least 15 minutes.  
If the wound is deep, a doctor may use a special tool to flush it out.  
Do not close the wound with stitches or cauterize it right away.  
This can trap the virus inside.

**Important:**  
Symptoms can take weeks or even years to appear.  
If you were bitten and did not get the vaccine right away, you can still get it later.  
But only if you have not yet shown any symptoms.

---

## What Are the Symptoms of Rabies?

The time between being bitten and showing symptoms is called the incubation period.  
It usually takes 3 to 8 weeks.  
But it can be as short as a few days or as long as several years.  
The closer the bite is to your head or spine, the faster symptoms appear.

Rabies has three main stages.

### Stage 1: Early Symptoms

At first, you may feel like you have the flu.  
You feel tired, weak, and have a headache.  
You may lose your appetite.  
You might feel sick and throw up.  
The area around the bite may hurt, burn, or itch.

### Stage 2: Brain and Nerve Problems

The virus now attacks the brain and nerves.  
Two main forms of the disease can develop.

**Furious form:**  
You become very anxious.  
You may fear water.  
Just hearing or seeing water can cause panic.  
You may have muscle spasms when trying to swallow.  
You may drool or foam at the mouth.  
Your mood swings between being aggressive and depressed.

**Paralytic form:**  
You feel numb or weak.  
You may have trouble moving or breathing.  
You may have trouble swallowing.  
Muscles can become paralyzed.

### Stage 3: Final Stage

The brain stops controlling breathing and heart function.  
You fall into a coma.  
You cannot breathe on your own.  
The disease is always fatal.  
Death usually happens within a few days after symptoms start.

---

## How Is Rabies Diagnosed?

Doctors can test for rabies in several ways.  
They may take blood and spinal fluid samples.  
They look for antibodies — the body’s defense against the virus.  
But these tests are not always accurate.

A more reliable test uses a small skin sample from the back of the neck.  
This sample is sent to a lab to check for the virus’s genetic material.

---

## Can Rabies Be Treated?

There is no cure for rabies once symptoms appear.  
If you are suspected of having rabies, you must go to an intensive care unit.  
Doctors will try to ease your symptoms.  
But the disease is always deadly.  
Treatment cannot stop the virus once it reaches the brain.

**The only way to stay safe is to act fast after a bite.**  
Preventive vaccines and quick wound care are your best protection.

# High Blood Pressure (Hypertension)

Many people have high blood pressure.  
But most do not feel any symptoms.  
This means it can go unnoticed for years.  
Over time, high blood pressure can harm your blood vessels.  
It also raises your risk of a heart attack, a stroke, or kidney problems.

## Quick Facts

- Many people have high blood pressure without knowing it.  
- It usually causes no symptoms.  
- High blood pressure damages blood vessels over time.  
- It increases the risk of heart attack, stroke, and kidney issues.  
- Blood pressure is too high if the top number is 140 or more.  
- Blood pressure is too high if the bottom number is 90 or more.  
- Both numbers can be high at the same time.  
- In many cases, doctors do not find a clear cause.  
- Exercise, weight loss, and eating less salt can help lower blood pressure.  
- If lifestyle changes are not enough, medicine can help.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is High Blood Pressure?

High blood pressure means your blood pressure is too high most of the time.  
It often causes no symptoms.  
So you may not know you have it.  
This can lead to damage in your blood vessels over time.  
High blood pressure increases your risk of heart attack, stroke, or kidney disease.  
The higher your blood pressure, the greater the risk.

Blood pressure readings have two numbers.  
The first number is the pressure when your heart beats.  
The second number is the pressure when your heart rests between beats.  
For example: 128 over 85.

Blood pressure is considered high if:
- The first number is 140 or higher, or  
- The second number is 90 or higher, or  
- Both numbers are too high.

These numbers are general guidelines.  
They help doctors decide when treatment is needed.  
But recommendations can vary from person to person.

## What Are the Symptoms?

High blood pressure usually has no symptoms.  
You may not feel anything at all.  
Only if your blood pressure is very high might you feel dizzy or have blurry vision.

## What Causes High Blood Pressure?

Your body naturally changes blood pressure.  
It goes up during exercise or stress.  
It goes down when you are relaxed or sleeping.  
It often increases with age.

These changes are normal.  
But if blood pressure stays high for too long, it can harm your blood vessels.

In many cases, doctors do not find a clear cause.  
This is called primary or essential hypertension.

Certain habits can raise blood pressure:
- Being overweight  
- Eating too much salt  
- Drinking too much alcohol  
- Not getting enough physical activity

But even healthy people can get high blood pressure.  
This can happen if it runs in the family.

Some medicines can also raise blood pressure.  
These include:
- Certain mental health medicines  
- Some herbal remedies like St. John’s wort  
- Nasal sprays or drops for a stuffy nose  
- Birth control pills

## How Is High Blood Pressure Diagnosed?

Doctors measure your blood pressure on both arms while you are sitting quietly.  
Measuring both arms helps get a clearer picture.  
Blood pressure is checked on different days to get a more accurate result.

The highest reading from each number is used to decide if blood pressure is high.

Blood pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury (mmHg).

Normal blood pressure for adults is less than 140 over 90.  
High blood pressure is diagnosed if:
- The top number is 140 or higher, or  
- The bottom number is 90 or higher, or  
- Both numbers are too high.

Sometimes doctors use a 24-hour blood pressure monitor.  
This device is worn during daily activities.  
It takes readings at regular times.  
This helps if your blood pressure changes a lot during the day.

For more details, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

## How Can High Blood Pressure Be Found Early?

In Germany, health insurance covers a free health check-up every three years starting at age 35.  
This check-up includes a blood pressure test.  
The goal is to catch early signs of heart disease, diabetes, or kidney problems.

But studies have not shown that these check-ups prevent illness or help people live longer.

## How Is High Blood Pressure Treated?

You can take steps to lower your blood pressure on your own.  
Some people succeed by:
- Losing a small amount of weight  
- Reducing salt in your diet  
- Moving more every day

If these changes are not enough, medicine can help.  
Before starting medicine, talk to your doctor.  
Consider the benefits and possible side effects.  
Not everyone needs medicine.  
Some people benefit more than others.  

For more information about blood pressure medicines, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

# Short-sightedness

Short-sightedness is a common vision problem. It often starts in childhood or the teenage years. People who are short-sighted see things that are far away as blurry. But they usually see things up close clearly. Glasses or contact lenses can help fix this.

---

## Quick Facts

- Short-sightedness is very common. Some people are born with it. Others develop it later in life.
- It usually begins when children start school. It often gets worse during the teenage years.
- People who are short-sighted see distant objects as blurry. Close-up objects are usually clear.
- Glasses or contact lenses can correct short-sightedness.
- **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Short-sightedness?

Short-sightedness means your eyes cannot focus properly on distant objects. Doctors call it “myopia.”  
When you are short-sighted, light focuses in front of the retina instead of on it. This makes distant images blurry.

The main reason is that the eyeball is too long.  
In some cases, the lens or the front surface of the eye (the cornea) is too curved. This also causes light to bend too much.

The opposite happens in long-sightedness. People with long-sightedness see close objects as blurry but can see distant objects clearly.

Short-sightedness usually starts in school-aged children. It often gets worse during puberty, when the body grows quickly. After young adulthood, the condition usually stops getting worse.

Doctors measure how strong short-sightedness is in units called diopters.  
- Mild short-sightedness starts at minus 1 diopter.  
- Severe short-sightedness begins at minus 6 diopters or more.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

People with mild short-sightedness may not notice any problems.  
They might only realize something is wrong when they need to see far away — like when driving.

With moderate short-sightedness, distant objects look blurry.  
For example, you can read a book easily. But you cannot read words on a classroom board a few meters away.

With severe short-sightedness, only objects very close — a few centimeters away — are clear.  
You cannot read a book at a normal distance.

People with severe short-sightedness have a higher chance of developing other eye problems later in life. These include:
- Retinal degeneration
- Retinal detachment
- Cataracts
- Glaucoma

---

## What Causes Short-sightedness?

In normal vision, light enters the eye through the lens and cornea. These parts bend the light so it lands exactly on the retina. This creates a clear image.

In short-sightedness, the light bends too much. It focuses in front of the retina. This makes the image blurry.

The most common cause is an eyeball that is too long.  
In some people, the lens or cornea is too curved. This also causes too much bending of light.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

Short-sightedness can run in families. If your parents are short-sighted, you may be more likely to be too.

Other things that raise the risk include:
- Spending a lot of time on screens (phones, computers, tablets)
- Reading for long periods
- Holding books too close to your eyes

---

## How Common Is It?

Short-sightedness is very common.  
About one in four people worldwide are short-sighted.  
The number has grown fast in Europe and the United States over the past few decades.

Experts believe this rise is due to lifestyle changes.  
More people now spend long hours indoors. They read more and look at screens up close.

---

## How Can It Be Caught Early?

Many young children do not notice short-sightedness.  
Doctors check children’s vision during regular health visits called U check-ups.

If a doctor suspects short-sightedness, the child should see an eye specialist.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

An eye specialist will ask about your symptoms.  
For example:
- When do your eyes get blurry?
- Do things look better up close or far away?

They will test your vision with a chart.  
You will read letters or numbers of different sizes.  
One eye is tested at a time, while the other is covered.

If you cannot read the small letters, the doctor will try different lenses.  
They will keep changing the lenses until your vision becomes clear.  
This shows how strong your short-sightedness is.

The doctor will also use a special machine.  
It sends a light into your eye and measures how much the light bends.  
This gives an exact number for your short-sightedness.  
It does not depend on what you say. It is an objective test.

People with short-sightedness have more bending of light than normal.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Glasses or contact lenses can correct short-sightedness.  
The choice depends on how severe your condition is.

The lenses used are concave.  
This means they are thinner in the middle and thicker at the edges.  
They spread out the light before it enters the eye.  
This helps balance the over-bending of light.

For adults with severe short-sightedness, surgery is an option.  
A laser is used to gently reshape the cornea.  
This makes the cornea flatter and reduces its bending power.

But surgery is not risk-free.  
Possible side effects include:
- Scarring
- Worse vision at night
- Trouble seeing distant objects clearly

If your vision gets worse after surgery, or if you develop presbyopia (a condition that makes it hard to see up close as you age), you may need to wear glasses again.

# Glandular Fever

Glandular fever is a viral infection.  
It is caused by the Epstein-Barr virus, also known as EBV.  
EBV is a type of herpes virus.  
Almost everyone carries this virus at some point in their life.  
Most people get infected during their teenage years or early adulthood.  
For people with a healthy immune system, the infection is usually mild and harmless.  

## Quick Facts

- Glandular fever is a contagious illness caused by a virus.  
- The virus responsible is the Epstein-Barr virus, or EBV.  
- EBV spreads through saliva. This often happens when people kiss.  
- Common symptoms include swollen glands, high fever, and a sore throat.  
- Most people recover fully within 2 to 4 weeks.  
- Some people may feel very tired for several months after the infection.  
- The infection can be serious for people with weak immune systems.  
  - This includes people with HIV or those who have had an organ transplant.  
  - These individuals should avoid close contact with infected people.  

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always see a doctor.

## What Is Glandular Fever?

Glandular fever is also called infectious mononucleosis.  
It is often called “mono” for short.  
It is caused by the Epstein-Barr virus, or EBV.  
This virus belongs to the herpes family.  

Most people get EBV through contact with saliva.  
Kissing is the most common way the virus spreads.  
Children may get it from kissing their parents.  
The virus can also spread by sharing drinks or eating utensils.  

In rare cases, a pregnant woman can pass the virus to her unborn baby through the placenta.  

Most people who get EBV do not get sick.  
If they do get sick, the illness is usually mild.  
It often goes away on its own in 2 to 4 weeks.  

Once you have had EBV, you are protected for life.  
The virus stays in your body in a quiet state.  
It can wake up again if your immune system becomes weak.  

If the virus wakes up in a healthy person, it usually causes no symptoms.  
But the person can still pass the virus to others without knowing it.  

## What Are the Symptoms?

Not everyone who has EBV gets symptoms.  
Some people feel fine and never know they are infected.  

If symptoms do appear, they may include:  
- A sore throat  
- Swollen tonsils  
- High fever  
- Headache  
- Feeling unwell  
- Extreme tiredness  

Swollen lymph nodes in the neck are common.  
The spleen may also become enlarged.  
Other lymph nodes in the body can swell too.  

Sometimes, the only symptom is a sore throat.  

Children under 10 years old usually have mild or no symptoms.  
They often do not feel sick at all.  
The infection may go unnoticed.  

In some people, tiredness, fever, sore throat, and swollen glands can last longer than 6 months.  
This is very rare.  

## What Causes Glandular Fever?

Glandular fever is caused by the Epstein-Barr virus, or EBV.  
This virus is part of the herpes family.  

The virus first attacks the lining of the nose and throat.  
It multiplies quickly in these areas.  
Then it moves into white blood cells, which are part of the immune system.  

These infected cells travel through the blood and lymph system.  
They reach the lymph nodes, spleen, and liver.  
This can cause swelling in these organs.  

The virus spreads mainly through saliva.  
Kissing is the most common way.  
Sharing drinks or utensils can also spread it.  

In rare cases, a pregnant woman can pass the virus to her baby during pregnancy.  

## How Common Is Glandular Fever?

Over 90 percent of people around the world have been infected with EBV.  
But not everyone who has EBV gets glandular fever.  

The illness is most common in people aged 15 to 24.  
Experts believe almost everyone gets infected with EBV by age 30.  
After that, most adults have no symptoms when they come into contact with the virus.  

## What Is the Outlook?

Most people recover fully from glandular fever in a few weeks.  
Some people still feel very tired for several months after the infection.  

Complications can happen, but they are rare.  

### Possible Complications

- Some people get a secondary bacterial infection.  
- The spleen often swells during the illness.  
  - If the spleen becomes very large, it can burst.  
  - A burst spleen is life-threatening and needs emergency care.  
  - To prevent this, avoid sports and physical activity for 4 to 6 weeks.  
  - Wait until the spleen returns to normal size before resuming activity.  

- Swelling in the throat and tonsils can block the airway.  
  - This is rare but can happen in children.  
  - It needs urgent medical treatment.  

Other rare complications include:  
- Inflammation of the brain lining (meningitis)  
- Inflammation of the heart muscle (myocarditis)  
- Kidney inflammation  
- Liver inflammation (hepatitis)  

People with weak immune systems may have severe swelling in the lymph nodes.  

EBV infection may increase the risk of certain cancers.  
This includes Hodgkin’s lymphoma.  
This risk is higher in people with severely weakened immune systems.  

## How Can Glandular Fever Be Prevented?

There is no vaccine for glandular fever.  
But you can reduce your risk by following good hygiene habits.  

Avoid close contact with people who have the infection.  
Do not share:  
- Drinking glasses  
- Eating utensils  
- Toothbrushes  

Avoid kissing someone who is infected.  

## How Is Glandular Fever Diagnosed?

A doctor will look for signs like:  
- Fever  
- Swollen glands in the neck  
- Sore throat  
These are most common in young adults.  

The doctor will check if your lymph nodes, spleen, or liver are swollen.  

If the spleen or liver is enlarged, the doctor may order an ultrasound scan.  

To confirm the diagnosis, a blood test is needed.  
The test looks for antibodies to EBV.  
If these antibodies are found, it means you have an active EBV infection.  

Blood tests can also show changes in white blood cells.  
These changes help confirm the diagnosis.  

## How Is Glandular Fever Treated?

There is no specific medicine to cure glandular fever.  
Treatment focuses on easing symptoms.  

Rest and drinking plenty of fluids help your body recover.  

Pain and fever can be treated with anti-inflammatory medicines like ibuprofen or diclofenac.  

If swelling in the throat makes breathing hard, doctors may use medicine to reduce swelling.  
This is usually a type of steroid, like cortisone.  

If a bacterial infection develops, antibiotics can help.  
But some antibiotics can cause a rash in people with EBV.  
So your doctor will choose the right one.  

### Important: Avoid Physical Activity

To prevent a burst spleen, avoid all sports and physical activity for 4 to 6 weeks.  
This is especially important for athletes.  

Wait until your doctor says it is safe to return to sports.  
Do not rush back.  
A full recovery takes time.  

Always talk to your doctor before resuming physical activity.

# Acne

Acne is a common skin problem. It often starts during teenage years. This article explains acne vulgaris — the most common type of acne in teens and young adults.

---

## Quick Facts

- Acne is the most common skin issue in teenagers.
- It can be upsetting, especially during puberty.
- Acne lasts longer than occasional pimples, blackheads, or whiteheads.
- Most people see their acne improve by age 20.
- Many treatments are available. Some go on the skin. Others are pills.
- Treating acne takes time and patience.

> **Note:** This article is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Acne?

Pimples are normal during puberty. Most teens get a few now and then. But some teens get more severe acne that lasts for months or years. This can be hard to deal with emotionally.

This article focuses on acne vulgaris — the most common form of acne in teens and young adults.

---

## What Does Acne Look Like?

Doctors divide acne into three levels: mild, moderate, and severe. They also look at whether the acne is inflamed (red, swollen) or not.

### Mild Acne

- The skin has blackheads or whiteheads.
- Blackheads form when a pore is open and the oil inside turns dark.
- Whiteheads form when a pore is closed and the oil stays under the skin.
- These are not yet inflamed.
- If oil builds up, bacteria grow and cause redness and swelling.

Mild acne means only a few small pimples appear.

### Moderate Acne

- More pimples appear.
- Some are red and swollen bumps called papules.
- Others are pus-filled bumps called pustules.

### Severe Acne

- A large number of papules and pustules form.
- Painful, hard lumps called nodules may appear under the skin.
- Severe acne can leave scars or lasting marks.

---

## What Causes Acne?

During puberty, the body makes more hormones called androgens. These hormones make the skin produce more oil, called sebum.

- Sebum helps keep the skin soft and protected.
- If dead skin cells block a pore, a blackhead or whitehead forms.
- If bacteria grow in the blocked pore, it becomes inflamed and turns into a pimple.

**Important:** Acne mostly appears on the face, chest, shoulders, and back. These areas have many oil-producing glands.

Acne is most common in teens because of hormone changes. Most people stop having acne by their early twenties.

Genetics and the body’s immune system may also play a role.

---

## What Makes Acne Worse?

Acne is not only caused by internal hormones. Other things can make it worse:

- **Hormone medicines:** Some muscle-building drugs (anabolic steroids) can cause acne.
- **Certain medicines:** Cortisone and some epilepsy drugs may trigger acne.
- **Oily skin products:** Creams, lotions, and oils that are too greasy can clog pores.
- **Harsh rubbing or squeezing:** This can irritate the skin and make acne worse.

### Myths About Acne

Some common beliefs about acne are not true:

- **Hygiene:** Cleaning your skin more does not prevent or fix acne.
- **Diet:** No strong proof links acne to meat, dairy, or chocolate.
- **Carbohydrates:** Foods like sugary snacks, white bread, and potatoes raise blood sugar fast. Some think this may make acne worse, but science has not confirmed this.
- **Smoking:** It is not clear if smoking causes acne.
- **Stress:** Many people say stress makes their skin worse. Some studies suggest stress might trigger acne.

---

## How Common Is Acne?

- Acne is the most common skin problem in teens.
- Most teens have only mild acne.
- Between 15% and 30% of teens have moderate to severe acne.
- Boys are more likely to get acne than girls.

---

## How Long Does Acne Last?

- For most people, acne goes away by age 20.
- Some adults still have acne after age 30.
- In some cases, acne leaves scars or dark marks on the skin.

---

## How to Treat Acne

Many products and treatments are sold for acne. Not all of them work. Some can even irritate the skin.

### Skin Care Tips

- Use gentle cleansers that do not contain soap.
- Choose products that match your skin’s natural pH (around 5.5).
- Use light lotions or water-based gels.
- Avoid greasy creams and oils. They can clog pores.

### Medicines

- **Topical treatments:** Creams, gels, or lotions applied to the skin.
- **Oral medicines:** Pills taken by mouth.

Some proven treatments include:
- Antibiotics
- Benzoyl peroxide
- Retinoids (like tretinoin)

**Important:** Acne treatment takes time. You may need to use it for months or even years. Results are not quick. Some treatments can cause side effects like dryness, redness, or irritation.

For more details on acne and skin care, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## Living with Acne

Teens often feel unsure about their looks. Acne can make this worse. Mood swings are common during puberty — with or without acne.

Even mild acne can cause strong feelings of distress. The level of upset does not always match how bad the acne looks.

How teens handle acne depends on their confidence.

- Some feel only a little bothered.
- Others may feel sad, withdrawn, or anxious.
- They may avoid friends or argue more with family.

Acne is linked to:
- More anxiety
- More thoughts about being sad or hopeless
- Lower self-worth

### Support and Coping

- Friends and family can help a lot.
- But teens with acne don’t want to talk about it all the time.
- Some ways to feel better:
  - Wearing makeup
  - Using sunglasses
  - Wearing long sleeves
  - Trying a hairstyle with bangs

These can help you feel more confident.

For real stories from teens who lived with acne, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Hepatitis C – Simple Explanation

Hepatitis C is a liver problem caused by a virus.  
The virus spreads through blood.  
Most people who get infected will have the virus in their body for a long time.  
If not treated, it can lead to serious liver damage or liver cancer.  
Today, over 95 out of 100 people with hepatitis C can be cured with medicine.  
There is no vaccine to prevent hepatitis C.  
You can get infected more than once.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Hepatitis C?

Hepatitis C is an infection that causes swelling in the liver.  
It is caused by a virus called the hepatitis C virus.  
Doctors found this virus in 1989.  
The main way people get it is through contact with infected blood.  
People who inject drugs and share needles are at high risk.  
The virus can also spread through shared drug tools like spoons, pans, or snorting tubes.  
Healthcare workers can get infected by accidental needle sticks, but this is rare.  
In Germany, blood supplies are now tested, so this is no longer a common way to get infected.  
The virus can be found in saliva, sweat, tears, and semen, but it is very unlikely to spread through these.  
Sexual contact can spread the virus in some cases, especially if there is injury.  
A pregnant woman with hepatitis C can pass the virus to her baby during birth or even before birth.  
But this happens in only a few cases.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people with hepatitis C do not feel sick at first.  
About 75 out of 100 people have no symptoms or only mild ones.  
These mild symptoms can include:  
- Feeling tired  
- Loss of appetite  
- Nausea  
- Muscle or joint pain  
- A slight fever  

In the remaining 25 out of 100 people, the skin and the whites of the eyes turn yellow.  
This is called jaundice.  
Stool becomes pale.  
Urine becomes dark.  
Itching can also happen with jaundice.  

If the infection becomes long-term, it often causes no clear symptoms.  
Some people feel tired, itchy, or have joint pain.  
A dull ache on the right side of the belly near the ribs can also happen.

---

## How Do People Get Infected?

The main way hepatitis C spreads is through blood.  
People who inject drugs and share needles, syringes, spoons, or pans are at high risk.  
Sharing snorting tubes for cocaine can also spread the virus.  
Healthcare workers can get infected by accidental needle pricks, but this is rare.  
Blood supplies in Germany are now tested, so this is no longer a common risk.  
The virus is not easily spread through everyday contact.  
It is very unlikely to spread through saliva, sweat, tears, or semen.  
Sexual contact can spread it, especially if there is injury.  
A pregnant woman can pass the virus to her baby, but this happens in only a few cases.

---

## How Common Is Hepatitis C?

Hepatitis C is found all over the world.  
About 1 in 100 people have a long-term infection.  
Infection rates are higher in some regions, like parts of Africa, the Middle East, and Central Asia.  
In Germany, only about 3 out of 1,000 people have hepatitis C.  
Some groups are more affected:  
- People in prison  
- Migrants from countries with high infection rates
