- People who use drugs  

Studies in Germany show that between 1 in 3 and 3 in 4 people who use drugs have hepatitis C.

---

## How Does the Infection Develop?

After infection, it can take 2 weeks to 6 months for the body to make antibodies.  
Symptoms usually appear around 7 to 8 weeks after infection.  
A person can spread the virus as long as the virus is in their blood.  
This can happen even before symptoms start.  
In 15 to 40 out of 100 people, the infection goes away on its own.  
But people who recover can get infected again because the body does not build lasting protection.  
In 60 to 85 out of 100 people, the infection becomes long-term.  
If not treated, some of these people will develop liver scarring (cirrhosis) over 20 to 30 years.  
The liver slowly turns into scar tissue, and its function gets worse.  

Some factors make the disease worse:  
- Being older  
- Being male  
- Drinking alcohol over a long time  
- Being overweight or having diabetes  
- Having hepatitis B or HIV at the same time  
- Taking long-term medicines that weaken the immune system  

People with liver scarring from hepatitis C have a higher risk of liver cancer.  
Hepatitis C can also affect other organs.  
It can lead to kidney disease, blood vessel problems, lymph node cancer, or heart disease.

---

## How Can You Prevent Hepatitis C?

There is no vaccine for hepatitis C.  
But you can protect yourself.  
If you inject drugs:  
- Always use your own syringe and tools.  
- Never share needles, spoons, pans, or snorting tubes.  

If you live with someone who has hepatitis C:  
- Do not share razors, razor kits, nail clippers, or toothbrushes.  
- Avoid contact with blood or blood traces.  

If you have many sexual partners:  
- Use condoms every time.  

In hospitals and clinics:  
- Standard hygiene and safety rules are enough to prevent spread.

---

## How Is Hepatitis C Diagnosed?

Hepatitis C often has no symptoms.  
It is often found by chance during a routine blood test.  
For example, if liver values are high, the doctor may suspect hepatitis C.  
A blood test checks for antibodies to the virus.  
If antibodies are found, another test checks for the virus’s genetic material (HCV-RNA).  
This tells if the infection is active or if it was cleared.  
An ultrasound of the liver may also be done to check for damage.

---

## How Is Hepatitis C Treated?

Some people with acute hepatitis C get better on their own.  
No treatment is needed in these cases.  

If the infection becomes long-term, treatment is usually given.  
Medicines are used together to stop the virus from multiplying.  
Different types of drugs are used:  
- Protease inhibitors  
- Polymerase inhibitors  
- NS5A inhibitors  

Treatment usually lasts 8 to 12 weeks.  
Sometimes it takes longer.  
Today, more than 95 out of 100 people who get treatment are cured.

# Acute Middle Ear Infection

This is a common illness in babies and young children. Most children get it at least once in their first three years. The pain and infection usually go away on their own in two to three days. Serious problems are very rare.

---

## Quick Facts

- About 8 out of 10 children have a middle ear infection by age three.
- You cannot always prevent these infections.
- A child with an infection may have ear pain, a high fever, cry a lot, and have trouble sleeping.
- Most infections clear up by themselves in two to three days.
- You can help your child feel better by giving pain relief medicine, reducing fever, and offering comfort and care.
- Antibiotics are only used if the infection is caused by bacteria.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat your child on your own.

---

## What Is a Middle Ear Infection?

Most babies and young children get at least one middle ear infection in their first three years. The child will feel pain and have a fever. They may cry often and not sleep well. While this can be stressful for parents, the infection usually gets better on its own in just a few days. Serious problems are very rare.

The main treatment is pain relief medicine and fever reducers. You can also help by giving your child extra care and attention. Watch your child closely. If symptoms get worse or last longer, see a doctor.

---

## Signs of a Middle Ear Infection

Common signs in young children include:

- Severe ear pain
- Fever over 38 degrees Celsius
- Trouble hearing because fluid is trapped in the middle ear

The illness starts suddenly. Some children may also vomit. Young children often cannot say “my ear hurts.” Instead, they may act upset, complain about a tummy ache, or seem irritable.

Look for these clues:
- Rubbing or touching the ear
- Shaking the head often
- Not sleeping well at night
- Crying more than usual
- Not eating much

Some children may become quieter than normal. This is also a sign of discomfort.

> **Note:** Most children with a middle ear infection have trouble hearing. This can make them restless and hard to comfort.

---

## What Happens in a Middle Ear Infection?

The middle ear becomes inflamed. This is often caused by a virus or bacteria. These germs can come from a cold, flu, or sore throat.

Here’s how it works:

- Germs enter the throat and cause swelling in the lining of the nose and throat.
- The same swelling happens in the Eustachian tube. This is the small tube that connects the middle ear to the back of the throat.
- The tube gets blocked. Fluid can no longer drain out of the middle ear.
- Fluid builds up behind the eardrum. This creates pressure.
- The pressure causes pain and makes it hard to hear.

Babies and young children are more likely to get these infections because their Eustachian tubes are short and narrow. This makes it easier for germs to travel from the nose and throat to the middle ear.

By age seven, the tube is longer and stronger. The immune system is also more developed. This means infections become less common.

Other things that can increase the risk:

- Enlarged adenoids (tissue at the back of the nose)
- Allergies
- Sinus infections

Factors that raise the risk of infection:

- Using a pacifier
- Being around other children, such as in daycare
- Bottle feeding instead of breastfeeding
- Exposure to secondhand smoke

---

## How Common Are These Infections?

Middle ear infections are one of the most common reasons parents take their child to the doctor. About 80 percent of children have had one by age three. Up to one third of these children will have more than one infection.

---

## How Does the Infection Progress?

Most infections go away on their own in two to three days. But sometimes, too much fluid builds up behind the eardrum. This pressure can cause the eardrum to burst.

If this happens:
- The ear pain will go away.
- Thick fluid, sometimes with mucus or blood, will leak from the ear.

This is called ear discharge. It can last for days or even weeks. The tear in the eardrum is usually small. It heals by itself.

If the fluid stays in the middle ear for weeks, it is called a chronic middle ear infection. The pain and fever may go away, but fluid still leaks from the ear. This can cause lasting hearing problems.

> **See a doctor** if you notice your child has trouble hearing after an ear infection.

---

## Can You Prevent a Middle Ear Infection?

You cannot always prevent these infections. But you can lower the risk by:

- Limiting pacifier use
- Keeping your child away from secondhand smoke
- Breastfeeding instead of bottle feeding
- Avoiding close contact with sick children

A smoke-free home is especially important. Secondhand smoke makes it easier for children to get infections in the nose, throat, and airways. It also weakens the immune system.

For more tips on prevention, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

The doctor will ask about your child’s symptoms and medical history.

Then they will examine:
- Both ears
- The throat
- The neck

They use a tool called an otoscope. It has a light and a magnifying lens. This lets the doctor see inside the ear canal.

They may also use a tympanometer. This device checks how well the eardrum moves. It sends sound and changes air pressure in the ear.

The doctor will also take your child’s temperature.

It can be hard to be sure of the diagnosis. But the following signs suggest a middle ear infection:

- Sudden illness with strong ear pain, fever, and feeling unwell
- A red eardrum
- A swollen, stiff, or cloudy eardrum — this may mean fluid is behind it

---

## How Is It Treated?

The main goal is to relieve pain fast.

You can use:
- Paracetamol
- Ibuprofen

These are available as liquid medicine or suppositories. They help reduce pain and fever. Most children feel better after taking them.

Antibiotics only work if the infection is caused by bacteria. Signs of a bacterial infection include:
- Pus mixed with fluid coming from the ear
- Infection in both ears, especially in children under two years old

Nose drops that reduce swelling may help with a blocked nose. But they do not make the infection go away faster. They may only help for a few hours. Do not use them for more than a few days.

Home remedies like:
- Warm leg wraps for fever
- Onion packs for ear pain
- Herbal or homeopathic treatments

Have not been proven to work. There is no strong evidence that they help.

For more information, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Heart Defects Present at Birth

Heart defects that are present at birth are the most common type of birth defect. One of the most common types is a hole in the heart wall. If doctors find the problem early, most children can recover fully.

---

## Quick Facts

- Heart defects are the most common type of birth defect.
- A ventricular septal defect is a hole in the wall between the two lower chambers of the heart.
- Some small holes close on their own without treatment.
- If a large hole is not treated, it can be life-threatening.
- Most heart defects like this are easy to treat.
- Children who get treatment early can live a normal life.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself or your child.

---

## What Is a Septal Heart Defect?

A septal heart defect means there is a problem with the wall (septum) that separates the left and right sides of the heart. This wall keeps oxygen-rich blood and oxygen-poor blood from mixing.

The heart has four chambers: two upper and two lower. The septum runs between the left and right sides. If there is a hole, blood can leak from one side to the other.

### Types of Septal Heart Defects

- **Ventricular septal defect (VSD):** A hole in the wall between the two lower chambers of the heart.
- **Atrial septal defect (ASD):** A hole in the wall between the two upper chambers of the heart.
- **Atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD):** A hole in both the upper and lower chambers, often with problems in the heart valves.

---

## Can Children with These Defects Live a Normal Life?

Yes. Children who get treatment early for a ventricular or atrial septal defect usually live a full, healthy life. They can do normal activities and have no lasting health problems.

Children with an atrioventricular septal defect can also live into old age if they get proper care.

---

## What Are the Signs of a Heart Defect?

Symptoms depend on the size and type of the hole.

- Small holes often cause no symptoms at all.
- In 75 out of 100 babies with a small ventricular septal defect, the hole closes on its own within two years.
- Babies with a large ventricular septal defect may show signs of heart failure by 3 to 4 weeks old. These signs include:
  - Breathing very fast or struggling to breathe
  - Poor feeding and not gaining weight
  - Fast heartbeat
  - Pale skin
  - Wheezing sounds in the chest
  - Frequent lung infections

Some children with a small hole may not have symptoms until they are older. They may get tired more easily than other children.

Children with an atrioventricular septal defect may also have signs of heart failure.

Some children develop **cyanosis**. This means their lips, fingernails, skin, or mouth turn blue or purple. This happens because the blood does not carry enough oxygen.

---

## What Causes These Defects?

The heart wall does not form properly before birth. Doctors do not know exactly why this happens in most cases.

However, some defects are linked to genetic conditions.

- Atrioventricular septal defects often happen in children with Down’s syndrome.
- About half of all children with Down’s syndrome have a heart defect, usually an atrioventricular septal defect.
- In rare cases, a specific gene change can cause a hole in the heart.

---

## How Common Are These Defects?

About 1 in every 100 babies is born with a heart defect.

Of these:
- 50 out of 100 have a ventricular septal defect
- 17 out of 100 have an atrial septal defect
- 3 out of 100 have an atrioventricular septal defect

---

## What Is the Long-Term Outlook?

- A small ventricular septal defect often closes on its own and causes no problems.
- A larger hole makes the heart work harder. This can cause the heart to grow bigger.
- The blood pressure in the lungs can also rise. This forces blood to flow the wrong way through the hole.
- If left untreated, a large hole can be deadly.
- Thanks to modern medicine, most children in Germany with a ventricular septal defect can live a normal life after treatment.

For an atrioventricular septal defect:
- The heart and lungs can become overworked in the first year of life.
- Some children have blue skin or lips because their blood lacks oxygen.
- They may also have trouble breathing.
- Without treatment, life expectancy is much shorter.

An atrial septal defect may close on its own without causing harm. But if it stays open, the heart must work harder. This can lead to:
- Less energy and stamina
- Irregular heartbeat
- Higher risk of blood clots

---

## How Are These Defects Found?

Some heart defects can be found during pregnancy.

### Before Birth

- Doctors use a special ultrasound called a **fetal echocardiogram** to check the baby’s heart.
- This test shows how the heart is working, how blood flows, and if there are any problems.
- A color Doppler ultrasound may also be used to check blood flow between mother and baby. This helps find smaller defects.

### After Birth

- Doctors listen to the heart with a stethoscope. A heart murmur may be a sign of a defect.
- An echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) is the main test used after birth.
- In some cases, a heart catheter test is done. This involves inserting a thin tube into a blood vessel and guiding it to the heart. It helps plan surgery.

---

## How Are These Defects Treated?

- Small holes in the ventricles or atria often close on their own. No treatment is needed.
- Children with a large ventricular septal defect or an atrioventricular septal defect usually need surgery in infancy.
- Surgery closes the hole using a patch. If valves are damaged, they are repaired or replaced.
- If a child has signs of heart failure, medicine can help ease symptoms.
- Large or symptomatic atrial septal defects can be closed using a heart catheter. A small device is placed through a blood vessel to seal the hole.

---

## What Happens After Surgery?

Children who have heart surgery need regular check-ups with a pediatric heart specialist.

Even after a successful operation, there is a small risk of:
- Irregular heartbeat
- Leaking heart valves

Regular visits help catch any problems early.

---

## What Rehab Options Are Available?

Rehabilitation helps children with heart defects get stronger and healthier after treatment.

Family-centered rehab programs focus on:
- Making sure treatment works well
- Building the child’s strength and energy
- Supporting the child’s mental health and confidence

These programs also look for stress in parents and siblings. They offer help when needed.

These services are available at special centers for children and teens up to age 17 with heart conditions.

Ask your child’s heart doctor if your family can join.

---

## Where Can I Get Help?

If your child has a heart defect, you are not alone.

- **Self-help groups** let parents share experiences and get advice.
- You can find these groups through the **NAKOS** website (National Contact and Information Point for Self-Help Groups).
- The website **herzklick.de** offers practical support and information for families.
- This site is run by the **Federal Association for Children with Heart Diseases**.

---

## Where Can I Learn More?

For more medical information and support:
- Visit the website of the **Federal Association for Children with Heart Diseases**
- Visit the website of the **German Heart Foundation**

These sites provide details on care, treatment, and where to get help.

# Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease

More and more people in Europe are getting a condition called non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.  
It often happens because of poor eating habits and not being active enough.  
This article explains what causes it, how it develops, and how you can prevent or manage it.

---

## Quick Facts

- Being overweight or having type 2 diabetes increases your risk.  
- About 20 to 30 out of every 100 adults in developed countries have this condition.  
- Among people who are severely overweight, up to 80 to 90 out of 100 have it.  
- Most people do not know they have it because it often causes no symptoms.  
- Eating better and moving more can help improve or even reverse the condition.  

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

---

## What Is Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease?

Fatty liver disease means fat builds up in the liver.  
This is also called hepatic steatosis.  
It usually starts without causing harm.  
But if not treated, it can lead to serious liver damage over time.

You are more likely to get it if you are severely overweight, have type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, or have changes in how your body uses energy.

A fatty liver is not dangerous at first.  
But it can be a warning sign for more serious liver problems like cirrhosis.

---

## What Are the Signs and Symptoms?

Most people with fatty liver disease feel fine.  
They do not notice any symptoms at all.

Some people report:
- Feeling tired all the time  
- Drinking more water than usual  
- Feeling bloated  
- Trouble sleeping

In later stages, the skin and eyes may turn yellow.  
This is called jaundice.  
It is a sign that the liver is not working well.

---

## What Causes Fatty Liver Disease?

The main causes are:
- Not getting enough physical activity  
- Eating too many high-calorie foods

Certain health conditions also raise your risk:
- Being severely overweight (obesity)  
- Having type 2 diabetes  
- Insulin resistance (when your body does not use insulin well)  
- Metabolic syndrome (a mix of being very overweight, having blood sugar or fat problems, and high blood pressure)  
- Dyslipidemia (a problem with how your body handles fats in the blood). This can be inherited or caused by lifestyle.

Some medicines and genetic factors can also lead to fatty liver disease.

---

## How Common Is It?

- In developed countries, 20 to 30 out of every 100 adults have fatty liver disease.  
- Among people who are severely overweight, 80 to 90 out of 100 have it.  
- Among children with a normal weight, 3 to 10 out of 100 have it.  
- Among children who are overweight, 40 to 70 out of 100 have it.

---

## How Does It Progress?

Fatty liver disease develops slowly.  
It can take years for fat to build up in the liver.  
It usually causes no symptoms at first.  
And it can be reversed if you make healthy changes.

In about 3 out of 10 people, the condition gets worse.  
The liver becomes inflamed. This is called steatohepatitis.  
Inflammation damages liver cells and causes scar tissue.  
Doctors call this fibrosis.

If not treated, fibrosis can get worse.  
It can lead to cirrhosis.  
Cirrhosis is serious scarring of the liver.  
It cannot be undone.  
It can be life threatening if not treated.

---

## How Can You Prevent It?

You can lower your risk by:
- Eating a healthy diet  
- Being physically active every day

For more on how to stay active and healthy, read the article called *Health through exercise*.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use blood tests to check for signs of liver problems.  
An ultrasound scan can show if fat is building up in the liver.

If the ultrasound is unclear, or if the doctor wants to know how advanced the disease is, they may take a small sample of liver tissue.  
This is called a biopsy.  
It helps check for inflammation or scarring.

The doctor will also rule out other causes of liver fat.  
These include:
- Alcoholic fatty liver disease (caused by heavy drinking)  
- Chronic hepatitis (caused by hepatitis B or C viruses)  
- Wilson’s disease (a rare inherited condition where copper builds up in the liver)

---

## How Is It Treated?

The best treatment is to:
- Stop drinking alcohol  
- Lose weight

Doctors will give advice on healthy eating.  
They may also help you create a physical activity plan.

Most people are told to lose up to 7% of their body weight.  
If the liver is already inflamed, losing up to 10% is recommended.

Sometimes, medicine is used to help with weight loss.  
But lifestyle changes are the most important part of treatment.

# Psoriatic Arthritis

Psoriatic arthritis is a long-term condition that causes joint pain and stiffness. It often happens in people who already have psoriasis. The condition can make daily life harder. Medicine can help reduce pain and swelling.

---

## Quick Facts

- Psoriatic arthritis causes joint pain, stiffness, and tiredness.
- It often affects the hands, feet, elbows, knees, neck, or spine.
- About 1 in 4 people with psoriasis will get psoriatic arthritis at some point.
- The body’s immune system wrongly attacks its own joints, causing inflammation.
- Doctors usually treat it with medicine. Physical therapy or occupational therapy may also help, depending on the person’s needs.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Psoriatic Arthritis?

Psoriatic arthritis is a long-term joint inflammation. It can happen in people who have psoriasis. Psoriasis is a skin condition that causes red, scaly patches.

This joint condition causes pain, stiffness, and swelling. It can also cause tiredness. Over time, it can affect sleep, energy levels, and the ability to focus.

There are treatments that can ease symptoms. These treatments also help protect the joints from lasting damage.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main signs of psoriatic arthritis are:

- Pain in the joints
- Swollen joints
- Stiff joints
- Feeling very tired

Swollen joints often feel warm and hurt when touched. Stiffness is usually worst in the morning. Moving around usually helps reduce the stiffness.

Many joints can be affected. Some people have swelling in more than five joints. Commonly affected areas include:

- Hands
- Feet
- Elbows
- Knees
- Neck
- Spine

In later stages, the small joints at the tips of fingers and toes may become deformed.

In some people, the tendons and the sheaths around them also become inflamed.

---

## What Causes Psoriatic Arthritis?

The body’s immune system is supposed to protect against illness. In psoriatic arthritis, the immune system goes wrong. It attacks the body’s own joints.

This is called an autoimmune response. When this happens, the body makes extra chemicals that cause inflammation. The joints become inflamed and painful.

---

## Who Is at Risk?

You are more likely to get psoriatic arthritis if:

- A parent or sibling has psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis.

---

## How Common Is It?

About 25 percent of people with psoriasis will develop psoriatic arthritis. It can start at any age, but it most often begins between the ages of 30 and 50.

---

## What Is the Long-Term Outlook?

In most cases, joint problems start many years after skin symptoms appear. But sometimes, joint pain shows up before any skin changes are seen.

There is no clear link between how bad the skin rash is and how bad the joint pain is.

Psoriatic arthritis is a lifelong condition. It does not go away. The course of the disease is hard to predict.

Some people only have a few joints affected. Others may have more joints involved over time.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several methods to confirm psoriatic arthritis:

- They ask about your health history and your family’s health.
- They do a physical exam to check for joint changes, especially in the hands and feet.
- Blood tests can show certain proteins. These help tell psoriatic arthritis apart from rheumatoid arthritis.
- Blood tests also check uric acid levels. This rules out gout as a cause of joint pain.
- X-rays and ultrasound scans help doctors see joint damage and distinguish between types of arthritis.

> **Important:** About 1 in 10 people with psoriatic arthritis do not have visible skin changes. This makes diagnosis harder.

---

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure for psoriatic arthritis. Treatment focuses on:

- Reducing pain and swelling
- Keeping joints working well
- Preventing long-term joint damage

Medicine is a key part of treatment. For mild joint pain in the knees, elbows, or hands, painkillers like diclofenac, ibuprofen, or naproxen may help.

If pain does not improve, or if the doctor thinks the condition may get worse, stronger medicines are used. These medicines reduce inflammation and can slow or stop joint damage.

Physical therapy or occupational therapy can help with movement, strength, and daily tasks. Orthopedic aids like special insoles can also ease discomfort.

---

## Living with Psoriatic Arthritis

You can take steps to feel better and slow the condition’s progress:

- Stay active with regular exercise.
- Do not smoke.
- If you are severely overweight, try to lose weight.

Learning about your condition helps. Knowing what to expect makes it easier to manage. Accepting the condition as part of life can also help reduce stress.

For more information on lifestyle changes and treatment, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

# Testicular Cancer – Simple Explanation

This page explains testicular cancer in clear, everyday language. It is not a substitute for medical advice. Always talk to a doctor if you have concerns.

---

## What Is Testicular Cancer?

Testicular cancer is a type of cancer that starts in the testicles.  
It happens in men.  
The cancer usually begins in the cells that make sperm.  
Doctors call this a germ-cell tumor.

There are two main types:
- **Seminoma**: This starts only in the sperm-making cells.
- **Non-seminoma**: This is a mix of different tumor types. It can include cells like embryonic cancer, yolk sac cells, or teratomas. Sometimes it also has seminoma parts.

---

## What Are the Signs of Testicular Cancer?

Many men notice changes in their testicles themselves.  
A painless lump or swelling in the scrotum is a common sign.  
Some men feel a heavy or dragging feeling in the scrotum or groin.  
You might feel a hard spot inside the testicle or on its surface.  
Pain in the testicle can happen, but it is not always present.  
Some men develop larger breast tissue or chest pain. This is due to hormones made by the tumor.  
Fluid can build up around the testicle. This is called a hydrocele.  
Some men may have trouble getting a partner pregnant.

---

## Who Is at Risk?

Certain things can raise your risk of getting testicular cancer. These include:
- Having had cancer in one testicle before.
- Having a testicle that did not move down into the scrotum during childhood. This is called an undescended testicle. Even if it was fixed, the risk stays.
- Having a brother or father with testicular cancer.
- Having fertility problems.

Men with these risk factors should check their testicles regularly.  
They should also see a urologist (a doctor who treats the urinary and reproductive system) as advised.

But remember:  
Even men with no known risk factors can get testicular cancer.  
Sometimes it happens for no clear reason.

---

## How Common Is It?

About 4,100 men in Germany get testicular cancer each year.  
It is the most common cancer in men aged 25 to 45.  
In this age group, it makes up about one in four cancers.

---

## Is There a Screening Test?

There is no official screening program for testicular cancer in Germany.  
But men aged 45 and older can have a free yearly check-up that includes a testicle exam.

**For younger men (under 45):**  
If you are at higher risk, talk to your doctor about whether you need regular checks.

**Self-exam is important:**  
Boys from puberty onward and all men should check their testicles regularly.  
Look for any changes.  
If you notice anything unusual, see a doctor right away.

You can learn how to do a self-exam and what to look for on the website of the German Society of Urology.

---

## What Should You Do If You Suspect Cancer?

If you notice any change in your testicles, see a doctor.  
The doctor will:
- Feel your testicles with their fingers.
- Use an ultrasound machine to look at the testicles.
- Check your abdomen and groin area.
- Take a blood sample to check for certain markers that can be high in testicular cancer.

---

## How Is the Diagnosis Confirmed?

If the doctor still suspects cancer after the first tests, surgery is needed.  
The surgeon makes a cut in the groin to see the testicle.  
They can look at it directly.  
If needed, they take a small sample of tissue (a biopsy) to test.  
If cancer is confirmed, the entire affected testicle is removed.

---

## Has the Cancer Spread?

The doctor will check if the cancer has spread to other parts of the body.  
This usually includes:
- An ultrasound of the abdomen.
- A CT scan of the pelvis, abdomen, and chest.

You can learn more about CT scans on the website of the German Cancer Research Center.

---

## How Is Testicular Cancer Treated?

The good news is that testicular cancer has a very high cure rate.  
Even if the cancer is advanced, it can still be cured.  
It is best to be treated at a center that specializes in testicular cancer.

Treatment depends on the type of tumor and how far it has spread.

### Surgery

The main treatment is surgery to remove the affected testicle.  
This is done through a cut in the groin.  
The surgery is called orchiectomy.  
You will be asleep during the operation.

In some cases, the doctor may also remove lymph nodes in the back of the abdomen.

### After Surgery

What happens next depends on the type and stage of cancer.  
Options include:
- Chemotherapy (medicine to kill cancer cells).
- Radiotherapy (high-energy beams to destroy cancer cells).
- Monitoring without further treatment.

Monitoring is becoming more common.  
It helps avoid unnecessary treatment and side effects, especially in young men.

**Important:**  
Before treatment starts, talk to your doctor about saving your sperm.  
Sperm can be frozen and stored.  
This allows you to have children later, if needed.  
Since July 2022, health insurance covers the cost of freezing sperm.

You can find more about treatment options and side effects on the website of the German Cancer Research Center.

---

## Can You Have Rehabilitation?

Yes. Cancer can be hard on your body and mind.  
Rehabilitation helps you recover.  
It can help you return to work and daily life.  
Some rehab clinics specialize in helping young men.

Talk to your doctor about rehab.  
They can recommend a program and confirm your need.  
Hospital social workers, cancer advice centers, and your health insurance can also help.

More information is available on the website of the German Cancer Research Center.

---

## What Is Aftercare Like?

Aftercare aims to:
- Catch a return of cancer early.
- Prevent or treat any side effects from the cancer or treatment.

The risk of cancer returning is highest in the first two years after treatment.  
But rare late returns can happen even 5 to 10 years later.

Aftercare is close and regular at first.  
You will have many check-ups each year.

Your doctor will:
- Examine you physically.
- Test your blood for tumor markers.
- Use imaging tests like CT or MRI scans.

### Long-Term Aftercare

After 5 years, you may still need follow-up care for life.  
The type and frequency of checks depend on your health, treatment, and lifestyle.

---

## How Does Testicular Cancer Affect Daily Life?

### Fertility

Many men already have reduced fertility when they are diagnosed.  
Surgery, chemotherapy, and sometimes radiotherapy can make it worse.

Before treatment, talk to your doctor about freezing your sperm.  
This is now covered by health insurance.

### Low Testosterone

Some men develop low levels of testosterone after treatment.  
This can cause:
- Weight gain.
- High blood pressure.
- Low energy.
- Mood changes.

This can be treated with testosterone medicine.

### Testicular Prosthesis

Some men feel self-conscious after losing a testicle.  
You can choose to have a fake testicle implanted.  
This is called a prosthesis.  
Check with your health insurance to see if it covers the cost.

---

## Where Can You Get Help?

Look for hospitals with certified specialists in testicular cancer.  
Some centers offer second opinions.

You can find a list of certified centers on the **OncoMap** website.

The German Society of Urology has a website called **Hodencheck**.  
It gives clear advice on:
- How to spot early signs.
- How to do a self-exam.

For more help with daily life and support, visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center**.

You can also contact them:
- By phone: **0800 420 30 40** (free call)
- By email: **krebsinformationsdienst@dkfz.de**

They are available to answer your questions.

# Seborrheic Dermatitis

Red, flaky patches on the scalp or face are signs of seborrheic dermatitis.  
The symptoms can be mild one time and worse another.  
Men are more likely to get this condition than women.  
It is not contagious.  
It is a long-term skin problem.  
Special creams and shampoos can help reduce the symptoms.

---

## Quick Facts

- Seborrheic dermatitis is a long-term skin inflammation.  
- It is a type of eczema that comes back over time.  
- It causes red patches with oily, yellowish flakes.  
- These patches are most common on the scalp and face.  
- The patches are usually not itchy.  
- Doctors think it may be caused by too much oil on the skin.  
- It may also be linked to a yeast that lives on the skin.  
- A weak immune system can also play a role.  
- If it starts during teenage years or adulthood, it often comes back.  
- Anti-fungal creams or cortisone creams can help treat the skin.  

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Seborrheic Dermatitis?

Seborrheic dermatitis is also called seborrheic eczema or seborrheic psoriasis.  
It causes red patches with oily, flaky skin.  
It mostly affects the scalp and face.  
The patches are not usually itchy.  
Doctors believe it happens because of too much oil on the skin.  
It may also be caused by a yeast called Malassezia furfur.  
Other possible causes include stress, genetics, hormones, and weak immunity.  
People with weak immune systems may get a more severe form.  
This form can affect the whole body and is harder to treat.  
In babies, the rash often goes away on its own within a year.  
It does not come back in most cases.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may see yellowish, shiny, oily flakes on the skin.  
On light skin, the patches look red.  
On dark skin, the patches look lighter than the rest of the skin.  
Itching is rare.  

The patches often appear in areas with many oil glands, such as:  
- The scalp and hairline  
- Between the eyebrows  
- The cheeks, especially near the nose and mouth  

The rash can also spread to other areas.  
Common spots include:  
- Above the breastbone  
- On the back near the spine  
- Under the breasts  
- In the armpits  
- In the groin area  
- In men, sometimes in the genital area  
- In babies, usually on the head  

---

## What Causes It?

Multiple things may cause seborrheic dermatitis.  
Too much oil from the skin’s oil glands is one factor.  
A yeast called Malassezia furfur is also involved.  
Other possible causes include:  
- Bacteria on the skin  
- Stress  
- Family history  
- Hormones  

Nervous system problems like Parkinson’s disease can make it worse.  
A weak immune system can also increase the risk.  
People with weak immunity may get a more serious form.  
This form affects the whole body and is harder to treat.

---

## How Common Is It?

Seborrheic dermatitis affects between 3% and 10% of people.  
Men are more likely to get it than women.  
Most people first notice it in young adulthood or after age fifty.  
It is a long-term condition.  
Symptoms can come and go.  
Some people have no symptoms for a while.  
This often happens in the summer.  
But the condition usually returns in winter or during stressful times.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor can usually tell if you have seborrheic dermatitis by looking at your skin.  
They will check for flaky, red patches in common spots.  
They will ask about your medical history.  
They will do a physical exam.  

They may rule out other skin problems, such as:  
- Atopic dermatitis (neurodermatitis)  
- Psoriasis  

These other conditions usually cause itching.  
Atopic dermatitis often causes blisters.  
On light skin, the red patches have blurry edges.  
On dark skin, the patches look darker than the rest.  
Atopic dermatitis also causes small hard bumps instead of blisters.  

Tests are rarely needed.  
A skin swab may be taken if a bacterial infection is suspected.  
A skin sample (biopsy) is not usually required.

---

## How Is It Treated?

For teens and adults, you can use special treatments on the skin.  
Examples include:  
- Shampoos with tar  
- Creams with salicylic acid  
- Anti-fungal creams or shampoos  
- Creams or gels with cortisone  

Oral medicine is usually not needed.  
Some people use UVB light therapy.  
Sunlight can help improve symptoms.  

There is no cure yet.  
The condition can last a lifetime.  

Most babies do not need treatment.  
The rash usually goes away on its own.

---

## Living With Seborrheic Dermatitis

The condition is not dangerous.  
But it can be hard to live with.  
Flaky patches on the face are easy to see.  
This can affect self-confidence.  
The condition can last for years.  

If it causes a lot of stress, talk to your doctor.  
They may suggest behavioral therapy.  
This can help you manage your feelings and reduce stress.  

Avoid covering the patches with thick makeup.  
This can clog pores and make things worse.  
Light makeup now and then is okay.  

Use mild, non-greasy skin care products.  
They are best for sensitive skin.  

You do not need special sun protection.  
Use regular sunscreen based on your skin type.  
Sunlight and fresh air can help ease symptoms.  
Use non-greasy sunscreen for best results.

# Kidney Stones and Ureteral Stones

Kidney stones are small, hard pieces that form in the kidneys.  
They can move from the kidneys into the tubes that carry urine to the bladder.  
These tubes are called ureters.  
When a stone moves into a ureter, it is then called a ureteral stone.  

Most people who get kidney stones are between 40 and 60 years old.  
Larger stones can cause strong pain.

---

## Quick Facts

- Kidney stones form in the part of the kidney that collects urine.  
- If a stone moves into a ureter, it is called a ureteral stone.  
- Many small stones pass out of the body in the urine within a few days.  
- Larger stones often cause pain and usually need treatment.  

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

---

## What Are Kidney Stones?

Kidney stones are hard, solid pieces that form in the kidneys.  
They can move into the ureters and become ureteral stones.  
Doctors also call them urinary stones.

Not all kidney stones need treatment.  
Very small stones often move into the bladder and pass out in the urine.  
This can happen within days or weeks.  
For small stones, doctors often recommend:  
- Drinking plenty of water  
- Taking pain relief medicine  
- Staying active  

For medium-sized stones, certain medicines can help.  
These medicines relax the muscles in the lower urinary tract.  
This makes it easier for the stone to pass.

Larger stones usually need medical treatment.  
They may need to be removed with surgery or broken apart using sound waves.  
A large stone can get stuck in the ureter or at the opening of the kidney.  
This can cause severe pain and other problems.  
The best treatment depends on the size, type, and location of the stone.

Many people get kidney stones more than once.  
To prevent this, it is important to find out what caused the stones.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Small stones often cause no symptoms at all.  
Some people feel a dull ache in the back or side.  
They may not even know they have a stone.  
Sometimes stones are found by chance during an X-ray or ultrasound scan.  
Others only notice a stone when they pass it in the urine.

Symptoms usually start when a stone blocks the flow of urine or moves through the ureter.  
The main symptom is pain.  
The pain can be mild or very strong.  
Where you feel the pain depends on where the stone is.

The pain is often worst when the stone moves through narrow parts of the ureter.  
One such narrow spot is where the ureter joins the bladder.  
At this point, the pain often starts in the side.  
It can spread to the lower belly and groin.  
This type of pain is called renal colic.

Renal colic comes in waves.  
It gets worse, then eases, then comes back.  
It can last from 20 to 60 minutes.  
Some people also have a high temperature or headaches.  
They may bend over or move around trying to find a position that feels better.

Other possible symptoms include:

- Pain when urinating  
- Needing to go to the bathroom often or urgently  
- Blood in the urine  
- Pain that spreads to the genitals

---

## Why Do Kidney Stones Form?

Kidney stones are like tiny crystals.  
They form when certain substances build up in the urine.  
Most stones are made of calcium salts.  
But some are made of uric acid or other minerals.

- About 80 out of 100 stones are made of calcium.  
- 5 to 10 out of 100 stones are made of uric acid.  
- 10 out of 100 stones are made of a mineral called struvite.  
- Stones made of other materials are rare.

Normally, these substances stay dissolved in the urine.  
But in some people, the levels rise too high.  
This can happen because of certain health problems.

For example:  
- Overactive glands in the neck (parathyroid glands) can raise calcium levels in the urine.  
- Gout can raise uric acid levels in the urine.  
- Some people inherit a condition that causes stones made of a substance called cysteine.

Some substances in the urine help prevent stones.  
One of these is citrate.  
If there is not enough citrate, stones are more likely to form.  
Chronic diarrhea can lower citrate levels.

Diet can also play a role.  
Foods like rhubarb have a lot of oxalic acid.  
Liver and other organ meats can raise uric acid levels.  
Eating these foods may increase the risk of stones.

Not drinking enough water is another risk.  
Low fluid intake makes the urine more concentrated.  
This increases the chance of stones forming.

The acidity of the urine also matters.  
Most stones form when the urine is too acidic.  
Stones can also form if the body loses too many acids, for example due to a urinary infection.

Some medicines can change the urine or even form crystals.  
This raises the risk of kidney stones.

Some people are born with kidney problems.  
For example:  
- Kidney cysts (fluid-filled sacs in the kidneys)  
- Horseshoe kidney (when the two kidneys are joined at the bottom)  

These conditions can increase the chance of stones.

---

## How Common Are Kidney Stones?

Kidney stones are fairly common.  
In the United States, at least 1 in 10 people will get a kidney or ureteral stone in their lifetime.  
In Germany, 1 to 2 out of every 100 people get them each year.  
Men are more likely than women to get them.  
They can happen at any age, even in children.  
The most common age group is 40 to 60.

---

## How Long Does It Take to Pass a Stone?

The time it takes to pass a stone varies.  
Small stones often pass within a week or two.  
If a stone has not passed after 4 weeks, treatment is usually needed.

Stones only cause symptoms when they enter the ureter.  
The size of the stone affects whether it can pass on its own:

- Stones smaller than 5 millimeters usually pass on their own.  
- About half of stones between 5 and 10 millimeters pass without treatment.  
- Stones larger than 10 millimeters usually need treatment.

> **Important:** Up to half of people who have had a kidney stone will get another one within 5 years.  
> Prevention is key.

If stones are not treated, they can block the ureters.  
This can lead to infection.  
Urine may build up and press on the kidneys.  
This is rare, though, because most stones are treated before problems happen.  
Signs of infection include:  
- High temperature  
- Shaking chills  
- Pain in the side or lower back  
- Nausea and vomiting

---

## How Can You Prevent Kidney Stones?

If the cause is not found and fixed, stones will likely come back.  
Prevention depends on the type of stone and what caused it.  
Doctors test the stone in a lab to find out what it is made of.  
To help with this, collect any stones you pass in the urine.  
Use a sieve or filter to catch them.

Based on the results, your doctor may suggest:  
- Eating less meat or salt  
- Taking medicine to change the pH of your urine  
- Reducing calcium or uric acid in your urine  

Your doctor will also consider your personal risk of getting more stones.

Another key step is drinking enough fluids.  
Doctors recommend at least two liters of fluid a day.  
Talk to your doctor to find the right amount for you.

For more details on prevention, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## How Are Kidney Stones Diagnosed?

The most common symptoms can point to kidney stones.  
But they are not always clear enough to be certain.  
An ultrasound scan can show most kidney and ureteral stones.  
It is safe and does not use radiation.

Sometimes doctors use a CT scan.  
This gives a more detailed picture of the stone’s size and location.

An X-ray of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder is less accurate.  
It can show calcium stones well.  
But it may miss struvite stones.  
Uric acid stones do not show up at all on X-rays.  
Still, X-rays can help check if treatment worked.

Blood and urine tests are also important.  
They can show signs of infection.  
They can also reveal high levels of calcium or uric acid.

---

## How Are Kidney Stones Treated?

Treatment depends on the size and location of the stone.

- Small stones that are not causing pain can be left to pass on their own.  
- Pain can be managed with over-the-counter painkillers like ibuprofen, paracetamol, or diclofenac.  
- For severe pain, stronger medicines (like opioids) may be used.

For stones in the ureter that are between 5 and 10 millimeters:  
- Doctors may try medicine to relax the muscles in the ureter.  
- This can help the stone pass more easily.

Larger stones usually need treatment.  
The method depends on the stone’s size and location.  
Options include:

- Using sound waves to break the stone into small pieces  
- Using a small camera (endoscopy) to remove or break up the stone
