# Type 1 Diabetes

Type 1 diabetes is a long-term health condition. People with this condition must take insulin every day. Their body no longer makes insulin or makes very little of it.

Insulin is a natural substance in the body. It helps the body use food for energy. Without insulin, the body cannot use food properly.

Today, insulin treatment can fit into daily life more easily than in the past.

---

## Quick Facts

- Diabetes mellitus is a health condition that affects many parts of the body.
- In type 1 diabetes, the body makes little or no insulin.
- Insulin is a hormone. It travels in the blood and helps control how the body uses food.
- Without insulin, the body cannot get energy from food.
- People with type 1 diabetes must take insulin every day.
- Insulin treatment can be adjusted to fit each person’s needs.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Diabetes Mellitus?

Diabetes mellitus is a condition that affects how the body uses energy from food. There are two main types: type 1 and type 2.

In type 1 diabetes, the body stops making insulin.  
In type 2 diabetes, the body does not use insulin well.

Insulin is a hormone. It acts like a key that opens the doors to cells so sugar from food can enter. Without insulin, sugar builds up in the blood.

---

## What Are the Signs of Type 1 Diabetes?

If not treated, blood sugar levels stay too high. At first, this may not cause obvious symptoms.

Common signs include:

- Needing to urinate more often  
- Feeling very thirsty  
- Feeling tired and weak  
- Feeling sick to the stomach  
- Feeling dizzy

If blood sugar gets very high, a person may lose consciousness. This is called a diabetic coma. It is a serious emergency.

For more on high and low blood sugar, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

---

## What Causes Type 1 Diabetes?

In most cases, the body’s immune system attacks the cells in the pancreas that make insulin. These cells are called beta cells.

Over time, the immune system destroys these cells. This means the body can no longer make insulin.

Some people have a higher chance of getting type 1 diabetes if it runs in their family. This is called a genetic risk.

It is not yet clear how much other factors, like certain infections or environmental conditions, play a role.

---

## How Common Is Type 1 Diabetes?

In Germany, about 200,000 people have type 1 diabetes.  
This includes around 30,000 children and teens under 19.

Each year, about two out of every 10,000 children are diagnosed with type 1 diabetes.

---

## How Does Type 1 Diabetes Progress?

Type 1 diabetes usually starts in childhood, adolescence, or early adulthood.  
Because of this, it is sometimes called juvenile diabetes.

It is rare in older adults.

Without treatment, high blood sugar can cause serious problems quickly.  
Symptoms include extreme thirst, needing to urinate often, and feeling very weak.

Taking insulin helps relieve these symptoms fast.

### Possible Long-Term Effects

If blood sugar stays too high for a long time, it can damage blood vessels.

Damage to small blood vessels can lead to:

- Vision problems, including blindness  
- Nerve damage, causing numbness or pain  
- Kidney damage

Damage to large blood vessels increases the risk of:

- Heart attack  
- Stroke

Poor blood flow and nerve damage can also cause small cuts or sores on the feet to go unnoticed.  
If not treated, these can become serious. This condition is called diabetic foot.

---

## How Is Type 1 Diabetes Diagnosed?

If doctors suspect diabetes, they test blood sugar levels throughout the day.

They check blood sugar before eating and again several times after meals.

They also do a blood test called HbA1c.  
This test shows the average blood sugar level over the past two to three months.

---

## How Is Type 1 Diabetes Treated?

People with type 1 diabetes check their blood sugar several times a day.  
They take insulin every day using a syringe, insulin pen, or insulin pump.

Insulin replaces the missing hormone. It helps lower blood sugar.

It is important to take the right amount of insulin.  
Too little insulin can raise blood sugar too high.  
Too much insulin can lower blood sugar too much.

When insulin treatment works well, symptoms go away.  
It also helps prevent long-term health problems.

There are many types of insulin and treatment tools.  
Insulin pumps and continuous glucose monitors can make treatment easier.

Blood sugar levels are affected by:

- What you eat and drink  
- How much physical activity you do  
- The time of day  
- Illness or infections  
- Other medicines  
- Hormonal changes

### Important Tips for Treatment

To stay healthy, people with type 1 diabetes must:

- Understand their condition  
- Manage their health carefully every day  
- Work closely with their doctor

It is also important to check blood pressure regularly.  
In addition to insulin, other medicines may help prevent heart and blood vessel problems.

For more on how to use insulin pumps, pens, and syringes, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

---

## What Is Life Like with Type 1 Diabetes?

There is no cure for type 1 diabetes.  
But most people can live a normal, active life with it.

In the past, people with diabetes had to follow strict schedules.  
They had to time insulin, meals, and exercise very carefully.  
This made daily life very rigid.

Today, treatment is much more flexible.  
People can adjust insulin and meals more easily.

Still, managing diabetes takes effort, focus, and care.  
This is not always easy. It can be harder for young people.

Like with any long-term condition that needs daily medicine, some people forget to take their insulin or medicine.

Some people feel fine even when they skip treatment.  
But this can be dangerous.  
Skipping treatment can lead to serious, lasting health problems.

# Hernias

A hernia happens when part of the bowel or a thin layer inside the belly pushes through a weak spot in the belly wall.

## Quick Facts

- Whether a hernia causes problems depends on its size and location.
- The most common type is an inguinal hernia. It mainly affects men.
- Most hernias do not go away on their own if you do nothing.
- Lifting heavy things, coughing, or straining can make a hernia bigger.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Hernia?

Most hernias happen when part of the bowel or the lining of the belly pushes through a weak spot in the belly wall. The lining of the belly is called the peritoneum. It covers most of the organs inside the belly.

Most hernias look like a bulge or pouch on the outside of the body. The bulge is called the hernial sac. Inside it can be part of the bowel, the stomach, or other organs.

Not all hernias cause symptoms. But some cause pain, a burning feeling, pressure, or a pulling sensation. These feelings often get worse when you strain, lift, or push hard.

Some hernias are large and clearly visible. They can be uncomfortable and upsetting.

If the bowel gets stuck in the hernia, you may have belly pain, constipation, or a blockage in the bowel. In men, an inguinal hernia can push into the scrotum and make it swell.

Sudden, severe pain in the hernia area, along with nausea or vomiting, can mean the hernia is trapped. This is serious. It can lead to infection in the belly lining (peritonitis).

Hiatal hernias are different. They happen inside the body. The opening in the diaphragm (the muscle that separates the chest from the belly) gets bigger. Part of the stomach or belly lining moves up into the chest. These hernias are not visible from the outside.

Hiatal hernias can cause heartburn, trouble swallowing, or trouble breathing. These symptoms can be treated with medicine.

Surgery can fix most hernias.

---

## What Causes Hernias?

Some people are born with weak belly muscles or weak tissue. Others get weaker tissue as they age.

Illnesses or surgery can also weaken the belly wall.

Being very overweight increases pressure in the belly. This raises the risk of incisional and umbilical hernias. But it does not raise the risk of inguinal hernias.

Tumors or fluid buildup in the belly can also increase pressure.

Hernias are more common in pregnant women.

Smoking and conditions like diabetes can slow healing after surgery. This increases the risk of incisional hernias.

Coughing, straining, or lifting heavy things can make an existing hernia grow. It is not clear if these actions can cause hernias in the first place. For example, it is not certain if lifting heavy things causes inguinal hernias.

---

## How Common Are Hernias?

Inguinal hernias are the most common.  
- About 25 out of 100 men will get one in their lifetime.  
- About 2 out of 100 women will get one.

The next most common types are umbilical and incisional hernias.

After belly surgery, up to 15 out of 100 people get an incisional hernia.

Epigastric, femoral, and hiatal hernias are less common.

---

## How Do Hernias Develop?

If left untreated, hernias usually get bigger over time. They may become more visible and cause more problems.

Sometimes the hernia gets trapped. This can block the bowel. This causes severe pain, nausea, and vomiting.

Femoral hernias are more likely to get trapped than inguinal hernias. This is because the weak spot is narrower.

If blood flow is cut off, the tissue in the hernia can die. This can cause infection in the belly lining (peritonitis).

In rare cases, the skin over the hernia can thin and break. The area may become inflamed or the hernia may burst through the skin.

A trapped hernia is an emergency. It must be treated with surgery within a few hours. If you think you have a trapped hernia, call emergency services (112) right away or get to the hospital.

---

## How Can Hernias Be Prevented?

Prevention depends on the type of hernia.

After open belly surgery, avoid heavy lifting for a while. This helps prevent incisional hernias.

If the risk is high, doctors may place a synthetic mesh during surgery to strengthen the belly wall.

People who are overweight can lower their risk of incisional and umbilical hernias by losing weight. But weight loss does not lower the risk of inguinal hernias.

It is not clear if lifting heavy things causes inguinal hernias.

Stopping smoking helps wounds heal better. This lowers the risk of incisional hernias after surgery.

Treating medical conditions like diabetes and anemia also helps wounds heal. This reduces the risk of incisional hernias.

---

## How Is a Hernia Diagnosed?

Doctors can often see a hernia just by looking and feeling.

You will be asked to stand. Then the doctor will ask you to tighten your belly muscles and cough. This makes the hernia more visible.

Next, you will lie down. This helps the doctor feel the size of the hernia and check if it can be pushed back into the belly.

The doctor may use a stethoscope to listen for bowel sounds inside the hernia.

Sometimes an ultrasound scan is done. X-rays, CT scans, or MRI scans are rarely needed.

---

## How Is a Hernia Treated?

Surgery is the only way to fix a hernia.

The surgeon pushes the hernia back into the belly. They close the weak spot with stitches. A thin synthetic mesh is usually added to strengthen the belly wall and prevent the hernia from coming back.

There are two types of surgery:

- **Open surgery:** A larger cut is made at the hernia site.
- **Minimally invasive surgery (keyhole surgery):** The surgeon makes a few small cuts. A tiny camera and tools are inserted through these cuts.

The type of surgery used depends on the kind and size of the hernia.

**Important:** Not all hernias need surgery.

If a hernia is not causing pain or problems, and the risk of complications is low, surgery may not be needed.

This is often true for very old, weak, or seriously ill people with a hernia that is not an immediate danger.

But most men with an inguinal hernia are advised to have surgery.

Hernia supports or belts were once used. These are tight, belt-like bandages meant to hold the hernia in place. Doctors no longer recommend them. They do not fix the hernia. They can cause pressure sores and other problems.

# Dengue Fever – Simple Explanation

Dengue fever is a serious illness caused by a virus. It spreads when certain mosquitoes bite infected people and then bite others.

Some cases are very serious and need hospital care. If you are traveling to areas where dengue is common, protect yourself from mosquito bites.

---

## Quick Facts

- Dengue is common in tropical and warm regions.
- It spreads through bites from Aedes mosquitoes.
- Most people get flu-like symptoms. Recovery can take weeks.
- In rare cases, dengue can cause severe bleeding and dangerous drops in blood pressure.
- There is no medicine to kill the dengue virus.
- Doctors can treat the symptoms to help you feel better.
- Before you travel, check if dengue is a risk in your destination. Take steps to avoid mosquito bites.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Dengue Fever?

Dengue fever is a virus that spreads through the bite of a mosquito.

The virus is found in tropical and warm areas of Asia, Latin America, and Africa. That’s why it is called a tropical disease.

There have been a few cases in non-tropical areas, like southern Europe.

Around 400 million people get infected with the dengue virus each year. Travelers to high-risk areas are at risk too.

Always learn about dengue before you travel. Take steps to protect yourself.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Dengue can be mild, severe, or cause no symptoms at all.

Symptoms usually start 4 to 10 days after being bitten.

### Mild Dengue

Most people have flu-like symptoms or no symptoms.

Common signs include:
- High fever
- Chills
- Severe headaches
- Pain in bones, joints, and muscles
- Nausea and vomiting
- A rash that looks like measles

Most people feel better after 2 to 7 days. But it can take weeks to feel fully well again.

### Severe Dengue

Some people get a dangerous form of dengue. This is more likely in children, young adults, and people who had dengue before.

This severe form is called hemorrhagic dengue. It means serious bleeding can happen.

It usually starts about 5 days after the fever goes down.

Signs of severe dengue include:
- Feeling restless or anxious
- Cold sweats
- Fast heartbeat

The blood vessels become leaky. The number of platelets (cells that help blood clot) drops. This makes bleeding worse.

Blood pressure falls. The body does not get enough blood. Organs like the lungs, liver, kidneys, and later the heart and brain, do not get enough blood.

This can lead to shock and organ failure. This is called dengue shock syndrome.

Without treatment, severe dengue is often deadly. But if treated in a hospital, 99 out of 100 people survive.

---

## How Does Dengue Spread?

Dengue spreads mainly through bites from Aedes mosquitoes. These mosquitoes are active during the day.

The most common carrier is the Egyptian tiger mosquito (Aedes aegypti).

The virus can also spread from people to mosquitoes. For example:
- An infected person is bitten by a mosquito.
- The mosquito gets the virus.
- The same mosquito bites others and spreads the virus.

This is why dengue spreads easily in homes where one person is infected.

In rare cases:
- A pregnant woman can pass the virus to her unborn baby.
- The virus can spread through blood or organ donations, but this is very rare.

### Four Types of the Virus

There are four different types of the dengue virus: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4.

After recovering from one type, you are protected for life against that type.

You may also get some short-term protection against the other types. But this only lasts one to two years.

Because there are four types, you can get dengue up to four times.

The second infection is more likely to be severe. The body’s first response to dengue can actually make the next infection worse.

---

## Who Is at Risk?

Dengue does not occur in Germany. It only happens in tropical and warm countries.

Your risk when traveling depends on:
- Where you are going
- How long you stay
- The time of year
- Whether you use mosquito protection
- How common dengue is in your destination
- If you have had dengue before

> **Important:** If you had dengue before, you are more likely to get a severe case if you get infected with a different type of the virus.

Always check the dengue risk in your travel area before you go. Take steps to avoid mosquito bites.

For current health information about foreign countries, visit the website of the German Federal Foreign Office (Auswärtiges Amt).

---

## How Common Is Dengue?

About 4 billion people live in areas where dengue can spread.

Nearly 130 countries are at risk. Most are in Asia. Others are in Central and South America.

### Worldwide

- Around 400 million people get infected with the dengue virus each year.
- Only 1 in 4 people get sick. The other 3 in 4 have no symptoms.
- The number of cases has increased sharply over the past 20 years. It is now eight times higher.
- Deaths from dengue have quadrupled between 2000 and 2015.

Possible reasons:
- More people living in big cities
- Easier travel around the world
- Climate change

### In Germany

Each year, 600 to 800 people in Germany get dengue after returning from travel.

Most cases come from South and Southeast Asia, and Central and South America.

So far, very few severe cases have been reported in Germany.

---

## How Can You Protect Yourself?

The best way to avoid dengue is to avoid mosquito bites.

Use several methods together for the best protection.

### Protect Your Body

- Use mosquito repellent on your skin. Choose products with DEET, IR3535, or icaridin.
- Wear light-colored clothes with long sleeves and long pants.
- Use repellent on your clothes too.
- Be extra careful during the day. Aedes mosquitoes bite during daylight.
- They can also bite in the evening or at night near lights.

### Protect Your Home

- Use air conditioning.
- Keep windows and doors closed or covered with screens.
- Sleep under mosquito nets.
- These steps help keep mosquitoes out of your living and sleeping areas.

The German Foreign Office has a free leaflet with more tips on how to avoid insect bites.

### Vaccination

Some vaccines against dengue are approved in Europe.

Talk to your doctor before traveling to a high-risk area. Ask if vaccination is right for you.

---

## How Is Dengue Diagnosed?

If you get sick while traveling or after returning home, tell your doctor:
- Where you went
- When you were there

### Early Diagnosis

- A doctor takes a blood sample.
- The lab checks for the virus using PCR testing. This finds the virus’s genetic material.
- Or, a rapid test can detect the virus right in the doctor’s office.

### Later Diagnosis

- If you suspect dengue later in the illness, or if you had dengue before, a blood test can check for antibodies.
- These are proteins your body makes to fight the virus.
- Antibodies show up about one week after infection.

---

## How Is Dengue Treated?

There is no medicine to kill the dengue virus.

Doctors treat the symptoms to help you feel better.

### Home Care

- Rest in bed
- Drink plenty of fluids (water, broth, oral rehydration solutions)
- Use paracetamol for pain and fever

> **Do not use:**  
> - Acetylsalicylic acid (like aspirin)  
> - Ibuprofen  
> These medicines can make bleeding worse and make the illness more serious.

### Hospital Care

Go to the hospital if you have:
- Trouble drinking enough fluids
- Little or no urine
- Feeling very weak, restless, or confused
- Low platelet count
- Any signs of bleeding (like nosebleeds, blood in vomit or stool)

Hospital treatment can save lives in severe cases.

# Cluster Headaches

Cluster headaches cause very strong pain that always happens on one side of the head.  
They usually affect the area around the eye or temple.  
Most people find relief with special migraine medicine or by breathing pure oxygen.

---

## Quick Facts

- The pain always happens on one side, usually near the eye or temple.  
- Attacks come in groups called “clusters.”  
- These headaches cause extra symptoms like watery eyes, a runny nose, or a droopy eyelid.  
- Most people feel better with special migraine medicine or pure oxygen.  
- Men get cluster headaches three times more often than women.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Are Cluster Headaches?

People with cluster headaches have very intense pain attacks.  
The pain always happens on one side of the head.  
It often starts near the eye or temple.

Unlike other headaches, cluster headaches come with other clear signs.  
These include:  
- One eye watering  
- A runny or blocked nose  
- A smaller pupil in the affected eye  
- Sweating on the forehead or cheek  
- A droopy or swollen eyelid  
- Being very sensitive to light or sound

They are called “cluster” headaches because the attacks happen in cycles.  
These cycles are called clusters.  
Between clusters, most people feel no pain at all.  
Some may go years without any symptoms.

Doctors do not know what causes cluster headaches.  
They are a type of primary headache, like migraines and tension headaches.  
But cluster headaches are much less common and usually more painful.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The pain starts suddenly and feels like a sharp stab, burning, or piercing.  
It builds up fast around one eye.  
The pain can also spread to the temple and forehead.

Many people say it feels like a nail is being driven into their eye.

The affected eye often looks red and watery.  
Other possible signs include:  
- A runny or stuffy nose  
- A smaller pupil  
- Sweating on the face  
- A droopy or swollen eyelid  
- Trouble with light or sound

During an attack, many people cannot sit still.  
They may walk around or pace.  
Moving can help ease the pain a little.

An attack can last from 15 minutes to 3 hours.  
The pain usually goes away as fast as it came.  
It always affects the same side of the head.

---

## What Triggers Cluster Headaches?

Doctors do not know the exact cause.  
But they think the brain’s nerve cells, which control sleep and body rhythms, may be overactive.

There may also be a family link.  
Some people with cluster headaches have relatives with the same condition.

Like migraines, certain things can trigger attacks.  
But only if you are already in a cluster phase.

Common triggers include:  
- Drinking alcohol  
- Being at high altitudes  
- Using certain medicines, like nitroglycerin (used for chest pain in heart disease)

Some people say strong smells can trigger attacks.  
Certain foods, like aged cheese or processed meats, are often blamed.  
But science has not proven that these foods cause attacks.

---

## How Common Are They?

Only about 1 in 1,000 people have cluster headaches.  
This makes them rare compared to tension headaches and migraines.

Men are affected three times more often than women.  
Most people first get cluster headaches between the ages of 20 and 40.  
But they can start at any age.

---

## How Do Cluster Headaches Develop?

Cluster headaches happen in cycles called clusters.  
These cycles can last from a few days to several weeks.

Between cycles, most people feel no pain.  
Some go years without any attacks.

The cycles often happen in spring or autumn.

During a cluster phase, attacks can happen every other day or several times a day.  
They often happen at the same time each day.  
Common times are early in the morning or one to two hours before bedtime.

---

## How Can You Prevent Attacks?

There is no known way to stop cluster headaches from starting.  
But you can try to avoid things that trigger attacks.

Keep a diary.  
Write down what you ate, drank, or did before an attack.  
This can help you spot patterns.

Medicine can help prevent frequent attacks.  
The most common medicine contains a drug called verapamil.  
But verapamil can cause heart problems.  
It is not officially approved for cluster headaches in Germany.  
Doctors can still prescribe it if needed (this is called “off-label use”).

Other medicines used for prevention include lithium or cortisone.

---

## How Are They Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and medical history.  
They will do a physical exam.  
This includes checking your touch, strength, and reflexes.

An MRI scan of your head is usually done.  
This helps rule out other causes of headache, like a brain tumor or blood vessel problem.

---

## How Are They Treated?

Painkillers like ibuprofen or paracetamol do not help with cluster headaches.  
But breathing pure oxygen often works.  
You use a special mask connected to an oxygen machine.  
Make sure the mask covers both your mouth and nose.

Some migraine medicines (called triptans) can help.  
They work faster when given as a shot or nasal spray than when taken as a pill.  
You may need to go to the hospital at first to start this treatment.

For more details on what helps during an attack, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## What Is Life Like With Cluster Headaches?

Cluster headaches are often described as unbearable.  
During an attack, it is hard to focus, work, or do normal tasks.  
Family life and hobbies can suffer.

Many attacks happen at night.  
This can keep people awake for hours.  
Some people do not realize they have cluster headaches for a long time.  
They may fear they have a serious illness like a brain tumor.

The pain can be so bad that some people lose hope or feel like giving up.

A correct diagnosis and knowing that treatment works can bring relief.  
But treatment may require changes.  
For example, you may need to learn how to use an oxygen mask or give yourself injections.

People with cluster headaches share their stories at: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Campylobacter Infection

Campylobacter infection is a type of food poisoning caused by bacteria. It leads to diarrhea, a high temperature, and stomach pain. The infection usually gets better on its own within a week. But it can be dangerous for babies, young children, older adults, and people with weak immune systems.

## What You Need to Know at a Glance

- Campylobacter infection is a bacterial illness that causes diarrhea and fever.
- It spreads through food that comes from animals and is contaminated with bacteria from the animal’s gut.
- Severe diarrhea can be life-threatening for babies, young children, older adults, and people with weak immune systems.
- Most people recover fully within a week.
- Rarely, it can lead to long-term problems like joint pain or paralysis.
- You can protect yourself by following good hygiene rules.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Campylobacter Infection?

Campylobacter infection is an illness caused by eating food that has been contaminated with bacteria. The most common symptom is diarrhea. In most cases, the diarrhea goes away on its own after a few days.

But in babies, young children, and older adults, the diarrhea can cause serious dehydration. This means the body loses too much water and salt. It can become life-threatening if not treated.

Some people may develop long-term problems after the infection. These include joint pain or muscle weakness.

The bacteria usually come from animal products. The most common sources are chicken and raw milk. Good hygiene can prevent the infection.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms usually start 2 to 5 days after eating contaminated food.

Some people feel unwell before the diarrhea starts. They may have a high temperature, headache, or joint pain.

Common symptoms include:

- Stomach pain and cramps
- Loose or watery stools
- Stools that may contain blood
- Nausea and vomiting

---

## What Causes Campylobacter Infection?

Campylobacter is a type of bacteria. It lives in the intestines of animals. It is found all over the world.

The two most common types are *Campylobacter jejuni* and *Campylobacter coli*. These bacteria do not grow on food. But they can survive for a long time, even in a freezer.

Even after a person feels better, they can still pass the bacteria in their stool for 2 to 4 weeks. This means they can still spread the infection during this time.

Babies and people with weak immune systems may carry the bacteria for even longer.

---

## How Does the Infection Spread?

The infection spreads when you eat food that has tiny amounts of animal feces on it. This often happens during slaughter or milking.

High-risk foods include:

- Chicken and other poultry
- Raw or undercooked meat
- Raw sausages
- Raw (unpasteurized) milk
- Unpasteurized dairy products

Other possible sources:

- Pet feces
- Well water
- Water in lakes or swimming areas

Even a very small amount of bacteria can cause illness.

It is rare for the infection to spread from person to person. But it can happen, especially among babies.

---

## How Common Is This Infection?

In Germany, about 60,000 to 70,000 people get campylobacter infection each year.

The infection is more common in warmer months. It affects children under 5 and young adults between 20 and 29 most often.

Campylobacter bacteria are found worldwide.

---

## What Are the Possible Complications?

Most people recover without any long-term issues. But in some cases, problems can develop later.

### Reactive Arthritis

Some people develop joint pain and swelling a few days or weeks after the infection. The body’s immune system attacks the joints by mistake. This is called reactive arthritis.

It usually gets better after about 6 months. Medicine to reduce inflammation can help.

### Guillain-Barré Syndrome

This is a rare condition where the nerves in the body become inflamed. It starts in the hands and feet and can spread to the arms, legs, and chest.

It can cause muscle weakness or paralysis. It may affect breathing. The body’s immune system attacks the nerves.

This condition is not fully understood. But it can follow a campylobacter infection.

### Irritable Bowel Syndrome and Chronic Intestinal Problems

Some people develop ongoing digestive issues after the infection. These include bloating, stomach pain, and changes in bowel habits.

Doctors believe that campylobacter infection may trigger long-term gut problems in some people.

---

## How Can You Prevent Campylobacter Infection?

You can protect yourself and others by following simple hygiene rules.

### Wash Your Hands Often

Wash your hands with soap and water in these situations:

- After using the toilet
- Before eating
- Before preparing food
- After handling raw food
- After changing diapers
- After cleaning up after pets

Dry your hands with a clean towel.

### Avoid Raw Animal Foods

Do not eat raw or undercooked animal products. This includes:

- Raw (unpasteurized) milk
- Raw dairy products
- Raw sausages like meat paste
- Any raw or undercooked meat

**Special advice:**

- Babies, young children, pregnant women, older adults, and people with weak immune systems should avoid raw animal foods.
- Always boil raw milk before drinking it. This includes milk labeled “direct from the farm” or “Vorzugsmilch.”

### Keep Your Kitchen Clean

- Wash all fruits and vegetables before eating or cooking.
- Cook meat, especially chicken, all the way through until it is no longer pink.
- Throw away any ice that melts from thawing meat. Clean all surfaces and tools that touched raw meat.
- Do not wash chicken before cooking. This can spread bacteria around your kitchen.
- Clean work surfaces and tools with dish soap and warm water after each step.
- Use separate cutting boards and utensils for raw and cooked food.
- Replace sponges and dish brushes regularly. Wash kitchen towels and cloths at 60 degrees Celsius or higher.

For more information, visit the website of the German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR).

### Stay Home if You Are Sick

Children under 6 with diarrhea should not go to school or daycare.

- Parents must tell the school or daycare about the illness.
- The child can return after being symptom-free for 48 hours.
- A doctor’s note is not needed.

### If You Work with Food

If you have diarrhea, stop working in food preparation or service.

- You can return to work once your symptoms are gone.
- But you must follow strict handwashing rules for 4 weeks.
- This is because you can still pass the bacteria in your stool even after feeling better.

### No Special Steps for Contacts

People who have been near someone with campylobacter infection do not need special treatment.

- Only take action if they develop symptoms like diarrhea or vomiting.

---

## How Is the Infection Diagnosed?

A doctor can test for campylobacter by checking a fresh stool sample.

- The sample must be sent to a lab quickly.
- The lab can grow the bacteria or detect it directly.
- The test can also show which antibiotics might work.

---

## How Is the Infection Treated?

Most people get better with simple steps:

- Drink plenty of fluids to replace lost water and salt.
- Eat light, easy-to-digest foods.
- Rest.

The infection usually clears up on its own in a few days.

Hospital care may be needed if:

- Diarrhea lasts more than 2 to 3 days.
- The person is very dehydrated.
- The person is a baby, young child, older adult, or has a weak immune system.

In these cases, doctors may give fluids through a drip (infusion).

Antibiotics are only used in rare cases. They are not needed for most people.

> **Important:** Severe diarrhea can become life-threatening quickly in babies, young children, older adults, and people with weak immune systems. These people often need hospital treatment to replace lost fluids and salts.

# Bipolar Disorder – Simple Explanation

Bipolar disorder is a mental health condition. It causes strong mood swings. People feel very high and full of energy at times. At other times, they feel very low and sad. These mood changes can happen over days, weeks, or months.

The condition usually lasts a lifetime. But with treatment, most people feel much better and can live full, meaningful lives.

---

## Quick Facts

- People with bipolar disorder swing between feeling very high (manic) and very low (depressed).
- These mood swings can make daily life hard. They can affect work, school, and relationships.
- Doctors do not know the exact cause. But family history may play a role.
- Most people need treatment for life.
- A mix of medicine and talking therapy helps most people feel better.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Bipolar Disorder?

Bipolar disorder is a long-term mental health condition. It causes extreme mood changes. These changes are not just normal ups and downs. They are strong and can disrupt life.

People with this condition often go through two main types of episodes:

- **Manic episodes:** Feeling overly confident, energetic, and excited.
- **Depressive episodes:** Feeling sad, tired, hopeless, and unmotivated.

Between these episodes, some people feel normal. Others may still have mild symptoms.

When someone is manic, they may:
- Think they can do anything.
- Need very little sleep but still feel full of energy.
- Talk fast and a lot.
- Take big risks without thinking.
- Have strange beliefs or see/hear things that are not real (psychotic symptoms).

When someone is depressed, they may:
- Feel tired all the time.
- Lose interest in things they once enjoyed.
- Feel worthless or guilty.
- Stop wanting to be around others.
- Have thoughts about ending their life.

Some people have both manic and depressive symptoms at the same time. This is called a mixed episode. It can be very dangerous. The risk of suicide is higher during these times.

A milder form of mania is called **hypomania**. It is not as strong as full mania. But it still affects behavior and mood.

---

## What Causes Bipolar Disorder?

No one knows the exact cause. But research shows that:
- Some people are born with a higher risk.
- Traumatic events, stress, or major life changes can trigger the illness.
- It often runs in families.

---

## What Makes the Illness Worse?

Certain things increase the chance of having a severe form of bipolar disorder:

- Trauma or emotional pain
- Using drugs or alcohol
- Having psychotic symptoms (like delusions or hallucinations)

Women and people who get the illness young are more likely to have severe symptoms.

---

## How Common Is It?

About 2 out of every 100 people worldwide have bipolar disorder. Most people first notice symptoms before age 25.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Bipolar disorder affects each person differently.

- Some people have only a few episodes in their life.
- Others have many episodes over time.

There are different types of bipolar disorder:

- **Bipolar I:** People have at least one full manic episode. They may also have depressive episodes.
- **Bipolar II:** People have hypomanic episodes and depressive episodes. They never have full mania.
- **Rapid cycling:** A person has four or more mood episodes in one year. Mood changes happen fast.

Relapses are common. But early treatment helps reduce how often they happen.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose bipolar disorder through:
- A detailed talk with the patient.
- A physical exam.
- Questions about past mood changes and life history.
- Checking if any family members have the same condition.

Many people are not diagnosed for 5 to 10 years after symptoms start. This is because early symptoms can look like other problems:
- A first depressive episode may be seen as regular depression.
- A manic episode with strange thoughts may be mistaken for schizophrenia.
- Mild mania (hypomania) may not seem serious enough to notice.

Early diagnosis and treatment can help stop the illness from getting worse. The sooner treatment starts, the better the outcome.

---

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure. But treatment can help control symptoms and prevent future episodes.

Two main goals of treatment:
1. **Relieve symptoms quickly** during a mood episode.
2. **Prevent future episodes**.

Treatment usually includes a mix of:

### 1. Medicine
- **Mood stabilizers** help balance mood swings.
- **Antidepressants** are used only when needed and carefully, because they can trigger mania.
- **Antipsychotic medicines** help if someone has hallucinations, delusions, or severe mania.

### 2. Talking Therapy (Psychotherapy)
- **Psychoeducation:** Teaches people about the illness and how to manage it.
- **Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT):** Helps change negative thoughts and behaviors.
- **Family therapy:** Helps family members understand the illness and support the person better.

### 3. Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT)
- Used only for severe depression that does not respond to other treatments.
- Done under general anesthesia.
- A small electric current is sent through the brain to cause a brief seizure.
- Usually takes 6 to 12 sessions.
- Can help with both depression and mania.
- Often used with medicine and therapy to prevent relapse.

### 4. Sleep Restriction
- Used for severe depression.
- The person stays awake for a full day and night, or sleeps only half the usual time for a few days.
- Many people feel better quickly.
- But the effect is often short-term.
- Best used with medicine.

---

## Support and Help

You are not alone. Many people with bipolar disorder and their families find support through:

- **Support groups:** Meet others who understand what you’re going through.
- **Sharing experiences:** Talking with others helps reduce feelings of isolation.
- **Getting advice:** Learn from others’ experiences.

You can find local support groups through the **National Contact and Information Point For Encouraging and Supporting Self-Help Groups (NAKOS)** website. This site has a database of self-help resources.

# Mumps

Mumps is a viral illness that spreads easily from person to person.  
It often causes a high fever and painful swelling of the salivary glands near the ears.  
Some people may have no symptoms at all.  
Complications can happen, especially in teens and adults.  
Vaccination is the best way to prevent mumps.

---

## Quick Facts

- Mumps is caused by a virus.  
- It causes fever and swelling of the salivary glands.  
- The virus spreads through tiny droplets in the air when someone talks, sneezes, or coughs.  
- You can get mumps from touching saliva or breathing in droplets from an infected person.  
- It is rare to catch mumps from objects like doorknobs.  
- Teens and young adults are now more likely to get mumps than children.  
- Vaccination protects you from getting mumps.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Mumps?

Mumps is a contagious illness caused by a virus.  
It can affect children, teens, and adults.  
The most common sign is painful swelling of the parotid glands.  
These glands are located in front of the ears, under the jaw.  
Swelling can happen on one or both sides of the face.  
Some people may have only mild symptoms or none at all.  
In older patients, mumps can lead to serious problems like swelling of the testicles, brain membranes, or hearing loss.

> **Important:** In Germany, mumps is much less common now because most children are vaccinated.  
> But outbreaks still happen.  
> The age of most cases has shifted from young children to teens and young adults.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Early signs of mumps include:  
- Headache  
- Body aches  
- High fever  
- Loss of appetite  

The most noticeable symptom is swelling of the salivary glands.  
This makes the cheeks look puffy.  
The swelling usually starts near the ears.  
It can affect one or both sides.  
Sometimes the glands under the jaw or under the tongue are also swollen.  

Some people have no symptoms.  
This is more common in babies and young children.  
Others may feel like they have a bad cold.

---

## What Causes Mumps?

Mumps is caused by the mumps virus.  
The virus only lives in humans.  
It cannot be caught from animals.  
The virus spreads from person to person.

### How Do People Get Infected?

The virus spreads through tiny droplets from the nose and mouth.  
These droplets are released when someone talks, sneezes, or coughs.  
Other people can breathe in these droplets.  
You can also get infected by touching saliva from an infected person.  
For example, by sharing a drink or kissing.  
It is very rare to catch mumps from touching objects that have the virus on them.

### Who Can Get Mumps?

Anyone who has not had mumps before and has not been fully vaccinated can get it.  
Even people who have had two doses of the vaccine can get mumps.  
But their illness is usually much milder.

---

## How Common Is Mumps?

Mumps happens all over the world.  
In Germany, it is much less common now because most children are vaccinated.  
But outbreaks still happen.  
On average, about 500 cases are reported each year in Germany.  
The age group most affected has changed.  
It used to be children aged 5 to 9.  
Now it is more common in teens and young adults.

---

## How Does Mumps Develop?

Symptoms usually appear 2 to 3 weeks after infection.  
The swelling of the glands lasts about 3 to 8 days.  
People can spread the virus even before they show symptoms.  
You can pass the virus from 7 days before the swelling starts to 9 days after it appears.  
Even people with no symptoms can spread the virus.

---

## What Complications Can Happen?

The older you are, the more likely you are to have complications.

### Problems with the Brain and Nervous System

Mumps can affect the brain and its covering.  
This can happen a few days after the swelling starts.  
It can also happen before or be the only symptom.

Possible issues include:

- **Encephalitis** (inflammation of the brain):  
  This happens in less than 1 out of 100 cases.  
  It can cause paralysis.  
  In very rare cases, it can be deadly.

- **Meningitis** (inflammation of the brain’s covering):  
  This happens in up to 1 in 10 cases.  
  Symptoms include severe headache, stiff neck, and vomiting.  
  It usually does not cause lasting damage.

- **Temporary hearing loss** (high-pitched sounds):  
  This happens in about 4 out of 100 cases.

- **Permanent hearing loss in one ear**:  
  This happens in about 1 in 20,000 cases.

### Swelling of the Testicles

This can happen 4 to 8 days after the gland swelling.  
It lasts 1 to 2 weeks.  
The fever comes back.  
The testicles become painful and swollen.  
About 15 to 30 out of 100 infected males (teens and adults) get this.  
In rare cases, it can lead to infertility.

### Swelling of the Breasts or Ovaries

Up to 30 out of 100 infected women get breast swelling.  
Up to 5 out of 100 get swelling of the ovaries.  
Mumps in pregnant women does not increase the risk of birth defects.

### Other Possible Complications

- Inflammation of the pancreas (pancreatitis)  
- Kidney inflammation  
- Joint pain or swelling (arthritis)  
- Low red blood cell count (anemia)  
- Inflammation of the heart muscle (myocardial inflammation)

---

## How Can Mumps Be Prevented?

Vaccination is the best way to prevent mumps.

### Vaccination for Children

- The first dose should be given between 11 and 14 months of age.  
- The second dose should be given between 15 and 23 months.  
- The two doses must be at least 4 weeks apart.  
- If a child misses a dose, it should be given by age 18.  
- The second dose gives long-term protection.  
- No booster shot is needed later.

### Vaccination for Adults

Adults born after 1970 who work in certain jobs should get two doses of the mumps vaccine.  
This includes people working in:  
- Hospitals and care homes  
- Community centers  
- Shelters for refugees  
- Technical and vocational schools  
- Universities

The vaccine is usually given as a combination shot called MMR.  
This protects against mumps, measles, and rubella.  
There is also a version called MMRV that adds protection against chickenpox.

For more information, visit the website of the Robert Koch Institute.

### What Should You Do After Contact with Someone Who Has Mumps?

If you are not vaccinated, had only one dose, or are unsure about your vaccination status:  
- Get one dose of the MMR vaccine.  
- Do this within 3 days of being around the infected person.

---

## How Is Mumps Diagnosed?

Doctors often suspect mumps based on the swelling of the glands.  
But lab tests are needed to confirm it.  
Tests can be done using:  
- A swab from the throat  
- A urine sample  
- A blood test to check for virus antibodies

---

## How Is Mumps Treated?

There is no medicine that kills the mumps virus.  
Treatment focuses on relieving symptoms.

You can take:  
- Pain relievers that reduce fever and swelling  
- Rest  
- Drink plenty of fluids

> **Important:** If you have mumps, do not go to school, work, or any group setting.  
> Stay home until your symptoms are gone.  
> You must stay away for at least 5 days after the illness starts.  
> This helps stop the virus from spreading.

# Chronic Pain

Chronic pain can make daily life hard. It does not always go away, even if the original injury has healed. Treatment focuses on reducing pain and helping you live better.

---

## What Is Chronic Pain?

- Pain that lasts more than 3 to 6 months is called chronic pain.
- It can continue even after an injury has fully healed.
- Everyone feels pain differently. Your mood, thoughts, and life situation can affect how you feel pain.
- Chronic pain can lead to anxiety, depression, or trouble sleeping.
- These problems can make the pain feel worse.
- Treating chronic pain works best when it includes both physical and mental health care.

**Important:** Treating pain early and well can stop it from becoming long-term. This is especially true after surgery.

---

## What Does Chronic Pain Feel Like?

Pain can feel different depending on where it is in the body.

- **Pain in organs** (like the stomach or kidneys) may feel dull, deep, or crampy. You may not know exactly where it starts.
- **Pain in muscles and bones** often feels sharp, heavy, or burning. It is easier to point to the exact spot.
- **Nerve pain** can feel like sudden electric shocks. It may come with tingling, numbness, or extra sensitivity.
- Older adults may struggle to describe their pain. They often say they feel “uncomfortable” or “not right.”
- People with dementia may not be able to speak about pain. Signs of pain include:
  - A face that looks strained or in pain
  - Moaning or groaning
  - Holding the painful area tightly
  - Hard or fast breathing
  - Confusion

---

## What Causes Chronic Pain?

Chronic pain can come from many sources.

- Problems in the nervous system
- Long-term inflammation
- Damage to nerves or the way the brain processes pain

Common conditions linked to chronic pain include:

- Osteoarthritis (wear-and-tear joint disease)
- Back problems
- Rheumatoid arthritis (an autoimmune joint disease)
- Fibromyalgia (widespread body pain)
- Diabetes

Different types of pain have different causes:

- **Nociceptive pain**: Comes from tissue damage. Examples: injuries, burns, kidney stones, heart attacks.
- **Inflammatory pain**: Happens when tissues are inflamed. This can be caused by infections or autoimmune diseases.
- **Neuropathic pain**: Comes from nerve damage. Causes include nerve injuries, diabetes, alcohol use, or shingles.
- **Central pain**: Happens when the brain or spinal cord misreads pain signals. This can occur in fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, or chronic pelvic pain.

Pain can become a habit. Even after the cause is gone, the pain may stay. Over time, nerves can become more sensitive. This means pain signals travel faster and easier. The brain may even “remember” pain, making it worse.

Stress can also make pain feel stronger or come on sooner.

---

## Who Is More Likely to Get Chronic Pain?

Certain factors increase the risk:

- Family history of chronic pain
- Past pain that was not treated well
- Mental health issues like depression or PTSD
- Living in difficult social or economic conditions
- Being older
- Using painkillers for a long time, especially strong ones like opioids
- Alcohol or drug misuse

---

## How Common Is Chronic Pain?

- About 3 out of every 10 people in developed countries have moderate to severe pain lasting more than 6 months.
- Over 40% of older adults have chronic pain.
- The most common causes in older adults are joint pain and back pain.
- Children can also have chronic pain.

---

## What Can Happen If Chronic Pain Is Not Treated?

- Life quality often stays limited, even with treatment.
- Pain relief is often not complete.
- Most people need more than one type of medicine.
- People often take more pills over time, and the doses may increase.
- These medicines can cause side effects.

For example:
- Too much paracetamol can harm the liver.
- Using strong painkillers like opioids regularly can lead to addiction.
- Overdosing on opioids can stop breathing and be deadly.
- Some people become more sensitive to pain after using opioids.

---

## How Is Chronic Pain Diagnosed?

Finding the cause of pain is the first step.

- Doctors may use imaging tests like X-rays, CT scans, or MRI scans.
- Blood tests can help find signs of inflammation or other issues.
- Nerve tests or nerve blocks may be used to check nerve function.

But sometimes, even with severe pain, doctors cannot find a clear cause.

To understand your pain, doctors will ask:

- When and where did the pain start?
- What does it feel like?
- On a scale from 1 to 10, how bad is it?
- How does it affect your daily life?

They will also do a physical exam. They check for movement problems and ask about:

- Your mood
- How well you sleep
- Stress at home or at work

This helps them see if your life situation is affecting your pain or being affected by it.

---

## How Is Chronic Pain Treated?

The best approach uses several methods together. This is called multi-modal therapy.

It includes:
- Medical treatment
- Psychotherapy (talk therapy)
- Physiotherapy (movement therapy)
- Occupational therapy (helps with daily tasks)

Treatment should be led by pain specialists. Social medicine experts can also help.

### Non-Medical Treatments

- **Behavioral therapy**: Helps you manage pain and sleep better.
- **Exercise and movement**: Done with a physiotherapist. Helps improve strength and reduce pain.
- **Acupuncture**: Used to ease pain in specific areas or all over the body.
- **Diet and weight loss**: Helpful if extra weight is causing pain.
- **Support tools**: Like walking sticks, braces, or special shoes.
- **Nerve stimulation**: Small electrical pulses reduce pain. A minor surgery is needed to place the device.

### Medicines

- Local anesthetics or anti-inflammatory creams can help with pain in one spot.
- Antidepressants can help with pain, even if you are not sad. It may take weeks to work.
- Anti-epileptic drugs are used for nerve pain.
- Muscle relaxants help with cramp-related pain.
- Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen or paracetamol are best for short-term flare-ups. Try different types to see what works best.
- Strong painkillers like opioids or sedatives should only be used for a short time.

**Important:** Long-term use of opioids is only considered if:
- There is a clear physical cause of pain
- Other treatments have not worked

For back or joint pain, opioids are not more effective than other painkillers over time.

Always talk with your doctor before starting or changing treatment. A good relationship with your doctor is key to successful care.

---

## How Can You Manage Chronic Pain Every Day?

Chronic pain often comes and goes. It needs long-term care.

You can learn to manage it better by finding what helps you feel better.

Support is available from:
- Doctors and therapists
- Information centers
- Self-help groups

You can find local self-help groups through the **National Contact and Information Point for Encouraging and Supporting Self-Help Groups (NAKOS)**.

---

## Where Can You Learn More?

For more information, visit:

- **German Society for Psychological Pain Therapy and Research**  
  (Deutsche Gesellschaft für psychologische Schmerztherapie und -forschung e.V.)

- **German Pain Association**  
  (Deutsche Schmerzgesellschaft e.V.)

- **German Brain Foundation**  
  (Deutsche Hirnstiftung e.V.)  
  This site has clear summaries of different pain conditions and answers to common questions.

# Prostate Cancer

About 60,000 men in Germany are diagnosed with prostate cancer each year. This is the most common type of cancer in men.

This article explains screening, diagnosis, treatment, and care for prostate cancer.

---

## Quick Facts

- Prostate cancer is also called prostate carcinoma.
- The biggest risk factors are getting older and having a family history of the disease.
- In Germany, men can get a free check-up for prostate cancer starting at age 45. This includes a physical exam and a digital rectal exam.
- The test for prostate-specific antigen (PSA) in the blood is not part of the national screening program.
- Health insurance does not pay for PSA testing. Men can pay for it themselves if they want.
- Most men with prostate cancer have no symptoms in the early stages.
- Most men with prostate cancer can be cured. Even if it cannot be cured, the cancer often grows slowly.
- Some treatments can cause side effects like leaking urine, trouble getting an erection, or bowel problems such as pain or bleeding.

> **Important:** This article is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Prostate Cancer?

Prostate cancer is a type of cancer that starts in the prostate gland. The prostate is a small organ inside a man’s body that helps make semen.

Doctors divide prostate cancer into three stages:

- **Localized:** The cancer is only in the prostate.
- **Locally advanced:** The cancer has spread beyond the prostate, for example into nearby tissues.
- **Advanced or metastatic:** The cancer has spread to lymph nodes, bones, or other organs.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most men with prostate cancer do not have symptoms at first. Even when symptoms appear, they are often mild and can be caused by other conditions.

Possible symptoms include:

- Trouble starting to urinate or feeling like the bladder is not empty.
- Pain or discomfort when urinating.
- Aching in the bones.
- Blood in the urine or semen.
- Problems during sex.

Many older men have trouble urinating because the prostate naturally grows larger with age. This is called benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). It is not cancer, but it can cause similar symptoms.

If symptoms last for more than a few weeks, see a doctor. The doctor can check what is causing the problem and decide if further tests are needed.

---

## What Causes Prostate Cancer?

The main risk factor is age. Most men diagnosed with prostate cancer are between 70 and 80 years old. It is rare before age 50.

Another major risk factor is family history. If your father, brother, or other close male relative had prostate cancer, your risk is higher.

If you have a family history, you may want to start screening earlier than age 45. Talk to your doctor about your options.

---

## What Screening Options Are Available?

In Germany, men can get a free annual check-up starting at age 45. This includes:

- A discussion about symptoms.
- A physical exam of the external genitals.
- A digital rectal exam (DRE), where the doctor feels the prostate with a gloved finger.

The national screening program does **not** include a blood test for PSA (prostate-specific antigen).

Health insurance does not cover PSA testing. You can pay for it yourself as an individual health service (IGeL). But studies have not shown that nationwide PSA screening helps more than it harms.

If you are thinking about a PSA test, talk to your doctor. Learn about the benefits and risks. This will help you decide if the test is right for you.

For more information about screening and PSA testing, visit the website of the **German Cancer Research Center’s Cancer Information Service** (in German).

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Prostate cancer behaves differently in different men.

In most cases, it grows slowly. Some men live with it for years without any symptoms. Many men with prostate cancer live a normal life span.

In some men, the cancer grows quickly. It may already have spread when first found. This type of cancer is usually not curable. But it can often be controlled for a long time.

Cancer can come back after treatment. In some cases, doctors can treat it again.

---

## How Is Prostate Cancer Diagnosed?

If prostate cancer is suspected, doctors use several tests.

The first steps include:

- Talking to the patient about symptoms, health history, and family history.
- Doing a physical exam, including a digital rectal exam.
- Measuring the PSA level in the blood.
- Using MRI to scan the prostate (multi-parametric MRI).
- If needed, using ultrasound (TRUS).
- Taking a small sample of prostate tissue (biopsy) for lab testing.

Your general practitioner can start the process. Specialists like urologists and radiologists do the next steps.

A biopsy is needed to confirm the diagnosis. Urologists usually take 10 to 12 samples using a standard plan. Some samples may also be taken from suspicious areas seen on imaging.

The biopsy results and PSA level help doctors decide if the cancer has spread beyond the prostate.

If the risk of spread is high, doctors may use more imaging tests:

- CT scan
- MRI
- Bone scan
- PET scan (especially PSMA-PET/CT)

For more details on diagnosis, visit the **German Cancer Research Center’s Cancer Information Service** website (in German).

---

## How Is Prostate Cancer Treated?

Treatment depends on several factors:

- How far the cancer has spread.
- The PSA level.
- How aggressive the cancer is.
- The man’s overall health.
- The man’s personal goals and values.

### **Localized Prostate Cancer (Only in the Prostate)**

If the cancer is only in the prostate, it can often be cured.

Treatment options include:

- **Surgery:** Removing the entire prostate (radical prostatectomy). This can be done with a robot or without.
- **Radiation therapy:** Using high-energy rays from outside the body (external radiotherapy).
- **Brachytherapy:** Placing radioactive material inside the prostate.

**Active surveillance** is another option. This means no treatment at first. Instead, you have regular check-ups. If the cancer becomes more aggressive, treatment starts then.

Minimally invasive focal therapy may be used in some cases. But it is not yet clear if it works as well as standard treatments.

Sometimes, doctors combine treatments. For example, surgery followed by radiation. Or radiation given at the same time as hormone therapy.

For more information on treatment and decision-making, see the **patient guide from the Cancer Information Service**.

Videos are available to explain:

- Open prostatectomy
- Laparoscopic prostatectomy
- Robotic prostatectomy

### **Advanced or Metastatic Prostate Cancer (Spread to Other Areas)**

At this stage, the cancer is usually not curable. But it can be controlled.

**Hormone therapy** is a key treatment. It lowers testosterone, which cancer cells need to grow. This helps slow the cancer.

Other treatment options include:

- **Chemotherapy:** Drugs that stop cancer cells from growing or dividing.
- **Targeted therapy:** Drugs called PARP inhibitors that damage cancer cells’ DNA repair.
- **Radionuclide therapy:** Drugs that go directly to cancer cells and destroy them with radiation.
- **Supportive treatments:** Medicines for bones and radiation to the bones. These help relieve pain and prevent broken bones.

In some cases, doctors may recommend **watchful waiting**. This means no treatment if the man has no symptoms. This is often suggested for older men or those with other serious health issues.

For more details on treatments and terms like “castration-resistant” or “oligometastatic,” visit the **German Cancer Research Center’s Cancer Information Service** website (in German).

---

## Rehabilitation and Aftercare

Cancer treatment can be hard on the body and mind. Rehabilitation helps men recover strength and cope with side effects.

Prostate cancer rehab is specialized. It includes:

- Pelvic floor exercises to help control urine.
- Advice on treating weak erections.
- Exercise to prevent problems from hormone therapy, like weak bones or metabolic issues.
- Psychological support.
- Nutrition advice.

### After Treatment

After treatment, regular check-ups are important. They help find a return of cancer early and catch long-term side effects.

Check-ups include:

- Talking about symptoms.
- Physical exams.
- Blood tests to measure PSA levels.

The frequency of check-ups starts high and then decreases over time.

For more information on rehab, aftercare, and how PSA levels change after treatment, visit the **German Cancer Research Center’s Cancer Information Service** website (in German).

---

## Living Well with Prostate Cancer

Many men want to stay active to help themselves feel better.

Ways to improve quality of life include:

- Rehab and physiotherapy can help with urine leakage.
- Talking to doctors or joining rehab programs can help with sexual problems.
- Exercise can reduce tiredness. It should match your fitness level.
- Eating a healthy, balanced diet supports well-being and prevents poor nutrition.
- Counseling can help if you feel anxious or worried.

If the cancer can no longer be cured and is getting worse, good medical and nursing care is essential. Pain, shortness of breath, and other symptoms can be managed. Emotional and social support can help you live well for as long as possible.
