# Tick-Borne Encephalitis (TBE)

Tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) is a virus that spreads through tick bites.  
It causes swelling in the brain and the layers around the brain and spinal cord.  
People in high-risk areas should consider getting vaccinated to stay safe.

---

## Quick Facts

- TBE is a virus spread by ticks.  
- It is rare in Germany. Fewer than 600 people get it each year.  
- Only about one in three people who get the virus will notice any symptoms.  
- Mild symptoms are like the flu: tiredness, headache, fever, and body aches.  
- About half of all infected people develop swelling in the brain, spinal cord, or the lining around them.  
- Vaccination is the best way to protect yourself if you live in or often visit high-risk areas.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is TBE?

TBE is a virus that causes swelling in the brain and the protective layers around it.  
The virus lives in small wild animals like wood mice.  
Ticks pick up the virus from these animals.  
When an infected tick bites a person, it can pass the virus into the blood.  

The name “Frühsommer-Meningoenzephalitis” means “spring meningoencephalitis.”  
This name suggests the illness only happens in spring.  
But ticks can spread the virus any time of year.  

In Germany, the risk is highest from May to October.  
This is when ticks are most active.

---

## What Are the Symptoms of TBE?

Symptoms usually appear 7 to 14 days after being bitten.  
Sometimes it can take up to 28 days.  

Only about one in three people will feel sick.  
People with TBE cannot pass the virus to others.

Symptoms happen in two stages:

### Stage 1: Mild TBE

You may feel very tired.  
You might have flu-like symptoms:  
- Headache  
- High fever  
- Aching muscles and joints  
- Stomach pain  
- Vomiting  

These symptoms usually go away after a few days.  
About half of all infected people feel better and stay well.

### Stage 2: Severe TBE

The illness may seem to improve, but then returns.  
You may get a high fever again.  
You may develop swelling in the brain, spinal cord, or the lining around them.

The most common problem is swelling of the lining around the brain (meningitis).  
This causes:  
- Severe headaches  
- High fever  
- Feeling very unwell  

Children may seem dull, quiet, or have seizures.

In about 40 out of 100 people, the brain is also inflamed (meningoencephalitis).  
This can cause confusion and trouble staying awake.

In about 10 out of 100 people, the brain, spinal cord, and lining are all inflamed (meningoencephalomyelitis).  
This can cause:  
- Weakness or paralysis in arms and legs  
- Facial drooping  
- Trouble speaking, swallowing, or hearing  

---

## What Causes TBE?

TBE is caused by a virus carried by two types of ticks:  
- Castor bean ticks  
- Meadow ticks  

These ticks live in grass, bushes, and undergrowth.  
They are usually found 30 to 60 centimeters above the ground.  
They do not fall from trees.  
In mountain areas, they can live up to 1,500 meters above sea level.

Ticks become active when the air is moist and the temperature is around 6 to 8 degrees Celsius.  
Meadow ticks can even be active at 4 degrees.

Not every tick bite causes TBE.  
Even in high-risk areas, only about 5 out of 100 ticks carry the virus.

Rarely, TBE can be caught by drinking raw milk from infected animals.  
But milk that has been heated (pasteurized) is safe.

---

## What Is the Outlook for TBE?

Many people recover after the first phase of illness.  
Some get better, then feel sick again after about a week.

Swelling in the brain lining (meningitis) usually goes away without lasting harm.  
But if the brain is also inflamed, about 20 out of 100 people have lasting damage.

If the spinal cord is also inflamed, the damage is more serious.  
Some people may be left with paralysis or seizures.

In rare cases, TBE can be deadly.

Children are more likely to recover fully from severe TBE than adults.  
Adults over 60 and people with weak immune systems are at higher risk of serious illness.

---

## Where and How Common Is TBE?

TBE is rare.  
In 2023, 475 cases were reported in Germany.  
In 2022, there were 565 cases.

Men are twice as likely as women to get TBE.

TBE is found in these regions of Germany:  
- Bavaria  
- Baden-Württemberg  
- South Hesse  
- Saxony  
- South-east Thuringia  
- South-east Brandenburg  

It is also found in these areas:  
- Central Hesse  
- Saarland  
- Rhineland-Palatinate  
- Lower Saxony  
- North Rhine-Westphalia  

### How High Is the Risk?

You can only get TBE in areas where infected ticks live.  
But not all ticks carry the virus.  
Even in high-risk areas like Bavaria, only about 1 in 10 ticks has the virus.

Not everyone who gets the virus will feel sick.  
Only about 1 in 3 people will have symptoms.

For the latest list of high-risk areas, visit the website of the Robert Koch Institute.

---

## How Can You Protect Yourself from TBE?

TBE can cause serious problems like paralysis.  
Prevention is very important, especially if you live in or visit high-risk areas.

There are two main ways to protect yourself:

- Get vaccinated  
- Avoid tick bites

### Vaccination Against TBE

The Robert Koch Institute recommends vaccination for:  
- People who live in high-risk areas  
- People who often go into forests or meadows (e.g. for work)  
- Travelers going to high-risk areas outside Germany  

Vaccination schedule:

- You need three doses for full protection.  
- After the three doses, 99 out of 100 people are protected for at least 3 years.  
- Booster shots are needed every 3 to 5 years, depending on your age and the vaccine used.  
- Even if you’ve had TBE before, you should still get a booster 3 to 5 years after recovery.  
- Children can be vaccinated from 12 months old.  
- Health insurance usually pays for the vaccine if you live in or travel to high-risk areas.  
- Employers pay for the vaccine if your job involves working in forests or fields (e.g. forestry workers).

The vaccine is given as an injection into the muscle.  
It is safe and well tolerated.  
About 10 out of 100 people have mild side effects:  
- Pain, redness, or swelling at the injection site  
- Flu-like symptoms (fever, tiredness, aches)

For more information, visit the Robert Koch Institute website.

### Avoid Tick Bites

To reduce your risk:

- Wear long pants and tuck them into your socks  
- Stay on paths and avoid tall grass and bushes  
- Use insect repellent on your skin and clothes  

For more tips, visit the website of the Federal Center for Health Education (BZgA).  
(Website is in German only.)

---

## How Is TBE Diagnosed?

If TBE is suspected, your doctor will ask:

- Have you been in a high-risk area?  
- Do you remember a tick bite?  
- Do you have flu-like symptoms like headache or fever?

To confirm the diagnosis, your doctor will test your blood or spinal fluid.  
The lab looks for special antibodies that fight the TBE virus.

In some cases, your doctor may order an MRI scan of your brain or spinal cord.  
This helps see if there is swelling caused by the virus.

---

## How Is TBE Treated?

There is no medicine that kills the TBE virus.  
Doctors can only treat the symptoms to help you feel better.

Treatment may include:

- Painkillers for headaches  
- Medicine to reduce fever  
- Anti-seizure drugs if you have seizures  

Do not take cortisone medicine. It can weaken your body’s ability to fight the virus.

Anyone with suspected TBE should be hospitalized.  
Your condition can get worse quickly.  
You may need intensive care.

---

## What Rehab Options Are Available?

People with severe TBE often need medical rehabilitation after treatment.  
This helps them recover from lasting effects.

Rehab may include:

- Physical therapy to improve movement and strength  
- Speech therapy to help with speaking and swallowing  

---

## How to Remove a Tick Correctly

If you find a tick on your body, remove it as soon as possible.  
You cannot tell if a tick is infected, so it’s best to remove it.

Follow these steps:

- Stay calm and work carefully.  
- Do not use oil, glue, or fire.  
- Use tweezers, a tick hook, or a tick removal card from a pharmacy.  
- Grasp the tick as close to your skin as possible, near its mouth.  
- Do not squeeze or crush the tick.

# Common Cold

A common cold is usually not serious. It often gets better on its own.  
It is not the same as the flu.  
This article explains the usual signs of a cold and how to feel better.

---

## Quick Facts

- A common cold is usually harmless.  
- It usually goes away without medicine.  
- Colds are caused by viruses.  
- Antibiotics do not work against viruses.  
- People often mix up a cold and the flu.  
- The flu causes much stronger symptoms.  
- The flu often starts suddenly.  
- Colds are very common, especially in children.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Common Cold?

A common cold is not the same as the flu.  
It is usually mild and gets better by itself.  
Common symptoms include coughing, a sore throat, and a runny or blocked nose.  
Some people feel tired or unwell during a bad cold.

Most colds go away in one to two weeks.  
Some symptoms, like a sore throat or runny nose, may fade in just a few days.  
Coughs can last longer — sometimes up to three weeks.

You do not need medicine to treat a cold.  
Medicine can only help ease symptoms a little.  
Antibiotics do not help with colds.  
This is because colds are caused by viruses, not bacteria.  
Antibiotics only work against bacteria.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

A common cold is a group of symptoms caused by a virus in the nose and throat.  
Symptoms usually appear over a few days.  
The most common signs are:

- Runny or blocked nose  
- Sneezing  
- Coughing  
- Sore throat  

Other possible symptoms include:

- Feeling tired  
- A slight fever  
- Headaches  
- Body aches  

Sometimes people confuse a cold with the flu.  
The flu can have similar symptoms, but it is usually much worse.  
Flu symptoms often come on fast.  
They include high fever, chills, and strong body aches.

---

## What Causes a Common Cold?

Colds are caused by viruses that infect the nose and throat.  
There are many different cold viruses.  
This means you can get a cold more than once.  
Your body reacts in a similar way to most of these viruses.  
That is why different colds cause similar symptoms.

---

## How Common Are Colds?

Colds are very common.  
Children get them often — especially those in school, nursery, or daycare.  
A child might get a cold 6 to 8 times a year.  
Adults usually get 2 to 4 colds each year.  
Colds are more common in colder months.

---

## How Does a Cold Progress?

A cold often starts with a sore or scratchy throat.  
Soon after, your nose starts to run or get blocked.  
Your body’s immune system fights the virus on its own.  

Even if you feel very unwell, the worst symptoms usually pass within a week.  
Full recovery can take longer.  
Coughs are often the last symptom to go.  
In adults, a cough may take about 18 days to clear.  
Children can also have a cough for up to three weeks.

---

## What Can Happen After a Cold?

After a cold, bacteria can sometimes grow in the nose or throat.  
This can lead to problems such as:

- Sinus infections  
- Middle ear infections  
- Hoarseness  

In babies, a condition called croup can sometimes develop.

Serious problems like pneumonia are very rare.  
But you should see a doctor if you have:

- A very high fever  
- Symptoms that get worse  
- Chest pain  
- Trouble breathing  
- Shortness of breath  

This is especially important for people with long-term lung problems, such as COPD.

---

## How Can You Prevent a Cold?

Colds are caused by many different viruses.  
Once you recover, you are not protected from getting another cold.  
Your body must learn to fight each new virus separately.  
There is no vaccine for common cold viruses.

The best way to avoid a cold is to stop the virus from spreading.  
Cold viruses spread through tiny droplets in the air.  
These droplets come from sneezing or coughing.  
They can land on surfaces like door handles, keyboards, or handrails.  
If you touch these surfaces, the virus gets on your hands.  
Then you can pass it to your nose or mouth by touching your face.

**Important:**  
- Avoid touching your face, especially your eyes, nose, and mouth.  
- Wash your hands often with regular soap and water.  
- Throw used tissues away right away.  
- Do not share cups, glasses, or other items that others have touched with their mouth or nose.

Some people take vitamin C or echinacea to prevent colds.  
But studies show these have little or no real benefit.  
Probiotics may help reduce colds, especially those affecting the upper airways.  
Vitamin D supplements may help prevent colds in people who are low in vitamin D.

---

## How Is a Cold Diagnosed?

You do not need special tests for a cold.  
A doctor can usually tell you have a cold by asking about your symptoms and looking at your throat.  

Colds are so common and have clear signs.  
It is unlikely that your symptoms are from something else.  
But if the doctor suspects the flu or another serious illness, they may do:

- A swab from your nose or throat  
- A test for the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2  

This can help rule out other conditions.

---

## How Is a Cold Treated?

There is no medicine that can cure a cold or make it go away faster.  
This is because many different viruses cause colds.  

But some treatments can help ease symptoms:

- Painkillers like ibuprofen, paracetamol, or acetylsalicylic acid (ASA)  
- Decongestant nasal sprays (for short-term use only)  

Antibiotics are not helpful for a cold.  
They can cause side effects.  
They should only be used if a bacterial infection develops, such as a sinus infection.

Some people use remedies with zinc, vitamin C, or echinacea.  
But studies have not proven they work well.  
Results are unclear or even mixed.  
Vitamin D does not seem to help treat colds.

Honey and herbal remedies with ingredients like:

- Geranium root  
- Primrose root  
- Thyme  
- Eucalyptus  
- Ivy leaves  

May help ease coughs.

For more information on colds and how to relieve a runny nose or cough, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

# Broken Ankle

A broken ankle is a serious injury. It often happens during sports. When the foot twists too much, the bones in the upper ankle can break. One or more bones may be affected.

## What You Need to Know at a Glance

- Most broken ankles happen while playing sports.
- The foot can roll or twist too far, causing the ankle joint to break.
- You cannot put weight on the foot after a break.
- The injury can affect one or more bones.
- Most broken ankles heal well over time.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical care. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is a Broken Ankle?

When the ankle twists too hard, the soft tissues around it can get hurt. This is called a sprain. But if the twist is too strong, the bones in the ankle joint can break. Doctors call this an ankle fracture.

This is a serious injury. One or more bones in the ankle may be broken. The ligaments around the ankle are often torn. The cartilage inside the joint can also be damaged.

Most broken ankles heal well with time.

## What Are the Signs of a Broken Ankle?

- The foot swells up.
- It hurts a lot.
- Bruises (dark marks) appear.
- You cannot walk on it.
- The foot is hard to move.
- The bones may shift out of place. This is called a malposition.

## What Causes a Broken Ankle?

Most often, broken ankles happen during sports. For example:

- You fall suddenly.
- You land badly after jumping.
- You run on uneven ground.
- You trip and twist your foot.

These actions can cause the ankle to twist too far and break.

## How Does a Broken Ankle Heal?

- Swelling takes days or weeks to go down.
- Full healing can take months.
- You can only put a little weight on the foot during recovery.
- Moving the foot is hard at first.

If you put weight on the foot too soon, the bone may not heal right. This can lead to more problems. But if the foot stays still too long, it can lose strength and flexibility.

Most broken ankles heal well. But some people may have long-term issues, such as:

- Osteoarthritis (a type of joint pain and stiffness).
- The ankle stays unstable. This makes it easier to twist the ankle again.

## How Is a Broken Ankle Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask how the injury happened. Then they will check your foot and ankle. They will look for swelling, pain, and movement problems.

If a break is suspected, an X-ray is taken. X-rays show the bones clearly.

Sometimes the X-ray is not clear enough. Then other tests may be needed:

- A CT scan gives a detailed picture of the bones.
- An MRI shows soft tissues like ligaments and cartilage better.

These tests help find hidden injuries.

## How Is a Broken Ankle Treated?

The first steps are:

- Keep the foot still.
- Raise it above heart level.
- Use cold packs if needed to reduce swelling.

Immobilizing the foot with a cast, bandage, splint, or brace is key. It protects the ankle and helps it heal. These devices are usually worn for about six weeks.

If the bones are out of place, the doctor may move them back into position. This is called realignment.

Surgery may be needed in some cases. This is more likely if:

- The break is severe.
- The bones are not in the right place.
- The skin is broken (open fracture).
- Nerves or blood vessels are damaged.

During surgery, the doctor may use screws and metal plates. These hold the bones in place so they can grow back together.

After surgery, the ankle is still immobilized with a splint, bandage, or cast. Some of these can be removed later.

Once the bones are healed, the screws and plates may be taken out. This depends on your situation.

## When Can You Start Moving Again?

You can begin light movement and exercises after a while. The right time depends on how bad the break is.

- In some cases, light exercises can start a few days after the injury or surgery.
- In other cases, you must wait until the cast or splint is removed.

Because the foot is still for a long time, your doctor may give you medicine to prevent blood clots. This is called a thrombosis prevention injection.

## Do You Always Need Surgery?

No. Surgery is not always needed. Your doctor will decide based on:

- How bad the break is.
- Where the break is in the ankle.
- If the skin is open (a break in the skin).
- If nerves or blood vessels are hurt.
- If the bone pieces have moved.

# Tuberculosis (TB)

Tuberculosis is an infection caused by bacteria.  
It mainly affects the lungs, but it can also affect other parts of the body.  
Around 10 million people get TB every year around the world.  
TB is hard to treat because some of the bacteria do not respond to many medicines.

---

## Quick Facts

- TB is caused by bacteria that spread through the air.  
- You can catch TB by breathing in tiny droplets from an infected person’s cough or sneeze.  
- Only 5 to 10 out of every 100 people who get infected will actually get sick.  
- Young children and people with weak immune systems are most at risk.  
- Treatment usually lasts 6 months and works well if taken correctly.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always see a doctor.

---

## What Is Tuberculosis?

TB is an infection caused by bacteria.  
It usually starts in the lungs, but it can spread to other organs.  
The bacteria spread through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes, talks, or sings.  
About one in four people worldwide have been infected with the TB bacteria.  
Most of them do not feel sick. Their body fights the bacteria and keeps them under control.  
This is called a latent TB infection.  
The bacteria can stay in the body for years without causing harm.  
Only a small number of people will develop active TB disease.

TB can start with symptoms like:
- Losing weight without trying  
- Feeling weak or tired  
- Sweating a lot at night  
- Having a long-lasting cough

In the past, TB was called “consumption” because it caused people to lose weight.

Treating TB takes a long time.  
The bacteria are tough and grow in different ways.  
Doctors must use several medicines together to kill them all.

You can learn more about TB from:
- The German Agency for Quality in Medicine  
- The German Central Committee against Tuberculosis

---

## What Are the Symptoms of TB?

The lungs are most often affected.  
But TB can also affect the lymph nodes, kidneys, bones, brain, and other organs.

### No Symptoms

In about 90% of people, the body stops the bacteria from growing.  
The bacteria are trapped in small areas of the body called tuberculomas.  
This is called latent TB.  
The bacteria stay alive but do not cause illness.  
They can stay hidden for years.

### Symptoms Appear

When TB becomes active, it usually starts within the first 1 to 2 years after infection.  
But it can also start decades later.  
Over 70% of people with active TB have lung problems.  
Other possible sites of infection include:
- Lymph nodes  
- Lining of the lungs (pleura)  
- Kidneys and bladder  
- Bones  
- Brain (meninges)

Early symptoms include:
- A mild fever  
- Feeling weak  
- Losing weight without trying  
- Sweating at night

The most common lung symptom is a cough that lasts for weeks.  
The cough may bring up thick mucus (phlegm).  
In rare cases, the cough brings up blood.  
Some people also have chest pain or trouble breathing.

Other general symptoms may include:
- Poor overall health  
- Not feeling hungry  
- Feeling very tired

A first-time infection with symptoms (called primary TB) usually happens when the immune system is already weak.  
This is common in young children and people with HIV.  
Even if the body has controlled the bacteria before, a weak immune system can wake them up again.  
This is called reactivation TB.

In rare cases, especially in people with weak immune systems, the infection can spread through the blood.  
This is called sepsis.  
It can be life-threatening.

> **Important:** If you have a cough that lasts more than three weeks, see a doctor.  
> If you cough up blood, see a doctor right away.

---

## What Causes TB?

TB is caused by bacteria that spread from person to person.

### The Bacteria

TB is caused by rod-shaped bacteria in the Mycobacteria family.  
The most common type is *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*.  
It was discovered by Robert Koch.  
Other types include *Mycobacterium bovis* (which affects cows) and *Mycobacterium africanum*.

### How It Spreads

TB spreads mainly from people with “open” TB.  
This means the bacteria are in their lungs and can be released into the air when they cough or sneeze.  
Other people can breathe in these tiny droplets and become infected.

If TB is in organs other than the lungs, it is very unlikely to spread through normal contact.

### From Milk?

TB can be passed through unpasteurized milk.  
But in Germany, most cows are free of TB.  
So this risk is very low.

### How Contagious Is TB?

People with open TB are most contagious when bacteria are seen in their phlegm under a microscope.  
They are less contagious if the bacteria are only found after growing them in a lab or using special tests.  
Children under 10 usually do not show bacteria in their phlegm.  
Also, children are less likely to spread TB because they cough less strongly.

---

## Who Is at Higher Risk?

Some people are more likely to get TB.  
These include:
- People who live or work closely with someone who has open TB  
- People who did not finish their TB treatment  
- Young children  
- People with HIV or other immune system problems  
- People on medicines that weaken the immune system (like after an organ transplant or for rheumatism)  
- People with alcohol or drug problems  
- Homeless people  
- People with long-term health issues like diabetes  
- People with silicosis (a lung disease from breathing in silica dust, common in construction and ceramics workers)

---

## How Common Is TB?

TB is common worldwide.  
It spreads easily in places where many people have HIV.  
HIV weakens the immune system, making it harder to fight TB.  
In some areas, treatment is not good enough.  
And the bacteria are becoming resistant to medicines.

### Worldwide

- About 10 million people get TB each year.  
- Around 1.5 million people die from TB each year.  
- TB is the leading cause of death from a bacterial infection in adults and teens.  
- It is also a major cause of death in people with HIV.  
- Most new TB cases happen in Africa, Southeast Asia, and the Western Pacific.

### In Europe

- Europe has about 3% of all new TB cases worldwide.  
- In Western Europe, fewer than 15 people per 100,000 get TB each year.  
- In the Balkans, it’s about 20 per 100,000.  
- In Eastern Europe, it’s over 100 per 100,000.  
- In most Western European countries, TB cases have been going down for years.  
- In Eastern Europe, drug resistance is a growing problem.

### In Germany

- In 2019, 4,791 cases were reported.  
- That’s about 6 cases per 100,000 people.  
- Most cases happen in people born in countries where TB is still common.  
- About 60% of cases are open TB, which means they can spread to others.  
- Local health authorities keep track of TB cases.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

### People with Healthy Immune Systems

Only 5 to 10 out of 100 infected people will get sick.  
The risk is highest in the first two years after infection.

### People with Weak Immune Systems

TB can develop quickly in people with weak immune systems.  
The bacteria can spread to other organs through the blood or lymph system.  
Even if the infection was quiet for years, a weak immune system can wake it up.  
This is called reactivation TB.

### Babies and Young Children

Babies and young children are at high risk.  
Their immune systems are not fully developed.  
They are more likely to get infected and to get sick.

---

## How Can TB Be Prevented?

The Standing Committee on Vaccination (STIKO) stopped recommending it in 1998.  
Reasons include:
- The vaccine only helps in areas with high TB rates.

- The vaccine lasts a lifetime, so side effects can happen later.

# Nummular Eczema

Nummular eczema causes itchy, round rashes on the skin.  
It often appears on the arms or legs.  
The rashes can come and go over many years.  
Most people can get relief from the symptoms with proper treatment.

---

## Quick Facts

- Nummular eczema is a skin condition that causes inflammation.  
- It leads to itchy, round spots on the skin.  
- The spots are usually between one and ten centimeters wide.  
- They most often appear on the arms or legs.  
- It is more common in men over fifty.  
- Women can get it too, but usually at a younger age.  
- Children can also develop this condition.  
- The rashes often return in episodes over months or years.  
- Anti-inflammatory creams and good skin care can help reduce symptoms.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always see a doctor.

---

## What Is Nummular Eczema?

Nummular eczema is a long-term skin problem.  
It causes itchy, round patches on the skin.  
The patches are often reddish-brown and shaped like coins.  
They are most common on the legs and arms.  
Sometimes they appear on the hands, feet, or lower part of the body.

The condition often starts in men over fifty.  
It is less common in women, but when it does occur, it usually starts in teens or young adults.  
Children can also get it.

The rashes come and go over time.  
They may last for weeks or even months.  
Doctors often treat it with cortisone creams that reduce swelling and itching.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main sign is round, itchy spots on the skin.  
They look like coins and can be one to ten centimeters across.  
The spots may burn or feel sore.  
They can weep clear fluid at first.  
Then they form a crust on top.

If the crusts turn yellow, it may mean the skin is infected with bacteria.  
Some people have just one rash.  
Others have many rashes at once.  
They usually appear on the arms, legs, hands, or feet.  
If they appear on the body, they are most often on the lower stomach, lower back, or buttocks.

Over time, the rashes dry out and become flaky.  
Sometimes the center of a spot becomes lighter.  
This can make the rash look like a ring.

The rashes often return in the same place or nearby.  
This happens during flare-ups.

---

## What Causes Nummular Eczema?

Doctors do not fully understand what causes it.  
But several things may play a role.  
These include:

- A skin condition called neurodermatitis  
- Allergies to certain metals, like nickel  
- Very dry skin  
- Poor blood flow or swelling in the legs  
- Skin injuries, such as insect bites  
- Bacterial skin infections  
- Some medicines

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors usually recognize nummular eczema by the look of the rashes.  
They are shaped like coins and appear in typical places.  
No special blood tests are usually needed.

If the doctor thinks there is a bacterial infection, they may take a small sample from the skin.  
This is called a skin swab.  
They may also do an allergy test.  
This helps find possible triggers for the eczema.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Doctors often prescribe cortisone creams.  
These reduce swelling and itching.  
If the skin is infected with bacteria, they may also give an antibiotic.  
This fights the infection.

Some people take antihistamines.  
These help reduce itching, especially at night.  
They also help people sleep better.  
Antihistamines work by blocking allergic reactions.

Good skin care is very important.  
Here are some helpful tips:

- Use mild soaps that do not irritate the skin  
- Take short showers with warm (not hot) water  
- Put moisturizing cream on your skin right after showering  
- Keep your skin damp while applying cream  
- Avoid things that irritate your skin  
- Stay away from known allergens that cause flare-ups

# Neurodermatitis

Neurodermatitis causes a rash that itches badly.  
The rash often comes and goes.  
It is a long-term skin problem that is not contagious.  
It often starts in childhood and can get better over time.  
It is rare in adults.  
Some people with neurodermatitis also have allergies.  
Doctors can treat the worst symptoms with special ointments and creams.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What is neurodermatitis?

Neurodermatitis is a long-term skin condition that causes inflammation.  
The main signs are a rash and strong itching.  
It is most common in children.  
It is not caused by germs.  
When it is linked to allergies, it is called atopic dermatitis or atopic eczema.

Over time, many people get better.  
Some even stop having symptoms completely.  
Good skin care, medicine, and avoiding irritants can help most people live a normal life.

But during bad phases, the itching can be very strong.  
It can make it hard to sleep.  
It can also make it hard to focus.  
Some people feel embarrassed because of the rash.

---

## How do you know if someone has neurodermatitis?

The main sign is a constant itch.  
When symptoms are bad, the skin turns red and itches.  
Sometimes small blisters form.  
These blisters can break open and leak fluid.

Over time, the skin becomes dry, cracked, and thick.  
Different types of rashes can appear at the same time.

The condition usually comes in waves.  
Some days, there are few or no symptoms.  
Other days, the rash and itching are very bad.  
The skin is rarely inflamed all the time.

> **Important:** Where the rash appears and how it changes depends on the person.  
> Age matters a lot.

- **Babies:** The rash usually shows up on the cheeks and the outside of arms and legs.  
  It is less common on the back, stomach, or chest.

- **Children, teens, and adults:** The rash often appears in the inside of elbows, the back of knees, and on the neck.  
  Hands and feet are also often affected.  
  Face rashes are rare.

---

## What causes neurodermatitis?

Many things can lead to neurodermatitis.

The skin’s natural barrier is damaged by inflammation.  
This weakens the outer layer of the skin.  
The skin can no longer protect the body well.

Changes in the skin’s natural bacteria may also play a role.  
Genes can be involved too.  
Some people inherit a gene that stops the body from making a protein called filaggrin.  
This protein helps keep the skin strong and moist.  
Without it, the skin dries out.  
Dry skin is more likely to get irritated, infected, or inflamed.

We do not yet fully understand how all these factors work together.

> **Important:** About 30 to 40 percent of cases are linked to allergies.  
> People with allergic neurodermatitis often have hay fever or asthma too.  
> Common triggers include dust mites, pollen, milk, eggs, nuts, and fish.

Other things can also irritate the skin.  
These include:  
- Very hot or cold weather  
- Rough fabrics like wool  
- Cigarette smoke

---

## What increases the risk of neurodermatitis?

Having a family member with neurodermatitis raises your risk.  
But other factors may also play a role.  
The number of people with neurodermatitis has gone up in recent years.  
This suggests that environment and lifestyle matter too.

Some experts think that too much cleanliness may be a cause.  
The “hygiene hypothesis” says that children who grow up with more germs have a lower risk.  
For example, children with many siblings, those who went to daycare early, or those who grew up with pets often get neurodermatitis less often.  
Their immune systems are better trained to handle germs.

---

## How common is neurodermatitis?

About 1 in 7 children get neurodermatitis.  
In adults, it affects 2 to 5 out of 100 people.  
Adults often have more severe symptoms.

---

## How does neurodermatitis start and change?

Most children get it in the first two years of life.  
The first signs often appear between 3 and 6 months.  
Some children develop it later.  
It is rare for it to start after age five.

How it changes depends on the child’s age.

- Children who get it in the first year: about half no longer have it after 3 years.  
- Children who get it between ages 2 and 5: it often lasts longer.  
- Over 80 percent of children see a big improvement or no symptoms at all by age 10.

In some people, the condition returns in adulthood.  
When it does, it often affects the hands.  
In adults, it is usually a long-term condition.  
Symptoms come and go in waves.

It is rare for someone to first get neurodermatitis as an adult.

---

## Can neurodermatitis be prevented?

There is no proven way to prevent neurodermatitis.  
The risk is partly genetic.  
But we cannot predict who will get it.  
Many different factors interact to cause it.

Some weak evidence suggests that probiotic supplements might help.  
Breastfeeding may lower the risk, but studies are not clear.  
We still do not know exactly why children get neurodermatitis.  
We only know that several different causes are involved.

There is no strong proof that avoiding certain foods helps children without a known food allergy.  
There is little research on whether special diets help adults.  
There is no proof that using special skin care products in the first year of life prevents neurodermatitis.

But it is a good idea to vaccinate children with neurodermatitis.  
Illnesses like chickenpox can be worse for them.

> **Important:** If you are thinking about removing foods from your child’s diet, talk to a doctor first.  
> More information is available at [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## How is neurodermatitis diagnosed?

Other skin problems can look like neurodermatitis.  
Doctors only diagnose it if the rash itches badly and lasts for months or keeps coming back.  
The rash must appear in areas typical for the person’s age.

Doctors also check to rule out other conditions like psoriasis.  
In babies, neurodermatitis can be mistaken for seborrheic dermatitis.  
That condition causes less itching and usually goes away on its own in a few weeks or months.

Allergy tests are not very helpful for diagnosing neurodermatitis.  
Testing for many allergens is not useful unless there is a real suspicion.

---

## How is neurodermatitis treated?

Neurodermatitis cannot be cured.  
But good treatment can greatly reduce symptoms like itching and rash.

### Main treatments:

- **Daily skin care:** Use moisturizing creams or ointments every day.  
  These help keep the skin from drying out.  
  They can reduce itching, protect the skin, and prevent new flare-ups.  
  Apply at least twice a day.

- **Avoid irritants:** Many soaps, shampoos, and shower gels dry out the skin.  
  Try special products made for sensitive skin.  
  Regular skin care can help replace lost moisture.  
  Also avoid rough clothes, strong chemicals, and extreme temperatures.

- **Cortisone ointments:** These are used for sudden flare-ups.  
  They reduce itching and swelling fast.  
  Some people use them on 2 days a week as a preventive measure.  
  This is called proactive or interval therapy.  
  It helps reduce how often flare-ups happen.

- **Pimecrolimus and tacrolimus:** These are creams or ointments used on the skin.  
  They help when cortisone does not work or causes side effects.  
  They are safe for sensitive areas like the face and neck.

> **Important:** Other treatments include wet wraps, UV light therapy, and medicines that calm the immune system.  
> These are used only when other treatments fail or the condition is very severe.

Antihistamines (allergy medicine) are sometimes used to ease itching.  
But studies show they do not help much with the main symptoms.

Some people try herbal products or supplements like evening primrose oil, borage oil, vitamins, or zinc.  
But research shows these do not work.

Many other treatments, like laser therapy or desensitization, have not been studied enough.  
Medical groups do not recommend them.

For more details on skin care and neurodermatitis, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## What is life like with neurodermatitis?

The impact of neurodermatitis is often underestimated.  
It takes time and patience to find the right treatment.  
But most people learn to manage it well, both physically and emotionally.

For children, the condition can be tough.  
Some days are stressful for both the child and parents.  
But bad phases are usually followed by better times.  
Many children grow out of it or see big improvements.

Parents may feel overwhelmed or helpless.  
Special training courses are available to help families.  
For severe cases, outpatient or inpatient rehabilitation may be an option.

# Shoulder Pain

Shoulder pain is very common. It affects many people, but it is not always easy to find the exact cause.

Most people with sudden shoulder pain should rest the shoulder. Some treatments can help reduce the pain. Surgery usually does not help.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Shoulder Pain?

Shoulder pain is one of the most common joint problems.

Your shoulder has many parts. These include muscles, ligaments, tendons, small fluid-filled sacs called bursae, and bones. Because so many parts work together, pain can come from many different places.

Most shoulder pain happens in a space above the shoulder joint and below the top of the shoulder blade. This area is called the subacromial space.

Pain in this area is often called impingement syndrome. But other conditions can also cause shoulder pain. These include frozen shoulder and arthritis.

Many people feel better within six months. But some have pain for longer.

Avoid lifting your arm high or doing movements that strain the shoulder until the pain gets better.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Pain often happens on the outside of the shoulder.

It can hurt when you raise your arm out to the side.

Nighttime pain is common. Lying on the painful shoulder can make the pain worse. Some people wake up because of the pain.

---

## What Causes Shoulder Pain?

There are many possible causes.

The space above the shoulder joint can get smaller. This can happen because of bone spurs, wear and tear, or calcium deposits in a tendon.

Other causes include:

- Swelling in the bursae (the cushioning sacs in the shoulder).
- A curved or downward-sloping shoulder blade bone (called a type III acromion).
- Weak or unbalanced shoulder muscles.

When the arm is raised, parts of the tendons or bursa can get squeezed between the top of the upper arm bone and the shoulder blade bone. This is called impingement.

Different names are used depending on the cause. These include:

- Shoulder impingement syndrome
- Rotator cuff syndrome
- Calcific tendinitis

Studies show that scans often show changes even in people with no pain. For example, some people have calcium deposits or worn tendons on an X-ray or MRI but feel no pain.

Because of this, many doctors now use the term **subacromial pain syndrome** instead of impingement syndrome.

---

## Who Is at Risk?

People who work with their arms above shoulder height are more likely to get shoulder pain. This includes:

- Painters
- Electricians
- Warehouse workers
- Shelf stackers

Sports that involve raising the arm overhead also increase the risk. These include:

- Tennis
- Basketball
- Throwing sports
- Swimming (especially crawl and butterfly strokes)

Intensive training can make shoulder pain worse.

Weak shoulder muscles, ligaments, or tendons can also lead to pain. The shoulder joint is very movable. It depends mostly on muscles to stay stable. If the muscles are weak, the upper arm bone can move out of place. This can press on soft tissues and cause pain.

---

## How Common Is Shoulder Pain?

Shoulder pain is one of the most frequent reasons people see a doctor for joint problems. It is as common as neck and back pain.

Up to 70 out of 100 cases of shoulder pain are due to subacromial pain.

Outlook varies:

- About half of people feel better within six months.
- Some people still have pain for years.

---

## How Is Shoulder Pain Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms. They will want to know:

- When the pain started
- When it hurts most
- If you had an injury
- If you do certain jobs or sports

They will then do a physical exam. This includes:

- Moving your arms in different directions
- Checking how your elbows turn
- Pressing on parts of your shoulder

These tests help the doctor find the cause. They also help rule out other problems, such as neck pain or frozen shoulder.

In some cases, your doctor may order a scan.

- An ultrasound can show tears in the rotator cuff.
- An X-ray shows bones and calcium deposits.
- An MRI gives a detailed image of soft tissues.

Scans are not always needed. There is often no clear link between what the scan shows and how much pain you feel.

Scans may be helpful if:

- The pain does not improve with treatment
- Surgery is being considered
- Another cause of pain is suspected

For example, an X-ray can help if arthritis is suspected.

---

## How Is Shoulder Pain Treated?

For sudden shoulder pain, follow these steps:

- Rest the shoulder. Avoid work or sports that require raising your arm above your head.
- Use cold packs on the shoulder to reduce swelling and pain.
- Take non-steroid anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen if needed. Do not use them for more than 1 to 2 weeks.
- If the pain is severe, a cortisone injection may help.

Rest does not mean keeping your arm completely still. Gentle movement is important.

A physiotherapist can guide you through exercises. These help strengthen the shoulder and improve movement.

Studies show that doing these exercises at home works just as well as doing them with a therapist.

> **Important:** Surgery does not usually help with shoulder pain. Research shows that surgery is no better than a fake surgery (placebo). Every surgery carries risks. It can even cause new problems. So, surgery should only be considered after careful thought.
