# Greenstick Fractures

A greenstick fracture is a type of bone break that happens mostly in children. The outer part of the bone and the layer around it get damaged. But the inner part of the bone stays whole.

This kind of fracture only happens in children. It is rare in adults.

## Quick Facts

- A greenstick fracture means the outer bone and the covering around it are damaged.
- The inner bone stays solid and whole.
- These fractures mostly happen in children under 10 years old.
- They most often affect the forearm or upper arm bones.
- They usually happen when a child falls on an outstretched hand.
- Doctors check for this injury with a physical exam and imaging tests.
- An ultrasound scan can help find the fracture.
- An X-ray confirms the diagnosis by showing a partial break.
- The injured arm is held still with a cast or splint.
- Surgery is very rare.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical care. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always see a doctor.

## What Is a Greenstick Fracture?

A greenstick fracture is a partial break in the bone. The outer layer of the bone and the tissue around it are damaged. The inner part of the bone remains intact.

This type of injury only happens in children. Their bones are still growing and softer than adult bones. They are more flexible and less likely to break completely.

Think of a green twig. If you bend it, it may crack on one side but not snap all the way through. That is how a greenstick fracture works.

These fractures usually happen in long bones, like the ones in the arms and legs.

The most common places are the forearm bones (radius and ulna) or the upper arm bone (humerus).

They can also happen in the thigh or lower leg bones. But they are rare in the face, ribs, collarbone, or shoulder blades.

Most greenstick fractures heal well with no lasting problems.

## What Are the Symptoms?

You may notice these signs after a fall or injury:

- Trouble moving the arm or leg.
- Pain when you touch the injured area.
- Small bruises under the skin.

If the injury is more serious, you might also see:

- Swelling from fluid buildup.
- Scrapes or damage to the skin and soft tissues.

If your child has any of these symptoms after a fall, see a doctor right away.

## What Causes a Greenstick Fracture?

The most common cause is falling on an outstretched hand. This often happens during play or sports.

When children fall, they often put out their hands to catch themselves. This puts strong pressure on the forearm. The bone twists and breaks on one side.

Sports that raise the risk include:

- Skateboarding
- Rollerblading
- Horseback riding
- Snowboarding

Wearing wrist guards can help reduce the risk.

Other causes include:

- Car accidents where the child is hit from behind.
- Being hit on the arm with a hard object.

## What Are the Possible Problems?

Most greenstick fractures heal without any lasting issues.

But if the bone is not treated properly, or if it heals crooked, problems can happen. These include:

- The arm or leg not moving as well as before.
- The bone not lining up correctly.

Children who have had a greenstick fracture are more likely to break the same bone again.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

The doctor will ask how the injury happened.

They will check:

- If the area is painful.
- If there is any damage to the skin or soft tissues.
- If the injury is open (skin broken) or closed (skin intact).

They will also check blood flow and nerve function.

To confirm the fracture, the doctor will use imaging:

- An X-ray shows a curved break that does not go all the way through the bone.
- An ultrasound scan can also be used. It is especially helpful for children.

## How Is It Treated?

The first step is to keep the injured arm or leg still.

Pain can be managed with common pain relievers like ibuprofen or paracetamol.

After a few days, a cast is applied. The type of cast depends on where the break is:

- If the break is near the wrist, a short cast may be used.
- If the break is in the upper arm, a full arm cast is needed.

The cast must stay on for three to six weeks. The length depends on the location.

After about three weeks, a long cast can sometimes be changed to a shorter one.

In some cases, a splint is used instead of a cast. A splint can be taken off temporarily, for example when bathing.

Surgery is only needed in rare cases. This includes when nerves, blood vessels, or joints are damaged.

## What Happens After Healing?

After the cast is removed, do not let your child use the injured arm or leg right away.

Doctors recommend waiting two to four weeks before returning to sports.

Most children do not need physiotherapy. Their natural activity helps the limb recover.

If the arm or leg still does not move fully after this time, see the doctor again.

An ultrasound may be done to check healing. Additional therapy might be needed.

# Heart Failure

Your heart pumps blood to all parts of your body.  
In heart failure, your heart can’t pump enough blood.  
This means your organs and muscles don’t get enough oxygen.  
Heart failure can happen suddenly or slowly over time.

---

## Quick Facts

- Your heart can’t pump enough blood.  
- This means your body doesn’t get enough oxygen.  
- Common signs include shortness of breath, tiredness, and swelling in the feet, ankles, or belly.  
- Heart failure can start suddenly after a heart attack.  
- It can also build up over time, often because of another health problem.  
- Treatment includes medicine, exercise, and treating the root cause.  
- Not smoking, limiting alcohol, and staying active help protect your heart.  

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Heart Failure?

Your heart is not pumping blood well enough.  
This causes blood to back up in your body.  
Organs and muscles don’t get enough oxygen.  
This condition is also called cardiac insufficiency or congestive heart failure.

Heart failure can happen fast — for example, after a heart attack.  
It can also develop slowly — for example, from long-term high blood pressure.

Mild heart failure may not cause obvious symptoms.  
In advanced cases, even simple tasks like walking or climbing stairs become hard.  
Some treatments can ease symptoms and help you live longer.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Common symptoms include:

- Trouble breathing, especially when lying down or during activity  
- Feeling very tired or weak  
- Swelling in the feet, ankles, or legs  
- Swelling in the belly or genital area (less common)  
- Gaining weight quickly due to fluid buildup  

Other possible signs:

- Fast or irregular heartbeat  
- Needing to urinate often at night  
- Trouble focusing or thinking clearly  
- A dry, hacking cough

These symptoms can also come from other health problems.  
Many people with heart failure have other conditions too.  
This makes it hard to spot early signs.

---

## What Causes Heart Failure?

Most of the time, heart failure is caused by another heart problem.  
These are the most common causes:

- Coronary heart disease (narrowed heart arteries)  
- Heart attack (blocked artery)  
- High blood pressure  
- Damaged heart valves  
- Irregular heartbeats (like atrial fibrillation)

In coronary heart disease, the blood vessels feeding the heart get narrow.  
This reduces blood flow to the heart muscle.  
If blood flow stops completely, part of the heart muscle dies — this is a heart attack.

High blood pressure forces the heart to work harder.  
Over time, the heart muscle thickens and stiffens.  
This makes it harder to pump blood.  
Eventually, the heart can’t keep up.

Other causes include:

- Infections of the heart  
- Birth defects in the heart muscle  
- Heart valve problems  
- Irregular heartbeats  
- Heavy alcohol use  
- Illegal drugs  
- Some cancer medicines

---

## What Increases the Risk?

You are more likely to develop heart failure if you:

- Have type 2 diabetes  
- Smoke  
- Drink too much alcohol  
- Are severely overweight  
- Don’t get enough physical activity  
- Take certain cancer medicines

If heart problems run in your family — especially rare genetic heart diseases — your risk is higher.

---

## How Common Is Heart Failure?

Heart failure mostly affects older adults.  
It usually starts after age 65.  
More than 10 out of 100 people over 70 have heart failure.  
Men and women are affected about equally.

---

## How Does Heart Failure Develop?

There are two main types:

### Acute Heart Failure  
This happens suddenly.  
It often follows a heart attack.  
It is a medical emergency.

### Chronic Heart Failure  
This develops slowly over months or years.  
It may not cause symptoms at first.  
Symptoms appear as the heart gets weaker.

There are four stages:

#### Stage 1: No Symptoms  
You feel fine.  
But tests show the heart is not working well.

#### Stage 2: Mild Symptoms  
You feel tired or short of breath when climbing stairs or walking uphill.  
Light activity does not cause problems.

#### Stage 3: Moderate Symptoms  
Even normal daily tasks — like walking on flat ground — cause tiredness or breathlessness.

#### Stage 4: Severe Symptoms  
Symptoms happen even at rest.  
Even small movements cause problems.  
Some people can no longer leave their bed.

Doctors also check how well the heart fills with blood and how much blood it pumps with each beat.

How heart failure progresses varies from person to person.  
It depends on the cause and other health issues.  
For some, symptoms stay stable for years.  
For others, the heart gets weaker quickly.

> **Important:** Advanced heart failure can make daily life very hard.  
> Simple tasks become difficult or impossible.

If heart failure is caused by a treatable condition — like high blood pressure or damaged heart valves — treating that condition may stop or even reverse heart failure.

But for most people, heart failure cannot be cured.  
The heart gets weaker over time.

---

## How Is Heart Failure Diagnosed?

Doctors look for signs like:

- Trouble breathing  
- Tiredness  
- Swelling in the legs or belly  
- Unusual sounds when listening to the heart  
- Rattling or crackling in the lungs

To confirm the diagnosis, they may do:

- An ECG (electrocardiogram): checks the heart’s electrical activity and rhythm  
- A blood test: checks for signs of heart problems  
- An echocardiogram (ultrasound of the heart): shows how well the heart pumps and how the valves work

Doctors also try to find the root cause.  
This helps them treat the underlying condition if possible.

For more details on types of heart failure, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## How Is Heart Failure Treated?

Treatment has several parts:

### 1. Treat the Underlying Cause  
If heart failure is due to high blood pressure or another heart disease, doctors treat that first.

### 2. Medication  
Medicines help reduce strain on the heart and ease symptoms.  
Common types include:

- Beta blockers  
- ACE inhibitors  
- Diuretics (water pills)

The exact medicine depends on your type of heart failure.

### 3. Physical Training  
Special heart exercise programs help build strength and stamina.  
They are tailored to your needs.  
These programs improve fitness and quality of life.

### 4. Medication Plan  
Work with your doctor to create a clear plan.  
This helps avoid dangerous drug interactions.  
It should include over-the-counter medicines.  
Some painkillers — like diclofenac or ibuprofen — can make heart failure worse.

### 5. Implantable Devices  
For severe cases, doctors may recommend devices.  
These can prevent sudden heart death or help the heart pump better.

### 6. Lifestyle Changes  
You can help your heart by:

- Not smoking  
- Drinking alcohol in small amounts  
- Staying as active as possible  
- Reducing daily fluid intake (if advised)

Reducing fluid can help prevent swelling and tiredness.

> **Note:** Always follow your doctor’s advice.  
> Do not change your treatment without talking to your healthcare provider.

# Cirrhosis of the Liver

Cirrhosis is a serious condition where healthy liver tissue is slowly destroyed. It is replaced by scar tissue. This scar tissue does not work like normal liver tissue. Over time, the liver can shrink and stop working properly.

Cirrhosis often develops over many years. It may not cause symptoms at first. This means people may not know they have it until serious problems appear.

## What Causes Cirrhosis?

The most common causes are:

- Drinking too much alcohol over many years.
- Long-term liver infections, especially hepatitis B or hepatitis C.
- Fatty liver disease that is not caused by alcohol.
- Autoimmune hepatitis – a condition where the body’s immune system attacks the liver.
- Wilson’s disease – a rare inherited condition where copper builds up in the liver.

## What Are the Symptoms?

In the early stages, cirrhosis may not cause any symptoms. Up to 4 out of 10 people do not notice anything at first.

Early signs include:

- Feeling very tired.
- Losing weight without trying.
- Not feeling hungry.
- Itchy skin.

As the disease gets worse, more serious symptoms appear:

- Yellowing of the skin, eyes, and mouth (jaundice).
- Severe itching.
- Redness on the palms of the hands.
- Spider-like blood vessels on the face and chest.
- Cracks at the corners of the mouth.
- Lips that look red and shiny.
- In men: breast growth, less hair on the belly, lower sex drive.
- In women: irregular periods.

## How Does Cirrhosis Progress?

Doctors divide cirrhosis into two stages:

**Compensated cirrhosis:** The liver is damaged, but it still works well enough to keep the body healthy. There are no major problems yet.

**Decompensated cirrhosis:** The liver is so damaged that it can no longer do its job. Serious complications can happen. These include:

- Bleeding from swollen veins in the esophagus (esophageal varices).
- Fluid buildup in the belly (ascites), which can lead to infection.
- Liver cancer.
- Brain problems due to toxins building up in the blood (hepatic encephalopathy).

Hepatic encephalopathy can cause:

- Confusion.
- Slowed thinking.
- Mood swings.
- Feeling sleepy or weak.
- Shaking hands.
- Changes in handwriting.
- In severe cases, loss of consciousness (liver coma). The person does not respond to sounds or pain.

## How Is Cirrhosis Diagnosed?

If cirrhosis is suspected, your doctor will:

- Do a physical exam. They may feel for an enlarged liver.
- Look at your skin for signs of liver disease.
- Use imaging tests. One common test uses sound waves to check how stiff the liver is. This helps show if scarring is present.
- Sometimes, a small sample of liver tissue is taken with a needle. This is tested in a lab to confirm cirrhosis.

Blood tests are also used to:

- Check how well the liver is working.
- Test for hepatitis B or C infections.

Doctors also check for complications and try to find the cause of the cirrhosis.

## How Is Cirrhosis Treated?

The main goal of treatment is to stop or slow the damage to the liver.

Treatment depends on the cause:

- If the cause is hepatitis B or C, antiviral medicines can help.
- If alcohol is the cause, you must stop drinking completely.
- If you are overweight, losing weight can help reduce liver damage.

You should avoid alcohol, drugs, and smoking — even if your cirrhosis was not caused by alcohol.

Medicines should only be taken when needed. Your doctor may need to change your dose because the liver does not work as well.

Some complications are life-threatening. Early treatment is key.

For example:

- Antibiotics may be given to prevent infection in the belly (peritonitis).
- Other treatments can help manage fluid buildup, bleeding, or brain problems.

If the liver is severely damaged and no other treatment works, a liver transplant may be the only option.

## How Can You Prevent Cirrhosis?

You can lower your risk by:

- Drinking alcohol in small amounts.  
  - Women should not have more than 12 grams of pure alcohol a day.  
    This is about one small beer (300 ml) or one small glass of wine (125 ml).  
  - Men should not have more than 24 grams of pure alcohol a day.  
- Getting vaccinated against hepatitis A and B.
- Using condoms during sex to reduce the risk of hepatitis infection.
- Maintaining a healthy weight and eating well.

## Important Note

This information is not a substitute for medical care. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor if you have concerns about your liver.

# Scarlet Fever

Scarlet fever is a bacterial illness. It mostly affects children and teens. It is caused by a type of bacteria called group A Streptococcus. These bacteria can make a toxin that causes a red rash. The rash gives the illness its name.

This illness can be treated. Most people get better with medicine. But it is important to see a doctor for proper care.

---

## Quick Facts

- Scarlet fever is caused by group A Streptococcus bacteria.
- Common signs are a sore throat, high fever, a red rash, and a tongue that starts white and then turns red and bumpy (called "strawberry tongue").
- It mainly affects children and teens between 5 and 15 years old. But adults can get it too.
- Doctors often use antibiotics to treat it. These help shorten how long a person is contagious.
- Serious long-term problems are rare in Central Europe today.
- Good hygiene can help stop the spread of the illness.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Scarlet Fever?

Scarlet fever is a bacterial infection. It usually happens in children and teens between 5 and 15 years old.

The bacteria that cause it are called group A Streptococcus. These bacteria can make a special poison. This poison causes the red rash that is the main sign of the illness.

Other common signs include:
- A sudden high fever
- A very sore throat
- Red, swollen tonsils
- Trouble swallowing

Doctors treat the fever and throat pain with medicine. They may also prescribe antibiotics.

Antibiotics help people feel better faster. They also reduce the time a person can spread the illness to others.

In rare cases, scarlet fever can lead to long-term health problems. These can affect the joints, heart, or kidneys. But these problems are now very uncommon in Central Europe.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms usually start suddenly, one to three days after infection.

Common early signs:
- High fever
- Chills
- Feeling unwell
- Severe sore throat

The throat looks bright red. The tonsils may have a white coating. The neck glands can swell up.

Younger children may also have:
- Belly pain
- Vomiting

The bacteria make a toxin. This causes a red rash. The rash usually appears on the chest, neck, and face on day one or two. It can spread to the rest of the body.

The rash feels like sandpaper. It does not appear on the palms of the hands or soles of the feet.

The cheeks are red. The area around the mouth is pale.

The tongue starts with a white coating. Then it turns dark red and bumpy. This is called "strawberry tongue."

The rash lasts about six to nine days. After that, the skin starts to peel. This is most common on the hands and feet.

> **Important:** There are many types of the bacteria that cause scarlet fever. Each makes a different poison. After one infection, a person is only protected against that one type. They can get scarlet fever again from a different type.

Some group A Streptococcus bacteria do not make the poison. If someone gets infected with one of these, they can still have a sore throat and fever. But they will not get the red rash.

---

## How Do People Get Scarlet Fever?

Scarlet fever is caused by group A Streptococcus bacteria.

The main way it spreads is through close contact with an infected person.

When someone with scarlet fever talks, sneezes, or coughs, tiny droplets with the bacteria come out. These droplets can be breathed in by others.

It can also spread if someone touches a surface with the bacteria and then touches their mouth or nose.

In rare cases, the bacteria can spread through contaminated food or water.

---

## How Common Is Scarlet Fever?

Scarlet fever is one of the most common bacterial infections in children.

It mostly affects children and teens between 5 and 15 years old.

About 5 out of every 1,000 children get it each year.

It is more common in winter and early spring. Children in schools or daycare centers are more likely to get it.

> **Important:** Some people carry the bacteria in their throat but do not get sick. They are very unlikely to spread the illness. But people who are sick can pass it on easily.

---

## How Does Scarlet Fever Progress?

The illness can be mild or severe.

Some people have a high fever and pus-filled tonsils. Others have only mild symptoms.

In Germany today, mild cases are more common than serious ones.

---

### Possible Short-Term Complications

The bacteria mainly stay in the throat. If they grow unchecked, they can cause:

- A pus-filled abscess near the tonsils
- Sinus infection
- Pneumonia
- Middle ear infection
- Blood poisoning (sepsis) — this is rare

---

### Possible Long-Term Complications

These are rare in Germany. But they can happen after scarlet fever.

#### Kidney Inflammation

In rare cases, the kidneys become inflamed. This usually happens one to three weeks after the illness.

Most cases are mild. The outlook is good, especially for children.

Permanent kidney damage is very rare.

When the kidneys are inflamed, they let blood parts pass into the urine. This can make the urine look brown and foamy.

Other signs include:
- Swelling around the eyes
- High blood pressure
- Feeling tired
- Belly pain
- Headaches
- Fever
- Blurry vision

#### Rheumatic Fever

This can happen in children and teens aged 3 to 15. It usually shows up two to three weeks after the sore throat goes away.

It causes:
- Swelling and pain in large joints
- Heart problems
- Skin rashes
- Nervous system issues

People may also have a fever and feel very weak.

This condition can cause lasting damage. It may lead to heart valve problems.

---

## How Can Scarlet Fever Be Prevented?

There is no vaccine for scarlet fever.

To lower your risk:
- Avoid close contact with sick people.
- Wash your hands often with soap and water.
- Clean toys and surfaces with disinfectant.

People with serious health problems or weak immune systems may be given preventive antibiotics if they are at high risk.

For people who have had a strep infection before, doctors may give long-term antibiotics to prevent new infections.

---

## How Is Scarlet Fever Diagnosed?

Doctors often recognize scarlet fever from the symptoms.

A quick test can check for strep bacteria. A swab is taken from the back of the throat.

If the test is negative or unclear, a lab test may be done.

If a doctor suspects long-term problems, they may take a blood sample. This checks for antibodies to the bacteria.

---

## How Is Scarlet Fever Treated?

Rest, pain relief medicine, and throat rinses help ease symptoms.

Antibiotics like penicillin are often used. They help shorten the illness and reduce the risk of spreading it.

It is important to take the full course of antibiotics. Even if you feel better, keep taking the medicine.

Taking antibiotics can reduce the illness by about 16 hours.

Not every case needs antibiotics. In mild cases, doctors may suggest not using them.

Antibiotics should only be used when needed. Overuse has led to bacteria becoming resistant to these drugs.

---

### How to Stop the Spread of the Illness

**If you are sick:**
- Do not go to school, daycare, or work.
- Tell your school or workplace about your illness.
- You are no longer contagious 24 hours after starting antibiotics.
- You can return when you no longer have a fever and feel well.
- You do not need a doctor’s note to return.

**If you have been around someone with scarlet fever:**
- No special steps are needed unless you develop symptoms.
- If you get a sore throat, fever, or rash, see a doctor right away.

> **Important:** Always follow your doctor’s advice. They will decide when it is safe to return to normal activities.

# Osteoarthritis of the Knee

Osteoarthritis of the knee is a condition where the cushioning tissue in the knee wears down. This can cause pain and stiffness. It often starts with pain when you use your knee. If the condition gets worse and does not improve with exercise or pain medicine, a knee replacement might be an option.

---

## Quick Facts

- Knee pain that only happens when you use the knee is often the first sign.
- You can help your knees by doing exercises to strengthen and move them.
- If you are overweight, losing weight can reduce pressure on your knee.
- It is not true that you should rest your knee. In fact, moving it helps.
- A knee replacement may be considered if the pain is severe and affects daily life.
- Many products and treatments are sold for osteoarthritis, but many have not been proven to work. Some may even cause harm.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Osteoarthritis of the Knee?

Your knee has a smooth surface inside that lets the bones move easily. This surface is called cartilage. When this cartilage wears down, it causes osteoarthritis. The knee may feel stiff after sitting or lying down. It may hurt when you move.

It is a myth that you should rest your knee when you have osteoarthritis. Resting makes things worse. Strong muscles help protect your knee. Movement helps feed the cartilage with nutrients.

The best treatment is staying active. Exercises help keep the knee and cartilage healthy. If you are overweight, losing even a little weight can help reduce pain.

If the condition is advanced and causes serious pain, a knee replacement may be an option. This is especially true if pain medicine and exercise do not help enough.

> **Important:** Many treatments are advertised for osteoarthritis, but their benefits are not proven. Some may even be harmful.

---

## Symptoms of Osteoarthritis of the Knee

- Pain that starts when you use your knee.
- The pain may get worse over time. It can happen even when you are not moving.
- You may feel pain at night or when resting.
- Your knee may feel stiff, especially in the morning or after sitting.
- Pain can be on the inside, outside, or under the kneecap.
- Pain under the kneecap often happens when standing up or going up stairs.
- In severe cases, pain is constant and can be sharp, burning, or throbbing.
- The knee may swell, feel hot, and become stiff during flare-ups.
- Flare-ups can come suddenly and last several days. They are hard to predict.
- Less movement weakens the muscles and ligaments. This can make the knee feel unstable.

---

## What Causes Osteoarthritis of the Knee?

The knee joint connects the thigh bone to the lower leg bone. The ends of these bones and the back of the kneecap are covered in cartilage. Healthy cartilage lets the knee move smoothly.

Osteoarthritis happens when the cartilage breaks down. It cannot heal itself well. Once damaged, it stays damaged.

Osteoarthritis can affect three areas of the knee:
- The inside of the knee
- The outside of the knee
- The area under the kneecap

---

## Risk Factors

- Everyone’s cartilage wears down a little with age. But this is not the same as “wear and tear” from normal use.
- Cartilage needs movement to stay healthy. Movement helps it get nutrients.
- Injuries to the knee can cause osteoarthritis. Examples include:
  - A torn meniscus
  - A torn anterior cruciate ligament
  - A dislocated kneecap
  - A bone fracture near the knee
- Being very overweight increases pressure on the knee. A body-mass index over 30 is considered obese.
- Jobs that require kneeling, squatting, or lifting heavy things increase risk.
- Leg length differences or bad knee alignment (like knock knees or bow legs) can increase risk.

> **Important:** Exercise does not harm the knee. In fact, not moving is worse. Lack of movement weakens muscles and stops the cartilage from getting nutrients.

---

## How Common Is Osteoarthritis of the Knee?

We do not know the exact number of people in Germany with this condition. But in other countries, about 4 out of every 100 adults have it.

The chance of having it goes up with age. About 10 to 15 out of every 100 people over 60 have it. Women are slightly more likely than men.

---

## How Does It Progress?

Osteoarthritis does not always get worse. Many people live with mild pain for years. Others see faster changes.

A large Dutch study followed people with knee osteoarthritis for 5 years. The results showed:

- About 60% had moderate pain that stayed the same or got a little better.
- About 25% had mild pain that did not change much.
- About 10% had severe pain that stayed about the same.
- About 5% had mild pain that got much worse over time.

Pain can come and go. Some days are worse than others. Sudden movements or small injuries can make pain worse. But it often goes away on its own.

> **Important:** In very advanced cases, the cartilage may be gone in places. This can expose bone. Other problems can develop, such as:
- Damage to the meniscus
- Weaker muscles
- Loose ligaments
- Extra fluid in the joint (called joint effusion), which can cause pain

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms. They will check your knee for pain, stiffness, and movement. They will look at your leg shape and rule out other causes like meniscus or ligament injuries.

An X-ray of the knee is usually enough to confirm the diagnosis. You usually do not need more detailed scans like CT or MRI.

If the diagnosis is clear, you do not need regular X-rays. Treatment is based on your symptoms, not on what the X-ray shows.

You may need more tests only if:
- The condition gets worse very fast
- New symptoms appear that suggest another illness

Before a knee replacement, special images are taken. These help the surgeon plan the operation.

---

## How Is It Treated?

There are many ways to treat osteoarthritis of the knee. The best choice depends on how bad it is, your health, and what you hope to achieve.

### Stay Active
- Moving your knee helps. It keeps the cartilage healthy.
- Strengthening and flexibility exercises reduce pain and improve movement.
- Studies show this works well.

### Lose Weight
- If you are overweight, losing even a small amount helps.
- Losing more than 5% of your body weight can improve movement and reduce pain.

### Wear Good Shoes
- Choose shoes that fit well.
- They should have cushioned soles and support the arch of your foot.
- Avoid high heels.

> For more information on knee exercises, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

### Other Treatments

- **Arch supports, knee braces, or special shoes:** These are safe to try. But there is not enough good research to prove they help. One study found that a special offloading shoe worked no better than a regular cushioned shoe.
- **Pain-relief gel (like diclofenac):** This can help many people. It has few side effects.
- **Pain pills (like diclofenac, ibuprofen, etoricoxib):** These can reduce pain. They are effective for many.
- **Paracetamol:** This does not help with knee osteoarthritis.
- **Opioid painkillers:** These are not better than anti-inflammatory medicine. They have more side effects and can be addictive.
- **Acupuncture:** Some studies say it helps. But it works no better than fake acupuncture (where needles are placed in the wrong spot or just lightly).
- **Injections into the knee:**
  - **Cortisone:** Can help for up to 8 weeks. But repeated use can harm the cartilage.
  - **Hyaluronic acid:** Studies show it is no better than a saltwater solution. It is not covered by health insurance.
  - **Autohemotherapy (using your own blood):** No proof it works.
- **Knee replacement:** This is an option for advanced cases. It helps most people with severe pain. After surgery, you need rehab and time to adjust.
- **Knee osteotomy:** A surgery to correct uneven wear on one side of the knee. It may be an alternative to replacement.
- **X-ray therapy (orthovoltage):** This uses low-dose radiation. There are no good studies to show it helps.
- **Radiosynoviorthesis (RSO):** A small amount of radioactive material is injected. Studies show no benefit. Some people had serious side effects like joint inflammation.
- **Surgery on the cartilage:** These procedures (like Pridie drilling, microfracture, or transplants) are not recommended. They can make symptoms worse and have no proven benefit.
- **Arthroscopy (knee washing and shaving):** This has been tested in many studies. It does not help people with osteoarthritis.

> **Important:** If you are thinking about a knee replacement, get a second medical opinion first.

> The decision aid on _gesundheitsinformation.de_ can help you decide.
