# Tendinitis

Tendinitis is a common problem for people who do sports. It causes pain in areas of the body that are used a lot. The pain happens when a tendon becomes inflamed or irritated.

## Quick Facts

- Tendinitis happens when a tendon is used too much or too hard.
- It often affects the shoulders, elbows, knees, and heels.
- Resting the painful area helps it heal.
- Most people need physical therapy after resting.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Tendinitis?

Tendons are strong cords that connect muscles to bones. When you use a tendon too much, it can get overworked and hurt. This is tendinitis.

Repeating the same motion over and over can cause tendinitis. For example, playing tennis or volleyball can irritate the tendons in your elbow or shoulder. Running a lot can hurt the Achilles tendon in your heel. Jumping sports like basketball or volleyball can hurt the tendons in your knees.

When a tendon is irritated, you must rest it. After resting, slowly start using it again. Stretching exercises help the tendon get used to normal use.

Tendinitis becomes more common as you get older. It is especially common in people who play sports.

## What Are the Symptoms?

The main symptom is pain. The pain may make it hard to move the area. The area may also feel stiff or slightly swollen.

The pain usually happens where the tendon meets the bone. It hurts most when you stretch the tendon, when the muscle is tight, or when you press on the area.

For example, if the Achilles tendon is irritated, it hurts when you stand on your toes. But the pain can also happen even when you are not moving.

## What Causes Tendinitis?

Using a tendon too much can cause small injuries. It can also reduce blood flow to the area. This can lead to scar tissue forming or calcium building up in the tendon. These changes cause irritation and pain.

Doing the same movement over and over is the most common cause. For example, swinging your arm to hit a tennis ball can irritate the elbow tendon. Running hard every day can hurt the Achilles tendon. Jumping a lot can hurt the knee tendons.

Other activities can cause tendinitis too. Using a computer mouse a lot, for example, can strain the tendons in your wrist.

In rare cases, some medicines, like certain antibiotics, can cause tendinitis as a side effect.

## What Increases the Risk?

Some things make tendinitis more likely. These include:

- Flat feet or other foot problems  
- Shoes that do not fit well  
- Diabetes  
- Joint diseases like arthritis  
- Autoimmune diseases that make the body attack its own tissues  
- Smoking  
- Being overweight  

Tendinitis is more common as you age. It is especially common in people who play sports.

## What Is the Outlook?

When a tendon is irritated, it hurts. Most people stop using the area, which helps it heal. The pain usually goes away in a few weeks.

But if you use the tendon too soon, the problem can come back. If the tendon does not rest long enough, it may not heal properly. This increases the risk of a partial or full tear.

## How Is Tendinitis Diagnosed?

Your doctor will look at the painful area. They will ask about your job and hobbies. This helps them see if your activities are causing the problem.

If the symptoms match tendinitis and you have used the area too much, the doctor can usually make a diagnosis.

Sometimes, an ultrasound scan is used. It can show small calcium deposits or other signs of tendinitis. X-rays or MRI scans may be used to rule out other causes of the pain.

## How Is Tendinitis Treated?

The first step is to protect the tendon. A brace or bandage may help. Rest for 3 to 6 weeks is usually needed.

After resting, slowly return to normal use. Stretching exercises help the tendon heal.

Other treatments can help too. These include:

- Ultrasound therapy  
- Massage  
- Electrical stimulation  

Pain medicine can be used for a short time.

If the pain does not go away, the doctor may suggest:

- Cortisone injections  
- Surgery  

Surgery removes damaged tissue or scar tissue.

For more information, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

## How Does Tendinitis Affect Daily Life?

It can be hard to protect your arms and legs in daily life. But you should avoid putting extra strain on the affected tendon.

Try to put off heavy tasks. For example, delay cleaning windows, weeding the garden, or carrying heavy bags.

Ask family, friends, or neighbors for help.

Learn which movements to avoid. A physiotherapist can teach you which movements hurt the tendon and which are safe.

Occupational therapy can help you change how you do work tasks. This can reduce strain on the tendon.

# Conjunctivitis

Conjunctivitis is when the eye becomes inflamed.  
The conjunctiva is a thin, clear layer that covers the white part of the eye and the inside of the eyelid.  
This layer protects the eye.  
When it gets inflamed, the eye turns red.  

Conjunctivitis can spread easily.  
It is usually not serious.  
But it can be annoying.

---

## Quick Facts

- Most cases are caused by viruses or bacteria. This is called infectious conjunctivitis.  
- Some cases are caused by allergies. This is called allergic conjunctivitis.  
- Symptoms include red eyes, watery eyes, itching, and a sticky discharge.  
- Viral and bacterial conjunctivitis can spread from one person to another.  
- Allergic conjunctivitis and conjunctivitis from irritants do not spread.  
- Most cases go away on their own in one to two weeks.  

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor.  
> Do not use this to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Conjunctivitis?

Conjunctivitis means the conjunctiva is inflamed.  
The conjunctiva is a thin, moist layer that covers the white of the eye and the inside of the eyelid.  
It helps protect the eye.  
When it becomes inflamed, the eye turns red.

There are many causes.  
The most common are viruses or bacteria.  
This is called infectious conjunctivitis.  
Allergies can also cause it.  
This is called allergic conjunctivitis.

> **Important:** If you touch an infected eye, you can spread the infection to the other eye.  
> Avoid touching your eyes.  
> If you do touch one eye, wash your hands right away.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on the cause.

### Bacterial Conjunctivitis

- Eyes turn red.  
- Eyes water a lot.  
- You may feel itching or a burning sensation.  
- A thick, yellowish-white fluid builds up.  
- This fluid can stick your eyelids together, especially in the morning.  
- The eye may hurt when you move it.

### Viral Conjunctivitis

- Eyes turn red.  
- Eyes water a lot.  
- The fluid is thin and watery.  
- Itching and burning may happen.  
- Symptoms are similar to bacterial conjunctivitis, but the fluid is clearer.

### Allergic Conjunctivitis

- Both eyes are affected.  
- Eyes water.  
- Itching and redness are common.  
- You may also have a runny nose or sneezing.  
- This type is not contagious.

> **Warning:** See a doctor if you have:  
> - Blurry or poor vision  
> - Pain when looking at light  
> - A feeling like something is in your eye  
> - A severe headache with nausea

These could be signs of a more serious problem.

---

## What Causes Conjunctivitis?

### Infections

- Viruses or bacteria can cause conjunctivitis.  
- These germs spread through touch.  
- You can pass the infection from one eye to the other by touching both eyes.  
- Germs can also spread through shared items like tissues, washcloths, eye drop bottles, or binoculars.

### Allergies

- Allergies to pollen, dust mites, or other things can cause conjunctivitis.  
- This type is not contagious.

### Irritants

- Dust, dirt, dry air, or strong liquids can irritate the eye.  
- Damage to the eye or not enough tear fluid can also cause inflammation.  
- These cases are not contagious.

---

## How Does It Develop?

- Bacterial conjunctivitis usually gets better on its own.  
- In most people, symptoms go away in one to two weeks without treatment.  
- Viral conjunctivitis also often clears up in a few weeks.  
- If symptoms last longer than four weeks, it is called chronic conjunctivitis.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms.  
They will check for:  
- Itching  
- A feeling like something is in your eye  
- Sticky eyelids  
- How long the symptoms have lasted  

They will also look at your eyes and eyelids.  
They will check for injuries or signs of irritation.

- The symptoms usually show if it is viral or bacterial.  
- If the cause is unclear, the doctor may take a small sample of fluid from your eye.  
- This sample is tested to find the exact cause.

---

## How Is It Treated?

### For Bacterial Infection

- Doctors often prescribe antibiotic eye drops or ointment.  
- Antibiotics only work against bacteria.  
- They do not help if the cause is a virus.

### For Viral Infection

- There is no cure for viruses.  
- Treatment focuses on easing symptoms.  
- You can use cold or warm compresses.  
- Over-the-counter eye drops may help with discomfort.

### For Allergic Conjunctivitis

- Antihistamine eye drops can help.  
- Mast cell stabilizer eye drops may also be used.  
- These reduce itching and swelling.

### Other Treatments

- Some eye drops are available that do not contain antibiotics.  
- Cold or lukewarm compresses may ease discomfort.  
- But there is not enough research to say if these treatments help or harm.

> For more information on conjunctivitis and whether antibiotics are needed, visit:  
> [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Inflammation of the Eardrum

This condition affects the thin membrane inside the ear called the eardrum. It can happen suddenly or last for a long time. Both types can be treated well.

## Quick Facts

- Doctors tell the difference between sudden (acute) and long-lasting (chronic) inflammation.
- Sudden inflammation usually happens with a middle ear infection. It is caused by viruses or bacteria.
- Symptoms may include ear pain, trouble hearing, and a high temperature.
- Pain and swelling usually go away on their own in a few days.
- Treatment includes pain relief and antibiotics if a bacteria is causing the problem.
- Long-term inflammation lasts at least one month. It often causes no pain but may lead to fluid coming out of the ear.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is an Inflammation of the Eardrum?

The eardrum is a thin, tight membrane. It sits between the outer ear and the middle ear. It protects the inner ear and helps carry sound to the hearing organ.

When the eardrum becomes inflamed, it can cause pain and fever. This is called myringitis. It often happens with a middle ear infection. Viruses or bacteria cause the problem.

Pain and swelling usually get better on their own in a few days. Pain medicine and antibiotics (if needed) can help. Serious problems are rare.

Chronic inflammation is milder. It lasts for at least one month. You may not feel pain. But you might notice fluid leaking from the ear. The exact cause is not known.

## What Are the Symptoms?

### Sudden Inflammation

- Sharp ear pain that starts quickly
- Trouble hearing, often because fluid builds up in the middle ear
- Small blisters filled with fluid or blood on the outside of the eardrum
- Possible fever

Sudden inflammation almost always comes with a middle ear infection.

**Important:** If not treated, the infection can spread to the inner ear. This can cause dizziness, hearing loss, and nausea. Inner ear hearing loss changes how sounds and voices sound.

### Long-Term Inflammation

This lasts for at least one month. It is usually mild. Symptoms may include:

- Ear pain or itching
- A feeling of pressure in the ear
- Fluid leaking from the ear (called a “draining ear”)

Without treatment, new infections can happen. The eardrum may also tear.

## What Causes It?

Sudden inflammation is caused by viruses or bacteria. These are the same germs that cause middle ear infections.

The cause of long-term inflammation is not clear. Some things may damage the eardrum. For example:

- Using cotton swabs to clean inside the ear
- Ear surgery

These actions can harm the eardrum and lead to ongoing problems.

## How Common Is It?

Inflammation of the eardrum is not very common.

- About 6 out of every 100 children under 2 years old get it each year.
- Boys are more likely to get it than girls.
- In adults, women are more likely to get it than men.

## What Is the Outlook?

- With sudden inflammation, pain usually goes away in 3 days.
- Fluid leaking from the ear may last for weeks, even after the eardrum is healed.
- Most people recover fully.

- With long-term inflammation, symptoms last at least one month.
- You may have times with fluid leaking and pressure, and times with no symptoms.
- Repeated infections can lead to hearing loss.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and past ear problems. Then they will examine your ear.

They use a tool called an otoscope to look at the eardrum. This helps them see if there is inflammation. They can also check for a middle ear infection.

They will decide if the problem is sudden or long-term. This guides treatment.

In rare cases, a CT scan may be needed. A hearing test checks for hearing loss. A lab test may be done to find the germ causing the infection.

## How Is It Treated?

### Sudden Inflammation

- Pain medicine
- Anti-inflammatory medicine
- Decongestant nose drops (only for a few days)
- Antibiotics if a bacteria is the cause

Nose drops help open up the middle ear. But using them too long can harm the nose lining.

Antibiotics can be taken as ear drops or pills. Sometimes they are used with steroid medicine.

If there are blisters on the eardrum, the doctor may gently open them with a small tool. This reduces pain by relieving pressure.

### Long-Term Inflammation

- Antibiotics if a bacteria is causing the problem
- But symptoms often come back after treatment

If medicine does not help, doctors may use a carbon dioxide laser. It removes the damaged tissue layer by layer.

If that does not work, the damaged part of the eardrum can be removed. A new membrane made from artificial material is used to replace it.

**Important:** If long-term inflammation is not treated, the outer ear canal can narrow or close. This can lead to deafness.

# Kidney Cancer

About 15,000 people in Germany are diagnosed with kidney cancer each year. This article explains the risks, common signs, how doctors diagnose it, and what treatments are available.

---

## Quick Facts

- Kidney cancer is also called renal cell cancer or renal cell carcinoma.
- It is not a common type of cancer. Some people inherit a higher risk.
- In the early stages, kidney cancer often causes no symptoms. Doctors usually find it by chance during another test.
- If the cancer is still only in the kidney, doctors aim to remove it completely and cure the patient.
- If the cancer has spread, it is usually not curable. Doctors treat it with targeted drugs and immunotherapy.
- Chemotherapy does not work well for kidney cancer.

> **Important:** This article is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Kidney Cancer?

Kidney cancer is a type of cancer that starts in the kidneys. There are different kinds, but this article focuses on the most common one: renal cell carcinoma.

This cancer usually starts in just one kidney. It is rare for both kidneys to be affected at the same time.

---

## What Are the Signs of Kidney Cancer?

Most people do not feel sick when kidney cancer is first found. Doctors often discover it by accident during an ultrasound or scan done for another reason.

Later, some people may notice these signs:

- Blood in the urine
- Pain in the side or back
- New high blood pressure
- Swelling in the legs
- Long-lasting fever, tiredness, or weight loss

Some of these symptoms can also happen with other, non-cancerous conditions. But if they last for more than a few weeks, see a doctor.

Your general practitioner can help figure out what is causing the symptoms. They may refer you to a specialist for further tests.

---

## What Causes Kidney Cancer?

Doctors know some things that increase the risk of kidney cancer. These include:

### Things you can change:
- Smoking
- Being overweight
- High blood pressure (keeping it under control can lower your risk)

### Things you cannot change:
- Family history of kidney cancer
- Being diagnosed before age 46
- Having tumors in both kidneys
- A close family member with kidney cancer

If you have any of these signs, talk to your doctor about genetic counseling. A blood test can check for certain gene changes linked to kidney cancer. If you have one of these changes, doctors can offer early checks to catch cancer sooner.

There is no national screening program for kidney cancer in Germany.

---

## How Is Kidney Cancer Diagnosed?

If kidney cancer is suspected, doctors use several tests together to confirm the diagnosis.

### First steps:
- They ask about your health, symptoms, and family history.
- They do a physical exam.
- They check your blood for signs of problems.
- They use imaging tests like ultrasound, CT scan, or MRI to look at the kidneys.

### Sometimes, they take a small sample of the tumor (a biopsy):
- This is not always needed.
- If the doctors are sure it is cancer and plan surgery, they may skip the biopsy.
- If surgery is not possible, they will take a sample to confirm the diagnosis.

For more details on the tests, visit the website of the Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center (in German).

---

## How Is Kidney Cancer Treated?

Treatment depends on how far the cancer has spread.

Doctors divide kidney cancer into three stages:

1. **Early stage:** The cancer is only in the kidney.
2. **Localized advanced:** The cancer has grown beyond the kidney but is still inside the protective layer around it.
3. **Metastatic:** The cancer has spread outside the kidney, possibly to other organs.

### Treating Early and Localized Advanced Cancer

If the cancer is still in the kidney or its outer layer, surgery is the main treatment. Doctors try to remove the tumor and keep the kidney.

- Surgery is the best chance for a cure.
- In some cases, the cancer comes back later. Then other treatments can help.

If surgery is not possible (for example, because of age or health), doctors can destroy the tumor using heat or cold. This is called ablation. It only works for small tumors (no bigger than 4 centimeters).

### Treating Metastatic Cancer

When the cancer has spread, a cure is usually not possible. But treatment can slow it down and help with symptoms.

Doctors use systemic therapies — treatments that work throughout the body. These include:

- **Targeted therapy:** Drugs that attack specific parts of cancer cells. Healthy cells are not affected.
- **Immunotherapy:** Drugs that help the body’s own immune system fight the cancer.
- **Supportive care:** Treatments to ease side effects and improve daily life.

> **Note:** Chemotherapy does not work well for kidney cancer. Radiation therapy is only used in special cases, such as when cancer has spread to the lungs, bones, or brain.

For more information on treatments, visit the website of the Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center (in German).

---

## What Happens After Treatment?

Cancer treatment can be hard on the body and mind. Rehab helps patients recover strength and adjust to life after treatment.

Kidney cancer rehab is specialized. It includes care focused on the kidneys and urinary system.

A rehab program may include:

- Exercise and physiotherapy to strengthen the stomach and back after surgery
- Advice on healthy habits to protect kidney function
- Nutrition and drinking tips
- Training in relaxation techniques
- Psychological support

### Follow-Up Care

After treatment, regular checkups help find any return of cancer or late side effects early.

- You will be seen often at first, then less often over time.
- Doctors will ask about symptoms, check your blood pressure and blood tests, and do imaging scans if needed.
- If you feel unwell, you can visit your doctor sooner.

If the cancer cannot be cured, regular visits help manage symptoms early. The goal is to keep your quality of life as good as possible.

---

## Life with Kidney Cancer

Many people want to stay active during and after treatment. Here are some ways to help:

- Stay as active as you can. Movement can reduce tiredness and weakness.
- Eat a balanced, healthy diet. This helps prevent poor nutrition.
- Talk to a counselor who works with cancer patients. This can help with fears and worries.

When the cancer is no longer curable and gets worse, good care is essential. Doctors and nurses can help with pain, shortness of breath, and other symptoms. Emotional and social support can also help you live well for as long as possible.

---

## Where to Get Help

Kidney cancer care involves doctors from different fields working together.

### Certified Cancer Centers:
- Hospitals with special experience in kidney cancer can earn certification.
- The German Cancer Society checks these centers regularly.
- Find certified centers at [OncoMAP](https://www.oncomap.de).

### Urology Clinics and Doctors:
- You can find urologists and clinics on the patient portal of the Urological Health Foundation (Urologische Stiftung Gesundheit) at the German Society of Urology website.

### More Information and Support:
- Visit the website of the Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center for detailed, reliable information (in German).
- Call the free helpline: 0800 - 420 30 40
- Email: krebsinformationsdienst@dkfz.de

# Alzheimer’s Disease

Alzheimer’s disease is a serious brain condition. It slowly gets worse over time. It affects memory, thinking, and the ability to do everyday tasks. People with Alzheimer’s need more help as the disease progresses.

There is no cure for Alzheimer’s disease. But treatments can help slow its progress and improve quality of life.

---

## What Is Alzheimer’s Disease?

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common type of dementia.  
Dementia means a person loses important brain functions over time.  
Memory and concentration are usually the first things to get worse.  
As the disease gets worse, it becomes harder to live on your own.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Everyone forgets things sometimes. This is normal as we age.  
But Alzheimer’s disease causes more serious problems.

### Early signs:
- Forgetting recent events or conversations.
- Trouble remembering names or words.
- Difficulty learning new things.
- Feeling confused or anxious about forgetting things.

### Later signs:
- Trouble with long-term memory.
- Getting lost in familiar places.
- Difficulty speaking or understanding others.
- Changes in mood or behavior.
- Becoming more anxious, quiet, suspicious, or even aggressive.

---

## What Causes Alzheimer’s Disease?

Scientists do not yet know the exact cause.  
But they believe several things may play a role.

- Brain cells slowly die over time.
- The brain has less of a chemical called acetylcholine, which helps brain cells communicate.
- Small protein clumps build up in the brain. These may damage brain cells.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

The chance of getting Alzheimer’s increases with age.  
Most people who get it are over 65.

Some health and lifestyle factors may raise the risk:
- Diabetes
- High cholesterol
- Smoking
- Depression
- High blood pressure
- Being overweight or obese
- Not having much social contact
- Hearing problems
- Low level of education

Genes also play a role.  
In rare cases, a family history of Alzheimer’s can increase the risk.  
Some families have multiple members affected from middle age.  
Special tests can check for these genetic risks.

---

## How Common Is Alzheimer’s?

In Germany, about 1.6 million people have dementia.  
More than two-thirds of them have Alzheimer’s disease.

Women are more likely to have dementia than men.  
This is mainly because women live longer.  
Most cases start in older age.

- In people aged 65 to 69, over 1 in 100 have dementia.
- In people aged 80 to 84, about 1 in 10 have dementia.

---

## How Does Alzheimer’s Progress?

Alzheimer’s disease gets worse slowly over many years.  
Most people first notice symptoms after age 65.

### Early Stage
- You may forget things more often.
- It becomes harder to focus or plan.
- Simple tasks like cooking or paying bills become difficult.
- You may feel stressed, anxious, or ashamed.
- Some people feel sad or irritable.

### Middle Stage
- You can no longer live alone.
- You may still eat and wash yourself, but need reminders.
- You need help with shopping, cleaning, or going out.
- You may get lost easily.
- You might forget to turn off the stove or iron.
- Your sleep pattern may become confused.
- You may have trouble understanding or speaking.
- You may mix up past and present events.

### Late Stage
- You need constant care.
- Talking becomes very hard or impossible.
- You cannot feed or drink yourself.
- You may not recognize family or friends.
- You may see things that are not there (hallucinations).
- You may confuse past and present.
- You may lose control of your bladder or bowels.

---

## How Is Alzheimer’s Diagnosed?

There is no single test to confirm Alzheimer’s disease.  
Doctors use many tools to make a diagnosis.

The first step is seeing your family doctor.  
You may then be referred to specialists like neurologists, psychiatrists, or radiologists.

Doctors will:
- Ask about your symptoms and medical history.
- Do memory and thinking tests.
- Check your brain with scans like CT or MRI.
- Run blood tests to rule out other causes.

A diagnosis of Alzheimer’s is only made if:
- Symptoms have lasted more than six months.
- Other possible causes (like thyroid problems or vitamin deficiency) are ruled out.

**Tip:** A visit to a memory clinic can be very helpful in the early stages.

---

## How Is Alzheimer’s Treated?

There is no cure. But treatment can help slow the disease and improve life quality.

Treatment includes:
- Medicines
- Non-drug therapies
- Support from family and caregivers

### Medicines
These drugs may help slow memory and thinking problems in mild to moderate cases:
- **Cholinesterase inhibitors**: Help brain cells communicate better.
- **Memantine**: Protects brain cells from damage caused by too much glutamate.
- **Ginkgo biloba extracts**: May improve blood flow and protect brain cells.

**Important:** These medicines may have side effects.  
It is not clear which one works best for everyone.

### Non-Drug Treatments
These can help keep the mind active and improve mood:
- Memory and orientation exercises
- Group activities every day
- Art, music, or animal therapy
- Aromatherapy
- Physical activity like walking
- Massage
- Training for family members

For more information, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## What Is Life Like with Alzheimer’s?

Every person’s experience is different.

Some people accept the disease and stay active and happy for years.  
Others feel sad, hopeless, or withdraw from others.

Some try to hide their symptoms.  
But many find it easier and better to be open about their condition.

When people talk about their illness, family and friends can help more.  
This support becomes more important as the disease gets worse.

Daily life changes.  
Hobbies and social activities may become harder.  
Roles in the family shift.  
This can cause stress or arguments.

Caregivers often need help too.  
They may feel overwhelmed or exhausted.

### Helpful Steps:
- Join a support group to share experiences.
- Keep doing things you enjoy: walking, cooking, crafting, singing.
- Stay connected with others.

On [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de), people with Alzheimer’s and their families share their stories.

---

## What Can You Do in Advance?

As the disease progresses, you will need more help.  
You may not be able to make important decisions later.

It is wise to plan ahead while you still can.

### Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA)
This lets you choose someone to make decisions for you if you can no longer do so.  
You can name a trusted person and set rules for when the power takes effect.

You can download the official form in German from:  
[www.bmjv.de](https://www.bmjv.de) (Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection)

### Advance Healthcare Directive (Living Will)
This lets you say what medical care you want if you become very ill.  
For example, whether you want life support or resuscitation.

### Support for Family Caregivers

As the disease gets worse, caregivers need help too.

Local services can help with:
- Day care centers
- Hourly home care
- Training for caregivers
- Support groups for family members

The main caregiver can also ask for short-term relief care if they are sick or need a break.

For more information, visit:
- [Wegweiser Demenz](https://www.wegweiser-demenz.de) (Federal Ministry for Family Affairs, Senior Citizens, Women and Youth)
- [Online Guide to Long-Term Care](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de/long-term-care) (Federal Ministry of Health)
- [German Alzheimer Association](https://www.alzheimer.de) (information and self-help groups)

# Lymphedema

Lymphedema is a condition where fluid builds up in the body’s tissues. This happens when the lymph system does not work properly. The lymph system helps remove waste and extra fluid from the body. When it fails, fluid collects and causes swelling.

This condition can happen at any age. It is often linked to cancer or cancer treatments. But it can also be caused by other health problems or injuries.

---

## Quick Facts

- Lymphedema causes swelling in the arms, legs, or other body parts.
- There are two main types: one you are born with (primary), and one that develops later (secondary).
- Common signs include swelling, pain, pressure, heaviness, skin changes, and trouble moving.
- It often affects the arms or legs.
- The most common cause is cancer or cancer treatment, such as removing lymph nodes or radiation therapy.
- Treatment usually includes special massage, compression bandages, exercise, and skin care.
- Surgery is rarely needed.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Lymphedema?

The lymph system moves fluid through the body. This fluid carries proteins, salts, and white blood cells. These white blood cells help fight infections.

The lymph system also cleans out waste and harmful substances. It helps keep the body’s fluid levels balanced.

Lymphedema happens when the lymph fluid gets stuck in one area. This causes swelling. It can happen if the lymph vessels or lymph nodes are damaged.

Lymphedema is a long-term condition. It does not go away on its own. Doctors divide it into two types:

- **Primary lymphedema:** You are born with it. It is caused by genes.
- **Secondary lymphedema:** You develop it later. It is caused by injury, illness, or treatment.

The most common cause of secondary lymphedema is cancer or cancer treatment.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Lymphedema can cause:

- Swelling in the arms, legs, or other areas
- Pain or aching
- A heavy or tight feeling
- Pressure in the affected area
- Changes in the skin, like thickening or hardening
- Trouble moving the arm or leg

These symptoms can appear alone or together. They may affect one or more parts of the body.

While any area can be affected, lymphedema most often happens in the arms or legs.

---

## What Causes Lymphedema?

**Primary lymphedema** is caused by genes. It is present from birth or appears later in life.

**Secondary lymphedema** can be caused by:

- Injuries
- Infections
- Surgery
- Radiation therapy
- Cancer

The most common cause is cancer treatment. This includes removing lymph nodes or having radiation.

Other risk factors include:

- Being overweight
- Arthritis
- Skin infections like dermatitis

These conditions can slow down or block the flow of lymph fluid.

---

## How Common Is Lymphedema?

Lymphedema can happen at any age.

- Primary lymphedema is rare. It affects about 1 in every 6,000 babies.
- It is more common in girls than boys—about ten times more often.

Secondary lymphedema is much more common.

- In developed countries, it affects about 0.1% to 2% of people.

---

## How Does Lymphedema Develop?

Lymphedema is a long-term condition. It lasts a lifetime. But treatment can stop it from getting worse.

Doctors divide lymphedema into four stages:

- Stage 0: No visible swelling, but fluid may already be building up.
- Stage 1: Swelling that goes down when you rest or elevate the limb.
- Stage 2: Swelling that does not go down with rest. The skin may feel firm.
- Stage 3: Severe swelling. The skin becomes thick and hard. This is also called elephantiasis.

With proper treatment, even severe lymphedema can improve.

---

## How Can Lymphedema Be Prevented?

If you are at higher risk, you can help your lymph system by:

- Doing regular physical activity
- Eating a healthy diet
- Keeping a healthy weight

If you have other health problems that affect the lymph system, such as diabetes or poor blood flow in the veins, get them treated by a doctor.

---

## How Is Lymphedema Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about:

- Your family history of swelling or blood vessel problems
- Past surgeries
- Any existing health conditions
- History of cancer
- Changes in your skin

Then your doctor will check:

- Where the swelling is
- If the skin looks different
- If you are short of breath or sweating
- How well you can move
- The size and feel of your lymph nodes
- The type of swelling
- The condition of your blood vessels
- The skin’s temperature
- How well your joints move

If the diagnosis is not clear, your doctor may use imaging tests:

- Ultrasound
- Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
- Lymphangiogram (a special X-ray of the lymph vessels)

A test called **functional lymphoscintigraphy** can show how well lymph fluid moves. A small amount of safe, radioactive material is injected. It travels through the lymph system and is tracked.

If primary lymphedema is suspected, genetic testing may be done.

---

## How Is Lymphedema Treated?

The main treatment is called **Complex Physical Drainage (CPD)**. It helps the fluid drain away. CPD includes:

- Manual lymph drainage: A special type of massage that moves fluid.
- Compression therapy: Wearing special bandages or stockings to help push fluid out.
- Exercise: Gentle movement, especially group or rehab exercises.
- Education: Learning how to care for yourself at home.
- Skin care: Using moisturizing creams to keep skin healthy.
- Immediate treatment for cuts or wounds: Clean and disinfect them right away.

Treatment often starts in the hospital. Later, your doctor will decide which steps to take and how often, based on your needs.

> **Important:** CPD may not be safe if you have:
> - Heart failure
> - A blood clot in a deep vein (deep vein thrombosis)
> - A severe skin infection like erysipelas

For people who are overweight, losing weight and doing strength, flexibility, and endurance exercises can help.

Surgery is only considered if CPD does not help after 6 months.

---

## How Does Lymphedema Affect Daily Life?

Lymphedema can make daily life harder. Swelling and limited movement can make simple tasks difficult.

The look of the affected limb can also affect your mood and confidence.

The treatment takes time and effort. You may need to change how you do everyday things.

Many people find that talking to a counselor or joining a support group helps. This kind of support can also improve physical symptoms.

# Tension Headaches

Most people have had a tension headache at some point.  
It feels like a dull, pressing pain in the head.  
These headaches are not serious.  
They can often be eased with over-the-counter painkillers if needed.  
Regular exercise or relaxation techniques may help stop them from coming back.

---

## Quick Facts

- More than 40 out of 100 people have tension headaches again and again.  
- The pain is dull and pressing. It can be mild or moderate.  
- Tension headaches are not as bad as migraines or cluster headaches.  
- Doctors do not know exactly what causes them.  
- But things like stress can often trigger the pain.  
- If the pain is strong, you can take over-the-counter painkillers.  

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Are Tension Headaches?

Tension headaches are very common.  
Many people feel them from time to time.  

Even though they are called "tension" headaches, they are not usually caused by tight muscles.  
The exact cause is still unknown.  

Tension headaches are one type of primary headache.  
This means they are not caused by another illness.  
Migraines and cluster headaches are also primary headaches.  

Tension headaches are less severe than migraines or cluster headaches.  
But they can still make life hard, especially if they last a long time.  

If the pain is strong, you can take over-the-counter painkillers.  
But do not take them too often.  
Using them too much can make headaches happen more often.

---

## What Do Tension Headaches Feel Like?

Most people feel a dull, pressing pain.  
The pain can be in the whole head.  
Some feel it mostly in the forehead.  

The pain can also feel like a tight band around the head.  
It may feel like wearing a hat that is too small.  

The pain is usually mild to moderate.  
It can last from a few minutes to up to a week.  

The pain does not get worse when you move, exercise, or climb stairs.  
Unlike migraines, tension headaches do not come with nausea or sensitivity to light.

---

## What Causes Tension Headaches?

Doctors do not know the exact cause.  
But certain things can trigger the pain.  
Stress is one common trigger.  

Tension headaches often run in families.  
They are also more common in people who have depression or other mental health issues.

---

## How Common Are They?

Almost everyone has a tension headache at some point.  
More than 4 out of 10 people have them more than once.  
About 1 out of 100 people have them very often or all the time.  

Anyone can get them, at any age.  
But they usually start in young adulthood.  
Women are slightly more likely to have them than men.

---

## How Do They Develop?

Most people have tension headaches only now and then.  
Doctors call this episodic tension headache.  

If headaches happen 15 or more days each month for 3 months in a row,  
or more than 180 days a year,  
and last for hours or are constant each time,  
then doctors call it chronic tension headache.

---

## How Are They Diagnosed?

If you have headaches often, see a doctor.  
The doctor will ask questions and do a physical exam.  

They will check your muscle strength and how you feel sensations.  
This is part of a neurological exam.  
It helps rule out other health problems that could cause the pain.  

If the doctor is still unsure, they may order more tests.

---

## How Are They Treated?

If your headaches are mild, you may not need medicine.  
Some people find relief by using peppermint oil on their forehead, temples, or neck.  
A walk in fresh air can also help.

If you want to take medicine, use over-the-counter painkillers.  
These are available at any pharmacy.  
But they can cause side effects.  
For example, they may upset your stomach.

> **Important:** Taking painkillers too often can make headaches happen more often.

To prevent tension headaches in the long term, try:  
- Light endurance exercise (like walking or swimming)  
- Manual therapy (such as massage or chiropractic care)  
- Relaxation exercises or yoga  
- Biofeedback therapy  

For more details on which medicines help, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

# Fifth Disease

Fifth disease is a common viral illness. It mostly affects children but can also affect adults. It is usually mild and not serious. Once you have had it, you are protected for life.

However, getting fifth disease during pregnancy can harm the unborn baby. It can also be more serious for people with certain health conditions.

---

## What Is Fifth Disease?

Fifth disease is caused by a virus called parvovirus B19.  
It spreads easily, especially among children.  
It is most common in children between the ages of 4 and 10.  

Many people do not notice they have it.  
Some may only have mild symptoms, like a fever or headache.  

The most common sign is a bright red rash on the cheeks.  
This gives the face a “slapped cheek” look.  
The rash can later spread to the arms, legs, and body.  
It often looks lacy or net-like.  

The rash usually lasts 1 to 6 weeks.  
It may come and go, especially when the person is warm or stressed.  

Once the rash appears, the person is no longer contagious.  
They can go back to school or kindergarten.  

Most people get better on their own.  
No special treatment is needed.  

You cannot get fifth disease again after having it once.  
About half to four out of five adults have immunity.  
But 30 to 40 percent of pregnant women do not have immunity.

> **Important:** If a pregnant woman gets fifth disease, it can harm the baby.  
> It may cause miscarriage or serious problems with the baby’s blood supply.  
> Women who work with young children should get tested early in pregnancy to check their immunity.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people have no symptoms at all.  
Some may feel like they have the flu.  
Symptoms can include:

- A high temperature  
- Headache  
- Sore throat  
- Runny nose  

These symptoms usually appear 4 to 14 days after infection.  

The first visible sign is redness on the cheeks.  
The skin around the mouth may look paler.  

Later, a rash appears on the arms, legs, and body.  
It may be itchy.  
It often looks like a lace pattern.  

In adults, the virus can cause joint pain.  
It usually affects the hands, wrists, knees, and feet.  
The pain can last for weeks or even months.

---

## What Causes Fifth Disease?

Fifth disease is caused by a virus called parvovirus B19.  
This virus attacks the cells that make red blood cells.  
It can cause a temporary drop in red blood cells.  

But in healthy people, the body makes new red blood cells quickly.  
The blood count returns to normal within 10 to 14 days.

---

### How Does the Virus Spread?

The virus spreads in several ways:

- **Through the air:** When an infected person sneezes or coughs, they release tiny droplets.  
  You can catch the virus by breathing in these droplets.  
  Close contact or kissing can also spread it.

- **By touch:** The virus can live on hands or surfaces.  
  If you touch a contaminated surface and then touch your eyes, nose, or mouth, you can get infected.

- **Through blood:** The virus can be passed through blood.  
  This can happen during blood transfusions or tattoos.  
  But donated blood is tested for the virus before use.  
  This helps prevent spread.

---

## Who Is at Higher Risk?

People who work with young children are more likely to get infected.  
This includes teachers, childcare workers, and nurses.  

Pregnant women who are not immune are at high risk.  
If they get infected, the virus can pass to the baby.  
This can cause serious problems, especially in the first and second trimesters.

People with certain health conditions are also at higher risk.  
These include:

- Anemia caused by low iron levels  
- Weak immune systems (from illness, medicine, or HIV)  
- Blood disorders like sickle cell anemia or thalassemia  

These conditions can make the illness worse.

---

## How Does the Illness Progress?

Fifth disease is most contagious before the rash appears.  
Once the rash shows up, the person is no longer contagious.  
Children can return to school or daycare at this point.

The rash usually fades within 1 to 6 weeks.  
It may come back when the person is warm, stressed, or in the sun.

---

### Possible Complications

In healthy people, the drop in red blood cells is short-lived.  
The body recovers quickly.

But in people with blood disorders or anemia, the drop can be severe.  
This can lead to a condition called an aplastic crisis.  
This means the body stops making red blood cells for a time.  
It can cause extreme tiredness, dizziness, and pale skin.

In such cases, a blood transfusion is needed right away.

---

## How Can You Prevent Infection?

There is no vaccine for fifth disease.  
But you can lower your risk with good hygiene.

These steps help protect you and others:

- Avoid close contact with people who are sick  
- Wash your hands often and thoroughly  
- Do not touch your eyes, nose, or mouth with unwashed hands  
- Do not share food, drinks, or utensils  
- Do not share personal items like toothbrushes or razors  

These steps are especially important for pregnant women and people with health conditions.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors often recognize fifth disease by the rash.  
The red cheeks and lacy rash on the body are very typical.

In some cases, a blood test is needed.  
This is done if the diagnosis is unclear.  
It can confirm whether the virus is present.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Fifth disease does not need special treatment.  
It usually gets better on its own.

You can help recovery by:

- Getting plenty of rest  
- Drinking enough fluids (like water or unsweetened tea)  
- Eating when you are hungry  

If you have a fever or feel unwell, you can take:

- Paracetamol  
- Ibuprofen  

These can help with fever, headaches, and body aches.

During pregnancy, the virus can harm the baby.  
So, pregnant women who get infected are closely monitored.  
Doctors may do regular ultrasounds to check the baby’s health.

If the virus causes a very low red blood cell count, a blood transfusion may be needed.  
This is rare but can be life-saving.

---

> **Note:** This information is for general knowledge only.  
> It is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.  
> Always talk to a doctor if you are unsure.

# Chronic Kidney Disease

Chronic kidney disease is common in older adults.  
It often starts without any symptoms.  
This means many people do not know they have it until the disease is far advanced.  
The main causes are diabetes and high blood pressure.  
There are treatments that can slow down the damage to the kidneys.

---

## Quick Facts

- The kidneys clean the blood and help your body work properly.  
- They are very important organs.  
- This condition is most common in people over 60.  
- It often goes unnoticed at first because there are no early symptoms.  
- Most cases in adults are caused by diabetes or high blood pressure.  
- More than two million people in Germany have long-term kidney problems.  
- Treatments are available to slow down further kidney damage.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Chronic Kidney Disease?

Your kidneys clean your blood and help your body stay healthy.  
Some conditions can make the kidneys work less well for a short time.  
For example, an enlarged prostate or kidney stones can block urine flow.  
Poor blood circulation can also reduce kidney function temporarily.

Chronic kidney disease means the kidneys have not worked well for more than three months.  
Or they have permanent damage.  
The most common causes in adults are diabetes and high blood pressure.

This disease is more common in older people.  
It often goes undetected for years because it does not cause symptoms early on.

---

## What Are the Signs?

You may not notice any symptoms at first.  
The disease is often found only when kidney function is very low.  
Or when complications cause health problems.

When the kidneys do not work well, waste and water build up in the body.  
This can lead to symptoms such as:

- Swelling in the legs, feet, or face  
- Feeling sick, vomiting, or having diarrhea  
- Losing your appetite or losing weight  
- Pale skin or itchy skin  
- Feeling tired, weak, or lacking energy  
- Trouble concentrating, confusion, or even passing out  
- Muscle cramps or weakness in the limbs  
- Shortness of breath

---

## What Causes It?

Most cases in adults are caused by:

- Diabetes  
- High blood pressure

Other causes include:

- Inflammation in the kidney tissue  
- Long-term use of certain painkillers  
- Kidney stones, tumors, or scars blocking urine flow  
- Birth defects in the kidneys, such as polycystic kidney disease

---

## How Common Is It?

More than two million people in Germany have long-term kidney problems.  
Most of them are over 60 years old.  
About 90,000 people each year need dialysis because their kidneys no longer work.  
More than half of all organ transplants in Germany are kidney transplants.  
Over 2,000 donor kidneys are transplanted every year.  
Around 10,000 people die each year from complications of this disease in Germany.

---

## How Does It Progress?

In the early stages, the kidneys may still clean the blood well.  
This can last for years.  
Sometimes the kidneys even recover on their own.

But in other cases, kidney function gets worse over time.  
This can lead to kidney failure.  
If the kidneys stop working completely, it becomes life-threatening.

---

## How Can You Lower Your Risk?

Diabetes and high blood pressure are the main causes.  
So, reducing your risk of these conditions helps protect your kidneys.

Key steps include:

- Keeping a healthy weight  
- Exercising regularly

If you already have diabetes or high blood pressure, your doctor may prescribe medicine.  
The goal is to keep your blood sugar and blood pressure at safe levels.  
This helps prevent kidney damage.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several methods to check for chronic kidney disease:

- They ask about your medical history.  
- They do a physical exam, including checking your blood pressure.  
- They may do an ultrasound scan of your belly and kidneys.  
- Blood tests check for creatinine, blood sugar, hemoglobin, and acid levels.  
- A urine test checks for protein and other signs.

These tests show how well your kidneys are working.  
They also help find out if the disease is caused by diabetes or if it has led to other problems.

If the results are unclear, doctors may use:

- CT scans  
- A kidney biopsy (a small sample of kidney tissue is taken)

---

## Can It Be Screened For?

People with diabetes or high blood pressure are at higher risk.  
They should have regular kidney checks with their doctor.  
This helps catch kidney problems early.

Under the **Check-up 35** program, anyone over 35 with public health insurance can get a free checkup every three years.  
The goal is to find early signs of heart disease, diabetes, or kidney disease.

---

## How Is It Treated?

If the kidneys are still working reasonably well, treatment can slow the disease.  
Medicines to lower blood pressure are key.  
They also help prevent heart and blood vessel problems.  
People with diabetes must check their blood sugar regularly.

Other medicines help with complications, such as:

- Anemia (low red blood cells) – iron supplements or medicines that boost blood production  
- Bone problems – phosphate binders and bicarbonate of soda to balance body chemicals

Diet and fluid intake must be adjusted based on the stage of the disease.  
Staying active is also important.

When the kidneys fail completely, two options are available:

- Dialysis (a machine cleans the blood)  
- Kidney transplant (a healthy kidney from a donor)

Most people need one of these treatments.  
Some choose not to have either.  
In such cases, palliative care is recommended.  
This focuses on comfort and quality of life in the final stages.

For more on dialysis: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)  
For more on kidney transplants: [BZgA website](https://www.bzga.de)

---

## Rehabilitation and Support

Living with kidney disease changes daily life.  
You may need to follow special rules about food, drink, and medicine.  
Special diet advice is available for patients and their families.  
Many kidney doctors offer this support.

If you are on dialysis, you must limit how much fluid you drink.  
Your kidneys cannot remove water well, so fluid builds up.  
To help with thirst:

- Suck on a lemon slice  
- Chew sugar-free gum or a sour candy  
- Avoid dry rooms  
- Drink slowly  
- Use small cups  
- Take medicine with meals instead of with extra water

You will likely need to take several medicines every day.  
A daily schedule can help you remember when to take them.

Some medicines, like ibuprofen, can harm your kidneys.  
Talk to your doctor about safer alternatives.  
You may also need to start new treatments, like insulin injections for diabetes.

---

## What Is Life Like with This Disease?

Living with chronic kidney disease can be stressful.  
You must follow strict rules about food, drink, and medicine.  
Dialysis takes a lot of time and affects work and personal life.

A free hotline is available for support:  
The German Kidney Centers and the Federal Kidney Association offer help.

Knowing you will need treatment for life can be hard on you and your family.  
It can lead to sadness or anxiety.  
Talking to others with the same condition helps.  
You can join a self-help group or share experiences during dialysis.  
If you feel very down or stressed for a long time, psychotherapy can help.

# Compartment Syndrome

Compartment syndrome often happens after a broken bone. Fluid builds up in muscle groups. This causes swelling and intense pain. If treated fast, the muscles and nerves can heal fully.

---

## Quick Facts

- Fluid builds up in muscle groups called compartments.
- This raises pressure inside the muscle area.
- High pressure can stop blood from reaching the muscles and nerves.
- Signs include extreme pain and swollen, tight muscles.
- It often follows a broken bone.
- People under 35 are more likely to get it.
- The condition can be treated successfully.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical care. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Compartment Syndrome?

The muscles in your arms and legs are grouped into sections called compartments. Each section holds several muscle strands side by side. These groups are wrapped in tough, tight connective tissue called fascia. Blood vessels and nerves pass through and between these sections.

When compartment syndrome happens, fluid builds up inside one of these muscle compartments. This can happen after a broken bone, such as in the lower leg or forearm. The extra fluid causes the muscles to swell. This swelling increases pressure and cuts off blood flow. It can also harm nerves.

This condition most often affects the legs or forearms. But it can also happen in the feet, hands, buttocks, belly, or chest.

If not treated, blood flow to the muscles can be blocked. This can cause serious damage. But with quick treatment, full recovery is possible.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms come on slowly and get worse over time. After a broken bone, they may start within a few hours and grow worse fast.

Common signs include:

- Deep, burning pain that does not go away
- Tingling, numbness, or strange feelings in the area
- Muscles that feel hard and swollen

---

## What Causes Compartment Syndrome?

The connective tissue around muscle compartments is tight and does not stretch much. If the muscles inside swell after an injury, pressure builds up fast. This stops blood from flowing through the area. Without blood, the tissue does not get enough oxygen.

The shinbone and forearm bone are often broken during sports or accidents. These breaks are the main cause of compartment syndrome in most cases. About three out of four cases are linked to broken bones.

Other causes include:

- Crush injuries from accidents
- Burns
- Tight bandages, splints, or casts
- Bleeding inside the muscles
- Blood vessel problems or blood clots

In children, it often happens after a broken bone near the elbow or forearm.

---

## How Common Is It?

Compartment syndrome is most common in people under 35. Men are about ten times more likely to get it than women.

Up to 1 in 10 people who break their shinbone will develop compartment syndrome.

Among athletes, about 1 in 3 people who have leg pain after long or hard exercise may have this condition. Runners are especially at risk.

---

## How Does It Develop?

If treatment starts within 6 hours of injury, the muscles and nerves often heal with no lasting damage.

If not treated early, serious problems can happen:

- Ongoing pain
- Muscles that become shorter
- Weak muscles
- Numbness or paralysis
- Infections

In rare cases, movement in the arm or leg may be permanently limited.

Even more serious risks include:

- Death of muscle tissue (necrosis)
- Breakdown of muscle tissue (rhabdomyolysis), which can lead to sudden kidney failure

These serious problems can be life-threatening. In some cases, amputation of the affected limb may be needed.

---

## How Is It Treated?

If there is a risk of compartment syndrome after an injury:

- The injured limb should be kept at heart level.
- Any tight bandages, casts, or splints should be removed.

If the pressure stays too high, surgery is needed. A doctor makes a cut in the tight connective tissue around the muscle. This lets the swollen muscles expand and lowers pressure fast.

Doctors also give supportive care, such as:

- Pain relief medicine
- Fluids and oxygen through a drip to protect the tissue

---

## What Kind of Rehabilitation Is Needed?

After treatment, some people may have weak or stiff limbs. Physical therapy or occupational therapy can help.

These exercises help rebuild strength and improve movement.

After a few weeks, most people can move their muscles without pain.

# Vocal Cord Nodules

If your voice sounds hoarse, you might have vocal cord nodules.  
Your voice may also sound weak or rough.  
These nodules are not dangerous.  
They often go away if you rest your voice or do voice therapy.  
They are more common in people who talk or sing a lot and loudly.

---

## Quick Facts

- Vocal cord nodules often cause hoarseness.  
- The voice may sound weak or throaty.  
- Resting the voice or doing voice therapy usually makes the nodules go away.  
- People who use their voice a lot are more likely to get them.  

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Are Vocal Cord Nodules?

When you use your voice too much or too hard, nodules can form.  
Your voice will sound different.  
You may become hoarse.  

If you rest your voice or do voice therapy, the nodules usually go away.  
Only in very rare cases do they need surgery.

The vocal folds are two bands of tissue in the middle of your voice box.  
They move together when you speak or sing.  
Air from your lungs makes them vibrate and creates sound.  

If the vocal folds are overused, they swell.  
This swelling can lead to nodules.  

> **Important:** Hoarseness is not always caused by nodules.  
> Most often, it is due to a sore throat (laryngitis).  
> Smoking and nerve problems in the voice box can also affect your voice.  
> In rare cases, a cancerous growth or mental health issues can cause voice problems.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

- Your voice is hoarse.  
- It sounds weak or rough.  
- You can no longer sing in tune for long.  
- You cannot speak or sing in very high or very low tones.

---

## What Causes Vocal Cord Nodules?

Using your voice too much or too hard causes swelling in the tissue.  
This swelling makes the vocal folds not fit together properly.  
They vibrate unevenly.  
This changes your voice and makes it hoarse or weak.

Causes of overuse include:
- Talking loudly or often.  
- Singing a lot.  
- Speaking loudly because you have trouble hearing.  
- Crying a lot, especially in babies and young children.  

Some people strain their voice without knowing it.  
This can happen if:
- You are under a lot of stress.  
- You breathe from your chest instead of your belly.  
- You have poor posture.

Jobs that require a lot of talking increase the risk.  
This includes:
- Teachers.  
- Call center workers.  
- Daycare staff.  
- Singers.  

Singers often get nodules from poor singing technique.  
These are sometimes called “singer’s nodules.”

---

## How Common Are They?

Vocal cord nodules are most common in women and children.  
In children, they are one of the most common reasons for hoarseness.

---

## How Do They Develop?

When the voice is overused, the edges of the vocal folds swell.  
This happens most in the front and middle parts.  
This swelling causes early voice problems.  

If the strain continues, small nodules form on the swollen edges.  
They are about the size of a pinhead and face each other.

These nodules usually do not cause serious health problems.  
But if they do not go away, voice problems may keep coming back when you use your voice.

---

## How Can You Prevent Them?

If you talk or sing a lot, give your voice regular breaks.  
This can help stop nodules from forming.

If your voice gets tired or hoarse quickly, voice therapy can help.  
A speech therapist can teach you:
- How to use better posture.  
- How to breathe properly.  
- How to coordinate breathing and speaking.  
- How to strengthen your voice.

These exercises make your voice more resilient.

---

## How Are They Diagnosed?

See a doctor who specializes in ear, nose, and throat problems (ENT).  
Or see a specialist in voice and speech disorders (phoniatrist).  

The doctor will look at your vocal folds using a laryngoscopy.  
This uses a thin tube with a camera (endoscope) that goes into your throat.  
The tube can be flexible or rigid.  
Sometimes, a numbing spray is used to make the throat less sensitive.

The doctor may also use a special device called a laryngostroboscope.  
It uses flashes of light to slow down the movement of the vocal folds.  
This lets the doctor see how they move in slow motion.

---

## How Are They Treated?

Rest your voice as much as possible.  
For example:
- Use text messages instead of phone calls.  
- Ask for help if you have a child who cries a lot.  
- Talk less when you are tired.

For older children and adults, voice therapy with a speech therapist is very helpful.  
It teaches you how to:
- Protect your voice.  
- Relax your body.  
- Improve your posture.  
- Breathe and speak together better.  

This makes your voice stronger and more lasting.

You can learn more about voice therapy at [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

Doctors may sometimes prescribe:
- Inhalations to keep the throat moist.  
- TENS (a type of electrical therapy).  

Medicine is rarely used to treat nodules.

If the nodules do not go away after therapy, surgery may be needed.  
Surgery carries the usual risks of anesthesia and operation.  
In rare cases, it can cause scarring that changes your voice permanently.

---

## What Is Life Like with Vocal Cord Nodules?

If your job requires a lot of talking or loud speaking, nodules can be very hard to manage.  
You must find ways to rest your voice.  
For example:
- Share speaking tasks with coworkers.  
- Ask for quieter workspaces.  
- Use microphones or speakers to reduce the need to shout.

With voice therapy and smart changes at work, many people can manage their voice problems well.  
Ignoring voice issues can lead to frequent sick days or even a job change.  
Take voice problems seriously to protect your voice and your career.

# Non-melanoma Skin Cancer – Simple Explanation

This guide explains non-melanoma skin cancer in clear, everyday language. It covers who is at risk, what it looks like, how it is treated, and how to protect yourself.

---

## What Is Non-melanoma Skin Cancer?

Non-melanoma skin cancer is a type of skin cancer that is different from melanoma. It mainly includes two types:

- **Basal cell carcinoma (BCC)**
- **Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)**

Both types grow from different kinds of skin cells. They are usually slow-growing and rarely spread to other parts of the body.

BCC is less aggressive than SCC. But if not treated, both can grow and damage nearby skin, tissue, or even bone.

---

## Where on the Body Does It Appear?

Non-melanoma skin cancer most often shows up on skin that gets a lot of sun. This includes:

- The face
- The ears
- The scalp (if not covered by hair)

BCC can also appear on areas not often in the sun, like the chest or back.

---

## What Does It Look Like?

The appearance can vary a lot. Sometimes it is hard for even doctors to tell the difference just by looking.

### Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC)

BCC often looks like:

- A small, shiny, pearly bump with tiny blood vessels.
- The bump may sink in the middle.
- Later, it can turn into a raised edge with small bumps that look like a string of pearls.
- In rare cases, it may look like a flat, white scar-like patch.
- It can also appear as a red, scaly, flat patch.
- Very rarely, it may look like a dark spot, similar to melanoma.

If not treated, BCC can break open, ooze, or form an open sore.

### Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)

SCC often looks like:

- A thick, horn-like patch of skin.
- A flat sore with a raised edge.
- A hard lump, with or without an open sore.

Other signs of SCC include:

- Fast growth
- Crusting
- Hardened skin
- Bleeding
- Redness
- Flaking

---

## What Causes Non-melanoma Skin Cancer?

The main cause is too much exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation.

This includes:

- Sunlight
- Tanning beds
- Tanning lamps
- Other artificial UV sources

The more UV exposure you have over your lifetime, the higher your risk.

BCC is also linked to strong sunburns during childhood or teenage years.

Other causes include:

- Long-term contact with harmful chemicals like arsenic or coal tar.
- Exposure to X-ray radiation.

---

## Who Is at Higher Risk?

You are more likely to get non-melanoma skin cancer if you:

- Have fair skin, light hair, or blue eyes.
- Have a history of sunburns.
- Have a family history of skin cancer.
- Have had a previous skin cancer.
- Have a skin condition that makes your skin sensitive to sunlight.
- Are taking medicine that weakens your immune system (like after an organ transplant).
- Have HIV or another illness that affects your immune system.
- Have actinic keratoses (pre-cancerous skin spots).

---

## How Common Is It?

Non-melanoma skin cancer is the most common cancer in Germany.

In 2018, nearly 200,000 new cases were reported.

But very few people die from it. In 2018, fewer than 1,000 deaths were linked to it.

It is most common in older adults.

---

## How Does It Progress?

### Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC)

- Grows slowly.
- Stays in one place for a long time.
- Rarely spreads to other parts of the body.
- If not treated, it can grow deeper and damage nearby tissue.

### Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)

- Grows at the original site.
- More aggressive than BCC.
- In about 4 out of 100 cases, it spreads to other parts of the body.

If left untreated, both types can grow into deeper skin layers and destroy nearby tissue.

---

## Can It Be Prevented?

Most cases are caused by too much UV exposure. You can lower your risk by protecting your skin.

### How to Protect Yourself

- Avoid strong sunlight between 11 am and 3 pm.
- Stay in the shade or under a parasol, especially at midday.
- Wear protective clothing, a hat, and sunglasses.
- Use sunscreen on all uncovered skin.
- Do not use tanning beds.

Parents should protect children from the sun. People who work outdoors should follow their company’s sun safety rules.

The **Federal Office for Radiation Protection** gives daily UV forecasts for Germany.

For more information on UV rays and sun protection, visit the website of the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## Screening for Skin Cancer

In Germany, people aged 35 and over with public health insurance can get a free skin cancer check every two years.

This is part of the national cancer screening program.

During the check, a trained doctor examines your entire skin and mucous membranes.

You should also check your own skin regularly. See a doctor if you notice any changes.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors often spot non-melanoma skin cancer by looking at the skin.

They may use a special magnifying tool called a dermatoscope to see details.

If cancer is suspected, the doctor may:

- Take a small sample of skin (a biopsy).
- Remove the whole tumor during surgery and check it under a microscope.

Imaging tests like ultrasound or CT scans are only used in rare cases. They are needed if the tumor is deep or if there is concern it has spread.

---

## How Is It Treated?

The main goal is to remove the cancer completely.

### Common Treatments

- **Surgery**: The tumor is cut out. A microscope checks the edges to make sure all cancer is gone.
- **Radiation therapy**: Uses high-energy rays to kill cancer cells.
- **Photodynamic therapy**: Uses special light and medicine to destroy cancer cells.
- **Cryotherapy**: Freezes the tumor with liquid nitrogen.
- **Laser treatment**: Uses a focused beam of light to remove the cancer.
- **Topical creams**: Medicines applied directly to the skin.

The best treatment depends on:

- The type of cancer
- The size of the tumor
- Where it is on the body
- How advanced it is
- Your overall health

### Advanced Cases

If the cancer has spread or is growing deep into the skin, special medicines may be used.

- For advanced BCC: Targeted therapy drugs stop cancer cells from growing.
- For advanced SCC: Immunotherapy helps your body’s own immune system fight the cancer.

For more details on treatments, visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## After Treatment

After treatment, you will have regular check-ups.

These help catch any new or returning cancer early.

- The doctor will examine your entire skin at each visit.
- If you had SCC, you may have an ultrasound of your lymph nodes.
- CT or MRI scans are only used if needed.

You should also check your own skin regularly.

For more information on tests like ultrasound or CT scans, visit the **Cancer Information Service** (in German).

---

## Living with Non-melanoma Skin Cancer

Most people recover well. Treatment usually works well, and life expectancy is not affected.

Advanced cases are rare.

After recovery, it is important to:

- Protect your skin from the sun.
- Check your skin often for new changes.

---

## Where to Get Help and More Information

### Certified Skin Cancer Centers

Hospitals that are certified by the German Cancer Society (DKG) meet high standards for treating skin cancer.

Find them on the **OncoMAP** website.

### Dermatology Clinics

You can search for dermatology clinics in Germany on the website of the **German Dermatological Society**.

### General Support and Advice

For help with daily life, emotional support, or more information, visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

You can also contact them directly:

- Freephone: 0800 420 30 40
- Email: krebsinformationsdienst@dkfz.de

---
