# Measles

Measles is a serious virus that spreads easily. It causes a high fever and a red rash on the skin. It can lead to very serious health problems, especially in babies and older adults. Getting vaccinated is the best way to stay safe.

---

## Quick Facts

- Measles is a virus that causes fever and a rash.
- The rash starts on the face and spreads all over the body.
- It can cause serious health issues, including brain swelling (encephalitis), which can be deadly or cause lasting damage.
- Vaccination works well to prevent measles.
- Since March 2020, people born after 1970 must show proof of protection against measles if they work in healthcare, childcare, or community care settings. This also applies to children and teens in these settings.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Measles?

Measles is a virus that spreads quickly. It can affect both children and adults. The virus causes a rash that starts on the face and moves across the body.

Measles can lead to serious health problems. One of the most dangerous is brain swelling (encephalitis). This happens in about 1 out of every 1,000 cases. It can be deadly in 10 to 20 percent of those affected. It can also cause lasting damage in 20 to 30 percent of people.

Vaccination stops most people from getting measles. If you were vaccinated or had measles before, you are protected for life. A very small number of people who get the vaccine may still get a mild case, but it is not serious.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Measles has two main stages. The rash appears in the second stage.

### Stage 1: Early Symptoms

About 10 days after catching the virus, you may feel sick. Symptoms include:

- High fever
- Red, watery eyes (conjunctivitis)
- Sneezing
- Runny or blocked nose
- Cough

Inside your mouth, you may see small white spots on the inner cheeks. These look like tiny grains of chalk. They are a clear sign of measles.

### Stage 2: Rash

Two to four days after the first symptoms, a red-brown rash appears. It starts on the face and behind the ears. Then it spreads to the rest of the body. The rash lasts 4 to 7 days. It may leave behind skin that peels off in flakes.

The fever lasts about one week.

> **Important:** You can spread measles up to 4 days before the rash appears. You stay contagious for 4 more days after the rash starts. The risk of spreading it is highest just before the rash shows up.

---

## How Does Measles Spread?

The measles virus spreads from person to person. It only lives in humans, so it cannot come from animals.

Measles is extremely contagious. Almost everyone who comes into contact with an infected person will get sick. Once you have had measles, you are protected for life. The same is true if you were vaccinated.

### How It Spreads

- **Through droplets:** When an infected person talks, sneezes, or coughs, tiny droplets can land in the nose or mouth of someone nearby.
- **Through the air:** Tiny particles (aerosols) can float in the air. They can infect people even hours after the sick person has left the room.
- **Through touch:** You can catch the virus by touching surfaces or objects that an infected person has touched. The virus can live on surfaces for a few hours.

---

## How Common Is Measles?

Measles happens all over the world. It is most common in places where many people are not vaccinated. In these areas, almost everyone gets measles at some point in life.

Measles is a leading cause of child death worldwide, especially in places with poor nutrition and low vaccination rates.

In Germany, 3 to 7 people die from measles or its complications each year. Thanks to high vaccination rates, measles is rare. But outbreaks still happen in groups with low vaccination rates.

Measles is often thought of as a child’s disease. But in recent years, more than half of those infected are 15 years old or older. This is because many people in this age group are not protected. Babies under one year old can also get measles before they are old enough to be vaccinated.

The goal is to stop measles completely by vaccinating everyone. Some countries have already achieved this.

---

## What Complications Can Happen?

Measles weakens the immune system. This makes it easier to get other infections. It can also lead to serious brain problems.

### Bacterial Infections After Measles

Because the immune system is weak for months or even years, people can get bacterial infections. These include:

- Pneumonia (lung infection)
- Middle ear infection
- Diarrhea

### Brain Swelling (Encephalitis)

One in every 1,000 people with measles gets brain swelling. This can be deadly in 10 to 20 percent of cases. In 20 to 30 percent of people, it causes lasting damage, such as memory problems or paralysis.

### Rare Long-Term Brain Disease (SSPE)

In very rare cases, a slow brain disease called SSPE can develop 6 to 8 years after measles. It is almost always fatal. It starts with changes in behavior and thinking. It ends with total loss of brain function. Children are at higher risk.

---

## How Can Measles Be Prevented?

The best way to prevent measles is vaccination.

Most people get the MMR vaccine. This protects against measles, mumps, and rubella. There is also a vaccine (MMRV) that adds protection against chickenpox.

### Vaccination for Children

- First dose at 11 months of age.
- Second dose at 15 months.
- The two doses must be at least 4 weeks apart.
- The second dose gives lifelong protection.

If a child is in a daycare or kindergarten, they can get the first dose at 9 months. Then, the second dose should be given shortly after their first birthday.

> **Important:** Since the Measles Protection Act, children aged 1 and older must show proof of at least one vaccine dose to attend a community facility. By age 2, they must show proof of two doses. Alternatively, they can show proof of having had measles before, or a medical reason why they cannot be vaccinated.

### Vaccination for Adults

Adults born after 1970 should get the measles vaccine if:

- They were never vaccinated.
- They only got one dose as a child.
- They are not sure about their vaccination history.

People born after 1970 who work in certain jobs need two doses. This includes people in:

- Healthcare
- Community or care facilities
- Vocational schools and universities
- Refugee or asylum accommodations

### Side Effects of the Vaccine

Some people may have:

- Redness, swelling, or pain at the injection site.
- Fever, headache, or body aches for a few days.

About 5 percent of people get a mild rash after the vaccine. This looks like the measles rash but is not contagious and goes away in a few days.

> **Important:** There is no link between the MMR vaccine and autism or Crohn’s disease.

To check if you or your child needs a vaccine, use the **Impfcheck** tool from the Federal Center for Health Education (BZgA).

For more information, visit the Robert Koch Institute website.

---

## What Does the Measles Protection Act Say?

The Measles Protection Act helps protect people in group settings like schools and hospitals.

It says that certain people must show proof of protection against measles. This proof can be:

- Two doses of the measles vaccine.
- A blood test showing past measles infection (measles antibodies).
- A medical reason why they cannot be vaccinated.

> **Important:** A doctor’s note or personal history is not enough proof. A blood test is needed to confirm past infection.

### Who Must Show Proof?

People born after 1970 who work in:

- Healthcare, community, or care facilities
- Vocational schools and universities
- Refugee or asylum accommodations

This also includes apprentices, trainees, students on placement, and volunteers.

Asylum seekers and refugees must show proof of protection within 4 weeks of arriving in a community accommodation.

### Rules for Children

- Children aged 1 and older must show proof of at least one vaccine dose to attend a community facility.
- By age 2, they must show proof of two doses.

For more details, visit the BZgA website.

---

## How Is Measles Diagnosed?

Measles symptoms can look like other illnesses, such as rubella or scarlet fever. To be sure, doctors need to test for the virus.

They may take:

- A swab from the throat
- A urine sample
- A blood sample

These tests can show if the measles virus is present or if your body has made antibodies against it.

---

## How Is Measles Treated?

There is no medicine that kills the measles virus. Treatment focuses on managing symptoms.

### For People Who Are Sick

- Rest in bed.
- Use medicine to reduce fever and relieve pain.
- If a bacterial infection develops, antibiotics are needed.

> **Important:** People with measles must not go to childcare, school, or work for at least 5 days after the rash starts. The doctor will decide the exact time.

### For People Who Have Been Exposed

- Anyone 9 months or older who is not vaccinated or unsure of their immunity

# Cervical Cancer – Simple Explanation

Cervical cancer used to be common in women. But now, thanks to screening and early treatment, it happens much less often. It can often be cured if found early. A vaccine can also help prevent it.

---

## Quick Facts

- Doctors sometimes call cervical cancer "cervical carcinoma."
- Most cases are caused by certain types of human papillomaviruses (HPV).
- Germany has a national program to screen women for cervical cancer.
- Early cervical cancer is usually treated with surgery.
- Advanced cases are treated with radiation and chemotherapy together.
- Cervical cancer and its treatment can affect a woman’s sex life.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Cervical Cancer?

Cervical cancer is a type of cancer that starts in the lower part of the uterus, called the cervix.

Before cancer develops, there are often changes in the cells of the cervix. These changes are called precancerous lesions. They usually happen in a special area where the inside of the cervix meets the vagina.

Most cervical cancers start in the surface cells of the cervix. These are called squamous cell carcinomas. A condition called cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is a warning sign for this type of cancer.

Less often, cancer starts in the gland cells of the cervix. This is called adenocarcinoma. Its early stage is called ACIS.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

In the early stages, cervical cancer often causes no symptoms.

But if symptoms do appear, they may include:

- Unusual vaginal discharge
- Bleeding after sex or between periods

In later stages, symptoms can include:

- Back or pelvic pain
- Pain when urinating or passing stool
- Swelling in the legs

These symptoms can also happen with non-cancerous conditions. But if they last for several weeks, see a doctor. A gynecologist can check what is causing the problem and order more tests if needed.

---

## What Causes Cervical Cancer?

Cervical cancer is usually caused by a long-lasting infection with certain high-risk types of human papillomaviruses (HPV), especially types 16 and 18.

When HPV stays in the body for a long time, it can cause abnormal cell changes. These changes can turn into cancer if not treated.

For more information about HPV and cancer, visit the website of the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## What Increases the Risk?

Certain things can raise your risk of cervical cancer:

- Smoking
- Other sexually transmitted infections, such as chlamydia, herpes, or gonorrhea
- Having many pregnancies
- Using birth control pills for more than five years
- A weak immune system

---

## How Common Is It?

In Germany, cervical cancer is the 13th most common cancer in women.

About 2 out of every 100 new cancer cases in women are cervical cancer.

Around 4,400 women are diagnosed with it each year.

The precancerous changes are much more common — about 100 times more common than actual cancer.

---

## Can It Be Prevented?

Yes. A vaccine against HPV can prevent infection with the virus that causes most cervical cancers.

The German vaccination committee (STIKO) recommends the vaccine for girls and boys aged 9 to 14. Health insurance covers the cost, even for catch-up vaccinations up to age 17.

Even if you get the vaccine, you should still take part in the cervical cancer screening program. The vaccine does not protect against all cancer-causing HPV types.

To learn more about the HPV vaccine, visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## How Does Cervical Cancer Spread?

If precancerous changes are not treated, cancer can grow.

The cancer cells can spread into nearby tissues. This is called invasive cancer.

At first, the cancer usually stays in the pelvis. Later, it can spread to nearby lymph nodes or to other organs.

Cancer can come back after treatment. It may return in the pelvis, in lymph nodes, or in distant organs. The chance of recurrence depends on the treatment and how advanced the cancer was.

---

## Can Cervical Cancer Be Screened For?

Yes. In Germany, all women over 20 can get free cervical cancer screening.

The main test is the Pap smear. The doctor takes a small sample of cells from the cervix. The lab checks the cells under a microscope.

Since 2020, women over 35 can get a combined test: an HPV test and a Pap smear every three years instead of a yearly Pap smear.

### Treating Precancerous Changes

If the screening shows something abnormal, the doctor may do more tests.

One test is colposcopy. The doctor uses a special magnifying glass to look at the cervix. If needed, they take a small tissue sample (biopsy).

If the results show precancerous changes, the doctor can treat them. The most common treatment is cervical conization. This means removing a cone-shaped piece of tissue from the cervix.

For more information about screening, including benefits and risks, visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

You can also read the **patient brochure** from the Joint Federal Committee (G-BA) for full details.

---

## How Is Cervical Cancer Diagnosed?

The first step is a gynecological exam.

The doctor checks the cervix and vagina. They use a spatula and a brush to collect cells from the cervix and the cervical canal.

The doctor also feels the vagina, uterus, and rectum during the exam.

If anything looks abnormal, the doctor may do a colposcopy. This uses a magnifying glass to look closely at the cervix. If needed, they take a tissue sample (biopsy).

An ultrasound of the pelvic organs (vaginal ultrasound) and kidneys is often done.

To see how far the cancer has spread, the doctor may use MRI or CT scans.

The final diagnosis is confirmed by examining the tissue under a microscope.

---

## How Is Cervical Cancer Treated?

Doctors choose the best treatment based on:

- How advanced the cancer is
- The patient’s overall health and life situation (e.g., whether they want to have children)
- The type and behavior of the tumor

Before treatment, doctors may do a surgical staging procedure. This helps check if the cancer has spread to lymph nodes or other areas. It is usually done using keyhole surgery.

### Treatment Options

Treatment depends on the stage of the cancer.

#### Early Stage

If the cancer is still only in the uterus and upper vagina, surgery is usually the first choice.

- For women who still want to have children, doctors may remove only part of the cervix to keep fertility.
- For women who do not want children or are past menopause, doctors usually remove the whole uterus, nearby tissues, and part of the vagina.
- In postmenopausal women, the fallopian tubes and ovaries are also removed.
- Younger women may keep their ovaries to keep hormone production going.

During surgery, doctors often remove lymph nodes from the pelvis and sometimes from the aorta.

Some women get extra treatment after surgery (called adjuvant therapy) if the cancer has spread to small blood vessels or is very large. This is usually radiochemotherapy.

#### Advanced Stage

For more advanced cancer, doctors usually recommend a combination of radiation and chemotherapy (radiochemotherapy).

If the cancer has spread to other organs, treatment is chosen based on the individual case. Options may include:

- Radiochemotherapy
- Chemotherapy alone
- Surgery to remove pelvic organs (in rare cases)

For more details on treatments, side effects, and options for advanced cancer, visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## Aftercare After Treatment

After treatment ends, regular check-ups are important.

The goal is to:

- Catch any return of cancer early
- Manage side effects from the disease or treatment
- Help women live well and stay healthy

Check-ups start often and become less frequent over time.

During follow-up visits, the doctor:

- Asks about symptoms
- Does a Pap smear of the vagina and cervix (if still present)
- May do an HPV test or colposcopy if needed

---

## Coping With the Effects of Cancer and Treatment

Many women want to take an active role in their recovery.

Supportive care is tailored to each person.

- **Psychological counseling** can help if you feel anxious or overwhelmed.
- Removing the uterus means you can no longer have children. Talk to your doctor — younger women may still be able to have children after treatment.
- Removing the ovaries causes early menopause. There are ways to reduce symptoms like hot flashes and mood swings.

### How Does Cervical Cancer Affect Sex Life?

Cancer and its treatment can affect how you feel during sex. You may have less sensation or trouble with sexual function.

This can be hard on you and your partner.

Talk to your doctor. Specialists in sexual health and psycho-oncology can help. Some health centers also offer advice.

---

## Where to Get Help

Cervical cancer is treated by doctors from different fields working together.

Hospitals with experience in treating gynecological cancers can become certified centers. The German Cancer Society checks these centers regularly.

Find certified centers on the **OncoMAP** website. Choose “gynecological cancer center” under “center.”

Have questions about daily life or support? Visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

# Vascular Dementia – Simple Explanation

Vascular dementia is the second most common type of dementia.  
It happens when blood flow to the brain is reduced.  
This affects thinking, memory, and other mental abilities.  
Treating risk factors like high blood pressure can help prevent it.

---

## Quick Facts

- Vascular dementia affects about 15 to 20 out of every 100 people with dementia.
- It is caused by problems with blood flow in the brain.
- It often follows a stroke.
- Main risk factors include high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, smoking, and older age.
- Treating these risk factors can help stop or slow the disease.
- Treatment focuses on slowing the disease and giving good care.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Vascular Dementia?

Vascular dementia means dementia caused by poor blood flow to the brain.  
It is one of the most common types of dementia, along with Alzheimer’s disease.  
It can be hard to tell the difference between Alzheimer’s and vascular dementia.  
Many older people have symptoms of both. This is called mixed dementia.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on which part of the brain is affected.  
Memory loss is not always the main problem — it is less common than in Alzheimer’s.

The most common type, linked to small blood vessel problems, causes:

- Trouble focusing or paying attention  
- Slower thinking  
- Forgetting things  
- Difficulty doing daily tasks  
- Feeling tired or unmotivated  
- Getting tired quickly, both mentally and physically  

Other physical signs may include:

- Unsteady walking  
- Needing to go to the bathroom often or leaking urine  
- Trouble swallowing or speaking  
- Laughing or crying without reason  
- Feeling dizzy or faint

If a large area of the brain loses blood suddenly, you may have stroke symptoms like:

- Weakness or paralysis  
- Numbness  
- Vision problems  

Dementia causes a slow loss of mental abilities, including:

- Remembering recent events  
- Remembering long-term memories  
- Staying focused  
- Understanding things  
- Knowing where you are and what time it is  
- Planning and organizing tasks  
- Having motivation  
- Speaking and understanding language  
- Behaving normally  
- Feeling emotionally stable  

---

## What Causes Vascular Dementia?

Poor blood flow to the brain causes vascular dementia.  
This can happen in several ways:

### Narrowed Small Blood Vessels

This is the most common cause.  
The small blood vessels in the brain become blocked or narrowed.  
This happens because of thickened walls or deposits.  
The brain areas they feed get too little oxygen.  
This can happen slowly over time.  
It can also cause small strokes.

### Blood Clots

Blood clots from the neck or heart can block brain blood vessels.  
When a blood vessel closes suddenly, brain tissue dies.  
This is called a stroke or brain infarction.

Clots often form because of:

- Hardened neck arteries (arteriosclerosis)  
- Irregular heartbeat (atrial fibrillation)

If several small strokes happen in different brain areas, it can lead to vascular dementia.  
One major stroke in a key brain area can also cause dementia.  
If a large artery is blocked, a large part of the brain can die.  
At least 25% of people who have this kind of stroke later develop dementia.

### Bleeding in the Brain

This is rare.  
It happens when blood vessels in the brain burst.  
This usually happens after years of high blood pressure.  
The burst vessels cause bleeding in the brain — a hemorrhagic stroke.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

About 1 in 4 people who have a stroke later develop vascular dementia.  
The same things that raise stroke risk also raise dementia risk.

Main risk factors:

- Older age  
- High blood pressure  
- Diabetes  
- High cholesterol  
- Heart problems like irregular heartbeat or heart disease  

Unhealthy habits also increase risk:

- Smoking  
- Not being physically active  
- Poor diet  
- Being overweight or obese  
- Drinking too much alcohol  

---

## How Common Is It?

About 250,000 people in Germany develop dementia each year.  
Vascular dementia makes up 15 to 25% of these cases.  
Women are slightly more likely than men to get dementia.

---

## How Does It Progress?

The course of vascular dementia depends on the cause and brain areas affected.

- If small blood vessels are affected, mental decline happens slowly and steadily.  
- If it is caused by single strokes, symptoms may stop getting worse or even improve a little.  
- But if more strokes happen, health gets worse over time.

People with vascular dementia often live shorter lives than those with Alzheimer’s.  
On average, people live 3 to 5 years after diagnosis.

---

## How Can It Be Prevented?

You can lower your risk by:

- Staying physically active  
- Not smoking  
- Eating a healthy, balanced diet  

Other helpful habits:

- Getting a good education  
- Staying socially active  
- Doing mentally stimulating activities every day  

These habits may help keep your mind sharp longer.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors use several tools to check for dementia.

### Mental Ability Tests

These tests measure memory, attention, and thinking.  
They give numbers to show how well you are doing.  
Doctors compare your results to average scores for your age group.

These tests help:

- Confirm if mental problems are real  
- Show what kind of symptoms you have  
- Help find the cause of dementia  

### Brain Scans

Doctors use imaging to see the brain.  
This helps spot:

- Long-term blood flow problems  
- Old or new strokes  
- Bleeding in the brain  

Common scans:

- CT scan (computed tomography)  
- MRI scan (magnetic resonance imaging)  

They also check neck arteries with ultrasound.  
Special scans can show blockages in brain arteries.

### Heart and Blood Tests

Doctors check:

- Blood pressure  
- Blood sugar levels  
- Cholesterol levels  

They may do a long-term heart monitor (ECG) to check for irregular heartbeats.  
An ultrasound of the heart (echocardiography) can find heart valve or muscle problems.

---

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure for dementia.  
Treatment aims to slow the disease and ease symptoms.

### Treating Risk Factors

You can treat high blood pressure, diabetes, and high cholesterol with:

- Healthy lifestyle changes  
- Medicines  

Heart problems like irregular heartbeat or heart disease can also be treated.

If blood clots are found:

- Medicine to prevent clots (like aspirin or anticoagulants)  
- Surgery or a stent to open a narrowed neck artery  

These steps can prevent more strokes.

### Medicines for Dementia

Medicines used for Alzheimer’s disease (like cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine) do not help with vascular dementia.  
They may cause side effects and are not recommended.

If needed, doctors may prescribe medicine for:

- Restlessness  
- Fear or anxiety  
- Irritability  
- Aggression  
- Sleep problems  
- Depression  

But doctors must first rule out other causes of these symptoms.

### Non-Medical Support

People with dementia need long-term care and support.  
A team of experts helps, including:

- Doctors  
- Psychologists  
- Care workers  
- Occupational therapists  
- Physiotherapists  
- Social workers  

Family caregivers also need information and support.

---

## What Does It Mean for Patients and Families?

Dementia gets worse over time.  
People lose the ability to do daily tasks.  
They may need help with everything.  
In later stages, most need full-time care.

For more on home care and support services, see the article: *“Caring for people with dementia.”*

### Plan Ahead: Legal and Care Decisions

As dementia gets worse, people may not be able to make their own decisions.  
It is wise to plan early.

You can:

- Choose a **lasting power of attorney** (LPA)  
  - This lets someone you trust make decisions for you later  
  - You can set rules for when it starts  
- Make an **advance healthcare directive** (living will)  
  - This says what medical care you want if you become very ill  
  - You can say if you want life-sustaining treatment  

You can download the official German form for lasting power of attorney (Vorsorgevollmacht) from the website of the **Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection**.

### Support for Caregivers

In later stages, support for the person with dementia and their family becomes very important.

Local services can help with:

- Day care centers for people with dementia  
- Hourly home care  
- Training for caregivers  
- Support groups for family members  

The main caregiver can ask for:

- Short-term care (respite care)  
- Breaks when they are sick or need time off  

Self-help groups let caregivers talk to others in similar situations.

---

## Where Can I Find More Information?

- **Federal Ministry of Health (BMG)**:  
  Online guide on dementia and a care guide (in German)

- **German Alzheimer’s Society (Deutsche Alzheimer Gesellschaft e.V.)**:  
  Information and support for patients and families

- **German Brain Foundation (Deutsche Hirnstiftung e.V. – DHS)**:  
  Detailed information on dementia  
  Free online and phone consultations for personalized advice

# Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)

People with obsessive-compulsive disorder often feel a strong need to repeat certain actions.  
For example, they may wash their hands many times because they fear germs.  
These actions can take over their daily lives.  
OCD can be treated and managed with the right help.

---

## Quick Facts

- A person with OCD has strong, unwanted thoughts and feels driven to do certain actions.  
- If the disorder is very bad, it can make normal life very hard or even impossible.  
- The thoughts and actions are hard to stop on purpose.  
- They often cause strong feelings of anxiety.  
- Therapy can help people live better with OCD.  
- Medicine may also be used as part of treatment.  

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

---

## What Is OCD?

You leave the house and suddenly wonder: Did I turn off the stove? Did I lock the door?  
Most people feel this worry once in a while.  
But for some, this fear becomes so strong that they feel they must check things again and again.  
Over time, these checks can take over their whole day.

> **Important:** With proper treatment, people with OCD can live a life that feels normal again.

---

## Signs of OCD

OCD shows up as two main things:  
- Unwanted, repeating thoughts  
- Repeating actions to feel better

### Unwanted Thoughts
These thoughts come back again and again.  
They are hard to ignore.  
Common ones include:
- Worrying you forgot something important  
- Fear of getting sick from germs

### Repeating Actions
These are routines people feel they must do.  
They do them to calm down the anxious thoughts.  
Examples:
- Washing hands many times a day  
- Cleaning the house constantly  
- Arranging things in a very specific way  
- Checking doors, stoves, or locks over and over

Some people feel their actions are silly or pointless.  
But they still feel they must do them.  
This can make them feel helpless.  
Some even fear they are losing their mind.

---

## What Causes OCD?

No single cause explains OCD.  
It likely comes from a mix of:
- Family history (some people are more likely to get it if a close family member has it)  
- Brain chemistry  
- Life events

For example:
- Trauma or a major life crisis can trigger OCD.  
- Some people with OCD had serious problems as children, like abuse or losing a parent.  
- People who are very careful, responsible, or afraid of making mistakes may be more likely to develop OCD.

---

## How Common Is OCD?

About 3 out of every 100 people in Germany will have OCD at some point in their lives.  
It often starts in childhood or the teenage years.  
But it can start at any age.

---

## How Does OCD Develop?

OCD does not happen overnight.  
It grows slowly over time.  
At first, the rituals may seem small.  
But they slowly take up more and more time and energy.

Over time, OCD can hurt:
- Work or school  
- Relationships  
- Daily routines

Eventually, the person’s whole life may be ruled by their rituals.

No two people experience OCD the same way.  
Symptoms can come and go.  
Some people have no symptoms for weeks or months.  
Others may have different types of rituals over time.

If not treated, OCD can last for years.  
Many people need help to manage it and live a full life.

---

## How Is OCD Diagnosed?

OCD can be hard to tell apart from other mental health issues.  
For example, constant worry can also be a sign of general anxiety.  
OCD often happens with other problems, like depression.  
When both happen together, they can make each other worse.

### Getting a Diagnosis

The first step is to talk to a doctor.  
You can see your family doctor or a mental health therapist.  
They will ask questions like:
- Do you keep having the same thoughts over and over?  
- Do you do certain things to make those thoughts go away?  
- Do you feel your actions are pointless or too much?  
- Do you feel forced to do things again and again?

> **Important:** A doctor can only diagnose OCD if:
> - The symptoms have lasted at least two weeks  
> - They happen on most days  
> - They interfere with daily life

OCD can also cause physical problems.  
For example, washing hands too much can cause cracked or sore skin.

---

## How Is OCD Treated?

OCD cannot be cured, but treatment can help a lot.  
People can learn to live well with it.

### Therapy
The most effective treatment is **cognitive behavioral therapy**.  
This helps people:
- Understand their thoughts and actions  
- Learn to face their fears  
- Reduce the need to repeat rituals

Therapy also includes:
- Relaxation techniques like deep breathing  
- Training to stay calm during anxiety

### Medicine
Antidepressants are often used.  
These are medicines usually used for depression.  
They can help reduce OCD symptoms.  
Doctors may prescribe them while waiting for therapy to start.

For more information, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## What Is Life Like With OCD?

OCD can be exhausting and hard to manage.  
Rituals can take hours each day.  
In severe cases, normal life becomes impossible.

Many people feel ashamed of their thoughts or actions.  
They hide them from others.  
This secrecy is stressful and tiring.

Most people wait a long time before asking for help.  
Some fear others will judge them.  
Others worry it will hurt their job or family life.  
After treatment, many say they wish they had asked sooner.

### How OCD Affects Loved Ones

Family and friends may also be affected.  
They might:
- Follow certain rules to avoid upsetting the person  
- Feel stressed or confused

Parents may feel guilty for not noticing the signs earlier.  
But this is normal.  
People with OCD often hide their symptoms.  
Some don’t even realize they have a problem.

Still, loved ones can be a big help.  
They can:
- Be patient and understanding  
- Join therapy sessions  
- Support the person through hard times

When family and friends are involved, treatment often works better.

---

## Where Can I Get More Help?

You are not alone.  
Support is available.

### Self-Help Groups
These groups let people with OCD and their families:
- Share experiences  
- Learn from others  
- Get advice and encouragement

### Books and Websites
Good, reliable books and websites can help you understand OCD better.

### Find Local Support
You can search for self-help groups at:  
[National Contact and Information Point for Self-Help Groups (NAKOS)](https://www.nakos.de)

# Atrioventricular Block (AV Block)

AV block is a heart rhythm problem. It happens when the heart’s electrical signals do not travel properly. This can cause the heart to beat too slowly.

Some people with AV block have no symptoms. Others may feel dizzy, weak, or faint. These symptoms can get worse if the heart is already under stress.

---

## What Is AV Block?

Your heart has a natural pacemaker. It sends electrical signals to make your heart beat. These signals travel from the top chambers (atria) to the bottom chambers (ventricles) through a part called the AV node.

When AV block happens, the signals slow down or stop. This can cause the heart to beat too slowly.

There are three levels of AV block:

### Grade 1 AV Block
- The signal is delayed, but it still reaches the lower chambers.
- The heart rhythm stays normal.
- Most people do not feel anything.

### Grade 2 AV Block
- Some signals do not reach the lower chambers.
- The heart may skip beats.
- You may feel your heart racing or fluttering.

### Grade 3 AV Block
- No signals get through to the lower chambers.
- The heart beats very slowly — fewer than 40 times per minute.
- The lower chambers make their own slow signals to keep the heart going.
- This is the most serious form.
- Most people with this need a pacemaker.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on how severe the block is. They also depend on whether you have other heart problems.

### Grade 1 AV Block
- Most people have no symptoms.
- It is often found by chance during a routine check-up.

### Grade 2 AV Block
- You may feel dizzy or weak.
- You may feel your heart racing or skipping beats.
- You may have trouble breathing, chest pain, or faint during exercise or stress.

### Grade 3 AV Block
- The heart beats very slowly.
- Symptoms happen even when you are resting.
- You may have swelling in your legs or feet.
- You may feel tired or faint.

---

## What Causes AV Block?

Many things can cause AV block:

- Some heart medicines can cause it.
- Hormone problems can affect the heart’s signals.
- Autoimmune diseases (where the body attacks itself) can damage the heart.
- Infections like Lyme disease can harm the heart.

A serious, long-term AV block is often caused by heart disease. Examples include:

- A heart defect you were born with.
- Inflammation of the heart muscle (myocarditis).
- Coronary heart disease (narrowed heart arteries).

Risk factors for heart disease also raise the chance of AV block. These include:

- Being older.
- Being overweight.
- Having high blood pressure.
- Having diabetes.

Some athletes have a mild AV block when resting. This is normal and not a concern.

---

## How Common Is AV Block?

AV block is fairly common. But it is hard to know exactly how many people have it.

Mild AV block is more common in younger people. Severe AV block is more common in older adults.

---

## How Does AV Block Progress?

- Mild AV block may come and go. It can disappear during exercise but return when you rest.
- Mild AV block can sometimes get worse over time.
- If heart disease is the cause, the block usually stays permanent.
- If a medicine is causing the block, stopping it may fix the problem.

---

## How Is AV Block Diagnosed?

Doctors may first notice AV block when checking your pulse or listening to your heart.

To confirm the diagnosis, you will need an electrocardiogram (ECG). This test records your heart’s electrical activity.

Sometimes, you may need more tests, such as:

- A stress test (checking your heart during exercise).
- A long-term ECG (wearing a small monitor for 24 hours or more).

To find the cause, your doctor may order:

- An echocardiogram (ultrasound of the heart).
- Heart catheterization (a test to check blood flow in the heart).

---

## How Is AV Block Treated?

Treatment depends on how serious the symptoms are.

- Mild AV block often needs no treatment.
- Severe AV block usually needs a pacemaker.

A pacemaker is a small device implanted under the skin. It sends signals to keep your heart beating at a safe rate.

- Pacemakers can be temporary or permanent.
- They do not cure the underlying problem.
- The main goal is to treat the cause of the block.

In emergencies, medicine like atropine can be used to speed up the heart.

---

## What Is Life Like with AV Block?

If you have severe AV block, you may feel tired or short of breath. You may worry about fainting or having a serious event.

Even with a pacemaker, life changes. You will need regular check-ups. You must always carry a pacemaker ID card.

Some people feel uncomfortable seeing the device under their skin. But most get used to it over time.

---

## Where Can I Find More Information?

If you need a pacemaker, talk to your doctor. They can help you understand what to expect.

You can also get help from your health insurance provider.

If your doctor recommends a pacemaker, you may want to use a decision aid. This tool helps you make informed choices. You can find it at **gesundheitsinformation.de**.

# Generalized Anxiety Disorder

Fear helps protect us when we are in danger. It prepares our body to act fast. For example, if you are driving and a car suddenly swerves in front of you, fear helps you react quickly.

But for some people, worry does not go away. It stays with them every day. They worry about almost everything. This can make life very hard.

This article explains what generalized anxiety disorder is. It also covers how it is diagnosed and treated.

---

## Quick Facts

- It is normal to feel worried or afraid sometimes.
- Fear helps protect you in dangerous situations. It makes your body ready to act.
- Some people feel constant worry about many things in life.
- Generalized anxiety disorder affects both emotions and the body.
- The condition is hard to manage alone. But help is available.

> **Note:** This article is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Generalized Anxiety Disorder?

It is normal to feel anxious now and then. Fear can help you stay safe. For example, fear can make you more careful at work or at home.

But when worry takes over, it can become a problem. Some people feel anxious all the time. They cannot stop thinking about possible dangers.

Their anxiety is not about one specific thing. It is about many things. They worry about their health, their family, their job, and even small daily events.

This kind of constant worry can take over a person’s life. It can make normal activities hard or impossible.

Even though people with this disorder know their fears are too strong, they cannot stop them. They feel stuck and overwhelmed.

But help is available. Many people get better with the right support.

---

## Signs of Generalized Anxiety Disorder

Generalized anxiety disorder shows up in both the mind and the body.

### Mental Signs
- You feel worried all the time.
- Your worries are strong and not based on real danger.
- You worry about many different things, not just one thing.
- The fear does not go away, even when there is no reason for it.

For example:
- You worry your child might get hurt on the way to school.
- Then you worry your partner might have an accident at work.
- Then you fear you might have a heart attack.

These thoughts happen over and over. They make daily life hard. They can also lead to sadness or depression.

### Physical Signs
- Feeling foggy or spaced out
- Feeling nervous or restless
- Dizziness
- Shaking or trembling
- Sweating
- Tense muscles
- Fast or irregular heartbeat
- Upset stomach

Being anxious all the time can cause:
- Tiredness
- Trouble focusing
- Sleep problems

In some cases, anxiety can lead to thoughts of suicide. This risk is higher if depression is also present.

If you only feel anxious in certain situations, it is likely not generalized anxiety disorder.

Panic attacks are not common in this condition. But they can happen sometimes.

> **Important:** When you are afraid, your body releases adrenaline. This makes your heart beat faster and your body ready to act. In people with generalized anxiety disorder, this state of alertness can last all the time.

---

## What Causes Generalized Anxiety Disorder?

Doctors do not yet know the exact cause. But several factors may play a role.

### Life Experiences
- Some people had a serious trauma in childhood or later in life.
- Losing someone close can trigger anxiety.
- Long-term stress at home or at work can also be a factor.

### Life Crises
- Big changes, like job loss or divorce, can lead to anxiety.
- Some people are more likely to develop anxiety if it runs in their family.

### Other Conditions
- Anxiety can happen with depression.
- It can also be linked to panic disorder or addiction.
- In some cases, no clear cause can be found.

---

## How Common Is It?

Generalized anxiety disorder usually develops slowly. It may not be obvious at first.

The condition can last for months or even years. People often have good days and bad days.

Most people who develop this disorder are adults in middle age.

But many people do get better over time. One study found that about one in four people recovered within two years.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

There are many types of anxiety. Each has different symptoms. This makes diagnosis tricky.

Doctors may check for:
- Phobias
- Panic disorder
- Obsessive-compulsive disorder
- Depression

A diagnosis can only be made after a full talk with a trained professional. This can be a psychologist or a psychiatrist.

To diagnose generalized anxiety disorder, the person must have:

- Worry that happens most days
- Worry that lasts at least six months
- Worry that feels out of control
- Worry that makes daily life hard

And at least three physical symptoms, such as:
- Fast heartbeat
- Shaking
- Tense muscles
- Stomach problems

> **Important:** These physical symptoms can also be caused by other health problems. For example:
- Overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism)
- Certain medicines
- Drugs like amphetamines (speed)

Doctors will check for these other causes before making a diagnosis.

It can take time to get a clear diagnosis. Many people first visit a doctor because of physical symptoms, like trouble sleeping. Only one symptom may be treated at first.

---

## How Is It Treated?

There is no quick fix. But treatment can help over time.

People can learn to manage anxiety and stress better. Medication can also help reduce symptoms.

There are four main treatment approaches:

### 1. Therapy
- Cognitive behavioral therapy helps people change their thinking.
- It teaches how to face fears in a healthier way.
- It helps people understand their anxiety patterns.

### 2. Relaxation Techniques
- Autogenic training helps calm the body.
- Progressive muscle relaxation teaches you to release tension.
- These methods are often used with therapy.

### 3. Medication
- Some antidepressants are used to treat anxiety.
- Some people use natural remedies like valerian root.
- Medication should always be taken under medical supervision.

### 4. Self-Help
- Joining a support group helps you share experiences.
- Reading books or trusted online resources can help you understand the condition.
- Being informed can reduce fear and help you feel more in control.

> **Important:** Many people learn to manage strong anxiety over time. It is not easy. But with proper treatment, most people see improvement in just a few weeks.

Therapy helps you understand the patterns behind your worries. This can make a big difference.

For more information on treatment options, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Brain Aneurysm

A brain aneurysm is a weak spot in a blood vessel in the brain. It can bulge out like a small balloon. Many people live their whole lives without knowing they have one. Some aneurysms are found by accident during tests for other problems. If an aneurysm bursts, it can cause serious bleeding in the brain. This is a life-threatening emergency.

---

## Quick Facts

- Doctors use the word aneurysm to describe a bulge in a blood vessel. It often looks like a small berry or pouch.
- The bulge happens when part of the blood vessel wall becomes weak and loses its strength.
- Aneurysms can happen in different parts of the body. When they happen in the brain, they are called brain aneurysms or cerebral aneurysms.
- Most brain aneurysms do not cause any symptoms.
- If a brain aneurysm bursts, it can cause a dangerous brain bleed.
- Risk factors for a burst aneurysm include the size and location of the aneurysm, high blood pressure, smoking, and being older.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Brain Aneurysm?

A brain aneurysm is a bulge in a blood vessel in the brain. It forms when the wall of the blood vessel weakens and stretches out. This can happen if the vessel loses its natural strength and flexibility.

Aneurysms can form in any blood vessel. For example, they can happen in the large blood vessel in the belly, called the abdominal aorta. When they happen in the brain, they are called brain aneurysms.

These bulges often form where blood vessels split into smaller branches. These are the places where blood flows with the most pressure. If a brain aneurysm bursts, it can cause a dangerous brain bleed.

Not all brain aneurysms burst. Many people never know they have one. Some aneurysms cause no problems and stay the same for years. But if symptoms appear, or if the risk of a burst is high, treatment is needed.

---

## What Are the Signs of a Brain Aneurysm?

Most people with a brain aneurysm have no symptoms. Doctors call this an asymptomatic aneurysm.

If the aneurysm is large or in a sensitive area, it can press on nearby brain tissue or nerves. This can cause symptoms such as:

- Headaches
- Blurred or double vision
- Weakness or paralysis in the eye muscles

Less common symptoms include:

- Seizures
- Problems with speech
- Hearing problems
- Numbness or tingling

---

## What Causes a Brain Aneurysm?

A brain aneurysm forms when the wall of a blood vessel becomes weak. This can happen because of:

- High blood pressure
- Smoking
- Inflammation in the blood vessels
- The natural aging process

As we age, blood vessels lose their strength and flexibility. This makes them more likely to bulge.

In rare cases, a brain aneurysm can be caused by a genetic condition. For example, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome weakens connective tissue. This includes the walls of blood vessels, making them more likely to bulge.

---

## Who Is at Risk?

Certain people are more likely to develop a brain aneurysm.

- Women are more likely than men to have one.
- People with a family history of brain aneurysms are at higher risk.
- Other risk factors include:
  - High blood pressure
  - Smoking
  - Older age

These same factors also increase the chance that an aneurysm will burst. But the size and location of the aneurysm also play a big role.

---

## How Common Are Brain Aneurysms?

About 3 out of every 100 adults have a brain aneurysm. Some people have more than one aneurysm in the brain at the same time.

---

## How Does a Brain Aneurysm Develop?

Most brain aneurysms do not cause any symptoms. They stay small and do not change over time.

But if the aneurysm grows larger, it may start to cause problems. The bigger the aneurysm, the higher the risk of it bursting.

If the aneurysm bursts, it causes bleeding inside the brain. This is called a brain hemorrhage. The bleeding increases pressure inside the skull. This pressure can damage brain tissue.

A sudden, very severe headache is a key sign of a burst aneurysm. The pain often starts at the back of the head and neck. It then spreads to the whole head and down into the back.

Other signs of a brain hemorrhage include:

- Stiff neck
- Nausea and vomiting
- Confusion or loss of consciousness

> **Important:** A brain hemorrhage is a medical emergency. It needs immediate treatment.

Another rare problem is a stroke. This can happen if a blood clot forms inside the aneurysm. The clot can break loose and block a small blood vessel in the brain. This cuts off blood flow and can cause a stroke.

---

## How Is a Brain Aneurysm Diagnosed?

Many brain aneurysms are found by accident. For example, a doctor may see one during a scan done for another reason.

If you have frequent headaches or vision problems, your doctor may order a scan. Two common types are:

- MRI scan: uses magnets and radio waves to create detailed images.
- CT scan: uses x-rays to create images of the brain.

The best way to see a brain aneurysm is a special test called digital subtraction angiography. This test uses x-rays and a special dye. The dye makes blood vessels show up clearly on the images. The computer then removes everything except the blood vessels.

---

## How Is a Brain Aneurysm Treated?

The best way to lower your risk is to avoid things that make aneurysms worse. This includes:

- Treating high blood pressure
- Quitting smoking

> **Important:** Treatment is only needed if the aneurysm causes symptoms or if the risk of it bursting is high. Deciding whether to treat is not always easy. Many factors are involved.

If you and your doctor decide not to treat the aneurysm, you will have regular scans every 1 to 3 years. These scans check if the aneurysm has changed or if the risk of bleeding has increased.

If treatment is needed, there are two main options:

### 1. Endovascular Coiling
- A thin tube called a catheter is guided through a blood vessel in the leg up to the brain.
- Tiny coils made of platinum are placed into the aneurysm.
- The coils cause the blood inside the aneurysm to clot.
- This seals off the aneurysm and stops blood from flowing into it.

### 2. Surgery
- A surgeon opens the skull and places a small metal clip at the base of the aneurysm.
- The clip blocks blood flow into the aneurysm.
- This prevents it from bursting.

Both treatments stop blood from entering the aneurysm. This lowers the risk of a burst. But both procedures carry risks. You should talk to a specialist before deciding on treatment. A neurologist or neurosurgeon can help you make the best choice.

# Heartburn and Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)

This article explains what GERD is, what causes it, and how to manage it. It is not a substitute for medical advice. Always talk to a doctor for diagnosis and treatment.

---

## What Is GERD?

GERD is a long-term condition where stomach acid flows back into the tube that connects your throat to your stomach. This tube is called the esophagus.

Many people have heartburn now and then. But if you have heartburn often or it is very strong, you may have GERD.

GERD is also called chronic acid reflux.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The most common symptom is heartburn. This feels like a burning pain that starts in your upper belly or behind your breastbone. It moves up into your throat.

Other symptoms include:
- Burping often
- Trouble swallowing
- A sour or bitter taste in your mouth
- A feeling of fullness in your stomach
- Nausea or vomiting
- A dry, hacking cough
- Hoarseness or a raspy voice
- Asthma-like symptoms
- Tooth pain

If stomach acid reaches your throat or mouth, it can damage your teeth.

---

## What Causes GERD?

GERD happens when the muscle at the bottom of the esophagus does not close properly. This muscle is called the lower esophageal sphincter.

When this muscle does not work well, stomach acid can flow back into the esophagus. This causes irritation and heartburn.

Some people have a condition called a hiatal hernia. This happens when part of the stomach pushes up through the diaphragm. The diaphragm is a muscle that separates your chest from your belly. When the stomach moves up, the muscle at the top of the stomach cannot close tightly.

Other things that may make GERD worse include:
- Being overweight
- Smoking
- Drinking alcohol
- Stress
- Eating large meals
- Lying down or bending over soon after eating
- Certain medicines, such as some blood pressure drugs or birth control pills

Some people have an esophagus that does not clear acid well. Or their esophagus may be more sensitive to acid.

---

## How Is GERD Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms. They will want to know:
- How often you have heartburn
- When it happens
- What makes it better or worse

If your symptoms match GERD, your doctor may give you medicine to reduce stomach acid for two weeks. This is called empiric therapy.

If your symptoms improve, it is likely you have GERD.

In some cases, your doctor may do further tests. These can include:
- A test to check the inside of your esophagus
- A test to measure how much acid is in your esophagus

---

## How Is GERD Treated?

There is no cure for GERD, but you can manage it. Treatment includes lifestyle changes and medicine.

### Lifestyle Changes

You may need to:
- Avoid foods and drinks that trigger symptoms (like spicy food, coffee, alcohol, or citrus)
- Eat smaller meals
- Avoid eating at least three hours before lying down
- Raise the head of your bed by 6 to 8 inches
- Lose weight if you are overweight
- Stop smoking
- Avoid tight clothing around your waist

These changes can help reduce symptoms over time.

### Medication

If lifestyle changes are not enough, your doctor may prescribe medicine. Common types include:
- Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) – these reduce stomach acid
- H2 blockers – these also lower acid production
- Antacids – these neutralize acid quickly

Take medicine as your doctor tells you. Do not stop without talking to your doctor.

### Surgery

Surgery is an option for people with severe GERD who do not get better with other treatments. It strengthens the muscle at the bottom of the esophagus.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

GERD is usually a long-term condition. Symptoms come and go. You may have times with no symptoms and times with bad flare-ups.

Not everyone with GERD gets inflammation in the esophagus. In up to two out of every three people, the esophagus stays healthy.

### Possible Complications

In rare cases, long-term acid exposure can cause changes in the esophagus. This is called Barrett’s esophagus. It happens in about 5 out of 100 people with GERD.

Barrett’s esophagus increases the risk of esophageal cancer. But the risk is still low:
- Out of 1,000 people with GERD and no Barrett’s esophagus, fewer than one will get esophageal cancer in ten years.
- Out of 1,000 people with Barrett’s esophagus, about ten will get esophageal cancer in ten years.

Another possible problem is a narrowed esophagus. Severe inflammation can cause scar tissue. This scar tissue can make swallowing hard.

---

## What Should You Watch for in Daily Life?

GERD can make life harder. It can:
- Keep you awake at night
- Make eating and drinking uncomfortable
- Make you feel tired or stressed
- Cause you to miss work or avoid social events

Treatment takes time. You may need to be patient. But many people feel much better after starting treatment.

You are not alone. Many people live well with GERD.

For more support and real stories from people with GERD, visit:  
[gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Bird Flu (Avian Influenza)

Bird flu is a virus that mainly affects birds. It can cause serious illness in some birds and, very rarely, in people.

## Quick Facts

- Bird flu is caused by certain types of influenza A viruses.
- In birds, it can lead to large numbers of deaths.
- People can get infected, but this is rare.
- When people do get infected, the illness can be very serious.
- Symptoms in people include high fever and breathing problems.
- Severe lung infections (pneumonia) can happen.
- Most cases happen in people who work with poultry or touch infected birds.
- Good hygiene can stop the spread of the virus, especially for people who work with birds.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Bird Flu?

Bird flu is a virus that mainly infects birds. Doctors also call it avian influenza. The virus comes from certain types of influenza A. These viruses can sometimes spread to people.

Most people who get bird flu have worked on poultry farms, in breeding or fattening farms, or in slaughterhouses. They had close contact with infected birds.

There are two main types of bird flu:

- One type causes only mild illness in birds.
- The other type is very dangerous. It causes severe disease and many deaths in poultry and some wild birds. This serious form is also called fowl plague.

Both types can spread to people.

Influenza viruses can infect many animals, including pigs and horses. They also cause regular flu in people. When a virus jumps from an animal to a person, it is called a zoonotic flu. Bird flu viruses can cause very serious illness in humans.

Bird flu in people is a reportable disease. This means doctors must tell public health officials if they suspect a case. The virus can change over time. New versions can appear that might cause a global flu outbreak.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Bird flu can cause different outcomes. Some people have no symptoms. Others become very ill and may die.

Symptoms usually start 1 to 5 days after infection. In some cases, they may take up to 14 days to appear.

People who are infected often have:

- A high fever
- Coughing
- Trouble breathing

They may also feel sick to their stomach, vomit, or have diarrhea. Sore throat, headache, and body aches are less common with bird flu than with regular flu.

**Important:** Bird flu viruses often settle deep in the lungs. This can lead to pneumonia.

## What Causes Bird Flu?

Bird flu is caused by influenza A viruses. These viruses come in different types. The ones that can infect people today are mostly H5N1, H5N6, H7N9, and H9N2.

In nature, these viruses are mostly found in wild water birds. Birds can get infected through bird droppings. The virus can then spread to farm birds.

Mild forms of the virus spread quickly. Birds may not show any signs of illness. But some versions of H5 and H7 are very dangerous. They can kill large numbers of poultry and some wild birds.

Both mild and severe forms can infect people. People usually get the virus through close contact with infected birds. This includes:

- Breathing in dust from bird droppings
- Touching infected birds or their droppings with bare hands

Most human cases have happened in people outside Europe who work with poultry. Very few cases of person-to-person spread have been recorded.

## How Common Is Bird Flu?

There have been no confirmed cases of bird flu in people in Germany. But there have been repeated outbreaks of the dangerous H5 virus in poultry and wild birds in Germany over the past five years. So, infection is still possible.

Traveling to certain areas increases the risk. These include Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Bird flu is more common in people in these regions.

Major outbreaks have happened in the past:

- From 2006 to 2014: H5N1 virus. Around 850 people got sick. About 450 died.
- From 2013 to 2018: H7N9 virus. Over 1,500 people got sick. At least 600 died.

Many people with mild flu symptoms do not get tested. So, the real number of cases may be higher. The death rates are based on people who were very sick and needed hospital care.

## What Is the Outlook?

Bird flu caused by H5N1 or H7N9 can be very serious in people. About half of those who are hospitalized die. This is often due to multiple organs failing.

The virus also weakens the body’s immune system. This makes it easier for bacteria to cause secondary infections. These can make the illness worse.

People who survive often have lasting lung damage. Some may also have long-term kidney problems.

## How Can Bird Flu Be Prevented?

To avoid bird flu:

- Do not touch sick or dead birds.
- If you find a dead wild bird, report it to the local veterinary office. Do not touch it.

If you work with poultry:

- Follow all safety rules at work.
- Practice good hygiene.
- Report any signs of bird flu in birds to the local veterinary office right away.

Birds are only vaccinated in areas where bird flu is common all year. This does not happen in Germany or most of Europe.

If you are traveling to Southeast Asia, the Middle East, or North Africa:

- Check the Foreign Office website for up-to-date risk information.
- Avoid visiting animal markets or poultry markets.
- Only eat poultry and eggs that are fully cooked.
- Wash your hands well with warm water and soap after handling poultry.

**Important:** If you have been near someone with bird flu or near infected birds, you can take a flu medicine called oseltamivir for 7 to 10 days. This can help prevent you from getting sick.

## How Is Bird Flu Diagnosed?

A fever and breathing problems do not always mean you have bird flu. A doctor must test for the virus to be sure.

You may be tested if you have:

- Breathing problems
- Recently traveled to a high-risk area
- Worked with poultry

The doctor will take a swab from your nose and throat. This sample can be tested quickly. But this test only shows if you have a flu virus. It may miss bird flu.

To confirm bird flu, a lab must do a PCR test. This test looks for the virus’s genetic material in the sample.

## How Is Bird Flu Treated?

Bird flu in people can be serious. Early treatment is important.

Medicines that fight viruses, like oseltamivir or zanamivir, should be started as soon as possible. Ideally, within 48 hours of possible exposure.

Other helpful steps:

- Take medicine to reduce fever and pain.
- Drink plenty of fluids.
- If you are in the hospital, you may get fluids through a drip.

If pneumonia develops:

- You will get extra oxygen.
- In severe cases, a machine may help you breathe.

Very sick patients need care in an intensive care unit.

## Where Can I Get More Information?

The Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR) gives advice on food safety and how to protect yourself from bird flu.

# Gestational Diabetes

Gestational diabetes means having high blood sugar during pregnancy.  
It can raise the chance of rare birth problems.  
But most of the time, changing your diet can lower this risk.  
In most cases, the pregnancy goes well and the baby is healthy.

---

## Quick Facts

- Women with gestational diabetes have a higher chance of rare birth problems.  
- Changing your diet usually lowers this risk.  
- A small rise in blood sugar can turn into gestational diabetes.  
- Most women with gestational diabetes have normal pregnancies and healthy babies.  
- Gestational diabetes is not the same as diabetes mellitus, which is a long-term condition.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Gestational Diabetes?

Most women have normal blood sugar during pregnancy.  
But if blood sugar goes above a certain level, doctors call it gestational diabetes.  
About 5 out of every 100 pregnant women have it.

A small rise in blood sugar can become gestational diabetes.  
This happens because your body changes during pregnancy.

After eating, sugar moves from the blood into your body’s cells more slowly.  
This means high blood sugar is common in many pregnant women.  
After the baby is born, blood sugar usually returns to normal.

Gestational diabetes is not the same as diabetes mellitus.  
Diabetes mellitus is a long-term condition that lasts for life.

Gestational diabetes slightly raises the risk of rare birth problems.  
But changing your diet can usually reduce this risk.

Most women with gestational diabetes have normal pregnancies and healthy babies.

---

## What Symptoms Can Happen?

Most women with gestational diabetes have no symptoms.  
If blood sugar rises very high, you might feel tired, weak, or very thirsty.  
These signs are similar to other types of diabetes.  
But they are usually mild.  
Many women think these feelings are just normal pregnancy changes.

---

## What Causes Gestational Diabetes?

Pregnancy hormones change how your body works.  
Your body cells take in sugar from the blood more slowly.  
This causes blood sugar to rise.  
If your blood sugar stays high over time, doctors call it gestational diabetes.

---

## What Raises the Risk?

You are more likely to get gestational diabetes if you:

- Are very overweight  
- Have had gestational diabetes before  
- Have a close family member with diabetes  
- Are older when you become pregnant

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Gestational diabetes usually does not cause lasting problems for mother or baby.  
On average, babies born to mothers with gestational diabetes are a bit heavier.  
But this alone is not a reason to worry.

When babies are larger, it can take longer for the shoulders to come out after the head.  
Sometimes the baby’s shoulder gets stuck in the mother’s pelvis.  
This is called shoulder dystocia.  
It can reduce the baby’s oxygen supply.  
Doctors and midwives are trained to act fast if this happens.

Shoulder dystocia happens in about 4 out of 100 babies when the mother does not treat gestational diabetes.  
Serious injuries or emergencies are rare.

Women with gestational diabetes also have a higher chance of getting pre-eclampsia.  
This is a rare condition where the body holds too much fluid.  
It causes high blood pressure and extra protein in the urine.  
If not treated, pre-eclampsia can harm both mother and baby.

Women who had gestational diabetes are more likely to develop type 2 diabetes later in life.

---

## Can It Be Prevented?

Eating a lot of sugary or starchy foods and being overweight increases the risk.  
Women who stay active and eat balanced meals are less likely to get it.  
But every pregnant woman’s body changes.  
So even healthy women can develop high blood sugar during pregnancy.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

The best way to find gestational diabetes is a sugar test.  
This test checks how your body handles sugar.  
It is usually done between the 24th and 27th week of pregnancy.

The test has two parts:

1. **Screening test:** You drink a sweet drink.  
   Then a blood sample is taken from your arm.  
   If the result is high, you need a second test.

2. **Diagnostic test:** This test is more detailed.  
   You must not eat or drink anything for several hours before.  
   You drink a sweet drink and have blood drawn at different times.

For more details, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

---

## How Is It Treated?

In most cases, changing your diet lowers blood sugar enough.  
Talk to your doctor for help.  
You may also get advice on healthy eating and safe exercise.

For some women, blood sugar stays too high.  
Then they may need insulin shots.  
In rare cases, they may need diabetes medicine.

After the baby is born, you will have another blood test.  
If the result is normal, you do not need more treatment.  
But all women with gestational diabetes should see a doctor after birth.  
They may need more tests or advice on staying healthy.

---

## What Else Should You Know?

Gestational diabetes often has no symptoms.  
So many women are surprised when they are diagnosed.  
You might worry about your baby’s health or birth problems.  
Some fear the diabetes will stay after the baby is born.  
These worries are normal, but most babies are born healthy.

It may take time to get used to new eating habits or more exercise.  
But soon, healthy eating and activity can become part of your daily life.  
These changes also help you stay healthy after the baby is born.

# Rhabdomyolysis

Rhabdomyolysis means muscle fibers are breaking down. This can happen for many reasons. It can be mild or very serious. Some people need strong medical care in the hospital.

---

## Quick Facts

- Rhabdomyolysis is the breakdown of muscle tissue.
- Common causes include muscle injuries, overdoing exercise, infections, certain medicines, and using alcohol or drugs.
- Symptoms can range from mild muscle pain to serious problems like sudden kidney failure.
- Severe cases need fast treatment in the hospital.
- Most people recover well with close care in the hospital.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Rhabdomyolysis?

Rhabdomyolysis happens when muscle fibers break down. This can be caused by a muscle injury, too much exercise, infections, or certain medicines.

Some people feel muscle pain. Others feel nothing at all. In some cases, the breakdown can lead to serious health problems. These include sudden kidney failure. This needs urgent hospital care — sometimes in an intensive care unit.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Mild cases may not cause any symptoms. If symptoms do appear, they can include:

- Pain in the muscles
- Weakness in the muscles
- Urine that looks reddish or brown

The pain often happens in muscles near the center of the body. This includes the shoulders, upper thighs, and lower back. Muscles may also cramp.

More serious cases can cause:

- Feeling very unwell
- High fever
- Fast heartbeat
- Stomach pain
- Nausea or vomiting

### Fun Fact:
Rhabdomyolysis can change the color of your urine. A protein called myoglobin leaks from damaged muscles into the blood. The kidneys then remove it through urine. Myoglobin gives muscles their red color. That is why the urine turns reddish-brown.

---

## What Causes Rhabdomyolysis?

Many things can cause muscle breakdown. Common causes include:

- A hard hit or bruise to the muscle
- Lying in one position for a long time
- Surgery
- Extreme exercise, like running a marathon without training
- Drinking too much alcohol or using drugs
- Some medicines, especially cholesterol-lowering drugs (statins) when taken with other drugs (fibrates)
- Infections, especially in children
- Imbalanced salt levels in the blood
- Overheating the body, such as from heat stroke
- Some mental health medicines (neuroleptics)
- Reactions to anesthesia
- Compartment syndrome — when swelling in the muscle traps fluid and causes severe pain

Often, more than one thing happens at the same time to cause rhabdomyolysis.

---

## How Common Is It?

Anyone can get rhabdomyolysis. But it is more common in children under 10 and adults over 60. People who are overweight and men are also more likely to get it.

---

## What Complications Can Happen?

When muscle fibers break down, small pieces enter the blood. Mild breakdown causes little harm. Severe breakdown can lead to life-threatening problems.

One common problem is sudden kidney failure. The protein myoglobin blocks the tiny tubes in the kidneys. It also harms kidney cells. Blood flow to the kidneys drops. This can stop or reduce urine production.

The breakdown can also cause too much or too little of certain salts in the blood. For example:

- Low calcium can cause muscle cramps.
- High potassium can lead to dangerous heart rhythm problems.

In rare cases, the released substances cause blood clots throughout the body. This can lead to failure of several organs, including the lungs and liver.

Most people recover well with close hospital care. The muscle damage usually heals without lasting effects.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors start by asking about your symptoms and health history. If rhabdomyolysis is suspected, they do blood and urine tests.

A high level of a protein called creatine kinase in the blood is a strong sign. This protein leaks from damaged muscles. The higher the level, the more severe the muscle damage.

A simple urine test can check if myoglobin is in the urine. This is called myoglobinuria.

An electrocardiogram (ECG) is also done. Muscle breakdown can affect the heart rhythm. The ECG checks for this.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Doctors first try to fix the cause. If a medicine is causing the problem, they stop it. If overexertion is the cause, rest and drinking plenty of fluids may be enough for mild cases. But a doctor must decide.

If there is a risk of serious problems, hospital care is needed. A thin tube is placed into a large vein. This lets doctors give fluids to help flush out harmful substances and protect the kidneys.

In severe cases, patients may need:

- Dialysis (a machine to clean the blood when kidneys fail)
- Care in an intensive care unit
- Close monitoring of potassium levels, which can be dangerous if too high

If compartment syndrome is the cause, surgeons may need to operate.

### Important:
Even though complications can happen, most people recover. About 80 out of 100 people with severe muscle damage and kidney failure get better.

# Hepatitis A

Hepatitis A is an infection that causes the liver to become inflamed.  
It is caused by a virus called the hepatitis A virus.  
The virus spreads through dirty water, contaminated food, or close contact with an infected person.

Many people get hepatitis A when they travel to countries with poor sanitation.  
You can prevent the infection with a vaccine.  
Most people can recover at home.  
Once you have had hepatitis A, you are protected for life.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Hepatitis A?

Hepatitis A is a sudden inflammation of the liver.  
It is caused by the hepatitis A virus.  
The virus spreads through the fecal-oral route.  
This means the virus gets from one person’s stool into another person’s mouth.

The word “hepatitis” comes from the Greek word “hepar,” which means liver.  
There are several types of hepatitis, labeled A through E.  
Hepatitis A is one of them.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms of hepatitis A can be very different depending on age.

**Children** often have no symptoms at all.  
They may not even know they are sick.

**Adults** usually feel unwell at first.  
They may have:

- Headaches  
- Muscle pain  
- Joint pain  
- Feeling tired  
- Loss of appetite  
- Nausea  
- Rarely, vomiting  
- A mild fever  
- Pain on the right side of the belly, near the liver

This early stage is called the prodromal phase.  
It can last a few days to a week.

Some people then develop jaundice.  
Jaundice means the whites of the eyes and the skin turn yellow.  
This happens because the liver is not working well.  
It cannot process a substance called bilirubin properly.

When the liver does not process bilirubin, it builds up in the blood.  
This causes the yellow color.

Other signs of jaundice include:

- Light-colored stool  
- Dark urine  
- Itching  
- Sometimes a mild rash

---

## How Do People Get Infected?

The hepatitis A virus is passed in the stool of infected people.  
It spreads when the virus gets into someone else’s mouth.

This can happen in many ways:

- Not washing hands after using the toilet  
- Touching dirty surfaces like door handles  
- Sharing food or drinks  
- Close contact in homes, schools, or daycare centers  
- Sexual contact, especially anal sex

Poor sanitation can also spread the virus.  
For example:

- Contaminated drinking water  
- Fruits and vegetables washed in dirty water  
- Seafood like mussels and oysters from polluted water  
- Fertilizing crops with human waste

In rare cases, the virus can spread through blood.  
This can happen if people share needles when using drugs.

Pregnant women can pass the virus to their baby during pregnancy.

---

## How Common Is Hepatitis A?

Hepatitis A happens all over the world.

In developing countries, most people get infected as children.  
They often do not know they are sick.  
But they become immune for life.

In developed countries with good hygiene, fewer people get infected.  
So many teenagers and adults have no immunity.

When they travel to areas where hepatitis A is common, they can get sick.

In Germany, about 1,000 to 1,500 cases are reported each year.  
Around 40 to 50 percent of these cases are linked to travel.

---

## How Does the Disease Progress?

After infection, it takes 2 to 7 weeks for symptoms to appear.  
On average, symptoms start about 25 to 30 days after exposure.

People can spread the virus **before** they even feel sick.  
They are contagious one to two weeks before symptoms start.  
They can still spread it for up to one week after symptoms begin.

If jaundice develops, it can last from a few days to several weeks.

After that, the body slowly recovers.  
This recovery phase lasts one to four weeks.

Most people get better without any problems.

In up to 10 percent of cases, symptoms last longer — sometimes for months.  
But hepatitis A never becomes a long-term (chronic) illness.

In very rare cases, the infection can be severe.  
It can lead to serious liver failure.  
Older people with pre-existing liver problems are at higher risk.

Once you recover, you are immune for life.

---

## How Can Hepatitis A Be Prevented?

The best way to prevent hepatitis A is vaccination.  
The vaccine contains dead hepatitis A viruses.  
It is given as an injection into the muscle.

You start to build protection within two weeks.  
A second dose is needed at least six months later.  
This gives long-term protection.

There are also combination vaccines that protect against both hepatitis A and hepatitis B.
