The vaccine is especially recommended for:

- People traveling to areas where hepatitis A is common  
  (such as most tropical regions, the Mediterranean, and Eastern Europe)  
- People with liver disease  
- People whose sexual behavior puts them at higher risk  
- People with hemophilia who need regular blood products  
- Residents of psychiatric hospitals or other care facilities  
- Workers who may come into contact with the virus  
  (such as healthcare workers, daycare staff, or wastewater workers)

If someone in your household has hepatitis A, you can get a vaccine or a special antibody shot (immunoglobulin) to prevent infection.

---

## How Is Hepatitis A Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose hepatitis A with a blood test.  
The test checks for:

- High levels of liver enzymes (a sign of liver inflammation)  
- Specific antibodies that show you have been infected  
- The virus itself in the blood or stool (in active cases)

---

## How Is Hepatitis A Treated?

There is no medicine that kills the hepatitis A virus.  
But you can treat the symptoms.

You can take medicine for:

- Fever  
- Headache  
- Nausea

The most important steps are:

- Rest and avoid physical activity  
- Eat light, low-fat meals  
- Do not drink alcohol

Most people can recover at home.  
Hospitalization is very rare.  
Liver failure is extremely uncommon.

---

## More Information

Are you planning a trip?  
You may need a hepatitis A vaccine.  
The Robert Koch Institute offers reliable advice on travel vaccinations.  
They also provide links to more information.

# Coronary Heart Disease

Coronary heart disease means the main blood vessels that carry oxygen to the heart are narrowed.  
This narrowing can stop the heart from getting enough oxygen.  
When this happens, you may feel chest pain, shortness of breath, or nausea.

## Quick Facts

- The main blood vessels to the heart become narrow.
- Chest pain, shortness of breath, and nausea can be early signs.
- Symptoms can be managed well with treatment.
- Preventing other heart problems is very important.
- Even if you have this condition, you can still do many things every day to keep your heart healthy.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Coronary Heart Disease?

Coronary heart disease happens when the main blood vessels that feed oxygen to the heart become narrow.  
These blood vessels are also called coronary arteries.  
The narrowing can lead to other heart problems like heart failure or irregular heartbeats.  
But these risks can be lowered with the right actions.

When the blood vessels are very narrow, you may feel shortness of breath or chest pain when you move or are stressed.  
This is because the heart muscle does not get enough oxygen.  
If a blood vessel suddenly closes, it can cause a heart attack.  
A blood clot can cause this blockage.

> **Important:** Chest pain or tightness can be a sign of a heart attack.  
> If you are unsure, call 112 right away.  
> Ask for an ambulance with a doctor.  
> Do not wait.  
> Getting help fast is critical during a heart attack — even at night.

## What Are the Signs?

Symptoms can include:
- Shortness of breath
- Nausea
- Dizziness
- A tight, heavy, or painful feeling in the chest (called angina)
- Pain that spreads to the arms, neck, back, upper belly, or jaw
- A strong sense of fear or anxiety

These symptoms usually happen during physical activity or stress.  
They often go away after resting or taking medicine.

In women, older adults, and people with diabetes or heart failure, chest tightness is less common.  
Instead, they may feel shortness of breath, pain in the upper belly, or a racing heartbeat.

Symptoms can appear suddenly without any effort. This is called unstable angina.  
It is an emergency. The blood vessel may suddenly close, leading to a heart attack.

Symptoms can also stay the same for a long time. This is called stable angina.  
It is less urgent but still needs medical care.

## What Causes Coronary Heart Disease?

Coronary heart disease is caused by a buildup of fatty deposits in the heart’s blood vessels.  
This process is called atherosclerosis.  
It starts with small areas of inflammation in the blood vessel walls.  
Over time, cells, fats, and other materials collect in these spots.

At first, the deposits do not cause any problems.  
But as they grow, they can block blood flow.  
This means the heart muscle does not get enough blood and oxygen.  
When you move or feel stressed, your heart needs more oxygen.  
This can cause chest pain or tightness.

If chest pain happens even when you are resting, a blood clot has likely formed.  
This usually happens when a hard deposit breaks open.  
If the clot is large enough, it can block the blood vessel completely.  
This causes a heart attack.  
If not treated quickly, part of the heart muscle can die.

## What Increases the Risk?

Your risk goes up as you get older.  
Other risk factors that are not related to age include:

- Smoking
- Being very overweight
- High cholesterol
- High blood pressure
- Diabetes

## How Common Is It?

Coronary heart disease becomes more common with age.  
About 2 out of every 100 people aged 40 to 49 have it.  
About 22 out of every 100 people aged 70 to 79 have it.  
Men are more likely to have it than women.

## How Does It Progress?

The disease usually develops slowly over many years.  
It often first shows up as chest pain during physical activity or stress.  
This is called angina.  
But sometimes, it can cause a heart attack without any warning signs.

For more details on long-term effects, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

## How Can I Prevent It?

You can lower your risk by following simple steps:

- Do not smoke
- Stay physically active
- Eat a balanced diet
- Avoid gaining weight

There is no strong proof that special diets or vitamin supplements prevent the disease.

For more tips on keeping your heart healthy, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Chest pain can have many causes. These include:
- Problems with the chest muscles or bones
- Inflammation of the heart muscle
- Irregular heartbeats
- Lung or breathing problems
- Esophagus issues
- Stress or mental health problems

The main test is an electrocardiogram (ECG).  
It checks the heart’s electrical activity.  
It can be done while you are at rest or during exercise.  
In some cases, an ultrasound of the heart (called an echo test) helps.

Your doctor will decide which tests you need.  
This depends on your age, health history, and symptoms.

If coronary heart disease is found, your doctor will do more tests.  
These help check your risk of future problems like a heart attack.  
They also help plan your treatment.

Tests may include:
- Measuring blood pressure: higher pressure increases your risk of other heart problems.
- Physical exam: the doctor listens to your heart. This can show if there are valve problems or other issues.
- Blood tests: to check for conditions like type 2 diabetes or high cholesterol. These increase your risk.
- Reviewing your family history: heart attacks or circulation problems in your family raise your risk.
- Talking about your lifestyle: such as smoking, diet, and exercise habits.

## What Screening Is Available?

If you are over 35 and have public health insurance, you can have a health checkup every three years.  
The goal is to find early signs of heart disease, diabetes, or kidney problems.  
During the checkup, your doctor may:
- Test your blood and urine
- Measure your blood pressure

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment has two main goals:
- Reduce symptoms
- Prevent future heart problems

If your condition is stable, medicine can help.  
Common medicines include:
- Beta-blockers
- Calcium channel blockers
- Nitrates

If medicine is not enough, your doctor may widen the narrowed blood vessel using a heart catheter.  
This is done during a procedure called angioplasty.  
A stent may be placed to keep the vessel open.

If more than one vessel is blocked, a bypass surgery may be needed.  
In this surgery, a healthy blood vessel from another part of your body is used to go around the blocked one.

You can help prevent future problems by:
- Staying active
- Eating a healthy diet
- Quitting smoking if you smoke
- Taking certain medicines

These medicines include:
- Low-dose acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) to prevent blood clots
- Statins to protect blood vessels

For more on medicines and heart catheter procedures, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

## What Rehabilitation Options Are There?

Cardiac rehabilitation helps people with coronary heart disease.  
It can improve your strength, reduce future risks, and improve your quality of life.

Rehab is especially helpful after:
- A heart attack
- A bypass surgery or stent placement
- Heart failure
- High risk of other heart problems
- Depression after a heart attack
- Symptoms that make daily life hard

Rehab is run by a team of experts.  
This includes doctors, physiotherapists, dietitians, and psychologists.  
It includes:
- Exercise training
- Education on managing your condition and risk factors
- Psychological support

You apply for rehab through your doctor.  
Usually, your public health insurance or pension fund covers it.

After rehab, you can join an outpatient heart group.  
These meet at least once a week.  
They offer guided exercise sessions.

## What Helps in Daily Life?

Many people with heart problems feel they must change everything overnight.  
They get lots of advice, but big changes are hard to keep.  
It works better to set one goal at a time.  
Small, steady steps are often more effective than big changes all at once.

Coronary heart disease is a long-term condition.  
But it does not have to take over your life.  
Understanding it helps you manage it better.  
It also helps you notice problems early.

> **Important:** Some people with this condition wonder if they could have done more to prevent it.  
> But lifestyle is only one part of the story.  
> Family history also plays a big role.

## Where Can I Get More Support?

If you have public health insurance and coronary heart disease, you may qualify for a structured treatment program.  
These are also called disease management programs (DMP).  
They aim to improve your quality of life and ensure good care.

To join a DMP, contact your health insurance provider.

For detailed information, visit the patient guideline titled **“Chronic Coronary Heart Disease”**.  
It is made for adults with the condition, their families, and trusted people.

# Liver Cancer – Simple Explanation

This page explains liver cancer in plain language. It covers what liver cancer is, its symptoms, causes, how it is diagnosed, treatment options, and where to get help.

---

## Quick Facts

- The most common type of liver cancer is called hepatocellular carcinoma.
- Another type is cancer in the bile ducts inside the liver.
- In the early stages, liver cancer often causes no symptoms.
- The biggest risk factor is long-term liver damage, called cirrhosis.
- Men are more likely than women to get liver cancer.
- Treatment depends on how far the cancer has spread.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

---

## What Is Liver Cancer?

Liver cancer is a serious growth of abnormal cells in the liver. Doctors call it primary liver cancer when it starts in the liver.

Most liver cancers are hepatocellular carcinomas. These start in the main liver cells.

Other types include:
- Cancers in the bile ducts inside the liver.
- Rare cancers like sarcomas.

About 9,800 people in Germany are diagnosed with liver cancer each year.

> **Note:** Liver metastases are not primary liver cancer. These are cancer cells that spread to the liver from another organ, like the colon or breast. Doctors call this secondary liver cancer.

---

## What Symptoms Can Liver Cancer Cause?

In the early stages, liver cancer usually causes no symptoms.

When symptoms do appear, they are often general and not specific to cancer. They may include:
- Pain or pressure in the upper belly.
- Feeling tired all the time.
- Loss of appetite.
- Losing weight without trying.

Later in the disease, more serious signs may show up:
- Yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice).
- A very large liver (hepatomegalia).
- Fluid buildup in the belly (ascites).

Bile duct cancer in the liver (also called cholangiocarcinoma) causes similar symptoms. It may also cause:
- Dark urine.
- Pale-colored stools.
- Severe itching.

These symptoms can also happen with non-cancerous illnesses. But if they last for more than a few weeks, see a doctor.

Your general practitioner can help figure out what is causing the symptoms. They may refer you to a specialist for further tests.

---

## What Causes Liver Cancer?

The main cause of hepatocellular carcinoma is long-term liver damage, known as cirrhosis.

In Germany, this is most often due to:
- Long-term hepatitis C virus infection.
- Heavy alcohol use.

Other risk factors include:
- Fatty liver disease (caused by poor diet or overeating).
- Being overweight or obese.
- Type 2 diabetes.
- Chronic hepatitis B or C infection.
- Some inherited metabolic disorders.
- Smoking.

The risk factors for bile duct cancer in the liver are similar. Additional risks include:
- Long-term inflammation of the bile ducts.
- Cysts in the bile ducts outside the liver.
- Bile duct stones.

---

## Can Liver Cancer Be Prevented?

Yes, some steps can lower your risk:

- Eat a healthy, balanced diet.
- Stay physically active.
- Avoid alcohol.
- Keep a healthy body weight.

Other preventive actions:
- Get the hepatitis B vaccine as recommended by health experts.
- Treat chronic hepatitis B or C infections early.
- Quit smoking.
- Drink coffee if you have chronic liver disease.
- For people with type 2 diabetes, the drug metformin may reduce liver cancer risk.

---

## Is There Liver Cancer Screening?

There is no routine screening for liver cancer in healthy people.

This is because liver cancer often causes no symptoms early on.

But people at high risk should be checked regularly. High-risk groups include:
- People with cirrhosis.
- Those with chronic hepatitis B or C.
- People with fatty liver disease.
- Those with rare inherited liver disorders.

For these people, doctors recommend:
- Regular ultrasound scans of the liver.
- Blood tests when needed.
- Tests to check liver damage (fibrosis stage).

These checks help doctors spot cancer early.

---

## How Is Liver Cancer Diagnosed?

Doctors use several methods to find liver cancer.

### Step 1: Ultrasound Scan
An ultrasound of the belly gives a first look at the liver. It can show if there is a suspicious lump.

### Step 2: Imaging with Contrast
If a lump is found, doctors use special imaging tests. They inject a contrast agent into a vein and take pictures at different times.

The most common method is:
- Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with contrast.

Other options:
- Computed tomography (CT) scan with contrast.
- Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS).

### Step 3: Biopsy (If Needed)
If imaging is not clear, doctors may take a small sample of the tumor.

This is done through the skin using a needle. A local anesthetic is used to numb the area.

The tissue is sent to a lab and examined under a microscope. This confirms the diagnosis.

Biopsies are especially useful when:
- The tumor is small.
- The liver does not have cirrhosis.

### Step 4: Molecular Tests
In some cases, doctors test the tumor cells to learn more about them. This helps plan future treatment.

---

### Diagnosing Bile Duct Cancer in the Liver

The same methods are used as for liver cell cancer. Additional tests may be needed:

- 3D MRI of the bile ducts with contrast.
- Endoscopic-retrograde cholangio(pancreato)graphy (ERC/P): a tube is passed through the mouth to look at the bile and pancreatic ducts.
- Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography (PTC): a thin needle is used to inject contrast into the liver’s bile ducts.
- Laparoscopy: a small camera is used to look inside the belly and take tissue samples.

If it’s unclear whether the cancer started in the liver or spread from another organ, doctors may also examine the stomach and intestines.

For more details on these tests and their risks, visit the website of the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## How Is Liver Cancer Treated?

Treatment depends on the stage of the cancer and the patient’s overall health.

Doctors use a system called the **Barcelona Clinic for Liver Cancer (BCLC)** to decide the best treatment. This system looks at:
- How many tumors there are and how big they are.
- Whether the cancer has spread beyond the liver.
- The patient’s general health.
- How well the liver is working.

If you have hepatitis B or C, doctors will treat that infection too.

---

### When a Cure Is Possible

If the cancer is found early and the liver is still healthy, a cure may be possible.

Treatment options include:
- Surgery to remove part of the liver.
- Liver transplant.

If surgery is not possible, doctors may use heat to destroy the tumor. This is called:
- Radiofrequency ablation (RFA).
- Microwave ablation (MWA).

These treatments are used when the tumor is small and in a hard-to-reach spot.

Sometimes, treatment is given before surgery to shrink the tumor. This is called **downstaging**.

If a liver transplant is planned, other treatments are used to keep the cancer under control until a donor liver is available. This is called **bridging therapy**.

---

### When a Cure Is Not Possible

If the cancer cannot be cured, treatment focuses on relieving symptoms and improving quality of life. This is called **palliative care**.

For cancer that is not too advanced:
- Internal radiotherapy (radiation placed inside the body).
- Chemotherapy focused only on the liver.

These treatments slow tumor growth. They are only used if:
- The patient is in good health.
- The liver is working well.
- There are no distant metastases.

For advanced cancer that has spread:
- Systemic treatment is used. This means medicine that travels through the whole body.
- Options include:
  - Immunotherapy: helps the body’s immune system fight cancer.
  - Targeted therapy: drugs that attack specific features of cancer cells.

Doctors check every 6 to 12 weeks with imaging scans to see if the treatment is working.

In the final stage, treatment focuses on comfort. This includes:
- Managing pain.
- Treating nausea, vomiting, and fatigue.
- Supporting mental and emotional well-being.

---

### Bile Duct Cancer in the Liver

For early-stage bile duct cancer:
- Surgery is the main treatment.
- The surgeon removes the tumor and part of the liver.
- Nearby lymph nodes are also removed.
- Liver transplant is not recommended outside of research studies.

After surgery, some patients get **adjuvant therapy** to lower the risk of cancer returning. This is usually chemotherapy.

If surgery is not possible, heat-based treatments may be used to destroy the tumor.

For advanced disease:
- Treatment depends on the patient’s overall health.
- Goals are to control the cancer and maintain quality of life.

Options include:
- Chemotherapy.
- Local treatments to destroy the tumor.
- Targeted therapy (if suitable).
- Supportive care to relieve symptoms.

---

### What If the Cancer Comes Back?

If the cancer returns after treatment, this is called a **relapse**.

If the cancer is still only in the liver, another surgery may be possible.

If not, doctors may use local treatments like heat or radiation.

For more information on surgery, chemotherapy, and side effects, visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## After Treatment: Rehabilitation

Rehabilitation helps patients recover after cancer treatment.

A rehab program may include:
- Counseling to support mental health.
- Advice on healthy eating.
- Help returning

# Non-Specific Physical Problems (Conditions with No Clear Medical Cause)

Sometimes doctors cannot find a physical reason for certain symptoms. For example, many people have ongoing pain, stomach issues, or problems with blood flow, but no clear cause can be found. If these problems last, it is important to look again at how you handle stress and difficult situations.

---

## Quick Overview

- Some people have long-lasting physical symptoms that doctors cannot explain.
- In most cases, these symptoms go away on their own after a few weeks.
- Not finding a physical cause does not mean the symptoms are not real.
- About 1 in 10 people have symptoms with no clear medical explanation.
- When symptoms last a long time, they can cause strong mental stress and emotional strain.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Are Functional Somatic Syndromes?

Many people get headaches, diarrhea, or dizziness. These can be uncomfortable, but they usually go away after a while. Often, doctors can find a reason for long-term symptoms. But sometimes, no clear physical cause is found — like an injury or infection. When this happens, it is called a functional somatic syndrome.

Not finding a cause can be worrying. But these symptoms often improve within a few weeks. People with these conditions should try to keep doing normal daily activities. They should also find ways to manage their symptoms.

If the symptoms continue and become very hard to live with, help from a mental health professional may be useful. Long-term medicine usually does not help much.

It can be frustrating when doctors cannot find a reason for your symptoms. But this does not mean the symptoms are fake or that nothing can be done.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

There are many types of functional somatic syndromes. Common ones include:

- Pain, especially in the head, stomach, back, or muscles
- Stomach and bowel problems like nausea, vomiting, bloating, diarrhea, or constipation
- Blood flow issues: these can cause tiredness, fast heartbeat, or anxiety
- Feeling very tired, weak, or unable to focus
- Dizziness
- Shortness of breath or sudden fast breathing (hyperventilation)
- Muscle cramps or tightness
- Skin sensations like itching, tingling, or numbness
- Urinary problems like a strong urge to pee or pain when urinating

These physical symptoms can come with anxiety or depression. Some people feel like something strange is inside their body or that something is physically wrong with them.

Conditions like fibromyalgia or irritable bowel syndrome often cause symptoms with no clear cause. That is why they are similar to functional somatic syndromes.

---

## What Causes These Syndromes?

Just because no physical cause is found does not mean the symptoms have no reason. Usually, a mix of physical and mental factors is involved. These can include:

- Being overwhelmed by work or life
- Past illnesses
- Family history
- Hard personal situations
- Conflicts in relationships

People feel these symptoms differently. Some find them very severe and disabling. Others pay less attention to them. How much the symptoms affect your life depends on how you respond to them.

The term “functional somatic syndromes” is used because an organ can be healthy but still not work properly. For example, your intestines might be fine, but stress can still cause diarrhea, bloating, or constipation.

---

## How Common Are These Syndromes?

About 1 in 10 people have symptoms with no clear cause. Women are affected twice as often as men. One reason may be that hormones affect how we feel pain. Social and cultural differences also play a role. For example, men and women may be raised to handle pain differently. Women are also more likely to see a doctor when they feel unwell.

---

## How Do These Syndromes Develop?

Functional somatic syndromes are usually not dangerous. They are often mild and temporary. But in some cases, they can last a long time and cause serious problems.

These syndromes can affect both your body and your mind. They can make family life, work, or daily routines very hard. Some people even lose their jobs.

Many people with ongoing symptoms stop being active. They believe they must rest because of the pain. But staying inactive can make things worse. For example, muscle and joint pain often gets worse when you do not move.

Long-term symptoms can lead to serious mental stress. About half of people with these syndromes develop depression or anxiety.

But many people also stay calm and hopeful. Knowing that symptoms come and go can help. Staying positive and believing the symptoms will improve can also help.

Some people feel doctors do not take their symptoms seriously. This can make them seek many different doctors or change doctors often.

Even though these syndromes can reduce quality of life, they do not shorten your life. On average, people with these conditions live just as long as others.

---

## How Are They Diagnosed?

Doctors start by talking to you about your symptoms. Then they do a physical exam to learn more. They may take a blood test or do an ultrasound. These tests help them check if there is a clear cause.

They first look for common reasons. They also check for signs of serious illness.

Whether more tests are needed depends on several things. For example, how bad the symptoms are and how they change over time.

Because symptoms often improve after a few weeks, doctors may not do all possible tests right away. They usually only do more tests if symptoms continue or get worse.

It is rare to find a real illness after all tests are done.

> **Important:** Doing too many tests is not always helpful. Some tests carry risks. More tests also increase the chance of finding something that looks like a problem but is actually harmless. This can cause unnecessary worry. It can also lead to more tests that are not needed.

If symptoms last, it is important to keep seeing your doctor. Even if no cause is found, you can still talk about what might be making symptoms worse. You can also discuss ways to feel better. The goal is to find a possible explanation and plan helpful steps. These plans can be reviewed and changed later.

Working with your doctor to understand your symptoms and find useful strategies is often the best approach.

If symptoms are long-lasting and very hard to manage, it can help to see a specialist in psychosomatic medicine or a psychotherapist. These clinics often focus on treating functional somatic syndromes.

---

## How Are They Treated?

Symptoms without a clear cause often get better on their own within a few weeks. So doctors usually wait before starting treatment.

If symptoms are mild, they may just give you simple tips to help you cope.

Doctors often suggest:

- Stay physically active
- Keep up social life — see friends, do hobbies
- Avoid things that are too stressful or tiring
- Work on solving personal conflicts
- Learn how to manage stress
- Notice what helps reduce your symptoms
- Eat well, sleep enough, and live a healthy lifestyle

Medicine can help sometimes — for example, for pain or stomach issues. But it is usually only used for a short time.

If symptoms last a long time or affect many parts of the body, talking to a therapist can help. Other options may include physical therapy, diet advice, or job coaching. Relaxation techniques or mindfulness training can also help you handle stress better.

> **Important:** It is better to stay active than to rely only on things like massages. Massages can help a little, but only for a short time. Long-term benefits come from regular exercise and better stress management. Some people need to push themselves at first. But most get used to it quickly and feel better. Exercise should be enjoyable, not painful.

If symptoms are severe and long-lasting, patience is key. Set small goals. Try to stay active even when you feel unwell. This means moving your body, distracting yourself, and being happy when symptoms slowly improve.

Your general doctor is the best person to talk to about these issues.

Many general doctors have extra training in psychosomatic care. This means they are specially prepared to help with these conditions. If needed, your doctor can connect you with other specialists.

More information is available at [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

---

## Is Rehabilitation Helpful?

Only a few people with these symptoms need rehabilitation. But it can help if you are unable to work. It can also help you return to work.

Other goals of rehabilitation can be:

- Preventing symptoms from getting worse
- Helping you stay socially active
- Keeping your ability to work

Rehabilitation plans are different for each person. They always include both physical and mental support.

The type and severity of your symptoms decide if you need outpatient or inpatient care.

In Germany, the German Pension Insurance (Deutsche Rentenversicherung) usually handles medical rehabilitation. But health insurance or accident insurance providers may also help.

---

## Where Can You Find More Help?

People with these conditions often search online for information. But be careful. Not all online sources are reliable. Always question the quality of what you read.

You can also contact support services or self-help groups.

The German Psychotherapists’ Association has a website with a tool to find qualified therapists.

The National Association of Statutory Health Insurance Providers (Kassenärztliche Bundesvereinigung) can help you find and book appointments with doctors.

The Alliance of Rare Chronic Diseases (Allianz Chronischer Seltener Erkrankungen – ACHSE) is a good source of information for rare conditions.

# Premature Ejaculation

If a man almost always reaches orgasm too soon during sex, this is called premature ejaculation.  
This can make sex frustrating and affect a man’s confidence and relationship.  
The good news is that exercises, medicine, or talking to a therapist can help.

---

## Quick Facts

- Premature ejaculation means a man reaches orgasm either before or just after sex starts.  
- On average, men take 5 to 7 minutes to reach orgasm.  
- About 4 out of every 100 men ejaculate very quickly almost every time they have sex.  
- Exercises, medicine, or sex therapy can improve control and help.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

---

## What Is Premature Ejaculation?

Many people have wrong ideas about how long sex should last.  
There is no single “right” time for orgasm.  
It can vary from one time to the next.  
It depends on many things, like mood, stress, and how long it has been since the last time.

Some men reach orgasm in less than a minute.  
Others take more than 30 minutes.  
Both are normal.

How much a quick orgasm affects a man depends on the person.  
Some feel upset. Others do not mind.

Studies show men often think they take longer to reach orgasm than they actually do.  
In some cases, they are off by 25 or even 50 percent.  
So, comparing yourself to others is not helpful.

About 4 percent of men ejaculate very quickly almost every time.  
This happens even before or just after sex starts.

Doctors call this premature ejaculation if it causes real problems.

---

## What Causes Premature Ejaculation?

Scientists do not fully understand what causes it.  
Some think it may be due to physical reasons.  
For example, the penis might be too sensitive.  
Or the nerves and hormones in the body might not work together properly.

Others believe it is linked to mental or emotional issues.  
These can include stress, low self-confidence, or problems in a relationship.

It is also possible that both physical and mental factors play a role together.

Some men have had this problem since they first had sex.  
Others start having it later in life.  
When it starts later, doctors call it “acquired” or “secondary” premature ejaculation.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

If you think you have premature ejaculation, talk to your doctor.  
You can see a general doctor or a urologist.

The doctor will ask:
- How long it usually takes you to reach orgasm.
- How often you ejaculate too soon.
- How much this bothers you.
- Whether you can delay ejaculation.

Tests are only needed if the doctor suspects another health problem.

You may be diagnosed with premature ejaculation if:
- You almost always ejaculate within one minute of starting sex.
- This has been happening for more than six months.
- It causes you a lot of distress.
- No other medical condition is causing it.

You do **not** have premature ejaculation if:
- You only ejaculate too soon sometimes.
- You have not had sex in a long time. It is normal to come quickly after a break.
- You think you come too soon, but your time is actually within the normal range.

The doctor will also check for other possible causes.  
For example, an inflamed prostate (prostatitis) can cause early ejaculation.  
Signs of this include pain or frequent urination.

> **Important:** Premature ejaculation can sometimes be a sign of another problem.  
> For example, if a man comes quickly because he is afraid he will lose his erection, the real issue may be erectile dysfunction.  
> Treating the real problem can help with premature ejaculation.

---

## How Is It Treated?

You decide whether you want treatment.  
There are several options:

- **Exercises:** These help you learn to control your body.  
  One common method is to stimulate the penis until you feel close to orgasm, then stop.  
  Repeat this several times. This can help you delay ejaculation.

- **Medicine:** Some medicines can help you last longer.  
  They can be taken by mouth or applied as a numbing cream to the head of the penis.  
  But they can also cause side effects.

- **Sex therapy:** This helps men and couples feel more confident.  
  It can reduce fear and anxiety about sex.

> **Important:**  
> Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are the most common medicine used.  
> In Europe, only one SSRI, called dapoxetine, is approved for this use.  
> It only adds about one to one-and-a-half minutes on average.  
> Other SSRIs are cheaper and work better. Doctors can prescribe them even though they are not officially approved for this use.

> **Note:** Health insurance does not cover the cost of medicine for premature ejaculation, even if it is approved.

For more information, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## Other Important Points

Sex is important to many people’s sense of self.  
Men with premature ejaculation may feel pressure from myths about “good” sex.  
They may hear others brag or get advice that is not helpful.  
Remember: Your problem does not make you less of a man.

If premature ejaculation affects your sex life, it can be very frustrating.  
Some men worry they are not good enough in bed.  
But a relationship is not just about sex or how long it lasts.

There are many ways to enjoy intimacy and feel pleasure.  
For many people, happiness in a relationship matters more than how long sex lasts.

Some men avoid talking about this issue.  
But keeping quiet can make it worse.  
Talking to your partner or a doctor can help you feel better.

# Vitamin D Deficiency

Vitamin D helps keep your bones strong and healthy.  
If you do not get enough vitamin D for a long time, your bones can become weak.  
Vitamin D also helps your immune system work well.  
Your body makes vitamin D when your skin is exposed to sunlight.  
Spending time outside regularly can help you avoid a vitamin D deficiency.

---

## Quick Facts

- A vitamin D deficiency means your body has not had enough vitamin D for a long time.  
- This can lead to health problems that need treatment.  
- A low level of vitamin D without symptoms is not the same as a deficiency.  
- Your body makes vitamin D when your skin is in sunlight.  
- To stay healthy, expose your face, hands, and arms to sunlight 2 to 3 times a week from spring to autumn.  
- You can get a small amount of vitamin D from food.  
  Good sources include oily fish, liver, eggs, and mushrooms.  
- **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Vitamin D Deficiency?

A vitamin D deficiency happens when your body lacks enough vitamin D over a long time.  
It causes symptoms that need medical care.  
If you have low vitamin D but no symptoms, it is called an insufficient supply.  
This does not always need treatment.

---

## What Is Vitamin D?

Vitamin D is a group of fat-soluble vitamins.  
The most important forms are vitamin D2 and vitamin D3.  
The active form in your body is called calcitriol.  
Vitamin D helps your body absorb calcium from food.  
Calcium is needed to build strong bones.  
Vitamin D also helps your muscles work well.  
It supports your immune system.

---

## How Does the Body Make Vitamin D?

Your body makes vitamin D in steps.  
It starts in the skin, then moves to the liver and kidneys.  
Sunlight is the main source.  
When your skin is in direct sunlight, it produces most of the vitamin D you need.  
This happens when you spend time outside.  

The amount of vitamin D your skin makes depends on:  
- Where you live (latitude)  
- The time of year  
- The time of day  
- The weather  
- Your skin color  
- What you wear  
- Whether you use sunscreen  

Because of this, the time you need in the sun can vary a lot.  
Your body can also store extra vitamin D in spring and summer.  
This helps you get through winter when the sun is weaker.

---

## What Are the Symptoms of a Vitamin D Deficiency?

You may not notice any symptoms if you have low vitamin D for a long time.  
But a true deficiency can cause several problems.  
These are mostly due to weak bones.

### Symptoms in Children

Low vitamin D can harm bone growth in children.  
It can cause permanent bone deformities.  
This condition is called rickets.  
Signs include:  
- Bent or deformed bones, especially in the spine, ribs, and legs  
- Swelling where bones meet cartilage  
- Soft skull in babies  
- Delayed closing of soft spots on a baby’s head  
- Weak muscles that make standing and walking hard  
- Delayed motor skills (like sitting, crawling, walking)  
- Seizures  
- More frequent infections

### Symptoms in Adults

In adults, weak bones can lead to a condition called osteomalacia.  
This means bones become soft and painful.  
It also causes muscle weakness.  
A vitamin D deficiency increases the risk of osteoporosis.  
Osteoporosis means bones become thin and weak, especially in older people.  
Symptoms in adults include:  
- Bone and leg pain  
- Weak muscles, muscle pain, or muscle twitches  
- Falling or breaking bones easily  
- Feeling tired and drained quickly

---

## Who Is at Risk?

Your body makes most of the vitamin D it needs from sunlight.  
If you spend little time outside, you are more likely to be low in vitamin D.  
Some groups are at higher risk:

- People with limited mobility or long-term illnesses  
- Older adults: your body makes less vitamin D as you age  
- Babies: their skin is very sensitive and should not be in direct sun  
- People who cover their skin for cultural or religious reasons  
- People with dark skin: they need more sun exposure than people with light skin to make the same amount of vitamin D.  
  This is harder in northern and central Europe, where sunlight is weak in winter.

Certain health conditions also raise the risk:  
- Long-term digestive problems  
- Chronic kidney disease  
- Liver disease, such as cirrhosis  
- Some medicines, like epilepsy drugs and chemotherapy

---

## How Can You Prevent a Deficiency?

To stay healthy, follow these steps:

- Expose your face, hands, and arms to sunlight 2 to 3 times a week.  
- Do not use sunscreen during this time.  
- Stay in the sun for half the time it would take to get sunburned without sunscreen.  
- The exact time depends on your skin type, time of year, and time of day.  
  For example, people with light skin should be in the sun 5 to 60 minutes daily from March to October.

From October to March in Germany, the sun is not strong enough to make vitamin D.  
Your body relies on stores from spring and summer.

**Important:**  
- Do not use a tanning bed to get vitamin D. It increases your risk of skin cancer.  
- Avoid sunburn, especially in children and teens.  
- Use sun protection if you stay in the sun for a long time.  
- Do not expose babies directly to sunlight.

You can get a small amount of vitamin D from food.  
Good sources are oily fish, liver, eggs, and mushrooms.  
But food alone cannot meet your full vitamin D needs.

---

### Using Vitamin D Supplements

Take vitamin D supplements only if a doctor says you need them.  
This is usually after testing shows a deficiency that cannot be fixed with sun and food.

In Germany, doctors recommend giving vitamin D drops to babies until their second summer.  
The daily dose is 10 to 12.5 micrograms (400 to 500 international units).  
Premature babies and sick children may need different doses.  
A pediatrician will decide what is best.

For adults in high-risk groups, such as those with chronic illness, in care, or very elderly, a daily supplement of 20 micrograms (800 IU) is advised.

Talk to your family doctor before starting any supplement.  
They can help you decide if you need one and how much.

**Important:**  
- Taking more than 100 micrograms of vitamin D per day for a long time can cause harm.  
- This can lead to nausea, stomach pain, and vomiting.  
- In serious cases, it can damage your kidneys or cause heart problems.  
- Sunlight and food do not cause this kind of overdose.

---

## How Is a Vitamin D Deficiency Diagnosed?

If your doctor suspects a deficiency, they will:  
- Ask about your symptoms and lifestyle  
- Do a physical exam  
- Order a blood test to check your vitamin D level and other values  
- Use X-rays to look for bone changes

---

### How Is Vitamin D Level Measured?

The blood test measures 25-hydroxy vitamin D3.  
This is a form of vitamin D that shows your body’s supply.  
It is also called calcidiol.  
The result is shown in nanomoles per liter (nmol/l) or nanograms per milliliter (ng/ml).

Here is how the level is interpreted:

- **Over 50 nmol/l (20 ng/ml):** You have enough vitamin D for healthy bones.  
- **30 to 50 nmol/l (12 to 20 ng/ml):** Your supply is low. This may affect your bones.  
- **Below 30 nmol/l (12 ng/ml):** You have a deficiency. This raises your risk of rickets, osteomalacia, and osteoporosis.

---

### Are Home Test Kits Useful?

Some pharmacies sell quick tests you can use at home.  
These tests are not reliable.  
Experts do not recommend them.

---

## How Is a Vitamin D Deficiency Treated?

If a blood test confirms a deficiency, your doctor will prescribe vitamin D supplements.  
These are usually vitamin D3.  
The dose depends on how low your level is and your health risks.  
In some cases, your doctor may also recommend calcium.

You will need follow-up blood tests.  
This helps your doctor adjust the dose.  
This is especially important if you take high doses.  
Too much vitamin D can cause serious harm.

---

## Where Can You Learn More?

For more information about vitamin D and when to take supplements, visit:  
[klartext-nahrungsergaenzung.de](https://klartext-nahrungsergaenzung.de)

# Aortic Stenosis

Heart valve diseases damage the heart’s valves. This makes it harder for the heart to pump blood properly. These problems are most common in older adults. The most frequent heart valve issue is aortic stenosis. This means the valve between the main pumping chamber of the heart and the main blood vessel leaving the heart becomes narrow.

## Quick Facts

- Heart valve problems usually develop slowly over many years.
- Aortic stenosis is the most common type of heart valve disease.
- In aortic stenosis, the valve between the left lower heart chamber and the main artery (aorta) gets narrower.
- Men are slightly more likely than women to have heart valve problems.
- If the valve is only mildly affected, regular checkups with a doctor may be enough.
- If symptoms appear or the condition gets worse, treatment options are available.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Aortic Stenosis?

The heart has four valves. These act like one-way doors. They let blood flow in only one direction. This keeps blood moving in the right direction through the heart and body.

Oxygen-poor blood goes to the lungs. Oxygen-rich blood comes back from the lungs and goes out to the body.

Over time, heart valves can become damaged. This is usually due to aging and wear and tear. Doctors call this acquired heart valve disease.

The aortic valve sits between the left lower chamber of the heart and the aorta. If this valve becomes narrow, the heart must work harder to push blood out.

Treatment is not always needed. But if symptoms appear or the condition gets worse, doctors often replace the damaged valve with a new one. This new valve can be put in during open heart surgery or through a thin tube inserted into a blood vessel.

> **Important:** If a valve does not close tightly, it is called valve leakage or regurgitation. If a valve is both narrow and leaks, this is called mixed heart valve disease.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people with aortic stenosis do not feel sick at first. The heart can often make up for a small narrowing by beating harder.

But if the valve becomes severely narrowed, blood can back up. This can cause fluid to build up in the heart, lungs, and body.

Symptoms may include:

- Feeling weak or tired
- Swelling in the legs
- Heartbeat that feels too fast, too slow, or irregular
- Coughing or shortness of breath, especially at night
- Chest tightness or chest pain
- Fainting

## What Causes Aortic Stenosis?

The main cause is aging. Over time, calcium builds up on the valve. This makes it stiff and narrow.

Some people are born with heart valves that are shaped differently. This makes it more likely the valve will become narrow or leak later in life.

Damage to the heart muscle near the valve can also affect how it works. For example, a heart attack can harm the area around the valve.

## How Common Is It?

Heart valve problems from aging are most common in older adults.

About 1 in 8 people aged 75 or older have a heart valve problem. Men are slightly more likely than women to have these issues.

## What Is the Outlook?

In many people, the heart can keep working well for years—even decades—even with a narrowed valve. But the heart muscle must work harder all the time.

This extra strain causes the muscle to thicken and the heart to grow larger.

Over time, the heart muscle becomes stiff and less able to pump. The heart chambers wear out. The heart gets weaker.

At first, symptoms only happen during physical activity. Later, they can happen even when resting.

Without treatment, this can lead to serious heart failure that can be life-threatening.

## Can It Be Prevented?

Smoking raises the risk of heart problems, including valve disease. Quitting smoking is one of the best ways to lower your risk.

Infection in the lining of the heart (called endocarditis) can also damage heart valves. This infection is often caused by bacteria.

People with a birth defect in their valve or a new valve prosthesis may be given antibiotics before dental work or certain medical procedures. This helps prevent bacteria from entering the blood and causing infection.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors start by listening to your heart with a stethoscope. This can reveal unusual sounds that suggest a valve problem.

An ultrasound of the heart, called echocardiography, confirms the diagnosis. It shows how badly the valve is damaged.

Sometimes, a special ultrasound through the throat (transesophageal echocardiography) is used. A small tube with a probe is passed down the throat to get clearer images.

Once the diagnosis is confirmed, the doctor checks your overall health. This helps decide the best treatment.

Tests may include:

- An ECG at rest and during exercise
- Blood pressure check
- Blood tests
- X-ray, CT scan, or MRI if needed
- A heart catheter test if there is concern about blocked heart arteries

In a heart catheter test, a dye is injected into the heart’s blood vessels. This lets the doctor see the vessels on a screen.

## How Is It Treated?

Mild valve changes often do not need treatment. Doctors just monitor them over time.

If symptoms appear or the condition worsens, treatment options are available. Many people with aortic stenosis get a new valve.

The type of treatment depends on:

- Your age
- How bad the valve problem is
- The cause of the problem
- Other health conditions you may have

A new valve can be placed during open heart surgery or through a thin tube inserted into a blood vessel.

There are two main types of new valves:

### Mechanical Valve

- Made of plastic and metal.
- Very strong and long-lasting.
- Used mostly in younger people, but rarely.
- Can cause blood clots to form.
- To prevent clots, you must take blood-thinning medicine for life.
- This medicine can cause rare but serious bleeding in the stomach or brain.

### Biological Valve

- Made from animal tissue (pig or cow) or human donor tissue.
- Not as long-lasting as mechanical valves.
- Usually lasts 10 to 15 years.
- After that, it may need to be replaced.
- Does not require lifelong blood-thinning medicine.
- Often used in people over 60 or in younger people who cannot take blood-thinning medicine.

## What Happens After Surgery?

After heart valve surgery, most people go through a rehabilitation program.

Rehab helps you slowly return to normal activities. It improves your strength and quality of life.

During rehab, your doctor adjusts your medicines. Your heart is checked regularly.

## Living with Heart Valve Disease

Aortic stenosis can be hard to live with. Feeling weak and tired can make daily tasks harder.

Deciding on treatment can be stressful. Talk to your doctor and family about your choices.

After surgery, it may be harder to handle stress for a while. It helps to talk to family and friends early about who can help and how.

You can also ask your health insurance for support before surgery. For example, you may get help with housework or other tasks.

# Flu (Influenza)

Many people say they have the flu when they really just have a cold. But the two are different. A cold usually starts slowly. Flu often comes on fast and feels much worse.

## Quick Facts

- Flu causes symptoms like headaches, sore throat, chills, high fever, and body aches.
- Flu is caused by viruses.
- A cold builds up slowly. Flu hits suddenly and makes you feel very sick.
- Washing your hands often can help stop the spread of flu.
- A flu vaccine is available and can help protect you.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Flu?

You can feel fine in the morning. By the afternoon, you may be shivering in bed with a high fever and feeling very ill. This sudden start is common with flu. A cold, on the other hand, gets worse slowly and is usually mild.

Flu is more serious than a cold for some people. But not everyone gets sick with flu. Some people have only mild symptoms. Others have no symptoms at all.

Even though flu can be serious, most people get better on their own. There is no cure for flu. But treatment helps ease the symptoms.

## What Are the Symptoms of Flu?

Flu affects the whole body, not just the nose and throat. It often starts fast and with strong symptoms. Most symptoms improve in about a week. But tiredness and coughing can last longer.

Common flu symptoms include:

- Fever of 38°C or higher
- Body aches in muscles and joints
- Headaches
- Sore throat
- Chills
- Extreme tiredness and feeling very unwell
- Dry cough (no mucus)
- Stuffy or runny nose
- Loss of appetite
- Feeling very weak

Only about one in three people with flu have the classic symptoms like fever, pain, and tiredness. Another third have mild symptoms like a cold. The last third feel no symptoms at all.

## What Causes Flu?

Flu is caused by viruses. Viruses are tiny germs that are smaller than bacteria. Once inside your body, they multiply fast.

Your body fights back by making special proteins called antibodies. But it takes time to make enough of them.

There are many types of flu viruses. The most dangerous are Influenza A and Influenza B.

After you have had flu, your body is protected against that exact virus. But this protection does not last forever. The viruses change every year. New types can appear each season.

## How Does Flu Progress?

Flu often leads to sinus infections. This means the spaces around your nose become inflamed and filled with fluid. You may get headaches and a blocked nose.

In babies and young children, flu can cause ear infections. This happens when the middle ear becomes inflamed.

Severe flu is rare. But it can happen. Pneumonia is a possible complication. It is most dangerous for:

- Babies and young children
- People with lung problems
- People with weak immune systems
- Adults over 60

In rare cases, flu can be life-threatening.

## How Can Flu Be Prevented?

Flu spreads through tiny droplets in the air. When someone coughs or sneezes, they release these droplets. You can catch the virus by breathing them in.

You can also spread the virus by touching your nose or mouth after touching contaminated surfaces. For example, doorknobs on buses or trains can carry the virus.

To stop the spread of flu:

- Wash your hands often with soap and water.
- Cough or sneeze into your elbow, not your hand.
- Open windows to let fresh air in.
- Throw used tissues away right away.
- Avoid close contact with others when you are sick.

Even after you start feeling better, you can still spread the virus for up to a week. Try to stay home from work or school during this time.

A flu vaccine can help protect you. But flu viruses change every year. That means you need a new vaccine each year.

It takes about two weeks after vaccination for your body to build up protection. The best time to get the vaccine is in autumn. But getting it later in the year—like in January or February—can still help.

For more details on who should get the flu vaccine and how it works, visit **gesundheitsinformation.de**.

## How Is Flu Treated?

Rest is the most important step. Stay in bed until you feel better.

Many people use home remedies like chicken soup or herbal tea. Drinking fluids is also common. But there is no strong proof that these help fight flu. You do not need to drink more than you want to.

There are many over-the-counter products for colds, coughs, and flu. These include vitamin pills and inhalers. But there is no good evidence they help you recover faster.

Pain relievers like paracetamol, acetylsalicylic acid (ASA), and ibuprofen can help with pain and fever.

**Important:** Do not give acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) to children or teenagers. It can cause a rare but serious condition called Reye syndrome. This affects the brain and liver and can be deadly.

There are also prescription medicines for flu. One common one in Germany is oseltamivir.

- It must be taken within 2 days of the first symptoms.
- It does not help if you start it later.
- It may shorten the illness by about a day.
- It can cause nausea and vomiting.

Antibiotics do not work for flu. They only fight bacteria, not viruses. So antibiotics will not help if you have flu.

# Cancer of the Gallbladder and Bile Ducts

This article explains gallbladder and bile duct cancer in simple terms. It covers causes, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment, and support.

---

## Quick Facts

- Doctors also call these cancers **biliary tumors**.
- These cancers are rare. About 5,130 people in Germany get them each year.
- Women are more likely to get gallbladder cancer.
- Men are more likely to get bile duct cancer outside the liver.
- Symptoms often do not appear until the cancer is advanced.
- The exact cause is not known, but some risk factors are linked to it.
- The only way to cure these cancers is to remove the entire tumor with surgery.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Gallbladder or Bile Duct Cancer?

Cancer in the gallbladder or bile ducts is called a **biliary tumor**.

- Gallbladder cancer starts in the inner lining of the gallbladder.
- Bile duct cancer can happen in different places:
  - Inside the liver: called *intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma*.
  - Outside the liver: called *extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma*.

This article focuses on **bile duct cancer outside the liver**.

Cancers in the bile ducts are grouped by location:
- **Klatskin tumor**: at the point where the right and left bile ducts meet.
- **Ampullary carcinoma**: near the opening of the bile duct into the small intestine.

Cancer inside the liver is covered in a separate article about liver cancer.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

### Bile Duct Cancer

Symptoms often appear only when the cancer is advanced.

Common signs include:
- Yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice).
- Itching all over the body.
- Light-colored stools.
- Dark urine.
- Pain in the upper right side of the belly.
- Nausea and vomiting.
- Loss of appetite and weight loss.
- Feeling very tired.
- Fever.
- Infection in the bile ducts (cholangitis).

A painless, swollen gallbladder that you can feel through the skin may also be a sign.

### Gallbladder Cancer

This cancer often causes no symptoms early on.

Later, you might feel:
- Nausea or vomiting.
- Loss of appetite.
- Pain in the upper right side of the belly.

Yellowing of the skin and eyes usually means the cancer is advanced. It may be felt through the belly wall.

> **If symptoms last for weeks or months, see a doctor.** Your family doctor can help find the cause. They may refer you to a specialist if needed.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

### For Bile Duct Cancer (outside the liver):
- Being older.
- Congenital (born with) bile duct problems (like Caroli disease).
- Bile duct stones.
- A cyst in the bile duct.
- Chronic bowel inflammation (like Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis).

### For Gallbladder Cancer:
- Gallstones.
- Being severely overweight.
- Large non-cancerous growths in the gallbladder (polyps).
- Abnormal bile duct development.
- Long-term gallbladder inflammation.
- Chronic bile duct inflammation (especially primary sclerosing cholangitis).
- Diabetes.
- A hard, calcified gallbladder after repeated inflammation (called “porcelain gallbladder”).

---

## Can You Prevent This Cancer?

There is no guaranteed way to prevent it. But you can lower your risk by:
- Eating a healthy diet.
- Staying at a healthy weight.
- Avoiding smoking.
- Limiting alcohol.

These healthy habits help reduce the risk of many cancers.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

If cancer is suspected, doctors use several tests:

### Step 1: Talk and Exam
- The doctor asks about your health history and symptoms.
- They check your right upper belly by touch.

### Step 2: Blood Tests
- No single blood test confirms cancer.
- But abnormal results can show a blockage in the bile flow.

### Step 3: Imaging Tests
These help see the tumor and how far it has spread:
- **Ultrasound**: first test to look at the abdomen.
- **MRI or CT scan**: most important for confirming cancer.
- **MRCP**: special MRI that shows the bile ducts in 3D.
- **Dynamic MRI with contrast**: helps see how the tumor grows.

### Step 4: Biopsy
- A small sample of tissue is taken.
- It is checked under a microscope to confirm cancer.
- This is especially important if surgery is not possible.

### Step 5: Additional Tests
- Doctors may test the tumor for specific changes in the cells.
- This helps decide if targeted drugs can be used.

### Other Procedures
Depending on the case, doctors may use:
- **Endosonography**: ultrasound probe inside the body.
- **ERCP**: a tube is passed through the mouth to the small intestine. Dye and X-rays help see the bile ducts.
- **Cholangiography**: direct imaging of the bile ducts.
- **PTC**: a thin needle is used to inject dye into the bile ducts from outside the body.
- **Laparoscopy**: a small camera is used to look inside the belly.

Tissue samples are taken during some of these tests to confirm the diagnosis.

Sometimes, gallbladder cancer is found by accident. For example, if a doctor removes the gallbladder for gallstones and finds cancer during the operation.

> For more details on tests and side effects, visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## Is There Screening?

There is no national screening program for gallbladder or bile duct cancer in healthy people.

But experts recommend:
- Regular ultrasounds for people with gallbladder polyps.
- In some cases, doctors may remove the gallbladder as a safety step.

For people with **primary sclerosing cholangitis** (a long-term bile duct inflammation):
- Have imaging scans every 6 months.
- Alternating between ultrasound, MRI, and MRCP.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on:
- How far the cancer has spread.
- The type of tumor.
- Your overall health.

### Can It Be Cured?

Yes, only if:
- The tumor is still in the bile duct or gallbladder.
- It has not spread to other organs.
- There are no distant metastases (cancer in other parts of the body).
- You are healthy enough for surgery.

Surgery is the only cure. The operation may include:
- Removing the gallbladder.
- Removing part of the bile duct.
- Removing parts of the liver, pancreas, or small intestine.
- Removing nearby lymph nodes.

Before surgery, doctors may:
- Use chemotherapy first (only in clinical trials).
- Drain bile if there is an infection (biliary drainage).

After surgery, most doctors recommend **chemotherapy** to lower the risk of cancer returning.

### If Surgery Is Not Possible

If the cancer is too advanced for surgery, doctors may:
- Use chemotherapy.
- Try treatments that use heat or light to destroy the tumor (less invasive).

### Borderline Operable

If the cancer is large but has not spread, doctors may:
- Give chemotherapy first.
- Recheck the tumor after a few cycles.
- If it shrinks, surgery may become possible.

In some cases, a **liver transplant** may be considered in clinical trials.

### If Cure Is Not Possible

When cancer has spread or is too advanced, treatment focuses on:
- Managing symptoms.
- Improving quality of life.
- Respecting your wishes.

Treatment options include:
- **Chemotherapy**: to slow cancer growth.
- **Palliative treatments**: to relieve pain or blockages.
  - For example, a small tube (stent) can be placed in the bile duct to keep it open.
  - High-precision radiation can shrink tumors.
- **Targeted therapy**: drugs that attack specific changes in cancer cells.
  - Only used if the cancer has certain markers and standard treatments no longer work.
- **Supportive care**:
  - Pain relief medicine.
  - Nutrition support if you are losing weight.
  - Psychological help.

If cancer is found by accident during gallbladder removal, treatment planning still follows the same steps.

> For more on surgery, chemotherapy, and side effects, visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## After Treatment: Rehabilitation

Rehab helps you recover after cancer treatment.

A rehab program may include:
- Counseling to help with stress or anxiety.
- Advice on healthy eating.
- Work-related rehab for younger patients to return to work.

The **Cancer Information Service** lists local support services, including psycho-oncologists and social law advisors.

---

## Follow-Up Care

If the cancer was completely removed, you will have regular check-ups. These include:
- Physical exams.
- Blood tests.
- Imaging tests (CT, ultrasound, or MRI) of the belly and chest.

### If the Cancer Cannot Be Cured

You will still have regular check-ups. Doctors will:
- Check your general health.
- Review blood test results.
- Use imaging to track how the cancer is progressing.

These visits help catch and treat symptoms early, such as:
- Blocked bile ducts.
- Digestive problems.

The goal is to keep your quality of life as good as possible for as long as possible.

> For more on aftercare, visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

# Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS)

Premenstrual syndrome, or PMS, is a condition that affects some women before their monthly period.  
It causes a mix of physical and emotional symptoms.  
These symptoms usually start a few days to two weeks before the period begins.  
They go away once the period starts and are gone by the end of the period.

## What Is PMS?

Many women feel worse before their period.  
They may have stomach pain, headaches, or feel sad or irritable.  
Some feel bloated or just not well.  
This is called premenstrual syndrome, or PMS.

Most women have only mild symptoms.  
They can still do their usual activities.  
But some women have strong symptoms.  
Their daily life can be hard during this time.  
They may not be able to work, study, or enjoy time with family and friends.

## What Are the Symptoms?

PMS includes a mix of physical and emotional signs.  
Common symptoms are:

- Breast tenderness  
- Belly pain or cramps  
- Headaches  
- Back pain or joint pain  
- Muscle aches  
- Swelling in hands, feet, or face (water retention)  
- Trouble sleeping  
- Digestive problems  
- Skin breakouts  
- Strong hunger or cravings

Emotional symptoms can include:

- Mood swings  
- Feeling tired or low in energy  
- Trouble focusing  
- Feeling anxious, sad, or hopeless  
- Feeling angry or irritable  
- Feeling insecure or overwhelmed

**Important:** When symptoms are severe, they can hurt relationships with family, friends, and coworkers.

A more serious form of PMS is called premenstrual dysphoric disorder, or PMDD.  
PMDD causes strong mental health symptoms.  
It can lead to deep sadness, panic, or feeling unable to cope.

## What Causes PMS?

Doctors do not know exactly what causes PMS.  
But they think it may be linked to changes in hormones during the menstrual cycle.

The body makes more of the hormone progesterone in the second half of the cycle.  
Estrogen levels drop at the same time.  
Even if hormone levels are normal, some women may react more strongly to progesterone.

Scientists believe brain chemicals like serotonin play a role.  
Serotonin helps control mood and sleep.  
If it is out of balance, it can cause emotional symptoms.

Genetics and life stress may also affect how bad PMS is.

## How Common Is PMS?

Most women have mild PMS symptoms sometimes.  
But they do not feel badly affected.

About 20 to 40 percent of women have more severe symptoms.  
These symptoms interfere with daily life.

About 3 to 8 percent of women have a very severe form of PMS.  
This is called PMDD.  
Their mental health symptoms are so strong that they struggle to live normally.

## What Is the Outlook?

PMS only happens in the second half of the menstrual cycle.  
It starts after ovulation and ends when the period begins.

Symptoms go away once the period starts.  
They do not last beyond the end of the period.

Some women have symptoms in some cycles but not others.  
The severity can change over time.  
No one can predict how symptoms will change.

PMS will stop for good at the latest when a woman reaches menopause.

## How Is PMS Diagnosed?

Doctors will ask about your symptoms and when they happen.  
They want to make sure the symptoms are not caused by another health problem.

They may check for conditions like:

- Depression  
- Thyroid problems  
- Irritable bowel syndrome

Keeping a symptom diary helps.  
Write down all your symptoms every day for at least two to three months.  
This shows patterns and helps the doctor make a diagnosis.

More information about keeping a diary is available at **gesundheitsinformation.de**.

## How Is PMS Treated?

There is not enough strong research on what treatments work best.  
But many women find relief with simple changes.

### Lifestyle Changes That May Help

- Exercise regularly  
- Drink less alcohol and coffee  
- Eat less salt  
- Eat more whole grains, fruits, and vegetables  
- Get enough sleep

### Other Helpful Approaches

- Relaxation techniques like deep breathing or meditation  
- Warm baths or gentle walks  
- Acupuncture (some women find this helpful)  
- Herbal remedies or supplements like chasteberry, St. John’s wort, calcium, or vitamin B6

**Important:** Some medicines can help with severe symptoms.  
But many are not approved for PMS.  
They may have side effects.

Common medicines include:

- Birth control pills or hormonal patches: These change hormone levels and can reduce PMS and PMDD symptoms.  
- Antidepressants (SSRIs): These help if mood symptoms are very strong.  
- Painkillers: These help with strong period pain. They are usually safe. But there is little research on whether they help with other PMS symptoms.  
- Diuretics: These help if you have bad swelling from water retention.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) may help women with strong mental health symptoms.  
But it is not yet proven to help with PMS.

More details on treatments are available at **gesundheitsinformation.de**.

## What Can You Do in Daily Life?

If you have PMS, try to take it easy when symptoms come.  
Give yourself more time and space to rest.

Try these simple things:

- Go for a short walk  
- Take a warm bath  
- Read a book or watch a calm show in the evening

Talk to your partner, family, or close friend about how you feel.  
This can help them understand and support you.

Some women worry that talking about PMS will cause problems.  
For example, if they feel angry or sad, others might think they are just “acting out” because of their period.  
Some people still believe that women are out of control during PMS.  
This is not true.  
PMS is a real condition, not a sign of weakness.

You are not alone.  
Many women go through this.  
Help is available.

# Epilepsy

Epilepsy can happen at any age.  
The brain or parts of it become overactive.  
This means too many signals are sent.  
These signals can cause a seizure.  

Learn more about what causes epilepsy, how it is diagnosed, and how it is treated.

---

## Quick Facts

- During a seizure, a person may have muscle jerks or the whole body may shake.  
- Some people pass out during a seizure.  
- A seizure does not cause lasting harm.  
- Doctors only call it epilepsy if seizures happen more than once.  
- Medicine can help stop seizures from happening.  
- If you are helping someone during a seizure, stay calm.  
- Protect the person from getting hurt.  
- Call emergency services at 112 if the seizure lasts more than five minutes.  
- Call 112 if someone has several seizures in a short time.  

**Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Epilepsy?

Epilepsy means the brain or parts of it are overactive.  
Too many signals are sent at once.  
This can cause a seizure.  

A seizure may cause just one muscle to twitch.  
Or it may cause the whole body to shake.  
Some people stay awake during a seizure.  
Others lose consciousness.

Epilepsy can start at any age.  
Some people have their first seizure as children.  
Others have their first seizure later in life.  
Between seizures, most people feel normal.  
But the fear of having another seizure can be stressful.

---

## What Are the Signs of Epilepsy?

Seizures can happen in many ways.  
One arm or leg may jerk.  
Or the whole body may shake.  
Some seizures last only a few seconds.  
Some are so mild they go unnoticed.

During a seizure, some people stay aware.  
Others lose awareness for a short time.  
Most seizures end quickly.

If a seizure lasts more than five minutes, it is an emergency.  
This is called “status epilepticus.”  
It needs fast treatment with medicine.  
If someone has several seizures in a row, it is also an emergency.

Most people feel normal between seizures.

---

## What Causes Epilepsy?

Different parts of the brain control movement, speech, feelings, and thoughts.  
Billions of nerve cells send signals using electricity and chemicals.  
During a seizure, this system gets out of balance.

The brain becomes overactive.  
Nerve cells send too many signals.  
This can cause a seizure.  
Doctors sometimes call this a “brain storm.”

It is often hard to find the exact cause.  
But some known causes include:  
- Head injuries  
- Brain infections  
- Strokes  
- Brain tumors  

When a cause is found, it is called “symptomatic epilepsy.”

Some people have a family history of epilepsy.  
This means it can run in families.

---

## How Common Is Epilepsy?

Doctors only call it epilepsy if a person has more than one seizure.  
About 1 in 100 people have epilepsy.  
If you include people who had just one seizure, about 10 in 100 have had a seizure at some point.

The first seizure can happen at any age.  
Many people first have a seizure as children.  
In rare cases, the first seizure happens between ages 40 and 59.  
After age 60, more people have their first seizure.

---

## What Happens Over Time?

Some people only have one seizure.  
Others have seizures for a few months or years.  
About half of people who have one seizure will have a second.  
After a second seizure, the chance of a third is higher.  
About 7 in 10 people have a third seizure within a few years.

These numbers are averages.  
The real risk depends on the cause.  
If a brain problem is known, the risk of another seizure is about twice as high.  
If the cause is unknown or genetic, the risk is lower.

Some people take medicine and stay seizure-free for years.  
They may even stop medicine and stay seizure-free.  
Others need to keep taking medicine to prevent seizures.  
About 3 in 10 people still have seizures even after trying different treatments.

---

## How Is Epilepsy Diagnosed?

Doctors usually diagnose epilepsy if:  
- A person has had at least two seizures  
- At least 24 hours passed between seizures  
- There is no sign of a one-time event (like a fever or low blood sugar)

Doctors may also diagnose epilepsy if there is a high risk of another seizure.  
This can happen if a person has a brain problem.

Some rare types of epilepsy are called epilepsy syndromes.

The most important part of diagnosis is the patient’s medical history.  
Doctors ask:  
- When did the seizure happen?  
- What was the person doing?  
- How did the seizure start and end?

People often do not remember their own seizure.  
So it helps if someone who saw it comes to the doctor’s visit.  
They can describe what happened.

Doctors also do a physical exam and a brain check.  
Blood tests are done to rule out other causes.

An electroencephalogram (EEG) measures brain activity.  
It can show patterns that suggest a higher risk of seizures.  
But an EEG alone is not enough to diagnose epilepsy.

A brain scan (MRI) is usually done.  
It can show if there are any brain changes that could cause seizures.

If a brain infection is suspected, a sample of spinal fluid may be taken.  
This is done with a needle in the lower back.  
It is called a lumbar puncture.

---

## How Is Epilepsy Treated?

Treatment depends on the type of epilepsy and how it progresses.

Most people take medicine called anti-epileptic drugs.  
There are many types of these medicines.  
They come from different groups of active ingredients.

If a low dose does not work, the dose can be raised.  
If that does not help, doctors may try a different medicine or combine two medicines.

Not everyone needs treatment right away.  
If a person only has one seizure, treatment may not start.  
But if there is a high risk of another seizure, treatment may begin after the first one.

Medicine is usually taken for several years.

Most care happens in a hospital.  
Some clinics and outpatient centers specialize in epilepsy.

If medicine does not work, other options are available:

- **Surgery:** If a specific part of the brain causes seizures, it may be removed.  
  This is not always possible.  
- **Vagus nerve stimulation:** A small device is placed under the skin in the chest.  
  It sends electrical signals through a wire to the vagus nerve in the neck.  
  This may help reduce seizures.  
  But research on this treatment is still limited.

Psychotherapy can also help.  
It can improve a person’s mental health and quality of life.  
There is no strong proof that it reduces seizures.

For more information on adult treatment, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## What to Do If Someone Has a Seizure

If someone has a seizure:  
- Stay calm.  
- Protect them from injury.  
- Do not try to hold them down.  
- Do not put anything in their mouth.  
- Turn them gently onto their side if possible.  
- Stay with them until they are fully awake.

Call emergency services at 112 if:  
- The seizure lasts more than five minutes  
- The person has several seizures in a row  
- The person does not wake up after the seizure

A long or severe seizure may need hospital care.

# Norovirus Infection – Simple Explanation

Norovirus is a common virus that causes stomach and gut problems. It spreads easily and can make people very sick.

---

## Quick Facts

- Norovirus is very contagious.
- It causes strong vomiting and bad diarrhea.
- People lose a lot of fluid when sick. They must drink plenty of fluids.
- The virus spreads fast in places like care homes, hospitals, kindergartens, and cruise ships.
- Good hygiene is key to stopping the spread.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Norovirus?

Norovirus causes sudden stomach and gut illness. It leads to strong waves of vomiting and severe diarrhea.

The virus was first found in a school in Norwalk, Ohio, in 1968. That’s how it got its name. In 2002, scientists started calling it "norovirus."

It causes most non-bacterial stomach infections.  
- In children, it causes about 30% of these cases.  
- In adults, it causes up to 50% of these cases.

Children under 5 and adults over 70 are most likely to get sick.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms come on suddenly and include:

- Severe vomiting
- Bad diarrhea
- Stomach pain
- Nausea
- Headaches
- Muscle aches

Some people only vomit. Others only have diarrhea.

Most people feel very weak and unwell.  
Body temperature may rise a little, but high fever is rare.  
Symptoms usually go away in 1 to 2 days.

---

## How Do People Get Infected?

Norovirus spreads only from person to person.

The virus changes often, so there are many different types. Only three types affect humans: types I, II, and IV. Type IV causes most adult infections.

The virus leaves the body through vomit and stool.  
You can catch it by:

- Touching surfaces that are contaminated (like door handles)
