- Breathing in tiny droplets from vomit
- Eating food or drinking liquids that are infected

Just 10 to 100 virus particles can make someone sick.

Infected food is a common source. Raw foods like salads, crabs, mussels, and drinks can carry the virus.

---

## How Common Is Norovirus?

Norovirus is found all over the world.  
It can happen any time of year, but it is most common from October to March.

---

## How Does the Illness Develop?

The time between catching the virus and getting sick is 6 hours to 2 days. This is called the incubation period.

People are most contagious while they are sick.  
But the virus can still be in the stool for 7 to 14 days after symptoms go away. In rare cases, it can last weeks.

So, good handwashing and toilet hygiene are important even after feeling better.

---

## Is There a Vaccine?

No vaccine is available yet. Scientists are working on one, but it is not ready.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor may test a stool sample to confirm norovirus.

Diagnosis is needed when someone has vomiting or diarrhea with no other clear cause.  
This is especially important in group settings like care homes, hospitals, and kindergartens.

Confirmed cases must be reported to public health authorities.

---

## How Is It Treated?

There is no medicine that kills the norovirus.  
Treatment focuses on managing symptoms.

Because vomiting and diarrhea cause fluid loss, drinking plenty is essential.

Children under 5 and adults over 70 are especially at risk from dehydration.

If vomiting is severe, medicine can help reduce nausea.

---

### When Should You See a Doctor?

See a doctor if you or someone you care for:

- Is an infant
- Is pregnant
- Is elderly or weak
- Has frequent diarrhea or vomiting that lasts more than 2 to 3 days
- Has a high temperature

> **Important:** There is no scientific proof that lemon juice helps against norovirus. Do not rely on it.

---

## What Should You Do at Home?

If you are sick:

- Rest as much as possible.
- Stay away from others.
- Drink plenty of fluids to replace lost water.

To help with salt and mineral loss:

- Use electrolyte drinks from the pharmacy. These contain salts, minerals, and sugar.

Eat only light, easy-to-digest foods. Add a little salt to your meals.

Use a separate toilet for at least 2 days after recovery.  
Wash your hands with soap and water after every bathroom use.  
Keep doing this for up to 2 weeks after feeling better.

Clean up vomit or stool right away.  
Wash your hands thoroughly after cleaning.

Wash clothes, bedding, towels, and washcloths often.  
Use hot water — at least 60 degrees Celsius.

Clean toilets, sinks, door handles, and floors regularly.  
Use disposable cloths and gloves for extra protection.  
Regular cleaning products and water are usually enough.

---

## What Should Group Homes and Facilities Do?

Follow strict hygiene rules in places like care homes, hospitals, kindergartens, and kitchens.

To prevent food-related spread:

- Cook all food thoroughly.
- Pay special attention to seafood.

The best time to stop the spread is from the first symptom until 48 hours after symptoms end.

If there is any suspicion of norovirus, take action right away — even before test results come back.

During illness, use these extra steps:

- Keep sick people apart from others.
- Wear gloves, aprons, and face masks when helping someone who is vomiting.
- Wash hands often and use hand sanitizer.
- Disinfect surfaces like toilets, sinks, and door handles near sick people.

Use cleaning products labeled “begrenzt viruzid PLUS” or “viruzid.”

---

### When Can Children Return to Kindergarten?

Children under 6 who are sick or suspected of being sick with norovirus must stay home.

They can return only 48 hours after all symptoms have stopped.

---

### Who Must Follow Special Rules at Work?

Anyone working with food — like in a kitchen or canteen — must not go to work if they are sick.

They can return to work at the earliest 2 days after symptoms are gone.

Good handwashing is very important at work for the next 4 to 6 weeks.

# Multiple Sclerosis

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a long-term condition that affects the brain, spinal cord, and optic nerves. It is one of the most common neurological diseases in young adults in Western countries. The symptoms vary widely from person to person. There is no cure, but treatments can help slow the disease and manage symptoms.

---

## What Is Multiple Sclerosis?

MS is a condition where the body’s immune system mistakenly attacks the nervous system. This attack damages the protective covering around nerve fibers. Over time, this damage leads to scarring in the nerves. This scarring is called sclerosis.

The nervous system includes the brain, spinal cord, and optic nerves. When these areas are damaged, nerve signals do not travel properly. This causes problems with movement, vision, balance, and other body functions.

MS can affect almost any part of the body. Because symptoms vary so much, it is sometimes called the “disease with a thousand faces.”

---

## Can MS Be Cured?

No, there is no cure for MS at this time. But new treatments have been developed that can slow the disease’s progress. These treatments help many people live better and longer.

---

## What Are the Symptoms of MS?

Symptoms of MS can be very different from one person to another. They depend on which part of the nervous system is affected.

Common symptoms include:

- Feeling very tired, even after little activity  
- Weakness, paralysis, or shaking in the arms or legs  
- Numbness, tingling, or crawling sensations on the skin  
- Pain, such as burning in the arms or legs  
- Cold or hot feelings in the hands or feet  
- Vision problems, like blurred or double vision, or tunnel vision  
- Trouble with balance or coordination  
- Problems with bladder or bowel control  

**Important:** Feeling extremely tired is very common in MS. This tiredness is not due to laziness. It is a real symptom of the disease.

Most people with MS have flare-ups. These are times when symptoms get worse. After a flare-up, symptoms may improve or go away completely. This pattern is called relapsing-remitting MS.

Some people do not have flare-ups. Instead, their symptoms slowly get worse over time. This is called primary-progressive MS.

---

## What Causes MS?

The exact cause of MS is not known. But experts believe it happens when a person’s genes and environment interact in a way that triggers the immune system to attack the nervous system.

Immune cells travel to the brain and spinal cord. There, they damage the myelin sheath — the protective layer around nerve fibers. This damage causes inflammation and can harm the nerves themselves.

When nerves are damaged, they cannot send signals properly. This leads to the symptoms of MS.

---

## What Increases the Risk of MS?

Certain factors make it more likely a person will develop MS. These include:

- Being female  
- Living in northern regions (like northern Europe or North America)  
- Having a family member with MS or another autoimmune disease  
- Smoking  
- Being overweight during childhood or teenage years  
- Low levels of vitamin D  
- Having had glandular fever (caused by the Epstein-Barr virus)

**Important:** Some people worry that vaccines cause MS. But research shows no link between vaccines and MS. Vaccines do not cause the disease.

---

## How Common Is MS?

MS is fairly common in young adults. It usually starts between the ages of 20 and 40. It is about three times more common in women than in men.

In Europe, about 125 out of every 100,000 people have MS. It is more common in Europe and North America than in other parts of the world.

---

## How Does MS Progress?

MS has two main phases:

1. **Inflammatory phase** – The immune system attacks the nervous system. This causes damage and swelling.
2. **Degenerative phase** – Nerve damage builds up over time. This leads to worsening symptoms.

Doctors classify MS into four types based on how it progresses:

### Clinically Isolated Syndrome (CIS)
This is a single episode of symptoms that lasts at least 24 hours. The symptoms go away on their own. About half of people with CIS go on to develop MS.

### Relapsing-Remitting MS (RRMS)
This is the most common form. People have flare-ups of symptoms, followed by periods when symptoms improve or go away. Most people start with this type.

### Secondary Progressive MS (SPMS)
After years of relapsing-remitting MS, the disease slowly gets worse. Flare-ups may still happen, but they are less common. About 80% of people with RRMS eventually develop SPMS.

### Primary Progressive MS (PPMS)
Symptoms get worse slowly and steadily from the start. There are no clear flare-ups. This type affects about 10 to 15% of people with MS.

**Important:** It is hard to predict how MS will progress. Some people have mild symptoms and do well with treatment. Others have more severe symptoms even years after diagnosis.

---

## How Is MS Diagnosed?

Diagnosis starts with a detailed medical history and a physical exam. The doctor will check:

- Vision and eye movement  
- Muscle strength and reflexes  
- Walking and balance  
- Sensation (touch, pain, temperature, body position)

### Additional Tests

If MS is suspected, the doctor will likely order:

- **MRI scan** – This checks the brain and spinal cord for signs of damage. It is the most reliable test for MS.
- **Lumbar puncture** – A small sample of spinal fluid is taken from the lower back. This helps detect signs of inflammation in the nervous system.
- **Evoked potentials** – These tests measure how fast nerve signals travel. They can show if there are delays in the nervous system.
- **Blood tests** – These help rule out other conditions with similar symptoms, such as thyroid problems or type 2 diabetes.

---

## How Is MS Treated?

There is no cure for MS, but treatments can help:

- Slow down the disease  
- Reduce symptoms  
- Delay disability  

Treatments fall into three categories:

### 1. Treatment for Acute Flare-Ups

When symptoms suddenly get worse, doctors use strong anti-inflammatory medicines. The most common is methylprednisolone, given through a drip in the vein for several days.

If this does not help, a second dose may be given. In rare cases, a low dose of the same medicine is taken by mouth over time.

If these treatments fail, a blood purification method may be used. This removes harmful antibodies from the blood.

**Important:** Flare-ups are very tiring. People should rest and avoid stress. Hospital care is often needed.

### 2. Long-Term Treatment

These medicines help prevent new damage to the nervous system. They work by calming or changing the immune system.

Options include:

- Injections under the skin or into muscles (like interferon or glatiramer acetate)  
- Pills (like teriflunomide, dimethyl fumarate, cladribine, fingolimod, ozanimod, siponimod, ponesimod)  
- Infusions (like natalizumab, ocrelizumab, alemtuzumab)

For primary-progressive MS, only one medicine (ocrelizumab) is approved. But doctors may use other medicines in special cases.

The right medicine depends on the type and severity of MS, and on possible side effects.

### 3. Symptomatic Treatment

This treats specific problems caused by MS. It is tailored to each person.

Common issues and treatments:

- **Fatigue** – Treated with physical therapy and gentle exercise  
- **Muscle stiffness (spasticity)** – Treated with medicine and physical therapy  
- **Walking and balance problems** – Treated with physiotherapy and occupational therapy  
- **Bladder or bowel issues** – Managed with medicine and lifestyle changes  
- **Speech or swallowing problems** – Treated with speech and language therapy  

Physical therapy and occupational therapy are key parts of care. They help prevent or reduce disability.

---

## What Is Life Like with MS?

Living with MS is challenging. The disease is long-term, and symptoms can affect daily life. Many people feel tired all the time or have trouble moving. This can make work, hobbies, and social life harder.

### Talking to Others

Many people find comfort in talking with others who have MS. Support groups help share experiences and coping strategies.

You can find support groups through the **National Contact and Information Point for Encouraging and Supporting Self-Help Groups (NAKOS)**.

### Staying Active and Eating Well

Even with MS, staying active is important. Regular physical activity and a healthy, balanced diet can improve energy and mood.

### Quitting Smoking and Reducing Stress

Smoking makes MS worse. Quitting is strongly advised. Support programs can help.

Stress can also make symptoms worse. Taking time to rest, relax, and know your limits can help.

### Regular Check-Ups

It is important to see your doctor regularly. This helps catch and treat other health problems early.

Conditions like being overweight, high blood pressure, type 1 diabetes, and high cholesterol can make MS symptoms worse.

---

## Where Can I Find More Information?

For more details on diagnosis and treatment, see the **Patient Guide to Multiple Sclerosis** by the German Neurological Society, published by the German Brain Foundation.

You can also visit the website of the **German Multiple Sclerosis Society, National Federation** for answers to common questions.

# Diverticulitis (Diverticular Disease)

## What Are Diverticula?

Diverticula are small pouches that form in the wall of the intestine.  
They happen when the inner lining of the intestine pushes through weak spots in the muscle layer.  
These pouches often look like small balloons.  
Stool can get stuck inside them.

Most of the time, diverticula do not cause any problems.  
But sometimes they lead to pain or other symptoms.  
This is called diverticular disease.

When the pouches become inflamed, it is called diverticulitis.  
Inflammation is caused by bacteria.  
It can be treated with antibiotics.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## Types of Diverticular Disease

There are three main types:

- **Diverticulosis**: Pouches form in the intestine.  
  They do not cause symptoms.  
  Most people do not know they have them.

- **Diverticular disease**: The pouches cause symptoms like pain, bloating, or changes in bowel habits.

- **Diverticulitis**: The pouches are inflamed.  
  This causes sudden, strong pain and other signs of infection.

If symptoms last for a long time, it is called chronic diverticular disease.  
Diverticulitis can usually be treated well.  
But if the infection spreads, it can become serious.

---

## How Do You Know If You Have Diverticula?

Most people with diverticula feel no symptoms.  
When symptoms do occur, they often affect the lower left side of the belly.  
Rarely, they happen on the right side.

Common symptoms include:
- Belly pain
- Bloating
- Constipation
- Diarrhea

Pain often gets worse after eating.  
It may improve after a bowel movement.  
Some people also have bleeding from the rectum.

When diverticulitis is present, symptoms are more severe:
- Sudden, dull pain in the belly
- Mild fever
- Constipation or diarrhea
- Bloating
- Nausea
- Cramps (less common)
- Vomiting (rare)

During a physical exam, the doctor may press on the belly.  
If the muscles tense up in response, it is a sign of inflammation.  
When the pressure is released suddenly, the pain may get worse.

---

## What Causes Diverticulitis?

Diverticula form where the intestine is weak.  
They most often appear in the sigmoid colon — the S-shaped part of the lower intestine.  
This area has the highest pressure from stool pushing against the wall.

Some people are more likely to get diverticula because of their genes.  
The condition is more common in older adults and in people who are overweight.  
Other risk factors include weak connective tissue and poor bowel movements.

A diet low in fiber may increase the risk.  
Fiber helps keep stool soft and easy to pass.  
Without enough fiber, stool can become hard and cause more pressure in the intestine.

Other possible risk factors:
- Eating too much red meat
- Smoking
- Not getting enough physical activity

It is not fully clear why some people get diverticula and others do not.  
One theory is that poor blood flow and hard pieces of stool in the pouches may play a role.

---

## How Common Is Diverticulosis?

Many people have diverticulosis without knowing it.  
The chance of having diverticula increases with age.

- About 10% of people under 50 have them.
- About 50% of people over 70 have them.

Men and women are equally likely to develop diverticulosis.

Out of every 100 people with diverticulosis, about 1 will develop diverticulitis within 10 years.  
Inflammation can happen at any age.

---

## How Can You Prevent Diverticulitis?

You can take steps to reduce your risk of symptoms or inflammation.

- Eat more fiber.  
  Good sources include whole grains, vegetables, beans, and fruits.  
  Fiber helps keep stool soft and easy to pass.

- Stay active.  
  Exercise helps your digestion and bowel movements.

There is no strong proof that these steps prevent symptoms.  
But they are still good for your overall health.

Some older advice said to avoid nuts, seeds, corn, and popcorn.  
The idea was that small pieces could get stuck in the pouches and cause inflammation.  
But recent studies show this is not true.  
You do not need to avoid these foods.

---

## How Is Diverticulosis Diagnosed?

Your doctor will start by asking about your health history and medicines.  
They will do a physical exam.  
They will feel your belly and listen to your intestines.

They may also:
- Take a blood test
- Test your urine
- Check your temperature

An ultrasound of the belly is usually done next.

If the diagnosis is still unclear, your doctor may order:
- A CT scan (computed tomography)
- A colonoscopy (a test that looks inside the large intestine)

During the exam, the doctor checks for other conditions that can cause similar symptoms.  
These include:
- Irritable bowel syndrome
- Appendicitis

A colonoscopy should not be done while you are having an active case of diverticulitis.  
Wait four to six weeks after symptoms go away.  
This test helps rule out polyps or colon cancer.

---

## How Is Diverticulitis Treated?

If diverticula do not cause symptoms, no treatment is needed.

The treatment depends on how severe the condition is.

Goals of treatment:
- Stop infection from spreading
- Ease pain and other symptoms
- Prevent future flare-ups
- Help with long-term symptoms

**Antibiotics** are used to treat diverticulitis.  
They work because the inflammation is caused by bacteria.

If symptoms do not improve with antibiotics, or if you have ongoing problems, surgery may be needed.  
The surgeon removes the damaged part of the colon.  
This is a major operation and carries risks.  
It is only done when necessary.

Surgery is always needed if there are serious complications, such as:
- Peritonitis (infection in the belly cavity)
- A hole in the intestine

For long-term symptoms, a high-fiber diet may help.  
The effect of probiotic foods (like yogurt) is not fully clear.

New research shows that antibiotics and surgery are not needed as often as once believed.

For more information on treating acute diverticulitis, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

# Bursitis

Bursitis happens when a bursa gets too much pressure.  
This causes pain and swelling.  
It often affects the knee or elbow.

## Quick Facts

- Bursae are small, fluid-filled sacs in the body.  
- There are over 100 bursae in the body.  
- Many are near the joints.  
- Bursitis can make movement hard.  
- It can be very painful.  
- It often happens when a bursa is under too much pressure.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor.  
> Do not use this to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Bursitis?

Bursitis comes from the word *bursa*, which means “bag” in Latin.  
It can cause pain and limit movement.  
It happens when a bursa gets too much pressure.

Bursae are small, fluid-filled sacs made of tough tissue.  
They act like cushions where bones rub against skin or other tissues.  
For example, when you rest your elbows on a hard table, the bursae protect the bones.  
There are over 100 bursae in the body.  
They are often found around joints.

Bursitis can also be caused by an infection.  
Most often, this is due to bacteria.

## What Are the Symptoms?

When a bursa becomes inflamed, it holds more fluid than normal.  
This causes swelling.  
Doctors call this extra fluid buildup an effusion.

The swollen area is easy to see or feel.  
It is especially painful when you move it.  
It also hurts when you press on it.  
The skin may look red.  
It may feel warm to the touch.  
You might also have a fever.  
You may feel generally unwell.

## What Causes Bursitis?

Bursitis often starts after an injury.  
For example, a hard hit or fall.  
It can also happen from repeated rubbing or pressure.

This is why people in certain jobs are more likely to get bursitis.  
Tilers who kneel on hard floors often get bursitis in the knee.  
Cleaners, carpenters, roofers, and gardeners are also at higher risk.  
Sports like volleyball can increase the risk.  
Sitting at a desk for long periods can also lead to bursitis.

Bursitis can also happen if bacteria enter the bursa.  
This often follows an injury.  
But doctors are not always sure how the bacteria got in.

Sometimes, long-term health problems like gout or rheumatic fever can cause bursitis.

## How Common Is Bursitis?

Every year, at least 1 in 10,000 people get bursitis in the knee or elbow.  
One third of bursitis cases are caused by bacteria.

Bursitis is most common in middle-aged men.  
This may be because they are more likely to do jobs that cause bursitis.

In many cases, the swelling goes down in two to three weeks.  
This only happens if you rest the area.  
But if you keep doing the same activity, the problem can last forever.

Long-term health issues like diabetes or rheumatic fever can slow healing.  
They can also make the inflammation worse.

## How Is Bursitis Diagnosed?

If the bursa is close to the skin, doctors can often see the problem right away.  
The area will be swollen, tender, and painful.  
The skin may be red or warm.

Bursitis is most common in the knees, elbows, feet, shoulders, and hips.

Doctors need to check if the cause is an infection.  
Signs of infection include a fever or a wound near the swollen area.

To test for infection, the doctor will use a thin needle to draw fluid from the bursa.  
They will send this fluid to a lab for testing.

Blood tests can also help.  
They can show if the bursitis is due to a condition like gout.

Imaging tests like ultrasound, X-rays, or other scans can rule out other problems.  
They can also show if the bursitis has damaged nearby tissue.

## How Is Bursitis Treated?

The main treatment is to rest the affected area.  
Avoid any activity that puts more pressure on it.  
This helps the bursitis heal.

You can use cool compresses to reduce swelling.  
Painkillers can help with pain.

Once the swelling goes down, avoid overusing the area.  
This helps prevent it from coming back.

People who work on the floor can use knee pads.  
An occupational therapist or workplace health expert can give advice on other helpful steps.

If the bursitis does not improve, or keeps coming back, a doctor may inject cortisone into the bursa.  
If the bursa stays inflamed, it may need to be removed in surgery.

If the bursitis is caused by a bacterial infection, antibiotics are usually enough.  
If not, surgery is often needed quickly.  
Cortisone is not used for bacterial bursitis.  
It can make the infection worse.

If bursitis is caused by gout or rheumatic fever, other medicines may be needed.

For more detailed treatment advice, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Rare Types of Cancer – Simple Explanation

This guide explains rare types of cancer in clear, everyday language. It covers diagnosis, treatment, recovery, and support.

---

## What Are Rare Types of Cancer?

- A rare cancer affects fewer than 6 people out of every 100,000 each year.
- There are about 200 different rare types of cancer.
- Around one in four cancer patients has a rare type of cancer.

Cancer is called rare if:
- It affects only a small number of people.
- It starts in an unusual part of the body.
- It happens in unusual situations, like during pregnancy or in men with breast cancer.
- It occurs in people who are much younger or older than usual for that cancer type.

Some rare cancers are hard to treat because of other health problems. Doctors then create a plan just for that person.

If you are told your cancer is “rare,” ask your doctor what they mean. This can help you understand your situation better.

---

## What Symptoms Can a Rare Cancer Cause?

- There is no single symptom that means you have a rare cancer.
- Symptoms depend on where the tumor is in your body.

For example:
- A tumor near the skin may feel like a painless lump or bump.
- If it grows, it may press on nerves or tissues and cause pain or tightness.
- A tumor inside the body may not cause any symptoms at first.
- It may only cause problems when it grows into nearby organs or tissues.

If you have swelling, pain, or discomfort that lasts more than four weeks, see a doctor.

You can start with your family doctor or a specialist, depending on where the problem is. The doctor will check your symptoms and decide what to do next.

---

## What Causes Rare Types of Cancer?

- Cancer starts when a single cell in your body changes in a way that makes it grow out of control.
- This leads to a tumor.
- If the cancer spreads into nearby tissues or travels to other parts of the body, it is called invasive or malignant.

Most of the time, doctors do not know exactly why this happens.

It may be due to:
- Age (chance increases with age).
- Lifestyle choices like smoking, poor diet, or lack of exercise.
- Exposure to harmful substances in the environment.
- Inherited genes from your parents.

**Important:** Living a healthy life helps lower your risk. This includes:
- Exercising regularly.
- Eating a balanced diet.
- Avoiding known cancer risks.

But even a healthy lifestyle does not guarantee you will never get cancer.

---

## How Is a Rare Cancer Diagnosed?

Diagnosing a rare cancer can be hard because there are so many types and they can appear in many places.

A correct diagnosis is very important. It helps doctors choose the best treatment.

If you think you might have cancer, go to a center that specializes in treating cancer in your body area.

These centers have teams of experts who work together. The team usually includes:
- Doctors who treat cancer (oncologists).
- Surgeons.
- Lab experts (pathologists).
- Doctors who use imaging (radiologists).
- Radiation therapists.

To make a diagnosis, doctors may:
- Ask you about your health history and symptoms.
- Do a physical exam.
- Test your blood or urine.
- Use imaging tests like CT scans, MRI, ultrasound, or X-rays to see how far the cancer has spread.
- Take a small sample of tissue (biopsy) and examine it under a microscope.

If the lab finds the cancer might be rare, they may send the sample to a special reference lab. A second expert opinion can help confirm the diagnosis.

Want to learn more about diagnosis?  
Visit the website of the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## How Is a Rare Cancer Treated?

The first step is to know exactly what type of cancer you have.

Doctors also need to know:
- Is the tumor in one place only?
- Has it grown into nearby tissues?
- Has it spread to other organs (metastasized)?

This helps decide the best treatment.

### If the cancer is in one place and has not spread:
- The main goal is to remove the tumor completely, including the tissue around it.
- After surgery, you may also get chemotherapy or radiation therapy to lower the chance of the cancer coming back.

### If the cancer has spread to other organs:
- In some cases, surgery can still remove the main tumor and any separate spots of cancer.
- You may also need chemotherapy, radiation, or special drugs.
- Clinical trials may be an option.
- But often, curing the cancer is no longer possible.
- Then the focus shifts to slowing the cancer’s growth, preventing complications, and easing symptoms.
- This is called **palliative care**.
- The main goal is to help you live as well as possible.

### If the cancer is not limited to one area (like some rare blood cancers):
- Treatment may include chemotherapy, radiation, or special drugs.
- The goal is to stop the cancer from growing and to relieve symptoms.

For some rare cancers, doctors have clear treatment guidelines from clinical trials or published cases.

Some patients take part in clinical trials. These are research studies that test new treatments.

Your age, overall health, and other medical conditions also affect your treatment plan.

**Important:** Not all hospitals can treat rare cancers well. Ask your doctor if a specialized center is recommended.

Specialized centers have more experience and often offer clinical trials.

Going to a specialized center may require extra travel and cost. Talk to your health insurance provider ahead of time.

Want to learn more about treatment and how to find a specialized center?  
Visit the website of the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## How Do You Recover After Cancer Treatment?

Cancer treatment can be long and exhausting.

After treatment, you may benefit from rehabilitation (rehab). This helps you get back to your daily life.

Rehab can include:
- General programs to rebuild strength and energy.
- Personalized plans based on your needs. For example:
  - Help with movement problems (orthopedic).
  - Support after gynecological treatment.
  - Care for nerve or brain-related issues (neurological).
  - Help with bladder or kidney problems (urological).
- Advice on how you can help your recovery through:
  - Healthy eating.
  - Exercise and sports.
  - Complementary therapies (like acupuncture or massage).

What is medical, professional, and social rehab? Who can get it?

Find more information on the **German Cancer Research Center’s Cancer Information Service** website.

---

## What Happens After Treatment? (Follow-Up Care)

After treatment ends, you will need regular check-ups.

The type and frequency of follow-up care depend on:
- The kind of cancer.
- Where it was in your body.
- The treatment you received.

Follow-up care focuses on:
- Finding and treating side effects from treatment.
- Checking for new problems that may appear after treatment ends.
- Looking for signs that the cancer has returned (relapse).
- Watching for new cancers (secondary tumors).

You will be seen by your doctor regularly at first, then less often over time.

During visits, your doctor will:
- Ask about your symptoms.
- Do a physical exam.
- Order blood tests and sometimes urine tests.
- Use imaging tests (like CT or MRI) if needed.

Talk to your doctor about how often you need to come back and which tests are necessary.

If the cancer cannot be cured, regular check-ups help catch problems early. You and your doctor can discuss new treatment options and support services. The goal is to keep your quality of life as high as possible.

---

## What Is Life Like with a Rare Cancer?

Many people want to stay active during and after treatment.

Here are some ways to help manage your health and well-being:

- Stay as active as your body allows. Movement can help reduce tiredness and weakness.
- Eat a balanced, healthy diet. This can prevent poor nutrition.
- Get support for your mental health. Talking to a counselor can help if you feel anxious or overwhelmed.

---

## Where Can You Get Help and Support?

Treating rare cancers often involves doctors from many different fields.

But not all centers that treat rare cancers are officially certified. There may be only a few such centers in Germany for some rare cancers.

### How to Find a Treatment Center

Use the **Health Care Atlas for People with Rare Diseases** (Versorgungsatlas für Menschen mit seltenen Erkrankungen).  
This online tool helps you find:
- Care facilities.
- Reference centers.
- Support groups.

You can search by:
- Typing “cancer” or the name of your cancer type.
- Looking for centers across Germany.

This tool was made by partners in the **National Action Plan for People with Rare Diseases** (NAMSE). It covers all rare diseases, not just cancer.

At the European level, use the **RARE CANCERS EUROPE** network to find centers (information in English).

Want more help with daily life and support?  
Visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## Need More Help?

You can contact the **Cancer Information Service** directly:
- Call the free phone number: **0800 420 30 40**
- Email: **krebsinformationsdienst@dkfz.de**

They can answer your questions about rare cancers.

# Canker Sores (Aphthous Ulcers)

Canker sores are very common in the mouth.  
They start with a tingling or burning feeling.  
Then they become painful.  
The sores are creamy-white with a red edge.  
They usually go away on their own.  
Gels, creams, or mouth rinses can help with the pain.

---

## Quick Facts

- Canker sores are open sores inside the mouth.  
- They are not contagious.  
- They are usually painful but heal without problems.  
- Some people get them again after a few weeks.  
- Others may go months or years without another sore.  
- Doctors do not know what causes them.  
- So far, there is no way to prevent them.  
- Pain relief gels, creams, or mouth rinses can help.  

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Are Canker Sores?

Many people get canker sores from time to time.  
They are open sores inside the mouth.  
The sores are creamy-white with a red border.  
You often get two to four sores at once.  
They hurt, but they usually heal on their own.  
Some people get them again soon after.  
Others may not get another one for months or years.

The exact cause is still unknown.  
That means we cannot yet stop them from happening.  
Pain relief gels, creams, or mouth rinses can help.  
If the sores are very large or do not heal, see a doctor or dentist.

See a doctor or dentist if you also have:  
- Bad breath  
- Swollen glands in the neck  

These could be signs of another health problem.  
The doctor or dentist will check to see if something else is causing the sores.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Canker sores usually appear as round, creamy-white spots.  
They show up on the lips or inside the cheeks.  
They are less common on the roof of the mouth, gums, or tongue.

The main symptom is pain.  
Before the sore appears, the area may tingle or burn.  
It may feel raw.

Certain foods can make the pain worse.  
These include:  
- Crusty bread  
- Sour fruits  
- Spices  

Chewing and talking can also hurt more.

Canker sores are usually small.  
They are a few millimeters wide.  
They are slightly sunken.  
They have a red, raised edge.

There are three types:

- **Minor canker sores:** Small sores. These are the most common.  
- **Major canker sores:** Larger sores, between one and three centimeters.  
- **Herpetiform canker sores:** Many tiny sores, like pinheads. These are rare.

---

## What Causes Canker Sores?

No one knows exactly why some people get canker sores and others do not.  
Experts think genetics may play a role.  
Other possible causes include:  
- Stress  
- A weak immune system  
- Hormone changes  

These same factors may cause sores to come back after a long break.  
Low levels of iron or vitamin B may also trigger them.  
Injury to the inside of the mouth can cause a sore too.

Some diseases can cause mouth sores that look like canker sores.  
These include:  
- Crohn’s disease  
- Ulcerative colitis  
- Behçet’s disease (a rare condition affecting blood vessels)

---

## How Common Are Canker Sores?

Canker sores are one of the most common mouth problems.  
Experts think about 1 in 10 people get them.  
We do not know how many people have recurring sores.

Most people first get canker sores as teens or young adults.  
Women are more likely to get them than men.

Types of canker sores:

- 85% are minor sores  
- 10% are major sores  
- 5% are herpetiform sores

---

## How Do Canker Sores Develop?

You may feel tingling or burning in the mouth.  
This happens in the first few hours.  
The area turns red and swells.  
It becomes painful.

Over one to three days, the swelling turns into a small pit.  
It has a creamy-white center.  
The pain starts to go down after a few days.  
The sore usually disappears in about one week.

Major canker sores last longer and hurt more.  
They can take up to four weeks to heal.  
They may leave a scar.

Most people get canker sores 3 to 6 times a year.  
Some go years without another one.  
The time between sores tends to get longer with age.

Severe cases are rare.  
In these cases, sores may last much longer.  
They can be so painful that eating or drinking is hard.  
Some people also get sores on the genitals.

---

## How Are Canker Sores Diagnosed?

Doctors or dentists can usually tell if you have a canker sore just by looking.  
The signs are very typical.

See a doctor or dentist if:  
- The sore does not heal in two weeks  
- The sore is very large or very painful  

They will examine your mouth.  
They may ask about your diet and symptoms.

If another illness might be causing the sores, they may do tests.  
These could include:  
- A swab from the sore  
- A blood test  
- A small tissue sample  
- Tests of organs like the bowel

---

## How Are Canker Sores Treated?

Most canker sores go away on their own.  
You do not need treatment.

To ease the pain:  
- Use pain-relief gels or creams  
- Rinse your mouth with special mouth rinses  

Only use stronger treatments like laser therapy or anti-inflammatory tablets in severe cases.

For more information on treatment, visit: [gesundheitsinformationen.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformationen.de)

# Surfer’s Eye (Pterygium)

## What is Surfer’s Eye?

Surfer’s eye is a growth of tissue on the clear surface of the eye.  
This surface is called the conjunctiva.  
The growth often looks like a cloudy white patch.  
It usually starts in the inner corner of the eye, near the nose.  
It can grow slowly over time.

The name “surfer’s eye” comes from the fact that it often affects people who spend a lot of time in bright sunlight.  
It is also called a pterygium.  
The word “pterygium” means “wing” in Greek.  
This is because the growth often has a triangle shape, like an insect’s wing.

Doctors do not know the exact cause.  
But they believe strong sunlight is the main reason.  
The condition is more common in warm, sunny places.  
It may also be linked to wind, dust, or dry air.

Some research suggests a link to certain types of human papillomavirus (HPV).  
These viruses can cause warts or changes in the cervix.  
People who have had HPV may be more likely to develop surfer’s eye.

## What Are the Symptoms?

In most cases, surfer’s eye causes no symptoms.  
You may not feel any pain or discomfort.  
But the growth can be hard to ignore because it changes how the eye looks.

Some people feel like something is stuck in their eye.  
It may feel dry, itchy, or irritated.  
The eye may look red.  
Rubbing the eye can make it worse.

The growth may make it harder to wear contact lenses.  
It can also cause blurry or distorted vision.  
This happens if the growth spreads onto the front of the eye, called the cornea.

If the growth changes the shape of the cornea, it can cause astigmatism.  
Astigmatism means the eye cannot focus light properly.  
This leads to blurry or fuzzy vision.

## What Causes Surfer’s Eye?

The main cause is long-term exposure to strong sunlight.  
UV rays from the sun may trigger the growth of extra tissue on the eye.  
This is why the condition is more common in sunny, tropical, or southern regions.

Wind, dust, and dry air may also play a role.  
Some studies suggest that certain viruses, like HPV, may increase the risk.

## How Does Surfer’s Eye Develop?

Most people with surfer’s eye do not have symptoms.  
They may not even know they have it.  
The growth can stay small and harmless for years.

Over time, the growth may get bigger.  
It can start to affect tear production.  
This leads to dryness, irritation, and redness.

If the growth reaches the cornea, it can block light.  
This can cause vision problems.  
It can also change the shape of the cornea.  
This change can lead to blurry or distorted vision.

## How Can Surfer’s Eye Be Prevented?

Protect your eyes from strong sunlight.  
Wear sunglasses that block UV rays.  
Choose sunglasses with wide or wrap-around frames.  
They protect your eyes from the side as well.

Wear a wide-brimmed hat or a cap with a visor.  
This helps block sunlight from above.  
These steps can reduce your risk of developing surfer’s eye.

## How Is Surfer’s Eye Diagnosed?

A doctor can see surfer’s eye during a simple eye exam.  
The growth has a unique shape.  
It looks like a triangle or wing.  
This makes it easy to recognize.

An eye specialist may do a more detailed check.  
They will look at how big the growth is.  
They will also test your vision.  
This helps to see if the growth is affecting your sight.

## How Is Surfer’s Eye Treated?

If you have no symptoms, you may not need treatment.  
But you should have regular check-ups with a doctor.

If your eye feels dry or itchy, you can use eye drops.  
These are called lubricating eye drops or artificial tears.  
They help keep the eye moist and reduce irritation.

Use 1 to 2 drops in the affected eye 3 to 4 times a day.  
If you are sensitive to preservatives in the drops, ask your doctor for preservative-free drops.

For more severe inflammation, your doctor may prescribe anti-inflammatory medicine.  
This can be a steroid or a non-steroidal medicine.  
But these medicines can have serious side effects.  
They may cause eye infections, glaucoma, or cataracts.

If the growth is blocking your vision, surgery may be needed.  
The surgeon removes the growth from the eye.  
But there is a high chance it will grow back later.

## Important Notes

This information is for general knowledge only.  
It is not a substitute for medical advice.  
Do not use this to diagnose or treat yourself.  
Always talk to a doctor if you have concerns about your eyes.

# Corns

Corns are common on toes and the soles of the feet.  
They form where the skin gets constant pressure or rubbing.  
Most of the time, corns go away on their own if the pressure stops.  
You can help the skin heal by softening the corn and removing it carefully.

---

## Quick Facts

- Corns grow where the skin is often pressed or rubbed.  
- They often go away if you stop the pressure. For example, if you wear better-fitting shoes.  
- Corns can hurt, especially when standing or walking.  
- They usually form near bones under the skin.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Corn?

Corns are very common, especially in older adults.  
They happen when skin is pressed or rubbed over and over.  
At first, the skin gets thicker and forms a callus.  
If the pressure continues, the callus turns into a painful corn.  
Corns often appear on toes and the bottom of the feet.  
They usually go away if you stop the pressure.  
Soaking the skin can help soften it. Then you can gently remove the hard part.

Doctors call a corn a *clavus*.

---

## What Does a Corn Look Like?

Corns are often painful.  
A corn on the foot hurts when you stand or walk.  
It looks like a small, hard lump of skin.  
The center is usually hard and shiny, like a bird’s eye.  
This center is very sensitive to pain.  
Corns stand out because they are raised and yellowish or beige.  
Corns between the toes are often white.  
They are softer than other corns because moisture from between the toes makes them swell.

---

## What Causes a Corn?

Corns form when skin is pressed or rubbed again and again.  
This makes the outer layer of skin grow more cells.  
The skin gets thicker and has more keratin.  
Over time, a round or oval patch of hard skin forms.  
Corns usually form near bones.  
That’s why they are more common on hands and feet.  
Hands and feet are more likely to be pressed or rubbed.  
People with joint problems or foot shape issues are more likely to get corns.  
Their feet may carry more weight on certain spots.  
Bent toes can press against each other or rub against the inside of shoes.  
This can make the toes squeeze into tight shoes.

---

## How Common Are Corns?

Corns are very common.  
They are especially common in older people.

---

## How Does a Corn Develop?

If pressure or rubbing continues, the corn gets thicker and harder.  
The hard skin grows deeper into the skin.  
It can press on nerves and tissues.  
The center of the corn grows even harder and can feel like a thorn.  
This causes more pain and can lead to long-term inflammation.

---

## How Is a Corn Diagnosed?

Most people and doctors can tell a corn just by looking at it.  
If the hard lump is in a spot that gets pressure or rubbing, it is likely a corn.  
Corns can look like warts, but they are different.  
Warts often have small brown dots on them.  
Corns have a hard, glassy center.  
This helps tell them apart.

---

## How Is a Corn Treated?

The most important step is to stop the pressure and rubbing.  
For example, switch to shoes that fit well and are not tight.  
This often makes corns go away on their own.  
You can also use small, ring-shaped pads.  
These protect the area from pressure and rubbing.  
Insoles in your shoes can help if foot shape causes pressure.  

Soak your feet or hands in warm water to soften the skin.  
After soaking, gently rub off some of the hard skin with a pumice stone.  
Do not use sharp tools like razors or callus shavers.  
They can cause cuts and infections.

People without other skin problems can use creams or patches with urea or salicylic acid.  
These help remove the thick skin.

> **Important:** If you have diabetes or poor blood flow in your feet, do not try to treat corns yourself.  
> You are at higher risk of injury and slow healing.  
> See a medical foot specialist (podiatrist) for safe removal.

For more details on treating corns, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

# Acute Appendicitis

The appendix is a small pouch attached to the first part of the large intestine. When it becomes inflamed, it causes serious health problems. This condition is called appendicitis.

## What You Need to Know at a Glance

- The most common signs of appendicitis are:
  - Belly pain
  - Nausea
  - Vomiting
  - High fever

- Appendicitis happens when the appendix swells and becomes infected.

- The most common and best treatment is surgery to remove the appendix.

- If left untreated, the appendix can burst. A burst appendix can lead to life-threatening infections or serious blood problems.

> **Important Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical care. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always see a doctor if you think you have appendicitis.

---

## What Is Appendicitis?

The appendix is a small tube that sticks out from the large intestine. When it gets inflamed, it can cause severe pain and other serious symptoms.

Inflammation can lead to pus building up inside the appendix. If the wall of the appendix breaks, the infection can spread into the belly. This is dangerous and can be life-threatening.

Because of this risk, doctors usually treat appendicitis quickly with surgery.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Appendicitis often starts with pain near the belly button or in the upper belly.

Later, the pain usually moves to the lower right side of the belly. It becomes sharp and severe.

Other common symptoms include:

- Loss of appetite
- Nausea and vomiting
- Constipation or sometimes diarrhea
- High fever

Some people do not have typical symptoms:

- Pregnant women often feel pain in the upper belly.
- Children and older adults may only have mild pain.

The appendix is not always in the same place. Sometimes it is behind the intestines or deep in the pelvis. This can cause pain in unusual spots or discomfort when urinating.

The longer the symptoms last, the higher the chance the appendix will burst.

> **Warning sign:** If the belly feels very hard or you are bent over because of pain, this could mean the appendix has burst. This is an emergency. Go to the hospital right away.

---

## What Causes Appendicitis?

The appendix has a small opening. If this opening gets blocked, the appendix swells up. This cuts off blood flow. The tissue in the wall of the appendix dies. Bacteria from the intestines then cause infection and inflammation.

The infection can eat through the wall. This creates a hole. This is called a burst appendix.

When the hole opens, bacteria and pus can spread into the belly. This can cause a life-threatening infection.

In some cases, the body walls off the burst area. This creates a pocket of pus called an abscess.

### Why Does the Appendix Get Blocked?

The appendix has a strong local immune system, especially in young people. If it is triggered by an infection, the lining swells and blocks the opening.

In older people, the immune system in the appendix weakens. Blockages are more likely due to:

- Hardened stool (fecal matter)
- Changes in the intestinal wall
- Rarely, worms or tumors

---

## How Common Is Appendicitis?

Appendicitis is one of the most common reasons for emergency surgery worldwide.

It can happen at any age, but it is most common in people between 10 and 19 years old.

About 1 in every 1,000 people gets appendicitis each year.

- Men and boys have about a 9 percent chance of getting it in their lifetime.
- Women and girls have about a 7 percent chance.

---

## How Does Appendicitis Progress?

Sometimes the inflammation goes away on its own. But if it gets worse, several things can happen:

- **Uncomplicated appendicitis:** The appendix is inflamed but has not burst. This is the most common form.

- **Burst appendix:** A hole forms in the appendix wall. This lets pus, stool, and bacteria leak into the belly. This causes a serious infection called peritonitis. Signs of a burst appendix include:
  - A hard belly
  - Bending over to protect the belly
  - Pale skin
  - Fast heartbeat
  - Feeling dizzy

- **Abscess or phlegmon:** If the hole is small, the body may trap the infection. This forms a pus-filled lump (abscess) or a swollen area of tissue (phlegmon).

---

## How Is Appendicitis Diagnosed?

Doctors start by checking your belly. They press on different areas to see where it hurts.

Pain when pressing on the lower right side of the belly is a strong sign of appendicitis.

But many other conditions can cause similar pain, such as:

- Inflammation in other parts of the intestines
- Bladder infections
- Problems with the reproductive organs

Because no single sign confirms appendicitis, doctors often do more tests:

- **Blood test:** Checks for signs of infection in the blood.
- **Ultrasound:** Looks at the appendix and checks for swelling or pus.
- **CT scan or MRI:** Gives a detailed image of the belly. Helps confirm appendicitis and rule out other causes.
- **Laparoscopy:** A small camera is used to look inside the belly. This is done only in some cases.

---

## How Is Appendicitis Treated?

The most common and effective treatment is surgery to remove the appendix.

There are two types of surgery:

- **Open surgery:** A single cut is made in the belly.
- **Laparoscopic surgery:** Several small cuts are made. A camera and tools are inserted through them.

If an abscess has formed, the surgeon will drain the pus and remove the abscess.

The timing of surgery depends on how serious the case is and whether the person is stable. Surgery usually happens within 24 hours of diagnosis.

Before surgery, you will get antibiotics to stop the infection from spreading. You may also get pain relief medicine.

In some cases, doctors can treat uncomplicated appendicitis with antibiotics instead of surgery. But this does not always work. In about 20 out of 100 people, the inflammation comes back.

For more information about surgery to remove the appendix, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Lyme Disease – Simple Explanation

Lyme disease is an infection caused by bacteria.  
It spreads when a tick bites a person.  
In Germany, about three out of every 10,000 people get Lyme disease each year.

---

## Quick Facts

- Lyme disease is caused by bacteria.
- It spreads through tick bites.
- Removing a tick quickly lowers the risk of infection.
- A red rash that spreads in a ring shape can appear at the bite site.
- Flu-like symptoms like fever, headache, tiredness, or body aches may also happen.
- Doctors usually treat Lyme disease with antibiotics.
- In Germany, around three people in 10,000 get Lyme disease every year.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Lyme Disease?

Ticks live in forests, gardens, and grassy areas.  
They can carry bacteria that cause Lyme disease.  
The bacteria are called Borrelia.  
Lyme disease is also known as Lyme borreliosis.

The first sign is often redness and swelling around the bite.  
The bacteria can later spread to joints, nerves, or other organs.  
But most people do not have serious problems.

---

## Signs of Lyme Disease

The skin around a tick bite may turn red and itch.  
This is normal and not always a sign of Lyme disease.

But if redness appears days or weeks after the bite, it could be Lyme disease.  
A Lyme rash often grows outward in a circle.  
It usually gets bigger than five centimeters across.  
This rash is called erythema migrans or EM rash.

You may also get flu-like symptoms within six weeks of the bite.  
These include fever, headache, tiredness, or muscle pain.  
These symptoms can be signs of Lyme disease even without a rash.

If symptoms appear one or two weeks after a bite, it could be tick-borne encephalitis.  
But this is rare.

---

### Post-Lyme Syndrome – What Does It Mean?

Some people feel tired, have joint or muscle pain, or have trouble remembering things.  
These symptoms can start months or even years after a tick bite.

Some people and doctors think this is a delayed effect of a Borrelia infection.  
This is sometimes called post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome or “chronic Lyme disease.”  
But most experts do not accept “chronic Lyme disease” as a real medical condition.

These symptoms can happen even if a person was not bitten by a tick.  
Blood tests may also show no sign of infection.  
In such cases, the symptoms are likely due to another health issue.  
Many other conditions can cause similar symptoms.

---

## What Increases the Risk of Lyme Disease?

The chance of getting Lyme disease depends on:

- How long the tick stayed attached.
- The size and age of the tick.

Larger ticks are more likely to carry the bacteria.  
They are older and have fed on more animals.

Borrelia bacteria are found all over Germany.  
But the number of infected ticks varies by region.

Not every tick bite leads to infection.  
The bacteria live in the tick’s gut.  
The bacteria can only pass to a person after the tick has fed for a long time.

That is why removing a tick within 24 hours greatly reduces the risk.

---

## How Common Is Lyme Disease?

About 1 in 100 people who get bitten by a tick develop Lyme disease.  
In Germany, around three people in 10,000 get Lyme disease each year.

---

## How to Prevent Lyme Disease

Your risk depends on where you are and what you do outdoors.

Wear closed shoes when walking in tall grass or bushes.  
Wear long pants and long-sleeved shirts.  
Cover as much skin as possible.  
This makes it harder for ticks to attach.

Light-colored clothes help you see ticks more easily.  
Ticks may crawl on your body for hours before biting.  
Check your body soon after being outside.  
Remove any ticks you find.

Children often forget to check themselves.  
Help them.  
Ask someone to help you check hard-to-see areas like the back, neck, or scalp.

If you get a tick bite, watch for symptoms.  
If you feel sick, see a doctor.

> **Important:** Tick sprays (repellents) can help for two to four hours.  
> You must reapply them if you stay outside longer.

---

## How Is Lyme Disease Diagnosed?

If you have the typical ring-shaped rash, a doctor can often diagnose Lyme disease just by looking at it.  
Tell your doctor about the tick bite.

If the rash is not clear, a blood test may be done.  
This test checks for signs of Borrelia bacteria.

---

## How Is Lyme Disease Treated?

Lyme disease is treated with antibiotics.  
Treatment usually lasts two to three weeks.  
Most people get better without problems.

Sometimes, the first antibiotics do not work well.  
Then a different antibiotic may be needed.

Some people get better without antibiotics.  
But this increases the risk of serious problems later.

---

### Possible Long-Term Effects

If the bacteria spread in the body, you may feel burning pain near the bite.

About 3 out of 100 people develop neuroborreliosis.  
This means the infection reaches the brain or nerves.  
It can cause facial paralysis, nerve pain, or meningitis.

About 2 out of 100 people develop Lyme arthritis.  
This happens when the infection spreads to the joints.  
It causes pain, swelling, and stiffness.

Very rare complications include heart problems or long-term skin inflammation.

Both neuroborreliosis and Lyme arthritis can be treated with antibiotics.  
Most people recover fully.

---

## How to Remove a Tick

Remove the tick as soon as possible.

Use special tools like:

- Tick tweezers  
- Tick removal cards  
- Tick hooks  

These tools are designed to slide under the tick without squeezing it.

You can also use regular tweezers.  
But only if the tips bend inward.  
Flat-tipped tweezers can squeeze the tick.  
This may push bacteria into your body.

For more details, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## Where to Get Support

Self-help groups can help people with Lyme disease and their families.  
They offer information, advice, and a chance to share experiences.

You can find a group through the **National Contact and Information Point for Self-Help (NAKOS)** website.

# Bedsore (Decubitus Ulcer)

A bedsore is an open wound on the skin. It happens when pressure stays on one spot for too long. Bedsores can be very painful. They often happen to people who stay in one position for a long time, such as lying in bed or sitting in a chair.

## Quick Facts

- A bedsore is an open wound caused by constant pressure on the skin.
- It can hurt a lot and takes a long time to heal.
- Bedsores usually form over bones that are close to the skin.
- People with paralysis may not feel pressure or pain in the affected area.
- Moving the person regularly can help protect vulnerable spots.
- Special cushions or mattresses can reduce pressure.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is a Bedsore?

A bedsore is a break in the skin. It forms when pressure stays on the skin for too long. These wounds are often painful. They heal slowly.

People who are very weak, paralyzed, or unconscious may stay in one position for long periods. This increases their risk of getting a bedsore.

## What Causes Bedsores?

Bedsores usually form over bones that are close to the skin. Common places include:
- The tailbone
- The heels
- The hips
- The elbows
- The shoulder blades
- The back of the head

When a person lies or sits in one position, the weight of the body presses on the skin. This pressure cuts off blood flow. Without enough blood, the skin does not get oxygen or nutrients.

Over time, the skin gets thinner. In some cases, the skin dies. The open wound that forms is a bedsore. It hurts more if the person keeps lying or sitting on the sore.

## What Increases the Risk of Bedsores?

Most people feel when pressure is too strong on a part of their body.

But some conditions make it harder to feel pressure. This raises the risk of bedsores.

- People with paralysis may not feel pressure or pain in the affected area.
- People with long-term diabetes may not notice pressure on their skin.
- Poor blood flow makes the skin more vulnerable. This happens in people with narrowed blood vessels.
- Poor nutrition weakens the skin. This is a risk for people who are bedridden.
- Friction and pulling (shearing) can damage the skin. This can happen when a person is dragged across a bed sheet.
- If the skin stays wet from urine, stool, or sweat for hours, it can get irritated and damaged.

Once a bedsore has formed, it is more likely to return in the same spot. Prevention is key.

## How to Prevent Bedsores

People who must stay in one position for long periods should move or change position often. Even small movements help. This is true even if the person is only bedridden for a few days.

Use special cushions or mattresses to reduce pressure. These can help protect the skin.

Check vulnerable areas often. Look for early signs of pressure, such as redness or warmth. A mirror can help reach hard-to-see spots.

When moving someone at risk, avoid pulling or dragging them. This can cause friction and shearing.

Keep the skin moist if it is dry. Use moisturizer if needed.

Change diapers or pads quickly if the person has incontinence. Wet skin is more likely to break down.

Dehydration and poor nutrition weaken the skin. Drink enough fluids and eat a balanced diet.

For more details on prevention, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

## How Are Bedsores Diagnosed?

Some people can check their own skin for early signs of a bedsore. A mirror can help with hard-to-see areas.

People who cannot move much may not notice changes. They may need help from a caregiver or nurse to check the skin.

Common spots for bedsores are on the back, especially the buttocks and heels.

## How Are Bedsores Treated?

The treatment depends on how bad the bedsore is.

It is very important to stop pressure on the sore. Move the person regularly. Use cushions, special beds, or positioning aids.

There are many types of wound dressings. They keep the wound moist, protect it, and prevent infection. The dressing is changed regularly. The wound is cleaned during each change.

If the wound is deep, dead tissue may be removed. This is called debridement.

Pain relief can include:
- Local anesthetics
- Dressings with ibuprofen
- Proper body positioning

For mild to moderate pain, medicines like acetaminophen (paracetamol) or ibuprofen can help. If these are not enough, a doctor can prescribe stronger pain medicine.

For more information on treatment, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

## How to Reduce Risk in Daily Life

The more movement a person can do, the better. Caregivers should encourage movement as much as possible.

If you see redness, swelling, or a sore spot, relieve pressure right away. Show it to a doctor or nurse.

Bedsores can cause pain and emotional stress. People with bedsores need good medical and personal support.

Family members can learn how to move and position the person safely. Many health insurance and long-term care providers cover the cost of medical aids. These may include special beds or cushions.

Many cities have nursing care offices. They can answer questions about preventing bedsores.

# Cataract (Gray Star)

A cataract makes the lens inside your eye cloudy.  
This cloudiness blurs your vision.  
It feels like you are looking through fog or a dirty window.  
Some people notice only a small change in their sight.  
Others find their vision gets much worse over time.  
In the end, the only way to improve vision is through surgery.

---

## Quick Facts

- A cataract is a condition where the eye’s lens becomes cloudy.  
- Cloudy vision makes it hard to see fine details.  
- Some people have only mild vision problems. Others lose their sight quickly.  
- Doctors can remove the cloudy lens and replace it with a clear artificial one.  
- Cataracts mostly happen in people over fifty years old.

> **Important Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

---

## What Is a Cataract?

A cataract is a condition where the lens inside your eye gets cloudy.  
This cloudiness makes your vision blurry.  
You may not see small details clearly.  
The old name for this condition is “gray star.”

The name “gray star” comes from the gray color of the cloudy lens.  
People with severe cataracts may look like they are staring blankly.  
Not everyone has the same level of vision loss.  
Some people have only a little trouble seeing.  
Others lose their sight fast.  
How quickly the cataract gets worse depends on the type.

Most people get cataracts after age fifty.  
The chance of having a cataract goes up with age.  
About 20 out of every 100 people aged 65 to 74 have cataracts.  
In people over 74, more than half have cataracts.

Cataracts are the top cause of blindness in poorer countries.  
In wealthier countries, fewer people go blind because surgery can fix the problem.  
During surgery, the cloudy lens is removed.  
A clear artificial lens is put in its place.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Your vision gets worse slowly over time.  
The only symptom is blurry or foggy sight.  
There is no pain or other physical discomfort.  
Your vision always feels less sharp.  
It is like looking through a dirty window.

Colors may look duller.  
You may notice less contrast between objects.  
Some people become very sensitive to bright light.  
This can happen when driving at night or in strong sunlight.  
Driving becomes harder and more dangerous.  
You may also be more likely to trip or fall.  
Your ability to judge distances may get worse.

Sometimes, people who wear glasses notice they can see better without them.  
This happens because the cataract changes how your eye focuses.  
But this improvement does not last long.  
It is temporary and not a good sign.

---

## What Causes a Cataract?

About 90 percent of cataracts are caused by aging.  
Doctors call this age-related cataract or senile cataract.  
As you grow older, the lens in your eye slowly becomes cloudy.

Some people have a higher risk because of their family history.  
Cataracts can be present at birth, but this is rare.  
A baby can be born with a cataract if the mother had measles or rubella early in pregnancy.

Certain things may raise your risk of getting a cataract.  
These include:
- Long exposure to sunlight (especially UV rays)
- X-rays
- Smoking
- Diabetes

Eye infections or injuries can also cause cataracts.  
Eye surgery may lead to cataracts later.  
Long-term use of certain medicines, like cortisone, can increase the risk.

---

## How Does a Cataract Develop?

Your vision gets worse slowly over time.  
At first, you may notice you are more short-sighted.  
People who used to be long-sighted (far-sighted) may suddenly see better without glasses.  
This is only temporary.

As the cataract grows, your vision becomes more blurred and cloudy.  
If left untreated, a cataract can lead to blindness.  
But this does not have to happen.  
Both eyes are usually affected.  
One eye may get worse faster than the other.

Cataracts progress in different ways.  
Some people lose their sight quickly.  
Others have only mild problems for years.

There are three main types:

- **Cortical cataract:** Causes blurry vision and strong sensitivity to bright light.  
  This can make night driving very hard.

- **Posterior subcapsular cataract:** This type often affects younger people.  
  It gets worse fast.  
  The cloudiness starts at the back of the lens.

- **Nuclear sclerotic cataract:** This type mainly affects far-sightedness.  
  The center of the lens becomes cloudy.  
  Vision may stay clear for a long time.  
  This type usually gets worse slowly.

---

## Can Cataracts Be Prevented?

There is no proven way to prevent cataracts.  
But some steps may help lower your risk.

- Quitting smoking may reduce your risk.  
- Wearing sunglasses with UV protection can help if you spend a lot of time in the sun.  
- Long-term use of cortisone medicine may raise your risk.  
  Ask your doctor if you can switch to a different medicine.

Some products claim to prevent eye problems.  
But studies show that dietary supplements do not help prevent cataracts.

---

## How Is a Cataract Diagnosed?

Blurred vision can have many causes.  
Your eye doctor will check for other possible reasons first.  
They will ask about your symptoms and medical history.  
They will also do eye tests and exams.

The doctor uses a special light called a slit lamp.  
This tool lets them see inside your eye.  
They shine a thin beam of light into your eye.  
This helps them check the lens and other parts like the retina and vitreous.

The exam is painless and quick.

To see the back of your eye, the doctor may put drops in your eyes.  
These drops make your pupils wider.  
After the drops, your vision may be blurry.  
You may also be more sensitive to light.  
This effect lasts for a few hours.  
Do not drive for at least four to five hours after the exam.  
If you are unsure, it is best to avoid driving.

---

## How Is a Cataract Treated?

Some people can manage with glasses or contact lenses.  
These can help for a while, or even for many years.  
There is no medicine that can cure a cataract.

The only effective treatment is surgery.  
During surgery, the cloudy lens is removed.  
A clear artificial lens is put in its place.  
The surgery takes about 20 to 30 minutes.  
It is usually done as an outpatient procedure.  
You can go home a few hours after the operation.

Whether to have surgery depends on how much the cataract affects your daily life.  
Your doctor will also check if you have other eye problems.  
These could affect the surgery or recovery.

For more information about cataract surgery, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Vaginal Yeast Infection

A vaginal yeast infection is a common condition. It happens when yeast fungi grow too much in the vagina. This causes irritation and discomfort. Most women who get this infection are of childbearing age.

You can often treat it quickly with medicine you put in the vagina or apply on the skin.

---

## Quick Facts

- You may feel itching, burning, or notice unusual discharge.
- The skin around the opening of the vagina and the lips of the genitals may become red and swollen.
- Some women have no symptoms at all.
- The most common cause is yeast fungi, especially a type called Candida albicans.
- A short course of vaginal suppositories or creams usually clears the infection.
- In pregnant women, the infection may slightly raise the risk of early labor, miscarriage, or early birth.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Vaginal Yeast Infection?

A vaginal yeast infection is also called vaginal mycosis. It happens when yeast fungi grow too much in the vagina. This causes inflammation and irritation.

You may feel itching, burning, or notice a thick, white discharge. The skin around the vagina may become red and swollen. Some women have no symptoms.

Yeast fungi are normally present in small amounts in the vagina. But when the balance of good and bad microbes changes, the yeast can grow out of control.

Certain things make yeast infections more likely:
- Being pregnant
- Using birth control pills
- Having a weak immune system
- Taking certain medicines, like antibiotics or cortisone
- Having diabetes

In most cases, a short treatment with vaginal suppositories or creams is enough. Sometimes a single tablet helps.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Common symptoms include:
- Itching or burning in the vagina
- Pain during sex
- Pain when peeing
- A thick, white, crumbly discharge that looks like curdled milk
- Redness and swelling around the vaginal opening

Symptoms often get worse just before your period. If the infection spreads to the outer genitals, the lips of the vagina may become red and swollen.

---

## What Causes a Vaginal Yeast Infection?

The main cause is an overgrowth of yeast fungi, especially Candida albicans. These fungi are part of the normal balance in the vagina. But they can grow too much if the balance is disturbed.

Things that can cause this imbalance include:
- High levels of estrogen during pregnancy
- Birth control pills (they change hormone levels like pregnancy does)
- Diabetes or other health problems that weaken the immune system
- Antibiotics, cortisone, or other medicines
- Radiation or chemotherapy
- Stress
- Wearing tight or synthetic underwear
- Sweating a lot
- Using plastic-backed pads or panty liners
- Poor hygiene, like washing the inside of the vagina with soap or sprays

You can also get a yeast infection from a partner who has a fungal infection on the penis. This can happen during sex.

---

## How Common Are These Infections?

Vaginal yeast infections are very common. They are the second most common cause of vaginal irritation after bacterial infections.

About 75 out of every 100 women will have at least one yeast infection in their lifetime. Most are between the ages of 15 and 45.

Some women have no symptoms. Others have mild or severe symptoms. If you get infections often—more than four times a year—or if you have a weak immune system, you may need stronger treatment.

---

## How Does the Infection Progress?

If you scratch the itchy skin, you can damage it. This can let other germs enter and make things worse. The urethra (the tube you pee through) may also become inflamed.

Serious problems are rare. They usually only happen in people with very weak immune systems, such as those with cancer or AIDS. In these cases, the infection can spread and become more serious.

In pregnant women, yeast infections may slightly raise the risk of:
- Early labor
- Miscarriage
- Early birth

The baby can also get infected during delivery. This can cause:
- Mouth sores
- Diaper rash

> **Important:** Many women feel shy about genital health issues. But delaying treatment can make the infection last longer. It can also spread to a partner. It’s best to talk to your doctor and your partner if needed.

---

## How Can You Prevent Yeast Infections?

You do not need special prevention if you are healthy. But you can take steps to lower your risk:
- Avoid douching (washing inside the vagina) or using intimate sprays. These can harm the natural balance.
- Wear loose, cotton underwear.
- Avoid tight clothing and synthetic fabrics.
- Change out of wet clothes quickly after swimming or exercising.
- Use breathable pads or panty liners.
- Manage stress and keep your blood sugar under control if you have diabetes.

Some women take probiotics (good bacteria) to support the natural balance in the vagina. These come in pills or vaginal suppositories. But there is not enough strong evidence that they work.

Some women try home remedies like:
- Tea tree oil-soaked tampons
- Garlic
- Natural yogurt

But there is no good proof that these are safe or effective. They can cause irritation or allergic reactions.

Do not rinse your vagina. This can make the problem worse.

---

## How Is a Yeast Infection Diagnosed?

Your doctor can often tell you have a yeast infection by your symptoms and a quick exam. They will look at the vagina and check for redness, swelling, or discharge.

If they are not sure, they may take a small sample of vaginal fluid. They will test it for yeast fungi.

If you get infections often or have severe symptoms, your doctor may check for:
- Immune system problems
- Diabetes
- Other health issues

If you keep getting infections, your partner may also need to be checked.

---

## How Is a Yeast Infection Treated?

Most cases are treated with antifungal medicine. You can use:
- A cream applied to the outside of the vagina
- A suppository inserted into the vagina
- A single tablet taken by mouth

These medicines work well and usually clear the infection in a few days.

If you have:
- Very bad pain
- Frequent infections (more than four times a year)
- A weak immune system
- Are pregnant and have severe symptoms

Then you should see a doctor. They may prescribe stronger treatment.

You do not usually need to treat your partner unless they also have symptoms.

Some people use suppositories with live lactic acid bacteria (probiotics). But there is not enough proof that they help.

Home remedies like tea tree oil, garlic, or yogurt are not proven safe or effective. They may cause irritation or allergic reactions.

> **Never rinse your vagina.** This can make the infection worse.

---

For more information on how to feel better during a yeast infection, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Heart Attack

A heart attack happens when a blood vessel that supplies the heart gets completely blocked.  
This stops oxygen from reaching part of the heart muscle.  
Without oxygen, that part of the heart can die.  
This is very dangerous and can lead to death.  
Getting help quickly is essential.

## Quick Facts

- A heart attack happens when a heart blood vessel is fully blocked.  
- Without fast help, part of the heart can die.  
- In Germany, about 75 out of 100 people survive a heart attack.  
- Women often have mild or unusual symptoms.  
- This means heart attacks in women are often missed or not recognized.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical care.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is a Heart Attack?

A heart attack happens when a blood vessel that feeds the heart becomes completely blocked.  
This stops oxygen from reaching part of the heart muscle.  
If the blockage lasts too long, that part of the heart dies.  
This can be life-threatening.  
You must get medical help right away.

## What Are the Signs of a Heart Attack?

The main signs of a heart attack are:

- Pain in the chest  
- Trouble breathing  
- Feeling sick to your stomach  

Chest pain often starts suddenly or gets worse over time.  
It does not go away when you rest.  
It lasts more than five minutes.  
It can spread to one or both arms, the back, neck, or upper belly.

Other signs include:

- A heavy or tight feeling in the chest  
- Pain or numbness in the upper body that moves to the shoulder blades, neck, or jaw  
- Sweating  
- Pale or grayish skin  
- Feeling dizzy or faint  
- Feeling very weak or lightheaded  

Some women only have nausea, vomiting, or extreme tiredness.  
These symptoms can be easy to miss.  
This is why heart attacks are often not noticed in women.
