**Important:** If you or someone else has signs of a heart attack, call emergency services right away.  
Dial 112 and ask for an ambulance with an emergency doctor.  
Do not call a doctor on call or a standby doctor.  
If symptoms happen at night, do not wait until morning.  
Get help immediately.

For more information, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_

## What Causes a Heart Attack?

Most people who have a heart attack already have a condition called coronary heart disease.  
This disease causes chest pain or shortness of breath during physical activity.  
Some people have no warning signs at all.  
They only learn they have a heart problem when they have a heart attack.

Coronary heart disease happens when the blood vessels to the heart become narrow.  
This is due to a buildup of fat, cells, and other material on the inside of the vessel walls.  
This buildup is called plaque.  
Over time, the plaque hardens and narrows the blood vessel.

A heart attack can happen if a plaque suddenly breaks open.  
A blood clot can form at the break.  
If the clot is large enough, it blocks the blood vessel completely.  
This causes a heart attack.

## What Increases the Risk of a Heart Attack?

The same things that raise the risk of heart disease also raise the risk of a heart attack.  
These include:

- Smoking  
- Being very overweight  
- High cholesterol  
- High blood pressure  
- Diabetes  
- Getting older  

Both men and women are at risk.  
But women usually have heart attacks later in life than men.  
More women die from heart attacks than from breast cancer.

## How Can I Prevent a Heart Attack?

You can lower your risk by making healthy lifestyle choices:

- Stop smoking  
- Exercise regularly  
- Keep a healthy weight  
- Eat a balanced diet  

These steps help keep your heart and blood vessels healthy.

## How Is a Heart Attack Diagnosed?

The main test is an electrocardiogram, or ECG.  
It records the heart’s electrical activity.  
The ECG pattern helps doctors tell what kind of heart attack it is.

There are two main types:

- **STEMI** – The ECG shows a clear rise in a part of the curve called the ST segment.  
  This means a large area of the heart is damaged.  
  It is a serious type of heart attack.

- **NSTEMI** – The ECG does not show a rise in the ST segment.  
  This usually means a smaller area of the heart is affected.

## How Is a Heart Attack Treated?

The most important step is to call 112 right away.  
Ask for an ambulance with an emergency doctor.  
The blocked blood vessel must be opened as fast as possible.

- **For a STEMI:**  
  Doctors usually do a procedure called angioplasty.  
  A thin tube is guided to the blocked artery.  
  A small balloon is inflated to open the vessel.  
  A stent may be placed to keep it open.  
  This restores blood flow and oxygen to the heart.

- **For a NSTEMI:**  
  Treatment depends on the person’s symptoms, other health problems, and age.  
  Most people still get a cardiac catheter (angioplasty) to open the blocked artery.

After the emergency phase, further treatment helps prevent another heart attack.  
This may include medicines, lifestyle changes, and follow-up care.

# Ebola Virus Disease

Ebola virus disease is a serious illness that can be deadly. It has only ever happened in Africa. Scientists have now created vaccines and treatments that work well.

---

## Quick Facts

- Ebola is a virus that can cause death in 30 to 90 out of every 100 people who get it.
- So far, all Ebola outbreaks have happened in Africa. It is very unlikely to happen in Germany.
- You can catch Ebola through contact with infected animals, people, or things that have been touched by their body fluids.
- Two vaccines are now available and they protect against one type of Ebola virus.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Ebola Virus Disease?

Ebola virus disease, also called EVD or Ebola, is a dangerous infection caused by the Ebola virus. There are five known types of the virus: Zaire, Sudan, Tai Forest, Bundibugyo, and Reston.

All known outbreaks have happened in sub-Saharan Africa.

The virus spreads mainly from person to person. But it can also spread from animals to people.

Two vaccines are now available. They protect against the Zaire type of Ebola. Two medicines are also approved in the United States for treating this type of infection.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

At first, Ebola feels like the flu. You may have:

- A high fever
- Feeling very tired
- Body aches
- General feeling of being unwell

After a few days, you may also get:

- Pain in the upper belly
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Loss of appetite
- Diarrhea

As the disease gets worse, you may have:

- Headaches and chest pain
- Joint and muscle pain
- A skin rash
- Trouble swallowing
- Problems with thinking, balance, or seizures
- A slow heartbeat
- Bleeding inside or outside the body
- Trouble breathing

### After Recovery: Post-Ebola Syndrome

Some people still feel unwell after they recover. This is called post-Ebola syndrome. Symptoms can include:

- Feeling tired or sleepy
- Muscle and joint pain
- Body aches
- Trouble remembering things
- Hearing or vision problems
- Depression or anxiety

---

## How Do People Get Infected?

The Ebola virus lives in wild animals, especially certain kinds of fruit bats. When people hunt or handle these animals, they can get infected.

The virus spreads from person to person through body fluids.

### How It Spreads Between People

You can catch Ebola by touching someone who is sick with Ebola. You can also catch it from the body of someone who has died from Ebola.

The most dangerous fluids are blood, saliva, sweat, urine, feces, and vomit.

Only people who are showing symptoms can spread the virus. It usually takes 8 to 9 days after infection for symptoms to start. But it can take as few as 2 days or as long as 3 weeks.

The more sick a person becomes, the more likely they are to spread the virus.

Once a person’s symptoms go away, they are no longer contagious — but the virus can still stay in their sperm for several months. This means they can pass it on through sex.

### How It Spreads Through Objects

The virus can live on objects that have touched infected fluids. This includes:

- Needles
- Surgical tools
- Clothes
- Bed sheets

If these items are not cleaned properly, they can spread the virus.

### How It Spreads From Animals

You can get Ebola by touching infected animals or eating their meat. This often happens during hunting, butchering, or cooking wild animals called “bushmeat.” This kind of contact can start a new outbreak.

---

## When Is the Risk of Getting Ebola Highest?

You are at high risk if you are not vaccinated and you have direct, unprotected contact with:

- A person who is sick with Ebola
- The body of someone who died from Ebola
- The body fluids of a sick person or someone who died from Ebola (like blood, saliva, sweat, urine, feces, or vomit)

Because Ebola is so deadly, strict safety rules are followed when caring for sick people or handling the bodies of those who died.

The death rate is between 30% and 90%.

---

## Where Does Ebola Happen?

Ebola has only ever been seen in sub-Saharan Africa.

Outbreaks have happened many times in Central Africa since 1976. The most affected countries are:

- Democratic Republic of the Congo
- Gabon
- Republic of the Congo
- South Sudan
- Uganda

The biggest outbreak ever happened from 2014 to 2016. It mainly affected:

- Guinea
- Sierra Leone
- Liberia

It also reached Mali and Nigeria.

Some infected people were found in the United States and Europe during this outbreak. But the virus did not spread widely in those places.

> **Important:** The chance of an Ebola outbreak in Europe is very low. Germany has strong safety rules to stop the virus from spreading and to keep patients safe.

---

## How Does Ebola Progress in the Body?

Ebola infection happens in stages.

### Stage 1: Early Fever Phase

About 8 to 9 days after infection, symptoms start. These include:

- High fever
- Headache
- Body aches
- Extreme tiredness

Symptoms can start as early as 2 days or as late as 3 weeks after infection.

### Stage 2: Gastrointestinal Phase

A few days after symptoms begin, you may also have:

- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Diarrhea
- Pain in the upper belly

Some people also get:

- Eye irritation (conjunctivitis)
- Sore throat
- Hiccups
- Confusion (delirium)
- A rash

As the disease gets worse, bleeding can happen inside the body and outside. This often affects the gut, lungs, and gums.

### Stage 3: Recovery or Deterioration

Some people start to get better during this stage. Others get worse.

If the condition gets worse, fluid loss, bleeding, and organ failure can lead to death.

Between 30% and 90% of people infected with Ebola die.

> **Important:** We do not yet know how long immunity lasts after recovery. But experts believe it lasts for several years.

---

## How Can You Protect Yourself?

There are different types of Ebola virus. Right now, two vaccines are available. They only protect against the Zaire type. Both are approved in Germany.

One of the vaccines can be given to people who have been near someone with Ebola. If given quickly, it can help prevent infection.

> **Fun Fact:** Scientists are testing other vaccines for the other types of Ebola virus.

If you are not vaccinated, avoid:

- Touching sick people
- Touching the bodies of people who died from Ebola
- Touching their body fluids

Healthcare workers protect themselves by wearing protective gear and following strict hygiene rules.

---

## How Is Ebola Diagnosed?

Doctors test blood or other body fluids in a lab to check for Ebola.

A test called PCR can find parts of the virus in the blood.

It may take up to three days after symptoms start before the virus shows up in tests.

If an early test is negative, doctors may repeat the test later.

---

## How Is Ebola Treated?

In the United States, two medicines are approved for treating Ebola. They only work for the Zaire type.

Both medicines use lab-made antibodies. These are special proteins that can find and stop the virus. If given early, they can cure about 90% of patients.

These treatments are not yet approved in Germany.

If medicine is not available, or if the infection is caused by a different type of Ebola virus, doctors can only treat the symptoms.

The most important thing is to replace lost fluids, sugar, and salts. Patients are given fluids through a tube in the vein. These fluids contain salt, sugar, and water.

# Clostridioides difficile infection

Clostridioides difficile is a type of bacteria that lives in the intestines.  
It often does not cause any problems.  
But if the balance of good and bad bacteria in the gut is disturbed, it can cause serious issues.  
This can lead to inflammation in the intestines and diarrhea.  
Read on to learn how this happens and what treatments are available.

---

## Quick Facts

- Clostridioides difficile bacteria make harmful substances called toxins.  
- When they grow too fast, they can cause swelling and irritation in the intestines.  
- The main sign of infection is sudden, watery diarrhea.  
- In rare, very serious cases, the intestines can tear open.  
- Infected people can spread the bacteria through their stool.  
- This can happen when they touch things like doorknobs, hands, or clothes.  
- Most people get sick only if their gut bacteria are out of balance.  
- The most common cause of this imbalance is taking antibiotics.  
- Washing hands well is one of the best ways to stop the spread.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What is a Clostridioides difficile infection?

A Clostridioides difficile infection happens when these bacteria grow too much in the intestines.  
They release toxins that damage the lining of the gut.  
This causes inflammation and diarrhea.

---

## What are the symptoms?

The most common symptom is sudden, watery diarrhea.  
It usually smells bad.  
It is very rare to have this infection without diarrhea.  
Blood in the stool only happens in the most severe cases.

Other signs include:

- A high fever (in about one in three people)  
- Pain in the lower belly (in about one in five people)  
- Loss of appetite  
- Nausea  
- Vomiting

---

## What causes the infection?

People with a Clostridioides difficile infection often have diarrhea.  
They pass large amounts of the bacteria in their stool.  
This lets them spread the bacteria to others.

The bacteria form tough spores.  
These spores can live on surfaces for a long time.  
They can survive on doorknobs, bedrails, and toilet handles.

Healthy people with strong immune systems and good gut bacteria may carry the bacteria but not get sick.  
But if the gut bacteria are out of balance — for example, after taking antibiotics — the Clostridioides bacteria can take over.  
They then cause inflammation and diarrhea.

The toxins they make damage the cells in the gut lining.  
This leads to diarrhea.

If antibiotics caused the problem, diarrhea usually starts during treatment or shortly after.  
But sometimes it can start weeks or even months later.

> **Important:** Antibiotics kill harmful bacteria, but they also kill helpful bacteria in the gut and on the skin.  
> These helpful bacteria are part of the body’s natural microbiome.  
> They help protect the body from infections.

---

## Who is at higher risk?

The biggest risk factor is taking antibiotics.  
They upset the balance of good bacteria in the gut.  
This makes it easier for harmful bacteria like Clostridioides difficile to grow.

Other risk factors include:

- Being older  
- Having a long-term digestive problem  
- Having liver or kidney disease  
- Taking medicine that weakens the immune system  
- Receiving chemotherapy  
- Staying in the hospital for a long time

---

## How common is Clostridioides difficile?

- Up to 80 out of 100 small children have Clostridioides difficile in their intestines.  
- Most of them do not have any symptoms.  
- In adults, up to 5 out of 100 carry the bacteria without symptoms.  
- This number can rise to up to 40 out of 100 in people who are in the hospital.  
- Still, most of these people do not get sick.

Clostridioides difficile causes about 15 to 20 out of every 100 cases of diarrhea linked to antibiotics.  
On average, 1 out of every 100 people who take antibiotics gets a Clostridioides difficile infection.

---

## What is the outlook?

Not everyone with Clostridioides difficile gets sick.  
Some people have no symptoms.  
Others have mild gut irritation.  
But some people develop a very serious form of gut inflammation called pseudomembranous enterocolitis.

Serious complications can include:

- A dangerously swollen large intestine (toxic megacolon)  
- Blockage in the intestines (ileus)  
- Blood poisoning (sepsis)

Up to 5 out of every 100 people with the infection die.  
This is more common in older adults and those with other health problems.  
Complications make death more likely.

After treatment, the infection can come back.  
Up to 20 out of every 100 people get sick again later.

---

## How can the infection be prevented?

Most Clostridioides difficile infections happen in people who are taking or have taken antibiotics.  
So, antibiotics should only be used when truly needed.  
This also helps prevent antibiotic resistance.

In hospitals and care homes, the spread can be stopped by:

- Finding infected people quickly  
- Keeping them isolated  
- Treating them early

When caring for infected people, staff must follow strict hygiene rules.  
This includes wearing gloves and gowns.

Good hand hygiene is key — not just in hospitals, but in daily life.  
Wash your hands with soap every time you use the toilet and before eating.  
This protects you and others.

> **Important:** Wash your hands with soap for at least 20 to 30 seconds.  
> This is one of the most effective ways to prevent Clostridioides difficile and many other infections.

---

## How do doctors diagnose the infection?

To confirm a Clostridioides difficile infection, doctors usually test a stool sample.  
The lab checks for the bacteria or their toxins.

If the case is very serious, or the test result is unclear, doctors may start treatment right away — without waiting for the lab result.

---

## How is the infection treated?

Doctors prescribe special antibiotics for Clostridioides difficile.  
Common ones are vancomycin, fidaxomicin, and metronidazole.  
The choice depends on how severe the illness is and the patient’s age.

In very serious cases — like a hole in the intestine or a swollen large intestine — surgery may be needed.

> **Important:** Treatment is only needed if you have symptoms.  
> If you carry the bacteria but feel fine, you do not need treatment.

Other treatment options include:

- **Bezlotoxumab:** A medicine made in a lab. It blocks the toxins made by the bacteria.  
- **Stool transplant:** A healthy person’s stool is transferred into the patient’s intestines.  
  This helps restore good bacteria.  
  But it carries risks, like passing on other infections or causing side effects.

> **Interesting fact:** Stool transplants work very well for people whose infection keeps coming back.  
> They help up to 90 out of every 100 patients.

# Scabies

Scabies is a skin disease that spreads easily from person to person.  
It is caused by tiny mites that live in the skin.  
The female mites dig small tunnels in the top layer of the skin.  
They lay their eggs in these tunnels.  
The mites only live on human skin.  
They can move to other people during long, close skin contact.  
Scabies causes intense itching.  
This is why the mites are also called itch mites.  
The condition can be treated well with medicine.

---

## Quick Facts

- Scabies is a contagious skin disease caused by a type of mite called the scabies mite or itch mite.
- The female mites burrow into the skin and lay eggs in the tunnels they make.
- The body reacts to the mites by developing a rash.
- Severe itching is common, and it often gets worse at night.
- Scabies can be treated with creams or tablets.
- To avoid getting scabies again, all close contacts must be treated at the same time.
- A quick handshake or brief touch usually does not spread scabies.  
  But the longer and closer the skin contact, the higher the risk of infection.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Scabies?

Scabies is a skin disease caused by tiny mites.  
These mites are parasites that live only on human skin.  
They cannot survive on other animals or in the environment for long.  
The female mites burrow into the top layer of the skin.  
They lay eggs and leave waste in the tunnels they make.  
The body reacts to the mites and their waste.  
This reaction causes a rash.  
The rash is often itchy.  
The itching is usually worse at night.  
The word *scabies* comes from a Latin word meaning “to scrape.”  
Scabies can be treated with medicine.  
Most treatments are applied directly to the skin as creams.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

It can take 2 to 5 weeks after first contact for the rash and itching to appear.  
This is because the body needs time to react to the mites.  
But a person can spread scabies even before the rash shows up.  
If someone has had scabies before, the rash can appear in just a few days.  
This is because the body already knows how to react to the mites.

The main symptom is strong itching.  
It can affect the whole body.  
It often gets worse at night.  
The rash includes small bumps, blisters, and pus-filled spots.  
This rash is caused by the body’s immune system reacting to the mites.

The tunnels the mites make look like thin, raised lines on the skin.  
They are usually less than a centimeter long.  
They often look like a comma.  
They are hard to see without a magnifying glass.  
The mites themselves can only be seen with a microscope or a special tool called a dermatoscope.

These tunnels are often found in:

- Between fingers and toes  
- On ankles, wrists, and elbows  
- In the armpits, around the nipples, and near the belly button  
- In the groin and on the buttocks  
- On the penis  

In rare cases, especially in babies and young children, the rash can also appear on the head (if hair is present), face, palms, or soles.

People with weak immune systems may get a more serious form of scabies.  
This is called crusted scabies.  
It causes thick, scaly, red patches on the skin.  
In this form, the itching may be mild or even absent.

---

## How Do People Get Scabies?

Scabies spreads mainly through direct skin contact.  
The mites move very slowly.  
You need at least 5 to 10 minutes of close contact to get infected.  
This can happen during activities like hugging, sleeping together, or playing closely.  
A quick handshake or brief hug usually does not spread the mites.

An exception is crusted scabies.  
In this form, a person has millions of mites on their skin.  
Even brief skin contact or touching skin flakes can spread the disease.

There are other mites that affect animals.  
These are called mange mites.  
They can sometimes move to humans.  
But they do not survive long on human skin.  
They die quickly and do not multiply.  
The skin irritation they cause usually goes away on its own in a few days.

> **Important:** Scabies mites cannot live more than one or two days away from human skin.  
> They die within 10 minutes at 50 degrees Celsius.  
> This means washing clothes at high heat kills them.  
> Transmission through clothes or bedding is rare — unless someone has crusted scabies.

---

## How Common Is Scabies?

Scabies can affect people of all ages around the world.  
It is more common in children and sexually active adults with multiple partners.  
Older adults and people with limited mobility or weak immune systems are more likely to get a severe form called crusted scabies.

Outbreaks can happen in places where people live closely together.  
Examples include kindergartens, nursing homes, hospitals, shelters for the homeless, and prisons.

There are no official numbers for how many people in Germany have scabies.  
This is because doctors are not required to report cases.  
But studies suggest scabies affects hundreds of thousands of people in Germany each year.  
The number can change from year to year and from region to region.

---

## How Can Scabies Be Prevented?

Scabies often spreads before symptoms appear.  
This makes prevention hard in early stages.

But if someone is diagnosed with scabies, their close contacts should be checked.  
All of them should be treated at the same time.  
This helps stop the mites from spreading further.

If you must care for someone with scabies, wear long-sleeved clothes and disposable gloves.  
This protects your skin.

To stop mites from spreading through shared items:

- Wash the infected person’s clothes and towels every day at 50 degrees Celsius or higher.  
- Change bed sheets after treatment.  
- Vacuum furniture and carpets with a strong vacuum cleaner.

You can also store contaminated items in sealed plastic bags for at least 3 days at room temperature (21 degrees Celsius).  
This kills the mites.  
Alternatively, you can freeze items for 2 hours at minus 25 degrees Celsius.  
This works for regular scabies, but not for crusted scabies.

People with scabies or suspected scabies should not go to school, kindergarten, or work until treatment is complete.

---

## How Is Scabies Diagnosed?

A doctor can often tell if someone has scabies by looking at the skin and asking about symptoms.  
To confirm the diagnosis, the doctor may take a small skin sample.  
This is scraped from the skin and checked under a microscope.  
A special magnifying tool called a dermatoscope can also be used to see the mites directly on the skin.  
No lab tests are needed to diagnose scabies.

---

## How Is Scabies Treated?

Scabies is usually treated with medicine applied to the skin.  
Permethrin is the most common treatment.  
Other options include benzyl benzoate or crotamiton.  
In some cases, a tablet with ivermectin is used.  
But ivermectin should not be used in pregnant women or young children.

Most people are no longer contagious after the first full treatment.  
To be safe, a second treatment is recommended one week later.

After treatment, the itching usually goes away within 1 to 2 weeks.

In severe cases of crusted scabies, more treatments are needed.  
You must also avoid close contact with others for a longer time.

---

## More Information

The Robert Koch Institute (RKI) has a lot of useful information about scabies on its website.

# Rheumatic Heart Disease

This condition happens when the body’s immune system overreacts to a strep infection. It can damage the heart valves. The disease can usually be prevented with antibiotics.

---

## Quick Facts

- Rheumatic heart disease starts after an infection with strep bacteria.
- Strep bacteria cause sore throats and other throat infections.
- The immune system fights the bacteria but sometimes attacks the body’s own tissues by mistake.
- The heart valves are most often damaged.
- In Germany, doctors treat strep infections with antibiotics. This stops the disease from developing.
- In poorer countries, the disease is common. It can lead to heart failure and sudden death.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## How Common Is It?

- In Germany, the disease is now very rare.
- It mostly happens in places with weak health care systems.
- It also affects people who cannot easily get medical help.

---

## What Happens If Someone Gets It?

- The valve between the left upper and lower heart chambers often becomes narrow.
- The valve between the lower heart chamber and the main artery may not close properly.
- The heart must work harder to pump blood.
- At first, you may not notice any problems.
- After years, the heart muscle weakens.
- This can lead to heart failure. The heart can no longer pump blood well.
- Other problems include:
  - Irregular heartbeat.
  - Inflammation of the inner lining of the heart.
  - Blood clots in the heart.
  - Clots can travel to the brain and cause a stroke.

---

## How Can It Be Prevented?

- The best way to prevent it is to treat strep throat with antibiotics.
- If your doctor prescribes antibiotics, take them exactly as told.
- Finish the full course, even if you feel better.
- This stops rheumatic fever and prevents heart damage.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

- A doctor listens to your heart with a stethoscope.
- Abnormal sounds may mean valve problems.
- An ultrasound of the heart (echocardiogram) shows valve or muscle damage.
- A history of rheumatic fever is a strong clue.
- Blood tests can show if the heart muscle is inflamed.
- In the past, doctors took a small piece of heart tissue to check. This could cause side effects.
- Now, doctors often use imaging scans like MRI instead.

---

## What Is Rheumatic Heart Disease?

- It is a long-term result of a strep infection.
- Strep bacteria cause painful throat infections.
- Strep bacteria look similar to some of the body’s own cells.
- The immune system makes antibodies to fight the bacteria.
- After about two weeks, these antibodies may also attack the body’s own tissues.
- This causes rheumatic fever.
- Rheumatic fever can inflame the heart muscle, inner lining, outer lining, and especially the heart valves.
- Damaged valves do not close well.
- Over time, this leads to heart failure.
- In rare cases, heart failure can happen suddenly.

> **Fun Fact:** In other autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system can also attack the heart.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

- Many people do not notice symptoms for 10 to 20 years after having rheumatic fever.
- When symptoms appear, they may include:
  - Feeling your heart beat strongly or irregularly.
  - Feeling very tired.
  - Trouble breathing, especially when active.
  - Chest pain.
  - Fainting.
  - Swelling in the legs or ankles.

- You may also remember past episodes of:
  - Rheumatic fever.
  - Heart muscle inflammation.
  - Joint pain.
  - Nervous system problems.
  - Skin rashes.

---

## What Causes It?

- The disease is a late result of rheumatic fever.
- Rheumatic fever is caused by group A strep bacteria.
- The first sign is often a sore throat.
- Some people also get a red rash on the skin.
- The body makes antibodies to fight the bacteria.
- Because the bacteria look like body cells, the antibodies can attack the body by mistake.
- This causes inflammation.
- The heart is especially affected.
- The inner lining, outer lining, and heart muscle can become inflamed.
- The heart valves may be damaged.
- The damage does not heal.
- Over time, this leads to rheumatic heart disease.

---

## How Is It Treated?

- The main goal is to stop the disease from getting worse.
- Doctors give antibiotics long-term to prevent the immune system from reacting again.
- This helps protect the heart.
- **Important:** You can get strep bacteria without knowing it. Even a silent infection can trigger more damage.
- So, it is vital to keep taking preventive antibiotics as directed.

- If the heart valves are damaged, they may need repair or replacement.
- Surgeons can fix them during open-heart surgery.
- Or, they can use a thin tube (catheter) inserted through a small cut in the groin.
- The tube travels through a blood vessel to the heart.
- The method used depends on which valves are affected.

- If the heart muscle is inflamed, medicine helps the heart work better.
- Medicine also helps control the heartbeat.
- Limiting physical activity is an important part of treatment.

# Legionnaires’ Disease (Legionellosis)

Legionnaires’ disease is a serious lung infection caused by bacteria called Legionella.  
It can cause flu-like symptoms or lead to severe pneumonia.  
The bacteria live in water and spread through tiny water droplets in the air.  
You get infected by breathing in these droplets.

---

## Quick Facts

- Legionnaires’ disease is a lung infection caused by Legionella bacteria.  
- It can cause flu-like symptoms or serious pneumonia.  
- The bacteria grow in warm, still water.  
- Common sources include showers, hot tubs, and poorly maintained water systems.  
- You get infected by breathing in tiny water droplets.  
- Older adults and people with weak immune systems or long-term health problems are at higher risk.  
- If pneumonia develops, hospital treatment with antibiotics is usually needed.  

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Legionnaires’ Disease?

Legionnaires’ disease is a lung infection caused by Legionella bacteria.  
It can cause pneumonia, or it may not.  
The bacteria grow in warm, still water, like in pipes or water tanks.  
They spread into the air as tiny water droplets when water is sprayed or heated.  
These droplets are invisible to the eye.  
When you breathe them in, the bacteria can enter your lungs.

People at highest risk include:
- Older adults
- People with weak immune systems
- People with long-term health problems like diabetes, heart disease, or lung disease
- Smokers

There is also a milder form called Pontiac fever.  
It feels like the flu and usually gets better on its own in a few days.

**Fun fact:** The disease got its name from a 1976 event.  
Many older men at a veterans’ meeting fell ill with severe pneumonia.  
The source was a contaminated air conditioning system in the hotel.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

If you are infected with Legionella, you may have flu-like symptoms.  
This is called Pontiac fever.  
Symptoms usually start within 5 hours to 3 days after exposure.  
They include:
- Dry cough
- Headache
- Body aches

If the infection leads to pneumonia, it is called Legionnaires’ disease.  
Symptoms appear 2 to 10 days after exposure.  
They are much more serious and include:
- Sudden high fever and chills
- Feeling very unwell
- Trouble breathing
- Coughing up mucus

Other possible symptoms:
- Stomach pain
- Diarrhea
- Confusion

---

## How Does Legionella Spread?

You get Legionnaires’ disease by breathing in tiny water droplets that contain the bacteria.  
These droplets come from water systems like showers, hot tubs, or cooling towers.  
The bacteria are common in natural water sources like lakes and rivers.  
But they usually do not cause harm in nature.

The bacteria grow fast in warm, still water.  
This happens when water sits in pipes for a long time and is between 25°C and 45°C.  
This temperature range is ideal for growth.

Common sources of infection:
- Taps
- Showers
- Hot tubs (jacuzzis)
- Humidifiers
- Cooling systems

Old or poorly maintained hot water systems are especially risky.  
They can develop a slimy layer called biofilm, which helps bacteria grow.

In rare cases, infection can happen if water with bacteria goes into the windpipe instead of the stomach when swallowed.  
But drinking water is safe. The stomach’s acid kills the bacteria.  
You cannot pass Legionnaires’ disease to someone else.  
It does not spread from person to person.

---

## How Common Is It?

In Germany, over 2,000 cases are reported each year.  
In Europe, about 4.5% of all pneumonia cases not caught in hospitals are caused by Legionella.  
But many cases go undetected because not everyone is tested.  
So the real number is likely higher.

Most cases affect just one person.  
But small outbreaks can happen, especially in hotels or on cruise ships.  
More cases occur in summer and autumn than in winter and spring.

People most at risk:
- Older adults
- People with weak immune systems
- People with diabetes, heart disease, or lung problems
- Smokers

Men are two to three times more likely to get the disease than women.

---

## How Can It Be Prevented?

Preventing Legionella means stopping the bacteria from growing in water systems.  
Good design and regular maintenance of water systems are key.

Tips to reduce risk:
- Use water pipes regularly. Do not let water sit for long periods.  
- Avoid water tanks or basins that collect still water.  
- Remove unused pipes or fix dead-end sections.  
- Keep hot water above 55°C at all times.  
- Set your water heater to at least 60°C.  
- Insulate cold water pipes so they do not warm up in summer.  
- Clean and dry devices that make mist, like humidifiers.  
- Do not lower hot water temperature to save energy.  
  This increases the risk of bacteria growth.

There is no vaccine to protect against Legionella.

> **Important:** Never turn down your hot water temperature to save energy.  
> Keep it at least 55°C in all hot water pipes to stop bacteria from growing.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors will ask about your symptoms and do a physical exam.  
If pneumonia is suspected, they may take a chest X-ray.  
But an X-ray alone cannot confirm Legionnaires’ disease.

To confirm the infection, doctors use lab tests.  
Common tests include:
- A quick urine test to check for Legionella proteins.  
- A sputum (phlegm) sample tested in a lab to grow the bacteria.  
- A PCR test to find Legionella DNA in the sputum.

These tests help confirm the diagnosis.

---

## How Is It Treated?

If you have pneumonia from Legionnaires’ disease, you need antibiotics.  
Treatment should start as soon as possible.  
Most people need to stay in the hospital.

Common antibiotics used:
- Fluoroquinolones like levofloxacin or moxifloxacin  
- Macrolides like azithromycin or clarithromycin

These are often given through a vein (IV) at first.

Treatment usually lasts 1 to 2 weeks, sometimes longer.  
Most people recover fully.  
But in up to 10% of cases, the infection can be fatal.  
This is why early treatment is so important.

People with Pontiac fever do not need antibiotics.  
The illness usually gets better on its own in a few days.

# Constipation in Children – Simple Guide

Constipation means a child has trouble passing stool. It is common in young children, especially those in preschool.

Most cases are not due to a serious illness. They happen because the bowel is not working the way it should.

Treatment focuses on softening stool, helping the child go to the toilet regularly, and changing habits. This takes time and patience.

---

## What Is Constipation?

Constipation means a child has fewer bowel movements than usual. Stool may be hard, dry, or painful to pass.

It often happens during toilet training. A child may feel pain when going to the toilet. That pain can make them want to avoid it.

This can lead to a cycle: hard stool → pain → avoiding the toilet → more hard stool.

Some children may have small amounts of poop in their underwear. This is called a "stool smear." Larger amounts are called fecal incontinence.

---

## Signs of Constipation

Look for these signs in your child:

- Fewer than three bowel movements per week (except for breastfed babies)
- Hard or lumpy stool
- Straining when trying to go
- Stool that is very big or blocks the toilet
- You can feel a lump in the child’s bottom
- Pain when passing stool
- Small cuts or tears around the anus
- Blood on the stool
- Small traces of poop in underwear
- Accidents in underwear, especially if the child is over 4 years old and has been trained
- Belly pain that goes away after a bowel movement
- Fidgeting, squirming, or squeezing the buttocks together when they need to go

If your child has any of these signs, they may be constipated.

---

## When to See a Doctor

See a doctor right away if your child has:

- No bowel movement and also has a fever
- Severe belly pain
- No appetite
- Is not growing well (not gaining weight)
- Stool that is very thin, like a pencil
- Blood in the stool without cuts around the anus
- Vomiting green liquid (bile)
- A very swollen belly

These signs may mean there is a serious problem.

---

## Why Does Constipation Happen?

Some children are more likely to get constipation. But many things can trigger it.

### In Babies and Young Children

- Switching from breast milk to formula or cow’s milk
- Not eating enough fiber (like fruits and vegetables)
- Pressure from parents during toilet training
- Feeling anxious or scared about using the toilet
- Deliberately holding in stool

### In Older Children and Teens

- Not wanting to use dirty or unfamiliar toilets at school
- Being too busy playing to stop and go
- Pain during bowel movements
- Eating disorders like anorexia
- Taking certain medicines, such as antidepressants

### Rare Causes

In very rare cases, constipation is caused by:
- Birth defects in the bowel
- Food allergies or intolerances
- Problems with the thyroid, nerves, or spine

---

## What Makes Constipation Worse?

Constipation can get worse if a child holds in stool. The longer stool stays in the bowel, the more water it loses. This makes it harder and bigger.

Over time, the bowel stretches. The muscles weaken. The child loses the urge to go.

This can lead to long-term constipation.

---

## Who Is at Risk?

Children are more likely to be constipated if:

- A parent or sibling has had constipation
- They drink too little or too much fluid
- They eat too many salty snacks, sugary treats, or processed foods
- They don’t eat enough fruit, vegetables, or whole grains
- They don’t move around much
- They are overweight
- They are going through a stressful time (like starting school or a new baby in the family)
- They refuse to use the toilet at school or preschool

Note: Active children before puberty may be more likely to have constipation due to their high activity levels.

---

## How Common Is It?

Constipation is most common in young children.

In Germany, about 7 out of every 100 children aged 5 to 8 have constipation.

Two out of every three children with accidents in their underwear also have constipation.

If constipation is caused by another condition, it usually shows up in the first few weeks of life.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

The sooner treatment starts, the better the chance of full recovery.

### What Happens If It’s Not Treated?

- Hard stool builds up in the bowel
- The bowel wall stretches and weakens
- The child may have accidents (fecal incontinence)
- The child may get urinary tract infections
- Bedwetting can happen
- The child may feel sad, anxious, or embarrassed

These problems can affect the whole family.

### How Long Does Treatment Take?

Most children need treatment for several months. Some need it for years.

After 5 years, up to 75% of children are fully recovered and no longer need stool softeners.

About 1 in 4 children who need hospital treatment for constipation still have it as adults.

---

## How to Prevent Constipation

Prevention starts with healthy habits.

### For Babies (0 to 2 years)

- Breastfeed only for the first 6 months
- Continue breastfeeding as long as possible
- Start solid foods at 6 months, slowly and gently
- Feed when the child is hungry
- Offer a wide variety of fruits and vegetables
- Avoid sugar, soft drinks, salty snacks, and fried or processed foods

### For School-Aged Children

- Make sure they drink at least 3 glasses of water a day
- Give them plenty of fruits, vegetables, and whole grains
- Encourage regular physical activity

---

## How Is Constipation Diagnosed?

A doctor will:

- Ask about your child’s symptoms
- Check the child’s body, especially around the anus
- Use an ultrasound to see if there is stool buildup in the bowel
- Ask about eating habits, toilet behavior, and family life
- Use a special questionnaire to help find the cause

If the doctor suspects another illness, they may do blood tests, imaging, or take a small sample of bowel tissue.

If treatment does not help, more tests may be needed.

---

## How Is Constipation Treated?

Treatment depends on the child’s age and how long they’ve had constipation.

### For Babies (First Year)

- If constipation is due to a medical problem, see a specialist
- Some babies are allergic to cow’s milk protein. Removing cow’s milk may help
- For mild cases, give small amounts of apple, plum, or pear juice. These help soften stool
- Stool softeners like lactulose, sorbitol, or polyethylene glycol (macrogol) can help
- Glycerin suppositories can help, but may irritate the skin

**Do not use:**
- Enemas
- Bisacodyl (a strong laxative)
- Mineral oil

These are not safe for babies.

### For Preschoolers and School-Aged Children

- Treat constipation early to stop it from becoming long-term
- Use stool softeners like polyethylene glycol (macrogol) to help
- If there are cuts or redness around the anus, use a pain-relief ointment
- For long-term constipation, aim for soft stool every day or every other day

**Treatment steps:**

1. Clear the bowel completely using macrogol or an enema
2. Use stool softeners daily for months or years to keep stool soft
3. Use macrogol or lactulose as the main softener
4. In some cases, use laxatives like bisacodyl or senna pods to help the bowel move
5. Use softeners consistently. If the child has no constipation for 6 months, slowly reduce the dose
6. Stop completely if no symptoms return

**Toilet training is key:**

- Have the child sit on the toilet 5 to 10 minutes after meals, 2 to 3 times a day
- Even if they don’t feel the urge, sitting helps train the bowel
- Use a small stool under the feet to help the child sit in a squatting position
- This helps the bowel empty fully

**Diet changes help:**

- Eat more fruits, vegetables, and whole grains
- Drink enough water every day

**Do not give:**
- Wheat bran, psyllium husks, or similar fiber supplements
- These can make constipation worse if the child doesn’t drink enough water

### For Teens

- Use stool softeners like macrogol or lactulose for several months
- Eat a high-fiber diet and drink plenty of fluids
- If constipation has lasted a long time, there may be another issue (like a bowel disease, mental health problem, or eating disorder)
- Treat the underlying condition
- Some adult medicines may be used if needed
- Special training programs can help with accidents

---

## What Parents Can Do

Help your child get better by being patient and supportive.

### Keep a Poop Diary

Write down:
- When your child has a bowel movement
- How soft or hard the stool was
- Which stool softener was used and how much

This helps the doctor adjust treatment.

# Phlebitis

Phlebitis most often affects the veins just under the skin in the legs. It is often linked to varicose veins. The affected vein feels hard and hurts when you press on it. The skin above the vein turns red. Several steps can help ease the symptoms quickly.

---

## Quick Facts

- A common sign of phlebitis is a vein that feels hard and hurts when pressed. The skin above it is red.
- The veins in the legs are most often affected. Varicose veins are a common cause.
- Blood clots can form. These can lead to serious health problems.
- You should see a doctor if you think you have phlebitis.
- A special ultrasound test can show if there is a blood clot and where it is.
- Symptoms usually improve quickly with treatment.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Phlebitis?

Phlebitis means the vein wall is inflamed. Often, a blood clot forms in the vein. This clot blocks blood flow. Because of this, phlebitis is also called thrombophlebitis.

While it usually affects veins near the surface of the legs, any vein can be affected. With proper care, the condition usually gets better in a short time. But if the blood clot moves into deeper veins, it can cause serious problems. These include a blood clot in the lungs, which is life-threatening.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

When a surface vein becomes inflamed, a hard, sometimes bumpy line forms under the skin. It hurts when you press on it. The skin over the vein is red, swollen, and feels warm. Some people may also have a mild fever.

Most cases go away without problems. But complications can happen, such as:

- Bacteria spreading into the vein and surrounding tissue. This can cause a high fever and pus.
- A blood clot moving into deeper veins. This can cause deep vein thrombosis. The leg swells. The skin looks shiny and tight. The calf may hurt.
- A piece of the blood clot breaking loose. This can travel to the lungs. This causes sudden shortness of breath and chest pain.

> **Important:** Because blood clots can cause serious harm, always see a doctor if you think you have phlebitis.

---

## What Causes Phlebitis?

Up to 90 out of 100 cases of phlebitis are caused by varicose veins. The bulging veins cause blood to move slowly and swirl. This can lead to tiny blood clots forming. These tiny clots cause the vein wall to become inflamed.

When the inside of a blood vessel is no longer smooth, blood cells called platelets gather there. This leads to a blood clot. The clot grows as more blood parts stick to it.

Other causes include:

- Injury to the vein
- Needles used for IV drips
- Not moving enough

Lack of physical activity can also raise the risk of blood clots.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

Anything that slows blood flow, makes blood more likely to clot, or damages the inside of blood vessels increases the risk of phlebitis.

Risk factors include:

- Varicose veins
- Poor blood flow in the veins
- Damage to the vein wall
- Vein surgery
- IV drips
- Injecting drugs into veins

Other common risk factors are:

- Being in bed for long periods after surgery or illness
- Not being active enough
- Pregnancy and the weeks after giving birth
- Hormonal birth control
- Hormone therapy during menopause
- Blood disorders that make clots more likely
- Cancer
- Severe obesity
- Getting older
- Inflammation of blood vessels (vasculitis)
- Autoimmune diseases
- Having had phlebitis before

---

## How Common Is Phlebitis?

About 5 to 8 out of every 1,000 adult men and women get phlebitis each year. The chance goes up as people get older.

---

## How Does Phlebitis Progress?

Most symptoms go away in a few days. If there are no other health issues, complications from blood clots are unlikely. But the vein may stay thickened for several months.

If the phlebitis is simple and not linked to other problems, a follow-up visit with a doctor 7 to 10 days after diagnosis can help check progress. If the phlebitis is caused by another health issue, the outcome depends on how that condition is treated.

---

## How Is Phlebitis Diagnosed?

Doctors can often tell if someone has phlebitis just by looking at the symptoms and how the leg looks. But they usually do a Doppler ultrasound. This test checks for larger blood clots and shows exactly where they are. It also helps track whether the clot is getting better or worse.

If there are no complications, no other tests are needed. If a blood clotting problem is suspected, a blood test can check for it. More tests are usually only done if the person does not have varicose veins or if phlebitis keeps coming back.

---

## How Is Phlebitis Treated?

There are several ways to treat phlebitis. The main goal is to reduce pain and discomfort.

Treatment options include:

- Raising the leg often, but not staying in bed or keeping it still
- Using cold or warm compresses on the area
- Wearing compression stockings or bandages to apply gentle pressure
- Taking non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medicines like ibuprofen or diclofenac
- Using antibiotics if there are signs of infection
- Taking blood thinners if there is a risk of a large blood clot

In rare cases, the affected vein may be removed or tied off during surgery.

# Molluscum Contagiosum

Molluscum contagiosum causes small, wart-like bumps on the skin.  
These bumps are usually harmless but can spread to others.  
The condition is caused by a virus.  
The bumps often go away on their own within a few months.

---

## Quick Facts

- The bumps look like small, flesh-colored or white spots.  
- They are about the size of a pinhead.  
- They often appear alone or in small groups.  
- They are most common in children and teens.  
- They are less common in adults.  
- The virus spreads through direct skin contact.  
- It can also spread through shared items like towels or toys.  
- The bumps usually disappear on their own in 6 to 12 months.  
- Most people do not need treatment.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always see a doctor.

---

## What Is Molluscum Contagiosum?

Molluscum contagiosum is a skin infection caused by a virus.  
It creates small, firm bumps on the skin.  
These bumps are sometimes called "Dell’s warts" or "mollusca."  
They are not the same as regular warts.  
Regular warts are caused by a different virus.

Each bump has a small dent in the center.  
Inside the dent is a soft, white or yellowish fluid.  
This fluid contains the virus and can spread the infection.

The infection is usually mild and does not cause serious health problems.

---

## How Do You Recognize Molluscum Contagiosum?

The bumps are:
- Solid and shiny.  
- White, pink, or the same color as your skin.  
- About the size of a pinhead.  
- Have a small dimple in the middle.

Most people do not feel pain.  
But some may feel itchy.  
The skin around the bumps can be red or swollen.  
In rare cases, the bumps themselves may become red and swollen.

Children usually get bumps on:
- Their torso  
- Arms and legs  
- Head and neck

Adults usually get bumps on:
- The genital area  
- Inner thighs  
- Lower belly

People with weak immune systems — such as those with HIV — may get very large or many bumps.

---

## How Do People Get Molluscum Contagiosum?

The virus spreads through:
- Touching someone else’s skin who has the bumps.  
- Sharing towels, clothing, or toys.  
- Swimming in pools, especially if the water is not clean.

The virus enters the skin through tiny cuts or scratches.  
Bumps can appear as early as a few days after exposure.  
Or they may take up to 6 weeks to show up.

Children often get it while playing together.  
Young adults often get it through sexual contact.

---

## What Increases the Risk of Getting It?

You are more likely to get molluscum contagiosum if:
- You have close contact with someone who has it.  
- You have a weak immune system. This can happen with HIV or certain medicines.  
- You have skin allergies or eczema.  
- You swim in public pools.

---

## How Common Is It?

Molluscum contagiosum is very common in children.  
About 5 to 12 out of every 100 children get it at some point.  
Teens and adults can also get it.

---

## Will It Go Away on Its Own?

Yes, the bumps usually go away on their own.  
Each bump may disappear in about 2 months.  
But new ones can appear.  
It can take 6 to 12 months for all bumps to go away.  
In some cases, it may take several years.

When the skin around a bump turns red and swells, it may mean the bump is healing.  
This reaction is normal.  
It usually does not leave a scar.  
But sometimes it can.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor can usually tell it is molluscum contagiosum just by looking at the bumps.  
The bumps have a unique look.

In rare cases, the doctor may take a small sample of skin.  
This is done to check under a microscope.  
It helps rule out other skin problems.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Most people do not need treatment.  
The bumps go away on their own.  
Some treatments do not work well.  
They can cause side effects like redness, swelling, or scars.

Treatment is usually only needed if:
- The bumps are very itchy or painful.  
- You want them gone for cosmetic reasons.  
- You want to stop the infection from spreading.  
- The bumps are in the genital area.  
- You have a weak immune system.

### Treatment Options

**For children:**
- A doctor may use a small tool to gently remove the bump.  
- This is called curettage.  
- The area can be numbed first.  
- Or the doctor may freeze the bump with liquid nitrogen.  
- This is called cryotherapy.  
- A special cream or ointment may be applied to the bump.

**For bumps in the genital area:**
- Cryotherapy is an option.  
- A medicine called podophyllotoxin may be used.  
- This is a plant-based treatment used for genital warts.

**Other treatments:**
- Some creams or ointments cause a mild skin reaction.  
- This may help the body clear the virus faster.  
- But their effectiveness is not proven in many cases.

Always talk to your doctor before starting any treatment.  
Weigh the benefits and risks carefully.

---

## How to Live With Molluscum Contagiosum

- Do not pick at or scratch the bumps.  
- This can spread the virus to other parts of your skin.  
- It can also spread it to others.

- If you swim, cover the bumps with a waterproof bandage.  
- Avoid contact sports or using shared mats if the bumps are exposed.  
- If you cannot cover them, it is best to wait until they heal.

- Do not share towels, toys, or baths with others.  
- This helps stop the virus from spreading.

- Children can still go to school or kindergarten.  
- They do not need to stay home.

---

**Remember:** Molluscum contagiosum is common and usually not serious.  
Most people get better without treatment.  
But always talk to a doctor if you are unsure.

# Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)

A scary or shocking event can deeply affect a person. Sometimes, the memory of such an event stays with someone and causes post-traumatic stress disorder. This condition can lead to flashbacks and trouble sleeping.

## Quick Facts

- PTSD is a mental health condition.
- It happens after a person goes through a traumatic event like a disaster, violence, abuse, or a serious accident.
- People with PTSD keep reliving the event in their mind. These memories come back suddenly and feel real again.
- PTSD can affect someone’s life for years after the event.
- Support from family, friends, and professionals is very important.
- Talking with a therapist can help a person understand and cope with what happened.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is PTSD?

PTSD is a mental health problem.

It starts after a person experiences something very frightening. Examples include war, a violent attack, sexual abuse, a car crash, or a natural disaster.

The event is called a trauma. A trauma is like a deep emotional wound.

Both people who lived through the event and those who saw it can develop PTSD.

People with PTSD cannot let go of the memory. The event keeps coming back in their mind. This causes strong stress. Some people feel their life has fallen apart.

Support from others is key during this time. Therapy can help a person process the event and regain control.

---

## What Are the Signs of PTSD?

The following symptoms may mean someone has PTSD:

### Flashbacks

The person relives the event as if it were happening again. These flashbacks are very vivid and hard to stop. They can include strong feelings and images.

Many people also have nightmares about the event. These dreams cause fear, helplessness, or shame. Some people feel physical pain again, even if they are not hurt.

### Being Easily Irritated

People with PTSD often feel on edge. They have trouble focusing. They sleep poorly. They get angry quickly. They react strongly to things that remind them of the event.

For example, a certain smell, sound, or image can trigger a strong reaction. This may cause a fast heartbeat, tight chest, trouble breathing, or shaking.

### Avoiding Triggers

People with PTSD try to avoid anything that reminds them of the event. This includes places, people, conversations, or activities linked to the trauma.

### Pulling Away from Others

Some people with PTSD stop seeing friends or family. They lose interest in things they once enjoyed.

They may feel disconnected from their own life. Some feel empty or numb inside. Others block out the memory so much that they forget parts of the event.

This makes it hard to understand or make sense of what happened.

### Negative Thoughts and Feelings

Many people with PTSD lose trust in themselves and others. They feel weak and powerless.

They may ask themselves:  
- Why did this happen to me?  
- Could I have stopped it?  
- Am I to blame?

PTSD can also lead to other mental health problems. These include depression, anxiety, or addiction. Some people develop a dissociative disorder. This means they lose parts of their memory or feel like they are not in their own body.

Some people also suffer from long-term pain, eating problems, or psychosis.

- If PTSD is mild, symptoms may only happen in certain situations. Life can still be lived normally.
- If PTSD is severe, the person may struggle to live day to day without help.

Symptoms depend on the event and how well the person handles stress.

### Children and Teens

Children and teens often show PTSD differently than adults.

They may act out the event over and over in play or stories. They might use different characters or scenes to reenact what happened.

Many become anxious or aggressive. Teens with complex PTSD often have trouble managing their emotions.

They may see themselves or others in a negative way. They may struggle to trust people or form healthy relationships.

> A brochure about trauma in children and teens is available at **gesundheitsinformation.de**.

---

## What Causes PTSD?

PTSD starts after a traumatic event that felt life-threatening. It can be dangerous for the person or for others.

Examples of such events include:

- War
- Violent crime
- Sexual abuse
- Car crashes
- Natural disasters
- Serious medical emergencies like a heart attack or severe bleeding

Even news about a loved one’s death or serious illness can be traumatic.

Events like losing a job, a breakup, or being bullied do not cause PTSD. But they can cause some symptoms that feel like PTSD. These events may also lead to depression or anxiety.

---

## What Increases the Risk of PTSD?

Several things affect whether someone develops PTSD and how severe it is:

- What exactly happened – for example, violence vs. an accident
- How intense and long the event was
- Whether the event happened more than once
- How strong the person’s mental health was before the event
- Whether they had support from others

How a person feels about the event matters a lot. Strong feelings of fear, helplessness, or loss of control increase the risk.

If the event felt life-threatening or involved violence from another person, the risk is higher.

People with existing mental health issues like depression, anxiety, or addiction are more likely to develop PTSD.

Personal strength and emotional support also play a big role.

Some jobs involve frequent exposure to trauma. These include police officers, firefighters, train drivers, and emergency workers.

People in war zones are also at much higher risk.

---

## How Common Is PTSD?

About 2% to 3% of people in Germany will have PTSD at least once in their life.

The chance depends on the person’s life and the type of trauma.

PTSD is more common in:

- 50% of war survivors, rape victims, and torture survivors
- 25% of people who were violently attacked
- 20% of soldiers after combat
- 10% of people who survived a serious car crash or life-threatening illness

But PTSD is not common for everyone who has been through trauma.

Many people feel sad or upset when memories return. But their daily life stays normal. These feelings usually fade over time.

---

## What Is the Outlook for People with PTSD?

Symptoms can start right after the event or weeks or even years later.

Some people develop PTSD years after a war or childhood trauma. This is more common in soldiers. But it can also happen in older adults who remember past events as stressful.

Symptoms may go away in a few weeks. Or they may last for years and become long-term.

Symptoms can come and go. Some days are better. Other days are harder.

Many people recover over time. They learn to live with their memories.

Some get better within a year, even without therapy.

About 30% of people have symptoms for 3 years or longer. These people may develop other problems, like addiction.

Severe symptoms can make daily life very hard. People may lose their jobs. They may not be able to focus or sleep well. They may keep thinking about the event at work.

After abuse, some people also have problems with intimacy or sex.

---

## Can PTSD Be Prevented?

After a traumatic event, emotional and practical support helps.

A safe, calm environment where the person feels protected is helpful.

Support can include comfort, reassurance, or help with daily tasks. What is best depends on the event.

Medication is not used to prevent PTSD.

---

## How Is PTSD Diagnosed?

Doctors only call it PTSD if symptoms last more than 4 weeks.

Right after a trauma, most people feel very upset. This is normal. These early reactions are called an acute stress reaction.

To diagnose PTSD, a doctor or therapist talks to the person.

They ask about:

- How bad the symptoms are
- How much the symptoms affect daily life
- The person’s family, job, and home life

A self-check questionnaire may be used.

For children, therapists may use drawing or play to understand what happened.

Parents or caregivers are also asked for their input.

After a serious accident, doctors often focus on physical injuries. This can mean PTSD is missed.

Some people do not connect their mental symptoms to a past event. Others find it hard to talk about what happened.

So building trust is very important. The therapist will not push for details. They will go slowly.

Other mental health problems can happen after trauma. These include anxiety and depression. The doctor will check for these too.

---

## How Is PTSD Treated?

The best treatment depends on the person.

Before starting therapy, it helps to ask:

- What are the main symptoms?
- What goals are realistic?
- What kind of help is needed?
- Is therapy really necessary?

A therapist can help answer these questions.

Some people need therapy to process the trauma. Others get enough support from family, friends, or counseling.

Medication is only used in certain cases. In hospitals, other options like art therapy, music therapy, or physical therapy may be offered.

> **Important:** Trauma-focused therapy is the most effective treatment. It helps the person face and understand what happened.

### Types of Therapy

- **Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT):** This helps change negative thoughts and feelings about the trauma. It is the most common therapy for PTSD.
- **Psychodynamic Therapy:** This looks at how past and present relationships affect the person’s feelings and behavior.
- **EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing):** During therapy, the person follows a moving object with their eyes, like a therapist’s finger. This may help the brain process the trauma.

If PTSD comes with other mental health issues, the therapist decides which problem to treat first.

For more on medication, visit **gesundheitsinformation.de**.

---

## What Is Life Like with PTSD?

A traumatic event can change a person’s life.

# Knee Pain in the Front of the Knee

Pain in the front of the knee is often caused by overuse. This means the knee has been used too much or too often without enough time to rest and recover. It is common in people who do a lot of physical activity, such as running, hiking, or cycling.

There is no single cause for why some people get knee pain and others do not, even when they do the same activities.

You can take steps to feel better. Here’s what helps.

---

## What You Should Know at a Glance

- Pain in the front of the knee is usually due to overuse.
- It often happens in people who run, climb hills, or cycle.
- Doctors do not know exactly why some people get knee pain and others do not.
- If the pain is sudden or sharp, stop training for a while.
- Doing regular exercises to strengthen your thigh and hip muscles can help in the long run.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Anterior Knee Pain?

Pain in the front of the knee, especially around the kneecap, is often due to overuse. This happens when the knee is used too much without enough rest. It is common in runners, hikers, and cyclists.

There is no cure for this type of knee pain. But research shows that strengthening your thigh and hip muscles can reduce the pain.

If you have sudden or sharp knee pain, reduce your training. Take a break from sports to let your knee heal.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The pain usually happens behind or around the kneecap. Doctors call this patellofemoral pain or patellofemoral pain syndrome.

The word “patellofemoral” means the area between the kneecap and the thigh bone.

The pain starts mild but can get worse over time. It feels dull and happens when you put pressure on the knee. It is common when:

- Climbing stairs
- Squatting
- Sitting for a long time

You may also hear cracking, crunching, or grating sounds when you move your knee. These sounds are normal. They do not mean you should stop moving. In fact, movement helps keep your knee healthy.

Your knee joint needs pressure to get nutrients. Bones also stay strong when they are used regularly.

---

## What Causes This Pain?

Too much strain on the knee can cause small injuries in the kneecap area. These can affect ligaments, bones, or tiny nerves.

Why some people get knee pain and others do not, even with the same activity, is not fully known. One possible reason is how the kneecap moves in the groove of the thigh bone.

Other possible causes include:

- Tight muscles
- Weak thigh and hip muscles
- Legs of different lengths
- Feet that roll inward too much when walking
- Knock knees or bow legs
- A larger angle between the thigh and lower leg (called the Q angle)

It is not clear how much each of these factors contributes. Most experts believe that several factors together cause the pain.

---

## What Increases the Risk of Knee Pain?

The biggest risk is doing too much physical activity too quickly.

Common causes of overuse include:

- Running, hiking, climbing stairs, or bending the knees often
- Cycling, especially uphill
- Increasing training too fast — this often happens with new runners or competitive athletes
- Jobs that require a lot of squatting or lifting heavy things

---

## How Common Is This Pain?

Front knee pain is one of the most common knee problems. It mainly affects young people and those who are very active, especially runners.

---

## How Does the Pain Develop?

The way the pain changes varies from person to person.

- About half of people have pain for only a few weeks or months.
- The other half have pain for years or it comes back again and again.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your pain and check your knee. They may ask you to stand on a step and slowly step down with your healthy leg. If this causes pain, it suggests anterior knee pain.

Some doctors use questionnaires to track your symptoms.

In some cases, the doctor may do further tests to rule out other problems, such as:

- Arthritis
- Tendon problems
- Broken bones
- A torn knee cartilage

Tests like ultrasound, X-rays, or MRI scans may be used.

A diagnosis of anterior knee pain is made if:

- You have pain behind or around the kneecap
- The pain happens when you climb stairs, run, squat, or do similar activities
- No other cause for the pain can be found

---

## How Is It Treated?

If the pain is sudden or sharp, rest is best. Stop training or reduce your activity level. Let your knee heal.

For short-term relief, use pain-relief and anti-inflammatory creams or gels. These are safer than painkillers in pill form.

In the long term, strengthening your thigh and hip muscles helps. Stronger muscles take pressure off the knee. Many people find their pain goes down and their knee works better with regular exercise.

If your feet roll inward too much when walking, special insoles may help. They can reduce pain for some people. But there is not much strong evidence that they work for everyone.

> **Important:** Do not take painkillers to keep doing high-intensity sports. Even if the pain goes away, your knee still needs rest to heal.

---

## How Can You Manage the Pain?

It is frustrating when you can’t do the things you love because of knee pain. Sometimes, even doctors cannot find the exact cause. That means they cannot offer a specific medical treatment.

But you can still help yourself. Healing takes time. You must stay active in your recovery.

If you have to stop your usual sport for a while, try a different activity that does not hurt your knee. Good options include:

- Light cycling
- Aqua jogging (running in water)
- Swimming

These activities keep you fit without stressing your knee.

---

## More Information

For more advice on dealing with knee pain, visit the website: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Depression

Feeling sad sometimes is normal. It usually passes after a while.  
But for someone with depression, the sadness does not go away.  
It lasts for weeks or months.  
It takes over their life.  

This can make daily tasks hard.  
Work, school, and hobbies become difficult.  
The person may pull away from friends and family.  

## What Is Depression?

Everyone feels down now and then.  
These feelings usually fade.  
But in depression, the sadness stays.  
It does not go away on its own.  
The person feels low all the time.  
They may feel empty or hopeless.  
They may lose interest in things they once enjoyed.  

## What Are the Signs of Depression?

Depression can show up in many ways.  
Here are common signs:

- A deep, lasting sadness  
- Feeling tired all the time  
- No energy to do anything  
- Not caring about things anymore  
- Feeling bad about yourself  
- Always thinking about past mistakes  
- Trouble focusing or making decisions  
- Pulling away from people you care about  
- Feeling hopeless about the future  
- Thinking about ending your life  

Physical signs can also happen:

- Feeling worn out  
- Trouble sleeping or sleeping too much  
- Not feeling hungry or eating too much  
- Losing or gaining weight  
- Less interest in sex  
- Stomach problems like constipation  
- Feeling more pain than usual  

Older adults often show depression through physical problems.  
For example, they may complain of pain that has no clear cause.  

You can read real stories from people who have lived with depression at _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

## What Causes Depression?

Doctors do not know exactly what causes depression.  
But they believe several things play a role:

- Some people have a family history of depression.  
- Traumatic events like abuse, loss, or separation can trigger it.  
- Having anxiety for a long time as a child or teen increases risk.  
- Brain chemistry may be different.  
  - Messages in the brain travel slower.  
  - Chemicals like hormones and neurotransmitters may not work right.  
- Serious health problems like stroke, heart attack, cancer, or an underactive thyroid can cause depression.  
- Long-term stress or feeling overwhelmed can lead to it.  
- Not having enough challenges in life can also be a factor.  
- Feeling lonely increases the risk.  
- Some people get depressed in winter when there is less sunlight.  

## How Common Is Depression?

Depression is very common.  
About 1 in 5 people will have depression at some point in their life.  
Some people have it only once.  
Others have it over and over.  
Some have a long-term low mood called dysthymia.  

Women are more likely to get depression than men.  
Older adults are more likely than younger people.  

## How Does Depression Start?

Depression changes how a person feels and acts.  
Many people blame themselves.  
They may avoid others.  
They may stay home most of the time.  
This can make the symptoms worse.  

Depression can appear in different ways:

- Some people get better without treatment.  
- Others go through times of depression and times without symptoms.  
- Some have mild to strong symptoms that come and go over years.  
- Some have long-term depression that lasts more than two years.  

Depression is diagnosed when symptoms last at least two weeks.  
They can go on for many months.  
The episode ends when symptoms fade.  

About half of people who get treatment feel much better after 3 to 6 months.  

If symptoms return within 6 months after getting better, it is called a relapse.  
If symptoms come back after more than 6 months — or even years later — it is called recurrent depression.  

For more details on types of depression, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

## Can Depression Be Prevented?

Some stress, like losing a partner or long-term pressure, can lead to depression.  
You can reduce some stress.  
Learning how to handle tough times can help lower your risk.  
Having strong relationships with family and friends also helps.  
People with good social support get depression less often.  

For those at high risk of getting depression again, long-term treatment with medicine can help.  
Long-term talk therapy is another option.  

## How Is Depression Diagnosed?

Some people think depression is just weakness or a short phase.  
Others are so unwell that they cannot ask for help.  

Family and friends often notice changes first.  
They can help by encouraging the person to see a doctor.  

Doctors ask questions about symptoms.  
They also check for other health problems that can cause similar signs.  
A physical exam may be needed.  

Doctors look for two types of symptoms:

**Main symptoms:**
- Feeling sad or hopeless  
- Losing interest in things  
- Feeling tired or slow  

**Other common signs:**
- Not eating well or eating too much  
- Trouble sleeping  
- Hard time focusing or deciding  
- Low self-worth  
- Feeling guilty  
- Thinking the future is bad  
- Thoughts about suicide  

Doctors use questionnaires to help make a diagnosis.  
If a person has several main and other symptoms for two weeks or more, they may have depression.  

The doctor will decide how serious the depression is.  
They may call it mild, moderate, or severe.  
Then they create a treatment plan.  

## How Is Depression Treated?

There are several ways to treat depression.  
The most common are:

- Talk therapy, like cognitive behavioral therapy  
- Medicine  

The best treatment depends on:

- The person’s life situation  
- How bad the symptoms are  
- How long they last  

You can talk to your doctor or therapist about the pros and cons of each option.  
You can also discuss what results to expect.  

For more on treatment, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

## What Can Family and Friends Do?

Family, partners, and friends often notice changes first.  
They are often the first to see signs of depression.  

Their support is very important.  
But helping someone with depression can be hard.  
You may feel tired or overwhelmed.  
It is okay to ask for help too.  

Support groups can help.  
So can talking to a doctor or therapist.  

If someone talks about suicide, take it seriously.  
Most people with these thoughts do not act on them.  
But they still need help.  

You should not ignore these thoughts.  
Talk to someone you trust.  

There are many places to get help:

- Social psychiatric services  
- Crisis centers  
- Phone helplines  

These services often keep your name private.  
They are available 24 hours a day.  

For tips on how to talk to someone with depression, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

## Where Can I Get Help?

Most people start with their family doctor.  
Even for mental health issues, the doctor is a good first stop.  

You can also go to:

- Psychological counseling centers  
- Psychotherapists  
- Psychologists  

You do not need a doctor’s referral to see a therapist.  

**Important:** If someone is in immediate danger — for example, if they are thinking about suicide — go to a psychiatric clinic with emergency care.  
Or go to the emergency department of a psychiatric hospital.  

For more on therapy, how to find an appointment fast, and what your health insurance covers, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.  

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.  
> Always talk to a doctor or mental health professional.

# Tooth and Jaw Misalignments

Everyone’s teeth look a little different.  
When teeth or jaws are clearly out of place compared to most people, this is called a tooth or jaw misalignment.  

Some people have only one tooth that is out of line.  
Others have several teeth or even their jawbones that are misaligned.  

Misalignments can cause problems with chewing, speaking, or breathing.  
They can also cause pain in the jaw joints or muscles over time.  
Some people feel stressed or self-conscious about their teeth.  
This can affect their confidence and make them avoid social situations.  

Misaligned teeth are harder to clean.  
This increases the risk of gum disease and tooth decay.  
They may also be more likely to get damaged, especially during accidents.  

**Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.
