Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor or dentist.

---

## What Are Tooth and Jaw Misalignments?

Your teeth are unique.  
If they look very different from most people’s, it may be due to a misalignment.  

Sometimes just one tooth is affected.  
Other times, several teeth or the jawbone are out of place.  

Severe misalignments can make eating, drinking, or talking hard.  
They can also make breathing difficult.  
Teeth may press into the gums or lips and cause pain.  
They can even become loose.  

Because misaligned teeth are harder to clean, they are more likely to get cavities.  
They may also be more easily damaged in an accident.  

Over time, misalignments can cause jaw pain or muscle tension.  

Many people feel insecure or less attractive because of their teeth.  
Children and teens may feel this especially strongly if others tease them.  
Some avoid smiling or speaking in public.  

For more details on how misalignments look, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

---

## What Causes Tooth and Jaw Misalignments?

Misalignments can happen for many reasons.  

They may be due to how teeth or jawbones develop.  
They can also be caused by how the tongue, lips, cheeks, or facial muscles grow.  

Some people inherit a tendency to have misaligned teeth or jaws.  
Losing teeth early can also lead to misalignment.  
Injuries or bone diseases can cause teeth to shift or grow abnormally.

---

## What Increases the Risk of Misalignments?

Habits like sucking a pacifier, thumb, or finger can increase the risk.  
This is normal in babies and young children.  
But if it continues past age three, it can affect tooth and jaw development.  

Children who breathe through their mouth instead of their nose are also at higher risk.  
This can happen if the tonsils are too big and block the nose.

---

## How Common Are Misalignments?

Misalignments are very common.  
More than half of all children and teens in Germany have them.  

Baby teeth are replaced by permanent teeth as children grow.  
The jawbones keep growing until the end of puberty.  
This means misalignments can get better or worse during this time.  

Even adults can develop misalignments.  
This can happen if teeth are lost or if someone grinds their teeth at night.

---

## How Can Misalignments Be Prevented?

Parents can help young children stop bad habits.  
For example, painting a face on the thumb or using a bitter-tasting liquid can help.  

After a dental check-up, a doctor may suggest a vestibular plate.  
This looks like a pacifier but sits between the teeth and lips.  
It helps stop the habit and protects the teeth.  
In Germany, health insurance often covers the cost of this device.  

It is also important to care for baby teeth.  
They act as placeholders for permanent teeth.  
If they are lost too early, misalignments can occur.

---

## How Are Misalignments Diagnosed?

Parents often notice a problem first.  
Dentists or doctors may also spot it during a check-up.  

If a misalignment needs treatment, the child is usually referred to an orthodontist.  
The orthodontist checks the teeth, jaw, and face.  
They ask about habits and look at how the mouth opens and closes.  

X-rays are often taken.  
Dental impressions are also made.  
The child bites down on two small trays filled with soft plastic.  
This creates a mold of the teeth.  

Some clinics now use digital scans instead.  
These create a 3D model of the teeth without needing trays.  
This helps the doctor plan treatment better.  

In some cases, other specialists are needed.  
For example, if breathing is affected, an ear, nose, and throat doctor may be consulted.

---

## How Are Misalignments Treated?

Most misalignments are treated with braces.  
There are two main types: fixed and removable braces.  
Sometimes both are used in sequence.  

Fixed braces are attached to the teeth.  
Removable braces can be taken out.  
Treatment usually lasts about two years.  
This is called the active treatment phase.  

Fixed braces can be uncomfortable at first.  
They pull on the teeth and may cause soreness.  
People with fixed braces must be careful what they eat.  

Good oral hygiene is very important during treatment.  
Food can get stuck in the braces.  
This raises the risk of tooth decay and gum disease.  

Brush your teeth carefully with a regular or electric toothbrush.  
Use special floss or interdental brushes to clean between the teeth and around the braces.  

Treatment is usually recommended if the misalignment is severe.  
For example, if the top front teeth cover more than 3 millimeters of the bottom teeth.  
Or if side teeth bite past each other.  

But some people choose treatment just to improve their smile.  

There is no clear proof that braces are needed as often as they are recommended.  
No studies have shown for sure whether braces prevent future dental problems or just improve looks.

---

## What Else Should You Know?

Braces can help fix misalignments and reduce pain or discomfort.  
But the treatment can be stressful.  

Wearing braces may hurt at first.  
Fixed braces can make eating difficult.  

Some teens think braces are cool.  
Others feel embarrassed, especially when eating.  
Some worry about damaging the braces.  

Treatment only works if the child or teen takes part.  
They must keep their teeth and braces clean.  
Removable braces must be worn every day.  

Doctors can help by showing progress during check-ups.  
Seeing how the teeth are improving can boost motivation.  

In Germany, health insurance covers treatment for children and teens under 18 if the misalignment is severe.  
The patient pays a small fee upfront.  
This fee is fully refunded if treatment is completed on time.

# Medication Allergy

A medication allergy happens when your body’s defense system wrongly sees a medicine as a threat. It then attacks the medicine, causing an allergic reaction.

Some people can switch to a different medicine. But not all medicines have a safe alternative.

---

## Quick Facts

- A medication allergy happens when your immune system reacts to a medicine.
- Symptoms usually show up within one hour of taking the medicine.
- Allergies are most common in young adults and middle-aged people.
- Medicines given through a needle, IV drip, or applied to the skin cause more allergies than pills taken by mouth.
- **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Medication Allergy?

Medicines can have side effects. Some side effects are not allergies. They are just the body’s way of reacting to the medicine.

An allergy happens when your immune system overreacts to a medicine or one of its parts.

People with a medication allergy often do not know which medicines are safe for them. If you need a specific medicine, finding a safe alternative can be hard. Sometimes, the alternative medicine does not work as well.

A medication allergy can make it harder to treat your illness. It can slow down recovery.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most allergic reactions happen within one hour after taking the medicine. But some reactions can happen later — even days or weeks after.

### Immediate Reactions (within one hour)

- Skin turns red and feels hot
- Patchy rashes appear
- Itching
- Swelling in the mouth or throat
- Swelling in the hands, feet, or face (fluid buildup)
- Hives (raised, itchy red spots on the skin)

### Severe Reaction (Anaphylaxis)

This is rare but dangerous. It can cause:
- Trouble breathing
- Dizziness or loss of consciousness
- Heart stopping

### Delayed Reactions (after a few days or up to two weeks)

- Rash
- Fever
- Swelling of the face
- Skin peeling
- Damage to organs (very rare)

To help doctors treat you quickly in an emergency, you can save your allergy details in the **emergency data section** of your **electronic health record**.

---

## What Can Cause a Medication Allergy?

Common causes include:

- Antibiotics (especially penicillin)
- Pain and arthritis medicines
- Dye used in X-rays (contrast agents)
- Local anesthetics and sedatives
- Cancer medicines
- Epilepsy medicines
- Blood pressure medicines (ACE inhibitors)
- Mental health medicines (like antidepressants or antipsychotics)
- Additives in medicines (like dyes or preservatives)

How you take the medicine matters. Injections, IV drips, and skin applications cause more allergies than pills. IV medicines carry the highest risk.

Medication allergies are more common in young adults and middle-aged people. Women are more likely to have them than men. People with certain genes or those with HIV/AIDS are also at higher risk.

---

## How Is a Medication Allergy Diagnosed?

Many allergy symptoms look like other problems. For example, a rash can be from measles or rubella. So, a rash alone does not mean you have an allergy.

Doctors ask questions like:

- When did the symptoms start?
- What medicines did you take?
- How much did you take?

If you take many medicines, give your doctor as much detail as possible. Your health records or hospital notes can help.

Do not forget to mention:
- Over-the-counter medicines
- Herbal remedies
- Dietary supplements

These can also cause allergies.

Doctors may do tests to find the exact cause. But tests are not always clear or easy to interpret.

---

## How Is a Medication Allergy Treated?

You can often avoid the medicine that causes the allergy. But you cannot cure the allergy with allergy shots.

Medicines like antihistamines or cortisone can help prevent or reduce reactions.

If you have a severe reaction, you may need an adrenaline shot.

If you go into anaphylactic shock, call emergency services right away at **112**.

Many people can find a safe alternative medicine. For example, if you are allergic to a certain antibiotic or painkiller, another one is usually available. Your doctor can suggest a safe option.

But be careful about cross-reactions. You might react to medicines that are similar to the one you are allergic to.

Some medicines are essential and hard to replace. If no alternative exists, your doctor may slowly give you small doses of the medicine. They will watch you closely. The goal is to help your body get used to it over time.

This method is risky. It is only used when the medicine is very important — for example, for cancer or serious infections.

It is **very important** to keep a list of medicines you are allergic to. Carry this list with you at all times. This is called an **allergy passport**. It helps doctors treat you safely in an emergency.

---

## Why Must Diagnosis Be Careful?

Not every bad reaction to a medicine is an allergy.

For example, some antibiotics cause rashes. This is not always an allergy.

Many people think they are allergic to penicillin. But tests often show they are not.

False beliefs can cause problems. If you avoid penicillin when you do not need to, doctors may use a stronger antibiotic. This can lead to **resistant germs** — bacteria that are hard to treat.

So, it is important to get a proper diagnosis before assuming you are allergic.

# Diphtheria – Simple Explanation

Diphtheria is a serious bacterial infection. It mainly affects the skin or the airways. The bacteria make a poison that can travel through the blood and harm vital organs. In rare cases, it can be deadly. Vaccination can prevent it.

---

## Quick Facts

- Diphtheria is a dangerous infection caused by bacteria.
- The bacteria usually attack the skin or the airways.
- The bacteria make a poison that spreads through the body and can damage organs.
- Doctors treat diphtheria with an antitoxin and antibiotics.
- Vaccination is the best way to protect against diphtheria.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Diphtheria?

Diphtheria is a bacterial infection that happens all over the world. It is very rare in Germany today because most people are vaccinated.

The bacteria can infect the skin or the lining of the airways. They also make a poison that spreads through the blood and can harm the heart, nerves, and other organs.

Vaccination protects you from diphtheria.

---

### Two Main Types of Diphtheria

**1. Respiratory Diphtheria**  
This type affects the throat, nose, or voice box.  
- It can be life-threatening.  
- About 5% to 10% of people with this type die.

**2. Skin Diphtheria**  
This type happens after small cuts, scrapes, or insect bites.  
- It is more common in places with poor hygiene.  
- Animals like pets and farm animals can carry the bacteria and pass them to people.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on the type of diphtheria.

### Symptoms of Respiratory Diphtheria

You may feel:
- Weak
- Have a sore throat
- Run a fever
- Struggle to swallow
- Cough with a barking sound (like a seal)
- Wheeze or have trouble breathing
- Speak with a hoarse voice or lose your voice completely
- Have swollen glands in the neck
- Breathe out a sweet, bad smell
- Have blue or purple skin (especially around the lips)
- Feel restless or anxious
- Look pale

The poison destroys tissue in the throat. Within 2 to 3 days, dead tissue forms a thick, gray-brown layer. This layer can block the airway and make breathing very hard. This can be deadly, especially in young children.

Doctors call this layer a "pseudomembrane." It can cover the tonsils, throat, or nose.

### Symptoms of Skin Diphtheria

You may see:
- Swelling around a wound
- Redness
- A wound that looks like it was punched out
- A slimy coating on the wound

---

## How Do People Get Diphtheria?

**Respiratory diphtheria** is caused by *corynebacterium diphtheriae*. This bacteria only lives in humans.

**Skin diphtheria** is caused by *corynebacterium ulcerans* and *corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis*. These bacteria live in animals. This means skin diphtheria is a zoonotic disease — it can pass from animals to people.

---

### How Is Diphtheria Spread?

**Respiratory diphtheria** spreads through droplets in the air.  
- If an infected person coughs or sneezes, they release tiny droplets.
- These droplets can be breathed in by others nearby.
- Rarely, someone with skin diphtheria can pass the infection to another person through the air.

**Skin diphtheria** spreads through direct contact.  
- You can catch it by touching an open wound of an infected person.
- You can also catch it by touching objects that have the bacteria on them.
- This is more likely in places with poor hygiene, such as shelters for homeless people.

---

## How Common Is Diphtheria?

Diphtheria happens in many countries around the world. It is most common in warm, tropical areas like India. It also occurs in parts of Africa, Asia, the South Pacific, and Eastern Europe.

Thanks to childhood vaccination programs, serious cases have dropped sharply.

### Diphtheria in Germany

Diphtheria must be reported to health authorities in Germany.  
- The number of skin diphtheria cases has gone up since 2010.
- In 2020, there were 16 cases in Germany:
  - 15 cases were skin diphtheria
  - 1 case was respiratory diphtheria

---

## What Complications Can Happen?

The poison from the bacteria enters the blood and can harm internal organs. This is called toxic diphtheria.

Possible complications include:
- Airway blocked by the gray layer
- Lung infections, from mild pneumonia to breathing failure
- Inflammation of the heart muscle
- Nerve damage (polyneuropathy)
- Paralysis
- Coma

---

## How Can Diphtheria Be Prevented?

If someone has diphtheria, they must stay away from others to stop spreading it.

The best way to prevent diphtheria is vaccination.

The vaccine does not stop the bacteria from growing. But it protects against the poison the bacteria make.  
- So, even if you get the vaccine, you might still have a fever or feel weak.
- The vaccine is made from the poison of the bacteria that causes respiratory diphtheria.
- It also works against the poison from the bacteria that causes skin diphtheria.
- But we are not sure how well it protects against skin diphtheria.

The German vaccination committee (STIKO) recommends that all babies, children, teens, and adults get vaccinated.

---

### Recommended Vaccinations

- Babies get their first shots at 2 months, 4 months, and between 11 and 14 months.
- These are usually given as a 6-in-1 vaccine. It also protects against:
  - Tetanus
  - Whooping cough (pertussis)
  - Polio
  - Hepatitis B
  - Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib)

Immunity from the first shots fades over time.  
- A booster is needed between ages 5 and 6.
- A second booster is needed between ages 9 and 17.

After that, a booster every 10 years is recommended.  
- There are different vaccines available for boosters.

> **Important:** If you missed any shots, you can still get them later in life. Talk to your doctor about the best option.

For more information on vaccines and STIKO recommendations, visit the Robert Koch Institute website.

---

## How Is Diphtheria Diagnosed?

Doctors suspect diphtheria based on symptoms and a physical exam.

To confirm the diagnosis, they take a swab from the throat or from a wound.  
- The sample is sent to a lab.
- The lab grows the bacteria to check for the pathogen.
- They can also use a test called PCR to find the bacteria’s genetic material.

---

## How Is Diphtheria Treated?

There is a medicine called an antitoxin that fights the poison.  
- But it only works if the poison has not yet attached to body cells.
- So doctors start treatment right away if diphtheria is suspected — even before test results come back.

### Antitoxin Treatment

- For skin diphtheria, the antitoxin is only used if the wound is larger than a Euro coin and has the gray-brown coating.
- The antitoxin comes from horses. Some people are allergic to it.
- Allergic reactions can be serious. In rare cases, they can be deadly (anaphylactic shock).
- Because of this risk, people with suspected diphtheria are treated in hospitals with intensive care units.

### Antibiotic Treatment

Doctors also give antibiotics to kill the living bacteria.  
- After starting antibiotics, most people are no longer contagious after 48 hours.
- But you must keep taking antibiotics for two weeks.
- This makes sure all bacteria are gone.
- Doctors test again to confirm the infection is gone.

People who were near someone with diphtheria may also get antibiotics to prevent infection.  
- This is called post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP).

> **Important:** Do not go to schools, workplaces, or group homes if you might still spread the bacteria.

# Head Lice

An itchy head can mean you have head lice.  
Head lice are annoying but not dangerous.  
You need to treat them to get rid of them and stop them from spreading.

---

## Quick Facts

- Head lice are tiny insects that live in hair.  
- They feed on blood from your scalp.  
- You may feel a tickling or itching on your scalp if lice are in your hair.  
- Head lice are most common in children from preschool to elementary school.  
- Lice spread mainly through head-to-head contact.  
- They can also spread through shared items like combs or hats.  
- There are steps you can take to stop lice from spreading.  
- Medicine to treat lice is available and most health insurance plans cover it for children under 12.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Are Head Lice?

Head lice are small, wingless bugs.  
They live in your hair and feed on your scalp blood.  
Their bites can cause itching, but they do not cause serious harm.  
Unlike ticks, head lice do not carry diseases.

The eggs of head lice are called nits.  
Nits stick tightly to the hair shaft, close to the scalp.  
A new generation of lice can hatch in just one week.  
Lice spread quickly once they are in a group.

They are often found in daycare centers, preschools, and schools.  
Once lice are in your hair, they will not go away on their own.  
But there are safe and effective ways to get rid of them.

---

## What Are the Signs of Head Lice?

You may not notice lice right away.  
But you might see these signs:

- A feeling of something moving on your scalp.  
- Itchy spots or small red marks from bites.  
- Scratches or small wounds on your scalp.  
- Trouble sleeping because the itching gets worse at night.

---

## How Do Head Lice Spread?

Head lice mostly affect children.  
They spread through direct contact.  
For example, when kids play together and touch heads.

Some people think lice mean poor hygiene.  
This is not true.  
Lice do not care if hair is clean or dirty.  
Anyone can get lice.

Girls may get lice more often than boys.  
This may be because girls often sit close together and put their heads together.  
Hair length does not affect the risk.  
But lice are harder to see in long, thick, or curly hair.

---

## How Common Are Head Lice?

Head lice are common in children aged 3 to 12.  
Exact numbers in Germany are not known.  
Experts estimate that 1 to 3 out of every 100 children have lice.

Outbreaks often happen in schools and daycare centers.  
They are most common in late summer and early fall.  
This is usually after summer vacation.

---

## How Can You Prevent Head Lice?

There is no 100% way to prevent lice.  
But you can help stop them from spreading.

Lice need to feed on blood every 2 to 4 hours.  
They do not live long away from the scalp.  
Lice that fall out dry up in a few hours.  
Lice eggs need warmth near the scalp to hatch.  
This means lice usually do not spread through objects.

Still, it is best to avoid sharing:

- Hats  
- Scarves  
- Combs  
- Brushes  
- Hair clips

To reduce the risk, you can:

- Wash combs, brushes, and hair clips in hot, soapy water.  
- Do not use them for a few days.  
- Wash bed sheets, pajamas, clothes, and towels at 60 degrees Celsius.  
- Or put them in the dryer.  
- For items that can’t be washed, seal them in a plastic bag for 3 days.

> **Important:**  
> - Lice only live on people. Pets do not get lice.  
> - You do not need to disinfect your home.  
> - Spraying insecticide is not needed.

---

## How Do You Know If You Have Head Lice?

Parents often check their child’s hair after a “lice alert” from school or daycare.  
A special lice comb helps find lice and their eggs.

You can buy lice combs at drugstores or medical supply stores.  
Wet the hair before using the comb.  
Go through the hair strand by strand, from the scalp to the ends.  
Do this at least twice.  
Wipe the comb on a paper towel after each pass to check for lice or nits.

Adult lice are only 2 to 3 millimeters long.  
They are gray-brown, flat, and have no wings.  
They cannot jump like fleas.  
They use their six legs to crawl through hair.

Young lice are easier to see with a magnifying glass.

Lice usually lay their eggs behind the ears or at the back of the neck.  
The eggs stick tightly to the hair, no more than one centimeter from the scalp.

Nits can look like dandruff.  
But dandruff flakes fall off when you shake your hair.  
Nits stay stuck to the hair.

---

## How Do You Treat Head Lice?

You only need treatment if you find live lice or live eggs.  
Start treatment right away to stop the lice from spreading.

Effective treatments include:

- Medicines with insecticides  
- Products with silicone oil

Some people use natural treatments like coconut oil.  
Others try home remedies such as olive oil or mayonnaise.  
But these have not been well studied.

Some insecticides are no longer as strong as they used to be.  
Today, silicone oil treatments are more common.  
They work by covering the lice in oil.  
This blocks their breathing and kills them.

Most treatments need to be repeated after 7 to 10 days.  
Always follow the instructions on the package.

Health insurance covers most treatments for children under 12.  
Doctors can prescribe them.

> **Important:**  
> - Use the lice comb after each treatment to check if the lice are gone.  
> - Repeat the treatment and combing every 3 days for at least 2 weeks.  
> - If you see no lice but a few nits remain, the infestation is likely gone.  
> - Nits can stay in the hair for weeks after treatment.  
> - Nits more than 1 centimeter from the scalp are likely old eggs.  
> - Hair grows about 1 centimeter per month. So nits far from the scalp are from a past infestation.

For more detailed treatment tips, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Hay Fever

Many people get hay fever when trees and plants start to bloom in spring. The symptoms happen because the body reacts badly to pollen in the air. This affects the nose, throat, and eyes. Sneezing and itchy eyes can be very bothersome. These problems are worse on warm, dry days.

## Quick Facts

- About one in four people in countries like Germany has hay fever.
- Allergies can run in families.
- It is almost impossible to avoid pollen unless you go to a place where no pollen is in the air.
- Medicines can help reduce symptoms.
- Some people with hay fever later develop asthma.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Hay Fever?

Hay fever happens when the body overreacts to pollen in the air. It usually starts in spring or early summer. The nose, eyes, and throat are most affected.

You may sneeze a lot. Your nose might run or feel blocked. Your eyes may water and itch. Your eyelids can swell up. This is called allergic rhinoconjunctivitis.

Some people also get coughing, wheezing, or trouble breathing. These are like asthma symptoms. If the symptoms are bad, you may feel weak and tired.

These symptoms only happen during pollen season. They are much worse than the symptoms of a dust mite allergy, which can happen all year.

Hay fever is also called allergic rhinitis.

## What Are the Signs of Hay Fever?

- You sneeze often.
- Your nose runs or feels blocked.
- Your eyes water and itch.
- Your eyelids swell.
- You cough or have trouble breathing.
- You feel weak or tired.

These symptoms only appear when pollen is in the air. They go away when the pollen season ends.

## What Causes Hay Fever?

Your body sometimes reacts too strongly to things that are not harmful. Pollen is one of these things. It is called an allergen.

When you are exposed to pollen, your immune system makes special proteins. These proteins remember the pollen. The next time you meet pollen, your body reacts fast. It releases chemicals like histamine. These chemicals cause the symptoms of hay fever.

## What Increases the Risk of Hay Fever?

- Climate change is making the weather warmer. Plants now bloom earlier and longer. They also make more pollen.
- Air pollution and cigarette smoke can make allergies more likely.
- Allergies can run in families.
- Some experts think that cleaner living and fewer childhood infections mean the immune system is not trained well. This may make allergies more common.

## How Common Is Hay Fever?

In countries like Germany, about one in four people has hay fever. Most people first notice symptoms before they turn 20.

## How Can Hay Fever Get Worse?

Some people with hay fever later develop allergic asthma. This means they have trouble breathing and wheeze more often.

Pollen allergies can also lead to food allergies. This is called cross-reactivity. For example, someone allergic to birch pollen might also react to apples or carrots.

Severe hay fever can lead to sinus infections. The lining of the nose and throat can become very sensitive. This means you may react more to dry air, smoke, or other irritants.

## How Can You Prevent Hay Fever?

It is very hard to avoid pollen completely. The only real way is to go to a place with no pollen in the air.

The German weather service gives daily updates on pollen levels. Use this to plan your day.

You can reduce your exposure by:
- Keeping windows closed when pollen counts are high.
- Washing your hair before bedtime to remove pollen.

## How Is Hay Fever Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about your symptoms and your health history. They may do a skin test.

In a skin test:
- Small amounts of possible allergens are placed on your forearm.
- The skin is gently pricked.
- If the spot turns red and swells, you are allergic to that substance.

Sometimes doctors use blood tests or a provocation test.

In a provocation test:
- A small amount of allergen is sprayed into your nose or dropped into your eyes.
- If your nose swells, you start sneezing, or your nose runs, this suggests hay fever.

## How Is Hay Fever Treated?

There are several medicines that can help:

- **Antihistamines** – reduce sneezing, itching, and runny nose.
- **Corticosteroids** – reduce swelling and inflammation in the nose.
- **Leukotriene receptor antagonists** – help with breathing and reduce mucus.
- **Chromones** – help prevent allergic reactions.
- **Decongestant nasal drops or sprays** – clear a blocked nose.

Non-drug options include:
- Saline (salt water) nasal sprays.
- Nasal washes (rinsing the nose with salt water).

These can help with symptoms. But they usually do not work as well as medicine.

**Desensitization** is a long-term treatment. It helps your body get used to the allergen over time. It can reduce or even stop your symptoms.

This treatment:
- Works like a vaccine.
- Involves regular injections under the skin or drops under the tongue.
- Takes at least 3 to 5 years to complete.

For more details on medicine for hay fever, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

## More Information

You can find more about hay fever at [allergieinformationsdienst.de](https://www.allergieinformationsdienst.de).

# Syphilis – Simple Explanation

Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection. It is caused by a type of bacteria. The infection can go through several stages. It often has no symptoms, so people may not know they are infected. If found early, syphilis is easy to treat. If not treated, it can cause serious harm to the body. This article explains what syphilis is, how it spreads, how to prevent it, how it is diagnosed, and how it is treated.

---

## Quick Facts

- Syphilis is also called lues or venereal syphilis.
- It is caused by a bacteria called *Treponema pallidum*. This bacteria only lives in humans.
- Untreated syphilis can go through three stages. It can also get better on its own.
- If caught early, syphilis can be cured with antibiotics.
- If not treated, syphilis can damage the heart, brain, and other organs.
- Condoms, femidoms, and dental dams can help prevent transmission.
- **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Syphilis?

Syphilis is a sexually transmitted disease. It spreads through close contact during sex. It can affect the skin, genitals, mouth, and anus.

The infection can go through three stages. But some people have no symptoms at all. Others may not notice the early signs. This means they can pass the infection to others without knowing it.

In Germany, syphilis is most common among men who have sex with men. One reason is that some men have used condoms less often since HIV prevention drugs became available.

The bacteria can spread in these ways:

- Through direct sexual contact, especially with open sores or small cuts.
- Through contact with infected skin or mucous membranes.
- From a pregnant woman to her unborn baby (called congenital syphilis).
- Through blood transfusions — but this is very rare today because all blood is tested.

---

## What Are the Signs of Syphilis?

About half of people with syphilis do not have any symptoms. If symptoms do appear, they can come and go. The disease can go through three stages.

### Stage 1: Primary Syphilis

A small bump appears where the bacteria entered the body. This is usually on the penis, labia, mouth, or anus — depending on the type of sex.

The bump turns into a hard, painless sore. Nearby lymph nodes may swell. The sore usually heals on its own in 4 to 6 weeks.

Even though the sore heals, the infection is still in the body.

### Stage 2: Secondary Syphilis

The bacteria spread through the body. Symptoms can include:

- Fever
- Headaches
- Joint or muscle pain
- Swollen lymph nodes
- Hair loss in patches
- Skin rashes — spots, bumps, or scaly patches
- Sores on the skin or inside the mouth or anus
- Thickened skin on the palms or soles

These symptoms can last for years. They may come and go.

**Important:** The first year after infection is called early syphilis. People in stage 1 or 2 can pass the infection to others. All sexual partners from the last 3 months (stage 1) or 12 months (stage 2) should be tested.

After this, the disease may have no symptoms for years. This is called latent syphilis. There is still a small risk of passing it on during this time.

In later stages, the person is no longer contagious.

### Stage 3: Tertiary Syphilis

This stage can happen years after the first infection. It can cause serious damage. Symptoms include:

- Lumps on the skin
- Sores inside the body (called gummas)
- Problems with blood vessels, including weak spots in the aorta that can burst
- Brain and nerve problems, such as:
  - Pain or numbness in the legs and lower body
  - Weakness or loss of movement
  - Trouble speaking
  - Seizures
  - Eyes that do not react to light
  - Confusion, mood swings, hallucinations, or loss of consciousness

If not treated, this stage can lead to death in about 4 to 5 years.

**Important:** Today, syphilis is easy to treat. Stage 3 is now very rare. But people with HIV are more likely to get early brain problems from syphilis. The disease can also progress faster in these people.

---

## What Causes Syphilis?

Syphilis is caused by a bacteria called *Treponema pallidum*. It only infects humans.

You are more likely to get syphilis if you have unprotected sex or have many sexual partners.

**Want to know your risk?**  
The center *WIR – Walk In Ruhr, Zentrum für Sexuelle Gesundheit und Medizin* offers a free online test to check your risk for syphilis and other sexually transmitted infections.

---

## How Common Is Syphilis?

The number of syphilis cases has been rising since 2010. In Germany, about 8,000 people get syphilis each year.

Globally, around 12 million people are infected. Most of them live in developing countries.

---

## How Does Syphilis Progress?

Syphilis moves through stages. It can get better on its own. But if not treated, it can cause serious harm.

If caught early, it can be cured with antibiotics. If not treated, it can lead to long-term damage or even death.

---

## How Can Syphilis Be Prevented?

You can reduce your risk by using protection during sex.

- Use condoms, femidoms, or dental dams every time you have sex.
- Use them correctly and consistently.
- Syphilis can also spread through mouth-to-mouth contact or from mouth to genitals or anus.

If you have syphilis, avoid all sexual contact until your treatment is finished.

**Important:** If you or your partner notice any unusual sores, rashes, or changes in the skin or mouth, see a doctor right away. Early treatment is simple and effective. It also stops the infection from spreading.

---

## How Is Syphilis Diagnosed?

If syphilis is suspected, your doctor may:

- Take a swab from a sore and look at it under a special microscope.
- Do a lab test to find the bacteria directly.

If the bacteria are found, treatment is needed.

Blood tests can also detect antibodies. These are proteins your body makes when fighting an infection.

- Some antibodies show you have been exposed to syphilis.
- Others show the infection is still active.

These tests help doctors decide if treatment is needed and if it worked.

To check for brain or nerve problems, doctors may take a sample of spinal fluid and test it for antibodies.

Rapid tests can give a quick idea if you might have syphilis. But they are not always accurate. A lab test is needed to confirm the result.

**Important:** Early symptoms usually appear about 3 weeks after infection. If you think you might have syphilis, your sexual partners should also be tested.

---

## How Is Syphilis Treated?

Syphilis is caused by bacteria. It can be cured with antibiotics.

- Penicillin is the main medicine used for all stages.
- For early syphilis, you get 1 to 3 injections into the buttocks, once a week.
- For syphilis that affects the brain, you need IV antibiotics for 2 to 3 weeks.

After treatment, blood tests check if the infection is gone.

Sometimes, the bacteria die quickly after treatment. This can cause a strong reaction in the body. Symptoms like fever, chills, and headaches may happen.

To help with these side effects, doctors may give a steroid medicine (cortisone) just before treatment starts.

After treatment, you will have check-ups every 3 months. The doctor will check if symptoms are improving and if antibody levels are dropping.

- In early syphilis, symptoms usually go away quickly.
- You should avoid sex until fully recovered.
- In late syphilis, some damage to organs may be permanent.

---

## Other Useful Information

Syphilis is a reportable disease. This means doctors and labs must report cases to health authorities. The reports are anonymous.

---

## Where to Get Help

- **Liebesleben** – A website by the Federal Center for Health Education (BZgA). It has clear information about love, sex, and protection.
- **WIR – Walk In Ruhr, Zentrum für Sexuelle Gesundheit und Medizin** – A center that provides helpful information about syphilis and other sexually transmitted infections.

# Acute Kidney Injury

Acute kidney injury means your kidneys suddenly stop working well or stop working completely.  
This can be dangerous if not treated.  
But with early treatment, most people get better.

---

## Quick Facts

- Your kidneys may work less or stop working suddenly.  
- In most cases, this happens within 48 hours.  
- A key early sign is less urine than usual.  
- Many things can cause this, like serious blood loss from an accident.  
- Some medicines or long-term health problems can also harm your kidneys.  
- If not treated, kidney failure can be life-threatening.  
- Most people recover if treatment starts early.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical care.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Acute Kidney Injury?

Acute kidney injury (AKI) was once called acute renal failure.  
It means your kidneys stop working fast — usually within two days.  
In serious cases, they may stop working completely.

Your kidneys clean your blood.  
They remove waste products from your body.  
They make urine to carry these wastes out.

When your kidneys stop working, waste builds up in your blood.  
This can cause a condition called uremia.  
Uremia can be life-threatening if it gets worse.  
Fluid can also build up in your body, causing swelling.

You can get acute kidney injury after a major accident with heavy blood loss.  
Some medicines or long-term health problems can also harm your kidneys.  
If caught early, most people recover fully.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Acute kidney injury often has no obvious signs at first.  
The first clue may be less urine than normal.

Later, you may notice swelling.  
This often starts in your legs.  
If fluid builds up in your lungs, you may have trouble breathing.  
Fluid can also collect in your belly, causing bloating.

You may feel tired, have a headache, or feel sick to your stomach.  
You might vomit.  
These signs can mean waste is building up in your body.

This buildup of waste in the blood is called uremia.  
Other signs include itchy skin and a yellowish-brown skin color.  
Your breath may smell like urine.  
You might get muscle cramps.  
As the condition gets worse, you may feel confused.  
You could have seizures or lose consciousness.  
In severe cases, you may fall into a coma.

---

## What Causes Acute Kidney Injury?

Doctors divide the causes into three types: before the kidneys (prerenal), in the kidneys (intrarenal), and after the kidneys (postrenal).

### Prerenal AKI

This happens when blood flow to the kidneys drops.  
This causes about 60% of cases.

It can happen after a serious accident with heavy bleeding.  
It can also happen after severe burns.  
It may happen with long-lasting diarrhea or vomiting.  
A heart attack can also cause this if the heart stops pumping well.

### Intrarenal AKI

This means the kidneys themselves are damaged.  
This happens in about 35% of cases.

The most common cause is acute tubular necrosis.  
This means part of the kidney’s tiny tubes are damaged.  
This can happen if blood flow to the kidneys is low for too long.  
If the blood flow stays low, the kidney cells can die.

Some medicines, like certain antibiotics, can harm the kidneys.  
Heavy metals and strong inflammation can also cause damage.

### Postrenal AKI

This is the least common type — only about 5% of cases.  
It happens when urine cannot flow out of the kidneys.

This can be caused by kidney stones or stones in the tubes leading from the kidneys.  
Tumors, blood clots, or blockages in the urethra can also stop urine flow.

---

## How Common Is AKI?

Up to 7 out of every 100 people in the hospital have acute kidney injury.

---

## What Are the Possible Outcomes?

Most people with acute kidney injury get better if treated early.  
About 15 out of every 100 people need long-term dialysis.

Dialysis is a treatment that takes over the job of the kidneys.  
It removes waste and extra fluid from the blood.

Your outlook depends on the cause.  
If doctors treat heavy blood loss after an accident quickly, your kidneys usually return to normal.

Your age and how long the injury lasts also affect recovery.

Some complications make the condition worse.  
For example, high levels of potassium in the blood (hyperkalemia) can cause dangerous heart rhythm problems.

Fluid buildup in the body can lead to swelling in the lungs (pulmonary edema).  
This makes it hard to breathe.

> **Important:** If you have fluid in your lungs, your body does not get enough oxygen.  
> This is a medical emergency. You need urgent care.

---

## Can We Catch AKI Early?

People at high risk for AKI get regular blood tests.  
These tests check the level of creatinine.

Creatinine is a waste product.  
Healthy kidneys remove it from the blood and put it in the urine.  
When kidneys are not working well, creatinine builds up in the blood.  
A fast rise in creatinine levels is a sign of acute kidney injury.

---

## How Is AKI Diagnosed?

Doctors check how much urine you pass.  
If the amount drops below normal, it may mean you have AKI.

They also test your blood for creatinine.  
If the level goes up quickly, this is another sign of AKI.

Sometimes the cause is clear — like after a major accident with heavy bleeding.  
If not, more blood and urine tests are needed.

An ultrasound scan can show if kidney stones or a tumor is blocking the flow.  
In some cases, a small sample of kidney tissue (a biopsy) is taken to check for damage.

---

## How Is AKI Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause.

It is important to keep fluid levels balanced.  
Too much fluid can cause dangerous swelling.  
Too little fluid can harm the kidneys.  
If needed, fluids are given through a drip.

If a medicine is causing the problem, your doctor may switch to a different drug or lower the dose.

If kidney stones or ureteral stones are blocking urine flow, they must be removed.

If kidney function does not return quickly, dialysis may be needed.  
Dialysis helps remove waste and extra fluid from the blood.

In some cases, the kidneys are too damaged to recover.  
Then, long-term dialysis is needed.  
In some people, a kidney transplant may be an option.

---

## What Aftercare Is Needed?

After treatment, you should see your family doctor regularly.  
They will check your kidney function.

This is especially important if you are at higher risk for long-term kidney problems.  
This includes older adults and people with existing kidney issues.

---

## Where Can I Get Support?

If you have long-term kidney disease, support groups can help.  
They offer information, advice, and a chance to share experiences.

You can find local support groups through the **National Contact and Information Point for Encouraging and Supporting Self-Help Groups (NAKOS)**.  
Visit their website to search for groups near you.

# Bedwetting

It is common for children and even teenagers to wet the bed sometimes.  
Most children around age five can stay dry at night.  
Some children take longer to learn how to stay dry.  

## Quick Facts

- Many children and some teenagers wet the bed.  
- Most children are dry by age five.  
- Bedwetting usually happens because the child does not wake up when their bladder is full.  
- There are ways to help the child and improve the situation.  
- A child’s age of becoming dry at night is partly due to their genes.  

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself or your child.

---

## What Is Bedwetting?

Many children and some teenagers wet the bed now and then.  
But people often do not talk about it.  

Children around age five usually sleep through the night or wake up when they need to pee.  
Some children just take a little longer to learn this.  

If a child over five wets the bed regularly and there is no physical reason, it is called bedwetting.  
This is also known as “nocturnal enuresis.”  

It can be upsetting for the family, especially if it happens often.

---

## Why Does Bedwetting Happen?

Most children wet the bed because they do not wake up when their bladder is full.  
The muscle that holds urine in the bladder relaxes while they sleep.  
This causes the bladder to empty without the child knowing.

This is not the child’s fault.  
They cannot control it because their body is still growing and developing.

For a child to stay dry at night, three things must happen:

- The brain must notice when the bladder is full.  
- The child must be able to wake up and go to the bathroom.  
- The child must be able to control the muscle that holds urine.

Also, the body must make enough of a natural hormone at night.  
This hormone helps the kidneys make less urine at night.  

The bladder must also be big enough to hold the urine made during the night.

Studies show that bedwetting often runs in families.  
This means genes play a role in when a child learns to stay dry.

---

## How Often Does Bedwetting Happen?

Over 15 percent of children wet the bed at age five.  
The number goes down as children grow older.

Some children wet the bed once or twice a month.  
Others do it several times a week.

Boys are more likely to wet the bed than girls.  
Most children grow out of it on their own.

---

## When Does Bedwetting Start Again?

If a child has been dry for more than six months and then starts wetting the bed again, it is called secondary bedwetting.

This can be a sign of stress.  
Stress may come from family problems or big changes, like a new baby in the house.

But secondary bedwetting can also be caused by physical health issues.  
These include bladder or kidney infections, or diabetes.

---

## How Is Bedwetting Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose bedwetting if a child over five wets the bed more than once a week for at least three months.

Other health problems can cause bedwetting, but this is rare.  
Possible causes include:

- Urinary tract infections  
- Kidney problems  
- Diabetes  
- An overactive thyroid  
- Sleep apnea (pauses in breathing during sleep)

The doctor will talk to the child and parents.  
They will also do a physical exam.

They will check for signs of other problems, such as:

- Wetting during the day  
- Trouble starting or stopping the flow of urine  
- Pain when peeing  
- Peeing less than three times a day or more than eight times a day  
- A weak stream of urine  
- Feeling the bladder is not empty after peeing

It helps to keep track of:

- What and how much the child eats and drinks  
- When and how often the child goes to the bathroom

Doctors may suggest keeping a “bladder diary” to record this.  
They can give advice on how to do this.

A quick urine test can check for infections or diabetes.  
More tests are only done if there is a clear reason to suspect a medical problem.

---

## How Is Bedwetting Treated?

There is a lot of advice about stopping bedwetting.  
But not all of it works.

The most important thing is to help the child feel calm.  
Make it clear that bedwetting is not their fault.

You can try:

- Giving the child less to drink two hours before bedtime  
- Avoiding drinks with caffeine or sugar, like soda or lemonade

Alarm systems can help.  
These include special underwear or mats that make a sound when the first drops of urine are detected.  
The sound wakes the child so they can go to the bathroom.

But these alarms do not work for every child.  
Some sleep too deeply to wake up.

Another method is to gently wake the child during the night and take them to the bathroom.  
This is called “dream peeing.”

> **Important:** Medicine is not usually recommended for children under seven.  
> A medicine called desmopressin is used for older children.  
> It works like a natural hormone in the body.  
> It helps the kidneys make less urine at night.  
> The medicine works fast, but only while the child takes it.  
> It can help for short times, like when staying away from home.  
> It may also be used if alarm systems do not work.

For more details on treatment, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## How to Live With Bedwetting

It helps to know that bedwetting is common and usually goes away on its own.

You can make nighttime easier by preparing ahead:

- Use a waterproof mattress cover or protector  
- Keep clean sheets ready to change quickly  
- Use diapers or diaper pants if needed

The child can shower and change clothes in the morning.  
This removes any smell.  
They will not be teased at school.

To remove the smell from clothes and bedding:

- Use washing soda (sodium bicarbonate)  
- Use eucalyptus oil

For more tips on making daily life easier, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Excessive Hair Growth (Hypertrichosis)

Excessive hair growth is called hypertrichosis.  
It can happen all over the body or just in certain areas.  
It can be present from birth or develop later in life.  
Finding the cause is important for treatment.

## Quick Facts

- Hypertrichosis means too much hair growth.  
- It can affect the whole body or just one area.  
- It can be present from birth or start after birth.  
- Some medicines can cause it.  
- If the cause is found and fixed, the hair often goes away.  
- Laser treatment or root removal (epilation) can remove hair permanently.  

**Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Hypertrichosis?

Hypertrichosis means more hair than normal.  
It can happen in one spot or all over the body.  
It can be present from birth or start later in life.

There are three types of hair:

- Soft, fine hair that babies have (lanugo).  
- Light, soft, downy hair (vellus hair).  
- Thick, dark hair like the hair on your head, underarms, or genitals (terminal hair).

In a rare form called congenital hypertrichosis lanuginosa, the whole body is covered in long, fine, silver-gray or blond hair.  
This is the most noticeable type.

**Important:** Hypertrichosis is not the same as hirsutism.  
Hirsutism means women grow thick, dark hair in areas where men usually grow hair, like the face or chest.

## How Does Hypertrichosis Look?

Too much hair can cover the whole body.  
This is called generalized hypertrichosis.  
If it only happens in one area, it is called localized hypertrichosis.

The hair can look different:

- Thick and dark like head, underarm, or genital hair — this is terminal hair.  
- Light, soft, and downy — this is vellus hair.  
- Fine, soft hair that babies have — this is lanugo.  
  Lanugo usually goes away after birth.  
  But it can grow back if there is a serious illness like cancer.

Some areas that can have extra hair from congenital localized hypertrichosis include:

- Forearms  
- Elbow crease (cubital fossa)  
- Palms of the hands  
- Soles of the feet  
- Ears  
- Tip of the nose  
- Front and back of the neck

In congenital hypertrichosis lanuginosa, the whole body has up to 10 centimeters of long, fine, silver-gray or blond hair.  
Other symptoms may include:

- Teeth problems  
- Narrowing of the stomach opening (pyloric stenosis)  
- Eye problems

Sometimes, the whole body has more normal-looking hair.  
This means more thick hair on the back, arms, legs, and around the ears.

If the cause is a genetic problem, hypertrichosis may be part of a larger condition with other symptoms or physical differences.

The location and timing of the hair growth depend on what caused it.

## What Causes Hypertrichosis?

Different things can cause hypertrichosis, depending on the type.

### Hypertrichosis on the Whole Body

Some rare inherited conditions cause abnormal hair growth.  
In children before puberty, too much male hormone (testosterone) can cause it.

In adults, medicines are often the cause. These include:

- Antibiotics like streptomycin  
- Anti-inflammatory medicines like cortisone  
- Acetazolamide — a water pill (diuretic)  
- Phenytoin — a medicine for seizures  
- Cyclosporine and mycophenolate mofetil — medicines that lower the body’s immune response

If the extra hair is fine and soft like baby hair, it may be a sign of cancer.  
This is most often lung cancer or bowel cancer.

### Localized Hypertrichosis

Some birthmarks (moles) are very hairy.  
Some rare birth conditions also cause it, such as:

- Cornelia de Lange syndrome  
- Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome

Repeated skin injuries, chafing, or inflammation can also cause extra hair.  
For example:

- People who work with heavy lifting often get more hair on their backs.  
- After a limb is in a cast, pressure sores can lead to more hair growth.

## How Is Hypertrichosis Diagnosed?

Doctors can see hypertrichosis easily by looking at the hair.

First, they check if the hair growth was present from birth or started later.  
They ask about your family history and any medicines you take.

Next, they look at the type of hair.  
They also check for other physical differences or health problems.

If a rare genetic condition is suspected, they may do genetic tests or brain scans.  
If cancer is possible, they may use ultrasound, X-rays, or CT scans.

## How Is Hypertrichosis Treated?

Medically, hypertrichosis does not always need treatment.  
Some people are not bothered by it.

Others feel self-conscious and want to remove the hair.  
There are several ways to do this.

The easiest and fastest way is using hair removal creams.  
These remove hair at the surface.  
But the hair grows back quickly.  
They can also irritate the skin.

Laser treatment is the best way to remove hair permanently.  
It targets the hair root.  
This method works best when done by a trained professional.

Another method is electrolysis.  
This removes hair by destroying the root.  
It is also effective but takes time and needs a specialist.

If the hair growth is caused by a medicine, it often goes away when you stop taking the medicine.  
If the cause is found and removed, the hair usually stops growing.

If the hair growth is present from birth, it usually lasts a lifetime.  
It can also be passed on to children.

If the hair is very visible, it can cause emotional distress.  
In such cases, counseling or psychological support may help.

# Duodenal Ulcer

A duodenal ulcer is a sore in the first part of the small intestine. It can cause pain or no symptoms at all. This page explains what it is, how it shows up, how it is found, and how it is treated.

---

## Quick Facts

- Most duodenal ulcers are caused by a bacterial infection called *Helicobacter pylori*.
- Some ulcers happen from using painkillers like ibuprofen or aspirin for a long time.
- Ulcers from painkillers often cause no pain until they bleed.
- Common signs include stomach pain, feeling full too soon, not wanting to eat, nausea, and vomiting.
- The chance of getting an ulcer goes up with age.
- Doctors usually diagnose it with a gastroscopy, which uses a camera to look inside the stomach and small intestine.
- Treatment often includes medicines that reduce stomach acid. Sometimes antibiotics are added.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Duodenal Ulcer?

A duodenal ulcer is a deep sore in the lining of the duodenum. The duodenum is the first section of the small intestine. It connects the stomach to the rest of the intestine.

Most ulcers form just behind the opening where the stomach empties into the duodenum. The main causes are:

- Infection with *Helicobacter pylori* bacteria.
- Long-term use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen, aspirin, or diclofenac.

The risk of getting an ulcer increases with age.

Many people have no symptoms for a long time. Some only notice the problem when it causes serious issues like bleeding. Doctors usually find ulcers during a gastroscopy. A small tissue sample is taken to check for infection, inflammation, or cancer.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many people with a duodenal ulcer feel nothing at first. When symptoms do appear, they can include:

- A heavy or full feeling in the upper stomach.
- Not feeling hungry.
- Nausea, sometimes with vomiting.
- Gas, bloating, or irregular bowel movements.
- Heartburn or sour burps.

Unlike stomach ulcers, duodenal ulcers often hurt when the stomach is empty. Eating usually makes the pain go away.

---

## How Does a Duodenal Ulcer Develop?

Two main causes lead to duodenal ulcers:

1. **Infection with *Helicobacter pylori* bacteria.**
2. **Long-term use of NSAIDs** (like ibuprofen or aspirin).

These painkillers stop the body from making a natural substance called prostaglandin. Prostaglandin helps protect the stomach and duodenum from acid. Without it, stomach acid can build up and damage the lining.

In some cases, both the bacteria and painkillers cause the ulcer together.

> **Warning:** Taking cortisone along with NSAIDs can make the damage worse.

---

## What Complications Can Happen?

If left untreated, a duodenal ulcer can lead to serious problems.

### Bleeding
- Black or tarry stools.
- Vomiting blood (red or black).
- Feeling very tired, weak, or short of breath.
- Pale skin.

These signs mean you need to see a doctor right away.

### Narrowing of the Stomach Outlet
- Repeated vomiting after eating.
- This happens if scar tissue forms around the opening between the stomach and the intestine.
- The opening gets too small, so food cannot pass through.

### Perforation (Hole in the Wall)
- Sudden, severe stomach pain.
- This is a medical emergency.
- Call emergency services (112) immediately if you think this is happening.

---

## How Can You Prevent a Duodenal Ulcer?

We do not yet know for sure if things like diet, smoking, or stress cause ulcers. But some people notice that their symptoms get worse with:

- Greasy or spicy foods.
- Alcohol.
- Stressful situations.

If you notice this, try to avoid those triggers.

If you take painkillers often, talk to your doctor. They may suggest medicines that reduce stomach acid to protect your stomach.

Always talk to your doctor about your personal risk and safe treatment options.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

If your doctor suspects an ulcer, they will:

1. Feel your stomach with their hands to check for tenderness.
2. Perform a gastroscopy. This is a test where a thin tube with a camera goes down your throat into your stomach and small intestine.

During the test, the doctor takes a small tissue sample. This sample is checked for:

- *Helicobacter pylori* bacteria.
- Signs of inflammation.
- Changes that could be cancer.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the test results.

### Some ulcers heal on their own in 2 to 3 months. But they often come back.

### If no bacteria are found:
- You will take a medicine called a proton pump inhibitor (PPI), such as omeprazole or pantoprazole.
- These reduce stomach acid.
- You take them for 4 to 8 weeks.

### If *Helicobacter pylori* is found:
- You take two different antibiotics plus a PPI (called triple therapy).
- This treatment lasts 1 to 2 weeks.
- After that, you may continue the PPI alone if needed.

### If the ulcer is caused by painkillers:
- Stop or switch the painkiller if possible.
- Quit smoking and avoid alcohol, or at least take a break.

### If antibiotics don’t work (due to resistance):
- A quadruple therapy may be used. This includes three antibiotics and a PPI.
- This also lasts 1 to 2 weeks.

### After Treatment:
- A test is done 4 weeks after finishing antibiotics.
- A special breath test (13C breath test) checks if the bacteria are still in your stomach.
- If they are still there, the treatment is repeated with different medicines.

### For Severe Bleeding:
- Doctors use a small camera (endoscopy) to stop the bleeding through a tiny cut in the belly.
- In rare cases, open surgery is needed.

---

> **Always follow your doctor’s advice.** Do not stop or change your treatment without talking to them.

# Postpartum Depression

Many women feel sad or low for a few days after giving birth. This is normal and usually goes away on its own. But postpartum depression is stronger and lasts longer. It can make you feel very mixed emotions about your baby.

This condition can be very hard on you. It can affect how you care for your baby and how you feel about yourself. If you do not get help, the sadness may last for months.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor or mental health professional.

---

## What Is Postpartum Depression?

Most women look forward to being with their new baby. But some feel sad or upset after the baby arrives. If these feelings last only a few days, it is called the "baby blues." This is common and usually gets better with rest and support.

If the low mood lasts more than two weeks, it may be postpartum depression. This is a real illness. It can affect your health and your relationship with your baby.

You should take strong feelings of sadness or mood swings seriously. Get help if they do not go away.

---

## What Are the Signs of Postpartum Depression?

Postpartum depression has the same symptoms as regular depression. But it often includes strong feelings of guilt. You may feel like you are failing as a mother. You may worry that you are not good enough for your baby.

Many women feel too ashamed to talk about their feelings. They may feel alone and scared. Some say they feel like a stranger to themselves.

The baby blues are different. They are a short-term low mood that most women feel after giving birth. It usually lasts only a few days. Sometimes it can last up to two weeks.

Common baby blues symptoms include:
- Mood swings
- Crying
- Feeling irritable

Most women feel better with support and understanding.

Postpartum depression is much stronger. The symptoms last longer and are harder to shake. They include:

- Feeling deeply sad or empty
- Crying often
- Feeling hopeless
- Losing interest in things you used to enjoy
- Feeling anxious
- Trouble sleeping
- Not feeling hungry
- Trouble focusing or making decisions
- Doubting yourself
- Having negative thoughts
- Thinking about hurting yourself or your baby

These symptoms must last at least two weeks to be considered postpartum depression.

---

## What Causes Postpartum Depression?

Becoming a mother is hard. It is both physically and emotionally tough. Some women feel overwhelmed by the stress. This can lead to depression.

Certain things make it more likely:
- You have had depression or anxiety before
- You had a lot of stress during pregnancy or after birth
- You are in a bad relationship
- You live alone
- You have no support from family or friends
- You have experienced violence at home

The role of hormone changes after birth is still not fully understood.

---

## How Common Is Postpartum Depression?

About 15 out of every 100 women feel depressed in the first three months after giving birth. Some have mild symptoms. Others have more serious symptoms.

---

## How Does It Progress?

Without treatment, postpartum depression can last for months. It often lasts between 4 and 6 months. In some cases, symptoms can still be there after a year.

Getting help early can stop the depression from lasting a long time.

---

## Can It Be Prevented?

Yes, support can help prevent postpartum depression. Regular visits from a midwife or trained helper can make a big difference.

Talking to a therapist can also help. It can stop your mood from getting worse.

In Germany, there is a program called “Early Support” (Frühe Hilfen). It helps women and families who are under stress. This includes:
- Mothers who have little help from others
- Parents who feel unsure about caring for their baby

The program is free. It offers things like:
- Support from a family midwife
- Parent meetings
- Advice and guidance

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor or therapist will diagnose postpartum depression after talking with you.

They will:
- Ask about your symptoms
- Check if other health problems could be causing your feelings

They may do a physical exam to rule out other causes.

---

## How Is It Treated?

For mild cases, more emotional support and help with daily tasks may be enough. The people around you should be kind and understanding. They should encourage you.

Talking to other women who have been through the same thing can help. You can talk to friends, family, or join a self-help group.

For moderate to severe cases, professional help is needed. A therapist or trained counselor can help you:
- Feel better about yourself
- Build a stronger bond with your baby

Studies show this kind of help makes life easier for many women.

Antidepressants can also help. But they are usually only used if:
- Your symptoms are very strong
- support from family or a therapist is not enough

If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, talk to your doctor before taking any medicine. Most antidepressants are safe, but doctors use the lowest possible dose. This is because small amounts can pass into breast milk.

Other helpful things include:
- Exercise, especially walking, cycling, or swimming
- Running regularly
- Yoga

These activities can improve your mood.

For more information, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## Where Can You Get Help?

Many people with depression find it hard to ask for help. Their family may also feel lost and unsure what to do.

But there are people who can help. You are not alone.

You can start by visiting:
- Your family doctor (general practitioner)
- A gynecologist
- A psychotherapist

You can see a psychotherapist without a doctor’s referral. You do not need to contact your health insurance first.

Pregnancy and parenting advice centers also offer support after birth.

To find a local advice center, visit: [BZgA – Bundeszentrale für gesundheitliche Aufklärung](https://www.bzga.de)

The website [elternsein.info](https://www.elternsein.info) has information in German about life with a baby, including feelings after birth.

The organization “Schatten & Licht e. V.” offers detailed help and information about mental health after childbirth. Visit their website for more.

# Vitiligo

Vitiligo is a skin condition that causes white patches to appear on the skin.  
The exact cause is not known.  
It does not hurt and it cannot be passed from one person to another.  
Many people feel upset about how their skin looks.  
Some feel judged or treated differently because of the changes in their skin.

## Quick Facts

- Vitiligo stops the skin from making its natural brown color.  
- The skin cells that make this color are called melanocytes.  
- In vitiligo, the body’s immune system may attack these cells.  
- This leads to white patches on the skin.  
- Vitiligo often starts between the ages of 10 and 30.  
- The first patches usually appear on the face, hands, or feet.  
- If patches are only in one or a few spots, it is called localized vitiligo.  
- If patches appear in many places, it is called generalized vitiligo.  
- Some treatments can help restore some color to the skin.  
- Special makeup can cover the white patches.  
- It is important to protect the white areas from sun and other skin irritants.  

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor.  
> Do not use this to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Vitiligo?

Vitiligo is a skin condition that causes the loss of natural skin color.  
The skin normally gets its color from a pigment called melanin.  
Melanin is made by special skin cells called melanocytes.  
In vitiligo, these cells are damaged.  
This damage may happen because the body’s immune system attacks them.  
When the cells stop working, the skin loses color and turns white.  
The white patches can appear anywhere on the body.  
They are often more noticeable on people with darker skin.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Vitiligo does not usually cause pain or itching.  
Some people feel itchy when new patches are forming.  
The white patches stand out clearly against normal skin.  
They are usually small at first — a few millimeters to a few centimeters.  
They can be round, oval, or shaped like lines.  
Over time, patches may grow and join together to form larger areas.  
The most common places for patches are around the mouth and eyes, on the hands, feet, and genitals.  
Friction or pressure on the skin can cause new patches to appear.  
This is called the Koebner phenomenon.

## What Causes Vitiligo?

Doctors do not know the exact cause.  
But some people with vitiligo have family members with the same condition.  
This suggests that genes may play a role.  
It may also be linked to other health problems involving the immune system.

## How Common Is Vitiligo?

Vitiligo is fairly common.  
It affects up to 2 out of every 100 people worldwide.  
It can happen in people of all races and ages.

## How Does Vitiligo Change Over Time?

Vitiligo is a long-term condition.  
It can change in different ways for different people.  
If it starts at a young age, it often spreads faster.  
Some people have times when the skin stops losing color.  
Other times, the skin loses more color.  
In some cases, the skin may regain color on its own.  
Treatments can help improve the skin’s color.  
But there is no cure for vitiligo.

## How Is Vitiligo Diagnosed?

A doctor can usually tell if someone has vitiligo by looking at the skin.  
They will ask about:  
- When the patches first appeared  
- How the patches have changed over time  
- Other health problems, such as thyroid issues  
- Exposure to chemicals or radiation  
- Medicines being taken  
- Whether other family members have vitiligo  

A special light called a Wood’s lamp may be used.  
It helps doctors see changes in skin color that are not visible under normal light.

## How Is Vitiligo Treated?

If the patches are spreading fast, doctors may prescribe anti-inflammatory creams.  
These creams help slow down the spread.  
They can be used alone or with light therapy using UVB rays.  
The white skin does not tan and burns easily in the sun.  
This increases the risk of skin cancer.  
Use sunscreen with high protection against both UVA and UVB rays.  
Apply it every day, even on cloudy days.  
Wear long sleeves, pants, or special clothing with UV protection when outside.  
If you have another health problem, such as Hashimoto’s disease, treat that too.

## How Can You Live Better with Vitiligo?

Many people with vitiligo feel sad, anxious, or embarrassed.  
Children may be teased or bullied at school.  
This can hurt self-confidence and lower quality of life.  
Talking to a counselor or joining a support group can help.  
Some people find it helpful to use special makeup to cover the patches.  
This is especially useful for the face.  
It can boost confidence and make daily life easier.

# Sepsis

Sepsis is a serious condition that happens when your body’s response to an infection goes wrong.  
It is also called blood poisoning, but it is not the same as being poisoned by a chemical.  
Sepsis always starts with an infection that your body can no longer control.  
The infection causes your immune system to overreact.  
This overreaction releases chemicals that damage your own organs.  
Sepsis can be life-threatening and must be treated as an emergency.

---

## Quick Facts

- Sepsis happens when your body’s reaction to an infection harms your own organs.  
- It can affect many vital organs at once.  
- About one in three people in Germany who get sepsis or septic shock die from it each year.  
- Sepsis is more common than stroke, breast cancer, or bowel cancer.  
- Any case of sepsis is an emergency.  

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Sepsis?

Sepsis always starts with a local infection.  
The infection is most often caused by bacteria.  
But viruses, fungi, and parasites can also cause it.  
Sepsis is not poisoning. It is your body’s immune system going into overdrive.  
The germs and the chemicals your body releases spread through your blood.  
They can damage your lungs, heart, liver, kidneys, and other organs.  
You need hospital treatment right away to survive.  
Sepsis is the third most common cause of death in Germany.  
Each year, about one third of people who get sepsis or septic shock die.

Would you like to learn how to prevent sepsis or spot it early?  
Check out the infographic on the website of the Robert Koch Institute.

For help recognizing sepsis and avoiding serious harm, visit the website of *Deutschland erkennt Sepsis* (Germany recognizes sepsis).  
This is a patient safety initiative.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

At first, sepsis may feel like a bad cold or the flu.  
These early signs can include:

- A fever above 38 degrees Celsius  
- A body temperature below 36 degrees Celsius  
- Shaking or chills  
- A fast heartbeat  
- Feeling very unwell  
- Body aches

Warning signs that sepsis may be developing:

- Sudden confusion or disorientation  
- Low blood pressure: systolic below 100 mmHg  
- Breathing faster than 22 times per minute

If you or someone else has at least one of these warning signs, get medical help right away.  
Sepsis is always an emergency.

> **Important:** Systolic blood pressure is the pressure in your blood vessels when your heart beats.  
> It is the first number when blood pressure is measured.  
> A normal value is between 110 and 130 mmHg.  
> A value below 100 mmHg is dangerous, especially for older adults.

A red streak slowly spreading on the arm can be a sign of sepsis.  
But most people with sepsis do not have this symptom.  
The red streak happens when a lymph vessel becomes inflamed.  
This can happen after an infected wound.  
It may lead to sepsis, but it does not always do so.

---

## What Causes Sepsis?

Sepsis is always caused by an infection.  
Most often, it is caused by bacteria.  
Viruses, fungi, and parasites can also cause it.  
As long as the infection stays in one place, sepsis does not happen.  
But if the infection spreads into the blood, the body’s immune system overreacts.  
This can damage organs and cause a dangerous drop in blood pressure.

Any kind of infection can lead to sepsis.  
Examples include:

- Infected skin wounds or boils  
- Mosquito bites  
- Tooth infections  
- Infected artificial joints or implants  
- Pneumonia  
- Meningitis  
- Urinary tract infections  
- Severe diarrhea

Sepsis is the final stage when your body can no longer control the infection.

---

## How Does Sepsis Develop?

Sepsis can become life-threatening very quickly.  
But it does not always get worse.  
Doctors divide sepsis into two stages:

### Sepsis

This happens when the body’s immune response harms your organs.  
Your immune cells and chemicals attack your lungs, heart, liver, kidneys, and other organs.  
This can reduce how well they work.

### Septic Shock

This is a more serious stage.  
Your blood pressure drops so low that your organs do not get enough blood.  
This can cause multiple organs to fail.  
Many people die from septic shock.

---

## How Can Sepsis Be Prevented?

You cannot be protected directly against sepsis.  
But you can prevent the infections that can lead to sepsis.  
These steps help reduce your risk:

- Wash your hands often and well.  
- Take care of cuts, scrapes, and skin infections.  
- Keep wounds clean and use antiseptic.  
- Do not scratch infected areas.  
- See a doctor if you think you have an infection.  
- If your doctor prescribes antibiotics, take them exactly as told and for the full time.  
- Treat long-term health problems like rheumatism or diabetes properly.  
- Stay healthy by eating well, exercising, and getting enough sleep.  
- Get recommended vaccinations to avoid certain infections.

---

## How Is Sepsis Diagnosed?

Doctors look at your symptoms and medical history.  
They take blood samples to check how your organs are working.  
They also test for germs in the blood.

---

## How Is Sepsis Treated?

Sepsis must be treated in a hospital.  
It is always an emergency.  
The faster treatment starts, the better your chances of recovery.  
The less damage you may suffer.

Before test results come back, doctors give you antibiotics.  
These work against the most common germs that cause sepsis.  
You also get fluids through a vein to help your blood pressure.  
Once the test results are in, doctors switch to the best medicine for your specific infection.

If your blood pressure drops too low or your blood has too little oxygen, you will need intensive care.  
If doctors do not know where the infection started, they will do more tests.  
They need to find the source so they can treat it properly.

---

## Where Can I Get Help After Sepsis?

Many people who survive severe sepsis face long-term problems.  
These can include physical weakness, memory issues, or mental health challenges.  
High-quality aftercare is not always available.  
For example, there may not be enough spots in rehabilitation centers.

Organizations like *Deutsche Sepsis-Hilfe e.V.* offer support.  
They provide information, help you find services, and connect you with others who have been through sepsis.

Visit the website of *Deutsche Sepsis-Hilfe e.V.* for more help.

---

## Other Useful Information

Every year on September 13th, there is a *World Sepsis Day*.  
This day raises awareness about how common sepsis is.  
It also highlights how many people die from it.  
The goal is to improve early detection and treatment so more lives can be saved.

# Frozen Shoulder
