Frozen shoulder happens slowly. It starts with mild pain. Over time, the pain gets worse. It can even keep you awake at night. The shoulder becomes stiff. Eventually, it is hard to move the arm at all. Most people get better without treatment. But it can take months or even years.

---

## What Is Frozen Shoulder?

Frozen shoulder means your shoulder becomes stiff and painful. It often starts around age 50. The cause is not always clear. The shoulder joint gets tight because of extra scar tissue. This tissue forms inside the joint capsule. The joint capsule is a strong layer of fibers around the shoulder joint.

Doctors call this condition "adhesive capsulitis" or "periarthritis." The name "frozen shoulder" comes from how the arm feels stuck and hard to move.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

- At first, the pain is mild.
- Over time, the pain gets worse.
- You may feel pain at night, even when not moving.
- The pain can feel dull or deep. It may spread to the biceps.
- The shoulder becomes harder to move.
- You may struggle to raise your arm or reach behind your back.
- Simple tasks become hard. These include:
  - Dressing
  - Cooking
  - Cleaning
  - Reaching into your back pocket
  - Changing gears while driving
- Some people can no longer do their job, especially if they work with their arms above shoulder level.

Other people may not understand how bad it is. There is no visible injury. No swelling or bruising. This can make it hard to get support.

Frozen shoulder often goes unnoticed until the symptoms are severe.

---

## What Causes Frozen Shoulder?

Joints connect bones. In the shoulder, the top of the upper arm bone fits into a socket in the shoulder blade. A strong layer of fibers, called the joint capsule, surrounds this joint.

In frozen shoulder, too much scar tissue forms inside the joint capsule. This tissue tightens and shrinks. The shoulder becomes stiff. Inflammation likely plays a role. But doctors do not yet know exactly why this happens.

In rare cases, frozen shoulder follows:
- An injury
- Surgery
- A period of not moving the shoulder (like after surgery)

When it happens after another problem, doctors call it "secondary frozen shoulder."

---

## How Common Is It?

- Most people get frozen shoulder between ages 40 and 60.
- About 2 to 5 out of every 100 people will have it in their lifetime.
- Women are slightly more likely than men.
- People with diabetes are at higher risk. Up to 1 in 5 people with diabetes get frozen shoulder.
- The reason for this link is not yet known.

---

## How Does It Progress?

Frozen shoulder has three stages. They overlap and can last for months or years.

### Stage 1: Painful Stage
- Pain starts and gets worse over time.
- Pain may happen at night or when the shoulder is still.
- The shoulder is still somewhat movable.

### Stage 2: Frozen Stage
- The shoulder becomes very stiff.
- Movement is very limited.
- Pain often gets better, even though the shoulder is frozen.

### Stage 3: Thawing Stage
- The shoulder slowly starts to move again.
- Mobility improves over time.
- Many people feel much better after a few months.

No one can predict how long it will take. Some people feel better in a year or two. Others take much longer. One study found that about 6 out of every 100 people still had serious symptoms after 4 years.

Most people only get frozen shoulder once. But 6 to 17 out of every 100 people go on to get it in the other shoulder within 5 years.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Not all shoulder pain means frozen shoulder. Doctors diagnose it by:

- Talking to you about your symptoms
- Examining your shoulder

During the exam:
- The doctor feels the shoulder.
- They check how far you can move your arm and shoulder.
- You stand with arms out to the side at shoulder height.
- The doctor watches how your shoulder blade moves.

In frozen shoulder, the shoulder blade on the affected side lifts all the way up. In a healthy shoulder, it does not.

Sometimes, doctors order:
- A shoulder X-ray
- An MRI scan

These help rule out other problems like arthritis. They can also help find the cause if it is unclear.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Frozen shoulder often gets better on its own. But treatment can help with pain and movement.

### First Step: Reduce Pain
- Cortisone tablets or injections into the shoulder can help reduce pain.
- Heat or cold packs may feel good to some people.

### Later Step: Improve Movement
- Stretching exercises and physiotherapy help restore movement and strength.
- Start gently. Do not force the arm.
- Stop if you feel sharp or severe pain.

### Medication
- Painkillers like ibuprofen (in tablets or creams) are not very helpful for frozen shoulder.

### Surgery
- Surgery is rarely needed.
- It carries risks, including from anesthesia.
- There is no strong proof that surgery helps more than other treatments.
- Doctors may suggest surgery only if symptoms do not improve after months of conservative treatment.

If surgery is suggested, you have the right to get a second medical opinion.

> **Tip:** The decision aid from gesundheitsinformation.de can help you choose the best treatment for your situation.

# Oral Thrush (Oral Candidiasis)

Your mouth may feel fuzzy or furry. This could be a sign of oral thrush. It is usually not serious. But it can be very uncomfortable. A weak immune system makes you more likely to get oral thrush. Learn more below.

---

## Quick Facts

- Oral thrush is not always easy to spot right away.
- It is caused by a type of yeast called candida. The most common type is called Candida albicans.
- The condition is usually not dangerous. But it can cause a lot of discomfort.
- The yeast can grow fast if your immune system is weak.
- Other things can also make it more likely. These include dentures, diabetes, and some medicines.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Oral Thrush?

Oral thrush is caused by a yeast called candida. The most common type is Candida albicans. It is also called oral candidiasis.

This yeast lives in the mouth of many people without causing harm. But under certain conditions, it can grow too much. This can happen if your immune system is weak. It can also happen after certain treatments.

Oral thrush is not always easy to see. It is usually not painful. But it can still make life hard and uncomfortable.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The most common sign is white patches in the mouth or throat. These patches can be gently scraped off. Underneath, the skin looks red and swollen. It may bleed a little.

Even if you brush your teeth well, your mouth may still feel fuzzy. Your sense of taste may change. You may feel pain or a burning feeling on your tongue.

These symptoms can make eating and drinking hard. If the infection is severe, it can be hard to swallow or speak.

---

## What Causes Oral Thrush?

Oral thrush often happens during or after an illness. It can also be a side effect of treatment.

It is common in people getting cancer treatment. Chemotherapy can damage the mouth lining. It can also weaken your immune system. This makes it easier for yeast to grow.

Radiation therapy to the head or neck also raises the risk. The stronger the treatment, the higher the risk.

Other causes include:

- Dentures that do not fit well
- Diabetes
- Long-term use of strong antibiotics
- Weak immune systems, such as in people with HIV/AIDS

People who are very weak, eat little, drink little, or need feeding tubes are also at higher risk.

---

## How Can You Prevent Oral Thrush?

Healthy people do not need special steps to prevent it.

If you are at higher risk, you can take action. For example, people with cancer or HIV/AIDS may take antifungal medicine to prevent infection.

Antifungals are medicines that stop fungi from growing or kill them.

There is not enough research yet on other ways to prevent oral thrush. But good oral hygiene helps. Brush your teeth and clean your mouth every day.

For more tips on prevention, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## How Is Oral Thrush Diagnosed?

If you are at risk, tell your doctor or nurse right away if your mouth burns or hurts.

They will look inside your mouth. If they are not sure, they will take a small sample. They use a clean cotton swab to collect a bit of the white patch. Then they send it to a lab for testing.

People with cancer or HIV/AIDS should have their mouth checked often. This helps catch any infection early.

You can also check your own mouth in a mirror. Look for white patches or red, sore areas. A family member or nurse can help you look.

---

## How Is Oral Thrush Treated?

Doctors treat oral thrush with antifungal medicines.

Some medicines are applied directly to the mouth. Others are swallowed or drunk. The swallowed medicines travel through your body.

Even when you apply medicine to the mouth, some of it goes into your stomach through saliva. Some of it is absorbed there and spreads through your body.

Studies show that swallowing antifungal medicine works better than applying it directly. But it can cause side effects. These include:

- Headaches
- Skin rashes
- Nausea
- Bloating
- Diarrhea

The right medicine depends on your health and how bad the infection is. Most people take the medicine for 1 to 2 weeks.

To help your mouth feel better:

- Eat soft foods
- Avoid hot drinks
- Do not drink alcohol
- Use honey instead of sugar to sweeten food and drinks

# Meniscus Tear

A meniscus tear is a common knee injury, especially in sports like soccer. It happens when the knee twists while under pressure. This can happen suddenly during sports or over time due to wear and tear.

---

## Quick Facts

- The meniscus is made of two C-shaped pieces of cartilage in the knee.
- One is on the inside of the knee. The other is on the outside.
- These pieces help the knee move smoothly and absorb shock.
- Meniscus tears are very common in sports, especially ball sports.
- Some small tears do not cause immediate pain or swelling.
- Treatment depends on the size, type, and location of the tear, and on your symptoms.
- About one in every 1,000 people gets a meniscus tear each year.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Meniscus Tear?

A meniscus tear happens when the knee twists while bent, especially if the foot is planted on the ground. This often occurs during sports.

- Tears from sudden injuries usually happen in younger people.
- Most of these tears need surgery.
- Sometimes, they can be treated without surgery using pain relief, bandages, and exercises.

There are also tears caused by aging and wear and tear. These are called degenerative tears.

- These tears are common in older adults.
- They often do not cause pain or problems.
- Surgery usually does not help with these types of tears.
- People with knee osteoarthritis often have meniscus damage from wear and tear.
- For these cases, staying active and managing osteoarthritis is key.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

If the tear is from a sudden injury, you may feel:

- Pain when twisting or bending the knee.
- Swelling in the knee.
- A popping or cracking sound at the time of injury.

Smaller tears may not cause pain right away. You might only feel pain hours or even days later. Some people do not notice the injury for weeks.

Larger tears usually cause:

- More pain.
- Swelling.
- A feeling that the knee is stuck or locked.
- Trouble moving the knee normally.

Age-related meniscus tears often cause no symptoms at all. For example:

- 20 out of 100 people over age 40 had meniscus tears or changes without any pain.
- In people with knee osteoarthritis, about 60 out of 100 have meniscus damage seen on X-rays.

---

## What Causes a Meniscus Tear?

The meniscus is a cushion between the thigh bone (femur) and the shin bone (tibia). It helps the knee move smoothly and absorb impact.

- The inner meniscus is on the inside of the knee.
- The outer meniscus is on the outside.
- The inner meniscus is less flexible and more likely to tear.

Acute tears happen when the knee twists while bent. This often occurs during sports when you stop suddenly and change direction.

- The force can be strong enough to tear the meniscus.
- The inner meniscus is more likely to tear because it is less mobile.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

You are more likely to get a meniscus tear if:

- You play sports like soccer, basketball, tennis, or handball.
- You often run fast and then stop or change direction suddenly.
- You have had a previous injury to the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).
- Your job requires a lot of bending or kneeling.
- You are very overweight.
- You climb many stairs regularly.
- You are a man (wear-related tears are more common in men).

---

## How Common Are Meniscus Tears?

- Exact numbers in Germany are not known.
- About one in 1,000 people gets a meniscus injury each year.
- Age-related changes in the meniscus are very common.
- These changes often do not cause symptoms and do not need treatment.

---

## How Long Do Symptoms Last?

Recovery time depends on:

- The size and type of tear.
- Whether other knee ligaments were injured.
- The treatment you receive.
- Your overall health.

- If the damaged part of the meniscus is removed, you can usually walk and jog again after about 6 weeks.
- But it may take several months to feel fully confident in all activities.

- If the meniscus is stitched back together, recovery takes longer.
- You may need 4 to 6 months before returning to most activities.

Some people still feel mild pain when climbing stairs, squatting, or kneeling after surgery.

---

## What Can Happen If a Meniscus Tear Is Not Treated?

Untreated meniscus tears can lead to:

- Severe pain.
- Swelling that limits movement.
- A higher risk of developing knee osteoarthritis over time.
- Even more risk of osteoarthritis if part of the meniscus is removed during surgery.

---

## How Is a Meniscus Tear Diagnosed?

Your doctor will:

- Ask how the injury happened.
- Check your symptoms.
- Feel your knee to find tender spots.
- Move your knee in different ways to test for pain or clicking.

They may also use imaging tests:

- **MRI scan:** Shows detailed images of the meniscus. It is useful if:
  - Other knee injuries are suspected.
  - Surgery is being considered.

- **Ultrasound:** Can only show the outer part of the meniscus.
- **X-rays:** Do not show meniscus damage. But they can help if a bone injury is suspected.

---

## How Is a Meniscus Tear Treated?

For the first few days after injury:

- Rest the knee.
- Keep the leg raised to reduce swelling.
- Apply cold packs to the knee.

Avoid:

- Squatting.
- Kneeling.
- Twisting the knee.
- Any activity that causes pain.

### Conservative Treatment (Without Surgery)

This may be enough if:

- The knee does not lock or get stuck.
- The tear is minor and only causes temporary pain.

Options include:

- Painkillers that reduce inflammation, like ibuprofen or diclofenac.
- Wearing a knee bandage for support.
- Losing weight if you are very overweight.
- Exercises to strengthen the leg muscles and improve balance and movement.

### Surgery Is Usually Needed If:

- The knee cannot straighten fully (like a bucket handle tear).
- Pain is severe and keeps coming back.
- The tear could lead to osteoarthritis.
- Other knee structures, like the cruciate ligament, are also damaged.

During surgery:

- A small camera is used to look inside the knee (arthroscopy).
- Damaged parts of the meniscus are removed or trimmed.
- The doctor tries to keep as much healthy meniscus as possible.

For more information, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## What Happens After Surgery?

Rehabilitation is important to help your knee work well again.

- A physiotherapist will guide you through exercises.
- You will learn how to strengthen your leg muscles in daily life.
- Your doctor and physiotherapist will work together to make a plan.

Recovery time depends on the type of surgery:

- If part of the meniscus was removed:
  - You can walk normally after about 1 week.
  - You can return to sports after about 6 weeks.

- If the meniscus was stitched:
  - You must not put weight on the leg for 6 weeks.
  - This is to protect the stitches.
  - You can usually start jogging after 4 months.
  - You can return to ball sports after about 6 months.

Even after recovery, some people still feel mild pain when climbing stairs, squatting, or kneeling.

# Inflammation of the Epiglottis (Epiglottitis)

Epiglottitis is a serious condition where the tissue around the epiglottis swells.  
The epiglottis is a small flap of tissue at the back of the throat.  
It closes off the windpipe when you swallow.  
This keeps food and drink from going into your airway.

When the epiglottis becomes inflamed, the swelling can block your airway.  
This makes it hard to breathe.  
In severe cases, it can lead to life-threatening breathing problems.  
This is a medical emergency.  
You must get help right away.

A vaccine can prevent this condition in children.

---

## Quick Facts

- Epiglottitis is usually caused by a bacterial infection.
- It is rare. It mostly affects young children and people with weak immune systems.
- It can happen in children between the ages of 6 and 12.
- Swelling around the epiglottis can cause a sore throat and trouble breathing.
- In serious cases, it can lead to suffocation.
- If you think someone has epiglottitis, call emergency services immediately.
- In Germany, the vaccination committee recommends the Hib vaccine for children up to age 4.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Epiglottitis?

Epiglottitis is an infection that causes swelling in the epiglottis.  
The epiglottis is a small, flexible piece of cartilage at the top of the windpipe.  
It acts like a lid.  
It closes when you swallow to keep food and drink out of your lungs.

Most cases are caused by bacteria.  
The infection leads to swelling in the tissues around the epiglottis.  
This swelling can block the airway.  
It makes breathing very difficult.  
In some cases, it can stop breathing completely.

This is a life-threatening situation.  
It needs emergency medical care.

Other common signs include:
- High fever
- Trouble swallowing
- Feeling very tired or weak
- Feeling anxious or restless
- Drooling

In young children, the most common cause is a bacterium called *Haemophilus influenzae type b*, or Hib.  
Children who have not been vaccinated against Hib are at higher risk.

People with weakened immune systems are also more likely to get epiglottitis.  
This includes people with cancer or HIV.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Children with epiglottitis often have trouble breathing.  
They may struggle to breathe in.  
They may not cough, even though they are having breathing problems.

You might hear a high-pitched sound when they breathe in.  
This is called stridor.  
It sounds like a whistle or a raspy noise.

Children often sit up or stand.  
They lean forward with their head tilted back.  
This position helps them breathe better.

Other symptoms include:
- High fever
- Feeling very tired
- Restlessness or anxiety
- Drooling

In adults, the main symptoms are:
- Severe sore throat
- Trouble swallowing
- Drooling because they cannot swallow saliva
- Difficulty speaking clearly

---

## What Causes Epiglottitis?

In children, the most common cause is the bacterium *Haemophilus influenzae type b* (Hib).  
This same bacterium causes about one in four cases in adults.

Other causes include:
- Different types of bacteria
- Viruses (less common)
- Fungi (rare)
- Injury to the throat

---

## How Common Is It?

Epiglottitis is rare.  
Since the Hib vaccine was introduced in 1990, cases have dropped sharply.

Before the vaccine:
- About 10 out of every 200,000 children under age 4 got epiglottitis each year.

Now:
- Only about 1 out of every 200,000 children under age 4 gets it.

In adults, the number of cases has stayed about the same.  
There are 2 to 4 cases per 200,000 adults each year.  
This is now higher than the rate in children.

---

## How Can It Be Prevented?

You can prevent epiglottitis by getting the Hib vaccine.  
This vaccine protects against the bacterium *Haemophilus influenzae type b*.

In Germany, the vaccination committee recommends this vaccine for children up to age 4.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

If you suspect epiglottitis, call emergency services right away.  
Do not wait. Dial 112.

Doctors will check:
- How the person is breathing
- How much oxygen is in the blood
- Whether the child has had the Hib vaccine

They may use a small mirror to look at the throat.  
This is called a laryngoscopy.  
They may also take a swab from the epiglottis to test for bacteria.

**Important:** Swelling in the throat can also happen with a condition called false croup.  
But false croup usually causes a barking cough.  
It does not cause trouble swallowing.  
False croup is more common in winter.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Epiglottitis must be treated in a hospital.  
Some people need care in an intensive care unit.

The main goal is to keep the airway open.  
Doctors will reduce the swelling and help the person breathe.

They may give medicine to reduce swelling.  
This is usually anti-inflammatory medicine.

If the person is not getting enough oxygen, they will get oxygen through a mask.

In serious cases, doctors may need to:
- Use a breathing machine (ventilator)
- Make a small hole in the windpipe (tracheotomy) to help breathing

If the cause is a bacterial infection, antibiotics are given.  
These medicines kill the bacteria.

With fast treatment, symptoms usually improve in a few days.  
The epiglottis heals without lasting damage.

# Cruciate Ligament Rupture

A cruciate ligament rupture often happens during ball sports or skiing. Women are more likely to get this injury than men. Whether you need surgery depends on how bad the injury is, how stable your knee feels, your age, and other personal factors.

---

## Quick Facts

- The anterior cruciate ligament is one of four major ligaments in the knee. It is the most commonly injured.
- Most injuries happen during sports, like falling while skiing or twisting your knee while playing soccer.
- Women are more likely to suffer this injury than men.
- Surgery is not always needed. Your doctor will decide based on the injury, knee stability, and your age and lifestyle.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Cruciate Ligament Rupture?

The anterior cruciate ligament helps keep your knee stable. It stops the lower leg bone from sliding forward. It also helps prevent the knee from twisting.

Most ruptures happen during sports. The injury often occurs when the knee twists suddenly or when you land badly after a jump.

You do not always need surgery. Whether you have surgery depends on how bad the injury is, how stable your knee feels, and your age. Your job, hobbies, and sports goals also matter.

Ruptures of the back cruciate ligament are rare. This article does not cover that type.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

When the ligament tears, you may hear a pop or snap. Your knee will likely swell quickly. It will hurt, especially when you move it.

Many people can still walk after the injury. But the knee feels wobbly. It may feel like the upper and lower leg are sliding a little. This happens when you bend your knee, turn sideways, or go up stairs.

In about 90% of cases, other parts of the knee are injured too:

- 50 to 75% of people also injure one or both menisci (cushioning pads in the knee).
- About half have damage to the joint cartilage.
- About 15% injure the inner or outer knee ligaments.
- Bones near the knee are often bruised. This causes strong pain and discomfort.

---

## What Causes a Cruciate Ligament Rupture?

The cruciate ligaments connect the thigh bone to the shin bone. They help keep the knee stable.

The anterior cruciate ligament:

- Stops the shin bone from moving forward.
- Works with the back cruciate ligament to prevent twisting.

It also has special sensors that help your muscles react quickly to keep the knee steady.

The ligament can tear if it is stretched too hard. This can happen when:

- The knee twists suddenly — for example, when stopping fast, changing direction quickly, or when your leg gives way inward.
- You land badly after a jump with your leg straight.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

Cruciate ligament injuries are common in sports like soccer, handball, volleyball, basketball, and skiing.

Women who play ball sports have a higher risk than men. Doctors think this may be because women often have weaker thigh muscles at the back of the leg (hamstrings).

---

## How Common Is This Injury?

Most ruptures happen during ball sports. People aged 15 to 45 are most at risk.

A review of over 50 studies found:

- 3 to 4 out of every 100 women who play ball sports will injure their cruciate ligament at some point.
- 2 out of every 100 men who play ball sports will have this injury.

---

## What Happens After the Injury?

With proper treatment, 80 to 90 out of 100 people get their knee working normally again.

Most people return to sports after healing. But about 20 to 30 out of 100 people choose to switch to less intense sports or different activities. This is often due to fear of re-injury — even though it may not be needed.

### Long-Term Risks

A cruciate ligament rupture increases the chance of getting knee arthritis later in life. This risk is higher if the meniscus was also damaged.

Studies over 10 years showed:

- About 20 out of 100 people had clear signs of arthritis on X-rays after a rupture.
- Only about 5 out of 100 people without a rupture showed this on X-rays.

But having arthritis on an X-ray does not always mean you have pain. Some people feel fine even with changes on the X-ray.

Exercises can help keep your knee working well after the injury.

---

## How Can You Prevent This Injury?

Doing special warm-up and strength exercises before sports can help prevent ruptures.

These programs include:

- Warm-up exercises.
- Strength training for your core and leg muscles.
- Balance and coordination drills.
- Exercises to improve quick, powerful movements.

Two well-known programs are:

- **FIFA 11+** – from the German Football Association.
- **Stop-X** – from the German Knee Society.

These are made for sports like soccer and handball, which carry a higher risk. They are especially helpful for active people, as injury risk goes up with intense training and many games.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask about the injury and your symptoms. They will check your knee by touching and moving it.

They will test how stable your knee is by moving the upper and lower leg.

If needed, they may use:

- **MRI** – gives clear pictures of the ligaments and meniscus.
- **X-ray** – shows broken bones, but not torn ligaments.

---

## How Is It Treated?

After the injury, rest your knee. Elevate it and apply cold packs right away. This helps reduce pain and swelling.

A compression bandage can help. Pain relief medicine like ibuprofen may also be useful.

Later, a walking aid (like crutches) can help if your knee feels very unstable.

There are two main treatment options:

### 1. Conservative Treatment (No Surgery)
- Work with a physiotherapist to strengthen your leg muscles.
- Strong muscles can take over the job of the torn ligament.
- This option works best if no other knee parts are badly damaged.

### 2. Surgery
- The torn ligament is replaced with a new one.
- Surgery is done using a small camera and tools through tiny cuts (arthroscopy).
- Surgery usually happens 2 to 4 weeks after the injury. This gives time for swelling to go down.

If your knee is still stiff or swollen during surgery, it may become stiff later. So, do exercises to improve movement before surgery.

After surgery, you need 4 to 12 months of healing and training, depending on your sport.

### What Does Research Say?

One major study compared surgery and conservative treatment:

- Conservative treatment worked well for over half of people.
- Surgery had a success rate of 80 to 90%.

It is safe to start with conservative treatment and only have surgery later if needed. But conservative treatment may lead to a slightly higher risk of further injuries, like to the meniscus.

---

## What Is the Recovery Process?

After surgery, it takes months for the new ligament to heal and work properly.

Strong thigh muscles are key. They help protect the new ligament and keep the knee stable.

Rehab aims to:

- Build up muscle strength.
- Help your knee get used to the new ligament.
- Restore normal movement and feeling.

It may take time before your knee feels natural again.

If you do not have surgery, rehab helps you build strong muscles so your knee stays stable. Physiotherapy is helpful no matter which treatment you choose.

### When Can You Return to Sports?

- After surgery: gentle sports can start after 4 to 6 months.
- After surgery: ball or combat sports usually wait until 9 to 12 months.
- With conservative treatment: recovery time is about 2 to 3 months shorter.

Recovery takes time and effort. Patience is just as important as training.

For more details on rehab, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

---

## What Else Should You Do Before Surgery?

Preparing ahead helps make recovery easier. Consider:

- Practicing walking with crutches before surgery.
- Removing trip hazards at home. For example, avoid stairs by sleeping in another room.
- Arranging a different way to get to work, school, or university. You may not be able to drive for weeks.
- Asking for help with shopping or chores.
- Getting a small shower stool so you can shower while sitting.

Using crutches a lot can cause soreness in your back, neck, or shoulders. Doing light exercises before surgery can help prevent this.

# Fungal Nail Infection

A fungal nail infection is a common condition. It happens when fungi get into the nail. These fungi usually live on the skin. The infection often starts in the big toes. It can make the nails look yellow or brown. The nails may also become weak, thick, or break easily.

Many people with a fungal nail infection also have athlete’s foot. This is a skin infection that often affects the feet.

---

## Quick Facts

- About 3% to 12% of people have a fungal nail infection.
- The infection is usually caused by fungi that live on the skin.
- Most people with this infection also have athlete’s foot.
- You can lower your risk by:
  - Keeping your feet dry
  - Wearing shoes that fit well and let your feet breathe
  - Wearing flip-flops in public showers, pools, and saunas

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Fungal Nail Infection?

Fungi can get into a toenail or, less often, a fingernail. Once inside, they grow and cause damage. Over time, the nail becomes weak and breaks. It may change color, turning yellow, brown, or white. The nail can also thicken and become uneven.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor may suspect a fungal nail infection if the nail is discolored, thick, or crumbling. The nail may hurt or come loose from the nail bed.

The infection often starts on the top or side of the big toe. It can also start at the base of the nail, especially in people with diabetes or a weak immune system.

Sometimes, the infection looks like other nail problems, such as psoriasis. To be sure, the doctor will take a small sample of the nail. They will send it to a lab for testing.

In the lab, the sample is examined under a microscope. A special dye helps make the fungus easier to see. To find the exact type of fungus, a culture is grown. This takes about three weeks. In some cases, more tests are done on the nail tissue.

---

## What Causes Fungal Nail Infections?

Most fungal nail infections are caused by skin fungi. Some are caused by mold or yeast. Yeast infections are more likely to affect the fingernails.

The infection often starts with athlete’s foot. The fungus spreads from the skin to the nail. This is why treating athlete’s foot can help prevent nail infections.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

These factors may make you more likely to get a fungal nail infection:

- Having athlete’s foot
- Spending a lot of time in pools, saunas, or showers
- Injuring your nails (e.g., from tight shoes or trauma)
- Wearing tight or poorly ventilated shoes
- Having skin conditions like psoriasis
- Poor blood flow in the legs, which can happen with diabetes or peripheral artery disease
- A weak immune system, due to illness or certain medicines
- Getting the infection from a family member

Fungal nail infections on the hands are more common in people who often get their hands wet, such as cleaners or dishwashers.

---

## How Common Are They?

Between 3% and 12% of people have a fungal nail infection. Older adults are more likely to get it than younger people.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

For healthy people, a fungal nail infection is not dangerous. But it rarely goes away on its own. Without treatment, it may stay the same or spread to other nails.

If you have diabetes or a weak immune system, the infection can lead to a skin infection around the nail. A thick, painful nail can also make walking difficult.

---

## How Can You Prevent It?

Fungal nail infections often start with athlete’s foot. So, preventing athlete’s foot helps prevent nail infections.

Fungi grow best in warm, damp places. Keep your feet dry to reduce your risk.

Here’s how:

- Dry your feet well after showering, bathing, or swimming. Use a towel and a hair dryer.
- Wear shoes that fit well and let your feet breathe.
- Take off your shoes often when you’re at home.
- Wear flip-flops in public showers, pools, and saunas.
- Do not share shoes or towels.
- Wash socks, bed sheets, and towels at 60 degrees Celsius or higher.

Nail injuries can also increase your risk. If you walk or run a lot, wear well-fitting shoes and special socks to protect your feet.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Fungal nail infections are hard to treat. Toenails grow slowly, so treatment takes time. It may take several months to see improvement.

But with consistent treatment, the healthy nail will grow in. The infected part will grow out over time.

### Topical Treatments (Applied to the Nail)

- A clear nail polish with medicine can be bought without a prescription.
- It contains active ingredients like amorolfine or ciclopirox.
- These stop the fungus from growing or kill it.
- You must use it every day, as directed.

Some kits include:
- A cream with urea to soften the infected nail
- A small tool to gently scrape away the soft part
- A cream with bifonazole to treat the skin under the nail

These treatments work best when used every day for several weeks.

### Oral Medicines (Pills)

Topical treatments alone may not be enough. Pills may be needed to clear the infection completely.

These medicines are prescribed by a doctor. They usually contain itraconazole or terbinafine.

- Toenail infections need treatment for more than 12 weeks.
- Fingernail infections may need only 6 weeks of treatment.

These pills can cause side effects, such as stomach upset. Always talk to your doctor about risks and benefits.

### Home Remedies

Some people try tea tree oil or vinegar. But there is no strong scientific proof that these work.

---

## Where to Learn More

For more detailed information on treatment options, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Autism

Autism is a condition that affects how a person thinks, feels, and interacts with others. It is present from birth and affects how people understand and respond to the world around them.

## What You Need to Know at a Glance

- Autism is a lifelong condition that people are born with.
- It affects how people connect with others and how they communicate.
- People with autism often repeat certain behaviors or follow strict routines.
- There is no medicine that can cure autism.
- But there are many ways to help people with autism improve their communication and social skills.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose yourself or others. Always talk to a doctor.

---

## What Is Autism?

Autism is a brain development condition. It affects how a person sees and understands the world. Everyone with autism is different. Some people can live on their own. Others need more help with daily life.

In the past, doctors used different names for autism, like Asperger’s syndrome or early childhood autism. Now, most experts use the term **autism spectrum disorder**. This means autism can show up in many different ways.

People with autism often find it hard to understand other people’s feelings. They may also struggle to share their own thoughts and feelings. This can make it harder to make friends or build relationships.

But with the right support, people with autism can live full, happy lives. They can take part in school, work, and social activities.

---

## What Are the Signs of Autism?

Autism shows up in three main ways:

1. Trouble with social interaction  
2. Problems with communication and language  
3. Repetitive or rigid behaviors

### Trouble with Social Interaction

- People with autism may avoid eye contact.
- They may seem distant or lost in their own thoughts.
- Some are very friendly but act in ways that seem odd to others.
- They may not understand jokes, sarcasm, or body language.
- They might not react when someone else is sad or happy.

### Communication Problems

- Some people with autism learn to talk late or not at all.
- They may use fewer hand gestures when speaking.
- Their voice may sound flat or monotone.
- Some repeat words or phrases over and over.
- Others speak in a very formal or precise way.

### Repetitive or Rigid Behaviors

- They may flap their hands, rock back and forth, or spin in circles.
- They like to do things in the same order every time.
- They may have very strong, narrow interests that they focus on intensely.
- They often need routines and get upset if things change.
- They may be very sensitive to sounds, smells, or touch — or not notice them at all.

> **Note:** Not everyone with autism shows all of these signs. Some may have only a few. The signs appear in different ways and at different times for each person.

### Other Common Challenges

People with autism may also face other difficulties, such as:

- Trouble sleeping  
- Eating problems  
- Anxiety or obsessive thoughts  
- Tics (sudden, repeated movements)  
- Attention problems or hyperactivity (ADHD)  
- Seizures (epilepsy)  
- Depression  

Some people may act out with anger, aggression, or self-harm. This usually means they are overwhelmed or struggling to be understood.

About half of all people with autism have learning difficulties. The other half have average or above-average intelligence. A few are highly gifted.

---

## What Causes Autism?

Autism is not caused by bad parenting or vaccines. It is a brain development condition that people are born with.

Scientists do not yet know the exact cause. But they have found some things that can increase the risk.

### Family History

- Autism can run in families.
- If a parent has autism, their child is more likely to have it too.
- If one child in a family has autism, the chance that a second child will have it is about 10 to 20 percent.
- The older a parent is, the higher the risk. This is because older parents are more likely to pass on genetic changes.

### Events During Pregnancy

- Infections during pregnancy, like rubella, can raise the risk.
- Premature birth is also linked to a higher risk.
- Taking certain epilepsy medicines during pregnancy — especially those with valproate — increases the risk.

> **Fact:** Vaccines do not cause autism. This idea has been proven false by many studies.

---

## How Common Is Autism?

In Germany, about 1 in every 100 people has autism.

Boys and men are about twice as likely to have autism as girls and women.

The number of people diagnosed with autism has gone up in recent years. But this is mostly because doctors now spot it earlier. We do not know for sure if autism is becoming more common.

---

## What Is the Outlook for People with Autism?

Autism lasts a lifetime. But how it affects a person can change over time.

Some symptoms may get better with age. Others may stay the same or even get worse. Many children and teens learn to talk better and get along with others over time.

Some signs of autism can appear as early as age 1 or 2. But others may not be noticed until much later — even into adulthood.

In some cases, early signs fade away. Or they turn out to be caused by something else. This is more common in children who show only mild signs.

Some children develop normally at first, then start showing autism signs later.

Many people with autism need support their whole lives. But many others can live independently, work, and raise families. They may still need help with certain tasks.

---

## How Is Autism Diagnosed?

If you notice unusual behavior in a child, talk to a doctor. The first step is usually a visit to a pediatrician. This can happen during regular check-ups.

For adults, start with your family doctor. You can also go directly to a psychologist or psychiatrist.

Only a specialist in mental health — like a psychiatrist or psychologist — can diagnose autism.

The diagnosis process is detailed and takes time. It includes:

- Talking with the child and parents  
- Filling out questionnaires about the child’s behavior  
- Watching how the child plays and interacts  
- Testing the child’s language and thinking skills  
- Checking for other possible causes with medical tests

Multiple appointments are needed. Sometimes, doctors wait to see how the child grows before making a final decision.

Children can be diagnosed as young as 1 year old. But a clear diagnosis often comes later, depending on how clear the signs are.

For adults, diagnosis is harder. Many have learned to hide their autism over time. This is called “masking.” Also, other mental health conditions can look like autism.

It’s a good idea to review the diagnosis after a few years — especially for children with mild signs. Doctors will keep checking the child’s development.

For more information, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## How Is Autism Treated?

There is no cure for autism. But treatment can help people live better lives.

The main goals of treatment are:

- To improve quality of life  
- To help people take part in society  
- To support independence and self-confidence

Treatment works best when it is tailored to the person’s needs. It also depends on when treatment starts and how much support is available.

### For Children

After diagnosis, a personalized plan is made. It may include:

- Behavioral therapy (to improve social skills)  
- Speech therapy (to help with talking)  
- Occupational therapy (to help with daily tasks)  
- Education and support for parents (called psychoeducation)

Early therapy — especially for children under school age — can make a big difference. Parents are often part of the treatment.

### For Teens and Adults

Therapy helps people accept autism as part of who they are. It also helps them adapt their lives to their needs.

Treatment may also focus on managing other conditions, such as anxiety, ADHD, or sleep problems.

> **Important:** There is no medicine that treats autism itself.  
> But medicine can help with other issues, such as:
> - Severe repetitive behaviors  
> - Anxiety  
> - ADHD  
> - Sleep problems  
> - Depression  
> - Seizures

---

## How Does Autism Affect Daily Life?

Autism affects people in many different ways.

Some people with autism struggle to make friends or find work. Others live independently and have strong relationships.

The level of support needed depends on:

- How autism affects the person  
- Whether they have learning difficulties  
- Their life situation and environment

### Support and Benefits Available

- Equal treatment in school and work  
- Support assistants in daycare or school  
- Family support programs  
- Help for parents and caregivers  
- Medical or assistive devices (like special tools or apps)  
- Personal help at work  
- Group homes with support  
- Care benefits

Most of these services are paid for by **integration assistance** (Eingliederungshilfe), not by health insurance.

To apply, contact your local youth welfare office (Jugendamt) or social services office (Sozialamt).

For more information, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

See also: [Support for children and adolescents in need of care](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## Where Can I Get Help?

You are not alone. Many groups offer support and advice.

Parent groups and self-help organizations help people with autism and their families. They share experiences and provide information.

For contact details, visit:

- **Autism Germany (Autismus Deutschland e.V.)**  
- **Aspies e.V.**

# Muscle Strain

A muscle strain is a common injury. It happens when a muscle is stretched too far. This causes pain and makes the muscle feel tight. The thigh, back, or neck are often affected. Here’s what you can do to prevent it.

---

## Quick Facts

- Muscle strains happen most often during sports.
- They occur when muscles are stretched too much. Tiny injuries happen in the muscle fibers.
- You feel sudden pain and the muscle feels hard.
- Most strains heal on their own. But it can take days or weeks to fully recover.
- In the first few days, rest the muscle. Cooling, a bandage, and raising the area help reduce swelling and pain.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Muscle Strain?

A muscle strain happens when a muscle is stretched too far. It is also called a pulled muscle. It often happens during sports like soccer. These sports involve sprinting, quick stops, or changing direction fast.

When a muscle stretches too much, small parts inside the muscle fibers get damaged. These small parts are called myofibrils. They help the muscle contract and shorten.

If the stretch is even worse, one or more muscle fibers can tear. This is called a torn muscle fiber. If the whole muscle tears, it is called a torn muscle.

---

## Symptoms of a Muscle Strain

You may notice:

- Sudden pain
- The muscle feels hard or tight

These symptoms often happen during sports or other hard physical work. The thigh, back, or neck are most often affected.

Other signs can include:

- Muscle cramps
- Swelling
- Bruising
- Weakness in the muscle
- Trouble moving the area

Pain can get worse quickly. Bruising may not show up right away. It can take up to 24 hours for swelling and bruising to reach their worst.

---

## What Causes a Muscle Strain?

A strain happens when a muscle is under stress and then stretched too far. This often occurs during sports like soccer, basketball, or tennis. These sports require sprinting, jumping, or sudden changes in direction.

Strains are most common in the thigh or calf muscles.

Even long-distance runners can get a strain. It often happens in the calf, especially when running uphill or downhill.

**Important:** When muscles are tired, they are more likely to get strained. Injuries often happen near the end of a game or race.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

- Not warming up before physical activity raises the risk.
- Older adults, especially those who are not active, are more likely to get a strain.
- People over 40 who haven’t trained before doing hard activity are at higher risk, especially for calf strains.
- Having had a muscle injury before increases the chance of another strain.

---

## How Common Are Muscle Strains?

Muscle strains are among the most common sports injuries. They affect both professional and amateur athletes. More than 90 percent of sports injuries are either muscle strains or bruises.

---

## How Does a Muscle Strain Heal?

Most strains heal on their own. But full recovery can take days or weeks.

A special exercise plan or physical therapy can help speed up healing.

Most people can return to normal daily activities 4 to 8 weeks after the injury. Athletes can usually go back to training after this time.

---

## How Can You Prevent a Muscle Strain?

- Always warm up your muscles before playing sports.
- Regular fitness training helps muscles stay strong and less likely to tire quickly.
- Strength training and stretching improve muscle strength and flexibility.

---

## How Is a Muscle Strain Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose a strain by asking about your symptoms and doing a physical exam. They will:

- Feel the injured area
- Check muscle strength
- Test how well the muscle moves

Imaging tests like X-rays or MRI scans are usually not needed. But they may be used if the injury is serious. They help rule out broken bones or a full muscle tear.

An ultrasound may be done to confirm the diagnosis and see how bad the injury is.

---

## How Is a Muscle Strain Treated?

Use the RICE method in the first 48 hours after injury:

- **Rest:** Keep the injured area still.
- **Ice:** Apply cold to reduce pain and swelling. Use a cold pack for 10 to 20 minutes every 2 hours. Put a thin cloth between the ice and your skin to avoid frostbite. Let the skin warm up between uses.
- **Compression:** Use an elastic bandage to reduce swelling. Do not wrap it too tight. If it feels tight or numb, loosen it.
- **Elevation:** Raise the injured muscle above heart level. This helps reduce swelling.

If pain is strong, you can take pain medicine like ibuprofen for a few days.

**Important:** Rest the muscle for at least 2 days. Then slowly start gentle movement. The sooner you move safely, the less stiff the muscle will become.

---

## How Long Does It Take to Recover?

Start with light, pain-free activities as soon as the pain allows. These should help improve movement and protect the healing muscle.

A doctor or physical therapist can help you pick safe exercises.

You can usually return to light training after 2 to 6 weeks. Once you can move the muscle fully without pain, you can slowly return to harder activities.

**Important:** Wait until the muscle is fully healed before doing intense exercise or playing sports. If you return too soon, you risk injuring it again.

# Cystic Fibrosis

Cystic fibrosis is a rare, inherited condition.  
It cannot be cured.  
It affects how the body handles salt and water.  
This causes thick mucus to build up in the lungs and other organs.  
The thick mucus leads to long-term coughing and frequent lung infections.  
New treatments are helping people live longer and feel better.  

---

## Quick Facts

- Cystic fibrosis is passed down through families.  
- It often shows up in teens or adults, but not always at birth.  
- It mainly affects the lungs, pancreas, and intestines.  
- All newborns in Germany are now tested for cystic fibrosis.  
- There is no cure, but symptoms and related health problems can be managed.  
- The average life expectancy is about 40 years.  
- With good care, this number is rising.  

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself. Always talk to a doctor.

---

## What Is Cystic Fibrosis?

Cystic fibrosis is a lifelong condition you are born with.  
It is also called mucoviscidosis.  
It affects several organs, including the lungs, pancreas, and intestines.  

A change in a gene causes the body to lose its balance of salt and water.  
This leads to thick, sticky mucus.  
When mucus builds up in the lungs, it causes a long-lasting cough.  

Newborn screening helps find cystic fibrosis early.  
This allows treatment to start sooner.  
Today, people with cystic fibrosis live longer than before.  
The average life span is about 40 years.  

In Germany, about one baby in every 4,500 is born with cystic fibrosis.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most babies with cystic fibrosis look healthy at birth.  
One exception is meconium ileus.  
This is a blockage in the bowel caused by thick stool.  
It happens in about 1 in 5 newborns with cystic fibrosis.  

Most people start showing symptoms in their teens or adult years.  
Symptoms can be mild or severe.  
Common signs include:

- A cough that lasts three months or more  
- Wheezing or shortness of breath  
- Coughing up mucus  
- Frequent lung infections  
- Long-term inflammation in the nose and sinuses  
- Swollen fingertips (called “clubbed fingers”)  
- Skin that tastes salty when kissed  

Many people with cystic fibrosis are born with a weak pancreas.  
This means the pancreas does not make enough digestive juices.  
This causes poor digestion and weight loss.  
Over time, it can lead to diabetes.  

Signs of a weak pancreas include:

- Children who grow slowly  
- Unexplained weight loss in children, teens, or adults  
- Stools that are oily, smelly, and large (called steatorrhea)

---

## What Causes Cystic Fibrosis?

Cystic fibrosis is caused by a change in a gene called CFTR.  
Everyone has two copies of this gene.  
Cystic fibrosis only happens if both copies are changed.  

The CFTR gene helps control salt and water in certain cells.  
When the gene is faulty, mucus becomes thick and sticky.  

In the lungs, thick mucus blocks airways.  
It is hard to cough up.  
This leads to long-term coughing and lung infections.  
Bacteria can grow in the mucus and cause repeated infections.  

Thick digestive juices damage the pancreas.  
This reduces the body’s ability to absorb nutrients.  
It can lead to poor growth and being underweight.

---

## How Likely Is It to Inherit Cystic Fibrosis?

Cystic fibrosis is inherited.  
It only happens if a child gets a changed gene from both parents.  

If both parents carry one changed gene, their child has:

- A 25% chance of having cystic fibrosis  
- A 50% chance of being a carrier (but not having the disease)  
- A 25% chance of not having the gene change at all  

If one parent has cystic fibrosis and the other is a carrier, the child has a 50% chance of having the disease.  
This is rare.

---

## How Does Cystic Fibrosis Progress?

The course of the disease varies from person to person.  
It is hard to predict.  
Lung and digestive problems are common.  
Fertility issues can also happen.

### Lung Problems

Thick mucus builds up in the airways and lungs.  
This causes a long-term cough.  
It can also lead to sinus infections and growths in the nose or sinuses (called nasal polyps).

### Digestive and Metabolic Issues

Many people have a weak pancreas.  
This means food is not digested well.  
They may lack important vitamins and minerals.  
Children grow slowly and may start puberty later.  

Over time, some develop diabetes.  
This is rare in children under 10.  
Some also get blocked bowels, which can be painful.  

Bones in people with cystic fibrosis often have less mineral.  
This increases the risk of broken bones and weak bones (called osteoporosis).

### Fertility Problems

Over 95% of men with cystic fibrosis cannot have children naturally.  
This is because the tube that carries sperm does not develop properly.  
But they still make sperm.  
With medical help, they can still become fathers.  

Women with cystic fibrosis can get pregnant naturally.  
But it is harder than for women without the condition.  
This is because the mucus at the cervix is thick and blocks sperm.

> **Important:** People with cystic fibrosis who want to have children should get special advice.

### Other Health Problems

Some children with cystic fibrosis develop anemia (low red blood cells).  
Up to one in three may develop long-term liver disease.

---

## How Is Cystic Fibrosis Screened?

Since 2016, all newborns in Germany are tested for cystic fibrosis.  
A small blood sample is taken 36 to 72 hours after birth.  
The blood is tested for certain proteins and for changes in the CFTR gene.  

This helps find cystic fibrosis early.

### How Accurate Is the Blood Test?

The blood test is not perfect.  
About 4 out of 5 babies who test positive do not actually have cystic fibrosis.  
This is called a false positive.  
A positive result must be confirmed with more tests.

---

## How Is Cystic Fibrosis Diagnosed?

A blood test is not enough.  
Doctors also ask about family history.  
If someone in the family has cystic fibrosis, the risk is higher.  

If the blood test or family history raises concern, doctors do a sweat test.  

In the sweat test:

- A small area of skin is stimulated to sweat  
- The sweat is collected and tested  
- High levels of chloride mean cystic fibrosis is likely  

If the sweat test is unclear, doctors do genetic tests.  
They may also do more tests if needed.

---

## How Is Cystic Fibrosis Treated?

There is no cure.  
But treatment can help manage symptoms and improve quality of life.  
Treatment is tailored to each person.  

Special clinics offer medical care, psychological support, and advice for families.

> **Important:** The earlier cystic fibrosis is found, the sooner treatment can start.  
> Early treatment helps children grow better and live longer.  
> That is why all newborns are now tested.

### Medicines

People with cystic fibrosis often take several medicines at once.  
These include:

- Inhaled medicines that help loosen mucus  
- Antibiotics to treat lung infections  
- Anti-inflammatory medicines to reduce swelling in the airways  
- Drugs like ivacaftor that help fix the salt and water balance in cells

### Breathing Exercises and Physiotherapy

Daily breathing exercises help loosen mucus.  
They make it easier to breathe.  
A physiotherapist teaches the exercises at first.  
Then the person does them at home.  

Trained physiotherapists or family members can also use chest treatments.  
These help loosen mucus so it can be coughed up.

### Other Treatments

People with cystic fibrosis need extra nutrients.  
They may need vitamin and mineral supplements.  
But always talk to a doctor before taking any supplements.  

If lung damage is severe, a lung transplant may be an option.  
This can extend life.

### Ongoing Care

Regular check-ups are essential.  
They help doctors spot problems early.  
This includes worsening lung function or new health issues.  
Early treatment can prevent serious complications.

# Magnesium Deficiency

Magnesium is a mineral your body needs to stay healthy.  
It helps your muscles and nerves work properly.  
It also helps keep your bones and teeth strong.

Most people get enough magnesium from their food.  
But some people do not have enough in their blood.  
This is called a magnesium deficiency.

---

## Quick Facts

- Magnesium helps your muscles, nerves, and bones work well.  
- Your body cannot make magnesium. You must get it from food.  
- A poor diet or kidney problems can cause a deficiency.  
- Pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers, athletes, and people with certain health issues need more magnesium.  
- Common signs include muscle cramps, tingling, or numbness in the arms and legs.  
- Eating green vegetables, beans, and whole grains often can help prevent a deficiency.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice.  
> Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Magnesium Deficiency?

Magnesium is a mineral your body uses in many ways.  
It helps your muscles work, including your heart.  
It also helps build strong bones and teeth.  
It helps control levels of calcium and potassium in your body.

A healthy, balanced diet usually gives you enough magnesium.  
Many plant-based foods contain magnesium.  
Good sources include nuts, seeds, green vegetables, beans, and whole grains.

But some things can stop your body from getting or keeping enough magnesium.  
These include:

- Eating very little or only certain foods  
- Severe diarrhea  
- Long-term kidney problems  

When blood levels of magnesium drop too low, doctors call it hypomagnesemia.  
This is the same as a magnesium deficiency.

If you have a deficiency, you need treatment.  
This can include taking magnesium tablets or getting it through a drip into your vein.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

A magnesium deficiency may not cause symptoms at first.  
You might not notice anything until the deficiency is serious.

When symptoms do appear, they can include:

- Cramps in your calf muscles  
- Tingling or numbness in your arms and legs  
- Feeling cold often  

Other possible signs are:

- Headaches  
- Fast or irregular heartbeat  
- Digestive issues like nausea or stomach pain  

Some people feel tired, unmotivated, or lose interest in daily life.  
They may seem quiet or uninterested in things.

---

## What Causes a Magnesium Deficiency?

You get a deficiency when your body takes in too little magnesium or loses too much.

Your body usually keeps magnesium levels stable.  
But in rare cases, a genetic condition can stop this from working.  
For example, Gitelman syndrome is a rare inherited kidney problem.

In most cases, the cause is something else. These include:

- Eating disorders or extreme dieting  
- Drinking too much alcohol  
- High stress levels  
- Physical activity or sports  
- Pregnancy  
- Severe diarrhea or frequent vomiting  

Certain health conditions can also lower magnesium levels.  
These include:

- Long-term kidney disease  
- Diabetes  
- Pancreatitis (inflammation of the pancreas)  
- Bowel diseases like Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis  
- Thyroid problems, such as underactive parathyroid glands  

A magnesium deficiency can also happen after:

- A kidney transplant  
- Surgery on the small intestine  
- Taking certain medicines, like diuretics (water pills)  
- Some antibiotics used to treat infections  

---

## How Common Is It?

About 2 out of every 100 people have low magnesium levels.

Pregnant women, people with diabetes, and those who drink a lot of alcohol are more likely to have a deficiency.

---

## What Can Happen If You Have a Deficiency?

A low magnesium level often comes with low calcium and low potassium.  
These imbalances can affect your bones and heart.

Calcium helps keep bones strong.  
Without enough magnesium, your body cannot store calcium well in your bones.  
This can weaken your bones over time.

A very low magnesium level can also cause serious heart rhythm problems.

---

## How Can You Prevent It?

Eating a variety of healthy foods usually gives you enough magnesium.

If you have a higher need for magnesium, eat more of these foods:

- Spinach and other green vegetables  
- Beans, lentils, and peas  
- Whole grain bread, pasta, and rice  
- Poppy seeds, sesame seeds, and sunflower seeds  
- Nuts like almonds and cashews  

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor can check for a deficiency by asking about your health and symptoms.  
They will also do a blood test to measure your magnesium levels.

If you have heart symptoms like palpitations or skipped beats, your doctor may do an electrocardiogram (ECG).  
This checks how your heart is working.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on the cause and your overall health.

If the deficiency is mild and you have few symptoms, changing your diet may be enough.

Try these steps:

- Cook meals with fresh vegetables and fruits  
- Eat vegetables every day  
- Add a small handful of nuts to your meals  
- Sprinkle seeds like sunflower or flax seeds on your cereal or salad  

For a more serious deficiency, your doctor may recommend magnesium tablets.  
Do not take these without talking to a doctor.  
Over-the-counter supplements may not have the right amount.

People with kidney disease or severe symptoms may need magnesium given through a drip into a vein.  
This is done in a hospital or clinic.

# Infection with Cytomegalovirus (CMV)

Most people do not get sick from CMV. But it can cause serious problems for unborn babies, premature babies, and people with weak immune systems. Good hygiene can help lower the risk of getting CMV.

---

## Quick Facts

- CMV is a type of herpes virus.
- Most healthy people do not get sick from CMV. They may not even know they are infected.
- After the first infection, CMV stays in the body for life. It usually does nothing and stays quiet.
- The virus can become active again later under certain conditions.
- CMV can cause serious health issues in unborn babies, premature babies, and people with weak immune systems.
- There is no vaccine for CMV.
- You can take steps to lower your risk of infection.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is CMV and What Happens When You Get Infected?

CMV is a virus from the herpes family. Once you get infected, the virus stays in your body for life. It hides in your cells and does not cause symptoms most of the time.

Sometimes, the virus wakes up and starts to grow again. This is called reactivation.

In Germany, about half of all adults have had a CMV infection at some point.

> **Important:** All herpes viruses stay in the body for life after the first infection.

Most healthy people do not get sick from CMV. If they do, symptoms are mild.

But CMV can cause serious harm to unborn babies, premature babies, and people with weak immune systems.

Pregnant women can pass CMV to their unborn baby. This is most likely if they get infected for the first time during pregnancy or shortly before.

---

## What Are the Symptoms of CMV?

You can get CMV at any age. Many people get it as children. Symptoms usually appear 4 to 6 weeks after infection.

Most healthy people have no symptoms or only mild ones. These may include:

- Feeling tired
- Fever
- Cough

Premature babies and people with weak immune systems are more likely to get very sick.

Severe CMV infection can lead to:

- Pneumonia (lung infection)
- Liver inflammation (hepatitis)
- Intestinal inflammation (enteritis)
- Eye inflammation that can damage the retina and cause blindness

Babies infected before birth may have:

- Poor growth
- Brain or nerve damage
- Hearing loss

These problems affect up to 15 out of every 100 babies born with CMV. Some may not show signs right after birth.

The virus can reactivate or a new infection can happen later in life. This can cause symptoms again.

---

## How Is CMV Spread?

CMV spreads from person to person through close contact. This is called smear infection.

The virus can be found in:

- Saliva
- Tears
- Urine
- Genital fluids
- Blood
- Breast milk

Children under 3 years old often carry large amounts of the virus. They can spread it easily.

CMV can also spread through:

- Blood transfusions
- Organ transplants

Pregnant women can pass CMV to their unborn baby. This is more likely if they are infected for the first time during pregnancy. It can also happen if the virus reactivates during pregnancy.

---

## Who Is at Higher Risk?

Some people are more likely to get very sick from CMV.

These include:

- Babies still in the womb
- Premature babies
- People with weak immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS or advanced cancer
- People taking drugs that weaken the immune system, such as chemotherapy patients or organ transplant recipients

---

## How Common Is CMV?

Many factors increase the chance of getting CMV. These include:

- Caring for young children
- Poor hygiene
- Having many sexual partners

We cannot know the exact number of people with CMV. But blood tests show that nearly half of adults in Germany have had CMV.

More than half of all pregnant women in Germany have not had CMV before. About one in four people who get a kidney transplant have not had CMV.

CMV is the most common viral infection in unborn babies.

---

## How Can You Prevent CMV?

Most healthy people do not need to worry about CMV. But people at higher risk should take steps to protect themselves.

This includes:

- Pregnant women who have not had CMV before
- Premature babies
- People with weak immune systems
- People taking immune-suppressing drugs

About 1 in 200 pregnant women get CMV for the first time during pregnancy. Most do not notice any symptoms. But it can harm the unborn baby, especially in the first three months.

### For Pregnant Women Without CMV Antibodies

Good hygiene can help prevent a first-time CMV infection during pregnancy. This is especially important when around young children.

**Follow these hygiene tips:**

- Wash your hands often with soap and warm water.
- Wash hands after:
  - Changing diapers
  - Washing children
  - Feeding children
  - Wiping tears or noses
  - Cleaning toys that children have put in their mouths
- Clean toys and surfaces that touch children’s saliva or urine.
- Wear gloves when cleaning, or have someone else do it.
- Do not kiss babies or young children on the mouth or cheek.
- Do not share:
  - Plates, cups, or utensils
  - Towels or cloths
- Do not put a pacifier in your mouth.
- Do not eat food that a child has chewed.

> **Important:** Women who work with children under 3 years old are at higher risk. Some may need to avoid certain tasks during pregnancy. This may apply to kindergarten teachers or healthcare workers.

Women trying to get pregnant can get a blood test to check for CMV antibodies. But German public health insurance does not always pay for this test. Some do, so ask your doctor.

---

### Babies and Mothers Who Have Had CMV

If a mother has had CMV before, the virus can come back during breastfeeding. It can pass to the baby through breast milk.

This is not a problem for full-term babies. But it can cause serious issues in premature babies.

Hospitals take special care to protect premature babies from CMV in breast milk.

---

### Safety with Blood and Organs

- Bone marrow donors are tested for CMV.
- Blood products are not always tested.
- Blood products without white blood cells are considered safe, even without testing.

- Organs are tested for CMV before transplant.
- CMV can cause serious illness in transplant recipients.
- It can also cause the body to reject the new organ.
- If the donor or recipient has CMV, preventive antiviral medicine may help protect the recipient.

---

## How Is CMV Diagnosed?

Doctors can find CMV in the lab.

There are two main ways:

1. **Antibody test (blood test):**  
   - This checks for antibodies in the blood.  
   - It shows if you have had CMV before.  
   - It can tell if the infection happened recently or a long time ago.  
   - Used for healthy people, including pregnant women.

2. **Direct virus test:**  
   - This finds the virus in urine, saliva, or blood.  
   - Used for people with weak immune systems or newborns who were infected before birth.

---

## How Is CMV Treated?

Most healthy people do not need treatment for CMV.

People at high risk of serious illness may get antiviral medicine. One example is ganciclovir.

If a newborn baby had CMV before birth, antiviral medicine may be used. But only after talking to a specialist neonatal care center.

Antiviral medicine is not recommended for pregnant women or those who are breastfeeding.

Using special antibodies (hyperimmunoglobulin) to prevent or treat CMV is still being studied. Experts are not sure if it helps.

# Typhoid and Paratyphoid

Typhoid is an infection caused by a type of bacteria.  
It spreads through dirty water or food.  
It is very rare in Germany.  
People who travel to high-risk areas should get a vaccine to prevent it.

---

## Quick Facts

- Typhoid is caused by bacteria.  
- The bacteria spread through the waste (poop or pee) of infected people.  
- You can get typhoid from eating food or drinking water that has been contaminated.  
- In Germany, most cases happen in people who traveled to high-risk areas.  
- Before traveling to a high-risk area, get vaccinated.  
- Once you arrive, be very careful about what you eat and drink.  
- Typhoid must be treated with antibiotics.  

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Typhoid?

Typhoid is an infection caused by a specific kind of salmonella bacteria.  
The bacteria spread through contaminated water or food.  
Germany has good hygiene, so typhoid is very rare here.  
Most cases in Germany happen in people who were infected while traveling in Asia.

There are two types:

- **Typhoid fever** – also called enteric fever. This is the more serious form.  
- **Paratyphoid** – similar to typhoid but less severe.

Both need to be treated with antibiotics.  
Without treatment, they can lead to life-threatening problems.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Typhoid and paratyphoid start similarly, but the timing and symptoms differ.

### Symptoms of Typhoid

- The time between infection and symptoms can be 3 to 60 days.  
- Usually, it takes 8 to 14 days.  
- At first, you may have a headache, body aches, and a mild fever.  
- After 2 to 3 days, your fever rises to 39 to 41 degrees Celsius.  
- You may feel very tired, dizzy, and weak.  
- You may have stomach pain and body aches.  
- Some people have constipation instead of diarrhea.  
- The high fever can last up to three weeks.  
- Later, you may get:  
  - Diarrhea  
  - Small, light red spots on your stomach  
  - A slower heartbeat

### Symptoms of Paratyphoid

- The time between infection and symptoms is 1 to 10 days.  
- You may have:  
  - A high fever (up to 39 degrees)  
  - Diarrhea  
  - Nausea and vomiting  
  - Stomach pain

---

## What Causes Typhoid?

Typhoid is caused by a type of bacteria called *Salmonella enterica*.  
There are two main types:

- **Typhi** – causes typhoid fever  
- **Paratyphi** – causes paratyphoid

### How Do You Get Typhoid?

- Infected people pass the bacteria in their poop or pee.  
- The bacteria can get into water or food if waste is not properly handled.  
- You can get sick by drinking contaminated water or eating contaminated food.  
- Person-to-person spread is rare.  

> **Important:** About 2 to 5 out of every 100 people who recover from typhoid still carry the bacteria in their body.  
> These people can spread the disease even if they feel fine.  
> They are not allowed to work in food handling jobs, restaurants, or places where they touch food.

---

## How Common Is Typhoid?

Typhoid and paratyphoid happen worldwide.  
They are more common in countries with poor sanitation.  
This includes parts of Africa, South America, and Southeast Asia.

### In Germany

- Between 50 and 100 cases of typhoid are reported each year.  
- In 2019:  
  - 86 people got typhoid  
  - 36 people got paratyphoid  
- Most of these people were infected while traveling in Asia, especially in Pakistan or India.  
- In 2020, cases dropped by about two-thirds.  
  - This was because travel was limited during the coronavirus pandemic.

### Worldwide

- The World Health Organization estimates:  
  - 11 to 21 million people get typhoid each year  
  - Up to 160,000 people die from it  
- About 5.5 million people get paratyphoid each year.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Typhoid starts with mild symptoms.  
Then the fever stays high for days or weeks.  
Without treatment, recovery takes longer.  
The illness can come back after you start feeling better.  
This can happen more than once.

Babies are more likely to have serious problems.

Paratyphoid is similar but less dangerous.

### Possible Complications

If typhoid is severe, it can cause life-threatening problems:

- Bleeding or holes in the intestines  
- Infection in the belly (peritonitis)  
- Inflammation of the gallbladder  
- Blood clots that break loose and block blood vessels  
- Bone infections  
- Infection of the heart lining (endocarditis)  
- Infection of the brain and spinal cord (meningitis)

> **Important:** After recovering, you are protected from getting typhoid again for about one year.

---

## How Can You Prevent Typhoid?

The best ways to prevent typhoid are:

- Be careful about food and water when traveling to high-risk areas  
- Get vaccinated before traveling

### Food and Water Safety

- Avoid tap water and ice made from tap water.  
- Do not eat raw or undercooked food.  
- Avoid:  
  - Salads  
  - Seafood  
  - Fruits that are not peeled  
  - Fresh juices  

> **Rule to remember:** “Peel it, cook it, or forget it.”

### Vaccines

You should get vaccinated before traveling to high-risk areas like:

- South and Central Asia (e.g. Pakistan, India, Nepal, Afghanistan, Bangladesh)  
- Any part of Asia, Africa, Central or South America with poor hygiene  
- Areas where living conditions are basic (e.g. during trekking, relief work, or after disasters)  
- Long stays in areas with high disease rates and poor hygiene

There are two types of vaccines:

1. **Injection (shot)**  
   - Made from dead bacteria  
   - Given into the muscle  
   - Works for up to 3 years  
   - Does not protect against paratyphoid  
   - Side effects: soreness at the site, headache, tiredness, body aches

2. **Oral capsules (taken by mouth)**  
   - Made from weakened live bacteria  
   - Taken as 3 capsules, one every 2 days  
   - Gives about 60% of people protection for at least 1 year  
   - Also gives some protection against paratyphoid B  
   - Side effects: nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, headache, fever, rash, diarrhea after fever

> **Important:**  
> - People who took the oral vaccine and travel again to a high-risk area should get the full vaccine again after 3 years.  
> - If you live permanently in a high-risk area, get a booster every 3 years.

Many health insurance plans cover travel vaccines.  
Check with your provider before getting vaccinated.

---

## How Is Typhoid Diagnosed?

Typhoid can look like the flu.  
If you’ve been in a tropical area, it can be mistaken for malaria.

Blood tests may show changes, but they are not enough to confirm typhoid.

To be sure, a doctor must find the bacteria.  
They do this by:

- Taking a blood sample  
- Growing the bacteria in a lab  
- In rare cases, testing bone marrow, urine, or stool

---

## How Is Typhoid Treated?

The sooner you start treatment, the better.  
Typhoid is treated with antibiotics.

The right antibiotic depends on the bacteria.  
Doctors test the bacteria to make sure the medicine works.

> **Important:**  
> Since November 2016, some typhoid bacteria in Pakistan are resistant to all common antibiotics.  
> This means the usual medicines do not work.  
> Because of this, getting vaccinated is strongly recommended before traveling to Pakistan.

---

## Where Can You Get More Information?

If you want to get vaccinated or think you might have typhoid, see a doctor who specializes in tropical medicine.  
Some university hospitals have special tropical medicine departments that offer advice.

# Rheumatoid Arthritis
