Rheumatoid arthritis is a long-term condition that causes joint pain and swelling. It is also often called rheumatism. The disease slowly damages joints, making them stiff and sometimes deformed. There is no cure, but treatment can help manage symptoms and slow the disease.

---

## Quick Facts

- Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease.
- About 1 in 100 adults in Germany has this condition.
- Women are two to three times more likely to get it than men.
- Over time, joints can become deformed and stiff.
- Muscles weaken as the disease progresses.
- Treatment includes medicine, physiotherapy, and sometimes surgery.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Rheumatoid Arthritis?

There are many types of joint diseases. But when people say "rheumatism," they usually mean rheumatoid arthritis. This condition causes long-term inflammation in multiple joints. The inflammation can damage the joints over time, leading to pain, stiffness, and deformity.

The disease can also affect other parts of the body. For example, it may harm blood vessels or organs. People with advanced rheumatoid arthritis often feel constant pain and extreme tiredness. Simple tasks like washing, eating, or buttoning clothes can become hard.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The first sign is often swelling in one or more joints. This causes pain and stiffness. Swelling usually happens in the small joints of the fingers and toes. It often affects the same joints on both sides of the body.

Common symptoms include:

- Warm, swollen joints – the same joints on both hands or both feet are usually affected.
- Pain in the joints.
- Stiff joints – especially after resting, like in the morning. It may take more than an hour to move the joints again.
- Weak muscles – people move less because of pain, so muscles lose strength over time.
- Feeling tired – the disease affects the whole body, so many feel weak and exhausted.
- Rheumatoid nodules – small hard lumps under the skin. They are usually not painful.

Symptoms vary from person to person. Not everyone has the same symptoms. Some people have more pain, others have more fatigue.

> **Important:** Rheumatoid arthritis is not the same as osteoarthritis.  
> - Rheumatoid arthritis is caused by the body attacking its own joints.  
> - Osteoarthritis is caused by wear and tear on the joints.  
> The two diseases are treated differently and progress in different ways.

---

## What Causes Rheumatoid Arthritis?

Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease. This means the body’s immune system mistakenly attacks the lining inside the joints. The exact reason for this is still unknown.

Some people have a higher chance of getting the disease because of their family history. Certain infections with viruses or bacteria may also trigger the immune system to react in the wrong way.

Smoking increases the risk of getting rheumatoid arthritis. It also makes the disease worse over time.

---

## How Common Is It?

About 1 in 100 adults in Germany has rheumatoid arthritis. Most people develop it after age 50. But it can start earlier, even in teens, though this is rare.

Women are much more likely to get it than men. On average, women develop it about 10 years earlier than men.

---

## How Does It Progress?

The disease often starts in the small joints of the fingers, hands, or toes. It can also affect elbows, ankles, or knees. Joints near the center of the body, like shoulders or collarbones, may also become inflamed.

The course of the disease varies. A study of people with rheumatoid arthritis found that:

- Almost half had only minor problems in daily life.
- About 4 in 10 had moderate problems.
- About 1 in 10 had serious difficulties.

Examples of hard tasks included getting out of bed, dressing, or opening jars, bottles, or packages.

Some people get worse over time. Others stay the same for years. Some have flare-ups – sudden increases in pain and swelling – followed by periods of relief.

In later stages, the disease can affect more than just joints. Inflammation can harm blood vessels. This raises the risk of heart and blood vessel diseases.

But this risk depends on other factors too, such as high blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, and high cholesterol.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask questions and examine your joints. They will look for swelling, pain, and stiffness. Swelling in finger or toe joints is a strong sign. Swelling in larger joints like shoulders or knees also matters.

The doctor will check how long symptoms have lasted and how many joints are affected.

A blood test can help. It may show certain antibodies and signs of inflammation. But these results are not always clear. Other conditions can cause similar results.

> **Important:** Early signs are often mild and not obvious. It can be hard to spot in the first weeks or months.  
> If you think you might have rheumatoid arthritis, see a doctor as soon as possible. A specialist called a rheumatologist is best for diagnosis.

---

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure for rheumatoid arthritis. But treatment can help control symptoms and slow the disease.

Medicines reduce inflammation. They can also slow joint damage. These drugs help ease pain, swelling, and stiffness. They help keep joints working as long as possible.

Physical therapy and exercise are very helpful. They improve movement, strength, and joint function. Good choices include:

- Walking
- Cycling
- Swimming
- Water aerobics
- Dancing
- Strength training
- Aerobics

If medicine does not help and joints are badly damaged, surgery may be needed. For example:

- The inflamed lining of the joint (synovium) can be removed.
- A joint prosthesis (artificial joint) can be inserted.
- Bones in a joint can be fused together to reduce pain.

Treatment depends on:

- How bad the inflammation is.
- How many joints are affected.
- How far the disease has progressed.
- How well past treatments worked.
- Whether the person needs help managing pain and daily life.

Psychological support can also help people cope with pain and limitations.

For more information on exercise, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

---

## Can Rehabilitation Help?

If rheumatoid arthritis is hard to control, or if it stops you from working for a long time, rehabilitation may be helpful.

The goal is to help you live better every day. It supports you in staying active, working, or returning to work. For older adults, it helps maintain independence and avoid needing long-term care.

Rehab usually lasts three weeks. It includes:

- Rheumatology (joint care)
- Physiotherapy (movement therapy)
- Ergotherapy (help with daily tasks)
- Social work
- Psychology

There are two types:

- **Inpatient rehab:** You stay at the clinic during treatment.
- **Outpatient rehab:** You stay at home and go to the clinic each day.

Costs are covered by health, pension, or accident insurance. But a doctor must first say rehab is needed. The insurance company must also approve it.

---

## What Is Life Like with Rheumatoid Arthritis?

Living with rheumatoid arthritis means dealing with pain, tiredness, and physical limits. Medicine can cause side effects. All of this affects daily life.

Many people need more time for simple tasks. They must rest more often. Doctor visits, treatments, and taking medicine take up a lot of time.

Because of fatigue, many people need more sleep. They may struggle to focus or get started in the morning.

The disease can also cause emotional stress. You might feel afraid, sad, or angry. These feelings can be hard for others to understand.

Still, many people learn to manage their symptoms. They find ways to live full and meaningful lives, even with limitations.

# Adolescent Scoliosis

Scoliosis in teenagers causes the spine to curve sideways and twist. The exact cause is not known. Mild cases often only need regular check-ups. More serious cases need treatment.

---

## Quick Facts

- Scoliosis makes the spine curve and twist.
- Doctors do not know what causes it.
- Mild scoliosis may not need treatment, but it should be checked often.
- Moderate scoliosis is often treated with a special brace.
- Surgery is only needed if the curve is very bad.
- Exercise and sports help strengthen back muscles.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Scoliosis?

Scoliosis causes the spine to curve sideways and twist. It usually starts during growth and has no clear cause. Because the cause is unknown, doctors call it "idiopathic."

Most of the time, the curve stays small and does not need treatment. But the spine should be checked every few months until growth stops. This helps catch any worsening early.

If the curve gets worse or is moderate, a brace may help. The brace stops the spine from curving more.

If the curve is very bad, surgery may be needed. During surgery, doctors connect several spine bones together to straighten the spine.

---

## What Are the Signs of Scoliosis?

Most teens with scoliosis do not have symptoms. Some may feel back pain or tightness in the shoulders. But many people without scoliosis also have back pain, so it’s hard to say if scoliosis is the real cause.

The most common sign is visible changes in the body. The back, shoulders, hips, or chest may look uneven or tilted. When bending forward, the ribs may stick out on one side, forming a bump.

The spine can curve more or less. Doctors measure the curve using a number called the Cobb angle. This number comes from an X-ray.

---

## What Causes Scoliosis?

Doctors do not know what causes adolescent scoliosis. That is why it is called "adolescent idiopathic scoliosis."

"Adolescent" means it happens during teenage years. "Idiopathic" means the cause is unknown.

Scoliosis usually starts between age 10 and when the spine stops growing.

It is not caused by poor posture. Teens cannot prevent it by sitting or standing better. No treatment has been found to stop it from starting.

Some families have a history of scoliosis. About 1 in 10 teens with scoliosis has a parent with the same condition. Doctors also think that if parts of the spine grow at different speeds, the risk goes up.

---

## How Common Is Scoliosis?

About 2 out of every 100 teens between ages 10 and 16 have scoliosis. Most have only a small curve.

Of all teens with scoliosis:

- 75% have a mild curve (10 to 20 degrees)
- 15% have a moderate curve (20 to 30 degrees)
- 5% have a severe curve (30 to 40 degrees)
- 5% have a very severe curve (over 40 degrees)

Girls are more likely to get scoliosis than boys. And when girls do get it, it is more likely to be severe.

---

## How Does Scoliosis Progress?

It is hard to predict if a curve will stay small or get worse. But doctors can make a guess based on:

- How big the curve is (Cobb angle)
- How mature the bones are

The bigger the curve and the younger the bones, the more likely it is to get worse.

Bone maturity is checked with an X-ray of the hip bone (iliac crest). This is called the Risser stage. There are 6 stages (0 to 5). Stage 0 means bones are still growing fast. Stage 5 means growth is done.

Once bone growth is complete, the spine only curves more if the curve is very large — 50 degrees or more.

> **Important:** People with scoliosis may have more wear and tear on their spine. This can lead to back pain in adulthood, especially in the lower back. But back pain is common, so it’s hard to know if scoliosis is really the cause. Studies have given mixed results.

---

## How Is Scoliosis Diagnosed?

Doctors first rule out other causes of spine problems, like legs of different lengths.

During the exam, they ask about:

- Any pain or discomfort
- Past health problems
- Family history of scoliosis
- When the curve was first noticed
- How it has changed over time

They then check posture and body shape.

To learn more, doctors may do:

- A standing X-ray of the spine: shows how bad the curve is and helps calculate the Cobb angle.
- A check of growth stage: doctors measure height and ask about growth spurts.
- An X-ray of the hip bone (iliac crest) or hand: helps determine bone maturity (Risser stage).

---

## How Is Scoliosis Treated?

There are several treatment options:

- **Regular check-ups:** The spine is checked every 4 to 6 months while growing. If the curve gets worse, treatment starts.
- **Physical therapy:** Special exercises like the Schroth method help with posture, breathing, stretching, and muscle strength. These may help the spine stay straighter. But there is not much strong evidence yet.
- **Brace (orthosis):** A brace holds parts of the spine in place. It stops the curve from getting worse. The brace is worn until growth stops.
- **Surgery:** If the curve is very bad, surgery can straighten the spine. Doctors use rods, wires, hooks, or screws to hold the spine in place.

> **Important:** Exercise and sports do not stop scoliosis. But they help keep the back strong and healthy. There is no proof that chiropractic care or electrical stimulation works for scoliosis.

For more details on treatments, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

---

## What Happens During Rehabilitation?

Most teens with scoliosis can be treated at home. But if symptoms are severe or quality of life is affected, inpatient rehab may help.

In Germany, there are special centers for scoliosis rehab. Treatment lasts 3 to 6 weeks. It includes:

- Physical therapy
- Help with emotional or mental health
- Training on how to use the brace

---

## Living with Scoliosis Every Day

Finding out you have scoliosis can be scary. Teens often worry about fitting in. Treatment can feel long and hard. You may wonder:  
- How will I wear a brace?  
- What can I still wear?  
- How will friends react?

But in reality, scoliosis and its treatment usually do not stop you from enjoying friends, hobbies, or fun activities.

It may take time to get used to the brace or daily exercises. Be patient. It becomes easier with time.

Remember: scoliosis can be treated successfully. Most people know when treatment will end.

Talking to others your age who have scoliosis can help. Join a support group or online community.

Parents should listen to their child’s worries. Involve them in every step of treatment decisions.

# Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD)

This condition affects blood flow in the arms or legs. It can cause pain and other serious problems. This article explains the signs, causes, and treatment of PAD.

---

## Quick Facts

- PAD means the blood vessels in the arms or legs are narrowed.
- Poor blood flow can cause pain when walking.
- The main cause is hardening of the arteries (called arteriosclerosis).
- Pain often goes away when you rest.
- PAD is more common in older adults.
- Smoking makes PAD worse.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Peripheral Artery Disease?

PAD is a condition where blood flow to the arms or legs is reduced. It mostly affects the legs, but sometimes the arms.

It happens when blood vessels become narrow due to buildup of fatty deposits. This is called arteriosclerosis.

In the early stages, most people feel no pain or other symptoms.

Later, you may feel pain in your legs or arms when walking. The pain goes away when you stop and rest.

If the blood flow gets very bad, the tissue can die. In extreme cases, doctors may need to remove a limb to stop infection.

Even mild PAD should be taken seriously. It can be a sign of other heart or blood vessel problems.

**Fun fact:** Because people with PAD often stop walking to rest—like looking in store windows—this condition is sometimes called “window-shopper’s disease.”

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

In the early stages, you may not notice any symptoms.

As PAD gets worse, you may feel pain in your calves, thighs, feet, buttocks, or arms. The pain usually starts after walking a certain distance.

In advanced cases, the pain can happen after walking less than 200 meters. It goes away after resting for a few minutes. This is called intermittent claudication.

Later, the pain may happen even when you are sitting or lying down. It often affects the front of the foot and toes.

Some people find that moving around helps ease the pain.

As blood flow gets worse, sudden sharp pain can occur. This may lead to numbness or even paralysis.

You might also feel like bugs are crawling on your skin. This is called “formication.”

Other signs include:
- Skin that looks pale or cold
- A weak or missing pulse in the leg or foot
- Wounds that do not heal
- Sores on the feet, especially in people who are bedridden
- Gangrene (dead tissue), which can turn black—especially on the toes. This is sometimes called “smoker’s leg”

---

## What Causes PAD?

The most common cause is arteriosclerosis. This is when fatty deposits build up inside blood vessels. Over time, this makes the vessels narrow and stiff.

Less blood flows through the narrowed vessels. This means less oxygen reaches the legs and arms.

The more the vessels are blocked, the worse the blood flow becomes.

Other causes can include:
- Tumors pressing on blood vessels
- Inflamed blood vessels
- Blood clots (thrombosis)

---

## What Increases the Risk of PAD?

You are more likely to get PAD if you:
- Smoke
- Have diabetes
- Are older
- Have a family history of PAD
- Have high blood pressure
- Have high cholesterol

Smoking makes the disease worse and increases the risk of serious complications.

---

## How Common Is PAD?

About 3 to 10 out of every 100 people in industrialized countries have PAD.

The chance of having PAD increases with age. Among people aged 70 and older, 15 to 20 out of every 100 have PAD.

---

## How Does PAD Progress?

In the early stage, the blood vessels are only slightly narrowed. The body still gets enough blood and oxygen.

As the narrowing gets worse, symptoms appear. At first, pain only happens when walking. Later, it can happen even when resting.

Poor blood flow also makes it hard for wounds to heal. This can lead to long-lasting sores (chronic wounds) and infections in the bones.

If blood flow stops completely, the tissue dies. This is called ischemia.

**Important:** If you keep smoking after being diagnosed, your condition is likely to get worse faster.

---

## Can PAD Be Screened For?

Yes. If you are at higher risk, doctors recommend screening even if you have no symptoms.

You should consider screening if you:
- Smoke
- Have diabetes
- Have a family history of PAD

Doctors check blood pressure in your arm and ankle. They compare the two numbers. This is called the ankle-brachial index. It helps show if blood flow is poor.

---

## How Is PAD Diagnosed?

Your doctor will start by asking about your symptoms and risk factors.

They will ask about:
- Whether you smoke
- How much physical activity you do
- Whether close family members have had similar problems

Next, they will do a physical exam. They will check for:
- Cold or pale skin
- Bluish color in the limbs
- Weak or missing pulse
- Open sores, ulcers, or dead tissue—especially on the feet or lower legs

If the results are unclear, they may do an ankle-brachial index test. This measures blood pressure in your arm and ankle. The ratio helps confirm if PAD is present and how severe it is.

They may also do a treadmill test. You walk on a treadmill at a fast pace with a slight incline. The test lasts about 5 to 10 minutes. Blood pressure is checked before and after. A drop of 20% or more means PAD is likely.

To see where the blockages are, doctors use imaging tests:
- Ultrasound (duplex sonography) to see blood flow
- X-rays with a special dye (contrast agent) to highlight blocked areas

---

## How Is PAD Treated?

There are several ways to treat PAD:

- Treat other health problems
- Walking exercises and medicine
- Surgery to open blocked blood vessels
- Living a healthy lifestyle

### Treating Other Health Problems

If you have other conditions, treating them can help PAD. This includes:
- Lowering high blood pressure with medicine and exercise
- Using medicine to control cholesterol
- Managing diabetes well. Good blood sugar control helps protect blood vessels

### Walking Exercises and Medicine

If you have pain when walking, you may have intermittent claudication.

The best non-drug treatment is structured walking. Do this 3 times a week for 30 to 60 minutes. It works best if you start with expert guidance for at least 3 months.

If walking doesn’t help, your doctor may prescribe medicine to improve blood flow.

### Surgery to Open Blood Vessels

If walking and medicine do not help, surgery may be needed.

Doctors can use a thin tube (catheter) to insert a balloon into the blocked artery. They inflate the balloon to open the vessel. This is called vascular dilation.

They may also place a stent—a small metal tube—to keep the artery open.

In some cases, a bypass is done. A healthy blood vessel from another part of your body is used to go around the blocked area. This lets blood flow freely again.

If tissue has already died, infection can become life-threatening. In such cases, amputation may be needed.

### Living a Healthy Lifestyle

Doctors recommend:
- Not smoking
- Eating a balanced diet
- Exercising regularly

These habits help prevent heart attacks, strokes, and other heart problems.

If you struggle to quit smoking, you can:
- Use nicotine patches, gum, or lozenges
- Ask your doctor for help with a smoking cessation program

---

## What Aftercare Is Needed?

PAD is a long-term condition. Regular check-ups are important.

- Have your first follow-up visit 3 months after treatment.
- If symptoms haven’t improved or the disease is getting worse, more treatment may be needed.
- If treatment is working well, an annual check-up with your family doctor is usually enough.

# Oral and Throat Cancer – Simple Explanation

This guide explains oral and throat cancer in plain language. It covers causes, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment, and support. Always talk to your doctor for personal advice.

---

## What Is Oral and Throat Cancer?

Oral cancer and throat cancer are serious diseases. They start in the lining of the mouth or throat. They can also start on the lips or in the salivary glands.

Doctors call these cancers squamous cell carcinoma. This means they begin in the flat cells that line the inside of the mouth and throat.

### Salivary Gland Cancer

Cancer can also start in the small salivary glands inside the mouth and throat. It can also start in the larger salivary glands near the ears or under the jaw. These cancers come from different types of cells and behave in different ways.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

In the early stages, oral and throat cancer often causes no symptoms. You may not feel any pain or notice anything wrong.

If you have a change in the lining of your mouth or throat that lasts more than two weeks, see a doctor. Do not wait.

As the cancer grows, symptoms may appear. These depend on where the tumor is.

- If the tumor is in the mouth: You may have pain, trouble moving your tongue, or difficulty swallowing and speaking.
- If the tumor is in the back of the nose (nasopharynx): You may have trouble breathing or nosebleeds.
- If the tumor is in the throat (oropharynx): You may have trouble swallowing, a sore throat, or ear pain. A lump in the neck is often the first sign. This means the cancer may have spread to the neck lymph nodes.
- If the tumor is in a large salivary gland: You may notice a painless swelling. Later, you may feel pain or numbness, or your face may droop. This happens if the cancer affects the facial nerves.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

Cancer happens when cells in the body change in a harmful way. These changes can happen by chance over time. But some things make this more likely.

The main risk factors are:

- Smoking tobacco
- Drinking alcohol
- Having red or white patches in the mouth that do not go away (these are called precancerous changes)
- Infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV)

For cancer in the back of the nose (nasopharynx), another risk factor is:
- Infection with the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)

For lip cancer, another risk factor is:
- Too much sun or tanning bed exposure (UV radiation)

Even after treatment, tobacco and alcohol stay dangerous. They raise the risk of the cancer coming back or new cancers forming.

---

## How Does the Cancer Spread?

Oral and throat cancer often starts from abnormal tissue that is not yet cancer. Over time, it can turn into cancer.

### Spread to Lymph Nodes

The cancer can spread early to nearby lymph nodes in the neck. Doctors often treat these nodes even if they look normal.

### Spread to Other Organs

In some cases, the cancer spreads through the blood. The most common places are the lungs. Less often, it spreads to the liver or bones. Bone spread is more common in nasopharynx cancer.

### Second Cancers

If you smoke or drink, you are more likely to get another cancer later. This could be in the head and neck, lungs, or esophagus.

---

## What Happens If Cancer Is Suspected?

If a doctor suspects cancer, they will examine your mouth, throat, nose, and voice box.

Specialists like ear, nose, and throat doctors or oral surgeons usually do the exam. Sometimes your regular doctor or dentist finds the problem first.

If they see a suspicious area, they take a small sample of tissue. This is called a biopsy. A lab checks the sample under a microscope to see if it is cancer.

For salivary gland tumors, a thin needle is used to take the sample. This is called a fine needle biopsy.

### Tests to Check the Spread

To see how far the cancer has spread, you may need imaging tests. These include:

- Ultrasound of the neck, throat, and belly
- CT or MRI scans of the neck, throat, and chest
- X-ray of the jaw
- Bone scan
- PET/CT scan

These tests help doctors plan your treatment.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on where the cancer is, how big it is, how fast it grows, and your overall health.

### Surgery

Surgery is an option if the doctor can remove the whole tumor. Your health must allow for surgery.

Sometimes, a tube is placed in your windpipe to help you breathe during and after surgery. This tube may stay in place permanently if the voice box is removed. This usually happens in advanced cases.

After surgery, some patients need radiation or chemotherapy. This is especially true if the cancer is advanced or if there is a high risk of it coming back.

For salivary gland cancer, surgery is often the main treatment. The goal is to remove the tumor completely. Radiation may follow, but chemotherapy is less common.

### Removing Lymph Nodes

Doctors often remove lymph nodes from the neck. This is called a neck dissection. Even if the nodes look normal, cancer may be hiding in them.

### Radiation and Chemotherapy

If surgery is not possible or not wanted, radiation therapy is an option. Often, it is combined with chemotherapy.

Cancers in the back of the nose (nasopharynx) respond very well to radiation and chemotherapy.

### Side Effects of Treatment

Surgery and radiation can cause side effects.

- You may have trouble chewing, swallowing, or speaking.
- If the voice box is removed, you will lose your natural voice. You can learn to speak again using special tools or techniques.
- Radiation can dry out your mouth, make swallowing hard, or damage your teeth and jaw.
- Surgery or radiation to the neck can cause swelling in the face and neck. This is called lymphedema.

---

## What If the Cancer Cannot Be Cured?

When a cure is not possible, the goal is to improve quality of life. This is called palliative care.

The treatment aims to:
- Slow down the cancer
- Help you live longer
- Reduce pain and other symptoms

Options include:
- Chemotherapy
- Targeted therapy
- Immunotherapy
- Radiation
- Surgery to relieve symptoms

Supportive care is very important. This includes:
- Pain relief
- Help with eating and drinking
- Psychological support

Talk to your doctor about all your options.

---

## Can Patients Get Rehab?

Yes. Rehabilitation helps you recover after treatment.

Rehab can help with:
- Speech and swallowing problems
- Nutrition advice
- Returning to work

Talk to your doctor about rehab. They can recommend a program and confirm your need.

Choose a hospital with experience in voice, speech, and swallowing rehab.

For more information, visit the Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center (in German).

---

## What Aftercare Is Available?

After treatment, you will need regular checkups. These help monitor your health and catch any return of cancer early.

- At first, checkups are close together.
- Later, they are spaced further apart.

During each visit, your doctor:
- Checks your symptoms
- Does a physical exam
- May order imaging tests like ultrasound, CT, MRI, or PET/CT

They will also check:
- How well you chew, swallow, and speak
- If you need help with nutrition
- If you need psychological support

You may be referred to:
- A speech therapist
- A nutritionist
- A psychologist

### Quitting Smoking and Alcohol

Aftercare often includes help to quit smoking and stop drinking alcohol. These habits increase the risk of cancer returning or new cancers.

---

## How Does This Affect Daily Life?

Cancer and its treatment can make everyday tasks harder.

You may have trouble:
- Chewing food
- Swallowing
- Speaking clearly

Some people find it hard to hide these changes. This can affect social life and confidence.

But you can improve with:
- Exercises for chewing and swallowing
- Speech therapy
- Support from professionals

### Financial Challenges

This illness can affect your job. You may need time off or change your work.

Get advice early on from a social worker or legal expert. This can help avoid financial problems.

---

## Where Can You Get Help?

Look for hospitals with special experience in treating head and neck cancers. The German Cancer Society (DKG) certifies such centers.

You can find a list at the OncoMap website.

For more information on daily life and support, visit the Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center (in German).

### Need More Help?

Call the Cancer Information Service:
- Phone: 0800 - 420 30 40 (free of charge)
- Email: krebsinformationsdienst@dkfz.de

They can answer your questions about oral and throat cancer.

# Lazy Eye in Children

Lazy eye is common in children. It happens when one eye sends a blurry image to the brain. The brain then pays more attention to the clearer image from the other eye. This causes the weaker eye to stop developing properly.

This article explains how to spot lazy eye and how it can be treated.

---

## Quick Facts

- One eye sends a clear image. The other sends a blurry one. The brain ignores the blurry image.
- If this happens during childhood, the brain may keep favoring the stronger eye.
- About 60 to 70 out of 100 children with a squint also have lazy eye.
- Only about 2 out of 100 children without a squint have lazy eye.
- Around 3 out of every 100 children and young people in Europe have lazy eye.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Lazy Eye?

Your brain usually uses both eyes together to build a clear picture. This helps your eyesight grow strong. But in some children, one eye sends a clearer image than the other. The brain starts to ignore the weaker eye. This stops the eye from developing fully.

Doctors call this condition lazy eye or amblyopia. The word comes from Greek and means "dimness of vision."

---

## Signs of Lazy Eye

If your child squints or if you think they have an eye problem, see an eye doctor right away.

Other signs include:
- Trouble seeing objects clearly.
- Holding toys or books very close to the eye.
- Turning the head to one side when looking at things.

These signs can show that one eye is not working well.

---

## What Causes Lazy Eye?

Lazy eye happens when the two eyes send different images to the brain. The brain cannot make one clear picture. This stops the eye from developing properly.

The most common cause is a squint. A squint means one eye looks straight ahead while the other eye turns in a different direction. The brain sees two different images. To avoid double vision, the brain blocks the image from the squinting eye.

Other causes include:
- Refractive errors: the image on the retina is blurry.
  - Short-sightedness: only close-up things are clear.
  - Long-sightedness: only distant things are clear.
  - Astigmatism: all things look blurry because the eye’s lens or front surface is shaped oddly.

---

## How Common Is Lazy Eye?

Lazy eye is most common in children. In Europe, about 3 out of every 100 children and young people have it. Among preschool children, the number is higher — about 6 out of every 100.

Most cases start before a child turns 8 years old.

---

## How Can We Spot Lazy Eye Early?

A child’s eyesight grows fastest in the first five years of life. Finding and treating vision problems early can prevent lifelong vision problems. It can also help with school and social life.

All children with public health insurance in Germany now get a special eye check at age 3 years and 4 months (U7a). This test looks for vision problems. It is part of regular child health checks.

---

## How Is Lazy Eye Diagnosed?

An eye doctor can use several tests to check for lazy eye:

- **Eye charts:** These test how well a child can see. Special charts are used for babies and young children.
- **Eye position test:** A squint may not be easy to see. The doctor covers one eye at a time. They watch if the other eye moves to adjust.
- **Eye exam:** The doctor checks for other causes like cataracts. They may use a tool called a retinoscope. It shines a light into the eye. The doctor sees how the light reflects off the retina. They then try different lenses to measure how much correction is needed.

These tests are safe. Before the retinoscopy, the child may get eye drops to widen the pupils. These drops can cause a mild burning feeling or skin irritation in some cases.

---

## How Is Lazy Eye Treated?

Glasses alone cannot fix lazy eye. But there are several ways to help the weaker eye improve.

Treatment options include:
- Prescribing glasses to correct vision problems.
- Covering the stronger eye with a patch. This forces the weaker eye to work.
- Using eye drops that blur the stronger eye. This also makes the weaker eye work harder.

Some children improve in just a few weeks. Others need treatment for months or longer. But most children get better with treatment.

If another problem causes the lazy eye — like a droopy eyelid — that problem is treated first.

For more details on treating lazy eye in children, visit [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de).

# Rosacea

Many people have redness on their face, small bumps, or visible tiny blood vessels. This could be a skin condition called rosacea. Learn how to recognize it and what might make it worse.

---

## Quick Facts

- Rosacea is a long-term skin problem that causes inflammation on the face.
- It is not contagious. You cannot catch it from someone else.
- The symptoms can be mild or severe.
- It often shows up on the cheeks, chin, forehead, or nose.
- Doctors do not yet know exactly what causes it.
- Most people find out over time what makes their symptoms worse.
- It usually starts after age 30.
- About 2 to 5 out of every 100 adults in Germany have rosacea.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Rosacea?

Rosacea is a common skin condition that causes redness, visible small blood vessels, and small pus-filled bumps on the face. It often comes and goes.

Many people do not realize their red face is due to a medical condition. Like other visible skin issues, rosacea can affect how someone feels about themselves. But there are ways to reduce symptoms and avoid flare-ups.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms can vary. They may appear on the cheeks, chin, forehead, or nose.

There are four main types:

- **Type 1:** Redness on the face, sometimes with visible small blood vessels.
- **Type 2:** Redness plus small bumps and pus-filled spots.
- **Type 3:** Thickened skin, especially on the nose. This can make the nose look swollen or bulbous.
- **Type 4:** Eye problems such as redness, itching, watering, or sensitivity to light. The eyes may feel dry or like something is in them.

Some people also have dry, itchy, burning, or peeling skin. The skin becomes more sensitive than normal.

The condition can look different in each person. Some have more than one type at the same time. In rare cases, the neck, chest, or scalp can also be affected.

---

## What Causes Rosacea?

Doctors do not fully understand what causes rosacea. But these factors may play a role:

- Inflammation and immune system reactions.
- Changes in the tiny blood vessels in the skin.
- A family history of rosacea.
- A weak skin barrier that does not protect well.
- Overreaction to tiny mites or bacteria on the skin.

Flare-ups can be triggered by:

- Sunlight.
- Hot or cold weather.
- Stress.
- Alcohol.
- Spicy foods.
- Hot drinks.
- Harsh soaps or cosmetics.
- Skin injuries.
- Some medicines, like those that widen blood vessels.
- Long-term use of steroid creams (but this is rare if used correctly).

> **Important:** Rosacea is not acne. It does not cause extra oil in the skin. The bumps are not caused by clogged pores.

---

## How Common Is Rosacea?

Rosacea usually starts after age 30. It affects about 2 to 5 out of every 100 adults in Germany. It is more common in women than men. People with fair skin are more likely to get it.

Many people with long-term facial redness do not know they have a skin disease.

---

## How Does Rosacea Progress?

Rosacea often comes and goes. There are times when the skin is worse, followed by times when it improves or clears up.

Over time, the skin can change. New symptoms may appear. But in many cases, the symptoms stay the same for years.

In men, the nose can become thick and swollen over time. This is called rhinophyma.

Rosacea can also affect the eyes. Symptoms include:

- Red, itchy eyes.
- Watery eyes.
- Sensitivity to light.
- Dry eyes.
- Pain or a feeling like something is in the eye.

Inflammation can happen in the eyelid edges, the lining of the eye (conjunctiva), or the clear front part of the eye (cornea).

---

## How Can You Prevent Rosacea Flare-Ups?

Many people learn over time what makes their rosacea worse. Anything that causes facial redness can also make rosacea worse.

Common triggers include:

- Alcohol.
- Hot drinks.
- Harsh soaps or irritating cosmetics.
- Skin injuries or cuts.
- Certain medicines, like those that widen blood vessels.
- Spicy foods.
- Sunlight.
- Extreme heat or cold.

Keeping a diary of your symptoms and what you do each day can help you find your triggers. Once you know them, you can avoid some of them.

For more tips on prevention, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## How Is Rosacea Diagnosed?

A dermatologist (skin doctor) can diagnose rosacea by looking at your skin. If your eyes are affected, you may also need to see an eye doctor.

---

## How Is Rosacea Treated?

Treatment depends on the type and how bad the symptoms are.

For mild cases:

- Use gentle skin care.
- Protect your skin from the sun.
- Use mild, soap-free cleansers with a low acid level.
- Avoid products that irritate the skin.
- Use makeup that is safe for sensitive skin to cover redness.

For more severe cases, doctors may prescribe:

- Creams, gels, or lotions with active ingredients like azelaic acid, brimonidine, ivermectin, or metronidazole.
- These are applied directly to the skin.

If the skin does not improve with topical treatments, or if symptoms are severe, a doctor may prescribe the antibiotic doxycycline to reduce inflammation.

For rhinophyma (swollen nose), surgery may be needed to reshape the nose.

---

## What Is Life Like with Rosacea?

Rosacea is not dangerous. But the redness can affect your feelings and confidence.

Some people stare or make assumptions, like thinking the redness is from drinking too much alcohol. This can be upsetting.

Unlike acne, rosacea is not well known. Talking about it with family, friends, or coworkers can help others understand.

Makeup with good coverage can help hide redness. But some makeup can make symptoms worse. Try different products carefully. A dermatologist can help you choose safe ones.

# Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)

ALS is a serious condition that affects the nerves controlling your muscles. These nerves slowly stop working over time. This leads to muscle weakness and eventually paralysis. There is no cure for ALS right now. But treatments can help ease symptoms and improve quality of life.

---

## Quick Facts

- ALS is a disease that slowly destroys nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord.
- These nerve cells are called motor neurons. They send signals to your muscles to make them move.
- The exact cause of ALS is still unknown.
- ALS often starts with weakness in one arm or leg, or trouble speaking or swallowing.
- Over time, more muscles become weak and paralyzed. Eventually, the muscles used for breathing can be affected.
- There is no cure, but treatments can help slow the disease and make life easier.
- Treatment focuses on keeping you as comfortable and independent as possible.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is ALS?

ALS stands for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. It is a disease that slowly damages the nerves that control your muscles. These nerves are called motor neurons.

The reason why these nerves break down is not fully known. As the nerves die, scar tissue forms in the spinal cord and brain stem. The muscles they control shrink and weaken. This is called atrophy.

ALS usually starts with weakness in one arm or leg. Some people first notice it when they have trouble speaking or swallowing. Other early signs include muscle twitches, stiffness, or cramps.

The weakness spreads over time. It may start in one arm, then affect the other arm, then the legs. Eventually, the muscles used for breathing become weak.

Most people live 3 to 5 years after diagnosis. But some live longer than 10 years.

There is no cure. But treatments can help you stay active and comfortable for as long as possible.

---

## What Are the Symptoms of ALS?

ALS shows up when the nerves that control movement begin to fail.

Because these nerves are in different parts of the brain and spinal cord, symptoms can vary.

Common symptoms include:

- Weakness in a limb that gets worse over weeks or months
- Loss of muscle size (muscle wasting)
- Muscle twitches, spasms, or stiffness
- Trouble speaking clearly (slurred speech)
- Trouble swallowing
- More saliva than normal (drooling)
- Shortness of breath or trouble breathing
- Feeling very tired or sleepy
- Laughing or crying without reason
- Changes in behavior or mood
- Trouble thinking clearly, or even memory loss (dementia)

> **Important:** In about 7 out of 10 people, ALS starts in the arms or legs. In about 1 in 4 people, it starts with speech or swallowing problems.

Symptoms usually get worse over time. For example, if one arm is weak, the other arm will likely become weak later. Then the legs are affected.

Eventually, the muscles used for breathing stop working. This can be life-threatening.

---

## What Causes ALS?

ALS damages motor neurons in the brain stem and spinal cord. These are the nerves that control movement.

In some cases, it may also affect nerves involved in thinking and memory.

The exact cause is still unknown. Scientists believe several things inside the cells may go wrong.

About 1 in 10 cases of ALS is inherited. This means it runs in families due to changes in genes. Several genes have been linked to ALS.

Environmental factors may also play a role, but this has not been proven.

---

## What Increases the Risk of ALS?

The only proven risk factors are:

- Getting older (most cases happen after age 40)
- Having a family member with ALS

Some people think certain chemicals or toxins in the environment cause ALS. But there is no solid proof yet.

---

## How Common Is ALS?

ALS is rare. About 1 to 3 people in every 100,000 are diagnosed each year.

It becomes more common with age. Most people diagnosed are between 60 and 75 years old.

Men are slightly more likely to get ALS than women.

---

## What Is the Outlook for ALS?

ALS causes a steady decline in muscle function. It often starts in one arm or leg and spreads to other parts of the body.

It is hard to predict how fast the disease will progress. That is why it is important to get support early. This helps you stay involved in daily life as long as possible.

Many symptoms can be managed with tools, medicine, or therapy.

The disease becomes life-threatening when the breathing muscles are affected.

People with ALS should talk to their family early about whether they want to use a breathing machine if their breathing gets too weak.

> **Important:** A living will (also called an advance healthcare directive) lets you say in advance what medical care you do or do not want.

---

## How Is ALS Diagnosed?

Many diseases have similar symptoms to ALS. There is no single test that can confirm ALS.

Doctors must rule out other possible causes before making a diagnosis.

Diagnosis is based on:

- Physical exam findings
- How symptoms spread over time
- Tests to check nerve and muscle function

ALS is suspected when both upper and lower motor neurons are damaged. Upper motor neurons are in the brain. Lower motor neurons are in the spinal cord.

- Damage to upper motor neurons causes muscle weakness and shrinking.
- Damage to lower motor neurons causes stiffness and twitching.

To diagnose ALS, doctors look for:

- Damage to both upper and lower motor neurons
- Symptoms in more than one part of the body
- No other explanation for the symptoms

Doctors use several tests:

- Checking reflexes and muscle strength
- Electroneurography (ENoG) to test nerve signals
- Electromyography (EMG) to check muscle response
- MRI scans to rule out other conditions (like tumors or spinal problems)

Genetic testing may be done in some cases.

---

## How Is ALS Treated?

There is no cure for ALS. But treatments can help manage symptoms and improve quality of life.

Your care team will include specialists such as:

- Neurologists
- Physiotherapists
- Occupational therapists
- Speech and language therapists
- Nurses
- Dietitians
- Social workers

Medicines like riluzole or edavarone may slow the disease a little.

As paralysis increases, physiotherapy helps keep your limbs moving and prevents stiffness.

Staying connected with friends and family improves your well-being.

Treatment depends on your symptoms:

- If breathing becomes hard, breathing exercises and special devices can help.
- Excess saliva (drooling) can be reduced with tablets or injections.
- If swallowing is hard, food can be changed to softer or thicker forms. A feeding tube can be used if needed.
- If speaking is hard, communication devices can help.
- Muscle spasms and pain can be treated with medicine and therapy.
- As movement becomes harder, a wheelchair may be needed.
- Anxiety, depression, or sleep problems can be treated with medicine.

There are also clinical trials testing new treatments. You can find information about current trials on the website of the **Outpatient Clinic for ALS and Other Motor Neuron Diseases at Charité University Hospital in Berlin**.

---

## Where Can I Get Support for Advanced ALS?

As ALS gets worse, you may need more care. If you can no longer be cared for at home, a hospice is an option.

Hospices provide expert care at the end of life. They help you stay comfortable and respected.

It is important to talk to your family early about your wishes for care at the end of life.

> **Important:** A lasting power of attorney (LPA) or guardianship directive lets you choose who makes decisions for you if you are no longer able to.

---

## Where Can I Find More Information?

An ALS diagnosis changes your life and your family’s life. Knowing what to expect and how to cope is important.

For more information on diagnosis, treatment, and research, visit the website of the **Outpatient Clinic for ALS and Other Motor Neuron Diseases at Charité University Hospital in Berlin**.

For detailed support on coping with the diagnosis and living with ALS, visit:

- The **German Society for Muscle Diseases (Deutsche Gesellschaft für Muskelkranke e.V.)**
- The **German Brain Foundation (Deutsche Hirnstiftung e.V.)**

# Alcohol Poisoning (Being Very Drunk)

Alcohol poisoning happens when someone drinks too much alcohol in a short time. It mainly affects the brain. If someone is wobbly and speaks unclearly, they are very drunk. If they pass out, call an emergency doctor right away.

---

## Quick Facts

- The symptoms depend on how much alcohol is in the blood.
- People who wobble and slur their words are clearly drunk.
- Very high levels of alcohol can lead to coma or stop breathing.
- Young people and teens often get alcohol poisoning when they drink a lot quickly.
- Small children can get very sick from even a small amount of alcohol. They may have dangerously low blood sugar.
- People with alcohol poisoning are watched closely in the hospital until their body breaks down the alcohol.
- Always talk to a doctor if you think someone has alcohol poisoning.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical care. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Alcohol Poisoning?

Alcohol poisoning happens when someone drinks a large amount of alcohol in a short time. The harmful part of alcohol is called ethanol. This can be dangerous and even deadly.

Most people who need hospital care for alcohol poisoning are teens and young adults. This often happens because of binge drinking. Binge drinking means men drink more than five standard drinks in a few hours. Women drink more than four standard drinks in the same time.

- Drinking more than two small beers a day for men is high-risk.
- Drinking more than one small beer a day for women is high-risk.
- If drinking causes health problems, it is called harmful drinking.
- If someone cannot stop drinking and it controls their life, they may be dependent on alcohol.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Symptoms depend on how much alcohol is in the blood. Even a small amount can be harmful. The faster the blood alcohol level rises, the worse the symptoms get. People react differently to alcohol, so these are general signs.

### Blood Alcohol Level Up to 0.5 per mille:
- Feeling relaxed and less shy.
- Talking more than usual.
- Trouble with small, careful movements.

### Blood Alcohol Level 0.5 to 1.0 per mille:
- Poor judgment.
- Trouble with movement and balance.
- Slower reactions.

### Blood Alcohol Level 1.0 to 2.0 per mille:
- Wobbly walking.
- Slurred speech.
- Mood swings and strange behavior.

### Blood Alcohol Level 2.0 to 4.0 per mille:
- Nausea and vomiting.
- Cold body.
- Hard to understand speech.
- Memory gaps.
- Confusion.
- Double vision.
- Shaking eyes.

### Blood Alcohol Level Over 4.0 per mille:
- Breathing stops.
- Unconsciousness or coma.
- Heart stops.
- Death.

> **Important:** People with long-term alcohol problems may not show serious symptoms until their blood alcohol level is extremely high.

---

## How Does Alcohol Poisoning Affect Small Children?

Children usually get alcohol poisoning by accident. They might:
- Find and drink alcohol left where they can reach it.
- Mistake strong drinks for water.
- Drink mouthwash, cough syrup, or fermented fruit juice.
- Have high-alcohol products rubbed on their gums to stop tooth pain.

Children react faster than adults. Even a small amount can cause a dangerous drop in blood sugar. If not treated, low blood sugar can cause seizures or coma.

In young children, the usual signs of being drunk—like confusion or trouble walking—may not appear until the blood alcohol level is very high. At first, they may just:
- Complain of stomach pain.
- Act strangely.
- Stop eating or drinking.
- Have trouble sleeping.

> **Important:** If you think your child has drunk alcohol, take them to the hospital. Doctors can give them fluids and sugar through a needle if needed.

---

## What Causes Alcohol Poisoning?

There are two types: drinking a lot in a short time (acute) or drinking too much over weeks or months (chronic).

Acute alcohol poisoning happens when someone drinks a large amount quickly. This is called binge drinking.

Chronic drinking means drinking too much over a long time. In these cases, poisoning symptoms may only show up at very high blood alcohol levels.

Teens and young adults often binge drink because of:
- Their personality.
- What their friends do.
- Pressure from others.
- Problems at home, school, or with friends.
- Alcohol is cheap and easy to get.

---

## How Does Alcohol Affect the Body?

Alcohol goes into the blood through the stomach and intestines. How fast it enters the blood depends on:

- The stronger the drink, the faster the blood alcohol level rises.
- Food in the stomach slows down alcohol absorption.
- Women’s blood alcohol levels rise faster than men’s. This is because women have less water in their bodies and more fat.
- Larger, heavier people have more body mass to spread the alcohol. So their blood alcohol levels stay lower even if they drink the same amount.

Alcohol spreads through the body in the blood. It mainly harms the brain. It slows down nerve activity, like an anesthetic. This makes it hard to think clearly, move well, or keep balance.

Alcohol blocks certain brain receptors. These are normally used by natural brain chemicals. If someone drinks heavily for a long time, the body makes more of these receptors. This means more alcohol is needed to feel the same effect. This is called developing a tolerance.

Alcohol also affects blood vessels. It makes blood vessels in the skin open wider. This makes you feel warm. But if it’s cold outside, you lose body heat fast. Alcohol also lowers blood sugar. Without enough sugar, the body can’t make enough heat. This raises the risk of hypothermia.

Alcohol makes you pee more than you drink. This leads to dehydration. It also changes the balance of minerals in the blood. Alcohol stops the liver from sending sugar into the blood. This can cause low blood sugar.

These effects cause thirst, weakness, and headaches after drinking. This is what people call a hangover.

Alcohol and its waste products are toxic. They can damage cells in the body. The heart, liver, and brain are especially at risk. Long-term drinking can cause:
- Inflammation of the pancreas.
- Inflammation of the stomach and intestines.
- Cancer.

> **Important:** If you take medicine, drinking alcohol can cause serious side effects. Always check the medicine label. It is best to avoid alcohol when taking medicine.

---

## How Common Is Alcohol Poisoning?

Alcohol is widely used and accepted in many cultures, especially in Western countries.

In Germany:
- About 18% of adults drink in a risky way.
- About 3% drink in a harmful way.
- About 3% are dependent on alcohol.

Alcohol poisoning is most common in teens and young adults.

In 2018, nearly 20,500 children and young people aged 10 to 20 were hospitalized for alcohol poisoning in Germany. The number was lower than in previous years, but the number of 10 to 15 year olds increased.

A 2014 survey found:
- Almost 13% of 12 to 17 year olds binge drink at least once a month.
- Over 35% of 18 to 25 year olds do the same.

Men binge drink about twice as often as women. The most common age group for regular binge drinking is 18 to 29. People with higher education tend to binge drink less than those with less education.

---

## How Is Alcohol Poisoning Diagnosed?

Doctors can check for alcohol in breath, blood, or urine.

If someone is clearly drunk and shows serious symptoms, they likely have alcohol poisoning. A blood test can confirm the level.

If someone is acting drunk, doctors must rule out other causes, such as:
- Head injury from a fall or accident.
- Blood infection (sepsis).
- Brain inflammation (encephalitis).
- Seizures.
- Poisoning from other substances.
- Low body temperature (hypothermia).
- High fever.
- Thyroid problems.
- Lack of oxygen.
- Other body chemical imbalances.

Doctors often check other blood values at the same time. These can show if someone has been drinking too much for a long time.

In some cases, a brain scan (like a CT scan) is done. This helps find hidden head injuries from an accident.

Because alcohol can cause an irregular heartbeat, doctors may do an ECG (heart test).

---

## How Is Alcohol Poisoning Treated?

The main treatment is watching vital signs until the body breaks down the alcohol.

It is very important to keep the airway clear. If someone is unconscious, place them on their side (recovery position). This prevents choking on vomit.

Cover them up to keep them warm. They can get cold quickly.

> **Important:** Severe alcohol poisoning is life-threatening. It must be treated in a hospital. If the person has long-term alcohol problems, withdrawal symptoms may appear when the alcohol level drops. These must also be treated in hospital.

Many people with alcohol poisoning are dehydrated and have low blood sugar. Doctors give them fluids and sugar through a needle.

If long-term alcohol use is suspected, doctors also give vitamin supplements—especially vitamin B1—to protect the nerves.

After the person wakes up, doctors will talk to them. They may offer follow-up appointments. The goal is to help change drinking habits and reduce alcohol use.

---

## What Happens After Alcohol Poisoning?

The outcome depends on how severe the poisoning was.

Mild drunkenness in healthy people usually causes no lasting harm.

But severe alcohol poisoning can be deadly—even for healthy people. Death can happen from:
- Accidents

# Heart Rhythm Problems

Heart rhythm problems are common, especially in older adults and people with other heart issues. Not all heart rhythm problems need treatment. If treatment is needed, doctors may use medicine or a heart procedure.

---

## Quick Facts

- The heart’s beat starts with electrical signals from the right upper chamber.
- Even healthy hearts do not beat perfectly regularly. It is normal to feel a skipped beat a few times a day.
- Doctors call a heart rhythm problem when the heart beats too irregularly or does not match your activity level.
- These problems can start suddenly and go away in seconds or minutes.
- Some people do not need treatment.
- Others may need medicine, heart surgery, or a device like a pacemaker.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Heart Rhythm Problem?

Your heart beats because of electrical signals. These signals start in the right upper chamber of the heart. They usually travel in a steady rhythm—about 60 to 80 beats per minute when you are at rest. The signals spread through the heart muscle. The heart then beats faster or slower depending on how active you are. This keeps blood flowing properly through your body.

Even healthy hearts can have small irregularities. You may feel a skipped beat now and then. These are called extrasystoles.

Doctors call it a heart rhythm problem when the heart beats too irregularly or does not match your activity level. For example:

- The heart beats too slowly. This is called bradycardia. One common cause is an AV block, where signals between the upper and lower heart chambers are delayed or blocked.
- The heart beats too fast. This is called tachycardia. People often call this a racing heart. It can be harmless, but it can also be a sign of a serious problem like atrial fibrillation.
- The heart beats in an uneven pattern. This is called arrhythmia. It can happen even if the heart is beating at a normal speed.

Sometimes more than one problem happens at once. For example, people with atrial fibrillation may have a fast and irregular heartbeat.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

If the heart rhythm is off for just a short time, you may not notice anything. Others feel:

- A skipped beat
- A pounding or fluttering feeling in the chest (called palpitations)
- A fast heartbeat, even when you are not moving

If the heart rhythm is so bad that blood does not pump well, you may feel:

- Dizzy
- Light-headed
- Faint

The heart muscle also needs oxygen. If it does not get enough, you may have:

- Chest pain
- Shortness of breath
- Feeling weak

---

## What Causes Heart Rhythm Problems?

A slow heartbeat (bradycardia) is often caused by an AV block. This means signals between the upper and lower heart chambers are delayed or blocked. It can also happen if the heart’s natural pacemaker (the sinus node) stops working well.

A fast heartbeat often happens with atrial fibrillation. It can also be caused by atrial flutter or scarring in the heart.

These conditions usually come from heart disease. Common causes include:

- Coronary heart disease
- Heart attack
- Heart valve problems
- Inflammation of the heart muscle (myocarditis)
- Heart failure

Other risk factors include:

- High blood pressure
- Smoking
- Drug use
- Drinking too much alcohol

Other possible causes:

- An overactive thyroid
- Chronic kidney disease
- Diabetes
- Electric shock from an accident
- Birth defects in the heart’s electrical system
- Inherited heart cell problems

Some people with healthy hearts still get heart rhythm problems. These are called idiopathic arrhythmias.

Certain medicines can also cause heart rhythm problems. These include:

- Some blood pressure medicines
- Heart medicines
- Antidepressants
- Antibiotics
- Cancer medicines

---

## How Common Are Heart Rhythm Problems?

Heart rhythm problems are common, especially in older adults and people with other heart issues. These people often need treatment.

Younger, healthy people may have mild rhythm problems that are not dangerous. But some inherited heart rhythm disorders can be life-threatening.

Problems can start suddenly and go away quickly. Some people have them again and again. Others have ongoing issues.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Some people pass out during a heart rhythm problem. This can lead to falls and injuries.

Heart rhythm problems can cause heart failure or make it worse.

With atrial fibrillation, blood can form clots in the heart. If a clot breaks loose, it can travel to the brain and cause a stroke.

Serious complications usually only happen if the heart is already damaged. Then, a rhythm problem can lead to:

- Poor blood flow
- Cardiac arrest
- Ventricular fibrillation (a very fast, chaotic heartbeat)

In ventricular fibrillation, the heart beats so fast that it cannot pump blood. Without quick treatment, this can cause sudden death.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

You may feel a fast or irregular heartbeat. Or you may feel a skipped beat.

Your doctor may check your pulse or listen to your heart with a stethoscope. They may find your heart is too slow, too fast, or irregular.

An electrocardiogram (ECG) can show the type of heart rhythm problem. If the ECG is normal but you still have symptoms, the problem may only happen sometimes or during exercise.

In that case, your doctor may ask you to wear a 24-hour ECG monitor. Or you may do an exercise ECG.

Other tests can help find the cause or check for complications. For example:

- An echocardiogram (ultrasound of the heart) can show if you have heart failure.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on:

- The type of problem
- The cause and whether it can be fixed
- How serious the problem is
- Whether it causes symptoms
- The risk of serious complications like stroke or ventricular fibrillation

Treatment options include:

- No treatment at all, if the problem is mild and not causing symptoms
- Medicine to help stabilize the heart rhythm
- Electric shocks (cardioversion) to reset the heart rhythm
- A heart procedure called catheter ablation. This destroys small areas of heart tissue that are causing the problem
- A pacemaker or defibrillator if the heart needs long-term help

Choosing the right treatment can be hard. A decision aid can help you and your doctor make the best choice.

---

## What Is Life Like With a Heart Rhythm Problem?

People with heart rhythm problems may feel:

- Tired
- Short of breath
- Weak

They may not have the energy for daily tasks. They may need help with things like cooking or walking.

Treatment can also be hard to manage. For example:

- Taking blood-thinning medicine every day can be a burden.
- Living with a pacemaker or defibrillator can limit some activities.

But many people live well with treatment and make adjustments to their daily lives.

# EHEC Infections

EHEC infections can cause serious diarrhea.  
They are usually caused by eating food that is contaminated.  
They can also happen from close contact with animals that carry the bacteria.  
In rare cases, these infections can lead to serious problems like sudden kidney failure.

---

## Quick Facts

- EHEC stands for enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli.  
- These are bacteria that live in the guts of animals like cows and sheep.  
- In people, EHEC can cause diarrhea and serious health problems.  
- Most infections come from food or surfaces that have animal poop on them.  
- A serious complication is called hemolytic uremic syndrome, or HUS.  
- HUS mainly affects young children.  
- You can reduce your risk by washing your hands often and keeping your kitchen clean.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is an EHEC Infection?

EHEC is a type of harmful E. coli bacteria.  
Some E. coli live naturally in the human gut.  
But EHEC lives in the gut of animals like cows, sheep, and deer.  
It makes poisons that can make people very sick.  

Some people get infected but have no symptoms.  
Others get severe diarrhea.  
A rare but serious problem is hemolytic uremic syndrome, or HUS.  
HUS can cause sudden kidney failure.  
This condition usually goes away over time.  
But some people may have long-term health issues later.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

You might not have any symptoms at all.  
Or you could get very sick.  
Symptoms usually start 2 to 10 days after infection.  
Common early signs include watery diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and stomach pain.  
Fever can happen, but it is rare.

### Severe Cases

In 10 to 20 out of every 100 people, the diarrhea turns bloody.  
You may also have strong stomach cramps and fever.  
Babies, young children, older adults, and people with weak immune systems are most at risk.

### Cases with Complications

In 5 to 10 out of every 100 people, HUS develops 5 to 12 days after diarrhea starts.  
Children are most likely to get HUS.  
HUS destroys red blood cells and causes sudden kidney failure.  
Toxins build up in the blood, which is dangerous.  
It also destroys platelets, which help blood to clot.

---

## What Causes an EHEC Infection?

EHEC infections happen when you are exposed to EHEC bacteria.  
These bacteria are found in the intestines of ruminant animals like cows, goats, sheep, and deer.  
The animals pass the bacteria in their poop.  
You can get infected by touching animal poop and then touching your mouth.  

You can also get infected indirectly.  
This happens when you eat food that has been contaminated.  
Or when you touch something that has the bacteria on it.  
For example, touching an animal at a farm or petting zoo.  
Handling raw meat or unwashed vegetables can also spread the bacteria.  

Even healthy animals can carry EHEC and spread it.  
The bacteria can survive in the environment for a long time.  
You only need a very small number of bacteria to get sick.  

Common sources of infection include:
- Swimming in lakes with dirty water
- Drinking unpasteurized milk
- Eating raw sausages or undercooked meat
- Eating raw leafy greens like lettuce, spinach, or sprouts

People with diarrhea can pass the bacteria to others.  
This is especially true in the same household.  
EHEC bacteria can stay in your stool for days or weeks.  
In children, they can stay for over a month.  
But the risk of spreading the infection drops over time.

---

## How Common Are EHEC Infections?

EHEC infections happen all over the world.  
We do not know the exact number because not all cases are tested.  

In Germany in 2020, 1,370 cases were reported.  
Children under 5 years old, especially one-year-olds, are most often affected.  
Two deaths were linked to EHEC.  
Both were in older adults.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

EHEC infections can be mild or very severe.  
Most people recover fully, even after severe diarrhea.  
Even serious cases with HUS can be treated successfully.  

In rare cases, children may need long-term dialysis.  
But most recover without lasting damage.  
Still, some people may have long-term health problems.

The toxins from EHEC attack small blood vessels throughout the body.  
This means HUS can affect many organs at once.  
The kidneys and digestive system are most affected.  
But the brain, nerves, pancreas, muscles, and heart can also be harmed.

This can lead to:
- Nervous system problems
- Pancreas issues, such as type 2 diabetes
- Higher risk of kidney disease later in life
- High blood pressure

---

## How Can You Prevent EHEC Infections?

EHEC bacteria can survive in the environment for a long time.  
Even a tiny amount can cause illness.  
Follow these hygiene rules to stay safe:

- Wash your hands with soap after using the toilet.  
- Wash your hands before eating or preparing food.  
- Wash hands thoroughly after touching animals, especially at farms or petting zoos.  
- Make sure children wash their hands before putting fingers in their mouth or eating.  
- Follow kitchen hygiene rules carefully.  
- Avoid close contact with people who are sick, especially siblings.

If you or someone in your home is infected, take extra care:

- Use a separate toilet if possible.  
- Wash hands well after changing diapers.  
- Infected people should not go to school or daycare.  
- Doctors decide when it is safe to return.  
- People who prepare food or work in kitchens must not work until they are no longer passing the bacteria in their stool.

For more prevention tips, visit the consumer advice from the Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR).

---

## When Should You See a Doctor?

Not all diarrhea is caused by EHEC.  
But doctors may test for EHEC if you have:

- A child under 6 with diarrhea needing hospital care  
- Bloody diarrhea  
- A colonoscopy showing bleeding in the gut  
- Diarrhea in someone who works with food  
- Signs of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS)  
- Close contact with someone who has HUS  
- A child with sudden kidney failure  

A stool sample is tested for EHEC and its toxins.  
Blood tests can also check for signs of HUS.

> **Important:** If EHEC is found or HUS is suspected, public health officials must be informed right away.

---

## How Is an EHEC Infection Treated?

There is no specific cure for EHEC.  
Treatment focuses on keeping your body strong.  
You need to drink enough fluids and replace lost minerals.  
If you are very sick, you may need fluids through a vein in the hospital.  
This can help protect your kidneys.

If HUS develops, doctors will give medicine to help your kidneys flush out waste.  
If your kidneys stop working, you will need dialysis.  
This is a machine that cleans your blood.  
You may also need blood transfusions to replace red blood cells, platelets, or plasma.

> **Important:** Antibiotics are not used to treat EHEC.  
> They can make the illness worse.  
> They can cause the bacteria to make more toxins.  
> This increases the risk of HUS.

# Mitral Valve Insufficiency

This is a condition where the valve between the left upper chamber and the left lower chamber of the heart does not close properly. Because of this, some blood flows backward instead of moving forward into the body.

## Quick Facts

- Heart valve problems usually develop slowly over many years.
- Mitral valve insufficiency is the second most common heart valve problem after aortic valve stenosis.
- The leak in the mitral valve means some blood returns to the left upper chamber instead of going out to the body.
- This can happen due to aging or poor blood flow to the heart muscle.
- If the problem is mild, you may only need regular check-ups to monitor your heart.
- If symptoms appear or your heart gets worse, several treatment options are available.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Mitral Valve Insufficiency?

Your heart has four valves. These valves act like one-way doors. They make sure blood flows in the right direction and does not leak back.

Damage to heart valves usually happens over time. Doctors call this an acquired heart valve problem. It mostly affects older adults because of wear and tear.

Mitral valve insufficiency is the second most common valve issue after aortic valve stenosis. When the mitral valve leaks, some blood flows back into the left upper chamber. This increases the amount of blood in that chamber. The heart must then work harder to pump blood out.

Treatment can include replacing the valve. But in most cases, doctors try to fix the existing valve instead of replacing it.

## What Are the Symptoms?

Your heart can often handle a leaky mitral valve for years without any symptoms.

Symptoms only appear when the heart can no longer pump enough blood to the body. This means organs and the heart itself do not get enough oxygen.

Possible symptoms include:

- Feeling weak or tired
- Swelling in the legs or ankles
- Heartbeat that feels too fast, too slow, or irregular
- Trouble breathing, especially at night
- Coughing at night
- Chest pain or pressure
- Fainting

## What Causes Mitral Valve Insufficiency?

The most common cause is aging. Over time, the valve wears out.

Some people are born with heart valves that are shaped differently. This makes it more likely the valve will not work well later in life.

Damage to the heart muscle near the valve can also cause problems. For example, a heart attack can harm the area around the valve and lead to leakage.

## How Common Is This Condition?

Heart valve problems from aging are more common in older adults.

About 13 out of every 100 people aged 75 and older have a heart valve issue. Men are slightly more likely than women to have this problem.

## How Does It Progress?

The heart can often adjust to a leaky valve for years or even decades.

To do this, the heart muscle must work harder. Over time, the muscle gets thicker and the heart grows larger.

If the heart stays overworked, the changes become permanent. The muscle loses its flexibility. The heart chambers wear out. The heart becomes weaker.

At first, symptoms only happen during physical activity. Later, they can occur even when resting.

If not treated, this can lead to serious heart failure.

## How Can It Be Prevented?

Smoking raises your risk of heart problems, including mitral valve insufficiency. Quitting smoking is one of the best ways to lower your risk.

Infection in the inner lining of the heart (called endocarditis) can damage heart valves. This infection is often caused by bacteria.

People with a birth defect in their heart valve or those with a new valve may be given antibiotics before dental work. This helps prevent bacteria from the mouth from entering the blood and causing infection.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will start by listening to your heart with a stethoscope. This can reveal unusual sounds that suggest a valve problem.

An ultrasound of the heart, called echocardiography, confirms the diagnosis. It shows how bad the valve leak is.

Sometimes, a more detailed ultrasound is needed. This is done by placing a small tube with a probe down the throat. This is called transesophageal echocardiography. It gives clearer pictures than a regular ultrasound.

Once the diagnosis is confirmed, your doctor checks your overall health. This helps decide the best treatment.

Tests may include:

- An ECG at rest and during exercise
- Blood pressure measurement
- Blood tests to check your blood count
- X-ray of the chest, and sometimes CT or MRI scans
- A heart catheter test if there is concern about blocked heart arteries

In a heart catheter test, a special dye is injected into the heart’s blood vessels. This allows the doctor to see the blood flow on a screen.

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on several things:

- The type of valve damage
- Your symptoms
- Your age
- Your general health
- Your personal needs

Like with aortic valve stenosis, a new valve can be used. But in most cases, doctors try to fix the existing valve.

Surgery can be done in two ways:

- Open surgery through the chest
- Minimally invasive surgery using a catheter

The goal is to repair the valve instead of replacing it. This is called valve reconstruction.

Repair methods include:

- Using your own tissue (like the lining around the heart) to strengthen the valve
- Using strong threads to reattach the valve to the heart muscle
- Placing a plastic ring around the valve to make it tighter and help it close properly
- Using a small metal clip to pull the leaking parts of the valve together

This clip can sometimes make the valve close completely again.

## What Happens After Surgery?

After heart valve surgery, most people go through a rehabilitation program.

Rehab helps you get back to normal physical activity. It also improves your quality of life.

During rehab, your doctor checks your heart regularly. Medications are adjusted as needed.

Some people worry about doing too much after surgery. Rehab includes counseling to help you manage these fears. Many people learn to better understand their body and limits.

## Living With Heart Valve Disease

Heart valve disease can be hard on your mind and emotions.

Symptoms like tiredness and weakness can make daily life harder.

Choosing a treatment can be stressful and confusing. Talk to your doctor and family about your concerns.

After surgery, it may be hard to handle stress for a while. It helps to talk to family and friends early about who can help and how.

You can also ask your health insurance for support before surgery. For example, you may qualify for help with housework or other tasks.

# Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML)

Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a rare type of blood cancer.  
It happens when certain white blood cells grow out of control.  
These cells come from the bone marrow, blood, spleen, and liver.

New treatments have made a big difference in how CML is managed.  
Many people with CML now live nearly as long as people without the disease.

This article explains what CML is, how it is diagnosed, and how it is treated.  
It is not a substitute for talking to a doctor.
