Do not use this information to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Chronic Myeloid Leukemia?

CML is a type of cancer that starts in the bone marrow.  
It causes certain white blood cells to grow too fast.  
These abnormal cells build up in the blood, spleen, and liver.

CML is caused by a change in the genes of a blood stem cell.  
This change creates a new chromosome called the Philadelphia chromosome.  
Almost all people with CML have this chromosome in their leukemia cells.

---

## What Are the Symptoms of CML?

CML often develops slowly.  
Most people do not notice symptoms at first.  
It is often found by chance during a routine blood test.

Some people may feel tired, weak, or have less energy.  
They might lose their appetite and lose weight without trying.  
They may feel full quickly in the upper belly because the spleen is enlarged.  
Some have a mild fever or sweat a lot at night.  
Others may have bone pain.

These symptoms are not unique to CML.  
They can happen with many other illnesses.  
If you feel unwell for a long time, lose weight without trying, sweat heavily at night, or have a low-grade fever, see your doctor.

Your doctor can check what is causing your symptoms.  
They may refer you to a specialist if needed.

---

## What Causes CML?

CML starts when a blood stem cell in the bone marrow gets a genetic change.  
This change creates a new chromosome called the Philadelphia chromosome.  
It forms when parts of two chromosomes swap places: chromosome 9 and chromosome 22.

This swap creates a new gene called BCR-ABL.  
This gene tells the cell to make a protein called BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase.  
This protein makes the blood cells grow and divide too fast.

The Philadelphia chromosome was first found in Philadelphia, USA.  
That is why it is named after the city.

---

## Are There Risk Factors for CML?

In most cases, doctors do not know what causes CML.  
But one possible risk factor is exposure to high levels of radiation.  
Most people with CML have not been exposed to radiation.

CML is considered an occupational illness for people who work with certain chemicals.  
These include butadiene, benzene, and benzene-related substances.

---

## How Common Is CML?

About 1,000 to 1,200 people in Germany are diagnosed with CML each year.  
This makes it a rare type of cancer.

More people are living with CML today.  
This is because new treatments help patients live longer.

---

## How Does CML Progress?

CML usually goes through three stages:

### 1. Chronic Phase

This is the earliest stage.  
Most people are diagnosed here.  
There are few or no symptoms.  
The disease grows slowly.

The goal of treatment is to keep CML in this stage.  
With good treatment, life expectancy is almost the same as for healthy people.

### 2. Accelerated Phase

Symptoms get worse.  
White blood cell counts go up.  
More immature blood cells (called blasts) appear in the blood and bone marrow.  
The spleen gets larger.

### 3. Blast Phase

This stage is like acute leukemia.  
The disease grows very fast.  
The body cannot make enough healthy blood cells.  
This leads to a higher risk of infections, bleeding, and anemia.

Without treatment, this stage can be life-threatening.  
It can lead to death within weeks or months.

---

## How Is CML Diagnosed?

Doctors use blood and bone marrow tests to diagnose CML.

A blood sample is taken from a vein in your arm.  
For a bone marrow test, a doctor numbs a small area on your lower back.  
They use a needle to take a small sample of bone marrow from the hip bone.

Doctors look at the blood and bone marrow under a microscope.  
They also test for genetic changes in the leukemia cells.

---

## How Is CML Treated?

The main treatment for CML is a type of medicine called tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs).  
These are also called targeted therapies.

TKIs stop a protein called BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase.  
This protein is made by the abnormal cells.  
By blocking it, the drugs stop the cancer cells from growing.

There are several different TKIs.  
Your doctor will choose the best one based on:

- How well it works  
- Possible side effects  
- Your overall health and other medical conditions

Doctors recommend starting treatment as soon as possible after diagnosis.  
The goal is to reduce the number of cancer cells as much as possible.

If treatment works very well and lasts, some people may stop taking the medicine.  
But it is not yet clear if this means the disease is completely gone.

**Important:** CML should only be treated by experienced specialists.  
Treatment should be done in a center that specializes in blood cancers.

---

### Regular Testing Is Needed

You will need regular blood and bone marrow tests.  
These tests help doctors see how well treatment is working.

Doctors use three main measures:

- **Hematologic remission:** All blood counts are normal. The spleen is back to normal size. You have no symptoms.
- **Cytogenetic remission:** No Philadelphia chromosome is found in the bone marrow.
- **Molecular remission:** The test can find even one cancer cell among thousands of normal cells.  
  If the number of cancer cells is very low, doctors call this deep molecular remission.  
  This is the best treatment goal.

---

### Stem Cell Transplant: Another Option

If TKIs stop working, your doctor may switch to a different TKI.  
If TKIs are no longer effective, a stem cell transplant may be an option.

In a stem cell transplant, healthy blood stem cells from a donor are given to you.  
The donor’s cells take over and make healthy blood cells.

This treatment is strong and has risks.  
But it can offer a chance for a cure.

---

### Want to Learn More?

For more information about CML treatment, side effects, and how to manage them, visit the website of the **German Cancer Research Center’s Cancer Information Service**.

---

## What Happens After a CML Diagnosis?

If treatment works well, most people with CML live a normal life span.  
But you must take your medicine every day as prescribed.

If you have side effects, talk to your doctor.  
They may suggest switching to a different drug.

You will need regular check-ups.  
If the treatment stops working, your doctor will act quickly to change it.

Women with CML should not get pregnant while on TKI treatment.  
These drugs can harm the unborn baby and cause birth defects.  
If you want to have a child, talk to your doctor.  
They can help you plan your options.

For more information about having children during or after cancer, visit the **German Cancer Research Center’s Cancer Information Service** website.

---

## Where Can You Get Help?

You can find patient information about CML on the website of the **Acute and Chronic Leukemia Competence Network**.  
The German CML Study Group is part of this network.

CML should be treated by a team of specialists.  
Hospitals that are experts in treating blood cancers can become certified as centers for hematological neoplasms.

The German Cancer Society and the German Society for Hematology and Medical Oncology check these hospitals regularly.

You can find certified centers on the **OncoMAP** website.  
Go to the search tool and select “Hematological Neoplasms” under “Centre”.

**Note:** Certification is not required in Germany.  
Some excellent clinics may not yet be certified.

# Neck Pain

Neck pain is very common. Most of the time, it is not serious. About one in three adults has neck pain once a year. Women are more likely to have it than men.

Most neck pain goes away in one to two weeks. Some people feel it again after certain activities. These include long hours at a desk, heavy lifting, or intense sports.

---

## What Is Neck Pain?

Neck pain often comes from tight muscles. This can happen if you sit too long at a computer. It can also happen if you sleep in a bad position. Sometimes, the exact cause is not clear.

The pain usually gets better on its own in a few days to two weeks. But some people have it come back after doing certain things.

If the pain lasts more than three months, it is called chronic neck pain. This kind of pain is often linked to stress or emotional strain.

Many people worry that moving will make the pain worse. In most cases, this is not true. Staying active is usually safe and helpful.

You can reduce your risk of neck pain by doing exercises to strengthen your neck muscles.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

There are two main types of neck pain:

- **Axial pain**: This hurts in the neck area, especially around the neck bones. It can sometimes spread to the shoulders.
- **Radicular pain**: This pain travels along the nerves. It may go into the back of the head or down the arm. It often happens when a nerve is irritated. For example, a disk in the neck may press on a nerve. This can cause weakness, numbness, or tingling in the arm or hand.

In rare cases, neck pain can be a sign of a serious problem. See a doctor right away if you have:

- Been in a car accident or other injury
- Trouble bending your head down to your chest (stiff neck)
- Loss of control over your bladder or bowels
- Headaches with nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or sensitivity to light
- Constant, severe pain that does not go away, even when you are resting
- Unexplained weight loss, fever, or chills
- Numbness, weakness, or trouble moving your arms or fingers
- Signs of paralysis

Also see a doctor if you have:

- Tingling that lasts a long time
- Hands or legs that often go numb (like “pins and needles”)
- Weak legs
- Trouble staying balanced when walking

---

## What Causes Neck Pain?

Many things can cause neck pain. These include:

- Weak neck muscles and too much strain. Sitting at a desk for long periods can cause neck and shoulder pain. It can also cause headaches.
- Normal wear and tear on the spine. Over time, the disks between the neck bones get thinner. Small bone growths can also form on the edges of the bones.
- Whiplash. This injury often happens in car accidents, especially rear-end crashes.
- Narrowing of the spinal canal or a slipped disk. If the space around the spinal cord gets smaller, it can cause pain that spreads to the shoulders or arms. A disk that bulges or breaks open can press on a nerve and cause similar symptoms.
- A slipped disk can cause neck pain, but it does not always do so.

Neck pain can also happen with other health problems. These include:
- Inflammation in the spine
- Jaw joint problems
- Severe headaches

It is often hard to find the exact cause. The neck bones, ligaments, and nerves are packed closely together. This makes it hard to know exactly where the pain starts.

---

## How Common Is Neck Pain?

Neck pain is very common. About one in three adults has it once a year. It affects more women than men.

Most cases are not serious. They go away on their own. But some people have it come back often.

Older people are more likely to have long-lasting neck pain. People who already have back pain or a slipped disk are also more likely to have ongoing neck pain.

After a whiplash injury, how long the pain lasts depends on how hard the impact was. People who are upset or very worried about the accident often have worse and longer-lasting pain.

---

## How Is Neck Pain Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask questions. They will want to know:
- If you had an accident
- Where the pain is
- If any activity made it worse

Then, your doctor will do a physical exam. They will:
- Feel your neck from the front and back
- Check your neck movement
- Test your reflexes
- Check the strength in your arms and shoulders

**Important:** X-rays, CT scans, or MRI scans are usually not needed. They are only used if your doctor suspects a serious problem.

Even if the scan shows changes in your neck bones, this does not mean you will have pain. Many people have these changes but feel no pain. On the other hand, some people with real pain show no clear changes on the scan.

---

## How Is Neck Pain Treated?

There is not enough strong evidence for most treatments. But you can try:

- Applying heat to the neck, such as with a hot water bottle or heated pillow
- Gentle stretching and strengthening exercises
- Massage
- Pain relief medicine

More information is available at _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

**Important:** Surgery is only considered if a clear cause is found that surgery can fix.

Surgery is usually not helpful for pain from a slipped disk. This problem often gets better on its own. Also, surgery in the neck area carries risks. Always talk to your doctor about the benefits and risks before deciding.

For long-term, severe neck pain, pain management therapy can help. This is a type of treatment offered by mental health specialists. It teaches you how to live with pain so it does not take over your life.

# Diabetic Foot

High blood sugar over a long time can lead to a diabetic foot. This condition can cause serious problems if not managed well. This article explains how to prevent it and how to treat foot wounds that do not heal.

---

## Quick Facts

- A diabetic foot can happen if diabetes is not well managed.
- High blood sugar can hurt nerves and blood vessels in the feet.
- Early signs include dry skin and thickened skin (calluses).
- You can avoid serious problems by taking care of your feet.
- Wear good shoes, avoid injuries, and check your feet every day.
- Even small cuts or sores should be treated right away.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is a Diabetic Foot?

When diabetes is not controlled, it can lead to a condition called diabetic foot syndrome. This means the feet can develop serious problems.

The first warning signs are dry feet and extra thick skin. Over time, these can turn into open sores that do not heal.

About 1 in 5 to 1 in 3 people with diabetes will get a diabetic foot at some point in their life.

But this does not have to happen. Good blood sugar control and daily foot care can stop serious wounds from forming. Doctors, family members, caregivers, or foot specialists (podiatrists) can help.

---

## What Are the Signs of a Diabetic Foot?

Dry feet and thick skin are early signs. The symptoms depend on whether nerves or blood vessels are damaged.

### If nerves are damaged:
- You may not feel pain, pressure, heat, or cold.
- Your feet may feel numb or tingly.
- The skin may feel very dry and warm.
- Sores on the bottom of the foot may not heal.

### If blood vessels are damaged:
- Your feet may feel cold.
- The skin may look pale or blue.
- You may not feel a pulse in your foot.
- Sores often appear on the toes or heel.
- Your legs may hurt when walking.

---

## What Causes a Diabetic Foot?

People with diabetes have high blood sugar. If blood sugar stays high for too long, it can damage nerves and blood vessels.

When nerves are damaged, you may not feel pain or pressure. This means small injuries can go unnoticed. You might not protect your feet or treat them in time. Tight shoes, calluses, or foot shape problems can cause injuries.

When blood vessels are damaged, blood flow to the feet slows down. This makes it harder for wounds to heal.

---

## What Makes Diabetic Foot More Likely?

Some things make blood flow worse and healing harder. These include:

- Smoking
- High blood pressure
- Not being active or exercising

These factors increase the risk of serious foot problems.

---

## What Can Happen If It Is Not Treated?

If a diabetic foot is not caught early, a wound can become chronic. These wounds often happen on the toes, the bottom of the foot, the heel, or the ankle.

They can get very deep and infected. Black spots in the wound mean dead tissue. In severe cases, part of the foot or toe may need to be removed.

> **Important:** Nerve damage means you may not feel pain. This makes it easy to ignore injuries. That can lead to worse problems.

---

## How Can You Prevent a Diabetic Foot?

You can take many steps to keep your feet healthy. The most important ones are:

- Keep your blood sugar under control.
- Wear shoes that fit well and never pinch.
- Never walk barefoot.
- Check your feet every day.
- Get regular foot exams from a doctor.
- Treat high cholesterol and high blood pressure.
- Do not smoke.

To avoid pressure points and injuries:

- Wear shoes with plenty of room.
- Choose shoes with soft inner soles.
- Avoid seams or straps that rub.
- Use custom-made shoes or special insoles if needed.
- Fix or replace worn-out shoes.
- Always check your shoes before wearing them — look for stones, sand, or sharp objects.

If your feet are badly shaped, surgery may help reduce pressure on certain areas.

Even if a wound has already formed, it can still be healed with proper care. Early treatment stops it from becoming a long-term problem.

For more tips on foot care, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## How Can You Spot It Early?

Check your feet every day. Use a hand mirror to see the bottom of your feet.

Take any small cut, sore, or red spot seriously. See a doctor right away.

If you have trouble seeing or feeling your feet, ask a family member or caregiver to check them regularly. A doctor or foot care center can also help.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Your doctor will examine your feet. They will check:

- Skin color and temperature
- Blood flow in the foot
- Nerve sensitivity (using a tuning fork or thin thread)
- Any sores, pressure points, or foot shape changes

If there is a wound, the doctor will check how deep it is and whether it is infected.

To check blood flow, your doctor may use:
- Ultrasound
- Angiography (a special X-ray of blood vessels)

To check for bone damage, they may use:
- X-ray
- CT scan
- MRI scan

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treating wounds early is key. This helps prevent serious damage and lowers the chance of amputation.

Treatment includes:
- Taking all pressure off the wound
- Treating any infection
- Improving blood flow in the leg

If blood flow is poor, surgery may help. This can include:
- Opening up blocked blood vessels
- Creating a new blood vessel (bypass)

Healing time depends on the size and depth of the wound. Small wounds may heal in a few weeks. Large or deep wounds can take months.

In some cases, a skin or tissue graft may help speed healing.

Amputation may be needed if:
- The damaged area cannot be saved
- The wound will never heal
- The infection has spread
- Pain is unbearable

> **Important:** If amputation is suggested, get a second opinion. It helps to understand all your options.

The decision aid on [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de) can help you choose the best treatment.

# Acne Inversa

Acne inversa is a long-term skin condition. It causes painful lumps, pus-filled sores, and deep infections under the skin. Over time, it can damage the skin and leave scars. The condition can also affect your mood and mental health. Doctors do not yet know what causes it.

---

## Quick Facts

- Acne inversa is a long-term skin problem.
- It mainly affects the armpits, groin, and areas around the genitals and anus.
- The skin becomes very painful and may leak fluid.
- The exact cause is not known.
- There is no cure, but treatments can reduce symptoms and slow the condition.
- Treatment depends on how severe the condition is.
- **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Acne Inversa?

Acne inversa is also called hidradenitis suppurativa. It is a condition that affects the hair roots in the skin. Hair roots are the parts of the hair that grow under the skin.

When the condition flares up, the hair roots become inflamed. This leads to hard lumps, abscesses (pockets of pus), and tunnel-like holes under the skin called fistulas. These changes damage the skin and often cause scarring.

The condition causes more than just physical pain. It can also lead to stress, anxiety, and depression. Some people stop going out or avoid social situations.

There is no cure, but treatments can help reduce pain and slow the disease.

**Important:** Acne inversa is not caused by being unclean. It is not contagious.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The hair roots become inflamed again and again. This leads to:

- Blackheads and pus-filled bumps
- Hard lumps under the skin, about half to two centimeters wide
- Pockets of fluid in the skin (cysts)
- Pus-filled pockets (abscesses)
- Tunnel-like holes under the skin (fistulas)
- Scars over time

The painful areas often last for months. They may leak pus or a bad-smelling fluid if pressed or broken open.

About half of people with acne inversa feel burning, pain, itching, or warmth in the area 12 to 48 hours before a new flare-up.

The most common places for symptoms are the armpits, groin, and around the genitals and anus. But it can also appear on the buttocks, stomach, and breast folds.

---

## What Causes Acne Inversa?

The condition starts when hair roots become inflamed. This blocks the root, so oil (sebum) cannot escape. When the blocked root bursts under the skin, the oil spreads into nearby tissue. This causes more inflammation.

The skin’s sweat glands and connective tissue can also be damaged. This can lead to abscesses and fistulas.

Doctors do not know why the hair roots become inflamed.

But these factors may play a role:

- **Family history:** About 4 out of 10 people with acne inversa have a close relative with the same condition. Some genes may increase the risk.
- **Hormones:** The condition is much more common in women. It often starts after puberty and can continue until menopause.
- **Immune system problems:** Some experts believe the body’s defense system may react in a way that causes the condition.

So far, research shows that bacteria do not cause acne inversa.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

The exact cause is unknown. But if a parent has acne inversa, their child is more likely to get it. This suggests a family link.

---

## How Common Is It?

Experts estimate that up to 4 out of every 100 people worldwide have acne inversa. It usually starts between the ages of 11 and 50. It is three times more common in women than in men.

---

## What Are the Long-Term Effects?

If not treated early, acne inversa can lead to lasting problems.

- The skin damage can cause ongoing pain and make movement hard.
- Some people develop anemia (low red blood cells) or high levels of protein in the blood.
- Joint problems may also occur.
- In rare cases, it can increase the risk of a certain type of skin cancer (non-melanoma skin cancer).

The pain, bad smell, and appearance of the skin can hurt your quality of life. Many people feel sad, ashamed, or isolated. Some develop depression.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

In the early stages, acne inversa is often mistaken for other skin problems. It can take years to get a correct diagnosis.

There is no single test to confirm acne inversa. Doctors rely on a detailed medical history and a physical exam.

The doctor will ask:

- When the symptoms first started and how long they have lasted
- If the pain goes away and then comes back
- If anyone in your family has had the same condition

The doctor will look at the skin. They will check if the inflammation is deep, painful, or has caused scars.

Doctors divide acne inversa into three stages:

- **Stage 1 (mild):** One or more abscesses. No fistulas or scars.
- **Stage 2 (moderate):** Recurring abscesses. Fistulas and scars are present.
- **Stage 3 (severe):** Many abscesses that connect under the skin. Multiple fistulas and scars. Large areas of skin are affected.

**Important:** Early signs of acne inversa are often mistaken for boils. But acne inversa lumps are deeper and break open under the skin, not on the surface.

---

## How Is It Treated?

There is no cure, but treatment can help reduce pain, delay flare-ups, and slow the disease.

It is important to see a doctor as soon as you notice new symptoms.

Treatment depends on how severe the condition is.

- **Pain relief:** Doctors may prescribe painkillers in the form of creams or tablets.
- **Anti-inflammatory and antibacterial medicines:** These are used for mild to moderate cases. They come as creams or pills.
- **Hormone therapy:** For women, birth control pills may help reduce symptoms.
- **Surgery:** In some cases, doctors remove the inflamed skin.
- **Laser therapy:** This is another treatment option.
- **Combination therapy:** Many people need more than one treatment at the same time.

---

## How Can You Manage It Daily?

Living with acne inversa is easier with some daily habits:

- Eat a healthy diet.
- Keep a normal body weight.
- Quit smoking.
- Wear loose, soft clothing that does not rub the skin.

Even though poor hygiene does not cause acne inversa, using a gentle antiseptic body wash on high-risk areas may help.

The condition can deeply affect your life. Many people suffer from pain or feel embarrassed about their skin. Mental health matters.

If you feel down or stressed because of the condition, consider:

- Talking to a therapist
- Joining a support group for people with acne inversa

You are not alone. Sharing your experience with others can help.

For more information on therapy and how to find a provider, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

# Hodgkin’s Lymphoma – Simple Explanation

This page explains Hodgkin’s lymphoma in plain language. It covers what it is, what symptoms to watch for, how it is diagnosed, treated, and what you need to know after treatment.

---

## What Is Hodgkin’s Lymphoma?

Hodgkin’s lymphoma is a type of cancer that starts in the lymphatic system.  
It is sometimes called lymph node cancer or lymph gland cancer.  
The cancer begins in white blood cells called lymphocytes.  
These cells grow out of control and collect in the lymph nodes.  
The cancer can also spread to other organs like the liver.

The disease is named after a British doctor, Sir Thomas Hodgkin, who first described it in 1832.

---

## Hodgkin’s vs. Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma

There are two main types of lymphatic system cancers:  
- Hodgkin’s lymphoma  
- Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma

Hodgkin’s lymphoma has a special type of cell called a Reed-Sternberg cell.  
Doctors can see these cells under a microscope.  
Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma includes many other types of lymphatic cancers.

**Important:** If cancer spreads to the lymph nodes from another part of the body, it is not called a lymphoma.  
This is called a metastasis. It is treated differently.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

The most common early sign is a painless lump in the lymph nodes.  
These lumps are often in the neck, under the arms, or above the collarbone.  
They feel firm or rubbery when you touch them.

Other possible symptoms include:

- Fever for no clear reason  
- Sweating heavily at night  
- Losing weight without trying (this is called “B symptoms”)  
- Itching all over the body  
- A dry cough or pressure in the chest if lymph nodes behind the breastbone are swollen  
- Pain in the abdomen if the liver or spleen is enlarged  
- Back pain if lymph nodes in the back of the abdomen are swollen  
- Bone pain  
- Getting sick more often  
- Pain in swollen lymph nodes after drinking alcohol (this is rare)

These symptoms can also happen with other illnesses, like infections or other cancers.  
They are not always a sign of Hodgkin’s lymphoma.

**Important:** If a lymph node stays swollen for more than four weeks, or keeps getting bigger, see a doctor.  
A doctor may remove a small piece of the lymph node to check it.

---

## What Causes Hodgkin’s Lymphoma?

Doctors do not know the exact cause for most people.  
But they believe it comes from a mix of factors.

People with weak immune systems — for example, after an organ transplant or with HIV — are more likely to get it.  
Heavy and long-term smoking may also raise the risk.

An infection with the Epstein Barr Virus (EBV) is linked to some cases.  
Most people get EBV in childhood. It often causes no symptoms.  
In some cases, it causes glandular fever.  
After infection, the virus stays in the body for life.

**Important:** EBV is very common. Hodgkin’s lymphoma is rare.  
Only a very small number of people with EBV go on to develop Hodgkin’s lymphoma.  
And not all cases involve EBV.

---

## How Common Is It?

Hodgkin’s lymphoma is rare.  
About 2,500 people in Germany are diagnosed each year.  
It can happen at any age.  
It is most common in teenagers and young adults, or in people over 70.

---

## How Does It Develop?

Hodgkin’s lymphoma usually starts in lymph nodes in the neck or throat.  
It can also start in the chest or belly.  
The cancer cells can travel through the lymph system and blood to other parts of the body.

If left untreated, Hodgkin’s lymphoma can be life-threatening.  
But today, most people can be cured with treatment.  
Even if the cancer comes back after treatment, another round of treatment can still cure it.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

If a doctor suspects Hodgkin’s lymphoma, they will take a small sample of a swollen lymph node.  
This is done with a small cut under local anesthesia.  
You can go home the same day.  
Sometimes, the procedure needs to be done in hospital under general anesthesia.

### Confirming the Diagnosis

The tissue sample is sent to a lab.  
Experts check:

- Is it cancer?  
- If yes, what kind of cancer is it?

Most people have the classic type of Hodgkin’s lymphoma.  
A rare type is called nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma.  
Knowing the exact type helps doctors choose the best treatment.

**Important:** A blood test cannot show if you have Hodgkin’s lymphoma.

### Finding Out How Far It Has Spread (Staging)

If the diagnosis is confirmed, doctors check how far the cancer has spread.  
This is called staging. It helps decide the best treatment.

Tests include:

- A detailed medical history and physical exam  
- Blood tests  
- Imaging scans: chest X-ray, CT scan of the neck, chest, and belly, or PET-CT scan  
- Sometimes, a bone marrow test

The cancer is grouped into one of four stages.  
Doctors use the Ann Arbor system.  
They also add “A” or “B”:

- “A” means no general symptoms  
- “B” means you have symptoms like fever, night sweats, or weight loss

Staging is very important for planning treatment.

---

## Is There Screening?

There is no routine screening test for Hodgkin’s lymphoma.  
It is too rare to justify testing healthy people.

**Important:** If you have symptoms, see a doctor right away.  
Early diagnosis means treatment can be less intense and more effective.

---

## How Is It Treated?

The goal is to cure most people with Hodgkin’s lymphoma.  
Treatment should start soon after diagnosis to stop the cancer from spreading.

All patients get chemotherapy.  
This is medicine that stops fast-growing cells from dividing.  
Doctors usually use several types of chemotherapy together.  
The strength of treatment depends on how far the cancer has spread and other health factors.

Radiotherapy (targeted radiation) may also be used, especially if the cancer is in one area.

Treatment is grouped into three levels:

- Early stage  
- Intermediate (middle) stage  
- Advanced stage

Less intense treatment is often given in outpatient clinics.  
More intense treatment may require hospital stays.

Both chemotherapy and radiotherapy can cause side effects.  
Many side effects go away over time.  
Doctors can help manage them with medicines or other support.

**Important:** Surgery cannot cure Hodgkin’s lymphoma.  
Doctors only remove a lymph node to check for cancer, not to treat it.

### Clinical Studies

Doctors are always working to improve treatment.  
In Germany, the German Hodgkin Study Group (GHSG) leads this work.  
They run studies to make treatment more effective while reducing side effects.

Ask your doctor if you can join a study.  
It may offer new treatment options.

For more on chemotherapy, visit the Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center (in German).

---

## Why Is Long-Term Aftercare Important?

Most people with Hodgkin’s lymphoma are now cured.  
But regular check-ups are still needed because:

- Doctors can catch a return of the cancer early  
- They can treat side effects from treatment  
- They can prevent or treat long-term problems early

Aftercare includes:

- Talking about symptoms  
- Physical exams  
- Blood tests

Check-ups start often at first, then become less frequent over time.  
But experts recommend lifelong follow-up care.

---

## Possible Long-Term Effects

Treatment can cause lasting damage to organs.  
Doctors watch for:

- Getting sick more often (weakened immune system)  
- Feeling very tired (fatigue)  
- Problems with the thyroid gland  
- Heart problems  
- Lung problems  
- Hormone imbalances and infertility  
- New cancers (secondary tumors)

**Important:** Not everyone has these problems.  
The benefits of treatment far outweigh the risks.

---

## What Should You Do After Treatment?

Relapses are rare after 5 years.  
After 5 years, the cancer is usually considered cured.  
But you should still keep going to check-ups.  
Treatment side effects can show up years later.

Doctors should explain the risks and benefits of follow-up care.  
This helps you stay motivated to keep coming to appointments.

---

## Who Handles Aftercare?

Your general doctor or specialist is usually the first contact.  
Some hospitals offer special follow-up clinics for former cancer patients.  
This is especially helpful if you were treated as a child or young adult.

---

## Want to Have Children?

Hodgkin’s treatment can affect fertility.  
If you want to have children later, talk to your doctor before treatment.  
There are ways to protect your fertility, such as freezing sperm or eggs.

For more information, visit the Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center (in German).

---

## Where to Get Help

For diagnosis and treatment in Germany, contact:

- **German Hodgkin Study Group (GHSG)**  
  Part of the Competence Network Malignant Lymphomas

You can also contact:

- **Competence Network Malignant Lymphomas (KML)**  
  For all questions about lymphomas

Hodgkin’s lymphoma should be treated by a team of specialists.  
Hospitals that are experts in this area can become certified as oncology centers for blood cancers.

The German Cancer Society (DKG) and the German Society for Hematology and Medical Oncology (DGHO) check these hospitals.

# Diarrhea

Diarrhea is a common illness. It often happens when you have a virus in your body. If diarrhea lasts a long time, it can cause serious problems. The body can lose too much water and salt. This can be dangerous, especially for young children and older adults.

---

## Quick Facts

- Diarrhea is often caused by a virus. The most common viruses are norovirus and rotavirus. These viruses spread easily.
- Doctors call it diarrhea when you have very loose or liquid stool at least three times in 24 hours.
- Acute diarrhea usually lasts a few days to one week.
- Your body loses water and salt (electrolytes). You must replace these to stay healthy.
- If diarrhea lasts longer than two weeks, it is called persistent diarrhea. This needs treatment.
- Some types of gut infections must be reported to health authorities.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Diarrhea?

Diarrhea is very common. Most adults get it about once a year. Children get it more often.

Most cases are caused by a virus. The main viruses are norovirus and rotavirus. Bacteria like salmonella or campylobacter can also cause it. These are called gastrointestinal infections.

For mild diarrhea, you just need to drink fluids and wait. But if diarrhea lasts a long time or is very bad, it can cause serious fluid and salt loss. This is especially risky for babies and older people.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Diarrhea often starts suddenly. You may vomit strongly or have very loose or liquid stool.

You may also have:
- Belly pain or cramps
- A bloated stomach
- Fever
- Headaches or body aches

If you feel dizzy or weak, you may have lost too much fluid and salt. This is serious. See a doctor right away.

Call a doctor if you have:
- No improvement after 48 hours
- A high fever
- Blood in your stool (red or black)
- Mucus in your stool
- Severe pain

---

## What Causes Diarrhea?

The most common cause is a virus. Norovirus and rotavirus are very contagious. They spread easily, especially among children and older adults.

In Germany, bacteria like campylobacter and salmonella are common causes. Traveling to other countries can also cause diarrhea. In some places, dirty water or food can carry germs like shigella, certain types of E. coli, or parasites.

Diarrhea can also happen for other reasons:
- Eating unfamiliar food, especially when traveling
- Food intolerances, like lactose or gluten intolerance
- A sensitive gut (irritable bowel syndrome)
- Long-term gut diseases like Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis
- Side effects from some medicines. Antibiotics can upset the balance of good bacteria in your gut and cause diarrhea

---

## How Does Diarrhea Progress?

Acute diarrhea usually lasts a few days to one week.  
If diarrhea lasts longer than two weeks, it is called persistent diarrhea.

---

## How Can You Prevent Diarrhea?

Germs can spread through stool, vomit, food, water, or dirty surfaces. You can catch them by touching a toilet, door handle, or clothes. Then touching your mouth can make you sick.

To protect yourself and others:
- Wash your hands often and well with soap and water.
- Use hand sanitizer if soap and water are not available.
- If possible, let the person with diarrhea use a separate toilet until they are well.
- Wash clothes in hot water (at least 60 degrees Celsius).

When cooking:
- Be very careful about hygiene.
- If you have diarrhea, do not prepare food for others.
- This rule applies to all food workers.

**Tips to avoid traveler’s diarrhea:**
- In tropical or subtropical countries, avoid raw or unpeeled fruits and vegetables.
- Drink only bottled or boiled water.
- Eat meat and fish only when they are cooked well and hot.

For babies under six months: The Standing Vaccination Committee recommends a rotavirus vaccine. This is given by mouth. It helps protect your child for about two to three years.

More information is available at [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)

---

## How Is Diarrhea Diagnosed?

Your doctor will ask:
- When your symptoms started
- How long the diarrhea has lasted
- How often you have loose stool
- What your stool looks like
- If you have other symptoms like pain, vomiting, or fever
- What you ate before the diarrhea started

They will also ask:
- If you recently traveled abroad
- What medicines you are taking
- If you have allergies or intolerances
- If you have long-term health problems like diabetes

If you have blood or mucus in your stool, or if diarrhea lasts a long time, your doctor may take a stool or blood sample. This helps find the cause.

---

## How Is Diarrhea Treated?

Diarrhea causes you to lose water and salt. You must drink fluids to replace what you lose.

For mild cases:
- Drink tea with a little sugar
- Eat a salty cracker
- Try rice, bananas, or dry bread (rusk)

Avoid:
- Coffee
- Fruit juices
- Lemonade
- Alcohol
- Fatty foods

These can make your gut worse.

For children and adults with mild diarrhea, no special treatment is needed. But young children and older adults need extra care. Severe diarrhea needs a rehydration solution.

Rehydration solutions are available as powder at pharmacies. Mix the powder with water. These solutions contain salt, minerals, and sugar (dextrose).

If you are traveling and do not have a rehydration solution, you can make your own:
- 1 liter of bottled or boiled water
- 4 teaspoons of sugar
- ¾ teaspoon of table salt
- 1 glass of bottled orange juice

Some people take probiotics (good bacteria). These are sold as food or supplements. But studies show they do not shorten the illness much.

Other treatments may be used depending on the situation:
- Medicines like racecadotril or loperamide can calm the gut. They reduce how often you need to go to the bathroom. But only use them after talking to a doctor. Racecadotril needs a prescription. It is not usually used in children under 5.
- Yeast tablets (like Perenterol) may help clear the infection and restore good gut bacteria. But they are not safe for very sick people or those with weak immune systems. The yeast itself could cause an infection.
- Charcoal tablets may help with symptoms. They are dissolved in water before use. But there is not enough strong evidence to prove they are safe and effective.

Antibiotics only work against bacteria. They do not help with viral infections. So they are only used when a bacterial infection is confirmed.

---

## What Else Should You Know?

Some gut infections must be reported to health authorities. This includes:
- Norovirus or rotavirus infection
- Salmonella or campylobacter infection

If a child under six years old has a gut infection and goes to daycare or preschool, it must be reported. The doctor must tell the local health office within 24 hours.

The child can only return to daycare or preschool after being diarrhea-free for two full days. This helps stop the infection from spreading.

In Germany, the Protection Against Infection Act applies. It helps stop the spread of disease.

Food workers with a suspected or confirmed gut infection must not work until:
- They have had three negative stool tests
- They are no longer carrying the germ

For four to six weeks after recovery, food workers must pay extra attention to hand hygiene. This helps protect others.

# Melanoma Skin Cancer – Simple Explanation

Melanoma skin cancer is a type of skin cancer that starts in the cells that give skin its color. Doctors also call it malignant melanoma or just melanoma.

If found early, melanoma skin cancer can usually be treated successfully.

This article explains the risks, signs, how it is found, how it is treated, and how to stay safe.

---

## Quick Facts

- Melanoma skin cancer is also called malignant melanoma or just melanoma.
- Too much sun or UV light can raise your risk of getting it.
- People with fair skin or many moles are more likely to get it.
- A new mole or a mole that changes in size, shape, or color may be melanoma.
- Early treatment works well.
- The main goal of treatment is to remove the cancer completely.

> **Important:** This article is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Melanoma?

Melanoma starts in skin cells called melanocytes. These cells make the pigment that gives skin its color.

Most melanomas start in the skin. But in rare cases, they can start in the eye or in the lining of the mouth or anus.

Melanoma spreads to other parts of the body more often than other types of skin cancer.

---

## What Are the Signs of Melanoma?

Melanoma can look very different from one person to another. It often shows up as:

- A new dark spot on the skin
- A mole that changes in size, shape, or color
- A mole with uneven edges or blurry borders
- A mole that itches, bleeds, or hurts
- Skin around a mole that is red or swollen
- A mole that looks different from all the others on your body

Some melanomas are dark brown, black, red, blue, or even colorless.

Melanoma can grow slowly at first. But it can also grow fast and go deep into the skin.

Melanoma can appear anywhere on the body. This includes the scalp, under fingernails or toenails, and inside the mouth or anus.

It can also appear on skin that does not get much sun.

In the early stages, melanoma does not usually cause pain. But if it spreads, it can cause many different symptoms, depending on where it goes.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

The biggest risk factor you can control is exposure to UV light.

UV light comes from:
- The sun
- Tanning beds or sunlamps

Getting a severe sunburn, especially as a child or teenager, increases your risk.

You are more likely to get melanoma if you:
- Have fair skin
- Have many moles
- Have a close family member with melanoma
- Have already had melanoma before

---

## How Common Is It?

In Germany, about 23,000 people were diagnosed with melanoma in 2016. Men and women are affected about equally.

The number of cases has been rising over the years. This may be because more people with fair skin are getting strong sun exposure without protection.

But it may also be because doctors are finding melanoma earlier, thanks to skin cancer screening programs.

---

## What Is the Outlook?

Melanoma can grow slowly or very fast.

If the cancer is only in the top layer of the skin, it is called "melanoma in situ." This stage does not spread. But it can become invasive and grow deeper.

Once it grows deeper, it can spread through the body via the lymph system or blood.

---

## How Can You Prevent Melanoma?

Too much UV light raises your risk. Protect yourself from the sun and avoid tanning beds.

There is no 100% way to prevent melanoma. But these steps help:

- Avoid strong sun between 11 am and 3 pm, especially in summer.
- Stay in the shade or under a sun umbrella.
- Even in the shade, some UV light reaches your skin.
- Wear protective clothing, a hat, and sunglasses.
- Use sunscreen on all exposed skin.
- Never use tanning beds.

Parents should protect children well from the sun. People who work outside should follow their company’s sun safety rules.

The Federal Office for Radiation Protection gives daily UV forecasts for Germany.

Want to learn more about UV rays and sun protection? Visit the website of the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## Skin Cancer Screening

The earlier melanoma is found, the better the chance of recovery.

In Germany, people aged 35 and over with public health insurance can have a skin cancer check every 2 years. This is part of the national cancer screening program.

During the check, a trained doctor looks at all your skin and mucous membranes.

You should also check your own skin regularly. See a dermatologist if you notice anything unusual.

Doctors use the **ABCDE rule** to check moles:

- **A** – Asymmetrical shape (not the same on both sides)
- **B** – Uneven or blurred edges
- **C** – Multiple colors (brown, black, red, blue, or white)
- **D** – Larger than 5 millimeters across (about the size of a pencil eraser)
- **E** – Has changed over time (size, shape, color, or texture)

Want to learn more about skin cancer screening? Visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## How Is Melanoma Diagnosed?

Doctors often spot melanoma by looking at the skin with their eyes.

A special tool called a dermatoscope helps them see the skin more clearly.

If melanoma is suspected, the doctor removes the whole spot. They also take a small amount of healthy skin around it.

The tissue is sent to a lab. There, a specialist checks it under a microscope to confirm if it is cancer.

If melanoma is confirmed, the doctor checks if it has spread.

This may include:
- Removing and testing nearby lymph nodes (sentinel lymph node biopsy)
- Ultrasound scan
- MRI or CT scan
- Blood tests

Want to learn more about these tests? Visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## How Is Melanoma Treated?

The main goal is to remove the cancer completely.

If a doctor suspects melanoma, they remove the suspicious area in one surgery. The tissue is checked under a microscope.

If it is melanoma, a second surgery removes more skin around the first area.

For very small tumors, one surgery is enough. No further treatment is needed.

If the tumor is at least 1 millimeter wide, the doctor removes nearby lymph nodes. These are tested for cancer.

If cancer is found in the lymph nodes, all the lymph nodes in that area are removed.

The stage of the cancer determines if more treatment is needed. The stage depends on:
- How big the tumor is
- If the skin over the tumor is broken (ulcerated)
- If cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes or skin
- If cancer has spread to distant organs

If surgery is not possible or if the cancer has spread, radiation therapy may help.

Other treatments may be used, depending on the cancer type and stage.

Some patients get drugs after surgery. This is called adjuvant therapy. It helps lower the risk of the cancer coming back.

---

### Treating Advanced Melanoma

Even if melanoma has spread, there are treatments available.

These treatments aim to slow the disease and ease symptoms.

The right drug depends on the cancer’s features and how it has been treated.

Some drugs target specific changes in the cancer cells. They stop the cancer from growing.

Other patients get a type of immunotherapy called immune checkpoint inhibitors. These drugs help the body’s own immune system attack the cancer.

If these drugs do not work, chemotherapy is another option.

All treatments have side effects. For more details on side effects and how to manage them, visit the **Cancer Information Service of the German Cancer Research Center** (in German).

---

## Recovery After Treatment

Cancer treatment can be hard on the body and mind.

Rehabilitation helps patients get back to normal life. It also helps prevent or reduce side effects.

Rehab is tailored to each person’s needs.

It may include:
- Physical therapy to improve movement and strength
- Exercises to build muscle
- Lymph drainage or compression bandages to reduce swelling
- Support for mental health, such as dealing with anxiety or depression

More information on rehab after cancer is available at the **German Cancer Research Center’s Cancer Information Service** (in German).

---

## After Treatment: What Happens Next?

Melanoma can come back even after successful treatment.

Follow-up care helps find a return of the cancer early.

Experts recommend regular check-ups for up to 10 years after treatment.

People with more advanced cancer need more frequent visits.

At each visit, the doctor checks:
- All skin areas
- The surgery site
- Lymph node areas
- Nearby lymph nodes

For early-stage melanoma, a physical exam is usually enough.

For others, extra tests may be needed, such as blood tests or ultrasound.

Anyone who has had melanoma should check their own skin regularly.

---

## Living with Melanoma

Everyone should protect their skin from too much sun.

If you’ve had melanoma before, your risk of getting it again is higher.

You should:
- Check your skin often
- Attend all follow-up appointments
- See your doctor if you notice any changes

Early detection means better outcomes.

---

## Where to Get More Help

Hospitals that specialize in skin cancer can earn special certification. The German Cancer Society checks these centers regularly.

Find certified centers at the **OncoMAP** website.

You can also search for dermatology clinics

# Tooth Decay (Caries)

Tooth decay happens when you eat a lot of sweets and do not clean your teeth well.  
Bacteria in plaque can harm your teeth.  
This can cause pain and may lead to losing teeth.  
Today, tooth decay is much less common than it was in the past.

## Quick Facts

- Tooth decay happens because of plaque, sugary foods, and not cleaning your teeth well.
- It can hurt and damage your teeth. In bad cases, you may lose a tooth.
- The first sign is a white or brown spot on a tooth.
- In Germany, about 8 out of 10 children aged 12 have no tooth decay.
- Brushing your teeth every day with fluoride toothpaste and eating less sugar help prevent tooth decay.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for seeing a doctor. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is Tooth Decay?

Tooth decay is a disease of the teeth.  
It is caused by plaque bacteria, eating too much sugar, and poor cleaning habits.  
It damages the teeth.  
It can hurt.  
It may lead to tooth loss.

Tooth decay is also called tooth rot.  
It is much less common now than it was a few decades ago.  
This is because more people use fluoride toothpaste and take better care of their teeth.  
These habits help keep teeth healthy and stop tooth decay.

## What Are the Signs of Tooth Decay?

The first sign is a white or brown spot on a tooth.  
As the decay gets worse, holes form in the tooth.  
If the decay reaches deeper parts of the tooth, it can hurt the nerve and root.  
The tooth may become sensitive to cold or sweet things.  
In serious cases, the tooth may need to be removed.  
It can be replaced with a dental implant or a bridge.

## What Causes Tooth Decay?

Tooth decay usually happens when three things are present:  
- Plaque on the teeth  
- Eating sugary foods often  
- Not cleaning your teeth well  

Plaque is a sticky film that covers your teeth.  
It feels fuzzy when you run your tongue over it.  
It is made of bacteria, saliva, and food bits.  
Bacteria on the teeth break down sugar and food.  
This process makes acid.  
The acid attacks the tooth surface.  
If you do not clean your teeth, the acid can slowly destroy the tooth.  
Bacteria that cause tooth decay can pass through saliva.

Children are more at risk.  
Baby teeth have softer enamel than adult teeth.  
If a child eats too many sweets or drinks too many sugary drinks, tooth decay can start early.  
This includes even very young babies who drink sweet tea or juice from a bottle.  
It can be hard to clean the teeth of babies and young children.

Permanent teeth are also at risk when they first come in.  
The enamel is not fully hardened yet.  
This makes them more likely to get decay.

## How Common Is Tooth Decay?

Many children and teens have healthy teeth.  
In Germany, only about 2 out of 10 children aged 12 have tooth decay.  
That means they have at least one tooth with decay.

Among children aged 6 to 7 who still have baby teeth, about half have had tooth decay at least once.

Adults get tooth decay more often.  
People aged 35 to 44 usually have about 11 teeth that are decayed, filled, capped, or missing.

## How Can You Prevent Tooth Decay?

Both children and adults can lower their risk by brushing their teeth every day with fluoride toothpaste.  
Fluoride helps strengthen tooth enamel.  
This makes teeth more resistant to decay.  
Brushing also removes plaque and the acids in it.  
It is best to brush at least twice a day, after meals.

For babies in their first year:  
- Give fluoride tablets **or**  
- Brush their teeth with fluoride toothpaste  

But too much fluoride can cause side effects.  
So children must not take in too much.

What you eat matters a lot.  
Eating fewer sugary foods lowers your risk.  
Sweets, soft drinks, fruit juices, and even ketchup have a lot of sugar.

Regular visits to the dentist are also helpful.  
They can find tooth decay early and treat it before it gets worse.

For more details on how to prevent tooth decay, visit _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

## How Is Tooth Decay Diagnosed?

Dentists usually spot tooth decay by looking closely at your teeth.  
They may also take an X-ray.  
An X-ray shows how far the decay has gone.  
It also shows exactly where the decay is.  
For example, it can show decay between teeth or under a filling.

## How Is Tooth Decay Treated?

If tooth decay is caught early, you may see white or brown spots.  
At this stage, brushing with fluoride toothpaste every day may be enough.  
Your dentist can also apply fluoride directly to your teeth.

If a hole has formed, the dentist will drill out the decayed part.  
They will then fill the hole.  
Fillings can be made of plastic, metal, ceramic, or precious metal.

If the tooth is badly damaged, it can be saved with a partial or full crown.

If the decay reaches the nerve, a root canal treatment is usually needed.

In some cases, the tooth must be removed.  
It can later be replaced with a bridge or a dental implant with a crown.

New treatments are now available that do not always require drilling.  
For example, a method called caries infiltration uses plastic to harden the tooth.  
This works well for early decay.

## Other Important Tips

Many people go to the dentist not just when they have pain, but also for regular check-ups.

For help finding the right dentist and preparing for your visit, go to _gesundheitsinformation.de_.

# Blockage in the Gallbladder

A blockage in the gallbladder usually happens because of gallstones or narrowed bile ducts.  
You may feel sharp pain in the upper right side of your belly.  
If not treated, the blockage can cause swelling and inflammation.  
Medicines or surgery can help.

---

## Quick Facts

- When the gallbladder is blocked, bile builds up because it cannot move in or out.  
- The most common causes are gallstones and narrowed or blocked bile ducts.  
- Sharp, cramp-like pain in the upper right belly is a typical sign.  
- If the blockage is not treated, the gallbladder or bile ducts can become inflamed.  
- Doctors usually use an ultrasound scan to find the blockage.  
- Most people have the gallbladder removed to stop symptoms from coming back.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is the Gallbladder?

The gallbladder is a small, hollow organ under the liver on the right side of your belly.  
Your liver makes about one liter of bile every day.  
Bile is a yellow-green to brown fluid.  
It flows from the liver into the gallbladder through tubes called bile ducts.  
The gallbladder stores and concentrates the bile.  
When you eat, especially fatty food, the gallbladder releases bile into the small intestine.  
Bile helps break down fats so your body can absorb them.  
Bile contains salts, water, cholesterol, fats, and a pigment called bilirubin.  
Bilirubin comes from the breakdown of old red blood cells in the liver.

A blockage happens when the bile ducts are blocked.  
This stops bile from flowing in or out.  
The main cause is gallstones.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Many people with gallstones feel no pain.  
But a blockage in the gallbladder usually causes pain and discomfort.  
The pain is in the upper right side of the belly.  
It can spread to the right shoulder or back.  
The pain often comes in waves.  
It starts suddenly and is very strong.  
It lasts at least 30 minutes.  
Then it slowly gets better and goes away after a few hours.  
These pain episodes can happen again and again, but not every day.

Other possible symptoms include:

- Feeling sick to your stomach  
- Vomiting  
- Sweating  
- Bloating or gas  
- Trouble eating fatty or spicy food  
- Fever  
- Losing weight without trying  

If the blockage affects the liver, you may notice:

- Yellow skin or eyes (jaundice)  
- Dark yellow or brown urine  

---

## What Causes a Blockage?

Possible causes of a blocked gallbladder include:

- Gallstones or thick bile (called bile sludge) in the gallbladder or bile ducts  
- Injury to the belly  
- Inflammation in the bile ducts, gallbladder, or pancreas  
- Poor blood flow to the bile ducts  
- Damage to the bile ducts during a medical test  
- Rarely, a bacterial infection in the bile ducts  

It is very rare for someone to be born with a tendency to get gallbladder blockages.  
One rare condition, called LPAC syndrome, is linked to genes.  
People with this condition often develop gallstones at a young age.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

You are more likely to get a blockage if you:

- Do not move much or are not physically active  
- Eat a diet high in calories and low in fiber  
- Are overweight or obese  
- Lose a lot of weight quickly  
- Are on a feeding tube for a long time  
- Have type 2 diabetes  
- Have had past inflammation in the gallbladder or bile ducts  
- Have high levels of cholesterol or other fats in your blood  
- Are a woman (women are more likely to have gallbladder problems than men)  
- Are pregnant  
- Take birth control pills that contain estrogen  
- Have a family history of gallbladder issues  

---

## What Can Happen If It’s Not Treated?

If the blockage is not treated, bile can build up.  
This can lead to:

- Sudden or repeated swelling in the gallbladder or bile ducts  
- Inflammation of the pancreas (pancreatitis)  
- Long-term liver problems  
- Pus in the liver (abscess)  

---

## How Can You Prevent It?

You can lower your risk by:

- Staying physically active  
- Eating a healthy, balanced diet  
- Keeping a normal body weight  

If you are at high risk, your doctor may prescribe cholesterol-lowering medicine (statins).  

After losing a lot of weight quickly — for example, from dieting or weight-loss surgery — you are more likely to get gallstones.  
A medicine called ursodeoxycholic acid can help prevent gallstones.  
It may even dissolve small ones.  
But you must take it only as your doctor tells you.

> **Important:** Never take medicine for gallstones without talking to your doctor.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

The symptoms depend on how long the blockage has been there.  
The gallbladder or bile ducts may already be inflamed.

If you have pain, see your family doctor or go to the emergency room.

Tell your doctor exactly what you feel.  
They will press on your belly.  
If you pull away or flinch when they press, it may mean the gallbladder is inflamed.

An ultrasound scan of the belly can show:

- Changes in the gallbladder  
- Blocked bile ducts  
- Large gallstones  

Sometimes, the ultrasound does not show anything.  
If doctors still suspect gallstones or thick bile, they may do an endosonography.  
This uses a thin, flexible tube with a camera.  
The tube goes through your mouth, into your stomach and small intestine.  
This lets doctors see the gallbladder and pancreas up close.

Other tests include:

- Magnetic resonance cholangiography (MRC): takes detailed pictures of the bile ducts  
- Computed tomography (CT): gives clear images of the organs  

Blood tests can also help.  
Doctors check for:

- High levels of enzymes like lipase. These help digest fat. If the bile ducts are blocked, lipase builds up in the blood.  
- High bilirubin levels. This yellow pigment does not drain properly when the ducts are blocked.

In young people with suspected gallbladder problems, a genetic test may show if they have a family tendency to form gallstones.

---

## How Is It Treated?

Treatment depends on how bad the symptoms are.  
It is especially important if the gallbladder or bile ducts are inflamed.

Treatment options include:

- Medicines  
- Endoscopic procedures  
- Surgery  

### Medicines

- Painkillers like Diclofenac can help with pain.  
- Ursodeoxycholic acid may dissolve small gallstones.  
  But only if the gallbladder is working well.  
- If bacteria cause an infection, antibiotics are used.

### Endoscopic Procedures

- A procedure called ERC removes stones from the bile ducts.  
  A thin tube (endoscope) goes through the mouth, stomach, and into the small intestine.  
  A special dye is injected to make the ducts visible on X-ray.  
- If stones remain in the gallbladder, it may be removed later.  
- ERC can cause side effects in 5 to 10 out of 100 people.  
  These include pancreatitis or damage to the bile ducts or gut.

### Surgery

- The most common treatment is removing the gallbladder.  
  This is called a cholecystectomy.  
- Doctors usually do this through small cuts in the belly.  
- If the gallbladder is inflamed or you have severe pain, surgery is done within 24 to 72 hours.  
- Sometimes, doctors remove the gallbladder even if they cannot find a clear cause.  
  This is if you have repeated, serious symptoms.

> **Important:** You can live a normal life without a gallbladder.  
> You can eat most foods.  
> But after very fatty meals, you may have gas or loose stools.

# Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease

This condition happens when too much fat builds up in the liver. It is linked to heavy drinking over time. Many people do not know they have it. But it can lead to serious liver problems if not taken seriously.

---

## Quick Facts

- Alcoholic fatty liver disease starts as a mild condition.
- It can lead to severe liver scarring (cirrhosis) if not treated.
- Most people with this condition have no symptoms.
- Drinking a lot of alcohol every day is the main cause.
- Being overweight also raises the risk.
- About 9 out of 10 people who drink heavily will develop this condition.
- Stopping alcohol can reverse the damage.

> **Important:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

---

## What Is Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease?

Your liver stores fat. When you drink too much alcohol over time, fat builds up in liver cells. This is called alcoholic fatty liver disease.

At first, this condition does not cause harm. But it can get worse. It may turn into liver inflammation or serious scarring.

If you stop drinking alcohol, your liver can heal. This is true even if you have been drinking heavily for years.

If you are dependent on alcohol, you will need treatment for that too.

---

## What Are the Symptoms?

Most people with this condition feel fine. They do not notice any changes.

Some people may have:
- Loss of appetite
- Nausea
- Vomiting

These symptoms are not always present. Many people do not know they have the condition.

---

## What Causes Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease?

Your liver breaks down alcohol. Drinking too much can damage liver cells.

When alcohol is processed, it creates fatty substances. These fats build up in the liver.

If you drink large amounts every day, fat can pile up in your liver.

Binge drinking also increases the risk.  
Binge drinking means drinking a large amount of alcohol in a short time.  
For men: about 1.25 liters of beer or 0.6 liters of wine in a few hours.  
For women: about 1 liter of beer or 0.5 liters of wine in a few hours.

---

## What Increases the Risk?

Besides heavy drinking, these factors raise your risk:

- Being very overweight (obesity)
- Family history of liver problems
- Other liver diseases, like long-term viral hepatitis
- Smoking

Women are more likely than men to develop fatty liver from alcohol.

> **Did you know?**  
> According to the German Center for Addiction Issues, women who drink more than 12 grams of pure alcohol a day and men who drink more than 24 grams a day are at higher risk.  
> 12 grams of alcohol is about one small beer (0.3 liters) or a small glass of wine (0.125 liters).

---

## How Common Is It?

We do not have exact numbers because most people have no symptoms.

But studies show that about 90 percent of people who drink heavily for years develop fatty liver disease.

For a man, this means drinking two or more bottles of beer a day, or more.

---

## How Does It Progress?

If you stop drinking alcohol completely, your liver can return to normal.

Alcoholic fatty liver disease is the mildest form of alcohol-related liver damage.

But it can get worse. It may lead to:
- Liver inflammation (steatohepatitis)
- Serious scarring of the liver (cirrhosis)

Cirrhosis can be life-threatening.

---

## How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors look for signs such as:
- A liver that feels larger than normal when touched
- High levels of a certain liver enzyme in blood tests

An ultrasound scan can confirm the diagnosis in most cases.

A liver biopsy (taking a small tissue sample) is rarely needed.

To tell the difference between alcoholic and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, doctors ask patients about their drinking habits.

---

## How Is It Treated?

The only way to treat this condition is to stop drinking alcohol.

If you stop completely, your liver can heal fully.

If you are dependent on alcohol, you must get treatment for that.

Heavy drinking often leads to poor nutrition.  
So, it is important to eat a healthy, balanced diet with plenty of nutrients.

---

## Where Can I Get Help?

If you are worried about your drinking, visit **kenn-dein-limit.de**.  
This is a website run by the Federal Center for Health Education.

You can:
- Learn how to manage your alcohol use
- Take a free self-test to check if your drinking is too high

For more detailed help, including support for family members, go to **gesundheitsinformation.de**.

# Dislocated Kneecap (Patellar Dislocation)

A kneecap can slip out of place during a sudden twist or a bump. Sometimes it slips back in on its own. But even if it does, you still need to see a doctor. This is because the bones, cartilage, or ligaments around the knee can be damaged.

## Quick Facts

- Most kneecap dislocations happen during sports.
- They are most common in teenagers and young adults.
- The kneecap may pop back into place by itself.
- You should still see a doctor no matter what.
- Surgery is only needed in some cases, especially if there is serious damage.
- The knee must rest for several weeks to months, depending on the injury and treatment.

> **Note:** This information is not a substitute for medical advice. Do not use it to diagnose or treat yourself.

## What Is a Dislocated Kneecap?

A dislocated kneecap means the small bone at the front of the knee has moved out of its normal groove in the thighbone. This bone is called the kneecap or patella.

When you bend or straighten your knee, the kneecap moves up and down in a groove in the thighbone. A sudden twist or a side bump can push it out of the groove. This often happens during sports, especially in teens and young adults.

The kneecap often slips back into place on its own. But even then, you should still see a doctor. Damage to bones, cartilage, or ligaments can still happen.

After a dislocation, the kneecap may feel unstable. It might slip out again later.

## Signs of a Dislocated Kneecap

- You will feel sharp pain.
- The kneecap will look out of place.
- You may hear a pop when it happens.
- The knee may feel like it is not in the right spot.

The knee can swell up. This happens if the joint capsule or the inner ligament (called the medial patellofemoral ligament) tears. This ligament helps keep the kneecap in place. The kneecap usually slips to the outside of the knee.

If the kneecap keeps slipping out over time, swelling may not happen every time.

## What Causes a Dislocated Kneecap?

The kneecap can pop out when the knee turns inward while the leg is slightly bent and the foot is flat on the ground. This often happens during sports. This type of injury is called acute or traumatic dislocation.

Sports where this is common include football, handball, dancing, and gymnastics.

About 80 percent of cases are acute dislocations. A less common issue is patellar subluxation. This means the kneecap moves sideways in the groove but does not fully come out. This can happen after a past injury or if the ligaments are too loose.

## Risk Factors

Some people are more likely to have a kneecap dislocation. These include:

- Knock knees or other leg shape problems
- A shallow or oddly shaped groove in the thighbone
- A higher-than-normal kneecap
- Weak inner thigh muscles
- Very flexible joints or weak ligaments

## How Common Is This Injury?

Kneecap dislocations mostly happen in people aged 10 to 20. Girls and young women are more likely to get this injury. This is because they often have more flexible ligaments and weaker muscles than boys.

## How Does the Injury Heal?

Recovery time depends on how bad the injury is and how it is treated.

If there is no major damage, most people can return to normal daily activities in about 6 weeks.

Returning to sports usually takes 3 to 4 months. If surgery is needed, it can take over a year.

You do not have to stop playing sports forever. Studies show that about half of people can return to their sport at the same level after resting and rehab.

Before returning to sports, it is a good idea to talk to a doctor or a physiotherapist.

After a dislocation, the kneecap may feel wobbly. You may feel pain in the front of the knee, especially when putting stress on it.

In 15 to 45 percent of people, the kneecap slips out again after the first time. This can happen weeks, months, or even years later.

We do not yet know all the long-term effects. But there is some evidence that this injury can increase the risk of knee arthritis later in life.

## How Is It Diagnosed?

A doctor can usually see a dislocated kneecap right away. They will look at and feel the knee.

After the kneecap is put back in place, an X-ray is taken. This checks for broken bones.

To check for ligament or meniscus damage, the doctor will do physical tests. An MRI scan may also be used. This scan shows soft tissues like ligaments and cartilage. It can also show bone shape problems or cartilage damage.

## How Is It Treated?

Sometimes the kneecap slips back in on its own. If it does not, call emergency services right away (dial 112).

If the kneecap pops back, you can go to the emergency room by car.

**First aid right after the injury:**

- Stay calm.
- Sit down or lie down to rest the leg.
- Keep the knee still to avoid more damage.
- Apply cold to the knee to reduce swelling and ease pain.

In the hospital, you will get fast-acting pain relief. Then the doctor will move the kneecap back into place. This may be done by slowly straightening the leg. Sometimes the doctor needs to use a special technique.

After the kneecap is back in place, you will wear a special bandage for a few weeks. This helps keep the kneecap stable. Crutches may help you walk without putting weight on the injured knee.

Surgery may be needed if:

- The kneecap slips out again.
- There is a high chance it will slip out again.
- There is serious damage to the cartilage or bone.

## How Does Rehabilitation Work?

After hospital treatment, the knee is kept still for a few days. Then rehab begins with physiotherapy.

The first step is to gently start moving the knee again. Swelling can be reduced with special massage techniques (lymph drainage).

Next, you will do exercises to strengthen the leg muscles. This helps stabilize the kneecap. Strengthening the inner thigh muscle is especially important. This muscle connects to the ligament that holds the kneecap in place.

Strong muscles in the hips, pelvis, ankles, and torso also help support the knee.

If some muscles are tight, stretching exercises can help. This prevents uneven strain on the knee.

For more information on physiotherapy for this injury, visit: [gesundheitsinformation.de](https://www.gesundheitsinformation.de)
